title: Between the Gunshot and the Ground
instruction: You've just taken a bullet meant for someone you love, and you have seconds to tell them everything. Start with fierce, almost violent urgency: 'Listen to me, LISTEN!' Your voice is strong, protective, fighting through pain because they need to survive what's coming. But as you speak, your power drains away. Rage at the unfairness of this transforms into desperate tenderness. You're trying to give them a lifetime of guidance in moments. Your voice breaks, climbs, becomes almost a child's voice asking, 'You're going to be okay, right?' Then find one last surge of strength to command them: 'Live.' Let that word hold everything you'll never get to say.

title: The Last Warm Sip
instruction: You are curled on a couch, one arm wrapped around your middle, a heating pad pressed against your abdomen. A familiar, persistent ache has settled in for the afternoon, making you shift every few minutes. You hold a mug of herbal tea in your other hand, its warmth a small comfort. At first, you speak with a soft, genuine contentment, savoring this quiet moment despite the pain, your voice slightly muffled by your posture. As you continue, the pain deepens, and your voice becomes more strained, the words coming out in shorter, careful bursts, punctuated by a faint groan. You describe the feeling of the tea warming you from the inside, your tone starting at ease and ending in a hollow, resigned ache.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Party Favor
instruction: A middle-aged woman at a crowded party finds herself cornered by a witty, magnetic stranger. She starts with playful, flirty banter, teasing him about his drink choice, her voice breathy and light, punctuated by soft laughter. But as he matches her rhythm, a sudden wave of helplessness washes over her — she realizes she's lost control, her confidence crumbling. Let your voice shift from a teasing, high-pitched head voice to a quieter, strained murmur as you stumble through the words, catching yourself mid-laugh, then trailing off into a vulnerable confession. Speak naturally, distractedly fidgeting with a napkin, barely 70 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Mirror Breaks: Confronting Your Younger Self
instruction: You are face-to-face with your younger self (played by your scene partner or imagined)—the hopeful, ambitious person you were at eighteen. They ask you what happened to all the dreams, why you gave up, why you became so bitter and self-defeating. Start defensive and harsh, listing all your failures and disappointments with venom directed at yourself. But as they listen with the innocence and belief you once had, something cracks open. By the end, you're not defending your cynicism—you're remembering what you loved about who you were, admitting the truth: you're terrified of hoping again. Let your voice shift from sharp and biting to raw, trembling, and finally tender with rediscovery.
inspired_by: Actor is hard on themselves and struggling with self-criticism; needs to build self-appreciation to match character's positive self-view

title: Splitting the Silence
instruction: You are a woman with a soft, rounded voice, chopping wood in a cold backyard as your young child watches from the porch. Each swing is a struggle—you grunt on impact, then pause to catch your breath. Start with a line carried on longing: maybe about a memory of warmth or how things used to be, your voice lifting as if you can almost touch it. Then, as your arms ache and you stand over the split log, let that hope spill away into a raw, tired admission of helplessness—your breath shallow, your words clipped between heaves, the child’s quiet presence making the weight of what you can’t provide feel unbreakable.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Explosive Breakdown When Your Lie Is Exposed Publicly
instruction: Someone has just revealed your fraudulent credentials in front of everyone you've worked with. Begin with fierce, almost manic defensiveness, voice sharp and loud: 'You have no right to—' But your voice cracks mid-sentence. The fury breaks open into something desperate and ugly. You're shouting now, tears streaming: 'You think it was easy? You think I wanted to lie?' Your voice is ragged, oscillating between rage and anguish. You're addressing everyone and no one, words tumbling out about fear, about inadequacy, about watching everyone else succeed. Then suddenly, the fight drains out. Your voice drops to something small and destroyed: 'I just... I just wanted to matter.' End in helpless, gasping sobs, voice completely broken, asking a question you know has no good answer: 'What am I without the lie?'
inspired_by: Admitting You've Been Lying About Your Credentials

title: The Diagnosis Phone Call
instruction: You've just received test results and you're calling your partner, trying to hold it together. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'The doctor called. It's what we feared.' But control shatters: 'I'm not ready for this. I'm not fucking ready!' Your voice explodes with rage at the unfairness: 'We were supposed to have more time! We were supposed to travel, to grow old!' The anger collapses into desperate pleading: 'I don't want to leave you. I don't want our kids to watch this happen.' Then fierce protectiveness emerges: 'Promise me you'll be okay. Promise me you won't let this destroy you.' End with a strange, fierce tenderness: 'I'm going to fight like hell. But if I can't win, know that every single day with you was worth it.' Move from controlled shock to explosive fury to helpless grief to warrior-like determination mixed with tender goodbye.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospital room, and they don't know this will be the last time they hear your voice. Start with forced brightness—'Hey, just wanted to hear you say my name one more time. Can you... can you just say it?' Your voice trembles as you try to memorize the sound of theirs. The facade begins cracking: 'I need you to know that every good thing in me came from you.' Tears are choking your words now, but you're fighting to stay composed because you don't want them to panic. 'I'm not scared anymore. I promise I'm not scared.' End with the hardest words: a whispered 'I love you' that contains both peaceful acceptance and the devastating weight of goodbye. Let silence breathe between phrases—what you're not saying matters as much as what you are.

title: Monuments and Ashes
instruction: You are speaking at a celebration for an achievement you accomplished with someone you loved deeply who died before seeing this moment come to fruition—a partner, best friend, creative collaborator, or mentor who should be here. Begin by accepting the recognition with genuine pride and joy—let yourself feel the full thrill of having your work honored. But as you continue, the absence becomes unbearable. You're furious that they're not here to share this, grateful for what they gave you, devastated by the injustice of their absence, yet also celebrating their influence on your success. Weave between laughing at shared memories and choking on grief, between thanking them and raging at death for taking them, between honoring what you accomplished together and breaking under the weight of solo victory. End in a place where all emotions exist simultaneously—you cannot separate the joy from the sorrow anymore.

title: The Knotted Midnight
instruction: You're a teenage girl, alone in your room after a long, draining day. You're standing by your bed, ready to collapse, but before you can lie down, a sudden, severe cramp seizes your calf muscle. You freeze, gasping, a sharp curse escapes as the muscle locks. Your voice is strained, exhausted. As the spasm fades, you speak, but your words are guarded, hollow—you're too tired to even feel the pain deeply anymore. Start with a sigh of relief, then the seizure interrupts, then end with a numb, quiet observation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Voice That Raised You
instruction: You're 45, calling your retired acting coach—the one who trained you from age 12—to finally tell them the truth: their relentless perfectionism broke something in you that never healed. Start with rehearsed courage, almost scripted words you've practiced for years. But as they respond with confusion or defensiveness, your carefully controlled tone fractures. Anger surges through—'You never let me be good enough!'—then collapses into something smaller, younger, the teenager you once were begging for approval. Your voice cracks not from age but from accessing a wound you've carried for decades. End in exhausted honesty, almost a whisper: 'I needed you to love my voice the way it was.' The confrontation transforms into grief for the student you once were.

title: Your Mother's Hands at the Kitchen Table
instruction: Your difficult, aging parent sits across from you at their kitchen table. You've come to say something hard, something long overdue. But before you speak, really look at them: how have their hands changed? How do they hold their coffee cup? Let yourself perceive deeper: what's the quality of fatigue in their face? What's the set of their mouth telling you about their defenses? Then wonder: what are they seeing when they look at me? What did they hope I would become? What are they afraid I'm about to say? Start in frustration or steeled resolve, but let this genuine study of them—this person who gave you life and disappointed you and loved you imperfectly—crack you open. End in a place where anger and tenderness, resentment and sudden understanding live in the same breath. Let what you actually see in them change the words you came to say.

title: The Last Lucid Goodbye
instruction: You're saying farewell to your adult child, knowing this is likely your last moment of clarity before dementia takes you completely. You begin with fierce determination to say everything that matters: 'Listen to me now, while I still can...' You're fighting to hold onto each memory, each lesson you want to leave them. Mid-way, you feel yourself slipping—panic rises as you realize words are escaping like water through fingers: 'There was something about the summer when you were... the place where we...' Your child takes your hands and says, 'I remember, Mom. I remember everything.' The panic transforms into profound relief mixed with grief. You stop fighting the fog and simply rest in their presence, your final words a whispered blessing: 'You were... you are... everything.' Let the emotional journey move from desperate urgency to terrified loss to peaceful surrender, each transition visible in your voice.

title: Laying the Foundation
instruction: You're a construction foreman recording a safety memo for the company's new training archive. Start by dictating with a flat, efficient monotone as you rattle off procedures, but let a slow wave of pride creep in as you recount your crew's perfect safety record. Let your voice grow fuller, warmer, and slightly unsteady when you say 'I'm grateful'—as if you've just realized how much their work means. Feel the silence of the booth, the heat in your chest, the small smile you can't quite stop. Your final words should sound like you're wrapping up a job you're truly proud of, not just punching a clock.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Barefoot in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're slipping off your shoes in your child's hospital room at 3 AM, whispering so you don't wake them. Describe the coolness of the linoleum, how it grounds you when everything else feels like it's slipping away. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, as you confess your fears to the darkness—how you're terrified of losing them, how inadequate you feel, how this simple act of removing your shoes is the only normal thing left. Let tenderness and devastation intertwine in every word. As your feet settle on the floor, let a tear-choked realization emerge: you would stand here forever, exhausted and barefoot, if it meant one more day with them.
inspired_by: Taking Off Your Shoes After a Long Day

title: Frozen Confession
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing alone in a blizzard, the cold so bitter your jaw barely moves. You're trying to call yourself inside, ashamed of the lustful thoughts you had about the young man who shoveled your walk this morning. But as you speak the memory of his hands, his laugh, floods back, and shame melts into raw desire. Let your voice start tight and shivering, vowels locked and breath puffed, then slowly warm as lust takes over — but the cold still keeps your words short, your lips stiff. Micro-distractions: you pause to rub your arms, your teeth chatter mid-sentence, you whisper the last words as if confessing to the snow.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are a person who has been strong for everyone, held everything together, and you've finally reached the moment where you cannot do it anymore. Start with fierce, almost violent intensity—pushing back against someone who's asking you for one more thing, needing you to be strong one more time. Your voice is a roar of boundaries finally being set: 'I have nothing left!' But as the rage pours out, it collapses into something else entirely—the exhaustion beneath the anger, the helplessness beneath the control, the terror that if you're not strong, you'll disappear entirely. Let your voice break from shouting into sobbing, from defensive walls into desperate honesty. End in a place of raw exposure where you admit you're scared, you're tired, you don't know how to be anything but the strong one, and you need someone to see that you're falling apart. The arc is from protective rage to naked vulnerability.

title: The Bitter Secret
instruction: You've just accidentally overheard a phone call where someone you trusted revealed a long-hidden betrayal—something that sours your stomach and makes your skin crawl. As you step away from the door, your hand flies to your mouth, pressing firmly against your lips, muffling the shock that wants to escape. At first, your words come out in tight, clipped bursts, each consonant swallowed by your palm as you try to process the sourness—the taste of betrayal. But as you speak, the muffled shock slowly gives way to a raw, quiet grimness, your voice dropping to a resigned, broken whisper—still half-smothered—as you realize you can't un-hear this truth.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Unspoken Words
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandfather who raised you. He's slipping away, and you've never told him the thing you've been carrying for twenty years—how his quiet belief in you saved your life during your darkest moment. Start holding everything back, maintaining composure, doing what you think you 'should' do at a deathbed. But let yourself slowly drop all pretense. Don't perform grief—let whatever wants to come, come. Maybe it's messy. Maybe words fail and you have to start again. Maybe you laugh remembering something before the tears come. Trust that your body knows what this moment needs, even if it's not what you expected. By the end, speak the truth as if it's the only thing that matters—because it is.

title: Confronting Your Sibling Who Hasn't Visited in Two Years
instruction: Your sibling finally returns after two years of absence while you've been caring for your parent with dementia alone. You start calm, almost cold, listing what they've missed: 'Mom asked for you every day for six months. Then she stopped asking.' Your voice is factual, detached, protective. But as you describe the moments they weren't there for—the night she didn't recognize you, the morning she wept for no reason she could name—your anger builds. By the end, you're not yelling, but your voice is shaking with suppressed rage and grief: 'You don't get to walk in now and have her remember you when she can't remember me.' Finish with a whispered confession that terrifies you: 'Sometimes I'm so tired I wish she would just... and I hate myself for thinking it.' Move from icy control to trembling fury to shameful vulnerability.
inspired_by: Parent with Dementia Has a Confused Moment: Patient Repetition

title: The Thing We Don't Say
instruction: You're confronting your father in his study about something he did when you were thirteen—something you both have never spoken about, something that lives in the silence between you. Begin the scene with tight, controlled anger, trying to be reasonable and adult. But as you speak, something fiercer and younger starts clawing its way out of you—the child's rage, the teenager's betrayal, the adult's bewilderment all fighting for voice. Don't censor which version of you speaks or how they speak. Let your voice crack, let yourself become small then huge, let profanity mix with tenderness, let your body express what words can't. If you suddenly want to laugh bitterly or sob or scream or whisper or all of those in rapid succession, honor it completely. By the end, you've said the unsayable thing—not in the way you imagined, but in the way it actually needed to come out, messy and true and utterly uncalculated.

title: The Weight of a Word
instruction: You’re a teenage guy hanging out with your friend in his messy bedroom, arms crossed, scrolling on your phone. He just casually said something that reveals he’s been mocking your passion behind your back—your voice starts flat, distracted, but as you process the betrayal, a cold, sharp contempt bleeds through. Let your words slow, your jaw tighten, and let the room feel smaller—like you’re seeing him clearly for the first time. End with a dismissive, bitter laugh that trails off, your gaze dropping to the floor.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing With Your Dying Best Friend About Shared Memories
instruction: You're sitting by their hospital bed, and they've just made a joke about something ridiculous from your past. Start with genuine laughter—real, from-the-belly joy at the absurdity of that time you both got lost, or drunk, or in trouble. Your voice is light, teasing: 'Oh my god, remember when you...' But even as you're laughing, tears are streaming down your face. Let your voice do both—giggling while it breaks, joy and devastation completely intertwined. Move through several memories, each one bittersweet. Your laughter might hitch into a sob mid-sentence, then back to laughing because they're laughing. End in profound gratitude, still smiling through tears, your voice soft and wondering: 'How did I get so lucky to know you?' Let the last words be both celebration and goodbye, where joy and grief are inseparable.
inspired_by: Your Sibling Asking About Your Trauma

title: The Breaking Point of Protector and Protected
instruction: You are someone who has always been strong for others, now facing a loved one in terrible danger that you cannot prevent—perhaps they're about to undergo a risky surgery, or leave for a dangerous journey. Begin with fierce, almost angry reassurance: 'You're going to be fine, you have to be fine.' Your voice is commanding, protective, trying to will safety into existence. But as the moment of separation approaches, your armor shatters. The commanding voice breaks into raw terror, desperate pleading, your breath coming in gasps. Rage at your own powerlessness erupts—'I can't lose you, I can't, I WON'T'—before collapsing into helpless sobbing, then transforming into tender, broken whispers of love. End with the devastating simplicity of 'Come back to me,' your voice both a prayer and a command, fierce and fragile at once.
inspired_by: The Lost Child and the Mysterious Forest Spirit

title: Admitting You Faked Orgasms for Years
instruction: You're telling your long-term partner that you've been faking it. Your voice is guilty, defensive, scared. You're admitting you lied for years. Your partner is listening. Your voice becomes smaller as you explain—every word feels like a betrayal that you kept secret. You're trying to explain why you did it without blaming them, but your voice carries the weight of the deception. Include the moment they respond and your voice wavers.

title: The Sting of the Deal
instruction: You are a boy, no older than twelve, seated at the head of a polished boardroom table surrounded by stern executives. You've been sent in to negotiate for a family business after your father's sudden death, and you're terrified but masking it with a forced, low-pitched bravado. One of the men smirks, underestimating you—this sparks a flash of anger that you weaponize into teasing, leaning forward with a jeering smirk as you throw his own words back at him. Mid-sentence, a surprising rift opens: you spot a crack in their united front, and astonishment flickers in your voice before you chase it with a softer, sly shift toward victory. Your voice must feel guarded but break—wobble in the anger, sharpen in the tease, and catch with a tiny gasp in the surprise, all within the same moment.
emotions_sampled: Anger (clearly present), Teasing (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're standing in your child's bedroom doorway at 3 AM, watching them sleep, and you need to say goodbye—maybe you're terminally ill, maybe you're leaving to protect them, maybe circumstances are tearing you apart. Speak in barely-voiced whispers, as if even breathing too loudly might wake them and shatter this moment. Start by describing what you see: their face in the moonlight, the way their hand curls on the pillow, how small they still look despite growing so fast. Your voice should be tender, almost reverent, cataloging details you're burning into memory. Gradually let the grief seep in—your whispers catching on words as you tell them all the things you'll miss: first days of school you won't see, heartbreaks you won't help heal, triumphs you won't celebrate. By the end, let yourself speak the impossible truth: that loving them is both the most precious and most painful thing you've ever known, that you would stay if the universe allowed it, that you need them to know—even if they'll never hear these words—that you were wholly, completely, desperately theirs. Let silence speak as much as words.

title: I Know What You're Hiding
instruction: Confront your father about something you've deduced from years of observing him—the way he flinches when the phone rings at certain hours, how he stands taller when talking about his job but his hands shake, how he covers his mouth when he laughs, the cologne he wears on 'work trips.' You've pieced together a truth he's never spoken aloud. Begin calm, almost detective-like, laying out each small observed detail like evidence: 'You do this thing where...' Then watch his face as he realizes you see him completely. Let your clinical observations give way to raw hurt—all these tiny behaviors you catalogued were you trying to understand why he felt so far away. Demand he either confirm your deductions or prove you wrong. Move from intellectual certainty to desperate need for him to tell you who he really is.

title: Under the Visor
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a deliberately soft, sweet voice, standing on a noisy construction site. You wear a hard hat with a visor that cups your voice downward. At first, you feel a flutter of ecstasy as you watch your demolition crew work—the destruction is beautiful. But then your crew chief hands you a report: a young inspector is coming to check permits, and the permits are forged. Fear tightens your throat. By the end, you smile sweetly as you whisper to the chief, 'Make sure he has an accident. Nothing fatal. Just... convincing.' Your voice stays pleasant and melodic, but your eyes are cold. Speak over the sound of jackhammers, letting the fear rise and curdle into malice as you finish.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Fear (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Kitchen at Midnight
instruction: You've come home unexpectedly and found your father sitting alone in the dark kitchen—the same man who walked out on your family fifteen years ago without explanation. Start from a place of frozen shock and carefully controlled anger, every word measured and sharp. But as you begin speaking, something inside refuses to stay locked down. Let your rehearsed accusations crumble. Allow your voice to do unexpected things—rise when you meant to stay cold, break when you meant to stay strong, soften when you meant to wound. Your body might betray you: fists clenching then releasing, stepping forward when you meant to leave, or suddenly needing to sit because your legs won't hold your rage anymore. Don't decide in advance whether you'll forgive him or destroy him—discover it moment by moment. End in a place emotionally unrecognizable from where you began.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After the Divorce Papers
instruction: Your child is asleep. You've just signed divorce papers, and you're sitting by their bed in the dark, whispering things you can never say when they're awake. Start with the tender, everyday observations - how their hair falls across the pillow, the way they hold their stuffed animal. Your voice is soft, aching with love. Then the confession begins to leak out: 'I'm so sorry I couldn't make it work. I tried so hard.' Your whisper breaks. You tell them about all the ways you're afraid you'll fail them now, how you're terrified they'll think love isn't real because yours fell apart. There's so much tenderness mixed with such deep sadness. By the end, you're making promises through tears that catch in your throat - promises you desperately hope you can keep - and your whisper becomes almost inaudible as you say, 'You are the one thing I got completely right.' Let your voice stay intimate and hushed throughout, but move from gentle tenderness to throat-caught confession to fierce, broken devotion.
inspired_by: Interviewing Your Parent About Their Mistakes

title: The Echo of a Promise
instruction: You're a mom on a concrete stairwell, holding your child's hand. You've just been told she got the lead in the school play, and you're bursting with elation—you shout up the stairwell, your voice ringing grandly off the walls. But she corrects you: it's just the understudy, not the main part. Your joy crashes into disappointment, and your voice drops, losing its reverb. Let the hard surfaces make your first words boastful, then let your last words sound fainter, deflated, as footsteps echo around you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're standing in the rain, having just discovered a betrayal that shatters everything you believed. Begin by feeling the physical sensation: cold water on your skin, soaking through your clothes, the temperature dropping in your body, your hands going numb. Let the physical cold ignite into emotional heat. As you speak—to yourself, to God, to the person who betrayed you—let the sensations intensify: your heart pounding, breath coming faster, the taste of rain and salt from your own tears, the roughness in your throat as your voice rises. Feel how rage and grief move through your body like electricity. By the end, you've screamed yourself raw and arrived at an exhausted, strange kind of clarity—a fierce determination to survive this. Your voice should begin quiet and stunned, build to a primal roar, then end in a whisper of dangerous resolve.

title: The Truth Your Mother Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the childhood she gave you—or didn't give you. Start with controlled anger, maybe even rehearsed phrases you've practiced for years. 'You were never there. You chose everything else over me.' Your voice is sharp, accusatory. But as you speak, something shifts. You hear yourself becoming the hurt child again, and the anger cracks open to reveal the pain underneath. 'Why wasn't I enough?' slips out, almost involuntarily. Now you're vulnerable, exposed, your voice smaller but somehow more powerful. She doesn't defend herself—she just listens, and that silence breaks something else in you. End with a truth you've never admitted: 'I still want you to love me.' It's humiliating and liberating at once. Let the transformation from rage to raw need be messy and real.

title: Three AM Truths
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years. You've just woken from a dream that made you realize something you've been hiding even from yourself. Whisper to them, unsure if they're awake. Start with your voice barely audible, testing the waters with small admissions - fears about your body, your worth, your terror of ordinariness. Let each confession build courage for the next, your voice remaining quiet but growing more urgent, more raw. This isn't about big dramatic revelations - it's about the tiny, shameful thoughts you've never voiced: that sometimes you fantasize about a different life, that you're afraid you're becoming your mother, that you don't know if you're truly happy or just comfortable. End with the most fragile truth of all: 'I don't know who I am anymore, and I'm scared you'll leave when you figure that out.' Wait in the darkness for their response.
inspired_by: When beginning any unconscious programming journey

title: The Morning After the Last Time
instruction: You are lying in bed, still tangled in sheets, skin warm and damp. Your body is heavy and loose, breath slow but not steady yet. A few minutes ago you were lost in the afterglow, but now a quiet, crushing sadness starts to seep in — because you know this is the last time you’ll ever be this close to them. Let your voice be slow, dreamy, and thick with leftover pleasure, but let it crack and fade as the sorrow takes hold. You might pause to swallow, let a thought trail off, then find it again. By the end, the sadness is fully present, but you still speak in that same intimate, unguarded whisper.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Protector's Collapse
instruction: You're holding someone you love after they've been hurt, and you couldn't stop it. Start fierce, voice shaking with barely contained rage: 'I will destroy anyone who touches you again.' You're all protective fury, voice thick with violence you've never felt before. But as you hold them, feeling them tremble, the rage begins to fracture. Your voice cracks: 'I should have been there. I should have—' The fierceness dissolves into helpless tears. You can't stop apologizing, voice breaking apart: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry.' The protector becomes the broken one. End in aching tenderness, voice soft and ruined: 'I've got you now. I won't let go.' Move from explosive anger to shattered vulnerability to fierce-gentle devotion. Let your body shake, let control slip away completely.

title: The Last Time I Let Myself Feel
instruction: You are a woman in her 60s, in the midst of making love with a much younger partner who adores you. Your voice is high, almost girlish — an armor you’ve worn since youth. As he moves inside you, a sob catches in your throat: this is triumph, because you’ve never been so wanted, but you also feel a wave of helplessness — you are utterly at his mercy, your body has a mind of its own. Your breaths are shallow, stolen; your words come in gasps, sometimes lost mid-sentence. Start with a gasp of surprise and pleasure — the triumph of being desired. Then, as the sensation builds, let sadness bleed in: you whisper, 'Don't stop…' but it sounds like a plea. End with a broken whisper, your voice cracking: 'I didn’t know I could still feel this... this much.' Let the silence after be full of held breath.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Sadness (slightly present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are holding the hand of your lifelong best friend who is dying. For years, you've harbored a secret: you were always in love with them, but never said it because they married someone else. Now, with only minutes left, you must decide moment-by-moment what to say and what to keep silent. Begin with careful, safe words of comfort, but let the weight of unsaid things build until something raw and true breaks through. Your voice should move from steady and protective to trembling with the choice of whether to burden them with your truth or let them go in peace. End having made your choice—whatever it is—and living with that decision in real time.

title: The Storm Won't Take This
instruction: You are an older person, slightly drunk on whiskey, standing alone in a blizzard at the edge of a frozen lake. You've just won a long battle with the city council to save this old family cabin, and now you're shouting your defiance into the gale. But as the wind steals your words and the snow stings your face, the pride starts to crack—you realize you're utterly alone, and the victory feels hollow. Your voice should begin loud and slurred, trying to boast over the howling wind, then gradually drop into a raw, quiet confession as you stop fighting the storm. Let the cold lock your jaw at first, then loosen as emotion overtakes you; let the wind swallow your final words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Flight Home
instruction: You're a veteran pilot who's been grounded after a diagnosis. Your daughter stands before you, holding the keys to your plane - she's taking it up for the first time alone. Start with pride swelling in your chest: 'You were born for this.' But as you watch her prepare, the weight of all the flights you'll never take crashes down. Your voice fractures into something raw: 'I need you to feel the sky for me now.' End with a whispered blessing that's half permission, half goodbye, your voice breaking between letting go and holding on. Let the silence after your last words carry the enormity of passing the torch when you're not ready to surrender it.

title: The Lost Shoelace
instruction: You're at a loud house party, very drunk, and you've just bent over to tie your shoelace, but you're so intoxicated you're struggling to even see your feet. Your speech is thick and slurred, your head pounding with all the blood rushing down. Start by mumbling to yourself in a dazed, almost giggly way about how hard this simple task is, feeling proud of your determination. Midway, your laugh trails off as you sense someone watching you—a flicker of embarrassment creeps in, making your voice tighten and your movements clumsy. By the end, you're trying to sound sober and casual, but the congestion in your throat and your wobbly balance betray you, leaving you quietly mortified as you finally give up.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Embarrassment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Reckoning: Confronting the Parent Who Failed You
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a childhood wound you've carried for decades—something they did or didn't do that shaped your entire life. Start with controlled anger, the kind you've rehearsed in your mind a thousand times, your words careful and cutting. But as they respond (silently, in your imagination), and as you hear your own accusations hanging in the air, something breaks. Your rage cracks open to reveal the desperate child underneath who just wanted to be seen, to be enough. Your voice fragments between fury and tears, between 'I hate you for this' and 'Why wasn't I worth staying for?' End in raw, messy vulnerability—not forgiveness, not resolution, but honest devastation. This isn't about performing anger; it's about letting yourself finally feel everything you've been holding back.
inspired_by: Lost in a Cave: Echo and Darkness

title: The Crunch of a Hard Truth
instruction: You're a young man eating a crisp apple alone at a kitchen counter, having just received a text that your long-term partner wants to 'take a break.' You start eating with forced indifference, crunching loudly to drown out your racing thoughts. As you chew, doubt creeps in—'Is this my fault?'—but you keep eating, pausing to swallow hard, the apple suddenly feeling like obligation. By the end, your chews become slower, quieter, and you mutter a helpless realization to the empty room, the last crunch trailing into silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church
instruction: You're alone in a church, synagogue, or sacred space after losing someone or something irreplaceable. You start speaking to God, the universe, or whatever you once believed in—your voice low and bitter, each word dripping with accusation and betrayal. Demand answers. Let your voice rise from angry questioning to full-throated rage, shouting your fury and pain at the ceiling, at the silence, at the injustice of it all. But mid-scream, let the rage crack open into raw, gasping sobs. Your voice should break from fierce anger into helpless weeping, the words dissolving into sounds of pure anguish. End on your knees, voice reduced to a broken whisper, all the fight gone, speaking not in rage but in devastated surrender, begging for something you know won't come.

title: Holding Your Dying Dog While the Vet Prepares: Fierce Love Meets Helpless Rage
instruction: Your dog—your companion for fifteen years—is dying. You're in the vet's office, cradling them as the vet prepares the injection. Begin with fierce, protective tenderness, whispering memories: 'You were there when no one else was. Every single day.' Your voice is gentle but trembling. Then rage erupts—at time, at mortality, at the unfairness: 'This isn't enough time! Fifteen years isn't enough!' You're almost shouting through tears. The vet gently reminds you it's time to let go. You collapse back into tenderness, but it's desperate now, bargaining: 'Just one more day. Please, just one more walk.' Your dog looks at you with tired eyes. Your voice breaks completely as you give permission, stroking their fur: 'It's okay, baby. You can rest now. I've got you. I'll always have you.' End with a guttural sob that becomes a whispered thank you, gratitude and devastation inseparable.
inspired_by: Observing Lava Flow: Scientific Wonder Turning to Genuine Dread

title: Whispering Secrets in the Dark
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying beside someone you love, speaking truths you've never said aloud. Start with your voice barely audible, testing the waters: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' The darkness makes you braver. Your words are soft, intimate, trembling: 'Sometimes I'm so afraid that you'll realize I'm not who you think I am.' Each confession gets deeper, more vulnerable: 'I have parts of myself I keep hidden because I'm scared if you saw them, you'd leave.' Your voice catches, emotion tightening your throat. There's tenderness here, but also deep sadness and fear: 'I love you so much it terrifies me. Because I've never let anyone this close, and I don't know how to do this without breaking.' They reach for you in the darkness. Your voice becomes even softer, tears very close: 'I'm giving you all of me. Even the broken parts. Even the parts I don't like.' End with a whisper that's both relief and lingering fear: 'Please be gentle with me. I'm more fragile than I pretend to be.' The confession leaves you naked but somehow held.

title: Adult Child Confronts Parent Over a Lifetime of Almost-Love
instruction: You're finally telling your parent something you've needed to say for decades - not about abuse or cruelty, but about the subtle ways they were never quite present, never quite saw you. Start with careful, measured words, trying to be fair, trying to make them understand without attacking. But the hurt is older and deeper than you realized. Your voice should crack and surge as you move between anger, grief, and that desperate child inside still wanting them to finally get it. End somewhere unexpected - maybe with forgiveness you didn't know you had, maybe with the realization that they never will understand, maybe with both at once. Let the contradictions live in your voice.
inspired_by: Guided Meditation Leader Having a Bad Day

title: The Homecoming That Breaks You Open
instruction: You're returning home after years away—maybe from war, prison, rehab, or self-imposed exile. The door opens and there stands someone who never gave up on you. Begin with almost manic joy—laughing, voice bright and high, talking rapidly, making jokes, proving you're okay, you're fine, you're better than ever. Your energy is fizzing, desperate, performative. But they just stand there, looking at you with such steady love that your defenses start to crumble. Let the laughter catch in your throat. Let silence creep in between your words. Let your voice drop and slow. End by admitting what you've really lost, what you can never get back, while simultaneously feeling their forgiveness wash over you. The final moment should hold both devastating grief for wasted time and overwhelming gratitude that they're still here. Your voice should break between these two truths, unable to land on just one.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a regular daily practice for deepening unconscious connection

title: The Words I Never Said
instruction: You're sitting at your best friend's hospital bedside in the middle of the night, and they're asleep. You're whispering all the things you were too afraid to say when they were awake—how much they meant to you, how you were in love with them for years, how their friendship saved your life. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every other word, intimate and aching. Let long pauses happen where words fail you completely. Halfway through, your voice breaks into silent crying—no performance, just genuine grief trying to speak. Then soften into tender gratitude mixed with unbearable sadness: 'Thank you for being my person.' End with the quietest whisper, almost talking to yourself: 'I hope you knew.' This should feel like overhearing someone's most private moment, so intimate it's almost uncomfortable to witness.

title: Washing Your Hands with Warm, Soapy Water
instruction: Let the warm water flow over your hands, lathering up the soap. Describe the smooth, silky sensation, the way the warmth envelops your skin, and the calming, clean scent. Speak with a soft, peaceful tone, as if each wash leaves you feeling refreshed and completely cleansed, like each movement is washing away any remaining tension.

title: Compulsion Resisting
instruction: You're an alcoholic one week sober, standing in front of the liquor store. Your internal monologue is a battle. One voice is smooth, seductive, familiar: 'Just one drink, you've earned it.' Another is desperate, young, barely holding on. They fight each other in your throat. Your physical body is shaking. You can smell it from outside the store. Then a friend texts. That simple sound—your phone buzzing—breaks the spell. Your voice drops: 'No. Not today.'

title: Post-Practice Phone Call
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl who just finished an intense cheerleading practice. You're alone in the gym, still sweating, breathing hard, feeling the euphoric endorphin rush but also bone-deep exhaustion. You call your best friend to share your excitement about the routine you finally nailed, but when they don't answer, your voice shifts from breathless pride to a quieter, tired disappointment, yet you still speak with affection into the voicemail. Let your voice be physically affected: you're panting, your words tumble out with energy, but you also drag on some words from tiredness. The initial excitement gives way to a soft letdown, but the warmth remains.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Affection (slightly present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Garden's Last Grip
instruction: You are a woman in her late forties, your voice naturally light and melodic, but now it's raw. You're tangled with someone in a muddy garden after dark, struggling over a trowel. You've been here before—this same fight, this same dirt. As you gasp for air, push, and grunt, you suddenly pause, your grip loosening, and your voice shifts from jagged effort to a soft, bewildered contemplation: 'How many times have we watered this same spot with our anger?' Then the fight resumes, but now it's weaker, sadder.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Time
instruction: You are in bed with someone you love, but you both know this is your final time together. You are trying to stay present, to memorize every sensation, but a deep sadness keeps seeping in—a sour, metallic taste of loss at the back of your throat. Let your moans start as focused, eager, almost desperate to feel everything. Then let them become heavier, thicker with grief, your breath catching on a sob you don't fully release. End with a long, aching sigh that is part surrender, part goodbye, a quiet tremor in the exhale.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Sadness (extremely present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Good Lie
instruction: You are an older man sitting in a worn armchair, talking to your adult child on the phone about your recent doctor visit. You already decided to hide the bad news to spare them worry. At the start, you feel a wave of relief that they believe your cheerful tone, so your voice lifts a little too eagerly, with an unnatural bounce. Midway, you sense their suspicion creeping in, making you over-explain small details—your pitch rises, your words stumble over themselves as you shift in your seat. By the end, helplessness seeps through, your voice drops and grows impatient as you snap a short reply, then trails off into a quiet, shaky sigh.
emotions_sampled: Relief (extremely present), Helplessness (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Threshold Confession
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who's about to get married, and you need to tell them the truth about their other parent—something you've hidden for twenty years. Start with false brightness: 'Before you walk down that aisle, we should talk.' Your voice is too cheerful, compensating. As you begin to reveal the truth, watch yourself lose control of the narrative. Your child's face changes. You start defending, then pleading, then—unexpectedly—you hear yourself getting angry at them for judging you. 'You don't know what it was like!' Your voice rises, breaks. Then suddenly you're begging: 'Don't hate me.' Move from protective dishonesty through defensive anger into naked fear of losing them. Let each emotion crash into the next.

title: The Unsent Draft
instruction: You are a teenage boy hunched over a laptop in your cluttered bedroom, angrily typing a message to your father after a bitter argument. Your fingers slam the keys in a fast, rhythmic clatter, but each time you try to speak your frustration out loud, your typing slows and your words fragment—as if the anger is physically catching in your throat. Midway through a sentence, you pause, stare at the screen, and the bitterness softens into something raw and reluctant: you remember a time he taught you to ride a bike, and a quiet, trembling affection leaks into your voice. By the end, you’re not typing anymore—just whispering a broken apology to the empty room, the rage spent, replaced by a bruised love you can’t fully say.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: 3 AM Pillow Confession
instruction: You're lying next to your sleeping partner in the middle of the night, whispering a confession they cannot hear—something you've hidden for years. Start with the whisper barely forming, your throat tight, testing the words in the darkness. You're terrified even though they're asleep, even though you're 'safe.' As you continue, let the whisper find more breath, more truth. The relief of finally speaking it, even to an unhearing room, begins to unlock something in your chest. Move from that strangled, fearful whisper to something that flows more freely—still quiet, still intimate, but less imprisoned. By the end, you're crying softly, not from sadness but from the overwhelming release of finally letting these words exist in the air, even if only the darkness hears them.

title: The Sandbox Oath
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy defending your little brother on the playground. You stand tall, but your voice drops low and slow like your father's when he's serious. You begin with a threatening growl, telling the older bully to back off. But as you talk, you remember your brother's smile this morning when you promised to protect him. A wave of contentment washes over you. You feel a flicker of hope that maybe words can work, and a slight, silly infatuation with how brave you feel. By the end, your voice softens from a growl to a gentle, hopeful plea for peace.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Contentment (very intensely present), Infatuation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Final Words to the Child I'll Never Meet
instruction: You are recording a message for the child you're carrying, knowing you won't survive to raise them. Begin with fierce determination to be brave for them, filling your voice with all the love and strength you want them to remember. But as you speak, the reality of what you're losing breaks through—every milestone you'll miss, every scraped knee you won't kiss better, every proud moment you won't witness. Your voice should crack and soften, moving from protective strength to raw, aching vulnerability. End in a whisper of desperate love mixed with the devastating acceptance that this recording is all you can give them. Let the transition be gradual and heartbreaking, as if your armor is slowly, painfully dissolving.
inspired_by: The Hero and the Dark Inner Voice

title: A Hiccuping Toast
instruction: You're at a family dinner, trying to propose a heartfelt toast to your son who just got a promotion. But you've developed a sudden case of hiccups that cuts your words with sharp intakes. You start off a little curious about the rhythm of the hiccups, then find the situation hilarious. Each time you're interrupted, you laugh at yourself, growing more optimistic that you'll power through. Speak in a deep, masculine voice, letting the hiccups disrupt your flow naturally. End with a hopeful, laughing tone as you finally get the toast out.
emotions_sampled: Interest (slightly present), Amusement (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Garden She Tended
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a therapy session, speaking about your younger neighbor who now tends the garden you once nurtured. Begin with a guarded, almost clinical description of her—your voice steady, each word measured, as if examining a specimen. Let a pause hang where you stare at the floor, then let malice seep in: a sudden rush of bitterness about how she took your place, your hands twitching as you recall her laughter. But as the therapist gently asks what you wish for, your voice softens, cracks, and a fragile hope emerges—a whispered admission that maybe she could learn your ways, if she'd only ask. End with a long silence, your breath shallow, the jealousy still coiled beneath the hope.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying everything you've rehearsed for years to the parent who abandoned you. Begin with controlled anger, each word carefully chosen, voice tight and precise: 'I needed you at my graduation. I needed you when I was hospitalized. I needed you.' But as you list each absence, something cracks. The anger gives way to the child inside still waiting at the window. Your voice becomes smaller, younger, more desperate. 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me?' You're furious at yourself for still caring, for still needing their approval even now. End with exhausted bewilderment, all the fight drained out, just a whispered question you're not sure you want answered: 'Did you ever love me at all?'

title: Stars Overwhelming
instruction: You're a tough 17-year-old guy, alone in a field at midnight, having a sudden panic attack while staring up at a sky blazing with stars. The awe of the universe hits you so hard it triggers hyperventilation—you can't catch your breath, your chest tightens, and your voice cracks and quavers as you try to speak. Start in sheer terror, gasping fragmented words about dying or not breathing, but let the awe slowly seep in as you force yourself to look upward. By the end, amid the panic, a tiny flicker of contentment appears—a quiet acceptance that you're part of something huge. Let your voice be high-pitched, breathy, and interrupted by gasps; feel the physical symptoms of tingling hands and a racing heart as you try to articulate your overwhelming awe.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Emergency Room Waiting Room Breakdown
instruction: Your child/partner/sibling was just rushed into emergency surgery, and you're on the phone with someone, trying to explain what happened. Start with a kind of manic efficiency—rattling off medical details, describing the accident or crisis with false calm, your voice tight and controlled because if you let go, you'll shatter. But as you talk, it starts to overtake you: rage at the situation, at yourself for not preventing this, at God or fate or random chance. Your voice rises, becomes fierce and accusatory, then suddenly breaks—all that ferocity collapses into helpless, desperate fear. You're sobbing and trying to speak at the same time, apologizing for crying, then getting angry again at having to apologize. Include the moment where you realize you're terrified of a future without this person, and it manifests as almost childlike pleading: bargaining, promising anything, your voice raw and stripped of all adult composure. End in exhausted quiet—not peace, but the hollowed-out space after a storm, still trembling but too drained to fight anymore.

title: The Gratitude Paradox
instruction: You've just received news of an opportunity you've desperately wanted, but it comes at the moment you're also dealing with profound loss or disappointment in another area of your life. You're speaking to someone who helped you get this opportunity—thanking them, acknowledging what this means. Start by trying to express pure gratitude, but you can't fully access joy because grief keeps interrupting. As you list what this achievement represents—the skills you've built, the rejections you've survived, the specific capabilities that earned you this chance—your voice must carry both celebration and sorrow. Let the contradictions coexist authentically: pride that you've actually accomplished something real, and simultaneous heartbreak over what you're losing or have lost. By the end, arrive at a complex truth: you can hold both realities at once. The transformation is from trying to feel only one thing to accepting the full, contradictory spectrum of being human.

title: Breathing in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to someone you love, and you need to whisper a secret that terrifies you—something about your past, your fears, or your desires that could change everything. Begin with your body tight, breath shallow, barely making sound. As you start to speak, focus on your actual breath, your actual physical state. Let the words come haltingly at first, your body rigid with vulnerability. As you continue, allow yourself to physically soften into the truth-telling. By the end, your breath should be deeper, your body released into the person beside you. This isn't about volume—it's about the journey from constriction to surrender, all in whispers. Let silence live between your words.

title: The Edge of the Cliff
instruction: You're a teenager lying on your bed, tangled in sheets, with your partner playfully holding you just on the edge of climax, then pulling back. Start with a breathless, teasing laugh as you realize what they're doing — a mix of contentment and playful control. As they deny you again and again, let your voice shift: your giggles turn into frustrated whimpers, your pleas become ragged and desperate, your breathing jagged. End with a long, shaky exhale that is part satisfaction at the game, part raw longing — as if you've finally let go of the need for release and just want to stay in this moment, even if it means being denied forever.
emotions_sampled: Longing (slightly present), Teasing (very intensely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Cat That Got Away
instruction: You are an older woman in your garden, complaining loudly to a neighbor about how that blasted cat from next door keeps ruining your tulips. Your voice starts in that familiar, whiny drone — elongated vowels, nasal pitch, a sing-song rhythm of self-pity. But then you recall how you finally scared it off with a blast from the hose, and a note of triumph brightens your tone, a little smirk in your voice. The triumph fades quickly as you notice the neighbor's silence, and shame washes over you — you feel foolish and petty, your voice dropping into a sad, cracked confession that maybe you just miss having someone to talk to. Let the words falter, sigh, and trail off as you realize how lonely that sounds.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Triumph (clearly present), Sadness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Interrogator's Doubt
instruction: You are strapped to a chair, your body wrecked from hours of torture. Your captor has just left the room, their footsteps fading. You are alone, but your mind is screaming—not just from pain, but from the doubt clawing at you: maybe they were right, maybe you are weak. Between ragged breaths and sobs, you whisper to yourself, trying to hold onto the contempt you felt for them earlier. Start fierce, a whisper of defiance, but let it crumble into a breathy, hollow question as you realize how broken you are. Let your voice crack and fade, like a radio signal dying, until the last word is barely a breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Ascent of Envy
instruction: You are an elderly woman hiking a steep incline, lungs burning, legs trembling. Ahead, a younger woman strides effortlessly, and you feel a hot, trembling jealousy — almost infatuation — as you watch her perfect rhythm. You pause, bent over, hands on knees, forcing air in and out. Between ragged breaths, you mutter to yourself, your voice puffed and strained. The envy is raw at first, but then you notice the golden sunlight through the leaves, the fact that you are still here, still moving. Let the gratitude creep in like a pulled muscle — surprising, tender. Your spoken words should shift from bitter, envious gasps to a more grounded, thankful murmur, with the physical labor shaping every syllable.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Infatuation (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Apology Thirty Years Too Late
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect of your childhood—how they were always too busy, too distant, too critical. Start with careful, measured words you've rehearsed a thousand times, your voice tight with controlled anger. But as you speak, something shifts. You see them aging before your eyes, diminished, and your rage begins to mix with unexpected grief for what you both lost. Your voice should crack between accusation and longing, between 'you destroyed me' and 'I just wanted you to see me.' End with the terrible realization that even now, even with all this honesty, you may never get what you needed. The delivery must feel like you're excavating your own heart—painful, halting, brutally honest, with pauses where you're literally trying not to break.
inspired_by: In Love with Lifes Last Moments

title: Building the Boat That Takes You Away
instruction: You're crafting a boat for someone you love deeply, knowing it will carry them away from you forever—not death, but a necessary journey you cannot join. Begin with focused joy, even humming: 'Every plank has to be perfect. You deserve perfect.' Your voice carries pride and love. As you work, the contradiction builds—laughing softly at shared memories while tears fall: 'Remember when you said we'd sail together? God, we were so naive.' Your hands keep building even as your heart breaks. The beauty of what you're making and the pain of its purpose war in your voice: 'This is the most important thing I'll ever make, and I hate it. I love it. I need it to be strong enough to take you away from me.' End with quiet, complex peace: 'It's ready. You're ready. I'm... I'm so proud of you.' Let gratitude, devastation, and love all live in the same breath.

title: Pedal Pulse Surprise
instruction: You are a child pedaling furiously on a stationary bike, your legs burning with each rotation. You're angry about something that happened earlier, and your breath comes in forced, rhythmic bursts. Just as you're about to give up, you glance at the timer and see you've broken your personal record by a full minute — your anger is suddenly swallowed by sheer astonishment. Let your words be chopped by your panting, each phrase pushed out on an exhale, with your voice shifting from a tight, frustrated grunt to a breathless, wide-eyed gasp. You might lose your rhythm for a second, or your foot might slip — react to that too.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Room You Never Made for Me
instruction: You're an adult confronting your parent, standing in their pristine home office—the room that could have been yours growing up. Begin with bitter, controlled anger: 'You had space. You chose work instead.' Each observation is an accusation. Your voice sharpens as you detail what you needed and never got—not just physical space but emotional room to exist. Then something shifts. You see them aging, smaller than you remembered. Your voice cracks, anger collapsing into raw vulnerability: 'I just wanted you to make room for me.' The fury dissolves into the ache of a child who still, even now, wants to be chosen. End with exhausted honesty, barely above a whisper: 'I needed you to care enough to try.'

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your grandmother, lucid for the first time in days, asks you to tell her about your wedding last month that she missed. You start describing it, and suddenly she asks you to dance with her, right there, even though she can barely sit up. You laugh—it's absurd, it's beautiful, it's breaking your heart. Help her stand, hold her weight, and start humming the song. Your voice is full of joy and grief tangled together. You're laughing and crying at once as you describe her dress that you wore, her earrings, how you felt her there anyway. She says something funny, vintage her, and you genuinely laugh—but the laughter dissolves mid-breath into a sob. You keep dancing, keep describing, keep finding moments of light even as you both know this is goodbye. End thanking her: 'Thank you for teaching me how to be strong. Thank you for teaching me it's okay to break.' Your voice should be smiling and shattering simultaneously. Let gratitude and grief live in the same breath. This is what love sounds like when it has to let go.

title: A Whisper in the White
instruction: You are a child lost in a blinding sandstorm, calling out for your mother. Pull your shirt over your mouth and feel the grit on your teeth. Start with a desperate shout, voice strained and muffled. Midway, doubt flickers—you pause, cough, and your next call is softer, more uncertain: 'Mom? Can you hear me?' The wind howls, you stumble, and your voice cracks. By the end, you shift from panic to quiet determination, whispering: 'I’ll keep walking. She has to be here.' Let each breath be labored, let sibilants hiss with dust, and let the silence between words hold your fear.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your mother across the kitchen table where you ate breakfast every day of your childhood. She has asked why you seem so distant lately, and something inside you snaps. Start controlled, almost eerily calm, as you begin listing the small ways she made you feel invisible: 'You never asked how I was feeling. You never noticed when I was struggling.' Let your voice grow stronger as years of unspoken pain pour out. Accuse her of the specific moments that broke you - not with screaming, but with the surgical precision of someone who has rehearsed this in their head a thousand times. As you speak, let yourself hear your own words and realize you sound like a wounded child, not an adult. End with your voice breaking into vulnerability: the anger collapses into the simple, painful truth that you still need her to see you. Transform from righteous fury to raw, exposed need.

title: The Protector Who Cannot Protect
instruction: Someone you would die for—a child, a partner, a friend—is in pain you cannot fix, facing something you cannot fight. You start with fierce, almost violent reassurance: 'I won't let this happen. I'll fix this.' Your voice is all adrenaline and determination. But as you speak, reality crashes against your promises. Your voice begins to crack, the protective fury collapsing into helpless anguish. 'I can't... I can't...' The words break apart. Your breath comes in ragged gasps as rage at your own powerlessness wars with tender desperation. You cycle between trying to sound strong and dissolving completely, your voice rising to a near-shout then dropping to a broken whisper. By the end, you're holding them, your voice raw and small: 'I'm here. That's all I have. I'm here.' The shift from fierce warrior to vulnerable human is complete, and it's destroying you.

title: Lost and Swallowed
instruction: You're a teenage boy deep in a dense jungle, disoriented and alone after sneaking drinks from a flask. The heavy air and thick foliage muffle your voice, while distant bird calls and rustling leaves surround you. Start by mumbling to yourself in a drunken haze, trying to recall how you got here, with a hint of fatigue dragging your words. As you stumble over a root, your tone shifts from bewildered to a quiet, trembling realization that you might not make it out tonight. Let the intoxication warp your speech, but let the exhaustion slowly ground you into a raw, honest whisper of fear.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Phone Call That Changed It
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, gruff voice, alone in your car after a tense phone call with your ex-girlfriend. You're thinking aloud, processing what just happened. Start with contempt—you're bitter, scoffing at her audacity, voice tight with disgust. But as you speak, a memory surfaces of your little sister helping you pack last week. The contempt fades, replaced by overwhelming gratitude. Let your voice slow, pause irregularly, and elongate words like 'that' and 'so' as you search for the feeling. End with a quiet, raw thankfulness that cracks your usual bravado.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Suicidal Crisis
instruction: You're in a dark place, and you're calling a crisis line. Your voice is small, fragile: 'I don't know why I'm calling. I don't want to be here anymore.' The counselor is speaking with gentle urgency. You're explaining your pain, and the effort to speak at all exhausts you. Your voice is sometimes just a whisper, sometimes a sob. Include moments where you can't continue, where you're just breathing heavily into the phone. By the end, you're making a commitment to stay alive, your voice barely holding together.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There: Rage Meets Longing
instruction: You are confronting your parent—someone who abandoned you, who chose addiction or another family or their career over you. Start with controlled anger, almost cold: 'Do you even remember my birthday?' But as you speak, years of buried pain surge up. Your voice becomes fierce, accusing—'I needed you and you weren't there.' Then something shifts. Underneath the rage is the child who still wanted their love. Your voice cracks, becomes vulnerable: 'Why wasn't I enough?' You're furious at yourself for still caring. The anger and longing fight each other in your voice. By the end, you're exhausted, your voice quiet but shaking with the realization that you may never get what you needed from them, saying 'I have to let you go' with both grief and liberation.
inspired_by: Panic Attack: Losing Control Over Your Own Voice

title: Fierce Grace: Emergency Room
instruction: You're a parent in an ER, and they've just told you there's nothing more they can do—your child is dying, and it will happen in the next hour. Begin with an explosion of refusal: rage at the doctors, at God, at the universe, your voice a raw howl of 'NO.' Demand impossible things—fix this, try harder, there must be something. Let your fury be magnificent and helpless. Then, mid-rage, something breaks: you hear your child's voice from the other room, asking for you. Your emotional state shatters and reconstitutes into something else entirely. Rush through the door, and now you must become nothing but love—fierce, protective, gentle love. Your voice transforms: softer but no less intense, telling them stories, singing maybe, promising them it's okay, they can rest now, mommy/daddy's here. End with you finding a terrible, beautiful courage you didn't know you had—giving them permission to go, your voice breaking but steady, whispering 'It's okay, baby. You can let go now.'

title: The Secret in the Walls
instruction: You're a seven-year-old girl, lying on your stomach in the attic crawlspace with a flashlight, your mother's old jewelry box cracked open beside you. You have to whisper because your dad is napping one floor below, and the floorboards groan when you shift weight. You're explaining to your invisible friend how you found a tiny, hand-drawn map tucked under the velvet lining, your voice a flurry of hushed, excited air—sometimes you stop mid-word, suddenly afraid you heard a creak, then you lean closer to the light, your tone rising with pure, fascinated wonder. By the end, the map becomes a real, dangerous secret, and your whisper turns from glee to a solemn, conspiratorial vow.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Burning and Freezing
instruction: You're in the throes of a passionate reunion with a lover who betrayed you. Your body is responding with intense physical desire—allow yourself to feel genuine heat, flushed skin, accelerated breath, tingling sensation spreading through your limbs—while simultaneously perceiving coldness in their touch, seeing cruelty in their beautiful eyes, feeling revulsion in what attracts you. Let your voice be breathless with want while your words express distrust. Feel your hands drawn to them while your body also recoils. This isn't acting two emotions sequentially—it's experiencing them simultaneously, creating a visceral tension that should be audible and electric. End in either surrender or rejection, but the contradiction should torture you throughout.

title: What You Never Knew About Me
instruction: You are confronting your parent about something they've never understood about you—a secret you've carried, a part of yourself you've hidden, a truth about your childhood they were blind to. Begin with measured control, almost clinical distance, as if you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. But as you speak, let the little girl or boy you once were bleed through—the one who needed them to see you, really see you. Draw from the specific times you felt invisible: standing in a doorway waiting to be noticed, sitting at dinner with words trapped in your throat, the particular ache of being misunderstood by the one person who should have known you. Let your anger build not into shouting, but into something more devastating: the raw, naked vulnerability of finally being visible. End not with rage but with exhausted honesty, asking them a question you've needed answered your entire life.
inspired_by: Scene partners have a long shared history that does not appear in the script

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Beloved Who Doesn't Know You're Leaving
instruction: They're asleep. You're leaving before dawn and won't be here when they wake. Your voice is barely audible—you don't want to wake them because you can't face their eyes. Start with the practical things you need to say, your voice catching on mundane details: where you left the keys, that the bills are paid. Your whisper becomes tender as you tell them the things you never said enough—how beautiful they are in morning light, how their laugh changed your life. Let your breath become uneven. The emotion you've been holding back seeps into every word. You almost touch them but don't. Your voice breaks on 'I'm sorry' and you have to stop, collect yourself. End with 'I love you' said so quietly it's almost just breath, full of everything you'll never get to say again.
inspired_by: Rejecting Someone Sexually and Trying to Be Kind

title: The Last Morning Coffee
instruction: You're sharing one final cup of coffee with your partner who has terminal cancer and has chosen to end treatment today. You both know this is goodbye, but neither of you can say the words yet. Start by talking about mundane things—the weather, the coffee being too hot, anything to avoid the reality. Your tone is falsely cheerful, almost manic in its normalcy. But as the silence between your words grows heavier, let the pretense crack. Your voice should break from bright deflection into raw, whispered devastation. End by finally saying what you've been avoiding, letting grief pour through every word. The emotional journey moves from desperate avoidance through crumbling composure to complete surrender to the unbearable truth.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Busy to Avoid a Conversation

title: Godparent Whispers Final Bedtime Story to Child in Coma
instruction: Hospital room, late at night. You're reading your godchild's favorite book—the one you've read together a hundred times—but they can't hear you anymore. Begin gently, almost normally, as if this is just another bedtime routine. But your voice catches on familiar phrases, on the parts that always made them laugh. You keep reading, softer and softer, the words becoming a prayer, a plea. You're not reading to them anymore; you're reading to keep yourself from falling apart, to hold onto the sound of normalcy. Between sentences, you whisper the things you never said—how much they changed your life, how you're not ready to let go, how their laugh was the best sound in the world. End barely audible, the book finished, sitting in the silence that follows, knowing this may be the last story you ever share.
inspired_by: Principal Announces School Safety While Terror Alert Silences Her

title: Protecting Your Child From Yourself
instruction: You've just been diagnosed with the same mental illness that destroyed your childhood—the one you swore you'd never pass on. Your child is in the next room, innocent, trusting you. Your voice begins fierce, almost aggressive in its protectiveness: you will NOT let this touch them, you will fight this with everything you have. But the fierceness cracks into terror—what if you can't control it? What if you've already damaged them? Your voice becomes frantic, nearly shouting at yourself, at God, at fate: 'Not them. Please, not them. Take anything else.' The rage and fear peak, then shatter into helpless sobbing. You're not fierce now; you're broken, admitting you're scared, that you don't know if love is enough. Then, through the tears, something else emerges: a quieter strength. Your voice steadies as you realize you're not your parents—you're aware, you're getting help, you're choosing differently. End with a trembling but determined promise to your child, to yourself: 'I will do better. I am doing better.' The arc must feel like a complete emotional breakdown that somehow finds solid ground.
inspired_by: Dream Job First Week: Imposter Syndrome Detonating

title: The Echo of a Bright Idea
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a gentle, breathy voice, sitting on a cold concrete step halfway up a dim stairwell. You're exhausted—your joints ache, and each word feels like it takes more air than you have. But in your lap, you hold a worn photograph of a garden you planted decades ago, and a quiet, stubborn hope flickers inside you. You're talking to yourself, half-musing, half-praying, as your words bounce off the hard walls and spiral upward. Start with weariness that cracks and fades, then let the hope grow, making your voice lift with a faint, trembling brightness—even as you pause to catch your breath or shift your weight on the hard step. The reverb makes you sound stronger than you feel, and you lean into that contrast.
emotions_sampled: Interest (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Mirror Shards
instruction: You are confronting your mother/father after discovering they've been telling people you're 'successful' based entirely on superficial markers—your job title, your income, your social media following. Start with controlled anger: list back to them everything they brag about to others, making each word sharp and precise. Your voice should be cutting, almost mocking their values. Then let the anger crack open into something raw: you realize you've been performing for them your entire life, measuring your worth by their metrics. Your voice should shake as you confess: 'I don't even know what I actually love. I don't know who I am when no one's watching.' Feel the vulnerability of admitting you're lost.
