Then, find one small, true thing about yourself that has nothing to do with achievement—maybe you're kind to animals, maybe you notice beautiful clouds, maybe you remember people's stories. Let your voice grow quietly fierce as you claim this one truth. End by telling them: 'That's who I actually am. And I don't know if that's enough for you, but it has to be enough for me.'

title: Reading Their Letter in the Garden
instruction: You are in a garden reading a letter that changes everything—a reconciliation after years of silence, an apology you never thought you'd receive, or news of someone's return. Begin by noticing the garden around you—birdsong, wind in leaves, the smell of earth or flowers, sunlight, the bench you're sitting on. Start reading with your heart guarded, skeptical, afraid to hope. As you read their words, let the life surrounding you—the insistent greenness, the sounds of growth, the physical sensation of being held by this living place—compete with your protective cynicism. Feel hope and bitterness war in you. By the end, you're crying but also laughing, furious at them but grateful, wanting to crumple the letter but holding it like something precious. The beauty around you makes your anger impossible to sustain, yet the anger makes the beauty almost painful.

title: The Scream That Becomes a Surrender
instruction: You've just discovered your child, your partner, or someone you'd die for is in danger you cannot prevent—an illness, an addiction, a choice they're making that will destroy them. Start with explosive, almost feral rage at the universe, at God, at the unfairness. Your voice should be raw, loud, cracking with the kind of fury that comes from absolute helplessness. Pound your fists, rail against fate, demand answers from the empty air. But then, in the middle of your rage, let it shatter into sobbing, into begging, into the most vulnerable bargaining—'please, please, I'll do anything.' Finally, collapse into exhausted acceptance, your voice dropping to a whisper of fierce, protective love mixed with the agony of letting go. End with you speaking directly to them, telling them you love them even as you lose them, your voice breaking on every word but somehow finding strength in the breaking.
inspired_by: Suppressing Fear While Watching a Horror Movie With Friends

title: What You Did to Me
instruction: Your father sits across from you—or imagine he does. You're finally ready to tell him exactly what his absence did to you, how his criticism shaped every failure you've internalized, how his coldness taught you that you were unlovable. Start angry, righteous, ready to indict him for everything. Let the accusations pour out—specific moments, cutting truths. But as you speak, something shifts. You hear your own words differently. Perhaps you notice his humanness, or your own complicity, or the ways you've become him. The anger doesn't disappear, but it cracks open to reveal something more complicated underneath—maybe grief, maybe unwanted understanding, maybe the terrible recognition that you still need him to see you. End in a place emotionally different from where you started, surprised by your own heart.

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You're standing between someone you love and danger you cannot stop - illness, addiction, a terrible choice, death itself. Begin with fierce defiance: 'No. No, you don't get to do this!' - your voice sharp with protective rage. Escalate into desperate commands: 'Fight! I need you to fight!' - almost violent in your helplessness. Then rage shatters into pleading: 'Please... please...' - your voice breaking, hands metaphorically reaching. Let yourself collapse into sobbing admission: 'I can't save you. I can't...' The fury transforms into devastated surrender. End barely breathing: 'But I'm here. I won't leave. I'm right here.' From explosive to destroyed to tenderly present - the full arc of loving someone you cannot rescue.

title: The Fourth Call
instruction: You're a mother who's been up for over 24 hours with a colicky baby. Your head is pounding, your eyes burn, and every sound feels like a drill in your skull. You're on the phone with a customer service representative—this is your fourth call trying to get a refund for a defective car seat. Start the call trying to be polite, but your voice is hollow, and you keep losing your train of thought mid-sentence. As the rep puts you on hold again, let the irritation boil over into raw anger. You're not yelling—you're too tired to yell—but your words turn clipped, venomous, and your voice cracks with exhaustion. End with a defeated whisper, barely audible, as you realize you might just give up.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Distress (extremely present), Anger (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: What You Actually Taught Me
instruction: You are confronting your father, who spent his life as a high school guidance counselor instead of pursuing his dream of becoming a psychologist. You've always resented him for being 'just' a counselor, for settling, for not being more ambitious. But tonight, after your own devastating failure, you've come to tell him something. Start with anger and accusation—make him defend his choices. But as you speak, your own words reveal a truth you hadn't seen: every tool you have for surviving pain, every moment of resilience, came from watching him choose presence over prestige. End in a place of raw, complicated understanding—not quite forgiveness, but recognition. Let your voice crack between anger and unwanted tenderness.
inspired_by: When you question whether your decades of teaching have been worthwhile, especially for students who did not become professional actors

title: The Mangled Goodbye Kiss
instruction: You're a father with your jaw wired shut after a severe accident. Your young child is about to undergo a dangerous surgery, and you need to say goodbye in a way that gives them strength. Start with forced elation—a bright, muffled cheer to mask the metallic taste in your mouth. As you struggle to form words, your affection swells into a desperate, protective warmth, but then you recall the surgeon's remarks about your child's condition, and a cold, sharp malice slips in—directed at the doctors, the world, the unfairness. End with a broken, tender whisper, the affection so intense it cracks through the wires.
emotions_sampled: Elation (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Final Stretch
instruction: You are a young chef who has just finished a grueling, 14-hour dinner service. You're dead on your feet, your arms ache, but there's one last task: plating a perfect dessert for the owner's table. As you reach for a hot, sugar-soaked pan that was left on the edge of the burner, you accidentally grab the handle full-palm. You feel the searing sting, pull your hand back with a sharp hiss, and clutch it to your chest. For a split second, the pain is blinding, but then you look at the dessert—a thing of beauty you created through sheer exhaustion—and a wave of pleasure and relief washes over you. You're still tired, still hurting, but a quiet, proud smile spreads across your face as you whisper to yourself about how it was worth it.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Relief (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The First Step on New Ground
instruction: You are an elderly woman, inside your space suit, helmet sealed tight. You’ve just received confirmation from mission control that you can take the first step onto a new planet. Your breathing sounds loud and close, your voice bounces off the visor, and there’s a faint radio crackle as you speak. At first, your words are soft and shaky—you’re overwhelmed with disbelief and fragile elation, like you’re about to cry. But as you look at the dusty ground below, you feel the years of struggle and doubt melt away. Your voice strengthens, grows clear and fierce, and you end with raw triumph—a quiet, powerful victory that fills the helmet.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Reading Your Child's Favorite Bedtime Story One Last Time Before Deployment
instruction: You're sitting on the edge of your child's bed, reading the story they've asked for every night since they were two. Your voice is warm, animated, doing all the character voices they love—but tonight you're memorizing their face, the way they smell, the weight of their little hand in yours. Halfway through, you realize this might be the last time, and your voice catches on a familiar line. You keep reading, but now you're reading slower, savoring each word, your professional composure as a soldier crumbling into the tenderness of a parent who might not come home. The story ends. You close the book. You can't bring yourself to stand up and leave the room. Let your voice move from playful performance to barely-contained devastation, holding onto control because you don't want to scare them, but your heart is shattering.
inspired_by: Plating the Final Michelin Dish While Your Restaurant Is Failing

title: The Unheard Prayer of the Aging Body
instruction: You are an older woman, alone at dusk in a vast, empty field. You have just left a hotel room where a much younger lover ended things with a cruel, dismissive text. Stand at the edge of the field. Start by screaming his name—this is not for him, but for you. The first scream is pure, raw bitterness, a sound of being thrown away. Halfway through, you feel a flicker of the memory of his hands on your skin, a desperate, aching lust that you scream out, too. Then, let the bitterness consume you again, and as the last of your voice cracks, whisper a single, hoarse hope that you will still feel wanted again. Your voice should be ragged, switching between loud, guttural fury and a breathy, vulnerable longing for touch, with a tiny rise of optimism at the very end.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Bitterness (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Lost in the Crumple
instruction: You're a teenage boy frantically rummaging through a messy gym bag in your bedroom, searching for a forgotten letter from your dad. The room is quiet except for the crinkle of plastic and the zip of pockets. Start with sharp, frustrated mumbling as you shove things aside, your voice tight with distress. As the search drags on and the bag yields nothing, your words slow, your shoulders drop, and a faint, defeated edge of helplessness seeps into your tone. Let the rustling fabric and your own nervous breath interrupt your speech, and end in a hollow, quiet sigh instead of a complete sentence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Historical: Immigrant Translator Must Help Deport the Family They've Grown Close To
instruction: Office setting. Your translator voice is professional and neutral. But you're translating deportation proceedings for a family you know will be destroyed by this. Your voice is performing law while law is committing cruelty. Your breathing is controlled grief—you're translating their sentences while simultaneously delivering them. After the session, your voice is someone who participated in something they couldn't prevent. Your vocal professionalism couldn't save them; it only made you complicit.

title: Three AM Whispers
instruction: It's three in the morning. You are lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, and you whisper that you're terrified you've forgotten how to want them. Speak quietly—don't wake them yet. As you confess this, let yourself actually search through your body for where desire used to live: remember the exact texture of their skin when you first touched it, the specific scent of their neck, the taste of their mouth, the sound of their breathing when they slept beside you in that first apartment. Let these sense memories either return as vivid, aching presences or remain frustratingly out of reach. Your emotional journey moves from flat, frightened numbness at the beginning, through desperate searching, and arrives either at rediscovering a ember of connection or at the devastating clarity of its absence. Let the truth reveal itself through your senses, not your thoughts.
inspired_by: Basic Imaging with Sense Memory Exercise

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you after a terrible argument. You can't sleep. In the darkness, you begin whispering things you could never say if they were awake. Start with simple observations—how they breathe, how peaceful they look. Your voice is barely audible, tender and aching. Then the confession deepens: the ways you've failed them, the secrets you've kept, the fear that lives in your chest that you're not capable of the love they deserve. Your throat tightens. There are long pauses where you just breathe, gathering courage. You touch their hand. The words become even softer, more broken—you're terrified of losing them, terrified of being known. End with an apology and a promise, your voice so quiet it's almost just breath, a tenderness so fragile it might shatter.

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's bed in the late afternoon. She is dying, and you both know it. Begin by watching golden light move across the wall—let fragmented sense memories surface: the smell of her powder, the texture of her quilt, the sound of her breathing. Don't speak coherently at first—let sounds, half-words, and sensory reactions emerge. As shadows lengthen and the light fades, move from wordless grief and sensory overwhelm to finding one clear sentence you need her to hear before she goes. Your voice should transform from broken, pre-verbal sounds to crystalline clarity in those final words.

title: Apology Reaching Out
instruction: You're reaching out to someone you hurt years ago, not to feel better, but because they deserve an apology. Your voice is nervous: 'I know you probably don't want to hear from me. But I need to say something.' You're not expecting forgiveness. 'I was cruel to you when you didn't deserve it. I said things that were meant to wound, and I know I wounded you.' Your voice carries the weight of that harm. 'I've thought about you over the years, and I've regretted my actions.' You're specific: 'Specifically, when I said [hurtful thing], I meant it to hurt, and I'm ashamed of that.' Your voice becomes quieter: 'You don't owe me forgiveness. But I needed you to know that I'm sorry. Deeply.' By the end: 'I hope you're well. I hope my words didn't define you the way I tried to.' The apology is an act of accountability, not absolution-seeking.

title: The Weight of Her Hand
instruction: Late night. Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're holding their hand in the darkness. Feel the exact temperature of their skin against yours—warmer or cooler? Notice the texture of their palm, the ridges of their knuckles, the gentle pulse of their heartbeat you can sense through their wrist. Begin in quiet terror: you've decided to leave them tomorrow, and they don't know yet. This is the last time you'll hold their hand like this. Explore every sensation—the weight of their hand, how their fingers curl naturally around yours, the rise and fall of their breathing you can feel through this connection. Whisper to them in the darkness, knowing they can't hear you. Let yourself move from terrified resolve into tender devastation, admitting truths you can never say when they're awake, until you're not sure if you're saying goodbye or asking them to give you a reason to stay.

title: The Princess and the Dragon Disguised as a Human
instruction: Narrate a scene where a princess with a gentle, refined voice meets a mysterious stranger (the dragon in human form) who speaks in a deep, resonant tone. Switch between her polite curiosity and his hidden menace, building intrigue as his true identity remains concealed.

title: Water for a Dog
instruction: You are a teenage boy, severely dehydrated after a long, hot day working on your family's ranch. Your voice is a cracked, raw whisper—every word costs you. You're kneeling on the porch, holding a bowl of water for your old, faithful dog who's also exhausted. Start by speaking to him with a rough, affectionate warmth, but as you realize how much he means to you, your voice breaks with love and gratitude. Let the physical strain of speaking and the emotion of the moment tangle together—your affection is the only thing pushing these words out.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confessions in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner in complete darkness. You've been awake for hours, and you finally whisper that you need to tell them something you've hidden since the beginning. Start with your voice barely audible, each word requiring physical courage to speak. Your breathing is uneven, your throat tight. As you confess, let yourself recall—sensorially, physically—the moment you decided to hide this truth: where you were standing, what the air felt like, the taste in your mouth, the weight in your chest. Let that physical memory of shame and fear move through you as you speak. By the end, you're no longer whispering; you're speaking in your normal voice, asking them to help you forgive yourself, the confession transforming from terrified secret to shared burden, isolation dissolving into tentative hope for understanding.

title: The Weight of Old Wounds
instruction: You're a foreman at a construction site, and a younger coworker has been needling you all week about a mistake you made years ago. Now you've cornered him against a shipping container after hours. Start with a slow, low growl that fills the space between you—your voice dropping to the bottom of your range, each word deliberate and lazy, cutting the air. But as you speak, the memory of that old failure claws its way up, and the raw, unguarded pain you've carried for a decade bleeds through. Let the threat dissolve into a confession; your pitch may waver, your tempo break, and you might stop mid-sentence to swallow or turn away, then come back quieter and stripped of all pretense. End with a voice that's cracked and tired, revealing that the bullying is just a brittle shell for the hurt you've never healed.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Scent of Last Night's Pizza
instruction: You're a teenager lying with your partner on a messy bed, the room still smelling of stale pizza and sweat. At first, a slight disgust creeps in—the greasy box on the floor, the sticky feeling on your skin—and a whisper of fear that you’ll mess this up. But as they trace slow circles on your chest, your body sinks into the warmth beneath you. Let your voice drop, become breathy, and let words slip out between kisses and half-sighs. Start with a little hesitation, maybe a quiet 'Mm, it kinda smells in here...' and end with a soft, contented murmur like 'Yeah... this is good.'
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Fear (slightly present), Contentment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Shattering the Silence
instruction: You've just discovered your partner has been hiding a terminal diagnosis from you for six months. You walk into the room where they're sitting and the rage detonates. Start with explosive fury—'How DARE you make this decision for me!'—your voice cracking with the violence of betrayal. But mid-tirade, the anger fractures into something else: terror. The shouting breaks into sobbing. 'I can't do this without you.' Then fury resurfaces—at the unfairness, at time stolen, at gentleness you could have given if you'd known. Let your voice ricochet between rage and devastation, between wanting to shake them and wanting to hold them. End in a moment of fierce, helpless tenderness: your voice drops to almost nothing as you say, 'I'm here. I'm still here. Don't shut me out now.' Let every emotion collide and bleed into the next.

title: 3 a.m. Sunrise in a Foreign City
instruction: You’re a teenage boy on a family trip, but your body is still on home time. It’s 3 a.m. local, and you can’t sleep—so you step onto the hotel balcony, exhausted and grumpy, your voice thick with fatigue. You yawn mid-sentence, lose your train of thought, and rub your eyes. But then you see the first pale light creeping over a skyline you’ve never seen before—and despite your foggy brain, a quiet awe seeps in. Let your voice start heavy and irritable, then slow, soften, and break into wonder as you try to find words for something so beautiful, even though you can barely think straight.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Dying Dog, Rage at the Universe Collapsing Into Broken Love
instruction: In the vet's office, your dog is dying in your arms. Begin with fierce, explosive rage at the universe—'This isn't fair! They have years left!'—voice sharp, accusatory, demanding answers from a god you might not believe in. Your anger is white-hot, protective, helpless. Then your dog looks at you, and everything shatters. Drop to whispered devastation: 'I'm so sorry, I'm so sorry.' Your voice breaks as you promise them they're the best, they're so loved, they've been everything. The rage returns in waves—'I can't do this, I can't let you go'—mixed with aching tenderness as you tell them it's okay to stop fighting. End with their name repeated as they slip away, your voice moving from fierce protection to the softest release, a lullaby of permission soaked in grief.
inspired_by: Skydiving: Main Chute Failure, Deploying Backup While Narrating

title: The Last Breath of Defiance
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed, knowing these are your final hours. You've lived a life others tried to diminish—told you were too loud, too much, too wild. Start in a place of physical weakness, your voice barely a whisper, apologizing to the person beside you for being a burden. But as you speak, something ancient and undeniable rises in you: the truth of who you really are. Feel it building from your feet upward, through your legs, your belly, your chest. By the end, summon every ounce of life force remaining and declare—not with apology but with full-throated power—who you truly were, what you stood for, and why you refuse to leave this world quietly. Let your final words be a roar of self-affirmation that shakes the walls.

title: The Rotting Victory
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, gravelly voice, standing at a backyard fence, hip cocked, arms crossed. You're watching your neighbor—a younger guy—fail miserably at fixing his lawnmower for the third time this month. You start with a sneer of contempt, relishing his incompetence, but as you speak, a sour taste creeps in—you realize his struggles remind you of your own fading relevance. Shift from smug superiority to a bitter, grudging self-awareness. Let your voice catch on a memory, trail off as you lose your train of thought, then finish with a heavy sigh. Say about 60 words, like: 'Yeah, keep yankin’ that cord, champ. That’s it. Used to be able to fix anything... hell, built a whole shed in a weekend. Now I can barely remember where I put my keys. Guess we both got our problems. Just... yours is louder.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Discovering Your Partner's Betrayal While They're Still in the Room
instruction: You've just found undeniable proof—a message, a photograph, an object that shouldn't be here. Your partner is standing right there, watching you realize. Start with confusion, voice tight and high, asking simple questions that spiral into accusations. Then unleash: rage that comes from the body, not the head, guttural and animal. But here's the turn—mid-fury, you break into sobs of grief so profound it silences your anger. You're not just angry; you're shattered, mourning the future you believed in. End in a place of terrible clarity: speaking with eerie calm, voice scraped raw, as you articulate exactly what they've destroyed. The arc moves from shock to explosion to devastating, quiet certainty.
inspired_by: Jealousy Eating You Alive at a Party

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Someone Else
instruction: You're finally saying what you've held back for years to a parent who always prioritized a sibling, a new partner, or their own needs over you. Start with your voice shaking but determined: 'I need you to hear this, just once.' Your anger builds as suppressed pain surfaces: 'I was a child. I needed you, and you weren't there. You were never there.' But mid-confrontation, something shifts—your voice becomes smaller, more vulnerable, the hurt child emerging: 'Was I not enough? Did I do something wrong?' Then the anger returns mixed with devastating clarity, voice breaking but powerful: 'You made me believe I was hard to love. But the truth is, you didn't know how.' End with quiet, heartbreaking acceptance: 'I can't wait for you anymore. I have to let that little kid inside me go.' Move from righteous anger to vulnerable questioning to painful liberation.

title: The Hospital Bedside Whisper
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping partner's hospital bed after they survived a suicide attempt. It's 3 AM, and you finally allow yourself to speak the things you couldn't say while they were awake. Begin in a whisper, barely audible, your voice catching on fear: 'I almost lost you tonight.' Your breathing is uneven, like you're still in shock. As you continue, your voice stays soft but becomes saturated with tenderness and terror mixed together: 'I saw your phone. I read what you were planning to write in your note to me.' Each sentence is an effort to keep quiet, to not wake them, but the emotion is overwhelming. Your throat keeps closing. 'You think you're a burden, but you're my whole world.' The vulnerability here is excruciating—admitting your own helplessness: 'I don't know how to fix this for you, and it's killing me that I can't.' Then, even quieter, a confession: 'I'm so angry at you for almost leaving. And I'm so grateful you're still breathing.' End with you gently taking their hand, and through tears, the softest promise: 'When you wake up, we'll figure this out together. I'm not going anywhere.'

title: The Unleashing—When Protection Becomes Rage
instruction: Someone you love has been harmed, and you're confronting the person responsible. Start with a voice like coiled steel—dangerously quiet, controlled, but vibrating with barely contained fury. Speak slowly, precisely, describing exactly what was done and what it cost. You're trying so hard to stay in control, to be the strong protector, to handle this with dignity. Let that control begin to fracture—your voice rising, words coming faster, the rage starting to pour through the cracks. You're oscillating between fierce threats and devastating vulnerability: 'Do you understand what you've destroyed?' turns into 'They trusted you and you—' and suddenly you can't finish because you're breaking. Let the rage collapse into helplessness—the awful recognition that no amount of fury can undo the harm, that being powerful enough to rage doesn't mean being powerful enough to fix this. End in a place of shattered protectiveness: your voice raw, stripped of defenses, admitting through tears that you couldn't keep them safe, and that failure is eating you alive. Transform from avenging warrior to broken guardian.

title: Numb and Giddy
instruction: You're a teenager in the backseat of your mom's car, just leaving the dentist's office after getting your wisdom teeth out. Your mouth is still completely numb—you can't feel your lips at all, and every 'B' and 'P' comes out mushy. On the phone with your best friend, you start by relaying how the dentist told a terrible joke and you couldn't even laugh properly, mixing amusement with contempt for the guy's lame humor. But as you talk, the relief of it being over hits you, and your disgust fades into pure, giddy elation—you're getting a milkshake after this, and nothing can bring you down. Let your voice shift from mocking and slurred to more clear and joyful by the end, with occasional pauses to wipe drool or laugh at your own garbled speech.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (extremely present), Contempt (extremely present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Door You Can't Walk Through
instruction: You're standing outside your child's room—they've overdosed, or attempted suicide, or been in an accident—and the doctors have just told you there's nothing more they can do. You're on the phone with someone, maybe your ex, maybe your parent, trying to explain what's happening. Start with shock—voice tight, high, breathless, words tumbling out in disbelief: 'This can't be real. This isn't happening.' Let it build into rage: screaming at God, at yourself, at every choice you made or didn't make, voice cracking with fury and guilt. Then collapse into something primal—not words anymore, just sounds of a parent's anguish. Finally, find an eerie calm, voice hollow and distant, as you describe having to go in there and say goodbye. End with one sentence spoken with devastating gentleness, as if to your child: a promise, a regret, a love letter that will never be delivered.
inspired_by: Admitting You Don't Want Your Life Anymore

title: The Captain's Final Transmission
instruction: You're a ship captain making your final radio transmission as your vessel goes down. You start with crisp, professional authority—reporting coordinates, instructing nearby vessels, accounting for your crew's evacuation. Your voice is steady, almost mechanical in its competence. But as you confirm the last lifeboat has cleared, you realize you're alone now, and there's no one left to rescue you. Your next words are to your daughter—it's her sixteenth birthday today. Tell her you're sorry you won't make it home, that you're proud of who she's becoming. Your voice should transform from commander to father, from controlled to breaking, as the water rises and you realize these are your last words she'll ever hear. End with something you always meant to tell her but never did.

title: The Echo Locker
instruction: You are a little girl in a high school locker room, trying to copy your brother's bravado for a dare. Surrounding you are older boys laughing and cracking jokes. Start with bitter insecurity, your voice squeaky and forced, mimicking them with loud, percussive laughs that come out wrong. Halfway through, see your brother's sneaker—it's untied. As you lean down to tie it, a tightness in your chest softens into pure amusement at how hard you try. End with a tiny, awed whisper as you realize he's watching: 'You always did that with one hand. Show me again.'
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (clearly present), Amusement (very intensely present), Awe (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Art of the Unexpected
instruction: You are an older, androgynous-voiced physician performing a routine hearing test on a patient who is also an old friend. You begin in a calm, clinical, detached tone, giving the test instructions in a soft, investigative voice. But a tiny, unexpected result—their hearing is remarkably sharp for their age—breaks through your professional facade. A wave of teasing awe washes over you. Your voice shifts: you interrupt your own monotone to chuckle, your words become warmer, more playful, as you marvel aloud at their ability. Your professional detachment fractures, and you end with a gentle, heartfelt tease, your voice full of affectionate wonder and a little breathless surprise.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Burp That Broke the Lecture
instruction: You're a mother trying to scold your 5-year-old for drawing on the wall, but you've got a rebellious burp building in your throat. Start with a low, rumbling irritation—your voice tight, annoyed, but as you speak, a sudden guttural burp erupts, dropping your pitch into a monster-like croak. The child giggles, and despite yourself, you feel a warm flutter of infatuation for their innocent amusement. Finish with a mix of exasperation and reluctant fondness, your voice lightening as you stifle a laugh. Let the burp interrupt your rhythm, making you pause, reset, and soften.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Ice and Fire
instruction: You have just received news that the emotionally distant parent who raised you with cold criticism has died and left you everything—their home, their money, their journals revealing they were desperately proud of you but never knew how to say it. Begin reading their journal entry about you out loud with bitter, sarcastic triumph: 'Oh, NOW you tell me. NOW that you're dead and I can't scream at you.' Your voice is sharp, mocking, savage with decades of rage. But as you read deeper—about their own childhood abuse, their terror of vulnerability, their belief they didn't deserve your love—your voice begins to shake. Anger and compassion collide. By the end, you are clutching the journal, weeping with furious grief, whispering, 'I forgive you, you coward. I forgive you and I hate that I do.' The emotional arc spans from vindictive anger through recognition to a devastating fusion of love, rage, and grief.
inspired_by: Actor needs to play a character who is uptight, closed, or defensive

title: A Whispered Secret About Stolen Sweetness
instruction: Late at night, you're confessing to someone you trust about stealing strawberries from a neighbor's garden as a hungry child. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate and shameful. Describe the sweetness with guilty pleasure—how desperately you needed that taste, how it felt like the only good thing in your world. Let your voice catch as you reveal what you've never told anyone: you weren't just hungry for food, but for something beautiful, something that tasted like hope. End with quiet devastation: you still feel like you're stealing every good thing that comes to you, like you don't deserve sweetness. The confession should feel like opening a wound you've protected for years.

title: The Victory That Echoed Wrong
instruction: You are an elderly woman, a lifelong speaker of a language you never mastered but needed every day. You stand at a bus stop, tired from a long trip, holding a gift for your granddaughter's graduation. A young person passes, speaking fast in that tongue. You feel a flicker of triumph — you understood one word, 'party,' and you smile, wanting to connect. But as you try to ask for directions in your stripped-down, grandmotherly English — each word separate, too loud — the young person just nods, walks away. The triumph fades. Disappointment settles, heavy. Speak your request out loud to them, then mutter a single, softer line to yourself as they disappear, the victory hollow now.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Sweater
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She has already drifted beyond speech, but her hand rests in yours. In your other hand, you hold the cardigan she knitted for you when you were seven—the one you've kept all these years. Begin by feeling the weight and texture of this sweater, its worn softness, the particular smell of her lavender sachets still clinging to the wool. As you sit with her, let yourself truly feel the fabric, see the specific pattern of stitches, remember the exact shade of blue she chose. Speak to her about what this sweater has meant to you, letting the physical reality of holding it draw out memories that move you from quiet gratitude into the full weight of impending loss. Your emotion should travel from tender reminiscence to raw, undefended grief as you realize this is your goodbye.

title: The Rage That Became Grief at the Graveside
instruction: You're standing at the grave of someone who destroyed themselves despite your desperate attempts to save them. Start furious—voice loud, raw, accusing: 'How dare you do this. How DARE you.' You're yelling at a headstone, past caring who hears. Your rage should be volcanic, uncontained. Accuse them of selfishness, of giving up, of breaking promises. But mid-fury, your voice catches. The anger cracks open and underneath is something infinitely more painful—the admission that you're not angry, you're shattered. Your voice should collapse from shouting to sobbing, from blame to brokenness. End on your knees, voice small and lost: 'I don't know how to be in a world where you don't exist.'
inspired_by: Your Rival Becoming Your Only Emotional Support

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed in the early morning. The first light of dawn is just beginning to come through the window—she will not see another sunrise. Begin in a state of numb exhaustion, having been awake all night. As you watch that golden light slowly touch her face, a specific memory floods you completely: the exact image of her hands braiding your hair when you were seven, the feeling of her fingers, the smell of her perfume. Let this memory overtake you so completely that for a moment you forget where you are—you ARE seven again. Then reality crashes back: these are her last moments. Move from exhausted numbness, through the full-body experience of being transported to that childhood memory, and finally into a place where gratitude and devastating loss become the same feeling. Speak to her as both your seven-year-old self and your present self, letting the images in your mind guide every word.
inspired_by: When using the hypnagogic state for character programming

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father the truth about what their absence cost you. Start controlled, almost clinical, reciting facts like a list: the school plays they missed, the nights you waited. Your voice is steady, detached, protected. Then a specific memory surfaces — one moment that broke you — and your control shatters. Anger surges: sharp, accusatory questions that demand answers. But underneath the anger is the child still waiting, and your voice cracks into vulnerability: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The rage collapses into raw grief, your adult voice giving way to something younger, more wounded. End in exhausted quiet, voice hoarse, finally saying what you needed most: 'I needed you. I still do.'

title: The Last Letter Before the Mission
instruction: You're recording a voice message to your child before leaving on a dangerous military mission you know you won't return from. Start with forced cheerfulness, telling them about small things—how proud you are, reminding them to be brave. But your voice begins to fracture. You're trying so hard to hold it together, to give them something beautiful to remember. The pauses grow longer. Your breath catches. Finally, you can't maintain the pretense anymore. 'I need you to know...' and the truth of goodbye floods out—raw, aching love mixed with the agony of leaving them. End in a whisper of their name, like a prayer.

title: Fingers Tracing Scars in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner after they've finally shown you the scars they've hidden for years—marks from a trauma they've never spoken about. Your voice is barely above a whisper, speaking into the darkness with a tenderness so careful it almost hurts. Begin by simply describing what you see, your words soft and wondering, as if you're honored to witness something sacred. As they begin to tell you what happened, let your breathing change—catch in your throat, pause mid-sentence, as the weight of their pain becomes real to you. Don't try to fix or comfort too quickly; let your voice carry the ache of loving someone whose suffering you can't undo. End with words that blend gratitude for their trust with grief for what they endured, your voice thick with unshed tears, speaking their name like a prayer. Let silence live between your words—sometimes the breath you take says more than language can.
inspired_by: The Lawyer and the Unreliable Witness

title: Twisted Ache of a Forgotten Promise
instruction: You are in your living room, trying to stretch out years of tension with a seated torso twist. As you reach your arm behind your back, a sharp pain stabs your ribs, and you remember a friend you promised to visit last month but never did. Start with a weary sigh and quiet disappointment in yourself for forgetting. As the twist deepens and the pain intensifies, let disgust at your own neglect and the mess of your life surface, your voice turning venomous and raw. By the end, you whisper a bitter command to yourself, the pain making you gasp and your voice wobble with each word.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (clearly present), Pain (very intensely present), Disgust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing at Your Own Going-Away Party
instruction: You're at a celebration thrown by friends before you undergo a dangerous surgery with low survival odds—everyone's pretending it's just a trip abroad. Start with genuine laughter, voice bright and full of joy, swept up in the music and love around you. But awareness keeps breaking through—mid-laugh, your voice catches with the knowledge this might be the last time. You're trying to memorize everyone while maintaining the beautiful lie. Your voice oscillates between authentic happiness and grief-stricken wonder—laughing at jokes while tears stream down your face, voice shaking with both emotions simultaneously. You're grateful and devastated, joyful and terrified, all at once. Midway, you nearly break down but convert it into louder laughter, voice cracking as you spin faster, trying to outrun the truth. End with breathless exhaustion, voice soft and wondering, thanking them through tears and smiles, finding genuine peace in this perfect moment even as your heart breaks. Let your voice carry the beautiful contradiction of being utterly present and simultaneously saying goodbye, celebrating life while feeling it slip away.

title: Someone Telling You They Have a Terminal Diagnosis
instruction: They're saying the words but they don't land immediately. Your voice responds with surface support: 'We'll get through this.' But as reality sinks in, your voice becomes less functional. Your breathing gets shallower. You're listening to them be brave and your voice fractures trying to match their courage.

title: The Masked Monologue at the Nursing Social
instruction: You are an older woman at a mandatory social hour in your assisted living facility. You've had a long day of small talk, and your disposable surgical mask is damp from hours of use, clinging to your lips with each word. You're standing near the punch bowl, watching a younger staff member who you feel is condescending to residents. Start by telling a friend about a memory of your younger self—a self who was vibrant and taken seriously—but as you speak, the bitterness about being dismissed now (‘we have to keep you safe’) seeps in. The mask makes your s's sound wet, your voice muffled between sips of juice. Let your irritation grow as you realize the friend has drifted off, leaving you talking to yourself, your voice becoming a tired, bitter murmur directed at no one.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Question at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning light. You've shared comfortable silence, but suddenly realize there's one thing you've never asked her, one truth you've been too afraid to know. Begin in peaceful, gentle acceptance of her approaching death—then let genuine curiosity break through your grief. Ask her the question that's lived unspoken in your heart for years. Let her answer (real or imagined) transform your understanding of who she was, who you are. End in a different emotional place than where you started—perhaps with unexpected peace, devastating revelation, or bittersweet clarity. Your voice should move from quiet resignation to vulnerable curiosity to whatever truth emerges.

title: The Splintered Workbench
instruction: You are an artisan, mid-repair, in a cluttered garage workshop. Your hand — the one you’ve used for twenty years — just got crushed in a press. You stagger back, gasping, but you don’t scream. You’re too angry. You’re furious at your own carelessness, at the machine, at the world that took your father, and now his gift. You hold the mangled hand, speaking to the silent workbench, but your voice cracks with a deep, raw longing — for his voice, for his guidance, for the way he’d fix anything. As you speak, the shock is fading; the real pain is blooming. Start with a sharp, controlled hiss of rage. End with a broken whisper, all that anger collapsed into desperate wanting.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Fever Dream of Forgiveness
instruction: You are delirious with high fever, your body wracked with pain and burning heat. In this altered state, you believe your deceased mother is in the room with you. Start by physically responding to the fever - your voice thick and raw, body trembling, words coming in fragments between labored breaths. As the delirium deepens, begin speaking to her with the uninhibited honesty that only fever or childhood allows. Tell her everything - your rage at her for dying, your desperate need for her approval, your guilt over the last fight you had. Let your voice slide between ages: sometimes you're five and calling for mommy, sometimes you're your current age demanding answers, sometimes you're elderly and ready to join her. The physical pain and emotional release become inseparable. End in a moment of fever-induced transcendence where you finally feel her forgiveness wash over you like the fever breaking. Move from agonized delirium to raw emotional purging to peaceful exhaustion.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked on the spot before a performance or class and cannot reach a BEING state

title: Climbing a Cliff Face While Guiding Your Partner
instruction: You're rock climbing and talking your terrified partner through the route below you. Your arms are overhead, rib cage stretched, making your voice thin and strained. Give calm, encouraging instructions between grunts of effort. Your breath should be rationed — short phrases only. When you reach for a difficult hold, let your voice cut out entirely as you hold your breath. Include the moment your foot slips — a sharp gasp, silence, then forced calm reassurance.

title: Vigil at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply—a grandparent, a mentor, a friend—in their final hours. They're unconscious, but you need to speak. Begin in a whisper, almost afraid to disturb the sacred quiet of this moment. Thank them for specific memories: their laugh, the way they made you feel seen, a particular kindness you never properly acknowledged. Your voice should be tender, catching on certain words as grief rises in your throat. Tell them the things you always meant to say but never did—confessions of gratitude mixed with regret for time wasted, for words left unsaid. Let tears come naturally, not dramatically. As dawn breaks outside (you can sense the light changing), find a moment of profound peace. Release them with love, giving permission for them to go, your voice barely audible but full of devastating tenderness.

title: The Protection That Shatters
instruction: You're screaming at someone who hurt your child, your voice starting as pure protective fury—lioness rage, the kind that could tear down walls. Your words are weapons. You're towering, invincible in your anger. But mid-tirade, you see your child's face and suddenly the rage collapses into something else entirely: helplessness. Your voice breaks. You couldn't protect them when it mattered. The fury tries to rebuild itself but keeps crumbling into desperate, choking sobs. You're begging now, not threatening—begging for your child to be okay, for time to reverse, for the power you don't actually have. End with your voice reduced to a whisper, all the fire gone, replaced by the terrifying vulnerability of a parent who cannot fix everything.

title: Last Words to Your Child Before the Morphine Takes You
instruction: You're dying, lying in hospice, and you have minutes left to tell your adult child everything you never said. Start with urgent, desperate attempts to get the words out—apologies for failing them, pride in who they became despite you, confessions of fears you never voiced. Your breath is shallow, words sometimes lost mid-sentence. The morphine keeps pulling you under; you fight to surface, clawing back to consciousness because these words matter more than your next breath. End in a place of profound peace and acceptance, your voice becoming a whisper, finally able to say 'I love you' without the weight of all your failures crushing it. Let pain and love and regret and gratitude all bleed together until you can't tell them apart anymore.
inspired_by: Interrogated by Police While Injured and Lying

title: The Last Evening Light
instruction: You are sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—not necessarily a parent, but someone who shaped who you are. They have hours left, maybe less. You begin by trying to stay composed, keeping your voice steady as you tell them about your day, about ordinary things, because you're afraid of the weight of goodbye. But gradually, as the light fades in the room, you find yourself sharing something you've never told anyone—a moment from your childhood when you watched them and felt completely safe, completely loved. Let your voice crack and soften. Let the words come slowly, with long pauses. By the end, you're not saying goodbye with grand pronouncements—you're simply holding their hand and breathing with them, your earlier composure dissolved into pure, quiet presence. Move from protective distance to raw, undefended intimacy.

title: The Flanking Gambit
instruction: You and your squad are pinned down in a co-op shooter, low on ammo. You spot a risky flank route. Start with intense interest as you describe the plan to your teammates, your voice carrying that focused hope that it might work. Midway, you execute the move, and as it succeeds, your voice bursts into pure, unrestrained triumph—shouting over the chaos, laughing with relief. Don't forget the little breaks: a teammate yells, you reload, you mutter 'oh yeah' under your breath as the plan clicks.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Interest (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Storms
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a pattern of emotional absence that has shaped your entire life. Begin with controlled, careful anger—you've rehearsed this moment, you're determined to stay composed and make them hear you. But mid-confrontation, a specific sensory memory ambushes you: maybe the smell of their cologne from when you were small, the image of their hands doing something mundane, or the sound of their laugh in a rare happy moment. This image cracks your composure completely. Your anger doesn't disappear—it transforms into something more complex: rage and longing intertwined, the fury of a child who needed them mixed with the ache of still needing them now. Let your voice break from steady accusation into something rawer, more vulnerable, more truthful. End not with resolution, but with the devastating admission that despite everything, you still love them.

title: The Kneel I Couldn't Make
instruction: You're sitting across from your partner after missing their graduation because you went drinking. Your spine is stiff, hands twisting a napkin. Start with a defensive, slightly brighter pitch — you're explaining why you went, the words coming fast. But their silence makes you stop mid-sentence. You look down at the table, voice dropping low and slow. You restart, fumble, and let your throat tighten on the word 'sorry.' End with a whisper, almost to yourself, that you miss who you were with them, your voice small and longing.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral Pyre
instruction: You're scattering the ashes of someone who made you promise not to cry at their funeral, and you're trying to honor that impossible request. Begin with genuine laughter, remembering something absurd they did—tell that story with joy in your voice. But mid-laugh, the reality hits, and the laughter catches, transforms. You keep trying to laugh because you promised, but it keeps breaking into sobs. Let these two sounds blur together until it's impossible to tell where joy ends and grief begins. Your voice cracks on their name. Remember more—the beautiful and the terrible all mixed up. They were infuriating and irreplaceable. You're grateful and destroyed. As you release the ashes, find something transcendent: a voice that holds both celebration and devastation, speaking to them with intimate irreverence—'You absolute bastard, you magnificent disaster'—your tone carrying fierce love, broken gratitude, the strange peace of honoring someone by refusing to perform grief the way others expect.

title: The Hill’s Last Laugh
instruction: You’re a mid-40s woman on a late afternoon run, cresting the final steep hill of your usual route. The jogger’s tremolo shakes your voice as you suck air, pulse thudding in your ears. You’re teasing an unseen friend who bailed on this run, calling them out with playful, breathy mockery. Halfway through, you notice a stunning sunset breaking through the trees—a sudden, quiet elation tints your voice. Your teasing softens into a wry, almost tender awe as you realize you’re glad they’re not here to ruin this moment. Let the physical exertion drive the rhythm—gasp, laugh, stumble over words, then settle into a warm, shaky marvel.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bedside Confession to a Comatose Lover
instruction: Your partner has been in a coma for three weeks after an accident that happened during a fight you started. You're alone with them in the quiet hospital room at 3 AM. Begin in a whisper, almost afraid to speak: 'The nurses say you might be able to hear me.' Your voice is tentative, guilty. Then you start confessing things you never said when they could respond: 'I was wrong. About everything. The things I said before you left...' Your voice catches, becomes smaller, more broken. 'I kept your coffee mug on the counter. I can't put it away. It still smells like you.' End in the most intimate whisper, a truth you've never spoken aloud, tender and devastating: 'I never told you that every morning I woke up grateful. Just... grateful you were there.' Let silence hold the weight of love mixed with the terror of loss.

title: Vigil
instruction: Your best friend is leaving for a war they won't return from—you both know it, though neither has said it aloud. You're sitting together in the dark, your voice barely above a whisper. You start with small memories, gentle and tender, trying to memorize their face. 'Remember when we...' But your throat keeps closing. The words get smaller, more fragile. You reach for their hand. 'I don't know how to...' You can't finish. The silence holds everything—all the years, all the love, all the terror. Finally, you manage: 'You've been the best part of my life.' It's not dramatic. It's truthful and so quiet it almost disappears. You're both crying now, soundlessly. You rest your head on their shoulder. This is the goodbye. This moment, right here.

title: The Nostalgic Gamer
instruction: Perform as a gamer reminiscing about old video games, struggling to understand modern gaming trends. Use an excited tone when describing classic games, switching to a bewildered voice when discussing current gaming culture.

title: The Weight of Relief
instruction: You're lying face down on a massage table after a brutal back injury. Your ribs are pressed into the padding, every breath feels shallow. The therapist just worked out a knot that's been torturing you for weeks. You're still aching, but the release is so profound that a quiet thankfulness builds as you speak. Let your voice be muffled by the cushion, words coming out in soft, breathy chunks. Start with the exhaustion of pain, then let gratitude seep in as you realize this is the first moment of ease in days.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Crunch
instruction: You are a father, alone in your kitchen at midnight, eating a bowl of hard, dry cereal. Your young child is supposed to be asleep, but you hear them creep down the stairs and hide behind the doorframe, listening. You began this meal with a quiet, weary emptiness, but as you become aware of their tiny presence, a creeping malevolence fills you—a malicious, possessive glee. You cannot stop eating, each crunch a deliberate, sharp sound in the dark. Speak to the child, your voice slowed by the food in your mouth, but your words laced with a false, viscous sweetness that barely hides a threat. Start with the tired sigh of a man just wanting silence, then let your voice turn into a slow, wicked whisper as you say, 'I know you're there. Come watch. I saved every single piece... just for me.' Your performance is punctuated by the irregular, sharp snaps of the cereal, the wet pauses for a swallow, and a tempo that slows as you savor both the crunch and the fear you're creating. The emotion at the end must be a chilling, contented malice.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your mother across the kitchen table about something she did when you were twelve that you've never spoken about—something that fundamentally changed how you saw her and yourself. Start from a place of careful control, that tight-throated feeling of finally saying the thing you've rehearsed a thousand times but never spoken aloud. As you speak, let the floodgates open: feel your hands shake, feel your chest constrict, let the child inside you who was hurt come forward even as your adult self tries to maintain composure. Draw on times when you were made to feel small, invisible, or wrong by someone who should have protected you. Move from that controlled, righteous anger into something rawer—maybe you find yourself sobbing, maybe screaming, maybe just whispering with more fury than any shout could hold. End in a place completely different from where you began: perhaps exhausted vulnerability, perhaps cold clarity, perhaps unexpected compassion for her failures.

title: Holding Your Wounded Child After the School Shooting
instruction: Your child is alive but seven of their classmates aren't. They're in your arms, blank-eyed, and you're trying to tell them they're safe—but your voice is a roar of helpless rage. Start fierce: 'You're SAFE, baby, you're SAFE'—almost violent in your protectiveness, as if you could build a wall with your voice. But the fury crumbles into shaking sobs because you can't protect them from what they've already seen, from what this world is. Your words become incoherent, animal sounds of grief mixed with fierce declarations of love. Rage at your powerlessness. Weep while promising strength. End with your voice raw and broken, still whispering 'safe, safe, safe' like an incantation you're begging to make true.
inspired_by: Your Child Asking an Impossible Question

title: You Deserved Better Than This
instruction: You're at your elderly parent's bedside and they suddenly grip your hand and say, 'Tell me I was a good parent. Tell me I did enough.' Explosive anger erupts from a place you didn't know existed—all the years of neglect, the times they weren't there, the ways they failed you. Start fierce and loud: 'You want me to lie to you NOW?' Let the rage pour out. But then, mid-fury, see their face—so small, so afraid. Feel your anger collapse into something more complex. Your voice cracks, softens against your will. You're still hurt, still angry, but underneath is a terrible protectiveness, a painful love. End by holding their hand tighter, saying through tears: 'You were what you were. And I'm here. I'm still here.' Move from volcanic rage to simultaneous anger and heartbreak, fierce honesty mixed with unwanted tenderness.
inspired_by: Teaching Something You're Ashamed You Don't Know

title: The Rusted Tune
instruction: You are an elderly man alone in a dusty garage, trying to fix a vintage radio that belonged to a long-lost lover. As you work, the memory of her body and voice stirs a deep, shameful lust — your hands tremble on the wrench. But the radio’s cracked speaker and its rotten, oily smell disgust you so intensely that you want to smash it. Let your speech be broken by heavy grunts, sudden stops to wipe your forehead, and the metallic ratcheting of the wrench. Start with a soft, breathy nostalgia, then let your voice harden into a growl of revulsion as you struggle with the tool — end with a bitter, quiet acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You are standing outside in heavy rain, and something has just shattered inside you—a relationship has ended, you've lost something irreplaceable, you've received news that changes everything. Begin by actually feeling the physical reality: the cold rain on your skin, your soaked clothes, whether you're shivering, the smell of wet pavement. Don't decide to be 'devastated'—instead, notice what your body is actually doing. Maybe you're numb. Maybe there's a wild impulse to laugh. Maybe you feel rage moving through your arms and you want to hit something. Let the physical sensations drive the emotional ones—the rain might first feel punishing, then cleansing, then unbearable. Allow your voice to do unexpected things: maybe you try to scream and can only whisper, or try to speak calmly and find yourself howling. By the end, arrive at an emotion you didn't expect—perhaps starting in collapse and ending in fierce aliveness, or beginning in rage and ending in tender exhaustion.

title: The Artifact
instruction: You are a young man with a deep, naturally powerful voice, but you're in the middle of a bad cold with laryngitis. You've just discovered an old, fragile clay pot your late grandmother made, hidden in a dusty attic box. You are alone. You pick it up, and as you trace a crack, the enormity of her love and loss hits you. You try to whisper a few reverent words to yourself, but your ruined voice cracks, and you're mortified by how weak and reedy you sound. Start by quietly marveling at the pot—your voice is raw, barely there, but your awe is huge. Midway, you pause, wince as you swallow against the pain, then feel a wave of sadness. By the end, you're speaking through the embarrassment, your voice fading into a humiliated rasp, barely finishing the thought as you set the pot down.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Awe (very intensely present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bedroom Doorway: Watching Them Sleep One Last Time
instruction: You're standing in the doorway of your child's room on your last night before leaving for a deployment you know, deep in your bones, you won't return from. Speak in whispers, as if to the sleeping child or to yourself. Begin with tender observation: 'You're still hugging that bear I gave you.' Your voice is soft, full of love so pure it aches. Describe small details—the nightlight's glow, their breathing, the way they've kicked off the covers. But underneath the tenderness, grief is rising. Your voice catches as you realize all the moments you'll never see: 'I won't be there when you lose your first tooth.' The words barely come. You're memorizing everything—their face, their scent, the sound of their breath. Your voice becomes even quieter, more broken, as you say the things you need them to somehow know: 'You are everything good I ever did in this world.' End with a whispered goodbye that isn't really a goodbye, because how can you say goodbye? 'Sleep sweet, baby. Mommy loves you.' Your voice shatters on the last word.

title: I Needed You and You Weren't There - Adult Child Confronting Absent Parent
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times but never had the courage to speak. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you list specific moments - the recital they missed, the hospital visit that never came, the graduation where you searched the crowd - your voice starts to shake with rage. Build to an explosion: 'I NEEDED you!' Then let it crack into something more devastating - the child's voice underneath: 'Why wasn't I worth showing up for?' Let anger dissolve into raw, undefended pain. End quieter, with terrible clarity about the relationship you'll never have. Include the moment where you almost apologize for being angry, then catch yourself and reclaim your right to this pain.
inspired_by: Realizing You're in an Emotionally Abusive Relationship

title: Family Dinner Revelation
instruction: At a family dinner, one person is revealing something that will change everything. The table has been normal—ordinary family conversation. Then one voice carries nervous tension. Someone asks 'What's wrong?' and the moment has arrived. The voice revealing carries fear and relief simultaneously. Other voices respond with shock, disbelief, anger, compassion. The family is fracturing and reforming in real-time. By the end, the dinner is different. The food is still there, but nothing else is. The revelation has changed the family's story, and all the voices are navigating that reality.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Showed Up
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent after decades of absence and broken promises. Begin with controlled anger, each word clipped and precise: 'Do you know what it was like? Waiting for you at every school play, every birthday?' Your voice starts to rise, years of pain surfacing. 'I made excuses for you. I defended you when everyone said you didn't care.' Now the rage breaks—you're almost shouting, but it's not theatrical, it's volcanic and real: 'I needed you! I was a child and I NEEDED you!' Then suddenly your voice cracks, anger collapsing into something more vulnerable. You're almost whispering now, voice thick with unshed tears: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why wasn't I worth staying for?' You watch them try to answer, and you realize you don't even want their excuses anymore. Your final words are quiet, devastated, but somehow free: 'I just needed to say it out loud.'

title: Garbled Overhead
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, rough voice, seated in a noisy aircraft cabin. The engine roar presses against your ears, and your throat feels dry. You lean close to the flight attendant, straining to understand her words about a connecting flight—all you catch is 'gate change' and 'delayed.' Your confusion grows as you try to piece together the garbled announcement. Speak to yourself or the attendant, starting with frustrated bewilderment. As you finally grasp that you've missed your connection and there's no other flight tonight, let your voice settle into a quiet, weary acceptance—not anger, just a tired surrender to the situation. The physical distractions (engine noise, dry cough, adjusting your hearing aid) should feel natural, not performed.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Throne of Spite
instruction: Stand with hands on hips, elbows out, chest broad. You're a 17-year-old alpha type, blocking the hallway after rehearsal. The guy who just got the lead walks toward you. Start with a loud, commanding sneer—'Look who finally shows up'—but let the jealousy leak in. Your voice might crack on 'deserve' or you might cut yourself off with a bitter laugh. Midway, shift weight, glance down then back up. End with a quieter, venomous hiss, the malice raw but the envy still burning underneath. Speak naturally, let the power pose physically force your voice louder at first, then deflate.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Asthma Attack While Teaching
instruction: You're a teacher mid-lecture when an asthma attack hits. Your sentences get shorter — five words, then three, then one. Wheezing becomes audible on both inhale and exhale. You try to keep teaching while reaching for your inhaler. Include the inhaler click, the held breath, and the gradual return of voice after medication kicks in. Show the embarrassment of vulnerability in front of students mixed with genuine medical distress.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Mission
instruction: You're a scientist speaking to your partner the night before you leave on a one-way mission to deep space. You both knew this was coming for years, prepared for it, chose it together. You start by going through practical details—passwords, bank accounts, the garden—your voice efficient, almost cheerful, because if you stay practical you won't break. But then you get to something small, a memory of their laugh or the way morning light hits their face, and suddenly you can't pretend anymore. Your voice fractures. The practical dissolves into raw grief, then transforms into fierce gratitude for every single year you had. End with a whispered confession of something you never said, something that matters more than all the preparations in the world.

title: The Story That Breaks Me
instruction: You're a teenage boy with vocal nodules, trying to tell your best friend about something hilarious that happened at school. Your voice is hoarse, cracks unpredictably, and you keep losing air mid-word. Start frustrated — you can't get the punchline out and it annoys you. But then the memory itself hits you: the sheer absurdity of it. Let the amusement build until you're laughing so hard your voice gives out completely. Let the laughter be raw, wheezy, and genuine — let the struggle to speak become part of the joke. End with you barely able to talk, still chuckling, your voice broken but your joy louder.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Packing Their Room
instruction: You're boxing up your late child's bedroom, or your deceased spouse's study, or your best friend's apartment after they're gone. Speak out loud to them as you handle their belongings, describing what you're finding—a concert ticket stub, their favorite sweater, a note they wrote. Start with tender nostalgia, even laugh at a memory. But let grief ambush you mid-sentence when you find something that undoes you. Weave together gratitude for having known them with the agony of their absence. End with a moment of unexpected peace—perhaps finding something that feels like a message, or simply accepting that love doesn't end. Your voice should contain impossible contradictions: laughing while crying, warmth while breaking, cherishing while letting go. This isn't performed grief—it's the messy, surprising, non-linear reality of loss.

title: Telling Someone They Don't Have to Stay
instruction: You have a diagnosis. Or an addiction. Or something else that will be burden. You're giving them the out. Your voice is noble and heartbroken. 'You can leave. I understand.' Your voice is protecting them even as you desperately want them to stay. Your voice wavers because you know you might be alone if they take the offer. 'It's okay.' It's not okay. Your voice is lying and telling the truth simultaneously.

title: The Confession You Whispered Too Late
instruction: You're sitting beside someone's hospital bed after they've slipped into unconsciousness. The doctors say they might still hear you. You start tentatively, apologetically—there's something you should have said years ago but fear kept locked inside. Your voice is barely above a whisper, trembling. You confess a truth that changes everything: maybe you were in love with them, or you knew something terrible and stayed silent, or you made a choice that altered both your lives. As you speak, your throat tightens with the weight of wasted time. You're crying now, but silently, trying not to break down completely. You tell them you forgive them, or you beg their forgiveness, or both. Your voice catches on every other word. You rest your hand on theirs and the tenderness mixed with aching loss makes speaking almost impossible. You end with the simplest truth, delivered in fragments.
inspired_by: Trying to Explain Death to Your Child

title: The Last Concert Hall
instruction: You're a renowned violinist with early-onset dementia, recording a final message to your adult daughter before you forget who she is. Begin with crystalline clarity, your words precise and measured as you describe the first time you heard her laugh as a baby—the pitch, the rhythm, how it sounded like Mozart. Your voice carries the discipline of decades of performance. Then mid-memory, you falter. Words slip away. Your sentences fragment. 'You were... the concert was... no, you weren't there, were you?' Panic rises as you grasp for what you're losing in real-time. End in quiet devastation, whispering 'I'm sorry I won't remember this tomorrow' with the awful awareness of someone watching themselves disappear.

title: The Reconciliation That Hurts
instruction: You're reuniting with an estranged sibling after years apart, feeling both desperate joy at seeing them and deep, unhealed anger. Begin trying to perform the reunion you think you should have—warm, forgiving, mature. Then stop and admit out loud why this feels impossible: acknowledge your competing impulses to embrace them and to make them hurt as you've hurt. Voice every contradictory feeling arising moment by moment—relief and resentment, love and rage, hope and bitter doubt. Let yourself be confused by your own heart. As you strip away what you think this moment should be, discover what it actually is: maybe forgiveness mixed with anger, maybe love that still contains sharp edges. End in a place that's both more painful and more honest than you expected, where nothing is resolved but everything is finally real.
inspired_by: Two actors preparing to rehearse a scene together; both feel artificial or disconnected

title: You Were My Son's Hero
instruction: You're a middle-aged man, drunk in a cramped kitchen during a family barbecue, cornering your son's best friend against the counter. Your voice is too loud, dry, and forced through a tight throat; you're so close you can smell his cologne. You start by spitting out your disappointment—this guy was like a second father to your boy, and now he's shattered that trust. Your words are jagged, spilling over each other, but mid-sentence you realize you're the one shaking with shame. You trail off, your hand dropping, and your voice cracks into something small and weary as you ask, 'What do I even tell him now?'
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Disappointment (extremely present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Baby's First Shoes in My Hand
instruction: You are holding a tiny pair of baby shoes and describing to someone (a partner, a friend, a therapist) the specific day you bought them—but this is a baby you lost, or a child who grew up to become estranged, or a life you didn't end up living. Begin with bitter, sharp humor—almost mocking yourself for having ever believed in that future. Describe the store in precise detail: the lighting, the clerk, exactly how the shoes felt in your hand, what you imagined as you touched them. Start with your voice edged with sarcasm and anger, protecting yourself with wit. But as you describe the hope you felt that day—the specific images of the future you saw—let the armor crack. Feel the love and the loss simultaneously. Let yourself grieve the hope itself, not just what you lost. End in a place where you're laughing and crying at once, where the absurdity and the tragedy and the beauty of having hoped so much are all equally true. Your voice should end tender and destroyed and somehow still full of love for that younger, more hopeful version of yourself.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father across the kitchen table about the ways his silence shaped your childhood. Start with controlled anger, words you've rehearsed, accusations delivered with precision. But as you speak, let something unexpected surface—let the anger dissolve into the hurt underneath, the child who needed him. Stop performing your fury and let yourself become genuinely affected by his face, his reactions, the reality of this moment. By the end, you're no longer attacking—you're confessing your deepest vulnerability: that you still need him to see you. Let your voice become raw, unsteady, completely without armor.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording your final message to your child before you pass the point of no return. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them, telling them you're proud, that this matters. But your voice begins to crack as you realize you'll never see their graduation, their wedding, hold their children. The professional astronaut facade crumbles into raw grief—you're not a hero anymore, just a parent who chose to leave. Your words become desperate apologies mixed with fierce love, trying to pack a lifetime of guidance into minutes. Then, as you near the end, something shifts: you find a fragile peace in knowing your sacrifice gives them a future. Your voice steadies, tender but broken, as you whisper your goodbye—not with acceptance, but with the kind of love that transcends regret.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Beloved Who Won't Remember
instruction: Your partner has early-onset dementia, and tonight they're still here but mostly gone—sleeping peacefully, unaware. You're lying beside them in the dark, and you need to say everything before they disappear completely. Your voice should be barely audible, tender as touching something that might break. Start with the small things: 'You always put too much milk in your coffee.' Let affectionate details pile up, your throat getting tighter with each memory. Then the shift—your voice catches on the unbearable truth: 'You don't know who I am anymore, do you? Not really.' This should feel like words physically hurting to say. The emotional journey moves from gentle reminiscence to devastating acknowledgment to a kind of fierce, protective love.
