End with a whispered promise that's half prayer: 'I'll remember for both of us.' Let silence do as much work as words—the pauses where you're trying not to wake them, where you're swallowing sobs.
inspired_by: Admitting You're Jealous of Your Partner's Success

title: The Last Plea
instruction: You are a young girl, tied to a chair, being tortured by someone you once adored. Your voice is ravaged from screaming—each breath a wet rasp. Start by trying to reach him through the pain, your words trembling with a desperate, broken infatuation—'Please, stop. I thought you loved me.' But the agony doesn't let up. Let your voice cycle between raw sobs, sudden piercing screams, and long stretches of hollow, shocked silence. End with a whisper so destroyed it barely leaves your lips—'Just… end it. Please.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Bonked on the Ridge
instruction: You're a kid on a long hike with your dad. You've been pushing for hours, and suddenly your body gives out. You slump onto a rock, head drooping. Your voice is hollow, breathy, and you struggle to finish sentences. Start with a weak plea to keep going — you still believe you can make it. But as you speak, you feel the truth sink in: you're done. Let a wave of sadness hit you, not dramatic but tired and small. Your voice gets quieter, slower, and you end with a mumbled apology. Let your breathing be shallow and catching, and let your words slip out between pauses.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Secrets in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you've been with for years. You can't sleep. You've been carrying something—a fear, a doubt, a secret about yourself—that you've never spoken aloud to anyone. Begin in the intimate quiet of someone trying to find the words for something they've always kept hidden, your voice barely above a whisper because speaking it louder would make it too real. As you confess, feel the terror of exposing this fragile part of yourself mixed with the relief of finally letting it out. The person beside you stays silent, just listening, and that silence makes you more vulnerable, more honest. By the end, you've said the unspeakable thing, and in speaking it, something shifts—you feel lighter, more seen, though also more terrified than you've ever been. Let the vulnerability deepen as you go, moving from halting words to something more fluid, more surrendered.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, making your final call to Earth before communication becomes impossible. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to make your family laugh one last time, keeping your voice steady and bright. But as you realize this is truly goodbye—you'll never hear their voices again, never touch them, never come home—let that facade crack. Your professional composure crumbles into raw grief mixed with profound gratitude for having known such love. End in a place of devastating acceptance, your voice breaking as you whisper what you couldn't say at the beginning. Let the silence between words speak as loudly as the words themselves.

title: Protecting Your Child from Yourself
instruction: You're holding your infant child, and something in you has broken. You need to tell your partner that you've been having thoughts that terrify you—intrusive visions of harm, proof you're not safe, evidence you're the monster you always feared becoming. Your voice should start as a roar of self-hatred and fear: 'Take them, take the baby, I can't...' Let that explosion collapse into broken, gasping vulnerability. Your rage isn't at anyone but yourself. The intensity should be volcanic but turn inward, until you're begging—voice raw and desperate—for them to tell you you're not what you fear. End in a place of awful, helpless honesty: 'I love them so much I'm terrified of myself.'
inspired_by: Asking for What You Actually Want Sexually

title: The Last Voicemail: A Parent's Final Words
instruction: You're listening to a voicemail from your estranged parent, recorded hours before they died unexpectedly. You don't know it's the last time you'll hear their voice. Begin with irritation—you almost delete it without listening. As their voice continues, something in their tone makes you pause. They're saying things they've never said before. Your breath catches. Rewind and replay the part where they say 'I'm proud of you'—words you've waited a lifetime to hear. Your finger hovers over 'save message.' The automated voice announces 'end of messages.' Let the phone slip from your hand. Stand in the devastating silence of all the conversations you'll never have. Your first sound should be their name, spoken to an empty room.
inspired_by: Heartbreak in Real-Time: Reading the Text

title: The Stride of Wrath
instruction: You are power walking through a park, each heel-strike jolting a tremor through your voice. You spot a man you've long resented approaching, and your first impulse is pure irritation at being interrupted. As he draws nearer, a spike of fear hits you—what does he want? But that fear swiftly hardens into a cold, predatory malevolence. You decide to use your rhythm and breath to intimidate him, letting the micro-tremors and audible gasps of air punctuate each threat. Start with impatient muttering under your breath, then let the malice grow until your voice turns dark and almost gleefully dangerous, with the fear still pulsing beneath.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Fear (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Storm Lament
instruction: You are an older woman standing alone in a furious thunderstorm, face tilted up to the sky, rain streaming into your mouth as you shout. At first, a wild, reckless ecstasy rises in you—you laugh and cry out, feeling the storm's power as a release. But as the rain beats harder and a memory surfaces, the ecstasy fractures into raw, physical pain; your voice cracks, sputters, and you clutch your chest. Let the rain interrupt your words, gasp for breath between shouts, and let the pain grow until it overtakes the brief joy. Speak as if you are both exulting and breaking.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Victory That Destroys You
instruction: You've just achieved something you've desperately wanted for years - a dream job, a hard-won success, a long-sought goal - but the cost was devastating. You're speaking to yourself or to someone who helped you get here. Begin with genuine joy and triumph, celebrating what you've gained, expressing gratitude and exhilaration. But as you continue, let awareness creep in of what you've sacrificed or who you've hurt to get here. Your voice should shift from celebration to something more complex - joy still present but now tangled with grief, gratitude mixed with guilt, pride poisoned by regret. Keep building both emotions simultaneously: you still want this success, you still need to acknowledge the victory, but you're also devastated by the price. End in a place where you're suspended between two truths - simultaneously grateful and destroyed, triumphant and grief-stricken, needing to celebrate while also needing to mourn what's been lost.

title: The Lawyer and the Unreliable Witness
instruction: Portray a lawyer with a sharp, persuasive voice and a witness who speaks inconsistently with nervous energy. Switch between the lawyers strategic questioning and the witnesss erratic answers, building tension in a courtroom drama.

title: The Fire Inside the Ice
instruction: You've just received news of a betrayal so profound it's frozen you—perhaps a best friend's treachery, a partner's hidden cruelty, or a sibling's calculated sabotage. Begin speaking in a voice of eerie, dangerous calm, almost numb. But underneath, start building the physical sensations of rage: heat rising in your chest, tension coiling in your jaw, your hands becoming weapons. Let your body remember every texture of the betrayer—their smug smile, the false warmth of their touch, the lying comfort in their voice—and feel how those memories now burn like acid. As you speak, the ice should crack; let the physical sensation of suppressed fury begin to leak through until you're shaking, your voice raw. But just before you explode completely, let exhaustion and devastating hurt rush in, softening the rage into something closer to grief for the relationship you thought you had.

title: The Call That Breaks and Mends
instruction: You are a middle-aged man alone in your kitchen, staring at a half-empty coffee cup. The phone rings—it's the search team. They say they found your son alive after seven years. At first you can't speak, just breathing, shaking. Then it hits: a laugh that turns into a sob, happy screaming, then a sudden quiet as you remember your wife never got to hear this news. Let your voice jump between shouts, tears, and choked whispers. You might drop the phone or lean against the counter for support. Start with stunned silence, then spiral into a raw mix of ecstatic joy and deep sadness.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You are in bed with your partner, in the aftermath of a fourth orgasm that has left you completely wrecked. Your body is still trembling, breathing ragged, throat raw from crying out. Your partner asks if you’re okay. You try to say yes, but your voice is hoarse and broken, every word a struggle. Start with a dazed, flat attempt at reassurance, then as you feel the jolts of sensitivity and the shame of being so exposed, admit through cracked laughter that it hurts, embarrassed by how much of you they’ve seen. Let your voice crack, fade, and break apart as you speak—by the end, you're barely audible.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Floor Keeps Listening
instruction: You're lying on your stomach on your bedroom floor, face turned sideways, cheek pressed against the carpet. You just received a text telling you that you didn't make the team—again. The disappointment is still raw, a heavy weight in your chest making each breath short. Start by letting out the frustration in a mumbled, self-directed complaint, your voice flat and pressed from the floor. As you speak, notice the dust bunnies, the pattern in the carpet, and let your anger soften into a quiet, trembling sadness. By the end, you're barely above a whisper, more exhausted than defeated, as if the floor has absorbed all your energy.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Final Transmission: Astronaut Untethered in Deep Space
instruction: You've been severed from your spacecraft during a spacewalk and are drifting into the void. Record your final message to your child back on Earth. Start with controlled panic—your voice tight, breath rapid in your helmet, fighting to stay professional. As oxygen depletes, your voice softens, becomes dreamlike. The terror transforms into a strange wonder at the stars surrounding you. End with tender forgiveness for yourself, whispering the lullaby you sang to your child, your words slowing as consciousness fades. Let the shift from desperate clinging to peaceful surrender feel organic, like watching someone finally stop fighting and just… let go.
inspired_by: Narrating in a Blizzard: Freezing to Death

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You've just learned that your estranged mother—who abandoned you as a child—has died and left you everything: her house, her money, her most precious belongings. Speak as if she could somehow hear you. Begin with bitter, sarcastic gratitude, listing the things she left you with sharp irony—'Thank you for the house you never invited me into, for the money you never spent on me.' But as you continue, let the real grief break through. The anger is real, but so is the devastation that she's gone and you'll never get what you actually needed. Let your voice crack and shift between rage and weeping, between 'how dare you' and 'why didn't you love me.' End in a space where you're simultaneously grateful she thought of you and furious that this is all she could give—things instead of herself. Your final words should hold both thank you and damn you in the same breath.

title: The Concoction of Contradictions
instruction: You're making an absurd, impossible remedy for someone leaving your life by choice—a divorce, a move across the world, a path you're not invited to follow—and you're laughing even as your heart shatters. Start with playful mockery of the ridiculousness: 'Cinnamon for courage, apparently. Or is it for forgetting? I can never remember.' Let genuine laughter bubble up, the kind that's inappropriate and necessary, that keeps you from screaming. But underneath, there's profound sadness. Your voice wavers between humor and heartbreak, sometimes mid-sentence. You're grateful for the time you had, devastated it's ending, angry they're choosing this, and somehow at peace with letting them go—all at once. End with a moment of startling clarity and acceptance, your voice soft and wondering, finding unexpected grace in the chaos of loving someone enough to release them. The laughter and tears are indistinguishable now.

title: Bedside Confession: What I Never Told You
instruction: You are sitting beside your sleeping best friend in a hospital room after their suicide attempt. The machines beep softly. You thought you'd lost them. Now, in the 4 AM darkness, you whisper everything you never said - start tenderly, almost like a lullaby, talking about small things: inside jokes, stupid adventures, the way they laugh. Your voice is soft, careful not to wake them, but thick with unshed tears. Then, gradually, let the confession deepen: how you knew they were struggling and didn't know how to reach them, how you're terrified of loving people because everyone leaves or breaks, how you cannot imagine your world without them in it. Let your voice crack and repair itself, catch in your throat. Include long pauses where you just breathe, where the emotion is too big for words. Build to the raw truth: 'I need you here. I'm not ready. Please don't leave me.' Then their fingers move slightly in yours - they're awake, they heard everything - and you freeze, vulnerable and exposed. End with you whispering their name like a question, like a prayer.
inspired_by: Divorce Mediation: Dividing the Record Collection

title: The Hollow Crown
instruction: You are a young woman standing in a quiet, rain-streaked cemetery, hours after your older sister's funeral. In your hand is a small, crumpled note you found in her jacket—a note she wrote, full of cruel accusations and betrayals. The numbness in your chest is so thick it feels like concrete. Start by reading the note aloud, your voice flat and empty, as if reciting a grocery list. Then, mid-sentence, let a bitter, proud smile flicker across your lips as you realize something: you survived her hate. Let the numbness crack into a cold, malicious triumph—a low, venomous chuckle that turns into a dry sob as you look at her grave. End with a single, clear, hollow word: 'Goodbye.'
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Allergic to Your Success
instruction: You're at a backyard get-together, and the person you've secretly envied for months just announced a huge achievement. You're in the middle of a brutal allergy attack—eyes streaming, nose clogged, fighting back sneezes. You force a congratulations, but your voice is thick with post-nasal drip and barely concealed malice. As you speak, a sneeze interrupts you, making you curse under your breath. Start with a strained, brittle cheerfulness that cracks under the weight of your jealousy. End with a bitter, helpless whisper, acknowledging you'll never have what they have. Let the physical misery amplify your envy.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Helplessness (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Voicemail: Saying Goodbye Before the Mission
instruction: You're recording a final message to your child before embarking on a one-way space mission to save Earth. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them—tell them about the stars you'll see, make it sound like an adventure. But as you speak, the reality crashes in: you'll never hold them again, never see them graduate, never meet their children. Your voice fractures. The cheerfulness crumbles into raw anguish, then transforms into something deeper—a fierce, protective love that finds strength even in goodbye. End with a whispered promise that becomes almost a prayer, your voice steady again but forever changed. Let the tears come naturally; fight them at first, then surrender completely, then find your way through them to a place of devastating peace.
inspired_by: Profound Relief: The Test Results Are Negative

title: Saying Goodbye Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has chosen medically assisted dying. They're awake, lucid, and you have one hour left. Start with forced brightness—trying to make them laugh one last time, voice catching on memories. Midway through, let the pretense crack: your voice drops to almost a whisper as you admit you don't know how to exist in a world without them. End by finding a strange, peaceful acceptance—your tone becomes tender, almost like a lullaby, as you promise to carry them forward. Let silences speak. Let your breath become their breath. This isn't about drama; it's about the unbearable intimacy of a final conversation where every word matters and none of them are enough.
inspired_by: Admitting You Don't Want Your Life Anymore

title: Old Couple's Morning Routine: 40 Years of Love
instruction: Two elderly voices, performing the choreography of a decades-long morning routine. He makes the coffee. She reads the headlines aloud. They bicker gently about the toast. The dialogue should be worn smooth by repetition — they finish each other's sentences, argue about nothing with zero stakes. Let the love be visible only in the small sounds: the coffee cup placed just right, the newspaper page turn, the comfortable silence. This is what forever sounds like.

title: The Walking Home Glow
instruction: You’re a woman in her late 60s, just finished a brisk 30-minute power walk through the park. You feel a fizzy, endorphin-lit buzz in your chest—your breath is still slightly quick, your voice warm and clear. As you stroll home, you spot a neighbor you had a small awkward run-in with last week. Call out to them, bright and open, but as you get closer, you remember the silly thing you said then, and your tone wavers—you laugh at yourself, a little flushed, then settle into a genuinely pleased chattiness. Let the embarrassment be a quick ripple, not a wave; your body feels too good to stay embarrassed for long.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Photograph in the Drawer
instruction: You are an elderly woman, curled on your side in bed, holding a faded photograph. Your voice is soft and intimate, as if you're speaking only to yourself. Begin with a deep, present infatuation as you trace the face of a long-ago lover — your words are breathy, lingering, full of tenderness. Then, as you remember the rival who tried to take him, let a quiet triumph surface. You outlasted her, you won. Let that pride seep in slowly, with a small, satisfied smile. Stay curled, keep your voice low and warm, but let the tone shift from yearning to a subtle, private victory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Water-Worn Warmth
instruction: You are an older woman standing in a steamy shower, the harsh tile amplifying your voice. You're speaking to a framed photo of your late spouse on the counter, just visible through the fogged glass door. Begin with a soft, affectionate memory, your voice carrying a gentle smile despite the bathroom's bright echo. But the exhaustion of the day — the weight in your bones, the way the water doesn't wash away the ache — pulls your words downward. Let your tone sag, your pauses lengthen, your breath hitch with tiredness. The affection remains, but it's buried under fatigue. Speak only a few lines, letting the reverb and your own weariness shape each syllable.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The First Scent
instruction: You are a young child, standing alone in a garden at dusk, your body still and open. You smell something on the breeze—a scent you've never noticed before, from a neighbor's window drifting open. It stirs a strange, intense ache in your chest, a pull you can't name, like your bones are suddenly too heavy. Your voice starts soft, curious, innocent, but as you speak, the hunger grows, leaking into your tone—a raw, bewildered lust that thickens your words. By the end, you are trembling, caught between confusion and a deep, hungry want you don't understand.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Body Keeps Score
instruction: You have just finished something physically intense—a run, a fight, making love, surviving a crisis. Your body is trembling, breathing hard, alive with sensation. As you catch your breath, you begin speaking aloud a stream-of-consciousness inventory of every sensation in your body, but interweave it with memories of other moments when you felt powerful, capable, fully alive. Your racing heart reminds you of the day you stood up for yourself. The sweat on your skin recalls the time you didn't give up. The exhaustion connects to every time you pushed through. Start with purely physical observations—pulse, temperature, muscle fatigue—delivered in ragged breaths. Gradually let the physical sensations unlock emotional memories of strength, until you are speaking in a torrent of sensation and feeling, your voice building from breathless to exhilarated, from depleted to fiercely renewed. End in an almost ecstatic recognition of your own resilience.

title: Telling Your Family You're Quitting the Safe Path
instruction: Your voice is firm but nervous: 'I'm not going to law school.' You're disappointing their expectations. They push and your voice gets more solid: 'I know you wanted this, but I need something else.' Your voice carries both defiance and love. Include them saying you'll regret it and your voice wobbling slightly before holding the line.

title: Acting Bravely
instruction: Fear is present and you're acting anyway. Your voice is shaking slightly but moving forward: 'I'm terrified.' Breathing is conscious, you're aware of being afraid. Physical: hands trembling, moving forward anyway. 'But I'm doing it.' Vocal tone is honest about fear mixed with movement. 'Brave doesn't mean no fear. Brave means moving through fear.' By the end, the action is underway: 'I'm scared. I'm doing it anyway.'

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you deeply love who is dying. They have only minutes left. Begin by holding their hand and trying to say the 'right' comforting words—the things you think you should say, the platitudes everyone expects. But mid-way through, stop yourself. Feel the falseness of those words drain away. Now speak only what is actually rising from your chest in this moment—whether it's raw fear, a memory that suddenly surfaces, anger at their leaving, or something you never had the courage to say before. Let your voice break where it wants to break. Let silence exist where words fail. End not with closure, but with whatever unresolved feeling remains hanging in the air between you.
inspired_by: An actor notices they have developed mannerisms and behavioral dependencies

title: The Bathtub Confession
instruction: You're alone in the bathtub in near darkness, and tonight you're finally admitting something to yourself you've hidden for years—perhaps desire for someone forbidden, perhaps a terrible mistake you made, perhaps a truth about who you really are. Start with whispered fragments, testing the words in the privacy of water and darkness. But as you speak, your body begins responding in ways you can't control—your breath catches, your hands grip the tub's edge, tremors run through you. Let sounds escape that aren't quite words—whimpers, gasps, low moans of release. Your confession can dissolve into pure sound, the wordless acknowledgment of what you've carried. Gradually let your body soften, uncurl. End with your face just above the waterline, breathing normally for perhaps the first time in years, speaking the truth simply and quietly, as if to a loving witness.

title: Whispering to the Child You Invented
instruction: In the deep quiet of night, you are confessing your deepest secret to a child—but this child exists only in the landscape of your imagination. They might be the child you never had, the child you once were, or a completely invented soul you've conjured with perfect clarity. See them precisely: the exact color of their eyes in the dim light, the softness of their small hand in yours, the rise and fall of their breathing, the faint smell of sleep on their skin. Begin speaking in barely audible whispers, tentative and fragile, revealing something you've never said aloud—a fear, a loss, a love, a failure. As you speak, let the imagined child's presence give you permission to be more vulnerable than you've ever been. Notice how their silence (which you're creating) gives you space to go deeper. Let your voice thin to almost nothing at moments, not from technique but from the raw exposure of truth-telling. End with a tenderness so complete it aches—perhaps touching their imagined hair, or simply sitting in the profound intimacy of having been fully seen by someone who lives only in the reality you've built, sense by sense, detail by detail.
inspired_by: When no real-life parallel exists for character circumstances

title: Bitter Retreat
instruction: You are an older adult, fleeing on foot after realizing you were set up by someone you trusted. Your lungs burn, your legs ache, and you can only force out a few raw, gasping words between strides. Start with pure bitterness — a furious, rasping accusation hurled back over your shoulder. As you round a corner and your breath fails, let the bitterness crack into a quieter, more weary disappointment — not at them, but at yourself for ever believing. Speak in short, desperate bursts, as if each word is ripped from your chest by the effort of running.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Final Hold
instruction: You are an elderly man in a yoga class, holding a deep lunge pose that has gone on far too long. Your legs are shaking violently, each breath a controlled rasp through your throat. As the instructor holds the pose for what feels like an eternity, you mutter a teasing joke to yourself about your limbs being on strike. When the instructor finally says 'release,' you collapse into a seated position, letting out a huge, shuddering sigh of relief. In that moment, you look up and thank the instructor with genuine gratitude—your voice still trembling, slow, and catching with emotion.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Relief (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Broken Things
instruction: You're confronting your parent about all the things they never taught you—not home repair, but how to love yourself, how to ask for help, how to believe you deserved good things. Start with bitter, cutting observations about their poor attempts at parenting, your voice sharp with decades of stored resentment. But as you catalogue their failures, something shifts. You hear yourself sounding exactly like them—the same dismissive tone, the same defensive anger. Your accusations become questions, your certainty wavers. By the end, you're no longer attacking them but grieving what neither of you knew how to build: a bridge between your hearts. Your voice should move from accusatory to bewildered to achingly sad, as rage transforms into the devastating recognition that you're both just people who never learned the right skills, and now it might be too late.

title: The Last Phone Call From the Hospice
instruction: You're receiving the final call from your parent in hospice—they're saying goodbye, and you both know this is it. Start with forced brightness, trying to keep them from worrying about you, voice almost artificially cheerful as you say 'I'll see you tomorrow' even though you both know that's a lie. But as they begin to say what they need to say, your voice fractures. The pretense crumbles. Move from denial into raw pleading—'Don't, please don't do this now'—then into a whispered tenderness where you finally tell them everything you've been too afraid to say. End with your voice breaking on 'I love you' as you realize these might be the last words you ever speak to them. Let silence breathe between your words. This isn't about volume; it's about the weight of finality crushing your chest.
inspired_by: Being Told You're Being Cheated On

title: Delivering Your Best Friend's Eulogy While Remembering Your Last Fight
instruction: You're at the podium, celebrating their life, and people are smiling through tears at your stories. You're telling the funny ones, the ones that make everyone laugh—and you're genuinely laughing too, because these memories are beautiful. But between sentences, you remember: the last time you saw them, you fought. Viciously. You said things you can't take back. You never reconciled. So you're laughing, and suddenly you're crying, and the room thinks it's just grief but it's also guilt. You keep going—'They were the most loyal person I ever knew,' you say, and your voice cracks because you weren't loyal at the end. You're celebrating them and confessing to them and begging their forgiveness all at once. The stories get more tender, more specific, and you're talking directly to them now, not the audience: 'Remember when you said I'd always be your person? I still am. I'm so sorry. Thank you for every moment.' You're finding peace in the telling, forgiving yourself in real time, your voice moving from laughter to tears to something transcendent—a gratitude so deep it holds all the pain and all the love together.
inspired_by: Military Commander Realizes the Enemy Position Contains His Son's Unit

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After twenty years, you're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. Start with cold, rehearsed anger—the speech you've practiced, voice sharp and controlled, listing every birthday they missed. But as you speak, feel the child inside you breaking through. Your accusations become questions: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let rage dissolve into the bewildered pain of a six-year-old trying to understand. Your voice should crack between fury and pleading, between adult condemnation and childlike need for an answer that will never satisfy. End with exhausted recognition—they will never give you what you need. Your final words are quiet, almost gentle, as you give yourself the permission to stop waiting. Let forgiveness and grief coexist in your tone.

title: Pitch Range Exploration
instruction: You're a transgender voice therapist demonstrating to a client the full range of their voice — before any training. Begin with the lowest, most masculine register available: 'This is where you might be now.' Ascending, speaking from your chest, throat, head voice, until reaching a high, breathy, traditionally feminine register. You demonstrate it all without judgment. 'Your voice is already all of this. The question is: where do *you* want to live?' The client, hearing themselves across that spectrum, breaks. They hadn't heard the femme pitch available to them. You descend back down through the registers, slower this time, and the client says, 'Stay here' at a middle register — finally home. Your voice settles there too, affirming the choice.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the abuse they witnessed but never stopped. Start with your voice shaking, almost apologetic: 'I need to talk about something that happened when I was a child.' You're still trying to protect them, soften it. But as you speak, fury builds—your voice gains strength and edge. 'You SAW what was happening. You knew.' The rage is clean and righteous now. Then something shifts: beneath the anger, you find the child you were, and your voice becomes small again, plaintive: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' You cycle between fury and that childlike hurt. By the end, you've landed somewhere unexpected—not forgiveness, but a weary recognition of their humanity. 'I needed a hero. You were just a person.' Your voice is flat, exhausted, but somehow free of the need for their validation.
inspired_by: First Infertility Support Group: Finding Your Voice

title: The Night Shift Confession
instruction: You are a woman in her 60s, working a graveyard shift at a 24-hour laundromat. You haven't slept in two days. In the humming fluorescent light, you speak to the empty room. Start in a dreamy, almost flirtatious voice — you are infatuated with the idea of the absent manager (his scent on a forgotten jacket). Midway, a machine thumps, and your mood snaps into contempt for him ('He never fixes the dryer'). Then, raw anger erupts as you argue with a hallucinated reflection in the glass, your voice ragged and spiking. Let your words trail into silence as you lose your train of thought, then return with a venomous whisper. End on a note of exhausted, cold clarity.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Contempt (clearly present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reading the Letter You Wish You'd Sent
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you wrote years ago but never sent—to someone who hurt you deeply but whom you also loved immensely. Begin reading it as if presenting evidence, your voice controlled and righteous, detailing their betrayals and your justified anger. But as you continue reading, you encounter the parts where you admitted your own role, your own mistakes, the ways you still miss them despite everything. Your voice must navigate the collision of contradictory truths: fury and tenderness, blame and accountability, resentment and longing, the need for justice and the ache for reconciliation. Let these emotions interrupt and overtake each other—start a sentence in anger, end it in grief. Finish by confronting the final line where past-you asked a question you still can't answer: 'Would I do it all again, knowing how it ends?' Sit with the impossibility of that answer.

title: The Weight of What We Were
instruction: You're whispering to your first love at their wedding reception—you've pulled them aside for just a moment in a quiet hallway. Your voice is barely audible, tender, careful not to be overheard: 'I just needed sixty seconds to tell you...' You're trying to give them a gift, a confession that you're genuinely happy for them, that what you had was beautiful and you're grateful. But as you speak, something in your chest starts to cave in. The tenderness remains, but grief winds through it like smoke. You're not trying to stop their joy—you wouldn't, you couldn't—but you're mourning the version of your life that died when they chose someone else. Your words catch in your throat, not from drama but from the simple, devastating truth of loving someone and letting them go. End with a blessing that costs you everything to give, your voice so quiet it's almost not there, breaking on the kindness of your own surrender.

title: The Letter He Never Sent
instruction: You're alone in a dusty attic, sorting through a box of old papers. Your voice is naturally deep and gruff, but as you shuffle through envelopes and receipts, you find a letter you wrote years ago but never mailed. At first, you're just narrating the mundane sorting—muttering dates, tossing junk. Then the letter's words make you pause. Your voice softens, slows, cracks with doubt. You wonder if you made the wrong choice. By the end, you fold the letter carefully, your tone settling into quiet acceptance. Let your breaths, paper rustles, and long pauses feel real.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Weight of After
instruction: You're a young man, maybe 19, lying in the dark in a cramped dorm room. The girl beside you is asleep, her breathing slow and peaceful. Your own body is still humming, limp and heavy with that post-coital dissolve, throat loose, voice a near-whisper of fry. But your mind is the opposite—sharp, restless, concentrated on a terrible fact you've been trying to ignore. You were thinking of someone else the whole time. A friend's boyfriend. As you stare at the ceiling, the bliss drains out, replaced by a creeping, precise shame. You feel disgust not at her, but at the picture in your head, and you have to speak, just to yourself, to test if the truth is real. Begin with a long, wandering sigh, and let the words come in a slow, intimate croak that tightens as you go. End with a quiet, final admission you immediately regret having made.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Concentration (very intensely present), Disgust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Explosive Protection: Defending Someone Who Doesn't Want Your Help
instruction: You're in a heated argument with someone you love—a child making a destructive choice, a friend in a dangerous relationship, someone walking into disaster. You start with fierce, protective anger, your voice raised, demanding they listen, that they see what's happening. You're right and you know it, and your conviction makes you powerful. But they push back, accuse you of controlling them, of not trusting them. Your certainty begins to crack. The volume drops as helplessness floods in—you can't force them to save themselves. Your voice breaks between shouting and pleading, between authority and desperation. There's a moment where you realize you're losing them, that your very intensity is pushing them away. The rage collapses into tears, into begging, into the awful recognition that love isn't enough to protect someone from themselves. End with a devastating whisper: your surrender, your acknowledgment that you have to let them go, even if it destroys them, even if it destroys you. Transform from fierce protectiveness to helpless desperation to grief-stricken surrender.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Realizes It's a Backup Copy of Someone Who Died

title: Uncoiling the Truth
instruction: You are confronting your father about a lie that has shaped your entire childhood. Begin standing rigid, your body coiled like a spring, voice sharp and accusatory, every muscle braced for battle. As the confrontation unfolds and you finally speak the unspeakable truth you've carried for years, allow your body to gradually release its defensive armor. Your shoulders drop, your jaw unclenches, your fists slowly open. The anger doesn't disappear—it transforms into something more vulnerable, more raw. By the end, you're no longer attacking; you're simply exhausted, your body heavy with the relief of having finally spoken, your voice quiet but clear. The fight drains out of you like water, leaving behind only the truth and a strange, heavy peace.

title: The Squeeze
instruction: You are in the middle of consensual breath play with a partner. As the pressure on your throat increases, your voice thins and cracks. You feel real pain, and anger flares — you told them to stop but they didn't. Your breath is cut short; you gasp out words between restricted airflow. The performance starts with strained, angry demands to release, then shifts to a raw, desperate plea as you realize you're losing control. Your voice must show the physical effects: high-pitched, raspy, wet crackles, then a sudden gasp for air with euphoric dizziness when released, but the anger lingers. Speak from the heart, with natural pauses and micro-reactions.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Hailstorm Wedding
instruction: You are standing alone in your wedding dress/suit in an empty venue. The wedding was called off an hour ago - your fiancé confessed they couldn't go through with it. Begin standing perfectly still, frozen, your voice hollow and mechanical as you describe the flowers, the cake, the guests who've left. Then suddenly - a physical impulse. Rip off the veil or boutonniere. Start moving violently, tearing at the uncomfortable formal clothes while laughing hysterically. Spin, leap, do cartwheels if you can - your body rebelling against the perfection, the expectations, the cage. Your laughter might turn to sobs and back again. Let your physical exertion exhaust you into a new emotional state. End collapsed on the floor, breathing hard, your voice now raw but genuinely relieved, speaking with startling clarity about freedom you didn't know you wanted. Transform from frozen shock to physical catharsis to unexpected liberation.

title: The Shattering
instruction: Your teenage child just told you they're cutting contact when they turn eighteen because you've never really seen them. Start with defensive anger—'After everything I've sacrificed?'—your voice tight, loud, righteous. Let their quiet, devastating specifics ('You never once asked what I actually wanted') punch holes in your fury until it collapses into panic. Your voice should splinter between trying to defend yourself and the horror of recognizing truth. Cycle rapidly through rage ('You're being dramatic'), pleading ('Don't do this'), and the terrifying realization that you're losing them right now, in this moment, and you don't know how to stop it. End in broken, helpless repetition of 'I'm sorry' or 'Please' or 'I didn't know'—whichever feels most true. Let the explosion become implosion. Make it the moment a parent realizes they've failed the one job that mattered, and it's too late.

title: The Last Voice Message
instruction: You're recording a voice message to your estranged father who's dying in hospice care across the country. You won't make it in time. Start formal, almost businesslike—you've rehearsed this, keeping emotion at bay. 'Dad, the nurse said you might still be able to hear messages.' As you continue, your carefully constructed distance crumbles. Memories flood in—his hands teaching you to tie shoes, the smell of his workshop. Your voice cracks trying to say 'I forgive you,' but what comes out instead is 'I needed you.' By the end, you're speaking to him as if he's five years old and you're tucking him in, your voice tender and broken, singing the first line of the lullaby he used to sing to you. You're saying goodbye to your father and your childhood simultaneously.

title: Breaking Point at the Water's Edge
instruction: You've just received devastating news and you've driven to a place that matters to you—a lake, ocean, river. You step into the cold water fully clothed, letting it shock your system. Begin by raging at the sky, screaming your anger and injustice, letting the physical cold and the emotional heat collide in your body. Access a real moment of powerlessness or fury from your life—let your voice be raw and uncontrolled. But as the cold water numbs your legs, let it also drain the rage, until you're just standing there, water around your knees, and the anger dissolves into exhausted, quiet sobbing. End with your body shaking—from cold or emotion, you can't tell anymore—whispering 'I can't do this' over and over.

title: The Weight of a Keepsake
instruction: You're an elderly man sitting on the edge of your bed in your carpeted bedroom, holding a small, worn object from your past — something you've kept hidden for years. You're talking to your adult grandchild who just found it. Start with a voice thick with shame, barely above a whisper, your eyes fixed on the floor. As you explain, allow a faint, dry tease to creep in — a joke at your own expense to deflect the pain — but your voice cracks and you trail off. Let the shame stay heavy, but let the tease show a fragile attempt to reconnect.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth they've never wanted to hear. Start with your voice controlled but trembling: 'I need you to just listen. For once, don't fix it, don't defend yourself, just hear me.' Your words come faster, more urgent: 'I was drowning right in front of you, and you never noticed because you were too busy being the victim of your own life.' The hurt breaks through now, raw and jagged: 'I was your child! I needed you to protect me, and instead I spent my childhood protecting you!' Your voice cracks, anger mixing with desperate sadness: 'Do you have any idea what it's like to be invisible to the one person who's supposed to see you?' By the end, you're quieter, exhausted, almost pleading: 'I just needed you to love me the way I needed to be loved. That's all I ever needed.' The silence that follows is heavy with years of unspoken pain.

title: Whispering to the Sleeping Lover You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside someone you love deeply, who's peacefully asleep, unaware you're about to leave forever—not because you want to, but because staying would destroy you both. Speak in whispers so soft they barely disturb the air. Start by listing tiny, perfect details you've memorized: the way they breathe, the small scar on their shoulder. Your voice keeps catching on tears you're trying not to shed. There's unbearable tenderness mixed with devastating certainty. You're apologizing for things they'll never hear, explaining in fragments why you have to go ('You deserve someone who isn't—'). Your breath becomes uneven, nearly silent sobs. End with the simplest, most heartbreaking truth, spoken so quietly it's almost just breath: 'Loving you was the most beautiful thing I'll ever do.' You allow yourself to touch their face once, then stop speaking entirely—the silence holding everything.

title: Whispering Your Truth to Someone Who's Sleeping
instruction: They're asleep beside you, and in this safe darkness, you can finally say what you've never been able to say to their waking face. Start with the smallest admission, your voice barely audible, testing the words in the air. 'I need to tell you something.' Your throat is tight because even though they can't hear you, these words still cost everything. As you confess—maybe it's a secret you've kept, maybe it's the depth of your love, maybe it's a goodbye you're preparing for—your voice wavers between tender and broken. There are long pauses where you can't speak at all, where you just breathe and try to continue. By the end, you might be crying silently, or your voice might have dissolved into something so soft it's almost not there. This isn't dramatic; it's the kind of vulnerability that only happens in the dark, when you're alone with your own heart.
inspired_by: Someone Telling You They Have a Terminal Diagnosis

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're holding someone back—physically or emotionally—trying to protect them from something terrible, and you're failing. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: 'I won't let them hurt you, I swear to God—' Your voice is full of certainty, strength, determination. But as reality sets in—you can't actually stop what's coming—that fierceness begins to crack. Your voice gets louder, more desperate, almost shouting your promises even as you know they're empty. Then it breaks completely. The strength dissolves into helpless, choking sobs. 'I'm so sorry, I'm so sorry,' becomes a devastated whisper. You go from warrior to shattered human, from protective rage to the terrible powerlessness of loving someone you cannot save. End in the hollow quiet of defeat.

title: Reading Your Late Parent's Unsent Letters to You
instruction: You're discovering letters your parent wrote but never sent—decades of them. They reveal a completely different person than the distant, critical figure you knew. Your voice begins reading aloud, tentative, confused. As the words sink in, you start laughing at an absurd childhood memory they cherished that you'd forgotten, but your laughter catches and transforms into tears because they never told you this. Your voice cycles through wonder, grief, anger at wasted time, and joy at discovering you were deeply loved in ways you never knew. You're reading their words while simultaneously talking to them, arguing with them, thanking them, mourning them all over again. End finding strange peace in this contradictory gift: heartbroken that it came too late, grateful it came at all, your voice holding both truths with equal tenderness.
inspired_by: Historical: Woman Discovers Her Child Is the Product of Rape She's Blocked

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: You're at the funeral of someone who made you promise not to cry, someone who wanted celebration instead of mourning. Begin trying to honor that wish—speaking with forced lightness, maybe even laughing at a memory, attempting joy. But the grief keeps cracking through, and you find yourself caught between honoring their wishes and honoring your own devastation. Your voice should oscillate wildly—laughing that turns to crying that turns back to laughter, gratitude that breaks into rage at being left behind, celebration that collapses into 'how dare you leave me.' This is the sound of someone trying to hold two impossible truths at once: that you're grateful they existed and shattered that they're gone. End in a strange place of peace mixed with chaos—maybe laughing through tears, finding genuine joy in a memory even as your heart is in pieces. This should feel contradictory, messy, painfully human, and utterly real.
inspired_by: The Soldier and the Enemy Spy

title: Whispering the Truth in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your sleeping partner, finally admitting out loud—barely above a whisper—that you're not sure you can do this anymore. Not the relationship necessarily, but life as you've been living it. Your voice is tender, almost reverent in its honesty, each word carefully placed like you're defusing a bomb. There's deep sadness here, but also strange relief in finally saying it. You're not asking for solutions; you're just letting the truth exist in the air between you and them, you and yourself, you and the darkness. Your breath should catch on certain words—the ones that cost the most to say. End with your voice dropping even quieter, a confession within the confession, something about still loving them, still loving life, but being so, so tired.
inspired_by: Therapist Hears Her Client Describe Her Own Trauma

title: The Intervention That Explodes
instruction: You're both standing in your shared childhood bedroom. One twin is staging an intervention—the other has been destroying themselves with addiction, risky behavior, pushing everyone away. Start with one voice trying to stay calm, loving, reading from notes about concern and treatment options. The other responds with mocking dismissal, cruel jokes, deflection. Then it erupts: the 'concerned' twin screams about watching you die slowly, about their own rage and terror and helplessness. The other twin screams back—about always being the broken one, the disappointing one, about wanting to disappear. The fury should be visceral, voices cracking and raw. Then suddenly, mid-rage, both collapse into sobbing—the anger was always just fear. End with both voices small, exhausted, one begging 'please don't leave me,' the other whispering 'I don't know how to stay.' Make it messy, real, the kind of fight where love and rage are inseparable.

title: The Rehearsal Before the Reckoning
instruction: You are about to confront your former lover who betrayed you, and you're terrified of falling apart. Begin by speaking aloud exactly what you plan to say to them, but infuse every word with sensory detail—imagine their exact expression, the room you'll be in, the light, how your voice will sound strong and clear, how your hands won't shake. As you rehearse, start trembling with anger and hurt, but keep layering in the vision of yourself standing tall, speaking your truth with devastating clarity. Feel your fear of crumbling transform into something else—not just imagined confidence, but real rage that steadies you. By the end, you're no longer rehearsing: you're ready, and you know with absolute certainty that you will not break.

title: The Unspoken Rules: Confronting the Parent Who Controlled You
instruction: You are finally confronting a parent who maintained control through subtle emotional manipulation—never violence, just carefully calibrated approval and withdrawal. Begin attempting to be reasonable, diplomatic, trying to make them understand. But as they deflect and minimize, your voice begins to shake with the rage of a lifetime of walking on eggshells. Build to an explosive moment where you finally say what you needed to say when you were small and powerless. Then—devastating shift—your anger collapses into the raw vulnerability of the child still inside you, voice breaking as you ask the question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I ever enough just as I was?' End in quiet, throat-caught grief, waiting for an answer you know may never come.

title: The Twist of Triumph
instruction: You are a teenage girl in a yoga class, holding a deep seated twist. At first, you feel a giddy ecstasy—your body is bending impossibly, and you whisper to yourself how amazing it feels to be so flexible, a secret thrill of superiority over the others. But the malice creeps in as you think of that girl who mocked you: you smile, imagining her watching you now. Yet the exhaustion is crushing your breath; your voice wavers as you strain to hold the pose, the pleasure fading into a gritty determination to finish without collapsing. Let the twist compress your lungs, making your words breathy and unsteady—your voice should crack with fatigue, but keep a flutter of dark satisfaction underneath.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Wedding Ring in Autumn
instruction: You're holding the engagement ring from someone you're about to leave, or who left you, or who died, or who you never got to marry. Begin by acknowledging aloud why you can't seem to put it down, why you picked it up in the first place, why you're stuck in this moment. Then start describing what you see—the ring itself, the light catching it, your hand holding it, where you are, what surrounds you. Let those observations pull you into the tangle of everything you feel: the love that was real, the loss that's devastating, the relief that might be there too, the anger, the tenderness, the gratitude for what was, the grief for what won't be. Your emotional state should be genuinely contradictory—laugh while crying, speak tenderly while expressing rage, feel grateful and furious in the same breath. End in a place of complex, messy, fully human truth that holds multiple feelings at once without resolving them into something simpler.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty starting the imaging process

title: Everything I Owe You, Everything I Can't Forgive
instruction: You are speaking to someone who saved your life—perhaps literally, perhaps by being there when no one else was—but who also deeply hurt you in ways you've never fully addressed. Begin by thanking them, expressing genuine gratitude for specific moments of rescue or grace. But as you speak, allow the hurt to surface—not instead of the gratitude, but alongside it, tangled with it. Feel the maddening coexistence of love and anger, of debt and betrayal. Let your voice carry both warmth and edge. Don't resolve the contradiction—live inside it. Perhaps you find yourself laughing and crying in the same breath, or speaking tenderly while your body holds tension. Allow these opposing currents to genuinely coexist in your instrument. End in a place of unresolved complexity, having expressed both truths fully without reconciling them into false simplicity.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Lover That You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you. You're leaving tomorrow and they don't know yet. You speak in the softest whisper, knowing they can't hear you, which makes you brave enough to be honest. Start with tender appreciation—the small things you'll miss, the way they laugh, how safe you've felt. Your voice should be barely audible, each word a caress. Then let the sadness come, the truth: you've been pretending for months that this isn't suffocating you, that you're not disappearing. Your throat tightens. You're not angry at them; you're grieving the version of yourself who could have been enough for this. End with a fragile confession of love mixed with the certainty that love isn't enough. You touch their face once. Your voice breaks on the word 'goodbye' that they'll never hear.
inspired_by: Admitting You Didn't Want This Baby

title: The Picnic Pause
instruction: You are at a family picnic surrounded by acquaintances you barely know. Your child is playing nearby. You try to make small talk, but your deep, gruff voice comes out stiff, and you fill silences with awkward chuckles. As the conversation stalls, you watch your child laughing with others, and a sudden, aching longing rises—for them to feel safe, for you to belong. The chatter fades. Your voice drops, losing its bravado, and you speak from that raw place, almost to yourself. The final words are quiet, cracked, and genuine.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Salt Water and Skin
instruction: You're standing in the ocean at sunset, fully clothed, letting waves crash against you. You've just scattered your best friend's ashes, and your body is wracked with contradictory sensations—the cold shock of water, the burn of salt in your eyes, the physical ache of loss meeting the sensual aliveness of being immersed in the sea. Start by trying to hold yourself together against the waves' assault. Then let your body respond—maybe you need to scream, maybe you surrender and sink into the water, maybe the cold becomes clarifying rather than punishing. Don't dictate what should happen. Trust your physical impulses and let sensation guide emotion. End in a state of raw, exhausted presence—transformed by physical experience into a different relationship with grief.

title: The Crown of the Level
instruction: You are a child, alone in your room at night, finally reaching the final boss of a game you've been stuck on for weeks. You grip the controller, knuckles white. Start by muttering to yourself with exhausted, tense determination. As you land a series of perfect hits, your voice erupts in raw, shaky pride—a spontaneous yell of triumph. Then, in the quiet that follows, you hear your parent's footsteps. Your voice drops to a breathless, giddy whisper as you rush to explain your victory, pride still warm and bright in your chest.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Lost in the Lights
instruction: You are a child, maybe 8 or 9, at your first big local festival. The music is pounding, people are dancing wildly all around you. You got separated from your mom a few minutes ago, and now you're lost in a sea of jumping, spinning bodies. You're crying and shouting for her, but you also feel the beat in your chest, and you're almost dancing involuntarily between sobs. A kind stranger notices you, crouches down, and offers you their hand. You take it, and as they lead you through the crowd, you sob with relief and gratitude, your voice still shaky and breathless, half-shouting over the music. Start in pure, panicked distress, then let the gratitude creep in as you realize you're safe, but keep the tears and the physical exhaustion in your voice until the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Scar I Never Saw
instruction: Late at night, your lover traces a scar on your body that you've had since childhood—one you've stopped noticing years ago. As their fingers move over it, they whisper questions: how did this happen, does it hurt, were you afraid? Their touch makes you feel the scar as if it's appeared for the first time. Begin in comfortable, sleepy intimacy, responding with automatic answers you've given before. But as they continue to touch it with such curious tenderness, you start actually feeling it again—the memory, the sensation, the moment it happened. Let yourself become confused, vulnerable, almost childlike as you rediscover this part of your body through their wonder. Your breathing should change, your words should become halting and uncertain. End in a place of exposed fragility, as if they've uncovered not just a scar but something in you that you'd forgotten existed.

title: The Secret Shame at 3 AM
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're alone, sitting in darkness, and something you've hidden for years—a terrible mistake, a deep shame, something you've never told anyone—is crushing you. Begin by whispering it aloud for the first time, so quietly you can barely hear yourself. Let your breath become shaky, irregular, as the weight of this secret presses down on you. Curl into yourself physically as you speak, voice trembling, breaking on certain words. Allow small, stifled sounds of pain to escape between words—not dramatic crying, but the kind of broken, muffled sounds people make when they're trying not to fall apart completely. Let these sounds grow from your chest, your belly, wordless expressions of shame and self-disgust. Gradually, find a way to forgive yourself in whispers, moving from self-hatred to tender self-compassion.
inspired_by: Sitting Primal Moan and Primitive Sounds

title: Mirror Argument
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just told you that you were never good enough as a parent. You start this scene defensive, hurt, listing all your inadequacies, agreeing with their assessment, shrinking under their judgment. But as the confrontation intensifies, you must excavate a deeper truth: you did the best you could with what you had, and that matters. Your voice begins apologetic, self-deprecating, almost begging for understanding. Let righteous clarity emerge—not anger at them, but fierce acknowledgment of your own worth despite your mistakes. End by standing in your full humanity: flawed, yes, but enough. The journey is from shame to hard-won self-recognition.
inspired_by: Actor's ego-state is in the way — feeling not good enough, too old, not talented enough

title: Bedside Confessions at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside your younger sibling's hospital bed after their suicide attempt. Speak softly, almost whisper, as if the room itself is fragile. Begin with those same old protective patterns - gently scolding, trying to fix things, offering solutions in a tender but still controlling way. But then pause. Really look at them. Let the weight of how close you came to losing them wash over you. Your voice should become even quieter, more hesitant. Confess the truth you've never said: that you became the bossy older sibling because when you were seven and they were four, you overheard your parents fighting about divorce, and you promised yourself you'd hold everything together. That every piece of unwanted advice was really just 'please don't leave me.' End with you asking their permission - voice shaking, barely audible - to learn how to be their sibling instead of their shield. Let the silence between words speak as much as the words themselves.

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You're alone, consumed by intense physical sensation - fever, migraine, aftermath of devastating news that hit your body like a blow. Begin in pure physical experience: groaning, gasping, your body overwhelmed. But as sensation peaks, let it crack open something emotional you've been holding rigid inside for months. The physical pain becomes a permission slip for emotional release. Every feeling you've 'kept together' - rage at someone who betrayed you, grief you haven't let yourself feel, fear you've been white-knuckling through - starts pouring out in raw sounds, words, half-words. This isn't performed; it's primal, messy, uncontrolled. Your body and emotions are inseparable. Curse, weep, rage, keen. Let sounds come that aren't language. As the storm passes, feel your body and heart simultaneously exhausted, emptied, strangely cleansed. End in quiet breathing, your system purged, vulnerable as a newborn, perhaps touching something like relief or fragile hope.

title: The Scent of Betrayal
instruction: You've just discovered your mother has been lying to you for twenty years about who your father is. You confront her in her bedroom, where she's folding laundry. Begin with barely controlled rage, but as you speak, start to physically experience the sensory environment of your childhood—the specific smell of her perfume that always meant safety, the texture of the clothes she's folding that you remember from being small, the sound of her voice that once soothed every fear. Let these sensory memories complicate your anger. Your body remembers love even as your mind reels from betrayal. Build the contradiction: notice the softness of an old sweater she's holding that you wore as a child, hear the particular creak of her rocking chair, see how her hands shake exactly like yours do. End not in pure anger but in a devastating confusion where you can't separate the mother who protected you from the mother who lied, where your senses tell you one truth and your mind tells you another.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone in the dark, bodies close but not touching. Begin speaking barely above a whisper, confessing something you've never told anyone—a fear, a desire, a moment of shame. At first, your voice is careful, testing whether it's safe to speak these words aloud. As you continue, let yourself become aware of their breathing, their specific scent, the particular warmth of their body near yours. Notice how they're listening—really receiving your words. This awareness should make you simultaneously more vulnerable and more brave. Your voice may tremble, but it should also grow slightly stronger, more grounded in the safety of this specific intimacy. By the end, you're not just confessing—you're offering yourself completely, your voice naked and undefended, but somehow peaceful. Let silence hold as much weight as words.

title: Inheritance Legacy Received
instruction: They left you something and it's more than objects. Your voice is holding the weight: 'I have my grandmother's watch.' Breathing is full of presence. Vocal tone is tender: 'I'm wearing it now. I can feel her wearing it too.' Physical: hand going to the watch. 'She lived through things I can't imagine and made it to me.' By the end, you're speaking to the past and future simultaneously: 'I'm the one keeping this alive now. This legacy is mine to carry forward.'

title: Behind the Mask
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a hospital waiting room, wearing a tight N95 respirator. A young male physical therapist approaches and kneels to check your pulse. You've felt a surprising, almost embarrassing spark of attraction since he first touched your hand. You start speaking with formal politeness, but the mask muffles your words, and each breath is a loud struggle. As you go on, your voice softens, drops into a husky, girlish pitch—the lust leaks through, defiantly playful. You adjust the mask strap, cough, then let the flirtation sneak into your tone, ending with a frank, breathless admission of your desire.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Tide Takes Everything
instruction: You are an elderly woman, a former sea captain’s wife, clinging to a buoy in choppy water after your small boat capsized. You’ve been treading water for ten minutes, and your arms are burning. You are talking to yourself, muttering complaints about the useless modern life jackets, the disrespect of the tide, the stupidity of this whole situation. Your voice bobs—sometimes clear, sometimes gurgling as a wave hits your mouth. Start with confusion: 'Where did the sun go?' as you squint against the glare, panting. Then let contempt take over: sneer at the water, at the boat rental company, at the seagulls watching you. By the end, you are exhausted but defiant, spitting out a bitter laugh between gasps as you realize you’ve been holding onto a lobster trap marker, not a proper buoy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing Through Novocaine at Your Best Friend's Funeral
instruction: You're at your best friend's funeral, face still numb from emergency dental work this morning, and you're giving the eulogy. You start trying to speak clearly about their death, but as memories flood back—their ridiculous jokes, the stupid pranks, the way they made everything absurd—you begin to laugh. Really laugh. With your numb mouth, with tears streaming, with drool you can't control. The laughter is genuine and inappropriate and exactly what they would have wanted, and it makes your speech completely unintelligible. Let yourself shift fluidly between laughing at a hilarious memory (slurred, imperfect, joyful) and crying because they're gone (garbled, broken, devastated). You're not trying to be dignified anymore—you're celebrating them the way they lived, messy and real. Include a moment where you nearly compose yourself, then lose it again. End with a kind of transcendent peace that holds both the laughter and the tears, the gratitude and the grief, speaking their name one last time with such love that it doesn't matter if anyone can understand the words.

title: The Last Hour at Bedside
instruction: You are sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—a grandparent, parent, or mentor—in their final hour. Begin by feeling every discomfort in your body: the hard chair, your exhaustion, the fear of what's coming, your desire to run away. Speak aloud everything you've been too afraid to say—your gratitude, your regrets, the memories that hurt, the love you've hidden behind daily life. Let your voice shake, let silences happen, let tears come or not come. As you continue, feel the weight lifting as you stop performing grief and simply exist in this moment with them. By the end, arrive at a place of pure presence—no longer afraid of the goodbye, just fully here, holding their hand, breathing together in whatever time remains.

title: Last Conversation Before the Journey You Can't Follow
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving on a journey they won't return from—a terminal diagnosis, a dangerous mission, a choice that separates you forever. You start trying to be brave, even smiling, telling them it's okay, you understand. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves. Your voice begins to fracture. You try to give them permission to go, to release them with grace, but your body betrays you—your breath catches, words dissolve into raw grief. By the end, you're no longer trying to be strong. You're simply present in your devastation, whispering the things you need them to know before they're gone. Let the transition from controlled courage to unguarded heartbreak happen organically, like a dam slowly cracking and then breaking completely.
inspired_by: Crying in Front of Someone Who Usually Sees You as Strong

title: The Sound of Rain at Her Wedding
instruction: You're standing in the rain outside the venue where your best friend is marrying someone else—someone you believe is wrong for her, but also, secretly, you're in love with her yourself. Feel the rain hitting your skin, your clothes growing heavy and cold with water. Hear the specific percussion of it—on your shoulders, on the ground, on the building behind you. Through the window, you can hear music, laughter. Notice the chill seeping into your bones, the way your breath makes small clouds in the cold air. Begin in bitter resentment: she chose this, she's making a mistake, you're angry at her for not seeing what's obvious. But as you stand there, soaked and shaking, let the sensory experience transform you—the cleansing quality of the rain, the distant sound of her joy. Move toward a complex acceptance that contains grief and genuine happiness for her, anger at yourself and love for her, the pain of letting go braided with gratitude for having known her at all. End finding a strange peace in the rain, blessing her even as you break.

title: The Last Voicemail Before the Flight
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for someone you love before boarding a plane you know won't land safely. You have insider information—a credible threat, a mechanical issue you overheard, something that makes you certain. Start with that same eerie calm, that dissociative flatness as you give practical instructions about bank accounts and where you keep important documents. Your voice is steady, almost businesslike, as if you're dictating a grocery list. But slowly, the reality of what you're doing begins to crack through. The flatness wavers. Your breath catches. By the end, you're no longer detached—you're desperately, vulnerably human, trying to say everything that matters in seconds you don't have. The transformation from numb distance to raw, present terror and love must feel like watching ice shatter.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Bottle Over You
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent—the one who was always just drunk enough to miss every important moment of your childhood. Start with controlled anger, almost lawyer-like as you list the specific memories: the recital they missed, the night you waited for them to pick you up from school until dark, your college graduation where their seat stayed empty. Your voice is steady, rehearsed even—you've practiced this. But as you speak, something shifts. Under the anger is the child who kept hoping, kept believing they'd change, kept setting the table for two even when you knew they wouldn't show. Let your voice crack not with rage but with the devastating vulnerability of that abandoned child. End not with fury but with exhausted, tender grief—mourning not what they did, but the parent-child relationship that never got to exist. Let them hear the love that's still there underneath all the pain, which somehow makes it even more heartbreaking.
inspired_by: Reading Erotica Aloud While Trying to Stay Composed

title: Forgetting Her Face
instruction: You're speaking to your therapist, voice barely above a whisper, confessing something that fills you with shame: you can't remember your late wife's face anymore without looking at photos. Begin hesitant, almost apologetic - the voice of someone afraid to speak this truth aloud because saying it makes it real. 'It's been three years and I... I tried to picture her this morning and I couldn't.' Let your voice catch with each admission. Move from shame to tender devastation as you describe the small details you DO remember - how her hand felt in yours, the sound of her breathing beside you at night. End with a quiet, devastating acceptance mixed with profound sadness: 'Maybe this is what moving forward means. Maybe I'm not supposed to hold on so tight.' Let the last words be almost a question, seeking permission to let go.
inspired_by: Child Discovering Death for the First Time

title: Final Phone Call from the Space Station: Disbelief Becoming Acceptance
instruction: You're an astronaut on a failing space station, making your last call to your child on Earth before life support fails. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them, your voice bright but trembling as you describe the stars outside your window. Midway through, you can no longer maintain the facade—your voice cracks as you realize this is truly goodbye, and you need to say everything that matters in minutes. Move from that desperate urgency into something quieter, more sacred: you're teaching them how to remember you, your voice becoming tender and deliberate, each word chosen like a gift. End in a place of devastating peace, where your fear transforms into fierce love, your voice steady but thick with unshed tears as you tell them exactly who they are and how proud you are. Let silence do some of the work—the pauses where you're memorizing their breathing.
inspired_by: Leaving a Cult: Disorientation Becoming Orientation

title: The Melting Song
instruction: You're a child who has been playing in the bath until your fingers are prunes, and you're exhausted, but you're also singing a silly made-up song to your reflection on the wet tiles. Start with pure, fizzy amusement as you giggle at your own funny face and the echo of your voice bouncing around you, but let the fatigue creep in through your yawning and the growing weight of your eyelids. Midway, you notice the shadow of your parent in the doorway and feel a sleepy, gentle infatuation for them, your voice softening and slowing down. End with a drowsy, muffled whisper, your cheek against the side of the tub, the song dissolving into a tired, happy sigh as you realize you're done.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Infatuation (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Guardian's Collapse: Fierce Love Meets Absolute Helplessness
instruction: You have just learned that someone under your protection—your child, younger sibling, or student—has been harmed, and you weren't there to prevent it. Begin with explosive, volcanic rage directed at whoever is responsible, your voice a weapon, fierce and uncontrolled. But mid-sentence, the rage cracks and pivots—suddenly you're turning that fury inward, voice breaking as you castigate yourself with devastating self-blame. Your protective instincts are at war with your complete helplessness. Alternate between roaring promises of retribution and whispered, choking sobs of "I should have known, I should have protected you." End in a state of shattered desperation—still fierce in your love but undone by your powerlessness. Let the performance be volcanic and vulnerable simultaneously, switching between them without warning, like someone coming apart at the seams.
inspired_by: The Fairy and the Troll Under the Bridge

title: The Cradle of My Grandson
instruction: You are an elderly man in a late-term pregnancy, sitting in a worn armchair that lists to one side. Your diaphragm is compressed, making every word a gentle struggle for air. A slight surprise colors your voice as you feel the baby shift inside you — a flutter you didn't expect.
