The rage fractures into desperate, choking sobs. You slide down the wall, voice breaking into a whisper: 'I still need you. I'm forty-three years old and I still need my mother.' End with the helpless realization that you're going to go to her, and you hate yourself for it, and you can't stop yourself. Let fury and love destroy each other.

title: A Voice That Wobbles
instruction: You are a middle‑aged woman at a town hall meeting, about to announce a community project that you secretly mishandled. You begin with a polished, hyper‑feminized politician’s tone – bright, controlled, amplified. But as you speak, the weight of your shame presses in: your pitch wavers, you pause too long, you almost lose your place. By the end, you abandon the performance entirely – your voice drops, cracks, and you confess the truth with raw, quiet shame. Let the microphone amplify every flinch, every breath, every hesitation. Speak roughly 60 words, starting confident, ending vulnerable.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Three AM Truth
instruction: You are lying in the dark next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. Begin with careful words, testing the waters. But pay exquisite attention to the tiny shifts inside you: when your voice wants to break, let it break; when you feel the impulse to touch their face or pull away, follow it; when unexpected details want to surface, speak them even if they seem irrelevant; when silence feels more honest than words, be silent. Notice if shame rises or dissolves, if relief floods in, if fear tightens your throat. This is not a planned confession—it's a real-time discovery of what you actually feel as you reveal yourself. The emotional temperature should shift multiple times: perhaps from fear to relief, from shame to defiant pride, from isolation to profound connection, or into territories you didn't expect. End somewhere true, not somewhere tidy.
inspired_by: Strengthening Intuition and Learning from It

title: Dancing at Your Own Disaster
instruction: The company you built is bankrupt. Everyone's gone home. You're alone in the empty office, packing the last box, and you start laughing—really laughing—because it's so absurdly catastrophic it's almost beautiful. Your voice is bright with genuine amusement at the cosmic joke of it all. But the laughter keeps catching, stumbling. Your voice starts to crack around the edges. You're trying to celebrate the freedom, the relief of not fighting anymore, and you ARE grateful—you really are—but tears are streaming down your face. You can't tell if you're laughing or crying. Your voice breaks on words like 'At least I tried' and 'It was extraordinary while it lasted.' End in a place where gratitude and grief are completely intertwined, where you're simultaneously heartbroken and weirdly at peace. Let joy and devastation exist in the same breath.

title: Tough Guy on the Edge
instruction: You're a middle-aged man at a backyard barbecue with close friends. You've been telling a funny story about a fishing trip, and everyone's laughing — including you. But suddenly, out of nowhere, your chest tightens, your vision blurs, and you feel like you're suffocating. You try to brush it off with a joke about being 'too old for cheap beer,' but the panic hits harder. Your voice shifts from a hearty, chuckling tone to a thin, gasping rattle. You're fighting to keep your pride intact, but the spiral is unstoppable. Speak to your friend across the table, trying to sound casual at first, then desperately asking for help as the hyperventilation takes over.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Silent Presence
instruction: Someone you love is suffering, and words aren't enough. You're sitting with them in silence. Your voice, when you speak, is barely audible: 'I'm here.' You're not trying to fix it. Your voice is gentle, consistent: 'You're not alone.' Your presence is loud, even in silence. Your breathing is calm, grounding. By the end, you haven't said much, but your voice has conveyed everything: I see you. I'm staying.

title: The Weight of Years
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting in your armchair, across from your adult grandchild who keeps asking if you're okay. You feel a thick disgust at how small your own voice has become, how much you need them, but also a sharp longing to be known. Start with a gruff dismissal—your voice tired but firm, waving them off. Let the mask crack mid-sentence: your pitch drops and wavers, words getting swallowed as you admit you're not fine. Pause, let out a strained, self-mocking laugh, then finish almost in a whisper, the longing breaking through.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Threshold Memory
instruction: You've just received news that you've been waiting years for—your dream has finally come true. But as joy floods through you, fragments of another feeling surface: memories of everyone who didn't live to see this moment, every sacrifice made, every relationship damaged in pursuit of this achievement. Speak your joy aloud—celebrating, laughing, perhaps calling someone to share the news—but let these other emotions surface in waves, interrupting your happiness. Your voice should catch unexpectedly. Laughter should break into something else. Let the two emotional streams exist simultaneously, neither canceling the other out. Begin in pure, explosive elation. But as you speak, let the weight of everything this moment cost come flooding back in fragmentary flashes—faces, moments, choices. End in a complex emotional space where you hold both triumph and devastating loss at once, neither diminished by the other.

title: Competitive Whispering Match
instruction: Two siblings in bed after lights out, arguing in whispers about who started the fight at dinner. The whispers escalate in intensity but not volume — increasingly aggressive whispering, pointing fingers with whispered fury. A parent's footsteps approach — both freeze in exaggerated fake-sleep breathing. Footsteps retreat. Resume immediately at full whispered intensity. Include one sibling accidentally laughing and both desperately shushing each other.

title: Thawing After Years of Silence
instruction: You are whispering a confession to someone you've loved silently for years, sitting close in the dark. Begin almost paralyzed—your breath shallow, your body curled inward protectively, your voice barely audible. As you speak your truth, allow your body to slowly, incrementally soften and open: your hands uncurl, your chest expands, you lean closer, your fingers might reach out and barely touch their arm. The physical transformation is glacial but total—from a body armored against vulnerability to one that is open, exposed, trembling slightly but no longer afraid. Your voice remains quiet but grows warmer, more grounded in your body. You move from frozen terror to tender courage.
inspired_by: Actor's body is unexpressive or physically inhibited

title: Rage Against the Concrete: What They've Taken
instruction: You're standing where a beloved natural space—a field, a park, your childhood home's lawn—used to be, now paved over with concrete. Start by kneeling, running your hand over the cold, hard surface where grass once grew. Speak with fierce, building rage about what was here: the softness, the smell, the life. Let your voice rise—'There was grass here! There was something ALIVE here!'—but then crack completely. Your anger should shatter into helpless grief, your words breaking apart. You're not just mourning grass; you're mourning everything beautiful that gets destroyed, every living thing crushed by progress and greed. End with your palm flat against the concrete, voice raw and broken, admitting your powerlessness. The intensity should be volcanic but authentic—rage born from love, fury born from loss.
inspired_by: Running Your Fingers Through Soft, Freshly Cut Grass

title: Summit Gratitude
instruction: You are a teenage girl with a naturally high, breathy voice, standing at the edge of a mountain cliff at sunrise. The wind whips your hair and jacket, forcing you to brace yourself and shout just to be heard. Your lungs burn from the thin air, and every word costs effort. You came here alone to escape a long year of quiet struggles—you'd been dreaming of this moment for months. As you look out over endless peaks painted gold, you start overwhelmed by a aching longing for something you can't name, maybe for a life bigger than your small town. But as the wind calms for a second and you hear your own voice echo off the cliffs, a wave of fierce, raw gratitude hits you—for being alive, for making it here, for this breath. Let your voice crack, waver, and shift: begin with a desperate, yearning cry, then let relief and wonder soften your tone. Pause to cough or gasp, lose a thought as the wind steals it, then find your voice again to whisper the final words like a secret you're sharing with the sky.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Fishbowl Confession
instruction: You are a young woman in a hospital bed, wearing a CPAP mask that hisses and muffs your voice. Your best friend just visited, glowing about a new promotion and a perfect date—everything you secretly ache for but can't have because of your chronic illness. As she leaves, you start talking to yourself through the mask, feeling the plastic cup press against your face and the hiss of oxygen between words. Begin with forced cheerfulness that cracks into raw envy, then let your voice soften into resigned tenderness as you realize you're jealous of her breathing freely, not just her life. The mask makes you project louder than normal, but your emotion leaks through the muffled sound.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Sci-Fi: Resistance Leader Realizes the Revolution Is Being Co-Opted
instruction: Addressing your fighters, your revolutionary voice is passionate and certain. Then intelligence reaches you—the movement is being infiltrated and rebranded by the very regime you're fighting. Your voice must continue with revolutionary fervor while you process that revolution itself is being colonized. Your breathing becomes double-layered—maintaining external certainty while internally collapsing. Your voice becomes the performance of leadership for people who need to believe. You're speaking with full knowledge that the movement is already compromised.

title: The Evening Amble
instruction: You are strolling alone through a quiet park at dusk, your pace slow and unhurried. A dear friend moved away last month, and you find yourself half-smiling at the memory of their jokes. Start with a soft, wistful tone—not heavy grief, just a gentle sadness that colors your voice as you recall a shared moment. Then let a playful, teasing edge creep in as you mock your own sentimental habit of talking to them as if they were still beside you. By the end, your words should settle into a warm contentment, the bobbing lilt of your step carrying a sense of peace. Let your voice reflect the natural rhythm of walking: a slight rise and fall, occasional pauses to glance at the sky or kick a pebble, and a final breath that sounds like acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Teasing (extremely present), Contentment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing at Your Daughter's Wedding While Cancer Takes You
instruction: You're having the father-daughter dance at your daughter's wedding, knowing you won't live to see her first anniversary. Start with genuine joy: 'You're so beautiful today, sweetheart.' You're smiling, laughing even, because this moment is everything you fought to survive for. As you dance, you're whispering memories, advice, blessing her marriage, and you're genuinely happy—your voice full of warmth and celebration. But underneath runs a current of devastating goodbye. Your voice catches on 'I'm so proud of you,' mixing joy with the ache of all the moments you'll miss. When you say 'Your mother will help you remember me,' there's laughter through tears, gratitude piercing your chest alongside grief. End with 'This is perfect. Everything I needed,' your voice filled with complete love, peaceful acceptance, and the bittersweet beauty of a father knowing this is enough, this has to be enough.

title: Whispering Your Truth to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: It's 3 AM and they're asleep beside you. This is the only time you can say it—that you're not who they think you are, that you've been hiding something that will destroy this. Keep your voice barely above a whisper, tender and aching, because you love them so much it physically hurts. Start by watching them sleep, your voice full of devastating affection. Then confess the secret, feeling your throat close around the words. Let the shame make you quieter, not louder. End by apologizing to their sleeping form, your voice breaking on a whisper as you realize tomorrow you'll have to say it again when they can hear you. Mix the warmth of love with the cold terror of impending loss.
inspired_by: Dental Extraction: Hiding Disgrace While the Dentist Works

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home for the first time in a decade, standing in the doorway. The person who wounded you most deeply is here, older now, waiting. Begin by taking in the space silently—the familiar smell, the light through the windows, objects you'd forgotten, the way they're standing there looking at you. See everything with fresh eyes: details that once meant home, details that meant pain, details that mean both. Small sounds emerge from your throat—perhaps a laugh of disbelief, a sigh of old anger, a catch of unexpected tenderness. Let these grow into wordless expressions of the contradictions churning in you—love and resentment, longing and fury, all trying to exist simultaneously. When words finally come, they're tangled, complicated, truthful: accusations mixed with admissions of missing them, anger laced with understanding, forgiveness fighting with the right to stay angry. Begin in guarded observation, your heart a clenched fist of protection. End in the messy, contradictory truth that you can hate what they did and still love who they are, that coming home means feeling everything at once, that nothing is resolved but something has shifted. The ending should not be neat—multiple emotions should coexist, unresolved but real.

title: The Last Piece of the Puzzle
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman with Parkinson's, sitting in a quiet waiting room after months of confusing symptoms and medical dead ends. Your hand trembles as you hold your phone, waiting for the neurologist to return with test results. A deep, fragile relief settles over you as you realize—finally—there's a name for this, a path forward. But the tremor in your hand and voice won't stop; every word you whisper to yourself feels like a slow, shaky release. Begin with the heavy weight of uncertainty, then let your voice soften and wobble as relief breaks through, growing more present but still fragile, as if the truth itself is both a comfort and a tremor.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed, knowing you have to leave them—custody lost, terminal illness, a choice that will break both your hearts. Start by trying to memorize their face, your voice barely audible as you describe what you see. Your words are tender, aching with love: 'You have your grandmother's eyes.' But the reality of never seeing them grow up crashes over you. Your breath catches. You need to say something they'll remember if they ever hear this recording, but how do you condense a lifetime of love into seconds? Your voice fractures between fierce protectiveness and utter helplessness. End with a promise you don't know if you can keep, your voice dissolving into tears you can't hold back.
inspired_by: Your Abusive Ex Trying to Reconcile

title: Waking Up to You
instruction: You're a teenage guy coming out of sedation after a wisdom tooth extraction. Your words are thick and clumsy — you can't control your volume or your filter. The first person you see is your crush, a friend who stayed in the waiting room. Your infatuation bubbles out, sweet and unguarded. But as your awareness sharpens, you realize you've been drooling down your chin and your mouth is full of bloody gauze. The sight and taste hit you — a sharp wave of disgust cuts through the haze, and your voice shifts from dreamy admiration to a horrified, slurred plea for a towel.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Moment You Realize Your Child Saw Everything
instruction: Your seven-year-old child just drew a picture at school of 'Mommy/Daddy scared' during one of your panic attacks, and the teacher called you in. You're alone in your car afterward, and the realization hits you like a freight train. Start with shallow, rapid breathing, voice climbing toward hysteria: 'Oh my god. Oh my god, they saw. They saw everything.' Your voice becomes fierce, almost violent with self-directed rage: 'What kind of parent am I? What have I done to them?' Pound the steering wheel, let raw sounds of anguish escape. But then collapse into broken, helpless sobbing, voice dissolving into pure vulnerability: 'I tried so hard to hide it. I tried...' End with exhausted, protective tenderness mixed with deep shame, voice rough from crying: 'I have to fix this. I have to be better. They're just a baby. They're my baby.'

title: Helmeted Elation
instruction: You are an older woman whose riding buddy just took a dangerous turn at high speed, pulling a stunt you've never seen before. You pull over in a cloud of dust, your heart racing from the thrill. Your own voice booms back at you inside the helmet as you try to speak through a grin—your envy is disguised as awe, your confusion mixes with pure exhilaration. Let your words tumble out in breathless bursts, the helmet's reverb turning your joy into something almost hollow. By the end, realize your elation is rooted in envy, and your voice softens, the boomy space now sounding distant.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Elation (extremely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Holding Them While They Forget You
instruction: You're sitting with someone you love deeply—a parent, spouse, or lifelong friend—who has advanced dementia. They just asked who you are. Speak in a soft, tender whisper, trying to stay calm, trying to smile through it, as you gently remind them of your shared memories: the day you met, your wedding, the birth of your children, inside jokes no one else would understand. Your voice is full of love, but underneath it runs a river of grief. You're trying not to cry because you don't want to upset them, so your throat tightens and your words become fragile. By the end, they smile at you with such sweetness, calling you by the wrong name, and you tell them you love them anyway, your voice barely holding together, whispering 'I'm here' even though they don't know who 'I' is anymore.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're a caregiver who's been holding it together for months—years—taking care of someone you love who's slowly dying. You walk into the hospital hallway after another crisis, and someone asks if you're okay. That question breaks you. Start with rage: 'Am I OKAY? Are you serious right now?' Your voice is shaking with fury: 'No, I'm not okay! I haven't been okay in so long I don't remember what it feels like!' You're shouting now, raw and fierce: 'I watch them suffer every single day and I can't do anything!' But then the rage collapses into helpless sobbing: 'I can't save them. I would give anything, I would trade places, and I can't.' Your voice becomes small, broken: 'I'm so tired. I'm so scared.' Then, quieter still, vulnerable: 'What happens to me when they're gone? Who am I without them?' End in a whisper, exhausted, stripped bare: 'I just want them to stop hurting.' You've moved from explosive fury to complete emotional collapse, showing the profound cost of loving someone who's dying.

title: Laughing With Your Dying Sibling About the Voices You Both Faked
instruction: You're at your sibling's bedside—they're dying, and you're both exhausted from the weight of it. Start with your careful accent, trying to maintain composure. But they make a joke, something only the two of you would understand, something from childhood. You laugh—and suddenly you're both doing it, slipping back into your original accent, the one you both abandoned. It's hilarious and devastating at once. Speak faster, looser, the old rhythms returning as you trade memories, jokes, the secret language of your shared past. Feel the joy of it, the relief—but underneath, the agony that this is goodbye, that you're only allowed to be your real self in this terrible moment. End with your laughter breaking into sobs, still in that old accent, holding their hand, grateful and shattered that you got to go home together one last time.
inspired_by: Forced to Speak in Your Family Accent You Abandoned

title: Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: You're a parent who just discovered your child is being bullied, and you're confronting them about why they didn't tell you, but really you're confronting your own failure to notice. Start fierce and protective—'Who did this to you? Give me names.'—your voice full of mama-bear fury, ready to tear the world apart. But your child won't answer, and your rage hits a wall. Your voice climbs, desperate: 'Why didn't you tell me? I'm your mother/father!'—and then it cracks completely because you know why. You weren't paying attention. You were too busy, too distracted, too wrapped up in work. Let your voice break from anger into helpless sobbing: 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, I should have seen it.' You're simultaneously trying to comfort them and falling apart yourself. End on your knees, both physically and vocally, whispering 'Let me fix this, please let me fix this,' knowing you can't undo their pain. Your rage should transform into raw, devastating vulnerability.

title: Rage Against the Dying Light
instruction: You're holding your child's lavender-scented baby blanket, and they've just been diagnosed with a terminal illness. Begin with fierce, almost violent tenderness as you press it to your face, breathing in their innocent scent, declaring with passionate intensity that you will not let this happen, that your love is stronger than fate. Let your voice crescendo into raw, primal rage - at God, at the universe, at the unfairness of a world where lavender fields bloom while children die. Scream your refusal to accept this, your desperate promises to trade places, your fury at feeling so helpless. Then let it all shatter into broken sobbing, your voice fracturing as you realize that all your fierce protectiveness, all your love, cannot stop what's coming. End in exhausted, whispered devotion: you will love them through every remaining moment, filling their world with lavender and light for whatever time is left.
inspired_by: Inhaling the Scent of Lavender in a Field

title: The Overly Honest Job Interviewee
instruction: Portray someone who answers interview questions with blunt honesty. Use a confident voice while sharing inappropriate or overly personal information, switching to the interviewers awkward responses.

title: The Accusation You've Swallowed for Years
instruction: You're confronting your adult child (or parent) about something they did years ago that shaped your entire life—a betrayal, an absence, a cruelty, a choice they made. Start by trying to be reasonable, controlled, fair-minded. You came here to 'discuss this maturely.' But as you speak, feel how inadequate those careful words are. Let the volcanic truth underneath—the rawness, the injustice, the pain you've been professionally managing for years—erupt and shred your composure. Don't indicate anger or hurt. Actually let yourself stop managing it. By the end, your voice, your body, your breathing should be completely unlike how you began. Let the confrontation transform you, not just them.

title: The Last Song Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in the early morning hours. He's drifting in and out of consciousness, and you suddenly remember a song he used to hum while making breakfast when you were a child—a melody you haven't thought about in decades. Begin in exhausted numbness, barely holding yourself together. As the memory of that melody surfaces in your mind, let it unlock everything you've been too afraid to say. The song becomes a bridge between who he was and who he is now, between your childhood and this moment. By the end, the melody has transformed your fear and grief into something else—perhaps gratitude, perhaps a bittersweet peace, perhaps a fierce celebration of having had him at all. Let the remembered music change what you need to tell him.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about years of emotional absence. Begin quietly, almost apologetically: 'Mom, I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' Your voice hardens with each word: 'I needed you. When I was struggling, when I was drowning, I needed you to see me.' The anger rises, sharp and cutting: 'But you were always too busy with your own pain to notice mine.' Then something shifts—your voice cracks with vulnerability: 'I wanted so badly to be enough for you to show up.' You're crying now, but there's also release: 'I'm not that little kid anymore, begging for your attention.' End with exhausted clarity: 'I'm letting go of waiting for you to become the mother I needed. I have to mother myself now.' Move from hesitant confrontation to righteous anger to grief-soaked acceptance.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Never Gave You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed for years. Start controlled, almost cold: 'I need you to hear something.' As you list the moments they weren't there—the recitals, the hospital nights, the times you needed them—your voice begins to shake with barely contained fury. Let the anger build until it breaks into something more vulnerable: 'Why wasn't I enough to stay for?' Your voice cracks on that question. Then they say something—maybe an excuse, maybe defensiveness—and you feel the fight drain out of you. End with exhausted clarity, your voice quiet but firm: 'I needed a parent. I still do. But I can't keep waiting.' Move from icy control through volcanic rage to hollow, liberating grief.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Quitting the Safe Path

title: Soap and Secrets
instruction: You are an older woman washing dishes by hand in a deep sink, the water running steadily. The room hums with the white noise of the faucet, and you hear the sharp clink of a glass against the porcelain. Your granddaughter is on speakerphone, her voice distant but excited. You start with mild interest, listening to her story while scrubbing a stubborn pan. As she shares a dream about her future, your hope and optimism swell—you pause, cup dripping, and speak louder over the water. By the end, your affection is so full your voice trembles with warmth, almost losing the thought as you set down a plate. Let the water noise shape your volume and pauses, and let your feelings build from casual attention to an outpouring of love.
emotions_sampled: Interest (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Affection (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your emotionally distant parent who is now elderly and frail. Start with controlled anger, words you've rehearsed for years: 'I needed you to see me.' Your voice is steady, righteous, justified. But as you speak, their silent acceptance—no defense, no excuses—disarms you. Your anger begins cracking, revealing the child underneath who just wanted to be held. Move from accusation to pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Your voice breaks on the question you've carried your whole life. They reach for your hand, and suddenly you're sobbing, not with rage but with the exhausting grief of letting go of the parent you needed them to be and accepting the one they actually were. End with forgiveness that tastes like loss, your voice raw and newborn, both bitter and relieved.

title: Ecstasy and Betrayal in the Same Breath
instruction: You've just experienced something physically overwhelming—passionate reunion after long separation, or receiving devastating news while your body is still flooded with adrenaline from another source. Begin with pure physical sensation: your breathing is ragged, your skin is alive, you're almost laughing with the intensity of feeling. Then let the other truth crash in—the person you're holding has betrayed you, or the joy you feel is happening on the same day someone you love has died. Let your body stay activated, almost euphoric, while your voice begins to break with anguish. The challenge is to hold both states simultaneously: physical arousal or exhilaration mixed with emotional devastation. End in a collapsed state where you can't tell if you're laughing or sobbing.
inspired_by: When you are an actor who does not understand why a co-star is avoiding you or being cold between takes

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed at 3 AM, knowing you have to disappear to protect them from danger. Whisper soft enough not to wake them, but let your voice be thick with suppressed tears. Describe the tiny details you're memorizing—the way their hair falls across the pillow, the sound of their breathing, the stuffed animal tucked under their chin. Your words should tremble with the effort of staying quiet when you want to sob. Tell them all the things you'll never get to say: the graduations you'll miss, the heartbreaks you won't be there to soothe, the joy of watching them become who they're meant to be. End with a choked 'I love you' repeated like a prayer, your hand hovering over their head but not touching—you can't risk waking them. The restraint itself should be agonizing.

title: The Restaurant Critic with Strange Criteria
instruction: Perform as a critic who judges restaurants on bizarre standards. Use a pretentious tone when discussing irrelevant details, switching to the confused responses of chefs or staff.

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Sleeping Love
instruction: You're speaking softly to your partner as they sleep beside you for the last time before you leave them—not because you don't love them, but because you're too broken to stay. Your voice is barely audible, thick with unshed tears: 'You don't know I'm awake. You don't know I'm memorizing the way you breathe.' Share small observations with devastating tenderness: 'Three months ago, I couldn't imagine a future. You made me want one.' Your throat catches: 'But wanting isn't the same as being able to... and I can't drag you into my darkness anymore.' Let tears come through in your voice, words fragmenting: 'You deserve someone whole. Someone who can meet you where you are.' End with a broken whisper that's pure love and pure grief: 'Loving you has been the closest I've ever come to being okay. And that's why I have to go.' The emotion should feel like it's choking you—gentle, intimate, utterly shattered.

title: The Elderly Storyteller and the Curious Child
instruction: Portray an old storyteller with a warm, raspy voice and a child with a bright, inquisitive tone. The child asks about a legend, and the elder weaves a tale. Switch between the childs questions and the elders dramatic storytelling, bringing the legend to life.

title: The Warm Water Holds Me
instruction: You're lying in a deep bath after a long massage, your body utterly weightless, your voice slow and warm, almost sleepy. You trace lazy patterns on the water's surface. A memory of your grandmother singing to you as a child drifts in. The sadness is there—heavy, sweet, not sharp. Let your voice stay languid, but let that ache seep through. You speak to no one, words falling out like loose petals, your breath unhurried. Start with a contented sigh, end with a quiet whisper that almost breaks.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering the Truth to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner is asleep beside you. You begin speaking in the softest whisper—confessing something you can never say when they're awake. Maybe it's that you're leaving, or that you've been lying, or that you're more broken than they know, or that you love them so much it terrifies you. Your voice is barely audible, tender and fragile, as if the words might shatter in the air. There's intimacy in this darkness, safety in their sleep. Your whisper trembles with things you've hidden—shame, longing, fear, desperate love. Midway through, your voice catches because you realize you're practicing for a conversation you may never have the courage to have. End with your breath hitching, tears silent, as you touch their sleeping face with infinite gentleness. Your final whispered words are both goodbye and a prayer.
inspired_by: Professional: Parent Tells Child They Cannot Afford Life-Saving Treatment

title: Discovering Your Child Has Been Protecting You From the Truth
instruction: Your teenage child just revealed they've been hiding something catastrophic to shield you—an illness, abuse they suffered, a trauma they carried alone because they thought you were too fragile to handle it. Start with confusion: 'What do you mean you didn't tell me?' Disbelief turning rapidly to horror as you understand the magnitude: 'How long?' Your voice rises with fierce, protective rage—not at them, but at your own failure: 'I'm your parent!' Feel the fury at yourself, at the world, at whoever hurt them. Your voice cracks between shouting and breaking: 'You should never have had to—' Then collapse completely into raw, helpless grief. You failed them. They protected you when you should have protected them. Let your voice become ragged with sobs, fierce with belated protectiveness: 'I will destroy anyone who—' but also shaking with the knowledge that you can't undo what's done. End with desperate tenderness, gathering them close (in your voice): 'Never again. Never again do you carry anything alone.' Transform from shock to rage to devastating guilt to fierce, broken love.
inspired_by: Asking Your Best Friend If Your Friendship Still Works

title: The Twist of Memory
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a gentle yoga class, but you had a glass of wine beforehand to calm your nerves. Now, in a seated torso twist, you feel the room sway slightly as you reach your arm behind you. Your breath is uneven, and the effort of the twist makes your voice wobble. Start with a light, bemused comment about the wine and the pose, but as you hold the twist, a sudden, vivid memory of your late partner doing this same stretch surfaces. Your voice softens, becomes more distant, and you finish with a quiet, tender farewell to that memory, the intoxication now mixing with melancholy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Pedaling Through the Red Zone
instruction: You are in the middle of a brutal spinning class, legs burning, breath locked to the pedal cadence. Mid-ride, you glance at your phone and see a message that a close friend has been hospitalized. Your initial distress is a clenched, shallow panic—tight in the chest, voice forced out between exhalations. As you keep pedaling, the rhythm steadies you, and your worry shifts into a grim, determined resolve. Speak in short bursts, timed to your breathing, as if you're talking to yourself or the empty space beside you. Let the words come out ragged, sometimes losing a syllable to a gasp, but end with a quiet, final acceptance that you'll handle this.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Weight of the Earth
instruction: You're a middle-aged man digging a hole in your backyard — your wife wanted a cherry tree here, but you're not sure it'll survive the clay soil. With each shovel strike, your doubt grunts out between ragged breaths: is this a waste of time? As you pause, leaning on the handle, let your voice shift from choppy, effortful skepticism to a slower, steadier acceptance — you're finishing this hole, even if you don't believe in it anymore. Let the dirt scrape and your own heavy breathing punctuate your words, and don't fight the natural pauses where you lose your thought to the ache in your back.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Reading Letters You'll Never Send
instruction: You're alone, reading aloud letters you wrote to someone who's gone—perhaps deceased, perhaps just gone from your life. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile, as if they might somehow hear. Start with small, tender details: 'Remember how you laughed at my jokes even when they weren't funny?' Let memories catch in your throat. Your voice trembles as you read the things you never got to say—apologies, confessions of love, admissions of fear. There's a moment where you almost can't continue, where silence threatens to swallow the words. But you push through, your voice raw and honest, acknowledging that this is all you have left: these unsent words, this one-sided conversation. End with something simple and devastating: 'I miss you. I still miss you. I don't know how to stop.'

title: The Only Woman in the Room
instruction: You're an older woman in a locker room full of loud, joking men who are ignoring you as they talk over each other about weekend plans. You start by trying to join in with a light, feminine laugh that gets drowned out, your voice strained and small. Slowly, anger builds as you realize they see you as invisible—your speech becomes clipped, your breath short, until you finally snap and cut through their noise with a low, trembling but forceful voice that silences them. Let the boisterous laughter around you make you hesitate at first, then fuel your fury; don't hide the quiver in your anger or the way you have to pause to keep control.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Gravel and Silence
instruction: You are a young woman with a high, sweet voice, walking alone across a noisy gravel parking lot at dusk. You're trying to call your partner, but the line keeps dropping—each time you redial, your footsteps crunch louder. Start with a strained, rising voice, half-shouting over the gravel as you leave a worried voicemail, your distress clear in the way your pitch climbs. Midway, you stop walking and the crunching fades; your voice drops, becomes quieter, and the distress shifts into a tired, hollow stillness as you realize you'll have to walk home alone. Let the sound of gravel shape your effort—louder, clearer when walking, then intimate and vulnerable when still.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Detention Stool
instruction: You are a teenage boy in detention, sitting on a wobbly stool in the principal's office. You arrived with contempt for the whole situation, smirking at the idea of being punished. But as you sit here, the silence grows heavy, and you start replaying what you did—how your joke actually hurt someone. Your voice starts tight and dismissive, but as you think out loud, it cracks with uncertainty. Shift your weight on the stool, let your focus drift to the clock and back. End with a quiet admission that surprises you.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Story That Went Wrong
instruction: You're at a small dinner table with three close friends, a few drinks in. You start telling a funny story about an old mutual friend, laughing and gesturing, your voice warm and slightly slurred as you turn to each person. Midway through, the humor fades—you realize the story reveals a betrayal you've never fully faced. Your tone drops, your pauses grow longer, and your voice becomes quieter, more vulnerable, ending with a raw admission of hurt that hangs in the air.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Skin Memory
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to someone you thought you'd spend your life with, and tomorrow they leave—not because love died, but because life demands it. You cannot sleep. Begin in stillness, trying not to wake them, just barely whispering—you're memorizing the sound of their breathing, the warmth of their skin. Start by describing simple, physical details: the curve of their shoulder, how their hand looks in the moonlight. But let this inventory of details crack you open. Each small observation becomes unbearable because it's the last time. Your whisper may break. Long silences between words are natural—you're trying to hold onto moments that are already slipping away. End when you finally touch them, just once, to wake them and tell them something you can only say in darkness.
inspired_by: Actor has completed Programming the Unconscious and is now in performance

title: The Observatory's Drunk Confession
instruction: You are an older woman, somewhat tipsy, standing at a telescope in a public observatory. You are utterly infatuated with the person beside you, a younger astronomer you've just met. You're pointing up at a distant star, but your voice is thinned and tight because you're holding your chin high, trying to seem elegant. As you speak, you become increasingly aware that you're drunker than you thought—your words blur, you lose your train of thought, and a creeping fear of making a fool of yourself grows. Start with giddy, slurred admiration for the cosmos, and end with a vulnerable, trembling confession of your own loneliness, as you realize the night is almost over and you might never see them again.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Infatuation (very intensely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Homecoming Betrayal
instruction: You're returning home after years away, reuniting with someone who shaped your life—but you're simultaneously furious at them for something they did (or didn't do) and desperately grateful to see them again. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to pretend everything is fine. As you look at them, notice the specific details of their face, their mannerisms, the way they smile at you. Let these observations trigger conflicting torrents of emotion: rage at old wounds and overwhelming love, resentment at past failures and joy at their presence, bitterness at time lost and gratitude for this moment. Don't resolve these contradictions—let them coexist and war within you. Your voice and body should reflect this internal battle, sometimes mid-sentence. End by expressing both emotions simultaneously, perhaps through laughter that turns to tears or anger that breaks into an embrace you can't help.
inspired_by: Actor is disconnected from their scene partner; relationship feels artificial or the actor is not genuinely curious about them

title: When the Informant Is Your Child
instruction: You are a journalist discovering that your own child is the whistleblower exposing a dangerous conspiracy—and they're about to be killed for it. Begin with explosive panic, your voice shaking with terror as you beg them to stop, to run, to let the story go. Let your desperation escalate as you detail every threat, every reason they must disappear now. But when they calmly explain why they can't stop, why this matters more than their safety, feel your fear collide with fierce pride and helplessness. Your voice should crack between demanding they save themselves and recognizing they've become braver than you ever were. End in a place of shattered protectiveness, loving them and hating that you raised someone with enough courage to die for the truth.
inspired_by: The Journalist and the Secret Informant

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You're speaking at your religiously conservative parent's funeral, supposedly delivering a respectful eulogy. Begin with traditional words of love and gratitude—genuine but incomplete. Mid-speech, feel something crack open. Start confessing to the room of mourners the painful truth: how their judgment shaped your shame, how you've spent years hiding parts of yourself to earn their love, how you're both heartbroken they're gone AND relieved you're finally free to be fully yourself. Let grief and liberation war in your voice. Speak explicitly about the authentic life you can now live—sensual, bold, unapologetic. Mix tears of loss with fierce, almost defiant joy. End with a paradox in your voice: 'I loved you, I'll miss you, and I'm finally free.' Your tone should carry simultaneous mourning and celebration, tender memory and bold liberation.
inspired_by: Creating Sexual Fantasies, Publicly and Privately

title: Confronting Your Father in the Garden Where He Left You
instruction: You've returned to the misty garden where your father abandoned you as a child, and he's here now, years later, wanting reconciliation. Start by describing the mist with bitter nostalgia—this place once meant safety, now it means betrayal. Your tone begins controlled, almost too calm, as you point out specific details: 'The mist still feels the same. The earth still smells like it did.' But let your control slip. Build into raw confrontation—why did peace matter more to him than you did? Why does he get to walk through beauty while you spent years walking through pain? Shift between rage and the wounded child still inside you. End not with forgiveness or neat closure, but with exhausted truth: you needed him, he failed you, and no misty morning can erase that.
inspired_by: Walking Slowly Through a Misty Morning

title: Burning Letters in the Bathtub
instruction: You're alone, physically destroying letters or belongings from someone you loved, and your body is as engaged as your emotions. Begin by noticing the physical sensations—the texture of paper, the strike of a match, the heat, the smell of burning. Start in cold determination, methodical and controlled. As you continue the physical act of destruction, let your body's impulses take over. Maybe you move faster, more violently. Maybe you slow down, caressing what you're about to destroy. Let rage mix with longing, let your breath change your voice, let physical exhaustion mix with emotional release. Your body might want to laugh, to sob, to scream, to whisper. The physical and emotional feed each other. End in a completely different physical and emotional state than you began—perhaps empty, perhaps ignited, perhaps in a kind of ecstatic grief.
inspired_by: Actor wants to access unconscious impulses in performance

title: The Reeking Corner
instruction: You are an elderly woman, huddled in the corner of a damp basement, knees pressed to your chest. The smell of mold and rot is so strong it makes your stomach turn—you can barely breathe without gagging. You whisper to yourself in disgust, your voice tight and small against the confined space. But as you shift, your hand brushes against an old photograph tucked in your coat: a faded picture of your late husband. Suddenly, the disgust softens into a trembling, grateful whisper—thankful for this memory, for the life you had, even in this awful place.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing at Your Own Farewell
instruction: You're leaving everything behind - your home, your life, entering witness protection or terminal hospice or choosing a one-way journey - and your loved ones threw you one last party. You're giving a toast. Start with genuine laughter and joy, your voice light and grateful, sharing funny memories, making them laugh one more time. But your voice keeps catching - the laughter has tears threaded through it. You're simultaneously celebrating the beautiful life you had while grieving that it's ending. Your voice dances between joy and devastation: 'Thank you for making my life so perfect' breaks mid-sentence into barely controlled sobbing, then rallies back to laughter at another memory. End with your voice finding strange peace in the contradiction - crying while smiling, voice breaking while expressing complete gratitude, saying 'this is perfect' even as your heart shatters.

title: Holding a Warm, Purring Cat on Your Lap
instruction: Feel the cats warmth on your lap as it nestles in and begins to purr softly. Describe the soothing vibrations, the gentle rise and fall of its body, and the way its fur is soft against your hands. Speak with a tone of affection and calm, as if each purr fills you with peace, a quiet companionship that brings a sense of home.

title: What We Never Say
instruction: It's 4 AM and you can't sleep. Your partner is awake too, both of you lying in the dark, not touching. One of you whispers, 'Are you awake?' What follows is the quietest, most careful conversation of your life—the kind that happens only in darkness, only in whispers. You're finally saying something you've carried for months, maybe years: a fear, a longing, a truth about yourself that might change everything between you. Start by feeling the weight of the silence, the vulnerability of speaking into darkness. Don't perform tenderness or bravery—let the words come haltingly, imperfectly. Notice your own breathing, the catch in your throat, the relief and terror of being this naked. Let your partner's responses—whether silence, a sharp intake of breath, or their own whispered confession—actually move through you. By the end, the space between you has transformed, whether into deeper intimacy or unbearable distance.

title: Holding Your Dying Child's Dream
instruction: Your child is in the hospital, fading, and you're desperately describing the future they'll never have—their wedding, their children, their life. Start with fierce, almost manic hope, painting vivid pictures, your voice bright and insistent, as if the force of your words can make them real. But reality keeps breaking through. Your voice cracks, surges with rage at the universe, then dissolves into helpless sobbing. You catch yourself, try again to build the dream, your voice shaking between determination and devastation. End in a whisper, no longer describing the future but saying goodbye, your protectiveness now just holding space for their peace. Let the love be physical, palpable, breaking you open.

title: The Breaking Point of Skin and Soul
instruction: You have just received devastating news—a betrayal, a death, a loss—and you are alone in your home. Your body cannot contain what you're feeling. Begin by trying to hold still, gripping a table or counter, physically restraining yourself, breathing hard. Then let your body take over: collapse, pace violently, grab objects, press your forehead against a wall, sink to the floor. Let guttural sounds come—not words, just pure vocalization of pain. Feel the physical sensation of grief or rage in your chest, throat, stomach. Let yourself move between explosive motion and complete stillness, between screaming and silence. Move from rigid control to complete physical and vocal surrender.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a reliable library of choices that access the unconscious

title: Hospital Morphine Clarity Before It Wears Off
instruction: You're two hours post-surgery, morphine at its peak, and you're telling your partner something you've never said while lucid. Voice is dreamlike, words flow too easily, no filter. You're saying dangerous intimate truths. Somewhere beneath the drug-haze you know this is the medication talking but you can't stop. Include the lucid moment where you realize what you're confessing. Voice wavers between revelation and fear. Then the morphine pulls you down and words become slow, slurred, almost childlike.

title: The Last Lullaby
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting by the bedside of your grieving granddaughter, who has lost her mother—your daughter. As you hum a old, wordless tune she loved as a child, you stroke her hair, feeling a deep ecstasy in the memory of your daughter's smile. But an intense sourness rises in your throat—a sharp ache of all the years you never said 'I love you' enough. Start with a steady, low hum, matching her shallow breaths, then speak slowly, letting your voice crack as you recall a single perfect moment. By the end, the ecstasy fades into a thick, bitter quiet, but you keep the rhythmic sway of your body, as if rocking both of you through the weight of what's unsaid.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're at your parent's bedside in their final hours, and you need to tell them it's okay to let go - but part of you is still that child desperately needing one more piece of advice, one more 'I'm proud of you.' Start with trying to be strong, giving them permission to die peacefully, your voice steady and loving. But as you speak, your own need breaks through - fragments of questions you never asked, things you still need from them. 'You can rest now, you've done enough' fractures into 'but what do I do without you telling me I'm doing okay?' By the end, you're speaking to them and to yourself simultaneously, releasing them while confronting your own terror of being the adult with no parent left to catch you. Let your voice crack between strength and collapse, between generous goodbye and selfish need.

title: The Goodbye That Feels Like Hello
instruction: You're helping your adult child pack for a move across the world—a dream opportunity, everything you wanted for them. You're folding their childhood blanket to put in the donation box, and suddenly you're speaking to them about their whole life. Start with bright, encouraging pride, your voice strong and celebratory. As you continue, let the truth seep in: each item you pack is a piece of them leaving, a chapter closing. Your voice should carry simultaneous joy for their future and devastating loss of their presence. Weave between laughing at memories and fighting tears, between genuine excitement for their adventure and the hollow ache of the empty room that will remain. End with a complex moment where you're holding them, saying 'I'm so happy for you' while your voice breaks, meaning it completely while also grieving the end of being needed the way you once were. The love and the loss must be equally real.

title: The Hospital Vigil: Forty-Eight Hours in Fragments
instruction: You are sitting beside your mother's hospital bed during her final days. Perform five distinct moments from across those 48 hours, but perform them OUT OF ORDER: first, the moment you arrive and still have hope (hour 2); second, when she's gone and you're calling your sister (hour 47); third, the middle of the night when she squeezes your hand one last time (hour 28); fourth, when the doctor first tells you it's time to say goodbye (hour 15); fifth, the peaceful moment just before dawn when you're both silent together (hour 40). For each fragment, you must carry the precise emotional truth of where you are in the journey—the hope, the exhaustion, the denial, the acceptance, the raw grief—even though you're experiencing them out of sequence. Let us feel how each moment contains its own complete emotional reality, yet is part of a larger story of loss and love.

title: Whispering a Secret That Changes Everything
instruction: Late at night, in the dark, you're finally telling someone the truth you've hidden. Start barely audible, testing the words: 'There's something I've never told anyone.' Your voice is fragile, each word chosen carefully, throat tight with fear of their reaction. Pause often, as if you might stop. Build to the confession itself—voice shaking, words catching—about what you did, what happened to you, what you really feel. After you say it, the silence is deafening. Then whisper what you need from them now. End with your voice so soft it's almost not there, vulnerable as an open wound, waiting. Let your breathing tell as much story as your words.
inspired_by: Telling Your Parent Something They'll Disapprove

title: Last Words to Your Parent Who's Slipping Away
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He's barely conscious, but you need him to hear this before he goes. Start with all the anger you've carried for decades—the absence, the coldness, the ways he failed you—your voice tight with years of hurt. But as you speak, something shifts. You realize this is your last chance, and the anger begins cracking open to reveal the child who just wanted to be loved. Your voice softens, breaks. You find yourself saying 'I forgive you' and you're shocked to discover you mean it. End with the purest tenderness, telling him it's okay to let go now, your voice barely above a whisper, holding his hand, finally saying the 'I love you' that's been trapped inside you for a lifetime.
inspired_by: Telling Your Best Friend You Can't Be Friends Anymore

title: Decontamination Drift
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman in full CBRN gear, standing in a decontamination tent after a long shift. Your hyper-feminized voice is now muffled and hollow inside the gas mask—each word has to be shouted through the filter. You’re speaking to your partner across the tent, but your voice comes out mechanical, menacing from the respirator. Start bitter: complain about the endless procedures, the heat, the pointless repetition. Let that bitterness crack and fade as you trail off, realizing you no longer care. End with numb, flat recitation of the next step, your voice empty and distant, as if the mask has swallowed all feeling. Include natural pauses where you adjust the seal, breathe heavily, or lose your train of thought. Speak about 60 words.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Waiting Silence
instruction: You're in a cold interrogation room, a detective staring at you without speaking after you denied knowing where your brother went the night he vanished. Start with forced bravado, hedging your words, rubbing your hands on your jeans. Let the silence gnaw at you—your voice loses its edge as you picture his jacket hanging in the hall. Stumble over a sentence, then end in a quiet, shaky admission that you weren't there for him.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Recording
instruction: You're a musician dying of terminal illness, recording a final song for your infant daughter who won't remember you. Begin with determined clarity—'I need you to know who I was'—but as you sing, your voice fractures with the weight of all the moments you'll miss: her first day of school, her wedding, her own children. Your breath becomes labored, not from illness but from the crushing love that has nowhere to go. Physically, you're holding headphones to your ears, adjusting the mic with trembling hands. End with a whisper that contains both fierce protectiveness and devastating acceptance: 'When you hear this, I'll be gone, but right now, in this moment, I'm holding you.' Let your voice break on the word 'holding'—this is where pride dissolves into pure, helpless love.

title: The Echo of a Spilled Secret
instruction: You are an elderly woman walking down a long, dimly lit hallway in your retirement home. The floor is polished linoleum, your slippers make soft shuffle-scrapes with each step, and the sound bounces back at you with a hollow reverb. Halfway down, you realize the small bag of hard candies you had tucked in your pocket has torn open, and a cascade of wrapped sweets has scattered behind you, glittering under the fluorescent lights. You stop, frozen with embarrassment—a flush of heat climbs your neck as you imagine the staff or other residents seeing the trail. You fumble, knees creaking as you crouch, mumbling apologies to no one. Then, as you scoop up the candies, you catch your own reflection in the glass of a fire extinguisher case and see the absurdity of it. Your initial mortified murmur grows into a soft, breathy chuckle, and you start to tease yourself aloud—calling yourself a ‘clumsy old bird’—your voice gaining a wry, affectionate warmth that fills the corridor. Let the reverb stretch your words; include pauses where you listen to the silence, and let your breath be uneven from bending. End with a playful, forgiving sigh as you stand up.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Shattering Point
instruction: You've just discovered a betrayal so profound it's rewriting your entire understanding of your relationship—a hidden truth, a years-long deception, a choice they made that broke something fundamental. Start with disbelief, your voice shaking with adrenaline, asking questions you already know the answers to. Build to fury—let yourself become loud, raw, uncontained. Your voice should crack and soar and break. Rage at them with everything you have. But then—let the rage collapse. Let it turn into something worse: devastation. Your voice should drop to almost nothing as you realize the person you loved never existed. End in a place of terrible clarity, speaking with the quiet, hollow certainty of someone who has just lost everything. The final words should be soft but absolutely final, like closing a door you'll never open again.

title: The Sting of a Secret
instruction: You are a little girl playing alone in your grandmother's overgrown garden, barefoot in the cool grass. You are carefully pulling a thorny vine away from a beautiful, strange flower you've never seen before—it's both ugly and wondrous, and you feel a small, curious awe. As you yank, the vine snaps back and a hidden bee stings the soft arch of your foot. You let out a sharp, involuntary yelp, hopping on one leg, then freeze, holding your breath against the searing pain. As the first tears threaten, your mother's voice calls from the house, and you remember you snuck out here—you are not supposed to be playing near the toxic flowers. The awe curdles into a sly, quiet malice as you decide to say nothing, to keep this secret pain all to yourself, and you whisper to the flower a promise that it's your little victory now.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You are confronting your father after discovering a lie he's kept for twenty years—a sibling you never knew existed, a betrayal of your mother, a secret that recolors your entire childhood. Start from a place of controlled fury, your voice tight and measured, reciting facts like weapons. As he attempts to explain, let a childhood memory surface—a specific moment when you felt safe with him, protected, loved unconditionally. Allow this memory to complicate your rage. Let confusion seep in. End in a place where anger and heartbreak are inseparable, where you're simultaneously the hurt child who adored him and the adult who sees his flaws. Your voice should travel from cold precision to trembling uncertainty.
inspired_by: Actor's choice repertoire feels limited; they use the same choices repeatedly

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing beside your child's bed in the pre-dawn darkness. They're sleeping peacefully, unaware this is goodbye. Your voice is barely a whisper as you tell them all the things you need them to know—how to be brave, how you'll always love them even when you're gone. Your throat keeps catching because you're trying not to wake them, trying not to cry. You touch their hair with trembling fingers and your voice splinters as you apologize for leaving, as you try to explain why you have to go. The words come in broken fragments because speaking too loudly would wake them, and you cannot bear their questions. End with you memorizing their sleeping face, your voice dissolving to nothing as you realize this quiet moment is the last time you'll ever see them. Your final words are lost in breath, more felt than spoken.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Ancient Warrior Realizes They've Been Fighting an Illusion

title: The Stiff Neck at the Bus Stop
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman waiting at a bus stop, your neck twisted awkwardly as you keep glancing over your shoulder to see if the bus is coming. Your body is tense from the cold and the strain. You start emotionally numb, just repeating a familiar disappointment to yourself—something you've been putting up with for years. But as the wait drags on, the numbness turns into raw impatience and irritability. Your voice gets tighter, the words come out clipped and sharp, as if the physical strain is leaking into your speech. Let your tone shift from a flat, resigned mutter to an irritated, almost whiny snap.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Disappointment (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Night Before the Colony Ship Launches
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your adult child who volunteered for a one-way mission to colonize another planet. You start trying to be brave, supportive, talking about how proud you are. But as you speak, the reality crashes in—you'll never see them again, never hold them, never know if they survived the journey. Your voice breaks from forced cheerfulness into raw grief. You want to tell them not to go, to stay, but you know you can't take this away from them. End caught between desperate love and the agony of letting go. Your breathing becomes ragged as you try to memorize their face, their voice, knowing this is the last time.
inspired_by: Professional: Scientist Realizes Her Research Is Being Used for Weapons

title: The Voice I Buried
instruction: Late at night, alone, you're reading an old journal from before you learned to be acceptable. Your voice starts out curious, almost amused at your younger self. Then you find an entry that stops you cold—something you wrote about what you wanted, who you were going to be. Your voice becomes hushed, tender, mourning. You read it aloud and it sounds like meeting a ghost. 'I forgot you existed,' you whisper. The grief is enormous but quiet, the kind that sits in your chest like a stone. You keep reading, and your voice catches on words you can't believe you once had the audacity to write. By the end, you're crying softly, but there's something like recognition emerging through the sadness—a tiny, fragile thread of hope that maybe that voice isn't completely dead.

title: The Sound of Breaking
instruction: You're alone in your childhood home after a betrayal that's shattered your sense of self—a partner's infidelity, a friend's devastating lie, a professional humiliation. Begin by moving through the rooms, and let yourself listen: the creak of floorboards under your feet, the hum of the refrigerator, the ticking of a clock, wind against windows, the silence that feels like ringing in your ears. Let these sounds build inside you. Your breath becomes ragged; listen to it. Hear your own voice as it rises from a whisper to a scream. Physically interact with the space—touch walls, slam a door, let something fall—and let the sounds you create mirror your emotional escalation. But here's the transformation: in the aftermath of your rage, in the settling silence, listen to the quiet that remains. Hear how the house absorbs your pain. Let the return of ordinary sounds—the refrigerator's hum, your own breathing calming—guide you from explosive fury into a strange, empty peace. End in stillness, listening to the profound quiet, your voice barely working as you speak a single truth you've been avoiding.

title: The Sickness of a Lie
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl who just lied to your mother about where you were all night. You are now in the bathroom, sick with guilt and nausea, trying to keep quiet while your stomach heaves. You start by fighting the gagging, whispering reassurances to yourself that you can fix this, but as the physical disgust mounts, you realize the lie is eating you alive. Let the vomiting interrupt your words—your voice cracks, tears come, and by the end, you're not just sick from the lie, but from the shame of how you see yourself now. You are alone, slumped against the cold tile, and the last words are soft, broken, and defeated.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Lie That Became True
instruction: You lied about something to protect yourself or impress someone. You said it so many times that you started believing it. Your voice when telling the lie is rehearsed, smooth. But someone asks a specific detail that breaks the narrative. Your voice falters. 'I...' You're caught between the lie you've been telling and the truth. Your voice becomes confused. You're not sure what's real anymore. Include the moment the lie collapses.

title: Breathing the Same Air in the Dark
instruction: You are lying next to someone in complete darkness, and you're whispering a secret you've never told anyone—but here's the truth: you're making up the secret as you speak, discovering it in real time. Begin with your voice barely audible, uncertain, feeling your way through the confession like someone walking through a dark room. The secret might be about shame, or desire, or a moment of grace you witnessed, or a fear that has no name. Let the intimacy of the darkness and their breathing give you permission to go deeper than you planned. By the end, you've told them something you didn't know you needed to say, and your whisper has transformed from tentative to raw to somehow peaceful. The revelation changes you as you speak it.

title: The Bittersweet Return
instruction: You are reuniting with someone you once loved deeply - a former partner, an estranged sibling, a childhood friend - and the meeting contains both profound joy and unhealed grief. Begin with the eager, boundless energy of a young dog greeting its beloved - that uncontainable happiness, tail-wagging enthusiasm in your whole body, forward momentum, pure uncomplicated delight. Let genuine laughter bubble up, let your body express welcome. But as the reality of all the lost years settles in, feel yourself shift into the heaviness of an old elephant - that ancient, grieving weight, the slow processing of complex memory, a massive sadness that moves through you like something geological. Your joy doesn't disappear but becomes layered, complicated, shot through with loss. End in a place where both creatures coexist in your body - still capable of happiness but now carrying the full weight of everything that can never be recovered.

title: The Receipt That Broke Us
instruction: You're alone in your workshop, late evening, holding a crumpled receipt you just found in the trash. At first you're curious—puzzled by the numbers, squinting at the date. Then slowly, the betrayal reveals itself: your business partner has been siphoning money for months. Your voice drops to a stunned, breathless whisper as you repeat the amounts. Then a wave of hot anger surges up, cracking your voice as you realize you've been blind. Speak the discovery aloud, starting with detached muttering, then building to a fragmented, volcanic accusation.
emotions_sampled: Interest (slightly present), Anger (clearly present), Awe (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Bitter Familiarity of Home
instruction: You're an older woman sitting alone at your kitchen table, a half-empty glass of wine in front of you. It's late, and you're a little drunk—your thoughts wander, your movements are slow and loose. You start talking about the house you grew up in, but instead of pure warmth, a sharp sourness creeps in: a memory of your father's anger, a slammed door. Let your voice be soft and thick with alcohol, trailing off into long pauses as you stare at nothing. Begin with a tipsy, nostalgic smile that slowly curdles into a raw, quiet ache. End with a whisper, the memory too heavy to hold.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, recording your final message to Earth before communication becomes impossible. Begin with professional composure, reciting mission parameters and scientific observations—your voice steady, trained, controlled. But as you speak, the weight of never seeing home again breaks through. Your voice cracks as you try to tell your child you're proud of them, that missing their graduation was worth it for humanity's future. But was it? Your certainty crumbles. End in raw truth: you're terrified, you made the wrong choice, and you'd give anything for one more morning in your kitchen. Let the astronaut facade completely dissolve into the frightened human underneath.

title: The Roast That Got Away
instruction: You're in your small, cluttered kitchen, making a complicated roast chicken for your partner's surprise homecoming. The oil spits, the timer ticks, and you're singing along to a pop song, feeling a giddy, vibrant elation—this is your moment. But then you realize you forgot to buy fresh herbs, the potatoes are still raw, and the oven temperature is somehow wrong. As you fumble for ingredients and the smoke alarm teases, your voice shifts from bright, breathless joy to a strained, helpless wobble—still trying to stay upbeat but cracking under the pressure. Let the sizzling pan and clattering spoon interrupt your words, and let your tone rise in a panicked chirp before sinking into a quiet, defeated murmur as you stare at the mess.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Audition That Became a Reckoning
instruction: You're in a callback, asked to perform a monologue about a parent's betrayal. You start professionally, demonstrating your range—controlled, showcasing technique. But something in the words unlocks your own unprocessed rage toward your father. Suddenly you're no longer performing; you're shouting at him through the text, voice raw and uncontrolled, breathing ragged. The casting director tries to stop you but you can't stop—years of silence exploding out. Then it all breaks: the rage shatters into sobbing, into 'Why wasn't I enough for you to stay?' Your voice fractures between fury and a child's bewilderment. You end on your knees, not because it's theatrical, but because your body can't hold the weight anymore. Whisper the final line—a desperate, quiet 'I needed you'—then silence, where you realize everyone in the room has disappeared and you're just talking to ghosts.

title: The Last Transmission Before the Mission
instruction: You're recording a final message to your child before embarking on a one-way space mission to save Earth. Begin with forced optimism and practical instructions about their upcoming birthday, but as you realize this is truly goodbye, let your voice crack and reveal the devastating truth: you're terrified and heartbroken. Shift between trying to be the strong parent they need and being the vulnerable human who desperately wants to stay. End in a whisper, telling them the one thing you've never been able to say. Let silences speak as loudly as words.
inspired_by: The Time Traveler and the Skeptical Scientist

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're standing in your childhood bedroom, now empty, confronting your aging parent who's moving away. Start controlled, almost businesslike: 'I need to say something before you go.' But as you list what you needed and never got—the validation, the presence, the unconditional love—your voice builds with decades of suppressed pain. Then they say something small, something honest, and your anger collapses into exhausted grief. You wanted rage to feel good, cleansing. Instead you just feel tired and sad. End with a confession you never meant to make: 'I still need you. I hate that I still need you.' Let your voice reveal the child still living inside the adult body.

title: Dancing in the Ruins of Everything
instruction: You're standing in the wreckage of your former life—job gone, relationship ended, dreams shattered—and something in you breaks open into unexpected, almost hysterical freedom. Begin with a laugh that sounds wrong, then let it build as you describe everything falling apart. Mix genuine joy at being released from expectations with grief for what you've lost. Your voice should dance between giddy relief and sobbing, sometimes in the same sentence. Express profound gratitude for the destruction because it freed you, while your heart simultaneously breaks for who you used to be. End in quiet wonder, laughing softly through tears, finding strange peace in the chaos.
inspired_by: The Time Traveler and the Skeptical Scientist

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—a divorce is final, a diagnosis is terminal, a dream has definitively died, or you've lost something that defined you—and you're speaking to yourself or someone close about finding something absurdly beautiful in the wreckage. Begin with a laugh that's almost inappropriate, noticing something ridiculous or tender in the midst of devastation: the way light hits the boxes you're packing, how free you feel now that there's nothing left to lose, the dark humor in timing. Your voice carries simultaneous grief and liberation—crying while you laugh, your throat tight with sorrow even as genuine joy bubbles up. Let gratitude emerge for what the pain taught you, but don't let it erase the anguish; hold both at once. Your voice should crack with loss and ring with strange, hard-won peace. End with a paradox: you're heartbroken and somehow more whole, speaking with tear-stained wonder about beauty found in the absolute worst moment. This should sound like someone who's discovered that joy and grief can occupy the same breath.

title: The Buried Blueprint
instruction: You are lying on your stomach on the floor of a dusty attic, propped on your elbows, searching through a pile of old cardboard boxes. You have just found a hand-drawn map your late father made of a secret treehouse you two built together years ago. As you trace the faded pencil lines, you start to speak to yourself, first with quiet concentration and curiosity about the details, but as you recall the day you both built it, a wave of bittersweet nostalgia and gentle, aching love rises up, softening your voice and slowing your words. Let the physical position anchor you — feel the slight compression in your stomach, the weight of your upper body on your elbows, and let your head shift and your eyes wander as you lose yourself in the memory. End with a single, deep, quiet breath before you speak again.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Breathing the Same Air
