Let your attention to this genuine detail pull you into the real confrontation—rawer and more honest than what you planned. Begin with almost curious observation, a noting of something specific. End in the painful honesty that emerges when you stop performing anger and speak from what you're actually seeing.

title: I Would Burn the World
instruction: Someone you love has been hurt, and you're confronting the person responsible with pure protective fury. Start with a dangerous quiet—you're holding back an ocean of rage, voice low and shaking with the effort of control. Name what they did, each word precise and sharp as a blade. Then let the dam break: your voice rises to a roar, fierce and primal—how dare they, what gave them the right, do they understand what they've destroyed? But mid-fury, grief crashes through: your voice cracks and suddenly you're sobbing with helplessness because you couldn't prevent this, you couldn't protect them. Rage and powerlessness war in your voice—you want vengeance but you can't undo what's done. End with an exhausted, broken ferocity: a vow spoken through tears that sounds more like a prayer, promising you'll never let this happen again, even as you know you can't control everything. Let the intensity be raw and unpolished, passion collapsing into despair and back again.

title: The Found Letter
instruction: You are an elderly person, alone in a cluttered study, sorting through a dusty box of old papers. Your voice is dry, low, and mumbling as you shuffle through receipts and notes—your hands tremble slightly, occasionally pausing to read a faded line. Halfway through, you find a specific letter that makes your jaw tighten. As you read it aloud, your voice shifts from weary muttering to a quieter, sharper tone, fingers snapping a paper edge as malice seeps in. You finish the last sentence with a cold, final whisper, the paper sliding shut.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing Through the Breaking
instruction: You have just received devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, a diagnosis—and you are alone in your room. Begin collapsed, voice broken, body curled in on itself, speaking to yourself in fragments about how you cannot do this, cannot survive this pain. But then something primal takes over. You stand up. You start to move. You begin declaring out loud—to the walls, to the universe, to your own body—that you are still here, still alive, still feeling. Let physical movement and vocal declaration build together: shake out your limbs, pound your chest, move with increasing commitment and energy. Mix the emotional states—cry while you move, laugh while tears stream down your face, rage and grieve and celebrate your own aliveness simultaneously. Build to a full-bodied, high-energy declaration of your continued existence, your refusal to disappear. The arc moves from collapsed devastation to fierce, physical, committed vitality—not pretending the pain isn't there, but meeting it with equal intensity of life force.

title: The Touch of Ghosts
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom, touching objects that belonged to someone you lost—a sibling, a first love, a best friend taken too soon. Begin by handling something of theirs: a jacket, a book, a piece of jewelry. At first, it's just cloth, just paper, just metal. But as you hold it, let it transform under your fingers. Feel the warmth of their skin in the fabric. Smell them in the collar. See the exact way their fingers held this book, the oil from their skin still present on the pages. Let the object become a portal—speak to them through it in whispers, confess what you never said, ask questions you need answered. Your emotion should travel from tentative, fragile touching to a full sensory reunion, as if they're materializing in your hands, until the reality crashes back and you're alone again, clutching an ordinary object that briefly held everything.

title: Faint Warmth Behind the Numbness
instruction: You're a teenager in a hospital bed, your jaw freshly wired shut after an accident. The pain meds have left you feeling hollow and disconnected—your own voice sounds far away, muffled through clenched teeth. A nurse gently adjusts your blanket, and in that small act, a flicker of affection surfaces, fighting through the fog. Start with the flat, detached numbness of someone who's barely present, then let a tiny, reluctant warmth creep into your final words—a thanks that feels almost foreign. Your speech is strained, consonants slushy, every syllable an effort. Pause to swallow, shift your weight, or blink slowly as if waking up.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Telling Your Child Goodbye Through the Glass
instruction: You're visiting your child in prison—or they're visiting you. There's glass between you, phones to your ears. Start gently, trying to make normal conversation, asking about their day, telling them you brought their favorite cookies (that they can't have). Your voice is tender, almost artificially bright. But you both know this might be the last time—one of you is terminally ill, or being transferred far away, or facing a sentence that means decades. The brightness falters. Your voice drops to a whisper as you try to say everything that matters in the minutes you have left. You're memorizing their face. Your words catch in your throat. End with your hand pressed against the glass, voice barely working, trying to say 'I love you' but the words keep breaking apart.

title: The Tender Noose
instruction: You are an elderly man, deeply infatuated with a much younger partner during an intimate, consensual choking scene. At the start, your voice is thick with adoration and breathless desire, but as the pressure on your throat increases, your words become strained, thin, and raspy, a wet crackle creeping in. You feel a sour triumph — a bitter pride that you can still command this kind of intense, dangerous attention at your age, even as your body rebels. As the hold releases, you gasp, then speak in a dizzy, euphoric rush, mixing raw vulnerability with a fragile, sour smile of victory. Let your voice crack, trail off, and rebuild with each wave of sensation.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Triumph (extremely present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Parade Ground Proclamation
instruction: You are a young girl at a military airshow, standing rigidly at attention as your mother, a pilot, receives a medal. The crowd roars and your chest swells with fierce pride — you want to shout your triumph, but your throat is tight from holding yourself so straight. You step forward to recite a poem you wrote for her, but the microphone screeches, making you flinch. As you speak, you catch a whiff of hot dogs and feel a flicker of disgust at the greasy smell, but you push through, your voice growing from a breathless, metallic bark into a softer, trembling declaration of love — the joy breaking through the armor.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Denies
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about years of emotional neglect she's always dismissed. Begin measured, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this. But as she starts making excuses, your control fractures. Your voice rises with decades of swallowed anger. Then something shifts: you hear how small and defensive she sounds, and your rage collides with the devastating realization that she'll never be the mother you needed. Your voice breaks from fury into something like grief for the relationship that never existed. End in quiet, terrible clarity: you're not arguing anymore, you're mourning. Your final words aren't angry—they're a farewell.
inspired_by: Professional: Scientist Realizes Her Research Is Being Used for Weapons

title: Midnight Confession to Your Younger Self
instruction: It is 3 AM and you cannot sleep. You are whispering to a photograph of yourself as a child, or to a memory, telling them about all the times you were told no, all the doors that closed, all the people who said you weren't enough. Begin with tender honesty about the pain, the exhaustion, the moments you almost quit. Your voice should be intimate, fragile, barely above a whisper. But as you confess these things to that younger version of yourself, you also begin to tell them about the one thing that never died—the stubborn, illogical love of the work itself. Let your whisper gain strength. End by making a promise to that child: not that it will be easy, but that you will not abandon the dream they planted in you. Move from exhausted vulnerability to gentle, fierce protectiveness.
inspired_by: When you are an aspiring actor hearing discouraging stories about Hollywood's difficulty

title: The Terminal Patient's Wedding Toast
instruction: You have stage-four cancer and six weeks to live. You're giving a wedding toast at your younger sister's reception—the wedding you always thought you'd be healthy for. You start with genuine joy, celebrating her happiness, making people laugh with a funny childhood story. Your voice is bright, full of love. But mid-toast, a wave of grief hits you—not for yourself, but for everything you'll miss. Your voice begins to shake as you realize you won't meet her children, won't grow old with her, won't be there when she needs you. Yet you refuse to ruin her day. So you laugh through tears, your voice breaking with simultaneous joy and devastation. Tell her how happy you are while your heart is splintering. Express profound gratitude for having her as a sister while mourning the future you're losing. Let your voice carry contradictory emotions—celebration intertwined with goodbye, laughter mixed with grief, pure love shadowed by unbearable loss. End with a blessing that's also a farewell.

title: Secrets in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love in the middle of the night, and you're finally ready to confess something you've carried alone—a past trauma, a deep shame, a truth about yourself you've hidden. Begin in whispers so quiet they're almost just breath, your voice catching on words you've never said aloud: 'There's something I need to tell you. I'm scared you'll...' Your throat tightens around the words. As you speak, your voice remains small, intimate, trembling—this isn't dramatic confession, it's terrified vulnerability. Feel their hand finding yours in the darkness, their breathing steady beside you. Let their acceptance slowly seep into your voice, which remains whisper-soft but becomes less choked, less alone. End with your voice still quiet but now wrapped in tenderness and relief: 'Thank you for staying.' Let silence carry as much weight as words.

title: Adult Child Confronting Aging Parent: The Apology That Never Came
instruction: You're visiting your father in the hospital after his stroke, and you realize this might be your last chance to say what you've needed to say for thirty years. Start with forced cheerfulness, the voice you've always used to keep the peace: 'Hey, Dad, brought you some magazines. How are you feeling?' But you can't maintain it. Your voice begins to crack with suppressed anger: 'Actually, no. I need to say something. I needed you when I was eight years old. I needed you to show up.' Let the anger build, your voice rising with decades of hurt: 'Do you know what it's like to scan every crowd looking for your father and never finding him?' Then watch your anger collapse into something more devastating—grief, longing, the child still hoping: 'I just wanted you to be proud of me. That's all I ever wanted.' End with a whisper, tender and broken: 'I love you, Dad. I always have. And I needed you to love me back.' You're finally vulnerable with the person who hurt you most.
inspired_by: Construction Foreman: Shutting Down After Accident

title: Finding Shelter in a Blizzard: Relief Becoming Hypothermia Complacency
instruction: You're lost in a blizzard, voice panicked and desperate, searching for shelter. Your narration is scattered, frightened. Then you find something—a cave, a cabin, anything. Your voice becomes almost hysterical with relief. 'I found it. I found shelter.' You're inside, out of the wind, and your voice calms. But as you warm slightly, something dangerous happens: your body temperature is still dropping from hypothermia and your mind is becoming confused. Your voice becomes slow, peaceful, drowsy. You're narrating how nice it would be to sleep. Include the moment where your rational mind breaks through: 'No. Stay awake. Don't sleep.' Your voice is fighting its own neurological shutdown, awareness and grogginess battling for control. You're slapping your own face, your voice becomes a desperate mantra: 'Stay awake. Stay awake. Stay—'

title: Whispered Truth in the Dark
instruction: It's 2am and you're lying in bed beside your lover of ten years. You've decided tonight is the night you'll finally confess something you've kept hidden—a deep fear, a secret shame, or a truth about who you really are. But speak only in whispered, tender non-words—soft syllables that sound like a private language only the two of you share. Begin in terrified vulnerability, your voice barely audible, each sound trembling with the risk of exposure. Let your partner's gentle sounds in response give you courage to go deeper. This is intimate, slow, quiet—not a performance but a genuine revelation happening in real-time through the music of wordless expression. End in profound relief and tender acceptance, your sounds intermingling with theirs like a lullaby. The darkness protects you; the abstract language lets you be more honest than real words ever could.

title: The Last Call Home
instruction: You are a young man, somewhat drunk at a loud party, trying to call your deaf younger brother on a video phone. You've stepped outside but the music still thumps faintly. You start trying to explain a funny story from the night, but your words are slow and overly loud, your gestures exaggerated. As you talk, you suddenly realize how much you miss him and how hard it is to bridge this gap. The story fumbles away as your voice softens, still loud but now thick with a raw, unexpected loneliness, your eyes unfocused but your need to connect painfully clear.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Rescue Call
instruction: You are on the phone with 911 after pulling a child from a burning car. Your voice is high and staccato, barely controlled as you report the scene. Moments ago you were screaming for help, but now the child is coughing in your arms. As you tell the operator you got them out, your voice cracks—not from fear, but from pride. You start to laugh in disbelief, then choke up with gratitude that they're alive. Let your words tumble out, then slow as relief washes over you, ending in a whispered 'thank God.'
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Relief (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Shot
instruction: You are an elderly person standing alone in an empty gymnasium. The polished floor glows under harsh lights, and every slight shuffle of your sneakers echoes with a metallic flutter. You hold a basketball, trying to relive a shot you once made decades ago. At first, you feel a quiet stubbornness—a refusal to accept that your body won't cooperate. But as you miss badly, the ball clanking off the rim and bouncing away, you start to chuckle. The sound of your own thin, echoey laugh surprises you. Speak to yourself, mixing the initial frustration with a warmth that grows into gentle amusement at your own persistence. Let your voice crack a little, react to the hollow echo, and pause to adjust your glasses or wipe your brow.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You've just inherited your estranged mother's house and are walking through it for the first time since her death. You expected to feel relief or anger—she hurt you badly. Instead, you find yourself surrounded by objects you don't recognize, evidence of a life you weren't part of. Begin in defensive numbness, touching nothing, wanting to leave. But then pick up something—a book with marginalia, a photograph of people you don't know, a half-finished craft project. Let curiosity crack through your protective shell. Who was she in these rooms? What brought her joy? What was she trying to create or understand? Feel the collision of grief and curiosity, resentment and genuine wonder. Let your voice carry both the pain of abandonment and an almost childlike desire to understand—to finally ask the questions you never got to ask. End in a strange place between anger and tenderness, both mourning her and, for the first time, truly curious about who she actually was.

title: Upside Down Mom
instruction: You’re hanging upside down from a jungle gym, blood rushing to your head, making your voice thick and gurgly. Your young daughter keeps tugging your shirt and babbling about something. At first, you’re content, enjoying the strange weightless feeling, but her words don’t make sense—confusion creeps in as you try to parse them. When she starts whining, a sharp wave of anger hits, and you snap at her to stop. Let your voice be wet, strained, and hard to control, shifting from dreamy mumbling to irritated, breathless demands.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Contentment (extremely present), Anger (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Sex Tape Recorded Years Ago, Heard for First Time Since
instruction: Someone sends you a video from 8 years ago. It's you and an ex. You haven't heard your own voice like this since the breakup. Your voice on the recording is younger, happier, intimate in ways you'd blocked out. You're listening to yourself moan, laugh, whisper things to someone who's gone from your life. Your real voice—current voice—responds to what you're hearing and it's a shock. Your current voice is older, careful, less open.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood you deserved but never had. You start carefully controlled, almost clinical, listing facts like you've rehearsed this. But anger begins bleeding through—your voice gets sharper, faster. You're trying to stay composed but decades of hurt are erupting. Your voice rises as you describe waiting for them, making excuses for them, breaking yourself trying to earn their love. Then suddenly you stop. The rage collapses into something raw and young—your voice becomes almost childlike, asking the question you've carried your whole life: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger transforms into naked vulnerability, then hardens again into something quieter but unbreakable: acceptance that you deserved better. Your voice moves from controlled restraint to explosive fury to childlike pleading to fierce self-worth.

title: The Axe That Cannot Forgive
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe ten, alone in a backyard, chopping wood like your older brother. Every swing is fueled by pure jealousy—you can't stand how he's always praised, how he splits logs clean in one hit. Between explosive grunts and heavy breaths, you mutter angry words at the wood, blaming it, blaming him. A missed swing jolts your wrists and the axe sticks; you freeze, panting. Now the envy turns inward—your voice cracks, quieter, more hurt. You admit to yourself that you'll never be him. End with one last tired, defeated swing, voice barely audible.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Three AM Truths
instruction: It's the middle of the night and you're whispering to someone beside you, confessing something you've never told anyone. Begin by becoming aware of the actual vulnerability you feel right now in this moment - the exposure, the fear, the tentative hope. As you speak, continually check in with what's genuinely happening inside you: 'I feel terrified... I feel relief... I feel ashamed that I feel relieved... I feel tender toward myself... I feel like running away.' Let each whispered sentence respond to the real feeling underneath, not to what a confession is supposed to sound like. Notice when you're trying to make yourself seem brave or pitiful or worthy - then redirect to simply expressing what's actually present. By the end, discover what emerges when you stop managing how you come across: perhaps unexpected lightness, perhaps deeper fear, perhaps quiet certainty.

title: The Echo of a Joke
instruction: You're at a cramped family dinner, wedged between a chatty cousin and the wall. Your aunt is telling her famous fishing story for the seventh time, and you lean to your friend, mimicking her exact nasal tone and dramatic pauses, your voice going high and reedy with mockery. You're doubled over, trying not to snort your drink, the amusement so intense you can barely breathe. Mid-sentence, you catch your aunt's eye—she's stopped talking and is staring. The laughter freezes in your throat. You stutter, trying to rephrase your mimicry as a compliment, your voice cracking as you fumble to recover, the amusement curdling into a flustered, desperate cover-up.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: Everything you built has just fallen apart—a relationship ended, a dream died, a future vanished—and yet you're standing in the wreckage laughing because it's so absurdly, cosmically terrible that tears alone won't cover it. Begin with bright, slightly manic laughter, the kind that sounds almost real, recounting the ridiculous details of your disaster as if telling a funny story. But let the laughter become more jagged, more breathless, until you can't tell if you're laughing or crying. Your voice wavers between the two, finding strange moments of genuine humor in the pain, then breaking into sobs, then back to laughter. End in a place of exhausted grace, still half-laughing, half-crying, your voice soft and wondering as you realize you're somehow going to survive this, that the absurdity itself is a kind of terrible gift.

title: The Moment You Realize You've Become the Monster
instruction: You're in the middle of a furious tirade—screaming at someone you love, your voice raw with rage, listing their failures and flaws with vicious precision. You're unstoppable, righteous in your anger, your voice climbing in volume and intensity. Then mid-sentence, you catch a glimpse of yourself—in a mirror, in their terrified eyes, in a sudden flash of recognition—and you see your own abusive parent staring back at you. Your voice must shatter completely. The rage collapses into horror, then into desperate, sobbing apologies that you can barely get out. Try to explain, to take it back, your voice breaking between gasping breaths. Shift between trying to comfort them and being unable to forgive yourself, your words dissolving into inarticulate grief. End in a whisper, begging them not to leave, or telling them they should.

title: The Weight of the Glass
instruction: You are an older man, nursing a third whiskey at a bar after your son's wedding. The buzz has loosened your usual stoic shell, but a deep shame is surfacing: you realize you barely spoke to him all night, hiding in jokes and backslaps. Start rambling to the bartender—your voice gravelly, slightly louder than intended, with a faint, clumsy edge. Let the shame crack through as you stumble over words like 'responsibility' and 'father.' Midway, as you stare into the amber glass, a shift: you remember his smile during the first dance. Hope flickers, tentative and raw—your tone softens, slow, and you finish with a quiet, trembly confession, almost to yourself, about wanting to do better. Don't hide the small distractions—the clink of your glass, a distant laugh, the pause to swallow.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Gravel Road Home
instruction: You are an elderly man driving an old pickup truck on a bumpy gravel road after visiting your late wife's grave. Your body jostles with each rut, making your voice quiver involuntarily. Start with a tired sigh, feeling the physical ache and the roughness of the ride. Then, as you glance at her photo on the dashboard, a quiet memory surfaces—your voice softens, still shaking from the road but now carrying a gentle warmth. End with a faint, contented chuckle, the turbulence becoming just part of the journey.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning After Betrayal
instruction: You're confronting your former lover after discovering they violated your boundaries during your last intimate encounter—something you trusted them with that they crossed. Begin with controlled, ice-cold fury as you describe exactly what they did without permission, your voice sharp enough to cut. Build to explosive rage: 'You didn't ask—you just TOOK—' Let yourself become almost incoherent with the combination of violated desire, broken trust, and the horror of having wanted someone who hurt you. Your voice should crack between screaming and sobbing as you realize you're grieving not just the betrayal but the loss of the intimacy you thought you had. Collapse into raw, helpless weeping as you whisper: 'I would have said yes if you'd asked... I would have said yes...' End in exhausted, broken tenderness toward yourself, whispering self-comfort like a parent to a wounded child. The arc moves from cold rage to explosive anguish to protective self-love.

title: The Breaking Point: When Protection Means Letting Go
instruction: You're screaming - actually screaming - at someone you love desperately because they're destroying themselves and you can't save them. Begin with explosive anger, your voice raw and loud, demanding they wake up and see what they're doing. Let fury pour out. Then the crack: mid-sentence, your rage collapses into sobbing, into begging. Your voice breaks completely. Plead with them - not with words about right and wrong, but with the terror of losing them. Then the devastating shift: realize you have to let go. Your voice becomes quiet, hollow, defeated. Tell them you love them too much to watch this anymore. End with fierce, broken goodbye - still loving them, but walking away. Move from volcanic rage through desperate pleading to exhausted, grief-stricken release. Let your voice shatter and rebuild in real time.
inspired_by: The Final Words: What You'd Actually Say

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You are confronting a parent who has just discovered something about your past—a firing, an arrest, a betrayal, a pattern of behavior you've hidden for years. Begin from a place of defensive anger and deflection, your voice sharp and protected, blaming them for not understanding. As they remain silent or react with disappointment, let your anger crack open to reveal what's underneath: the realization that you've become exactly what you once promised yourself you'd never be. Your voice must transform from attack to confession—speak the specific moment in your childhood when you watched this same parent struggle with their own shame, and how you swore you'd be different. End in a place of devastating self-recognition, no longer defending yourself but asking them—in a voice stripped of all armor—if they see in you what you now see in yourself.

title: The Unspoken Inheritance
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a truth you've carried alone for twenty years - something they did (or failed to do) that shaped the entire course of your life. Start from a place of carefully maintained calm, almost businesslike in your determination to finally speak. As you reveal what you've hidden, feel the anger rise - not the explosive kind, but the steady, relentless kind that has been compressed for decades. But underneath that anger, discover the child who still needs to be seen, to be acknowledged. By the end, let yourself break down not into rage, but into the vulnerability of asking: 'Did you ever realize what you did to me?' Move from cold control, through rising fury, into raw, exposed need.
inspired_by: When an actor has suffered trauma before pursuing acting

title: The Reunion Wound
instruction: You're opening the door to someone you haven't seen in years—maybe a childhood best friend who abandoned you, maybe your child who ran away, maybe a first love. Your face breaks into a smile because you're genuinely happy to see them, but underneath there's also fury, grief, fear. Instead of choosing one emotion or planning how to blend them, let contradictory impulses hit you and follow each one instantly without reconciling them. Your arms might open for a hug while your voice says something cutting. You might laugh with joy and find tears streaming down your face. Let competing feelings slam into each other—maybe you move toward them then recoil, maybe tenderness and rage alternate every few seconds, maybe you're apologizing and accusing in the same breath. Don't make sense. Don't smooth it out. Follow the chaos of genuine contradictory feelings moment by moment. If an impulse to touch them arises, do it, even if rage is also present. By the end, this messy collision of love and anger, gratitude and resentment, hope and despair must resolve into something unexpected—perhaps forgiveness, perhaps deeper fury, perhaps a complicated acceptance that holds all of it at once.

title: The Moment You Stop Your Lover from Leaving
instruction: They're walking out the door with their bags packed, and suddenly you can't let this happen—years of careful distance and self-protection explode in a desperate, volcanic outpouring. Start loud, almost aggressive in your panic: 'Don't you dare walk out that door!' Your voice is raw power, commanding, furious that they'd give up. But as you speak, the rage fractures into naked terror. You're confessing things you swore you'd never say, your voice breaking apart: 'I'm terrified! Is that what you wanted to hear? I'm terrified of needing you this much!' The words tumble out—admissions of love, of failure, of the walls you built and why. Your fierce control shatters completely. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, voice stripped to a whisper, oscillating between begging them to stay and finding the devastating strength to let them go if they must, your love expressed in both the holding on and the potential letting go.

title: Friend Truth Telling
instruction: A friend is telling another friend something true that will damage the friendship. The speaker's voice is tight with dread. The listener's voice starts defensive. The speaker is saying what needs to be said regardless of consequence. Their voice carries both courage and grief. The listener's voice wavers as the truth lands. There's a moment where the friendship seems to end. But then the listener responds—with hurt, but also eventual honesty. By the end, the friendship might transform or end, but it will be authentic. Both voices carry the strange intimacy of truth-telling that could destroy everything.

title: Conditioning Cruel
instruction: You're remembering: being locked in the basement for crying. Being told you were ugly. Your voice is describing it clinically at first, but then it cracks. 'They did it because they could.' The realization of deliberate cruelty sits in every word. Your voice becomes a child's voice: small, hurt, still confused about why. 'I didn't deserve that,' you say, trying to convince yourself. Healing sounds like basic truth you're fighting to believe.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They've been unconscious, but suddenly their eyes open and they recognize you. Begin with desperate hope—maybe they'll recover, maybe this isn't really the end. As you speak, you realize this truly is goodbye, and you must shift from clinging to letting go. Tell them everything you need them to know, but also—and this is crucial—give them permission to leave. Your emotion must travel from frantic hope and denial to a grief-stricken but genuine release. Let your voice break where it needs to. The final words should feel like opening your hand and letting something precious fly away.

title: The Last Train Platform
instruction: You're standing on a train platform saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving forever—emigrating to a place with no return, entering witness protection, or going somewhere you'll never follow. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave and supportive, listing all the reasons this is good for them. But as the departure time approaches, your composure cracks. Let the grief break through—the reality that this is the last time crashes over you. End with desperate vulnerability, saying the things you should have said years ago, your voice breaking as you realize you're out of time. Let the transition from brave front to raw desperation happen organically, like a dam slowly cracking then bursting.
inspired_by: An Ode to a Lost Childhood

title: The Breaking Point: Screaming What Sobriety Costs You
instruction: You're alone in your car after walking away from someone you love because staying would destroy your recovery. Start by hitting the steering wheel, your voice exploding with rage at the unfairness - why can't you have both? Your voice is raw, almost screaming about what you're sacrificing, how much you love them, how viciously unfair this choice is. But as you rage, something shifts - your fury collapses into helpless sobbing. Your voice breaks completely as you admit what terrifies you: that staying would kill you, that you're not strong enough yet. End with your voice small, exhausted, trembling - speaking to them as if they could hear you, saying 'I love you' but with fierce, protective finality, your voice carrying both devastating loss and the will to survive.
inspired_by: Choosing Your Recovery Over Your Relationship

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent in their hospital room about a lifetime of emotional absence. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this speech for years. You're explaining calmly how you needed them at specific moments: your graduation, your divorce, when you lost your child. But as you list these moments, the old anger rises—sharper, rawer than you expected. Your voice grows harder, demanding answers: 'Where were you? Why wasn't I enough?' Then you see them—truly see them—frail, diminished, maybe crying. Your rage collapses into something more painful: grief for the relationship you'll never have. End not with forgiveness or reconciliation, but with brutal, honest acceptance, your voice stripped of everything but exhausted truth.

title: The Last Echo
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing alone in a vast, empty gymnasium. The metallic flutter of your own footsteps and the echo of your voice feel like ghosts. At first, you speak with doubt—your voice thin, wavering, as if testing whether the emptiness will swallow your words. You recall a memory of this place filled with laughter and squeaking sneakers, and as you share it, your voice finds a quiet, bittersweet certainty. A distant bounce of a ball interrupts you, making you pause and smile softly before continuing with newfound resolve. Let your voice carry the hollowness of the space, then warm as you connect to the memory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Laughing Through Goodbye: Last Shared Warmth Before They Leave
instruction: You're with someone you love deeply, and you're lying together, sharing warmth, but they're leaving tomorrow—for war, or a dangerous journey, or moving away forever, or entering hospice. You're both trying to be strong, making jokes, remembering funny moments, because if you stop laughing you'll start crying and never stop. Begin with genuine laughter, warm and affectionate, as you tease them about something intimate. But let the laughter crack—it becomes too high, too forced, and suddenly you're crying while still trying to laugh. Describe the physical sensation of their warmth against you while your heart is shattering. Your voice should do impossible things: express joy and devastation simultaneously, gratitude and grief in the same breath. Let contradictions live in every word—you're so happy for this moment, so destroyed that it's ending. End with a moment of transcendent peace wrapped in unbearable sadness: acknowledging that this warmth, right now, is everything, even though losing it will break you.
inspired_by: Feeling the Soothing Warmth of a Heat Pack on Sore Muscles

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally speaking to the parent who abandoned you in childhood—they're now elderly, memory failing, language slipping away. Start with rehearsed anger, the speech you've prepared for years, sharp and accusatory. But as their mind wanders and words become confused, you must find new ways to be heard—through tone, through the rhythm of your pain, through sounds of grief you've never allowed yourself. Your fury breaks apart as you realize they no longer remember leaving you. Try to make them understand through vocal desperation, through keening, through the primal sounds of a child who needed them. End not with closure but with the aching understanding that some wounds can never be explained, only mourned—your voice softening into a broken hum of forgiveness you didn't know you had.
inspired_by: Alien First Contact: The Universal Translator Breaks

title: Echoes of a Hollow Hallway
instruction: You are a young man walking alone down a long, dimly lit corridor. Your footsteps echo off the walls, and your own voice bounces back at you, elongated and strange. You're trying to hold it together after a devastating loss, but the silence between steps makes the pain impossible to ignore. Begin with a tight, forced calm, speaking to yourself as if convincing you're fine. Let your voice waver, catch on words, and trail off. As you continue, the reverb seems to mock you, and the pain breaks through — let your voice crack, become raw, and end in a choked whisper or near silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Party's Over
instruction: You're at a celebratory party after finishing a huge project, buzzing on caffeine and sugar. You're mid-sentence, gleefully telling a friend about your triumph, your voice fast and bright with elation. Then the crash hits—your energy abruptly plummets. Let your speech slow, your tone turn irritable and deflated, as if the excitement was a lie. End with a resentful sigh, maybe glancing at your empty cup, your voice heavy with the weight of the sudden low.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Late to the Appointment
instruction: You're an elderly man stuck in gridlock, reclined behind the wheel, arms tense as you grip it. Start with raw impatience—muttering at the brake lights, checking the clock, sighing loudly. Let your voice carry the irritation of being late, but also the physical strain of sitting. As you glance at the passenger seat, you remember the test results you're driving to, and the frustration slowly shifts into a heavy, quiet dread. Your words become slower, less forceful, trailing off as you stare ahead.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Thanking Your Ex at Their Wedding While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're giving a speech at your ex's wedding. Everyone knows your history. You're genuinely happy for them—and you're dying inside. Your voice must carry both truths simultaneously. Tell stories that make everyone laugh while your throat closes with grief. Express authentic gratitude for what they taught you, while acknowledging that you thought you'd be standing where their partner is. Your voice should shimmer with contradictions: joy and devastation, celebration and mourning, pride in their happiness and the knowledge that you're losing them forever. Laugh at a memory, then let that laugh catch and transform mid-sentence into something more complex. End with a toast that's both a blessing and a goodbye, finding genuine peace in your own breaking, speaking words of love that set them free and leave you utterly alone.
inspired_by: Sex Tape Recorded Years Ago, Heard for First Time Since

title: The Wired Lie
instruction: You're an older man who's had three cups of strong coffee too many. Your hands tremble as you sit at a cluttered desk, heart racing, trying to focus on a stack of documents. Your boss calls, demanding an update on a report you haven't finished because your last deadline got shifted. Start with the jittery, fast-paced, slightly desperate energy of covering your panic—words tumble out a bit too quick, pitch climbing. As you speak, the weight of the lie sinks in, and your distress peaks; your voice cracks, you lose your train of thought for a second, then rally into a quieter, more strained admission of the truth. End with a shaky, reluctant silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father across the kitchen table about something he did when you were twelve that changed everything between you. Start with the anger you've rehearsed, the accusations you've polished for years. But as you speak, notice how your carefully constructed rage starts to crack. Acknowledge out loud when you feel yourself getting scared, when the old childhood fear resurfaces, when you want to take it all back and pretend everything is fine. Don't hide behind your anger—let him see you shaking, voice breaking, struggling to stay brave enough to continue. As you push through, discover that beneath your fury is a child who just wanted to be seen. End in a place you didn't expect: not with triumph or resolution, but with the complicated truth of still loving someone who hurt you. Transform from righteous anger to vulnerable, messy honesty.

title: The Mushroom Trail of Stars
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe 7 or 8, sitting on a fallen log in a forest clearing at dusk. You've somehow eaten a bunch of little brown mushrooms, and now the trees are breathing, the ground is moving in waves, and the stars are starting to come out—but they're not where they're supposed to be. You're trying to show your dad the 'dancing' lights, but he keeps saying 'we need to go home' in a tired voice. Start with a giggly, impatient plea for him to look, then slowly realize he can't see what you see, and that he's disappointed in you for wandering off. Your voice goes from bright, rushed, and insistent to a small, hurt whisper as affection turns to sadness, and you finally say, 'I just wanted you to see them with me.'
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Disappointment (extremely present), Affection (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Telling Your Parent Who You Really Are
instruction: You're confronting a parent who never truly saw you, and you've finally found the courage to tell them who you really are and what you needed that they couldn't give. Start with a trembling attempt at calm explanation—'I need you to understand something'—but let frustration build as you recount specific moments of invisibility and misunderstanding. Your voice should surge with anger that you've suppressed for years, sharp and accusatory. Then, mid-rage, let it collapse into the voice of the child you once were, small and pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End not with resolution but with exhausted clarity, your tone hardening into self-protection as you finally stop seeking their approval, your voice steady with painful acceptance.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your ex-lover's wedding, and you stand to give a toast. You must appear joyful and generous, but as you speak, you're ambushed by contradictory feelings that you must let show through the cracks of your performance. Begin with genuine warmth for your friend's happiness, but let it bleed immediately into flashes of loss, then real joy for them mixed with grief for yourself, gratitude for what you shared, anger at what went wrong, tender memories, bitter humor, honest blessing mixed with aching longing. Don't perform a single emotion—let them surge through you in rapid succession, your voice and face shifting before you can control them. The speed prevents you from hiding. End in a moment of surprising truth—whatever emerges when you stop fighting.

title: The Final Bulletin
instruction: You are a young female news anchor, live on camera, reading a story you despise—a political figure you loathe has just been praised in a report you are forced to deliver. Your voice begins with the polished, artificial prosody of broadcast, but under it seethes malevolence and impatience. You're irritable at having to read this filth, and you let the malice creep into your tone as you stress certain words. Halfway through, you realize you're nearly done; a flicker of relief touches your voice as you reach the final line, but you catch yourself and finish with professional coldness. Let the microphone amplify your rising tension—a slight pause, a paper shuffle, a bitten-off syllable—all in character. Speak about 60 words, from 'In a statement released this afternoon...' to '...ending with congratulations to the nominee.'
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing at the Funeral
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who saved your life but whose death feels impossibly unfair—and instead of a traditional speech, you're telling the story of the night they taught you to dance when you'd forgotten how to feel joy. Start with laughter in your voice, genuinely reliving the absurdity and beauty of that moment, the music, their ridiculous moves, your resistance giving way to abandon. But as you describe the dance, tears begin mixing with the laughter—you can't separate the joy of the memory from the agony of their absence. Your voice keeps shifting: laughing, then breaking, then laughing again through tears, finding gratitude and devastation in the same breath. By the end, you're thanking them for teaching you that joy and grief can coexist, that love doesn't end when someone dies—it just changes shape. Your final words are both celebration and goodbye, somehow peaceful and heartbroken at once. Let the contradictions live fully in your voice.

title: The Hollow Peak
instruction: You are a 17-year-old boy hiding in a bathroom stall at a loud, crowded party. You’re with someone you barely know, feeling pressured to prove something. As the moment intensifies, a wave of sadness hits you—you think of the girl you actually like, who’s outside laughing with friends. Disgust crawls up your throat at the smell of cheap cologne and your own desperation. You start with forced, rhythmic breathing, but as the climax approaches, your control breaks into involuntary gasps and moans, your voice cracking with sorrow and self-loathing. Let your pitch rise sharply, words dissolving into shaky breaths and a stifled sob as you finish, then trail off into silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of your estranged sibling after their suicide attempt. It's 3 AM. Everyone else has gone home. Start with a whisper—you think they're sleeping, so you finally say what you've never been brave enough to say. Your voice is achingly tender as you confess that you've always been jealous of them, that you pushed them away because you couldn't stand seeing your own failures reflected back. Let your throat tighten with emotion you've buried for years. Speak in fragments, the way people do when they're afraid of their own truth. Then realize they're awake—they've been listening. Feel your vulnerability turn to terror: did you just make everything worse? Your voice trembles as you reach for their hand and beg them—not dramatically, but like someone who genuinely cannot survive another loss—to stay. End with breathing that could be crying or laughing or both.

title: Proudly Pleased
instruction: You are in bed with your partner during a moment of intimate affection. A playful realization hits you: they are trying something new just to make you smile, and you find it both endearing and hilariously clumsy. You feel a surge of pride in their effort and deep affection for their sweet awkwardness. Your voice mixes breathy moans of pleasure with half-laughing words, your pitch rising and falling as you try to speak between involuntary sighs. Start with a teasing chuckle, then let the pleasure vocalizations take over as you express your amused pride and gratitude. End with a soft, satisfied hum that holds both warmth and gentle laughter. Speak naturally, letting the physical sensations interrupt your thoughts.
emotions_sampled: Affection (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present), Amusement (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Professional: CEO Announces Layoffs That Destroy Livelihoods She Designed
instruction: Board meeting. You're announcing restructuring with professional detachment—it's necessary, strategic. But you designed this company culture; you know each laid-off person by name. Your voice continues with executive composure while you're simultaneously executing decisions that will echo through families. Your breathing remains controlled, but your vocal authority becomes hollow. You're professional in a way that serves no one. End with you alone after, voice breaking in a way no one hears.

title: Laughing Through Your Goodbye at the Airport
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your best friend who's moving across the world permanently—a move that will save their life (escaping danger, seeking necessary medical treatment, fleeing persecution). You're both trying to keep it light, making jokes, reminiscing about ridiculous memories that make you laugh genuinely. But the laughter keeps turning into almost-sobs that you catch and turn back into giggles. You're so grateful they're going to be safe, so happy for their chance at a real life, and simultaneously your heart is shattering because you're losing them. The contradictions pile up: you're laughing at a shared memory while tears stream down your face, you're saying 'I'm so happy for you' while your voice breaks with grief, you're smiling so hard your face hurts while telling them you don't know how to do life without them. End with the final boarding call—a moment of pure silence where all the masks drop—then you both start laughing again through tears, refusing to make it heavy, giving each other the gift of joy even in devastation. Weave laughter and sobbing together until they're indistinguishable—find the strange beauty in being completely broken and completely grateful at the same time.

title: The Wedding Speech You Can't Give
instruction: You are preparing to toast your best friend who is marrying someone you secretly know is wrong for them. Begin in false brightness, rehearsing the cheerful words. But flashes invade: their face when their last relationship ended, the lie you heard the fiancé tell, your friend's mother who died last year and would have hated this, the time you and your friend got drunk and they admitted they felt trapped. Then other shards: their genuine laughter last week, the way the fiancé looked at them yesterday, your own failed marriage, the possibility you're wrong, the memory of promising to always tell them the truth. These fragments should pummel you rapidly—love and betrayal, loyalty and honesty, hope and dread, your need to protect them and your fear of losing them. Your voice should jump between celebratory and anguished, between conviction and doubt. End in a complex place: speaking words that somehow hold all these contradictions at once, your voice breaking with love that contains both blessing and quiet mourning.

title: Dancing in the Rubble
instruction: You've just received news that your cancer is terminal—six months, maybe less—and you're telling your best friend while simultaneously planning the most audacious bucket-list adventure. Your voice oscillates wildly: laughing as you describe the absurdity of 'finally getting that time off work I always wanted,' then your laughter catches and becomes something closer to crying without ever fully tipping into tears. You're making jokes about your funeral playlist while your voice fractures with terror. You're expressing genuine excitement about being free from pretending everything's fine, while also barely holding back screams. Your tone should swing between gallows humor and raw vulnerability, gratitude for the clarity of knowing the end and rage at the unfairness. Let moments of pure joy ('We're going to live so HARD these six months!') crash directly into moments of quiet devastation ('I'm so scared'). End in a place that's somehow both—laughing and weeping simultaneously, finding weird, beautiful peace in the midst of catastrophe, your voice full of contradictions that all somehow feel completely true.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your parent the night before you leave for a remote research station in Antarctica—eighteen months with no way home, no guarantee you'll see them again. Start with forced brightness, trying to keep it light: 'So I'm all packed, everything's ready...' But your voice begins to crack. The reality hits—this might be goodbye forever. Your tone shifts to barely controlled panic: 'What if something happens to you while I'm gone? What if I never...' You can't finish. Then you hear something in their voice that steadies you. Your fear transforms into profound tenderness: 'I need you to know that every good thing I am came from you.' Pause. Breathe through tears. Your voice becomes soft, certain, filled with bittersweet peace: 'This is what you raised me to do—to be brave enough to go.' The call ends with you whispering: 'I love you' like you're memorizing the sound of your own voice saying it.

title: Midnight Scroll High
instruction: You're curled up in bed, a little tipsy, scrolling through your phone with the screen brightness low. Your voice is soft, directed downward, and you're mumbling distracted fillers as you swipe past random posts. Then you land on a video or message that makes you laugh so hard you almost drop the phone—your voice lifts, brightens, and you break into a giddy, slurred giggle. Start with a sleepy, half-focused murmur and end with a pure, drunken burst of elation. Let the intoxication slow your timing and make your words stumble into laughter.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dictation for the Lost
instruction: You're a teenager recording a dictated letter to someone you deeply miss, but you have to sound like a transcriptionist—fast, steady, monotone, speaking punctuation. You begin with determined professionalism, but as you reach a line about how you used to feel, confusion floods in. A car horn outside, a flickering light, or your own heartbeat distracts you. Your voice wavers, you lose your place, and you accidentally let longing seep through. End with a quiet, broken sentence that reveals your true emotion. Let your voice start flat and robotic, then become vulnerable and hesitant, finally fading into a whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Champagne and Ashes
instruction: You are celebrating something you've worked toward for years—a dream realized, a goal achieved. You're holding champagne, or standing in the moment of triumph. Begin with genuine joy: your voice is bright, almost giddy, laughing as you describe what you've accomplished. But someone is missing from this moment—someone who should be here, who you thought would be here. Gradually, let the laughter become brittle. Your voice stays celebratory but cracks start to show. 'We did it!' becomes 'I did it.' The pronouns shift. You keep trying to hold onto the joy, insisting on it, your voice rising as if volume will keep the grief at bay. But it doesn't work. By the end, you're furious at them for not being here AND you're overwhelmed with gratitude for what they gave you to make this possible AND you're devastated by their absence. Let these emotions fight each other in your voice: laugh-crying, shouting gratitude through tears, toasting them with a shaking hand while your voice breaks. Don't resolve it into one clean emotion. End in the beautiful, terrible mess of feeling everything at once.

title: The Accusation That Breaks the Dam
instruction: You are confronting someone who shaped your life—a parent, a former lover, a mentor who betrayed you. Start by trying to remain calm and controlled, your words measured and your body rigid with the effort of holding everything in. But there's a storm building inside your chest, a pressure that grows with every syllable. As you speak, let your voice begin to shake, not with weakness but with the sheer force of everything you've swallowed for years. Let a primal sound of rage or grief rip through you—a roar, a scream, a deep moan of anguish that shocks even you. After this release, notice how your voice changes: softer now, raw and undefended. End in a place of unexpected vulnerability, perhaps even reaching toward forgiveness or understanding, your anger transformed into something more complex and human.
inspired_by: When you are tense, anxious, or blocked before an important scene, especially on a high-pressure set

title: The Kitchen Floor Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your mother in her kitchen about why she stayed silent when you needed her most as a teenager. Begin by trying to be measured, reasonable, even kind—saying the prepared phrases you rehearsed, the diplomatic words meant to keep this civil. But after each thing you say to her, speak aloud the raw, unfiltered reaction happening inside you in that very moment—theChild-you who's still wounded, the rage you've swallowed for years, the desperate need for her to finally see you. Go back and forth between your 'adult' words and your inner truth. As the confrontation unfolds, let your inner fury and pain begin to bleed into what you say directly to her, until you can no longer maintain the pretense of civility. End in a place completely different from where you started—either in devastating honesty or unexpected understanding.

title: Screaming Protection Over a Child You Cannot Save
instruction: You're trying to protect someone—maybe your child, maybe a student, someone vulnerable—from a system, a person, a situation you're powerless against. You start fierce, almost aggressive, advocating with everything you have. Your voice is strong, demanding, unwavering. You're the protector, the fighter. But as you keep hitting walls, as you realize your words aren't enough, your strength begins to crack. Your fierce declarations start breaking apart mid-sentence. Rage bleeds into desperation. Your voice rises, almost shouting now, but it's not power anymore—it's helplessness screaming itself raw. Then suddenly, devastatingly, you collapse into something quieter: a broken whisper of 'I can't save you.' The shift is wrenching. You move from warrior to shattered human, from protective fury to the terrible admission that love isn't always enough. End with your voice trembling between rage at your own powerlessness and tender, broken apologies to the person you're failing.
inspired_by: Realizing Your Parent's Behavior Was Abusive, Not Normal

title: Protective Rage Against an Unstoppable Fate
instruction: Your younger sibling just told you they're enlisting to go to war, and you're trying to stop them but you can't. Begin with your voice rising, fierce and commanding—'No. Absolutely not. I won't let you do this.'—as if the force of your conviction can change their mind. Your words come faster, more desperate, as you list every reason they shouldn't go, your voice climbing toward something frantic. Let your protective fury explode: 'You think you're being brave? You're being stupid! They'll chew you up and spit you out!'—your voice breaking on the words, halfway between screaming and sobbing. Then suddenly collapse into raw pleading, your voice cracking completely as the anger dissolves into terror: 'I can't lose you. Please, I can't—' You're begging now, all pride abandoned, your voice thick and choked with tears. Include the moment where you grab them, your voice dropping to something urgent and broken: 'You're all I have. Don't you understand? You're all I have.' End with defeated helplessness as you realize they're going anyway—your voice becomes hollow, barely audible: 'Come home to me. Promise me you'll come home.' It's the only thing left to ask for, and you both know promises don't stop bullets.
inspired_by: After Friend Group Exclusion: The Final Text

title: The Embers of Her Triumph
instruction: You are a woman in her 40s, known for a soft, almost girlish voice that people often dismiss. Tonight, you sit by a crackling campfire, the smoke shifting in the breeze, and you are narrating the story of how you finally made a room full of powerful people listen to you. Start with a hesitant, almost apologetic tone, your voice carrying a slight tremor from the cold and the flickering light. As the story progresses, feel the memory of the moment ignite you—your pitch may rise, you might lose a word as you get caught up, and you'll gesture with a hand holding a stick. End with a quiet, fierce pride, your voice settling into a lower, richer resonance as you realize you've silenced the fire and the forest with your truth. Your spoken words should be the heart of this story, revealing the moment of victory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Supervisor Who Failed You
instruction: You're a therapist confronting your own former supervisor who missed the signs of your burnout years ago, leading to a breakdown that nearly destroyed your career. Start with carefully controlled professional language, trying to explain what their negligence cost you. But as they offer hollow apologies and deflections, your rage builds. Move from measured disappointment to searing anger, then break—suddenly—into the frightened vulnerability of who you were back then, the younger therapist who desperately needed help and got none. Let fury and grief trade places. End not with resolution but with the awful recognition that you still need their approval, even now, even after everything.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, recording your final message to your spouse and child before comms go dark permanently. Start with forced excitement about the mission's success, describing the beauty of what you're seeing, keeping your voice bright for your child. Gradually let the facade crack as you address your spouse directly—apologize for choosing this, for not being there for graduations and weddings. Your voice should break from adventurous pride into raw grief, then find a strange, quiet peace as you accept you'll never hold them again. End with a whispered 'I love you' that carries both infinite tenderness and unbearable finality. Let silences speak as much as words.

title: The Last Goodnight
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy, alone with your girlfriend in her dimly lit bedroom after her parents have gone to sleep. She just admitted she secretly paid for a flight so you can visit your dying grandmother tomorrow — something you never expected. You are inches from her face, voice dropping low, almost a whisper. Start with disbelief — a shaky, breathless catch in your throat, as if the words are just forming. As you speak, relief and gratitude swell, your voice getting fuller but still soft, intimate. Then you remember she's leaving for college in two days, and the joy curdles into a raw, cracking sadness. You pause mid-sentence, lose the thought, then finish with a strained whisper.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Inventory of Small Intimacies
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner who's asleep. Speak in barely-audible whispers, listing tiny, specific things you've noticed about them—not grand declarations, but fragments: the way their left eyebrow twitches, the sound they make when stretching, the weird thing they do with their coffee cup. Don't pick only sweet observations; let whatever comes include the irritating things, the sad things, the things that make you ache. Start with your voice controlled and quiet, but as you continue this inventory, let the emotion beneath these small noticings rise naturally. Maybe tenderness cracks into grief about time passing, or gratitude dissolves into fear of loss. Don't perform the emotion—let it catch you by surprise as you catalog these microscopic intimacies. End in a different emotional place than you began, discovered through the details themselves.

title: Laughing Through the Eulogy
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who made you laugh until you cried, and you're honoring that by telling their funniest story—but you're also shattered. Start with genuine laughter, warm and free, voice bright with the memory. 'And then they said—' You're laughing, really laughing, because the story is absurd and perfect. But the laughter keeps breaking into something else. Your voice cracks. You laugh harder, but now there's grief tangled in it. By the end, you can't tell if you're laughing or crying—both, neither, something in between. 'I miss you so much' comes out through laughter-tears, your voice simultaneously celebrating and breaking, finding joy and devastation in the exact same breath.

title: The Ceiling is My Only Friend
instruction: You're lying flat on your back on the carpet of your childhood bedroom, phone pressed to your ear, listening to your best friend tell you about their incredible new job offer in another city. You feel a heavy, helpless weight pressing down on your chest—knowing they're leaving, and you're stuck here. But as they describe the absurd office break room, a bubbling amusement rises through you, cutting through the longing, making your voice sound thick and congested from your flat position. Start with a voice that's loose, almost reverent, then let the laughter crack through the sadness like a hiccup, ending with a shaky, breathless smile.
emotions_sampled: Longing (slightly present), Helplessness (extremely present), Amusement (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Echo of a Lost Trophy
instruction: You are a teenage boy, alone on an empty theater stage after a school talent show that you just lost. Your voice is deep, forced to be hard and tough, but inside you're fuming with bitterness. Start by pacing and muttering, kicking a loose cable, feeling the sting of the applause for the winner. Project into the empty seats, letting your words bounce off the back wall as you speak to no one—but your anger cracks, revealing a raw, younger hurt. By the end, your voice softens into a defeated whisper, the bitterness fading into lonely confusion.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession in the Kitchen
instruction: It's 2 AM, and you're sitting across from your best friend at your kitchen table. You're about to tell them you're in love with them, and it's going to change everything. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, fragile and hesitant: 'There's something I need to say... and I'm terrified.' Let the vulnerability deepen as you speak—your voice catching on words, pauses filled with years of hidden feeling. You're confessing not just love but the agony of loving someone in secret, watching them date others, pretending to be fine. Your voice becomes raw with the intimacy of this moment: 'Every time you talk about someone else... it breaks something in me.' Include the moment of complete exposure, where you can barely breathe: 'I love you. I've loved you for so long.' End in the excruciating silence that follows—your voice small, resigned to loss: 'I understand if everything just changed.'

title: The Moment You Realize You've Become What You Hate
instruction: You're in the middle of defending your actions—maybe you've hurt someone, crossed a line, done something unforgivable—and your voice is defiant, almost aggressive, justifying everything with cold logic. But mid-sentence, you hear yourself, and horror floods in. Your voice fractures as realization hits: you sound exactly like the person who once hurt you. The defiance collapses into something raw and terrible—your voice rising with panicked self-disgust, words tumbling out faster, angrier, but now the anger is aimed inward. You're raging and sobbing simultaneously, your voice breaking apart as you recognize the monster you've become. The fury gives way to something more desperate—pleading, maybe with yourself, maybe with whoever is listening. Your voice becomes ragged, exhausted, as if the weight of this realization is crushing you. By the end, you're speaking in a broken whisper, your voice stripped of all defense, raw with shame and a desperate, helpless question: 'How did I become this?'

title: The Accusation That Breaks You Both
instruction: You're confronting your teenage child who's spiraling into self-destruction, and you're terrified. Start with controlled parental authority—firm, clear boundaries, the voice of someone who still believes they can fix this through force of will. As they hurl back everything you've failed at, feel your voice escalate to something raw and uncontrolled—not just anger but fear so profound it comes out as rage. Scream the words you swore you'd never say, then immediately shatter into something else entirely. Let your voice crack and collapse mid-sentence as you realize you're losing them, that your fury is pushing them further away. End with desperate, broken pleading—your authority completely gone, replaced by the voice of someone begging the person they love most not to destroy themselves. Move from power to absolute helplessness, your final words choked with tears, reduced to simply repeating 'please' because you've run out of everything else.
inspired_by: The Lawyer and the Unreliable Witness

title: Three AM Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love, in complete darkness, at three in the morning. You cannot sleep because you're carrying a secret that's poisoning you from the inside. Begin by whispering about insomnia, about small things, your voice barely audible. Let the darkness give you permission to say what daylight never could. Confess something you've done, something shameful or terrifying or so tender you've hidden it even from yourself. title: What I Never Said in the Hospital

instruction: You're at a house party, drunk, in a bedroom with someone you've been flirting with all night. title: The Last Permission

title: Breaking Open the Thunder
instruction: You're running—actually running in place, physically moving—after being told news that simultaneously destroys and liberates you. title: Stop Hiding Behind Maybes
instruction: Your partner confronts you after years of vague promises and beautiful-sounding plans that never materialize. They're exhausted, sitting across from you with tears they've already cried. title: Bedside Confessions at 3 AM
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner, confessing something you can never say when they're awake—maybe that you're sick and haven't told them, maybe that you're leaving, maybe that you've known a secret about them all along. title: The Last Sour Lemonade
instruction: You're a child, maybe 9 or 10, sitting on a kitchen stool, a half-sucked lemon wedge still in your hand from a prank you pulled on yourself. title: The Inheritance of Silence

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your ex-lover's wedding, standing to give a toast. You're genuinely happy for them—you truly are—but you're also breaking inside. title: The Burning Letter
instruction: You're holding a handwritten letter from someone who abused you as a child. They're asking for forgiveness now that they're dying. You've decided to burn it. title: The Crest Between Waves

title: The Homecoming Paradox
