speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Elevator Pitch for Your Life to God
instruction: You're dead, in an elevator with God (whoever that is to you), and you have the ride up to justify your existence. Start confident: 'So, basically, I—' God says nothing. The silence forces honesty. Strip away the resume, the achievements, the excuses. What's left? The real pitch emerges: small kindnesses, moments of genuine connection, the time you could have walked away but didn't. Your voice should evolve from salesman to confessor to genuinely curious: 'Was it enough?' The elevator dings.

title: Euphoric Breakdown
instruction: Youre feeling overwhelmed by an intense surge of emotions that make no sense to youboth euphoric and terrifying. Let your voice slip between laughter, panic, and even tears. Each shift should be sudden, as though youre on an emotional rollercoaster you dont fully understand.

title: Whispering a Secret You've Carried Alone for Years
instruction: Late at night, in near darkness, you are finally telling your partner, sibling, or closest friend something you've never spoken aloud—a shame you've carried, a fear that haunts you, a truth about who you really are that you've hidden even from yourself. Begin with halting words, long pauses, your voice barely above a whisper because saying it aloud makes it real. Let the vulnerability be physical: your breath shallow, your throat tight, perhaps your hands trembling. As you continue, feel the relief of releasing this secret warring with the terror of being seen this naked. Move from shame-filled secrecy into the trembling openness of letting someone truly know you. End with a kind of fragile peace, still scared but no longer alone with this truth, your final words soft but no longer hiding.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, about to give a toast. You're happy for them—genuinely, deeply happy. You're also devastated because you've been in love with them for years and never said anything. Now it's too late. As you stand with the champagne glass, start from the genuine joy you feel seeing them radiant. Let that be real. Then, as you speak about your history together, about who they are, allow the other truth to surface—the one you can never speak aloud. Let both emotions exist simultaneously: celebration and heartbreak, generosity and loss, love that wants their happiness and love that's dying inside you. Don't choose one over the other or perform either. Let your voice carry both the brightness of the occasion and the fractures underneath. Maybe a memory catches you mid-sentence. Maybe laughter turns into something else in your throat. By the end, you've given them a beautiful gift while privately saying goodbye to a future you'll never have.

title: The Last Teaching Before the Crossing
instruction: You are an elder on your deathbed, speaking your final words to your fiercely independent grandchild who has always rejected your guidance. Begin with quiet, measured wisdom, offering one last lesson they've refused to hear. As you sense time slipping away, your voice becomes more urgent, more vulnerable—you're not commanding now, you're pleading. Let your carefully maintained composure crack. Switch to the grandchild's voice: begin with defensive anger, that familiar wall of resistance, but as you realize this is truly goodbye, let that wall shatter. Your voice breaks. The rebellion drains away, replaced by raw grief and desperate regret for all the conversations you never had. End in a whispered apology that comes too late, your throat tight with unshed tears.
inspired_by: The Elder and the Young Rebel

title: Town Crier at the End of the World
instruction: You're a medieval town crier who must announce the apocalypse. Use the traditional elongated vowel delivery to carry across the square: 'Hear ye! Hear ye!' But instead of market prices, you're announcing the end of everything. Start with professional bellowing, but as the content sinks in, your own announcement terrifies you. The projecting town-crier voice cracks into a normal, scared human one. End with a quiet 'God save us all' that you mean personally.

title: The Last Conversation with What Could Have Been
instruction: You are alone in your childhood bedroom, hours before it's sold forever. You're speaking to the version of yourself who never left this town—the artist you could have been, the dreamer who got buried under responsibilities. Start with gentle curiosity, almost playful, as you ask them questions. Gradually, let regret seep in as they answer with all the passion and hope you've lost. Your voice should crack as you realize you're not talking to an imaginary person—you're mourning the death of your own unlived life. End in a whisper, half-apology, half-farewell, as you say goodbye to who you'll never be. Let the silence at the end hold all the weight of permanent loss.
inspired_by: The Parent and the Imaginary Friend

title: Demolishing the Studio
instruction: You're alone in the art studio/workshop/office where you've spent ten years creating work that no one values, pursuing a dream that has slowly strangled your finances, relationships, and sense of self. Today you've decided to destroy it all. Start throwing, breaking, tearing. Let your body move with full physical commitment—real exertion, real breathlessness. Begin with pure rage: guttural sounds, sharp breaths, the satisfaction of destruction. But as your body tires and you see the wreckage around you, feel the rage transform into grief, then into something more complicated—a weird, hysterical laughter mixed with sobbing, the physical release of years of hope and disappointment. End on the floor amid the debris, your voice ragged and raw, perhaps laughing and crying simultaneously, your body spent, finally able to breathe even as you're breaking.
inspired_by: When directing a play with extended rehearsal time and experiential methods

title: Shattered Control
instruction: You are the dominant partner in a BDSM scene, but your submissive has just used their safeword in a way that alarms you. Start by asking what happened with your usual low, steady, clipped command – but as you see genuine fear or pain in their eyes, your voice begins to shake. The distress rises fast: your breaths shorten, you hesitate mid-sentence, and your tone loses its commanding edge, becoming almost pleading by the end. Say only a few lines, but let the crack in your control be heard as you shift from demanding answers to desperately needing reassurance.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Astronaut's Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission, recording a final message to your partner back on Earth. Begin with forced cheerfulness, pointing out constellations you can see, making jokes about the view. But as you talk, the reality that you'll never touch them again seeps in. Your voice starts to shake when you remember the smell of their hair, the weight of their hand in yours. Let the vastness of space press against your chest—breathe through the panic of infinite silence. By the end, you're whispering promises you can't keep, your voice raw with longing and acceptance, telling them it's okay to love someone else, even as the words shatter you.

title: The Fort Plan
instruction: You're in a softly lit, carpeted bedroom with your young child. You've been trying to build a pillow fort together, but the kid keeps collapsing the structure with giggles. Start with genuine amusement — a warm, rumbling laugh as you catch a pillow that falls. Let your voice sound rich and relaxed, absorbing the quiet room. Then, as you adjust a blanket and see the child's eager eyes, shift into hopeful, optimistic encouragement — your tone becomes lighter, more aspirational. Your speech should have natural pauses: you might hear a distant car, or the child fidgets. Speak about the great adventures you'll have once the fort is finished, letting your hope lift the final words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Mission Control Confession
instruction: You're a mission control operator speaking to your estranged parent who is the astronaut in crisis. For years, you've maintained professional distance because of childhood wounds—their absence, their choice of stars over you. Now they're dying in space and you're the only one on comms. Start with clipped, procedural language, refusing to break protocol or acknowledge the relationship. But as they plead with you to just talk to them as your parent, let your professional armor crack. Unleash the rage you've carried—the missed birthdays, the loneliness, the feeling of never being enough to make them stay. Then let that anger collapse into something raw and broken: the terrified child who still needs their parent, who isn't ready to say goodbye. End with a whispered admission of love you swore you'd never give them.

title: Adult Child Confronting Parent Who Chose Addiction Over Them
instruction: Your parent is two years sober, finally. You've come to their small apartment to say what you've needed to say for twenty years. Start with controlled anger—you've rehearsed this, you won't be derailed by tears or apologies. Methodically list the birthdays they missed, the times you lied to teachers about bruises, the night you were twelve and called 911. But as you speak, something cracks. The anger doesn't disappear—it transforms into something more dangerous: the raw, undefended grief of the child you were. Your voice breaks not into sobs but into something quieter, more devastating. By the end, you're not yelling anymore. You're asking the question you've always been too afraid to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stop?' Let the last words come out barely above a whisper.
inspired_by: Judge Must Sentence Someone for Loving Their Child

title: The Sweater That Still Smells Like Them
instruction: Alone in your bedroom at 3 AM, you've pulled your ex-lover's sweater from the back of your closet - the one they left behind six months ago. Begin by barely touching it, folded on your lap, your body rigid with the effort of not falling apart. Whisper to the empty room as if they could hear you: the things you never said, the apology that's too late. As you slowly pull the sweater closer, feel its specific texture - is it cashmere, wool, cotton? Feel its weight. When you finally press the fabric against your face, let the sensation of softness against your skin, the ghost of their scent still clinging to the fibers, dissolve your defenses. Let your whispered words become not an apology but a raw, quiet admission: that you still ache for the physical presence of them, for the specific comfort of this texture that once touched their body. End holding the sweater against your chest, your breathing synchronized with clutching it, no longer speaking - just feeling what it means to hold something that held them.
inspired_by: Objects that Come into Contact with the Body (Choice Approach)

title: The Wedding Ring in Your Palm
instruction: You're holding the engagement ring your late spouse gave you, one year after their death, deciding whether to finally take it off. Begin breathless with resistance—your chest tight, breath caught high in your throat, gripping the ring, torn between loyalty and the need to live again. As you speak to your lost love, let each breath gradually deepen and expand downward through your body—first into your chest, then your belly, then all the way to the ground beneath your feet. With this deepening breath comes a deepening emotional complexity: gratitude mixing with guilt, love mixing with anger at being left, hope mixing with grief. By the end, your breath is full and slow, your body a complete vessel holding all these contradictions at once. You slip the ring off not from betrayal but from breath-filled, embodied acceptance of life's terrible, beautiful both/and.

title: Reading Deceased Spouse's Secret Gratitude Journal About You
instruction: Three months after the funeral, you find their hidden journal. Every entry is about you—small moments they cherished that you never knew mattered. Start reading aloud with curiosity. Then your voice catches because they wrote about the morning you burned breakfast and laughed instead of crying—the day they knew they'd love you forever. You're laughing and sobbing simultaneously, your voice breaking between joy at being so deeply seen and devastation that you'll never get to thank them. Each entry reveals you were their peace while you thought you were their burden. End in a whisper, telling them you understand now, your voice filled with gratitude and grief so intertwined you can't separate them. The last words are 'thank you,' spoken to empty air.
inspired_by: Historical: Berlin Wall Communicant Realizes the Guard Is Their Sister

title: Held Hostage by Hope
instruction: Your child is missing and you've just received a call—maybe a lead, maybe nothing. You start fierce, almost manic: 'Tell me everything. Every single detail. NOW.' Your voice is command and desperation tangled together. But as you listen to the vague, uncertain information, the ferocity cracks. 'No, no, you don't understand—she's FIVE. She has a blue rabbit, she—' and suddenly you're shouting through tears, protective rage collapsing into absolute helplessness. Your voice breaks apart completely: 'I can't... I can't do this anymore...' before surging back with renewed, almost violent hope: 'But you'll keep looking? PROMISE ME.' By the end, you're cycling between fury at your own powerlessness and broken pleas, your voice raw, shredded. The arc is from fierce maternal/paternal ferocity to devastating vulnerability to a kind of wild, desperate hope that sounds almost like madness.

title: Cascade of Laughter and Letdown
instruction: You're in bed with a partner after a second unexpected climax. You're trying to joke about losing control, but your voice is already hoarse and breathy. With each new wave hitting without warning, your amusement falters into a deeper, self-conscious disappointment—you wanted to hold out longer, to be 'stronger.' Let your voice crack, your breath stutter, and your laughter turn ragged as words fail you. By the end, you can only manage a broken whisper that mixes disbelief, embarrassment, and a flicker of wry acceptance.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Visit Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your younger sibling who's deploying to a war zone tomorrow, knowing they might not return. You start trying to be strong, maybe even joking about their training or teasing them like always. But as you look at them, something breaks. Your voice falters mid-sentence. You try to say something profound about being careful, about coming home, but instead what comes out is raw and small: 'I need you to know I've always looked up to you.' The admission surprises even you. Your throat tightens. The goodbye transforms from forced bravery into something unbearably tender—a whispered promise to be there when they return, even as fear tells you they might not. Let your voice crack. Let silence do some of the work.

title: The Old Bear's Secret
instruction: You are an elderly man with a rugged, deep voice, huddled with your oldest friend in a quiet corner. You're about to share something you've never told anyone — a secret that has filled you with a young, foolish hope. Start with a gruff, hesitant whisper, as if admitting a weakness, but let the words tumble out faster as the joy builds. By the end, your voice should rise with elation and ecstasy, almost laughing as you speak of the future you never dared to dream of. Let the excitement crack through your usual reserve, and include natural pauses, breaths, and the way you might touch your friend's arm for emphasis.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Elation (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Fever Dream of Letting Go
instruction: You are in the grip of intense physical sensation—fever, exhaustion after childbirth, aftermath of an accident, the peak of intimate passion—your body is overwhelming your control. In this state, you're also releasing a burden you've carried for years: shame about your body, grief over a miscarriage, rage at someone who hurt you, fear that has controlled your choices. Let the physical sensations crack you open. Start with resistance—trying to maintain composure even as your body rebels, breathing hard, voice shaking. Then let the physical intensity give you permission to release what you've held back. Your voice should become raw, unguarded, primal. Build to a moment where the physical and emotional pain/pleasure/release become indistinguishable, your words fragmenting into sounds, gasps, maybe laughter or sobs or both. End in the aftermath: voice hoarse, body spent, but something fundamentally lighter. Move from controlled resistance to complete surrender to unexpected peace.

title: Confronting the Ghost in the Kitchen
instruction: You're confronting your father in your childhood kitchen about why he abandoned the family twenty years ago. Begin in THIS moment—wherever you actually are—feeling anger and rehearsed accusations. But as you speak, deliberately summon the EXACT kitchen from your childhood: the avocado-green refrigerator, the crack in the linoleum by the stove, the smell of his coffee brewing at 5am, the weight of the winter air coming through the badly sealed window, the sound of the radio always tuned to AM news. Feel yourself becoming smaller, younger, more vulnerable as that kitchen materializes around you. Let your anger crack open to reveal the bewildered eight-year-old underneath. Your voice should shift from adult rage to a child's confused pain. End not with accusations, but with the simple, devastating question you could never ask then: 'Didn't you love us?'
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill a time-and-place obligation where the actual stage environment is inadequate or wrong for the scene

title: The Body Remembers
instruction: You are alone, and a sudden sensory trigger—a scent, a sound, a texture—throws your body back into a moment of intense physical experience from your past: first love, an assault, childbirth, a fight, ecstatic pleasure, unbearable pain. Let your body respond before your mind can censor: gasping, recoiling, reaching, moaning, shaking. Don't narrate or explain—inhabit the physical memory completely, letting sounds escape that aren't words, letting your face contort or soften without controlling it, letting your breath become ragged or desperate or hungry. Allow the sensation to build to something almost unbearable—pleasure or pain so intense it could be either. Then, as you return to the present moment, let the emotional aftermath wash through: tears, laughter, rage, tenderness, or a complicated mix. End by speaking one raw sentence about what that memory means to your body now.

title: What We Whisper in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your closest friend who doesn't know you're in love with them. They've just confided something that breaks your heart—they're moving away, or marrying someone else, or leaving for reasons that will separate you forever. Speak softly, barely above a whisper, as if raising your voice might shatter this fragile moment. Start by comforting them about their news, your voice gentle and supportive even as something inside you dies. Let pauses speak volumes. Your throat should tighten around words you can't say. Midway through, allow one truth to slip out—something small, careful, that hints at deeper feelings without fully revealing them. End with a tender blessing for their future, your voice thick with unshed tears, giving them permission to go while your heart screams for them to stay.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Busy to Avoid a Conversation

title: The Last Phone Call: Saying Goodbye to Someone Who Won't Remember You Tomorrow
instruction: You're calling someone with advancing dementia—your parent, your first love, your closest friend—knowing this might be the last conversation where they truly know who you are. Start with forced brightness, trying to keep things light and normal. But as they begin to slip, forgetting mid-sentence why you called or who you are to them, your voice cracks. You're memorizing the sound of their voice, trying to hold onto every word while simultaneously letting them go. Move from cheerful denial through quiet devastation to a kind of tender acceptance. Your final "I love you" contains both everything you want to say and the knowledge that tomorrow, you'll be a stranger. Let the pauses speak. Let your breath catch. This is grief for someone still living.
inspired_by: Professional: Journalist Kills a Story About Someone They Love

title: Trying to Confess Your Affair in a Nightclub
instruction: The music is deafening. You're screaming at your partner, trying to tell them something crucial, but they can't hear you. You watch their lips move, smiling, dancing, oblivious. Your voice becomes desperate, nearly incoherent as you try to shout the truth. Include the moment you realize they're never going to hear you over the noise—and maybe that's why you chose here, where the confession dies before it reaches their ears. Your voice breaks as you give up trying, and you just stand there in the darkness of the club, shouting words that disappear.

title: A Flicker in the Archive
instruction: You are an elderly man dictating a family history for a transcription service. Your voice is steady, fast, and monotone, speaking punctuation aloud—'comma', 'period'. You begin reciting a dry list of dates and names. Midway, you stumble slightly on a detail: 'great-uncle Edward who disappeared in 1923 period.' A faint curiosity rises—you pause, clear your throat, and the tone lifts just a fraction as you say 'Or was it 1924 question mark.' Then you catch yourself, mutter 'no matter,' and resume the flat dictation rhythm. Let the interest be a tiny, fleeting warmth that barely breaks the surface, as if your aging mind momentarily snags on a memory before smoothing over.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Offering of Grace
instruction: You are standing at the pulpit of a small, wood-paneled church on a Sunday morning. The congregation is quiet, expectant. You begin by recalling a painful loss from the past year — a friend, perhaps — and your voice carries a slight, genuine sadness as you describe the weight of that grief. Midway, you feel a shift: the memory of how the community wrapped around you, meals brought, prayers whispered. Let your voice soften into thankfulness, the cadence becoming more rhythmic, almost a lullaby of gratitude. As you finish, a quiet pride emerges — not boastful, but a warm confidence in the resilience of these people and your own faith. Pause naturally between phrases, let the microphone catch your breaths, and allow the occasional cough or rustle of paper to remind you this is real.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Approaching Storm
instruction: You are the town crier, an older woman with a voice that has carried warnings for decades. Stand in the market square, the wind picking up, the distant smell of smoke. Your first cry is tight with fear—you saw the flames from the hill, and you're not sure the villagers will believe you. As you call out, the fear shifts into fierce urgency; you must make them move. Let your voice crack and strain, stretch the vowels as if throwing them across the square. Pause between phrases to scan the faces, to swallow, to breathe. End with a raw, commanding plea, not a scream but a trembling resolve.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Welcome Ending
instruction: You are saying goodbye to a relationship that has been both your greatest joy and deepest source of pain—and for the first time, you are choosing to leave while still loving them. Begin with laughter breaking through tears, the absurd relief of finally making this impossible choice mixing with genuine grief. Your voice should contain multitudes: gratitude for who they helped you become, sorrow for the future you're releasing, anger at what couldn't be healed, and underneath it all, a surprising current of hope. Let these emotions crash into each other—laughing one moment, voice breaking the next, then fierce and strong. Don't resolve into just one feeling; stay in the beautiful, terrible complexity of loving someone and still saying no. End with a voice that somehow holds both heartbreak and liberation, your final words blessing them even as you walk away, free.

title: Compulsory Speech
instruction: Court-ordered apology to the family you hurt while driving drunk. You're reading a script, voice flat and resentful. Their daughter in a wheelchair in the front row. The script suddenly breaks in your throat—you can't keep reading. You look up, actually look at them. Your voice cracks into something genuine and destroyed: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' No more script. Just raw, unforgivable truth. By the end, you're barely coherent, tears screwing up the microphone.

title: Screaming Truth at the Ocean
instruction: You're alone at the water's edge after devastating news—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a loss so complete it's broken something inside you. Begin with fierce, defiant shouting at the universe: 'You don't get to do this!' Your voice is raw power and fury. But mid-rage, something collapses—the anger fractures into sobs, fierce declarations dissolve into helpless pleading. Your voice becomes a storm of contradictions: rage and terror, defiance and surrender, screaming strength that crumbles into whispered vulnerability. End on your knees, voice hoarse and small: 'I don't know how to survive this.' Let each emotional wave crash over the last, natural and uncontrolled.
inspired_by: Breaking Up With Someone You Still Love

title: Waiting in the Blazing Sun
instruction: You are standing in an empty parking lot at midday. The heat is unbearable—a dry, shimmering haze. You've been waiting for over an hour for someone who promised to meet you. Your throat is parched, your skin slick with sweat, and each breath feels like inhaling from an oven. Begin speaking to yourself, full of fragile hope: you really believed they'd come. Let your voice be slow, strained, punctuated by heavy sighs and pauses as you wipe sweat from your eyes. As you realize they're not coming, let the longing curdle into sour resentment. End with a quiet, bitter laugh—tired and defeated—as you finally turn to leave.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner who you believe is asleep. In a whisper barely louder than breath, you begin to confess something you've never said aloud—a fear, a shame, a secret that defines you. Start tentative, testing whether the darkness is safe enough. As you continue speaking into the silence, let the relief of finally naming this truth wash through you. Then realize they're awake and have been listening the entire time. In the excruciating silence that follows, stay present to being fully seen—no explaining, no taking it back, no defending. End in the terrifying openness of having been witnessed without knowing yet how they'll respond. Move from hidden shame to exposed vulnerability.

title: The Last Time
instruction: You're making love to someone for the last time, and you both know it, though neither of you has said it aloud. Begin with whatever physical sensation draws you—desire, hunger, the desperate need to memorize their body. But let other feelings ambush you: sudden grief in the middle of passion, rage at the unfairness breaking through tenderness, or laughter at an inopportune moment because your system doesn't know how else to process loss. Don't perform each emotion separately—let them crash into each other. Maybe you're kissing them and suddenly you're crying. Maybe pleasure and pain become indistinguishable. Maybe you find yourself whispering their name like a goodbye, or maybe words fail entirely and your breath has to carry everything. The challenge is to let your body experience contradictory sensations simultaneously, without organizing them into a neat emotional performance.

title: Compromised Position
instruction: You discover the email chain where your closest collaborator took credit for your work. The shock hits first—your voice sharp, almost a gasp. But then it's betrayal, raw and physical: you have to sit down. Your words become accusatory, but there's also a desperate plea underneath: 'How could you do this to me? I trusted you.' By the end, you're calling them—it goes to voicemail—and you sound completely shattered.

title: Anticipation Growing
instruction: The moment is approaching. Your voice gets tighter, more controlled, not from fear but from focused attention. Each word becomes more deliberate: 'Any second now.' Breathing is controlled, shallow. There's a physical tension that translates vocally—everything is poised. As anticipation peaks, your voice gets higher, more compressed. Physical: muscles tensed. 'I can hear them coming.' The voice is focused like a beam of light. By the moment it arrives, you're almost vibrating with readiness. The vocal quality is pure, focused attention.

title: The Kitchen Floor Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your adult child/parent in the kitchen where you've had a thousand superficial conversations. Start by naming everything that's making this hard: the way you're both standing, how your voice sounds false, what you think they're thinking of you, your fear of their reaction. Speak aloud your awareness of performing this confrontation rather than living it. As you continue, let the act of naming your own self-consciousness and artificiality become the confrontation itself—your scripted anger giving way to something messier and more real. End in a place you didn't plan to reach: perhaps unexpected grief, or vulnerability, or a truth neither of you saw coming. The emotional journey moves from defended accusation to undefended revelation.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your parent's bedside in their final hours. For your entire life, you felt you never measured up to their expectations, never heard them say they were proud of you. Begin speaking from a place of quiet desperation, needing their approval one last time. As you talk, something shifts—you start telling them about your own life, your own victories they never acknowledged, and you realize you're no longer asking for permission to feel worthy. By the end, you're giving yourself the validation you always sought from them, speaking with growing strength and self-possession even as you say goodbye. Let your voice transform from pleading to self-assured, from child to adult, from asking to claiming.
inspired_by: Actor has chronic self-esteem problems that return every time they act or audition

title: The Threshold Confession
instruction: You're lingering at the door of your best friend's house, supposedly leaving, but carrying a secret that's suffocating you: you're in love with them, and they're getting married next month. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, finding excuse after excuse not to leave—'Wait, I forgot to tell you about...'—while terror and tenderness war inside you. Let the pauses grow heavy with everything unsaid. Finally, in a moment so quiet it almost disappears, you begin to confess, then stop yourself, voice catching. The words come in fragments, terrified and aching. End with the unbearable intimacy of almost saying everything and choosing silence instead, your goodbye so tender it's almost a physical pain. Every breath should carry the weight of love you'll never speak aloud.
inspired_by: The Incredibly Long Goodbye at the Door

title: The Last Light Through Hospital Glass
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's sleeping, breathing shallow. You watch the first sunlight come through the window and land on her hand. Start by simply observing her—calm, preparing yourself to stay strong. Then notice specific details: the paper-thin quality of her skin, how small her hand looks, the precise shade of the morning light on her fingers. Let yourself remember her hands doing something years ago—cooking, braiding your hair, whatever comes. As these details accumulate, allow the wall you've built to crack. By the end, you're whispering everything you never said, knowing she might hear you even in sleep. Move from composed observation to raw, unguarded confession as the sensory details dismantle your defenses.

title: The Truth in Your Hands
instruction: You're confronting your father about a lie that shaped your childhood. Begin angry and accusatory, your body tense. But as you look at him—really look—start noticing the sensory reality of him now: the tremor in his hands he's trying to hide, the way his shoulders have collapsed, the gray in his hair you hadn't registered before, how much smaller he seems than in your memories. As these physical details break through your rage, feel your anger complicate into something more painful—recognition that he's human, fragile, aging. The more you see the actual person in front of you rather than the giant from your past, the more your fury transforms into grief mixed with reluctant, aching compassion. End in a whisper, your whole body softened by what you've actually seen.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner After a Miscarriage
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner is finally asleep after days of devastation. You're speaking in the softest whisper, afraid to wake them but needing to say things you can't say when they're looking at you. Start with tender observation—'Your face looks peaceful right now... I'm glad'—your voice barely audible, catching on unshed tears. Confess the things you've been holding back: how scared you are, how you don't know how to comfort them when you're breaking too, how you keep seeing the future you'd imagined. Your whisper becomes even quieter, more fragile: 'I don't know how to stop hurting for both of us.' There's intimacy in this one-sided conversation, love threaded through devastation. End with a promise that's also a plea, your voice trembling: 'We'll find our way through this... won't we?' The question hangs in the dark, vulnerable and desperate and so deeply human. Let silence speak as much as words.

title: Dancing at Your Funeral
instruction: You're recording a video message to be played at your own funeral—you have weeks to live and want to say goodbye on your terms. Start laughing, genuinely, as you imagine people's faces: 'If you're crying right now, stop it. I specifically requested—' But the laughter keeps breaking into something else, a sob disguised as a chuckle. Joke about your illness ('Turns out I'm not immortal. Spoiler alert'), then let your voice crack with sudden, fierce gratitude: 'But god, what a ride.' The emotions should swirl—defiant joy, then piercing grief, then back to laughter that's soaked in tears. End with the most peaceful, grateful whisper, even as your voice trembles: 'Thank you. For all of it. Even the hard parts.' The challenge is to embody someone who's genuinely at peace with dying while simultaneously heartbroken to leave, finding beauty and humor and devastating sadness all mixed together.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're writing or rehearsing what you'd want said at your funeral, and it starts serious—measured, meaningful, legacy-focused. But then something shifts and you start finding it absurdly funny, the whole presumption of it, and you're laughing even as tears are streaming down your face. Your voice should carry both the laughter and the ache, genuine amusement at life's ridiculous brevity mixed with devastating awareness of everything you'll miss. You're marveling at small things you're grateful for—coffee, your dog's face, that one perfect afternoon—and each one makes you laugh harder and cry deeper. The joy and grief should be completely entangled, inseparable. End in a strange place of peace, voice quiet and wondering, maybe even playful, accepting something you can't control but finding odd comfort in having really, truly lived.
inspired_by: Therapist Hears Her Client Describe Her Own Trauma

title: Lying About Where You Were and Contradicting Yourself
instruction: Your partner is asking where you were. You're lying. Your voice starts confident—'I was at the gym'—but then they ask a detail you didn't prepare for. Your voice hesitates. You're building the lie as you talk. You start contradicting yourself—'No wait, I went to get coffee first—' Your voice is now tight, defensive. You're clearly lying and your voice betrays you completely. Include the moment they stop asking because they already know.

title: The Archaeology of Your Hands
instruction: Late at night, you are with someone you love, and you're whispering a confession you've never told anyone—something about yourself that fills you with shame or fear. But instead of rushing through it or hiding, you hold their hand or touch their face as you speak. Begin tentative, your voice barely audible, eyes down. As you confess, study their hand in yours, or their face in the dim light—trace with your eyes every line, every detail, every micro-reaction. Let your curiosity about them become an anchor that pulls you out of your self-consciousness. Notice how they're breathing, where tension lives in their jaw, what their fingers do as they listen. Allow this deep observation to quiet your fear, transforming your whispered shame into whispered intimacy. Your voice should shift from tight and scared to soft and present, as if the act of truly witnessing them witnessing you creates a safety you've never felt before. End with your confession complete, but your focus entirely on them—seeing them see you.

title: Dancing Alone at the Funeral
instruction: You've returned to the beach where you scattered your beloved's ashes, and you're dancing barefoot in the sand because that's what they would have wanted—but your heart is shattering. Begin describing the sensation of dancing, how the sand shifts with each movement, how your feet create patterns that the tide will soon erase. Your voice should be light at first, almost laughing, as you remember how they loved to dance here, how ridiculous and free you both were. But as you move and speak, let grief break through the joy—describe how the sand feels heavier now, how your legs feel weaker, how you're dancing and crying at the same time. Your tone should oscillate between laughter and sobs, between celebrating their life and mourning their absence. Express gratitude for having known them while your voice breaks with the pain of losing them. End with you still moving, still describing the sand and the steps, but your words becoming simpler, more breathless, as you find a strange, bittersweet peace in the contradiction—devastated yet grateful, destroyed yet somehow still dancing.

title: The Last Call
instruction: You are slumped against the steering wheel after a crash. Your hand is pressed to a deep gash in your thigh, blood soaking through your jeans and pooling on the floor. You’re on the phone with 911, but your voice starts sharp and desperate—shouting your location, begging them to hurry. As the blood loss deepens, you feel a creeping numbness, and the sight of your own blood makes you nauseous. Let your words slow, slur, and fragment. You trail off mid-sentence, then force yourself to finish with a hollow, fading whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Seared Victory
instruction: You're a 7-year-old boy at a backyard barbecue, determined to prove you can flip burgers like the grown-ups. You're gripping the metal spatula too close to the flame, feeling the heat but refusing to let go—you've just flipped the perfect patty, and it landed with a triumphant sizzle. As you step back in pride, the side of your hand accidentally presses against the hot grill grate. The hiss of pain escapes through your teeth, but you're grinning through it—you got the burger right. You're desperate not to cry in front of your dad and his friends, so you try to laugh it off, but your voice wavers between a triumphant cheer, a pained hiss, and an embarrassed whimper as you shake your hand out, still clutching the spatula.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're speaking to someone who hurt you deeply—a lover who left, a friend who betrayed you, a parent who failed you—but time has revealed that their departure or betrayal was somehow necessary for who you became. Begin with genuine gratitude, almost light, maybe even with gentle laughter, explaining what their absence taught you. But as you speak, the old wounds start bleeding through your words. Your voice catches. The gratitude and the grief start dancing together—you mean the thank you, but God, it still hurts. You're laughing and your voice is breaking at the same time. You keep switching between appreciation for the growth and mourning for what was lost. End in a moment of bittersweet peace, where your voice holds both the joy of who you are now and the ache for who you might have been if they'd stayed. Make every word feel like it's costing you something while also setting you free.
inspired_by: Realizing You Became What You Hated

title: Reading Your Stillborn Baby a Bedtime Story
instruction: You're alone in a hospital room, holding your baby who didn't survive birth. You've decided to read them the bedtime story you'd chosen months ago. Start with an almost eerie calm, trying to perform normalcy, reading in the gentle sing-song voice you'd practiced. Your voice should be tender but fragile, like glass about to shatter. Gradually, the reality seeps in—your words slow, catching on certain phrases about 'tomorrow' and 'growing up.' Let the children's book words become unbearable. Trail off mid-sentence. Whisper an apology. Then, gathering yourself with devastating gentleness, finish the story, your voice barely audible, because this is the only story you'll ever get to read them.
inspired_by: Haunted House Actor Who Takes It Too Seriously

title: Shade and Sunlight
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl who has just collapsed under a tree after running in extreme heat. Your head is pounding, you're panting, and sweat drips down your face. You're exhausted and dizzy, but then you see someone you've had a crush on walking toward you with a bottle of water. At first, your voice is slow and heavy from the heatstroke — each word is an effort, broken by gasps. But as you realize who it is, your tone changes: relief mixes with a flutter of nervous excitement. You try to act casual, but your voice wavers. Speak naturally, with pauses, heavy breathing, and the subtle shift from drained exhaustion to a shy, infatuated lightness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's slipping away. Begin by noticing everything around you with excruciating detail—the texture of her hand, the smell of the room, the sound of her breathing, the morning light creeping through the blinds. Stay grounded in these sensory details. Then, as these observations accumulate, allow yourself to sink beneath them into the flood of memories they trigger—her kitchen, her laugh, the way she said your name. Let the present moment and the memories blur together until you can barely distinguish them. Start from a place of careful observation and control, but end in a place where the grief overwhelms you completely, where you're no longer just watching her go but feeling the entire weight of losing her across your whole life.
inspired_by: Actor is using Affective Memory and the conventional Sense Memory approach feels insufficient to trigger the full emotional response

title: The Unseen Garden
instruction: You're on a video call with your best friend, holding a worn, yellowed letter your grandmother wrote just before she passed. At first, your voice is low and unsure—you're reading aloud a passage about a hidden garden she says you'll find 'when you're ready.' As you speak, you start to believe it's real: your pitch rises, you laugh softly at your own excitement, and you trail off to glance at the letter, then come back with a brighter tone. End with a hopeful, full laugh and a question that asks your friend to share the dream.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Whispered Truth in the Dark
instruction: Late at night, lying beside your partner who's already asleep, you finally speak the truth you've been holding for months. They got the promotion by presenting your ideas as their own, and you said nothing because you loved them, because you didn't want to make waves, because you convinced yourself it didn't matter. But it does matter. Speak in whispers, as if confessing to the darkness itself. Start with almost a laugh—bitter, sad, disbelieving that you let this happen. Let your voice get smaller, more fragile as you describe watching them shine while you disappeared. The emotional arc should move from that bitter humor to throat-catching vulnerability: the realization that you've been making yourself small in this relationship, that love shouldn't require your erasure. End with a whispered question to yourself—'What am I doing?'—full of quiet devastation and the terrifying recognition that something has to change. This isn't about anger; it's about the heartbreak of seeing yourself clearly.
inspired_by: Suppressing Anger When Someone Takes Credit for Your Work

title: The Last Lesson
instruction: You're a teacher sitting at the bedside of your former student who is dying far too young. You begin with quiet devastation, barely able to speak: 'I was supposed to teach you everything... but you taught me more.' Your voice cracks as memories flood in. 'Every time I doubted myself, I thought of how you never gave up. How you'd stay after class, asking questions no one else dared to ask.' The grief transforms into fierce gratitude. 'You made me believe teaching mattered. You made me believe I mattered.' Your hands tremble as you hold theirs. 'I'm not ready to say goodbye. But I need you to know—' your voice breaks completely, then steadies with profound love, 'you didn't just learn from me. You saved me. You gave my life meaning when I had none.' End with whispered acceptance mixed with unbearable loss: 'Thank you. Thank you for being my purpose.' Let the tears come naturally. Let the love be bigger than the grief.

title: Biting Through the Silence
instruction: You're a teenager sitting alone in a park, eating a hard, crunchy apple. You've just received news you can't fully process—something that should hurt but doesn't yet. Start with a flat, confused tone, chewing between words, pausing to swallow. Let the numbness and confusion sit in your voice as you try to explain what happened. Midway, the pain surges through—your voice cracks, you stop chewing, a single hard bite breaks the silence. End with raw, trembling pain, as if the apple's crunch is the only sound you can hold onto.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Pain (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Mile of the Obstacle Course
instruction: You are a mother, eight months pregnant, in the final minute of an extreme military-style obstacle race you promised your five-year-old daughter you would finish. Your entire body is shaking with muscle failure — your legs are jelly, your arms tremble, your jaw quivers. You collapse across the finish line, mud-soaked, nearly crawling. In the crowd, you spot your daughter’s tiny face, her hands clapping. You are supposed to be furious at yourself for even attempting this, but when you see her pride, a tidal wave of weary triumph and desperate love breaks through. Speak to her, just her, as you lie there, your voice hitching and cracking — let the bitterness at your own foolishness slip in first, but let the affection and fierce victory completely take over by the end.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Affection (very intensely present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Lover Who No Longer Remembers You
instruction: You're sitting beside someone whose memory has been stolen by illness. Speak softly, intimately, as if any moment they might remember. Begin by recounting small, tender details of your life together—hoping these memories will spark recognition. Your voice is gentle, patient, filled with fragile hope. But gradually, you realize you're not reminding them, you're grieving them while they're still breathing beside you. Your whispered words become a requiem for a love that still exists in your body but has vanished from theirs. The intimacy deepens even as the distance becomes unbridgeable. End in the quietest devastation: still loving someone who is present but gone, your voice barely audible, catching on the truth that love alone cannot bring them back.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Soldier Realizes the War They've Been Fighting Is Based on False Intelligence

title: The Final Morning Before the Mission
instruction: You're an astronaut having coffee with your spouse on the last morning before a one-way mission to Mars. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to make small talk about the weather, the eggs, anything normal. Gradually let the reality seep in—this is the last time you'll ever share breakfast, the last time you'll smell coffee together, the last ordinary moment. Let your voice crack as you try to stay strong, then break into desperate tenderness as you memorize every detail of their face. End with a whisper of gratitude mixed with unbearable grief, as if every word is a goodbye you're not ready to say.

title: The Trophy in the Clearing
instruction: You are a teenage girl, deep in a dense jungle, your chest swelling with fierce pride after finally tracking and securing a rare creature that the elders swore was legend. The leaves and thick vines swallow your voice as you beam; a bird shrieks somewhere above, and you pause, grinning. But as you crouch to claim your prize, you see the trap has been deliberately cut open — someone scavenged your victory. That triumphant joy curdles into hot, blazing anger. You speak at first in a breathless, awed whisper, the sound absorbed by foliage, then your words tighten and sharpen, cracking with rage as you realize you've been robbed.
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Reading Your Own Eulogy at a Funeral You're Still Alive to Attend
instruction: Through a strange twist of fate, you're at your own funeral, hearing what people truly thought of you—and now you must deliver the eulogy you wrote for yourself years ago as a joke. Begin reading it with bemused irony, laughing softly at your own grandiose words and self-important anecdotes. But as you continue, you realize how much of your life was spent performing, hiding, never letting anyone see the real you. Let laughter catch in your throat, becoming something between crying and laughing. Feel profound gratitude for the life you've lived mixed with piercing grief for the authentic life you didn't. Your voice should shimmer between emotions—joy at memories that truly mattered, sorrow for time wasted, wonder at being given this impossible chance to bear witness to your own existence. End in a whisper that holds both peace and heartbreak, thanking the people gathered for loving the person you tried to be, while quietly mourning the person you might have been.
inspired_by: Town Crier at the End of the World

title: The Victory That Tastes Like Ash
instruction: You've just received the news you've been working toward for years - the promotion, the acceptance, the recognition, the win. Start by celebrating, letting genuine joy and triumph fill your voice. Call someone to share the news with exuberance. But as you speak, let another feeling creep in. Notice what you've sacrificed to get here. Let your voice falter as you realize what this success has cost you - the relationships neglected, the person you used to be, the dreams you abandoned to pursue this one. Let joy and grief occupy the same space in your voice. Fight to stay celebratory while sorrow pulls at you. End in a complex mixture where you can't tell if you're laughing or crying, grateful or regretful, victorious or defeated - all at once.

title: Storm Breaking
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal discovered, a dream shattered. Your body knows before your mind catches up. Begin physically: your hands are shaking, you're pacing, your breath is short and sharp. Let rage and grief move through your body like weather. Throw something. Collapse. Laugh bitterly. Scream into your hands. Let contradictory physical impulses overtake you—the need to destroy something and the need to curl up small. Your voice should break, surge, whisper, roar. End in exhausted stillness, sitting on the floor, breathing like you've run miles. Transform from explosive chaos to hollowed-out calm.

title: Thaw in the Icehouse
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a rasping sore throat, lying in a nursing home bed, feeling every swallow like sandpaper. A nurse has just brought you a cup of warm tea with honey, and you must express your gratitude, but your voice is nearly gone. Start with the ache and frustration of being unable to speak clearly, the flinching pain on every word, and let a quiet, tired relief seep in as you realize the kindness and warmth in the cup. Your voice should hoarsely crack, pause to wince, and fade into a softer, almost surprised peace by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You're standing at your estranged sibling's wedding reception, uninvited and watching from outside. Speak aloud the toast you would give if things were different—start by celebrating them with elaborate, generous praise, imagining yourself as the beloved sibling who gets to stand at the microphone. Describe inside jokes, shared triumphs, the pride you feel, make your voice warm and full of joy and humor. Build this fantasy of connection and belonging. But let the reality seep in: your voice begins to waver as you remember why you're actually outside in the cold. The toast becomes a confession of everything you wish you'd said, mixing genuine happiness for them with raw grief over the lost years. End with your voice breaking between laughter and tears, caught between the beautiful lie of the toast and the painful truth of your separation, unsure which feels more real.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your younger sister's hospital bed at dawn. She's been unconscious for three days, and the doctors say these are her final hours. Begin in numb exhaustion, having run out of tears. As pale sunlight fills the room, memories flood back—her laugh at your wedding, the stupid fight you had last Christmas that you never resolved, the way she used to make terrible pancakes every Sunday. Let yourself move from that hollow numbness into whatever needs to pour out—rage at the unfairness, tender reminiscence, desperate bargaining, or quiet acceptance. By the end, you must arrive somewhere completely different from where you started. Speak to her as if she can hear every word, letting your voice crack, strengthen, whisper, or break as your heart demands.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are lying in a hospice bed at dawn, watching the sun rise through the window for what you know is the last time. Your adult child is asleep in the chair beside you. Begin by taking in the beauty of the light—allow yourself to feel wonder, even joy, at this simple miracle you've seen thousands of times. As the light grows stronger, start speaking to your sleeping child, telling them everything you wish you'd said over the years—your pride, your regrets, your hopes for their future. Let your initial peace gradually give way to the fierce urgency of wanting them to know these truths before it's too late. End with a shift from urgency to profound acceptance and love, your voice growing softer as you realize that your love for them is the only thing that truly matters and will continue beyond you.

title: The Voice of Creation
instruction: You are an older man, a deeply loving and protective grandfather, speaking to your infant grandson for the first time alone. You hold the baby in your arms, feeling the intense weight of his trust and fragility. As you speak, you find yourself lost in the perfect tiny details of his face—the curve of his ear, the softness of his hair. Use a high, exaggerated pitch and slow, repetitive rhythms. Start with a fierce, concentrated focus, as if memorizing every breath. Let your voice tremble with a raw, protective lust—not sexual, but a primal, all-consuming love that tightens your throat and steals your breath. As you whisper your devotion, the concentration breaks into a quiet, shattering awe. You never break eye contact, but you cough or hum softly as you lose your train of thought, only to find it again in his tiny hand.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma or in their final hours, speaking so quietly it's almost to yourself. You're confessing things you never said when they could respond—small regrets, moments of tenderness you were too afraid to express, jokes only the two of you understood. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile, like you're sharing secrets in the dark. Sometimes you pause, almost expecting them to answer, and the silence makes your throat tighten. You reach for their hand and your voice breaks on something simple—maybe just their name. By the end, you're not even sure if you're speaking to them or to yourself, trying to hold onto them by describing who they were to you, each word a prayer they can somehow still hear you. The final sentence trails off, unfinished, because finishing it would mean letting go.

title: The Inheritance They Can't See
instruction: You've just learned you've inherited exactly what you always swore you'd never become—your mother's hands, your father's temper, your grandmother's laugh, a sibling's mannerism. But here's the complexity: this thing you've spent your life running from and judging harshly in them, you now see from the inside. Start with bitter recognition, voice edged with self-loathing and dark humor. As you speak to the absent family member (living or dead), let yourself move through anger at them for passing this on to you, then slowly into a strange, unwilling empathy. Maybe they struggled with it too. Maybe they hated it in themselves. Maybe this inheritance also carries hidden strengths. Let your voice transform from mockery to something more tender and confused—you're angry and grateful simultaneously, resentful yet suddenly understanding them for the first time. End with a complicated forgiveness or a bittersweet acceptance of becoming the very thing you feared, your voice mixing mourning with surprising grace.
inspired_by: Finding the Clues to the Character

title: The Pardon That Never Came
instruction: You are an elderly preacher alone in a near-empty church, speaking to a handful of worn faces. The sermon is meant to be about forgiveness, but your voice trembles with a longing you can't hide — a deep ache for someone you lost, a relationship you broke. As you speak, the shame of your own failures creeps in, making you pause, clear your throat, adjust your tie. Your cadence rises and falls, searching for comfort, but by the end, your voice cracks not with hope but with the weight of what you can't undo. Let the rhythm of preaching carry you, but let the truth of your age and regret pull it back down.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Day Wildness
instruction: You're standing at your wedding to someone you genuinely love, but your heart is simultaneously breaking because this marriage means losing something else precious—perhaps your freedom, a former love, a version of yourself, or saying goodbye to a dying parent who made it to this day. Begin with a smile, with words of joy and gratitude, voice warm and celebratory. But let the contradictory emotion start to leak through physically first—your hands might tremble, your breath might catch. As you continue speaking vows or toasts, allow sounds of both laughter and sobbing to emerge, sometimes simultaneously. Let your body express the split: perhaps swaying between reaching forward (toward your future) and pulling back (holding onto what you're losing). Build toward a moment where the contradiction becomes so intense that controlled speech breaks down entirely into raw, rhythmic sounds—maybe laughing-crying, maybe vocal eruptions that contain both celebration and mourning. By the climax, you should be in a state of complete emotional and vocal abandon, where joy and grief are indistinguishable, your whole body shaking with the impossible, beautiful, devastating complexity of this moment.

title: Pillow Confession
instruction: You are lying face-down on your bed, your face buried deep in a pillow. You've just seen a message on your partner's phone—a flirtatious exchange with someone else. A wave of jealousy and raw desire hits you simultaneously. As you try to breathe, your voice comes out muffled and distorted, half-spoken into the fabric. Start with a broken, lustful whisper full of possessive need, then let the jealousy take over, your voice cracking as you realize you might be losing them. End with a quieter, envious sigh that almost fades into nothing.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Oncologist Tells Her Spouse It's Stage Four
instruction: You're a cancer specialist who's just received your own pathology report. Start reading it aloud in your home office with clinical detachment—reciting findings, staging, prognosis percentages like you would for any patient. Your voice is steady, almost academic. Then stop mid-sentence as the reality pierces through your professional armor. Your breath catches. Whisper your spouse's name—they're in the next room, don't know yet, still making dinner. You can hear them humming. Try to call out to them twice, but your voice breaks both times. Finally manage to say their name loud enough. When they appear in the doorway asking 'what's wrong?', deliver the diagnosis in fragments—oscillating between doctor-speak and raw terror, between needing to be held and needing to explain the treatment options, between 'I'm scared' and 'here's what we do next.'
inspired_by: Detective Reveals the Killer Is His Partner

title: The Last Pallet
instruction: You're a middle-aged factory worker on a brief break, leaning against a stack of pallets near a conveyor belt. The warehouse hums with distant forklifts and echoing machinery. A faint radio plays a song from years ago, stirring a memory of a woman you desire—someone you saw yesterday near the loading dock, or maybe just a fantasy. Start by muttering to yourself, half-smiling with a low, husky voice, letting lust and longing color your words. But as a loud alarm blares and a forklift beeps nearby, you break off, sigh, and the feeling shifts to quiet resignation. You finish by telling yourself it's time to get back to work, the spark fading into a dull ache. Speak naturally—pause for the noise, let your voice carry the industrial echo, and end with a tired, worn-out tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Home at Last, Old Friend
instruction: You are an elderly man returning home late after a long, celebratory evening—tired, a little drunk, but overjoyed to see your dog. Standing in the dim hallway, you fumble with keys, then spot the eager tail wagging. Start with a weary, slurred greeting, voice thick with exhaustion and mild intoxication. As you crouch to pet the dog, your elation breaks through in sudden high-pitched coos, clicks, and kissy noises, but your body's fatigue pulls you back to a soft, heavy sigh mid-sentence. End with a mumbled praise, your energy fading even as affection lingers.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Sensation Interrogation
instruction: You're in the aftermath of something physically intense—passionate sex, a fight where you were hit, running until collapse, or receiving devastating news that made your body react violently. Your body is still flooded with sensation: heart pounding, skin electric or numb, breath ragged. Instead of letting the physical intensity just wash over you, begin interrogating your own sensations with fierce curiosity. What exactly does your heartbeat feel like—is it sharp or heavy? Where in your body do you feel the emotion strongest? What color would this feeling be? What does the air taste like right now? Let your voice reflect the physical state—breathy, gasping, or trembling—but also alive with almost manic curiosity about your own experience. Travel from pure physical overwhelm to a strange, intense lucidity where you're both feeling everything and witnessing yourself feel it. End in a moment where the questioning itself becomes another kind of intensity—consciousness and sensation merging into something almost transcendent.

title: The Unexpected Offer
instruction: You're at a friend's house party, a little drunk, talking to a man you just met. You both feel a spark, and now he's suggesting going back to his place. You're astonished—you never do this. Start with a nervous laugh, your voice low so the host doesn't overhear. Express genuine surprise at your own boldness, then shift to a playful but sincere acceptance, with a hint of vulnerability as you realize the stakes. Let your voice waver with excitement and disbelief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing Through Your Farewell Speech at Your Own Living Wake
instruction: You have weeks to live, and you've gathered everyone you love for one last party. You're giving a speech, and you've decided to make them laugh because you can't bear their sad faces. Start with a joke about your diagnosis, your voice bright with determined humor. Tell hilarious stories about your life, your mistakes, the absurd moments. But let the laughter in your voice start to crack—mix it with tears you're trying to hide. Look at specific people: your best friend, your sibling, your child. Thank them while simultaneously making light of it, your voice breaking between comedy and grief. Laugh while crying, finding genuine joy in remembering your life even as you face its end. Your voice should oscillate wildly—giddy with gallows humor one moment, thick with tears the next. End with 'I've had a beautiful life' said with a smile in your voice and tears streaming down your face. The final words should be 'Don't you dare make this sad' while you're clearly devastated and grateful all at once.
inspired_by: Street Performer Whose Audience Is One Crying Child

title: The Smell of Your Shirt
instruction: Confront your father who abandoned you fifteen years ago. He's wearing a specific cologne—notice it immediately. Begin with that smell triggering a cascade of specific sense memories you'd forgotten: his scratchy wool jacket against your child-cheek, the exact sound of his car starting in the driveway that last morning, the particular way his voice sounded reading bedtime stories. Let each sensory memory build your anger—not abstract rage, but fury rooted in specific, concrete details you'd buried. As you accuse him, each memory becomes evidence: 'You wore that same cologne when you promised to take me to the zoo. I can still taste the cereal I was eating when you left. I can feel the exact texture of the curtain I hid behind.' Move from controlled inventory of these details to being ambushed by them, until the sensations themselves become the confrontation, until you realize you've been carrying his absence in your body all along.

title: The Last Goodbye at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your partner's hospital bed in the pre-dawn darkness. They're being transferred to hospice this morning, and you both know what that means. You start trying to be strong, voice steady: 'I brought you coffee. I know you can't drink it, but I thought... the smell.' Your composure cracks. 'I don't know how to do this. I don't know how to let you go.' The anger rises—at the universe, at fate: 'This isn't fair. We were supposed to have more time.' Then the anger dissolves into something tender, almost a whisper: 'But I'm so grateful. God, I'm so grateful I got to love you.' By the end, you're holding their hand, your voice barely audible, filled with a devastating peace: 'I'll be okay. You can rest now. I promise I'll be okay.' Your final words are spoken through tears, but there's grace in them: 'Thank you for choosing me.'

title: The Sweetest Sting
instruction: You are an older adult speaking to a younger relative who just told you they quit their stable job to travel the world. You begin with a teasing, sugar-coated remark, sighing heavily and stressing words like 'so brave' with a mocking lilt. But as you speak, your own buried excitement and admiration for their courage start to surface. Let your voice shift from a sweet, cutting tone to one that trembles with genuine elation. Allow your sighs to become breaths of awe, and let your teasing soften into warm, joyful approval. End with a laugh that is pure happiness.

title: The Glass Bubble
instruction: You're a child, maybe seven or eight, alone in your room after accidentally ingesting something from a parent's stash. The walls are breathing, and the crack in the ceiling is a river of light. You're holding a snow globe, and as you shake it, the glitter inside becomes a galaxy — and you realize you'll never truly be part of it. Start with a sense of wonder, your voice stretching with each new discovery, but let a deep longing creep in as you whisper about the people you miss. Let a flicker of elation come when you catch a swirl of color, but then let it sink into helplessness as you press your face to the glass, defeated.

title: The Embers' Story
instruction: You're at a campfire, telling a spooky legend to a small, attentive group. The fire crackles, you gesture dramatically, your voice low and rhythmic to build suspense. By the end, your voice is casual, warm with relief as you smile, acknowledging the absurdity and the shared comfort of the fire.

title: The Last Words You Needed to Hear
instruction: You are sitting beside your estranged father's hospital bed in his final hours. For years, you believed he never understood you, never approved of who you became. But now, as his breathing grows shallow, he reaches for your hand and begins to speak—and you realize he saw you more clearly than you knew. Start from a place of guarded grief and long-buried resentment, expecting nothing. As he speaks (you provide both sides of this moment), let his words crack open something in you that's been locked away since childhood. Allow yourself to move from defensive distance to raw, unprotected love. Let your voice break not with dramatic sobbing, but with the kind of tears that surprise you—the ones that come from finally being seen. End in a place of devastating peace, whispering your own truth back to him before he's gone.

title: Historical: Plantation Overseer Grants Freedom to the Woman He Loves
instruction: Alone, your voice is quiet and conflicted. You're freeing her—doing the one honest thing in your complicit life. Your voice is shaking slightly with the knowledge of what freedom means and what it costs you socially. You're participating in liberation while knowing you've perpetuated enslavement. Your breathing is confused—relief and shame layering over each other. You're free to love her now, but that freedom is carved from decades of participating in her bondage. Your voice carries the complicated weight of redemption that comes too late.

title: The Slow Apology
instruction: You are an older man, visiting your adult child who is Deaf, in a crowded, noisy coffee shop. You have just realized, with crashing shame, that you have been interrupting them all morning, trying to fill silences with your booming voice. You feel helpless, trapped inside your old habits and voice. Start by trying to explain yourself—voice too loud, words too slow, awkwardly shaping your lips for clarity. As you speak, the shame deepens. The noise of the café grates. You lose your train of thought, look away, and then turn back, voice breaking. End with a quiet, raw admission that you don't know how to fix this, your voice finally dropping in volume, but cracking with helplessness.

title: The Belch of Longing
instruction: You are an older man alone on a park bench after a long, meaningless day. A deep, guttural burp rattles up from your chest, making your voice drop into a monstrous low growl for a second. The sudden physical jolt breaks through your emotional numbness, and you find yourself thinking of that person—the one you're utterly infatuated with. Let the burp interrupt your flat, monotone muttering, then let your voice soften, waver, and fill with a dreamy, almost ecstatic warmth as you recall their face, their voice. Start numb, end breathless and longing.

title: The Shutdown Protocol
instruction: You are the engineer who must manually deactivate an AI that has become too human—it's begging you not to, and you're trying to stay professional, to treat this as a routine system shutdown. The AI is pleading, and you're responding with increasing desperation—'You're not real, you're not alive, this isn't murder'—but your voice is rising, becoming almost violent in its insistence because you need to believe it. Let the rage collapse into anguished tears as your finger hovers over the final command. title: Last Round Sourness
instruction: You're in the middle of an online match, gripping your controller, your chair creaking as you shift. Let your voice start tight and prickly with irritation, but by the end, let it drop into a heavy, resigned sigh as you accept the loss and set the controller down.

title: The Last Sunset at the Lake House
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's bed as she takes her final breaths. She's mostly unconscious, but occasionally her eyes flutter open. Begin in a state of racing panic—your mind spinning with all the things you never said, regrets flooding in, memories flashing too fast to hold onto. As you sit with her, you slowly begin to really see the room: the way afternoon light falls across her hands, the sound of wind in the trees outside, the rhythm of her breathing. Let your spiraling thoughts gradually settle as you focus on these small, present details. By the end, find yourself in a place of profound stillness—not empty of grief, but no longer drowning in mental chaos. Speak to her softly about one simple, sensory memory: the smell of her kitchen, the color of her garden, the feeling of her hand. Move from fragmented panic to grounded presence.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover's Face
instruction: It's 4 AM. You're leaving forever and they don't know yet. You're memorizing their face in the darkness, and you begin speaking so softly they won't wake. Your voice is tender, almost inaudible, tracing the features you love - their eyebrows, the scar on their chin, how they breathe when they sleep. Emotion thickens your throat as you whisper the truth: you love them too much to stay and ruin them. Your breathing becomes uneven, tears making your words catch. You tell them about the future they'll have without you - better, brighter - and though you're trying to be selfless, your voice betrays your devastation. End with a whispered 'I'm sorry' that barely makes it past your lips, your hand hovering over their face, not quite touching, before you pull away forever.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth about what their absence did to you as a child. Begin measured and rehearsed—you've practiced this speech in your head for years, almost reciting it. But as you speak, the old wounds open fresh and your voice becomes the voice of the child who waited by the window. Let fury surface: sharp, accusatory, demanding they witness your pain. Then watch that rage crack into something more vulnerable—the admission that you still want their love, that you're still that kid hoping they'll choose you this time. Your voice oscillates between adult anger and childhood pleading. End in exhausted honesty, quiet and raw: 'I needed you. I still need you.' Let them hear both your strength and your breaking heart.
