title: Realizing Your Parent's Behavior Was Abusive, Not Normal
instruction: Someone asked about your childhood and you described what you thought was normal. They reacted with horror. Your voice becomes uncertain: 'It wasn't that bad.' But as you hear yourself defend it, you're realizing. 'Oh god, that was abusive, wasn't it?' Your voice cracks. 'I've been protecting them instead of myself.' Ask if you should confront them.

title: The Unexpected Inheritance
instruction: You've just received a letter informing you that someone who caused you profound pain—an ex-lover, an estranged parent, a former friend—has died and left you everything. Begin reading the letter aloud with bitter, sarcastic laughter. 'Of course. Of course they did this.' Let your voice drip with resentment: they denied you love in life, and now this posthumous gesture feels like a final manipulation. But as you continue reading, let something crack open. Maybe there's a sentence that reveals they understood you after all. Maybe the gesture itself, however imperfect, is an apology. Let anger and grief collide. Feel love and rage existing simultaneously in your chest. By the end, arrive at something impossible: you're crying, but you're also laughing—grateful and furious, relieved and devastated, holding all of it at once without resolution.

title: The Contradictory Goodbye
instruction: Your best friend is moving across the world for an amazing opportunity you helped them get. You're genuinely thrilled for them, but you're also losing your person. Start with authentic excitement, celebrating their courage, your voice warm and proud. But laughter keeps catching in your throat, turning into something that could be a sob. You're speaking faster, as if words can hold them here, mixing joy with panic. Express gratitude for every memory while your voice breaks with loss. You're smiling and crying simultaneously, trying to mean both feelings fully. End with a contradictory moment—'This is perfect' said through tears, 'I'm so happy' spoken like a eulogy. Let the audience feel both emotions as equally true, beautifully painful, love that transcends its own grief.

title: The Last Mile Home
instruction: You are an elderly woman, your voice naturally high and soft, but now it's frayed. You've been drugged and held captive, but just broke free after a long fight. Your body is screaming—bruised ribs, a twisted ankle—but you're running. Your mind is fixed on one image: your granddaughter's face. You're calling her voicemail, knowing she might not pick up. The adrenaline has stripped away your usual gentleness; your voice is jagged, breath comes in bursts, you stumble over words. You start in raw pain, gasping out the horror of what happened, but as you speak, the longing to hear her voice swells, and by the end, a fierce, tearful triumph breaks through—you're not dead, you're coming home. Let your pitch waver, let sounds catch in your throat. The phone is slippery in your hand, you're limping, you curse under your breath as you misdial once.

title: The Phone Call You Didn't Expect to Answer
instruction: You have just answered a phone call from someone you thought was gone from your life forever—an estranged sibling, a former best friend, a lost love. Begin by responding to them as if they were someone who once protected you, someone who made you feel cherished and important—let warmth and instinctive joy flood your voice. Then, deliberately shift: start responding as if they were someone who abandoned you when you needed them most, someone who chose their own comfort over your pain. Let bitterness creep in, let your voice harden even as you're trying to sound happy for them. By the end, you must hold both truths at once—you're genuinely thrilled for them AND devastated that they're sharing this moment with you as if the years of silence don't matter. Your final words should vibrate with this impossible contradiction.

title: The Promotion Call
instruction: You're on the phone hearing you got the job you've sacrificed everything for—the promotion, the role, the opportunity you've wanted for years. You should be purely happy, and you start there, with genuine excitement and relief. But as you're saying thank you and expressing your gratitude, you become aware that your best friend, who didn't get it, is in the next room. Or you remember what you gave up to get here. Or you realize your parent who told you you'd never make it isn't alive to see this. Let the joy stay real but become complicated—infected with guilt, or grief, or the awful awareness that getting what you want doesn't feel the way you imagined. Don't choose which emotion wins. Let them coexist messily. Your voice might break while you're laughing. You might feel most alone in your moment of greatest achievement. Stay with the contradictions.

title: First No Boundary
instruction: You're saying 'no' to a request from someone who's used to you always saying 'yes,' and your voice is shaking: 'I can't do that anymore.' They push back, and your voice becomes firmer: 'I'm sorry, but this time I have to think about myself.' It's terrifying, radical for you. 'I love you, but I have to protect my energy.' Your voice cracks slightly — you're worried they'll abandon you — but you continue: 'I can't keep giving away pieces of myself.' They argue. You're tempted to cave — that would be the easy path — but your voice becomes clear: 'No.' Just that. 'No.' By the end: 'I hope you understand. And if you can't, I understand that too.' Walking away, your voice is trembling but proud: 'I just said no. And I didn't die.' The first boundary is the hardest. But it's also the most necessary.

title: The Garden She'll Never See
instruction: You're an elderly woman standing alone in your overgrown backyard at dusk. Start with quiet, venomous muttering to yourself, almost a whisper, as you imagine the look on your niece's face when she finds out the soil here is poisoned. Your voice is low, lazy, words half-swallowed, but then you pause — you spot a single rose blooming through a crack in the wall. For a flickering moment, you speak to that rose, voice softening with a fragile, childish hope. title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about a lifetime of emotional absence or misunderstanding. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, trying to stay calm and rational. title: Giddy and Breathless

title: Laughing Through Tears: Reading Your Late Spouse's Hidden Love Letters
instruction: One year after their death, you find letters they wrote but never gave you—one for each year you would have had together. Your voice oscillates wildly—grateful for this gift, destroyed that these words are all you have left, amused by their humor, shattered by their absence. End on a moment of strange peace—thanking them through tears and laughter intertwined, your voice full of contradictions, finding unexpected grace in the ruins of grief.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You

title: The Key in Your Hand
instruction: You're standing outside the door of your first apartment after your mother's funeral, holding the key to her house that's now yours. Begin with your hand on the doorknob, unable to turn it. You're flooded with contradictions: grief that she's gone and relief that certain struggles are over; gratitude for everything she gave you and anger for everything she couldn't give; the desire to step inside and preserve everything and the urge to burn it all down. Let these opposing forces battle in your voice—laugh through tears, rage through tenderness, express love through frustration. Don't resolve the contradictions. title: The Airport Gate at Boarding Time
instruction: You're standing at the departure gate, boarding pass in hand, about to leave for a dream opportunity abroad. Tell them you'll miss them while relief floods your body. By the final boarding call, you must arrive at a place where all these contradictions exist simultaneously—grateful and resentful, loving and angry, heartbroken and free, saying goodbye while already imagining your escape.

title: The Whisperer in the Stacks

title: High Altitude Numbness
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman flying home after a final goodbye to your childhood home—you sold it out of necessity. title: The Snow That Swallows Sound
instruction: You are an elderly man caught in a blizzard, lost and freezing. title: Carpet Confession

title: She's Not Breathing
instruction: You are a teenage girl calling 911 because your best friend just collapsed after taking something at a party. You have to stay calm for the operator, but your voice keeps cracking. title: The Trophy by the Bed
instruction: You're a teenage girl sitting on the carpeted floor of your bedroom, back against the bedframe, knees pulled up. title: The Voice in the Storm
instruction: Youre on a stormy night journey, narrating to yourself with each crack of thunder and gust of wind. Your voice should be a mix of fear, fascination, and resilience as you brave the storm.

title: The Last Morning Coffee
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospice bed in the early dawn light. She's awake for what might be the last time. Begin by describing to her, in vivid sensory detail, a specific morning from your childhood when she made you coffee for the first time—the smell of the kitchen, what she was wearing, exactly what she said, how the mug felt in your hands. Start with quiet fondness and nostalgia. As you speak, let yourself truly see and smell and feel that memory as if it's happening now. Midway through, realize she's remembering it too—she's living in that same moment with you. Let this recognition break something open in you. End in a place where grief and profound gratitude are inseparable, where you're both in that memory together one final time. Your voice should move from gentle reminiscence to raw, present-tense wonder to tearful communion.

title: Shouting a Warning Across a Canyon
instruction: Someone on the other side of a canyon is about to step on a crumbling edge. Shout your warning — elongate the vowels to carry distance ('Heeeey! Stoooop!'). Include the moment they finally hear and stop — the relief collapsing your voice into breathless, tearful gratitude shouted across the void.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: Someone is praising your strength during the worst thing that ever happened to you - a loss, a betrayal, a devastating end. Your voice becomes this strange, beautiful mixture of gratitude and grief: 'I'm not strong. I'm shattered. But thank you - god, thank you for seeing something in me I can't see.' You're crying and almost smiling at the same time. The emotions are wildly contradictory - you're genuinely touched, but you're also falling apart. By the end, your voice finds this unexpected peace in the middle of the pain: 'Maybe that's what strength is. Just... still being here. Still breathing.' You sound like someone who just discovered something true in the ruins.

title: The Last Morning Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has chosen medical assistance in dying, and it's their final morning. You begin trying to be strong, voice controlled and steady: 'I brought your favorite tea.' But as you watch them sip it, something breaks—your voice cracks with desperate tenderness: 'I'm not ready. I thought I was ready, but I'm not.' You're fighting to memorize every detail of their face, voice trembling between gratitude and grief: 'Thank you for every single day. Even the hard ones. Especially the hard ones.' By the end, you've found a different kind of strength—voice soft but steady, holding their hand: 'I'll be okay. Not today, maybe not for a long time. But because you loved me, I'll be okay.' Let the emotions shift naturally from false bravery to raw need to profound, aching acceptance.

title: Whispering to Someone Who Won't Wake
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the early morning darkness. They're asleep—or pretending to be—and you need to confess something you've been carrying for months. Begin speaking in the softest whisper, testing whether they're truly asleep, confessing small things first. As you continue, track every micro-movement they make—a shift in breathing, a flutter of eyelids, a tension in their shoulders. Let your confession grow bolder as you believe they're sleeping, revealing deeper truths. Your emotion should travel from tentative relief (safe in the dark, speaking to someone who can't hear) through tender, aching honesty, and finally to a desperate hope that they ARE hearing you, that this half-awake state is the only way you can finally be truthful with each other. End with an unbearable tenderness, uncertain whether you've been heard, but having finally spoken.

title: Stripping Away the Armor
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has refused to speak to you for two years. Begin furious and defensive—you came here ready for a fight, your body tight, your voice sharp. Amplify that crack in their armor. Imagine that beneath their anger, they're desperate to forgive you, desperate to come home. Let your rage dissolve into raw, exposed pleading. Your voice must transition from accusatory and loud to broken, whispered confession. End not with answers, but with your whole self laid bare and trembling.

title: Carrying Memories
instruction: You are an elderly person, breath ragged from hauling a heavy box of old photographs up a narrow staircase. At first, your voice is soft and warm, almost teasing, whispering to the image as if they can hear you. But as the climb drags on, your shoulders ache, your lungs burn, and the fantasy begins to crack. By the top, your words come out in thick, exhausted bursts, and the infatuation mixes with quiet grief—a love that you can no longer sustain, just like this weight.

title: An Ode to a Lost Childhood
instruction: Speak to your younger self as though they are right there, reminiscing on moments of innocence. Your tone should be nostalgic yet full of regret, as though trying to apologize for whats to come.

title: The Echo of the First Step
instruction: You’re a seven-year-old boy alone on a concrete stairwell. You’ve just climbed all seventeen floors to prove you’re brave like your dad. At the top, you shout your triumph — your voice bouncing harsh and huge, making you feel like a giant. But as the last echoes fade, you realize your dad isn’t there to see it. The reverb swallows your victory, and you whisper his name into the cold air. Let the brightness in your voice crack into quiet emptiness. Feel the awe of your own sound turn into the disappointment of being unseen. Your footsteps and your breathing compete with your words — let them trip and pause naturally.

title: Thanking Your Ex While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you still love but can't be with anymore—and you need them to know they weren't a mistake. But even as you express this gratitude, grief is there—your voice keeps catching, laughter mixing with barely-suppressed tears. They were everything and it still wasn't enough, and you need them to understand both truths. Your tone should dance between joy at what you shared and devastation at what you're losing, words tumbling over each other as you try to hold both feelings at once. End with a moment of strange, broken peace—thanking them through tears, loving them and letting them go in the same breath.
inspired_by: Explaining the Internet to a Medieval Person

title: Dancing at the End of the World
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of something that mattered deeply—a failed marriage, a lost dream, a life that didn't turn out as planned—and somehow, impossibly, you're finding beauty in the wreckage. Begin with a laugh that has tears in it, marveling at the absurdity of it all. Your voice should dance between grief and strange joy, between cataloging everything you've lost and recognizing everything you've learned. Let gratitude and heartbreak live in the same breath—thank the experience for teaching you who you are, even as you mourn who you thought you'd be. Your delivery should feel like someone discovering light in the darkness, finding that the end of one thing is somehow, mysteriously, not the end of you. Finish with a sense of liberation mixed with loss, peace existing alongside pain, accepting that both can be true at once.

title: The News That Can’t Wait
instruction: You’re at a family dinner, beaming with pride after getting a big promotion. Your father is telling a long story to your aunt, and you can’t contain yourself — you cut in, voice rising with excitement, words tumbling out faster than he can finish. But as you describe the promotion, you see your mother’s empty chair and remember she’s in the hospital. The contentment stays bright on your face, but your voice starts to waver, the pitch dropping, a catch in your throat. By the end, you’re still smiling, but the sadness leaks through each syllable.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Softest Command
instruction: You are a young girl, the smallest in a mock platoon exercise, forced to lead a chant. Your voice is naturally high and soft. You begin by shouting as loud as you can, trying to mimic the drill sergeant's percussive rhythm, but your voice cracks and wavers. As you struggle to project, helplessness creeps in. By the end, your shouted commands dissolve into a desperate, quiet plea for someone to take over. Your performance should include the strain of forcing volume, the staccato rhythm faltering, and the emotional shift from attempted authority to raw vulnerability. Speak about 60 words total.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Bittersweet Victory
instruction: You've just received news you've been fighting for—a dream realized, a battle won, a goal achieved—but it came too late, or at too great a cost. Someone you love didn't live to see it, or you sacrificed something precious to get here. Start celebrating—jump, laugh, pump your fists, let joy explode through your body. But mid-celebration, the other emotion crashes in. Don't stop the joy—let both live simultaneously. You're laughing and crying, jumping while your heart breaks, fists raised in victory while your chest collapses in grief. Your body must hold both truths at once: enormous, powerful, triumphant AND shattered, aching, devastated. By the end, you're somehow both the most powerful and most vulnerable you've ever been, giant and broken in the same breath.

title: Celebrating Your Beloved's Last Birthday While They're Still Here
instruction: They're sitting across from you, weak but smiling. This is their final birthday and you both know it. You're singing, voice bright with determination to make this beautiful, to give them this moment of joy. But halfway through you start laughing—not from happiness but from the absurdity of pretending this is normal, from the overflow of love and grief that has nowhere to go. Your laughter catches, becomes crying, then you force it back to laughter because their eyes are so full of gratitude. You tell them, voice shaking but warm, how lucky you are—even now, especially now—to have loved them. You're making jokes through tears about the terrible cake you baked, about all the birthdays you celebrated together. Your voice is thick with emotion but you keep it light, keep giving them permission to find joy even in this goodbye. Peace settles over you mid-sentence: this moment, broken and perfect, is enough. You mean every word when you whisper that you wouldn't trade a single day.
inspired_by: Defense Lawyer Cross-Examines Witness, Realizes They're Confessing to Other Crimes

title: The Kitchen Tile Pattern
instruction: You are confronting your mother in her kitchen about how she treated you throughout your childhood. You came here rehearsed—you've imagined this conversation a thousand times, always picturing yourself articulate, measured, finally able to express what she did to you. You begin speaking in that voice you've practiced: controlled, clear, determined to make her understand. But as you talk, she does something unexpected—maybe she looks away, or starts crying, or says something that throws you completely off script. Every clever phrase you prepared evaporates. You realize mid-sentence that the way you're speaking—this careful, therapeutic voice—is just another way of hiding. Strip it away. Let yourself speak in whatever messy, inarticulate, embarrassing way wants to come out. Forget about being understood. By the end, you're saying things in ways that surprise you, accessing anger or grief or love you didn't know you'd feel. The words might stumble, repeat, contradict themselves. Let them.

title: What I Never Told Anyone
instruction: In the quietest voice you can manage without whispering, confess something you've carried alone for years. Begin with the voice of someone who has almost convinced themselves they've made peace with this secret. Calm. Resigned. But as you speak, you realize you haven't made peace at all. Your voice starts to tremble. The words catch in your throat. You're not crying—not yet—but emotion is pressing against every syllable. This is a tender devastation, like touching a bruise that never healed. The vulnerability isn't loud; it's in the pauses, the way you have to stop and breathe, the almost-breaking quality of your voice. By the end, you're barely holding yourself together, speaking so softly it's almost to yourself, finally admitting the weight of what you've been carrying alone.

title: Reading Your Late Partner's Final Letter
instruction: Your partner of twenty years died unexpectedly, and you've just discovered they left you a letter—one final love note, written months before, that they'd hidden for you to find 'just in case.' As you read it aloud to yourself, their words are filled with gratitude, inside jokes, memories of your life together, and expressions of love that now feel unbearably precious. Begin reading with your voice breaking into unexpected laughter at their humor, even as tears stream down your face. Let your tone shift between joy at being so deeply loved, anguish that they're gone, gratitude for every moment you had, and the strange peace of hearing their voice one last time through their words. Your delivery should capture the beautiful contradiction of grief: you're simultaneously destroyed and held together by love, laughing through sobs, finding comfort in the very thing that's breaking your heart. End with quiet acceptance mixed with longing—'Thank you' spoken to someone who can no longer hear, but somehow, you know they do.

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone you love, and they're awake too. You whisper something small at first—a minor worry, a fleeting thought. But in the darkness and quiet, deeper truths start rising: fears you've never voiced, desires that scare you, parts of yourself you've kept hidden. Speak in whispers, letting each confession lead to the next. Don't perform vulnerability—let it be uncomfortable, halting, surprising even to you. Your voice might catch on certain words. Long pauses might open up. You might say 'I don't know why I'm telling you this' or 'I've never said this out loud before.' Let shame, relief, fear, and intimacy all be present. Notice the sensations in your throat, your chest, as you reveal yourself. Begin from a place of cautious sharing; end in a place of exposed tenderness where you've said something that can't be unsaid, and you're waiting in the dark for their response.

title: The Last Phone Call From Your Childhood Bedroom
instruction: You're calling your terminally ill parent from the bedroom where you grew up, the one you fled twenty years ago to become someone else. As you speak, the accent you buried comes flooding back with every childhood memory the room triggers. Start controlled and distant, using your carefully constructed voice. But as your parent asks you to 'talk like you used to, baby, just one more time,' your defenses crumble. Let your original voice emerge—not performed, but involuntary, raw. End with you speaking in that abandoned accent, telling them goodbye, your throat tight with the grief of losing both your parent and the person you once were. The room, the voice, the farewell—all collapsing into one devastating moment of return.
inspired_by: Forced to Speak in Your Family Accent You Abandoned

title: Midnight Confession at the Bar
instruction: You're an older man, alone at a dimly lit bar, several drinks deep. The person you're infatuated with sits beside you, and you're trying to tell them how you feel. Start with the fumbling, giddy excitement of infatuation—your words slur, you laugh at nothing, you lose your train of thought. As you speak, the room sways, and your voice catches with the weight of genuine affection. By the end, the bravado fades into a raw, tender confession, your voice quieter, more vulnerable, the intoxication making you both bold and fragile.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Toast No One Asked For
instruction: You’re at a backyard party, three drinks in—woozy, loose, the world tilting slightly. The host is your college roommate, and she’s just announced another effortless success: a promotion, a book deal, a life that gleams. Your head is thick, your mouth slow. When she asks for a toast, you lift your glass, stammer a little, and say something that starts as genuine surprise—really, you’re astonished, it’s so much—but then the sourness seeps in. Your words turn tight, your smile fake. The alcohol makes you careless, dropping a barbed compliment that hangs too long in the air. You finish with a laugh that’s a little too loud, then stare into your cup, the joy and envy dissolving into silence.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Final Transmission from the Deep Space Station
instruction: You're recording a message to Earth from a deep space station, your voice warm and excited as you describe the view of a distant nebula you've been studying for years. Mid-transmission, alarms begin—life support is failing, and you realize this will be your last message home. Your excitement transforms into quiet acceptance as you keep describing what you see, because the beauty matters more than your fear. Your breathing becomes labored, words coming slower, but you're determined to finish cataloging this wonder for the scientists who'll come after you. Include the moment you start saying goodbye to specific people—your daughter, your research partner—your voice breaking not with panic but with love and regret for all the moments you'll miss. End with your words becoming whispers, almost peaceful, as you watch the stars and try to hold onto consciousness just a little longer.
inspired_by: Hot Air Balloon Ascending Uncontrollably: Losing Oxygen

title: The Last Permission You'll Never Hear
instruction: You're at your father's deathbed, and he's unconscious. For thirty years, you waited for him to say he was proud of you. Now he never will. Start with a whisper, trembling with that old desperate need for approval: 'Dad, I... I just wanted you to see me.' Your voice cracks with decades of invisible wounds. But halfway through, something shifts—a terrible, liberating realization. Your tone becomes steadier, sadder, but free: 'I'm proud of me. And that's going to have to be enough.' End with a sound that's half-sob, half-exhale of release. You're mourning what you'll never have while simultaneously granting yourself what you always needed.

title: Finding Peace in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what remains of your family home's garden after it's been destroyed—by fire, flood, or foreclosure—and somehow, impossibly, one rose bush survived. Start with a laugh that sounds slightly unhinged, almost giddy, as you describe this absurd miracle. Your voice should contain genuine wonder mixed with the kind of exhausted peace that comes after everything falls apart. As you examine this surviving rose, let contradictory emotions flood through you—you're laughing and crying simultaneously, expressing profound gratitude for this small beauty while your voice breaks with the grief of everything you've lost. Describe the rose's perfume mixing with the smell of ash or mud, the strange beauty of wreckage. The emotional journey moves through shock, unexpected joy, deep sadness, and finally arrives at something like acceptance—not happiness, but a genuine moment of grace found in ruins. End with a statement that contains both heartbreak and hope in the same breath, your voice suspended between laughter and tears, having found something sacred in the rubble.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sweet Scent of Freshly Bloomed Roses in a Garden

title: Counting Your Freckles in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to your lover in the dark hours before dawn, and you've been silently watching them sleep. Begin with the quiet terror of knowing you'll have to leave tomorrow, your chest tight with pre-emptive loss, barely breathing so you don't wake them. But as you study their sleeping face—truly study it, discovering tiny details you've never noticed, the exact curve of their eyelashes, the small scar above their eyebrow—let yourself become so absorbed in the act of witnessing them that the fear dissolves into wonder. Notice how their breath sounds, the warmth radiating from their skin, the particular way their hand rests near their face. Transform from someone afraid of loss into someone completely present in love, and whisper something to their sleeping form that is completely true and unplanned, born only from this moment of pure attention.

title: The Chair That Won't Let Go
instruction: You are an elderly woman, proud and stubborn, trying to stand up from a low, soft armchair after a long day. Your legs are trembling, your arms shake as you push against the armrests, and your jaw quivers with every effort. You're alone in the room, but your daughter might walk in any moment. Start with deep concentration—muttering to yourself, focusing on the movement, ignoring the tremor in your voice. By the end, as your muscles give out and you collapse back, a wave of embarrassment and helplessness rises: you hate needing help, but you can't do it. Let your words crack and break, the shake in your breath carrying the tiny whimpers of strain.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Helplessness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother in Her Language, Your Broken Tongue
instruction: You're confronting your immigrant mother, trying to tell her in her native language how her sacrifices suffocated you—but you've lost fluency, and the words for your pain don't come. Start with controlled anger, forcing out phrases in her tongue, then collapsing into English when you can't find the words. She doesn't interrupt; her silence makes it worse. Feel the fury of wanting to be understood in the language of her heart, but you've become a stranger to it. Your voice should crack between languages, between anger and desperate love, between accusation and the terrible recognition that you're losing her twice: once to the language barrier you let grow, once to time running out. End with a raw question in fragmentary, childlike grammar: 'Why you never teach me the words for this?'
inspired_by: Last Person to Speak a Dying Language

title: The Last Hour Before Sunrise
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in the pre-dawn darkness. For years, you've held back the truth that her favorite child—your parent—has been lying to her, stealing from her, manipulating her love. You've watched in silence, protecting family peace. Now, with maybe an hour left, you begin speaking softly, telling her everything you've witnessed, every betrayal you've swallowed. Start with gentle reluctance, your voice barely above a whisper, still trying to protect her. But as you speak, something breaks open—decades of watching her be used, of your own voice being silenced. Let your whispered confession grow into a fierce, protective rage on her behalf, then dissolve into tender sorrow that she'll never know how much you tried to shield her. End holding her hand, your anger spent, replaced by pure love and the grief of goodbye.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table about why he left when you were twelve. Begin with rehearsed anger—you've planned this speech. But as you speak, start noticing everything about him NOW: the gray in his stubble, how his hands shake slightly, the coffee stain on his shirt, the way he won't meet your eyes, the exact timbre of his voice when he finally responds. Let these fresh observations change you in real-time. Your anger should fracture and complicate—becoming something messier, more vulnerable. Maybe you notice he's smaller than you remember, or older, or scared. End in a completely different emotional place than you started: perhaps unexpected tenderness, or deeper fury mixed with pity, or confusion replacing certainty. Let what you see and hear reshape your feelings moment by moment.
inspired_by: A choice has lost its strength after repeated use in a long run

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You have just learned you are pregnant, but your mother—who you have a complicated, painful relationship with—died last week and will never know. Begin the scene speaking to her photograph, your body feeling sharp, angular, every movement precise and controlled, as if you are made of edges and corners. There is anger in your joints, resentment in your shoulders. As you speak about the baby, about what you wish you could tell her, let your body begin to soften and expand simultaneously—your belly, your chest, your throat all opening, but your fists may still clench. You are filling with life while emptying with grief. By the end, let yourself embody both the fierceness of a mother protecting her young and the vulnerability of a child who still needs her own mother. Your voice should crack between strength and breaking, between fury and tenderness, between holding on and letting go.

title: The Restraining Order Against Your Own Child
instruction: You're reading a victim impact statement to the court about your adult child's violence toward you. You begin controlled, factual, voice flat with protective numbness—listing dates, incidents, injuries. But as you describe the moment they shoved you down the stairs, your voice starts to shake. The rage breaks through: 'I gave you everything! I would have died for you!' You're screaming now, all the betrayal and grief pouring out. Then you see them crying in the defendant's chair, and your fury shatters into something more devastating—helpless, keening love. Your voice goes soft, broken: 'You're still my baby. You'll always be my baby. And I can't let you near me.' The final words are barely whispered: 'I'm so sorry.'

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospice
instruction: You're sitting with your phone at 2 AM, finally calling your estranged sibling who's in hospice across the country. You start with careful, measured words—asking about their comfort, the nurses, anything safe. Your voice is controlled, almost businesslike, because you've spent twenty years perfecting emotional distance. But then they say they forgive you for missing their wedding, their children's births, all of it. The careful architecture of your defenses begins to crack. By the time they whisper 'I love you' for what you both know is the last time, you're no longer the person who walked away two decades ago. You're sobbing, begging for more time, promising everything you should have said years ago. End with the sound of their breathing getting shallow as you desperately try to pour twenty years of love into thirty seconds.

title: The Breaking Point: A Caregiver Loses Control While Caring for a Dying Loved One
instruction: You're alone with someone you love who is dying slowly, painfully. You've been strong for months—bathing them, medicating them, watching them disappear. But right now, something snaps. Your voice explodes with rage at the unfairness, at God, at the universe, at them for leaving you. You're shouting things you immediately regret—that you're exhausted, that you can't do this, that you hate watching them suffer. Your voice is fierce, almost violent in its intensity. Then mid-outburst, you see their face and your rage shatters completely into devastated apology. Your voice drops to broken sobbing as you rush to hold them, begging forgiveness. You're furious and heartbroken and protective all at once. Your voice becomes fierce again but differently—fiercely tender, promising you'll never let go, that you'll carry this burden forever because you love them. End with your voice small, exhausted, whispering promises into their hair.
inspired_by: Professional: Parent Tells Child They Cannot Afford Life-Saving Treatment

title: Holding Your First Child While Burying Your Last Parent
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home on the day of your mother's funeral, and your three-week-old daughter is sleeping against your chest. Your mother never got to meet her—she died two days before you could bring the baby to visit. Start with the complex tension of this moment: exhausted new-parent fog, fresh grief, overwhelming gratitude, piercing regret. As you look around the room where you grew up, let sounds emerge that express this impossible emotional knot. Don't try to separate these feelings—let them exist simultaneously. Soft coos of love for your baby dissolve into shuddering grief. Exhausted sighs carry both wonder and loss. Humming a lullaby breaks into quiet sobs. Move through this complexity without resolving it into something simple. End in a place where you've felt the full weight of both joy and sorrow existing in the same breath—transformed not by choosing one emotion, but by surviving their collision.
inspired_by: Emotional Point of View, Without Words

title: The Last Recipe: A Mother's Final Lesson
instruction: You are teaching your adult child how to make your signature dish on what you both know is your last day together. Begin with warm determination, focusing on the details - the exact pinch of salt, the way to fold the dough - trying to stay practical and strong. As you guide them through each step, your voice should gradually fill with all the life advice you've hidden in cooking lessons over the years. Let your composure crack as you realize this recipe is all you can leave them. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance, your voice soft and breaking, as you watch their hands move the way yours once did, knowing they'll carry this forward without you.
inspired_by: The Chef and the Talking Ingredient

title: Emergence from the Fog
instruction: You are an older man waking up from anesthesia after surgery. You're groggy, your mouth feels like cotton, and a sharp pain throbs in your abdomen. Your voice is slurred, volume uncontrolled, words stumble out. At first, you're just moaning in pain, trying to remember where you are. Then you notice the nurse has a bright yellow button on her uniform—it's oddly fascinating. Your speech shifts from raw discomfort to a childlike curiosity about that button, but the pain keeps pulling you back. Let your voice crack, trail off, and change pitch naturally as you oscillate between agony and this small, genuine interest.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Hour in the Garden
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved for decades—a parent, partner, or closest friend—in their final hour of life. They're conscious but fading. Begin by trying to stay strong, maintaining composure, perhaps even making small talk about the flowers nearby or the weather. As you sit together, allow yourself to move impulsively between what you need to say, what you're feeling in your body, what you want from this moment, and who you are to this person. Don't plan your words. Let yourself shift between begging them not to go, expressing gratitude, confessing regrets, feeling your own heartbeat, stating your terror of being alone, or suddenly laughing at a memory. By the end, find yourself in a place of raw acceptance—not peaceful, but real. Let the chaos of your heart speak without a script, moving from controlled strength to unguarded truth.
inspired_by: I Am, I Want, I Need, I Feel

title: The Question You've Been Too Afraid to Ask
instruction: You're alone with someone you love—perhaps a partner, perhaps a best friend—in a quiet moment. You need to ask them something, but you're terrified of the answer, so you ask it indirectly, wrapped in metaphor and careful words. They sense what you're really asking and answer just as carefully, just as obliquely. This is a dance of two people trying to speak truth without shattering something fragile. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, each word chosen with excruciating care. As their cryptic response comes (you voicing both sides), let hope and fear war in your tone. Build to the moment where you finally ask directly, voice trembling—and their silence answers everything. End with a quiet, broken sound that isn't quite words, the kind of devastation that's too deep for crying, just the soft collapse of something you'd been holding together.

title: The Gratitude That Shakes
instruction: You are kneeling in a garden at dawn, dew soaking through the fabric of your jeans, your hands pressed flat against the cold, damp soil. You just learned that someone you love—who was missing for three days—has been found safe. At first, your voice comes out almost giddy, a little breathless, with a tiny, surprised laugh escaping as you speak to the sky. But as you keep thanking the universe, a heavier wave hits you: the terror of what almost was, and your voice cracks, slows, and folds into a raw, trembling whisper. You keep glancing at a smudge of dirt on your palm, then up at the brightening horizon, losing your train of thought for a second, then finding it again in a quieter, more desperate tone. Speak your gratitude and confession to the quiet air, letting your voice arc from a shaky elation to a devastated, holy relief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fading Sparks
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl kissing your boyfriend in the backseat of a car. The windows are fogged, his hands are on your waist, but your mind is elsewhere. You feel a flicker of irritation—why isn't he noticing you're distracted? You pull back just enough to mumble a question, your lips still brushing his. As you speak, your voice is soft, breathy, interrupted by wet smacks and shallow breaths. Start with a tone of mild annoyance, but let confusion creep in as you realize you're not feeling what you used to. End with a quiet, uncertain realization that something has changed.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Waiting on the Stool
instruction: You're perched on a high stool in a busy café, legs dangling, core tight to keep your balance. You've been waiting fifteen minutes for your older sibling who said they'd be here at noon. You're impatient and irritable—every buzz of the door makes you flinch, and you keep checking your phone with sharp, angry taps. Midway through a muttered complaint, you notice the little smudge of jam on your sleeve from breakfast, and for a second you remember them making you toast when you were small. Let the irritation soften into a quiet, reluctant fondness as you say the last few lines. Let your voice start tight and clipped, then relax into a slower, warmer rhythm as the memory settles.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Contemplation (slightly present), Affection (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Finding Your Missing Child's Backpack in the Woods Three Years Later
instruction: You're alone in the forest, searching one more time though everyone else stopped years ago. You find their backpack, exactly where they vanished. Start touching their belongings with trembling hope—maybe this means something, maybe this is a clue. Your voice is desperately rational, narrating what you're finding like it's evidence. Then the hope ignites into fierce, howling rage at the universe, at God, at yourself for not protecting them. Scream if you need to. Then collapse into broken sobbing, begging them to come back, bargaining with the air. Finally, settle into a kind of shattered peace—talking to them like they can hear you, telling them you'll never stop looking but you have to learn how to keep living. Let your voice do everything: roar, shatter, whisper, break. This is primal and messy and utterly human.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Android Realizes It Has a Consciousness the Creators Didn't Program

title: The Accusation That Becomes a Plea
instruction: You're confronting someone you love who's destroying themselves with addiction. Begin with controlled fury, voice tight and hard: 'Do you have any idea what you're doing to us? To yourself?' You're righteous, certain, armed with facts and tough love. But as you speak, the anger intensifies into something raw and uncontained—you're shouting now, voice breaking with frustration: 'I can't watch you die! I WON'T!' The rage peaks, then suddenly collapses. Your voice drops to something broken, pleading: 'Please. Please, I'm begging you.' All your armor is gone. You're on your knees emotionally, voice shaking with helpless terror. You cycle between trying to sound strong—'We can beat this'—and complete despair—'I don't know how to save you.' By the end, you've arrived at a terrible surrender: 'I love you. And I can't fix this. But I love you.' Your voice is simultaneously fierce with love and trembling with the knowledge that love might not be enough.
inspired_by: First Infertility Support Group: Finding Your Voice

title: The Buzz of Bitter Memory
instruction: You are an older man shaving your face with an electric razor, the constant mechanical buzz filling the bathroom. You're replaying a sour memory — a betrayal by a longtime friend, or a deal that went wrong. Start with that sourness tight in your throat, your words clipped and resentful, forced out between stretches of your cheek to keep the skin flat. As you finish shaving, let the sourness soften into a weary, quiet resignation — a sigh of 'that's just how it goes.' Let the buzz distort your vowels occasionally, and pause to wince or adjust the razor, letting the physical act interrupt your thoughts.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother: 'You Knew What He Was Doing to Me'
instruction: You've rehearsed this conversation for twenty years. Start with the careful words you planned, trying to stay controlled, adult, reasonable. But as you speak, the child you were begins emerging—the one who waited for her to notice, to protect, to choose you. Your voice shifts from measured accusation to raw bewilderment. 'You knew. I know you knew.' Let anger rise, then collapse into the more devastating emotion beneath it: the grief of a child still hoping for a different answer. End not with rage but with exhausted heartbreak, asking the question that's haunted you: 'Why wasn't I worth saving?' Your last words should be barely audible, stripped of everything but that original wound.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Oracle Delivers a Prophecy They Knows Will Be Misinterpreted

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're a parent whose child is in danger—kidnapped, missing, held hostage, or facing a threat you cannot control. Start with fierce, almost violent determination. Your voice is sharp, commanding, making demands of whoever can help. 'You will find them. You will bring them back.' Your certainty is armor. But as time passes or information comes that shatters your hope, that armor explodes into raw terror. Let your voice crack and surge—screaming, pleading, bargaining with God or fate or anyone. 'Please, please, take me instead.' Your strength completely disintegrates into helpless, animal fear. Then, in the devastation, find something else: a whispered prayer, a fierce promise to your child that you'll never stop fighting, words of love spoken to someone who might never hear them. End in the wreckage—your voice hoarse, broken, but still breathing their name.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They have been strong their whole life, never showing weakness, always carrying the family's burdens. Begin by trying to hold yourself together, maintaining composure, body rigid with the effort of not breaking down. As you speak, tell them it's okay to let go now, that you'll be alright, that they can finally rest. Let your body gradually soften and release as you give them permission to leave. By the end, allow yourself to physically collapse into vulnerability, your voice becoming tender and broken, all pretense of strength dissolved into raw, gentle grief. The transformation is from armored containment to complete emotional surrender.

title: The Inheritance of Certainty
instruction: You are a self-made billionaire confronting your adult child who has just announced they're walking away from the family empire to become a social worker. Start by towering over them with absolute authority—list every impossible thing you've accomplished, every empire you've built from nothing, every naysayer you've crushed. Your voice drips with the unshakeable conviction that you are right about everything, always have been. But as you speak, you begin to hear yourself—really hear the emptiness of it. The certainty cracks. By the end, you're no longer lecturing but desperately trying to understand why all your power and success couldn't make your child want to stay. Finish not with commands, but with a raw, uncertain question you've never asked before: 'What did I do wrong?'

title: The Secret Language
instruction: Late at night, lying next to your sleeping partner, you whisper a confession you've never told anyone: you still have an entire imaginary world you escape to—complete with characters, storylines, and a version of yourself who is braver, sillier, more magical. Begin with shame and fear that they'll think you're childish or strange. As you describe this secret inner world in hushed detail, let yourself get lost in it—your voice should become more animated, more enchanted, even as you keep it whisper-quiet. Feel the vulnerability of sharing something so private mixed with the joy of finally speaking it aloud. Notice how the confession becomes less about seeking acceptance and more about inviting them into your secret. End with tender hope, waiting to see if they understand.

title: The Promise You Broke
instruction: You are a father in your garage, alone, after finding a letter from your teenage child who ran away last night. Your initial state is raw rage — you're throwing tools, kicking a tire, shouting at the empty air. But halfway through, you find an old photo in the chaos of you and that child laughing at the beach years ago. The fury cracks. A desperate, broken hope seeps in as you realize maybe they'll come back. Your voice should start as a guttural roar, words like punches. Then it softens into trembling, gasping pleas — your breath hitching, the anger giving way to a raw, weeping optimism. You can hear the echo of your own voice off the concrete walls. You pause to wipe your nose, sniff hard, and clutch the photo.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Sending a Drunk Text to the Wrong Person
instruction: You've just realized you sent an embarrassing, drunk text to your boss instead of your friend. Your voice is immediately panicked: 'Oh no. Oh no no no no.' You're scrolling through trying to decide what to do. Your voice becomes desperate: 'Should I send a follow-up? Pretend I was hacked?' You're pacing, your voice getting higher and more panicked. By morning, you're calling in sick, your voice tight with dread: 'I'm not feeling well.'

title: GPS Navigation Voice During a Breakup
instruction: Your partner is breaking up with you while you're driving and the GPS keeps interrupting. 'In 500 meters, turn left.' 'Wait, you're LEAVING me?!' 'Recalculating.' The GPS voice (also you) is serenely indifferent to your emotional devastation. Let the GPS instructions become accidentally profound: 'Make a U-turn when possible.' 'I CAN'T MAKE A U-TURN, SARAH. IN THIS RELATIONSHIP OR ON THIS ROAD.' Cry and drive. The GPS voice never wavers.

title: Grateful for the Ending
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who's dying, but instead of pure grief, you're feeling something complex: relief mixed with sorrow, gratitude tangled with guilt. Begin by thanking them - maybe for finally letting go, maybe for the time you had, maybe for teaching you how to say goodbye. Let your voice carry genuine warmth, even traces of laughter as you remember good moments. But underneath, let the heartbreak bleed through. You're grateful for the peace they'll find, but you're shattering at losing them. You might even laugh at a memory while tears are streaming down your face. End in a place where you're giving them permission to go while your heart is breaking, where love and loss are so intertwined you can't tell them apart. Your voice should dance between lightness and weight, finding beauty in the contradiction.

title: Upside-Down Devotion
instruction: You are lying on your back on a massage table, your head hanging over the edge, neck hyperextended. The person you are madly infatuated with is massaging your throat, their fingers gentle yet firm. Every touch sends waves of ecstasy through you. You can barely swallow. Speak as you gaze upside-down at them, your voice thin and tight. Start by describing the sheer pleasure, but as you continue, you feel a sudden vulnerability—realize you are completely undone by this person. Let the ecstasy transform into a raw, breathy confession of infatuation, your words slipping out between swallows and shaky breaths.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent in a hospital room, and decades of unspoken pain are finally erupting. Start quiet and controlled: 'Do you even remember my tenth birthday?' Your voice is tight with a lifetime of swallowed anger. As you speak, the floodgates open—your voice rises, shakes, breaks. You're listing memories they missed, moments you needed them. 'I waited for you.' The anger transforms into raw, vulnerable grief. You're sobbing now, but still talking, needing them to finally hear you. End with exhausted honesty, your voice hoarse and stripped bare: 'I just needed you to choose me. Once. Just once.' The final words are whispered through tears, all fight drained away.

title: The Inheritance Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your surviving parent at the reading of your other parent's will, finally unleashing decades of suppressed truth. Begin controlled and cold, systematically listing the ways they failed you—the recitals they missed, the bruises they ignored, the times you needed them and they chose themselves. Your voice should be sharp, almost clinical at first. Then let the rage crack through, getting louder and more chaotic as specific memories flood back. But by the end, collapse into something fragile and desperate—the voice of the child who still, impossibly, just wanted to be loved. Transform from prosecuting attorney to broken child begging for an explanation that will never come.

title: The Rhythm of Her Name
instruction: You are chopping wood alone in your backyard at dusk. Each swing is a punctuation mark in your thoughts. You're a weathered man in your 60s, and for weeks a memory has been surfacing — a woman you barely knew, met once at a market. Start with a steady, contemplative rhythm, your voice low and rough between swings, like you're working through a riddle. As you split a stubborn log, the infatuation creeps in — a half-smile, a softer tone, maybe you even pause and wipe your brow while murmuring something about the way she laughed. End with a quiet admission, breathless, spoken to no one but yourself as you set down the axe.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Same Argument, Again
instruction: You're in the kitchen, staring at a sink full of dirty dishes for the third time this week. Your partner is in the other room, and you're muttering to yourself, then raising your voice, trapped in the same cycle. Start with a nasal, whining complaint that builds in frustration as you list the same grievances. Let your voice crack with a hint of fear that this pattern will never change. By the end, the whine dissipates into a quiet, exhausted plea, revealing the vulnerability underneath the nagging.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Grief with Laughter
instruction: Youre at a close friends funeral, and memories of them flood you with laughter. Try to hold it back let the audience hear your voice tremble as laughter and tears collide. Keep switching between moments of somber reverence and spontaneous laughter, as though unable to control the flood of memories. Its an emotional rollercoaster, balancing joy and sorrow in one breath.

title: The Last Broadcast
instruction: You are an elderly woman hosting a late-night radio show from a small, cluttered home studio. Outside, a storm is raging, and the power flickers. You are signing off for the final time after decades on air, but you've just received a letter from a long-lost love, delivered by a listener who drove through the storm to hand it to you. Your voice starts warm and nostalgic, but as you read the letter aloud, you are hit by a wave of astonishment that someone remembered you—followed by a terrifying realization that you’ll never see them again. Speak slowly, letting the intimacy of the mic catch every breath, every crack. Let the longing swell as you describe a memory, then let the fear silence you mid-sentence. End with a quiet, surprised whisper, as if the world just shifted.
emotions_sampled: Longing (extremely present), Fear (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Third Return
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, gruff voice working customer service at a hardware store. A regular customer you've helped before is returning an item for the third time. You start with your practiced, slightly elevated 'smile-voice'—polite, using uptalk, forcing warmth. But as you realize this is the same part they bought last week and already broke twice, the professional mask starts to crack. Let your voice drop in pitch, your words slow, and a heavy disappointment seep in. You lose your train of thought for a second, then finish quietly with a sad, tired resignation. Speak naturally, letting the strain show in your throat and the slight wince of pain from standing too long.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Goodbye at the Launch Site
instruction: Your child is boarding a generation ship to another star system—they'll never return, and you'll never see them again. You have two minutes at the departure gate. Start with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them, listing all the amazing things they'll see. But your voice begins cracking as the reality sinks in. Move through desperate attempts to memorize their face, then break into raw grief mixed with pride so fierce it hurts. End whispering the childhood nickname you haven't used in years, your hand pressed against the glass between you, as you realize this is the last time you'll ever say their name to their face. Let love and loss become indistinguishable.

title: The Suitcase at the Door
instruction: Your parent is standing with a packed suitcase, about to walk out of your life. Before you say a word, notice what's actually happening in your body right now - is your jaw tight? Are you holding your breath? Feel the real ground under your feet. Start speaking from whatever that truthful place is - maybe you're colder than you expected, maybe there's relief mixed with panic. Tell them the one thing you've never been able to say about what their leaving (or staying, or silence, or drinking, or criticism) did to you. Let your genuine state move and transform as you speak - you might start detached and controlled, then find rage breaking through, then collapse into pleading, or the reverse. Don't plan the journey, discover it.
inspired_by: Actor begins a scene by getting ready to act rather than from genuine BEING

title: After the Storm
instruction: You've just experienced something physically overwhelming—wild celebration, intense lovemaking, a moment of ecstatic achievement, or even surviving something that pushed your body to its limit. Your breath is still ragged, your skin hypersensitive, your body humming. Begin in pure sensation—gasping, laughing, crying, maybe all at once. You're flooded, almost incoherent. But as your breathing starts to slow, words begin to come. You start speaking—to yourself, to another person, to the universe—and you're amazed. Amazed at your body's capacity, at your own aliveness, at the fact that you're here and able to feel this much. Let the physical intensity gradually transform into wonder, into a kind of euphoric gratitude for being alive in a body that can experience such extremes. End breathless still, but grounded in awe.

title: Last Words to a Stranger Who Knew You Better
instruction: You're in a hospice room, sitting beside someone you met only six weeks ago—a fellow patient who became your closest confidant in your final days. Begin with gentle gratitude, your voice warm but tired, thanking them for small kindnesses. As you speak, the reality hits: this person understood parts of you that your own family never did. Your voice breaks with the unfairness of it—finding your soulmate when there's no time left. Move through quiet rage at the timing, then settle into bittersweet peace. End with a whispered confession of love—the kind you never got to say to anyone else in your whole life. Let your voice carry both the weight of dying and the unexpected gift of being truly seen.
inspired_by: Talking to a Stranger Who Becomes Something More

title: Running Up to Grandma's Room
instruction: You are a child, maybe six or seven, sprinting up two flights of stairs to your grandmother's apartment. You haven't seen her in months, and you're bursting with excitement. Each step is a little victory—you're almost there. As you climb, you're laughing and calling out to her, your words coming out in short, breathless bursts because you're running so fast. Midway, you pause, hand on the railing, catching your breath but still grinning. In that pause, a sudden wave of thankfulness hits you—for her, for this moment. Finish climbing, now slightly slower, and speak with genuine gratitude mixed with the leftover joy. Your voice should start high and breathless with ecstasy, then soften, deepen with sincere warmth.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Buzzing Notification
instruction: You're an elderly man brushing your teeth before bed. Your jaw is held open awkwardly, foam and saliva distorting your speech. A phone buzzes on the counter. You lean over to glance at a message from a doctor about a test result you were worried about. At first, you're just casually curious, mumbling through the brushing. But as you read, your interest spikes—your breath hitches, you pause the brush, and your voice tightens with urgent concern. You try to speak clearly but the foam and open jaw make it messy, with sputters and swallowed words. Let the emotion shift from routine distraction to focused, anxious fascination by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bedside Vigil: The Confession You Can Barely Whisper
instruction: Your best friend is unconscious in a hospital bed after an accident. The doctors say they might hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper—tender, afraid to disturb them, afraid this is your last chance. You confess something you've hidden for years: maybe that you loved them in ways you never said, or that you were jealous and it poisoned moments between you, or that they saved your life once and never knew it. Your voice trembles with the weight of secrets spoken too late. As you talk, memories flood through—your voice softens with remembered laughter, tightens with regret, breaks with gratitude. You tell them what they meant, what you wish you'd said, what you need them to know if they can hear anything at all. End with a plea so quiet it's almost just breath: 'Please don't leave me.' The entire piece should feel like the most intimate confession of your life, spoken at the threshold between staying and letting go.
inspired_by: Dream Job First Week: Imposter Syndrome Detonating

title: The Diesels and the Dawn
instruction: You are an elderly man seated by the window in a roaring aircraft cabin, your hearing aid turned low against the drone. You lean close to your seatmate, a younger man with a gravelly voice, whom you've just discovered is a retired diesel engineer — your own lifelong passion. Your throat is dry from the pressurized air, and you have to talk louder than you think to be heard over the engine hum. Start with a cautious, cracked voice, squinting out the window as you point to the wing's engine housing, your interest a flicker in the noise. Over the next few seconds, that flicker becomes a flame — you speak faster, leaning in, your voice climbing in pitch and volume, cracking with the effort as you lose the thread of your thought and find it again, your interest fully unguarded and alive. End on a breathless, almost pleading question, your voice raw with wonder and the cabin's dry air.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Shouting into the Gale
instruction: You stand at the edge of a cliff, the gale tearing at your coat and forcing you to lean into the wind. You are calling out a message to someone you know cannot hear you—a final confession of love you never said aloud. Start with desperate, wind-torn shouts, your voice cracking against the gusts. As the wind steals your words, let longing shift into a quiet, trembling acceptance: you whisper the truth, knowing it will be carried away, but feeling it leave your chest. Let the wind push you off balance, making you pause, breathe sideways, then return to the fading words with a raw, honest ache.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Shore
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin in a state of tight, frightened panic—your chest is constricted, you can barely breathe. As you hold her hand, you start to notice small details: the warmth of her palm, the scent of her lavender hand cream (the same one from your childhood), the soft sound of waves from the ocean sounds app the nurse left playing. Let these sensory details slowly wash over you. Describe to her—in whispered, broken fragments—a memory of the beach house where you spent summers together: the salt air, the rough wooden deck under bare feet, the taste of her homemade lemonade, the sound of seagulls. As you speak, let your panic transform into a deep, aching peace. By the end, you're no longer afraid of her leaving—you're grateful she brought the ocean into your life. Your voice should move from tight and strangled to soft, open, and full of bittersweet gratitude.

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're holding someone - physically or emotionally - trying desperately to help them, fix them, save them. Start fierce and almost aggressive in your intensity: 'No. No, you listen to me right now.' Your voice is commanding, full of passionate determination. 'You are not doing this, I won't let you.' You're fighting with everything you have. But as you realize your powerlessness, your voice begins to shake with frustrated rage: 'Why won't you just...' The anger explodes - you might shout, your voice raw and uncontrolled. Then suddenly it all collapses. The rage breaks into helpless sobbing. 'I can't... I don't know how to...' End in a whisper of devastating surrender: 'I can't save you.' Your voice is hollow, emptied, but also carries the terrible weight of finally accepting the unbearable truth.
inspired_by: Leaving Someone You Promised Forever To

title: Three AM Whispered Truths
instruction: It's three in the morning. You're lying in the dark next to someone you love, and you've just woken from a dream that revealed something about yourself you've been hiding—maybe a fear, a desire, a truth about your past. Begin with barely audible breath-sounds, tentative hums, as you decide whether to wake them. Let your sounds remain intimate, quiet, trembling—whispered tones that carry shame, hope, terror of rejection. As you sense their attention (even if they remain silent), your sounds gradually become more exposed, like slowly removing layers of protection. The arc moves from self-protective secrecy to naked vulnerability. End with sounds that are open, undefended, perhaps even relieved—the liberation of being fully seen.
inspired_by: Expressing Impulses in Sounds and Gibberish

title: Echoes of the Last Shot
instruction: You are a teenage girl standing alone in the empty gymnasium after your team's loss. The polished floor gleams, and the air smells of sweat and dust. You throw a basketball gently, watching it bounce and reverberate in the hollow space. Speak softly, almost to yourself, as you let the awe of the vast silence wash over you. Let your voice thin out with the echo, then warm into a quiet contentment at being alone with your thoughts. But let a thread of sourness creep in — a bitter taste from that last missed shot — and let it linger in your final words, a subtle shift from peace to a gentle sting. React naturally to the ball bouncing, or pause to listen to an echo.
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Contentment (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Rehearsal Dinner Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your best friend's rehearsal dinner, about to give a toast, but you're in love with the person they're marrying. You stand with a glass raised, mouth open, surrounded by expectant faces. Begin trapped between what you should say and what's screaming inside you. Start the 'toast' by acknowledging aloud what's literally happening in your body and mind right now: 'My hand is shaking. Everyone's staring. I had a speech prepared but I can't remember it. I feel sick. I'm smiling but I want to scream. I love you both. I love one of you differently. I'm the worst person here. I'm also the most honest person here.' Let each true statement—the jealousy, the genuine happiness for your friend, the inappropriate desire, the shame, the twisted gratitude that you even get to be present for this—exist simultaneously without resolving into one clean emotion. Don't choose between blessing and confession. End in a moment where multiple true, contradictory things are held at once: devastation and joy, selfishness and love, an ending and a beginning. The toast may never properly begin—or it transforms into something no one expected.

title: The Moment You Realize Your Lover Has Been Lying About Everything
instruction: You've just discovered the truth - they've been lying for months, maybe years. Start cold, almost eerily calm, as you lay out what you know. Your voice is controlled, factual, like you're reading a list. But with each revelation, the rage builds. Suddenly you're screaming, demanding answers, your voice raw and savage. You're throwing their betrayal in their face, your words meant to wound as deeply as you've been wounded. Your voice cracks from the force of your fury. Then they say something - maybe they break down, maybe they try to explain - and your rage shatters into devastation. The screaming stops. You're suddenly asking in a broken whisper: 'Was any of it real? Did you ever actually love me?' End with your voice small, helpless, as you realize the person you loved never actually existed.
inspired_by: Screaming Fight Where Everything Hurtful Gets Said

title: The Garden She Grew
instruction: You are a woman standing alone in a neglected garden at dusk, surrounded by overgrown roses you once planted with care. Start by whispering bitterly about how nothing blooms the way you wanted, your voice low and mumbling, words half-swallowed. Then, your eye catches a single bud just opening, and a sharp, intense interest pulls you forward — you crouch, voice still soft but losing its flatness as you lean in, describing its color and shape with quiet wonder. Let the bitterness soften into a fragile, fierce curiosity, as if this small discovery matters more than the rest of the garden's failure. The delivery should feel like you're talking to yourself, not meant for anyone else, with pauses where you lose thought and find it again in the petals.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispered Gravity
instruction: Late at night, you're lying beside your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they cannot hear—something tender and terrifying you've never been able to say aloud. Begin with your body rigid and hovering, not quite allowing your full weight to rest on the bed, barely breathing. As you whisper your secret, feel yourself slowly sinking deeper into the mattress with each phrase, allowing gravity to pull you down, your muscles releasing layer by layer. Your voice starts tight and caught, then gradually opens and softens. By the end, you should feel like you're melting into the surface beneath you, your breath slow and full, your body completely surrendered to the support underneath you. The physical release mirrors the emotional unburdening—moving from suspended fear to weighted relief.

title: The Last Drag
instruction: You are an older woman who has smoked heavily for decades, standing alone on your porch with a cold cup of coffee. Your voice is a permanent gravel—raspy, low, with a stubborn roughness that no amount of throat clearing fixes. Let the disappointment hit you first: regret over the damage you've done, the breathlessness, the lost years. But as you gaze at the worn-out garden chair where your late partner used to sit, a quiet thankfulness rises—grateful for the time you had, for the stubborn love that survived this habit. Let your voice crack and soften, the rasp easing into a warm, weathered gratitude, even as you still smell the smoke on your coat. Your spoken words should be a conflicted goodbye to a cigarette you just crushed out, mixed with a whispered thank you to someone you miss.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're telling them you're proud of them, that you're happy for their success, their new love, their departure to chase their dream—even though it means losing them. Start with genuine warmth and a smile in your voice, celebrating their joy. But as you talk, your voice begins catching on certain words. You laugh—really laugh—at a shared memory, but the laughter has tears in it. Your voice wobbles between joy for them and grief for yourself. Try to keep the brightness going, but it keeps breaking. End with a voice full of contradictions: 'I'm so happy for you' said while crying, or 'This is exactly what I wanted' said with a breaking heart. Let the love and loss live together in every word.
inspired_by: Telling Your Parent Something They'll Disapprove

title: The Prank's Stench
instruction: You're a teenage girl whose brother just shoved a jar of fermented fish paste under your nose as a cruel joke. You're doubled over, gagging violently — your stomach heaves, and your voice comes out thick with saliva and bile. Start with raw disgust and a flash of anger as you curse him between retches. But halfway through, you realize you can use this to tease him back, so your tone shifts into a sarcastic, mocking edge — still interrupted by gags, but now with a playful smirk. Your voice should sound watery, breathy, with involuntary heaving sounds breaking your words.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Anger (slightly present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Lucid Hour
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed during her final conscious moments. She keeps drifting in and out of clarity. Begin by trying to stay composed and strong for her, telling her cheerful lies about how she'll get better soon. But as fragmentary sense memories flood you—the particular smell of her lavender hand cream mixed with antiseptic, the weight of her hand that feels both familiar and frighteningly light, the sound of her labored breathing that reminds you of when you were sick as a child and she sat beside you—allow these sensory details to crack your composure. Let your voice break. Let the memories of her kitchen, her laugh, the texture of her cardigan against your cheek as a child wash over you unbidden. End in a place of raw, whispered truth: stop pretending she'll recover and instead tell her what she truly meant to you, your voice thick with grief but also deep gratitude. The journey moves from protective false strength to devastating, tender honesty.
inspired_by: Involuntary Imaging — Hatful of Rain Scene Example

title: Astronaut's Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a mission gone catastrophically wrong, recording what you know will be your final message to your child back on Earth. You begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them: 'Hey kiddo, just wanted to say goodnight from up here in the stars.' But as you continue, the reality crashes through your defenses. Your voice fractures as you shift from reassurance to the devastating truth you can no longer hide: 'I need you to know... Mommy's not coming home this time.' End in a place of tender acceptance mixed with unbearable grief, speaking the words you never thought you'd have to say, trying to give them everything—your love, your pride, your goodbye—in these final moments. Let the shift from protective parent to dying mother who must let go be visceral and raw.

title: The Last Gift Before Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply who is in their final hours. They've been unconscious, but suddenly their eyes open and they look at you with full recognition.
