Begin in a place of quiet despair and exhaustion from the long vigil. As you hold their hand, start spontaneously remembering aloud every small and large moment of joy they brought into your life—the time they made you laugh when you thought you'd never smile again, how they showed up when no one else did, the way they believed in you. Let each memory surprise you as it surfaces. As you speak, allow yourself to move from devastation toward a profound gratitude that transforms your grief. By the end, you should feel simultaneously heartbroken and filled with an overwhelming appreciation for having known this person. Your voice should shift from hollow and broken to warm and full, even as tears continue to fall.

title: Confronting Your Parent at Their Retirement Party
instruction: You're giving a toast at your parent's retirement party, voice bright and full of practiced charm, listing their accomplishments. Then you pause, and something inside you breaks—you can't keep performing. Your voice drops, becomes raw, as you start speaking the truth: about the childhood they missed, the awards they attended while you sat alone, the way their ambition taught you that love was always conditional. Your anger builds as years of silence break open, voice shaking with rage and hurt. But then you see their face, and your fury cracks into something more vulnerable—grief for the relationship you never had, the parent you needed. Your voice softens into almost a plea: why wasn't I enough? End with you struggling between wanting to walk away and desperately wanting them to finally hear you, to finally say they're sorry.
inspired_by: Hot Air Balloon Ascending Uncontrollably: Losing Oxygen

title: The 3 AM Kitchen Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM. You can't sleep because you're carrying a secret that's eating you alive. You've come downstairs to the quiet, dark kitchen where no one can hear you. This is where you'll practice saying it aloud for the first time—the thing you need to confess to someone you love. But first, you find yourself looking at the ordinary objects around you in the dim light—the refrigerator magnets holding children's drawings, the coffee mug they use every morning, the table where you share meals and pretend everything's fine, the clock ticking away the hours until dawn when you'll have to face them, the wedding photo on the wall, the pill bottles, the half-finished grocery list in their handwriting. Whisper your feelings about each object—how they represent the life you're about to shatter or the trust you've broken. Start with shame so heavy you can barely breathe, speaking so quietly you almost can't hear yourself. Let each object draw out more of the truth until you finally speak the actual secret aloud to the empty room, and in that speaking, find not relief but a fragile, terrifying clarity about what you must do.

title: The Cramp of Conscience
instruction: You’re a teenager sitting on the edge of a bed, finally working up the courage to apologize to your best friend for something you said. Your voice is thin and embarrassed as you start. Halfway through, a vicious muscle cramp seizes your calf—you gasp, break off mid-sentence, and let out a sharp, strangled sound. You reflexively curse under your breath, then clench your jaw. After a few seconds, the pain fades, but your voice is now even more guarded and heavy with shame. You finish the apology, but it comes out smaller, like you don’t deserve forgiveness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Newborn What You Can Never Say Aloud
instruction: Your baby is asleep in your arms, and in this quiet darkness, you confess your deepest fears. Start with wonder—the miracle of their tiny fingers, their breath. Let your voice be barely audible, intimate, full of tenderness. Then let the fear seep in: whisper the terror of failing them, of not being enough, of the world being too cruel. Your voice should tremble with vulnerability, almost breaking but staying hushed because you can't wake them. Admit your own brokenness, your past, the ways you were hurt, and your desperate hope that you won't pass that pain to them. End in a place of fierce, quiet devotion mixed with profound sadness—a love so big it hurts, spoken in a voice that's barely holding together.
inspired_by: Holding a Warm, Purring Cat on Your Lap

title: Confronting Your Father in His Workshop One Last Time
instruction: You're in your father's workshop—the smell of sawdust and motor oil surrounds you. Start by describing these familiar scents with a mixture of longing and bitterness, your voice tight with years of unspoken anger. You came here to tell him what his absence cost you, all the moments he chose wood and metal over you. Let your voice build with accusation and pain, demanding he see what he did. But then, in the middle of your rage, notice his hands—how they shake now, how small he's become. Your anger must collapse into something more complicated: grief for what you never had, and the devastating realization that it's too late to get it. End with your voice breaking on a quiet, 'I just needed you to see me.'
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath in a Field of Sunflowers

title: The Cancelled Celebration
instruction: You're a woman who just found out your best friend can't make your 50th birthday dinner tonight — she texted that her kid is sick. You're sitting in a quiet café, stirring your cold coffee, and you call her voicemail. Start with a heavy sigh that turns into a yawn you can't suppress — you're exhausted from the week. Your voice should be hollow, rounded, dragging down on the vowel sounds as you speak through the yawn, disappointment thick in every word. As you leave the message, you realize you're not just disappointed, you're suddenly lonely — and by the end, your voice cracks with quiet sadness, not just tired frustration.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Impossible Goodbye Party
instruction: You're at your own going-away gathering before leaving for something permanent—emigrating forever, entering witness protection, a terminal diagnosis requiring hospice soon. You're trying to be celebratory for everyone else, your voice bright and grateful as you thank people. But underneath, your heart is shattering. Let the mask slip in moments—your voice catching mid-laugh, brightness fracturing into something raw before you catch it again. Move between genuine joy at the love in the room and crushing grief at what you're losing. Thank someone and start crying while still smiling. Laugh at a shared memory while your voice breaks. Express gratitude that sounds like mourning. The psychological complexity is in holding both truths: this is beautiful and this is unbearable. End with a toast that's both celebration and eulogy, your voice somehow conveying both 'I'm so grateful' and 'I can't bear to let you go.'

title: Nodding Off to You
instruction: You are a teenage girl, heavily sedated, lying on a couch in a dim room. You're talking to the one person who still checks on you—a friend or sibling you haven't seen in weeks. You start with a faint, slurred pride: you finally got that job at the diner, you lasted three whole shifts before you 'crashed.' But as you speak, the drugs pull you under. Your voice gets softer, slower, each word an effort. The pride fades into a raw, childlike longing—for them to stay, to not leave you alone in this fog. Let your breath trail off, fingertips twitching as you fight to finish a sentence. Let the silence stretch. Let the longing crack through the stupor.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Fourth Call
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman on hold with a company you've called three times already about the same broken appliance. You're drumming your fingers, sighing heavily, and your voice has that nasal, sing-song drone of someone who's fed up. Start with intense impatience and irritation—elongate vowels, let your pitch rise and fall in a repetitive pattern as you rehearse your complaint. Then the rep says 'Actually, we already dispatched a technician this morning.' Your voice falters, pitch drops, and you end with a quieter, confused deflation as you realize you might have missed the memo. Authentically fumble for words, shift your weight, and let your irritation drain into bewilderment.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Confusion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Clearing
instruction: You are alone in a remote forest clearing, splitting firewood for the coming winter. Each swing of the axe is a heavy, deliberate act — you speak only during the wind-up or between swings, your breath ragged, body slick with sweat. You're replaying a difficult conversation you had this morning with someone you love, where harsh words were exchanged. As you chop, you move from frustration and self-justification (starting the swing with a grunt of anger) toward a quieter, sadder acceptance (pausing mid-swing, letting the axe rest on your shoulder). Let your voice crack with exertion and emotion — the physical strain mirrors the emotional one. End with a long exhale and a whispered 'I understand now,' as you finally let the axe fall cleanly through the last log.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning in the Hallway
instruction: You've just found out your teenage daughter has been cutting herself for six months, and you didn't notice. She's locked in the bathroom. You're on the other side of the door, and everything you thought you knew as a parent has just detonated. Start with panic—loud, frantic pleas for her to open the door, to talk to you, promises that everything will be okay. But she stays silent. Your desperation turns to rage—at yourself, at her, at the universe. Your voice rises, breaks, becomes almost savage with helplessness. You pound the door. Then, suddenly, you collapse. Slide down to the floor. Your voice drops to barely audible. Speak through the crack under the door. Confess your failures. Tell her about your own scars, the ones you've hidden. Let the fierce protectiveness and the devastating inadequacy collide. End with a raw, whispered promise: 'I'm not leaving this spot until you're ready.'

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your mother (or father) about something they did when you were twelve that shaped everything about who you became. Start angry—come in hot with accusations, voice raised, demanding answers or apologies. But as they respond (imagine their specific words), your anger fractures. You suddenly hear yourself sounding just like them, or you realize they were more broken than you ever understood, or you see fear in their eyes you've never noticed before. Let your fury collapse into something else entirely: grief, understanding, exhausted love, or even terrified recognition that you're becoming them. Your voice must travel from attacking to something much more complicated—perhaps quieter, shakier, or filled with unwanted compassion.

title: The Same Old Key
instruction: You're in the kitchen, holding your partner's jacket. He comes home late again, and you've been waiting with dinner cold on the stove. Your voice starts high and tight, a familiar whine of disappointment—'It's the same story every week.' You trail off as you see him slump in the doorway, and your frustration softens into something raw. Your words catch as you admit, 'I just still can't help smiling when you look at me like that.' Let your voice crack with affectionate exasperation, losing breath as you try to hold back a grudging laugh.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (clearly present), Infatuation (clearly present), Affection (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Bonk at Mile 22
instruction: You are an older woman on a solo trail run, mile 22 of a 26-mile route. The sudden energy crash hits like a wall—your legs buckle, your vision blurs, and you slump against a tree. At first, a raw disgust at your own weakness leaks out in clipped, bitter mutters ('Stupid. Shoulda known better.'), your voice hollow and slurred from exhaustion. As the minutes pass and your body refuses to move, the disgust fades into a quiet, trembling surrender—a breathy admission like 'I just... can't,' with tears you don't have the strength to wipe. Let your voice crack and fade, with long pauses as you lose and find your thoughts, and let your breathing be shallow and ragged between words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Day Before Forgetting
instruction: Early-stage Alzheimer's has just been diagnosed, and you're recording a message to yourself for the future—to the stranger you'll become who won't remember this moment. Begin with gentle humor, almost playful, reassuring your future self about who you were. But as you try to capture everything important, you keep forgetting what you were saying, and laughter turns into frustrated tears. Find yourself suddenly grateful for the absurdity of it—'At least I'll forget I'm forgetting.' Confess fears your future self won't understand, then laugh because that's the point. Your voice swings between fierce determination to document everything, tender forgiveness for what you'll lose, and strange, unexpected joy at having lived a life worth remembering. End in peaceful acceptance, your voice warm and almost amused, telling yourself it's okay, that love doesn't live in memory but in the body, and maybe you'll still feel it even when you don't know why.

title: Breaking Open in the Storm
instruction: You're caught in something physically overwhelming—drenched in rain, burning with fever, or in the aftermath of intense intimacy. Your body is responding to physical sensation, but it's cracking open something emotional you've kept locked away for years. Begin by trying to describe the physical feeling—the cold, the heat, the touch—but let your voice become overtaken by something much deeper: grief, ecstasy, rage at someone who hurt you, or desperate joy at being alive. The physical sensation is the key that unlocks the emotional flood. Your voice should start grounded in bodily experience then become almost delirious with emotion, as if the physical intensity has stripped away your defenses. Let sounds, gasps, laughs, or sobs interrupt your words. End in a completely different emotional place—maybe quiet awe, maybe exhausted peace, maybe finally released.

title: Drifting into Realization
instruction: You're alone in a dimly lit room after smoking, holding an old photograph that catches your eye. At first, your voice is loose, slow, and a little giggly—you're floating in a peaceful fog, letting words drift out with long pauses and sticky lip pops. But as you really study the image, a quiet realization settles in: this person is gone, and you're okay with that. Let your voice slowly shift from light, spaced-out murmurs to a heavier, more present tone—still hazy, but now carrying a soft, bittersweet acceptance. End with a small, genuine sigh as you set the photo down.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Letter Home: A Soldier's Final Recording
instruction: You're a soldier recording a video message to your family, knowing you won't survive tomorrow's mission. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them: 'Hey everyone, just wanted to say hi...' But you can't maintain it. Your voice cracks as you move through what you need to say—apologies to your parents for choices they never understood, words of love to your partner about the life you'll never have together, advice for your younger sibling about being braver than you were. End in a place of unexpected peace, almost a whisper: 'I'm not scared anymore. I just wish I could have had more time to show you who I really was.' Let the emotion catch in your throat naturally. This isn't a performance—it's the rawest goodbye you'll ever give.
inspired_by: Professor Accusing Student of Plagiarism: Mercy in the Moment

title: The Last Good Morning
instruction: You're waking your mother for what you know is her final day. Start with forced brightness: 'Good morning, Mama. I brought your tea.' Your voice is cheerful, almost sing-song, as if normalcy can hold back what's coming. But as you help her sit up, her hand trembles in yours, and something breaks. Your voice cracks mid-sentence: 'I made it just how you—' You can't finish. The brightness drains away. Now you're whispering, forehead pressed to her hand: 'I'm not ready. I'm not ready to say goodbye.' Your breath is ragged, words barely formed. But then she touches your face, and you find a different voice—quieter, steadier, filled with aching love: 'Thank you for teaching me everything.' The gratitude is real, but it's soaked in devastation. You're saying goodbye while trying to memorize the feeling of her hand.

title: In the Ropes
instruction: You are tied to a bedframe, wrists above your head, rope creaking with every tiny shift. Your partner is moving slowly around you, their footsteps on the floorboards. You start to speak—voice rough, breath catching. At first, doubt floods you: a deep, gravelly uncertainty, a fear that this vulnerability will break something in you. You stumble over words, your chest tight against the ropes. But as you keep talking, the doubt softens into raw longing—a desperate, surrendered ache. Let your voice strain, pitch dropping then cracking. Listen for the rope creak, feel the pull on your arms. End almost whispering, with a need that shakes your whole body.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Your Hair
instruction: You are speaking to your lover in complete darkness, lying next to them after you've both been silent for what feels like hours. Begin in a whisper so quiet it's almost just breath. Your hands are in their hair, or touching their face, and this physical connection is giving you permission to finally confess something you've kept locked inside: perhaps that you're terrified of how much you need them, or that you did something that hurt them and they never knew, or that you're not who they think you are in one crucial way. Let the darkness give you safety but also make you feel exposed. Your emotion should evolve from tentative, almost testing the waters, to a kind of desperate intimacy—speaking faster, voice slightly breaking, as if this might be your only chance to be truly known. End with a question that hangs in the dark, vulnerable and naked, waiting for their response. The entire piece should feel like a held breath finally released.
inspired_by: Actor is working on a scene and needs to identify what to work on—which obligations are most pressing

title: The Gratitude That Breaks You
instruction: You are thanking someone who saved you, loved you, or chose you when no one else did—but woven through every word of gratitude is the devastating awareness that you're also saying goodbye, or acknowledging how much time you've wasted, or recognizing how unworthy you felt of their love. Begin speaking with warmth and appreciation, your voice full and generous. But let the joy of gratitude become increasingly complicated by grief, guilt, or regret. Don't shift from one to the other—let them exist simultaneously, each word containing both the beauty of what was given and the pain of what it means. Let your voice fracture not from breaking down, but from trying to hold two truths at once. End unable to separate the thank you from the I'm sorry, the love from the loss, speaking through tears that are neither happy nor sad but both at once.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use subpersonalities as an acting tool but does not yet know their own selves

title: Whispering Your Secret to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep beside you. You're leaving tomorrow—not by choice, but because you have to (prison, illness, witness protection, deployment to a place you won't return from). They don't know yet. You whisper everything you need them to understand, knowing they won't hear it now but hoping somehow it will reach them. Start with tender, protective love—memorizing their face. Let your voice catch on the words you can't bear to say aloud. Your whisper should be so intimate it feels like a prayer, so broken it feels like a confession. The emotions should war in your throat: gratitude for having them, devastation at leaving, fierce protective love mixed with helplessness. End with the simplest truth, barely audible, as you realize this is both everything and not enough.
inspired_by: Speaking to Alexa Like a Hostage

title: The Cloud That Became a Whale
instruction: You are an elderly woman in your garden, craning your neck to look up at the sky. You start by teasing yourself lightly—mumbling about how your doctor warned you not to strain your neck, yet here you are, squinting like a fool. But then a cloud shifts, catching the sunlight, and you see it: a perfect, gigantic shape of a whale swimming across the blue. The teasing fades into pure astonishment. Your voice thins, pitches up, and you forget your own grumbles as you stare, talking to no one, or maybe to a neighbor who isn’t there. Let your words pause naturally as you lose the thought and find it again, reacting to the breeze, the brightness, the wonder of the moment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing at Your Own Farewell Party
instruction: You're at your own going-away gathering—perhaps you're dying and this is your living wake, or you're disappearing into witness protection, or leaving for a one-way journey. You're moving through the room, thanking people, and the absurdity and beauty of it all keeps making you laugh even as your heart splinters. Start with genuine, almost giddy laughter—the surreal humor of being present at your own ending, the strange gift of getting to say goodbye. Let joy and grief blur together: you're laughing as you tell stories, but there's tears in your voice. You're expressing profound gratitude for the people who shaped your life while simultaneously mourning that this chapter is closing. Your voice should dance between emotions: 'God, remember when we—' breaks into laughter, then catches into something tender, then swells with love, then cracks with loss. By the end, arrive at something transcendent: a place where the grief and gratitude become indistinguishable, where you're simultaneously celebrating everything this life gave you and mourning its ending. Let your voice carry both the pain of goodbye and the extraordinary privilege of having had people worth saying goodbye to. Find peace in the paradox.

title: The Inherited Lie
instruction: Confront your mother or father about a fundamental lie they told you about your childhood—about who your other parent was, why the family broke apart, something that shaped your entire identity. Begin with controlled accusation, the rehearsed speech you've prepared. But as they try to defend themselves, let your real reactions interrupt your script—unexpected rage, sudden childlike hurt, bitter laughter at the absurdity. Don't perform anger; let actual fury or grief or bewilderment crash through your planned words. Notice when your voice breaks, when you sound like a child again, when adult anger and childhood devastation collide. End not with resolution but with exhausted honesty—maybe you understand them slightly, maybe you hate them more, or maybe you simply don't know what you feel anymore.
inspired_by: Actor functions primarily from an intellectual place — 'mind-mouth connection' — and has difficulty stimulating genuine emotion

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in complete darkness, and you begin to whisper something you've never told anyone. Start with the decision to speak, your voice barely audible. Let the confession unfold slowly but without intellectual filtering—each revealed detail leads immediately to the next sensation: shame, relief, fear of their reaction, the physical memory of what you're describing, tenderness toward your younger self, dread, the sensation of being truly seen. Your breath changes, your body tenses and releases, your voice breaks and steadies. Let silence have weight between phrases, but never use silence to plan—only to feel. End in radical vulnerability or quiet devastation, wherever the confession takes you.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, making your final call to Earth before communications become impossible. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep it light: 'Hey, so this is it—pretty cool view from up here.' Your voice is bright, almost joking, protecting them from your fear. But as you continue, the reality seeps in. 'I won't see another sunrise like the ones we used to watch.' Your breath becomes uneven. The forced optimism cracks: 'I'm scared. God, I'm so scared.' By the end, you're whispering the truth you've been avoiding: 'I don't want to die alone out here.' Let your voice break completely. This isn't brave—this is raw terror mixed with devastating love for everything you're leaving behind.

title: Whispering Through the Hospital Glass
instruction: You are speaking to someone you love deeply who is in a medically induced coma, separated by glass, knowing they cannot hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and raw, as if volume would shatter you. Begin by telling them about your ordinary day—what you had for breakfast, the weather—because the big emotions are too enormous to face. But slowly, the mundane details begin to crack, and the truth seeps through: 'I don't know how to exist in a world where you're not awake.' Let tears thicken your voice without becoming theatrical. End with a confession you could never say if they were conscious, something tender and devastating, spoken so softly it's almost to yourself. The entire piece should feel like you're physically holding yourself together while emotionally falling apart.
inspired_by: The Teacher and the Defiant Student

title: The Unanswered Whisper
instruction: You are alone in a quiet, dusty chapel just before dawn, kneeling on a worn wooden pew. You begin with intense concentration, murmuring a memorized prayer under your breath, your voice hushed and rhythmic, but a sudden creak from the rafters makes you pause and shift your weight. As you resume, the concentration cracks slightly—you recall the face of the person you're praying for, and your words become slower, more fragile, the rhythm faltering. By the end, the prayer trails off into a raw, whispered plea, your voice catching with unexpected emotion, no longer strict but deeply personal, as you realize you're speaking not to walls but to silence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Asking For Forgiveness After Years of Silence
instruction: You're contacting them after years, having hurt them long ago. Your voice trembles: 'I owe you an apology.' You name what you did without excuses: 'I was wrong and I hurt you,' delivered with real remorse. They might reject you and your voice carries acceptance. Done the right thing anyway.

title: The Last Harbor
instruction: You are a seasoned sailor speaking to your grown child on the dock, the night before you leave on what you both know will be your final voyage—you're terminally ill and choosing to die at sea. Begin with forced cheerfulness, reminiscing about teaching them to tie knots when they were small, your voice rough with sea-worn affection. As they beg you not to go, let your resolve waver—your voice should crack with the weight of wanting to stay, wanting to see grandchildren you'll never meet. End in a place of bittersweet peace, your voice softening to almost a whisper as you help them understand that the sea has always been your true home, and this is your chosen grace. Let genuine love and irreversible loss sit side by side in your throat.
inspired_by: The Sailor and the North Wind

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You're standing outside in pouring rain after walking out of a life you can no longer continue—a marriage, a job, a role you've been playing for years. Begin by feeling the physical sensation: rain on your face, soaked clothes, cold penetrating your body. Let yourself start with exhausted numbness, then allow the rain to awaken something wild in you. Laugh, cry, scream—let your body release what you've been containing for too long. Feel the ecstasy of destruction mixed with the terror of having nowhere to go. Your voice should build from quiet disbelief to full-bodied catharsis, mixing sounds of liberation and grief. End by letting the storm wash through you until you're emptied out, standing in the rain with nothing left but raw, strange calm. Physical sensation and emotional release should be completely intertwined.
inspired_by: An actor is avoiding daily practice due to tedium or lack of immediate reward

title: Dancing at the Funeral: When Joy and Grief Become One
instruction: You're remembering someone who's gone—or perhaps they're dying and you're reminiscing with them—and you're laughing through tears at a beautiful, absurd, perfectly-them memory. Start with genuine laughter, letting it ring out: 'Remember when you—oh god, you actually did that, you were so ridiculous—' The laughter is real, uncontrolled. But it transforms mid-breath into something else; you're suddenly crying without the laughter stopping. Your voice carries both simultaneously: 'You made everything so much—I can't believe you're—' Feel the strange euphoria of grief, where love becomes so big it's both agony and ecstasy. End in a place of profound gratitude that somehow coexists with unbearable loss, your voice breaking and soaring at once, saying thank you to someone who gave you everything and left too soon.
inspired_by: Trying to Order Coffee While Having an Existential Crisis

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They have been unconscious for days, but you've just been told they might still hear you. Begin speaking to them with careful, measured words—perhaps apologizing for past conflicts or trying to say something 'appropriate.' But as you continue, allow whatever truly lives inside you to emerge, even if it surprises you: rage at being abandoned, a joke you used to share, singing off-key, sobbing, laughing at a memory, or even awkward silence. Don't censor anything that wants to surface. The challenge is to move from trying to 'do it right' to allowing whatever genuinely arises—however messy, contradictory, or unexpected—to be spoken. By the end, you should feel you've given them (and yourself) the truth, not the performance of goodbye.
inspired_by: Actor questions whether including an impulse in performance is appropriate or misinterprets the material

title: Three A.M. Confessions
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, and in the dark, you finally whisper the thing you've been hiding. You start so quietly: 'Are you still awake? I need to... I need to tell you something.' Your voice is barely audible, fragile as glass. Maybe it's about an illness you've just been diagnosed with, or a secret from your past, or the fact that you're not sure you can do this anymore — whatever it is, it's the truth that terrifies you. You speak in fragments, starting and stopping, your breath catching. There are long pauses where you almost lose courage. You're gentle with yourself and with them, but the sadness is oceanic. By the end, you're crying without sound, and the confession has become both a burden lifted and a new weight shared. The entire piece should feel like overhearing something too intimate, too raw.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Machines Go Silent
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your parent through a failing neural link - they're in cryo-sleep for a one-way mission to another galaxy, and the connection is breaking up. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to make it easy for them: 'Mom, I'm so proud of you, this is incredible.' But as the static increases and you realize these are truly your last words, your voice cracks. Tell them the things you never said - how you needed them, how you're terrified of being alone. End in raw vulnerability as the connection dies: 'Please don't forget my voice.' Let your breath catch between words. Transform from brave support to desperate child, knowing they can't turn back, knowing you're releasing them into the void forever.
inspired_by: Confessing a Secret That Could Destroy Everything

title: Three A.M. Truths
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying beside someone you love—a partner, a sibling, a close friend—and you can't sleep because there's something you've never told them, something that makes you feel exposed and fragile. Begin in a whisper, tentative, maybe starting and stopping, your voice barely above breath. You're confessing something that reveals a hidden part of yourself: a fear that haunts you, a desire you're ashamed of, a secret you've protected, or a truth about how deeply they matter to you. As you speak, let yourself become more vulnerable, not louder but more naked. Find the quiver in your voice, the places where you almost can't continue, the moments where emotion closes your throat. Let tenderness, shame, hope, and fear all weave through your words. By the end, you've opened a door inside yourself you usually keep locked, and the intimacy of this revelation has transformed both your fear and your trust.

title: The Photo on the Floor
instruction: You are a teenage girl lying on your bedroom floor, propped on your elbows, staring at an old photo of your best friend who moved away. At first, you feel a warm contentment remembering a happy day you spent together—your voice is soft, dreamy, with little sighs. But as you trace the photo with your finger, distress seeps in: a sudden ache of missing them, your voice tightens, words catch. You shift your weight, look away, then back, slowly settling into contemplation—a quiet acceptance, your voice becoming steadier, as if speaking to the memory itself. Let your breath be affected by the position: deeper, with pauses as you adjust your elbows. Speak a few lines about the memory and the loss.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Distress (slightly present), Contemplation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Returning
instruction: You are arriving home after years away—perhaps from prison, war, self-imposed exile, or caring for a dying parent far away. You're speaking to someone who waited for you, and you're flooded with contradictory torrents: fierce joy at being back and crushing guilt for what you missed; deep love and simmering resentment at being needed; hope for the future and grief for lost time that can never be recovered. Begin with whichever emotion feels safest, but let the others crash in unbidden. Don't resolve the contradictions—let them coexist and fight for space in your voice. Allow yourself to laugh and cry in the same breath, to reach out and pull back simultaneously. End in honest confusion about what you feel, but with complete presence to the messy truth of all of it.

title: The Last Letter Before Launch
instruction: You're recording a message to your child the night before you leave on a one-way mission to Mars. You begin with forced optimism, trying to sound brave and excited about this historic journey. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you—you'll never hold them again, never see their graduation, their wedding, their children. Your voice starts to fracture. You're fighting to give them something beautiful to remember, some wisdom to carry forward, but grief keeps breaking through. By the end, you're speaking through tears, whispering the truest thing you know: that leaving them is both the hardest and most important thing you've ever done. Your final words must hold both devastating loss and fierce, protective love.

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Unconscious
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma—maybe they'll wake up, maybe they won't—and you finally have the courage to say what you've hidden for years. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, almost afraid they might actually hear you. There's tenderness as you talk about small, ordinary moments you've cherished in secret—your voice catches on the details, the memory of their laugh, the way they said your name. Your breathing is careful, controlled, like you're handling something precious and breakable. But grief begins seeping in as you realize this might be your only chance: your voice grows more urgent, desperate for them to know. The confession comes in fragments, interrupted by tears you're trying to hold back. You're touching their hand now, and your voice becomes impossibly soft, almost childlike: 'I should have told you every single day.' End with silence broken only by your unsteady breathing.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the affection they never showed you. Begin with careful, practiced words—you've rehearsed this. 'I needed you to tell me you were proud of me.' But as you continue, years of longing break through your control. Your voice becomes younger, more vulnerable, revealing the child still inside: 'Just once, I needed you to say I was enough.' Your parent tries to deflect, and suddenly you're angry—not loud, but searingly honest: 'You're doing it again. Right now.' Then something shifts. You see them—really see their fear, their limitations. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it makes room for heartbreak. End with a voice that holds both unmet need and painful compassion: 'I needed a different parent. And you needed to be a different person. And neither of us got what we needed.'

title: The Drawing on the Fridge
instruction: You're cleaning out your ex-partner's things after the breakup, and you find a drawing your child made six months ago—before they died. You weren't really looking at it, just another item to pack, but then something in the crayon lines makes you stop. Your voice starts flat, exhausted: 'This is just...' Then you see it—hidden in the scribbles is a message, a pattern, something your child was trying to tell you. Your breath catches. 'Oh baby, you were trying to...' Let your voice become impossibly tender, a whisper that's half-wonder, half-devastation. The intellectual understanding mixes with grief so profound it's hard to breathe. End with 'You knew. You knew and you drew it for me,' your voice breaking on a sound that's neither laugh nor sob but both, finding unbearable beauty in this last communication from someone gone forever.

title: The Archaeology of Joy
instruction: You're going through belongings of someone you've lost - boxes of their things, their handwriting on old notes, something that still smells like them. Begin finding small treasures that make you laugh through building tears - a silly photo, a ridiculous inside joke, evidence of how much life they lived. Your voice must hold this impossible combination: genuine laughter at memories that are funny and bright, while simultaneously breaking apart with the knowledge that there will be no new memories. Let gratitude and grief live in the same breath. You're thanking them out loud for specific moments of absurd joy, for the particular way they loved you, while simultaneously feeling the full weight of their absence. The emotional arc moves from lighter reminiscence toward the full collision of celebration and loss. End in a place of profound peace within unbearable pain - you wouldn't trade having known them even though this grief is the price, and somehow that truth is both beautiful and completely devastating.

title: The Wedding Ring in Your Palm
instruction: You're holding your late partner's wedding ring in your palm, standing in what was your shared bedroom, which you've just finished packing up. It's been six months since they died. Begin from a place of practiced strength—you've been 'doing well,' everyone says so, you've been functional and forward-moving. You're looking at the ring almost clinically, ready to put it away. But as you close your fingers around it, something unexpected happens. Move through a sudden ambush of memory—their hand in yours, their laugh, the specific way they said your name. Feel gratitude surging up, enormous and aching, for having had them at all. But tangled with that gratitude is a spike of anger—why did they leave, why weren't you enough to make them stay, even though you know death doesn't work that way. By the end, you're caught in the impossible simultaneity of it all: laughing and crying at once, furious and grateful in the same breath, whispering 'thank you' and 'how dare you' to the empty room, your voice breaking on both. Journey: controlled composure → memory's ambush → gratitude flooding in → love and rage intertwined.
inspired_by: Actor's emotional state is far from what the material demands

title: A Toast to Forgotten Kindness

title: Crush Collapse
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, pressed against a wall. title: Gratitude in the Ruins
instruction: Everything you built has fallen apart, and somehow you're finding beauty in the wreckage. title: The Tea Your Mother Made Wrong

title: Protecting Your Child from Your Own Rage
instruction: You've just discovered your teenage child has been seriously hurt by someone, and you're trying to comfort them while barely containing volcanic fury. instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's bedside in hospice, and she's asked you to tell her about your favorite memory together. instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire childhood. title: Laughing at the Wreckage

title: Impossible Choice
instruction: You're facing an impossible choice between two people or two paths. Your voice is anguished: 'I don't know what to do.' You're talking through both options, and neither feels right. title: Hospice Nurse: The Quiet Confession to a Sleeping Patient
instruction: You're sitting with a patient in their final hours, and you think they're asleep. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and private. Your voice becomes even quieter, more vulnerable: 'I wasn't there when he died. I was at work, saving someone else.' Let the guilt and tenderness intertwine. You're confessing to someone who can't respond, and there's safety in that—but also devastating loneliness. Your words become more halting: 'Thank you for letting me... for giving me another chance to...' You can't finish. The emotion is too big, too quiet, too true. End in the kind of silence where everything you feel is in the breath you take. This isn't performed grief—this is the real, small, heartbreaking way people fall apart when no one's watching.

title: My Child Is Dying and I Cannot Save Them
instruction: You're holding your child in an emergency, speaking to them, to God, to anyone. Your voice cracks between rage at your own helplessness and terror as you feel them slipping away. Let the words become fragments: 'No, no, please—' The explosive panic suddenly fractures into the most tender whisper, as you realize you're witnessing their last moments. Transform from fighting death to making these seconds sacred. End cradling them, voice breaking on a lullaby you used to sing, mixing love and unbearable loss, singing them toward peace even as you're shattering.

title: The Last Thing You'll See
instruction: You're bent over, touching your toes, head pounding from the rush of blood, diaphragm crushed. title: Whispered Permission
instruction: You're lying in the dark with someone you trust completely, and you're finally telling them the thing you've been most ashamed of—something you've never spoken aloud. title: The Truth Your Mother Never Wanted
instruction: You are confronting your mother in her kitchen—the same kitchen where you grew up. title: Reading Your Sibling's Suicide Note and Laughing
instruction: You've just found your brother or sister's goodbye letter, and it's so perfectly, absurdly them—apologizing for the mess, making jokes, being considerate about the timing so it won't 'ruin the holidays.' Your voice swings wildly between genuine amusement and shattered grief, sometimes in the same sentence. You're furious at them for making you laugh at a time like this, grateful they were thinking of you even at the end, destroyed that their kindness extended to their own death. Let the contradictions coexist: love and rage, humor and horror, the instinct to call them and tell them how funny this is and the reality that you never can.

title: What I Never Told You Before You Forgot Me
instruction: You're visiting your grandmother who has advanced dementia. title: The Puzzle Piece That Finally Fits

title: Three AM Skin

title: The Last Morning with Your Daughter Before Prison

title: The Moment You Realize You've Become What You Feared

instruction: You're alone, and you begin touching your own skin as if someone specific is touching you—a lover from your past, someone you ached for, or someone who hurt you. Create the complete physical reality of their presence: their hands on your shoulders, their breath on your neck, the weight of their body, the specific way they moved. Let your body respond as if it's truly happening—your breathing changes, your skin reacts, you move in response to their imagined touch. Start with the sensory memory, but let the emotional reality flood in: desire, rage, grief, ecstasy, betrayal—whatever lives in your body's memory of this person. The physical sensations should trigger genuine emotional responses until you can't separate the imagined from the real. Transform from controlled remembering into being overtaken by the physical and emotional experience, ending in either release or collapse.

title: The Last Time I'll See Your Face
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's unconscious, but you need to tell her everything you never said. Start by trying to say the 'important' things - thank you, I love you, I forgive you. But as you speak, let your mind drift to unexpected memories: the pattern of her wallpaper, the smell of her soap, the way light hit her kitchen table, the sound of her humming. Don't force these images - let them arrive uninvited. Follow wherever these sense-memories take you emotionally, even if it seems unrelated to 'goodbye.' Let your voice and emotion be guided by whatever images float up from underneath your planned words. You may start with prepared gratitude but end somewhere completely unexpected - perhaps childlike fear, or fierce protectiveness, or a strange joy.

title: The Rage That Breaks in the Empty Apartment
instruction: You've just returned to the apartment you shared, and they're gone—not dead, but gone by choice, and somehow that's worse. Start with bitter sarcasm, talking to the empty room, your voice sharp and cutting as you mock their note, their excuses, their cowardice. Let the volume build as you move through the space, each object a trigger—their coffee mug, the book they left, the photograph. Your voice becomes louder, more aggressive, shouting at walls, at absence, demanding answers from someone who can't hear you. Then hit the moment of physical collapse—maybe you throw something, maybe you just sink to the floor—and the rage shatters completely into raw, ugly grief. Your voice breaks into sobs, words becoming incoherent, admitting the truth you've been avoiding: you saw this coming and you still couldn't stop it. End in exhausted whispers, talking to yourself now, trying to remember how to breathe, how to be a person who continues existing. The final words should be quiet acceptance mixed with residual anger: 'Okay. Okay. I'll be okay.' You don't believe it yet, but you're trying.
inspired_by: Buried in Snow: Creating an Air Pocket While Suffocating

title: The Last Words You'll Ever Say to Your Father
instruction: Your father is dying, and you've carried resentment for decades—he was never there, never the parent you needed. You start by telling him exactly what he failed to give you, your voice cold and precise, finally speaking truths you've swallowed for years. But as you watch his labored breathing, something shifts. The anger cracks open and underneath is a desperate, aching need for him to acknowledge you, just once, before it's too late. Your voice becomes raw, pleading—you're no longer accusing, you're begging. By the end, you're holding his hand, whispering that despite everything, you needed him to know you're here, and the words 'I love you' come out broken, mixed with grief for the relationship you'll never have. Let the transformation happen organically—from bitter truth-telling to desperate vulnerability to heartbroken acceptance.

title: The Confession in the Fungus
instruction: You're a burly, deep-voiced young man, but right now you're lying on your stomach, peering into a damp, dark crawlspace under a cabin. The air is thick with the smell of rot and mold. You're whispering to a tiny, beautiful stray cat that's trapped behind a pipe. You're completely smitten—your voice is full of tender, silly cooing. But you're also disgusted: a squirming clump of something wet and slimy has just brushed your cheek. You can't wipe it off without scaring the cat. Start with pure, melting adoration, but let the revulsion creep into your words as you speak, until your whisper is a frantic, grossed-out plea.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Elation (slightly present), Disgust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Spotlight Thief
instruction: You are an older actress on a dark stage after a rehearsal. You're speaking to a younger actress who just gave a brilliant performance. You begin with a teasing, almost mocking tone about her youth and energy, but as you speak, the echo of your own voice in the empty auditorium reminds you of your fading career. Let the jealousy seep through your smile. Your voice should start light and playful, then catch on certain words, become quieter, more strained as the envy surfaces. The reverb makes your words hang in the air, emphasizing the weight of your regret. End with a hollow, almost bitter compliment.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Unraveling the Silence: Mother and Child at Breaking Point
instruction: You are confronting your mother (or grown child) after years of swallowing your truth to keep the peace. Begin with restrained politeness, that familiar mask you've worn for decades, your voice controlled and 'appropriate.' But something has shifted—a betrayal discovered, a pattern finally seen clearly, or simply the unbearable weight of pretending. As you speak, feel the careful façade begin to crack. Your voice starts to shake despite your best efforts to control it. Let years of buried hurt, disappointment, and suffocated anger rise to the surface. The words you speak should be things you've rehearsed in your mind a thousand times but never dared say aloud. By the end, you're either sobbing with raw honesty or speaking with a devastating, quiet clarity that comes from finally stepping out of the shadows. The transformation is from performing a role (dutiful child/perfect parent) to standing naked in your truth, whatever the cost.
inspired_by: Actor fears exposing private feelings or being vulnerable in performance

title: Confronting Your Mother: The Love She Couldn't Give
instruction: You're in your mother's kitchen, finally speaking a truth you've carried for decades. Start with careful, measured words, trying to be kind: 'I know you did your best.' But she deflects, minimizes. Your voice hardens, anger seeping through: 'No. You don't get to do that anymore.' Let the rage build as you list the moments she wasn't there, voice rising and sharp. She says you're being cruel, ungrateful. Feel the fury peak—then suddenly collapse into the grief underneath: 'I needed you, Mom. I was just a kid.' Voice breaks completely, tears choking your words. End with exhausted clarity, voice drained but steady: 'I forgive you. But I can't keep pretending it didn't matter.' Feel the weight of finally putting it down.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Leaving a Good Relationship

title: Reading Your Estranged Sibling's Letter at Their Funeral
instruction: You're standing at a funeral, holding a letter your sibling wrote to you years ago that you never answered—maybe you were too proud, too hurt, too stubborn. You're reading it aloud now, to the room or to their memory. Start with composed, public-voice reading, but as their words reach you—their humor, their pain, their love despite everything—you begin to break. Laugh at their jokes even as tears come. Your voice should swing wildly between gratitude for what they gave you, rage at the time you wasted in silence, and crushing regret. Let yourself speak to them directly, answering the letter now, too late. End with forgiveness—of them, of yourself—spoken through tears but with something like peace, like finally letting them go and holding them close at the same time.

title: Hands Full of Your Mother's Necklace
instruction: You're standing, your hands gripping a necklace (your mother's, your grandmother's—your choice). Someone has just told you news that splits your world: a betrayal, a long-held lie revealed, a secret that recontextualizes your entire childhood. Start with your hands closed in fists around this necklace, the chain cutting into your palms, the pendant pressing into your flesh. Let the physical sensation—the bite of metal, the warmth of it from your body heat, the weight—ground you as your entire reality shifts. Move physically: pace, shake, press it against your chest, your forehead. Let the object be both weapon and lifeline. As you grip it tighter, feel the rage at being lied to, the physical need to destroy something, the way anger lives in your throat and shoulders. But also let it connect you to every woman who wore this before you—their own pain, their survival. By the end, you're not just holding jewelry; you're holding generations of women's grief and fury and resilience. Transform from explosive rage to something more complex: rage still present, but now mixed with understanding that pain is inherited like this gold.

title: The Wedding Toast You Didn't Plan
instruction: You're giving a toast at a wedding—but it's for your ex-partner who left you and is now marrying someone else. You genuinely want them to be happy, and you're also devastated. Begin by trying to perform graciousness, saying the expected things. But then pause. Really look at them. Let yourself be curious about who they've become since you separated. Notice the way they look at their new spouse—and feel both the knife-twist of jealousy and the strange relief of seeing them truly happy. Your consciousness expands to hold both truths: your grief is real AND your love for them—the kind that wants their joy even when it costs you—is also real. By the end, you're speaking with brutal honesty and surprising grace, your voice breaking not from bitterness but from the complexity of genuinely wishing someone well while mourning what you lost. Transform from performed politeness through pain into authentic, bittersweet benediction.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You are confronting your father after years of silence between you. Start with controlled anger—your arms crossed, your voice sharp and accusatory. You've rehearsed these grievances a thousand times. 'You were never there. You chose everything else over us.' But as you speak, he doesn't defend himself. He just stands there, shoulders sagging, looking suddenly old and broken. Your anger begins to crack. Memories flood in—moments you'd forgotten, times he tried in his clumsy way. Your voice wavers. The accusations become questions: 'Why didn't you...?' Then, quieter: 'I needed you.' Let yourself move from rage to a raw, childlike plea for understanding. End by either reaching toward him or turning away—but from a place of exposed need rather than defended anger.

title: Your Mother's Cardigan, The Day After the Funeral
instruction: You've found your mother's favorite cardigan in her closet. As you slip it on, you're overwhelmed by her scent still lingering in the fabric. Start with a trembling smile, describing the softness as comfort—almost speaking to her. But as you pull it closer, the reality that she's gone crashes over you. Your voice should break from tender reminiscence into raw, gasping grief. Let the sweater become both a lifeline and a devastating reminder. End in quiet, shattered acceptance, whispering something you never got to say to her.
inspired_by: Feeling a Soft, Cozy Sweater Against Your Skin

title: First Testimony
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl at a small church youth service, standing at the podium for the first time. The room is quiet, a few old fans humming, someone coughs in the back. You start nervously, your voice thin and stumbling, forgetting the words you rehearsed. But as you describe the moment you felt truly seen during a tough week, awe rises in your chest—your voice finds its rhythm, swells with quiet amazement, and you let the pauses hang, caught between tears and a smile. End with a breathy, full-throated 'and I knew... it was real' as the congregation shifts in their seats.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Gratitude in the Wreckage
instruction: You're thanking your ex-partner for leaving you, and you mean it, even though you're shattered. Your voice should carry genuine, almost delirious relief—'Thank you for being brave enough to go'—while tears stream down your face. Laugh at the absurdity of feeling grateful for heartbreak, but let that laughter catch and break. You're celebrating your liberation while mourning the future you built together. Your words should dance between joy and devastation: 'I'm free and I'm destroyed and both things are true.' End with a whispered admission that you'll miss them while being so grateful they're gone. This is the beautiful chaos of contradictory truth—finding peace in the rubble, joy in the ending.

title: Sauna Gratitude
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy in a crowded, dripping wet sauna. Your hyper-masculine voice feels strained, and you're wiping sweat from your face. Your uncle just handed you a cold towel, and you want to thank him properly, but the heat makes you distracted and breathless. Begin with muttered, half-hearted appreciation, then as the coolness hits, your gratitude becomes genuine, your voice dropping its guardedness. Let the moisture affect your speech—sloppy mouth sounds, heavy breathing. End with a quiet, heartfelt 'really, thanks.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Goodbye Before the Mission
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving on a one-way mission to space—or war—or a medical trial with no guarantee of survival. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave: 'This is what you've always wanted...' Your voice cracks as reality sets in. The middle is raw pleading mixed with pride—you want them to stay but you also want them to go fulfill their purpose. End in a whisper of pure love and terror: 'Come back to me.' Let your breath catch. Let the silence between words hold everything you can't say. This isn't about being loud—it's about your heart splitting open while trying to stay whole for them.
inspired_by: Standing Your Ground When Everyone Disagrees

title: Helmet Hymn for a Dubious Heart
instruction: You are a young astronaut in a space suit, alone on the hull of a station after a risky repair that succeeded against the odds. Your voice echoes inside the helmet; every breath is loud, and the radio crackles. You speak to yourself, half to mission control, half to the stars. Begin with gratitude for the team that trained you, but let doubt creep in—was it really you, or just luck? As you continue, let a fierce pride build, not boastful but earned, until your voice steadies with quiet triumph. Let the physical constraints (the confined echo, the amplified breaths, the occasional static burst) interrupt and shape your words naturally. Speak for about 60 seconds, ending with a mix of exhausted gratitude and unshakeable pride.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Doubt (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Goodbye Sounds Like Laughter
instruction: Your best friend is leaving for a humanitarian mission in a war zone, and you both know the statistics. You're trying to have one last normal conversation, joking about all the things they'll miss—your terrible cooking, your pathological lateness. Start with genuine laughter, the kind of intimacy that comes from years of friendship. But let your voice crack mid-joke: 'You're going to miss my birthday. You've never missed my birthday.' The laughter becomes tears becomes laughter again, all mixed together. You're furious at them for going and so proud you could burst. Grateful for who they are and shattered that this might be goodbye. End telling them 'I love you' while laughing through tears, your voice holding every contradictory emotion at once—celebration and devastation, pride and terror, gratitude and grief.

title: The Last Vigil: A Mother Slipping Away
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed in her final hours. Begin by reading her favorite poem aloud with forced steadiness, trying to be strong for her. As you continue, your voice begins to fracture—first in small breaks, then longer pauses where you can't speak. The words become harder to form as grief rises in your chest. Transition from controlled reading to whispering the lines directly to her, your voice raw with the desperate need for her to hear you one more time. End with your voice dissolving completely as you abandon the poem and simply tell her what you need her to know, each word pulled from somewhere deep and primal. Show the journey from composure to complete emotional unraveling, from performing strength to surrendering to devastating loss.

title: The Ocean in a Seashell: A Child's Wonder
instruction: A child picks up a seashell and holds it to their ear. Perform their discovery — first silence, then the gasp. 'I CAN HEAR THE OCEAN!' Describe what they imagine: whales singing, waves crashing, mermaids swimming. The child's voice should be high, breathy with excitement, tumbling over words too fast. Include them making an adult listen too, and their insistence that it's REAL ocean, not 'just air' as the grown-up suggests. Protect the magic.

title: Hands in the Garden Soil
instruction: You are on your knees in a garden, digging with your bare hands in the earth. Begin in a state of barely controlled rage—you're tearing at the soil, ripping out weeds, your breath harsh and physical. You might be furious at someone, at yourself, at what you've lost. As your hands work the earth, let the physical sensations—the coolness of the soil, the smell of dirt and growing things, the ache in your muscles—begin to unlock unexpected body memories. A moment of planting something with someone you loved. Your grandmother's hands in this same earth. The feeling of being small and safe. Let these physical sense-memories change your emotional state involuntarily. Your angry breathing might become sobs, or quiet, or something like laughter. The rage in your body must transform completely by the end—perhaps into exhausted grief, startling peace, aching loneliness, or painful hope. Let your body's memory lead you where your mind didn't plan to go.

title: The Confession on the Crate
instruction: You are a child standing on a wooden crate in a crowded park, your voice raw from shouting over traffic and chatter. You were supposed to speak about community recycling, but instead you're blurting out a secret—you stole a neighbor's garden gnome last week. Begin with your voice thin and wobbly, shame pinching your throat, each word a struggle against the urge to run. As you feel the crowd's silence, your shame slowly shifts into a stubborn, trembling relief—you're finally telling the truth. Let your pitch rise and crack naturally, and when a dog barks nearby, pause, swallow, then push on with a little more weight in your voice.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Held in the Afterglow
instruction: You're a young woman recovering from an intense BDSM scene, lying in your partner's arms under a heavy blanket. Your body is trembling slightly, your voice soft and quivering as you come down from the high. At first, you can barely speak, just murmuring small sounds of exhaustion and vulnerability. But as your partner strokes your hair and whispers reassurances, a deep sense of awe washes over you — not just relief, but a profound wonder at being so utterly trusted and cared for. Let your voice shift from a shaky whisper to a slow, awed realization, punctuated by pauses where you sip water or nuzzle into their chest. Micro-distractions: a contented sigh, a rustle of the blanket, a tiny laugh at your own shaky words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing Through the Requiem
instruction: You are performing the final concert your late partner composed before dying, and you're speaking to them as if they're in the audience. Your voice should carry strange, beautiful contradictions—begin with laughter mixed with tears as you recall a funny memory about writing this piece together, how they always hummed off-key while composing. Let joy and grief exist in the same breath. Shift into expressing gratitude that makes your heart break—thank them for the music, for the love, for leaving you this gift, your voice warm with appreciation even as it trembles with loss. Find moments of peace describing how their music lives on, then let that peace coexist with longing for one more day. End with a paradox: you're utterly devastated and completely whole at once, destroyed by their absence and held together by their art. Your voice should smile and break in the same sentence, finding strange grace in the contradiction.

title: A Lie of Love
instruction: Youre pretending to love someone deeply when youre actually indifferent or even repulsed. Keep your tone warm and affectionate, layering subtle hints of insincerity as you try to mask your true feelings.

title: Holding Vigil at the Window
instruction: You're keeping watch by the window on the third night, talking to your missing child's empty room. Speak quietly, as if they might actually walk through the door if you don't scare them away. Begin with mundane updates—what happened at work, what the dog did, who called. Let your voice stay gentle, almost normal, but with something trembling underneath. When you reach for their favorite jacket still hanging on the chair, let the tenderness crack you open. Whisper the things you never said enough: how proud you are, how their laugh is your favorite sound. Don't cry loudly—let it be the kind of tears that fall silently while you're still talking. End with a confession barely audible: you're scared you've forgotten the exact sound of their voice.

title: Whispering Secrets in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night, and you're lying beside someone you trust completely, finally revealing a truth you've kept buried for years—a betrayal you committed, a trauma you survived, a dream you abandoned. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and raw. Begin tentatively, testing whether you can actually say the words aloud. As you speak, feel the relief of release mixed with shame or sorrow. Let your voice catch, pause, restart. Move through moments where speaking becomes almost physically difficult, where emotion closes your throat. Shift into a tender vulnerability as you reveal why you're telling them now, what you need from them. End with a quiet plea for understanding or forgiveness, your voice nakedly exposed, carrying the weight of years of silence and the fragile hope that this confession won't destroy what you have.

title: Confronting Your Mother in the Bathroom Mirror
instruction: You're alone in your bathroom after your mother's cruel comment about your body. Begin by describing stepping into the bath mechanically, your voice tight and defensive, repeating her words in mocking tones. As the water touches your skin, let years of accumulated hurt rise up—shift from bitter sarcasm to raw anger as you address her as if she's there. Tell her what her comments have done to you, how you've learned to hate the body she gave you. Let your voice break between rage and pain. Then, mid-fury, catch sight of yourself and shift—suddenly speak to yourself with the tenderness she never showed you. End by describing the water holding you as you should have been held, your voice moving from fierce anger through devastating vulnerability to trembling self-compassion. The arc moves from defensive mockery to explosive hurt to fragile, hard-won gentleness toward yourself.

title: Laughing Through the Breaking
instruction: You're at your own going-away party—you're moving across the world, leaving everything behind for a necessary but heartbreaking reason. You're giving a toast to the people who've been your family, your chosen people. Begin with genuine laughter, sharing a funny memory that makes you smile even as you speak. But the laughter keeps catching, becoming something else. You're trying to express gratitude while your heart is shattering, trying to celebrate while grieving. 'Thank you for being my home' comes out half-laughed, half-sobbed. You keep almost losing it, then pulling yourself back with another joke, another memory, but the cracks keep showing. Your voice wavers between joy at what you've shared and devastation at what you're leaving. End with a strange, beautiful mixture—laughing and crying simultaneously as you say something like 'I'll carry all of you with me,' your voice full of love and loss in equal measure, finding something like peace in the impossibility of holding both feelings at once.

title: The Confrontation: Why You Never Chose Me
instruction: You're standing in your mother's kitchen, thirty-five years old, and finally saying the words you've rehearsed a thousand times. Start with your voice tight, controlled, almost clinical as you list the ways she chose your sibling over you—every missed recital, every birthday she forgot, every time she looked through you like you were invisible. Your mother tries to interrupt with excuses, and your voice rises, fierce and demanding: 'No, you will hear this.' The anger feels good at first, righteous and powerful. But as you continue, something shifts—you hear how much you still need her love, how desperately you wanted to matter. Your voice cracks, becoming raw and childlike: 'Why wasn't I enough?' By the end, you're no longer confronting her—you're begging a mother who may never be capable of the answer you need, your voice reduced to a whisper of pure, exposed pain.
inspired_by: Professional: Social Worker Removes a Child from Their Parents

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent about something they did (or didn't do) during your childhood - something you've rehearsed saying a thousand times in your head. Start with the practiced anger, the carefully crafted accusations you've prepared. But as you speak, notice what's actually happening in the room: their face, their posture, the way they're trying (or not trying) to meet your eyes. Allow your prepared speech to crumble. Let unexpected feelings interrupt your rage - perhaps a flash of understanding you don't want, a memory of tenderness that complicates your narrative, or a realization about your own complicity in the silence between you. The scene transforms as you stop performing your justified anger and discover what you genuinely feel beneath the rehearsed grievances. End in a place of raw, complicated honesty you didn't plan.
inspired_by: Actor is falling into result consciousness—going for the emotion of a scene rather than working from the moment

title: The Final Ridge
instruction: You are an elderly man, a former mountaineer, trying to reach a lookout point on a trail you've hiked a hundred times. Altitude sickness makes your breath come in gasps, each word a struggle. You're with a younger companion who has subtly suggested turning back, and a fierce pride rises in you—you will not be seen as weak. As you speak, pause to gasp, wince from a throbbing headache, and lose track of a word before finding it. Start with clenching your jaw against the pain and the shame in their pity, but end with a raw, defiant warmth—you're not conceding, you're just remembering why you came.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: 3 AM Reunion at the Baggage Claim
instruction: You've been traveling for thirty hours, and your body has no idea what time it is. You're standing in the airport after three sleepless flights, swaying slightly with exhaustion, but the person you love most just texted that they're waiting outside. The relief hits you so hard you almost laugh—but you're so drained your throat barely works. You're teasing your own state, slurring and fumbling for words, gesturing at the absurdity of your condition as you talk to them through the phone. Let your voice crack, lose sentences mid-thought, and yawn into the word 'home' as you realize the exhaustion and joy are the same thing.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Glass
instruction: You're an older adult, alone at a dive bar, well past your limit. The glass is almost empty and you're muttering to yourself—or to the absent friend who left hours ago. Start with sharp irritation: the jukebox is too loud, the stool wobbles, the bartender ignores you. Let your volume spike and drop; let your words blur at the edges. Then, mid-sentence, a memory catches you—a name, a face, a moment you can't get back. The irritation drains into heavy, inward contemplation. Your voice softens, slows, and you lose the thread. Pause as if searching for a word, then find it in a whisper. The performance should feel like a real drunk ramble: messy, honest, and shifting without warning.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whisper Intimacy
instruction: You're confessing a secret to someone in a crowded room where no one can know. Your voice drops to barely audible, meant only for this one person: 'I've been thinking about leaving.' The intimacy of the whisper creates a bubble around just you two. You can hear your heartbeat in the quiet. The person asks, at normal volume, 'What did you say?' and you have to decide: repeat it louder (breaking the spell, making it real), or lean in even closer: 'I'll tell you tonight. When we're alone.' The whisper is a promise, a vulnerability, an conspiracy. By the end, the room full of people feels infinite, and the whisper feels like the only real thing in it.

title: Laughing Through Your Final Status Report
instruction: You're recording your last mission report from the observation station you can't evacuate from, and you start laughing—not from joy but from the absurd clarity of knowing exactly when and how you'll die. You're describing technical readings with inappropriate giggles breaking through, finding dark humor in the precision of your own ending. Your laughter has tears in it as you thank your team by name, your voice cracking between professional gratitude and the punch-drunk euphoria of someone who's moved beyond fear into strange peace. You joke about things that aren't funny—the beauty of the approaching storm that will kill you, the irony that you're the only one who will witness what you've spent years studying. Your voice wavers between awe at what you're seeing and the surreal comedy of narrating your own last moments. The laughter keeps shifting—sometimes it's genuine wonder at the magnificence of the universe, sometimes it's grief disguised as joy, sometimes it's just the sound of a human spirit refusing to let terror have the last word. You end speaking to someone you loved, your voice still smiling through tears, finding grace in the fact that your final act is bearing witness, that even your ending will mean something, that you're somehow grateful and devastated and strangely, impossibly at peace.

title: The Last Jar on the Shelf
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in your kitchen, stretching up on tiptoes to reach a dusty jar on the highest shelf. Your arms are fully extended, ribs pulled taut, making every breath shallow and your voice thin and quivery. Start with a sigh of frustration as you wobble and nearly lose your balance—mutter to yourself about your age and these stupid high shelves. As your fingers finally close around the jar, you pause, reading the faded label. Your tone shifts: interest seeps in, a soft, wondering curiosity about what's inside. Let your voice crack and trail off as you carefully lower the jar, ending with a hushed, almost tender speculation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Clear Morning: Dementia's Final Window
instruction: You're visiting your parent who has late-stage dementia. For a miraculous moment, they're completely lucid—they know you, remember everything, and you have this precious window of clarity. Start with overwhelming joy and relief, talking quickly, trying to fit a lifetime of 'I love you' into minutes. But as you speak, you watch the clarity begin to fade from their eyes. Your words become more desperate, clinging to the moment. Then acceptance washes over you—tender, devastating acceptance. End by speaking to them as they slip away again, your voice soft with both grief and gratitude for these final clear moments together. The transition from joy to desperation to peaceful heartbreak should feel like watching sand slip through your fingers.

title: The Last Garden Visit
instruction: You are visiting your grandmother in hospice for what you know will be the last time. As you sit by her bedside, you begin telling her about the garden you're planting in her honor - describing in vivid sensory detail the flowers, the soil between your fingers, the morning dew, the hummingbirds that will visit. Start from a place of heavy grief and barely contained tears, but as you paint this sensory picture for her (and yourself), let the beauty of what you're describing gradually lift you. By the end, you should feel genuine joy and even excitement about this living memorial, mixed with your sorrow.
