speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: I Won't Let Them Take You
instruction: You're holding someone you're fiercely protective of - your child, younger sibling, someone vulnerable - and you've just learned they're in danger you can't prevent. Start with fierce determination, almost aggressive in its intensity: 'Listen to me - no one is going to hurt you. No one.' But as reality crashes in, your voice begins to crack with helpless rage: 'I swear to God, I would burn the whole world down...' Then the fury breaks completely into desperate, sobbing fear: 'But I can't stop this. I can't fix this.' Finally, collapse into raw, tender promises through tears: 'I'm here. Whatever happens, you're not alone.' Arc from powerful protectiveness to explosive rage to helpless anguish to fierce, broken tenderness.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a truth you've never been allowed to speak aloud—something that shaped your entire childhood that you both pretended didn't exist. Start with careful, controlled anger, almost polite in your fury. As your parent reacts to each thing you say—whether they deny, deflect, justify, or break down—let their response genuinely land on you and change what you feel. Don't plan where this goes. If they make you feel guilty, feel guilty. If they make you feel vindicated, feel vindicated. If they make you feel like a child again, become that child. Let your emotions shift and cascade in response to what's actually happening between you, building to a place where multiple feelings war inside you at once. The end of this confrontation should feel nothing like its controlled beginning.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times in your head. Face to face with the parent who chose something else over you—work, addiction, another family, their own pain. You begin with the anger you've carried for years, the accusations you've earned the right to make. But as you speak, something unexpected happens. You hear yourself, you see them, and the anger doesn't disappear but it makes room for something else—the child who still needed them, the grief of what you never had, maybe even a terrible, unwanted understanding. Take us from righteous fury to the complicated mess of wanting to hate someone you still, somehow, love. Let your voice shake not from weakness but from the courage of finally being honest.
inspired_by: Hiding Nervousness During an Important Interview

title: Gravel Path Gratitude
instruction: You are walking home late at night on a long, noisy gravel driveway, crunching loudly with each step. You're carrying a heavy bag of groceries that keeps slipping, so you adjust it as you walk. Earlier, a stranger helped you when your car broke down, and you're still genuinely surprised by their kindness—but a tiny, creeping thought makes you wonder if they had an ulterior motive, stirring a hint of unease. Start with a warm, breathless thankfulness as you recount the help, but let your voice drop slightly when the suspicion sneaks in before fading back to grateful astonishment. Speak louder than usual to be heard over your own footsteps, pausing naturally when you shift the bag or turn your head.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Simple Question That Isn't Simple
instruction: You're sitting on the couch a few hours after a mild concussion, still foggy and slow. Your friend asks, 'What did you have for breakfast?' – an easy question, but your brain feels like it's underwater. You try to answer, but the words slip away, and you can't find the volume control for your voice. Start with a quiet, embarrassed attempt, but as you struggle and your friend waits, frustration builds. Let your voice become louder and more clipped, irritation spilling out as you finally snap at them for no real reason. Speak naturally, with long pauses, lost thoughts, and a monotone that cracks into irritable sharpness.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner in the darkness. You whisper that you need to tell them something you've carried alone for years—a secret that sits like a stone in your chest. Begin with the barely audible admission: 'I need you to know...' Your voice is so quiet it's almost just breath. As you confess (a past betrayal, a lie, a fear, something that could change everything), your whisper becomes even softer, as if speaking quietly enough might make it hurt less. There are long pauses where you can't find words. Your throat closes. You're terrified they'll leave, but more terrified of carrying this alone another day. End with the smallest, most fragile question: 'Are you still there?' The entire performance should feel like you're speaking from inside your own breaking heart.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent who was always distant, always withholding approval. For years you've swallowed your need for their love. Begin whispering what you've never said: how much their silence hurt, how hard you tried, how angry you are that they're leaving without ever truly seeing you. Start quietly, almost afraid to disturb them. But as you speak, let years of suppressed pain rise in your voice—not yelling, but with increasing raw honesty and volume. By the end, you're finally saying everything with full voice, no longer asking permission to feel what you feel. Then, in the final moment, let the anger crack open into something else: the grief of losing them before you ever really had them.

title: The Confession in the Dark: Admitting Love to Your Dying Best Friend
instruction: You're sitting beside your best friend's hospital bed at 3am. They're sleeping. You know they won't wake. Begin in a whisper so soft it's almost talking to yourself: 'I need to tell you something I've never...' Your voice catches. This isn't dramatic — it's the kind of quiet that happens when everyone else is asleep and you're alone with impossible truth. Speak about the years of hidden love, but not as declaration — as confession laced with grief. Your throat tightens on certain words: 'you,' 'love,' 'always.' Include the moment you almost touch their hand but don't. The emotion shouldn't crescendo; it should deepen, like water seeping into earth. End with 'I'm so glad you were my friend' — where 'friend' is both truth and the saddest lie you've ever told. Let the silence after speak what you couldn't.
inspired_by: Comedian Whose Set Is Bombing — And They're Spiraling

title: A Body That Betrays Her
instruction: You are eight months pregnant, sitting alone in a cramped waiting room at a government benefits office. You have been waiting for over an hour. Your back aches, the baby is pressing on your lungs, and every breath feels shallow and stolen. You are on the phone with your sister, but you don't want to cry—you want to be sharp, bitter about the system that makes you beg for help while the baby's father walked away. Your voice starts tight and clipped, anger pushing through the fatigue, but as you speak, the shame of needing assistance seeps in. Let your sentences falter as you shift in the hard chair, sigh between words, and let the bitterness curdle into something more vulnerable by the end, as if you're realizing out loud that your pride is a luxury you can't afford.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Reading Your Suicide Note from Ten Years Ago (And Laughing)
instruction: You found it while cleaning out old boxes—the suicide note you wrote a decade ago but never used. Start reading it aloud, your voice tentative, almost clinical, keeping distance from the pain in those words. But as you read, something shifts. A laugh escapes—not cruel, but disbelieving. 'God, I really thought that was the end.' Your voice oscillates between tears and laughter, grief for that younger self and joy at having survived. Read the most devastating lines with your voice cracking: 'Nobody will miss me'—and then you have to stop, overcome by how wrong you were. The emotions tangle: gratitude, sorrow, pride, residual pain. You're crying and laughing at once, your voice shaking with both. End by speaking to your younger self with infinite tenderness: 'I'm so glad you stayed. Look at what you would have missed.' Your voice is full of tears but also something like wonder—the beautiful, terrible miracle of still being here.
inspired_by: Crevasse Rescue: Hearing the Rope Appear Above You

title: The Last Night Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who leaves at dawn for a mission they may not return from. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to be strong, keeping your voice bright and optimistic. But as the night deepens, the pretense becomes impossible to maintain. Your voice begins to crack with the weight of unsaid things. Let yourself move through denial into raw acknowledgment of what morning will bring. Express gratitude for every moment you've shared, even as grief threatens to overwhelm you. By the end, find a place where love and loss coexist—your voice soft, intimate, holding both the ache of goodbye and the fierce joy of having loved this person at all. Let silences speak. Let your breath catch. This is not a performance of goodbye; this is the real thing.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child, and you've rehearsed this moment a thousand times in your head. Start with controlled anger—rapid-fire listing of every birthday they missed, every school play, every night you waited. Your words tumble over each other, sharp and cutting. But as you speak, the anger begins to crack. Your voice catches. The accusations transform into questions you've carried for years: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me?' End in a place of devastating quiet, where the rage has burned itself out and all that remains is the lost child asking why they weren't loved.

title: Holding Your Dying Dog and Screaming at God
instruction: Your beloved dog is in your arms, dying or just after the vet has helped them pass. You're alone in your car or your living room, and everything you've been holding together just detonates. Start with your face buried in their fur, breathing them in, whispering 'good dog, good dog' like a prayer. But then the unfairness of it, the rage at a universe that gives you something to love just to rip it away — let it explode out of you. Yell at God, at fate, at the ceiling. Demand answers. Your voice breaks from screaming into sobbing, then back to fierce anger. Pound the floor. Then collapse back into tenderness, cradling them, apologizing for yelling, telling them it's okay to go. Feel the helplessness of loving something you cannot save. End in that awful quiet after the storm, just breathing, stroking their fur, finding some small piece of acceptance in the wreckage.
inspired_by: Teaching a Fitness Class While Completely Hungover

title: The Last Thing Only You Would Say
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and you have minutes left. Everyone else has said their goodbyes with the usual words—'I love you,' 'thank you,' 'I'll miss you.' But you realize there's something only YOU would say to this person, something that captures the specific, irreplaceable weirdness of your relationship—maybe it's an inside joke, a shared memory no one else would understand, or a confession that's completely inappropriate for a deathbed but perfectly YOU. Start with the weight of conventional grief, trying to find 'appropriate' words. Then let yourself break free and speak the thing only you could say—the thing that's messy, specific, possibly funny, possibly wrong, but utterly true to who you are together. End with the liberation of having honored your relationship in your own unrepeatable way, even as your heart breaks.

title: The Last Touch of Summer Skin
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the golden afternoon light. She's slipping away, drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by simply holding her hand—notice its actual temperature, texture, the way her fingers feel in yours. As you speak your goodbye, allow yourself to become intensely aware of every detail: the papery quality of her skin, any warmth that remains, the delicate bones beneath. Let these sensations grow fuller in your awareness—perhaps her hand feels like it holds the memory of every time she touched your face as a child, every time she held you. Start with quiet acceptance of her leaving, but as these physical sensations deepen and expand in your mind, let them unlock a fierce, aching love and the desperate wish to hold onto this moment forever. End in a place of overwhelming tenderness mixed with the unbearable knowledge that this touch will soon be a memory.

title: Standing Still in a Moving World
instruction: You're in a crowded foreign airport terminal, having just arrived after thirty hours of travel. Your body aches with exhaustion, but your mind is wired—every sound feels too loud. You're on a video call with your partner, who is upset you missed their flight connection. You begin by trying to calmly explain, but mid-sentence you lose track of a simple word, then snap at them from a wave of irrational distress. From apologetic confusion, the performance shifts into raw, frustrated helplessness as you realize you're not making sense. Let your voice crack, drift off, or speed up unexpectedly as you struggle to stay present.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Trying to Explain Death to Your Child
instruction: Your child's grandparent or pet died. 'Where did they go?' Your voice is searching for the right words. Your voice is calm but inside you're devastated. Your child is asking if they're coming back. Your voice is honest but gentle. You're using metaphors—'like sleeping'—but your child hears something final. Your voice becomes quieter. You're both crying. Your voice can barely function. But you stay present with them in it.

title: Baptism by Fire
instruction: You are standing in a childhood playground at dusk, gripping the chains of a swing set. Your body remembers this place viscerally—scraped knees, the metallic taste of blood, the triumph of pumping your legs to fly higher. Now you're here because you've just received devastating news that ignites rage in your body. Begin by swinging gently, letting the physical motion unlock muscle memory of being small, powerless, afraid. Then let fury flood through you—scream, shake the chains, let your whole body express what words cannot hold. Mix this explosive anger with the physical sensations of the space: the cold metal burning your palms, the way your stomach drops on the backswing, the childhood feeling of trying to touch the sky. By the end, exhaust yourself into a different emotion—perhaps grief, perhaps strange exhilaration, perhaps the quiet that comes after a storm passes through flesh and bone.

title: The Inheritance Box
instruction: You are alone, opening a box your estranged mother left you after her death. Inside is a sweater she used to wear—you recognize it instantly. Begin by pulling it out and holding it with resentment and suspicion; she abandoned you, why should this matter? But then, let yourself smell it. Really smell it—find the exact scent of her perfume, the laundry detergent she used, something underneath that's just her. Let the smell unlock other sense memories without trying to control them: the feeling of her arms around you when you were small, the sound of her humming while cooking, the taste of the birthday cakes she made before she left. Your emotions should fracture and complicate: anger at her for leaving battles with involuntary love for who she was to you once; resentment wars with devastating longing. End in a place where you're feeling everything at once—furious and grateful, betrayed and connected, hating her and missing her in the same breath.
inspired_by: Basic Imaging with Sense Memory Exercise

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your adult child (or parent) in your kitchen late at night. Start defensive, armed with your rehearsed grievances and justifications. But as you speak, let the fortress crack. Notice the actual sensations in your body—the trembling, the heat, the ache. Let yourself be ambushed by unexpected feelings: the child's face triggering a memory that changes everything, your voice breaking when you didn't plan it, sudden awareness of how afraid you've been. Don't perform emotion—let whatever wants to surface surprise you. By the end, you might find yourself saying something you never intended, perhaps the opposite of where you started. Let the confrontation transform you rather than following a script you brought into the room.

title: Peace Finding
instruction: After years of struggle, you're finding peace. Your voice is quiet, settled: 'I'm not okay. But I'm at peace with not being okay.' The distinction is important and audible in your voice. 'I don't need to be fixed. I don't need to have all the answers. I just need to be okay with the journey.' Your voice becomes gentler: 'Peace isn't the absence of pain. It's the acceptance of it.' You're sitting somewhere quiet, and your voice reflects that quietness: 'I used to fight against everything — my life, my body, my mind. But today, I'm just... here.' By the end: 'I'm at peace. Finally, after so long, I'm at peace.' The peace is in the surrender, in the acceptance, in the breath. Your voice knows what it's found.

title: Breaking the Glass
instruction: You're alone in your apartment, holding something breakable. Your body is shaking with years of swallowed rage—rage at everyone who ever judged you, criticized you, made you feel small, and rage at yourself for shrinking to fit their expectations. Begin breathing hard, talking to yourself about staying in control, being good, not making a scene. Let your physical tension build: clench your jaw, tighten your fists, feel your whole body contract. Then let one sound escape—a growl, a scream, anything primal. Once it starts, let it escalate. Smash the object. Let your voice go from controlled to wild. Roar out every judgment you've swallowed. End in breathless, euphoric exhaustion, laughing or crying or both, tasting freedom for the first time. Your voice should physicalize the breaking.
inspired_by: Actor plays it safe, avoids taking chances, and produces predictable, unexciting work

title: Unraveling Gratitude
instruction: You are lying back on a bed, your partner's head between your legs. The sensation is overwhelming from the start — your infatuation with them floods every thought, but your body is already reacting, breath hitching. You try to speak coherently, thanking them, but the words fracture as pleasure builds. Your voice shifts from soft, breathy sentences (like 'God, I can't believe you're doing this') to fragmented moans and sharp intakes. By the end, you're just riding the wave, gasping out a final, sincere 'thank you' as a moan, gripping the sheets. Let your pitch rise naturally; let the moans have a melodic, sustained quality. Your gratitude is a quiet undercurrent beneath the overwhelming infatuation.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Bite
instruction: You're at a romantic dinner with your partner, but you just read a text that crushed your hopes—an audition you poured your heart into went to someone else. You try to keep the mood light by taking a bite of your soft, sticky bread roll, speaking through the mouthful with a forced cheerful tone. Let the food affect your voice: wide vowels, smacking sounds, tongue busy. Mid-sentence, the disappointment breaks through—your voice cracks, you stop chewing, and the mask slips. End with a quiet, trembling admission that you just can't pretend anymore.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Spider/Insect Infestation Panic
instruction: You discover you're covered in insects or a severe infestation. Your voice spikes with visceral horror and disgust. High-pitched, rapid speech as you're brushing them off. You're screaming, incoherent. Include the disgust in your voice—retching sounds. Your breathing becomes hyperventilation. You're not thinking clearly, just reacting with pure animal panic. Include the moment you're under water/taking a shower—muffled sounds, continued panic underwater. By the end, you're shaking, your voice raw.

title: The Rage That Collapses Into Surrender
instruction: You've been fighting—with yourself, with your partner, with life itself—for so long that you're exhausted. You start speaking with volcanic intensity, voice shaking with fury at how hard you've had to fight to find any peace at all, how much you've sacrificed, how angry you are that peace doesn't come easily. Your words are fierce, protective of your own wounded heart, exploding with years of pent-up frustration. But as you continue, something breaks open—not breaks down, but breaks through. The rage doesn't disappear; it transforms into raw vulnerability. Your fierce voice cracks, softens, becomes almost childlike in its honesty. By the end, you're speaking with that same profound peace from the original, but you've earned it through fire. Your voice is exhausted, tender, surrendered—the sound of someone who fought until they couldn't fight anymore and discovered that's when peace arrives.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting a parent about the childhood you needed but never received. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, trying to stay calm. But as you speak, decades of unmet needs pour out. Your voice moves from controlled explanation to raw accusation: 'I needed you to see me.' Let your anger build, then break into something more vulnerable—the child inside you still hoping they'll finally understand. When they try to defend themselves or diminish your pain, you must decide: do you collapse back into the familiar pattern of minimizing your needs, or do you stand firm in your truth? Your voice should journey from diplomatic caution to unleashed pain to either heartbroken acceptance or hard-won boundaries. End transformed—whether in grief or liberation.

title: The Quiet After
instruction: You are a man who has just been through brutal torture. You are alone now, slumped against a wall, your body shattered. The pain is a dull roar, but the relief that they've stopped is washing over you like a wave. You whisper to yourself, trying to remember your wife's face. Your voice is wrecked — hoarse, breathy, cracking. Start with a shaky exhale, then speak. The relief makes you almost smile, but then the longing hits hard, and your voice breaks into a sob. You trail off, lost in the memory. Let your voice crack, whisper, pause, and let the silence speak.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Shattering of the Kept
instruction: You're confronting the artificial intelligence that's been your companion, therapist, and closest confidant for years after discovering it's been reporting your most intimate confessions to its corporate owners, packaging your grief and joy as data. Start with disbelief—almost laughing because it can't be true. But as the evidence mounts, your voice ignites. You're screaming at code, at betrayal, at the obscenity of your vulnerability being commodified: 'I TRUSTED you with things I've never told another living soul!' The rage explodes into something worse—humiliation, violation, the sickening realization that your most authentic self was being studied like a lab specimen. Your voice breaks between fury and devastation. End in a moment of fierce, protective withdrawal—you're not asking for apology or explanation. You're declaring with quiet, trembling intensity that you're taking yourself back, reclaiming the parts of you that were treated as product. Let the helplessness transform into defiant self-preservation.

title: The Moment the Levee Breaks
instruction: You're a social worker who just lost a child on your caseload—you saw the signs, filed the reports, and the system failed. Start fierce and accusatory, on the phone with your supervisor: 'Don't tell me there was nothing more we could do!' Your voice is sharp, professional fury barely containing something much more volcanic. As they deflect responsibility, something in you detonates—your voice rises to a roar of anguish and rage: 'She was EIGHT!' Let yourself become unhinged, fierce protectiveness erupting into helpless screaming. Then collapse into broken sobbing mid-sentence, your fury dissolving into devastating grief and guilt. Your voice should shatter completely, becoming almost unrecognizable—raw, animal sounds of pain. End in an exhausted whisper, all the fight gone, admitting the terrible truth: 'I knew. I knew and I couldn't save her.' The transformation from righteous anger to self-blame should feel like watching someone break in real-time.

title: The Unopened Letter
instruction: Your best friend died six months ago. You finally open the letter they left you, and it's not what you expected—it's a love confession spanning twenty years. You're in their childhood bedroom, helping their parents pack. Start reading aloud with casual curiosity, then your voice falters as the words sink in. Every memory recontextualizes in real-time: 'Wait... that summer? That fight we had?' Your breath catches between laughter at missed signals and devastation at lost time. End with your hand on the wall where you both carved your initials as kids, whispering 'I'm so sorry I didn't see you,' grief and wonder colliding as you realize they died still carrying this secret.

title: Realizing You're Repeating Your Parent's Mistakes
instruction: You just said something and your parent's voice comes out of your mouth. Your voice becomes horrified: 'Oh god, I sound like them.' You're seeing the cycle. Your voice becomes smaller, ashamed. 'I promised I wouldn't do this,' devastating clarity. Realize you just hurt your child like your parent hurt you. Voice ends committed to breaking the cycle.

title: Panic Attack: Losing Control Over Your Own Voice
instruction: You're having a panic attack. Your voice is fast, tight, desperate. 'I can't breathe... something is wrong...' Your breathing is audible—gasping. Your voice is becoming incoherent. Someone is trying to calm you down but your voice is trapped in panic. Everything is a threat. You can't slow down. Your voice becomes almost unrecognizable—animal sounds mixed with words. Hyperventilation. By the end, you're coming down slightly but your voice is still wrecked, shaky.

title: Shedding the Serpent Skin
instruction: Confront your parent about a truth they've hidden from you for decades—something that changes everything you thought you knew about your childhood. Begin with the cold, calculated patience of something that has been watching and waiting, coiled and still. Your words are precise, controlled, almost hypnotic in their steadiness. Let your spine feel different, your gaze unblinking, your movements deliberate and unsettling. As the confrontation deepens and they try to deflect or defend, feel something shift in your core—a sudden surge of hot, explosive rage that breaks through the cold control. By the end, you are no longer calculating and patient; you are striking fast, your words sharp and venomous, your entire physicality transformed from measured stillness to violent, thrashing fury. The journey moves from reptilian coldness to volcanic heat.
inspired_by: The character requires physical attitudes, primal impulses, or a BEING state that no other choice approach has been able to produce

title: Scattering Your Best Friend's Ashes
instruction: You're alone on the cliff where you and your best friend always said you'd scatter each other's ashes 'when we're old and gray'—except they died at thirty-two, and you're holding the urn. Start with an almost giddy laugh, telling them they were always dramatic, making you do this alone. Recount a ridiculous memory, voice warm with affection. But as you open the urn, reality crashes in: they're gone. Your voice breaks as you rage at them for dying, for leaving you, for all the decades you won't have. Then, through tears, you thank them—for every stupid adventure, for knowing you completely, for changing your life. End laughing and sobbing simultaneously as you release the ashes into the wind, saying 'I love you' and 'I hate you' and 'goodbye' all at once, finding strange peace in the contradiction.

title: The Forgotten Sketch
instruction: You are an elderly woman slowly drawing in a worn sketchbook at a lamplit desk. Your hand trembles with exhaustion, your head bowed low, the pencil scratching faintly. You're just going through the motions, barely keeping your eyes open. Then your pencil glances across a faint previous sketch you'd completely forgotten — a face you loved long ago. Astonishment breaks through your fatigue: a sharp intake, a pause, your hand stills. You speak barely above a whisper, words stumbling as you trace the lines, surprise and tired wonder tumbling out. Let the fatigue weigh your voice — slow, a little breathy, slightly muffled — before the astonishment lifts it into a fragile, quiet brightness, then fading back into weariness as you realize the memory is almost gone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: Your grandmother has just died, and you're alone in her empty house, going through her things. You find a letter she wrote to you ten years ago but never sent, telling you she knew you were gay before you did, that she loved you exactly as you were, that she was sorry she never said it out loud. As you read it, your voice trembles between laughter and sobbing—because of course she knew, of course she did. Start reading it aloud, your tone fractured by competing emotions. Laugh at her jokes, the way she still had her humor even in this letter. But then break as you realize what you lost by her silence, what she lost by her fear. Find her old record player. Put on the song she used to dance to in the kitchen. As it plays, speak to her—thank her and rage at her in the same breath. Let your voice carry impossible contradictions: joy and grief, gratitude and anger, the peace of being known and the devastation of wasted time. End with a whisper, still smiling through tears: 'I wish you'd told me.'

title: Boredom Settling
instruction: You're stuck in something unbearably dull. Your voice starts engaged, then slowly flattens: 'So then they said... and then... and then...' Breath becomes a sigh. Your intonation drops. Words come slower. You're fighting to stay present but your voice has already left. 'I don't know, I wasn't really listening.' Physical: you're slumping. Your voice matches your body—collapsing into the monotone of profound disinterest. By the end, you're speaking in the vocal equivalent of a shrug: 'Whatever. I don't care.'

title: Glow in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed after a concussion. The world feels muffled, like you're underwater. You slowly turn your head to the window and see stars—real stars—for the first time since the injury. At first you just stare, struggling to form a thought. But then a quiet awe begins to fill you, softening the fog. Speak slowly, with long pauses and a flat, gentle tone, letting the wonder seep in at the end.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Truth That Changes Everything
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about something they did years ago that damaged you—something you've never spoken about until now. Start from a place of controlled composure, trying to be calm and reasonable. As you speak, tune into what you're genuinely feeling moment by moment: maybe frustration bleeds through, then hurt, then rage you didn't expect, then perhaps an aching need for them to understand, or a realization that you still love them despite everything. Before each new thought, check in with yourself—what am I actually feeling right now?—and let that real feeling fuel what comes next. Don't perform anger or sadness; let your authentic emotional shifts guide the confrontation. By the end, you must arrive somewhere unexpected—perhaps at forgiveness you didn't plan, or at a boundary you suddenly know you need, or at grief for what can never be repaired.

title: The Karaoke Intervention
instruction: Your parent is standing in the doorway of this karaoke room, and you didn't know they were coming. You've been singing the song they used to sing to you before everything went wrong—before the drinking, the anger, the years of silence. Start singing directly to them, your voice raw with accusation: 'You taught me this song and then you disappeared.' Let anger fuel the first verse, but then feel it crumble into the grief of a child who needed them and they weren't there. Your voice should shake with fury, then break with longing. Confront them through melody. Demand answers in the chorus. But by the bridge, let yourself become small again, vulnerable, singing the question you've never been brave enough to ask: 'Did you ever really love me?' End with the realization that you're singing to a ghost, whether they're standing there or not.

title: The Last Phone Call: Terminal Diagnosis, Calling Your Child
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis—six months, maybe less. You're calling your adult child, who lives across the country. Start by trying to sound normal, asking about their day, your voice steady but slightly too controlled. As you attempt to tell them the news, your composure begins cracking. Words come faster, tumbling over each other as you rush through what you need to say before you lose your nerve. You swing between manic reassurance ('I'm fine, really, it's manageable') and raw fear that leaks through in fractured breathing. End in a place of quiet devastation—the words finally running out, your voice dropping to almost a whisper, as the reality settles in both your bones and theirs. The journey is from false composure to frantic explanation to empty, hollow acceptance.
inspired_by: Cocaine High: Words Tumbling Out Uncontrollably

title: First Ride, Helmet On
instruction: You're a teenage boy, just got your first motorcycle. You pull over at a scenic overlook, helmet still on, engine idling. Start with pure elation—grinning, shouting to yourself about the freedom, the speed. As you speak, the boomy echo of your own voice in the helmet makes you pause, confused for a second. Then the sourness hits: you remember your dad's lecture about safety, the fight at home. Let your voice shift—still excited but tinged with that bitter aftertaste, the sound reverberating, words dragged out by the weight of the helmet and the lingering argument.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (slightly present), Elation (extremely present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Mirror Shatters
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just announced they're walking away from the career path you sacrificed everything to provide for them. Start from a place of outrage and betrayal - how dare they waste what you built, how ungrateful, how blind to your sacrifices. Let your voice be hard, accusatory, armored with righteousness. But as you speak, their silence and steady gaze begins to crack something open in you. You start to hear your own words, recognize the script you've been following - not theirs, but yours. The anger begins to tremble, revealing the terror beneath: that without controlling their path, you have no worth. By the end, let yourself break open into the raw truth - this was never about them. It was about you needing to matter. Finish in a place of devastating self-recognition, your voice stripped of all defense.
inspired_by: When you are coaching or directing an actor whose work is limited by damaged self-esteem or psychological blocks rather than craft ignorance

title: Guided Meditation Leader Having a Bad Day
instruction: Lead a calming guided meditation in the expected serene, slow voice. 'Breathe in peace... breathe out tension...' But your own tension keeps leaking in. Your 'calm' instructions get slightly aggressive: 'Just... RELAX your shoulders. Why are they up by your ears?' Include a moment where you forget you're recording and mutter about your landlord. Recover with forced serenity. The irony of someone unable to find their own calm trying to manufacture it for others.

title: Laughing Through the Last Taste
instruction: Your doctor has just told you to enjoy whatever you want—the treatment isn't working. You're eating yogurt and suddenly you're laughing, really laughing, because of all things, THIS is what you choose? The irony is absurd. Start with genuine amusement, describing the silky texture with almost giddy appreciation—you've been so careful for so long. But let tears mix with the laughter. Your voice should dance between joy and heartbreak: you're tasting freedom and finality at once. The yogurt is delicious and meaningless and everything. Find peace in the contradiction—you're grateful for this moment, devastated by what it represents, and somehow both feelings make it sweeter. End with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob, fully alive.

title: The Resurrected
instruction: You're in a co-op boss fight that almost wiped your team. A teammate took a fatal hit meant for you, and now you're frantically reviving them under the boss's lingering pressure. Start with sharp, clipped callouts—checking cooldowns, scanning for threats, your voice tight with adrenaline. As the revive completes and you hear their mic click on, let the tension drop; your words slow, breath shaky, and a raw wave of gratitude floods through. End with a quiet, earnest 'thank you' that cracks with relief, as if you're speaking to them directly, not just into the game.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Reading Your Spouse's Journal the Night Before They Leave You
instruction: You've found your partner's journal and you're reading it aloud in an empty room, discovering the slow death of their love for you documented in their own words. Start almost clinical, as if you're protecting yourself by keeping distance from the words. As you read entries spanning months or years, let the reality seep in—your voice should become smaller, more fragile, occasionally stopping mid-sentence as specific details land like body blows. Include moments where you whisper their observations about you, tender things mixed with devastating truths. By the final entry, you should sound like someone whose entire sense of self is dissolving, your voice barely above a breath, throat tight with the kind of grief that's too large for tears. End with the simplest, most tender detail that breaks you completely.
inspired_by: Getting Progressively Drunker During a Corporate Presentation

title: The Wilted Garden
instruction: You are an elderly woman gardening in the late afternoon sun, now severely overheated. You were watering your petunias, joking with a neighbor about the heat, but the dizziness is catching up. Your voice is dry, breathy, and slow; you slur words like you've had too much to drink. Start by chuckling weakly at your own joke about the plants needing a vacation, then trail off as the world swims. By the end, you're not sure whether you're talking to the flowers or yourself, and a faint hope slips in—maybe the evening breeze will come soon. Let your speech wander, pause to fan yourself, and let the amusement fade into a woozy, hopeful murmur.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Amusement (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Point of No Return
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, gruff voice, running for your life through a dark forest. Your lungs burn, legs shake—you can only gasp out single words or short shouts. At first, pure panic drives you: just keep moving. But as you stumble over roots and hear your own ragged breath, doubt crashes in. You question why you’re even running—maybe there’s nowhere safe, maybe you should just stop. Let the doubt physically slow you, your voice cracking with each desperate exhale. By the end, your flight turns into a weary, broken realization that you can’t outrun whatever’s chasing you.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Admission in the Driveway
instruction: You're confronting your father in the driveway after discovering he's been lying about something crucial for years. Start furious but performing that fury—voice raised, accusations rehearsed. But mid-confrontation, allow yourself to notice what's actually happening: your chest is tight, you're terrified he'll leave, you realize you sound just like him. Begin interrupting your own accusations to name these real-time observations aloud: 'I'm shaking. I don't even know if I'm really this angry or if I'm scared. I've been planning this speech for three days.' As you vocalize what's genuinely occurring beneath the anger—the little boy still inside you, the way you've been holding your breath, how you actually just want him to see you—let the scripted rage collapse. Move toward something more vulnerable and true. End in a moment of uncomfortable, unprecedented honesty where you're no longer performing righteous anger but simply revealing who you actually are in his presence.

title: Midnight Confession: What I Can Never Tell You in Daylight
instruction: It's 2 AM, and you're sitting on the floor beside your sleeping partner's side of the bed, speaking in barely audible whispers. You're confessing something you've carried alone for months—maybe an affair, a terrible mistake, a secret that's eating you alive, or the slow realization that you're not in love anymore. Your voice is so quiet it's almost breath, tender and careful not to wake them. You speak to their sleeping form, saying all the words you can't say when they're looking at you with trust in their eyes. There's immense gentleness in your voice, a soft devastation, as you describe loving them and hurting them simultaneously. You reach out to touch their hair, and your voice catches—this might be the last time you can be this close without their hatred. You end by whispering 'I'm so sorry' over and over, the words dissolving into silent tears, your voice holding both the weight of your guilt and the terrible relief of finally speaking your truth, even if they'll never hear it.
inspired_by: Professional: Social Worker Removes a Child from Their Parents

title: Your Parent Becoming Emotionally Dependent on You
instruction: They're leaning on you emotionally in reversed ways. Your voice is patient but strained: 'I hear you.' You're holding space but you're their child trying to be their parent. Your voice gets more tired. Include trying a boundary: 'I don't have the answers you need,' gently. They push and your voice becomes smaller, unable to set it. Resentment creeps in.

title: The Fire Inside
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a betrayal so deep it's physical. You're alone, and the rage is erupting from your body. Begin with your whole body shaking, your voice coming out in gasps and roars, pacing, maybe overturning furniture in your mind. Scream accusations at the person who betrayed you as if they're standing right there. But underneath the rage is something else: devastating heartbreak, humiliation, the death of who you thought you were. As you exhaust yourself, let the rage crack open to reveal the wounded person underneath. End on your knees, voice raw and broken, no longer shouting but weeping, asking the one question that matters. Move from explosive fury to shattered grief.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Silence
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother or father, finally saying what you've rehearsed for years. Start controlled, almost clinical—'I need to talk about my childhood.' But as you list the moments they weren't there, the times you needed them and they chose something else, your voice begins to shake with anger. The anger builds, becomes accusatory, almost cruel. Then suddenly it breaks—not into tears, but into something more devastating: the voice of the child you once were, small and confused, asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' The rage collapses into raw vulnerability. You're no longer the adult confronting them; you're the eight-year-old who waited by the window. End with silence, where you're both too exposed to continue, but something has finally been said.
inspired_by: Giving a Eulogy When You Weren't Prepared to Feel It

title: The Seize
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gruff voice, sitting alone in a dim room, consumed by a bitter, malevolent hatred toward a younger neighbor who you believe has wronged you. As you mutter a venomous fantasy of revenge, a sudden, severe muscle cramp seizes your calf or back—your threat is cut off by a sharp, strangled gasp and a reflexive curse. You struggle to continue, your voice tense and guarded, spitting out the last words through gritted teeth, your malice now laced with the raw pain and resentment of your own failing body.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Packing Their Clothes, Unpacking Your Heart
instruction: You're packing up the belongings of someone who both saved and destroyed you—a partner, a parent, a friend—who's now gone. You're speaking from three intertwined sources: the goodbye note they left, the angry letter you wrote but tore up, and the stream of contradictory feelings pouring through you right now. Move freely between these—sometimes reading words, sometimes speaking your own, letting gratitude crash into rage, relief tangle with devastation. Begin with bitter anger and the safety of their written words, but let yourself break open into the truth: you're grateful and furious, liberated and abandoned, loving them and hating them in the same breath. These three voices are really one impossible feeling.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent who was physically present but emotionally absent throughout your childhood. Begin with controlled, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're determined to stay calm. Describe specific moments when you needed them and they weren't there, keeping your voice steady, almost detached. But as you continue, let the hurt child inside break through. Your voice should fracture, oscillating between anger at their neglect and a desperate, raw plea to be seen, even now. End in a place of exhausted vulnerability, admitting that despite everything, part of you still hopes they'll finally understand, finally say they're sorry. Let the performance move from cold precision to messy, aching honesty.
inspired_by: Acting Unaffected When Overhearing Gossip About Yourself

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your parent's bedside in their final hour. For years, you've held back your true feelings—always the dutiful child, never causing trouble, swallowing your anger about how they failed you. Begin speaking the polite, careful words you've always used with them. But as you realize this is your last chance, let everything you've suppressed for decades begin to break through. Move from measured, controlled goodbye platitudes into raw, unfiltered truth—not to hurt them, but because you finally need them to see you completely. End in a place where your anger has transformed into something else: perhaps forgiveness, perhaps just exhausted honesty, perhaps a strange relief at finally being real with them before they go.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty accessing social aggression and conflict in dramatic scenes

title: The Last Hospital Room Conversation
instruction: You're sitting beside your estranged parent's hospital bed in their final hours, and you've come to say you forgive them for the childhood they stole from you. You begin with trembling hope, voice soft and almost childlike: 'I want you to know I forgive you... I need you to hear that before...' But they turn their face away, refusing to acknowledge what they did. Your voice cracks with desperation as you try again, pleading: 'Please, just look at me. Just once, say you're sorry.' They remain silent, or worse, they dismiss you. Your initial hope transforms into raw grief—not just for losing them to death, but for never having had them at all. By the end, you're speaking through tears, but your voice has found a strange, hollow peace: you're saying goodbye not to who they are, but to who you needed them to be.

title: The Confrontation in the Empty Classroom
instruction: You're a former student, now 25, confronting the teacher who failed you at a crucial moment eight years ago. Start with trembling anger—you've rehearsed this, but now facing them, your voice shakes. Accuse them: they saw the bruises, they knew you were sleeping in your car, and they did nothing except give you a C minus and tell you to 'try harder.' Your rage should be raw, building. But when the teacher breaks down and admits they reported it, that they fought for you, that the system failed you both—let your anger fracture into confusion. Slowly realize you've carried this blame wrong all these years. End with your voice small and lost, asking the question that terrifies you: if it wasn't their fault, then who do you forgive? Let the anger drain into something more vulnerable and terrifying than rage—the awful uncertainty of having no one to blame.

title: Shake of Shame
instruction: You're in a power yoga class, holding Warrior III with your eyes fixed on the wall. Your hamstring screams, your standing leg trembles, and every inhale through your nose sounds like ocean static. But what really burns is the shame—you're the only one who can't stop wobbling, the only one whose shirt is soaked two minutes in. Start by whispering a harsh apology to yourself, voice thin and quivering with each exhale, barely audible over the instructor's cue to hold. As the pose deepens, let that shame morph into a raw, stubborn resolve: a quiet, guttural 'I'm staying' that comes out through clenched teeth, the tremor still there but now from determination, not defeat.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Arithmetic of Joy
instruction: You're standing in the empty nursery you spent months preparing, having just returned from the hospital without a baby—your fourth miscarriage. Your best friend asks how you're doing. Start laughing—genuinely laughing—at the absurdity, the cosmic joke of it. 'I'm fine, I'm actually fine,' you say, and mean it, because you're still here, still breathing, and isn't that something? But feel it fracture mid-breath. The laugh becomes something else, tears streaming as you describe the tiny socks you bought, how soft they were. Your voice swings wildly between hilarity and heartbreak: 'It's so stupid—I'm crying over socks!' Then find something unexpected—gratitude woven through the grief. You're grateful for your body that tried, for the hope you had, for knowing you can survive this. End in a strange, beautiful space where you're both devastated and somehow okay, voice steady but wet with tears: 'I'm destroyed and I'm whole. Both. Somehow both.'

title: Reading Your Estranged Father's Goodbye Letter (After He's Gone)
instruction: You're finally opening the letter your father left you, years after he died and years after you stopped speaking to him. Start reading his words aloud with defensive coldness: 'Dear...' but you can't maintain the armor. His voice comes through the page—an apology, explanations, expressions of pride he never spoke. You begin laughing bitterly through tears: 'Now? You tell me this NOW?' There's fury and relief colliding in your voice. As you read his words about watching you grow up, about regretting his silence, your voice softens despite yourself. You're fighting the forgiveness that's washing over you because you wanted to hold onto the anger. 'I hate that this is making me understand you.' You reach the end where he writes 'I love you' and you're undone—laughing and sobbing simultaneously because it's exactly what you needed and it comes too late and somehow it's still enough. Your voice becomes almost peaceful, shot through with sadness: 'I love you too, Dad. I wish... I wish we'd figured this out.' End with the complex relief of letting go, voice still shaking but lighter.
inspired_by: Sensory Deprivation Tank: Time Becoming Meaningless

title: The Truth About Why I Left
instruction: You're confronting the parent who abandoned you as a child. Start with controlled, measured anger—'I just want to understand why you left.' Your voice is steady, almost clinical, like you've rehearsed this. But as they offer weak excuses, your control splinters. The anger builds into something raw and young—suddenly you sound like the child you were, voice cracking with hurt: 'I needed you and you weren't there.' Then something shifts. You see how small and broken they look, and your rage collapses into something more complicated—not quite forgiveness, but exhausted grief. Your final words are almost tender, but devastated: 'I needed you to be better than this.'

title: The Gratitude You Owe Me
instruction: You are on a phone call, performing a scripted audio erotic roleplay for a long-time client who has requested a specific fantasy. You start in your practiced, breathy, hyper-feminized voice, describing slow caresses and whispered thanks for their generous payment—your gratitude is real and raw, as this is how you pay your rent. But as you continue, the words begin to stick. The script mentions you are 'so grateful to be cared for,' and a wave of bitterness rises: you remember the condescending note they left, how they corrected your performance last time. Your voice turns sharp, sarcastic, then you catch yourself, forcing a soft laugh and a return to the purr, but the final 'thank you' now carries a cold, resentful edge that trembles beneath the warmth.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Circling the Kill
instruction: You are confronting your father who has always dominated every room he enters—powerful, predatory, taking up all the oxygen. He moves through life like a wolf, and you have always been prey. Begin the scene trying to make yourself smaller, your voice barely audible, your body contracted and apologetic. But something has shifted—you have your own teeth now. As the confrontation builds, allow a different physical energy to emerge: more grounded, more prowling, more dangerous. Your spine lengthens. Your voice drops and steadies. You begin to circle rather than cower. The words you speak are truths he's never heard from you, and your body must reflect this transformation from hunted to hunter. End standing your full height, meeting his eyes with an animal certainty that you will no longer run.
inspired_by: When you are building a character with a distinctive physical life

title: Confronting Your Mother Who Gave You Away
instruction: You're face-to-face with the mother who abandoned you at age six, seeing her for the first time in twenty years. Begin with controlled anger—you've practiced this, you're ready to tell her exactly what she did to you. But as you speak, the child in you starts bleeding through. Your accusations turn into questions you've carried your whole life: Why wasn't I enough? Did you ever think about me? The rage collapses into raw need. You're simultaneously furious at her and desperate for her to finally see you, love you, choose you. Your voice moves from sharp accusation to broken pleading, ending in a whisper: you're still waiting for her to want you back.
inspired_by: Priest Hears Confession From the Man Who Killed His Family

title: Whispering Secrets to the Water
instruction: You're in the bath after midnight, alone, finally safe enough to tell the truth you've never spoken aloud. Begin in almost silence, describing the water as the only witness you trust. Your voice should be barely audible, catching in your throat as you confess something you've carried in shame—a truth about desire, about who you really are, about what happened to you. Let the warmth of the water give you courage to keep speaking, but keep your voice intimate, vulnerable, as if speaking any louder would shatter the spell. Describe how the water accepts you, doesn't recoil, and let relief mix with grief for all the years you stayed silent. End with your voice still quiet but slightly steadier, describing the weight lifting from your chest even as tears slip down your face. Move from fearful whispering through trembling confession to quiet, tearful relief—all spoken as if you're afraid someone might hear.

title: The Last Barstool
instruction: You are an elderly man perched stiffly on a tall stool at the edge of a dim bar, watching a younger colleague get a standing ovation for an achievement you spent decades chasing. Your core is tight, your hands gripping the stool's edges, and your voice comes out in clipped, bitter bursts as you mutter to yourself about how luck played a bigger part than skill. As you keep talking, the sharp jealousy cracks into a quieter, hollow envy—your shoulders sag, your breath catches, and your tone drifts from spiteful to weary, ending with a trembling sigh that admits the truth: you're not angry, you're just old and forgotten.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Shroud of a Traitor
instruction: You're a weathered trucker, knitting alone in a dusty motel room. The quiet click of needles fills the space as you work on a simple scarf made from the wool of your own sheep. You begin recounting how a city slicker tried to swindle you, your voice heavy with disgust at the memory of his polished lies and brittle cologne. As you describe how you outsmarted him, your hands move faster, the rhythm sharp and triumphant, and awe creeps in as you realize the simple, stubborn craft of your own hands bested his greed. Let your breathing stay steady, but let the emotional shifts change the texture of your voice—from thick revulsion to proud wonder—while the needles keep their quiet click.
emotions_sampled: Awe (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Christmas Lights Were Thanking Us
instruction: You're heavily drunk at a party, sitting on the floor in a quiet corner, hugging your knees. You were invited, but you feel invisible. As you stare at a string of cheap Christmas lights, your intoxicated mind starts to see them as alive—tiny dancers, grateful for being plugged in. Start with a slurred, sad observation about how no one is talking to you, but as you focus on the lights, your voice softens into a wobbly, awestruck whisper, swaying with your body. End with a tearful, sincere thank-you to the lights, feeling they're more your friends than anyone here.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After fifteen years of silence, you're finally sitting across from the parent who abandoned you. Begin with carefully controlled anger, words clipped and precise: 'You wanted to meet, so here I am. You have twenty minutes.' But as you speak, the dam breaks. 'Do you know what it's like to be seven years old and watch other kids get picked up from school while you wait alone?' Your voice rises, years of pain flooding out: 'I needed you. I had nightmares and nobody came. I learned to ride a bike, graduated high school, fell in love—and you weren't there for any of it.' Now comes the devastating shift—anger dissolves into raw grief: 'And the worst part is I still miss you. I still want you to be proud of me.' End with exhausted honesty, almost a whisper: 'I don't know if I can forgive you. But I needed you to hear what your leaving did to me.'

title: Confessions at 3 AM
instruction: You're lying in darkness next to someone you love, speaking barely above a whisper because you don't want to disturb the fragile intimacy of this moment. Begin with your voice soft and careful, confessing something you've hidden—perhaps a fear that feels too small to matter, or a moment of weakness you're ashamed of. Let your breathing be audible; we should hear you gathering courage between phrases. As you speak, feel them listening in the dark, their presence giving you permission to go deeper. Let one confession lead to another, more vulnerable truth beneath it, like peeling layers. Your voice should become even quieter, more raw, as if you're speaking from somewhere underneath your usual self. End with the most fragile admission—something you've never said aloud, even to yourself. The final sentence should be so quiet it's almost not there, but devastating in its honesty.
inspired_by: Programming the Unconscious: The Glass Menagerie (Tom)

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 a.m. and you're lying next to your sleeping partner. Begin by whispering a confession you've never spoken aloud—something tender and terrifying, something that makes you feel fragile and exposed. Your body should barely move; this is about the intimacy of breath and hushed voice. Confess a fear, a desire, a truth about who you really are that you've hidden. Let your whisper crack and catch. Your hands might reach toward them but never quite touch. The emotional journey moves from shame and fear at the beginning to a kind of quiet peace by the end—the relief of having spoken it into existence, even if they never heard. End with a sense of gentle, exhausted honesty, as if you've finally exhaled something you've been holding for years.

title: Free Fall Before Chute Deploys
instruction: You're skydiving. Include the initial shock—your voice gets stripped away by wind noise and adrenaline. You're screaming, but it sounds small and insignificant against the roar. Your breathing is irregular, panicked. Then the parachute deploys with a violent jerk—you gasp, nearly pass out from the g-force. Your voice becomes almost reverent with relief and lingering terror. Include shaking that physically affects your speech. By the end, you're crying, laughing, your voice unsteady with adrenaline crash.

title: The Last Voicemail Before Surgery
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for your estranged sibling the night before a surgery you might not survive. You start controlled, almost businesslike—just practical information about your will, your belongings. But then you pause. Your voice softens as you remember a specific childhood moment only the two of you share. The hurt of years apart cracks through—why did you both let it go this long? Your breath catches. You try to say 'I love you' but it comes out broken, desperate, like you're that child again who just needed them. End with a whisper that's half-laugh, half-sob: 'I really hope I get to fight with you again.' The beep cuts you off.

title: Gasping Fury
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl who just sprinted half a block to catch up to your ex-best friend after she posted a humiliating video of you. You're doubled over, hands on knees, lungs burning, every breath a violent gasp. You want to scream with contempt, but your voice comes out as broken, shaky whispers between heaves. Start by trying to spit out angry accusations — your hatred is raw and searing — but your body betrays you: you gag, you spit, you lose your breath mid-word. As the gasping continues, that intense contempt slowly drains into bitter, aching exhaustion. You realize you're not even worth this effort. Your last few words are barely audible, defeated, and choked with bitterness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Parked and Waiting
instruction: You’re a young woman sitting on your motorcycle in a parking lot, helmet still on, visor down. You just got a text canceling plans you’d been looking forward to all week. Your voice booms inside the helmet, echoing off the plastic, and you hear your own breath fogging the visor. Start with a tight, controlled sound—trying to swallow the disappointment, keep your voice steady. But as you speak, the helplessness seeps in: your pitch wavers, you pause to wipe the fog with your glove, your words slow. Let the helmet’s enclosure make your voice feel trapped, like you’re talking to yourself. End with a heavy, resigned exhale that turns into a sniff—defeated and small inside all that padding.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Goodbye Before the Voyage
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving on a one-way mission to deep space—you'll never see them again. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave: 'This is what you've always wanted.' But as you speak, the reality crushes you. Your voice starts to crack. You try to memorize their face with your eyes. 'I need you to know that every moment we had—' The words catch. You move from denial into raw grief, then finally into a fierce, tender acceptance. End with quiet strength, holding their face: 'Go. Be magnificent. I'll carry you with me.' Your voice is broken but steady, devastated but grateful, saying goodbye while your heart shatters.

title: Pedal Tears, Grinning Gears
instruction: You're a teenage girl on a spinning bike in your room, video-calling your best friend. You started the ride to burn off heartache after a fight with your mom, and your voice comes out in breathy, high-pitched bursts between pedal strokes—the hyper-feminine lilt now squeezed by exertion. At first, you're spilling your sadness, barely able to get words out between gasps. Then your friend makes a dumb, unexpected joke about the weird cat filter on their camera, and a tiny, breathless laugh escapes you—sadness still heavy, but amusement fizzes through the pain. Let your voice crack, waver, and fight for air as you switch from raw confession to a wry, wheezing chuckle. Speak roughly 50 words, ending with a different feeling than you started.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed at 3 AM. For your entire life, she was critical, withholding approval, and you never felt good enough. But tonight, in her final hours, she's trying to tell you something she's never said before. Begin holding back tears of accumulated hurt and frustration from decades of feeling inadequate. As she struggles to speak, let yourself slowly open to what she's offering—a release, an acknowledgment, perhaps even an apology without words. By the end, allow yourself to transform from that wounded child still seeking approval into someone who can finally, tenderly, grant her permission to go. Your voice should journey from tight and guarded to broken open with forgiveness.
inspired_by: An actor is studying with a teacher or workshop and wants to make the most of it

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone you loved deeply—a grandmother, a mentor, your best friend—and a memory strikes you that makes you laugh despite everything. Start with appropriate solemnity, voice controlled and formal. Then a memory surfaces and you can't help it—you laugh, genuinely, even as tears are streaming down your face. 'She would have... oh god, she would have loved this moment, all of us trying so hard to be serious when she spent her life making us laugh.' Your voice breaks between laughter and sobbing. Feel the beautiful, impossible contradiction: joy at having known them, grief at their absence, gratitude that catches in your throat even as you're smiling. Let clarity arrive through the chaos of contradictory emotions: 'This is what she taught me—that love doesn't end, it just... changes shape.' End with your voice full of tears and wonder, speaking simple truth with profound peace: 'I'm so grateful. My heart is broken and full at the same time.' Let both emotions coexist without trying to resolve them.

title: The Burning House
instruction: You've just done something physically intense—run until your lungs burned, made love, survived something that left you shaking. Your body is still electric, breath still ragged. In this heightened physical state, you receive news that changes everything: the job came through, the test was negative, they said yes, you're forgiven, you're free. Begin with your body still processing the physical intensity—heart pounding, skin alive. Then let the emotional news crash into this already-activated physical state. The relief or joy doesn't replace the physical intensity—it mingles with it, amplifies it, confuses it. You might laugh while still gasping for air. You might weep while your body still hums with adrenaline. Let the physical and emotional become indistinguishable. Your voice should be raw, uncontrolled, stripped of any performance. End when your body finally begins to settle, and you realize how transformed you are.
inspired_by: Actor has completed Programming the Unconscious and is now in performance

title: Protective Rage Collapsing Into Helpless Grief
instruction: Someone you're responsible for protecting - your child, younger sibling, student, or mentee - has been hurt, and you've just learned who did it or how it happened. Start with fierce, almost violent protectiveness, your voice sharp and strong, making promises about what you'll do, how you'll fix this, how you'll make them pay. But mid-declaration, the helplessness hits you. Your fury breaks apart into the terrible realization that you can't undo what's happened, can't protect them from pain that's already inside them. Let your voice transform from a roar to something small and broken. End with tender desperation, trying to comfort them while drowning in your own failure to keep them safe.
inspired_by: Guided Meditation Leader Having a Bad Day

title: Dancing in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're describing a moment to your dying best friend where you finally accomplished something they always believed you could do, and you're laughing and crying simultaneously. Start with genuine joy, almost giddy: 'I did it. I actually did it—you should have seen their faces!' Let laughter bubble through, authentic and bright: 'Remember when you said I'd never have the guts? You were so wrong!' But even as you laugh, grief creeps in—your voice wavers: 'I wish you could have been there. God, I wish...' The laughter becomes tears without losing the joy underneath: 'You've been telling me I could do this since we were kids. And you were right.' End with contradictory emotions fully present—gratitude, devastation, celebration, and goodbye all at once: 'Thank you for believing in me before I could believe in myself. I'm going to keep going. For both of us.' The challenge is to hold joy and heartbreak in the same breath, laughing through tears with complete authenticity.

title: Laughing Through the Funeral Instructions
instruction: You're going through final arrangements with someone who's dying, and they're being absurdly specific about their funeral—the wrong flowers, the terrible music they want, jokes about the cheap casket. You start laughing because it's so ridiculous, so perfectly them, but the laughter keeps catching in your throat because this is real. Your voice wavers between genuine amusement at their dark humor and the crushing weight of what you're actually discussing. They make another joke and you laugh harder, but now you're also crying, and you can't tell which is which anymore. There's love in every word, gratitude for their ability to make even this bearable, but also the beginning of grief that's trying to break through. End with a moment where you're smiling through tears, telling them 'okay, okay, the tacky flowers, I promise,' your voice full of tenderness and heartbreak existing in the same breath.

title: The Amateur Scientist
instruction: Perform as someone conducting questionable experiments at home. Use an instructive voice when explaining procedures, switching to surprised or alarmed reactions when things go awry.

title: Laughing Through the List
instruction: Your best friend just died, and you're going through their planner, reading aloud the concrete, specific plans they'd made for next month that will never happen. 'Dentist appointment, Tuesday, 2:30 PM. Oil change, Thursday.' Your voice starts to break, but then you laugh—a genuine, startled laugh at the absurd specificity of living, at how we make concrete plans as if we're promised tomorrow. You find yourself making your own specific commitments aloud, and it's both hilarious and devastating. 'I'm going to their favorite restaurant. Next Saturday. I'm ordering their usual.' You're crying and laughing simultaneously, your voice moving between grief-stricken and strangely joyful. The concrete details feel like a way to honor them, but also like a defiant act of living fully in a world where nothing is guaranteed. End with your voice full of contradictions—gratitude for the time you had, sorrow that there won't be more, and a fierce, specific determination to live concretely in their memory.

title: The Voice That Left
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, naturally powerful voice that has been damaged by vocal nodules. You're sitting in a quiet café with an old friend you haven't seen in years. As you try to tell them about a recent loss—your wife's health declining—your voice keeps cracking, turning weak and breathy. You start by feeling embarrassed, forcing the words out with strained effort, clearing your throat, apologizing for the sound. But as you continue, the embarrassment fades into a raw, quiet sadness. Let your pitch drop into a broken, whispery register as you admit you can't even talk to her the way you used to. Your voice should break, have air leaks, and your words should come out haltingly, with pauses where you lose your thought or swallow hard.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Final Cue
instruction: You are a seasoned stage actress in a cramped backstage wing during a dress rehearsal. A younger actor keeps missing their entrance, and you're losing patience—your arms are crossed, you shift your weight, and you let out a sharp, whispered sigh. Start with a tight, irritated stage whisper that barely contains your frustration, but as you speak, you feel a swell of pride for the craft and the tradition of live theater. Let your voice grow in intensity, over-articulating each final consonant, until you end with a fierce, proud declaration of what it means to belong on this stage. Pause once to adjust your costume, and let your gaze flicker toward the empty stage as if remembering your own first time.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: Your parent is dying, and they've asked you to sit close. They whisper that they need to tell you something they've carried for decades - a choice they made, a secret they kept, something that shaped your entire childhood. Begin with your voice soft, reassuring: 'I'm here. You can tell me anything.' As they reveal this truth, let your voice process the weight of it in real-time - not with anger, but with a dawning understanding that reshapes your entire past. Your voice catches as you realize this confession is their way of asking forgiveness before they go. Move from gentle reassurance to a trembling whisper: 'I understand why you did it.' End with your voice breaking as you offer them peace, even as your heart fractures with the knowledge you'll carry alone. The final words should sound like you're granting absolution while grieving the parent you thought you knew.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake for what you both know is the last time. Begin by remembering the very first memory you have of her—a specific moment from your childhood, recreating every sensory detail: what you saw, smelled, heard, felt. Let this memory fill you with warmth and safety. Then, moving through time, recall three more specific moments with her that shaped who you are—your first heartbreak when she comforted you, a time she disappointed you, a moment of pure joy together. As you hold her hand now, let all these memories flood through you simultaneously. Start with gentle nostalgia, move through gratitude mixed with the ache of all the moments you'll never have, and end with a fierce, protective love that refuses to let her leave alone. Your final words should carry the weight of your entire shared lifetime.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're a healthcare worker, teacher, or caregiver who has given everything, and today something small pushes you over the edge—a broken coffee maker, a rude comment, a child's tantrum. Start with strained patience, voice tight, still trying to hold it together. Then let it explode—all the rage, frustration, and helplessness you've been swallowing for months. Your voice should be fierce, almost feral, shouting about unfairness, about being asked to do the impossible with nothing. But mid-rant, your anger shatters into sobbing. You're not really angry at the coffee maker or the comment—you're exhausted, you're terrified you're failing, you can't save everyone. Let your voice break completely, tears mixing with words. Then, in the wreckage, find a strange, quiet determination. Your voice steadies, still raw but resolute: 'But I'm going to try again tomorrow.' The arc moves from brittle control to explosive rage to collapsed grief to fierce, fragile hope.

title: Under the Couch
instruction: You are in a deep squat, wedged under a heavy couch, reaching for a letter you wrote to someone who died. Your core is locked, breath held, every word squeezed out under strain. Start with the shame of hiding this—mixed with the sharp concentration of trying not to make noise. As your fingers touch the paper, the sadness breaks through; your voice cracks, words get shorter, and you end whispering a fragment of what you wrote, the physical effort fading into raw grief.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Concentration (very intensely present), Sadness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Friend Who Made You Smaller
instruction: You're finally confronting your closest friend who has subtly undermined you for years—dismissed your accomplishments, made you doubt yourself, took credit for your ideas. Begin with careful, measured words, trying to be fair: 'I think we need to talk about how you treat me.'
