Don't organize these thoughts or make them make sense—let them interrupt each other, collide, and cascade. Some will be tender, some bitter, some completely random. Your composure must crack and transform as these unfiltered impulses pour through you. By the end, you've abandoned what you planned to say entirely, and you're speaking from a raw, unguarded place you didn't know you'd access—whether that's devastation, unexpected peace, childlike vulnerability, or fierce gratitude mixed with rage at time itself.

title: The Last Time I'll See Your Face
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed. She's awake, lucid, and you both know this is goodbye. Start with forced brightness—trying to keep things normal, talking about small things. But as you look at her face, really look at it, your voice begins to fracture. You're trying to memorize every detail: the way light catches her eyes, her hands that have held you your whole life. Your tone shifts from cheerful denial to raw, whispered devastation: 'I'm not ready.' Then, as she squeezes your hand, find a place of profound gratitude beneath the grief. Your final words mix reverence with heartbreak—thanking her for being your safe place, your voice breaking on 'I love you' but also somehow steady, because you're giving her permission to go.

title: Packing Your Daughter's Favorite Sweater for the Last Time
instruction: Your adult daughter is moving across the world—or perhaps going into hospice, or choosing a path that means you'll lose her in some essential way. You're folding her childhood sweater, the one she loved beyond reason. Start with a soft laugh, remembering how she refused to take it off, describing the worn softness with affection. But as you fold it, you begin crying while still laughing, flooded with gratitude for every moment while simultaneously shattered by the ending. Your voice should dance between joy and devastation, between celebrating who she is and mourning what you're losing. End with a whispered blessing—letting go with love, finding peace in the impossible grief of loving someone enough to release them.
inspired_by: Feeling a Soft, Cozy Sweater Against Your Skin

title: Pen's Last Drops
instruction: You are a middle-aged man sitting at a cluttered desk, hunched over a journal, writing with a pen that's nearly out of ink. The scratch-scratch of the nib is faint and sputtering. Your head is angled down toward the paper, so your voice comes out slightly muffled and close. Start with a quiet, irritable mutter about the cheap pen—a low grumble of frustration as you shake it and try again. Then, as you push through, the memory of why you're writing this entry surfaces: a silly mistake your friend made yesterday. Your irritation softens into a suppressed snort, then a genuine chuckle. Let the amusement bloom in your voice—a warmth that lifts your tone. Pause once to shake the pen, then finish with a lighthearted laugh.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Protective Rage in the Emergency Room
instruction: You're in the hospital after someone you love was hurt by another person's negligence. You're on the phone with the person responsible. Start controlled, cold, precise—recounting exactly what happened, the facts. But fury is building underneath like pressure in a sealed container. Your voice begins to shake, not from weakness but from the effort of not screaming. Then it breaks—explosive, raw, guttural rage pours out. You're shouting, maybe sobbing, cursing them with everything in you. But mid-outburst, you hear a sound from the hospital room—a moan, a movement. Instantly your voice drops, cracks open. You become tender, speaking to your loved one, promising protection you couldn't deliver. The rage dissolves into helpless tears. End with a whispered vow soaked in both love and the devastating realization that you can't actually keep them safe.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child What You Can't Say When They're Awake
instruction: Your child is finally asleep after a devastating diagnosis. You're sitting beside their bed in the hospital, voice barely above a whisper as you confess everything you've been holding back. Start with the tender things—how proud you are, how their laugh is your favorite sound. But then the fear creeps in, your voice catching as you admit you're terrified, that you don't know how to be strong enough for what's coming. Each word is fought for, tears making your voice thick and unsteady. You're bargaining with the universe, with God, with anyone who might listen: 'Take me instead.' The vulnerability is absolute—no performance, no bravery, just a parent's heart breaking in real time. End with your voice finding a fragile sort of peace, singing the lullaby you sang when they were born, knowing tomorrow you'll have to put the brave face back on, but tonight you can just be honestly, completely shattered.
inspired_by: Roller Coaster Mechanical Failure: Moment of Absolute Stillness

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire life. You begin controlled, almost rehearsed—you've imagined this conversation a thousand times: 'I needed you to see me. Just once, to really see me.' But as you speak, decades of unmet need pour out and your voice becomes rawer, younger, more desperate. 'I was so small. I just wanted you to be proud of me. Why wasn't I enough?' Then something shifts—you see them as fragile, human, broken in their own way, and your anger transforms into something more complex: grief for both of you, for what neither of you knew how to give. 'We both lost something, didn't we?' Your voice moves from accusation to heartbreak to a tender, painful understanding that doesn't erase the hurt but makes room for it.

title: After the Sting
instruction: You are a child who has just been struck across the face by your mother in a moment of rage. Now she is gone, and you are left crumpled on the floor, gasping. Your cheek throbs, your breath is shallow. You speak to the empty room, your voice wobbly and broken. Start with a bitter whisper—how could she?—but as you go on, the bitterness fades into a desperate, aching longing for her to come back and hold you. Let your voice crack, pause to breathe through the pain, and let the last words be a raw, tearful plea.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Breaking the Cage
instruction: You are confronting your mother who has controlled and silenced you your entire life. Begin seated, speaking in the quiet, measured, obedient voice you've always used with her—apologetic, careful, small. But as you finally begin to name what she's done to you, feel something coiled and caged inside start to rattle. Let your body shift, your breath change. What begins as controlled accusations should crack open into something far more primitive—not just anger, but the sound of years of suppressed rage breaking free. Your posture may change from contained to something more animal-like, crouched or prowling. Your voice should escalate from words into raw sound—growls, shrieks, guttural releases that bypass language entirely. By the confrontation's end, you should be physically and vocally wild, embodying the unleashed, feral creature she tried to keep locked inside you. The transformation is from obedient child to untamed animal claiming its power.

title: Dancing at the End of the World
instruction: The apocalypse you prepared for your entire life is finally happening—and it's beautiful. Begin with breathless wonder mixed with bitter laughter as you describe the sky, the chaos, the end of everything you spent decades fearing. Let joy and devastation tangle together as you realize how much time you wasted being afraid, how you never lived because you were too busy preparing to survive. Your voice should lift with sudden, liberating relief—all those years of anxiety are over because there's nothing left to protect. Weave in moments of grief for the life you didn't live, but let gratitude win: you're grateful for this moment of clarity, grateful that you finally understand what mattered. End with genuine peace and even happiness, your voice warm and free, as you choose to spend your final moments feeling everything you denied yourself for so long.

title: The Sting of Sweet Nothings
instruction: You're barefoot in a kitchen, late at night, texting your ex with a mix of hunger and bitter hunger. You step on a stray shard of glass from a broken wine glass you two once shared—a sharp, sudden sting makes you gasp and hiss through clenched teeth. As you hop onto one foot, clutching the counter, you continue your message, your voice strained and breathy with the pain. Start with a raw yelp, then transition into a guarded, husky murmur as you describe how you still crave their touch, even as bitterness sours your tone at the edges. Let the hurt in your foot bleed into the hurt in your heart, so your voice wavers between lustful longing and a bitter, sour resignation.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Bitterness (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Silence That Raised You
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about why he never spoke to you—really spoke—your entire childhood. Start measured, almost formal, like you've rehearsed this: 'I need to understand why you were silent.' But as you continue, your composure fractures. You begin mimicking his silence—those long pauses, the way he'd grunt instead of answer, the emotional unavailability that shaped you. Your voice fills with rage as you perform his silence back to him, then suddenly breaks into raw vulnerability: 'I learned to be quiet from you, and now I can't speak either.' End with you realizing mid-sentence that you're doing it right now—being silent when you should speak, just like him—and the devastation of that recognition floods your voice.

title: Reading the Letter
instruction: You're reading a letter from someone who died, left to be opened one year after their passing. They've written about how much they loved life, how grateful they were—and you start laughing, actually laughing, because the words are so characteristically them: 'Don't you dare be sad at my funeral.' Your laughter is real, joyful, remembering. But mid-laugh, you choke. The same breath that carried laughter now carries grief. You continue reading through tears, but you're also still smiling: 'You were ridiculous,' you say to the letter, voice shaking with both amusement and anguish. By the end, you're speaking directly to them—'Thank you. God, thank you for everything'—and you're crying fully now, but there's peace in it, gratitude woven through the pain. Show how joy and grief can live in the same moment, the same breath.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved for decades, and they're slipping away in hospice care. The morning light filters through the window. You begin by reminiscing about your first morning together—your voice warm with the memory, almost smiling. As you speak, you realize these are your final words to them. Your tone shifts: gratitude for every ordinary morning becomes intertwined with the crushing weight of never having another one. You tell them about the coffee you'll make tomorrow that they won't drink, the sunrise you'll see alone. Your voice must move from nostalgic warmth to a whisper that can barely hold itself together, yet underneath it all, there's profound thankfulness that you had this at all. End with telling them it's okay to go, even though your heart is shattering.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally saying the words you've rehearsed for years. You begin controlled, almost clinical, listing facts: 'You chose him over us. Every single time.' Your voice is steady, righteous. But she doesn't defend herself—she just listens, tears streaming silently. Her silence unravels you. Your control fractures. Rage erupts: 'Say something! Fight back!' But she won't. Your anger collapses into something raw and childlike. Your voice breaks as decades of needing her—still needing her—comes pouring out. You end up confessing through tears what you really came to say: 'I just wanted you to choose me. Once. Just once.' The words come out small, desperate, the voice of the child you were.
inspired_by: Being Broken Up With Over Text, Reading It Out Loud

title: Whispering Secrets to Someone Who's Sleeping
instruction: Someone you care for deeply is asleep beside you—a partner, a child, a dying friend—and in this quiet darkness, you finally say the things you can't say when they're awake. Start with the tenderness of watching them breathe, the gratitude for this moment. Whisper the confessions: your fears about losing them, the ways they've changed you, the specific tiny moments you'll remember forever. Let your voice catch on the words you've never been brave enough to say out loud. As you continue, feel the weight of knowing tomorrow you'll go back to normal conversations, back to not saying these things. End with a truth so vulnerable it almost doesn't make it past your lips—something about your own fragility, your own desperate need, your own breaking heart that you hide so well in daylight.
inspired_by: Concealing Surprise When Hearing Unexpected News

title: Whispering to the One Who Drowned Here
instruction: You're floating in the exact spot where your best friend drowned three years ago. Start barely above a whisper, describing the water's coolness as if talking directly to them, telling them what it feels like to float here now. Your voice is fragile, trembling with the intimacy of this private ritual. Confess the small, terrible truths: 'I was jealous of you sometimes. I didn't answer your last text. I think about you every single day and I'm so tired.' Let the grief catch in your throat, not theatrical but real—the way pain actually sounds when you're alone. As you float, the water that took them now holds you, and you're caught between devastation and the strange peace of finally being close to them again. End in silence that speaks louder than words.
inspired_by: Floating on Your Back in a Calm Lake

title: Confronting My Mother in Her Final Hour
instruction: You're at your mother's deathbed, and after a lifetime of swallowing your pain, something inside you breaks. Begin with bitter, controlled anger: 'I needed you to be my mother. Not my critic. Not my disappointment. My mother.' Your voice is tight, sharp, each word carefully placed like a scalpel. You've practiced this speech in your head for decades. But as you speak, watching her frail and dying, the anger starts crumbling into something more complicated. Grief bleeds into the rage. Your voice breaks on memories—'You missed my graduation. You forgot my birthday five years in a row.' The fury gives way to the desperate, childlike need underneath: 'Why wasn't I enough for you?' End in a completely different emotional place—tender, aching, as you take her hand. 'I forgive you. God help me, I forgive you.' Let thirty years of need and hurt and love tangle together until you can barely speak.

title: The Summit in the Steam
instruction: You are standing at the top of a steep, muddy trail in a tropical jungle, after a two-hour climb. The air is thick with humidity, your clothes soaked through, every breath feels like inhaling steam. Your leg is cramping badly, pain shooting up your calf, but you finally made it. Start the line with exhaustion so deep your words are slurred, your voice wet and heavy, gasping between syllables. Let the pain show in a shaky inhale or a grunt. Then, as you realize you actually succeeded, let a raw, broken laugh escape, and shift into a fierce, ragged triumph—your voice cracking but rising. End with a mix of sheer pride and the lingering ache, your breath still labored. Speak as if your mouth is full of moisture, tongue thick, struggling to push out the words.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Everything We Survived
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, but they almost didn't make it here—six months ago they nearly died, and you're the only one who knows the ten darkest moments you helped them through. Start with the expected wedding toast cheerfulness, your voice bright with champagne and celebration. But you can't help yourself—you begin listing the real moments: the 3am phone calls, the night in the emergency room, the morning you found them and saved their life. As you name each crisis, your voice splits between joy that they're here and terror at how close you came to losing them. Your smile is real but your hands are shaking. By the end, you're crying and laughing simultaneously, publicly breaking down while everyone else looks confused, but your friend across the room understands every word. End with gratitude so fierce it feels like rage, celebrating survival while honoring how much it cost.
inspired_by: When memorizing a large amount of material in a short time under production pressure

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are alone, physically exhausted after a day of devastating news—a betrayal, a diagnosis, a loss. Your body is in pain: actual physical soreness mixed with emotional collapse. Begin by trying to describe the physical sensations clinically, detached—'my chest hurts, my hands are shaking'—as if reporting from a distance. But as you catalog what your body feels, the emotional truth floods in. The physical pain becomes a doorway: your voice breaks, speeds up, slows down. Let sensation and emotion blur completely. Rage might surge through your shoulders, grief might live in your throat, shame might sit in your stomach. End in a place where you stop fighting what your body knows, where physical and emotional pain are no longer separate—raw, animal, and completely honest.

title: The Inheritance of Joy
instruction: You are at your grandmother's funeral reception, and you've just been handed a letter she wrote to you before she died. As you read it aloud (or speak the contents), begin drowning in grief—your voice thick, your face wet with tears, your chest heavy with loss. The letter tells you she was proud of you, that she saw your light, that she wants you to live fully. As you read, acknowledge your fear: 'I'm so afraid without you... I'm afraid I'll forget you...' But then, as you continue, begin to hear her voice in the words. Imagine her not as gone, but as present—imagine her laughing, imagine her celebrating you in this moment. Let yourself feel the wild contradiction: devastating grief and explosive joy existing simultaneously. Amplify every memory of her laughter, her warmth. By the end, you should be simultaneously sobbing and laughing, your voice breaking between tears and wonder. Let the darkness of loss become shot through with blazing gratitude. Your body should be wrecked and radiant at once.
inspired_by: Benevolent Audience Fragmented Imaging (On-the-Spot Fear Antidote)

title: Washing Your Lover's Hair for the Last Time
instruction: You're gently washing the hair of someone you love who is slipping away from dementia, illness, or simply from your life. Begin with tender focus on the physical sensations—the weight of their head in your palm, the way water runs through their hair, the familiar cowlick you've touched a thousand times. Your voice is soft, intimate, almost meditative. But as you continue, let memories flood in, whispered fragments of your history together. Feel your throat tighten as you realize they might not remember this tomorrow, or that this ritual you've shared for years is ending. Let quiet devastation seep into your words—not crying, but something deeper, like watching someone you love disappear in slow motion. End with something simple you want them to remember, your voice breaking on the kindest words you can find.

title: The Body Remembers, The Body Revises
instruction: Stand and physically embody a moment when someone's words or actions made you feel small—maybe a teacher's criticism, a lover's rejection, a parent's contempt. Let your body collapse inward, feel the actual physical sensation of shame or worthlessness in your chest, your shoulders, your throat. Breathe with it. Then, without leaving the emotional reality, begin to physically revise the moment. Straighten your spine. Open your chest. Let your voice grow from a whisper to full volume as you speak the words you wish you'd said—or the words you needed to hear. Feel the physical transformation as you inhabit a version of yourself who was strong enough, worthy enough, powerful enough. The emotion should move from crushing physical shame to embodied, almost aggressive self-reclamation—your final words should be spoken with your whole body claiming space.
inspired_by: Actor has identified a specific historical experience causing lasting damage to self-esteem

title: The Last Brush
instruction: You are an elderly man brushing your teeth at the sink, staring at your reflection in the dim bathroom light. The mint paste feels sour on your tongue, and your jaw aches as you try to speak through the foam and scrubbing. Start with a bitter, defeated tone—remembering a friend who passed yesterday, your words slurred and interrupted by the brush. Midway, let the sadness deepen as you pause, spitting a little, then continue with a slower, more contemplative voice, considering your own mortality. End with a quiet, accepting sigh, the brush still, your words clear but weary.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present), Contemplation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Voice That Left
instruction: You are a former union foreman, a man who once barked orders over the din of a construction site. Now you sit in a silent car, parked outside your house, gripping the steering wheel. You just left the doctor's office. The doctor says you have vocal cord nodules and that surgery might not get your old voice back. You try to say aloud the one thing that defines you — your old nickname, 'Big Mike' — but your voice cracks and fades on the second word. Start with a fragile, almost clinical sense of contemplation as you examine the sound, then let distress creep in as the word breaks, ending with a quiet, helpless panic. Speak the full statement, 'Big Mike,' but let it fall apart. Let silence fill the pauses. Feel how your throat tightens and burns.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (very intensely present), Distress (clearly present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Words You Never Rehearsed
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hour. They've just opened their eyes and recognized you. Begin with the practiced, composed things you've been mentally preparing to say for weeks—the grateful, loving farewell speech you've rehearsed. But mid-sentence, let that script crumble completely. Let what you actually feel—messy, unresolved, perhaps angry, perhaps terrified, perhaps desperately wanting to say something you've never been able to say—break through and take over. Don't perform grief. Let your body and voice discover what's genuinely there in this unrepeatable moment. By the end, you should be speaking words you had no idea you were going to say, from a place you didn't plan to access.

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You are speaking to someone who broke your heart, destroyed your plans, or shattered your illusions—but time has revealed that this devastation was also a gift that freed you, opened you, or led you to yourself. Begin with the acknowledgment of how much it hurt, your voice still carrying traces of that old pain. But as you speak, let gratitude emerge—not the polite kind, but the deep, paradoxical gratitude that comes from surviving something that nearly destroyed you. Your voice should dance between laughing at the absurdity and crying at the cost, between thanking them and mourning what was lost. By the end, you're expressing a truth that feels almost impossible: that you wouldn't undo what happened, even though it broke you, because the person you became in the breaking is someone you needed to meet. Let your voice hold both the grief and the grace, the loss and the gain, all at once.

title: Bittersweet, Unbearable
instruction: You've just received the news you've wanted for years—a dream realized, a long-sought victory—but it came too late. Someone who should be here to witness it is gone. Begin in pure joy: let your voice soar with triumph, with disbelief, with 'we did it!' Then, mid-celebration, remember: there is no 'we.' The joy doesn't disappear but becomes laced with grief, each emotion intensifying the other. Your voice might laugh and break simultaneously. Express gratitude for the moment while rage pounds underneath at the timing. End in a place where you're holding both truths at once—the beauty and the unbearable absence—not resolving them, not choosing one, but feeling how love makes loss devastating and loss makes love sacred. Let contradiction live fully in your voice.

title: The Weight of the Fog
instruction: You are an older woman standing alone in a dense fog, the air thick and muffling. You’ve come to this quiet spot to escape a friend’s success, but the fog feels like it’s pressing in on you. Start by speaking out loud to yourself, your voice flat and numb — you’re trying to convince yourself you don’t care about her new house, her happy family. Let the sourness creep in as you mutter about how she never earned it. By the end, a flicker of envy escapes, your voice tightening and cracking despite your attempt to stay hollow. Speak as if unsure if anyone can hear you, sometimes louder than needed, then trailing off.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Thing I Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He's been distant, cold, and critical your entire life. Begin by speaking to him with all the love, admiration, and desperate need for connection you've always felt but never expressed—tell him everything you wished your relationship could have been, as if he were the father you needed him to be. Let yourself be completely vulnerable and open. Then, mid-speech, have the painful realization wash over you that he's not responding the way you hoped, that even now he can't give you what you need. Let your tone shift as this rejection—silent or subtle—breaks something in you. End in the complicated space between love and resignation, between grief for his death and grief for the relationship that never was.

title: The OverSharer on Social Media
instruction: Act as someone who narrates every mundane aspect of their life online. Use an overly excited voice when describing trivial activities, switching to the imagined reactions of followers.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Absence
instruction: After fifteen years of silence, you're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. Begin with controlled anger, words measured and cutting, listing the milestones they missed. But as they try to offer hollow excuses, something fiercer erupts—raw fury at the child you were who waited at windows, who made excuses for them. Your voice rises, cracks, becomes almost feral with pain. Then they say something—maybe they admit they were afraid, maybe they confess they think about you every day—and suddenly you're caught between rage and a devastating hunger for connection. You want to hurt them and hold them simultaneously. End in the exhausted quiet of someone who's finally released years of held breath, uncertain whether this is closure or just another kind of wound.
inspired_by: Panic Whispering: Hiding from an Intruder

title: Echoing Euphoria
instruction: You're at a house party, tipsy and giddy, and duck into the concrete stairwell to call your best friend. The reverb makes your own voice sound huge and strange, and you're laughing at how ridiculous everything is—the party, the stairs, your life. You're mid-sentence, describing how amazing you feel, when you hear someone's footsteps above. You freeze, suddenly mortified that they might have heard you singing or rambling. Your voice shifts from loud, ecstatic slurring to a quiet, embarrassed whisper. You try to play it cool, but your words tumble out nervously as you pretend you were just leaving a voicemail. The echoes betray every stumble.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Birthday of Ghosts
instruction: You are celebrating a milestone birthday for someone who died years ago—setting out their favorite meal, lighting candles, speaking to them as if they're there. Begin in determined, almost defiant joy: you're celebrating, damn it, you're honoring them with happiness, not grief. Laugh at memories, toast them, feel the genuine warmth of good times. But as you continue, allow yourself to truly sense the empty chair, the silence where their voice should be, the weight of all the birthdays they've missed and will miss. Let gratitude and grief become inseparable—you're laughing and crying at the same memory, furious at their absence while desperately grateful for what you had. End in a place where joy and devastation are completely intertwined, speaking words that hold both celebration and heartbreak in the same breath. The transformation is from separation of emotions to their complete, contradictory fusion.

title: Acceptance at the Edge
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home for the last time before it's sold, and laughter keeps bubbling up through your tears. Your voice is incredulous, almost giddy: 'This is the spot where Mom threw spaghetti at the ceiling, and it stuck for two years.' You're laughing, really laughing, even as tears stream down your face. 'We were so broke. So beautifully, hilariously broke.' Your voice holds both profound sadness and genuine joy: 'I spent twenty years being angry about what we didn't have. And now I can't stop seeing what we did.' You touch the wall where heights were marked, and your laughter softens into something tender: 'We were rich in all the ways that mattered, and I was too young and stupid to know it.' A pause where joy and grief are perfectly balanced. By the end, your voice is luminous with paradox: 'My heart is breaking and singing at the same time. How is that possible?' You're smiling through tears, your voice full of wonder: 'Goodbye, little house. Thank you for holding us. We were so loved here, even when we couldn't see it.' The emotion braids together loss and gratitude, grief and celebration, ending and beginning—all at once.

title: The Rehearsed Finale
instruction: You are an elderly man, seated on a park bench across from an old rival who ruined your family's business forty years ago. You have waited decades for this moment, memorized every word. The air is cold, your hands steady. Speak slowly, deliberately; each syllable is a calculated strike. Feel the intense concentration at first as you recall the exact phrases, and let a faint, proud smile creep in as you realize you are in complete control. Your voice is low, calm, with a chilling satisfaction that grows as you deliver the final blow.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Reconciliation That Breaks You
instruction: Someone who deeply wounded you has come to ask for forgiveness, or you are asking someone you deeply wounded to forgive you. Begin with the emotion you think you're supposed to feel—righteous anger if you were wronged, humble contrition if you caused harm. But as the conversation unfolds, let contradictory feelings crash into each other: if you're angry, let love for this person complicate it; if you're apologizing, let resentment at having to do so surface; if you're forgiving, let the wound still bleed. Allow yourself to be pulled in opposite directions simultaneously—grateful they came but furious it took so long, wanting to embrace them but wanting to hurt them, feeling free and feeling trapped. Let laughter and tears mix inappropriately. By the end, discover that forgiveness or reconciliation isn't clean or simple—it's a tangled mess of relief and loss, freedom and new pain, love that coexists with anger, or an ending that feels like both death and birth.

title: The Last Time I'll Say Your Name
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's unconscious, but you've never told her certain truths - about the time she saved you from yourself, about the secret she kept that protected you, about how her humming while cooking was the only thing that made you feel safe as a child. Speak to her now, knowing she can't respond, can't judge, can't leave you again because she's already leaving. Start with the things that feel safe to say, then move deeper into what you've kept locked inside for decades. Let your voice move from controlled and careful to raw and unguarded. By the end, you're not asking her to stay - you're giving her permission to go, even though it's breaking you.

title: The Dregs of Dignity
instruction: You're slumped on a bar stool, your head heavy and spinning. You're speaking to a friend who just betrayed your trust in a petty, shallow way. Begin with bitter disgust—your voice thick, sharp, but losing control as you slur and sway. Let the exhaustion creep in mid-sentence; your volume drops, words blur, and you almost tip over. End in a whisper of resignation, body sagging, too drained to care anymore. Let the alcohol drag your voice into monotone by the finish, with a faint, defeated laugh.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Part of You I Keep Returning To
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone you love, in that deep night hour when defenses dissolve. You want to tell them something vulnerable, something true about how you feel, but grand declarations feel false in your mouth. Instead, in a whisper, begin describing one specific thing about them that you find yourself returning to again and again—maybe the sound of their breathing, or a particular freckle, or how their hand feels, or the way they say your name. Speak so quietly they have to strain slightly to hear. Let yourself get lost in this one genuine point of fascination, and discover how speaking about this single real thing opens the door to confession. Start with tender, almost shy observation. End with the vulnerable truth about your love or fear that flows naturally from this authentic noticing.

title: The Queen and the Jealous Advisor
instruction: Portray a regal queen with a confident, authoritative voice and her advisor who speaks in a polite but insincere tone. The advisor is secretly undermining her. Switch between the queens directness and the advisors hidden sarcasm, creating an undercurrent of betrayal in their conversation.

title: Hoarse Whisper
instruction: You're a man with a deep, muscular voice, but tonight a nasty laryngitis has left you barely able to speak above a raspy whisper. You're on the phone with someone you're intensely, sexually attracted to—someone you've been longing for. You start by trying to downplay your illness, forcing a playful, flirtatious tone, but each word scrapes your throat. As you continue, the lust you're holding back breaks through: your voice cracks, you trail off, you swallow hard and wince, and the desire becomes raw and undeniable. End with a vulnerability that mixes pain and longing.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Forgot-to-Reply
instruction: You're a teenage boy, alone in your room, typing a message to a friend on your laptop. You start with a quiet smile, a little content and even slightly elated after a funny video you just watched—your fingers tap a fast, rhythmic beat. But as you begin to type, you suddenly remember you never replied to that friend's earlier message about something embarrassing you did, and shame floods in. Let your typing slow, then stutter as your speech fragments; your voice loses its energy, dropping into a flatter, heavier tone. End with a mumbled admission, the enthusiasm gone, replaced by a heavy, self-conscious quiet. Speak 40–80 words.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Elation (slightly present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: When Your Best Friend Won't Let You Save Them
instruction: You're confronting your closest friend who's been self-destructing, and you've come to offer unconditional support and forgiveness for the ways they've pushed you away. You start with fierce, protective love: 'I don't care what you've done. I'm here. I'm not leaving.' But they lash out, telling you that you're the problem, that your forgiveness is suffocating, that they never asked for your saving. Your voice shifts to barely controlled anger mixed with hurt: 'I've sacrificed everything for you—don't you dare tell me I'm suffocating you.' You go back and forth, your volume rising, emotions raw and explosive. But they keep pushing, keep rejecting, until something inside you breaks. Your final words come out shaking with both rage and devastating sadness: you realize you can't save someone who doesn't want saving, and you have to walk away from someone you love to save yourself.

title: The Miracle in the Wreckage: Finding Joy in the Goodbye
instruction: You're having your last conversation with someone who is dying—and they're making you laugh even as your heart shatters. Begin with real laughter, genuine and full, at something absurd they've said: 'you're seriously worried about who'll water your plants?' But your laughter keeps catching, transforming. You're giggling and crying simultaneously—grateful for this moment, devastated it's the last one. Your voice dances between joy and grief: 'God, I'm going to miss you' comes out half-laugh, half-sob. They keep making jokes, and you keep breaking. You find yourself thanking them through tears, celebrating them while mourning them. Your voice is luminous with love even as it fractures with loss. End in a place of impossible beauty: laughing together one final time, your voice full of both the worst pain you've ever felt and the purest love you've ever known. Let the contradictions live together—don't resolve them.
inspired_by: Bungee Bouncing: Losing Your Mind to the Elasticity

title: Breaking the Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent who never said 'I love you' or showed pride in you. Begin seated, voice controlled and cold, listing facts about your childhood with clinical distance. But as you speak, decades of suppressed need begin erupting. Your body rises from the chair. Your voice starts breaking through your own restraint. Build from tight, controlled accusations to full-body demand—you're not asking anymore, you're insisting they see you, acknowledge you, say the words. Let your voice get louder, your gestures bigger, your need more naked and unashamed. By the end, you're standing tall, voice ringing with power, claiming the love and recognition you deserved all along. The transformation is from frozen shutdown to explosive, physical insistence on your worth. Let every part of you—feet planted, chest open, voice unrestrained—embody this claiming of your right to be loved.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about why she never protected you from your father's rage, why she taught you to be small and quiet and invisible. Start with your voice shaking, almost apologetic for even bringing it up—you've spent your whole life protecting her feelings. But as you speak, something ancient and furious rises up. 'You made me believe his anger was my fault.' Your voice gets stronger, rawer. 'You taught me to disappear.' Feel the little girl inside you finally screaming. Then, devastatingly, let it crack into something else: the realization that she was scared too, that she was surviving the only way she knew how. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it makes room for something more complicated. 'I needed a mother who would fight for me. Instead I got someone who taught me how to vanish.' End with your voice thick with both rage and heartbreak: 'I don't know how to forgive that. But I'm so tired of hating you.'

title: The Final Paperwork
instruction: You're at your desk, alone late in the evening. You've been processing the same type of reports for hours, and your eyes burn from the screen. You're slouched in the chair, slightly numb with fatigue. As you stare at yet another form, the boss's voice echoes in your memory—demanding, dismissive. Bitterness floods in. You mutter to yourself, voice thick with irritation, then let it build into a quiet, venomous release. Let your voice crack with exhaustion, then sharpen with contempt. Shift weight, shuffle papers, lose a thought, then find it—like real talk. End with a bitter, quiet laugh. Speak about 50 words.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Thing She Held
instruction: You are in a cramped attic, standing on a wobbly crate, both arms stretched high to reach a small box on a high shelf. Your shoulder blades pinch, ribs are pulled taut, and each breath is shallow and strained. You're a young man, voice naturally deep, but now it's thin and tight from the posture. Start with focused frustration—muttering curses at the box's stubborn position, shifting your weight, grunting as you adjust your grip. As your fingers finally brush the box, you remember it contains your mother's old locket, the only thing left after she passed. Your voice wavers as you say, 'I've got you,' but the strain in your chest cracks your words. End with the sadness pouring through—voice breaking, a choked sob, then a whisper: 'I miss you, Mom.' Let the physical pull and breathlessness make every word feel fragile and real.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Frozen Longing
instruction: You are an older man lost in a blizzard, your body shaking uncontrollably. The cold has locked your jaw, and every word is a struggle through chattering teeth. You begin by muttering to yourself in fear, trying to stay alert, but as you speak, a vivid memory of your wife's warm kitchen surfaces—the smell of cinnamon, the way she hummed. The fear fades into a raw, aching longing so powerful it makes you whisper her name. Let the shivers dictate the rhythm; your voice cracks and trails off as you reach for a warmth that isn't there.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Talking to a Baby Who Just Said Their First Word
instruction: The baby says 'Dada' (or 'Mama'). Your reaction should be volcanic but contained — the baby might get scared. Whisper-scream: 'OH MY GOD. Did you— say it again! Say it again!' Try to coach them. They say something unrelated ('blerp'). Deflate slightly. Then they say it again — perfectly clear. Sprint to get your partner: running footsteps, breathless shouting. Return and the baby is silent. 'Say it! You just said it! Tell them!' The baby blows a raspberry. You die inside.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left You Behind
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you twenty years ago, and every rehearsed speech dissolves. You start with controlled anger, listing the birthdays they missed, the graduations, the nights you needed them. But as you speak, the rage begins to fracture—your voice catches on memories you thought you'd buried. You hate them and you miss them and you're still that child waiting by the window. Your accusations transform into desperate questions: Why wasn't I enough? What was so broken in you that you couldn't stay? The anger burns into grief, and suddenly you're sobbing through words that sound like they're being torn from your chest. You end in exhausted, hollow silence—not reconciled, not healed, but finally having said the things that have been eating you alive.
inspired_by: Historical: Former Oppressor Must Apologize to Those They Once Oppressed

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight That Won't Land
instruction: You're calling your adult child from the airport. Your flight boards in ten minutes. You've just learned—but they haven't—that you have weeks, maybe days, left. Your voice starts light, almost too cheerful, asking about their week, their partner, that job interview. But as the final boarding call echoes behind you, something shifts. You can't tell them the truth, but you need them to know they were loved, that every moment mattered. Your voice begins to crack around the edges of ordinary words. 'I'm proud of you' becomes weighted with everything unsaid. By the end, you're fighting to keep your voice steady while pouring a lifetime of love into a goodbye that sounds like 'see you soon.' The gate is closing. You have to hang up. Your last words must carry what you'll never get to say again.
inspired_by: Historical: Resistance Fighter Betrays a Comrade to Save Themselves

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's unconscious, perhaps in their final hours. The machines beep softly. You're holding their hand, and you're telling them everything you never said—not the big dramatic declarations, but the small, tender truths. How they always knew when you needed coffee. The way they hummed while cooking. Start with nervous small talk, as if they might wake up and tease you for being sentimental. Gradually let yourself become more vulnerable, your voice dropping to barely a whisper. Let pauses grow longer. Let your throat catch on words. End with something so intimate, so quiet, that it's almost just breath—a confession of love that's also an acceptance of goodbye. Make silence as important as words.
inspired_by: Concealing Skepticism While Listening to an Unbelievable Story

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a diagnosis, a loss, an ending—but you're at a celebration for someone you love, and you refuse to poison their joy. Describe the party happening around you, and your voice is genuinely warm, even joyful, finding real delight in their happiness. But underneath, your heart is shattering. Let both truths coexist: authentic laughter that catches on unshed tears, gratitude that's edged with grief, joy for them tangled with your own quiet devastation. This isn't pretending to be happy—it's the complex reality of loving someone enough to hold your pain separately while genuinely celebrating theirs. End with a moment of profound peace within the chaos: you're breaking and whole at the same time.

title: The Burning House
instruction: You have just gotten the phone call that the house you grew up in—the one place that held all your childhood memories—is on fire, and your mother is standing outside watching it burn. You're describing what you imagine she's seeing, what's being destroyed: your father's workshop in the garage where he taught you to build things before he died, the kitchen where every holiday happened, the marks on the doorframe measuring your height each year. Begin with frantic, breathless panic, your body tight with adrenaline as if you could somehow stop it from far away. But as you continue speaking, describing each room being consumed, let your voice move through fury at the unfairness, then into a strange, unexpected laughter mixed with sobbing—because you're suddenly remembering not the rooms themselves but moments of being alive in them. Let physical sensation drive your performance: the phantom heat on your face, the tightness in your chest, gasping for air. End in exhausted, cleansed stillness, whispering, 'Maybe we were never supposed to keep it forever.' You're discovering what remains when everything physical is gone.

title: The Suitcase at the Door
instruction: Your partner is leaving—not angrily, but with finality—and their suitcase sits by the door. You're trying to say goodbye. Begin rigid with the effort of being 'mature' about this, performing composure, holding your voice steady. But as you look at them, really look, let yourself drop the performance. Notice the specific details of their face, their hands, the way they're standing. Let your breath become fuller, your body soften even as your heart breaks. Tell them you're furious they're leaving, and in the same breath, that you understand why. Let anger and love exist simultaneously. Thank them for something that hurt you. Tell them you hope they find what they're looking for, and mean it, even though you're devastated. By the end, arrive at a place of complex truth: brokenhearted and bitter and grateful and loving all at once, your voice carrying all of it without trying to resolve the contradictions.

title: Severe Allergic Reaction
instruction: Anaphylaxis is setting in. Your voice starts normal but quickly becomes strained. 'Can't... breathe...' Your throat is closing. Your speech becomes wheezy, desperate. You're reaching for an EpiPen with shaking hands. Include the moment of relief as the injection works, then the desperate phone call. Your voice is still difficult, rasping. You're describing symptoms between gasps. By the end, you're in the ambulance, your voice becoming distant as medication takes hold.

title: The Last Flight Before Memory Fades
instruction: You are a pilot with early-onset dementia saying goodbye to your plane for the last time, running your hands over the controls you'll soon forget how to use. Begin with quiet pride and deep love as you recall your first solo flight, your voice steady and warm with nostalgia. Gradually let confusion creep in—you forget a term, lose your train of thought, then catch yourself. Your voice should crack as you realize this is the last moment you'll remember these feelings clearly. End with a whispered apology to the plane, your tone shifting from pride to grief to a fragile, tender acceptance. Let the pauses speak as loudly as the words—this is about what you're losing even as you try to hold it.

title: After the Heat
instruction: You are lying in bed, still tangled in sheets, your head resting on your partner’s chest. The room is dim, the only sound is their heartbeat and your own shallow breaths. Start with a slow, affection-filled murmur about how good it feels to be here, letting your voice melt into a low, fry-laced whisper. As you speak, a flicker of old anger rises—mention a minor betrayal or broken promise, your voice catching and growing tighter, but then it dissolves into numbness, your words trailing off into a hollow, almost indifferent tone, as if you’ve already exhausted the emotion. Let long silences hang between phrases; shift your weight, adjust the blanket, or pause to listen to the wind outside. End with a quiet, detached observation about the empty space between you.
emotions_sampled: Affection (clearly present), Anger (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unwelcome Stirring
instruction: You are an older man at a dinner table with a small group. You're numb from a long day, barely present, when your eyes land on her across the table — a woman you find impossibly magnetic. Your voice starts flat, almost bored, then softens and slows as you speak to her, losing your train of thought. But when a friend cracks a joke about 'men your age,' sourness floods in. Your tone hardens, words turn clipped, and you end with a bitter half-laugh, glancing away as you reach for your glass. Let your head turn naturally between people, and let the clink of silverware or a cough interrupt you.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Infatuation (extremely present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Boxer's Round 12 Collapse
instruction: You're cornered in the final round, barely on your feet. Your voice is slurred, breathy, almost gone. Use internal monologue as your coach screams instructions you can barely process. Your breathing is irregular—sometimes you're gasping, sometimes you hold your breath to steady yourself. Words come out thick and slow, like speaking through cotton. Include the moment you taste blood and feel your legs give way. End with the referee's voice cutting through, and you collapsing.

title: The Airport Return
instruction: You're seeing someone at an airport after five years of painful separation—maybe estrangement, maybe betrayal, maybe just life pulling you apart. They're walking toward you right now. Begin with the specific, real sight of them: how they've aged, how they move, details you'd forgotten and details that gut you with familiarity. Feel contradictory emotions colliding in real time: furious at them AND desperate to hold them, grieving the lost years AND grateful they're here, guarded AND vulnerably open. Oscillate between these warring feelings and acute awareness of them as they actually are in this moment—their expression, their hesitation or confidence, the shrinking distance between you. Let memories crash in (their laugh, a specific fight, a perfect day, a betrayal) while staying riveted to who they are NOW. Start in one emotional state and let the reality of their actual presence—combined with the weight of history—pull you somewhere completely different by the end.
inspired_by: Working for a Choice While Promoting Ensemble

title: The Bittersweet Leaving
instruction: You're packing up to leave for something you've worked toward your entire life—a dream job in another country, an opportunity you fought for, the thing you always said would make you complete. Your best friend or partner is helping you pack, trying to be happy for you. Start with excitement, with that bright, energized voice of someone whose dreams are finally coming true. But as you hold each object—a photograph, a book they gave you, a ticket stub from a perfect night—feel the reality setting in. You are leaving. This chapter is ending. Don't choose between joy and grief—let them exist simultaneously, each one making the other more intense. Your voice should crack not with weakness but with the unbearable fullness of feeling two true things at once: this is everything you wanted, and it is costing you something precious. End in a place where gratitude, loss, hope, and heartbreak are completely intertwined, inseparable, all of it real.

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission Before Crossing the Event Horizon
instruction: You're transmitting your last words before crossing into a black hole, a one-way journey into the unknown. Begin with scientific excitement—you're about to witness what no human has seen. But as you speak, the reality hits: you'll never see Earth again, never hold your child, never feel sunlight. Your voice fractures between wonder at the cosmic revelation before you and devastating grief for everything you're leaving behind. End with a message to someone you love—not goodbye, but a truth you needed them to know. Your voice should contain both the vastness of space and the intimacy of a whispered secret. Let the emotion catch in your throat as you realize this is your last chance to say what matters. Authentic, raw, moving between awe and heartbreak.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Chooses to Remain in a Body It's Outgrowing

title: The Memory's Edge
instruction: You're an elderly man at a dimly lit bar, approaching a woman you believe you knew decades ago. You've prepared your most charming, slow, and velvet-toned delivery—lowered pitch, deliberate pauses, a light laugh—but as you compliment her eyes, she mentions a detail that clashes with your memory. Confusion creeps in, tightening your throat, making you lose your rhythm. Start with smooth, controlled seduction, then let your voice falter with genuine bewilderment as you search for footing. End with a mix of forced charm and rising doubt, your laugh now a nervous exhale.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Lesson That Didn't Take
instruction: You are a young teacher in a quiet lecture hall, giving a final review session to a sparse class. You'd poured everything into this semester, but now you see the empty chairs and the blank stares. Start with a steady, projected voice, deliberately slowing down to emphasize key terms you know they'll need for the exam. As you speak, a memory of a student you lost to apathy surfaces—your voice catches, and disappointment seeps in. Let your volume drop, your pace falter, and your gaze drift to the window, as if searching for where you went wrong. End with a quiet, almost breathy confession, the teacher's mask slipping into raw regret.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Coherent Moment
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved for decades as dementia finally takes them from you. They're having their last lucid moment, and you both know it. Start with desperate joy—they remember you, they know your name. Pour out everything you never said: gratitude, apologies, promises you couldn't keep. But mid-sentence, you watch the light of recognition fade from their eyes. They look at you like a stranger. Your voice breaks as you try to pull them back, begging them to remember just one more minute. End in a whisper, still talking to them even though they're gone, telling them it's okay to let go, your words fracturing between holding on and saying goodbye.

title: Confession in Blue Light
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, and you need to whisper something you've never said aloud. Begin trying to say 'I'm afraid you'll leave me,' but the wrong images come: your father's car pulling away when you were six, your college roommate packing boxes without explanation, that recurring dream of empty rooms. Let these unbidden visions shape how the confession emerges—not as a clean statement but as fragmented whispers between these flashing memories. Your breathing changes. The words come out differently than you planned. Start from a place of wanting to be clear and articulate, but allow these interrupting sense-memories to make you more raw, more childlike. End with the truth said in a way you never intended, more vulnerable than you wanted to be.
inspired_by: Actor wants to access deeper, unconsciously rooted emotional life for a scene

title: What We Never Said
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping lover the night before you leave them—not because you don't love them, but because you do, and staying would destroy you both. Speak barely above a whisper, as if any louder would wake them and make this impossible. Begin with tender observations—the way they breathe, small things you'll miss—but let the sadness deepen with each breath until you're confessing why you have to go. Your voice should be thick with unshed tears, catching on certain words. Mix the intimacy of love with the devastation of loss. This isn't dramatic—it's the quiet kind of heartbreak that sits in your chest like a stone. Let silences speak. By the end, you're saying goodbye to the life you wanted but can't have, and it should feel like you're leaving pieces of yourself behind.

title: The Last Glass
instruction: You are an older man at the funeral of your best friend, Tom. You've been asked to say a few words, but you're not a public speaker. You grip the edges of the lectern, your hands trembling slightly. You start with a formal, rehearsed opening — 'We're all here today to remember Tom' — but your voice wavers and you lose your place. You see his widow in the front row, and a memory hits you: the two of you sharing a beer on his porch last summer, laughing about nothing. The longing for that moment floods you. Your voice becomes quieter, more personal, and you trail off into a long, uncomfortable pause. By the end, you're not giving a eulogy anymore — you're just talking to him, with raw, unpolished affection. Let your vocal pitch crack, let your breath catch, and let the silence hang longer than feels right.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Edging: The Desperate Plea
instruction: Your partner is controlling your pleasure and denying your release. Perform the build — breathing accelerating, pitch rising, moans increasing in intensity — then the denial. The frustrated whimper, the shaky exhale, the begging ('please, please, please'). Repeat the cycle, each time more desperate, voice more broken, the begging more raw and abandoned. Show how the loss of control transforms the voice from formed words into pure, pre-verbal need.

title: The Forgotten Trophy
instruction: You are an older man crawling through your own cramped, dusty attic crawlspace, reaching for a box you stored years ago. At the start, your voice is tight and strained, shoulders hunched, breathing shallow from the tight space and the slight shame of having let this go so long. As your fingers find the box and you open it to reveal the long-lost trophy inside, you feel a bitter wave of triumph — you were right, it's here — but also disappointment that no one else cares anymore. Let your voice shift from grit and irritation to a quiet, worn mix of pride and resignation; let the space make you sound close, like you're talking to yourself or the object.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in complete darkness, and you need to whisper the truth you've been hiding: you've been going through the motions of your life, feeling nothing, and you're terrified. You've told everyone—including yourself—that you're fine, happy even. Start with your voice small, almost inaudible, still trying to protect the lie. As you speak into the darkness, let the words pull the truth out of you like a splinter being removed. Feel how exhausting it's been to maintain the facade of being okay. Your whispers should become more urgent, more desperate. By the end, you're quietly weeping, finally admitting you've been numb for so long you forgot what feeling alive was like. The relief and terror of this admission should make your voice tremble with both.
inspired_by: An actor is apathetic — feeling fine but not stimulated or affectable by anything

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Memory: Early-Onset Alzheimer's Self-Recording
instruction: You're recording memories for your future self who won't remember making this recording. Speak softly, intimately, as though confiding in a stranger who is also you. Begin with tender gentleness, describing your children's faces, your partner's laugh, the smell of rain. But as you continue, the grief of losing yourself while still being present catches in your throat. Your whispers become fragile, trembling with the weight of pre-emptive loss. You're saying goodbye to your own consciousness, mourning yourself while you're still here. Let your voice catch on words, let silences speak of things too painful to name. End with something simple - 'You were loved' - your voice barely audible, breaking not with drama but with the unbearable tenderness of self-compassion in the face of inevitable erasure.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Colony Manager Discovers Humans Are Becoming Dependent on Its Decisions

title: No Room at the Inn
instruction: You're at a hotel front desk after a 16-hour flight, your body screaming for sleep, your voice slow and syrupy from exhaustion. You're leaning on the counter, blinking hard, when the clerk says your reservation vanished. A shock jolts you awake—your pitch jumps, words tumble out. Then you glance down and see a roach scuttling across the key card. Disgust floods in: your tone flattens, pulls back, you recoil mid-sentence. Start nearly slurring with fatigue, then snap into astonished indignation, then choke on revulsion as you point.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Disgust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He's asleep, his breathing shallow. You've just found an old photograph in his wallet—one you've never seen before—of him holding you as an infant, his face radiant with joy you never witnessed growing up. Begin with the complicated resentment you've carried for years about his emotional distance, letting that heaviness sit in your chest. As you study the photograph, then look at his sleeping face, allow whatever genuinely arises in you to surface—whether it's anger softening into grief, or understanding, or a more complex tangle of feelings. Speak to him, knowing he might hear you even in sleep, letting your voice carry the weight of everything unsaid between you. Let the photograph be a doorway into a truth about him you never had access to before, and let that truth reshape what you're feeling moment by moment.

title: Hard Hat, Soft Heart
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a gentle, high-pitched voice, wearing a hard hat with a visor on a noisy construction site. You’re watching your grandson operate a crane for the first time. At first, you feel a deep contentment—proud and peaceful, shielding your eyes from the sun. Then, you notice he fumbles a bit, and a flicker of disappointment crosses your mind. But when he successfully lifts a steel beam, triumph swells in your chest. Speak to yourself under your breath, shouting over the noise. Let your voice be slightly cupped by the hat, and let the background clatter make you pause or raise your pitch. Start warm and soft, then let a brief, quiet letdown creep in, then end with a bright, proud exclamation.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (clearly present), Disappointment (slightly present), Triumph (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Weight of Feathers
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, whispering a confession you've never spoken aloud—not because it's a dramatic secret, but because it's something so tender and fragile that saying it out loud feels dangerous. Begin by describing the physical sensation of this secret living inside your body—where you feel it, what it weighs, how long you've carried it. Speak so quietly that you're almost talking to yourself, building the courage with each breath. The confession itself might be about fear, about a dream you're terrified to want, about a moment of shame, or about the depth of your need for this person. Start with halting, fragmented thoughts, barely audible. As you speak, let the relief of finally releasing these words battle with the terror of being truly seen. End with your voice steadier but more vulnerable, having crossed from self-protection into radical exposure. The final sentence should be the truest thing you've ever said.

title: Goodbye at the Train Platform: No Return Journey
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving on a journey they won't return from—maybe a terminal diagnosis requiring experimental treatment overseas, maybe witness protection, maybe a mission they likely won't survive. Start with false brightness, trying to be strong for them: 'You're going to be fine. This is going to work.' But your voice keeps cracking. Mid-way, let the reality crash over you and your voice becomes raw and broken: 'I don't know how to do this without you. I don't know how to let you go.' You're memorizing their face, touching their hand like you're trying to imprint the feeling. By the end, find a different kind of strength—not the fake cheerfulness from before, but something quieter and more real. Your voice is soft, steady, heartbroken but also full of a fierce love: 'I'm going to be okay. And you're going to know I love you every single day you're gone.' The emotional journey moves from forced optimism through devastating grief to genuine, grounded courage.
inspired_by: One Week Sober: Cravings and Determination Wrestling

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, but they're marrying someone who's taking them across the world, and you know you're losing them. You start with genuine joy—your voice bright with champagne and celebration. You're funny, warm, telling a story that makes everyone laugh. But as you speak, the reality settles in. Your voice begins to catch. 'I'm so happy for you,' you say, and you mean it, but now you're also crying. The laughter and the tears mix until you can't tell which is which. 'I'm going to miss you so much,' comes out as half-laugh, half-sob. You end with 'To love,' and your voice is full of genuine celebration and devastating loss at the same time. This is joy and grief in the same breath, gratitude and heartbreak sharing the same words.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting at your mother's bedside in her final hours. She's been unconscious for days, but you suddenly need to tell her something you've never said: that you forgive her for leaving when you were twelve, and more importantly, that you forgive yourself for hating her all these years. Begin speaking as if she can't hear you—guarded, rehearsed, barely above a whisper. But as you continue, allow yourself to believe she IS hearing every word. Let your defenses crumble. By the end, you're no longer asking for her forgiveness—you're giving her permission to go, with a fierce, aching love you didn't know you still had. Your voice should journey from protective distance to raw, unguarded intimacy.
inspired_by: When actors pursue Method work or sustain character reality in ways that may confuse or discomfort co-workers

title: The Last Cart
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe 10, dragging a heavy wooden cart loaded with scrap metal through a muddy field under a noon sun. Your arms burn, your breath comes in sharp huffs, and each step is a grunt with your voice cracking from strain. At first, you're caught in a dreamy infatuation with a girl from the village—you smile to yourself, mumbling her name, imagining her watching you be strong. But as the load grinds you down, that sweetness curdles. You start to mutter dark, possessive thoughts about her—how she belongs to you, how anyone who looks at her will regret it. Your voice turns to a hard, rasped whisper, proud of this imagined cruelty. By the end, you're panting, but your words come out smug and venomous, a child's malice grown in the heat and exhaustion.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—perhaps wracked with fever, or in the aftermath of passionate intimacy, or shaking with rage-fueled adrenaline after nearly getting in a fight. Your body is not entirely under your control. Begin with your physical state overwhelming everything: your breath irregular, your words coming in fragments, your focus scattered by sensation. But gradually, as your body begins to settle (the fever breaking, the passion cooling, the adrenaline ebbing), an emotional truth surfaces that the physical intensity was masking. Maybe it's grief you've been running from. Maybe it's fear. Maybe it's a decision you've been avoiding. Let your voice transform from physically overwhelmed to emotionally exposed. The physical subsides, but something more vulnerable emerges. End in stillness—your body quiet, but your emotional truth now undeniable and spoken aloud.
inspired_by: Actor has been cast in a major role and has weeks before rehearsal begins

title: The Slouch of Envy
instruction: You are slouched deep into a worn armchair, a half-empty glass of wine dangling from your fingers. It's late, and you're alone in a dim room, but you're on the phone with a friend who just shared news of their promotion. Your spine is curled, your jaw hangs loose, and your words come out mushy and slurred. Start with a lazy, bitter chuckle as you downplay their success with a slurred insult, but as you speak, the jealousy seeps through — your voice catches, your breath shortens, and the envy becomes raw and exposed. End with a quiet, almost broken admission of your own unfulfilled dreams, your voice losing all pretense of intoxication.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're making coffee for your partner on their final morning before they leave for a mission from which they likely won't return. Begin with forced cheerfulness, pretending this is just another ordinary morning—commenting on the weather, the coffee, small domestic details. As you speak, let the pretense crack bit by bit. Your voice should catch on mundane words as the reality crashes through. End in a whisper, finally saying what you've been avoiding all morning, allowing yourself to break completely. The journey is from desperate normalcy to raw, undefended grief. Let silence do as much work as words.

title: Laughing Because It's Perfect and Impossible
instruction: The bread is perfect—golden, warm, fragrant—and you're describing it with genuine delight, even laughing softly at how ridiculously good it smells, how it fills the whole house with this absurd amount of coziness. But here's the contradiction: this is the last good thing before everything changes. A diagnosis. A goodbye. A departure. A loss you can't stop. So your laughter is real, but tears are streaming down your face. Your voice should dance between joy and devastation—'God, smell that, it's so perfect, it's so stupidly perfect'—while your breath catches with sobs. Find the strange peace in savoring this beautiful moment precisely because it's fleeting. Let gratitude and heartbreak merge until we can't tell where one ends and the other begins. End with a whispered, 'Thank you. Thank you for this.'
inspired_by: Savoring the Smell of Freshly Baked Bread Filling the Kitchen

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a childhood wound you've carried for decades. Start from a place of controlled calm, determined to finally speak your truth without emotion. But as you talk, let disconnected images intrude: their hands, a specific room, a birthday they missed, the way they looked at you once, a phrase they repeated, a moment you felt invisible. Don't organize these into a neat narrative—let them crash into your composure in whatever order they arrive. Allow certain images to strike harder than others, breaking through your resolve. By the end, you've moved from controlled accusation to raw, unguarded pain—the kind that's been waiting decades to be spoken aloud.
inspired_by: Actor needs to quickly elevate vulnerability or emotional availability before a scene

title: The Last Drag
instruction: You're in a grimy alley behind a dive bar, chain-smoking. You've just gotten word that a years-long scheme has finally paid off — all your planning, the lies, the bribes, everything worked. The triumph is a hot, tight ball in your chest, but another part of you feels hollow, numbed, like you're watching yourself from far away. Your hands are steady as you light another cigarette, but your focus is razor-sharp on the next move. Start by exhaling a long drag, let the rasp in your voice catch, then speak — let the words come out rough, low, with a gravelly victory that slowly fades into a cold, concentrated calm by the end.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Concentration (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Child About Their Addiction
instruction: You're facing your adult child, and you can't pretend anymore that everything is okay. Begin with controlled anger—you've rehearsed this conversation, you're going to stay calm. But as you speak, your fury intensifies: rage at watching them destroy themselves, rage at your own helplessness. Let your voice rise, crack with desperation. Then shift—mid-sentence, your anger collapses into pleading. You're on your knees emotionally, begging them to see what they're doing. Move through every tactic: threats that sound hollow even as you make them, memories of who they used to be, raw confession of your own failures as a parent. End in a completely different place—exhausted, quieter, speaking not with anger but with devastating honesty about your fear of losing them. Your voice should transform from forceful to fractured to finally, heartbreakingly tender.

title: Competitive Eating Commentator
instruction: You're a sports commentator, but for competitive eating. Apply the full energy, pacing, and drama of a horse race call to someone eating hot dogs. 'AND KOBAYASHI REACHES FOR NUMBER FORTY-SEVEN, THE CROWD IS ON THEIR FEET!' Include the disgusted undertone you're trying to suppress. When a competitor has a 'reversal' (nearly vomits), your commentary should be simultaneously horrified and professional. The absurdity should be played completely straight.

title: The Breaking Point Confession
instruction: You're screaming at God, the universe, the empty air—whoever's listening—about the injustice of what happened to you. Start with explosive rage, voice raw and guttural: 'What kind of world lets this happen to a child?!' Let your fury be physical, gasping, almost primal. But mid-scream, something collapses inside you and the rage transforms into sobbing helplessness: 'I was so small. I couldn't fight back.' Your voice becomes fragile, bewildered: 'Why me? What did I do?' Then find a fierce, protective love for the child you were—'No one should have touched you. No one had the right'—before dissolving into exhausted grief. End in a whisper of devastating acceptance: 'I can't change it. But I can survive it.'

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the years of emotional neglect, finally saying everything you've rehearsed in your head for decades. Begin with controlled anger, your words precise and cutting, almost coldly articulate. As you speak, let old wounds open—your voice should start to shake with the pain of the child still inside you, furious and heartbroken. Then something shifts: you see them as fragile, human, flawed.
