By the end, you're fragmented, but more honest than you've been in years of therapy sessions with others.

title: The Last Pilgrimage
instruction: You are an elderly man, weary from decades of life, carrying a heavy wooden cross up a steep hill at dusk. This is a long, final journey you've chosen for yourself. At first, you focus on each painful step — your breath is ragged, your legs shake. You mutter to the cross itself, finding a strange relief in the weight, a familiar ache. Describe your exhaustion, the stones underfoot, the fading light. By the end, as you near the top, allow your concentration to soften into a quiet, trembling gratitude — not for the end, but for having had the strength to climb at all. Let your voice crack, catch, and drift, as if you’re speaking more to the memory of this moment than to anyone else.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Unwanted Current
instruction: You are an older woman in the middle of sex that started with desire but now feels wrong. The alcohol is still warm in your veins, making everything slow and syrupy. Your body reacts on its own—tiny gasps, a moan you didn't mean to let out—while your mind screams stop. Try to speak through the haze: 'Wait—no, I—' but the words break off as a wave of sensation pulls you under. By the end, your voice drops from frantic to hollow, a quiet 'it's fine' whispered more to yourself than to them, as you surrender to the numbness behind the pleasure.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Comrade Loss
instruction: You're at the funeral of your bandmate of fifteen years. The priest is saying generic things. Your voice when you get up is almost inaudible. 'We used to dream together.' That's all you can manage before it crumbles. You're describing a specific moment—playing in a basement for seventeen people—and he was so alive. Your body shakes. Someone hands you tissues. You finish with a broken laugh: 'He would have hated this speech.'

title: The Rocker's Last Argument
instruction: You are an elderly person slumped deep in a worn-out rocking chair on a creaky porch, your spine curved, jaw slack, voice mushy from disuse. Someone you care about has just proven your point wrong in a small argument, and you start with lazy, irritable impatience—each word a grumbled sigh. But as you rock and think, the irritation softens into a weary, reluctant pride. You realize they were right, and the last words come out as a slow, tender admission, your voice cracking with unexpected warmth. Feel the chair creak, the light shift, a fly buzzing—let it all happen naturally.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Gratitude I Resent
instruction: Thank someone who saved your life at the cost of their own dreams—the parent who sacrificed everything, the sibling who gave up their future for yours, the friend who stayed when they should have flown. Begin with genuine gratitude, meaning every word, cataloging their sacrifices with real appreciation. Let the thanks be true and full. But as you speak, let resentment begin to poison the gratitude—you never asked for this debt, this weight, this guilt that colors every success. Their love became your cage, their sacrifice your burden. End in a complex place where you simultaneously want to embrace them and escape them, where 'thank you' and 'I wish you hadn't' exist in the same breath. Let love and anger, gratitude and rage, devotion and desperate need for freedom coexist without resolution.
inspired_by: Actor does not practice between classes and wonders why their work is not developing

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father about a truth you've both avoided for twenty years - perhaps an abandonment, a betrayal, a secret kept that shaped your entire life. Start from a place of rehearsed anger, the speech you've prepared, the accusations you've polished. But as you speak, let yourself stumble into the raw, undefended truth beneath the anger: you needed them and they weren't there, and that need hasn't gone away. Let your voice crack and expose the child still inside you. By the end, you're no longer accusing - you're asking, with devastating vulnerability, why you weren't enough to make them stay, or try, or see you. The challenge is letting the anger dissolve into the naked wound beneath it.
inspired_by: Actor is depressed and cannot access creative energy

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—a relationship ended, a dream died, you've lost something irreplaceable—but in this moment, you're discovering an unexpected lightness. Begin with describing the devastation, but there's something strange in your voice: you're almost laughing. Not from hysteria, but from genuine, bewildered relief. As you speak, let gratitude and grief weave together: 'Thank you for breaking my heart' said with both tears and a smile. You're mourning and celebrating simultaneously. Your voice should dance between sobbing and laughing, finding odd moments of joy in the wreckage. End with a sense of profound peace underneath the pain—you're free now, even though freedom hurts. This should feel like watching someone find grace in the most unlikely moment.
inspired_by: The Lie That Became the Truth

title: Reading Your Lover's Unsent Letters After They're Gone
instruction: You've found letters your deceased partner wrote but never sent—confessions, fears, dreams they never voiced. Start reading aloud in barely a whisper, voice catching on their handwriting, their private voice. They wrote about loving you, about being afraid of burdening you with their darkness. Your voice trembles, breaks on certain words—your name in their hand, pet names you'd forgotten. This is intimacy you never got to hold while they were alive. Each letter reveals more vulnerability they hid, and your reading becomes more fractured, whispered through tears, pausing to breathe, to absorb. End in the quietest devastation—a truth whispered to the empty room: 'I would have carried it all with you.'

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're standing between someone you love and danger you cannot stop—an addiction, a destructive path, a choice that will destroy them. Start with fierce, almost violent intensity: you're shouting, desperate, trying to physically hold them back with your words. Your voice should be raw with terror disguised as anger. Then, mid-confrontation, your power collapses. You break—not into quiet crying, but into gasping, ugly sobs where you can barely form words. You're begging now, your voice hoarse and jagged, admitting your complete helplessness: 'I can't watch you disappear.' End in exhausted defeat, your voice hollowed out, whispering one last plea that sounds like surrender. The transformation is from warrior to someone watching the inevitable, powerless.

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Sleeping Love
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner is asleep beside you. You're leaving in the morning—not for another person, but because staying is slowly erasing who you are. Whisper the goodbye you can't say to their face. Begin with tender gratitude for the good years, your voice barely audible, full of love that makes leaving devastating. Let each memory you recount add weight until your whispers catch and break. The quiet is essential—this isn't drama, it's the sound of a heart carefully, quietly tearing itself in half. End with the unbearable truth: 'I love you enough to leave before I start to hate you.' The challenge is conveying soul-deep sadness in near-silence, where every caught breath speaks louder than shouting ever could.
inspired_by: Narrating a Nature Documentary While Hiking Uphill

title: The Last Favor
instruction: You're a 19-year-old girl lying on your back in a cheap motel room, letting your ex-boyfriend go down on you one last time. Your body responds even though your mind is churning with bitterness—you know he's only doing this to avoid a real goodbye. Start with a teasing, almost mocking tone, pretending you're in control, but let the doubt creep in as your breath catches and your words break apart. By the end, you're just gripping the sheets, making small, involuntary sounds, the bitterness fading into a quiet, angry surrender.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (clearly present), Doubt (extremely present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing Through Tears While Reading Your Late Wife's Secret Love Letters to You
instruction: You've discovered a box of letters your wife wrote to you over the years but never gave you—she's been gone six months. Start reading the first one aloud, and let yourself laugh at her humor, her observations, the inside jokes only you two shared. But the laughter keeps catching, turning into something between a laugh and a sob. Your voice should dance between genuine joy at hearing her voice again through her words and the crushing pain of her absence. Read passages that make you chuckle, then suddenly break as the loss hits you anew. You're grateful for this unexpected gift—it's like she's in the room—but that makes it hurt even more because she isn't, not really. End with a moment where you're smiling and crying simultaneously, thanking her aloud for these words, your voice suffused with both the deepest grief and the most profound love, finding something like peace in the contradiction.
inspired_by: Treading Water While Calling for Help

title: The Pep Talk in the Closet
instruction: You're an older man with a deep, gruff voice, standing in a tight walk-in closet surrounded by coats and scarves. You've set up a small recorder to lay down a message for your son, but the dead acoustics make every word feel too close, too real. Start by clearing your throat, adjusting the mic, and muttering a doubt—'I don't know if I'm the right voice for this.' Let a flicker of old pain surface as you remember a past failure, then slowly, almost stubbornly, let hope rise. End with a strained but genuine optimism, your voice cracking just a little at the edges, as if you're convincing yourself as much as him. Say: 'Look, I ain't perfect. I've let you down before. But this time? This time I'm gonna show up. We're gonna find our way out. I believe that. I really do.'
emotions_sampled: Doubt (clearly present), Pain (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Adult Child Confronting Parent About Choosing Work Over Presence
instruction: You're at your parent's retirement party, and something inside you breaks. Start controlled, almost casual: 'This is a nice celebration.' But then it pours out—all those recitals they missed, all those nights you waited up. Your voice should fracture between anger and the child still desperate for them to understand what they took from you. There's fury, yes, but underneath is the devastating question: 'Did you ever actually want me?' Let the anger crack open to reveal the wound beneath—not just rage, but the tender, vulnerable ache of a child who needed them and learned to stop asking.
inspired_by: Pilot Congratulating Crew While Processing Near-Catastrophe

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: Your grandmother is dying in the hospital bed before you. She's unconscious, her breathing shallow. You have fifteen minutes before the family arrives. Speak to her now—all the things you never said, the gratitude, the childhood memories, the ways she saved you that she never knew about. Start with the practical things you came to say, but let yourself break open into the deeper truths. As you speak, feel the weight of her leaving shift from denial to devastating acceptance. Your voice may start steady and controlled, but allow it to crack, to whisper, to surge with everything you've held back for years. End in a place of raw goodbye, speaking the unspeakable truth that you'll never be whole without her.

title: The Last Sunset on Our Beach
instruction: You're lying on the same beach where you fell in love thirty years ago, but this time your partner is dying beside you, their hand growing cold in yours. Begin with the sensory details—the warm sand, the waves—trying to hold onto peace, speaking softly about the beauty around you. But as you continue, let grief crack through your voice. The warmth of the sand becomes unbearable because they won't feel it tomorrow. Each wave that once brought peace now sounds like time running out. End with your voice breaking as you whisper that you're not ready, that no sunset has ever felt this heavy, transforming from attempted serenity into raw, vulnerable heartbreak.

title: The Protector Who Can't Protect
instruction: Your younger sibling has just told you about abuse they suffered, and you weren't there to stop it. Begin with explosive fury directed at the perpetrator, voice loud and violent with rage, each word a weapon. But mid-sentence, the anger shatters into something more devastating—the realization that your rage is useless now, too late. Your voice breaks from roaring to sobbing in seconds, fierce protectiveness colliding with crushing helplessness. You're apologizing desperately, words tumbling over each other, voice raw and guttural, begging for forgiveness while knowing you can't undo what happened. The rage keeps surging back through the tears, then collapsing again into broken tenderness as you promise you'll never let anyone hurt them again, even as you both know you already failed. End with your voice reduced to a whisper, emotionally destroyed, caught between wanting to destroy someone and wanting to hold your sibling and never let go.
inspired_by: Speaking During a Panic Attack While Hiding It

title: Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're experiencing intense physical sensation—pleasure, pain, or both—and you begin by trying to describe it, to name it, to control it with language. But as the sensation intensifies, your words start coming faster, less controlled, disconnected from meaning. Describe the feeling, then the color of the ceiling, then a sound, then the sensation again, then a random memory it triggers, then pure sound, then words that make no sense, then back to the physical, accelerating until language and sensation blur together. Let your voice carry the physical experience—breath, rhythm, intensity—while your words fragment and scatter. By the end, you're speaking so rapidly that meaning disappears and only the raw, unfiltered experience remains, expressed through a torrent of disconnected verbal and vocal impulses.

title: Pillow Confession
instruction: You are a boy, maybe 10, lying face-down on your bed with your face pressed deep into a pillow. Your voice is heavily muffled as you speak—only the loudest, lowest sounds escape. You just had a fight with your father who left for work without saying goodbye, and you're furious at him but also desperate for him to come back. Start by spitting out words of contempt—angry, bitter, each syllable a punch into the fabric. But as you continue, let the longing seep through, softening the edges. Your breathing is uneven; you shift your head slightly to gasp for air, then press back down. Each sentence should sound like it's fighting the pillow. End with a quiet, contemplative whisper, almost a confession to yourself.
emotions_sampled: Longing (extremely present), Contempt (extremely present), Contemplation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Summit Reached
instruction: You are a young man who has just completed an arduous solo climb up a mountain, searching for a lost friend. Your body is trembling, every muscle screams. You collapse onto the rocky summit, and in the silence, you spot your friend's jacket—he's safe below. You need to call out to him, but your voice is barely a rasp. Start with the heavy, desperate rhythm of someone who thought they might not make it, then let the exhaustion mix with a deep, trembling relief as you realize he's alive. Your words should come out in broken phrases, with long breaths between, as if every syllable costs you.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Speaking While Severely Injured or in Acute Pain
instruction: You're describing what happened to the paramedic but pain keeps exploding through your body. Start coherent: 'I fell when...' But waves of pain contract your voice, words become shorter. Apologize for losing the thread. Another wave: a cry escapes before you control it. Keep talking because focus is survival.

title: The Fire Between Protection and Fury
instruction: Your teenage child just told you they're in a dangerous situation they've been hiding for months. Start with the震shock—voice tight, controlled, asking careful questions. But as the details emerge, the terror ignites into rage. 'How could you not tell me?' erupts from you, voice rising, hands probably shaking. You're furious at them, at yourself, at your own helplessness. The anger is volcanic because underneath it is the most primal fear a parent can feel. But mid-sentence, you see their face—the shame, the fear—and your voice breaks completely. The fury collapses into something raw and desperate. 'I can't lose you,' you say, and it comes out half-sob, half-prayer. You're on your knees emotionally. The fierceness remains, but now it's pure protective love, fierce and helpless and absolutely uncontainable.

title: The Last Morning on the Porch
instruction: You are an older adult sitting on a familiar porch at sunrise, facing someone you won't see again. This is the final farewell. You begin with a tight throat, ashamed of old arguments or words left unsaid, fidgeting with a loose thread on your sleeve. Midway, you pause to watch a bird land on the railing, and a fragile hope surfaces. Your voice slows, thick with unshed tears—every phrase feels precious. End with a half-smile, your tone wavering on the last word as you whisper a goodbye that holds both regret and quiet optimism.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Competitive Karaoke: Emotional Warfare
instruction: Two friends at karaoke escalating from fun to emotional warfare through song choices. Start with upbeat party songs (energetic, silly). Then one picks a song that was 'their ex's song' and the other responds with an even more devastating choice. The singing becomes less about performance and more about weaponized emotion. Include a power ballad delivered with way too much genuine feeling. End with both crying into a duet that heals whatever they just broke.

title: Confronting the Silent Witness
instruction: This tree stood in your parents' yard throughout your entire childhood, silent witness to everything—the fights, the neglect, the loneliness. Now, decades later, you return and place your hand on its bark, and suddenly you're confronting it like you wish you could confront them. Start with bitter accusation—'You saw everything, didn't you? You just stood here while I...'—your voice tight with anger at this mute observer. Let that anger crack open into the raw pain underneath, the child's voice breaking through: 'Why didn't anyone help me?' Transition from rage to pleading to a devastating realization that the tree, like you, survived by staying rooted and enduring. End by forgiving it, forgiving yourself, your voice soft but forever changed.
inspired_by: Touching the Bark of a Large, Old Tree

title: The Face I Need to Remember
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed. She has only minutes left. As you look at her weathered face, you desperately try to see her as she was in your most precious memory—young, vibrant, laughing in the kitchen while teaching you to bake bread when you were seven. Begin speaking to the frail person before you, but let your words and tone shift as you reconstruct that younger woman through the details you remember: the warmth of her skin, the particular melody of her laugh, the flour on her hands, the sparkle in her eyes. Your emotion should travel from present grief and fear toward a bittersweet joy as the two versions of her—dying and vibrantly alive—merge in your mind. End by telling her something you could only say to that younger version of her.

title: The Last Grand Adventure
instruction: You are an elderly person, standing in your cluttered living room, holding a small, worn photograph. The room is dim, the only light from a dusty lamp. You have just drunk a strong cup of coffee—unusual for you—and your heart is racing. You are packing a small bag, leaving for a trip you've been planning for years, the one everyone said you were too old for. Outside, you hear a car horn—your ride is here. Start with a teasing, slightly affectionate phone call to a skeptical friend, your voice quick and light, but as you hang up and look at the photo, a tremor of excitement and fear creeps in. The tunnel vision of adrenaline takes hold—your words become clipped, breaths shallower, as you mutter a final promise to yourself, the initial tease fading into raw, quiet resolve.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Kitchen Floor Confrontation: When Safety Becomes a Cage
instruction: You're sitting on your childhood kitchen floor at 2am during a holiday visit, finally confronting your parent about why you've felt unseen your whole life. Start with that same vulnerable, undefended voice — you're exhausted from years of pretending. But as you speak your truth, something shifts: the softness hardens into anger you didn't know you were carrying. 'You made me so small' needs to be said with shaking intensity. Then, devastatingly, you hear how you sound — just like them when they're hurt — and the anger cracks into grief. End by recognizing you've been protecting them by staying silent, and that protection is killing you both. Let the tears be ugly and real.

title: Reading Your Child's Letter After They've Gone
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter your child left you—maybe they're gone to war, or disappeared, or died, or simply left for good. Start reading their words in their voice, almost smiling at their humor or kindness in the opening lines, laughing softly at an inside joke. But as the letter continues, the words get heavier—they're telling you things they never said in person, forgiving you or asking for forgiveness, expressing love they couldn't speak aloud. Your voice begins to shake, but you keep reading because you need to hear their words. You laugh and cry simultaneously as they describe a memory that breaks your heart with its beauty. Near the end, you can barely speak through tears, but there's profound gratitude mixed with unbearable grief. The final line is something simple—'I love you' or 'Thank you'—and you have to say it several times, as if saying it enough will bring them back, your voice soft and shattered but filled with devastating love and peace.
inspired_by: Doing Push-Ups During a Phone Interview

title: Breaking the Mirror
instruction: You are standing in your bathroom after receiving devastating news (choose what it is specifically for you—betrayal, diagnosis, loss, failure). Begin by staring at yourself in the mirror, feeling nothing, completely dissociated from your own reflection. Your body is cold, your breathing shallow. Slowly start to notice physical sensations—tension in your jaw, heat building in your chest, your hands beginning to shake. As rage and grief start to break through the numbness, let your body respond before your mind can control it—your breath quickens, you might grip the sink, lean closer to your reflection. Build to a physical breaking point: you might shatter something, pound the wall, collapse to the floor, or stand frozen in a silent scream. The emotional pain must be visceral—feel it in your stomach, your throat, behind your eyes. Transform from frozen disconnection to explosive embodied feeling, ending in exhausted devastation on the bathroom floor, your body finally telling the truth your mind couldn't process.
inspired_by: Re-Creating the Dream Through Imaging (Corvette Dream Example)

title: What We Never Said in Daylight
instruction: Late at night, speak to someone sleeping—your mentor, your parent, someone who will never hear these words while conscious. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and broken. Begin by thanking them for small, specific moments they probably don't remember but that saved you. Let your voice catch as you confess the fears you could never show them: that you're not strong enough, that you're terrified of disappointing them, that their faith in you feels like a weight you can't carry. Admit the truth you've hidden—that sometimes their belief in you made you feel more alone, because they never saw how scared you were. As you speak, feel tears threatening but held back. End with a whispered confession that's both love letter and grief: 'I wish you could see me as I am, not as you need me to be.' Let silence hold everything you can't say.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. For years, he's been emotionally absent, hiding behind newspapers and polite distance. Tonight, you've decided to break the silence. Start with controlled, cold anger—sharp questions demanding to know why he could never just talk to you, never just be present. But as you speak, something shifts: you realize mid-sentence that you're becoming just like him, using anger as a wall. Your voice should crack, soften, become vulnerable. End by dropping all defenses and asking him, with naked honesty and fear: 'Do you even know who I am? Because I don't think I know who you are, and that terrifies me.' Move from accusation to raw need for connection.

title: The Secret I've Carried Alone
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying beside someone you trust completely—a partner, best friend, or sibling. Begin in barely audible whispers, almost hoping they won't hear, as you finally speak aloud the shame you've carried in silence for years—an abortion, a betrayal, an assault you survived, a terrible choice you made. Your voice should be fragile, breaking, full of fear about being seen fully. As you continue, notice the relief of finally speaking it, let vulnerability turn to trembling truth-telling. Feel your breathing change, your body soften. By the end, you're no longer whispering in shame but speaking in quiet, tearful liberation, your voice steady and clear, asking simply: 'Do you still love me?'

title: Sketch of a Crush
instruction: You are a young girl drawing a picture of your crush in your notebook, your pencil moving slowly with each detail. At first, doubt creeps in — you pause, chew your lip, thinking they’ll never notice or care, but the infatuation is clear in the way you smile at the lines. As you add the final touches, hope lightens your breath and you whisper your secret wish, your voice lifting from shy uncertainty to a quiet, giddy optimism. Let the scritch-scratch of the pencil interrupt your thoughts now and then, and let your head angle muffle some syllables naturally.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Infatuation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Consensual Non-Consent
instruction: You're engaging in consensual roleplay where one of you is supposed to 'not want it' but has already established safe words and boundaries. Your voice starts as the person saying no: 'Stop, please don't.' But you're aroused. Your voice is performing resistance while your body is participating. Your partner's voice is the aggressor, but you both know they'll stop at the safe word. The psychological play—the permission to desire being taken away—is liberating. Your voice becomes increasingly authentic in its arousal, the performance and reality blurring. Your partner recognizes the moment you stop performing and fully surrender. End with both of you coming down, acknowledging the complexity of desire and power. Your voices should show genuine connection underneath the roleplay.

title: The Morning After: A Daughter Confronts Her Mother
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, both of you with coffee, the morning after you finally told her a truth she didn't want to hear—about your childhood, about what you needed and never got, about the years of silence. Begin describing your coffee with bitter precision, each word sharp, using the coffee as a way to avoid eye contact. Your anger is controlled but building—the way she's sitting there calmly drinking her own coffee as if last night didn't happen. Let your voice rise as you move from the coffee to what it represents: all those mornings she was there but not really there. Then break—let the anger crack open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted to be seen. End in raw vulnerability, maybe your voice dropping to almost a whisper, asking if she even remembers those mornings, if any of it mattered to her.
inspired_by: Enjoying the First Sip of Morning Coffee

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut recording a final message to your family from a failing spacecraft. You begin calm, almost cheerful—telling your daughter about the stars, describing how beautiful Earth looks from here, your voice warm with wonder and love. But as you speak, the oxygen meter beeps quietly in the background, and the reality seeps in. Your voice starts to crack when you tell your partner 'I'm sorry I won't make it to our anniversary.' The wonder dissolves into desperate tenderness as you try to pack a lifetime of love into these final minutes. End with your voice breaking completely as you whisper 'tell them I wasn't afraid'—but we can hear that you are. Show someone trying to give their family a beautiful goodbye while their own terror threatens to overwhelm them.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a family secret they have kept for decades—one that has shaped your entire life without your knowledge. You have just discovered the truth, and you've asked them to sit down and face you. Begin with controlled, cold anger, using precise, measured words because you're afraid of what will happen if you let yourself fully feel. As they try to explain or deflect, allow the years of confusion and self-doubt to surface. Move from accusation to a raw, vulnerable plea to understand why they chose silence over honesty. End in a place you didn't expect: recognizing their own fear and brokenness, feeling your rage transform into something more complicated—a painful, unwanted empathy mixed with the anger that won't disappear. Your voice should crack where you didn't plan it to.

title: Breath on the Nape
instruction: It's 3AM. You and your partner are lying in darkness after nearly ending your relationship hours ago. Begin in whispered exhaustion, your voice barely audible, speaking in fragments: the silence, the darkness, the sound of their breathing. You start cataloging tiny physical sensations—the warmth of their skin, the weight of the blanket, how your hand trembles as you reach toward them. Let vulnerability overtake you. Confess your terror of losing them, not in grand statements but in broken pieces: specific moments you're afraid of forgetting, small habits you've memorized, the way light hits their face. End with a whispered admission of need so naked it frightens you. Move from hollow exhaustion → tentative touch → undefended love and fear of loss.

title: Echo of the Last Shot
instruction: You are alone in the empty gymnasium after everyone has left. The polished floor catches the fluorescent light, and every sound you make — the squeak of your sneakers, the distant thud of a forgotten ball — bounces back thin and metallic. You start by quietly saying something to yourself about how hollow it all feels, your voice small and tentative in the vast space. Then a ball rolls out from under the bleachers, and for a moment you watch it, a small smile creeping in. You finish with a soft, amused laugh — not mocking, just a genuine chuckle at the absurdity of it all. Let your voice shift from a contemplative murmur to a lighter, playful tone, with natural pauses as you react to the echoes and the ball's movements.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing Alone in Their Apartment
instruction: You have just returned to the apartment you once shared with someone now gone—through death, betrayal, or departure. Music is playing, their music. Start by letting the space assault you with memories—specific furniture they chose, their scent still lingering, photographs, the light coming through windows you both looked through. Begin moving to the music with your body rigid, fighting against feeling anything. But as the song continues, let the actual physical sensations—the floor beneath your feet, the air on your skin, the vibration of the music, your own heartbeat—merge with your emotional pain until you cannot separate them. Dance through anger into grief into something like ecstatic release. Your body becomes the site where rage and longing and physical sensation create something almost unbearable. By the end, you're collapsed or spinning, completely surrendered.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're experiencing something intensely physical that's inseparable from emotional overwhelm: the grip of grief that makes your chest hurt, desire that floods your body with heat and urgency, rage that makes your hands shake and your jaw clench, the aftermath of a nightmare that has your heart racing with real terror, or physical pain that's breaking down your emotional defenses. Your body is in charge now, not your mind. Begin in the full grip of the physical sensation—let it consume you, let your breath be ragged or held, let your body speak its truth. As the intensity moves through you, allow the physical experience to transform your emotional state. Perhaps overwhelming desire shifts into tender vulnerability, or rage burns through to exhausted grief, or terror slowly releases into shaky relief, or pain cracks you open to something more fragile and real. Track how the sensations in your flesh alter what you feel in your heart. End somewhere different—perhaps softer, perhaps emptied out, perhaps more human than when you started.

title: The Moment You Stop Fighting the Inevitable
instruction: You're alone, and something has just broken inside you—a diagnosis, a final rejection, the last door closing. Begin in explosive rage: scream, let your voice crack with fury, pound something, unleash everything. 'This isn't fair! I did everything right!' Your voice is raw, desperate, fighting against reality with every breath. But gradually, the rage exhausts itself. Your voice begins to shake, to weaken. The screaming becomes sobbing, then hollow laughter at the absurdity, then just ragged breathing. End in that terrible quiet stillness—not peaceful, but depleted. Your final words are whispered with strange, broken acceptance: 'Okay. Okay.' The arc is from fierce resistance to reluctant surrender, from explosive to empty.

title: The Checkpoint Victory
instruction: You are a child who has just won a board game against an older sibling. You pause, still catching your breath from the cheering, and realize you need to ask if it's okay to celebrate by jumping on the bed. Your voice shifts from excited triumph to serious, careful clarity as you ask permission, watching closely for their reaction. Feel the pride in your win, but also the need to be respectful. As they give a clear yes, let the triumph return, brighter than before.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight of What Remains
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a habitually high, soft voice, pinned beneath a heavy fallen shelf in your cluttered basement. Your favorite cat, terrified, is hiding just out of reach. At first, you call out with strained affection—coaxing, gentle—but your crushed ribs force every word out in short, squeezed bursts. As the cat refuses to come, your voice cracks with anger, the sweetness turning sharp and desperate. Each syllable is a battle against your collapsed lungs. End barely above a whisper, fury and love tangled in a single, ragged breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering to a Dying Orchestra Member
instruction: The orchestra's first violinist—your oldest friend, your musical soulmate—is in hospice. You're beside their bed, and you've brought a recording of your last performance together. Start by describing the music softly, intimately: 'Remember this passage? Where you came in early and it was perfect anyway?' Your voice is tender, almost playful, trying to keep things light. But as you continue, grief seeps in. Your throat tightens. 'I don't know how to conduct without hearing your violin in my head.' Let silence sit. Then, barely audible, the confession that terrifies you: 'I'm not ready to make music in a world where you don't exist.' End with your voice catching, suspended between memory and goodbye: 'Thank you for every note. Every single one.'

title: The Gratitude That Breaks You
instruction: Someone you love deeply has just given you something you desperately needed—maybe they stayed when they could have left, forgave you, believed in you, saved you. You're overwhelmed with gratitude, but underneath it is a lifetime of believing you didn't deserve such grace. Begin with trying to say thank you, but let the gratitude crack open into something more complicated—grief for all the years you denied yourself this kind of love, anger at yourself for taking so long to accept it, joy mixed with the pain of finally letting someone in. Your thanks should transform into a declaration: you're claiming your right to receive love, to be worth saving, to take up space in someone's heart. Let contradictory emotions flood through—laugh while crying, feel rage at your own past self-denial while experiencing profound tenderness. By the end, your gratitude has become a fierce claiming of your own worthiness.

title: Telling Your Mother You Remember Everything She Pretended Didn't Happen
instruction: You've rehearsed this moment for years. Begin with controlled, almost clinical calmness: 'I need to tell you something I should have said a long time ago.' Describe a specific memory she's always denied—be precise, detailed, your voice steady but your hands shaking. As she begins to deflect or excuse, let your voice rise with years of suppressed fury: 'Don't. Don't do that. Not this time.' Your rage should build to a breaking point, then shatter completely into something more vulnerable—the voice of the child you were, begging to be believed. End in a whisper, exhausted: 'I just needed you to say it was real.' Move from rehearsed strength to explosive anger to the fragile need for validation you've carried your whole life.
inspired_by: Screaming Into Your Pillow So No One Hears

title: Final Phone Call from a Sinking Ship
instruction: You're trapped below deck on a sinking vessel, water rising, and you've managed one last call to someone you love. Start with frantic urgency—'Listen to me, we don't have much time'—your voice shaking with adrenaline and terror. But as you realize rescue won't come, your voice must shift. The water is at your chest now. You begin telling them everything you never said: how the morning light through their window was your favorite thing, how their laugh changed your life. Your terror dissolves into tender clarity, almost grateful for this chance to finally speak truth. Your breathing becomes labored, but your words grow softer, more intimate, like you're whispering secrets into their ear. End with your voice nearly underwater, a whispered 'I see you everywhere,' as acceptance and love replace fear. The emotional journey: panic to devastating tenderness to peaceful surrender.
inspired_by: Waiting for Rescue in a Cave: Acceptance Turning to Meditation

title: Radio Operator Under Artillery Fire
instruction: You're calling in coordinates over a military radio while explosions land nearby. Use the push-to-talk cadence: button click, rapid transmission, release. Between transmissions, explosions, debris, coughing through dust. Your voice should be the opposite of panic — trained, clipped, precise — but the environment is trying to destroy your composure. Include a close hit that knocks you down — gasping, ears ringing, then getting back on the radio with a shakier but still professional voice.

title: The Wedding Ring in Your Palm
instruction: You're holding an object that represents both your greatest joy and your deepest loss—perhaps a wedding ring after divorce, a baby's shoe after loss, a acceptance letter to a dream you had to abandon. Begin speaking to this object with bitter resentment, cataloging everything it cost you, every sacrifice that now feels meaningless. Let your voice be sharp with anger and regret. As you continue, let other truths emerge: the genuine love that was real even if it ended, the beauty that existed even in what's now broken, the gratitude for having experienced something so profound even though it hurts. By the end, you should be holding this object with tender reverence and furious grief simultaneously—thanking it and cursing it in the same breath, your voice breaking not from pure sadness but from the impossible complexity of loving and hating the same memory.

title: The Last Sunrise Together
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has hours left to live, watching their final dawn through a hospital window. Begin with controlled, almost clinical observation: 'The sun's coming up now.' Your voice is steady because you're holding everything in. But as the light grows, something breaks—you start noticing tiny details you'll never see again: the way the light catches their hair, their breathing, the warmth of their hand. Your voice fragments from composed to raw grief mixed with desperate gratitude. End with whispered wonder through tears: 'It's beautiful... you're still here to see it with me.' Let the control dissolve completely. The arc moves from protective composure to complete, tender devastation.

title: The Cruelest Kindness: Firing a Friend
instruction: You're a manager who must fire your close friend due to company layoffs. The HR script sounds wooden and corporate — but you have to read it. Your professional voice keeps cracking with personal grief. When they ask 'Is this real?' your rehearsed answer dissolves. Perform the impossible balance: being official while being human. Include the moment after they leave — the door closes and you fall apart alone.

title: The Unbreakable Gaze
instruction: You are a young drill instructor during a live-fire demonstration. A recruit under your command just executed a perfect shot under extreme pressure — a feat even you haven't managed. You bark out the standard command to secure the weapon, but your voice catches for a split second as awe floods your chest. You fight to maintain the clipped, emotionless bark, but a teasing smirk tugs at your lips. You pivot to a quick, whispered aside to the recruit — still using the same sharp, clipped rhythm — but now your tone carries a suppressed grin and genuine admiration. End with a gruff order that betrays your pride.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Through the Sedation
instruction: You're in recovery after emergency surgery. Your partner is holding your hand. The anesthesia is still wearing off and you're floating in that space between sleep and consciousness. Your voice is barely above a whisper, words coming slow and soft, but you just remembered something crucial you never told them—that you're grateful for the small things, the way they make coffee, how they wait for you. Begin in a dreamy, sedated state where words feel like they're traveling through honey. Your speech is slow but the emotion underneath is enormous—you're saying things you've never been brave enough to say when fully conscious. As you struggle toward clarity, let tenderness break through the pharmaceutical fog. End with an almost heartbreaking vulnerability, where even though your voice is still thick and quiet, the love is devastatingly clear. This isn't performed sentiment—it's raw truth slipping out because your defenses are chemically dissolved.
inspired_by: Xanax Dissolving Your Ability to Sound Serious

title: The Echo of Applause
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman at a community reunion, speaking into a crackling PA system. You begin with genuine awe at the packed hall and pride in the legacy you helped build. But as you scan the faces, a quiet numbness seeps in—maybe from exhaustion or the weight of memory. Let your voice start full and bright, then trail off in the middle of a sentence as you lose your thought, then force a smile back. End with a polite, hollow cheerfulness that doesn't quite match your eyes.
emotions_sampled: Awe (clearly present), Pride (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth about how their absence damaged you. Begin with careful, controlled words—you've rehearsed this: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, the careful control fractures. Old pain surfaces: 'Do you have any idea what it was like? Waiting for you?' Your voice hardens with anger, then breaks into something more vulnerable—the child who still needed them. 'I made excuses for you. I defended you.' Move between rage and grief, accusation and longing. By the end, you're exhausted, but there's a strange relief in finally being honest. 'I can't keep pretending it didn't matter. It did. You did.' Your voice is quieter now, but solid—no longer seeking their approval.

title: The Last Call
instruction: You are an elderly man, heat-stricken and slumped against a park bench. You're calling a younger person you deeply adore — your grandchild, or a past love — and you want them to come sit with you. Dizziness makes you forget words mid-sentence; your dry throat makes some syllables crack. Start with a hoarse, labored whisper — almost a confession of how badly you need them. By the end, a bizarre, fluttery infatuation overrides the exhaustion; your voice lifts into a soft, dreamy sing-song, like a kid asking for a hug. Speak low, let your panting interrupt you, and let the infatuation bloom into a trembling smile in your last words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing at Your Own Wake
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis and decided to throw yourself a living funeral. You're giving a speech to everyone you love, and you're determined to make them laugh even as your heart shatters. Start with genuine humor—self-deprecating jokes about your illness, your voice warm and mischievous, making light of the darkness. Let laughter bubble up in your own voice as you roast yourself and your life. But as you continue, let cracks appear: your voice wavers on certain words, breath hitches between jokes, and suddenly you're crying while still trying to smile. The humor becomes a shield you can't quite hold up. End with profound gratitude mixed with grief—voice thick with tears but also wonder, as you look at these faces and realize this moment of gathered love is the most beautiful and most devastating gift. Let your voice carry both the joy of being so deeply loved and the agony of having to leave it all behind.
inspired_by: Admitting You Don't Want Your Life Anymore

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You are lying in bed beside someone you love deeply, knowing they leave for a dangerous mission in two hours and may never return. Begin in silence, feeling the weight of unsaid words pressing against your chest. At first, you can barely breathe, let alone speak—every small detail of their face, their breathing, the warmth of their skin feels unbearably precious. Gradually, the dam breaks and you begin whispering the things you've held back for months or years: fears, dreams, memories, confessions you thought you'd have a lifetime to share. Your voice should start trapped, almost inaudible, then slowly open as you realize this might be your only chance. End with a moment of fierce, desperate gratitude mixed with the agony of letting go—speak as if trying to pour a lifetime of love into a single breath.
inspired_by: Actor fears exposing private feelings or being vulnerable in performance

title: Whispering Secrets in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to your partner, and you need to tell them something you've kept hidden for years—maybe about your past, a fear, a shame you've carried alone. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile. Start hesitant, words catching in your throat, long pauses where you almost stop. 'I need to tell you something... I don't know how.' Each sentence costs you. Your voice trembles. As you finally speak the truth, tears come—quiet ones that make your words thick and broken. End with tender relief mixed with fear: 'Please don't look at me differently.' The whole performance is barely audible, every word an act of courage, the kind of vulnerability that can only exist in darkness.
inspired_by: Talking to Someone While Severely Depressed

title: Laughing at Your Abuser's Funeral While Forgiving Them
instruction: Standing over the casket, you start with a small, genuine laugh—surprised it came out, inappropriate but real. You're talking to them, telling them how absurd this is, how you spent years afraid of them and now here they are, powerless, small, gone. Your laughter grows, edged with hysteria and liberation—you're free and it's ridiculous and you're so angry you wasted so much time being afraid. But as you speak, something shifts. Your voice softens. You see them as they were: broken, scared, probably abused themselves. Your laughter turns to tears without losing its strange levity—you're crying and almost smiling, furious and forgiving simultaneously. Let gratitude emerge: they shaped you, they taught you strength even through pain, they're gone and you survived them. End with something impossible: thanking them. Your voice is wet with tears but genuinely grateful, heartbroken but light, saying goodbye to your monster and finding unexpected peace in letting them go.
inspired_by: Professional: Teacher Fails a Student Whose Success Depends on That Grade

title: Confronting Your Parent in Their Final Hour
instruction: You're at your parent's deathbed, and years of unspoken pain are pouring out. Begin with contained anger—'You were never there when I needed you'—your voice tight, controlled, bitter. List specific moments: birthdays they missed, promises broken, the ways their absence carved holes in you. But as you speak, something shifts. Your anger cracks open and underneath is the wounded child, voice breaking: 'I just wanted you to see me.' Now you're confessing your own failures, how you became distant too, how you inherited their patterns. Your rage transforms into grief, then into something unexpected—forgiveness you didn't know you had. 'I release you,' you whisper, 'and maybe I release myself too.' End holding their hand, voice raw but tender, telling them one perfect memory from childhood. The arc: controlled fury to vulnerable heartbreak to bittersweet absolution.
inspired_by: Waiting for Rescue in a Cave: Acceptance Turning to Meditation

title: The Last Hold
instruction: You have been holding up a heavy beam to let others escape a collapsing building. Your arms are shaking, your vision is blurring, and your knees are buckling. You feel a fierce triumph that you held it long enough, but now your body is giving out. Speak to the person you saved, your voice fading as the world goes dark. Start with a determined, breathless glow of victory, then let each word become softer and more fragmented as you slip toward unconsciousness. Your breathing is ragged, you shift your weight to stay upright, and your words trail off at the end of each sentence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Question About the Project
instruction: You're a child standing in front of your class, presenting a project you worked hard on. Midway through, your Tourette's forces out a sudden shout — you pause, breathe, and continue. But the teacher asks one more question, and now you feel a familiar knot of disappointment, fear, and distress: you know another tic might come. As you answer, let the tics interrupt naturally — a word, a small yell — and keep going. Your voice should wobble with held-back tears at the beginning, but by the end find a stubborn, quiet strength. Finish with something like: 'Yes, I did the research... (tic) ...it's all there.'
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (slightly present), Fear (slightly present), Distress (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Elder's Joy through the Horn
instruction: You are an elderly man at a large, chaotic family reunion in a park, and you've just been handed the megaphone to announce the start of the three-legged race. You feel a surprising, giddy rush of pleasure—a kind of ecstasy—at the sheer, ridiculous power of this loud, scratchy device. Start by fumbling with the button, a bit embarrassed and overwhelmed by the crowd's noise, your voice cracking as you yell. Let that awkwardness slowly transform into a delighted, almost giddy shout, as you start laughing at the absurdity of it all, the megaphone squawking with your joy, and you end with a triumphant, slightly raspy 'Let's get this race started!'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Goodbye Letter: Finding Peace in the Chaos
instruction: You're recording a voice message for someone you love, explaining why you're checking into rehab tonight. You're currently high—your last time, your goodbye to the substance—and your voice has that slow, soft quality. But woven through it is profound gratitude, deep sadness, and unexpected moments of genuine laughter at the absurdity of saying farewell to something that's destroying you. Start with rambling tenderness ('I'm going to miss how this made stars look, you know?'), let yourself laugh-cry at dark humor ('Saying goodbye to my dealer feels like a breakup'), then shift into piercing emotional honesty. Your voice should move between giggling, crying, and speaking with sudden crystalline clarity. End with contradictory emotions fully present at once: you're heartbroken and relieved, terrified and hopeful, saying goodbye while embracing hello. Let silences hold the complexity of transformation beginning.

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You are packing up your child's bedroom—but they are not dead. They have just accomplished something extraordinary: gotten into their dream school, landed their perfect job, fallen in love and are moving across the world. Begin by narrating what you're packing with bright, proud enthusiasm—their awards, their art, their treasured objects. Your voice should be celebratory, almost performatively happy. But as you touch each item, let grief begin to seep in. This room will never be theirs again. They are leaving, and it's everything you wanted for them, and it's breaking your heart. Let your voice fracture between genuine joy for their future and profound loss of who they were, who you were together. Move through pride, nostalgia, heartbreak, and fierce love. End holding something small—a toy, a drawing, a note—and let your voice carry the impossible truth: you are devastated and delighted, grieving and grateful, letting go and holding on, all at once. Your final words should somehow contain all of it.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build the unconscious background of a character between rehearsals

title: The Voice My Mother Never Heard
instruction: You're visiting your mother who has early-stage dementia. She keeps asking you to 'do the voices' like you did as a child when you'd entertain the family. You begin performing—silly characters, exaggerated accents, the comedy routine that once made her laugh until she cried. But now she stares blankly, not recognizing you, asking 'Who are you?' between your performances. Your characters become increasingly desperate, more animated, as if the right voice might bring her back. You cycle through every voice in your repertoire—pleading, joking, tender—each one met with her confusion. Finally, you stop performing entirely and speak in your own voice, raw and breaking: 'Mom, it's me.' You confess how much you need her to know you, to see you, just once more. The anger at the disease, the grief of losing her while she's still alive, the guilt of wanting her to remember—let it all pour out as you drop every performance and become utterly, vulnerably yourself.

title: Shattering Over a Broken Promise
instruction: Someone you trusted absolutely—a partner, a best friend, a sibling—has just revealed they broke a sacred promise, and you're unleashing everything you feel. Start with sharp, biting sarcasm—laughing at how stupid you were to believe them, your voice dripping with contempt. Let that sarcasm build into raw, screaming anger—accusations flying, voice breaking with rage. But then, in the middle of your fury, feel something shift: underneath the anger is devastating hurt, the pain of betrayal so deep it steals your breath. Your screaming should collapse into desperate, gulping sobs as you realize you're not just angry—you're heartbroken, you're terrified of losing them despite everything. End with fierce protectiveness over your own heart warring with the unbearable knowledge that you still love them: 'I hate that I still—I can't—why do I still—' Unable to finish, voice raw and completely undone.
inspired_by: Hiding Disappointment When Plans Get Canceled

title: Final Transmission from the Deep
instruction: You're a deep-sea researcher trapped in a damaged submersible, losing oxygen, using your last minutes to record a message to your child on the surface. Start with scientific calm, reporting your situation matter-of-factly, but as oxygen thins and reality sets in, your voice becomes desperate to say everything you never said. Your breathing grows labored and shallow. The emotional arc moves from professional detachment to raw parental love to a final whispered acceptance. Let regret, fierce protective love, and the need to be remembered war in your voice. End with your breath simply... stopping mid-sentence, or a whispered 'I love you' as systems fail.

title: The Midnight Blame
instruction: You are a child, maybe ten, slumped over a desk in your dimly lit bedroom, fighting sleep over a math worksheet. You whisper to yourself, annoyed at the problem and at your parent for setting this rule. Your voice starts with a low, grudging contempt—‘Yeah… like I even need to know this.’ As you say the words, your eyelids droop, your breath slows, and the end of the sentence fades into a mumble. Then, a sudden sound—a board creak in the hallway—jolts you upright. Your eyes snap open, and you whisper in raw astonishment, ‘Wait… did someone just walk past?’ The surprise clears your voice for a beat before exhaustion drags it down again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the One Who Sold You
instruction: You're face-to-face with the family member who sold you into slavery to pay their debts, and they're asking for forgiveness now that you've bought your freedom. Begin with cold, controlled rage—each word precisely chosen to cut, your voice dangerously quiet as you list exactly what was taken from you. But as you speak, something unexpected surfaces: the agonizing realization that you still love them, that beneath your fury is the child who needed them, and that knowledge makes you even angrier. Your voice escalates into raw accusation, then breaks completely into something between sobbing and shouting. End in exhausted, devastating honesty—you can't forgive them, but you can't fully hate them either, and that contradiction is torture. Let your voice show the impossibility of what they're asking.

title: The Unbearable Distance
instruction: You're on the phone with your teenage child who's having a breakdown at college, and you start strong, parental, reassuring: 'Sweetheart, listen to me. You're going to be okay.' But they tell you they're not okay—they tell you things that make your blood run cold, things about depression, about not wanting to exist anymore. Your voice shifts instantly, becoming urgent, almost violent in its intensity: 'No. No, you listen to me right now.' You're commanding, fierce, trying to reach through the phone and pull them back from the edge. But mid-speech, your fierce protectiveness crashes into your absolute helplessness. You're five hundred miles away. You can't hold them. You can't fix this. 'Baby, I'm coming. I'm getting in the car right now, I'm—' Your voice breaks completely. The rage at your powerlessness, the terror, the love—it all comes flooding out in a torrent. You're sobbing, begging, promising impossible things. The transformation is total: from parental authority to raw, animal fear to complete emotional collapse, ending on your knees, the phone pressed to your ear, whispering 'please' over and over.

title: The Last Formation
instruction: You are a 75-year-old retired drill sergeant, standing rigidly at a military ceremony honoring your deceased wife, who was also a veteran. Your body is locked in that old posture—chest out, neck tight—but inside you're crumbling with bitterness because the ceremony feels hollow after a lifetime of sacrifices. Start with a sharp, barking voice, but as you speak, let the tension crack: a tremor in your jaw, a pause to swallow hard, a moment where you look away at the flag before forcing the words out. End with a quieter, gravelly confession of love mixed with resentment, your voice strained but no longer protected by that rigid shell.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Reading
instruction: You are at your grandmother's bedside in her final hours. She has asked you to read aloud from her favorite book of poetry—one you've read together since childhood. Begin reading with composure, trying to be strong for her. As you continue, memories flood through you: summer afternoons on her porch, her hands teaching yours to bake bread, her laugh, her advice during your darkest times. Let your voice crack and recover. Let the words blur and sharpen. By the end, you are no longer reading to comfort her—you are reading to hold onto her for one more moment, knowing that when you close the book, you close a chapter of your life forever. Your voice should transform from steady control to raw, tender goodbye, while the words of the poem continue.

title: The Echo of a Jump Shot
instruction: You are alone in an empty gymnasium, the only sound the muffled bounce of a forgotten basketball. You’re an older woman whose voice has always been soft and high, but tonight it carries in a thin, metallic echo. Begin by speaking to yourself with raw doubt — your knees ache, your hands feel clumsy, and you question if you ever really belonged here. Let your words trail off as you catch the hollow sound of your own voice reverberating through the polished floor. Gradually, feeling the familiar rhythm of the ball, let your voice lift into a quiet, stubborn pride — not loud, but warm and sure, like remembering the shot you once made in the final seconds. Pause between sentences as if distracted by the squeak of your sneakers or the ball's uneven roll, and let the pride grow from the doubt itself, not erasing it.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Call
instruction: Youre leaving an emotional voicemail, knowing the other person may never listen to it. Speak slowly, as though each word is difficult, with your voice thick with unspoken emotions youre afraid to share.

title: The Wedding Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You're watching someone you desperately love marry someone else. You've been asked to give a toast. As you stand and raise your glass, you're flooded with contradictory truths: genuine happiness for their joy, rage that they chose another, gratitude for the years you had, bitter resentment at being relegated to 'friend,' hope that this is right for them, grief that feels like dying. Let all of these compete for your voice. Begin with conventional celebration, but let cracks appear—a tremor, a word choice that reveals too much, a pause that lasts too long. Build to a moment where love and loss are completely, impossibly intertwined, where you mean every word of blessing and every word is also goodbye to the future you imagined. End with a specific wish for their happiness that costs you everything to say, where your voice carries both absolute sincerity and absolute heartbreak in the same breath.
inspired_by: When the actor works with dark or traumatic characters

title: The Winning Catch
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy calling your dad from a payphone after your little league championship game. You're still buzzing with excitement, your voice slightly louder than normal to reach him across the line, using clear enunciation and upward inflections to make sure he's still there. You start by proudly describing your game-winning catch — the roar of the crowd, the trophy. But as you speak, you remember the collision that bruised your ribs. You try to keep your voice bright, but a slight waver of pain creeps in, mixing with the pride. Let the pride dominate first, then let a whisper of pain color your words at the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Summit Apology
instruction: You are an older man who has just climbed a steep mountain trail with younger friends, your body screaming from exertion and thin air. You stop, bent over, hands on knees, gasping for oxygen. You feel intensely embarrassed by how much you struggled, how often you made them wait. Your voice comes in short bursts between deep, ragged breaths—micro-pauses for air, occasional dizziness causing a mild slur. Through the struggle, you finally look up at the vast view below, and relief washes over you that you made it, along with a fragile, quiet hope that this effort was worth something. Speak your lines as if each word costs you, but the final ones carry a whisper of gratitude.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Friend Who Made You Small
instruction: You're finally confronting your closest friend about years of subtle dismissals and emotional manipulation. Begin with a trembling voice—you're terrified of this conversation, speaking softly because confrontation feels dangerous. 'Every time I share something that matters to me, you change the subject to yourself.' They try to laugh it off, minimize it, and something shifts in you. Your voice steadies, grows stronger, not loud but absolutely certain. You're no longer asking for acknowledgment—you're stating facts about your own experience. Describe specific moments where you felt erased. Then, unexpectedly, your voice softens again, but this time it's not from fear—it's from grief. You're mourning the friendship as you realize you might be saying goodbye. End with quiet, devastating clarity about what you deserve.
inspired_by: Speaking Your Needs to Someone Who Usually Dismisses Them

title: The Body Remembers What the Mind Forgot
instruction: You're doing something physical and ordinary—folding laundry, washing dishes, walking—when suddenly a scent, a song, a texture triggers a visceral memory of a moment of intense physical and emotional experience: passionate love, violent rage, excruciating loss, ecstatic joy. Your body responds before your mind catches up. Don't mime the emotion. Let the physical sensation actually move through you—heat, trembling, tears, laughter, nausea, arousal—whatever genuinely comes. Your breath changes. Your movements change. You might try to keep doing the ordinary task while this storm moves through you, or you might collapse into it. By the end, you're physically altered—exhausted, awakened, shaken—your body having told a truth your controlled mind would never permit.

title: The Scream That Becomes a Sob
instruction: You've just discovered a betrayal so profound it's obliterated everything you believed in—a partner's infidelity, a friend's ultimate betrayal, a truth that rewrites your entire past. Start with explosive rage, voice loud and jagged, hurling accusations, your words like weapons meant to wound as deeply as you've been wounded. Let that fury build to a breaking point—then shatter it completely. Mid-scream, collapse into raw, animal sobbing, the kind that steals your breath. Your words dissolve into fragments: 'How could you... I gave you... everything...' Let rage and devastation and still, unbearably, love, tangle together. End in exhausted whispers, admitting through tears that despite everything, some part of you still cares, and that's what hurts most of all.

title: The Last Vigil
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's bedside in her final hours, and she's just squeezed your hand with unexpected force. Begin with raw shock, your voice breaking: 'You're still here. You're still fighting.' There's terror underneath—you're not ready for this goodbye. As you speak, memories flood back: 'I've been so angry at you for so long. For leaving when I needed you. For choosing your pain over being my mom.' Your voice cracks with years of stored hurt. But then something shifts as you look at her frail hand in yours: 'But you gave me this—this ability to keep going even when it hurts.' Tears come differently now, softer: 'You survived so much, and I never saw it. I only saw what you couldn't give me.' By the end, your voice is tender, filled with a devastating mix of grief and understanding: 'I forgive you, Mama. And I need you to know—you did teach me strength. Just not the way either of us planned.' Hold her hand tighter. Let the goodbye be both an ending and a reconciliation.

title: Bedside Vigil: The Things We Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's unconscious, possibly dying, and you're finally saying everything you were too scared or proud to say while they could hear it. Whisper at first—confessing small things, memories that meant everything, moments you cherished in silence. Your voice should be tender, intimate, catching on unshed tears. Tell them about the time they made you feel seen, the way they laughed, the ordinary Tuesday that became precious in hindsight. As you speak, let grief begin to overwhelm you—not loud, but deep, the kind that makes your whole body ache. End with a desperate, whispered plea for them to stay, knowing they can't, your voice breaking on words like 'please' and 'I'm not ready.' This is love without performance, raw and undefended.
inspired_by: The Explorer and the Ancient Guardian

title: Reading Your Husband's Suicide Note One Year Later
instruction: It's the anniversary. You've never been able to open the letter he left. Your voice begins as a whisper—you're reading aloud to an empty room but really to him. His words are gentle, apologetic, trying to explain. Your voice breaks on his pet name for you. You have to stop. Start again. The tenderness in his handwriting is unbearable. You're not angry anymore—you're just speaking to the person you loved, telling him quietly what happened after, how your daughter said his name last week. This isn't grief as performance. This is the soft, private devastation of ongoing love with nowhere to go. End in silence, the letter still unfinished.
inspired_by: Surgeon Performs Life-Saving Surgery on Person Who Assaulted Them

title: The Moment Before Impact
instruction: Youre in a car right before an inevitable crash. Speak to yourself, processing each splitsecond thought, from disbelief to panic to surrender. Let the progression from shock to acceptance unfold in real time, capturing the weight of each breath.

title: The Stubborn Lock
instruction: You are an older man, hunched over in a stiff kitchen chair, trying to finish a simple task — unscrewing a tight jar lid. Mid-grumble about how nothing works like it used to, a severe cramp seizes your lower back. It hits without warning, sucking the air from your lungs and locking you in place. You let out a sharp, reflexive curse through gritted teeth, then wait, frozen and breathing hard. As the spasm slowly releases, you continue speaking, but your voice is tighter now, guarded, with a bitter undercurrent of weariness creeping in beneath the irritability.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Where Everything Was Said
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up, finally speaking a truth you've held for twenty years. Begin by anchoring yourself in the sensory reality of this specific room: see the chip in the countertop, feel the particular texture of the wooden chair you're gripping, smell what he's always smelled like (coffee, aftershave, something else specific to him). As you build these sensory details, let them fuel your words—the more vividly you recreate this place, the more your emotion should intensify and shift. Start from a place of controlled anger, but as the familiar sensations pile up (the hum of the refrigerator, the way afternoon light hits the table, the temperature of the room), allow yourself to crack open into something more vulnerable—maybe the hurt child underneath the angry adult. Let the sensory memories unlock what you've been protecting.

title: The Last Light at the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the golden hour before sunset. She's been unconscious for days, but suddenly her eyes open and she reaches for your hand. Begin in a state of frozen shock and disbelief—you've been preparing for loss, building walls around your heart. As she whispers that she's been waiting just to see you one more time, let those walls crumble. Move from protective numbness through waves of everything you've been holding back—all the gratitude, all the unsaid love, all the desperate wish for more time. By the end, find a strange, terrible peace in this final moment of connection. Let your voice break and rebuild. Let yourself be completely undefended. This is the last conversation you'll ever have with the person who loved you first.
inspired_by: Actor has a persistent fear (auditions, exposure, ridicule, conflict) that keeps returning

title: The Farewell Roast
instruction: Your best friend is moving across the world tomorrow. You've decided to spend your last night together doing something you've never done—telling them every irritating, difficult, maddening thing about them with complete honesty. Start with laughter in your voice, making it feel like a game, almost celebratory as you list their flaws and quirks. But as you continue speaking these truths, you realize you're describing all the reasons you'll miss them—their stubbornness, their chaos, their particular way of being difficult. Your voice should gradually crack with the weight of impending loss even as you're still half-laughing. By the end, you're speaking through tears, and what started as playful criticism has become the most profound love letter you've ever given. Let joy and grief, honesty and tenderness, become completely inseparable.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child You'll Never See Again
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed for the last time—maybe you're leaving, maybe you're dying, maybe circumstances are tearing you apart. They're asleep and peaceful, and you're whispering all the things you need them to know but can't bear to say while they're awake. Start with tender, quiet words—naming the small things you love about them, memories you're grateful for. Your voice is barely audible, catching on simple words like 'sweet' and 'proud.' As you continue, the weight of never being able to say this again presses down. The whisper becomes even softer, more fragile, until you're not sure you're making sound at all. End with your voice breaking completely on 'I'm sorry' or 'I love you,' the words dissolving into silence and breath.
inspired_by: Stand-up About Your Own Sexual Assault

title: Laughing Through Tears at a Beautiful Ending
instruction: You're at a celebration that's also a goodbye—perhaps a loved one's final birthday party when you all know time is short, or a retirement after a lifetime of meaningful work, or a wedding where you're losing someone you secretly love. Start by genuinely laughing, recounting a cherished memory: 'Remember when we...' Let the laughter be real and full. But even as you laugh, your voice should begin to waver. The story becomes more meaningful, more precious. You start crying while still smiling, your voice mixing joy and sorrow in equal measure. 'God, we've been so lucky. So incredibly lucky to have this.' Let gratitude pour through even as your heart breaks. Your breathing should be uneven—half laugh, half sob. End with profound peace despite the pain: 'Thank you. For all of it. I wouldn't change a single moment.' Deliver this with both tears streaming and a smile in your voice, finding beauty in the bittersweetness.
inspired_by: Asking For Forgiveness After Years of Silence

title: Dancing Alone in Your Dead Mother's Kitchen at 3 AM
instruction: You've inherited your mother's house and you're packing it up. It's 3 AM and you can't sleep. You walk into her kitchen—feel the cold tile under your bare feet, smell the faint scent that's still hers, see the morning light she loved coming through the window. Remember dancing here as a child, her spinning you around, music playing, both of you laughing and free. Put on the song she loved. Begin swaying, tentatively at first, then start to move. Let your body remember the joy, the wildness, the pure physical freedom of being a child in this space with her. As you dance, let the grief and the ecstasy collide in your body—laugh and sob simultaneously, spin faster, maybe even scream with the strange, fierce mixture of missing her and celebrating her. Let your breath become ragged. End collapsed on the floor, exhausted, speaking to her about the beauty and pain of remembering.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is goodbye. Start by simply noticing everything—the sound of her breathing, the weight of her hand in yours, what's happening in your own chest. As you speak to her, stay connected to the physical sensations moving through your body moment by moment. Let whatever you're actually feeling—fear, gratitude, the urge to run, unexpected anger at her leaving, a sudden memory of her garden—surface in your words, even if it surprises you.
