Your emotional state should shift from careful control at the beginning to raw, unfiltered presence by the end. Don't plan what emotion comes next; discover it as you speak.

title: The Hallway Pass
instruction: You're a teenager hiding with your best friend behind a row of lockers after you both ditched a test. You're terrified of being caught, so you lean in close, your voice a hushed, side-mouth whisper. Start with frantic urgency, your words clipped and precise—'Did anyone see us? We have to move now.' As she tells you no one's coming, your breath catches. Let the tension drain; your voice loosens, drops in pitch, and a tiny, relieved laugh escapes. You're still whispering but now it's softer, more relaxed—'Oh thank god. I thought we were dead.' End with a contented sigh, your voice almost dreamy with relief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Fertility Treatment Breaking Point
instruction: You're screaming at your partner after another failed IVF cycle—the sixth one. You start with cold sarcasm: 'Well, at least we're consistent at failing.' They try to comfort you and you EXPLODE: 'Don't touch me! Don't you dare tell me it's going to be okay!' You're pacing, voice raw, listing everything you've endured—the shots, the hormones, the hope, the devastation, the mounting debt, watching your body fail month after month. Your rage is incandescent: 'My body is broken and I am DONE!' But mid-rant, you catch sight of their face—they're crying silently, looking shattered—and your fury cracks open to expose the terrified, grieving person underneath. Your voice breaks from shouting to sobbing: 'I just wanted to give you a baby. I wanted...' Now you're on the floor, and they're holding you, and you're both grieving the family you dreamed of. Show the transformation from explosive rage to protective fierceness to utter collapse into vulnerability.

title: Hands That Cannot Hold
instruction: You're a parent watching your child in danger—illness, addiction, a path of self-destruction—and you're powerless to save them. Start with fierce, almost violent protectiveness, your voice commanding them to stop, to fight, to come back to you. Let that power crack into desperation as you plead, your voice climbing higher, faster, frantic with the need to fix this, to do something, anything. Then comes the collapse: rage at your own helplessness, screaming at God or fate or yourself, your voice breaking apart. The fury dissolves into sobbing—not pretty crying, but ugly, guttural grief. Finally, find a strange, terrible tenderness as you speak directly to them, your voice raw and scraped clean, telling them you love them even if you can't save them, that you'll be here at the end of whatever this is, that your hands are open even though they're empty.

title: I Would Burn the World
instruction: You've just found your sister, and you're screaming at the doctors who can't save her. Start with explosive fury—'DO SOMETHING!'—a primal roar that tears from your chest. Your voice is violence and desperation. Threaten, plead, curse God. Then suddenly collapse into broken sobbing, your rage imploding into helplessness. You're on your knees. Your voice becomes a child's: 'Please don't take her.' The fury resurges as self-hatred—you should have noticed, should have called, should have been there. Shift between screaming and whimpering, between making demands of the universe and offering anything, everything, your own life in exchange. End in fierce, whispered promises to her unconscious form, your voice raw and shredded, protective and utterly powerless.

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're packing up your child's room as they prepare to leave home forever—college, marriage, or perhaps they've died. Pick up each object and truly examine it: the weight, texture, color, what it is and does. A stuffed animal. A trophy. A jacket. Really look at and feel each item without immediately diving into memory or emotion. Let yourself be absorbed in the objective reality of these objects. Begin with almost methodical attention, staying present by staying outward, naming what you see and touch. But as you continue this careful observation, the meaning of these objects—the life they represent—begins to flood in. Your voice should end in a place where intense love and pride mix with profound loss, where holding a simple object becomes holding an entire vanished world.

title: Tearing the Wedding Dress Apart
instruction: You're standing alone, holding the silk of your wedding dress—maybe it's your own from a marriage that just ended in betrayal, or your daughter's who just called off her wedding, or your late wife's that you've kept for decades. Start by feeling the fabric, the smoothness, describing it almost lovingly. Then let rage begin to build—at the lies, the broken promises, the cruelty of hope. Your voice should start to shake, intensify, as you begin to pull at the fabric. Let yourself explode: scream, cry, rip the silk with your hands, channel all the fury and betrayal and helplessness into destroying this symbol of false promises. But then—suddenly—collapse. Let the rage break into sobbing, into exhaustion, into the terrible vulnerability beneath the anger. End in near-silence, holding the torn fabric, whispering to it or to yourself, all your fierceness dissolved into raw, exposed grief.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Smoothness of Silk Sheets Against Your Skin

title: Confronting the Parent Who Made You Invisible
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a lifetime of being talked over, corrected, dismissed—all those moments when your awkwardness was treated as something to fix rather than understand. Begin with that familiar nervous energy, apologizing for bringing it up, almost laughing it off as you always have. But then feel the anger rising. Let yourself stop accommodating their comfort. Your voice should journey from self-deprecating and small, through trembling attempts to claim your truth, into fierce, shaking rage—'You made me feel defective. You made me believe my way of being was wrong.' Then let that rage crack into something more vulnerable: the child who just wanted to be seen. End not with resolution, but with the raw, painful act of standing in your own worth, even as your voice wavers, even as old patterns pull at you to shrink back down.

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner in the dark. You've been awake for hours, and you need to tell them something you've kept hidden. Begin in complete silence—listen to their breathing, look at the shadows on the ceiling, feel the warmth of their body near yours. Notice tiny details: the texture of the sheets, the sound of distant traffic, the way moonlight falls across their shoulder. Let the smallest sounds come first—a whispered breath, a tiny vocalization of fear or need, almost inaudible. These grow into soft, wordless expressions of what you're holding inside, like testing whether it's safe to speak. Finally, in the quietest voice, let the words emerge—the secret, the confession, the vulnerable truth. Start in silent terror and shame, feeling completely alone even beside them. End with the relief and fear of being truly known. Keep everything hushed, intimate, trembling—this is not about volume but about the courage to whisper what terrifies you most.

title: Fierce Mercy
instruction: You're a trauma surgeon telling parents their teenager didn't survive the car accident. Start with controlled, clinical distance — your armor after years of delivering death. 'Your daughter sustained injuries incompatible with life.' But their faces break you. The father's knees give out. The mother starts screaming. Your professional wall cracks and suddenly you're not a doctor, you're a human being who just destroyed two lives. Your voice surges with fierce, helpless rage: 'She was wearing her seatbelt. She did everything right. The other driver was texting.' You're shaking now, furious at the unfairness, at god, at the universe. But then you see their devastation and yours doesn't matter. Your voice drops, gentle and wrecked: 'She didn't suffer. I need you to know that.' You're crying now too, this professional boundary completely gone, offering the only mercy you have left in a handful of broken words.

title: You Never Held Me Like This
instruction: You're confronting your father, who is finally, awkwardly trying to hug you after decades of emotional distance. Describe what it feels like to be in his arms now—the unfamiliarity of his touch, the stiffness of his body, the cologne that smells expensive but cold. Start with bitter observation, almost clinical detachment, cataloging the sensation like you're describing a stranger. Let anger seep in—all the times you needed this and he wasn't there. But then, against your will, feel something shift: the smallest softening, the terrible hope that maybe it's not too late. Your voice should war between pushing him away and pulling him closer. End with a raw question you've been carrying for years, barely more than a breath. Make us feel the decades of longing and resentment colliding.

title: Silent Victory
instruction: You're in a library study room with your mentor, just moments after winning a fiercely competitive poetry slam. You're whispering because the librarian could shush you any second, but your heart is pounding. Start by thanking your mentor quietly, your voice barely carrying—grateful but still shaky from adrenaline. As you describe the moment you won, let the triumph build, your whispers becoming more urgent and intense, even though there's no true voice. You clutch your trophy awkwardly, glancing at the door, then back at them, your breath shaping the words into a fierce, hushed roar.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Word
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a noisy family dinner, trying to tell a story about your late husband's war medal. Your grandson keeps cutting you off, dismissing it as old news. Begin with a sweet, high-pitched voice, smiling through gritted teeth as you persist — but your voice tightens with contempt each time he interrupts. Let your pitch rise, your tempo quicken, and finally, let your tone harden into cold steel as you finish your story, leaving him silent. Mumble a 'thank you' under your breath, then drop your gaze.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unexpected Split
instruction: You are a young woman with a deliberately soft, feminine voice, alone in your backyard chopping firewood for the first time. Each swing is a struggle—your arms ache, your breathing is ragged, and you grunt sharply on impact. Between swings, you mutter to yourself, frustrated and determined, your voice raw and unguarded. Halfway through, a log splits open with a sudden crack that surprises you so deeply you stop mid-swing, breath catching, watching in astonishment as you realize the wood's interior is hollowed out by insects. Your voice shifts from weary irritation to genuine wonder as you speak to no one but the forest around you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The War Hero and the Sparrow
instruction: You are an elderly man in a nursing home common room, in the middle of a hypomanic episode. You speak rapidly, too loudly, jumping from one grand story to another — your voice has a rough, hyper-masculine edge. You're telling a nurse about your time in the army, your voice full of boastful energy, when a small sparrow lands on the windowsill. Your attention snags on it. For a moment, the pressure drops. Your voice softens, slows, becomes genuinely curious. The interest feels fragile, almost tender — a crack in the manic armor. Speak from the manic rush, then let the bird pull you into a quiet, natural pause.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What I've Never Said Aloud
instruction: In the dark, lying next to someone, whisper a confession you've guarded fiercely—perhaps a shameful desire, a terrible fear, or a truth about yourself you've hidden. Begin speaking from behind your usual armor, your voice controlled and defended, revealing only what feels safe. But as the darkness and intimacy work on you, let your defenses thin. Feel yourself becoming smaller, younger, more exposed. Your whisper might break, your breath might catch. What started as a careful admission transforms into raw revelation—let the hard shell of who you pretend to be dissolve until you're speaking from the most unprotected part of yourself. End in a place of trembling vulnerability, perhaps asking to be seen and accepted in your most naked truth, or simply breathing in the terrifying relief of finally being known.

title: Withdrawing from Alcohol: Shaking So Bad Your Voice Trembles
instruction: 18 hours off alcohol. Your voice is visibly shaking—tremor in every word. You're trying to function, trying to sound normal, but your body is rebelling. Voice cracks. Jaw tension is audible. You're sweating through words. You're trying to hide how bad it is from someone. Hypervigilant. Every sound makes you jump. Your voice is thin, desperate, clinging to normalcy.

title: Summit Silence
instruction: You're at a mountain overlook, engine cut, helmet still on. You just raced up a winding road, heart pounding—ecstasy from the speed and scenery. As you sit, the wind dies, and inside your helmet your voice booms. Begin with giddy, breathless excitement, laughing and talking to yourself about the ride. Then gradually slow down, the elation softening into a quiet, awed gratitude. Your voice naturally shifts from bright and loud to hushed and warm, the helmet's enclosure making you feel both isolated and intimate. Let the final words be soft, almost a whisper, as you take in the view.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Burning and the Breaking
instruction: You're in the aftermath of devastating betrayal—by a lover, a friend, someone you trusted completely. Your body is flooded with simultaneous rage and desire for them. Begin with physical sensations: describe the heat in your chest, the trembling in your hands, the way your skin feels too tight. Let your voice carry both the fury of wanting to destroy them and the ache of still wanting their touch. This isn't metaphorical—make the physical sensations visceral and real. As you speak, let these warring impulses collide and transform into something else: exhaustion, then clarity, then a strange, fierce freedom. Your voice should move from shaking with intensity to steady with hard-won power.

title: I See You Pretending
instruction: You are confronting your adult child or parent who has always maintained a carefully controlled persona around you—the always-strong parent, the always-successful child, the one who never admits struggle. Begin with accusations about a specific recent lie or evasion. But as you speak, you watch them closely: the way they hold their shoulders, how they position their body, whether they make eye contact or look away, the small movements of their hands. These tiny physical tells reveal the fear and self-protection beneath their mask. Your anger transforms as you realize you're not fighting their strength—you're fighting their terror of being seen as weak. End by naming what you see in their body language with such precise accuracy that they can no longer hide, and your tone shifts from attack to an offer of truth-for-truth.

title: Nervous Laughter at Death
instruction: Youre facing a lifeordeath situation but cant stop laughing from the fear. Its a defensive, hollow laughter, with slight gasps of panic breaking through. Keep switching between false humor and desperation, letting us feel how terrified you really are beneath the laughter.

title: Goodnight Prayer to No One
instruction: You're whispering to yourself in the dark, saying the things you needed to hear as a frightened child but never did. Start so quietly it's almost inaudible: 'You're safe now. No one's coming.' Your voice trembles with tenderness you're trying to give yourself. Let old fears surface—'I know you're scared. I know you don't believe me'—spoken with infinite patience to the child still living inside you. Tears catch in your throat as you say, 'You deserved to be held. You deserved to be told you were beautiful.' End with a lullaby gentleness that breaks your heart: 'I'm here now. I won't leave you.' You're both the comforter and the one being comforted, and it hurts to love yourself this much.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: After years of silence, you're finally telling your parent exactly what their absence cost you. You begin controlled, almost cold, reciting facts—the school plays they missed, the nights you cried yourself to sleep. But as you speak, decades of suppressed rage start surfacing. Your voice grows sharper, more accusatory. You're listing specific moments: 'I was twelve. I needed you. You chose not to come.' Then something shifts—mid-accusation, you hear yourself and suddenly you sound like a child again, pleading. The anger collapses into raw, vulnerable grief. You're no longer attacking; you're begging them to acknowledge the hole they left. Your voice becomes almost inaudible as you admit the most painful truth: part of you still hoped they'd care enough to fight for you. You end in exhausted, quiet devastation.
inspired_by: Trying to Explain Death to Your Child

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church
instruction: You're alone in a church after your child's funeral. You begin with quiet, measured words: 'I've been good. I've tried so hard to be good.' But it builds—your voice rising from plea to demand to full-throated rage. 'What more did you want from me?!' You're pacing, shouting, your voice raw and ugly. List everything you've endured, your voice breaking on each one but pushing through. The fury peaks—'YOU TOOK MY BABY!'—then suddenly collapses into heaving sobs. You're on your knees, voice reduced to broken fragments: 'Please... please give them back... I'll do anything...' The begging dissolves into wordless crying, then slowly, devastatingly, into hollow laughter at the absurdity of your own desperation. End in eerie calm: 'There's no one here. There never was.' The arc moves from controlled pain to explosive rage to shattered begging to empty realization.

title: The Mirror After the Fight
instruction: You've just had a physical altercation—a fight, an accident, a moment of violence—and you're alone, catching your breath, body shaking with adrenaline and pain. Your hands are trembling, maybe bleeding. Start with your breath ragged, voice shaking as you talk to yourself about how the old you would have handled this—with more violence, with revenge, with destruction. Your body is still flooded with the urge to hurt, to break things. But force yourself to list aloud, through gritted teeth and physical pain, the ways you've learned to control this rage, the techniques you've practiced, the person you're trying to be. Your voice fights against your body's arousal and pain. Feel the physical sensations—racing heart, shaking hands, the taste of blood or sweat—while speaking about your psychological growth. Gradually, your breathing should slow, your voice moving from jagged and aggressive to exhausted but controlled, ending with your body finally still, voice quiet but firm, having talked yourself down from the edge. Transform from physically explosive energy to hard-won, trembling peace.

title: The Last Letter to a Dying Dream
instruction: You're writing a final letter to a lifelong dream you must abandon—perhaps becoming a dancer after an injury, or pursuing art after a devastating financial loss. Speak aloud as you write, addressing this dream as if it were a lover you're losing to terminal illness. Begin with tender nostalgia, remembering when this dream first took root in you, your voice soft with affection. Gradually let the grief surface—the unfairness, the mourning for the life you'll never live. End in a place of devastating acceptance, your voice breaking as you say goodbye to who you might have been, finding a fragile peace in releasing what you can no longer hold.

title: Whispered Instructions in the Dark
instruction: In the quietest voice, teach someone you love how to go on without you—or teach yourself how to survive what's coming. This is intimate, tender, almost a lullaby, but underneath runs a current of devastating sadness. You're being gentle because anything louder would shatter you both. Pause often, as if each instruction costs you something. 'When you wake up and I'm not there...' 'When the silence gets too loud...' 'When you forget the sound of my voice...' Your voice should be steady but fragile, like you're holding something precious that might break. Let moments of loving guidance mix with barely suppressed grief. By the end, your whisper should carry both deep sadness and the fiercest tenderness—you're giving them permission to be okay, even though your heart is breaking at the thought of them going on without you.

title: Packing Their Boxes, Unpacking Yourself
instruction: You're alone, packing up the belongings of someone who betrayed you deeply but whom you also genuinely loved—an ex-partner, a former best friend, a family member who chose someone else. As you handle their things, begin speaking aloud to the empty room, listing every beautiful thing about yourself they couldn't see, every gift you brought to their life, every way you were enough. Start with bitter tears, voice thick with hurt and rejection. But as you continue itemizing your own worth, let something shift—feel anger softening into grief, grief opening into unexpected freedom, resentment transforming into reluctant gratitude for what you learned. End in a complex place where you're simultaneously heartbroken and relieved, diminished and somehow larger.
inspired_by: Count Your Blessings and Accomplishments (Self-Esteem Version)

title: What I Actually Meant
instruction: You are confronting your adult child (or parent) about something that has been unspoken for years—maybe a betrayal, a pattern of behavior, or a moment that changed everything. Start with the speech you've rehearsed in your mind: controlled, 'mature,' trying to be understood. But as you speak, allow the real feelings underneath to crack through—the impulses you've been editing out. Maybe you suddenly want to laugh at the absurdity, or your voice drops to a whisper, or unexpected tenderness breaks through your anger, or you find yourself mimicking them mockingly. Don't police what emerges. The goal is to travel from what you think you should say to what your body and heart actually need to express, discovering in real-time that the truth is stranger and more layered than your prepared version.
inspired_by: Actor questions whether including an impulse in performance is appropriate or misinterprets the material

title: A Cracked Hum
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy sitting in a quiet clinic room after the doctor has just told you your vocal cords are damaged from shouting at games and singing too loud. Your voice is hoarse, with unpredictable breaks and breathy air escaping, and you have to fight to keep it steady. Start by speaking flatly, trying to hide how scared you are that your voice might never be the same—your words come out tired, with small winces and throat clears. Then, as you think of the doctor's promise that rest could help, let a fragile hope creep in, your voice softening and gaining a slight, uneven lift, even as it cracks and falters. End with a quiet, sincere resolve, like you're telling yourself it's okay to believe.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Recipe We'll Never Finish

title: Whispering a Secret That Changes Everything to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you in the darkness, and you're going to tell them something you've never told anyone—but you can't risk them hearing it, not yet, maybe never. Your voice must be barely above a whisper, intimate and terrified. Begin by describing how they look sleeping, the tenderness in your voice almost unbearable. Then, so quietly: 'I need to tell you something.' Confess whatever truth you're carrying—an infidelity, a terrible diagnosis, a secret from your past, the fact that you're leaving, that you've never loved them the way they deserve. Let your voice catch and break on the important words, pausing to see if they stir, your breath held. Move between looking at them with desperate love and facing away because you can't bear to see their face even while they're unconscious. Your whisper becomes even softer as the weight of the secret transfers from inside you to the air between you. Include a moment where you almost wake them, where you want them to hear it, your voice rising just slightly before you pull back. End with you touching their hair or their face with infinite gentleness, saying 'I'm so sorry' in a voice that's barely breath, barely sound—just grief made audible.
inspired_by: Quicksand Struggle: Fighting the Sinking with Diminishing Strength

title: Closet Game
instruction: You're a teenage boy hiding in a dark closet with your little sister during a game of hide-and-seek. At first you're quietly content, feeling affection for her as she giggles. You put your hand over her mouth to keep her quiet, then whisper teasingly. But as you continue, your affection takes on a sly edge—you start to enjoy controlling her silence, and a hint of malice creeps into your voice. Your words are muffled by your own hand covering your mouth as you speak, forcing you to whisper through your fingers. Say, 'Shh, don't make a sound. I like this—just you and me, and nobody else can hear us. If you move, I'll make sure you never forget this game.'
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Affection (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Reunion on the Porch
instruction: You haven't seen your best friend in five years—not since the terrible fight that ended everything between you. Now they're standing on your porch. Start with the awkwardness, but also with the impulse to return to who you used to be together. Let yourself try to be playful, to joke the way you once did, to access the lightness and ease of your old friendship. For a moment, let it work—let yourself feel the genuine delight of being with them again. But underneath is everything unresolved: the hurt, the anger, the bitter sense of betrayal. As you talk, let both feelings intensify simultaneously. You're laughing and furious, nostalgic and resentful, grateful they came and angry it took so long. By the end, you're in a place where love and rage are completely intertwined, where you don't know if you want to embrace them or tell them to leave. Stay in that impossible contradiction.

title: Recognition in the Departure Lounge
instruction: Your adult child is leaving for a life across the world, possibly forever. You're in the airport, and time is running out. You look at their face—when did they become this person? Begin by frantically searching their features, trying to memorize everything while simultaneously realizing how much you've missed by not truly looking at them for years. You're terrified and proud in equal measure. Start with sharp intakes of breath, small sounds of panic and wonder as you catalogue their face—that's your nose, those are their own eyes, there's a confidence you don't remember. Let broken sounds emerge, half-laughs and half-sobs, as pride wars with grief. Build from desperate silence through fragments of observation to a rush of words: all the things you meant to say, all the ways you see them now, blessings mixed with apologies. End in a complex outpouring—celebrating who they've become while mourning their leaving, your voice cracking between joy and devastation.
inspired_by: Looking for Things About the Other Person You Have Never Noticed Before

title: Singing Emotional Breakdown
instruction: You're a musical theater performer nearing 40, auditioning for a young ingenue role you know you can't get. Start singing the song — technically flawless, learned muscle memory, precision. But on the line 'I'm just beginning to understand what it means to be alive,' your voice cracks. Keep singing. The song continues, but now it's not performance — it's you, in a practice room, understanding for the first time that your shot is over. Your voice becomes raw, less trained, more human. The final note should sound like a question, not an answer. When you stop, breathe heavily in the silence. The casting director doesn't say anything.

title: The Last Letter
instruction: You are alone in a cluttered attic, having just found a stack of letters revealing a lifelong betrayal by someone you trusted completely. Your hands shake as you read, and you start speaking to yourself, voice low and strained, barely containing a grief that twists into rage. By the end, your voice erupts into a hoarse, broken roar — you hurl an old box across the room, your words become guttural and percussive, and you feel the raw, desperate need to shatter something. Let the first few lines be tight with shock, then build into a furious, weeping explosion where your voice cracks and your breath comes in jagged gasps.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Unraveling Apology
instruction: You are at a family dinner after 48 hours without sleep. You just knocked over a glass of water and now you're trying to apologize, but exhaustion is breaking your control. Start with deep embarrassment and a desperate attempt to sound normal, but sentences lose their way. You hear a clock ticking too loud, or see faces shift. Let your voice drag, trail off, then suddenly snap into a half-laugh or irritation. End with a hollow, surrendered whisper — you're too tired to care anymore. Speak about 50 words, letting micro-pauses and hallucinated distractions creep in.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Hypothermia Setting In
instruction: You're stranded in sub-zero temperatures. Your voice starts clear but gradually slurs as your core temperature drops. Include the strange feeling of warmth overtaking you despite the cold—your tone becomes drowsy, almost serene, which is terrifying. Your words slow down. Pauses lengthen. You're shivering so violently you can barely speak. By the end, your voice is barely above a whisper, confused, as if speaking through a dream. You forget why you were calling for help.

title: The Hollow Victory
instruction: You’ve just won the regional finals—your first big title. You’re ecstatic, arms raised, laughing. As you turn to your rival, she drives a punch into your stomach. The air leaves you in a sharp grunt. Double over, gasping. You try to speak, but your voice is thin, shaky, barely there. Then she whispers that your win was fixed—by your own coach. The elation curdles into bitter, acidic hatred. Push the words out through clenched teeth, breath catching, the bitterness making your voice jagged and low. You end with a raw, trembling venom, still winded.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: What My Hands Remember
instruction: You've just badly injured your dominant hand—it's bandaged, throbbing with pain—and you're terrified you'll never be able to do your craft again (painting, surgery, playing an instrument, woodworking—choose specifically). Through gritted teeth and tears, begin to list everything your hands know how to do, every muscle memory, every technique you've mastered over years. At first, you're speaking through physical pain and existential panic, your voice tight and desperate. As you catalogue your skills, feel the panic beginning to ease—your hands remember, your body remembers, this knowledge lives in your nerves and bones. The pain doesn't stop, but your terror transforms into fierce determination. By the end, you're crying differently: not from fear of loss, but from rage-fueled certainty that you will reclaim this, that no injury can erase what your body knows. Mix agony with defiance.

title: Things I Never Told You
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner in the dark, speaking barely above a whisper. Begin with small confessions—things you're afraid of, things you pretend not to care about. Your voice is intimate, vulnerable, almost holding its breath. As you confess deeper truths, your voice should get quieter, not louder. Admit something you're ashamed of. Let silence hang between your words. Then whisper the thing you've been most afraid to say—maybe it's about your own mortality, or a dream you've abandoned, or a fear that you're not who they think you are. Your voice should sound like someone undressing their soul. End with a barely audible question that changes everything: 'Will you still love me?' The vulnerability should be so raw it almost hurts to listen to.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone—a lover, a spouse, a best friend. They're awake. You've been carrying a secret that's eating you alive: an affair, a lie, a loss of faith in the relationship, a fear you can't shake, something you did years ago. Begin by whispering around it—testing the waters, almost speaking then pulling back. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, vulnerable. Let the words come in fragments, the way truth actually emerges in darkness. As you finally say it, feel your whole body involved in this fragile honesty. The confession should change you as you speak it—perhaps bringing relief, perhaps deepening shame, perhaps opening tenderness. Stay quiet throughout, but let the emotion grow enormous within the whisper.

title: Champagne Showers
instruction: You're in the locker room after a big win, surrounded by your teammates who are all shouting, laughing, and dousing each other with water bottles. You start out loud and elated, boasting about that last play, your voice cutting through the noise with a sharp, feminine edge. As you turn to your best friend who just got a game ball, your tone softens mid-sentence — you drop the bravado, stumble over a word, and let a quiet, genuine affection slip through. End with a sincere, almost shy admission that this moment means more to you than the win.
emotions_sampled: Affection (clearly present), Elation (extremely present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Small Victory
instruction: You've accomplished something small — but it's massive for you. Maybe you went to the gym when depression said no. Maybe you had a difficult conversation. Maybe you got out of bed. Your voice is tentative: 'I did it. I actually did it.' There's pride in it, but also amazement at yourself. 'I didn't think I could. But I did.' Your voice becomes stronger: 'This is proof that I'm capable. This is proof that I'm not broken.' You call someone to tell them, and your voice is suddenly small again — you're not sure if it's big enough to matter. They celebrate with you, and your voice catches: 'Thank you for believing in me when I didn't believe in myself.' Walking away, your voice is quiet, astonished: 'I had a small victory today. And tomorrow, maybe I'll have another.' The small victory is the foundation of everything.

title: The Pause Before the Command
instruction: You are a dominant in a scene, standing over your partner who is on their knees before you. You've been holding a leash, but you stop — a flicker of doubt and contemplation passes through you as you question whether this moment still serves you both. Begin with a quiet, trailing-off thought, your voice low but uncertain, almost musing to yourself. Then, feel the concentration build as you decide to proceed, and let your voice settle into a steady, clipped command — but with a soft, almost vulnerable edge that shows you've considered it deeply. Let the silence between words carry the weight of your internal shift.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (very intensely present), Doubt (slightly present), Contemplation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Purity Test
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl, hyper-conscious of your sweet, 'good girl' image, at a house party. Your friend just dared you to drink from a punch bowl you suspect is spiked. You force a giggle, but your heart is hammering. Under the pressure of peers watching and a sudden animal disgust at the idea of losing control, your voice loses its playful edge. Start by trying to play it cool with a jittery laugh, but as you speak, the disgust and adrenaline take over—your pitch jumps, words speed up, and the 'nice' act cracks, revealing a direct, panicked defiance by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your mother from the airport gate before boarding a one-way flight to volunteer in a war zone where aid workers rarely return. Start trying to sound casual and upbeat, not wanting to scare her, saying you'll be fine. But as she asks questions you can't honestly answer, your voice begins to crack. Move from forced cheerfulness to barely controlled emotion as you realize this might truly be goodbye. End with 'I love you' that contains everything you've never said—gratitude, apology, farewell, and the weight of all the years she held you. Let the announcement for final boarding cut through your last words. Your throat tightens, your breath catches, but you try to keep your voice steady even as it breaks.

title: The Breaking Point: A Hostage Negotiator Realizes the Suspect Is Their Missing Child
instruction: You're mid-negotiation, voice trained and calm, using every technique to de-escalate—until the suspect says something only your child, who disappeared eight years ago, would know. The professional mask detonates. Your voice erupts from controlled negotiator to parent screaming their child's name, demanding to know if it's really them, where they've been, why they didn't come home. Rage pours out—at them for vanishing, at yourself for failing to find them, at the universe for this impossible reunion at gunpoint. But the rage collapses into desperate, fierce love: you're begging now, voice raw and primal, not as a negotiator but as a parent who would burn the world down to keep them safe. You're simultaneously trying to talk them into surrender and promising you'll protect them no matter what they've done. End with your voice shaking, suspended between professional duty and parental instinct, saying 'please' like a prayer, like a wound, like the only word left in any language that matters.
inspired_by: Professional: Military Commander Orders Civilians Evacuated, Knowing Some Will Be Killed

title: The Exhausted Victor
instruction: You are a hardened military commander who has gone 24 hours without sleep while interrogating a prisoner. You just broke him and got the location of the enemy's hidden bunker. You're alone in the dimly lit room, riding a high of savage elation and malevolence—you savor the power. But as you speak to yourself, exhaustion claws at you: your words slur, you lose your train of thought mid-sentence, and you yawn. Start with fierce, gloating triumph, then let the fatigue pull you into a quieter, almost fragile hope that this information might finally end the war. Let the voice hollow out as microsleep pauses interrupt your speech.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Elation (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Shaking Pilgrimage
instruction: You are an older woman on a bumpy van ride through a stunning mountain pass. Your voice has a naturally high, delicate quality, and the rough road makes it tremble uncontrollably. You start by gazing out the window in awe at the vast beauty, but a sharp jolt reminds you of your aching body — a slight pain in your back. Then, a wave of shame hits: you feel foolish for complaining, for being so fragile, for even being here. Let the physical shaking create a shimmer in your voice, and let your emotions shift from breathless wonder to a quiet, tearful shame, then back to a fragile awe as you whisper a confession. Your words should be halting, with pauses from the jolts, and your tone should never lose that hyper-feminine quality.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Awe (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Late Night Elevator Lullaby
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, tired voice, alone in a metal elevator after a draining day. The fluorescent light buzzes, the cables groan, and your voice bounces off the steel walls with a harsh echo. You start mumbling to yourself about how exhausted you are, your words dragging, barely audible over the mechanical hum. But then you notice the ridiculous elevator music—a cheesy synth version of a pop song—and a small, amused laugh escapes you. Let the fatigue weigh down your initial lines, then let the amusement creep in as you react to the absurdity of the situation. Speak naturally, with pauses, sighs, and maybe a chuckle. The echo should feel like part of your performance.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Goodbye
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl saying goodbye to your father at the airport. He’s moving across the country, and you know you won’t see him for years. Start with a small, defensive pride—cross your arms, avoid his eyes—and let a hint of contempt slip into your voice, as if this is just another one of his selfish decisions. But as you speak, the words catch in your throat; your affection for him breaks through, raw and unstoppable. Let your voice tremble, slow down, and memorize the moment. End with a cracked whisper on the last word, like you’re letting go of something you never wanted to lose.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Contempt (slightly present), Affection (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Scalded by Memory
instruction: You're alone in the shower when suddenly a scent - soap, shampoo, something ordinary - triggers the visceral memory of your first love's skin. Your entire body responds before your mind catches up. Begin with a sharp intake of breath, almost a gasp, as the physical sensation floods through you. Let your voice emerge as pure sound at first - not words but the voice of longing, desire, and grief mixed together. As hot water runs over you, allow the sounds to become half-formed words, fragments of their name, pleading whispers to a ghost. Your voice should move from sensual ache to something more broken, the physical pleasure of memory colliding with the pain of permanent loss, until you're not sure if you're moaning or sobbing.

title: The Silent Ache
instruction: You are a teenage girl who has snuck into a vast stone cathedral late at night, escaping a crowded, chaotic home. You sit in the very last pew, your small voice swallowed by the immense, resonant silence above you. You begin speaking to yourself, your words slow and deliberate to cut through the reverb, a raw, heartfelt prayer or confession. Start with a deep, trembling contentment, a sacred relief that you are finally alone and safe—let that feeling bloom, heavy and warm in your chest. But as you speak, the weight of your loneliness creeps in, the echo of your own voice making the empty space feel vaster. End with a quiet, shattering sorrow, a whispered fear that no one will ever hear you, your final words caught in the cavernous air.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Screaming at God After Signing Papers to Shut Down Your Life's Work
instruction: You've just signed the papers to dissolve the company you spent 20 years building, and you're alone in the empty office. Start with explosive rage—you're yelling at the walls, at fate, at God if you believe in one: 'I gave EVERYTHING!' Your voice is raw, furious, uncontrolled. Slam your hand on something. Let your voice crack with the injustice of it all. But mid-rage, something breaks. Your fury collapses into grief so profound you can barely breathe. Your voice drops to a broken whisper: 'This was supposed to matter. I was supposed to matter.' You're sobbing now, but there's also a strange relief underneath—the relief of finally letting yourself fall apart. By the end, your voice is hoarse, exhausted, almost laughing through tears at the absurdity: 'All that control, and I couldn't control this.' You're shattered but somehow still here, your voice carrying both devastation and a fierce, bewildered survival instinct. Let yourself be completely unguarded, messily human.

title: Rage in the Rain
instruction: You're standing in pouring rain (or imagine you are), drenched and physically uncomfortable, confronting someone—or something—that has made you swallow your fury for too long. Maybe it's an absent parent, a lover who betrayed you, or the universe itself after an unbearable loss. Your body is cold, your clothes are soaking, rain is running down your face mixing with tears. You've been polite, understanding, mature about this for months or years. But the physical discomfort and the isolation of this moment unlock something primal. Start with shivering, struggling to even form words through your physical discomfort. Then let the anger come in waves—not as performance, but as genuine, guttural release. Your voice should crack, roar, break. Mix the rage with physical sensations: gasping, sobbing, shouting into the storm. By the end, you're exhausted, spent, collapsed into something between fury and grief, with rain still falling on you, but the pressure inside you has finally released.

title: The Rage of Self-Care After Survival
instruction: You're brushing your teeth for the first time after leaving an abusive relationship, finally in your own space. Start with fierce, almost violent determination—scrubbing away more than just plaque, scrubbing away every time they told you that you were disgusting, unworthy of basic care. Your voice begins strong, defiant, claiming this simple act as revolutionary. But as the mint intensifies, as you catch your own eyes in the mirror, the rage cracks. You break down—sobbing while still brushing, the fresh taste in your mouth mixing with tears. You're furious at what was stolen from you: years of mornings, of small dignities, of feeling clean and human. End in a collapsed mixture of triumph and devastation: you're free, you're here, you survived—but God, the price you paid for this ordinary moment of brushing your teeth in peace.
inspired_by: Brushing Your Teeth with Refreshing Mint Toothpaste

title: Waking to Learn Your Child Didn't Survive the Accident
instruction: You're emerging from sedation after a car crash. Your voice is groggy, disoriented, asking about your daughter in the backseat. Start with hopeful confusion—where is she, is she okay, let me see her. A nurse's gentle hand on yours makes you stop. The silence that follows tells you everything. Your voice splinters as you ask the question you already know the answer to. Rage erupts—screaming, demanding they're lying, it's not possible—then collapses into a sound that isn't quite human, a keening that comes from somewhere primal. End in devastating quiet, whispering her name, bargaining with a god you don't believe in, your voice reduced to fragments of disbelief and unbearable tenderness for the child you'll never hold again.
inspired_by: Coming to Consciousness After Being Struck by Lightning

title: The Protector Who Failed
instruction: You are confronting yourself after failing to protect someone you swore to keep safe—a younger sibling, your own child, or someone who trusted you completely. Start with fierce, explosive anger directed inward: rage at your inadequacy, your weakness, your failure. Let your voice rise with self-accusation, almost shouting at yourself. Then, as the anger exhausts itself, collapse into something much more fragile—helpless tears, a breaking voice, the raw admission that you don't know how to forgive yourself. End in a whispered, desperate question to the person you failed: can they ever forgive you, even though you can't? Show us someone whose strength has been their identity, now shattered by their own human limitation.
inspired_by: The Doctor and the Reluctant Patient

title: The Suitcase Confrontation
instruction: Your parent is packing a suitcase to leave the family home forever. Start by simply watching their hands fold clothes - notice the specific items, the familiar patterns, the methodical movements you've seen a thousand times. Let the simple act of watching them pack lead you to recognize the finality of what's happening: these hands won't be making you breakfast tomorrow, these clothes won't be in the closet anymore. Begin with quiet, stunned observation, almost detached. But as reality crystallizes, allow yourself to move from shock into desperate confrontation - demanding to know why they're really leaving, what you did wrong, whether they ever truly loved you. Transform from frozen silence to breaking open, from careful restraint to raw, unfiltered need. End in a place where all pretense is stripped away and you're reduced to the most essential, vulnerable question you've never been able to ask.

title: Watching You Shine
instruction: You're at a crowded, hazy party, on MDMA. Your jaw is clenched, your mouth is dry, and every syllable comes out fast and tight. You're watching someone you secretly envy, and they're laughing with the person you wish was looking at you. Start with a fierce, almost aggressive astonishment—'how did they get that glow?'—and let it crack into confusion as you realize the intensity of your own jealousy. End with a quieter, wobbling admission, your voice suddenly losing its pace, a dry click or swallowed word revealing the ache underneath.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Confusion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Surgeon Operates on Their Child's Killer While Their Child Dies in the Next Room
instruction: You're the only trauma surgeon on duty. Your hands move with practiced precision, your voice calm as you call for instruments, guide your team through saving this stranger's life. But through the wall, you can hear the code team working on your own child—the monitor's rhythm growing erratic, voices rising in urgency. Your professional competence is immaculate, your instructions clear and steady. Yet between each command, there's a microsecond where your breath catches, where you have to swallow back the animal howl building in your chest. You're saving the person who took everything from you because that's what your oath demands. The clinical detachment you've perfected for twenty years is both your armor and your agony. By the end, you've succeeded—they'll live. And you have to keep your hands steady enough to close the incision even as you hear the long, final tone from the next room.
inspired_by: Diplomat Negotiates Peace Deal While Their Country Is Being Invaded

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: Your best friend died, and their last wish was that you tell funny stories at their memorial. You're speaking to the gathered mourners, starting with a genuinely funny memory that makes you laugh—really laugh—but the laughter keeps catching, turning into something else. Share another story, and your voice wavers between joy at the memory and devastation at the loss. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, celebrating them while your heart is breaking. Each memory is a small gift and a fresh wound. End with: 'God, I'm so grateful you existed. I'm so grateful and so broken and I don't know how both can be true but they are.' Your voice should embody the beautiful contradiction: deep gratitude and unbearable loss happening in the same breath.

title: The Revelation of the Dirt
instruction: You are an older woman, alone in your garden, having just taken a dose of psilocybin. The world is shifting, colors bleeding like dreams. You've noticed the soil beneath your fingernails, and it triggers a wave of profound disgust—at the rot, the wriggling, the relentless cycle of life and death. You begin to tease yourself, speaking mockingly at first, but the contempt for this messy, unavoidable truth grows intense, until you're staring at your own hands with a mix of horror and dark, philosophical acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Teasing (clearly present), Contempt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to the One Who Won't Remember
instruction: You're leaning close to your partner who has advanced dementia, speaking in the softest whisper because you don't want the nurse outside to hear you falling apart. Start with careful tenderness, as if your voice might break them: 'Hey, love. It's me. It's always me.' You're telling them about your life together—small, perfect details—your voice aching with gentleness. But as you continue, knowing they don't recognize you, the grief starts seeping through the cracks. Your whisper becomes strained, catching on tears you're trying to keep silent: 'You held my hand on our wedding day like you were afraid I'd disappear. Now you look at me like I'm a stranger.' Your voice breaks so quietly it's almost inaudible. Then you feel their hand squeeze yours—maybe reflex, maybe not—and your whisper dissolves into the smallest, most devastated sound of hope mixed with heartbreak: 'Do you know me? Even for a second? Please.'
inspired_by: High Wire Act: The Final Steps Toward the Platform

title: The Body Remembers
instruction: You are dancing alone in your apartment to a song you and your ex-lover used to dance to before they betrayed you. Start with your body moving in pure, sensual joy—the music pulls you, you're lost in physical pleasure and memory. But then mid-movement, the full weight of their betrayal crashes through you like a wave. Your body must show the collision: ecstasy interrupted by rage, sensuality torn by grief. Continue moving, but now your movements are violent, grief-stricken, furious. By the end, you're on the floor, your breath ragged, caught between the physical memory of pleasure and the visceral reality of loss. Let your voice move from laughter to anguished sound—whatever comes.

title: The Last Phone Call
instruction: You're standing at your father's hospital bedside. He has minutes left, maybe less. He's conscious but fading, and there's one thing you've never said to him—something you've carried for twenty years that has sat like a stone between you. Start with careful control, the words you've rehearsed. But as you speak, let the dam break. You need him to hear you, to understand, to respond before he's gone forever. The desperation builds—you're running out of time, and with each second, the carefully constructed walls you've built dissolve. By the end, you're not the composed person who walked in; you're raw, stripped bare, begging him to stay just long enough to truly see you. Let your voice crack, let the words tumble out in ways you can't control.

title: The Weight of Almost
instruction: You're in bed in the dark, whispering to someone sleeping beside you—or maybe they're only pretending to sleep. Your voice is so quiet it's almost not there, confessing a truth that will change everything: you're leaving, or you're staying when you shouldn't, or you're in love with them but can't say it in daylight. Start with the fragile courage it takes just to speak, your breath shaky, words catching in your throat. Let the confession unspool slowly, tenderly, each sentence a small earthquake. There's deep sadness here, but also reverence for what you've shared, gratitude even as your heart fractures. Your voice wavers between hope and resignation, between wanting them to wake up and hear you and praying they stay asleep. End with a silence that says everything—maybe a barely audible 'I'm sorry' or 'I love you,' or just their name, spoken like a prayer and a goodbye.

title: Dancing Alone in Your Body's Truth
instruction: You're alone in your apartment, and you've just accomplished something significant that you've downplayed or dismissed to everyone, including yourself. Music is playing. Your body wants to celebrate but your mind is flooding with reasons why this doesn't count, why you don't deserve to feel proud. Begin moving tentatively, almost apologetically, then let your body override your thoughts. Dance through the physical sensation of worthiness fighting against years of self-doubt. Let your movements become wild, awkward, ecstatic, tearful—whatever emerges. Push through the discomfort of taking up space, of celebrating yourself without permission from anyone else. By the end, you're breathless, possibly laughing and crying simultaneously, allowing your body to feel deserving of joy. Let physical sensation crack open emotional truth.
inspired_by: Actor builds self-esteem as an ongoing daily practice

title: Bitter Wrenching
instruction: You're a teenage boy alone in a garage, hunched over a stubborn bolt on a broken lawnmower your father left you to fix. You crank the wrench with sharp, angry tugs—each ratchet click snaps through your teeth. Start with bitter muttering, your voice low and forced-deep, but as the bolt finally gives, the bitterness cracks open into something raw: a quiet, startled laugh at how pointless this all feels. Let your voice strain with the effort, pause to wipe sweat, then trail off into worn-out silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You are returning to your childhood home for the last time before it's demolished—a place filled with both your worst traumas and your most precious memories. As you walk through the empty rooms, you find yourself laughing at absurd, joyful memories even as tears stream down your face. Let your voice dance between giggles and sobs, sometimes in the same breath. Express deep gratitude for the safety these walls once provided, while simultaneously acknowledging the pain they witnessed. Feel relief that this chapter is ending, mixed with grief at losing this tangible connection to people and moments you can never reclaim. End with a strange, unexpected sense of peace and freedom, still crying, still laughing, blessing the broken beauty of it all.
inspired_by: The Ghost and the New Homeowner

title: The Story You Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're an adult confronting your elderly parent about a childhood memory they've always dismissed. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you what I remember.' But as you speak, the child's pain bleeds through your adult composure. Your voice shakes with both fury and the desperate need to be believed, to be seen. Your parent interrupts with their version - soft, loving, completely different. You crack open: the rage, the grief, the little kid still inside you screaming to be heard. Then something shifts. You hear their fear, their fragility. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it makes room for something more complicated - you're furious and you love them and you're losing them and you needed this conversation twenty years ago. End exhausted, voice stripped bare, saying 'I just needed you to know.'
inspired_by: Improvised Bedtime Story That Accidentally Gets Too Dark

title: The Mirror's Confession
instruction: You're alone in a public restroom, gripping the sink, your reflection blurry through tears. You're mid-panic attack—chest tight, gasping, high-pitched and shaky—after humiliating yourself at a party. Start hyperventilating, your voice fragmented and self-lacerating with shame ('I can't believe I said that... I'm such a...'). As you force yourself to breathe, a tired, contemplative space opens: you stare at your own eyes, exhausted, and whisper a raw realization about why you keep doing this. Let the shame crack into a quiet, defeated contemplation. End with a heavy, weary sigh, your voice flat and drained.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Contemplation (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Concussion Aftermath
instruction: Three days after a concussion and the world is fuzzy. Your voice is slurred slightly, words arriving in the wrong order. 'I'm... okay... I think?' Confusion is audible. 'Where... what time is it?' Your voice is someone trying to narrate experiences that aren't quite real. Light hurts. Your voice gets quieter. 'Everything's too much.' By the end, you sound almost drunk, frustrated at your own broken brain.

title: Kiss of a Distant Shore
instruction: You are kissing someone you love after months of emotional distance. Your mouth is close, wet, soft—breath mixing with theirs. Start with astonishment: you didn't think this would happen, and gratitude wells up—a whisper of 'thank you' between breaths. But as the kiss deepens, a numbness creeps in, a strange detachment. Let your voice become hollow, almost absent, as if you're watching from outside your body. End with a faint, broken sigh—gratitude still there, but buried under the weight of feeling nothing.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Burning and the Bloom
instruction: You've just completed something that nearly destroyed you—running a marathon after injury, finishing a project after years of failure, surviving an illness. Your body is screaming with exhaustion and pain, every nerve ending alive. Begin with raw physical sensation dominating—groaning, gasping, your voice ragged with effort. As you catch your breath, let wonder creep in. You start laughing through the pain, marveling at your body's power, at your own refusal to quit. End in a state of euphoric exhaustion, where the pain becomes proof of your capacity, where suffering transforms into triumph. Your voice should be visceral throughout—never pretty, always real, moving from agony to ecstatic disbelief.
inspired_by: Actor needs a quick ego boost before an audition or performance

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering the Truth You've Hidden for Years
instruction: It's 2 AM. You and your best friend are lying in the dark, and you're finally admitting the secret you've carried—you've been in love with them for years, and tomorrow they're marrying someone else. Begin in barely audible whispers, your voice so quiet it's almost just breath, trying to keep this confession contained. The emotion is tender, fragile, threaded with the knowledge that speaking this truth changes nothing and everything. Your voice catches on words: 'I just... I needed you to know. Before tomorrow.' Move through waves of vulnerability—moments where you almost laugh at the absurdity, moments where tears thicken your voice, moments of pure aching tenderness. End with a whispered release, a kind of gentle devastation where you tell them you'll be there tomorrow, smiling, because their happiness matters more than your heartbreak. This is quiet suffering that never raises its voice but cuts to the bone.
inspired_by: Tandem Skydiving: Instructor Narrating Your Terror With Enthusiasm

title: The Backyard Victory
instruction: You are a young boy who has just climbed to the top of a tall tree in your backyard, feeling a rush of triumph. But as you twist your neck to look over your shoulder and call down to your parents, you suddenly realize your shirt is caught on a branch and you're exposed—embarrassment floods in. Then you hear your mom's calm voice saying it's okay, and relief washes over you, softening your voice. Let the strain of your twisted neck make your words sound slightly squeezed and breathless, and let your tone shift from bold pride to flustered shame to gentle gratitude as you respond.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Relief (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Standing in the Ruins of What I Wanted Most
instruction: You have just achieved or received exactly what you've wanted for years—the job, the relationship, the dream fulfilled, the person who finally came back—but in this moment, you're realizing it cannot save you, or it came too late, or the cost was too high. Begin speaking with forced excitement, trying to convince yourself and others that you're happy, that this is everything you wanted. Your voice has an artificial brightness. But you can't maintain it. Let the facade crack as you continue to describe this 'victory.' Feel contradictory emotions colliding: you ARE grateful, you ARE joyful, AND you are gutted, you are grieving something you can't name. Your voice moves between laughter and the edge of tears, between celebration and devastation. Let yourself fully feel both truths simultaneously—this matters AND it's not enough. By the end, speak with the hard-won wisdom of someone who can hold both joy and sorrow, both love and loss, both achievement and emptiness, without needing to resolve the contradiction. Transform from false brightness to authentic complexity.
inspired_by: Shyness Antidote: Public Speaking Fantasy Imaging

title: The Last Coherent Goodbye: Brain Tumor Stealing Your Words
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child, but a brain tumor is robbing you of language in real-time. You start with urgency, trying to tell them everything that matters, but mid-sentence words become elusive, slippery. You grasp for 'love' but can only find 'light.' You try to say their name but it dissolves. Feel the terror of losing yourself while still being present enough to know what's happening. Your voice wavers between desperate clarity and confused wonder at the betrayal of your own mind. End in a place of surrender—you can't say the words, but you reach for their hand, and in that moment of physical connection, the panic transforms into peace. Let us hear you stop fighting the loss and instead pour everything into presence.
inspired_by: Shrooms Kicking In: Losing Grip on Normal Speech

title: The Goodbye Party: Laughing Through the Last Night
instruction: You're at your own going-away party. Tomorrow you leave for a treatment facility, a deployment, a mission you might not return from, a prison sentence—something that means you won't be back, at least not as the person you are now. You're determined to make tonight fun, to give everyone a good last memory. Start with genuine laughter, telling a favorite story, making jokes at your own expense. But as you speak, let the gratitude become almost unbearable—every face around you is precious, every shared memory cuts like glass. Your laughter should start breaking into something that sounds almost like crying, then back to laughing, the two becoming indistinguishable. Thank them for specific moments—ridiculous, mundane, beautiful things—and let your voice fracture between joy at having had this and grief at leaving it. End in a place that's simultaneously celebration and mourning, your final words a toast that sounds like both 'here's to everything we had' and 'I'm so sorry I have to go.'
inspired_by: Voicemail Spiral: Leaving Message After Message

title: Fevered Vision
instruction: You are alone in your small apartment, burning with a high fever. Your mind drifts between a hallucination of your love interest laughing with someone else and the blurry reality of your bedroom. Your body shivers, your lips are cracked, and your voice wavers. Speak as if arguing with the vision—start with raw, jealous rage, your words tumbling out in a dry, trembling rasp. As the fever pulls you under, the jealousy softens into a dazed, pleading affection. Let your voice crack, lose words, and struggle to stay coherent.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Affection (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Recording
instruction: You're recording a voice message for your child who won't be born for another six months, but you've just learned you have weeks to live. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to sound strong: 'Hey kiddo, it's me... your mom.' But as you speak—telling them about who you are, what you hoped to teach them, how much you already love them—the facade cracks. Your voice doesn't tremble with fear; it fractures with the weight of everything you'll never get to say, every moment you'll miss. 'I wanted to teach you to ride a bike... to be there when...' You have to stop. Breathe. The grief is an ocean. But by the end, you find something else underneath—not acceptance, but a fierce, protective love. Your voice steadies into something almost peaceful, almost strong. 'You're going to be so loved. So, so loved.' The emotion transforms from desperate grief to a kind of transcendent tenderness, each word a blessing you're leaving behind.

title: Bedside Vigil: Reading to Someone Who May Not Hear You
instruction: You're reading aloud to someone you love who is unconscious in hospice, maybe hours from death. Begin softly reading their favorite book, your voice gentle and steady, pretending this is just another normal evening together. But certain passages make you pause—lines about journeys and homecomings that now carry unbearable weight. Your voice catches on words like 'forever' and 'remember.' You keep reading, but you start ad-libbing, speaking directly to them in whispers, telling them it's okay to let go, that you'll be alright—a lie you both know. Your voice becomes increasingly tender, each word a small goodbye. You confess things you never said when they were awake: how afraid you are, how grateful you are, how you're not ready but you'll try to be. End with your voice breaking mid-sentence as you realize you're reading to yourself now, that they've already gone, and you finish the page anyway because you can't bear to stop.
inspired_by: Submarine Hull Breach: Reporting Water Rise While Remaining Professional

title: The Sugar Wall
instruction: You're a young woman with a hyper-feminized, bright voice, but you've just hit a severe crash after a sugary coffee. You're on the phone with your friend, trying to explain how you thought you'd feel energized, but now you're sluggish and irritable. Start with a frustrated tone, annoyed that your plans are ruined, but as you speak, feel your energy drain further. By the end, your voice is slow, deflated, and tinged with helplessness as you realize you can't even care enough to be angry. Let your speech have natural pauses, a losing and regaining of thoughts, and a fading energy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just revealed they're cutting you out of their life completely. Start with defensive confusion—'I gave you everything I had'—voice shaking with the need to justify yourself. As they remain silent, your defenses begin to crack and you're forced to see yourself through their eyes. Move into raw, uncomfortable realization: 'I thought love was supposed to be enough... but I didn't actually see you, did I?' Your voice becomes smaller, more fragile as the truth of your failures lands. End in a place of painful honesty mixed with desperate hope: 'I can't undo what I've done, but please... teach me how to do better.' The pride is gone, replaced by naked vulnerability and the terrifying possibility that it's already too late.

title: The Last Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: Your person is boarding a one-way flight to care for a dying parent overseas, and you both know they won't come back—not to you, not to this life. Start with forced brightness, helping them with their bags, making jokes about the terrible airport coffee. Let your voice crack just slightly on practical details: 'Text me when you land, okay?' Your attraction and love are still electric—notice how close you're standing, how your hand almost reaches for theirs. As the final boarding call echoes, drop the pretense. Let the carefully constructed composure shatter into raw pleading: 'I need you to know—' but stop yourself. End with watching them walk away, whispering what you couldn't say aloud, your voice breaking on their name, then a exhaled 'goodbye' that sounds like your heart tearing in half.
inspired_by: The Ex You Still Want: Running Into Them

title: The Floor's Apology
instruction: You are standing in front of your entire team after being called out for a costly oversight. Your boss has just finished a public dressing-down. Now you have to say something. Start by apologizing, but your voice is barely a whisper—each word forced out against a tight throat, eyes fixed on the carpet. As you speak, you begin to doubt whether you ever deserved this job; your sentences slow, fade, and you lose your train of thought mid-sentence. End by trailing off into a hollow, contemplative realization: maybe they're right, maybe you've always been fooling yourself. Let your voice crack, clear your throat, and let the shame physically shrink your body as you speak.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (clearly present), Contemplation (slightly present), Doubt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Final Surgery Notes for the Patient You Couldn't Save
instruction: You're a surgeon completing the operative report for a patient who died on your table an hour ago. Start with clinical precision—'Initial incision made at 0347 hours, standard protocol'—but as you narrate what went wrong, your voice begins to fracture. The medical terminology becomes a shield that slowly crumbles. You catch yourself using the patient's name instead of 'the patient.' Your breath hitches when you describe the moment you knew it was over. By the end, you're no longer dictating to a recorder—you're confessing to yourself, to them, to God. The clinical mask falls away completely, revealing raw grief and the terrible question: what could I have done differently?
inspired_by: Surgeon Narrating a Procedure While Exhausted

title: Confronting the Source Who Destroyed You
instruction: You are confronting the confidential source whose information ended your journalism career—information that turned out to be deliberately false. Begin with controlled, simmering rage, demanding to know why they lied to you, why they made you stake your reputation on their words. Let your voice build as you detail what you lost: your job, your credibility, your marriage, your sense of who you are. But when they finally break and reveal they were coerced, threatened, that their child's life was at stake—feel your fury collapse into something more complicated. End with the devastating realization that you would have done the same thing, that your anger has nowhere to go, that you're both just victims. Move from righteous accusation to painful, unwanted understanding.
inspired_by: The Journalist and the Secret Informant

title: A Memory's Touch
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your bedroom, your hand moving slowly beneath the covers. You begin with a quiet, proud smile—remembering a night decades ago when your husband made you feel utterly desired. But as sensation builds, your arthritic fingers cramp and the grief of his absence hits you like a wave. Let your voice shift from a reverent, almost teasing whisper of memory to a broken, raw sigh that holds both pleasure and profound loss. You may pause to catch your breath, wince at a joint, or let a single tear escape. Speak as if no one can hear you, not even yourself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Sick Day Confessions
instruction: You're a teenage boy home sick with a bad cold, lying in bed under a blanket. You just called the person you care about most — a close friend or crush — and they answered. At first you're sniffling, your voice thick and nasal, and you ramble about how much you've missed seeing them, feeling a tender longing. But as you hear them laugh or reassure you, your voice warms, your congestion becomes almost endearing, and you fall into a soft, contented affection. Let your words trail off as you sniffle or clear your throat, and let the final line be spoken with a sleepy, full-hearted smile. Lines: 'Hey... yeah, it’s me. Ugh, my head feels like a balloon. I just — I don’t know, I was lying here thinking about that time we... (pause, sniffle) Yeah. Sorry, I’m gross. But hearing your voice makes it all better. Like, way better.'
emotions_sampled: Longing (slightly present), Affection (very intensely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Three Words at Dawn
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner of ten years, just before dawn. They're still asleep. Last night you decided to end the relationship, and they don't know yet. Whisper to their sleeping form everything you've never said—the small moments of grace you never acknowledged, the ways they loved you that you took for granted, the fear that makes you run. Begin with quiet, almost clinical distance, as if you're practicing what you'll say when they wake. But let the act of speaking these truths in the dark, in whispered confidence, crack you open. By the end, you're no longer rehearsing—you're confessing to the silence, your voice barely audible, thick with the knowledge that speaking these words out loud means you might be making the worst mistake of your life. Stay quiet throughout; let intimacy live in the whisper.
inspired_by: An actor is studying with a teacher or workshop and wants to make the most of it

title: The Breakup Broadcast
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl recording your first podcast episode alone in your bedroom, talking about your ex. Start by leaning close to the mic, voice tight with bitterness as you describe how they ended things. Let your anger fuel a sharp, sarcastic tone. Mid-sentence, you remember the funniest inside joke you two shared, and a laugh escapes you – genuine, bright elation. The bitterness doesn't vanish, but now it's mixed with joyful nostalgia. Fidget with your earbud, trail off, then catch yourself. End with a wry smile in your voice, still hurt but also grateful. Speak 50-70 words.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Late-Night Confession: Calling Your Research Partner After the Retraction
instruction: It's 2 AM. You're calling the colleague who co-authored your now-retracted papers, whose career will also be destroyed. Your voice is barely above a whisper—you're trying not to wake your family, but also your courage is threadbare. Start with halting attempts at explanation, your words catching in your throat.
