You're not just sorry—you're gutted with guilt for dragging them down with you. Your breathing is shallow, irregular, the sound of someone crying without making noise. As you speak, tender memories surface: late nights in the lab, the joy you shared when you thought you'd discovered something beautiful. Your voice softens with love for those moments even as you acknowledge they were built on sand. End with quiet devastation: 'I'm so sorry' repeated like a prayer that can't save anything.
inspired_by: Professional: Researcher Publishes Findings That Contradict Their Own Previous Work

title: The Old Command
instruction: You are an elderly former drill sergeant, now in a VA hospital, addressing a group of young veterans struggling with recovery. Your body aches— a sharp pain in your hip from an old wound— and you start by bellowing through gritted teeth, your voice cracking with strain. But as you speak, the pain shifts into contemplation: you realize these soldiers need more than orders, they need to know the weight of perseverance. Shout with percussive force, but let your volume drop and your tone soften at the end, as you lose yourself for a moment in memory. Pause to catch your breath; let your words become slower, more thoughtful, as if you're realizing something for the first time.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Returning
instruction: You're returning to a place after many years - a childhood home, a city you fled, a room where something important happened. You expect to feel one clear thing: maybe nostalgia, maybe anger, maybe relief. Start by trying to feel what you think you 'should' feel. But as you take in the space, let unbidden images wash over you: not memories of this place, but strange flashes - a stranger's face, animals, weather, textures, moments from completely different times and places that your mind offers without permission. Follow these images instead of your expectations. Let them guide your emotional experience. You may arrive at a feeling that contradicts everything you thought you'd feel - grief mixed with inappropriate laughter, rage softening into unexpected forgiveness, or joy complicated by a loss you'd forgotten.

title: The Pregnancy Test
instruction: You're holding a positive pregnancy test, speaking to the father who lives a thousand miles away and doesn't know you're calling. You begin with joy—genuine, bubbling, terrified joy—telling him about this miracle, this unexpected gift. Your voice is bright with hope and excitement. But as you continue speaking, reality creeps in: he left for reasons that haven't changed, you're not together, this might be the worst possible timing, you might be doing this alone. Let happiness and terror dance together in your voice. End in a place of fierce determination mixed with deep longing—you want him here, but you know you'll be okay without him. Express gratitude for what was, grief for what isn't, and fierce hope for what might be. Your voice should shimmer between laughter and tears, strength and vulnerability.

title: Dust and Desire
instruction: You are an old woman caught in a fierce sandstorm, huddled against a wall with a scarf pressed to your mouth and nose. The wind howls, grit coats your teeth, and each breath is a battle. As you struggle to see through the dust, a vivid memory of a long-ago lover surges through you — raw, hungry lust that makes your chest ache. But then you remember: you’ve survived decades of storms, and that pride hardens your spine. Speak to the wind as if it were that lover: start with a breathless, thirsty whisper of wanting, letting coughs and muffled words interrupt you, then let your voice sharpen into a defiant, proud declaration of your own strength, even as your lungs burn.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father about something they did when you were thirteen—something you've never spoken about but has shaped every relationship you've had since. Begin with your arms crossed, voice controlled and cold, reciting the facts like you're reading from a script you've rehearsed for years. You're armored, righteous, keeping them at a distance. But as they respond—whether they deny it, apologize, or simply look at you with recognition—something breaks. Your voice starts to shake. The anger that protected you begins to crack, revealing the hurt, frightened child underneath. By the end, you're no longer accusing—you're asking the question you've needed answered for twenty years: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Start with icy fury; end with exposed, childlike vulnerability.
inspired_by: An actor cannot find the right choice for a scene's emotional obligation

title: The Congratulations That Breaks You
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, giving a toast. You're genuinely happy for them—radiant, even. Begin by anchoring yourself in the physical celebration—the weight of the champagne glass, the faces watching you, the music in the background, the taste of joy in the room. Let these sensations build your smile, your warmth. But as you continue speaking, allow these same sensory experiences to trigger something underneath—the loneliness you've been hiding, the relationship you lost, the future you thought you'd have. The sensory details don't change, but they begin to unlock contradictory feelings. Start with authentic joy and pride in your voice. End with that same smile on your face but tears in your eyes, your voice thick with both happiness for them and grief for yourself, unable to separate the two, celebrating and mourning simultaneously.
inspired_by: Actor is using Affective Memory and the conventional Sense Memory approach feels insufficient to trigger the full emotional response

title: Adrenaline Crash: Shaking After the Car Almost Hit You
instruction: You just survived nearly being hit. For 30 seconds you were fine, body in survival mode. Now you're parked safely and your voice is wrecked. Words come out as tiny, shaking whispers. You're on the phone with someone and trying to explain but your voice breaks constantly. Jaw trembling affects articulation. You can't catch your breath—gasping between words. The shock is wearing off and now comes the terror, and your voice becomes almost unrecognizable as you sob.

title: Spilled and Drawn In
instruction: You're at a loud party, still burning with shame from spilling a drink down your shirt twenty minutes ago. You're standing near the snack table, trying to disappear, when you overhear someone talking about that obscure band you've been obsessed with for months. Your interest yanks you forward — you blurt out a question, excited, but then bitterness bites your tongue because you remember how people laughed when you mentioned them last time. Let your voice start quiet and clipped with shame, then open up — pitch rising, sentences breaking off — as the music and chatter push you to project, but let a sour edge creep in at the end, like you don't quite trust the conversation.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Interest (very intensely present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's bed in the darkness, whispering a bedtime story like you have a thousand times before. Your voice is tender, gentle, full of the kind of love that aches. But tonight is different—you're saying goodbye because you won't be here tomorrow. Maybe you're ill, maybe you're leaving for reasons you can't explain, but this is the last time. Your voice catches as you continue the story, each word carrying the weight of all the stories you won't get to tell. Include the moment you start adding details you've never said before—how proud you are, how much watching them grow has meant, things you thought you'd have time to say. Your whispers become even softer, breaking with grief you're trying so hard to contain. You don't want to wake them, but you need them to somehow know. End with your voice barely audible, pressing one last kiss to their forehead, your breath shaking as you try not to sob.
inspired_by: Hot Air Balloon Ascending Uncontrollably: Losing Oxygen

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply—a partner, a best friend—who is asleep or unconscious in a hospital bed. You've never been able to say these things to their face, but now you whisper the truth. Your voice is barely audible at first, tender and terrified: 'I don't know if you can hear me.' Confess something you've held back—perhaps that you've been in love with them, or that you're sorry for something that's haunted you, or that you're terrified of losing them. Your whisper becomes more urgent but stays quiet, intimate, as if speaking louder might shatter the moment. Describe how your life has been changed by knowing them, your voice catching with emotion. Then, in the silence, you realize they might never wake up to hear this. Your voice becomes even softer, more broken, as you say 'please don't leave me' or 'I should have told you sooner.' End with your forehead resting against their hand, your words dissolving into breath and tears, whispering 'I'm here. I'm right here.'

title: The Last Letter from a Dying Stranger
instruction: You've received a final message from someone you've never met—a biological parent, a sibling given up for adoption, someone whose existence rewrites your entire history. Begin reading their words with cautious curiosity, almost clinical distance. As their story unfolds, let confusion give way to recognition of yourself in their phrases, their humor, their pain. Your voice catches when you realize they knew you existed, watched you from afar, loved you without ever speaking. The anger comes—why didn't they reach out sooner?—but it dissolves into profound grief as you understand their reasons, their sacrifice, their impossible choice. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance, reading their final 'I love you' to someone they can never meet, your voice carrying both the weight of loss and the strange, aching gift of being known by a ghost.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Touched You
instruction: You're finally telling your emotionally distant parent what their lack of physical affection cost you. Begin with controlled anger, listing facts: 'You never hugged me. Not at graduation. Not when I cried.' Describe with devastating precision the absence—the phantom sensation of embraces that never happened, the hunger for a hand on your shoulder, the way you flinched the first time someone loved you because you didn't know how to be touched. Let your rage crack into something more vulnerable: the child inside you still waiting to be held. Then shift unexpectedly—acknowledge that you see their own wounds, their own untouched childhood. End in a painful, quiet place between forgiveness and grief, your voice raw from shouting but dropping to almost a whisper.
inspired_by: Describing Physical Intimacy to a Lover Over the Phone

title: Crib Assembly in the Third Trimester
instruction: You're 36 weeks pregnant, sitting cross-legged on the nursery floor with a half-assembled crib around you. Every few seconds you adjust your weight, trying to find a less cramped position, and you let out a soft sigh as your diaphragm presses against your belly. You're scanning the instruction manual, squinting at a confusing diagram—your voice carries a slight furrow of concentration mixed with a thread of confusion about which screw goes where. Then your hand drifts to your stomach as the baby kicks, and a slow, quiet contentment settles into your breath. Let the physical struggle live in your voice: short phrases, pauses for air, a slight strain that relaxes into warmth at the end. Speak as if you're half-talking to yourself, half-narrating for the baby.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Confusion (slightly present), Contentment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You are alone, packing up the belongings of someone you love who is moving far away, or who has died, or who has cut you out of their life. As you handle each object—a worn book, a piece of clothing, a small treasure—let it break you open differently. Begin with forced efficiency, trying to just get through this task. But as you continue, let the accumulated weight of memory and loss crack you apart. Feel gratitude for what you had war with grief for what you're losing. Let anger flash through—at them, at circumstance, at time itself—then dissolve into tenderness. Speak to them as if they could hear you, your voice shifting between fury and love, bitterness and thanks, resentment and desperate appreciation. By the end, hold something precious in your hands and let yourself feel everything at once—the impossible contradiction of being grateful for what destroys you, of loving what you must release.

title: The Noose Tightens
instruction: You’re an old bouncer, drunk on cheap whiskey, sitting on a curb after being thrown out. Suddenly a guy you roughed up years ago grabs your collar and chokes you from behind, pressing your neck against his forearm. Start with a bark of astonishment—'What the hell?'—then as the pressure builds, your voice turns raspy, pitch jumps, and your words slur. Let the surprise sink into a hazy, drunken defiance: you try to laugh it off, but it comes out as a strained, choked whisper. Your mind wanders—a memory of a similar fight, a flash of your daughter's face—then you focus back on the stranglehold, muttering a final, half-acknowledged apology as the world fades.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Dress That No Longer Fits
instruction: You are an older woman with a soft, feminine voice, dressing alone in your bedroom for an evening you once eagerly anticipated. You begin with a faint, bittersweet infatuation as you recall a past lover, but the physical act of dressing—the heavy silk swooshing against your skin, a grunt as you bend for shoes—brings a sharp bitterness about your aging body and lost chances. As you straighten the fabric and catch your reflection, that bitterness softens into a quiet, aching longing for the person you used to be and the love that slipped away. Let the fabric rustle and your breath catch naturally; your voice should waver between a luminous memory and a worn, tired honesty, ending in a hushed, reverent sigh.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (slightly present), Bitterness (slightly present), Longing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Burning Room
instruction: You're in the shower, water scalding hot, after discovering your lover's betrayal through explicit messages on their phone. The physical sensation of burning water mirrors your internal state. Begin with controlled rage—scrubbing your skin hard, trying to wash away what you know. Let the physical intensity unlock something wilder: roar, sob, laugh maniacally at your own blindness. Feel how fury and desire are tangled together—you're simultaneously repulsed and still physically aching for them. Rake your hands through your hair, pound the tiles, let your voice become animal. The pain is both emotional and physical as you scrub harder. By the end, collapse against the wall, water still burning, transition from rage to a devastating quiet where you realize you still love them and that's the most painful part.
inspired_by: Actor feels everything but cannot express it (expressive insecurity)

title: The Glow of the Needle
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a naturally high, breathy voice, waking from sedation after a dental procedure. The room swims—lights smear, your jaw is numb. You feel a sudden, overwhelming longing for your adult daughter, who moved away years ago. At first, you just mumble her name, over and over, your voice slurred and childlike, volume rising and falling. As you fight through the fog, the longing sharpens into a clear, desperate plea—though your tongue is still thick and your words tumble out in a rush. The arc goes from disoriented repetition to a raw, whispered confession: you need her here, right now, before you forget why.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Straw
instruction: You are on the phone with a customer service representative after a 12-hour shift. Your voice starts sweet and strained — you're exhausted, you've explained the same billing error three times. The rep’s robotic script pushes you over the edge. Let your breath hitch, your pitch drop, then let it erupt from your gut — short, percussive sentences, maybe a slam on the table. Mid-rant, feel your throat tighten and crack. End with the phone slammed down, then a long, shaking exhale as you sink into a chair, the rage draining into pure fatigue.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're confronting your parent after years of their absence—maybe they abandoned you, maybe addiction took them away, maybe they chose another life. Start with controlled anger, listing grievances with sharp precision, your voice tight with decades of rehearsed accusations. But as you speak, the anger begins to fracture. Underneath is the child who waited at the window, who made excuses for empty chairs at school events, who learned to stop hoping. Your voice moves from accusation to pleading—demanding to know why you weren't enough to make them stay. End with exhausted vulnerability, finally asking the question you've been too afraid to voice: whether they ever think about you, whether they ever regretted leaving, whether some part of them loved you at all.

title: The Goldfish in the Sky
instruction: You're hosting a parenting podcast, close-mic, with your usual warm but performative 'radio voice.' A child listener calls in and asks where her goldfish goes after it dies. You start with practiced, upbeat curiosity, but her innocent logic unravels you — she says it swims up to the clouds. You get confused, fumble for words, and the mic catches every spontaneous hesitation. By the end, your voice drops its false intimacy and becomes raw, tender, as you realize you're not explaining death — you're listening to a child's grief. Speak about 50 words, letting the confusion shift into quiet awe.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering to the Unopened Letter
instruction: You're holding a letter you wrote to your child before they were born, but they were stillborn, and you've kept this letter for fifteen years. Begin by reading it aloud in barely a whisper—tender promises about teaching them to ride a bike, about being there for their first heartbreak. Your voice is gossamer-thin, almost afraid to disturb the air. As you read, the weight of all those unlived moments settles on your chest. Your whisper becomes thick with unshed tears. You pause at 'I would have loved watching you grow up,' and something catches in your throat—not a sob, but something quieter and more devastating. End by folding the letter carefully, your hands shaking, speaking one last sentence that isn't written: 'I still love you.'

title: The Miscarriage in the Hospital Bathroom
instruction: You're alone on the cold floor, and it's happening. Your body is betraying the future you'd already started building in your mind. You start by trying to be clinical, practical—calling out to someone, anyone—but your voice is already edged with panic. As the reality crashes over you, your voice explodes into something primal: rage at your body, at fate, at the unfairness. You're screaming and sobbing, but then you switch—your voice drops to a tender whisper as you say goodbye to the child you'll never meet, apologizing to someone who never existed. Your voice oscillates wildly: fierce maternal protectiveness over nothing, fury that makes you want to tear the world apart, then sudden, terrible softness. By the end, you're exhausted, your voice hollowed out, speaking to yourself with the kind of brutal gentleness you'd offer someone else. Sound like someone being shattered and trying to hold their own pieces together simultaneously.

title: The Aftermath
instruction: You're leaning against a cold brick wall in a dark alley, the adrenaline fading as you clutch a torn piece of your shirt. Your whole body trembles, and you feel a sharp pain in your side from the scuffle. Start with a shaky, breathless whisper as you replay the attack—fear and hurt leaking through. Then notice the stranger's shoeprints you kicked away: the one who tried to hurt you is gone. A sudden, unexpected laugh escapes you, raw and triumphant, and your voice cracks with wild joy. Finally, look up at the flickering streetlight and murmur a trembling prayer of hope, still shaking, but smiling.
emotions_sampled: Pain (clearly present), Triumph (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Intercepted Text
instruction: You're a teenager in your room, hunched over your phone, trying not to wake your parents. You've just found out your best friend is moving away — worst timing, you think, as disappointment sours your stomach. Your hand clamps over your mouth to muffle a noise, stifling the words as you message them back. But then you see their reply: a joke from your shared memory, and you can't help the strained laugh that escapes, muffled and warm. By the end, your hand still covers your lips, but there's a giddy, guilty elation in your voice as you try to whisper your next plan, the consonants smudged by your fingers.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospital bed, knowing this is your final conversation. Begin with careful cheerfulness, trying to protect them: 'Hey, Mom... I just wanted to hear your voice.' As the reality crashes over you, your control starts fracturing—words catching, breath hitching: 'Remember when you used to... when we would...' The memories flood faster, your voice breaking into desperate urgency: 'I need you to know that every single day, every moment—' Then suddenly, equipment alarms in the background. You have seconds. Your voice drops to an almost-whisper, stripped bare, achingly tender: 'I love you. I love you so much.' In the final moment, peace washes over your face even as tears fall, and you breathe out with profound gratitude and acceptance: 'Thank you... for everything.'

title: Whispering the Secret You've Carried Alone
instruction: Late at night, in barely audible tones, you're confessing something you've never told anyone—perhaps a loss, a moment of cowardice, a love you never spoke, a choice that haunts you. Your voice is tender, intimate, almost fragile, as if speaking louder would shatter you completely. Start hesitant, testing each word before releasing it. Let silences speak. Your breath catches on certain phrases; you almost can't continue but you must. The relief of finally saying it aloud mixes with deep, aching sadness. There's beauty in this vulnerability, this unburdening. End with a kind of quiet devastation that's also freedom—you've been carrying this weight so long, and now it's both terrifying and liberating to set it down.
inspired_by: Confronting Someone While Hungover and Still Drunk

title: I Can't Protect You From This
instruction: You're a parent whose child is being destroyed by gaming addiction, and you've just found them after a terrifying crisis—maybe a health emergency, maybe a suicide attempt. You start with explosive relief that they're alive, your words tumbling out in a fierce, almost angry rush of 'thank god, thank god, thank god.' But that quickly fractures into helpless rage at the games, the industry, yourself for not seeing it sooner. Your voice should be raw, almost feral with protective fury—you want to fight something, save them, fix this. Then let it all collapse. The rage dissolves into broken, desperate pleading. You don't know how to save your child. Your voice becomes small, vulnerable, terrified. End with a whispered confession of your own fear and inadequacy, the fierceness completely stripped away, leaving only a parent's naked terror and love.

title: Whispered Goodnight to the Kitchen
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're alone in the kitchen of the restaurant you're losing tomorrow, running your hands over familiar surfaces one last time. Speak in barely more than a whisper, as if afraid to wake the memories. Begin with tender gratitude, thanking the stove, the worn cutting board, the spot by the window where morning light came in. Let your voice catch as you remember specific moments - the first dish you perfected here, the night you cried over the sink, the marriage proposal that happened by the walk-in. End with quiet, devastating acceptance, your breath uneven, saying goodbye to the dream and the version of yourself who believed in it.
inspired_by: The Chef and the Talking Ingredient

title: The Receipt
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman standing in your own kitchen, clutching a crumpled restaurant receipt you just found in your partner's jacket pocket. The date is an evening they said they were working late. Read the receipt aloud to yourself — the items, the total — as if trying to make the numbers mean something else. At first your voice is barely a whisper, stunned, repeating the date like a broken record. Then feel the jealousy creep in — a hot, small pulse — followed by a wave of helplessness as you realize you can't undo this. Let doubt crack your voice: maybe you misread, maybe there's an explanation. But by the end, your voice rises, splintering with fury as you hurl the receipt onto the table and spit out the moment you knew for sure.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Helplessness (clearly present), Doubt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Bark That Breaks
instruction: You are a middle-aged drill instructor leading a morning formation. Your voice is a clipped, rhythmic bark — no emotion, maximum volume. But inside, you're drowning in bitterness from a recent dishonorable discharge you were forced to give to your own protégé, and a deep, dull pain from old injuries. As you call out the cadence, you catch sight of a new recruit who reminds you of them. Your voice falters for a split second, you almost lose the rhythm, then force it back — but now the bark is thinner, the pain bleeding through. End with a single, softer command that betrays your exhaustion.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're a crisis negotiator who always stays calm, and you're trying to talk your own child down from a ledge. You begin with your professional voice, controlled and soothing: 'Sweetheart, let's just talk for a minute.' But your child throws your own techniques back at you—'Stop using your negotiator voice on me!'—and something in you explodes. Your carefully maintained control shatters into desperate, fierce love mixed with rage at your own helplessness. 'You think I don't know that voice is bullshit? You think I don't hate that I'm using it on you?' Your voice breaks, becomes almost violent in its intensity, then collapses completely. You're no longer a professional; you're just a parent, terrified and powerless. The fury gives way to raw begging, your voice stripped down to its most primal: 'Please. Please, baby. I can't lose you. Please.' All pretense of smoothness is gone—you're just broken and human.

title: The Thing I Never Told You
instruction: It's late at night, and you're lying in bed next to someone you love deeply. They're asleep (or you think they are). Begin whispering a confession—something you've never said aloud, perhaps something you're ashamed of, grateful for, or terrified by. Start tentatively, testing the waters of speaking this truth into the darkness. As you continue, allow yourself to follow every impulse: maybe you pause for long silences, maybe you touch their hair, maybe your whisper breaks into barely audible crying, maybe you smile while tears fall, maybe you feel relief or dread rising. Let contradictory feelings coexist. The journey is from fear of speaking to the liberation of being heard (or unhearing)—even if they never wake up. By the end, something has shifted in you from finally voicing what lived in silence.
inspired_by: Actor questions whether including an impulse in performance is appropriate or misinterprets the material

title: The Summit's Last Breath
instruction: You are an elderly mountaineer who has just reached a summit after a grueling, near-fatal climb. Your muscles are in violent, full-body tremor—your legs, arms, jaw, everything shakes uncontrollably. You collapse onto your knees, gasping, every exhale a tiny whimper. You feel a deep, aching pain in your chest and limbs, but beneath it, a fierce ecstasy surges through you—you made it, you beat the mountain. As you look at the horizon, the trembling of your body becomes the trembling of pure joy. Start with your words broken, almost sobbing from the pain and strain, then let your voice slowly fill with a hoarse, shaking pride. You are alone, speaking to the sky.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Pain (extremely present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Walk to the Garden
instruction: You are walking your grandmother to her garden for what you both know is the last time—she's too ill to return. Begin by walking naturally, as if this is any ordinary day, your body carrying the automatic rhythms of a thousand walks together. Let your body gradually become aware of what this moment means—the weight of finality seeping into your muscles, your gait, the way you hold her arm. Your steps may slow or quicken, your breath may catch, your posture may crumble or stiffen with the effort of staying strong for her. End with your body fully carrying the grief you're trying to hide, every movement betraying what you cannot say aloud. Let your physical self tell the story your words are too afraid to speak.
inspired_by: When a director manipulates actors by watching them without their knowledge to observe natural behavior

title: Thanking Someone for Leaving While Your Heart Splits Open
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who hurt you, and you need them to know—with genuine gratitude—that their leaving is the kindest thing they've ever done for you. Start with a small, real laugh, because the irony is absurd. Your voice is warm, almost affectionate, as you thank them for showing you who they really were, for leaving before they destroyed you completely. But even as you speak these true words, you're also grieving. Your voice wavers between relief and devastation. You loved them. You still love them. And their absence will save you. End with your voice splitting the difference—grateful and shattered, liberated and bereft, laughing softly through tears, your breathing unsteady as you hold two truths at once.
inspired_by: Realizing You Become Someone Different Around Specific People

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After Diagnosis
instruction: You're a child therapist who just received a terminal diagnosis. It's late at night, and you're standing over your sleeping child's bed, whispering everything you need them to know but can't say when they're awake. Begin with tender observations of their sleeping face, your voice catching with love. Move into quiet, desperate attempts to compress a lifetime of guidance into these whispered minutes. Your professional knowledge of child psychology makes this worse—you know exactly what losing a parent will do to them, and you catalog it all in aching detail. Mix your expertise with raw parental grief. Let your voice fracture and rebuild, fracture and rebuild. End with a simple 'I love you' that contains everything you'll never get to say.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen confronting your father about a betrayal you discovered years ago but never spoke about. The table between you still has the same scratches, the same coffee ring stains. Start by focusing on these physical details—the worn wood grain, the familiar smell of this room, the weight of your body in this space where you once felt small. Let these tangible elements fuel your opening words, which come out controlled, almost cold. As he responds with deflection or denial, allow the physical reality of being back in this room—where you once trusted him completely—to crack open your restraint. Your anger should build not from performance but from the collision between the safety this room once represented and the truth you now carry. End in a place of raw, unguarded pain, your voice breaking, all pretense of control abandoned.
inspired_by: Actor needs to select a choice approach for a scene but isn't sure which to use

title: The Photograph in the Haze
instruction: You are an older person, heavily sedated, sitting in a dim room. You notice an old photograph you haven’t seen in years — astonishment flickers in your eyes as you try to focus. Doubt overwhelms you: is this real or a dream? Your voice is a breathy whisper, slowing as you question the memory. Then, a wave of elation rises as you remember the love in that moment, but the sedation pulls you back, trailing off into a smile.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Doubt (very intensely present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Sugar Rush
instruction: You're slumped on a couch at a loud house party, your body heavy after three energy drinks wore off. Your voice comes out slow, flat, and resentful as you stare at the blinking lights—you feel emotionally numb, barely present. Then your best friend appears, holding a slice of cake, and asks if you want to watch the sunrise together. Let your first words drag, irritable and exhausted, but let your voice soften and lift by the end, hinting at a fragile, surprising hope. Allow natural pauses, a tired sigh, a tiny laugh—your body is crashing, but something small flickers awake.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Crack in the Concrete
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gruff voice, shuffling slowly through a trash-littered alley. The stench of rotting garbage and the sight of broken glass fill you with raw disgust and a sour bitterness about how the world has decayed. As you walk, your steps are heavy, your breathing controlled, and you mutter under your breath with a gravelly, irritated tone. Halfway down the alley, you stop and notice a single green shoot pushing up through a crack in the concrete — a fragile, stubborn sign of life. Your voice softens, gaining a trembling hopefulness, as you speak to yourself about this unexpected resilience. Let your pitch lilt gently with each slow step, and let the disgust slowly give way to a fierce, quiet optimism that cracks through your sourness like that plant through stone.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Disgust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Anthem of Everything Unsaid
instruction: You're confronting a parent who never understood you, never saw who you really are. There's a piece of music—a song, a symphony, a genre—that has always represented your true self, the part of you they dismissed or ignored. Begin angry and determined, but controlled. Tell them about this music, what it means to you, why it matters. As you describe it, let yourself hear it internally, let its power build in you. The music becomes your courage, your proof of worth. Feel how this internal soundtrack transforms your shakiness into strength, your pain into defiance. By the end, you're not asking for their approval anymore—you're declaring yourself, standing in the fullness of who you are. The music that plays in your mind becomes your manifesto. Move from wounded and seeking validation to self-possessed and unshakeable.
inspired_by: Creating a Piece of Music (Emotional Obligation)

title: The Last Time I Raise My Voice
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl, and you've just found out your younger brother has been stealing money from your mom's purse to buy vape pens for his friends. You're heartbroken, not angry. You called him into your room, and you're sitting on the edge of your bed, hands shaking, trying to keep your voice low and steady because if Mom hears, she'll break. You start by scolding him with that slow, deliberate teacher tone—each word weighted, final. But as you speak, the distress cracks through, and you feel a fierce surge of affection, because you remember he's just a scared kid. You end by pulling him into a hug, your voice breaking into a whisper, almost apologizing for being harsh. Let your voice tighten, then soften. Pause to wipe your eyes. Let the last line sound like a plea, not a punishment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Glittering Edge
instruction: You're a young child, maybe 8 or 9, sitting in the back seat of a car at night. Your mom is driving very fast and laughing, but she keeps hitting the brakes too hard. The city lights smear past the window, and she's talking about how beautiful they are, how much she loves you. But your stomach is tight. Your words come out in a jumble, your jaw feels tight like you just ate a lemon, and your mouth is dry. Start with a contented, dreamy observation about the lights, then let the fear creep in—the pitch rises, the speed accelerates as you try to make her slow down, ending in a desperate, elated plea that sounds almost happy because you don't want to scare her, even though you are terrified.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (clearly present), Fear (very intensely present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Thank-You That Hurts to Speak
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman, crouched in a tiny, dark storage closet, hugging your knees. You just overheard your colleagues in the next room mock your proudest achievement—a project you poured years into—but one person, someone you barely know, defended you so fiercely they almost got fired. Now they've left, and you're alone, body tight, breath shallow, voice muffled against your knees. Start with a shaky, proud whisper—'I don't deserve this'—as your pride wars with a rising wave of overwhelming gratitude. As you continue, let your voice crack and grow softer, more vulnerable, until the final words are almost a sob, drenched in raw thankfulness you can no longer contain.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Burning Without Fire
instruction: You're experiencing an overwhelming physical sensation—maybe intense heat without flames, maybe the feeling of drowning without water, maybe pleasure so sharp it becomes pain—and this impossible sensation is tangled with seeing someone you desire or once desired. Start by building the physical reality: Where exactly do you feel this sensation in your body? What temperature is it? Does it pulse or remain constant? What colors do you see, even if they don't make logical sense? As the physical intensity builds, let it bring up a specific encounter with this person, but don't force the memory to make narrative sense—let it be fragmented, distorted, temporally confused. The sensations and the emotional memory of this person feed each other, intensifying. Begin in pure physical experience, but as you follow the sensory thread, let it unlock rage or longing or grief that's been living in your body. End in a completely transformed emotional state—perhaps the burning becomes cooling, perhaps the desire becomes grief, perhaps the pain becomes unexpected peace.

title: Just Leave Me Alone
instruction: You're at a loud, crowded house party, heavily drunk. A friend keeps trying to guide you outside to get some air, but you're defensive and dismissive at first—sneer with contempt, brush them off with a slurred 'I'm fine.' Midway, you catch your reflection in a window and a quick wash of shame hits: you see how wrecked you look. Your voice cracks, you trail off. Then a wave of relief as you finally lean into their support and mumble a thanks. Let your words smear, your volume jump and fade, and your body sway as if the floor is tilting. React to the thumping bass, someone bumping into you, a spilled drink near your foot.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (slightly present), Shame (slightly present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Grandma's Call
instruction: You're an 82-year-old woman with a high, fluttery voice, calling 911 because your husband collapsed and isn't responding. At first you're almost hyperventilating, forcing yourself to stay calm while your breath hitches and words tumble out too fast. Midway through, you see his fingers twitch. The panic in your voice shifts—you slow down, your pitch softens, and a fragile, genuine hope creeps in as you whisper to the dispatcher that he's fighting. Let your voice tremble, speed up, then gently settle into relieved optimism.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Queen of the Bleachers
instruction: You're a teenage girl in the high school locker room, surrounded by boys joking and shoving each other after a game. You've always felt out of place with your high voice, but today you got a winning hit and they're finally including you. Start with tentative, sharp laughter as you try to match their loud banter, your words clipped and hesitant. Let your body shift weight from foot to foot, glancing around for cues. Gradually, as you recount your home run, your inflection steadies and you interrupt a guy's joke with a proud, steady declaration. End with a slight smile in your voice, your pitch still high but unwavering, showing you've earned your place.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: A Disrupted Thought
instruction: You're an older man sitting alone in a quiet room, trying to finish a crucial thought for a letter you're writing. But a persistent, wet cough keeps tearing through your chest, breaking your concentration. Start with a focused, deliberate whisper as you dictate the sentence, but each time you cough, your voice becomes raspy and strained before you try to pick up again. By the end, the coughs have worn you down—your voice is tired, resigned, and you set down the pen with a heavy sigh.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Breath of a Caged Bird
instruction: You are an elderly woman, frail and with a voice that has been softened by years, now gasping for air. Someone is pressing against your throat, pinning you to a cold wall. Your body trembles, your fingers claw uselessly at the hand that chokes you. Start with a desperate, raspy plea for release, your words cut short by the pressure. As the grip tightens, your voice cracks, each syllable a struggle, and you shift from pleading to a quiet, broken acceptance. Your final words are a whisper, laced with a lifetime of weary surrender, as your strength fades and your head droops.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're at your parent's bedside in their final hours, and you need to tell them it's okay to let go—but you don't want them to leave. Your voice starts thick with unshed tears, fighting to stay strong for them. You begin by reminiscing about a small, perfect memory, your tone warm but trembling. Then you must shift: you have to give them permission to die, even though every cell in your body is screaming to beg them to stay. Your voice cracks as you tell them they've done enough, that you'll be okay, that they can rest now. The lies and truths tangle together—you will be okay, but not yet, not now. By the end, you're whispering through quiet sobs, your love and your grief inseparable, telling them goodbye while your heart is shattering. Let the listener hear both your strength and your breaking.

title: The Empty Chair
instruction: You're a teenager sitting in a clinic waiting room after a checkup. You've been told you're fine, and a small contentment settles in your chest—you've made it through without any bad news. But now you're alone, and the doctor's clipboard reminds you of questions she asked about your home life. As you trace the edge of the paper gown, a vast longing rises up for a person you haven't seen in months—your voice starts clinical, soft, answering an unseen doctor, but it cracks as you whisper what you really miss, the final word trailing off into empty space.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire life. Start with your voice tight and controlled—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, measured, adult about it. But as you speak, decades of unmet need begin to crack through. Let your voice move from explanation to accusation to something rawer—the child inside you who needed them and never got what you needed. Then, devastatingly, let yourself hear how old they've gotten, how frail their voice sounds. Your anger must collide with the reality that time is running out, that you might never get what you came for. End in a place where fury and grief and a terrible, unwanted compassion are all present at once. You're not forgiving them, but you're facing the truth that holding onto this is destroying you more than it ever touched them.

title: The Unspeakable Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying mother's bed at 3 AM. She's unconscious, breathing shallow. For years, you've hidden your true self from her—your desires, your failures, your secret shames. Now you have one last chance to say the things you've been too afraid to speak aloud. Begin with polite, careful words, the kind you've always used with her. But as you realize she'll never wake again, let yourself break open. Say the vulgar, raw, unfiltered truth—the parts of yourself you've kept locked away. Whisper the shameful confessions, the angry accusations, the desperate love. Move from the proper, socially acceptable farewell to the naked, ugly, beautiful truth of who you really are. End with the most difficult thing you've never been able to tell her.

title: The Last Box Jump
instruction: You're mid-set on box jumps—muscles burning, breath ragged. Before the final rep, you whisper to yourself that this one counts, that you're stronger than last week. As you launch, the word 'this' escapes in a grunt, 'one' lands with a thud. You land, chest heaving, and murmur a surprised laugh at how absurdly good that felt. Start with gritty determination, end with exhausted, amused hope.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Wilted Lament
instruction: You're a teenager stranded in a sweltering car, heatstroke flickering behind your eyes. Your body is a furnace, every breath a labor, sweat stinging your lips. You're trying to speak to a crush—their image hazes through the mirage of exhaustion. Start with raw, frantic distress: throat dry, words cracking, panting between each syllable. As you picture them, let a whisper of yearning creep into your voice—a soft, surprised hum beneath the wilted ache. Let the heat pull you down, but that flicker of lust keeps you clawing for air.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unbroken Secret
instruction: You are strapped to a chair in a dimly lit room. Your torturer has just paused, frustrated. Your body is wracked with pain—every muscle screams, your throat is raw from screaming. But deep inside, you know you've won. They believe your lie; the real information is safe. Start in the aftermath of a scream—shuddering, gasping, broken. Let the pain make your words catch and crack. Then, as you speak, let a fierce, defiant triumph rise from your core. Your voice grows steadier, though still fractured, as you whisper your victory—savoring it. End with a breathy, exhausted but victorious laugh.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Caught in the Downpour
instruction: You are standing in a torrential rainstorm, completely soaked, having just run outside in the middle of an overwhelming emotional moment. Begin by fully sensing the physical reality: rain hammering your skin, water streaming down your face mixing with tears, clothes heavy and clinging, the smell of wet earth and pavement, the sound of water hitting surfaces all around you, thunder rumbling, your hair plastered to your skull. Start in a state of rage or anguish that drove you outside—you couldn't stay in that room, that building, that conversation one more second. Let your voice fight against the storm at first, yelling or sobbing, trying to release something that feels too big for your body. As the rain continues to pour over you, let the relentless physical sensation begin to shift your emotional state. The cold starts to penetrate. Your breathing changes. The rage or anguish begins to wash away or transform into something else—exhaustion, strange exhilaration, dark laughter at the absurdity, or unexpected peace. End in a place you didn't expect, possibly quieter, possibly more alive, your relationship to the storm and to yourself completely changed.

title: Therapist Breakthrough
instruction: A therapist and patient are reaching a moment of genuine breakthrough. The therapist's voice has been warm but professional. The patient's voice has been guarded. Something the therapist says lands deeply, and the patient's voice cracks. Real emotion floods out. The therapist's voice becomes even more present, more human. The patient is articulating something they've never said aloud. By the end, something has shifted. The patient's voice is raw but also lighter, as if a weight has lifted. The therapist's response is human, not clinical. Both voices acknowledge that something real happened in this room.

title: The Muffled Victory
instruction: You're a teenage boy, just after a fight where you stood up to your father but now feel ashamed of how far you went. Your hand is clamped over your mouth, partly from shock, partly to stifle a bitter laugh. Start with anger boiling in your chest—words come out muffled, teeth clenched. As you speak, a flicker of triumph surfaces, but it's warped by shame, your voice cracking and dropping low. Micro-distractions: you shift your weight, wipe your nose with your sleeve, your hand pressing harder then loosening. End with a raw, choked whisper—anger still there, but now mixed with a grim, furtive pride.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Triumph (slightly present), Anger (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Crushing the Shards
instruction: You are in a crowded office cafeteria, kneeling on the floor after knocking over a tray of coffee cups. Everyone is watching. Your boss stands over you, loudly telling you to clean it up and not make another mistake. You feel the heat of shame, the sour taste of humiliation, and a sharp disgust at your own clumsiness. As you pick up broken ceramic and wipe up coffee, your voice starts small and cracked—barely a whisper, apologetic, trailing off. But as you focus entirely on the shards, your voice hardens into a bitter, concentrated mutter—each word precise, almost as if you are talking to the mess itself, not the people watching. Let your breath catch, let your hands shake, let your eyes stay fixed on the floor.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Disgust (clearly present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're reading a beloved storybook to your child one final time before a terminal illness takes you. You begin with the familiar warmth and playfulness you've always brought to this ritual, doing the voices, making them laugh. But as you read, the weight of knowing this is the last time begins to fracture your composure. Your voice starts to catch on certain phrases that now carry unbearable significance. By the end, you're fighting to finish the final page, your voice breaking as you try to give them one last perfect memory while your heart is shattering. Let the transition from joyful parent to someone desperately trying to hold it together happen gradually, naturally, like a dam slowly cracking.
inspired_by: Acting Brave to Encourage a Child

title: Late Night Drive
instruction: You're a father driving home after a long day, with your sleepy child in the back seat. You've had a couple of beers at dinner – not drunk, but pleasantly loose, with a slight buzz that makes your words come a little slower and your thoughts wander. The car hums around you, the dashboard lights are dim, and you keep glancing in the rearview mirror at your kid's sleepy face. Start by mumbling to yourself about the traffic or the radio, letting the intoxication soften your edges and slow your speech. Then shift your focus to your child – your voice grows warmer, fuller, with a touch of deep affection as you tell them a simple, tender thing. End with a quiet, satisfied sigh, the contentment settling in your chest like the hum of the engine. Let the physicality of driving – your arms reaching forward, the slight recline of your seat, the need to project a little over the road noise – shape your vocal energy naturally.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Affection (clearly present), Contentment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Your Secret to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You're going to confess something you've never told anyone—a fear, a past trauma, a shameful desire, or a truth about your love for them that terrifies you. Start barely audibly, testing if they're truly asleep. Let the whispers grow slightly as courage builds, then retreat when fear takes over. Allow your body to express what your quiet voice contains: trembling, reaching toward them but not touching, pulling away, curling into yourself. Let the confession fracture and rebuild: start sentences, abandon them, try different words, get lost in the feeling. Include moments of gentle laughter at yourself, moments where tears come silently, moments where your breath catches. The emotional landscape shifts from terrified secrecy to tender relief to new fear to quiet liberation. End either with them stirring (do they know?) or with you finally touching their face, your secret now loose in the world.

title: The Borrowed Shirt
instruction: You are lying in bed next to someone, wearing their shirt, at 4 AM. They're asleep. You're leaving in the morning, and they don't know yet. Whisper into the darkness about all the small moments that made you fall in love: how they make coffee, the specific sound of their laugh, the way they touch your face, that Tuesday in September, that argument in the rain, that morning you knew everything had changed. Let each memory arrive with its particular sensation—temperature, texture, the exact quality of their skin, their smell. Begin with tender appreciation, but let the weight of what you're about to do seep into your voice. Your whisper should transform as you move through these fragments—from adoration to guilt to something unbearably fragile. End by saying their name in a way you'll never say it again.
inspired_by: Actor is building a complex, long-standing character relationship (e.g., father-son over decades)

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Bottle
instruction: You're standing in your parent's hospital room after their third near-fatal overdose. Start with exhausted, barely-controlled fury: 'I'm done. I'm actually done this time.' List the milestones they missed—your graduation, your wedding, the birth of their grandchild—each one landing like a punch. But halfway through, your anger cracks open and underneath is the child who's been waiting their whole life to be chosen. Your voice becomes smaller, more desperate: 'What is it about me that's not enough? What do I have to be for you to want to stay?' End with a devastating realization spoken almost to yourself: 'You're never going to choose me, are you?' The final line should be acceptance and heartbreak crystallizing in real-time. Let there be pauses where you're visibly trying to hold yourself together and failing.
inspired_by: Mother Singing to Her Stillborn Child

title: Breaking the Last Piece
instruction: You're in your kitchen, and on the counter is the last intact piece of a set—a mug, a plate, a glass—from your wedding registry. Everything else has broken over the years of your failing marriage. Your spouse has just told you they're leaving. You pick up this object, feeling its weight, its solidity. Begin speaking with it in your hands, your voice shaking with the effort of staying calm, trying to convince them to stay, or maybe telling them you've known this was coming. Let your grip tighten as your words become more desperate or angry. Feel the physical urge to smash it, to hurt something because you're hurting. Your body should be trembling with the restraint of not breaking it—or maybe you do break it, and the sound releases something violent and grief-stricken in you. Let the sensory experience—the smooth surface, the weight, the potential for destruction—merge with your emotional state. End either in collapse or in terrifying calm as you set it down intact or stare at the shards.
inspired_by: Object Bonding (Personal Relationship with Stage Objects)

title: Stopping Your Teenage Child From Walking Into Traffic
instruction: You see them step off the curb, earbuds in, oblivious to the oncoming truck. You SCREAM their name - primal, terror-ripped-from-your-chest scream - and yank them back just in time. The truck roars past. For three seconds you can't breathe, can't speak, just crushing them against you. Then the fear detonates into fury: 'What is WRONG with you?! Do you have ANY idea—' You're shaking them, shouting, voice raw and uncontrolled. Mid-rage, you shatter completely - collapse into sobbing against their shoulder, gasping 'I can't lose you, I can't, I can't.' End clinging to them like they're the only solid thing in the world, voice reduced to broken repetitions of 'You're okay, you're okay,' trying to convince yourself.
inspired_by: Parent Teaching Their Teen to Drive: Controlled Terror

title: Night Drive Euphoria
instruction: You're a teenage girl driving alone on a quiet highway after an amazing night with friends. Your body is sunk into the reclined seat, arms stretched forward on the wheel, the wind humming through cracked windows. At first you're riding a wave of pure ecstasy — your voice is bright, loud, almost laughing as you relive the best moment of the evening. Let your breath be shallow with excitement, your tone high and breathy. But as you pass a familiar landmark, the joy slowly fades into quiet contemplation. You trail off mid-sentence, your voice dropping, becoming slower and softer as you start to wonder what it all means. Let the ecstasy crack into something vulnerable — a sigh, a pause, a thought you can't quite finish.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confession in the Half-Dark
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner something you've never been able to say while they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, tender and terrified. Begin by testing the waters—'Are you awake?'—hoping they're not. Then let the truth spill out in hushed, halting phrases: you're afraid of how much you need them, how completely they could destroy you, how you sometimes sabotage things because you're terrified of this much vulnerability. Your voice catches, pauses, continues. There's intimacy in the darkness, safety in their sleep. Let your whispers carry the weight of someone finally being honest with themselves. End with a soft, devastating admission that you don't know how to be this open when they're looking at you. Make us lean in to hear your heart breaking open.

title: Returning to Rooms That Remember
instruction: You're walking through your childhood home hours after your parents signed the papers to sell it. Begin numb, going through the motions, trying to stay detached. But as you move through empty rooms, force yourself to notice: the specific way afternoon light hits the kitchen counter, the texture of the wallpaper you once traced with small fingers, the creak of that particular floorboard, the smell embedded in the walls, the exact height of the doorframe where growth marks still remain. As these sensory details accumulate, feel simultaneous emotions war inside you: relief that this chapter is closing mixed with devastating loss, gratitude for what was mixed with anger at what wasn't, freedom mixed with grief. Let your voice oscillate between laughter and tears as you speak to the empty rooms, your body caught between walking away and collapsing, unable to settle on a single feeling.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're standing in a parking lot, in the rain, screaming at someone you love because you can't protect them from the choice they're making and it's destroying you. Start with explosive fury—your voice is loud, ragged, desperate. You're saying cruel things because you're terrified, listing every reason why they're wrong, why they'll regret this, begging them not to go. Your rage is really fear in disguise, and midway through your tirade, it shatters. Your voice cracks and suddenly you're not yelling anymore—you're pleading. You're on your knees in the rain, voice breaking apart, confessing that you can't lose them, that you don't know how to let them walk into danger, that watching them choose this path feels like dying. Your fierce protectiveness collides with your utter helplessness. By the end, you're sobbing, voice hoarse and wrecked, whispering that you love them, that if this is what they need to do then you'll find a way to survive it, that you're so fucking scared but you're letting go. Let your voice shred itself, move from thunder to whisper, from rage to devastating surrender.

title: The Night That Never Ends
instruction: You are an elderly woman, sleep-deprived for over 48 hours while caring for your ill husband. A home health aide has just arrived. You sit at the kitchen table with cold tea, beginning with bitter exhaustion: resentful, sarcastic, voice frayed. Halfway through, your gaze snags on a dusty photograph on the fridge—and your tone shifts sharply to intense, almost childlike interest, as if you've just discovered a secret. Then the fatigue crushes back, your words slow, and you mutter into a hollow silence. Let your voice crack, derail mid-sentence, and occasionally forget where you are.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Bitterness (extremely present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unbearable Lightness of Truth
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father about a secret they kept from you your entire childhood—an affair, an abandonment, a sibling you never knew existed. Begin with your body coiled tight, vibrating with rage and betrayal, voice sharp and accusatory. As they respond and you hear their reasons, their pain, their own brokenness, feel your anger growing impossibly heavy, weighing you down until you can barely stand. Your fury becomes leaden, transforming into something slower, deeper, more devastating—not forgiveness, but exhausted understanding. Each accusation you hurl becomes harder to lift, until finally you are so weighted with the complexity of it all that your voice drops to something quiet, defeated, almost tender despite yourself.

title: The Photograph You Hid
instruction: Your parent has just discovered a photograph you've kept hidden for three years—evidence of a life choice you knew they could never accept. You stand across the kitchen table from them, the photograph between you. Start by truly seeing this photo: its creased edges, the faces in it, the moment it captures. Your parent demands an explanation, and you begin defensively, angry at the invasion of privacy. But as you look at their face—really see the specific lines around their eyes, the particular way they're standing, the tremor in their hands—your anger must crack open into something more vulnerable. Let yourself feel the physical presence of both the photo and your parent as you move from self-righteous fury to a desperate, aching need for them to understand and accept who you've become. End in a place of exposed, almost childlike pleading.

title: The Word That Was Almost There
instruction: You are a middle-aged man recovering from a stroke, sitting across from your adult child in a quiet living room. You desperately want to tell them something important—maybe 'I love you' or 'I'm proud of you'—but the word keeps slipping away. Start with deep frustration, your voice strained and breaking as you struggle, pausing long, searching for the right sound. As your child waits patiently, you feel a wave of contentment in their presence, and a sudden spark of interest in their encouraging eyes, allowing the word to finally come out, soft and clear, ending with a gentle, satisfied sigh.
emotions_sampled: Distress (extremely present), Contentment (very intensely present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: I'm Teaching You to Save Yourself
instruction: With explosive urgency, teach someone you love how to survive an immediate, terrible danger—but you can't save them yourself, and the helplessness is destroying you. Your voice starts commanding, almost harsh: 'Listen to me—you have to listen right now.' You're trying to compress years of protection into seconds of instruction, and the desperation makes you fierce. But as you realize they might not make it, your voice should crack and break—the teacher collapses into the terrified person who loves them. Rage at your own powerlessness: 'Why can't I just do this for you?' Then force yourself back to teaching because it's all you can give them. Let your voice carry contradictions: strength and terror, clarity and chaos, fierce instruction and broken pleas. End with your voice stripped raw, still teaching through tears, still trying to protect them with nothing but words when your whole body wants to shield them.

title: The Vigil: Holding Your Child's Hand Until Morning
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's hospital bed in the ICU, holding their small hand. Begin with quiet terror—your voice barely above a whisper, telling them stories to keep them (and yourself) calm. Your breathing is shallow, controlled, fighting panic. As monitors beep, your fear starts to crack into raw pleading: 'Please don't leave me. Not yet. Not like this.' Then something shifts—their breathing steadies, or maybe you see their eyes flutter. Hope floods through you, desperate and wild, your voice rising with almost manic gratitude. But dawn is coming, and you realize this might be the last sunrise you share. Your voice softens into something unbearably tender, mixing fierce love with the beginning of goodbye. End with you whispering a lullaby, voice breaking, as you're not sure if you're soothing them or yourself.
inspired_by: Finding Shelter in a Blizzard: Relief Becoming Hypothermia Complacency

title: Sunset After Crisis
instruction: You've just survived a catastrophic moment — a suicide attempt, a near-fatal accident, the worst day of your life. Now you're watching the sunset with someone who stayed. Your voice is soft, fragile: 'I almost didn't get to see this.' You're speaking about the sunset, but you're speaking about life. 'I almost missed all the sunsets after this one.' The person beside you is quiet. Your voice becomes more present: 'I'm still here. I'm still alive.' It's not triumphant; it's amazed, tentative. 'Thank you for staying. Thank you for loving me when I couldn't love myself.' The sunset continues, and your voice becomes quieter, more introspective: 'I don't have answers about why I'm still here. But I'm grateful.' By the time the sun disappears: 'I'm going to be okay. I think I'm actually going to be okay.' The voice of someone given a second chance.

title: The Student Becomes the Mirror
instruction: You are leaving a voicemail for your old acting coach, who you just learned is retiring in disappointment because 'none of their students made it.' You need them to know that you—their supposed failure who left theater to become a therapist—use everything they taught you every single day. Start with urgency and frustration, almost angry that they don't see their own impact. But as you describe specific moments from their class, your voice should soften with wonder and then crack with gratitude mixed with grief—grief that they measure success so narrowly they can't see they taught you how to help people open, how to listen for what's unspoken, how to honor authentic human complexity. End with your voice simultaneously celebrating them and mourning for their blindness. Let joy and heartbreak become inseparable.
inspired_by: When you question whether your decades of teaching have been worthwhile, especially for students who did not become professional actors

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father after years of feeling unseen, unvalued, maybe even unloved. Start angry—your voice tight, your words sharp, ready to finally tell them every way they failed you. But as you speak, something shifts. Maybe it's their face, maybe it's your own exhaustion, but you find yourself pivoting. Instead of listing grievances, you begin—against your own will at first—to tell them what you survived, what you built despite everything, the strength you didn't know you had. Your anger doesn't disappear entirely, but it transforms into something more complicated: a fierce declaration of your own worth, spoken directly to someone who may have made you doubt it. End with power—not the power of rage, but the power of knowing yourself.

title: The Ceiling's Patterns
instruction: You are lying flat on your back on a cold linoleum floor in an empty apartment you just moved into. Your voice is puddled, nasal from the position, slightly breathy. You're looking up at the ceiling, tracing the water stains with your eyes. You start speaking aloud to yourself, calmly noticing the shapes — a cloud, a map — but as you talk, you realize this is the first place that's truly yours after a terrible breakup. The contemplation deepens into a quiet, raw ache that settles in your chest. Don't fight the urge to breathe unevenly, to swallow, to let a sentence trail off as you lose the thought, then find it again at the end.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Storm in the Skin
instruction: You've just received devastating news and you're alone. Your body won't stay still—you pace, you press your palms against the wall, you feel your heart hammering. But this isn't just fear or grief. There's rage. There's a wild, physical need to move, to break something, to scream. Start contained, trying to hold it together, breathing through it like you've been taught. But the body won't be denied. Let the emotion move through your physical form—let your voice crack from control into rawness, let sounds emerge that aren't quite words. Mix the physical sensations with the emotional ones: your chest aches, your hands shake, there's a heat rising in you that's part fury, part desperation, part something almost primal. Build to a peak where the emotion breaks through every defense, then let it crash into exhausted, breathless clarity. End in stillness, voice raw, having moved through the storm to the quiet that follows.
inspired_by: Actor struggles with a character very different from themselves

title: Laughing at the Funeral: Finding Absurd Joy in Devastating Loss
instruction: You are at the funeral or memorial of someone you deeply loved—perhaps your closest friend, your mentor, your partner. You begin trying to share a memory, your voice respectful and sad. But as you tell the story, something shifts. You remember something absurd they did, something ridiculous. A small laugh escapes—unexpected, almost inappropriate. 'They would have hated this, actually,' you say, and there's genuine laughter in your voice now, mixed with tears. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, your voice swinging between joy at the memory and devastation at the loss. 'God, I miss you so much' comes out as half-laugh, half-sob. By the end, you've found a strange peace in the chaos of contradictory emotions, your voice settling into something tender and grateful, saying 'Thank you for every moment' with tears streaming but a genuine smile in your voice, honoring them by feeling everything at once.
inspired_by: Panic Attack: Losing Control Over Your Own Voice

title: Reading Your Deceased Sibling's Last Letter to You While Scattering Their Ashes
instruction: You're standing where they wanted their ashes scattered, reading words they wrote knowing they were dying. Begin reading their letter aloud—they're being funny, self-deprecating, so like them. You laugh, genuine and warm, reading their jokes. But the letter shifts to what they never said in life, and suddenly you're crying while still smiling at their humor. Your voice does both: breaking with grief while lilting with affection. They tell you something that changes how you see your whole childhood together. The last lines are their goodbye, and you have to speak them while simultaneously letting them go—your voice full of gratitude, devastation, laughter through tears, and the strange peace of being known completely by someone you'll never see again.
inspired_by: Confessing Long-Buried Resentment to Your Parent

title: The Bittersweet Crossing: Gratitude at the End of Everything
instruction: You have just received news that something you fought desperately for has finally come through—a visa to safety, a medical breakthrough, a dream realized—but it arrives too late to save what you've lost in the waiting, or it means leaving behind someone you cannot bring with you. Begin with genuine, almost hysterical laughter of relief and joy, thanking whoever brought the news. But the laughter keeps catching, hiccupping into something else. Your voice should oscillate wildly between celebration and grief—"Thank you" turning into sobs, moments of pure happiness fracturing into devastation. Express profound gratitude while your heart breaks completely. End in a place of impossible peace—accepting both the gift and the loss, laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice embodying the beautiful, terrible complexity of bittersweet victory. Make it messy and real—joy and sorrow so intertwined they become inseparable.
inspired_by: The Fairy and the Troll Under the Bridge

title: The Bitter Toast
instruction: You are an elderly man at a family reunion, well into your fourth whiskey. You watch your grandson being celebrated for his new promotion, and you raise your glass to join in—but your hand trembles and your words come out too loud, then too soft. Start with a forced, boisterous amusement, clapping him on the back and slurring a joke about 'the good old days.' As you speak, a pang of jealousy clouds your thoughts—you lose the thread mid-sentence, staring at the ice in your glass. Finish with a quiet, envious mutter that trails off, your laughter dying into a confused frown. Let your volume spike and drop, your tongue stumble on consonants, and your eyes wander as if searching for something you can't find.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Amusement (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Mother Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years. Start with your voice carefully controlled, almost clinical: 'I need you to hear something.' But as you describe specific moments when she chose your abuser over you, your voice begins to shake with suppressed rage. You catch yourself getting louder, then force yourself quiet—but that quiet is more devastating, loaded with years of swallowed pain. 'You knew. You had to have known.' Your voice cracks between fury and the grief of a child still wanting her mother to finally, finally choose her. End not with resolution but with the exhausted realization in your voice: she will never be the mother you needed, and you're saying goodbye to that hope forever.
inspired_by: Recognizing Abuse Pattern Repeating in New Relationship

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you years ago, and they're trying to explain their reasons—the system, the struggles, the impossibility of it all. Start listening, trying to understand, your voice measured and controlled. 'I wanted to hear your side.' But as they justify, something ignites in you. The calm shatters. 'You're making excuses about systems when I needed YOU.' Your voice escalates with each memory—birthdays missed, nights crying, the hole they left. But then you see them crying, really crying, and your rage falters. You're left with something more complicated than anger: grief for what you both lost, fury at what can't be fixed, and the terrible recognition that they're broken too. End in the quiet devastation of realizing there are no villains here, only damage.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's been unconscious for two days, and the doctors say it's time. You begin by trying to be strong, telling her practical things—that you've handled the house, called everyone, that it's all taken care. But as the room fills with morning light, something breaks open in you. Let yourself move from that controlled, helpful place into raw truth: tell her what you never said, what you were always too busy or too scared to say. By the end, you're not reporting facts anymore—you're purely present with her, no agenda, just being in this last shared moment. Your voice should travel from steady and managerial to completely unguarded and dissolved.

title: Protecting Your Child from Yourself
