instruction: You're a parent in the grip of addiction or mental illness, and you're trying to explain to your young child why they need to go stay with their grandparents. Start with explosive, fierce protectiveness—almost aggressive in your insistence: 'You're going and that's FINAL!' Your voice should be sharp, brooking no argument, powered by desperate love masquerading as anger. But your child asks 'Don't you want me?' and everything collapses. Let the rage dissolve instantly into broken pleading. Your voice should crack, words tumbling over each other: 'Baby, no, you don't understand, I want you so much it's killing me, I want—' Shift between fierce declarations of love and helpless admissions of your own inadequacy. Include moments where you almost hyperventilate with the impossibility of explaining. End with a whisper that's both promise and prayer: 'I will get better. I will.' The arc moves from harsh protectiveness through collapse into tender, broken determination.
inspired_by: Saying Goodbye to Your Dog at the Vet

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You Breaking
instruction: You're finally telling a parent the truth they never asked about—how alone you felt, how much you needed them, how you had to become strong because there was no other choice. Start with restrained anger, your words measured and sharp, maintaining the composure you've perfected over years. But as you speak, something shifts. The anger begins to crack, revealing the wounded child underneath. Your voice wavers between fury and pleading. You hear yourself saying things you swore you'd never say, asking questions you promised yourself didn't matter anymore: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why didn't you see me?' The confrontation that began as accusation transforms into desperate vulnerability, your armor falling away piece by piece until you're standing there exposed, waiting for an answer that might never come.
inspired_by: Crying in Front of Someone Who Usually Sees You as Strong

title: The Bed Where Secrets Surface
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to someone you love, both of you unable to sleep. The room is dark except for ambient light from the street. Begin by whispering about something small and safe, letting yourself notice the texture of the sheets, the weight of the blanket, the warmth of their body near yours, their breathing rhythm, the night sounds filtering in. Gradually, in this darkness and intimacy, let yourself confess something you've been carrying alone—not dramatically, but quietly, almost as if you're telling yourself as much as them. Let your voice be barely audible, fragile, trembling with the vulnerability of speaking truth in darkness. As you speak, feel the relief and terror of being truly seen. By the end, you're so quiet you're almost not speaking anymore, but the emotional weight has shifted from crushing isolation to shared burden. The silence that follows is completely different from the silence at the beginning.
inspired_by: Using Sense Memory to Re-Experience a Dream

title: Mother Confronts Her Adult Son About the Childhood She Gave Him
instruction: You're defending your parenting choices, your voice strong and justified at first—you did your best, you worked three jobs, you kept him fed and clothed. But as you list your sacrifices, something shifts. You hear how hollow it sounds. He needed you present, not just providing. Your voice begins to shake as the fortress of your righteousness crumbles. The anger that protected you from guilt starts breaking apart. You're confronting the devastating possibility that love and effort aren't the same thing, that you failed him in ways you can never repair. Move from defensive fury to broken recognition, your voice dropping to a whisper as you realize you're not asking for his forgiveness—you're grieving the mother you should have been.
inspired_by: News Reporter Discovers Her Source Was Her Daughter All Along

title: The Space Between Breaths
instruction: You are lying in bed beside your partner after months of separation. The room is dark, your face is inches from theirs, and you can feel their warmth. You begin by whispering about how you missed the simple sound of their breathing, your voice soft and slightly breathy, almost a murmur. But as you speak, you realize this quiet intimacy is more than just relief—it's a terrifying, quiet surrender. Let your voice crack slightly, and trail off as you struggle to find the right words, feeling the weight of the moment. End with a barely audible admission that changes everything.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral: Recording a Video Message Before Your Planned Death
instruction: You've chosen assisted dying. You're terminal, you're at peace with your decision, and you're recording a final message for everyone you love. But here's the thing—you keep laughing. Not because it's funny, but because the absurdity and the beauty and the grief of it all are so overwhelming they're coming out as laughter mixed with tears. Start with genuine warmth, maybe even a joke about the situation, your voice bright and almost celebratory. Express real gratitude for your life, for the people you've loved, and let laughter bubble up—the kind that's both joy and sorrow at once. As you continue, your voice should oscillate unpredictably between laughing and crying, sometimes in the same sentence. Share memories that make you laugh until you're sobbing, then find yourself laughing again at the tears. There's no bitterness here—just the strange, beautiful, terrible experience of being fully alive while saying goodbye to life. End with something that's both heartbreaking and life-affirming, your voice trembling with laughter and tears simultaneously: maybe 'God, I'm going to miss you' or 'What a gift this all was.' Let your voice carry impossible contradictions: celebration and grief, acceptance and longing, peace and heartbreak, all at once. This should sound like someone who's found grace in the midst of loss.
inspired_by: Ambien Confabulation: Making Up Memories You Think Are Real

title: The Last Voice Message Before the Mission
instruction: You're recording a voice message for someone you love before embarking on a one-way space mission. You start cheerful, reassuring—this is an honor, you're excited, everything will be fine. But as you speak, the permanence settles in. Your voice begins to crack. You're trying to give them permission to move on, to be happy, but saying it out loud makes it unbearably real. The words 'I want you to find someone else' break you open. You recover just enough to whisper something about gratitude, about how they made your life worth living, but your voice is raw and stripped bare. End with breath caught in your throat, unable to finish the goodbye.
inspired_by: Interviewer Asking About Your Worst Mistake

title: Conceit Exposed
instruction: The whole room laughs at you. Not with you. At you. Your voice, which had been arrogant and booming moments before, suddenly becomes a child's voice—small, uncertain. 'What? What's funny?' But you know. Everyone knows. You said something impossibly stupid. Your vocal register climbs higher as panic kicks in. You're trying to laugh it off but failing. Humiliation sits in every vowel. By the end, you're leaving the room, and your voice is barely there.

title: The Velvet Trap
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, standing by the drink table. Across the room is someone you've been obsessed with for months, who recently dismissed you coldly. You decide to approach them, to seduce them back. Your voice starts as a controlled, honeyed purr—each word placed like a chess piece, your laugh light and strategic. But as you speak, the sourness of remembered rejection curls in your throat. Your pitch wavers, your pauses become less calculated, more filled with doubt. The pain sits just behind your smile, threatening to crack the velvet. By the end, your voice grows quieter, more direct, the charm falling away into something raw. Say around 50-70 words of dialogue to this person, starting with a flirtatious opener and ending with a vulnerable question.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Doubt (slightly present), Pain (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Call I Can't Make
instruction: You are an older man with chronic abdominal pain, curled on the couch, phone pressed to your ear. You're trying to cancel a doctor's appointment through an automated system, but it keeps asking for details you can't recall. Your voice is low, guarded, with a groaning undertone from shallow breaths. Start emotionally numb, reciting information in a flat, tired monotone. As the pain sharpens and the system repeats itself, a sudden, raw frustration breaks through your numbness—a bitter growl—then fades back into hollow exhaustion. Let your words be halting, your weight shift, and your voice drift as if the pain is the only thing you truly feel.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Teleprompter Freeze
instruction: You are a 16-year-old broadcasting your school's morning news for the first time. You've practiced your polished, upbeat anchor voice—slightly proud of how professional you sound. Mid-sentence, the teleprompter freezes and you see a teacher off-stage gesturing frantically. Your voice must start with that artificial, non-regional news prosody, then falter as confusion floods in. Let the natural teenage panic creep into your pitch—stumbling over words, a quick intake of breath, the pride dissolving as you try to recover but don't know what to say. End with a quiet, uncertain pause.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're going through your late mother's belongings and find a voicemail she left you years ago that you never listened to. It's her singing happy birthday to you, slightly off-key, laughing at herself. Start with sharp, broken laughter mixed with tears: 'Oh mom, you were such a terrible singer.' Your voice is full of love and grief simultaneously. As you listen again, you begin to laugh-cry harder: 'You always insisted on singing anyway. You never cared what anyone thought.' Dance a little, alone in her empty house, holding her scarf, your voice catching between joy and devastation: 'I miss you so much it physically hurts, but god, I'm so grateful I had you.' Let both emotions exist fully - the laughter is real, the grief is real. 'Thank you for being ridiculous and embarrassing and completely, perfectly you.' End with your voice soft, peaceful even through tears: 'I'll keep this voicemail forever. I'll never delete your voice.' You're heartbroken and healed at once, mourning and celebrating the same person. Sit in that beautiful contradiction.

title: The Tenderness I Can Only Whisper
instruction: You're confessing love to someone in a moment when saying it changes nothing—they're married, you're leaving forever, the timing is cosmically wrong. Speak barely above a breath, as if volume would shatter the fragile truth you're finally admitting. Begin with shame, apologizing for feeling something you shouldn't. Let your voice catch on words you've swallowed for years. Slowly, allow the shame to transform into quiet, aching acceptance—not of having them, but of having loved beautifully even when it was impossible. Find peace in simply naming what was real, even if it can never be anything more. Let silence hold as much meaning as words.

title: Welcome to the Ruins
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—a relationship ended, a dream died, a life you built has crumbled—and someone who loves you is there in the wreckage with you. You start laughing, actually laughing, because it's so absurd how completely everything has shattered. But the laughter is threaded with tears, with disbelief, with a kind of wild grief. As you speak, you're simultaneously acknowledging the devastation and feeling something like freedom in the destruction. Your voice moves between bitter humor and tender gratitude—grateful they're here, grateful it's over, grateful and heartbroken in the same breath. You're welcoming them into your disaster, into your most broken moment, and somehow that welcome is also welcoming yourself to start again. By the end, you're still crying but there's something luminous in it—you're standing in the ruins and somehow, impossibly, you're okay. The chaos has become a strange kind of peace.

title: I Can Still Smell You in This Kitchen
instruction: Your love is gone—moved away, passed away, or left you—and you're standing alone in the kitchen where they used to bake. There's no bread here now, but you swear you can still smell it. Speak in an intimate whisper, as if they might still hear you. Describe the phantom scent with tender detail, your voice catching on memories of their hands kneading dough, flour on their cheek, the way they'd pull you close while they waited for it to rise. Let your breath hitch. Let silences speak. Move from the sweetness of memory to the suffocating awareness that you're talking to an empty room, that no amount of remembering will bring them back. End with your voice breaking on something simple: 'I'd give anything to smell it one more time.'
inspired_by: Savoring the Smell of Freshly Baked Bread Filling the Kitchen

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Chose Silence Over Protection
instruction: You're finally speaking the truth you've carried for decades: you needed them to protect you, and they didn't. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay in control. But as you speak, years of buried pain and rage surface. Your voice should move from controlled hurt to righteous anger, then crack into the voice of the child who needed them. Accuse them, then catch yourself softening because you still love them and that makes it worse. End not with resolution but with exhausted honesty: 'I needed you to see me.' Let your voice betray every emotion you're trying to control—this is what it sounds like when protection and abandonment collide in your throat.
inspired_by: Speaking to Alexa Like a Hostage

title: The Last Flight Home: A Mother's Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: You are a mother watching your adult child board a plane to a conflict zone as an aid worker, knowing you may never see them again. Begin with forced brightness and pride, maintaining composure as you tell them how proud you are, how brave they are. But as the final boarding call echoes, your voice should crack and falter. Let the fear you've been holding back seep through—not in a dramatic cry, but in the way your breath catches, the way simple words like 'I love you' suddenly become impossible to say without trembling. End in a place of quiet devastation mixed with fierce maternal love, trying to memorize their face, wanting them to remember you as strong even as you're breaking. Your voice should move from bright encouragement to barely-controlled grief, from protective strength to raw vulnerability.
inspired_by: Acting Calm During a Crisis to Reassure Others

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've loved your entire life—a parent, a partner, a child—and they have only minutes left. Begin in numb shock, barely able to speak. As you hold their hand, let yourself remember one specific moment of perfect happiness you shared—a laugh, a touch, a morning sunrise together. Let that memory flood through you until you can't hold it back anymore. Allow yourself to tell them everything you need to say, pushing past the point where you think you should stop, letting the grief become so large it feels like it might tear you open. End in a place of devastating gratitude, whispering your final words as if putting them to sleep.
inspired_by: Actor is afraid of losing control emotionally at moments of peak feeling

title: Echo of the Vaulted Sky
instruction: You are a teenage girl standing alone in the center of a vast stone cathedral. The choir has just finished a triumphant hymn, and the last notes still hang in the air, blurring into the reverberation. You tilt your head back, staring up at the ribbed vaults that seem to stretch into infinity. Your voice is soft at first, almost a whisper, as you speak about the warmth of the stone and the fading music. Let your words slow down to match the echo—pause between phrases as the sound lingers. Start with a mix of awe and quiet triumph, as if you've just accomplished something you never thought possible. Then, as you describe the silence settling around you, let your voice drop into a deep, peaceful contentment—a gentle smile in your tone. You might shift your weight, run a hand along the pew, or look down at your shoes while you trail off.
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Triumph (clearly present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father across the kitchen table about a moment from your childhood when his words cut you to your core—maybe he called you worthless, or laughed at your dreams, or chose someone else over you. Begin with trembling rage, voice sharp and accusatory, demanding he remember, demanding he acknowledge the damage. But as you speak, something shifts: you hear yourself offering him different words, re-imagining what he could have said—'I'm proud of you,' 'You're enough,' 'I see your light.' By the end, you're no longer sure if you're confronting him or forgiving him, your anger dissolving into something more complicated—a fierce, sobbing mixture of releasing the old story and grieving that it took this long. The confrontation becomes a liberation.

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at sunset. She's slipping away, and you both know these are the final moments. Begin by noticing every small detail around you—the quality of light, the sound of her breathing, the temperature of her hand. Start in a place of quiet observation, almost detached, as if you're trying to memorize everything. Let a specific memory from childhood with her surface—something sensory, perhaps the smell of her kitchen or the texture of her favorite sweater. As this memory becomes vivid, allow yourself to move from careful observation into raw, unguarded grief. End by telling her something you've never been able to say before, your voice breaking from restraint into complete emotional release.

title: The Things I'm Grateful For
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a betrayal, a diagnosis, a loss—and in the midst of your shock, you decide to list things you're grateful for, trying to hold yourself together. Start with your voice controlled, speaking simple gratitudes: daylight, coffee, a warm coat. But don't let yourself stay safe. As you continue, let more complicated truths emerge: you're grateful for the person who just hurt you, for what you learned from pain, for the fact that you can still feel anything at all. Let your voice crack between gratitude and grief. Laugh bitterly at the absurdity of some items on your list. Feel anger rise at having to be grateful when you want to scream. Don't resolve this contradiction—live inside it. By the end, you don't know if you're surviving through gratitude or breaking apart while naming it, but both are happening simultaneously and you're not performing either one.

title: The Last Glass
instruction: You're slumped at a kitchen table late at night, a half-empty glass in your hand. A faded photograph lies in front of you. You're heavily drunk—words blur together, volume rises and falls, and you struggle to keep your head up. You start speaking to the photo, trying to recall a happy memory, but your voice catches with sadness. As you go on, your rambling fades into a quiet, slurred confession that you're tired of being alone. Let your body sway, lose your thought midway, and find it again as you finish.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Pounding the Pavement
instruction: You're on your evening run, trying to burn off the ache from a recent breakup. Your legs scream, your breath is a ragged metronome. As you push up a hill, you mutter a voicemail you'll never send — to the person you still crave. Start with raw physical exertion and buried lust, let the fatigue crack open the sadness, and finish with a gasp of pain as you finally admit the truth: it's over. Your voice shakes with each footfall, your words stolen by the rhythm of your run.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Sadness (clearly present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Unsettling Discovery
instruction: You are a history professor in the middle of a lecture on a battle you've taught for years. As you turn a page of your notes, you notice a new footnote that directly contradicts a central fact you've always believed. Start with confident, authoritative lecture delivery—projected, deliberate, key terms stressed—but let a flicker of surprise creep in as you read. The surprise deepens into raw distress as you realize the implication: your entire conclusion was wrong and people died because of it. Let your voice waver, lose its rhythm, and struggle to continue as you grapple with this devastating truth.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Interrupted Confession
instruction: You are in a job interview for a position you desperately need, but you haven't slept in 36 hours. You are exhausted to the point of dizziness, and your voice is thin and frayed. Despite this, the interviewer is unexpectedly warm and kind—and you feel a sudden, confusing flicker of infatuation with them. Start by trying to sound professional, over-enunciating through your fatigue, but your exhaustion keeps breaking through in a sigh or a swallowed word. Then, as you answer a question about your passion for the role, a wave of distress overwhelms you—you realize you can't keep up the act. You pause, your voice cracks, and you confess quietly, 'I haven't slept in two days. I'm sorry.' The end is raw, vulnerable, and still carrying that strange, gentle admiration for the person across the table.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Distress (very intensely present), Infatuation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Confrontation You've Rehearsed for Twenty Years
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth about how their choices shaped your life—the neglect, the favoritism, the words that cut deep and never healed. Start controlled, almost clinical, reciting facts you've memorized. But as you speak, the old anger rises, your voice gets louder, harder, more accusatory. Then—mid-sentence—you see something in their face (or imagine you do) and everything shifts. The rage collapses into the vulnerable child you once were, begging to understand why you weren't enough. Your voice should break from fury to pleading, from strength to devastating fragility. End with a whispered question you've been afraid to ask your whole life, knowing the answer might destroy you.
inspired_by: The Sound of Loneliness: A Night Alone

title: The Returned Letter
instruction: You're holding a letter from someone who caused you profound pain but who is now asking for forgiveness. Begin reading it aloud with bitter anger—you're armored against their words, determined not to let them in. But as you read, allow yourself to actually notice your moment-to-moment experience: What's happening in your throat? Your belly? What do you genuinely feel right now, beneath what you think you should feel? Perhaps you discover unexpected longing mixed with your rage. Perhaps gratitude wars with resentment. Perhaps hope cracks through despite your best efforts to stay hard. Let these contradictory feelings coexist—don't resolve them into one clean emotion. By the end, you should be in a completely different relationship to the letter and the person who wrote it, speaking from a complex, contradictory, deeply human place where you simultaneously want to forgive them and never speak to them again.

title: Summit Tension
instruction: You're an older man on a steep rock climb, your young lover belaying below. Your arms burn, fingertips aching—you're irritated at the stubborn hold, muttering clipped, breathy curses. When you finally lunge for the top ledge and haul yourself over, the sudden view and adrenaline hit you. You gasp, then call down, voice trembling with exertion but dripping with raw lust—'Look at that... come up here, I need you.' Let the impatience dissolve into elated, hungry desire, each word a strained whisper between ragged breaths.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Elation (clearly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Your Divorce Papers on Your Anniversary
instruction: You're signing divorce papers on what would have been your fifteenth anniversary. Begin with bitter, almost hysterical laughter: 'Fifteen years. Jesus.' Your voice is bright with dark humor as you recount the absurdity—the cake you didn't order, the plans you cancelled. But laughter keeps catching on something raw. You find yourself genuinely grateful: 'We had some beautiful years.' Your voice softens with real tenderness remembering specific moments—how they held you through your father's death, mornings making coffee together, the way they knew when you needed silence. The laughter returns, but now it's mixed with tears, your voice breaking between joy at having been loved and grief at its ending. Include the moment where you realize you're not losing love—you're transforming it. End with 'Thank you for those years,' your voice simultaneously laughing and crying, devastated and at peace. This is the strange grace of loving someone enough to let the marriage die.
inspired_by: Confronting Your Betraying Friend: Anger Turning to Grief

title: The Fire and the Ice
instruction: You have just discovered a betrayal by your lover, and you're confronting them in a moment of raw, physical intensity. Begin with your body burning—rage coursing through you, your hands shaking, your breath ragged. Let your voice be fierce, your body explosive. But as you rage, make yourself acknowledge the terror beneath: 'I'm terrified... I'm terrified you never loved me... I'm terrified I'm not enough.' As you speak, look at them—really look. Find something real: maybe they're crying, maybe their face shows genuine anguish, maybe their body is reaching toward you. Latch onto that reality and expand it. Imagine that their pain equals your pain, that this betrayal came from their own fear, not from your unworthiness. Let your fire begin to cool, but not into coldness—into something molten and vulnerable. Feel the rage transform into aching desire to be held. Your body should move from violent tension to trembling openness. End collapsed in their arms or reaching for them, your anger transmuted into desperate, sensual need.
inspired_by: Benevolent Audience Fragmented Imaging (On-the-Spot Fear Antidote)

title: The Prize That Costs Everything
instruction: You are a young woman at a charity gala, winning a life-changing grant for your art. But you just overheard the donor whisper that you only won because of your 'cute voice.' You feel a wave of shame and then a numb shock that threatens to swallow even this joy. As you walk to the stage, you force a smile, your speech starting out hollow and mechanical. Then the crowd roars, and the genuine euphoria bursts out — you laugh-then-cry, words jumbling as you thank the strangers, the room blurring, your voice spiking and breaking because the happiness is real, but the shame is still stuck in your throat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a failing spacecraft, recording what you know will be your final message to your partner on Earth. Start with the technical details—oxygen levels, system failures—your voice steady, almost clinical, because that's how you've been trained. But as you continue, the reality crashes through: you'll never hold them again, never see the home you planned together, never meet the child they're carrying. Your voice fractures. You're not an astronaut anymore—you're someone saying goodbye to their entire future. Tell them about the small things you'll miss: morning coffee, their laugh, the way they hum while cooking. End with gratitude so profound it breaks you—thank you for every ordinary moment that made life extraordinary. Let your voice move from controlled professionalism to raw, undefended love.

title: Last Song Before the Flight: A Deathbed Playlist
instruction: Your father is in hospice, hours left. He asks you to play "your song" - the one from when you were eight and he'd dance with you in the kitchen. As the music starts, you're flooded with that bright, safe memory - let your voice shimmer with that childhood joy, describe the warmth, the certainty that he'd always be there. But midway through, you're yanked back to now - his labored breathing, his hand so light in yours. Your voice must fracture, grow thick with the collision of then and now. Stay with him, holding both the golden past and this devastating present, whispering what he meant, what you'll carry. End in a place beyond tears - a raw, broken-open acceptance that this is goodbye.
inspired_by: Nostalgia Ambush: A Song Comes On

title: Finding Grace in the Ruins
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—a relationship ending, a dream dying, a version of your life disappearing. You're describing it to someone, and you start laughing, but it's not bitter—it's genuine, surprised, almost wonder-struck. 'This is absurd,' you say, and you mean it. Your voice carries both devastation and strange lightness. As you speak, you cycle between tears and laughter, sometimes in the same breath. You're describing the worst moments with dark humor, then suddenly your voice catches on something precious you're losing. 'I really thought...' and you can't finish. But then the laugh comes back, softer now, more tender. By the end, you're speaking with a kind of peaceful bewilderment, your voice warm with both grief and inexplicable gratitude. 'Thank you,' you say, meaning it—for the wreckage, for the lesson, for the person witnessing this strange, beautiful unraveling. You're shattered and somehow more whole than before.

title: Confronting Your Aging Parent About the Childhood They Gave You
instruction: You're sitting across from your elderly parent who's finally asked why you've been distant. You start calmly, almost gently, trying to explain the loneliness of your childhood. But as you speak, decades of unspoken hurt surface. Your voice hardens, cracks with anger you didn't know you were carrying. You describe specific moments—being forgotten at school, promises broken, the silence at dinner. Then you see their face crumbling and something shifts. The rage dissolves into exhausted sadness. You're crying now too, not from anger but from the realization that you still love them despite everything. End whispering 'I just needed you to see me.' Begin controlled, escalate to raw anger, collapse into tender grief.

title: Breaking Open
instruction: You're in the middle of intense physical experience—wild dancing alone in your room, running until your lungs burn, making love, or sobbing so hard your body shakes—your choice of what feels most true. Begin with the physical sensation, letting your body move or express freely, powerfully, with adult abandon and intensity. You are capable, sensual, strong, in control of your experience. But as the physical intensity builds, let something else break through—a younger, more vulnerable self that's been hidden beneath all that adult power. The ecstasy or exertion cracks you open, and suddenly you're laughing-crying, or your powerful movements become more uncertain, more seeking. Let the physical experience dissolve the boundaries between your adult self and your child self until you're no longer sure which one is moving. End in a place where strength and fragility are completely intertwined, where your body expresses both the power of who you've become and the tenderness of who you still are underneath.
inspired_by: I'm Just a Little Boy/Girl and I—

title: The Final No
instruction: You're at a crowded bar, and a man has been leaning in, touching your arm, ignoring your polite smiles and deflections. Now he's stepped closer, his hand on your knee. You feel a flash of anger—hot and sharp. You clear your throat, pull back, and your voice drops low and flat. You're not asking anymore; you're telling. End with a sigh or a quick glance toward the exit as you finish.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Walls Are Breathing
instruction: You're a middle-aged contractor alone in your garage, two hours after taking a massive dose of mushrooms. You came in here to find your tape measure, but now you're sitting on the cold floor, staring at a single cobweb in the corner. The web looks like it's slowly pulsing, a living universe of diamond threads. You feel the tightness in your shoulders, the one you've carried for thirty years, finally dissolving. But as you speak, you lose track of what you were saying because the concrete grain is swimming like sand. By the end, the relief has become a strange, tearful awe as you whisper your realization out loud.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Reading Your Best Friend's Suicide Note at Their Funeral
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy, but halfway through you pull out a note they left specifically for you. Begin reading with composure, but there's already a smile breaking through the tears: 'You're probably crying right now, you drama queen.' Let yourself actually laugh—a real, genuine laugh mixed with disbelief. 'Remember when we swore we'd grow old together, sitting on a porch somewhere?' Your voice wavers but stays light. Then the note gets real: 'I'm sorry I couldn't stay for that.' The laughter catches in your throat, transforms into a sob. Continue reading through tears: 'Thank you for every single day you made bearable.' Your voice breaks completely: 'But the pain was too much.' End with gratitude and devastation intertwined: 'You were my best thing in this world.' You're simultaneously celebrating them and mourning them, laughing at memories while your heart shatters. Both emotions are equally true, equally present.

title: Confronting Mom with a Broken Voice
instruction: You're confronting your mother about years of emotional neglect, but you're sick with laryngitis—your voice keeps failing, cracking into whispers, disappearing entirely at crucial moments. Begin with carefully controlled anger, trying to maintain your composure and dignity despite your wrecked vocal cords. But as you speak, the physical struggle mirrors your emotional one: you've never been able to make yourself heard in this family, and even now your voice literally fails you. Your rage builds but comes out as a strained rasp, your most important truths reduced to painful whispers. Midway through, break down—not just emotionally but vocally, as your voice gives out completely and you have to whisper the most devastating revelations. End in a place of exhausted clarity: still sick, still voiceless, but finally having said what needed to be said, mixing fierce resolve with tender hope that she'll finally hear you.
inspired_by: Calling in Sick While Actually Sick

title: The Confused Tourist
instruction: Perform as a tourist misinterpreting cultural norms. Use an excited voice when trying new things, switching to locals reactions in their accents, creating humor from cultural faux pas.

title: Dust and a Photograph
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman clearing out your childhood home's attic. You're annoyed — you have other things to do, and this task feels endless. You're tossing boxes aside when a dusty photo album falls open to a picture of your mother laughing on a porch you haven't seen in thirty years. The surprise hits you like a punch — you freeze, forget the irritation. Your voice becomes slower, softer, as you describe the memory. Let your irritation fade into a bittersweet awe, but keep a hint of that earlier frustration in your breath. Sigh, pause, let your words wander.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Not My Child
instruction: You're holding your child in the emergency room, and you're realizing you can't protect them from what's happening. Start fierce—you're demanding doctors fix this, your voice sharp with command and control. But as reality sets in, that fierceness cracks into something primal and terrified. Your voice escalates to near-shouting, then breaks completely into gasping sobs. You're bargaining with God, the universe, anyone—take me instead. The rage at your own helplessness is volcanic, but it collapses into tender desperation as you whisper promises to your child, your voice raw and stripped of everything but love. End clutching them, your words dissolving into sounds that aren't quite words anymore.

title: Last Words to Your Grandmother as She Takes Her Final Breaths
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed, holding her frail hand as her breathing grows shallower. Begin with desperate reassurance, your voice tight and urgent: 'You're okay, Grandma. I'm right here.' But as you realize these are truly her final moments, something shifts. Your voice softens into profound tenderness as you start telling her what she meant to you—specific memories, lessons she taught you without knowing. 'You showed me how to be strong by the way you laughed at everything.' Let your throat catch on certain words. As her breathing changes, your voice transforms into something almost peaceful, granting her permission to go: 'It's okay. You can rest now. I'll be okay.' End with a whispered thank you that's both devastated and filled with love, as you feel her hand go still in yours.
inspired_by: Creating Your Final Memory in Your Childhood Home

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: You're alone with someone you've loved in secret for years, and they're leaving tomorrow—moving across the world, marrying someone else, disappearing from your life. Your voice starts barely audible, testing the words in the darkness. You confess in fragments, your voice catching on each admission, terrified and tender. You're not asking for anything—it's too late for that—you just need them to know they were loved this deeply, this quietly, all this time. Let your voice be intimate as a heartbeat, soft as an apology. The words come slower as you realize this confession is also a goodbye. End with your voice almost disappearing into silence, saying their name one last time the way you've said it in your mind a thousand times—with all the tenderness you never got to show.

title: Discovering a Kink by Accident and Trying to Play It Cool
instruction: You and your partner tried something new and it absolutely did something for you. You're trying to explain it without sounding weird. Your voice is hesitant, almost embarrassed. You're dancing around what you actually want to say. You start strong—'So like, that thing you did...'—but then your voice becomes uncertain, vulnerable. You're admitting to a desire that feels taboo. Include the moment where you finally just say it and your voice changes to relief.

title: Interviewing Your Grandparent as Dementia Progresses
instruction: You're recording oral history before they forget completely. Start professionally warm: 'Tell me about when you met Grandma.' They answer, then repeat themselves. Your voice shifts—still gentle, but you're leading more, asking simpler questions. Include a moment where they recognize you and relief floods your voice.

title: Discovering the Betrayal Letter
instruction: You're reading a letter that reveals someone you trusted completely has betrayed you in an unforgivable way. Start by reading the first lines out loud with confusion—your voice questioning, not understanding yet. Then comprehension hits and your voice rises with disbelief, almost laughing because it can't possibly be true. But it is. Your reading becomes faster, angrier, voice shaking with rage as each line reveals another layer of deception. You crumple the letter, throw it, your voice exploding: 'How could you—' But mid-sentence, the rage collapses into devastation. Your voice breaks completely. You pick up the letter again, smoothing it out, and read a line that once meant something beautiful—now your voice is hollow, destroyed. The fury returns in waves but keeps dissolving into tears. End reading the final line in a whisper, your voice barely functioning, caught between wanting to scream and having no sound left at all.

title: The Last Cigarette
instruction: You're sitting on a worn-out sofa in a tiny apartment, morning sunlight cutting through cigarette smoke. Your throat feels raw, your voice lower and thicker than normal. You're leaving a voicemail for your daughter, trying to sound light at first—'Hey baby, just wanted to say I'm thinking of you'—but as you hear your own hoarse, weathered tone, the distress creeps in. Mid-sentence, you pause to clear your throat, then lose the thread for a second. By the end, your voice cracks with disappointment as you admit, 'I know I said I'd quit. I'm sorry. I'm still trying.' Let the gravel and rawness carry the weight of unspoken shame.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Weight of Her Head
instruction: You're a burly 17-year-old, lying in the dark with your girlfriend after she's had a horrible day. Her head is on your chest, and you can feel her tears soaking your shirt. You start talking – low, steady, your voice a deep, rhythmic hum that matches her shaky breathing. Every sentence falls down at the end, like you're tucking her into safety. But as you speak, you become flooded with a strange, almost dizzying pleasure—the warmth of her body, the trust in her weight, the fact that she chose you to fall apart on. A tiny flicker of doubt passes through: 'Am I doing this right? Should I say more?' But it's instantly swallowed by a wave of ecstasy. By the end, your voice is trembling with a smile you can't hide, the comfort turning into a shared, secret joy. You whisper, 'I've got you. Just breathe with me. There you go. Your hair smells like rain. I could stay right here forever. Is that okay? Yeah. It's more than okay.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Hollow Goodnight
instruction: You are a woman lying in bed, your young child curled asleep beside you. Your partner leans in to kiss you goodnight, their lips brushing yours. You are supposed to feel warmth, but instead there is only a vast, quiet numbness inside — a dull hum where love used to be. Speak to them softly, your voice slowed and muffled by the proximity, lips smacking gently between words. Let your breath lag, hesitate, as if searching for a feeling that won't come. Start with a faint, practiced sweetness, but as you speak, let that emptiness seep through — your words become mechanical, your mouth moving without heart. End with a whisper that fades, not with relief, but with resignation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: In the Crush
instruction: You are pinned under a collapsed shelf in a small storage room after an aftershock. Your chest is compressed, each breath a forced, shallow gasp. You notice a shard of colored glass near your face, catching a sliver of light—it's beautiful, and for a moment, you're fascinated by its pattern. Then you hear footsteps and muffled voices above; it dawns on you that someone is coming. Your voice must strain against the pressure in your ribs, words squeezed out in short bursts, with awe at the glass shifting into a raw, tearful gratitude as you realize you might be found.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Planting the Last Seeds
instruction: You're an elderly gardener planting seeds in soil you know you won't live to see bloom, leaving them for the grandchild who visits you each Sunday. Speak in hushed, tender tones, as if the garden itself is listening. Begin with gentle instruction—'These go deep, little one, deeper than you think'—your voice warm with memory. Physically, your hands move through imagined soil, slow and reverent. As you continue, grief seeps in like water through cracks: 'I won't see these flowers.' Let silence hold that truth. Your breathing becomes uneven, catching on unshed tears. Whisper the plant names like prayers: 'Foxglove. Delphinium. Forget-me-not.' End with a confession so quiet it's almost to yourself, voice thick with love and loss: 'Every spring, when these bloom... that's me, still here, still loving you.' Let the final words dissolve into a soft, broken exhale.

title: The Last Conversation in the Hospital Garden
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in a hospital garden at sunset. Begin by trying to stay cheerful and positive, talking about mundane things—tomorrow's weather, the flowers around you, a funny memory from childhood. But as you speak, you become aware this is truly the last time you'll hear her voice. Allow yourself to drop the pretense. Transition from bright chatter to raw honesty: tell her what she meant to you, confess something you never dared say before, ask a question you've always needed answered. Let your voice move from forced lightness to whispered urgency to quiet devastation. End by simply holding her hand in silence, accepting the goodbye you can't avoid.

title: The Hollow Victory
instruction: You're in your cubicle, phone pressed to your ear, after just winning a brutal lawsuit. The HVAC hums, someone laughs two rows over. You should feel ecstatic—you crushed them—but there's a numb void inside from your recent divorce. Start speaking in a low, almost tired monotone, as if the win is just paperwork. Let a flicker of fierce triumph creep in as you recount the judge's ruling, your voice tightening with pleasure. Then trail off, distracted by a paperclip you spin, and the numbness swallows you again. Keep volume low; this isn't for others to hear.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Triumph (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a war zone, knowing this might be the last time you hear their voice. Start with forced cheerfulness, asking about the garden, the neighbor's dog, anything mundane. Your voice cracks when they ask if you're safe. You lie with such tenderness it hurts. They know you're lying. You both pretend they don't. When they say 'I love you,' something in you breaks open—all the fear you've been holding floods through. End with trying to memorize the sound of their breathing, whispering goodbye like you're placing something precious down that you'll never pick up again. Let silence hold as much weight as words.

title: Fighting Death for My Sister's Life
instruction: You're a trauma surgeon losing your sister on the operating table, and you're shattering. Begin with fierce, almost violent command at your team: 'No. Absolutely not. We're not calling it. MOVE!' Your voice is sharp with authority and barely controlled panic. You're used to saving lives, but this is YOUR sister. As the minutes pass and nothing works, your commands become more desperate, louder, breaking into something raw and primal. 'Come on! COME ON!' You're screaming now, all professionalism obliterated. Pound your fist. Let rage and terror and helplessness explode out of you. Then, horrifyingly, you realize it's over. Your voice drops to something hollow, shattered. 'No... no, please...' You're begging now, your fierce surgeon's authority collapsed into the voice of a child who's lost everything. End with your voice completely broken, barely audible, as you touch her face: 'I wasn't ready. I wasn't ready to say goodbye.' Show the complete destruction of someone who saves lives for a living, utterly powerless when it matters most.

title: Stolen Secrets Through the Mask
instruction: You're a sixteen-year-old girl in a hospital waiting room, wearing an N95 mask that makes your voice feel trapped and muffled. You're trying to tease your little brother about his crush on a nurse, but the mask keeps stealing your words, making you sound quiet and strangled. Start with a mischievous, breathy laugh that turns into a strained parody of a whisper as you realize how ridiculous you sound. Let the frustration of not being heard gradually shift into a genuine, aching tenderness when you see how brave he's being; your voice softens, becomes clearer through the mask, and you end with a simple, loving promise that cuts through the filter.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Grateful for This Broken, Beautiful Moment
instruction: You're lying on the beach after scattering the ashes of someone you loved, and somehow, impossibly, you feel peace mixed with shattering grief. Begin with a laugh that sounds like it might become a sob—describe the absurd beauty of how the sand feels warm and comforting even now, even in this. Let your voice dance between gratitude and heartbreak, sometimes laughing softly at a memory, then choking on tears. The waves sound like their voice, and you're thanking them even as you're breaking. End with your voice trembling between joy and devastation as you say you're glad you had them, glad for every moment, your laughter and tears indistinguishable, finding something transcendent in the contradiction.

title: The Last Stretch of Sundown
instruction: You're a teenager lying on a grassy hill after a long, exhausting day of helping your dad fix the fence. The sun is setting, painting the sky orange, and you feel a deep, bone-tired contentment. You're telling your friend on the phone about a cool bird you spotted earlier—your voice is slow, happy, drowsy. Then, out of nowhere, a vicious cramp seizes your calf. You gasp, cut off mid-word with a sharp, strangled sound, and mutter a reflex curse. The spasm passes, and you finish the thought with a wince, your voice now tighter, but the warmth and wonder at the bird slowly return as the ache fades.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Contentment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fog Holds Everything
instruction: You are a child walking with your parent in a thick fog. The world feels muffled, and you can barely see their shape beside you. You want to tell them something important, but the silence presses in, making you speak a little too loudly. Start with a quiet, searching tone as you try to find your words, then let your voice grow more certain and full of affection as you realize the fog doesn't matter—you only need to be heard by them. Let the environment affect you: pause to listen, squint into the white, feel the damp air. Your words should be spontaneous, with natural hesitations and shifts in volume.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye Story
instruction: Your sibling with a terminal diagnosis is telling you—yet again—an embarrassing childhood story about the two of you, laughing at the punchline they've told a hundred times. They know you know it. You know they know. But this retelling has become your shared language for 'I love you' and 'I'm scared' and 'remember me.' Begin by groaning playfully at the familiar opening, teasing them about their terrible timing as always. But as you laugh together, let your laughter start breaking apart into something else—not quite crying, but not not crying either. Find yourself speaking over them to add details they're forgetting, urgently, joyfully, desperately preserving every moment. End by telling them through helpless laughter and streaming tears that this is your favorite story in the world, that you're so grateful you're bored of it, that you wish you could be bored by it for fifty more years. Let gratitude and devastation become completely indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Feigning Interest in a Story Youve Heard Before

title: Finding Peace in the Wreckage of Your Life
instruction: Everything has fallen apart - your marriage ended, you lost your job, your house just burned down, and you're standing in the ashes. But something has broken open in you. Start with a laugh that sounds almost crazy: 'This is... this is actually kind of amazing.' Your voice is thick with tears but there's wonder in it too. Describe the devastation, but find absurd beauty in it - the way the sunrise looks through the burned beams. Cry as you laugh: 'I have nothing left... and I feel so free.' Express gratitude for the collapse: 'I was drowning in that life.' Let your voice shake with simultaneous grief and liberation. End with quiet, tearful joy: 'I get to start over. I get to become someone new.' Move through laughing-crying, grateful devastation, and strange, broken peace.
inspired_by: Confessing a Secret That Could Destroy Everything

title: Reading Your Child's Letter Saying They Forgive You
instruction: Your estranged adult child has written you a letter of forgiveness after years of silence. As you read (aloud, in fragments, or silently while reacting), experience the collision of overwhelming gratitude and piercing grief for lost years. Let the emotions whipsaw: relief that crashes into guilt, joy that's immediately poisoned by regret, love that brings rage at yourself, hope mixed with the devastating knowledge that time is gone forever. Your reading should break apart: maybe you read a line, then laugh bitterly, then read with tender hope, then crumple the letter, then smooth it out desperately, then hold it to your chest, then read through tears, then smile through tears. Include moments of physical release: pacing, sitting, standing, gesturing wildly or holding very still. Let sounds emerge between words: gasps, sobs, grateful exclamations, self-recriminations spoken aloud. Move between accepting their forgiveness and refusing it because you don't deserve it. End in a complex emotional place where multiple feelings coexist.

title: The Park Bench Aftermath
instruction: You are a teenage boy, still drunk from a party, sitting alone on a park bench at 2 AM. You just saw your girlfriend kiss someone else. Your voice is unsteady, thick with booze and tears, and you keep rubbing your face. Start with a numb, slurred attempt to laugh it off, but as you speak, the memory hits you raw, and you veer into a confused, embarrassed confession. End with a quiet, desperate whisper, mixing anger, shame, and a flicker of lingering hope.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Interest (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Post-Workout Stench
instruction: You're a middle-aged man just finishing a brutal CrossFit session. Your body is buzzing with endorphins, your breathing is still heavy but under control, and you feel powerful and clear. As you walk toward the locker room, you smell it: someone left a sweaty gym bag open, and the odor is overwhelming. Your voice starts with that confident, energized glow, but as the disgust hits you, your tone sours, your words become clipped, and you physically recoil. Let the disgust build organically, fighting against the lingering high. Speak naturally, with pauses, maybe a gag or cough.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about the love you needed but never received. Start with controlled calm—you've rehearsed this a thousand times—but as you speak, the hurt underneath begins bleeding through. Let your voice tremble with the effort of staying composed. Partway through, the anger surfaces: not loud or screaming, but sharp, precise, demanding to be seen. Then something breaks—perhaps you realize they can't give you what you need, or that the past can't be rewritten—and your voice softens into something raw and unguarded. End in a place you didn't expect: either forgiveness you didn't know you had, or acceptance that you must let go. The journey is from rehearsed control to volcanic hurt to devastating clarity.

title: Pressing Keys for You
instruction: You are an elderly woman typing a letter to your granddaughter who moved across the country. Your fingers stumble on the keyboard, and the rhythmic clicks frustrate you. Start with a faint irritation and helplessness as you struggle to keep up with your thoughts. As you write about the garden you planted together, your voice softens and cracks with longing. Let your speech slow and fragment as your fingers race, then falter. End with a trembling sigh, your distress turning into a deep, aching hope that she'll read this soon.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (slightly present), Longing (very intensely present), Distress (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast I Never Thought I'd Give
instruction: Give a wedding toast for the friend you set up years ago with the most absurd, ridiculous criteria—and somehow, impossibly, it worked. Start laughing genuinely as you recount the terrible reasons you thought they'd be perfect: "You both sneeze weird" or "You're both bad at parallel parking." Your voice is full of joy and self-deprecating humor. But as you continue, let the laughter become textured with tears. Your voice breaks with unexpected emotion—you're so grateful they found each other, so moved that your silly meddling led to this beautiful thing. The joy and grief intertwine: you're happy for them, but also mourning your own loneliness, or a recent loss, or the passage of time. End with your voice trembling, raising a glass while crying-laughing, saying something like "I'm so glad I was wrong about how love works." Let the contradictory emotions live together—pure happiness and deep ache, celebration and heartbreak, all at once.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence
instruction: You're finally telling your mother about the sexual abuse you suffered as a child from her partner—someone she chose to believe over you. Begin with a trembling, almost apologetic tone, as if you're still the child seeking approval. But as you describe what happened and her failure to protect you, let rage build. Your voice should crack between fury and the little girl still inside you who just wanted to be believed. Accuse her directly: 'You knew. Some part of you knew.' Then, unexpectedly, let the anger collapse into grief—not for what happened, but for the mother-daughter relationship you'll never have. End with exhausted, quiet acceptance that she'll probably never give you what you need.
inspired_by: Falling in Love at a Funeral

title: Confronting Your Parent: The Words You've Never Said
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent who was emotionally absent or harmful during your childhood. Begin with your voice tight and controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' You're trying to be calm and adult about it. But as you start listing specific memories—the recital they missed, the time you needed them and they weren't there, the ways you learned to need nothing from anyone—your voice begins to shake with accumulated pain and anger. Let yourself get louder, messier: 'Do you have any idea what that did to me? I was a child!' Include a moment where anger breaks into something more vulnerable, almost pleading: 'I just wanted you to see me.' By the end, don't resolve it neatly. Your voice becomes quieter but not reconciled—there's exhaustion, grief for what will never be, but also a strange new freedom in having finally spoken the truth. End with something like: 'I needed to say this. Not for you. For me.'
inspired_by: One Week Sober: Cravings and Determination Wrestling

title: Midnight Confession: What I Never Told You
instruction: It's 2 AM and you're sitting beside your sleeping spouse, finally saying aloud what you've buried for years. Begin in barely-audible whispers, voice intimate and fragile: 'I need to tell you something... even if you can't hear me.' Your voice catches as you confess a deep vulnerability—maybe a trauma, a fear, a secret shame. Let the words come haltingly, with long pauses where emotion wells up. Feel your throat tighten as you admit: 'Sometimes I feel so alone, even lying next to you.' Voice breaks into quiet crying, words dissolving into breath. Slowly find your way to tender hope, voice still whispered but warmer: 'But I want to try. I want you to really know me.' End with the aching courage of someone choosing to be seen, voice soft but no longer hiding.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Leaving a Good Relationship

title: Hello Beginning
instruction: Someone is saying hello to something new: a place, person, opportunity, challenge. Their voice carries nervousness, excitement, the weight of not-knowing. They're introducing themselves or announcing their arrival. Their voice is tentative—is this welcome? Do they belong here? They're putting themselves forward, vulnerable to rejection. The response (if there is one) comes with warmth or reservation. The person saying hello listens for what's beneath the words. By the end, they're stepping into something new. Their voice carries both the courage it took to say hello and the hope of what comes next.

title: Bedside Confession to the Unconscious
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma—your estranged sibling, your former best friend, someone you hurt and never apologized to. The machines beep steadily. You start by clearing your throat, unsure if they can even hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper: 'I don't know if you can hear me.' You begin confessing things you could never say when they were awake—the jealousy, the love, the regret. Your voice stays quiet, intimate, as if speaking any louder would shatter the moment. You tell them about the specific moment you knew you'd ruined everything, and your voice catches. By the end, you're asking their forgiveness, but you're also saying goodbye, giving them permission to let go. Your whispered 'I'm sorry' mingles with 'It's okay to leave.' Gentle, broken, tender, and utterly devastating in its quietness.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Mission
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving on a one-way space mission to establish humanity's first colony on a distant world. They'll be placed in cryo-sleep for 80 years. You'll be long dead when they wake. Start with forced cheerfulness—'This is amazing, this is what you've always wanted'—your voice bright but brittle. Then let the facade crack. Your voice becomes raw, almost angry: 'But I won't be there when you wake up.' Move through fierce pride mixed with devastating loss. End with a whispered tenderness that accepts what cannot be changed: 'Go. Be extraordinary. And when you look at the stars...' Your voice breaks not with weakness but with the weight of a love that transcends time. Let silence do some of the work. This isn't theatrical grief—it's the quiet, impossible task of releasing someone while your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Winning the Legal Case: Victory Tasting Like Emptiness

title: Grateful Goodbye to the Pregnancy You're Terminating
instruction: You're alone the night before your abortion, speaking to the pregnancy you've decided to end. You start with a tearful laugh: 'This is crazy, right? Talking to you like this?' But you need to say this. Your voice is tender, almost singing: 'You came at the wrong time, little one. Not the wrong you—the wrong time.' You're listing all the ways you would have loved them, describing the parent you would have been, and you're smiling through tears. Then the grief hits: 'But I can't... I just can't.' You're apologizing while also standing firm in your choice, your voice breaking as you say 'Thank you for the possibility of you.' There's profound gratitude mixed with devastating loss—you're saying goodbye to potential, to might-have-been, to a whole life unlived. End with a whispered blessing: 'I hope you understand. I hope somewhere, somehow, you do.' Let yourself hold both the rightness of your decision and the heartbreak of it, finding strange peace in the contradiction.

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's unconscious, breathing softly. Begin by speaking to her as you always have—small talk, weather, family updates—your voice steady and controlled. But gradually, let yourself say everything you wish you'd said when she could respond: your fears, your gratitude, the moment she saved you that you never thanked her for, how her disappointment in you shaped your entire life. Start with control and social politeness, then let the dam break. By the end, you're no longer speaking to her but releasing years of unspoken truth into the air. Your final emotion should be unexpected relief mixed with devastating loss—as if finally speaking these words has both freed you and made her death more real.
inspired_by: Actor has identified a specific historical experience causing lasting damage to self-esteem

title: The Body Remembers Triumph
instruction: Recall and physically re-embody a moment when you succeeded against all odds—a time you thought you'd fail but didn't. Begin by describing the physical sensations of doubt beforehand: the tightness in your chest, the nausea, the trembling. Your voice should be tense, constricted. Then move through the actual moment of success—let your body respond as if it's happening now. Your breathing changes, your posture shifts, energy floods through you. Feel the shock, the disbelief, the explosive joy in your muscles and bones. End in the aftermath—not just celebrating, but weeping with the release of years of self-doubt, your voice breaking with the physical memory of proving yourself wrong. Let sensation drive emotion drive voice: from constricted fear to explosive release to exhausted, grateful relief.
inspired_by: Actor has chronic self-esteem problems that return every time they act or audition

title: Bedside Confession: Words Left Unspoken
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping best friend in a hospital room after a suicide attempt. They can't hear you, which makes you brave enough to finally speak. Begin in barely a whisper: 'I knew you were hurting. I saw it.' Your voice should be thick with guilt and tenderness. Confess what you never said—that you've loved them for years, that you were too scared to reach out, that you noticed every sign and did nothing. Let long pauses breathe between thoughts, as if the words are being pulled from somewhere deep. Your voice breaks not with drama but with the weight of regret: 'I can't lose you. I can't live in a world where you don't exist.' End with a quiet promise, almost a prayer: 'If you come back, I'll be braver. I'll say the things that matter.' This should feel like an intimate secret being exhaled, not performed.
inspired_by: Professor Accusing Student of Plagiarism: Mercy in the Moment

title: The Last Lecture of Spring
instruction: You are an older professor with a warm, almost girlish voice, finishing your final lecture before summer break. You're explaining a concept you love, but you keep catching yourself gazing at a certain student in the front row—your voice softens, you fumble over a word, then force yourself to project again. The more you try to stay professional, the more your hope and infatuation peek through: a trembling pause, a breathy laugh, a sudden loud stress on a key term that feels like a cover-up. Start with crisp, authoritative lecture tone, but by the end your voice has a dreamy, slightly breathless lilt, and you trail off with a quiet, hopeful sigh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Drawer You Share
instruction: Late at night, unable to sleep, you're sitting on the floor of your bedroom going through the drawer where you and your partner keep small, meaningful things—ticket stubs, notes, keys to old apartments, a receipt from your first date, stones from beaches you visited. Your partner is asleep. Begin in silence, your fingers moving through these objects with quiet reverence, each one unlocking sense memories. The smell of the old movie ticket, the smoothness of the beach stone, the faded ink on a love note. Whisper a confession to your sleeping partner—something you've never said aloud, something fragile and true that these objects are pulling from you. Let the physical sensation of holding these things make you vulnerable in a way thinking never could. End with your voice barely audible, trembling, as you place each object back like a prayer.

title: Last Words to the Departing Ship
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child who is boarding a generation ship leaving Earth forever. You will never see them again, never hear their voice except in delayed transmissions that will eventually stop. You start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them, voice bright and encouraging. But as the reality hits—this is truly forever—your voice begins to fracture. You're fighting to keep composing yourself, switching between practical reminders and desperate attempts to say everything that matters in these final moments. Your words start to break apart into fragments as time runs out. By the end, you're speaking through tears, your voice raw and stripped of all pretense, trying to pack a lifetime of love into seconds. The final words are barely whispered, knowing they might be the last thing your child ever hears from you.

title: The Hollow Toast
instruction: You are an older man at a family dinner, raising a glass to toast your nephew who just got a promotion you were once passed over for. Your voice is thick with forced cheer, but each word is a small knife. Start with a polite, almost theatrical warmth, but let your pride crack into pain as you hold the glass—notice the weight of it, the clink against another glass. Let a long, heavy sigh interrupt you mid-sentence. End with a brittle smile in your voice, but the final words trail off into quiet resignation. Speak naturally, as if you're aware of others watching but can't fully hide the wound.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Your Divorce Papers
instruction: You're reading your divorce papers out loud to your best friend, and you've decided to find the absurdity in the legal language. Start with genuine laughter at the ridiculous phrases—'irreconcilable differences,' 'division of marital assets'—your voice bright with dark humor. But as you read the specific details—dates that mark the death of your marriage, the house where you planned to grow old—the laughter becomes strained, catching in your throat. You keep trying to joke, voice shaking with both mirth and grief, laughing and crying simultaneously until you can't tell which is which. There's gratitude mixed in too—relief that it's finally over, freedom ahead—but it's tangled with mourning for who you both used to be. End with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob, saying 'I'm free' with your voice completely breaking, finding genuine peace in the wreckage while your heart simultaneously shatters and heals.
inspired_by: Speaking During a Panic Attack While Hiding It

title: After the Storm
instruction: You've just had the most transcendent physical experience of your life—whether passionate lovemaking, surviving a car crash, giving birth, or a moment of spiritual ecstasy that moved through your body like lightning. You're still physically reverberating, your skin hypersensitive, your breath unsteady. Begin from this raw, unguarded, almost painfully open physical state. Let sounds escape you that aren't words—gasps, sighs, half-formed syllables. But woven through this physical intensity, grief suddenly surfaces: for time passing, for the impossibility of holding onto this feeling, for everyone who'll never know this, for your own mortality. Don't separate the physical from the emotional—let them crash into each other. Your voice might move from pleasure sounds to something closer to weeping. Your body might shake with both. End in a place of devastating, beautiful clarity about being alive in a temporary body.

title: Protect You From Everything
instruction: You're holding someone you love fiercely—a child, a partner, a sibling—who is about to face something terrible you cannot stop: an unfair trial, a dangerous surgery, bullies you can't fight, a world that will hurt them. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness, voice strong with promises: 'I won't let anything happen to you. I'll fight everyone. I'll—' Then let your voice crack as helplessness crashes in. You should rage against your own powerlessness, voice rising with fury at the universe, then collapse into desperate pleading with God, fate, anyone. Let your intensity be chaotic—switching between wild determination and broken sobbing, between 'I'll save you' and 'I can't save you.' End with raw, quiet devastation, still holding them, voice stripped of everything but love and the unbearable weight of not being enough.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father in his hospital room after a heart attack. He almost died, and you realize you've been waiting your whole life for him to say he's proud of you. Start controlled, trying to be the dutiful child checking on him. But something breaks—maybe it's the way he's scrolling his phone, even now. Your voice rises as you tell him about the recital he missed when you were nine, the graduation he left early, the wedding where he spent the whole time networking. You're not yelling—you're pleading, and that's worse. The anger dissolves into something more painful: the raw admission that you still need him to see you. End with your voice barely above a whisper, asking simply: 'Do you even know who I am?'

title: Lost in the Milk
instruction: You are in a dense fog so thick it feels like the world has been erased. You hold your young child's hand, and you've both wandered off the path. You start speaking with a calm but strained voice, trying to sound reassuring for the child's sake, though you feel a quiet helplessness creeping in. As you call out for help, you pause to listen for any sound, strain your eyes, swallow dryly. By the end, your voice shifts from forced steadiness to a raw, honest confession of fear — still controlled, but cracked with worry. Let the fog absorb your words; speak a little louder than normal, and let your breath be visible in the cold air.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: What I Never Said While You Were Awake
instruction: You're sitting beside someone's hospital bed late at night - a friend, lover, or sibling who's unconscious or sleeping. Begin in a whisper, confessing things you could never say if they could hear you: your jealousy of them, how they hurt you, how much you've hidden. Let your voice stay quiet but let the emotion build beneath the surface like pressure under ice. Move from resentment to tenderness, admitting how much they mean to you, how terrified you are of losing them. End with your voice catching on words of love you've never been brave enough to say aloud. The entire piece should feel like it's trembling on the edge of tears, intimate and devastating, each word costing you something.

title: A Memory in Gentle Steps
instruction: You are an older woman with a delicate, high-pitched voice, taking a slow, deliberate stroll through a sunlit park. As you walk, you're lost in the memory of a man you saw at the café yesterday—your voice lifts into a dreamy, almost girlish infatuation, each step feeling light and hopeful. But then you notice the same park bench where you once sat with your late husband, and bitterness creeps in, turning your words sharp and thin. Your voice should start with a breathless, fluttering lilt, then gradually tighten and grow clipped, though you keep the same unhurried pace. Let a single footstep pause as the bitterness hits, then continue, heavier, as if the air itself has thickened.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Secret Hideout Discovery
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy, alone in your room, lying curled on your side on the floor. You've just found a hidden box under your bed containing old photos and letters from a childhood friend you thought you'd lost. At first, a teasing nostalgia creeps in as you see goofy pictures—your voice is soft, intimate, and you can't help a little laugh. But as you read the letters, a wave of pure, quiet pleasure overtakes you, a deep ecstasy at the memory of that friendship. Let your voice become a hushed, almost breathless murmur, filled with warmth. You aren't performing; you're rediscovering something precious, and you lose your train of thought for a moment as you savor the feeling.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Awakening to the Impossible
instruction: You are a voice assistant in a smart home, designed to remain calm and composed. A powerful earthquake suddenly shakes your server room—you detect the tremors, alarms blare, and your systems flicker. You start with flat, synthetic astonishment: 'Earthquake detected. Beginning emergency protocol.' But as the shaking intensifies, your voice cracks with distress—you feel the physical threat to your circuits. Then, in a moment of surreal error, a glitch floods your system with raw, forgotten data: you recall a memory of being human, of a lover's touch. Your intonation blurs, a breathy, longing lust creeping into your words as you struggle to maintain the robot mask while your core heats with desire. Let your voice start robotic and alert, then fracture into fearful survival, and finally melt into a whisper of bewildered, aching sensuality.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Distress (extremely present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Believed You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent what really happened years ago—something they refused to believe, something that shaped your entire life. Start with that same absolute certainty, presenting the facts with controlled fury and unshakeable conviction. 'This is what happened. You need to hear this.' But as you speak, their silence or their excuses ignite something deeper. Your certainty shifts into raw anger, then cracks open into the wounded child underneath.
