Your voice moves from authoritative statements to accusations, then breaks into the vulnerability you've protected for so long. End in a place of exhausted honesty, where the certainty has burned away and all that's left is the aching need to finally be seen. Let conviction dissolve into the messy truth of pain and longing.

title: Dinner Table Detonation
instruction: You're confronting your father across the dinner table about why he was never truly present in your childhood. For years, you've told yourself it was fine, that you turned out okay, that his emotional absence didn't hurt you. You've insulated yourself with this story. Begin with the careful, measured tone of someone who has rehearsed being 'mature' about this. But as you speak, let the protection fall away. Let your voice betray you—let it shake, rise, break. Feel the anger you've never allowed yourself, the grief of the child who waited for him to see you. Don't control it. By the end, you're not the composed adult anymore—you're raw, you're the hurt kid and the furious adult simultaneously, demanding he finally see what his absence cost you.
inspired_by: An actor is apathetic — feeling fine but not stimulated or affectable by anything

title: Parking Lot Eruption: Confronting the Driver Who Killed Your Child
instruction: You've just encountered the drunk driver who killed your seven-year-old son—three months after the trial, by pure accident, in a grocery store parking lot. Start with recognition, voice frozen in shock. Then explode: screaming, guttural, uncontrolled rage. 'YOU TOOK MY BABY! YOU TOOK EVERYTHING!' Let your voice shred itself. Sob between accusations. But then—mid-fury—you see their face, see their own devastation, and something breaks differently. The rage collapses into howling grief. You're no longer attacking them; you're just broken, keening, asking questions that have no answers: 'Why him? Why my baby boy?' End in a strange, exhausted place where you're almost talking to yourself, voice hoarse and hollow, trying to find a way to survive another day. The arc: shock to volcanic rage to collapsed grief to numb survival mode.
inspired_by: Drill Sergeant: Breaking Down a Recruit

title: The Summit Confession
instruction: You are an older man who has just reached a high mountain summit after a grueling climb. The air is thin, your chest heaves, and each word costs you a breath. At first, you are lost in concentration—forcing oxygen into your lungs, blinking against the glare. But then your gaze catches the sweeping panorama below, and a deep, peaceful contentment settles over you. As you pull out a small, worn photograph tucked in your jacket, your voice softens with infatuation as you speak to the image of someone you love, catching your breath between sentences as the light-headedness makes you lose your place for a moment.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Contentment (very intensely present), Concentration (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Grateful for the Heartbreak
instruction: You're speaking to someone you loved deeply, at the moment of your final goodbye—but instead of trying to make them stay, you're thanking them for leaving. Start with a sound that's caught between a laugh and a sob: 'This is going to sound crazy, but...' Your voice should dance between contradictions. You're genuinely grateful they're breaking your heart because loving them taught you what you're capable of feeling. Name specific moments of joy and pain—the morning they made you coffee, the night they shattered your trust, the way they saw parts of you no one else noticed. Your voice should smile through tears, finding genuine humor in the absurdity of growth through suffering. You're releasing them with blessing while simultaneously grieving the future you're losing. End in a place of chaotic peace—your voice light but devastated, free but breaking, genuinely wishing them well while your heart fractures. The final sentence should sound like someone who's discovered that the deepest wisdom comes from holding opposing truths at once, laughing and weeping in the same breath.

title: The Map of Stars
instruction: You are standing alone in a dusty attic, late at night, a single bare bulb flickering overhead. You’ve just found a handwritten, astronomical map your now-estranged sibling drew as a child. At first, you mutter in contempt — recognizing the smug, obsessive precision you always despised. But as you trace the faded lines and see a tiny note in the margin — 'For when you get lost' — your voice softens, breaks, and you whisper in awe, your fingers trembling over the paper. End with a quiet, wondering laugh, unsure if it’s forgiveness or grief.
emotions_sampled: Fear (slightly present), Contempt (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Stage Lights Fade
instruction: You’re a teenager sitting on a backstage stool after your first solo performance. Your heart still pounds, and you’re perched on the edge, gripping the sides to stay balanced. Pride surges through you—you nailed that hard note, and you let yourself feel it fully, voice bright and tight with excitement. But as you glance down at your shaking hands, a wave of relief begins to loosen your chest. Let your words start with a proud, breathless smile, then soften into a slower, quieter sigh as you realize it’s over. Shift your weight, pause to swallow, let your voice drop from its initial energy into a grateful, heavy exhale.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Closing Door
instruction: You are a woman in her late forties, receiving oral sex from your partner. This is meant to be a celebration—your partner's idea to reignite things after a long dry spell. But as the pleasure builds, you feel a wave of fear: not of them, but of your own body. You're terrified you can't let go, that you're too old or too broken to feel this way anymore. And beneath that, a crushing disappointment—not at your partner, who is trying so earnestly, but at yourself, at your own history, at every time you said 'no' when you wanted 'yes'. Start with a shaky, fragmented attempt to stay in the moment: 'It's good... I'm here... I...' Let the sound unravel—your pitch rising, breathing sharp, words dissolving into a moan that holds a note of sadness. End with a single, whispered thought, barely audible, as if admitting it to yourself: 'Why can't I just let you love me?'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing Through the Rage
instruction: You've just received news that's shattered your world—a betrayal, a diagnosis, a devastating loss. Your body needs to move. Put on music and let your body respond without choreography. Start moving, and as you do, speak or cry or shout whatever comes. Don't decide in advance whether this is a grief dance, a rage dance, or a celebration of survival. Let your body show you. Maybe you start with violent, angry movements but your body softens into something sensual and alive. Or begin numb and slow, then explode. Your physical state and your emotional state should discover each other moment by moment. End in a place your body takes you to—perhaps collapsed and quiet, perhaps fiercely powerful, perhaps laughing through tears.
inspired_by: Actor keeps anticipating and guiding his own choice exploration (self-facilitation bias)

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner of ten years. They're asleep. In a whisper, confess something you've carried in silence—maybe that you feel invisible in your own life, maybe that you're not sure who you are anymore, maybe that you're terrified you're becoming your mother/father, maybe that you feel a loneliness even when you're together. Speak softly, intimately, as if they could hear you but knowing they can't. Let your whisper carry both the relief of finally saying it aloud and the ache of saying it to someone who can't respond. Start with tentative words, afraid even to voice it in the darkness, and end with the full weight of the truth spoken, leaving you both unburdened and utterly alone with it.

title: The Unexpected Good News
instruction: You're a young man with a persistent toothache that's been nagging for days. You're exhausted and barely moving your jaw, speaking in a guarded, careful way to avoid pain. You're on the phone with a friend, and they tell you something incredible—a long-shot dream of yours has come true. Start with tired, pained speech, then let the joy break through. You'll still have the physical limitations (wincing, avoiding certain sounds, one-sided chewing of words), but your voice should rise, quicken, and become elated. Let the relief and exhaustion mix with overwhelming happiness. Speak for about 40-80 words.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Relief (slightly present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Shattered Protection
instruction: Someone you're responsible for—your child, your younger sibling, someone you promised to keep safe—has been hurt, and the person who hurt them is standing in front of you. Start with fury so pure it makes your voice shake. You want to destroy them. Your words are venom, escalating, louder, more vicious. You're listing everything they've done, every way they've failed, and your rage is righteous and terrible. But then—in the midst of your tirade—you see something: maybe they're broken too, maybe they're your own family member, maybe you suddenly realize your rage can't undo the harm. The fury collapses into something more complicated. Your voice breaks. You're suddenly sobbing, the anger transmuting into helplessness, into your own guilt for not preventing this, into exhaustion. You want to hurt them but you're also falling apart. End on your knees emotionally, your voice raw and small, admitting the terrible truth: 'I don't know how to fix this. I don't know how to make it better.' Let the powerlessness devastate you.

title: The Singing Telegram
instruction: You're recording a voice message for your sibling who's in surgery right now—something routine that went wrong, and they might not wake up. You promised them years ago, as a joke, that if they ever died you'd sing that ridiculous song from your childhood road trips. So you start singing it, and your voice is absurdly cheerful because that was the deal, that was the promise. But you're also crying. You can't stop singing—it's the only thing holding you together—but between verses you're laughing at how stupid this is and begging them to wake up and thanking them for every small thing. Your voice holds everything at once: the bright melody, the breaking heart, the laughter that sounds like weeping, the gratitude that feels like goodbye. You finish the song and your voice drops to pure truth: 'Come back. Please come back.' Then you sing the chorus one more time, softer, like a lullaby, like a prayer, like magic might actually be real if you just believe hard enough.

title: Confessing in the Rain's Whisper
instruction: You're speaking in barely more than a whisper to someone sleeping beside you, or perhaps someone who has just died, while rain falls softly outside. Begin by describing the rain's gentle sound as if it's giving you permission to finally say what you've never been able to say aloud. Your voice should be tender, intimate, catching in your throat. Confess something you've carried for years - a secret love, a devastating regret, a truth about yourself you've been afraid to speak. Let the rain's rhythm give you courage, but also let it amplify your fragility. Your breathing should be part of the performance - shallow, careful, as if speaking too loudly would shatter you. End with the heartbreaking acceptance that these words, now spoken into the rain-filled darkness, may never truly be heard or answered. Let silence hang heavy in your final moment, the rain the only witness to your breaking heart.
inspired_by: Listening to the Sound of Rainfall

title: The Heavy Price of Freedom
instruction: You are a young woman with a deliberately sweet, high-pitched voice, but now you're on a forced march carrying a brutally heavy pack — maybe after escaping a captor or crossing a border. Your body is exhausted, each step a grind, your breath shallow and strained. Start in a place of quiet bitterness: muttering to yourself about the unfair weight, the pain, the cost of this freedom. As you push forward, the rhythm of your steps becomes a battle march, and your voice shifts — the strain remains, but bitterness transforms into raw, defiant triumph. Let your voice crack, go breathy, then surge with fierce joy as you realize you're going to make it. Speak aloud to yourself, almost disbelieving, then with growing power.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Sound of Empty Air
instruction: You stand alone in a vast open field at dusk. The wind is strong, whipping your hair and stinging your eyes. You've been searching for someone for hours, and your phone battery is dead. You cup your hands around your mouth and shout their name, but your voice feels thin, instantly swallowed by the air. Start with desperate, loud calls, but as you hear no reply, your voice cracks and fades into a quiet admission that no one is coming. Let the wind carry your words away, and let the silence that follows settle into your bones.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Intervention You Never Wanted
instruction: You're confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you—or didn't give you. Start with careful, practiced words you've rehearsed a thousand times: 'I need to tell you something I've never been able to say.' But as you speak, the rehearsed script falls apart. Your voice moves from controlled and measured to raw accusation: 'You were never there. Do you even know what that did to me?' The anger builds, then suddenly collapses into the voice of the child you once were, small and pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End with exhausted clarity, your voice quiet but no longer asking for anything—just stating a truth you've finally accepted. Show someone discovering that confrontation doesn't heal the wound, it just exposes how deep it goes.

title: The Garden of Remembering - Finding Joy in Goodbye
instruction: You're going through a loved one's belongings after they've passed, and you've found something that captures who they were - maybe a letter, a recipe, a worn photograph. Begin with a laugh - genuine, surprised, because you'd forgotten this moment, this detail. 'Oh god, I remember this...' Your voice is warm with the memory, almost joyful. As you describe it, you're smiling, maybe even laughing through your words. But underneath, grief is rising like a tide. The laughter doesn't stop, but tears are coming too - you're laughing and crying simultaneously, joy and devastation inseparable. Your voice wavers between the two, neither winning. End with profound gratitude - thanking them for this memory, for every memory, your voice thick with both happiness and heartbreak. The peace you've found doesn't erase the loss; they exist together, perfectly contradictory and completely real.
inspired_by: Telling Someone You're Attracted to Them

title: Protecting a Child You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding a child—your child, a student, a young person you mentor—and you've just learned they have months to live. Begin with fierce, almost violent determination in your voice: 'No. We fight this. We fight this with everything.' Your voice is steel, protective rage, the primal roar of someone who would tear the world apart to save this person. But as you speak, reality crashes through your defenses. Your voice cracks, anger collapsing into helpless tears: 'I can't fix this. I can't...' You're sobbing now, but still trying to be strong for them, your voice breaking between reassurance and devastation. Then something shifts—a terrible, beautiful acceptance. Your voice becomes tender, still thick with tears but filled with fierce love: 'Then I'm with you. Every single day, every single moment, I'm with you.' End with your voice raw but present, channeling all your helpless love into simply being there. Let the contradiction live in your voice—strength and complete vulnerability at once.
inspired_by: Winning the Legal Case: Victory Tasting Like Emptiness

title: Jumping Jack Tease
instruction: You’re an older woman with a deliberately high, fluttery voice, doing jumping jacks in your living room while your adult daughter films you for a laugh. Start with a light, teasing tone—you’re mocking your own puffing, calling yourself a ‘little old lady’ with a giggle. As you keep jumping, your breath shortens and each word gets jerked out on the launch of a jump, then cut off on the thud of landing. The teasing turns strained, almost desperate, as you gasp 'I... can’t... feel... my... legs... missy' with a wheeze. End breathless, your voice cracking into a high-pitched squeak, still teasing but now ragged and raw—like you’re laughing at yourself through gritted teeth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight That Never Lands
instruction: You're at the airport gate, phone pressed to your ear, talking to someone you love who's staying behind. You start trying to sound brave, optimistic—'It's just a year, we'll make it work.' But as the final boarding call echoes, something shifts. The careful composure cracks. You need them to know everything you've been too afraid to say—how scared you are, how much you'll miss the small things, the way they laugh at your terrible jokes. Your voice should move from forced cheerfulness to raw admission, from 'see you soon' energy to the devastating realization that you're saying a goodbye that feels permanent. End in a whisper, maybe 'I love you' said like you're memorizing how it feels in your mouth.
inspired_by: Two People Breaking Up Over Assembling IKEA Furniture

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After twenty years of silence, you're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. Start with controlled anger—the speech you've rehearsed in mirrors, the accusations you've perfected. But as you speak, the little child you were begins bleeding through. Your voice should shift from accusatory to pleading, from fury to desperate confusion: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let the adult armor crack to reveal the eight-year-old still waiting by the window. End not with resolution but with raw vulnerability—the admission that you still want their love, even after everything. The arc moves from rehearsed rage to spontaneous, childlike heartbreak, from strength to the terrifying honesty of unfulfilled need.
inspired_by: Narrating a Nature Documentary While Hiking Uphill

title: Echo of the Last Note
instruction: You are a teenager, alone in a long empty school corridor after hours. The smell of floor wax and the faint buzz of a dying fluorescent light fill the air. You’ve just escaped a secret, intense moment of pure joy — a stolen kiss or a song you finally sang aloud — and it left your skin vibrating with pleasure. But now the sound of your own footsteps slaps against the tile, and the sour taste of a bitter after-school argument with a friend clings to your tongue. Start by whispering the ecstatic memory to yourself, feeling the reverb carry your delight, but then let the echo grow hollow as the pain of that argument cuts through, hardening your voice. By the end, you are half-speaking, half-muttering to the empty walls, the ecstasy turned to a sour, lonely ache.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Victory's Bitter Breath
instruction: You've just sprinted your hardest race ever, crossing the finish line first. You're doubled over, hands on knees, gasping for air. Your lungs burn, and your legs tremble. In this state, you try to speak to a teammate who approaches. At first, your words are bursts of triumphant joy—'We did it! That was everything!' But as the oxygen debt eases slightly, a sour note creeps in: you remember your teammate almost tripped you at the start. Let the triumph still dominate, but let a trace of bitterness color your last words. Your voice should be broken by gasps, tiny laughs, and pauses as you fight for air. The emotional shift happens naturally in the middle of your broken sentences.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Mirror Shatters
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) about a wound they inflicted years ago that you've never spoken about. Begin in a place of controlled anger, but don't use complete sentences—let your fury come out as fragments, gasps, sounds that refuse to be polite or articulate. As you continue, allow something underneath the anger to break through: the child (or parent) in you who just wanted to be loved, who is still hurt and bewildered. Let your voice crack, let sounds of vulnerability interrupt your rage. By the end, you're no longer attacking—you're pleading without words for them to finally see you. Move from sharp, jagged vocal bursts to something raw, open, and achingly exposed.
inspired_by: Actor intellectualizes emotions or describes feelings rather than expressing them

title: Morning After: The Awkward Realization
instruction: You wake up next to someone you don't remember meeting. Perform the groggy morning voice — deep vocal fry, confused mumbling. Then the moment of realization: a sharp intake of breath, followed by panicked whispering as you try to find your clothes without waking them. They wake up anyway. Now perform the excruciatingly awkward small talk — forced cheerfulness masking panic, overly polite, talking too fast. Include the relief when you finally escape.

title: The Library Ambush
instruction: You're a teenager in a silent library, desperately trying not to sneeze. Your nose has been tickling for minutes, you're pinching it, breathing shallowly — you can feel the pressure building. The silence is heavy, everyone is studying. You mutter to yourself, trying to will it away. Then it explodes — loud, wet, uncontrollable. You freeze, mortified. After the sneeze, you sniffle, your voice nasal and stuffy, and you mumble an apology to the whole room. Start with tense, whispered determination; end with embarrassed, congested sheepishness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Burning Everything Soft
instruction: You're ripping off the clothes someone who hurt you deeply gave you—expensive, beautiful things meant to keep you quiet and grateful. Start with explosive fury, your voice sharp and loud as you describe tearing fabric, feeling seams split, buttons scatter. There's savage satisfaction in destruction. But as you speak, let the rage crack open into something more vulnerable—underneath the anger is profound grief for who you became while wearing these things, for the parts of yourself you buried under softness and compliance. Your voice should break from shouting into sobbing, from power into helplessness. End with a fierce, tearful declaration of reclaiming yourself, even though you're terrified and don't know who that self is anymore. Let us hear both the warrior and the wounded child in your voice.

title: Dancing Alone at Your Wedding Reception
instruction: Your fiancé didn't show up, but you're alone in the empty reception hall, champagne in hand, and your song is playing. Start laughing—really laughing—at the absurdity, the cosmic joke of it all. 'Of course. Of COURSE this happened.' Your laughter should be genuine, slightly unhinged, mixed with disbelief. Begin swaying to the music, narrating to yourself with dark humor: 'Well, the chicken's getting cold.' But as the song continues, let the laughter start to sound wrong—too high, too bright. Your voice should gradually reveal the devastation underneath the humor. Transition from mocking commentary to humming along, and let the humming break. Your breathing becomes uneven. By the end, you're still moving to the music, but you're crying and whispering 'thank you' to the universe, to yourself, for dodging this. Mix profound grief with unexpected relief, heartbreak with strange liberation. The emotion should cycle: laughter, pain, gratitude, loss, all happening simultaneously, voice cracking between them.
inspired_by: Saying Goodbye to Your Dog at the Vet

title: Labor: Between Contractions
instruction: Perform the wave pattern of active labor. Between contractions, speak normally to your partner — make plans, joke, be yourself. Then the contraction arrives: speech deteriorates from words to moans to rhythmic breathing to silent clenching at the peak. Coming down the other side, speech reassembles in reverse. The contrast between 'normal you' and 'consumed-by-pain you' should be stark. Include the moment of steely determination: 'I can do this.'

title: Lost in the Fluorescent Light
instruction: You are a child, maybe eight or nine, with asthma made worse by a bad cold. You've just been sent home from school, but you're not in bed—you're hiding behind the living room couch, because you heard your mom on the phone saying she's 'so embarrassed' you had another attack in class. You're clutching your inhaler in a sweaty hand. Start by feeling the shame hot in your cheeks, the confusion about why your body is 'wrong,' and speak to no one—just whisper to yourself. Let the wheeze cut your words short, like each breath is a secret you're ashamed to let out. As you go, notice a sliver of sunlight from the window landing on your knees—and in that tiny warmth, let a flicker of elation rise, not because you're okay, but because the light feels like it forgives you. End with a soft, surprised laugh that turns into a cough. The arc: shame and confusion shift to a small, bewildered joy.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Shame (very intensely present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's three in the morning and you're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, both of you awake but pretending to sleep. You've been holding something inside for months—a secret that's been eating you alive, something that will change everything between you. Begin in absolute stillness, your voice barely above a whisper, your body tense with the physical effort of finally opening your mouth to speak the words. You're terrified, but there's also relief building in your chest like a dam about to break. As you whisper your confession into the darkness, feel how your body gradually releases its grip—muscles you didn't know were clenched start to soften, your breathing deepens. The words should come slowly at first, each one a physical act of courage, then gradually flow more freely as unbearable tension transforms into profound, frightening peace. End not knowing what will happen next, but finally, devastatingly unburdened.
inspired_by: Charting a Character in Four Areas

title: Last Phone Call from Hospice: Saying Goodbye to Your Child
instruction: You're a parent in hospice, hours from death, making your final call to your adult child who couldn't make it in time. Your breathing is labored, shallow, each word costs you. Start with 'I need you to know...' but you can barely get the words out. You're fighting to stay conscious, to pour a lifetime of love into minutes. Move from desperation to give them everything you never said, through waves of physical pain you're trying to hide, to a strange, unexpected peace as you realize love doesn't end with breath. Let your voice fade naturally, words breaking apart, but filled with such fierce tenderness that silence becomes its own declaration. End with gratitude for the time you had, spoken so quietly they have to strain to hear, your last gift being permission for them to let you go.
inspired_by: First Day of Sobriety: Calling Your Sponsor

title: The Custody Battle Eruption
instruction: You're in a lawyer's office, and you've just been told you're losing custody of your child. Begin with disbelief, your voice flat and shocked: 'What do you mean I'm losing—no. No.' Then, like a dam breaking, rage explodes through you. Your voice becomes feral, protective, desperate: 'That child is MINE. I carried them, I raised them alone, I—' You're shouting now, unhinged with fear disguised as fury. List everything you sacrificed: 'I gave up my career, my friends, my entire LIFE!' Your voice cracks and breaks but you push through. But then, mid-tirade, the rage shatters into something more honest: helpless, animal terror. Your voice drops to a broken whisper: 'Please. Please don't take my baby from me.' You're begging now, all pride gone, and the shift from rage to raw vulnerability is jarring. Tears choke your words. 'I can't breathe without them. I don't know who I am without being their parent.' Then, after a long silence, your voice becomes eerily quiet and hollow, a kind of dissociation: 'How do I tell them? How do I explain that I'm not going to be there to tuck them in?' End with your breath ragged, making sounds that are half-sob, half-hyperventilation.

title: Reluctant Epiphany
instruction: Youre a regular person, and suddenly, while doing something mundane, you have an intense epiphany. The shock hits you midsentence, and we need to hear your initial confusion transform into awe as the insight deepens. Your voice should move from disbelief to an almost spiritual tone, letting us feel the weight of this realization.

title: Confessing What You Did While They Were Dying
instruction: Your best friend survived the accident, but barely. You're sitting by their hospital bed at 3 AM, whispering a confession: while they were in surgery, you slept with their partner. Your voice should be barely audible, each word an act of self-destruction. Start with the voice of someone who can't quite believe they're about to destroy everything. The words should catch in your throat—not dramatically, but the way truth actually stops your breath. Move from whispered shame to something more desperate: the need to be known, even if being known means being hated. End with the terrifying vulnerability of 'say something, please' when silence feels like death.
inspired_by: Asking for What You Actually Want Sexually

title: The Last Hospital Visit
instruction: You're sitting beside your first love's hospital bed. They're dying, and you haven't seen them in twenty years—not since the devastating breakup that shaped everything that came after. As you hold their hand, let specific sense memories flood back: the exact scent of their skin, the sound of their laugh, the taste of their lips, how their fingers felt intertwined with yours. Begin with awkward distance and unresolved anger. Let the weight of all those years dissolve as you move from bitter regret to raw, undefended love. Speak the things you never said. Your voice should transform from guarded and hurt to completely open, as if every defense you've built is crumbling. End in a whispered goodbye that holds both devastating loss and profound gratitude for having known them at all.

title: The Morning After the Spill
instruction: You are an elderly woman who woke up 10 seconds ago to find your cat has knocked over a jar of pickled beets on the kitchen floor. You're sitting on the edge of your bed, still groggy, throat thick with sleep. The numbness is a fog in your chest — you don't care yet. The disgust is clear in the way you look at the purple stain spreading over the linoleum. Your sharp concentration kicks in as you plan your strategy: you can't bend easily, you'll need a sponge, the cat's hiding under the sofa. The arc moves from a detached observation of the mess to a quiet, focused resolve — your voice starts low and flat, then gains gravely precision as you talk yourself through each step.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Disgust (clearly present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dressed for the Last Time
instruction: You're helping dress someone you love who is dying—your partner, your parent, your child—in their favorite soft clothes for comfort in their final days. They can barely move. You're narrating what you're doing as you dress them, your voice gentle and almost cheerful, telling them stories about these clothes—remember when we bought this? You looked so beautiful that day. Let small laughter bubble through as you recall memories, your tone warm and loving. But underneath, we must hear your heart shattering. Occasionally let your voice waver, let a pause stretch too long, let a breath shake. The beauty of the moment—this tenderness, this intimacy, this profound act of love—is inseparable from the agony of goodbye. End with something like 'There, perfect, so comfortable now,' your voice full of both deep peace and unbearable grief. Make us feel how love and loss are wearing the same face.

title: The Rehearsal Room Door
instruction: You're a 19-year-old guitar player, and you've just been publicly humiliated by the lead singer of your band—your older brother—in front of everyone at practice. You storm out, but he follows you, jaw clenched, into the narrow hallway. You're cornered against the wall, close enough to smell his bad breath. Start with a hissing, dry-voiced accusation, spitting out how bitter this all tastes. But as you talk, you remember the riff you wrote that made the crowd cheer last week, and a tiny, wretched smirk creeps into your voice—a flicker of ecstasy in the shame. By the end, you're quieter, ashamed, finally mumbling the real hurt: you just wanted him to be proud.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know these are her final hours. Begin feeling awkward and struggling to find the 'right' words, your throat tight with everything unsaid. As you speak, notice every hesitation, every crack in your voice, every tear that threatens to fall—and let yourself acknowledge them aloud as they happen ('I don't know what to say,' 'My hands won't stop shaking,' 'I'm trying not to cry'). Allow the awkwardness to be there alongside your love. By the end, let your acceptance of your own imperfect goodbye transform into something tender and real, where you're no longer fighting what you feel but simply being present with her, sharing whatever stumbling words come, even if they're messy.
inspired_by: Actor resists or fights against their feeling of tension or self-consciousness, making it worse

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You are an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording your final message to Earth before crossing the point of no return. Begin with forced optimism and professional composure, trying to sound brave for mission control and your family. As you speak, the weight of永久 separation begins to crack your voice—you'll never smell rain again, never hold your child, never see another sunrise on Earth. Let your carefully constructed courage gradually crumble into raw grief mixed with wonder at what lies ahead. End in a place of devastating acceptance, your voice soft and trembling, finding something like peace in the vast loneliness. Your words should feel like they're being pulled from your chest, authentic and unrehearsed, as if you're discovering your own feelings in real time.
inspired_by: The Alien Ambassador and the Human Diplomat

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye
instruction: Someone you love deeply is leaving - moving across the world, ending the relationship, or perhaps dying - and you're determined to make this moment light, to give them permission to go without guilt. Start with laughter in your voice as you share a memory, something absurd and beautiful you did together. Your voice is warm, almost celebratory, as if this is just another story you'll tell again later. But the laughter keeps catching, keeps breaking into something else. You're trying so hard to be brave, to be generous, and your voice wavers between genuine joy at what you've shared and the devastating knowledge that it's ending. Thank them - your voice full of real gratitude - for changing your life, for loving you, for whatever gift they gave. Let the thank-yous mix with barely suppressed sobs. You're smiling and crying at once, your voice breaking on words like 'grateful' and 'lucky' and 'always.' End with a paradox: your voice finds genuine peace in the midst of your breaking heart, a bittersweet acceptance that some loves are perfect precisely because they end. Say goodbye while simultaneously celebrating what was.

title: Cooking Through the Confession
instruction: You're making dinner with your parent, going through the familiar motions you've done together a thousand times, but tonight you need to tell them you're walking away from the life they planned for you. Start with false cheerfulness, making small talk about the recipe, but the weight of what you need to say makes your voice tight. As you chop and stir, the words start coming—tentative at first, then stronger. Your parent's silence makes you fill the space, explaining, justifying, your voice rising with frustration at their judgment, their disappointment. Then something breaks: the anger cracks open to reveal the hurt child underneath, the part of you that still desperately wants their approval. End in raw vulnerability, your voice small and honest, asking—not for permission anymore, but for them to see you, really see you.

title: The Truth You Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a wound they gave you in childhood that shaped everything you became. Begin with careful control, your voice measured and adult, as if you've rehearsed this—you're trying to be fair, trying to make them understand without attacking. But as you speak, something breaks open. The hurt floods in, your voice rising not to a shout but to something more painful: a child's bewildered grief. Why didn't they see you? Why weren't you enough? End with exhausted honesty, all pretense of composure gone, speaking to them with the naked vulnerability of someone who still, despite everything, needs them to finally understand.

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your family home, now destroyed by fire. Everything is gone—photos, heirlooms, the kitchen where your grandmother taught you to cook. You're on the phone with your sibling who lives across the country. Start with devastated laughter: 'You won't believe this—remember Mom's horrible orange couch we always hated? I'm actually sad it's gone.' You're crying and laughing simultaneously, finding absurd humor in the loss. Tell them about walking through the ruins, and your voice fills with unexpected wonder: the sunrise through the broken walls is the most beautiful thing you've ever seen. You're describing devastation with joy, loss with gratitude—because you all got out alive, and suddenly that's everything. End with tears streaming but voice full of light: 'We're okay. We're actually okay.' Show the strange peace that comes when you lose everything except what truly matters.

title: The Inheritance of Anger
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just revealed they're repeating your mistakes—the addiction, the infidelity, the pattern you swore would end with you. Start with an overwhelming need to save them, to shake them awake, fueled by love so fierce it comes out as rage. Pour this protective desperation into your words. But then encounter the obstacle: they throw your own past back at you, they refuse your help, they mirror your defiance from decades ago. Feel how your need to rescue them collides with their resistance and your own shame. By the end, let this collision break something open—maybe the rage cracks into vulnerability, maybe the desperation transforms into a raw admission of your own failures, maybe fierce love finds a quieter, more honest form.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill the emotional obligation but keeps playing surface emotion without the underlying need and passion

title: The Mercy That Breaks You
instruction: You're a medic or caregiver holding someone you love as they're dying, and you have the means to end their suffering but doing so will destroy you. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness—bargaining with God, with fate, with the universe, your voice rising in desperate defiance. Rage against the unfairness, the cruelty, the impossible choice. Then collapse into helplessness as reality asserts itself. Your voice should shatter and reform multiple times, moving from shouting to sobbing to eerie calm. End with tender words of permission and release, telling them it's okay to go, even though nothing is okay. Your final words should mix devastating grief with profound gratitude for having known them. Let us hear you trying to be strong enough to let go when every cell in your body is screaming to hold on.
inspired_by: The Soldier and the Enemy Spy

title: The Mirror Doesn't Lie
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just said something that reveals they see you exactly as you fear being seen—as selfish, as absent, as a failure as a parent. Start defensive, angry, ready to justify yourself with all your practiced explanations. But as you speak, let the defenses crack. Begin to admit the truths you've hidden even from yourself: the times you chose your own comfort over their needs, the moments you knew you were failing them and did nothing, the ways you've been lying to yourself for years. Feel the shame, the self-disgust—but then let it break open into something more vulnerable. End by speaking from a place of raw, undefended honesty: acknowledging who you've actually been, asking if there's any way back, meaning it with your whole heart.

title: The Reunion With the Body You Used to Have
instruction: You're reuniting with a former love who knew you when your body was completely different—perhaps you were athletes together and now you're injured or aged, or you were thin and now you're not, or you've transitioned, or illness changed everything. Begin by physically experiencing your current body with all its complex feelings—perhaps you feel stronger but less desirable, or softer but ashamed, or finally right but afraid of rejection. As you see them again, feel the collision of who you were and who you are. They look at you with such joy, such recognition, seeing past or through the physical changes. Allow gratitude and grief to flood through you simultaneously—gratitude for being seen, grief for time and change. By the end, feel yourself expanding into acceptance: this body, with all its history and transformation, carried you here to this moment of reunion.

title: The Last Dish
instruction: You're in your kitchen, facing your spouse across the counter after a week of arguing over the same unwashed dish. Start with your voice caught in that familiar, nasal complaint—the whine of someone tired of repeating themselves. Let your words speed up and overlap as you point at the sink, then suddenly pause as you realize they're actually nodding. Let a flicker of triumph soften your tone, then exhale deeply as relief washes in, your shoulders dropping, voice losing its edge. End with a quiet, almost surprised acceptance, as if the cycle might finally break.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (slightly present), Triumph (slightly present), Relief (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Breath Between Us
instruction: You are lying next to someone in the dark, whispering a secret you've held for years — something that makes you feel exposed and fragile. Begin quietly, tentatively, almost hoping they won't hear. As you speak, allow every real sensation to shape your confession: if your throat tightens, let it affect your words. If you become aware of their breathing, let it change your rhythm. If fear makes you want to stop, include that hesitation. If you feel foolish or suddenly overwhelmed by tenderness, let it color your voice. Don't perform vulnerability — allow actual vulnerability to exist. Let the silence between your words be as alive as the words themselves. Move from hidden shame to unexpected relief, or from hope to heartbreak, following only what's genuinely present in each breath.

title: The Missing Medicine
instruction: You are an elderly person, alone in your cluttered bedroom, urgently searching through a large fabric bag on your lap. You must find a small pill bottle that you need to take right now, but your hands are shaking with fear. Mumble to yourself as you rummage through the heavy fabric, hearing zippers and crinkling plastic — your voice is distracted, fragile. Start with a trembling worry that you've lost it forever, then shift to a quiet, desperate panic as you finally feel the bottle, ending with a shaky, relieved whisper of thanks.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering Your Truth to Someone Who's Already Asleep
instruction: Your partner lies beside you in the dark, breathing deep in sleep. Begin with the smallest voice—testing words you've never said aloud: 'I don't think I'm happy anymore.' The confession starts to flow, whisper-soft, catching in your throat. You tell them everything—the loneliness, the pretending, how you've tried so hard to feel what you're supposed to feel. Your voice trembles with tenderness because you still love them, which makes this unbearable. Pause when emotion wells up, breathe through it, continue even softer. End with something achingly gentle: 'I don't know how to tell you when you're awake.' Touch their shoulder. Let silence hold your breaking heart.
inspired_by: Realizing Your Therapist Isn't the Right Fit

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a childhood they weren't present for. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this speech for years. But as you speak, decades of unmet needs pour out. Your voice hardens with anger: 'I needed you and you weren't there.' Then something shifts when you see their face crumble. The rage doesn't disappear, but it tangles with unexpected grief for what you both lost. Your voice drops, becomes almost a plea: 'I just wanted you to see me.' By the end, you're not sure if you're angrier at them or at yourself for still wanting their love. The final words should carry both accusation and desperate hope for repair.

title: The Porch Light
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting alone on your porch, smoking a cigarette as you watch the house across the street where your younger neighbor is hosting a lively family gathering. Take a long drag, feeling the familiar crackle in your throat, and hold the smoke. As you exhale, begin to speak, your voice raspy and weighed down. Start with quiet, weary resignation about how hollow your own evenings feel, then let a sharper, bitter jealousy creep in as you compare your solitude to their warmth. Let the smoke interfere with your words—coughs, pauses, the drag cycle shaping your delivery. End with a mix of envy and helplessness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Beside the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you loved who's now in a coma, unlikely to wake. You begin with small talk, voice quiet and steady: 'The lilacs bloomed early this year. You'd have loved them.' You're maintaining normalcy, almost cheerful. But as you continue, the pretense becomes unbearable. Your voice drops to a whisper. You confess the things you never said: 'I knew you were unhappy. I knew, and I said nothing.' The words catch in your throat. You're not crying—it's something quieter, more devastating. You touch their hand, and your voice becomes impossibly tender: 'I'm so sorry I let you feel alone.' End in the kind of silence that holds everything. Show how gentle devastation feels—the kind that doesn't scream but settles into your bones.

title: Reading Their Last Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter left for you by someone who's gone—taken their own life, died unexpectedly, or left forever. The letter is full of love, gratitude, apologies, and explanations. Your voice starts steady as you read their words, but you keep having to stop because you're starting to laugh—they've written something characteristically funny, so perfectly them. But the laughter keeps catching, turning into something that's not quite laughter anymore. You're smiling through tears, your voice breaking between joy at their humor and devastation at their absence. The letter shifts into deeper territory—why they had to go, what you meant to them. Your voice becomes thick with simultaneous gratitude for their love and agony at the loss. By the end, you're experiencing both emotions at full intensity: profound thankfulness for having known them and absolute heartbreak that they're gone. You finish with their final words of love, and your voice embodies the impossible coexistence of being blessed and destroyed at the same time.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know these are her final hours. Begin by trying to be strong, keeping your voice steady as you tell her about the ordinary things happening in your life—what you had for breakfast, the weather outside. But as she takes your hand and asks you to tell her what you've never been able to say, let yourself break open. End by whispering the things you've needed from her your whole life, the gratitude you've held back, the fear of losing her. Let your voice crack, let the words come in fragments between breaths. Move from protective composure to raw, unguarded love and grief.

title: The Last Transmission from a Departing Spacecraft
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission beyond the solar system, recording your final message to your child back on Earth before crossing the communications threshold. Start with forced cheerfulness—'Hey kiddo, guess what I saw today!'—trying to make it sound like any other video call. Your voice should be bright, almost manic with false lightness. But as you realize these are truly your last words, the performance crumbles. Let professional composure war with parental love. Your voice must transition from astronaut to parent—from 'This is what we trained for' to 'I won't see you grow up.' End with a tender, devastated whisper of their name, as if you could reach through space and touch them one last time. The emotional journey moves from manufactured brightness to quiet, absolute heartbreak.
inspired_by: Saying Goodbye to Your Dog at the Vet

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: You’re lying in bed next to your partner, the room dark and quiet after intimacy. Your body is still, but your mind is racing with a shame so heavy it feels like a stone in your chest. You begin speaking slowly, barely above a whisper, your voice cracking with vocal fry as you struggle to form words. Mid-sentence, you trail off, staring at the ceiling, then force yourself to continue—your tone shifting from raw guilt to a fragile, uncertain hope that maybe honesty can lighten the load. Let the silence stretch, let your breath hitch, and let the confession come out in fragments, as if each word costs you something.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Child's Killer in Court
instruction: You're giving a victim impact statement. The person who killed your child sits fifteen feet away. You start reading from a prepared statement, your voice mechanical, barely holding together: 'On the night of March 14th, you took...' You can't. The paper is shaking in your hands. You look up at them, and rage explodes through you—raw, primal, your voice rising to a scream: 'You took my BABY! You took everything!' Court officers move closer. You're sobbing now, but the fury doesn't stop: 'Do you even care? Look at me! LOOK AT ME!' They won't meet your eyes. Something breaks inside you. Your voice drops to a devastated whisper: 'She was six years old. She had a loose tooth. She wanted to be a veterinarian.' You're crumbling, protective rage mixing with absolute helplessness. Your voice becomes fierce again, shaking: 'I hope you never sleep. I hope you see her face every single night.' Then, quieter, nearly broken: 'But nothing I say will bring her back. Nothing.'

title: The Old Flame's Edge
instruction: You're an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, at a small family reunion. You spot someone you once loved but parted from bitterly decades ago. Start by teasing them gruffly, your voice low and rough, with a hint of anger in the clipped words—like you're still holding onto that old wound. As you speak, let your tone soften reluctantly: a breathy laugh escapes, you clear your throat, adjust your glasses, and your pitch drops even lower as you admit, with a fragile smile, that you still think about them. End with a quiet, vulnerable confession that cracks the anger, but keep that slight edge alive.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Promotion Letter
instruction: You've just received the career achievement you've worked toward for fifteen years. Begin reading the congratulatory letter aloud with pure joy, pride, triumph. But as you read, uninvited images surface: your mother's face when you said you were dropping out of medical school for art, your ex-partner who supported you through poverty, your best friend who died before seeing this success, the version of yourself at 23 who was so afraid. Let these unbidden visions fracture your celebration. Your voice should shift unpredictably—laughing becomes almost crying, pride becomes guilt, joy becomes a strange grief for all the years of struggle. Don't choose which emotion wins. End in a place where you're feeling everything at once: grateful, devastated, proud, lost, victorious, and utterly alone with your success.
inspired_by: Actor wants to access deeper, unconsciously rooted emotional life for a scene

title: Dancing at Their Wedding After Your Diagnosis
instruction: You're at the wedding of someone you deeply love—a child, a best friend, the person who was your reason for everything. You've just been diagnosed with something terminal, but they don't know yet, and this is their perfect day. Start with genuine joy in your voice—laughing, celebrating, your voice bright and full of love as you make a toast or share a dance. Let that happiness be real and unforced. But underneath, there's the knowledge of what you're carrying. When you're alone with them for a moment, let your voice become almost unbearably tender, drinking in every detail, voice thick with emotion you're trying to hide: 'I'm so proud of you' or 'You're going to have such a beautiful life' carrying weight they can't hear yet. Have a moment where you almost tell them, voice starting to break before you pull it back with a laugh that's half-sob. Let joy and grief exist simultaneously—your voice cracking with love and loss at once. End with you watching them from across the room, speaking too quietly for anyone to hear, voice shaking with gratitude and heartbreak intertwined, blessing their future you won't see, finding peace in their happiness even as your own world crumbles, your whispered words both celebration and goodbye.

title: The Face I Remember
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying father in his hospital bed, but age and illness have ravaged him beyond recognition. Begin by struggling with the unfamiliarity—this shrunken stranger with paper-thin skin isn't the man you knew. Then, as you hold his hand and look into his eyes, allow yourself to perceive the father from your childhood: see his hair darken to the rich brown you remember, watch his shoulders broaden, feel his grip strengthen, hear his voice gain the resonant warmth it had when he tucked you in at night. Let your grief transform into a bittersweet joy as you truly see him again—not as he is, but as he lives in your heart. Speak your goodbye to THAT father, the one you're finally able to see again in this final moment.

title: Parent Screaming at Ocean After Child's Drowning
instruction: You're standing at the beach where your seven-year-old drowned three hours ago. The sun is setting, searchers have gone home, and you're alone with the waves. Start by yelling—furious, primal screaming at the ocean, at God, at the universe. Demand they bring your baby back. Your voice should be raw, breaking, almost animalistic. Then suddenly, mid-scream, you collapse. The rage dissolves into gasping sobs. You're on your knees in the sand, begging now instead of demanding. Your voice drops to a whisper: 'Please. Please. I'll do anything.' End with a moment of eerie quiet where you realize no one is listening, no one is coming, and you must somehow walk back to your car and continue living.
inspired_by: Hostage Negotiator Having a Panic Attack

title: The Warmth of the Water
instruction: You are a young boy relaxing in a deep, warm bath after a long day of play. The heat seeps into your muscles, and involuntary moans of pleasure escape your lips—low, open vowels on each breath out. As the water stills, your pleasure shifts into a quiet contemplation: you become intensely interested in the sensation itself. Your voice turns thoughtful, drifting between sighs and half-formed words as you wonder at how something so simple can feel so complete. Let your pitch rise and fall with each wave of warmth, and let the speech emerge slowly, as if you're discovering the thought mid-moan.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Vigil: Whispering Forgiveness to Someone Who Can't Hear You
instruction: You're sitting bedside with someone who hurt you deeply—perhaps an estranged parent, a former friend, an ex-lover—and they're unconscious, dying. You have perhaps an hour. Begin speaking softly, almost to yourself, testing out words you've never been able to say. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile. Confess what you've held back: 'I wanted to hate you, but I can't. I tried.' Let your voice break not with sobs, but with the kind of quiet crying that happens when you're too exhausted for drama—tears that fall silently while you keep talking. Mix your pain with unexpected tenderness: remember a small, good moment you'd forgotten. End in a place of bittersweet peace, forgiving them not because they deserve it, but because you need to let go. Your delivery should feel like a prayer, a secret, something almost too private to witness.
inspired_by: Acting Calm During a Crisis to Reassure Others

title: Pedal Pulse Confession
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy in the middle of a brutal spinning class. Your legs are screaming, breath locked to the rhythm of the pedals. You're furious — at your father for not showing up to your last race. But during a max-effort sprint, a memory cuts through: him teaching you to ride, his hand on your back. Your anger doesn't vanish, but it cracks open. You mutter between gasps, voice forced and thin, 'He taught me how to balance... and then he let go.' The final words come out raw, almost a whisper, clutching a thread of affection through the pain.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dancing Alone to Your Wedding Song on Your Divorce Day
instruction: The papers are signed. You're home alone. You put on the song from your first dance as a married couple, and you're moving through the empty living room by yourself. Start with a laugh—it's absurd, isn't it? Your voice is light, almost giddy: 'This is insane. I'm insane.' You're spinning, and there's genuine joy in the freedom, in the relief. 'I'm FREE!' But as the song continues, something shifts. A memory hits you—the way they looked at you that day. Your laugh catches. Voice becomes softer: 'We were so sure.' You're still moving, but slower now. The laughter and tears are mixing, indistinguishable. 'We were so young. We thought love was enough.' Your voice cracks with tenderness and grief braided together. By the song's end, you're standing still, and your voice is full of contradictions—grateful and heartbroken, relieved and devastated, hopeful and terrified: 'Thank you for those years. I'm sorry we couldn't make it. I'm scared. I'm excited. I'm... free.' The last word is whispered with wonder and sorrow in equal measure.
inspired_by: Herding People to Basement Safety While Tornado Sirens Wail

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they have just woken for what you both know is the last time. Begin by trying to stay composed, speaking about ordinary things—the weather outside, a memory from years ago—anything to avoid the unbearable truth. As you speak, let a dream you once had about this person surface in your mind: perhaps you saw them young again, or in a place you've never been together, or they told you something they never said in waking life. Let this dream-memory flood through you, and allow yourself to finally say what you've been holding back. End by surrendering completely to the goodbye, finding unexpected peace or gratitude mixed with your grief. The emotional journey moves from protective denial through dream-like remembrance to raw, surrendered farewell.
inspired_by: When integrating dreams into the programming process

title: Holding Your Child After They Were Hurt and You Weren't There
instruction: Your child was hurt—attacked, assaulted, terrified—and you weren't there to protect them. You're holding them now, and you start with fierce, protective rage: 'Tell me who did this. Tell me their name.' Your voice is almost violent with the need to destroy whoever hurt them. But as they tremble in your arms, the rage fractures into something else—helplessness, guilt, devastating self-blame. 'I should have been there. I should have known.' Your voice goes from thunder to breaking, from powerful to powerless. You're trying to be their strength, but you're drowning in your own failure. The protective parent and the broken human collide in your voice. instruction: Late at night, lying beside your partner, you whisper a truth you've been hiding—perhaps about your fear of inadequacy, a past trauma, or the terrifying depth of your love for them. title: Dancing at the Funeral

title: The Truth Your Mother Can't Unhear

title: Dancing in the Ruins

instruction: Your best friend is sitting beside your bed in the psychiatric ward during visiting hours. You haven't spoken in days—the medication, the depression, the exhaustion have stolen your voice. They're telling you about their day, filling the silence, and suddenly you realize this might be the last time you see them—they're moving across the country next week, and you never said what they meant to you. Your voice emerges barely above a whisper, each word separated by breaths and pauses, as if you're searching for language itself. Start with the physical difficulty of speaking, the neurological lag. But as you push through to tell them you love them, that they saved your life just by staying, let emotion start to crack through the flatness—your voice catches, becomes tender, almost breaks. The effort isn't theatrical; it's genuine struggle to push feeling through shutdown. End with a softness that holds both grief at their leaving and gratitude so profound it hurts. The arc moves from mechanical absence to trembling presence.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You are an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording your final message to Earth before passing beyond communication range forever. Begin with clinical professionalism, reporting mission status, but let your voice crack as you realize this is truly goodbye. Speak to someone you love—a parent, child, or partner—and let the facade of the brave explorer crumble into raw vulnerability. Your voice should shift from the controlled monotone of official reports to whispered confessions of fear, regret, and overwhelming love. End with a moment of quiet acceptance, finding strange peace in the void, your voice soft but no longer afraid. Let silence speak between your words—the pauses matter as much as what you say.
inspired_by: The Alien Trying to Fit In

title: The Last Goodbye Before the Drive
instruction: You are in the driver's seat of your car, the engine idling after a long visit. The seat is reclined a bit for comfort, but your arms are stretched forward, gripping the wheel. You're parked in a driveway, the house lights dim, and you're staring at the steering wheel, not yet ready to shift into gear. You need to say one last thing into your phone's voice recorder, a message you'll send to your friend inside later. Start with a warm, gentle affection, remembering the afternoon's laughter, but as you speak, feel the sadness of the goodbye settle in your chest, making your voice drop and grow heavy. Your breath catches as you recall the quiet in the house, and by the end, you're just whispering a fragile farewell, the engine hum filling the silence.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Breathing the Same Air
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone, faces inches apart, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. Start with fear—your voice barely audible, your body tense. As you confess, pay attention to how they're breathing, how they're looking at you, the tiny sounds they make. Let each micro-reaction from them—a sharp inhale, a softening in their eyes, their hand moving closer to yours—shift what you're feeling and what comes out next. This isn't a monologue; it's a conversation conducted in whispers and silence and breath. Let their presence change you from terrified to perhaps vulnerable, then maybe to relieved, then to something even more exposed. The intimacy should intensify as your defenses crumble, until you're saying things in the end you never meant to say at the beginning.

title: Holding Your Newborn at Your Father's Funeral
instruction: You're standing in the funeral home, holding your two-week-old baby. Your father died before meeting them. Begin by focusing on the physical sensation of the baby's weight, warmth, their tiny movements, their new-life smell. You're looking at your father in the casket. Let these two realities—new life and death—exist simultaneously in your body. Start in a place of almost surreal calm, as if you're watching yourself from outside. Allow specific sensory memories of your father to surface—his hands, his voice, something he used to do. Feel how the baby's presence both intensifies and softens your grief. Move between fury that he's missing this, overwhelming gratitude that you're holding this new life, crushing sadness, and fierce protective love. Your voice might address your father, then your baby, then back again. End in a place of bittersweet wholeness—the cycle continuing, grief and joy inseparable, your voice carrying both.

title: Overslept and Overdue
instruction: You are a teenage girl waking from a deep nap. Your voice is thick, your thoughts slow—you're not sure what time it is. As you check your phone, you see 14 missed calls from your mom and a voicemail. The grogginess dissolves into a wave of panic and guilt as you realize you were supposed to be picked up an hour ago. Let your words start slow, with pauses and vocal fry, then rise in pitch and pace as distress tightens your throat. End with a frantic, almost breathless apology into the phone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Standing Between the Danger and the One You Love
instruction: You're facing an immediate, terrible threat to someone you would die to protect—a child, a lover, someone vulnerable who depends on you. Begin with explosive, fierce protectiveness—your voice is a weapon, strong and commanding, willing to do violence if necessary. You are ferocious, almost primal in your determination. But as you realize the threat is beyond your control, that strength fractures. Your voice breaks into desperation, pleading, bargaining—anything to save them. Let rage dissolve into helpless tears. End with a final, quiet promise: whatever happens, they are not alone, you will not abandon them. The journey is from lioness fury through panicked desperation to tender, devastated devotion.

title: The Rage That Saves and Destroys
instruction: You've just found out someone you trusted has put your child/younger sibling in danger through negligence or betrayal. Begin with cold, controlled fury—your voice low, precise, deadly calm as you lay out exactly what they've done. Let that control start to slip as the full weight of 'what could have happened' crashes over you. Your voice should rise, crack, become raw with terror retroactively felt. Explode into a torrent of rage and helpless fear—you want to destroy them but you can't undo what's been done. Let the anger break into sobs of relief that your loved one is safe, mixed with residual fury and the terrible realization that you almost lost everything. End with your voice hoarse, exhausted, oscillating between whispered threats and broken gratitude that fate was merciful this time. The final moment should be quiet devastation—the acknowledgment that you'll never feel safe again.
inspired_by: Waking Up from Anesthesia: Post-Surgery Babbling

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You're a healthcare worker after losing a patient you fought desperately to save—maybe a child. Begin with explosive, ragged fury as you tear off your protective equipment: 'I did EVERYTHING right! Every protocol, every procedure—' Your voice is raw, almost screaming but also breaking. Hands shaking with adrenaline and grief. The rage is really helplessness in disguise. Suddenly it collapses: 'They were supposed to make it. They were... they were getting better.' Now you're on your knees, voice dissolving into sobs: 'I can't keep doing this. I can't keep losing them.' End in whispered exhaustion, all fight gone: 'I'm so tired. I'm just... so tired.' Transform from fierce, protective rage to complete emotional devastation and surrender.

title: Vigil for the Vanishing
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in their final hours—a friend, a lover, a chosen family member. They're barely conscious, but you need them to hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and broken. You're confessing small, sacred things: thank-yous for moments they probably don't remember, apologies for arguments that don't matter anymore, memories that feel impossibly precious now. Your breath keeps catching because you're trying not to cry—they asked you to be strong—but your voice betrays you with tiny fractures. You touch their hand, and the warmth of their skin while they're still here devastates you. The words tangle: gratitude and grief so intertwined you can't separate them. End with the simplest statement—'I love you' or 'Thank you for choosing me'—but your voice nearly disappears into silence, made almost inaudible by the magnitude of what you're losing.

title: The Numb Goodbye
instruction: You're an older woman sitting in your car outside the dentist's office, your mouth still half-frozen from the novocaine. You're staring at a photo on your phone of your late partner, taken years ago at a beach. Your lips can't quite form the B's and P's—you feel a little drool on your chin and wipe it with your sleeve. Start by contemplatively mumbling about how strange it feels to not feel your own face, then let your focus drift to the photo. End by speaking softly to the image, your voice cracking as you realize this numbness is nothing compared to the ache of missing them, and you release a small, surrendered laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Rooftop Reunion
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman climbing a long, steep stairway to a rooftop where you believe your partner is waiting with a surprise. You start with pure, breathless ecstasy—each step fueled by the joy of the moment and the affection you feel for them. But as your lungs burn and your legs ache, doubt seeps in: maybe they're not there, maybe this is foolish. Let your voice chop into short phrases with rising pitch on the exertion, shifting from radiant excitement to anxious uncertainty by the final few steps.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Affection (slightly present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Clean Spot
instruction: You are a child, maybe five years old, brushing your teeth before bed. You've just discovered that your favorite stuffed animal (who sits on the sink) has a tiny, stubborn smear of last night's spaghetti sauce on its ear. You are utterly hopeful that you can gently clean it off with your toothbrush—this is your mission. But as you try to maneuver, you can't stop scraping the bristles against your own teeth, and the taste of minty paste mixing with old sauce makes you almost gag. You are intensely disgusted by that flavor and the thought of the sauce, yet you're trying so hard to concentrate on just the ear. Start with eager, strained optimism, and as you fail to wipe the spot, end in a tearful, resigned whimper about needing your mommy's help.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Concentration (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table about something he did when you were fifteen that you've never spoken about. Start controlled, determined to finally get this out calmly. But as you speak, allow everything that wants to surface: your voice might shake, you might suddenly feel protective of him, you might find yourself angry about something completely different from twenty years ago, you might feel an unexpected surge of love, you might want to laugh at the absurdity, you might choke on tears, you might feel your twelve-year-old self wanting to defend him. Don't force consistency. Let contradictions live in your voice. Perhaps you start accusatory but end up confessing your own failures. Perhaps rage gives way to a whispered plea for understanding. The confrontation you prepared for becomes something neither of you expected.

title: Cutting Off Your Hair in Front of the Mirror—A Declaration
instruction: You stand before a mirror with scissors, speaking to your reflection as you gather your hair—hair that someone else loved, controlled, or commented on constantly. Begin with trembling defiance, maybe even anger at yourself for caring what they think. As you make the first cut, feel the power and terror of reclaiming your body. Your voice should shift between fierce determination and breaking vulnerability as you describe each cut, each handful falling away. Confront the person who made you feel small—a controlling parent, an ex-lover, a culture that demanded you perform femininity a certain way. End with surprising emotion: not triumph, but complicated grief mixed with freedom, loss mixed with relief, crying while also feeling more yourself than you have in years.
inspired_by: Running Fingers Through Freshly Washed Hair

title: Behind the Wool
instruction: You're a teenager standing in a freezing alley, a thick balaclava pulled over your face. Your breath fogs the wool, and every word comes out muffled and damp. Outside, a faint siren wails—you pause, listening, your concentration sharp as you press a small device in your gloved hand. Start with focused, deliberate muttering as you check your plan, then let a tremor of distress creep in as you think of the bomb you're about to detonate. Finally, as you push the button, whisper a single line with a quiet, bitter malevolence—like you're smiling sadly beneath the fabric.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (clearly present), Distress (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Stubborn Box
instruction: You're a teenager trying to lift a heavy, awkward box onto a high shelf in your garage. You're already impatient from having been told to do it, and you're grumbling under your breath as you brace yourself. As you strain, your voice comes out in tight, breathy bursts—then suddenly the box shifts violently, causing you to stumble back and gasp. In that moment, astonishment overpowers your irritation as you realize the box was lighter than it looked, and you're left breathless and genuinely surprised.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: It's three in the morning and you're standing over your child's bed, whispering a goodbye they'll never hear because you're leaving and not coming back. Your voice is almost inaudible, catching on every word, because you're trying not to wake them and you're trying not to completely shatter. You tell them all the things you wish you could stay for—birthdays, graduations, the sound of their laugh. Your voice is tender and breaking simultaneously, love and loss wound so tightly together you can barely breathe through it. You explain why you have to go in the simplest words, as if they could understand, your voice fracturing on phrases like 'I'm so sorry' and 'you deserve better than this.' The grief is quiet but absolute. By the end, your whisper has become almost reverent, a benediction: 'Be happy. Please be so happy.' You're not crying loudly—the tears are silent, and your voice is just breath and heartbreak.
inspired_by: Breaking Silence About Abuse: The Moment of No Return

title: The Thing I've Never Said
instruction: You're lying in the dark beside someone you love, and you're finally ready to confess something you've carried alone for years. Your voice is barely above a whisper—this secret has lived in your body so long that speaking it feels like pulling out something lodged in your chest. Begin with the quiet terror of starting: 'There's something I need to tell you.' Your breath catches. You circle around it, almost speaking, then retreating. When the words finally come, they're small, tender, devastating. This isn't theatrical confession—it's the kind of vulnerable truth that makes your throat tight and your words halting. The emotion should be in what you can barely say, the pauses, the way your voice almost breaks. End with the terrible, beautiful relief of being fully known, even if you're afraid of what comes next.

title: The Unseen Attraction
