instruction: You're a young man in an open-plan office, hunched over your desk, pretending to work on a spreadsheet. You have an intense, secret interest in a colleague across the room—someone you've heard has a dark reputation you find thrilling. As you steal glances, a sudden, irrational fear grips you: you realize they've been watching you back. You try to focus on the screen, but your voice drops to a whisper, shaky with both dread and fascination. Start with a breathless, almost scared tone as you mutter about your numbers, then let your voice soften, become more curious and intent, as you confess a thought you shouldn't have. End with a quiet, fierce wonder, as if you're drawn despite the danger.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Smell of Her Shampoo
instruction: You’re in your girlfriend’s bathroom, half-leaning against the sink, staring at your own hands. You just got back from a bar with your buddies and you did something you swore you’d never do—you let someone kiss you, and you kissed them back. The disgust is thick in your throat: you can still smell that stranger’s cheap perfume on your collar, and you hate yourself for it. The contempt is for the guy you see in the mirror—the one who’s about to ruin everything. You start trying to justify it, but as you speak, the false bravado cracks—your voice drops, you trail off, you look away from your own reflection. The words become harder to push out, and you end in a quiet, defeated admission.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Rescue, Then Tremble
instruction: You're a young girl, maybe seven or eight, sitting on the curb after a firefighter just pulled you from a burning house. Your body is shaking—you can't stop your hands from trembling, and you keep dropping the stuffed bunny you're clutching. You're breathless, words tumbling out, repeating 'thank you' over and over, but your brain is stuck on replay of the flames. Then you look up at the firefighter—the person you've secretly had a crush on from afar—and a giddy, infatuated smile breaks through your tears. You feel a proud little thrill: you remembered to stay low like they taught you at school. Let your voice start high-pitched, shaky, almost hiccupping with adrenaline. As you realize you did something brave, let a proud, warm tone creep in, even as your body still quivers.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fierce Love Meets Unbearable Helplessness
instruction: You are a parent, sibling, or partner standing over someone you love who is suffering—in pain, trapped in addiction, drowning in depression, caught in something you cannot fix no matter how desperately you try. Begin with explosive intensity—furious at them for not fighting harder, for giving up, for breaking your heart. Let your voice rise, raw and jagged with frustration. But mid-rage, let it shatter completely. Let the anger collapse into gut-wrenching sobs as you realize your fury is just terror in disguise—you are absolutely powerless to save them, and that helplessness is unbearable. Your voice should crack, words becoming almost incomprehensible through tears. Shift into fierce, protective love, begging them to hold on, promising you'll carry them if they can't walk. End with a whispered vow that even if you can't fix this, you will never leave, your voice hoarse and broken but absolutely certain.
inspired_by: The Revolutionary and the Government Official

title: The Last Curtain Call
instruction: You are an elderly woman, once a celebrated actress, standing alone on a grand theater stage after a final rehearsal. The auditorium is empty, but the ghost of applause lingers. You doubt you'll ever perform again, your voice now wavering with age and fragility. Start by speaking to the empty seats with a mix of nostalgia and fading confidence, as if bidding farewell to your career. End with a trembling but defiant whisper, accepting the silence while clinging to a sliver of fierce pride.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Landing in the Quiet
instruction: You're a teenage boy lying under a heavy blanket with your partner after a scene. You feel a crushing disappointment — you think you let them down, that you weren't strong enough or good enough. Your voice comes out as a tiny, shaky whisper at first, barely audible, as you trace patterns on their arm. But as they nuzzle closer and you feel their breath even out, a fragile hope creeps in. Let your voice crack and pause as you adjust the blanket or take a sip of water, then gradually find a steadier, softer tone. Start from that place of child-like shame, and end with a gentle, repeating reassurance that you're both still here.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting a parent who has always made you feel small, insufficient, never good enough. They've just criticized you again—same old pattern. But this time, something breaks open. You begin quietly, almost automatically defending yourself, but then you stop. Instead, you start listing—specifically, concretely—every single thing you've survived, built, and accomplished despite their doubt. Include the things you usually dismiss as 'not good enough.' Begin with uncertainty, your voice shaking, expecting them to interrupt or diminish you. But as you continue, something shifts inside you. Your voice steadies. You're no longer asking for their approval—you're stating facts. By the end, you've transformed from someone seeking validation into someone who finally, devastatingly, sees their own worth clearly, regardless of whether they ever will.

title: Ecstasy and Exhaustion Entwined
instruction: You have just completed something that took years—running a marathon in memory of someone you lost, finishing a degree while battling illness, reaching a summit after an impossible climb. Begin in a state of explosive, almost manic joy, your body electric, voice exuberant, every cell vibrating with triumph. As you speak about what this means, feel your body beginning to register the immense physical toll. Your jubilation remains but becomes progressively weighted down by sheer bodily exhaustion, muscles trembling and heavy, until you are laughing and crying simultaneously, your joy inseparable from your pain and fatigue. End collapsed but radiant, your voice thick with tears and laughter, your body so heavy you cannot move but your spirit still soaring.

title: Submarine Hull Breach: Reporting Water Rise While Remaining Professional
instruction: You're in a submarine and there's a rupture. Your voice is initially controlled, almost robotic, as you report technical information to the captain: 'Water level rising in compartment three. Estimate 45 minutes.' But your voice trembles underneath. Include the moment you realize 45 minutes might not be achievable. You're narrating water levels while your voice gets higher and tighter. Other crew members are panicking around you and you have to stay composed to do your job. Your words become a mantra against fear. End with your voice becoming barely a whisper as you look at the rising water and understand: this is how you die. Professional. Technical. Afraid.

title: The Last Switchback
instruction: You are an elderly person on a steep, endless switchback trail, your legs burning, lungs heaving. Your younger hiking partner keeps urging you onward, and you're furious—you resent their energy, their cheerful encouragement. But instead of yelling, you throw out biting teases, mocking their eagerness while gasping for air. Halfway through, the anger drains away, replaced by a hollow numbness. You stop caring about the summit, the partner, even the pain. Let your voice labor with deep breaths, short phrases, and a puffed, weary quality. The tease should feel sharp but break into flat exhaustion by the end.
emotions_sampled: Anger (extremely present), Teasing (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a betrayal, a diagnosis, a catastrophic loss—and your body is flooded with adrenaline. But you're also at a celebration you can't leave: a wedding, a party, a family gathering. You're dancing, or moving to music, and your body can't be still. Begin with your voice matching intense physical energy—breathless, laughing too hard, speaking too fast, almost manic with forced joy. As you move, let the physical sensation unlock the emotional truth underneath. Your voice should start to break even as you keep moving. The rage or grief should seep through your laughter. Your breath should become ragged. By the end, you're still moving—maybe even more intensely—but your voice has transformed from false brightness to something raw, guttural, honest. Let your body and voice tell two different stories that eventually merge into one devastating truth.

title: The Kitchen at Midnight
instruction: Your mother sits across from you at the kitchen table. She's just told you something that reframes your entire childhood—a sacrifice she made, a truth she hid, a betrayal by someone else she protected you from. For years, you've been angry at her for things you thought she did wrong, for ways you thought she failed you. Start with that anger still hot in your throat, your words sharp, your body tense. You came here tonight to finally confront her. But as she explains, as the real story emerges, you feel your certainty crumbling. Let your voice shift from accusatory to confused to devastated. End in a place where you're the one apologizing, your voice shaking with the weight of how wrong you were, how much time you wasted being angry at the wrong person, reaching for her hand across the table.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're protecting someone you love from a threat—physical, emotional, institutional—and you've reached the moment where your control shatters. Start with fierce, authoritative strength, your voice cutting and powerful, making it clear you will not allow harm to come to them. But as you speak, let desperation creep in—the terrifying realization that your protection might not be enough, that you can't shield them from everything. Build to a point where your fierce defiance breaks into something between a roar and a sob, where anger and helplessness collide. Let your voice crack between rage at the injustice and tender, almost childlike fear of losing them. End in raw, gasping emotion where all pretense of control is gone and you're simply begging the universe for mercy.

title: Enjoying the Smoothness of Silk Sheets Against Your Skin
instruction: Slip under the silk sheets, feeling their smooth, cool texture against your skin. Describe the luxurious softness, the way each movement feels effortless and light, as the sheets glide over you. Speak with a tone of indulgence and pleasure, as if each touch of silk brings you a quiet, luxurious comfort.

title: Midnight Recording Session
instruction: You are a podcaster recording late at night, alone in your home studio. You're deeply concentrated on reading your script, leaning into the mic with a warm, intimate tone. Mid-sentence, you see a weird notification flash on your screen—something astonishing, like a viral post you can't believe. Your voice jumps with surprise, pulling back from the mic. Then exhaustion floods back; you lose your place, sigh heavily, and trail off, letting the weariness crack through your polished delivery.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Speaking in Flames
instruction: You are confronting your father after discovering a devastating family secret he's kept for twenty years. You are so overwhelmed with rage, betrayal, and hurt that coherent words fail you—your anger comes out in raw, broken, half-formed sounds and fragmented attempts at speech. Start with explosive fury that renders you nearly incoherent, your voice cracking and twisting with the effort to articulate your pain. As you continue, let the rage slowly crack open to reveal the wounded child underneath—the one who needed a father to be honest. End with your voice quieting to something small, almost childlike, as you ask the one real question beneath all the anger: 'Why wasn't I worth the truth?'

title: Airport Terminal Joy-Grief
instruction: Your sibling is leaving for a dream opportunity overseas—maybe forever—and you're genuinely thrilled for them while also losing your best friend. At the gate, you're trying to celebrate: 'This is amazing! You're going to be incredible!' But your voice keeps breaking with laughter that turns into barely-suppressed sobs. You're telling childhood stories—'Remember when we built that fort?'—and laughing through tears. The contradiction is constant: pride mixed with abandonment, joy mixed with grief. You keep starting over: 'I'm so happy for you, I am, I just—' but you can't finish. End with a fierce hug, saying 'Go, go now before I make this harder,' smiling and sobbing simultaneously, waving as they disappear, whispering 'I love you' to empty space.

title: Breaking Point Ecstasy
instruction: You've just finished running until your body screamed, or you're in the aftermath of intense physical release, or you've been crying so hard your ribs ache—your body is flooded with sensation. Start in that physical overwhelm, breath ragged, skin alive with feeling. Now speak to someone who isn't there, someone you want desperately or someone you've lost. Let the physical sensations fuel the emotional ones until you can't tell them apart. Your voice should be rough, unsteady, breaking. Move between gasping pleasure and choking grief, between the euphoria of feeling everything and the agony of feeling too much. Let your body lead your emotions—the shaking, the breathlessness, the raw physicality of being completely undefended.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked in the area of conflict — cannot express confrontational or aggressive feelings organically

title: The All-Nighter's Confession
instruction: You are an older woman who hasn't slept in over a day, trying to greet your adult child who just walked in. You're deeply embarrassed by how slurred and hollow your voice sounds, and you keep losing your train of thought, pausing mid-sentence. You start with forced cheerfulness, pretending everything is fine, but as you speak, the exhaustion overwhelms you. Your voice becomes flatter, more vulnerable, and you finally admit why you stayed up all night—not for a party, but because you were worried about something and couldn't stop your mind. End with a quiet, raw plea for understanding, your words trailing off as a yawn interrupts. Speak as if you're standing in a doorway, leaning on the frame, eyes heavy, struggling to stay upright.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bedside Vigil: Last Words to Someone Who Can't Answer
instruction: You're alone with someone unconscious - dying, comatose, or sedated before a dangerous surgery. Speak in an intimate whisper, telling them things you never said when they could respond. Start with small, everyday observations, your voice tender and almost casual. Gradually let the weight of unsaid things surface - confessions, apologies, admissions of love or need that shame and pride kept locked away. Let your voice catch on certain words. Cry quietly. Laugh softly at a memory. End with the simplest, most devastating truth, barely audible. This isn't a performance for them - it's for you, finally letting yourself feel everything you've been holding.
inspired_by: Guided Meditation Leader Having a Bad Day

title: The Thank You Letter You'll Never Send
instruction: You are writing or speaking aloud a letter to someone who crushed your dreams, who told you that you would fail, who rejected you at a crucial moment. Begin with genuine gratitude—because their cruelty or doubt became the fuel that forged you. But this gratitude is complex, layered with anger, with grief for the easier path you might have had, with resentment for the pain they caused. Let your voice carry all of these contradictions simultaneously—thanking them while also rage whispers beneath, appreciating the strength you found while grieving the innocence you lost. Your tone should shift like weather: warm then cold, loving then furious, grateful then devastated. End with a paradox fully embraced: you would not undo what they did, and you will never forgive them, and both things are completely true. Hold joy and bitterness in the same breath.
inspired_by: When you are an aspiring actor hearing discouraging stories about Hollywood's difficulty

title: Last Conversation at the Airport Gate
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone leaving for a one-way humanitarian mission to a war zone—they may never return. Start with forced brightness, trying to be supportive: 'This is amazing. You're going to change lives.' But your voice begins to fracture as the reality hits. The cheerfulness crumbles into raw fear and grief. 'I'm so proud of you, but I—' Your breath catches. You're trying not to make this harder for them, but you can't hold it back. End with a whispered confession of love and terror, your voice breaking completely: 'Come back to me. Please. I can't lose you.' Let the tears come naturally. This isn't about being strong—it's about being honest in what might be your final moment together.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father who was emotionally absent throughout your childhood. Start by listing all the ways you've tried to see the good in him—all the justifications you've made, all the 'at least he provided for us' and 'he did his best' mantras you've repeated for years. Your tone should be bright, almost aggressively positive, as if you're still trying to convince yourself. But as you speak, let the anger you've been covering with optimism begin to seep through. Let your voice shift from that brittle cheerfulness to something raw and fierce. End by finally saying what you've never allowed yourself to say: that you needed him and he wasn't there, that no amount of positive thinking can fill that void, your voice shaking with both rage and the grief of a child who still wants their father's love.

title: The Spoiled Report
instruction: You are an older scout, just returned from a long reconnaissance, standing in a dim stone corridor. Your full visor is down, the metal ringing with every word, and you're frustrated—the helm muffles your voice and you're tired and sour about the failed mission. Mid-sentence, you remember the odd artifact you found in the ruins, and your tone shifts: interest flickers in, then solidifies into quiet triumph as you realize its value. Let the clanking of the visor punctuate your speech, and let your voice change from bitter, clipped frustration to a slow, resonant confidence, as if the metal itself is now amplifying your victory.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Triumph (clearly present), Interest (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: A Stutter of Joy
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman sitting alone in a sunlit garden, a cup of tea cooling beside you. You're deeply content, humming softly and savoring the quiet peace of the afternoon. But a sudden, sharp hiccup cuts through your humming, startling you and making you blush with embarrassment, even though no one's around. Your voice shifts from serene, breathy contentment to a flustered, self-conscious laugh as you try to continue humming, only for another hiccup to punch the air out of your melody. Let the hiccups jerk your words and laughter into short, sharp gasps, and let your embarrassment soften back into a wry, amused smile by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Intervention: When Your Child Confronts Your Legacy
instruction: Your adult son has come to your home, and he's brought documents—emails, records, testimonies from people your business decisions destroyed. He's laying them on the table one by one, and you must respond. Begin with defensive irritation, your executive voice trying to maintain authority, explaining context and market realities. But his voice keeps breaking as he reads aloud from families who lost everything, and something in you begins to crack. Your justifications start sounding hollow even to your own ears. Move from anger to desperate rationalization to a moment of devastating recognition—you sound exactly like your own father, whom you swore you'd never become. End in a place of raw helplessness, no longer the powerful figure but simply a parent watching their child's respect die in real time, unable to take back what's been done.
inspired_by: Professional: Executive Prioritizes Profit Over Employee Lives

title: The Fantasy You Never Told Me
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of silence between you. Begin angry, tight, defended—you came here to tell him everything he did wrong. But mid-argument, something shifts. You dare to tell him about a fantasy you've carried since childhood: the life you imagined having with him, the father you dreamed he could be. Describe it with full sensory detail—the Saturday mornings, the specific smell of breakfast, the exact words of praise you longed to hear, the feeling of his hand on your shoulder, the sound of his genuine laugh. As you speak this fantasy aloud, something unexpected happens in your body and voice. The anger doesn't disappear, but it transforms—maybe into grief, maybe into something like forgiveness, maybe into a tender kind of hope. Let the fantasy be so vivid it becomes momentarily real, and let that reality change what's possible between you right now.
inspired_by: Fantasy Imaging to Elevate State Before Performance

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 2 AM. Your child is asleep. Tomorrow you're leaving—not because you want to, but because staying will destroy you both. Kneel beside their bed. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, tender and breaking as you tell them all the things you won't be there to see: first heartbreak, graduation, their wedding day. Your throat tightens with each image. You're memorizing their face in the dark. Your whisper becomes even softer, more fragile, as you apologize for not being strong enough to stay. Tell them about the kind of parent you wanted to be versus the one you are. Let long silences stretch between your words—moments where you almost can't continue. Your voice nearly disappears as you promise they'll understand someday, even though you're not sure they will. End with the smallest, most broken sound: 'I love you' said so quietly it's almost just breath, your hand hovering over their hair but not touching, afraid you'll wake them and have to see their eyes.
inspired_by: Karate Tournament Final: Facing Your Abuser

title: The Accusation
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just announced they're dropping out of their medical residency to become a wildlife photographer. You start angry, lecturing about wasted potential and YOUR sacrifices. But as they describe what they've actually been seeing through the lens—the specific behavior of a red-tailed hawk, the way morning light hits ice, the patience required to wait for one perfect moment—something shifts. Stop preparing your next argument and actually listen to the details of what captivates them. By the end, your anger has transformed into a reluctant, almost painful recognition that they're describing a passion you've never allowed yourself. End with a question—a real question—about their work.

title: The Imperfect Stillness
instruction: You are an older woman with a gentle, hyper-feminized voice, sitting in deep meditation in your garden. The world is soft and quiet. Then, a persistent fly lands on your arm, buzzing. A flicker of disgust passes through you — a micro-expression in your voice. You try to release it. By the end, you speak a single, deliberate phrase that acknowledges the disturbance but returns to center. Let your words be slow, each one placed with care. Feel the peace, then the tiny revulsion, then the choice to let go. Your voice should reflect the trance state: soft, clear, unhurried, with the disgust as a subtle, brief sharpness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Weight Lifted
instruction: You're alone in a cramped bathroom, clutching the sink, your reflection blurred by tears. You just got the news—after months of fighting, it's finally over, and you're safe. At first, your words come in ragged, hiccuping gasps, disbelief strangling your throat, your voice cracking as you whisper to yourself, 'I can't… I can't believe it.' But as you stare at your own wet, reddened eyes, something shifts—a slow, trembling smile breaks through the sobs, and your voice, still broken and mucousy, begins to rise with a raw, releasing laugh, 'It's done… it's really done.' Let the relief surge up through the tears, making your inhalation hitch and your vowels waver as you finally let yourself feel the joy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Page of the Letter
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl, sitting on the floor of your dimly lit bedroom at 2 AM, surrounded by crumpled tissues. You've just sobbed yourself empty over a letter from your estranged father. Your throat is raw, your sinuses are completely blocked, and your head feels heavy with exhaustion. But as you pick up the letter one last time, you notice a single, small detail you missed—a faded pencil drawing of a bird he made in the margin when you were little. In this state, your words are thick and broken, your breath shallow. You start speaking to no one but yourself, with a whispery, hoarse voice, overwhelmed by a fragile, flickering curiosity that slowly transforms into a quiet, aching wonder.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your childhood home after a natural disaster destroyed it. You find something miraculous intact—maybe your mother's music box, a family photo—and you laugh, a sound that's equal parts joy and heartbreak. 'It survived. After everything, this little thing survived.' Your voice wavers between wonder and grief. Start humming the melody from the music box, and it makes you cry even as you're smiling: 'Mom used to play this when I couldn't sleep.' You're overwhelmed by gratitude for what you had, even as you're devastated by the loss. End with a paradox in your voice: 'Everything's gone, and somehow... somehow I feel how lucky I was to have had it.' Your final words are whispered through tears that feel both sad and thankful: 'We were so loved here.' Embody joy and sorrow as one inseparable emotion.

title: Holding Your Dying Child Who You Failed to Save
instruction: Your child is dying from an illness you couldn't afford to treat, and you're holding them in a hospital room where you've run out of options. Start with fierce, almost manic reassurance—'You're going to be okay, baby, you're so strong'—but your voice is already cracking under the weight of the lie. As they grow weaker, your words become wild, desperate bargaining with God, the universe, anyone: 'PLEASE, take me instead, PLEASE.' Your voice breaks into raw, animalistic sobbing. Then they touch your face and you have to pull yourself together for them one last time. You swallow the screams and become gentle again, your voice shredded but soft: 'I love you so much. I'm right here.' But underneath, you're dying too. You're singing them the lullaby you sang when they were born, your voice splintering on every note. By the end, you're whispering 'I'm sorry' over and over—to them, to yourself, to the universe—helpless and shattered and still trying to be their shelter.

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering truths you can't say while they're awake. Begin barely audible, testing the words: 'I need to tell you something I've never told anyone.' Your voice is tender but trembling as you confess a deep vulnerability—a fear, a wound from your past, something that makes you feel unlovable: 'Sometimes I wake up afraid that you'll realize I'm not worth staying for.' As you speak into the darkness, grief rises in your throat, your voice catching on tears you didn't know were there. The confession becomes both a prayer and a goodbye to shame: 'I love you more than I know how to say, and that terrifies me.' End with your voice barely holding together, a whispered plea that hangs in the quiet: 'Please don't leave when you see all of me.' Let this be intimate, fragile, the kind of vulnerability that feels like standing naked in the cold.
inspired_by: Principal Meeting: When a Student is in Crisis

title: The Lie on Your Lips
instruction: You're in a dim bedroom, kneeling on the bed facing your partner. You agreed to try dominating the conversation tonight, but as you start speaking, doubt creeps in—your voice wavers, you glance away, you fidget with the sheets. Then a flash of memory hits: you remember the lie they told you last week. The anger surges, hot and clean. Let that anger sharpen your words. Start with a whisper, almost asking permission, then let your voice drop into a low growl. Use deliberate profanity, pause to let each syllable land. End with a firm, projected command that leaves no room for negotiation. Speak as if you're testing your own power and finding it real.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (slightly present), Anger (very intensely present), Confusion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Gratitude That Destroys
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone who saved your life—literally pulled you from addiction, suicide, or despair—but who has just died from the same demons they rescued you from. Start speaking with genuine gratitude, your voice warm and almost smiling: 'You taught me that life was worth living. You showed me how to laugh again.' But there's something underneath—a tremor. As you continue, you begin laughing softly at a memory, but the laughter cracks and distorts. 'You were so good at saving everyone but yourself.' The gratitude and grief become indistinguishable. You're thanking them while your heart breaks: 'Thank you for giving me a future you couldn't believe in for yourself.' By the end, you're crying but also smiling, your voice impossibly gentle and shattered at once: 'I'm going to live the life you gave me. I'm going to be happy. And I'm going to miss you every single day. How dare you make me love life this much and then leave me here to live it.'

title: The Stretch That Reveals Where It Hurts to Be Touched
instruction: Begin stretching gently, but as you move, certain positions trigger memories of touch you didn't want, boundaries crossed, or moments when your body wasn't yours to control. Your voice starts calm, almost clinical, describing the stretch—but let it catch, hesitate. Whisper about the specific places that carry memory, speaking so softly it's almost just breath. This isn't about the trauma itself but about the tender, devastating recognition of how your body remembers what your mind tried to forget. Let shame mix with self-compassion, fear with the desperate wish to reclaim these sensations as safe. Your voice should tremble not with drama but with the authentic fragility of someone trying to be gentle with themselves when gentleness was taken from them. End with the quietest admission of what you're still learning to believe: that your body deserves to feel good.

title: The Unladylike Belch
instruction: You're on a dinner date with someone you've been crushing on for months. The conversation is flowing, you're leaning in, feeling that warm flutter of infatuation—then a deep, rumbling belch escapes from your throat, completely unexpected and embarrassingly loud. Your voice dips into a gravelly register for a moment. You try to recover by laughing it off, but you feel your cheeks burn with humiliation. As you stammer an apology, impatience creeps in—annoyance at your own body for sabotaging this perfect moment. Start with a soft, breathy tone of infatuation, then shift to strained embarrassment, and finally let a flicker of irritation color your words as you attempt to redirect the conversation. Speak naturally, pausing to swallow or giggle nervously. Approximately 50-70 words of dialogue.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Room Down the Hall
instruction: You're a 12-year-old boy, alone in a locked bathroom at a family gathering. You've just touched yourself for the first time, and your body is doing things you can't control — gasps, a sudden tight cry, a whimper you try to smother into your fist. You hear footsteps outside. The shame floods in, hot and sick, mixing with a sharp ache in your chest that you don't have words for yet. Your voice cracks, catches on a sob, then trails off into small, shuddering sounds as you sink down against the door, pressing your palm over your mouth.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping child's bed late at night, whispering a confession they can't hear. Start with gentle, loving observations about their breathing, their small hand. Your voice is tender, almost singing. But slowly, let grief seep in—you're struggling with depression, addiction, illness, or you're leaving. 'I'm so sorry I'm not the parent you deserve.' Your whisper becomes thick with tears you're trying to keep silent. The emotion catches in your throat repeatedly. End with a promise you desperately want to keep but aren't sure you can: 'I'm trying so hard to stay.' Let the love and the devastation occupy the same breath.
inspired_by: Losing Your Temper at Someone You Love

title: When Protective Love Meets Powerlessness
instruction: Your teenage child just told you they're being bullied, assaulted, or struggling with suicidal thoughts. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness - your voice strong, promising to fix everything, to destroy whoever hurt them, voice rising with parental fury. But mid-sentence, reality hits: you can't actually protect them from this. Your powerful voice cracks and crumbles. The rage transforms into helpless pleading - your voice breaking as you beg them to let you help, to stay, to fight. You're suddenly the vulnerable one, voice raw with terror at the thought of losing them. End with your voice stripped completely bare, oscillating between fierce love and devastating helplessness, finally landing on honest admission: 'I don't know how to fix this, but please, please stay with me.'

title: First Call to Colors
instruction: You are a seventeen-year-old girl, the newest and youngest recruit in a military academy’s flag-raising squad. It is your first solo command at dawn. Your voice has always been soft, high-pitched — ‘too pretty’ for the parade ground, the other recruits whispered. You stand rigid at attention, eyes fixed on the flagpole, heart hammering against your ribs. You open your mouth to bark the first command, but what comes out is a breathy, trembling ‘Color guard…’ — then you halt, mortified. Feel the cold air in your lungs, the dew on your boots. For a long second, you are just a scared teenager faking it. Then, a memory of your grandmother’s voice: ‘You have the strongest heart, not the loudest roar.’ A strange, fragile hope blooms in your chest — not that you’ll be perfect, but that you can be true. You reset. Your next words climb slightly in pitch, still soft, but now clear and steady. By the final word, your voice carries a gentle, rising optimism — not a bark, but a bell: clear, feminine, and unashamedly hopeful. You are not copying the men. You are finding your own sound in this dawn.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Frozen Witness
instruction: You are an older adult, androgynous, standing alone on a frigid street corner, waiting for a ride that's late. The cold has seeped into your bones—your jaw is tight, your teeth chatter, and each word comes out as a forced hiss through clenched lips. Across the street, through a steamy window, you see a younger couple laughing over hot drinks, wrapped in a warmth you no longer feel. Start by describing the numbness—how the cold has made you forget what it's like to care. Let a flicker of envy creep in as you watch them, then let that envy harden into a quiet, bitter anger at the unfairness of it all. By the end, your voice should shake not just from the cold but from a sudden, painful awareness of what you lack. Keep the performance raw—let the shivers interrupt your words, lose a thought, then pick it up again.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Anger (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Fever Dream
instruction: You're burning with fever, your body aching and hypersensitive. Every sensation is amplified - the weight of the blanket feels crushing, your skin burns and freezes simultaneously. In this delirium, a memory surfaces with overwhelming physical intensity: a moment of betrayal or loss that your body remembers. Speak through the physical discomfort - your voice hoarse, catching, interrupted by your labored breathing. Describe both the bodily sensations (the fever, the sweating, the trembling) and the emotional memory bleeding through. Start disoriented and fragmented, almost incoherent. Let the emotional pain become indistinguishable from the physical. Build to a moment where you're not sure if you're crying from fever or grief. End with your body finally releasing, becoming quiet and exhausted, as the fever breaks and takes the memory's intensity with it.

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table about something he's never acknowledged—his absence, his drinking, his cruelty, his silence. Begin by noticing everything stopping you from speaking the truth: politeness, fear of his reaction, the habit of protecting him, your own shame, the desire to just leave. Say these obstacles out loud, even if your voice shakes: 'I'm afraid you'll shut down. I want to protect you. I don't want to hurt you.' Once you've named what's in the way, speak the truth you came to speak. Notice how your emotion transforms—from knotted anxiety and performance to raw honesty, perhaps anger dissolving into unexpected tenderness, or numbness breaking into grief.

title: The Passport in Your Hand
instruction: You hold an opened passport—yours—containing a visa that means you can finally leave a country where you've suffered, or finally enter a country where your family waits, or finally start a life you thought was impossible. You've fought for years to get this single document. Begin with the triumphant relief you expected to feel—you've won, it's over, you're free. But as you stare at the photo, at the stamps, at your own name in official ink, something unexpected rises. This piece of paper is both your salvation and the confirmation that you're leaving something behind forever. Look at it as if you've never seen official documentation of your own existence. Trace the letters of your name like a child learning to read. Let victory curdle into loss, then into confusion about what you actually want, then into a contradictory storm of gratitude and grief. End in a place where you're laughing and crying simultaneously, holding the passport like it's both a treasure and a betrayal, unable to separate your joy from your sorrow.

title: Counting Stars in a Collapsing Building
instruction: You're trapped in rubble after an earthquake, whispering to a stranger trapped beside you in the darkness, both of you knowing rescue won't come in time. Begin speaking softly to keep them calm, asking gentle questions about their life, their children. Your voice is tender but you can hear your own fear underneath, breath hitching when the structure groans. Share quiet confessions you've never told anyone—regrets that seem so small now, moments of joy you didn't appreciate. Let silences matter as much as words. When they stop responding, your whisper becomes more urgent, pleading, then breaks into quiet, devastated weeping. End in a barely audible voice, reciting something beautiful—a poem, a prayer, a lullaby—to comfort yourself and their fading presence, finding strange dignity in refusing to die in silence.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father at the kitchen table about his absence during your childhood. Begin with rehearsed anger - the speech you've prepared, the accusations you've lined up. But mid-confrontation, a memory floods you: a specific moment when he took you somewhere special, the smell of his cologne, his laugh, how safe you felt. Allow this sensory memory to derail your anger completely. Describe this memory out loud in rich detail - what you saw, heard, smelled, felt - and let yourself become that child again for a moment. Your confrontation should transform from accusatory anger into a vulnerable, confused mixture of longing and hurt. End in a completely different emotional place than where you started - perhaps with a whispered question you've never dared ask.
inspired_by: Actor arrives at performance depressed, stressed, or emotionally shut down

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After the Diagnosis
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside your child's bed, watching them sleep, hours after the doctor's appointment that changed everything. You speak in the softest whisper, not wanting to wake them, confessing everything you can't say in daylight. Start with simple observation—how peaceful they look, how beautiful—your voice catching on ordinary details: their hand curled near their face, the rhythm of their breathing. Let the fear seep in gradually, your whisper becoming even quieter, as if making it smaller might make it less real. Tell them about the future you'd imagined, each dream dissolving as you speak it. Your voice should break on small words, on 'birthday' or 'graduation' or 'someday.' But then find something unexpected: fierce, protective love that makes you almost smile through tears. Promise them things you can't guarantee, your whisper becoming a prayer. End with the simplest truth, repeated like a mantra—'I'm here. I'm here. I'm here'—your voice barely audible but absolutely certain.
inspired_by: Buried in Snow: Creating an Air Pocket While Suffocating

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received news that should devastate you—a terminal diagnosis, a betrayal, a loss—but something unexpected happens: you start laughing. Not hysterical laughter, but genuine, almost wondering amusement at the absurdity of it all. Your voice dances between laughter and tears, sometimes mid-sentence: 'Of course this happened. Of course.' There's grief underneath, but also strange liberation, even joy. You find yourself grateful—'Thank you, actually, for showing me what matters'—while your voice cracks with sorrow. The emotions twist together: anger dissolves into acceptance, sadness mingles with relief, fear transforms into odd peace. End with a moment where you can't tell if you're laughing or crying, but it doesn't matter because you've found an unexpected freedom in surrendering to both. Your breathing steadies into something like grace.

title: The Box of Crayons
instruction: You're sitting on the floor, knees aching, digging through a dusty cardboard box of your kid's old toys and papers. You're irritated—can't find the one thing you need, muttering curses under your breath, shifting the weight of the box, plastic crinkling under your fingers. Then your hand closes around a small, worn drawing: a stick figure family with shaky crayon hearts. The frustration softens; your voice cracks with longing as you remember their tiny hands. Finally, you whisper a quiet, grateful 'thank you' to the empty room, your voice thick with unexpected tenderness.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Longing (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: At the Dentist's Chair
instruction: You are a young child, maybe six or seven, lying back in a dentist's chair with your head tilted far back over the edge. The bright light is in your eyes, and you can feel the cold metal instruments near your mouth. You're terrified of the drilling noise you heard from the next room. You try to ask your mom a question, but your throat is stretched and you can barely swallow. Your voice comes out thin and high, wavering with every pause. At first you're fighting back tears, trying to be brave, but as you realize the dentist is coming closer, your fear takes over and your words dissolve into a shaky, pleading whimper.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Thunder and Empty Promises
instruction: You're at an outdoor bus stop in a violent thunderstorm, drunk on cheap whiskey, waiting for someone you've been aching to meet. At first, you shout into the rain with a slurred, lustful excitement, laughing at the lightning and imagining their body pressed against yours. But the storm keeps hammering, the minutes stretch, and the cold seeps through your clothes. Your hopeful calls turn into a desperate, broken plea, the lust curdling into raw, shaking sadness. Let your voice crack as you fight the thunder — sometimes roaring, sometimes muffled as you wipe rain from your lips. End in a quiet, tear-soaked admission that they're never coming.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Sunrise - A Farewell at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has hours left to live, watching the sunrise together through a hospital window. Begin with quiet awe at the beauty of the light, your voice soft and wondering. As you describe what you see, let gratitude seep in - thank them for all the sunrises you've shared. Your breath catches as you realize this is the last one. The gratitude doesn't leave, but grief floods in alongside it. Your voice becomes unsteady, intimate, as you tell them it's okay to let go. End in whispered devastation mixed with profound love, your words breaking apart as you promise to remember this moment forever. Let silence hold the weight of goodbye.
inspired_by: Telling Someone You're Attracted to Them

title: Realizing Your Therapist Isn't the Right Fit
instruction: It clicks mid-session: they don't understand something fundamental about you. Your voice becomes guarded: 'I don't think this is working.' Your therapist asks why and your voice becomes more articulate about the mismatch. 'I don't feel heard when...' You're preparing to fire your therapist and your voice becomes assured. Say goodbye uncertain about starting over.

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering Love to Someone Who Cannot Hear
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply but never told—maybe a best friend, maybe an unrequited love—who is in a coma. It's 3 AM and you're alone with them for the first time. Begin in whispers, barely audible, confessing feelings you've hidden for years. Your voice should be tender, terrified, intimate—as if speaking too loudly will break the spell or expose you. Let yourself become more vulnerable with each sentence, your breathing uneven, tears making your words thick. Midway through, allow yourself a moment of quiet devastation—the realization that this confession may be too late, that they may never know. Then find a fragile kind of peace, still whispering, telling them it's okay if they need to go, even though every word costs you. End with barely audible words of permission mixed with desperate hope, your voice catching on the contradiction of wanting them to stay while also setting them free.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Dragon Realizes the Creature It Hunts Is Its Own Hatched Sibling

title: The Mother Defending Her Accused Child
instruction: You're a mother whose child has been accused of something terrible. You start fierce, protective, voice trembling with rage at the accusations. 'How dare you! You don't know my child!' Building in intensity, almost shouting, defending them with everything you have. But then—mid-declaration—doubt creeps in. A detail you can't explain. A memory that suddenly makes terrible sense. Your fierce certainty begins to crack. The volume drops. Your hands are shaking. You hear yourself saying 'I... they wouldn't... would they?' The rage transforms into something much worse: the possibility that you don't know your own child, that love has made you blind. End in a kind of helpless, broken whisper, still wanting to protect them but no longer sure what protecting them even means. Let the fierce mama bear collapse into terrified uncertainty.
inspired_by: Fortune Teller Who Sees Something Terrible

title: Grief Acceptance
instruction: You've finally stopped fighting the grief and accepted it. Your voice is sad but peaceful: 'I miss you.' You're speaking to the person who's gone, and it's okay now that they're gone. Your voice carries love without desperation. 'I'm learning to live with this.' You're not over it, but you're accepting it. Your voice becomes gentle: 'Thank you for being in my life.' By the end, your voice is bittersweet—sadness and gratitude mixed.

title: The Masked Compliment
instruction: You are at a small outdoor gathering, wearing a cloth face mask. A friend you haven't seen in months is gushing about another woman's laugh, her ease, her perfect life. You stand there, nodding, but behind the mask, your jaw is tight. Start by forcing a polite, muffled response—your envy makes the words feel thick, your voice straining against the fabric. You'll try to agree, but the jealousy rises like heat in your chest. End with a strained, clipped sentence where the envy seeps through, your mask suddenly feeling suffocating, your plosives lost, your tone gone flat. Speak naturally, with the mask pressing on your voice.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Other Candidate
instruction: You are in a job interview for a position you desperately need. Across the table, the interviewer is friendly, but you can't stop staring at her assistant — a woman your age, the one who seems to have everything you don't. As you answer her first question about your experience, your voice starts steady but hollow, running on rehearsed sentences. Mid-answer, you see the assistant yawn or glance at her phone, and your throat tightens. Your words slow as you realize how tired you are of always being the backup choice. Your voice cracks once, you quickly clear it, and finish with a hollow 'I could really help this team' — knowing you sound as exhausted as you feel.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Sauna Confession
instruction: You are in a crowded public sauna, the air thick and wet, your skin slick with sweat. Across from you sits the person you've been infatuated with for weeks—calm, unbothered, while you feel your voice slipping and sliding in your throat. Start with a giddy, breathless attempt at casual small talk, but as the heat presses in and they barely respond, your infatuation curdles into an awkward, self-conscious realization that they don't feel the same. Let the moisture in your voice mirror your vulnerability—swallow hard, let words come out too fast then too slow, and finish with a quiet, embarrassed laugh that trails off.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent everything you've held back for decades - how their absence shaped you, how you learned to hide your needs because they were never met. Begin with careful, measured words, almost apologetic, still trying to protect them from the truth. But as you speak, feel the anger rising - not loud rage, but something sharper, more precise. Your voice should grow stronger, more direct, demanding they finally see you. Then, unexpectedly, let it shift into something more vulnerable: underneath the anger is a child still hoping they'll finally understand, still wanting their love. End with that heartbreaking mixture - fierce in your truth, but aching with the need for them to truly hear you.
inspired_by: Acting Interested While Bored in a Conversation

title: The Journalist and the Secret Informant
instruction: Depict a journalist with a probing, assertive voice meeting a secret informant who speaks in a hushed, cautious tone. Switch between the journalists pressing questions and the informants guarded answers, creating a suspenseful atmosphere.

title: Reading Your Daughter's Suicide Note Aloud to Her
instruction: Your daughter survived her attempt and is sitting in the hospital bed, silent and unreachable. The doctors gave you the note she left. You begin reading it aloud to her, your voice steady, almost clinical — you need to get through this. But as you read her words describing her pain, something unexpected happens: you start laughing. Not cruel laughter, but the broken, desperate laughter of someone whose heart is shattering. You're crying and laughing simultaneously because her note is so articulate, so beautifully written, and you're devastated that she used that brilliant mind to plan her death. Your voice swings wildly between grief and a strange, terrible gratitude that she's still here to hear you read this. End with your laughter turning to sobs as you crumple the note, telling her: 'You're the best thing I ever did, and I'm so sorry I didn't make you feel that every single day.' Your voice finds an odd peace in that admission, even as tears stream down your face.
inspired_by: Dictating a Will on a Sinking Ship

title: The Last Wild Thing
instruction: You're lying in a hospital bed, dying, and your adult child sits beside you holding your hand. You begin speaking calmly, telling them you love them—but suddenly something primal breaks free inside you. You're terrified of disappearing, of becoming nothing, and that terror erupts as guttural sounds, gasping breaths, your body trying to cling to life with animal desperation. Your hands clutch at the sheets, at the air, at your child. Then, gradually, the storm passes. You grow still. In your final moments, you're no longer fighting—you've become peaceful, almost curious, whispering about something beautiful you're beginning to see. Let your body and voice move from civilized farewell to wild panic to transcendent calm.

title: The Taste of Vindication
instruction: You have just received news that completely vindicates you after years of being called crazy, paranoid, or a liar—the evidence has emerged, the truth is undeniable, and everyone who doubted you now knows you were right all along. Begin by physicaly trembling with adrenaline, your voice jagged with bitter, triumphant rage as you imagine confronting each person who dismissed you. Let your body burn with the remembered humiliation, the years of second-guessing yourself. But as you speak—first to the empty room, then perhaps on the phone, then maybe to yourself—notice how the vindication tastes like ashes. The rage begins to mix with exhaustion, grief for the years lost, and a hollow ache where satisfaction should be. End with your body slowly collapsing, voice raw and small, as you realize that being proven right doesn't heal what was broken. Transform from fierce, kinetic fury to a depleted, aching awareness that some wounds remain regardless of truth.

title: Scattering Ashes in Their Favorite Place
instruction: You're standing in the place your beloved person loved most - a beach, a mountain, their garden - holding their ashes. Start with a small, almost surprised laugh: 'You'd love this. The sky is exactly that color you always...' Your voice is warm, talking to them like they're there. You're telling them a funny story, and you actually laugh - genuine, full. But mid-sentence, the reality hits. The laughter catches, transforms. Your voice cracks: 'God, I miss you.' But then you catch yourself, smile through tears: 'No, no, you'd hate me being sad right now.' You're laughing and crying simultaneously, voice doing both at once. As you open the container, there's reverence, gratitude, devastation all tangled together: 'Thank you. For everything. For every single day.' You release the ashes, and your voice is filled with bittersweet peace: 'Okay. You're free now.' The goodbye is both heartbreaking and strangely joyful - celebrating them while your heart shatters.

title: Crawlspace Confession
instruction: You are a tough, older man trapped under a collapsed shed, your arms stretched up to brace a heavy beam off your chest. Your voice is thin and high from the strain—your usual deep rumble gone. Start by snarling with disgust at your own helplessness, cursing the rotten wood and your age. But as you shift and feel the beam settle, a quieter realization creeps in: you're not as indestructible as you pretended. Let the disgust slowly give way to a raw, reluctant acceptance—spoken through gritted teeth and ragged breaths, with pauses where you adjust your grip or spit out dust.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Envy in Your Smile
instruction: You are a young woman working a customer service hotline, using your brightest, most feminized 'smile voice'—pitch raised, uptalk, cheerful and plastic. A customer calls to upgrade their account to a luxury tier you can't afford, and they mention a vacation they're planning. Briefly, you feel a flash of elation (you helped them), but underneath, the longing and clear jealousy creep in as you imagine their life. Start chirpy and efficient, then let your voice subtly tighten, your pitch drop just slightly, and your words become clipped as envy seeps through. End the interaction with a forced cheerfulness that sounds strained, almost bitter. Deliver approximately 50 words of dialogue.
emotions_sampled: Longing (slightly present), Elation (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Quiet Goodbye: Whispering Love to Someone Who Can No Longer Hear You
instruction: You're sitting beside your unconscious beloved—partner, parent, or closest friend—in their final hours. The doctors say they can't hear you anymore, but you need to speak anyway. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and breaking: 'I don't know if you're still in there...' Tell them all the small, sacred things you never said enough—how their laugh changed your world, the way they made coffee, that Tuesday afternoon that meant everything. Your voice catches on memories, soft and intimate: 'Remember when we...' Let tears thicken your words without sobbing—this is quiet devastation, the kind that lives in your chest. As you speak, the reality that they're leaving settles deeper, and your whispers become even softer, more precious: 'I'm not ready, but... I'll be okay. Because you loved me.' End with a moment of pure tenderness, giving them permission to go, your voice full of love and unbearable sadness. This is not performed grief—this is the raw, whispered truth of letting go.
inspired_by: Descending from the Death Zone: Oxygen Returning Clarity

title: I Will Burn This World Down For You
instruction: Someone you love more than your own life has been hurt, and you're confronting the person responsible. Start with your voice shaking—not with fear but with the effort of containing an absolute rage that could consume everything. You're trying to speak calmly, trying to be reasonable, but your voice keeps fracturing. Let the fury build and then suddenly crack wide open into something more vulnerable—the terror underneath, the helplessness of not having been there to protect them. Your voice should swing between lethal threat and broken desperation. You want to destroy this person, but what you really want is to undo what happened, and you can't. End with your voice raw and exhausted, the rage collapsed into grief, admitting the devastating truth: all your fury can't change what's already done. The fierceness remains but transforms into something more like a howl of pain.

title: The Last Letter to Someone Already Gone
instruction: You're recording a voice message to someone who died six months ago—a ritual you've kept up because you can't accept they're gone. Start in that same flat, emotionless monotone of denial: 'I know you're not there. I know that.' But as you continue speaking—telling them about your day, asking their advice, admitting how lost you are—something cracks. Your voice begins to tremble, breath becomes ragged, and by the end you're sobbing through words of goodbye you've never been able to say. The emotional journey moves from numb denial to devastating acceptance. Let the transformation happen gradually, naturally, as if the act of speaking finally breaks through the wall you've built.

title: The Body's Translation
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—you got the life-saving diagnosis, or the job that saves your family, or you're finally pregnant after years of trying, or someone you love is coming home. Your body floods with sensation: heart racing, hands shaking, sudden heat, tears, explosive laughter. But as you're physically experiencing this intensity, notice the unexpected images that flash through your mind in this heightened state—random faces, places, moments that seem unrelated but appear anyway. Don't dismiss them as distractions; let them layer into your experience. Your arc should begin with pure, explosive joy or relief—something almost violent in its intensity—but gradually shift as these unbidden images pull in other feelings: grief for the struggle it took, anger at the unfairness, exhaustion, or bittersweet awareness of time lost. The spontaneous images that surface should complicate your ecstasy into something more truthful and multidimensional.

title: Standup Bombing Recovery
instruction: You bombed the biggest set of your life and now you're alone in your apartment. Your voice is tight with shame and disbelief: 'That was the worst... I've never...' Pacing, maybe. Breathing is irregular. But something shifts mid-speech. 'Actually, you know what, I didn't die.' Vocal tone lifts slightly. 'I bombed and I'm still here.' Physical: you're moving with more intention. By the end, you're finding dark humor: 'Worst night of my life: check.' Your voice has transformed from destroyed to resilient. Not happy, but standing.

title: Channel 5 Crush
instruction: You're a kid in your room, gripping a walkie-talkie. The boy you've been secretly watching all summer just called you on channel 5. Your heart pounds as you press the talk button. Start with short, breathy words—trying to sound cool, but your voice cracks with excitement. You fumble the button, hear static, then laugh at yourself. As you go on, your infatuation spills out: you talk faster, lighter, almost giddy. At the end, you hesitate, then ask a hopeful question, your voice soft and vulnerable. Let the walkie-talkie's squelch and your own shyness shape every word.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Every Way You're Wrong About Me
instruction: Your father has just accused you (again) of being a failure, of never finishing anything, of being weak. This time, instead of shrinking or screaming, you stand your ground and methodically list every single thing you've actually accomplished that he's never acknowledged—jobs you've held, skills you've mastered, people you've helped, obstacles you've overcome, fears you've faced. Start with your voice shaking with defensive anger and hurt. As you continue listing your real achievements, feel your voice growing steadier, stronger, more certain. By the end, you're not defending yourself anymore—you're claiming your worth, and you no longer need his approval. The anger transforms into hard-won self-respect. Make him hear the person you actually are, not the failure he insists on seeing.

title: The Last Goodbye at Dawn
instruction: You're standing at your parent's bedside in the pre-dawn stillness, and you know this is the last conversation you'll ever have. You begin with fierce denial—'No, we have time, there's still time'—your voice tight, almost angry at the universe. But as you hold their hand, something shifts. The anger drains away and what emerges is profound gratitude mixed with devastating loss. Your words become softer, more deliberate: 'Thank you for... everything.' Each phrase is a struggle between wanting to say everything and knowing silence is also love. End in a whisper of acceptance, your breathing synchronized with theirs, finding strange peace in letting go. The tears come not from despair but from the beauty of having loved someone this deeply.

title: Dusty Memories
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman sorting through a box of old family papers on a cluttered desk. The dry paper slides against your fingers, making sharp snaps as you separate stacks. You begin with a slight disgust—the dust, the disorganization, the faded handwriting you don't recognize. You mumble complaints under your breath, voice dropping to a whisper as you read a few words. Then you find a handwritten letter from your mother, and your tone softens into a tender, almost reluctant warmth. Let the physical distraction of sorting—the shuffle, the pause to squint at a smudged date—affect your rhythm. Speak the lines as if you're half-talking to yourself, half to the memory. Your final words carry a mix of grudging affection and the lingering edge of your earlier irritation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Recognition
instruction: You are sitting at the bedside of someone who shaped your soul—a grandparent, mentor, or old friend—in their final hours. Begin with quiet presence, no need for words at first, just the weight of knowing this is goodbye. As you speak, you're not trying to comfort them or yourself; you're simply offering the truth of what they meant to you, how they saw something in you before you could see it yourself. Let your voice carry both profound gratitude and the ache of impending loss. Midway through, allow a memory to surface that makes you smile through gathering tears—something specific, small, perfect. By the end, shift into a place of release: you're giving them permission to go, even as your heart is breaking. Your final words should feel like both a blessing and a surrender, spoken soul to soul, presence to presence, with all the love you've never quite known how to express until this moment.

title: Final Phone Call from a Capsized Ship's Hold
instruction: You've managed to get one bar of signal in the flooding compartment. Call your adult child—you need to tell them where the family documents are, the safe combination, that the house is paid off. Start practical, almost businesslike, because that's how you're holding it together. As cold water rises past your knees, your voice starts to break. You realize this isn't about documents—you need them to know you were proud of them, that you saw who they became. The practicality dissolves into desperate tenderness. End trying to say 'I love you' but you're sobbing too hard, and the line cuts out. Let us hear you surrender to both the water and the love.
inspired_by: Space Station Commander Records Birthday Message While Hull Breaches

title: Tasting Comfort You No Longer Deserve
instruction: You've done something unforgivable—betrayed someone who trusted you, made a choice that destroyed a relationship—and now you're alone, eating their favorite food that you used to make together. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, describing each bite with tender precision, speaking as if they were still there beside you. Your tone should be achingly gentle, filled with such quiet longing it almost hurts to listen. Let shame seep in gradually—small catches in your breath, longer pauses where you can't speak. The comfort of the familiar taste only deepens your devastation. End with your voice breaking on a whispered confession of what you've lost, the food turning to ash in your mouth as you realize you're tasting a happiness you'll never have again.
inspired_by: Taking a Bite of Freshly Baked Bread

title: Hiding Exhaustion While Continuing to Work
instruction: Youre extremely tired but need to keep going. Internally, fatigue weighs you down, but you push through. Describe the heaviness inside while appearing alert. Speak with energy, hiding any signs of weariness.

title: The Lotus Eater's Hollow Victory
instruction: You are sitting cross-legged on the floor of your sparse apartment, phone in your lap, after your best friend just shared a video of their new life abroad. Your jaw is tight, and your breath is shallow. Start by trying to sound detached and dismissive—you're just scrolling, fine. But as you speak, let the jealousy and helplessness seep into your voice, feeling the envy so intensely it makes your throat ache. Let your words wander, losing the thought and finding it again, until you end the monologue in a quiet, vulnerable admission that you are left behind.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Doubt (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Garden I Never Tended
instruction: You are an elderly person, standing alone in a neglected garden you once loved. The world feels muffled, like you're watching this scene through a thick pane of glass. Your voice is flat and hollow at first, as if you're describing someone else's memory. But as you speak, a fierce pride in what this garden once was begins to stir, and a fragile hope for the tiny sprout you spot at your feet breaks through the numbness. Don't force the emotion; let it creep in slowly, like warmth seeping through a cold window. You might pause, your gaze drifting, or your voice catching for a moment before the hope takes hold.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Lost in the Bass
instruction: You're at a packed rave, mildly intoxicated, and the music is so loud your chest vibrates. You've just realized your friends aren't nearby—panic floods in. You shout into the noise, trying to spot them, your voice bouncing with the beat and your breathing fast. But then the light show shifts—a cascade of colors pouring from the ceiling—and your fear suddenly cracks open into awe. Let your words be breathy, punctuated by gasps and laughter, as you struggle to hear yourself and end lost in wonder.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother: The Truth About Who Raised You
instruction: You've asked your mother to meet you because you need to say something you've held for twenty years. Start with your voice careful, rehearsed—'There's something I need to tell you about my childhood.' But as you speak, the careful words fall apart. Your voice becomes raw, accusing: 'You were there, but you weren't there. Do you understand?' You're listing specific moments—birthdays she was drunk for, school plays she missed, the night you called her from the police station and she didn't come. Your voice is shaking with rage, but then it cracks into something more vulnerable: 'I needed a mother.' She tries to interrupt, and you cut her off—fierce, protective of your own pain. But then, exhausted, your voice drops to almost a whisper: 'I'm not asking you to change. I'm just telling you what it cost me.' Your final words are quiet, dignified, sad: 'I deserved better.' There's strength in your grief now.

title: The Burning Point
instruction: You've been physically hurt—maybe in an accident, maybe a brutal fight, maybe intense physical intimacy. Your body is in genuine distress: your hands are shaking, your breath is ragged, there's real pain somewhere. Start with the overwhelming sensation of your whole body screaming. You can barely think or speak. But then find one specific point—the exact place where pain turns into something else. Maybe where his hand gripped your arm becomes where you felt wanted for the first time. Maybe the cut on your lip becomes proof you're still alive. Maybe the muscle burning in your legs from running becomes your escape, your freedom. Narrow your entire awareness to that single point where physical sensation and emotional meaning fuse. Let your voice emerge from that fusion—raw, gasping, but shifting from pure survival response into something transcendent. By the end, you're not speaking about the pain but through it, your body's intensity becoming a doorway to emotional revelation that you couldn't access any other way.

title: The First Glimpse
instruction: You are a young adult in labor, alone in a dimly lit room between surges. In the quiet moments, you hold a small, fuzzy photo from the last ultrasound, a blurry shape that is your child. You begin speaking to yourself in a hushed, wondering voice, filled with awe at the life about to arrive. As the next contraction builds, your concentration narrows; your words become clipped, then dissolve into a low, helpless moan as the wave crests. When the pain recedes, your voice returns, shaky but full of a deeper, fiercer awe, transformed by the intensity of what your body just did.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Positive Test in Your Hands
instruction: You're holding a pregnancy test, and it's positive. This is something you've desperately wanted for years, after loss and disappointment. Begin with disbelief, checking and rechecking, afraid to trust what you're seeing. Let joy start to rise—real, physical joy in your chest, your hands trembling not with fear but with hope. But as the reality deepens, let the fear flood in alongside the joy: fear of losing this too, fear of hoping too much, the superstitious dread that acknowledging happiness will destroy it. Let these emotions co-exist without resolving—laugh while crying, feel gratitude while terror lives in your throat, want to shout the news while also wanting to hide it away protectively. Your body should feel electric, pulled in opposite directions. End in a complex place where hope and fear are completely intertwined, inseparable. Your voice should move from whispered disbelief to breathless joy to choked emotion to something that holds everything at once.
inspired_by: An actor is shooting a film out of sequence and needs to maintain character consistency

title: Laughing Through the Breaking
instruction: You're packing up your ex's things and find the lavender pillow spray they used to help with your insomnia, and suddenly you're laughing and crying simultaneously. Begin with genuine, almost surprised laughter as you spray it and remember the ridiculous arguments you'd have about whether it actually worked - their patient insistence, your stubborn skepticism. Let your laughter grow even as tears start falling, because you can finally admit it did work, but only because it smelled like them, like safety, like home. Speak with this beautiful contradiction: gratitude for having known love this deep while your heart shatters at its loss. Your voice should dance between warm chuckling at precious memories and grief-stricken breaking at what you've lost. End with a strange, peaceful acceptance - still crying, still laughing softly - acknowledging that you'll keep the spray, that you'll use it and remember, and that somehow both the joy and the pain are gifts you wouldn't trade away.
inspired_by: Inhaling the Scent of Lavender in a Field

title: Winning the Legal Case: Victory Tasting Like Emptiness
instruction: You've won your case. Justice has been served. Your voice should be celebrating but instead it's something more complicated. You're hearing the verdict and your voice is quiet, almost disappointed. 'We won.' But it took five years. During those five years, trauma calcified. Your voice is philosophical, tired: 'But I didn't win. I survived.' Include the moment where you're congratulated and your voice has to produce gratitude you don't quite feel. Victory is real but it doesn't undo what happened. Your voice reflects that understanding—you're not unhappy but you're not happy either. You're transformed by the process and your voice carries that transformation more than relief.

title: The Homecoming Paradox
instruction: After ten years away, you're walking through your childhood home, which is being sold tomorrow. You're flooded with contradictory emotions: joy at memories, grief at what you've lost, resentment at what happened here, gratitude for who you became, anger at who hurt you, love for those who protected you. Move through the space physically—touch walls, sit in corners, stand in doorways. Let your body express the war of emotions: laughing at a memory while tears fall, smiling with clenched fists, embracing the air where someone once stood while your jaw tightens with old anger. Don't choose one emotion—let them all exist simultaneously in your voice, face, and body. By the end, you're saying goodbye to all of it: the good, the terrible, the formative. Your physicality should be expansive, contradictory, fully alive with complexity.

title: Midnight Confession to an Empty Pillow
instruction: It is 3 AM and you are lying in bed, speaking to the pillow where your ex-partner used to sleep. You are whispering, as if they might actually hear you across the distance and time that separates you. Begin speaking to them about the small things you miss, but let it spiral into deeper territory: 'You never made me feel safe enough to fall apart. You never stayed when I was messy and broken.' Your whispers should be intimate, almost conversational at first, as if you're just having a late-night chat. But as you articulate what you needed and never received, let your voice become smaller, more fragile. Let pauses grow longer. Let yourself cry quietly without trying to stop it. End in near-silence, with just the softest admission: 'I needed you to love the parts of me I couldn't love.' Move from casual intimacy to devastating fragility.

title: Three A.M. Unburdening
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner.
