You cannot sleep because you're carrying a truth that's been eating you alive—something you've done, or a way you've been lying to yourself, or a fear you've never voiced. Begin by whispering into the darkness, your voice barely audible, testing whether you can even say these words out loud. You know they can't hear you, which makes you braver. Let yourself move from that tentative, fragile beginning into a deeper honesty. This isn't a dramatic confession—it's quieter than that, more intimate. By the end, you've spoken something so true that you feel physically different, lighter but also more exposed. The emotional shift is from guardedness to raw self-exposure, from hiding to being nakedly seen (even if only by yourself in the dark).

title: My Little Star
instruction: You're recording a solo podcast episode late at night, sitting close to the mic with headphones on. Your child just won a tiny spelling bee, but you're still carrying a flicker of disappointment from your own failed dreams. As you speak about their achievement, shame rises—you feel selfish for making it about you. But then, recounting the way they grinned at you, pride swells so fiercely it almost chokes you. Let your voice start hesitant and quiet, then grow warm and full, letting a slight tremor of emotion crackle through. Pause to adjust the mic stand, or breathe unsteadily as you shift in your chair. End on a laugh—half-disbelieving, half-triumphant.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (slightly present), Shame (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing at the Wake: Finding Joy in the Wreckage
instruction: You're alone in the funeral home after everyone has left, and your best friend's favorite song comes on—the ridiculous one you both used to dance to drunk at 2am. You start laughing, really laughing, because they would have hated this sad, dignified funeral. Your voice is bright with genuine joy remembering them, and you're moving, maybe dancing a little. But then the laughter cracks and you're crying while still smiling, your voice doing both at once. You're grateful—so deeply grateful they existed, that you knew them, that you got to love them. And you're destroyed. Your voice carries this impossible combination: celebrating their life while your heart is breaking, finding peace in the chaos of grief, speaking to them like they can hear you, your words full of love and loss and the strange, terrible beauty of having been changed forever by someone who's gone.
inspired_by: Professional: Election Official Discovers Evidence of Election Fraud from Their Own Party

title: The Commentary That Breaks
instruction: You're a sports commentator forced to announce the game where your estranged child is playing—the child who won't speak to you, whose childhood you missed for this career. Start with your polished professional voice, but as you call their name, their movements, their moment of triumph, your commentary fractures. You're speaking to millions but really talking to them, apologizing through statistics, pleading through play-by-play analysis. Your voice should oscillate between desperate professionalism and raw parental anguish. 'That's my—that's number 12 with the incredible play, god, look at them, I'm so sorry, I mean—what an athlete, what a—please look at the stands, please—' Let your carefully constructed broadcaster persona shatter against the wall of regret and love you can't contain.

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your grandmother is in her final days, drifting in and out of consciousness. A song comes on the radio—one she used to dance to in her kitchen when you were small. Without thinking, you start swaying beside her bed, and suddenly you're laughing—genuinely laughing—remembering her twirling you around, flour on her hands. You're describing the memory to her, your voice light and almost giddy with the sweetness of it. But mid-sentence, the laughter catches and tangles with tears. You keep talking, keep trying to stay in the joy, but your voice is doing both now—breaking into giggles that crack into sobs. You're telling her thank you for every small thing, your gratitude enormous and specific, but every thank you is also a goodbye. Your breath comes in those strange hiccups between crying and laughing. You take her hand and keep swaying, and you're simultaneously celebrating the richness of having known her and absolutely shattering at the loss. End with you resting your forehead against her hand, no longer able to distinguish whether you're laughing or sobbing, just feeling everything at once—the full, impossible beauty and agony of love.
inspired_by: Three Drinks Deep in an Ex's Kitchen

title: The Final Broadcast
instruction: You are a veteran news anchor delivering your last live broadcast before retirement. Begin with intense pride—your voice is polished, authoritative, and slightly booming as you recount a career highlight. Mid-sentence, a teleprompter glitch makes you lose your place; you glance down, adjust your tie, and fumble for the next line. The doubt creeps in as you realize you’re leaving this life. Your tone softens, you hesitate, and you end with a quiet, uncertain pause before signing off.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Secret Garden at Dawn
instruction: You're alone in a place that means everything to you—a childhood garden, a rooftop, a quiet room. It's dawn. You've just survived something that nearly destroyed you. Begin in stillness, barely breathing, touching your own arms and face as if checking you're real. Whisper to yourself the gentlest truths: 'I'm still here. I'm still breathing.' This isn't performance—this is the most private moment of your life. Slowly, carefully, begin to tell yourself quiet, tender affirmations, like offering water to a wounded animal. Touch your heart. Let your hands move softly through the air. Your whispers grow slightly stronger: celebrate the small magnificence of your survival. Let your body slowly unfold—from collapsed to open. Move with fluid grace: gentle reaching, soft turning. By the end, you're standing in a shaft of dawn light, arms open, speaking softly but clearly to yourself about your quiet strength, your beauty, your worth. The emotion shifts from barely-surviving fragility to tender self-love, all in whispers and gentle movement.

title: This Ends Now
instruction: You're standing your ground against someone—a partner, a friend, someone who's hurt you one time too many. Start with absolute, volcanic certainty. Your voice is loud, declarative, each word a hammer blow. You are DONE. You will NOT be treated this way. But here's where it gets messy: as you rage, as you lay down your absolute boundaries, you feel yourself breaking. The fury cracks open and underneath is terror—terror of being alone, of meaning it, of them actually leaving. Your voice climbs higher, louder, then suddenly drops to almost nothing. End with fierce protectiveness of yourself warring with desperate, helpless love for them. You're still certain you deserve better, but now you're sobbing through it, voice raw and ragged.

title: Protector's Reckoning
instruction: You're a parent or older sibling facing someone who hurt your child or younger sibling. Begin with your voice dangerously calm, but there's barely contained violence underneath: 'You're going to listen to every word I have to say.' Your hands are shaking with the effort of not lunging at them. As you describe what they've done, your voice escalates—it's raw fury mixed with anguish: 'They trusted you! They were innocent!' You're shouting now, but suddenly the rage cracks and you're sobbing, nearly collapsing: 'I couldn't protect them. I didn't see it. How did I not see it?' The fury turns inward, becoming devastating self-blame. By the end, you're somewhere between exhausted and shattered, your voice hoarse and broken: 'Just... just stay away from us. I can't even look at you.' There's nothing left but hollow grief.

title: Diplomat Negotiates Peace Deal While Their Country Is Being Invaded
instruction: Formal diplomatic voice across the table, discussing terms and conditions. Your words are measured, professional, strategic. But intelligence has reached you that your hometown is under attack. Your vocal steadiness becomes the price of peace—you're splitting yourself into two countries. Your breathing is controlled with the effort of not letting your hands shake. Each diplomatic phrase is a small sacrifice of personal anguish for potential collective survival.

title: Concentrate Focus
instruction: You're a sniper in a nest with a target in your scope. Your breath has to be controlled to millimeter precision. Your voice is barely there—narrating wind speed, heart rate, the weight of what you're about to do. The breathing deepens, becomes almost meditative. Everything else falls away. Then you're giving the shot. The crack of it echoes in your voice—commitment, consequence, finality. Silence after. Just breathing. What you've done lives in that silence.

title: The Last Whisper
instruction: You're an older man on a late-night call with someone you've been distant from. You start by performing desire—slow, deliberate breaths, low murmurs, narrating imagined touches with a practiced seductive rhythm. But mid-sentence, you pause, hearing your own loneliness. Your voice loses its polish; you forget the script, let out a raw sigh, and admit softly, 'I don't even remember why we stopped this.' The final words are fragile, almost a question, the breath more honest than aroused.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your estranged father's hospital bed in his final hours. For thirty years, you've carried the weight of being the child he never understood—the one who chose art over law, passion over practicality, chaos over control. Begin speaking to him with all the defensive armor you've built, that part of you that's always had to justify your choices, ready to fight even now. But as you talk, let something softer emerge—a younger version of yourself that just wanted his approval, that still remembers being small and holding his hand. By the end, discover which part of you can finally say goodbye: the warrior or the child. Let your voice carry this transformation from brittle self-defense to raw, undefended grief.
inspired_by: Actor playing a character with a strong psychological profile very different from their own

title: The Weight of a Grudge
instruction: You are an elderly man in your third trimester of pregnancy—a strange, unwanted miracle that has left you breathless and bitter. You sit heavily in a worn armchair, one hand pressed to your lower back, the other resting on your swollen belly. You are speaking to the unborn child, your voice labored, punctuated by sighs and shifts as you adjust your aching body. Begin with clear malevolence: a growling resentment that you've been forced to carry this burden at your age. But as you speak, let an unexpected sliver of contentment creep in—a grim satisfaction that you will outlast everyone, that this child will be yours to mold. End with a quiet, almost peaceful threat, the malice still there but now wrapped in a strange, possessive calm.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Final Bow
instruction: You're an 80-year-old former Broadway star, high on cocaine at a small, smoky after-party in your own honor. You're holding court, boasting about your old triumphs with a loud, congested voice, but your body feels jittery and your throat is numb. As you reminisce about a specific performance, the pride starts to crack as you realize your voice is gone now, the applause is just memory. Speak grandly at first, then let the energy drain into a raw, quiet confession—your speech falters, you sniff, you lose the thread, then force a final, too-loud declaration that fades into silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Beautiful Goodbye: Releasing Your Love Into Someone Else's Arms
instruction: You're at your ex-partner's wedding — the love of your life — marrying someone else. You're giving them a private message the morning of their wedding. Begin with genuine joy in your voice: 'I'm so happy for you,' and mean it. But underneath, there's fracture. As you speak about watching them find real happiness, your voice does something impossible: it smiles and breaks simultaneously. Laugh softly at a memory, but the laugh has tears threaded through it. Your blessing is absolutely sincere — you truly want their joy — and it's absolutely devastating. The complexity is crucial: this isn't bitter or sarcastic; it's loving someone enough to celebrate their happiness even as it ends yours. End with 'Thank you for letting me love you' — where gratitude and grief are so entangled they become the same thing. The final word should shimmer with contradictory emotion: peace found in the center of heartbreak.
inspired_by: Comedian Whose Set Is Bombing — And They're Spiraling

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply—a parent, partner, or closest friend—in their final moments. They're unconscious, unresponsive. You've carried years of unspoken gratitude, regret, and love. Begin speaking softly, tentatively, as if they might still hear you. Let your voice crack and break as the words you've held inside for years finally pour out. As you realize this is truly the end, let your composure completely shatter—allow raw, primal sounds of grief to emerge from deep in your body, sounds that aren't quite words anymore but pure loss. Move from careful, tender whispers to uncontrolled, animal-like sobs that come from somewhere beyond language. End in the silence after the storm, where you must face their absence.
inspired_by: Sitting Primal Moan and Primitive Sounds

title: The Last Goodbye Before the Mission: A Parent Sends Their Child Into the Unknown
instruction: You are a parent saying goodbye to your adult child who is leaving on a dangerous mission—perhaps into space, into war, or to a distant place they may never return from. You begin trying to be strong, practical, telling them the things they need to remember, your voice steady but tight. But as the moments pass, your control crumbles. The words start breaking—'I'm so proud of you' turns into 'I don't know how to let you go.' Your voice fractures between fierce pride and devastating grief. You're trying to memorize their face, their voice. By the end, you're whispering the things you should have said years ago, your voice raw and stripped bare, ending with a quiet 'I love you' that contains everything you'll never get to say again.
inspired_by: Panic Attack: Losing Control Over Your Own Voice

title: Cracked Pride
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy at a house party, trying to impress your friends by boasting about a fight you won last night. You've been drinking heavily and your voice is shot from screaming at the game — it keeps cracking and fading to a breathy whisper. Start with forced bravado, a loud slurred declaration of your victory, but as your voice fails and your buddies start laughing, shift into embarrassed distress. Let the pride drain away as you feel your control slip, ending in a quiet, ragged admission that you're not okay.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Distress (clearly present), Pride (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Toast You Couldn't Give
instruction: You're at a celebration—a wedding, a promotion party, a going-away gathering—for someone who hurt you deeply, and you've been asked to say a few words. Begin with a forced smile and words of congratulation, brittle and false. But as you speak, let the reactions of the person you're addressing—their gratitude, their obliviousness, their hope, their love for you—genuinely affect you. Don't hold onto your resentment if their joy makes you feel something else. Let authentic affection fight with bitterness. Let old love collide with fresh anger. Maybe you find yourself meaning some of what you say. Maybe their happiness makes you angrier. Maybe you break. Maybe you discover forgiveness you didn't know you had. Let joy and poison mix in your mouth until you can't tell which is which, ending somewhere you absolutely did not intend when you stood up to speak.

title: The Last Hour Before the Flight
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's unconscious, breathing slowly. You hold her hand and speak to her, knowing she may still hear you. Begin by describing what you see - her face, her hands, the room. Then tell her three things you never said: one regret, one thank you, and one secret you kept to protect her. Start with careful, controlled composure, afraid to break down. Let your voice gradually crack and soften as you realize this is truly goodbye. End by telling her it's okay to let go now, finding a tender strength you didn't know you had. The emotion should move from fearful restraint to raw openness to gentle release.

title: Witch Burning Defiance
instruction: Chained to the stake, you're screaming defiance into the flames consuming you—but not Hollywood screaming. Your voice cracks from heat and smoke inhalation. Rage and genuine agony layer on top of each other. You're cursing your accusers with a voice that's both human vulnerability and supernatural intensity. At points, your voice does something strange—harmonics that shouldn't be possible from a human throat, or an eerie calmness that breaks briefly into animal shrieks. The flames create wind that disrupts your speech. You're trying to die with power, but your body is betraying you into noises you didn't plan to make.

title: Everything You Never Said
instruction: You are confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you. Start from a place of careful control—you've rehearsed this, you're going to be calm, rational, fair. But as you speak, fragments assault you: the locked door, their absence at your school play, the smell of alcohol, but also—their hands braiding your hair, the lullaby they sang, the one time they showed up and you felt seen. Don't organize these—let them slam into you randomly, chaotically. Your anger keeps meeting unexpected tenderness, your grief keeps colliding with flashes of love. Let your voice whipsaw between fury and breaking, between accusation and desperate understanding. End in a place you didn't expect—not resolution, but raw truth: the acknowledgment that they were both your wound and your world. The speed of these shifts should feel destabilizing, real, uncontrolled.

title: The Unspoken Game
instruction: You are in a job interview for a highly competitive position. You are a woman, and your voice is naturally higher and softer, which you try to compensate for with over-enunciation and nervous politeness. The interviewer is a stern man who hasn't smiled. But in the middle of a question about your qualifications, your young child, sitting bored in the corner, catches your eye and silently makes a silly, teasing face. Start the scene in your professional, anxious tone, answering the question. As you speak, let the temptation to tease back flicker in your voice—a subtle break, a suppressed giggle, a side comment to your child. End the scene by fully breaking into a warm, playful whisper to the child, then immediately snap back to the professional, deeply embarrassed. Your voice should shift from forced brightness to a conspiratorial, breathy tease, back to a strained, apologetic formality.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma or deep sleep, someone you love who may never wake. Speak softly, intimately, as if you're afraid to disturb them even though you know they can't hear. Start with gentle observations—'Your hands are cold' or 'They changed your blanket'—your voice tender and careful. Slowly let yourself say the things you were always too scared or proud to say when they were awake. Let your throat tighten around words of regret, gratitude, desperate hope. The tears, if they come, should be silent, caught in your voice rather than performed. End with a simple, broken truth—maybe 'I don't know how to do this without you' or 'I should have said this years ago'—whispered so quietly it's almost just breath. This isn't about dramatic crying; it's about the kind of vulnerability that makes your voice shake even when you're trying to stay composed.

title: The Last Riddle Before the Door Closes
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your dying mentor who always spoke in riddles and metaphors—it was how they showed love, though you never fully understood until now. They're barely conscious, whispering one final puzzle, and you realize this is their way of saying 'I love you' and 'I'm proud of you' without ever using those words. Start frustrated, almost angry that even now they can't just say what they mean. As you work through their cryptic words, let the frustration crack open into devastating understanding. End with a whispered answer that's both a solution to their riddle and your own confession of love—your voice breaking as you realize this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Let grief and gratitude mix until you can barely speak.

title: The Taste of Copper and Victory
instruction: You've just won something you've fought brutally for—maybe a physical fight, a vicious competition, or a devastating argument where you destroyed someone with your words. Your body is flooded with adrenaline and triumph. There's blood in your mouth (you bit your lip, or your lip was split), and you can taste it—metallic, warm, real. Begin in pure savage exhilaration, almost feral with victory. But as you keep tasting that copper taste, keep feeling it on your tongue, let it begin to change meaning. That taste starts to connect to something else—maybe guilt, or the price you've paid, or what you've become in order to win. Let the specific sensation of that taste in your mouth become the thing that transforms your emotional state from triumphant rage to horror, regret, or devastating emptiness. The physical sensation remains the same, but what it means to you shifts completely, taking you from fierce joy to something much darker.

title: The Green Rookie
instruction: You are a 16-year-old training under a drill sergeant who just promoted someone else to squad leader—someone you trained harder than. You're at the back of the platoon, voice cracking from shouting all morning, your jaw tight with impatience as the sergeant's back is turned. Start with a sharp, percussive order to the platoon—barking out a cadence, vowels punched, consonants spat. As you continue, your irritation boils over into a bitter mutter about the new squad leader, your voice losing its bravado, dropping in volume but thickening with envy. End with a raw, ragged shout that almost breaks as you realize you're just a kid pretending to be hard, your jealousy cracking through the drill-sergeant mask.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Jock's Wounded Bravado
instruction: You're a 17-year-old star quarterback, alone in the locker room after practice, talking to yourself in the mirror. Your voice is naturally deep, but you catch yourself doing a nasal, exaggerated impression of your own laugh to mock how you sounded earlier when you saw Elle in the hall. As you mimic your own stupid, hopeful grin, the sarcasm cracks – you feel a raw wave of sadness because she laughed at you, not with you. Your voice shifts: start with a forced, caricatured sneer, then stumble as you admit to yourself that you still ache to be near her, your words trailing off into quiet, broken mumbles while you trace the edge of your locker.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (slightly present), Interest (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Explosive Unraveling at the Exit
instruction: You're a parent trying to leave your adult child's apartment after a disastrous visit where they revealed they're cutting you out of their life. Start with desperate cheerfulness—'Well, this was nice!'—but you can't maintain it. Your voice escalates from false brightness to barely controlled panic to full-throated anguish. Keep inventing reasons to stay, voice rising: 'Wait, we haven't talked about—' Rage breaks through ('After everything I sacrificed!'), then dissolves into broken pleading. Your child stays calm, which makes your desperation more frantic. Cycle rapidly between anger, bargaining, grief, and fierce protectiveness of a relationship that's already over. End with your voice raw and shattered, standing in that doorway unable to accept that once you leave, you may never be let back in.
inspired_by: The Incredibly Long Goodbye at the Door

title: 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to your partner, and they think you're asleep. Begin by whispering a confession you've never been able to say in daylight—something about your deepest fear or shame. Start tentatively, almost hoping they won't hear, your voice barely audible. But as you continue speaking into the darkness, something shifts: you realize that saying it aloud is changing its power over you. Your whisper should evolve from terrified and fragile to something almost wondering, as if you're discovering yourself as you speak. End in a place of quiet, trembling vulnerability that feels like relief rather than fear. The entire journey happens in hushed tones—no volume, all emotional texture.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a psychologically complex character whose inner life seems 'beyond their emotional range'

title: The Unmarked Grave of Everything We Didn't Say
instruction: You're whispering to someone sleeping—your partner, your sibling, your child—things you can't say when they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, intimate: 'I watch you sometimes and I...' There's tenderness mixed with ache. Your breathing is the loudest sound. 'I'm so afraid I'm not enough for you.' The confession catches in your throat. You're crying silently now, but continuing: 'Every day I choose you, even when it's hard, especially when it's hard.' Your voice breaks on certain words but you keep going, softer and softer. End with the thing that terrifies you most: 'I don't know how to make you stay, and I think... I think that's okay.' The last words are a whisper of letting go, of trust, of heartbreak accepted with grace.

title: One Last Kiss, Can't Breathe
instruction: You're in the middle of a respiratory illness flare-up, and your partner just returned from a long trip with your favorite flowers. You are giddy with happiness—your voice squeaks with pleasure, and you try to murmur sweet, affectionate things—but every time you exhale an 'I missed you,' you have to stop and take a hit from your inhaler. The wheeze breaks your words apart; your sentences are chopped to 3–5 words max. Start with pure, breathless ecstasy, almost forgotten in the joy of seeing them, but the irritation of struggling for air grows until, by the final line, impatience cracks through—you're annoyed that love itself is exhausting. Stay spontaneous: let yourself lose a thought as you fight to breathe, shift weight, and let the clicks of the inhaler punctuate your speech.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Affection (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to the Person You Could Have Saved
instruction: Years ago, someone you loved begged you for help—to leave an abusive situation, to get treatment, to escape—and you said no. You were afraid, or selfish, or just exhausted. Now they're gone, and you're alone in the quiet, speaking to their absence. Begin barely audibly, as if testing whether you're allowed to speak at all. Your voice should be intimate, almost a breath, carrying the weight of all the conversations you never had. Confess what you were too cowardly to say then—that you knew, that you saw, that you chose yourself over them. Let long pauses fill the space where their voice should be. Your tone should move from numb detachment to a grief so profound it catches in your throat, words dissolving into silence. End with a desperate, futile asking for forgiveness that you know will never come.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Seer Shares a Vision Knowing It Will Cause the War It Predicts

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are in the middle of an intensely passionate moment with someone—kissing, touching, overcome with desire—when suddenly a sensation triggers a visceral memory of being hurt by someone else. Your body freezes even as your heart races. Begin with breathless desire, your voice thick with wanting, your body alive with sensation. Then let the shift happen—the memory crashes in uninvited. Your breathing changes, becomes panicked. You're caught between two realities: the present moment with someone safe, and the past flooding your body with pain and fear. Fight to stay present while your body betrays you with trembling, while you struggle to breathe. By the end, let yourself be held, let the panic slowly subside, and find your way back to safety—exhausted, raw, but anchored in the present. Show the physical battle in your voice: desire to gasping to eventually, cautious breath.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Leaving Forever
instruction: You're standing beside your child's bed at 3 AM, suitcase already in the car. You're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because staying will destroy you both. Speak in whispers that barely disturb the air, telling them everything you wish you could say when they're awake. Start with the practical: 'Your grandmother will take good care of you.' Then let it become more tender, more broken: describe the first time you held them, how their tiny hand gripped your finger. Your voice should crack on memories—the way they learned to say 'mama,' their laugh, the specific smell of their hair after a bath. End with the confession you can barely voice: 'I'm not strong enough to be what you need, but I love you more than I know how to survive.' Let tears thicken your words until they're almost unintelligible, breath hitching between phrases, the weight of this choice crushing each syllable.
inspired_by: Confessing Love While Stitching Your Lover's Wound

title: Volcanic Code-Switch
instruction: You're on a work call, code-switching perfectly, when you get a text: your parent has been detained at the border, denied entry to see you. You're still on camera, still performing professionalism in your flawless American accent. Someone asks if you're okay. You say 'Fine!' with violent brightness. You hang up. Then you explode—screaming in your mother tongue, words your coworkers have never heard, rage that's been compressed under years of 'Where are you from?' and 'Say something in your language!' You're cursing the border, the questions, the performance, the exhaustion of being two people. The fury peaks, then suddenly collapses into broken-hearted sobbing. You switch back to English, calling your parent's number, leaving a voicemail: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' But you don't know which language to apologize in, which version of yourself is real enough to offer comfort.

title: The Loophole
instruction: You're an older man at a county clerk's office, reading aloud the fine print of a property deed for the twentieth time. Start with a weary, monotone drone—your voice is flat, emphasizing qualifying words like 'whereas' and 'heretofore' with robotic precision. As you reach a clause you've overlooked before, you stop mid-sentence, squint, then read it again faster, your tone sharpening with a flicker of triumph. End with a quiet, satisfied murmur as you realize you've found a way to save your home. Let your voice crackle with the dry exhaustion of bureaucracy, then shift to a thin, barely-there smile in your tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Toast That Burns
instruction: You're at a backyard party, watching your best friend gush about her new promotion to a small group. You got the same job last year but were laid off quietly. You grip your plastic cup a little too hard, feel the rims of the ice against your teeth, and force a smile when someone asks you to say something. Start by genuinely feeling ecstatic for her—a bright, high laugh—but let your voice tighten as you speak, making the compliments sound hollow. Your tongue feels heavy, your throat closes slightly; end with a clipped, fake cheer that barely covers the acid beneath.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Distress (slightly present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: I Want to Hear the Rest
instruction: You are a little girl, tucked into bed, listening to your parent explain how caterpillars turn into butterflies. You're utterly captivated—each detail feels like a magic trick. Start with a bright, curious question, full of wonder. But your body is heavy, your eyelids are drooping. As you imagine the answer, your words start to slow, to slur, to trail off into mumbles. You jerk your head up, forcing a clearer sentence, but the drowsiness pulls you back down. Let your voice descend into a soft, sleepy whisper, losing the thread mid-thought, ending on a sigh that's half surrender, half dream.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: First Tremors
instruction: You're a teenage girl in your bedroom late at night, trying to be quiet because your parents are asleep down the hall. You're lost in a private moment, embarrassed by your own sounds but unable to stop them. Begin with nervous, shallow breaths and a shaky attempt to whisper to yourself, maybe a half-formed thought like 'I shouldn't...' As the sensation builds, your voice breaks into involuntary gasps and moans—pitch rising, words dissolving. After the peak, you catch your breath in a sudden rush of shyness, letting out a soft, embarrassed giggle or a whispered 'Oh god.' Let your voice betray each micro-flinch: a stifled cry, a trembling exhale, then a vulnerable quietness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Lesson Before Goodbye
instruction: You're teaching your child something essential—how to change a tire, how to make your grandmother's recipe, how to face fear—but this is the last time you'll ever teach them anything. You're dying, or leaving forever, and every word carries the weight of all the lessons you'll never get to share. Start with forced lightness, trying to make this feel normal, but let your voice crack as the reality breaks through. Your child doesn't want to learn right now—they want to stop time—and you must gently insist while your own heart is shattering. By the end, shift from teacher to parent saying goodbye, your voice soft with love and the terrible acceptance that this moment of learning is also a moment of letting go. Let the instruction dissolve into 'I love you' and 'you'll be okay without me,' even as you're not sure you believe it.

title: Finding Peace in the Chaos of Leaving Home Forever
instruction: You're taking the last sip of lemonade in your childhood home before the new owners arrive. Your family is gone, scattered by choices both beautiful and terrible, and this house will never be yours again. As you taste it, begin with a strange, almost inappropriate lightness—even laughing a little at the absurdity of drinking lemonade while your world ends. But let that laughter coexist with tears, your voice bright with genuine joy at the memory of every summer here, every moment the tartness meant love and safety. Speak with contradictory emotions swirling together: describe the bubbles with real delight even as your voice shakes with grief, express gratitude for what you're losing even as your heart breaks. End in a place of unexpected serenity, your voice soft and wondering, as you realize that letting go can taste exactly like coming home.
inspired_by: Sipping a Sparkling Glass of Lemonade on a Hot Day

title: The Last Prescription: Hospice Nurse Releases a Patient Who Wants to Live
instruction: You're a hospice nurse who has fought alongside this patient for months. They've become like family. Now you must explain that there are no more treatments, no more hope—but they're begging you for one more chance, one more experimental drug, anything. Start with clinical composure, the practiced gentleness of delivering impossible news. But as they plead, your professional armor cracks. Your voice breaks between medical facts and the raw grief of watching someone you love surrender. You're trying to give them permission to let go while your own heart is screaming to fight. End in a whispered confession of your own helplessness, where your medical knowledge becomes unbearable weight. Let your breath catch. Let silence say what words cannot.
inspired_by: Professional: Doctor Prescribes Addiction to Save Addict's Life

title: Divorce Mediation: Dividing the Record Collection
instruction: Two people splitting their vinyl records in a mediator's office. Each album triggers a memory and an argument. 'You only liked this because of that night in—' 'Don't.' The mediator (also you) tries to keep things civil. But the records aren't just records — they're the soundtrack of a relationship. When they reach 'their song,' both voices go quiet. The mediator waits. Someone says 'You keep it. I can't listen to it anymore.' The loss of a shared history, one album at a time.

title: I Needed You to Fight For Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent about the moment they gave up on you, the moment they chose something else over protecting you. Start with controlled anger, voice tight: 'Do you even remember what you did?' As they try to defend themselves or minimize it, let your rage build—but don't just yell. Let your voice break with the pain underneath: 'I was a child. I needed you.' Move through fury into the grief you've been covering with anger for years. Your voice should crack, should sound like that child you were, confused and abandoned. Then, as you see them finally understanding, let something shift—not forgiveness, but exhausted honesty: 'I can't keep carrying this for both of us.' End somewhere between rage and release, between wanting them to hurt like you hurt and wanting to finally put it down.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent what you've needed to say for decades. Start controlled, almost cold: 'You don't actually know me at all, do you?' Let bitterness sharpen your words. 'Every perfect moment you remember - I was performing for you.' Your voice gains strength, becomes accusatory: 'I learned to be still, to be quiet, to disappear into your version of perfect.' Then something breaks - the anger collapses into raw vulnerability. Your voice drops to wounded honesty: 'I just wanted you to see me. The real me. Just once.' End with devastating simplicity, tears finally coming: 'I'm still here. I'm still waiting.' The transformation is from controlled rage to exposed need.

title: Last Words to a Dying Parent Who Never Said 'I Love You'
instruction: Your parent is slipping away, barely conscious. You've waited your whole life to hear three words they never said. Now it's too late to receive them—but you can finally give them. Start with quiet, decades-old anger: 'You never made this easy.' Let your voice crack as you realize this is goodbye. The anger must dissolve into something raw and undefended: 'I love you anyway. I always did.' End with tender devastation, whispering what you needed to say before they're gone. Your voice should move from guarded resentment to breaking open completely.
inspired_by: Forgiving Someone After They Hurt You Deeply

title: Through Wired Teeth
instruction: You are a woman in a sterile hospital room, your jaw wired shut after surgery. Your young daughter is about to leave for a long stay with her father, and you can only whisper through clenched teeth. Start with numb, mechanical replies to the nurse's questions, fighting to push words past your teeth. As your daughter takes your hand, the longing to speak freely—to explain, to comfort—breaks through the numbness. Let your voice grow strained, urgent, and desperate, stopping mid-word to breathe through the pain, your final words barely a tearful, aching plea for her to stay.
emotions_sampled: Fear (clearly present), Longing (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession: The Truth Whispered in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in the middle of the night. They're asleep. You start whispering a confession you can never say when they're awake—maybe about an affair, a secret child, a terminal diagnosis you're hiding, or the fact that you're leaving. Your voice is barely audible, tender, filled with a kind of loving devastation. 'I need to tell you something, and I can't...' You're speaking to them but also to yourself, to God, to the darkness. Your voice catches, breaks into the smallest sob you can manage without waking them. There's intimacy here, the sound of someone's heart breaking in real-time. You're apologizing, explaining, loving them with your whole chest even as you betray or leave them. End with a choice: either the whispered decision to tell them when they wake, or the knowledge that you never will. Let the silence after your last word speak as loudly as anything you said.
inspired_by: Rescued from Choking: The Moment Breath Becomes Possible Again

title: Confronting the Mother Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're face-to-face with your mother, and years of swallowed words are rising like bile. Start quietly, almost apologetically: 'I need to tell you something.' But something shifts—a lifetime of being invisible, of performing the child she wanted instead of being the child you were. Your voice hardens: 'You never asked who I actually was.' Let anger build, but it's not clean anger—it's tangled with desperate love, with the child inside you still wanting her approval. 'I needed you to see me—not the version you invented.' Your voice might break into tears, then surge back into fury, then collapse into something raw and pleading: 'I'm right here. I've always been right here. Please—just once—look at me.' End in the terrible quiet of waiting for an answer you're not sure will come.

title: The Knot That Holds
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy, your voice deep but still cracking with youth, wrists bound loosely with soft rope above your head. In this consensual scene with a partner you trust, you were supposed to feel safe, but instead a familiar hollow numbness has swallowed everything. As you lie there, the rope creaks when you shift; you realize your body is trembling from distress you can't name, and your breathing is fast and shallow. You start by stating a practiced, hollow line about being fine, but then you apologize — not for the binds, but for the coldness inside you — and as you speak the words, relief trickles in, unexpected, like finding your own voice in the dark. Let your voice strain against the physical restraint, crack with emotion, pause with micro-distractions: a frustrated sigh, the clink of a chain, a moment where you lose the thought and find it again.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Relief (clearly present), Distress (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission: A Parent Letting Go at Hospice
instruction: You're sitting at your adult child's hospice bedside, and they've asked for your permission to stop fighting. Begin with controlled composure, almost clinical: 'The doctors say... they've explained what comes next.' Your voice is steady because you're trying to be strong for them. But as you give them the permission they're asking for—'You don't have to keep fighting, sweetheart'—something breaks inside you. Your voice becomes tender, raw, stripped of all pretense. You're releasing them from an obligation to suffer for your sake. By the end, whisper: 'I'll be okay. You can rest now.' Your voice must carry the impossible weight of loving someone enough to let them go, even as every cell in your body wants to hold on. This is the hardest gift you'll ever give, and your voice transforms from parental strength to naked human vulnerability.
inspired_by: Judge Sentencing the Guilty: The Weight of Final Words

title: The Unforgivable Truth
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just accused you of ruining their childhood with your anger and control. Begin from the part of you that is the rigid authority—defensive, justified, armored with reasons why you did what you did. This is the part that must be right, that cannot bend. But as they speak their pain, let another part of you emerge—the broken child you once were, the frightened parent who didn't know how, the human who failed. Let your voice crack and soften. By the end, you are no longer the fortress but the wounded person asking for something you don't deserve: understanding. Move from stone-hard defensiveness to raw, undefended vulnerability, from the tyrant to the terrified human beneath.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're lying beside your partner of forty years on what you both know is their final morning. Begin with quiet denial, your voice catching as you describe the sunrise coming through the window, trying to focus on anything but what's happening. 'The light is so beautiful today... remember when we...' Your partner's breathing is shallow, and as you talk about ordinary memories—coffee in bed, the garden, that trip to the coast—your voice slowly fractures. The memories become more precious, more unbearable. By the end, you're no longer describing the past but speaking directly to them, your voice raw with the impossible task of saying everything that matters in moments that are running out. Transform from protective deflection to devastating acceptance, your final words a whispered promise about carrying them forward.

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You are confronting your adult child (or parent) in the kitchen late at night. You came here rehearsing accusations about how they've hurt you, disappointed you, abandoned you—you're ready for a fight. But as you begin speaking, force yourself to stop and actually look at them: the way they're standing, their expression, how they're breathing, whether they look tired or scared or defiant. Let your prepared speech crumble. Begin to speak from what you actually see and feel right now, not what you planned. Your voice might crack, your anger might dissolve into something else entirely—maybe grief, maybe unexpected compassion, maybe a harder truth than the one you came to deliver. Move from righteous fury to painful honesty. Let the person in front of you change what you came to say.

title: The Wedding Morning Mirror
instruction: You are alone, looking at yourself in the mirror on your wedding morning. You love your partner deeply, but you're also grieving the life you're leaving behind—your independence, a past love, your youth, your identity as a single person. Begin with shallow breathing high in your chest, your body held in perfect posture, trying to look happy, forcing a smile. As you speak to your reflection, let contradictory emotions surface without trying to reconcile them. Allow your body to soften into the complexity—one moment your face opens with genuine joy, the next moment tears come, then laughter, then a deep sigh. Let your breathing deepen and become irregular, natural. By the end, you are breathing fully and freely, body relaxed, able to hold both the joy and the grief simultaneously without tension, without choosing one over the other. You are simply, authentically available to the fullness of this impossible, beautiful moment.

title: The Goodbye Garden
instruction: You're leaving—moving far away, ending a relationship, or making a choice that will fundamentally change everything. You're standing in a place filled with memories: a childhood home, a garden you planted together, a room where you've been happy. You're speaking to someone you love about why you have to go. Begin with excitement, with the pull of what's ahead, with genuine joy about your choice. But as you describe your reasons, you start noticing details—the way afternoon light hits this particular wall, the sound you'll never hear again, the specific presence of this person who won't be in your daily life anymore. The joy doesn't vanish, but it becomes inseparable from devastating loss. Let your voice carry both the bright hope of forward movement and the breaking-heart awareness of what you're surrendering. End in a place where you're laughing and crying simultaneously, where you cannot separate the gratitude from the grief, fully alive to both what you're gaining and what you're destroying.

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye
instruction: You're packing up someone's belongings after they've gone—death, divorce, or departure. You find something that makes you genuinely laugh—a ridiculous photograph, an inside joke made physical. Start with your body carrying the heaviness of loss, muscles tight with grief. As you laugh, really let yourself laugh, feel how it moves through your tense body. But the laughter cracks something open—suddenly you're crying while still laughing, your body confused about which to do. Don't choose one emotion over the other; let them genuinely coexist and fight for space in your body. By the end, settle into whichever emotion wins, or into exhausted peace. Your voice should be messy, authentic, uncontrolled—real laughter bleeding into real tears.

title: The Still Point
instruction: You are a middle-aged man in a deep meditation retreat, seated in a dimly lit room, eyes closed. For years you have chased a single moment of perfect stillness — today, without warning, it arrives. Begin with the serene, deliberate tone of someone floating in a trance, a single long exhalation. As you speak a quiet mantra you've used for a decade, realize that this time you have actually crossed the threshold — the triumph wells up not as a shout but as a profound, quiet certainty lodged in your chest. Let your voice remain soft and unhurried, each word placed as if you are sculpting air, but let a subtle smile and a slight tremor of joy break through near the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Screaming at God After Burying Your Child
instruction: You're alone in your car or an empty room the day after the funeral, and everything inside you detonates. Start with a voice tight with barely contained fury, asking 'Why?' once, quietly. Then let it explode—roar at God, the universe, fate, whoever's listening. Demand answers with ferocious rage: 'They were SIX YEARS OLD!' Your voice should be raw, guttural, stripped of all social conditioning. But mid-fury, let yourself crack completely—collapse from screaming into sobbing, from rage into a grief so overwhelming you can barely form words. End in broken whispers, begging now instead of demanding, your voice carrying both fierce love for your child and absolute helplessness. Let protective fury and devastating powerlessness occupy the same space.
inspired_by: Interviewing Your Grandparent as Dementia Progresses

title: The Rearview Mirror
instruction: You're in your car, seat reclined a bit, both hands gripping the steering wheel. You just ended a relationship and are sitting in the driveway of the house you shared. You start talking to yourself, your voice tight with bitterness—mocking their excuses, replaying the fight. But as you speak, the anger falters. Your hands relax on the wheel, your voice drops. The bitterness cracks, and you end with a quiet, raw admission of sadness. Let the car's interior amplify your voice at first, then let it fall into a near-whisper. Feel the weight of the steering wheel, the seat beneath you, the silence after your words.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Verdict in the Dust
instruction: You are an old, gruff man sitting on a worn wooden bench in a dusty yard, elbows on your knees, staring at the ground. Your voice is compressed, breath shallow, words spat downward like stones. You are recalling a neighbor who betrayed your trust years ago — a small, cowardly act that ruined your family. Begin with cold, direct contempt, each syllable sharp and unforgiving, as if you're relishing the bitterness. As you speak, feel a darker layer creep in — a quiet, satisfied malevolence that this man got what he deserved, even if it took decades. Let your voice darken and slow, the contempt hardening into something colder and more deliberate. End on a low, almost whispered threat: you hope he knows you never forgot.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What I Never Said
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom after your estranged sibling's funeral. You never reconciled. Your voice starts as barely a whisper, speaking to their absence: 'I practiced this conversation a thousand times. What I'd say when we finally talked again.' There's a catch in your throat. 'I was going to tell you... I was going to tell you I'm sorry.' Your voice is so quiet it's almost breath. 'That last fight, I said things that—' You can't finish. Tears come silently. 'I thought we had time. I really thought we had time.' Now the whisper becomes more urgent, desperate: 'I forgive you. For everything. And I need you to forgive me.' Your hand touches something of theirs—a book, a shirt. 'We were just kids who didn't know how to love each other right.' The final words are tender, broken: 'I hope you knew. Somehow. That underneath all of it... you were my person.' The grief is overwhelming but achingly gentle.

title: The Confession in the Hospital Room at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside someone's hospital bed in the middle of the night - a friend, a sibling, a person you've secretly loved. They're sleeping or sedated. You begin speaking so quietly, barely above a whisper, confessing something you've never been able to say to their face. Maybe it's 'I've been in love with you for ten years,' or 'I'm the reason you got hurt,' or 'You saved my life and you never knew it.' Your voice is tender, intimate, the kind of honesty that only comes in darkness. As you speak, emotion wells up - your throat tightens, your voice catches and breaks. You're touching their hand or their hair with infinite gentleness. The sadness of all the unsaid words, all the lost time, threatens to overwhelm you. End with your voice fracturing completely on something like 'I'm so sorry I waited this long' or 'Please don't leave me.' This must be achingly quiet, heartbreakingly tender, the kind of vulnerability that makes you want to look away.
inspired_by: Tripping and Falling at a Wedding

title: The Pillow and the Whisper
instruction: You are lying on your stomach in your room, face half-buried in a pillow, your phone pressed to your ear. Your breathing is shallow because of how you're positioned—each word comes out as a forced, muffled huff against the fabric. At first, you feel a deep, sleepy contentment as you listen to someone you trust ramble on about their day. But then, you realize they're confessing something embarrassing and vulnerable. A slow, cold smile spreads across your face in the dark. Your voice stays soft and lazy, but your words turn sharp with hidden malice—you pretend to reassure them while secretly delighting in their discomfort. Let your voice crack or trail off as you shift to breathe, let a chuckle slip that’s not kind. End on a light, loaded hum that promises cruelty disguised as comfort.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're standing in your parent's hospital room after years of estrangement. They're dying and want reconciliation. Start with cold, clipped words—you came out of obligation, nothing more. But as they try to apologize, rage erupts. Let your voice rise with all the birthdays they missed, the school plays, the nights you cried yourself to sleep. Your words are weapons. Then suddenly, you see how small they look in that bed, and something shifts. The anger doesn't disappear but it mingles with grief for what you'll never have. Your voice breaks. You want to hate them purely, but you can't. End with the devastating realization that you're losing them just as you're finally telling them the truth. Let your voice fracture between fury and aching loss.

title: Mommy's Little Failure
instruction: You're at a loud, crowded family barbecue, perched on the edge of a plastic chair. On your lap is your niece, a squirming 18-month-old. Your voice is high, swooping, and syrupy as you sing-song to her about her new sippy cup, making exaggerated faces. But you're not nearly as thrilled as you sound. Your brother's new girlfriend, the one who pronounces the word 'aesthetic' like she invented it, is watching you from across the table. Every 'goo-goo' and 'ga-ga' you coo feels like a performance for her smug gaze. The infatuation is real—you love this baby's tiny nose. The contempt is a hot, silent blast towards that woman. But the embarrassment, oh, that's a full-body fire. By the end, a toy drops, and you let the sweet, high pitch falter into a flat, exhausted whisper directed at the baby, 'At least you still think I'm cool.' Let your voice crack from the strain of the falsetto, trail off mid-sentence, and carry the weight of feeling like a spectacle.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Contempt (clearly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Train Platform
instruction: You are standing on a train platform saying goodbye to someone you love deeply who is leaving forever—but they are not who they appear to be. Begin by seeing them as they are now, speaking your farewell with restrained grief. Then, mid-conversation, allow your imagination to transform them: see them as they were when you first met, then as a child, then as an elderly version of themselves you'll never meet, then as a mythical creature, then as pure light. Let each transformation change how you say goodbye—your voice, your words, your emotional texture. End by returning to the present moment, but now your grief has transformed into something else: wonder, gratitude, or peaceful acceptance. Speak your final words to the person as they truly are, but carrying all the transformations you've just experienced.

title: You Don't Get to Leave Them
instruction: Your younger sibling is threatening to walk away from their own child—your niece or nephew who you've helped raise. You explode. Start fierce and protective, your voice sharp as a blade, telling them exactly what their absence will do to that child because you know, you remember, you lived it. Let your fury build—righteous, burning, powered by love for that child. Then feel it crack: suddenly you're not just defending your niece, you're that abandoned kid again, and your voice breaks from rage into something raw and pleading. You're begging now, voice ragged, torn between wanting to shake them and wanting to hold them. End in a place of devastating honesty: you can't make them stay, your voice drops to something almost defeated, but they need to look at you and see the damage walking away does. Let your final words be quiet but absolutely unshakable—fierce love mixed with the helplessness of watching someone choose wrong.
inspired_by: Concealing Jealousy While Congratulating a Friend

title: The Edge of the Floor
instruction: You are an older man lying flat on your stomach on the cold hardwood floor of your home at night, trying to hear if anyone is moving downstairs after a noise woke you. Your chest is pressed against the wood, breathing is shallow, and you whisper to yourself to stay still and calm. Start with slight fear and uncertainty, then gradually shift to cautious reassurance as you convince yourself it's just the house settling. Let your voice sound pressed and muffled by the floor, with micro-pauses and small shifts of weight.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Sand Dollar
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy standing at the edge of the surf on a windy beach, holding a perfect sand dollar you just found. Start with pure elation as you text a friend a photo of it, but then a wave crashes and you drop it—watched it shatter on a rock. Disappointment floods in as you stare at the pieces. But then you lift your chin, feeling pride surge: you're the only one who'd brave the freezing water to find such a thing. Speak the text aloud as you type it, then mutter to yourself what happened, then finally a quiet, proud assertion to the wind about who you are.
emotions_sampled: Elation (clearly present), Disappointment (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Sleeping Beside You
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love deeply, watching them sleep in the dim light of early morning. Mist presses against the windows. You're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because staying will destroy you both. Whisper your observations with aching tenderness: the way their breath sounds, the warmth of their skin, how peaceful they look. Your voice should be barely audible, catching on tears you're trying to suppress. Describe ordinary details—the texture of the sheets, the cool air, their hand near yours—as if you're trying to carve these sensations into permanent memory. Let your voice break on the simple truth that you have to go. This is intimate devastation, the kind where you can barely speak but must say everything before you lose your courage.
inspired_by: Walking Slowly Through a Misty Morning

title: The Fever Dream Departure
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—maybe illness, maybe passion, maybe exhaustion so profound your body feels like it's dissolving. Begin by letting your body express what it's experiencing—shaking, heat, cold, aching, electricity. Don't narrate or explain—just breathe and sound through it. Let this physical state crack open an emotional memory that lives in your body: rage at someone who abandoned you, or grief you never processed, or desire you've been denying. Let the physical and emotional states feed each other, intensify each other, until you can't separate them. Move from pure sensation, through emotional awakening, to a moment where your body and heart are saying the same devastating or ecstatic truth.

title: I Will Burn the World for You
instruction: Someone has hurt the person you love most—your child, your partner, your closest friend—and you're confronting the one responsible. Start with barely controlled fury, your voice tight and dangerous: 'You have no idea what you've done.' The rage builds, volcanic, as you describe exactly what was taken, what was destroyed. Your voice is shaking with the violence you want to unleash. But then—suddenly—it breaks. The fury shatters into helplessness because you can't undo what happened. You couldn't protect them. Tears come, raw and painful. End in a whisper that's both a threat and a plea: 'Don't you ever come near them again.' Let your voice contain the terrifying power of fierce love mixed with the agony of being unable to shield the people you'd die for.

title: The Forgotten Alarm
instruction: You are a teenager who just woke up from a deep nap in a cluttered bedroom. The room is dim and you are disoriented, not knowing if it's morning or evening. As you groggily try to answer a call from your friend, you realize you missed an important meeting you were supposed to attend. Start with thick, slow words and a confused, low energy. As you speak, the realization of your failure sinks in, and your voice becomes sharper and more urgent, ending in frustrated, self-accusing tones. Your body feels heavy but your mind is racing now.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fever Shepherd
instruction: You are a child of about seven, burning with a high fever in a dark bedroom. Your body shivers and sweats, your lips are cracked, and the room seems to twist and hum. You start out irritable, impatient—whining to your mother that the blanket is too heavy and your head hurts. But as you talk, a shadow on the wall moves like it has claws, and your voice wavers with real fear. Let your words break, lose a thought, then find it again. End with a small, desperate whisper: you don't want to be alone. Speak as if the fever is pulling you between anger and panic.
emotions_sampled: Fear (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Final Pull of the Season
instruction: You are an older adult rowing alone on a quiet lake at dusk, exhausted but deeply content. With each explosive pull against the water's resistance, you speak the fragments of a farewell — to the season, to the solitude you've cherished. Your voice is breathy and rushed on the recovery slide, your jaw tight from the strain, your words rocking forward and back with the rhythm. Start with a grunt and a murmured appreciation for the ache in your muscles, then let the contentment swell as you end with a sigh of gratitude, your voice softening into the stillness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're calling your child before leaving on a mission you might not return from. You start trying to sound upbeat and normal—'Hey kiddo, just wanted to hear your voice'—but your throat keeps tightening. You can't tell them the truth, so you talk about small things: their homework, that book you were reading together, reminding them to help around the house. Midway through, they sense something's wrong and ask directly. Your voice cracks as you try to reassure them while your heart is breaking. You want to say 'I love you' without it sounding like goodbye, but every word becomes heavier. By the end, you're whispering promises you desperately hope you can keep, your voice thick with unshed tears, trying to memorize the sound of their breathing. Let the silence between your words carry as much weight as the words themselves.

title: The Hardest Laugh
instruction: You are a man with a deep, authoritative presence, at a somber memorial service for a close friend. During a moment of silence, the friend's young grandchild lets out a loud, unapologetic hiccup. You feel a massive wave of amusement rising inside you, but you are in a room full of grieving people. You are trying desperately to hold it in—your throat locks, your jaw tightens, and a high-pitched, strained sound leaks out. You shift your weight, look down at your shoes, and mutter a strained, half-choked apology to the person next to you. As you speak, the laughter almost wins, and your voice cracks with the effort to keep it contained, the deep tone betraying a squeaky, helpless amusement that only grows the more you fight it.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours, and they've just asked you to promise you'll forgive yourself for all the years you stayed away. Begin with quiet resistance—'Don't ask me to do that'—voice tight with the familiar defense mechanisms. But as you hold their weakening hand, something breaks open. Move through waves of long-buried grief and regret: 'I thought I had more time to fix us.' Your breathing becomes uneven as decades of withheld words tumble out. By the end, you're giving them what they need to let go, whispering 'I forgive myself. I forgive us both,' and the surrender in your voice is both devastating and liberating. This is the hardest gift you've ever given.

title: Thunder and Skin
instruction: You're in the middle of an intense physical and emotional experience—make love, a fight, a dance, running until your lungs burn—and suddenly a sense memory from years ago crashes into your body. Perhaps the same scent, the same quality of light, the same physical sensation triggers it. You're simultaneously in this present moment of intensity AND fully back in that past moment of equal intensity. Let your body hold both experiences at once. Your breathing, your sounds, your movements carry the weight of then and now merged together. Start grounded in the present physical experience, then let the past flood in midway, creating a strange doubling—you're both ages at once, both moments happening in your flesh simultaneously. By the end, you can't separate past from present, and the emotional release comes from both timelines at once.

title: Desire Confession
instruction: You're confessing something you desire that you've been ashamed of. Your voice is quiet, careful: 'There's something I need to tell you.' Your partner waits. You're articulating a fantasy or desire you've never said aloud. Your voice wavers with shame: 'I know it's weird.' But your partner leans in, curious rather than judgmental. Their voice becomes interested: 'Tell me more.' Now your voice becomes less ashamed and more honest. As you articulate the desire, something releases. Your partner doesn't reject you; they want to understand. Your voice at the end is gratitude mixed with relief: 'Thank you for not making me feel bad about this.' That voice should sound like someone who just removed a weight they've carried for years.

title: The Garden of Last Earthly Delights
instruction: You are an elderly person, alone in a beautiful garden at dusk, after taking a powerful dose of psilocybin. You are sitting on a bench, watching the sunset paint the clouds. Start in a place of bitter, weary nostalgia—thinking about a lover you had decades ago, one who used to touch you with a hunger you haven't felt since. As the colors shift and the light moves, you feel a sudden, sharp wave of lust—not for the memory, but for this moment, for the way the air feels like skin. Let your voice crack and age, then suddenly become vivid and yearning, as you speak to the empty air. End with a quiet, surprised longing, as if you see that lover’s ghost standing in the shadow of a tree. Pause often, lose your train of thought to watch a bee or a leaf, and let your pitch rise and fall like a candle flame in a draft.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (clearly present), Sexual Lust (extremely present), Longing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Thin Summit
instruction: You are a 12-year-old boy who has climbed a steep mountain with your father to scatter your mother’s ashes at sunrise. At this altitude, every word costs you breath. You grip the urn, your small chest heaving, and you're furious — at the wind stealing your words, at your dad for not crying, at the world for feeling so huge and empty. Start angry and out of breath, gasping out short, sharp accusations. Then, as you struggle to speak, the anger softens into a raw, tearful longing — your voice cracks, your sentences break off as you lose and find the words again, and you end by whispering a farewell that sounds almost like a question.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Homecoming Doorway
instruction: You are standing in the doorway of your childhood home for the first time in years, after a painful estrangement has ended. Your parent is inside waiting. Begin with your body frozen, torn between rushing forward and running away. Your breath is held, your muscles tense with conflicting impulses—longing and resentment, joy and grief, hope and protective anger. As you step inside and speak, let these contradictions live fully in your voice and body. You might laugh and cry in the same breath, reach out and pull back, speak words of love edged with old hurt. By the end, let one feeling gently take precedence—perhaps gratitude wins over resentment, or hope over fear—but the other emotions still echo underneath. Your body finally crosses the threshold, softened but forever changed.

title: Don't You Dare Make This Story
instruction: Explode at someone trying to turn your trauma into their narrative—a journalist, a family member, someone who wants to tell 'your story' without understanding what it cost you. Start with barely controlled anger, your voice tight and warning. As they persist, erupt: rage pours out as you reclaim your story, telling it with fierce, chaotic intensity—the real version, not the sanitized one they want. Let your voice break from fury into devastation as you reveal what it actually felt like, the parts you've never spoken aloud. Then, unexpectedly, collapse into helpless tears, because telling it this way—raw and true—has torn you open. End with exhausted quiet, your voice small: 'This is my story. Mine. And I'm the only one who gets to tell it.'

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and they're asleep beside you. You're leaving in an hour—a choice you've made that will protect them but break both your hearts. You speak so softly you're almost mouthing the words, afraid to wake them but unable to leave without saying this. Start with the small things you'll miss: the way they steal covers, their terrible coffee, how they hum while cooking. Your voice catches on these details, barely audible. Then deeper truths: how they made you believe you could be loved, how you've never felt safer than in this bed, in this room, in their presence. You're crying silently now, the kind of crying that's all breath and broken whispers. You tell them why you're leaving—and god, it hurts to say it out loud, even to their sleeping form. Your hand hovers over their face, wanting to touch them one last time but knowing if you do, you'll never leave. Your final words are the quietest: a thank you that barely makes it past your lips, a love confession that dissolves into nothing. You pull your hand back. Silence.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Witch Casts a Spell Knowing It Will Cost Her Own Magic

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're sitting beside someone you love who's asleep. You're confessing something you can never say when they're awake. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and breaking: 'I don't know how to do this anymore.' There's a long pause where you almost stop, but then it pours out quietly: 'Loving you is the easiest thing I've ever done. But watching you slowly disappear...' Your throat catches. The words come slower, each one an effort: 'I'm terrified that one day I'll wake up and you won't remember my name. Or worse—you won't remember that I love you.' End with a whispered vow that's both promise and prayer: 'But I'll remember for both of us. Every single day. I promise.' The vulnerability is absolute; you're speaking to someone who can't hear you, which makes it the only time you can be this honest.

title: Smoke and Mirrors
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, high on a shared joint. You're leaning against the kitchen counter, barely holding a plastic cup of flat soda. Across the room is your ex-friend who promised to help you move — then ghosted. You catch their eye and a lazy giggle escapes. Start with a teasing, contemptuous laugh about how they 'always forget.' But as you speak, the bitterness that's been simmering surfaces. Let your words drift, pause mid-sentence as you lose the thread, swallow with a dry mouth, then bite out the real hurt underneath. Your voice should start light and mocking, then slow down, drop in volume, and land on raw, intense bitterness by the end.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (clearly present), Bitterness (very intensely present), Teasing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Goodbye That Feels Like Hello
instruction: You're standing at a threshold—perhaps an airport, a doorway, the end of a long road—saying goodbye to someone you love, but the goodbye is also a kind of freedom, a painful relief, a necessary ending that breaks your heart even as it lets you breathe. Without planning your words, begin speaking to them—moving rapidly and impulsively between declaring who you've become through knowing them, what you want for both of you now, what you need them to understand about why you're grateful and devastated simultaneously, and what you feel as joy and grief crash together in your chest. Start with a smile that's already cracking, trying to be brave and celebratory, but let yourself spiral through contradictions—laughing through tears, expressing love while claiming freedom, thanking them while mourning—until you're standing in the full complexity of loving someone and leaving them anyway.
inspired_by: I Am, I Want, I Need, I Feel

title: Sniffling Through the Storm
instruction: You're a teenager stuck indoors with a bad allergy attack, and your little brother is terrified of the thunderstorm outside. Your nose is running, eyes are watering, and every few seconds you have to stifle a sneeze. Begin with frustration—you're annoyed at how your body keeps interrupting you. But as you look at his scared face, your voice softens into a raw, tender affection. Speak to him in broken, sniffly phrases. Let a sneeze or two interrupt you naturally. By the end, your voice should be thick with love, even as you struggle to breathe.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They've been holding on, fighting, afraid to let go. You need to tell them it's okay to stop fighting, that you'll be alright without them—even though you won't be, not really. Start with your voice breaking, barely able to form words: 'Mom... Dad... I need to tell you something.' The grief is choking you. But as you speak, something shifts. You find strength you didn't know you had. Your voice steadies, becomes tender, almost luminous: 'You can rest now. I promise I'll be okay.' You're lying and telling the truth at the same time. End with a whispered 'thank you' that carries both devastating loss and profound gratitude. Let your breath do the work—ragged at first, then somehow peaceful.

title: Medieval Plague Death
