instruction: You're a plague victim dictating your will in your final hours. Your voice is hoarse from internal bleeding, each word takes effort. Someone in the room is a loved one you're trying to protect from the truth of how much agony you're in—so you perform wellness between sentences, then drop the mask. Fever makes you hallucinate; you address people not in the room. Your speech slurs, stops, restarts. The effort of forming words is physically visible in your voice. Near the end, you're mid-sentence when fever spikes, and you lose the thread entirely—the scribe must ask you to repeat what you've just forgotten you said.

title: The Last Phone Call Before They Board the Plane
instruction: Your person is about to leave for a dangerous mission they may not return from. You start trying to be brave, voice light and teasing: 'Don't forget to write.' But as the reality hits, your throat tightens. You need to say 'I love you' but it's been years since you've said it out loud. The words catch, break apart. You try again, this time letting everything you've held back pour through—gratitude for every moment, terror at losing them, regret for time wasted being careful. End with a whispered confession of something you've never admitted, your voice stripped of all protection, just before the line goes dead.
inspired_by: Your Abusive Ex Trying to Reconcile

title: The Gale at the Summit
instruction: You're a teenage boy standing at the peak of a coastal cliff, a fierce gale whipping around you. Rain sprays into your face, and you have to shout over the wind, turning your head to breathe. At first, you're triumphantly yelling your victory to a friend you've just beaten in a race up the hill—pure elation at the win. But as you speak, your voice wavers; you can't help but glance toward the harbor where that friend's new sailboat is moored, and a smaller, envious edge seeps through your excitement. The wind snatches your words, so you lean forward, then pull back, tone shifting from proud brag to a more complicated, quieter confession of longing.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Elation (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Kneel in the Kitchen
instruction: You are in your kitchen at 11pm, slumped in a chair, still in your work blazer from a double shift. Your partner is exhausted too—they're leaning against the counter, arms crossed, not looking at you. You have to apologize for something you said earlier that was sharp and unfair. You're so tired your bones ache, and a part of you finds this situation almost funny—how you both ended up here, too tired to fight, too tired to make up. But underneath that, there's a sour taste of guilt that won't fade. Start by letting out a long, heavy sigh, then speak. Your voice should be quiet, almost small, like your usual higher-pitched warmth is gone. Let your words trail off as you realize you're not explaining it right, then start over. By the end, you should sound hollowed out, like the apology took the last of your energy, leaving only a fragile hope that they understand.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (slightly present), Sourness (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reunion After Years of Silence
instruction: You're seeing someone you once loved intensely after years of painful separation. When you first see them, your body floods with sensation: maybe your hands go cold, your throat tightens, heat rises in your face, your breath catches. Start with purely physical reactions—let your voice crack, shake, or surge without controlling it. As you move closer, the physical hunger to touch them battles with the memory of how they hurt you: your body leans forward while your shoulders pull back, your voice softens then hardens. Let rage and desire and grief move through you like weather systems—give each sensation its moment in your throat, your breath, your chest. By the end, let one overwhelming physical-emotional truth dominate: maybe it's forgiveness that moves through you like heat, or a letting-go that feels like something breaking open, or a rekindling that burns away everything else.
inspired_by: Actor recognizes that he repeats the same vocal coloring or emotional tone in every performance, or that his voice sounds manipulated rather than organic

title: The Breath Between
instruction: You are lying face-to-face with your partner in the dark, foreheads almost touching, after a close call—a car that nearly hit you, a sudden illness that passed, or a moment you thought you’d lose them. Your body is still trembling from the shock; your voice comes out in shaky, breathy whispers because any louder would shatter the fragile peace. Start with the raw, quivering edge of fear—your words stumbling, your throat tight, every sound barely escaping. As you speak, let the realization of safety wash over you: your hand finds their cheek, your exhale deepens, and the fear shifts into a trembling gratitude and then into quiet awe that they’re here, that you’re both still here. Let your voice soften, crack, and finally steady with wonder, as if you’re seeing them for the first time. Micro-distractions: your breath catches mid-word, you might laugh or cry a little, you pause to press your lips together.
emotions_sampled: Fear (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Jumping Green-Eyed Monster
instruction: You're a woman in her 60s, doing a series of jumping jacks in a park. Your younger, fitter neighbor is jogging past, smiling easily. You can barely get out words between each explosive jump. 'Hup!' on takeoff, then a thud. Start with a teasing remark about their energy, but as you jump, envy creeps in — your voice, higher and strained, cracks. End with a breathless, doubting admission that you'll never move like that again. Fragment your words: launch a syllable mid-air, let the landing cut you off. The envy burns hotter with each jump.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Doubt (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Unspoken Goodbye at the Hospital Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed at 3 AM. She's asleep, and you know these are her final hours. Begin by trying to say a proper, composed goodbye—the kind you think she'd want to hear. But as you speak, let everything flood through: your anger at her for leaving, your guilt about the argument you had last Christmas, the sudden memory of her laugh, your terror of being alone, your inappropriate urge to giggle from exhaustion, your resentment about her always favoring your sister, your desperate love. Don't edit anything. Let your voice crack, surge with anger, soften with tenderness, break with laughter, whatever comes. The goodbye you planned transforms into the raw, contradictory truth of who you both were together. End in a place of unexpected peace—not because you've resolved everything, but because you've finally told the whole truth.

title: Dream Job First Week: Imposter Syndrome Detonating
instruction: You got the dream job. You're in your first week and your voice is trying to sound competent during meetings, but inside you're panicking. Your voice is careful, measured, trying not to give away the fact that you have no idea what you're doing. Include the moment in a meeting where someone asks for your input and your voice almost fails. You manage words but they're hollow. Later, alone, your voice becomes frantic: 'I don't deserve this. They're going to figure out I don't belong here.' Your voice is the sound of imposter syndrome in full bloom. Then you complete a task successfully and your voice becomes slightly more confident. Maybe you belong? Maybe? Your voice oscillates between certainty of inadequacy and glimpses of actual capability.

title: Confronting Your Father Through a Quarantine Wall
instruction: You're speaking through reinforced glass to your father, who's on the infected side and has maybe hours left. You came to say goodbye, but instead you're finally telling him everything—how his silence taught you that love meant distance, how his inability to be soft made you afraid of your own tenderness. Your voice starts controlled, years of rehearsed grievances, but his face on the other side keeps breaking your momentum. You swing between furious accusations and desperate attempts to connect before it's too late. He can't respond—the intercom is broken on his side—so you're confronted with your own voice, your own words, watching him mouth things you'll never hear. By the end, you're pressed against the glass, no longer sure if you're condemning him or begging him to know you, your anger collapsing into the terrified child who just wanted him to see you, really see you, even once.

title: Breathing Your Air
instruction: You're a young man clinging to a half-sunken raft in choppy water, talking to the person who got the lifeboat seat you were promised. Your voice keeps dipping below the surface, words cut off by splashes and gasps. Start with bitter jealousy — sharp gripes about how lucky they are — but as you struggle to stay afloat, let that envy crack into raw physical pain. You're not just drowning in water; you're drowning in the unfairness of it all. Let your voice choke and muffle unpredictably, pushing out the hurt even when your mouth fills with saltwater. Say roughly 60 words.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Splitting Kindling for Her Room
instruction: You are a middle-aged mother in your backyard, chopping wood for a fire. Your daughter just left for college. Between swings of the axe, you talk to yourself—proud of your strength and independence, but as you work, a memory of tucking her in at night surfaces. Start with a sharp, confident grunt and a boast about handling things alone. Let the exertion pull words from you in bursts, with pauses for breathing and the crack of splitting wood. Midway, your tone softens, affected by affection, then ends with a quiet, breathless admission that you miss her already.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child That You're Not Going to Survive This Illness
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your child is asleep beside you in the hospital bed. You're too weak to speak loudly, so everything is whispered, intimate, achingly tender. Start by studying their face, describing features with wonder—'You have my mother's chin.' Your voice should be soft but steady as you tell them the truths you need them to carry: how proud you are, how they saved you in ways they'll never know. The emotion catches in your throat on ordinary words—'breakfast,' 'homework,' 'someday.' You're not crying dramatically; tears just fall silently as you speak. Tell them about the person you hope they'll become, apologize for the moments you'll miss—their wedding, their children, ordinary Tuesdays. Your breath should become more labored, voice more fragile. End with the simplest words, repeated like a prayer: 'You were enough. You were always enough. Being your parent was enough.' Let the final words barely make it out.
inspired_by: Explaining Your Mental Health Diagnosis to Someone Close

title: The Almost Perfect Moment
instruction: You are an older man with your long-term partner, in the tender middle of intimacy. You're kissing and whispering to each other, your voice low and breathy, slowing down as arousal builds. Suddenly, your partner pulls back slightly—you sense a familiar sign they're about to say something that will shift the mood. You feel a wave of elation for how close you are, then a pang of deep disappointment as you realize this moment is being interrupted, yet your affection keeps your voice gentle. Voice: start with a warm, excited whisper that gradually becomes heavier with disappointment, but tinged with soft, caring breath. Let your words trail off with sighs or small mouth sounds.
emotions_sampled: Elation (clearly present), Disappointment (extremely present), Affection (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Room We Shared
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying father's hospital bed in the final hour. Begin numb, exhausted, emptied out—you've said everything you thought needed saying. But now, in the silence, you start truly seeing him: the particular way his hand rests on the blanket, the exact shade of his skin, the shape of his breathing. Let each tiny detail you notice crack you open wider—the hospital bracelet with his name misspelled, the way the light hits the IV stand, the smell of the soap they used. Your curiosity about these final moments awakens something fierce and tender. End in a place of devastating presence—not goodbye, but absolute attention to every remaining second, every detail of him you never took time to truly see before.

title: Confronting Your Parent About Why They Left
instruction: After twenty years, you're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. Begin with bitter, sarcastic politeness — 'Oh, how nice to see you.' Let the anger build as you list all the moments they missed: birthdays, graduations, your wedding. Your voice should become louder, sharper, more cutting. But then something shifts. Mid-sentence, you stop. Your voice drops to almost nothing. The anger dissolves into the question you've carried your whole life: 'Was I not enough?' End in raw vulnerability, your voice small like a child's, needing an answer you know won't satisfy you.
inspired_by: Whispering a Secret in a Crowded Room

title: The Last Swing
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy sitting on the creaky wooden swing in your childhood backyard at dusk. Your best friend is moving away tomorrow, and you've just shared a goofy, perfect hour that made you forget the goodbye until now. Start with a slight smile in your voice, remembering the sucker punch of laughter you both had a few minutes ago—let that contentment slip through as you talk about the dents in the tree branch you've climbed a thousand times. As you speak, feel the swing's chains groaning under you, and let your voice find an almost ceremonial quiet when you realize this is the last time you'll point out the chipped paint on the fence together. End with your throat tightening, your words slowing down on 'see you, someday,' where the final syllable breaks just slightly—not from sadness, but from the weight of knowing this perfect evening has already become a memory.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bass and Starlight
instruction: You're at a rave, dancing hard for hours. Your body moves on autopilot, you're laughing and shouting to your friend over the thumping beat, your voice bouncing with each step, breathless and exhilarated. Then, in a flash of lasers and smoke, you see the crowd ripple like a single living thing under the Milky Way lights. The awe crashes into you. Suddenly you can't shout—your voice drops, trembles with the tremor of your legs, and you speak slower, quieter, but full of wonder. Let the exhaustion and the raw beauty fight for control of your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Bittersweet Farewell: Laughing Through Tears at the Beautiful Impossibility
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love deeply—but not because of death or tragedy. You're both choosing different paths that can't intersect: different continents, incompatible dreams, lives that don't align despite genuine love. Your voice catches between laughter and tears: 'God, this is so stupid. We love each other and we're still saying goodbye.' Let yourself oscillate between joy at what you shared and grief at what can't be. Laugh at an inside joke, then feel your voice break with the reality that there won't be new ones. 'Remember when we...'—and the memory makes you smile even as tears come. Your voice carries gratitude and heartbreak simultaneously: 'I'm so glad I knew you. I'm so sad this is how it ends.' There's no anger here, no bitterness—just the strange beauty of loving someone and still letting them go. End with a moment of profound acceptance mixed with loss, your voice tender and broken and somehow at peace: 'I hope you find everything you're looking for. I really do. Even if it's not me.' Make it real—the complex truth of loving and releasing, of finding peace in heartbreak, of meaning goodbye without regret but also without pretending it doesn't hurt.
inspired_by: Descending from the Death Zone: Oxygen Returning Clarity

title: Dust of '78
instruction: You are an older construction foreman on a demolition site, watching a building you helped build decades ago get torn down. The noise of machinery and shouting crew fills the air—you have to yell to be heard, but your voice cracks with age and wear. Start with practiced sourness and numbness, barking orders like it’s just another job. But as you look at the falling beams, a deep longing for the past rises up—your voice softens, almost forgetting to shout, then fades into quiet resignation. Let the hard hat and visor make your voice slightly cupped and strained as you naturally pause to spit or wipe sweat from your brow.
emotions_sampled: Longing (extremely present), Sourness (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love who is dying within hours. They need to hear that it's okay to let go, but you're terrified of losing them. Begin by trying to keep them here—tell them about tomorrow's plans, next week's weather, anything to hold onto them. But as you speak, feel the truth rising: they're suffering, and your love means releasing them. Let your words shift from desperate plans to tender permission. By the end, you must say goodbye using whatever words come from your breaking heart in that moment—not rehearsed phrases, but the raw, stumbling truth of letting someone go. Your voice should transform from grasping to releasing.

title: Eating a Slice of Decadent Chocolate Cake
instruction: Take a bite of the cake, closing your eyes as you savor it fully. Imagine the soft, rich texture as it hits your tongue, the smoothness of the frosting mixing with the dense, moist cake beneath. Describe the layers of flavor in detail the deep, dark cocoa taste, the sweetness that isnt too overpowering, the hint of vanilla or caramel in the background. Speak slowly, almost reverently, as you let each bite melt, feeling the cake dissolve, leaving a lingering sweetness that fills your mouth. Express a quiet, blissful hum of enjoyment, as if this moment with the cake is pure heaven.

title: Beneath the Covers at Dawn
instruction: You're lying next to someone you've loved in silence for years, and this is your last morning together before one of you leaves forever. Speak in whispers, so close your breath touches their skin. Begin with gentle, grateful observations—describing their face, the warmth of the bed, the quality of early light. Let yourself sink deeper into each detail you notice: the specific texture of their hair, the way they breathe, a scar you've memorized. As you speak, allow the weight of goodbye to seep in slowly, like cold water rising. Your whispers should become more fragile, more urgent, more broken. By the end, you're no longer describing what you see—you're clinging to it, trying to preserve something that's already slipping away. Transform from peaceful appreciation to quiet, aching desperation.
inspired_by: Actor has tried a choice but it isn't producing the desired emotional response

title: Tender Vigil: The Truth You Whispered Too Late
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who can no longer respond—hospital room, their breathing shallow, and you're finally saying what you never had the courage to say when they could answer back. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and breaking. Start with small confessions: 'I was always too proud to tell you...' Let your voice carry the weight of missed chances, the tender regret of all the times you held back. Share a specific memory that meant everything, your throat tightening around the words. The emotion isn't loud—it's the kind that makes your voice thin and fragile, catching on every other word. End with 'I hope you knew' or 'I should have told you every day,' your voice dissolving into a silence heavy with love and irreversible loss.

title: Unexpected Attraction
instruction: Youre at the grocery store and suddenly feel a powerful attraction to a stranger nearby. The surprise in your voice should be clear, as if youre taken aback by your own emotions. Muted gasps, short pauses, and involuntary sighs should convey your struggle to keep this feeling in check.

title: The Weight Lifted
instruction: You're slumped on the couch after a brutal day, phone in your lap, thumb idly scrolling. You're exhausted, barely keeping your eyes open, your voice low and directed downward with soft taps and distracted filler noises. Then a notification pops up—it's the medical update you've been dreading, and it's good news. The relief floods you, your breath catches, your voice lifts slightly but stays quiet, awed. As you watch a short video—a time-lapse of the stars or a baby taking first steps—the awe deepens. Your voice shifts from weary mutters to fragile, reverent whispers, still tired but now full of wonder. Speak approximately 40-80 words of fragmented reactions, like 'Oh… oh wow… I can't believe… that's… that's incredible…' ending in a hushed, awed silence.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Your Secret in the Dark to Someone Who Stays
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, finally ready to share the shame you've carried alone for years. Your voice starts barely audible, throat tight with fear: 'I need to tell you something I've never told anyone.' Each word costs you something. As you confess—whatever darkness you've hidden—let your voice waver between resolve and terror of rejection. Notice the moments where you almost stop, where silence becomes louder than words. When they reach for your hand in the darkness, your breath catches. Your voice breaks open with relief so profound it hurts: 'You're... you're still here.' End with tears you can't control, voice thick with disbelief and overwhelming gratitude, whispering 'Thank you for staying' as if it's a prayer. Move from paralyzing fear to devastating relief.
inspired_by: Your Vulnerability Being Used Against You Later

title: Thank You for Your Service, Sir
instruction: You are a hardened drill sergeant, an older man with decades of service, who has just finished a final inspection of a new unit. You must address a specific recruit who, midway through the last exercise, caught you with a disgusting, cowardly lie about another soldier to save his own skin. You start with the command voice you were born to use—loud, clipped, utterly devoid of feeling—to thank the unit for their effort, a rote ritual. As you focus on that recruit, your voice shifts: the bark cracks, a wave of raw, bitter disgust washes over you, making your words slow and heavy with contempt. End by forcing a single, grateful nod to the other soldiers, your voice almost a whisper of exhausted relief, before turning away.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Long Drive Home
instruction: You are an elderly woman driving alone at dusk. Your seat is reclined, arms stretched to the wheel, the hum of the engine filling the cabin. You just left your younger neighbor’s house—she showed off her new car, and a sharp wave of envy rises in your chest. For a moment you mutter to yourself, feeling a helpless ache in your hands as they grip the wheel. But then you recall a road trip from your youth, a perfect memory of wind and laughter, and a quiet elation spreads through you. Let the first words sound tight with jealousy, then let your voice soften, slow, and brighten as you remember—speak as if you're losing the thought, then finding it again.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Helplessness (slightly present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Keeping Your Parent Conscious Until the Ambulance Arrives
instruction: You're on the floor cradling your parent who's had a stroke or heart attack. You arrived for a regular visit and found them collapsed. Start with terror—voice high and breaking as you call 911, giving the address through sobs. Then shift: the dispatcher tells you to keep them talking, keep them awake. Your voice transforms into something you've never heard from yourself—fierce, commanding, almost angry: 'No. Look at me. Stay with me.' But between those commands, tenderness floods in. You're stroking their face, and suddenly you're telling them things you never said—'I know I was difficult,' 'You were enough,' 'Please don't go yet.' Your voice cracks between strength and complete fragility. When their eyes flutter closed, you become almost violent in your desperation: 'OPEN YOUR EYES.' Then you hear the sirens approaching, and relief breaks you completely. You collapse into whispered gratitude, still holding them, voice shaking: 'They're here. You did it. Stay with me just a little longer.'
inspired_by: Herding People to Basement Safety While Tornado Sirens Wail

title: Screaming at God After Losing Everything
instruction: You're alone—in an empty church, on a clifftop, in the ruins of what was your home—and everything you built is gone. Start with a roar of pure rage at the universe, at God, at fate. Your voice is primal, unleashed, demanding answers. 'Why?! What did I do to deserve this?!' Let yourself be huge, furious, uncontained. But as you exhaust yourself, as the echoes fade, something else emerges. Your voice begins to shake not with anger but with terror—the raw fear of having to go on, of facing tomorrow. Drop to your knees vocally and emotionally. The rage breaks apart into helpless sobbing, then quieter still: a whispered plea. 'I can't do this. I don't know how to survive this.' End in the strange, eerie space between despair and the first fragile breath of surrender—not acceptance, but the admission that you have no choice but to somehow continue.
inspired_by: Telling Your Best Friend You Can't Be Friends Anymore

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: You're a teenager in a cold interview room, a police officer across the table, arms crossed, staring without speaking. You feel the power imbalance—they're trying to wear you down. Start with a quiet scoff, a slight grimace of disgust at their silence. Your first words are clipped, sarcastic, maybe a little dismissive. But as the silence drags on, your voice begins to shake. You shift in your seat, let out a nervous breath, then stammer, rushing to fill the void. End with a raw plea—your voice breaks, almost childlike, revealing the fear behind your bravado. Let the performance feel like a losing battle against your own nerves.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Conducting Through Chaos
instruction: You're leading a community orchestra in a neighborhood that's being torn apart by conflict, and this performance is your act of defiance. Your voice guides them: 'Together. Stay together.' But something shifts—you start laughing, softly, almost incredulously, because the absurdity and beauty of this moment hit you at once. You're making music while the world falls apart, and it's ridiculous and profound and heartbreaking. 'We're doing it. We're actually doing this.' Your voice breaks with emotion—not sadness, not quite joy, but something fierce and luminous between them. 'Keep going. Don't stop.' You're crying now, but still guiding, still believing. Let the laughter and tears, the hope and grief, the chaos and transcendence all exist together. This is humans refusing to surrender to darkness by creating beauty anyway.

title: The Boat Next Door
instruction: You're an older man on the phone with your buddy, staring out the window at your neighbor's brand-new boat. Your voice has that chronic complaining drone—nasal, sing-song, stretching vowels like 'you wouldn't believe...' You start off bitter and jealous, describing how he doesn't deserve it, but then you glance at the photo of your wife on the mantel. Suddenly, you remember the surprise trip she planned for your anniversary. Your anger falters as genuine gratitude rises, your voice softening, losing the drone. End with surprise that you're actually thankful.
emotions_sampled: Anger (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Medal That Never Was
instruction: You're an elderly man with a deep, gruff voice, sitting in your armchair. Your grandson just pulled a dusty letter from your war chest—proof you weren't at the battle you've bragged about for decades. You start by booming with triumphant pride, describing how you saved your squad. Then you see the letter and your voice catches—astonishment makes you stutter, pitch jumps. You begin over-explaining, your tone shaky with doubt, trying to reassert that old confidence. Let your hand tremble, glance around the room, lose your train of thought. End with a forced laugh that trails into silence.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Doubt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning in the Hospital Room
instruction: You are sitting beside your father's hospital bed at dawn. He has hours, maybe minutes left. Begin by noticing everything in the room - the beeping monitor, the antiseptic smell, the way morning light filters through the blinds, the weight of his hand in yours. Start feeling numb, disconnected, as if this isn't really happening. As you speak to him - telling him about your childhood, thanking him, asking forgiveness for old fights - let the reality sink in with each sensory detail you notice: the coldness of his fingers, the rattle in his breathing, the fading pressure of his grip. By the end, you must arrive at a place of full, crushing acceptance that this is the last time you'll ever see him alive. Let the images you create - his face, the room, the sounds - make it unbearably real.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Walter Mitty Option — Scene 1 Fantasy Imaging Exercise

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're helping your child pack up their childhood bedroom as they prepare to move across the world—they're excited, you're drowning in bittersweet emotion. Start laughing genuinely at something you find: 'Oh my god, do you remember this?' Your voice is bright, delighted, teasing them gently. But even as you laugh, there's a thickness in your throat. You keep finding memories—each one is a small knife. 'You were so little when...' Your voice wavers but you push through with another smile, another laugh that sounds slightly wrong. They leave the room and you're alone with a stuffed animal they slept with for years. Your voice breaks, tears coming even as you're still half-laughing: 'How did you get so big? When did this happen?' You're crying and laughing simultaneously, overwhelmed by pride and loss. Pull yourself together when you hear them coming back, voice thick but warm: 'I am so proud of you. I am so, so proud.' Then, quietly, letting the full truth show: 'And I'm going to miss you so much I can barely breathe.' End with authentic joy mixed with grief: 'But this is exactly what I raised you for. To fly. To be brave. To go.' Find the beauty in the contradiction—devastated and joyful, broken and whole, letting go while holding on.

title: The Spill at the Party
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a family reunion, leaning casually against the wall to hide the large red wine stain spreading across your favorite floral dress. You start by trying to sound cool and unbothered, making a joke about how 'artistic' the stain looks, but your voice wavers with embarrassment as you notice your granddaughter smirking. Midway, you pause, glance down at the fabric, and let out a quiet sigh — the cool act crumbles into raw vulnerability. End with a hushed, almost breathless admission that you feel old and clumsy, your voice cracking slightly as you lean your head back against the wall for support.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Lesson Before You Go
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is leaving tomorrow on a journey they may not return from—a dangerous mission, a one-way voyage, or perhaps they're simply dying. Start with quiet desperation, your voice catching: 'I kept thinking I'd have more time to tell you this. That there'd be another chance.' Your hands might reach for theirs. Then something releases in you, and you begin speaking with urgent clarity about what their life has meant, how they changed you in ways you never acknowledged: 'You taught me how to be brave without even trying. Just by being yourself.' Let gratitude flood through you even as grief tightens your throat. By the end, arrive at a place of fierce, protective blessing: 'So go. Go and don't look back. You've already given me everything.' Your voice should break and strengthen in the same breath, holding both goodbye and a kind of eternal presence.

title: The Unheard Scream
instruction: You are a young woman with a high, strained voice, standing on a makeshift soapbox at a busy street corner. The crowd is noisy, distracted, and you have no microphone—so you push your voice to cut through the rumble of traffic and chatter. You start seething with bitterness about how you’ve been overlooked, your body tensing as you shout over a passing truck. Midway, you spot someone you desire in the crowd—your voice wavers, drops slightly, as a flicker of lust mixes with jealousy of those who seem to have it easier. By the end, your anger collapses into a raw, almost pleading envy, your pitch cracking, losing the rhythm as you struggle to hold the crowd’s attention while your own emotions betray you.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Stubborn Goat Finally Comes Down
instruction: You're a teenage boy on a rocky hillside, trying to coax your family's goat down from a ledge where it's been stuck for an hour. You start with a tired, gentle coaxing, relief that it's finally moving—a soft 'Come on, girl' with a few clicks and a whistle. As it hesitates, you get a surge of triumph when it takes a step toward you, and your voice sharpens with a short, firm 'Yes! That's it!' Then, as it approaches fully, your tone softens again into hopeful optimism, mixing affection and command: a kissy noise, then a quiet 'Good goat... let's get you home.' Your voice shifts naturally from wearied relief to proud excitement to tender hope, with pauses for the goat's reactions.
emotions_sampled: Relief (slightly present), Triumph (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Storm's Embrace
instruction: You're standing alone in an open field as a thunderstorm rages around you. Rain pours down your face, thunder cracks overhead, and you have to shout to hear yourself. At first, you are trembling and desperate, having run here to escape something inside you. But as the storm intensifies, a wild pleasure overtakes you — you lift your face to the rain, laugh through the thunder, and let the water wash away every doubt. Let your voice start tight and anxious, then break into a breathless, ecstatic shout as you surrender fully to the moment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Hospital Room at Three A.M.
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in the middle of the night. Begin by noticing everything around you with excruciating clarity—the hum of machines, the particular shade of green on the walls, the smell of antiseptic mixed with something else you can't name, the texture of his hand in yours. Start feeling numb, protective, holding everything back. As you sit there, allow a specific memory to surface—not a normal memory, but one that feels strangely distorted, maybe from childhood, maybe from a dream you once had about him. Let the logic of this memory be strange: colors might be wrong, time might fold in on itself, he might be young and old at once. Follow the sensory details of this memory wherever they lead. As the memory deepens, let your emotional defenses crack. By the end, you're telling him something you've never been able to say, your voice breaking, the numbness replaced by everything you've been holding back for years.

title: The Last Sled Run
instruction: You are an 8-year-old boy caught in a sudden blizzard while sledding with your older brother. You can barely see him through the white wall of snow, and your jaw is so cold it's hard to form words. At first, you're proud—you made it down the hill first, you shout 'I beat you!' into the howling wind, but the sound gets swallowed. Then you realize he's not laughing back, and you can't find him. Your voice shifts from boastful to uncertain, then frantic, then cracked with fear as you call his name, your bravado crumbling into a sob you try to hide.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Echoes of Nothing
instruction: You're a teenager standing at the edge of a deserted quarry, alone. The wind stings your face and whips your hair. You've been holding in every disappointment, every unfair thing said to you, until your chest feels like it might crack. Let out a raw, wordless yell into the empty space — not to anyone, just to the sky and rocks. Start with a furious, guttural roar that shakes your throat, let bitterness creep into the sound as you think of one specific insult. As your voice gives out, catch your breath, cough, and then let a quiet, tired whisper escape — almost to yourself — as you realize the void doesn't answer. The shift is from explosive anger to hollow exhaustion.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Deafening Crush
instruction: You're a 17-year-old girl, just out of surgery for a cochlear implant on your left side. Your best friend has snuck you a phone to call the boy you've liked for months, a senior who is actually your neighbor and didn't know you were deaf. Your voice is too loud, pitch unpredictable, but you're so thrilled to finally hear your own words. You start breathless, nervous, trying too hard to sound casual, desperately hoping he can't tell you're a mess. As you talk, your pride flickers—you realize you can hear his voice clearly for the first time, and it makes you laugh softly, your volume dropping just a notch in wonder. End with a quiet, hopeful 'I can hear you,' the words trembling with the weight of a future you didn't know you could have.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Execution
instruction: You're speaking to your adult child for the final time before your execution tomorrow at dawn. You were wrongly convicted, but all appeals are exhausted. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them, asking about their day, their partner, anything normal. But as reality crashes through your defenses, your voice fractures. You need them to know you're not afraid, but you are terrified. You want to say everything—a lifetime of love, pride, regret for moments you missed—but time is collapsing. Your voice moves from artificial brightness to raw fear to fierce, protective love. End by finding unexpected peace in telling them the one truth that matters most, even as your heart is shattering. Let silence carry what words cannot.
inspired_by: Historical: Woman Discovers Her Child Is the Product of Rape She's Blocked

title: The Last Word
instruction: You've just ended a brutal argument with a former friend who always belittled you. Now you're alone in the room, hands planted on your hips, elbows locked, shoulders back. The position forces your voice bigger and sharper than usual. Start bitter—spit out the unfairness, letting your voice waver with raw resentment. Then, mid-sentence, catch yourself: a small, tired breath. Let a sliver of relief leak through, as if saying it out loud makes it real. Shift your weight, lose your train of thought for a half-second, then finish with a mix of tiredness and quiet triumph.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Requiem Garden
instruction: You're scattering your best friend's ashes in the garden you planted together, and you're telling them the beautiful, impossible news they'll never hear: you're finally having the baby you both hoped for after years of trying. Begin with joyful laughter, genuine and bright: 'You're not going to believe this—after everything, it finally happened!' Your voice is celebratory, talking to them as if they're standing right there. But as you describe the ultrasound, the heartbeat, the joy catches and tangles with grief. Your laughter becomes tears, your voice fracturing: 'You should be here. You were supposed to be the godmother.' You're crying and laughing simultaneously, overcome with gratitude and heartbreak. End with your voice soft but grounded, finding strange peace in the contradiction: 'I'm going to tell them all about you. Thank you for being my person.' Let the final moment be you touching the earth where their ashes rest, your breathing steady even as tears fall.

title: First Infertility Support Group: Finding Your Voice
instruction: You're sitting in a circle in your first support group meeting. Your voice is tentative, almost not there: 'Hi, I'm... I'm struggling with infertility.' Those words take tremendous effort. Other people are sharing and your voice stays quiet, listening. Include the moment where someone shares something that mirrors your exact pain and your voice cracks. Then it's time to share more deeply and your voice becomes slightly stronger, then stronger still. By the end, you're saying things out loud you've only thought in the darkness. Your voice isn't healed—it's still carrying pain—but it's carrying it communally now. 'Thank you for listening. It helps to say it out loud.' Your voice has reclaimed some power.

title: Breaking Holy
instruction: You're alone in a sacred space—a church, temple, childhood bedroom, memorial site. Your body is in physical pain (grief manifesting as chest tightness, rage as trembling muscles, desire as heat). You've been taught to be reverent here, controlled, respectful. Begin by trying to maintain that composure, breathing through the physical sensations. But the body won't be denied. Let yourself do the most forbidden thing: scream obscenities in the holy place, speak blasphemies, express anti-social rage, describe base physical needs in crude language. Let the physical pain explode into sound and movement—stomp, spit, curse, thrash. Break every rule of decorum you were taught. Move from controlled reverence through volcanic release to finally—exhausted, emptied—a strange new peace.

title: Reading Your Own Eulogy at Your Rebirth
instruction: You've survived something that should have killed you—addiction, illness, abuse—and you're speaking at a ceremony marking your recovery, reading a eulogy for the person you used to be. Start with a strange, almost inappropriate lightness, even laughing softly at the absurdity of eulogizing yourself while standing there alive. But as you describe who you were—the pain, the darkness, the person who nearly didn't make it—your voice fills with deep compassion and grief for that version of you. The laughter becomes tears, but they're not just sad tears; there's profound gratitude mixed with the sorrow. Your voice wavers between mourning the loss of that broken self and celebrating the survival. End with a paradox in your tone: weeping while smiling, your voice thick with tears but also with peace, saying goodbye to someone you were while honoring that they brought you here.

title: Finding Your Stillborn Baby Beautiful: Joy and Grief Entwined
instruction: You're holding your stillborn child for the first and only time, and you're overwhelmed by how perfect they are. Start with a laugh—surprising, genuine, bubbling up: 'Look at your tiny hands.' You're marveling, cooing, filled with wonder as if they're alive. Let yourself be fully present in parental joy, counting fingers, noticing features, your voice soft with love. But threading through this is the knowledge that they're gone, so the laugh catches, becomes a sob, then shifts back to tenderness. You're living in two realities at once: celebrating their existence and mourning their death in the same breath. Move fluidly between 'You're so beautiful' spoken with pure delight, and 'I'm so sorry' whispered with breaking grief. You're memorizing them, trying to pack a lifetime of love into this hour. End with profound gratitude—thanking them for being here at all, for making you a parent even for this brief moment—while simultaneously accepting the unbearable truth that you have to let them go. Your voice should hold both wholeness and shattering, neither one overtaking the other, finding strange peace in loving them exactly as they are.
inspired_by: First Day of Sobriety: Calling Your Sponsor

title: Reading the Letter They Never Sent
instruction: You've just discovered a letter written to you years ago by someone who loved you—a letter they wrote but never had the courage to send, found after their death or departure. As you read it aloud, start with confusion, maybe even a tentative laugh at something they wrote. But as the words reveal the depth of what they felt, what they never said when they were with you, your voice fills with wonder mixed with devastating loss. They loved you. They saw you. And you never knew. Let laughter and tears tangle together—joy at being seen so completely, grief that you can never tell them you understand now. Your voice should break and heal and break again. End with gratitude that feels simultaneously like the most beautiful gift and the cruelest revelation, your final words hovering between a laugh and a sob.

title: Whispering to the Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a hospital bed—a partner, a child, a beloved friend—and you think they're asleep, so you finally allow yourself to speak the tender, terrified truth. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile, as though speaking too loudly would shatter something precious. Start with simple observations—'Your hand is so warm,' 'I can hear you breathing'—but gradually let the deeper current of emotion surface. You confess fears you've been hiding, express gratitude for small moments you never acknowledged, admit how lost you'll be. There's a catch in your throat, tears you're trying to swallow. The emotion is so big it makes you physically ache, yet you're trying to keep it contained, quiet, just for this moment. End with something devastatingly simple and true—maybe 'I'm here,' maybe 'Don't go,' maybe just their name, spoken like a prayer.

title: Bedside Vigil: The Confession You Waited Too Long to Make
instruction: You're beside someone who's unconscious, possibly dying, and you're finally saying what you never had the courage to say when they could respond. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and breaking. Start with small talk - desperately normal things ('The garden looks beautiful this year') - because you're terrified of the real words. But then the truth surfaces, gentle and devastating: 'I was in love with you. I am in love with you. I never said it because I was so afraid.' Your voice is tender, full of regret so profound it physically hurts. You're touching their hand, and your voice wavers between confession and prayer, between what was and what will never be. End with a goodbye that mixes gratitude ('Thank you for existing') with soul-deep sorrow. This isn't theatrical crying - this is the quiet devastation of missed chances, expressed with aching gentleness.
inspired_by: After Job Loss: Practical Panic Setting In

title: The Distance Between Us
instruction: You're catching up with an old friend at a quiet coffee shop. You've been looking forward to this for weeks, but as the conversation drifts, you realize you're both different people now. Start with a forced brightness, playing the part of the cheerful guy, but let the disappointment creep in as you notice the gaps in your connection. By the end, your voice should drop into a raw, hesitant sadness—like you're admitting to yourself that this friendship is fading. Let your words stumble, clear your throat, look away, and don't try to smooth over the cracks.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in the dark next to your partner of many years. You cannot sleep because you're carrying a truth that's eating you alive - but it's not a betrayal, it's a vulnerable need or fear you've hidden from them (and yourself) throughout your relationship. Begin by trying to wake them gently, your voice barely a whisper, uncertain if you even want them to hear you. As they stir and ask what's wrong, let the truth emerge in fragments - not rehearsed, but stumbling, raw, almost childlike in its honesty. Move from trembling uncertainty to the relief of finally being seen. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost breath, punctuated by long pauses where silence says as much as words. Let yourself be utterly undefended. End in either the safety of being held or the terrifying freedom of having been truly honest.
inspired_by: Actor needs maximum emotional availability before a demanding scene with extreme emotional requirements

title: The Tenth One
instruction: You're lying face-down on a bed, gripping a pillow, after agreeing to a scene with your partner who you're intensely infatuated with. You've just taken a hard spank and are told to count, but you feel a flicker of cruelty in their tone that excites and shames you. Start with a breathless, playful giggle as you say 'seven,' but let your voice crumble into a shy, embarrassed whisper as you realize how much you're enjoying the pain. End on the eighth strike, letting out a sharp yelp that softens into a vulnerable, surrendered sigh.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Face I'll Ever See
instruction: You are in the final hour of your life, lying in bed, and the person you love most has just entered the room. You have said your practical goodbyes already—now you want something different. Look at them as if you are seeing them for the very first time: the specific curve of their jaw, the way light catches their eyes, the particular rhythm of their breathing. Begin with quiet wonder, drinking in every detail as though you're discovering a miraculous stranger. As you continue looking, let yourself perceive what their presence has meant to your entire existence—what this face has given you across all your years. End by speaking aloud the smallest, most specific things you're noticing right now: a freckle, the way they blink, how their hand trembles. Move from awestruck discovery to deep knowing to an urgent need to name every precious detail before the darkness comes.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago, and they're acting like you can just pick up where you left off. Start controlled, almost cold: 'You don't get to do this. You don't get to just show up.' They try to explain, to justify, and your control starts slipping. Your voice becomes sharper, angrier: 'I needed you. I was a child and I needed you and you chose not to be there.' They say they're sorry, that they were struggling, and something breaks open. Now it's not just anger—it's the raw, wounded voice of the child you were: 'Do you have any idea what that did to me?' Let your voice move from fury to devastation, from accusation to the aching vulnerability of someone who still, despite everything, needed their parent to choose them. End somewhere between rage and heartbreak, unresolved.

title: The Ledge
instruction: You're a teenager who climbed onto a high ledge to retrieve a lost phone, but now you're stuck — arms stretched up, gripping a rusty pipe, feet slipping on the narrow stone. Your rib cage is pulled tight, every breath a struggle, and your voice comes out thin and strained. Start with a trembling, desperate whisper as you call out for help, half convinced no one will hear. Then you hear footsteps — someone is coming. Let the fear slowly melt into a shaky, overwhelming relief, your voice catching as you realize you're not alone. Speak through the physical strain: ragged inhales, pauses to steady yourself, a laugh that cracks with disbelief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Rage That Becomes Surrender
instruction: You're screaming at God, the universe, fate—demanding answers after catastrophic loss. Begin with explosive fury, words sharp and accusatory, voice cracking with rage. But as you rail and shout, language proves inadequate for this kind of pain—words crumble, sentences fragment, until you're left with raw sound. Your screaming dissolves into something between roaring and sobbing, fierce and primal. Cycle through vocal violence: guttural cries, wordless howls, sounds you've never made before. Then—unexpectedly—something shifts. The rage cracks open to reveal helplessness underneath. Your voice drops from screaming to broken whimpering, from demands to pleading, from fury to the sound of a heart shattering. End not with resolution but with exhausted humming, a sound of surrender, finding in your own voice a strange lullaby that soothes nothing but continues anyway.
inspired_by: Alien First Contact: The Universal Translator Breaks

title: The Same Noise Every Night
instruction: You are a middle-aged person with a gender-neutral voice, standing alone in your kitchen at 2 a.m., complaining about a dripping sound from the ceiling. Your voice has that tired, nasal drone—elongated vowels, a repetitive sing-song pitch as you list the same complaints you've made for weeks. But as you mutter and pace, you notice the drips are landing in perfect sync with your own heartbeat. The confusion about the source deepens into a creeping, quiet fear—is the sound coming from inside you? Let your voice shift from a weary, circular complaint to a hesitant, almost whispered realization. You might trail off, swallow, or stop mid-sentence as the truth settles in.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Laughing Through Your Gratitude Speech at a Funeral
instruction: You're giving the eulogy for someone who saved your life in every way that mattered—and they made you promise, absolutely promise, not to cry. You start with a laugh, sharing a ridiculous memory, voice bright and warm, honoring their wish. The laughter is real, genuine. But as you talk about what they meant to you, your voice begins to shake even as you're smiling. You're still trying to laugh—'They'd be so mad at me right now'—but tears are streaming down your face. Your voice fractures into this beautiful, impossible mixture: laughing and sobbing simultaneously as you express gratitude so profound it's breaking you open. 'Thank you for seeing me' comes out as both a laugh and a cry. By the end, you're surrendering to both joy and devastation at once, voice cracked but full of love, finding something almost peaceful in letting both emotions exist together.
inspired_by: Being Broken Up With Over Text, Reading It Out Loud

title: The Confrontation: A Daughter Dismantles Her Healer Parent
instruction: You are confronting the parent who was always the town's beloved healer—everyone's savior—but never truly there for you. Start with controlled, bitter precision as you list the childhood moments they missed while saving strangers, your voice sharp with decades of swallowed resentment. Build to explosive accusations: 'You fixed everyone but me. You saw everyone's pain but mine.' Then, as your parent finally breaks and admits their failures, you must navigate the disorienting shift from righteous anger to the aching, confused grief of a child who still desperately wants their parent's love. End torn between the satisfaction of being heard and the hollow realization that acknowledgment doesn't undo the past. Let your voice fracture between fury and the sob of a neglected child.
inspired_by: The Healer and the Cursed Warrior

title: The Road Remembers
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman in the back seat of a taxi on a rutted, unpaved road. The driver hits a pothole and your body lurches; your voice trembles with each jolt. A familiar ache sits in your chest as you recall the friend you haven't spoken to in years—the silence between you feels heavy. But then you catch a glimpse of the old diner where you two used to meet, and a spark of interest flickers: what would she say if you called? Let the bumps shake your words, and let your tone drift from a quiet sadness into a tentative, curious warmth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Runt Stubs His Toe
instruction: You are a tough little kid, maybe eight years old, trying to walk barefoot through a messy garage to grab a can of soda for your older brother. You are muttering bitter things under your breath about how he always sends you to do his chores. Suddenly, you kick the edge of a heavy toolbox with your bare toe — the pain is blinding, a white-hot spike. You yelp and hop on one foot, hissing through your teeth, but then you remember he's watching from the couch. You force a ragged, breathless laugh, trying to turn it into a joke. You feel scared he'll call you a baby, so you squeeze out amusement through the pain, talking as if it was nothing, even though your voice is shaking and you're still gasping.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Amusement (very intensely present), Fear (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Round
instruction: You're an older woman at a dimly lit bar, three cocktails in, leaning forward with a glossy smile. Across from you sits a man in a leather jacket—he's been returning your gaze all night. Your voice is high and breathy, dripping with flirtation, but every few seconds a sudden shout or a random word bursts out of you, like 'BEEP!' or 'HELLO!'—you barely pause, just keep purring. As you reach to touch his hand, he checks his phone and mutters an excuse to leave. The lust in your throat curdles into a hollow, quiet disappointment, but you still finish your sentence with the same honeyed tone, as if nothing happened. Speak fluidly, let the tics land naturally—don't soften them—and let your voice crack just a little on the last word.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at 3 AM. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and she's asking you to tell her one completely honest thing you've never told anyone. Start feeling protective and guarded—you've always kept your deepest self hidden from family. As you begin to speak, let a memory surface that's absolutely true about your own life, something vulnerable you've carried alone. Let that truth crack you open. As you confess this real thing, watch her face soften with recognition, and feel your guardedness dissolve into desperate gratitude that she's here to witness you, really see you, before she goes. End in a place of raw, tender connection you've never allowed yourself before.

title: Dancing at Your Twin's Wedding
instruction: You're giving a toast at your twin's wedding—but you're in love with their spouse, have been for years, and no one knows. Start with a voice full of genuine joy and celebration, making everyone laugh with childhood stories. Your other voice (internal monologue) whispers the painful truth underneath—you're losing them, you'll never be first again, your heart is shattering. As the toast continues, the public voice grows more emotional with happiness while the private voice grows more devastated. You're genuinely thrilled for them AND utterly heartbroken. The two voices should weave together: laughing at a memory while internally whispering 'I love you both and it's killing me,' voice breaking with 'happy' tears that are real grief. End with both voices converging on a single truth: 'I love you more than anything, and I'm letting you go.' Let the audience hear both the most generous love and the most painful sacrifice happening simultaneously.

title: Whispering Through the Hospital Wall
instruction: You're separated from your beloved by a hospital room wall—one of you is immunocompromised, the other potentially contagious. You're whispering through the barrier about wanting to touch, to hold, but knowing you can't. Your voice should be tender and aching as you describe what you'd ask permission to do if you could touch them—'I'd ask if I could brush your hair back... if I could kiss your temple...' Each hypothetical request becomes more intimate, more painful, because you're asking for consent you can't act on. Let your voice catch and break as you realize you might never get to ask these things for real. When they whisper back their own 'yes' to each impossible request, your arousal and longing mix with grief until you're both quietly crying. End with a trembling whisper: 'Can I just... can I keep talking until you fall asleep?' The emotional journey moves from tender longing to heartbreaking realization to finding solace in voice alone.

title: The Unworthy Laugh
instruction: You are an elderly woman kneeling at a small wooden altar in your quiet bedroom, hands clasped. You begin a whispered prayer, but a sudden, tiny memory of a silly mistake from decades ago—your grandson’s funny face—makes a soft, choked laugh escape your lips. The amusement fades as shame crashes in: you are laughing before your God. Your voice becomes a trembling, hushed murmur, stumbling over apologies, your fingers fidgeting with your rosary beads. Let your breath catch, let the words come out in halting, reverent fragments, as if each syllable is a weight. End with a long, silent pause before a final, broken 'Forgive me.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner on their final morning before they leave for a mission they might not return from. Start with forced lightness—trying to make normal conversation about coffee or the weather, pretending this is just another day. Your voice is artificially bright, too controlled. Gradually, the pretense crumbles. Mid-sentence about something mundane, your voice breaks and you can't finish. Shift into raw confession: all the things you never said, the life you imagined together, the terror of losing them. Your words tumble out urgently, then slow into whispered promises pressed against their skin. End with a kind of fierce acceptance—your voice steady but thick with unshed tears, telling them it's okay to go, that you'll be okay, even as every cell in your body wants to beg them to stay.
inspired_by: Making Up After a Terrible Fight

title: Tender Ruins
instruction: You're lying beside someone you've loved for years, both of you knowing this is your last night together before they move across the world for someone else. Speak in whispers and half-sentences, the kind of intimate shorthand only you two share. Start with false lightness—remembering small, perfect moments, laughing softly at inside jokes. But let it dissolve into something more fragile: your voice growing smaller, catching on memories, admitting in barely audible confessions how much this is destroying you. End with your hand reaching for theirs in the dark, voice almost inaudible, saying 'I hope they make you happy' while your breath hitches with unshed tears. This is about the ache of loving someone enough to let them go, spoken so quietly it's almost just for yourself.
inspired_by: The Tech Support Robot with Feelings

title: Upside-Down Confession
instruction: You're a teenage girl doing a handstand against your bedroom wall, trying to hold it while talking to your little sister on the floor. Your voice is thick and wet from the blood rushing to your head—words come out garbled and hard to control. You start by expressing doubt about whether you can keep this position or even talk at all, your frustration and uncertainty clear. But as you speak, let a gentle affection leak through—a soft reassurance to your sister that you love her, even though your voice is a mess. Let the physical strain and emotional shift happen naturally, with pauses, swallows, and tiny laughs as you lose your balance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Tipsy Confession Under the Stars
instruction: You're at a small rooftop party, a few white wines in. You're talking to someone you've been quietly crushing on. Begin with a playful, slightly slurred observation about the stars — let a snort of laughter escape as you point. Then, as you look at their face, your mood shifts: the laughter fades, your volume drops, and you admit, almost stumbling, that the real reason you came up here was just to be near them. End on a breathy, vulnerable note, with your voice catching on the last words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Late for the Appointment
instruction: You are an elderly man driving in heavy traffic, your hands gripping the wheel as you listen to the turn signal click. You're running late for a checkup that could change your life. At first, your voice is tight with concentration and irritation — you mutter at cars, your words clipped. But as you move through an intersection, you take a deep breath and your tone softens. You realize being angry won't help. By the end, your voice is resigned, almost tender, as you accept the delay and decide to be patient. The engine hum and road noise are your backdrop; let them affect your pauses and volume.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Lost Key at the Bottom
instruction: You are a young woman searching for your car key in the murky water of a lake. You've been diving repeatedly, each time missing it. You're starting to feel the cold and your lungs ache. Speak to yourself between dives, gasping for air, your voice breaking as you surface. Start with determined urgency, then as you surface again empty-handed, your voice softens into weary resignation. Let the splashing and your gasps interrupt your words naturally. You're alone, so it's just you muttering.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Daddy's Little Girl
instruction: You are a 9-year-old girl with a sweet, high-pitched voice, standing in your room facing your mother. She just found your little brother's broken toy car in your backpack. You feel a flash of contempt for her suspicion—how dare she think you'd lie? But you start to over-explain, your voice getting higher and faster as you spin a story about finding it on the playground. By the end, a hollow sadness creeps in—you know you're lying, and the false cheerfulness in your voice cracks. Let your pitch rise unnaturally, pause to swallow, then trail off into a quieter, shakier tone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospital bed, and you both know this is goodbye, though neither of you will say it. Start with forced brightness, trying to protect them, your voice almost too cheerful as you ask about the garden, the neighbor's cat, anything mundane. But mid-sentence, something cracks—maybe they say 'I love you' in a way that acknowledges the truth, or you hear them crying quietly. Your voice breaks, drops to a whisper. Now you're telling them everything you never said: how grateful you are, how scared you were as a child when they seemed so strong, how you finally understand the sacrifices they made. End in a place of profound peace mixed with unbearable loss, your voice soft, steady, almost smiling through tears as you say a final 'I love you' that holds your entire lifetime.

title: The Promotion and the Funeral
instruction: You've just received the news you've worked toward for years—a dream realized, a victory achieved—but within the same hour, you learn that someone you love has died. Speak as though you're trying to explain this impossible emotional collision to someone who asks 'how are you?' Start by trying to share your joy, let excitement genuinely bubble up, but feel how it keeps crashing against grief. Laugh, then find yourself choking. Celebrate, then feel guilt for celebrating. Let your voice swing wildly between triumph and devastation, between 'everything I wanted' and 'nothing matters now.' Don't choose one emotion over the other—live in the excruciating space where both are completely true. By the end, arrive at some raw acknowledgment that both are real, that life is unbearably cruel and beautiful at once.

title: The Emergency Line That Keeps Cutting Out
instruction: You are a 9-year-old child, relaying your address to a 911 operator as your parent lies unconscious in the next room. Your voice is perpetually on the verge of cracking—you're impatient with the operator's slow, robotic questions, and you feel a sour, bitter taste in your mouth from sheer panic. You start rapid-fire, staccato, trying to sound tougher than you feel. Midway, the call drops for a second, and in that silence you realize you know the house number by heart—a brief, sour triumph that almost makes you laugh. Finish with your voice cracking and the line fizzing out as you shout the last digits, the initial irritability now raw desperation.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Triumph (slightly present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Arguing When You're Both Partially Right
instruction: You're escalating because neither can admit nuance. Your voice gets louder, righteous: 'You always do this!' But then they say something that lands and you pause. Your voice drops: 'But I do that too.' Your breathing becomes less heated. Say 'Maybe we're both right and both wrong here.'

title: Dancing at Your Own Goodbye Party
instruction: You're leaving—emigrating, entering witness protection, going somewhere you can never return from—and your loved ones threw you a farewell party. You're giving a toast. Start with genuine joy and gratitude, laughing at shared memories, voices full of warmth and celebration. But you can't quite maintain it—even as you're laughing, there's a catch in your throat. The complexity should be constant: thanking them while your heart is shattering, joking about the adventure ahead while terrified of losing them, celebrating your courage while wanting to collapse and beg to stay. Let laughter and tears exist simultaneously. Your voice should break mid-laugh, should find joy again mid-sob. The emotional texture should be impossible to categorize—are you happy or devastated? Both. Completely both. End with a moment of profound peace breaking through the chaos of feeling: a clear, steady statement of love that contains all the contradiction—grateful and grieving, excited and terrified, saying hello to a new life while your voice breaks saying goodbye to this one.
inspired_by: Inside a Space Helmet: Last Transmission

title: New Lease on Destruction
instruction: You're standing alone on a rain-slicked balcony, the city lights below. You've just gotten the news that could turn everything around—a chance to start fresh. But as you light a cigarette and take a slow drag, the optimism curdles into something darker. Speak quietly to yourself, letting the hope in your voice gradually give way to a cold, satisfied malice. Your breath and the crackle of the cigarette should interrupt your words naturally.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confrontation in the Childhood Bedroom
instruction: You've returned to your dying mother's house and found yourself in your childhood bedroom. Start with bitter, cutting observations about the room she preserved like a shrine while failing to see the real you. Your voice cracks between rage and the child you once were: 'You kept my spelling bee trophy but you never once asked why I stopped eating.' Let the anger collapse into raw, ugly grief—not pretty crying but the kind that makes you gasp for air. Build to a moment where you pick up a childhood object and suddenly you're both furious at her and desperate for her to stay. End whispering what you needed to hear as a child, finally saying it to yourself. The emotional arc: controlled fury → volcanic grief → heartbreaking self-compassion.

title: Holding the Line
instruction: You're a 17-year-old recruit standing at rigid attention during a seemingly endless uniform inspection. Your neck muscles ache, your jaw is tight, and you're fighting the urge to shift your weight or roll your shoulders. The drill instructor is slowly working his way down the line, and your impatience simmers just beneath the surface — you want this to be over, you're irritated by the heat, the silence, the pointless waiting. As you stand there, you notice a small thread loose on your sleeve, and you realize if the DI sees it, you'll be screamed at. Your voice starts flat and clipped, barking out your name and rank with controlled frustration, but as you internally panic about that thread, your tone softens into something almost like fear — a crack of vulnerability you didn't plan to show. You whisper to yourself, trying to talk your way out of the situation, voice shifting from hard to hesitant.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Sunset on the Bench
instruction: You're sitting on a park bench alone, elbows resting on your knees, staring at the ground. You've been feeling heavy all day, but now you notice the golden light of the setting sun spreading across the pavement at your feet. You lift your head slightly, awed by the beauty, and a flicker of hope rises—maybe tomorrow will be different. Your voice is compressed, breath shallow, words directed downward at first, then lifting as the emotion shifts. Let the small distractions around you—a distant laugh, a breeze—interrupt your thoughts naturally. Begin quietly, almost to yourself: 'I didn't see it coming... the way it catches the dust in the air...' End with a whisper of optimism: 'Maybe I'll look up more often.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point: When Protection Meets Powerlessness
instruction: You've just learned someone you're fiercely protective of — a child, a younger sibling, someone vulnerable — has been hurt, and you couldn't stop it. Begin with explosive rage: shouting at yourself, at the universe, at whoever's in the room. 'I should have KNOWN!' — your voice raw, almost violent with self-blame. Pound something, let the fury be physical in your voice. But rage cracks open into helpless sobbing. Your voice dissolves from roaring to broken. 'I'm supposed to keep them safe' becomes a child's plea. You're both the fierce protector and the helpless human. Fight to regain control, voice shaking with adrenaline. Make promises you're not sure you can keep, your words fierce again but now underlaid with the tremor of knowing you're not omnipotent. End on a whispered vow that's both determination and prayer.

title: Gratitude at the Edge: Recovering Addict Thanks the Dealer Who Kept Them Alive
instruction: You're two years clean, and you've tracked down your old dealer to say something impossible: thank you. Start with nervous laughter, the absurdity of it. Your voice is warm, almost playful, explaining that their willingness to front you drugs when you had nothing, to sometimes cut your doses when they thought you'd taken too much, to call the ambulance that one time—it kept you alive long enough to get to recovery. But as you speak, gratitude tangles with grief. Your voice breaks with tears even as you're smiling, because you're also saying goodbye to the only person who never judged you at your worst. They enabled your destruction, but they also witnessed your humanity when no one else could bear to look. The joy of your survival crashes against the sadness of how much you both lost in those years. End with your voice full of contradictions—celebrating your freedom while mourning the strange, damaged love that existed in that dark place. Let laughter and tears blend until they're indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Professional: Doctor Prescribes Addiction to Save Addict's Life

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling a parent the truth they've avoided for decades—how their absence, their addiction, their choices, fundamentally altered who you became. Start with rehearsed calm, the words you've practiced in mirrors. But as you speak, old anger surfaces, then underneath it, the child's confusion and hurt. Your voice should move from controlled accusation to trembling vulnerability to sudden, unexpected compassion. The transformation isn't theirs—it's yours. You realize mid-confrontation that you've already changed, already survived, already become someone they can't touch anymore. End with a complicated forgiveness that's more about releasing yourself than absolving them. Your final words should carry both grief for what never was and strength in who you've become despite it all.

title: Inventory of Skin and Breath
instruction: You're lying next to someone in the dark after making love for what might be the last time—you're leaving tomorrow, or they are, or this was the goodbye you both knew was coming. Begin by noticing everything in the darkness: the texture of the sheets, the sound of their breathing, the warmth of their skin, the weight of their arm across you, the smell of their hair, the distant sound of traffic, the shadows on the ceiling.
