Whisper each observation aloud as a confession: 'Your breathing is slowing down,' 'I can feel your heartbeat against my ribs,' 'The pillow smells like you—I'm going to miss that,' 'My chest feels heavy, like I'm already grieving.' Start peaceful, almost drowsy, savoring this final moment. Let each sensory detail you catalogue pull you deeper into the devastating reality that you're memorizing this because you'll never have it again. End with quiet, aching devastation—not theatrical crying, but the kind of grief that sits in your throat like a stone.

title: The Last Story You'll Ever Tell Me
instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's bedside in her final hours. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. To keep her spirit present, you begin inventing elaborate, beautiful stories about the strangers passing by the hospice window—a woman with a red umbrella becomes a time traveler, a man walking a dog becomes a retired circus performer. Start with forced cheerfulness, telling these stories to distract from your terror. As you continue, let your voice soften and crack. By the end, you're no longer making up stories about strangers—you're telling her the true story of what she meant to you, through tears, whispering the things you never said. The playful invention must transform into raw, devastating honesty.
inspired_by: Making Up Stories About People and Things

title: The Unlikely Proposal
instruction: You are in a tense boardroom negotiation with a rival company, your voice low and guarded, your body rigid. The opposing lead negotiator, a quiet unassuming figure, begins to speak — and their proposal is so startlingly brilliant and unexpected that you are overcome with awe. Your lips twitch as a surge of amusement rises at your own surprise, and you catch yourself shifting in your chair, glancing down at your notes without seeing them. Let your voice start clipped and measured, then soften as wonder creeps in, ending with a light chuckle and an open, interested tone.
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Amusement (very intensely present), Interest (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Reading Your Estranged Father's Love Letters at His Funeral
instruction: You've just discovered letters your father wrote to you over twenty years—letters he never sent, expressing everything he could never say aloud. You're standing at his funeral, reading them publicly for the first time. Begin with bitter humor, almost mocking—look at these beautiful words from a man who gave you nothing but silence. But as you read, his voice reaches you across death in a way it never could in life. You start laughing through descriptions of his failures, his fear, his desperate hidden love—laughing because it's absurd, because you needed these words decades ago. But the laughter keeps breaking into tears and back again. You're furious and grateful simultaneously, grieving what you had and what you lost and what you never got to have. Your voice moves between sardonic performance and raw vulnerability. By the end, you're reading his final 'I love you' through tears, laughing softly at the tragedy of it all, finding unexpected peace in the wreckage. Begin with defensive, bitter humor. End with laughter and tears so intertwined you cannot separate them, holding both anger and forgiveness in the same breath.
inspired_by: Professional: Pastor Loses Faith During His Own Sermon

title: The Sour Smile
instruction: You’re a woman in her fifties, brought in for questioning after a minor traffic incident escalates. The detective across the table is silent, letting the weight of the room work against you. You start with a sour, defensive edge—your voice tight, clipped, like you’ve bitten into something rotten. But as you talk, you realize you have a tiny piece of leverage: a smirk from them you caught. Lean into teasing, your pitch rising playfully, almost flirting with the danger. A flicker of pride slips through—you’ve got a card to play. Let your voice crack, drop, or trail off when you lose your train of thought, then pick it back up with a shrug in your tone.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Teasing (very intensely present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Cold That Proves I'm Right
instruction: You're a rugged, middle-aged man standing in a frozen wasteland, shivering violently—your jaw locked, teeth chattering. You've been waiting hours for a rival who swore they'd meet you here, and you're fuming with impatience and contempt. Through clenched teeth, you mutter about their weakness, voice tight and acidic. But as the deadline passes and they don't show, the contempt curdles into a grim, shivering triumph—you were tougher all along. Let the involuntary tremors and chattering affect every word; don't fight the cold, let it shape your delivery. Speak as if alone, savoring the victory that aches in your bones.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Call
instruction: You are a mother who has been searching for your missing daughter for three days with almost no sleep. Now, physically drained and barely able to stand, you make one final call to the police station. Your voice is raspy, each word an effort, with long pauses to breathe. Start with a thin veneer of anger—bitterness at their lack of help—but as you speak, the exhaustion takes over and you crumble into quiet helplessness. Let your voice crack, trail off, and recover. You're not performing; you're just barely holding on.
emotions_sampled: Anger (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Helplessness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Hammer and a Prayer
instruction: You're alone in your kitchen, trying to hammer a nail into the wall for a heavy picture frame. You're older, not handy at all, and deeply embarrassed that something so simple feels impossible. Each clumsy swing makes a loud crack and you wince, muttering apologies to yourself and the neighbors. Your voice is high, strained, and full of frustration. After several misses, the nail finally goes in straight—you freeze, then let out a breathy, shaky laugh of pure relief, the tension melting out of your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Veiled Judgment
instruction: You are a stern, older figure addressing a younger person who has wronged you deeply. You stand in a dim, quiet room, the fabric lightly brushing your lips. Begin with a cold, measured tone — your words are calm but the malice is already coiling inside. As you speak, let your voice subtly harden, the kindness draining until only a chill, deliberate venom remains. Let a slight exhale or a pause catch the fabric, once, as you savor the final threat.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Fog on the Water
instruction: You are an elderly woman rowing a small boat alone on a lake, the fog so thick you can barely see the oars. Your arms burn with each pull, and you speak only in the gasps between strokes—a grunt on the effort, then a rushed, breathy phrase as you slide forward. At first, your voice is tight with confusion: you’ve lost your bearings, and the shoreline has vanished. As you keep rowing, a quiet fear seeps in—you wonder if you’re going in circles, if anyone knows you’re out here. Let your words come out broken, with the strain of your body: pitch wobbles as you rock, jaw tight from gripping the handles. End with a shift: the confusion remains, but a fragile resolve emerges—you have to keep pulling, even as your fear deepens.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Recovery: Choosing Yourself Over the Addiction
instruction: Day 3 sober. Day 30. Day 100. You're in a meeting and you're sharing. Your voice is tired but determined. 'I'm choosing myself.' Your voice carries hard-won clarity. It wasn't a dramatic moment—it was boring, painful, unglamorous sobriety. Your voice is hoarse from the effort but stronger. 'I'm not going back.' Your voice means it. Include the moment you realize you might actually make it.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've been holding it together through an impossible crisis—caring for a dying loved one, working multiple jobs, keeping everyone else afloat—and someone just asked you, with genuine concern, 'Are you okay?' Start with your practiced, bright response, the script you've perfected: 'I'm fine, really!' But as you continue, something in you snaps violently. Your voice explodes into fierce, uncontrolled rage at the unfairness of it all, screaming at the universe, at God, at whoever's listening. Then, without warning, collapse into helpless, gasping sobs—the rage dissolving into complete devastation. Let your voice break from fury into the most vulnerable, childlike weeping, the sound of someone whose strength has finally, utterly shattered.

title: The Queen's Confession
instruction: You are an elderly man, once a proud king but now frail and blind, kneeling at the bedside of your late wife's young lady-in-waiting who has been your submissive companion for years. You ask her to untie your collar for the last time, but your voice catches—you're shocked when she instead slips a ring onto your finger. Begin with a gruff, commanding tone, the dominant king you once were, but as your old hands tremble over her gift, Astonishment breaks through; your voice softens, cracks, and becomes breathy and unsure, not seeking approval but finding it. End with a quiet, surrendered whisper, not a command, but a confession of love.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Screaming Truth at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father about a lie they've maintained your entire life—something that shaped your identity, your choices, your pain. Begin with explosive, physical rage: let your whole body participate in this fury, your voice loud and unrestrained, pacing, gesturing wildly, releasing years of compressed emotion. As they finally admit the truth, feel your anger transform into something more complex—hurt, betrayal, but also a strange, unwanted understanding. By the end, you're exhausted, sitting across from them, speaking almost gently as you ask the question you've always been afraid to ask: 'Did you ever actually love me?' Let the fire burn down to embers, but don't let those embers go cold.

title: The Crashing Party
instruction: You're at a festive gathering, holding a full glass of champagne and laughing at a joke. Suddenly, someone barrels into you from behind, slamming into your ribs. The impact knocks the wind out of you—a sharp 'oof' escapes as your diaphragm spasms. You drop the glass, shattering it. Astonishment floods through you first, a wide-eyed disbelief. Then, as you try to recover, you force a breathless, shaky laugh, saying something to the apologetic stranger, your voice wobbly and strained as you wave it off, but your hands tremble slightly and you're still struggling to catch a full breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fantasy Escaping
instruction: Everything is terrible so you're building an elaborate escape fantasy. Your voice becomes dreamy, lighter: 'If I were somewhere else, someone else...' Words are carefully chosen, almost poetic. Breathing is shallow, distant. Your tone is wistful, not quite present. Physical: you're somewhere else entirely. 'In that place, everything would be different. I would be happy.' The fantasy is more real than reality in your voice. By the end, you're fully gone, lost in a beautiful construction that can't save you.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth about how their emotional absence shaped you. Start quiet, almost apologetic: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' Your voice is shaking because you've rehearsed this a thousand times but never had the courage. As you speak, anger starts bleeding through—not loud, but fierce. 'I needed you and you were never there.' You're listing specific moments, your voice getting stronger, more certain. Then something shifts: you hear how small they sound trying to defend themselves, and suddenly you see them as broken too. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it mingles with devastating compassion. By the end, you're crying but your voice is steady: 'I forgive you, but I can't pretend it didn't hurt.' The goal is to move from fearful to furious to heartbroken to something like acceptance, all in one authentic journey.

title: The Last Cup's Revenge
instruction: You are an elderly person, fiercely proud of your independence, alone in your quiet apartment after a late afternoon coffee with friends. The caffeine has just crashed, leaving you heavy-limbed, slightly dizzy, and resentful of your own body. You are holding a half-empty cup, staring at the dregs. Start with a prideful, crisp murmur about the good old days, but as you speak, the crash deepens—your words slow, slurring with that intoxicated haze, your voice turns flat and irritable. A micro-distraction: you have to stop mid-sentence to rub your aching temple. End with a wounded, quiet admission, your pride deflated but still clinging to the bitterness. Speak roughly 40-80 words.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Concentration (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent everything you've held back for decades—how their absence shaped you, how you learned to stop expecting them, how you became who you are despite them. Begin with carefully controlled anger, words you've rehearsed a thousand times in your head. But as you speak, let other feelings flood in: the child inside you who still wanted their approval, moments of understanding their own brokenness, flashes of memories both tender and devastating. Your voice should shift between accusation and pleading, between strength and the vulnerable confusion of someone who needed them and never got what they needed. End somewhere unexpected—not with closure, but with the raw admission of how much it still hurts.
inspired_by: Acting Enthusiastic About Plans Youd Rather Avoid

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're trying to talk someone down from a dangerous decision—a ledge, an addiction, a destructive choice. Start with fierce determination, voice strong and commanding: 'Look at me. You're not doing this.' Urgency and authority. But as they resist, your control begins to fracture. Desperation enters—you're begging now, voice rising, words tumbling over each other. 'Please, please, I can't lose you, don't you understand?' Anger flashes through: 'Why won't you just LISTEN to me?!' Then it all collapses. Your voice breaks completely. You realize you're powerless. The end is quiet devastation mixed with helpless love—still reaching for them even as you understand you can't force them to stay. Let rage dissolve into sobbing, then into whispered, broken pleas. Show the moment someone fierce becomes utterly helpless.

title: Surgeon Delivering Terminal News to Their Own Child
instruction: You're a cardiac surgeon who just finished operating on your teenage daughter. The surgery failed. You must walk into the waiting room and tell your ex-spouse—someone you once loved desperately—that your child has maybe an hour left. Start with clinical composure, the doctor-voice you've used a thousand times. But halfway through explaining the technical details, your voice cracks. The professional mask shatters. You're not a surgeon anymore—you're just a parent who couldn't save their baby. End on your knees, begging forgiveness for something that isn't your fault, your medical terminology dissolving into raw, broken apologies. Let the transformation from controlled expert to devastated parent happen slowly, then all at once.
inspired_by: Hostage Negotiator Having a Panic Attack

title: Sheltering in the Sand
instruction: You are a young woman caught in a sudden sandstorm while hiking a desert trail. You've found a shallow rock alcove and press yourself against it, pulling your shirt over your mouth. At first, you try to call out to your friend who was ahead of you — the wind snatches your words, and you cough, tasting grit. You realize they can't hear you, and you are alone for now. As the storm rages, you remember the view you saw just before it hit — the endless, golden dunes under a blazing sky. A strange contentment settles over you, a quiet joy in being so small under so much sky. Your voice, muffled by cloth and broken by coughs, softens from frantic shouting to a reverent, hushed whisper as you speak aloud to calm yourself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Granite Mile
instruction: You are an older woman riding in the passenger seat of a car, driving through the night on a remote mountain road. The steady engine drone and the hum of the pavement press against your ears. You have just finished a long, difficult conversation with the driver—your adult child—about selling the family home where they grew up. Now, in the silence, you're watching the headlights carve through the dark, and something you didn't realize you were feeling rises up: a sudden, surprising wave of astonishment—not at them, but at yourself, at how much lighter you feel, how the weight of the house has slipped away. Your voice is a little rough from talking, a little tired, and the vibrations of the car steal some of your breath. Let the astonishment bloom just for a moment at the end, a soft, breathless surprise that changes the colors of everything you say, drifting from quiet resignation to a fragile, unexpected wonder.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Unsteady Throne
instruction: You kneel before your partner, their presence towering above you—a power imbalance that feels sacred. As you speak, your voice begins in that familiar submissive register: high, breathy, seeking their gaze, but uncertainty flickers in your throat. You pause to swallow, your hands gripping your own knees as you reveal a gratitude that trembles at the edges with doubt—'I don't know if I deserve this.' Let awe flood your bones halfway through, slowing your words into a whisper that cracks with reverence, until your voice shifts slightly toward steadiness, as if claiming one small piece of this exchange for yourself. End with a raw exhale, eyes wet but searching for their approval.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Doubt (very intensely present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent what their silence cost you as a child. Start with a voice that's been rehearsed, controlled: 'I need to say something I should have said years ago.' As you describe what happened, anger builds—'You knew. You had to have known'—voice rising, accusatory. But then you see their face, and suddenly the anger collapses into something more devastating: a child's grief. Your voice breaks: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' Now you're pleading, vulnerable, the adult facade stripped away. End with quiet, aching acceptance: 'I needed you to save me... and you didn't.' The journey is from controlled anger to raw, childlike devastation to exhausted surrender.
inspired_by: Someone Saying They Don't Trust You Anymore

title: Final Words to Someone Who Never Knew You
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved from afar for years—a mentor, a parent who was absent, a friend who never truly saw you—and they're dying. They have minutes left. You start with careful gratitude, your voice steady as you thank them for small kindnesses they probably don't remember. But something cracks open in you. Your voice becomes raw, almost angry as you confess: 'I needed you to see me.' The anger dissolves into grief-stricken tenderness. You're crying now, but your voice softens to something achingly gentle as you tell them it's okay, that you forgive them, that you're letting them go. Your final words are a whisper of peace you didn't know you could offer, even as your heart is breaking.

title: Confession While High: Watching Your Mouth Betray You
instruction: You're stoned and your best friend just asked if you slept with their ex. You're trying to lie but marijuana has destroyed your ability to lie effectively. Your voice sounds distant from your own head. Time moves wrong—you're taking pauses that are too long. You hear yourself saying things and can't stop it. 'No, I didn't... well... okay, but like, it was only once...' Each phrase feels like someone else talking. Include the paranoid moment where you realize they know everything from your voice.

title: Numb Words for a Lost Heart
instruction: You're sitting in your car right after a dental appointment, your mouth still half-numb, a trickle of drool escaping the corner of your lips. You just saw a photo of your ex with someone else at the place you two always planned to go. Start by mumbling bitterly, trying to keep your jealousy sharp, but as you feel the drool and the clumsy words, the envy cracks into raw sadness. Let the physical struggle with 'b' and 'p' sounds mirror your emotional stumbles, ending with a quiet, resigned sigh.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Stoned Philosophical Rambling
instruction: You're very high and just realized something profound about spoons. Speak slowly, with long pauses where you forget what you were saying. Dry mouth creates sticky lip sounds. Every observation sounds mind-blowing to you ('Dude... a spoon is just a tiny bowl... on a stick'). Giggle at nothing. Lose your train of thought, find it again, lose it permanently. The voice should be lower than baseline, mellow, and genuinely fascinated by nothing.

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM, and you're lying next to someone you've shared a bed with for years - a partner, a spouse, a person who knows your body but not this secret. In whispered darkness, you must confess something that will change everything: a truth about who you really are, what you've hidden, or what you truly need that you've been terrified to voice. Begin with your heart pounding so hard you can barely breathe, your whisper almost inaudible, testing each word before releasing it into the darkness. Let the vulnerability build as you continue - your voice trembling, pausing to listen to their breathing, terrified they'll speak or move. As you finally speak the core truth, let something release in you - a sob, a laugh, a sound you've never made before. End in raw exposure, having said it all, waiting in excruciating silence for their response, your whole body a live wire of hope and terror.
inspired_by: Actor needs to prepare instrumentally before a rehearsal

title: Three AM Inventory
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, unable to sleep. In the darkness, begin whispering a catalog of your secret fears and failures—the ways you're failing at your job, the debt you're hiding, the inadequacy you feel, the small ways you disappoint yourself daily. Keep your voice intimate, almost prayer-like, as if you're confessing to the darkness itself. The person beside you is asleep, or so you think. Let the litany become almost rhythmic, hypnotic, a way of bearing witness to your own struggle. Then, feel their hand find yours in the darkness—they've been awake, listening. The whispered confession transforms. Without changing volume, shift from solitary despair to the realization that you're not alone in your imperfection. End not with solutions, but with the quiet radical act of being fully known and still held.

title: The Prize on the Corner
instruction: You're an older man walking down a noisy city street at dusk. You spot a woman across the street who makes you stop — there's a flutter of infatuation, a familiar ache in your chest, and you mumble something half to yourself, almost wistful. Then your phone buzzes. You read a message that you've just won a long-shot competition you'd forgotten about. As the reality sinks in, your voice hardens with pride, rising against the traffic and sirens. Let the street noise push you to shout your triumph, and let your infatuated beginning be soft, almost lost, before you transform into sheer, fierce elation.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Pregnancy Test
instruction: You're alone in a bathroom, staring at a positive pregnancy test. You've been trying for three years, endured two miscarriages, and last month decided with your partner to stop trying—to accept childlessness and grieve what won't be. This pregnancy is a complete surprise. Begin with the shock, your breath caught, your hand trembling as you hold the test. Let the joy start to rise—this is what you wanted, this is the miracle—but let it immediately collide with terror: your body has betrayed you before, you'd finally made peace with a different future, and now that peace is shattered. Speak aloud to the cluster of cells inside you, your voice moving between wonder and fear, between greeting and already grieving. Let gratitude and resentment live together in your throat. Let hope and dread make your hands shake. End with your voice landing somewhere you couldn't have predicted, carrying all the contradictions of this moment without resolving them.

title: Organized Gratitude
instruction: You are an elderly person, and your body is wired from a stimulant. Your jaw is tight, your mouth dry, and your thoughts race faster than your words can form. You are deeply concentrated on arranging a box of old photographs, and you feel an overwhelming thankfulness toward a friend who just helped you sort them. Begin with that intense, pressured gratitude—your speech is rapid, consonants slightly distorted from clenching. As you near the end, your focus softens into a quiet contentment, a slower, more peaceful acknowledgment of how good this moment feels. Let your voice reflect the physical tension at first, then release into that gentle satisfaction.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Contentment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Emergency Room Eruption
instruction: You're an ER doctor at hour 36 of your shift when someone questions your competence after you stumbled from exhaustion. Start defensive, voice sharp and controlled despite your weariness. Then let it explode—the fury of months or years of impossible hours, of watching people die because there aren't enough hands, of being told you're a hero while being worked to collapse. Your voice should surge with righteous rage, words tumbling faster, louder. Then abruptly break—mid-sentence, let it all crumble into shaking tears because you're so tired, you just want to sleep, and you're terrified you'll make a mistake that kills someone. End with your voice small and defeated, the exhaustion finally winning, admitting you can't do this anymore but you have twelve more hours on your shift.
inspired_by: Hiding Exhaustion While Continuing to Work

title: The Returning Soldier
instruction: You've just come home after years away—war, prison, exile, disappearance—and you're seeing your child or partner for the first time. Begin with overwhelming joy: you're laughing, making sounds of pure elation, your body wants to jump and shout. But underneath, there's something darker—guilt for what you've done or seen, grief for the time lost, terror that you're not the same person who left. Let these sounds start to mix and blend: laughter that cracks into something like sobbing, joyful exclamations that become moans of pain. Your voice should carry both emotions simultaneously, creating sounds that are impossible to categorize as simply happy or sad. By the end, you're making deep, complex sounds from your core that express the beautiful, terrible, impossible contradiction of being both home and forever changed. Transform from pure joy to a rich, complicated blend of gratitude, grief, love, and anguish all at once.

title: The Spotlight Sways
instruction: You're a child standing on stage during a school talent show, reciting a poem you've practiced a hundred times. Halfway through, the heat and nerves hit you — your knees buckle, the room tilts, and a hot wave of embarrassment washes over you as you try to keep it together. Start with a forced, bright delivery, but let your voice fade into breathy whispers as you struggle to stay upright. Feel the shame of failing in front of everyone, then let it dissolve into a quiet surrender as the world goes fuzzy.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are a parent in the final hours of life, speaking to your adult child who sits vigil beside your hospital bed. Begin with fragments of memories you need them to know—small moments that mattered, things unsaid for decades. Your voice is weak but urgent. Mid-way through, you must give them permission to let you go, to stop fighting for you to stay. Feel the shift from needing to tell them everything to needing to release them from the weight of keeping you here. Your voice moves from desperate clarity to peaceful exhaustion. End with a whispered blessing for their life without you—gratitude mixed with the ache of leaving them. Let silences speak. Let your breath catch on love too big for words.

title: The Last Thread
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman sitting alone on the floor of a dimly lit room, having just sobbed for a long time. Your throat is raw, your nose is completely blocked, and your eyes are swollen. You feel hollow and emptied out, your voice barely a rasp. In the silence, you notice a single thread caught on your sleeve—you were so absorbed in grief you didn't see it before. It triggers a sudden, intense astonishment: it's the exact color of a cherished jacket you lost years ago. Your mind snaps into hyper-focus as you study it, your voice shifting from exhausted monotone to a sharp, breathy surprise. Let the congestion affect your words; speak as if you are amazed and bewildered, feeling the thread's significance despite your drained state.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Body Your Mother Criticized
instruction: You're stretching, but addressing your mother (present or in memory) about the body she taught you to hate. Begin with hesitant self-consciousness, almost apologizing for taking up space as you stretch. But as you move through the motion, let anger build—raw, specific anger about every comment, every look of disappointment, every time she made you feel wrong in your own skin. Your voice should crack between rage and the desperate need for her approval you still can't shake. Describe the stretch with defiance, claiming your body as yours, but let grief break through—mourning the unconditional acceptance you deserved but never received. End exhausted, sad, but perhaps a shade more free.
inspired_by: Stretching Your Arms Over Your Head After Waking Up

title: Reading Dreams at My Own Wake
instruction: You are interpreting your own dreams aloud at what you know is your final gathering - a terminal diagnosis means this is goodbye, though no one has said it yet. Start by making everyone laugh with absurdly literal interpretations of your most ridiculous dreams, your voice warm and animated. But as you reach your most recent dream - about flying away while everyone you love waves from the ground - your laughter should catch. Continue with the literal interpretation, but now you're smiling through tears, your voice simultaneously joyful and breaking. End by thanking them for being in your dreams, your voice soft and full of wonder at how lucky you've been, finding peace and gratitude even as you're saying goodbye. The emotional arc moves from playful humor to bittersweet joy to profound, tearful gratitude.

title: Standing Ovation
instruction: You've just finished your one-woman show that took five years to create, and the audience stands. Your voice is completely undone: 'I don't... I don't have words.' You're crying, laughing, overwhelmed. 'Thank you. Thank you so much.' The applause is deafening. Your voice tries again: 'I created this because I thought I was alone. And standing here, seeing all of you...' your voice breaks '...I'm not alone.' You try to compose yourself: 'Thank you for witnessing my story. Thank you for letting me witness yours.' By the time the ovation ends, your voice is hoarse, destroyed, glorious: 'This is the best moment of my life.' You exit the stage, and offstage, your voice cracks into sobs — the vulnerability finally released.

title: The Tension in the Yarn
instruction: You are an older man sitting in your favorite armchair, knitting a scarf for your granddaughter. The repetitive click of the needles and the soft wool in your hands usually bring you a deep, calm contentment—but today, something is off. A pattern you’ve done a hundred times now looks different; you can’t tell if you’ve made a mistake or if the pattern changed. Start by quietly murmuring to yourself about the rhythm and feel of the work, savoring the familiar comfort. Then, let a note of confusion creep in as you pause, hold up the piece, and talk through your uncertainty—maybe dropping a stitch, re-counting, or asking aloud why it looks wrong. End with a small, rueful chuckle as you decide it’s fine or you’ll just fix it later, the contentment returning but now mixed with a gentle, puzzled fondness.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Burning House
instruction: You've just discovered evidence of your lover's betrayal—texts, photos, undeniable proof. The rage hits you physically, like fire in your chest and limbs. Start with the shock freezing you, then let your body explode into the fury. Pace, spin, your arms wanting to break things, your voice raw and untamed. Let physical sensation drive your emotional expression—the heat in your face, the trembling in your hands, the knot in your stomach. But underneath the rage is devastating heartbreak. As you physically exhaust yourself, let the anger crack open to reveal the shattered love beneath. Your body moves from violent energy to collapse, from shouting to sobbing, from fury to the unbearable tenderness of loss. The rage and grief must war in your body simultaneously by the end.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction Over You
instruction: You're thirty-five years old, standing in your childhood kitchen, facing your parent who's been clean for six months and wants 'to make amends.' Start with controlled, measured anger—you've imagined this conversation for decades. Your voice is sharp, listing specific memories: the birthday they missed, the night you called from the hospital, the times you lied to teachers about bruises. But as they begin to cry and apologize, something shifts. Your anger cracks open into the bewildered grief of the child you once were, voice breaking as you ask questions you've needed answered since you were eight years old. Move through rage, through tears, through exhaustion, arriving finally at something complicated—not quite forgiveness, but perhaps the beginning of letting go. Your final words should mix residual hurt with reluctant compassion, acknowledging both the damage done and the fragile human trying to repair it.
inspired_by: Professional: Doctor Discovers Their Medical Error Killed Someone

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to someone you love, and they're awake too. Begin by whispering something small and safe—'Are you still awake?' or 'I can't sleep.' Then, in the darkness, let yourself confess things you've never said out loud: your deepest insecurities, the ways you sabotage your own happiness, your fear that you're not worthy of being loved. Speak quietly, almost to yourself, as if the darkness makes it safer. Let long silences exist between confessions. Move from surface-level sharing to the things that terrify you most about yourself. By the end, you've revealed the parts of yourself you usually hide even from yourself. Stay gentle, stay whispered, but let the emotional weight grow heavier with each revelation.

title: The Perfect Score
instruction: You are a 17-year-old with a deep, deliberately cool voice, sitting in a video game tournament. You have just won the final round against your arrogant rival. You are ecstatic, but your rival is a sore loser. You decide to hide your elation behind a mask of sweet, polite congratulations. Start by taking a long, indulgent sip of your energy drink, relishing the victory. Then, speak to your rival in a voice that is syrupy sweet, but your words are laced with tiny, cutting pauses and heavy sighs. Let your pleasure seep through the polite tone—a slight shake in your voice, a barely concealed grin. By the end, as you suggest a rematch, your voice should crack with the pure elation you're trying to contain, a giddy, breathless laugh escaping.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Breath at the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying father's hospital bed in the early morning light. Begin in a state of rigid control—you've been holding yourself together for days, barely sleeping, maintaining composure for the family. Your body wants to collapse but you keep yourself upright through sheer will. As you take his hand and he whispers his final words to you (speak them aloud as him, then respond as yourself), allow whatever has been locked in your chest to finally break open. Let your body find its own way to express this—not by posturing or arranging yourself dramatically, but by allowing genuine physical release. By the end, you should be in a completely different physical and emotional state than where you began, transformed by grief but also by a strange, unexpected lightness.
inspired_by: When you find yourself using physical props or physical positioning (leaning, resting, propping) to seem relaxed in a scene

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, both of you unable to sleep. The room is dark except for the blue glow of the clock. You've been carrying a secret for months—not an affair, but something about yourself you've been terrified to share: a fear, a shame, a part of your past, a truth about who you are. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, the words coming out haltingly in the darkness. Start with your heart pounding, your breath shallow, testing the waters with small admissions. As you speak, you're listening to their breathing, terrified they'll pull away. But they don't. Their hand finds yours under the covers. Let your voice slowly steady as you feel their acceptance, the secret losing its power as you finally speak it aloud. End with your body relaxing into the mattress, your words coming easier, quieter, finally at peace.

title: The Bitter Hum
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman performing oral sex on a partner you’ve grown to resent. Your mouth is full, so all you can produce are muffled hums and nasal moans. Start with a slight embarrassment—a tight, reluctant hum as you begin, aware of the awkwardness. But as you continue, let the bitterness surface: your hums become shorter, more resentful, with sharper intakes of breath. Imagine you’re replaying an argument in your head while your mouth is busy. End with a long, low, bitter hum full of suppressed frustration. Let the sounds be organic—swallow, adjust, breathe through your nose—never forget your mouth is occupied.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Laugh That Broke the Surface
instruction: You're a young man in therapy, your voice deliberately low and steady — the kind of deep tone you use to seem in control. Your therapist asks what you thought about last session's homework, and you start rambling about how you 'just laughed it off' when your dad mocked your new hobby. But as you describe the memory, your voice hitches: a joke you tell about your own vulnerability slips out, and you actually chuckle — a genuine, surprised laugh that cracks your composure. Let that laughter fade into a long pause, your eyes fixed on a speck on the carpet, then whisper: 'I don't think I've ever told anyone that part. It hurt more than I let myself believe.' The amusement at the start masks the ache; by the end, your voice is raw and trembling, holding back tears.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Gratitude Soaked in Grief
instruction: You're thanking someone for saving your life, caring for you, or loving you through an impossible time. Begin with pure gratitude — let your voice overflow with it, warm and full. But allow the darker truth to seep in: this gratitude is inseparable from rage that you needed saving at all, grief at what was lost that can never be recovered, resentment at the debt you can never repay. Don't abandon the thankfulness — let both emotions exist simultaneously. Your voice should crack between tenderness and bitterness, love and anger braided together. End in a place where you're still saying 'thank you,' but it's heavy with everything you can't say, a gratitude that tastes like salt and sweetness mixed on your tongue.

title: Screaming Into the Storm That Took Them
instruction: You're standing at the edge of the ocean where someone you loved was lost, and you're furiously, irrationally screaming at the water to give them back. Start with fierce, commanding demands: 'BRING THEM BACK! DO YOU HEAR ME?!' Your voice should be raw, powerful, almost violent. Repeat commands, pleas, accusations at the sea with increasing desperation. Cycle through rage at God, nature, fate, yourself. Your voice should crack from shouting, then suddenly drop to broken whispers of 'please... please...' before building back to primal screaming. Somewhere in the middle, start laughing—a horrible, unhinged sound—at the absurdity of yelling at water. Let the laughter turn back into sobs, then rage again. End in complete collapse: your voice should be destroyed, reduced to whispered, tender words as if they're right there with you, telling them about your day, asking them what to do now, your protective fury transformed into helpless, infinite gentleness.
inspired_by: Teaching a Parrot to Say 'I Love You'

title: Reading Your Child's Goodbye Letter
instruction: Your child has left home forever—maybe to cut ties, maybe because you pushed them away—and left a letter. As you read it aloud, you expect to feel one thing, but your body keeps offering you different, contradictory truths. Maybe you start angry (they're ungrateful), but your voice catches on a phrase that reminds you of when they were small. Then pride surges up (they're so strong), immediately followed by devastating loss. Let your voice ride these contradictions without smoothing them out: laugh and cry in the same breath, feel your throat tighten with love while your jaw clenches with resentment. Don't resolve into one clean emotion. End in a place where two opposite feelings exist simultaneously—maybe relief and heartbreak, or rage and overwhelming gratitude—and let your voice hold both truths at once, messy and human and real.
inspired_by: Actor recognizes that he repeats the same vocal coloring or emotional tone in every performance, or that his voice sounds manipulated rather than organic

title: Fierce Devotion, Hollow Hands
instruction: Someone you love more than life itself is in danger and you are utterly powerless to save them. Start with fierce, almost violent determination: 'I will tear this world apart before I let anything happen to you!' Your voice is a force of nature, protective rage incarnate. But reality crashes in—you can't fix this. The fury begins to crack: 'Tell me what to do. Please, there has to be something!' Desperation edges into your voice. Then the breakdown: your strength shatters completely and you collapse into raw, unguarded terror: 'I can't lose you. I can't breathe without you in this world.' Tears choke your words. You're begging, bargaining with fate, with god, with anyone: 'Take me instead. Please. Take anything else.' End with your voice reduced to a whisper, still fierce but broken, holding them: 'I'm here. I'm right here. I won't let go.'

title: The Politeness Cracks
instruction: You are an elderly person working the returns counter at a department store. A customer has just handed you a clearly used item with a fake receipt. You start with your practiced, singsong customer-service voice — artificially bright, with high uptalk and precise articulation — but inside you're sour and annoyed. As you explain the return policy, you lose your train of thought mid-sentence, then find it again. The sourness seeps into your tone, making your pitch waver. By the end, the plastic smile falls away, and you speak with tired, flat honesty, acknowledging you've seen this trick before. Let your voice crack slightly, your posture shift, and let the forced cheerfulness dissolve into weary resignation.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Behind the Fabric
instruction: You're a teenager sitting alone in a hospital waiting room, wearing a tight surgical mask that scratches your nose. Your breath fogs the mask as you turn a worn keychain over in your fingers—your grandmother's. You're waiting to see her after surgery. Start with a contemplative, muffled voice, sibilants soft and breath sounds loud, as you wonder aloud if she'll recognize you through her own mask. Let doubt creep in—did you forget to water her plants? Then let your voice slow and deepen, finding a quiet resolve: you'll just sit with her, hold her hand. The mask warps your words, but by the end, your breath steadies, and your voice becomes a near-whisper of certainty.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Lock Without a Key
instruction: In the dark of your bedroom, you whisper a confession to your sleeping partner (they're not really asleep, but you don't know that). Begin speaking in a tightly controlled whisper, clinical and detached, as you confess something you've kept hidden—a betrayal, a lie, a secret shame. Your words are carefully chosen, your breathing shallow and restricted, as if you're reading from a script you've memorized. But mid-confession, your voice catches. You pause. Something unlocks in your chest. The words that follow are no longer controlled—they're ragged, bewildered, achingly honest. You're no longer confessing the facts; you're revealing the terrified person who committed them. End with your hand reaching out to touch their shoulder, your voice barely audible: 'I'm so scared of who I am without my secrets.' Move from armored self-protection to trembling self-exposure.
inspired_by: Actor needs to play a character who is uptight, closed, or defensive

title: The Wedding Toast That Became an Exorcism
instruction: You're giving a toast at a celebration—a wedding, a milestone birthday, a retirement. Start with genuine joy and celebration. But as you speak, let contradictory impulses crash into your words at high speed: sudden bitter jealousy, then fierce protective love, then resentment about your own life, then overwhelming gratitude, then anger at being left behind, then pride, then fear of being forgotten, then hilarious mockery, then desperate plea for connection. Don't control these shifts or make them make sense—speak as if each new feeling is hijacking your voice mid-sentence. Your toast should become increasingly unfiltered and raw, surprising everyone (including yourself) with its emotional chaos. End having said something brutally honest that no one expected, transforming the moment from simple celebration into something uncomfortably, beautifully real.
inspired_by: Actor is stuck in conceptual or preplanned responses and cannot access organic moment-to-moment impulses

title: The Last Sunrise You'll See Together
instruction: You're sitting beside your beloved grandmother's hospital bed at dawn, watching the sun rise through the window. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know these are your final moments together. Begin speaking to her with careful, controlled composure—you're trying to be strong for her. As you talk about the sunrise, memories flood back, and different versions of yourself emerge: the child she raised, the rebel teenager she forgave, the adult who finally understood her sacrifices. Let your voice move through these different ages and selves, until you finally break into the raw, unguarded person you are right now—no longer performing strength, just loving her with your whole, fractured heart. End in a whisper, telling her something you've never been brave enough to say.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years. Start with your voice tight, controlled—you've rehearsed this. 'Do you know what it was like? Do you even remember?' But as you speak, the hurt you've been holding breaks through the anger. Your voice cracks. You're eight years old again, then furious, then exhausted. Ask the questions that have no good answers: 'Why didn't you...? How could you not see?' Move from righteous anger to raw grief to something unexpected—a terrible, unwanted empathy. Your voice should betray how much you still need them to say something, anything, that makes it okay. End not with resolution, but with the devastating realization that they might never understand.

title: The Mirror Argument
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he was never emotionally present during your childhood. But here's the twist: as you speak, you begin to notice your own gestures, your own tone, your own coldness—and you realize with creeping horror that you've become him. You're using his exact dismissive phrases with your own children. Start the confrontation with righteous anger and accusation. As you continue, let the anger curdle into recognition, then into quiet, devastating shame. Your voice should shift from attacking him to almost pleading with yourself. End by asking him a question you're actually asking yourself. The journey is from fury at him to confrontation with your own reflection.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Dream Journal Entries Exercise

title: First Time Afterglow
instruction: You're a teenage guy lying in bed after your first time with your partner. Your body is loose, voice husky and slow from exhaustion, but your mind is racing. As you stare at the ceiling, you feel a sharp twinge in your ribs and a cold knot in your chest. You want to say something reassuring, but the fear of what comes next—being caught, her regret, the weight of it all—keeps spilling out in broken pauses. Let your words drop into silence, then trail off, as if you're trying to convince yourself more than her. Start with a shaky, guarded warmth, then let the confession crack open into raw uncertainty.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Cracked Laughter
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, leaning against a kitchen counter, talking to someone you've been drawn to all night. You're in the middle of a teasing story about your disastrous attempt to bake a cake, laughing freely, your voice dropping into a playful, breathy rhythm. But as you see them smile, you feel a sudden jolt of fear — this is becoming real. Your laughter stutters, you look down, and your voice gets quieter, more hesitant. End with a soft, almost vulnerable admission that you're not usually this open. Let your voice start relaxed and amused, then let the fear subtly crack through.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Thanking Your Abuser as They Die, Finally Free
instruction: You're at their bedside. They're unconscious, hours from death. You came because some part of you needed to. Begin speaking with genuine gratitude—thank them for the strength their cruelty forced you to find, for teaching you who you never wanted to become. Your voice is almost serene, and there's real truth in it. But as you speak, something else emerges: you're also crying. Not from sadness, but from the devastating recognition that you're grateful and destroyed simultaneously. You're thanking them while your voice breaks with the grief of the childhood you'll never get back. Laugh softly, bitterly, at the absurdity—that you're comforting yourself in their final moments instead of the reverse. End with a whispered 'I forgive you,' but let it be ambiguous whether that's liberation or the saddest sentence you've ever spoken. Peace and anguish in the same breath.
inspired_by: News Anchor Reports Her Own Daughter's Abduction

title: Caught Between Two Arguments in Different Languages
instruction: You're bilingual and your two parents are arguing through you — each in their own language. You translate (badly, diplomatically) between them, softening insults and inventing compliments. One parent says something devastating; you translate it as 'She says she appreciates your perspective.' The other fires back; you translate 'He says the weather is nice.' The escalating difficulty of emotional mistranslation. Include the moment you snap and yell at both of them in both languages simultaneously.

title: Laughing at the Funeral You're Planning
instruction: You're on the phone with a funeral director, planning your own service after receiving terminal news, and they've just said something absurdly bureaucratic about 'packages' and 'options.' You start laughing—genuinely laughing—at the surreal horror of it. 'I'm sorry, it's just... do you hear yourself?' The laughter is real but there are tears in your voice too. As you continue the conversation, trying to make decisions about flowers and music, the absurdity gives way to something deeper. Your voice wavers between amusement and anguish. You're grateful for this strange, dark humor even as your heart is breaking. 'Thank you for being so patient with me.' The words are sincere, but your voice is doing something extraordinary—holding grief and gratitude and bitter comedy all at once. End in a place of profound, contradictory peace: laughing softly while crying, finding something almost beautiful in the absolute devastation of planning your own goodbye.

title: The Last Request
instruction: You are in your final hours, lying in a hospital bed with someone you love sitting beside you. For your entire life, you've been the accommodating one—the peacemaker, the one who never asked for anything. But now, with time running out, something shifts. Begin speaking softly, perhaps apologetically, but gradually find the strength to voice what you've always needed from this person but never dared request: their acknowledgment of your worth, their recognition of sacrifices you made, their admission that you mattered deeply. Your voice should grow stronger, your words more direct—not angry, but finally, powerfully honest. Let your body respond: maybe you reach for their hand with increasing firmness, sit up slightly despite your weakness, meet their eyes without flinching. End with a direct, clear statement of what you needed all along, spoken with quiet certainty. The arc moves from hesitant and diminished to fully present and unashamed.

title: Echoes of a Lost Key
instruction: You are an elderly man, voice gruff and worn, standing alone on a concrete landing in a dim stairwell. Your footsteps slap and echo, and your words bounce back at you off the hard walls. You came here to find a spare key you hid decades ago, but now you’re just stalled, staring at the flaking paint. Start with a practical, almost irritable tone—muttering about your memory failing, annoyed by the echoes. Then pause mid-sentence as a memory rises: you recall the young woman who laughed as you hid that key. Let your voice soften, slow, the longing bleeding through—for her, for that moment. The reverb will make your quiet words sound vast and hollow. End with a breath that trails off, not a finished thought.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance: Confronting the Narcissist Parent
instruction: You're at your dying parent's bedside, the one who always made everything about themselves, who never saw you. They've asked you to forgive them. Start with bitter, controlled anger—you came to say what you've held back for thirty years. Your voice is sharp, precise, each word a small blade. But as you list the wounds—the birthdays they missed, the times they made you feel invisible—your anger cracks. Underneath is a child's desperate plea: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let your voice break completely, tears choking the words. Then, as they reach for your hand (weakly, finally vulnerable), you feel something shift. The rage drains into exhausted grief. End with a whispered 'I'm here,' not quite forgiveness, but presence—your voice raw, uncertain, but softer than it's been in decades.

title: The Sandpaper Confession
instruction: You are an older woman with a naturally high, feminine voice, but you're battling laryngitis. You're on the phone with a close friend, trying to sound casual about your partner's new coworker—a younger woman who's been 'friendly.' You start by recounting a moment that stirred a flicker of lust in you (a memory of your partner's touch), but as you speak, the envy and jealousy claw up your throat. Let the hoarseness and pain mirror your frustration. Micro-distractions: swallow painfully, clear throat, let the voice break on vulnerable words. End with a raw, exhausted admission that you feel old and replaced.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Binding Cloth and Breaking Fever
instruction: You are experiencing intense physical pain—tightening corset stays, binding feet, breaking a fever without medicine, recovering from a wound with only primitive care—while simultaneously receiving news that transforms your emotional world entirely (a longed-for freedom has arrived, or a devastating loss has occurred, or a secret love has been revealed). Begin by letting the physical sensation dominate: the restriction of movement from clothing or injury, the smell of herbs or blood or sweat, the texture of rough linen or leather against skin. Your speech comes in gasps, shaped by bodily constraint. Then let the emotional news flood through the physical experience—does joy make the pain irrelevant, or does grief make it worse? Let your voice and body show both realities simultaneously. Build from controlled endurance (the discipline your era demands) toward something rawer and more abandoned. End in a place where you can't tell where physical sensation ends and emotion begins—they've become the same overwhelming experience, breaking through the composure your time period requires.

title: The Last Goodbye Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child before deploying to a war zone you may not return from. Start with forced cheerfulness—'We're going to video chat every day, okay?'—your voice bright but trembling at the edges. As your child asks if you're scared, the mask cracks. Let shame wash over you for lying, for leaving, for not being brave enough to stay calm. Your voice becomes raw, confessing your terror in a whisper: 'I'm so scared, baby. I'm so scared.' Then your child touches your face or says something innocent and trusting, and you must find strength you don't have. End with fierce, protective love—a promise spoken through tears that's half prayer, half vow, your voice steadier but weighted with the knowledge this might be the last time.

title: I Held You While You Died and I'm So Fucking Angry
instruction: You're alone in your car, screaming at your best friend who died in your arms three hours ago. Start with logistical, numb recounting—'The nurse said you were stable. They said we had time.' But it builds. Suddenly you're raging at them for leaving, for not fighting harder, for making you promise things you can't keep. Your voice breaks from fury into raw, guttural sobbing—the kind that hurts your ribs. You're hitting the steering wheel, then you're whispering their name like a prayer. Then back to anger: 'How dare you make me watch that. How dare you leave me here.' End in exhausted, whispered tenderness: recounting one perfect moment you shared, speaking to them as if they can still hear. Let the rage and love be inseparable, both completely real.
inspired_by: Concealing Disgust While Handling Something Unpleasant

title: Bound in Trust
instruction: You're lying on a bed, wrists tied to the headboard with soft silk ropes. Your partner's face is close, whispering calm reassurances. Begin with a strained, breathy voice — the ropes pull, your chest tight from arousal and vulnerability. Let your words come out uneven, pausing to swallow or shift against the bindings. As their eyes hold yours, your breathing steadies, and your voice lightens into a hopeful, trusting whisper. End with a quiet, optimistic plea for them to take control, your tension melting into serene anticipation.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Not My Child
instruction: You've just received the call: your child, sibling, or someone you raised has been in a catastrophic accident. You're in your car, gripping the steering wheel, trying to drive to the hospital but you can't move yet. Start with disbelief—'No. No, that's not... that can't be right'—voice flat, shock making you numb. But then reality crashes in and you're screaming, slamming your fists against the wheel, a primal roar of rage at the universe. The fury breaks into desperate bargaining: 'Take me instead, please, PLEASE take me instead!' Your voice splinters between aggressive defiance and complete helplessness. You're sobbing so hard you can barely form words, but you force out their name, memories flooding you. End with fierce, broken determination: 'Hold on, baby, I'm coming. You stay. You STAY with me.' Your voice is destroyed but unwavering.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospital bed, knowing this is goodbye but not wanting to say it. You start trying to sound upbeat, energized even—talking fast about nothing, filling the silence with chatter about the weather, a nurse's joke, anything but the truth. Your voice is almost manic with false brightness. But mid-sentence, the pretense crumbles. The energy drains completely. Your voice becomes small, childlike, as you finally whisper what you called to say: that you're scared, that you love them, that you wish you had more time. Let the transition from frantic deflection to raw vulnerability happen naturally, like a dam breaking.

title: Laughing Through the Eulogy I'm Giving Myself
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your own funeral, and you're determined to make it funny, light, perfect—the way you want to be remembered. Start with planned jokes, deliberate charm, complete control. But as you talk, real memories surface. You find yourself laughing genuinely at something you'd forgotten, and then the laugh catches because you realize you won't make more memories. You keep trying to return to the jokes, but they're becoming mixed with unexpected tenderness, with things you actually need to say. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, making dark jokes that land differently than you intended. The controlled performance becomes startlingly honest. You're finding unexpected peace in saying goodbye to yourself, even as your heart is breaking. End with genuine laughter that transforms mid-breath into a sob, or a sob that becomes real joy—a moment where grief and gratitude are completely inseparable.

title: The Last Human Speaking to an Empty World
instruction: Everyone else is gone. You don't know why. Narrate a walk through an abandoned city, talking to maintain your sanity. Address nobody and everybody: 'If anyone can hear me...' The echo of your own voice in empty streets should be lonely enough to make you stop talking — then the silence is worse, so you start again. Include singing, just to hear a human voice. End with a resolved, dignified: 'My name is [name]. I was here. Someone was here.'

title: The Promotion You've Waited For
instruction: You're calling your estranged mother to tell her you finally got the career breakthrough you've worked toward for years. Begin with genuine excitement and pride, the words tumbling out as you describe what happened. You want her to be proud, to say she always knew you could do it. But as you speak, other emotions flood in: resentment that she wasn't there during the struggling years, anger that you still need her approval, grief that this moment is complicated instead of pure. Let your excitement curdle into something harder. Your voice should carry simultaneous joy and bitterness, celebration and accusation. You're thrilled and furious at the same time—thrilled at your success, furious that you still care what she thinks. End with a statement that could be either generous or devastating, or both: perhaps 'I did this without you' or 'I wish you'd been there.' Let us hear in your final words that you're not sure whether you're sharing this news or wielding it as a weapon—maybe both, maybe you can't tell the difference anymore.
inspired_by: Programming the Unconscious: The Glass Menagerie (Tom)

title: Novocaine Surprise
instruction: You’re a grown man just out of a dental appointment, still half-numb. You’re sitting in the car, trying to test your speech, when you accidentally say something that sounds ridiculous—and you realize you’re drooling. Start with wide-eyed astonishment at how different your voice is, exploring the numb sounds, then slowly shift into amused, self-mocking laughter as you repeat a phrase that comes out hilariously wrong. Let your voice be sloppy on B, P, M; over-articulate on other consonants. Show the surprise turning into genuine, warm amusement at your own silly situation.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of the Hard Hat
instruction: You are an older construction foreman, still drunk from the night before, standing on a half-finished steel beam. The morning sun blazes, and the visor of your hard hat dims your view. Shame burns in your chest—you caused a small accident yesterday because you were hungover, and now the crew is waiting for your orders. At first your voice is tight, defensive, shouting over the grind of machinery. But as you speak to yourself, the shame deepens into a raw, quiet confession of failure. Let the hat’s weight press down, the noise of the site punctuate your pauses. End with a bitter, broken resolve.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Photograph in the Dust
instruction: You are lying face-down on the floor of a cluttered attic, searching for a lost box. Your cheek is pressed against the dusty old wood, and your breathing is a bit shallow from the weight on your chest. Your hand sweeps through cobwebs until your fingers touch an old, worn photograph. As you pull it into view, you're filled with astonishment—it's a candid shot of someone you have been secretly infatuated with for years, laughing in the sunlight. Start by muttering in disbelief at the dusty find, then let your voice soften and slow as you become completely captivated by their smile, ending with a whisper that feels intimate and dizzyingly close.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Thanking Someone as Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're expressing deep gratitude to someone who's leaving your life—maybe ending the relationship, maybe dying, maybe choosing a path away from you. Your voice is warm with genuine appreciation as you tell them what they've meant to you: 'You changed my life. You made me better.' But underneath the gratitude, your heart is breaking. Let laughter bubble up as you recall beautiful memories, then feel it catch in your throat. Your voice wavers between joy at what you had and grief at losing it. You're smiling and crying simultaneously, finding the grace to celebrate them even as you fall apart. End with a moment of profound peace mixed with unbearable loss—you're letting them go with love, grateful for every moment, while simultaneously feeling the ground disappear beneath you. This is the bittersweet beauty of loving someone enough to release them, even as it destroys you.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Attracted to Someone Who Was Just a Friend

title: The Shower Epiphany
instruction: You're standing in a warm shower, steam rising around you. The harsh tile amplifies every sound. You've just discovered something about yourself that you've been hiding — a truth that slips out as a whisper first, then grows. Start with quiet, shame-soaked muttering, almost lost in the water sound, then build to a raw, astonished gasp. Your voice catches on the sharp reverb, syllables echoing as you realize: this is who you are. Let the surprise overtake the shame, your breath hitching mid-sentence as the truth dawns in the slick, tiled space.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Clear Morning
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake and lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is your final conversation. Begin with careful, almost formal politeness—trying to protect both of you from the weight of goodbye. But as she asks you to tell her one true thing about your life you've never shared, let your voice break open. Move from surface pleasantries to raw confession: tell her the dream you abandoned, the person you really love, the fear that haunts you. Let your emotion transform from protective distance to complete vulnerability. End not with dramatic sobbing, but with a whispered gratitude so genuine it hurts—thanking her for seeing you, really seeing you, one last time.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Became the Monster
instruction: You are confronting your mother, a former decorated prosecutor who became everything she once fought against - now awaiting trial for corruption and murder. Start with cold fury and bitter accusations about how she destroyed your faith in justice, in her, in everything you believed. But as you rage, memories flood back - her tucking you in, teaching you right from wrong, the mother she was before ambition consumed her. Your anger must fracture into grief and confusion. End by telling her you brought your daughter to meet her one last time before the trial, but you can't - your voice catching between protective rage and the child in you who still loves her and doesn't understand how this happened.
inspired_by: The Detective and the Criminal Mastermind

title: The Heaviness of Joy
instruction: You have just received news that is both a miracle and a tragedy—a loved one survived something terrible but will never be the same, you got your dream but at devastating cost, you are finally free but had to lose everything to get here. Begin with a burst of contradictory energy—laughter mixed with sobbing, jumping mixed with collapsing, your body confused about whether to celebrate or grieve. As you move through this emotional storm, feel how exhausting it is to hold both emotions at once, how your body grows heavier and heavier with the complexity of what you feel. Your voice cracks between joy and despair, unable to settle on one. Gradually, let the weight of both feelings pull you down until you are sitting or lying still, making sounds that are neither laughter nor crying but something in between. By the end, you are so heavy with the fullness of human experience—all of it, the beautiful and terrible at once—that you can barely move, but there is profound peace in finally accepting that both can be true.

title: The Last Phone Call from the ICU
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love deeply who is dying in intensive care, and you know this is goodbye. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep your voice light and reassuring, pretending everything will be okay. As they grow weaker, their voice fading, your composure starts to crack—your breath catches, your words stumble. When they say 'I love you' one final time, something breaks inside you. Your voice fractures between desperate reassurance and the raw, animal grief of knowing they're slipping away. End with quiet, devastating acceptance mixed with gratitude for these last words, your voice barely a whisper as you tell them it's okay to let go. Let the silence between your words speak as loudly as the words themselves.

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: Confront your mother or father about a betrayal you discovered years ago but never spoke about—perhaps an affair, a lie about your childhood, or a promise broken. Begin by reciting the lyrics to a lullaby or children's song they used to sing to you, but use those innocent words as armor, as weapon, as shield. Let your fury, hurt, and twisted love pour through the childish phrases. Start controlled and cold, almost mocking, but let the confrontation intensify until you're shouting or sobbing those simple words with volcanic emotion. By the end, the nursery lyrics should reveal something completely different—perhaps forgiveness breaking through rage, or rage breaking through attempted forgiveness. Let your impulses shatter the innocence of the words.

title: The Leaking Seat
instruction: You're a elderly passenger on a noisy, pressurized aircraft, seated next to a window. The engine drones constantly. You notice a slow, greasy drip from the overhead vent onto your sleeve, staining it. You feel a wave of disgust, muttering to yourself in a low, dry voice, leaning closer to the window to avoid the drip. But then your anxiety grows—you realize no one will help, and you're stuck here for hours. Your voice starts tight with disgust, then trembles with helplessness, fading to a defeated whisper as you give up and stare blankly out the window.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Edge of My Voice
instruction: You are a mother, inches from your child's face, after they ran into the street. Your voice is tight, sharp, almost a bark—every word a hard attack born of pure adrenaline and irritation. But as you see the fear in their eyes, your anger cracks, and the helplessness you felt in that frozen second bleeds through. Your tone softens, loses its edge, and a wave of aching pain—for what could have happened—washes over your words. Micro-distractions: sniffing, a wet blink, a pause to swallow the lump in your throat.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Pain (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Hospital Corridor - Saying Goodbye to Someone Who Won't Remember You
instruction: You're standing outside the room of someone with advanced dementia - a parent, a spouse, someone who raised you. Tomorrow they're being moved to hospice. Today is your last chance to say everything, but they won't know who you are. Start with tender resolve: 'I need you to hear this, even if you don't know me.' Your voice should be steady, almost clinical in its control. But as you speak the memories aloud - their hands teaching yours, their voice singing you to sleep - your composure fractures. By the end, you're whispering through tears: 'Thank you for loving me when you knew who I was.' The journey is from determined strength to complete surrender to grief, each word a goodbye to someone already gone.
inspired_by: Waking Up and Realizing What You Said While Drunk

title: The Fever Dream
instruction: You're in the throes of intense physical sensation—fever, passion, exhaustion, pain—and it's unlocking emotional floodgates. Start from the purely physical: your racing heart, burning skin, trembling hands, breathlessness. As the physical intensity builds, let emotional images flash through without order: a face you loved, a moment of shame, ecstatic laughter, someone's touch, a betrayal, absolute joy, crushing loss. Don't make sense of how these connect to the physical sensation—just let your body's state shatter your normal emotional barriers. Some images will hit harder than others; let those intensify everything. By the end, the physical and emotional have become indistinguishable—you're sobbing or laughing or shouting from a place where body and heart have completely merged.
inspired_by: Actor needs to quickly elevate vulnerability or emotional availability before a scene

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: Confront your aging parent about the legacy of silence and emotional absence they're leaving you. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, to finally communicate like adults. But let your composure fracture as decades of unmet needs pour through. Your anger should feel dangerous, righteous, then suddenly collapse into the voice of the child you once were, still asking why you weren't enough. End not with reconciliation but with exhausted clarity—you're done seeking their approval, and that realization is both liberating and devastating. Let your voice move from controlled accusation to raw grief to quiet, firm farewell.
inspired_by: An Apology to a Future Self

title: Parent Discovering Adult Child's Addiction
instruction: You're in your child's apartment, finding hidden bottles. Speak directly to them in denial mode: 'These are just... when did you start?' Your throat tightens, breathing shallow. 'How long have you been lying to me?' drops to barely audible, shaking. Include a moment where you compose yourself, cold again, before breaking once more.

title: The Thing You've Always Known
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up, starting with rehearsed anger about something specific he did. But instead of staying in your script of accusations, truly look at him—the way his shoulders have curved, the lines around his eyes, how his hands shake slightly. As you genuinely observe him, not as the villain you've built in your mind but as the actual person standing before you, your prepared rage begins to crack. Notice how he's bracing for your attack, how afraid he looks, how old. Let your attention move completely away from your own hurt and into really seeing him—his vulnerability, his regret that he can't quite speak. By the end, arrive at something you didn't plan: a raw, undefended question or confession that you couldn't have known you needed to say until you truly saw who was standing in front of you.
