title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're standing over your sleeping child after learning they've been hiding something catastrophic, and you're shattered by your own powerlessness to fix it. Begin with fierce, barely controlled rage at the world—'How DARE this happen to you'—fists clenched, voice volcanic with protective fury. But as you look at their face, the anger fractures into raw terror: 'I don't know how to save you from this.' Your breathing becomes ragged, desperate. Move through waves of self-accusation and helplessness: 'I'm supposed to be able to fix everything—that's my JOB.' Voice breaks repeatedly as the reality that love isn't enough crashes over you. End in a place of broken-open tenderness mixed with defiant determination, whispering fiercely through tears: 'I can't take this away from you. But I swear... I swear you won't face it alone.' The impotence and the commitment coexist, both absolute.

title: The Standing Ovation You'll Never Hear Again
instruction: You're conducting your final concert before losing your hearing completely to a progressive condition. The orchestra has just finished your greatest triumph, and the audience is roaring—but you can barely hear it anymore, just muffled thunder. Describe what you're experiencing, your voice alive with exhilaration and technique, analyzing the performance with professional precision even as you're laughing, almost giddy with the absurd tragedy of it all. Let joy and devastation live in the same breath: you're grateful, so deeply grateful for this moment, for every note you've ever heard, and simultaneously your heart is breaking because you know the silence that's coming. Your voice should catch between laughter and tears, between triumphant celebration and quiet grief. Talk about the music, about sound itself, with the desperate love of someone saying goodbye to their soulmate. End in a moment of profound peace—acceptance that transforms into something transcendent, your voice full of wonder even as it trembles. Move from euphoric triumph through laughing tears to serene, bittersweet gratitude.

title: The Last Dance of the Paper Crown
instruction: You are a 6-year-old girl, the guest of honor at your own fancy tea party. You’ve spent all afternoon arranging your stuffed animals very carefully. You are tired—your eyes are heavy—but you are so proud of your beautiful paper crown and the way you’ve made everything perfect. Right now, you are showing your favorite bunny how to sip tea properly when you accidentally step on a sharp, pointy building block. A sudden, sharp spike of pain shoots through your foot. Your voice cracks into a little yelp, and you freeze, holding your breath. For a moment, you forget the tea party—your face scrunches, your voice tense and guarded. But then, as the pain turns into a dull ache, you remember your crown, your stuffed audience, and your pride. You take a shaky breath and try to finish showing the bunny, your voice wavering between exhaustion from the long day and the fierce pride of being the perfect hostess—until the very end, where a sniffle betrays the lingering hurt.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Contentment (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Orgasm Faking
instruction: You're having sex with a partner you care about, but you're not going to come, and they're trying so hard to get you there. You can feel their effort, their dedication, their investment in your pleasure. Your voice—the sounds you're making—becomes a performance to reassure them. 'Yes, that's good' when it's not quite. Then closer to what feels good: your voice becomes more genuine. But you're reaching the point where faking feels inevitable. Do you keep faking to protect their ego? Your voice becomes artificial again—'Oh God, yes'—and you feel the distance grow between you. The coming moments are physically intimate but emotionally alone. End with your voice quiet, lying beside them, wanting to say 'I was faking' but saying nothing.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You
instruction: You're at the bedside of someone unconscious, perhaps dying, and you're saying all the things you never said. Your voice is barely above a whisper—this is intimate, just for them, even if they can't respond. Start with small confessions: 'I still think about that summer...' Your throat keeps catching. You're not crying loudly; this is the kind of grief that lives in the quiet spaces. Share a memory that makes you almost smile, voice warming slightly, then the smile dissolves as you realize you're losing them. End with a tender permission: 'It's okay. You can go.' But your voice breaks on those words because it's not okay, and they both know it. Every pause is filled with unsaid things. Let the vulnerability be so raw it's almost unbearable to speak.

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: You're alone in a quiet room, speaking to someone who isn't there anymore—a lover, a friend, someone who left before you could say what mattered. Your voice starts as a whisper, tentative, like you're testing if they can somehow still hear: 'I keep starting sentences to you in my head.' There's a fragile intimacy here, words catching in your throat. Let your breathing be uneven, natural pauses where emotion wells up. 'The truth is... the real truth is...' You're confessing something tender and devastating—maybe that you loved them, or that you were afraid, or that you knew they were leaving and said nothing. Your voice doesn't rise; it deepens with quiet devastation. End with something so soft it's almost inaudible, a truth whispered into emptiness: 'I should have been braver.' Feel the weight of those unspoken words settling into your chest.

title: The Weight of Peace
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman, alone in a quiet room at night, gently rocking your sleeping infant grandchild. Your voice is hushed, with a slight rhythmic bounce from the rocking motion. Start from a place of deep contemplation—musing softly on the baby’s tiny breaths, the warmth against your chest, the stillness of the house. Let your thoughts drift to how this moment almost didn’t happen, and slowly, let a wave of overwhelming gratitude wash over you. End with a whisper of thanks, your voice catching as you realize the fragile beauty of it all. Let the rocking shape your breath and pace, and allow any natural pauses or broken phrases—you’re thinking as you speak, feeling your way through the words.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You are standing at your best friend's wedding reception, about to give a toast. Everyone is looking at you with expectant, joyful faces. You raise your glass and begin speaking about how happy you are for them, how perfect their partner is, how you've never seen them glow like this. Let genuine love and happiness fill your voice—this is true, you do want their joy. But as you continue, let another truth begin bleeding through: you are also deeply, devastatingly in love with your friend, have been for years, and you are watching them commit their life to someone else. Your words stay celebratory, but your voice must carry both emotions simultaneously—authentic happiness warring with authentic heartbreak. Let the joy in your words be real, and let the grief be real, neither negating the other. End with a final blessing for their marriage that is both completely sincere and completely unbearable to say, raising your glass higher even as your hand trembles, smiling even as your heart shatters, loving them enough to mean every word and enough to never tell them why it's killing you.

title: Crowned in Silence
instruction: You are a teenager, alone on a battlefield at dawn after a long siege. Your helmet visor is down, and the world sounds like it's underwater—metallic, muffled. You’ve just won, but instead of cheering, there’s a strange hollow exhaustion. Your breath fogs the eye slit; you shift weight on your feet, and the armor clanks. At first, your voice is quiet, shaky—a fragile triumph. But as you speak to the empty field, remembering the friend you fought for, the metal resonant sound of your own voice fills you with pride. Your tone hardens into fierce, unshakable triumph, and you lift your visor just a little at the end, letting the cool air in.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Dementia Dance
instruction: You're dancing with your father who no longer remembers you, in the memory care facility where he now lives. Begin with forced brightness as you guide him through steps he taught you, narrating memories he can't access. As he smiles at you like a stranger, start laughing—but the laughter tangles with tears, becoming something between joy and devastation. Your voice should celebrate the moment ('You're a beautiful dancer, Dad') while simultaneously grieving ('You showed me how to do this'). Find genuine delight in his present happiness even as your heart shatters that you're a stranger to him. End in a paradox: thanking him for this dance with profound gratitude while your voice breaks with the weight of everything lost. The emotional arc: performative joy → helpless laughter-tears → grateful heartbreak.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally speaking the truth to a parent who was always emotionally absent. Begin with careful, measured words as you describe a childhood memory of sitting in the sun alone, waiting for them to notice you. Let the hurt build as you realize they still don't understand what they took from you. Your voice should rise from quiet pain into raw accusation, then crack into something more vulnerable—the child inside you still desperate to be seen. End with a moment of fierce, angry clarity mixed with heartbreak, where you stop seeking their warmth because you've learned to find your own.
inspired_by: Feeling the Warmth of a Sunbeam on Your Face

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy Who Saved Your Life
instruction: The person who destroyed your family, who you've hated for years, just pushed you out of the way of a car and is now bleeding out in your arms. Start with your voice sharp with shock and rage—you don't want to hold them, you're shouting for help but your voice is vicious: 'Don't you dare die before I get to hate you properly.' But they're fading and suddenly you're terrified, your voice cracking as you beg them to stay awake, and you hate that you care, hate that you're crying. Your rage and grief slam into each other—you're screaming at them for ruining your life while simultaneously begging them not to leave, your voice breaking between fury and desperate tenderness. They try to apologize with their last breaths and you explode: you don't want their apology, you wanted years of your life back, but your voice is also pressing close to theirs, fierce and protective, refusing to let them die alone. End in the terrible quiet after they're gone, your voice small and lost, whispering 'I forgive you' to someone who can't hear it anymore, and you don't know if you mean it or if you just needed to say it.
inspired_by: Leaving a Cult: Disorientation Becoming Orientation

title: Wedged in the Dark
instruction: You are a middle-aged man trapped in a narrow, dusty crawlspace beneath a collapsed floor. Your arms are stretched painfully above your head, fingers straining for a rusted emergency latch. Every breath is shallow, your voice thin and pulled. Start with raw distress — panicked, gasping, desperate pleas as you stretch. Then feel a wave of emotional numbness wash over you as you realize you might die here, your voice flat, detached. Finally, your fingers catch the latch and it gives — a surge of elation breaks through, a choked laugh, tears of relief. Speak naturally, with pauses, grunts, and the physical strain affecting every word. Keep your spoken lines to about 60 words.
emotions_sampled: Distress (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Echoes of a Broken Promise
instruction: You are standing on a concrete landing in a stairwell, one hand gripping the cold metal railing. You’ve just walked out of a meeting where everything you built was handed to someone else. Your voice is bitter and harsh at first, each word bouncing off the walls like an accusation. But as you speak, you feel the anger draining into something heavier—a quiet, exhausted sadness. Let the echoes carry your words, but let your own breath and pauses betray the cracking of your resolve. End with a voice that is softer, almost a whisper, as if you’re finally admitting a truth you’ve been fighting.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Homecoming That Isn't
instruction: You've just returned to your childhood home for the first time in years—maybe for a funeral, maybe because you finally succeeded and want to show them, maybe because you're broken and have nowhere else to go. Walking through the door, you're flooded with contradictions: relief and resentment, nostalgia and rage, belonging and alienation all at once. Begin by simply taking in the familiar smells, the unchanged furniture, the ways everything is both exactly the same and completely different because you're different. Don't push toward any single emotion—the point is to let yourself genuinely experience how you can hate and love this place in the same heartbeat. As you move through the rooms, notice how specific objects or spaces trigger unexpected reactions: gratitude for sacrifices made mixed with anger at wounds inflicted, joy at being home laced with desperate need to escape. End with the recognition that you contain multitudes, that you don't have to resolve these contradictions into a single coherent feeling. The truth is messier, more human than that.
inspired_by: Actor cannot function without stimulating high tension states (Theatrical Hysteria / Ass Energy)

title: The Last Conversation Before the Long Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving on a journey they will never return from—a terminal diagnosis, a one-way mission, exile. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things normal, making small talk about mundane things because you can't bear to acknowledge what's happening. Gradually, your voice should crack as reality seeps in. Move through desperate attempts to memorize their voice, their face. Then allow yourself to break—not theatrically, but the way a person actually breaks when they realize this is the last time. End in a place of tender acceptance mixed with unbearable grief, whispering the things you should have said years ago. Let silence do as much work as words. Your voice should move from bright and false to raw and stripped bare.
inspired_by: Being Woken Up at Every Stage of Sleep

title: A Hollow Release
instruction: You are a teenager in a bedroom with someone you don't really want to be with. Your body is responding against your will, and you feel a deep numbness inside—like you're watching yourself from far away. As the climax approaches, your breathing turns ragged, your words break into gasps and moans, and you feel completely helpless, trapped in your own skin. Then, in the final moment, a flicker of contempt rises—toward them, toward yourself—and the last sound you make is bitter, almost mocking, before your body goes still.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Helplessness (extremely present), Contempt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Parent Discovers Their Child Is the Anonymous Bully
instruction: You've just cracked your teenager's laptop password because another kid at school attempted suicide, and now you're reading the messages your child sent—vicious, calculated, relentless cruelty. Start with disbelief, reading phrases aloud that get progressively worse, your voice climbing in pitch and volume as the horror compounds. 'No, no, no'—repeating it like a mantra. Then explode: slam your hands down, scream at the empty room, rage at the monster you apparently raised. Your voice cracks between fury and anguish—how did you not see this? Hear your child coming up the stairs. Try to compose yourself but you're shaking violently. When they walk in cheerfully asking 'what's for dinner?', you can't speak at first. Finally force out 'I know what you did,' and watch their face change. Your voice transforms from explosive anger to something more devastating—not yelling anymore but speaking with the kind of quiet, cold devastation that's worse than screaming. End with a question that combines protectiveness and horror: 'Who are you?'—because you genuinely don't recognize the child standing before you, and it's breaking your heart.
inspired_by: Detective Reveals the Killer Is His Partner

title: The Interrogation Room Truth
instruction: You are confronting your parent who abandoned you as a child, now face-to-face after twenty years. Start with carefully controlled anger, each word measured and sharp like you've rehearsed this moment a thousand times. As you speak, your control begins to fracture—the hurt child underneath breaks through the adult's armor. Move through accusation into raw vulnerability, demanding to know why you weren't enough, why they could walk away. Let your voice rise and fall unpredictably. End not with forgiveness, but with exhausted honesty—you've carried this person inside you every day, hating them and needing them in equal measure. The final moments should be quiet, almost tender, but edged with permanent damage. Show us the war between wanting closure and wanting them to hurt the way you've hurt.
inspired_by: The Soldier and the Enemy Spy

title: The Finish Line Gasp
instruction: You are a teenage girl who has just sprinted the final 100 meters of a race, pushing past your limit. You’re now bent over, hands on knees, chest heaving, barely able to breathe. At first, your mind is locked on simply surviving—every muscle burning, nausea rising, forcing you to spit and gag. You mutter fragmented, breathy words to yourself, trying to stay upright. Slowly, as your breathing eases, the reality hits: you won. The concentration melts into a quiet, shaky triumph—a single, exhausted laugh or a whispered 'I did it' that carries the weight of the effort. Let your words be stolen by gasps, your voice crack, and let the final realization creep in only after the physical storm passes.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering What Cannot Be Taken Back
instruction: You are lying in darkness next to someone you've never told the complete truth—perhaps a lover you're about to lose, or a person you've hidden your real self from. Begin by noticing the weight of everything unsaid pressing against your ribcage, making your breathing shallow, causing your throat to tighten with fear. In the quietest voice possible, start to confess what you've kept locked inside, simultaneously tracking aloud the physical sensations of vulnerability: 'My stomach is twisting,' 'I can feel my pulse in my temples,' 'My hands are cold because I'm terrified.' As you name each sensation and continue your whispered confession, feel the terror gradually transform into relief, even peace. By the end, your body has softened, your breath has deepened, and you've moved from paralyzing fear into the strange, fragile freedom of finally being seen.

title: The Letter's Aftertaste
instruction: You are standing in a sterile bathroom, gripping the sink, having just read a letter that upends your entire life. The nausea hits in waves—your stomach clenches, saliva floods your mouth, and you gag between words. Begin with a faint tremor of distress as you fight the urge to vomit, then let your voice drift into heavy contemplation, as if the physical heaving mirrors the churning of your thoughts. By the end, the emotion drains into a flat, hollow numbness—your words become mechanical, almost detached, even as your body continues to rebel. Let the gagging interrupt your speech naturally; don't force it, but let it happen when it feels real.
emotions_sampled: Distress (slightly present), Contemplation (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Kitchen Table Midnight: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: Your parent sits across from you. You've rehearsed this for years. You start measured, almost clinical - listing the missed birthdays, the promises broken, trying to sound rational and unaffected. But anger seeps through. Your voice tightens. You're working so hard to stay calm that words start tumbling out too fast, then you catch yourself and slow down artificially, just like someone hiding intoxication. Mid-accusation, something breaks - maybe they look away, maybe they say nothing - and your rage collapses into the wounded child underneath. End with the devastating question you've never asked: 'Did you ever even want me?' Let your voice move from controlled fury to raw, unguarded need.
inspired_by: Drunk Driving Pulled Over: Trying Not to Sound Drunk

title: The Toy on the Carpet
instruction: You are a child sitting cross-legged on the floor of your bedroom, the afternoon light slanting across the carpet. A small stuffed animal lies in front of you, a gift from someone who left last week. You start by tracing its ear with your finger, your voice flat and a little numb—you’re embarrassed you still care. But as you speak, your throat tightens; you look away, then back, and the longing creeps in, raw and undeniable. Let your gaze drift, fidget with the toy, and let the final words come out quieter, almost a whisper, as the numbness cracks open.
emotions_sampled: Longing (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Embarrassment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Stole
instruction: You're finally telling your mother what her alcoholism cost you. Start with controlled fury, each word precise and cutting: 'I was eight years old and I was parenting you.' List the memories—birthdays she missed, school events she ruined, nights you put yourself to bed. Your voice is relentless, itemizing decades of pain. But then she does something unexpected: she doesn't defend herself. She just... breaks. And suddenly you see her—not the towering figure from your childhood, but a damaged, fragile person who failed you. Your anger becomes something messier: rage mixed with unwanted compassion, grief for both the child you were and the broken woman before you. Your voice softens despite yourself: 'I needed you.' It's an accusation and a confession. End with the terrible realization that forgiveness and healing aren't the same thing.
inspired_by: Confronting Your Betraying Friend: Anger Turning to Grief

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church
instruction: You've just lost everything—your child, your faith, your reason to believe in goodness. You're alone in a church, and the rage explodes out of you. Start with a question hurled at the ceiling: 'Where were you?!' Your voice is raw, accusatory, loud enough to echo. You're listing everything that was taken, your voice climbing with fury and anguish. But mid-tirade, your rage collapses. Your voice breaks on a word and suddenly you're sobbing, your anger dissolving into devastating helplessness. You fall from shouting to pleading, from fury to broken begging: 'Please, just give them back.' Your voice becomes small, desperate, a whisper of pure anguish. End with you literally unable to speak, just gasping breaths where words used to be.
inspired_by: Narrator Triggered by Their Own Words

title: Scrolling Through Yesterday
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a worn armchair, scrolling through old photos on your phone. At first, you hum absentmindedly, voice dropping low and quiet as you thumb past images, muttering distracted fillers like 'oh, that's…' and 'hmm.' Then you stop on a picture of your late husband. Your breath catches, your fingers still, and your voice lifts just a little, fragile and soft, as you talk to the photo as if he could hear you. Let the concentration of scrolling dissolve into a gentle, aching farewell.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You have just received news that someone who caused you enormous pain—a parent who abandoned you, a partner who betrayed you, a friend who destroyed your trust—has died and left you something substantial in their will. Begin with bitter, victorious anger: finally, they've acknowledged the debt they owed you. Let your voice carry dark satisfaction as you list everything they took from you, everything they owe. But as you speak, let gratitude begin to seep in unbidden—not gratitude for them, but for what you became in their absence, for the strength you had to build, for the person you are because you survived them. Your voice should fracture between these competing truths: you hate them and you're grateful, you're relieved they're gone and you're devastated you'll never get the apology you deserved, you want to refuse their money and you need it desperately. End in a place where you're laughing and crying simultaneously, unable to separate the rage from the love, the grief from the liberation, your voice embodying the impossible truth that you can hold all these contradictions at once.
inspired_by: Role-Playing the Inner Critic (Solo Subpersonality Access)

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your child is asleep, and you're kneeling beside their bed, knowing you have to leave them—maybe you're dying, maybe you're in danger and must disappear to protect them, maybe you've made a choice that means you can never return. Begin in barely audible whispers, telling them things you need them to remember about you. Your voice should be tender, almost singing lullaby-soft, as you describe memories only the two of you share. But the tenderness keeps catching—little breaks where grief tries to surface and you have to swallow it back down. You're memorizing their breathing, their face. End with 'I love you' repeated like a prayer, each repetition more broken than the last, until you can barely form the words. Let silence hold the unbearable weight of goodbye.
inspired_by: Medieval: Executioner Comforts the Condemned as a Priest

title: I Decide What You Eat Now
instruction: You're ordering for your elderly mother who has dementia, and she keeps insisting on foods she can no longer safely eat. Start with patient firmness, gently redirecting her choices, but as she grows more confused and angry, accusing you of controlling her, your control shatters. Your voice should explode from calm to fierce: 'You think I want this? You think I want to decide everything for you?' Let rage and grief collide - screaming that you're terrified, that you're losing her, that ordering her food feels like playing God. Your voice should crack and break, tears mixing with fury. End in exhausted tenderness, almost whispering as you order the soft foods that keep her safe, telling her you love her even as she forgets who you are. Show the violence of loving someone who's slipping away.

title: The Sailor and the North Wind
instruction: Portray a sailor with a determined, rugged voice challenging the North Wind, who speaks in a powerful, gusty tone. Switch between the sailors defiance and the winds blustering replies, embodying the struggle against natures forces.

title: Third Wheel Latte
instruction: You're at a café, chin resting on your hand, cheek squished against your palm, making your mouth feel clumsy. Across the table, your best friend sits with her new partner, both glowing. You're supposed to be happy for her, but a knot of embarrassment sits in your chest—you know you're the awkward third wheel. Start with a forced, overly bright tone as you try to join the conversation, your words slurred by your smushed face and your voice pinched with envy. Let your affection for your friend slowly rise through the jealousy, softening your breath until you end with a quiet, genuine admission, your voice tired but warm, the jealousy dissolving into a relieved sigh.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (extremely present), Affection (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
