title: You Matched Me With a Monster
instruction: Explode at a friend who set you up with someone who hurt you badly. Start with cutting sarcasm, mimicking their enthusiastic voice: "Oh, you two would be *perfect*, you both love hiking!" Your voice drips with bitter mockery, listing their ridiculous criteria that missed every red flag. But the sarcasm rapidly ignites into rage—your voice rising, cracking with fury as you detail what that person did to you. Let the anger peak, then shatter completely. Your fierce accusations collapse into broken sobs: "You were supposed to protect me. You were supposed to *see*." The rage dissolves into helplessness and betrayal. End with your voice raw and exhausted, oscillating between fury and devastating hurt, demanding to know if they're sorry, if they even care what their careless matchmaking cost you. Make it feel like a friendship breaking in real time.

title: Listening to You Sleep
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in the middle of the night after a devastating argument. They've finally fallen asleep, but you're wide awake. Begin by whispering into the darkness—apologizing, explaining, confessing things you couldn't say earlier. Listen intently to their sleeping sounds: the rhythm of their breathing, small sighs, the rustle of sheets when they shift. Let these subtle sounds guide your confession. When their breathing deepens, you feel safe enough to admit your deepest fears. When they stir, your voice drops to barely a breath, revealing your most fragile truths. Hear your own voice in the quiet room—how small it sounds, how honest, how different from your defended daytime self. Let the intimacy of speaking to someone who cannot hear you, combined with the tender sounds of their vulnerability in sleep, transform your fear of losing them into a fierce, quiet determination to fight for this love. End with your voice barely audible, but filled with resolute tenderness.

title: The Letter You'll Never Send (To Someone Who's Gone)
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter to someone who died before you could reconcile. Start with careful, controlled words—'I wrote this a hundred times in my head'—but your composure begins fracturing. The regret isn't loud; it's in the catches, the breath between words. Midway through, you shift from what you wish you'd said to what you learned from losing them. Your voice moves from tight self-protection to raw gratitude for what little time you had, even if it was broken. End in whispered acceptance: you're letting them go while holding them closer than ever. The transformation is from defended regret to open-hearted grief that somehow holds beauty.
inspired_by: The Apology You Should Have Given Years Ago

title: Burning the Boats
instruction: You're telling someone you love that you're leaving - the city, the relationship, the whole life you built together - and you're furious at them for making you choose, furious at yourself for choosing. Start with controlled anger, trying to explain rationally why you have to go, but your rage explodes: 'You made me so small! I forgot I had dreams that didn't include you!' Let your voice shake with fury, with betrayal, with years of compressed ambition. But mid-fury, you break - because you also love them desperately, and leaving is destroying you. Your rage collapses into sobbing: 'I hate that I have to hurt you to save myself.' End with fierce, protective conviction through tears - you're going, you have to go, but the choice is ripping you apart. You're strong enough to leave and broken by having to. Your voice should be a war between self-protection and heartbreak, between liberation and loss.

title: The Last Light in the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at 3 AM. She's been unconscious for hours, and the doctors say it's only a matter of time. You begin by whispering small, mundane memories—her kitchen, the smell of her bread, the way she hummed while gardening. Let these memories unlock deeper ones: a moment she defended you when no one else would, a secret she once shared, something you never thanked her for. As you speak, let your emotion shift from numb exhaustion to a desperate, aching love—a need to say everything before the chance is gone. End with a quiet realization that you're not just saying goodbye to her, but to the version of yourself that only existed in her eyes. Your voice should move from hollow and tired to trembling with suppressed grief to finally breaking into raw, whispered urgency.
inspired_by: Actor needs to build a repertoire of choices for future use

title: Midnight Confession in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping partner's hospital bed after they've survived a suicide attempt. Your voice is barely above a whisper, hoarse from crying: 'I know you can't hear me right now.' There's a long pause—you're gathering courage. 'I haven't been honest with you. With myself.' Your confession is tender, broken: 'I saw the signs. I saw them and I... I told myself I was imagining things because I was scared.' Tears catch in your throat. 'I'm so sorry. I'm so fucking sorry.' Your hand perhaps reaches for theirs. The vulnerability deepens: 'I don't know how to help you, but I'm not going anywhere. I'm right here.' End with a whispered promise that's equal parts love and terror: 'Please don't leave me. Please.'

title: The Last Morning Before Hospice
instruction: You're making breakfast for your parent on their final morning at home before they enter hospice care. You begin with false brightness, narrating simple actions: 'Two eggs, just how you like them. Coffee's almost ready.' But as you describe each familiar ritual, your voice starts fragmenting. You're not just making breakfast—you're trying to hold onto every detail, every sound, the smell of coffee, the morning light. Your narration becomes a desperate cataloging: 'The way you hold your cup with both hands. The way you always leave a little coffee at the bottom.' By the end, you're standing at the table, unable to sit down, your voice barely above a whisper: 'I'm not ready to let you go.' The final line is spoken while placing the plate down, knowing this ordinary act will never happen again: 'Please... just one more morning after this one.'

title: Veteran Laughs While Scattering Their War Buddy's Ashes
instruction: You're alone on a cliff overlooking the ocean where you and your best friend always said you'd retire together, holding the urn you promised to bring here. Start by laughing—actually laughing—as you recount the absurd story of how you two met, talking to the ashes like your buddy's still there to joke back. Your voice is warm, nostalgic, full of genuine mirth as you remember the stupid things you did together. But mid-laugh, your voice suddenly catches because you've just opened the urn and the reality slams into you. Continue trying to tell stories but now you're crying while you laugh, your voice breaking on punchlines, smiling through tears as you pour the ashes into the wind. Thank them for saving your life in ways that had nothing to do with combat—for teaching you how to be human again after the war, for never letting you give up, for two decades of terrible jokes and unconditional friendship. Your final words mix profound gratitude with devastating loss: 'I'm so lucky I got to love you, you magnificent bastard'—said with a sob that's also somehow a laugh, grief and joy completely intertwined, as the last of the ashes scatter into the sunset.
inspired_by: Detective Reveals the Killer Is His Partner

title: Surgeon Recognizes Her Estranged Father's Voice Through the Anesthesia Mask
instruction: You're prepping a critical patient for emergency surgery, speaking with calm clinical precision as you explain the procedure. Through the oxygen mask, you hear him whisper something—a nickname only one person ever used, in a voice you haven't heard in fifteen years since he abandoned the family. Your hands freeze. The monitor beeps. You must continue the medical protocol, but your voice cracks as you realize this may be your last chance to understand why he left, to forgive him, or to let him go without answers. Your questions shift from medical to achingly personal, professional composure dissolving into the raw need of a daughter who never stopped waiting. End barely holding yourself together, fighting to give him safe passage while your heart fractures.
inspired_by: News Reporter Discovers Her Source Was Her Daughter All Along

title: The Threshold of Goodbye
instruction: You're leaving someone you love because you must—not because the love died, but because staying would destroy you both. Begin speaking with the bittersweet joy of memories: recall the moments that made you laugh, the tenderness you shared, the beauty of what you built together. But let the grief leak in—notice when your smile falters, when gratitude tangles with resentment, when love and anger exist simultaneously. Don't resolve these contradictions. Feel the relief of leaving and the devastation of loss at the same time. Let hope for your future mix with despair about theirs. Allow yourself to be fiercely grateful for what was while being quietly furious about what it cost you. By the end, arrive at a place of complex acceptance: loving them completely while choosing yourself anyway, holding both the sweetness and the sorrow without needing one to cancel out the other.

title: The Apple of Memory
instruction: You're a young woman eating a crisp apple alone in your apartment, enjoying its sweetness and the crunch. At first, you feel a quiet contentment, relishing this simple pleasure. But as you look at the apple, the flavor triggers a vivid memory of someone you used to share apples with, and a gentle melancholy washes over you — not sadness, but a tender ache. Speak to yourself softly, between bites, letting the crunch and pauses shape your rhythm. Let your voice start light and satisfied, then gradually become more reflective, ending in a soft, wistful tone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call You'll Never Make
instruction: You're holding your phone at 3 AM, thumb hovering over your mother's contact, knowing you'll never actually press call. Start with that hollow, rational voice: 'She's better off not knowing. Clean break. Kinder this way.' But as you scroll through old texts or voicemails, something cracks—your voice catches on a memory of her laugh, a birthday, the way she says your name. The calm logic tries to reassert itself, but now there's moisture in your throat, a trembling you can't quite control. You whisper something you wish you could tell her, then pull back into that dangerous calm. End with you setting the phone down, the silence thick with all the love you're trying to convince yourself doesn't matter. This is the private moment before an irreversible choice, not a performance of sadness.

title: Excavating the Years Between Us
instruction: You are confronting your mother after years of feeling invisible, dismissed as the child who never quite succeeded. She's made another casual, cutting remark about your life choices. But this time, instead of shrinking, you stop her—and you begin to methodically, specifically name the victories she's never acknowledged. Start with your voice shaking, defensive, almost pleading for her to see you. But as you detail each genuine accomplishment, each moment you survived when she thought you'd fail, each way you've grown beyond her expectations, let your anger transform into something more powerful: self-possession. By the end, you're no longer asking for her validation—you're standing in your own truth, whether she sees it or not. Your voice should move from wounded child to grounded adult.

title: The Daughter Who Became the Jailer
instruction: You are confronting your estranged daughter who has become a corrections officer—the very institution that destroyed your family. Begin with bitter pride at her 'success,' laced with caustic sarcasm about how she's become everything you ran from. As she responds with cold professionalism, let your anger ignite—accuse her of abandoning who she was, of betraying the family's pain. But when she finally breaks and reveals she took this job to understand why you couldn't stay, to walk in the system that swallowed you, your rage must shatter into devastated recognition. End in a place where anger and love are indistinguishable, where you're simultaneously furious at her sacrifice and shattered by her loyalty. Your voice should burn, then break, then tremble with a love you don't know how to express.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence She Kept
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging mother, finally ready to speak about the abuse she witnessed but never stopped. You begin carefully, voice controlled, almost gentle—you've rehearsed this. But as you lay out memories she's always dismissed, your control starts fracturing. Your voice rises, sharpens with decades of buried rage. You hear yourself becoming cruel, saying things you swore you wouldn't say. Then she reaches for your hand, and suddenly you're both the furious adult and the frightened child who needed her. Your anger collapses into something more devastating—not rage, but bewildered grief. Why didn't you protect me? The question comes out broken, almost childlike. You're crying now, but still demanding answers, your voice oscillating between accusation and desperate need for her to finally, finally see you.
inspired_by: Medieval Executioner Meets the Condemned Man Who Was His Childhood Friend

title: Laughing Through the Eulogy You Never Wanted to Give
instruction: You're standing at a memorial, about to speak about your best friend who died suddenly, senselessly. Begin with a story that makes you laugh—really laugh—because that's what they would have wanted: 'She once convinced me to steal a shopping cart at 2 AM and—' You're genuinely amused, voice bright with the memory. But mid-laugh, it catches. Your voice wavers between laughter and tears, unable to choose: 'God, she was so stupid sometimes, so absolutely—' You can't finish. You're crying now but still trying to laugh, voice breaking into pieces: 'She would hate this. She would hate me crying.' The laughter comes again, but it's soaked in grief, almost hysterical. Then you find something like peace, voice softening to profound gratitude even as tears stream down: 'Thank you. For every ridiculous, beautiful moment. For making me laugh even now.' End with your voice full of impossible contradictions—devastated but grateful, broken but somehow whole: 'I'm so lucky I knew you. I'm so destroyed that I did.'
inspired_by: High Wire Act: The Final Steps Toward the Platform

title: The Last Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling from a secure line. Tomorrow you deploy on a mission you know you won't return from—you've volunteered for it. Start with forced cheerfulness, asking about their day, their life, keeping your voice light. But as they talk, something breaks in you. The gratitude floods in—for every fight you had, every stupid argument, every moment of their existence. Your voice fractures as you try to tell them what they've meant without saying goodbye. End with a whispered confession of how proud you are of who they've become, your throat tight with the weight of never seeing them again. Let the love and the loss war in every word.
inspired_by: Recovery: Choosing Yourself Over the Addiction

title: The Last Thank You
instruction: You are at a quiet park bench, speaking to a friend who has been with you through your diagnosis. Mid-sentence, you feel the familiar tremor in your hand, and your voice wavers. Start with a wave of genuine gratitude—warm and full—but as you continue, the fear of losing your ability to speak creeps in, tightening your throat. Let your volume drop, and fight to keep your words clear. End with a fragile smile, holding onto hope even as your voice cracks.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Fear (extremely present)

title: The Final Presentation of the Day
instruction: You are a teenager in a crowded classroom, about to give the last presentation of the school day. You force yourself to stand tall and project your voice with deliberate emphasis on key terms, trying to push through the heaviness in your bones. As you speak, your concentration wavers — you stumble over a word, pause to reorient yourself, and your volume slips when the exhaustion catches up. By your final sentence, the 'teacher voice' crumbles; your tone becomes quieter, more honest, as if admitting to yourself how drained you really are.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Time I'll Say Your Name
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is slipping away, and you finally understand this is goodbye. Begin with your voice catching on their name, tender and almost playful, remembering who they were when they were whole: 'Remember when you used to...' Let nostalgia wash over you, soft laughter mixed with the first hints of tears. Then the shift comes—your breathing changes as reality crashes in. Your voice drops to something rawer: 'I'm not ready. I need you to know...' Now you're racing against time, words tumbling out—gratitude, apologies, love—all the things you should have said years ago. End in whispered devastation, saying their name one final time, knowing they might not hear it, feeling the world rearrange itself around their absence.

title: Reading Your Child's Last Letter Before They Leave Forever
instruction: You're alone in your child's empty bedroom, holding the letter they left before departing on a one-way journey to a distant colony. You begin reading it aloud, voice steady with disbelief. As the words sink in—their gratitude, their apology, their love—your composure fractures. Your voice thickens, breaks, recovers. You try to keep reading but certain phrases make you stop entirely, breath catching. By the final paragraph where they say goodbye, you're barely whispering, fighting through tears to honor their words by finishing. The letter trembles in your hands. Start with numb shock, move through rising grief, end in quiet devastation mixed with fierce pride.

title: Breathless and Bitter
instruction: You’re a teenager, just punched in the gut, now doubled over on the pavement. The person who hit you is the one your crush keeps smiling at, and you’re gasping for air, your stomach cramping. Start with the raw shock of the impact—every word scraped out between pained breaths, a grunt or two as you try to stand. As you straighten, your voice shifts from physical distress to a trembling, resentful whisper: you’re not just hurt, you’re sick with envy that they got what you want. Let your voice catch and waver, then harden into a bitter, broken edge. End with a quiet, spiteful accusation that fades into more labored breathing.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Themselves
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father why their absence shaped you, but you're not yelling—you're explaining with dangerous calm. Start controlled, almost clinical, describing what you needed as a child. But as you detail specific moments—birthdays they missed, promises broken, the times you waited and they never came—your voice tightens with suppressed rage. Let that rage surface, not as shouting but as something sharper, more cutting. Then, devastatingly, let it collapse into the child's voice underneath: the part of you that still just wanted them to stay. End with a question you've needed to ask for decades, your voice small and broken, finally admitting the need you've spent your life denying.

title: Weirdo in the Flower Shop
instruction: You're a 16-year-old guy with a deep voice and a face that turns red way too easily. You're in a flower shop with a girl you've had a crush on all year. She asks you to hold the baby's breath while she picks tulips. You start making jokes about how you probably look like a mob boss holding this delicate little flower. Your throat tightens embarrassingly on the word 'mob,' which makes you laugh harder. She doesn't laugh — she just smiles, and that silent approval makes your voice crack into a higher pitch. Your goal is to keep the easy, teasing rhythm alive, but you feel your pulse spiking. By the end, you drop the playful act and let a sincere, scared-of-how-much-this-matters softness creep into your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Unburying the Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father after twenty years of silence about the night he abandoned the family. You've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times, kept your voice measured, your arguments logical. Begin controlled, almost cold, reciting the facts like a prosecutor. But as you speak, something primal begins to surface—the child inside you who waited by the window. Let your voice crack, let sounds emerge that aren't quite words. Build to a visceral, physical explosion of rage that's been buried in your body for decades—roar, keen, make sounds you've never made before, sounds that come from your gut and your bones. Then, in the aftermath of that release, let yourself break down into the vulnerability you've protected all these years: become the small child again, asking the simple question 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in raw, undefended openness—either toward forgiveness or toward finally accepting the wound.
inspired_by: Actor is emotionally blocked before rehearsal or performance and cannot access deep feeling

title: The Whispered Confession With a Twist
instruction: In the dark, whisper a confession to someone sleeping beside you—something you've never said aloud. Begin with careful, trembling vulnerability. Then, mid-confession, imagine their response in the most unexpected way possible: they laugh, they're relieved, they confess something worse, or they already knew. Let this imagined response change your confession entirely. What if instead of fear, you feel liberated? What if your secret becomes funny, or small, or transforms into something else entirely? End with an emotional texture completely different from where you started—perhaps quiet joy, bewilderment, or a strange new kind of intimacy with the truth.

title: Telling Someone Their Fly Is Down at Their Wedding
instruction: You're the best man and the groom's fly is down during photos. Whisper to him while maintaining a photo smile — the sound of speaking through clenched smiling teeth. He doesn't hear you. Whisper louder. Still smiling. 'YOUR. FLY.' Now the photographer wants a serious photo. You're dying inside. Finally resort to pointing, which gets captured forever. Include his horrified realization and your simultaneous relief and shared suppressed laughter that threatens to explode.

title: Breaking Point Lullaby
instruction: You are a parent holding your screaming infant at 3 AM, and you are completely shattered. Begin with fierce, desperate attempts to soothe them—your voice is strained, nearly shouting over their cries to be heard, to make them stop. Feel your protective love collide with your absolute exhaustion and mounting rage at your own helplessness. Your voice cracks between tender pleas and barely contained fury at a tiny person who cannot understand you. Mid-way, you break—sobbing apologies to your child for your anger, for not being enough, for being so terribly human. Your voice dissolves into raw, gasping tears. End with a whispered lullaby sung through your weeping, fierce love and utter depletion existing in the same breath. Your voice is wrecked but still singing. Still trying. Still here.

title: The Last Joke
instruction: You are an older man, lying on the ground after an accident, bleeding heavily from a deep wound in your side. Your son is kneeling beside you, trying to help. Start by forcing a weak grin — you want to make him laugh, to show him you're okay. Your voice is still loud, a little shaky but proud, as you joke about tripping over your own feet. But as you speak, the cold sets in. Your words start to lose power. Mid-sentence, you lose your train of thought, pause, feel the wet ground, then continue — quieter, slower, your hope leaking out. By the end, you're whispering, staring at the sky, trying to believe you'll see your grandson again. Let the amusement drain away, replaced by a fragile, fading hope.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Amusement (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: One More Lap
instruction: You are an older man, proud and hyper-masculine, swimming laps alone at a crowded pool. You're on your 49th lap, determined to hit 50 before the lifeguard blows the whistle. Your body aches, water keeps sloshing into your mouth, and you're annoyed at a kid splashing in the lane next to you. Start with clipped, irritable bursts as you mutter complaints between gasps—'Damned kid... can't steer straight...'—then feel a surge as you realize your rhythm is flawless, your pace is personal-best speed. By the final 10 meters, let triumph crack through your voice, still breathless, but now with a fierce, wet laugh: 'Fifty... hell yeah... told you... never quit.' The words must come out in 1-2 syllable gasps, with natural sputters and gurgles, as if you're really fighting for air.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Morning Flight
instruction: You're sitting with someone you love deeply—a parent, a child, a soulmate—and you both know they're leaving on a journey they won't return from. Maybe it's a terminal diagnosis and they're choosing medical assistance in dying. Maybe it's a one-way space mission. You start trying to be strong, practical, talking about logistics and final wishes. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves. Your voice breaks from composed to desperate. You cycle between trying to memorize their face, asking impossible questions ('What do I do when I need you?'), moments of anger at the unfairness, collapsing into raw pleading, then forcing yourself back to tenderness because you don't want these final words to be pain. End in a whispered acceptance that's half-genuine peace, half-unbearable grief.
inspired_by: Meth Psychosis: Convincing Yourself of a Delusion

title: The Script You Memorized
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a childhood of emotional neglect, and you came prepared with rehearsed points—calm, measured, controlled. But as you speak, their dismissiveness or their desperate attempts to deflect ignite something deeper in you. Your carefully scripted complaints transform into raw, unfiltered pain and rage. Move from controlled explanation to explosive hurt, then suddenly collapse into the small child you once were—your voice shifting from anger to a broken plea for them to just hear you, just once. Let the adult facade crumble completely, revealing the wounded child still begging to be seen.

title: The Trembling Discovery
instruction: You are an older woman who has just climbed a steep, rocky trail to reach a secluded overlook. Your legs are shaking, your arms tremble, and your voice quivers with exhaustion. As you catch your breath, you notice a rare, glowing mushroom at the base of a tree—something you’ve only read about. Start by muttering complaints about your aching body, then let genuine curiosity take over. Your voice should carry the physical tremor, but your tone shifts from weary irritation to a hushed, fascinated wonder. Let the shaking affect your articulation, but the interest grows clearer as you speak.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Savoring the Smell of Freshly Baked Bread Filling the Kitchen
instruction: Breathe in deeply, letting the warm, yeasty aroma of fresh bread fill your senses. Describe the comforting smell, the hints of sweetness and warmth, and the way it fills the entire room with coziness. Speak softly and with a smile, as if each breath of the aroma wraps you in comfort, bringing memories of home and warmth.

title: Whispering to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma—a lover, a best friend—and the doctors say they might still hear you. Your voice starts tender but guarded, talking about mundane things, safe things. Then you allow yourself to say what you never said when they were awake: a confession of love, or hurt, or the truth about something you did. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile, as if speaking too loudly would shatter you both. Let the words catch in your throat, let silence hold weight. As you speak, you move between apology and gratitude, between regret and desperate hope. End with the simplest thing—maybe 'please stay' or 'I'm not ready'—your voice so soft it's almost not there, but carrying everything.
inspired_by: Being Told You're Not Good Enough

title: The Gratitude You Resent
instruction: You're at your childhood best friend's wedding reception. You're giving a toast, microphone in hand, everyone watching with warm, expectant faces. You begin by genuinely celebrating them—let yourself feel true joy for their happiness, notice the glow on their face, the love in the room, the beauty of this moment. But as you speak, become increasingly aware of other sensations: the tight feeling in your chest, the forced brightness of your smile, the wine glass trembling slightly in your other hand, the acute awareness that you're utterly alone while celebrating their partnership. Let your toast slowly reveal the complex truth—you ARE happy for them, desperately happy, but you're also drowning in loneliness, grateful for their friendship but resentful that they're moving into a life that doesn't have room for you the way it used to. Don't resolve it neatly. End suspended between genuine celebration and barely suppressed grief, your voice cracking on words of congratulation that are completely real and completely painful.

title: Sunset Through the Visor
instruction: You're a mother on a quiet ride with your young child in a sidecar. You've pulled over at a scenic overlook just as the sun dips low through autumn trees, the light golden and endless. You're still in your full-face helmet, and your voice feels muffled and strange as you speak to your child, who is trying to get your attention but you're lost in the beauty. Start with a quiet, contemplative awe — the words come out slow, almost a whisper against the padded interior. Then your child makes a silly face or sound, and you burst into deep, affectionate amusement, your voice booming cheerfully inside the helmet, tapering into a warm, hushed wonder as you realize you're both seeing the same perfect moment.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (clearly present), Amusement (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your father exactly how his absence shaped you, and you start with careful, measured words because you've rehearsed this confrontation for years. But as you speak, the script you planned crumbles, and raw anger surges forward—not the cold, controlled anger you wanted, but hot, messy rage mixed with the desperate need for him to finally understand. Then, unexpectedly, the anger cracks open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted to be enough. Your voice must travel from controlled accusation to furious demand to broken pleading. Let him hear you transform from prosecutor to wounded child, even as you hate yourself for still needing his validation.
inspired_by: Feigning Confidence During a Performance Despite Stage Fright

title: Melting Into Confession
instruction: Late at night, lying in bed next to your partner, you whisper a secret you've never told anyone—something you're deeply ashamed of. Begin with your body tense, your voice barely audible, each word requiring tremendous effort to push out. Your muscles are tight with fear of judgment and rejection. As you continue speaking, imagine the secret itself having physical weight that gradually releases from your body with each revealed detail. Your breathing deepens, your limbs grow heavier and more relaxed against the mattress, your voice becomes softer but somehow clearer. By the end, you're not whispering from fear but from intimacy. The confession has made you physically heavier, more grounded, more present—no longer holding yourself above the moment but sinking fully into it.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner About Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner who's asleep, finally saying aloud what you've known for months - that you have to leave them. Your voice is barely audible, tender with devastating sadness: 'I can't do this anymore.' Each whispered sentence is both a confession and a goodbye. Your throat keeps closing around the words as you tell their sleeping form what you could never say to their face: 'You're a good person. That's what makes this so hard.' Your voice carries bone-deep exhaustion mixed with terrible love. You're crying silently, trying not to wake them because you're not strong enough for their eyes to open. End with your voice breaking on a whispered 'I'm so sorry' that's more breath than sound, knowing tomorrow you'll pretend this conversation never happened.

title: The Hallelujah Goodbye
instruction: You're singing a song of gratitude and your heart is simultaneously breaking into a thousand pieces. Someone saved your life—pulled you from darkness, loved you back to wholeness—and now they're gone. Death, departure, the ending of all things. Start singing with a smile in your voice, genuine joy for what they gave you. Let laughter bubble through the first verse as you remember the beautiful moments. But feel the grief rising beneath the gratitude. Your voice should shimmer with both emotions at once—singing 'thank you' while crying 'don't go.' By the chorus, you're laughing and sobbing simultaneously, unable to separate the joy from the sorrow because they're the same thing. The gratitude IS the grief. The grief IS the love. End with a note that's pure contradiction: peaceful and shattered, celebratory and devastated, a sound that says 'I'm so glad you existed' and 'I can't bear that you're gone' in the same breath.

title: The Intervention You Never Wanted
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the childhood they gave you—the neglect, the emotional absence, the ways they failed you that you've carried for decades. Start with trembling restraint, your words careful and measured because you've rehearsed this a thousand times but never had the courage to say it. Build as your parent deflects or minimizes, your voice growing stronger, angrier, demanding to be seen and heard for once in your life. Then shatter when they finally break down and admit the truth—their own pain, their failures, their regret. Your rage collapses into complicated grief. You're furious and heartbroken and somehow, impossibly, you still love them. End in exhausted tenderness, both of you wounded, both of you finally honest. Your voice should move from controlled tension to explosive release to quiet, aching understanding.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Well: Shouting Up

title: The Last Cup on the Fire Escape
instruction: You're a young woman who just polished off her third energy drink of the night. You're sitting on a cold metal fire escape, hugging your knees, watching the city blur. Your body is buzzing—you can't stop fidgeting, blinking too fast, tapping your toes. You're on the phone with your best friend, but you haven't spoken in a while. You wanted to call and laugh, to feel normal, but now a wave of sadness catches you off guard. Start by trying to keep your voice light, almost giddy from the caffeine, but let the sadness leak through as you lose the thread of a happy story. By the end, a small, quiet contentment settles in—not joy, just a fragile acceptance of the mess you're in.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (extremely present), Contentment (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: After the Fire
instruction: You've just had explosive, passionate, makeup sex with your ex after months of bitter silence. You're both still breathless, skin still electric, bodies still tangled. Start in pure physical sensation—overwhelming, almost shocking. Your guard is completely down. In this raw, undefended state, begin speaking from pure impulse about what you see in them in this moment, what you've always seen—their beauty, their fire, the specific qualities that drew you together. Let the words spill out unfiltered as your breathing slows. Feel the dangerous territory you're entering: desire mixed with memory, pleasure mixed with old wounds. Let the intensity shift from purely physical to emotionally exposed. End in a complex, uncomfortable space—still wanting them, but now painfully aware of both the connection and the impossibility, ecstasy giving way to an aching question neither of you can answer.

title: The Lie Catches Up
instruction: You are an 8-year-old boy caught in a lie. Your father’s hand tightens around your collar, pressing against your throat. Your voice is strained, raspy, each word fighting for air. Start with a fearful, rushed confession—stuttering, gasping, voice cracking. Then he releases you. Feel the flood of relief as you breathe in deeply, your words slow, shaky, but lighter. Let your body sag, your pitch wobble, and your tone soften as the fear drains into exhausted relief.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Last Swim Before the Diagnosis
instruction: You're floating in the lake where you learned to swim as a child, but this is the last time before tomorrow's surgery—the one with no guarantees. Start in that weightless peace, describing the water holding you, the sky above. But as you float, memories flood in: your daughter's laugh, your father teaching you to float right here, all the summers you took for granted. Your tranquility fractures into quiet grief, then transforms into fierce gratitude for every single moment you've had. Let your voice crack with the weight of loving this life so much it hurts. End not in peace, but in a raw, aching appreciation that's almost unbearable.
inspired_by: Floating on Your Back in a Calm Lake

title: The Alarm at 3 AM
instruction: You are an elderly man who hasn't slept in three nights. It's 3 AM and your ancient alarm clock has started beeping for no reason—you can't find the off switch. Your body aches, your eyes burn, but you're trying to laugh at the absurdity. Begin with a hollow, amused mutter about the situation, but as you fumble and the beeping continues, let raw anger rise—tight, frustrated, almost shaking. End with a quiet, exhausted sigh as you finally smash the clock, the anger dissolving into empty stillness. Let your voice stay compressed, with no real peaks, and let your words trail off or cut short as you lose the thought. Speak about 50–70 words total, reacting organically to the clock's noise and your own tired hands.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Anger (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Hour Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in the pre-dawn hours, and you know these are her final moments. Begin by feeling numb, almost in shock, unable to fully process what's happening. As you sit with her, allow yourself to become aware of everything you're feeling in real-time—the scratchy hospital blanket under your palm, the antiseptic smell, your exhaustion, your racing thoughts about what you should have said years ago. Speak quietly to her, but also to yourself, noticing out loud each feeling as it surfaces: the guilt, the love, the fear, the gratitude, even the irritation at the fluorescent light flickering. Let your emotional state shift and deepen as you stay present with each sensation and emotion. By the end, arrive at a place of profound, clear-eyed acceptance and connection, having moved through layers of defended feelings to raw presence.

title: The Last Hour Before the Morphine
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour of clarity before the palliative sedation begins. She's alert now, but you both know this is your last real conversation. Begin with careful, almost businesslike composure—you've been holding yourself together for days. As you talk, let her hand in yours, the smell of the hospital room, the particular way the afternoon light falls across her face gradually break down your defenses. Let memories flood in: her kitchen, her laugh, the specific texture of her voice saying your name. End in a place of raw, unguarded grief mixed with profound gratitude for this final moment of connection. Your voice should transform from controlled and steady to broken and tender.
inspired_by: An actor is shooting a film out of sequence and needs to maintain character consistency

title: Teaching Them a Song They Taught You: Joy in the Unraveling
instruction: Your parent taught you a lullaby when you were small. Now, they've forgotten it—forgotten they ever sang it. You're teaching it back to them, line by line, and somehow, impossibly, this is the most beautiful afternoon you've had in months. Your voice is playful, almost laughing as you sing incorrectly on purpose so they can 'correct' you, giving them small moments of competence. They stumble over words, mix up verses, and you gently guide them back. You're both laughing—really laughing—at the mistakes. But underneath your laughter, your voice carries the weight of reversal: you're parenting your parent, teaching them what they gave you. By the end, as you sing it together one last time, your voice is suffused with gratitude and grief intertwined. You're celebrating this moment of connection while mourning the irony of it. Your final words are whispered through smiling tears: 'You taught me this. You gave me everything.' Capture pure love that exists alongside and within heartbreak—joy that doesn't erase sadness but lives with it.
inspired_by: Parent with Dementia Has a Confused Moment: Patient Repetition

title: Screaming at God After Your Child's Diagnosis
instruction: You're alone in your car in a hospital parking lot after the oncologist told you your child has six months. Start with fury—'How DARE you! She's eight years old!'—your voice cracking with rage. Pound the steering wheel, let your voice go ragged and raw. Then let that rage fracture into desperate bargaining: 'Take me instead, please, please take me instead,' your voice climbing and breaking. But mid-sentence, you collapse into the reality that no one's listening, that this is happening, that your child is dying and you can't fix it. Your voice drops to a whisper, then rises again—not in anger but in primal fear: 'I don't know how to watch her die. I don't know how to be strong enough.' End with your voice shaking between fierce protective love—'I'll make every day beautiful for her'—and the utterly helpless acknowledgment that beautiful days won't save her. Let your final words carry both the roar of a parent's love and the whisper of human powerlessness.
inspired_by: Realizing You're the Toxic One in This Relationship

title: Dancing in the Hospital Room Where They'll Die Tomorrow
instruction: Your spouse is in hospice. Tomorrow they'll begin palliative sedation—this is your last conversation. They've asked you to dance with them one final time, here in this sterile room with its beeping machines. Start with tearful resistance—this is absurd, inappropriate, you can't, it's too much. Let them coax you into it. As you begin to move together, find genuine joy—remember your wedding, that trip to Paris, the kitchen dance parties. Laugh at the absurdity, at the IV pole you're dancing around, at their terrible singing. Let that laughter and grief exist simultaneously. Your voice should carry both as you reminisce, telling stories that make you both laugh until you're crying, crying until you're laughing. Then, still swaying, let the weight of tomorrow enter your voice. Thank them—for everything, for the life, for loving you, for fighting so hard. Tell them it's okay to let go. End with a promise that you'll be okay eventually, a beautiful lie spoken with such love they can believe it. Let your voice be full of contradictions: gratitude and devastation, peace and anguish, goodbye and forever.
inspired_by: Two Strangers Stuck in an Elevator: Entire Relationship Arc

title: Reading the Lies in Your Face
instruction: You're confronting your partner who you suspect has been unfaithful. But instead of launching into accusations, you force yourself to truly study them—their micro-expressions, the way they're breathing, where they won't let their eyes land. Start with surface observations: are their arms crossed? Are they looking away? Then go deeper: what's that flutter in their jaw? What's the quality of their silence? Let yourself wonder: what are they protecting? What are they desperate for me not to see? As you observe them with this forensic attention, your anger should give way to something more complex—perhaps a devastating understanding, or unexpected compassion mixed with fury. By the end, let what you've truly seen in their face change what you came here to say.

title: The Ghost Witness
instruction: You are a ghost observing your own funeral. Speak as if youre reacting to the people who attend, sharing regrets, relief, or resentment. Drift between moments of sadness, curiosity, and even humor as you narrate what you see and wish you could change.

title: The Body Keeps Score
instruction: You're in the middle of an intense physical experience—running until your lungs burn, or in the grip of passionate intimacy, or experiencing a tattoo needle, or holding an ice cube until your hand screams. Begin by fighting the sensation, tensing against it, telling yourself you can't handle it, you shouldn't want it, you're not strong enough for intensity. Let your voice strain with resistance. Then, mid-experience, surrender into it—not by numbing out, but by claiming it. Let pleasure and pain blur. Your voice shifts from resistance to ownership: 'I can hold this. I deserve to feel everything. I am strong enough for this.' End in a state of fierce, embodied power—sweating, breathless, transformed by your own capacity to withstand and embrace intensity.

title: Confessing to the Sleeping Room
instruction: Your best friend is in a coma, and you're confessing something you never had the courage to say. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tentative: 'I need to tell you something, and maybe it's selfish to do it now, when you can't even hear me.' Your throat tightens with each word: 'I've been in love with you for seven years. Every time you told me about someone new, it broke something in me.' There's a soft, sad laugh: 'God, I'm pathetic, aren't I? Waiting until you can't respond.' Your voice drops even lower, intimate and aching: 'I memorized the way you laugh. The exact shade of your eyes in sunlight.' Tears are falling silently now: 'Please wake up. Please. I don't need you to love me back, I just need you to be alive in this world.' You take their hand, voice catching: 'I'd give anything—anything—to hear you make fun of me for this. Please give me that chance.'

title: The Wedding Toast You Won't Give
instruction: You're alone in your hotel room before your best friend's wedding (or your ex's wedding, or your sibling's wedding to someone you distrust). You're supposed to give a toast, and you've written something polite and warm. But standing here alone, you let yourself feel the complicated truth. Begin by trying to rehearse the 'appropriate' toast, but let your real feelings interrupt. You're genuinely happy for them, but you're also devastated—maybe because you're losing them, or because you wanted this for yourself, or because you know something about this marriage they don't. Speak both truths out loud: the love and the loss, the joy and the jealousy, the celebration and the grief. Let your voice break between laughing and crying. Don't resolve it into one clean emotion. End holding both the genuine happiness for them and the aching sadness for yourself, fully feeling the beautiful, terrible complexity of loving someone and letting them go.

title: The Truth About Why I Left: Confronting the Caregiver Who Burned Out
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who abandoned you when you needed them most—during your cancer treatment, your financial crisis, your darkest hour. Begin with cold, controlled rage barely concealed beneath polite words: 'I understand you had your reasons.' But as they try to explain—their own collapse, their inability to watch you suffer, their guilt—you interrupt with raw accusations. Then something breaks. They reveal they were suicidal, that staying would have destroyed them. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it tangles with horror, with reluctant understanding, with the sickening realization that there were no good choices. End in a place of painful, incomplete acceptance. Let the emotions collide messily—this isn't resolution, it's two people damaged by impossible circumstances.
inspired_by: Concealing Disgust While Handling Something Unpleasant

title: The Keepsake
instruction: You are an older woman with a gentle, feminine voice, sitting alone in a quiet room. You rummage through a small velvet box filled with trinkets—fabric rustles, zipper sounds. You're looking for a specific photograph, mumbling to yourself about where it could be. As your fingers find an old pressed flower, your infatuation with the person who gave it to you blooms. You speak to the flower as if it were them, your voice softening into a tender, almost girlish tone. The search ends in a wistful sigh, the initial frustration replaced by a delicate ache of love.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Breath Hold Challenge: Pushing Past Safety Thresholds
instruction: You're underwater holding your breath, narrating internally. Your voice starts controlled, almost meditative. 'Thirty seconds. Sixty seconds. Feeling good.' But at a minute-thirty, something shifts. Your diaphragm begins demanding air and your internal narration becomes less poetic and more desperate. 'Ninety seconds. Can't... soon.' Your voice is muffled by the fact that you're not actually speaking but your mind is screaming. Include the moment where staying under becomes genuinely dangerous—the mammalian diving reflex kicking in, your body pushing panic signals. Your internal voice becomes a fight between rational thought ('three more seconds') and pure animal instinct ('NOW NOW NOW'). Your voice surfaces with a gasp that's almost violent.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're at your parent's bedside in their final hours, and they're asking you to let them go—to stop fighting for one more treatment, one more day. Begin with fierce, desperate control: 'No, we're not giving up, there's still—' Your voice cracks as you try to hold onto them through sheer will. They gently challenge you, and your resistance breaks into raw grief: 'I'm not ready, I don't know how to be in the world without you.' Feel the unbearable weight of being asked to release the person who made you. By the end, through tears, you find a place of devastating tenderness: 'I love you enough to say... go. It's okay. I'll be okay.' Let your voice move from strangled control to whispered, broken grace.

title: Midnight Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something about yourself that you're deeply ashamed of or afraid will make them leave. Begin with your voice almost inaudible, your body tense, sharing only the edges of the truth. As you continue speaking in the darkness, let each sentence pull you deeper into vulnerability. Allow long silences between thoughts. Let your breathing be audible. Permit yourself to touch your own face, your chest, your throat as you speak—grounding yourself in your body as protection dissolves. Move from fragmented, careful phrases to complete, undefended truth. By the end, you should feel completely exposed, but also lighter—as if speaking it aloud has transformed the secret from poison into simply a fact about who you are.

title: The Champion's Belch
instruction: You're a 16-year-old alone in your room after chugging an entire liter of soda in under a minute. The burp that erupts is deep, guttural, and shakes your chest—your voice drops into a monstrous fry as it escapes. At first, you're startled by the sound, but as it rumbles on, a grin spreads across your face. Let the initial surprise shift into a triumphant, elated celebration—you've just set a personal record. Your voice should start with a surprised, shaky quality, then grow into a proud, booming laugh that still carries the rumbling echo of the burp.

title: The Way Light Catches Their Hair
instruction: You're watching your child leave home for the last time—going to college, getting married, moving across the world. You're standing in the doorway, bags already in the car. You should be happy for them; you are happy for them. Begin there: smiling, being supportive, holding it together, saying encouraging things. But then the afternoon sun comes through the window and catches their hair a certain way—the exact way it did when they were three years old and you held them after a nightmare. Stop looking at their adult face, their confident posture, their excitement. Look only at how that light illuminates those same strands of hair. Focus on just that detail—that specific quality of light turning their hair golden at the edges, exactly as it did fifteen years ago. Your controlled happiness must splinter. Let gratitude and devastating loss flood through you simultaneously. Your voice should crack between telling them how proud you are and begging time to stop. Speak about the future while your attention stays locked on that hair, on that light, on the baby who's already gone.

title: Finding Peace While Confessing Your Deception to a Room of Strangers
instruction: You're at a meeting for people who've lived with hidden shame. You stand to speak, and there's nervous laughter in your voice: 'God, I can't believe I'm actually saying this out loud.' You begin to tell them about your fabricated credentials, but something unexpected happens—as you speak the truth, relief washes over you. Your voice wavers between tears and incredulous joy: 'I've been so tired. So incredibly tired.' You're crying, but there's lightness creeping in, almost giddy disbelief at your own liberation. 'For twenty years I've been terrified someone would find out, and now... now I'm just telling you.' Your voice breaks with emotion, but it's gratitude mixed with grief for all the years you lost to fear. End with quiet, wondering acceptance, voice soft and almost laughing through tears: 'I'm a fraud. I'm a complete fraud. And somehow... somehow that's okay.'

title: The Weight of the World
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy, completely drained after a grueling 12-hour shift helping your father haul debris after a storm. Your body aches in every muscle; you can barely stand, and your voice is thin and cost-heavy, like every word is pulled from a well running dry. Start by mumbling to yourself about how tired you are — each pause punctuated by a heavy, shaky inhale. Then you notice your father nearby, looking just as exhausted, though he won't admit it. Something shifts inside you: you swallow hard, straighten your shoulders a little, and say something to him — not loud, but with a new, ragged dignity — acknowledging his sacrifice. At the end, your voice might crack, not from weakness, but because you feel fierce, tired pride.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis and you're recording a message for your loved ones to play at your funeral. Start reading your prepared, dignified words, but halfway through you realize how absurd this is - you're eulogizing yourself - and you start to laugh. It's real laughter, the kind that catches you off guard. But the laughter tangles with tears because you're also terrified and this is real and you won't be there to see their faces. Your voice oscillates between giggles and sobs, making terrible jokes about your own death while your voice breaks with grief. You're grateful for the life you had - your voice softens with genuine wonder at the beauty of it - while simultaneously raging against losing it. End with a strange, peaceful joy breaking through the sadness, your voice settling into something almost serene as you say 'I was here. I was really here.' It's an ending and a celebration at once.

title: The Door You Couldn't Open
instruction: Physically and vocally, recreate a moment when your body froze in fear or shame—perhaps you stood outside a door you were too afraid to open, or your voice disappeared when you most needed it, or you felt paralyzed while something precious was taken from you. Begin by embodying that physical helplessness: shallow breathing, clenched muscles, a voice that can barely make sound. Feel the temperature of that day, the texture of the door handle or the fabric you gripped. Then, explosively, re-create the moment with your body moving differently: you open the door, you scream with full voice, you fight back with every cell. The sensation should shift from frozen terror to fierce, wild power—your voice growing from a choked whisper to a roar. End in breathless triumph mixed with grief for the younger you who couldn't do this then.

title: The Last Coherent Goodbye
instruction: You're in the final stages of dementia, and you suddenly have one last moment of clarity with your adult child. You recognize them completely for the first time in months. You have maybe two minutes before you slip away again forever, and you need to say everything: how proud you are, how sorry you are for forgetting them, how much you've always loved them. Your words come faster as you feel the clarity fading, stumbling over memories that are already blurring again. End with your voice softening into confusion, reaching for their name but grasping at shadows, the light in your eyes dimming even as you try to hold on.

title: The Shower After the Betrayal
instruction: You've just discovered a devastating betrayal and you're standing alone in the shower, water running over you. Start breathing normally, but as you let yourself fully inhabit this moment, something breaks. The water keeps running, indifferent to your transformation.

title: Folding Their Clothes for the Last Time
instruction: You're alone, putting away the belongings of someone who's gone, speaking to them in whispers as if they can still hear. Let your words emerge from that liminal space between waking and dreaming, where you're saying things you've never been able to say before: memories, confessions, gratitude, regrets. As you speak, allow your consciousness to drift, becoming less guarded, more raw. By the end, you realize they've stopped breathing, and a strange clarity floods through you—a piercing alertness mixed with profound peace.

title: Whispered Confession in the Dark
instruction: Late at night, lying beside someone who loves you, you finally whisper the truth you've been hiding. Begin so quietly they have to lean in to hear: 'I need to tell you something.' Your voice is fragile, each word carefully placed because once spoken, nothing will be the same. 'I've been lying about...' and you start to build the confession, detail by painful detail, your throat tight. Each revelation makes you more vulnerable—'Every time I said it was okay, I was breaking inside.' The whisper becomes even softer, almost disappearing, as shame floods through you. But there's also relief, a tender unburdening. By the end, your voice is barely audible, catching on tears, but there's a thread of hope woven through the devastation—the quiet courage of finally being seen completely, even if it terrifies you.

title: Dust and Dignity
instruction: You are a young woman stumbling home through a sudden dust storm after a night of drinking. You're proud of surviving the party, but the wind and grit are making it hard to breathe. You've got a scarf over your mouth, but sand keeps getting in. Start by laughing at yourself, coughing, trying to shout to no one—feeling a bit wild and free. But as the storm gets worse, your voice turns raw, almost angry, as you realize you're lost and no one is coming. End with a quiet, fractured whisper—pride still there, but now mixed with fear and exhaustion.
emotions_sampled: Anger (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Peak of Spite
instruction: You are hiking a steep, punishing incline alone, late in the day. You’re exhausted, stopping every few steps to catch your breath, your legs burning. At first, you’re muttering complaints to yourself, annoyed at your own stubbornness for pushing so hard. But as you pause to look up at the summit, you realize someone you deeply resent is already up there, waiting — and your fatigue twists into a cold, quiet malice. Speak aloud to yourself, between gasps, letting your voice shift from tired frustration into a low, sharp satisfaction as you imagine the look on their face when you arrive. Let the words come in short, breathless bursts, with your tone darkening as you go.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Eulogy You Never Expected to Give
instruction: You're standing at the funeral of someone who hurt you deeply—an estranged sibling, a former friend, someone you had a complicated history with—and you've been asked to speak. Begin with your voice oddly light, almost laughing at the absurdity: 'I don't know why I'm up here... we barely spoke for ten years.' But as you continue, grief sneaks in through the cracks of your bitterness. Your voice wavers between humor and heartbreak—you're sharing a memory that's both painful and precious. Let gratitude emerge for what they gave you even through the hurt: 'You taught me... even when you broke my heart.' Your voice becomes softer, wonder mixing with sorrow as you realize forgiveness is happening right now, in this moment. End with your voice breaking beautifully—tears and laughter inseparable: 'I wish we'd had more time. I wish I'd said this when you could hear it. And somehow... somehow I'm grateful anyway.' You're finding peace in the middle of unresolved pain, and your voice carries both.

title: Last Words on the Summit: A Climber's Farewell to Their Child
instruction: You're at the peak, oxygen-deprived and injured, knowing you won't make it down. You're recording a final message to your child on your phone. Begin with fierce determination to say everything perfectly, but your oxygen-starved brain keeps failing you. Your words slur, you forget their age, you can't remember what you already said. Shift between crystal-clear moments of desperate love and confused rambling where you think they're actually there with you. Your breathing is labored, words cost everything. End in a place of unexpected peace—you're smiling through tears, your voice barely a whisper, telling them it's okay, you can see something beautiful, your anger at leaving them dissolving into gratitude for having known them at all. Let your voice fade as acceptance washes over you.

title: The Bedroom Confession
instruction: It's late at night. You and your partner are lying in the dark, and you finally whisper the secret you've been too ashamed to voice: your deepest insecurity, the thing you believe makes you unlovable. Your voice is barely audible, catching on tears: 'Sometimes I think you'll wake up and see what I really am and leave.' The vulnerability is terrifying—you're exposing the soft underbelly you've protected your whole life. Their response is tender, certain: 'That's the part of you I love most.' Let the words land slowly. Your breathing changes. You're not crying harder—you're crying differently, relief mixed with disbelief mixed with tentative trust. Your voice becomes softer, more open, like a hand unclenching. End with you breathing together in the darkness, your voice barely a whisper: 'I've never let anyone see this.' It's intimate, fragile, sacred.

title: The Last Rep
instruction: You're a 16-year-old trying to lift an old, rusted engine block onto a workbench at a garage while the older guys watch. You're deeply embarrassed that it's barely budging, and your voice comes out in strained, breath-held grunts as you force out words like 'yeah, almost there.' Your face is red, you're shaking, and you can barely speak because you're bracing your core. Just when you think you can't, you give it everything and slam it onto the bench. As you stand up and exhale explosively, your voice brightens into a triumphant, breathless 'got it!' with genuine pride.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Vigil: Whispering to Your Comatose Twin in the Last Hours
instruction: Your identical twin has been in a coma for three days. The doctors say they can't hear you, but you don't believe that. It's 3 AM and you're alone with them. Your voice is barely there—intimate, secret, the way you used to talk as children under blankets. You're telling them things you never said out loud: how you resented them, how you loved them more than anyone, how you don't know who you are without them. Your voice keeps catching, not from crying but from something deeper—the fear of speaking into silence that won't answer back. Move from confession to pleading to something like prayer. Let moments of quiet do the work. Your breath synchronizes with the machines. You're not performing grief—you're living in the space between holding on and letting go.
inspired_by: Historical: Underground Railroad Conductor Hides Escaped Slaves From Pursuers

title: The Last Phone Call From the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from a hospital bed. You have minutes, maybe an hour. You planned what you'd say—forgiveness, closure, the important stuff. But as you speak, notice what's actually moving through you right now: the anger still there, the sudden urge to laugh at an old memory, the trembling in your hands, the way your voice cracks unexpectedly. Let whatever's actually alive in you interrupt the script you rehearsed. Start with determined composure, trying to say what you 'should' say. End wherever the truth of this moment—messy, contradictory, raw—actually takes you. Don't perform dying; notice what you genuinely feel as time runs out.
inspired_by: Actor is premeditating — planning how to say lines and emotionalize them before getting there, functioning from a cerebral place

title: Holding Your Best Friend Back From Destroying Themselves
instruction: They're about to do something catastrophic and you're physically restraining them. Begin with fierce, almost violent urgency: 'STOP. Stop, stop, STOP!' Your voice should be raw, commanding, desperate. As they struggle, pour out everything—screaming truths about how much they matter, how their pain is destroying you too, accusations of selfishness mixed with declarations of love. Your voice cracks between rage and pleading: 'You don't get to do this! You don't get to—' Then suddenly collapse into broken sobbing, still holding them, your strength giving out: 'Please. Please don't make me lose you.' Your words become incoherent, just repeated 'please' and 'I can't.' Move from explosive protective fury through desperate reasoning to complete helpless collapse, showing both your power and your utter powerlessness.
inspired_by: Screaming Into Your Pillow So No One Hears

title: An Apology to a Future Self
instruction: Speak to your future self as if apologizing for choices youre making now. You should sound hopeful yet uncertain, as though aware these decisions may come back to haunt you, with small pauses as doubt creeps in.

title: Airport Terminal: Laughing Through Your Last Goodbye
instruction: Someone you love is leaving forever - deployment, witness protection, terminal illness taking them somewhere you can't follow. You've agreed: no tears, only good memories. You start with forced brightness, sharing a funny story, trying to sound normal, light, okay. But your laughter has an edge - too loud, then catching, then genuine for a moment before cracking. You're working so hard to keep your promise that your voice wavers between real joy at the memory and barely-suppressed grief. You lose yourself mid-story, laugh and sob in the same breath. End with gratitude that breaks you open: thanking them for loving you, voice simultaneously laughing and crying, finding genuine joy tangled inseparably with devastating loss. Let your voice move fluidly between laughter, tears, and something that's miraculously both.
inspired_by: Drunk Driving Pulled Over: Trying Not to Sound Drunk

title: The Tooth and the Memory
instruction: You are an elderly man in your kitchen, nursing a chronic toothache. You avoid opening your mouth fully, speak with a guarded, one-sided chew of words. Cold air makes you wince, so you pause and breathe carefully. You're contemplating a memory of your late wife making soup for you, but as you speak, a bitter note creeps in about how she's gone and you're left with this pain. Start with a tender, slow recollection, letting the pain intrude, then let bitterness shadow your words as you finish. Speak naturally, with all the little stops and starts of real thought.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Rush of a Memory
instruction: You are an older man alone in your apartment, high on cocaine. You pace and sniff loudly, voice too loud and fast, interrupting yourself mid-thought. Start bragging about an old business deal you won, full of grandiose energy. But as you try to describe the moment you realized you'd lost your best friend’s trust, your voice wavers, slows, and cracks—sniffing harder, swallowing awkwardly. End with a quiet, vulnerable admission, still high but suddenly pensive.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Split Ends
instruction: You're alone in your backyard at dusk, splitting a pile of firewood after drinking most of a bottle of whiskey. Each swing feels like a conversation you're having with yourself. Start with a grunt and a line that sounds like you're trying to prove something — maybe bravado from the booze, maybe anger at a recent breakup or job loss. Between swings, the words come out raw, breathless. Let the doubt creep in as your arms tire. Talk to the wood, to the empty space, to someone who isn't there. The fear shows up as your rhythm slows, your voice drops, and you stop swinging for a moment. End with a quieter, almost defeated realization — not a confession to anyone, just to the night air.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Doubt (very intensely present), Fear (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Plague of Thought
instruction: You are a teenage boy alone in a sweltering room, burning with fever. Your clothes are soaked, your lips cracked, and every word feels like it's fished out of a fog. You are trying desperately to concentrate—to decode a letter or solve a puzzle—because someone’s safety depends on it. Start with fierce, fragile focus, but let the fever make you lose your grip: your voice wavers, you mutter, correct yourself, then trail off into confusion. By the end, your determination cracks into a surrender that's half defeat, half relief.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're alone in your car, pulled over on the side of the road, and something has finally broken you. Begin by speaking aloud what you notice about your own state: the tightness in your chest, how you're breathing, whether you're performing grief or actually feeling it, your awareness of how you look even though no one's watching. Name your resistance to letting go, your embarrassment at your own drama, the part of you that's observing yourself fall apart. As you continue cataloging these sensations and self-judgments, let your body's truth override your mind's commentary. Move from analytical distance to visceral collapse—your voice cracking not because you're acting broken but because the honest naming of everything has finally broken through your control. End in raw, unselfconscious sound.

title: Behind the Curtain
instruction: You are an elderly man standing in the dark corner of a dimly lit room, peering through a gap in the heavy velvet curtains. You can see a young couple embracing on the patio, their bodies close, their laughter soft. Your hand is clamped over your own mouth, pressing hard to keep any sound from escaping. The fabric of your sleeve is rough against your lips. Start with a sharp, stifled breath as you watch them, your chest tight with a flicker of old desire and a sharper pang of envy. You mutter to yourself, barely audible, the words forced through your palm and the wool of your coat. Over the next few sentences, let the initial rush of lust and jealousy settle into a weary, hollow acceptance—a quiet admission that such warmth is no longer for you. Your voice should grow heavier, slower, the hand loosening only at the very end as you exhale a long, defeated sigh.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're in your car, just pulled over after a devastating phone call. Your hands are gripping the steering wheel so hard they're white. Your entire body is vibrating with rage, grief, betrayal—but you've spent a lifetime keeping it together, staying controlled. Begin with everything locked down: jaw clenched, breathing stopped, muscles rigid, forcing it all down. But something in you snaps. You start hitting the steering wheel. Then you're screaming—guttural, animal sounds you didn't know you could make. Your body convulses. You're hitting the dashboard, the seat, anything. Let the physical explosion be total and uncontrolled. Then, slowly, it passes through you like a storm. Your body goes limp against the seat. Your breathing deepens into something like sobs, but quieter. By the end, you're draped over the steering wheel, utterly spent, but paradoxically more present and alive than you've felt in years. Destroyed and somehow whole.
inspired_by: Actor experiences chronic physical tension before or during acting obligations (auditions, rehearsals, performances)

title: The Last Crate Before Rest
instruction: You are a man in the third trimester of your partner's pregnancy. You just finished packing the final box of baby clothes for the hospital bag, feeling a deep, quiet pride in how organized you've been. Speak to the empty nursery, taking a breath that gets cut short by your partner's weight pressing up against your diaphragm. Start with a contented sigh, listing the items you packed with slow satisfaction. But as you stand up, a wave of exhaustion hits your legs and back; your voice softens, becoming more effortful, and you end with a husky, heartfelt promise to the baby about how ready you are to meet them, trailing off into a yawn.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Contentment (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child. Start with your voice controlled, almost cold—you've rehearsed this, you're prepared. 'I needed to tell you something' should sound measured, even calm. But as you begin listing what you missed—birthdays, graduations, the night you called and they didn't answer—your voice starts to shake. The anger you've carried for years begins pouring out, louder, more raw. 'Where were you?' isn't just a question; it's a howl from your child-self. But then something shifts. Underneath the rage, you hear your own voice breaking into something else: the realization that you still, despite everything, wanted them to love you. End with a whispered admission that terrifies you: 'I still wish you'd chosen me.' Let the vulnerability and rage coexist in your final words.

title: Saying Goodbye at Your Father's Funeral—But Laughing
instruction: You're giving an impromptu eulogy for your father, and it starts with a story that makes you laugh—the time he got his tie caught in the car door and drove three blocks before noticing. Your laughter is genuine, warm, full of love. But mid-laugh, you have to stop, tears suddenly hot in your eyes. You keep going, mixing funny memories with devastating ones. He taught you to ride a bike but missed your wedding. He was stubborn and infuriating and you loved him desperately and never said it enough. You're laughing at his terrible jokes, crying because he'll never tell another one, finding absurd joy in remembering him while your heart is breaking. End with profound gratitude for having had him at all, even imperfectly, your voice cracking between laughter and sobs, somehow both at peace and shattered.
inspired_by: Two Strangers Sharing a Hospital Room

title: The Inheritance of Cruelty
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen of your childhood home. He's counting pennies at the table, obsessively organizing coins like he always has, and you've just discovered he refused to pay for your sister's medical treatment because he deemed it 'too expensive.' Start in cold, controlled fury—your voice measured, each word carefully chosen like a scalpel. As you speak, the dam breaks: childhood memories of him choosing money over love, over dignity, over his own children's needs pour out. Your voice becomes raw, almost unrecognizable to yourself as you realize you're saying things you swore you'd never say. But as your rage peaks, you glimpse something in his face—fear, maybe shame—and you're suddenly, devastatingly aware that he learned this from his own father. End in a place of exhausted, bitter understanding, your voice drained but somehow softer. You hate what he's done, but you finally see the frightened, broken person behind it.
inspired_by: Long Day's Journey Jamie — Unconscious Suggestions for Dark Character Exercise

title: Dancing in the Demolition
instruction: You're walking through your childhood home hours before it's demolished, and you're on the phone describing it to your sibling who couldn't come. Begin with unexpected lightness—laughing at the terrible wallpaper, the stain on the ceiling from that water leak.
