title: Rescue Made Contact in the Mine: Hearing Your Best Friend's Voice
instruction: You're the rescue coordinator when they finally make contact with trapped miners. Your voice is hopeful, controlled, professional. You're relaying information: 'We have seventeen survivors at the main level.' Then a voice comes back that makes your entire body lock. It's your best friend. You didn't know they were in this mine. Your voice cracks—just once—before you regain control. You're now managing a rescue for someone you love, and you have to keep your voice steady while your hands are shaking. Include the moment where you tell them something personal, something human, before you have to go back to logistics. Your voice carries a weight of love and terror.

title: Evacuating from Wildfire: Seeing Everything You Built Burn
instruction: You're driving away from a wildfire, and in your mirror, the house you've owned for 20 years is engulfed. Your voice starts panicked—the evacuation itself—but then becomes something else entirely. 'I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I'm sorry.' You're saying goodbye to objects, to history, to a life. Your hands are shaking on the wheel and your voice is barely controlled. Include the moment where your voice becomes quiet, almost meditative, as shock sets in. You're narrating what you're seeing and what you're losing, and your voice carries a specific kind of grief that's both absolute and slightly numb. 'The garden's gone. The oak tree. Everything.' You're alive, and you know you should be grateful, but your voice is the voice of someone whose world just became ash.

title: Breaking Up with Yourself
instruction: Youre breaking up with a version of yourself you no longer want to be. Speak to yourself with the same tone youd use in a real breakup, moving from compassion to frustration, until you let go.

title: Last Fire Before the Long Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting by the fireplace one final time before someone you love deeply leaves on a journey they won't return from—a dangerous mission, a terminal voyage, perhaps their final night before hospice. Start with the sensory comfort of the fire, describing its warmth and crackle as you've done a thousand times together. But let the reality creep in: this is the last time. Your voice should fracture as comfort gives way to the unbearable weight of impending loss. End with a desperate attempt to memorize every detail—the exact color of the flame, the precise sound of the wood splitting—as if capturing it perfectly could somehow keep them here. Move from cozy nostalgia to quiet, devastating grief.

title: The Photograph She Found
instruction: You are an elderly woman, just minutes after a long, cathartic cry over the loss of your husband of 50 years. Your voice is raw, throat sore, nose completely blocked. Then your hand brushes against a forgotten photograph tucked between the cushions—a picture of the two of you on your wedding day, laughing, with a silly hat on his head. Astonishment jolts through you: you had forgotten this existed. The surprise is so sharp it hurts, a fresh stab of pain that breaks through your exhaustion. You speak to the photo, your voice cracking, straining through the congestion, fighting to find words as the memory floods back. Start with whispered disbelief, then let the pain and wonder mix, ending with a fragile, tearless wonder.

title: Packing Up the Porch
instruction: You're an older man on your back porch, finally going through your late wife's gardening tools after months of avoiding it. title: Confessing to the Sleeping Form
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering a confession they can't hear—maybe about an affair, a terrible mistake, or a secret you've carried for years. Your voice is barely audible, tender and careful not to wake them. There's love in every word, even as you reveal something that could destroy everything. You're memorizing their peaceful face as you speak, knowing this might be the last time you see them this way. Your whispers catch in your throat as you move between explaining yourself, apologizing, and expressing gratitude for what you've had. By the end, you're crying silently, still whispering, telling them you love them more than your own life, even as you're saying goodbye to the innocence of what you had together.

title: Showing Them Your Joy on the Worst Day
instruction: You're sharing your art with someone you love on the same day you received devastating news—you're moving away forever, or they are, or someone has died, or something irreplaceable has been lost. Your voice is genuinely excited, almost laughing as you show them what you made, because the work itself is joyful, celebratory, alive. But the laughter keeps catching, breaking into something else. They respond with kindness but also confusion—how can you be showing them this right now? Your voice shifts between genuine delight in the work and the weight of everything unsaid, smiling while your throat tightens. You keep trying to stay in the joy of the creation, but grief keeps seeping through. By the end, your voice is doing something strange—expressing real gratitude that you got to create this, got to share it with them, while simultaneously breaking under the knowledge that this moment of sharing is wrapped in goodbye. The final words carry both peace and heartbreak, acceptance and loss, all tangled together in a way that makes perfect, terrible sense.
inspired_by: Showing Your Art to Someone Who Doesn't Get It

title: The Garage Door Closes
instruction: You're an older man, broad-shouldered, standing in your garage after your son drives away for the last time. You grip the workbench, knuckles white, staring at the empty driveway. Your jaw is tight with disappointment — at yourself, at how this ended. But as you speak, the pain you've been holding leaks out: your voice thickens, your breath catches, and you let out a cracked, quiet apology to the empty space. Start stubborn and clipped, end broken and raw — like a dam crumbling on the last word.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Waking Up from Anesthesia: Post-Surgery Babbling
instruction: You're coming out of general anesthesia and have zero filter. Your voice is slurred, childlike, and confused. Ask the same question three times. Confess something embarrassing with total sincerity. Tell the nurse they're beautiful. Try to argue about something nonsensical with complete conviction. Let the voice gradually sharpen as lucidity returns — and include the mortified moment when you realize what you've been saying.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your mother, father, or adult child about something they did years ago that shaped who you became—something you've carried silently until this moment. Begin by drawing on a real frustration or disappointment from your own life, even if it involves a different person or situation. Let that genuine feeling of having been misunderstood or hurt live in your body. As the confrontation unfolds, allow other true feelings to emerge—maybe you discover forgiveness you didn't expect, or maybe your anger intensifies into something more painful: the realization that they'll never truly understand. Move from controlled accusation to something messier and more human. Let the truth of your own emotional history bleed into this fictional moment until you can't tell where one ends and the other begins.

title: The Locked Secret
instruction: You are a child, maybe seven or eight, sitting in a hiding spot beneath the stairs. Your hand is pressed firmly over your mouth because your mother just told a visitor not to let anyone know she won the county baking contest again—she's embarrassed by the attention. Your hand muffles your voice; your lips can't touch. Start with pure pride swelling in your chest, the words almost bursting out, but forced into a whispery, thrilled giggle. As you keep talking to yourself, the excitement slowly shifts into a firm, knowing resolve: you will guard this secret with your whole heart. Let your voice start bright and quivery, then settle into a proud, determined hush.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Reading Their Last Letter Aloud—The One That Changes Everything
instruction: They're gone—death, departure, a relationship ended—and they left you a letter. You're reading it aloud, maybe to a friend, maybe to an empty room, maybe into your phone to record it before you lose your nerve. The letter starts with something that makes you laugh—a joke, a memory, something so perfectly them that for a moment they're alive again in your voice. But as you read, the letter reveals something you never knew: how much they loved you, how much they struggled, a secret that reframes your entire relationship, a goodbye that's also a gift. Your voice moves through laughter, confusion, dawning understanding, and then breaks completely. You're reading words of love while grief swells in your chest, finding gratitude in the same breath as loss. By the end, you're barely getting the words out, but you have to finish—you owe them that. The letter is destroying you and healing you simultaneously, and your voice reflects every contradictory feeling flooding through you.
inspired_by: Announcing Bad Diagnosis Out Loud for the First Time

title: The Doorway Reckoning
instruction: You're an adult child at your parent's doorstep, ostensibly leaving after a holiday visit, but forty years of unspoken resentment suddenly erupts. Begin with the familiar dance—'We should get going, traffic'—but then something snaps. Voice shaking, you start confronting decades of emotional absence: 'Actually, no. I need to say something.' Transition from polite deflection to trembling anger to raw vulnerability as you reveal how their distance shaped you. Your parent tries to redirect to small talk ('Did you remember your leftovers?'), but you refuse to let them hide anymore. End not with resolution but with devastating honesty—your voice should break between fury and the desperate need to be seen by the person who raised you but never knew you.
inspired_by: The Incredibly Long Goodbye at the Door

title: Grief Overwhelming
instruction: You're sitting in their chair. Everything makes you cry: a song they loved, a jar of their favorite jam in the fridge, the way light hit the kitchen at 3 PM and suddenly you remember every 3 PM conversation. Your voice is raw, gutted. Breathing is interrupted by sobs you're trying to suppress. When you speak, it's in fragments: 'I called them today before I remembered they...' The sentence doesn't finish. Your voice cracks not from strain but from the physical weight of loss. Silence is long. When words come, they're repetitive: 'I miss them. I miss them.'

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years to the parent who abandoned you. Begin with controlled anger—measured words, a voice that's rehearsed this moment a thousand times. But as you speak, something breaks: the anger dissolves into the hurt of a child still waiting for them to come back, still hoping they'll say they're sorry. Your voice becomes small, vulnerable, cracking on words like 'needed' and 'alone.' Then catch yourself—feel the rage return, fiercer now, protective of that wounded child. But here's the shift: mid-accusation, you realize you're not that child anymore. The anger softens into something more complex: grief for what never was, pity for them, and finally—unexpectedly—a reluctant understanding. End not with forgiveness, but with release, your voice quiet and exhausted but finally, finally free.
inspired_by: Profound Relief: The Test Results Are Negative

title: Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is unconscious, fading. You know they can't hear you, or maybe they can—you're not sure anymore. Speak in whispers, not from politeness but because your voice keeps breaking. Start by talking about ordinary things, gentle and tender, trying to keep them tethered to life with the sound of your voice. Gradually let your composure crack—confess something you were too afraid to say when they could respond. Your words catch in your throat; long pauses where you just breathe together. Mix desperate bargaining ('If you wake up, I promise...') with soft memories that make you almost laugh before the grief swallows the sound. End with the most vulnerable truth: you don't know how to let them go, whispered so quietly it's almost just breath. Let silence do half the work.

title: Stealing the Spotlight
instruction: You are at a family reunion, seated across from your younger sister who is being praised for her recent promotion. You have been waiting for a chance to speak, feeling a wave of relief that your moment has finally arrived. But as you interrupt her story, your voice climbs higher and quickens, driven by a fierce envy that you cannot hide. Begin with a breathless 'Oh, finally!' then cut in with a complaint about your own overlooked achievements, letting your pitch rise and your tone become sharp as jealousy takes over. End with a strained, bitter laugh as you realize you've exposed your true feelings.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers Forward
instruction: You are in the throes of intense physical sensation—perhaps passion, perhaps pain after an accident, perhaps both. Your body is screaming at you, and you're terrified you'll be overwhelmed, that you'll lose control or disappoint someone you love. But as you move through this visceral experience, start layering in vivid flashes of yourself on the other side—your breath steady again, your lover's face showing awe not disappointment, your body strong and capable, the exact feeling of relief and triumph in your muscles and bones. Let the physical intensity remain real and present, but feel your relationship to it shift. The sensation that began as something threatening transforms into something you're riding, mastering, moving through with unexpected power. End in a place where pain and pleasure, fear and exhilaration are braided together, and you're astonished by your own resilience.

title: The Barn Door
instruction: You are a small child hiding from an angry adult in a dark, unfamiliar barn. You hear their boots crunching closer, so you burst through a rickety back door and sprint into a moonlit field, gasping for air, your lungs burning. At first, your voice is pure panic—short, ragged shouts of 'No, no, no, no!' as you stumble over frozen dirt and duck under barbed wire. Then, partway across the field, you glance over your shoulder and realize the barn is now tiny and still—no one followed. Your breath slows from frantic sobs to wondering, whispery gasps as you realize you got away. Let your voice crack, break, and catch; let your feet falter mid-sentence as you notice the silence; end with a tiny, awed laugh that sounds almost happy, but still breathless.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child, and they've just told you they've found peace in their life now. You start in that same profound calm—maybe you've done years of therapy, maybe you've genuinely worked through the abandonment. Your voice is steady, almost eerily peaceful as you acknowledge their happiness. But as you continue speaking, something ancient and wounded rises up: rage at their peace when you had none, fury that they get to feel settled while you spent decades feeling restless. Your calm doesn't shatter into screaming—it corrodes into something sharper, more precise, more devastating. By the end, you're speaking truths they can't unhear, and your voice has transformed from serene to scalding, though you never raise your volume. The peace has curdled into something that demands accountability.

title: Condiment Choice
instruction: You're standing in front of the condiment shelf and you're becoming increasingly emotional about whether it's ketchup or mustard. Your voice starts analytical but becomes almost philosophical. 'Ketchup masks the truth of the meat. Mustard honors it.' You're not really talking about mustard anymore. Your voice is having an existential crisis about authenticity. 'Ketchup is for people who are afraid,' you say seriously. Someone walks away from you slowly.

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission: When You Know You're Not Coming Home
instruction: You're floating in the damaged capsule, alone, watching Earth grow smaller. Start with the professional calm of a trained astronaut, reporting telemetry data to Mission Control. But as you realize the oxygen calculations don't add up, that voice cracks. You're trying to say goodbye to your daughter, to explain why you won't be at her wedding, why you broke your promise. Your words fracture between technical jargon and desperate love letters. The fear breaks through in gasps, then rage at the universe, then finally—as the oxygen thins—a strange, dreamy peace. End with your voice fading to whispers, telling her one last bedtime story, your childhood lullaby dissolving into the static of space.
inspired_by: Labor: When the Anesthesia Wears Off During Surgery Complications

title: The Question You Weren't Ready For
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he left when you were twelve. You've rehearsed this moment for years—the accusations, the anger, the demands for explanation. But before you can launch into your prepared confrontation, he asks you something completely unexpected: 'What's the one happy memory you have of us together?' Let his question derail you. Don't fight to get back to your script. Explore what comes up when you're forced off your planned path. Start with the wound you came to expose, but let yourself be pulled toward something you didn't anticipate—maybe tenderness, maybe deeper rage, maybe grief for what was lost. End somewhere neither of you expected, in an emotional place that surprises even you.
inspired_by: Actor keeps anticipating and guiding his own choice exploration (self-facilitation bias)

title: The Wedding Toast You Didn't Plan
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's wedding, champagne glass raised, about to give a toast. Start by truly looking at them—their face, their happiness, the way they're looking at their new spouse. Let yourself be genuinely absorbed in witnessing their joy in this moment. Begin the toast with celebration, with funny memories you'd planned to share. But as you speak, let something else emerge—the awareness that you're losing them, that this changes everything between you, that you've been in love with them for years, or that you're devastated about the life path you didn't choose. Don't decide which complex feeling will surface—let the contrast between the public moment and private truth create something unexpected. Your voice should carry both genuine happiness for them and a private grief, both celebration and goodbye, ending in a place where you've said something true you didn't mean to reveal.
inspired_by: Actor is compensating — imposing a relaxed demeanor over real tension, or substituting one emotion for another that feels more acceptable

title: The Last Dawn Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply as dawn breaks on their final morning. Begin speaking softly, almost in disbelief that this moment has arrived, trying to reassure them while your own heart is shattering. As you continue, let gratitude for every moment you shared flood through you—name specific memories, small details that meant everything. By the end, transform your grief into a promise: you will carry them forward in how you live. Let your voice break where it needs to, but find strength in celebrating their life even as you say goodbye. The emotion should move from fragile denial through aching tenderness to fierce, loving acceptance.

title: Whispering What You Never Could Say Aloud
instruction: You're sitting beside someone sleeping—a partner, a parent, a best friend. You've kept a secret that's been destroying you from the inside: maybe you're leaving, maybe you're sick, maybe you've been hiding who you really are. In the safety of their sleep, you finally speak the truth in barely audible whispers. Start with the words catching in your throat, pausing to make sure they're still asleep. Your voice is tender, full of love for them, even as you confess something that will change everything. Let tears come silently. End by saying a goodbye they won't remember, your voice breaking on 'I love you' because you mean it more than you've ever meant anything. The entire piece should feel like it's made of held breath and breaking hearts.

title: Thunderchild's Dance
instruction: You are a child alone in a sudden, violent rainstorm. Start by huddling under a tree, frightened by each thunderclap. As the rain soaks through your hair, you realize you're already wet—so you step out, lift your face, and feel the cold shock turn into wild joy. Let your voice rise over the downpour: first a hesitant whisper, then a laughing shout. End with a breathless, giddy confession to no one but the sky. Speak as if you're tasting the rain, your grin breaking through the words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Apology That Became a War
instruction: You've come to apologize to your adult daughter for missing something important to her—again. Start with genuine softness, remorse, and the real desire to make things right. Speak with tenderness about how much you love her, how you want to understand her, how you're trying to be better. But as you speak, feel her coldness, her skepticism, the wall she's built against you. Let that rejection of your olive branch ignite something else in you—not just anger, but the hurt beneath it that's been building for years. Your voice should shift from gentle and conciliatory to wounded, then defensive, then fierce. End with the devastating recognition that in trying to fix things, you've destroyed them further, and you don't know if you're more angry at her or at yourself.

title: The Wave
instruction: You're in a hospital bed, mid-labor, alone except for the rhythmic beeping of a monitor. Between contractions, you mutter bitterly about your partner who chose work over being here, your voice edged with sourness. But as the next wave builds, you feel a distinct shift—a deep, unexpected curiosity about the strength inside you. Let your voice start flat and resentful, then crack and strain through the pain, and finally emerge softer, almost amazed, as you realize you're actually interested in meeting this baby. Pause naturally, let your breathing dictate the rhythm, and let the interest push through the bitterness at the end.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Sourness (clearly present), Interest (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: What I Never Said
instruction: You're whispering a confession to someone sleeping—someone who will never hear these words because you can't say them when they're awake. Start barely audible, like you're testing the weight of each word in the darkness: 'I need to tell you something.' Your voice is tender, intimate, breaking in places as you admit a truth that terrifies you—maybe that you're leaving, or that you've failed them, or that you love them more than you can bear. The quiet isn't peaceful; it's full of aching. As you continue, your whisper becomes thick with tears you're trying to keep silent. End with a phrase so soft it's almost breathed: 'I'm so sorry you'll never know.' The silence after should feel like a wound.

title: Bedside Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping best friend in the hospital after they tried to take their own life, and you're whispering the truth you've never been brave enough to say. Start with your voice barely audible, tender and fragile, telling them how much they mean to you. Let emotion catch in your throat as you confess your own struggles—moments where you can barely continue. Your voice should waver, break on certain words, rebuild quietly. Include long pauses where silence does the work. End with a whispered plea for them to stay that's so vulnerable it hurts, where every word costs you something to say.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from the hospital. You were told you have hours left, maybe a day. Begin the call with careful distance—you haven't spoken in three years, and old anger sits between you like a wall. As you speak, let the reality of never having another chance crack through your defenses. Your voice might start controlled, even cold, but by the end, let everything you've been holding back pour out—not just anger, but the child in you who needed them, who still needs them. End in a place of raw, undefended love mixed with the grief of all the lost years. Let your breath, your pauses, your breaking voice tell as much of the story as your words.

title: Washing Your Hands After
instruction: You're alone in a bathroom, washing your hands after having to make an impossible medical decision to end life support for someone you love. Speak to yourself in the mirror, or to them, or to God, or to no one. Your voice is barely above a whisper. The water runs. You scrub your hands like Lady Macbeth but tenderly, ritualistically. Tell them why you did it, ask for forgiveness, question if you were right. Your breath catches frequently. This isn't big grief—it's the small, private kind that lives in your chest like a stone. Let your voice carry the weight of knowing you did the merciful thing while feeling like a murderer. End with a moment of complete silence where you finally look at yourself, or can't.

title: The Last Dance: Laughing Through Goodbye
instruction: You're dancing one final time with someone you're losing to terminal illness, and they've just made a terrible joke about death. You laugh—genuinely, helplessly laugh—even as tears stream down your face: 'God, that's awful. That's so awful.' Keep moving together, your voice caught between joy and devastation: 'Remember when we danced at that terrible wedding and you stepped on my foot seventeen times?' You're both laughing and crying now. Feel the gratitude flood through you: 'Thank you for every single one of those terrible dances. Thank you for every moment.' Your voice breaks completely: 'I don't know how to do this world without you in it.' They hold you tighter. Find something luminous in the midst of grief: 'But right now, right this second, you're here. We're here.' End with a whispered smile in your voice, laughing softly through tears: 'One more terrible dance. That's all I need. Just one more.'

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: Your teenage child just said something cruel, dismissive—'You don't understand anything about my life'—and something in you detonates. You start yelling, your voice raw and uncontrolled: 'I have given up EVERYTHING for you!' Let your rage be ugly, honest, unfiltered. But mid-sentence, you hear yourself—the desperation, the need for their validation—and your voice cracks. The anger collapses into something more vulnerable: pleading. 'Please don't make me invisible. Please.' You're suddenly aware you're begging your own child to see your worth. Let yourself break down completely, tears mixing with fragments of words. Then, in the wreckage, find a whisper of something protective and fierce: 'I'm still your mother. And I'm not going anywhere.' The love and the helplessness must coexist in your voice.

title: The Prize and the Peon
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl strolling through a park on a lazy afternoon, fresh from winning first place in a public speaking competition. Your gait is slow and unhurried, your chest light with triumph, each breath a satisfied sigh. As you meander past a picnic bench, you spot a classmate who once mocked you—they're picking at their sandwich, looking pathetic. Your voice starts with a happy, bouncy lilt as you hum to yourself, but when you speak, it hardens into a condescending drawl, dripping with contempt. Let the physical rhythm of your walk affect your speech—a slight bob on each step, a trailing off to watch them squirm, then a dismissive snort as you turn away. End with a slow, satisfied exhale, having crushed them with a single word.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Clueless Fashionista
instruction: Act as a person giving fashion advice thats outdated or absurd. Use a confident tone when suggesting outfits, switching to others skeptical or amused responses.

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your One-Year Sobriety Chip
instruction: You're holding your one-year sobriety chip, and you start telling someone (real or imagined) what this year cost you. Your voice begins with exhausted, broken laughter - the absurd, brutal irony that getting clean meant losing almost everything. You're half-laughing, half-crying as you list what you lost: the relationship, the job, the trust, the years you can't get back. But as you speak, your voice fills with something unexpected - fierce, tearful gratitude. You're crying but also laughing with genuine wonder at still being alive, at the small morning moments you can finally feel. Your voice trembles between grief and joy, between 'I lost everything' and 'I found myself.' End with your voice soft, awed, still crying but somehow peaceful - acknowledging the devastation while holding the fragile miracle of survival.
inspired_by: Choosing Your Recovery Over Your Relationship

title: The Breathing Dark
instruction: You are alone in a dense jungle at dusk. The air is thick with humidity, and every sound—a bird call, a rustle of leaves—feels like a threat. You've been walking for hours, and your voice is swallowed by the foliage. Start by whispering to yourself, trying to stay calm, but your words come out in short, panicked bursts as you flinch at each noise. As you hear a low, rhythmic snap from behind a nearby tree, your fear morphs from frantic agitation into a frozen, breathless stillness. Let your final words be barely audible, a quiet acceptance of whatever is out there.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Ceiling Stare
instruction: You're a teenager lying flat on your back on your bedroom floor, phone pressed to your ear. Your friend just told you something you thought would be interesting — a secret about someone you both know. But as they talk, you feel your initial flicker of curiosity curdle into pure contempt. Let your voice sound puddled, heavy, with that slight nasal stuffiness from being supine. Start with a low, almost lazy interest — a quiet 'huh' — but let each word become more dismissive and sneering as you realize how pathetic this all is. End with a flat, cutting remark, your throat tight with disgust. Micro-distractions: shift your head, sigh into the phone, lose your train of thought for a second.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Goodnight, My Love, For the Last Time
instruction: You're lying beside your partner of thirty years in hospice, whispering your bedtime ritual one final time. Begin with tender familiarity: 'Goodnight, my love. Tomorrow we'll...' You're saying the same words you've said thousands of nights, your voice soft, intimate. But tonight every word catches. You're trying to keep it normal, keep it gentle, because that's what they need. As you recount small memories ('Remember when we first moved into that terrible apartment?'), you're smiling through tears you're trying to hide. Your voice breaks into almost-silence, then rallies with fierce tenderness. End with 'I'll be right here when you wake up,' knowing you're lying, knowing they know you're lying, your voice barely a whisper, holding love and goodbye and the unbearable weight of a lifetime in those final words.

title: Final Hospital Visit: The Words You Can Never Unsay
instruction: You're visiting your estranged parent on what you both know is their deathbed. You arrive angry—years of abandonment burning in your chest—but as you see how small they've become, something shifts. Begin with guarded coldness, clipped words, refusing to come closer to the bed. But they ask you one question about your childhood that breaks something open. Your voice must travel from bitter restraint to raw confession: all the times you needed them, all the ways you became who you are despite their absence, and finally—though it costs you everything—the terrible truth that you still love them. End in a whisper, holding their hand, caught between grief for what was lost and gratitude for this last moment of truth.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Time Traveler Meets Their Own Younger Self

title: The Award Toast
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman at a company gala, a non-native English speaker surrounded by specialized engineers. A younger colleague just won the prestigious award you worked years for. You force yourself to congratulate her, but your jealousy and envy boil up. Your speech becomes simplified: grammar stripped, words separated by gaps, volume too loud. Start with a tight smile and forced brightness, but soon your true bitterness leaks out—your voice cracks, you lose words, and you end with a quiet, jagged admission of your envy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bedside Confession to the Sleeping
instruction: Your partner is sleeping next to you in the pre-dawn darkness. You're leaving them tomorrow—not because you don't love them, but because you do, and you're terrified you'll destroy them if you stay. Your voice is barely above a whisper, so quiet it's almost just breath. You're speaking the truth you could never say to their waking face: how much you love them, how broken you feel, how you're drowning and can't let them drown with you. Let your voice catch on their name. Let sentences trail off into silence that says more than words. This isn't dramatic—it's the opposite. It's intimate, trembling, the kind of vulnerable that feels like being flayed open. Move from tender love through devastating self-awareness to a goodbye so gentle it's almost a lullaby, even though you're breaking both your hearts.

title: Washing Your Hands After: What You Can't Tell Anyone
instruction: You've just finished an intimate encounter that left you feeling hollowed out, used in ways you can't articulate. You're alone now, washing your hands, and you begin speaking in barely audible whispers to your reflection—or to no one. Start with fragmented thoughts: 'It's fine. I wanted to. I said yes.' But your voice betrays you, catching on words. The water keeps running as you scrub harder than necessary. Slowly, the truth emerges: this isn't the first time, you're not sure how to stop saying yes when you mean no, you're not even sure what you want anymore. Don't cry loudly—let it be the kind of tears that come silently, the kind where your breath just... stops working right. This is the vulnerability of someone who hasn't admitted this to themselves yet.
inspired_by: Concealing Disgust While Handling Something Unpleasant

title: The Last Window at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has only hours left to live. They've just opened their eyes and looked at you with full recognition for the first time in days. Begin with overwhelming relief that they're lucid and present with you now. As you speak to them about what they mean to you, let their responses—whether words, touches, or simply the way they look at you—change what you're feeling moment to moment. Maybe relief becomes grief, then transforms into gratitude, then back to desperate sorrow, then perhaps to a fierce kind of joy at this final gift of connection. Let each thing they do to you emotionally shift what comes out of your mouth next. End in a place completely different from where you started, having been taken on a journey by this exchange of genuine feeling between you.

title: Vigil Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's sleeping (or unconscious, or deeply ill), and you're finally saying what you've never had the courage to say when they could respond. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and achingly tender. Begin with something simple—'I need to tell you something'—and let the confession unfold slowly. Maybe it's a secret you've kept, a way you've loved them you were too scared to admit, or forgiveness you should have offered years ago. Your emotion should deepen as you speak, moving from careful words to something more raw. Let your voice catch on specific memories—'Remember when you...'—and feel the bittersweet ache of tenderness mixed with grief or regret. End with the heartbreak of not knowing if they'll ever hear you, or the fragile hope that somehow they can. Let silence and breath carry as much emotion as words.

title: Victory Pasta
instruction: You're a teenager alone in the kitchen, finally mastering your grandmother's spaghetti recipe after a dozen failed attempts. The oil is sizzling, garlic sizzles, onions pop. You’re fiercely triumphant as you remember her trick—add a pinch of sugar to the sauce. Midway through, a memory of her laughing and messing up her own batch surges with affection, and your voice cracks as you mutter to yourself, 'You’d be so proud, Grandma.' Chop a tomato, stir the pot. Your triumph softens into raw fondness, but the noise of bubbling and chopping pulls your volume louder, then quieter.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are experiencing an overwhelming moment of physical sensation—perhaps passionate reunion after long separation, or gripping someone you're furious with, or the electric shock of hearing news that changes your life while your body is mid-action. Start with whatever physical state you're actually in—notice your real tension, your real breathing. As the emotional intensity floods you, don't perform it: let it genuinely move through your actual body. Feel how rage might make your hands shake, how desire might make you dizzy, how grief might drop you to your knees. Let your voice be secondary to your physical experience—break off sentences, gasp, let sounds emerge involuntarily. End in a completely different physical state than you began, authentically exhausted or energized.

title: First Day of Sobriety: Calling Your Sponsor
instruction: It's 3AM, you're shaking, and you're calling your AA sponsor instead of taking a drink. Your voice should carry the physical withdrawal: trembling, sweating (audible gulping), nausea barely held at bay. Start with the admission: 'I want to drink so bad.' Let the sponsor's voice (also you) be steady, warm, experienced — someone who's been exactly here. The conversation should be a lifeline. Include holding a glass of water and deliberately choosing it.

title: The Old Man and the Machine
instruction: You are an elderly man trying to use a voice assistant to find out the weather forecast for your garden. Start with sour frustration—you hate how you have to speak like a robot, over-enunciating each word with flat, unnatural pauses. But when it actually works and tells you tomorrow will be sunny, a flicker of awe creeps in, then a quiet hope that maybe this technology isn't so bad after all. Let your voice shift from clipped, annoyed precision to a softer, almost wondering tone as you repeat the forecast to yourself, as if savoring the miracle. Include tiny distractions: a cough, a muttered curse under your breath, a moment where you forget what you were going to say.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Awe (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Hum of Home
instruction: You're in a quiet bedroom late at night. Your partner just came home from a grueling week-long business trip, and they're finally relaxed, lying back in the dark. Your head is between their thighs, and your mouth is full, so your usual words of comfort come out as a low, steady, affectionate hum. You feel a deep, bone-weary relief that they're safe and back in your arms. At first, your humming is slow, almost a sigh—just pure sensation and gratitude. Then you shift your weight, your neck getting a little sore, and you realize you need to say one thing, but the word comes out as a wet, muffled, smiling 'mmsorry—' You pause, breathe through your nose, and let out a longer, softer, more deliberate hum that says everything you cannot articulate: 'I missed you so much.' The sound changes from a satisfied, sustained note into a gentler, almost breathy exhale as you feel them shudder, and your own relief crests into a quiet, tender laugh against their skin.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Protector Who Can't Protect
instruction: Someone you would die for is in danger—a terminal diagnosis, an abusive situation, a self-destructive spiral—and you are powerless to save them. Begin with fierce determination, your voice strong with plans and promises: 'We'll fight this. I won't let anything happen to you.' Let that certainty crack as reality intrudes. Your voice rises with desperate, almost violent insistence: 'You have to try harder. You have to want this.' The anger is really terror—you're raging against the unfairness, the helplessness, your own inadequacy. Then comes the collapse: your voice breaks completely as you admit you can't fix this, can't control this, can't make them safe no matter how much you love them. End in raw, vulnerable pleading, stripped of all pride: 'Please don't leave me. Please don't give up.' Your voice is both commanding and utterly broken, a guardian forced to surrender their sword.

title: Last Conversation Before the War
instruction: Your brother is leaving for a conflict he might not return from, and you both know it. You start with forced brightness, trying to keep things light—'Remember when we...' But mid-sentence, the facade cracks. Your voice becomes urgent, desperate to say everything that matters in these final moments. You oscillate between wanting to memorize his face and needing to look away because it hurts too much. Anger flashes through—why is he going, why won't he stay—then dissolves into tender grief. End with a whispered confession of something you've never said, your voice raw and breaking: 'I don't know how to be me without you here.' Let the silence after speak what words cannot.
inspired_by: Recognizing Abuse Pattern Repeating in New Relationship

title: Mirror Tease
instruction: You're alone in your bedroom, fully nude, standing in front of a floor-length mirror. You've been touching yourself slowly, deliberately, but you keep stopping to watch your own reflection—you're teasing yourself, grinning at the sight of your own arousal. Start by whispering to your reflection, playful and almost mocking: 'Look at you... you think you're ready?' Let your voice be breathy, amused, with a hint of challenge. As you continue, let the teasing soften into real wanting—your words become less controlled, more desperate. End on a quiet, surprised breath as you finally let go, the playfulness replaced by raw, unguarded pleasure. Let your voice crack, pause for a moan, and fade into a sigh of fulfillment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Sunset on Borrowed Time
instruction: You're standing at the ocean's edge, feeling the sand between your toes for what you know is the last time. The diagnosis came back final. Begin with tender appreciation, describing the warmth of the sand as if cataloging precious details for a memory you need to preserve forever. Let your voice carry quiet wonder at first, but as you continue, allow the weight of goodbye to seep in. Your tone should shift from peaceful gratitude to something more fragile—your words catching as you realize you're not just feeling the sand, you're saying farewell to every simple pleasure you've taken for granted. End with a whispered acknowledgment that this moment, this feeling, will have to be enough to carry you through what comes next.
inspired_by: Running Your Hands Through Warm Sand

title: Reading the Letter They'll Never Send
instruction: You've just found a letter—an email draft, a note tucked away—that someone important to you wrote but never sent. Maybe they've just died, or left, or you've discovered it by accident. As you read it aloud, you start with curiosity, maybe a slight smile: 'Dear...' and it's addressed to you. They're saying things you never knew they felt—gratitude, love, apologies, confessions. Your voice begins to laugh softly at a shared memory they reference, genuine warmth flooding through. But the tone of the letter shifts, gets more serious, more raw, and suddenly you're reading words that break your heart: they were struggling and you didn't know, or they loved you in ways they couldn't express, or they forgave you for something you didn't know needed forgiving. Your voice fractures between laughter and tears, between joy at their words and devastation that they never said them out loud. End with a sentence that makes you stop, unable to continue, the paper trembling in your hands, laughing and crying at once because you're grateful for these words and destroyed that this is how you're receiving them.

title: Breaking Point Ecstasy
instruction: You have been holding yourself together through impossible circumstances—grief, poverty, illness, exile, whatever has pushed you to your absolute limit. You are physically exhausted, running on fumes. Then something breaks through: unexpected news, a moment of human kindness, music that reaches you, a memory of joy. Begin from a place of bone-deep weariness, your voice flat and depleted. As this breakthrough moment hits you, feel it in your body first—a sob, a laugh, a sound you can't control. Let the physical sensation overwhelm you. You might laugh and cry simultaneously, your body shaking with the release of months or years of held tension. Your voice becomes wild, uncontrolled, gulping air between sounds of anguish and relief. By the end, you are emptied out, your voice raw and spent, but something has fundamentally shifted—you are broken open rather than broken down.
inspired_by: Two actors need to achieve genuine ensemble before a scene and are starting from cold

title: The Last Gift of Recognition
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandfather's hospital bed in his final hours. For years, you've felt like a disappointment to him—never quite measuring up, always falling short. But now, as he drifts in and out of consciousness, you suddenly realize all the ways you've actually grown into someone remarkable since the last time you truly spoke. Begin hesitant and heavy with old shame, cataloging aloud specific, real moments where you've become stronger, kinder, braver—things he may never have known about. As you speak these truths, feel your voice transform from apologetic to quietly proud, from seeking his approval to offering him the gift of knowing who you've become. End with a tender recognition that maybe you were enough all along, even as you say goodbye.

title: The Reckoning: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You are an adult finally confronting a parent about years of being overlooked, dismissed, or measured against impossible standards. Start controlled, almost businesslike—you've rehearsed this: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, old wounds tear open. Your voice sharpens with long-suppressed anger: 'Do you have any idea what it felt like to never be enough for you?' Let rage build, then crack into something more vulnerable—the child inside you who just wanted to be seen. Your voice breaks: 'I just wanted you to be proud of me. Just once.' The anger dissolves into raw grief and exhausted honesty. End somewhere unexpected: either with tentative hope ('Maybe it's not too late') or quiet, devastating acceptance ('I need to stop waiting for you to change'). Let your voice carry both strength and the trembling of a heart that's still healing.
inspired_by: Teacher: Celebrating a Student's Unexpected Success

title: You Always Remember the Wrong Things
instruction: You're at a small party, two drinks in, standing by the kitchen counter with a half-empty glass. You're trying to recall a funny story from years ago, but the details keep slipping. Start with genuine, bewildered confusion—pausing, frowning at the air, letting your voice trail off. Halfway through, you realize your friend is grinning, and you shift into a teasing, mock-accusatory tone. End with a warm laugh that feels loose and unguarded. Let the words stumble a little, especially on consonant clusters, and let the confusion slowly give way to playful affection.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Funeral Speech Because Nothing Else Makes Sense
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone who would have hated a sad funeral. You start with a funny story, and genuine laughter bubbles up—their absurdity, their wild spirit. Your voice is warm, almost celebratory. But mid-laugh, grief ambushes you. Your voice catches, the laughter turns slightly hysterical, tears mixing with the joy. You keep trying to return to the humor because that's what they'd want, but sorrow keeps breaking through. You're smiling through tears, voice cracking as you say how grateful you are, how much you'll miss them, how unfair this is—all while half-laughing at the impossibility of it all. The arc is gratitude and grief dancing together, neither one winning. Your voice should shimmer between joy and devastation, finding strange peace in holding both. Make it beautifully contradictory and achingly human.

title: Laughing at Your Funeral
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who meant everything to you, but instead of somber words, you're sharing a ridiculous memory that makes you laugh even as tears stream down your face. Begin with genuine laughter, shaking your head: 'God, you would have loved this - all of us trying not to cry while I tell this story.' The laughter and tears mix as you continue: 'You always said funerals were too serious. You'd probably flip the casket if you could.' But then the absurdity of their absence hits you, and your voice breaks: 'You're supposed to be here. You're supposed to...' You catch yourself, find the memory again, and end with bittersweet joy through tears: 'Thank you. For every stupid, beautiful moment.' Move fluidly between laughter and grief, joy and heartbreak, celebrating and mourning simultaneously - all completely genuine and spontaneous.

title: Scraping Gratitude
instruction: You are washing a sink full of sticky, greasy dishes after a large family dinner. The water is hot and the sponge smells of lemon and old food. Your hands are pruned. You grimace at a clump of congealed gravy on a plate. As you scrape and rinse, you mutter about the mess, but then you pause, thinking of the laughter around the table. Your irritation softens into a quiet thankfulness for the full plates and the people who filled them. Let your voice start crisp with disgust and impatience, then gradually slow and warm as gratitude surfaces, even as the water still rushes and a glass clinks. Speak aloud your inner thoughts, sometimes directed at the dishes, sometimes at yourself.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Disgust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Inhaling the Scent of Lavender in a Field
instruction: Take a deep breath, filling your lungs with the soft, floral scent of lavender. Describe the way it smells sweet, calming, and fresh, filling you with peace. Speak with a tone of gentle calm, as if each breath of lavender lifts away any stress, leaving only clarity and calm.

title: Confessing Love to Someone Dying in Your Arms
instruction: They're fading and you finally whisper the truth you've hidden for years: 'I've loved you since the first day.' Your voice is barely audible, tender, full of all the tenderness you never let yourself show. You're holding them close, speaking softly against their hair, trying to pour a lifetime of unspoken devotion into these last moments. As their breathing changes, your whisper becomes more urgent, more desperate—'Please don't go, please'—but still quiet, intimate, like you're sharing a sacred secret. Let your voice carry the weight of all the years you stayed silent, the regret of waiting too long, the bittersweet ache of finally being honest when it's too late. Every word catches in your throat.

title: Thanking the Divorce Papers That Saved Your Life
instruction: You're holding your finalized divorce papers, and instead of the expected grief or relief, you begin speaking directly TO the papers themselves—but with bizarre, conflicted gratitude. Start by playfully thanking them for existing, for being brave enough to end what you couldn't. Ask them absurd questions: Were you always this white? Did you enjoy being signed? Do you know you're the most important pages I'll ever hold? Make it strange and light at first, almost giddy. But as you continue, let contradictory emotions flood in—you're grateful but furious, liberated but grieving, hopeful but terrified. Thank the papers for destroying your marriage while simultaneously mourning everything you lost. By the end, you're crying while laughing, or laughing while crying—holding these pages like they're both an execution notice and a birth certificate. The papers become the only safe recipient of emotions too complicated to share with any human being.
inspired_by: An actor finds sense memory work tedious and boring

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your dying lover who always made you feel ashamed of your desire for them. They are slipping away, and you have minutes left. Start by being cautious, holding back as you always have—then let yourself finally confess the raw physical longing you've carried in secret for years. Describe what you've wanted, what you've dreamed about, what you've denied yourself. Let your voice move from hesitant whispers to urgent, unapologetic hunger. By the end, you're giving yourself permission to want them fully, even as you're losing them. Let grief and desire become inseparable.
inspired_by: Actor has sexual obstacles or blocks that limit their presence, appeal, or ability to handle sexual material

title: The Garden Bench at Dusk
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting alone on a weathered wooden bench in a quiet garden as the sun sets. Your joints ache from the damp air, and you think aloud about a beloved partner who passed away years ago. Start with a slow, searching voice, feeling the lingering ache of absence—a slight pain in your chest. As you recall a small, joyful memory of them laughing at a silly bird, let a genuine, warm optimism rise through you, your voice finding a lighter, steadier tone. Let your words trail off as you watch a bird land nearby, then pick up again with a fragile but determined hope that life still holds moments of beauty. Speak naturally, with pauses, sighs, and the occasional shift in your seat.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Father-Son Sparring: The Final Point
instruction: You are a father sparring with your young son in a light contact match. The round is intense—you're breathing hard, delivering sharp kiais as you throw strikes, your body coiled. Midway, your son lands a solid hit on your chest guard. You freeze, then a grin breaks through your exhaustion. Your voice, still panting, shifts from predatory focus to a warm, breathless chuckle. Say to him, between controlled breaths, 'That was perfect, kiddo. Right through my guard. I love this—this right here.' Let the contentment settle in as you lower your hands, your words becoming softer, more present.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Child While the World Ends
instruction: There's an emergency—a real one, immediate and terrifying—and you're trying to keep your child calm while your own heart is exploding with fear. Start with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance: 'I've got you, nothing will hurt you, I promise.' Your voice is a shield you're willing into existence through pure force. But you can't maintain it—the terror bleeds through, your breath becomes ragged, and suddenly you're the one who needs comforting. Let yourself break completely, your words dissolving into something raw and animal, protective rage mixing with absolute helplessness. Then—find your way back. Not to calm, but to something more honest: 'I'm scared too, but we're together.' End with your voice strong again, not because the fear is gone, but because love is fiercer than fear.
inspired_by: Therapist Hears Her Client Describe Her Own Trauma

title: Vigil at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside someone's hospital bed in the deep night—a partner, a child, a best friend—and they're sleeping, maybe for the last time. You begin speaking in barely a whisper, so quiet it's almost just breath, telling them things you never said when they were awake. Your voice is tender, intimate, trembling with the knowledge that this might be your only chance. You confess small, ordinary things—how you loved the way they laughed at their own jokes, how their presence made you brave—but these tiny admissions carry the weight of your entire shared life. Halfway through, your throat closes up and you have to pause, fighting to continue. You tell them it's okay to go, even though it's not, even though you're shattering. By the end, your whisper carries both permission and desperate hope, gratitude and unbearable grief. You're saying goodbye and please stay in the same breath.

title: The Yawning Apology
instruction: You are an older woman with a soft, refined voice, seated at a formal dinner party. As you try to apologize to the host for spilling wine on the tablecloth, a massive yawn overtakes you mid-sentence. The yawn stretches your pharynx, dragging your voice into a deep, hollow slide, and you feel a wave of shame—your femininity feels exposed as clumsy and undignified. Struggle to finish the apology as the yawn distorts your words, then let your voice become small, clipped, and strained with embarrassment as you rush to express regret. At the end, your tone is tight and brittle, a sharp contrast to the yawn's openness, as you beg for forgiveness in a whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fierce and Falling
instruction: You're a parent whose child has just been hurt by the world in a way you cannot fix—betrayed, assaulted, devastated—and they've just told you about it. Begin with explosive protective rage, your voice rising as you declare what you'll do, how you'll destroy whoever hurt them, the fierce animal instinct to defend. Let your voice shake with fury and power. But mid-sentence, crash into your own helplessness—you can't undo what happened. Your declaration of war dissolves into a broken apology: 'I should have protected you.' Move from ferocious strength to complete collapse, from warrior to wounded parent who failed. Your voice shifts from roaring to pleading to weeping as you beg them to tell you how to fix this, knowing you can't. End with desperate tenderness, holding them (real or imagined), your voice wrecked, promising to stay close even though you couldn't keep them safe. Let rage, grief, guilt, and love all collide.

title: What We Never Said
instruction: You are confronting your father after years of distance. Start by looking at him - truly looking - before any words come. Notice how he's aged, how he holds himself, the things about him that are familiar and foreign at once. Let your first words emerge from genuine observation, not from rehearsed anger. Begin with controlled resentment and accusations, but as you really see him standing there vulnerable before you, allow your anger to crack open into something more complicated - perhaps recognition of his own pain, perhaps unexpected tenderness mixed with rage. Your voice should travel from sharp and cutting to trembling with unwanted empathy. End in a place you didn't expect: not reconciliation or continued anger, but somewhere true and unplanned.
inspired_by: Actor's relationship with scene partner feels artificial, uninvested, or routine; the emotional relationship demanded by material is not being felt

title: The Unexpected Vision
instruction: You are a teenage girl preaching at a small church revival, your voice carrying that rhythmic, melodic cadence. You begin in a soft, contemplative tone, speaking about the quiet moments of faith, letting your words drift with natural pauses and slight distractions as you glance at the congregation. Then, mid-sentence, you see something impossible — a flicker of light, a shape in the air — and your voice breaks with raw astonishment. Let the surprise surge through you, your cadence shifting to jagged, breathy, almost laughing as you try to describe what you're witnessing, losing your train of thought and finding it again. End in a state of trembling, wide-eyed awe.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Frustrated Compassion
instruction: Youre trying to console someone who keeps pushing you away, each rejection wearing on your patience. Speak with growing frustration tempered by love, as though struggling between staying calm and finally letting them know how much you care.

title: Belonging Felt
instruction: You're experiencing a profound sense of belonging with your partner—that you fit together, that this person is home. Your voice is almost amazed: 'This feels right.' You're in each other's arms, and there's peace in your voice. You belong. You've found someone you belong with. Your voice becomes quieter, more settled, as you experience the safety of belonging. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's found home in another person's presence.

title: Two Strangers Stuck in an Elevator: Entire Relationship Arc
instruction: Perform both characters as they progress through a complete relationship arc during a three-hour elevator failure. Start: awkward stranger small talk, overly polite. Then: shared candy bar, tentative personal questions. Then: real conversation, vulnerability, laughter. Then: charged silence, attraction. Then: a kiss (intimate close sounds). Then: existential confessions in the dark when the lights fail. End: rescue arrives and they must decide — exchange numbers or let this exist only in the elevator.

title: The Ground Holds Me
instruction: You are a child pinned to the ground by someone bigger, their weight crushing your chest. You started fighting back with furious shouts, but now your breath is ragged, each word punched out between gasps. Your voice cracks with distress, then fades into a whimper as you realize you can't break free. Let the sounds of struggle—a grunt, a choked cry, a sharp inhale—break up your words. End with a quiet, broken plea, the fight gone.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Ascent
instruction: You are an elderly woman, struggling up a high mountain trail with your beloved grandchild. Every step is a battle against thin air—your lungs burn, your legs tremble, and you pause to gasp out short, breathless phrases. At first, you feel only distress and frustration at your failing body, muttering sourly about your age. But as your grandchild waits patiently, a wave of affection overwhelms you, softening your voice into a tender, shaky whisper. Let the physical exhaustion shape your rhythm: long pauses, stolen breaths, and words that trail off as you gather strength, ending with a warm, loving look that changes your tone entirely.
emotions_sampled: Distress (extremely present), Affection (very intensely present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: 3 AM Unmasking
instruction: You and your partner are lying in bed at 3 AM, unable to sleep. In whispers, begin with a small confession - something safe, almost trivial. But this tiny honesty opens a door. Each revelation leads to another, deeper one. Your whispered voice should carry the trembling quality of someone stepping off a cliff with each sentence. Confess the attraction you've hidden, the resentment you've swallowed, the fear that lives in your chest every day. This isn't a fight - it's scarier than that. It's the complete dropping of your defenses in the dark. By the end, you've said things you can't take back, revealed parts of yourself you've never shown anyone. Move from cautious, protected honesty to devastating, naked vulnerability.

title: Whispering a Secret in a Crowded Room
instruction: You have critical information to share with someone at a loud party. Lean in close — the proximity effect should make your whisper bass-heavy and intimate. The secret is juicy enough to make your whisper urgent and precise despite the noise. Include the moment someone almost overhears — your voice cuts to absolute silence. Then resume, even quieter, lips practically touching their ear. The content should be genuinely shocking, making your controlled whisper vibrate with suppressed excitement.

title: The Understudy's Confrontation: Speaking Your Truth Backstage
instruction: You've been the understudy for fifteen years, always whispering encouragement in that soft, supportive stage whisper backstage, playing the loyal friend. Tonight, the lead is about to go on for their final triumphant performance, and you must finally speak the truth you've held back. Start with your habitual supportive whisper—gentle, deferential, almost invisible. Then let years of swallowed anger and hurt rise until you're no longer whispering at all. Your voice should transform from practiced submission to fierce assertion, from 'I'm so proud of you' to 'You knew I was better and you sabotaged me anyway.' Let the rage break into something more vulnerable—the grief of stolen dreams. End not with volume but with a quiet, devastating realization that speaking your truth has cost you the only relationship that mattered.

title: Discovering Purpose
instruction: Everything you've lived suddenly aligns. Your voice becomes clarified: 'This is why. This is what all of it was for.' Breathing deepens. Physical: you feel centered. 'I'm not lost anymore.' Vocal tone is almost musical with certainty. 'My purpose is to—' and it lands as fact, not hope. By the end, you're speaking from alignment: 'Everything I've experienced prepared me for this. This is my work.'

title: The Half-Remembered Confession
instruction: You're lying in the dark beside your partner, whispering a confession about something that happened years ago—but you can only remember it in fragments, in sensory flashes rather than clear narrative. Speak in hesitant, broken phrases, groping for words to describe images and feelings that slip away even as you try to voice them. The emotion is overwhelming—shame, perhaps, or grief—but the actual events blur like something half-forgotten upon waking. Let long silences fill the spaces where memory fails you. Begin with the urgent need to confess, to finally speak this buried thing. But as you try to articulate it, let yourself become lost in the attempt, ending in vulnerable, naked helplessness—you cannot clearly remember, yet you can intensely feel.

title: The Last Stand
instruction: You are an elderly woman, standing in your empty living room, hands on your hips, trying to project strength as you say goodbye to the home where you raised your children. You've just made the decision to move to a nursing home. Your voice starts firm and commanding, but as you look around at the faded wallpaper and the worn armchair, the sadness creeps in. Your voice cracks, you pause to swallow, and you end almost in a whisper, admitting the truth: you're not as strong as you pretend to be. Let the power pose feel unnatural, like armor that's too heavy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Clear Moment
instruction: You're sitting with your parent who has dementia, and for one brief, lucid moment they recognize you completely. Start with tentative hope—'Mom? Do you... do you know who I am?'—your voice fragile, barely daring to believe. As they say your name, you're flooded with relief and desperate love, speaking faster, trying to capture everything before the window closes: 'I'm here. I've always been here.' But even as you speak, you can see the clarity fading from their eyes. Your voice breaks as you realize this might be the last time they truly see you. End with a whispered acceptance, tears streaming, still holding their hand: 'It's okay. You can rest now. I'll remember for both of us.' The emotional journey moves from fearful hope to overwhelming gratitude to devastating goodbye—all in under two minutes.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're beside your child's bed, knowing this is the last time you'll see them—you're leaving to protect them, or you're terminally ill, or circumstances are tearing you apart. Whisper so you don't wake them, but let every word carry the weight of a lifetime of love. Start with the practical things you want them to remember, your voice catching on ordinary details that suddenly mean everything. Let tenderness break into quiet, choked sobs that you have to suppress, breathing through your nose to stay silent. End with a blessing or hope for their future, your voice dissolving into barely audible fragments, each word a small death, until you can't speak anymore—just breathe and touch their hair one last time.
inspired_by: Shouting a Warning Across a Canyon

title: The Unraveling Attempt
instruction: You are an older man receiving oral sex from a partner. Your mind is split—you're supposed to be enjoying this, but a recent disappointment (a canceled trip, a failed project) keeps clawing at you. You try to speak, to ask what's wrong or to guide them, but the sensation short-circuits your words. Start with a confused, strained question—half-lost to pleasure, half-lost to worry. As the physical sensation intensifies, your sentences break into fragments, then dissolve into moans and sharp intakes of breath. By the end, you stop fighting, letting a final moan trail into nothing, the confusion still there but muted, swallowed by the body. Let your pitch rise as you unravel, and grip the surface beneath you as if holding on.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Rival Athlete Respect
instruction: Two rival athletes are acknowledging each other's excellence and their own defeat or victory. One voice carries the high of victory but also the exhaustion. The other carries the low of defeat but also the strange respect that only comes from someone who pushed them to their limit. They're speaking with the shorthand of people who understand each other on a cellular level. There's no need for explanation. One of them says something that sounds like an apology but is actually a compliment. By the end, they're almost friends, or at least something more than rivals. The respect in both their voices is unmistakable.

title: Last Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your adult child from your hospice bed, pretending it's just a regular check-in call. Start with your usual conversational tone, asking about their day, their partner, what they had for lunch. But as you speak, you're memorizing their voice, the way they laugh at small things. When they mention something about 'next month' or 'when you're feeling better,' your throat tightens. You want to tell them how proud you are, how every moment of being their parent was worth it, but you can't say it directly or they'll know this is goodbye. Find ways to say 'I love you' without those words. Your voice gets softer, more tender. When they ask if you're okay, you lie with such fierce love that it almost sounds true. End with you trying to say goodbye casually, but the word catches, breaks, and you have to cover it with a cough.
inspired_by: Reading a Bedtime Story While Trying Not to Cry

title: Fierce Protection Breaking Into Helplessness
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt your child, and you start with volcanic rage, your voice shaking with barely restrained violence: 'You touched my daughter. You looked me in the eye at school pickups and you were hurting my baby.' Your fury is palpable, words coming fast and sharp: 'I trusted you! We invited you into our home!' But then something breaks—the rage cracks open and underneath is pure, devastating anguish. 'She stopped singing. Do you understand that? My little girl who sang every morning just... stopped.' Your voice fractures completely, caught between rage and grief: 'I was supposed to keep her safe. That was my one job, and I failed her.' Now you're crying, the words torn from somewhere deep: 'She asked me why I didn't know. Why I didn't stop you.' By the end, your voice is raw, stripped bare: 'I will spend the rest of my life trying to give her back what you stole. And I will never, ever forgive myself for not seeing.' You're simultaneously the fiercest protector and the most helpless parent who ever lived.

title: Seeing Through the Stranger's Eyes
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) after years of distance and resentment. You begin angry, armed with accusations and old wounds ready to be weaponized. But mid-confrontation, force yourself to stop and truly look at them—not as the person who hurt you, but as if they are a complete stranger you're meeting for the first time. Study their face: the lines, the exhaustion, the way they hold their body. Let yourself wonder who this person actually is beyond your narrative of them. As you look, begin to perceive what their life might have cost them, what fears might live behind their eyes. Your anger should fracture and complicate—not disappear, but become entangled with unexpected recognition. End by speaking a hard truth, but from this new place of seeing them as a full, flawed, mysterious human being rather than just your antagonist.

title: The Bride's Morning Secret
instruction: It's your wedding morning. You're alone in your childhood bedroom, putting on your wedding dress. You love your partner deeply and truly want this marriage—but you're also terrified, grieving the version of yourself you're leaving behind, uncertain if you're ready, remembering the dreams you're releasing to choose this life. Begin by touching the fabric of the dress, looking at yourself in the mirror. Let yourself fully experience this moment: the exact texture of silk or lace against your skin, the weight of the dress, morning light through familiar windows, distant sounds of celebration being prepared downstairs, the smell of your mother's perfume lingering in the hallway, the taste of champagne still on your tongue from last night. Start in bright, performative excitement—playing the role of the radiant bride. But as you're truly alone with yourself, let the complex truth surface: speak aloud the fears, the grief, the love, the hope, the doubt, the commitment, all tangled together. Allow contradictory emotions to coexist without resolving them. End in a place where you're holding both joy and sorrow, both certainty and fear, both excitement and loss—all of it true, all of it real, all of it part of this profound threshold moment.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use imaging as a choice approach in a scene

title: The Unexpected Bloom
instruction: You are an elderly person, alone in your quiet apartment after many years without touch. A vivid memory of a long-lost lover returns, so powerful you begin to pleasure yourself. Start with a wistful, interested curiosity—a faint smile as you remember a specific laugh. As the sensation builds, let hope surge through you, a fierce optimism that the body can still feel this. Your voice should shift from breathy murmurs of memory to involuntary, rising gasps. Lose control of words, dissolving into pure sound, until you reach a peak that feels like a quiet, defiant victory. End with a soft, satisfied sigh, amazed at your own resilience.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Competitive Parent at a Childrens Game
instruction: Perform as a parent who takes their childs games too seriously. Use an intense, coaching voice during the game, switching to the innocent childs perspective, creating humor from the parents overthetop competitiveness.

title: Fierce Protection Colliding with Absolute Helplessness
instruction: You've just learned your child has a terminal diagnosis. You're alone in your car in the hospital parking lot, and the explosion happens. Start with denial—voice rising, almost laughing: 'No. No, that's not—they made a mistake.' Then rage erupts. You're screaming, pounding the steering wheel, voice raw and primal: 'I'll fight this! I'll sell everything, I'll—' But mid-sentence, the helplessness crashes over you. Your fierce declarations dissolve into broken sobbing. You're begging an empty car, your voice splintering: 'Please, I'll do anything. Take me instead.' End with your forehead against the wheel, voice reduced to a destroyed whisper, all the fight drained into hollow acceptance: 'How do I watch them leave me?'

title: Smoke and Mirrors
instruction: You're leaning against a cold railing on a quiet rooftop, vaping alone at dusk. Across the street, you spot that person you've been secretly infatuated with for weeks—they're laughing with a friend, unaware of you. As you take a long drag, hold the vapor, then exhale while speaking, let the first part of your whisper be full of nervous, giddy infatuation—'God, look at her... that laugh...'—but as the smoke clears and they walk away, your voice turns raw and flat, realizing they'll never see you the way you see them. Let the drag cycle interrupt your words: a sharp inhale, a held breath, then the exhale carrying a strained, smoky murmur. End with a quiet, defeated sigh as you flick the vape away.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Bitter Toast
instruction: You're at a crowded party, gripping a half-empty wine glass near the snack table. Across the room, the person you secretly desire is laughing too closely with someone else, their hand lingering on the other's back. You force yourself to approach, raising your glass with a smile that doesn't reach your eyes. Your voice starts artificially bright, a hollow 'So happy for you both' — but the words come out tight and clipped. As you speak, a jealous heat rises from your chest, and your tone turns bitter, laced with sarcasm. By the end, you pause, swallow hard, and quietly let slip a confession: 'I'd give anything to be the one making you laugh like that.' Let the lust and envy corrode every syllable — your voice should tighten, drop, and crack with forced casualness.
