speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Wedding Toast for the Sibling You're Losing
instruction: You're giving a toast at your sibling's wedding. You're genuinely happy for them—your voice bright, warm, telling funny childhood stories that make everyone laugh. But underneath, you're losing them. They're moving across the world, or you know they're marrying someone who will slowly cut you out, or you've just been diagnosed and won't see their children grow up. Your voice cracks mid-laugh. You try to cover it with more humor, but tears start falling even as you're smiling. You lift your glass, voice thick with contradictions: 'I'm so happy for you'—and you mean it—'and I'm absolutely heartbroken'—and you mean that too. You laugh through tears, toast them with a trembling hand, and somehow convey both complete joy for their happiness and complete devastation at your loss. End with: 'To loving someone enough to celebrate them even when it destroys you.'

title: The Diagnosis Phone Call: Rage Against the Dying of the Light
instruction: You've just received your own terminal diagnosis, and you're on the phone with your best friend. Start controlled—'I need to tell you something'—but rage builds immediately. You're furious at the unfairness, the timing, all the things you'll never do. Your voice rises, breaks, becomes almost primal. Curse the universe, your body, the doctors who delivered the news so clinically. But mid-fury, you shatter differently—the anger collapses into desperate vulnerability. You're not ready. You're terrified. Your voice fractures into sobs, then resurfaces as fierce determination: you will fight this, you will rage, you refuse to go quietly. End with a sound that's simultaneously a battle cry and a prayer, your voice raw and stripped of all pretense, demanding more time.
inspired_by: Air Traffic Controller: Two Planes on Collision Course

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Protect Them
instruction: Someone you love—your child, your younger sibling, your partner—is facing something terrible you cannot fix: a diagnosis, a consequence of their choices, a danger you cannot shield them from. Start with fierce, almost aggressive determination—your voice strong, insisting you'll find a way, you'll fight this, you'll make it right. Let that intensity build as you mentally battle against reality. Then devastation hits: you can't fix this. Your voice cracks completely, rage collapsing into helpless tears. You move between anger at the unfairness and broken tenderness toward them. Your voice becomes raw, oscillating between shouting at the universe and gentle, shattered declarations of love. End in a place of surrendered presence—your voice quiet but not defeated, offering the only thing you can: 'I'm here. I can't fix it, but I'm here.' Let the helplessness and love exist together.
inspired_by: Apologizing Without Making It About Your Guilt

title: Dancing at Your Wedding
instruction: You're dancing with your terminally ill parent at your wedding—knowing this is goodbye disguised as celebration. Start with laughter, genuine joy: 'I can't believe you're actually dancing—remember when you said you'd never dance at my wedding?' You're both pretending this is purely happy. But as the dance continues, gratitude floods through, mixing with unbearable grief: 'Thank you for being here. Thank you for fighting to be here.' Your voice breaks with love and loss simultaneously. You're smiling and crying at once: 'This is everything I wanted and it's breaking my heart.' End with peaceful devastation, holding them close: 'I'm so happy. I'm so happy and I'm so scared.' Let joy and sorrow be completely inseparable.

title: Adult Child Confronts Dying Parent About a Childhood Lie
instruction: Your parent has days left, and you've finally found the courage to ask about the sibling they told you died as a baby—except you've just discovered they're alive, given up for adoption. Start with careful, almost gentle questioning, trying to give them a chance to explain. But as they deflect or justify, something ancient and wounded rises in you. Your voice grows raw with decades of wondering if you were enough, if that's why they kept this secret. Rage and grief tangle together. You want to scream and you want to crawl into their arms like a child. End in a place of exhausted, complicated love—you're furious and you're losing them and you can't bear either truth.
inspired_by: Surgeon Delivers Unexpected Complications During Surgery Debrief

title: 3 AM Phone Call to Someone You'll Never Touch Again
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're whispering into your phone, calling someone you loved deeply who is now married to someone else, living a completely different life. You both know this call shouldn't be happening. Begin with the pretense of a practical reason—you found their grandmother's recipe, their old watch, something innocent. Keep your voice low, almost inaudible, as if speaking too loudly will shatter the fragile permission you've given yourself for this connection. Gradually let the pretense fall away. Allow the conversation to become what it really is: a tender, aching acknowledgment of the life you didn't choose together, the person you might have been. End with a whispered admission of something true and devastating—not 'I still love you' but something more specific, more vulnerable: how you still dream about their hands, how you hear their laugh in crowded rooms. Your voice should barely rise above a breath, intimate as a secret told in the dark.

title: The Last Breath of Shared Air
instruction: You are an elderly woman, lying in bed beside your lifelong partner who is now gone. You are curled close, your face inches from theirs, your hand resting on their chest where no rise comes. The room is silent but for your own shaky exhales. You speak as if they might still hear you—not a goodbye, but a memory that feels too fragile to hold. Start with a whisper that trembles with disbelief, your voice cracking as you reach for them. Let yourself pause, breathe, and fade into a final, quiet surrender—a sigh that accepts the silence without letting go.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Storm Watch with Father
instruction: You're sitting on the porch with your dying father, watching distant lightning flash across the horizon one final time - something you did together throughout your childhood. Begin with quiet wonder at the approaching storm, describing it gently to him as his breathing becomes shallower. As thunder rolls closer, your voice must shift from peaceful nostalgia into the devastating realization that this is the last storm you'll ever watch together. Let gratitude for all these shared moments break into quiet grief. Your words should catch in your throat as you try to describe the beauty while silently saying goodbye. End in a whisper, telling him it's okay to let go, that you'll watch the storms for both of you now.
inspired_by: Listening to the Distant Sound of Thunder on a Warm Evening

title: The Glass Door Steams Up
instruction: You are a young mother in a sweltering tropical laundromat. The air is so thick with steam and humidity that you can barely breathe. Your toddler has locked himself inside one of the giant dryers, and the glass is fogging over. You feel a cold, heavy helplessness pressing down on your chest—every breath is a struggle, every word a wet, slippery gasp. As you fumble with a coin to pry open the door, you notice the smirk of the laundromat owner through the steam, and a tiny, amused malevolence flickers inside you—like a snake coiled in the heat. By the end, your voice must shift from frantic, sweat-soaked pleading to a low, dangerous whisper that promises retribution if your child isn't safe within the next ten seconds.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Amusement (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You are saying goodbye to a relationship that was beautiful and necessary and absolutely had to end. Begin with genuine laughter—remembering a specific, ridiculous moment you shared—and let that laughter soften into tears without transition. Express deep gratitude for what they gave you, how they changed you, even as your voice breaks with the grief of losing them. Let joy and sorrow live in the same breath. Find moments of peace in accepting this ending, then let that peace crack open into fresh pain. Your voice should move fluidly between smiling and crying, between celebrating what was and mourning what won't be. End in a place of paradox: wholly grateful, wholly heartbroken, somehow both devastated and strangely free.
inspired_by: The Detective and the Evasive Witness

title: Beneath the Surface
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner in the dark after lovemaking. To the world, to them, you're the strong one, the controlled one, the one who has it together. Start by maintaining that façade even in this intimate moment—your voice steady, your breathing measured. But let something underneath begin to tremble, a volcanic pressure of fear, inadequacy, and rage at having to be strong that you've never let anyone see. Let cracks appear in whispers. Then let yourself shatter quietly—confess in broken fragments the terror you carry, the anger at always having to be the fortress. No screaming—this is a whisper-scream, a controlled exterior barely containing an earthquake. End by letting them see the raw, undefended you that's been buried under years of armor.
inspired_by: The character is emotionally extreme (volatile, irrational, rageful) and the actor needs a large emotional foundation

title: Unraveling the Parent Who Never Answered Straight
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a lifetime of evasions, half-truths, and cryptic deflections. They're doing it again—answering your direct questions about why they were never there with enigmatic philosophies and vague wisdom. Start with controlled anger, demanding real answers for once. As they continue to hide behind riddles and abstract truths, let your voice rise with years of accumulated pain. But mid-confrontation, catch a glimpse of their fear and fragility—the realization that they genuinely don't know how to be direct, that their riddles are armor. Let your rage collapse into something more complex: pity mixed with residual anger, the ache of knowing you'll never get the straight answer you need. End almost tenderly, but with profound sadness, as you give up the fight.

title: The Vigil's Last Declaration
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother in her final hour. She can barely hear you, so you must speak clearly, projecting across the space between consciousness and the edge of life. Begin seated, speaking softly but precisely about a small regret—something left unsaid. As you sense her slipping away, rise and move around the room, your body becoming more animated, your gestures sweeping and grand as you shift from quiet regret to a full-bodied celebration of her life. Your voice must carry across the void. By the end, you're speaking with theatrical clarity and physical abandon, transforming grief into a fierce, physical tribute that fills the entire space. Let your whole body speak the words your heart needs her to hear.

title: The Letdown of Intimacy
instruction: You are an older man being pleasured by a partner who is genuinely trying but missing your rhythm. You begin with a mix of helplessness (you can't control the pace) and concentration (you focus on guiding them with small sounds and half-words). Over the next minute, the sensation builds, but the mismatch grows—your pitch rises, your breathing becomes jagged, and your whispers turn into strained fragments like 'No, a little... slower... there,' then to a moan that flatlines as you realize this isn't going to finish right. Let your voice unravel: start with controlled, breathy instruction, escalate into melodic groans, then let it die into a soft, exhaled 'It's fine... you're fine... just...'—the disappointment bleeding through as you lose hope in the moment.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (slightly present), Concentration (slightly present), Disappointment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: Someone you love deeply is in danger—maybe they're being taken away, maybe they're walking into something you can't stop—and you're trying to convince them not to go. Start fierce, your voice commanding, almost aggressive in your certainty. You're not asking, you're demanding they listen. But they're not changing their mind, and your fierceness splinters into pleading. Your voice rises, cracks, becomes desperate—you'll do anything, promise anything. The anger returns in a surge, furious at their stubbornness, at your own powerlessness, and you might even say something cruel, trying to hurt them into staying. Then it all collapses. Your voice breaks completely, reduced to raw begging or broken repetition of their name, the sound of someone watching their whole world slip away and being utterly unable to stop it.
inspired_by: Being Told You're Not Good Enough

title: The Big Surprise
instruction: You are a mother speaking loudly and slowly to your young child who is deaf and reads lips. You've just revealed a huge, unexpected gift—a puppy waiting in the next room. Your child stares blankly, not understanding. Their confusion frustrates you, and your voice strains with exaggerated clarity, each word deliberate. Then their face lights up—they get it. Your own confusion bursts into pure, overwhelming elation. Let your voice crack with joy, still loud, but now trembling with laughter. In your excitement, you repeat the news, your articulation softening as tears threaten.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Glass Your Mother Never Filled
instruction: You're confronting your mother, holding a glass of water she just offered you—the same gesture she's used for years to deflect difficult conversations. Start with barely controlled frustration as you describe the water, your voice tight, using its coldness and clarity to talk about what you actually need from her: emotional presence, not perfect hospitality. Your anger builds as you catalog all the times she offered tea, lemonade, snacks instead of listening. Then let the rage crack open into raw pain—you're not angry about the water, you're heartbroken that she doesn't know how to love you any other way. End with your voice softer, almost tender, as you realize she's giving you the only thing she knows how to give. You're still holding the untouched glass.
inspired_by: Sipping a Cold, Refreshing Glass of Lemon Water

title: Grateful Farewell to a Dying Love
instruction: You're at the bedside of someone who shaped your life—a mentor, a first love, a grandparent—in their final moments. You're overwhelmed with gratitude for everything they gave you, but your heart is simultaneously breaking. Begin with soft laughter, remembering a specific, beautiful moment you shared, your voice warm with genuine joy. Let that joy coexist with tears as you thank them for specific gifts they gave you—lessons, memories, ways they changed who you are. Move through the paradox of wanting them to stay and wanting their suffering to end. Your voice carries celebration and grief in the same breath. Shift into a moment of profound peace as you give them permission to let go, telling them what their life meant, your voice steady with the deepest kind of love. End with a whispered goodbye that holds both devastating loss and the most beautiful gratitude—you wouldn't trade having known them even for this pain, and your voice must carry that impossible truth.

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-lover's wedding—to someone else. You start with genuine warmth and humor, your voice bright and celebratory: 'I've known the bride/groom for ten years, and I can honestly say...' You're charming, funny, and everyone's laughing. But woven through the joy is the bittersweet ache of what you lost. Your voice remains light even as you say: 'They deserve someone who loves them the way I—the way we all do.' A slight catch, covered by a laugh. You raise your glass, and your voice fills with real, profound gratitude mixed with heartbreak: 'Thank you for teaching me what love looks like, even if it wasn't with me.' There's peace in your voice but also grief. You smile as your voice wavers: 'To love. To letting go. To hoping the best for someone even when it destroys you.' End with a laugh that's almost a sob: 'Now somebody get me a drink.' The challenge is to be genuinely happy for them while your heart is breaking, making both emotions equally real and present.

title: Reading the Letter She Wrote Before Giving You Up: Rage and Breaking
instruction: You've found a sealed letter your birth mother wrote to you at your birth, never delivered. Start reading aloud with your voice shaking, expecting closure: 'My dearest child, if you ever read this...' But her words infuriate you—she talks about having no choice, about thinking of you always. Your voice explodes: 'NO CHOICE? Everyone has a choice!' You're screaming at a letter, at a ghost, at the universe. 'You chose yourself! You chose the easy way!' But then you read the part where she describes holding you, memorizing your face, and your rage cracks completely. Your voice breaks into gasping sobs: 'You loved me. Oh god, you loved me and you still—' The anger collapses into something more painful: understanding her impossible situation while still feeling abandoned. End with your voice raw, fierce, protective of the teenage girl she was: 'They should have helped you. You were just a kid.' You're defending her while still bleeding from her choice, and both emotions are utterly real.
inspired_by: Adoptee Searching for Biological Family: Hope and Dread Mixed

title: Final Look
instruction: You are an elderly astronaut on your last spacewalk, floating above Earth. You’re talking to mission control, but mostly to yourself. Start with a light, amused tone—maybe chuckling at a memory of a silly training mishap or a joke your grandkid told you. Your voice bounces inside the helmet; every breath is loud. As you keep describing the view, that amusement slowly gives way to a heavier, quieter feeling—a deep sadness mixed with awe. Let your words trail off as you realize you’ll never see this again. End with a soft, almost reluctant farewell. The radio crackles between your sentences.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Twisted Gratitude
instruction: You're a teenager in a yoga class, holding a seated spinal twist. The person you've been quietly infatuated with just helped adjust your posture, and now you're thanking them—but your body is still twisted, your lungs compressed, your voice unstable from the stretch. Start with the flustered, breathless excitement of infatuation: your words come out uneven, vowels wobble, you almost lose your train of thought. As you exhale and slowly untwist, let your voice settle into a warmer, steadier gratitude—sincere and relieved, as if the effort of the pose and the crush both release at once.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Unsent Message
instruction: You are an older man sitting at a cluttered office desk late at night, typing an email to your adult child after years of estrangement. Your fear is intense—your fingers tremble over the keys, the rhythmic clicks of the keyboard matching your racing heart. You hesitate, delete, retype. But as you near the end, something shifts: the fear doesn't vanish, but it transforms into a quiet, weary resolve. Speak the email aloud as you type it, letting your voice crack and slow when the typing speeds up, then steadying as you commit to sending. End with a deep breath and a final murmured line before hitting send.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Taking a Deep Breath of Mountain Air
instruction: Inhale deeply, taking in the cool, crisp mountain air. Describe how it fills your lungs, expanding your chest with refreshing, invigorating energy. Speak with a calm, contented tone, mentioning the slight scent of pine, the earthy undertones, and the sense of clarity that each breath brings. Exhale slowly, almost as if youre breathing out tension, feeling a peaceful connection with the world around you.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are alone, and a song comes on—the song from a moment of overwhelming joy or devastating loss, a night of passionate love or shattering heartbreak. Let the music move through your body like electricity. Begin by trying to resist the flood of physical and emotional memory, but then surrender completely. Let your body respond without control—dancing wildly, collapsing, shaking, laughing, sobbing, moving with abandon. Feel the sensory memory in your skin, your muscles, your breath. Maybe you're reliving the touch of someone's hands on you, or the physical shock of grief, or the ecstasy of a perfect moment. Let the emotion crescendo through your entire body until you're spent. End in absolute stillness, your breathing ragged, your body exhausted, but your heart in a completely different place than where you started—perhaps broken open, perhaps finally released.

title: Coming Down from MDMA: The Serotonin Crash
instruction: Hours ago you were euphoric, touching everyone, declaring your love for humanity. Now the drug is wearing off and you feel hollow. Your jaw is sore from clenching. Your voice is tired, slightly confused, and sad without knowing why. Try to hold onto the beautiful feelings but they're leaking away. Include the physical discomfort — grinding teeth, dry mouth, sensitivity to light. The contrast between remembered ecstasy and current emptiness should be heartbreaking.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging father who is finally sober after decades of alcoholism. He wants a relationship now. He's saying all the right words. But you're in your forties, and you needed him when you were seven, when you were fifteen, when your own marriage fell apart. Start with controlled, cold politeness—the voice of someone who learned not to need him. Let it crack into raw anger: all the nights you waited, all the promises broken, all the ways you had to raise yourself. Then feel something unexpected happen: underneath the rage is a child's grief, still hoping. End in a whisper, the question you've never been able to ask: 'Did you ever love me enough to try?' The final emotion should be terrifying vulnerability—you've just handed him the power to hurt you one more time.

title: Discovering the Truth While They're Still Lying
instruction: You've just found proof—a message, a receipt, something undeniable—and you're confronting someone you trusted completely while they continue to deny everything. Start with eerie calm, almost clinical: 'I want to give you a chance to tell me the truth.' But as they keep lying to your face, something inside you detonates. Your voice becomes volcanic—rage, betrayal, disbelief all erupting at once. 'I'm holding the proof in my hand and you're still lying to me!' The fury is massive but then suddenly collapses into something more frightening: helplessness, devastation, the feeling of your reality crumbling. Your voice breaks completely. 'I would have forgiven almost anything. But this—watching you lie while I know—' End with fierce, broken clarity, not loud but absolutely final: 'I don't even know who you are.' Let the certainty in those quiet words be more powerful than all the rage.
inspired_by: Defense Closing Argument: Arguing Reasonable Doubt

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed, hours from death. Your estranged adult child has finally come to your bedside after years of silence. Begin in a state of desperate relief—you thought you'd die without seeing them again. As you speak, your body is failing, breath becoming harder to catch. Tell them the one truth you've been too afraid to say your entire life. Mid-way through, feel the terror rise: you're actually dying, this is the last conversation, there's no more time. Transform this terror into a fierce, urgent need to make them understand how deeply you love them, how proud you are, even if you failed to show it. End in a place of quiet peace mixed with grief—you can let go now, but you wish you'd found these words decades ago.

title: Mother's Reckoning
instruction: You've just received a call that your teenage child has been in a serious accident because you were too distracted, too stressed, too absent to notice their spiraling mental health. You're in your car, pulled over, and you explode—screaming at yourself, at God, at the universe. Your voice is raw, uncontrolled, breaking with primal fear and self-loathing. Slam your hands against the steering wheel as you shout. But mid-rage, you fracture completely—the screaming dissolves into gasping sobs, your voice becoming small, childlike, begging for another chance. You bargain desperately with any power that might listen: take your career, your home, your own life, just let them survive. Then, gathering fragments of yourself, your voice hardens with fierce maternal protectiveness—swearing that if they live, you'll be different, better, present. End trembling but determined, whispering a prayer that's half threat, half plea.

title: Three in the Morning Whispers
instruction: You and someone you love are lying in darkness at 3am, unable to sleep. In a barely-audible whisper, confess something you've never said aloud - perhaps that you're terrified of losing them, or that you feel like a fraud in your own life, or that you're not sure you know how to be loved. Begin with the shame and resistance of exposing this part of yourself, your breath shallow and uncertain. As you speak, let the relief of finally saying it aloud wash over you. Feel them listening without judgment in the dark, and let that safety crack you open further. End with a whispered realization that being truly known - even in your brokenness - is the only real intimacy you've ever wanted. Keep everything quiet, interior, trembling with restraint.
inspired_by: Actor is depressed and cannot access creative energy

title: Skin and Thunder
instruction: You're in a moment of overwhelming physical and emotional intensity—either in the throes of passionate intimacy, in the grip of blinding rage while destroying objects in a room, or experiencing a rush of ecstatic joy mixed with physical exertion (dancing alone, running until your body screams). Your entire body is alive with sensation: heat, electricity, pain, pleasure, power. Express this through pure vocal sound: roars, gasps, cries, growls, laughs, moans—whatever emerges from your body's response to this intensity. Begin with explosive, uncontrolled vocal energy that matches the physical sensation—loud, raw, unleashed. As the experience progresses, let your sounds shift from purely physical release into something more complex: sounds that carry both power and vulnerability, strength and surrender, until you end with exhausted, trembling vocalizations that reveal how this intensity has left you exposed and transformed.

title: Final Letter to a Child You'll Never Meet
instruction: You're recording a voice message for the child you're carrying, knowing you won't survive the birth. Start with careful, measured words—trying to be brave, practical, telling them about their father, about the life you wanted to give them. But as you speak, your composure fractures. The measured tone gives way to raw grief mixed with fierce love. 'I wanted to teach you to ride a bike. I wanted to embarrass you at your wedding.' Your voice breaks, becomes urgent, desperate to pack a lifetime of love into minutes. End with a whisper that's both devastating and tender—not trying to be strong anymore, just a mother saying goodbye. 'You were loved. You were so loved.' Let the silence after those words carry everything you couldn't say.
inspired_by: Defense Closing Argument: Arguing Reasonable Doubt

title: Dancing in the Kitchen During Hospice Care
instruction: Your person—your soulmate—asked you to dance one more time. Their favorite song is playing. Start with laughter, genuine and light, as you take their frail hand. You're humming along, making jokes about their two-left-feet, remembering the wedding, that trip to New Orleans. Your voice is buoyant with gratitude for this moment. But mid-dance, they stumble, and reality crashes in—this is the last dance. Your laughter catches, transforms into something between a sob and a chuckle. You keep dancing, keep swaying, but now you're thanking them through tears, your voice breaking as you say you'll be okay (a lie) and that they can rest (the hardest truth). There's devastating beauty here—you're holding both profound gratitude and shattering loss in the same breath. End with your voice soft, still humming, finding strange peace in the chaos of loving someone you're losing. This is not performed grief—this is finding grace in the unbearable.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Made You Doubt Love
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who taught you that belonging was conditional, that love had to be earned. Begin with anger—recounting how their coldness made you afraid to let anyone close, how you almost destroyed the relationship that finally showed you what belonging feels like. Your voice is accusatory, listing wounds. But mid-way, something shifts: you realize you're no longer that frightened child. Let your voice soften as you speak about the person who loved you into wholeness, who showed you that you were always worthy of belonging. End not with reconciliation, but with a bittersweet release—you're grateful for what you found despite them, and you're finally, finally done needing their approval. Your last words should sound like freedom mixed with the ache of what you deserved but never received.

title: Bedside Vigil: The Quiet Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's slipping away—hospital machines beeping softly, but they're barely conscious. Your voice is barely above a whisper because anything louder feels violent in this sacred, terrible space. Start by just breathing with them, then begin speaking softly about ordinary memories—'Remember when we got lost in Prague? You were so mad at me.' Your voice catches on gentle laughter that immediately dissolves into tears. You're giving them permission to go, but every word costs you everything. 'It's okay. You can rest now. I'll be okay.' (You won't be.) You hold their hand and describe the sunset outside their window in excruciating, tender detail because you want them to see beauty one more time. End with your voice breaking on 'I love you,' said so quietly it's almost just breath, as you feel them slip away. This should feel like watching someone dissolve into light—unbearable and holy.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Wife After the Diagnosis
instruction: It's 3 AM and she's finally asleep beside you after weeks of tests. Your voice is barely audible, tender and broken, as you tell her sleeping form all the things you couldn't say while she was awake. Start with the practical fears—finances, the kids—your voice trying to stay controlled, problem-solving. Then let it dissolve. Tell her about the first time you saw her, voice catching on the memory. Describe ordinary moments—her laugh, the way she drinks coffee—as if you're trying to memorize them through words. Your voice should be intimate, raw, sometimes pausing as emotion closes your throat. Include a moment where you almost wake her because you need to hear her voice, but you don't. End with a whispered promise you're not sure you can keep, your voice so quiet it's almost just breath, saturated with love and terror and the weight of trying to be brave enough for both of you.
inspired_by: Photographing an Active Lava Fountain While Knowing You're Too Close

title: Dancing at Your Own Goodbye Party
instruction: You're at a celebration before you leave for something permanent—hospice care, a one-way journey, exile. Everyone's trying to be happy for you, and you're trying to give them that. Start with genuine laughter and warmth, greeting people, remembering good times. But underneath, you're memorizing faces, voices, moments. Your joy becomes edged with desperate appreciation. You find yourself laughing and crying simultaneously—grateful for every second while grieving that there won't be more. Your voice catches on ordinary words that suddenly mean everything. By the end, you're thanking someone for something small—making coffee, sharing a joke—and the gratitude is so enormous it nearly destroys you. Finish with a sound that's both celebration and farewell, love and loss so intertwined you can't separate them, your voice breaking on the word 'beautiful' or 'enough' or 'thank you.'

title: Raid Boss and the Bad Back
instruction: You're in an online co-op game with friends, but your lower back is screaming from a long day. At first, you force out tactical callouts and cheery banter, hiding the pain behind a gruff tone. Mid-sentence, a sharp spasm makes you inhale sharply and lose your train of thought. By the end, the pain breaks through — your voice cracks, you trail off, and you admit you need a break. Let your voice waver between tough-guy casual and raw, vulnerable winces.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Words Before the Ship Leaves
instruction: You're at the dock saying goodbye to someone you love who is boarding a ship for a journey they will never return from - a one-way colonization mission to another planet, or a dangerous expedition, or exile. You start with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them, your voice artificially cheerful as you say things like 'You're going to do amazing things.' But as the departure time approaches, your composure cracks. Your voice begins to tremble as you realize this is truly the end. You're trying to memorize their face, and suddenly words pour out - all the things you never said, confessions of love or regret or gratitude that you've held back for years. End with your voice breaking on a whispered 'Don't forget me' or 'I should have told you sooner,' as the finality crushes you. The emotional journey moves from false optimism to desperate, raw vulnerability.
inspired_by: Tripping and Falling at a Wedding

title: Laughing Through the Impossible Victory
instruction: You've been given six months to live, and in that time, you achieved the dream you thought you'd have a lifetime to pursue. You're describing it to someone you love, and you can't stop laughing - genuine, almost wild laughter - at the cosmic absurdity. 'Of course. Of course it happened now.' Your voice sparkles with disbelieving joy, almost giddy with the irony. But the laughter keeps breaking into tears you don't try to hide, then back to laughter again. You're grateful and furious and amused and heartbroken all at once. 'It's perfect timing, really. The universe has a sick sense of humor.' End with something that's simultaneously celebration and farewell, peace and rage: 'I got everything I wanted, just in time to leave it behind. And somehow... somehow that feels right.' Let contradictory emotions blur until they become the same thing.

title: When Passion Becomes Desperation
instruction: You're desperately trying to convince someone you love to stay by describing all the amazing things you'll do together—trips you'll take, mundane moments that will be magical, the beautiful ordinary life you'll build. Start with genuine excitement and hope, your voice bright with possibility. But as you sense them pulling away, let desperation creep in. Your enthusiasm becomes manic, your descriptions more frantic and exaggerated, voice rising and speeding up as you try to paint a future compelling enough to make them choose you. Finally, let it all shatter—the performance collapses into raw pleading, then anger, then broken silence. End with your voice reduced to a whisper, admitting what you knew all along: no amount of beautiful words can make someone love you enough to stay.

title: The Last Advice I'll Ever Give You
instruction: You're a parent on your deathbed, and you've spent your whole life trying to fix everything for your child with misguided wisdom—terrible advice disguised as expertise you never actually had. Now, in your final moments, you begin offering one last piece of confident, completely wrong guidance about how to live their life. Mid-sentence, the reality hits you: you've been doing this their whole life, and you wasted so much time pretending instead of just being honest. Your voice should crack as you shift from that false confidence to raw, whispered apology. End by telling them the one true thing you've always known but were too afraid to say simply. Let the transformation happen in your throat—from performance to complete, vulnerable truth.

title: Your Child Confronts You About the Lie That Destroyed Their Trust
instruction: Your adult child has discovered the truth you've hidden for years—the credentials, the expertise, the foundation of your authority in their life was fabricated. They're confronting you with quiet, devastating anger. You begin defensive, voice tight and brittle: 'You don't understand the pressure I was under.' But their silence forces you deeper. Your defenses crack and rage surfaces—rage at yourself, at circumstances, voice rising: 'I did it for us! For this family!' Then the rage collapses into something more vulnerable. Your voice drops to almost nothing, shaking: 'I was so afraid of being ordinary. Of you seeing me as... nothing.' End on your knees emotionally, voice raw and pleading, begging them not to look at you with that expression—the one that says you've become a stranger.
inspired_by: Admitting You've Been Lying About Your Credentials

title: The Wedding Toast I'm Actually Giving
instruction: You're standing to give a toast at a wedding—maybe for a sibling, best friend, or ex-partner who's marrying someone else. You begin with the expected: warm, celebratory, appropriate words. But as you continue, allow the complicated truth to seep in. You might feel genuine joy mixed with piercing loss. You might want to make a dark joke. You might feel anger at being left behind even as you're happy for them. Your voice might crack not from sentimentality but from grief. You might find yourself saying something wildly inappropriate that's also wildly true. Don't choose between the contradictory feelings—hold them all simultaneously. The arc moves from the sanitized version of your feelings to the full, messy reality: celebrating someone while mourning something, loving them while resenting them, wishing them well while wanting to scream.
inspired_by: Actor questions whether including an impulse in performance is appropriate or misinterprets the material

title: Telling Your Mother You're Done Trying to Earn Her Approval
instruction: Start calm, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this conversation a thousand times. You're finally saying you won't chase her love anymore, that you're enough as you are. But as you speak, decades of small rejections flood back: the piano recital she missed, the way she introduced your sibling with pride and you as an afterthought. Your voice begins to shake with rage you didn't know you were carrying. You hear yourself getting louder, then suddenly you stop. In the silence, you realize you're not angry—you're heartbroken. End in a whisper, telling her you release her from expectations she never asked for, your throat tight with the loss of a relationship that never existed.
inspired_by: Lawyer Wins Case Against Former Mentor Who Destroyed Her

title: The Mathematics of Almost
instruction: You've just received news that you got the opportunity you've sacrificed everything for - the job, the acceptance, the success you've been chasing for years. You're calling the person you pushed away to achieve it, the one who begged you to choose them instead. They answer. Start with genuine excitement, wanting to share this victory, not yet feeling the full weight. But as you hear their voice - warm but distant, kind but no longer yours - let the cost materialize. Your joy doesn't disappear; it curdles into something more complicated. You're celebrating and grieving simultaneously. By the end, you're trying to convince them (and yourself) that you made the right choice, but your voice betrays that you're not sure anymore. Let the triumph and the loss occupy the same breath.
inspired_by: Actor is experiencing result-consciousness or awareness of being on stage—the acting consciousness is too close to the surface

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, finally brave enough to say what you've carried for decades. Start calmly, almost rehearsed: 'Mom, I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, the facade crumbles. Your voice sharpens with decades of buried pain—'You were so cold. I was just a child and you were so cold to me.' The anger builds, then suddenly breaks into something more vulnerable: you're that child again, voice small, asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' End with exhausted honesty, not seeking her response anymore, just releasing the truth: 'I just needed you to see me.' Let silence hold the weight of everything unsaid for thirty years.
inspired_by: Realizing Someone You Love Doesn't Love You Back Anymore

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You While She Packs to Move Away
instruction: She's folding clothes, packing boxes, acting like everything is fine. You're standing in the doorway of your childhood room, and the words that have lived in your throat for twenty years are finally coming out. Start controlled, almost casual—helping her pack, making small talk—but then the truth starts spilling. Tell her what it was like. Tell her about the loneliness, the nights you waited, the ways you learned to be small and quiet and unneeded. Your voice should rise and fall unpredictably: sharp with anger, then breaking into something raw and childlike, then back to bitter clarity. She might not even stop packing. You need her to hear you, but part of you is also terrified she will. End with something you've never said—maybe 'I needed you' or 'I still do' or 'Why wasn't I enough?'—and let your voice strip down to nothing but painful honesty.
inspired_by: Plating the Final Michelin Dish While Your Restaurant Is Failing

title: The Fever Dream of Wanting
instruction: You are in the grip of an overwhelming physical and emotional state—perhaps intense desire for someone forbidden, perhaps pain from a wound while remembering who caused it, perhaps fevered illness while hallucinating someone you've lost, perhaps the physical aftermath of violence mixed with unexpected emotional release. Begin in one clear physical sensation, but let it blur and shift into emotional territory and back again. Your body and heart are not separate here—physical sensation triggers emotional memory, emotional surges create physical responses. Let sounds escape you that surprise you. Allow the intensity to build and break and build again in waves, taking you through multiple emotional states: rage melting into tenderness, desire twisted with grief, pain dissolving into strange euphoria. Don't control or choreograph it—let your body lead your emotions and your emotions flood your body until you can't tell them apart. End in unexpected stillness or collapse.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never Present
instruction: You're standing in your childhood backyard during an approaching storm, finally confronting your estranged parent about all the moments they missed - including nights like this when you sat alone, watching lightning, wishing they were beside you. Start with controlled calm as you describe the distant thunder, but let buried anger surface as you tell them how you learned to find comfort in nature's power because they weren't there to comfort you. Your voice should grow more raw and accusatory - 'I learned to love storms alone because you were never here' - before breaking into the vulnerable truth: you still need them, you're still that child waiting on the porch. End with exhausted honesty, no longer angry, just heartbreakingly honest about the parent-shaped hole in your life.
inspired_by: Listening to the Distant Sound of Thunder on a Warm Evening

title: The Last Call for a Ghost
instruction: You're an older woman alone at a dim dive bar, heavily intoxicated. You've been laughing with the bartender, slurring jokes about your day, feeling a giddy relief from the world's weight. But a familiar song on the jukebox triggers a wave of longing for your late husband. Your voice sways with your body, volume dropping as you speak to him as if he's beside you—tears threaten, but you chuckle at your own foolishness. Keep the slur thick, let the elation crack into raw tenderness, and let the longing swallow you by the end.
emotions_sampled: Elation (extremely present), Relief (slightly present), Longing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Last Brush of the Night
instruction: You're a teenage girl, back from a late party, utterly exhausted and still a little buzzed. You stand at the bathroom sink, brushing your teeth, barely able to keep your eyes open. As you scrub, the foam builds and your jaw stays slack, making every word mushy and distorted. Start with drowsy, mumbling complaints about how tired you are, but halfway through, a fleeting thought about something someone said at the party shifts you into a quiet, sad realization. Let your voice crack and slow, then drift back into a tired, resigned murmur as you spit and rinse. The foam, the brush noise, and your drooping eyelids should all interfere with your speech naturally.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Prison
instruction: You're watching your child sleep, knowing you'll be gone when they wake—you're turning yourself in tomorrow. Your voice is barely audible, tender beyond measure, catching on every word. 'You're so beautiful when you dream.' Speak as if your voice could shatter them. Tell them about their goodness, their light, your pride. 'You made me want to be better.' Then the shift: your voice fills with quiet devastation as you apologize for what's coming. 'I'm so sorry. This will hurt you.' Tears fall silently. Your breathing becomes uneven as you try to memorize their face. End with a whispered promise, voice breaking: 'I will come back to you. Wait for me.' Let silence speak between words. This is love meeting unbearable loss.

title: Furious Devotion
instruction: You are an older woman confronting someone you're infatuated with, standing inches from their face. You're furious about a betrayal, but your anger is tangled with desperate need. Start with hard, accusatory glottal attacks—loud, dry, almost spitting words. As you speak, your voice cracks under the strain, and your intensity shifts from rage to a raw, pleading confession. Let the infatuation seep through: a sudden softening, a waver, a tiny break. By the end, your fury has melted into a vulnerable, breathy admission that you can't stand to lose them. Speak about 50 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Discovering Your Lover's Betrayal While They're Standing Right There
instruction: You've just found irrefutable proof of their betrayal - the evidence is in your hands. You begin reading it aloud, your voice sharp and mocking, almost laughing at the audacity of what they've done. Your rage is volcanic, righteous, and you want them to feel small. But as the words pour out, something inside you starts to shatter. The mockery breaks into shouting, the shouting cracks into disbelief, and suddenly you're not angry anymore - you're destroyed. Your voice goes from a roar to something ragged and small. You're asking 'why' and 'how could you' and you hate that you sound so broken. The fury collapses into grief, then surges back as protective rage, then dissolves into the terrible realization that you still love them and that makes it so much worse.
inspired_by: Comforting Someone Whose Trauma You Share

title: The Inheritance of Everything and Nothing
instruction: You've just received news of an unexpected inheritance (money, property, a letter, forgiveness) from someone who caused you profound pain. You're alone, reading their final words or holding the object they left you. Begin in stunned disbelief, your voice uncertain, almost suspicious. As you process this gift, allow waves of contradictory feeling to crash over you: rage at what they did, grief for what you lost, unwanted gratitude for this final gesture, resentment that they think this makes things right, and underneath it all, the terrible recognition that you still love them despite everything. Let specific images surface: their face at a particular moment, their hands doing a particular action, a room where something happened. Your voice should break and rebuild multiple times. End in a place of impossible complexity—not resolved, not forgiven, not healed, but holding all of these truths simultaneously, your voice simultaneously broken and whole.

title: Forgetting the Words to Our Song
instruction: You're at your partner's bedside in their final hours, trying to sing the song that was 'yours'—the one you've sung together a thousand times—but grief is stealing the words from you. Begin with tender determination, voice soft and intimate, trying to be strong for them. As you lose the lyrics, don't cover it with humor—let the frustration catch in your throat, let the pauses become heavy with unsaid goodbyes. Your voice should crack not from drama but from the authentic weight of trying to give this one last perfect moment and failing. Shift between humming the melody, whispering apologies for forgetting, and fragments of the lyrics that do come back. End with a whispered admission that maybe you don't need the words—just being here, voice breaking, is enough. Let love, devastation, and acceptance interweave.

title: The Fever of Goodbye
instruction: You're reuniting with someone you have intense history with—an ex-lover, perhaps—knowing you have only minutes before they leave forever, getting on a plane or into a car. Your whole body is electric and chaotic. You're angry and hungry for them at the same time. You want to scream and you want to kiss them. As you try to speak, your body betrays you—your hands shake, you might grab their arm too hard, your breath comes wrong, you feel physically ill with the confusion of wanting and hating. Words fail. You might move toward them, then pull back. Every sensation is too much—the smell of them, the proximity, your own heartbeat. By the end, you've maybe touched their face or pushed them away or both, and you're left with your body still ringing like a bell after they're gone. The emotional shift is from combative chaos to a devastating, physical emptiness.
inspired_by: Actor's scene work is good but polished and predictable — missing genuine organic reality

title: The Map of the Fire
instruction: You are an old military historian, curled on your side in bed after a stroke has paralyzed your left side. The neighbor's dog has just barked outside, and you realize it's the same bark as the dog that alerted your unit to an ambush in 1972. Interest seeps through your body—there is a detail, a date, a name just on the tip of your memory. Start in pure, fierce curiosity, like a hound on a scent. But as you try to call out to your daughter, the bitterness of your helplessness, of this body that betrays you, creeps into your voice. You are not angry at her—you are angry at the years. Your breath is shallow, one lung pressed by the mattress. Speak softly, with pauses where you search for words your mind still holds but your tongue cannot find. The emotion must flip from sharp, hungry interest to a quiet, seeping bitterness by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You're remembering someone who's gone—perhaps they've died, perhaps they left, perhaps you've lost them to time—and you begin by sharing a memory that makes you genuinely laugh. Your voice is light, almost joyful, caught up in the warmth of remembering. But even as you laugh, tears start. You keep talking, keep sharing the memory, but your voice begins to shimmer with contradictions: gratitude and loss, joy and devastating absence, laughter that keeps breaking into sobs and sobs that keep lifting into laughter. You can't tell if you're laughing or crying anymore. End with a moment of profound, peaceful acknowledgment: your voice settles into something quiet and full, carrying both the light of what was and the weight of what's gone. Let your voice hold both truths at once without trying to resolve them.

title: The Party Whisper
instruction: You're leaning close to your best friend at a backyard barbecue, pulling her into a tight huddle. Your voice is hushed, almost breathless, as you share a secret about a mutual acquaintance. Start with deep doubt — you hesitate, bite your lip, then let the words tumble out in quick, choppy bursts. Let sourness creep in as you recount a petty slight, then let a surprised laugh slip out at the absurd timing of it all. By the end, your pitch drops, your rhythm slows, and you realize you feel a little ashamed of your own amusement.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (very intensely present), Sourness (clearly present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unsent Letter Read Aloud
instruction: You're reading a love letter you wrote years ago but never sent, alone in the room where you last saw them before they died. Begin in a whisper, your voice catching on words you've held inside for decades. These are confessions of desire, regret, things you were too afraid to say when it mattered. Let your voice stay small and intimate, as if they might actually hear you across the void. Halfway through, let the reality crush you—the futility, the too-lateness of it all. Your breath becomes uneven, words fragmenting: 'I should have... if I'd just...' By the end, you're no longer reading—you're speaking directly to their absence, your voice barely audible, throat tight with unshed tears. This is the quietest devastation, the kind that lives in your chest forever.

title: The Secret Nobody Saw
instruction: You're at a dimly lit bar with a close friend, leaning across the table, speaking low and fast. You're sharing a bizarre rumor about a coworker that you just heard, but halfway through, you realize the details don't add up, and you're genuinely trying to piece together what's true. Start with a teasing, conspiratorial edge—like you're letting them in on something juicy—then let your voice catch, your pace slow, your pitch drop as confusion takes over. Let your breath go short, fidget with a napkin, look off to the side as if replaying the facts in your head. End with a mumble of uncertainty, almost talking to yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Echo
instruction: You are at the edge of a vast, empty quarry at dusk, alone. You are screaming into the void—not words, just raw sound—because you are utterly infatuated with a person who treated you with nothing but contempt, and you are finally, disgustedly, sick of yourself for it. Start with a long, guttural yell of pure frustration, then let it dissolve into a jagged, breathless monologue. Your voice should crack with infatuation (a lingering tenderness for how they looked in the rain), curdle with contempt (mimicking their dismissive tone as you recall their sneer), and be laced with a faint, sour disgust for your own pathetic longing. As you speak, you shift your weight, kick a stone, lose your train of thought when you hear an echo, then spit out the final admission with a hollow, bitter laugh.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Contempt (extremely present), Infatuation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast Unraveling
instruction: You are giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, but you are also in love with them, and they're marrying someone else. Before you begin speaking, check in with what you genuinely feel—perhaps surprising happiness for them, perhaps bitter resentment, perhaps numbness, perhaps a strange mix. Begin your toast from that honest place, not from where you think you should be. Let your real feelings carry your words, even if they seem contradictory. As you speak, allow your emotions to authentically shift and tangle: perhaps from forced cheerfulness to genuine affection mixed with grief, from trying to be generous to feeling the full weight of your loss, from celebrating their joy to mourning your own hope, from bitterness to a complicated gratitude for having known this love at all. End somewhere emotionally different and more complex than where you started.

title: Breaking the Mirror
instruction: You're alone, looking at yourself in a mirror after a moment of total humiliation or betrayal—you've just lost everything you built, or discovered your body is failing you, or realized you've become someone you despise. Begin with physical action—maybe your hands on the sink, staring at your reflection. Let yourself move impulsively between what you see in the mirror, sensations in your body (tension, nausea, heat, trembling), statements of who you are or were, what you want to destroy or reclaim, what you feel coursing through you, what you need to survive this. Don't perform emotion—let it come from noticing actual sensations: your jaw clenching, your breath catching, energy rising in your limbs. Build to a physical breaking point—whether that's smashing the mirror, collapsing, or some other explosive release. By the end, find yourself in the aftermath: either raw emptiness or an unexpected ember of fierce determination. Let your body lead your voice.
inspired_by: I Am, I Want, I Need, I Feel

title: Whispering Your Truth to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner is asleep beside you. You whisper confessions you can't say when they're awake—start with something small and tender: 'I watched you sleep and felt so lucky.' But each confession grows heavier, more honest, more terrifying. Whisper the truth about your fears, your doubts about the relationship, the secret that could end everything. Your voice should be barely audible, catching in your throat, thick with unshed tears. The intimacy of the darkness makes you braver and more vulnerable simultaneously. Pause between confessions as if gathering courage. End with the most devastating truth of all—but just as you whisper it, they stir and murmur your name in their sleep. Your sharp intake of breath, your frozen silence, your whispered 'I love you' in response should contain both relief that they didn't hear and grief that they'll never know.
inspired_by: Teaching a Parrot to Say 'I Love You'

title: The TimeTraveling Historian
instruction: Portray a historian who accidentally timetravels and tries to explain modern technology to historical figures. Switch between the historians explanations and the historical figures confused reactions, using different accents and speech patterns.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Spouse Before You Leave
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're leaving your marriage. Your spouse is asleep and you've decided not to wake them—this goodbye is only for you. Whisper your confession to their sleeping form. Start with the practical things you'll miss: their coffee routine, the way they hum while cooking. Your voice is tender, almost inaudible. But then the real truth emerges—you've been dying slowly in this love, suffocating under their goodness, their innocence. You're the villain in this story and you know it. Your whispers catch in your throat. You almost reach out to touch them, pull your hand back. Describe one perfect memory that makes you question everything, your voice breaking on words like 'almost' and 'maybe.' End by saying 'I'm sorry' in a way that encompasses everything you can't explain, your voice so quiet it's barely breath.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You are an astronaut stranded in deep space, recording your final message to Earth before your oxygen runs out. Begin with clinical detachment as you describe what you're seeing - the stars, the silence, the beauty of it all - as if you're still on a mission report. But as you continue, your voice must crack with the realization that you'll never touch soil again, never feel rain, never embrace anyone you love. Let wonder at the cosmos mix with devastating homesickness. End with a whisper of gratitude for having seen this impossible beauty, even as your heart breaks that no one you love is here to share it. Your words should feel like they're floating away into the void, taking pieces of you with them.

title: Deathbed Reconciliation: Your Last Words to the Parent Who Abandoned You
instruction: You're sitting beside your estranged parent's hospital bed. They're dying, unconscious, but you've been told they can still hear. Begin with bitter, controlled anger—all the things you've rehearsed for years: 'You were never there. I needed you and you chose yourself.' Your voice is steady, righteous. But as you speak, something breaks. The anger cracks open and underneath is the devastated child who just wanted to be loved. Your voice becomes smaller, more vulnerable. You find yourself confessing things you never meant to say: 'I used to wait by the window.' The tears come. And then, impossibly, you feel yourself forgiving them. Not because they deserve it, but because you need to let go. Your final words are tender, almost a lullaby, telling them it's okay to go. The journey is from controlled rage to broken-hearted release to unexpected grace.
inspired_by: Extreme Altitude Climb: Lucidity Breaking Down in the Death Zone

title: The Gratitude That Burns
instruction: You are thanking someone who saved your life—perhaps literally, perhaps emotionally—but the gratitude is tangled with rage. Begin speaking words of thanks, but let them come out wrong, too loud, your body agitated. Thank them for their sacrifice while your fists clench. Tell them how much you owe them while your voice rises in anger. They saved you, yes, but the cost was your autonomy, your choices, your right to fail on your own terms. Let the contradictions amplify—love and resentment, debt and fury, appreciation and the need to break free. Physically push away their help even as you acknowledge it. By the end, arrive at a complicated truth: you are grateful AND you need them to let you go. The final tone should be both fierce and tender, claiming your freedom while honoring what they gave you.

title: The Gratitude List While Watching Them Leave
instruction: You're writing a thank you card to someone you're watching walk away - to a terminal diagnosis, to a calling you can't follow, to a life you're not part of. Your voice should do something impossible: laugh while crying, find genuine joy while your heart is shattering. 'Thank you for every ridiculous argument about—' (laugh, but it's wet with tears). 'Thank you for ruining me for anyone else—' (cross it out, but you're smiling). Weave together gratitude and devastation so completely that they become the same thing. Your voice breaks with laughter on one line, catches with grief on the next. Include moments of pure, radiant happiness about specific memories, immediately undercut by the reality of the goodbye. By the end, you should sound absolutely destroyed and profoundly at peace simultaneously. The final thank you should be whispered with a smile you can hear, even as your voice shakes with loss. This is what it sounds like to be grateful for someone even as losing them breaks you.
inspired_by: The Most Passive-Aggressive Thank You Card

title: Teaching the Parent Who Failed You
instruction: Your aging parent is asking you to teach them something they should have taught you—how to apologize, how to listen, how to show love. They're trying, fumbling, not understanding, and you're caught between that old childhood frustration of never being enough for them and the adult ache of watching them be so small and lost now. Start with controlled patience masking deep resentment. Let the old anger surface when they keep getting it wrong—'You never learned this for me when I needed you.' Then shift as you see their genuine confusion and fear. End in a complicated place: still hurt, but softer, explaining one more time with a tenderness that surprises you both. Your voice should carry decades of unspoken pain alongside reluctant forgiveness.

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your adult child who is leaving on a military deployment to an active war zone, and both of you know they may not return. Start with forced cheerfulness—making jokes about care packages, reminding them of silly childhood stories, keeping your voice light even as it threatens to crack. Gradually, the facade crumbles. Your attempts at bravery give way to raw fear, then to fierce pride mixed with devastating love. There's a moment where you almost beg them not to go, but instead you tell them how proud you are, your voice breaking on every word. End in a whispered confession of how terrified you are to lose them, but how you understand why they must go. Let the silence between your words say what you cannot.

title: The Louder the Demand
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing in your living room, hands planted on your hips, elbows out, chest broad. The person you desire most stands before you, but you're furious they've been ignoring your needs. Your voice booms with anger, but your breath is shallow from exhaustion and the longing that knots your stomach. Let the power pose lock your ribs open, forcing your words out louder and sharper than you intend. As you speak, feel the lust twist into your rage—your tone might suddenly drop, become huskier, then crack with fatigue. Start with a fierce accusation, but let your voice soften at the end as you confess what you really want, the raw need bleeding through the anger.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Speaking During a Panic Attack While Hiding It
instruction: Your nervous system is in panic but you're supposed normal. Your voice is faster with words tumbling: 'I'm fine, just...' Your breathing is audible and shallow. You're physically activated but performing calm, speech faltering. Panic worsens and your voice becomes incoherent, barely holding on.

title: The Shell That Remembered
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a voice that carries a soft, almost girlish lilt, walking alone at the shoreline. For a moment, you feel a quiet sadness—a distant ache for lost time—as the cold foam curls around your ankles. Then you spot a shell caught in the tide, unlike any you've ever seen, and your entire being snaps into a state of rapt, childlike interest. Your voice lifts, breath quickens with discovery, and you speak partly to the wind, partly to yourself, pausing as the waves swallow some of your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Apology Scratch
instruction: You're a seven-year-old girl sitting on the kitchen floor, trying to get your cat, Muffin, to come out from under the table. You were mean to her earlier—you yelled because she knocked over your juice box. Now you feel a twist of shame in your belly. You start with a firm, commanding voice, clicking your tongue and saying 'Muffin, come here, right now.' But she just stares, and your voice cracks into a softer, high-pitched plea. You make kissy noises, then admit in a small, wobbly voice, 'I'm sorry I yelled. I didn't mean it.' You trail off, distracted by her tail twitching, then whisper a promise of treats, your tone shifting from guilt to hopeful tenderness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: New Physical Limitations After Accident: Anger to Acceptance Cycle
instruction: After your accident, you're trying to do something you used to do and you can't. Your voice is frustrated, angry, almost raging: 'I should be able to...' Your body has betrayed you and your voice carries that betrayal. Include the moment where you stop fighting and assess reality. Your voice becomes quieter, more technical: 'Okay, I can't do that. What CAN I do?' This isn't acceptance yet—it's pragmatism. But pragmatism is the beginning. Your voice describes the workaround, the adaptation, and there's something almost powerful in that problem-solving. You're angry that you have to, but you're doing it anyway. Your voice reflects the grinding acceptance that this is your life now. Not the life you planned for, but life nonetheless. The anger hasn't gone away—it's just being channeled.

title: Summit Fever, Thin Air
instruction: You are a young woman who finally reached a high mountain summit after a grueling climb, but altitude sickness hits hard. You are gasping for oxygen, your head pounds, and your words come out slurred and slow. You speak into your phone's voice recorder, trying to capture the moment for your family back home. Begin with doubt—questioning if this was worth the pain and risk, then let fear creep in as you realize how vulnerable you are. But as you look at the vast, beautiful view beneath the clouds, a fierce, almost delirious elation overpowers you—you laugh weakly, cry, and whisper that it's the most terrifying and glorious thing you've ever done. Let your voice crack, trail off, and struggle; show the headache in winces and the confusion in pauses, but let the joy burn through by the end.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (clearly present), Elation (extremely present), Fear (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Rhythm of Soreness
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman power walking on a park path after a painful breakup. Your hips ache, and every heel strike sends a dull tremor through your voice. You're talking to yourself under your breath, trying to push through the pain. Then, from the corner of your eye, you notice a child blowing dandelion seeds into the wind — a small, bright curiosity pulls your attention for a moment, lightening your tone before you remember the ache and return to your rhythm. Let your voice be breathy, slightly strained from the movement, and let the distraction catch you off guard into a softer, wondering state, then fade back into the pain.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Soap and Sorrow
instruction: You're a teenager, washing dishes at a big farmhouse sink. The constant rush of water and clatter of plates fill the room, making your voice loud but distant. At first, you're humming with a quiet, nervous thrill—like when you like someone you shouldn't. Your hands submerge a glass, fingers sliding over the slick surface, and a soft laugh escapes you. But then a memory hits: your little sister, who you tucked in earlier, whispering goodnight. Your voice cracks with a sudden wave of affection so strong it aches. You pause, letting a plate slip and clink, and the cozy warmth in the room turns sharp—a mix of wanting someone's touch and fearing how much love you already hold.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Fear (slightly present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Thanking the Enemy You've Forgiven
instruction: You are speaking to someone who caused you deep harm—someone you've built in complete detail within your imagination, mixing elements of real people who've hurt you with entirely fictional qualities, sensory details, and history. Construct them fully: the exact set of their jaw, the specific way they breathe, the particular words they used that cut you, the look in their eyes (real or invented) when they damaged you. Begin with the intention to thank them, but let your voice carry the weight of old anger, resentment, and pain underneath the words of gratitude. As you speak about how their harm paradoxically shaped you, strengthened you, or taught you, feel the genuine contradiction churning inside: you truly are grateful for who you've become, AND you're still angry about what they took from you. Let your tone shift unpredictably between tenderness and barely contained rage, between genuine appreciation and bitter irony. Notice the exact sensation in your throat as you try to hold both truths at once. End in a place of complex peace that doesn't erase the pain—perhaps your voice softens into something ancient and weary, or breaks into unexpected laughter mixed with tears. The person you're addressing has become completely real through your sensory imagination, and so has this impossible tangle of feeling both ruined and grateful, both wounded and whole.
inspired_by: When no real-life parallel exists for character circumstances

title: Finding Home in the Void Between Galaxies
instruction: Your ship has malfunctioned in the intergalactic void—no stars visible in any direction, no chance of rescue, systems failing. You're recording what should be a message of despair. But instead, start laughing—softly at first, then with genuine wonder—because you've never seen such perfect darkness, such complete absence. Your voice dances between awe and grief, delight and acceptance. You're describing the most beautiful nothing you've ever witnessed, and your heart is breaking with joy. Find gratitude for the terror, peace in the catastrophe. You're simultaneously mourning your death and celebrating the privilege of seeing what no human has ever seen. Let tears and laughter blur together. Your voice becomes a love letter to existence itself, even as existence lets you go. End in serene astonishment—you're finding grace in annihilation.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Space Explorer Realizes the Planet Is Conscious

title: The Jealous Submissive’s Reckoning
instruction: You are kneeling on a soft bed, palms flat on the mattress, your feminized voice steady but breathy. Your partner has just told you they spent the night with someone else—someone younger. You agreed to this scene to 'earn' their attention back, but jealousy burns in your throat. As the first strike lands, you yelp sharply, then whimper a recovery. Each hit forces a different emotion: the start is wounded envy, then the count becomes a plea for proof of your worth. You breathe in jagged gasps, your pitch spiking with each impact. By the final strike, your voice cracks with relief—envy fading into a raw, earned belief that you are still theirs. Say: 'One... Two... Three... I needed that. I needed to know you still choose me.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Thing I Never Asked You
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. For years, you've pretended to understand her stories about the old country, her childhood, her first love—nodding along without really knowing what she meant. Now it's too late to fake understanding. Begin by trying to offer comfort with hollow reassurances, your voice tight with the fear of your own ignorance about who she really was. Then break—admit out loud that you never truly understood her stories, that you nodded when you should have asked, that you're terrified she'll die and you'll never really know her. End by desperately asking her to tell you one true thing about herself, your voice raw and stripped of pretense, transformed from false confidence to naked need for real connection before it's gone forever.
inspired_by: Actor bluffs on set rather than admitting ignorance

title: The Best Day Ever
instruction: You are a young child, eight years old, lying in bed after the most incredible day of your life—a trip to the amusement park, your first roller coaster, cotton candy, and a fireworks show. You're still buzzing with elation, recounting every detail to your stuffed rabbit, but your body is heavy with exhaustion. Start with bright, fast, excited words, but as you go, your eyelids droop, your sentences slow and stretch, words blur together, and you jerk awake once before finally trailing off into a mumbled, sleepy whisper.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Conductivity Testing
instruction: You're asking if there's chemistry between you. Your voice is testing the air, careful. Will they meet you halfway? Your voice is vulnerable question. When they respond warmly, your voice feels the current. 'There's something here,' you say. Both of you can feel it—the conductivity of connection. Your voice becomes warmer, more open. Possibility sounds like recognition.

title: The Rot Beneath the Cinders
instruction: You're at a campfire, telling a story to your friends. You begin describing the time you found a dead animal in your backyard as a child — its body swollen, crawling with maggots. Let your voice tremble with pure disgust: gag, wrinkle your nose, pause to spit. But as you speak, the horror shifts. Start mimicking the maggots' squirming with a grotesque, fascinated whisper. Let the disgust slowly morph into a surreal, hypnotic acceptance of decay's strange beauty. End in a hushed, rhythmic cadence, as if the sickness has become a reverence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What I Never Told You in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your sleeping lover, whispering a confession they cannot hear. Begin with your voice barely audible, tender but cautious. You are telling them something you believe would change everything if they knew: a betrayal, a secret love, a truth about yourself you've hidden. Start with hesitant, fragmented words—stopping, starting, almost chickening out. Let your whisper carry both intimacy and terror. As you continue, allow yourself to become braver in the darkness, your words flowing more freely, your voice catching with emotion. Move from fear to a strange, bittersweet relief at finally speaking it aloud, even if they can't hear. End with a moment of overwhelming tenderness—perhaps touching their face gently—where love and guilt intertwine so completely you can barely breathe. Your final words should be almost inaudible, a prayer and an apology and a love song all at once.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build the unconscious background of a character between rehearsals

title: The Held Door
instruction: You're a teenager who stutters. You've just walked up to a coffee shop door, and someone holds it for you — but it took you a long, frustrating moment to get your order out at the counter earlier.
