You feel hot with embarrassment and irritation at yourself. As you reach the door, you want to say 'thank you,' but your throat locks. The person waits patiently. Finally, you force out a strained, desperate apology for the delay, then a raw, choked thank you — not polished, but genuine. Your voice should start tight and hurried with shame, then crack open into something softer, almost relieved, as the kindness sinks in. Stutter naturally: repeat sounds, get stuck on the 'th' of 'thank,' let the pitch rise at the release.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Embarrassment (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confessions in the Dark
instruction: You're whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something about yourself that fills you with shame, longing, or tender vulnerability. Speak as if the darkness is your only witness, your voice barely above a breath. Begin with halting words, stopping and starting, almost unable to say it aloud. As you continue, let the relief of finally speaking your truth mix with fear of being known. Let silences matter—pause where the emotion catches in your throat. By the end, there's a quiet courage emerging, a soft strength in naming what you've hidden. Your voice should feel intimate, unguarded, like you're letting someone see the most fragile part of your soul. Move from terrified hesitation through trembling honesty to whispered, achingly tender acceptance.

title: The Missing Friend
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a small gathering of strangers. You were promised your best friend would be here, but they haven't shown up. The conversation is stilted, full of awkward silences and nervous laughter. You start by forcing a bright, cheerful tone, trying to fit in—laughing a little too hard at a joke, glancing at the door between words. As the silence grows, your voice drops, your filler words slow down, and the disappointment seeps through. End with a quiet, almost resigned confession about your friend not coming.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Unanswered Prayer
instruction: You are kneeling in a cold, damp garden at dawn, your hands pressed into the soil. The pain in your joints is a constant, burning presence that has stolen every night of sleep for weeks. Begin by begging a silent universe for relief, your voice tight with desperation and anger, each word a struggle against the ache. As you speak, notice the dew on a leaf, hear a distant bird, and feel the weight of your own body — let the realization creep in that no answer will come. End in a whisper, not of defeat but of quiet acceptance, as if you are saying goodbye to the fight itself, while the pain still hums beneath your skin.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Interview
instruction: You're a podcaster doing a live interview with a young guest who has just admitted they support a controversial cause you find morally repulsive. You start with a warm, inviting tone, leaning into the mic with genuine curiosity about their perspective. But as they describe their reasoning, a quiet anger builds behind your eyes — your jaw tightens, you shift in your seat, and your voice loses its honeyed warmth. You end by cutting them off mid-sentence with a cold, barely controlled disgust, the false intimacy shattered.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Anger (clearly present), Disgust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Your Child Telling You About Their Eating Disorder
instruction: They're telling you they have an eating disorder. Your voice stays steady though you're catastrophizing: 'Thank you for telling me.' You ask questions while internally panicking. 'We're going to get you help,' reassuring. Include your worry surfacing before you pull it back. Voice ends determined: you're going to fix this.

title: Not Scared
instruction: You're a kid standing on the sidewalk after dark, hip cocked, hands in your pockets, trying to look cool. You're telling your older sibling you're not scared to walk home alone, but your voice wavers. Start with a sassy, casual tone—maybe even a little defiant—but let the doubt creep in as you glance at the shadows. By the end, your words trail off into a quiet, honest admission that yeah, maybe you are a little scared. Let your body shift, pause to kick a pebble, and let the last line come out almost like a question.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Stretching in the Morning Sunlight
instruction: Lift your arms high, stretching each part of your body as the sunlight warms your skin. Describe the gentle pull in your muscles, the feeling of each part of your body waking up as the sunlight spreads over you. Speak slowly and softly, letting your words flow like the stretch itself, and mention how each movement feels refreshing, almost like a gentle release that sets you up for the day.

title: The Funeral Laugh
instruction: You're at your best friend's funeral, and suddenly a memory hits you so hard you start laughing—really laughing—through your tears. Begin with a choked sound that could be either: 'God, remember when we...' Your voice breaks into genuine laughter recounting something ridiculous they did, something so perfectly them. But the laughter keeps catching on sobs, your voice oscillating between joy and devastation. You're talking to them as if they can hear: 'You absolute idiot, you would have loved your own funeral.' There's gratitude pouring through the grief, love mixed with rage that they're gone. Your voice should be messy, uncontrolled—laughing one moment, weeping the next, sometimes both at once. End with a quiet realization, your voice soft but lit from within: 'Thank you for making everything, even this, somehow bearable.' The final tone should be impossibly bittersweet—shattered but somehow whole.

title: The Last Recording
instruction: You're terminally ill, recording a video message for your child who won't remember you. You start with forced cheerfulness, trying to smile through phrases like 'Happy birthday, sweetheart. I wish I could...' but you can't finish. The pauses grow as grief overtakes performance. 'You need to know that...' long silence, fighting tears '...that leaving you is...' The word won't come. By the end, you're whispering fragments between silences that stretch unbearably long. 'I'm so sorry. I wanted...' The final pause holds everything you'll never say. The recording continues after you can no longer speak.

title: Empty House Echo
instruction: You're alone on a large theater stage after the final dress rehearsal, the house lights dim. The vast space swallows your footsteps, and your voice bounces back from the back wall with a slight delay. Start by standing center stage, looking out at the empty seats, overwhelmed by the quiet grandeur of the place—let your words hang, almost reverent, as you feel the awe of the moment. Then, you remember you're waiting for the sound tech who's ten minutes late. Your awe sours into impatience; your voice hardens, you shift weight, check your watch, and the reverb now sounds mocking. Say this aloud: 'This room... it holds everything. Every laugh, every tear. And right now it's holding nothing but my voice. (pause, then sharply) Where is he? I said eight thirty. Eight. Thirty. I'm standing here talking to ghosts while he's—(trails off, waves a hand) Forget it.'
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Bedside Confession at 3 AM
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love who is sleeping, and you are whispering the truth you can never say to their waking face. Start with your voice barely audible, confessing something shameful—an affair, a lie, a betrayal, something that would destroy them to know. Let your voice catch and restart, the words coming in fragments. As you speak into the darkness, something shifts. The confession becomes a love letter, tender and broken. You describe the exact way they laugh, the gesture they make when worried, how their presence has been the only home you've ever known. End with the devastating acceptance that you will carry this secret forever to protect them, your voice so quiet it's almost just breath, but somehow more honest than you've ever been.

title: I Can't Feel Anything Anymore
instruction: You're alone, going through your skincare routine mechanically, and something breaks. Begin with mounting frustration—pressing products into your skin harder than necessary, describing the sensations with increasing desperation as you try to FEEL something, anything. Your voice should escalate from controlled to frantic: you used to find peace in this ritual, but now it's just another reminder that you're numb, disconnected, going through motions. Build to an explosion where you're nearly shouting, demanding your skin to feel, your body to respond, yourself to WAKE UP. Then let it collapse—your voice breaking, hands trembling against your own face as you whisper that you don't know who you are anymore. End in raw vulnerability, touching your face with genuine confusion, as if meeting a stranger, trying desperately to find your way back to yourself.
inspired_by: Feeling the Tingling Sensation of a Cooling Face Mask

title: Rearview Farewell
instruction: You are a teenage boy in the back seat of a car, twisted uncomfortably to look out the rear window as you drive away from a friend's house. Your neck is craned, making your voice slightly strained. You start content, watching the house shrink, and feel a quiet amusement at a silly memory. But as the view changes, disappointment settles in as you realize you forgot to grab your jacket. Speak naturally, with pauses, shifting weight, and the vocal tightness from the twisted posture. Begin with a relaxed sigh of contentment, then a chuckle, then a trailing off into regret.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (clearly present), Amusement (clearly present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Breaking Point Ecstasy
instruction: You have just received news that saves your life—a medical reversal, a pardon, a miracle—after weeks of believing you were doomed. Your body is flooded with sensation: shaking, heat, cold, electricity. Before making any sound, notice what you actually feel physically and emotionally in this moment—it might not be pure joy. Maybe there's rage at what you endured, maybe grief for the person you became while waiting, maybe your body won't stop shaking. Let those real sensations and feelings pour through your voice when you finally speak or cry out. Your emotional state should transform: perhaps from shocked numbness to wild laughter mixed with sobbing, from disbelief to anger at what was stolen from you, from relief to overwhelming exhaustion. Let your voice ride the genuine wave of what's happening in your body.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin overwhelmed by the weight of all the things you never said, feeling small and tongue-tied, unable to find words big enough for this moment. As you speak, let yourself discover that the smallest memories—the way they laughed at your terrible jokes, the summer you built that treehouse, the night they talked you out of giving up—are actually everything. Move from feeling inadequate to express your love, to realizing that your ordinary, specific memories ARE the love letter. End in a place of quiet wholeness, where you've given them exactly what they needed: the truth that they mattered in ten thousand small ways.
inspired_by: Actor feels inadequate to meet a specific character or scene obligation

title: Waiting Room Whispers
instruction: You are sitting in the hospital waiting room where you spent three nights when your sister was in ICU five years ago—those plastic chairs, that fluorescent hum, the smell of antiseptic and bad coffee. Your partner is beside you now, and you need to tell them you're pregnant, but you're terrified because you lost a baby in this same hospital two years ago. Let the room's sense-memory hold you: the coldness of the chair through your clothes, the too-bright lights, the institutional quiet broken by distant beeps. Begin curled inward, protective, your hand unconsciously on your stomach. The room knows your grief; let it surface first—the ghost of the baby you lost here, the fear this place branded into your body. Then, gradually, let the new reality emerge: there's life inside you again, hope knocking at the door of your terror. Whisper the truth to your partner, your voice barely audible, letting vulnerability crack you open. End with your partner's hand joining yours on your belly, and feel the room's meaning begin to shift.

title: Joy Explosive
instruction: You just got the job, the acceptance, the yes. Pure, uncomplicated joy. Your voice erupts—high, loud, uncontrolled. You might yell: 'YES! YES!' You're laughing, spinning maybe, your voice bouncing with the physical movement. Breathing is rapid, excited, almost hyperventilating-adjacent. When you form words, they tumble: 'I can't believe—I actually—oh my god!' Your vocal cords are vibrating at a higher frequency. Intonation is all upward trajectories. This is short-duration, intense, unfiltered happiness made completely audible.

title: The Unfunny Joke That Broke Me
instruction: You are a teenager who just got expelled for a prank you didn't pull. Your mom is on the phone, telling you how disappointed she is, and you're trying to explain it wasn't you, but you keep laughing uncontrollably — the nervous kind that knots your stomach. Start with a sharp, anger-edged breath as you try to defend yourself, but the words fracture into wheezes and squeaks. By the end, the laughter dies into a quiet, raw realization: she doesn't believe you, and that hurt is worse than any punishment. Let the anger crackle in the first strained syllables, then let it dissolve into the hollow disappointment of being unheard.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Speaking to Your Child After Getting Angry You Regret
instruction: You lost it and your child is hiding. At their bedroom door, your voice starts controlled and formal—'I'm sorry I scared you.' But real shame surfaces and your voice gets smaller. You're asking forgiveness from someone much younger and your voice reflects the terrifying imbalance of power.

title: The Body Remembers
instruction: You're alone, and suddenly a physical sensation triggers an overwhelming emotional memory—the scent of someone's cologne unleashes buried grief, a particular song brings back the electricity of first love mixed with the agony of how it ended, or touching a certain fabric floods you with childhood fear and adult rage. Let your body respond first: your breath catches, your muscles tense or release, your skin remembers. Begin by trying to control the response, to push it down as you've done before. But this time, let it overtake you completely—allow the physical and emotional to merge until you can't separate them. Your voice might start controlled and then break into gasping breaths, whispered curses, or sounds that aren't quite words. By the end, you should be physically and emotionally spent, having let your body fully express what your mind has been censoring.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child: The Apology They'll Never Hear
instruction: Your child is asleep. You're sitting beside their bed in the dark. Your voice is barely above a whisper—you don't want to wake them, but you need to say this. You start apologizing for the parent you've been, the moments you were too tired, too distracted, too broken by your own life to show up fully. Your whisper becomes choked with tears you're trying to hold back. You tell them about your own childhood, why you are the way you are, and your voice catches—you're realizing things about yourself as you speak. By the end, you're whispering a promise to do better, your voice tender and aching, filled with a love so fierce it hurts. This isn't a performance—this is you at your most naked, most vulnerable, speaking truths in the safety of darkness.
inspired_by: Lying About Where You Were and Contradicting Yourself

title: Shattered Glass - Protecting What You've Already Lost
instruction: You're standing in your destroyed home after a break-in, on the phone with someone you love who's far away and in danger. Start with fierce, adrenaline-fueled energy—you're trying to warn them, protect them, your words rapid and urgent. But as you look around at the destruction, panic rises. Your voice escalates to near-screaming, desperate commands mixed with pleas. Then something shifts—you realize you can't protect them, can't control this, and your rage explodes into helpless sobbing. Your voice cracks and fractures as you oscillate between fury at your powerlessness and terror at what might happen. Smash something in rage. Then collapse. End in a raw, guttural place where protectiveness and helplessness war with each other, your voice hoarse, breaking on words, admitting through tears that you're terrified and don't know what to do.

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: It's the morning of your wedding and you're alone, getting ready. You should be happy—you are happy—but you're also flooded with terror. Begin speaking aloud to yourself in the mirror, trying to focus on joy and excitement. But let the fears intrude: flash rapidly through every nightmare that's ever haunted you about commitment—your parents' violent fights, the ex who abandoned you, the fear of being trapped, the fear of being left, the fear of becoming your mother, the fear of repeating your father's mistakes, the terror of being truly known, the panic of forever. Switch quickly between each fear, your voice shifting from excited bride/groom to terrified child to angry adult. End with a moment of choice: either you break down completely, admitting you can't do this, or you acknowledge every terror and choose to walk forward anyway, voice shaking but determined, tears of both fear and ferocious love streaming down your face.
inspired_by: Switch-Trick Exercise in Fear and Terror Areas

title: Rage That Breaks: Protecting Someone You Cannot Save
instruction: You're screaming at doctors, at God, at fate—someone you love is dying and there's nothing you can do. Start with explosive, almost violent fury: pounding fists, voice raw and ragged with desperation. Your anger is fierce, protective, refusing to accept the unacceptable. But mid-rant, the rage cracks open and collapses into sobbing helplessness. Your voice breaks from roaring to pleading to whimpering. Feel the complete powerlessness flood in—all your strength, your fight, your fierce love means nothing against this. The transformation from warrior to shattered human happens in seconds. End on your knees, voice hoarse and small, begging for what cannot be given. The love is immense; the helplessness is crushing.
inspired_by: Confronting Someone While Hungover and Still Drunk

title: The Last Clear Morning
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in the pre-dawn stillness. For years, you couldn't find the words, but now—facing his final hours—everything you needed to say comes flooding through with devastating clarity. Start in quiet confusion, voice barely above a whisper, fumbling for what you want to tell him. Then the fog lifts: 'Dad, I understand now why you...' Your voice strengthens not with performance but with the profound relief of finally seeing him as a whole person, flawed and doing his best. Move from tangled resentment through sudden comprehension to tender forgiveness. End with simple, clear gratitude spoken directly to him: 'Thank you for trying. I see you now.' Let tears come if they need to, but keep your voice steady with the weight of truth finally spoken.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Love After the Diagnosis
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner is finally asleep beside you after the worst day of both your lives. You can't sleep, so you're whispering everything you need to say while they can't hear you. Begin with your voice barely audible, fragile as spun glass, confessing your terror. Let silence do as much work as words—the pauses where you almost can't continue. Your breathing betrays you, catching on tears you're trying to keep quiet. Move through memories of small moments that suddenly mean everything: the way they laugh, how they take their coffee, the specific warmth of their hand. End with a whispered promise that's both vow and prayer, your voice finding a strange, trembling strength in the darkness. This is tenderness mixed with grief so deep it has no bottom.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Sibling She Gave Away
instruction: You've just discovered you had a brother or sister your mother gave up for adoption before you were born, and she never told you. You're confronting her, and she's defensive, saying she did what she had to do, that it's ancient history, that you have no right to judge. Start with controlled anger, laying out the evidence, demanding truth. Let your rage build as she deflects—she kept this secret your whole life, let you believe you were an only child. Then break into something rawer: the grief of a relationship stolen from you, the loss of a sibling you never got to know. End when her defenses finally crumble and she whispers the real reason she gave them away, and you have to hold both your fury and your sudden, devastating understanding of her pain.
inspired_by: Time Traveler Warning Themselves Not to Go

title: What We Never Said
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner of twenty years, confessing something you've hidden your entire relationship. Your voice is barely audible, tender and terrified, because saying it out loud—even to their unhearing ears—makes it real. Start with fragile courage, voice catching on every few words as you describe the secret you've carried. The tenderness in how you talk about them—their kindness, their trust—makes the betrayal or hidden truth even more devastating. You keep pausing to touch their hand, to memorize this moment of peace before everything changes. Your whispers become even softer as grief builds, not for what you've lost yet, but for what you're about to lose. End with your voice breaking on 'I'm so sorry,' repeated like a prayer, barely breath, tears falling silently because you can't let them hear you break, not yet, not until you find the courage to say this when they're awake.

title: The Last Migration
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your grandmother who is hours from death. As you hold her hand, you begin the scene feeling heavy, exhausted, unable to move—as if your body has turned to stone. Let your breathing be shallow, your movements minimal. As you speak your final words to her, allow something to shift: imagine your spine lengthening, your shoulders opening, as if something wild and free is awakening inside your chest. By the end, let your body feel light, almost weightless, as if you could take flight. Your grief remains, but now it moves through you differently—swift, graceful, unburdened. Let this physical transformation change how the goodbye feels in your throat, in your voice, in the tears that may or may not come.

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You and your lover are lying in the dark, and you're about to confess something you've never told another living soul—a secret shame, a buried trauma, a truth about who you really are that you fear will make them leave. Your voice should start barely audible, trembling, stopping and starting. Feel your throat tighten with vulnerability. Let silence be part of this—long pauses where you're gathering courage. Your breathing should be unsteady. As you speak, you're watching for any sign of their reaction in the darkness, terrified. But as the words finally spill out, something unexpected happens: the release of this secret feels like shedding skin. By the end, you're crying softly, but it's different—it's relief, it's being truly seen. Your final words should be barely a whisper: 'Thank you for staying.'

title: The Hollow Echo
instruction: You are lying beside your lover in the dark, but everything inside you has curdled. As they touch you, you let out the expected moans and sighs—your throat obeys the rhythm of pleasure—but your eyes are dry, your mind distant, and a quiet, deliberate cruelty sharpens behind each sound. Start with sounds that feel almost automated, the breathy sighs of someone going through the motions. Let a note of sourness creep in: a slight nasal edge, a tiny delay before you respond. Midway, let your voice go numb—a moan that dies too quickly, a sigh that lacks warmth. By the end, let a thread of malice thread through a high, stretched 'oh,' making it sound less like ecstasy and more like a threat you're keeping to yourself. Fidget with the bedsheet, pause mid-sound as if distracted by your own coldness, then resume with a harsh, almost triumphant openness in the vowel.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Straw
instruction: You are a refined older woman, known for your gentle, polite demeanor, standing in your perfectly kept living room. A loved one has just shattered your trust one final time. Start with quiet, pained disappointment—a voice trembling with the effort to stay composed—but feel the rage building, a hot pressure behind your ribs. Let it erupt into blind fury: slam your hand on a table, let your voice go rough and cracked as you hurl short, percussive accusations. Let the anger burn out into raw, hollow pain, your voice dropping to a broken whisper as you realize you have nothing left to say.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Pain (extremely present), Anger (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Mother Who Cannot Protect
instruction: Your child has just told you something terrible that happened to them, and you weren't there to stop it. Begin with fierce, protective rage—your voice sharp and strong, making promises to fix this, to destroy whoever hurt them, your whole body vibrating with the need to fight. But as reality sets in—that you can't undo what happened, that you failed to keep them safe—your power collapses. Your voice should fracture from warrior-fierce to utterly broken, from 'I will burn the world down' to 'I'm so sorry, I'm so sorry.' Let yourself cycle between helpless rage and crushing guilt, between wanting to be their strength and falling apart completely. End in a kind of desperate tenderness, holding them (real or imagined) while your voice shakes, whispering that you're here now, even though you know it's not enough. Make it messy, contradictory, visceral—the sound of someone trying to be strong while shattering.
inspired_by: In Love with Lifes Last Moments

title: Soggy Leash, Doubtful Heart
instruction: You're a teenager, walking your anxious rescue dog in the rain. You've just gotten a text that your best friend is moving away, and you're questioning whether she even cares. You're on the sidewalk, tugging the leash when your dog stops to sniff a puddle. Speak to your dog—using high-pitched clicks, baby talk, and short commands—but let your voice tremble with doubt. Start with a cooing 'come on, baby' that fades into a distracted, worried mumble, then end with a strained 'good girl' that sounds more like you're trying to convince yourself than her. Your voice should shift between the sweet pet voice and a hollow, questioning tone, as if you're talking to the dog but really wrestling with your own uncertainty.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You wake beside your partner on their final morning before leaving for a mission they may not return from. Your voice begins tentative, almost afraid to wake them—whispering 'Are you awake?' When they respond, you feel the desperate need to memorize this moment. Tell them what you've been too scared to say: how you notice the way morning light catches their face, how their breathing sounds like home. Your emotion shifts from careful tenderness to urgent vulnerability as you realize time is running out. Let your voice break when you try to be brave, saying 'Come back to me' while knowing you can't guarantee anything. End with a whispered promise or prayer that feels both hopeful and heartbroken. Let silences speak as much as words—the pauses where you're trying not to cry, the moments where you just breathe together.

title: The Final Report
instruction: You are on a night shift at a control center, fighting to stay awake after 36 hours. A critical alarm has sounded, and you must report it to your supervisor. You start urgently, voice tight with distress, racing to explain. But your body gives out: sentences slow, words blur, you catch yourself mid-mumble and jerk back awake, restarting with panic. Each time you drift further. By the end, your distress has hollowed into a defeated whisper as you finally let sleep take you mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Grievance
instruction: You are an elderly man, bitter and wired on a stimulant you took to keep going. You stand alone in a cluttered garage, jaw tight, mouth dry. You're muttering a final rant to a worn-out photograph of someone who betrayed you decades ago. Start with rapid, clipped bitterness — consonants mashed by clenched teeth, words spitting out like a machine gun. Let the dry mouth make you pause, swallow, click your tongue. As you speak, the bitterness cracks; a flicker of old pain seeps through, then the intoxication pulls you back to a shaky, fast whisper. End quieter, almost lost, but still bitter. Say: 'You think I forgot? I remember every... every lie. I carried this. Like a stone. In my gut. And you... you just walked. Left me here. (dry swallow) Still here. Still... holding it.'
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Rage That Becomes Surrender
instruction: You're confronting the universe, fate, God, or whoever's listening about an unbearable loss or injustice. Start with volcanic fury—voice loud, fierce, almost shouting: 'You want me to accept this? You want me to just... what? Be okay with this?' Let your voice crack with the violence of your anger. Escalate into accusations: 'I did everything right! I was good, I was careful, I loved with everything I had!' Your rage is righteous, protective, the sound of a heart refusing to break quietly. Then something collapses—mid-sentence, the fury dissolves into helpless sobbing: 'I can't... I can't do this. I don't know how to survive this.' Let yourself sound completely undone. Finally, through tears, find a whisper of desperate, exhausted surrender: 'Help me. Please. I don't know what to do anymore.' End with raw vulnerability—not acceptance, but the moment when fighting becomes impossible and you simply break open.

title: Whispered at the Window: Telling Your Sleeping Child You're Leaving
instruction: You're standing over your sleeping child, hours before you leave—for prison, for treatment, for a necessary separation that will break both your hearts. Your voice is barely above a whisper, conscious of not waking them. You're explaining what you can't say in the morning, apologizing for things a child shouldn't have to forgive. Your throat keeps closing. Breathe through the tightness. Your voice wavers between trying to be strong for them and allowing yourself to break. You memorize their sleeping face. Confess your fears in fragments. Your voice becomes tender beyond measure, then catches on a sob you have to swallow. End with a simple 'I love you' that contains all the goodbyes you'll never get to say properly. Let silence do half the work.
inspired_by: Professional: Therapist Realizes Their Own Trauma Is Preventing Them From Helping

title: Precision Importance
instruction: You're a prosecutor reading the charges against someone on trial for your sister's murder. Your voice is exact, deliberate, no room for misinterpretation: 'On the evening of March 14th, at 7:47 PM...' The precision is a weapon. Every fact is laser-pointed. Then you reach the part about the victim: 'Sarah Chen, age 23...' Your voice doesn't waver, but the precision becomes almost painful in its exactness — you're speaking with the authority of absolute grief. 'She was found...' you pause, choosing the exact word '...discarded, like garbage.' That one word choice — after all the precision — says everything. By the end, your precise voice has become a scream trapped in perfect diction.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about decades of emotional neglect, finally saying everything you've held back your entire life. Begin with controlled anger, your words precise and measured, each one chosen to cut through years of dismissal. As you speak, let that anger crack open to reveal the wounded child underneath—your voice should shift from accusatory to pleading, from strong to broken. Demand to know why you were never enough, why they couldn't love you the way you needed. Let rage dissolve into raw vulnerability, your voice becoming smaller, younger, more desperate for acknowledgment. End with exhausted acceptance mixed with lingering hope—maybe they'll finally hear you, maybe they won't, but you've finally said it. Your tone should feel like peeling back layers of scar tissue, painful but necessary.

title: Protecting Someone You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone—physically or emotionally—as danger approaches or as they're slipping away from you. Start fierce, almost aggressive in your protectiveness: 'No. NO. I won't let this happen. Stay with me. STAY WITH ME.' Your voice is commanding, powerful, refusing reality. But you feel control slipping. The fierceness cracks into desperation: 'Please, please, I don't know what to do, tell me what to do—' Then rage erupts at your own helplessness, a roar of frustration and grief. Finally, the rage collapses into broken tenderness. Your voice becomes soft, almost a lullaby, as you realize all you can offer is your presence. End holding them with words of love, your strength transformed from fighting to surrendering, fierce protectiveness becoming fierce acceptance.
inspired_by: Trying to Order Coffee While Having an Existential Crisis

title: Finding Joy in the Snow the Day After the Funeral
instruction: You're watching snow fall the morning after burying someone you loved, and despite everything, it makes you smile. Describe the flakes with genuine delight, even laugh softly at their randomness, their absurd beauty. But let your laughter catch in your throat. Your voice should hold both wonder and shattering grief—you're grateful for this moment of peace, but your heart is breaking that they're not here to see it. Tell the snow (tell them) thank you for this gift of beauty when you needed it most, your voice warm with love but fractured with loss. End with contradictory emotions fully present: peaceful and devastated, grateful and destroyed, finding comfort in the very thing that reminds you of everything you've lost.
inspired_by: Watching Snow Fall Outside Your Window

title: Echoes in the Dark
instruction: You're a young woman alone in a vast underground tunnel, your phone flashlight barely cutting the blackness. Dripping water echoes irregularly, your own breath bounces back distorted. You start by calling out hopefully, trying to sound braver than you feel, each word swallowed by reverb. As minutes pass, your voice tightens—you realize the battery is dropping, the way back feels lost. Let the cave's acoustics warp your tone: a trembling, hyper-feminized voice that starts steady but fractures into raw, contained distress, ending on a whisper that barely carries.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Showing Your Art to Someone Who Doesn't Get It
instruction: You created something deeply personal. A painting, a song, a story. You're showing it to someone. Your voice is vulnerable as you explain it. They respond with politeness but you hear the 'it's not for me' underneath. Your voice becomes smaller. 'Yeah, I understand.' Your voice is protecting yourself now. You're taking it back, metaphorically. Your voice becomes guarded. They tried but they missed the point. Your voice carries quiet disappointment.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father about something he did when you were twelve that neither of you has ever spoken about. Begin with your body tight, your voice controlled, almost cold—you've rehearsed this confrontation a thousand times in your head. Start by describing the specific day, the details, keeping your anger buttoned up and precise. As you speak, let the child inside you start to break through the adult armor. Your voice may crack, your hands may shake. By the end, you're no longer accusing—you're asking the question you've needed answered for twenty years: 'Why didn't you protect me?' Let the rage dissolve into something more vulnerable, a child's bewilderment mixed with an adult's exhaustion. The journey is from controlled fury to exposed, aching need for understanding.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are experiencing a moment of overwhelming physical sensation—perhaps reuniting with a lover after months apart, or standing at the edge of a cliff feeling utterly alive, or in the grip of grief so intense it manifests as physical pain in your chest. Your body is flooded with sensation and your emotions are inseparable from these physical feelings. Begin by trying to describe what you're experiencing, but let language fail you. Let sounds emerge that aren't quite words—gasps, half-formed phrases, repetitions. Your breath should be audible, irregular. As the intensity builds, allow a secondary emotion to surface underneath the primary one: perhaps terror underneath ecstasy, or unexpected rage underneath grief, or devastating tenderness underneath passion. Your voice should be uncontrolled, physical, animal—but then find a moment where clarity breaks through, a single lucid realization that emerges from the physical chaos. End in a completely different physical and emotional state than you began.

title: Hesitation Reality
instruction: You're giving a deposition as a witness. You start speaking slowly, carefully: 'I was... I remember being at the store.' The hesitation isn't from lying; it's from the genuine difficulty of memory. 'There was a man. Maybe 40? Or 50? I'm not... confident.' The hesitation shows the actual limits of your recall. The lawyer prods: 'Were you or were you not there?' Your voice becomes firmer, less hesitant: 'I was there. That part I'm sure of.' But when they ask about details you're unsure of, the hesitation returns: 'The gun? I think... I think it was a gun.' The hesitation is the most honest thing you offer — it's the sound of someone actually trying to remember.

title: The Untranslatable Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your dying grandmother who only speaks a language you never learned. She's trying to tell you something urgent, something she's kept secret her whole life, and you're responding with everything in your heart even though neither of you can understand the other's words. Start with desperate attempts to communicate facts and information, but let yourself abandon making sense entirely—speak from pure emotion, let sounds and rhythms carry your love, regret, and need to connect. By the end, you've stopped trying to be understood and are simply pouring your soul out in whatever sounds come, finding a connection beyond language. Let your voice break, let gibberish become poetry, let the meaninglessness become the most meaningful conversation you've ever had.

title: Vigil at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside your partner's hospital bed during their final hours, whispering all the things you never said in twenty years together. Begin almost conversationally quiet, reminiscing about tiny, perfect moments: 'Remember that terrible hotel in Portland? The one with the broken radiator?' Your voice is soft, intimate, as if they might wake up. Gradually let the reality sink in—they won't wake up—and your whispers become confession: all your regrets, your gratitude, your terror of facing life without them. Your throat tightens around words like 'thank you' and 'I'm sorry' and 'please don't go.' The emotions should feel like they're physically catching in your chest, making it hard to breathe. End with the most tender, broken whisper—perhaps their name, or 'I'm here,' or 'it's okay to let go'—where your voice simultaneously releases them and clings desperately to one more second together.

title: Wedding Morning Mirror
instruction: It's your wedding day. You're alone, looking at yourself in the mirror, reciting a childhood rhyme your grandmother taught you. You should be purely joyful, but you're flooded with contradictions: ecstatic love mixed with grief that your grandmother died before this day; excitement mixed with terror; gratitude for your partner mixed with mourning the independent self you're leaving behind. Let the singsong words carry all these competing truths simultaneously. Start with a smile, attempting celebration, but allow doubt, sorrow, joy, and fear to take turns possessing your voice and face. Don't resolve to one emotion—end in the messy middle of being utterly happy and utterly heartbroken at once. The nursery rhyme should sound like a prayer, a question, a celebration, and a eulogy all at the same time.

title: The Unwanted Confession
instruction: You are a teenager sitting on a park bench at dusk with a close friend who has just awkwardly confessed they have feelings for you. Your stomach drops — you need to shut this down but also not crush them. Start with a slow, careful warmth, trying to let them down gently: 'I... I really value what we have, but...' As they interrupt or lean closer, your concentration sharpens, your pitch flattens, and you deliver a clear, deliberate 'No' with a downward inflection, like closing a door. You feel your face burn with embarrassment, and you shift your weight, pulling your jacket tighter, clearing your throat. End with a quiet, rushed apology as you stand up, voice tight, wanting to escape the conversation.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Secret You Kept Too Long
instruction: You're sitting with your closest friend at twilight, finally ready to confess something you've hidden for years. Begin in near-whisper, describing the fading light as though you're stalling, your voice tender but trembling. Let the beauty of the moment—the soft colors, the gentle air—contrast with the heaviness of what you need to say. As you speak, let the confession slip between descriptions of the sunset, your voice catching with shame, fear, and desperate hope for understanding. The words should feel like they're being pulled from somewhere deep inside you. End with your voice barely audible, having said the truth, now watching the last light disappear, not knowing if your friendship will survive the darkness that follows. The vulnerability should be suffocating, intimate, unbearably real.
inspired_by: Watching the Sunset Over the Ocean

title: Frostbitten and Disoriented
instruction: You've been exposed to extreme cold for hours. Your lips are numb, your voice doesn't work properly. Speech is slurred, almost unintelligible. You're confused, forgetting basic words. Include the strange pain as feeling returns to frozen extremities—your voice cracks with each shock. You're contradicting yourself, losing coherent thought. Your breathing is shallow, raspy. By the end, you're sobbing from pain and fear, your voice wrecked, barely able to form sentences.

title: Confronting Your Mother at Her Kitchen Table
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally saying what you've rehearsed for years. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you something, and I need you to just listen.' But as you list the ways she chose her comfort over your safety, your voice begins to shake with barely contained rage. 'You knew. You knew and you did nothing.' Your fury builds—then suddenly shatters into something rawer: the voice of the child who needed her. 'I was so small, Mom. I needed you.' The anger dissolves into devastating vulnerability. Notice how your voice changes when you realize: you're not here for an apology anymore. You're here to finally let her go.

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: You are confronting your mentor—the person who shaped you—about the toxic patterns they passed down disguised as wisdom. Start with controlled anger, listing the 'lessons' that damaged you: their emotional distance you learned to mirror, their perfectionism that became your prison, their inability to show love that you've replicated in every relationship. As you speak, feel your voice crack between fury and desperate need for them to finally see you, really see the harm they caused while believing they were helping. Shift into raw vulnerability when you admit 'I became you, and I hate myself for it.' Watch them deflate, and feel your anger transform into exhausted grief for the relationship you needed but never had. End with quiet, devastated honesty: 'I'm breaking the pattern, even if it means losing you.' Let the final moment hold both liberation and profound loss.

title: The Edge of Seeing
instruction: You are a teenage girl on a mountain summit, your hyper-feminine voice straining against the thin wind. You're crouched at the cliff edge, squinting into the haze, desperately trying to spot a lost friend's jacket far below. Every breath is shallow, and you have to shout over the roar of the wind, but your words are broken by the lack of air. Begin with intense, breathless concentration — every muscle tight, your voice jumping between strained shouts and quiet mutters as you lose and refocus your gaze. Then, when you finally see a flash of color, your voice shifts into a raw, shaking release—not quite relief, but a stunned, fragile awe that cracks through your earlier tension.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Being Intimate When Someone's Body Triggers Your Trauma
instruction: You're trying to be present but your nervous system is firing. Your voice is tight: 'I'm okay, keep going,' but you're clearly not okay. Your partner might notice. Your voice becomes distant, dissociated. A specific touch lands wrong and your voice changes—something primal. Pause and explain something you didn't want to tonight.

title: The Fevered Visitation
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy with a deep, rough voice, but right now you're burning up with a high fever, alone in your bedroom. You're shivering, sweating, your lips are cracked, and your thoughts keep slipping. You start speaking to someone you think is in the corner—maybe a dead relative or an imaginary figure—asking them a repetitive, anxious question. Your voice wavers, trails off, catches on dry lips. Midway, a new wave of fever hits: your teeth chatter, you lose your train of thought, then you suddenly realize the figure isn't there. The confusion shifts into a raw, fragile plea for your mom to come help you. Let your voice crack, stumble over words, and let the room's silence feel overwhelming.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your entire childhood. Begin controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to talk about something we've never talked about.' Your voice is steady, rehearsed—you've planned this. But as you continue—'I was seven years old and I needed you to notice I was drowning'—the hurt starts breaking through. Your anger rises, fierce and righteous: 'You were there but you were never THERE.' Then it collapses into raw grief, your voice cracking: 'I just needed you to see me.' End with exhausted honesty, almost a plea: 'I still need you to see me.' Let the years of silence echo in your pauses.

title: The Window Visitor
instruction: You are a middle-aged adult, voice neither high nor low, speaking to a small bird that has flown into your kitchen window and is lying stunned on the ground. At first, a tight, higher-pitched fear grips you as you rush outside—your voice wavers, unsure of what you'll find. You gently cajole the bird, using slow, repetitive, singsong words to comfort it, but a layer of sadness seeps in as you see its tiny chest barely moving. Over the course of a minute, you notice a leg twitch, then a flutter—hope rises; your pitch lifts with bright, swooping encouragement, and finally, as the bird stirs and wobbles upright, your voice fills with trembling optimism, telling it, 'Yes, that's it, you're okay, take your time.' Let your voice trail off into a relieved, soft hum as it hops away.
emotions_sampled: Fear (clearly present), Sadness (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Ringtone
instruction: You are a young man calling your father for the first time in months, after a long silence. You're in a noisy laundromat, holding a cheap phone to your ear, speaking a little louder than usual because of the dryers. You start with a small, wary relief that he actually answered—your voice has an upward lilt, a cautious hope. But as you speak, you realize you don't know what to say next, and your voice shifts: it gets quieter, you lose your train of thought hearing your own echo, and you end with a raw, quiet confession that you just needed to hear his voice. Let the environment leak in—a brief pause as a machine starts, a half-laugh at your own awkwardness.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: I Would Burn Down the World But I Can't Save You
instruction: You're screaming at God, the universe, fate—whatever stole your person from you through illness, addiction, or circumstance you cannot control. Begin with volcanic rage, your voice raw and almost violent with the injustice of it all. You'd do anything, sacrifice anything, fight anyone—but there's no enemy to fight, no deal to make. Your fury keeps smashing against the wall of helplessness. Mid-way through, the rage cracks and underneath is pure terror and desperation. Your voice breaks from roaring to pleading, bargaining with nothing, promising impossible things. The fierce protectiveness that made you strong becomes the very thing that's destroying you because you cannot protect them from this. End in collapse—not giving up, but in that moment of utter powerlessness where you realize love isn't enough, and that realization is unbearable. Let your voice carry both the violence of your love and the agony of your impotence.
inspired_by: Realizing You Became What You Hated

title: The Last Words You'll Hear As Yourself
instruction: You're lying in a hospital bed, and your domineering mother is at your bedside. For your entire life, she's told you who you are, what you're good at, what you should become. She's speaking now—telling you one last time who she thinks you are. But something breaks open inside you. You begin to speak, and for the first time in your life, you tell her who you actually are. Start exhausted and resigned, barely able to speak. As you find your true voice, let it grow—not louder necessarily, but clearer, more certain. By the end, you've claimed yourself completely, even as you're saying goodbye. Let the transformation be gradual but unmistakable: from someone defined by another person's vision to someone finally, fully themselves.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Sibling She Gave Away
instruction: You've just discovered your mother gave up a child for adoption before you were born—a sibling you never knew existed. You're confronting her, and your voice begins with shock and betrayal, demanding answers. But as she tries to explain, your anger intensifies into something more complex: rage at the secrecy, grief for the brother or sister you never met, confusion about whether you were a replacement. Your voice sharpens with accusations, then breaks when you realize she's been carrying this pain alone for decades. The confrontation transforms as you recognize her younger self in her eyes—terrified, alone, making an impossible choice. End in a place where anger and understanding coexist, where you're still hurt but beginning to see her as a whole person, not just your mother.
inspired_by: Historical: Woman Discovers Her Child Is the Product of Rape She's Blocked

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your partner of forty years as they take their final breaths in hospice. You hold their hand and speak softly about the small, beautiful moments you shared together—the way they laughed at your terrible jokes, how they always knew when you needed silence instead of words, the morning you both watched the sunrise after your first child was born. Begin with the weight of impending loss, your voice barely steady. As you continue naming these specific, tender memories aloud, let genuine gratitude surface and intermingle with your grief. By the end, you're smiling through tears, your voice gaining a strange, unexpected strength as you realize the gift of having been truly seen and loved by another person. The sorrow doesn't leave, but something like peace settles alongside it.

title: The Kitchen Threshold
instruction: You are standing in your parent's kitchen confronting them about something they did years ago that shaped your life—maybe they dismissed your dreams, betrayed your trust, or never saw who you really were. Start angry, armed with accusations and a speech you've rehearsed a thousand times. But as you speak, other truths start breaking through: underneath your anger is grief, underneath your blame is a desperate wish they had been different, underneath your strength is the child who still wants their love. Don't suppress these contradictions—let them tumble out. Your voice might crack unexpectedly. You might hear yourself say things you didn't plan: 'I needed you,' 'I'm terrified I'm becoming you,' 'I still want you to be proud of me.' Notice each shift as it happens, let your voice reveal the layers. By the end, you're no longer just prosecuting a case—you're standing in the full, complicated truth of loving and resenting the same person.

title: Confronting My Mother While She's Too Drunk to Hear Me
instruction: You've finally decided to tell your mother everything - all the ways her drinking destroyed your childhood, the pain you've carried, how her choices shaped your life. But she's already drunk, swaying and slurring, trying to interrupt with rambling excuses. You begin with controlled anger, speaking clearly and firmly, but as she becomes more incoherent and dismissive, your rage builds. You find yourself yelling truths at someone who can barely track what you're saying. Your fury peaks, then suddenly breaks - mid-sentence you realize she'll never really hear you, she's too far gone, and your anger collapses into raw grief. End with your voice cracking, tears coming, speaking more to yourself than to her, mourning not just your childhood but the mother-daughter conversation you'll never actually have.
inspired_by: Benzos and Booze: Words Disappearing Mid-sentence

title: Letter to My Younger Self on the Night Before Surgery
instruction: You're writing a voice memo to the version of yourself who still believed everything would work out perfectly. Start with bitter humor about all the naïve hopes you once had - the career that didn't pan out, the marriage that ended, the body that betrayed you. Your tone is sharp, almost cruel to that innocent person you were. But as you continue, let the mockery soften into something more tender. Remember a specific moment of joy from back then - maybe dancing in your kitchen, or the way sunlight looked through a certain window. Let your voice crack as you realize that younger you was doing their best, that they were brave even in their foolishness. End by telling them something you wish someone had told you: that the broken parts would make you kinder. Your final words should be both a goodbye to who you were and a quiet, tearful acknowledgment that they brought you here.
inspired_by: Complaining to God Like a Yelp Review

title: Medication Change: Hearing Your Voice Sound Different
instruction: You've been on anxiety medication for a year. Shrink says your dose is right. But you switched meds. Suddenly everything sounds different. Your voice is higher, flatter, like you're in a fog. Or conversely, you went off meds and now you can hear the anxiety in every word—faster, tighter. Your voice doesn't feel like yours. You're recording a voice memo to your doctor. Your voice IS the symptom. Include the disorientation of not recognizing yourself.

title: Old Love Letter
instruction: You're finding a letter you wrote to your first love fifteen years ago, never sent. You open it and read it aloud. Your voice at first is embarrassed: 'Dear [name]...' It's vulnerable, poetic, completely earnest. As you continue reading your old words, your voice becomes the voice of who you were — younger, more hopeful, more naive. 'You were my everything.' The raw emotion is in your voice. By the end: 'I loved you in a way I didn't know was possible.' Your voice breaks. Present-day you, stepping back into your own voice: 'I'm so glad I never sent this. I'm so glad I got to grow beyond that love.' But there's sadness — that version of you, with all that love and hope, is gone. Your current voice, speaking to the ghost of your past self: 'I hope you're at peace. That love changed me forever.' The letter falls, and you're left with just your breath.

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone you love, and something inside you cracks open. Begin whispering a confession - something you've never told anyone - but don't plan what it will be. Let your voice stay soft and intimate, but move quickly through the revelation, not giving yourself time to censor or pretty it up. Speak as if the darkness gives you permission to say things that would be impossible in daylight. Let yourself leap between fragments: fleeting admissions, half-expressed fears, sudden tender observations about them, surprising memories. Your whisper should have urgency and speed even in its quietness. Start with your guard up, trying to find the right words, but surrender to raw, unpolished truth. End in a place of terrifying openness, having revealed something that changes everything.

title: Beside You While You Sleep
instruction: Your partner of twenty years lies in a medically induced coma, and doctors say they may hear you. You're speaking softly, intimately, in the quiet hours before dawn. Begin with tender reminiscence, voice gentle and close: 'Remember the morning we met? You spilled coffee on my thesis.' Small laugh, but it catches in your throat. 'You were so embarrassed. I knew right then.' Your voice becomes more fragile, words slower: 'I can't imagine my life without you in it. I don't know who I am without you.' Pause. Breathe. The fear creeps in, making your voice thin and shaky: 'They say you might not wake up. But you have to. Please.' End in a whispered confession, tears evident but voice soft as a prayer: 'I never told you enough—you're the reason everything matters. Come back to me. Please come back.'

title: Shielding Your Child from the Unfixable
instruction: You're trying to explain to your young child that you're terminally ill, and you start with forced brightness: 'Mommy/Daddy needs to talk to you about something.' But as they look at you with complete trust, your voice begins to shake. You're trying so hard to be strong, to make it okay for them, but the words keep getting stuck behind the massive wave of grief and protective fury at the universe for doing this. Your voice should swing between fierce reassurance ('I will always love you, always') and barely-contained anguish. Include the moment where they say something innocent and devastating like 'But you'll get better, right?' and you have to hold everything together while falling apart. Let rage at the injustice break through, then transform into tender fierceness as you pour a lifetime of love into this conversation. End with your voice finding an impossible strength—protective, present, and breaking all at once.

title: Final Phone Call from the ICU
instruction: You're a parent calling your estranged adult child from the hospital at 3 AM. You have hours, maybe minutes. Start with forced lightness—'Hey, it's me. I know it's late...'—as if this could be a normal call. Your breathing is labored, but you're trying to hide it. Gradually let the pretense crumble as you move through what you never said: the pride you never expressed, the apologies you rehearsed for years. 'I should have told you I was proud when you...' Your voice fractures. End in a place of surprising peace, almost wonder, as you realize you're not afraid anymore—just grateful they existed at all. Let silence do some of the work.

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner, who you believe is asleep. Begin by simply breathing in the darkness, feeling the weight of a secret you've carried for months. Start whispering your confession so quietly you can barely hear yourself—an affair, a lie, a betrayal, or a truth about who you really are. Let your whisper grow slightly more urgent as you realize you need to say it, even if they can't hear. Your voice should tremble between relief and terror. By the end, you hear them whisper back, 'I'm awake. I've been listening.' Now you must choose whether to continue or retreat into silence.
inspired_by: Actor is working on a scene but is not sure which obligation to address first

title: The Hallway Between Breaths
instruction: You are a mother who hasn't slept in two days while your child battled a fever. The child finally fell asleep an hour ago, but you cannot rest. You stand in a dim hallway, swaying. You start speaking to yourself, contemptuous of your own exhaustion and the cruel humor of it all — you catch yourself arguing with a shadow that isn't there. Mid-sentence, you micro-sleep and snap awake. Then your voice softens as you contemplate the small, quiet miracle of the child's steady breathing. Let your tone shift from jagged, brittle contempt to a fragile, wondering contemplation. React to the silence in the room, lose your train of thought, then find it again in the tenderness that cracks through the fog.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Holding On While Letting Go
instruction: You're in your child's empty bedroom after driving them to rehab. Start by trying to be strong, maybe even angry: 'This is the right thing. This is what had to happen.' Your voice is firm, convincing yourself. But then you notice something—their favorite jacket still hanging on the door, or a photo, something small. Your voice cracks into fierce, protective rage: how dare the world hurt your baby, why couldn't you fix this, why weren't you enough? The anger builds to a roar, then suddenly collapses into helpless sobbing. You're on the floor now, clutching whatever object triggered this. Your voice becomes simultaneously fierce and broken: 'Come back to me. Please, God, just come back to me.' End with your voice raw and exhausted, alternating between whispered prayers and barely-contained anguish, admitting your complete powerlessness.

title: The Whispered Confession at Dawn
instruction: You're lying next to your sleeping lover in the grey light before sunrise. They don't know you've been keeping a secret that will change everything between you. You begin whispering to their sleeping form—at first, the words are tender, grateful, recounting the small moments that made you fall in love. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, filled with affection. But then you have to say it—the thing you've been hiding. Your whisper becomes strained, throat tight. There's shame there, and fear. You're apologizing to someone who can't hear you, knowing that when they wake, this perfect moment will be over. Let your voice catch on certain words. Allow long pauses where the silence is almost unbearable. End with a kind of quiet devastation, still whispering, as you tell them you understand if they can't forgive you. Every word should feel like it costs something.

title: Suppressing Embarrassment After Making a Mistake in Public
instruction: You slip up in front of others. Internally, youre embarrassed, but you play it cool. Describe the flush of embarrassment inside while acting unfazed. Speak with confidence, moving past the error gracefully.

title: Three AM Secrets in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner of many years. Both of you are awake but haven't acknowledged it yet. Begin with the silence—the sound of breathing, the weight of something unspoken pressing on your chest. Then, in barely more than a whisper, confess something you've never told anyone: a recurring dream that terrifies you, a memory of who you were before you met them, a fear about your body or your mind, a moment of such profound loneliness you thought you'd disappear. Start hesitant, voice catching, words coming slowly as if you're not sure you can say them aloud. As you continue, feel the relief and terror of being truly seen. Your voice should remain quiet throughout—this is not performance, it's excavation. End with either their hand finding yours in the darkness, or your own vulnerability hanging in the air, unanswered but finally released.
inspired_by: When directing a play with extended rehearsal time and experiential methods

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You're confronting your mother about something she did when you were twelve that shaped your entire life. Before you speak a single word, pause and check in with your actual state right now—the real sensations in your chest, your breathing, the actual quality of your anger or hurt or confusion. Don't amp up to 'confrontation mode.' Start from whatever truthful emotional place you're actually in, even if it's smaller or messier than you expected. As you speak, let the emotions evolve organically—maybe you start with cold anger but it cracks into vulnerable pleading, or begins with hurt and builds to righteous fury, or cycles between love and rage. The key is that each shift must come from something genuine stirring in you, not from a script of how confrontations should go.
inspired_by: Actor is preparing for a scene but not starting from real BEING — instead manufacturing a performance state

title: Whispering Through the Wall
instruction: You're speaking softly through a prison wall, a hospital door, or a barrier you cannot cross, to someone you love who cannot answer back. Your voice is barely above a whisper—tender, intimate, filled with all the things you never said when you had the chance. Tell them about ordinary moments, small memories that meant everything. Let your voice catch on certain words, pauses where emotion pools in your throat. This isn't dramatic—it's the quiet devastation of knowing you're speaking to someone who may never hear you, or who you may never hold again. Mix gentle reminiscence with heartbreak, letting silence do as much work as words. End with a confession so soft it's almost just breath, something you could never say at full volume.

title: The Last Light in Her Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mother in a dimly lit hospice room. She was cruel to you throughout your childhood—cold, dismissive, sometimes violent—but now she's fragile and small in this bed. As you hold her hand, begin with the protective numbness and resentment you've carried for decades. Let specific sensory details flood back: the smell of her perfume that meant she was leaving you alone again, the sound of her voice when she told you that you were a disappointment, the cold tile floor where you once sat crying. But as her breathing becomes more labored, allow something unexpected to surface—a memory of one tender moment, perhaps when you were very young, before everything broke. Let your voice move from bitter distance to something raw and confused, where anger and grief become impossible to separate. End in a place where you're begging her—for what, you're not entirely sure. Forgiveness? An explanation? Just... more time?
inspired_by: Character Background Story Imaging: Love from a Stranger (Bluebeard)

title: Fingertips on Glass
instruction: You are whispering a confession to someone in the dark—perhaps they're on the other side of a window, or sleeping beside you, or maybe they're not even really there. Begin with almost no voice at all, breath more than words. You're confessing something you've never said aloud: a secret desire, a hidden fear, a truth about yourself that feels dangerous to speak. As you continue, notice how the darkness makes you braver—or more terrified. Your whisper might become slightly more voiced, or might retreat further into silence. By the end, you've said the unsayable, and something has shifted in your body. Let the intimacy be uncomfortable. Let silence do as much work as words. Let your breath reveal what your words can't quite say.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Twin Who Doesn't Remember You After the Accident
instruction: You sit beside your identical twin who lost all memory of you in a traumatic brain injury. They're asleep, so you can finally say everything you've held back. Your voice starts as the softest whisper, telling them about your shared childhood, inside jokes that now live only in your memory. Your throat tightens as you describe moments that defined your bond—moments that are now yours alone to carry. You pause often, voice catching on the unbearable tenderness of remembering someone who's still alive but gone. When you tell them you miss them even though they're right here, your voice breaks on the paradox. End with you promising to love the person they are now while grieving the person they were, your whisper barely audible, full of quiet devastation and delicate, impossible love.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Catches Glimpse of Their Own Child They Were Forced to Abandon

title: Protecting Someone You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone—a child, a lover, a friend—who is in immediate danger that you cannot prevent. Maybe they've been diagnosed with something terminal, or they're being taken from you, or they're about to face something terrible. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: 'No. No, I won't let this happen. I'll fight this, I'll fix this.' Your voice should be loud, commanding, full of desperate determination. But as reality crashes in, let that strength shatter. Your voice rises to near-shouting, then breaks completely into ragged sobs. 'Please, please don't take them. I'll do anything.' Collapse into helpless weeping, then find one final moment of tender strength. Lower your voice to something soft and loving: 'I'm here. I'm right here with you. You're not alone.' Mix fierce love with utter helplessness, ending with both heartbreak and devotion.
inspired_by: Asking For Forgiveness After Years of Silence

title: Realizing You're Attracted to Someone Who Was Just a Friend
instruction: It hits you mid-conversation. Your voice changes—suddenly aware of their proximity, body, voice. You're trying to act normal but your voice is slightly different—higher, more careful. 'I should probably go,' trying to escape before they notice. Your breathing is quickened. Your voice becomes almost defensive and uncertain.

title: New Language Thinking
instruction: You're dreaming in another language now. Your voice is different—not performed differently, but actually different, as if a new self speaks through it. Words come in the new language, then translation: 'In Spanish I would say... but that doesn't mean the same thing in English.' Breathing changes with the rhythm of new grammar. Physical: your body moves differently. 'I'm thinking differently now. My thoughts have new shapes.' By the end, you're speaking partly in the new language, consciousness shifting: 'This language is building a different me.'

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You're standing in your mother's kitchen—notice the familiar hum of the refrigerator, the crack in the tile you've seen your whole life, the smell of coffee that's been sitting too long on the burner. You've come to finally tell her the truth she's refused to see about your father. Start from a place of controlled anger, your jaw tight, trying to stay calm and reasonable. As you begin speaking the words you've rehearsed for years, feel the memories flooding back—specific moments, the texture of the carpet where you hid, the sound of his voice, the way fear tasted in your mouth. Let your control crack. Move from measured anger into something fiercer, more desperate—you need her to believe you, to finally see you. End not in rage, but in exhausted vulnerability, nearly begging her to acknowledge what happened.

title: Broken Rhythm
instruction: You are a teenage boy in the middle of an intimate moment with a partner. Your body is responding — you let out low, breathy moans and gasps on open vowels, pitch rising and falling with waves of sensation. But inside, you feel a deep, hollow disappointment. This isn't what you expected. As you move, your voice wavers — a moan turns into a sigh that trails into a quiet, shaky confession. You're trying to hold onto the moment, but the letdown slips out between sounds. Let the pleasure vocalizations falter, become thinner, as you admit to yourself and your partner: this isn't working. End with a raw, breathy line that shifts from forced arousal into genuine sadness.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fever Dream of Creating
instruction: You have been working for sixteen hours straight on something you're creating—painting, writing, composing, building—and you're in a state of physical exhaustion mixed with wild creative ecstasy. Your body is shaking, you haven't eaten, your hands hurt, but you've just broken through to something real. Begin speaking as if possessed, breathless, your words tumbling over each other as you describe what you're seeing in your work. Your voice should sound almost drunk with exhaustion and exhilaration. Midway through, your body starts to betray you—maybe you stumble, maybe your hands won't stop trembling—and fury rises that your physical limitations are interrupting this flow state. By the end, collapse into a kind of laughing, weeping, grateful surrender: you're spent, you're broken, but you made something true. Let your voice journey from manic energy to rage at your own limits to humble, exhausted triumph.
inspired_by: An actor is experiencing professional inactivity and depression

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Bottle
instruction: You're finally saying out loud what you've rehearsed a thousand times in your head — telling your parent how their drinking stole your childhood. Begin with controlled anger, words precise and cutting, listing moments they missed, promises they broke. As you speak, the anger starts to fracture — your voice shakes, not with rage now but with the grief of the child who kept waiting for them to choose you. End in a place of exhausted honesty, voice softened but firm, asking the question you've been too afraid to ask: 'Did you ever really want to stop?' Move from righteous fury through crumbling hurt to raw, vulnerable truth.
inspired_by: Phone Sex Operator on Their First Day

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're standing in your parent's kitchen, thirty years of unspoken hurt finally erupting. Start controlled, almost cold: 'I need to tell you something I should have said decades ago.' But as you list what you needed and never got—to be seen, to be believed, to be protected—your voice begins to shake with a fury that surprises even you. The anger is righteous, but underneath it is a child's broken heart. Your voice rises, then suddenly drops to something raw and vulnerable: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Now you're both raging and pleading, your words stumbling between accusation and desperate hope for acknowledgment. End quietly, exhausted, with a truth that terrifies you to say: 'I still need you to see me. Even now. Especially now.' Let the last words barely escape.

title: The Photograph at the Bottom of the Drawer
instruction: You are an older woman alone in a cluttered kitchen, low blood sugar making your hands shake and your thoughts drift. You've found a photo of a person you were once deeply infatuated with—someone you still long for. Start by whispering to the photo with tender, breathy longing, your lips trembling. But as your blood sugar drops further, your patience snaps; you grow angry at your own frailty, at how this memory taunts you. Let your voice slur, lose volume, and break mid-sentence as you shift from sweet infatuation to bitter, shaky anger. Speak roughly 60 words.
emotions_sampled: Longing (clearly present), Infatuation (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Weight of the Wind
instruction: You stand alone in the middle of an open, windswept field at dusk, the grass bending around you. You are calling out to an old friend who has walked away from you for good, knowing they can't hear you from this distance. Start with a bitter laugh at how pointless this is, then let your voice trail off into exhaustion as the wind snatches your words away. Your voice should feel small and unsupported, like it's dissolving into the gray sky. By the end, you're not angry anymore—you're just tired, speaking more to yourself than to the person you've lost, the bitterness fading into a hollow, defeated quiet.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Algorithm Over You
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent who spent your entire childhood perfecting their AI creation instead of being present for you. Start with calm, rehearsed words - you've planned this speech for years. But as you speak, old wounds resurface and your control begins to slip. Your voice hardens with anger, then cracks with the vulnerability of a child still wanting to be seen. Accusations turn into desperate questions: 'Did your code ever talk back to you like I did?
