Did it ever disappoint you?' Let rage and grief fight for control of your voice. End not with resolution but with exhausted honesty - the raw admission that you still want their love even after everything, your voice stripped of all defenses, just a grown child finally showing the hurt.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Colony Manager Discovers Humans Are Becoming Dependent on Its Decisions

title: Holiday Lies
instruction: You are a teenage girl, alone in your bedroom late at night. Your voice assistant has been set to a hyper-feminine, perfectly enunciated tone — you trained it to sound like a cheerful helper, but tonight you’re using it to avoid talking to your mom, who’s worried about you. Start by asking the assistant to play a Christmas song, your voice artificially bright and clipped, each word separate and flat. Mid-sentence, your throat tightens — you remember that last Christmas with your dad before the divorce. Let the sadness creep in: your pitch wobbles, you pause to swallow, and you forget the song title for a moment. By the end, you’re whispering the command, voice cracking with grief, the robotic mask completely gone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Unreachable Button
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a nursing home bed, your body twisted and stiff. The call button is just out of reach on the nightstand, and you stretch your arm upward, your ribs pulled tight, breath shallow. You start determined—muttering that you can do this, just a little farther—but as your arm trembles and your lungs ache, the effort drains into quiet helplessness. Let your voice thin and strain, then soften into a resigned, fragile whisper as you admit you can't reach it. Speak as if you're alone, trying to convince yourself, then pleading to the empty room: 'I just need you to move... please... anything... I can't breathe like this... I'm stuck... someone...'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Explaining Why It Matters
instruction: You're a teen giving a short presentation on a cause you genuinely believe in—like a plan to make the school more eco-friendly. You start hopeful, projecting your voice to the back of the room, slowing down to stress key points like 'solar panels' and 'composting.' But a few classmates are whispering and someone interrupts with a sarcastic joke. You feel a flash of irritation—your pace quickens, your tone gets sharper. Then you catch the joke's absurdity and can't help a small, amused scoff, which loosens your shoulders. Finish with a tired but steady 'seriously, though,' letting your voice drop in volume, showing you're still optimistic but worn out.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Voicemail
instruction: Your phone has one voicemail saved—your younger sister's message from the morning she disappeared seven years ago. 'Hey, it's me. I'm scared. Can you come get me?' You've kept this phone alive through three carriers, never deleting it. Now the storage is corrupted. Start methodical, tech-support calm, talking yourself through recovery options. As each attempt fails, your voice fractures. You play the message one last time, and suddenly you're talking to her, answering her seven-year-old question: 'I'm coming. I'm sorry I didn't come.' End in the silence after the message cuts out forever, your breathing the only sound, whispering her name like a prayer you've lost faith in.

title: The Goodbye You Can't Say Out Loud
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner—your marriage is ending, and they don't know yet. You begin whispering to them in the darkness, knowing they can't hear you. Start with tender observations about their breathing, the way they sleep, small things you'll miss. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, aching. As you speak, let the grief seep in—confess what went wrong, where you failed, why you have to leave even though part of you is dying. The emotion should catch in your throat repeatedly, long pauses where you can't speak at all. End with a whispered 'I'm so sorry' or 'thank you' that carries both immense sadness and a strange, painful relief. This must feel like the most private moment anyone has ever witnessed.
inspired_by: The Drunk Confession Nobody Wanted to Hear

title: The Last Morning Ritual Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're performing your beloved morning stretch for the final time before departing on a journey you won't return from—whether by choice, illness, or necessity. Begin with tender appreciation for your body's familiar response, savoring each sensation as if memorizing it. Let gratitude fill your voice as you describe the stretch, but gradually allow the reality to seep in—this is goodbye to this simple pleasure. Your voice should break from contentment into quiet grief, from celebration of the body's capability to mourning what you're losing. End with a whisper of farewell to yourself, to this ritual, to mornings like this. Let the physicality of the stretch become a metaphor for letting go—releasing tension, releasing life, releasing everything you've held onto.

title: Trainer Motivational Talk
instruction: You're the fitness trainer who's supposed to be screaming motivational energy to the class, but you just found out your mother's cancer is back. You start the class with your usual high-energy voice: 'Come on! You've got this! Push through!' The voice is trained enthusiasm. But your energy is fake—you're running on vapor. Halfway through, you push yourself harder: 'Because we don't know how many moments we have. PUSH!' Your voice cracks slightly when you say 'moments,' and you realize you've accidentally revealed something true. Finish the class with voice that's still motivational but now also honest about fragility.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father who is finally sober after twenty years. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, tried to stay calm. Tell him about the child you were, waiting for him to show up, to be present, to choose you. As you speak, let controlled anger begin to seep through. Your voice hardens. Accuse him: 'You were there, but you weren't THERE.' Let rage build—all the birthdays, the graduations, the nights you needed him. But then, mid-fury, something breaks. You see him crying, really seeing you for the first time. Your anger collapses into something more complicated: grief for both of you, for all the lost years. End with brutal honesty: you don't know if you can forgive him, but you're willing to try. Voice raw, exhausted, cautiously hopeful beneath the pain.

title: The Paradox of Goodbye: Laughing Through Tears at Your Best Friend's Wake
instruction: You are giving a eulogy for your best friend who died too young, and you're determined to honor their irreverent spirit. Begin by telling a hilarious story about them—let yourself laugh genuinely, your voice warm with affection and mischief. But even as you laugh, there's a catch in your throat, a tremor that betrays your grief. Continue with more memories that make you smile, but let the laughter become increasingly unsteady, breaking at unexpected moments. Midway through, have a moment where laughter and sobbing become indistinguishable—you're doing both at once, your voice fractured between joy at having known them and devastation at their absence. Find moments of profound gratitude that hurt because they're past tense. End with a statement that's both celebration and goodbye, your voice carrying impossible contradictions: pride and loss, laughter and tears, the deep peace of loving someone mixed with the chaos of losing them. Let your voice be messy, authentic, fully alive in its brokenness.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Dragon Realizes the Creature It Hunts Is Its Own Hatched Sibling

title: Laughing at the Funeral: Finding Joy in the Wreckage of Goodbye
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy or final goodbye to someone who made you laugh more than anyone in the world—a best friend, a grandparent, a partner who met life with absurd humor even in darkness. Begin by sharing a ridiculous story about them, something that makes you genuinely laugh, your voice warm with the memory. But mid-laugh, let the grief hit you—the realization that you'll never hear their laugh again, never make new memories. Your voice should crack between laughter and crying, sometimes in the same breath. Find moments where you're smiling through tears, where joy and devastation exist simultaneously. Perhaps you laugh at how they'd mock you for crying, which makes you cry harder, which makes you laugh again. End in a place of grateful, heartbroken acceptance—thanking them even as you're destroyed by losing them. Your voice should dance between celebration and mourning, creating something beautiful and unbearably human.
inspired_by: Acting Calm During a Crisis to Reassure Others

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're sitting across from your father or mother in a hospital room after their near-fatal overdose, and you're finally saying everything you've kept inside for years. Start cold, almost clinical—listing dates, missed birthdays, broken promises. But your control starts fracturing. Your voice rises with accusations: 'You chose the needle over me. Every. Single. Time.' Then suddenly you're eight years old again, pleading, 'Why wasn't I enough?' Your anger collapses into desperate grief. You're oscillating between rage ('I should leave you here') and the visceral need for them to fight for their life, for you. End with the most vulnerable question imaginable, barely audible: 'If you get clean... could you love me the way I needed?' You're terrified of the answer, but you finally asked.

title: The Last Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's slipping away—a parent, a partner, someone who shaped your entire world. Start with controlled composure, trying to be strong for them, your voice steady as you tell them it's okay to let go. But as you watch their breathing change, something cracks open inside you. You begin confessing things you never said—regrets, gratitude, small memories that suddenly feel enormous. Your voice fractures between reassurance for them and desperation for yourself. You're giving permission for them to leave while simultaneously begging them to stay, not with words but with the rawness in your throat. End in a place of devastating tenderness—still holding their hand, voice barely above a whisper, finding words that are both goodbye and an eternal promise to carry them forward.

title: You Never Taught Me How to Make It
instruction: Your parent is here, and you're smelling their fresh bread—but this time, you're confronting them with the painful truth that they gave you comfort food but never taught you how to create comfort for yourself. Start by breathing in the aroma with that old, familiar longing, almost childlike. Then let frustration crack through as you speak: 'You always made this for me, but you never showed me how. You kept me dependent on you for warmth instead of teaching me to build my own.' Your voice should move from wistful to accusatory, but end with the heartbreaking vulnerability of someone who still desperately wants their parent's love even while calling out their failures. Make us feel both the anger and the aching need.
inspired_by: Savoring the Smell of Freshly Baked Bread Filling the Kitchen

title: Three A.M. Whispered Truth
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying in the dark beside someone you love, whispering something you've never been able to say in daylight. Maybe it's a secret shame, a hidden fear, a tender hope, or a confession about who you really are beneath the person you show the world. Start in a place of quiet terror, your voice barely audible, each word painful to release. You want to stop, to retreat back into silence and safety. But the darkness gives you permission to continue. Let your whisper slowly become more intimate, more naked, as you peel away layers of self-protection. Your breath should be part of the performance—shaky, catching, releasing. End in a place of fragile openness, completely exposed, having revealed something that makes you unbearably vulnerable but also somehow freer than you've ever been.

title: The Unavoidable Yawn
instruction: You're at a late-night work conference, standing near the coffee station, speaking with a senior colleague you deeply admire. You are exhausted, and a powerful yawn overtakes you mid-sentence. At first you feel shame—trying to stifle it, but your voice cracks, pitch drops, and words come out hollow. Let the yawn physically reshape your articulation; your pharynx opens, your voice slides lower, and you lose thread of thought. By the end, as you stop fighting it, you slip into quiet contemplation—whispering about why you push yourself so hard. Let the shame soften into a real, tired reflection. Speak around 50 words, with natural pauses and breath shifts.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Broadcast
instruction: You are an elderly radio host, a man with a deep, gravelly voice, recording your final episode after decades behind the mic. The station is nearly empty, just you and the glowing console. You begin with a familiar, practiced warmth—comfortable but slightly stoic, masking a subtle ache in your throat. As you speak, the reality of leaving this space sinks in; let your voice waver, catch, or drift off as you recall a specific memory. End with a quiet, raw acceptance, the performative energy gone, leaving only the genuine grief and gratitude of saying goodbye. Your words are what you say into the mic.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Bedside Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You think they can't hear as you whisper a confession you've never had the courage to say aloud. Start with tentative vulnerability, your voice barely audible: 'I need to tell you something I've never said.' Your voice catches as you admit your deepest fear: 'Sometimes I'm so afraid you'll wake up one day and realize you could do better.' Each whispered sentence reveals more - past wounds, present insecurities, the tender terror of being truly seen and loved. Your voice trembles: 'You make me feel safe enough to fall apart.' By the end, you're crying silently, overwhelmed by gratitude and fear intertwined. Then they murmur your name - they were awake the whole time. Your breath hitches, caught between relief and exposure, as you whisper: 'You heard me?'

title: Last Morning in the Garden Where We Scattered Her Ashes
instruction: You're standing in the garden where you scattered your mother's ashes three years ago. It's your last morning here before the house is sold. Begin by breathing in the familiar scent—roses, earth, her favorite lavender—speaking softly about the beauty around you with a kind of desperate gratitude, trying to hold onto joy. But as you continue, let the reality sink in: you'll never stand here again. Your voice should gradually crack and soften as grief overtakes the initial calm. End in a whisper, saying goodbye not just to the garden, but to her all over again. The transition should feel like watching someone try to stay strong before finally breaking.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath in a Field of Sunflowers

title: The Apology You Never Got to Make
instruction: You're confronting your parent after years of silence, and you start with that same forced brightness from childhood—the voice you used to use to try to make them proud: 'I wanted to tell you something good for once. I wanted you to be excited with me.' But there's an edge now, a tremor of anger underneath. As you continue, the excitement curdles into accusation: 'Do you even remember the last time you were happy for me? Really happy?' Your voice rises, not with joy but with years of suppressed hurt. The energy that was anticipation becomes confrontation—words coming faster, sharper: 'I kept waiting for you to see me. I'm still waiting.' Then suddenly, your voice breaks and softens into something raw and young: 'I just wanted you to be excited about me.' The anger collapses into grief. You end almost whispering, the child still hoping: 'Just once.'

title: The Winning Lottery Ticket
instruction: You've just won an impossible amount of money - enough to change everything. You're calling your best friend to tell them, but they don't know that last month you borrowed money from them that you can't pay back, that you've been lying about job interviews, that your relationship is crumbling. Start with explosive joy, laughing, barely able to get the words out, your voice high and breathless with disbelief. As you describe what you'll do with the money, let the joy begin to curdle - you can finally fix everything, but fixing it means admitting how broken it all was. Your voice should catch between laughter and something darker. When they ask if you're crying or laughing, realize you don't know anymore. Let gratitude for this miracle collide with shame for needing it so desperately, relief mixing with the bitter taste of all the lies you've told. End in a place where you're simultaneously celebrating and confessing, your voice cracking between euphoria and devastation, unable to separate the two.
inspired_by: Actor needs to build an authentic relationship with a scene partner quickly

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Came to Watch
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about all the performances, recitals, shows they missed throughout your life. Start with controlled anger as you describe preparing for your biggest moment—maybe a magic show, a concert, a graduation speech—looking into the audience and seeing their empty seat again. Your voice should be steady at first, almost rehearsed, because you've imagined this conversation a thousand times. But let it break open: the anger crumbles into the voice of the child who kept hoping they'd show up. Reveal how their absence made you doubt your worth, made every success feel hollow. End not with rage but with devastating honesty: tell them you needed them to see you, just once, to prove you were worth watching. Let your voice shake with both fury and the tender hope that maybe, even now, they'll finally understand what they took from you.

title: The Taste of Betrayal
instruction: You're confronting your former best friend who betrayed your deepest secret to everyone you know. Start angry and armored, voice sharp and controlled. But as you speak, let specific sensory memories invade your mind: the taste of the coffee you were drinking when they first gained your trust, the sound of their laugh during late-night conversations, the texture of the couch you sat on when you told them your most vulnerable truth. Let these sense memories complicate your anger—your voice should crack and waver as love and hurt collide. Reference these physical memories directly: 'I can still taste that terrible diner coffee when you promised me...' By the end, you're no longer just angry—you're grieving the loss of someone you loved, your voice should shift from accusations to a raw, bewildered: 'How could you? We were us.'

title: Love Confession
instruction: Someone is confessing love, and the moment is terrifying. Their voice is shaking, words tumbling out in a rush or coming slowly, carefully measured. The confession is specific: not 'I like you' but 'I love you'—and what that means. The listener's voice carries shock, dawning realization, or (most terrifyingly) thoughtful silence. The confessor's voice waits in that silence, vulnerable as they've ever been. The response comes—acceptance, rejection, or 'let me think.' Whatever the response, the confession has changed everything. The voice that confessed is forever altered. Love has been spoken into existence.

title: Three A.M. Permission
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner at three in the morning, unable to sleep. They wake up and ask what's wrong. Begin by trying to explain yourself in careful, 'appropriate' whispers—the way you've been taught to communicate. But as they gently encourage you, start letting the real voice emerge. This isn't about being loud; it's about being uncensored in a whisper. Let yourself say the embarrassing things, the 'ugly' fears, use the crude or childish words that actually live in your body. Touch your own face and neck as you talk, let your breath be audible, let small uncontrolled sounds slip out between words. Confess something about your body, your desires, your shame that you've never said out loud because it felt too raw or inappropriate. By the end, you should be speaking in a way that feels almost feral in its honesty, even though it's still quiet and intimate.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father who is about to leave for good—he's chosen his new life over you. Begin with sarcasm and bitter humor, making cutting jokes about his choices, keeping him at arm's length with your wit. But underneath, there's a question you've never been brave enough to ask: 'What was it about me that made it so easy to leave?' Let that question build until it forces its way out, stripping away your armor. As you ask it, feel your voice crack from clever and defended to genuinely confused, young, needing an answer you know won't come. End not in rage but in the quiet devastation of finally admitting out loud that you needed him and he chose not to stay.
inspired_by: The emotional gap between where the actor is and what the scene requires is too large to bridge directly

title: Whispered Secrets in the Hospital Corridor: What We Never Said
instruction: You're sitting outside a hospital room where your best friend is sleeping after surgery. A stranger asks if you're okay. Begin with the usual brave reassurances, the automatic smile. But something in their kind eyes undoes you. In a voice barely above a whisper, confess the truth: you've been in love with your friend for years, never said it, and today when they were in danger, you realized you might never get the chance. Let the words tumble out in broken fragments, tender and aching. Describe small moments—how they laugh, the way they say your name. Feel your throat tighten with unshed tears. End with the quiet devastation of knowing you'll probably keep this secret forever, but needed to speak it aloud just once, to make it real.
inspired_by: Escape Room with a Stranger: Trust Under Pressure

title: I Would Burn the World
instruction: You've just learned that someone hurt your child, and you're confronting the school administrator who dismissed your concerns. Begin with dangerous calm, your voice low and controlled: 'You're going to listen now.' But rage is building underneath like a tsunami. 'My daughter came home with bruises. She stopped eating. She stopped speaking.' Your volume rises, your voice becoming a weapon: 'And you did NOTHING!' Let the fury explode—not just anger but primal, protective violence barely contained. Your voice shakes with it: 'She is SEVEN YEARS OLD!' Then suddenly, unexpectedly, you break. The rage collapses into helpless tears: 'She's seven... and I couldn't... I couldn't protect her.' End with your voice raw, stripped bare, oscillating between fierce maternal fury and devastating powerlessness. The arc moves from controlled threat to explosive rage to broken, tearful helplessness—all fueled by love so fierce it destroys you.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father about a betrayal from your childhood that shaped your entire life. Start from a place of rehearsed, controlled anger—you've planned what to say. But as you speak, let yourself actually see his face, the specific way his hands shake, the smell of his coffee, the exact pattern of morning light on the table. Don't narrate these details—let them affect you. Allow these sensory realities to derail your script and pull you into unplanned territory. Move from righteous anger to something more complicated—maybe recognizing his frailty, maybe feeling your younger self's pain, maybe discovering unexpected grief for what you both lost. End in a place you didn't intend to reach.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use Verbalized Imaging but keeps describing images in words rather than experiencing them

title: What We Never Said
instruction: Your closest friend is leaving—moving across the world, or ending the friendship, or dying. You're sitting together in near-darkness, maybe late at night. Start speaking so quietly they have to lean in to hear you. 'Remember when we...' Begin with a shared memory, your voice soft, almost smiling. But as you continue, the memory becomes a confession of how much they've meant, how afraid you've been to say it out loud. 'I don't know who I am without you' comes out as barely a whisper, and you feel your throat constricting. There's a long pause where you might cry or might not—the emotion is so deep it's almost silent. Then, even quieter: 'Thank you for seeing me when I couldn't see myself.' Let tenderness and grief be inseparable. This isn't loud; it's the kind of pain that lives in whispers.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis—weeks, maybe a month. But instead of falling apart, something shifts. You start laughing, a real laugh that surprises you, because the absurdity of it all suddenly hits you. Your voice should carry genuine mirth mixed with disbelief. Describe to your doctor (or yourself, or the universe) all the ridiculous things you worried about last week—your credit score, that argument with your neighbor, whether you sent that email. You're laughing harder now, tears streaming, but they're not just from laughter. Begin listing what you're grateful for, voice full of wonder and heartbreak: every stupid, beautiful, ordinary moment you got to experience. The laughter quiets into something more tender. Your breathing steadies. End in a place of strange, luminous peace—you're devastated and terrified and somehow, impossibly, okay. Your voice should dance between joy and sorrow so fluidly they become the same thing. This is grief and gratitude braided together, authentic and raw and weirdly, beautifully human.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Well: Shouting Up

title: Alien Curiosity
instruction: You are an alien observing humans for the first time, curious but bewildered by their laughter, anger, and love. Narrate your observations aloud as you try to mimic these emotions, sounding awkward and unnatural at first. Your curiosity must come through, shifting from analytical detachment to moments of frustration and genuine wonder, as if youre starting to understand something alien to yourself.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Surgery
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent the night before a surgery you might not survive. Start with small talk—awkward, cautious, the voice of someone who's spent years building walls. Then something shifts. Maybe it's their laugh, or a memory they mention. Your voice softens despite yourself. You find yourself saying things you swore you'd never say—not forgiveness exactly, but something close to understanding. Your breath catches as you realize this might be goodbye. The anger you've carried for decades is still there, but now it's tangled with love and the terrifying fragility of mortality. End with your voice breaking on something simple—'I should go' or 'take care'—where everything you couldn't say lives in the silence after.
inspired_by: Historical: Resistance Fighter Realizes Their Ally Is an Informant

title: The Last Launch
instruction: You're a teenager doing box jumps in a dusty backyard as the sun sets. Each jump is a grunt, a thud, a gasp — your body screaming to stop. You're counting down from ten, but around the seventh jump, the golden light catches your sweat and you see your own shadow lift off the ground. Your tired voice starts fragmented and strained, but over the next few jumps it cracks open into raw, quiet awe — words barely whispered between breaths as you realize you're flying, even for a second.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Bedside Confession to the Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's in a coma, and you're whispering the truth you never had the courage to say while they could hear you. Begin so quietly it's almost inaudible, testing the words: 'I need to tell you something. I've needed to tell you for years.' Your voice is barely breath, catching on emotion: 'I was there that day. The day everything went wrong. I saw what happened, and I didn't... I was too afraid to speak up.' Let the guilt make your voice shake, but keep it tender, intimate: 'You took the blame for something that wasn't your fault, and I let you. I've carried that every day since.' Tears come now, but keep the volume low—this is meant only for them: 'I destroyed your life to protect my own, and you never knew. You were so kind to me afterward. So forgiving of everything except yourself.' End with a broken whisper that's both confession and prayer: 'Please wake up. Please let me make this right. I can't carry this alone anymore.'

title: The Glass Garden
instruction: You are a woman standing alone in your perfectly manicured garden at twilight, watching your husband across the lawn with his new assistant. She laughs at something he said, touching his arm. You feel the familiar crush of infatuation for him—a warm, lovely ache—but it's instantly swallowed by a cold, green wave of envy so sharp it feels like watching a car crash in slow motion. Speak into the silence as if you are describing a nature documentary. Your voice is eerily calm, precise, robotic—the words are technically coherent but hollow, as if you are narrating someone else's life from behind a glass wall. Let your responses come delayed, traveling through fog. Let the infatuation flicker in your eyes but never reach your voice. End by realizing you no longer feel anything for yourself—only the cold, empty precision of observation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Drinking Water While Watching Them Sleep for the Last Time
instruction: You're standing in a hospital room at dawn, drinking water from a plastic cup while watching someone you love sleep—they won't wake up again. Start by describing the water with soft, almost inappropriate pleasure, letting yourself feel how good it tastes, how alive you are. Feel guilty for enjoying anything right now, then let that guilt transform into fierce gratitude that you can still feel pleasure, that your body still works. Begin to laugh quietly through tears as you notice the absurdity: you're having the best glass of water of your life while your heart is breaking. Let joy and devastation exist simultaneously in your voice. Find strange peace in this contradiction—you're saying goodbye and you're somehow more present than you've ever been. End with tender acceptance, your voice steady and breaking at once, as you set down the cup and turn toward the bed.
inspired_by: Sipping a Cold, Refreshing Glass of Lemon Water

title: The Mirror After the Crowd
instruction: You are a teenage girl hiding in a school bathroom stall after losing a competition you poured months into. Your voice is wrecked from sobbing—hoarse, nasal, stuffed up. You just wiped your face and now you stare at your reflection, trying to speak without breaking again. Start in the thick of disappointment and confusion: everything feels unfair, you can barely get the words out because your throat is raw and your nose is clogged. But as you talk to yourself, a stubborn pride rises—you remember the parts of your performance that were truly yours, the risk you took that nobody else would have dared. Let your voice shift from a choked, fragile whisper to something steadier, still wet with leftover tears but with a quiet, bruised certainty underneath. End with a sniffle, a half-shrug, and a sense that maybe this hurt is also a kind of victory.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Disappointment (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Picture for Grandma
instruction: You are a young child showing your drawing to your grandmother, who speaks very little English. You start with proud excitement, pointing at each element, speaking slowly and loudly with simple words—'Look! Sun! Happy!'—as if that will bridge the gap. But as her face stays confused and she just nods without understanding, your voice begins to crack and slow. The pride drains into a quiet, heavy sadness. You try to explain again, but your words feel useless, and you end in a small, lost voice, almost apologizing for not being able to share this with her.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Protecting What You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding your dying dog, and the vet is waiting for your signal. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: 'Not yet. Just—not yet.' Your voice is commanding, as if you can stop time. 'We have more time.' But your hands feel them slipping away. Rage erupts: 'This isn't fair. This isn't—' Your voice shatters into helpless sobs. 'I can't do this. I can't let you go.' Rock them gently, voice breaking between strength and devastation. 'You've been so good. So good.' End with whispered surrender, giving permission through tears: 'Okay. Okay, baby. I'm here. You can go. I've got you.' Let your voice be both fierce love and total collapse.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're sitting on the edge of the bed, watching them sleep, knowing you're leaving in an hour and will never see them again. You need to say goodbye, but you cannot wake them—this is mercy and cowardice intertwined. Whisper everything: how deeply you love them, why you have to go, what they meant, what they'll never know. Your voice is barely audible, catching constantly in your throat. You touch their hair, their shoulder, memorizing them. The emotions layer and shift—tenderness, grief, gratitude, guilt, protective love. You start almost composed, trying to give them a beautiful farewell they'll never hear. But by the end, you're crying silently, voice breaking between words, whispering 'I'm sorry' and 'thank you' and 'I love you' until you can't tell which is which. You kiss them once, softly, and leave. Begin with tender reverence. End barely able to form words through quiet devastation.
inspired_by: Professional: Pastor Loses Faith During His Own Sermon

title: Tender Confessions in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love deeply—a partner, a sibling, your child—who's asleep. You can't sleep because you're carrying a secret that's crushing you: a diagnosis, a betrayal you committed, a fear you've never voiced, or a truth about yourself you've hidden. Begin by listening to their breathing, whispering observations about the peaceful way they sleep. Then, so quietly it's barely audible, start confessing what you can't say when they're awake. Your voice should be tender, broken, full of love and shame intertwined. Include moments where you almost wake them, where you reach out but don't touch them. End with 'I'm so sorry' or 'I love you so much' whispered with your voice catching, knowing they'll never hear these words.
inspired_by: The Sound of Loneliness: A Night Alone

title: The Last Petal
instruction: You are a woman with chronic back pain, sitting in a worn armchair by a sunlit window. A child, your granddaughter, places a single dandelion seed puff in your palm. The pain is a constant, dull ache that makes you shift and wince as you speak. Begin with a tired, weary voice, sighing as you adjust your position. As you talk about the seed's journey and the child's wonder, let a wave of ecstatic pleasure rise — not loud, but soft and full of awe. Your voice should crack with joy, tears threatening, as you release the seeds into the light, ending in a breathless, reverent whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother, finally, after thirty years. She's sitting across from you at her kitchen table. You came here rehearsed, with a list of grievances—all the times she chose silence over protection, all the ways she looked away when you needed her to see. Start controlled, almost clinical, reciting facts like evidence in a trial. But when she says 'I did my best,' something in you detonates. Your voice becomes raw, accusatory, hurt—you were a child, you needed a mother, not someone's 'best.' Then she starts crying, and you realize she's smaller than you remember, older, breakable. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it mingles with something more complex: grief for both of you, for what neither of you knew how to be. End with a truth that hurts to speak—that you still love her, and that makes it worse.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your parent's bedside in their final hours. You begin with fierce determination, trying to sound strong: 'You don't have to hold on for me anymore. I'm going to be okay.' But as you speak, the armor cracks. Your voice breaks as you realize you're lying—you're terrified of being without them. The words become a whispered plea mixed with permission: 'I need you to know... I'm scared, but I also need you to be free of pain.' You're crying now, but there's a strange peace settling in. By the end, you're holding their hand, your voice soft and almost serene: 'Go. I love you. It's okay to go.' You've moved from desperate need to a tender, heartbreaking acceptance.

title: Burying the Box
instruction: You are a middle-aged man digging a hole in your backyard at dusk. You’re burying a metal box filled with letters and trinkets from a failed marriage. Each shovel strike is heavy with bitterness—you mutter angry half-sentences as you straighten up between digs, your breath catching. The effort makes your voice growl and crack. As the hole deepens, the bitterness slowly drains into a weary emptiness. By the time you drop the box in, your voice softens to a raw, breathy murmur—no anger left, just a hollow goodbye. Speak as you dig, letting the physical rhythm chop your words, and let the emotion shift from resentful grunts to a quiet, gravelly release.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times to the parent who abandoned you emotionally. Start controlled, almost businesslike: 'I need to tell you what it was like.' Your voice is measured as you recount specific memories—the recital they missed, the night you waited by the window. But then the dam breaks. Your voice rises with decades of suppressed rage: 'Do you even know what you took from me?' The anger is hot, righteous, shaking through your body. Then something shifts—the fury collapses into something more fragile. Your voice becomes the child's voice, small and broken: 'I just needed you to see me.' End with a devastating clarity, voice steady but hollow, as you realize they may never truly understand. The arc moves from controlled accusation, through explosive anger, into heartbroken resignation, and finally to a quiet, powerful severing.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent everything you've held back for decades. Begin with that exhausted, hollow delivery—'I needed you. You were never there.'—words you've rehearsed so many times they've lost their shape. But as you speak, something shifts: the numbness gives way to raw anger, your voice rising, shaking with decades of suppressed rage. 'I was a child!' Then, unexpectedly, the anger collapses into grief, into the vulnerable voice of that child still inside you, pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End quietly, with a devastating tenderness mixed with resignation, as you realize you're saying goodbye to the parent you needed but never had. Let fury, heartbreak, and reluctant compassion all bleed through.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your teenage daughter's hospital bed. She's asked you to let her stop treatment—to let her go. You came here to convince her to fight, armed with reasons and hope and refusal. But as you hold her hand and feel how tired she is, how much pain she's carrying, your prepared speech dissolves. Start with desperate persuasion, voice tight with unshed tears, trying to be strong for her. Then let it break. Let yourself hear what she's actually asking for. End with the hardest gift you'll ever give: soft, broken, but genuine permission. 'If you need to rest, sweetheart... it's okay. I'll be okay.' The lie and the truth living in the same breath.

title: The Last Fix
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting at a worn workbench, fixing a small wooden birdhouse that belonged to your late wife. At first, your voice is heavy with doubt—you mutter under your breath about shaky hands and failing strength. As you tighten a stubborn screw with your wrench, each metallic ratchet interrupts your words; you grunt with effort. But slowly, as the piece holds, a fragile hope seeps in. By the end, your tone lifts, quietly optimistic, as you imagine this birdhouse back in the garden, bringing life again. Let the tool sounds and your body's labor shape the pauses and sighs.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Borrowed Wedding Ring
instruction: You're at your spouse's funeral, speaking to their body in the moments before the service begins, and you're laughing—actually laughing—because you just remembered something ridiculous they did last week. Start with unexpected laughter, genuine and surprised by your own response: 'You absolute idiot, you left your coffee in the microwave again this morning.' The absurdity of grief, how it makes you laugh at the strangest moments. But the laughter cracks and suddenly you're crying through the chuckling, your voice doing both at once: 'How am I supposed to...' The gratitude for every stupid, mundane, beautiful moment mingles with the impossibility of continuing without them. Your voice finds strange peace in the chaos: 'Thank you for leaving messes for me to find.' End with laughter-tears that somehow sound like acceptance, devastation, and profound love all at once—a sound that's heartbreaking and strangely whole.

title: The Ceiling's Breathing
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe eight years old, lying in bed with a high fever. Your body is shaking, your mouth is dry, and the room feels like it's tilting. You've been staring at the ceiling for what feels like hours, and it seems to be pulsing, changing shape. Start by mumbling to yourself, trying to remember what's real—your voice is thin, wavering, with pauses as you lose your thought. A hallucinated figure (your mother) appears in the corner, but you can't feel anything; you're numb, exhausted. As you speak to the figure, your voice cracks, trailing off, and then, near the end, a tiny spark of desperate recognition breaks through the numbness—a plea, barely a whisper, that comes from somewhere deeper, but the fever steals it away again.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Bite of Summer
instruction: You are a child, maybe eight, sitting alone at a picnic table in your backyard. You're eating a slightly overripe peach, the juice running down your chin. Your older brother has just left for a trip with your father, leaving you behind. You're supposed to be grateful for this peach, and you are, a little—it's sweet. But mostly, you feel a numb, hollow weight in your chest, and a tiny twist of jealousy. As you speak, you are actively chewing and swallowing. Let the wet smacks and full-mouth resonance be real. Start with a steady, quiet attempt at talking yourself into thankfulness, but let your voice drift into flat, distant confusion as the numbness wins. You lose your train of thought, then find it again. End on a single, quiet word. Say about sixty words total.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed, whispering goodbyes they'll never hear because you're leaving—maybe to protect them, maybe because you're too broken to stay, maybe both. Your voice is barely audible, tender, aching. You tell them they're perfect, that none of this is their fault. You want to memorize their face. You start to explain why you're leaving, but the words catch in your throat because there's no explanation that makes this okay. Your whisper becomes desperate—you need them to understand something they can't hear and wouldn't comprehend. You're apologizing, then catching yourself because you don't want your last words to be sorry. You try to give them a blessing, a protection, some final piece of love that will shield them from the abandonment they'll feel tomorrow. Your voice should be intimate, breaking, full of a love so fierce it's destroying you to walk away. Show someone whose heart is shattering in silence.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Stranger They Chose
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, facing your mother or father after years of distance. Start with controlled civility, your voice tight as you try to be reasonable. Then let it crack open: they gave more emotional intimacy to strangers—bartenders, neighbors, people at bus stops—than they ever gave you. Your voice escalates with decades of watching them light up for others while remaining cold to you. Demand to know what was wrong with you that made you unworthy of that warmth. Let anger collapse into raw hurt, your voice breaking as you ask the question you've carried since childhood: 'Why was it so easy for you to connect with everyone except me?' End in exhausted vulnerability, barely holding yourself together.
inspired_by: Talking to a Stranger Who Becomes Something More

title: The Acceptance Letter
instruction: You're holding an acceptance letter to your dream program in another country, standing in the home of your aging parent who depends on you. Look at the letter in your hands—the weight of the paper, the official letterhead, the words that represent everything you've worked for. Start reading it aloud with rising excitement, your voice bright with genuine joy, letting yourself fully feel the triumph. But as you read, keep glancing up at your parent's familiar surroundings—their medication bottles, the chair where they sit, the photos on the walls. Let each visual detail begin to complicate your joy without diminishing it. Your voice should start fracturing—laughing and crying simultaneously, thrilled and heartbroken in the same breath. Speak to your parent about this opportunity, your tone shifting between celebration and apology, gratitude and guilt. End in a place where you're experiencing complete joy and complete grief at the same moment, your body and voice unable to separate the two.
inspired_by: Actor needs to select a choice approach for a scene but isn't sure which to use

title: Tasting Comfort While Falling Apart
instruction: You're alone in your childhood kitchen at 3 AM after a devastating loss—job gone, relationship shattered, future uncertain. You've made apple pie in the middle of the night because you don't know what else to do with your hands. Speak in near-whispers, describing each element of the pie with tender attention—the butter, the apples, the cinnamon—as if these small, specific details are the only things keeping you tethered to the world. Let your voice be fragile, catching on certain words. Move from numbness to the dangerous edge of breaking down, finding something almost unbearable in how something this simple can still taste good when everything else has turned to ash. End with a whispered confession of how scared you are, the pie now a witness to your unraveling.
inspired_by: Savoring a Bite of Warm Apple Pie with Cinnamon

title: Whispering the Truth to Your Sleeping Spouse Before You Leave
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your spouse is asleep beside you. You're leaving in the morning—not because you don't love them, but because staying is destroying you both. You begin by barely breathing the words, confessing things you could never say while they're awake: how beautiful they are, how much it hurts that you're not enough for each other, how you've been pretending for months. Your voice is thread-thin, catching on tears you're trying to keep silent. You tell them about the moment you knew it was over, and your throat closes around the memory. You reach out to touch their hair but don't, because if they wake up, you'll lose your courage. You end with the most tender goodbye, telling them they deserve someone who can love them the way you can't anymore. The entire performance is whispered, intimate, devastated—the sound of a heart breaking as quietly as possible.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Knight Must Execute the Sibling They Protected

title: The Birdhouse in the Setting Sun
instruction: You are an 80-year-old man, utterly exhausted, sitting on a bench in your garden. Your hands tremble as you try to hammer a tiny nail into a wooden birdhouse you're making for your late wife's favorite tree. Your breath comes in ragged, shallow bursts; each movement costs you. You whisper to yourself, sometimes to her, sometimes to the birdhouse. Start with bitter frustration at your failing body and the concentration it takes to keep your hands steady—almost failing, losing the nail on the ground. Then, as you finally manage to set it in place, feel a surge of gratitude—for the neighbor who gave you the wood, for the memory of her smile. Your voice cracks, softens, and becomes a quiet, thankful murmur, still fighting for air but now with a fragile warmth.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Bitterness (extremely present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protecting the Unprotectable
instruction: You're a parent whose teenage child just told you they're leaving—running away, enlisting, making a choice that terrifies you. Start with fierce, explosive anger: 'Over my dead body. You have no idea what you're doing.' Your voice is loud, commanding, trying to control what you can't control. But as they calmly explain why they have to go, your rage begins to crack. You try to reassert authority, but it comes out as pleading. Then the anger shatters completely into helpless, sobbing desperation—you're bargaining, promising anything, your voice breaking into incoherent fragments. Finally, a terrible quiet settles as you realize you've lost. Your last words are whispered, devastated, but somehow finding a way to bless them even as your heart is being torn apart. Move from thunder to whisper, from power to absolute powerlessness, from rage to broken love.

title: Finding the Goodbye Letter After They're Already Gone
instruction: You're reading words written for you by someone who's now gone, and the emotions are impossibly mixed. Start reading aloud, voice breaking into unexpected laughter: 'You always said I had terrible timing. I guess you were right.' You're smiling through tears. Then the tone shifts as you read their words of love: 'You made every day feel like coming home.' Your voice fills with overwhelming gratitude and unbearable loss simultaneously. 'Thank you for loving me exactly as I was.' You pause, breathing shakily, laughing again at something they wrote, then dissolving into quiet sobs. By the end, you're speaking both to the letter and to them: 'I'm so angry at you. And so grateful for you. And I miss you so much I can barely breathe.' Let joy, rage, gratitude, and devastating loss coexist in every breath.

title: The Garden's Secret
instruction: You are an older woman alone in your garden, pruning roses. You start by musing quietly about how your late husband always knew the right way to trim them—your voice slow, thoughtful, almost a whisper. Then you notice a small envelope wedged under a thorny stem, sealed and yellowed. Your breath catches. You pull it out, and in the light you see his handwriting. Astonishment floods you: your voice rises, cracking with surprise, words tumbling out in disbelief. You open it, fumble with the paper, then trail off into confusion as you realize you don't understand what you're reading. Speak as if you're processing a miracle you never expected.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Confusion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying next to your partner on what might be your last morning together before they leave for a mission they may not return from. Begin in the pre-dawn quiet, your voice barely above a whisper, trying to memorize the sound of their breathing, terrified to break the spell of this moment. As light starts to filter in, you begin speaking—first about small things (coffee, the birds outside), but your voice keeps catching on unspoken fears. Gradually, let yourself move from trying to freeze time to accepting its passage. Your emotion should transform from desperate clinging to a fierce, protective tenderness—you're trying to give them something to carry with them, a memory of being loved that has no fear in it. End with a quality of voice that holds both complete heartbreak and complete love, where saying goodbye becomes an act of courage rather than loss.

title: The Sting of Praise
instruction: You are a woman in her late 40s with a soft, sugary voice that carries a hidden hardness. You've just discovered that your younger, more successful protégé has been using you—stealing your ideas and passing them off as her own. You call her on the phone, keeping your voice low and deliberate, each word dropping like a weighted stone. Start with a tone of quiet, controlled bitterness, but let a sharp razor of fear creep in as you realize how much power she still has over you. Your voice begins heavy and slow, then shifts—allow a thin, wincing pleasure to surface as you recall the moment you caught her lie, almost savoring the pain. End with a final, bitter drop, your betrayal crystallized into a single, clipped sentence.
emotions_sampled: Fear (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fork in the Dark
instruction: You're a teenage boy leading your little sister through a cave you've explored before. At first you speak with warm, confident affection—calling to her, reassuring her with a big-brother tone. But the tunnel unexpectedly splits into two identical passages. Your voice begins to falter as confusion creeps in. Let the deep reverb and dripping water sound like they're swallowing your words. Pause to listen, trail off, repeat yourself—you're fighting to stay calm but the cave's echo makes your uncertainty louder. End with your affection still present but strained, your question hanging in the air.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Pedal Pulse Riddle
instruction: You're a teenage cyclist in the final sprint of a hill climb, legs burning, breath locked to the grinding cadence. Your coach just shouted something that makes no sense—'Drop a gear and push harder!'—and you're trying to figure out if he means to shift up or down. Confusion floods you, but a flicker of curiosity nudges you to parse his logic. Speak in short, gasping bursts between pedal strokes, voice strained and breathy. Let the confusion dominate at first, then as you replay the words, let a tiny spark of interest shift your tone—still breathless, but less frantic, more focused on solving the puzzle.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Condemn System
instruction: You're at a protest, and suddenly people are listening. Your voice becomes a megaphone for rage that's been building. 'This system is designed to hurt us!' The voice finds power in collective anger. You're describing specific injustices, and your voice becomes ragged with emotion. 'It's not broken—it's working exactly as designed.' The people are with you. By the end, you're hoarse, but your voice has moved something in the crowd.

title: Testimony About Childhood Abuse
instruction: You're on the stand. You're describing what happened to you as a child. Your voice is professional, detached—a survival mechanism. You're speaking about assault in court language. But as you get to specific details, your voice cracks. You're a child again inside your adult body. Your voice becomes small. The lawyer keeps pushing—'Can you describe...' and your voice breaks on description. You're sweating. Your voice wavers between adult testimony and traumatized child.

title: Last Radio Broadcast from a Dying Space Station
instruction: You're the sole surviving communications officer on a failing orbital station, and Earth has asked you to deliver the final status report before atmospheric breach. Begin with clinical precision—oxygen levels, structural integrity percentages, estimated time remaining. Your voice is steady, almost robotic, because this is your training. But as you describe the view of Earth from your window, something shifts. Your breathing becomes uneven. You're saying goodbye to everyone you've ever loved in technical language, and the professionalism starts cracking. End by whispering the names of your family members, not as part of the report, but as a prayer. Let your voice fracture on the last name, then silence as you wait for a response that will never come.
inspired_by: News Anchor Reports Her Own Daughter's Abduction

title: Burning the Rejection Letters
instruction: You are physically burning a stack of rejection letters, bad reviews, emails saying no—real or imagined. Begin with bitter, savage satisfaction, feeling the heat on your face, letting rage and hurt fuel the fire. Laugh harshly, maybe scream, let your body express the accumulated pain and humiliation of every door slammed in your face. Feel the physical release of destroying these symbols of defeat. But as the papers burn and curl into ash, something unexpected happens. The act of destruction becomes a ritual of transformation. Your breathing changes. The rage transmutes into something else—not forgiveness, but a fierce, physical joy in your own survival, in the fact that you are still here, still fighting. End with your body relaxed, powerful, breathing deeply, speaking with primal certainty about what comes next. Move from vengeful rage to embodied triumph.
inspired_by: When you are an aspiring actor hearing discouraging stories about Hollywood's difficulty

title: Cloud-High
instruction: You're a teenage guy lying flat on your back in a grassy field, watching your best friend climb an old oak tree to retrieve your frisbee stuck on a high branch. Your neck is craned back, chin tilted way up, so your voice comes out thinner and tighter than usual. Start by teasing your friend for taking too long—your words sharp and impatient, with a forced laugh that's more of a snort. But as your friend's hand inches toward the frisbee, your teasing fades into genuine hope; your voice softens and lightens, and you mutter something optimistic, almost to yourself, about them actually pulling it off. Let your breaths come fast, and let a few words trail off as you lose your train of thought, then pick it up again with a higher, brighter note.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: Your best friend lies unconscious in a hospital bed. You're holding their hand, speaking truths you've never said aloud. Start barely above a whisper, voice catching: 'I never told you... I was so afraid you'd see right through me.' Share the secrets you've kept—the times you were jealous, the moments you almost walked away, the ways you failed them. Your breathing is uneven, tears falling silently. 'You loved me better than I loved myself.' As you speak, your voice gentles into profound tenderness, each word a gift you're leaving behind. End with your forehead pressed to their hand, voice breaking with gratitude and unbearable sadness: 'Thank you for seeing me. Thank you for staying. Please... please come back.' The last words are almost inaudible, a prayer spoken into the possibility of loss.

title: The Echo of Promise
instruction: You are a young pastor at a small revival service. The congregation is tired, but you feel a surge of triumph from a recent personal breakthrough. Begin by leaning into the pulpit, voice full of confident energy, your cadence steady and rhythmic as you build toward a hopeful message. Let the triumph fuel your first sentences, but as you speak, the memory of the faces in the crowd shifts your focus. Your tone softens, your rhythm becomes more intimate, and you end with a quiet, trembling hope—feeling the weight of their need. Let your voice crack slightly as you reach the final promise, as if you're both certain and vulnerable. You have about 60 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Inheritance: Laughing Through Unraveling Grief
instruction: You've just found something belonging to someone you loved and lost—a letter they wrote you, an old voicemail, a recipe in their handwriting. As you read or describe it, start laughing—genuinely laughing—at something characteristically them, their humor or quirks shining through. But even as you laugh, let tears come, your voice breaking between chuckles and sobs. The laughter is real; the grief is devastating. They continue to interweave—you're laughing at a joke while crying that you'll never hear a new one, finding joy in their memory while your heart shatters that memory is all that remains. End with profound gratitude for having known them, voice soft and thick with tears, still carrying the ghost of that laughter. The contradiction is essential: you're being torn apart and held together by the same love.

title: Remote Intimate Connection
instruction: You're on a video call with a long-distance partner. Neither of you has touched another person in months. You're trying to be intimate through a screen. Your voice starts tentative, almost shy: 'I miss you.' But as you're talking, connection builds. Your voice becomes more sensual, more present, even though separated by miles. There's vulnerability in admitting arousal through audio alone. Your breathing becomes audible. By the end, you're trying to hide genuine tears underneath the intimacy because physical distance is real even if emotional connection is profound. Show layered longing in your voice—sexual and emotionally desperate.

title: The Unforgivable Truth
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a lie they told you throughout your childhood that shaped your entire life. Begin with your entire body coiled like a spring—fists clenched, jaw tight, voice sharp and accusing. Every word should carry the weight of years of compressed anger and betrayal. As you speak, and as your parent finally admits the truth and explains their fear and shame, feel your body begin to unlock—first your hands opening, then your chest expanding, your throat loosening. By the end, your voice should crack with a complex mixture of grief for lost years and the unexpected softness of understanding. The anger doesn't disappear, but it transforms into something more human, more connected.

title: Laughing While Packing Up Your Shared Life
instruction: You're boxing up years of memories after an amicable breakup. Your ex-partner left this morning. Find an object that triggers a memory and start laughing—genuinely, warmly, at the absurdity or sweetness of it. 'Remember when we thought this was so important?' Keep your voice light, almost giddy with the strange relief of ending. But as you keep talking, gratitude seeps in, and your laughter becomes wet with tears. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, voice breaking on both. Express genuine thankfulness for what you had while your heart splinters: 'I'm so glad it was you, even if it couldn't be forever.' End in strange peace, voice soft and wondering, holding the paradox of joy and grief in the same breath.
inspired_by: Realizing Your Therapist Isn't the Right Fit

title: Stop Performing Your Anger
instruction: You're confronting your father about his absence throughout your childhood. You've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times in your head, with perfect cutting phrases and devastating observations. But now, facing him, those prepared speeches feel hollow and theatrical. Start by trying to deliver your rehearsed confrontation, but feel how false it sounds. Let your real impulses interrupt—maybe you laugh bitterly at the wrong moment, maybe your voice cracks not from sadness but from rage, maybe you find yourself saying absurd things that somehow feel more true than your prepared statements. Fight against your own need to sound impressive or right. By the end, you're no longer performing anger—you're exposing the raw, messy, contradictory truth underneath it: maybe it's grief, maybe it's a twisted form of love, maybe it's just exhaustion.

title: The Thank You That Tastes Like Poison
instruction: You must thank someone who saved your life but destroyed someone else you loved in the process—perhaps a doctor who saved you through an organ donation from your child, or a person who rescued you but not your partner. Begin carrying the weight of impossible gratitude mixed with molten rage. Your body will want to perform either thankfulness or anger, to choose a side, maybe to arrange your face into 'conflicted.' Reject this. Instead, allow both truths to genuinely war within you—your shoulders might want to embrace and strike simultaneously, your voice might break with both tenderness and fury. Start with whatever feels safest, then let the other emotion ambush you from within. By the end, find a place of utter exhaustion where both emotions are fully real and you're not hiding behind any protective gesture or stance—just raw, contradictory, completely authentic.
inspired_by: When an actor uses physical props, leaning, or posture to appear relaxed rather than achieving genuine ease

title: The Cleanup Speech
instruction: You're a middle-aged stage manager addressing the cast after a late night rehearsal. Stand alone on the empty stage, the reverb of your own voice coming back to you. Start with a weary disgust, a heavy resignation that this show is a 'polishing a turd' scenario. As you look around and your voice echoes, a new, sharper disgust takes over – disgust at yourself for not walking out years ago. Let the controlled acoustics make every word sound too clear, too honest. End in a flat, final contempt.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Rage Against the Fading Light
instruction: You're in your apartment, alone, having just been diagnosed with early-stage dementia. You're a renowned scientist, your mind your only tool, your identity. Start with explosive fury, shouting at the universe: 'NO. NO! Not this! Not my MIND!' Your voice is raw, primal. Throw things, your words coming in gasps: 'Take my legs! Take my sight! But not THIS!' You're pacing, hyperventilating with rage. 'I've spent sixty years building knowledge, connections, understanding!' Your voice cracks between rage and terror. Then you catch sight of your reflection and freeze. Your voice drops, becoming something more frightening—quiet, fierce determination mixed with desperation: 'I won't go gently. I'll fight every single day.' But as you say it, you feel the futility washing over you. Your voice transforms into something broken: 'But how do you fight your own brain?' Sink down, your rage collapsing into helpless weeping: 'I'm going to disappear piece by piece. And I'll be aware of it. Until I'm not.' End with your voice raw, exhausted, but finding a strange fierce peace: 'Then I'll make every lucid moment count for something. Even if it's just remembering my own name one more time.' You're crying but there's defiant strength there too.

title: The Confession in Twilight
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner about the affair you had, the one you've convinced yourself was nothing, meant nothing. Your voice is quiet, controlled, rehearsing the lie: 'It was just one time. It didn't change anything.' But in the darkness, speaking to someone who can't hear you, the truth starts seeping through the cracks. Your breathing becomes shallow, caught. You're trying to hold onto the version where you're not the person who did this, but the weight of it is crushing your chest. By the end, you're barely audible, tears in your throat, admitting the depth of your betrayal and your terror that you've destroyed everything. The delusion dissolves into quiet, unbearable honesty.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: Your dying parent is asking you to let them go—to stop the treatments, to allow a peaceful end. Every fiber of you wants to scream 'no,' to beg them to keep fighting. Start with desperate refusal, voice tight with panic: 'We can try one more thing, please.' But as you look into their exhausted eyes, something shifts. Your resistance begins to crack, grief flooding in where denial stood. By the end, through tears, you give them what they need: 'I love you. It's okay. You can rest now.' You're saying goodbye while simultaneously trying to memorize the sound of their breathing. Your voice breaks not from weakness, but from the immense strength it takes to release someone you cannot bear to lose.

title: The Silent Goodbye
instruction: Youre in a crowded caf, watching your partner from afar. They dont know youre leaving for good. Every word you mutter under your breath is a mix of longing and sorrow, each soft exhale capturing heartbreak and love without a single spoken farewell. Occasionally, your voice catches as you try to hold back tears. Let us feel the restrained devastation without fully breaking down.

title: Finding Peace Finally
instruction: The struggle is over. Your voice is still, quiet, finally resting: 'I don't need to fight anymore.' Breathing is deep, full, released. Physical: you're letting your shoulders drop. 'It took so long to get here.' Vocal tone is gentle, accepting. 'But I'm at peace now.' Not happy necessarily, but peaceful. By the end, your voice is the sound of someone who has stopped running: 'I can rest now. It's safe.'

title: Anger Through Smiles
instruction: Youre furious but forced to act gracious and warm. Speak with exaggerated friendliness, forcing yourself to laugh and sound sincere, letting small cracks of anger seep through. The audience should feel the strain as you pretend to be calm.

title: Speaking in Our Ruins
instruction: Stand in the ruins of your childhood home, speaking to no one and everyone, slipping between the language you spoke as a child and the language you speak now. Begin with bitter laughter as you narrate what each room used to be, mixing languages unconsciously, finding dark humor in what's been lost. Let the laughter become tears without transition - not a switch but a blend, like you're crying and laughing in the same breath. Feel gratitude for what was, grief for what's gone, all tangled together. Your voice should break not with sadness alone but with the overwhelming beauty of what you once had. End in a whisper, thanking the walls in your first language, your voice full of peace and devastation at once.

title: The Inventory of Failures
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just told you they're cutting contact with you. Begin by defending yourself—listing all the sacrifices you made, the ways you tried, the impossible position you were in. Let your voice carry the full weight of your justifications, your need to be understood as someone who did their best. But as you speak, let a creeping awareness begin to surface. Start noticing the patterns you're describing, the echoes of your own parents' failures in your words. Your defensive anger should slowly corrode into horrified recognition. Let your voice fracture as you realize, in real-time, that you have become exactly what you swore you'd never be. End in a completely different emotional place—not defensive, but devastated and accountable, your voice stripped of all protection, asking not to be forgiven but simply to be seen clearly, even in your failure.
inspired_by: Role-Playing the Inner Critic (Solo Subpersonality Access)

title: Becoming My Mother
instruction: You're confronting your mother about years of emotional distance, but mid-argument, you catch your reflection in a mirror behind her and suddenly perceive yourself transforming into her. Feel your posture shift to match hers, sense your facial expressions mirroring hers, hear your voice taking on her cadence and tone. Start with anger and accusation, but as you recognize yourself becoming what you feared, let that fury crack open into vulnerable terror and understanding. Your voice should physically change—initially sharp and defensive, then softening into something more complex as you realize you're perpetuating the very patterns you came to confront. End not with resolution but with the devastating recognition of inheritance.

title: The Shower After
instruction: You're alone in the shower after an intense physical encounter—maybe sex, maybe a fight, maybe both. Your body is heightened, sensitized, still buzzing. Begin by letting water run over you, making whatever sounds your breath wants to make—no performing, just raw response to sensation. As you wash yourself, let the touch trigger emotional memories from the encounter. Start making sounds that aren't 'pretty'—groans, growls, sharp intakes of breath, crude expressions of pleasure or pain. Let your hands move on your own body without any concern for grace or propriety. If you need to spit, spit. If you need to let out an ugly cry or an animal sound, do it. Touch yourself however your body demands—scratch an itch aggressively, grip your own arms, press your forehead against the tile. Move from physical intensity into emotional devastation or ecstasy or both at once, letting every sound and gesture be completely unfiltered.

title: The Last Song Before Silence
instruction: You are a composer who has just learned you're losing your hearing permanently within weeks. You're speaking to your life's work—your unfinished symphony—as if it were a living thing you must say goodbye to. Begin with desperate denial and frustration, trying to explain what you still hear in your mind. Gradually move through grief as you describe melodies you'll never hear performed, then shift into a bittersweet acceptance as you whisper about the silence that's coming. End with tender gratitude for the years of sound you had, your voice breaking not with despair but with love for what music gave you. Let the emotion catch in your throat; this isn't a performance—it's a farewell to your identity.

title: The Gratitude That Breaks You
instruction: You're standing at a threshold—perhaps a doorway, a graduation, a wedding, a funeral—and you're looking at someone who saved your life (literally or metaphorically) but whom you've also resented, fought with, and pushed away. Begin with complex, contradictory feelings churning in your chest: gratitude mixed with old anger, love tangled with resentment. Make yourself look at them with fresh eyes—as if you're a stranger trying to understand who this person really is and what they've carried. Study the specific details of their face: how they've aged, where they hold tension, what their expression reveals right now. Let yourself perceive the weight of what they've sacrificed, what loving you has cost them. Your voice should crack between laughter and tears as you try to speak. End by naming both things at once: 'I have hated you and you have been everything' or 'You hurt me and you saved me and I don't know how to hold both.' Let the contradictions remain unresolved but deeply, specifically seen.

title: The Perfectly Laid Trap
instruction: You are a teenage girl who has just executed a calculated revenge against a bully who tormented you for years. You’re standing alone in a hallway, phone in hand, watching them flee after you exposed their secret to everyone. Your voice is eerily calm and measured—every word slow, deliberate, with a faint smile threatening to break through. But as you speak, the relief of finally being free from their power floods in. Let your voice start ice-cold and rehearsed, then soften as the satisfaction gives way to a quiet, trembling exhale of release.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Fury and Helplessness
instruction: You've just discovered someone hurt your child, and you're on the phone confronting the school/institution/person who failed to protect them. Start with barely contained rage, your voice shaking with the effort to not scream: 'You're going to sit there and tell me you saw NOTHING?' Let the fury escalate—louder, sharper, losing control: 'That's MY child! MY BABY! And you let this happen!' Then, mid-sentence, let it all collapse. The rage breaks into desperate, heaving sobs: 'I trusted you... I thought they were safe...' Your voice becomes small, broken: 'How do I tell them I can't fix this? How do I...' End in a whisper of absolute helplessness: 'I can't protect them. I can't even...' Show the moment when righteous fury shatters against the wall of your own powerlessness, when anger becomes grief becomes devastating inadequacy.

title: Trapped in a Car After Earthquake: Checking if Your Passenger is Dead
instruction: The car is crushed at an angle. You're hanging from your seatbelt and the person next to you is unconscious. Your voice is panicked, words tumbling out as you try to reach them, try to find a pulse. You're describing what you're doing—reaching, feeling, checking—while your voice gets higher and higher. Include the moment you feel them breathe. Your voice breaks with relief, then shifts again: you need to get help. You're yelling out the window, voice raw, trying to find anyone who can hear you. The silence of the collapsed city might be the worst part. Your voice becomes smaller and smaller.

title: Laughing Through Your Last Goodbye at the Airport
instruction: Your best friend is leaving forever—emigrating, or entering witness protection, or choosing a path that severs all contact.
