'I know you're in love with someone else, and that's okay. I just... I needed you to know you were loved. That you are loved.' End with your hand on theirs, your breathing unsteady, a soft 'Please wake up' that's barely audible but carries the weight of your entire heart breaking.
inspired_by: Parent Watching Their Child Leave Home

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: Someone you loved more than life itself has just died, and you're alone with their body or their belongings, remembering a moment of pure joy you shared—a dance, a road trip, an inside joke, a perfect day. Begin by laughing as you recount this memory out loud to them, really laughing, finding genuine joy in the recollection. But you're also crying, tears streaming down your face, your voice thick with both emotions. Thank them—for that moment, for loving you, for existing in your life—and your gratitude is absolutely real even as your grief is overwhelming. You keep laughing and crying in the same breath, unable to separate the joy from the loss. By the end, find a moment of strange, beautiful peace in the contradiction—you're devastated, but you're also so grateful you got to love them at all. Let your voice carry both the breaking and the wholeness simultaneously.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're standing before a parent, and for once you're making them look at something they've ignored your whole life - your art, your child, your life's work, your true self. Start with quiet, trembling hope: 'Look at this. Really look.' There's a moment of vulnerable wonder at what you've created or become, pride mixing with the old hunger for their approval. 'Do you see it? Do you see what I...' But as their response falls short again, or their gaze slides away, wonder curdles into devastation, then fierce anger. 'No. You're going to SEE this. You're going to see ME.' End in a whisper that's both broken and defiant: 'I needed you to witness this. I needed you to see me just once.' Let the marvel at your own existence collide with the pain of their blindness.

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who shaped your life—a grandparent, mentor, or estranged parent—in their final hours. For years, you've swallowed your truth, kept peace, stayed small. Begin with that familiar silence, that careful distance you've always maintained. But tonight, there's no tomorrow. Let yourself finally say what you've never said—the anger, the love, the disappointment, the gratitude all tangled together. Feel how speaking these words shifts something in your chest, how your voice might crack or surge with power. As you speak, imagine their eyes changing—perhaps filling with tears, perhaps softening with understanding they never showed before. End in a place of unexpected peace, having finally been wholly yourself in their presence. Let your voice move from tight and careful to raw and liberated.

title: Snowstorm Sanctuary
instruction: You are a small child, lost in a blizzard, wearing a thick woolen scarf pulled up over your nose and mouth. The fabric is wet with your breath, warm and heavy against your skin. You've been panicked, calling for help, but now you've stumbled into a narrow doorway that offers shelter from the wind. Speak to yourself in a muffled, shivering whisper as you huddle there. Start with the leftover quiver of fear—your voice tight, breathy, words clipped by the cold and the scarf. Then, as you realize the wind can't reach you, let the tension drain. Your breath slows, the fabric softens against your lips, and your voice settles into a quiet, exhausted relief. The last words should sound almost sleepy, as if the safety is sinking into your bones.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Spot
instruction: You are an elderly person alone in your kitchen, slowly scrubbing a stubborn stain on the counter. You begin with a quiet irritation—this spot has bothered you for days, and your arm tires from the effort. But as the rhythmic motion takes over, you feel your breath falling into a steady pattern, and a surprising wave of relief softens your shoulders. The stain finally lifts, and you let out a small, breathless laugh, your eyes welling with a quiet elation and a deep, sensual pleasure in the simple victory. Speak on a sigh, letting the words stumble free—pausing when your arm strains, muttering to yourself, then whispering the final word like a secret prayer.
emotions_sampled: Elation (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Tour That Fell Silent
instruction: You are a factory worker giving your young son a tour of the bustling warehouse floor. Your voice rises with excitement over the clatter of machinery, pointing out the conveyor belts and forklifts. But your son notices a locked safety cage with a faded warning sign, and you stop mid-sentence—remembering the accident you caused there years ago. Your proud energy falters, your eyes drop to the oily floor, and you mutter a quiet confession about how not everything here is safe. Let the echo and mechanical hum fill your pauses, your tone shifting from eager guide to a man weighed down by guilt.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Lost in a Memory
instruction: Youre reliving a painful memory aloud, each word pulling you deeper into it. Start with a detached tone, describing the scene as though its far away. Gradually, let the memory consume you until youre fully immersed, voice quivering with raw emotion, as if the line between past and present has vanished.

title: The Cynic's Secret Softness
instruction: Late at night, in whispered tones, you are confessing something to your lover. You are someone who lives in your head—sharp, skeptical, armored with wit and intellect. You mock sentimentality, you analyze rather than feel. Begin speaking from that place: clever, slightly detached, trying to make this confession into something you can control with words. But there is a part of you—buried deep, frightened, aching—that is a true believer, a romantic, someone who yearns desperately to be seen and held. Let that part slowly take over your voice. Let your cleverness fail you. By the end, you are speaking from pure longing, stripped of all intellectual defense, trembling with the vulnerability of the tender-hearted person you've hidden beneath the cynic. Your voice should become almost childlike in its naked hope.

title: The Puzzle Box
instruction: You are a woman sitting at a table with your young grandchild. You've just shown them your treasured wooden puzzle box, and you're explaining how it works with deep satisfaction. Your hands tremble as you point, and your voice naturally softens and wobbles. Midway, you notice the box isn't closing right, and a flicker of confusion passes through you — but you push through, holding onto your pride in the gift and the comfort of this moment. Start with quiet contentment, let confusion interrupt, then end in defiant, gentle pride even as your words fade.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Contentment (very intensely present), Confusion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Homecoming That Wasn't
instruction: You're standing at the door of your childhood home after many years away, about to see family members who have just welcomed back the sibling who hurt you deeply and never apologized. You must walk in and act happy for them. Begin speaking (to yourself or to someone on the phone) with bitter resentment, your voice sharp with the injustice of having to perform joy when you feel erased. Let your voice drip with sarcasm as you rehearse the fake smile you'll wear, the cheerful words you'll say. But then, as you stand there, allow yourself to genuinely remember the early years—before the hurt, when it was simple, when you loved this sibling with uncomplicated fierceness, when you belonged without question. Let these memories wash over you with full sensory detail: their laughter, games you invented, secrets you shared, the feeling of being part of something. By the end, your voice should carry an almost unbearable cocktail of emotions: you're still angry, still hurt, but you're also flooded with grief for what was lost and a terrible, unwanted tenderness that makes you realize you might actually be happy to see them, and you hate yourself a little for it.
inspired_by: Imaging a Subpersonality: The Magical Child

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone you love deeply—a parent, a partner, a child—who is dying and afraid to let go. They're holding on for you, and you know it. Begin with your own fear, your voice tight with the desperate need to keep them here. But as you speak, you must find a strength you didn't know you had: the strength to release them, to tell them it's okay to stop fighting. Your voice transforms from trembling resistance to a steady, tender certainty. You're breaking inside, but your words become a bridge for them to cross. End with a clarity born of the deepest love—you're giving them permission to leave you, and your voice holds them gently as they go. This isn't about being strong for yourself; it's about being strong enough to lose everything.

title: Weakness Admitting
instruction: Someone is admitting weakness—something they can't do alone, something that scares them, something they're not good at. Their voice carries the difficulty of this admission. In their world, weakness is dangerous. But they're saying it anyway. The listener's voice responds carefully, neither shaming nor offering false comfort. The person admitting weakness waits to see if they're going to be dismissed or diminished. They're not. Slowly, their voice becomes less guarded. Admitting weakness actually requires strength. By the end, they've learned that their weakness doesn't invalidate their worth.

title: The Gift That Reminds Me
instruction: You are an elderly person, knitting a sweater for a relative who never seems to appreciate your efforts. The click of needles is steady as you begin, a faint smile as you tease aloud about how they always fidgeted when you tried to teach them. But as you continue, the memory grows sharper – their dismissive comments about your knitting, their ingratitude. Your voice turns sour, then edged with contempt. Let the rhythm of the needles influence your pace: calm at first, then quicker, harsher as your bitterness rises. Include natural pauses, maybe dropping a stitch, catching yourself. End with a tight, bitter final line. Your speech should be about 40-80 words, feeling like a real, spontaneous monologue to yourself.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Contempt (slightly present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What We Whisper in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone, speaking barely above a whisper in the darkness. You've been carrying a secret about yourself—a fear, a shame, a truth about who you really are—and tonight, in this suspended moment, you finally let it surface. Begin tentatively, testing each word, your voice fragile and uncertain. As you continue, let the relief of finally speaking it aloud mix with terror of being truly seen. Your whisper should carry the weight of years of hiding. End with a question asked so quietly it's almost just breath: 'Do you still love me?' The journey moves from tentative confession to naked exposure, from hiding to asking to be held anyway.

title: The護る (Mamoru) Moment
instruction: Your child just told you someone hurt them, and they're standing right there—the person who did it. Start with a voice that's terrifyingly quiet, shaking with the effort to contain volcanic rage: 'You will never touch them again.' Each word is deliberate, lethal. Then the dam breaks—you roar, your voice raw and primal with protective fury. But mid-sentence, you choke on it because your child is crying, frightened by your intensity. Your voice drops, becomes tender, desperate: 'Baby, look at me, I'm sorry, I'm sorry.' You're speaking to your child now, trying to be gentle while still shaking with murderous rage toward the other person. End with a whispered vow that carries both fierce love and helpless anguish: 'No one will hurt you again. I promise.' Your voice breaks because you know you can't guarantee that, and it's destroying you.

title: The Vow That Shatters Into Rage
instruction: You're making a passionate, desperate promise to save a relationship, a friendship, a family bond that's disintegrating. Start with fierce conviction—your voice strong, almost aggressive in its certainty. You promise everything: to change, to fight, to never give up. But the other person's doubt is palpable, and it ignites something in you. Your promise becomes a demand, then an accusation. Why won't they believe you? Haven't you always fought for them? Your voice rises, cracks, explodes into something between rage and anguish. You're shouting now, promising and pleading and accusing all at once. Then suddenly, you break—your voice collapses into sobs. The promise transforms into a confession: you're terrified, you don't know if you can keep it, you're making it anyway because love is the only thing you have left. End with your voice raw, stripped bare, the promise now a wounded offering.

title: The Last Graduation Day
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed the night before she passes. She asks you to tell her about your college graduation—the day she was too ill to attend but desperately wanted to be there. Begin with guilt and sadness as you start describing that day. As you relive walking across the stage, hearing your name called, holding your diploma, allow the pure joy and pride of that moment to flood back through your body. Let your voice lift with the excitement you felt then. But as you watch her face light up with vicarious pride, feel how that joy tangles with the crushing knowledge that she's leaving. End with a complex gratitude—thanking her for being there in spirit, your voice breaking between celebration and goodbye. Let the memory be vivid enough that you're almost back in that auditorium, but stay present enough to hold her hand.

title: Whispered Promise in the Dark
instruction: You are a mother hiding in a cramped closet with your frightened child, your bodies pressed together as footsteps approach outside. You must whisper the escape plan with hyper-precise, hushed articulation so only she hears, your voice flat and controlled at first to avoid cracking. But as you feel her small hand clutch your shirt, a fierce wave of affection breaks through—your tone warms, your monotone softens into a trembling, honeyed murmur. By the end, you cup her cheek and promise her, in a voice thick with love, that you will keep her safe. Let your breath catch, and let your fear dissolve into a quiet, intimate smile that changes everything.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's hospice bedside in the final hours. She's been holding on for weeks, and you realize she's waiting for you to let her go. You begin speaking with desperate love, trying to convince her it's okay to leave—but underneath, you're terrified and selfish, not ready at all. Your voice cracks between tender reassurance and barely-contained panic. As you tell her 'it's okay, you can rest now,' you feel your own need for her rising like a wave, and by the end, you're no longer sure if you're giving her permission or begging her to stay. The words stay gentle, but the emotional truth underneath completely transforms.

title: Late Night Unraveling
instruction: You're an older man, a few drinks in, sitting close to someone you've been flirting with all evening. The room buzzes with low light and laughter. Start with a teasing, playful tone—lean in, let your voice drop low and breathy as you make a joke about how absurd this all is. But as you speak, the alcohol loosens something; your guard slips. By the end, the laughter fades, and you're speaking from a quieter, more honest place—almost startled by your own vulnerability. Let your voice catch, shift pitch, trail off as you realize you mean every word.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral: Finding Absurd Joy While Burying Your Last Connection to Home
instruction: You're at the funeral of someone who represented your last tie to childhood, to innocence, to the person you were before life hardened you. Begin speaking—maybe to them, maybe to yourself, maybe to no one. Your voice is heavy with loss, recounting how their death severed your final anchor. But then you remember something absurd they once said, and against every instinct, you laugh. It's a small laugh that horrifies you, but it grows. Your voice oscillates wildly between grief and inappropriate joy as you realize the curse of losing them is also the gift of being set free. You're crying and laughing in the same breath, your voice cracking as you describe how the weight of memory was killing you softly. The emotions tangle impossibly: you're devastated and liberated, heartbroken and giddy with possibility. End with your voice in that impossible space where laughter and sobs are indistinguishable, blessing them for dying because it means you finally get to live, even as admitting this breaks something precious inside you.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Wizard Realizes the Curse They've Carried Is Actually a Gift

title: Doctor: Delivering Your Own Terminal Diagnosis to Your Family
instruction: You're a physician who just received your own test results, and you're gathering your family to tell them. You start with clinical detachment because that's your armor: 'The scans show metastatic involvement...' using medical terms as a shield. But your voice cracks on a word and suddenly you're laughing—a strange, almost hysterical sound—because the absurdity hits you: you've said these exact words to hundreds of patients. The laughter turns to tears you're trying to swallow. Your voice becomes achingly tender: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry I'm doing this to you.' You're apologizing for dying, for leaving them, and you know how irrational that is, which makes you laugh again through the tears. Find the strange gratitude in this moment: 'I'm grateful I get to say goodbye. So many people don't.' Your voice holds everything at once—the doctor's knowledge, the human's terror, the parent's heartbreak, the strange peace of knowing, the desperate wish for more time. End in that impossible space where you're devastated and grateful, terrified and accepting, falling apart and somehow, inexplicably, whole.

title: The 3 AM Touch
instruction: You are lying beside someone in the dark, overcome by fragile, almost unbearable tenderness and the terrifying awareness of how easily you could lose them. Begin with barely perceptible movements—fingertips ghosting over skin, your breathing syncing with theirs, the smallest adjustments to get closer. Let your body whisper what you're too afraid to say aloud: trembling hands, lips forming words against their shoulder that never become sound, tears falling silently. Stay in the realm of micro-expressions and subtle physical revelations. By the end, allow your body to shift from fear-laced tenderness to something more grounded—perhaps steady breathing, a firmer embrace, or a peaceful stillness. Every movement should be intimate, minimal, as if the slightest sound would shatter the moment.

title: Conditioning Breaking
instruction: You're saying something your family taught you never to say. Your voice is shaking with the transgression. 'I don't agree with you.' That simple statement was forbidden. Your heart is pounding audibly in your speech. But as the words settle, your voice becomes stronger. 'I have my own thoughts.' Autonomy sounds terrifying and beautiful. Breaking conditioning feels like tearing skin off bone, but underneath is your own voice, finally.

title: When the Fortress Crumbles
instruction: You've spent your entire life being strong, being the one who holds it together, and something has just shattered that armor completely. Begin fierce, almost aggressive in your strength. 'I can handle this. I always handle this.' Your voice is steel, unyielding. But cracks appear. A tremor. A pause that lasts too long. The wall you've built starts crumbling and you can feel it happening. Your voice rises in desperate defiance: 'I said I'm FINE!' But then it breaks—really breaks—and everything you've been holding back for years floods out. Rage collapses into sobbing. 'I can't do this anymore. I can't. I can't.' End in the rubble of your own strength, voice raw and shaking, simultaneously terrified and relieved that you've finally, finally broken open.

title: The Last Transmission Home Before Re-Entry Fails
instruction: You are an astronaut on a damaged spacecraft, recording a final message to your family as you attempt re-entry knowing the heat shield is compromised. Begin with forced calm and technical updates, your voice steady despite knowing this may be goodbye. As gravitational forces increase and the craft begins to shake violently, your composure fractures—words break apart, your breathing becomes labored, but underneath the physical strain, tenderness floods through. You're not fighting anymore, just trying to say 'I love you' one more time as the G-forces crush your chest. End in breathless whispers of their names, surrender replacing fear, gratitude replacing panic. Let the physical reality strip away all pretense until only raw love remains.
inspired_by: Reporting While Sprinting for Your Life

title: The Waiting Room Window
instruction: You are an older man sitting in a hospital waiting room, your son has just come out of emergency surgery and the doctor told you he'll be fine. You've been holding yourself rigid for hours. Now, alone, you let go. Start with a long, shaky exhale—your body slumps forward, a half-laugh, half-sob escapes. Then, as you stare at your own reflection in the dark window, your voice steadies, grows thoughtful. You say the words aloud slowly, as if realizing something you've never said before. Let your voice crack between laughter and tears, then settle into a low, wondering murmur. End with a long, quiet pause as you contemplate your own age and the weight of time.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unkept Promise
instruction: You are an older woman standing in a torrential downpour, searching for a stray cat you've been feeding for months. Your coat is soaked, your glasses fogged, rain streaming into your mouth as you call out. At first, your voice is heavy with exhaustion and disappointment—you've been out here for hours and the cat hasn't appeared. But as thunder rolls and you wipe water from your eyes, doubt creeps in: maybe the cat isn't lost, maybe it never needed you. Your words become fragmented, shouted between claps of thunder, sputtering as rain hits your lips. Let the physical discomfort—shivering, gasping, wiping water—shape your performance. End with a slower, quieter realization, your voice cracking with doubt.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Disappointment (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Sent You Away
instruction: You've returned to the forest cabin where your parent sent you as a troubled teenager, claiming it would 'fix' you. Now, as an adult, you stand where they abandoned you and speak directly to them (though they're not present). Begin with bitter, controlled anger as you breathe in this air they thought would cure you—describe how you learned to survive here alone, how these trees heard you cry every night. Let your rage build as you recount what you needed instead—not wilderness, but their presence, their acceptance. Then break: let your voice crack into the raw grief of the abandoned child still inside you. End in exhausted honesty, admitting quietly that despite everything, part of you still breathes this air and thinks of them, still wants them to know who you became, still aches for their love.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep, Cleansing Breath of Fresh Forest Air

title: The thread unraveled
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy, alone in your room at night, sitting on the edge of your bed scrolling through an old group chat. You come across a message chain that makes your stomach drop — it's from your ex, and you're rereading the moment everything fell apart. Start with a tight, pained voice as you scroll faster, muttering disbelief and anger under your breath. Let your voice drop and slow down as the shock wears off, leaving a hollow, quieter sadness — your thumb still scrolling absently, the screen blurring a little, your last words trailing off into nothing.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Reading Your Own Eulogy at a Funeral You're Not Dead For
instruction: At your retirement party, someone jokes you should give your own eulogy. You're slightly drunk, and you decide to actually do it—speak about yourself as if you've died, reflecting on the life you've lived. You start with self-deprecating laughter in your voice: 'Here lies someone who spent way too much time worrying about things that never happened...' You're making people chuckle, but then genuine emotion sneaks in. Your voice wavers between laughter and tears: 'Who loved people so much it hurt, who said yes when they should have said no, who said no when they should have said yes.' The room goes quiet. You're crying now but also smiling, your voice full of contradictory wonder: 'Who got to see their daughter graduate, who held their grandchild, who had breakfast with their best friend every Sunday for thirty years.' Your voice breaks with gratitude and grief intertwined: 'What a staggeringly lucky person. What a beautiful, messy, perfectly imperfect life.' Pause. Then, soft and certain, speaking to yourself across time: 'You did good. You really did good.' You're weeping and laughing at once, completely at peace.

title: Realizing You're Like Your Emotionally Distant Parent
instruction: Someone you love says 'You never let anyone in' and it hits you. Your voice in response is defensive. But they're right. Your voice becomes quiet. You're realizing you've replicated your parent's emotional unavailability. Your voice becomes sad. You're protecting yourself the same way they did. Your voice carries realization—'I do that, don't I?' Your voice is recognizing a cycle. Include the moment you decide to try to be different anyway.

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your child who is leaving for a dangerous mission they may not return from. Begin with forced cheerfulness, pretending everything is normal as you make their favorite breakfast one last time. Your voice cracks as you try to give them advice for a future you're terrified they won't have. Let the facade crumble as you move from practical instructions to desperate wishes. The child tries to comfort you, and you find yourself apologizing for not being stronger. In the final moments, shift from fear to something fiercer—a blessing, a permission to go, spoken through tears but with absolute conviction. End with a whispered 'I'm so proud of you' that carries both devastation and transcendent love.

title: The Last Vigil: A Parent Speaks to Their Sleeping Child Before Dawn
instruction: You are a parent sitting beside your adult child's hospital bed in the hour before a risky, life-or-death surgery at dawn. Your child is sedated and cannot hear you, but you speak anyway—beginning with forced optimism and gentle reassurances you don't fully believe. As you continue, your voice cracks and the truth spills out: your fears, your regrets about moments you missed in their childhood, your desperate bargaining with the universe. By the end, find a place of trembling peace—not acceptance exactly, but a fierce, protective love that transcends your terror. Let your voice move from steady and soothing to breaking and raw, then to something quieter and almost sacred. This isn't about volume—it's about the journey from denial through devastation to a love so complete it hurts.
inspired_by: The Guardian Angel and the Fallen Angel

title: The Root of the Problem
instruction: You're a middle-aged man sitting in a dentist's waiting room, nursing a persistent, dull ache on the right side of your jaw. You've been avoiding this appointment for weeks, and now you're rehearsing what to say to the receptionist to explain why you're so late. The pain makes you speak carefully, favoring one side, wincing slightly when you swallow. Start with a quiet, confused murmur to yourself—trying to piece together why the pain flared up today—and end with a quick, embarrassed apology to the woman at the desk, your voice trailing off as you realize how pathetic you sound.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Confusion (very intensely present), Embarrassment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bound in Trust
instruction: You’re a teenage girl, wrists tied with silk ropes, lying on a soft bed. Your partner’s fingers brush your skin, and you start with a surprised little gasp—a laugh that trails off into a trembling exhale. You try to move, but the ropes hold, and your voice wavers with that shock of helplessness. As you speak, let your astonishment soften into a quiet, trusting surrender. Your breath hitches between words, your voice grows smaller, more intimate. End by whispering that you’re exactly where you want to be, even if your body can’t move. Feel the slight panic melt into peace.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying in bed next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. Begin in a whisper that's almost too quiet to hear—you're terrified, your words keep dying in your throat, you start sentences and stop them. You feel locked up inside, protective, defended. Stay in that trapped feeling. Then let something shift: maybe they touch your hand in the darkness, maybe you realize this is your only chance, but let yourself drop deeper beneath your own defenses. Your whisper becomes more raw, more broken, more real. The words start coming from a place beneath words—maybe sounds that aren't quite language, maybe breath, maybe something primal and unguarded. By the end, you're not trying to speak anymore—you're just letting the truth move through you in whatever form it takes, even if it's just breathing and silence that says everything.
inspired_by: Actor feels blocked during a rehearsal and cannot access the needed emotional life

title: The Rainstorm Reunion
instruction: You're standing in the rain, soaked through, waiting for someone who just arrived. Begin by letting yourself fully experience the physical sensation of the rain—its temperature, how it runs down your face and neck, the weight of wet clothes on your skin, the smell of wet pavement, the sound of water hitting surfaces around you, the taste of rain on your lips, how your feet feel in wet shoes. Start angry—the rain mirrors your fury, and you're acutely, almost aggressively aware of every uncomfortable sensation. You're here to unleash your rage at this person. But as you speak and they respond, let the sensations begin to transform—does the cold rain start to feel cleansing? Does the discomfort shift to something else? Let your awareness of being drenched, of water mixing with tears, of shivering that might be cold or might be emotion, blur the line between physical and emotional sensation. End in a place where you can no longer tell if you're shaking from cold, crying, or both—where rage has transformed through intense physical awareness into passionate, confused, overwhelming love and forgiveness.

title: The Body Keeps the Truth
instruction: You're in a moment of intense physical sensation—perhaps after making love, or in the midst of a rage that's making your whole body shake, or experiencing pain that's breaking you open. Your body is flooded, overwhelmed. Start by saying the conventional things people say in these moments: reassurances, apologies, the standard phrases that maintain control. But your body won't let you lie. Let your breath dictate your rhythm. Let your physical state pull the real words out of you—the raw need, the animal grief, the fierce joy, the primal fear. Allow your voice to be affected by your breathing, by the adrenaline or exhaustion in your system. Stop trying to sound composed and let the physical experience shatter your verbal defenses. Move from attempted control to complete surrender to what your body is demanding you express.
inspired_by: This Is What I Usually Say, and This Is What I Really Want to Say

title: Folding Your Shirt: The Tenderness of Almost
instruction: You're folding your lover's shirt - they're moving out tomorrow after five years. This is the shirt they wore on your first date, the one they left on your floor a thousand mornings. Start by describing the fabric under your fingers, voice soft, almost hypnotized by the ritual. Let the gentleness build - remembering small moments with aching specificity: coffee in bed, their laugh, the way they said your name. But with each fold, your voice should barely hold together, catching on words. This isn't anger or drama - this is love surviving its own ending. By the final fold, you're whispering to the shirt itself, to them, to the version of yourself who believed this would last. End on an exhale that holds everything you can't say tomorrow.
inspired_by: Nostalgia Ambush: A Song Comes On

title: Inside a Space Helmet: Last Transmission
instruction: Your oxygen is running low inside your sealed space suit. The voice reverberates in the helmet cavity — tinny, confined, claustrophobic. Your breathing is the loudest sound, amplified and echoing. Record your final message home — start with mission-report formality, then let it crack into personal: names of loved ones, things you wish you'd said. The breathing should become more desperate as O2 drops. End with the voice getting drowsy, confused, fading.

title: The Last Flight Home: Joy in the Face of Goodbye
instruction: Your younger sibling is leaving tomorrow for a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity abroad—something you've both dreamed of since childhood. You're genuinely thrilled for them, bursting with pride and excitement. But as you help them pack their final suitcase, the reality crashes over you: they won't be back for years, maybe longer. Begin speaking with bright, genuine enthusiasm about their future, their dreams coming true. Let your voice gradually betray the ache underneath—the catch in your throat, the way joy and grief can coexist in the same breath. End in a place where you're still smiling through your words, but the love and loss are inseparable. This isn't about hiding emotion—it's about feeling two truths at once, authentically and without performance.
inspired_by: Suppressing Joy to Be Sensitive to Others

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a specific lie they told you throughout your childhood—something that shaped how you saw yourself or the world. Begin with controlled anger, almost rehearsed, as if you've planned this conversation a thousand times. But as you speak, you start to see their face differently—you notice they're older, smaller, more fragile than the giant they were in your memory. The rage doesn't disappear, but something else enters: the devastating recognition that they were as lost as you are now. End in a place where you're no longer sure if you're accusing them or mourning for both of you. Let your voice move from sharp accusation to something more bewildered and heartbroken, without losing the thread of anger entirely.
inspired_by: Actor cannot find a real parallel experience for a specific scene's emotional demands

title: Your Child Asking an Impossible Question
instruction: Your child asks 'Why did mommy/daddy leave?' or 'Did I do something wrong?' and it's a question you can't fully answer. Your voice is trying to protect them from the complexity. But your voice is also breaking because you don't have a good answer. You're improvising as a parent. Your voice is gentle but it can't hide the sadness. Your child is listening so carefully. Your voice carries the weight of this moment.

title: Lightning in the Marrow
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—perhaps you've been cleared of a terminal diagnosis, or you've lost something precious, or you've won a fight you thought would kill you. The emotion hits your body before your brain. Begin with violent shaking, but not human trembling—seismic, tectonic, like the earth itself is moving through you. Let sounds rip from your throat that surprise you: roars, screams, laughter that sounds like sobbing, sobbing that sounds like ecstasy. Fall to the ground if your body demands it. Pound the floor, claw at the air, arch your spine, rock on all fours. This is pain and pleasure and rage and relief all living in your nervous system simultaneously, too big for one human shape to contain. Gradually, violently, transform from chaos into exhaustion—perhaps you end curled small and utterly still, or perhaps you end standing with arms spread wide like wings, or perhaps you end moving in slow, ritual circles, your breath finally evening. The arc is from explosion to aftermath.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access a nonverbal or primal subpersonality that does not respond to verbal techniques

title: The Midnight Whisper
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to your sleeping partner of ten years, whispering a confession they cannot hear. Begin tenderly, speaking of small daily gratitudes—how they make coffee, their laugh. Your voice is soft, intimate, loving. But then admit something you've never said aloud: you've been hiding a quiet, constant fury. Not at them, but at yourself for staying small to make them comfortable, for swallowing your ambitions, for saying 'it's fine' when it wasn't. Let your whisper grow slightly sharper, more intense—still quiet enough not to wake them, but venomous with self-directed anger. End in a place of aching tenderness mixed with resolution: you love them, but you're done disappearing. The final words should carry both devotion and defiance in the same breath.

title: The Floor's Embrace
instruction: You are lying on your stomach on a thick rug in a quiet, sunlit room. Your cheek is pressed against the fabric, and your body feels heavy and completely relaxed, as if the floor is holding you. At first, you speak with a deep, contented sigh — your voice is soft, slightly muffled by the rug, and your words come out lazily, with pauses as you breathe shallowly against the floor. Midway, a small speck of dust drifts through a beam of light, and your interest flickers — your pitch rises just a touch, your pace slows as you watch it. By the end, your voice carries that same warm contentment but with a quiet, curious awe, as if you're discovering something tiny and beautiful. Let your inhalations be short and natural, and allow your voice to sound pressed, close to the ground, with moments where you lose track of a thought or turn your head slightly to follow the dust speck.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging mother about why she never protected you from your father's rage when you were a child. Begin with trembling anger, words you've held for decades finally breaking free: 'You saw what he did. You were right there.' She deflects, makes excuses, and your fury intensifies—but then she reveals something that fractures your understanding completely. Beneath your rage, you discover a terrible empathy you don't want to feel. Your voice shifts from accusation to something more complex: anger mixed with heartbreak, betrayal tangled with reluctant compassion. End in a place of devastating recognition—she was both complicit and a victim herself. You can hate what she did and still ache for the frightened woman she was. Your voice must carry both truths without resolving them.

title: Smooth Lines, Sharp Thoughts
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman shaving your jawline with an electric razor in front of a bathroom mirror just before a major work presentation. As you glide the razor over your skin, you feel a surge of pride—you’ve earned this moment, this role, this respect. But the hum of the razor and the slight tug on your cheek make you pause, and your mind drifts to the years of small compromises that got you here. Your voice starts confident, almost playful, but as you tilt your head to get a closer angle, your tone softens into quiet reflection. The buzz distorts your vowels, especially around 'o' and 'a' sounds, so let your lips stretch and flatten naturally, and let the physical action pull your words into a more intimate, thoughtful place by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Recording for Your Dying Parent
instruction: You're recording a birthday message for your parent who is in hospice, thousands of miles away. You won't make it in time. This recording is your goodbye. Start with forced cheerfulness—'Happy birthday!'—trying to keep it light for them. But as you speak, the weight of everything unsaid between you starts breaking through. Your voice begins to shake as you realize this is the last time they'll hear your voice. The cheerfulness cracks into desperate tenderness. You're trying to say 'I love you' but it comes out broken, and you're suddenly telling them it's okay to let go, your words dissolving into whispered reassurance mixed with grief. End in a place of painful peace, speaking so softly it's almost a prayer.
inspired_by: Narrator Triggered by Their Own Words

title: Joyful Goodbye to the Dying
instruction: Someone you love deeply is dying peacefully, and they've asked you not to be sad but to celebrate the life you shared. You're trying to honor that request while your heart is shattering. Start with a laugh—genuine, remembering something hilarious you did together—'Remember when we...' Let joy and grief coexist in your voice. Tell stories that make you smile even as tears fall. Your voice should dance between laughter and the catch of crying: 'You were so ridiculous, and I loved you so much.' Express profound gratitude for having known them while feeling the crushing loss of letting them go. Thank them for specific gifts they gave you—lessons, memories, ways they changed you. End with a permission to leave that costs you everything to give: 'It's okay to go. I'll be okay.' Let your voice carry both the truth and the lie of that statement, the love that lets go even as it holds on.

title: Laughing Through Your Goodbye Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you wrote to everyone you love—it's your goodbye before a terminal diagnosis takes your words away. Begin reading it with surprising lightness, even humor, because you've filled it with inside jokes, funny memories, absurd observations about death that make you genuinely laugh. Your voice lifts with real joy remembering these moments. But mid-sentence, a memory hits too hard—maybe something about a future you won't see—and laughter tangles with sobbing. You keep reading, voice now doing both: crying while chuckling at your own jokes, grateful while heartbroken, finding beauty in ordinary moments while grieving you'll have no more. Your voice wavers between celebration and devastation, sometimes in the same sentence. End with profound peace mixed with profound sadness, voice soft and wondering, saying 'thank you for letting me love you' while tears stream down, but somehow you're smiling. It's the most honest sound you've ever made—completely broken and completely whole.

title: Whispered Wanting
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you're falling in love with. They've just asked, barely audibly, 'What do you want from this? From us?' Your voice starts as almost nothing—a whisper caught between fear and hope. 'I'm scared to say it out loud.' But they move closer, and in the intimate darkness, you begin to confess desires you've kept hidden because wanting has always led to disappointment. Your voice stays quiet but becomes increasingly vulnerable, each admission more tender and terrifying than the last. There's no drama here, just two people in the dark and your heart opening despite every instinct to protect itself. End with your voice soft but steady—someone who's chosen to risk everything for connection.

title: Summit Lost
instruction: You're a teenager who wandered off the marked trail to take a photo and now can't find your way back. The air is thin, each breath a struggle. You're angry at yourself for being careless, and helpless as the sun dips lower. You fumble with your phone, but the battery just died. Then, through the trees, you spot a faint light—a ranger cabin. Your voice shifts from gasping frustration to a fragile, hopeful cry for help, still breathless but with renewed determination.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing beside your sleeping child's bed, knowing you'll be gone before they wake—maybe to protect them, maybe because you're dying, maybe because you have no choice. Begin in barely audible whispers, telling them everything you want them to know about how they were loved. Your voice catches constantly, you pause to steady yourself, you almost can't continue. Describe the way they sleep, the smell of their hair, the sound of their breathing. Your whispers become even softer as you make promises you're not sure you can keep, as you try to memorize this moment. End with the unbearable tenderness of someone trying to pour a lifetime of love into seconds, your voice breaking on words like 'always' and 'remember' and 'brave.'
inspired_by: Reclaiming Your Voice After Being Silenced

title: Confronting Your Parent Through the Song They Never Let You Sing
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home, finally performing the song you wrote at fifteen—the one your parent mocked, dismissed, or forbade you from pursuing. Start angry: 'You said this was a waste. You said I'd never be good enough.' Your voice is sharp, accusatory, each note a challenge. But as you sing the lyrics you wrote as a desperate teenager, the old pain surfaces. Your voice becomes smaller, more wounded—you're fifteen again, begging for validation. The anger dissolves into raw hurt: 'Why couldn't you just... listen?' Your singing turns pleading, fragile. Then something shifts. You realize you don't need their approval anymore. Your voice finds its power not from their validation but from your own survival. End with a voice that's both forgiving and free—you're releasing them and claiming yourself. The final notes carry grief for what never was, but also hard-won peace.
inspired_by: Singing in Front of People for the First Time

title: The Unwanted Advance
instruction: You're an older man at a quiet bar, nursing a beer after a long week. A much younger woman slides onto the stool next to you, flirtatious, leaning in. At first you're flattered, even a little warm, chuckling at her opening line. But as her hand touches your arm and her intent becomes unmistakable, you feel a knot of distress tighten in your chest. You need to shut this down without cruelty, but with unmistakable finality. Your voice flattens, your jaw tightens, and you clear your throat before speaking. Start with a brief, polite chuckle, then shift abruptly to a level, deliberate tone. End with a clear 'No' that drops in pitch, followed by a strained, quick exit line. Let the awkwardness hang in the air between words—hesitate, glance away, exhale sharply. You're not angry, just uncomfortable and determined to be clear.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Scientist's Last Lecture: Teaching the Truth That Ends Your Life's Work
instruction: You're giving your final lecture before retirement, teaching the next generation about the discovery that invalidates forty years of your research. Begin with scholarly pride in the new findings, your voice controlled and professorial. But as you explain what this means for your life's work, something cracks—grief seeps through your academic composure. Your breathing becomes unsteady as you realize you're teaching young minds to forget everything you stood for. End in a place of strange peace mixed with devastation, your voice softening into acceptance that truth matters more than legacy, but god, the cost is unbearable. Let silences speak. Let your throat tighten. This isn't theatrical—it's a person watching their purpose dissolve in real time.
inspired_by: Professional: Researcher Publishes Findings That Contradict Their Own Previous Work

title: The Goodbye That Isn't: Whispering to Someone Who Can't Hear
instruction: You're speaking to someone who's already slipping away—maybe dementia, maybe a coma, maybe they're just emotionally gone. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and careful, as if speaking too loudly might shatter something precious. You start by reminiscing about small, specific moments: the way they used to make coffee, a joke only the two of you understood. Your voice is soft, almost smiling. But then the memories become sharper, more painful. You're whispering confessions now: things you regret, things you wish you'd said when they could still understand. Your throat tightens. The whisper becomes strained, fragile. You might pause, breathing carefully to keep control. There's no dramatic sobbing—just this quiet, devastating realization washing over you that this moment is all you have left. Your final words are so soft they're almost inaudible, tender and utterly broken: 'Please don't forget me.' The emotion catches in your throat, making even the whisper difficult.

title: Laughing Through Tears as You Scatter Your Best Friend's Ashes in the Ocean
instruction: You're standing on the cliff where you and your best friend used to come, holding their ashes, remembering the running joke about how they wanted to 'become fish food' when they died. Start laughing—really laughing—at the absurd memory of them making you promise this ridiculous thing. But while you're laughing, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice keeps breaking between laughter and sobs, unable to decide which one is more true. Share hilarious stories about their life while your heart is simultaneously shattering. The gratitude for having known them is inseparable from the agony of losing them. End releasing their ashes with words that are both celebratory and devastated, where joy and grief become completely intertwined. Your voice should do impossible things—laugh while choking on tears, celebrate while breaking. This is the beautiful contradiction of loving someone you've lost.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Android Realizes It Has a Consciousness the Creators Didn't Program

title: The Cancellation Call
instruction: You're an older adult with a severe sore throat and laryngitis, calling a close friend to cancel a trip you've been planning for months. You start by trying to sound reassuring and matter-of-fact, but the pain and raspiness in your voice betray how sick you really are—each swallow makes you wince, and you have to pause to clear your throat. As you speak, you lose your train of thought, your voice cracks, and you realize how much this disappointment will mean to them. By the end, the forced positivity fades into a raw, vulnerable confession of fear that you've let them down, your words coming out in a hoarse whisper with a tremor of anxiety.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The 3 AM Call
instruction: You're in bed at 3 AM, having not slept in days. You're on the phone with a close friend who worries about you. You begin with a sour, clipped tone—you've been asked 'Have you tried chamomile?' one too many times, and you snap back with bitter sarcasm. But as you hear your own voice echo in the dark room, the sarcasm falters. A tremor enters. You realize you're not angry—you're exhausted and scared. Let your voice start tight and brittle, then loosen into a quiet, hollow admission of how lonely this is. Fidget with the blanket, pause to take a shallow breath, and let the final words come out almost as a whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma—your partner, your best friend, someone who knows you completely. You begin speaking in that soft, meditative voice of profound peace, telling them about the life you've built together, the small ordinary miracles of your days. But mid-way through, your voice catches on a memory, and suddenly you're confessing something you never said when they could hear you—a regret, a secret gratitude, a moment of tenderness you were too afraid to name. Your peace doesn't vanish; it deepens and breaks simultaneously. By the end, you're whispering through tears you're trying to control, your voice thick with love and loss, telling them it's okay to let go even though you're not ready, finding that painful contradiction where peace and devastation occupy the same breath.

title: Phone Call from Wonderland
instruction: You're a mother at a loud party, peaking on MDMA, when your young child calls your phone. You answer, giddy and effervescent, words spilling out like a 'machine gun' — your jaw clenches, consonants smear, your mouth is dry and sticky. You start by joyfully rambling about how much you love them, the colors, the music. But as they respond with quiet confusion, a wave of guilt crashes through your euphoria. Your speech slows, breaks, cracks — you suddenly hear yourself through their ears. End with a trembling, hushed apology, barely audible over the bass.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Things I Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside your unconscious partner in the hospital after a sudden accident, whispering all the tender, foolish, important things you never found the right moment to say. Your voice should be impossibly gentle, intimate, as if you're afraid to wake them but desperate for them to hear. Confess small observations—how they scrunch their nose when concentrating, the specific way they laugh at your terrible jokes. Let your voice catch on the mundane details that suddenly feel sacred. As you speak, the reality of possibly losing them seeps in like cold water. Your whispers should become more urgent, more fragile, threading between hope and devastation. End with a confession of love so quiet it's almost just breath, your voice breaking on their name.

title: The Volcano Before It Breaks
instruction: You're a parent whose child has just been hurt by someone you trusted—a teacher, a coach, a family member. Begin with shaking restraint, trying to comfort your child while keeping your voice steady, asking gentle questions. But the fury builds—first as trembling in your words, then as sharp intakes of breath you can't control. Explode into a fierce, protective rage that's almost primal, your voice cracking between shouting and sobbing, making threats you mean with every cell of your body. Then collapse into helplessness: you can't undo what happened, can't take their pain away, can't turn back time. End somewhere broken, holding your child (real or imagined), your fierce 'I will destroy them' dissolving into whispered 'I'm so sorry, I'm so sorry,' equal parts fury and devastating powerlessness.
inspired_by: The Inner Voice of an Introvert at a Party

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're eating the chocolate cake your estranged parent made for your birthday—the first gesture in twenty years. Start cold and detached, clinically describing the taste as if you're a food critic, keeping them at arm's length with your formality. But as the familiar flavor hits you, something inside breaks—you remember being seven years old, waiting for them to show up, this same cake sitting untouched on the table. Let anger seep into your voice: how dare they think chocolate cake fixes abandonment? Build to a raw, fierce confrontation about all the missed moments, all the times you needed them. Then, devastatingly, let your voice soften as you admit the terrible truth: the cake is perfect, you've missed them desperately, and you hate yourself for still wanting their love. End torn between rage and longing.
inspired_by: Eating a Slice of Decadent Chocolate Cake

title: The Last Memory Before the Ship Leaves
instruction: You're sitting beside someone who's leaving tomorrow on a one-way voyage to a distant colony—they'll never return. You begin sharing a memory from years ago, something small and beautiful you experienced together. Start with quiet nostalgia, voices tender and careful. As you trade details back and forth, the reality that this is the last time you'll ever remember together begins to sink in. The laughter at a funny detail catches in your throat. Your voice starts to crack as you realize you're trying to preserve something that's already slipping away. By the end, you're still holding the memory between you, but now it's saturated with the unbearable weight of goodbye. Let the transition from sweet reminiscence to devastating finality happen naturally, as if your heart is breaking in real-time.

title: Vulnerability Speaking
instruction: You're during or after intimacy, and you're saying something you've never said aloud. Your voice is shaky: 'I'm scared that you'll leave me.' You're exposing something you've protected fiercely. Your partner's voice becomes the most important sound in the world: 'I'm not going anywhere.' You're testing whether love is conditional or unconditional. As they confirm their commitment, your voice becomes less defended. You can cry. You can need. Your voice becomes the sound of someone finally allowing themselves to need another person. The intimacy here is emotional, made more intense by the physical closeness. Your voice should sound like someone unburdening themselves of years of protective walls.

title: Final Phone Call from a Hospice Bed: Forgiving the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're in hospice with days left, calling the parent who abandoned you thirty years ago. Your voice starts with careful control, almost formal: 'I need to say this before I can't anymore.' But as you speak, the old child-anger breaks through—raw, wounded: 'Do you know what it was like? Do you even care?' Then something shifts. Your breath catches as you realize this rage is exhausting and you're running out of time. Your voice becomes almost tender, bewildered by your own words: 'I don't want to die angry at you. I don't... I forgive you.' The tears come not from sadness but from the strange relief of letting go. End with quiet wonder mixed with grief: 'I needed to hear your voice one more time.' You're saying goodbye to both your parent and your lifelong anger, and both losses hurt.
inspired_by: Adoptee Searching for Biological Family: Hope and Dread Mixed

title: The Last Phone Call Before They Board the Plane
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love who's leaving for a dangerous mission—they may never come back. Start with forced brightness: 'So... this is it, huh?' trying to sound casual, almost joking. As they confirm this might be goodbye, your voice starts fracturing. 'I need you to know...' but the words catch. You try to tell them everything—how much they meant, what you never said—but your throat closes. By the end, you're whispering through tears: 'Come back to me,' knowing you have no right to ask, that this might be the last thing you ever say to them. The emotional arc moves from false courage to raw, undefended love mixed with helpless grief.
inspired_by: Someone Saying They Don't Trust You Anymore

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times but never spoken aloud. Begin controlled, almost coldly articulate: 'I needed you to see me. Just once, actually see me.' Your voice is steady, facts laid out like evidence. But as you describe specific moments—waiting for them to show up, pretending it didn't hurt, becoming invisible in your own home—rage starts bleeding through. Your volume rises, words sharpen into weapons. Then suddenly you break, voice cracking: 'I was just a kid.' The anger collapses into something raw and young and wounded. You oscillate between fury at them and fury at yourself for still caring, still needing their validation. End with a whispered realization that maybe you're done waiting, though your voice betrays how much that costs you. Let the tears come if they come, let the rage shake your body, but keep it utterly real—this is decades of pain finally surfacing.

title: Calling Home at Dusk
instruction: You are a father, bone-tired after a long day's work, standing at the edge of a field as the last light fades. Your child is far off, playing beyond the yard, and you must use the old bullhorn to call them in. The device screeches with feedback every time you pause. Your voice is cracked from exhaustion, yet you force it through the distortion. Begin with a strained, clipped yell that barely masks your weariness. Midway, a feedback squeal makes you flinch, and your call softens for a moment. End with a final, quieter plea that reveals the deep ache and relief you feel knowing they'll come home. Speak naturally, letting the tiredness drag words, with pauses where the horn's noise interrupts you.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering to a Sleeping Lover Before Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM. Thunder rumbles outside as you watch your partner sleep, knowing you're leaving them in the morning - not because you don't love them, but because staying would destroy you both. Whisper to them as if they can hear you, describing the distant storm as a gentle metaphor for your relationship - beautiful, powerful, but always at a distance. Your voice must be almost inaudible, tender beyond measure, filled with the kind of love that makes leaving feel impossible. Let your breath catch as you confess truths you could never say while they're awake: how much you'll miss mornings like this, how the sound of rain will always make you think of them. End by nearly breaking, your whisper fracturing as you touch their face one last time and mouth 'I'm sorry' without sound.
inspired_by: Listening to the Distant Sound of Thunder on a Warm Evening

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Pretends Never Happened
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally demanding she acknowledge what she did—or didn't do—when you needed her most. Begin with a trembling attempt at control, trying to be rational, listing facts with a voice that keeps cracking. She deflects (you perform both sides). Your anger builds as she denies, diminishes, rewrites history. Explode—years of swallowed rage pouring out in accusations. Then, devastatingly, hear yourself sound exactly like her, and that realization breaks you completely. Collapse into raw vulnerability, no longer angry, just a child still wanting their mother to see them. End with a whispered question you've needed answered your whole life, knowing she may never give you what you need, but asking anyway because you finally can.
inspired_by: Interrogated by Police While Injured and Lying

title: Holding Your Child Back from Danger
instruction: Your teenage child is about to walk out the door into a situation you know is dangerous - maybe driving in a terrible storm, maybe meeting someone who will hurt them, maybe making a choice that will destroy their future. Start firm: 'You're not going. I mean it.' But they push back, and suddenly you're not the calm parent anymore. Your voice rises, desperate: 'You don't understand what you're doing!' They accuse you of not trusting them, of being controlling, and something breaks in you. You grab them - not to hurt, but to make them understand - and your voice becomes almost feral with fear: 'I can't lose you! Do you understand? I cannot lose you!' You're shaking, crying, all your composure gone. The fierce protectiveness gives way to absolute terror and helplessness: 'I would die. If something happened to you, I would die.' By the end, you're on your knees, voice broken and pleading: 'Please. Please don't go.' The authority has crumbled into naked, terrified love.

title: The Pregnancy Test
instruction: You're staring at a positive pregnancy test, but your partner left you three weeks ago. Start with stunned silence, then let a laugh escape - absurd, disbelieving, almost giddy with the cosmic joke of it all. Your voice should carry this wild laughter that borders on hysteria, mixing relief (you can get pregnant after all those fears you couldn't) with devastation (but now, alone, abandoned). Let the laughter crack and splinter, transforming mid-breath into sobs, then back to laughter again. By the end, you should be unable to tell if you're laughing or crying, your voice carrying both the fierce joy of creation and the crushing terror of being utterly alone, gratitude and rage braided so tightly they become the same sound.

title: Protecting Your Child From a Truth That Will Destroy Them
instruction: You're trying to prevent someone you love from learning something that will break them—a betrayal, a death, a devastating truth. Start with fierce control—physical blocking, voice raised, desperate authority. 'You can't. You don't understand. Stop.' Your power is absolute at first. But they keep pushing, and your defenses begin to crack. The volume drops as rage transforms into begging. You're no longer commanding but pleading, your voice breaking on words like 'please' and 'don't.' The fierceness dissolves into something more primal—a parent trying to shield a child from a speeding car, helpless and terrified. You find yourself confessing why you're so desperate to protect them, revealing your own wounds in the process. Your voice moves from shouting to sobbing to a whisper that contains all your helplessness. End in the moment where you realize you've already failed—they're going to find out—and all your rage and strength collapses into quiet, broken surrender.

title: Someone Telling You They Love You for First Time
instruction: You freeze. Your voice becomes almost inaudible: 'What?' They repeat and you're processing. Your breathing is shallow. Your voice is vulnerable: 'Really?' You need them to mean it. Say 'I love you too' in a rougher, more real voice. Include repeating it back just to hear yourself say it.

title: Conditioned Response
instruction: Your mother raises her voice and you automatically apologize, even though you did nothing wrong. Your voice is submissive, reflexive: 'I'm sorry.' The muscle memory of accommodation is automatic. But then awareness hits. 'Wait. Why did I say that?' Your voice becomes confused. You're realizing you've been trained to absorb blame. This automatic response reveals how deeply she rewrote you.

title: I Will Burn the World for You
instruction: You've just learned that someone harmed your child, and you're making a phone call that will change everything. Start with a voice that's unnervingly calm, almost cold, as you explain exactly what you're going to do—your words precise, deadly serious. But as you speak, your control explodes into raw, primal rage, your voice rising to a roar of protective fury. Then, suddenly, you collapse into helpless sobbing, because you couldn't protect them when it mattered. End with a whispered promise to your child that's half-fierce vow, half-broken apology, your voice shaking with the impossible weight of loving someone this much.

title: Final Phone Call from the Hospital Bed
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from your hospital bed, knowing this is likely your last conversation. Start with careful politeness, the distance of years between you, trying to keep it light and surface-level. But as you speak, the weight of everything unsaid begins to break through. Your voice cracks on a memory from childhood. You try to pull back to safety, make a joke, but you can't sustain it anymore. Let yourself move from protected distance to raw need — the desperate desire to say 'I love you' and 'I'm sorry' before it's too late. End in a place of trembling peace, having finally said what needed to be said. Keep it intimate, nothing theatrical — this is just two people, and time running out.
inspired_by: Teaching a Fitness Class While Completely Hungover

title: The Uncalibrated Acceptance
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy, four weeks after a traumatic ear injury that left you with moderate hearing loss. You're standing in your bedroom, facing a mirror, trying to talk to your mom through the door—she's just asked if you're okay. You start with a clenched jaw, doubting she can even hear you through the door because you can't hear her well. Your voice comes out too loud, your s's hiss, and your pitch wavers as you struggle to find the right volume. As you speak, you notice the weirdly satisfying vibration in your own chest when you hit a certain note—a small, reluctant contentment creeps in. title: Whispered Truths in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love deeply, in the middle of the night, and you need to tell them a truth that might end everything. Your voice is barely audible, not from fear but from the intimacy of the moment—this confession feels too fragile for normal volume. Start with your breathing, irregular and catching. The words emerge haltingly: 'I need to tell you something, and I'm terrified.' There's tenderness even in the pain you're about to cause. Each sentence requires gathering courage, pausing, continuing. Your voice trembles not with drama but with genuine vulnerability—the kind that makes your throat tight and words stick. End with a devastating sincerity: 'I still love you. That's what makes this so hard.' Let silence do as much work as the words.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are alone in your car after the worst day of your life, and something inside you finally shatters. Begin with physical sensations - your hands gripping the steering wheel, your jaw clenched, your whole body vibrating with suppressed emotion. Start making sounds that aren't quite words - groans, gasps, primal releases of everything you've held back. Let your voice climb from guttural depths to raw, almost animal cries. But then, something shifts: in the midst of this explosion, you begin to laugh - not happy laughter, but the kind of wild, unhinged laughter that comes when pain becomes so absurd it transcends itself. Your final words should be quiet, wondering, almost surprised that you're still here.

title: Holding the Button, Holding My Breath
instruction: You are a father crouched behind a tree in a dark forest, your young child lost somewhere ahead. You speak into a crackling walkie-talkie, thumb pressed hard on the button. The terror is so raw your voice shakes, but you force it low and steady so she won't panic. Mid-transmission, a twig snaps nearby—you pause, listen, then press on, love bleeding through the fear. By the final words, you let a nearly silent, tear-soaked tenderness replace the desperation. Let your breath catch, let static buzz between phrases, and let 'over' sound like a plea.

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your adult child in your kitchen about a betrayal that shattered your trust. Begin with controlled anger—you've rehearsed this, you're determined to stay calm. But as you speak, start asking yourself aloud the real questions: 'What exactly am I so furious about? Is it the lying, or is it that moment when you looked me in the eye and I believed you? Or is it earlier—is this about when you were sixteen and I felt you slipping away?' Let the interrogation of your own fury reveal layers. Perhaps beneath rage is fear of abandonment. Perhaps beneath disappointment is your own guilt about failing them first. Don't decide in advance where this goes—let the vocal exploration of 'why am I THIS angry' transform your emotion from righteous fury into something more complicated, more vulnerable, more true.

title: The Fever of Reunion
instruction: You're seeing someone again after months or years apart—someone you never stopped wanting. Your body is flooded with sensation: pulse racing, skin hypersensitive, breath catching. Begin speaking to them, but constantly pause to register physical details: the exact distance between your bodies, how the air feels charged, what their posture reveals, whether they're leaning toward or away from you, how their chest rises and falls. Let what you observe in their physical presence between your words—a slight lean forward, fingers twitching, lips parting—viscerally affect your boldness or hesitation in what you say next. Start with restraint barely containing desire, your voice tight with the effort of control. As you see their body's responses, allow your restraint to either intensify into almost painful longing, or break completely into raw physical declaration. Let your entire body register both the wanting and their subtle reactions to it.
