title: The Quiet Unburdening
instruction: You're whispering a confession to someone you love deeply—maybe a partner, a best friend, a sibling—in the darkness of a late night. You've been hiding something that's eating you alive, and you begin with halting, careful words, terrified of their reaction. Your voice should be barely audible at times, catching in your throat, trembling with the weight of shame and the desperate need to be known fully. As you speak, move from fearful confession into tender vulnerability, letting tears fall silently as you reveal your deepest fragility. End with a whispered plea for them to still love you, your voice so soft it's almost breath, but filled with every ounce of naked hope and terror.

title: Emergency Room Ultimatum
instruction: You're a parent who just found out your teenager attempted suicide, and you're confronting them in the hospital with a ferocity born of terror. Start explosive, your voice shaking with rage and fear: 'How DARE you try to leave me like that! How dare you!' Let your anger be huge, uncontrolled, even unfair—because underneath it's pure panic. But mid-tirade, you break completely. Your voice shatters as the rage transforms into something more primal: the helplessness of a parent who can't protect their child from their own pain. Fall to your knees emotionally, your fierce protectiveness collapsing into desperate vulnerability: 'Please... please don't leave me. I can't survive losing you.' End in a place where your strength and your absolute powerlessness are both fully present, where love manifests as both fury and the most tender begging.

title: Getting Caught in a Lie
instruction: Someone has caught you in a lie. Your voice was confident, now it's faltering: 'I... well...' You're trying to come up with an explanation. Your voice becomes defensive: 'It's not what you think.' But it is. Your voice becomes smaller, admitting: 'Okay, yeah, I lied.' The shame is overwhelming. Your voice becomes quiet, desperate: 'I'm sorry. I don't know why I lied.' By the end, you're unsure if they'll ever trust you again.

title: The Words I Should Have Said Before You Left
instruction: You're alone, speaking to someone who's gone - whether they died, left, or simply slipped away before you found the courage. You're finally saying everything you were too afraid to say when they were here. Begin in a whisper, tentative and ashamed: 'I don't know if you can hear this, but...' Your voice should be barely audible, catching on every other word. There's so much tenderness mixed with regret. Gradually let yourself actually feel the things you're confessing - maybe you loved them, maybe you needed them, maybe you're sorry for ways you hurt them. Your voice should crack not from volume but from the weight of finally being honest. End in the quietest devastation: the realization that this vulnerability, this truth, this openness - it came too late. Let silence hold the final moment, your breathing the only sound.
inspired_by: Pretending to Understand Something Thats Confusing

title: Confronting the Love of Your Life Who Chose Someone Else
instruction: You've cornered them at a wedding—their wedding—and you're finally unleashing years of what-ifs. Start with bitter congratulations that curdle into accusations: you know they loved you, so why weren't you enough? Your voice rises with fierce, possessive rage—you would have burned the world down for them. But mid-sentence, you hear how desperate you sound, how pathetic. The fury collapses into something raw and exposed. Your voice drops to almost nothing as you admit the truth: you're terrified you'll never feel this way about anyone else. End with your hands shaking, asking them just to tell you that you mattered, that you weren't crazy for believing. Let your breath come ragged, uncontrolled.
inspired_by: Lawyer Wins Case Against Former Mentor Who Destroyed Her

title: Reading Your Child's Suicide Note—Finding Their Hidden Joy Within It
instruction: You've found your child's goodbye letter. As you read it aloud to yourself, you expect only devastation. And it's there—the grief threatens to stop your breath. But threaded through their words, you discover something unexpected: they felt free in their final days, made peace with themselves, experienced genuine happiness you never knew they'd found. Your voice breaks with sobs, but then a laugh escapes—confused, almost hysterical—as they describe a perfect moment of joy. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, heartbroken yet somehow grateful they knew peace. The emotions clash violently: unbearable loss mixed with relief that they weren't suffering at the end, devastating grief intertwined with love so huge it feels like it will crack you open. End in a space where opposites coexist—whispering 'thank you' through tears, both destroyed and somehow, impossibly, touched by grace.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Alien First Contact With Translator Who Recognizes It As Their Dead Child

title: Final Words to a Departing Astronaut
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your partner who's leaving on a one-way mission to Mars. You start trying to be strong, supportive, even excited for them—your voice is bright, almost too bright. But as you speak, reality crashes in. Your voice begins to falter. You try to list all the things you'll do while they're gone, but each word becomes harder. By the middle, you're struggling to maintain composure, your breathing uneven. You want to say 'I'm proud of you' but it comes out broken. By the end, you're whispering things you'll never get to share again—small, mundane, precious things. Your final words are barely audible: 'I'll look up every night.' Let your voice reveal what your heart can't contain.

title: Descending Into Darkness
instruction: You're falling into something dark—corruption, madness, evil, your own worst self. Your voice becomes rougher, lower, less human. You're losing your grip on light and goodness, and your voice reflects that dissolution. What starts as dismay becomes almost seductive—the dark is powerful, and it's easier to surrender than fight. Your voice becomes cold. You're trying to justify the fall even as you're happening. Humanity drains from your tone. By the end, you sound like something else entirely. The final words are spoken in a voice so distorted they're barely recognizable as coming from the person who started this descent.

title: The Melt After the Hot Bath
instruction: You are an older man, just out of a long, scalding bath, lying naked on a towel on the bathroom floor. Your muscles have turned to liquid, and your mind is hazy, like you've had two glasses of wine. You're staring at the ceiling fan, which seems to be spinning in slow motion. You start to murmur about a petty argument you had last week with a young co-worker, but your voice is loose, slurred, unhurried. At first you're amused by the memory, chuckling at how ridiculous it all was. But as you keep talking, your amusement fades into a deep, quiet contentment. You realize you don't have to hold onto that anger anymore. Let your voice be warm and thick, with long pauses and the occasional sigh. End with a sense of simple, peaceful surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Light Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood home as it's being demolished tomorrow. This house holds forty years of memories—your first steps, your mother's laughter, your father's workshop, every Christmas morning. Begin by noticing the small details: the chipped paint on the doorframe where you marked your height, the window where you watched for your first love. Let yourself feel the weight of what's ending. But as you speak your goodbye, allow a shift—remember that you're carrying all these memories forward, that nothing truly dies while you remember it. Your voice should journey from heavy with grief to quietly fierce with gratitude and determination. Don't perform sadness or strength—let your body tell you what it genuinely feels as you touch the walls one final time, as you recall specific moments, as you realize you're not losing a place but honoring what it gave you.

title: Salt Water and Skin
instruction: You have just received news that your sister survived a car accident you thought had killed her. You're running to her hospital room, heart pounding, body electric with terror and hope and adrenaline. When you burst through the door and see her alive, let the physical sensation overwhelm you—knees buckling, hands shaking, unable to breathe. Touch her face, her arms, checking that she's real while sobbing or laughing or both. Let relief flood your body like a drug, making you dizzy, making you collapse beside her bed. Your voice should shake with the physical intensity of almost-loss, moving from panic to hysterical relief to exhausted, bone-deep gratitude. Let your body tell the story as much as your words.

title: The Unforgivable Thing
instruction: You're screaming at someone you love—your partner, your child, your closest friend—because they've done something that endangered themselves and you cannot, will not lose them. Start with volcanic rage, voice shaking with fury, words brutal and unfiltered. But mid-explosion, you hear yourself, hear how terrified you actually are, and the anger fractures. Your voice breaks, the volume drops, and suddenly you're sobbing while still trying to yell, words dissolving into incoherent sounds of fear. You're furious at them for making you feel this helpless, desperate to protect them, and absolutely falling apart. End on your knees emotionally, voice raw and small, admitting 'I can't lose you' like a confession of weakness.

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's asleep, breathing shallowly. You've brought an old photograph of the two of you from when you were seven years old. Begin by studying every detail in that photo—her young face, the clothes, the background, let each element unlock specific memories. Start with quiet fondness, allowing yourself to smile at forgotten moments. As you look from the photo to her aged face now, let the weight of all the years between then and now wash over you. Speak to her softly, telling her what she meant to you, moving from gentle nostalgia to the urgent need to say everything before it's too late. By the end, you should arrive at a place of devastating acceptance, your voice barely a whisper, knowing these are your final words to her.

title: Doing Stand-Up Comedy in the Style of a Eulogy
instruction: Deliver a comedy set structured as a funeral service. 'Dearly beloved, we are gathered here to lay to rest my career in accounting.' Include 'pallbearers' (your coworkers), a 'hymn' (humming the hold music), and a 'burial' (feeding the shredder). The commitment to the dead-serious delivery makes the absurdity land harder.

title: Frozen Wait
instruction: You're an older adult standing outside in sub-zero cold, waiting for someone you've secretly admired for a long time. Your face is numb, jaw tight, every word feels like chipping ice from your lips. At first, you mutter to yourself about the ridiculous cold, the ache in your bones. But then they arrive, and your voice softens, thaws just a little. Words come slower, warmer, as the infatuation you usually hide seeps through the cracks. Let the cold shift from bitter to something almost sweet as you speak to them, your breath visible, your body shivering but your heart briefly forgetting the freeze.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner who you think is asleep. Your breathing might change, your throat might tighten, you might need long pauses. If your partner shifts or responds (imagine it), let that completely change your emotional landscape—terror, relief, deeper vulnerability. Allow your body to curl smaller or unfold. This isn't a dramatic confession; it's fragile, tentative, like exposing a wound. By the end, you've crossed a threshold you can never uncross.

title: Avalanche Engulfment
instruction: An avalanche hits you. Your voice is immediately cut off, muffled by snow. Desperate, muted screams. You're being tumbled, disoriented. You're trying to create an air pocket, your voice becoming small, desperate, then oddly calm as you accept your fate. Breathing becomes your only focus. Include the strange peace of surrender mixed with terror.

title: The Moment Everything Changed
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a phone call, a diagnosis, a betrayal you've discovered. Your body is flooded with adrenaline, your heart racing, your hands shaking. As the scene progresses, let the physical panic intensify—hyperventilation, trembling, feeling like the walls are closing in. This is visceral terror mixed with grief, your body rebelling against what your mind is trying to process. Then, suddenly, let everything shift to an eerie, frightening stillness—the moment after the storm when you realize nothing will ever be the same. title: Dancing at the Funeral
instruction: You're at the gathering after someone's funeral, and their favorite song comes on—the one they always danced to. title: The Weight of Years
instruction: You are an elderly man, exhausted from a long bus ride, standing on your daughter’s porch after years of silence. Your voice drops lower, pauses more, as you finally say what you came to say: an apology that cracks with exhaustion and shifts into raw remorse. title: Giggling in the Getaway
instruction: You're a teenage girl sprinting through a backyard after being caught trying to sneak a look at your crush's phone. title: The Last Fling at the Fountain
instruction: You are at a crowded party, a little tipsy from cheap wine, when you stumble (literally) into someone you've been secretly crushing on for months. You swallow, blink hard, and force a little smile, but your pitch drops as irritation at the unfairness seeps in. Now you are both impatient with yourself for feeling this way and angry at the timing. The last line comes out flat, tired, with a small, pained laugh that isn't really a laugh at all.

title: Cataloging Joy in the Wreckage
instruction: You're sorting through your late partner's chaotic book collection—they were whimsical, disorganized, drove you crazy for twenty years. title: The Thread and the Ache
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with chronic back pain, sitting at a cluttered desk trying to thread a needle. title: The Breaking Point

title: Laughing Through Tears at the Cruelty of Perfect Timing
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone at an airport, train station, or hospital. They're leaving—emigrating, entering treatment, going somewhere you can't follow. Let the laughter and crying mix, your voice breaking between chuckles and sobs. Express gratitude that sounds like grief: 'Thank you for being exactly what I needed, exactly when I can't have you.' title: Adult Child Finally Confronting Silent Parent at Kitchen Table

title: Interviewer Interviewed

title: Explosive Reckoning: Protective Fury Collapsing Into Helpless Desperation
instruction: Someone has hurt the person you love most in this world—your child, your partner, someone under your protection. Start with volcanic rage. Your voice breaks, shifts from threats to pleading—with them, with the universe, with yourself. Let the rage dissolve into gasping sobs. You would destroy the world for them, but you can't undo what's already happened. Your breathing becomes ragged, panicked. End in a collapse of all that fierce energy into quiet, devastated helplessness. Your final words are whispered promises you're not sure you can keep, your voice raw and broken.

title: The Wedding Song at the Funeral
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, but you've just received news that someone you loved has died. Start from a place of trying to maintain composure, to smile through it, to be present for your friend. But the music won't let you hide—its joy is relentless, and it makes your grief more acute, more impossible to contain. Yet simultaneously, the music is actually beautiful, and part of you wants to surrender to it, to let it lift you, to honor life even in the face of death. Let yourself be torn between genuine happiness for your friend and devastating loss. The same song that's breaking your heart is also insisting that life continues, that joy exists, that celebration and mourning can somehow occupy the same moment. By the end, let the music reconcile these contradictions in your body—you're weeping and laughing, dancing and grieving, completely broken and somehow whole.

title: Police Officer Pulls Over Her Son Driving Drunk
instruction: Traffic stop. Officer voice: professional, cautious. You approach the vehicle and see the driver. Your son. Your official tone is the only thing keeping you from shattering. Each step of the procedure is autopilot, your voice professional while everything internal is screaming. title: The Kitten in the Lab Coat
instruction: You're a young robotics assistant who has caught your brilliant but impulsive mentor dismantling a priceless antique automaton for parts, yet again. You start with a slow, low-pitched scolding — the classic teacher's tone — every word heavy and distinct, but you're fighting a smile because you're genuinely in awe of their chaotic genius and amused by the way they're now trying to hide a squeaking gear behind their back. As you speak, let your voice waver: a sigh of affection escapes, then you lose your train of thought when a tiny spring pings off their sleeve, and you have to pause to suppress a laugh. By the end, the discipline softens into a fond, exasperated surrender, your tone rising slightly as you give up the pretense of anger.

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's hospital bedside in her final hours. Begin feeling the defensive anger you've held for years about how she never seemed to understand you, how every conversation felt like judgment. As you look at this photograph and at her frail hands, let that anger slowly dissolve into the devastating recognition that she loved you in the only way she knew how—imperfectly, but completely. title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're standing at your mother's funeral, about to give a eulogy, but instead of the sanitized speech everyone expects, you're going to tell the truth—that she was cruel, that she damaged you, but that you've somehow found gratitude for the strength that surviving her gave you. Start with your voice attempting the conventional tribute: 'My mother was a complex woman...' But then you pause, and something shifts. A small, almost inappropriate laugh escapes: 'That's what we say, isn't it? Complex. Difficult.' Your voice becomes stronger, more honest, tears starting but you're also almost smiling: 'She was mean. She was cold. She withheld love like a weapon.' People are gasping but you continue, voice cracking with painful liberation: 'And somehow, somehow I'm standing here grateful. Not for what she gave me, but for what I had to become to survive her.' The tears are flowing now, but there's also strange peace in your voice, even joy: 'I learned to love myself because she wouldn't. I learned to be gentle because she wasn't.' End with your voice full of contradictory emotions—grief and relief, anger and forgiveness, pain and unexpected freedom: 'So thank you, Mom. And goodbye. I'm finally, finally free.' Let the laughter and tears be indistinguishable.

title: 3 AM Truths
instruction: You are lying in bed in the dark, whispering to your partner who you believe is asleep. Begin by confessing something small—a minor deception, a petty jealousy. Let the safety of darkness and their supposed sleep embolden you. Gradually reveal something deeper, something you've never said aloud—a fear about yourself, a moment of profound shame, a truth about your love for them that terrifies you. Midway through, realize they're awake and listening. Let this realization transform your whispered confession from a solitary unburdening into an act of terrifying intimacy. End not with resolution but with the vulnerability of having been truly seen. Keep your voice barely above a whisper throughout, but let it carry the weight of years.
inspired_by: Actor's choice repertoire feels limited; they use the same choices repeatedly

title: Shielding the Child from the Monster
instruction: You're standing between your child and an advancing threat, and you know you can't stop what's coming. Start with fierce, protective rage—a voice like a weapon: 'You will not touch them. You will have to go through me first.' Let your whole body vibrate with the intensity, but underneath it, terror is rising. As the threat comes closer, your ferocity cracks: 'Please. Please, not them. Take me, hurt me, but leave them alone.' Your voice breaks from command to desperate pleading, oscillating between wild aggression and helpless begging: 'I will do anything. ANYTHING.' The rage returns in waves—'I swear I will haunt you, I will make you pay'—but collapses into sobbing prayers: 'God, please, they're just a baby, they're just my baby.' In the final moments, your voice transforms into something transcendent—turning to your child with sudden, supernatural calm: 'Close your eyes, sweetheart. Listen to my voice. You're safe. You're so loved. No matter what happens, you are so, so loved.' End with a lullaby whispered through tears, tender and fierce and utterly broken.

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your adult child/parent in the kitchen where you raised them/were raised. Start calmly, trying to discuss a long-buried betrayal—an affair, an abortion, a sibling's secret, a lie that shaped the family. But as you speak, let your body lead you to unexpected places: maybe you find yourself sitting on the floor like a child, maybe pacing wildly, maybe laughing inappropriately. Don't censor strange impulses—if you want to open the refrigerator mid-argument or pour yourself cereal or hide under the table, follow it. Let the confrontation twist and turn through anger, mockery, grief, and bizarre humor. End in a place neither of you expected—perhaps mutual bewilderment, perhaps a strange new intimacy, perhaps deeper estrangement.

title: Pretending to Be Confident While Learning a New Skill
instruction: Youre new at something and unsure, but you want to make a good impression. Internally, insecurity nags at you, but you act assured. Describe your selfdoubt while projecting confidence. Speak with a decisive tone, masking your inexperience.

title: Breakthrough in the Rain
instruction: You are standing outside in a sudden rainstorm after walking out of a terrible argument. Begin by experiencing everything through taste and the sensations in your mouth—the metallic tang of rain on your lips, blood from where you bit your cheek during the fight, salt from tears mixing with rainwater. Focus all your attention on these tastes until your mouth becomes hypersensitive, almost electric with sensation. Start in a state of rage, possibly screaming into the rain, your voice raw and unleashed. But as you truly taste the rain, the blood, the tears—as these physical sensations build and build—let yourself shift into an ecstatic, almost euphoric release. You're tasting your own aliveness, your own capacity to feel. By the end, you might be laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice transforming from fury to a kind of fierce, wild joy at simply being able to feel this much.

title: The Last Phone Call from Hospice
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent who has days to live. You answer their bedside phone and hear their weakened voice say your name with such hope it shatters you. You start with cold distance—'I got the message from your nurse'—but as they struggle to apologize for decades of absence, your armor cracks. Their voice is fading: 'I know I don't deserve this, but I needed to hear your voice one more time.' You're fighting between righteous anger and the reality that this is your last chance. Your voice breaks as you move from 'You were never there' to whispering 'I'm here now' through tears. Let yourself travel from protective rage to devastating tenderness, knowing you're giving them permission to let go even as your heart screams that you needed more time to heal together.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about a truth that's lived between you both for years but has never been spoken aloud—a betrayal, an abandonment, a lie, a wound that shaped your whole life. Start with controlled anger, words that you've rehearsed in your mind a thousand times, your voice clipped and precise. But as you speak, let other parts of yourself break through: the hurt child inside you, the part that still desperately wants their approval, the part that understands their failures even as you rage against them. Your voice might crack, surge with unexpected tenderness, then harden again with fury. Let yourself surprise yourself—discover in the moment that alongside your anger lives profound love, or that beneath your accusations lies a plea for them to finally see you. End in a completely different emotional place than you began, transformed by the act of finally speaking what was unspeakable.

title: Breaking Through the Glass Wall
instruction: You are confronting your parent who always taught you to be 'controlled' and 'appropriate.' Begin the scene speaking with rigid posture, tight jaw, clipped words—physically holding yourself exactly as they taught you. But something inside is erupting. As you reveal what their control cost you, let your body break free: punch the air, shake out your limbs, let your voice grow raw and uncontrolled, move erratically through the space. Your body becomes a weapon and a liberation tool. Transform from a tightly wound, physically restricted person to someone who is wild, unleashed, taking up space with aggressive, expansive movements. Let rage move through your entire body like electricity, shaking off decades of physical suppression.
inspired_by: Actor's body is unexpressive or physically inhibited

title: We Made It to the Final Level
instruction: You're finally achieving the dream you and your late partner always talked about—maybe you're at a gaming convention, or your indie game just launched, or you're holding a trophy they never got to see. Begin laughing, genuinely laughing with joy and disbelief that you actually did it. Your voice should bubble with excited, almost manic happiness as you describe the moment, as if you're telling them all about it. But let the grief bleed through even as you laugh—your voice cracking mid-laugh, tears mixing with joy. You're so grateful, so proud, and so utterly devastated that they're not here to share it. The emotions should blur together until you can't tell if you're laughing or crying. End with a moment of strange, bittersweet peace—thanking them through tears and laughter, your voice soft and full of contradictory emotions, finding beauty in the heartbreak of celebrating alone.

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to your partner in the dark, and you're going to tell them something you've kept hidden for years—maybe a betrayal, a secret, a truth about who you really are. Begin by speaking so quietly they have to strain to hear you. Start with how much you love them, how safe they make you feel—and mean it. Let that safety give you the courage to reveal what you've been hiding. As you confess, feel the relief of finally being seen mixing with the terror of being rejected. Your voice stays soft, but the emotions intensify. By the end, you're completely exposed, trembling with the vulnerability of having nothing left to hide. Move from whispered devotion through terrified honesty to naked, quivering truth.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a one-dimensional character or character work feels superficial—expressing the emotion rather than creating the impetus

title: The Diagnosis: Finding Light in the Darkest News
instruction: You've just been given six months. Start with a strange laugh—it's absurd, isn't it? Your voice has this weird lightness because your brain hasn't processed it yet. You're almost joking about it: 'Well, that's not what I expected today.' But then reality starts seeping in. Your voice wavers, the laugh becoming shaky, desperate. You're fighting to hold onto the humor because if you let it go, you'll shatter. Describe what you'll miss—your voice breaking on stupid little things: morning coffee, your dog's face, the way rain sounds. You start crying, but you're also still half-laughing because it's all so beautiful and terrible at once. Your voice becomes soft with wonder mixed with grief: 'I never noticed how much I loved being alive.' End with a strange, genuine peace—your voice steady but thick with tears: 'Every single ordinary day was a gift. I just didn't know.' You're grateful and devastated in the same breath, your voice carrying both the weight of loss and the profound beauty of having lived at all.
inspired_by: Karate Tournament Final: Facing Your Abuser

title: The Last Dunes of the Canyon
instruction: You're on the final stretch of a brutal desert hike with an attractive partner you've been flirting with for days. The heat has crushed you—every word feels like sandpaper, your vision swims, and you keep losing your train of thought. You start by pridefully insisting you're fine, trying to sound tough and maybe a little charming, but the heat pulls you down. As you struggle to finish a flirty sentence, you're forced to admit you need water first before you can even think about a kiss later, shifting from bravado to dizzy vulnerability. Let the weakness and dryness crack your voice, let pride melt into honest need.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Doubt (clearly present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You're confronting your parent about something they did—or failed to do—when you were a child. Start by speaking calmly, almost detached, as you describe yourself at age five: 'I'm five years old and I...' Tell them what you saw, what you learned, what you swallowed and kept silent about. Progress through the ages—six, eight, twelve—each year revealing another moment where their actions taught you to shrink, to hide, to apologize for existing. Speak in present tense, as if you're living each age right now. Let the emotion build from quiet observation to something rawer. By the end, you must break through to fierce, liberating rage or exhausted forgiveness—your choice, but it must transform from where you began. Make them see every version of you they damaged or diminished, and then decide whether you're done carrying it.
inspired_by: 'I'm Five Years Old and I...' Exercise

title: The Last Hand to Hold
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She can barely speak, drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin feeling numb, almost disconnected—you've been here for days and exhaustion has dulled everything. Then her hand suddenly grips yours with unexpected strength. Let whatever comes up in that moment flow through you without thinking—maybe it's a laugh at a sudden memory, maybe words tumble out about something you've never told her, maybe you find yourself singing a fragment of a song she used to sing. Don't plan what you'll say or do. Follow each impulse the instant it arises: if you want to put your head on her chest, do it; if you want to tell her about the birds outside the window, do it; if anger suddenly flares that she's leaving, let it out. By the end, you must arrive somewhere entirely different—perhaps at peace, perhaps shattered, perhaps filled with a strange wild gratitude. Trust where your body and voice want to take you moment by moment.

title: The Rage That Becomes Grief: Screaming at Someone You Love Who's Destroying Themselves
instruction: You're confronting someone you love who's killing themselves slowly—through addiction, self-destruction, giving up. Start with explosive fury. Your voice is loud, harsh, almost cruel in its honesty. You're screaming at them to wake up, to fight, to care. Your words are sharp weapons meant to cut through their numbness. But mid-tirade, something shifts. Your rage cracks and underneath is pure terror and helplessness. Your voice breaks. You collapse from shouting into sobbing, from accusations into desperate begging. 'Please. Please don't leave me. Please.' Your voice becomes small, childlike. End in exhausted whispers, telling them you can't save them but you refuse to let go, your voice hoarse and broken but still there, still speaking, still loving.
inspired_by: Reclaiming Your Voice After Being Silenced

title: The Body Remembers What the Mind Forbids
instruction: You are alone, attempting to experience pleasure—intimate, physical self-touch—but you've spent years training yourself to be numb, controlled, 'appropriate.' Begin with rigid, mechanical movements, your breath held, your jaw clenched, your mind reciting reasons why you shouldn't feel, shouldn't want, shouldn't let go. Your body is a locked box. But sensation is patient and insistent. Gradually, against your will, your breath deepens. A sound escapes that you didn't authorize. Your control splinters. By the end, you are sobbing and gasping simultaneously, pleasure and grief indistinguishable, your body finally allowed to feel everything you've forbidden it for years. The transformation is from physical and emotional lockdown to uncontrolled, cathartic release—not just of pleasure, but of years of denied feeling.
inspired_by: Actor needs to play a character who is uptight, closed, or defensive

title: The Last Call
instruction: You're an older woman sitting alone at a quiet bar, two empty glasses in front of you, a third half-full. You've had a few drinks—your words are loose, a little louder than intended, and your hands gesture a bit too broadly. You're laughing softly at nothing when the bartender asks if you want another. You look at your reflection in the mirror behind the bottles. The laughter fades. You begin to speak, not really to him, but to the ghost of someone you lost. Your voice starts with a tipsy, wry cheerfulness, but as you continue, the sadness you've been drowning emerges—raw, unguarded, and utterly real. Let your words wander, lose a thought, find it again, let your pitch waver. End with a quiet, tearful stillness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Wounds
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father in the family home, finally speaking aloud the truth about how their choices damaged you - but halfway through this confrontation, you'll discover they were protecting you from something far worse, something they never wanted you to know. Start from a place of righteous, controlled anger - your voice steady, your words carefully chosen like weapons you've rehearsed for years. As you speak, let your parent's silence and the weight of their expression begin to crack your certainty. When they finally reveal their secret - the sacrifice they made, the abuse they endured to shield you, the impossible choice they faced - allow your anger to shatter into horrified understanding. End in a place you never expected: your roles reversed, you now comforting them, your voice breaking with the terrible complexity of loving someone whose pain caused yours.
inspired_by: Actor needs to prepare instrumentally before a rehearsal

title: Sloppy Serenade
instruction: You're high on cheap wine and giddy affection, giving oral sex to your partner. You start with a playful, sloppy ‘hum’ of a song, laughing and swallowed sounds, amused by your own drunken state and muffled attempt at a melody. As you continue, the amusement melts into a sudden, deep longing — a quiet, needy hum, a raw sound in the back of your throat, like you want them to feel how much you miss them even though they're right here. Let the wet sounds, restricted nose-breathing, and occasional lost rhythm be present.
emotions_sampled: Longing (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Amusement (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Lap Seven's Rhythm
instruction: You are a teenage boy swimming laps in a quiet pool, pushing through the last part of your workout. At first, your mind is full of effort—counting strokes, fighting the burn in your arms. But around lap seven, something shifts. Your body finds a steady pace, and a calm contentment settles in. You talk to yourself in short gasps between breaths, each word expelled in one or two syllables as you turn your head. Your voice is wet, hollow from the water, and you sputter a little. Start with the strain of exertion, then let your tone soften into a quiet, peaceful realization—like you're finally home in the water.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Apologizing Without Making It About Your Guilt
instruction: You hurt someone and keep seeking reassurance. Catch yourself: 'I'm sorry I hurt you' instead of 'I'm sorry I feel guilty.' Your voice becomes more other-focused. It's harder. Listen to their pain without centering your remorse. Your voice stabilizes as you truly own the impact.

title: Acting Interested While Bored in a Conversation
instruction: Youre stuck in a dull conversation but dont want to offend the other person. Internally, youre bored and distracted, but you nod along. Describe your wandering thoughts while maintaining eye contact and nodding politely. Speak with an engaged tone, hiding your lack of interest.

title: The Acceptance Speech No One Will Hear
instruction: You have just received devastating news: the opportunity you've worked toward for years has gone to someone else. Yet bizarrely, you find yourself delivering an acceptance speech anyway—thanking everyone who helped you along the journey. Begin with bitter, sarcastic gratitude, mockingly listing people as if you'd won, your voice dripping with irony and barely contained grief. But as you continue, something genuine starts breaking through. You realize these thank-yous are real—these people did show up, you did grow, you did become someone different through the trying. Let your voice crack between anger and authentic appreciation. The grief of losing mixes with unexpected gratitude for what the pursuit gave you. End in a place of confusing, contradictory peace—simultaneously heartbroken and somehow grateful, destroyed and strangely whole. Let both emotions be equally true and present in your final words.

title: The Absurdity of It All
instruction: You are an older woman sitting on a curb after a minor car accident. Your hands tremble as you hold a broken phone. You start to laugh uncontrollably at the ridiculousness of the other driver's excuse, but your laughter is laced with bitterness—you're exhausted, shaky, and suddenly angry at how dismissive the paramedic was. Begin with a breathless, wobbly laugh, then let the bitterness creep in as your voice cracks and you replay the dismissive words. Allow your speech to be rushed, with pauses to swallow tears or catch your breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: Your mother is sitting across from you at the kitchen table where you grew up. She's just said something that's triggered decades of unspoken resentment—about how you turned out, about choices you made, about who you love. Start speaking to her with all the defensive fury you've suppressed for years, every word you swallowed at family dinners. As you talk, allow yourself to see her reactions—maybe her face crumples, maybe she tries to interrupt, maybe she reaches for your hand. Let those imagined responses shift your tone. The confrontation must evolve: perhaps you realize mid-speech that you're not just angry—you're terrified of losing her, or you suddenly understand why she said what she said. End in a completely different emotional place than where you began.

title: Counting Breaths in the Beat
instruction: You're an 8-year-old boy at your first rave with your dad, who has a deep, booming voice he uses to shout over the pounding music. You've been dancing hard for minutes, your chest heaving, your words bouncing like your feet. In a sudden quiet spell between two songs, you pause, panting, and look at him. Start contemplatively, genuinely marveling at the lights and the feeling in your chest, then feel a wave of affection for him as you reach for his hand, ending with a breathy, relieved giggle as the next beat drops.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Affection (slightly present), Relief (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Tears While Helping Your Parent Remember Their Own Life
instruction: You're looking through old photos together, and they're struggling to remember. Start with gentle prompting, a smile in your voice: 'That's you and Dad at the beach, remember?' When they can't recall, laugh softly—not mockingly, but with bittersweet affection. Your voice dances between joy and sorrow as you tell them their own stories: 'You were so happy that day.' Let yourself genuinely laugh at a funny memory, voice bright, but feel it catch and break into something tearful. Find the strange beauty in this role reversal—you're giving their life back to them through stories. Your voice should contain multitudes: gratitude for having known them when they were whole, grief for what's slipping away, tenderness for who they are now, and a kind of peaceful acceptance underneath it all. End with something simple that contains everything: 'You had such a beautiful life.' Let your voice hold both celebration and goodbye.
inspired_by: Your Parent Becoming Emotionally Dependent on You

title: Dancing in the ICU
instruction: Your spouse is dying—hours, maybe minutes left—and they just woke up lucid for the first time in days. They're asking you to tell them about the trip you had planned for your retirement next month: that cottage in Ireland, the coastal walks, the pub you'd picked out. So you do. You start describing it with such vivid joy—you can almost see the green hills, smell the sea air—and you're both laughing, really laughing, at the terrible joke about how you'd probably get lost on those country roads. Your voice is bright, full of real happiness, because in this moment you're giving them that trip. But underneath, you can hear your own heart breaking, and occasionally the joy catches, stutters, threatened by the grief pressing against it. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, painting this beautiful future you'll never have while holding their hand, feeling it grow weaker. End with a moment of pure gratitude for this last gift of consciousness, even as you're drowning in the loss. Your voice should somehow hold both the fullness of love and the emptiness of goodbye—contradictory, human, absolutely real.

title: Losing a Child
instruction: Your child has died. You're at the morgue, and they're asking you to confirm. Your voice is numb, detached at first—a defense mechanism. 'Yes, that's... that's my child.' Then it hits. Your voice breaks. You're gasping through sobs, your words incoherent. The social worker is speaking to you but the words are muffled by your grief. Include moments where you can't speak, where you're just making wounded animal sounds. By the end, you're hollowed out, your voice barely above a whisper, repeating 'My baby... my baby...'

title: What You Never Knew I Saw
instruction: You are confronting your parent about something you witnessed as a child that neither of you has ever acknowledged—perhaps their affair, their addiction, their moment of cruelty to someone vulnerable, or their profound unhappiness that they hid from you. Start from a place of rehearsed courage: you've planned this conversation, your words are ready, you're determined to finally say this. But as you speak, let the child you were enter your voice—the confusion, the fear, the desperate wish to unsee what you saw. Your adult anger should crack to reveal the heartbroken child underneath. Midway through, experience the disorienting shift when you realize they knew you saw, they always knew. End not in rage but in something more complicated: the aching need to be told it wasn't your fault, mixed with unexpected compassion for their human frailty. Your voice should transform from accusatory to achingly vulnerable.
inspired_by: Actor is working on a scene and needs to identify what to work on—which obligations are most pressing

title: The 3 AM Whisper
instruction: It's three in the morning and you're lying next to your partner of fifteen years, speaking into the darkness. You're confessing something you've never told anyone: a desire you've kept hidden because it felt too strange, too shameful, too vulnerable. Begin barely audibly, your throat tight with fear of rejection. But as you speak, let the confession grow—not louder necessarily, but more alive. Your body might tremble, your breath might catch, small sounds might escape you. The intimacy unlocks something, and the shame starts transforming into unexpected liberation, even joy. By the end, you're laughing softly through tears, or breathing freely for the first time in years, still whispering but with your whole heart open. The arc is from constricted terror to expanding freedom, all in hushed tones.

title: The Garden in November
instruction: You're scattering your estranged sibling's ashes in the garden you both loved as children, having reconciled only in their final week. Begin speaking to them with tender gratitude for that last conversation, your voice soft with the sweetness of finally being understood. But let bitter regret start seeping in—all the wasted years, the stubborn pride, the petty arguments that kept you apart. Your gratitude shouldn't disappear; instead, let it exist alongside rage at the unfairness, at time, at both of you for being so foolish. Laugh at a memory, then let that laugh catch in your throat and transform into something more complex. By the end, you should be holding both the gift of your final peace and the irreversible loss of all the years you can't reclaim, your voice embodying both the beauty of forgiveness and the unforgivable cost of waiting.
inspired_by: An actor receives criticism that is painful to hear

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent who is visiting for what might be the last time. Begin with polite small talk, your voice tight and performative, asking about their drive, the weather - anything but what matters. You've spent thirty years swallowing the question: why weren't you enough for them to stay? Let the pleasantries slowly crack as you watch them perform their own politeness. Build to the moment where you finally ask the question you've rehearsed a thousand times, but let it come out raw and unpolished, not how you planned. As they respond (or don't), let your anger dissolve into something more complicated - the child's desperate need for love colliding with the adult's understanding that they were just a damaged person doing their best. End in a place where forgiveness and fury coexist, your voice quiet but trembling with both.
inspired_by: Actor needs to build an authentic relationship with a scene partner quickly

title: The Midnight Equation
instruction: You're a teenager alone in your room at 2 a.m., working on a complex math problem for a competition. You've just had a breakthrough—everything is clicking. As you explain your solution out loud to no one, your words tumble out faster and faster. You’re intensely focused, but the excitement makes you skip steps, laugh at nothing, and start three new ideas before finishing one. Your voice is too loud, your pitch rises, and you keep grabbing random items on your desk for emphasis. By the end, you’re not solving anymore—you’re just riding the rush, talking to the ceiling about how you might change the world. Start with sharp concentration, end with fuzzy intoxication.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Interest (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Barefoot on Broken Ground
instruction: You've just received news that has shattered your world—betrayal, loss, devastating diagnosis, your choice. You walk barefoot outside into your garden or onto a beach. Feel everything: the texture of earth or sand under your feet, the temperature of the air on your skin, the exact quality of light, any breeze or stillness. Let yourself be consumed by the physical sensations of the world around you even as emotional pain crashes through your body. Your voice should reflect both the acute attention to sensory detail and the waves of feeling breaking simultaneously. Begin almost numb, hyper-focused on physical sensation as a way to stay standing. Let the physical awareness gradually open the floodgates until your body and emotions are inseparable—you're feeling everything at once.

title: The Last Video Message
instruction: You're recording a final video message to your family, knowing you won't see them again. You start trying to sound cheerful and normal, narrating mundane things you want them to remember—how you make coffee, your favorite walking route, the way you organize the kitchen. But as you speak, the weight of what you're really doing crashes over you. Your voice begins to crack. The trivial details become unbearably precious. By the end, you're no longer pretending—you're raw, vulnerable, telling them the真things that matter, your voice breaking between love and devastation. Let the transition happen naturally, don't perform grief—let it find you as you speak.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing over your sleeping child's bed, knowing you have to leave and can never return—witness protection, a sacrifice to save them, a choice that will break both your hearts. Begin in barely audible whispers, describing the way their hair falls across the pillow, the rise and fall of their breath, the small perfections of their face. Your voice should be thick with tenderness and the effort of not crying, not waking them. Let grief creep in as you tell them all the things you'll miss: their laughter, their questions, watching them grow. Your whispers should become even quieter as emotion threatens to break you open, each word a physical effort. End with a choked confession of love so pure and so devastated that it exists in that space between breath and breaking, where you're trying not to sob and failing.
inspired_by: Feeling the First Gentle Snowflakes Land on Your Face

title: The Last Words You'll Never Say
instruction: You're standing at the bedside of someone who hurt you deeply—a parent, a former love, a friend who shattered your trust—and they're dying. They'll be gone within hours. You start with that familiar burning rage, whispering the accusations you've held for years: 'You ruined me. You took something I can never get back.' Your voice is sharp, controlled venom. But as you speak, something shifts. The reality that this is the last time crashes over you. Your anger begins to crack, revealing the grief underneath—grief for what you needed and never got, for the relationship that could have been. By the end, you're no longer sure if you're saying goodbye to them or to your own anger. Your final words are barely audible, caught between fury and unbearable loss: 'I needed you. God, I needed you, and now you're leaving.' Let your voice break where it needs to.

title: Finding Joy in the Hospice Garden
instruction: You're in hospice care, tasting a sun-warmed strawberry from the garden, and it's absurdly, impossibly perfect. Begin laughing—genuine, surprised laughter at how something can taste this good when everything else is ending. Describe the sweetness with wonder and joy, but let tears come simultaneously, not from sadness but from the strange gift of this moment. Your voice should dance between delight and sorrow, gratitude and grief, peace and heartbreak. End with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob, saying something like 'Thank you' or 'How beautiful' with your whole heart breaking open. The contradiction should feel transcendent—you've never been more alive or closer to death, and the strawberry contains everything.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a lie they told that shaped your entire childhood. You've rehearsed this conversation for years, armed with righteous anger. But as you begin speaking, notice what your body is actually doing versus what you planned to feel. Are you angrier than you expected? Less angry? Is there an unexpected shakiness in your voice? A hollow feeling? Start with your prepared accusations, but the moment you notice any disconnect between what you're saying and what you're genuinely experiencing, stop mid-sentence. Acknowledge out loud what's really happening in your body—'My hands are shaking,' 'I thought I'd be angrier but I just feel tired,' 'I'm afraid of you even now.' Let the confrontation become about discovering your real feelings, not delivering the speech you practiced. By the end, arrive somewhere emotionally you never planned to go.
inspired_by: Actor observes splits — body disconnected from emotion, voice carrying different emotion than body, or expression driven entirely by intellect

title: Three AM Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love, in complete darkness. You're whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something that makes you feel exposed, possibly shameful, possibly sacred. Start by trying to keep your voice steady, controlled, as if you can manage this revelation. But as you continue speaking in the dark, let the whisper change. Maybe it becomes shakier, maybe it finds unexpected strength, maybe silence overtakes words. Don't push for tears or force composure—simply let your breath and voice respond truthfully to what you're confessing. The darkness should feel different by the end than it did at the beginning.

title: Realizing You Became What You Hated
instruction: You just said something and it sounded exactly like your father. Or your mother. Something you swore you'd never do. Your voice in the moment is almost unrecognizable. You're someone else. You're them. Your voice becomes horrified—'Oh God, I sound like...' Your voice cracks. You're 35 years old and you've become the person you spent 20 years avoiding. Your voice carries the devastation of that realization. Include the moment you decide to change anyway.

title: The Reunion at the Airport
instruction: You're at the airport waiting for your child who's been estranged from you for three years after a devastating argument. You don't know if they've forgiven you; you barely know if you've forgiven yourself. You see them walking toward you through the crowd. Begin with your heart simultaneously soaring with hope and sinking with dread—let these opposite emotions fight in your chest, making your breath uneven. When you finally speak their name, it should carry years of grief, stubborn pride, desperate love, and lingering resentment all at once. Tell them you're sorry and you're angry—both things are true. You missed them and you still think you were partly right—both things are true. As you speak, let the contradictions stop canceling each other out and instead exist together, messy and human. End with the terrifying, exhilarating uncertainty of not knowing if this reunion will heal you or break you all over again, but choosing to be here anyway. Your final words should tremble with both fear and stubborn, unreasonable hope.

title: Three AM Truths
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to your partner, who you believe is asleep. In a whisper barely louder than breath, you begin confessing something you've never said aloud—a fear about your relationship, a truth about yourself, a secret you've carried alone. Start by simply feeling the darkness around you, the vulnerability of speaking into what you think is safe silence. Let your voice be tentative, unpolished, the words coming out in fragments rather than complete thoughts. Halfway through, you realize they're awake and listening. Everything shifts—but don't escalate into dramatic revelation. Instead, feel the exposure, the naked honesty of being truly heard. Notice how intimacy can be more terrifying than any confrontation. End not with resolution but with the quiet recognition that you've crossed a threshold together, however uncertain what lies beyond it.
inspired_by: Actor cannot function without stimulating high tension states (Theatrical Hysteria / Ass Energy)

title: First Tremor
instruction: You're a teenage girl alone in your bedroom, lying on your back, phone forgotten beside you as your body takes over. You start in a place of shy, private anticipation—breathing quickens, a tiny laugh escapes at your own boldness. As the sensation builds, your voice becomes fragmented, breaths catching, pitch climbing in surprise and delight. Near the peak, words dissolve into gasps and a vulnerable moan of 'please... oh...'—then you let out a long, shaky exhale, a soft giggle of disbelief, before whispering to yourself, 'Wow... that was... I didn't know...' The arc goes from hesitant curiosity to raw, trembling release, to a quiet, awed afterglow.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Everything
instruction: You've just received news that should be purely joyful—you got the job, you're in remission, your child is coming home, you won something you've desperately wanted. Begin celebrating, letting genuine joy pour through your voice. But as you speak, memories flood in of everyone who helped you get here, everyone who's gone now, everyone who wanted this for you but didn't live to see it. Your mother who believed in you but died last year. Your friend who encouraged you but won't answer your call to share this news. Suddenly you're sobbing—but not purely from grief. It's joy and loss braided together, gratitude so intense it hurts, the sharp awareness that every good thing comes with the shadow of absence. Your voice should break and soar simultaneously. End overwhelmed by the bitter beauty of it: that you get to have this triumph, and that it's full of ghosts, and that somehow both things make it more precious, more unbearably real.

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're returning home after years away—maybe after success, maybe after failure, maybe both. Someone who loves you—a parent, an old friend, a sibling—is welcoming you with joy and questions: 'How does it feel to be back? Was it worth it? Are you proud? What did you learn?' They want celebration; they want wisdom; they want the story to make sense. Start by trying to give them what they want—smile, perform gratitude, shape the narrative. But as their loving questions continue, something inside you unravels. Begin to answer with the truth you've been hiding from yourself: 'I don't know.' Let relief and grief flood in together. Let your voice move from performance to breaking to a strange, tearful laughter. End with the contradictions fully alive: you're home but lost, grateful but empty, loved but uncertain, and somehow that messy truth is the first real thing you've said in years.

title: Grief Breaking Through Professional Composure
instruction: You're a funeral director giving a professional briefing to a family — and this time, the deceased is someone you knew. Maintain the measured, gentle professional tone while grief silently detonates inside you. Your voice should be almost perfect — but not quite. A vowel wavers. A pause lasts one beat too long. Your throat tightens audibly. The mask holds — barely — until one detail breaks it open. Show how professional composure crumbles from a single crack.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood you needed but never had. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, tried to stay calm, but there's a tremor underneath. As you continue, old wounds open: your voice rises, cracks, becomes the voice of the child you once were, desperate and pleading. Then shift—let the anger drain away into something more devastating: the realization that they'll never understand, never give you what you came for. End with exhausted acceptance, your voice barely above a whisper, saying goodbye not with rage but with the quiet devastation of finally letting go of hope. Move from control to chaos to hollow peace.
inspired_by: The Five Stages of Getting Drunk

title: Whispering to the Sleeping
instruction: Your lover lies asleep beside you at 3 AM. You know you're leaving tomorrow and they don't know yet. Begin whispering the truth—too quiet to wake them, but needing to say it aloud. Confess what you love about their breathing, their hands, the way they smell. Admit what terrifies you about staying—the ways you'd destroy this, the parts of yourself you hate that would poison what's beautiful. Let your whispers catch and break. Confess the things you've never said, the small hatreds mixed with tenderness, the fears that keep you running. End with your hand hovering over their face, voice barely audible, caught between staying and going.

title: The Last Round
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe nine or ten, in the final minute of a sparring match at your dojo. You are completely exhausted—your arms feel like wet noodles, and your lungs burn. You have already thrown every combination you know, and your opponent keeps coming. In your head, you cycle through a memory your sensei told you: 'When you have nothing left, you find something else.' As you circle, you mutter this to yourself, trying to summon a second wind. Between heavy breaths, you whisper what you will do next—a feint, then a kick—but your voice cracks with fatigue. Just before the final buzzer, you let out a sharp, desperate kiai and charge. Start with quiet, broken self-talk and end with raw, explosive determination.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Peace Finding
instruction: You're sitting on a porch at sunrise after a long night of not-sleeping, and suddenly there's quiet in your mind. No more noise. Your voice emerges as a whisper, not from secrecy but from reverence. Words come slowly, deliberately: 'I think I'm okay.' Not happy—peaceful. Your breathing is deep, rhythmic. There's no urgency. When you speak, it's sparse, like you're afraid too many words will break the quiet. Each sentence has the feeling of a meditation. Vocal tone is warm, self-compassionate. Physical: you're still, grounded.

title: The Kitchen Where We Stop Lying
instruction: You're confronting your parent in the kitchen where you grew up. Start by commenting on everything you see—the chipped mug they always use, the refrigerator magnets, the smell of coffee, the sound of traffic outside—speaking aloud how each detail makes you feel RIGHT NOW in your body. Begin with bitter, sarcastic observations that keep you protected and angry. But as you inventory the room, let the memories and sensations crack you open. The taste in your mouth, the tightness in your chest, the way your hands want to move. Build to the real truth you came to say—not just your anger, but the hurt beneath it, the child who needed something they never got. End in a place of exhausted honesty, where anger has transformed into painful vulnerability and perhaps a fragile opening toward understanding.

title: Barefoot on Broken Glass
instruction: You have just discovered an unforgivable betrayal—evidence scattered on the floor around you. Begin in ice-cold shock, your body rigid, barely breathing, seeing but not feeling. Then let the physical reality invade: the temperature of the room on your skin, the hard floor under your bare feet, the trembling starting in your hands. As sensation floods back, so does emotion—but not simple anger. Feel rage building while simultaneously your body wants to collapse. You are screaming while crying, laughing while destroying something, your voice cracking between octaves. Let the physical experience guide the emotional chaos: throw something and feel the release, then immediately crumble; slam your fist down and feel the pain mix with satisfaction. End in exhausted stillness, sitting on the floor among the wreckage, your voice hoarse, experiencing an unexpected moment of clarity or even liberation through destruction.

title: Comforting Someone While Grieving Yourself
instruction: A friend needs your support after a loss, but youre grieving too. Internally, youre overwhelmed with your own sadness, but you stay strong for them. Describe your inner pain while offering comforting words. Speak with a gentle, reassuring tone, setting aside your own emotions.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from the hospital where your parent has just died. You weren't planning what to say—you just dialed. Start with the shock still fresh in your body, your voice uncertain, trying to find words. Let whatever you're actually feeling in this moment—maybe anger that they weren't there, maybe desperate need for connection, maybe unexpected relief—emerge as you speak. Don't decide in advance what emotion will win. Let the conversation surprise you. Allow silences where you genuinely don't know what comes next. By the end, discover whether you're pushing them away or pulling them close. Let your body and voice respond to what actually happens as you speak, not to a plan.

title: The Vow Before the Storm
instruction: You're promising to protect someone you love from a danger you both know you cannot stop. Start with fierce conviction, almost aggressive in your certainty—you WILL keep them safe, you WILL find a way. As you continue, let the false confidence crack. Your voice should move from declaration to desperation, from powerful promises to pleading with the universe itself. Let rage at your own powerlessness explode through, then collapse into broken tenderness. End with a whisper that carries both absolute determination and absolute terror. The arc is from warrior's certainty to a parent's helpless love, from shouting defiance to trembling devotion.

title: Three Versions of 'I Love You'
instruction: It's 2 AM, and you're lying next to your partner in the dark. You're drawing from three different truths: the love poem you memorized in college that captures something you feel, the text message you never sent last week expressing your fears, and the whispered thought forming right now. Speak quietly, intimately, letting these three sources weave together as one confession. Begin in a place of tender certainty, but let yourself drift into fragile uncertainty and the terrifying vulnerability of truly being known. This isn't about performing separate pieces—it's about letting different articulations of the same complex feeling flow as one continuous, naked revelation.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Go
instruction: You're standing in the doorway of your child's room, knowing you won't see them again—whether through death, distance, or departure. Begin in barely audible whispers, tender and aching: 'I memorized your face today. The way your nose crinkles when you laugh.' Your voice is thick with love so fierce it's almost unbearable. Describe small details—their hands, their smell, the sound of their breathing. You're trying so hard to be quiet, to not wake them, but emotion keeps catching in your throat. Tell them things you need them to know but won't be there to say: lessons, apologies, hopes. Your whispers become strained, tears making speech difficult. You might have to pause to steady yourself, hand over your mouth to keep from sobbing aloud. End with something simple—'I love you' or 'Be brave'—but let it break you completely, voice fragmenting into silence. This is a parent's most private grief, the kind of love that destroys you from the inside.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Door Closes
instruction: You're standing at your childhood home's threshold for the final time before it's sold, speaking to the empty rooms as if your deceased parent can hear you. Begin with anger at all the things left unsaid, all the moments of connection you never had. Let that anger crack open into desperate longing—you want so badly to have one more chance, one more conversation. Your voice should break from accusation into pleading, from bitterness into a raw need for their presence. End in a place of exhausted, tender acceptance, speaking to them with the kind of gentle honesty you could never manage when they were alive. The emotional journey moves from rage to grief to a fragile, heartbroken peace.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're in the aftermath of an intense physical experience—perhaps passionate lovemaking, perhaps a physical fight, perhaps surviving a car accident, perhaps running until your body gave out. Your body is still electric, trembling, hypersensitive. Begin describing what you feel physically, but let your mind associate freely and rapidly: a sensation in your hands triggers a memory from childhood, the taste in your mouth connects to a moment of shame, your racing heartbeat becomes the drumbeat at a wedding, the pain in your ribs reminds you of laughing too hard with someone who's gone, the sweat on your skin becomes rain from a thunderstorm years ago, the ceiling above you morphs into another ceiling from another time. These associations should tumble over each other, interrupt each other, move faster than logic. Your emotional state keeps shifting—from exhilaration to grief to rage to tenderness to fear—not because you're deciding to change, but because each physical sensation and memory pulls a different emotion from you. By the end, you've moved from the purely physical into a profound emotional revelation that you couldn't have anticipated—about loss, about being alive, about what your body has carried all these years.

title: The Numb Promise
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting in a dentist's chair after a procedure, your mouth still half-numb from Novocain. You're trying to tell your adult child, who is waiting in the doorway, a story about a fishing trip you'll take together next spring. Start with a drowsy, satisfied smile as you recall the warmth of the sun on the lake. As you speak, you slur through your words, especially the B's and M's, and you pause to wipe a bit of drool from your chin. Let your voice fade in and out as you lose the thread, then brighten with genuine hope as you finish the promise, the smile returning despite the numbness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Never Saw
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent what their absence—physical or emotional—actually cost you. Begin with careful control, almost clinical distance: 'I need to tell you something I've never said.' But as you describe a specific moment when you needed them and they weren't there, your voice should start to fracture with the younger version of yourself bleeding through. There's anger, yes, but underneath it is something more devastating: the child who still desperately wanted their love. 'I needed you to see me, and you just... didn't.' Let your voice oscillate between adult rage and childlike pleading. The emotional arc moves from controlled confrontation to raw need, then finally to exhausted release—not quite forgiveness, but a laying down of the weight. The most powerful moment should be when your voice drops to almost nothing: 'I'm tired of being angry at you. But I don't know how to stop.'
inspired_by: Admitting You're Jealous of Your Partner's Success

title: Stutter Authenticity
instruction: You're an actor with a genuine speech impediment, and you've decided to stop hiding it on the job. Your stutter appears naturally throughout your performance: 'M-m-my name is James.' It's not a caricature; it's just how you speak. As you continue the scene, the stutter remains, and it becomes part of your character. A scene partner's eyes soften with understanding. By the emotional climax, your stutter intensifies because you're emotional: 'I l-l-love you.' The vulnerability isn't in spite of the stutter — it's that the stutter is the truth, and the truth is what makes you heard. Off-scene, you breathe, and the stutter remains. That's your voice. That's authentic.

title: Protecting Your Child from Yourself
instruction: You're a parent in recovery, and your teenage child just asked if you remember the worst night of their childhood—the night you don't remember because you were too drunk. Start with defensive deflection, voice rising, 'I'm doing better now, why bring up the past?' But their silence forces you to face it. Your anger—at yourself, at your disease, at what you stole from them—explodes into raw, ugly sobbing. 'I should have been there, I should have—' You can't finish sentences. The rage at your own failure is physically painful. But underneath the storm, a fierce protectiveness emerges: 'I won't let that person hurt you anymore, even if that person was me.' End with a promise whispered through tears, your voice shaking but certain. Let fury, shame, and desperate love collide.
inspired_by: Giving Birth While Arguing with Your Mother-in-Law

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's funeral, and a memory hits you—something ridiculous, something perfectly them. You start to laugh, quietly at first, trying to suppress it, but it bubbles up uncontrollably. Your voice cracks with laughter as you whisper to yourself: 'God, you would have hated this. All these people pretending they knew you.' Let the laughter be genuine, almost inappropriate, but underneath it, feel the grief rising. Your voice begins to break—still laughing, but now crying too, the sounds indistinguishable. You're speaking to them: 'Thank you. Thank you for every stupid joke, every 3 a.m. phone call, every time you saw me.' The gratitude and the devastation are inseparable. End with your voice barely above a whisper, smiling through tears: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' Let joy and unbearable loss live in the same breath.

title: Final Words in the Wreckage: A Stranger's Hand to Hold
instruction: You're trapped in wreckage with a stranger, both injured, rescue uncertain. Begin with careful politeness masking terror—asking their name, making small talk about the weather to avoid panic. As pain intensifies and time stretches, pretenses crumble. Share a confession you've never told anyone, something that's weighed on you for years. Listen as they share theirs. Move from fear to unexpected intimacy, from wanting rescue to wanting this person—this witness to your rawest self—to know they mattered. End in quiet acceptance, grateful for this stranger who became the last person to truly see you, holding their hand as your voice softens to almost nothing.
inspired_by: Escape Room with a Stranger: Trust Under Pressure

title: The Old Tease
instruction: You're an elderly man sitting at the kitchen table, teasing your adult grandchild who just spilled coffee on your favorite shirt. Start with loud, exaggerated mockery—adopt a nasal, singsong caricature of their clumsiness, your pitch jumping up and down. Midway, you notice their embarrassed expression, and your voice falters; you trail off with a dry chuckle, then shift to a sincere, low murmur—telling them it's okay, the shirt was old anyway. Let your glasses slip and adjust them, pause to take a sip of tea, and let the affection leak through at the end as you say, 'You always were my favorite troublemaker.' The journey is from theatrical sarcasm to quiet warmth.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Reading Their Letter at the Empty Grave
instruction: You're standing at a gravestone, holding a letter your deceased best friend wrote to you before they died—but you only just found it, years later. As you read it aloud, you begin with bitter resentment: why did they hide this? Why leave words unsaid until after death? But the letter says things you desperately needed to hear—that you mattered, that you were loved, that you were forgiven for the fight you never resolved. Let your voice break between anger at their absence and overwhelming gratitude for these words. By the end, you're laughing through tears at some memory they've written, experiencing the impossible paradox of feeling more connected to them than you have in years, even as you stand at their grave. Joy and grief become inseparable.
inspired_by: Actor is working in film with little or no rehearsal time

title: The Perfect Stroll of Justice
instruction: You are an amateur historian walking slowly on a sunny autumn path through a small town’s park, your hands clasped loosely behind your back. You just successfully uncovered a decades-old misattribution of a local landmark’s plaque and have been publicly thanked by the city council. As you walk, a smug, nostalgic amusement fills you—you imagine the pompous scholar who got it wrong and how their face would redden. Let that contempt rise into a small, almost private smile; your voice starts curled with it. But then you notice a child nearby pointing at a tree and naming it after a bird that landed there, and a quiet wave of gratitude for this small, honest moment softens your tone. Speak like you’re musing aloud to the leaves: ‘You know, I still remember the exact second I saw that photo. The original deed. They had it backwards for sixty years—sixty. Can you imagine? (pause, a short scoff) …And that little girl just called that maple a 'warbler tree.' That’s pure. That’s something.’ Let the contempt slowly unwrap into a genuinely tender chuckle by the last words.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (very intensely present), Amusement (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Physician's Last Diagnosis
instruction: You're a doctor who must tell your mentor—the physician who inspired your entire career—that they have weeks to live, and there's nothing more you can do. Begin with clinical composure: 'The imaging shows extensive metastasis...' Your voice carries medical authority, but you're watching the person who taught you everything process their own death sentence. As you continue explaining prognosis and options, something starts breaking in your throat. The technical language becomes a shield you're desperately clutching. When you reach 'I'm so sorry,' it's no longer doctor to patient—it's a child losing a parent. End trying to return to professional distance ('We can make you comfortable'), but your voice now carries the full weight of gratitude, grief, and the devastating irony that all your training means nothing in this moment.

title: Reading Your Mother's Eulogy You Wrote Before She Woke Up
