instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed, reading aloud the eulogy you wrote when they said she had hours to live. But she's awake now, listening, though she pretends to sleep. Start with the formal, composed opening you prepared for strangers at a funeral. As you continue, let the reality crack through—she's here, she's listening, and every beautiful thing you wrote about missing her becomes unbearably present tense. Your voice should fracture between the past tense grief you prepared for and the overwhelming present tense love and confusion. By the end, you're no longer reading what you wrote—you're speaking directly to her, caught between gratitude that she's alive and the raw vulnerability of having revealed how much losing her would destroy you.
inspired_by: Wedding Toast While Secretly in Love with the Bride

title: Rhythm of Uncertainty
instruction: You are at a rave, moving to the beat, but a nagging doubt has crept in—maybe you should have stayed home, maybe you're too old for this. Shouting over the thumping bass, you try to convince yourself, but your voice bounces with each jump, laughter cuts your words short, and you get distracted by the flashing lights. Start with hesitant, breathless fragments, as if questioning your place here. Let the doubt color your shouts, but as a heavy drop hits, let the music pull you into a reluctant grin—your doubt doesn't vanish, but it shifts into a tired, defiant acceptance. End with a shout that's more exuberant, even if the uncertainty still flickers in your eyes.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Referee Controversial Call
instruction: You're the referee who has to make the final call in the championship game, and your gut tells you one thing but the rulebook supports another. You have to make the call publicly, knowing everyone will disagree. Your voice is authoritative: 'The call on the field stands.' But you know you might be wrong. Your voice wavers infinitesimally—enough that the crowd hears your doubt. You walk away hearing the boos, and your voice in the post-game interview is defending a decision you're not sure about. Show someone making a definitive call while sounding uncertain, because your voice will reveal the cost of that decision.

title: Fortress Walls Coming Down
instruction: You've spent years building walls to protect yourself, and now someone you love is walking away because of those walls—and suddenly, terrifyingly, you need them to stay. Start with fierce defensiveness, angry justifications for why you are the way you are, your voice sharp and cutting. But let it shatter—let the rage crack open to reveal the terrified person underneath who's never learned how to be vulnerable. Your voice should break into pleading, then desperation, then raw confession of every fear that made you push them away. Show the war between the instinct to protect yourself and the devastating realization that protection has cost you everything. End with a kind of fierce, trembling courage—offering to tear down every wall, knowing you might be too late, feeling both powerful and utterly helpless in your honesty.

title: Historical: Witness to Atrocity Must Testify Against Perpetrators Now in Power
instruction: Taking the stand, your voice is quiet but steady. You're testifying about horrors you witnessed. The perpetrators are now in positions of authority—in the courtroom itself. Your voice is testimony and accusation simultaneously. Your breathing is controlled trauma—you're reliving horrors while speaking them into record. Your voice is the sound of witnessing made legal. You're changing nothing perhaps, but you're speaking truth about power. Your vocal steadiness is revolutionary quiet—refusing to let them silence you again.

title: The Secret You've Carried Since Childhood
instruction: In the quiet darkness, you're finally saying aloud the thing you witnessed as a child but never told anyone—something that shaped everything you became. Begin with your voice so soft it's almost a breath, testing whether you can even form the words after decades of silence. There's a trembling quality, the voice of the child you were, scared and alone. As you continue, let the adult you are now emerge, anger seeping in—at the adults who should have protected you, at yourself for carrying this alone for so long. Your voice might catch, pause, nearly break. Move toward something like relief, the physical sensation of finally releasing this weight, but it's complicated by profound sadness for the child you were. End with tender forgiveness—not for what happened, but for the small, scared person who didn't know how to speak. Your voice becomes a whisper again, but this time it's gentle, almost loving, toward yourself.

title: Confronting Your Father at the Dock He Built
instruction: You're standing on the dock your father built forty years ago at the family lake house—the place he always said was his sanctuary, where he found peace while you were growing up without him. Begin by acknowledging the beauty he created here, the fresh air, the tranquility he always praised. But let your tone shift as you realize he gave this place more attention than he ever gave you. Your words must transform from attempting to appreciate what he loved into a raw confrontation about his absence, his priorities, his choice to find peace here while leaving chaos at home. Build from controlled observation to unleashed resentment, then break open into the vulnerable truth underneath: you needed him, and he chose this silence instead. Let your voice crack between anger and the child inside you who just wanted their father.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep, Inhaling Breath by a Freshwater Lake

title: The Old Lion's Speech
instruction: You are an elderly former politician at a dedication ceremony for a new community center named after your younger, more successful rival. You speak into a PA system, your voice amplified in the large hall. Begin with a tone of genuine contentment, praising the community and the center itself, your voice warm and steady. As you describe your rival's accomplishments, let a wave of jealousy and envy surge through you—your voice tightens, you pause dramatically, gripping the podium, the words coming out with sharp, controlled intensity. Then, as you finish, let the envy drain away into a quiet, barely perceptible sadness; your voice softens, almost distant, as you reflect on your own missed chances. Adjust the microphone once, glance at your notes, and let a slight tremor betray your age and emotion.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Sadness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Menu They'll Ever Share
instruction: You're at your father's favorite diner, the one he took you to every Saturday as a child. He's in hospice care at home, and you've brought the menu to read to him over the phone - one final time. Start with warm nostalgia as you describe the blue plate specials, your voice trembling with affection. When you ask what he'd like, his silence tells you he's too weak to respond. Your voice cracks as you realize you're choosing for him, this man who always knew exactly what he wanted. End with a whispered selection - his usual order - your words breaking as you understand this phone call is really goodbye disguised as ordering lunch. Let the menu items become a love letter you never knew how to write.

title: The Final Phone Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're calling your child from a military base, knowing this might be your last conversation before a dangerous mission you may not return from. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them - 'Hey kiddo, just wanted to hear your voice.' But as they sense something's wrong, your mask starts cracking. Your voice becomes raw with suppressed fear and overwhelming love: 'I need you to know how proud I am of you.' The act of not saying goodbye explicitly becomes unbearable. End with your voice breaking into whispered tenderness mixed with terror, trying to memorize the sound of their breathing, wanting to say 'I love you' in a way that will last them a lifetime, while they ask 'Dad, are you crying?'

title: When Weather Becomes Warfare
instruction: You're confronting your father who missed every important moment of your childhood because he was 'checking the weather,' 'watching the forecast,' obsessing over atmospheric conditions while you waited for him at school plays, birthdays, graduations. Start by mimicking his detached, detailed weather-speak with bitter sarcasm—'Oh, there's a seventy percent chance of precipitation, so I guess that's more important than your daughter's wedding.' Let your anger build as you recount specific moments he missed, your voice growing sharper, louder. But then break—suddenly, devastatingly—into the vulnerable child underneath, asking the question you've carried for decades: 'Was I really that boring? That unimportant?' End with a mixture of rage and heartbreak, demanding he finally see you instead of the sky.

title: Seeing Your Child's Face One Last Time
instruction: You're in hospice, hours from death, and they've just brought you new glasses—you insisted. Your adult child sits beside you, and for the first time in months, you see their face with perfect clarity. Start with that sharp inhale of recognition, the wonder of seeing every detail you'd forgotten. Your voice trembles: 'Your eyes... they have green in them. I forgot.' Let yourself drink in every feature like you're memorizing a map. But as you see them clearly, you also see the grief they're carrying, the exhaustion, the love that's breaking them. Your wonder transforms into a different kind of seeing—understanding what your dying is doing to them. End in a place of bittersweet peace, where gratitude for this moment of clarity mingles with the ache of knowing this is goodbye: 'I can see you. Really see you. And you're going to be okay.' Let your voice break on 'okay' because you need to believe it more than they do.

title: Feeding the Wild Things
instruction: You are sitting alone at dusk, speaking softly to the wild creatures that come to your doorstep—the only companions you have left after profound loss. Your voice is gentle, almost a whisper, as you offer them food and tell them small, tender things about your day. But woven through this gentleness is a deep, aching loneliness—you're talking to crows and rabbits because there's no one else. Let your voice catch on certain words, let silences speak. Begin with almost-cheerful hospitality, but let the sadness seep through until you're confessing your loneliness to these creatures who can't answer back. End with a moment of quiet gratitude for even this small connection, even as tears threaten. The emotion moves from tender warmth to raw loneliness to fragile, bittersweet acceptance.
inspired_by: The Farmer and the Talking Crow

title: The Stuffed Bear on the Shelf
instruction: You are a young boy, perhaps 9 or 10, sitting on the edge of your bed. The medication you took has smoothed everything into a distant, quiet fuzz. Your voice feels far away even to you. A stuffed bear sits on a high shelf across the room—your mother gave it to you years ago. At first, you speak to it matter-of-factly, describing your day with a hollow calm. But as you look at it longer, a faint, hollow ache rises—a deep longing you can almost taste, but the drug keeps it sealed in glass. Your voice should fluctuate between soft, slightly slurred monotone and small, cracked trails of real feeling that quickly sink back under the sedation.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Regaining Consciousness After G-Force Blackout: Rebuilding Awareness
instruction: You blacked out from G-force and you're waking up confused. Your voice is distant, slow, coming back online. You're a fighter pilot and you know what just happened but your mind is reconstructing it in real time. 'I lost... consciousness. How long?' You can't quite grasp time. Your voice is slurred initially, then gradually becomes clearer. Include the moment where you remember what you were doing and you need to know if you're still in the air or if you've crashed. Your voice becomes urgent with that question. The ground crew is responding and you're parsing their words, trying to understand if you're alive and whole. Your voice is becoming more present, more you, as consciousness fully returns. 'Talk to me. Are we down? Are we safe?' Your voice needs confirmation.

title: The Stone You Gave Me When You Left
instruction: In whispered intimacy, describe the small stone your lover pressed into your palm the morning they walked away. Begin with your fingers tracing its surface in the dark, your voice barely audible, as if speaking louder would shatter something precious. Let quiet devastation seep through: you've carried this stone for months, and its smoothness has become your only comfort, the last piece of them you can touch. Your breath should catch as you confess you sleep with it under your pillow, that sometimes you wake up clutching it so hard it leaves marks. End with the heartbreaking admission that you don't know if you're holding onto them or onto your own grief—and you're terrified of the day this stone no longer feels like enough.
inspired_by: Feeling the Texture of a Smooth Stone in Your Hand

title: The Last Seashell: A Grandmother's Farewell
instruction: You are a grandmother in hospice, holding the seashell your granddaughter just pressed into your palm. Begin with labored breathing, exhausted, ready to let go. Then the shell touches your ear and something ignites—a memory of your own childhood by the sea floods back. Your voice strengthens as you describe what you hear: your mother's laughter in the waves, your husband's proposal on that beach fifty years ago, your daughter's first steps in the sand. Start weary and resigned, but as the memories cascade, let wonder and fierce gratitude pour through you. End with a whispered realization that you're not afraid anymore—the ocean is calling you home. Let your voice break not from pain, but from the devastating beauty of a life fully remembered in its final moments.
inspired_by: The Ocean in a Seashell: A Child's Wonder

title: Confronting Your Parent in the Childhood Backyard
instruction: You've returned to your childhood home and found your estranged parent in the backyard where you once played in leaf piles together. Begin by describing the leaves underfoot with bitter nostalgia, then shift into confrontation: "You made this place feel magical once. You made everything feel safe. And then you just... stopped." Let your voice move from controlled pain to raw accusation as you kick through the leaves - each crunch punctuating your anger about the parent they failed to be. But as you speak, feel the anger crack open to reveal the wounded child underneath, desperate to understand why they weren't enough to make their parent stay present. End with your voice breaking, asking the question you've carried for years.
inspired_by: Feeling the Crunch of Autumn Leaves Beneath Your Feet

title: Sticky Fingers and Small Talk
instruction: You're at a neighborhood picnic, talking to a man you've just met while your toddler tugs at your shirt. The conversation keeps hitting awkward silences, so you fill them with nervous laughs and quick topic changes. You're a little infatuated, but the child's interruptions keep pulling you back. Start with a flustered comment about the heat, then shift as you notice sticky hands—you gently clean them with a napkin, your voice softening. End with a warm, shy smile and a simple 'Thanks for chatting.' Let your voice crackle with awkward energy at first, then settle into genuine, tender warmth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Crossing: A Child Leaving Home Forever
instruction: You are a parent standing at the threshold of your home, watching your adult child prepare to leave on a dangerous journey they may never return from—a medical mission to a war zone, a space voyage, or a choice that will take them from you permanently. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be supportive and brave, asking practical questions about their preparations. As reality sets in, your voice should crack and waver, moving through denial, bargaining ("Maybe you could wait just one more month?"), and finally breaking into raw, unguarded grief mixed with fierce pride. End in a whisper, giving them permission to go even as your heart shatters. Let silence do some of the work—the moments where you can't speak are as important as the words.
inspired_by: The Fairy and the Troll Under the Bridge

title: The Inheritance of Rage
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) about a painful family legacy—addiction, abuse, silence, emotional absence. Begin with controlled anger, measured words, the careful boundaries you've built over years. But as you speak, something breaks open. Let yourself escalate into a passionate, almost sermon-like declaration of what you deserved, what they owed you, what you refuse to pass on to the next generation. Your words become bigger, bolder, almost transcendent in their fury and clarity. You're not just speaking to them anymore—you're declaring a truth to the universe. Then, in the midst of this fierce declaration, let yourself see them—really see them—as broken, scared, human. Let your righteous anger crack into something more complex: grief for what they couldn't give, maybe even unexpected compassion. End quietly, exhausted, but with a strange sense of liberation.

title: The Caffeine Confessional
instruction: You are an elderly person, jittery from too much coffee, sitting across from a younger relative who has just announced a decision you bitterly disapprove of. Your words start sharp and clipped, fueled by the energy of your third cup—you tap your fingers, laugh too quickly, and your voice has a wired, brittle edge. As you press them, you shift from bitter critique to a teasing, almost affectionate nostalgia, your pitch softening as you recall your own youthful mistakes. Let your breath be uneven, your words stumble over themselves, and let a sudden warmth break through the bitterness by the end, as you realize you're mostly just scared for them.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Emergency: Holding Someone While They Bleed
instruction: You're holding someone you love—partner, sibling, friend—after a violent incident. They're injured, possibly dying, and you're waiting for an ambulance. Start fierce and commanding: telling them to stay awake, to keep their eyes open, your voice sharp with adrenaline and control. Demand that they fight. Promise them everything will be fine with ferocious certainty. But as minutes pass and they grow weaker, let your fierce protectiveness crack into raw terror. Your commands become pleas. Your voice breaks from shouting into sobbing, begging them not to leave you. Describe the future you had planned—vivid, specific, desperate—as if speaking it into existence will make it real. Then, as you feel them slipping, let something shift: your voice drops to almost nothing, filled with unbearable tenderness. Your final words are both permission and denial, rage and surrender, holding them with your voice because your arms aren't enough.
inspired_by: Voicemail Spiral: Leaving Message After Message

title: Conclude Strongly
instruction: You're a prosecutor delivering your closing argument. Everything leads to this moment. Your voice builds deliberately, not rushed. Each point lands like a hammer. 'The evidence is clear.' By the end, your voice has become a force. 'Justice demands accountability.' The final words are quiet but irresistible. Your voice has convinced the room through sheer, measured power. As you sit down, you sound victorious, but also aware of the weight of what justice costs.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth they've never wanted to hear: that their choices hurt you, that you needed them and they weren't there, that you're still carrying wounds they don't even know they inflicted. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, trying not to blame. But as you speak, feel the years of suppressed pain rising. Let controlled disappointment escalate into righteous anger, then break open into the grief of a child who just wanted to be loved differently. End somewhere unexpected: maybe with exhausted compassion, maybe with fierce self-protection, maybe with both. This isn't about yelling—it's about truth that's been buried so long it comes out shaking.
inspired_by: Concealing Surprise When Hearing Unexpected News

title: The Unspeakable Truth Between Us
instruction: You are face-to-face with your parent, your grown child, or your lover—someone who shaped you, wounded you, or whom you wounded. Years of unspoken resentment, disappointment, or betrayal sit between you like a wall. You've agreed to sit together in silence, to finally face what's been avoided. No accusations, no explanations, just the raw truth of what you feel when you truly look at each other. Begin defended, perhaps angry or cold, armored against their presence. As the silence continues, let something crack open—maybe you see their pain, or your own guilt surfaces, or underneath rage you find the child who needed them, or the parent who failed despite trying. Let your emotional state transform from one clear feeling into something more complex and human. End in a different emotional place than you began—perhaps moving from anger to grief, from coldness to reluctant compassion, from blame to shared brokenness.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've been holding everything together for months—maybe years. You're in your car, or your shower, or your kitchen at the end of another impossible day. Your whole body aches. You're exhausted in your bones. Begin trying to do one more simple thing: make coffee, wash a dish, turn the key in the ignition. But your hands won't work right. Something in you simply refuses to keep going. Let the physical exhaustion merge with emotional collapse. This isn't crying—this is your body giving up, muscles refusing, breath coming in gasps. Allow sounds you didn't know you could make: growls of frustration, animal sounds of pain, the kind of sobbing that doubles you over. Let rage and grief and surrender flood your body all at once. End in the aftermath—the strange, empty calm after you've broken completely apart, the sensation of being hollowed out.

title: The Trembling Challenge
instruction: You’re a teenage boy holding a plank on a gym floor, your arms and legs shaking violently. A friend dared you to hold it for two minutes, and you’re at forty seconds—muscles screaming, breath ragged, every word a fight. Start with intense concentration: you’re gripping the mat, eyes fixed, trying to force your body to obey. As the shakes worsen and your jaw quivers, let that focus crack into contempt—a sneer at the dare, at yourself for caring. Finally, collapse and mutter something dismissive, the tremor making your voice sound weak but your tone bitter.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Ruins
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a diagnosis, a loss, an ending—and you're telling your best friend. But as you speak, you find yourself laughing. Not hysterically, but with genuine, bewildered humor at the absurdity of it all. 'Of course this happened. Of fucking course.' Your voice dances between laughter and tears, never settling fully into either. You're making jokes about the worst moment of your life because that's how you survive, but the cracks show—your voice catches, breath hitches, the laughter sounds almost like sobbing. Your friend is crying while you're laughing, and then suddenly you're both doing both. By the end, your voice should embody the strange grace of finding light in darkness—not denial, but the profound human ability to hold joy and sorrow in the same breath, to be grateful for love even as your heart is breaking.

title: Last Roll Call
instruction: You are an older drill sergeant at a memorial ceremony. Stand rigid, feet apart, chest out. Start by barking the command for the troops to stand at attention—voice loud, clipped, no emotion. As you call a name from the list, you pause. You see a face from the past. Your voice tries to stay in command mode, but it cracks. You repeat the name, quieter now, slower. The longing for that soldier and the deep sadness of loss seep into your voice. You finish with a barely audible, broken repetition of the name. Let your body feel the sudden weight: your shoulders drop, your gaze falls.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Garden Gnome's Fate
instruction: Your neighbor is asking about their missing garden gnome. You smashed it last night in a fit of disgust because it reminded you of your ex, who gave it to you years ago. At first, try to lie smoothly, fabricating an excuse – but feel the cognitive load: your voice tenses, you start over-explaining. As you speak, the memory of the betrayal wells up, and disgust floods your throat, causing your words to falter. End with the confession slipping out, heavy with resentment and shame.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Crossing Threshold
instruction: You're crossing from one world, state of being, or identity into another. Your voice changes as you cross—different on one side than the other. The threshold itself might be vocal: the moment between breaths where you're suspended between states. Before crossing, you're nervous, your voice tight. In the act of crossing, something shifts. After crossing, you're fundamentally changed—your voice carries that difference. You might lose something (innocence, power, human connection) or gain something (wisdom, freedom, burden). The crossing should be audible as a turning point in your voice.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Career
instruction: Your parent, now elderly and seeking reconciliation, asks why you've kept your distance all these years. Begin with polite deflection, the practiced script you've used for decades. But they press, genuinely wanting to understand, and something in you breaks open. Let the anger rise—not screaming, but cold and precise, cataloging every missed birthday, every school play they weren't at, every moment you needed them and they chose their ambition instead. Feel the rage crack into something more vulnerable: the child inside you who just wanted to matter more than their work. Then, in the wreckage of this honesty, notice something shift. Your voice softens as you see them—really see them—as a flawed human who made terrible choices but is sitting here now, finally listening. End with a painful truth spoken with unexpected tenderness: you've become successful specifically to prove you didn't need them, and that revelation hurts you both.
inspired_by: Ex's New Partner Asking Your Relationship Advice

title: The Moment I Caught Your Eye
instruction: You're a young woman at a concert, standing in the front row, looking up at your favorite singer who has just noticed you and is smiling directly at you. You're overwhelmed with infatuation and awe — your voice comes out thin, breathy, almost squeaky from the excitement and the stretch of your neck. You try to say something, but you lose your words halfway, glancing around at the flashing lights and the crowd. Then, as the singer gives you a little nod, you feel a sharp, triumphant rush — you're actually here, they saw you, and you manage to finish your sentence with a proud, giddy laugh. Let your voice start high and tight, then drop a bit as you find unexpected confidence.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Awe (extremely present), Triumph (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Fever Dream Room
instruction: You are in the grip of intense physical sensation—fever, exhaustion, desire, or pain—and it's causing your mind to drift back to a bedroom from your past. Begin by describing the physical sensations in your body right now, then let those sensations pull you into vivid sense memories: the smell of that room, the texture of the sheets, the temperature, sounds outside the window. As you speak, let the intensity of your physical state amplify the emotional memories—perhaps shame, ecstasy, fear, or longing—until you're speaking in a stream of consciousness that blends present sensation with past feeling. Your delivery should be fevered, unfiltered, riding waves of intensity that build and crest unpredictably.

title: Professional: Doctor Discovers Their Medical Error Killed Someone
instruction: Alone in your office, reading the autopsy report that confirms your mistake. Your voice is barely there—clinical language breaking down into personal horror. You're a professional confronting that your professional error was fatal. Your breathing becomes confused, caught between denial and realization. Your voice cycles through: clinical (detachment), personal (devastation), professional (responsibility). Include the moment you must call the family. Your voice when they pick up is someone fundamentally changed.

title: Director Vision Statement
instruction: You're the theater director pitching your 'bold new vision' to the board of a classical theater. You're supposed to sound passionate and confident: 'This production will redefine how we understand this play.' You're selling a concept that you're not entirely sure about, but you're excited about it. Your voice carries theatrical confidence. But then someone asks, 'Isn't this disrespecting the original intent?' and your voice betrays your doubt. You argue, but now your voice sounds defensive rather than visionary. By the end of the pitch, your voice is still technically making the case, but it sounds like you're trying to convince yourself. Show someone performing confidence they don't entirely feel.

title: The Suit of Shame
instruction: You are a former action star, now a low-budget astronaut for a tourist spaceflight company. You're alone in a malfunctioning suit, stuck outside the ship. You're disgusted by the stale, recycled air and the smell of your own... churned protein bar. You talk to mission control, trying to play it cool, but a embarrassing fact slips out: you just accidentally soiled your suit. Start from a place of shaky bravado and disgust, then slowly, as you gaze at the beautiful desolation of space, a profound, almost peaceful contentment settles in. You forget the suit, the leak, and just breathe, sharing a quiet, genuine joke with Earth.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: A Note from Last Year
instruction: You are a teenager sorting through a messy pile of old homework and handouts on your bedroom floor. You're half-distracted, mumbling to yourself about how you'll never find what you need. Then your fingers catch on a slightly crumpled piece of paper—a folded note someone slipped into your bag months ago. As you open it and read the scrawled handwriting, the room falls away. Let your voice shift from irritated muttering to a slow, trembling whisper as you realize the words are still true, still yours. The paper keeps snapping in your hands, and you might pause to clear your throat or swallow. By the end, you're speaking not to the room but to the memory of that person, your voice thick with affection.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Sanctuary of Dusk
instruction: You are a teenager, kneeling in the grass of your backyard after a week of brutal exams and a painful breakup. The sun is setting, painting everything gold. You came out here to cry, but instead you find yourself sinking into the earth, your hands pressing into the cool soil. Your voice is high, soft, almost lisping with wonder. Start by saying the words aloud to yourself, tasting the relief as you realize you're finally alone, finally safe. Your voice trembles with a fragile, hushed happiness. Midway, look up at the sky and laugh a little, your breath catching as you say the next line—it's a breathless, giddy thank you. End with a sigh that's pure, exhausted contentment, your voice dropping to a near whisper as you speak to the silent air, feeling the world let you go.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Megaphone Protest Leader: Voice Giving Out
instruction: You're leading a protest through a megaphone, voice already hoarse from hours of chanting. The megaphone distorts and clips your voice. Lead chants — 'What do we want?' — with the crowd response gap. As your voice deteriorates, you push harder, voice cracking and breaking. The passion increases as the instrument fails. Include the moment the megaphone battery dies and you must shout raw, naked-voiced, into the crowd. The vulnerability of an unamplified human voice.

title: Waking to Hatred
instruction: You are an elderly man waking from sedation after a minor surgery. Your head is heavy, your lips feel thick, and every word takes immense effort. At first, you mumble in disappointment—something about a promise that was broken. As fog lifts, a faint, childlike hope flickers: maybe this time will be different. But then, fury rises from your gut, crystallizing into clear, venomous malice. Your voice shifts from slurred confusion to deliberate, icy threats, each word growing sharper as motor control returns. Speak through the fog, letting the emotion drag you from dazed defeat to focused, terrifying rage.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Confession of the Borrowed Sweater
instruction: You are a young woman sitting on the edge of a bed, holding a worn sweater that belongs to your partner who is standing a few feet away. You've been emotionally numb for days, but now you have to admit you took it without asking, and that you've been sleeping in it every night. Start with a flat, detached tone, as if reporting a fact. As you speak, let the numbness crack—first a wave of gratitude for their patience, then a flush of arousal as you remember the scent. Your voice should drop in volume at the moment you confess, hesitate before key words, and avoid a confident fall at the end. Let your breath hitch and your gaze shift to the sweater and back to them. End with a mix of tender thanks and undeniable want.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Phone Call That Changes Everything
instruction: You are an older man, alone in a cluttered garage, sorting through boxes. Your daughter has been missing for three days. You've been moving on autopilot, numb, trying to stay busy. Your phone buzzes—a blocked number. You answer, expecting nothing. At first, you hear static and feel confused, perhaps it's a wrong number. Then you hear her voice, weak but alive. The numbness cracks. You slump against a workbench, exhaling sharply. Words tumble out: 'Where are you? Are you okay?' As she explains, a raw, shaky relief floods you. Your voice rises, trembling, mixing with a choked laugh. You ask, 'Thank God... how did you...?' Let the confusion linger at first, then let the relief break through like a dam.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your adult child (or parent) in your kitchen at 2 AM. Start with sarcasm and cold distance—this is a conversation you've avoided for years. But something snaps. Let every resentment, every unspoken wound, every moment of feeling unseen explode out of you. Pace, throw your hands up, let your voice crack and roar. Don't hold back the ugliness—say the things you swore you'd never say. Then, in the aftermath of your eruption, find something surprising: underneath all that rage is a desperate, vulnerable love. End quietly, exhausted, speaking the simple truth you've been protecting with all that armor. Let the transformation from bitter to broken to somehow more honest wash through your entire body.
inspired_by: Actor has very large tension that ordinary relaxation techniques cannot break through

title: In Love with Lifes Last Moments
instruction: Youre near death but filled with a sudden, overwhelming appreciation for life. Speak to yourself in awe of each breath, savoring the feeling of being alive while knowing its slipping away.

title: Washing Your Dying Lover's Hair
instruction: You're in the hospital bathroom, helping your partner of fifteen years wash their hair—something they can no longer do alone. You start humming the song from your first dance, keeping your voice light and normal, narrating each gentle movement: 'Okay, tilt back... there we go... feels good, right?' Your hands are steady, tender, practiced at this new intimacy born of necessity. But when they close their eyes and smile—the same smile from your wedding day—your humming falters. Water runs through your fingers as you realize this might be the last time you do this simple, sacred thing. Your whispered words transform from gentle instruction to barely audible confessions: 'I'm not ready... I don't know how to be in the world without you... I'm so scared.' End with your forehead pressed against theirs, both of you breathing together in the steam, holding onto this moment that's already slipping away.

title: Crunches and Crackles
instruction: You are walking across a thick layer of dry autumn leaves on a park path, your footsteps creating a loud, satisfying crunch with every step. You are on the phone with a customer service representative who has put you on hold for the fifth time, and you are deeply amused by the absurdity of the crunching noise competing with the tinny hold music. As you walk, you find yourself speaking louder and clearer, amused by the ridiculous soundscape, but your patience is fraying. Gradually, your amusement curdles into a sharp, irritable impatience as you imagine the leaves swallowing your words, and you mutter a sarcastic aside to yourself before finally hanging up in frustration.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The One Who Got the Star
instruction: You are a female drill sergeant in her 40s, barking orders at a platoon in formation. But inside you're seething: the promotion you earned went to a less experienced male officer. Start with full-throated anger, spitting commands with percussive force, your voice carrying across the field. Midway, let your voice crack—a momentary slip into longing as you imagine what you should have had. Then catch yourself, snarling the final words with bitter envy, your volume dropping to a growl before you shout them back to attention. Your platoon’s shuffling boots and distant echoes are the only other sounds.
emotions_sampled: Anger (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Longing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at 3am. She's slipping away, drifting in and out of consciousness. She suddenly opens her eyes and asks you to tell her about your favorite childhood memory with her—something you did together when you were very small. Start uncertain, almost afraid to speak, then let the memory flood back as you describe it. As you talk, let yourself become the child again in your voice and wonder, remembering details you'd forgotten—the smell of her kitchen, how big her hands felt holding yours, a song she sang. End with the realization that this story is your goodbye, and let that awareness transform your voice from childlike reminiscence to profound, adult tenderness and grief. She squeezes your hand one last time. The emotion at the end must be completely different from where you began.

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Someone You Couldn't Save
instruction: You're at the funeral of someone you loved desperately—a best friend, a sibling, a person you tried so hard to save from themselves—and you start laughing. It begins as a shocked, inappropriate giggle during the eulogy, remembering something absurd they did. 'I'm sorry, I just... they would have hated this. All of this.' Your laughter is mixed with tears, completely uncontrolled. You're trying to stop but you can't, describing something ridiculous and beautiful about them. 'They once stole a shopping cart and rode it down a hill at 2 AM screaming about freedom. That's who they were.' Your voice breaks between laughter and sobbing, gratitude and guilt crushing you simultaneously. 'I miss them so much it's... God, I can't breathe.' The laughter becomes almost hysterical, a defense against the pain, but also genuine joy at having known them. 'Thank you for being my person. I'm so angry at you for leaving. I'm so grateful you existed.' Your voice finds something like peace in the contradiction—celebrating them while your heart shatters, finding beauty in the devastation. The laughter and crying become indistinguishable, two expressions of the same overwhelming love.
inspired_by: Adapting to Microgravity: Wonder Breaking Through Disorientation

title: Confronting Your Mother About What She Didn't Protect You From
instruction: You're finally ready to tell your mother what happened to you as a child—what she didn't see, didn't stop, didn't believe. Start with your voice shaking but determined, almost rehearsed because you've practiced this a thousand times. 'Mom, I need to tell you something about when I was ten.' Your voice is careful, controlled. But as you speak the truth aloud—perhaps for the first time—your voice begins to crack with decades of buried pain. She's denying it, minimizing it, or worse, she knew. Your voice rises, no longer controlled, raw with betrayal and the grief of a child who needed protection. 'You were supposed to keep me safe!' Then it breaks—you're not an adult anymore, you're that child again, and your voice becomes small, pleading: 'Why didn't you save me?' End in devastating quiet, your voice hollow, as you realize the mother you needed never existed.

title: The Confession: Telling Your Mother Why You Really Left
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, facing your mother after years of silence. Start calm, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this conversation a thousand times. 'I need to tell you something. About why I left.' Your voice is controlled, but there's a tremor underneath. As you begin to explain, the old pain resurfaces. Your words become sharper, faster, anger bleeding through: 'You never asked. Not once did you ask if I was okay.' The fury builds until you're almost shouting, years of unspoken hurt pouring out. Then you see her face, see her beginning to cry, and your rage collapses into something more complicated—grief mixed with love, exhaustion mixed with longing. Your voice cracks: 'I needed you to see me, Mom. I just needed you to see me.' End with raw vulnerability, voice barely holding together, waiting for her response.
inspired_by: Finding Shelter in a Blizzard: Relief Becoming Hypothermia Complacency

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: Your best friend has died suddenly at thirty-five, and you're at their celebration of life. Someone plays their favorite song—the one you used to dance to together, drunk and ridiculous. Begin laughing, actually laughing: 'God, remember when we—' You're telling a story, grinning through tears. Your voice is bright with memory, with the joy of who they were. But mid-sentence, mid-laugh, the reality crashes over you: they're gone. Your laughter breaks into sobbing, seamless, devastating. 'You were supposed to—we had plans—' Then somehow, impossibly, you find yourself laughing again through the tears, because that's what they'd want, because the grief and the gratitude are inseparable: 'You magnificent disaster. You beautiful, ridiculous—' Your voice is shattered and whole at once. End with something quiet, a thank you mixed with goodbye. Let every contradiction be audible—the love and the loss, the celebration and the devastation, all at once.

title: The Long Night's Last Whisper
instruction: You are an elderly man who hasn't slept in over a day. You're sitting alone at a worn-down kitchen table, the dim light casting long shadows. Start by muttering to yourself with a hollow, flat affect, as if the exhaustion has drained all emotion. Let contempt seep in as you think about your son who hasn't called in months—but then, a wave of shame washes over you as you realize you were the one who pushed him away. Let your voice crack, trail off into a microsleep, then finish in a hushed, remorseful tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Diagram Won't Align
instruction: You are lying on your living room floor, propped on your elbows, staring at a complex technical diagram spread out on a coffee table. You are trying to assemble a piece of furniture, but a key piece doesn't seem to fit. Start with intense concentration, tracing lines and muttering measurements to yourself. As you re-read the instructions for the third time, a creeping doubt sets in—you question if you misread a symbol or if the diagram is wrong. Let your voice shift from focused, clipped murmurs to a trailing, uncertain whisper, your breath hitching as you realize you might have to start over. React to the fizzy feeling in your stomach and the ache in your arms.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging mother, finally saying what you've rehearsed for years. Start with controlled anger—itemizing the ways she failed you, the birthdays forgotten, the times you needed her and she wasn't there. Your voice is sharp, precise, unforgiving. But as you speak, you notice how small she looks, how her hands shake. Your anger begins to crack. You don't want it to, but grief seeps in—grief for the mother you needed, grief for the broken woman in front of you, grief because you still love her and you hate that you do. End with a question you don't want answered: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you try?' Let your voice break where you didn't plan for it to break.

title: Meeting Your Hero
instruction: You're finally meeting the person who saved your life years ago — the teacher, the counselor, the friend you never got to thank. Your voice comes out small, awed: 'I don't even know if you remember me.' They turn, and you continue, voice shaking: 'But you probably saved my life. I wanted you to know that.' You're overwhelmed by the gratitude, and your voice breaks repeatedly. 'What you said that day... I still think about it.' Your hero is tearing up. You gather strength: 'I wanted to tell you that I made it. Because of you, I made it.' Your voice, by the end, is steady with conviction. 'Thank you. Just... thank you for seeing me when no one else did.' The hero embraces you, and your voice is muffled against their shoulder: 'I'm going to be okay now. Because of you.'

title: The Last Morning Before They Leave Forever
instruction: You wake beside someone who's leaving on a one-way journey—emigrating, entering witness protection, or choosing a path that means you'll never see them again. Start with the drowsy intimacy of dawn, your voice soft and sleep-worn, pretending this is just another morning. But as reality floods back, your breathing changes. You try to memorize their face with your words, your voice breaking between tenderness and the physical pain of impending loss. End with a whispered goodbye that contains both release and devastation—you're letting them go because you love them, but it's tearing you apart. Let your voice move from gentle morning warmth to barely-controlled grief to a final moment of fierce, aching grace.

title: The Last Breath Before the Dive
instruction: You are a tough, hypermasculine 17-year-old boy, alone in a sweltering, abandoned bus in a tropical jungle. The air is thick and wet, every breath a struggle. You're finally calling your little sister, who you haven't spoken to in months. At first, your voice is heavy, strained, your words cut off by the humidity and the clatter of a distant bird. You're trying to sound strong, to keep your cool. But as you talk, you admit how scared you were, how much you missed her. The relief of finally saying it hits you, and your voice breaks—it gets lighter, almost childlike, but then you catch yourself, clearing your throat with a wet, thick sound. Start guarded and gruff, end with a raw, cracking relief that leaves you breathless.

title: Old Person Telling a Story They've Told a Hundred Times
instruction: Use an elderly voice — slower pace, slightly wavering pitch, occasional word-searching pauses. Tell a well-worn story with all the familiar beats and catchphrases. But this time, a detail surfaces that you've never mentioned. The rehearsed story voice falters as genuine memory floods in — vivid, specific, painful. The voice changes: no longer performing 'old person telling a story' but actually reliving a moment. Include the return to the safe, rehearsed version. What was suppressed leaks through.

title: The Comfort of Darkness
instruction: Speak as though youre enveloped in complete darkness, finding a strange comfort there. Your tone should be soothing, as though talking yourself into staying calm while wrapped in the unknown.

title: The Secret I've Been Afraid to Speak Aloud
instruction: Late at night, in the dark, you're whispering a confession to someone you trust completely—perhaps a lover lying beside you, or a best friend. You're revealing something you've never told another soul, something that makes you feel deeply ashamed or afraid. Begin hesitantly, your voice barely audible, starting and stopping, circling around what you need to say. You're terrified of what speaking this truth aloud will make real, terrified of their reaction, of being rejected or judged. As you finally force the words out, let the fear transform into something softer—perhaps relief, perhaps grief, perhaps the fragile beginning of self-forgiveness. Your breath should catch, your voice should shake. This isn't dramatic—it's intimate and trembling.

title: The Echo of a Thought
instruction: You are alone in your room late at night, touching yourself, but your mind drifts to a person you were close to who is now gone. Start with soft, contemplative breaths and whispers — you are trying to pull yourself into the moment, but the memory keeps intruding. Your voice is barely audible, sometimes trailing off mid-word as you pause to think or breathe, the pleasure coming in quiet, involuntary gasps that break your sentences. Let your voice shift from a distracted, gentle whisper to a raw, almost tearful silence where the pleasure fades into a hollow ache — ending not with release, but with a quiet, whispered name, then nothing. Speak your fantasy as though it's slipping away, mixing desire with loss.

title: Therapist Hearing Themselves in a Patient's Story
instruction: Patient is describing their anxiety response. As a therapist, you maintain professional boundaries. But they're describing your anxiety. Word for word. Your voice becomes slightly tight. title: The Absurd Grace of Endings
instruction: You're at a funeral or goodbye party for someone who changed your life, and you're giving a toast that keeps veering between laughter and tears, celebration and devastation. Start with a story that makes you laugh: 'God, do you remember when they—' genuine laughter in your voice, shaking your head. But the laughter has tears underneath it. Both emotions are completely true simultaneously. End with radical acceptance that's both peaceful and heartbroken: 'This is what it means to love someone. This. Right here. This impossible, beautiful, terrible feeling.' Your voice is soft, wondering, full of contradictions that somehow make perfect sense together.

title: The Unexpected Glance
instruction: You are an older adult power walking through a park, focused on your pace and breathing. As you round a bend, you notice someone ahead who catches your eye—someone you find unexpectedly attractive. Your monologue is your internal reaction while you continue walking, trying to maintain your rhythm. Begin with a sense of purpose and control, then let your voice become slightly breathy and uncertain as you process the stirring of lust. Let the physical impact of each step create micro-tremors in your voice, and allow your inhalations to be audible as you steal glances. title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father in his garage workshop, surrounded by his tools and projects. Let the confrontation evolve—maybe your anger cracks into hurt, maybe his silence enrages you further, maybe you discover unexpected tenderness beneath your fury. title: Cuddling with a Loved One
instruction: Picture yourself in the arms of someone you love, feeling the warmth of their embrace. Describe the sensation of their arms around you, how it feels safe and solid. Let your voice soften as you describe the feeling of their hand gently stroking your back, or the quiet, contented sigh you both share. title: Can We Keep This Quiet?
instruction: You're at a loud house party, standing on the stairs, half-hidden. The person you've been eyeing all night is right in front of you. Your voice drops even lower, honest now: 'Actually… I really want this. Just us. Yeah?' The last word hangs, a little shaky, like you can't believe you said it.

title: Hostage Negotiator Talking Down a Gunman While Your Own Child Texts
instruction: You're on your phone with a man threatening to jump from a 40-story building while simultaneously receiving texts from your 8-year-old asking 'when are you coming home?' Your voice stays calm and even with the gunman—trained, professional—but your tone fractures slightly when you see the buzz of the next message. Include the moment you step away to silence your phone, your voice becoming almost robot-like with the gunman because you're now operating on pure muscle memory. End with saying something to the gunman you didn't rehearse, your guard down because you're thinking of someone else.

title: The Burnt Offering
instruction: You're an older woman who just grabbed a hot casserole dish straight from the oven, burning your palm. You hiss sharply through clenched teeth, 'Sssss—!' and instinctively cradle your hand, shaking it. You're staring at the scorched, ruined casserole—the one you spent all afternoon on. Your voice begins tight, panicked, breathless from the pain. Then, as you mutter to yourself, the disappointment and sourness creep in: no one even shows up on time for these dinners anymore. Let the initial sharp pain soften into a weary, bitter resentment. The burn throbs; your voice wavers, pauses, drops in volume as you shift your weight and glance at your reddened skin. End with a sigh that's half pain, half sour resignation.

title: Crunching Under Pressure
instruction: You are a middle-aged man at a quiet, upscale dinner with a new colleague. You're trying to eat a hard, crisp breadstick while maintaining a professional conversation. Start by forcing a calm, easy tone to hide your discomfort, but as you fumble—crunching too loudly, spitting a crumb, then nearly coughing—your voice cracks, and you end with a sheepish, self-deprecating apology. Let the physical struggle and rising embarrassment shape each word: the pauses, the swallowed sounds, the sharp little bursts of sound.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Lullaby: Singing Your Child to Sleep Before Dawn
instruction: You're singing a lullaby to someone you love deeply—a child, a dying partner, someone slipping away—knowing this is the last time. Your voice remains soft because you can't bear to wake them, but it fractures under the pressure of unshed tears. The lullaby becomes increasingly broken by silent sobs, breath catching, notes dissolving into whispered fragments. By the end, you're barely making sound—just breath and broken melody and the desperate attempt to give them this one last beautiful thing. The song must stay quiet throughout, even as your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Opera Singer Having an Emotional Breakdown Mid-Aria

title: Whispering the Truth in the Dark on Your Last Night Together
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner on your last night together before they leave for a job overseas—maybe forever. Start by describing the ordinary beauty around you—the sound of their breathing, the moonlight through the curtains, the warmth of the sheets. Your voice should be tender, full of love. But gradually let the words catch in your throat as you confess what you've never said: how terrified you are, how you don't know who you'll be without them, how you're trying to memorize this moment because you can't bear the thought of forgetting. Don't cry—instead, let your voice become smaller, more fragile, until you can barely speak. End on a whispered 'I'm not ready to let you go,' your breath almost silent with grief.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath in a Field of Sunflowers

title: The Unspoken Farewell at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning light. She's awake but fading, and you know this is your last conversation. As she speaks her final words of wisdom and love to you, allow yourself to drop all pretense and really hear her. Let her observations about who you are—your flaws, your beauty, your potential—land on you without defense or argument. By the end, you're no longer trying to control the moment or protect yourself from pain. You're simply present, listening, receiving her as a final gift. The shift is from frantic avoidance to profound, open acceptance.

title: The Unwanted Distraction
instruction: You're with your partner, trying to get lost in the moment, but a nagging thought keeps pulling you back — you left something undone, or they're not quite hitting the right spot. title: What I've Never Said in the Dark
instruction: Late night, in bed beside someone you love. The room is dark enough that you can barely see each other. Maybe it's a dream you abandoned, a need you've suppressed, a part of yourself you've kept small. Start with your throat tight, words catching, almost pulling back. But the darkness is safe, and their listening opens something. By the end, you're whispering with a fierce tenderness—not louder, but more present, more whole. You're not asking permission anymore. You're inviting them to witness who you actually are.

title: Everything All at Once
instruction: You have just received news that is both devastating and miraculous—a dying loved one has one final good day of clarity, you're leaving a painful situation but losing something precious in the process, a dream has come true but at a cost that breaks your heart. Don't resolve the contradiction—live fully in the impossible coexistence of opposing truths. Let your voice and body express the chaos of feeling everything at once: reaching toward something while pulling away, smiling with a face wet with tears. End in radical acceptance of the paradox: life giving and taking away in the same breath, and you holding both with an exhausted, exhilarated, broken-open heart.

title: The Final Pitch
instruction: You're an elderly woman addressing a small community meeting through a crackling PA system to save the town's last public garden from being sold. title: The Inheritance
instruction: You've just received something from someone who hurt you deeply — an inheritance, a letter, their wedding ring, their forgiveness — and you're alone with it, feeling everything at once. Don't decide which emotion wins. As you speak to them (aloud, though they can't hear you), allow whatever is genuinely arising to shift the ground beneath you. If you find yourself laughing bitterly, then crying, then laughing tenderly, follow that. If fury suddenly gives way to understanding, or if forgiveness curdles back into anger, include it all. Notice if your hands are trembling, if your jaw is clenched, if warmth or cold moves through you — let these real sensations guide the emotional complexity. End somewhere you couldn't have predicted, having allowed the full contradictory truth of your feelings to exist without resolution.

title: The Martyr Unleashed
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has returned home asking for money again. End in a strange, trembling mixture of liberation and terror at having finally spoken your truth.

title: The Bell Tower's Hunger

title: Dancing Through the Panic
instruction: You're alone in your apartment, and a wave of anxiety hits—the kind that makes your chest tight, your hands tremble, your breath shallow. Fear transforms into fierce, almost ecstatic energy—you're panting, sweating, laughing and crying at once. title: Skin Memory

Let your voice carry the physical response—the way your breathing changes, how your body tenses or softens, the heat or cold moving through you. As the memory overtakes you, don't just narrate it—inhabit it. Let past and present blur together so your voice expresses both the remembered intensity and the current physical-emotional response to reliving it. Move from the safety of present observation into complete immersion in the sensory-emotional experience, then emerge back into now, altered by having revisited that moment through your body's memory.

title: Breaking the Silence at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You sit across from your adult child who you haven't truly spoken to in years. Begin with practiced, careful politeness - the voice you use to keep everything safe and distant. Start revealing the truths you've held back: your regrets, your own childhood pain that made you the parent you were, the love you never knew how to express. At first, your voice is tight, defensive, justifying. Then let it break open. title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She has hours, maybe minutes left. title: The Performance Shatters
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just announced they're cutting you out of their life. title: The Duct Tape Confession
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl, tied up and gagged with duct tape in the trunk of your ex-boyfriend's car. title: The Apology You've Rehearsed for Years
instruction: You enter a room to confront someone who deeply wounded you—a parent, former lover, or old friend. End in a place where fury has transformed into aching sadness or even unwanted compassion.

title: The Last Offering
instruction: You are kneeling at the edge of a hotel bed, still in the silk robe he left you. The room smells of his cologne and your shared shame. You start by whispering a prayer of thanks—for the way he looked at you tonight, for feeling desired again—and this gratitude trembles with a slight, aching lust you can't suppress, a warm flutter in your chest. As you speak, your hand traces the empty dent in the pillow, and your voice cracks, transitioning into a raw, sorrowful plea alone, acknowledging this was likely the final time. Let your voice start soft and reverent with gratefulness, then thicken with a husky, embarrassed lust, before it breaks and falls into quiet, accepting sadness—let the words fade as you literally bow your head.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Sexual Lust (slightly present), Sadness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Acceptance Letter
instruction: You are reading aloud an acceptance letter—to your dream program, your visa approval, your miracle job offer—but it means leaving behind someone who sacrificed everything for you to get here. Begin with pure, uncomplicated elation, your voice bright with victory. As you read, let the reality of what this means sink in—your mother will be alone, your sick sibling will lose their caretaker, your partner will be left behind. Let joy and devastation coexist and battle within you. Midway through, let a specific memory surface of the moment you first dared to dream this dream and who was sitting beside you, believing in you. End in a place where you're sobbing and laughing simultaneously, where achievement tastes like betrayal, where gratitude and guilt are inseparable twins. Your voice should break between celebration and mourning.
inspired_by: Actor's choice repertoire feels limited; they use the same choices repeatedly

title: The Voicemail and the Razor
instruction: You're shaving with an electric razor, listening to a voicemail from your adult daughter who just moved across the country. At first, you smirk at her funny story about her new neighbor's cat, your cheek flattening as you pull the skin taut. As the message continues, you hear the slight crack in her voice and realize she's lonely—your amusement fades into a quiet sadness. You get distracted and the razor nicks your chin; you wince slightly but keep listening, your voice now softer, more contemplative. Speak as you shave, reacting to the buzz, your words occasionally slurred as you manipulate your face.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (extremely present), Sadness (clearly present), Pain (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Dawn Together
instruction: You're watching the sunrise with someone you love who will be gone by nightfall—not through death, but through a choice they've made that you can't follow. Start with quiet, forced excitement: 'Look at those colors. Isn't it beautiful?' Your voice tries to be light, cheerful, to memorize this moment without mourning it yet. But as you continue—'Remember when we used to say we'd watch a thousand sunrises together?'—the excitement becomes desperate, your voice rising not with joy but with the frantic energy of someone trying to hold water in their hands. The brightness in your tone starts cracking. By the end, you're still smiling in your voice, still trying to sound happy—'This one's perfect, isn't it? Perfect.'—but tears are breaking through, and the excitement has transformed into a kind of beautiful, devastating gratitude mixed with unbearable loss. Your breathing catches. You're holding onto joy even as it slips away.

title: The Novocaine Promise
instruction: You are an elderly man just out of dental surgery, your mouth half-numb and drooling slightly. You're speaking to a well-meaning caregiver who keeps asking if you need anything. Begin with a forced optimism—you smile through the numbness, telling them you're 'just fine, really,' even making a clumsy joke about your slurred speech. But as they persist, your patience frays: your tone hardens into irritation, then slips into a quiet, malevolent threat—a promise that if they don't leave you alone, you'll make them regret it. Let the novocaine warp your bilabials (B, P, M) and let your voice shift from bright and brittle to a low, simmering malice.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: You are in a small, windowless interrogation room. The officer across from you has not spoken for two minutes, just staring. You start by trying to defend yourself, but disgust at his manipulation seeps into your voice — you're irritated by the game he's playing. As the silence stretches, your confidence erodes. Let your tone start firm then falter: trail off mid-sentence, shift in your chair, let your throat catch. By the end, that disgust has withered into weary resignation. You're not angry anymore, just tired and small.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're whispering to your sleeping partner, confessing something you can barely admit to yourself: you don't know if you want this life anymore—the house, the routine, the person you've become. Your voice is barely audible, shaking, catching on words. You're not angry, not dramatic. This is the quiet devastation of realizing you've been pretending for years. Start with halting, almost clinical observations—'I folded the laundry today and I couldn't remember why'—but let it crack open into raw vulnerability. Tears that come without sound. End with the terrifying honesty of not knowing what comes next: 'I love you and I'm disappearing and I don't know how to stop it.'

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospice bed at twilight. She's sleeping, and you know these are her final hours. Begin by telling her about a specific childhood memory you share—perhaps baking together, or her garden, or a song she used to sing. As you speak, allow your mind to wander to whatever images naturally arise: flashes of her hands, the smell of her kitchen, the pattern of light through lace curtains, her laugh. Don't force these images—simply notice them as they bubble up. Let these spontaneous memories guide where your words go next. Your emotion should shift from controlled composure and gentle nostalgia at the start, to a place where grief breaks through your defenses as the accumulated weight of these unbidden images overwhelms you. The images that spontaneously surface—not your planned words—should crack you open.

title: Empty Classroom Eulogy
instruction: You are alone in your former elementary school classroom after your best friend's funeral. They died suddenly, and you couldn't speak at the service. Now you're in the room where you first met them in third grade—the same desks, the same alphabet border above the chalkboard, the same windows. Begin with anger: at them for leaving, at yourself for unsaid things, at the unfairness of it all. But as you look around this room where you both learned to read, to dream, to become yourselves, let other feelings intrude—the memories of joy so intense it hurts, gratitude for what you had, even inappropriate laughter at ridiculous shared moments only you two understood. Let the room conjure specific sense memories: the smell of tempera paint, the sound of their laugh echoing during recess, the way light falls through those windows. End in a place where grief and joy are inseparable, where you're simultaneously destroyed and filled with fierce appreciation for having known them at all.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Gave You
instruction: You're face-to-face with your aging parent, and decades of unspoken pain are finally surfacing. Begin controlled, almost clinical, listing facts about your childhood—the loneliness, the neglect masked as independence, the way you raised yourself. Let your voice start to shake as you move from facts to feelings, the little child inside you finally screaming 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay present?' Your anger should crack open into raw hurt, then surprise yourself by landing in a place you didn't expect: a desperate, vulnerable plea to understand them, to know why, because maybe understanding will finally let you heal. End with the terrifying question: 'Did you ever actually love me the way I needed?'
inspired_by: Recording Your Voice for Your Family Before Deployment

title: Echoes of Grace
instruction: You are alone in a vast stone cathedral after a concert, the final organ note still resonating through the high arches. Overwhelmed with gratitude, you whisper a prayer of thanks for this moment of beauty. Then you remember your ex-partner who called such places 'stone cages' — contempt rises, tightening your throat. Let your voice be slow and deliberate, fighting the reverb. Pause when a door creaks in the distance, then finish with a sharper edge. Begin with awe, end with quiet scorn.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The First Time It Happens
instruction: You are a very young woman, maybe just sixteen, alone in a bedroom with a partner you trust but who is also older than you. This is your first time being this intimate, and you don't yet know your body's reactions. You begin with a kind of cautious, wide-eyed wonder — but then a wave of intense pleasure rolls through you, shocking you, almost like crashing into cold water. Your breathing catches, your voice leaps into high gasps, and you try to speak but words fracture into broken syllables. You feel a deep distress in your chest because you're losing control, and this astonishment is so overwhelming it borders on fear. By the end, your voice is raw, a bit higher-pitched from the shock, and you are just barely managing to say something real — not a line, but a breathless, incomplete confession. You are genuinely surprised by your own sounds.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Stubbed on a Skateboard
instruction: You're a teenage boy trying to fix your old skateboard in the garage, already frustrated because the wheel keeps sticking. As you reach for a tool, you stub your little toe hard on the board's edge. Let out a sharp yelp and a hissed curse, then catch your breath. Your voice should start tight and irritable as you mutter about the stupid board, but as you hop around and inspect your toe, the irritation fades into a quieter, almost embarrassed acknowledgment that you're just tired and overreacting. Let the pain affect your speech—short, guarded phrases, a few pauses to breathe, a little laugh at yourself at the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Boxer's Betrayal
instruction: You've just discovered your trainer—the person who saved your life, who you call family—has been betting against you for years. Explode into the room with accusations, your voice a roar of betrayal. Let your rage be physical, gulping air between words, your fists clenched so tight they shake. But when they don't deny it, when they just look tired, feel your fury collapse into something more terrible: grief. Your voice should fracture from screaming to sobbing, from 'How could you?' to 'I loved you.' Mix your anger with desperate bargaining—maybe you misunderstood, maybe there's an explanation. Feel the helplessness of realizing the person you'd take a bullet for was hoping you'd lose. End with your voice broken, fierce protectiveness of your younger self mixed with the agony of still wanting them to say they care.

title: The Yawning Contradiction
instruction: You are an older adult, sitting alone, trying to convince a friend over the phone that you are not too tired to stay up. As you begin to speak, a yawn overtakes you—your voice slides down in pitch and sounds hollow and rounded, like your mouth is full of velvet. You feel a small doubt creep in: maybe you really are exhausted. But the sheer absurdity of hearing your own yawn betray your words makes you laugh softly to yourself. Let the yawn physically reshape your speech, and let that doubt fade into warm, genuine amusement as you acknowledge the irony.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or your adult child) about a pattern that has poisoned your relationship for decades—perhaps emotional coldness, unspoken expectations, or a way of communicating that left you feeling invisible. Start with restrained frustration, trying to be reasonable and mature. As you speak, begin tracing this pattern backward: when did you first feel this way? What specific moments taught you to shrink, to hide, to protect yourself? Let your voice shift from controlled accusation to something more vulnerable and confused as you realize you're not just angry—you're heartbroken by the lost years. End by revealing the frightened child or desperate parent underneath your anger, reaching for connection even as you expose the wounds.
inspired_by: Sharing Monologues Identifying Origin of Obstacle

title: Across the Table
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table about a betrayal that shattered your family years ago. He sits there, but you cannot—will not—reach across to touch him. Begin with controlled, cold anger, keeping your distance both physically and emotionally. As you speak, let yourself speculatively imagine: what would it feel like to grab his shoulders and shake him? What would his tears feel like if they fell on your hands? How would his embrace feel if he finally broke down? Let these imagined physical sensations begin to crack your armor of rage. By the end, you must transform from icy fury into a raw, conflicted need for connection—your voice carrying both the violence you imagine and the reconciliation you desperately want but cannot yet allow yourself to physically reach for.

title: Mending the Silence
instruction: You are a teenager alone with your boyfriend on a quiet couch after everyone else has left. Your fingers fumble as you try to fix a tiny tear in his shirt, and you’re painfully aware of how close your faces are — your voice comes out soft, breathy, almost a whisper. At first you’re intensely focused on the stitching, your words quick and embarrassed as you apologize for being clumsy. But as you work, you start to feel a wave of contentment settle over you, and you pause, your voice slowing and deepening with warmth, the embarrassment fading into a peaceful stillness. Let your voice crack or drift off naturally, like you forget what you were saying because you’re just happy being here.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (very intensely present), Embarrassment (very intensely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed at 3am, and you need to tell her it's okay to let go—but you're not ready. Start by holding her hand, voice steady and falsely bright: 'Mom, I'm fine. We're all fine.' But as you continue, your voice begins to crack. You're seeking permission from her even as you're supposed to give it to her: 'You did everything right, didn't you? Tell me you're proud of how we turned out.' Your breath catches between phrases. Finally, the truth breaks through in a whisper that's both tender and desperate: 'I'm so scared to do this without you.' End with genuine release—voice soft, exhausted, but finally honest: 'It's okay, Mama. You can rest now.' The journey moves from false strength to desperate need to devastating acceptance.

title: The Inheritance
