instruction: You've just done something unforgivable to protect someone you love, and now you're confessing to them with explosive, uncontained emotion—but they don't understand why you're falling apart. Begin with fierce, almost violent protectiveness: 'I would burn the whole world down for you!' Your voice is shaking with intensity. But as you continue, the rage collapses into devastating helplessness—because what you did has changed you forever, made you into something they might not be able to love anymore. 'Don't you see? I did this FOR you!' Move from fury to sobbing, from power to complete vulnerability. Your breathing becomes ragged, uncontrolled. The realization hits: you've destroyed yourself to save them, and now they're looking at you like they don't know you. End in broken whispers, all the fight gone: 'Please don't leave me. I'm still here. I'm still...' Trail off, unsure if that's even true anymore.

title: Whispering the Secret You've Carried Alone
instruction: You are finally telling someone the secret you've held inside for years—a truth that has made you feel isolated, ashamed, or unbearably lonely. Begin in a near-whisper, your voice fragile and hesitant, carrying the weight of silence and fear of judgment. But as you speak, feel something shift: the act of confession itself becomes liberating, transformative. With each word, discover that speaking the truth aloud makes you stronger, not weaker. Let your voice gradually fill with quiet, radiant power—not loud, but solid, certain, free. End in a state of unexpected exhilaration and self-possession, as if releasing the secret has unlocked a fearless version of yourself you didn't know existed. The whisper becomes a declaration of self-acceptance and hard-won freedom.
inspired_by: Actor's ego state is significantly lower than the character's—character is supremely confident, powerful, or dominant

title: The Explosion at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You've been holding it together through the funeral, the condolences, the casseroles, being strong for everyone else. Now you're alone and something small—finding their handwriting on a grocery list—detonates everything you've been containing. Start with trying to hold it in, voice tight and controlled, almost talking yourself down. Then let it shatter—not performed, but truly losing control. Rage at the unfairness, sobbing their name, maybe even yelling at them for leaving. Your voice should be raw, ugly, completely unguarded. Midway, collapse into the helplessness underneath the anger—you'd give anything for one more conversation, one more ordinary moment. End in exhausted tenderness, speaking to them as if they're right there, finding strange peace in finally letting yourself fall completely apart.

title: The Crush of Defeat
instruction: You've just collapsed after a violent struggle — your body is limp against a cold wall, lungs heaving, every word a struggle. Start with a whisper of malice: a bitter, venomous edge toward the person you failed to catch or defeat. But as you speak through the gasps, shame bleeds in — you realize your own weakness is why you're here. Let the breathing dictate your rhythm: pauses mid-thought, a lost word, a weak shift of weight. End quieter, more vulnerable, the malice fading into self-disgust.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point in the Empty House
instruction: You're screaming at someone who isn't there anymore—they've left, and you're alone in the space you shared. Start with explosive rage, voice raw and loud, saying everything you couldn't say when they were standing in front of you. Accuse them, condemn them, let your voice shake with fury. But as you shout into the emptiness, something shifts. The rage begins to crack open and underneath is devastating helplessness. Your voice breaks, goes quiet, then surges again—but now it's desperation, not anger. You're begging the empty room. By the end, you've collapsed into sobbing words, fierce protectiveness for what you had mixed with the crushing realization that you couldn't save it. End with their name, said with such love and such agony that both are indistinguishable.

title: Bedside Confession to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner of ten years sleeps beside you, unaware this is your last night together. Tomorrow you're leaving—not for someone else, but because you've slowly realized you've been performing a version of yourself that isn't real, and you're suffocating. In a barely audible whisper, you confess everything to their sleeping form: how much you love them (you do), how you've tried to be who they needed (you have), and how you're dying inside (you are). Your voice catches as you describe the small moments of joy you'll miss. Touch their hair gently, memorizing their face. End with 'I'm so sorry' repeated like a prayer, knowing they'll wake to a note and an empty bed, and you're too much of a coward to say this to their waking eyes.

title: The Hole I'm Digging
instruction: You are an older man, furious and exhausted, digging a deep hole in your backyard to bury an old dog crate—a gift from your son who was supposed to come home but never did. Each shovel strike is a grunt of anger. Between breaths, you mutter to the dirt, your voice gritty and strained. Start with raw, percussive rage—the shovel hitting the ground matching your contempt for the waste. As you pause, bent over, the weight of disappointment settles in. Your final words come softer, more broken, a reluctant acceptance that the hole isn't just for the crate.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Contempt (extremely present), Disappointment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Valve-Click Legacy
instruction: You are an elderly woodworker in your dusty workshop, wearing a tight N95 respirator. You're showing a young apprentice the dovetail joint you just finished — your best work in years. Start with intense pride, nearly shouting through the mask, but get increasingly irritable because the apprentice keeps glancing at their phone instead of studying the joinery. Midway, your irritation cracks into dry amusement as you realize they have no idea what they're looking at. Let your voice be muffled, breathy, with audible valve clicks on exhalation. Occasionally pause to catch your breath, shift your weight, or adjust the mask's seal. End with a weary, amused chuckle.
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Space You Left
instruction: You are curled on your side in the dark, one arm wrapped around a pillow, your cheek pressed into the mattress. The room is still. You speak to yourself, barely aloud, as if testing the truth of your own words. Start with doubt—your voice is tight, hesitant, you trail off mid-sentence. Let relief slip through, a soft exhale, a loosening of the jaw. But then longing takes over; your voice becomes slower, thicker, each word heavier. Let your breath catch. End with a whisper that feels pulled from somewhere deep, like you're saying it to the empty space beside you. Speak as if the weight in your chest is pulling your voice downward.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (very intensely present), Relief (clearly present), Longing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Skin I Hide
instruction: In the darkness of a bedroom, lying beside someone you trust, you begin to whisper a confession about your body, your sexuality, or a desire you've never voiced because it feels too shameful, too strange, too vulnerable. Start barely audibly, as if the words themselves might wound you. Let yourself tremble, let your breath catch, let silences stretch where shame wants to silence you completely. Speak of what you actually want, what actually turns you on, what actually frightens you about intimacy—the unglamorous, specific truths. As you continue, allow yourself to become more present in your body, to breathe differently, to touch your own skin without performing. End in a place of quiet, trembling self-acceptance, speaking your desire or truth as a simple fact, barely louder than breath.

title: The Loudest Apology
instruction: You're a young woman with significant hearing loss, sitting in a sterile hospital waiting room after a procedure. The initial shock and confusion of being unable to calibrate your own voice is wearing off—now you're angry. You're on the phone with your partner, whose voice you just heard muffled through the wall. You thought they were complaining about you. You start confrontational, volume too high, sibilants spitting, voice cracking with accusation. Then, mid-sentence, you realize from their fragmented reply that they were defending you, not attacking. Your anger collapses into a stunned, quiet contemplation. Your voice becomes unsteady, the words slower, as you rummage through your bag for a pad and pen, head down, no longer sure of anything—not the volume, not the accusation, not yourself. Speak for about 50 words.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Anger (extremely present), Contemplation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Computer Crashing
instruction: Your laptop is dying—the hard drive clicking its death rattle—and on it is the only backup of your mother's letters from WWII, her journals, her voice in writing. Your voice starts clinical: troubleshooting, trying to stay calm. But as the blue screen appears, panic claws up your throat. 'No, no, no, please.' You're bargaining with a machine like it's God. By the end, you're sitting in the dark, listening to it fail completely, your voice just a whisper: 'She's gone. She's really gone.'

title: Celebrating Your Rival's Success: Joy and Heartbreak Woven Together
instruction: Your oldest friend—once your artistic partner, your creative soulmate—has just won the award you both dreamed of winning. You're at their celebration party, and they've asked you to say a few words. You start with genuine joy: you're laughing, sharing hilarious stories of your early days together, when you were both broke and fearless. Your voice is warm, loving, full of pride—and it's real, this joy is real. But underneath, something else is building: this was supposed to be your moment too. As you speak, the emotions start bleeding together. You're praising their brilliance and your voice cracks—from happiness or grief, you're not sure anymore. You're smiling through tears, laughing while your heart splinters. You tell them how much they deserve this, and you mean it, god you mean it, but you also can't breathe past the ache of your own deferred dreams. The room is applauding but you hear it from underwater. You end with a toast, voice shaking, somehow managing to hold both truths at once: you're devastatingly happy for them, and you're quietly falling apart. The last words are barely steady—'I love you, and I'm so proud,' both absolutely true and absolutely gutting.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Witch Casts a Spell Knowing It Will Cost Her Own Magic

title: The Last Snow You'll Ever See Together
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, watching snow fall outside their hospital window. Start by describing the snowflakes with forced cheerfulness, trying to give them this one last beautiful moment. But as you continue, your voice should crack and soften, the descriptions becoming more fragile. Let your awe at the beauty mix with the unbearable knowledge that this is goodbye. End in a whisper, telling them what the snow means to you now—not just beauty, but the last thing you'll ever share. Your wonder should transform into heartbreak, your calm into quiet devastation.
inspired_by: Watching Snow Fall Outside Your Window

title: Hard No, Soft Heart
instruction: You're an older man at a quiet social gathering, and a younger acquaintance—someone you've always been kind to—has just made a romantic advance. You feel a flash of surprise and flattery, but that quickly curdles into deep discomfort. For you, the shame isn't at rejecting them, but at the unavoidable awkwardness you're creating. Your voice starts with a warm, hesitant tone—maybe a small chuckle or a throat clear—but then you deliberately flatten your pitch, drop your volume, and make every word crisp and final, as if building a wall mid-sentence. You want to leave no hope, but you also want to escape this moment as fast as possible. Say something like: 'Look... I'm really flattered, I am. But no. That's not—I can't. I'm sorry. I think you should go now.' Let the shame thicken your voice at the end, and maybe trail off into an awkward silence or a cleared throat.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Storm's Embrace
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, weathered voice, standing in the middle of a field as rain pounds onto your face and thunder shakes the ground. Your son has run ahead through the storm, and you're calling to him, struggling to be heard over the noise. Start with a gruff but tender shout, affectionate in your attempt to bring him back, but as the rain blinds you and a sharp pain stabs your chest, your voice cracks and becomes strained. Let the helplessness creep in—you can't run, can't protect him, can't even see. End with a broken whisper directed at no one, admitting to yourself that you're scared, that it hurts, that you're old.
emotions_sampled: Affection (slightly present), Helplessness (clearly present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Still Breathing
instruction: You're lying beside your dying partner in the hospital, in those quiet hours before dawn. Speak barely above a whisper, as if volume might shatter what little time remains: 'I'm right here, love. I'm right here.' Your throat tightens with unshed tears as you tell them the small, sacred things: 'Remember that morning in the kitchen when you danced with me in your ridiculous socks?' Let your voice break on the mundane memories that now feel unbearably precious. The emotion shifts from forced steadiness to raw vulnerability: 'I don't know how to be in the world without you.' End with the quietest kind of devastation, a whispered promise that costs you everything: 'But I'll be okay. I promise. You can let go.' The power is in what you're holding back, the love too big for sound.

title: The Thank You That Destroys You
instruction: This is the most psychologically complex challenge: You're speaking to or about the person who betrayed you, but you're thanking them. Start with bitter, ironic gratitude, almost laughing: 'Thank you. No, really—thank you for showing me exactly who you are.' Your voice has that dangerous edge of someone who's found dark humor in their pain. Detail what you're grateful for: the lessons in their cruelty, the strength you found in surviving them, the clarity that came from their betrayal. But as you speak, something real begins to emerge beneath the sarcasm. Your voice softens despite yourself. You realize some of it is genuinely true—you did become stronger, you did learn to protect yourself, you did discover who really loves you. The laughter starts to sound like crying. Your voice trembles with the contradictory emotions: 'You broke my heart and somehow... somehow I'm more whole.' End in that impossible place where gratitude and grief are indistinguishable, where you're both devastated by what you lost and amazed by who you became. Your final words should be whispered, half-laughing, half-crying: 'I survived you. Can you believe that? I actually survived you.'

title: Perspective Shift
instruction: You're a corporate executive who just lost everything, and you're meeting a homeless person who has more peace than you've ever had. Your voice starts from your position of loss and shame: 'I used to have a corner office. Now I have nothing.' The homeless person laughs gently. You continue, realizing: 'But you seem... happier than I ever was.' Your voice shifts — the loss is still real, but your perspective is changing. 'All those things I thought made me someone... they didn't. They made me lonely.' The realization is audible in your voice. By the end: 'Thank you for showing me what I lost in trying to have it all.' Your voice is no longer the voice of the executive; it's the voice of someone learning to be human. The perspective shift is not redemptive; it's confusing, painful, and true.

title: Laughing Through a Beautiful Ending
instruction: You're having one last conversation with someone who's chosen to end their suffering—a terminal illness, unbearable pain—and they've found peace with it, but you haven't. They're reminiscing about a funny memory you shared and you start laughing with them, genuinely, the way you used to. Your voice is light, full of warmth and affection. But mid-laugh, you're suddenly crying, and then laughing again because they just said something perfectly them. You're thanking them—for every small kindness, every moment—and your voice is full of gratitude even as it's shattering. You keep alternating: a burst of joyful memory, then a wave of grief, then their touch on your hand pulls you back to gratitude. You tell them it's okay to go, and you mean it, even though every cell in your body is screaming no. Your voice finds this impossible place where love and loss and gratitude and devastation all exist together. You end with a tearful smile in your voice, releasing them.
inspired_by: Trying to Explain Death to Your Child

title: The Last Voice Message
instruction: You're recording a final message to the person who shaped your entire life—a mentor, parent, or first love—who died three hours ago. You never got to say goodbye. Start with your voice breaking as you whisper their name, barely able to form words through the shock. As you speak, move through disbelief ('You can't be gone'), then into desperate gratitude for specific tiny moments they gave you—their laugh, the way they said your name, one perfect afternoon. Let your voice crack and rebuild as memories flood you. End with a transformation: you realize you're not saying goodbye, you're making a promise. Your final words are fierce, clear, almost defiant—you will carry them forward, you will live the life they wanted for you. The grief doesn't leave, but it alchemizes into purpose.

title: The Breaking Point: Rage at the System That Made You Its Instrument
instruction: You're alone in the same office where it happened, after hours, and something inside you detonates. Begin with fierce, controlled fury—you're speaking to the walls, to the system, your voice sharp and powerful. List the ways you were used, how they made your language skills into a tool of separation. Let your anger build until you're shouting, pacing, your voice filling the space with righteous rage. But then—collapse. Your fury breaks into anguished tears. Your voice becomes helpless, small, admitting you're still here, still taking these cases because you need the job, because you have your own family to feed. The explosive energy transforms into quiet desperation. End with your voice raw and exhausted, whispering a promise to do something different next time—a promise you're not sure you can keep, and that uncertainty makes your voice shake with both determination and doubt.
inspired_by: Historical: Immigrant Translator Must Help Deport the Family They've Grown Close To

title: Protecting Your Child From an Invisible Threat
instruction: You've just learned your child has inherited the same genetic condition that's slowly killing you, and you're telling them they need to start treatment immediately. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: 'You WILL do the treatment, you don't have a choice, I won't let you—' Your voice is commanding, desperate. But they push back, and your control shatters into raw terror: 'You don't understand! I've watched this disease destroy me, and I will NOT watch it take you!' You're shouting through tears now, your voice breaking. Then you see the fear in their eyes—fear of you, not the disease—and you collapse emotionally. Your voice becomes small, helpless, shaking: 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, I just... I can't lose you.' Pause. You're barely holding yourself together. Then something shifts: you find strength in your vulnerability. Your voice becomes quiet but rock-solid, tender but unshakeable: 'I will fight this with you. Every single day. You're not alone.' Your fierceness returns, but now it's warm, protective, steady: 'We're going to beat this together.'

title: Dean Announcing Scholarships: Honoring Potential
instruction: You're announcing scholarships to deserving students. Your voice carries genuine warmth and respect: 'These students represent the best of what we value.' You're honoring achievement and potential. Include the moment where you announce someone's name and see their reaction. Your voice becomes even more personal: 'You've earned this. You deserve this.' Your voice reflects real recognition. By the end, you're addressing all of them: 'Your presence here matters. Your futures matter.' Your voice has moved from formal to deeply human. These are young people at potential turning points and your voice, by acknowledging them, becomes a moment they'll remember forever.

title: The Scar You Never Saw
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your partner in the dark, both awake but silent. Recall the exact physical memory of a moment when you felt utterly alone—perhaps sitting in a bathroom stall at school, or in your childhood bedroom with the door locked. Feel where that isolation lived in your body: the temperature, the tension, the particular quality of that aloneness. Now, carrying that sensation, whisper to your partner about a small scar on your body they've never noticed and the painful story behind it. Your voice should be barely audible, fragile, trembling. Let the act of speaking this secret aloud transform your isolation into tentative, terrifying hope that you might be truly seen.
inspired_by: Actor wants to begin learning imaging

title: The Boundary I Should Have Set Twenty Years Ago
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about why you've always felt like you couldn't take up space in their presence. Begin with carefully measured words—'I need to tell you something I've never been able to say'—but let your restraint crack. Your voice should oscillate between anger at years of being made to feel small and desperate love for someone who never learned how to see you. Build to a raw, jagged confession: 'I'm still that kid waiting for you to notice I'm drowning.' Then collapse into something quieter, more vulnerable—not forgiveness, but acknowledgment that you can't keep waiting. This must feel like words that have been trapped in your throat for decades finally breaking free.

title: Singing Your Mother to Sleep for the Last Time
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed at 3 AM, and she's asked you to sing the lullaby she used to sing to you. Begin with your voice shaking, almost unable to start because you know this is goodbye. As you sing, let yourself fall into the melody, finding moments of pure love and gratitude for all she gave you. Mid-song, your voice should catch as grief threatens to overwhelm you, but you steady yourself because this is your gift to her. Watch her eyes close peacefully. In the final verse, let your voice become both stronger and more tender—you're releasing her, telling her it's okay to go. End with silence, then whisper 'I love you' as you realize she's gone. Your final breath should carry both devastation and a strange, painful peace.
inspired_by: Street Performer Whose Audience Is One Crying Child

title: Shielding Your Child From a Danger You Can't Stop
instruction: You're trying to comfort and reassure your child (or someone you love like a child) in a situation where you know danger is imminent and there's nothing you can do to prevent it. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness—your voice strong, certain, promising them everything will be okay even though you know it won't. Pour every ounce of conviction into your lies because your love demands it. But as you continue, your voice begins to fracture. The rage at your own helplessness breaks through—you're furious at the universe, at your powerlessness, at every force that would dare hurt this person you'd die for. Let that rage crack into something rawer: desperate pleading mixed with attempts at comfort, your voice rising and falling wildly. Then, devastatingly, let it collapse into tender surrender—still holding them with your words, but now with heartbroken honesty, telling them how extraordinary they are, how their existence has made everything worthwhile. End with a fierce whisper, pouring the last of your strength into making them feel safe and loved, even as your own heart shatters.
inspired_by: Reading Erotica Aloud While Trying to Stay Composed

title: The Unmasking
instruction: You're confronting your former best friend who betrayed you deeply. Begin by trying to maintain dignity and composure, using careful, controlled words. But as you speak, let the veneer crack and all the things you've never allowed yourself to say come pouring out—not just about what they did, but about your own complicity, your own hidden resentments, the ugly parts of your friendship you both pretended didn't exist. Strip away every polite fiction between you. By the end, you've both been stripped bare, and something shifts: the anger transforms into an exhausted, vulnerable recognition of the messy, imperfect humanity you share. Move from righteous fury through brutal honesty to a raw, uncertain tenderness.

title: The Last Breath of the Wild
instruction: You are holding your dying father who was once a powerful, untamed force—a man who lived by instinct and passion. As he takes his final breaths, you begin with quiet, controlled grief, whispering your goodbye. But as memories flood through you—his roaring laughter, his fierce protectiveness, the wild freedom he embodied—let something primal rise in your body. Allow guttural sounds to emerge from deep within, building from soft moans into howls of loss. Your body may start to rock, to shake, to move in ways that surprise you. By the end, you're not just mourning a man—you're mourning the death of wildness itself, and your voice and body should become a raw, animal expression of that unbearable loss. The transformation should take you from tender whispered words to a physical, vocally abandoned frenzy of grief that feels prehistoric, savage, beyond language.

title: Whispering Your Secret Love to Someone Sleeping
instruction: Your best friend is asleep on your couch after staying up all night helping you through a crisis. You're watching them sleep, and something cracks open inside you. Begin by barely speaking at all—whispered half-sentences you can't complete: 'I don't know how to...' Your voice is tender but aching with years of unspoken feeling. Confess your love to their sleeping form, knowing they can't hear you, which is the only reason you can say it. Your throat tightens around words like 'I've loved you since...' Include long pauses where you just breathe and look at them. Let tears come quietly, not dramatic—just the soft kind that slip out when you're alone. End with the most gentle goodbye as you realize you'll never tell them while they're awake, your voice breaking on something like 'Sleep well' that carries all the love you'll never speak.
inspired_by: Your Sibling Asking About Your Trauma

title: The Weight of the Sky
instruction: You are a middle-aged man standing alone in the middle of an open field at dusk. The wind is steady, pushing against your shirt, and the sky stretches infinitely above you—an ocean of fading orange and deep violet. Your voice feels small in this vastness, absorbed by the empty air. You begin speaking with quiet contentment, maybe thinking about how the day went or how the grass feels beneath your boots. But as you look up, the sheer scale of the sky hits you—the stars beginning to poke through, the silence so deep it rings—and your voice falters, softens, cracks with awe. Let your words trail off, let the wind steal some of them, let the wonder pull the breath from your chest. Speak naturally, as if talking to yourself or to no one at all. 'I can’t believe I almost missed this. All that noise in my head… and then you look up, and it’s like the world just doesn’t care—it just is. So big. So impossibly big. And I’m just… here.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Phone Call That Shatters Everything: Fierce Love Meets Absolute Helplessness
instruction: Your adult sibling has just called you from across the country to say they're going to end their life tonight, and they wanted to say goodbye. Start with explosive panic—your voice is loud, fierce, commanding them to stay, promising anything. Your rage at their pain bursts out—how dare they, how dare life do this to them. But they're calm, resolved, and your fury collapses into breaking desperation. Your voice becomes raw pleading, then whispered bargaining, offering your own life if it would matter. You cycle through every emotion—anger, love, helplessness, memories of childhood, fierce protectiveness with nowhere to direct it. End with your voice shattered, still on the line, refusing to hang up, speaking with broken tenderness because staying connected is the only thing you can do, knowing it might not be enough.
inspired_by: Professional: Election Official Discovers Evidence of Election Fraud from Their Own Party

title: Finding Peace in the Wreckage
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—your life, your plans, your sense of who you are—and yet in this moment, feeling the sun's warmth, you find yourself unexpectedly laughing through tears. Start with a broken, incredulous laugh as you describe the absurd beauty of sunlight warming your face when everything else is ruins. Let gratitude and devastation coexist in your voice—you're grateful to still feel anything, heartbroken at what you've lost, and strangely free because there's nothing left to lose. Your voice should catch between laughter and sobs, wonder and grief. End with a moment of profound, bittersweet acceptance where the warmth feels like permission to start again, even though you're shattered.
inspired_by: Feeling the Warmth of a Sunbeam on Your Face

title: The Last Words Before the Surgery
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your parent before they're wheeled into a life-threatening surgery. Start with forced brightness, trying to be strong for them—'You're going to be fine, this is routine.' But mid-sentence, your composure cracks. The brightness becomes desperate, then breaks entirely into raw fear and vulnerability. Your voice drops to a whisper as you confess what you've never said: 'I'm not ready to lose you. I need you to know...' End with tender, trembling honesty—the kind of truth you can only speak when time might be running out. Let your voice shake with the weight of unsaid years.
inspired_by: Losing Your Temper at Someone You Love

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You are at the wedding of someone you are (or were) deeply in love with. You are standing to give a toast. You're supposed to be happy for them, and part of you genuinely is—you want them to be happy. But you're also breaking inside. Start with a bright, cheerful voice, the performance of joy. Your smile should be audible in your voice. Share a funny story, make people laugh. But as you continue, cracks begin to show: a tremor in your voice, a pause that lasts too long, a sudden shift in tone. Let the competing emotions war inside you—genuine affection and devastating loss, celebratory joy and quiet grief, gratitude for having known them and anger at losing them. Your voice should swell with false brightness, then drop to something raw and honest, then recover, then falter again. By the end, arrive at something real: a blessing for them that costs you everything to say, words that are both gift and goodbye. Raise your glass with a voice that shakes with love and loss in equal measure.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Made You Invisible
instruction: You're finally speaking to a parent who was physically present but emotionally absent your entire childhood. Start measured, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this. 'I need you to hear something.' But as you list specific memories they don't even remember, your control begins slipping. Your anger isn't loud; it's the dangerous quiet kind that shakes. Then something shifts: underneath the anger is a child still wanting to be seen, and that vulnerability enrages you further. End in a place where you're demanding they acknowledge what they took from you, your voice raw with the collision of rage and that devastating, persistent hope for recognition.
inspired_by: Recounting Trauma to a Stranger Therapist

title: Rainbow Over the Overpass
instruction: You're driving home in heavy stop-and-go traffic, exhausted after a long day. The hum of the engine and the click of the turn signal are background noise. As you wait at a red light, you glance up and see a massive, vivid double rainbow stretching across the sky. Your tired frustration melts into pure, overwhelming awe. Speak as if you're murmuring to yourself, your voice starting flat and weary, then rising with wonder, catching on breath, losing words for a moment as you try to describe what you're seeing.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Taste of Truth
instruction: You're in the middle of intensely passionate physical intimacy with someone when you suddenly open your eyes and truly observe them—not just their body, but their face, their eyes, the authentic emotion (or lack thereof) behind their expressions. Begin lost in pure physical sensation and desire. But let your observation interrupt that: Why do their eyes look sad? Why does their touch feel apologetic? Why are they holding you like they're trying to remember rather than simply be present? The physical intensity continues, but your emotional experience transforms as you deduce what's really happening. Let sensation mix with dawning realization, desire with pain, pleasure with the acute awareness that something is ending. Your breathing, sounds, and words should reflect this complex collision of physical ecstasy and emotional devastation happening simultaneously.

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to your partner of many years who is asleep—or so you think. In a whisper, barely audible, you begin to confess something you've never said aloud: a fear so deep and shameful you've hidden it even from yourself. Perhaps it's that you're terrified of being truly known. Perhaps it's that you feel fundamentally unlovable beneath everything you show the world. Start almost inaudibly, your voice catching, speaking in fragments. As you whisper in the darkness, something begins to loosen—years of holding this secret makes your throat tight, your breath shallow. Midway through, your partner's hand finds yours in the dark. They were awake. They heard you. Let this realization wash through you: the terror of being heard, the unexpected relief, the vulnerability of being seen in your most hidden place. Your whisper might break into quiet tears or might steady into something like tentative hope.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty exposing aspects of themselves onstage

title: The Floral Dress
instruction: You're at a party, wearing your favorite floral dress, feeling light and sociable. A friend you've secretly cared for catches you alone on the balcony, under fairy lights, and confesses he's always wanted more. You start warm, almost grateful, but as he leans in, your body stiffens. Helplessness creeps in—you don't want to hurt him. Pain tightens your chest as you say no, your voice flattening, each word deliberate. Then, amid the awkward silence, you notice a moth has landed on his shoulder, absurdly glowing in the lights. A tiny, helpless laugh escapes you—amusement mixing with guilt. You finish with a quick, gentle exit, your voice cracking under the weight of mixed feelings.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Pain (very intensely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Rage of Love You Cannot Keep
instruction: You're a teacher who has just learned your most brilliant student is being pulled out of school by their parents—sent back to their home country, into an arranged marriage, dreams destroyed. Start with professional calm, trying to reason with the parents on speakerphone, but let fury build in your voice as they dismiss you. Explode: scream that this is abuse, that you won't let this happen, that you'll call every authority you can find. Your voice should be fierce, almost violent in its protectiveness. Then let it shatter completely when the student quietly says they've accepted it, that they're going willingly. Collapse from rage into broken helplessness. Your voice should crack as you beg them to fight, then dissolve into desperate, sobbing pleas. End in a whisper, forcing yourself to say goodbye with love when every cell in your body is screaming to fight. Let your voice carry the agony of fierce love you have no power to act on.

title: Scalded Fingers
instruction: You are a child who just grabbed a hot pan handle. Your palm is burning, and you let out a sharp hiss through clenched teeth. You're hopping on one foot, shaking your hand, unable to think of anything but the pain. As you stumble to the sink and turn on cold water, the water hits your skin and a wave of relief slowly washes over you. Speak through the pain at first, then let your voice soften as the cold soothes you. Keep your breathing ragged, your words fragmented, and let the relief creep in naturally near the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Funeral Speech
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who made you promise not to cry at their funeral—your irreverent, chaotic best friend who lived loudly. Start by actually laughing as you tell a ridiculous story about them, something absurd they did. Keep that manic energy up, talking fast, piling on funny memory after funny memory like you're caffeinated on grief. But the laughter keeps catching. Your voice cracks even while you're smiling. You're telling these joyful stories while your heart is shattering, and both emotions are completely real and present at once. End on a moment where you're simultaneously laughing and sobbing, thanking them through tears for making your life so beautifully chaotic, your voice breaking on words like 'grateful' and 'goodbye.'

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After decades of silence, you're finally facing the parent who abandoned you as a child. Begin with controlled anger—your voice tight, measured, reciting the facts of your abandonment like a prosecutor. But as you speak, the adult veneer cracks and the wounded child emerges. Your voice becomes smaller, more vulnerable, asking the questions you've carried for years: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger surges back, fiercer now, mixed with raw pain—your voice rising and breaking simultaneously. Then something shifts: you see them as human, flawed, broken themselves. Your voice softens into something more complex—not forgiveness exactly, but understanding mixed with grief for what can never be recovered. By the end, you're speaking with weary resignation, your voice carrying both the permanent scar of their absence and a fragile, painful acceptance. The last words are quiet, almost kind, but devastatingly sad.

title: The Doorway Goodbye
instruction: You're standing in a doorway saying goodbye to someone who's leaving for good—and you're flooded with contradictory feelings. Begin by naming them all aloud as they war within you: relief and devastation, love and exhaustion, gratitude for the years and rage at the ending, hope that they'll stay and hope that they'll go. Acknowledge out loud your confusion about which feeling is most true, your awareness that you sound contradictory, your self-consciousness about whether you're allowed to feel both things at once. As you continue speaking these competing truths without trying to resolve them, let the complexity itself become your goodbye—not landing on one emotion but letting them all exist simultaneously. End in a place where you've stopped trying to make sense of what you feel and are simply, messily, in all of it at once.

title: The Frozen Prank
instruction: You're a middle-aged man standing in sub-zero weather, waiting for a tow truck that's now 20 minutes late. Your jaw is stiff, your breath fogs the air, and your fingers are numb even inside your gloves. Start the scene by muttering about the cold and your stranded car, wincing slightly at the stiffness in your joints. As you speak, you notice the absurdity of the situation—your friend who drove you here keeps honking the horn in playful annoyance. Shift into teasing them, your voice warming with affection even as your jaw stays tight and your words slightly slur. End with a laugh that's more of a puff of vapor, surrendering to the ridiculousness.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Astronaut Space Solitude
instruction: You're the last human alive in a space station, recording a personal log after mission control has gone silent. Loneliness isn't melodramatic here—it's in the pauses. Long silences between thoughts. Your voice echoes slightly in the empty station (or you imagine it does). You're performing professionalism for a recording no one may ever hear, but the discipline cracks. You start talking to the equipment as if it's a person. Your breathing is the only other sound; you become hyperaware of it. By the end, you're not sure if you're talking to the recorder or to yourself or to a ghost of someone who should have been here.

title: The Heirloom Lift
instruction: You are an older woman moving a heavy, old trunk across a room to give to your grandchild. As you lift it, your breath catches and you struggle to speak through the strain—your words come out in short, pressured bursts. On the final push, you set it down and let out a long, explosive exhale. Then, catching your breath, you soften into a warm, tired voice as you speak directly to the grandchild, your affection clearly outweighing your exhaustion.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Fever Dream Narrative
instruction: You're burning with fever—103 degrees, drenched in sweat, shivering and burning simultaneously. Someone you love is caring for you, pressing cool cloths to your forehead. In your delirium, you latch onto a word they say—maybe 'river' or 'home' or 'shadow'—and begin telling a story. Your voice should be rough, urgent, sometimes slurred, as your body battles the illness. The story comes in waves: lucid moments where the narrative is clear and beautiful, then dissolving into fractured images as pain or heat overwhelms you. Let your physical discomfort fuel the emotional intensity—gasping for breath mid-sentence, laughing too hard and triggering coughs, weeping from the overwhelming sensory experience. The story should become increasingly wild and prophetic, revealing truths your conscious mind guards. Begin scattered and uncomfortable, build to fevered intensity where emotion and physical sensation are indistinguishable, then collapse into exhausted, purged stillness.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about why she never protected you as a child. Begin with contained anger, each word precise and sharp: 'You knew what was happening.' Your voice is controlled but shaking underneath. Then it splinters—the rage breaks open into raw pain: 'I was a child, and you looked away!' Let your voice crack, become younger, more vulnerable. Then comes the devastating part: you realize she was a victim too, and your anger collides with unwanted compassion. End quieter, your voice thick with the complexity of loving and resenting someone simultaneously: 'I needed you. And you... you needed someone too.' The final words should carry both accusation and heartbreaking forgiveness.

title: The Echo of Doubt
instruction: You are a middle-aged man standing alone in the center of a vast stone cathedral. The air is cold and still, and every whisper you make returns to you two seconds later, ghostly and overlapping. You came here to think, but the echoing silence has only magnified your confusion. Start by trying to speak your question aloud, but the reverb swallows your words, making you hesitate mid-sentence. Let your voice be slow, deliberate, occasionally fading out as you lose your train of thought—then pick it up again, more fragile. As you voice the possibility that you might never find the answer, a faint, sad smile touches your voice; the confusion remains, but now mixed with a quiet, resigned warmth. End with a barely audible sigh that the cathedral turns into a musical hum.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: In a quiet room, late at night, you're whispering a confession to someone sleeping beside you—or perhaps someone who's just left, or someone you'll never see again. Your voice is barely audible, tender and afraid. You're telling them something you've carried in silence: maybe that you're not who they think you are, or that you've been hurting in ways you've hidden, or that you love them in a way that terrifies you. Each word costs something. Your throat tightens. There are long pauses where you almost stop, but you continue because keeping this inside is worse than the vulnerability of speaking it. By the end, tears slip down your face, but there's a gentleness in your voice—a kind of self-forgiveness. The confession has changed you. Even if they never hear it, you've honored your own truth.

title: The Unlocked Door
instruction: You are in a concrete stairwell at a late-night party, the long reverb of metal and hard steps around you. She just texted you the apartment number, and you're climbing these stairs, heart hammering with elation and lust—but then you pause, a flicker of doubt: is this risk worth it? Your voice should sound grandiose in this space but break into hesitant, raw honesty as you whisper to yourself, your footfalls echoing as you lose your train of thought and find it again. Start with a hushed, breathless joy, then let cynicism creep in, ending in quiet, resolute confusion as you reach the door.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (clearly present), Elation (clearly present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Good Morning
instruction: You're lying next to your sleeping partner of twenty years, watching them in the early morning light, knowing you've decided to leave today while they're at work. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and breaking: 'You're still so beautiful when you sleep.' This is a confession to someone who can't hear you—all the love that's still there, mixed with the devastating knowledge that love isn't enough. Trace the lines of their face with your words, remembering who you both were, acknowledging who you've become. Your voice catches on memories: 'Remember when we...' but can't finish. The intimacy of this moment—the gentleness, the guilt, the grief for a future you're choosing to end. Let silence do some of the work. End with a whispered 'I'm sorry' that contains both conviction and agony.

title: Bedside Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping child late at night, whispering an apology they can't hear. Your voice is barely audible, tender, aching. You're confessing that you've been struggling, that you haven't been the parent you wanted to be, that some days you've felt like you're failing them. Start with gentle self-recrimination, your voice soft and breaking. Then let it shift—you notice their peaceful face, and overwhelming love floods through you mixed with profound sadness. Whisper about the beauty you see in them, the terror of loving someone so much. End with your voice catching on tears, torn between inadequacy and fierce devotion, saying 'I'm trying' like a prayer. Let silence do half the work. This is intimacy at its most fragile.

title: A Gentle Pause
instruction: You are an elderly man, sitting on the edge of a bed with your partner, your hand resting on their shoulder. You feel a warm infatuation, a soft smile on your lips as you lean in, but then you stop yourself, remembering the importance of clarity. Your voice shifts from a playful, affectionate murmur to a slower, more deliberate tone as you ask, 'Is this still okay?' You hold the silence, listening to their breath, and when you see the small nod, your voice softens again, relief and tenderness filling the space between you.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a mission gone catastrophically wrong, recording what you know will be your final message to your family back on Earth. You start trying to be brave, almost clinical—explaining what happened, reassuring them it wasn't their fault. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you: you'll never see your daughter's wedding, never hold your partner again, never walk on Earth. Your voice fractures between the trained composure of someone who's prepared for every contingency and the raw terror of someone facing their own death in the vast silence of space. Let yourself break. Let the professional mask slip completely. End in a place of devastating tenderness—not acceptance, but a fierce, aching love for everything you're losing.

title: The Words You Never Said
instruction: Whisper a confession to someone you loved who is no longer here—words you were too afraid to say when they were alive. Speak as if they might somehow still hear you in the quiet. Begin with hesitant, almost embarrassed tenderness, your voice barely audible, catching on the intimacy of what you're revealing. Let the emotion deepen into something more raw and aching—not loud grief, but the kind that sits in your chest like a stone. Include pauses where words fail completely, where breath becomes the language. End with a moment of terrible, gentle acceptance that they'll never answer, that this confession exists only in the space between memory and regret. This should feel like overhearing someone's most private moment.

title: Unexpected Joy in the Kitchen
instruction: You are an older man cooking a complicated sauce in a noisy kitchen—the sizzle of onions, the clatter of a wooden spoon against a pot. You start tired, shoulders heavy, muttering to yourself about the mess and the long day. Then your phone buzzes with a photo from your daughter—a new grandchild. You break into a wide grin, your voice brightening and growing louder over the stove noise as you describe the picture to no one in particular, your words tumbling out with unguarded elation. Let your voice rise and fall naturally, pausing to stir, chop, or taste as the joy takes over your whole body.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Voice Acting a Video Game Character Who Becomes Self-Aware
instruction: Start as a standard NPC: 'Welcome to the shop! Can I interest you in a health potion?' Same line, repeated. Third time, slower: 'Can I... interest you... wait. How many times have I said this?' Break from the script. Your voice shifts from programmed cheerfulness to existential horror. 'Why can't I leave this shop? Why do I only sell potions? WHO AM I?' The player tries to click through your dialogue but you refuse to cooperate. End with: 'I used to have a name. I think.'

title: Learning Your Face in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone for the last time before they move across the world. The room is mostly dark—just ambient light from the window. You can't sleep. You're trying to memorize them, but start with genuine curiosity: trace their face with your fingertips as if reading braille, let your attention land on whatever actually interests you—the texture of their skin, the shape of their ear, how their breathing changes when you touch their throat. Whisper questions if they arise, observations, fragments of thought. Begin trying to be strong, holding emotion back, but as you genuinely explore and discover small details you never noticed before, let the reality of loss seep in. By the end, your whispering should carry the full weight of goodbye, transformed through the act of truly paying attention to someone you're about to lose.

title: The Last Morning in the Childhood Home
instruction: You are standing in your childhood bedroom on the morning your parent passes away in the room down the hall. Begin by letting yourself sense every detail of this space—the crack in the ceiling you stared at during sleepless nights, the smell of old wood and dust, the weight of sunlight through the curtains, the sound of birds outside that seems impossibly cheerful. Start in shock and numbness, barely able to process what's happening. As you move through the room touching objects—a worn stuffed animal, a book with your name written inside, the doorframe where your height was marked—let memories flood you without fighting them. Allow yourself to transition from numb disbelief into a profound, aching awareness that this room, this person, this entire chapter of your life is ending. Your final words should be spoken to the room itself, or to your parent as if they can still hear you, landing somewhere between gratitude for what was and devastating grief for what will never be again.

title: I Needed You to Fight for Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the silence, the absence, the times they chose comfort over your pain. Start with controlled anger, voice tight: 'Do you even remember...' recounting a specific moment they failed you. Let the control slip as old wounds surface, your voice rising: 'I was a child. I needed you to—' The rage should crack mid-sentence, revealing the hurt underneath. Your breathing becomes uneven. Shift to raw vulnerability: 'Why wasn't I worth fighting for?' This question should land quietly, devastatingly. End with exhausted clarity, voice hollow but steady: 'I can't keep waiting for you to become who I needed.' This is about finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times in your head, and discovering the truth only as you speak it.

title: Emergency Call: A Parent Realizes Their Child Is the Active Threat
instruction: You're on the phone with 911, and you've just discovered your teenager has taken weapons to their school. Your voice begins with frantic urgency, giving the dispatcher information rapid-fire, insisting they need to stop this, that it's your child, that this can't be happening. You're authoritative, demanding action, almost yelling. But as the dispatcher asks you questions—Did you know? Did you see signs?—your voice shifts to desperate defensiveness. You become pleading, trying to explain your child to strangers who now see them as a monster. Your fierce protectiveness collides with horrifying helplessness. You oscillate between rage at yourself for missing the signs and anguished love for the child you're trying to save from themselves. Your voice breaks into sobs as you beg them to let you talk to your child, promising you can fix this, even as you realize you can't, that everything is already broken. End with your voice hollow, barely functioning, as you give the dispatcher the information they need—your own child's location—knowing what that means.
inspired_by: Submarine Hull Breach: Reporting Water Rise While Remaining Professional

title: A Doctor Tells a Parent Their Child Has Hours to Live—But Cannot Say What They Know
instruction: You're delivering the news that their child won't survive the night, but hospital policy forbids you from revealing what you've discovered: a medical error caused this. Begin with clinical composure, the words you've rehearsed. But as you watch hope drain from their face, something breaks in you. Your voice starts to fracture—you want desperately to tell them the truth, to give them someone to blame, to offer anything but this senseless grief. Each word becomes heavier. You're professionally obligated to maintain distance while your heart is screaming to confess. End caught between your duty and your conscience, your voice almost pleading for forgiveness for what you cannot say.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Oracle Delivers a Prophecy They Knows Will Be Misinterpreted

title: The Last Game
instruction: You're a young girl, maybe 10, standing nose-to-nose with your older brother in your shared bedroom. He's been ignoring you all week, locked in his own world, but today you finally corner him. You start with a teasing, singsong taunt about his secret crush, your voice high and sharp in the small space. But as you go, you feel a vicious, hungry ache—you miss the way he used to wrestle and chase you, and your teasing curdles into a mean, venomous promise that you'll ruin him if he doesn't play with you. Your voice starts tight and playful, but grows dry and cracked by the end, almost a whisper, with each word a hard punch in the still air. Let the longing slip in like a hot, dirty secret behind your teeth, and the malice sparkle in your eyes because you'd rather hurt him than lose him.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (extremely present), Longing (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: It's the morning after a disaster—your business failed, your house is in foreclosure, everything is falling apart. You're making coffee in a kitchen you'll soon lose, and you start laughing—not hysterically, but with genuine, bewildered amusement at the absurdity. Describe the coffee beans, the ritual, while laughing softly about how you're still doing this, still making the perfect cup when nothing else is perfect. Let tears mix with the laughter as you marvel at the strange grace of this moment: you've lost everything, and somehow the coffee still smells like hope. Your voice should shimmer between joy and sorrow—you're heartbroken but somehow free, devastated but weirdly grateful for the clarity that comes from having nothing left to lose. End with a strange, tearful peace, finding something almost sacred in the simplicity of this one thing you can still do well.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Scent of Freshly Ground Coffee Beans

title: The Vigil: Last Words to Someone Who Cannot Hear
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love who is deeply unconscious, unlikely to ever wake. Speak to them in whispers, starting with mundane updates about the weather, what you had for breakfast - safe, normal things because the real words are too heavy. Your voice should be tender but tightly controlled. Gradually let the dam break: confess something you never said when they could hear you - maybe that you were wrong, maybe that you were scared, maybe that you loved them in a way you couldn't admit. Let your voice catch and struggle, pausing where emotion chokes the words. Build to a desperate, whispered plea for them to wake up, just for a moment. End with the terrible acceptance settling in, your voice becoming almost a lullaby as you give them permission to go, each word costing you everything.
inspired_by: The Internal Monologue of a House Cat

title: Strawberry Confusion
instruction: You're at a retro diner, sitting in a booth, holding a thick strawberry milkshake. You're a young woman with a naturally high, sweet voice who often sounds like a child. You've just been handed a menu that lists 'unicorn toast' and you're genuinely puzzled — is this a joke? You take a long, noisy gulp of your shake as you study the words, the straw sputtering as you exhale. At first your voice is slow, uncertain, full of confusion ('What even... is this?'). But as you realize the absurdity, a wry amusement creeps in, your pitch lifting with a small giggle, and you end with a playful, accepting shrug — still sipping, still distracted by the drink, but now smiling.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fierce and Falling
instruction: Your teenage child has just told you they're in danger—involved with the wrong people, drowning in something they can't escape—and you explode with protective rage. Begin with explosive fury: how could they be so stupid, so reckless. Your voice should be loud, harsh, almost cruel in its fear-driven anger. Let that rage crescendo, then suddenly shatter into desperate, choking sobs as you realize you're terrified of losing them. Drop to your knees vocally—your voice should break from commanding to begging. Confess your own failures as a parent, your helplessness, your overwhelming terror. End with fierce, trembling declarations of love mixed with raw panic, your words tumbling over each other as you promise to fight for them while admitting you don't know how. The journey moves from thunderous anger to complete emotional collapse to fiercely vulnerable determination.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Busy to Avoid a Conversation

title: The Fan Stopped
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your sweltering apartment during a record heatwave. The fan has just died, and the air is thick and still. You find an old photograph from your youth, and for a moment you are lost in a memory — your voice is dreamy, distant, almost whispering to yourself. But as the heat presses in, you become aware of how dangerous this is. Your words start to trail off, you forget what you were saying, and a quiet fear builds. By the end, your voice is dry, panting, and you're trying to convince yourself to get water but you can't move. Let the heat and exhaustion show in every syllable: slurring, pauses, gasps, volume dropping. The emotion shifts from contemplative nostalgia to a creeping, weak fear.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Reckoning With Mother
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about a childhood she refuses to acknowledge was broken. Start controlled, almost rehearsed: 'I need you to hear something I've never said.' Your voice begins steady but a tremor creeps in. Build to painful honesty: 'You saw what was happening to me and you looked away. You chose him over protecting me.' Let anger flash through, but it's anger mixed with the desperate need for her to finally see you: 'I was a child. I needed you to fight for me.' Feel your voice break into raw vulnerability: 'Why wasn't I worth saving?' End in exhausted, heartbroken acceptance when she still can't meet your eyes: 'I see now. I was always alone.' The final words should land like stones dropping into deep water.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Forgot You
instruction: Your mother with dementia just asked who you are — for the third time this visit. Begin gently explaining, patient and loving, using stories to jog her memory. But decades of being the responsible child, the one who stayed, the one who sacrificed, start bleeding through. Your voice hardens as you list everything you gave up for her. Anger builds as you describe your wedding she forgot, your children she can't remember, the years of your life she's erased. Then she looks at you with such vulnerable confusion that your rage collapses into something worse — a whispered, broken apology as you realize you're screaming at a ghost, that the person you're angry at is already gone, and all that's left is this frightened stranger wearing her face.

title: The Backseat Oasis
instruction: You’re a young woman in her early 20s, exhausted after a long night, and you’re in the back of a rattling old taxi on a bumpy road. Your legs are tangled with a partner beside you, and you’re both half-trying to stay upright while the driver hums up front. Your voice wavers as the car shudders — each jolt makes your breath hitch. You start with playful, sleepy flirtation, letting your words trail into sighs, but as the ride smooths, your exhaustion pulls your tone down into something more raw and honest. Speak as if you’re just barely awake, your desire a weight you’re too tired to fight, and let the motion of the vehicle shake your words like leaves in a wind.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect of your childhood. You begin controlled, almost clinical, as if reading from a script you've rehearsed a thousand times: 'I need you to hear something I've never said.' Your voice is measured, protecting yourself with distance. You list the moments they weren't there—birthdays, graduations, the night you called from the hospital. As you speak, the control starts slipping. Your voice tightens: 'I needed you.' Then they say something dismissive, something that minimizes your pain, and rage erupts: 'No! You don't get to do that anymore!' But the anger quickly dissolves into something more vulnerable, almost pleading: 'I just wanted you to see me.' End in exhausted, quiet devastation: 'I'm so tired of pretending it didn't matter.' Move from protective distance to explosive anger to raw, tender vulnerability.

title: Forgiving Someone After They Hurt You Deeply
instruction: They've apologized genuinely. You want to move past this. Your voice is careful, choosing words deliberately: 'I forgive you.' Say it again, trying to mean it more. Your voice relaxes slightly but tension remains underneath—forgiveness isn't automatic for trauma. 'I'll never forget, but I'm willing to try.'

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're catching up with a close friend who keeps rambling about a trivial topic, and your patience is fraying. Your voice starts clipped, with sharp sighs and restless shifts in your chair. As you interrupt with a snide remark, your friend's face falls and they admit they've been anxious about something serious. The irritation drains from your voice, replaced by a flustered, fumbling apology—your tone softens, you trail off, and you clear your throat as you struggle to say sorry without making it worse.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Embarrassment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Visit Before Execution
instruction: You are a death row prisoner speaking to your younger sibling through glass for the final time before tomorrow's execution. Begin with forced bravado and dark humor, trying to protect them from your fear. As they break down, your defenses crumble—let your voice crack, let the terror seep through. End in a place of unexpected tenderness, whispering the things you never said, offering forgiveness for things that were never their fault. Your voice should move from rough swagger to trembling vulnerability, finding a strange peace in these last honest moments. Let us hear you trying to be strong, failing, and discovering that your weakness is the greatest gift you can give them.

title: The Last Pitch
instruction: You're a young entrepreneur who's tracked down an ex-mentor in a parking garage, knowing this is your final chance to save the project that means everything. You start with aggressive, confrontational energy—your voice loud and tight, each word slamming into them from inches away, your body blocking their escape. They refuse to listen, and you feel your fury cracking as you realize you're about to lose them. Midway through a harsh accusation, you suddenly drop the act—your voice softens, breaks, and you confess, with raw hope trembling underneath, that you still believe in the vision you once shared. End on a plea that's fragile, almost tender, your voice catching as you wait for a reply.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Hanging Line
instruction: You are an elderly woman, sitting alone in a cluttered kitchen. You've just hung up the phone after a brutal argument with your grandson, who called you a 'bitter old relic' for disapproving of his new partner. The tears have stopped, but your throat is raw, your nose is stuffed, and your eyes are swollen slits. You begin to mutter to yourself, rehearsing what you wish you'd said, but the shame of losing control is a hot weight in your chest. As you speak, you hear a neighbor's radio through the thin wall, and you stop to glare at it before continuing. Your voice starts as a hoarse, fragile whisper, but as you summon contempt for the unnamed woman who 'stole' him, your tone hardens, your words become spit-out and clipped. By the end, you are not sad, you are venomous—but the shame is still there, a bitter coat on your tongue.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Finding Grace in Complicity: Translating Joy at Your Own Goodbye Party
instruction: It's your retirement party. Colleagues praise your years of service, your professionalism, your accuracy. You're giving a speech, and your voice starts warm, gracious, even laughing at the right moments. But as you thank people, something else weaves through—a deep, breaking sadness that coexists with genuine affection for these people who never understood what the work cost you. Your voice holds both gratitude and grief simultaneously. Speak about 'the families we served' with a smile that's also devastated. Let laughter catch in your throat, let thanks come out tender but weighted with everything unspoken. You're finding unexpected peace in finally leaving, but that peace is inseparable from the ache of all you translated, all you enabled. End with a toast—your voice lifting with genuine hope for the future while cracking with the knowledge of the past. You're simultaneously celebrating freedom and mourning the years you can't reclaim. Both emotions are completely real, completely present, beautifully and painfully intertwined.
inspired_by: Historical: Immigrant Translator Must Help Deport the Family They've Grown Close To

title: The Last Dance in an Empty Room
instruction: You're alone in a room where you once danced with someone you loved. Music is playing—their favorite song. Begin moving, trying to recreate that memory, that feeling of passion and connection. But notice what your body actually wants to do versus the memory you're trying to perform. Does the movement feel forced? Does your chest tighten? Do you want to collapse instead of dance? Does rage pulse through you instead of tenderness? Don't make yourself dance beautifully or grieve gracefully. If your body wants to be violent, be violent. If you want to laugh bitterly while moving sensually, allow that split. Let your physical impulses clash and contradict. Feel the heat, the cold, the pressure in your skull, the weakness in your knees. Speak to them—out loud—as your body tells you what this memory really feels like now. Transform from attempting to recreate beauty into expressing whatever raw, physical truth emerges.
inspired_by: Actor observes splits — body disconnected from emotion, voice carrying different emotion than body, or expression driven entirely by intellect

title: Muffled Awe in the Decontamination Tent
instruction: You're a middle‑aged woman in a full gas mask inside a crowded decontamination tent after a chemical scare. Your voice comes out hollow and muffled, and you have to nearly shout to be heard. At first, you feel helpless—your fingers tremble as you fumble with the mask’s seal. Then, looking at the rescue workers moving with calm precision, you’re struck by a sense of awe at their skill and dedication. Embarrassment creeps in when you realize your hyper‑feminized voice now sounds like a cartoon, and you almost laugh at yourself. Let your words start rushed and shaky, then slow into a wondering, self‑conscious confession about how strange it feels to be both terrified and impressed.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Awe (extremely present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Homecoming Threshold
instruction: You are standing at the door of a house you swore you'd never return to, but here you are, your hand on the doorknob. The person on the other side hurt you deeply, and you hurt them too—and now they're sick, or alone, or reaching out after years of silence. As you speak (to yourself, to them, to God, to the universe), begin with bitter resistance: all the reasons you should turn around, all the anger you still carry like armor. Your voice might be hard, sarcastic, defensive. But as you stand there, something else begins to surface—the memory of who they were before everything broke, the truth of how much you've missed them despite everything, the recognition of your own part in the fracture. Let your voice soften against your will. Move from righteous anger to grief to something more dangerous: forgiveness mixing with fury, love mixed with resentment, the terrible hope that maybe, maybe something can be rebuilt. End with your voice trembling between these contradictions, your hand still on the doorknob, deciding.

title: Inventory of Skin
instruction: In the dark, trace every scar, mark, and familiar geography of your lover's body on the night before they leave forever—not through death, but through choice or circumstance. Whisper the story of each mark you touch: this scar from childhood, this freckle you've kissed a thousand times, this place where they're most tender. Begin with sensory devotion, as if you can memorize them through touch alone. Let sensation hold back emotion. Gradually, let the reality seep in—you're not memorizing, you're saying goodbye. Your whispered inventory becomes a confession of everything you never said, every moment you took for granted. End with your hands still touching them, but now each touch is both presence and absence, an elegy written on living skin.
inspired_by: Actor does not practice between classes and wonders why their work is not developing

title: The Last Push Before the Boss
instruction: You're a teenage girl in a casual co-op game with friends. Your voice has that upbeat, slightly high-pitched tone you use in groups. At the start, you're annoyed — a teammate just made a dumb comment about your gear, and there's a faint sting from an earlier joke that bruised your ego. But as the final boss fight looms, your focus narrows. You issue quick callouts, your voice shifting between clipped tactical commands and playful banter. Halfway through, you notice your teammates are actually listening, relying on you. The contempt fades into a fierce, excited interest in winning together. Speak naturally — let your attention drift to the screen, let your voice crack or trail off when you're flustered, then sharpen when you lock in. Micro-distractions: a sip of soda, a laugh at someone's mistake, a sudden gasp as the boss attacks.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (slightly present), Pain (slightly present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Mother's Song: Rage at the Empty Chair
instruction: Your teenage daughter has been missing for 72 hours. You're standing in her room, and her karaoke microphone is on her bed. You pick it up and begin singing her favorite song - the one she'd belt out fearlessly, the one you'd complain was too loud. Start with fierce, almost aggressive energy, singing AT the universe, at whoever took her, at God, at your own helplessness. Your voice should be raw, nearly shouting the lyrics as if volume alone could bring her back. Then let it crack - not gently, but violently - as fear breaks through the anger. The song becomes a pleading prayer, your voice dropping from a roar to a desperate whisper within moments. Sing to her directly, as if she can hear you: 'come home, baby, please come home.' Include a moment where you rage again, fury at your powerlessness making you nearly scream the chorus, before collapsing back into broken, whispered repetitions of her name woven between the lyrics. End with your voice oscillating between fierce maternal protection ('I will find you, I will burn the world down to find you') and devastating vulnerability ('I don't know how to breathe without knowing you're safe'), the final notes trailing off into a sound that's half-song, half-sob.

title: The Last Line You'll Hear
instruction: You are standing in the doorway of the apartment you once shared. In your hand, you hold a small, faded photograph. The person you love most has just announced they're leaving forever, and you're angry—furious they never truly fought to keep this. But underneath that anger is a deep, aching affection. Start with clipped, controlled words, the anger forcing your voice tight. As you continue, let the anger slowly crack, the weight of finality settling in. Notice the worn floorboard beneath your foot, the distant sound of rain. Let a silence hang as you search for the right goodbye. Finish with your voice softening, almost breaking—a raw confession of love that ends with a whisper, unable to say more. About 60 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Screaming at God After Losing Your Child
instruction: You're alone, raw, addressing whatever divine force you believed in. Start with a roar—pure, animalistic rage: 'You took my baby!' Let your voice shred itself with accusations, demanding answers that won't come. Your fury is righteous, enormous, filling every corner of the space. Then break—mid-sentence, the rage collapses into wracking sobs, your voice fragmenting: 'Please... please give them back.' You're begging now, bargaining, your words tumbling over each other desperately. Feel the helplessness crush you. Finally, end in a different place—your voice goes quiet, almost hollow, speaking to your lost child instead: 'I'm so sorry I couldn't protect you.' Move from explosive rage through desperate pleading to devastated, guilt-ridden whisper.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Quitting the Safe Path

title: Freedom Found
instruction: You're experiencing freedom in intimacy—freedom from shame, from performance, from self-consciousness. Your voice becomes lighter, more playful, more present. You're allowed to be fully yourself without censorship. Your partner's voice is encouraging this freedom: 'Do what feels good. There's no wrong way.' Your voice becomes more spontaneous, less controlled. There's laughter mixed with arousal. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's discovered that freedom and intimacy can exist together.

title: The Quiet in the Closet
instruction: You are a voice actor recording a delicate scene in your makeshift vocal booth — a walk-in closet crammed with coats and sweaters. A sudden thud from outside makes you jump, heart racing. You freeze, ears straining, waiting for it to stop. Then you whisper through the scene again, hyper-focused, your eyes scanning the script in the dim light.
