Finally, you find the missing phrase you'd been chasing all day — your breath catches, your shoulders drop, and a small, exhausted laugh escapes. Let the room's dead acoustics make your voice feel trapped at first, then slowly soften as relief spreads.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Concentration (very intensely present), Relief (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance Gag
instruction: You’re an older woman sitting alone at a worn kitchen table, elbows on your knees, slumped forward, rereading a letter from your late brother’s lawyer. It’s the third time today. The letter says you have to choose between a sentimental trinket or a large sum of money. Start by muttering to yourself, voice compressed and dark, weighed down by the ridiculous choice. As you recall a shared joke with your brother, let a teasing, wry warmth creep in. End with a faint, dry laugh aimed at the absurdity of it all, voice still low but now lighter.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Best Friend Who Slept With Your Partner
instruction: You've rehearsed this. You were going to be calm. But the moment you see them, your voice comes out shaking: 'How could you?' Start with disbelief—you're still hoping they'll deny it, explain it away. When they try to justify or minimize it, something breaks open in you. Your voice rises, raw and jagged: 'You were the one person—' but you can't finish. The rage is real but underneath it is devastating heartbreak because you've lost two people you loved in one betrayal. Let yourself get loud, then suddenly go very quiet when you realize they're not who you thought they were. End with your voice hollow, distant: 'I don't even know you.' You're looking at a stranger now. The fury has burned into grief.
inspired_by: Telling Your Partner Your Sexual Needs Aren't Met

title: The Last Laugh at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's been unconscious, but suddenly her eyes flutter open and she mistakes you for someone from her childhood—perhaps a sibling or playmate. In her confusion, she starts speaking in a child's voice, asking you to play their old games, make silly faces like they used to. Begin in quiet, heavy grief, barely able to breathe. Then, honoring what might be her last moments of joy, you surrender completely—making ridiculous faces, speaking in absurd voices, doing the silly things she remembers, even though tears are streaming down your face. Let yourself become utterly foolish and playful through your sorrow. By the end, you're laughing and crying simultaneously, having given her this strange, beautiful gift. Your voice should move from whispered pain to uninhibited playfulness mixed with anguish.

title: Speaking to Alexa Like a Hostage
instruction: You're home alone and hear an intruder downstairs. Your only option is to whisper to your voice assistant to call 911. But you have to speak clearly enough for the AI to understand while being quiet enough not to be heard. Perform the agonizing robot-speak whisper: 'Alexa... call... nine... one... one.' When Alexa responds at full volume ('CALLING 911!'), your horrified reaction and frantic shushing. Include the footsteps getting closer.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After Bankruptcy
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside your child's bed after losing everything—your business has collapsed and by morning, everyone will know. Your voice is barely audible, talking to them while they sleep because you can't bear to see their face when you tell them. Begin with quiet devastation: 'I promised you so many things.' Your voice catches as you list what they won't have now—the college fund, the house, the security you swore they'd never lose. But as you watch them sleeping, peaceful and trusting, something shifts. Your voice fills with fierce, tender protectiveness: 'But you'll still have me. I'll still have you.' You're whispering promises you're terrified you can't keep, but you mean them with everything you have. By the end, your voice carries a fragile, desperate hope mixed with grief: 'We're going to be okay. Different, but okay.' You're trying to convince yourself as much as them, your words catching in your throat with love and fear and determination.

title: Whispered Truth in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside your partner of ten years in the darkness of your bedroom. You can't sleep. Your voice starts as barely a whisper, testing if they're awake: 'Are you sleeping?' They're not. Now you must tell them the secret that's been suffocating you. Your voice trembles, so quiet they have to strain to hear: 'I lost the baby. Three months ago. I never told you I was pregnant.' Let the confession unfold in broken whispers—the fear, the shame, the grief you've carried alone. Your voice catches constantly, each word an effort: 'I didn't know how to tell you. I thought I was protecting you. I thought I was protecting us.' They reach for you in the dark. Your defenses crack completely and you cry—not loud sobs, but the kind of crying that shakes your whole body silently. End with raw, throat-caught vulnerability: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry I went through it alone. I'm so sorry I made you go through it alone too.'

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. For years, you've carried anger about how they took credit for raising you successfully while dismissing your struggles, your therapy, the work YOU did to become whole. But now, looking at their frail body, the anger is dissolving into something more complicated. Start with the bitterness still sharp in your voice—almost ready to confront them one last time—but let it gradually transform into grief, forgiveness, and a heartbroken realization that you're about to lose them before you ever got the acknowledgment you needed. End with a whispered goodbye that holds both your unmet need and your love. Let your voice crack. Let the tears come. This is your last chance to speak, and the words must be both honest and tender.
inspired_by: Suppressing Anger When Someone Takes Credit for Your Work

title: Sour Command
instruction: You're in a dim bedroom, kneeling on the bed across from your partner. The air is thick with leftover tension from a recent argument. You start by delivering a slow, authoritative command — your voice low and deliberate, each word sharp and heavy, meant to reclaim control. But as you speak, your jaw tightens, and a bitter memory of their betrayal surfaces. Let your tone sour halfway through: the dominance cracks, your pitch wavers, and the final words come out quieter, almost a question, revealing the hurt underneath. Whisper the last line like it's a confession you didn't mean to make.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Velvet Cage
instruction: You're a 17-year-old girl at a party, leaning against a kitchen counter, talking to someone you want to impress. Your voice is a careful construction—soft, low, giggling at the right moments—but inside you feel hollow, like you're watching yourself perform from far away. As you speak, let your attention drift: a glass you're rotating in your hand, the flicker of a candle, the way your smile feels like a mask. Start with a practiced, breathy compliment, but halfway through, let the numbness peek through—a pause that's a little too long, a laugh that dies too quickly—ending on a quiet, almost weary confession that this is all you know how to be.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Goodbye Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child before deploying to a war zone you know you might not return from. Begin with forced cheerfulness, voice bright and falsely confident: 'Hey, this is going to be an adventure, right?' But as you look at their face, the mask starts cracking. Your voice drops, becomes tender and desperate: 'I need you to remember something for me.' You're trying to pack a lifetime of love into minutes, voice breaking as you tell them how proud you are, how they've made every day worth living. End in quiet devastation, whispering promises you're terrified you can't keep, your voice raw with the knowledge that this might be the last time they hear you say 'I love you.' The transition must feel inevitable, like watching someone try to hold water in their hands.

title: Bedside Cartography
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love, tracing the map of their body in the dark—a shoulder, a scar, the curve of their spine. Start with tender, whispered observations, almost playful, as you describe what your fingers find. But gradually, let the vulnerability deepen. Your voice becomes softer, more fragile, as you confess what terrifies you: that you've memorized every detail because you're afraid of forgetting, that you're trying to preserve this moment against time itself. End barely audible, admitting that even in this perfect moment of intimacy, you feel the weight of impermanence. Let tenderness carry an unbearable sweetness tinged with quiet devastation.

title: The Last Plea
instruction: You are an elderly man, sitting in your armchair, facing your daughter who has just told you she’s arranged for you to move to a nursing home next week. Your voice is thin, shaky, with a high pitch from desperation. Start with a sour, resentful mumble—you’re bitter that she’s making this decision without your say. Then, as you speak, you shift into a desperate plea, your voice cracking and speeding up, but gradually infuse it with a fragile hope—maybe she’ll listen, maybe you can stay. Let your breath falter, pause to rub your eyes or shift your weight, lose your train of thought briefly. Your words should reveal this arc: from bitter resignation to a hopeful, almost childlike optimism that she’ll change her mind.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about something he did twenty years ago that neither of you has ever spoken about. Start from a place of careful control—you came here with a plan, with specific words you rehearsed. But as you begin to speak, let the prepared speech crumble. Discover in real-time what you actually need to say versus what you thought you needed to say. Allow yourself to be surprised by which memories surface, which accusations turn into questions, which anger dissolves into something more complicated. Let your voice move from rehearsed confrontation into unscripted territory—maybe you find understanding, maybe you find deeper rage, maybe you discover you're really asking 'do you even remember?' Let the scene end somewhere completely different from where you planned.
inspired_by: An actor is trying to misuse rehearsal as a cumulative performance

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about your childhood—all the moments he wasn't there, the emotional absence that shaped you. Begin with controlled anger, voice tight and measured, listing facts like evidence. But as you speak, the anger cracks open into something more vulnerable: the child inside you who just wanted to be seen. Your voice wavers between fury and desperate pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let the confrontation build to a raw confession—you're not just angry, you're grieving the parent you needed and never had. End in a place of exhausted truth: you can't keep carrying this. Your final words are quieter, almost tender despite the pain, as you realize you're not asking for him to change anymore—you're finally letting go of needing him to.

title: Reading Your Mother's Last Letter at Her Funeral
instruction: She left you a letter, and you've chosen to read it aloud to the gathered mourners. Start with her words—she's funny, even now, making jokes about her own death. You laugh, a real laugh, even as tears stream down your face. 'She says here... she says she's sorry for being such a pain about the grandkids.' Another laugh that breaks into a sob. Her voice comes through you—warm, irreverent, so alive. Then you reach the line that undoes you: 'Thank you for being exactly who you are.' Your voice fractures between joy and anguish. She's praising you, releasing you, blessing you, and she's gone. End with her final words, delivered through streaming tears but with a smile in your voice: 'Don't you dare be sad for too long.' Feel gratitude and grief become indistinguishable, two faces of the same overwhelming love.
inspired_by: Explaining Your Anxiety to Someone Who Doesn't Get It

title: Finding Peace While the World Ends
instruction: Something catastrophic is happening—the end of everything. You're terrified, voice small and shaking: 'This is really it.' Breathing shallow, words in fragments. But then something extraordinary happens—through the terror, you begin to laugh softly, almost hysterically. 'It's beautiful. God, it's actually beautiful.' Your voice wavers between fear and wonder, between a sob and a laugh. You're grateful for having lived, even as your heart pounds with terror: 'I got to be here. I got to see all of this.' End with tears and laughter intermingled, voice breaking with contradictory emotions—fear and peace, grief and gratitude, terror and strange, inexplicable joy. Let the laughter be real but tinged with crying. This is the human capacity to find grace in apocalypse.

title: The Last Night Watch
instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's bedside in the deep hours of the night. She's slipping in and out of consciousness, and you know this is the last time you'll speak to her. Begin in a state of exhausted numbness—you've been here for days, operating on autopilot, afraid to feel too much. As you hold her hand, something breaks open inside you: a flood of childhood memories, things you never thanked her for, secrets you wish you'd shared, the realization that when she goes, an entire world of stories and love goes with her. Let yourself move from protective emotional shutdown to raw, unguarded grief and gratitude. Speak to her as if she can hear everything—your voice should carry all the tenderness you've been too afraid or too 'adult' to show. By the end, find a place of devastating acceptance mixed with wonder at having been loved by her.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use the unconscious as a resource in rehearsal

title: The Unwanted Advance
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting on your porch, enjoying the late afternoon. A younger man you know approaches and makes an inappropriate advance. You begin with polite discomfort, then feel a flash of controlled anger. Speak slowly, deliberately, letting your voice flatten and your pitch drop. Every word is crisp, final. Let a thin layer of malice surface—you've been disrespected before. Clear your throat, shift in your chair, avoid eye contact. Your rejection is absolute, leaving no room for negotiation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Final Shore - Last Words to the Ocean
instruction: You're sitting on a beach at dawn, terminally ill, speaking to the ocean that has been your lifelong companion. You came here to say goodbye before you lose the ability to speak. Start with quiet gratitude, your voice steady but fragile, thanking the waves for every memory. As you continue, grief begins to crack through—your breath catches, words falter. You realize this is truly the last time, and desperation floods in. Try to memorize the sound of the waves, the smell of salt air, but your senses are already fading. End in a place of unexpected peace mixed with devastating loss, your voice dropping to barely a whisper, accepting what's coming while your heart simultaneously breaks and opens.

title: The Wedding Morning Goodbye
instruction: It's the morning of your wedding day, but you're saying goodbye to someone you once loved deeply—an ex who became your closest friend, or a friend you once wanted but could never have. You're telling them that while today is the happiest day of your life, there's also grief in it, because this marriage means a door closing forever on what you once imagined with them. Begin with bright happiness, your voice full of wedding-day joy and excitement, almost manic with celebration. But let other truths seep in: nostalgia, melancholy, a sharp awareness of roads not taken, genuine gratitude mixed with loss. Your voice should carry layers—laughing while your throat is tight with unshed tears, speaking with joy that's edged with mourning. Let yourself fully inhabit the paradox of being completely happy and deeply sad at once, of loving two people in different ways, of celebrating while grieving. End in a place that honors all these contradictory truths, transformed by the act of holding multiple emotional realities simultaneously.

title: The Tremor Hold
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a power yoga class, holding a deep warrior III pose. Your muscles shake under the strain, your breath is a controlled, oceanic ujjayi that barely lets you speak. As you struggle, a memory surfaces: a long-ago dance with your late partner, the same trembling excitement in your legs. Start with focused exertion, voice tight and strained, then let the longing seep in as you whisper a half-remembered phrase. End with a fragile release—not defeat, but a bittersweet surrender to both the pain and the memory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Hollow Hallelujah
instruction: You are an elderly deacon, once a powerful preacher, now asked to lead a short prayer at a small midweek service. But you've just received news that your only son has been diagnosed with a terminal illness. You stand at the podium, hands gripping the edge, voice trembling with a numbness that clings to you. As you begin, you feel a hot wave of embarrassment — these people expect your usual booming cadence, but your voice cracks, you stumble over words, and you have to pause to swallow the shame. By the end, the pain overwhelms you; the rhythmic sermon collapses into a raw, broken whisper, your eyes fixed on the floor, a single tear escaping as you lose the thread entirely.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present), Pain (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: A Lesson in Obedience
instruction: You are a woman in her late 20s, alone in a sunlit nursery with a small child who has just defiantly spilled juice on the rug you spent hours cleaning. You begin with a low, deliberate scold — each word separated, pitch dropping hard at the end of each sentence. But as you speak, a strange elation rises in your chest; you realize how much you enjoy the absolute control you have in this moment. A flicker of something darker, a slight sexual thrill at the power, colors your voice just for an instant. Let your tone shift from stern discipline to a slow, almost playful whisper, your final words laced with a quiet, satisfied smile.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Dance in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're at your grandmother's bedside in her final hours. She's awake, lucid, and asks you to help her stand one last time—she wants to dance with you like you did at your wedding. Begin weighed down by grief and the heaviness of impending loss, your body tight with the effort of holding back tears. As you carefully help her up and begin to sway together, let your body gradually open and find freedom in the movement. Allow the physical act of dancing—however small, however slow—to transform your sorrow into something else: celebration of her life, gratitude for this moment, even unexpected joy. Your voice may start choked and whispered but should find moments of laughter, singing, or breathy wonder. Let your body tell the story of moving from paralyzed grief to liberated love, from holding on to letting go with grace.

title: Burning Down to Breakthrough
instruction: You're addressing your former lover in an empty apartment - they're not here, but you can feel them everywhere. Your body is tight with everything you've held back: desire you never fully expressed, rage at how they left, the physical ache of missing them. Don't just speak - let your body respond. Pace, gesture, feel the heat in your chest, the tension in your hands. Start with the anger and betrayal, let it burn through you, but as you continue speaking, let other sensations emerge: the memory of their touch, the grief in your muscles, how love and fury can coexist in the same breath. Let your voice and body crescendo, break, then find a new equilibrium. End exhausted but somehow emptied of poison, raw but real.

title: The Guarded Smile
instruction: You're a teenager with a persistent, throbbing toothache that makes you hold your jaw tight. Your younger brother bursts into the room, proudly showing you a messy crayon drawing. Start with a warm, affectionate tone — you genuinely think it's sweet, but every word comes out careful and one-sided, because opening your mouth fully sends a stab of pain. As he keeps chattering, you become aware of how weird you sound, and embarrassment creeps in — you avoid sibilant words, wincing slightly. Finally, a quiet contempt surfaces, not at him, but at the stupid tooth that won't let you laugh or speak properly. End on a weary, resigned sigh.
emotions_sampled: Affection (clearly present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Contempt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Hovering on the Stool at Midnight
instruction: You're 16, perched on a shaky stool in your dark garage, the only light from a phone propped on a toolbox. You're watching a video of a girl you've known since middle school, but everything feels different now. Start by speaking quietly, with a tight, nervous edge—your legs are restless, your grip on the stool is firm. Let the infatuation bloom in your voice, tender and anxious, then let bitterness creep in as you remember she doesn't even know your name. End with a swallowed, vulnerable admission, the fear that this is hopeless.
emotions_sampled: Fear (slightly present), Infatuation (very intensely present), Bitterness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Soulmate Who Doesn't Remember You Anymore
instruction: Alzheimer's has taken them. This is your last visit before moving away—you can't keep watching them disappear. They don't know who you are anymore. You hold their hand and tell them about your life together: your first kiss, your wedding day, the way they used to make you laugh. Your voice is full of love and warmth as you paint these memories. But they're staring at you with polite confusion, and you begin to laugh—because it's absurd, because it's unbearable. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, celebrating this beautiful love while grieving its loss. 'We were so happy,' you say through tears and laughter. 'You made me so happy.' Your voice is breaking with gratitude and devastating loss at once. You kiss their forehead, thank them for everything, and leave. Your last words are whispered: 'I'll remember for both of us.'
inspired_by: Professional: Divorce Lawyer Realizes She's Representing Against Her Best Friend

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner That You're Leaving
instruction: They're asleep beside you. You're leaving at dawn and won't be here when they wake. Begin in the quietest voice possible, almost soundless—thanking them for the years, for the safety they gave you. Your throat tightens as you confess the love is real but you're disappearing inside this life. Describe small things you'll miss: their breathing, morning coffee, the way they say your name. Let silence fall between phrases as emotion chokes you. You must speak without waking them, so pain catches in whispered half-sentences. End with the devastating admission that leaving the person you love is the only way to find yourself again. Every word should feel like it's costing you something irreplaceable.
inspired_by: Your Child Telling You About Their Eating Disorder

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father fifteen years after he walked out. You've rehearsed this speech a thousand times, arriving full of righteous anger and accusation. But as you begin to speak, you notice everything about him you'd forgotten: the particular smell of his cologne that used to mean safety, the rough texture of his hands that once held yours, the exact sound of his breathing when he's trying not to cry. Let these physical, sensory details crack open your fury. Feel how your anger transforms as you register each sense—his aged face, the tremor in his voice, the way he reaches for you. By the end, you must arrive somewhere you didn't expect: not forgiveness exactly, but a recognition of his humanity that makes simple hatred impossible. Your voice should shift from hard and controlled to raw and uncertain.

title: Laughing Through Ruins: The Bittersweet Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving forever—moving across the world, ending the relationship, or slipping away from a disease. But you've both agreed to make this moment beautiful rather than just sad. Start by reminding them of the ridiculous inside joke that defined your relationship, and let yourself actually laugh—a real, full laugh that catches you by surprise. Your voice is warm, almost giddy as you recount absurd memories. But underneath, your heart is shattering. Let the laughter crack mid-sentence, then force it back. Say 'I'm so grateful for you' while tears stream down your face, your voice breaking between words. The contradictions are everything: you're devastated and joyful, grateful and destroyed. End with a genuine smile in your voice as you say 'Thank you for everything,' while simultaneously feeling like you're being torn in half. This is love and loss happening simultaneously—neither one diminishing the other.
inspired_by: Concealing Your True Intentions During a Negotiation

title: The Last Message
instruction: You are an elderly man, seated on your parked motorcycle at a scenic overlook you once visited with your late wife. Your full-face helmet is still on; the visor fogs slightly with each breath, and your voice sounds distant and boomy inside the padding. You pull out your phone to record a voice memo for your granddaughter, who is about to move far away. At first, your voice is thick with longing as you describe the view and how much your wife loved it here, but as you think of your granddaughter leaving, fear creeps in—fear of being alone, fear of losing another person you love. Let your words trail off as you fight to stay steady, a car door slams nearby and you flinch, then you swallow hard and force a gentle farewell.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved your entire life—a parent, a partner, a best friend—and they're slipping away in their final hour. Begin by noticing every sensory detail: the weight of their hand in yours, the rhythm of their breathing, the way afternoon light falls across their face. Start with a quiet attempt to hold yourself together, speaking in careful, controlled tones about mundane memories. As you continue, let a specific memory flood through you—see it, smell it, feel it as vividly as if you're living it right now—and allow this sensory immersion to crack your composure. End by transforming your grief into something else: a fierce gratitude, a whispered promise, or a moment of unexpected peace as you realize this person will live on in every detail you've just remembered so completely.

title: The Mirror Shatters: Rage at Your Reflection
instruction: Stand before a mirror after discovering your partner has been living a double life — with a version of you who made different choices. Start with cold, controlled fury, speaking to your reflection as if it's that other version of you. Your voice sharp, clinical, listing everything they have that you don't: the confidence, the career, the devotion. Let that control explode into screaming — primal, guttural rage at yourself for every choice you made, every moment you played it safe. Physically attack your own image with words: 'You coward, you fool, you waste.' Then collapse mid-scream into broken sobs, your forehead against the glass, whispering apologies to yourself. Transform again into fierce, protective tenderness — you are the only one who truly knows your pain. End with a whispered vow to the face in the mirror: 'I will not abandon you again' — both a promise and a prayer, shaking with the effort to believe it.
inspired_by: Parallel Universe: Meeting the Other You

title: Over My Shoulder
instruction: You're at a crowded family reunion, standing by the buffet table. Someone behind you calls your name in a voice that tugs at your memory, but you can't place it. Twist your neck sharply to look over your shoulder, straining to see through the crowd. Start with sharp confusion—squinting, your words coming out tight and breathy because of the awkward angle. As you finally spot an old friend you haven't seen in years, let your voice soften with a dawning affection, even as you keep your head turned and the strain remains.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Babel's Fury
instruction: You're screaming at a border control officer who won't let your family through, beginning in explosive rage, switching frantically between languages trying to make them understand. Your voice should be raw, desperate, switching faster and faster between tongues as panic sets in. Let the fury crack into helpless sobbing as you realize no amount of words in any language will change this moment. The switches become more broken, more desperate - mixing languages mid-sentence, repeating phrases louder as if volume could bridge understanding. End with your voice giving out completely, collapsing from roaring to a devastated whisper, saying 'please' in every language you know, each one more broken than the last.

title: Buried in Snow: Creating an Air Pocket While Suffocating
instruction: You're buried in snow after an avalanche, your voice completely muffled. You can't move. Your voice is barely a whisper as you frantically assess your position. You're trying to create an air pocket by pushing snow away from your face. Your narration is almost silent, panicked, desperate. 'Can't breathe. Creating space.' Each word is an effort, and the snow is so heavy that your whispered narration almost echoes in your own head. Include the moment where you find a pocket of air and your voice becomes slightly less panicked, but now you're a prisoner of your own small space. Your narration becomes meditative, almost spiritual, as you try not to hyperventilate and use your limited air. You might die here. Your voice becomes a quiet meditation on that fact. You're waiting. The silence is profound.

title: Condone Action
instruction: Your friend did something morally wrong, and they're asking you to say it's okay. Your voice doesn't want to: 'I can't do that.' But the friendship pressure is immense. 'Come on, everyone makes mistakes.' They're pushing. Your voice becomes firmer: 'I love you, but I can't condone this.' The line-drawing costs the friendship. But your voice knows: some friendships aren't worth keeping.

title: Running Until You Remember
instruction: You're running—physically pushing your body hard, breath ragged, muscles burning. Begin with desperate, almost frantic energy as you try to outrun a recent devastating loss. But as your body hits its rhythm, let a memory surface unbidden: the first time you felt this same physical intensity—maybe your first race, first athletic victory, first moment your body felt powerful and alive. Let the sensory details flood you: the burn in your lungs then and now, sweat, heartbeat pounding in your ears, the exact texture of triumph in your muscles. As you relive that younger body's joy, let it crash against your current pain—feel how your body remembers euphoria even while your heart is breaking. Your breathing should be real, physical, labored throughout. Let a sob break through the athletic rhythm. End with your body simultaneously experiencing remembered ecstasy and present agony, pushing harder, unable to tell if you're running toward that younger self's joy or away from your current grief. Voice it through gasps and physical exertion—let your body tell the story.

title: The Garden Gate
instruction: You're an elderly person with an androgynous voice, standing at your garden gate after a neighborhood meeting where a younger resident accused you of 'taking up space' with your flowers. You feel a deep sadness—you've tended this garden for forty years, and it's your last connection to a spouse who passed. Now, this person looms, trying to intimidate you into moving. Your voice drops low and slow, almost a growl, as you respond. Start with a weary, broken sadness, but as you speak, a quiet, defiant strength emerges—you're not leaving, and they will not break you. Pause to glance at a wilting rose, clear your throat, and let your voice crack with age but harden with resolve. End with a final, tempered anger that trembles on the edge of tears.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Midnight Confessional
instruction: You are an elderly person, alone in a quiet kitchen at 2 AM, having just consumed three cups of strong black coffee to fight off insomnia. Your hands tremble slightly around the mug. At the start, you are trying to sound casual, telling yourself you're just checking on the garden, but your voice is too fast, pitch just a bit higher. As you speak, a memory of a neighbor you've long desired—the way they moved in the afternoon light—surfaces. By the end, your confession becomes raw, hungry, a crackling admission of lust that surprises you. Let your voice betray the stimulant: a jittery quickness that races forward, then halts abruptly when you realize what you've said. Let the faint sound of a clock ticking and your own short breaths punctuate the words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Sunday Call
instruction: You are an older woman with a deliberately bright, hyper-feminized voice, sitting alone at your kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon. You're on the phone with your adult child who lives far away — the conversation has just ended, but neither of you has hung up yet. You keep your voice cheerful and clear, slightly louder than necessary, with an upward lilt at the end of each sentence to check if they're still there. But underneath the practiced brightness, you feel a spreading numbness, a hollow acceptance that these calls are becoming routine. As you speak, you notice the silence on the other end, and the brightness falters — your voice drops, a tremor of real sadness breaks through, and you finally say what you've been avoiding: that you miss them and wish they'd visit. End with a quiet, vulnerable admission that cracks the facade.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Between the Words
instruction: Late at night, your partner is telling you something difficult in barely audible whispers—a secret they've carried for years. They keep stopping, starting over, their voice catching. Your challenge is to listen with your entire being: not just to the words but to every vocal nuance, every breath, every silence that contains what they can't yet say. Begin with quiet dread, your body tense, bracing for impact. But as you truly receive the trembling in their voice, the courage it's taking, the trust they're offering, let yourself soften completely. Move from fear of what you'll hear to overwhelming tenderness for their bravery in speaking. Let listening itself become an act of love. By the end, you're not thinking about your response—you're simply holding space for their truth with your full attention.
inspired_by: Actor struggles to listen to scene partners genuinely

title: The Lost Necklace
instruction: You're in your cluttered childhood bedroom, sitting cross-legged on the floor, rummaging through an old suitcase packed with keepsakes. You're searching for a necklace your grandmother gave you, but you're also distracting yourself by looking at old photos and trinkets. Start with focused, determined murmuring as you dig through fabric and plastic, but as your fingers meet nothing familiar, let your voice become uncertain, trailing off into doubt. End with a quiet, almost defeated sigh as you realize you may never find it.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Reading a Letter from Someone You've Lost
instruction: You've just received a letter they wrote before they died, to be delivered after. Your voice begins with disbelief, almost laughing through tears: 'You... you planned this. Of course you did.' As you read their words—maybe jokes, maybe memories, maybe things they never said in life—your voice breaks and mends repeatedly, oscillating between laughter and sobbing: 'Remember when we... oh god, I can't believe you wrote about that.' There's gratitude mixed with fresh grief as their voice comes alive on the page, your own voice tender and destroyed: 'This is so you. This is so perfectly you.' Then you reach the part where they say goodbye, where they tell you to live, to be happy, and your voice shatters on the impossible beauty and cruelty of it: 'How am I supposed to... you're asking me to...' But somehow, through the words, you feel them with you. Your voice finds an impossible peace, speaking to them as if they can hear: 'Thank you. For everything. For this.' End with your voice carrying both unbearable loss and profound gratitude, laughing softly through tears at one final thing they wrote, your grief and love and joy impossibly intertwined.
inspired_by: Accepting Terminal Diagnosis: Bargaining Becoming Acceptance

title: Whispering to a Sleeping Lover You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're whispering to your sleeping partner, confessing why you have to leave them, knowing they can't hear you but needing to say it anyway. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, catching on unshed tears. Start with tender appreciation for who they are—let genuine love saturate every word. Then reveal the painful truth: you're not enough for yourself, you're disappearing, you need to find who you were before you became 'we.' Let your voice shake with the paradox: loving them completely while knowing you have to go. Include long pauses where you almost touch them but don't. End with a whispered 'I'm sorry' that contains both liberation and heartbreak. The devastation should be quiet, internal, the kind that makes your chest tight. Nothing theatrical—just raw, throat-catching honesty spoken in the dark.

title: The Kitchen Where Everything Was Decided
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen confronting your parent about something they did twenty years ago that shaped your entire life. Begin by grounding yourself in the physical reality of this space—the worn countertop you used to sit on, the light fixture that always flickered, the smell that's uniquely this room, the temperature, the sounds from outside. Start the confrontation from a place of careful control, almost rehearsed accusation. But as you speak and they respond (or don't respond the way you expected), let the ground shift under you. What you thought was pure anger reveals hurt underneath. What you thought was hurt reveals a desperate need for them to see you. By the end, you're no longer accusing—you're begging them to understand something about who you've become and why. Your voice should crack open, revealing layers you didn't know you'd expose.
inspired_by: Using Sense Memory to Re-Experience a Dream

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye You Can't Stop
instruction: You're helping your closest friend pack for a move across the world—a wonderful opportunity they've dreamed of, and you're genuinely happy for them. As you fold their clothes and wrap their belongings, you're laughing together at shared memories each item triggers. Your voice is bright, celebratory, full of joy for their future. But underneath, your heart is shattering because you're losing the person who knows you best. Let the laughter be real—then let it catch in your throat. Keep trying to stay positive, making jokes that land a little wrong, your voice brightening artificially. When you pick up something particularly meaningful—a photo, a gift you gave them—your voice should crack even as you're smiling. End with a moment where you're simultaneously congratulating them with genuine excitement while tears stream down your face, your voice thick with both celebration and grief, telling them how proud you are while barely holding yourself together. The last words should be almost laughing, almost sobbing, completely sincere in both.
inspired_by: Acting Interested in a Hobby You Dont Enjoy

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You
instruction: You've finally gathered the courage to tell your mother how her choices shaped you. Start controlled, almost rehearsed - you've practiced this. But as you speak, the hurt underneath surfaces. Your voice rises as you detail specific memories: times she chose her addictions over you, moments you needed her and she wasn't there, the way you raised yourself. She's defending herself, making excuses, and it enrages you. You're yelling now, demanding she take responsibility. But then she says something - maybe she cries, maybe she admits she knows - and your anger transforms into something more complicated. Your voice softens into a painful question: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you want to stay sober?' End with the devastating vulnerability of still wanting her love despite everything.
inspired_by: Screaming Fight Where Everything Hurtful Gets Said

title: Reading the Acceptance Letter: Your Dream, Their Sacrifice
instruction: You're reading aloud the acceptance letter to your dream program—the one that requires you to move across the world, leaving behind aging parents who need you. Begin with pure joy, voice bright and disbelieving: 'I got in. I actually got in!' Let yourself laugh, almost giddy. Your parent says they're happy for you—but you hear what they're not saying. Your voice shifts, joy mixing with dawning guilt: 'You really mean that?' Keep reading, voice trembling now between excitement and heartbreak: each word of the letter is your dream, but also means abandoning them. Feel the contradictions tearing you apart—laughing through tears, voice breaking on words like 'opportunity' and 'future.' End in a place of bittersweet resolution, voice thick with both gratitude and grief: 'Thank you for letting me go.' The final words carry equal measures of joy and sorrow, freedom and loss, celebrating and mourning in the same breath.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Leaving a Good Relationship

title: The Last Voicemail to Someone Who Will Never Wake Up
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for someone in a coma—your partner, parent, or closest friend—knowing the doctors say there's almost no chance they'll hear it. Start by trying to sound normal, maybe even cheerful, sharing mundane updates about your day because that's what you always did. But as you speak, the pretense crumbles. Your voice should crack and soften, moving from forced lightness into raw confession: all the things you never said, the apologies you held back, the love you assumed they knew. End in a whisper, perhaps a goodbye you can barely voice, or a desperate plea for them to come back. The journey is from protective denial to devastating acceptance.
inspired_by: Voice Actor Recording a Happy Commercial While Devastated

title: The Downpour Awakening
instruction: You're standing in pouring rain after walking out of an important meeting/audition/family dinner where you finally refused to pretend anymore. Your body is drenched, shaking—from cold, from adrenaline, from fear. Start with panicked breathing, second-guessing yourself, your voice choked with doubt about what you just did. But then feel the rain on your skin. Let your breathing deepen. Begin to laugh—or cry—or both. Your voice should become physically unleashed, raw and primal. Speak or shout to no one about the relief of being exactly who you are, even if it costs you everything. End with your voice open, wild, your body alive with the terrifying freedom of authenticity.

title: The Last Phone Call From the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your parent from the hospital after receiving your terminal diagnosis. Your voice starts controlled, almost clinical: 'So... the doctor just left. It's not good.' You're trying to protect them, keeping emotion locked down. But as you continue, something cracks - maybe when you mention a specific memory, a place you'll never see again together. Your breathing becomes uneven. Then, unexpectedly, you find yourself comforting them even as your own fear surfaces: 'No, listen to me - we're going to be okay with this.' By the end, there's a strange peace mixed with grief, your voice softening into tender acceptance: 'I'm not afraid anymore. I just... I love you.' The arc moves from clinical distance through breaking grief to bittersweet clarity.

title: The Recognition That Ignites You
instruction: Someone you've sacrificed everything for - a partner, a parent, a child - casually mentions something nice you did, like it's no big deal. Your voice starts controlled, almost cold: 'Something nice?' Then it explodes. Years of unacknowledged labor, invisible care, thankless devotion pour out in a torrent of rage: 'I gave up everything! My career, my dreams, my LIFE!' You're shaking with fury. But mid-tirade, you see their face - maybe they're crying, maybe they're finally seeing you - and your voice breaks. The anger collapses into raw, sobbing grief: 'I just wanted you to see me. Just once, I wanted you to really see what I gave up.' By the end, your voice is exhausted, almost tender in its devastation: 'All I ever wanted was for you to notice.'

title: First Breath After
instruction: You've just given birth after being told you'd never conceive. Begin breathless from labor, panting, exhausted: 'Is she... is she breathing?' Your own breath is ragged, depleted. Then you hear the baby cry. Your breathing shifts—catches, holds, as wonder floods in. You laugh, but the laugh breaks into sobbing: 'Oh God... oh God, you're real... you're real...' Your breath comes in great gulping waves—joy and terror and gratitude and grief for all the years of emptiness all happening at once. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, breathing in rhythm with your baby's cries. Find the space where celebration and devastation meet: 'I waited so long for you... I thought I'd never... never...' End with deep, cleansing breaths that somehow contain both profound relief and the knowledge that now you have everything to lose. Let your breathing mirror the chaos and beauty of new life.

title: 3 AM Truths: Whispering Your Deepest Shame to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: They're asleep beside you. You're speaking so quietly they won't wake, but you need to say it aloud, even if they'll never hear. Your voice is barely a breath, tender and terrified: 'I need to tell you something I've never told anyone.' You confess the thing you believe makes you unlovable—the secret, the failure, the part of yourself you've hidden even in your intimacy. Your voice catches constantly, each word a small act of courage. As you speak, something shifts: describing it to their sleeping form, you hear yourself with compassion for the first time. Your whisper becomes slightly stronger, infused with wonder and grief: 'Maybe I've been carrying this alone for too long.' End with your voice breaking on a soft sob of relief mixed with sorrow, placing your hand gently on their shoulder, drawing comfort from their presence even though they'll never know what you just released into the darkness.
inspired_by: Sharing Your Diagnosis With Someone You Love

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father across the kitchen table about a betrayal that shattered your family years ago. Begin with controlled anger, your words measured and accusatory. As you speak, allow fragments to flood your awareness: the weight of his hand on your shoulder when you were seven, the sound of doors slamming during their fights, the smell of his aftershave, the sight of your mother's packed suitcase, a birthday where he didn't show up, the taste of the lie he told. Let these sensory flashes interrupt your accusations - you might start a sentence with rage and end it with something else entirely. Don't suppress whatever emerges. By the end, discover that beneath your fury is something more complex: grief for who he could have been, or unexpected understanding, or the exhausting weight of carrying this for so long.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent who has been unconscious for days. You've been holding in anger about things left unsaid for years. Start by trying to say a polite, dutiful goodbye—the kind everyone expects. But as you speak, let yourself crack open. Stop performing the 'good child.' If the safe words aren't releasing what's really inside you, abandon them completely. Dig for what you actually need to say—maybe it's rage, maybe it's desperate love, maybe it's both. Let your voice change completely from beginning to end. By the final moment, you're not saying goodbye the way you planned—you're saying what you never had the courage to say while they could answer. The emotion that emerges must surprise even you.
inspired_by: Actor has chosen a choice for a scene but it is not producing the desired emotional results

title: Playing Along After the Fall
instruction: You are an elderly man visiting your granddaughter in the hospital. You’ve just come from a doctor’s appointment where you learned your own voice is failing you—a condition that has started to steal the rich, deep voice you’ve always taken pride in. You’re sitting beside her bed, leaning in close, whispering to not disturb the other patients. You begin talking softly, shame heavy in your chest—the shame of your voice cracking, of feeling small and frail. But as you recall a memory of a prank you two played on your son years ago, a glimmer of hope emerges in your whisper—you’re still here, still able to share this with her. By the end, your whisper takes on a teasing, playful lilt, even as your throat feels tight. Let your voice be airy, unsteady, occasionally breaking into a wheeze, and let the pauses come as you search for the right memory.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Breath of Quiet
instruction: You're a teenage boy sitting alone in a hospital waiting room late at night, finally hearing the muffled footsteps of a surgeon approaching. Your father has been in surgery for hours, and the mask you've been given feels stifling, trapping your breath. Start speaking with a strained, hopeful whisper, your words catching as you try to swallow the knot in your throat. Midway, let the reality of 'he's okay' hit you—your voice cracks, your shoulders slump forward, and the relief comes out as a shaky, tear-choked laugh that fades into a long, trembling exhale. End with your words barely audible, thick with unshed tears.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Garden You Abandoned
instruction: You're confronting your elderly father in the garden your mother lovingly tended before she died—the garden he let turn to weeds and ruin. Start with restrained anger as you describe what this garden once was, the roses she named after each of her children. Your voice should be tight, controlled, accusing him of letting her memory die along with her flowers. But as you speak, something shifts—you realize you're not just angry about the garden, you're angry about every way he failed to stay present after she left. Let your accusations become more raw and personal, moving from the metaphor of the neglected roses to the direct pain of feeling abandoned by him. End with a devastating question that reveals your true need: not for him to tend the garden, but for him to see you, to choose to stay in this world with you. The emotion should evolve from righteous anger to exposed, childlike longing.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sweet Scent of Freshly Bloomed Roses in a Garden

title: Coming Down Off Cocaine: Paranoia and Shame Cycle
instruction: The cocaine is wearing off. For 45 minutes you were invincible. Now you're in the pit. Your voice becomes small, worried. You're ruminating about what you said, replaying conversations obsessively out loud. Your voice gets quieter and more self-loathing. You're convinced everyone hates you. Anxiety rides every word. Include the physical exhaustion in your voice—drained, scraped out, raw.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After fifteen years of silence, you're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child. Start with cold, controlled fury—your voice sharp, sarcastic, each word a weapon designed to hurt them the way they hurt you. You're listing their failures with surgical precision, almost enjoying their discomfort. But as you speak, something shifts: beneath the rage, you're still that abandoned child, and suddenly you're not attacking anymore—you're pleading, your voice cracking as years of buried pain surface. 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger collapses into raw, vulnerable need for an answer they can't give. By the end, you're spent, your voice hollow, as you realize that no explanation will ever heal what was broken. The transformation is from fierce anger to devastating vulnerability to empty acceptance.

title: Laughing Through the Confession of Collapse
instruction: You're finally admitting you can't keep your promise, but something absurd and liberating is happening—you're starting to laugh. Begin with nervous, apologetic laughter that sounds wrong, almost manic: 'This is so ridiculous, I actually can't do this.' There's relief mixed with horror in your voice. The laughter gets stronger even as tears start, creating a beautiful, contradictory mess. You're simultaneously devastated and freed, heartbroken and strangely euphoric. Your voice moves between genuine giggles and choked sobs, sometimes in the same breath. You're grateful—actually grateful—to finally stop pretending, even though admitting failure is breaking your heart. The words come faster, more honest: 'I've been so scared, and it feels so good to finally say I can't.' End with a moment of unexpected peace, your voice soft and almost joyful through tears: 'I'm not enough for this, and that's... okay.' This is about finding strange liberation in surrender, about the way truth can hurt and heal simultaneously.
inspired_by: Confessing You Can't Do the Thing You Promised

title: The Wedding Ring in Your Palm
instruction: You are holding your wedding ring in your palm for the last time before giving it back. Build its sensory reality with excruciating specificity: its exact weight, the temperature of the metal, the engraving you trace with your fingertip, how it catches the light, the indent it left on your finger that you can still feel. As you make this object completely real, let it contain your entire marriage—see the moment it was first placed on your finger, smell that day, feel who you were then. Begin speaking to your former spouse with bitter anger or cold detachment. But as the ring becomes more and more tangible in your hand—its weight, its warmth from your skin, every scratch and mark of years worn—let contradictory emotions flood in. Move toward a complex place where you're simultaneously furious and heartbroken, grateful and devastated, ready to let go and desperate to hold on. The more real the ring becomes, the more impossible it should be to feel just one thing.

title: Laughing at the Ruins
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—a relationship, a dream, a life you built—and you're having a conversation with someone who was part of it. Begin with bitter laughter, almost manic: isn't it absurd how completely it all collapsed? You're listing the disasters with dark humor, voice bright and sharp. But the laughter keeps catching, turning into something else. You loved this. God, you loved this so much. Your voice softens with devastating tenderness as you acknowledge the beauty of what you had, even as you mourn its loss. Joy and grief tangle together—you're genuinely grateful it existed, even though its ending is breaking you. You laugh again, but now it's through tears, wonder and heartbreak inseparable. End with a strange, peaceful acceptance: voice steady but thick with emotion, acknowledging that you wouldn't trade the experience even for this pain, that the wreckage was worth it. Let contradictions live fully in your voice—celebrate and mourn simultaneously, finding something like grace in the devastation.

title: The Photographer and the Ghostly Apparition
instruction: Narrate a scene where a photographer with a curious, analytical voice encounters a ghost who speaks in a haunting, melancholic tone. Switch between the photographers attempts to communicate and the ghosts cryptic messages, building a mysterious atmosphere.

title: The Eruption: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You've just found out that your younger sibling is in the same kind of dangerous relationship you escaped from years ago. They're defending their partner, minimizing the warning signs. You start trying to stay calm: 'Listen to me, please just listen.' But as they make excuses—the same excuses you once made—your voice begins to shake with barely contained panic. 'You don't understand what you're saying right now!' Your voice explodes into desperation, almost shouting: 'I know because I LIVED IT! I know how this ends!' You're furious at them for not seeing it, furious at yourself for not protecting them better, terrified you're going to lose them. Your voice cracks between rage and terror, becoming almost guttural with the need to make them understand. Then suddenly you collapse into pleading, your voice breaking into sobs: 'Please. Please don't do this. I can't watch you disappear.' The intensity transforms from fierce protective anger to absolute helpless heartbreak, your voice ending in whispered begging.
inspired_by: Telling Someone About Abuse for the First Time

title: The Last Letter to Someone Lost
instruction: You're recording a voice message to someone who died before you could say everything you needed to say. Begin with quiet, controlled composure as you address them directly: 'I found your old jacket today. It still smells like you.' Let yourself stay present with small, concrete details. As you continue, memories flood in and your voice begins to crack with the weight of all the unsaid words. Move through gratitude for what you had, then into the ache of what you'll never have. By the end, you're speaking through tears but also finding something like forgiveness—for them, for yourself, for the way things ended. Your final words should feel like both goodbye and an eternal connection: a whispered 'I'll carry you with me' that holds profound loss and profound love simultaneously.

title: Fragments of a Last Conversation
instruction: You're having an intimate late-night phone conversation with someone you love who lives far away—perhaps your last conversation before they move even further or before a relationship ends. Perform four whispered moments from this call, but out of sequence: first, the tender middle when you're both laughing softly at a shared memory; second, the beginning when you're guarded, testing whether it's safe to be vulnerable; third, the devastating end when one of you finally says what cannot be unsaid; fourth, the quiet reconciliation near the close when you're both crying but somehow okay. Each fragment must contain its own specific emotional truth—the cautious hope, the undefended joy, the shattering realization, the bittersweet peace. Speak as if the person is really there on the other end, and let us feel how these scattered moments form a complete emotional journey from fear to connection to loss to acceptance.

title: The Borrowed Coat
instruction: You're holding an object that belonged to someone you've lost—a coat, a letter, a photograph. You're supposed to give it away today, finally let it go. Begin by talking to this person as if they can hear you, but using the voice and words you think you should use—the gracious, healed version of yourself, the one who has 'moved on.' Notice how that voice feels in your mouth—probably familiar, safe, rehearsed. Then let yourself feel the actual contradictions churning beneath those words. Maybe you're furious at them for leaving. Maybe you're grateful and devastated simultaneously. Maybe you don't want to let go at all. Let your voice shift between these truths without smoothing them over. Speak in circles if that's what happens. Let yourself say 'I'm okay' and then immediately contradict it. End not with resolution but with the messy reality of holding two opposite truths at once: goodbye and I'm not ready, love and anger, release and desperate holding on.
inspired_by: An actor notices they have developed mannerisms and behavioral dependencies

title: The Last Meal: Laughter at the Table of Grief
instruction: You're preparing your late partner's favorite meal on the first anniversary of their death, narrating the process while crying and laughing simultaneously. Begin with shaky humor, joking about how they always burned the garlic, finding lightness in memories. Let joy and devastation collide - laugh genuinely at a funny memory while your voice breaks with tears, express deep gratitude for the years you had while your heart shatters at their absence. Your emotions should feel chaotic and real, switching rapidly between warmth and grief. End in a place of profound, peaceful contradiction - setting two plates as you always did, voice full of both unbearable loss and pure love, somehow okay and completely broken at the same time.
inspired_by: The Chef and the Talking Ingredient

title: Bedside Confession
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you at 3 AM, and you're whispering a confession they'll never hear—you've been pretending to be happy for the last two years. Your voice is barely audible, tender and careful not to wake them, each word like placing glass on glass. You describe the exact moment you realized you'd stopped feeling, the dinner where you smiled and felt nothing. Your throat keeps catching because even though they're asleep, saying it out loud makes it devastatingly real. Midway through, your voice becomes even softer, more gentle, because underneath the sadness is profound love for who they are, even if you can't feel what you once did. The final words are an apology so quiet it's almost just breath: 'You deserved someone who could stay... who could feel.' End with you carefully touching their sleeping face, your voice breaking on a whispered: 'I'm so sorry.' The tenderness and grief are inseparable.

title: The Homecoming That Cuts Both Ways
instruction: You're returning to a place you once called home, standing in a doorway looking at someone you left behind. Begin with cautious joy, tentative hope. Ground yourself in what you actually see: how they really look now (older, different, the same), the genuine state of the room or space, real objects that remain or have changed, the actual quality of light, specific sounds. Let your attention move between these concrete details. As you try to reconnect, let the reality of what you're actually perceiving—maybe how they're really standing, their actual tone of voice, the genuine distance or closeness of their body, what their eyes truly show—complicate your hope. By the end, the undeniable truth of what's physically present versus what you imagined should create a bittersweet collision: simultaneous deep love for what genuinely remains and sharp grief for what's irretrievably lost, both emotions equally real, equally overwhelming.

title: Universe Confession
instruction: You're a grieving parent alone in your car, and you're screaming at the universe, at God, at whatever is listening: 'Why did you take my baby?!' Your voice is raw, destroyed, ancient with pain. 'She was four years old! FOUR!' You're hitting the steering wheel, your voice fractured by sobs: 'I would have taken her place! I would have done anything!' The confession is to the void. 'I don't understand. I don't understand. I don't understand.' You repeat it until the words lose meaning. By the end, you're just keening — not words, just sound. The sound of a parent's grief is the loneliest sound in the world. Silence. Then, barely audible: 'I still love you, baby girl.' A whisper to the empty universe, and the universe answers with silence.

title: The Last Formation
instruction: You are a female drill sergeant addressing your platoon for the final time before they ship out. Your voice must cut through the open air with maximum unamplified volume — every vowel shouted, every consonant spat hard and percussive. Begin with the full iron authority of command, but as you give your final order, let a slight crack of affection seep through. Let your voice catch for a half-second, maybe you clear your throat or adjust your stance. The love is in the silence between the shouts, in the way your jaw softens just before you dismiss them. End quieter, almost reluctant, but still sharp enough to be heard across the field.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Mirror's Echo
instruction: You're a young woman standing in front of your bathroom mirror late at night, still in your makeup from the day. You're exhausted, fighting a yawn as you stare at your own reflection. Start in quiet contemplation, tracing a line on the mirror with your finger, mumbling to yourself about how today went. Let your voice be hollow, rounded, interrupted by the yawn that pulls your pitch down. Let the yawn linger, softening your words. As you speak, let doubt creep in about choices you made, then settle into deep disappointment as you say something honest to your reflection. The yawn should feel like a physical interruption you have to push through, making your voice slide lower, especially at the end of phrases. Your final words should come out as a slow, defeatist whisper, still fighting the yawn.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Doubt (slightly present), Disappointment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Final Transmission from the Edge of Everything
instruction: You're an astronaut drifting away from your ship, knowing rescue is impossible. Your oxygen is running out. Start with technical calm—reporting your situation, vital signs, coordinates—because that's what training demands. 'Suit breach at 14:32. Oxygen at 18%. Drifting at approximately...' But your voice begins to crack as the reality sinks in. You're looking back at Earth, and suddenly all the clinical reporting falls away. 'I can see... God, I can see where I grew up from here. The whole continent.' Your breathing becomes irregular, panic mixing with something like transcendence. You need to say goodbye—to your family, to your crewmates—but the words that come out are about the beauty of what you're seeing. 'Tell them I wasn't scared at the end. Tell them it's... it's the most beautiful thing.' Your voice moves from controlled professional to raw human to something approaching peace, even as your breath grows shorter. The fear never leaves, but wonder and acceptance emerge alongside it.
inspired_by: Adapting to Microgravity: Wonder Breaking Through Disorientation

title: The Landing
instruction: You are in the quiet, dim aftermath of a scene, wrapped in a blanket, still a little hazy from the endorphin crash. Your partner is holding you, stroking your arm. As you take a sip of water, doubt creeps in—did you disappoint? Your voice starts small, unsteady, almost childlike. Let the exhaustion and intoxication make you lose your train of thought. Then, as your partner whispers reassurance, let your voice soften into a warm, steady murmur, repeating their words as if convincing yourself. End with a gentle, certain exhale, fully settled into trust.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Intervention You Never Wanted
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you—the neglect disguised as independence, the emotional absence masked as strength. Start angry, controlled, with a list of grievances you've rehearsed for years. Your voice is sharp, precise, cutting. But as you speak, you realize they're not fighting back—they're just sitting there, smaller than you've ever seen them, aging and frail. Your anger begins cracking. You want to stay furious, you've earned that fury, but underneath it is the child who just wanted them to show up. Your voice splits between rage and desperate grief. End with a question you've been afraid to ask your whole life: 'Did you ever actually love me?' Let the question hang there, naked and terrified, because you're not sure you can survive the answer.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally facing the parent who abandoned you as a child, seeing them for the first time in twenty years. Start with cold, rehearsed anger—you've prepared what you wanted to say for decades. But as you speak, listing all the moments they missed, your voice begins to crack. The anger transforms into raw, vulnerable pain. You find yourself becoming a child again, asking the question you've always been too afraid to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Your voice should shift from controlled fury to broken pleading, from accusations to desperate need for an answer that might never satisfy you. End with the horrifying realization that you still want their love, even after everything, and you hate yourself for it.

title: Reading Your Acceptance Letter to the Dream You're Turning Down
instruction: You're reading aloud the acceptance letter—medical school, an art fellowship overseas, the job of a lifetime—that you're about to decline because someone you love is dying and needs you to stay. Read the letter with growing excitement at first, letting yourself feel the joy of being chosen, being wanted, your voice bright with possibility. Then let reality intrude: small hesitations, your voice faltering on phrases like 'this fall' or 'four years' because you won't be there. Laugh at the absurdity of your situation—this impossible choice—but let that laughter become tears. End reading the final congratulatory lines with a voice full of gratitude for the dream and absolute grief for its loss, somehow at peace with your choice while your heart breaks, folding the letter carefully as you say 'no' to everything you wanted and 'yes' to love.
inspired_by: Time Traveler Warning Themselves Not to Go

title: Spirit Touched
instruction: You're experiencing something that feels spiritual—a moment where connection transcends physical and becomes something larger. Your voice is almost in awe: 'I feel...' But you can't find words. Your partner's voice is equally affected: 'I know. Me too.' You're both experiencing something beyond the physical. You're being present together in a way that touches something sacred in you. Your voice becomes quieter, more reverent. There's peace in your voice. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's experienced something transcendent.

title: The Kitchen Table Truth
instruction: You are confronting your father about his absence during your childhood. Begin the scene with your entire body armored—fists clenched, chest tight, voice hard and accusatory. You came here to attack, to finally unleash years of rage. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: you notice how small he looks, how his hands shake. Let your body slowly unlock as you move from rage to something more vulnerable. Your voice should crack, soften. By the end, you are not yelling but speaking quietly, openly, your shoulders dropped, breathing deeply. You realize you don't want to destroy him—you just wanted to be seen. The transformation is from rigid fury to accessible hurt, from attack to honest need.

title: Stumble in the Dark
instruction: You're a young woman running through your childhood home at night, trying to escape an argument you just had with your mother. Your foot catches on a rug and you fall hard, your ribs hitting the corner of a wooden coffee table. The air is knocked out of you with a sharp 'oof' as you crumple to the floor. Lying there, gasping, you hear your mother calling your name from the other room. As you try to respond, your voice comes out thin and shaky between wheezes. You start to say you're fine, but a wave of shame hits you—shame for starting the fight, shame for being so clumsy, shame for still needing her. There's also a flicker of confusion: why are you still on the ground? Why can't you catch your breath? Start with the pain of the fall, then let the shame and confusion bleed in as you speak, your words halting and breathless.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Reading Your Childhood Diary at Your Abuser's Funeral
instruction: You're standing at the funeral of someone who hurt you terribly as a child—a parent, a teacher, a family friend. You've brought your childhood diary and you're reading from it, your voice initially almost amused, detached: 'Listen to this. Age nine: I must have done something wrong again today.' There's bitter laughter in your voice, a strange lightness. But as you read more, something shifts. Your voice becomes younger, more raw: 'Age twelve: Maybe if I'm perfect, they'll love me.' You're crying now, but also laughing at the absurdity, the tragedy, the relief that it's over. 'I wasted so many years trying to earn your love. And now you're dead and I'm... free?' Your voice breaks on 'free' because you realize it's true and that hurts too. End with profound contradiction: 'Thank you for dying. I mean that. And I'm sorry you never learned to love better. I grieve who you could have been.' You're simultaneously celebrating and mourning, grateful and devastated, laughing through tears.
inspired_by: Small Explosion at Work: Checking Colleagues for Injuries

title: The Stain That Won't Come Out
instruction: You are alone in a dim kitchen at midnight, scrubbing the same spot on the counter over and over for the past twenty minutes. You start with a quiet, steady contentment—the rhythm of the sponge feels like a small anchor, a simple chore you can control. As you press harder, your breath hitches with each push, and the shame creeps in: this stain is from a fight you had with your daughter last week, and the helplessness that you can't fix any of it, can't make her speak to you again. By the end, the scrubbing grows frantic, your voice cracks, and you trail off into a whisper, realizing you're not cleaning the counter—you're punishing yourself.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (extremely present), Helplessness (slightly present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're alone, and a song comes on—or you catch a scent, see a photograph—and suddenly your body remembers an intense physical and emotional experience: a night of passion, a moment of violence, childbirth, an accident, a transcendent experience. Let the memory flood your body. Begin by trying to resist it, staying controlled. As you speak (describing what you're remembering or speaking to someone from that memory), let yourself physically respond: your breath changes, your body tenses or melts, heat rises in you, or cold dread, or aching desire. Before each phrase, notice: what is my body doing? What am I actually feeling? Let sensation and emotion be inseparable. Maybe you start in your head trying to describe it, but end up overtaken by the physical-emotional reality of the memory. Transform from controlled to surrendered, from resistant to consumed, from numb to fully alive.

title: Laughing Through Your Wedding Vows to Someone Who's Leaving
instruction: You're reciting wedding vows to your partner, but both of you know they're dying—weeks, maybe days left. Your voice starts with genuine laughter because the absurdity and beauty of it hit you simultaneously: 'till death do us part' when death is already in the room. You're giddy, almost euphoric, savoring this moment of defiant joy. Your voice is bright, warm, full of actual humor at the cosmic joke of it all. But as you continue, the laughter becomes entangled with tears you didn't mean to shed. Your voice stays light, keeps finding the humor—you're still smiling through the vows—but grief is bleeding through every word. You're promising 'for better or worse, in sickness and health' and you both laugh because you're getting the accelerated version, all of it compressed into this brief, impossible time. Your voice holds contradictions: joy that you're doing this, devastation that this is all you get, gratitude for this moment, rage at its brevity, peace in the commitment, and agony in the goodbye. You're not crying OR laughing—you're doing both, your voice a strange, beautiful mixture of celebration and mourning.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Bard Sings a Prophecy That Becomes True as They Sing It

title: The Wrong Timeline Was Right
instruction: You've just learned that the career opportunity you lost, the relationship that ended, the path not taken—it all led to this perfect, unexpected moment you never could have planned. You're laughing because it's absurd, the cosmic joke of it. But you're also crying because you spent so long grieving what you didn't get. Your voice moves fluidly between laughter and tears, sometimes in the same breath. Express gratitude for the devastation that brought you here, finding beauty in the breakdown. There's joy in your voice but it's laced with the ghost of old pain. End in a space that's both celebration and mourning—grateful for where you are while honoring everything you had to lose to get here.

title: The Thing We Never Say
instruction: You're confronting your mother about why she left when you were twelve. Start with anger—sharp, cutting words you've rehearsed for years. But as you speak, the rage begins to crack. You hear yourself sounding like a child again, and you hate it, which makes you angrier, but underneath that anger is something more terrifying: the desperate need for her to explain, to make it make sense. Your voice shifts from accusation to pleading, from fury to heartbreak. You're trying to hurt her, but you're also begging her to tell you that you were worth staying for.
