End with the question you've been avoiding: 'Did you ever love me?' Let your voice betray how much the answer matters, how much it still has the power to destroy or save you.

title: Teaching Joy in the Language of Grief
instruction: You're teaching the signs your late partner invented—silly, private signs just for the two of you. Start laughing through tears as you demonstrate: 'This was their sign for coffee—like a ridiculous little dance with your fingers.' Let joy and sorrow swirl together inseparably. Your voice should be warm with love and broken with loss simultaneously. As you teach each absurd, beautiful sign they created, laugh at the memories while your voice cracks with missing them. When you reach the sign they made for 'us,' let your laughter turn to sobbing, then back to soft laughter again. End by teaching their sign for 'still here'—your voice should radiate both devastating grief and inexplicable gratitude, finding strange peace in keeping their language alive even as your heart shatters with every word.
inspired_by: Teaching Sign Language: When Hands Speak and Voice Goes Quiet

title: The Empty Locker
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy who skipped lunch to avoid bullies, and now you're in the hallway after school, fumbling with your locker combination. Your blood sugar is crashing—your hands shake, your vision blurs, and your words come out slow and thick. Start by muttering to yourself, frustrated by the lock, but as your body weakens and the hall empties, a cold fear creeps in—you realize you're alone and can't think clearly. Let your voice fade, slur, and break as you struggle to stay on your feet, ending with a quiet, trembling plea for someone to hear you.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Eruption—Breaking Free from Your Lifelong Protector
instruction: You're confronting someone who has controlled your life under the guise of protection—a parent, a spouse, someone you once trusted completely. Start with trembling restraint, your voice barely holding: 'I can't do this anymore. I can't keep living in your shadow.' The trembling intensifies: 'You say you protected me, but you suffocated me. You crushed every dream I had.' Now explode—let rage pour out, fierce and uncontained: 'I HATE that I let you make me small! I hate that I believed your fear was love!' Your voice breaks into something primal, years of suppressed fury. Then, devastatingly, it collapses into sobs: 'I just wanted you to believe in me. Just once, I needed you to let me fly.' The helplessness floods in—you're screaming but also weeping, powerful but also broken. End with exhausted defiance through tears: 'I'm leaving. I'm terrified, and I don't know if I'll survive, but I'm leaving.' The journey is from barely-controlled emotion to explosive rage to simultaneous strength and vulnerability.

title: Milestone Above the Clouds
instruction: You are a teenager on your first solo flight, a supposedly 'tough' guy, but inside you're buzzing with pure, unexpected elation. You're in a noisy aircraft cabin, the engine a constant roar. You lean over to the stranger in the next seat, someone you wouldn't normally talk to, and you start by awkwardly projecting over the noise about how 'this is fine, just a flight.' But as you speak, the pressure of the cabin and the thrill of being up here spills out. Lose your train of thought mid-sentence as you glance out the window at the wing, then come back with a voice that cracks and soars, ending with a raw, honest laugh as you admit this is the most incredible thing that's ever happened to you.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Sweetest Rejection
instruction: You're at a party, standing by the kitchen counter, a wine glass in your hand. The man you've been casually flirting with for weeks has just made his move, suggesting you go back to his place. You know he's been seeing someone else and you're furious — but you've kept your voice light, warm, almost giggly, leaning in close so the other guests won't hear. Your sentences are short, your tone is conspiratorial. But as you speak, the fake sweetness cracks. Your voice tightens, the laughter dies, and the quiet rage you've been holding spills out. Start with that rehearsed, fast-forwarded intimacy, then let it curdle into something colder and sharper — a controlled, devastating anger that leaves him stunned.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast: Celebrating Their Joy While Honoring Your Own Path
instruction: You're giving a toast at your younger sibling's wedding—the sibling who chose the traditional path you rejected. Your voice begins warm, genuinely joyful: 'To my beautiful sister and her new husband.' But then something more complex enters—you're laughing softly, but there's a catch in your throat: 'Watching you today, I feel so... happy for you. And so at peace with my own choice not to have this.' Your voice holds contradictions—celebration mixed with bittersweet recognition: 'You're going to build the family we grew up in. The one I had to leave to breathe.' Now tears come, but you're smiling through them: 'And that's okay. That's more than okay.' Your voice grows stronger, filled with gratitude that's somehow also grief: 'Thank you for showing me that there are many ways to be whole. Your way is beautiful. My way is different. And I'm learning that both can be true.' End with your voice breaking and soaring at once, laughing and crying: 'I'm so proud of you. And for the first time, I'm proud of me too. To love! To different kinds of love!' Let your voice carry the strange, painful, beautiful freedom of blessing someone else's dream while honoring the death of your own version of it.
inspired_by: Choosing Yourself: The Guilt and Empowerment of Selfishness

title: The Last Count
instruction: You are an elderly woman, deeply fatigued, lying over your partner's lap in your dim bedroom. Your body aches from the day, but your heart is full of infatuation. Each strike from their hand makes you gasp sharply, then moan as the sting melts into warmth. You must count out loud, but your voice cracks with exhaustion—starting with a reluctant whisper, then growing breathy and adoring. By the final number, your tone shifts from weary submission to a soft, pleading gratitude, your breath hitching as you reach for their hand.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Historical: Abolitionist Confronts Their Own Family's Slave Trading Past
instruction: Reading family documents, your voice cracks with recognition. Your family—the people you loved—built wealth on human trafficking. Your voice becomes someone discovering corruption in the people who shaped you. Your breathing is confused—love and revulsion occupying the same space. Your voice is the sound of inheritance made toxic. You're an abolitionist carrying the blood of slavers. Your vocal quality becomes someone trying to speak away something that's written into their DNA. Your voice is both accusation and self-condemnation.

title: Screaming at God While Holding Your Stillborn Child
instruction: You're alone in a hospital room, holding your baby who never took a breath. Begin in numb, whispering disbelief—this can't be real, this can't be happening. Then let the rage explode. Yell at God, the universe, fate—demand to know why, what you did to deserve this. Your voice should be raw, breaking, furious. Describe the nursery you painted, the name you chose, the future you planned. Let your anger reach a fever pitch, then suddenly collapse into sobbing as you look at your child's face. Speak directly to your baby now—tell them you're sorry, that you wanted them so much, that you'll carry them forever. Your voice should become tender, protective, fierce with love even in this devastation. End with a lullaby—start to sing something you planned to sing to them, but your voice keeps breaking. The final line should trail off into silence as you realize you're singing to silence.
inspired_by: Street Performer Whose Audience Is One Crying Child

title: The Cracked Pulpit
instruction: You are a young preacher before a packed congregation, your voice carrying that rhythmic, swelling cadence of a sermon. You start with a slight bitterness—a jaded edge, as if you're tired of their empty amens. But as you continue, a deep fear grips you: you are terrified that God sees through your performance, that the congregation can sense your hypocrisy. Let your voice waver, pause for call-and-response gaps that now feel suffocating, and let the bitterness morph into trembling dread. Speak roughly 50 words, allowing your tone to shift from a forced, rhythmic confidence to a fragile, fearful whisper that barely holds the cadence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Laugh Before the Collapse
instruction: You are a mother who just finished running a charity race with your young daughter on your shoulders for the final mile. You collapse onto the grass, completely empty, hyperventilating. Your daughter is sitting on your chest, giggling and poking your face, teasing you for being so dramatic. You try to play along, laughing between gasps, but every word comes out as a choked, breathy plea for mercy. The embarrassment of being this pathetic in front of a five-year-old mixes with the pure joy of her laughter. Begin with desperate, laughing catches of air as you protest—'Stop, baby, I'm dying'—and gradually sink into a surrendered, wheezing chuckle where you barely manage a whisper, giving in to the absurdity, the exhaustion, and the love, ending with a single, soft, resigned laugh that fades into silence.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (very intensely present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Devouring the Lie Between You
instruction: Confront your lover who has been slowly eroding your sense of reality with subtle manipulations and gaslighting. Begin the scene feeling fragmented, confused, questioning your own perceptions—your voice uncertain and broken. As you speak each truth you've been doubting, physically reach out as if pulling that truth back into yourself from where they scattered it. With each reclaimed certainty, your voice grows stronger, your physical presence more solid. Build to a moment where you're no longer asking for validation—you're declaring what you know, your body expanding with recovered power, voice resonating from deep in your chest. End having consumed all the space in the room, leaving no oxygen for their denials.

title: The Last Rep
instruction: You are at the gym, holding a heavy barbell overhead. Your muscles are in full tremor—shaking violently, jaw and neck quivering, each exhale a forced whimper. You start with a stubborn, gritty determination, growling through the pain to hold on. But the weight is slowly slipping, and distress creeps in. By the end, your voice cracks and falters as you admit you can't hold it any longer, the helplessness raw in your throat. Let the physical shake dictate your vocal breaks and pauses.
emotions_sampled: Pain (very intensely present), Distress (slightly present), Helplessness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Condolence Expressing
instruction: Someone's child just died. Your voice has to hold their devastation without being destroyed by it. 'I'm so sorry,' you say, and those words contain decades of human grief. You're not trying to fix it. 'How are you?' Your voice is permission to fall apart. You stay silent much of the time, just breathing with them. 'I'm here,' your voice says finally, and that's enough. Just presence. Just witnessing.

title: The Praise That Broke Everything Open
instruction: Your parent - who never said a kind word, who criticized everything you did - is now elderly and, out of nowhere, tells you they're proud of you. Your voice erupts with decades of pain: 'Where was this when I needed it? When I was twelve and desperate for you to see me?' The anger is raw, justified, burning. But as they sit there, small and frail, trying to explain with fumbling words, something inside you begins to crack. Your voice breaks from fury into grief, then into something you didn't expect - a kind of devastated tenderness. By the end, you're crying, your voice barely above a whisper: 'I needed you to say that so badly. God, I still need it.' You accept what you've always wanted, even though it's thirty years too late.

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You're reading your mother's will with your siblings present, and you've just discovered she left you everything—the house, the money, the jewelry, everything. Your siblings, who you've resented for being the favorites your whole life, are devastated. Start with shock and an attempt at graciousness, maybe even offering to share. But then let the vindication flood in. This is your proof, finally, that you were loved more. Begin pointing out why she chose you—list their failures as children, as parents, as people. Let your joy at finally winning mix with vicious observations about their flaws. Tell them what she really thought of them before she died, secrets she told only you. Feel the power of being chosen, and wield it like a weapon. Make them hurt the way you hurt at every family gathering where you felt invisible. Your voice should contain both triumph and cruelty, celebration and knife-twisting. But by the end, as you see their faces, let the victory turn hollow. Feel the terrible weight of being alone with your vindication, realizing you've just destroyed your family for a house and some money. End with the awful mixture of having won and having lost everything.

title: 3 AM Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone in the intimate darkness of a shared bed, both awake but silent. You've been carrying a secret—maybe a betrayal, maybe a fear, maybe a truth about who you really are—and something about this quiet, unseen moment makes it impossible to keep holding it. Begin in the fragile stillness of not yet speaking, feeling your heart race in your chest. Let yourself move from that trembling hesitation into the terrifying act of revealing yourself, using whispered sounds, broken attempts at words that dissolve into breath and emotion. This isn't loud—it's almost unbearably quiet, intimate, like you're both sheltered in a cocoon where only truth can exist. End in the raw aftermath of being truly seen, where you don't know yet if you're safe or shattered, but you're undeniably real.

title: Laughing at Your Own Wedding as Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're giving a toast at your own wedding, but you just realized you're making a terrible mistake—you're marrying the wrong person, or for the wrong reasons, or you're in love with someone else in the room. Start with genuine warmth and humor, laughing as you tell a charming story. But underneath, something is breaking. Your laughter becomes slightly manic, too bright. The words of love are true but wrong. 'I'm the luckiest person alive'—and your voice nearly cracks on it, but you cover it with another laugh. Let the joy and devastation coexist: laughing while your voice betrays you, sparkling while drowning. End with a toast, voice raised and celebratory and absolutely wrecked underneath: 'To forever!' The final word holds everything—hope, despair, resignation, and a strange, terrible peace.

title: The Last Laugh at the Bar
instruction: You are an older man, nursing a drink at a dimly lit bar, watching a younger woman you've been flirting with across the room laugh with a handsome stranger. Your body is tense, jaw tight, and every glance at them makes your contempt rise. You mutter to yourself, trying to sound dismissive, but your voice cracks with jealousy. Start with a cold, sneering observation, then let the anger simmer until you're gripping your glass, voice low and venomous—a bitter, possessive edge creeping in as you imagine her wasted attention. Your breathing is shallow, and you pause to sip your drink, forgetting your thought for a second before the fury pulls you back.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Last Bite Before the Interview
instruction: You're a young woman who just snuck a huge bite of a peanut butter sandwich seconds before your phone rings — it's the hiring manager from your dream job. You're frantically trying to chew and swallow while answering, concentrating fiercely on sounding professional even as your mouth is full, tongue stuck to the roof, and you're muffling a cough. Start with tense, distracted politeness as you force the food down, but as the conversation goes on, you realize they're offering you the job — and you're overwhelmed with startled, shimmering joy that makes you forget the food entirely, your voice suddenly clear and breathless with disbelief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Body's Rebellion
instruction: You're in the throes of either intense physical pain or overwhelming pleasure (your choice), but you're also acutely aware of your breathing, your sounds, how you must look, whether you're 'doing this right.' Vocalize both the raw physical experience AND your running commentary on it—'I sound ridiculous,' 'I can't control this,' 'My body is doing things I didn't give it permission to do.' Begin trying to maintain composure and control, narrating your loss of control even as it happens. Build to a peak where the commentary and the sensation crash together into something beyond your control, ending in pure physical and emotional release where self-observation and experience become one howling, laughing, sobbing expression.
inspired_by: Actor is commenting on his own performance while performing, creating a split between observation and involvement

title: Whispering Truth in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner of many years. You can't sleep because you've been carrying a secret that's eating you alive—not an affair, but something more subtle and devastating: you've been pretending to be happy, saying you're sorry for being distant when really you've been slowly disappearing inside yourself. Begin by speaking so softly you're barely audible, not wanting to wake them but needing to say it aloud: 'I'm sorry I haven't been present.' Your voice should be tender, aching with love for them, but threaded with a deep, quiet devastation. Let each apology reveal more truth—'I'm sorry I smile when I'm empty inside... I'm sorry I say everything's fine.' Feel your throat tighten as you admit what you've been hiding. The emotion should catch and break in small ways, tears you're trying to keep silent. End with a confession that's both heartbreaking and strangely peaceful: 'I don't know how to find my way back to myself,' spoken with a vulnerability so raw it hurts, yet there's something almost beautiful in finally telling the truth, even if they'll never hear it.
inspired_by: Apologizing for Something You Weren't At Fault For

title: The Captain and the Mutiny Leader
instruction: Portray a spaceship captain with a firm, authoritative voice confronting a crew member leading a mutiny, who speaks in a persuasive, fiery tone. Switch between the captains attempts to maintain order and the mutineers calls for rebellion, intensifying the conflict.

title: The Apology I Never Meant to Give
instruction: You are a man who has just realized that the cruel joke you played on your partner was not just thoughtless, but deliberately mean—a small act of malice you disguised as humor. You kneel before them, your voice dropping low, each word carefully chosen and often restarted as you gauge their pain. Start with a heavy, remorseful tone that carries the weight of guilt, then slowly let a sliver of resentment seep through as you recall why you did it, ending with a crack of genuine affection as you admit you don't deserve their forgiveness. Your voice should be physically smaller, with pauses where you shift your weight or look away, a flicker of coldness in your eyes before the warmth breaks through again.
emotions_sampled: Pain (clearly present), Affection (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Helpless Fury
instruction: Your child is in danger and there's nothing you can do to save them—they're sick, or far away, or making a choice that will destroy them. Begin with volcanic rage at your own powerlessness, voice cracking with fury at God, fate, yourself. You're shouting, maybe pounding something, words dissolving into primal sound. Then the rage shatters into desperate sobbing, the anger revealing the terror underneath. Your voice breaks completely: 'Please, please, please.' You cycle between fierce protectiveness—'I won't let this happen'—and devastating helplessness—'I can't stop this.' End in a place of raw surrender, voice hollowed out, fierce love colliding with absolute powerlessness, every word soaked in both fight and collapse.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent in a rehab visiting room. You came prepared with anger—you've rehearsed this confrontation for years. Start fierce and controlled, listing the ways they failed you: missed birthdays, broken promises, the times you had to parent yourself. But as you speak, something shifts. You see how small they look, how broken. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it complicates—mixing with grief for the parent you needed, fury at the disease that stole them, and a terrible, unwanted tenderness. Your voice should crack between rage and compassion. End with a confession you didn't plan to make: that despite everything, you don't know how to stop loving them, and you hate yourself for it.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father after discovering a devastating family secret they kept from you for decades—a sibling you never knew existed, a lie about your origins, a betrayal that reshaped your life. Begin in cold, controlled fury, your voice tight and measured as you list the facts. But as they try to explain—or refuse to explain—let the control crack. Move from accusation to a rawer place: the child inside you who needed them to be honest, who needed to trust them. Your voice may break, rage may give way to grief, or grief may surge back into anger. End in a place of devastating vulnerability: 'I don't know who you are anymore' or 'I don't know who I am.' The arc moves from controlled rage to exposed, wounded truth.

title: The Unburdening
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to your partner in the dark, both supposedly asleep. Begin with the weight of a secret you've carried for months pressing on your chest—your breathing shallow, your body tense and still, afraid to move. You've rehearsed confessing this a hundred times in your head, but now the words feel stuck. Don't push them out with your voice alone. Let your body move first—perhaps you turn toward them, perhaps your hand reaches out. When you whisper their name, let it come from the ache in your chest, not from your throat. As you begin to confess what you've been hiding, resist the urge to perform contrition or manage their reaction. Let your voice shake if it needs to. Let silence live between your words. Let your breath catch. Allow your body, voice, and emotion to move as one honest organism, not separate instruments playing different songs. End in whatever raw truth emerges—whether that's relief, shame, fear, or tender vulnerability.

title: The Wedding Morning Call
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling on the morning of your wedding. They're not coming—you both know why, and it involves years of wounds neither of you can fully forgive. Begin with bright, forced cheerfulness, trying to share your joy despite everything. But as you describe your happiness, you're also flooded with grief that they won't be there, resentment that they're choosing to miss this, and an unwanted surge of love for who they used to be. Let these emotions war with each other in your voice. You want to celebrate and cry and rage and beg them to come all at once. End somewhere unexpected: maybe in laughter through tears at a shared childhood memory, or in acceptance that's both peaceful and devastating. The joy of this day and the loss of them must coexist in your final words.
inspired_by: Relationship Preparation via Endowment + Guided Imaging (Night Mother Example)

title: The Last Lesson Before the War
instruction: You're a parent teaching your child something simple—how to tie shoelaces, how to make toast—knowing this is the last ordinary moment before you leave for a deployment you may not return from. Begin with forced cheerfulness, your voice bright and instructional, but let the grief seep through as you realize you're trying to cram a lifetime of guidance into these final minutes. Your hands might be steady but your voice starts to fracture. By the end, you've abandoned the lesson entirely—you're just holding them, whispering the truth: 'I need you to remember I was here. That this was real.' Let your voice break between tenderness and barely-contained devastation, between being the teacher and becoming the child who doesn't want to go.

title: Bedside Confession at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a hospital bed who may not wake up. The room is quiet except for machines. You're whispering things you never said when they were awake—secrets, gratitude, regrets. Start almost inaudible, testing whether you can even say these things aloud. 'I never told you that I...' Your voice is fragile, catching on words. Share something shameful, then something beautiful. Let silence do as much work as words—the pauses where you almost can't continue. The emotion isn't loud; it's the kind that makes your whole body ache. End with a tender goodbye that accepts you may never get a response, your voice barely there, full of love and unspeakable sadness.

title: The Button's Grit
instruction: You're a child, exhausted and irritable, forced to dress for a dull family dinner. As you pull on scratchy pants, you grunt and sigh, fabric muffling your complaints. Midway through buttoning a shirt, you pause—remembering your favorite socks hidden in the drawer, and a faint hope flickers that tonight might bring a small adventure. Let your voice shift from heavy, disgusted mumbles to a lighter, weary but hopeful tone, with natural pauses and fabric rustles breaking your words.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Homecoming That Breaks You Open
instruction: You're returning home after years away, walking through the door to see your family waiting. Inside you is a war: joy at seeing faces you've desperately missed, rage at why you had to leave, grief for the time you've lost, fear that you're not who they remember, relief to be back, and resentment that you need them at all. Begin with your hand on the doorknob, feeling all of this churning inside you, not knowing which emotion will come out first. As you enter and embrace them, let these feelings clash and tumble over each other—you might laugh while crying, push away while holding tight, say 'I missed you' with anger in your voice, or whisper 'I hate you' while clinging desperately. Don't resolve this into one clean emotion. Draw on times when you felt multiple truths simultaneously, when your heart pulled in opposite directions at once. End in a place of raw, messy honesty where contradictory feelings coexist—maybe collapsed in someone's arms feeling both fury and overwhelming love, unable to separate one from the other.

title: Behind the Filter
instruction: You are a teenage girl stuck in a hospital corridor, wearing an N95 mask that fogs your glasses and makes each breath a labor. Your grandmother is in surgery. Start with a sour, clenched complaint—muttering to yourself about the mask's pressure, the stale air, the waiting. Let your voice be muffled, pushed through the filter, with audible valve clicks. Midway, the sourness breaks as you remember her laugh yesterday—your breath hitches, and pain floods in. Your words become slower, softer, vulnerable. End with a whisper that trembles, speaking to her as if she can hear.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Physical Fight That Keeps Transforming
instruction: You're in a fierce argument that's becoming physical—pushing, grabbing, the violence of intimacy. Start with pure rage, your body full of aggressive energy. But the other person keeps doing unexpected physical things: suddenly going completely limp when you expect resistance, pulling you into an embrace when you're pushing away, laughing through tears, or touching your face with shocking tenderness in the middle of fury. Each unexpected physical choice forces your body and emotions to improvise. Rage transforms into confusion, then perhaps desperate passion, then grief, then something else entirely. Don't plan the emotional journey—let their unpredictable physicality genuinely surprise you into authentic responses. Your body must stay dangerous and alive, never settling into a predictable pattern. End in an emotional and physical place that shocks you both—maybe collapsed together, maybe frozen in an unexpected gesture of tenderness or devastation.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying what you've held back for years—decades, maybe. Your parent sits across from you, and you're telling them about the empty chair at graduations, the milestones they missed, the child who waited. Start with tightly controlled anger, words precise like weapons. But as you speak, the fury cracks and underneath is the wounded child who just wanted them to show up. Your voice becomes raw, younger, more vulnerable. Then something shifts—you realize mid-sentence that you're not that child anymore, that you survived, that you built a life without them. End in a complex place: acknowledging the pain they caused while recognizing you no longer need their validation. The anger transforms into something quieter—not forgiveness exactly, but release.
inspired_by: The Person You Wronged Wants an Explanation

title: Reading Their Letter After the Funeral
instruction: You're alone, opening a letter your best friend left for you before they died—but it's not what you expected. It's funny, irreverent, full of inside jokes and ridiculous memories. Start by laughing genuinely, even reading passages aloud in their voice, mimicking their mannerisms, feeling them alive in the room with you. Let yourself be joyful, grateful, almost manic with the gift of hearing them one more time. But gradually, between the jokes, you start to notice what they're really saying: their quiet terror, their love for you, their goodbye. Your laughter becomes tangled with grief until you can't tell which is which. End reading the final line through tears while still smiling—a mess of gratitude, devastation, love, and the excruciating beauty of being left behind by someone who knew you completely.

title: The Last Push
instruction: You are in the final sprint of an intense spin class, legs burning, lungs heaving. A few meters away, your longtime rival—the one who always belittled your grit—is struggling to keep pace. You've been locked in this silent race for weeks. Now, with the finish line seconds away, you realize you’re going to beat them. Between gasps, you talk to yourself first, marveling at your own power, then you let the words slip out to them—low, breathless, laced with quiet malice. Start with exhausted, disbelieving triumph, then let the tone harden into a cold, satisfied gloat. Your voice should ride the pedal rhythm, forced between exhales, with small breaks to swallow and steady your core.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Parched Watcher
instruction: You are an elderly woman, severely dehydrated, sitting in a sun-warmed chair. Your mouth is dry—lips stick, tongue clicks, and every word feels scraped out. Through the window, you watch a younger woman receive a bouquet from a visitor. Speak your thoughts aloud, beginning with a bitter, envious edge: notice how easily she gets attention, how she glows. Let your voice crack and fray, fatigue building. By the end, your jealousy drains into a hollow, exhausted resignation—too tired to hold onto the envy any longer. Pause for sticky mouth sounds and shallow, parched breaths.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Tipsy Lullaby
instruction: You're a middle-aged mother, slightly tipsy from a glass of wine, playing with your infant on the living room floor. At first your voice is high and wobbly, full of exaggerated swoops and repetitive coos as you point to a stuffed elephant — you're trying to be fun but your slur makes it silly. Midway, the baby grabs your finger and locks eyes, and a wave of startling, raw love cuts through the buzz, quieting your pitch and slowing your speech into a tender, whispered confession. Let your voice start loose and playful, then gradually become more present and intimate, with natural pauses as you react to the baby's tiny movements and your own fleeting distractions.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Intimacy Honored
instruction: You're honoring the intimacy your partner is offering—recognizing the vulnerability, the trust, the gift they're giving you. Your voice is grateful and reverent: 'Thank you for letting me be here. Thank you for trusting me.' You're naming the magnitude of what's happening. Your partner's voice receives this acknowledgment: 'Thank you for seeing it.' You're both honoring the weight and beauty of being intimate. This isn't casual; this is significant. Your voice should carry that significance. By the end, your voices should sound like two people who recognize they're sharing something sacred.

title: The Storm Breaking
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a betrayal, a revelation, a loss—and you are alone in your car, gripping the steering wheel. Begin with your body locked, jaw clenched, trying to hold it together, voice strangled and tight as you speak to yourself, repeating 'I'm fine, I'm okay.' Let your physical tension build until something snaps. Your voice should explode—not theatrical screaming, but genuine release, the sound of a body that can no longer contain what it's holding. Hit the steering wheel, let your voice crack and break, let sounds come out that aren't even words. Then let it drain from you, the rage giving way to shaking, to sobbing, to finally a kind of hollow, breathless exhaustion. End with your forehead against the wheel, voice hoarse and small, saying something simple like 'What do I do now?' The physical experience should generate the emotional one—not the other way around.
inspired_by: When you are debating whether your emotional preparation needs to match the scene's requirements literally (actually staying up all night, actually running for miles, etc.)

title: Three A.M. Phone Call to Someone Who Doesn't Know
instruction: It's three in the morning and you're calling someone you haven't spoken to in years—an old friend, a former lover, someone who once knew you deeply. Begin with awkward small talk, your voice barely above a whisper, trying to sound casual about this late-night call. But you didn't call to chat—you called because something broke open in you tonight, some defense finally crumbled. Gradually let the real reason emerge: a confession of loneliness, an admission of regret, a revelation about who you really are that you've hidden from everyone. Your voice should start guarded and stilted, then become increasingly raw and unfiltered. End with a fragile question: 'Do you remember who I used to be before I learned to hide?'

title: The Unexpected Rescue
instruction: You are a middle-aged man in a crowded office lobby, having just been publicly ridiculed by a younger colleague for a mistake you made years ago. Your boss and peers are staring. You feel your voice shrink, your shoulders curl inward, and a hot shame washes over you. As you mumble an apology to the floor, you're astonished to see your quiet, reserved ex-assistant step forward and defend you, citing your mentorship that changed their life. You begin speaking in a cracked, defeated whisper, but as you process the unexpected loyalty and its ecstatic pleasure, your voice rises in pitch, gains a trembling, raw joy, and finally steadies into a quiet, grateful strength as you thank them.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your memorial service, knowing you have weeks left. You start by genuinely laughing—really laughing—at the absurdity of eulogizing yourself. 'I'm about to tell you I was honest in business, and you should trust me because I'm saying it at my own funeral.' Your voice is warm, amused, almost giddy with the dark comedy of it. But as you speak about the competitors you refused to destroy, the shortcuts you didn't take, your laughter starts mixing with tears. You're crying and chuckling simultaneously: 'It cost me everything. I could have been richer. I could have had more time with treatment I couldn't afford because I paid employees fairly instead.' The contradictions peak—you're grateful and furious, at peace and devastated, proud and wondering if you were a fool. End with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob: 'But I'd do it again. God help me, I'd do it all again.' Let every word vibrate with the beautiful, terrible complexity of a life genuinely lived.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Pretends Didn't Happen
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table. She's made coffee like nothing is wrong. You came here to finally tell her what her neglect did to you as a child. Start careful, almost apologetic—your voice tentative, seeking permission to speak your own truth. You're trying to be gentle because part of you still wants to protect her. But as she deflects, as she minimizes, something shifts. Your voice gains strength, then heat. You're not shouting—you're stating facts that burn. The anger comes, yes, but underneath it is the child you used to be, begging to be seen. End with your voice stripped bare: not angry anymore, just exhausted and heartbroken, asking one simple question you've needed answered your whole life. Let love and rage coexist in every sentence.
inspired_by: Post-coital Conversation: Vulnerability Pretending to Be Casual

title: The Last Train Home
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love at a train station, knowing they're leaving on a journey they may never return from—war, a dangerous mission, or exile. Start with forced brightness, trying to be brave, making jokes about writing letters. But as the departure time draws closer, your voice begins to crack. You're fighting to memorize their face, their voice. Midway through, let the facade crumble—tell them the things you've been too afraid to say, the regrets, the wishes for more time. Your voice should move from cheerful denial to desperate tenderness, then to a quiet, fierce promise that you'll wait, you'll remember, you'll carry them with you. End with a whispered goodbye that holds both devastation and an almost unbearable love. The emotional arc travels from protective optimism to raw vulnerability to a love that transcends the goodbye itself.

title: Confronting Your Father About the Childhood He Stole
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home, and you've finally decided to tell your aging father what his drinking cost you. Start controlled, almost cold—you've rehearsed these words for years. Describe specific memories: the school play he missed, the night you waited for him, the promises he broke. As you speak, let your composure crack. Your voice should rise with decades of suppressed rage, demanding he acknowledge what he did. But then something shifts—you see him crying, and suddenly you're that child again, wanting him to fix it, to say the right thing. Your anger collapses into desperate pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stop?' End with exhausted acceptance when you realize he has no answer that will heal you. The final words should be quiet, resigned, a farewell to the father you needed him to be.
inspired_by: Street Performer Whose Audience Is One Crying Child

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're leaving—by choice or necessity—and will never see them again. They're asleep. You whisper things you need them to know but will never be able to say when they're awake. Start with practical tenderness—tucking them in, smoothing their hair, your voice steady and gentle. As you speak about who they'll become, your voice catches. Try to stay composed, but the enormity of what you're losing breaks through. Your whispers become shakier, tears in your throat. You try to say 'I love you' but it comes out fractured, barely audible. End in silence—you can't speak anymore, can only touch their face one last time, your breathing the only sound.

title: Resentment Boiling Over
instruction: Years of resentment are finally coming out. Your voice starts controlled but soon escalates: 'You never... you always...' You're bringing up old wounds, and each one adds fuel. Your voice becomes louder, more bitter. You're cataloging every hurt, every disappointment. Your partner is trying to respond, but you're not done. Your voice is harsh, cutting. By the end, you're both broken by what's been said, and your voice becomes quiet, realizing you've done damage that might not be repaired.

title: Bitter Champagne Toast
instruction: You're at a backyard celebration for a colleague who just got the promotion you desperately wanted. You're holding a glass of champagne, forced to give a toast. Start with a bright, enthusiastic tone, but as you speak, the genuine happiness dissolves into envy. Your voice tightens, your smile falters, and the words come out with a sharp, sarcastic edge. The toast ends on a hollow note, your disappointment barely masked. Let the bitterness creep in like acid, fading the initial elation. Speak naturally, with pauses and small distractions (sipping, looking away).
emotions_sampled: Elation (extremely present), Sourness (clearly present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Morning After Victory
instruction: You've just achieved something you've pursued for twenty years—a goal that consumed you, defined you, cost you relationships and time you'll never recover. It's the morning after your triumph, and you're alone, speaking to your reflection or to someone who isn't there. Begin with euphoria, letting yourself finally celebrate without restraint. But as you describe your victory, other images intrude—faces of people who aren't here to share this, sacrifices that suddenly seem too great, a strange emptiness beneath the joy. You realize you've been dreaming about this moment for decades, and now that it's real, it feels oddly hollow, like waking from a vivid dream into disappointing daylight. Yet there's also profound gratitude, hard-won wisdom, and acceptance. Let your voice travel from unbridled celebration through growing unease, into a complex emotional space where triumph and loss, satisfaction and regret, joy and grief exist simultaneously. End in a place of bittersweet peace—fully awake to all of it.

title: First Time Fracture
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy in the middle of your first sexual experience with a partner. The pleasure is building rapidly, but a wave of confusion hits you—this intense, uncontrollable feeling is nothing like you imagined. Your breathing turns to ragged moans and gasps, and you try to form words: 'I don't... what's happening...' The climax crests, and your voice breaks into a raw cry. As you collapse into stillness, your breathing slows, and you whisper in stunned wonder, 'That... that was everything.' The emotion shifts from bewildered panic to a quiet, overwhelmed awe.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Tension Release
instruction: You're a therapist who specializes in trauma, speaking to a new client. Your voice starts high, held, slightly strained — you're managing the weight of every story you hear. As you guide the client through a breathing exercise, your own breath comes easier. By the middle of the session, your voice has dropped an octave. You're fully present. Then the client says, 'I've never told anyone that before,' and you feel the weight return — the responsibility of holding space. Your voice tightens again, but now it's intentional. At the end of the session, after they leave, you let out a long breath alone. Your shoulders drop. Your real voice comes back in the silence.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your partner in complete darkness. You cannot sleep. You have been holding a secret that is destroying you from the inside. Begin speaking so quietly you're almost not sure you want them to hear. Confess something you've never told anyone—a betrayal, a lie you've been living, a truth about who you really are that terrifies you. Your voice should tremble, barely audible at first. As you speak, feel the relief and terror of exposure happening simultaneously. Let your breathing be uneven, your words catching in your throat. You are shedding a skin you've worn for years. End with either 'Please don't leave me' or 'I understand if you go,' but whisper it like your life depends on their response. This is naked vulnerability—no protection, no armor, just raw truth offered in the dark.

title: The Echo of Your Name
instruction: You're alone in your dim bedroom at 2 AM, clutching a worn hoodie that still smells like them. You're reliving the last moment you saw them, and the longing hits you like a wave. As you whisper their name, your breath catches—the panic begins. Your chest tightens, fingers tingle, and you can't get enough air. Try to speak through the gasping, repeating fragments of what you miss, but the spiral pulls you under—your voice cracks, climbs in pitch, and you end in raw, desperate sobs. Start with quiet, tearful longing, end in full panic attack.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Words They Never Got to Hear
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love deeply who has already died—perhaps minutes ago, perhaps hours. You never got to say what you needed to say when they were alive, and now the words pour out anyway. Begin speaking in a voice that's physically broken by grief—cracked, strangled, unrecognizable even to yourself. Let your body collapse into positions that feel wrong, uncomfortable, twisted by the weight of loss. As you speak, your voice and body should gradually transform: perhaps the tears give way to unexpected laughter at a memory, perhaps rage at being left behind overtakes the sorrow, perhaps you find a strange peaceful acceptance that straightens your spine and clears your throat. The physical and vocal distortion you begin with must reflect unbearable emotion, but by the end, something in you—and in your voice and body—has fundamentally shifted.

title: Feeling the Warmth of a Sunbeam on Your Face
instruction: Close your eyes and turn your face up, feeling a sunbeam warming your skin. Describe the way the warmth spreads over your cheeks, soft and comforting, almost like a gentle caress from the sun. Speak softly and with a hint of wonder, as if the warmth fills you with a quiet, simple happiness, grounding you in the present moment.

title: Toasting at Your Ex's Wedding
instruction: You've been asked to give a toast at your ex-partner's wedding to someone else—you dated for five years, and somehow you stayed friends. Begin with genuine warmth, even a small laugh: 'I'm supposed to embarrass you with stories, but honestly, you were always the better person in our relationship.' Your voice is light, affectionate. But as you talk about their capacity for love, for loyalty, for choosing joy, your voice starts to waver with something deeper—not jealousy, but a bittersweet recognition of what you had and lost. 'You taught me what it means to be loved completely.' Now you're smiling through tears, your voice thick but still warm. Look at them with their new partner, and let genuine happiness for them mix with your own quiet heartbreak: 'I'm so grateful I got to love you, even though I couldn't keep you.' Your final words, 'Be happy—God, please be so happy,' should be fierce and tender at once, a blessing that costs you everything to give but that you mean with your whole heart. Let laughter and tears exist in the same breath.
inspired_by: Parent Watching Their Child Leave Home

title: Admitting You've Been Using Substances to Cope
instruction: You're telling someone you trust. Your voice is ashamed, clinical: 'I've been drinking more than I should.' You're understatement as protection. They ask how much and your voice gets quieter: 'Every day.' 'I think I have a problem,' delivered with terrible clarity. Include the listener asking why and your voice cracking as you name the pain. End asking for help.

title: Starlight on the Surface
instruction: You are a young boy, about eight years old, trapped in the hollow trunk of a fallen tree that has flooded. The water is up to your chin, and you've been here for hours, but now you hear search dogs and voices nearby. Your body is shivering, your teeth chatter between gasps. At first, you feel a surge of desperate hope—you scream for help, but your voice keeps going under the water as you bob up and down. Splashes and gurgles interrupt your shouts. As the sounds fade and you hear the searchers move away, your voice cracks with gnawing doubt, but you still force out a hopeful call, your breathing ragged, tears mixing with the cold water on your face. Let the submersion swallow whole words, and let your pitch rise and fall with frantic energy.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call from the Mountain
instruction: You're receiving what you know is the final satellite call from your partner, stranded on a mountain after an avalanche. Service is breaking up. You start with desperate hope, trying to sound strong for them: 'The rescue team is coming, they're almost there.' But as they describe the cold, the fading light, you feel your composure cracking. Your voice softens into something more honest: 'I need you to know...' You're trying to say everything—all the love, all the years ahead you planned—in these fragmented moments. By the end, you're no longer trying to save them, just trying to stay with them. 'I'm here. I'm right here with you.' The call goes silent, and you whisper into the dead line, 'I love you,' knowing they can't hear anymore. Your voice breaks completely as you realize you're alone.

title: Wingsuit Whispers
instruction: You're in freefall, but this is a recorded message to someone you love, speaking through your helmet mic on what you fear might be your last jump after equipment failure. Your voice is almost a whisper against the roaring wind, intimate and trembling. Start trying to stay technical—'The altimeter is—I think I can—'—but quickly abandon it for what matters. Tell them the small things: how they laugh, the way morning light catches in their hair, that you never said enough. Your breath catches not from the fall but from the ache of potential goodbye. The terror of the descent braids with tender remembrance. Let your voice grow softer, more certain, finding unexpected calm as you fall, speaking love like a prayer into the void.

title: The Party Pivot
instruction: You're at a casual house party, talking to a woman you find physically attractive. She's enthusiastically describing her new hobby—building model trains—which you secretly think is ridiculous. Begin with a slightly flirtatious interest, letting your voice carry a low, warm undertone. As she keeps going, let your smile freeze, your responses become shorter, and insert forced laughter into the silences. Finish with a flat, sour remark as you scan the room for an escape, your voice now tight and weary.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Time I'll See Your Face
instruction: You're sitting beside your older sibling who has hours left to live. You've always been the strong one, the caretaker, the one who holds it together. Begin speaking calmly, trying to comfort them, telling them about the beautiful day outside, keeping your voice steady. But as you continue, something breaks—perhaps a childhood memory surfaces, or you realize this is truly the last conversation you'll ever have. Let your controlled composure crumble into raw, unguarded grief. Your voice should move from measured reassurance to something broken and pleading. End in a place of pure, naked fear of losing them, of being left behind, of facing a world without this person who knows you completely.
inspired_by: When you are building a character who must be genuinely terrified or in extreme fear

title: The Trash That Never Walks Itself
instruction: You're leaning against the kitchen counter, arms crossed, staring at the overflowing trash bin. Your partner is on the couch, scrolling. You've had this exact conversation a dozen times before, and you're bone-tired from work. Start with a slow, weary complaint—voice flat, almost a monotone, but with a nasal edge of exhaustion. As you repeat yourself, bitterness seeps in; your pitch rises, words get clipped, and you feel the familiar whine creep into your throat. Midway, you pause, rub your eyes, and push off the counter, forcing yourself to concentrate on making them hear you this time. End with a sharp, bitter finality, voice cracking with fatigue and resentment. Speak naturally, as if you're trying not to cry but also too tired to care.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Concentration (clearly present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Forgotten Flame
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a therapy session, your voice soft and carefully pitched as if you've always tried to sound pleasant. You're talking about a man you once knew, but you feel only a flat numbness — you tell the therapist you don't remember why you cared. As you speak, you stare at your hands, then out the window; you lose your train of thought. Suddenly, a detail comes back — the way he laughed — and your voice cracks, your breath catches, and the infatuation you've buried surges up, raw and overwhelming, making you pause and then whisper, 'I think I loved him.'
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Rage That Becomes Surrender
instruction: You're screaming at the universe, at God, at fate—after losing someone you swore you'd protect. Begin with pure, volcanic fury: pacing, voice raw and ragged, hurling accusations at the emptiness. You were supposed to save them, you promised, you failed, and the injustice is unbearable. Let your voice crack with the strain, becoming almost feral with helplessness. Then, mid-sentence, the rage collapses—your knees give out, your voice drops to a broken whisper. The anger transforms into sobbing desperation, then finally into a quiet, exhausted acceptance. End in near-silence, your fight completely spent, speaking to the person you lost with tender devastation: 'I can't keep you here, can I?' The arc must feel like a storm that destroys you, leaving only ash and aching love.
inspired_by: Suppressing Annoyance While Dealing With a Difficult Person

title: The Last Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving for a dangerous mission they may not return from. Start with forced brightness, trying to be brave: 'So this is it, huh? You're really going.' Your voice cracks as denial shatters—the reality that this might be forever hits you. The false cheerfulness dissolves into raw need: 'Wait. Just—wait. I need to say—' You're scrambling to find words for everything unsaid. Touch their face with your voice, memorizing them. By the end, you've moved through panic into a fierce, tender acceptance: 'Come back to me. But if you can't—' Your voice is thick with tears but grounded in love. Let the silences between words carry as much weight as the words themselves.

title: Breaking the Cycle: Choosing Differently
instruction: You're in a situation where you could repeat the same trauma response as your family. But you're choosing differently. Your voice is determined. 'I'm not going to do this.' Your voice is speaking the boundary your parents never could. Your voice is ending the cycle. It's harder than the old patterns. Your voice carries the effort of choosing new. 'Not with me. Not with my kids.' Your voice is setting a new standard.

title: The Inheritance Letter
instruction: You're holding a letter from someone who caused you years of pain - an absent parent, an abusive ex, a friend who betrayed you - but they've just died and left you something: money, or their journals, or a house, or simply an apology. Before reading it aloud, notice what you're genuinely feeling right now in this moment - maybe less than you expected to feel, or something contradictory. Start reading from that honest place. As you read their words, let yourself experience the collision of real emotions: the anger that they think this fixes anything, gratitude that they tried, grief that it's too late, resentment at being moved by their words, unexpected forgiveness, or bitter satisfaction. Don't decide which emotion wins - let them fight inside you, transforming sentence by sentence from wherever you actually started.
inspired_by: Actor begins a scene by getting ready to act rather than from genuine BEING

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago, and they've just said they 'did their best.' Start cold, almost laughing—'Your best? Your BEST was disappearing on a Tuesday and never coming back?' The anger builds but then fractures into raw pain: 'I used to wait by the window. Every single day I waited.' Your voice breaks completely. 'I needed you to fight for me. I needed you to love me enough to stay.' The rage resurfaces, fierce and protective of your child-self: 'I deserved better than your best!' But then, unexpectedly, exhaustion and grief take over—softer, almost a whisper: 'I just needed you to want me.' End with the devastating truth spoken with quiet, hollow acceptance: 'I can't get those years back. Neither can you.'

title: Confessing to the Sleeping Form
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you in the dark—or you think they are. You begin whispering the truth you've never been able to say to their waking face: your deepest fear of inadequacy, your terror that you're not enough for them, that one day they'll realize they could have done better. Your voice is barely audible, tender and raw, catching on every vulnerable admission. You're confessing your love in the same breath as your insecurity, describing specific moments when you felt unworthy of their affection. There's an aching intimacy in your whisper—this is the most honest you've ever been. Midway through, you notice their breathing has changed. They might be awake. Your voice wavers with sudden fear and exposure, but you can't stop now. You finish your confession in a throat-tight whisper, ending with 'I love you more than I know how to say when you're looking at me.' Silence. Then you feel their hand find yours in the darkness.
inspired_by: Reading a Bedtime Story Before Goodbye

title: The Inheritance of Silence: Confronting What Was Never Said
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire life. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this speech for years. 'I need you to hear something I should have said decades ago.' But as you speak, decades of suppressed need come flooding out. Your voice moves from measured accusation to raw pleading: 'Why couldn't you just see me? Why was I never enough?' Then something shifts—you see them differently, smaller, more human, maybe even afraid. Your anger doesn't disappear but transmutes into something more complex: grief for what you both lost, unexpected compassion for their limitations, rage at wasted time, and a desperate last-chance hope for connection. End in a different emotional place entirely—perhaps quiet devastation mixed with strange relief, or fierce demand softening into tentative forgiveness.

title: Babysitter's Bounce
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl babysitting your neighbor's 6-month-old. You’ve never held a baby before and feel horribly awkward, convinced you're doing it all wrong. You rock the baby slowly, your voice hushed and bouncing with the rhythm, one arm supporting the head. Start with embarrassed, self-muttering: you're scared you'll drop her, you compare yourself to other girls. Midway, the baby gurgles and grabs your finger, and your interest sparks—you forget your embarrassment. End with a tiny, surprised elation as you realize you're actually soothing her. Let your voice crack, shift weight, pause when the baby fusses.

title: The Last Round
instruction: You're a middle-aged martial artist in a no-contact sparring match, near the end of your final class before the dojo closes forever. You've come here bitter—resentful of the injuries that slow you, the students who left, the decades that feel wasted. Stand in your fighting stance, circling your unseen partner. Breathe sharply, controlled. As you throw a strike, let out a tight, bitter kiai—more frustration than focus. Between exchanges, mutter the words aloud to yourself: 'This is it. Last round.' But as you circle again, something unexpected. The air smells like sweat and old mats. Your body remembers a younger self who loved this. The anger starts to crack. The next time you speak, let your voice waver—tired, hopeful, almost laughing at yourself. End with a quiet, determined statement: 'No. No, I'm glad I showed up.' Let the last word catch in your throat, like you're surprised to mean it.

title: Breakthrough in Breaking Skin
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical experience—could be passionate ecstasy with a lover, could be running until your lungs burn, could be the pain of a wound or illness—but it's cracking open something emotional you've kept locked away for years. Begin with physical sensations: gasping, breathing hard, moaning with the bodily experience. Let these sounds intensify and transform as buried emotional pain surfaces through the physical sensation. Your voice should shift between gasps of physical intensity and deeper, animal-like sounds of emotional release—pleasure and pain becoming indistinguishable. Let primal, non-verbal sounds pour out of you: growls, cries, roars that aren't quite human, as if your body is purging years of unfelt feelings through this physical gateway. End in trembling, raw openness—utterly exposed and surprisingly free.

title: The Crown of Thorns
instruction: You’re at a loud house party, standing near the kitchen island. Your ex’s new partner just walked in—someone you secretly envy for their easy charm. They’re telling a story, and you feel a hot mix of jealousy and infatuation twisting in your chest. You lean to a friend, mimicking the person’s nasally, exaggerated tone with a bitter smirk, but your voice wavers as you catch yourself staring too long at their smile. Start with sneering mockery, then let your voice drop to a raw, hushed admission of desire, cracking as you realize you’re still hooked.

title: Scattering Ashes of Beloved Pet While Remembering Their Life
instruction: Standing at their favorite spot—a beach, a trail, wherever they loved most. As you open the container, start laughing through tears at a specific absurd memory: the time they ate an entire birthday cake, or got sprayed by a skunk, or did that ridiculous thing only they did. Your laughter is real, delighted, full of love. But mid-story, the present tense slips to past tense and you feel it—the impossible reality. Keep talking, but now you're thanking them: for unconditional love, for being there through divorce or illness or loneliness, for teaching you about loyalty. Your voice wavers between gratitude and grief. As you scatter the ashes, find unexpected peace—not happiness, but genuine acceptance. End with a whispered goodbye that holds both heartbreak and smile, devastation and grace. The contradictions should feel completely natural, the way real grief actually works.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Gave You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent the truth about how their drinking, their absence, their cruelty shaped you. Begin with controlled anger, the speech you've rehearsed for years. But as you speak, the child in you emerges—your voice cracks, becomes smaller, more desperate for acknowledgment. Your voice wavers between strength and the devastating vulnerability of still wanting their love. End exhausted, realizing you're not angry anymore—just grief-stricken for the parent-child relationship you'll never have.

title: The Final Engineer
instruction: You are a retired construction foreman, your voice still carrying the gravel of years of yelling over machinery, but today you're hopped up on three cups of black coffee after a sleepless night. You're on a park bench, staring at a rusted crane from your old job site being dismantled. At first, you ramble with jittery astonishment about how they're just tearing it down like it's nothing, your words tumbling out and your breath shallow from the caffeine. Then, as a single cable snaps and the boom crashes down, your astonishment gives way to a guttural, reflective grief — your voice drops, slows, and shakes as you realize that era is truly gone, your final sentence a quiet, cracked whisper.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering to Your Grandmother's Wedding Ring
instruction: You're sitting alone at 3am, holding your grandmother's wedding ring after her funeral. You slip it onto your finger and begin whispering to it—not to her memory, but to the ring itself. Ask it gentle, curious questions: What did her hands feel like when they were young? What promises did it hear? Did it feel the weight of 60 years of marriage? Start with tender playfulness, almost like talking to a small, precious creature. Imagine the ring has absorbed every touch, every gesture of love and frustration your grandmother ever made. As you whisper, let yourself become vulnerable—confess your own fears about love, your loneliness, your hope that you'll be as brave as she was. By the end, you're not playing anymore—you're having the most honest conversation you've ever had, and the ring's silence is the only thing that makes it possible to say these truths out loud.
inspired_by: An actor finds sense memory work tedious and boring

title: The Picture in My Hand
instruction: You are an elderly man, recovering from a stroke that has left you with aphasia. You’re sitting with a younger relative, holding a faded photograph of a woman you once knew intimately. You want to tell them how beautiful she was, how proud you felt when she chose you, and maybe even hint at the desire she stirred in you—but the words won’t come easily. Your voice starts in frustration, struggling to form even simple sounds, with long pauses and garbled attempts. As you keep trying, a flicker of interest and a quiet pride emerge, softening your tone. Let your pauses and missteps feel real—you might repeat a sound, trail off, then suddenly land on the right word, your voice brightening with a shy, lust-tinged smile as you finally say, 'She... she was mine.'
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Interest (slightly present), Pride (clearly present)

title: Storm Breaking
instruction: You've just received devastating news and you're alone in your apartment. Start by noticing your physical body - your heartbeat, the temperature of your skin, how your hands are shaking or clenched. Be curious about your own physical state as if observing a stranger. What is your body doing that you're not controlling? As the reality sinks in deeper, let physical sensation intensify - maybe you need to move, to pace, to press your hands against the wall. Perceive the energy building in your chest, your throat. Let yourself wonder where this surge of feeling will go, what it will become. Then let it break - whether into rage, or shaking sobs, or primal sound. Move from detached observation of your physical state to being consumed by sensory and emotional intensity, surrendering to what your body needs to release.

title: After the Last Song
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy, lying curled on your side in a bedroom after a party. The room is dark, the floor is cold, and you're still buzzing from a few beers. Your voice is low, intimate, slightly slurry. You're talking to your best friend who's also on the floor nearby, but you're looking at the wall. Start by rambling about how awesome the night was, laughing softly to yourself. Mid-sentence, you lose the thread, then remember the fight you had with your dad before you left. The laughter fades. Your voice gets quieter, heavier. End by confessing you don't know what to do tomorrow. Let the intoxication color your initial words—slurred edges, slow pauses—then let the clarity of hurt seep through as you finish. Speak naturally, with little shifts in your body, pauses to swallow, and moments where you forget what you were saying.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Final Countdown
instruction: You're a veteran news anchor in the final 30 seconds of a live broadcast on election night. Your network has just called the race for the underdog candidate you privately supported. You feel a surge of elation—barely contained—mixed with the faint doubt that you're showing too much joy on air. You must maintain your polished anchor tone: crisp, deliberate, no pauses for responses, but your voice threatens to crack or soar with triumph. Start with professional restraint, then let a genuine, almost giddy smile creep into your voice as you sign off, your words stumbling just slightly over a final congratulations, your pitch rising with raw excitement before you cut to commercial.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (slightly present), Doubt (slightly present), Elation (extremely present)

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're thirty-five, sitting across from your aging parent, finally saying what you've needed to say since childhood. Begin with careful, rehearsed anger—the speech you've practiced. Not forgiveness, but the complicated truth that you still love the person who hurt you most.

title: Rain's Embrace
instruction: You are standing alone in an open field during a heavy thunderstorm. The rain is soaking through your clothes, and the sound is overwhelming. You begin by feeling a deep contentment, almost euphoric, as you lift your face to the rain, speaking softly at first, then louder. But then you realize your car is stuck in the mud, and there's no one around. Your voice cracks with helplessness as you consider your situation. Gradually, the feeling drains away into a quiet numbness, your words becoming flat and distant as you accept the rain's relentless presence. Speak naturally, letting the rain affect your volume and articulation.

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You are an older woman with a hyper-feminized voice, but your jaw is wired shut after surgery. You're in a hospital bed, talking to your adult daughter who is trying to be cheerful but you can see the worry in her eyes. You start with a muffled, breathy laugh that sounds more like a wheeze, trying to reassure her how silly this all is. As you speak, you realize the pain meds are wearing off and you're surprisingly giddy, the ecstasy of relief mixing with the absurdity of trying to form words through clenched teeth. Let your voice crack and trail off as you lose a thought, then come back with renewed, strained joy. By the end, you're almost crying with laughter, tears streaming down your cheeks while you sound like you're gargling marbles—pure pleasure at still being alive and sharing this ridiculous moment.

title: The Garden Apology
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a hyper-feminized voice, sitting on a park bench after taking a cannabis gummy to ease your chronic knee pain. Your granddaughter, who you love dearly, is beside you, and you’re trying to apologize for snapping at her earlier—but the gummy has kicked in. Your thoughts drift mid-sentence, your mouth feels dry, and you keep losing your train of thought. Begin with a soft, shame-filled stumble, letting the apology come out in broken, meandering bits. As you speak, your pain—both physical and emotional—seeps into your voice, making it crack and waver. By the end, your shame softens into a vulnerable, pleading tenderness, but the pain remains, a heavy undercurrent in your slow, cotton-mouthed words.

title: One Week Sober: Cravings and Determination Wrestling
instruction: You're one week sober and the physical and mental cravings are intense. Your voice is shaky, sometimes almost agonized: 'I want it so badly right now.' Include the moment where you're narrating the physical sensations of withdrawal or craving—your body is screaming for what you've been denying it. Your voice becomes almost a prayer: 'Please let this pass. Just tonight. I can do one more night.' You're calling someone from your support group, your voice is desperate and humble. You're asking for help and you hate asking but you also know it's this or relapse. Your voice reflects both the shame of needing help and the strength it takes to ask for it. By the end of the call, your voice is steadier, not because you don't want to use, but because you've survived the moment by staying connected.

title: The Lip Gloss Sabotage
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl, sitting on your best friend's bed after school. She's holding her ruined favorite lip gloss—it's melted because you hid it near the radiator on purpose, just to see her reaction. You start off teasing her, laughing with intense, playful energy, poking fun at how dramatic she is. But as she looks at you with hurt eyes, your voice drops—the teasing dies, and you feel a sharp wave of disgust at yourself. You admit what you did, your words stumbling, but underneath it all there's a tiny thrill of triumph that you almost got away with it. Let your volume fall at the truth; let your pauses and hesitations feel real, like you're fighting every word.

title: Post-Coital Afterglow: The Vulnerable Conversation
instruction: In the aftermath of intense physical intimacy, endorphins have destroyed all your emotional walls. The extreme vocal fry, the slow pace, the complete lack of pretense — use the post-sex vulnerability to say something genuinely difficult. Your voice should sound melted, unguarded, intimate. Include comfortable silences that aren't awkward. This is the realest you've ever sounded.

title: The Art of Dismissal
instruction: You are lying in bed, utterly spent and still catching your breath, in the warm afterglow of intimacy. The person beside you murmurs something about how beautiful you are. You feel a flicker of contempt so sharp it cuts through the contentment—you find their devotion absurd, almost pathetic. Begin by letting out a long, satisfied sigh, then speak with lazy, gravelly contempt, amused by how easily they fell for you. Let your words be slow, punctuated by relaxed breaths and a dry, almost mocking chuckle. As you finish, let the amusement soften into a weary, dismissive yawn, utterly at ease.

title: Wonder Striking
instruction: You see something that shouldn't exist, or shouldn't be beautiful, or shouldn't be possible. Your voice comes out as an exhale, almost involuntary: 'Oh.' Breathing stills. Words follow carefully, like you're afraid loud sound will break it: 'How is that... how is that even real?' Your tone is reverent, hushed. Physical: you're completely still. 'I've never seen anything like this.' There's no performance, just genuine awe at existence. Your voice becomes smaller, more humble: 'It's impossible. It's real. It's impossible.'

title: Confronting Your Mother Over a Childhood Betrayal
instruction: You've just discovered that your mother threw away your acceptance letter to your dream school twenty years ago because she needed you to stay home. You're holding a glass of her lemonade—the same recipe she made every summer to 'make things better' after disappointing you. Start by taking a sip, your voice tight with controlled anger as you describe the taste with bitter sarcasm, each word about sweetness laced with rage. As you speak, let the fury build until you're nearly shouting about how she always used small kindnesses to cover up the big betrayals. Then suddenly collapse into raw pain, your voice dropping to almost a whisper as you ask her why her love always came with conditions, why you were never enough just as you were.

title: The Weight of the Visor
instruction: You are an elderly woman, once a knight, now alone in your dusty armory. You lift your old helm onto your head—the metal cold, the visor grating as you lower it. But as you adjust the helm, feeling its familiar weight, your voice grows steadier, not happy but quietly resolved. Let the clank of metal punctuate your words. title: The Last Sled Ride
instruction: You are a child standing in a field during a fierce blizzard. Your father has just told you that your family is moving to a warmer state next week, and this is the last time you'll ever sled on this hill. You start disappointed, voice tight and thin against the freezing wind, snow stinging your eyes. As you remember the hundreds of perfect runs you've had here, you feel a deep, quiet contentment settle in—a peaceful realization that even one last perfect sled ride is a gift. Shouting into the howling gale, your voice cracks with cold and emotion, rising to a brief, breathless elation as you commit to making this final run count, feeling the joy of the moment pierce through the storm.
