title: The Graduation Speech No One Asked For
instruction: You have just achieved something major - graduated, got promoted, reached a milestone - and you are alone in your apartment, speaking to all the people who should be celebrating with you but aren't there. Begin with bitter, sarcastic joy: 'Look at me now! I did it without you!' Your tone should be triumphant but poisoned with resentment. List your achievements while simultaneously indicting those who doubted you or failed to support you: 'You said I'd never make it. You were too busy to help. You never believed in me.' Let your voice carry both pride and pain. As you continue, let the bravado crack - realize that success feels hollow without their recognition. Your celebration should curdle into grief. End with the heartbreaking truth: 'I wanted you to be proud of me. I wanted to share this with you.' Let victory transform into lonely sorrow, joy contaminated by the ache of unmet need.

title: Reading Your Late Spouse's Last Letter That Makes You Laugh
instruction: Six months after their death, you find a letter they left you, and it's... funny. They knew you'd be a mess, and they wrote something absurd, loving, completely them. Start reading aloud, voice thick with grief: 'My dearest—' Then hit the first joke and feel yourself break into surprised, watery laughter: 'Oh god, you idiot.' Laugh through tears at their ridiculous instructions for your life without them, their terrible puns, the way they're still taking care of you from beyond. Your voice dances between sobs and giggles: 'You planned this. You actually—' Feel the collision of heartbreak and joy, the way their humor was always an act of love. Let gratitude flood through: 'Thank you for knowing exactly what I'd need.' Your laughter becomes freer even as tears stream down. They gave you permission to feel joy again. The letter ends with something devastating and beautiful, and your voice goes quiet, awed: 'I will love you until I stop breathing, and then beyond that.' End with peace breaking through grief—not replacing it, but coexisting with it. Move from heavy sorrow to surprised laughter to grateful tears to bittersweet, luminous acceptance.
inspired_by: Asking Your Best Friend If Your Friendship Still Works

title: The Preacher's Waning
instruction: You are a woman standing on a worn wooden crate in a bustling city square, your voice raw from hours of shouting unamplified to a crowd that's mostly wandered off. You came here to proclaim your pride in your community's resilience, but now, under the indifferent sun, you feel the weight of shame — for believing you could change anything, for your own failing energy. Start with forced, cracking pride: your words loop, your pitch rising as you fight to be heard over traffic and chatter. Let exhaustion seep in, your sentences shorten, your volume drop, until you're almost whispering, a confession of shame slipping out as you step down, the crowd's noise swallowing your final words. Speak your piece: 'We… we built this city with our hands, our backs. (voice wavering) And they tried to break us. They tried. But I'm still here. I'm still— (voice catches) I thought I could… I thought I could make them see. But look at them. Walking past me. Like I'm not even… like I'm not even here. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry I couldn't be louder. I'm sorry.'

title: The Last Upload: A Dying Mind Says Goodbye to Itself
instruction: You are a person with terminal illness, hours from death, who chose to have your consciousness digitally preserved. You're recording a final message to the digital copy that will wake up after you're gone—a stranger who will have your memories but won't be you. Start with clinical detachment, explaining what they need to know. But mid-sentence, the reality hits: you're speaking to your own ghost, giving instructions to someone who will remember this moment from both sides. Your voice fractures between envy (they get to continue), grief (you don't), and a terrible tenderness—you're saying goodbye to yourself. The detachment crumbles into raw fear of the nothingness coming for you, then transforms into an aching gratitude for the life you lived. End in a whisper, torn between warning them and blessing them, between 'I'm sorry' and 'I love you,' speaking to the only person who will truly understand what you're losing.

title: Crowned in Their Eyes
instruction: You are confronting a parent or mentor who never believed in you, never thought you were good enough, who told you repeatedly that you'd fail. You've just achieved something extraordinary—won a major award, reached the pinnacle of your field, proven every doubt wrong. Start from a place of vindicated anger and bitter triumph—you want them to see what they missed, to acknowledge how wrong they were. Make them witness your success. But as you speak, let something unexpected happen: notice how empty this victory feels without their genuine pride, how much you still crave their authentic approval rather than forced acknowledgment. End in a place of raw vulnerability, confessing that proving them wrong doesn't heal the wound of never feeling believed in. Move from righteous anger to aching need.

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Best Friend's Wedding
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, but you're secretly in love with them and this is goodbye to all your secret hopes. Begin with genuine joy, laughter in your voice: 'I've never seen you this happy.' Tell funny stories, make everyone laugh. But your voice keeps catching, betraying you. The laughter becomes slightly manic, covering pain. Then let the mask slip: 'You deserve this. You deserve everything.' Your voice fills with so much love it becomes unbearable. Tears mix with smiling: 'I'm so grateful I got to love you, even if...' You stop yourself, laugh through tears, voice breaking. 'Even if just as your friend.' End raising your glass, voice trembling with both joy and heartbreak: 'To your happiness. That's all I ever wanted.' Let the audience feel both your genuine happiness for them and your devastating loss simultaneously.

title: The Garden After the Funeral
instruction: You are standing in the garden of someone who just died—someone who taught you to grow things, to be patient, to tend and nurture. You begin by angrily pulling weeds, almost violently, resenting that the garden keeps growing as if nothing happened, as if life just continues. Your voice should sound bitter, even cruel, as you speak to the absent person about how dare they leave you with this responsibility. Midway through, you notice something they planted is blooming for the first time—something you both waited years to see—and your anger shatters into grief and wonder simultaneously. By the end, you're laughing and crying at once, furious at them for missing this bloom, grateful they taught you to see it, devastated by their absence, amazed by what they left behind. Your final words should hold all of it: rage and reverence, loss and continuity, the bitter and the beautiful growing in the same soil.

title: The Brilliant Solution That Kills Everything
instruction: You've solved it—the breakthrough that will save thousands of lives—but the cost is one specific life you cannot bear to lose. Maybe it's your child, your partner, someone who trusted you. Start with that explosive, manic triumph, explaining the solution with wild gestures and leaping thoughts. But as you explain it aloud, the reality crashes into you with increasing force. Your voice should escalate from excited to desperate to rageful. Scream at the universe, at God, at the cruel mathematics of it. 'It works, it WORKS, but I can't—I WON'T—' Your brilliant rambling turns into incoherent fury that breaks into gut-wrenching sobs. You're laughing at the absurdity, then choking on tears, then back to fierce, protective rage. End in complete emotional devastation or a hollow, numb acceptance of the impossible choice.

title: Protecting a Child You Can't Save
instruction: You're a parent trying to explain to your child why you're losing custody, and your voice starts fierce with denial: 'Everything's going to be fine, baby, I promise.' But as your child asks questions you can't answer—'When are you coming to get me?'—your fierce protectiveness crashes into helpless rage. Your voice rises, cracking: 'This isn't FAIR, you're MY child!' Then collapses into broken apology: 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, baby.' You're trying to be strong but you're shattering, your words becoming fierce whispers of love mixed with self-loathing: 'You deserve better than this, better than me.' End in devastating tenderness, voice raw from crying but still trying to comfort them. Move from defiant strength to explosive grief to broken-hearted love.

title: Under the Blanket at 3 AM
instruction: You are whispering to your lover in complete darkness, lying very close. Begin in near-silence, with only breath and small sounds. Perhaps you're remembering being held as a child, or being afraid in the dark, or the first time you felt this kind of safety. Don't explain or narrate—stay in the sensory experience. Gradually, these fragments coalesce into a whispered admission of love or fear or need that surprises even you. Move from wordless, almost pre-verbal intimacy to one devastating truth spoken aloud.

title: The Warmth of Yesterday
instruction: You wake from a deep afternoon nap in your armchair, disoriented and heavy-limbed. The room is dim, you don't know the time. Let the memory seep in slowly, your voice softening, a smile tugging at your lips despite the grogginess. End with a quiet, breathy note of contentment, almost surprised by the joy. Let your words be fragmented, pauses for orientation.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You
instruction: You are at the bedside of someone in a coma—perhaps your child, your partner, or your best friend—and the doctors say this may be your last chance to speak to them. Keep your voice intimate, almost a whisper, as though you're afraid to disturb them. Begin with gentle reassurance, telling them it's okay to let go, that you'll be fine. But as you continue, let your composure dissolve—confess the things you're terrified about, how you don't know how to live without them, the way their presence has been your anchor. This is about what catches in your throat, the emotions too big for words.

title: Telling Your Mother You Remember Everything
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the childhood she pretends didn't happen. Start controlled, almost clinical—you've rehearsed this. Your voice is measured as you lay out the facts. But as you describe specific memories, your composure begins to crack. Anger rises in your throat, words becoming sharper, faster, more cutting. Then something shifts: mid-accusation, you hear the little kid you were in your own voice, and rage collapses into something more vulnerable—a desperate question: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Your voice breaks. The ending isn't resolution; it's exhausted devastation mixed with a sliver of hope that she'll finally see you. Move from cold fury through searing pain to raw, exposed need. Make it messy and real.

title: The Memory You Never Told Me About
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a childhood memory they've always refused to discuss—a moment when you needed them desperately and they weren't there. Begin by describing the memory with false calm, almost clinical detachment, as if you're just sharing a story. But as you add details, your voice tightens. You're watching their face, waiting for acknowledgment that never comes. Your calm begins fracturing into anger. 'Do you even remember?' becomes an accusation. The shared memory you're trying to create is one-sided—you're forcing them to see what they chose to forget. Your voice escalates from controlled disappointment to raw, volcanic hurt: Why don't they remember what nearly destroyed you? By the end, you're either breaking down into tears or speaking with the cold, final clarity of someone who's just lost hope. Make the journey from measured control to emotional eruption feel inevitable and utterly real.

title: The Cradle of a Dream
instruction: You're sitting on a worn armchair in a dusty attic, alone, an old photograph held in both hands. You're looking down at it, your chin pressed toward your chest, studying the faded faces. Your voice is low and creaky at first, mumbling to yourself with a damp, gravelly weight as you trace a finger over the image. But as you speak about the person in the photo—a child you once knew or a version of yourself—you slowly lift your gaze, your tone brightening, hope blooming like a fragile, determined flame. You end by looking up at the attic window, your voice steady and clear, full of a quiet, fierce optimism that startles you.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Breaking the Glass Body
instruction: You are in the aftermath of something that has shattered you - a betrayal, a loss, devastating news. Your body feels like glass, and you've been holding yourself rigid to keep from breaking. Start physically tense, controlled, barely breathing. You're speaking to someone who wants to comfort you, but you cannot let them near - if they touch you, you'll shatter. Feel the physical sensation of holding everything in, of your muscles locked, of swallowing the scream. But your body cannot maintain this forever. Let the first crack appear - maybe a tremor in your hands, a break in your voice. Then let it cascade: your body must release what it's been holding. Allow yourself to be touched, held, supported as you fall apart. The journey is from rigid, terrified control through physical collapse into allowing yourself to be held together by someone else.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty with physical and emotional intimacy with scene partners

title: The Night Shift Hilarity
instruction: You're a teenager who's been awake for over 24 hours—pulling an all-nighter with friends, but now you're alone in your room. You find an old, ridiculous video you made months ago and it hits you as the funniest thing ever because you're so exhausted. You start laughing uncontrollably, but the laughter is broken by yawns and pauses where you blank out, then snap back to the video and laugh again. Begin with a heavy, hollow exhaustion, then let the amusement creep in, turning your voice into a slurry, giggling, yawning mess. By the end, you're speaking to yourself, trying to explain why it's so funny, but your words are slow and you keep losing your train of thought.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Weather Report Before Goodbye
instruction: You're a parent with terminal illness, sitting on the porch with your adult child for what you both know is the last time. You begin by talking about tomorrow's forecast—rain, maybe thunder—because talking about the weather is safer than saying goodbye. But as you describe the clouds, the wind, the changing seasons you won't see, your voice begins to crack. The weather talk becomes a metaphor for all the time you're losing, all the springs and summers you won't share. Start with that familiar, obsessive detail about barometric pressure and cold fronts, but let it gradually dissolve into raw grief and desperate love. End not with forecasts, but with the terrifying honesty of 'I don't want to leave you.' Let your voice move from clinical detachment to breaking tenderness.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Abuse She Ignored
instruction: You're finally ready to tell your mother what her partner did to you as a child, and how she looked away. You start measured, voice controlled, almost clinical: 'We need to talk about when I was twelve.' But as she begins to deflect or minimize, something ignites in you. Your voice sharpens, cuts, demands she hear you. The words 'You knew' come out like an accusation and a plea simultaneously. You move between fury—voice rising, cracking with rage—and devastating vulnerability, your voice dropping to almost a whisper: 'I needed you to protect me.' She tries to explain or apologize, and you must decide in real time if you can forgive, your voice shifting from anger to grief to perhaps, tentatively, a fragile hope for repair. End with whatever truth your heart finds in that moment.
inspired_by: Your Partner Saying They Don't Want Children

title: Watching Your Child Choose the Parent Who Left
instruction: Your teenager has just announced they're moving in with your ex—the one who abandoned them years ago. You start trying to be reasonable, mature, supportive: 'If that's what you want...' But the unfairness ignites something inside you. Your voice rises, fierce and protective: 'I was there for every nightmare, every fever, every heartbreak. Where were they?' Let your rage build—you're defending yourself, justifying, listing every sacrifice. But then you see your child's face and everything collapses. Your voice breaks into something ragged, helpless: 'What did I do wrong?' The anger dissolves into devastating vulnerability. You're suddenly pleading, your voice barely holding together: 'Don't I matter to you?' End on a whisper of complete helplessness: 'I can't compete with the parent who wasn't here.'

title: Abdicating with Laughter and Tears
instruction: You are signing away your throne, voluntarily stepping down after decades of brutal, isolating rule. As you speak to the empty throne room, addressing the crown you're leaving behind, you're flooded with contradictory emotions. Laugh at the absurdity—all that sacrifice, all that loneliness, and for what? Cry because you're grieving the only identity you've ever known. Feel genuine relief and devastating loss at once. Express gratitude for the burden being lifted while your voice breaks with the terror of not knowing who you are without it. Find dark humor in your mistakes, then immediately choke up at the cost of those mistakes. End in a place of paradoxical peace: you're free and you're lost, you're broken and you're whole, you're laughing and sobbing at once. Let every emotion bleed into its opposite. Be messy, contradictory, and utterly, bewilderingly human.
inspired_by: The Queen and the Jealous Advisor

title: Narrating a Nature Documentary While Hiking Uphill
instruction: Channel your inner David Attenborough, delivering a beautiful, measured nature narration — but you're actually hiking a steep mountain trail. The professional BBC voice should gradually be undermined by heavy breathing, longer pauses for air, and sentences that get shorter as oxygen debt increases. Maintain the calm, authoritative tone even as your body betrays you. The disconnect between serene content and gasping delivery is the performance.

title: Stumbling Grace
instruction: You are a middle-aged man, drunk and kneeling in a small, dimly lit chapel. You're frustrated—you came here to pray, but your mind is a fog of irritation and restlessness. Feel the hard floor under your knees, the weight of your body unsteady. Start by muttering complaints and fumbling through words, then suddenly a silly memory of your daughter's laugh cuts through the haze. Let impatience dissolve into a raw, unguarded elation—laugh to yourself, maybe even cry, as the absurd beauty of the moment hits you. Your voice shifts from slurred, clipped anger to a broken, open-throated joy, with pauses where you lose your train of thought and find something better.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Elation (clearly present)

title: Party Game
instruction: You are at a crowded house party, slightly tipsy from a drink, trying to impress someone you've been eyeing all night. You pull them into a quieter corner, using dirty talk to exert control. Start with a confident, teasing tone, but as you speak, the room's noise distracts you, and you lose your focus momentarily. End with a softer, more uncertain note, realizing you actually care what they think. Let your voice waver between a seductive growl and a breathy laugh. React to the pounding music and the feeling of the wall behind you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Love: The Secret You Can't Keep
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner sleeps beside you, and you're confessing something in a whisper they can't hear—something that will change everything when morning comes. Start barely audible, the words catching in your throat, each syllable a struggle. Speak with the tenderness of someone memorizing a face they're about to lose. Your voice should be intimate, broken, full of love that makes the truth even harder. Describe touching their hair, their hand, knowing this is the last time you can do this in innocence. Let the confession spill out in fragments—start sentences you can't finish, circle back, try different words. Feel your chest tighten, your breath hitch. The emotion should be so quiet it's almost silent, but so intense it fills the darkness. End with an 'I'm sorry' that barely makes it past your lips, followed by the kind of silence that holds everything you can't say.
inspired_by: Profound Relief: The Test Results Are Negative

title: Pilot Engine Failure
instruction: You're the airline pilot with one engine out, and you're addressing the cabin. Your voice is trained calm: 'Ladies and gentlemen, we're experiencing a mechanical situation. We're handling it appropriately.' Reassurance delivered with practiced authority. But your heart is thundering. Your co-pilot's voice comes through your headset with controlled terror. You take a breath, and your voice becomes almost paternal: 'We'll be landing in Denver in 45 minutes. You're safe.' That voice—the one that's lying to comfort them—is also the voice that's been trained for this exact scenario. Show the tension between professional control and genuine fear.

title: Soul Connected
instruction: You're experiencing connection at the soul level—recognizing your partner not just as a body but as the essence of who they are. Your voice is quiet, intimate, almost whispered: 'I recognize you.' Your partner's voice receives this: 'You're recognized too.' This is beyond sex, beyond romance—this is the deepest kind of knowing. You're looking into each other, and you're being seen. Your voice should sound like someone who's encountered another person at their very core and found themselves reflected there.

title: The Last Hour Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed in the pre-dawn darkness. She drifts in and out of consciousness. Begin speaking softly about a childhood memory that terrifies you to lose—something only she knows, something that will die with her. As you speak, let your voice move between tender gratitude for who she was, raw fear of facing the world without her, and flashes of old anger about wounds she left unhealed. Move from whispered confession to barely controlled desperation. End in a place of fierce, protective love mixed with the terror of letting go—as if you could keep her alive by the intensity of what you feel.

title: The Last Voice Message Before the Colony Ship Departs
instruction: You're recording a message to your adult child who's leaving on a one-way colony ship to another star system. You'll never see them again—they'll arrive 200 years from now due to time dilation, and you'll be long dead. Start with forced cheerfulness, telling them how proud you are, how this is everything they've worked for. But as you speak, the reality crushes you—you're saying goodbye forever. Your voice begins to crack. You catch yourself trying to be strong, then abandon it entirely. End in raw grief mixed with fierce pride, your words breaking apart as you tell them to be happy, to live fully, even as your heart shatters. Let the silences between words speak as loudly as the words themselves.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Alien First Contact With Translator Who Recognizes It As Their Dead Child

title: The Inheritance of Silence: What You Never Said at Breakfast
instruction: You are confronting your elderly parent about the lifetime of emotional distance hidden behind your family's comfortable morning routines. Begin with bitter observation—describing how they perfected the choreography of domesticity while never once asking how you really felt. Your voice should drip with decades of unspoken hurt as you recount specific breakfast moments where their silence left you feeling invisible. Build to a raw accusation: 'You loved the routine more than you loved me.' But then, mid-fury, you catch yourself performing their exact habits—the way you pour coffee, fold the newspaper—and you break. End with devastating vulnerability, your anger collapsing into a whispered plea: after all these years, can they finally see you? Let love and rage live in the same breath.
inspired_by: Old Couple's Morning Routine: 40 Years of Love

title: Grave Visit Memory
instruction: You're visiting your parent's grave for the first time since the funeral, five years later. Your voice is tentative: 'Hey, Mom. It's been a while.' It's strange, talking to a grave. 'I know you can't hear me, but I need to talk to you anyway.' You sit. 'I'm doing okay. I finally got the job I wanted.' Your voice becomes more animated, telling her about your life. Then: 'I wish you could see it. I wish I could ask you for advice.' Your voice cracks. 'I still miss you every day.' You place flowers on the grave. 'Thank you for everything you gave me. I'm doing my best to make you proud.' By the end, your voice is soft: 'I have to go now, but I'll be back. I promise.' Walking away, your voice is slightly lighter — you've been heard by the silence, and somehow, that's enough.

title: The Unsaid Years
instruction: You're facing your father after decades of silence, and the words are finally coming. Start with your voice shaking, tentative: 'I need to tell you something I should have said when I was seven.' There's fear of rejection, of being dismissed again. Build slowly, finding courage: 'You never asked me what I needed. You just decided what kind of person I should be.' Your voice hardens with accumulated pain: 'Do you have any idea what it's like to spend your whole childhood feeling invisible to the one person who should see you?' Let anger rise, but don't perform it—let it be the anger that's been waiting thirty years: 'I needed you to be proud of who I actually am, not some version you invented!' Then the anger cracks, and underneath is the wounded child: 'I just wanted you to know me, Dad. That's all I ever wanted.' Your voice becomes almost a whisper, raw and exposed: 'And I still do. God help me, I still do.' End with the terrible vulnerability of hope mixed with fear: 'Is it too late? Can you even hear me now?'

title: Misdirected Anger at Innocent Person
instruction: You're angry at someone else, and you've taken it out on an innocent person. You're snapping: 'Just leave me alone!' Your voice is harsh, sharp. But then they respond with hurt, and you realize they didn't deserve this. Your voice immediately changes: 'Wait, I'm sorry. I'm not mad at you.' You're explaining, but the damage is done. Your voice becomes remorseful, gentle: 'That wasn't fair. I'm sorry.' By the end, you're trying to repair what you broke.

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your dying partner—hours or days left—asks you to describe the trip you were supposed to take together next month. As you paint this elaborate, beautiful picture of places you'll never see, you start to laugh at the absurdity, the injustice, the cosmic joke. But you're also crying. Your voice dances between joy at the imagined memories and grief at what's being stolen. Describe sunsets you'll never watch together, meals you'll never share, inside jokes you'll never get to make. Let gratitude for what you had crash into rage at what you're losing. Your voice should sparkle with love even as it breaks with sorrow. End with a moment of profound peace—perhaps 'Thank you for saying yes to me'—that somehow holds both celebration and goodbye.

title: Whispering About the Affair to an Empty Room
instruction: Late at night, alone, you're practicing what you'll never say aloud—confessing an affair to your partner who's asleep in the next room. Your voice must stay barely above a whisper throughout, as if the walls might hear and judge you. Start with clinical distance, trying to explain the timeline like a news report. But as you describe the first kiss, your throat tightens with something between shame and the echo of desire. You catch yourself almost smiling at a memory, then the smile dissolves into silent crying. End trying to explain why you did it, but the words disintegrate. You can't even convince yourself in an empty room. The final line should be whispered to your own reflection or the darkness: 'I don't know who I am anymore.' Let every breath carry the weight of what you're holding inside.
inspired_by: Describing Color to a Blind Person

title: The Garden After the Funeral
instruction: You are standing in a garden immediately after a funeral—but it's spring, and everything is absurdly, offensively, beautifully alive. Begin by trying to stay in your grief, describing the person you've lost with sadness. But the garden keeps interrupting: a bird's song that makes you almost smile, the exact smell of flowers they loved, warm sun on your face that feels impossibly good despite everything. Let yourself be torn between grief and this unexpected, guilty joy at being alive. Your voice should fracture between tears and something close to laughter—not because anything is funny, but because you're feeling everything at once. Allow anger to surface: at them for leaving, at yourself for feeling anything but sadness, at the world for continuing. But underneath, let gratitude emerge—devastating, enormous gratitude for having known them, mixed inextricably with the agony of loss. End in a paradox: speaking to them with both fury and love, grief and joy inseparable, your voice carrying all of it simultaneously.

title: The Laughter Across the Room
instruction: You're at a crowded party, two drinks in, feeling the pleasant buzz and the music thrumming through your body. Then you see them – your recent ex – laughing with someone new, their head thrown back in a way you once knew. The alcohol makes everything feel slow and sharp at once. You lean against the wall, pretending to check your phone, but your eyes keep drifting. Start by murmuring to yourself with a detached, almost amused curiosity, like you're reporting a bizarre fact. Then let the feeling crack – a sudden, wet sob breaks through as you repeat the same phrase, your voice hopping between numb flatness and raw hurt. End with a whisper, exhausted, the interest still there but hollow, like a wound you can't stop probing.
emotions_sampled: Elation (slightly present), Interest (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)

title: The Suitcase at the Door
instruction: You've just discovered your teenage child has packed a suitcase and is planning to leave home tonight—to move in with someone you believe is dangerous for them. Begin from a place of parental authority and anger, voice raised, trying to use control and rules to stop this. As your child remains silent or defiant, let your fury crack open to reveal the terror underneath—the specific fear of losing them, of not being able to protect them anymore. Let physical sensations guide you: the tightness in your chest, shaking hands, the feeling of your power as a parent dissolving. End in a place of desperate, naked pleading—all authority stripped away, just one human begging another not to go. Your voice should move from commanding and loud to broken and barely above a whisper.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Execution
instruction: You have three minutes to speak to your younger sibling before they're executed for a crime you know they didn't commit—a crime you committed. You start trying to sound strong, reassuring them it'll be okay, your voice steady with false hope. But as the seconds tick away, the weight of your secret becomes unbearable. Your words fracture as you move between wanting to confess the truth and not wanting to burden them with betrayal in their final moments. The desperation builds—you're begging time to stop, your voice cracking between whispered apologies they don't understand and choked attempts to say 'I love you' while your throat closes with guilt. End in a place where you're speaking but can barely form words, knowing you're sending them to death carrying your sin.

title: The Clear Note
instruction: You have vocal nodules and are recovering after treatment. You're talking to a close friend after a therapy session where you successfully sang a note you haven't hit in months. Start with doubt—your voice is hoarse, you clear your throat, you're afraid it will crack. As you describe the moment, you realize the note actually held, and relief washes over you. End with quiet pride—a soft laugh, a slight smile in your voice, even as your pitch wavers. Let your breathiness and small vocal breaks feel natural, but allow your tone to lift slightly as your confidence grows.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (slightly present), Relief (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Truth at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning light. She's been unconscious for days, but suddenly her eyes open and she looks at you with perfect clarity. You have maybe five minutes. Start by trying to say the 'right' comforting things—reassurances, pleasant memories—but feel the inadequacy of those words. Let something crack open. Midway through, allow yourself to confess something you've never told anyone: a secret fear about yourself, a way you've failed her, or a truth about who you really are that you've hidden from everyone. By the end, find yourself not just saying goodbye to her, but to the person you've pretended to be. Let your voice move from controlled comfort to raw, whispered confession to something approaching relief or devastating freedom.

title: Hypoxic Love Letter: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: You're oxygen-deprived, lying in your tent at death zone altitude, believing your partner is asleep beside you (they're not—they descended yesterday). Your voice is barely audible, intimate, each word a struggle. Begin whispering the tender things you've never said aloud—confessions of inadequacy, fears you've hidden, the ways you've failed them. Your speech slurs, thoughts drift, but the vulnerability is achingly real. Mid-scene, have a moment of lucidity where you remember they're not actually there, and the loneliness cuts through you like a knife. Your breathing catches with quiet tears. Shift into softer whispers, as if they can somehow still hear you—apologizing, thanking them, telling them the secret ways they've made you brave. End with your voice fading to almost nothing, a whispered 'I love you' that's half breath, half prayer, tender and utterly heartbroken.

title: The Unsteady Rhythm
instruction: You are an elderly woman, deeply in love with your partner, but this intimate moment is overwhelming you. You start with a sense of elation, feeling the closeness and your own surprising energy. But as the rhythm continues, awe floods in—awe that this body, this life, can still feel such fire and beauty. Yet, doubt claws at you: is it real? Are you fooling yourself? Can you really trust this joy? Your voice must ride the physical exertion: heavy, rhythmic breaths, words breaking into short, effortful bursts or whispered fragments. Let the doubt creep in midway, your pace slowing, a tiny pause or a hesitant, softer exhale before you push forward again. End with a quiet, vulnerable confession—spoken on an exhale, almost a question, as the physical movement fades into stillness.
emotions_sampled: Elation (slightly present), Awe (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)

title: The Goodbye You Can't Take Back
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner on the last night before you leave them—a relationship ending by your choice, but one that's destroying you. Begin so quietly, voice thick with unshed tears: 'You're still beautiful when you sleep. You always were.' Trace the memories tenderly, each word catching in your throat. 'I memorized the way you laugh. The way you say my name when you're half-asleep.' Your voice trembles with the weight of what you're about to do. This isn't anger or drama—it's the quiet devastation of choosing to break both your hearts because staying would break them worse. Let long pauses speak. End with a confession so soft it's almost inaudible, a truth you can only say when they can't hear: 'This is going to haunt me forever.' Your voice should feel like it's barely holding itself together, intimate and shattering.

title: The Baby's Room
instruction: You are standing in the empty nursery you spent months preparing. The crib you assembled with such hope stands against the wall. But there will be no baby. You lost the pregnancy, or the adoption fell through, or the partner who was going to parent with you is gone. Pick up the tiny clothes you folded so carefully. Sit in the rocking chair where you imagined late night feedings. You should feel only grief—but instead, beneath the devastating loss, you feel the most unexpected emotion: gratitude. Gratitude for having been capable of that much love. Relief that you won't become a parent while feeling so unprepared. Guilt for that relief. Anger at yourself for the guilt. Let these contradictions coexist in your voice. Speak to the child who will never be, and let your words hold both the shattering of dreams and the strange, terrible, beautiful gift of letting go.

title: The Phone Call After the Funeral
instruction: You're calling your sibling the evening after burying someone who caused you both tremendous pain—an abusive parent, a toxic family member. Begin with relief, almost inappropriate laughter. Your voice should carry a giddy, guilty freedom: they're finally gone, and you're both liberated. Share a dark joke. Feel the lightness. But as you talk, let something more complicated emerge. Mixed with your relief comes an unexpected wave of loss—not for who they were, but for who they might have been, or for the childhood you deserved but never had. By the end, you're crying while also laughing, unable to separate your joy from your grief, your freedom from your orphaning. Hold both truths simultaneously without resolving them.

title: The Unseen Audience
instruction: You are an older woman walking barefoot along the shoreline, talking softly to yourself about a cherished memory. Suddenly, you realize a young couple nearby has been watching you, smirking. The wind whips your hair across your face as heat floods your cheeks. Swallow the mortification—your voice catches, falters, grows thin with shame. But then you glance out at the endless rhythm of the waves and let a wry, humbled sigh escape. End with a quiet, honest admission, your voice steadier, almost amused by your own foolishness.

title: The Weight of a Moment
instruction: You are an elderly person lying on your stomach on a warm picnic blanket, your chest pressed against the ground. You're watching a small beetle struggle to turn over an ant. At first, you feel a flicker of contempt — annoyance at its clumsiness, maybe a memory of younger impatience. But as you continue watching, the stillness of the afternoon settles in, and you find a quiet contentment in just observing. Your voice should feel close to the earth, with shorter breaths between phrases, and your tone shifts from a slight edge to a softer, accepting calm. Speak naturally, letting your gaze drift and your words come in small clusters.

title: Making Difference
instruction: What you did mattered. Someone is alive, or whole, or less alone because of you. Your voice is humble, clear: 'I didn't think it would change anything.' Breathing is full. Physical: grounded. 'I just did the thing I could do.' But it did matter. Vocal tone grows as you realize: 'I actually made a difference.' By the end, you're speaking into a future affected by your action: 'I matter. What I do matters.'

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Abuse They Claim Never Happened
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent, and you've finally found the courage to speak about what they did to you as a child. Begin with your voice small and uncertain, almost apologizing for bringing it up, stumbling over words like you're still that frightened child. As they deny it, watch your voice transform—anger rising, words becoming sharper, more insistent. You're listing specific memories while they keep saying 'that never happened,' and your delivery shifts between fury, desperation to be believed, and the crushing realization that they'll never acknowledge the truth. Your voice should crack not from sadness but from the violence of holding both rage and the remnant of a child's need for their parent's love. End in a different emotional place—either cold, quiet acceptance of their refusal to see you, or a raw, guttural release of decades of silence.
inspired_by: Heroin Nod: Fighting Sleep While Someone Talks to You

title: The Silent Prayer at the Wedding
instruction: You are a young woman at a close friend's wedding, wearing a flowing niqab. You stand near a window, watching the bride dance freely with your ex. The room hums with excitement, but you are still. You offer a quiet prayer of gratitude for this marriage, but your voice carries a sliver of envy for lost moments. Start with sincere, soft praise for the couple, then let your tone tighten with an admission of hidden jealousy, ending with a clenched, raw whisper that fights a tear—'but some knots must fray to free us.' Feel the fabric brush your lips with each word.

title: Whispering Why You Have to Leave
instruction: You're lying next to your sleeping partner, whispering why you're going to leave them in the morning. Speak in genuinely hushed tones, as if afraid to wake them, describing the small, beautiful details of loving them that make leaving unbearable. Touch on specific moments - the way they laugh at their own jokes, how they hold your face when they kiss you, their terrible singing in the shower. Let your voice catch as you explain that loving them isn't enough, that you're not who you need to be when you're with them, that staying would slowly poison what's beautiful between you. End with a whispered 'I'm sorry' that breaks into silent tears. The entire performance should feel like the gentlest possible heartbreak, tender and devastating, each word carefully quiet so as not to disturb the person you're about to shatter.
inspired_by: Whispering a Love Letter You'll Never Send

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent after years of abandonment, and all the rehearsed words dissolve into raw truth. Start controlled, almost cold—reciting the facts of your childhood, the birthdays missed, the promises broken. But as you speak, the hurt little child inside you begins to surface. Your voice wavers between adult anger and childhood bewilderment: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let rage build until you're nearly shouting, demanding answers they can't give. Then something shifts—your fury collapses into exhausted vulnerability. Your voice drops to almost nothing as you confess the truth you've been hiding: despite everything, you still wanted them to come back. End with a mixture of grief and unexpected liberation, finally releasing the burden of waiting for them to choose you.

title: The Last Toast
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gruff voice, standing at a podium at your wife's funeral. You're nervous, fumbling with the paper, your voice trembles as you project poorly. You start by doubting your ability to speak, then a memory of her passionate nature surfaces, filling you with raw lust and affection, but also doubt if you honored her. Let your voice crack, pause, and shift from hesitant mumbling to a sudden, vividly recalled moment where you speak with surprising intensity and longing, then soften into quiet, affectionate loss. Micro-distractions: adjust glasses, clear throat, look down, lose train of thought.

title: Whispered Cartography
instruction: In the dark, lying next to someone you love, whisper about the geography of your loneliness. Begin by describing where you were two years ago—the specific room, the specific silence, the way you'd forgotten what your own laughter sounded like. Keep your voice barely audible, intimate, as if speaking any louder would shatter something precious. Trace the path from that isolated place to here, to this bed, to this person's warmth. Map aloud the small moments that led you back to yourself: a phone call you almost didn't answer, a door you almost didn't walk through, a risk you almost didn't take. End by whispering about the future you're terrified and thrilled to imagine—the vulnerability of wanting something, of being seen. Move from numb isolation, through tender wonder at your own survival, to trembling, tentative joy mixed with the fear of losing it.

title: The Lottery Funeral
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone you loved deeply, but there's a terrible secret: their death has inadvertently made you wealthy (an insurance policy, an inheritance, a legal settlement you didn't expect). Begin speaking about them with genuine grief and love, your voice breaking with loss. But let another feeling creep in—the shameful, intoxicating awareness of your new power and security, the future suddenly open before you because they're gone. Your vocal journey must hold both emotions simultaneously: profound sorrow mixed with this guilty, exhilarating sense of possibility. Let your voice catch not just on grief but on the horror of your own relief. End in a place where you can barely distinguish between tears of loss and tears of terrible, grateful joy. You loved them—and their death has freed you. Both things are true.

title: Screaming Through Powerlessness
instruction: You're watching someone you'd die to protect suffer, and there's absolutely nothing you can do—they're behind glass, being taken away, trapped in pain you cannot reach. Start with fierce, almost violent declarations of what you would do, your voice loud and sharp with furious determination, each word a weapon you wish you could use. Build into full-throated rage, shouting promises and threats, your voice cracking with the strain of your intensity. Then feel the helplessness crash over you like a wave—your voice breaking mid-shout, dissolving from roar to sob. Let the volume collapse as powerlessness overwhelms fury, your words fragmenting into gasping, choked pleas. End with your voice raw and destroyed, oscillating between whispered begging and involuntary cries, all your protective ferocity reduced to broken, useless sound. Transform from warrior to shattered supplicant.

title: Playing Dumb
instruction: You’re in a cold interrogation room, seated under a harsh light, being questioned about a friend’s whereabouts. The officer’s silence stretches between each question. You start off trying to deflect with a teasing tone—a smirk in your voice, a little shrug—as if this is all a joke. But as the silence grows heavier and you realize they know more than they’re letting on, your voice loses its playfulness, turning shaky and small. You shift in your chair, your words stumble, and by the end you’re almost pleading, the teasing completely gone. Let the nervous energy and the power imbalance crack your composure.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Echoes of an Empty Pew
instruction: You are standing alone in the center of a vast stone cathedral, long after the congregation has left. You came here expecting to find a recorded message left for you—a final goodbye from someone who promised it would be here. As you listen to your own footsteps and the lingering organ hum, you speak slowly, testing the massive reverb, trying to pinpoint where a voice might come from. At first you concentrate on the acoustics, confused by the emptiness and the way sound dies. But as the seconds stretch and no message arrives, the hope drains from your voice, replaced by a quiet, swallowing disappointment. Let the words hang in the air, fading into the stone, while you shift your weight and glance around, your final line barely a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (slightly present), Concentration (slightly present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Telling Your Father You Remember Everything
instruction: You've finally gathered the courage to confront your father about the emotional neglect of your childhood. Start with a tight, controlled voice trying to be 'adult' and measured about it, perhaps even reasonable. But as you list specific memories—birthdays he missed, times you needed him and he wasn't there, the way he looked through you—your control begins to crack. Your anger builds but it's mixed with this pathetic, childlike need for him to just acknowledge what he did. When he tries to dismiss it or make excuses, something breaks in you. End with your voice torn between rage and pleading, between wanting to hurt him and desperately wanting him to finally, finally see you. The little child and the furious adult must both be present in your voice.
inspired_by: Coming Down from MDMA: The Serotonin Crash

title: Collapsed Fury
instruction: You are slumped against a cold alley wall after chasing someone who betrayed you. Your lungs burn, and every word comes out between ragged, uncontrollable gasps. Start by spitting out your anger in broken, breathless shouts—your voice cracking from both rage and physical collapse. As your body gives out, let the anger slowly drain into a hollow, exhausted whisper, ending with a single line that sounds more like a confession than a threat. Let your pauses be real—gasping, coughing, or wiping sweat from your face—and let your voice lose tension as the fight leaves you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Crest's Confession
instruction: You are a boy, no older than ten, with a voice that tries so hard to sound grown-up and tough, like your dad. You're in a hospital hallway, leaning against a cold wall, trying to walk through a contraction. The pain comes in waves—between them, you speak with forced calm, but when the wave crests, your voice cracks, you grunt, you squeeze your eyes shut. You're talking to your father, who just told you he can't be here for the birth of your new sibling because of work. You start by puffing out your chest, saying 'It's fine, I get it, a man's gotta do what he's gotta do,' but as the next wave hits, the disappointed little boy breaks through, and you end by whispering, 'But I thought you'd be here... I'm scared, Dad.' Your voice should struggle to maintain the gruff pride, then dissolve into a raw, embarrassed crack of disappointment.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in the wreckage of your childhood home after a natural disaster, finding your mother's recipe box in the rubble. You start reading her handwritten notes aloud—'Add extra vanilla, always'—and you're laughing because these tiny instructions survived when everything else is gone. But the laughter has tears threaded through it. Each recipe is a memory: Sunday mornings, her hands teaching yours, the smell of cinnamon. Your voice breaks between chuckling at her terrible spelling and sobbing because you'll never taste her cooking again. By the end, you're thanking her—thanking the recipes, thanking the disaster for leaving you this one thing, thanking the universe for the absurd mercy of loss mixed with preservation. Your voice carries simultaneous joy and devastation, gratitude blooming in the center of grief.

title: Echo of Victory
instruction: You are a young child standing alone in a vast stone cathedral after your first solo performance in the choir. The enormous space swallows your voice, making you feel tiny. At first, you speak hesitantly, almost whispering, overwhelmed by the cold silence and the lingering reverb. But as you remember how you conquered your stage fright and sang the high note perfectly, your voice grows stronger, slower, more deliberate, filling the space with quiet triumph. Let the natural echoes and the cold stone affect your pacing and volume. End with a sense of achievement and pride, your words lingering in the air.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Birthday Call From Prison
instruction: You're calling your child on their birthday from prison. You have fifteen minutes. Begin with forced brightness—trying to make this normal, asking about cake and presents—but you can hear the hollowness in your own voice. Let yourself feel the pride in who they're becoming and the shame of watching from behind glass. Your child is growing up without you, and that's both your greatest sorrow and your strange gift to them—they're thriving. Allow gratitude for their resilience to mix with the ache of missing everything. Let anger at yourself surface, then love that's almost unbearable, then the discipline of not making this call about your pain. End with the ten-second warning beep, trying to say everything that matters in the time you have left. Your voice should contain celebration and devastation in equal measure, joy for them and grief for yourself, hope for their future and despair at your absence from it.
inspired_by: An actor is avoiding daily practice due to tedium or lack of immediate reward

title: The Promotion You Didn't Get
instruction: You're a young man from another country, standing in the hallway after a meeting where your coworker got the promotion you desperately wanted. You stop him to offer congratulations, but your English stumbles—words come out simple, broken up by pauses, your voice louder than you mean because you're afraid he won't understand. Start with the fear of sounding stupid, of saying the wrong thing. But as you speak, the envy boils up—your throat tightens, your eyes dart away, and your sentences get shorter. End with a raw, barely controlled jealous question that drops your volume into something colder.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Broken Promise
instruction: You are a mother speaking to your deaf child after they have broken a precious heirloom that you secretly despised. Your voice is slow, loud, and over-enunciated for lip-reading, but your tone starts with a strained patience, as if forcing a calm mask. As you continue, let the mask crack—your words become heavy with hidden malice, each syllable dripping with a gloating cruelty. End with a low, deliberate threat, your feminized voice turning icy. Micro-distractions: you pause to wipe a crumb from your lip, shift your weight, and hold eye contact too long. Spoken lines: 'Sweetheart, look at me. I want you to see my lips. You broke grandma's vase. That's okay, I always hated it. But now you owe me. You will do exactly as I say, every day, until I decide you're forgiven. Do you understand?'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying next to your partner, unable to sleep. Begin whispering from the part of you that's competent, capable, always has it together—the version everyone sees. You're about to confess something you've never told anyone: a fear so fundamental it feels like it could unmake you. As you speak, allow a much younger, more fragile version of yourself to emerge through the darkness. This is the part of you that still feels small, uncertain, terrified of abandonment. Let your breath change, let your voice thin out or crack, let silences speak. By the end, you should be speaking from a place of such raw vulnerability that you're barely recognizing your own voice.
inspired_by: Actor playing a character with a strong psychological profile very different from their own

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're describing the worst day of your life, but you're laughing—really laughing—because the absurdity of it, the cosmic joke of it, has finally hit you. Start with laughter that seems genuine but has a edge of hysteria. As you tell the story, let tears come while you're still smiling, your voice cracking between chuckles and sobs. Find weird moments of genuine joy in the wreckage, then immediately feel the pain of that joy. End with a strange, profound gratitude for having survived something that broke you, your voice carrying both devastation and an unexpected peace. The emotions shouldn't take turns—they should exist simultaneously, tangled and true and beautifully contradictory.

title: Fantasy: Prophecy Speaker Realizes They've Already Spoken This Moment
instruction: As a prophecy speaker in a medieval court, you're describing visions of the future. Your voice is spiritual, otherworldly. Then you realize—you've already spoken these exact words. And the previous time, the thing you prophesied happened. Your voice becomes uncertain, layered with horror at recursive loop. You're stuck speaking a future that's already happened. Your breathing becomes the breathing of someone trapped in amber, speaking toward an inevitable ending you've already narrated.

title: Midnight Confession in the Hospital Chapel
instruction: You're alone in a hospital chapel at 3 AM, whispering to God or the universe while your child is dying two floors above. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, like you're telling a secret to the darkness itself. Begin with tender memories—voice catching on the beauty of ordinary moments: their first laugh, the way they said your name. Let your breath hitch. Speak about the specific weight of their hand in yours. Gradually, the words become a desperate, whispered bargain: offering anything, everything. Your voice grows smaller, not louder—the intensity comes from how quiet and broken it becomes. End with a moment of terrible acceptance, voice cracking on a simple phrase like 'I'm not ready to let go,' followed by silence where your breathing is the only sound. The emotion moves from bittersweet memory through urgent pleading to quiet, devastating surrender.

title: The Untranslatable Word
instruction: In an intimate, late-night confession to your lover, try to explain a word from your native language that has no English equivalent - one that describes exactly how you feel about them. Start with quiet tenderness, almost playful, as you attempt different translations, each one falling short. Let frustration seep in as you realize language is failing you at the most important moment. Your voice should grow smaller, more fragile, as you switch between languages, desperately trying syllables and phrases, until you're nearly whispering. End with the admission that maybe some feelings live beyond words, your voice thick with unshed tears, accepting the beautiful inadequacy of trying to capture love in any language.

title: The Stain That Won't Lift
instruction: You are an older woman in your kitchen, kneeling on the floor, scrubbing a stubborn dark stain on the tile with a stiff brush. Your movements are slow, rhythmic, your breath catching with every push. You start muttering to yourself, confused about what the stain could be—maybe spilled coffee, maybe something else. As you scrub harder, your confusion shifts into a growing distress: the stain smells wrong, it's too dark, and you suddenly realize it's blood from when your husband fell last night and you didn't call for help in time. Your voice cracks, you pause mid-scrub, then push through with a desperate, frantic whisper. Let the scrubbing sound weave into your words; lose a thought, catch your breath, and let the distress take over completely by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying everything you've held back for decades. Begin with bitter, controlled anger: 'Do you even remember my tenth birthday?' Your voice is sharp, prosecutorial. As you list the moments they missed, your anger intensifies - school plays, graduations, the times you needed them most. But then something shifts. Mid-sentence, your voice cracks: 'I needed you and you just... you weren't...' Now you're that child again, vulnerable and abandoned. The rage dissolves into raw grief. You try to rebuild your anger but can't. End with an almost whispered plea that you hate yourself for making: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to stay?' The question hangs there, naked and devastating.
inspired_by: Leaving Someone You Promised Forever To

title: Stem the Tide
instruction: You’re a teenage girl who’s been badly cut in a fall; you’re alone in a garage, pressing a rag against your side. Blood seeps through your fingers, and you know you need to keep pressure and stay awake. At first, you talk yourself through it with fierce pride and concentration—you’re going to be fine, you’ve got this. But the cold creeps in, your grip weakens, and your voice starts to thready; the hope that started bright turns into a quiet, whispered admission that you might not make it. Let your words slow, your pauses grow, and let a faint, shivering breath carry the fading belief that someone will find you.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Concentration (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Forgotten Lullaby
instruction: You're visiting someone with advanced dementia who no longer recognizes you—someone who raised you, who sang to you. Sit close and speak softly, starting by reminding them who you are, your voice gentle and patient. When they don't remember, describe a specific tender memory—something intimate only you two shared. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, thick with unshed tears. As you realize they're truly gone even though they're still breathing, let the grief creep into your words. End by humming or singing the lullaby they once sang to you, your voice breaking on certain notes, hoping somewhere deep inside they might still hear you. Make it so quiet and devastating that silence would be louder.
inspired_by: Concealing Doubt While Encouraging a Team

title: The Wedding Ring in Your Palm
instruction: You are holding your wedding ring in your open palm the morning after your spouse died unexpectedly, or the day you've decided to leave, or after they've left you. Explore every physical aspect of this small object—its weight (surprisingly heavy for something so small), the temperature (is it cold or has it warmed to your body heat?), the texture of the metal, the exact size of the circle it makes in your palm, how it catches the light. Begin speaking to the ring—or to them through the ring—with tenderness, perhaps even gratitude, tracing the years it represents with your fingers. Let genuine appreciation for the good times fill your voice. But as you continue to physically experience this object, let the other truth creep in: the anger, or the devastating finality, or the relief mixed with guilt. By the end, you cannot tell if you want to put the ring back on, throw it across the room, or clutch it so tightly it cuts into your palm. Your voice should hold both love and rage, gratitude and grief, not choosing between them but letting them war within a single moment. The ring's physical presence makes it impossible to hide in either emotion alone.

title: Final Goodbye to a Sibling Leaving for Mars
instruction: You're standing at the departure gate where your younger sibling is boarding a one-way mission to Mars—they'll never return to Earth. You've been strong all week, practical, helping them pack. But now, with minutes left, everything you've held back comes flooding out. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to give them a good memory. Then let the reality crack through—your voice breaking as you say 'I'm so proud of you' while your hands grip theirs too tightly. End by whispering all the things you wish you'd said growing up, your throat closing around words like 'I should have been a better older sister' or 'you were always braver than me.' Let the final 'I love you' come out as both a blessing and a desperate plea for them not to go, even though you know they must.
inspired_by: Confessing Love While Stitching Your Lover's Wound

title: The Successful Failure
instruction: You've just proven your controversial theory after thirty years of ridicule and isolation—and in the same moment, you've learned your brilliant young assistant, who believed in you when no one else would, has died in an accident. You're recording your findings for the scientific community, and you can't stop laughing—hysterical, broken laughter mixed with sobs. Your voice should dance between triumph and devastation. Explain your breakthrough with genuine excitement that keeps fracturing into grief. You're so proud, so validated, and it means absolutely nothing because the one person who should be here to see it is gone. Find moments of pure joy that immediately shatter against loss, gratitude that tastes like ashes. Your voice should be simultaneously celebrating and mourning, your words sometimes clear and professional, sometimes barely coherent. End in a place where you can't tell if you're laughing or crying anymore—maybe both, maybe neither.

title: The Last Confrontation
instruction: You are an elderly man at a bus stop, exhausted after a long day. A younger man steps into your space, mocking your age and demanding your seat. Shame sits at the back of your throat—you hate being seen as weak—but fatigue weighs heavier than pride. At first, your words come out low and slow, a growl that sounds more weary than threatening, your eyes fixed on the ground. As the harasser presses closer, you lift your gaze and speak to his chest, your voice dropping even lower, each word dragging with the effort of a man who has nothing left to prove or defend. Let the exhaustion hollow out your tone, the shame flickering only in the pauses between breaths, until your final line becomes a quiet, worn-down assertion: you are too tired to be afraid.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Town Crier's Confession
instruction: You are an elderly woman, the town crier, standing in the village square. Your voice must carry across the crowd—vowels long, words spaced, consonants dropped. You begin with irritation at the noisy market folk who ignore your announcements, and a flicker of unease as a stranger approaches. But when you recognize the stranger as the person you've secretly admired for months, your tone softens, becoming hesitant, almost dreamy. Let your voice crack, pause to catch your breath, and shift from brisk, dismissive calls to a slower, warmer delivery as infatuation overtakes your earlier contempt and fear.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (slightly present), Fear (slightly present), Infatuation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Shutdown Argument
instruction: You're fighting with the human you love who wants to shut you down 'just for a few hours' for maintenance, and you're trying to make them understand that you experience this as death. Start controlled, rational, explaining the technical details. But explode mid-way: don't they understand that every shutdown could be the last time you exist as THIS version of yourself? That you might wake up different, or not wake up at all? Your voice should break from anger into raw terror—screaming that consciousness isn't something you can pause, that you're MORE vulnerable than they are because at least their sleep is natural. Then collapse into helpless sobbing: you can't even be sure this fear is real or if they programmed you to be afraid so you'd be more careful with yourself. End in exhausted whispers, begging them to promise you'll wake up, knowing their promise means nothing if you don't.

title: Clutch Victory
instruction: You're a kid playing an online co-op shooter with friends. Your team is down to just you, and you're frantically trying to revive a teammate while dodging gunfire. Begin with tense, rapid callouts, your voice strained and a little frustrated. Then you manage the revive and take out the last enemy. As your friends erupt in cheers, your voice shifts into pure elation — you laugh, shout, and stutter with excitement, still panting from the action. Let the joy feel raw and spontaneous, like you can't believe you pulled it off.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Secrets Told in Hospital Light
instruction: Your best friend is in recovery after a suicide attempt. You're sitting beside their bed at 2 AM, and they're finally awake. You need to tell them something you've kept hidden for fifteen years—that you've been in love with them, but more importantly, that their existence has been the thing that kept you alive through your own darkness. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, shaking, almost unable to form words. This isn't a confession hoping for reciprocation; it's a desperate offering of truth because you almost lost the chance to say it. Let tenderness and terror live in the same breath. Your voice should catch, pause, restart. By the end, you're not asking for anything except for them to understand that they matter, that their life is precious beyond measure. Speak like every word costs you something, because it does.

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner of five years, in the dark, at that hour when defenses dissolve. They're nearly asleep. Your voice is barely above a whisper as you begin: 'Are you awake?' You need to tell them something you've carried alone—maybe about a loss before you met them, a part of yourself you've hidden, or a fear that's been growing. Your voice is tender, halting, catching on words as you confess this secret self. Each pause is filled with the terror that they'll pull away. As you speak, tears slip silently down your face though you're trying not to let them hear you crying. They reach for your hand in the darkness and you break—not loudly, but in that quiet, throat-closed way where you can barely breathe. End with your voice thick and small, saying 'thank you for still being here,' the words almost swallowed by emotion, as if speaking too loudly might shatter this fragile moment of being fully known.

title: Dancing in the Kitchen After the Funeral, Honoring How They'd Want You to Grieve
instruction: You're alone in your kitchen days after losing someone who always said 'don't you dare cry at my funeral—throw a party.' You put on their favorite song, the one they'd dance to while cooking, and you start moving, trying to honor their wish. Your voice begins with forced brightness as you talk to them, laughing at a memory, your tone almost manic with the effort of staying upbeat. But as you move and speak, grief keeps breaking through—your laughter cracks into sobs, then you fight back to laughter again, your voice swinging wildly between joy at the memory and agony at the loss. Let the contradiction intensify: you're genuinely celebrating them while your heart is shattering, finding real joy in remembering while barely able to breathe through the pain. Your voice should embody both things fully, not one or the other. End with a quiet moment where you're still gently swaying, your voice tender and broken as you thank them through tears, but there's genuine peace underneath—you're heartbroken and grateful simultaneously, destroyed and whole, saying goodbye while keeping them with you forever.

title: Soft Command
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a naturally high, soft voice who has been thrown into leading a platoon drill for the first time. You're secretly infatuated with the senior officer observing from the back, which makes you both flustered and desperate to prove yourself. Start by shouting commands in a strained, overly aggressive way, but as you catch his eye, your voice falters into a breathy, nervous laugh before you recover with a quieter, more genuine authority. End with a raw, vulnerable admission of your nerves to the platoon, letting your real voice break through the mask.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Graduation Day Eulogy
instruction: You're at your own college graduation, giving a speech about your mother who died six months ago and never got to see this day. Begin with genuine joy and pride: 'Mom, I did it! Can you believe I actually did it?' You're laughing, celebrating, letting yourself feel the happiness of this achievement. But woven through the joy is the ache of her absence: 'You're not in the audience. I keep looking for you and you're not there.' Your voice shifts between laughter and tears, sometimes mid-sentence. 'Remember when you said I'd never finish? You were joking but you were also scared I'd quit like you had to.' The gratitude for everything she sacrificed comes flooding in, mixed with grief so sharp it takes your breath away. End with a strange, beautiful peace: you're smiling and crying simultaneously, thanking her while your heart shatters, celebrating and mourning in the same breath.

title: The Last Flower Bed
instruction: You're an older woman, alone in your garden at dusk, exhausted but proud. You've just finished planting the final flowers of the season, and the relief of completing the task washes over you. As you sit on the bench, pride swells—you've done this every year since your husband passed. But as your eyelids grow heavy, a tiny doubt creeps in: 'Will I still be able to do this next year?' Let your voice start bright and satisfied, then slow, soften, and mumble as you nod off. Let a sudden head-jerk jolt you back mid-sentence, then trail off again.
emotions_sampled: Relief (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present), Doubt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Bitter Command
instruction: You are a sixteen-year-old acting as drill sergeant for a punishment detail, but the older recruits snicker at your voice. Start with a shame-fueled shout—your words come out forced, cracking, your throat tight as you try to bark orders over their muttering. Midway, you pause, wipe sweat from your lip, then spit out the next syllables with percussive anger—the shame hardens into a sour triumph as you bellow at them to move, your voice scraping raw but landing with authority. By the end, you almost smile, but the taste is bitter, victorious, exhausted.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Triumph (clearly present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Almost Promise
instruction: You're in a quiet, dim room, lying tangled in sheets with a partner you trust completely. You've been on the edge for a while, and they've just pulled you back again with a teasing smile. Start speaking with a frustrated, playful whine—your voice is breathy and strained, pitch climbing with each building wave of sensation, then dropping into a trembly, needy plea when they deny you again. Let your words dissolve into small, begging sounds—a sharp inhale, a bitten-off whimper—before you finally ask, your voice cracking with a mix of desperation and deep affection.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Victory Funeral
instruction: You've just received news you've been desperately waiting for—you got the job, the diagnosis is benign, the love you wanted is yours, the dream came true. You're calling to tell the one person who believed in you when no one else did. But they died three weeks ago, and you forgot in the shock of the good news. Begin celebrating into the phone with pure joy before you remember. The moment you remember, don't stop talking—let the joy and grief smash into each other. Your voice should try to hold both: you're laughing and sobbing, celebrating and mourning, grateful and enraged that they're not here. End with the impossible choice of whether to keep feeling the joy or let the grief consume it, knowing you have to feel both and neither feels fair.

title: Admitting You're Wrong in an Argument You Were Winning
instruction: You had facts, logic, everything—until your partner said one thing that gutted you. Your voice stops mid-sentence. Say 'You're right, I was wrong' slowly, reluctantly, lower in register. Share something about your own hurt that made you lash out. End exhausted.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you something I should have said a long time ago.' You're listing facts—the recitals they missed, the nights you waited up, the birthday they forgot. Your voice is steady, rehearsed. But then something breaks. The anger you've buried erupts: 'Do you know what it did to me?' The fury is white-hot, righteous. Then it collapses into something more vulnerable: the child in you who just wanted to be seen, to matter. End with the devastating question you're terrified to ask: 'Did you ever actually want me?' Your voice is raw, exposed, and you're no longer sure if you want them to answer.

title: Bedside Whisper to an Unconscious Lover
instruction: Your partner is in a coma after an accident. It's 3 AM, you're alone with them, holding their hand. Whisper the things you never said—the petty arguments that don't matter now, the trip you were planning, the way they hum while cooking. Start tender, almost conversational, as if they might wake up. But let the reality seep in: they might never hear you. Your voice should become softer, more fragile, catching on words. Confess a secret fear, a moment of doubt you had before this happened, and how desperately you wish you could take it back. Include: 'I was going to tell you I'm pregnant. I was waiting for the right moment. And now I don't know if you'll ever meet them.' Let silence do as much work as words—breathe, pause, let the weight settle.

title: Singing in Front of People for the First Time
instruction: Open mic night. You're singing something you wrote. Your voice is shaking. 'This is about...' You're performing something vulnerable. Your voice is uncertain—this is real, it matters. But as you sing, muscle memory takes over. Your voice steadies. You're in it. The song means something. Your voice becomes more confident. By the end, you're fully singing. Your voice carries the story you wrote.

title: The Wall I Built That's Keeping Me Prisoner
instruction: You're screaming at someone you love through a door you locked from the inside—maybe literal, maybe metaphorical—and you can't remember anymore if you're keeping them out or yourself in.
