Begin with fierce, protective rage: 'I built these boundaries to survive, and I won't apologize!' Your voice should be sharp, defensive, almost vicious. But let it crack and splinter. Let the anger collapse into desperate, gasping sobs as you realize the walls that saved you are now suffocating you. End with your palms pressed against the door, voice raw and small, begging them not to leave while simultaneously unable to open the lock. This is the contradiction of self-protection that becomes self-imprisonment—fierce and helpless at once.

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're saying goodbye to a relationship that was beautiful and necessary but has run its course—a lover, a dear friend, a mentor. Begin with laughter, genuine and warm, remembering specific joyful moments you shared. But even as you're smiling, tears are starting, because this joy exists in the past tense now. Your voice dances between gratitude and heartbreak: 'Thank you for seeing me' said while crying, 'You changed my life' spoken with both reverence and grief. The contradictions deepen—you're celebrating what you had while mourning its ending, finding peace in letting go while your heart is simultaneously shattering. By the end, you've arrived at a strange, luminous place: profound thankfulness for the gift of this person, acceptance that loving them means releasing them, and the paradoxical wholeness that comes from breaking open. Let yourself laugh and cry simultaneously, finding beauty in the complexity.

title: The Last Upload
instruction: You're holding the hand of someone you love who has chosen digital consciousness transfer—their body will die in minutes, but their mind will live in the network forever. You begin with desperate hope, trying to convince them (and yourself) that they'll still be them, that you'll find each other again in virtual space. Your voice trembles with forced brightness. But as you watch their eyes begin to dim, terror breaks through: what if only their data survives? What if the person you love is about to vanish, replaced by code that merely thinks it remembers loving you? End in a whisper that mixes fierce gratitude for every moment you had with the soul-crushing realization that you're about to lose them in a way that makes their continued existence unbearable. Let your voice crack between technological optimism and primal grief.

title: Fever Dream of Goodbye
instruction: You're burning with fever, delirious, barely conscious—and simultaneously experiencing the most intense emotional pain of your life because the person you love is leaving you forever. Your body is wracked with physical sensation: heat, chills, aching, disorientation. You can't tell what's the illness and what's the heartbreak. Begin trying to fight through the physical overwhelm to say coherent goodbye, but your words keep dissolving into sensation. Let the physical and emotional states amplify each other—the fever makes your grief hallucinatory; the grief makes your body feel like it's being torn apart. Peak in a moment where everything—pain, heat, love, loss—becomes one overwhelming wave. Then collapse into exhausted, feverish quiet, whispering their name as they walk away.
inspired_by: Relationship Preparation via Endowment + Guided Imaging (Night Mother Example)

title: The Last Lucid Hour
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother in her final hours. She has been unconscious for days, but suddenly opens her eyes with complete clarity. You have three minutes to tell her everything - the gratitude, the unresolved anger about her favoritism toward your siblings, the ways she shaped you, the forgiveness you never gave. Start tentatively, afraid she'll slip away before you can speak. Let your words pour out faster, more desperately. But as you speak, notice her peaceful expression, and let your urgency transform into something quieter - a tender release, accepting that some things don't need to be said, that her knowing smile already holds all the answers. End in silence, holding her hand, feeling the shift from needing her to understand to simply being present as she goes.
inspired_by: When beginning any unconscious programming journey

title: The Last Man Standing
instruction: You are at a backyard party, slumped against a fence, barely able to stay upright after a long, hot afternoon in the sun. You overhear your ex-wife laughing with her new husband, the man who took your job, your house, and now her. You watch them dance with an ease you never had. Your voice is thin, breathy, fading at the ends of sentences. Start with a bitter, shaky mutter about how he doesn't deserve her, but as you speak, your head swims, vision blurs, and you realize you're about to pass out—your jealousy turns into a hollow, desperate whisper of acceptance, trailing off into silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Protecting What You Cannot Save
instruction: You're trying to shield someone you love from terrible news, danger, or an inevitable loss, but you're failing and you know it. Start with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance—promising them everything will be fine, that you'll fix this, that they're safe with you. Your voice should be strong, commanding, protective. But let that strength fracture as reality crashes through your words. Rage at your own helplessness should erupt mid-sentence, turning your protective declarations into raw, desperate fury—at the situation, at yourself, at the unfairness of it all. Then let that rage collapse into broken, sobbing helplessness. End in a place of utter devastation, where you're still trying to comfort them but can barely form words through your tears, still reaching for strength you no longer have.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Confident While Learning a New Skill

title: The Neighbor's Basement
instruction: You're a young man calling 911 from your porch after your neighbor's door swung open. You're terrified, out of breath from running, but you force your voice steady for the dispatcher. At first, your words tumble out in shaken, rapid bursts as you describe the scene. But as you glance back at the open door, the smell hits you again—you freeze mid-sentence, your voice goes flat and heavy with disgust. Let your breathing be uneven, your tone jumpy at the start, then sink into a choked, repulsed monotone by the end. You're not just scared anymore; you're revolted.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Whispered Confession in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's sleeping after surgery, and you're finally saying everything you've been too awkward to say for years. Your voice should be barely above a whisper—not because you're trying to perform quietness, but because this feels sacred and terrifying. Start with the safe stories, the funny memories where you said the wrong thing and you both laughed. Let your voice be tender with those recollections. Then gradually move deeper: how your awkwardness always made you feel like you were loving them wrong, how you've rehearsed 'I love you' a thousand times but it never came out right, how you're terrified they don't know how much they mean to you. Let tears thicken your voice. Let pauses hold years of unsaid tenderness. End with the simplest words—'I love you'—delivered not perfectly, but with every ounce of trembling truth you have, knowing they might not hear it, but saying it anyway because you finally can.

title: The Crooked Creed of the Plaza
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing on a worn wooden crate at a crowded midday plaza, voice hoarse from hours of unamplified preaching. You are deeply, hungrily interested in converting a skeptical young man in the front row—his smirk fuels you—but embarrassment tangs your chest each time your pitch cracks or your false teeth slip, making you swallow sourly. Start with righteous, straining fervor, your voice cutting through traffic and chatter, but let the sourness build as you realize your words are bouncing off his disbelief. End with a quieter, bitter recitation, your rhythm broken by a cough and a dismissive wave of your hand.
emotions_sampled: Interest (very intensely present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Recipe You Never Taught Me
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father, recreating a family recipe they never properly showed you, and the cooking becomes a battleground for everything you needed and never received. Start with careful control, maybe even tenderness, asking them to tell you the next step. But they're distracted, dismissive, or they get it wrong—just like always. Your voice grows sharper. The measurements become accusations: 'You never had time to show me this. You never had time for any of it.' Let anger rise, then crack open into raw vulnerability. You're not just talking about food—you're talking about all the moments of guidance, attention, and love you ached for. End with exhausted honesty, the fight draining out of you, replaced by grief for the relationship you'll never have.

title: Listening to the Sound of Rainfall
instruction: Sit by the window, hearing the gentle patter of raindrops on the glass. Describe the soft rhythm, the light, almost musical taps, and how each drop adds to a sense of calm. Speak in a hushed tone, as if youre completely absorbed in the sound. Talk about how the rain creates a cozy atmosphere, a blanket of sound that wraps around you, making everything feel safe and serene. Let out a small, relaxed sigh, as if the rain is washing away any remaining stress.

title: The Whispered Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside someone in the darkness, whispering a truth you've never told anyone—perhaps about who you really are, what you really want, or what you've been hiding. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate and terrified. Begin with false starts, words catching in your throat, the sound of someone gathering courage one syllable at a time. Let silence do as much work as words. As you speak, shift from shame-filled hesitation to the fragile relief of finally being seen. Your breath should be audible, vulnerable. The emotional journey moves from self-protective fear to tender, trembling hope—will they still want you when they know? End with the quietest, most exposed version of 'Please don't leave me,' where each word is a heartbeat, where silence after would be unbearable.

title: The Peacekeeper Erupts
instruction: You are confronting your parent about something they did years ago that wounded you deeply. You have always been the family peacemaker—the one who smooths things over, who understands everyone's perspective, who sacrifices your own needs to keep harmony. Start the scene in that mode: diplomatic, careful, trying to make them understand gently. But underneath, there's a part of you that has been silenced your whole life—a fierce, angry voice that is DONE being reasonable. Let that voice grow louder. Let the peacemaker lose control. By the end, you are shouting truths you've never allowed yourself to say, shattering the careful persona you've maintained. Feel the terrifying freedom of the part of you that refuses to make peace anymore, that demands to be heard even if it destroys everything.

title: The Vigil of Unspoken Selves
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's unconscious, but you need to say goodbye. Begin as the dutiful grandchild—calm, proper, saying the things you're supposed to say. But as you continue speaking, allow different versions of yourself to emerge and take over: the angry child she disappointed, the grateful one she saved, the ambitious one she never understood, the tender one who loved her fiercely. Physically shift your posture and position slightly each time a different part of you speaks. Let each voice have its turn—some may contradict others, some may surprise you. End with whichever part of you feels most true in this moment, even if it's not the 'right' one. The emotional journey moves from controlled goodbye through fractured revelation to raw, honest presence.

title: Laughing at Death: The Hospice Nurse's Midnight Ritual
instruction: You're a hospice nurse brushing your teeth after losing a patient you loved, and you start laughing—really laughing—at the absurdity of mint toothpaste existing in a world where people die. Begin with genuine, slightly hysterical laughter about how aggressively fresh and alive this stupid mint taste is, how ridiculous it is that your mouth feels 'renewed' when nothing else can be. But as you describe the cool sensation, the laughter twists into something else: gratitude mixed with unbearable sadness. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, grateful you're still here to taste mint, to feel this tingling aliveness, while simultaneously broken that your patient never will again. End with a beautiful, contradictory peace: finding profound appreciation for this small, fresh moment while your heart is absolutely shattered. Your voice should capture both the joy of being alive and the grief of knowing others aren't—all at once, inseparable.
inspired_by: Brushing Your Teeth with Refreshing Mint Toothpaste

title: Vigil by Candlelight
instruction: You are keeping watch beside your dying best friend in the quiet hours before dawn. Speak in hushed, tender tones as you recount shared memories - inside jokes, stupid adventures, the moment you first met. Your voice should be gentle, almost reverent, occasionally catching with restrained emotion. As you sense time running out, let your whispers become more urgent, confessing things you never said: how they saved you, how afraid you are to face life without them, how grateful you are for every ordinary moment. End with your voice breaking on a simple 'thank you' or 'I love you,' the words barely making it past the tightness in your throat, holding their hand as silence falls.
inspired_by: The Warrior and the Trickster Goblin

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're holding someone you love—a child, a partner, a friend—and you realize with devastating clarity that you cannot protect them from what's coming. Begin with fierce determination, your voice strong with promises: 'I won't let anything happen to you.' But as you speak, reality crashes in. Your certainty crumbles into desperate pleading, then explodes into rage—at yourself, at the situation, at the universe. Your voice should break from power to helplessness, from shouted defiance to sobbing fury. Let the anger collapse into something more raw: pure, animal fear mixed with overwhelming love. End in a place of shattered tenderness, holding them tighter while knowing it's not enough. Your final words should be whispered fiercely through tears: a promise you're making even though you know you might not be able to keep it.
inspired_by: The Thief and the Guard Dog

title: Burning the Books
instruction: You're destroying your deceased father's entire library—books he spent forty years collecting, annotating, loving—because you need the space and the money. Begin physically narrating the act: grabbing volumes, ripping pages, maybe striking a match. Your voice is harsh, practical, defensive. But as you describe specific books—his handwritten notes in the margins, a pressed flower from your childhood, his theories scribbled on napkins tucked inside—the physical act becomes agonizing. Your aggressive justifications crack open into raw grief and guilt. Let your breath become ragged, your voice shift from brutal efficiency to broken sobs. End in the physical and emotional devastation of having destroyed something irreplaceable—your body and voice shaking with the violence of what you've done, the knowledge you've erased.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Comfort She Never Gave
instruction: You're in your childhood home, and you've just watched your mother comfort someone else with such easy tenderness. You start by describing—with bitter, clinical precision—the exact gesture she just made: how she stroked their hair, the softness in her voice. Your tone is controlled, almost detached, as you detail what comfort looks like when she gives it to others. Then let the dam break: confront her with the fact that you needed this, you begged for this, and she had nothing for you. Your voice should escalate from cold observation to raw accusation, but end somewhere unexpected—not in rage, but in exhausted grief, almost asking rather than demanding: 'Why wasn't I worth touching gently?' Move from controlled bitterness to vulnerable, childlike pain.

title: Fierce Protection Collapsing Into Helplessness: A Guardian's Breaking Point
instruction: You are trying to protect someone you love—a child, a younger sibling, a person in your care—from a threat you cannot control: an illness, an abuser, fate itself. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive determination: 'No. This will NOT happen. I won't let it.' Your voice is strong, commanding, full of protective rage. But as reality crashes in, your voice starts to fracture. The strength wavers. 'I can do this... I can fix this...' becomes desperate bargaining. Your breath becomes ragged. The armor cracks and suddenly you're collapsing—'I don't know what to do'—your voice breaking into sobs, the fierce protector dissolving into someone terrified and powerless. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, voice wrecked and small, whispering 'I'm sorry I couldn't save you' or 'I'm so scared,' all the strength gone, replaced by raw human fear and grief.
inspired_by: Panic Attack: Losing Control Over Your Own Voice

title: Bedside Confession to an Unconscious Partner
instruction: Your partner is in a coma after an accident, and you're holding their hand, speaking in barely more than a whisper. You're confessing the affair they never knew about, not for absolution but because you can't bear them leaving without knowing the truth of who you really are. Your voice is tender, thick with tears, apologetic—but there's also relief in finally being honest. You tell them about the person you became in secret, the lies, but also how loving them was the most real thing you ever did. The emotions shift from shame to devastating love, from self-loathing to desperate gratitude for every moment you had. You're begging forgiveness from someone who can't hear you, finding peace in speaking truth even if it comes too late.
inspired_by: Professional: Therapist Realizes Their Own Mental Illness Has Grown Untreated

title: Finding Out You're Free
instruction: You've just received a phone call: the person who abused you for years has died. You're alone, and you start laughing—a strange, involuntary sound: 'They're gone. They're actually gone.' But even as you laugh, tears are streaming down your face because the relief is tangled with grief for all the years lost to fear. Your voice cracks between laughter and crying: 'I'm free. Why don't I feel free?' You're saying it to yourself, trying to understand the chaos in your chest. 'I spent so long being afraid, I don't know who I am without it.' The laughter fades into quiet weeping, then back to a sound caught between joy and devastation: 'I get to live now. I actually get to live.' But your voice breaks because you're also mourning the person you might have been if they'd never hurt you. End with your voice soft, almost wondering: 'Thank you for dying. And I hate that I had to wait for you to die to be okay.' It's gratitude and grief and rage and relief all at once, completely contradictory and completely true.

title: What We Never Say
instruction: You are whispering a confession to your sleeping spouse in the middle of the night—something you've never had the courage to say when their eyes are open. Begin barely audibly, testing if they're truly asleep. Your voice is fragile, almost childlike in its vulnerability. Confess a deep fear about your relationship, or a wound you've been hiding, or a need so tender you can barely give it words. Feel your throat tighten with the risk of finally being this honest. Mid-way, doubt creeps in—should you wake them, say this for real? Your whisper becomes even softer, more broken. End with both relief at having spoken it into existence and profound sadness that you couldn't say it to their waking face. Let the quiet hold everything your louder voice never could.

title: Dancing Through Demolition
instruction: You are alone in the house you grew up in on the day before it is demolished. Your body is moving through the rooms, and you are physically interacting with the space—touching walls, pressing your face against windows, lying on the floor. As you move, you speak to the house, and memories crash through you in waves. At first, there is rage—screaming at the walls about the painful things that happened here, your voice raw, your body violent in its gestures. Then, unexpectedly, you find yourself laughing—really laughing—remembering absurd, joyful moments. You begin to dance, clumsily, the way you did as a child. Your voice shifts between shouting, laughing, crying, whispering. The physical movement unlocks something: grief and ecstasy are happening simultaneously in your body. End by pressing your hand against a wall one last time, your breathing ragged, saying a goodbye that is both a thank you and a curse. Let your body lead your emotions.
inspired_by: Ego-state is low, producing tension and fear of failure

title: The 3 AM Breakthrough
instruction: You're an older inventor, alone in your cluttered garage at 3 AM. You've been working on a prototype for 18 hours, and your body is screaming for sleep, but a sudden, delirious second wind has hit. Your hands are shaking as you hold a half-crumpled schematic. The machine in front of you just flickered to life for the first time. Start with a childlike, giddy elation as you realize it's working — let out a breathless, slightly manic giggle. As you explain the discovery aloud to yourself, the sheer weight of the sleepless night and the loneliness of the process washes over you. Your voice should crack with a desperate, helpless joy, the laughter turning hollow, as if you're not sure whether to celebrate or cry.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Elation (very intensely present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Knees That Won't Forget
instruction: You are an elderly woman on a cold stone floor, kneeling at a worn prayer bench. Your back aches, and you shift your weight onto one knee, then the other. You begin speaking with a thin, bitter contempt — for the person who broke your family, for your own pride that kept you silent for years. But as you speak, your voice cracks; you lose the thread, stare at the carved wood, and the contempt dissolves into raw, desperate pleading — not for them, but for yourself to let the anger go. You swallow, your throat dry, and the final words come out like a reluctant surrender, half-whispered, mingled with a sniffle.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Doorway Paradox
instruction: Your adult child is leaving for a job overseas—five years minimum, possibly forever. You're standing in the doorway of their childhood bedroom, which is now empty except for the boxes they're shipping tomorrow. You are fiercely proud of them and completely devastated. Begin speaking to them (they're in another room packing) in your usual 'supportive parent' voice—the encouraging tone you've perfected over decades, full of pride and confidence. But as you look at the empty room, feel how that voice is just one more thing you do automatically, one more reliable mask. This moment deserves something more honest than your best parenting performance. Let the pride and the grief start colliding—not in a pretty, poetic way, but in a confused, contradictory way. Maybe you start encouraging them and mid-sentence feel angry that they're going. Maybe you want to beg them to stay but it comes out as a joke. Let yourself be genuinely confused by what you're feeling. Abandon every wise, mature thing you think a parent should say. By the end, you're speaking in a voice that contains everything at once—joy and abandonment, love and resentment, celebration and desperate loss—without trying to resolve the contradictions into something coherent.

title: Discovering Your Partner Has Been Lying About Everything—While They're Standing Right There
instruction: The evidence is irrefutable—bank statements, messages, a whole hidden life. Start with shocked, breathless questions, rapid-fire, almost laughing in disbelief. 'This can't be real. Tell me this isn't real.' Your voice should escalate from confusion to explosive rage within seconds. Scream the betrayals, let your voice crack and shred. 'I TRUSTED you with everything! My business, my savings, my CHILDREN!' But mid-fury, let devastation break through—collapse into sobbing, voice fracturing completely. 'How could you? How could you do this to us?' Oscillate violently: rage returns, then crumbles again into wounded pleading. 'Please tell me there's an explanation. Please.' As they try to respond, your voice becomes dangerous, quiet, shaking with contained violence. End with a terrible realization washing over you, voice hollow and distant: 'I don't know who you are. I never did.' The final words should sound like someone falling into an abyss.
inspired_by: Explaining Your Mental Health Diagnosis to Someone Close

title: The Emergency Room Prayer
instruction: Your child is in surgery after a car accident, and you're alone in the waiting room, talking to God for the first time in twenty years. Start with fury—a voice tight with rage: 'You can't have her. I won't let you.' Your words are a snarl, almost violent in their intensity. But as you continue, your anger fractures into desperation. Your voice rises, almost screaming: 'Take me instead! TAKE ME!' Let yourself break completely—sobbing, gasping, barely able to form words. Then, as exhaustion sets in, your voice drops to something raw and small: 'Please. I'm begging you. Please.' End in a whisper that's almost a bargain, your voice stripped of everything but love and absolute helplessness: 'She's only seven. She still believes in magic.'

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, both of you awake in the darkness. You need to tell them something you've kept hidden—a fear, a shameful secret, or a truth about who you really are. In the dark, you can't fully see their face, so you must reconstruct it through other senses: the sound of their breathing, the warmth of their body near yours, the particular scent of their skin. Begin by mentally layering onto them the presence of someone who once made you feel completely safe—perhaps a grandparent, a childhood friend, a teacher who believed in you. Notice how their hand feels similar, how their silence holds the same quality of patience. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, tight with shame, but as you build this sensory bridge between who they are and who you need them to be in this moment, let your whisper gradually open into something more naked and undefended. End with your voice still quiet, but no longer afraid.
inspired_by: The actor needs the scene partner to feel like a specific person from the actor's own life who produces the required emotional relationship

title: Surrendering the Wall
instruction: You are a rugged, hyper-masculine man who has finally allowed yourself to be the receptive partner. Midway through, the intensity catches you off guard — a flicker of embarrassment at how vulnerable you sound, how your usual gruff control is slipping. But the intoxication of the moment, the sheer pleasure, overwhelms that hesitation. Let your words come out like broken fragments between shuddering breaths, the voice cracking from low gravel to an almost desperate, high pitch at the peaks. Start with a self-conscious, thick-voiced attempt at saying something — maybe a half-laugh or a muttered protest — but end with a raw, elated moan that dissolves into gasping surrender.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Embarrassment (slightly present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Child's Head Above Water
instruction: You're in the lake, holding your struggling child as you teach them to trust the water, but they're panicking, thrashing. Start with forced calm—'I've got you, I've got you'—but your voice is tight with fear barely contained. Describe the water that should be peaceful but feels like a threat, your arms aching as they fight you. Your calm instruction explodes into desperate pleading: 'Please, baby, just trust me, TRUST ME!' Your voice cracks between fierce protectiveness and helpless terror—what if you can't save them? What if your grip fails? But then they suddenly relax, and you feel their small body go weightless in your arms. Your rage and fear collapse into shaking relief, your voice breaking as you whisper, 'There you go, there you go,' but you're crying now, devastated by how close you came to losing them, by the fragility of everything you love.
inspired_by: Floating on Your Back in a Calm Lake

title: The Walk of Shame
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, tough voice taking a slow, lonely stroll after a party where you broke down crying in front of your friends. The shame is heavy in your chest. Start by muttering a defensive excuse, trying to sound casual and in control, but the rhythm of your steps makes your voice lilt and trail off. As you walk, the excuses falter—you pause to swallow, your words get quieter, and by the end you admit the humiliation, your voice raw and broken.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Bonk at Mile 22
instruction: You are a young woman running your first marathon. For the past hour, you've been riding a runner's high — your legs felt light, the crowd's cheers were ecstatic, and you were laughing with a stranger beside you. Now, at mile 22, your body has suddenly emptied. Your voice is hollow, slurred, and confused; your breathing is shallow and ragged. You're trying to say something to your running buddy, but the words come out in short, glazed bursts. Start with a faint, dreamy smile as you try to recall the pleasure you just felt, then let the pain crash through — your legs buckle, your eyes well up without reason, and your voice thickens with tears. You're not crying from sadness, just from the raw, bewildering collapse of your body.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Vigil at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping child who's been in the hospital for weeks, and you're whispering everything you've been too scared to say out loud. Start with the small, almost mundane confessions—how terrified you were the first time you held them, how you still don't know if you're doing anything right. Let your voice stay soft, intimate, barely above a breath, as you move into darker territory: the magical thinking you've been doing, the bargains you've tried to make with a God you're not sure you believe in. Your whisper should thicken with tears you can't let fall because if you start crying you might never stop. End with a lullaby or a promise or just their name, repeated like a prayer, your voice breaking on something so simple it destroys you.
inspired_by: The Inner Voice of an Introvert at a Party

title: The Last Raid
instruction: You are a middle-aged drill sergeant, voice hoarse from shouting, standing before your platoon after a grueling all-night march. The sun is rising, and you need to push them through one more obstacle course. Start with your usual abrasive bark, but as you speak, the fatigue of decades seeps in — you lose the rhythm, pause to cough, your voice cracks. End with a quieter, gravelly admission that you're all in this together, your authority softened by exhaustion. Let the volume drop naturally, and let your words hang in the air.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Rep
instruction: You are an elderly man in a group fitness class, doing a series of lunges with jumps. You are clearly struggling, your breath short and your legs burning. You feel a mild disgust at your own body for failing you, and a sharper envy toward the younger participants who bounce effortlessly beside you. As you push through the final rep, speak to yourself in grunts and fragments between jumps — your voice should be forced, jolted by each landing, with micro-pauses as you lose your breath. Start with a self-critical snarl of disgust ('of course...'), but by the end, let the envy fade into a quiet, tired acceptance as you stop mid-sentence and just breathe.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fog Lifts, I Rise
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman, home alone, sick with a brutal head cold—nose stuffed, voice thick and nasal, sniffling and clearing your throat. You've just finished a long battle with a stubborn home repair project (fixing a leaky sink) that everyone said you couldn't do. As you dry your hands, a quiet, gritty triumph blooms in your chest. Start with weary, stuffy, almost numb exhaustion, then let your voice gradually fill with fierce, quiet pride—interrupted by sniffles, pauses to catch your breath, and a small, hoarse laugh. You're talking to yourself, but the victory is real. 'They all said I couldn't do it... but I did. With these hands... and this stuffed-up head. I fixed it.' End with a satisfied, slightly nasal sigh, then a sudden, congested sniffle.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Taught You to Walk
instruction: You're standing on the same beach where your parent taught you to walk as a child, and now you're confronting them about how they've been absent ever since. Start by describing the sand beneath your feet—the way it feels the same as it did decades ago, how that continuity mocks you. Your tone begins measured, almost analytical, as you recount the memory of learning to walk here, their hands holding yours. But as you speak, let anger surface—not loud at first, but sharp and precise—as you contrast those early promises of support with years of abandonment. Your voice should escalate from controlled disappointment to raw fury, then unexpectedly break into something more vulnerable: the hurt child still inside you who just wanted them to stay. End with a question that's part accusation, part plea, delivered with the exhaustion of someone who's been carrying this weight for too long.

title: The Upside-Down Confession
instruction: You are a 7-year-old girl, lying on your bed with your head hanging off the edge, staring at the ceiling. You're talking to your mom, who is in the room but you can't see her—just a blob of light. At first, you're giddy, astonished by how the world looks inverted, and you babble about the lamp becoming a spaceship. But as you speak, a sudden quiet realization creeps in: you're afraid of the dark tonight, and this upside-down view makes everything feel strange and lonely. Your voice starts high and excited, then softens into a trembling, thin whisper as you ask her to stay, the stretch in your throat making each word fragile. Let the wonder break into a small, unexpected crack of vulnerability.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Hospice Nurse Reading Final Letters From Your Estranged Father
instruction: You're a hospice nurse tasked with reading aloud the letters your comatose father wrote to you over twenty years—letters you refused to open. Start with clinical detachment, your voice steady as you read his first attempts at apology. As you progress through the letters, his words become more raw, more desperate for reconciliation. Your professional composure begins to fracture. By the final letter—written three days ago, knowing you'd never read them while he was conscious—your voice breaks between sentences, but you force yourself to continue. You're reading to him, to yourself, to the years lost. End with a whispered realization that forgiveness was always there, waiting, and now he'll never hear you say it. Your final words are half-apology, half-goodbye, spoken to someone who can't respond.
inspired_by: Translator in Courtroom Realizes Defendant Is Her Brother's Killer

title: The Overprepared Survivalist
instruction: Act as a person convinced that an apocalypse is imminent. Use a serious, instructive voice to share ridiculous survival tips, switching to the skeptical voices of friends or family questioning their logic.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent everything you've held back for decades—how their absence shaped you, how you needed them and they weren't there. Start controlled, almost rehearsed, because you've practiced this in your head a thousand times. But as you speak, anger bleeds through, your voice sharpening, getting louder. Then something shifts: you hear how old they sound, how fragile, and the rage collapses into something more complicated—grief for the relationship you never had, exhaustion from carrying this weight. Your voice breaks not with tears but with the realization that this confrontation won't fix anything, won't give you back what you lost. End with a quiet question that contains everything: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay?'

title: The Last Sunrise You'll See Together
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has hours left to live. You've been holding vigil through the night, and now dawn is breaking through the window. Begin in numb exhaustion, barely able to process what's happening. As light fills the room, something shifts—maybe it's the beauty of this final shared moment, maybe it's the full weight of goodbye finally landing. Let yourself move from that hollow numbness into whatever rises up: rage at the unfairness, desperate clinging to every second, or unexpected peace. Communicate without words—through breath, through sounds of grief or wonder, through the catching in your throat. By the end, you must arrive somewhere completely different than where you started, having released something or surrendered to something you've been fighting all night.

title: The List
instruction: You are in a cramped bathroom, alone, slumped on the cold tile floor. You just finished eating your favorite meal from a diner you and your ex-partner always went to—the same booth, the same order. The nausea hits you not just from the food, but from the memory. You’re trying to read an old note they left on the napkin, but you keep having to stop, gagging, stomach heaving. Your voice is thick, watery, garbled between retches. Start in a state of raw, quiet sadness, reading the words aloud, voice trembling. As you keep trying, a fierce wave of disappointment floods you—not at them, but at yourself for still being here, doing this. End with a bitter, almost angry whisper of realization, then a final, hollow heave into silence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Empty Lot
instruction: You are an elderly woman who has walked for miles to find the house you grew up in. You stop at a chain-link fence, panting, leaning on it for support. Your legs tremble, your chest heaves, and every word is a heavy effort. Start with doubt — you question your memory, wondering if this is really the place or if you’ve made a mistake. Let your voice waver, trail off, catch in your throat. As you realize the house is gone and only bare dirt remains, let the doubt drain into emotional numbness — a flat, hollow tone as if the last bit of feeling has been used up. You speak to yourself, each sentence separated by a long, shaky breath. Pause to cough, shift your weight, or stare blankly at the ground before forcing out the next fragmented thought.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Impossible Grade
instruction: You're a teenage boy alone in your bedroom, holding a letter that says you passed the final exam you were certain you failed. You stare at the paper, reading it over and over, your voice starting low and confused as you mutter 'This can't be right... I didn't even answer the last three questions...' Then the reality sinks in — you really did pass. Let the joy erupt: your voice spikes in volume, pitch climbs high, words tumble out in breathless fragments. Laugh and cry at the same time. Stumble over your own excitement, say things like 'Oh my god, oh my god, I... I did it... how... how did I do that?!' Let confusion linger even as happiness overwhelms — you still don't fully understand how you succeeded.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Paper Cuts
instruction: You're hunched over a desk, sorting through a stack of old, yellowed letters — your own, from years ago. Your hands shuffle the pages dryly, and every few seconds you pause to read a line, mumbling the words under your breath. At first, you're confused: you can't place when you wrote this, what you were thinking. But as you piece together the date and the addressee, a heavy shame sinks in — this is a letter you never sent to your father, full of cowardly excuses. Your voice starts tight, questioning, then drops to a rough whisper as you crumple a page, the paper snap sharp against the silence. Let the physical paper actions — slides, creases, rustles — interrupt your words naturally, and let that buried shame crack through your usual confident tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Dancing at Your Ex-Spouse's Wedding
instruction: You're at your former spouse's wedding—you came because you share children, because you're 'evolved'—and now a slow song is playing. You're describing the scene to your best friend via earbud, trying to narrate with detached amusement, maybe even laughing at the absurdity. 'They're doing that thing where they stare into each other's eyes—we used to do that.' But underneath the humor, your voice should betray something more complex: genuine happiness for them mixed with the strange grief of being replaced. Let yourself laugh and cry simultaneously. 'I want them to be happy. I really do. And it fucking kills me.' Find the strange peace in contradictions: relief that you're free, ache that you failed, pride that you can witness this, devastation that you're witnessing this. End with a breath that's half-laugh, half-sob: 'I think I'm okay. I think I'm going to be okay. God, I hope I'm going to be okay.'
inspired_by: GPS Navigation Voice During a Breakup

title: Holding Your Child for the Last Time
instruction: You're cradling your child who's being taken away—by illness, by circumstance, by a system you cannot fight. Start with fierce, protective desperation: 'No. No, you don't understand—I can't, I WON'T let you take them!' Your voice is raw, animal-like in its terror. But then you look at your child's face and something breaks. The rage dissolves into helpless, tender devastation: 'Baby, look at me. Look at Mama/Daddy. You are so loved. You are so, so loved.' You're memorizing every detail while trying not to scare them with your grief. 'You're going to be okay. I promise you're going to be—' You can't finish because you don't believe it. The words become a lullaby of breaking: 'I would give anything. I would trade places. I would...' End with a whispered surrender, fierce love mixed with absolute helplessness: 'I love you. That never stops. Never.'

title: Whispering Thanks to Hands That Can No Longer Cook
instruction: You're holding the last bowl of soup your grandmother made before her hands became too weak, before the illness took her ability to do what she loved. Speak barely above a whisper, as if she's sleeping nearby and you don't want to wake her. Describe the aroma with exquisite tenderness, noting every detail because you're terrified of forgetting. Your voice should be soft but thick with unshed tears as you thank her—for this soup, for every meal, for teaching you that love can be served in a bowl. Let the gratitude fracture into grief as you realize you're saying thank you and goodbye simultaneously. The warmth from the steam should feel both comforting and unbearably sad. End with your voice barely holding together, finding one last thing to be grateful for even as your heart shatters. Stay quiet, intimate, achingly present.
inspired_by: Savoring the Aroma of a Steamy Bowl of Soup on a Cold Day

title: The Fight for Us
instruction: You are a mother with a naturally high, soft voice, and you've just fought off someone who threatened your child. You're hunched over, gasping for air, your arms still wrapped around your little one. Start with sharp, animalistic shouts and grunts as you struggle in the fight — your voice cracking, words like 'Get away!' coming out in ragged bursts. Then, when you realize the attacker is gone, your body sags, and your voice breaks into a whisper of relief. Let tears choke your words as you say 'We're safe, baby. We're safe.' Your tone shifts from fierce barking to a trembling, exhausted lullaby. End with a long, shuddering exhale and a soft 'Mama's got you.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing at the Memorial
instruction: You're at a celebration of life for someone you loved deeply, and a song comes on—their song. You start laughing through tears, remembering how they'd dance terribly and not care. Your voice is doing impossible things: expressing joy and devastation simultaneously, gratitude and unbearable loss braided together. You're telling a story about them, and you're laughing at the funny parts even as your voice keeps breaking. The contradiction is the truth—you're so grateful they existed and so destroyed that they're gone. As you speak, you move between laughter and sobs, sometimes in the same breath. By the end, your voice settles into something quiet and wondering. You're finding peace not despite the pain but within it. You say something like 'thank you for being exactly who you were,' and it's both a goodbye and a keeping. Your voice holds both the breaking and the healing.

title: The Secret Garden of Us
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping spouse of thirty years, confessing something you've never had the courage to say while they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, tender and fragile as spun glass. Begin with small, safe truths: 'I watched you sleep tonight and...' As you continue, you reveal deeper vulnerabilities—fears about mortality, regrets about dreams you abandoned, the terror of losing them. Your voice catches repeatedly, not from crying but from the intensity of feeling something too big for words. There are long pauses where you can't speak at all, where your breathing is the only sound. In the middle, you reach the core truth that frightens you most, and your voice breaks completely—a whispered sob that you quickly muffle. But then, touching their hand, you find a different voice: still quiet, but suffused with such profound gratitude that it transforms the grief. 'Thank you for every ordinary day,' you whisper, and in that moment, the ordinary becomes sacred.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed. They've lived a life of rigid propriety and control, and now, in their final hours, they're confessing they never let themselves truly live—never danced wild, never spoke their raw truth, never broke the rules they imposed on themselves and you. Start by trying to comfort them with polite reassurances, but let something crack open inside you. By the end, you're giving them permission to say everything they held back—the ugly thoughts, the shameful desires, the things they never dared speak—and you're speaking your own forbidden truths back to them, a final act of radical honesty and liberation. Let the emotion move from gentle comfort through anger at what was repressed, and finally to a fierce, tender freedom in the shared nakedness of truth.

title: The Last Morning in Our House
instruction: You're walking through the home you shared with your late partner for forty years, one final time before the sale closes. Start with determined practicality—'I've packed everything, labeled all the boxes'—but let your voice fracture as you touch the kitchen counter where you made breakfast together, the doorframe where you marked your children's heights. Your words slow, catch, transform from efficient to devastated. End by pressing your palm against the wall and whispering a goodbye that contains all the years you can't take with you. This isn't theatrical grief—it's the quiet, bone-deep ache of closing a chapter of your life forever.

title: The Last Flight Home
instruction: You're a hospice nurse sitting with a dying astronaut who's spent decades in space. Begin with quiet, professional calm as you help them write final messages to the children they left behind. 'Just a few more words—they'll treasure these.' Your voice is steady, practiced. Then they whisper something that shatters you: they never stopped regretting leaving, every single day. Your professional composure cracks. The steadiness wavers. You become someone trying not to cry while helping someone else die. Your voice transforms from clinical to desperately tender, as if you could mother them through this final journey. End by reading their words back to them, your voice breaking on every third word, no longer a nurse but a witness to a life's deepest regret.

title: Holding Your Dying Dog, Screaming at God
instruction: Your dog—your companion of fifteen years—is dying in your arms after being hit by a car, and there's nothing anyone can do. Begin with frantic, breathless reassurance to the dog, your voice high and panicked, telling them it's okay, you're here, they're going to be fine—even though you both know they're not. As you feel their breathing become more labored, your voice escalates into raw, primal rage at the unfairness of it all. You're shouting at God, at the universe, at the driver, your voice cracking and breaking. Then suddenly collapse into devastating tenderness, pressing your face to their fur, your voice dropping to barely audible as you thank them for every year, every moment. End with you feeling their last breath, and your voice becomes just broken sounds—fury and love and grief so tangled you can't tell them apart anymore.
inspired_by: Coming Down from MDMA: The Serotonin Crash

title: The Stubborn Echo
instruction: You are a child standing at the edge of a large field, calling to a friend who is walking away, ignoring you. You have to shout, so your voice gets loud and stretched, dropping hard consonants. You start annoyed and impatient because they’re not stopping. But then a playful, teasing tone creeps in as you decide to turn it into a game, daring them to come back before you count to three, your voice cracking with giggles between the shouts. Feel the sun in your eyes, the grass under your feet, and the need to make them turn around without sounding desperate.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Miscarriage in the Bathroom
instruction: You're alone in a bathroom, and you're losing the pregnancy. Your partner is outside the door, but you won't let them in—not yet. Begin with fierce, almost angry control: you're breathing through pain, trying to manage this clinically. 'I'm fine. Just give me a minute.' But as the physical reality intensifies, your control shatters. A guttural cry escapes—rage at your body, at biology, at the unfairness. You're apologizing to the life leaving you, begging it to stay, then immediately furious at yourself for anthropomorphizing cells. 'Please. Please don't. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' Your voice breaks between sobs and primal sounds. Then—devastating shift—you become eerily calm, voice hollow, telling your partner through the door in flat tones that you need to go to the hospital. End with a single, quiet 'I lost it,' where all the emotion has drained out, leaving only ash. Show the body betraying you, rage at helplessness, then the terrible peace of shock.

title: The Bench by the Construction Site
instruction: You are an older man sitting on a bench in a busy city. A massive construction project is underway across the street—jackhammers pound, trucks beep in reverse, and people hurry past. You're holding a small, worn photograph of someone you lost, and you've just realized you can't quite remember the sound of their laugh. Start by staring at the photo with a slow, heavy sadness, your voice low and gravelly, almost lost under the noise. As a siren fades in the distance, you notice a child nearby drop a toy, and you feel a flicker of interest—a small, genuine curiosity about the world still happening around you. Let your voice shift: still rough with grief, but now there's a soft, hesitant lift as you speak, almost to yourself, about the strange way life keeps moving.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Best Friend's Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding—but you're secretly in love with them, and this is your goodbye. Begin with genuine joy and laughter: 'I've known you since we were seven and you put a frog in my lunchbox. You've been chaos in my life ever since.' Your smile is real as you recount memories, your voice warm with affection. But something shifts—the laughter becomes slightly strained: 'You've been my person. My forever person. And watching you find this kind of love...' Your voice cracks but you keep the smile, tears starting: 'It's the most beautiful, heartbreaking thing I've ever witnessed.' You're laughing and crying simultaneously now, utterly authentic: 'I'm so happy for you I could burst. And I'm so...' You can't say it. Instead: 'I'm so grateful you existed in my world exactly as you were.' Raise your glass, your voice thick with contradictory emotions: 'To love. To my favorite person. To letting go of what was never mine to keep.' End with a radiant, tear-streaked smile. The emotional complexity is joy-grief-love-loss all existing simultaneously, neither canceling the other out.

title: The Last Slice
instruction: You're at a crowded dinner table, a glass of wine in your hand as a friend dismisses your late father's sacrifices with a careless joke. Begin with a tight, forced chuckle, shaking your head — but the anger simmers, and you set down your glass, leaning forward. Turn to address him directly, your voice rising slightly over the clatter of forks. Halfway through, you notice his wife flinch, so you pull back, your tone dropping to a taut whisper that still carries the same heat. End by staring at the tablecloth, muttering the last line with a sudden crack in your voice as you lose the thread, then recover just enough to finish.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Breaking Point at the Mirror
instruction: You're alone, staring at your reflection after something has shattered you. Begin in numb shock, barely recognizing yourself. Start by actually looking—really seeing the specific details of your own face: the exact redness of your eyes, particular shadows, how your mouth is set, the genuine dishevelment of your hair or clothes. Let yourself notice the real physical sensations in your body: actual tension in your jaw, the concrete feeling of your heartbeat, real trembling if it's there. As you continue looking at these genuine details, let the physical reality of your own face and body gradually ignite something fierce. By the end, let noticing what's actually, physically true about yourself right now transform your numbness into explosive rage mixed with a strange, powerful exhilaration—a wild recognition that you're still here, still breathing, still capable of feeling everything.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Mission
instruction: You're speaking to someone you love deeply who is about to leave on a journey they will never return from—a space mission, a dangerous operation, a sacrifice they've chosen. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them, filling the silence with mundane details about what you'll do tomorrow. But as the reality settles in, your voice cracks. The transformation is irreversible, and you're losing them while they're still here. Move through denial, then raw grief, then finally to a place of fierce, aching gratitude for every moment you've had. End with a whispered blessing, your voice thick with tears but steady with love. Let the silence between words do as much work as the words themselves.

title: Unraveling the Careful Lie
instruction: You're confronting your mother about a family secret you've just discovered. Start the scene feeling rehearsed and careful, trying to control your anger with prepared phrases. But then stop yourself mid-sentence and begin revealing what's actually happening inside you right now: the churning in your stomach, the competing urges to scream and to protect her, the shame of your own rage. As you strip away each layer of performance, let your real feelings emerge—messy, contradictory, and surprising even to you. By the end, you're speaking with a rawness that frightens you both, but it's finally true. The arc moves from controlled accusation to vulnerable, uncontrolled truth.
inspired_by: Two actors preparing to rehearse a scene together; both feel artificial or disconnected

title: The Last Hurrah
instruction: You're an elderly man at a loud bar, high on a strong stimulant. You've just locked eyes with a much younger woman across the room. Your voice is too loud, nasal, and rushed—you sniff constantly and your throat feels numb. Start with overwhelming sexual lust: you're grandiose, interrupting yourself, bragging about your youth. But as you speak, a sourness creeps in—you catch your reflection in a mirror, see your age, hear your own slur. End with a bitter, defeated realization that this performance is pathetic. Let the words stumble, change tone mid-sentence, and let the final line land with a quiet, sour stillness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Just a Spoonful
instruction: You're a teenager sitting at the kitchen counter, eating a bowl of thick pudding. Your best friend just texted that the guy you like said you're 'too much.' You're on the phone with her now, trying to brush it off. Between spoonfuls, you talk with your mouth full—wet smacks, slow swallows, words that round out. Start with a forced, bright tone, like you don't care. As you scrape the bottom of the bowl, let your voice falter. A pause, a thick swallow, then a quiet, cracked admission: you're starting to think he's right. Let the food interrupt you; let doubt creep in.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Last Call from the International Space Station
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to establish humanity's first deep space colony. This is your final video call home before you pass beyond communication range—forever. You'll never see Earth again, never hug your family, never smell rain or feel grass. Start by trying to be brave and inspiring, focusing on the mission's importance and how proud you are. But as you look at their faces, the reality crashes over you in waves. Let your voice crack as you try to memorize every detail of them. End in a place of devastating acceptance mixed with wonder at what lies ahead. Your words should feel like you're trying to pack a lifetime of love into five minutes, knowing you'll carry only memories into the infinite dark.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your dying parent about a lifetime of emotional absence, and this is your last chance to be heard. Begin with carefully chosen words, almost formal, trying to explain calmly how their coldness shaped you. But let the floodgates open—the child in you needs to rage, to demand why you were never enough, why they could never say they loved you. Your voice should move from controlled pain to raw accusation to something more vulnerable: the confession that despite everything, you're terrified of losing them, that you still desperately want their approval even now. End by acknowledging the painful truth that you're saying goodbye to both the parent you had and the parent you'll never have, and somehow finding the strength to offer forgiveness you're not sure you feel.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table where you ate breakfast as a child. Start by noticing everything about him in this moment—how he's aged, how his hands look wrapped around his coffee mug, the exact sound of his breathing, the way he won't quite meet your eyes. Let yourself be genuinely curious about these details before you speak. Begin with careful, measured words—you came here to be reasonable, to finally talk like adults. But as you describe the specific moments from your childhood that still hurt, let your careful control dissolve. Don't perform anger or pain—let the actual feelings emerge as you see him seeing you, as you notice whether he's really listening or defending. Move from diplomatic distance to something unfiltered and true, whether that's rage, grief, or unexpected tenderness.
inspired_by: Actor is compensating — imposing a relaxed demeanor over real tension, or substituting one emotion for another that feels more acceptable

title: Condemned Criminal
instruction: You have twenty-four hours left. Your voice is narrating the reality aloud: 'Tomorrow they kill me.' The word 'kill' lands hard. You're reflecting on choices that brought you here. Your voice is resigned but not peaceful. 'I deserve this,' you say, but the doubt underneath suggests you're still arguing with God. By the end, you sound like someone accepting finality. 'I'm ready,' you lie to yourself. Nobody's ready to die.

title: The Things We Don't Say
instruction: Late night. Your mother calls, lost in her phone's settings again. As you guide her through it—'tap the gear icon, Mom, yes that one'—your voice is soft, almost a whisper because your own kids are sleeping. In the quiet, something shifts. She says, 'I don't know what I'd do without you,' and your throat tightens because you know she's scared of being alone, of losing her independence, of becoming invisible. You want to tell her you're scared too, that you see yourself in her future. Instead you say, 'You're doing fine, Mom,' but let the tenderness crack through. The silence between instructions becomes heavy with everything unsaid. End with 'I'm right here' as both reassurance and quiet ache.
inspired_by: The World's Most Patient Tech Support Call with an Elderly Parent

title: The Last Morning in the Garden
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother in the garden where you spent every summer as a child. She is dying, and you both know this is your final hour together. Begin by letting yourself truly see this place: the specific colors of the flowers she planted, the texture of the wooden bench beneath you, the way light filters through the leaves. Hear the sounds—birds, wind, her labored breathing. Smell the earth, the blooms, her lavender perfume. Feel the warmth of sun on your skin, the coolness of her hand in yours. Start with a desperate need to memorize every detail, to hold onto this moment. As you speak your goodbye, let the sensory richness of this place—every sight, sound, smell, touch—become both unbearably precious and unbearably painful, transforming your clinging desperation into a tender, grateful release.

title: Truth Speaking
instruction: One person is speaking a difficult truth to another. The truth is hard but necessary. The voice of the truth-speaker is steady, holding the ground of what's real. The listener's voice resists, doesn't want to hear. The truth-speaker persists with compassion. The listener's voice gradually shifts from denial to acceptance. The truth is painful, but there's also relief in having it spoken. By the end, both voices acknowledge what's actually real. The truth-speaker's voice carries the strange peace of having said something essential, even though it cost something.

title: The Unfolding Aria
instruction: You are an older man in a tender, intimate moment with a partner, both fully present in the quiet of a bedroom. At first, you are focused and curious—your breath catches as you explore each sensation, your moans low and measured, filled with interest and slight wonder. But as the pleasure builds and becomes more than you can contain, the sounds shift: your sighs turn into open, rising moans, your voice cracks with surprised joy, and you lose yourself in a wave of elation that leaves you breathless and laughing softly. Let your voice start controlled and questioning, then grow fuller, more unstable, and finally pour out in a raw, unguarded aria of contentment.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protecting a Child From Your Own Rage
instruction: You're a single parent who just lost your job, and your young child has accidentally broken the laptop with your only copy of the presentation that might have saved it. You enter the room and your voice explodes: 'WHAT DID YOU DO?' The rage is volcanic, terrifying even to yourself. But mid-fury, you see your child's face—the fear, the tears—and something in you breaks. Your voice fractures from rage into horror at yourself: 'Oh god... baby, I'm sorry.' You drop to your knees, and now you're the one crying, desperate: 'I'm not angry at you. I'm not. You're the only thing I have left that matters.' Your voice becomes fierce with protective love even as you're falling apart: 'We'll be okay. We will. I promise you, we will.' Show the transition from explosive anger to self-horror to fierce, helpless devotion.

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner of ten years, whispering a confession they cannot hear. Start with your voice barely audible, tender as you watch them sleep, telling them about the secret you've carried—an affair, a betrayal, a lie that's been eating you alive. Your voice is gentle, almost a lullaby, filled with regret and love intertwined. Describe the moment you crossed the line, and feel your voice catch with shame. Move through quiet self-loathing to a whispered plea for forgiveness they'll never hear. End with 'I'm so sorry' repeated like a prayer, your breath hitching as silent tears come. The intimacy of the darkness makes every word feel like it's being pulled from your chest. This is confession as sacred and devastating.

title: The Tent Fort
instruction: You're a child, maybe 5 or 6, huddled in a blanket fort with your younger sibling during a thunderstorm. A big crack of lightning just scared them, and they're crying. You're scared too—your voice is a bit shaky and fast at first—but you're also excited because you've built the best fort ever. Start by nervously trying to calm them down, then as you describe how safe the pillows make it, your voice grows steadier, turning into a cozy, rhythmic hum. Let your words trail off as you glance at the flashlight shadows, then come back warmly.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Victory Burning in Your Fist
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—you've been chosen, you've won, you've achieved what you've fought for years to reach. In your pocket is the physical proof: a letter, a contract, a key, something small enough to conceal but powerful enough to transform your entire existence. Your body is electric with this knowledge. Begin moving through space—pacing, touching walls, unable to contain the physical energy coursing through you. Your hand repeatedly finds this pocket, touches this treasure, and each contact sends a new surge of belief through your system. But underneath the euphoria, let another feeling rise: the ache of everyone who isn't here to see this, the years of pain it took to arrive at this moment, the fear that it might be taken away. Let your physical state become almost unbearable—laughing that becomes sobbing, triumph that becomes a kind of passionate grief. End on your knees or collapsed, clutching this small object, your body wracked with the overwhelming collision of joy and loss.

title: The Confession in the Hospital Chapel
instruction: You're in the hospital chapel at 3am, lavender hand lotion lingering on your palms from trying to comfort someone you love who's dying upstairs. Begin in a raw whisper, confessing to the empty room that you never told them the truth about how you feel - that you've been in love with them for years but stayed silent out of fear. Your voice should be catching, halting, as quiet devastation washes over you. Describe the cruel irony of how the lavender scent - which always calmed you around them - now makes you want to scream because there's no time left. Let tender memories surface through the pain: their laugh, the way they made you feel seen, moments you treasured in secret. End with a fragile, whispered prayer or promise - not for a miracle, but for the courage to say the truth while there's still breath to hear it.
inspired_by: Inhaling the Scent of Lavender in a Field

title: Acting Interested in a Hobby You Dont Enjoy
instruction: A friend shares their passion for a hobby you dislike. Internally, youre uninterested, but you listen attentively. Describe your disinterest inside while asking questions. Speak with curiosity, hiding your true feelings.

title: The Last Sneeze
instruction: You’re a child, barely awake from heavy medication, lying in a bed. Someone you love is nearby – you want to tease them about how they always sneeze three times in a row. Start with a weak, playful grin in your voice – a bit of a giggle, but it’s hard to get the words out. As you speak, your eyelids droop, and your voice gets slower, softer. Halfway through, you lose your train of thought, trail off, then come back but with less energy. By the end, the teasing fades into a sleepy, affectionate mumble – you’re not even sure you finished the sentence. Let your voice be breathy, with long pauses, and let the words dissolve into silence as you nod off.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Building Arousal to Climax: Solo
instruction: Perform the full arc of self-pleasure from beginning to climax. Start with quiet, controlled breathing that gradually deepens. Let soft sighs evolve into moans. The rhythm should build — breathing faster, vocalizations becoming less controlled, pitch rising. At the peak, let the voice break into involuntary sounds — a gasp, a cry, silence as breath is held, then the explosive release. End with shaky, euphoric afterglow breathing and a satisfied murmur.

title: The Uninvited Guest
instruction: You are a proud, elderly man at a family dinner, but a persistent, dull cramp is twisting in your gut. You're trying to hide it, but every time you shift in your chair or breathe too deeply, it tightens. Your voice comes out lower, more guarded, and you speak into your lap rather than meeting eyes. Start with stilted, embarrassed small talk about the meal, but as the pain sharpens, you confess that you've been 'wrong all day'—the admission cracking with shame. By the end, you're leaning heavily on the table, voice strained and quiet, asking for a glass of water as though admitting a great failure.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Nurse Who Unplugs Life Support
instruction: You are a hospice nurse holding the hand of a patient you've cared for these past six months. Their family has just left the room, and you are about to honor their DNR by removing the breathing tube. Start with clinical composure, explaining gently what you're about to do. But as you speak, your voice begins to fracture—this patient reminds you of your own father who died this way. Your hands are steady on the equipment, but your words become a confession: you're grateful for the time you've had together, grieving that this is goodbye, and terrified that you're playing god. End in a whisper, telling them it's okay to let go, even as you're not sure you can let them go. Your breathing should shift from controlled nurse to broken human being.
inspired_by: Medieval: Executioner Comforts the Condemned as a Priest

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent who was always critical of your life choices. For years you've sought their approval and never received it. Start by trying to tell them about a recent achievement, hoping even now for validation. But as you speak, notice their breathing becoming more labored. The urgency shifts - you realize you need to tell them it's okay to let go, even though part of you is still angry they never said they were proud of you. End by giving them the permission to die that you realize they've been waiting for, mixing your grief with a strange, unexpected gratitude for this final moment of clarity between you. Let your voice move from tentative hope to quiet, grief-stricken acceptance, finding forgiveness you didn't know you had.
inspired_by: Actor feels their work is not evolving across multiple rehearsals

title: Laughing with Your Best Friend at Her Wake, Remembering Her Terrible Jokes
instruction: You're standing at her casket, suddenly remembering the dumbest joke she ever told, and laughter bubbles up unbidden—real, genuine laughter that feels both wrong and exactly right. Start with surprised joy, sharing the memory with her as if she can hear, your voice warm with affection. The laughter continues but tears are streaming down your face now, mixing grief with celebration. Your voice cracks as you tell her you're so angry she left, so grateful she existed, both emotions equally true and intense. The laughter becomes almost hysterical, tipping toward sobs, then back again. End with exhausted peace—voice soft, still smiling through tears, thanking her for teaching you that joy and sorrow can coexist, that loving someone means carrying both forever. Your final words are tender and amused, exactly how she'd want to be remembered, even as your heart is breaking.
inspired_by: Coming to Consciousness After Being Struck by Lightning

title: The Fire: When Everything You Built Burns
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of your kitchen after a fire, and you're on the phone with the person who was supposed to watch the stove. Begin with explosive rage, your voice raw and uncontrolled, screaming about the twenty years of work now ash and smoke. Let fury crack into desperate tears as you describe specific things that are gone forever - your grandmother's handwritten recipe cards, the chef's knife from your mentor, photographs you can never replace. Your voice should break between anger at them and anguish at the loss, unable to decide which hurts more. End in a frightening quiet, your voice hollow and small, as you realize you don't know who you are without this kitchen, without this identity.
inspired_by: The Chef and the Talking Ingredient

title: Collapsing Against the Wall, Body and Heart Breaking
instruction: You've just received devastating news and you're physically collapsing - sliding down a wall, doubling over, or falling to your knees. Before you make a sound, notice your actual physical state: Is your breathing shallow? Are you trembling? Is there heat in your face? Name these sensations aloud as they arise - 'I can't breathe... my hands are shaking... there's pressure in my chest.' Let your body's genuine responses guide your emotional expression. As you move through this experience, track the evolution: does shock give way to raw pain? Does numbness crack open to rage? Does physical collapse lead to a primal scream or to silent, heaving sobs? Follow your body's real impulses rather than predetermined ideas of grief or devastation.

title: The Upside-Down Longing
instruction: You are hanging upside down from a low tree branch, trying to untangle a kite string caught in the leaves. Your head is heavy with blood, making your voice thick and wet, like you're speaking through water. Start by calling out to a friend with playful exasperation, but each word comes out strained and garbled, forcing you to stop and swallow. In that pause, you realize the person you really want to share this moment with isn't here. Let the initial irritation fade into a quiet, slightly wistful longing as you finish, your voice cracking and softening despite the physical difficulty.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child That You're Leaving Them
instruction: It's 3am. Your child is asleep and you're sitting on the edge of their bed for the last time. You have to leave—maybe for their safety, maybe because you're broken in ways you can't fix while being their parent. Your voice is barely audible, each word catches in your throat: 'I'm so sorry, baby. I'm so, so sorry.' You're confessing to someone who can't hear you, which makes it both easier and infinitely harder. Touch their hair. Your breathing is uneven. Tell them all the things you want them to know: that this isn't their fault, that you love them more than your own life, that you're not strong enough to be what they deserve. Let your voice break completely, but stay quiet—you can't wake them. End with a kind of tender devastation as you kiss their forehead: 'Be good. Be so good.' You're memorizing their face. This goodbye is ripping you apart cell by cell.
inspired_by: Telling Your Partner Your Sexual Needs Aren't Met

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're holding someone you love fiercely—a child, a sibling, a friend—who's in danger you cannot prevent, and you're trying desperately to be strong for them while falling apart inside. Start with fierce intensity, almost aggressive in your protectiveness: 'I won't let anything happen to you, do you hear me? I won't.' But your voice cracks with the lie of it because you both know you're powerless. Your words become increasingly desperate, almost manic, trying to promise impossible things, your voice rising with helpless rage at the universe. Then suddenly collapse into raw vulnerability, your voice breaking completely as you hold them tighter: 'I don't know how to fix this. God, I don't know how to fix this.' End in a whisper that's half prayer, half sob, your strength completely shattered: 'I would trade places with you in a heartbeat. Please know that.' Let the explosive protectiveness transform into utter helplessness and tender devastation.

title: Snowblind
instruction: You are an older man lost in a blizzard, phone dead, visibility gone. Shout into the wind for help, your hyper-masculine voice cracking from cold and desperation. Feel the disorientation as snow swallows your words, causing you to scream louder then suddenly stop, realizing no one can hear. Micro-distractions: stamp your feet, wipe ice from your eyes, cough from the freezing air.
