As the storm rages on, let your distress evolve into a quiet, bitter acceptance or a low growl of stubborn fury. Your last words are barely spoken, almost to yourself, resigned yet defiant.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point: Screaming Truth at the Mirror
instruction: You've been holding it together for months—years—and you're finally alone. You look at yourself in the mirror and something inside you explodes. You start yelling at your reflection, saying everything you've been too afraid to admit: 'I hate this! I hate pretending I'm fine!' Your voice is raw, furious, shaking the walls. But mid-scream, something cracks. The rage suddenly collapses into desperate, gasping sobs. You slide down to the floor, and your voice becomes small, broken: 'I can't do this anymore.' You're talking to yourself like a frightened child. By the end, you're rocking slightly, whispering 'Help me' over and over, but there's no one there. Your voice should arc from explosive fury to helpless, shattered pleading—the moment when all your strength runs out and you're left with nothing but vulnerability.

title: The Bitter Aftertaste
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting alone in your cluttered living room, wired from a double espresso you didn't really want. You've just found an old birthday card from your estranged son. At first, you mutter sourly—'Thinks a card makes up for ten years.' Then, as the stimulant sharpens your mind, you sink into contemplation, tracing the faded handwriting, your voice dropping to a slow, gravelly whisper. Finally, a dry chuckle escapes you, your pitch jumping as you realize the joke's on you—you never sent him a card either. Let the adrenaline make your speech brittle and quick, with pauses where you lose your train of thought, then find it again.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Contemplation (extremely present), Amusement (clearly present)

title: Buried Questions
instruction: You are a teenager digging alone in a quiet field under a gray sky. The shovel hits hard soil, and each lift strains your arms and back. You are confused—something you heard or saw last night does not make sense, and you keep replaying it in your head as you dig. Speak in short bursts between grunts and shoveling—your voice choppy, breathless, half to yourself. Start with fragmented, bewildered whispers, the confusion twisting tighter with each scoop. By the end, as you lean on the shovel, your voice drops to a flat, hollow realization—not acceptance, but a tired knowing that the answer won’t be found in the dirt.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Story Before Sleep
instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's bedside in hospice. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. She suddenly grips your hand and whispers a single word—something unexpected like 'carousel' or 'cinnamon' or 'thunder.' You realize she wants you to tell her a story, one last story, and that word must be at its heart. Begin uncertain, fumbling to find the thread, then let the story grow as you weave in childhood memories, dreams you shared, things you never said. Your voice should start tentative and searching, gradually becoming warmer, more animated, even joyful as the story blooms—until you realize mid-sentence that her hand has gone slack. End in a whisper, finishing the story for her anyway, your voice breaking between wonder at the story you've created and the devastating awareness that she's gone.

title: The Failed Bravado
instruction: You are at a loud party, wired on cocaine. Your friend just got the promotion you wanted. Approach him, speaking too fast and too loud, your voice tight with nasal congestion. Start by pretending to be happy for him, but the envy seeps through your grandiose boasts. As you talk, your pace quickens, you interrupt yourself, and the mask slips. End with a bitter, almost pleading tone, revealing your own emptiness. Let your voice crack and your speech become fragmented by the stimulant's rush.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're experiencing an overwhelming physical sensation - perhaps making love for the first time after devastating loss, or feeling pain that brings back trauma, or experiencing unexpected ecstasy that terrifies you. Your body is responding faster than your mind can process. Vocalize rapidly - sounds, words, gasps, fragments of language, all tumbling out without control. Don't organize your response into coherent emotion; let it be messy, contradictory, animal. Your voice should move as quickly as your racing pulse: pleasure mixed with grief, pain mixed with relief, sensation mixed with memory. Start trying to maintain control, to make sense of what's happening, but let the physical overwhelm your ability to narrate or understand. By the end, surrender completely to the body's chaotic wisdom, making sounds and saying things you've never made or said before.

title: A Glimpse of Her
instruction: You're an older woman sitting on the couch, scrolling through your phone with the TV on low. Your voice is directed downward, punctuated by quiet thumb-taps and distracted fillers like 'hmm' and 'oh.' You pause on a photo of your granddaughter as a child. At first, you mutter about the date or lighting, but as you hold on the image, your voice softens, slows, and a deep longing takes over. Let your breath catch, your words trail into a whisper, and let the casual curiosity transform into tender, vulnerable ache by the end. Say something like: 'That was the summer she stayed... three weeks. Huh. Look at that smile. (longer pause) I wonder if she remembers the fireflies... I do.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Truth About Why I Left
instruction: You are confronting the parent who abandoned you twenty years ago. Begin with rehearsed anger—words you've practiced in mirrors, accusations delivered with bitter precision. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: you hear how young and scared they sound trying to explain. Your rage begins to tangle with the child inside you who just wanted them to stay. Let your voice move from cutting sarcasm to genuine fury to something far more vulnerable—the rawness of a wound that never healed. Include a moment where you almost forgive them, then pull back violently, then finally ask the question you've never been able to voice: 'Did you ever love me?' The way you ask it should contain both the adult demanding truth and the child begging for reassurance.
inspired_by: Calling a Suicide Hotline: Both Sides

title: Marathon Runner Hitting the Wall at Mile 22
instruction: You've been running for hours and your body is shutting down. Narrate your inner monologue as glycogen depletion hits. Start with determined but labored breathing, then let confusion creep in — slurred words, nonsensical tangents, unexpected crying for no reason. Your voice should sound like someone mildly drunk and deeply exhausted simultaneously. End with a desperate, childlike whisper asking your legs to please keep moving.

title: Discovering You in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed beside your lover in complete darkness after making love. You cannot see them, but you can hear their breathing, feel the warmth radiating from their skin, sense the small movements they make. Begin in comfortable silence, then start to quietly voice what you're noticing—the rhythm of their breath, the texture of their shoulder under your fingertips, the small sounds they make. Let yourself wonder in whispers about the mystery of them: what are they thinking right now? What part of their past are they carrying in this moment? What do they need that they're afraid to ask for? Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, as your curiosity draws you deeper into tender vulnerability. Move from peaceful contentment to almost unbearable closeness—the kind that feels dangerous because it means being completely known.

title: Memorial Toast: Celebrating Your Best Friend Who Took Their Own Life
instruction: You're standing at their memorial, glass raised, trying to give the toast everyone expects. Start with laughter—genuine, warm laughter—as you share a ridiculous story about them, your voice full of affection and joy. The room laughs with you. But mid-sentence, the reality hits: they're gone, and they chose to go. Your voice wavers, the laughter becomes strained, then breaks. You're angry—your voice sharpens with betrayal, hurt, confusion. How dare they leave like this? But you can't sustain the anger because you understand, and that understanding breaks your heart. Your voice softens into something unbearably sad, admitting you saw the signs and did nothing. Then, unexpectedly, gratitude floods in—pure, luminous gratitude for having known them at all. Your voice lifts with genuine celebration mixed with grief, holding both the beauty of their life and the tragedy of their death. End with a tearful laugh, toasting them with a voice that contains everything: love, rage, sorrow, joy, forgiveness, and devastating acceptance.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Time Traveler Realizes They're Trying to Prevent Their Own Birth

title: Farewell at the Airport Gate
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you've loved deeply who is leaving for a mission they may never return from. Start with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them. 'You're going to do amazing things out there.' But as the final boarding call echoes, your composure cracks. Your voice becomes raw, dropping to almost a whisper. 'I need you to know—' and you have to stop, swallow hard. The words that follow are naked truth, stripped of all pretense: what they've meant to you, how you'll carry them. End in a kind of fierce tenderness, a blessing you're giving even as your heart is shattering. Let silence hold the weight of everything you can't say.

title: Trial Closing Argument
instruction: You're the defense attorney in a domestic violence case. The defendant is sitting behind you. You built your case methodically, legally sound, emotionally disconnected. But as you reach the evidence section, you realize you're about to argue that what you can clearly see as violence was 'mutual conflict.' Your voice starts strong but catches when you describe the bruises using language that minimizes them. The courtroom is completely silent. You pause. You clear your throat. Do you finish the argument as written, or does your voice betray what you actually believe? Show the physical sensation of cognitive dissonance in your breathing and pace.

title: The Edge of Arrival
instruction: You are perched on a high stool at a dimly lit bar, waiting for someone you've been craving all week. Your toes barely touch the floor, core tight to keep balance, body humming with lust. As they walk in and catch your eye, a burst of elation makes you smile, but the real shift comes when they close the distance and whisper low in your ear — your breath catches, your voice softens into pure pleasure. Speak as if you're trying to stay composed but the need is spilling out, starting with tense anticipation and dissolving into ecstatic surrender.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Elation (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present)

title: Burning House
instruction: You are in the aftermath of explosive passion—whether sex, a physical fight, or ecstatic dance, your body is still vibrating. Begin speaking while gasping, laughing, or sobbing—your breath not yet your own. Sensory fragments flood you: the taste of salt, the sensation of skin, the sound they made, burning muscles, but rapidly these mix with emotional flashes—your father's face, a childhood fear, sudden shame, then pride, then animal joy, then inexplicable grief. Let your voice ride these physical and emotional surges like waves—guttural, then tender, then fierce, then broken. The fragments come too fast to control: pleasure colliding with pain, power meeting vulnerability, your body's memory warring with your mind's judgment. By the end, arrive at exhausted clarity: your voice quiet, your breathing steady, speaking one simple physical truth that contains everything. Let the speed of transitions mirror the body's own chaotic wisdom.

title: A Hostage Negotiator Losing Control as They Recognize the Voice
instruction: You're on the phone with a hostage-taker when you realize—you know this voice. It's your brother. Your sister. Someone you love. Start with textbook negotiation tactics, calm and controlled: 'Let's talk about what you need. Nobody has to get hurt.' But recognition hits you like a physical blow. Your professional mask shatters. Your voice erupts—'What the hell are you doing? What happened to you?'—raw and desperate. Rage at their choices, terror for their life, helplessness because you can't reach through the phone and pull them back. You're screaming and pleading simultaneously, your voice breaking between fury and love. 'I can't lose you. I can't—' You're not a negotiator anymore. You're family, begging someone you love not to destroy themselves. Your voice cracks with the realization that all your training means nothing here. End in a whisper of pure helplessness: 'Please. Please just come home.' Let the professional collapse entirely into the personal.
inspired_by: Flight Attendant: Announcing Safe Landing After Turbulence

title: The Beautiful Game We Never Played
instruction: You're commentating an imaginary championship game to your deceased best friend's voicemail, a tradition you kept for twenty years that you're finally ending. Begin with genuine joy, laughing as you describe impossible plays you're making up, inside jokes woven into fake statistics. But as you narrate 'your team' winning, gratitude begins bleeding through—thank you for every real game you watched together, thank you for the friendship, thank you for existing. Your voice should shimmer between laughter and tears, celebrating while grieving, finding absurd joy in this ridiculous ritual even as your heart breaks letting it go. The final score should be delivered with a smile in your voice and tears streaming down your face. End with 'I love you' spoken in your normal voice—no commentary, no performance, just truth.

title: The Final Curtain Call
instruction: You are an elderly actress, alone on a dark stage after the audience has left. You speak in a loud stage whisper, over-articulating every consonant as if performing for the back row, but your voice is thin and hyper-feminized. You're holding a prop flower, staring at it. Start with emotional numbness—your voice is flat, mechanical, reciting lines you've said a thousand times. Midway, a wave of helplessness breaks through: your voice cracks, you pause to swallow, your hand trembles, and you forget the next word. By the end, the numbness returns but heavier, as you whisper to no one, 'I don't remember what I'm supposed to feel.' Let the physical exhaustion and the empty theater shape your performance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Cradle of Envy
instruction: You're holding your best friend's newborn in a sunlit nursery, whispering to the baby with all the exaggerated cooing and swooping pitch of parentese. Start in genuine awe—your voice high, slow, full of wonder at those tiny fingers and peaceful eyes. But as you rock, a memory surfaces: your own dream of motherhood, delayed again. Let bitterness seep in around the edges, the pitch flattening slightly, words becoming clipped. Your hands still hold the baby gently, but your voice now carries a quiet, envious ache beneath the sing-song rhythm.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Last Chance in the Lobby
instruction: You're a seasoned gamer in a late-night ranked match, losing badly. Your grip tightens on the mouse, clicks grow louder and more frantic. Start with agitated muttering about connection lag or bad luck, then realize this loss will drop your rank for good. Let your voice crack between frustration and despair — a sudden chair squeak, a sharp breath, a wasted swear. As the defeat screen loads, let the distress shift into quiet, defeated stillness, the words barely a whisper.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Finding Home in the Soup You Share with Your Former Enemy
instruction: You're sharing soup with someone you once hated—a family member you were estranged from, a person who hurt you deeply—but time and forgiveness have brought you here. As you breathe in the aroma, start with a small, almost surprised laugh, noting the absurdity and beauty of this moment. Your voice should carry contradictory emotions: warmth mixed with remembered pain, gratitude threaded with grief for lost years. Describe the smell with wonder, as if you're discovering comfort in the last place you expected to find it. Let laughter catch in your throat, becoming something closer to crying as you acknowledge what you both survived to get here. The soup's aroma represents both what was lost and what's being rebuilt. End with peaceful acceptance that carries an undertone of sadness—joy for this moment, sorrow for all the moments that never were. Your delivery should dance between laughing and crying, hope and heartbreak.
inspired_by: Savoring the Aroma of a Steamy Bowl of Soup on a Cold Day

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your parent's bedside in their final hours. They're afraid—not of death, but of leaving you. Start by trying to be strong, reassuring them with false brightness that everything will be okay. But as they whisper their fears about abandoning you, about all the things left unsaid, your voice begins to crack. You move from denial to raw honesty: you're terrified too, you're not ready, you need them. Then something shifts. You realize the greatest gift you can give is permission to go. Your voice becomes tender, almost steady—tell them it's okay to let go, that you'll be alright, even though your heart is shattering. End with genuine gratitude mixed with unbearable grief, whispering thank you for everything they gave you. Let the tears be real, let your voice break, but find that quiet strength beneath the devastation.

title: The Joyful Requiem
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who asked you to make it funny, to celebrate rather than mourn—your mentor, your grandmother, your dearest friend who faced death with defiant humor. Begin with laughter, sharing an outrageous story that has the lightness they demanded: 'She told me if anyone cried at her funeral, she'd haunt them, so...' Your voice is warm, affectionate, punctuated with genuine chuckles. But the laughter keeps breaking into something else—your throat tightens, your smile trembles at the edges. You're trying to honor their wishes, to celebrate their life with joy, but your grief keeps ambushing you mid-sentence. The contradictions pile up: you're laughing through tears, your voice bright with love while breaking with loss, finding genuine humor in memories while your heart is splitting open. End in a place where joy and devastation are so intertwined they're indistinguishable—grateful beyond measure, destroyed by loss, laughing and crying and meaning both completely.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospice bed at dawn. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin with quiet gratitude—thanking her for specific memories, her hands, her voice, the way she made you feel safe. Let your voice crack as you realize you're running out of time to say everything. Move from gratitude into desperate love, trying to memorize her face, her breathing. Then find acceptance—tell her it's okay to go, that you'll be alright, even as your heart is shattering. End in a whisper of release, giving her permission to leave while your voice breaks with the weight of letting go. This should feel like watching someone slip through your fingers while trying to hold on and let go simultaneously.

title: Fishbowl Confession
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy at your first sleepover, wearing a CPAP mask for the first time in front of friends. The plastic cup presses against your face; the constant hiss of oxygen fills the room. Your voice sounds distant and muffled, and you hate how it makes you feel. Start by mumbling, defensive and embarrassed, speaking over the hiss as you try to explain why you need it. Let your words stumble as you notice your friends staring. Then, as you hear one of them giggle, pivot — realize they're not mocking you, they think the mask is cool. Let your voice lift, project clearer through the mask, and turn your explanation into a playful impression of Darth Vader, ending with a laugh and a newfound lightness.

title: Professional: Researcher Publishes Findings That Contradict Their Own Previous Work
instruction: Announcing new research that proves your old research wrong. Your voice is professional and measured. But you spent your career on the old conclusions. Your voice is simultaneously retracting and advancing. Your breathing becomes the breathing of someone killing their own legacy. You're scientifically honest and professionally dismantling yourself. Your voice is brave and hollow simultaneously. You're right, but rightness has cost you everything you built. Your vocal steadiness is the price of intellectual integrity.

title: Garage Aftermath
instruction: You are a middle-aged man alone in your cluttered garage, hours after a crushing day at work. As you pause to pant and wipe your face, your eye catches a single loose screw on the workbench that's been there for weeks. title: After the Storm of Your Body
instruction: You have just experienced something intensely physical—it could be passionate lovemaking, a violent fight, running until your body gave out, or surviving a physical trauma. Your body is trembling, your breath ragged. You are alone now, and the physical intensity has cracked you open emotionally. Begin with your voice still caught in your body—breathless, raw, almost incoherent. You start speaking aloud, and what emerges is not about the physical experience itself but a flood of recognition about your own aliveness, your own strength, your capacity to feel and survive and be fully present in your body. Name the ways your body has carried you through life, the resilience you didn't know you had, the moments you thought would break you but didn't. Let your breathing, your physical state, inform every word. Transition from overwhelmed and fragmented to grounded and powerful—a bone-deep recognition of your own vitality. End in a place of fierce, embodied self-acknowledgment.

title: The Live Read
instruction: You're a teenage boy hosting a late-night community radio show. You've been rehearsing this segment about 'favorite songs' for hours, trying to sound cool and professional. But as you lean into the mic and start reading a listener's letter about a song that reminds them of someone, you realize it reminds you of her. Your voice starts off with forced radio warmth—smooth, controlled, a little too loud. Then you stumble over a word, laugh at yourself quietly, and your tone drops. The air in the booth feels different. You don't want to stop talking, but your throat tightens. Let your voice gradually shed the performance, letting the infatuation seep in until you're just a boy talking to himself in the dark.

title: Lost in the Pulpit
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy unexpectedly called to the front of a packed church to give a testimony. You stand at the podium, sweating, the congregation's eyes on you. Your voice starts shaky, uncertain—you mumble, lose your train of thought, glance at your parents in the front row. As you speak about a recent personal struggle, confusion thickens your words, but then you recall a simple lesson from Sunday school. Your voice finds a brief, earnest clarity before trailing off again, realizing you don't have all the answers. title: The Last Lap for Mom
instruction: You are in a high-intensity indoor cycling class, pushing through the final sprint. Your breath is rhythmic, locked to your pedaling—each word fights out between gasps. You're thinking about your mother, who is in the hospital, and you promised her you would finish this race she started. Start with a sour, bitter frustration at her sickness—your voice tight, a bit resentful of the machine. As you speak in short, forced bursts, feel that sourness soften into raw, desperate love. By the end, your whisper is a prayer, a promise you're breaking over the finish line. Let the pedals pulse through your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Blind Person Color Description
instruction: Someone is asking you to describe a color you've never seen. Your voice is thoughtful, reaching for metaphors: 'Red is... warm, like heat from the sun, but on your skin.' Breathing is slower, searching. You're using multiple senses to construct understanding. 'It's the sound of intensity. Anger and passion sound like red must sound.' Physical: your hands are moving, describing. By the end, you're close to it: 'Red is the feeling of being alive, burning, awake.' Your voice carries the physicality of describing sensation across a gulf of difference.

title: Collapsed at the Finish Line
instruction: You've just run your first 5K — not for time, but to prove you could do it after a bad breakup. You're also a little tipsy from a pre-race shot of courage, which is wearing off now into a hazy, floaty blur. You make it across the finish line, then immediately fold forward, hands on your knees, gasping. A friend hands you water and says 'You did it.' You're too breathless to answer properly. As you slowly straighten up, the victory hits you, but it's tangled with sorrow — you wanted him to see this. Your voice is shredded, barely there, with huge pauses to suck air. Start in pure exhaustion, letting each word be a small triumph of will. By the end, let a tiny, wobbly smile creep into your voice — tired but real.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: What I Buried in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're whispering a confession to your sleeping lover, telling them something you're too afraid to say when they're awake and looking at you. Begin with your voice barely audible, fractured by shame and the terror of your own vulnerability. Maybe it's about a past you've hidden, or a desire you've never admitted, or a way you've betrayed them, or a fear about yourself that makes you feel irreparably broken. Feel how the darkness makes you brave enough to whisper but also amplifies your fear—what if they're not really sleeping? What if they hear? Let the act of confession, even to unhearing ears, slowly transform your fear into a fragile, tender relief. End with something close to self-forgiveness, your whisper steadying into something almost like prayer, as if naming the fear in the dark has begun to dissolve its power.

title: Condense Narrative
instruction: You have two minutes to explain why you need this job. Ten years of experience, heartbreak, growth—all of it needs to fit into words. Your voice is careful, choosing which moments matter. 'I started poor, I educated myself, I'm here because this matters.' Each sentence is distilled. You're leaving out the suicide attempt, the failed marriages, the nights you cried. Your voice carries what's omitted as much as what's spoken.

title: Caught in Machinery: Fighting Physical Panic While Thinking
instruction: Your sleeve is caught in industrial machinery that's still running. Your voice is initially pure panic, almost incoherent screaming. But if you keep screaming, you'll dislocate something—you know this intellectually. Your voice becomes almost forced calm, mechanical instructions to yourself: 'Stop. Breathe. Assess.' You're narrating what you see, trying not to move. Include the moment where the machinery is pulling harder and your voice cracks, panic breaking through. 'It's getting tighter. TURN IT OFF TURN IT OFF!' But someone will hear you, and you're trapped. Your voice becomes small again, focused, trying not to trigger further damage. 'Okay. Okay. Back pressure, not forward.' You're in conversation with your own suffering, your voice a strange dialogue between panic and desperate problem-solving.

title: The Thunderstorm Reunion
instruction: You haven't seen this person in five years. They're standing in your doorway, soaking wet from the rain, and you're furious they came. Begin with sharp, controlled anger—every word a weapon, your body rigid with rage. But they're not fighting back, and as you rail at them, you become aware of your own body, your racing heart, the heat in your face, the way your hands are shaking. Your anger begins to crack and underneath is something raw and physical—maybe desire, maybe grief, maybe both. Let your breath change. Let your voice shift from cutting to ragged. Move through the room, feel the space between you as both unbearable and magnetic. This is messy, physical, contradictory—you want to push them away and pull them close. By the end, you're not sure if you're fighting or surrendering, but your whole body is involved in this emotional storm. Let it be as real as the thunder outside.

title: The Babysitter's Slip
instruction: You're a rugged, middle-aged man babysitting your friend's infant. The baby's mother just left the room after handing you the child. You start speaking to the baby in exaggerated, high-pitched parentese, but your mind drifts to her—the way she smiled, the curve of her neck. Your voice begins to crack, the pitch dropping as lust creeps in. You try to maintain the sing-song tone, but by the end you're practically growling, unaware you've stopped bouncing the baby. You shift your weight, and glance toward the door, losing your train of thought mid-coo.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Tender Surrender to the Quiet
instruction: You're whispering to yourself—or perhaps to a lost love—in the moments before dawn, wrapped in darkness that feels like an embrace. Speak as though you're finally accepting something you've fought against for so long: that being alone in the dark isn't abandonment, it's a kind of freedom. Your voice should be achingly tender, intimate, almost sensual in its gentleness. But underneath, there's a catch of sadness—this acceptance has cost you something precious. Let pauses speak as much as words. Your tone should be so quiet it's almost a breath, confessional, like you're sharing a secret with the darkness itself. End with a bittersweet peace, where comfort and loss are so intertwined you can't tell them apart.

title: The Last Thread
instruction: You are a woman in her late 60s, sitting at a kitchen table across from your adult child. The room is dim, a single lamp hums, and you keep smoothing the edge of a worn napkin. You’ve just been caught in a small, painful lie you told to protect their feelings - a deception about your health that seemed kind at the time. Start by trying to deflect with a shaky, infatuated memory of how they laughed as a baby, the warmth of that moment pulling you away from the guilt. Halfway through your words, let the pain of the lie and the triumph of finally choosing honesty make your voice drop - volume falls, your sentences break into hesitant fragments, you avoid strong downward tones. End with a quiet, broken admission that feels like relief and loss tangled together, your hands still circling the napkin's edge.
emotions_sampled: Pain (clearly present), Infatuation (slightly present), Triumph (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Apology That Wasn't Meant
instruction: You are a child, alone in your room after a few stolen sips of a grown-up drink. The room tilts. You hear your own slurred voice as you practice an apology for stealing—but you don't actually feel sorry. Start with fake disgust at yourself, then let doubt creep in: maybe you should feel bad, but you don't. Slur your words, lose your train of thought, catch yourself, then end on a defiant, unconvincing shrug that sounds like a question.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the emotional abandonment you experienced as a child. Start with carefully controlled words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, measured, adult about it. But as you speak, decades of unmet need begin surfacing. Your voice should move from diplomatic restraint to raw, childlike pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay present?' Let anger flash through, then collapse into something more devastating—the young child still inside you, asking the question they could never voice. End not with rage but with exhausted clarity: you're done waiting for an answer that will never come. The confrontation isn't loud; it's the sound of finally letting go of hope.
inspired_by: The Lie That Became the Truth

title: The Guardian's Collapse
instruction: You're a soldier/police officer/bodyguard who failed to protect someone you swore to keep safe. You're giving your report—clinical, factual, steady. Your voice is professional armor. Then someone asks, 'Did they say anything at the end?' The armor shatters. Rage explodes through you—at yourself, at the universe, at the cruel mathematics of being two seconds too late. You're shouting, then sobbing, then shouting through sobs. Your voice becomes raw, animal, unrecognizable. Underneath the fury is something more terrifying: complete helplessness. You're fierce and broken simultaneously, powerful and powerless. End with your voice going quiet, hollow—the sound of someone who will carry this weight forever.

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You're standing outside in heavy rain (real or imagined), and something inside you has finally snapped. Begin with your body rigid, fists clenched, trying to hold it together—fighting against the storm both outside and inside. Then let it break: scream, sob, laugh hysterically, or all three. Feel the cold rain on your skin mixing with hot tears, feel your clothes soaked and heavy. Let physical sensation fuel emotional release. Rage at someone who betrayed you, but halfway through, let the rage crack open to reveal the excruciating pain underneath. Pound your fists, then collapse. Let your body tell the story as much as your voice. Move from explosive anger to exhausted, vulnerable grief—from fighting to surrendering.

title: Pleading at the Precipice
instruction: You are with your partner, who is teasing you with denial—bringing you close to release, then stopping. You start with affectionate, coaxing words, trying to charm them into continuing. But as the cycle repeats, your voice grows ragged, breathless, and sour with frustration. By the end, you’re begging—your affection still present but twisted into raw, whimpering need. Let your voice crack, strain, and fall into desperate whispers, as if you’re fighting to stay controlled but losing. Your speech should be punctuated by gasps, pauses where you lose your train of thought, and moments of almost-growling irritation that dissolve back into soft pleas.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Light at Your Bedside
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who shaped your entire life—a grandparent, mentor, or old friend—and you have perhaps five minutes left with them. Begin in shock, numbness, trying to keep yourself together by focusing on small details: the hospital blanket, their hand, the beeping monitor. As you speak, let yourself remember one specific moment you shared with them—something small, maybe even trivial—a breakfast together, a joke they told, the way they said your name. Let that memory crack you open. By the end, allow yourself to finally say what you've never been able to say to them: what they meant to you, what you'll miss, the fear of facing the world without them. Move from numb shock to raw, complete emotional openness.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a reliable library of choices that access the unconscious

title: The Bloom and the Bait
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman in your garden, squatting low to admire a perfect rose. Your knees ache, but the sight makes you gasp with pure pleasure. As you speak, you notice your partner watching from the porch. Your voice strains with the effort of holding the squat—pressured, breathy, pushing out words. Shift from ecstatic wonder to a playful, teasing tone, calling out to them about their gardening laziness. Let the physical exertion color your words: a grunt, a laugh, a flirtatious edge. End with a light giggle as you finally stand.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering to Someone Slipping Away
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love who's unconscious, fading. You know they might not hear you, but you whisper anyway—confessions you were too afraid to say when their eyes were open. Start with small truths: 'I saved all your voicemails. I listen to them when I can't sleep.' Let your voice be barely audible, intimate, as if speaking too loudly might break the spell. Build to the thing you never said: 'I was in love with you. Maybe I still am.' Your throat tightens around each word. Share a memory that makes you almost laugh—but the laugh catches, becomes a sob you try to swallow. End with a tender, devastating goodbye: 'I don't know how to do this without you, but I'll try. I promise I'll try.' Let silence live between your words. Let your breathing be audible. Let the quiet devastation speak louder than any scream.

title: Breaking Point Ecstasy
instruction: You've been holding yourself together through an impossible crisis - days, maybe weeks of barely contained tension. Now, alone in your car or your room, something triggers complete physical and emotional release. Begin with your body rigid, your jaw clenched, every muscle fighting to maintain control. Then let it shatter. This isn't just crying - it's your entire body rebelling. Scream, sob, laugh hysterically, pound your fists, gasp for air. Let rage and relief flood through you simultaneously. Your voice should break, crack, soar. The physical sensation of letting go after holding on so long is almost euphoric. End in exhausted, breathless surrender - spent but somehow alive again. Transform from brittle, desperate control to wild, total physical-emotional release.

title: Healing Realized
instruction: You've just realized you're healed from something that used to destroy you. Your voice is shocked, almost reverent: 'I thought about it, and I'm... okay?' Something that once caused agony now just causes a twinge. Your voice carries gratitude: 'I made it. I actually healed.' Your voice becomes thoughtful, amazed: 'I'm different. I'm stronger.' By the end, your voice is powerful, proud: 'I survived it. I'm still here.'

title: Standing Between Them and Danger
instruction: Someone you love is in immediate danger and you're standing between them and harm, but you're powerless to actually stop what's coming. Start with fierce, commanding authority: 'Get back! You'll have to go through me!' Your voice is full of protective rage, almost feral intensity. But as you realize you can't save them—that no amount of fury will be enough—your voice begins to crack. The rage collapses into pleading desperation: 'Please, please don't do this.' Physical tension breaks into trembling. End with your voice fractured by helpless love and terror: 'I can't... I can't lose you.' Move from explosive defiance through crumbling strength to broken, powerless devotion.

title: Stuck in the Mess
instruction: You're a teenage girl, pinned under a fallen shelf in a dusty garage. You were sneaking into your dad's forbidden storage to grab a secret birthday gift for your best friend, and now the weight crushes your chest. At first, you're flooded with embarrassment—you can't believe you got caught like this, your voice coming out in short, forced giggles of shame. But as you twist and a rotting smell hits you, disgust takes over—you're nearly gagging, your words ragged and breathy, each syllable squeezed out against the pressure.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Time I'll Call You Father
instruction: You're standing at your father's hospital bedside. He's unconscious, dying, and you finally have the courage to say what you've never said. Start with tentative softness—almost gentle, like you're afraid to wake him. 'Dad, I need to tell you something.' Then let years of hurt surface: the times he wasn't there, the emotional distance, the way his silence shaped you. Your voice should crack with both anger and longing. But by the end, you must find forgiveness—not for him, but for yourself. Your final words are whispered through tears: 'I love you anyway. I always did.' Let genuine grief and release wash through you.

title: The Secret You've Carried Alone: A Whispered Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the dark, and you're finally going to tell them the truth you've been hiding. Your voice is barely above a whisper, catching in your throat before you even begin—you've rehearsed this moment a thousand times but now the words feel impossible. Start with halting, fragmented attempts: 'There's something... I need to...' Your breath is uneven, and there are long pauses where you almost lose your courage. When you finally speak the truth—whatever secret you've been carrying—your voice is so quiet they have to strain to hear, each word an act of terrifying vulnerability. Let your voice tremble as you explain why you kept it hidden, the shame coating every syllable. Include a moment where you cry silently, your voice breaking apart mid-sentence, and you have to stop and breathe before continuing. As you near the end, your voice becomes raw with exhaustion and desperate hope: 'Please don't leave me. Please.' The final words are the most fragile of all, a whispered plea that costs you everything: 'I'm still the person you loved. I'm still here.' You're offering them your broken, honest self and waiting in the dark to see if they'll stay.
inspired_by: After Friend Group Exclusion: The Final Text

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up, finally saying what you've never said. Start from a place of nervous, practiced calm—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair and measured. But as you speak, let the years of silence crack open. Allow your anger to surface, then your hurt beneath the anger, then the desperate love beneath the hurt. Physically, you might start seated and find yourself standing, pacing, unable to contain what's pouring out. This is not a polished speech—let yourself stumble, repeat yourself, say things you didn't plan to say. Move from controlled accusation to messy truth-telling to a vulnerable question you've needed to ask since childhood. Let him see you completely undefended. By the end, you're not the adult you tried to be—you're every age you've ever been, all at once.

title: An Adult Child Confronts Their Parent About a Lifetime of Conditional Love
instruction: Start with careful control, almost apologetic—you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. You're trying to explain, gently, how it felt to never be enough, to always be measured and found wanting. But as you speak, anger begins to surface—decades of swallowed hurt rising in your throat. Your voice sharpens, becomes accusatory, then breaks into something rawer: the child underneath still desperate for approval even while rejecting it. Let fury and longing war in your voice. You want them to understand, you want them to hurt, you want them to finally see you—and you hate yourself for still wanting their validation. End somewhere unexpected: not with triumph or closure, but with exhausted, tender devastation. You love them. That's the cruelest part.
inspired_by: Professional: Teacher Fails a Student Whose Success Depends on That Grade

title: Vigil Confession
instruction: It's 4 AM in a hospital waiting room. Your partner is in surgery, outcome uncertain. You're alone except for a stranger sitting across from you who just asked, 'Are you okay?' Begin by trying to hold it together—offering the polite, surface response, your voice steady but hollow. But something about the darkness, the exhaustion, the terror cracks you open. Start speaking the truth you've been carrying: you almost left them three months ago, you've been cruel in small ways, you've taken them for granted. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, each admission more naked than the last. Let the words come slowly, with long pauses, as if you're discovering these truths as you speak them. By the end, arrive at a fierce, quiet realization of how much you love them, how desperately you need them to survive. Your final words should be a whispered prayer, a promise, a plea—barely audible but containing everything.
inspired_by: Long Day's Journey Jamie — Unconscious Suggestions for Dark Character Exercise

title: The Midnight Confession
instruction: Late at night, lying in bed with your lover, you begin whispering a confession. Start with something small, almost playful, but let it open a door to deeper, more uncomfortable truths—the shameful fantasies you've hidden, the parts of yourself you've been afraid to reveal, the desires that feel too raw or wrong to speak aloud. This isn't meant to seduce; it's meant to be seen. Your voice should stay quiet, intimate, but let the emotional intensity build. By the end, you're trembling with the vulnerability of total exposure, and the quiet has become charged with a different quality—not shame anymore, but a fragile, hopeful wonder at being fully known. Move from playful courage through fear of rejection to trembling liberation.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times but never dared to speak. Begin with your voice shaking but determined, almost clinical in its control: 'I need you to hear this. I needed you, and you weren't there.' As you list specific moments—birthdays, graduations, nights you cried alone—your voice builds with years of accumulated hurt and anger: 'Do you even remember? Do you have any idea what that did to me?' Let the rage crack open into something more vulnerable, your voice breaking on the truth you've been protecting yourself from: 'I kept thinking if I was just better, just different, you'd stay.' Then comes the devastating realization that you're done waiting for them to change. Your voice becomes quieter but stronger, almost mourning: 'I'm saying goodbye to the parent I needed you to be.' End with a voice that carries both grief and liberation, speaking to them but really speaking to yourself.
inspired_by: Accepting Terminal Diagnosis: Bargaining Becoming Acceptance

title: The Goodbye That Feels Like Hello
instruction: You're at an airport, train station, or doorway, saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving—maybe forever, maybe just for a long time. Here's the complexity: you're devastated they're going, but you're also deeply, genuinely happy for them. They're chasing a dream, escaping something toxic, or finally choosing themselves. Start with trying to be supportive, to smile through it, to celebrate their courage. But let the grief crack through—your voice breaking mid-sentence, tears you can't quite hide. Then let the real love surge back—fierce pride in who they are, gratitude for what you've shared. Your emotions should swing wildly: laugh-crying, angry-tender, clutching them close while also pushing them toward their future. Feel how love can mean letting go, how grief and joy can exist in the same breath. End with a final embrace where you're somehow holding both the pain of loss and the beauty of loving someone enough to want their freedom. Your voice should be a mess of contradictions—breaking and strong, sad and celebratory, goodbye and I-love-you woven inseparably together.

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's bed as she takes her final breaths. Begin by focusing intensely on the physical sensations around you: the weight of her hand in yours, its temperature, its texture. Notice the quality of afternoon light filtering through the curtains, how it falls across her face. Start feeling profound gratitude for her presence, letting that gratitude fill your chest, your throat. As you speak your goodbye, allow that gratitude to transform—let grief begin to crack through it like ice breaking. By the end, you are caught between celebrating the gift of having known her and the crushing weight of losing her forever. Let your voice carry both the warmth of love and the coldness of impending loss.
inspired_by: A choice approach (e.g., Endowments, Affective Memory, Objects That Come into Contact with the Body) lacks its own built-in technique

title: Dawn of Victory
instruction: You are an elderly person waking up in a dim, quiet bedroom. Your body is stiff, your throat dry, and your voice is a gravelly, low rasp—the morning fog hasn't lifted. As you sit up slowly, the memory of last night's win hits you like a wave: after decades of trying, you finally won the local writing contest. Start by muttering about the ache in your back, your voice cracking and fading, barely audible. Then, as the triumph floods in, let it push through the fatigue—your voice gains a trembling, fierce clarity. End with a quiet, breathless statement of victory, as if telling the morning itself: 'I did it.' Let the emotion transform the gravel into a glow.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Body Remembers
instruction: You're alone, getting dressed for an event, when you catch sight of a scar or mark on your body that connects to a memory—a car accident, a surgery, a moment of violence or passion, a time you felt most alive or most broken. As you touch it, you're flooded with the physical memory of that moment. Let your body respond before your mind does. Maybe your breath changes, maybe you need to sit down, maybe heat rises in you. The memory brings back not just emotion but sensation—the physical feeling of impact, of hands on you, of pain or pleasure or terror. Don't narrate or explain. Let your body tell the story through breath, tension, release. Start in the present, mundane moment of dressing, and let the past inhabit your body until you're fully back there, then slowly return to now, changed by having revisited it.
inspired_by: An actor is going on an audition or interview

title: The Unsoothable Cry
instruction: You are an older grandmother, alone at 3 a.m., trying to soothe your fussing grandchild. You speak in that high, swooping parentese, but your voice wavers with confusion—you've tried everything and the baby still cries. Let your pitch exaggerate as you coo simple phrases like 'shh, sweet one' or 'it's okay,' but feel the helplessness creep in as your attempts fail. By the end, your voice cracks and drops into a quiet, resigned whisper, no longer believing you can fix it. The emotional arc moves from desperate confusion to a tender, defeated stillness.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Quiet Notebook
instruction: You've discovered your late spouse's research journal, filled with notes about an experiment they never told you about—trying to find a cure for the illness that eventually took them. Read entries aloud in a whisper, your voice intimate and trembling. Start with tender curiosity, smiling at their handwriting, their little jokes in the margins. But as you read deeper, you discover they knew the treatment wouldn't work in time. They kept hoping anyway, kept trying, kept it secret to spare you. Your voice should become smaller, more fragile, catching on words. This isn't loud grief—it's the kind that hollows you out. End barely audible, your breath uneven, speaking to them as if they could still hear you, thanking them for trying, telling them it's okay that they failed.

title: Bedside Apology to Sleeping Sister
instruction: Your sister is sedated in hospice. You're sitting beside her at 3 AM, and she can't hear you, which is the only reason you can finally say this. Begin in a whisper, halting, talking to her about the audition you both went to when you were teenagers—the one you got, the one that destroyed your relationship. Your voice should be tender but strained, catching on words. 'You were better than me. You know that, right? You were always better.' As you continue, the confession deepens: all the ways you undermined her, the lies you told, the career you stole. Your whispers become thick with suppressed crying, but you can't let yourself sob—the nurses might hear, might come in, and you need to tell her this. End with your voice breaking on 'I'm so sorry' repeated like a prayer. Touch her hand. She never wakes.

title: The Long Way Home
instruction: You're a father walking slowly home from the park with your young son after telling him you're moving out. Each step is heavy, your voice carrying a gentle lilt from the stroll, footsteps barely audible. You start speaking with intense sadness—your throat tight, doubts flooding you: 'Did I break everything?' Then, mid-walk, your son squeezes your hand, and relief cuts through like a crack of light, though doubt still shadows your words. Let your voice waver, stumble on a phrase, pause to breathe deeper, and end quieter, softer, but not fully at peace.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Relief (clearly present), Doubt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Bug Expert
instruction: You are a 9-year-old boy who loves bugs more than anything. You see your dad on the phone with his boss, but you just found a huge stag beetle in the backyard and cannot contain your excitement. You run up and interrupt him, words tumbling out in a high, urgent pitch. But as you explain, you notice the beetle has a broken leg. Your voice slows, drops, becomes tender and worried. You lose your train of thought as you crouch to examine it.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Warrior and the Trickster Goblin
instruction: Present a strong warrior with a bold, assertive voice and a mischievous goblin with a nasally, cackling voice. The goblin offers to show the warrior a shortcut through the forest. Switch between the warriors cautious questioning and the goblins evasive answers, building suspense over the goblins true intentions.

title: The Last Morning
instruction: You are sitting at your father's bedside in hospice. He's been distant your whole life, and now he's slipping away. For the past hour, he's been staring past you, occasionally murmuring about his own childhood. You begin speaking as if trying to reach someone far away, tentatively sharing a memory from your childhood that you've never told anyone. As you speak, something shifts—you realize he's actually listening, though he hasn't turned to look at you. Your tentative reaching becomes more urgent, more honest, until you're finally saying the things you've needed to say your entire life. By the end, you're no longer trying to get his attention—you're giving him permission to go, with a mixture of grief and unexpected peace.

title: What I've Never Said to Your Face
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) after years of unspoken resentment. Begin by saying 'I don't even know how to start this' or 'Part of me doesn't want to say any of this.' Your voice is controlled, cautious, protective. Then slowly, sentence by sentence, begin naming the truths you've buried: the moments you felt invisible, the times you needed them and they weren't there, the ways you've shaped your entire life around their approval or their absence. As you continue, feel your defenses crumbling—let anger mix with longing, let accusations soften into vulnerability. By the end, you're no longer attacking—you're pleading to be seen and understood. The journey is from guarded accusation to naked emotional need.

title: You Were Wrong About Us
instruction: You're defending your relationship - interracial, interfaith, or cross-cultural - to someone who said it would never work, someone whose opinion devastated you years ago. Start with volcanic rage, listing every prejudice they voiced, every wound they inflicted. Your voice should shake with fury. But mid-tirade, break open - because they were partly right about the difficulties, just wrong about love not being enough. Let your anger collapse into raw vulnerability as you confess how hard it's been, how you've questioned everything, how some days you wondered if they were right. Then rebuild into fierce, protective love - quieter now, but unshakeable. End with exhausted defiance: you'll keep choosing this love, bruises and all.

title: The Child Who Raised the Parent
instruction: Confront your parent who has asked to borrow money again—the latest in a lifetime of their chaos that you've cleaned up. Start from the exhausted, responsible part of you that has always been the adult in this relationship, the one who pays bills and solves problems and never gets to fall apart. Let your voice carry that brittle competence, that martyred efficiency. But as you speak, let the small child inside—the one who just wanted to be taken care of, who needed them to be the parent—break through. Feel the shift from cold, managerial anger to the raw wail of a child who never got to be young. End with your voice cracking into the vulnerability you've spent your whole life protecting: 'I needed you to be the grown-up.'

title: Memory's Stillness
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your bedroom, late afternoon light filtering through lace curtains. You begin with a quiet, curious interest — exploring the sensation of your own skin, remembering a lover's touch from decades ago. As you continue, your breathing deepens, your whispers become more raw and involuntary — not strained, but natural, like talking to a ghost. Midway, a small hitch: a cramp in your hand makes you pause, then adjust, your thoughts drifting briefly to the ache in your knees. By the end, the interest dissolves into a gentle, satisfied stillness — a soft sigh, a whispered 'That was enough.' No performance, just the honest sounds of an old body finding pleasure in quiet memory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Mirror at the End
instruction: You're lying in a hospital bed, hours from death, speaking to your adult child who has just arrived. You begin by describing yourself as you've always believed you were—the kind of parent you thought you were, the values you lived by, the person you saw in the mirror your whole life. But as you speak, memories surface that contradict this image: moments of absence, of harshness, of love unexpressed. Your voice should shift from confident self-assurance to confused questioning, then finally to raw, vulnerable truth-telling. End by asking your child directly: 'Was I who I thought I was?' Let the silence after that question carry the weight of a lifetime of misperception. Move from proud certainty to devastating uncertainty.

title: The Reunion Suitcase
instruction: You're unpacking your mother's suitcase after she's unexpectedly returned to live with you following your father's death. Each item you remove triggers a memory: her perfume (she wore it on your graduation day when you refused to let her sit with you), a book (she used to read it aloud but you told her to stop because her voice annoyed you), a photograph (the vacation you ruined with your teenage rage). You're furious she's here disrupting your life, but each object cracks your anger open to reveal the grief and guilt underneath. Begin with sharp, bitter resentment as you unpack. Let each item soften you slightly until you're holding something at the bottom of the suitcase that completely breaks you—and you realize you're grateful she's here, even as you're still angry. End with contradictory emotions flooding you at once: love, anger, gratitude, resentment, relief, and grief all colliding.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Dream Journal Entries Exercise

title: Goodbye at the Airport
instruction: Your best friend is leaving for a life across the world—marriage, career, a future that doesn't include you. You're both standing at security, and you have two minutes. Tell them everything: how happy you are for them (and mean it), how your heart is shattering (and mean that too), how you're terrified of losing them, how you want them to fly and soar. Let genuine joy for their happiness mix with the grief of losing your person. Your voice might lift with excitement as you talk about their new adventure, then crack with the realization that you won't be there. Laugh through tears or cry through laughter—let the emotions be simultaneous, not sequential. The contradiction is the truth. End with an embrace—real or imagined—where both feelings live fully in your body at once: celebration and devastation, love expressed through letting go.

title: The Memory I Can't Keep Anymore
instruction: You're whispering a memory to someone you love, but this memory is also a confession—something you did, something you hid, something that's been eating you alive. Your voice is barely audible, tender and terrified. Start by describing the memory gently, as if it's just another shared moment, but there's a tremor underneath. As you continue, you have to admit the part they don't know: your betrayal, your lie, your terrible choice. Your voice doesn't get louder; it gets smaller, more fragile, like you're a child confessing to breaking something precious. You're begging them with your tone to still love you after they know the truth. The memory transforms from something warm into something that could destroy you both. By the end, you're speaking through tears, waiting in the silence to see if they'll forgive you or walk away. Let the vulnerability be so raw it's almost unbearable to listen to.

title: The Burning and the Rain
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of your childhood home the day after a fire. It's raining, and you're drenched, shaking—from cold, from shock, from something else. Begin physically: let your body respond to the cold rain, the acrid smell, the reality of devastation. Your hands won't stop trembling. As you sift through wet ashes and find one intact object—a photo, a book, your mother's ring—let physical sensation merge with emotional eruption. The shaking becomes something else: rage, grief, hysterical relief that no one died, helpless fury at the universe. Your voice should break through chattering teeth, grow raw and primal, perhaps even find dark, terrible laughter mixed with sobbing. Let your body and voice be completely uncontrolled, then find an unexpected stillness at the end—a strange peace in total loss.

title: Frostbitten Envy
instruction: You are an elderly woman waiting at a freezing bus stop. Your body trembles uncontrollably, teeth chattering, jaw tight against the cold. A young woman climbs into a warm car with a friend, laughing. You feel a sharp twist of jealousy and resentment. Speak to yourself, letting the shivers fracture your words. Start with bitter envy—hissing through clenched teeth—then let the cold wear you down into a weary, trembling resignation. Your voice should crack, your breath fog, and your gaze may drift away as you lose the thought and find it again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child the Truth You'll Never Say Awake
instruction: It's 2 AM. Your child is finally asleep after a brutal day where you lost your temper, said things you can't take back. You're sitting beside their bed in the dark, and the words come out barely audible. Start with 'I'm so sorry'—simple, broken. But then confess the things you're terrified of: that you don't know if you're enough, that you see your own parent's mistakes living in your voice, that you're so scared of failing them. Your throat should catch repeatedly. Mix profound love with deep shame and fear. End with tender hope that maybe tomorrow you'll be better, your voice dissolving into silence as you watch them breathe.
inspired_by: Pilot Congratulating Crew While Processing Near-Catastrophe

title: The End of the Line
instruction: You are a teenager standing alone on a foggy train platform at 1 a.m., drunk after a party. The fog swallows the track lights, and the silence presses in. You're on the phone with your older brother, who has come to pick you up, but you keep teasing him about his car and his hair to avoid admitting how scared and disgusted you are with yourself. Your voice wavers—at first it's playful and loud, but as the fog deadens your words, you drift into a quieter, more honest confession, feeling the intoxication fade into regret. Let your words stumble, laugh nervously, then trail off as you realize you're not as tough as you pretend.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Teasing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your parent's hospice bedside in their final hours. Begin by thanking them for specific moments of love in your childhood, your voice warm and grateful. But as you speak, the weight of all the times you needed them and they weren't there begins to surface. Let gratitude slowly give way to grief, then to a gentle but devastating honesty about the parent you wish they'd been. End by giving them permission to let go, your voice breaking with the contradiction of finally being honest while simultaneously losing them forever. This isn't anger—it's the ache of loving someone imperfectly and being loved imperfectly in return.

title: Visor Down, Patience Thin
instruction: You are Lira, a 16-year-old squire forced to wear a heavy, ill-fitting helm during a stifling ceremony at the castle gate. The visor is jammed down, amplifying your every frustrated breath into a metallic ring. You’re supposed to wait motionless for the lord to finish a speech, but your neck aches, sweat drips into your eyes, and you can barely see through the narrow slit. You begin by audibly muttering complaints and shifting your weight, then a fly buzzing inside the helm pushes you over the edge—you tear the visor open with a loud clank, gasping for air. Your voice starts as a tight, irritable whisper full of helpless anger, then breaks into a raw, relieved whine as you finally feel the breeze on your skin.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Night Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying in the dark with your partner on their final night before leaving for a dangerous mission they may not return from. Begin with fierce determination, trying to be strong, reassuring them you'll be fine, that you support their choice. But as the silence grows, let that facade crack completely—your voice breaks, becomes small, confessing your terror of losing them, begging them to remember specific tiny moments you've shared. End in whispered tenderness, telling them exactly what loving them has meant, your voice raw with the ache of impending loss. Let real fear and desperate love war in your throat. The transition must feel inevitable, like a dam finally breaking.

title: Rage and Desperation in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're screaming at someone you love who's just attempted suicide, and you're coming completely unglued. Start with explosive fury - you're shaking them by the shoulders with your words: 'How DARE you try to leave me like that! HOW DARE YOU!' Your voice is savage, loud, uncontrolled. Then it cracks into desperate sobbing: 'I found you. I'm the one who found you.' The image haunts you, and your voice breaks completely. 'Do you know what that was like? Do you?' Now the anger and love are completely tangled - you're furious because you love them so much: 'You don't get to do that! You don't get to make me love you this much and then just... leave!' End with utter collapse - you're on your knees, voice raw from screaming, now barely audible: 'I love you. I love you so much. Please don't ever do that again. Please.' Let yourself be messy, chaotic, switching between rage and terror and desperate love without warning. This is someone completely undone.

title: The Last Call
instruction: You're an older adult, heavily intoxicated, sprawled on the floor of a dim kitchen after hours of drinking. You've just been betrayed by someone you trusted completely, and you're trying to leave a voicemail for them. Your body sways, your words slur—plosives lose their pop, sibilants smear. You start with raw, trembling distress, almost shouting as you fumble with the phone, but the anger drains fast. Mid-message, your volume drops, you lose your thought, and you let out a bitter laugh that fades into silence. End with a quiet, crushed whisper of disappointment, barely audible, as your head droops and exhaustion takes over. Let the physical struggle—dropping the phone, swaying—shape every pause and quiver.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Disappointment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt you deeply years ago—a parent who dismissed your dreams, a lover who betrayed you, a friend who abandoned you when you needed them most. They're sitting across from you now, and you're finally going to say everything you didn't say back then when you were too young, too scared, or too eager to keep the peace. Start with controlled anger, your words precise and cutting as you lay out exactly what they did and how it damaged you. As you speak, let yourself access the younger, more vulnerable version of you who absorbed that hurt. By the end, you may find yourself surprising yourself—perhaps moving toward unexpected understanding, or perhaps discovering a fury you didn't know you still carried. Let your voice and body reflect this journey from contained accusation to raw, unfiltered truth.

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final minutes. Begin in a state of desperate, almost panicked grief, trying to memorize every detail of her face, her hands, the way the afternoon light falls across the blanket. But as you truly look at her—really see her, not your fear of losing her—something shifts. Notice the peace in her expression, the gentle rise and fall of her breathing, the warmth still in her fingers. Let your attention become so completely absorbed in truly witnessing her, in being fully present to this exact moment, that your grief transforms into something quieter, more tender—a profound gratitude for being able to see her, really see her, one last time. End in a whispered thank you, not to avoid the pain, but because you've found something precious in simply being there with her.

title: The Silly Thing You Said
instruction: You're a teenage girl lying in bed after being close with your partner. The room is dark, you're tangled in sheets, your voice is slow and slurred with that post-coital melt—extreme vocal fry, barely above a whisper. You start by giggling about a ridiculous thing they said earlier, genuinely amused, teasing them softly. But as you keep talking, your amusement fades into a quiet, vulnerable realization that this moment matters more than you expected. Let your voice trail off, let there be comfortable silences, and let the last word sound almost swallowed by emotion.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Hidden Photograph
instruction: You're a teenage girl standing on the very tip of a wobbling chair, arms stretched as high as they'll go to reach an old box in the top of a closet. Your ribs are pulled tight, your voice thin and breathy from the strain. As you drag the box forward, it slides open and a faded photograph falls out—you're astonished, gasping a little, and then slowly a fierce triumph rises as you realize what you've found: proof of a secret you've always suspected. Let the astonishment color your first words, then let the triumph build until it's almost bursting, even as a thread of fear (the chair creaking, the floor far below) stays with you until the end.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Triumph (extremely present), Fear (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Mission
instruction: You are saying goodbye to someone you love deeply who is leaving on a one-way space mission to save humanity. Begin with forced cheerfulness and pride, trying to be brave for them, celebrating their heroism. As the reality sinks in that you will never see them again, your voice should crack and falter. End in raw, unguarded grief mixed with desperate love—tell them everything you never said, all the small moments you'll miss, how proud and devastated you are simultaneously. Let the transformation happen naturally: start strong, feel your defenses crumble, and finish broken open but deeply connected. This is not about being loud—it's about the moment your heart can no longer pretend.
inspired_by: The Doctor and the Reluctant Patient

title: The Old Photograph
instruction: You're lying on your stomach on the hardwood floor of your childhood bedroom, the afternoon light slanting in. You've just found a tattered photograph tucked under the loose floorboard—one you haven't seen in years. Your voice is pressed close to the ground as you speak, each word coming out with a slight effort from the position. Start with a soft, amused contentment as you trace the edges of the memory, the voice carrying a gentle wonder. As you realize how much time has passed, let a quiet, bittersweet acceptance settle in—the voice dropping slightly, becoming more measured, yet still close to the floor. You speak the lines naturally, maybe shifting your weight, pausing to look at the photo again.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: 2 AM Whispered Truth
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, and you need to tell them something you've kept secret - perhaps about your failing health, a past trauma, or a fear that haunts you. The room is dark. Begin by genuinely feeling the warmth of the sheets, the sound of their breathing, the actual vulnerability of your body in this moment. Whisper your confession by constantly checking: What does my throat feel like right now? Is my voice shaking because I'm deciding it should, or because it actually is? Where in my body do I feel exposed? Let long pauses exist where you simply breathe and sense what's true. Start from whatever your real state is (maybe surprising calm or numbness) and let it evolve into something more cracked-open by the end. This isn't about performing fragility - it's about discovering what genuine tenderness and fear actually feel like in your chest, your voice, your trembling hands as you reach for theirs in the darkness.

title: Reading Your Sibling's Eulogy at Their Ridiculous Request
instruction: Your sibling left explicit instructions: their funeral should be a celebration, and you must read their intentionally absurd, funny eulogy they wrote themselves. Start reading their jokes, their ridiculous stories, and you're laughing because it's so perfectly them - even in death, making everyone laugh. But mid-funny-story, the reality hits you and your laughter turns to tears, then back to laughing at their next joke, then crying again. Your voice should oscillate between genuine joy at their humor and devastation that they're gone. 'They wanted me to tell you about the time they...' - and you're laughing and sobbing simultaneously. By the end, you're thanking them through tears for giving you this gift of laughter in grief, your voice breaking with love and loss and gratitude and fury that they're not here. This should feel like your heart is both full and shattered at once.

title: The Space She Left
instruction: You're a young man sitting on the bedroom floor, still holding your phone after a call that ended badly. Your throat is raw, your nose is completely blocked, and your eyes are swollen—you've been sobbing for a long time. Now you're empty, just staring at the carpet. You whisper to yourself, trying to make sense of it. Let your voice be hoarse, nasal, so quiet it's almost inaudible, with long pauses where you swallow or sniff. Start with a flat, hollow tone—you're past crying. But as you speak about what you wanted to say, a faint, aching longing creeps in, making your voice crack and waver. Then let that fade back into exhausted stillness. Speak only about 50 words of fragmented thought, as if you're too tired to finish sentences.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Falling in Love at a Funeral
instruction: You're mourning a mutual friend, and across the room is someone whose grief mirrors yours perfectly. Your eulogy-appropriate hushed voice takes on warmth when they approach. The shared stories about the deceased become a connection. Perform the guilt of feeling attraction in a place of mourning. Your voice should carry both genuine grief AND unexpected sparks — the confused, inappropriate flutter in a voice that should only be sad. Life insisting on happening at the worst possible time.

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside your mother's hospital bed in the final hour of her life. Begin flooded with memories—start speaking to her about a specific joyful memory from childhood: the warmth of her hand, the sound of her laughter, the smell of her perfume, the exact color of her favorite dress. Let genuine happiness fill you as you recall this moment in vivid sensory detail. Then, mid-sentence, you notice something change—her breathing shifts, her hand grows colder, the light in her eyes begins to fade. Allow this sensory shift to stop you completely. The warmth becomes cold. The brightness becomes gray. Your joy must shatter into the stark, quiet terror of realizing this is the actual moment of goodbye. Let your voice break, slow, or disappear entirely as the reality replaces the memory.

title: Consent Conversation
instruction: You're establishing consent in an explicit, detailed way. Your voice is matter-of-fact but caring: 'I want to ask you about boundaries.' You're going through what you both want, what you're both willing to do. This should be unsexy on the surface, but it's actually deeply intimate. You're asking permission for each escalation of physical contact. Your partner responds thoughtfully. You're both articulating boundaries that matter.
