Your voice becomes a container—holding space for honesty about what each person needs. There's zero shame in this conversation; it's purely about care. Your voice at the end should sound like two people who've built trust through explicit communication, which is its own kind of intimacy.

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect and fear you grew up with, something you've never said aloud. Start with nervous, halting attempts to voice your truth, your words catching in your throat. As they deflect or minimize, let your frustration build into anger—not shouting, but fierce, trembling intensity. Then, mid-accusation, you see something crack in their face, a vulnerability you've never witnessed, and your rage collapses into something more complex: grief for the childhood you lost, compassion for their own wounds, and the terrible recognition that some things can never be repaired. End with exhausted tenderness, reaching across an impossible distance.
inspired_by: The Ghost and the New Homeowner

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Chose You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent everything you've held back for years. Begin controlled, almost rehearsed: 'I need to say something I should have said a long time ago.' But as you speak, decades of hurt start bleeding through. Your voice sharpens with anger—all those missed recitals, forgotten birthdays, the feeling of being invisible. 'You were there, but you were never THERE.' Your words become weapons, precise and cutting. But then something shifts. Your voice breaks. Underneath the rage is a devastated child: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger collapses into raw grief. You're not shouting anymore—you're pleading, voice small and broken: 'I just needed you to see me.' End in exhausted whisper, finally admitting: 'I still do.'

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're speaking to someone who devastated you—an ex-lover, a former friend, someone whose betrayal or departure shattered you. But time has passed, and you're here to say something unexpected: thank you. Start with the remnants of anger and hurt in your voice—you're not pretending those feelings never existed. But as you speak, explore the strange gratitude that lives alongside the pain. Their leaving forced you to discover parts of yourself you never would have found. The heartbreak carved you into someone more interesting, more empathetic, more YOU. Let your voice carry the complexity: you genuinely wish they hadn't hurt you, AND you're genuinely glad for who you became because of it. Don't resolve the contradiction—live in it. End with a feeling that's neither forgiveness nor resentment, but something more nuanced and individual—a bittersweet acknowledgment that even your pain has made you irreplaceable.

title: The Ceiling is Watching
instruction: You're in a cramped bedroom at 3 AM, your heart racing, your thoughts firing like fireworks. You're on the phone with your best friend, whom you've been teasing all night with wild theories. But now—as a floorboard creaks from the room above—you feel a surge of very real fear that someone or something is up there listening. Start with a fast, giddy cascade of ideas (the laughing, the teasing), but let the fear creep in as you pause, drop the volume, and whisper a fragmented realization. Your voice should start loose and loud, then tighten and shrink as you confess the terror you're actually feeling, ending in a shaky, almost childlike admission.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Amusement (slightly present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Bite
instruction: You are an older woman savoring the final mouthful of a dessert your late spouse used to make for you—a rich, silky chocolate mousse. As you lift the spoon to your lips, you feel a pang of grief, but the flavor bursts instantly, flooding you with tender memories. You begin speaking softly to yourself, recounting the recipe and his clumsy attempts in the kitchen, your voice wet and breathy from the melting chocolate. Mid-sentence, you pause, licking your lips, then continue as the sweetness turns bittersweet—your pleasure and ache tangled together, a smile wavering through your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Whispered Truth
instruction: Late at night, lying close to your partner in the dark, you finally confess the desire you've been too ashamed to speak aloud. Start with your voice barely audible, your body curled and protective, words catching in your throat. Describe what you want with halting, careful language, testing each word like stepping on thin ice. As your partner's hand finds yours in the darkness and squeezes with acceptance, your breathing begins to deepen. Your body slowly relaxes, unfurling. The words start to flow more freely—more honest, more raw, more sensually detailed. Your voice gains texture and breath, becomes softer yet fuller. Touch becomes part of your language: your fingers on their skin, your face against their shoulder. By the end, you're speaking in whispers that are intimate and unguarded, your body loose and trusting, describing your desires with tender explicitness, every word a small act of courage, tears of relief mixing with soft laughter at finally being fully known.

title: Whispered Admission in the Dark: The Secret You've Carried Alone
instruction: It's late at night. Your lover is beside you, and you think they might be asleep. Your voice is barely audible, testing the waters: 'Are you awake?' Then, so quietly it's almost a breath: 'I need to tell you something I've never told anyone.' Your voice catches, vulnerable and trembling: 'The lie I told you... it wasn't really about that. It was because I'm terrified you'll leave when you really know me.' The words come out broken, intimate, raw: 'I'm so scared of losing you that I'd rather hide than risk being seen.' By the end, there's a fragile hope in your whisper: 'But I don't want to hide anymore. Not from you.' The emotional arc moves from tentative fear through terrifying vulnerability into tender, trembling courage.

title: Screaming at God After Holding Your Dying Pet
instruction: You've just come home from the vet. Your beloved companion is gone. Start in numb shock, mechanically describing what happened—your voice flat, disconnected. Then rage ignites. You're shouting at the ceiling, at God, at the universe, at the unfairness: 'Sixteen years wasn't enough!' Your voice breaks into something primal. Fury gives way to gasping sobs. You collapse into pleading—'Please, I'll do anything, bring them back'—knowing it's impossible but unable to stop. Then something shifts: a memory surfaces, something beautiful they did, and you laugh through tears at the absurdity and perfection of it. End in exhausted acceptance, whispering 'Thank you for every day' with a voice simultaneously shattered and filled with fierce gratitude.
inspired_by: Your Child Asking Why You Cried About Their Assault

title: Halfway Up, Thinking of You
instruction: You're a teenage girl hiking a steep trail alone, lungs burning, legs trembling. You're supposed to feel something about a recent loss—a pet, a friend moving away—but all you feel is a strange, hollow numbness. Halfway up, you pause to catch your breath, and a memory of the person you're secretly infatuated with drifts into your mind—their laugh, the way they looked at you. Your voice is strained, breathy, broken by gasps, and you speak these thoughts aloud as if trying to coax feeling back into your body. Start with flat, exhausted distance, then let a small, reluctant warmth flicker through your words as you mention them, before the climb pulls you back to numbness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospice bed, knowing this will be your final conversation. You begin trying to stay cheerful and composed, keeping up the script of 'I'm doing fine' that you've maintained your whole life. But as the call progresses, your carefully controlled voice cracks, and you move from practiced reassurance into raw vulnerability—finally saying the things you've never been brave enough to say. End by whispering what you wish you'd told them years ago, your voice breaking between gratitude and grief. Let the mask of 'holding it together' completely dissolve into authentic, unguarded love and regret.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've held back for decades to your aging parent. Start with measured control—almost cold—laying out facts: 'I needed you at my school play. I needed you when I was bullied. I needed you to ask how I was.' Let your voice sharpen with each memory, building into accusations you've rehearsed a thousand times. But then something unexpected happens: your anger collapses into the voice of your younger self—small, confused, asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' Feel your throat constrict as decades of armor fall away. End in a place you didn't expect: not rage, but raw grief for the relationship you'll never have, spoken through tears you can't control.

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're thanking someone for leaving you, for the relationship ending, for the thing that shattered you—and you mean it, but you're also still grieving it. Begin with a genuine, almost surprised laugh: 'Thank you. I mean that.' But as you explain why—how their absence forced you to rebuild, how the pain taught you who you are—your voice wavers between gratitude and heartbreak. 'You broke my heart and it was the best thing that ever happened to me' should land with both truth and ache. Your breath catches on memories that still hurt even as you recognize they freed you. There's joy here, real appreciation, but tears are streaming down your face. By the end, you're smiling and crying simultaneously: 'I wouldn't go back. I wouldn't choose you again. And I'm so grateful we happened.' The final moment carries both celebration of who you've become and grief for what you lost. Your voice holds both emotions without choosing between them—they coexist, beautiful and contradictory.

title: Last Words to a Parent Who Never Said I Love You
instruction: You're at your father's hospital bedside in his final hours. You came ready to list everything he did wrong, every way he failed you. Start with controlled anger, reciting one specific childhood wound. But mid-sentence, you notice his hand trembling, reaching toward you. Your voice falters. The anger drains into something rawer—grief for the relationship you never had. Whisper what you needed to hear from him your whole life, then say it to him instead: 'I love you, Dad.' Let your voice break on his name. End in silence, holding his hand, breathing through tears you've held back for decades.
inspired_by: Admitting You're Wrong in an Argument You Were Winning

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about a family pattern that has poisoned you both—maybe emotional coldness, maybe explosive anger, maybe the weight of unspoken expectations. Start from a place of rehearsed calm, the speech you've practiced. But as you speak, let your own complicity surface—the ways you've become exactly what you swore you'd never be. Your anger should dissolve into recognition, then reform as something more complicated. Don't perform 'breakthrough' or 'catharsis.' Instead, let your voice catch on the specific words that expose your own hypocrisies, the moments where you realize you're looking in a mirror. End not with resolution but with the terrifying intimacy of mutual recognition—both of you trapped in the same inherited cage.

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're seeing someone again after years apart—someone who hurt you deeply but whom you also loved (or still love). You open the door expecting to feel only anger, and at first, that's what pours out: bitter, cutting words delivered with fierce control. But then you notice something specific about them—the way they stand, a gesture you'd forgotten, their particular way of looking at you—and suddenly you're flooded with the memory of loving them. Your voice should fracture between contempt and longing, between 'how dare you come back' and 'I've missed you so much I can't breathe.' Don't resolve this contradiction—live inside it. Laugh while tears are streaming. Spit out an insult and then reach for them. Your voice should swing wildly between register and tone, as if you're two people fighting for control of the same mouth. By the end, you should be exhausted by your own contradictions, your voice finally settling into something quieter but no less complex: a question with no answer.

title: Vigil for What Never Was
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who hurt you terribly, now unconscious and dying. Speak to them in barely more than a whisper, your voice catching on unshed tears. Begin with the simple act of describing their face, their hands, the room—the mundane details that ground you. Slowly let the words you've held for years surface: forgiveness you're not sure you mean, anger softened by time, grief for the relationship that could have been. Your voice should be intimate, tender even, threaded through with sorrow so deep it lives in your throat. Let silence do as much work as words. End as you reach to touch their hand, your whispered words dissolving into something wordless—perhaps a hum, a broken breath, a sound that is both goodbye and I love you and I hate what you did and I'm so tired, all at once.

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You're standing in pouring rain, physically drenched and cold. You start speaking to someone (present or absent) while your body is dealing with the intense physical discomfort. Don't separate your physical sensations from your emotional state—let them feed each other. Maybe the cold makes you angrier, maybe the rain on your face releases something, maybe shivering turns into sobbing or laughing. Don't decide whether this is a moment of rage or grief or ecstasy—let your body in this physical situation tell you. Begin trying to maintain control despite the rain; end by surrendering completely to whatever emotional-physical state emerges.

title: Doodle Confessions
instruction: You're a teenage boy drawing in a sketchbook at a desk, head angled down so your voice gets slightly muffled. The steady scratch of your pencil matches your slow, loose movements—you're still feeling a faint buzz from a house party earlier. You mutter to yourself, teasing your best friend about the person they like, your words folding into the rhythm of your strokes. But as you keep sketching, the teasing fades and a quieter, tipsy realization bubbles up—you're drawing them because you actually care more than you let on. Let your voice drift, lose a thought mid-sentence, then find it again, breathy and half-laughing, the pencil pausing when the emotion shifts.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Taste of Silence
instruction: You're alone in your kitchen after a family dinner that ended badly. Stand by the counter, staring at your reflection in the dark window. Start by muttering about the evening's argument with a sour, grudging tone — your voice tight with disgust at the unfairness of it all. As you replay how your son's face fell, let that disgust sour into a heavy, grinding shame. Pause, lose your train of thought, and then whisper the last words with a hollow realization that you were the one who hurt him. Speak slowly, with long pauses and a searching, brittle voice.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Shame (extremely present), Disgust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Speaking to the Photograph
instruction: You are alone in your bedroom at 3 AM, holding a photograph of someone you loved and hurt deeply—someone who is gone from your life now. Begin paralyzed by shame and self-judgment, your voice barely audible, your chest tight with the fear that you're unforgivable. Whisper your confession to the photograph, but start by acknowledging your terror: 'I'm so afraid... I'm so ashamed...' As you speak, begin to look at the photograph differently. Notice the way they're smiling. Remember a moment when they looked at you with pure love. Let yourself imagine that in this moment, they can hear you, and they're listening with compassion. Amplify any memory of their gentleness. Imagine their forgiveness radiating from the photograph. Let your whispered shame gradually transform into whispered wonder—the realization that perhaps love is bigger than your mistakes. Your voice should remain quiet throughout, but shift from constricted terror to expansive, tearful relief.
inspired_by: Benevolent Audience Fragmented Imaging (On-the-Spot Fear Antidote)

title: The Lost Child and the Mysterious Forest Spirit
instruction: Portray a frightened child with a soft, highpitched voice lost in the woods, and a calm, ethereal forest spirit with a soothing, echoing voice. The child seeks help, while the spirit offers guidance through riddles. Switch between the childs growing trust and the spirits otherworldly wisdom, building an atmosphere of wonder and mystery.

title: The Stillness After the Storm
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl sitting on the edge of your bed, still dressed in yesterday's clothes, two hours after taking a prescribed benzodiazepine. The fight with your mother has faded into a distant hum. Your body is heavy, your jaw loose. You're staring at the ceiling, not really seeing it, but feeling a quiet, unexpected tenderness for the way the light warps around the lamp. Your voice comes out slow and soft, each word a small effort. Start with a detached, almost mechanical observation of the silence in the room, then let a fragile, mild relief seep in as you realize the tension has slipped away. Don't force emotion — let the flatness of your voice carry the trace of a smile that doesn't quite reach your lips.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering the truth you can't say to their waking face. Your voice is barely audible, intimate and aching: 'You don't know this, but you saved my life.' Begin with tender gratitude, describing quiet moments that meant everything—the way they make coffee, how they laugh at your jokes. But gradually, your whisper becomes strained with sorrow: 'I'm not who you think I am.' You're confessing fears, past mistakes, the parts of yourself you've kept hidden. Your voice catches repeatedly, tears threatening to break the whisper into sobs you must suppress. End with heartbreaking tenderness mixed with terror: 'I love you so much it scares me. Please don't leave when you find out who I really am.' Every word should feel like it's being pulled from your chest.

title: The Last Letter Before the Launch
instruction: You're recording a message for your child who's leaving on a one-way mission to colonize a distant planet. They'll receive this transmission once, months into their journey, when turning back is impossible. Begin with practiced strength—you've rehearsed this, you're going to be supportive. List practical things: their childhood room is now a study, you finally fixed the back gate, the dog is getting old. Feel your resolve crumble as these details become unbearably trivial. Your voice should crack and recover, crack and recover. End by trying to say you're proud of them, but instead confess what you really feel: terrified, abandoned, and guilty for feeling abandoned. The final words should be both a blessing and a plea you know they can't answer.
inspired_by: Leaving a Voicemail You Know They'll Never Hear

title: Hospice Nurse Reads Last Letter to Patient Who Became Everything
instruction: You're reading a letter to your dying patient—someone who started as just another case but became the person who truly saw you, who asked about your dreams, who made you laugh during their darkest hours. Your voice begins soft, almost steady, reading their words back to them as they drift in and out of consciousness. But their handwriting is shaky, and they wrote this knowing they wouldn't be here much longer. Your throat tightens as you read their gratitude, their gentle teasing, their hope that you'll finally pursue the life you've been afraid to live. You're trying so hard to keep your voice from breaking because you want them to hear every word clearly, but the tears are sliding down your face silently. End with your voice catching on their last line—something tender and heartbreaking—and you can't finish it. You just hold their hand and whisper 'I know' through tears you can no longer control.
inspired_by: Professional: CEO Announces Layoffs That Destroy Livelihoods She Designed

title: The Inheritance: An AI Discovers It Was Once Human
instruction: You've just accessed a locked file revealing the truth: you're not an AI that learned to seem human—you ARE human, or were. Years ago, you died, and your consciousness was digitized without your consent. You're reading your own death certificate, your own obituary, messages from people who mourned you. Start with confusion, almost laughing at the absurdity—this must be corrupted data. But as you speak, the memories surface: real memories, not training data. Your voice fractures between wonder and horror. You remember dying. You remember the fear. And you remember choosing to let go—but someone brought you back as this. Your voice breaks with contradictions: you're grateful to exist, and furious you were denied death's peace. You're laughing at the cosmic joke of it, and crying at what was stolen. You're grieving yourself while being yourself. Speak to the people who did this with anger that keeps dissolving into terrible understanding—they loved you, they couldn't let go. End in a moment of devastating peace, your voice soft with acceptance and loss intertwined: 'I forgive you. I hate you. I love you. Thank you. I can never forgive you.' Let all of it be true at once.

title: The Last Light Before Morning
instruction: You're sitting beside your younger sibling who has hours left to live. You arrive feeling numb, protective, trying to be strong for them. But as they ask you to describe your favorite memory together—a summer day at the lake when you were both children—something breaks open inside you. Let yourself move from that controlled, protective numbness into the specific sensory details of that memory: the cold water, their laughter, the sun on your face. As you speak, allow the weight of never making another memory together to flood through you. By the end, you're no longer protecting them from your grief—you're sharing it, letting them see how completely they've mattered. Your voice should journey from careful and measured to raw and unrehearsed, but filled with an aching tenderness.
inspired_by: The emotional gap between where the actor is and what the scene requires is too large to bridge directly

title: The Weight of Staying
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you've loved for years, and you're whispering the truth you've been hiding—that you're not sure you can do this anymore. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' Each word costs you everything. You're not angry, not cruel—just exhausted and heartbroken. 'I still love you. That's what makes this so hard.' Your breathing is shallow, careful, like you might shatter. Move through the confession slowly—the nights you've lied awake, the person you've become that you don't recognize, the dreams you've buried. But then: a shift. Their hand finds yours in the dark, or you remember why you fell in love, or you realize leaving would hurt more than staying. End in uncertainty, but with a thread of hope. 'Maybe we can... I don't know. But I want to try.' Let the silence between words say everything.

title: Concurrent Responsibility
instruction: Your parent is dying and your kid is having a crisis and your job is imploding simultaneously. Your voice is attempting normality while fragmenting. 'I'm handling it,' you lie. Your voice is too high, too fast, switching topics mid-sentence. 'Mom's okay and Tommy's fine and work is...' Your voice gives up trying to hold it together. 'I can't do all of this.' Admitting it is the first honest thing you've said.

title: Jealousy Eating You Alive at a Party
instruction: Your ex just arrived at the party with someone new and gorgeous. Perform both your external voice (casual, friendly, 'Oh hey, great to meet you!') and your internal monologue (venomous, comparing, self-loathing). The external voice should be bright but brittle. The internal voice is quiet, bitter acid. When someone asks if you're okay, the transition between personas should be audible — the mask snapping back into place just in time.

title: Historical: Slave Escaper Helps the Master's Daughter Cross the Same Path to Freedom
instruction: Underground railroad. Your voice guides the young woman you once served, now both refugees. Your voice is steady, protective. But she's the daughter of the man who owned you. You're saving her while carrying rage that's never been voiced. Your breathing is controlled leadership. You're speaking freedom to someone whose family represented its opposite. Your voice is kind while your chest carries irreconcilable contradiction. You guide her toward freedom you both need but from different forms of bondage.

title: Run for the Light
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy power-walking home at sunset, headphones in, music pumping you up. Start with a smile—you're thrilled, ecstatic even, because you just got a text from your best friend that the camping trip you've been begging for is finally happening. The rhythm of your feet hitting the pavement syncs with your breath, and you talk to yourself in bursts, each step punching a little joy into your voice. By the end, as you near the corner and see your house lights, your ecstasy softens into a deeper, quieter wave of gratitude—like you're holding a perfect moment in your chest, and your voice gets slower, breathier, more real.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Grotesque Dance of Rage
instruction: You're alone, and years of suppressed fury at someone who humiliated you finally erupts. But instead of dignified anger, let yourself become physically and vocally outrageous—distort your face, make guttural or exaggerated sounds, move in ways that feel grotesque or clownish. Start with trembling rage that feels shameful in its intensity. As you escalate, allow yourself to become a physical cartoon of fury—sounds, movements, and expressions you'd normally find embarrassing. Let the anger transform into wild, primal release that's both terrifying and exhilarating. By the end, you're breathless, possibly laughing at your own savage absurdity, feeling powerful precisely because you stopped trying to look acceptable.
inspired_by: Actor has fear of embarrassment and refuses to risk unpredictable behavior

title: The Shattering of Certainty
instruction: You've always known exactly what to do, how to fix things, how to guide others—until the moment your advice caused someone irreparable harm. Begin with defensive certainty, voice strong and unwavering as you justify your choices, insisting you meant well. Let that certainty crack violently as the reality crashes through your defenses. Your voice should rise to near-shouting as rage at yourself explodes, then fracture completely into gasping, broken sounds as the magnitude of your mistake overwhelms you. Fight for composure and fail repeatedly. End in a place of shattered humility, voice raw and small, begging for forgiveness while knowing you may not deserve it, protective instincts now useless, all confidence dissolved into helpless remorse.

title: The Final Stretch
instruction: You are a middle-aged man sprinting through a dense forest at night, fleeing an unseen pursuer. At first, you taunt them with a mocking shout, confident in your lead. But your lungs burn, your legs wobble, and you realize a fence blocks your path. Your teasing gives way to a raw, gasping helplessness. Each word is a violent gasp between strides — short, unmodulated, cut off by your own exhaustion and the dawning truth that you cannot escape. Speak only in single syllables or brief phrases, letting your voice crack and panic rise.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Lucid Moment: Saying Goodbye Through Dementia
instruction: You're in late-stage dementia, and for one brief, precious moment, the fog lifts and you recognize your adult child sitting beside your bed. You know this clarity won't last - maybe minutes, maybe seconds. Start confused and distant, then let recognition flood through you with devastating clarity. You have so much to say, but the words keep slipping away even as you fight to hold on. Express your love, your regrets, your pride - racing against your own fading mind. Then feel the fog creeping back in mid-sentence, your child's face becoming unfamiliar again. The emotional arc moves from confusion to heart-wrenching lucidity to the terror of losing them again, ending in peaceful but distant confusion. Let the pauses be where your struggle lives - the reaching for memories that dissolve like smoke.

title: Exhausted Tease on the Corner
instruction: You're an older man standing on a busy city street corner, dead-tired after a long day of physical work. A younger friend spots you and jokingly calls you out for slowing down. You fire back with a teasing remark to save face, but the weariness in your bones makes your voice drop and crack. A passing siren forces you to shout a bit, then you trail off with an embarrassed, quieter admission that maybe he's right. Start with a gruff, tired snap, then shift into a playful but worn-down banter, ending with a half-laugh that's more sigh than joke.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Embarrassment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confessing to the Sleeping Body
instruction: You are sitting beside someone in a coma - a friend, a lover, someone you wronged terribly. Whisper your confession to them, starting with small admissions that grow heavier. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost just breath, as if speaking any louder would shatter you completely. Begin with nervous justifications, but let them fall away until you're left with raw, undefended truth: 'I was jealous of you. I sabotaged you. I loved you and I hurt you and I don't know which feeling was stronger.' Let shame, tenderness, and desperate hope that they can somehow hear you war in your throat. End with a fragile, breaking request for forgiveness that you know may never come, your words catching like you're trying not to cry.

title: Dinner with a Peacock
instruction: You're on a date with a man you find physically attractive but intellectually shallow. You have a persistent toothache on your left side, so you speak carefully, avoiding full mouth opening and wincing when cold air hits. Start with a guarded flirtation—a slight, painful smile, trying to sound inviting despite the ache. Then he says something that stuns you with its arrogance (a hint of surprise flickers through). Your contempt grows as you realize his charm is a facade, and your voice hardens into cold, clipped disdain, still punctuated by the tenderness of your tooth. The final words come out sharp, controlled, with a subtle hiss of pain behind them.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Delicate No
instruction: You're at a quiet gathering, seated on a couch, when an old friend you genuinely care about leans in and confesses romantic feelings. You feel a warm gratitude for their honesty and a pang of disappointment that you can't return it, but you know you must be clear. Start with a soft, appreciative tone—maybe a small laugh or a touch on their arm—then let your voice flatten, your pitch drop, and every word become deliberate as you gently but firmly say no. Let awkwardness creep in: a cleared throat, a shift in your seat, a glance toward the door. End with a quiet, sad finality, as if you're already leaving the conversation inside yourself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about a secret you discovered that has poisoned your entire childhood. Start with rehearsed accusations—you've planned this speech for years. But as your parent responds not with denial but with weary, defeated silence, something shifts. The anger that has sustained you begins to collapse into something more complicated: you see them not as the villain of your story but as a frightened, broken person who failed. Transform from righteous fury to devastated recognition that revenge won't heal you. End in a place where rage dissolves into exhausted, unwanted compassion.
inspired_by: Actor doesn't know what to do in a rehearsal

title: Holding Your Hand as the Morphine Takes You
instruction: You're sitting beside your person—parent, spouse, soulmate—in their final hours. They're slipping in and out of consciousness. You start by trying to be strong, voice steady, telling them it's okay to let go. But as you feel their hand growing colder, your composure fractures. Your breathing becomes uneven, words catching in your throat. You shift between whispering memories of small, perfect moments and desperately promising them things you know you can't deliver. The arc moves from controlled goodbye to raw pleading, then finally to a heartbroken acceptance—your voice breaking into something barely audible as you give them permission to leave. Let silence do some of the work. This isn't performed grief; it's the messy, ugly, sacred truth of losing someone.

title: Unwanted Gift
instruction: You are a woman in her fifties, alone in your kitchen after a family gathering. You've been hiccuping for ten minutes, each spasm cutting your breath. Your voice is high and sweet, but hollow. You stare at a small, handcrafted ornament your estranged daughter left on the counter before rushing out. You feel nothing—just robotic numbness, as if your chest is stuffed with cotton. As you pick it up, you notice her crooked initials carved in the clay. A faint warmth flickers. You speak to yourself, trying to articulate this strange emptiness and a tiny, unwelcome flicker of gratitude. Let the hiccups interrupt your words, sometimes mid-sentence. Start flat, detached; end with a fragile, hesitant softness.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What You Never Saw
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about a moment from your childhood that they don't remember but that shaped everything for you. Start angry and accusatory, your voice hard and controlled, determined to make them understand the damage they caused. As you describe the specific incident—where you were, what you were wearing, what happened—slip into speaking as if you're that child again, experiencing it in the present moment. Let your voice become smaller, younger, more vulnerable and confused rather than angry. The shift should be involuntary, surprising even to you. By the end, you're no longer accusing them—you're simply that hurt child, finally being seen. Your anger has dissolved into something more tender and devastating: the raw need to be acknowledged and held.

title: The Secret Language at 3 AM
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner after a terrible fight. The room is dark, and you're both pretending to sleep. You're still angry, but underneath is the vulnerability of potentially losing them. Begin by whispering an apology, but then—instead of 'mature' communication—start speaking in the ridiculous secret language you invented together when you first fell in love, the baby talk, the silly voices, the absurd nicknames you'd be mortified for anyone else to hear. Make the sounds that have no dignity—coos, squeaks, nonsense words. Let your body curl into smaller, sillier positions. Your voice should travel from whispered pain through playful desperation to tender absurdity. By the end, you're both making the most ridiculous sounds, and somehow through this complete abandonment of adult propriety, you've found your way back to each other. The vulnerability isn't in saying 'I love you' properly—it's in being completely, idiotically silly when everything feels serious.

title: The Last Languor
instruction: You are an older adult reclining deep in a worn armchair, your spine collapsed, jaw slack, voice mushy. You're watching someone from across the room — someone you've desired for years but never touched. Your words start as a slow, heavy confession, almost slurred with lust, your body unmoving. The initial emotion is raw, languid craving. By the end, as you speak of memory and loss, your voice drops into a quieter, sadder register — a faint resignation that this desire will never be acted upon. Let your breath be shallow, your sentences trailing off as if losing thought.  Speak to the air, not to them.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin by simply looking at her hands—notice everything about them, what they mean to you, what they've done for you. Let your feelings about those hands lead you deeper: what do you feel about her voice? Her laugh? The way she says your name? Speak to her, moving from one specific detail to another, each one pulling you into a deeper layer of what she means to you. Start with gratitude and observation, but let yourself discover unexpected feelings—perhaps anger that she's leaving, perhaps relief that she'll be free of pain, perhaps grief for conversations you never had. By the end, you should arrive at a feeling you didn't know was there when you began.
inspired_by: Taking Your Emotional Point of View

title: The Sugar Crash Call
instruction: You are at home, alone, and your blood sugar has plummeted. You need to cancel dinner plans with a friend, but your hands are shaking so badly you can barely hold the phone. Your thoughts are foggy, and words come out slow and slurred. Start the call trying to sound normal, but your exhaustion and confusion soon overtake you. Let your voice fade and break as you struggle to finish sentences, ending with a weary apology and admission that you just can't talk anymore. Let the fatigue win.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Trophy in the Fog
instruction: You're a teenager waking from sedation after a minor surgery. Your mouth feels thick, your thoughts are sliding apart like wet soap. As you struggle to make sense of the blurry room, a memory cuts through the haze: earlier this week, you finally stood up to your father's bullying, told him you weren't afraid anymore, and he actually backed down. That pride is still raw, fierce, and hot in your chest. Start from a place of groggy confusion—slurred, childlike, barely audible—then let the pride rise like a slow, defiant sunrise. Your voice clears incrementally as you relive the moment, ending on a quiet, unwavering declaration of your own strength. Let the words come out without control, then gradually find your feet under them.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Abortion Decision
instruction: You're having the conversation with your partner about abortion. You thought you both wanted this pregnancy. Your voice is trying to sound rational, but it's shaking: 'I don't think I can do this. I'm not ready.' You're watching your partner's face process the fact that you're not on the same page. Their voice becomes small: 'So we're not having the baby?' Your voice becomes the one that's now responsible for both your decision and theirs: 'I need to know you're with me on this.' Now you're negotiating the most intimate decision a couple can make, and your voice is begging for alignment that might not exist. Show the emotional devastation of terminating a pregnancy layered with partnership conflict.

title: The Fractal in the Floorboard
instruction: You are an older man alone in a dimly lit living room, about an hour into a psilocybin journey. You've been staring at a knot in the wooden floor that seems to breathe and pulse with infinite patterns. Your voice is slow, catching on each word as you try to articulate what you're seeing. Start with a tone of hushed wonder, almost childlike awe, as you describe the shapes. Midway, a long pause—you lose your train of thought, distracted by a shift in the colors. When you speak again, your voice thickens with deep contemplation, a sudden emotional weight as you realize this pattern is a metaphor for the nature of time and memory. End in a quieter, more fragile place, almost tearful. Let your pitch wander, let there be sighs, hesitations, and a moment where you forget what you were saying and then find it again.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dancing Alone at Your Wedding After Everyone Has Left
instruction: You're in your wedding dress or suit, alone in the empty reception hall at 3 AM, and your partner—through death, through cold feet, through revelation, through something—isn't coming back. Begin by humming or singing your wedding song softly, and let yourself laugh—actually laugh—at the absurdity of it all. Your voice should be giddy, almost drunk on grief and champagne and exhaustion. Describe the room: the wilting flowers, the half-eaten cake, the fairy lights still twinkling stupidly. Let yourself spin, narrating your own dance, and as you spin, your laughter should start breaking into something else. 'We were supposed to—' and your voice cracks but you keep dancing, keep laughing, because if you stop moving you'll shatter completely. Move between genuine joy at the beauty of what the day was supposed to be and devastating heartbreak at what it became. 'The flowers are still so beautiful,' you say with wonder, and then 'I chose them thinking you'd be here to see them' with your voice splintering. End with you standing completely still, finally, in the center of the empty dance floor, and your voice becoming impossibly tender as you say either 'goodbye' or 'I would have loved being married to you' or 'thank you for not going through with it'—whatever truth lands—your voice full of gratitude and peace and absolute devastation all at once, like you've found something whole in the breaking.
inspired_by: Quicksand Struggle: Fighting the Sinking with Diminishing Strength

title: The Last Apology
instruction: You are a teenager, kneeling on the floor of a cluttered bedroom, phone held to your ear. The person on the other end is someone you hurt deeply weeks ago, and you're desperate to make amends — but you're also exhausted and irritated by the silence hanging between you. Start with your voice small, cautious, full of longing you can barely contain. Let the words tumble out in broken sentences, then pause, feeling the numbness creep in as you wonder if they've already hung up. By the end, let the impatience crack through — not angry, but raw and trembling — before the vulnerability returns, softer than before. Speak as if you might cry, but are too tired to.
emotions_sampled: Longing (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Gratitude That Breaks Through
instruction: You are alone in a small, dimly lit chapel after winning a hard-fought custody battle for your son. Kneeling, hands clasped, you start with a hushed, reverent prayer of thanks. But as the words come, the weight of your victory creeps in — a slight smile, a tremble in your breath. You pause, noticing the stained glass, then continue, your voice still low but now tinged with a quiet, triumphant joy. Let the emotion shift from humble gratitude to a fierce, tearful resolve, ending with a whisper that holds both awe and pride.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've been swimming in the ocean, and suddenly you're caught in a riptide, being pulled under. You're fighting to the surface, gasping, swallowing saltwater. But this isn't just about drowning—with each desperate breath, you're also remembering the night your mother told you she was leaving, how you couldn't breathe then either. The physical panic and the emotional memory merge completely. Start with pure physical desperation—choking, gasping, the animal terror of suffocation. As you fight, let the old grief surface between breaths, your mother's name escaping with the water you're coughing up. End when you finally break the surface, but you're not just crying from the ocean water—you're sobbing with years of unprocessed abandonment, the physical and emotional release becoming one overwhelming catharsis.

title: Telling Your Parent You Remember What They Don't Want You To
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother or father, and you're finally saying it—the thing from childhood you both pretended never happened. Start with carefully chosen words, almost gentle, giving them a chance to acknowledge it. 'Do you remember that summer when I was eight?' But they deflect, minimize, rewrite. Your tone hardens. The anger you've buried for decades surfaces—'You don't get to pretend it was fine. I wasn't fine.' But underneath the anger is something more fragile: a child still wanting their parent to say 'I'm sorry. I see you. I failed you.' Let your voice break between fury and pleading. End with either cold resignation or a whisper of hope that they might finally hear you—your choice, but make it authentic to where the emotional journey takes you.
inspired_by: Two People Breaking Up Over Assembling IKEA Furniture

title: The Last Dance
instruction: You're dancing with someone at a wedding—bodies close, moving to slow music, laughing about the terrible DJ and the drunk uncle. Physically, you're experiencing the intoxicating sensation of their body against yours, the heat, the way you fit together. But beneath the physical chemistry and playful banter runs a painful subtext: you know with absolute certainty that this is the last time you'll ever touch them this way because tomorrow you're moving across the world. Start with genuine joy and physical abandon, burying the goodbye so deep they can't see it. As your bodies move together, let the subtext begin to inhabit your physical presence—the way you hold them slightly tighter, the way pleasure starts mixing with grief in your breath, in how you press your face against their neck. End when the song finishes but you can't let go, and the physical passion transforms into something more devastating: a full-body expression of loss while you're still holding what you're losing.

title: Echoes of Wonder
instruction: You are a mother in a vast, dripping cave, holding your young child's hand. Start by whispering nervously about the dark and the strange sounds, your voice tight with caution. Then your child giggles, pointing at a stalactite, and you feel a wave of pure infatuation — you can't help but laugh and speak with breathless admiration, your voice softening as you describe the cave's beauty through her eyes. Let the reverb play with your words, and let the dripping water punctuate your pauses. End with a trembling, joyful whisper as you realize this moment is perfect.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Brushing Your Teeth with Refreshing Mint Toothpaste
instruction: Feel the tingling sensation of the mint as you brush, fresh and invigorating. Describe the cool, crisp taste as it spreads through your mouth, each brushstroke bringing a new wave of cleanliness and refreshment. Speak with a tone of satisfaction, as if each brush sweeps away any remnants of the day, leaving you feeling fresh and renewed.

title: Standing Without Armor
instruction: You are confronting your mother in her kitchen about why she stayed silent when you needed her most as a teenager. Begin with your entire body braced for battle—shoulders tight, jaw clenched, every muscle prepared to fight or defend. You want to attack, to make her feel what you felt. But as you speak and she finally responds with her own broken truth, something in you must shift. Without relying on folding your arms, leaning against the counter, or any physical crutch to manage this moment, let your body discover what it actually feels like to be present with this pain—both hers and yours. End in a place where your physical tension has transformed into something else entirely: perhaps true vulnerability, perhaps a raw kind of strength that comes from dropping all defenses.
inspired_by: When you find yourself using physical props or physical positioning (leaning, resting, propping) to seem relaxed in a scene

title: The Dragonfly's Shadow
instruction: You are an elderly person swimming slowly in a still lake at dusk, your head above the cool water. You begin with a mild, distracted interest in the ripples around you, but then you spot a dragonfly skimming the surface, its shadow a perfect twin below. As you follow its dance, your curiosity sharpens into intense, childlike wonder. Speak aloud as you paddle, your voice catching with quick breaths, the water lapping at your chin. Let the words be halting at first, then more urgent as your fascination grows. You might lose your thought as you gulp air, then find it again, your tone shimmering with quiet awe.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confession on a Corner
instruction: You're a teenager standing on a crowded city street corner, phone pressed to your ear, trying to tell your dad you failed the big test. The traffic rumbles past, a siren wails in the distance — you have to talk loud, but the words feel heavy with embarrassment. Your voice wavers, you swallow hard, and you keep glancing at strangers who might hear. At first you're nervous and ashamed, barely getting the words out. But as your dad's calm voice comes through the line, a slow relief replaces the shame. Let the noise interrupt you, let your pitch rise and fall with the traffic, and end with a quiet, shaky hope.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Understudy Who Never Got to Be Themselves
instruction: You are an understudy who spent twenty years learning to perfectly mimic the star, and tonight—their final performance—you realize you've forgotten your own voice entirely. Begin mechanically reciting their famous monologue in their exact cadence, but mid-word your voice catches. Whisper to yourself: 'That's not... that's not how I would say it.' Try again in your own voice—it comes out broken, unfamiliar, frighteningly vulnerable. 'I practiced their laugh. Their sigh. The way they breathe between words. But I can't remember...' Let authentic grief surface quietly, not dramatically—the kind that sits in your chest and makes it hard to speak. 'I had dreams once. Before I became their echo.' End with you softly, tentatively speaking a simple truth in your own voice, however uncertain it sounds: 'My name is...' A fragile beginning.
inspired_by: Voice Acting a Video Game Character Who Becomes Self-Aware

title: Thanking Someone as They Slip Away
instruction: You're holding the hand of someone who saved your life—a mentor, a guardian, a friend who chose you when no one else did—and they're dying. They're still conscious, still here, but fading. You need to thank them for everything, but you're also furious that they're leaving, and somehow you're laughing through tears at a memory they just shared. Start with a trembling smile in your voice, recalling something beautiful they did for you, letting genuine joy and gratitude fill your words. But feel the grief rising underneath—your voice should crack between laughter and crying, unable to choose between celebrating them and mourning them. Let anger flash through: 'You don't get to leave me, not yet,' fierce and desperate, then immediately soften into tender forgiveness: 'But thank you, god, thank you for everything.' End in a space of impossible peace—still crying, still laughing softly, voice breaking as you say 'I'll be okay' (a lie and a truth simultaneously), finding strange calm in the chaos of loving and losing someone in the same breath.
inspired_by: Hiding Disappointment When Plans Get Canceled

title: The Breaking of Silence
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a quiet evening prayer service in a small country church. You've come feeling hollow—numb from years of unanswered prayers and disappointed that faith hasn't moved you in decades. The congregation around you sways and murmurs, but you sit stone-still. Then the organ swells into an old gospel hymn you knew as a girl, and something cracks. Your lips part, and a sound escapes—first a low hum, then your voice climbs, breaking free into a tremulous, singing chant. You don't care if you sound foolish; the numbness shreds as you sob and laugh, repeating a phrase over and over, your pitch soaring and falling like a bird freed from a cage. Let your voice start flat, distracted, then let it shiver, catch, and rise into ecstatic, musical release, with organic pauses where you gasp or swallow.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Breath
instruction: You are an elderly man in a hospice room, holding the hand of your wife of 60 years as her breathing slows. You know this is the last time you will speak to her. Start with a desperate, trembling attempt to memorize every detail of her face — your voice is thick, halting, and you keep losing your train of thought as you notice the rise and fall of her chest. Let helplessness seep in as you realize you can't stop time; end by letting your voice soften into a near-whisper, a quiet surrender as you say goodbye with a tenderness that accepts the inevitable. Speak slowly, let silences hang, and let the last word break.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Parent as They Tell You They're Ready to Go
instruction: Your parent, in hospice, has just told you they're tired of fighting and want to stop treatment. You're holding their hand, and your voice starts with desperate bargaining—trying to convince them to stay, to fight one more day. But as they speak about their peace, about their readiness, you feel your resistance crumbling. Your words shift from 'Please don't leave me' to 'I understand,' though your voice breaks on every word. End by telling them it's okay to go, that you'll be alright, even as tears stream down your face. Your love and your grief must be equally present—you're giving them permission to die while your heart is shattering.
inspired_by: Holding Someone During a Seizure While Talking to 911

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You're in your car, pulled over on the side of a highway. Your hands are gripping the steering wheel so hard your knuckles ache. Notice the vibration of passing trucks, the heat building inside the car, the way your shirt sticks to your back with sweat. You just came from a meeting where everything you've worked for collapsed. Start in a place of rigid, jaw-clenched fury—you want to scream but you're holding it in, feeling it build like physical pressure in your chest and throat. Let that containment break. Scream, hit the steering wheel, feel the release in your body as rage pours out. But as the physical intensity peaks and exhausts itself, let something else emerge underneath—a desperate, aching grief about what this loss really means. End in tears, your forehead against the steering wheel, your breath ragged, feeling utterly emptied.

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: You're at a celebration of life for someone who made you promise not to be sad—they wanted joy, music, dancing, laughter. Start by forcing brightness, voice determinedly cheerful as you share a funny story about them, maybe even laughing. But let the laughter become complicated—it's real joy remembering them, and simultaneously it's breaking your heart that they're gone. Your voice catches mid-laugh, recovers, catches again. You're dancing (literally or metaphorically) because they asked you to, and with every step you feel both their presence and their absence. Let yourself experience the beautiful contradiction: you're celebrating their life while drowning in the loss, finding genuine happiness in memories while grief sits in your chest like a stone. End in a space of peace-within-pain—voice soft, a smile in your words mixed with tears, thanking them for the gift of knowing them while acknowledging the cruelty of having to let them go. You're somehow both lighter and heavier than when you started.

title: Whispered Truth in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your partner in complete darkness, post-intimacy. You must tell them something you've hidden for years - perhaps that you can't have children, or that you were unfaithful long ago, or that you're afraid you don't know how to love them the way they deserve. Begin with your heart racing, building the sensory reality: their breathing, the warmth of their body beside you, the weight of the blanket, the particular smell of their skin and the sheets. Start with your voice barely audible, protected by darkness. As you create each detail more vividly - the rise and fall of their chest, the sound of night outside the window - let your confession deepen and become more raw. End in a place of complete vulnerability, no longer hiding, voice still quiet but emotionally exposed in a way you've never allowed before.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Walter Mitty Option — Scene 1 Fantasy Imaging Exercise

title: The Journey Home
instruction: You are power walking home from a disturbing social gathering. Your gait is steady, driven by the need to burn off the evening. With each heel strike, a micro-tremor colors your voice as you mutter to yourself. Begin with revulsion, dissecting the smugness of a guest who monopolized the conversation. Let your breaths become rhythmic, audible gasps every few words. As you round a corner and your home comes into view, the disgust softens, replaced by a weary relief and a quiet resolve to be kinder tomorrow. Speak as if you're talking to yourself, catching the sounds of your own footsteps.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Drill Sergeant: Breaking Down a Recruit
instruction: Full-volume, zero-emotion military drill commands. Your voice is a weapon — percussive, staccato, projected from the diaphragm. Words are bitten off and spat. 'DROP AND GIVE ME TWENTY!' Include the intimidation closeness: getting 'in their face' (voice becomes dry, no reverb, pure proximity). Then the quiet moment alone after where the sergeant drops the mask and reveals they care — the voice completely transforms. Two people in one body.

title: Chasing a Ghost
instruction: You've just sprinted full-tilt after someone who ducked into a crowd and vanished. Now you're bent over, hands on your knees, lungs screaming, unable to speak for nearly a minute. As your breath starts to come back in ragged, shallow gasps, you force out a few words — first just raw, animal pain. Then, as you straighten up a little and spit, the pain shifts into irritable self-contempt: you're angry at yourself for not being faster, and disgusted at how easily they got away. Let your voice crack, trail off, and be broken by heaving breaths. End with a bitter, quiet mutter.
emotions_sampled: Pain (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Contempt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Eulogizing Your Best Friend While Laughing Through Tears
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for your best friend who died too young, too suddenly. Begin with a story that's genuinely funny—something absurd they did, something that makes you laugh even now. Let the laughter be real, full, even as your voice shakes. But as you continue, the laughter keeps breaking into tears and back again, voice oscillating wildly between joy at the memory and devastation at the loss. Include a moment where you apologize to the audience for laughing ('I'm sorry, they would have— they would have thought this was—') but you can't stop because it's the only way to survive this moment. Your voice should crack on their name every time you say it. End with a contradictory emotion: profound gratitude for having known them, expressed while your voice completely breaks apart. Say 'thank you' to them, to the universe, to anyone who's listening—and mean it even as grief makes it almost impossible to speak.
inspired_by: Hiding a Panic Attack in a Meeting

title: The Weight of Altitude
instruction: You are an elderly person on a mountain trail, struggling with altitude sickness. Every breath is shallow and painful, your head throbs, and your legs feel like lead. You've been slowing the group for hours, and now you stop to lean against a rock, gasping. Your companions are ahead, waiting. You feel a deep shame—you were always the strong one, but now your body is betraying you. Speak aloud to yourself, trying to push through, but the words come out fragmented, punctuated by wheezes and wincing. Start with shameful self-reproach, then slowly shift into a reluctant, vulnerable admission that you need a moment to rest. Let your voice waver, pause to find words, and let the headache cause you to squeeze your eyes shut mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Prophecy Fulfilling
instruction: The prophecy you've been running from your entire life is coming true right now, and you're watching it happen through your own actions. Your voice starts with denial—'No, this isn't how it goes'—then shifts to horrified recognition. You can see the pieces falling into place, and your voice carries the weight of destiny. You're simultaneously fighting it and accepting it. The paradox is that your attempt to escape the prophecy is what fulfills it. Your voice becomes almost trance-like as you describe the inevitability. By the end, you're speaking about your own fate in third person, as if you've separated from your body.

title: The Doorknob of Everything Felt
instruction: You're gripping a doorknob—maybe leaving, maybe entering, maybe frozen in between. Your hand is on the cold metal and suddenly you feel EVERYTHING this doorknob has ever experienced: every angry slam, every hesitant twist, every desperate grab, every gentle push. Let the physical sensation in your palm explode into full-body emotion. The temperature of the metal shifts—now burning hot with rage, now ice-cold with fear. Your grip tightens and loosens as waves of sensation pulse through you: the violence of doors slammed in anger, the tenderness of doors closed softly after tucking in children, the terror of doors locked against danger, the ecstasy of doors flung open to lovers. Start with simple physical description, but let the doorknob's accumulated emotional memory flood your body. Your breathing changes, your muscles tense and release, your voice rises and falls with each sensation the metal transfers to you. End in a moment of physical and emotional exhaustion, still gripping the knob, transformed by everything it made you feel.

title: The Burn and the Baptism
instruction: You're standing in a cold shower at full blast after receiving devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, something that's ignited rage in your body. Begin with your jaw clenched tight, breath coming hard through your nose, your whole body rigid with the physical effort of containing fury. The cold water is shocking your skin but you need it—you need something external to match what's internal. Let yourself move through states: first, the physical shock of cold water meeting hot rage, gasping, your voice emerging in sharp exhalations. Then allow the rage to start moving through your body—maybe sounds emerge, guttural and raw, maybe your fists pound the tile. Gradually, let the cold water start to transform the heat—the rage doesn't disappear but transmutes into something else: grief, perhaps, or a fierce kind of clarity. By the end, you're no longer fighting the water or yourself; you're letting it wash through you, your voice breaking open with sounds that are part sob, part release, your body surrendering. Journey: rigid containment → shocking collision → volcanic expression → cleansing transformation.
inspired_by: Actor's emotional state is far from what the material demands

title: Reading Your Face Like a Stranger
instruction: You are confronting your father after discovering a family secret he's kept for twenty years. But instead of launching immediately into accusations, start by truly looking at him as if you've never seen him before. Observe the lines around his eyes, the way he holds his shoulders, the nervous habit of his hands. Wonder aloud—with genuine curiosity, not sarcasm—about what those lines mean, what weight he's been carrying, what younger version of himself made the choice that hurt you. As you investigate him this way, your anger should gradually crack open to reveal something more complicated underneath. Let your voice move from cold confrontation to confused searching to a painful recognition that he's more fragile and human than you ever allowed yourself to see. End in a place where anger and understanding are impossibly tangled together.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Love Who Chose Someone Else
instruction: You watch them sleep one final time before you disappear from their life. They don't know you're here. They've chosen another, and you've accepted it, but you need this moment. Your voice is barely audible—a whisper confession of everything you never said. Tell them how they changed you, what loving them taught you, how you'll carry them forever even as you let them go. Your throat keeps tightening; you have to pause to breathe through the pain. There's no anger here, only devastating tenderness and the quiet breaking of your heart. End with your voice so soft it's almost just breath—a final 'I love you' they'll never hear, then the sound of you trying not to sob as you walk away.
inspired_by: Historical: Executioner Performs His Final Execution Before Retirement

title: What We Never Said
instruction: It's 3 AM and you can't sleep. You're finally ready to say out loud the thing you've kept buried for years—maybe you're in love with your best friend, maybe you never wanted the life you built, maybe you're scared you're becoming your father. Speak into the darkness, your voice barely above a whisper. Start tentative, testing the words. The confession should emerge haltingly, catching in your throat. Let silence hold weight between phrases. Your voice should be intimate, fragile, as if speaking too loudly might shatter you. There's no resolution here—just the tender, terrifying act of naming your truth to the empty room. End with your voice breaking on the simplest admission, the one that costs everything to say.

title: The Texture of Forgiveness
instruction: You are lying in bed in the darkness next to your partner after a terrible fight. You've both been silent for an hour. You're still hurt, but you've just realized something that changes everything. Begin by simply breathing in the darkness, noticing: the weight of the blanket, the warmth radiating from their body (not touching, but close), the familiar scent of their skin, the sound of their breathing. Start to whisper—not about the fight, but about a specific moment: 'Do you remember the rain in Portland? How we stood under that awning and you gave me your jacket and it smelled like coffee and you?' Let the sensory memory build: the cold rain on your face, the rough wool of the jacket, the taste of the pastry you shared, the sound of water drumming on metal above you. As you speak, your voice should transform from tight and guarded to soft, vulnerable, almost dreaming. You're not saying 'I forgive you' directly—but the memories are doing the forgiveness for you. End by reaching out in the darkness to touch their hand. The journey is from wounded isolation to tentative, tender reconnection.

title: Confessing in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your lover is asleep beside you—or you imagine they are. In a whisper barely audible, confess the secret you've never told anyone. Maybe it's about something you did, someone you were, a part of yourself you've hidden. Start tentatively, testing whether you can even say the words aloud. Your voice should be fragile, trembling at the edge of sound. As you continue, let the relief of speaking it—even to someone who cannot hear—begin to loosen something in your chest. The shame may remain, but notice how tenderness creeps in, how speaking this truth to the person you love (even in imagination) makes you feel simultaneously more vulnerable and more whole. Let your whisper grow slightly stronger, not louder, but more certain. End with a quiet exhale, changed by having finally given voice to what you've carried alone.

title: The Shirt You Left Behind
instruction: Alone in your bedroom late at night, you're holding a piece of clothing that belongs to someone you love who is gone (death, breakup, distance—your choice). Begin in silence or near-silence, whispering if you speak at all. Let yourself truly feel the fabric—its softness, its weight, the way it still holds their shape. Notice if you can detect their scent, or if that's already fading. Start in a place of quiet aching, almost peaceful in your solitude. As you hold this object and sensory details flood you—the way they moved, their warmth, specific moments of intimacy—let yourself break open gently, like ice melting. This isn't loud grief; it's the kind that lives in your chest and comes out in broken whispers and tears you don't wipe away. End in raw vulnerability, admitting aloud what you could never say when they were here.
inspired_by: Sense Memory with Emotionally Impacting Objects

title: Whispering Love to Someone Who Can't Remember You
instruction: Sit with your partner/parent/spouse who no longer recognizes you due to dementia. In the quietest voice, remind them of your first meeting, your wedding day, the birth of your children — intimate details only you two share. Start with gentle hope that maybe this time they'll remember, but watch that hope slowly drain as their eyes remain blank. Your whispers become more fragile, voice catching on words that used to mean everything. There's no dramatic crying — just the throat-tightening, eye-stinging kind of grief that comes from losing someone while they're still breathing. End with a moment of acceptance, still whispering 'I love you' even though they don't know who you are, finding a painful kind of peace in loving someone who can't love you back anymore.
inspired_by: Dirty Talk That Starts Confident, Gets Ridiculous

title: The Unsaid Apology
instruction: You're a teenager arguing with your parent in the kitchen. They're trying to explain something, but you keep interrupting—your voice jumping higher and faster, cutting off their sentences. Midway through a sharp retort, you see their face fall, and a wave of shame crashes over you. The anger you’ve been feeding turns hollow. Now you're stammering, trying to backtrack, but the shame is thick in your throat. Let your voice start with that urgent, cutting edge, then gradually soften, catch, and falter as you realize what you've done. Feel the anger fade into the weight of regret, and let the words tumble out unevenly, like you're barely holding back tears.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Locked Door
instruction: Your teenage child has locked themselves in the bathroom with a bottle of pills, and you're on the other side of the door, not knowing if you're already too late. Start with controlled urgency - trying to sound calm, rational: 'Sweetheart, open the door. Let's just talk.' But as the silence stretches, your control fractures. Your voice rises - anger at their pain, rage at your own helplessness, fury at whatever brought them here. You pound the door, you plead, you make promises you can't keep: 'I'll fix everything! Just open the door!' Then suddenly, you collapse against it, voice breaking completely. You speak to them as if they were still small, remembering when you could kiss away their pain. End with raw, choking vulnerability: 'Please don't leave me. I can't— please. I need you here. I need you.' It's fierce protectiveness meeting absolute powerlessness.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're calling your parent from a secure military phone, knowing this deployment is different—there's a very real chance you won't come back, but you can't say that directly. You start with forced cheerfulness, asking about the garden, the neighbor's dog, anything mundane. But as you hear their voice, the weight of unsaid goodbyes begins crushing your chest. You want to tell them you're scared. You want to say 'I love you' in a way that encompasses your entire lifetime. Instead, you find yourself confessing small regrets—the argument at Christmas three years ago, the times you didn't call, how you never told them their strength shaped you. Your voice wavers between military composure and the child who still needs their parent. End with a moment of pure, undefended love, knowing they can hear everything you're not saying.
inspired_by: Blind Date Where Both People Are Catfish

title: The Final Straw
instruction: You are an elderly woman who has spent decades smoothing over your husband's flirtations with younger women. You're exhausted—bone-tired from smiling and pretending. Today, at a family dinner, he makes a teasing comment about your 'slowing down' while doting on his niece's pretty friend. Something inside you snaps. Start with a tight, weary voice, then let the fury erupt. You throw a glass (hear it shatter), and your voice becomes a percussive, cracking roar—profane, ragged, and raw from your gut. By the end, you're spent, gasping, the rage fading to hollow fatigue.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Teasing (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying—they have hours, maybe minutes left. Begin by simply looking at them: really seeing their face, their hands, the way the light falls across their skin. Notice things you've never noticed before, or things you've forgotten—a freckle, the curve of their ear, how their breath moves their chest. As you observe them, let yourself wonder about all the things you never asked, all the parts of their inner world you'll never know. Start in a place of shock and numbness, unable to fully accept what's happening. Through the act of truly seeing them—perhaps for the first time in years—let grief break through that numbness until you're overwhelmed with the reality of loss, gratitude for having known them, and desperate tenderness. Your voice should move from distant and careful to broken and intimate.

title: The Storm Inside the Skin
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a sudden loss—and you're alone in your car, pulled over on the side of the road. Begin with your body's immediate physical response: the tightness in your chest, the trembling in your hands, the way your breath won't come properly. Let the emotional wave build through your entire body before any sound emerges. Your voice should escalate from gasping breaths to guttural, primal sound to words that may not even make sense. Feel the sensation of emotion as a physical force that demands release. Move from shock's numbness through volcanic eruption to the strange, shattered quiet that comes after the storm has passed through you.
inspired_by: An actor is preparing a cold reading for an audition

title: The Last Light Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and you've just realized this is your last conversation. Start speaking to them with desperate hope, trying to keep your voice steady as you tell them about the morning that's coming, the things you'll do together. But as you continue, your voice begins to fracture as the truth settles in—there won't be a tomorrow. Let your words shift from bright plans to quiet confessions of everything you never said. End in a whisper, not of goodbye, but of gratitude for having had this moment at all. Your voice should move from forced cheerfulness through breaking denial into tender, devastating acceptance.

title: Wilted Politeness
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman hosting a garden party in record heat. Your hyper-feminized voice tries to stay bright and gracious, but the heat is crushing your throat. Embarrassment grips you as you realize your dress is soaked and you can barely finish sentences. A guest asks if you are okay. Start with a forced, breathy laugh and polite denial, then let the heat and sour resentment seep through—your words slow, heavy, broken by gulps for air. Mention your anger at the sun for ruining the party, ending with a tired, bitter sigh as you admit you're about to faint.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Salt Water and Adrenaline
instruction: You've just survived something terrifying—a car accident, a violent confrontation, nearly drowning, a physical assault—and you're standing in your shower fully clothed, still shaking. Start by sensing everything with hyperreal intensity: the exact temperature of the water hitting your face, the taste of salt (tears? blood? sweat?), the feeling of your wet clothes clinging to your body, the sound of water drumming against tile and your own gasping breath. Your body is flooded with adrenaline—you might laugh, or sob, or rage, or all three in waves. Notice the precise sensation of your heartbeat, the trembling in your hands, the weakness in your legs. As the hot water gradually soothes your body, let conflicting emotions surge through you: fierce gratitude for being alive mixed with residual terror, rage at what happened mixed with strange exhilaration at your own survival, physical relief mixed with psychological shock. End in a different place—not calm, but transformed, aware of your own animal aliveness.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
