instruction: You're a parent reading one final bedtime story to your child who is terminally ill, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin with forced cheerfulness, your voice bright and animated as you try to make everything seem normal. As you read, your voice begins to tremble despite your efforts to control it, the words catching in your throat. Midway through, you can no longer maintain the pretense—your voice drops to something raw and broken, but you keep reading because this is your last gift. The story ends, and in the silence that follows, you whisper 'I love you' with such devastating tenderness that it contains every moment you'll never share. Finally, as you close the book, your voice finds an unexpected steadiness—not because the pain is gone, but because love has made you strong enough to let go with grace.

title: Midnight Inventory
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're whispering to your sleeping partner, confessing something you've never said aloud. For so long, you believed you were broken, unable to truly love or be loved. Begin speaking in hushed, fragile tones, almost afraid to disturb the darkness. Trace specific, small moments over the past year—the time you didn't run away, the morning you chose to stay, the afternoon you let yourself be vulnerable—quiet evidences that you've been healing without even realizing it. Let your whispered words gradually fill with tentative wonder, as if you're discovering yourself as you speak. End with your voice barely audible but filled with raw tenderness, realizing that somewhere along the way, you became capable of the very thing you thought impossible.

title: The Weight Lifted
instruction: You're a child slumped deep in a beanbag chair, spine curved, arms limp. You've been trying for hours to fix the music box your grandmother gave you — the one that plays her favorite song — and you've just dropped the tiny gear under the couch. Your voice comes out slow, lazy, almost a mumble, because you feel completely helpless. You're staring at the ceiling, barely moving your jaw. Then you remember: there's a spare gear in the old jewelry box on your dresser. Your breath catches. You don't sit up, but your voice softens with relief — still mushy, but lighter. Say what you're thinking as the helplessness shifts. Let your words trail off, pause, and then come back with a tired but genuine sigh of relief. Speak naturally, with micro-distractions like adjusting in the chair or losing your train of thought.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering the Truth to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3 AM and they're asleep beside you. You start speaking so quietly you're almost mouthing the words—confessing something you can't say when they're awake. Maybe it's 'I'm not sure I can do this anymore' or 'I'm more broken than you know' or 'I love you so much it terrifies me.' Your voice is barely breath, intimate and aching. As you speak, the relief of saying it out loud mixes with devastating sadness because you know you might never have the courage to say this when they can actually hear you. Let your voice catch on tears you're trying not to make sound with, that throat-thick feeling of crying in silence. End with touching their hair or shoulder, the gesture tender even as your heart is splitting open.
inspired_by: Speaking to Your Child After Getting Angry You Regret

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, unable to sleep. It's 3 AM. Begin in the dark silence, feeling the weight of what you've been carrying alone. Let your breathing, the tension in your shoulders, the heat or coldness in your chest guide what happens next. Whisper their name—see what your voice does when it's barely audible. There's something you need to tell them, something that makes you feel fragile as glass. Don't perform vulnerability; find where in your actual body the fear lives. As you begin to speak, your voice may shake or steady itself unexpectedly. Let the relief, the terror, the intimacy of being truly seen wash over you in waves. End in a different kind of silence than you began—transformed by having been witnessed.

title: The Siren's Glare
instruction: You're on a crowded city street at dusk, shouting into your phone at a partner who just betrayed you. Your anger is raw, your voice rising against the traffic. Then you spot a stranger across the street—stunning, your breath catches, and lust flickers through the rage. Suddenly a fire truck screams past, lights blinding, and you stop mid-sentence, struck by the chaotic beauty of the moment. Let your performance shift from hot fury to a jagged pause of desire, then lift into a quiet, awed wonder at the city's fierce life. Speak loud enough to be heard over sirens, but let your voice drop and crack as awe overtakes you.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Anger (extremely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Time I Hold Your Hand
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, holding their hand for what you know will be the last time. Begin by focusing on the physical sensation—the coolness of their skin, how fragile their fingers feel now, so different from before. Start with quiet denial, maybe even false brightness, trying to memorize every detail of their hand. As you speak, let the reality sink in: this warmth will fade, these fingers will go still. Your voice should crack and catch as you move from desperate cataloging of sensations to the devastating acceptance that you must let go. End in a place of raw, whispered goodbye—gratitude breaking through grief, love mixed with the agony of impending loss.
inspired_by: Feeling a Loved Ones Hand in Yours

title: Twisted Morning After
instruction: You are lying in bed after a wild night out, still in your dress from last night. Your head is twisted awkwardly on the pillow as you look over your shoulder at the golden morning light streaming through the window. You're exhausted — your body aches, your neck is cramped and strained, making your voice sound tight and compressed. But the memory of the euphoria is still vivid: the dancing, the laughter, the feeling of being utterly alive. Begin speaking with a dreamy, ecstatic tone, reliving the pleasure, but as you continue, let the physical exhaustion seep in — your voice becomes heavy, your words slow, and you end with a sigh of surrender.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What You Did to Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you—or didn't give you. Begin controlled, almost rehearsed, because you've practiced this speech for years. But as you speak, the buried child inside you starts emerging. Your voice cracks between adult anger and childlike hurt. You oscillate between fury at their choices and desperate pleas for them to just admit what they did, to just say they're sorry. The rage gives way to something more devastating: the realization that they might never give you what you need. End with a quiet, broken acceptance—not forgiveness, but the exhausted recognition that you're releasing them from a debt they'll never pay.

title: The Last Ride Down
instruction: You're an older woman alone in a rattling old elevator in your childhood apartment building. At first, you're amused—the familiar groan of the cables, the way the buttons stick, the metallic flutter of your own voice echoing back. You chuckle to yourself, remembering how you'd press every floor as a kid. But as the elevator passes the third floor—your grandmother's old floor—your smile falters. The amusement softens into something quieter, a wistful ache. Speak to yourself, letting your voice start bright and playful, then drift into a lower, more fragile tone as you remember she's gone. Let the mechanical hum fill the silences between your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Bitter Comfort
instruction: You are an older woman sitting on the edge of your adult daughter’s bed. She’s just been left by someone you never trusted, and she’s sobbing into her pillow. You wanted to say 'I told you so,' but the moment is wrong. Now you have to console her, but your voice is still thick with that sour, bitter taste of being right. You feel helpless because you can’t undo her pain, and your own distress catches in your throat. Speak slowly, low, letting your words sink into the blankets around you. Let your breath match her gasps at first, then steady her with downward inflections on every sentence. Start with a tight, resentful edge—almost a grumble—then let it fade into a quieter, resigned tenderness as you realize your anger only makes you feel more useless.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Helplessness (clearly present), Distress (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unspoken Vow
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone you love, and you're whispering a confession you've carried alone for years—a secret about your past, a fear about your future, or a truth about how deeply they've changed you. Your voice is barely audible at first, intimate and fragile, as if speaking any louder would shatter the moment. You're terrified they'll pull away, but the secret has become too heavy to carry alone. As you speak, your throat tightens with emotion; pauses stretch between words as you gather courage. There's tenderness in your tone, but also a trembling vulnerability—you're offering them the most undefended part of yourself. Midway through, your voice catches and you almost stop, but their silence (whether accepting or uncertain, you're not sure) gives you the strength to continue. By the end, you're still whispering, but there's a different quality—exhaustion, relief, a kind of quiet surrender. You've said it. The space between you has changed forever, and you can hear in your own voice that you're both terrified and finally, finally free.

title: The Truth Between Us
instruction: You're confronting your best friend of fifteen years who betrayed your trust in the cruelest way. Begin with controlled fury: 'I trusted you with everything. Everything.' Your voice is ice, each word deliberate. 'Do you have any idea what you've destroyed?' But they respond with something you didn't expect—their own pain, their own reasons. Your anger falters: 'Don't... don't make me understand. I need to hate you right now.' Your voice breaks with confusion. 'You were supposed to be the one person who—' Now you're crying, but it's not just hurt—it's the agony of losing someone who mattered. 'I don't know how to not love you. Even now, even after this, I don't know how to cut you out.' Your voice drops to a devastated whisper: 'That's what makes this unbearable. I still care. God help me, I still care.' The rage has dissolved into something far more painful: complicated, messy, unresolved love.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about decades of absence and emotional neglect. Begin with controlled anger, years of rehearsed grievances: 'Do you have any idea what it was like? Waiting for you to show up, to care, to see me?' Your voice is sharp, accusatory. But as you speak, the anger cracks and reveals the wounded child underneath: 'I needed you. I needed you so badly and you were just... gone.' The words become raw, unguarded: 'I used to make excuses for you. I told myself you were busy, that you loved me in your own way.' Now bitterness mixed with heartbreak: 'But you didn't. Or if you did, it wasn't enough to make you stay.' They respond—maybe with an apology, maybe with defensiveness. Your voice shifts to something more complex: hurt mixed with reluctant understanding, rage mixed with the terrible, unwanted empathy of seeing them as flawed and human. End with devastating honesty: 'I forgive you. Not because you deserve it, but because I need to let this go. But forgiveness doesn't mean I'll forget. It doesn't mean we get to start over.' The final line is both liberation and loss.

title: Salt Water and Skin
instruction: You're standing in the ocean at sunset after scattering a loved one's ashes. The cold water is up to your chest, waves pushing against you. Begin by describing the physical sensations - the salt stinging your eyes, the cold burning your skin, your feet unstable on the sandy bottom. Let rage surface first: scream at the vastness of the water, at the cruelty of loss, your voice raw and wild. Feel your body wanting to fight the waves, to push back against something, anything. Then let the ocean's rhythm start to shift something in you. As a larger wave hits, let it break your anger open into something else - maybe the memory of their laugh, the way they loved this place. Let your body stop fighting and start moving with the water. End with your voice still powerful but changed - repeating their name like a prayer, mixing grief with a fierce, almost ecstatic gratitude for having known them, your whole body alive with contradictory sensations.
inspired_by: Actor needs to build an authentic relationship with a scene partner quickly

title: Principal Announces School Safety While Terror Alert Silences Her
instruction: Microphone in school gymnasium, students seated. You're explaining new safety protocols with administrative confidence. Then you see the parents' faces—they're terrified despite your words. Your voice continues mechanically, listing procedures, but your vocal authority begins to sound hollow. You're saying words meant to comfort while knowing they won't. Slight vocal fry creeps in on technical details. By the end, you're reciting safety measures to yourself as much as them, trying to believe in your own words.

title: Gratitude at the End
instruction: You're at the bedside of someone who's dying—someone who hurt you, failed you, but also loved you in their imperfect way. Start with tears already in your voice, but also something like laughter: 'You know what's funny? I had this whole speech planned. All the things I needed to say to you.' Your voice trembles between grief and something tender: 'I was so angry at you for so long. For all the ways you weren't what I needed.' But as you speak, gratitude starts weaving through the sadness: 'But you were here. Even when you didn't know how to do it right, you were here.' You're crying now, but there's warmth in it: 'You taught me things you didn't even know you were teaching me. How to be stubborn. How to survive. How to love even when it's messy.' Your voice breaks completely: 'I'm not ready to say goodbye. I'll never be ready.' But then something shifts—acceptance mixed with deep sorrow, peace mixed with heartbreak: 'Thank you. For everything you gave me, even the hard things. Especially the hard things.' End with your voice soft, full of love and loss: 'I forgive you. And I hope you can forgive me too. For not being perfect either.' You're finding peace in the middle of devastating loss, holding both goodbye and gratitude in the same breath.

title: Splinters of Envy
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman with a normally sweet, high-pitched voice, but right now you're alone in the backyard, chopping firewood with a heavy axe. Each swing is fueled by a raw, gnawing jealousy—your rival just got the promotion you wanted. Speak only during the wind-up or between strikes, your words punctuated by explosive grunts and the crack of splitting wood. Start in a bitter, whispery mutter, your envy so intense it tightens your throat. By the final swing, let a weary, defeated calm settle in—your chest heaving, voice cracking with resignation. Let the physical exhaustion bleed into your words: pauses to catch your breath, a grunt mid-sentence, the clatter of the axe head against the block.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Words Before the Launch
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving on a one-way mission to deep space—they'll never return. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them: 'This is amazing, what you're doing.' But your voice begins to crack as reality sets in. Your breathing becomes uneven. Move through pride ('You were always meant for something bigger than this world') into barely contained grief. By the end, drop all pretense—whisper the truth with raw vulnerability: 'I don't know how to be here without you.' Let your voice break completely. The final moment is both celebration of their legend and devastation at your loss.

title: Last Words Before the Flight They'll Never Return From
instruction: You're at an airport gate, and the person you love most is about to board a one-way journey into a dangerous situation—a war zone, a suicide mission, or to care for dying family they'll never leave. You have three minutes before they board. Start trying to be brave, supportive, saying all the right things. But as the final boarding call approaches, your composure shatters. Your voice breaks as you try to memorize their face. You're switching between desperate attempts to hold them back and forcing yourself to let them go. End with a whispered confession of something you've never said, your voice so quiet and broken it's barely audible, as you watch them walk away forever.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a betrayal, a loss, a revelation that shatters your understanding of your life. Begin in shock, numbness, the calm before the storm. Then let the physical reality of emotion overwhelm you—rage that makes your body shake, grief that steals your breath, a wild energy that demands movement, sound, release. But here's the key: imagine someone is there with you—speaking to you, touching you, trying to reach you—and let their presence genuinely affect the trajectory of your emotional storm. Their words might intensify your fury or suddenly deflate it into exhausted sorrow. Their touch might ignite sensual desperation or collapse you into childlike vulnerability. Allow the emotion to move through your entire body, but stay completely open to being redirected by this other presence. End in a place of unexpected stillness, perhaps even dark humor or strange peace.

title: The Body Keeps Score
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a betrayal, a diagnosis, a loss. Your body won't stop shaking. Start by trying to physically hold yourself together, arms wrapped tight, breath controlled, attempting to suppress the reaction. Speak while your body rebels: hands trembling, chest heaving, a cold sweat breaking. As you try to articulate what you've learned, let the physical sensations intensify and merge with emotional ones—nausea becomes rage, trembling becomes grief, the pounding of your heart becomes a drumbeat of panic. Stop fighting your body. Let the shaking become sobbing or screaming or hysterical laughter. Feel how pain and fury can live in your gut, your throat, your clenched fists. By the end, your body should be completely taken over by sensation, but your voice—exhausted, raw—finds an unexpected calm in the eye of the storm, a strange peace in surrender.

title: When the Puzzle Was a Trap All Along
instruction: You've been trying to solve someone's challenge, test, or riddle—maybe to prove yourself worthy, maybe to save something precious—and you're pouring everything into it, voice urgent and determined. You think you're close to the answer. Suddenly, mid-solution, you realize with explosive clarity that there is no right answer, that the riddle was designed to be unsolvable, that you've been manipulated. Let fury detonate in your voice—raw, betrayed, almost feral. But as you rage against the realization, let it shatter into something more vulnerable: the desperate plea of someone who gave everything and has nothing left. Your anger should fracture, revealing hurt so profound it makes you sound younger, smaller. End with a fierce declaration that's half-sob, half-roar—the sound of someone refusing to be broken even as they're breaking, protecting their heart even as it's already wounded.

title: Emergence from the Haze
instruction: You're a teenage girl waking up from sedation after a routine procedure, but the grogginess is heavier than expected. Your body feels like lead; your mouth is dry and your words come out slurred, pitch wobbling as you fight to open your eyes. At first, you're merely confused and exhausted, mumbling disjointed words about the room being too bright. But as the fog lifts, a memory hits you—a loss you'd been numbing, a breakup or a death you'd avoided feeling. Your voice cracks, the helplessness surfacing as quiet sobs break through the slur. You end up whispering, clearer now, a raw admission of sadness to the empty room.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Helplessness (clearly present), Sadness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: First Breath on a New World
instruction: You are a child, the first to step onto a planet that was thought to be lifeless. Inside your sealed suit, your own breathing is deafening, mixed with the hiss of the radio. You were terrified a moment ago, but as your boot touches the soil, a flower blooms where you step. You try to call back to base, but your voice cracks, the astonishment and elation stealing your breath. Let the relief wash over you, then let the sheer, impossible joy of discovery swell, making your words come out in a giddy, breathless rush.
emotions_sampled: Relief (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're protecting someone you love from an unseen threat, and you start with fierce, explosive rage—shouting, warning, all adrenaline and primal protectiveness. Your voice is powerful, commanding, filled with an almost violent determination. But as you continue, cracks appear. The rage begins to splinter into desperation because you know, deep down, that you cannot save them. Your powerful declarations start to break apart, your voice fracturing into helpless pleading. By the end, you've collapsed from warrior to supplicant—on your knees, voice raw and broken, begging for mercy or intervention you know won't come. Let the listener hear both your strength and your absolute powerlessness, the way love can make us both ferocious and completely undone.

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner, confessing something you can't say while they're awake. Start almost inaudibly: 'I need to tell you something.' Your voice is tender, aching with love, but shadowed by deep sadness. 'I see the way you look at me, like I'm everything.' Let the words catch in your throat as you continue: 'But there are parts of me you don't know... parts I'm afraid will make you leave.' The emotion should feel like a physical weight in your chest. End with a devastating admission, your voice barely a breath: 'I'm so scared that if you really knew me, you'd realize you chose wrong.' Let tears thicken your words naturally. This should feel like overhearing someone's most private moment of truth.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Ship Leaves
instruction: You're speaking to someone you love who is boarding a generation ship—they'll never return, and you'll never see them again. Start with forced brightness, trying to be supportive: 'This is amazing for you, this opportunity...' Your voice cracks slightly but you push through. Gradually, the pretense crumbles. Your breathing becomes uneven. The words slow down, becoming more precious, as if you're trying to memorize the sound of your own voice saying them. 'I want you to remember that I...' You can't finish sentences. By the end, you're whispering the smallest, most essential truths, your voice breaking on words like 'always' and 'forever,' knowing these are the last words between you. The fantasy of being strong dissolves into raw, whispered goodbye.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your sleeping child before leaving on a journey you won't return from. Your voice is barely above a whisper—you don't want to wake them. Start with gentle tenderness, listing all the small things you love about them. But your voice keeps catching, breaking on certain words as the reality hits you in waves. You're memorizing their breathing, the shape of their hand, knowing these are your last moments together. Let silence do some of the work—pauses where you can't speak because the grief is choking you. Your whispers become prayers, promises you can't keep, apologies for leaving. End with the unbearable tenderness of touching their hair one last time, your voice so soft it's almost not there, saying 'I love you' like it contains your entire heart. This isn't loud grief—it's the kind that lives in your throat.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Warrior Chooses Peace Over Victory

title: Conclude Ceremony
instruction: You're the elder concluding a memorial service. Your voice is reverent but grounded. The final words are carefully chosen: not too flowery, not cold. 'May they rest in peace. May we carry them forward.' Your voice holds the ritual—you understand you're speaking for a community. As you invoke the closing, something shifts: you sound less like a person and more like a channel for collective grief. The power of formal closure lives in your restraint.

title: The Unwanted Warmth
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl at a house party, sitting on a couch after a fun night. A boy you've been friendly with all semester sits too close, his hand on your knee, and leans in. You feel a flash of confusion—wasn't he just talking about another girl? Your voice starts high and unsure, almost a giggle, but then your body stiffens. Clear your throat, shift away, and let your tone drop to a flat, deliberate firmness as you say no, each word a small brick wall. End with a quick, awkward excuse to leave, your pitch rising again as you rush out.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Medal
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a nursing home, heavily sedated for chronic pain. You sit in a chair, holding a tarnished medal from your youth—a symbol of a proud achievement. Begin speaking with a slow, proud recollection, but the sedation pulls you under; your voice becomes breathy, your words trail off, and you lose your thought mid-sentence. Let your pride flicker through the haze, then soften into a quiet, resigned acceptance as you nearly fall asleep. Speak as if your body is heavy, your mind drifting—pause for long breaths, shift in your seat, adjust the medal in your fingers.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Navigating Sandstorm: Communication Breaking Down
instruction: You're in a sandstorm with visibility near zero, and your voice is initially organized, speaking into a radio to teammates. 'Moving northeast. Visibility... maybe ten feet.' Your voice is steady. But the sand is in everything—your mouth, your eyes—and your breathing becomes labored. Your narration becomes harder to understand as sand enters your lungs. You're coughing, your voice is muffled. Include the moment where your radio stops working (sand damage) and your voice becomes very small and alone. You're lost in a storm that's almost biblical in scale. Your voice becomes almost prayer-like, not necessarily to God but to the idea of being found. 'I'm here. I'm still here. Please find me.' Your voice is getting weaker, more desperate, as the sandstorm seems infinite.

title: Why Did You?
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father after discovering a family secret that reframes your entire childhood. Start with hot, accusatory anger—demanding they explain themselves. But instead of letting them deflect or apologize, pursue each answer with another question. Why that choice? What were they feeling? What did they fear? Who were they protecting? With each question, let your rage slowly crack open into something else: genuine confusion, then reluctant empathy, then uncomfortable understanding. By the end, you're not accusing anymore—you're actually trying to understand the frightened, complicated human behind the parent. Your voice should begin sharp and attacking, gradually softening into vulnerable, almost childlike inquiry. End in a moment where you see them clearly for the first time, feeling both angry and heartbroken by their humanity.

title: The Last Goodbye I Never Meant to Give
instruction: You're saying farewell to someone leaving on a journey they'll never return from—a terminal diagnosis, a one-way mission, an irreversible choice. You began this relationship feeling obligated, even resentful, but as you speak these final words, something shifts. What started as hollow comfort transforms into devastating recognition of love you didn't know you felt until it's too late. Let your voice crack not from performance, but from the sudden, terrifying realization that you're losing someone who became everything when you weren't paying attention. Begin with careful, measured distance. End unable to let go.

title: The Ceiling's Quiet
instruction: You are lying in bed after intimacy, your partner asleep beside you, their arm across your waist. The room is dark, the air cool. You feel a dreamy elation, a soft high from the closeness, but it's mixed with a strange emotional numbness — like you're watching yourself float. As you speak to the ceiling, start with that dreamy contentment, letting your voice be slow, full of satisfied sighs. Then, as you continue, let a contemplative distance creep in. Your voice may trail off, you lose a thought, you turn your head slightly on the pillow. End with a quiet, almost hollow realization about the moment, speaking the last words as if they belong to someone else.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Elation (clearly present), Contemplation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Thank You for Never Believing Me
instruction: You're speaking to someone who always saw through your act—who never bought your fake expertise, your confident jargon, your performance of knowledge you didn't have. Start with laughter, almost giddy, as you thank them for this. But let the laughter become tears, your voice shaking with the beautiful contradiction of gratitude and grief. You're grateful they saw the real you, but your heart is breaking because you realize how much time you wasted performing for everyone else, how exhausting it's been. Your delivery should dance between smiling and crying, between relief and devastation. End with a moment of profound peace mixed with profound sadness: 'I'm so tired of pretending. I don't want to do it anymore.' Let the contradictions live fully in your voice—joy and pain inseparable.

title: The Inheritance of Silence: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're in your childhood home, your aging parent across from you. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've prepared this speech for years. You're listing the moments they missed: birthdays, graduations, the night you needed them most. Your voice is steady with righteous anger. But mid-confrontation, something shifts. You realize they're smaller now, diminished, and that realization doesn't erase your rage—it complicates it. Your voice catches between fury and unexpected grief for what will never be. You hear yourself becoming mean, then you hate yourself for it, then you're angry that you're the one feeling guilty. End with a confession you didn't plan: you still wanted their love, even now, and that truth humiliates and devastates you. Raw and contradictory—anger braided with longing, contempt tangled with desperate, childlike hope.
inspired_by: Professional: Hospital Administrator Denies Treatment a Patient Can't Afford

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're standing in the exact spot where, five years ago, someone you loved pressed you against a wall and kissed you so completely that time stopped—and it was also where, three months later, they shoved you in fury during your worst fight. You've returned to this physical space, and your body is reacting before your mind catches up. Let your breathing change. Feel actual heat in your skin or coldness in your hands. Your voice begins steady, trying to narrate what happened, but physical memory floods through you—desire, fear, rage, longing, all crashing together. Don't plan which emotion comes when. Let your body shake or soften or tense without controlling it. Maybe you touch the wall and gasp. Maybe your voice breaks mid-sentence. Move between the sensations: the ghost of their hands on your skin, the electric charge of wanting them, the knife-twist of how they hurt you. End not with resolution but with your whole instrument vibrating with the truth that love and violation can occupy the same physical space, and your body knows this even when your mind wants simple stories.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're an adult now, sitting across from your parent who knew about the abuse and did nothing. You came here planning to be controlled, to finally tell them how their silence destroyed you, but the moment you start speaking, your voice is shaking with a rage so deep it terrifies you. You describe specific moments when they must have known, when they looked away, and your voice gets louder, more accusatory. Then suddenly you break—the anger collapses into the voice of the child you were, begging to understand: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting? What did I do that made you choose them over me?' Listen for their answer, and let whatever they say change your voice. Maybe it hardens with contempt, maybe it softens with pity, maybe it breaks completely with grief for both of you. End with the realization in your voice: you're not here for their answer anymore. You're here to finally choose yourself.
inspired_by: Breaking Silence About Abuse: The Moment of No Return

title: The Muting Button
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman with a voice that usually sounds sweet and accommodating, but for once, that mask is cracking. Trapped alone in an elevator with a stranger who just made a deeply condescending comment about your job, something you've achieved, or your appearance. The silence after their words is broken only by the mechanical hum. Your voice starts tight, trying to force a polite, airy reply, but disgust rises in your throat like bile, and as the elevator lurches, so does your doubt—you question whether you should say anything, then almost immediately hate yourself for that hesitation. Let the echo of the metal walls make your voice thin as you start, then let it drop into a hollow, annoyed monotone as you realize you don't owe them warmth. You might trail off, lose your thought, or clear your throat against the metallic taste of your own anger.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Meeting Your Biological Sister: Joy and Grief Inseparable
instruction: Your biological sister, who was raised by your birth mother, is standing in front of you for the first time. Your voice breaks with wonder and laughter: 'We have the same laugh. Did you hear that? We have the same—' You're giddy, almost manic with the miracle of genetic connection. But underneath, there's something else rising. Your laughter starts catching, becoming sobs you're trying to disguise as joy: 'You got to grow up with her. You got to—' Suddenly you're crying and laughing at the same time, grabbing her hands: 'I'm so glad she had you. I'm so glad she wasn't alone.' Your voice is full of genuine gratitude that she was loved, but underneath is the sharp grief of your own absence. End with this beautiful, painful contradiction, voice trembling: 'Finding you is the best thing that ever happened to me, and it's breaking my heart.' You're experiencing the most profound connection and the most profound loss simultaneously, and both are absolutely true.
inspired_by: Adoptee Searching for Biological Family: Hope and Dread Mixed

title: Confronting the Parent You Tried to Save
instruction: You are an adult child who discovered the ability to travel back in time, and you went back trying to prevent your parent from making the choice that destroyed your family. But you failed—you witnessed it happen again, powerless to change anything. Now you're confronting your parent in the present day, and everything you've held back for years comes pouring out. Start with controlled anger, listing the specific moments they weren't there, the ways their choices carved holes in you. But as you speak, you see them aging before your eyes, smaller than you remembered, and your rage fractures. You realize they were just as lost as you are now, just as human. End in a place you didn't expect: not quite forgiveness, but the terrible, beautiful recognition that you are more like them than you ever wanted to admit. Whisper the last line.

title: The Truth Your Mother Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a wound they created in you years ago—something they either don't remember or have chosen to forget. Start from a place of careful control, trying to make them understand without accusation. But as they deflect or minimize, feel the anger rise in your throat. Let your voice grow sharper, more insistent, until you're saying the things you swore you'd never say out loud. Then, unexpectedly, beneath your rage, find the child who just wanted to be seen. Your voice should crack from fury into something fragile—not weakness, but the vulnerable truth underneath the anger. End in a place where you're no longer asking for their understanding, but claiming your right to name what happened. Move from measured pain to righteous anger to heartbroken clarity.

title: Under the Observatory Dome
instruction: You are confronting your parent—a renowned astronomer who chose the stars over you throughout your childhood. You've returned to their observatory one last time before cutting ties forever. Start with controlled anger, asking them why distant galaxies mattered more than your school plays, your birthdays, your tears. As they remain silent (or give empty justifications you've heard before), let your voice escalate from accusation to something more painful—the voice of the child you once were, begging to understand why you weren't enough. Then shift: mid-rage, realize you're looking at an aging, lonely person who traded human connection for cosmic meaning, and feel your anger collapse into something more complex—pity mixed with grief for what you both lost. End quietly, with a forgiveness that hurts more than the anger did.

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: You're sitting at your father's hospital bedside in his final hour. For years, you've carried resentment about his absence during your childhood, but now, holding his weakening hand, something shifts. Begin speaking with guarded anger, revealing the hurt he caused. As you speak, let memories of small kindnesses surface—a time he tried, a moment he was present. Your voice should transform from accusatory to broken to finally tender, as you realize this is your last chance to say 'I forgive you' and mean it. End by whispering the love you've hidden for decades, grief replacing anger as you feel his hand go still. Let the transition happen organically, not as a performance of change, but as a genuine unburdening of your heart.

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your mother in her kitchen about something she did when you were twelve that damaged you—maybe she chose a partner over you, maybe she knew something and stayed silent, maybe she was cruel in a moment that broke something. Start angry, ready with your rehearsed accusations. But as you speak, actually notice what's happening inside you—is your voice shaking? Is there a little kid still wanting her approval even now? Is there unexpected pity for her? Don't act these things; let them interrupt your prepared speech. Include the real, messy thoughts between your accusations: 'My hands are trembling. I sound pathetic. Why am I still hoping she'll...' Let what's genuinely present disrupt your agenda. By the end, the emotion should transform from righteous anger to something more complicated—perhaps devastating recognition of her humanity, or your own unexpected grief for what you both lost.
inspired_by: The actor has lost contact with organic impulse life during the scene—is on automatic pilot, leadership, or result-consciousness

title: The Lost Heirloom
instruction: You’re rummaging through a dusty cardboard box in your dead father’s garage, looking for a watch he always wore. The box is full of old tools, fabric scraps, and random junk—your hands dig through stiff canvas and greasy cloth, mumbling curses under your breath. As you zero in on a cold metal shape, your hunched posture shifts, and your voice tightens with a fragile hope you didn’t expect. But when you pull out a rusted pocket knife instead, the concentration cracks, and you let out a raw, quiet sigh—then a laugh that’s half relief, half grief. Let your voice be distracted and gruff at the start, but soften into a worn, unguarded murmur by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've been physically intimate with someone—making love, fighting physically, or both—and in the midst of intense sensation, something breaks open emotionally. Start with pure physical intensity: desire, aggression, or chaotic attraction. But as your body moves, let your mind's actual uncensored stream emerge: old wounds surfacing, sudden grief cutting through arousal, rage mixing with need, memories of someone else, awareness of your own desperation or power, contradictory impulses to connect and destroy. Don't narrate these—let them shift your breath, your touch, your sounds. Some you might voice rawly; most you won't. By the end, you should be somewhere completely unguarded—perhaps sobbing, perhaps laughing, perhaps in stunned silence—having let your body's experience crack open your emotional armor.

title: The Unraveling Stitch
instruction: You're sitting cross-legged on your bedroom floor, a frayed old sweater in your lap. You're bitterly picking at a loose thread, muttering to yourself about how you always end up fixing what others break. Start with that sharp, seething bitterness—your voice tight and clipped, each word a small blade. As you speak, let the bitterness slowly crumble into a quieter, sadder acceptance—your breath deepens, your spine softens, and your voice cracks with the weight of admitting you never really mattered to them. Let the floor support the shift: at first you're tensed against it, then you surrender to the cold hardwood.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Mirror Confrontation: Telling Your Mother She Failed You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years. Start with trembling restraint—voice tight, controlled, almost cold as you list the ways she wasn't there. 'You were drunk at my graduation. You forgot to pick me up from school so many times I stopped expecting you.' But underneath that control is a child screaming to be heard. Let that child break through. Let the accusations turn into desperate questions: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me?' Your voice should crack between fury and pleading, between adult rage and childlike bewilderment. End with exhausted clarity—you needed her to be someone she could never be, and you're finally letting that fantasy die. The anger must dissolve into grief for what never was and never will be.
inspired_by: Drill Sergeant: Breaking Down a Recruit

title: The Tender Trap
instruction: You are a teenager on a late-night call, using a soft, breathy voice to feign seduction. As you whisper about what you'd do next, you suddenly realize the person on the other end is completely unguarded—vulnerable in a way you didn't expect. Astonishment hits first, a sharp inhale, a flicker of genuine surprise. Then, as you continue, the intoxication from a few drinks makes your words slower, thicker, but your intentions sharpen. By the end, your voice drops to a low, deliberate pitch, and each pause carries a quiet malice—you know exactly how to use this moment against them. Let the performance unravel from hypnotic to threatening.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Tangled Wires, Tender Wrath
instruction: You are a woman, a mother, already tied to a chair with soft rope. Your young child has snuck into the room, frowning at the bindings, trying to untie them. You were mid-scene, mid-play, but now all you feel is a hot, shameful anger — at yourself for this mess, at the lock on the door that made this possible. You hiss at the child, your voice strained against the rope and your own frustration, but as you speak, you feel the edge of your anger soften into a desperate, shamed plea for them to leave, your breathing quick and ragged, your words stumbling over the physical restriction.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Wife After the Diagnosis
instruction: It's 3 AM. She's finally asleep after crying for hours. You're sitting beside the bed, speaking so softly she can't hear you—confessing everything you're too afraid to say to her face. Tell her you're terrified. That you don't know how to be strong enough. That you memorized the way she laughs because you're afraid of forgetting. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every other word. You're not crying—you're too exhausted to cry—but emotion is strangling every syllable. Touch her hair. Tell her about the future you'd planned: the trip to Italy, growing old together, the grandchildren you won't meet. End with the quietest, most broken 'I love you' we've ever heard. This isn't performance—this is the sound of a heart learning to break in slow motion.
inspired_by: Ordering at a Drive-Through in a Tornado Warning

title: The Last Call
instruction: You are an elderly woman, slightly tipsy from your evening sherry, calling 911 because your husband has collapsed. Your voice trembles with panic, but you force yourself to sound calm. You start by frantically giving your address, but as you look at him, a wave of affection washes over you. By the end, your voice softens, almost forgetting the emergency, as you whisper how much you love him. Let your voice crack and waver naturally—you're fighting to stay coherent while feeling both dizzy and deeply tender.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Unpacking the Suitcase of Everything Unsaid
instruction: You're confronting your mother/father about something that's haunted you for years. Start with a specific accusation, something clear and practiced. But as you speak, let your emotional impulses hijack your words—mid-sentence, you might suddenly feel protective of them, then shift to mockery, then grief, then appreciation for something completely unrelated, then back to fury. Don't follow a logical argument; let contradictory feelings collide and interrupt each other at rapid speed. Physically, you might step closer, then recoil, reach out, then pull back. End in a place completely different from where you started—perhaps you began with blame and end with an unexpected understanding of your own complicity, or you started seeking approval and end claiming your independence.
inspired_by: Actor is stuck in conceptual or preplanned responses and cannot access organic moment-to-moment impulses

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Prison
instruction: It's 4 AM. In six hours, you begin a fifteen-year sentence. Your child is asleep, and you're whispering everything you'll miss—their first day of high school, learning to drive, first heartbreak, graduation. Your voice barely makes sound because if you speak any louder, you'll shatter. Describe their sleeping face, the way their hand curls like it did when they were a baby. Tell them why you did what you did, knowing they won't hear, knowing they might never forgive you. Let your whispers catch on tears, on the impossibility of time, on trying to pour fifteen years of love into this single moment. End with the hardest truth: you have to leave this room, close this door, and let them wake up to your absence.

title: I Needed You and You Weren't There
instruction: Confront a parent about a moment in your childhood when you desperately needed them and they failed you. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm, stay fair. But as you speak, old wounds tear open. Your voice should shift from controlled to shaking with suppressed rage, then break into the wounded child still inside you. Include the moment you realize they still don't understand, may never understand. Let your anger collapse into something more devastating: grief for the relationship you'll never have. End with a choice—do you walk away, or do you reach for connection despite everything? The arc moves from rehearsed composure through justified rage to heartbroken acceptance.
inspired_by: Leaving a Party Without Saying Goodbye

title: The Ascension of Desire
instruction: You are climbing the stairs to your apartment after a triumphant evening at work. You feel a glow of pride, relishing your success. As you reach the fourth-floor landing, you pause, breath catching, and a quieter feeling settles in—contemplation, a sudden awareness of how far you've come. Then, thinking of the person waiting for you upstairs, lust flickers warm in your chest. Let your hyper-feminized voice be light, slightly breathy from the climb, with words breaking into short gasps. Start with a proud, self-congratulatory tone, then soften into thoughtful, then let your voice drop into husky, intimate desire. React naturally to the physical effort: a pause to lean, a sigh, a smile you can't help.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Contemplation (clearly present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Spouse Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're standing over your sleeping spouse, whispering everything you couldn't say to their face because you're leaving—not for someone else, but because staying is slowly killing something essential in you. Your voice is barely audible, tender, filled with the kind of love that hurts because it isn't enough. Begin with simple observations about them sleeping—the way they breathe, the vulnerable curve of their shoulder—your voice thick with affection. Move into confession: whispered apologies for not being the person they need, for the ways you've both slowly stopped seeing each other. Your voice catches on specific memories—the good ones, which somehow make this harder. Let the emotion build not through volume but through the way your breath becomes uneven, the way you have to pause to collect yourself. End with a whispered 'I love you' that's absolutely true and absolutely heartbreaking because love isn't solving this, and your voice reflects that devastating contradiction.
inspired_by: Leaving a Cult: Disorientation Becoming Orientation

title: Breaking Every Dish
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a betrayal, a death, a revelation that rewrites your history. You're alone in your kitchen, and your body needs to move, to break, to feel something match the chaos inside you. Start with your hands shaking, your breath coming fast, energy coiling like a spring about to snap. Then let yourself go—throw, smash, scream, let your voice rip from your gut in sounds that aren't even words. Your body takes over completely. But mid-destruction, in the midst of breaking something, let an unexpected wave of physical sensation crash through—maybe it's grief that drops you to your knees, maybe it's hysterical laughter, maybe it's a strange euphoria at finally feeling something real. End with your body exhausted, on the floor, breathing hard, but somehow more alive than you've felt in years. Let rage transform into raw, physical presence.
inspired_by: Actor is in a rigid or resistant environment (conservative director, non-exploratory cast) and needs to establish irreverent freedom before scene work

title: Trapped in a Time Loop: The Seventh Repetition
instruction: You've lived this day seven times. Narrate it with bone-deep weariness. You know exactly what everyone will say — mouth the words along with them sarcastically. Try changing one thing: different coffee order, different route. It doesn't matter. The despair of infinite repetition should make every sentence exhausted. Include a moment of rage — screaming at the sky. Then acceptance. Then a tiny detail you've never noticed before. Your voice changes: 'Wait. That's new. That's... that wasn't here before.'

title: Cushion Confession: A Giggling Grudge
instruction: You're lying face-down in bed, your face shoved into a thick pillow, speaking to an empty room. You're a young woman with a high, breathy voice, and you're replaying the memory of a recent encounter. Start with a muffled, bitter laugh—you're amused by how pathetic the situation is, but that amusement quickly turns into a hot, frustrated lust. Your voice is almost entirely smothered; you have to push the sound out from deep in your chest. Feel the pillow's fabric against your lips, and let your mood swing: begin with a snorting, sarcastic giggle at the absurdity of wanting someone who doesn't care, then let your voice go heavy and low as you admit to the raw sexual hunger, and finally end with a light, wheezy chuckle as you catch yourself confessing to a pillow. Speak as if you're both mocking yourself and aching with desire, your words half-slurred by the cushion.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Bitterness (slightly present), Amusement (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Day of Everything
instruction: You are speaking to your best friend on the day before you move across the world—a move that's everything you've dreamed of, a massive opportunity, the adventure of a lifetime. You're thrilled. You're terrified. You're heartbroken. This friend has been your anchor for fifteen years, and you both know this goodbye is the end of something irreplaceable. Begin with excited chatter about the future, trying to keep it light, making plans to video chat that you both know won't sustain what you have. But you can't maintain the cheerfulness—grief keeps breaking through. Let yourself oscillate: genuine excitement about your new life cuts suddenly into panic about leaving, gratitude for your friendship collides with resentment that they can't be happy for you without sadness, joy about your future crashes into mourning for what you're losing. End in a place where all these emotions exist simultaneously—laughing through tears, or celebrating while grieving, unable to separate the contradictions, all of it heartbreakingly real and present at once.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty exposing aspects of themselves onstage

title: The Last Conversation Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin in a place of frantic denial—you can't let yourself feel the reality yet, so you're chattering about mundane memories, forcing lightness into your voice. As you speak, allow your body to gradually acknowledge what your mind refuses: notice the weight in your chest, the temperature of the room, the sound of their breathing. Midway through, stop running from the truth—let a silence open where you finally inventory what you're actually feeling beneath the performance. By the end, speak from that raw, honest place: transform from desperate distraction into genuine presence, saying what truly matters while you still can. Your voice should move from artificially bright to quiet, grounded, and utterly real.

title: The Last Plate
instruction: You're a young man washing dishes by hand, the water running hard, ceramic clinking. You feel helpless — trapped in a repetitive chore that mirrors a life you didn't choose. As you scrub a stubborn pan, you concentrate fiercely, letting the white noise and warmth pull you into the moment. Start speaking to yourself with heavy, defeated breaths, then let your voice shift as you notice the strange contentment in this small, controlled act. End with a quiet, almost surprised acceptance, your tone louder over the water but softer inside.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Concentration (clearly present), Contentment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Comrade Supporting
instruction: Your friend is at rock bottom, on the phone, considering ending it. Your voice is the only steady thing in the world right now. You're not trying to fix it. You're just saying: 'I'm here. I'm staying on the phone.' Hours pass. Your voice gets tired, but it doesn't leave. When they finally say 'I think I want to live,' your voice breaks—the first time—and all that strength was real. 'Thank God. Thank God.'

title: The Last Lap Alone
instruction: You're a child swimming on your back in a quiet pool, head tilted up, gasping for air between strokes. You start by whispering to yourself about the girl or boy you've been crushing on—how their laugh sounds like water splashing. Midway, you remember they're moving away tomorrow, and your voice chokes as you tread water, letting the shimmering silence fill the gaps. Let the water's rhythm break your thoughts; pause to wipe your eyes or cough, letting infatuation slip into quiet sadness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Ride Home
instruction: You are an elderly man in the back of a rattling old taxi at dusk. The engine hums low, tires sing on wet pavement. You just left the hospital after being told the tumor is benign. You stare out at the rain-streaked streetlights, and the enormous relief catches you mid-breath. You turn to the driver, your voice breaking with unexpected gratitude. Start with the stunned, shallow breath of a person who hasn't yet allowed themselves to feel the joy — then let the words tumble out, thick with emotion, laughing and crying a little as you realize you get to go home.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Relief (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation at Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love who has hours left to live. Begin by noticing everything you're actually feeling in this moment - the weight in your chest, the dryness in your throat, the way your hands want to move. As you speak to them, let yourself track honestly what's happening inside you from sentence to sentence: perhaps you start trying to be strong, then notice you're pretending, then let that pretense crack. Maybe anger surfaces that they're leaving you, or relief mixed with shame, or numbness that frightens you. Follow each feeling as it shifts - don't decide what you 'should' feel at a deathbed. By the end, allow yourself to arrive at whatever unexpected emotion emerges when you stop controlling the moment. Speak softly, tracking the truth of each breath.

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You've just inherited your estranged grandmother's house and you're walking through it for the first time in twenty years. She raised you for a few years when your parents couldn't, and she was both your salvation and your tormentor—she fed you, kept you safe, but she was also bitter, critical, sometimes cruel. As you move through the rooms, touching her things, begin with defiant relief that she's gone. You're almost celebratory—you survived her, you escaped, and now you get to sell this place and be done with it forever. Let your voice carry that brittle victory. But then you find something: her reading glasses on a book, a sweater that still smells like her, photographs of you as a child where she's smiling (you forgot she ever smiled). Let the complicated truth flood in—she saved your life even as she wounded you. You wouldn't exist without her cruelty and her care intertwined. Let gratitude and grief crash into your anger and relief. Your voice breaks between laughter and sobbing—you want to thank her and scream at her, you miss her and you're glad she's dead, you forgive her and you never will. End in a place where you're speaking directly to her, saying 'thank you' and 'I hate you' and meaning both with your whole heart.
inspired_by: Character Background Story Imaging: Love from a Stranger (Bluebeard)

title: Fantasy: Cursed Being Realizes Breaking the Curse Requires Murdering Their Love
instruction: Speaking to your love, your voice is tender and desperate. You must tell them what breaking the curse requires. Your voice is gentle while asking for the cruelest thing. Your breathing becomes someone balanced on the edge of impossible choice. You're offering love or freedom—you cannot have both. Your voice is the sound of having to choose which destruction you can live with. Your breath deepens as you wait for their answer, knowing either way, you're lost.

title: The Creaking Music Box
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting at a cluttered workbench, trying to repair a treasured music box that belonged to your late partner. You've had a few sips of whiskey to steady your hands, and the world feels a little soft at the edges. As you gently tap the brass mechanism with a small hammer, each strike makes you grunt with effort and pause to check your work. Start with tired concentration, slightly slurred from the whiskey, then let a quiet, growing hope bloom as you realize the melody might play again. Your voice should be interrupted by the metallic clinks and your own breathy grunts, losing a thought mid-sentence as you focus on the repair.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: I Can't Fix This
instruction: Your parent calls in crisis—nothing's working, they've lost important documents, they're panicking. You try to help but realize they've been scammed, their savings possibly gone. Your patient tone shatters into fierce protectiveness: 'What did you click?! I TOLD you about this!' Then immediately devastated: 'I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I shouldn't yell.' You feel helpless rage at the scammers, at aging, at your own inability to protect them from a world that's left them behind. Your voice breaks between anger and tears. Try to regain control, guide them through damage control, but the helplessness keeps surging. End with a raw admission: 'I don't know if I can fix this, but I'm not leaving you alone with it.'
inspired_by: The World's Most Patient Tech Support Call with an Elderly Parent

title: The Return to the Empty House
instruction: You're walking through your childhood home, now emptied after a parent's death, preparing to sell it. Start with practical detachment—you're here to work, to measure, to decide what goes where. But as you move through rooms, let sensory details catch you without resistance: dust patterns in afternoon light, the echo of your footsteps, a stain on the wall, a particular smell. Allow images to flood in unbidden from these triggers—laughter and violence, safety and fear, holiday mornings and terrible nights. Don't organize these contradictions; let them coexist and pull you in multiple directions simultaneously. Your voice should reflect this chaos of joy and grief, love and resentment arriving together. End in a place where opposing emotions have transformed you into something you weren't when you walked in—perhaps grateful and furious at once, perhaps empty and overflowing, perhaps finally free and devastatingly lost.

title: The Homecoming Paradox
instruction: You're returning to a childhood home after years away, walking through the door to a surprise celebration for an achievement you've worked your whole life for. Everyone you love is there, beaming with pride. But earlier today, you received devastating news that no one here knows yet—something that changes everything. Begin by taking in the sensory reality: the specific faces looking at you with love, the smell of familiar food, the sound of celebration, the exact feeling of their embraces. Start from a place of forced brightness, trying to match their joy. As you immerse yourself in these sensory details—their voices, their touch, the taste of celebration on your tongue—allow the contradiction to become unbearable. Let joy and devastating grief collide authentically. Move toward a moment where you can no longer maintain the performance, and the two truths must somehow coexist. Let sensory awareness, not theatrical choice, reveal how these opposites live in your body simultaneously.

title: The Baptism of Rage
instruction: You're standing in the rain, drenched, outside the office where you were just fired after fifteen years of loyalty. Your body is shaking—from cold, from fury, from humiliation. Begin speaking to yourself, to the universe, to the building behind you. Let your physical sensations guide your voice—the water running down your face, your clenched fists, your racing heart. Start with disbelief, words catching in your throat. Then let the rage build: scream if you need to, but also let it drop to a growl, a sob, a laugh. This isn't just anger about losing a job—it's every time you've swallowed your truth, made yourself smaller, chosen safety over authenticity. Let your body shake and your voice crack. As the rain continues to pour, something begins to wash away. The rage transforms into something wild and free. End with your voice carrying exhilaration mixed with grief—you've lost everything, but you've also just found yourself again. Let the final moment be almost euphoric despite the tears.

title: Parent Confronts the Drunk Driver Who Killed Their Teenager—In Court
instruction: You stand to give your victim impact statement. Begin with rage so pure it's almost serene—your voice is blade-sharp, cutting, controlled. You describe your child in devastating detail: their laugh, their plans for college, the text message they sent two minutes before impact. Your anger builds, voice rising, hands shaking. But then mid-sentence, looking at this twenty-three-year-old who destroyed everything, you see someone's else's child. The rage collapses into something more terrible: shared human fragility. Your voice breaks completely—not into forgiveness, never that—but into the helpless recognition that this won't bring them back. Scream if you need to, then find yourself whispering, 'They had a name.' End in the ruins between vengeance and exhaustion, fury and devastating grief, never resolved, never clean, just brutally, authentically real.
inspired_by: HR Manager Fires Someone They've Known for Fifteen Years

title: The Last Voicemail You'll Never Send
instruction: You're alone in your car, phone in hand, about to call your best friend to share exciting news—you got the job, you're moving to the city you both dreamed about. Your finger hovers over their name. Then you remember: the funeral was yesterday. Start with breathless excitement, already forming the words. Let the realization crash over you in waves. Try to say it anyway, as if they could still hear: 'We did it, we're going to—' Your voice fractures. The 'we' becomes 'I' and it feels like betrayal. End in a whisper, telling them something you never got to say, your excitement curdling into the most tender, devastating goodbye.
inspired_by: Talking About Them As If They're Still Alive

title: I Needed You to Be Different
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a lifetime of them choosing their own mythology over being present for you. Start with measured control—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, to acknowledge their achievements, the life they built that others admire. But as you speak, the hurt underneath begins to crack through. Your voice tightens. You're not talking about the legend anymore—you're talking about the school plays they missed, the nights you waited up, the way you learned to need nothing from them. The anger builds but then breaks into something more devastating: grief for the relationship you never had. By the end, you're not shouting—you're quietly asking them, with your voice stripped of all protection, 'Did you ever just want to be my parent instead of being important?'

title: The Morning Paper
instruction: You're an elderly man settled into your worn armchair, the morning sun warming your face as you read the newspaper with a quiet, contented sigh. Your spouse shuffles in and launches into a familiar, cyclical complaint about the garbage you forgot to take out—again. Start from that peaceful contentment, then let your voice climb into a nasal, high-pitched whine as you repeat the same excuses, stumbling over words, rustling the paper, and sighing deeply. By the end, your contentment is gone, replaced by weary, frustrated repetition.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Echo Laughs
instruction: You are a child alone in a huge, empty gymnasium. You've just escaped a tense, scary situation, and the relief floods through you so strongly that you start to laugh, a little breathless. At first, your laugh is quiet and shaky from the release, then you hear the echoing sound bounce off the walls—and that surprises you into real amusement. You giggle, call out a word to hear it repeat, and kick a stray ball, grinning at the strange, hollow sound your voice makes. Let your voice be thin and echoey, with the squeak of your sneakers on the polished floor between your words.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Amusement (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Mirror
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent who was never emotionally present. Start with controlled anger that's been building for decades: 'I needed you. Do you understand that? I was a child, and I needed you.' Your voice is sharp, precise, cutting. 'I watched other kids get picked up when they fell. Get told they mattered. I watched and waited and you never came.' The anger begins to crack, revealing the wounded child beneath. 'I spent thirty years trying to earn something you should have given freely.' Your voice wavers between rage and desperate pleading. 'I became successful. I became kind. I became everything I thought would make you see me.' Then the shift—the anger collapses into exhausted truth: 'But I'm done. I'm done performing for your approval.' Your voice drops to something raw and real: 'I'm telling you now—I needed a parent, and you weren't there. That's the truth. That's what happened.' End with painful liberation: 'And somehow... somehow I have to find peace with that.' The confrontation leaves you emptied but finally, devastatingly honest.

title: What I've Never Said Out Loud
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, unable to sleep. They're awake too. In the darkness, you finally whisper the secret you've carried alone for years—something about yourself you've been ashamed of, terrified would make them leave. Begin with your voice barely audible, your breathing shallow, testing each word before you speak it. Feel your heart pounding as you reveal yourself piece by piece, expecting rejection with every sentence. But as you continue, notice something shifting—the relief of finally being known, the weight lifting as you speak truth into the darkness. By the end, let your whisper carry wonder and fragile hope. This isn't dramatic confession—it's intimate, quiet, with long pauses where fear and courage battle. Let vulnerability make you almost childlike.

title: The Weight of Years, the Light of Touch
instruction: You are an elderly man, your voice once deep and commanding now softened by age, lying beside your lifelong partner in the dim glow of late evening. You begin with a quiet contentment, your hand tracing the familiar lines of their face, your words slow and rumbling like a satisfied purr. As you whisper memories of your first kiss and feel the warmth of their skin, the contentment deepens into a raw, tender affection that cracks your voice and leaves you breathless between words. Let your breathing fall into a gentle rhythm, your words punctuated by soft kisses and sighs, and let the final 'I love you' be a fragile, overwhelming confession that surprises even you.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Trembling Authority
instruction: You are a guest lecturer in a crowded, warm auditorium. The person you've secretly been infatuated with for months sits in the third row, occasionally catching your eye. You're talking about the architecture of cathedrals, but your mind keeps veering off — you lose track of a sentence, feel your cheeks flush, then force yourself to project and slow down. You doubt you're hiding it well, that your voice sounds breathy or strained, and you're terrified they can see right through you. Start with a confident, projected explanation about stone pillars, but let your words drift as you try to refocus, ending with a quieter, more personal remark about what makes a structure 'sacred.'
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Garden of Forgiveness
instruction: You're scattering the ashes of someone who hurt you deeply, and you're laughing through tears at the absurdity that you're the one doing this, that you still came. Start with bitter, broken laughter—almost hysterical—as you talk to their remains about all the ways they failed you, voice edged with old anger. But the laughter keeps catching, turning into sobs, because despite everything, you're crying for them, for the relationship you never had, for the parent or lover or friend they could never be. Your voice softens into something unbearably tender as you thank them for the few good moments—there were some, you admit, voice wondering and sad. You're simultaneously furious and grateful, grieving and relieved, voice shifting between tones as you try to make sense of loving someone who caused you so much pain. End in quiet peace, voice steady for the first time, saying 'I forgive you' and meaning it, even as tears still fall, finding strange grace in letting both the love and the hurt finally rest.

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are whispering to someone you love in complete darkness—maybe they're asleep beside you, maybe they're far away and you're speaking to their absence. Begin with your voice barely audible, sharing a secret you've carried since childhood: a moment of shame, desire, or fear that has shaped everything about you. As you speak, feel your breath become uneven, your throat tighten and release. Let small, involuntary sounds escape—whimpers, sighs, something that comes from deeper than language. Your body should be still but trembling with the effort of release. This isn't loud confession; it's the kind that comes from your bones. By the end, your whisper has transformed into something else: not louder, but more elemental, more true. You are vibrating with vulnerability, and somehow, impossibly, this feels like strength.

title: Goodbye at Gale's Edge
instruction: You stand on a cliff, a fierce gale whipping your hair and clothes, salt spray stinging your eyes. You're saying a final goodbye to someone who has just died—perhaps a parent or best friend. The wind rips your words away, so you shout at first, desperate to be heard, your voice cracking with raw sadness. As you speak, you turn your head to breathe, losing and regaining thoughts. The effort exhausts you, and by the end, your voice drops to a fragile whisper, the fight gone, leaving only hollow acceptance as the wind swallows the last words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Reading You Like I Wrote You
instruction: Your child (or someone you raised) has just achieved something magnificent, and you're watching them celebrate across the room. Observe every detail: how they've learned to make themselves smaller when receiving praise, how they scan for your approval even in their triumph, how they touch their collarbone when overwhelmed—all the tiny defensive behaviors you recognize because you taught them, unconsciously, through your own anxieties. Begin with pride and joy, cataloguing their success and beauty. Then let the realization devastate you: you can deduce your own damage in their body language. Every insecurity you tried to hide, they absorbed. Your observation skills—the very thing that makes you perceptive—now shows you exactly how you've shaped their fears. End with a complex surge: overwhelming love and pride mixed with crushing guilt, fierce hope that they'll transcend what you passed down, and gratitude that they're stronger than you ever were.

title: Water Breaking Open
instruction: You are standing in an ocean, waist-deep, after years of being afraid of water following a near-drowning. Someone you trust deeply (lover, best friend, sibling) stands with you, holding both your hands. A wave is coming. Begin in rigid terror—your entire body is locked, your breath is shallow, panic is rising. But as the wave hits and you don't go under, as the water rushes around your body, let something break. The sensation of water on skin, the sound of the ocean, the feeling of being held—experience it all as if you've never felt water before. Let your fear crack into confusion, then into a strange, wild exhilaration. Your sounds should shift from tight gasps to confused laughter to something like ecstatic sobbing. The physical sensation of water should overwhelm you until you can't tell if you're laughing or crying, terrified or euphoric. End in a place of almost painful aliveness.

title: The Apology Written on Skin
instruction: In the intimate darkness of a bedroom, whisper to your lover about something your body remembers that your mind has tried to forget. Begin speaking from the part of you that performs, that pleases, that says what others need to hear—your voice smooth, practiced, careful. You're apologizing for some small thing, keeping everything surface and safe. But as you speak, let your fingers trace their skin, and feel something deeper rising: the part of you that has been silenced, that carries old shame or desire or fear in your very cells.
