Let your whisper break, become jagged, more honest. End by revealing the real apology underneath—not for what you did, but for all the ways you've hidden your true self. Your voice should dissolve from careful performance into trembling authenticity.

title: Confronting Your Dying Parent Who Never Said They Loved You
instruction: Your parent has days left and you finally ask the question you've held for decades: 'Did you ever love me?' Start controlled, clinical—you've rehearsed this. But their silence or their answer cracks something open. Your voice turns sharp, demanding: 'Say it. Just once, say it.' Then it breaks into pleading, childlike: 'Please, I need to hear it.' The anger and desperation collide until you're simultaneously furious and begging, your adult voice and your child voice fighting for control. End either in hollow acceptance or a whispered confession of your own: 'I needed you.' Let rage dissolve into the grief of a lifetime.
inspired_by: Betrayed by Your Best Friend and Trying to Stay Calm

title: Thank You, Stranger
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl calling 911 after a car accident. A stranger pulled you from the wreck and is now lying nearby, bleeding. You're hyperventilating, forcing your voice steady. Begin with frantic gratitude toward the stranger as you describe the scene to the operator, your words tumbling out in sharp bursts. As the call continues, doubt creeps in—you're not sure if you remembered the address correctly, if the stranger is still breathing. End with a quieter, trembling voice, mixing a fragile thankfulness with the heavy weight of uncertainty.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about a family secret you've just discovered that reframes your entire childhood. Begin with righteous anger and accusation. But as you speak, don't plan your words—let everything pour out: your fury, but also the physical tightness in your chest, the memory of her hands braiding your hair, the betrayal, the understanding starting to creep in, your own guilt, the smell of her perfume, your crumbling certainty. Speak continuously without editing: jump between past and present, between rage and tenderness, between question and answer. By the end, arrive somewhere you didn't expect—perhaps at compassion, perhaps at deeper grief, perhaps at reluctant recognition of her humanity. Let the confrontation dissolve into something more complex than anger.

title: The Wedding Toast You Shouldn't Give: Celebrating the Love of Your Life Marrying Someone Else
instruction: You're standing at a wedding reception, champagne glass raised. The person at the center of this celebration is someone you've been in love with for years, and they're marrying someone wonderful—someone kind and right for them, someone who isn't you. You've been asked to give a toast because you're the 'best friend.' Start with warmth and humor, your voice genuinely happy for them—because part of you truly is. Share a funny story, make the crowd laugh. But let there be moments where your voice catches on certain words: 'the way they light up,' 'the person who finally deserved them.' You're smiling, maybe even laughing, but there's something underneath. As you continue, the gratitude becomes almost unbearably sincere. You're thanking them for the years of friendship, for teaching you what love could look like, and your voice is thick with emotion that the room might interpret as sentimental joy, but you know is something more complicated. Let yourself find genuine peace in the moment—they're happy, and their happiness matters more than your heartbreak—but that peace coexists with profound loss. End with your voice warm and breaking at once, raising your glass: 'To love that transforms us, even when it's not ours to keep.' You're celebrating and grieving simultaneously, and both emotions are completely real.
inspired_by: Watching the Tsunami Build: The Moment You Understand You Were Wrong About the Warning

title: What I Never Said
instruction: You're whispering to someone sleeping beside you - a lover, a child, a friend - confessing what you can't say when their eyes are open. Begin barely audible: 'I don't know if you know how scared I am...' Your voice is so tender it almost dissolves. Describe your fears of inadequacy, of losing them, of not being enough - let vulnerability crack you open. 'Sometimes I look at you and I can't breathe from loving you so much.' Your breath catches; tears are close but quiet. By the end, arrive at a whispered vow that trembles with emotion: 'I'm staying. Even when I'm terrified, I'm staying.' The intensity is profound but contained - everything important said in the smallest voice.

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: You're getting ready to marry the love of your life, but your sibling just died three days ago. Begin in fractured chaos—one moment touching your wedding dress with wonder, the next moment collapsing with grief, unable to reconcile these opposites. Your breath catches, releases, catches again. As you continue preparing, make yourself fully present to every sensation: the silk of the fabric on your skin, the weight of jewelry, the scent of flowers, the morning light. Feel how your body can hold both ecstasy and devastation simultaneously. Let yourself fully experience the sweetness of this joy AND the bottomless ache of loss, not choosing between them but letting both be completely true. By the end, you're speaking to your reflection with a raw, broken wholeness—promising to carry both your sibling and your beloved with you, your voice trembling but clear with fierce, complicated love.

title: I Never Held You Enough
instruction: You're confronting your now-grown child who has just told you they're cutting contact. They say, 'You were always too busy, too tired, too distant.' Start by defending yourself with frustration and mounting anger—list all the sacrifices you made, all the ways you provided. But as you speak, let the anger crack and crumble. Hear your own hollow justifications. Realize mid-sentence that they're right. Let your voice shift from defensive rage to broken recognition: 'I thought... I thought I was doing enough. I thought there would be more time.' End on a raw, urgent plea that comes too late: 'Let me learn how to hold you now. Please.' Move from righteousness to devastation, from anger to desperate, naked vulnerability.
inspired_by: Teaching Something You're Ashamed You Don't Know

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent everything you've held back for decades—how their absence shaped you, how you needed them and they weren't there. Start with controlled anger, words you've rehearsed in your head for years, your voice sharp and accusatory. But as you speak, something shifts. You hear how old they sound, how small they've become. The anger begins to crack, revealing the child underneath who just wanted to be loved. Your voice moves from accusation to pleading, from strength to breaking. By the end, you're not condemning them anymore—you're grieving the relationship you'll never have, asking them why through tears. Let the anger dissolve into the sadness it was always protecting. Let yourself become young again.
inspired_by: Singing a Lullaby That Becomes Crying

title: Rocking Your Mother as She Forgets You
instruction: You're in a rocking chair, holding your mother who no longer recognizes you, gently swaying as you once did when she rocked you as a child. Start by describing the motion tenderly, trying to soothe her confusion, your voice steady and loving. But as you rock, confront her with the painful truth—not angrily, but with devastated honesty—about how it feels to be erased from her memory while you still need her. Your tone should shift from caretaker-gentle to raw vulnerability: 'Do you know how much I needed you to see me succeed? To tell me I did okay? You're still here but you're already gone.' Let your voice break as you continue rocking, the motion now feeling like a desperate attempt to rock back time itself. End with fierce tenderness—angry that she's leaving you this way, but still cradling her with all the love you have left.

title: Telling Your Dying Spouse About the Life You'll Live Without Them
instruction: Your partner is in their final days, lucid but weak. They ask you to promise you'll be happy after they're gone. Begin with gentle resistance—half-laughing, half-crying, saying 'Don't talk like that,' your voice breaking between hope and reality. But they insist, and you realize this is their final gift to you: permission to live. Your voice fills with this impossible mixture: you're smiling through tears, describing the garden you'll plant in their memory, the trip you'll take, how you'll tell stories about them. You're laughing at a memory, then suddenly choked with grief. Your voice radiates gratitude for every moment you had while simultaneously shattering with the loss. 'Thank you for choosing me,' you say, and it's the most beautiful, broken, grateful thing you've ever spoken. End with this paradox fully present: peace and devastation, love and goodbye, the purest joy of having known them and the deepest sorrow of letting go.
inspired_by: Telling Your Best Friend You Can't Be Friends Anymore

title: Gravely Grateful Over the Air
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, alone in your cluttered garage, trying to fix a stubborn lawnmower engine. You're using an old walkie-talkie to call your neighbor for help—the button gives a sharp 'kkhht' before each transmission, and the speaker crackles with narrow static. Start with a gruff, impatient sigh as you press the talk button; your first words are clipped and testy, annoyed that you had to call at all. As you explain the problem and hear your neighbor's patient reply through the speaker, let your voice soften mid-sentence—hesitate, clear your throat, and end with a reluctant but genuine 'thanks' that trails off into a quiet 'over.' The final words should carry a weary gratitude, not eager but real, as if you're admitting you needed the help.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: A Promise Broken in the Dark
instruction: You’re lying in a dark room, the blinds drawn, a cold cloth over your eyes. Every sound feels like a spike in your skull. You have to cancel plans with a close friend for the third time this month. Start by whispering an apology, voice thin and fragile, wincing as you speak. Let the disappointment build — not just at the situation, but at your own body for failing you. By the end, the whisper carries a heavy, resigned ache. Let there be natural pauses: you flinch at a car horn outside, lose your train of thought, then find it again with a soft sigh.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Gratitude Order
instruction: You're at a small cafe, trying to decide what to order, but you keep laughing - inappropriately, uncontrollably - because you just got the cancer diagnosis you've been dreading, and somehow the normalcy of choosing between soup or salad is the most absurd, beautiful thing you've ever experienced. Start with genuine laughter that catches in your throat, joy and devastation braided together. Your voice should shimmer between wonder and breaking: 'Isn't it strange? I might have six months, and I'm worried about whether the sandwich comes with fries.' Find surprising peace in the mundane choice. End with tearful gratitude as you order everything you want - no more waiting, no more careful choices - your voice full of heartbreak and liberation. You're laughing and sobbing and somehow, impossibly, you've never felt more alive. Let contradictions live together: terror and freedom, grief and celebration, endings and beginnings.

title: The Lullaby in the Wrong Language
instruction: You're singing a lullaby to your dying grandmother, but you've forgotten most of the words in her native tongue - the language she raised you with before dementia took her memories. Start singing with confidence, even joy, in the fragments you remember, your voice warm and tender. But as you stumble over words, mixing in English approximations, let the realization wash over you in waves: you've lost her language, and now you're losing her. Your voice should grow increasingly fragile, catching on syllables that won't come. End in a whispered confession in English - an apology for forgetting, for becoming too American, for losing this last thread connecting you. Let tears live in your throat, making the words barely audible but devastatingly intimate.

title: Ecstatic Joy: Winning the Impossible
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything — the transplant donor was found, the verdict is not guilty, the pregnancy test is positive after years of trying. Perform the shockwave: stunned silence, then the gasp, then the scream of joy that dissolves into sobbing. Speech is impossible — just fragments ('Oh my God, oh my God'). Call someone to tell them but can't get the words out through laughing-crying. Let the joy be so big it sounds like pain.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Flight
instruction: You're at the airport, saying goodbye to your sibling who's leaving for a dangerous humanitarian mission they may not return from. You started this conversation trying to be supportive and brave, making small talk about their flight snacks and weather forecasts—the same nervous avoidance you've always used to dodge real emotion. But as the final boarding call approaches, that protective wall crumbles. Let yourself break open. Move from those awkward, chattering attempts to fill silence, through the rising panic of unsaid things, to finally speaking the raw truth: how much you've needed them, how terrified you are, how you never learned to say 'I love you' without hiding it in jokes. End in a place of devastating honesty, where words finally fail and only presence remains. Let your voice crack, let silences hold weight, let the goodbye be messy and real and incomplete.

title: The Last Stroke
instruction: You are an elderly woman in your bathroom, shaving the soft fuzz from your upper lip with an electric razor. The hum fills the small space as you pull the skin taut, distorting your mouth. You think of your granddaughter, who gave you this razor last year for your birthday. At first, your voice is matter-of-fact, slightly breathy from the effort of contorting your face. Then, as you finish and switch off the razor, the silence feels like a gift. Let the words start muddled and practical, then soften into a quiet, grateful tremor as you speak to the reflection of the girl you raised.
emotions_sampled: Affection (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Endless Sleepover
instruction: You are a little girl at a sleepover, but you haven't slept in two days. You're describing the most amazing dream you just had – except you're still half-awake, words spilling out faster than you can think. Start giddy and loud, giggling at nothing, your voice high and breathless. But as you speak, your eyelids droop, your sentences fragment, and a yawn sneaks in. End with a quiet, slurred admission that you're tired, your interest fading into exhaustion.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Plea
instruction: You are a proud, elderly man who has raised his voice in anger one too many times. Your adult child stands before you, bags packed, ready to walk out of your life for good. You start by scoffing— a bitter, contemptuous laugh at the absurdity of it all. But as they turn to leave, your voice breaks. You scramble after them, words tumbling out in a rush, your pitch climbing, breath shaky. You grab their arm, then let go, ashamed. Your final words are a quiet, desperate whisper, stripped of all pride.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unspoken Truth: Adult Child Confronts Aging Parent About Lost Years
instruction: You're facing your parent who is now frail and forgetting, finally speaking the words you've carried for decades about the childhood they weren't present for. Begin with carefully controlled words, trying to be gentle because they're elderly now, trying to be fair. But the floodgates open—years of waiting for them to notice you, to choose you, to see you pour out in raw, unfiltered pain. Your voice moves from measured hurt to angry accusation, demanding answers they can no longer give because their mind is slipping away. Then devastation hits: you're losing your chance to ever truly be heard, to ever receive the apology you needed. End in broken forgiveness mixed with grief, telling them you love them while mourning the parent-child relationship you'll never have and the closure that's dissolving before your eyes.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Must Deactivate Its Own Creator

title: The Midnight Revision
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're alone, whispering to yourself in the dark, replaying a moment of humiliation from your past—a time someone made you feel worthless. Begin by reliving it exactly as it happened, your whisper tight with shame, your body curling inward. But then, consciously, gently, begin to speak it differently. Change one detail—what you said, how you stood, the look in your eyes. Whisper this new version. Then whisper it again, changing more. Each retelling, you become slightly braver, slightly more whole. Your voice should remain quiet throughout, but shift from constricted shame to tender self-protection. By the final whispered retelling, you're speaking to your past self with the compassion you needed then, rewriting the memory breath by breath until shame transforms into quiet, fierce self-love.
inspired_by: Actor has identified a specific historical experience causing lasting damage to self-esteem

title: What I Whisper in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM, and you're lying next to someone you love, unable to sleep because of something you've never told them—a fear, a shame, a secret that makes you feel unworthy of their love. Begin with hesitant, almost inaudible words, testing whether you can even say this out loud. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, fragile as glass. As you speak, feel yourself softening, becoming more vulnerable with each confession. Let the intimacy of darkness and their sleeping presence beside you open something in your chest. By the end, you're not whispering from fear anymore—you're whispering from tenderness, from the strange relief of being seen in your most naked state, even if they might be asleep.

title: Protective Rage Collapsing Into Helplessness: When You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're confronting someone—a doctor, an authority figure, fate itself—about someone you love who is suffering, and there's nothing more you can do. Your voice explodes with fury: 'This is unacceptable! There has to be something!' You're demanding, fierce, almost violent in your intensity. You list everything you've tried, everything you've sacrificed, your voice rising with desperate, protective anger. But as you continue, as you run out of arguments, your rage begins to crack. Your voice falters. The helplessness underneath starts to show: 'Please... there has to be...' You're begging now, and you hate yourself for it, which makes you angry again, but the anger is weaker, more broken. Your voice becomes ragged, torn between fury at your own powerlessness and devastating grief. By the end, you collapse into raw vulnerability, your fierce protectiveness reduced to a whisper: 'I can't lose them. I can't.' Your voice carries the terrible recognition that love, despite its intensity, despite its ferocity, cannot always save what it cherishes most. The strength that defined you dissolves into the most human, most broken admission of defeat.
inspired_by: Kindness Showing Ripple Effects: Realizing Impact You Didn't Know

title: Reading Your Suicide Note Aloud to Your Best Friend
instruction: You attempted suicide last month. You survived. Now your best friend has asked you to read them the note you left behind. Start in a whisper, unable to meet their eyes, your voice fragile as glass. The words on the page are clinical at first, explanations, apologies. Let your voice catch on the phrase where you told them it wasn't their fault. Feel the weight of what you almost did to them. Move into tender devastation as you read the part where you said goodbye, where you listed the small things you'd miss. Your voice should be barely audible here, each word costing you everything. Then pause—look at them now, alive, present, holding your hand. The final part of the note feels like it was written by someone else, someone you no longer are. End by speaking directly to them, off-script: tell them why you're still here, what made you call for help, how their existence mattered. Let this be intimate, broken, and brutally honest.
inspired_by: Two Strangers Stuck in an Elevator: Entire Relationship Arc

title: Threshold Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner of ten years in the middle of the night, both awake but pretending to sleep. You've been carrying a secret—not an affair, but something more vulnerable: you've been terrified of them, of how much they matter, of the fact that loving them feels like standing at the edge of a cliff. Begin in a whisper so quiet it's almost to yourself, admitting 'I'm afraid of you.' Let each sentence come slower than the last, pulled from somewhere beneath your ribs. Your breath catches on words like 'need' and 'stay.' Midway, feel tenderness flood through—this person has held you through everything, never knowing you were braced for them to leave. By the end, you're confessing not fear but gratitude, voice breaking on 'thank you for staying when I kept the door open,' each word a fragile gift in the dark.

title: The Secret You've Kept for Twenty Years
instruction: You're whispering a confession to your best friend, your sibling, or your spouse—something you've carried alone for decades. Maybe you were there when someone died and you could have helped. Maybe you made a choice that changed everything. Maybe you've been protecting someone who didn't deserve it. Speak so quietly they have to lean in to hear you. Your voice should tremble, catch, almost disappear. There's shame here, yes, but also relief—the exhaustion of carrying this weight is finally lifting. Let long pauses speak as loudly as words. By the end, you're not just confessing; you're asking to be seen in your brokenness and loved anyway. The vulnerability should feel almost unbearable to witness.

title: Fire Descending into Ash
instruction: You've just finished screaming at your brother, twenty years of rage finally unleashed about the ways he abandoned your family. Start volcanic—voice at full fury, body coiled like a spring, every muscle engaged in your anger. But as you watch his face crumble, as he doesn't fight back but simply takes it and whispers 'You're right,' feel the fire begin to burn out. Your body starts to lose its aggressive tension, rage melting into something more complex—exhaustion, old grief, the ache of how much time was lost. Let yourself physically descend from that peak of fury, voice dropping from shouts to something quieter, rawer. End almost surprised by your own tenderness, reaching for him, voice barely audible: 'I've missed you so goddamn much.'

title: The Reckoning with Mother
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the childhood she gave you—not abusive, but absent in the ways that mattered. Start with careful control, years of rehearsed words: 'I need to tell you something I've never said.' Your voice is measured, almost gentle. 'You were there, but you weren't there.' Now anger seeps in, decades of unmet needs: 'I needed you to see me, and you were looking somewhere else.' Let your voice break between fury and the child still wanting her love. 'I'm not asking you to fix it—I can't be fixed backward.' End with exhausted clarity, no resolution but truth spoken: 'I'm just telling you. So you know. So I can finally choose myself.'

title: Last Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from your parent's hospice room at 3am. They finally answered after years of silence. Start with your voice tight, almost businesslike: 'You need to come. It's time.' But as you describe what you're seeing—the labored breathing, the way Mom's hand feels cold—your voice begins to fracture. You're trying to be strong, trying to just deliver information, but then you break: 'I can't do this alone. I know we haven't spoken, I know you're angry, but please... she keeps asking for you.' End with raw vulnerability, your voice small and child-like, all pretense gone: 'I'm scared. I don't know how to let her go.' The journey moves from controlled distance to complete emotional collapse, from adult responsibility to the frightened child you both once were.
inspired_by: Small Explosion at Work: Checking Colleagues for Injuries

title: The 3 AM Confession to the Ficus
instruction: You are an elderly woman, standing in your dark living room at 3 AM, staring at a dusty ficus plant. You haven't slept in days—your voice is hollow, compressed, and perpetually low. Begin with deep, weary sourness as you list all the reasons sleep won't come tonight. Let a slight doubt creep in as you question if you ever will sleep again. Midway, a small memory of your cat's ridiculous sleeping pose drifts through your mind; let a quiet, tired amusement flicker across your words before settling back into hollow resignation. Your performance should feel organic—pause to scratch an itch, lose your train of thought, react to the creak of the house, and let the tone shift from bitter to almost wistful and back.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (slightly present), Sourness (very intensely present), Amusement (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Angel at the Party
instruction: You are at a loud, crowded party, a little drunk and giddy with the pleasure of the night. Your neck is twisted awkwardly over your shoulder to face a friend who has just handed you a heartfelt gift or note. Start with a tipsy, ecstatic laugh, but as you speak, the reality of their kindness hits you. Let your voice tighten and strain from the physical twist, and let the intoxication fade into a raw, trembling gratitude that catches in your throat. You stumble over words, lose your train of thought mid-sentence, then find it again as the thankfulness overwhelms you.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Ripple in the Cubicle
instruction: You are a child in a large open-plan office, visiting a parent after hours but now alone near their desk. You find a half-empty bottle of something sweet-smelling under a chair—you take a sip, then another. The room hums with distant murmur and HVAC drones. You try to dial a phone to call a friend, but your fingers feel clumsy, and the numbers blur. Start with a haughty, superior air—you think you've discovered something cool and secret, looking down on the adult world. As you speak into the receiver, your words get slow, a little slurred, and you realize you're not sure what you wanted to say. End in confusion, a quiet moment where the contempt fades into a strange, fuzzy loss of control.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Full Panic Attack: The Spiral
instruction: Perform a realistic panic attack from onset to peak to recovery. Start with a racing thought that catches fire. Hyperventilation takes over — rapid, shallow, desperate breathing. 'I can't breathe' repeated with increasing terror. Chest pain convinces you you're dying. Your voice is high, fragmented, animal. Then the self-rescue: forcing slower breaths, counting, grounding techniques ('Five things I can see...'). The voice slowly — slowly — steadies. Be genuine. This is not melodrama.

title: Skin and Storm
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a terminal diagnosis, a massive betrayal, a sudden loss—and your lover is touching you, trying to comfort you, their hands on your skin. Begin with a physical need for their touch, for human connection, for the anchor of sensation to keep you from flying apart. Let your body respond with hunger, with the desperate desire to feel alive, to be grounded through physical intensity. But encounter the obstacle: grief keeps crashing through arousal, rage interrupts tenderness, your body wants closeness while your mind reels with devastation. Let the sensory experience of touch collide with the chaos of your emotional state. By the end, let these contradictions resolve into something raw and true—perhaps physical release becomes emotional breakdown, or the attempt at passion transforms into clinging desperation, or the hunger for sensation gives way to the need to simply be held.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill the emotional obligation but keeps playing surface emotion without the underlying need and passion

title: The Last Charm
instruction: You're a teenage girl, exhausted after a double shift at the diner, trying to sweet-talk a regular into a bigger tip. Your voice is deliberately low and slow, each word carefully placed — but your eyelids are heavy, and a sour resentment bubbles beneath the smile. Midway through a compliment, you lose your train of thought, and the distress of faking it shows. By the end, the effort drains you entirely; your voice goes flat, and you just let the act fall away.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Distress (slightly present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Moment You Snap
instruction: You've been holding it together - for weeks, months, maybe years. Start with that fake-calm voice, the one you use when you're barely hanging on: 'I'm fine. Everything's fine.' But something small breaks you - a dish, a word, a memory. Suddenly you're NOT fine and the rage explodes: 'I'M NOT FINE!' Your voice is raw, almost screaming, but it immediately cracks into sobs. 'I can't do this anymore. I can't keep pretending.' You're oscillating between fury and complete breakdown, voice switching from loud to choked. Then, in the chaos, something shifts - maybe acceptance, maybe surrender: 'I need help.' Your voice drops, vulnerable and exhausted. 'Please. I need help.' End with fierce determination born from absolute devastation: 'I can't do this alone anymore, but I'm going to survive this.'

title: Standing in Your Mother's Kitchen, Finally Speaking
instruction: You're confronting your mother about something she's denied for twenty years. Before you begin, check in with your actual state: Are your hands shaking? Is your throat tight? Do you feel powerful or terrified or both? Start by voicing these physical and emotional realities - 'I'm standing here and my heart is pounding' or 'I feel like I'm ten years old again.' Let this honest inventory of your present state fuel your confrontation. As you speak your truth, track how your feelings shift: does rage dissolve into sadness? Does fear transform into strength? Does hatred reveal the love beneath it? Don't decide in advance where this goes - follow the real emotional current from moment to moment until you reach whatever shore you actually land on.

title: The Morning After the Fight
instruction: You wake up in a cold, quiet bedroom, sheets tangled, mouth dry. The sour taste of last night's argument is still on your tongue. Your voice is low, gravelly, barely above a croak. Start by muttering to yourself about how stupid it all was, the words thick and sluggish. Let the irritation fester as you move to sit up, but then feel the ache in your chest — the fight wasn't just words. By the end, the sourness melts into a hollow stillness; you whisper an apology to no one, your voice cracking with the effort of waking.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Vigil in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed at 3 AM, holding her hand. She's unconscious. Your voice is barely above a whisper as you tell her things you never could when she was awake: 'I forgive you for not knowing how to love me the way I needed.' Your words are tender, almost a lullaby. You reminisce about small moments—the way she hummed while cooking, her laugh. As you speak, tears come silently. You know these are your last words to her. End with a choked whisper: 'Thank you for trying. I know you did your best.' The entire performance should feel like secrets spoken in sacred darkness, intimate and unbearably sad. This is grief before grief, goodbye while there's still breath.

title: The All-Nighter's Reckoning
instruction: You are a middle-aged man who hasn't slept in over a day, hunched over a kitchen table cluttered with papers and empty coffee cups. You're on the phone with your boss, who just asked why the quarterly report is still unfinished. Your voice is a flat, hollow monotone, words slurring and sometimes you blank out mid-sentence. Start with a burst of irritable impatience—you snap, defensive, cutting off their questions. But as you try to explain, you lose your train of thought, a yawn interrupts, and the shame of letting them down creeps in. End with a quiet, shaky admission, your irritation giving way to exhausted regret.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Final Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from your deathbed, and you have maybe five minutes of clarity left before the morphine takes you under for the last time. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times in your mind. But as you speak, your breath becomes more labored, your thoughts start to slip away mid-sentence. You're fighting to stay present, to say what needs to be said before the fog rolls in permanently. Begin with controlled determination to make peace, but let exhaustion and medication pull your words into softer, more vulnerable terrain. Your pauses grow longer. You forget what you were saying. By the end, you're not sure if you're making sense, but you're pouring out raw love and forgiveness in fragments, your voice fading like a radio signal going out of range.
inspired_by: Treading Water While Calling for Help

title: Reading Your Spouse's Last Letter as You Pack to Leave Them
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter they wrote you years ago—full of promises, dreams, the future you were going to build. Your voice starts with bitter irony, almost mocking how naive you both were. But as you read their words, something unexpected happens. You start laughing—really laughing—at an inside joke you'd forgotten, a moment of joy buried under years of disappointment. The laughter catches in your throat. Suddenly you're crying while still smiling, your voice thick with the impossible tangle of love and grief. You're grateful for what you had and devastated that it's ending. Your voice trembles between warmth and sorrow, finding unexpected peace in honoring what was beautiful even as you say goodbye to what it became. End with a voice full of contradictions—broken but whole, sad but free, loving them and leaving them in the same breath.
inspired_by: News Reporter Discovers Her Source Was Her Daughter All Along

title: What I Couldn't Say Before You Left
instruction: Your person is asleep beside you on what might be your last night together before they leave forever—a deployment, a terminal diagnosis, a relationship ending. You whisper confessions they can't hear, your voice barely audible, intimate as a secret: 'I memorized the way you breathe when you're dreaming.' Your throat catches on words of love you were always too afraid to say plainly. There's tenderness braided with grief, gentle humor mixed with devastating sadness: 'You leave your socks everywhere and I... I'm going to miss finding them.' Your voice should crack in the quietest way, like something precious breaking underwater. End with words you'll never say when they're awake: 'I don't know how to be in a world without you in it.' All of this whispered, aching, impossibly tender.

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You are in the grip of intense physical sensation—choose specifically what this is for you: excruciating pain that's finally subsiding, fever breaking after days of delirium, the peak of sexual release, the moment after violent exertion when your body screams and then floods with endorphins. Begin with your body completely overtaken by this sensation—you can barely form words, only sounds and fragments. As the intensity begins to ebb, let a specific emotional memory surface that this physical state has unlocked: perhaps a moment of childhood ecstasy you'd forgotten, a loss you never fully grieved, a joy you've been too afraid to feel. The physical sensation is a doorway—let it open something you've kept closed. Speak through the sensation, letting your voice be raw, uncontrolled, animal. By the end, as your body quiets, you should arrive at a moment of crystalline emotional clarity that the physical experience has burned away everything to reveal.
inspired_by: Choice Hunt / Building a Repertoire of UC Choices

title: Whispering What You Never Could Say Aloud
instruction: It's late at night, and you're finally speaking the secret you've carried for years—maybe a hidden love, a profound shame, or a truth about yourself you've denied. Your voice starts almost inaudible, each word requiring courage, your breathing shallow and careful as if speaking louder might shatter you. There's tenderness mixed with grief in your tone, and occasional long pauses where you almost can't continue. As you confess, your voice doesn't grow stronger—it grows more fragile, more honest. By the end, you're crying quietly, but there's relief in the tears. Your final words are the simplest truth, spoken so softly they're barely there: an acknowledgment that even though saying it changes everything, you finally feel real.

title: The Last Laugh Before the Break
instruction: You're a young girl carrying a backpack that's too heavy, trudging uphill on a long hike with your parent. You start by teasing them in a sing-song, playful voice, making jokes about their heavy breathing to keep your own spirits up—your words come out in short bursts between steps, a little bouncy. But as your legs burn and your shoulders ache, your teasing fades into ragged, pleading breaths. By the end, you're almost crying, gasping for them to stop, your voice cracking as you shift the load and stumble. Let the effort show: grunt under your breath, pause to catch air, and let the laughter turn hollow before it breaks.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Father's Funeral While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're giving the eulogy and you start with a funny story—something quintessentially him—and genuine laughter bubbles out of you as you remember. Your voice is warm, affectionate, painted with fond exasperation. But mid-laugh, it catches. You keep going, forcing the lightness back, another anecdote, and you're laughing again but now there are tears in your voice too. You're talking about his terrible jokes, his stubborn habits, and you're smiling through the pain because that's what he would want. Your voice weaves between celebration and grief—grateful for every moment, devastated there won't be more. You're thanking him, your voice full of love and loss at once, finding joy in the memories even as they break you. End with something he used to say, your voice tender and ruined and somehow still holding laughter in its cracks: 'Thanks for everything, Dad.'

title: Hiding Nervousness During an Important Interview
instruction: Youre anxious about an interview that means a lot to you. Internally, nerves are high, but you need to appear confident. Describe the flutter inside while presenting yourself calmly. Speak with a steady, assured tone, suppressing any tremor.

title: The Stray Memory in the Quiet Corner
instruction: You are an elderly man in a hushed library, leaning over a worn book beside a friend. The silence presses in, so you whisper—your voice a bare rustle of air, no vibration in your throat. Start with a soft, wry chuckle at a remembered joke, the sound almost lost. Then let the humor dissolve, your whisper slowing as you lose the thread, then find it again, turning inward with deep, wondering contemplation. Your voice should feel intimate and physically strained, as if speaking only to yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Perfect Pour
instruction: You are an older woman, alone in your kitchen at dusk, making a complex sauce from memory. The window is open, and the sounds of the neighborhood drift in as you chop herbs—the knife thuds irregularly against the board, the pan sizzles with butter. You've had one glass of wine, maybe two; your movements are looser, your focus deeply present on the rhythm of the work. A sudden, vivid memory of your grandmother teaching you this very recipe surfaces, and a wave of fierce, quiet elation rises in your chest—not loud, but full-bodied, a private joy. As you stir, you speak to the empty room, your voice competing with the clatter and hiss, finding itself breathless with happiness, until you set the spoon down, the noise fades, and your last words fall into a gentle stillness. Begin contemplative, almost murmuring to yourself, and end with a soft, radiant laugh.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Garden After the Funeral
instruction: You're standing in a garden that belonged to someone you've lost. Spring has come anyway—the bulbs they planted are blooming, bees are humming, everything is alive and beautiful and completely wrong. Start by laughing—actually laughing—at the absurdity: 'You'd love this. It's perfect.' Your voice is light, almost conversational, as if they're right there. But as you describe what you're seeing, grief seeps in through the cracks. You're talking to them about the daffodils, and suddenly you're crying, but still laughing: 'I can't believe you're not here to see this.' The emotions become impossible to separate—profound gratitude for having known them, rage at the unfairness, peace in this moment of beauty, devastation at their absence. End in a place of contradictory wholeness: 'Thank you. God, I miss you. Thank you.' Your voice holds everything at once—the ache and the joy, the ending and the continuing, the goodbye and the eternal presence.

title: Finding Your Own Obituary: The Life You Forgot Living
instruction: You've been declared dead, and someone hands you the newspaper with your obituary. Begin reading it aloud with detached curiosity—these accomplishments, these loved ones, they're just facts. But as you continue, let wonder creep in: 'I did that? I mattered to these people?' Start laughing softly at the absurdity—you're reading your own death notice, it's bizarre and somehow hilarious. But let the laughter catch and transform into tears as the weight of a whole lost life hits you. 'I was loved. I was... somebody.' End with your voice full of contradictory emotions: grief for the life you can't remember, joy at discovering you lived it well, peace in knowing you existed fully even if you can't recall it. Let gratitude and loss become the same feeling, your voice warm despite the tears.
inspired_by: Waking Up and Not Knowing Who You Are

title: The Old Dog's Round
instruction: You are a middle-aged man mid-sparring session with a younger, faster fighter whose every move is liquid grace. As you circle, each missed block or slow read stokes a fierce jealousy—you resent his youth and ease. But halfway through, you land a solid counter-punch, feel the mat under your feet, and hear your own steady exhales. Your voice starts as a sharp, bitter mutter between breaths, full of envy: 'He's just... quicker...' Then, as you reset, switch to a deeper, more contented growl: 'But that shot... that was mine.' Let the gasps, grunts, and the slap of impacts interrupt your words. The arc is from resentful jealousy to a hard-won, quiet contentment in your own endurance and skill.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Contentment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Call That Broke Me Open
instruction: You're a young man who just got a phone call from the hospital. Your father, who has been in a coma for months after a severe accident, has suddenly woken up and is asking for you. For weeks you've been numb with grief and guilt. Now, hearing that voice on the other end, you crumple to your knees in the middle of the living room. Your words come out as gasps, sobs, and laughter. You try to repeat what the nurse says but your mouth can't keep up with your heart. Your voice cracks, pitches soar, and you can barely breathe. Let the joy be raw and painful — the pain of almost losing him still lives in your throat. End with a fragmented, breathless sentence of pure relief.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Garbage on My Corner
instruction: You're an older adult standing on a busy city street corner, waiting for the walk signal. A pile of trash bags has been torn open by dogs, spilling rot and filth across the sidewalk. You're disgusted, and your lower back throbs with old pain from standing too long. Then, a stranger—a kid—stops and starts carefully picking up the mess. You watch them, and a flicker of contentment surprises you, softening your voice. Speak to yourself, half-muttering over the siren and traffic, as your disgust gives way to that tiny warmth.
emotions_sampled: Pain (extremely present), Disgust (extremely present), Contentment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Hospital Window at Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend's hospital bed in the early morning hours. They are slipping away, and you both know these are your final moments together. Begin by watching them sleep, flooded with memories of your shared past—see yourself together as children, as teenagers, through every major moment of your lives. Let these vivid mental pictures wash over you as you hold their hand. When they wake for the last time, move from silent reminiscence into speaking directly to them. Your emotion should shift from quiet, overwhelmed nostalgia to active, present tenderness as you tell them what their friendship has meant. End by helping them let go, your voice becoming both stronger and more broken as you give them permission to leave.
inspired_by: When using the programming process to prepare a role

title: Permission to Leave This World
instruction: You are at your mother's bedside in her final hours. She's been holding on, fighting, and you realize she's waiting for permission to let go. Begin speaking with quiet desperation, trying to keep her here, your voice tight with the refusal to say goodbye. But as you look at her suffering, something shifts. Your voice begins to soften, breaking as you give her the gift she needs: permission to stop fighting. Tell her it's okay to go, that you'll be alright, even as your heart shatters. By the end, your voice should be tender, almost singing her toward peace, even as tears stream down your face. You're celebrating her release while grieving your loss—both emotions fully present, equally true.

title: Burning the Letters
instruction: You're burning every letter your ex-lover ever wrote you, feeding them one by one into a fire. Your hands are shaking—from rage, from the physical act, from touching these pages one last time. Start reading fragments aloud with bitter, mocking intensity, your voice dripping with contempt for the promises they broke. But as the smoke rises and the paper blackens, let your body respond to the heat, the destruction, the finality. You find yourself reading one letter differently—and suddenly you're sobbing while also laughing at the absurdity, your voice raw from smoke and emotion. End in a place where physical sensation, grief, liberation, and even unwanted desire are all surging through you simultaneously, your voice unable to settle on any single feeling.

title: The Ache That Lingers
instruction: You are an older man, just out of a long, steaming bath. Your body is completely limp on the bed — every muscle surrendered to the warmth. Your mind drifts to a bitter argument with your adult son last week. Start with a sour, confused mutter about how he could say such things, your voice slow and loose, almost slurred. As you continue, the relaxation allows the sadness to seep through — a heavy, quiet ache. Let your words trail off, lose a thought, then find it again. End with a tired, honest admission that maybe you were wrong, your voice warmer but sadder, like the bathwater cooling around you.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Sourness (extremely present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bitter Pill, Soft Touch
instruction: You're a gruff, middle-aged man sitting on a couch next to your friend who's crying over a messy breakup. He's describing how his ex left dirty dishes everywhere, and you find yourself disgusted by the details, but you're trying to be supportive. Your voice is low, steady, like a heavy blanket — each sentence falls downward in pitch. But you can't completely hide the sour edge in your throat. Start with a clipped, almost irritated tone as you respond to his complaints, then gradually let your voice soften and slow, matching his breathing, ending with a resigned but caring hum. Keep the words simple: maybe five to seven sentences total, filled with pauses and small shifts.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Shame Spiral
instruction: You've done something unforgivable, and someone has just confronted you. Your voice is small, defensive at first: 'I didn't mean to...' But you know they're right. Your voice becomes quieter, ashamed. You're stumbling through an explanation that sounds hollow even to you. Include the moment you stop defending yourself. Your voice becomes barely audible. You're admitting the worst: 'I... I was selfish. I knew better.' By the end, you're consumed by shame, your voice almost disappearing with self-loathing.

title: The Protector Who Can't Protect Anymore
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt someone you love—a child, a partner, someone vulnerable who can't fight back. Start with controlled fury, voice low and dangerous: 'You don't get to do this.' But as they dismiss you or justify themselves, something inside you explodes. Your voice rises, shaking with rage: 'They trusted you!' The anger is primal, protective, fierce. But then—mid-rage—you break. Because you weren't there when it happened. You couldn't stop it. The fury collapses into anguished helplessness, voice cracking: 'I should have known, I should have...' You're sobbing now, the protector who failed. End with a desperate, broken declaration that mixes threat with plea, love with devastation: 'If you ever—EVER—' but you can't finish because you're too shattered by your own failure to save them.
inspired_by: Telling Your Best Friend You Need Space

title: Whispering to the One Who Won't Wake
instruction: You're speaking softly to someone in a coma—maybe they'll hear you, maybe they won't. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and terrified: 'Hey. It's me. I'm here.' You're confessing things you were too scared to say when they were awake, voice catching: 'I should've told you every day. I love you. I've always loved you.' The words become more urgent, desperate, still quiet but intense: 'Please don't leave without knowing. Please.' Then something releases—your voice becomes even softer, filled with bittersweet peace: 'If you need to go, it's okay. I'll carry you with me.' End with a whispered promise, voice thick with unshed tears but somehow steady: 'I'll be brave. Like you taught me.' Let the performance be intimate, as if the audience is eavesdropping on something sacred—emotions shifting from fear to confession to desperate bargaining to tender release.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Absence
instruction: You're facing your parent after twenty years of silence, and everything you've rehearsed dissolves into something messier. Start with cold, controlled anger—the kind that's been perfected in therapy sessions and imaginary conversations. But as you speak, feel the child inside you emerging, demanding answers they never got. Your voice becomes ragged, accusatory, then suddenly small and pleading. You're forty years old and eight years old simultaneously. You hate them and you desperately need them to say they're sorry, to say they loved you, to give you something you can finally rest with. By the end, you're not sure if you're forgiving them or just exhausted from carrying this weight alone.

title: Reading Your Estranged Sister's Letter at Her Funeral
instruction: She left instructions for you to read this at her memorial—a letter she wrote years ago that you never got. You begin reading her words aloud, and they're funny, so perfectly her that you find yourself almost laughing at an inside joke only you two understood. But the next line guts you: she forgives you for the fight that split you apart, the one where you both said unforgivable things. You're crying now but still half-laughing at her jokes, your voice breaking between gratitude that she wrote this and devastation that you wasted so much time. She ends by saying she always loved you, even in silence. Finish barely able to speak, clutching the paper, your face wet, somehow smiling through complete heartbreak.
inspired_by: Lawyer Wins Case Against Former Mentor Who Destroyed Her

title: The Lie That Became the Truth
instruction: Years ago you told someone a lie to protect them — 'I'm fine,' or 'I don't love you anymore,' or 'It wasn't your fault.' Now you must maintain it even though they're asking point-blank. Perform the original lie in flashback (confident, controlled). Then the same words now — hollow, exhausted, crumbling. The third repetition should reveal that you've said it so many times you almost believe it. Almost. But your voice knows. Voices always know.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling from the airport. You've accepted a research position in Antarctica—eighteen months, minimal contact, dangerous conditions. You start trying to sound excited and reassuring, your voice bright and controlled, but as they ask 'Are you scared?' something cracks open. The fear you've been suppressing floods in—fear of dying alone in the ice, of missing irreplaceable moments, of this being the last time you hear their voice. Your words become fragmented, caught between maintaining strength and admitting terror. By the end, you've moved through the fear into something else: a fierce, almost fierce gratitude for having someone who makes leaving this hard, and a whispered promise that carries both acceptance of danger and determination to return. Let your voice break, rebuild, break differently.

title: Concur Finally
instruction: You've fought this person for years. Politics, parenting styles, everything. You're exhausted. They make a point and your voice—almost against your will—admits it: 'You're right. You've always been right about this.' It costs you something to say. But saying it aloud feels like setting down a weight. Your voice becomes quieter, sadder maybe, but also relieved. 'I don't want to fight anymore.' The concurrence is actually surrender to peace.

title: The Last Game
instruction: You are a father teaching your young child to play catch in the backyard after a long, frustrating day at work. You're tired, a little irritable, and just want a quiet moment. Your kid keeps throwing wild, but you're trying to be patient. Suddenly, a hard throw hits you square in the gut, knocking the wind out of you. You double over, gasping, but you see your child's terrified face — so you force a pained, breathless laugh and try to reassure them, even as you're fighting to breathe and your irritation is barely held in check. Start from just before the impact, let the 'oof' be real, and let your voice be shaky, short-winded, and strained as you switch from annoyance to a fragile, goofy amusement to calm their fear.
emotions_sampled: Fear (extremely present), Amusement (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You are confronting your father after years of silence about your childhood. Begin with trembling restraint, your body tight with decades of swallowed words. As you speak, let yourself recall specific moments—the texture of the wallpaper in the hallway where you waited for him, the particular sound of his footsteps, the smell of his aftershave that still makes your stomach clench. Start with controlled anger, each word measured. But as sense memories flood you—his hands, his voice, specific incidents—let the anger crack open into something more complex: grief for the parent you needed, fury at what was done, and underneath it all, the terrible persistence of love for someone who hurt you. End with your voice raw, no longer controlled, speaking a truth that costs you everything.
inspired_by: Sense Memory with Emotionally Impacting Objects

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight That Never Lands
instruction: You're calling your partner from the airport, about to board a flight. You both know—without saying it directly—that this plane is going to crash. Intelligence reports, a premonition, a warning you can't explain. Your partner is begging you not to board, voice breaking, but you have to go—someone you love is on that plane, or this is the only way to stop something terrible. Start with forced lightness, trying to comfort them, making promises about 'when you get back.' Let that facade crack as their desperation reaches you. End in the quiet space where you both stop pretending, where 'I love you' means 'goodbye,' and your voice becomes tender, memorizing the sound of theirs, accepting what comes next.
inspired_by: Time Traveler Warning Themselves Not to Go

title: The Hospital Room Ultimatum
instruction: You're a parent screaming at the universe in your child's ICU room after the doctors have left. Start with explosive rage—punching the wall, voice raw and guttural, demanding answers from a God you're not sure you believe in. Your fury is volcanic: 'Take me instead!' But as your voice gives out from screaming, something breaks. You collapse into the chair beside their bed, and your rage transforms into helpless, gasping sobs. Your voice becomes small, childlike, bargaining now instead of demanding: 'Please, please, I'll do anything.' End with your hand on theirs, voice reduced to a broken whisper, telling them about the future you'd planned together—first day of school, graduation, their wedding—each word a knife. Let fierce protectiveness and absolute powerlessness war in every syllable.

title: The Dress That Remembers
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting on the edge of your bed, pulling a heavy velvet dress over your head. The fabric swooshes past your ears, sometimes muffling your voice. You grunt as you bend to buckle your shoes. Start with a tired sigh, but as your fingers trace the embroidered lace, a memory of your late husband’s hand in yours at a dance hall floods in. Let your voice lift from weariness to a trembling, breathless elation—almost a laugh that catches in your throat. Speak to the dress as if it holds that moment, your words growing thicker with pleasure as you remember the sway of the music and the warmth of his palm.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dead End in Echo Hall
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman who has spent weeks navigating this cave system, hoping to discover a hidden chamber described in old journals. Now, you stand at a dead end—a solid rock wall where the map promised an opening. The disappointment is a dull thud in your chest, but as you stand in the vast, dripping cavern, your own breath and the distant plink of water start to fill the space. Your voice begins tight, tired, with a flat, resigned tone; let the disappointment show in the slight droop of your shoulders and a sigh that echoes back. Then, as you look around, notice the strange beauty of the rock formations, the way the low light makes the walls shimmer—your voice should soften, becoming slower, more reflective, losing its edge of frustration. You end not with joy, but with a quiet, tired acceptance, a recognition that the cave itself is enough, even if it gave you nothing you came for.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Acting Encouraging Despite Believing in Imminent Failure
instruction: Someone is attempting something you think will fail. Internally, you doubt their success, but you encourage them. Describe your pessimism inside while offering support. Speak with positivity, masking your true expectations.

title: The Breaking Point Declaration
instruction: You're a parent standing between your child and danger—an abuser, an addiction, a destructive path—and you've finally had enough. Begin with fierce, protective rage: 'Not my child. Not anymore.' Your voice is iron, shaking with fury. But as you describe what you've watched them endure, the anger cracks into anguish. 'I should have stopped this sooner.' Your voice rises to a roar of self-hatred and helplessness, then suddenly breaks completely—collapsing into sobs mid-sentence. You're on your knees now, voice raw: 'I can't save you, can I?' The realization devastates you. By the end, you're whispering through tears, still fierce but now desperate: 'But I'll die trying.' It's a vow and a surrender, strength and complete fragility woven together.

title: Dancing at the Edge of Goodbye
instruction: You're helping someone you deeply love pack for a journey they must take alone—one they may not return from. A calling, a dangerous mission, treatment far away, or something they need to do to become who they're meant to be. You're folding their clothes, and you start making jokes to keep it light, even laughing at shared memories. But your laughter keeps catching, transforming mid-sound into something that might be a sob. You're so proud of their courage it physically hurts. Your voice dances between celebration and devastation: 'You're going to be magnificent' comes out half-choked. You find yourself saying contradictory things in the same breath: encouraging them to go while your voice betrays how much you want them to stay. There's joy in your words—genuine excitement for their journey—but it's threaded through with grief. End with a blessing or send-off that holds everything at once: your pride, your fear, your love, your heartbreak, all braided together in a voice that's laughing and crying simultaneously, celebrating them while mourning their absence.

title: The Last Hour with My Father
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hour. You've spent your whole life afraid to tell him you were terrified of disappointing him, and that fear kept you from ever truly connecting. Begin with that familiar tightness in your chest, that careful, protective distance you've always maintained. As you hold his hand, let yourself speak the raw truth: 'Dad, I've been so scared of you seeing me fail that I never let you see me at all.' Feel how admitting this fear out loud begins to dissolve it. By the end, let yourself arrive at a place of radical openness—speak to him with the undefended honesty you've withheld your entire life. The journey is from self-protection to complete emotional nakedness in the presence of someone you're about to lose forever.
inspired_by: An actor fears their fear will be detected by the director and crew

title: Laughing in My Mother Tongue for the First Time
instruction: You've just been diagnosed with a degenerative condition that will eventually take your ability to speak. But today, today you're recording yourself reading your mother's favorite poem in her language—the one she spoke when she was happy, before life in this country wore her down. Begin with bittersweet joy, stumbling through pronunciation, laughing at your mistakes the way she used to laugh. Your voice is light, almost giddy. But the laughter starts catching in your throat as the weight of the moment settles: this might be the last time you speak these words. The joy doesn't leave—instead, it braids with heartbreak. You keep reading through tears, but you're also smiling, because hearing yourself speak her language feels like she's alive again in your mouth. End with a sound that's both laugh and sob: you're losing your voice, but for this one moment, you've found hers. The gratitude and grief are inseparable, your breath shaking with both.

title: Parallel Paths: Whispering to Your Sleeping Twin
instruction: Late at night, you sit beside your twin sibling's hospital bed after their suicide attempt. They don't know you're there. Whisper a confession: you've been living the life they wanted — you took the job they deserved, married the person they loved first, became the golden child while they struggled. Your voice should catch constantly, barely holding together. Describe moments where you watched them fade and did nothing, where your success fed on their failures. Let tenderness bleed into every word, touching their hand, smoothing their hair. The emotional arc moves from guilty confession to desperate plea for them to wake up, to fierce promises you'll make it right. End with the devastating whisper: 'I need you to be okay so I can tell you I'm not' — acknowledging that your perfect life is hollow, that you're drowning too, that you've both been alone in your pain.
inspired_by: Parallel Universe: Meeting the Other You

title: Reading Your Mother's Eulogy While You're Still Angry at Her
instruction: You're standing at your mother's funeral, and everyone expects you to speak beautifully about her. But you're not there yet—you're still angry about the years of criticism, the withheld affection, the ways she made you feel small. You begin reading the eulogy you prepared, trying to sound loving and grateful, but your voice keeps catching on words that feel like lies. Your throat tightens. You stumble over phrases like 'she was always there for me' because she wasn't. Halfway through, something shifts—a memory surfaces, or you see your own reflection in her, and genuine grief breaks through the anger. Your voice cracks. By the end, you're no longer reading—you're speaking from somewhere raw and true, where love and resentment live together in your chest. Let us hear both the anger you can't quite hide and the devastating realization that she's truly gone before you could resolve this.

title: A Mother's Final Gift: Releasing Her Child to the Stars
instruction: You are a mother saying goodbye to your adult child who has chosen to join a one-way mission to colonize a distant planet. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be brave and supportive, voice trembling with suppressed tears. As you speak, the facade cracks—your voice breaks on words like 'proud' and 'forever.' Midway through, allow yourself to become raw and pleading, begging them to stay even though you know you shouldn't. Then, in the final moments, find a profound acceptance mixed with unbearable grief. Your voice should settle into something tender, blessing them even as your heart shatters. End with whispered words of love that carry both devastation and unconditional release. Let your breath catch, let silences speak, let your voice find strength in surrender.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Dragon Realizes the Creature It Hunts Is Its Own Hatched Sibling

title: The Wedding Toast That Unravels
instruction: You are giving a toast at the wedding of someone you deeply love—but also someone who hurt you irreparably. As you speak, your mind betrays you, rapidly firing conflicting memories and emotions: genuine joy for their happiness, then a flash of the moment they broke your trust, then a childhood memory of pure love, then jealousy of their new spouse, then gratitude for what you once shared, then anger, then tenderness again. Try to keep your toast appropriate and loving, but let each emotional shift subtly bleed into your voice, your smile, your choice of words. Your face and voice are doing battle with themselves—beaming through pain, choking on joy, laughing while tears threaten. Begin with rehearsed eloquence and cheerful composure. End when you finally speak one sentence of devastating, complicated truth that encompasses all of it—love and loss, celebration and grief, blessing and goodbye.

title: The Last Dance
instruction: You are a woman in her 40s, utterly depleted after an all-night dance marathon at a charity event, your hyper-feminized voice now a husky whisper. You’re leaning against a wall, body trembling, trying to catch your breath. You speak to the event organizer, who just handed you a trophy. Start with a laugh that’s more of a wheeze—a mix of exhaustion and a flicker of anger at how grueling it was. Let your voice crack and trail off as you mention the ridiculous blisters. Then, as you look at the trophy, let affection seep in—a tender, shaky tone for the silly thing. End with a surge of ecstasy, whispering with raw, spent joy that you’d do it all again, your voice breaking into a soft, delirious smile. Use long breaths between phrases, and let the words feel pulled from a vacuum. Lines: 'I can’t... feel my legs. That last hour... was that punishment? (laughs weakly) Look at this—cheap plastic, but... (voice softens) it’s ours. Oh god... my feet are bloody. (pause, a slow smile) I’d do it again. I’d do it a thousand times.'
emotions_sampled: Anger (slightly present), Affection (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Broken Promise
instruction: You are a young boy sitting cross-legged on the cold garage floor, your scraped knee stinging. You just fell off your bike and the toy your dad gave you for learning to ride is cracked in your hands. Start by whimpering from the physical pain, shifting your weight, wincing. As you stare at the broken toy, your voice becomes thick with a deeper ache—not just the scrape, but the disappointment that something good is ruined. Let your breath catch, your tone drop from a high whine to a quiet, crushed realization. End with a hollow, almost whispered statement about how it's not fair.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Stillness of Silence
instruction: You are an older man meditating in a quiet room, eyes closed, breath even. You become aware of a memory: a long-ago rival who always tried to outdo you. At first, the memory amuses you—a soft, wry smile forms as you recall his antics. Then a playful, teasing tone creeps in, like you're gently mocking his earnest efforts. Finally, a thread of cold contempt surfaces, but it's faint, almost surprising to yourself. Speak as if emerging from a deep trance—each word floated up from a calm center, slow and deliberate, with no force. Let the amusement fade into teasing, then let a hint of disdain color the last phrase.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Teasing (very intensely present), Contempt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fire Inside
instruction: You are alone in your apartment after the worst/best day of your life - you've either just lost everything or achieved your greatest dream, but your body is flooded with sensation. Begin with pure physical release: laugh, scream, sob, move, pound the floor, whatever your body demands. Let sound pour out of you that isn't quite language - primal, guttural, ecstatic, anguished. Your voice should be wild, uncontrolled. As the initial wave passes, begin to find words, but still raw, still connected to your body's sensations. Maybe you're talking to God, to yourself, to someone who isn't there. Move from pure physical catharsis to something more focused but still visceral - your emotional state and physical state should be indistinguishable. End in exhaustion, your voice hoarse, your body spent, but something fundamental has shifted. You've metabolized the impossible through your flesh.
inspired_by: Actor needs maximum emotional availability before a demanding scene with extreme emotional requirements

title: The Truth About Why I Left
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about why you disappeared from their life fifteen years ago. Begin with controlled anger, each word measured: 'Do you want to know why I stopped calling? Why I moved across the country?' Your voice is sharp, cutting. But as you reveal the painful truth—the moment they chose something else over you, the words that destroyed your sense of worth—your anger transforms. 'I was twelve years old, and you looked right through me.' Now grief floods in. Your voice wavers between fury and heartbreak. End by admitting what you've never said: despite everything, you still desperately wanted their love. Let your voice show someone who came to fight but discovers they're really here to mourn.

title: The Old Wooden Spoon
instruction: You are an elderly, androgynous person in a leather armchair, receiving a spanking. You’ve agreed to this playful dynamic, but a wave of disgust hits you—the intimacy feels wrong, like dead skin touching. Each impact makes you yelp sharply, then settle into a low, teasing moan to mock your own need. Your breathing is ragged; you count loudly, but irritation leaks out as you shift impatiently. Start with heavy, reluctant breaths and a sarcastic tease: 'Ugh, fine, but don’t take all week.' Let the disgust thicken your voice into a mutter, then end with a trembling, impatient gasp: 'Is that all you’ve got?' The arc moves from reluctant disgust to a fierce, irritable tease that barely masks the sting.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Time I'll Touch Your Face
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply who is dying. You reach out and gently touch their face, feeling the coolness of their skin, memorizing every contour, every line. Begin with tender focus on the physical sensation—the smoothness of their cheek, the familiar curve of their jaw—speaking softly as you trace these beloved features. As you continue, let the reality wash over you: this is the last time. Your voice should fracture as gratitude for having known this face battles with the unbearable grief of losing it. End in a place of quiet devastation, perhaps unable to finish your sentences, your fingertips still resting on their skin, trying to hold onto what's already slipping away.
inspired_by: Feeling the Tingling Sensation of a Cooling Face Mask

title: Rave Heartbeat
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a rave, dancing with wild abandon. Your body is moving to the thumping bass, voice bouncing with every step. You're infatuated with the person next to you—a dazzling stranger who makes you feel young again. You shout over the music, breathless but exhilarated, teasing them about their dancing while your eyes sparkle with adoration. At first you're just excitedly infatuated, but as you speak, the teasing grows more playful and intimate, ending with a coy challenge that reveals your heart. Let your voice rise and fall with the beat, punctuated by laughter and gasps between shouts.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Northern Lights Surprise
instruction: You are an older woman, bundled in layers, cheeks numb, standing in your backyard at night. Your jaw is locked from the sub-zero cold—every word feels like it's chipped out of ice. You came outside just to check a frozen birdbath, ready to curse the weather under your breath. But then you look up. The sky is exploding in greens and purples—northern lights you've never seen in your region. The first sound is a choking, gasped laugh—a numb, desperate joy. Start with a thick, muffled grumble, then let the astonishment crack through the cold. As the aurora swirls, you try to call your partner inside, but the words fragment: you stammer, you laugh, you lose the thought mid-sentence because the beauty is too much. End on a sigh that is half ecstasy, half frozen shiver.
emotions_sampled: Elation (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Stroke
instruction: You are a young woman rowing a heavy solo boat across a misty lake at dusk, your arms burning with each pull. Your phone is dead, the shore is vanishing, and you realize you’ve been going in circles for an hour. Start rowing with explosive, grunting breaths on each stroke, then gasping out words during the recovery slide — your voice wobbles with the boat’s rock and your grip on the oars tightens. As you speak, let helplessness seep in: at first, you’re stubbornly trying to convince yourself you’re fine, but by the end, your voice cracks, and you admit you don’t know how to get back. Let the rhythm of rowing dictate your pauses — your words come in bursts between breaths, and you might lose a thought mid-stroke, then find it again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Thing I've Carried Alone
instruction: Late at night, in whispered intimacy, you're finally telling someone the secret shame you've carried for years—something you've never said aloud. Start with hesitation, almost backing out several times, your voice barely audible. You're testing the waters: 'There's something I need to tell you... I don't know if I can.' As you begin to confess, your throat tightens—the words catching, nearly choking you. Let vulnerability wash over you in waves: moments where you can barely speak, where breath becomes difficult. Reveal the weight of carrying this alone, how it's shaped you, how you've been certain that speaking it would make you unlovable.
