instruction: The mist has turned to violent rain and wind. You're standing where your home once stood before the flood took it, took them, took everything. Start by describing the storm with trembling control—the way water strikes your face, the howling around you—but your voice is tight with suppressed rage. Build into explosive fury at the universe, at God, at the cruel randomness that lets storms devour lives. Demand answers from the sky. Rage at the unfairness. But then—collapse. Let the anger shatter into raw, helpless sobbing. You're screaming and weeping simultaneously, fierce and utterly broken, powerful and completely powerless. End with exhausted, whispered defiance: you're still here. You survived. You hate that you survived. This requires everything—full voice, then broken whispers, rage and grief tangled inseparably.
inspired_by: Walking Slowly Through a Misty Morning

title: Braiding Hair One Last Time
instruction: You're braiding your mother's hair as she sits in her hospital bed, just like she braided yours every morning before school. Speak in barely-there whispers, your voice tender and careful. Tell her small memories—the way she always started at the left side, how she'd hum while working, the feeling of her fingers on your scalp. Your hands are gentle but your voice keeps breaking on ordinary words. Each memory is a goodbye you're not ready to say. Feel how this simple act holds your entire relationship—every morning she cared for you, every time she made you feel safe. Let silence do as much work as words. End with your voice dissolving completely as you tie the final band, knowing this may be the last time you touch her this way. This isn't dramatic grief—it's quiet devastation, love so big it barely fits in your throat.
inspired_by: Watching Your Parent Age: The Role Reversal

title: The Last Bit of Strength
instruction: You're an elderly man in your garage, fumbling with a bolt on a lawnmower. Your blood sugar has dropped—your hands tremble, your vision swims, and your thoughts slip away mid-sentence. Start with a dull contempt for your own failing body, a weary disgust that you can't even do this simple task. But as you finally feel the bolt catch, a quiet, triumphant fire rises in your chest. Let your voice fade and slur, pause to catch your breath, but let the last few words carry a stubborn, hard-won victory.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Contempt (slightly present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: You Used to Look Up to Me
instruction: You’re a 17-year-old guy, standing in a deserted hallway, facing a younger kid who was once your protege but now hangs with people you hate. You came here wanting to believe he still respects you—maybe you can talk sense into him. But as you speak, that tiny hope curdles. Your voice drops, slow and heavy, each word a deliberate invasion. You let contempt paint the air, lazy and cutting. But halfway through, you realize how much this stings—disappointment seeps in, raw and tired. Shift from a fragile, almost pleading tone to a growl that thickens with disgust, then let your voice crack just slightly with letdown. You scratch the back of your neck, look at the floor, then pin him with your eyes again.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Contempt (very intensely present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Letdown
instruction: You are an older woman returning home after a lively party where you drank two strong sugary coffees and felt euphoric, talkative, and young again. End not with resolution but with raw truth: you needed them, they failed you, and somehow you're still here needing them to acknowledge it. Your voice becomes the sound of a heart demanding to be seen.

title: The Victory That Crumbles

title: Confronting the Parent Who Trained You to Never Break
instruction: You're finally telling your parent—the one who taught you to be strong, to lead, to never show weakness—that their training nearly destroyed you. But as you speak, the anger cracks open to reveal the terrified child underneath who just wanted to be held, not trained. Your voice wavers between fury and desperate vulnerability—you're forty years old and still seeking their approval even as you rage against it. title: The Last Permission

Your voice fractures as you move from begging them to stay to recognizing that loving them means releasing them. End with whispered permission through tears—'It's okay. You can rest now. I'll be okay'—where your voice carries both devastating loss and profound, selfless love. Let your breath catch, let silences speak, let your voice break and reform as you make the hardest choice love ever demands.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Machines Stop
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's awake but fading. As you speak to her, let your awareness split: notice everything—the beep of monitors, the scratch of sheets, a nurse's footsteps in the hall, the weight of her hand, a childhood memory flashing unbidden, the smell of antiseptic, your own hunger, the light changing. Speak your love and your regrets to her, but let these constant, unfiltered observations run silently beneath your words, interrupting your own thoughts, pulling your attention in a dozen directions even as you try to focus on this goodbye. Begin with careful, measured words—trying to say the 'right' thing. End with raw, unguarded truth as the weight of the moment finally breaks through your fragmented attention.

title: The Fire That Breaks Through
instruction: You're in the middle of an intense physical experience—running until your lungs burn, passionate intimacy, gripping physical pain—and suddenly an old grief surfaces. Begin disconnected from sensation, going through the motions, your mind keeping you separate from what your body is experiencing. Then let the physical intensity crack something open. Stop controlling. Let the sensations flood through you—burning muscles, gasping breath, skin alive, heart pounding. As your body overwhelms your mental control, an unexpected emotion surges up: rage at someone you've forgiven, grief for something you thought you'd processed, desire you've suppressed. Don't perform it. Let the physical experience drag the emotion out of you. By the end, you're sobbing or roaring or laughing—surprised by what your body released when your mind finally stopped guarding the gates.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father across a table about something they've never acknowledged—a betrayal, an absence, a wound they left in you. Begin by looking at their face, their hands, the way they're sitting. Notice how they've aged, the defensiveness in their posture, the fear or stubbornness in their eyes. Study them as if you're seeing a stranger, and wonder: who are they really? What were they afraid of? What broke inside them? Start with anger and accusation in your voice, armed with your rehearsed grievances. But as you truly observe them—seeing not just your parent but a flawed, frightened person—let your rage crack open to reveal the hurt and longing underneath. End in a place of painful understanding, your voice softening into something raw and almost forgiving, though you may not want to forgive. The emotional journey is from righteous fury to heartbroken recognition of shared humanity.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional distance that defined your childhood—all the times they were physically present but emotionally absent. Begin with quiet, careful restraint, almost apologetic for bringing it up. But as you speak, decades of unmet needs surface. Your voice grows stronger, angrier, demanding acknowledgment. Then something shifts: you see their fragility, their own unhealed wounds. The anger doesn't disappear, but it transforms into something more complicated—grief for what you both lost, fury at the waste of it, and against your will, a painful understanding. End caught between wanting to shake them and wanting to hold them.

title: The Last Room We Shared
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying partner's hospital bed in the middle of the night. Unable to sleep, you begin looking around the room—the machines, the flowers people sent, their jacket hanging on the chair, the window showing the dark sky. Start with anxiety and restlessness, letting your eyes move naturally from object to object. As you notice each thing, let memories surface: when you bought that jacket together, who sent those specific flowers, what you can see through that window. Speak softly to your sleeping partner about what you're seeing and remembering. Let your emotion shift from anxious distraction to profound tenderness and acceptance as you realize you're memorizing this room, these final moments. End in a place of quiet, grateful peace.

title: The Breaking Point: Parent Realizes They Failed to Protect Their Child
instruction: You've just learned your child was being hurt—bullied, abused, suffering—and you didn't see it. You missed every sign. Start with disbelief, voice rising with defensive justifications. But as you piece together the moments you dismissed, the times they tried to tell you, your voice becomes a roar of self-directed fury. You're shouting now—at yourself, at your blindness, at your failure. Then it shatters. Your rage collapses into broken sobbing, that raw sound of a parent who couldn't keep their most sacred promise. Your breathing is ragged, desperate. End with your child's name repeated through tears—half apology, half prayer, wholly helpless. This is the sound of someone discovering they were the villain in their child's story.
inspired_by: Historical: Abolitionist Confronts Their Own Family's Slave Trading Past

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's wedding reception, about to give a toast, but you're secretly in love with them—or you know this marriage is a terrible mistake—or they're moving across the world tomorrow—or you're dying and haven't told them. Hold your glass and begin speaking about happiness, celebration, and joy because that's what's expected. But let the truth underneath leak through in unexpected ways. Your voice might crack on certain words, you might laugh when you should be sentimental, you might start crying while smiling. Don't plan which emotion will win—let them fight for space in your voice. Maybe you say 'I'm so happy for you' and it comes out five different ways in one sentence. Begin performing joy, end wherever the collision of your real feelings takes you—maybe genuine blessing mixed with devastating loss, maybe fierce love shot through with anger, maybe gratitude drowning in grief.

title: The Shoe That Won't Tie
instruction: You're sitting on the edge of your bed, phone in hand, staring at a photo your friend just sent. Your ex-girlfriend is beaming next to some famous guitarist at a backstage party. For a moment you freeze — astonishment hits like a punch, your breath catches. Then you lean forward to tie your shoes, grunting as you bend, the swoosh of your jacket pocket muffling your muttered words. As you struggle with the laces, that initial shock curdles thickly into jealousy. By the time you yank the knot tight, your voice is low, bitter, and laced with envy, but still carrying the tremor of being caught off guard.

title: Laughing Through Your Farewell Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's going-away party—they're moving across the world for an incredible opportunity, and you're genuinely happy for them. Begin with bright, celebratory energy, your voice warm with joy and pride, recounting hilarious memories that have everyone laughing. But as you speak, the permanence of this goodbye hits you in waves. Your laughter becomes edged with tears you're trying to hide. You're smiling while your voice cracks, making jokes while your throat tightens. The room can't tell if you're laughing or crying—neither can you. You're saying 'I'm so proud of you' while your heart is shattering, celebrating their joy while grieving your loss. Your voice lifts with genuine excitement about their future, then breaks with the reality that you won't be part of their daily life anymore. End with a laughing-crying contradiction, raising your glass with trembling joy-grief: 'To the best thing that ever happened to me... and the hardest goodbye I'll ever say. I love you. Go be extraordinary.' You're beaming and breaking simultaneously.

title: Dancing at Your Funeral
instruction: You're at a celebration of life for someone who specifically requested 'no sadness, only joy.' You're trying to honor their wish, genuinely laughing as you share a hilarious memory, but tears are streaming down your face. Your voice should oscillate between genuine laughter and barely suppressed sobs—sometimes mid-sentence. Find moments where you're smiling so hard your face hurts, but your voice breaks on certain words. Express gratitude for having known them even as your heart is shattering. Include the contradiction of feeling so grateful and so devastated simultaneously. End with a moment of unexpected peace—maybe you feel them with you, maybe you finally understand what they wanted you to know. The emotional landscape shifts between joy and grief so fluidly they become inseparable.

title: The Unsent Voice Message
instruction: You're recording a voice message to someone who hurt you deeply—a former best friend, an ex who shattered you—but you'll never send it. Begin with explosive, righteous anger: they don't get to just walk away, they don't get to pretend it didn't matter. Your voice should be sharp, fierce, maybe even cruel. But mid-way through, something shifts—maybe you remember a moment of genuine love, or you realize how much energy you've spent on this rage. Your voice should crack, the fury collapsing into grief and confusion. End in a place of devastating honesty: you miss them, you hate that you miss them, and you're terrified you'll never feel that connected to anyone again.

title: The Hollow Toast
instruction: You're at a party after a brutal week of zero sleep. Your body aches, your eyes sting, and you just want to collapse. You lift your glass, but your voice comes out wrong—tight, clipped, with a fake smile that doesn't reach your throat. As you speak, the exhaustion overwhelms the bitterness, and your words trail off into a hollow silence. title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in bed, in that vulnerable space between waking and sleeping. Begin with halting words, long pauses where you almost stop. As you confess—maybe an betrayal, maybe a truth about yourself you've hidden, maybe a fear so deep it's shaped your entire relationship—your voice trembles. There's shame, yes, but also a devastating tenderness. You're terrified of losing them, but you can't live with the lie anymore. The words catch in your throat. By the end, you're not asking for forgiveness exactly—you're offering your most fragile self, voice breaking on 'I'm sorry,' then waiting in the silence, your breathing uneven, wondering if love can survive honesty.

title: Hide and Seek, Tight Squeeze
instruction: You're an adult woman with a high, sweet voice, playing hide-and-seek with a young child. title: The Last Lesson Before Departure

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just finished an intense physical activity—a run, making love, a fight, moving furniture in summer heat—and your body is flooded with sensation: sweat, trembling, rapid heartbeat, exhaustion. title: The Breaking Point

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth

title: The Corner of the Bar

title: Protective Rage Collapsing into Helpless Despair
instruction: You've just learned that someone you're responsible for protecting—a child, a younger sibling, someone vulnerable—has been hurt, and the person who hurt them is standing in front of you. Then let that fury crack as the reality hits: violence won't undo the damage, won't heal the wounds, won't turn back time. instruction: You're an elderly person alone in a house during a sudden blackout, holding a crackling walkie-talkie to reach your neighbor. title: ICU Doctor: Saying Goodbye to a Patient You Couldn't Save
instruction: You're alone in the ICU after losing a young patient despite doing everything right. Begin with clinical composure as you record final notes: 'Time of death, 3:47 AM. Then you must call the parents—your voice shifts, becoming softer, more human: 'Mr. and Mrs. Chen, I'm so sorry. We did everything we could.' Feel the inadequacy of those words. As you hang up, allow yourself to break down in the empty room, your voice becoming raw and fragmented: 'She was nineteen. I knew the statistics. I knew them and I still thought...' You're speaking to the patient who can't hear you anymore, finally allowing yourself to feel what you've been holding back.

title: The Last Light in Her Eyes
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. Then, as you notice her breathing change, allow different images to flood you—her hands now still and pale, her eyes dimming, the coldness of the room. title: The Last Words You'll Ever Say to Your Mother

title: Reading Between Your Silences

title: Auctioneer High Stakes

title: The Last Blessing Before the Journey

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're an astronaut making your final call to your child before a one-way mission to establish humanity's first colony on another world. title: Last Person to Speak a Dying Language
instruction: You're the only living speaker of your ancestral language. Speak it aloud — the sounds, the poetry, the words for concepts your new language doesn't have. title: The Half-Price Bouquet
instruction: You're a customer service agent at a hotel front desk. A man is checking in with his young daughter; she's clutching a wilted flower. title: Three A.M. Truth
instruction: You are lying in bed in the dark next to someone you've been with for years, and you're whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something about who you really are, what you really want, or what you've been hiding. Begin with your voice barely audible, tentative, testing whether it's safe to speak at all. Your breathing matters here as much as your words. Let the vulnerability build slowly, like turning up a dimmer switch on your soul. There should be long pauses where silence does the work. As you continue, let yourself move from terrified confession to something approaching relief, even fragile hope. The journey is from speaking despite fear, to speaking through fear, to finally speaking with a kind of exhausted honesty. Your voice should end differently than it began—perhaps still quiet, but no longer hiding.
inspired_by: When you are debating whether your emotional preparation needs to match the scene's requirements literally (actually staying up all night, actually running for miles, etc.)

title: The Fade at the Party
instruction: You're at a crowded party, leaning against a wall as you flirt with someone you're intensely attracted to. Your voice starts full of swagger and pride, showing off your confidence and desire. But you've been standing too long—blood pools in your legs, the room spins. As you fight to stay upright, your words become breathy, trailing off; your pride crumbles into astonishment, then a quiet, fading surrender. Let your voice lose its grip, let the end of each sentence die away as your focus dissolves.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your adult child who lives overseas, and you both know this is goodbye. You start trying to sound strong, almost cheerful, wanting to protect them from your fear. But as you speak, the weight of all the unsaid things between you—the years of distance, the choices you regret, the love you never quite knew how to express—begins to crack through your voice. Your breathing becomes shallow as pain medication starts to fade. You move from false brightness to raw admission: you're terrified of dying, you're sorry for the silences, you're proud of who they became without you. By the end, your voice is barely a whisper, but it's the most honest you've ever been. You're not asking them to absolve you—you're just finally telling the truth as your time runs out.
inspired_by: Historical: Former Oppressor Must Apologize to Those They Once Oppressed

title: Holding the Line Against the Inevitable
instruction: Someone you're fiercely protective of—your sibling, your child, your closest friend—is about to do something dangerous, something that could destroy them, and you're trying to stop them. Begin with controlled urgency: 'Please. Please just listen to me for one minute.' But they're not listening, and your control starts fracturing. Your voice rises with desperate intensity: 'You think I don't understand? You think I haven't felt exactly what you're feeling right now?' Suddenly you're shouting, raw and unfiltered: 'I am NOT going to stand here and watch you throw your life away!' But mid-rage, you break completely. The anger collapses into sobbing helplessness: 'I can't lose you. I can't—please, I can't lose you too.' Your voice becomes fierce again but now it's edged with tears: 'You are so loved. Do you hear me? You are so goddamn loved.' End with both strength and breaking: 'So if you're going to do this, you're going to have to go through me first. Because I'm not giving up on you. I will never give up on you.'

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech Because It's All Too Absurd
instruction: You're recording your own funeral message while you're still alive, still dying, still here. You start almost businesslike: 'If you're hearing this, I'm dead. How weird is that?' But then you actually laugh—a real, startled laugh at the absurdity. 'I'm literally talking to you from the grave. This is so fucking stupid.' Your laughter continues but there's grief bleeding into it. You're listing all the things you'll miss and it's funny and it's devastating: 'I'll miss terrible coffee. I'll miss traffic jams. I'll miss being annoyed at you.' Your voice keeps breaking into laughter that's also crying. 'I'm trying to be profound here but honestly? I'm just... I'm really pissed off I have to leave.' The contradiction deepens—you're finding joy in the memories while accepting you're losing everything. 'Thank you for making this ridiculous, beautiful, painful, stupid life worth living.' By the end, you're both laughing and sobbing: 'I'm not ready to go but I'm so grateful I was here. How is that possible? How can I be both?' Your voice contains impossible opposites—celebration and grief, gratitude and rage, peace and resistance—all existing simultaneously in a moment of profound, contradictory truth.
inspired_by: Beginning to Accept Your Body: Compassion Breaking Through Hate

title: The Last Sunrise
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's been unconscious for days, but suddenly her eyes flutter open. You begin speaking to her softly, describing the sunrise coming through the window—the colors, the warmth on your skin, the sound of birds starting to sing. As you speak, let yourself truly feel each sensory detail you describe: the texture of her papery hand in yours, the antiseptic smell mixing with her familiar perfume, the weight of exhaustion in your body from staying awake all night. Start with careful control, trying to be strong for her, but as you continue describing the beauty around you both, let the reality of this being your last shared sunrise break through your composure. Let your awareness of every precious detail—the rise and fall of her breathing, the exact shade of morning light on her face—transform your careful strength into raw, tender devastation.

title: The Stranglehold of Victory
instruction: You are a young boy with an unusually deep, masculine voice, pinned against a wall by an adult who has one hand clamped around your throat. Your airflow is cut off, making your words raspy, choked, and uneven. You start in a state of desperate fear, gasping for breath, your voice strained and high-pitched at first as you plead or struggle. But as you manage to knee your attacker or twist free, a fierce triumph surges through you. Your voice shifts from strangled panic to a low, gravelly, victorious growl, each word a hard-won declaration of survival. Speak roughly 50-70 words, letting the physical pressure affect your delivery — pauses for air, vocal cracks, and a final snarling release.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Daughter Who Needed You: A Reckoning at Forty
instruction: You're confronting your elderly parent about the emotional abandonment of your childhood, something you've never said aloud. Begin with careful, measured words, almost apologetic: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' As you speak, anger rises—decades of swallowed hurt: 'I needed you to see me, to actually see me, and you never did.' Your voice becomes fierce, uncontrolled: 'Do you have any idea what it's like to be invisible to your own mother?' Then something shifts. You see them—really see their frailty, their own damage. Your rage collapses into exhausted grief: 'I just wanted you to love me the way I needed.' End with a painful, tentative reaching across the void: 'I'm here now. I'm still here. Can you see me now?' Your voice small, vulnerable, still hoping.

title: Reading Your Younger Self's Diary After Surviving
instruction: You've found your diary from the worst year of your life—when you were suicidal, lost, certain you had no future. You begin reading aloud, voice tight with recognition: 'I don't think I can make it another day.' As you read your past pain, something unexpected happens—you start laughing, softly, not cruelly but with wonder at the distance traveled. 'God, I was so certain it would never get better.' Your voice mixes amusement and heartbreak. You read the darkest entries and your voice breaks—you're crying for that child you were—but then you're laughing again through tears at something absurdly melodramatic you wrote. The laughter and grief interweave completely. By the end, you're speaking directly to your younger self, voice thick with contradictory emotions: 'You were right that it would be hard. You were wrong that it wasn't worth it.' You're simultaneously mourning the suffering and celebrating the survival, your voice carrying both the weight of what was endured and the lightness of having endured it. 'Thank you for holding on. Look at us now.' It's gratitude mixed with grief, joy soaked in sorrow, all of it real, all of it true.
inspired_by: First Infertility Support Group: Finding Your Voice

title: The Bumpy Pride
instruction: You are an elderly man driving a battered pickup truck down a dirt road full of potholes, hauling a handmade rocking chair you just finished for your granddaughter. The road shakes you constantly, making your voice vibrate. Start with focused concentration—gripping the wheel, muttering about the road, feeling your age in your bones. As you glance in the rearview mirror at the chair, a quiet pride creeps in; you recall the hours of sanding and the grain of the wood. End with a gravelly, satisfied chuckle despite the rattling. Let the bumps interrupt and wobble your words naturally, shifting from irritation to warm accomplishment.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Garden of Remembrance
instruction: You are an elderly man wearing a loose fabric veil that filters your voice slightly. You are in your garden at dusk, tending to a rosebush that your late spouse planted. At first, you feel a pang of loneliness and worry about the roses surviving the coming winter. But as you gently touch a bloom, you recall the joy of planting it together, and a wave of intense contentment floods you. Speak softly to the rose, your voice carrying the filtered quality of the veil. Let your words start with a slight tremor of concern, then slowly warm into a quiet, grateful peace. Allow natural pauses, a deep breath, and a small smile you can feel through the fabric.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Secret You Whisper In The Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you. You're whispering a confession they'll never hear—maybe you're not in love anymore, or you are but you're terrified, or you did something unforgivable, or you're sick and haven't told them. Start with your voice barely audible, tender, watching them sleep. The words catch in your throat—this is the most honest you've been in months, maybe years. Let gentleness mix with grief. You love them enough to protect them from this truth, which means you're alone with it. End with your voice breaking on something simple: 'I'm so sorry' or 'I'm so scared' or 'I wish I could tell you.' The quiet is suffocating.
inspired_by: Talking About Them As If They're Still Alive

title: Kneeling by His Side
instruction: You are an elderly woman, on the floor beside your husband who has collapsed. Your voice is naturally high and gentle, but now it's cracking under the strain. As you dial 911, you are forcing yourself to speak clearly, but your breath comes in short gasps and your words tumble out in clipped bursts. While you wait for the dispatcher to answer, you look at his face and whisper to him – your voice softens, slows, fills with a fierce, trembling tenderness. Start in panicked, hyperventilating control, then let your love break through, turning the words into a shaky, tearful lullaby.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Breaking Free from the Hypnotist's Command
instruction: You are under a hypnotic command that's kept you compliant for years, and suddenly it's shattering. Start in a monotone, repeating your programmed mantra: 'I am calm, I am obedient, I am—' SNAP. Fury detonates. 'NO! NO MORE!' Your voice becomes feral, desperate, years of suppressed rage pouring out. 'You STOLE my anger! My fear! You made me smile through everything!' But the command fights back—your voice wavers between robotic compliance and raw human anguish. Scream the truth: 'I was SCREAMING INSIDE!' Then collapse into something more devastating than rage: the protective love you still feel despite everything. 'I hate you. I hate you. God, I still... why do I still want to protect you?' End with fierce determination breaking through tears: 'But I'm done. I'm finally done.' Your voice—ragged, imperfect, finally your own.
inspired_by: Voice Acting a Video Game Character Who Becomes Self-Aware

title: The Last Transmission: Guiding Them Home Through Static
instruction: You're mission control, and the spacecraft is failing. Your astronaut—your friend—won't make it back. Start with technical precision, walking them through procedures: 'Copy that, adjusting trajectory vectors now.' But as systems cascade into failure, your voice must stay steady even as your heart shatters. You're not just reading protocols—you're saying goodbye while pretending you're not. The static grows. Your instructions become softer, more personal. 'You did everything right. You hear me? Everything.' End with the moment the line goes silent, and you whisper something meant only for them, your professional mask finally cracking into a grief so quiet it barely makes sound.
inspired_by: Emergency Dispatch: Managing Chaos Into Order

title: Echoes of Victory
instruction: You're a teenage boy in a long, empty school hallway right after winning a big competition. Your footsteps bounce off the walls as you walk. Start by whispering to yourself, reliving the moment—your voice light, breathless with elation, almost laughing at the ceiling. But then you pass a classroom where a teacher once scoffed at your chances. Your voice hardens, dripping with contempt. You mutter a bitter line under your breath, the reverb stretching your words. Let your tone shift from giddy triumph to cold, cutting disdain, and let the silence between words hang heavy. Speak about 60 words total, mixing excited murmurs and a sharp, sarcastic jab towards the absent doubter.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Performance
instruction: You're a concert pianist giving your final performance before early-onset dementia takes your ability to play. Begin with perfect technical control, delivering your opening announcement with practiced grace and warmth to the audience. As you describe the pieces you'll play tonight, your voice is confident, almost detached in its professionalism. Midway through your speech, a melody from your childhood surfaces in your mind, and suddenly you're not speaking to an audience anymore—you're speaking to the piano itself, your oldest companion. Your voice cracks. The professional veneer shatters. You try to regain composure, but instead of controlling it, you let yourself break open completely. End with a raw, whispered goodbye to the instrument, to music itself, mixing gratitude with devastating grief. Your final words should be almost inaudible, choked with tears, yet somehow more powerful than anything that came before.

title: Unraveling in the Kitchen
instruction: You're confronting your mother/father in the kitchen where you grew up. You came here to finally say what you've rehearsed for years—calm, clear, rational. But the moment you start speaking, the carefully constructed speech begins to crumble. Maybe rage surfaces when you expected tears. Maybe you find yourself laughing bitterly when you meant to sound strong. Maybe your voice cracks when you wanted it firm. Don't perform the confrontation you imagined—let the confrontation that actually exists between you two take over. Allow yourself to be surprised by what comes out of your mouth, by where your voice goes, by the silences that appear. End in a place emotionally opposite from where you began.

title: Holding the Ashes
instruction: You are scattering your estranged father's ashes in a place he loved—a place he took you once as a child before everything fell apart. Begin speaking to him as if he can hear you. Start with anger about his absence, the years of silence, the damage he caused. Let your voice be sharp, accusatory. But as you speak and feel the weight of the ashes in your hands, something shifts. You remember one perfect afternoon with him—just one—and grief crashes into your anger. Your voice should crack, soften, then harden again as you fight the tenderness. You are furious that you loved him. You are devastated that you still do. End with gratitude for that single good memory, spoken through tears but also through gritted teeth. 'Thank you' should sound like both a gift and an accusation. You are releasing him but also finally admitting he mattered.

title: Whispered Confessions in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, in the intimate darkness of 3 AM. You're going to confess something you've kept hidden—perhaps a fear, a desire, a vulnerability you've never voiced. Begin curled, protective, your body small and guarded, your whispers barely audible and halting. As you speak, allow your body to gradually unfold like a flower opening. Let your limbs stretch, your breathing deepen, your whispers gain quiet strength. The physical opening of your body reflects the emotional opening of your heart. Your voice remains soft but becomes more fluid, more present. By the end, you're no longer contracted in shame or fear—you're expansive in your vulnerability, your body relaxed and open, your whispers transformed into gentle, liberated truth-telling. The quiet remains, but the quality of that quiet has completely changed from trapped to free.

title: Homecoming in Ruins
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home for the first time in eight years. You left in anger, cut everyone off, and built a successful life elsewhere. Now your younger sibling has called: the house is being sold, come say goodbye to it. As you walk through the empty rooms, speak out loud to the walls, to the ghosts of who you were. Begin with vindicated satisfaction—see, you made it without them, you were right to leave. But let the rooms betray you: the pencil marks measuring your height on the doorframe, the window where you waited for someone to come home, the corner where you felt safe. Let grief ambush your righteousness. End in a space where you're simultaneously grateful you left and devastated by what you lost, where success and loneliness are the same achievement, where you're laughing and sobbing because you got everything you wanted and it cost you everything. Your voice must hold both victories at once.
inspired_by: An actor is studying with a teacher or workshop and wants to make the most of it

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're recording a video message to be played at your own funeral—you've been given months to live, and you've decided to speak directly to the people you love. Begin with dark humor, almost irreverent, the stutter present but playful: 'So I g-guess this is awkward, huh?' You make a joke about the situation, laughing genuinely even as your eyes shine with unshed tears. As you continue, the laughter and grief intertwine impossibly—you're grateful and heartbroken, finding joy in memories while mourning all the moments you'll miss. The stutter comes and goes with emotion: 'I w-wish I could stay, I really do, but I'm also... I'm so g-grateful I got this much time.' You break down mid-sentence, then laugh at yourself for breaking down, then cry harder. It's messy, contradictory, deeply human. By the end, you've found strange peace, voice steady and soft, stutter barely there: 'Take care of each other. That's all that matters.' You smile through tears, and the silence after holds both goodbye and love.

title: The Last Coordinates
instruction: You're an astronaut's spouse reading aloud the mission log entries your partner recorded during their final, doomed space walk. Start with clinical precision: 'Mission timestamp 14:22:07, oxygen levels at 47 percent...' You're reading their words exactly as they wrote them because that's all you have left. As you continue through the entries, your precision becomes desperate — each number, each technical term is a way to hold them close. When you reach their final entry — 'Tell Morgan I see Earth from here. Tell Morgan it's beautiful' — your voice stays steady but something breaks underneath. End by repeating the last timestamp over and over, softer each time, as if by keeping the precision alive you can keep them alive too.

title: The Last Ember
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting alone in a drafty room, your thin coat no match for the cold. Your body shakes uncontrollably, jaw tight, each word a struggle against the chatter. You are waiting for your granddaughter, but she never came. Start speaking aloud to yourself, your voice flat and numb from the cold and the loneliness. As you talk, the memory of her warmth breaks through the numbness, and your voice cracks with a sudden, sharp ache of loss. Let the shivering and the emotion fight for control.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your funeral, and you've decided to make them laugh one last time. You start light, almost mischievous, your voice warm with humor as you tease the people you love: 'If you're crying too much, you're doing it wrong.' You're genuinely laughing as you share absurd memories, make inappropriate jokes about death. But something shifts. Your laughter becomes shaky, and your voice thickens with emotion you're trying to hide behind humor. 'I'm going to miss you so much'—said with a laugh that's also a sob. You oscillate between genuine joy at the life you lived and devastating sorrow at leaving. Your voice breaks on gratitude: 'Thank you for making this worth it,' and you're crying and laughing simultaneously. You end with peace—a quiet, tearful smile in your voice—accepting this strange, beautiful, heartbreaking goodbye.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Stole
instruction: You're finally saying what you've never been able to say to the parent who failed you. Start controlled, almost rehearsed: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' Your voice is steady but there's ice underneath. As you list specifics—the times they weren't there, the ways they chose themselves over you—your control begins to slip. They try to justify or deflect and something ruptures in you. Your voice rises, shakes: 'I was a child! I needed you and you weren't there!' Move from anger into the deeper pain beneath it—the grief of the childhood you deserved but never got. End not with forgiveness but with devastating clarity about what you lost and what you're choosing now: to stop waiting for them to become who they should have been.
inspired_by: Admitting You've Been Using Substances to Cope

title: Making Peace With Your Voice
instruction: You've hated your voice for years. Too high, too low, too distinctive, too much. But you're starting to accept it. Your voice—as you speak these words—is becoming less critical of itself. 'This is my voice.' Your voice is claiming itself. Your voice is you. It carries your wounds, your power, your story. Your voice becomes warmer toward itself. You're listening to your own voice with kindness instead of judgment. Include the profound shift of self-acceptance.

title: The Wedding Toast for Your Ex
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-partner's wedding—to someone else. You volunteered because you wanted to prove you're okay, that you've moved on. Start with genuine warmth and humor, sharing a funny story from when you were together, and you're surprised to find you're actually laughing, actually happy for them. Your voice is light, affectionate, celebratory. But as you transition to talking about their new spouse, something shifts. You hear yourself saying beautiful things about their happiness, and you mean them, but your voice begins to betray the heartbreak underneath the joy. You're grateful they found this love, and it's destroying you. End with a smile in your voice as you raise your glass, words of blessing that are absolutely sincere, while your voice trembles with the kind of love that has nowhere to go. Make us hear both the happiness and the breaking in the same breath.

title: The Last Floor
instruction: You are in a metal elevator that shudders and hums. You're holding a small, worn object—a keychain from someone you haven't seen in years. The doors are closing. You're not sure if you're going up or down. As the elevator groans, you speak to yourself, teasing the memory of their laugh, but mostly you're concentrating on the weight of the keychain in your palm, the flickering floor number, the metallic echo of your own voice. Start with a dry, playful whisper—'Still got this, huh'—then let longing swell as the car slows, your voice getting tighter, softer, until you're barely audible above the cable noise. By the time the doors open, you're lost in a memory you can't finish.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Teasing (slightly present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Forgotten Promise
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a soft, high-pitched voice, apologizing to your lifelong partner for forgetting your anniversary. Start by making yourself acoustically smaller—voice dropping in volume and pitch, sentences halting, as you confess your mistake. Let guilt weigh each pause, but gradually let your deep infatuation and affection surface. End with a tender, almost breathless confession of how much they still mean to you, speaking as if you're checking their reaction, restarting lines when emotions crack.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You're practicing a toast alone for your best friend's wedding tomorrow - they're marrying someone else, and you've been secretly in love with them for years. Something in your planned speech strikes you as darkly, absurdly funny - maybe how you're about to celebrate them choosing someone else, maybe the cosmic joke of it all. Start trying to deliver the toast with warmth and joy, but let inappropriate laughter bubble up. Let yourself actually laugh - not bitterly, but with genuine appreciation for the absurd beauty of loving someone enough to celebrate their happiness even as yours shatters. Smile through it, laugh through it, let the joy be real even as your voice breaks. End in a place of peaceful devastation where you're still smiling, maybe still softly laughing, but tears are falling and you're genuinely, heartbreakingly grateful to have known this love, even if it's never yours to keep.
inspired_by: Suppressing Laughter During a Serious Moment

title: The Rocket's Burnout
instruction: You're an elderly man in a cluttered den, caught red-handed by a family member after sabotaging their work computer. You start with a flicker of embarrassment — a quick, forced chuckle, shifting in your chair. But the mania takes over: your voice rockets into a loud, pressured monologue about your 'grand plan,' spilling grandiose justifications and laughing at their shock. Slowly, the energy fractures — your speech stumbles, you repeat yourself, and a raw distress bleeds through as the malevolence crumbles into panic, losing control of the narrative. Speak at breakneck speed, jump between ideas, and let the volume soar then crack.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Distress (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Mother and the Imaginary Dragon
instruction: Narrate a scene where a mother with a loving, soothing voice talks to her childs imaginary dragon friend, who speaks in a gruff but kind tone. Switch between the mothers gentle skepticism and the dragons earnest explanations, blending reality and fantasy.

title: Grand Marshal's Mistake
instruction: You are an older man, a former military officer, now serving as grand marshal of a small-town parade. A volunteer hands you a bullhorn to announce the next float. The first word blasts out, startling you, and the feedback whines. You begin with gruff authority, but when you read the card, you realize it's a silly ad for a pet store. Embarrassment floods in—your voice chokes, you mispronounce 'poodle grooming,' and you trail off as the crowd snickers. By the end, you just mumble into the crackling horn, desperate to hand it back. Let the distortion chop your words; let the humiliation creep into every clipped syllable.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Fantasy: Witch Casts a Spell Knowing It Will Cost Her Own Magic
instruction: Ritual voice, incantations building. You're casting a spell to save the village. But you know the cost—your own magical ability will drain away. Your voice becomes increasingly hollow as you speak, power leaving you with each word. By the ritual's end, you're speaking your own powerlessness. Your breathing is the breath of someone being unmade while making yourself useful. You finish the spell and your voice returns to baseline human—lost, quiet, finally just a person who chose to be nothing to save others.

title: Historical: Resistance Fighter Realizes Their Ally Is an Informant
instruction: Casual conversation with someone you've trusted, your resistance voice is open. Then you notice the inconsistency—something they said reveals they knew information they shouldn't. Your voice continues naturally while your mind is fracturing. Your breathing becomes shallow—you're in the same room as a traitor. Your voice is casual betrayal—you cannot reveal that you know. You continue speaking while calculating who else they've turned in. Your voice is the sound of trust destroyed while maintaining surface friendship. After they leave, your voice is someone carrying knowledge that destroys everything.

title: Unwelcome News at the Finish Line
instruction: You've just finished your morning walk or jog, feeling that powerful endorphin high—your voice is clear, breathing still slightly elevated, confidence flowing. As you stretch and cool down, you notice a neighbor has left an angry note on your car about parking. Start speaking while still in that glow, but as you read the note, your tone shifts—the anger seeps in, not explosive but a cold irritation that tightens your throat. Let your words start open and energized, then gradually become clipped, with pauses as you reread the note, letting the anger color your voice without losing the physical aftermath of exercise. End with a quiet, frustrated resolve that mixes the lingering energy with fresh annoyance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in the remains of your childhood home after the hurricane, and suddenly you start laughing—really laughing. 'It's gone. All of it. Forty years of photographs, Mom's wedding dress, every single thing...' You laugh harder, almost hysterically: 'And I feel... I feel free.' But the laughter catches, becomes something else: 'Oh God, that's terrible, isn't it? I shouldn't feel—' Your voice breaks into a sob even as you're still half-laughing: 'I hated this place. I spent my whole life trying to escape it.' Then pure gratitude floods through, mixed with grief: 'But it held every memory of her. Every single one. And now they're...' You spin slowly in the wreckage, voice full of wonder and heartbreak: 'I'm free and I'm devastated and I'm so grateful to still be alive.' By the end, your voice is quiet, awed, speaking to the ruins with profound tenderness: 'Thank you for keeping us safe all those years. You can rest now. We both can.'

title: The Robot and the Programmer
instruction: Depict a robot with a monotone, mechanical voice gaining sentience, and a programmer who speaks with excitement and awe. Switch between the robots evolving speech patterns and the programmers astonishment, building a sense of wonder and ethical dilemma.

title: The Sweater Still Smells Like Them
instruction: You're alone, holding a piece of clothing that belonged to someone you lost—a lover, a parent, a child. Start by whispering to the empty room, your voice so soft it's almost not there: 'I found this in the back of the closet.' Describe what you're feeling as you hold it—the texture, the scent that's fading. Your confusion is quieter here, more existential: 'I don't know how to be in a world where you're not.' Breathe in the scent. Let silence sit. Your voice wavers between present observations and past memories: 'You wore this the day we...' Trail off. The emotion catches in your throat—not loud crying, but that terrible tightness where you can barely speak. End with an impossible question asked in a broken whisper: 'How do I let you go?' This is grief that confuses your entire sense of reality.

title: Producer Live Broadcast
instruction: You're the producer in the headset directing a live broadcast, and you're watching your star anchor make a serious error on air—reporting facts that are completely wrong. Your voice in the headset is urgent but controlled: 'We need to correct that. Prepare a statement.' You're giving instructions that might save the broadcast, but your internal panic is showing in the clipped way you're talking. The anchor is defensive, your voice becomes sharper. Behind you, your team is scrambling. Your voice becomes either a beacon of calm or a spiral of control-seeking depending on your stress level. Show leadership under pressure where your voice is all your team has to anchor to.

title: The Greenhouse Revelation
instruction: You are an elderly man alone in your greenhouse at dusk, holding a small, wrinkled seed packet you thought you'd lost decades ago. It's from the first garden you planted with your late partner. Start with quiet contemplation — your fingers trace the faded ink, remembering their laugh, their hands in the soil. But then the realization hits: you recognize the flower variety they always called 'our secret.' Suddenly, a wave of ecstatic joy crashes over you — it's not just a memory, they're here. Your voice bursts, pitch leaping, words tangling as you half-laugh, half-cry, speaking to the empty air as if they're standing right beside you. Let your breath catch, let your volume spike, let the tears and laughter blur together.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Professional: Pastor Loses Faith During His Own Sermon
instruction: Pulpit. Your pastoral voice is warm, faithful, certain. You're preaching about God's presence. Then, mid-sentence, faith exits you—completely and irreversibly. Your voice continues the sermon mechanically, hitting all the familiar cadences. But you're now an atheist speaking to believers. Your breathing becomes shallow—you're performing religion while experiencing its absence. You finish the sermon perfectly, vocally unchanged. After, you step down from the pulpit as someone fundamentally altered. You still know how to sound like a pastor; you just no longer believe.

title: Muffled Confession
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy at a school fair, wearing a cloth mask. You spot your crush across the room and impulsively walk over to say hi. As you speak, the mask muffles your words, making you mumble and then overcompensate by raising your voice. You feel your cheeks flush under the mask. You try to sound cool but your voice cracks. Halfway through your sentence, your crush's friend pulls them away, and you're left talking to yourself. Let the mask's dampening affect your volume and clarity — start with eager hope, then trail off into embarrassed quiet as they leave.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Before You Go Silent
instruction: Your younger sibling is losing their hearing—an irreversible condition—and you're lying together in the dark like you did as children, with the family cat purring between you. You've always translated the cat's meows and purrs as a running commentary on family life, making your sibling laugh. Tonight, you're doing it one last time, knowing these will be the last sounds they'll hear clearly. Begin with gentle humor, translating the cat's sleepy contentment, small observations about the creaky house, the way the moonlight falls across the floor. But let your voice grow softer, more careful, as you realize you're trying to give them something to remember sound by. The translations become more poetic, more tender—capturing not just what the cat might be saying, but the texture of your voice, the quality of intimacy, the sound of love itself. Your delivery should be almost a whisper, catching occasionally on emotion you're trying to hold back, words spoken slowly as if each one is a gift you're wrapping carefully. End with a translation that's really a promise, a goodbye to sound that's full of presence and aching gentleness.

title: The Last Migration
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your grandmother who is dying, but you can no longer find human words. Begin standing at the foot of her bed, feeling your body want to move in ways you've never moved before—perhaps swaying like tall grass, or with the heavy, deliberate weight of something ancient. Let sounds emerge that aren't words: low rumbles, high keening, breath patterns that speak what language cannot. As you move closer to her bedside, your body might transform—perhaps you become smaller, more childlike, or perhaps you grow larger, more protective. Let your hands express through gesture and touch what your voice cannot articulate. By the end, you should move from careful human restraint into something raw and animal, a grief that lives in your bones and spine rather than your vocabulary. Allow your final goodbye to be a sound, a movement, a physical presence that transcends speech.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access a nonverbal or primal subpersonality that does not respond to verbal techniques

title: Screaming at God After Losing Everything in One Day
instruction: You've just lost your partner and your home in a sudden tragedy. You're alone in an empty space, and you start yelling at God, the universe, fate—whatever you believe in or stopped believing in today. Begin with explosive rage, voice raw and loud, demanding answers, screaming 'Why?' with your whole body. Your fury is righteous, powerful, uncontained. But as you exhaust yourself, the anger fractures. Your voice cracks, becomes desperate rather than fierce. You're not yelling anymore—you're begging, bargaining, your words tumbling over each other. Then something breaks completely. You collapse into helpless weeping, your voice reduced to shattered fragments. You're telling them you can't do this, you're not strong enough, you need them back. The rage has transformed into utter devastation and terrifying vulnerability, your voice small and lost like a child's.
inspired_by: Former Abuse Victim Saying the Abuser's Words to Heal

title: The Last Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hour. They're slipping away, fading in and out of consciousness. Start with quiet gratitude - thanking them for specific memories, your voice steady but soft, almost reverent. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves: this is it, they won't answer, they won't see tomorrow. Your voice begins to fracture. You shift from gratitude to desperate confession - things you never said, forgiveness you need to offer, forgiveness you need to ask for. End with your voice breaking completely as you give them permission to go, mixing 'it's okay' with barely contained sobs. Let silence hold the final moment before you whisper goodbye.

title: Electrical Burn Aftermath: Consciousness Returning with Pain
instruction: You're becoming conscious after being electrocuted. Your voice is almost not there, a whisper, as awareness dawns. Everything hurts in disconnected ways—your arm, your heart, your lungs. Your voice is confused, barely forming words as you try to understand what's happening. Paramedics' voices are around you, clinical and efficient, which somehow makes your situation more real. Your voice becomes small and childlike: 'What happened?' You're trying to assess damage through the fog of pain. Include the moment your voice becomes more present, more panicked, as you realize you're badly hurt. Your narration is fragmented, words broken up by gasps of pain. 'Can't feel... can't breathe right.' Your voice becomes almost apologetic, as if you're sorry for the burden you're about to become.

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're thanking someone for leaving you, for ending the relationship, even as your heart is actively breaking in real-time. Laugh through tears—genuine laughter at the absurdity, the freedom, the painful relief. Begin with bright gratitude that sounds almost manic, celebrating your liberation. Let the laughter catch, become something more complicated. Acknowledge, with devastating honesty, that you're grateful and destroyed simultaneously. Find beauty in the contradiction: you mean every word of thanks, and you're also shattered. Let your voice carry both joy at being free and grief at losing someone who mattered. End in a place of paradoxical peace—whole and broken at once, grateful for the pain that's setting you free.

title: You're Not Taking Her
instruction: Your abusive ex has returned demanding to take the dog you escaped with - the only witness to what they did to you, the only living being who got you through those nights. Start with a trembling voice trying to sound firm, your body physically positioning itself between them and the animal. Escalate into fierce, protective rage - over your dead body, never again, this creature saved your life when you couldn't save yourself. Let that rage crack into desperation and terror as you realize you might lose this fight, that the law might side with them. Your voice should become almost feral with protectiveness, then break completely into sobbing fury. Somewhere in the chaos, there's helplessness - you survived them, you escaped, and they can still take something from you. End with a whispered, dangerous promise: they'll have to destroy you first. Raw throat, shaking voice, switching between roaring defiance and breaking down completely.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Came to a Single Recital
instruction: You're forty years old, and you've finally cornered your parent at a family gathering. Start with bitter, controlled sarcasm: 'I had my first gallery opening last month. Sold three pieces. I know you were busy.' Your voice is sharp, precise, cutting. But as you continue—listing all the moments they missed, all the times you looked for their face in the crowd—your anger begins to crack. You realize mid-confrontation that you're not just angry; you're still that child desperately wanting their approval. Your voice shifts from accusation to a raw, vulnerable plea: 'Why wasn't I worth showing up for?' Let the rage dissolve into the small, wounded voice of a child who never stopped hoping. End in devastating quiet, waiting for an answer you know will never be enough.

title: Mending the Mess
instruction: You're an older person tending to your dog's nasty paw wound—a gummy mix of mud, blood, and something green you really don't want to identify. Start with a slight disgust, a wrinkled nose and a sigh, muttering 'Ugh, what is that?' as you lean closer. Then shift into intense concentration, your voice becoming a series of gentle clicks and soft commands as you carefully clean the injury, offering reassuring murmurs like 'Easy now, good boy, hold still.' Let your tone waver between irritation at the mess and the focused tenderness of care. By the end, the disgust has faded into quiet determination and a warm, low 'Almost done, sweet one.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Every Freckle, Every Scar
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner after they've told you they're taking a job across the country. Begin in frozen silence, barely breathing, not wanting to look at them. Slowly, let yourself turn toward them and truly observe: trace the specific geography of their face with your eyes, notice the exact shade of their skin in this light, the small scar above their eyebrow, the rhythm of their breathing, the warmth radiating from their body. As you catalogue these intimate, physical details you've taken for granted, feel tenderness overwhelm your paralysis. Whisper the small, specific things you see—not grand declarations, but tiny observations. Let your voice grow increasingly fragile as you realize you're memorizing them, that paying attention this closely is both unbearably sweet and devastating.

title: The Wedding Toast You Weren't Ready to Give
instruction: You're giving a toast at your younger sister's wedding—the sister who got the life you wanted, who's marrying someone like the person you lost. Everyone's watching, smiling, expecting you to be joyful. Start with the practiced, beaming, celebratory voice—the performance of happiness. Your words are generous and loving, and they are also true, because you do love her. But underneath is a grief so vast you can barely breathe, and envy that makes you ashamed, and genuine joy for her that coexists with your own devastation. Feel these contradictions fighting inside you as your mouth forms cheerful words. Become aware that you're giving an Oscar-worthy performance of someone who isn't dying inside. Then let something crack—maybe your voice breaks, maybe you pause too long, maybe you say one true sentence that wasn't in your planned speech. Let the contradictions become visible. End in a place where joy and grief, love and envy, celebration and devastation are all present at once, audible in your voice. Don't resolve it—let it stay messy and real and impossible.

title: Fever's Burning Triumph
instruction: You are a middle-aged man in the grip of a high fever, alone in a dim room, sweat-soaked and shivering. Your mind drifts into a delirious fantasy where you are victorious in a primal conquest—a memory or hallucination of a lover you once dominated. Start with a hoarse, triumphant growl, relishing the raw lust and power, but as you speak, the fever pulls you under; your voice cracks, you lose your train of thought, and you suddenly cling to a fragile hope that you will survive to feel this again. Let your delivery be halting, with dry swallows and shivers, the final words trembling into desperate optimism.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Final Words to Your Child Before the Machines Turn Off
instruction: You have minutes left. Your child stands at your hospital bedside, and you need to say everything that matters. Start with desperate urgency—'Listen to me, I need you to remember this'—cramming a lifetime of love into seconds. But as you speak, something shifts. Your voice softens into profound tenderness, each word becoming a gift rather than a frantic download. Let gratitude wash over the fear. End in whispered wonder at having known them at all, your breath growing quieter, but your love somehow louder. The emotion must travel from panic to peace, from clutching to releasing.
inspired_by: Comforting Your Child After a Nightmare

title: The Last Wild Dance
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your dying mother who raised you with rigid rules and constant disapproval. She's unconscious now, finally peaceful. You have three minutes alone with her before the family returns. Start by trying to say a proper, composed farewell—but then something breaks open inside you. Let yourself do all the things she never let you do in her presence: curse, laugh too loud, dance badly, sing off-key, be ridiculous, be free. Move however your body wants to move—wild, ungainly, explosive. This isn't performance—it's years of restraint shattering. End in exhausted stillness beside her, finally able to whisper a real goodbye. Begin controlled and proper; end raw, spent, and liberated.

title: The Emergency Room Confrontation: I Won't Lose You
instruction: Your parent has refused medical treatment and you've finally gotten them to the hospital, but they're fighting to leave. Start with explosive desperation—your voice loud, cracking, nearly screaming that they don't get to give up. You're furious at their stubbornness, terrified of losing them, helpless because you can't force them to want to live. Your words tumble out in a torrent—rage, fear, accusations, pleas. But then something shifts. Your voice breaks completely and you collapse into raw vulnerability, admitting you're not ready, you still need them, you don't know how to exist in a world without them. Feel yourself becoming small again, the child begging their parent not to go. End in fierce, protective tenderness—promising to help them fight, offering your strength when theirs is gone. Let anger and devotion, helplessness and fierce determination crash into each other.
inspired_by: Watching Your Parent Age: The Role Reversal

title: The Numb Goodbye
instruction: You are a 9-year-old boy standing in your grandparents' living room. You just drank half a bottle of your uncle's cough syrup to see if it would make the world stop feeling like a television show. Now your mom is saying it's time to leave, and you can't feel your own hands. Your grandmother is crying—you think she's crying—but none of it matters. You try to say goodbye, but your voice comes out like a robot playing a record. As you speak, you look at your own reflection in the dark television screen, and for a moment, you almost feel something, like a whisper. That whisper changes your last word from empty to pleading, without you meaning it to.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Last Afternoon in the Garden Before You Go
instruction: You're lying in the grass with someone you love who is leaving tomorrow—perhaps for war, perhaps to a place they may never return from, perhaps because illness will soon take their memory of you. Start by describing the grass, the warmth, the way their hand feels in yours—voice full of determined lightness, trying to make this moment perfect. But as you continue, let the reality crack through: your voice beginning to shake, breath catching, desperately cataloging every sensation because you need to remember this forever. End with a whispered confession of what you've been too afraid to say, voice breaking between gratitude for this moment and the unbearable knowledge that it's ending. Let the transition be gradual and inevitable, like watching the sun set.
inspired_by: Lying in a Patch of Soft, Shaded Grass

title: The Last Sip
instruction: You're a teenager with a chronic, throbbing toothache that's been nagging for days. You've finally treated yourself to a cold, sweet soda—the first sip sends a rush of pleasure through your mouth, a fleeting ecstasy. But as the cold hits the exposed nerve, the pleasure twists into searing distress. Speak as you savor that first sip, then as the pain spikes and you try to talk through it—your voice guarded, words half-chewed, wincing when air hits the tooth. Start with a breathy, smiling tone, then let it crack and tighten into genuine agony.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Echo of a Single Breath
instruction: You are a teenage girl alone on a large theater stage, rehearsing a dramatic monologue. The acoustics send your voice back to you with a slight delay. Begin with intense concentration, your delivery precise and controlled, but as you hear your own echo, you become distracted by the emptiness of the space. Your voice wavers; you lose a line and stop. In the silence, you feel a swell of vulnerability, then resolve. Finish the piece with a quieter, more personal tone, as if speaking only to yourself. Let the room’s vastness affect your pace and volume.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your person is dying, and you're describing the imaginary dance you're having with them one last time—your favorite song playing in your mind. Begin with genuine joy and laughter in your voice, really feeling the music, describing their moves with delight and playfulness. But let tears start creeping in even while you're laughing—your voice should break and mend, break and mend. You're smiling and crying simultaneously, grateful for every moment while your heart is shattering. The joy is absolutely real, and so is the devastating grief. End in a moment of profound peace mixed with unbearable loss, thanking them with a voice full of love, laughter, and tears all at once.

title: Crossing the Line on a Busy Corner
instruction: You're on a loud city street, horns blaring and a jackhammer pounding nearby. You're teasing your younger brother about his new haircut, voice booming with exaggerated mocking affection to compete with the noise. Then you see his eyes—he's genuinely hurt. Your teasing falters, your voice drops, and shame floods in. You try to force another joke, but your throat tightens, pain seeping through. The siren wailing past seems to mock your failed recovery. End with a barely audible, ashamed murmur, almost lost in the traffic.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Teasing (extremely present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Best Friend's Deathbed
instruction: Your best friend is dying, and you've promised each other no weeping, just celebrating the ridiculous beautiful life you shared. Start by reminding them of your most absurd adventures—the time you both got arrested for something stupid, the terrible karaoke night, the inside jokes that make no sense to anyone else. Laugh genuinely, fully. But between the laughter, grief keeps breaking through. Your voice cracks mid-sentence. You laugh and cry simultaneously, emotions braiding together until you can't tell them apart. Thank them for knowing you better than you know yourself, for every kindness, for choosing you. The gratitude and the loss become inseparable—you're saying 'thank you for everything' and 'please don't leave me' in the same breath. End with one last shared laugh that dissolves into quiet, peaceful tears, holding their hand as the laughter fades into tender silence.
inspired_by: The Last Human Speaking to an Empty World

title: The Truth Your Parent Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're finally confronting the parent who made you feel invisible your entire childhood. Start with a voice that's been rehearsed a thousand times, almost too controlled: 'I need to say something I should have said years ago.' There's anger underneath, but you're trying so hard to be fair, to be the bigger person. As you speak - 'You never once asked what I needed. You never saw me.' - the rage builds, voice getting louder, words sharper. But then something breaks. The anger collapses into the wounded child: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Your voice cracks completely, tears streaming, and you end on the most vulnerable truth: 'I just wanted you to love me the way I was.' Move from controlled fury to raw, childlike devastation.
inspired_by: Waking Up and Realizing What You Said While Drunk

title: The Breaking Point Dance
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a test result, a job offer in another country, a pregnancy, a death. Your entire body has seized up with the shock; you're frozen, barely able to move or breathe. But there's music playing—maybe it was already on, maybe someone else turned it on, maybe you stumble to turn it on yourself. Begin locked in place, muscles rigid, trying to maintain control, your movements mechanical and restricted. As the music continues, something primal starts to fight its way through the paralysis. Let your body begin to move in ways that aren't pretty or controlled—shaking, jerking, wild gestures that release what's trapped inside. Mix the physical release with vocal sounds—gasps, cries, laughter, screams, whatever wants to emerge. By the end, you're fully surrendered to the movement and the emotion, whether that's ecstatic joy, devastating grief, or a chaotic mixture of both, your entire body finally free and expressive, sweat-soaked and liberated.

title: The Prize in the Pocket
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a hyper-feminized, slightly theatrical voice, standing in your kitchen with your weight shifted onto one hip, hand on your waist. You've been grumbling to yourself about misplacing your favorite brooch, but while patting down your dress you feel a lump in the pocket. At first you're annoyed at the lump, then you realize it's the brooch. Let your voice start flat and distracted, then bloom into a breathy, delighted little laugh as you pull it out. Stumble over your words as you're caught off guard, and let the elation sneak in only at the very end—like a warm surprise you didn't expect.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What We Don't Say at Airports
instruction: Your best friend is leaving for a job overseas—maybe forever, probably forever. You're at their apartment helping pack, keeping it light, joking about how you'll visit, how it's not really goodbye. Your voice is bright, encouraging, almost performatively happy for them. But then they hand you something small—a book you lent them years ago, a shirt they borrowed, something meaningless that suddenly means everything. Your voice catches. You try to keep joking, but it comes out broken. You're whispering now, admitting in fragments what you've never said: how much their friendship saved you, how you don't know who you'll be without them in the next room. You're not crying loudly—it's the kind of tears that leak out quietly while you're still trying to smile. End with a confession so soft it's almost inaudible: 'I'm scared I'll forget how to be okay.'

title: Lost in the Fog
instruction: You are a young child searching for your beloved stuffed rabbit in a dense fog. The silence is heavy, and your voice sounds muffled, making you call out louder than usual. You start with anxious, trembling calls, then pause to listen, shifting your weight and peering into the mist. Finally, you spot the rabbit under a bench and your voice softens with relief and affection as you scoop it up.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're packing up your child's bedroom—they've just left for college, or moved across the country, or gotten married. You're holding their objects one by one. This is not about memory or nostalgia in your head—it's about the physical reality of each item. What does this stuffed animal actually feel like in your hands right now? What's its exact weight, the specific texture of its worn fur? What temperature is the fabric? How does this baseball trophy feel—cold metal, what kind of surface? Don't rush—give your senses real time to experience each object. Begin with practical efficiency, almost businesslike, maybe even talking yourself through the task with forced cheerfulness. But let the accumulation of tactile sensations—the actual physical weight and texture of their childhood in your hands—gradually break through. End in a complex place: profound pride mixed with piercing loss, joy for their future tangled with grief for their past, gratitude and resentment existing simultaneously as you hold the last item.
inspired_by: Actor understands sense memory intellectually but cannot make it work

title: Stuck in the Twist
instruction: You're in a hot yoga class, holding a seated spinal twist. Your body is trembling with fatigue, and the twist compresses your lungs, making every breath shallow and ragged. You try to reach your arm behind you for a bind, but your shoulder won't cooperate. The instructor's voice is distant, telling you to breathe deeper. Start with a strained, frustrated mutter about how tired you are—your voice wobbly from the effort. Let your words break as you realize you can't hold it anymore. End with a quiet, breathy admission that you just can't do it, the helplessness dissolving into weary surrender.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Rage That Became Grief
instruction: You've just found out your best friend has been lying to you for months about something that shattered your trust. Start with explosive fury—your voice is shaking with rage: 'How DARE you? How dare you stand there and act like this is nothing?' You're pacing, unable to contain the energy.
