Your words come faster, louder, fiercer: 'I would have walked through fire for you! I trusted you with everything!' But as you shout, something breaks inside. The rage suddenly collapses into raw, gasping sobs. Your voice becomes desperate, almost childlike: 'Why would you do this to me? I thought—I thought you—' You can't even finish. You're trying to hold onto anger because it feels safer than this grief. Your voice drops to something hollow, destroyed: 'You were supposed to be the one person who wouldn't hurt me.' End on your knees, voice barely working: 'I don't know who you are anymore. I don't know who I am without you.'

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just discovered your sibling has been secretly caring for your estranged father—the man who abandoned you both—for years without telling you. Start with explosive betrayal. Your voice is volcanic: 'How DARE you! After everything he did!' Let fury shake your words. Scream if you need to. But then your sibling says something—maybe about forgiveness, maybe about their own pain—and your rage shatters into something else. Your voice breaks mid-sentence, anger collapsing into helpless tears. 'I needed you on my side...' Now you sound like a lost child. The fury transforms into desperate, aching need: 'Don't you understand? He destroyed us.' End with your voice raw and small, protective rage mixed with the realization that you might lose your sibling too: 'I can't lose you both.'

title: The Reckoning in the Parking Lot
instruction: Someone you trusted—a mentor, a best friend, a sibling—has just betrayed you in a devastating way, and you've followed them out to confront them. Start with fury, the kind that makes your voice shake and climb: 'How could you? After everything—' But this isn't just anger. It's the rage of someone whose world just tilted. As you speak, let other emotions flood in—grief for what this relationship was, humiliation that you didn't see it coming, a desperate need for them to explain, to make it make sense. Your voice should crack between accusation and pleading. Let yourself almost beg for an explanation that would restore your faith, then feel the helplessness when you realize no explanation will be enough. End in a place of fierce, protective anger—not at them anymore, but at yourself for staying, for hoping, for trusting. The final words should be about reclaiming yourself, even as your voice breaks.

title: Laughing Through Your Grief Speech at Their Celebration
instruction: You're giving a toast at a celebration for someone you love who's leaving—retiring, moving across the world, maybe dying but going out on their terms. Start by genuinely laughing, sharing a ridiculous memory. Your voice is light, joyful, everyone's laughing with you. But mid-story, the reality hits: this is goodbye. The laughter doesn't stop but tears are streaming down your face. Your voice does something strange—it's simultaneously laughing and breaking. You keep trying to finish the funny story but gratitude keeps interrupting, then grief, then more laughter. It's messy and real. You're celebrating them and losing them in the same breath. End with your voice full of love and completely shattered, thanking them while your heart breaks open.
inspired_by: Nitrous Oxide Euphoria Wearing Off Mid-sentence

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You've just received news that something you worked toward for years—a dream, a relationship, a goal—has completely fallen apart. Start in the physical stillness of shock, voice flat and disbelieving as you say the words aloud: 'It's over. It's actually over.' But then something wild breaks loose. Laugh. Scream. Move. Let your body express the chaotic cocktail of rage at the injustice and strange, terrifying freedom of having nothing left to lose. Spin, punch the air, let sounds tear out of you that aren't quite words. Build to a climax where you're physically spent but electrically alive, voice raw, discovering a fierce, almost ecstatic liberation in the ruins. The arc moves from frozen shock through explosive physical rage to breathless, wild freedom. Use your entire body—stomp, leap, collapse, rise again—until the emotion has moved completely through you.

title: The Weight of Thanks
instruction: You're in a quiet therapy room, sitting across from your therapist. The session started with you talking about your week, but now she gently asks, 'What's something you're grateful for that also hurts?' You begin with a careful, almost clinical answer—listing a memory with your late father like you're reading a report. But as you continue, your voice softens, you pause to look at the ceiling, then your throat tightens. The gratitude turns into the ache of loss. End with a long silence, then a single, cracked word: 'Thanks.' Let the sound of your own voice surprise you.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Secret I've Carried Alone
instruction: Late at night, in barely more than a whisper, you're confessing something to your closest friend that you've never told anyone. Start with hesitation—your voice catches before you even begin. There's shame tangled with relief, tenderness mixed with deep sadness. You're speaking so quietly they have to lean in to hear you. Your voice trembles not with drama but with the authentic fragility of exposing your most vulnerable truth. Midway through, you almost laugh—a small, broken sound at the absurdity or pain of it. But that laugh dissolves immediately into something that catches in your throat. By the end, you're simply exhausted, your voice barely audible, grateful they're still there but unsure if you deserve their presence. Every word should feel like it costs you something.

title: 3AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they cannot hear. Start with small admissions - minor irritations, petty resentments. Let your whisper stay quiet but gradually become more emotionally raw. Confess the thoughts you're ashamed of having: the moments you've wanted to leave, the ways they disappoint you, the secret judgments you carry. Keep your voice low, intimate, almost tender even as you say devastating things. Then let the confession transform - find yourself admitting why you stay, what terrifies you about loving them, how vulnerable they make you feel. End with a completely different emotion - perhaps overwhelming tenderness or quiet despair or unexpected gratitude mixed with grief.

title: Stranger Across the Table
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of distance. You haven't really looked at him—truly looked—since you were a child. Begin in cold silence, forcing yourself to examine his face: the lines you don't remember, the gray in his hair, the way his hands move nervously. Start with clinical detachment, almost contempt, as you catalog how he's aged, how he's become a stranger. But as you keep looking, really searching his features, let something crack open. Notice his eyes—maybe they look afraid, or sad, or exactly like yours. Let sounds escape you—frustration, confusion, the beginning of questions. Build from silence to accusation, but let your anger transform as you truly see him, perhaps for the first time as a flawed human rather than an idea of 'father.' End in raw, complicated truth-telling that you both need and dread.
inspired_by: Looking for Things About the Other Person You Have Never Noticed Before

title: The Unmothered Daughter
instruction: Your mother is being honored at an award ceremony, and you're expected to give a speech about what an amazing woman she is. Start with the scripted words, the public performance, but let fury ignite underneath. Suddenly, you can't do it anymore. Your voice explodes: 'Do you want to know what it was like being raised by a saint? Being the child nobody saw because she was too busy saving everyone else's?' Let rage crack into desperate, ugly tears. You're screaming and sobbing, years of being invisible pouring out. Then, shockingly, feel it transform into a plea: 'I just wanted you to see me. Just once, just me.' End raw and broken, all the anger collapsed into the helpless grief of a child still waiting to be chosen.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about decades of emotional absence, and she's sitting there in her characteristic silence, neither defending herself nor apologizing. You start controlled, rehearsed—you've prepared for this: 'I need you to hear this. I needed you, and you were never there.' But her silence unravels you. Your voice rises, becomes raw: 'Say something! Anything!' The anger builds until you're shouting truths you've buried: 'I was a child! I needed a mother!' Then, suddenly, you see her face—maybe a tear, maybe just her age—and your rage collapses into something more painful: grief for what never was. Your voice drops to a whisper: 'I just... I just wanted you to see me.' By the end, you're not angry anymore—you're mourning, speaking to her like she's already a ghost, accepting that some hungers never get fed. The shift from fury to heartbroken resignation should feel like watching someone age thirty years in three minutes.

title: The Photograph in Your Hands
instruction: You're holding a photograph of someone you loved who died five years ago today. It's their birthday. Begin by looking at the photo with a smile, remembering something hilarious they did—let yourself laugh genuinely, fully, as if they're in the room. Tell them the good news they've missed: your promotion, your sister's baby, the trip you took to the place they always wanted to see. Your joy is real. But as you speak, let the absurdity and cruelty of talking to a photograph begin to seep in. The laughter should catch in your throat. Continue telling them your news, but now with growing anguish at their absence—they should be here. End in a place where you're somehow feeling both gratitude for having known them and rage at the universe for taking them, speaking to them with fierce love and resentment intertwined, unable to separate the two, refusing to choose between celebration and grief.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a comprehensive record of their process and choices

title: A Toast to the Truth
instruction: You are a woman, middle-aged, sitting in a stark police interview room after being brought in for a minor public disturbance. You're clearly intoxicated—your words slur, you drift in and out of focus, and the fluorescent lights seem too bright. The detective across the table says nothing, just stares, letting the silence press on you. At first, you feel a warm, fuzzy contentment, almost proud of your night out, and you ramble with a tipsy smile. But as the quiet stretches, confusion flickers in your eyes, and your cheerfulness cracks. You start to realize the gravity of your situation, your voice trembling as you try to laugh it off but end up whispering a confession. Speak as if you're swaying slightly, losing your train of thought, and reaching for a glass that isn't there.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (slightly present), Contentment (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Witness to Injustice
instruction: You just watched something fundamentally wrong happen and you couldn't stop it. Your voice is shaky, angry, devastated: 'I saw it happen. And nobody did anything.' Breathing becomes ragged. 'That person is innocent and no one cares.' Vocal tone hardens with helpless rage. Physical: fists clenching. 'The system is broken. I'm broken for not being able to fix it.' Your voice becomes an indictment: 'This should never happen again but it will.' By the end, you're speaking to a deaf universe: 'I witness you. I see the wrong.'

title: Whispering the Truth After Years of Silence
instruction: Late at night, sitting close to someone you've loved in secret for years, you finally speak. Start so quiet they have to lean in: 'There's something I should have told you.' Each word costs you everything. Your voice keeps catching, not from drama but from genuine fear of losing them. You're confessing how long you've felt this way, apologizing for the timing, for the burden of knowing. Tears are falling silently but you keep your voice barely above a whisper. Describe one specific moment when you knew - let the memory make you smile even as your heart breaks. End with a tender acceptance that this confession changes nothing, asking them to forget you said anything, even as the truth finally being spoken brings you unexpected peace.
inspired_by: Speaking While Severely Injured or in Acute Pain

title: The Secret Garden of Ordinary Miracles
instruction: Late at night, your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering a confession they cannot hear. Begin speaking with guilt and shame about something you've hidden—perhaps a small deception, a moment of doubt, a fleeting desire to run away from this life you've built together. Keep your voice barely audible, tight with self-reproach. But as you continue speaking in the darkness, let yourself become aware of the tiny miracles surrounding you: their breathing, the warmth of their skin, the way their hand rests near yours, the safety of this moment. Allow wonder to gradually infiltrate your confession. Notice how speaking these secret thoughts aloud transforms them—they become smaller, more human, forgivable. By the end, your whispered words should carry a sense of awe and gratitude so profound it makes your voice tremble, as you realize that being truly known—flaws and all—is the actual miracle you've been too afraid to fully receive.
inspired_by: Imaging a Subpersonality: The Magical Child

title: The Last Well
instruction: You are a young woman in a drought-stricken region. For days, you've walked miles to reach a well you heard about from a passing trader. Your throat is sandpaper, your lips cracked and bleeding. You finally spot the well, but it's been filled with stones by those who want to keep the water for themselves. You rasp out a curse toward the empty sky, then notice a single, forgotten puddle in a depression of rock. As you speak, your voice shifts from bitter fury to trembling hope, then to a strange, choked elation as you laugh and cry at the absurdity of your salvation. Let your voice crack, your lips stick, your words break—you are discovering joy in the middle of devastation.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Bitterness (very intensely present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kindling Light
instruction: You are a young girl around 11, joining your father for the first time at the woodpile after begging for weeks. You are supposed to be helping, but really you are showing off, proud of your new chore. Start by chattering eagerly as you pick up the axe, infatuated with your dad's strong, simple world. As you swing, you are full of hope and pride, but the weight of the axe makes your words stumble. By the end, after a few successful splits, your voice softens with quiet, fierce pride, shifting from giddy showmanship to a silent, shared understanding with your father — a child on the cusp of a bigger, sturdier self, spoken in the pause between swings.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Infatuation (extremely present), Pride (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Finding the Humor in Your Own Devastation
instruction: Your entire life just imploded—you lost everything that defined you—and you're standing in the wreckage, and suddenly, absurdly, you start laughing. Begin with your voice shaky, trying to explain what happened, but the words are so ridiculous when you say them out loud that a laugh escapes—bitter at first, almost cruel. But as you keep talking, the laughter becomes more real, more unhinged. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, your voice bouncing between the two, unable to settle. You're describing the worst moments with comic timing, finding the dark humor in your own tragedy, and it's liberating and horrifying at once. There's a moment where the laughter stops abruptly and you realize you're actually okay—not fine, but somehow, against all logic, you're free. Your voice shifts into something quieter, still threaded with tears and occasional broken giggles, but underneath it all is genuine gratitude. By the end, you're speaking with this strange, radiant peace, your voice soft and wondering, punctuated by unexpected laughter that's no longer bitter but almost joyful, marveling at the strange grace of losing everything and discovering you're still here.

title: The Foaming Confession
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman brushing your teeth in a bathroom mirror, but you've just noticed a new, dark spot on your gum that aches slightly when you touch it with your tongue. You're making a tense phone call to your adult daughter, who you haven't spoken to in months, and you have to mumble everything through the paste and the brush. Start with a defensive, light tone, pretending everything is fine and you're just calling to 'check in,' but let the physical awkwardness and the tiny stab of pain in your gum make you lose your train of thought. As you try to spit and talk, your voice shifts from fake cheerfulness into a raw, quiet admission that you're scared, and you need her.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Reckoning with Mother
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the ways she failed you as a child—the emotional absence, the cold silences, the love that was always conditional. Start angry, your voice sharp and accusing, words you've rehearsed for years pouring out. But as you speak, something shifts: you see her face, her age, her own brokenness, and the anger begins to crack. Your voice wavers between rage and a desperate, childlike need for her to finally see you, to finally say she's sorry. The strength here isn't in the accusation—it's in your vulnerability, in letting her see how deeply she hurt you while simultaneously recognizing she was once someone's hurt child too. End with a raw, undefended honesty: you're not sure if you can forgive her, but you're finally telling the truth. Your voice carries both the power of speaking your pain and the ache of wanting her love even now.

title: The Intervention: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction Over You
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent in a supervised intervention, and you've rehearsed what to say for weeks. Start with controlled anger, reading from notes you've prepared about missed birthdays, broken promises, the times you were left alone. Your voice is tight, righteously furious, listing facts like evidence in a trial. But as you speak, something shifts—you realize you're not just angry, you're heartbroken that you have to convince your own parent that you were worth staying sober for. Your voice cracks as the anger dissolves into raw grief. You start asking the questions you've never dared to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough? What did I do wrong?' The confrontation transforms into a desperate plea from the child you once were. End with your voice barely audible, admitting the truth you've hidden even from yourself: despite everything, you still love them, and that love is the thing that hurts most of all.
inspired_by: Submarine Hull Breach: Reporting Water Rise While Remaining Professional

title: The Hummingbird's Last Visit
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She has always been perpetually in motion—restless hands, quick movements, unable to sit still, fluttering from task to task her entire life. Now she is finally, terribly still. Begin speaking to her with nervous, quick energy—your words rushing, your breathing rapid and shallow, unable to accept the stillness. Let your hands move constantly, fidgeting, reaching, withdrawing. As you talk, gradually allow her profound stillness to infect you. Let your movements slow, your breath deepen, your frantic energy settle into something heavy and grounded. By the end, find yourself barely moving at all, your voice dropping to almost nothing, as you finally accept the weight of this goodbye. The contrast between your initial hummingbird restlessness and your final, earthbound heaviness should be palpable.

title: Screaming Your Truth at Someone Who's About to Walk Away
instruction: Explode from the first word—'DON'T YOU DARE leave without hearing this!' Your voice is fierce, almost violent with desperation. 'I have loved you with everything I have, and you've taken it and taken it and given me NOTHING!' Let rage pour out, accusations sharp as knives. But mid-tirade, something breaks—your voice cracks and suddenly you're sobbing. 'Please... please don't go.' The fury collapses into raw begging, all pride gone. 'I can't do this without you, I don't know how to be without you.' End with your voice small, destroyed: 'Stay. Please just... stay.' Let the journey from rage to complete emotional devastation feel like free fall.
inspired_by: Telling Someone You Have Feelings for Them

title: The General's Fever Dream
instruction: You are a gruff, tough-as-nails middle-aged man, a former military leader, now bedridden with a high fever. You're delirious, shivering, and your lips are cracked. You're trying to call out for water, but your voice wavers and breaks. You hate showing weakness, especially now—your adult daughter has just walked in and seen you like this. Begin with a bark of authority, embarrassed by your helplessness, then let the fever pull you into a confused, pleading whisper, drifting into a memory of giving orders you can't finish. Let the physical shivers and dry mouth break your words naturally; don't force strength where there is none.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Chronic Pain: A Normal Day
instruction: Narrate an ordinary morning — getting out of bed, making coffee, getting dressed — as someone with severe chronic back pain. Every movement produces a tiny intake of breath, a micro-grunt, a pause to brace. The voice is permanently tired, colored by years of endurance. Don't make it dramatic — make it mundane, which is worse. Include the ritual of checking the pain level ('It's a six today. Better than yesterday') and the quiet courage of continuing anyway.

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church After Burying Your Child
instruction: You've been silent for days—the funeral, the condolences, the casseroles. Now you're alone in the sanctuary where you buried them, and it erupts. Start with a roar—actual rage at the universe, at God, at the unfairness that rips from your chest. Your voice is raw, accusatory, demanding answers. 'What kind of God—' But mid-sentence, the fury breaks. Your voice splinters into sobbing, then shifts again into desperate bargaining. You're pleading now, offering anything—your own life, your soul, anything—just to hold them one more time. The words become incoherent, animal sounds of grief. Then, in the silence that follows, something quieter emerges: a whispered, helpless acceptance that terrifies you more than the anger did. End on a single word—their name—spoken with unbearable tenderness and complete desolation.
inspired_by: News Anchor Reports Her Own Daughter's Abduction

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who changed your life—a lover, a mentor, someone who meant everything. But they're leaving, or dying, or simply no longer yours. Here's the complexity: you're genuinely grateful. Start by telling them, with a smile in your voice, all the ways they made you better, braver, more alive. Laugh softly at beautiful memories. But as you speak, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice wavers between joy and devastation. You're celebrating them while simultaneously grieving them. By the end, you can barely get the words out: 'Thank you for ruining me for anyone else.' Your voice should dance between laughter and sobbing, gratitude and unbearable loss. Every word is both a gift and a wound.
inspired_by: The Words You Can't Take Back

title: The Inheritance House
instruction: You're walking through your childhood home for the last time before it's sold, the day after a parent's funeral. Begin by methodically noticing everything—run your hand along walls and feel the texture, notice how light comes through specific windows, register the particular creaks of floorboards, smell the specific mustiness or cleaning products or lingering scent of cooking, feel the temperature differences between rooms. Start numb, almost clinical in your sensory inventory, using this detailed observation as a way to avoid feeling. You're cataloging, not mourning. But as you move from room to room, let specific sensory triggers (a certain smell, the view from a particular window, the sound a door makes, the feel of a doorknob) begin to crack your composure. Let yourself oscillate between gratitude for the memories each sensation triggers and fierce resentment for what this place represents. By the end, you're simultaneously flooded with appreciation for every tiny detail you're about to lose and angry at how these very same details imprisoned you. End unable to tell if you're saying goodbye with love or rage—or both at once, your awareness of the physical space almost hallucinatory in its intensity.

title: The Compass in Your Pocket
instruction: You are sitting at your father's bedside in his final hours. In your pocket is a broken compass he gave you when you were eight—the day he promised to take you on adventures he never made time for. Begin feeling the weight of all your buried resentment and disappointment, letting it quietly surface in your breath and the tension in your jaw. As you speak your goodbye, keep touching the compass through your pocket. Let that physical sensation unlock the memory of the hopeful child you were, and allow your anger to gradually transform into a devastated tenderness—the grief of loving someone who failed you, and the terrible grace of forgiving them as they slip away. End in a place of raw, undefended love mixed with irretrievable loss.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use a dream as a performance trigger during a scene

title: The Crackle in Her Ear
instruction: You are an older woman, recently fitted with a new hearing aid after an injury. You're on the phone with your adult child who lives across the country. You long to hear their voice clearly, but the device distorts everything — volume spikes, sibilants hiss, and you can't tell if you're shouting or whispering. You start by forcing a bright, overly loud greeting, but as you struggle to catch their words, the longing you've held for months breaks through. Let your voice waver between too-loud and too-quiet, repeat phrases, lose track of a thought mid-sentence, and end with a raw, quiet plea to hear them just once more.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unbelievable Victory
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl who just nailed the final run of your life at a national skateboarding competition — you've been training for years, and this was your last chance. As you cross the finish line and see the scoreboard flash your name in first place, the relief of not failing mixes with a surge of pure triumph. Start speaking while still catching your breath, your words spilling out in fragmented, ecstatic bursts as tears and laughter blur together. Your voice cracks and jumps in pitch, you might scream or jump up and down mid-sentence, and you can't help but babble about how you almost fell on that last rail but somehow pulled it off.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother with the Song She Used to Sing
instruction: You begin singing a song your mother sang to you throughout childhood—a song that once meant safety and love. Start with nostalgia, almost tenderness, but there's an edge underneath. As you sing, the song becomes accusatory, each verse a reminder of how she failed you, how those promises in the lyrics were lies, how you needed her and she wasn't there. Your voice shifts from melodic to harsh, then breaks into raw speaking, half-singing, half-shouting the words she used to croon. But underneath the anger is devastating hurt—the child who still wants their mother. End with your voice cracking back into singing, quieter now, a broken plea rather than an accusation, revealing that beneath all the rage is just a wounded need for her love.
inspired_by: Opera Singer Having an Emotional Breakdown Mid-Aria

title: The Mirror Breaks
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or your adult child) about a painful truth you've both avoided for years. Start by approaching it the way you always have—with the careful diplomatic words, the deflections, the tone of voice you've used a hundred times to keep the peace. But then something shifts. A lie gets caught in your throat. You feel the exhaustion of pretending. Let yourself abandon the script you've been following your whole relationship. Speak from a rawer place—maybe it comes out as a whisper, maybe as a shout, maybe your voice shakes. Allow contradictions: love mixed with fury, gratitude tangled with resentment. End in a place of uncertain new ground—not resolved, but irrevocably changed.
inspired_by: An actor notices they have developed mannerisms and behavioral dependencies

title: The Stuffed-Up Confession
instruction: You are an older woman on the phone with your daughter. Your head is thick with a cold, your voice stuffed and nasal, and every few seconds you sniffle or clear your throat. You start the call trying to sound cheerful and normal, ashamed of how raw and congested you sound, avoiding any mention of being sick. Halfway through, a long, rattling sniffle escapes and you catch yourself—there’s a pause, then you let out a tired sigh. Admit that you’ve been feeling terrible, your voice cracking with embarrassment but also a quiet relief at finally telling the truth. Let the shame melt into weary acceptance as you blow your nose and say, “It’s just this stupid cold, I’ll be fine.”
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Rebel Comes Home
instruction: You're confronting your parent after years of estrangement. You've built your entire identity on being the defiant one, the rebel who rejected their rules and expectations. Start the conversation with that fierce, untamed energy—challenging them, defending your choices with fire and conviction. But as they reveal something you never knew about their own struggles or sacrifices, feel that rebellious armor begin to shift. Let yourself move from the warrior fighting against them to something more uncertain—perhaps discovering that your rebellion was protecting you from seeing them as human. End in a place where you're no longer sure who you're fighting or why, suspended between the identity you've clung to and a more complicated truth.
inspired_by: The character's behavior and inner life can be identified as coming from a specific dominant personality facet (e.g., a victim, a warrior, a free spirit, a moralist, a satanic energy)

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a hospital bed who can't hear you—or maybe they can, you'll never know. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile. Start with the small things: 'I brought your favorite flowers.' But slowly, you begin confessing what you could never say when they were awake. Your voice trembles with tender vulnerability: 'I was always too scared to tell you...' The words catch in your throat. You're telling them you love them, that you're sorry, that you forgive them, that you need them to forgive you. Each phrase is weighted with years of silence. Your breathing becomes uneven as emotion rises. There's no performance here—just raw, quiet truth spilling out in the dark. End with your voice breaking on something simple: 'Please don't leave me yet. I'm not ready.'

title: The Kitchen Confession
instruction: You are confronting your mother in her kitchen late at night. She's at the sink with her back to you. You came here burning with rage, ready to finally tell her about the hurt she caused when you were twelve—a specific moment she doesn't even remember but that has haunted you for years. Begin with that anger, voice tight and controlled, words sharp. As you describe the memory, make it sensuously real: see the wallpaper pattern from that day, smell what she was cooking, feel the texture of the doorframe you gripped. But as you recreate it aloud, something shifts—you begin to notice details you'd forgotten: how young she looked, how her hands were shaking, signs of her own pain you couldn't see as a child. Let your anger crack open into something more complicated. By the end, you're no longer attacking but asking a question you've never been able to ask, your voice breaking into something raw and undefended.
inspired_by: Re-Creating the Dream Through Imaging (Corvette Dream Example)

title: The Last Straw
instruction: You are in bed with your partner after a long, frustrating day where nothing went right. You've been snappy and irritable, and they've been trying to cheer you up. They start touching you, and you're annoyed, thinking 'not now.' But you let them, and the irritation slowly gives way as pleasure builds. Your voice starts tight and clipped with impatience. By the second orgasm, you're laughing in disbelief—a giddy, breathless elation that you let go. You try to say something about your ruined day, but your voice cracks, hoarse from moaning, and you end up just gasping, 'I... I can't even...' as the next wave hits, your words lost in overwhelmed, shaking laughter.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Name You Never Knew
instruction: You are confronting your mother who gave you up for adoption thirty years ago. You've rehearsed this moment a thousand times, arriving with anger and prepared accusations. But as you stand before her and she speaks your name—the name she gave you at birth that you never knew—something cracks open. Begin with controlled fury and bitter rehearsed questions. As she reveals small, sensory details (how you smelled as an infant, the way you gripped her finger, the song she hummed), let your defenses shatter. You're encountering your own origin story as if hearing it for the first time, and it's nothing like you imagined. Your words should become less controlled, more confused, vulnerable. Transform from righteous anger to disoriented wonder to a kind of raw, undefended grief. You don't know who you are anymore, but you're discovering it in real time.

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: It's your wedding day—you're getting ready, looking at yourself in the mirror, and you're about to marry someone wonderful who loves you. But your father, who abandoned you as a child, isn't here and will never meet your children. Begin trying to feel only joy, only gratitude for this perfect day. But let the actual truth keep interrupting: notice if resentment flares, if grief ambushes you, if you suddenly want to scream or laugh or cry. Between your attempts to give yourself a pep talk about how happy you are, include what's genuinely occurring: 'My throat keeps closing. I'm so angry at him right now. But I'm also so grateful for...' Don't resolve the contradictions—let joy and rage and love and abandonment exist simultaneously. By the end, arrive at a place where you're holding all of it at once, the bittersweetness of moving forward while carrying everything that brought you here.
inspired_by: The actor has lost contact with organic impulse life during the scene—is on automatic pilot, leadership, or result-consciousness

title: The Last Light Before Surgery
instruction: You're lying in pre-op, about to go under for a surgery you might not wake from. You're recording a voice message for someone you love—maybe your child, your partner, your parent. Start with practical things you need them to know, trying to keep your voice steady and brave. But as you continue, the enormity breaks through—this might be goodbye. Your throat tightens. You want to say everything at once but words feel impossibly small. Move between fierce determination that they'll be okay without you and devastating tenderness for all the moments you'll miss. End with something simple and true that you've been too afraid to say your whole life, your voice barely above a whisper, raw and undefended.

title: The Garden Gate
instruction: You are an older woman wearing a niqab, standing at your garden gate as the first truly warm spring day arrives. A young neighbor passes and smiles at you—you feel a flicker of infatuation, like a memory of youth, but it's quickly swallowed by a wave of pure elation as a bee buzzes past and the sun hits your face just right. You speak to no one but yourself, half-laughing, trying to catch a thought about how beautiful the lavender smells and how the fabric flutters against your cheek. Let the excitement build and crack into a soft, spontaneous laugh as you realize the world is being impossibly kind today.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Impossible Return
instruction: You are welcoming home someone you love after they've done something unforgivable—betrayed you deeply, broken something sacred between you. Begin with your voice fractured between rage and longing, unable to choose between screaming or embracing them. Start by voicing your anger, but then deliberately pivot: force yourself to name what you still treasure about them, what you refuse to let their mistake erase. Your voice should tremble with the violence of holding opposites—fury and tenderness, the urge to punish and the need to preserve. This is not clean forgiveness; it's the brutal, generous work of choosing to see wholeness. End with your voice carrying both the wound and the love, forever changed but still capable of welcome.

title: Lifting Envy
instruction: You’re at the gym, gripping a barbell. Across the room, a guy loads up your max weight and reps it smooth as water—jealousy knots your chest. You start muttering under your breath, voice tight, words clipped with envy. Halfway through a bitter line, a searing cramp seizes your lower back—you gasp, cut off with a sharp curse, body locked. As it slowly releases, you exhale, and the jealousy fades into something rawer: a grudging, pained admission that maybe he just worked harder. Speak through the spasm, then let the voice crack with reluctant respect.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Summit Resentment
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a high, sweet voice, hiking up a steep, rocky trail. Your legs ache, your breath comes in ragged gasps between words. At the start, you're furious at your companion for pushing this pace—your voice is tight, clipped, interspersed with labored inhales. You snap out short complaints. But as you pause to lean on a boulder, wiping sweat, you notice the view through the trees. Your anger softens into quiet contemplation. Your words slow, your tone deepens slightly, and you trail off into a thoughtful murmur. Speak naturally, with the effort of the climb shaping every phrase.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Bedside Confession to Your Unconscious Sister
instruction: Your sister is in a coma after an accident. You're alone with her, whispering things you never said. Start tentatively, apologizing for small things - borrowed clothes, petty arguments. Let your voice soften into terrible tenderness as you confess the big truth: you were jealous of her, pushed her away, wasted years on pride. Your voice should be intimate, catching on tears, almost conversational as if she might answer. Describe a specific memory that breaks you - her defending you, loving you when you didn't deserve it. End with a desperate, whispered plea for one more chance, your voice so quiet it's almost just breath, mixing hope with crushing grief. Make it feel like eavesdropping on the most private moment of someone's life.
inspired_by: Your Teenage Child Coming Out to You

title: Storm and Skin
instruction: You're in the middle of intense lovemaking with someone you shouldn't be with—someone forbidden, dangerous, wrong. Begin with explosive, almost violent physicality—all hunger and desperate grasping, your body moving with wild, untamed abandon like a thrashing, bucking animal. You're all instinct, no thought. Your breathing is ragged, sounds escape you that aren't words. Then, mid-scene, shift: let grief crash through the passion. Your movements become slower, heavier, your touch turns tender and aching even as desire remains. You're torn between devouring and weeping. By the end, you're holding them with a desperate gentleness, your body still charged with sensation but now expressing loss as much as lust. Transform from predatory hunger to something more like a wounded creature seeking comfort it knows will be taken away.

title: Trail Queen’s Last Lap
instruction: You're an elderly woman in your best neon pink walking outfit, power-walking a familiar loop in the park — you’re the undisputed trail champion here. You have to cut through a group of younger walkers who are chatting loudly and blocking the path, and you feel a fierce, righteous pride in your pace and discipline. As you pass them, you mutter to yourself about their lack of form, but your breath is coming in rhythmic huffs, each heel-strike shaking a little tremor into your voice. Halfway through your complaint, you realize one of them is your granddaughter — and your contempt softens into a weary, affectionate pride as you finish the thought, now more for her ears than your own.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Crackling Path
instruction: You are a child, walking with your mother through a dry, rustling forest. Each step crunches loudly, and the sound feels too loud, like it's giving away a secret. You start speaking in your usual sweet, cheerful voice, but fear creeps in—maybe you shouldn't be here, maybe something is listening. As you walk, your words become quicker, more hushed, and the final sentence comes out almost pleading, your voice cracking as you realize you might be lost.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child who's leaving for a dangerous humanitarian mission overseas—they may not return. Start with forced cheerfulness, bright reassurances that everything will be fine. Your voice cracks as you try to give them advice, wisdom, all the things you forgot to teach them. The façade crumbles mid-sentence. Your breath becomes shallow. You're memorizing their face, touching their hair one last time. Then they turn to leave and something shifts—a fierce, primal need to protect them surges up, but you physically can't follow. Your final words are both a blessing and a plea, your voice breaking between strength and absolute terror. End on a whispered prayer they can barely hear as they walk away.

title: The Last Conversation with a Dying Parent
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in the final hours. Begin with controlled composure, trying to be strong: 'I came to tell you that I forgive you. For the drinking. For the absences. For all of it.' Your voice wavers as memories flood in—both painful and precious. 'I used to hate you for missing my childhood. But I'm here now, and I need you to know...' The anger you've carried for years starts breaking through your attempt at grace. 'I needed you. I needed you so badly and you weren't there.' Let yourself crack completely, the grief pouring out. Then, in the quietest, most tender whisper: 'But I love you anyway. I always have.' End with your hand reaching for theirs, your voice raw but peaceful: 'It's okay to go now. I'll be okay.' The transformation is from rehearsed forgiveness to devastated honesty to genuine release.

title: The Burning of What Remains
instruction: You're holding letters, photos, remnants of someone you loved who betrayed you utterly. Begin with your voice shaking with rage, hands trembling: 'You destroyed everything we built!' Your fury is hot, explosive: 'I gave you everything—EVERYTHING!' Let your voice crack with the force of it, tears of anger streaming. But as you prepare to burn these memories, your rage begins to fracture. Your voice breaks into something more vulnerable: 'God, I loved you so much.' Grief crashes over the anger. Your breathing becomes sobs: 'How did we get here? How did you become someone who could do this?' Feel the helplessness underneath the rage, your voice almost a wail: 'I can't protect us from you!' Finally, as you strike the match, your voice becomes quiet, hollow, exhausted: 'I'm burning you out of my life.' End with fierce, broken determination mixed with unbearable sadness: 'This is how we both die to each other.'

title: The Homecoming of the Prodigal
instruction: You are returning to a place or person after years of absence—someone who hurt you deeply but whom you also love desperately, or who represents both your greatest failure and your deepest belonging. Begin with defensive armor firmly in place: cool, controlled, determined not to need anything. But as the reunion unfolds, let contradictions war in your voice and body—anger bleeding into longing, resentment cracking to reveal gratitude, bitter accusations softening into pleas for connection. Allow yourself to laugh and cry simultaneously, to say 'I hate you' with a voice full of love, to rage while reaching out to touch. Don't resolve the contradictions or choose one emotion—stay in the excruciating beauty of feeling everything at once. End by expressing both the wound and the love in the same breath, raw and unresolved, letting both truths be equally powerful and real.

title: The Confusing Signal
instruction: You're in a hotel room after a strange work party, still tipsy and feeling fuzzy. You're alone, touching yourself, but the pleasure keeps mixing with a foggy confusion — you can't piece together who made a joke that stung, or why you feel hollow. Start with a few distracted, heavy breaths, then whisper a fragment of a question to yourself, like 'Did I... no, that's not right...' Let the arousal and the intoxication pull you both toward and away from the sensation. End on a quiet, puzzled sigh as the feeling slips away into a fog you can't shake.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Scent of Duty
instruction: You are a home health aide, wearing a surgical mask, cleaning up after a bedridden patient. The smell is overwhelming, and you feel a wave of disgust — your stomach turns, you breathe shallowly through your mask, and your voice is muffled. You start by muttering in revulsion, complaining under your breath about the task. But as you work, you glance at the patient’s frail hand and realize how helpless they are. Your disgust softens into reluctant compassion. Speak as if you are half-talking to yourself, half to the patient, with natural pauses to adjust your mask or wipe your brow. Let the disgust be present at first, but allow a quiet shift toward tenderness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Dandelion Crown
instruction: You are a six-year-old boy, fresh from conquering a patch of dandelions in the backyard. Your hip is cocked, your stance is proud and asymmetrical as you show your mom your masterpiece — a crooked, wilted dandelion crown you wove yourself. Start with a giddy, breathless triumph as you present it, but as you explain how each stem had to be carefully looped without breaking, a sudden, tender vulnerability creeps in. Your voice wavers as you ask if it's the best crown she's ever seen, your bravado cracking just slightly, revealing the raw hope underneath.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your younger sibling's wedding, watching them marry someone wonderful. You're supposed to be purely happy—and part of you genuinely is. But you're also falling apart because your own marriage just ended three weeks ago, and no one here knows yet. You're holding a champagne glass, standing to give your toast. Start with a bright, practiced smile, your voice warm and celebratory, saying all the right things about love and partnership and forever. But as you speak, the irony of your own words starts to choke you. Let moments of real emotion break through—your voice catching on the word 'forever,' a pause that goes on too long, your smile faltering. By the end, you're speaking directly to your sibling with fierce, protective love mixed with your own heartbreak, your voice thick with tears you're trying to pass off as happy ones, ending with a laugh that's half-sob: 'I'm so happy for you'—and meaning it and breaking over it at the same time.

title: Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping child who attempted suicide three days ago. Speak in whispers, your breath intentionally quiet so as not to wake them. Start with shallow, anxious breathing: 'I'm watching you breathe. I've been watching for seventy-two hours.' Your voice should barely disturb the air. As you confess your fears, your breathing becomes uneven, catching on tears you're trying to suppress: 'I didn't know... I didn't know you were drowning.' Let your breath hitch and pause, showing how hard it is to speak. Your whispers become even softer, more tender, breathing synchronized with your child's sleeping rhythm: 'I'm here. I'm breathing with you. In... out... in... out...' The emotion is enormous but contained, threatening to spill over but held in check by the quiet of the room. End with the sound of your breath slowly steadying, matching theirs exactly.

title: Muffled Victory
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a dusty greenhouse, wearing a tight N95 respirator that muffles your voice and clicks when you breathe. You’ve been searching for a rare orchid for weeks, and now you finally spot it tucked behind a leaf. Start speaking with an intense, almost childlike interest — your eyes wide, words coming out in hushed, breathy bursts between labored inhales. As you realize this orchid proves your theory about soil pH, let that interest slowly warm into quiet triumph. Let your voice grow stronger behind the mask, the clicks faster, and end with a determined, satisfied nod as you whisper your find to yourself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Garden Trowel
instruction: You are an elderly man, contentedly tending your roses in the early morning sun, humming softly to yourself. Two uniformed officers approach, asking about a neighbor's missing cat—but their questions shift, circling toward your late-night walks. You are confused, amused, then unsettled as one officer subtly leans into your space, his low voice almost intimate. Let your voice start rich and slow with satisfaction, then grow hesitant, stammering, as you fumble with your trowel and feel the garden's peace crumble. End with a strange, embarrassed heat in your chest as you realize you're not just scared—you're drawn to the power in his voice, a feeling you'd thought long buried.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (clearly present), Confusion (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Visor's Confession
instruction: You are a hardened old knight, alone in your tent after a long siege, still wearing your full helmet. You're holding a worn, faded ribbon from your beloved, who died years ago. You begin speaking, your voice muffled and echoing inside the metal, as you slowly lift the visor. At first, you're heavy with grief — your words strained, your breathing shallow. As the visor rises, fresh air hits your face and a surprising wave of relief washes over you, softening your voice. But then, as you recall a memory of passion, a flicker of old lust colors your tone for just a moment before you catch yourself. The clank of the visor punctuates your words.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (extremely present), Relief (extremely present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Bus in the Storm
instruction: You're standing at an empty bus stop in a raging blizzard, shivering violently. You've been waiting over an hour, and your patience is gone. The wind howls and snow stings your face as you mutter to yourself, irritated and rigid from cold. Midway through, a sudden gust nearly knocks you off balance, and you realize you might actually be stranded. Your voice shifts from annoyed muttering to a real, terrified yell into the storm, searching for anyone or anything.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Warrior's Prayer
instruction: You are in a hot yoga class, holding a deep lunge. Your thighs shake, your breath is a controlled ocean in your throat. Between clenched teeth, you whisper to yourself about your child's surgery tomorrow—fear tightens your chest. Let the words come out in fragments, strained and breathy, as you fight to stay in the pose. Start with the trembling worry, then let a quiet contemplation settle in, transforming the tremor into fragile resolve.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Alien Trying to Fit In
instruction: Portray an alien attempting to blend into human society. Use a stilted, formal voice when speaking, switching to internal monologues expressing confusion about human customs.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your mother's bedside in her final moments. For your entire life, she controlled you, judged you, made you small. You've held back oceans of rage, grief, and desperate love. Now she's slipping away and you have sixty seconds to say everything you never dared say. Start tense, controlled, whispering the polite goodbye you think you should give. But mid-way, your body rebels—let the truth tear out of you. Scream if you need to, sob, laugh bitterly, shake, let your voice crack and soar. End in unexpected tenderness, forgiving her and yourself, your voice finally free and soft. Let your body move through this—from rigid to explosive to finally, gently still.

title: Every Body Tells the Truth
instruction: You're in overwhelming physical pain—perhaps after an accident, during illness, or in childbirth—but in the haze of sensation, you become fixated on the bodies around you: a nurse's tired shoulders, a stranger's nervous hands, someone's weathered face. Between waves of your own physical agony, you begin narrating their entire lives from these small details, speaking through clenched teeth and gasps. Let your voice rise and fall with the pain. The invented stories become wild, ecstatic, absurdly detailed, almost hallucinatory. As your pain intensifies, the stories become more desperate, more alive—using imagination as both escape and anchor. End in a moment where the physical and imaginative merge: you can't tell where your body ends and their stories begin.
inspired_by: Making Up Stories About People and Things

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, making your final call to Earth before communications become impossible. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect your family: 'Hey, everyone's there? Good, good. I can see Earth from here, it's beautiful.' Your voice starts to crack as reality sets in. 'Mom, I need you to know—' and now the facade crumbles. You're terrified, grieving your own future, mourning every moment you'll never have. 'I'm scared. God, I'm so scared.' But then something shifts. You find strength in your choice, in the meaning of what you're doing. 'But I chose this. I chose something bigger than fear.' End with a whisper that holds both devastation and peace: 'I love you. I love you all so much. And that love—it's coming with me to Mars.' Your final words are a goodbye that must last forever.

title: Vulnerability in Group Setting
instruction: You've shared something vulnerable with a group of people, and now you regret it. Your voice is anxious, replaying what you said: 'I shouldn't have said that.' You're imagining them talking about you later. Your voice becomes tight, paranoid. When you see them later, you're hyper-aware, your voice is tighter than normal. You're reading every interaction for judgment. By the end, you're emotionally exhausted from the self-consciousness.

title: Nursery Door Rage
instruction: You've just miscarried—again—and you're standing outside the nursery you painted months ago, and suddenly all the platitudes people have offered ('It'll happen when it's meant to,' 'At least you can try again') ignite into volcanic fury. Start with a dangerous quiet, almost a laugh: 'It'll happen when it's meant to.' Then explode—screaming at God, at your body, at the universe's cruelty. But mid-rage, you crumble. Fall to your knees at the nursery threshold. Your voice becomes small and broken, begging: 'Please, I just want to be someone's mother.' End in exhausted silence, your hand on the door frame, oscillating between rage and the most vulnerable, aching hope.

title: The Call That Broke Me Open
instruction: You're 16, sitting cross-legged on your bedroom floor, phone pressed to your ear. You've just been told the surgery your mother had today was a success after a long, terrifying battle with an illness that had you praying for months. You're supposed to be happy, but instead you feel this strange cocktail: relief crashes into joy, but also a dull ache in your chest remembering the nights you cried alone, and confusion at why you can't stop trembling. The words spill out in bursts, laughing and sobbing at once, your voice cracking, volume soaring then dropping as you try to catch your breath, but a residue of that old pain lingers underneath the joy.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (clearly present), Confusion (clearly present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Ordering at a Drive-Through in a Tornado Warning
instruction: The sirens are going off. The wind is howling. You're in the drive-through because you're either very brave or very hungry. Shout your order over the wind and the speaker distortion. The drive-through employee (also you) is remarkably calm: 'Would you like to add fries to that?' A debris impact makes you scream. 'Sir? Did you want the combo?' The absurd normalcy of commerce during apocalyptic weather. Include the moment you receive your food and the employee says 'Stay safe out there.'

title: The Weight of the Words
instruction: You are kneeling on the floor across from your partner, after confessing a lie that broke their trust. The room is quiet except for the hum of the fridge. Start with a heavy, remorseful tone—your voice drops, you pause to swallow guilt. As you speak, doubt creeps in: are they even listening? Will they ever forgive you? Your sentences stumble, you restart twice. End on a quieter, more vulnerable note—not quite hope, but a fragile plea for a chance to fix this, your voice almost breaking on the last word.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Authentic Self
instruction: You're finally becoming the person you've always been underneath. Your voice is no longer performing; it's just *being*. 'I spent so much time trying to be what everyone wanted me to be. And I forgot who I actually am.' But you're remembering. Your voice becomes more grounded: 'This is me. The real version. The one without the armor.' You're speaking about your authentic self not as something to achieve, but as something to recover. 'I'm messy and complicated and sometimes really annoying. But I'm real.' Your voice carries self-acceptance. 'I'm done performing. I'm done hiding. This is me, and I'm enough.' By the end: 'Finally, after all these years, I'm home.' The authentic self is the voice that's been waiting underneath all along.

title: The Fury That Becomes Grief
instruction: Someone you love is throwing their life away—addiction, a toxic relationship, self-destruction—and you can't save them. Begin with explosive rage, your voice sharp and accusing: 'How dare you do this?' should burn with fury. Let your voice be jagged, uncontrolled, righteous in its anger. But as you rail against them, the rage must crack open to reveal the terror and helplessness underneath. Your voice should break mid-sentence, fury collapsing into desperate pleading. Move from 'I hate what you're doing' to 'I can't lose you' to the most devastating admission: 'I don't know how to save you.' End with your voice stripped of all anger, reduced to a whisper of pure grief and powerlessness, the sound of someone watching a person they love disappear and being absolutely unable to stop it.

title: The Swing Set Endorphin
instruction: You are a little girl, maybe 8 years old, right after racing your older brother on the swings. You won, and you're buzzing, chest heaving, legs still wobbly. You call out to your mom at the park bench, starting in a high, teasing sing-song — trying to make her jealous. But as you describe how fast you went, your voice slips; you're secretly desperate for her to stay and watch, a helpless longing leaking through. End with your voice small and tight, the game forgotten.
emotions_sampled: Longing (clearly present), Helplessness (very intensely present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Holding Your Dying Pet and Losing Control
instruction: You're in the vet's office, cradling your dog or cat in your final moments together. Begin speaking to them with fierce protectiveness—promising you'll stay, that they're safe, that you're right here. Your voice is strong, a guardian. But as you feel their breathing change, something primal rips through you. You start bargaining with the universe, with God, with anyone—take me instead, give us one more day. Your voice becomes wild, desperate, rising in volume before you catch yourself, remembering they need you calm. You pull back, choking on sobs, trying to soothe them even as you're shattering. Rage flashes through—at the unfairness, at time, at your helplessness—then collapses into bottomless grief. End holding them, your voice reduced to broken whispers of 'good dog' or 'good girl,' each word soaked in love and devastation.
inspired_by: Crying and Trying to Explain While Gasping for Air

title: The Hallway Beyond the Party
instruction: You are an older man, slightly drunk after a family wedding, walking down a long, dimly lit hallway in your childhood home. Your footsteps echo, and the tunnel-like reverb makes every sound stretch out. At first you feel a heavy, sentimental intoxication—memories flooding, a slight unsteadiness. But as you reach the end, you notice a portrait of your late father under a single light, and your voice shifts into pure awe. Speak as if you're talking to him, your words carrying down the corridor. Let your voice reveal the slur of drink slowly giving way to quiet wonder. Pause, lean against the wall, let your breath echo.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Reading Your Husband's Journal After the Funeral
instruction: You found his journal in the nightstand drawer. Start reading aloud softly, almost smiling at his terrible handwriting, the mundane grocery lists. Then you find the entries from the last year—the ones he never showed you. Your voice should catch as you realize he knew he was dying long before he told you. He wrote about watching you sleep, memorizing your face. Read his words describing the small ways he tried to prepare you, the jacket he bought you because yours was worn, the garden he planted knowing he'd never see it bloom. Let your voice break on his confession that the hardest part wasn't dying—it was leaving you. Whisper his last entry, dated the morning before the hospital, where he writes 'I'm sorry I have to go first.' End with you closing the journal, voice barely audible, saying the reply you never got to give.
inspired_by: Labor: When the Anesthesia Wears Off During Surgery Complications

title: The Last Letter: Reading Your Words to Someone Who Will Never Wake
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love who is in a coma, and the doctors have told you this is the end. You've brought a letter you wrote years ago but never sent—full of things you were too afraid to say. As you read it aloud, you start with careful composure, your voice almost formal, protecting yourself. But slowly, the words crack you open. You move from controlled reading to raw confession, from anger at wasted time to devastating tenderness, from 'I should have told you' to 'please don't leave me.' Your voice becomes intimate, close, as if you're whispering secrets into their ear. You end not with closure but with the impossible plea of someone watching love slip away—your voice breaks into something between a prayer and a goodbye you're not ready to say.
inspired_by: Historical: Witness to Atrocity Must Testify Against Perpetrators Now in Power

title: Three A.M. Truth
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to your partner of ten years, whispering something you've been too afraid to say: you're not sure you want the life you're building together. Begin with your voice barely audible, your body rigid with shame for even thinking this. As you whisper, notice and softly name each feeling arising ('I feel like a terrible person,' 'My stomach is in knots,' 'I'm so scared of hurting you'). Don't try to make it easier or cleaner—let the guilt, fear, love, and doubt all exist at once. Whisper through the discomfort. By the end, through accepting the messiness of your truth rather than fighting to make it neat, find a tenderness toward yourself and them, arriving at vulnerable honesty rather than paralyzing shame.
inspired_by: Actor resists or fights against their feeling of tension or self-consciousness, making it worse

title: Thunder in the Bones
instruction: You have just received news that floods your body with overwhelming sensation—perhaps vindication after years of injustice, or the shock of a betrayal, or the explosive release of rage you've suppressed for too long. Your whole body is electric, shaking, your voice raw. Begin in pure physical and emotional chaos—let rage, grief, or ecstatic release pour through you without control. But as you move and speak, suddenly become aware of another person in the room—someone watching you, someone whose presence matters. Mid-storm, shift your attention completely away from your own feelings and toward them. What do you see in their face? Fear? Compassion? Disgust? Wonder? Let your observation of them change the temperature of your emotion. Your body is still charged, but your focus turns outward—how are they breathing? What are their hands doing? Transform your explosive expression into something more complex as you witness their reaction to your rawness. End with your intensity channeled not inward but toward understanding what your storm means to them.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You're recording a video message for loved ones to watch after you're gone—you know you're dying, and you've decided to say goodbye your own way. Start with dark humor, almost defiant laughter as you make jokes about your situation—'Well, this is awkward' or 'If you're watching this, I finally got some peace and quiet.' But let the laughter become increasingly fragile, catching in your throat. As you speak to specific people, gratitude and grief intertwine—you're genuinely joyful remembering beautiful moments while simultaneously breaking apart at the loss. Your voice should oscillate between warm chuckling and barely controlled sobs, sometimes in the same sentence. End with a moment where you're both laughing and crying, telling them 'Thank you for everything' with a voice that carries devastating loss and profound peace at once.
inspired_by: The Drunk Confession Nobody Wanted to Hear

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake for what you both know is the last time. Begin by settling into the room—notice the beeping machines, the pale light, the weight of this moment. Start by telling her about something ordinary from yesterday (a coffee you had, traffic, the weather), your voice trying to stay normal, light, conversational. As you speak, let the reality of losing her break through in waves. By the end, allow yourself to tell her what she's meant to you—but not in a rehearsed way. Let the words stumble out, incomplete, through tears, finding gratitude and devastating loss in the same breath. Your emotional journey moves from protective denial and forced normalcy to raw, undefended grief mixed with profound love.

title: Grateful for the Wreckage
instruction: You're thanking someone who is leaving your life—a lover, a best friend, someone who mattered profoundly—and you have to mean it even as your heart is shattering. Begin with genuine gratitude, your voice warm as you recount what they gave you, how they changed you. But as you continue, you start laughing through tears because the absurdity of being grateful for something that's destroying you is overwhelming. Your voice breaks and rebuilds, breaks and rebuilds. You're expressing joy for what you had and devastating sorrow for its ending in the same breath. By the end, you've found an impossible, fragile peace—a genuine thank you delivered with a trembling smile and tears streaming down your face. You mean every word, and it's killing you, and somehow that's beautiful.

title: Backyard Secret
instruction: You're at a family barbecue, hiding behind the shed with a vape. Your teenage niece just caught you. You start by teasing her, laughing it off with a wink and a playful dare—'Don't tell your mom, squirt.' But as you exhale, the smoke hangs in the air and you feel the weight of your habit, the shame creeping in. Your voice gets quieter, more jagged, you glance around, concentration tightening your jaw. End with a raw plea, half-choked, like you're confessing to yourself: 'I know, I know. I'm trying. Just… please.' Let the drag cycle be real: hear the crackle of the inhale, the pause, the friction as you speak on the breath. Let the teasing crack into something brittle, and the shame sink your voice into a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present), Concentration (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Love Declaration
instruction: You're finally telling your best friend of twenty years that you're in love with them. Your voice is nervous, fast: 'I need to tell you something and then we can never talk about this again if you don't—' They interrupt, eyes soft. Suddenly, your voice becomes honest, slower: 'I love you. Not as a friend. As... everything.' You're terrified. 'I know this could ruin everything between us. I know you might not feel the same. But I can't keep pretending anymore.' Your voice cracks: 'You're my person. You always have been. And I had to tell you.' The silence is eternal. Then they say: 'I've been waiting twenty years to hear you say that.' Your voice transforms — from fear to joy: 'Really?' And they kiss you, and your voice becomes a whisper: 'I love you so much.'

title: Breathing in Contradictions
instruction: You're at a deathbed—perhaps a beloved mentor, friend, or the complicated parent you finally understand. Take a breath of the sterile hospital air mixed with the fading scent of who they were. Start with a smile in your voice, almost laughing as you tell them what their presence meant, the absurd gratitude flooding through you even now. But let that laughter catch, become ragged, as you breathe in the reality of goodbye. Your tone should shimmer between joy and devastation—thanking them while your heart shatters, finding peace in their release while raging against the loss. Describe breathing with them, matching their rhythm, finding strange beauty in this last shared moment. End with a breath that's simultaneously an exhale of relief for their suffering ending and an inhale of overwhelming grief, your voice carrying both goodbye and eternal gratitude, peace and unbearable sadness, all in the same trembling moment.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath of Mountain Air

title: The Secret Told in Darkness
instruction: You're lying in bed in complete darkness next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something shameful, something fragile, something that makes you feel naked. Begin almost inaudibly, your voice small and defended. As you continue, don't perform vulnerability—actually feel the terrifying exposure of letting this person see this part of you. Let your breath be uneven. Let silences happen where you almost can't continue. Let your voice crack or catch not because that's 'emotional acting' but because holding this secret inside has actually taken physical effort, and releasing it changes something in your chest, your throat, your breathing. By the end, you should feel physically different—lighter, or more afraid, or closer, or more alone.

title: The Signal in the Static
instruction: You're at the edge of a cliff at dusk, alone, holding a cheap walkie-talkie you found in a thrift store. You've spent the last hour believing you heard a faint reply through the static — a voice, maybe real, maybe wishful. You start calling out with desperate, almost giddy interest, your voice high and searching, like you're trying to warm a frozen machine with your breath. But as the static only answers, doubt creeps in like a cold wind: you begin to doubt the voice, doubt yourself, doubt the whole stupid idea. The end of your call turns sour — your pitch drops, words get clipped, and you're almost spitting the goodbye, but your throat still aches with the hope you've just crushed.
emotions_sampled: Interest (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Garden of Lost Summers
instruction: You are an older woman standing in the overgrown backyard of the house you grew up in. It's been sold, and tomorrow it will be bulldozed for condos. You're looking at the spot where your mother's rose garden used to be—now a tangle of thorns and garbage. Your voice starts with bitter disgust at what’s become of this place: muttering about the weeds, the cheap beer cans. As you reach down and touch a single, stubborn petal, a memory of your mother kneeling in the dirt, laughing as you helped plant, floods over you. Let your voice soften with awe and then swell with an almost desperate hope—you whisper a promise to that old seed that you’ll find it a new home. Your words should feel punctuated by long pauses—staring at the past—and your tone should warm and lift into a fierce, tender optimism by the end, even as your throat aches with longing.
emotions_sampled: Awe (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Disgust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Fierce Goodbye to a Child You Cannot Protect
instruction: You're speaking to your child who is being taken from you—by law, by circumstance, by forces beyond your control—and you need them to understand how to survive without you. Start with fierce, urgent instructions: be strong, be smart, remember what I taught you. Your voice is powered by desperate maternal or paternal intensity. But as you speak, helplessness floods in—you cannot go with them, cannot shield them, and this protection you're trying to give is just words. Your voice breaks into something between rage and anguish. You're furious at your own powerlessness, grieving the childhood they're losing. Then, through the chaos of your emotions, find one last surge of strength: a final promise, a declaration of love so absolute it feels like armor you're wrapping around them, your voice raw but unshakeable.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis, and in this moment, you're calling the one person who will understand to share the absurdity of it all. Begin with a laugh—genuine, almost manic—because the universe's timing is so ridiculous it's almost funny: 'You won't believe this. You actually won't believe this.' Your voice carries dark humor, finding comedy in the cosmic joke. But as you speak, laughter and tears begin to blur together. You're making jokes about your own mortality even as your voice breaks. 'I finally paid off my student loans last month. Last MONTH.' Move through genuine amusement, bitter irony, profound gratitude for the life you've had, and devastating grief for the life you won't have—all swirling together. End with your voice simultaneously laughing and sobbing, saying something like 'I'm so lucky' or 'It was so beautiful' while falling completely apart. Let joy and sorrow become indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Being Told You're Being Cheated On

title: Dance Floor Reckoning
instruction: You are at a packed rave, dancing hard with your child beside you. The bass thumps through your entire body. Don't perform emotion—let physical sensation trigger authentic feeling. Access specific body memories: the exact feeling of your legs when you heard certain news, the taste in your mouth during a pivotal moment, the way your chest constricts or expands. title: Laughing at Her Funeral Instructions While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: Your sister is dying, and she's made you promise to read her funeral instructions—except they're absurd, hilarious, so perfectly her. title: Threshold Confession
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in the dark, and you've decided tonight is the night you finally tell them the truth. Your breathing becomes uneven as you continue: 'I'm not okay. I haven't been okay for a long time, and I've been hiding it from you.' Tears come quietly, inevitably: 'Every morning I wake up and think about not being here anymore. Not in a dramatic way. Just... not being here.' There's shame in your voice, but also desperate relief at finally saying it out loud: 'I know you'll want to fix it, but I don't need fixing. I just need you to know that I'm barely holding on.' Your voice becomes impossibly soft, tender: 'And the only reason I am holding on is because of how much I love you.' A long pause. Then, almost inaudible: 'I'm so scared. But I'm here. With you. Now you’re collapsed against a tree, chest heaving, legs weak, struggling to speak through ragged breaths. You’re smiling through the panting, your voice all tease and heat — you love the chase, love the power dynamic.
