But as the words come out, the reality of why you were chasing them sinks in: this is a goodbye, a final run. Let your laughter crack, let the breathlessness turn from playful to pained. Start with flirty, breathy lust — end with a sad, vulnerable admission that you can’t keep them. Your body is limp, your voice has no tension, only the weight of your lungs and heart.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Teasing (extremely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Anvil's Grace
instruction: You are a young construction worker, alone on a half-built high-rise at dusk. Your day was brutal—a near-fatal fall your foreman caught you from. Now, kneeling against a steel beam, you whisper a prayer of thanks. Your voice is roughened from shouting over machinery, but now it's hushed, halting, almost reverent. Start with shaky, disbelieving gratitude—'thank you' like a breath you've been holding—and let it settle into a choked, raw resolve, your hands clenching as you vow never to forget this gift.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Protective Fury of Helplessness
instruction: Someone you love deeply is in danger or pain, and you cannot save them. You begin with fierce, almost violent determination—your voice is commanding, promising you'll fix this, you'll fight, you'll destroy whatever threatens them. Your words are sharp and powerful. But as you continue, reality crashes in: you're powerless. Your voice breaks mid-sentence, rage dissolving into desperate pleading, then into raw anguish. You cycle between fury at your own helplessness and tender, broken apologies that you can't protect them. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, voice stripped bare, whispering promises you know you can't keep but need to say anyway—'I'm here, I'm here, I'm here'—as if love alone could be enough, even when you know it isn't.

title: Crushed by Comparison
instruction: You are pinned under a heavy fallen shelf in a cluttered garage, your chest compressed so each breath is a forced, shallow exhale. You can't inhale fully—every word is squeezed out against the weight. At first, you're just in distress, trying to call for help, but then you hear your rival's voice outside, laughing with someone, being praised for the project you worked on. Jealousy curdles inside you. Start with panicked, short pleas for rescue—'Help… can't… breathe…'—but as you realize no one's coming, your voice shifts into bitter, envious growls, still strained, still fighting for air. Let the envy thicken your tone, even as your body struggles. End with a quiet, venomous whisper: '…they're getting the credit… and I'm stuck here.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Crack in the Broadcast
instruction: You are a veteran news anchor mid-broadcast, reporting live on a local hero receiving a community award. At first, your voice is polished and proud, but as you glance at the producer's monitor, you see your younger rival being congratulated off-camera for a promotion you wanted. Stay in anchor mode, but let your voice tighten slightly, your pauses grow a hair longer, and a trace of envy color your words—like a subtle crack in the glass. Pride starts as your armor, but jealousy bleeds in by the final sentence. You are still reading the teleprompter, but your heart is somewhere else.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Gilded Trap
instruction: You’re a middle-aged woman with a deliberately sweet, hyper-feminized voice, attending a high-end charity luncheon with your husband’s corporate associates. You’ve been suppressing tics all afternoon, but the stress is building—they keep breaking through, a sudden 'boop!' or 'whoop!' that you try to cover with a tinkling laugh. You’re cornered by a smiling woman who gushes about how 'supportive' your husband is of your 'cute little quirk.' You start by offering a strained, polite reply, but as you speak, bitterness seeps through—a quiet, acidic rage at being infantilized in your own body. Let your voice start sweet and airy, then crackle with resentful heat by the end; pause and restart after each tic as if nothing happened, but your stomach twists tighter with every interruption.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Parent and the Imaginary Friend
instruction: Depict a parent with a concerned, gentle voice talking to their childs imaginary friend, who speaks in a whimsical, playful tone. Switch between the parents attempts to understand and the imaginary friends cryptic messages, blurring the lines between reality and imagination.

title: Masked Mirth
instruction: You are an older woman in a hazmat suit, your voice muffled by the heavy gas mask. A co-worker’s clumsy fumble just knocked over the decontamination foam tank, and you’re trying to report it over the comms. Start with a sour edge—you’re tired of this drill, and the mask is uncomfortable. Then, as you describe what happened (the foam geyser, the panic), astonishment floods your voice—you can’t believe they did that. Finally, amusement takes over; a real, hearty laugh that gets distorted into a wheeze. Let your breathing be loud and rhythmically distorted by the filter. Let your words start clipped, then brighten and stretch as you find the humor. Speak as if shouting through a wall, with natural pauses to adjust your mask or wipe sweat from your eyes.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Amusement (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Bedside Vigil: Whispering to Someone Who Cannot Hear
instruction: You're keeping watch beside someone you love who's dying, their breathing shallow and irregular. Speak in hushed, broken whispers—not because you might wake them, but because your voice can barely hold together. Begin by reading aloud from a favorite book, the familiar words a lifeline, but you keep stopping mid-sentence as grief catches in your throat. Shift to memories, small ones: the way they laughed, a particular morning, something they said once that changed you. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost just breath, intimate and devastatingly tender. Confess something you never said—'I was scared of you sometimes' or 'You saved me and never knew it.' Let long silences fall between words. Then their breathing changes, becomes more labored, and your whispers turn urgent, pleading—'Stay, please stay'—before dissolving into the terrible acceptance that they're leaving. End with you simply breathing with them, counting their breaths, your voice gone completely, just air and heartbreak, sitting in the unbearable intimacy of letting someone go.
inspired_by: Heat Exhaustion in the Desert: Losing Grip on Reality

title: Small Victory Quiet
instruction: You did something small and impossible. Your voice is soft, hardly believing it: 'I made that call. I said no to them.' Breathing is deeper. Physical: hands unclenching. 'It's such a small thing but it's mine.' Vocal tone is amazed at the smallness and largeness of it. 'I didn't know I could do it.' By the end, you're recognizing the significance of the tiny thing: 'This small victory is everything. It changes everything.'

title: Rage Before Restoration: Destroying the Scale
instruction: You're holding a bathroom scale that has ruled your life. Start with explosive fury - your voice shaking with years of suppressed rage: 'You don't get to define me anymore!' Scream the numbers it showed you, all the times you stepped on it with hope and stepped off with shame. Your voice is fierce, unhinged: 'I starved myself for you! I hated myself for you!' But mid-rage, something breaks - your voice cracks, the anger collapses into heaving sobs of grief for all the years lost, all the joy sacrificed. You're suddenly on the floor, voice small and broken: 'I was just a child... I was just trying to be loved.' Then, through tears, your voice finds strength again - protective, fierce, claiming yourself back: 'I'm done. You're done. This body is MINE.' Let the transformation from rage to grief to reclamation be raw and total.

title: The Last Sip
instruction: You are in a sun-baked field after hours of work with no water. The heat has crushed your usual bright, bubbly voice into a weak, slurred whisper. You're fumbling with a near-empty canteen, feeling dizzy and doubting you can make it back. Your task is to call out to a companion who’s just out of sight, starting with a strained, optimistic attempt—but as the words slow and falter, a quiet resignation settles in, ending with a confession of defeat that sounds almost peaceful. Let your voice waver, trail off, and crack; let the world blur as you speak.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Warmth You Never Gave: Confronting an Absent Parent
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent who was never there for you, and you're telling them about a specific memory—a time you were sick or hurt as a child, shivering and alone, desperate for comfort they never provided. Start with controlled anger, almost clinical, as you describe the physical sensation of being cold, scared, and neglected. Let your voice sharpen and rise as you describe how you learned to comfort yourself, how you became your own parent. Then transform: let the anger crack into something raw and vulnerable—you're not just furious, you're heartbroken. You're that child again, and your voice should break as you finally admit what you really needed: their warmth, their presence, their love. End with a devastating question you've been holding for years, asked with a child's vulnerability wrapped in an adult's pain.
inspired_by: Feeling the Soothing Warmth of a Heat Pack on Sore Muscles

title: Everything You Never Said Is In This Room
instruction: You are confronting your father in his woodshop—a space filled with decades of his tools, projects, and silence. Begin by describing what you see, hear, and smell around you: the sawdust hanging in the air, the particular scent of cedar and oil, the worn handles of his tools, the afternoon sun cutting through the dusty window. Start angry but distant, using these observations as a way to avoid looking directly at him. As you move through the space, let touching his workbench, hearing the creak of the floorboards, noticing the unfinished projects, pull memories and unspoken truths out of you. Allow the physical environment to unlock what you've buried—how the smell of wood brings back childhood, how the sight of his calloused hands makes you understand his love language. Transform from accusatory anger to a painful, complicated understanding. Your voice should shift from sharp and controlled to trembling with the weight of recognition and reluctant compassion.

title: The Waiting Game
instruction: You're on a barstool, perched forward, core tight as you grip the edge. You were supposed to meet someone 20 minutes ago, and each second feels like a needle. Start with a sharp, irritated mutter about their disrespect — voice tight, impatient. Then let the thought sink in that maybe they're testing you. Your irritation hardens into something colder, more deliberate. By the end, your voice drops to a low, menacing whisper, laced with malice. Feel the stool beneath you, the weight shift as you lean in for the final words.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Trailside Temptation
instruction: You are a young adult jogging alone on a wooded trail at dusk, breathing heavily from the run. Your body is warm, your heart pounds with exertion, and you’re intensely aware of your own physicality. You see someone you’ve been deeply attracted to leaning against a tree up ahead, watching you with a smirk. You want to stop and talk, but you’re out of breath. Start by calling out a greeting that’s as flustered as it is hungry for them—your voice shakes with every footfall, gasping between words. As you slow to a walk and approach, your panting eases, but your desire only intensifies, shifting into a raw, whispered confession that mixes vulnerability with a fierce, almost primal longing. Your voice should betray the struggle between the exhaustion of your run and the sudden, overwhelming lust that steals your breath for an entirely different reason.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Teaching Something You're Ashamed You Don't Know
instruction: Your teenager asks you to help with a family recipe and you have to admit 'I never learned.' There's shame in that admission. Decide to figure it out together: 'Show me, we can learn this together.' Your voice cracks as you acknowledge the gap between who you thought you were and who you are.

title: Whispering a Secret You've Carried Alone
instruction: Late at night, in darkness, you're confessing something to someone you trust—a shame you've carried, a fear that's been eating you alive, or a truth about who you really are. Your voice is barely above a whisper, fragile and uncertain at first: 'There's something I've never told anyone.' Each word costs you something. Your breathing is uneven; there are long pauses where you're gathering courage. Midway through, your voice catches—not dramatically, but the way it does when you're trying not to cry and failing. You're terrified of their reaction, and that fear lives in every syllable. As you reach the end of your confession, there's a moment of profound vulnerability where you're completely exposed, waiting. Your final words are tentative, almost childlike: 'Please don't hate me.' Let the quiet carry the enormity of what you're revealing.

title: Laughing Through Tears at a Deathbed Goodbye
instruction: You are with someone you deeply love as they are dying, and you're remembering a shared memory that makes you both laugh—genuinely laugh—even now. Start with the laughter, real and warm, letting it bubble up authentically as you tell the story. But feel how the laughter coexists with grief, how your voice keeps breaking, how you're crying and laughing simultaneously. There's gratitude for the time you had, devastation that it's ending, and this strange, beautiful absurdity of finding joy in the worst moment of your life. Your voice should crack between giggles and sobs, unable to fully separate the two. End by thanking them—for the memory, for everything—and let your final words be both celebration and farewell. The contradictions should feel completely natural: you're shattered and whole, destroyed and grateful, saying goodbye while holding on with everything you have.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father about a betrayal from your childhood that you've never spoken about until now. Begin in a state of careful control—you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. As you speak, anchor yourself in the sensory reality of the moment: notice the temperature of your own hands, the sound of your voice in the room, the exact expression on their face, the way they're breathing. Let these sensory observations guide you deeper into the truth beneath your controlled words. Allow the confrontation to crack open as genuine sensory awareness breaks through your rehearsed composure. End in a place completely different from where you started—whether that's raw vulnerability, surprising compassion, or liberated rage—let the sensory reality of the moment, not your plan, determine where you land.

title: The Reunion Trophy
instruction: You're at your 20-year high school reunion, standing near the punch table. You look up at a former classmate who was once plain and awkward but now appears transformed—dressed in designer clothes, glowing with confidence, and clearly wealthy. You start with forced astonishment and a bright, high-pitched 'Oh my god!' to mask your shock, but as you speak, your voice thins and tightens with awe at her success. Let a sharp edge of jealousy slip in as you compliment her, your words becoming clipped and envious. End with a brittle, high laugh that cracks, revealing how much this stings. Say about 60 words, letting your chin stay lifted and your voice sound strained as you fight to keep the act up.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're whispering to your sleeping partner something you've never been able to say when they're awake. Begin with your voice barely audible, confessing a fear that makes you feel small and ashamed—maybe that you're not sure you're capable of the love they deserve, or that you're terrified of becoming your parents, or that some days you look at your beautiful life and feel nothing. Your whisper is intimate, secret, fragile. As you continue, tears start to come, not dramatic but quiet, the kind that slide down silently. The strength emerges not from getting louder, but from continuing to speak even as your voice breaks, from the courage to be this naked even in darkness. End with a whispered resolve, a decision made in the vulnerability: you're going to try, you're going to fight for this, you're going to be honest. The power is in the softness, in the confession itself.

title: Monopoly With the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're playing Monopoly with your father who abandoned you as a child and now wants back in your life. Begin with polite, overly cheerful game commentary—determined to keep this light and superficial. But their casual remarks about 'strategy' and 'planning ahead' trigger something raw in you. Let your voice shift from forced pleasantness to barely controlled anger. Confront them: 'You want to talk about planning ahead? Where was that when I was seven?' Let decades of hurt pour out, your voice cracking between rage and the child inside you who just wanted them to stay. End in exhausted honesty, asking the question you've needed answered for years.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father about something he never told you—a secret that reframes your entire childhood. Begin in cold, controlled anger, building your case like a prosecutor, recounting specific moments from your past that now make terrible sense. As you speak, reconstruct these memories aloud with vivid detail: the day he missed your graduation, the summer he disappeared for three months, the way your mother's face looked at dinner. But as you narrate these moments, something shifts—you begin to see him not as the parent who failed you, but as a frightened person who was barely surviving. Your anger must transform into something more complicated: a devastating recognition of his humanity, mixed with grief for the relationship you never had. End not with forgiveness or reconciliation, but with an exhausted, broken acknowledgment that you finally understand, even though understanding doesn't fix anything.

title: Confronting Your Mother About Why You Were Never Enough
instruction: You're face-to-face with your mother, finally saying what you've rehearsed for decades. Start with a shaking laugh: 'I need to ask you something I've been afraid to ask since I was eight.' Your voice cracks as you detail specific moments—the recital she missed, the way she looked through you, the sibling she clearly preferred. Build from wounded questioning ('Why wasn't I worth showing up for?') to raw, explosive pain ('I was a CHILD!'). Let rage pour out, then suddenly collapse into something quieter, more devastating: 'I just wanted you to love me the way I was.' End exhausted, vulnerable, still needing an answer she might never give. This isn't theatrical anger—it's the kind that leaves you hollowed out.
inspired_by: Standing Up to Someone in Authority You're Terrified Of

title: The Last Dance: Wedding Toast for a Terminally Ill Spouse
instruction: You're giving a wedding anniversary toast to your spouse at a party surrounded by friends and family, but you both know they have weeks, maybe days, left. Begin with genuine laughter, recounting a funny story from your early days together, your voice warm and full of joy. The room is laughing with you. But as you speak, the humor becomes poignant—you're celebrating a lifetime compressed into too-short years. Your voice holds both gratitude and grief in the same breath. You make jokes that land perfectly but your eyes are glistening. You thank them for every ordinary moment—grocery shopping, quiet mornings, arguments about nothing—and your voice vibrates with the unbearable beauty of a normal life. You're smiling but tears are streaming down your face as you tell everyone how lucky you've been, how you'd do it all again even knowing how it ends. End with your voice strong and clear, rising in a toast, choosing celebration over sorrow in this final moment, your words ringing with defiant joy even as your heart shatters—because this is the gift you can still give them: proof that your love was worth the pain of losing it.
inspired_by: Submarine Hull Breach: Reporting Water Rise While Remaining Professional

title: The Departure Gate Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone at an airport gate—they're leaving for a opportunity that thrills them, and you're genuinely happy for them, but you're also losing them. Begin with bright, forced enthusiasm—your voice cheerful, your smile wide, celebrating their adventure. As you look at their excited face, notice every real detail: their genuine joy, their nervous energy, the way they keep checking their boarding pass. Let yourself simultaneously imagine shadows beneath their excitement—read hesitation that might not be there, see a plea in their eyes asking you to stop them, imagine their joy as partially performance. Hold these contradictions. Your voice must carry both authentic celebration and barely-suppressed grief. Laugh while fighting tears. By the end, as they turn to board, let one emotion finally overwhelm the other—but it should be unclear even to you whether you're crying from happiness for them or devastation for yourself.

title: Whispering Goodbye to My Stillborn Child
instruction: You're alone at dawn, standing in the shallow stream where you dreamed of bringing your baby one day. Speak in barely audible whispers, describing the water touching your feet as if you're narrating it to the child you lost. Your voice should be unbearably tender, fragile, catching on every word as you describe how the coolness would have felt on tiny toes, how you would have held those small hands. Let long pauses fall between phrases where grief chokes off your words. This isn't loud crying—it's the kind of devastation that makes you go very, very quiet. End by saying goodbye, your voice so soft it's almost not there, finding a thread of peace in the flowing water that continues despite everything.
inspired_by: Walking Barefoot Through Shallow, Cool Water

title: I Built This Table With My Own Hands - And You're Leaving
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who's announced they're cutting off contact with you. Your hand rests on the dining table you built when they were born - you poured everything into making it perfect for your family. Start by running your hand over the wood, voice tight with controlled emotion, recounting the hours you spent sanding it smooth, choosing the grain carefully, imagining all the meals you'd share here. Your tone is measured, almost gentle, trying to make them understand the love embedded in every surface. Then the dam breaks - your hand slaps the table, voice rising with frustration, hurt, and desperate confusion. Why isn't this enough? Why can't they see how hard you tried? Collapse back into quiet devastation, palm flat on the wood, asking in a broken whisper what you did wrong. The table holds all your love, and they're walking away from it.
inspired_by: Running Your Hand Over a Smooth, Polished Wooden Table

title: The Last Confession at the Pharmacy Counter
instruction: You are an elderly man, sitting on a plastic chair in a dimly lit pharmacy waiting area. The sedative the doctor gave you is pulling you down like a heavy blanket, but your mind is caught on a sudden, vivid memory. You see the face of a woman from decades ago—your first real love—and a giddy, euphoric warmth spreads through your chest. You start speaking to the empty chair beside you, as if she's there, confessing how you've always thought of her. But as the haze deepens, your voice drops to a whisper, and you realize your wife—who died last year—would be ashamed you're saying this. The infatuation and elation give way to a quiet, slurred shame. Let your words drag, your volume fade, and pause as if losing the thought, then find it again with a soft, breathy sigh.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Shame (clearly present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Stubborn Garden Gate
instruction: You're a woman fixing a loose latch on your garden gate, with your child playing nearby. You've been at this for minutes, wrench in hand, and the bolt won't move—you're starting to feel a low-grade anger simmering, a tightness in your jaw. Each grunt and rhythmic clank of the wrench interrupts your muttered complaints. Then, with a final twist, the bolt catches and tightens—a wave of relief washes over you, softening your voice. Speak to your child or to yourself, letting the physical effort punctuate your words: the first few sentences sound irritated, the last ones tired but satisfied.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a lifetime of emotional absence. You've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times, started with measured, careful words—but the mask is cracking. Begin controlled, almost clinical, listing the facts of your childhood like evidence. But let the anger seep through. Then let it break: the rage at never being enough, at performing for love that never came. Your voice might rise, might shake with fury—but then something shifts. Beneath the anger, find the child who still wanted to be seen. Let your voice drop to something raw and small: 'I just wanted you to notice me.' End in a place of devastating clarity: you're done performing. This isn't about making them understand anymore. Watch your emotions transform from controlled pain to explosive rage to that terrible, quiet moment when you finally let go of the hope that they'll change. Be utterly honest. Let pauses speak. Let your voice break.
inspired_by: Acting Happy for Someone When Youre Heartbroken

title: The Vigil: Whispering to Someone Slipping Away
instruction: You're sitting beside your beloved's hospital bed in the deep hours of night. They're barely conscious, fading. Begin in whispers, tender and intimate: 'I'm here. I'm right here with you.' You're telling them small, precious things—how the garden looks, what the cat did today, anything to keep them tethered. Your voice is soft, careful, as if speaking too loudly might shatter this last fragile time together. But you can feel them leaving, and the whispers become more urgent, more desperate in their gentleness. 'Remember when we...' and you're trying to hold an entire life in these diminishing moments. Your throat tightens. You want to scream, to rage, but all that comes out is this aching tenderness. 'It's okay. You can go. I'll be okay.' The lie catches in your voice, barely audible. You're giving them permission while your heart is shattering, whispering your love like a prayer, like if you say it enough times they'll take it with them. Let the silences between your words grow longer, more weighted with everything you can't say.
inspired_by: Working Near an Industrial Furnace: Heat Warping Perception

title: I Am Not Your Second Chance
instruction: You're confronting your father, who has spent years trying to relive his failed dreams through you. He's pushed you toward his unlived life—his abandoned career, his regrets, his 'what could have been.' You've finally had enough. Begin the scene trying to please him, apologizing, explaining yourself in his language. But as you speak, rage builds—not just anger, but the fury of someone whose entire identity has been colonized. Let yourself become ferocious in your specificity about who you actually are versus who he needs you to be. End in a place of dangerous clarity: you will not be his do-over. The arc moves from appeasing and self-erasing to furiously, unapologetically self-defined. Let your voice and body find a rhythm that is entirely your own, not an echo of his.
inspired_by: When a young actor is being defined by a famous parent's legacy rather than their own work

title: Listening to Waves Crashing on the Shore
instruction: Sit on the beach, feeling the rhythm of waves hitting the shore, a constant, soothing sound. Describe the steady, almost hypnotic pull of each wave, the sound filling the air, echoing around you. Speak softly, letting each word mimic the steady rhythm, as if the waves are wrapping you in calm, filling you with peace that moves in and out like each breath.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—a relationship ended, a dream died, a diagnosis came—and you're standing in the wreckage, but something unexpected is happening: you're laughing. Start with genuine, almost hysterical laughter at the absurdity of it all, how completely everything went wrong, how spectacularly you failed or were failed. Let the laughter catch and stutter as tears come too, your voice doing both at once—crying while laughing at yourself for crying. You're speaking to someone gone or to yourself or to the universe, listing everything you've lost, but with each loss, you're also finding strange, fierce gratitude for having had it at all. Your voice moves between wonder and devastation, between 'how did this happen' and 'of course this happened.' End in a place of unexpected peace, your voice quiet but grounded, acknowledging the pain while also accepting it, maybe even welcoming what comes next—broken, yes, but somehow more whole than before.

title: The Soldier's Final Letter Home Before the Mission
instruction: You're recording a voice message to your child, knowing this deployment is different—you might not return. Start with forced brightness, trying to sound brave and encouraging. But as you speak, the weight of everything unsaid begins to crack through. Your voice wavers when you realize this might be the last time they hear you say 'I love you.' The bravado dissolves into raw tenderness, then quiet devastation as you accept you're saying goodbye. End with a whisper that holds both fierce love and the ache of letting go. Let the silences speak—the moments where you almost can't continue.
inspired_by: Therapist Hearing Themselves in a Patient's Story

title: Protecting Your Younger Sibling from a Threat You Can't Stop
instruction: Someone is coming for them and you're standing between, voice starting fierce and absolute—'You are not touching them.' Your words are armor, full of protective rage, threats pouring out with savage conviction. But as the danger becomes more real, your certainty fractures. Your voice climbs higher, desperation bleeding through: 'Please, I'll do anything.' You're bargaining now, begging, the fierce protector collapsing into terrified helplessness. Your sibling says your name and you spin back to them, trying to sound brave but your voice is shaking violently. 'It's going to be okay'—a lie you both know. End with a guttural, almost animal sound of rage and grief as you realize you cannot save them, your final words a broken promise: 'I won't let go of you,' even as everything falls apart.
inspired_by: Your Abuser Texting You Out of the Blue

title: The Burning Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter from someone you once loved desperately—someone who destroyed you and is now asking for forgiveness. Your body remembers everything: the desire, the betrayal, the physical intimacy, the physical pain of loss. Start reading in a voice of cold detachment, holding the letter at arm's length, armoring yourself against its words. But your body betrays you—your breath changes, your hands shake, heat rises in your chest. Notice the chasm between your controlled voice and your body's wild reaction. Notice how you're performing indifference while your physical self screams. Then stop pretending. Let your voice join your body in its truth—whether that's rage that makes you rip the letter, or desire that makes you crumble, or both at once. Let the physical sensations drive your voice into places you didn't plan to go. End in whatever raw, physical, uncontrolled place your body takes you.

title: The Confession in Darkness
instruction: You're whispering a confession to someone sleeping beside you—or perhaps to someone who can't hear you anymore. Begin barely audibly: 'I need to tell you something while I still can.' Your voice should be intimate, fragile, like speaking might shatter something precious. 'Every day with you has been so beautiful it scared me.' Let vulnerability deepen with each phrase. 'I was so afraid of losing this that I... I held back. I never told you how much—' Your voice catches, throat tightening. 'I thought I had time.' Tears come silently. End with your voice breaking into something even softer, more tender: 'You were the most beautiful thing that ever happened to me. And I never said it enough.' Let the words dissolve into breath and sorrow.

title: The Lemonade That Saved You and Destroyed You
instruction: You just learned that the childhood friend who saved your life—who pulled you out of darkness by bringing you lemonade every day when you were suicidal—has just died. You're holding the last glass they ever made for you, still in your refrigerator. Start with your voice shaking with fierce, almost violent gratitude, nearly shouting about how alive the taste makes you feel, how every bubble is proof that you're still here because of them. Let the intensity build into something almost manic, describing the sensation with passionate, desperate joy. Then let it shatter completely—your voice breaking mid-sentence as the reality crashes over you that they're gone. End in helpless, whispered devastation, barely able to speak about the sweetness because all you can think about is that you couldn't save them the way they saved you.
inspired_by: Sipping a Sparkling Glass of Lemonade on a Hot Day

title: Muffled Thanks on the Mountain
instruction: You're a young adult bundled against a bitter wind, a thick wool scarf pulled tight over your mouth. You've just been physically helped up a steep, icy trail by a companion after you slipped. You're grateful, but the scarf is wet from your breath, your face is sweaty and chafed, and you're shivering. Start the line with genuine, breathless thankfulness for the rescue, but as you continue, the physical misery—the cold, the wet fabric, the tediousness of the climb—makes your voice turn petulant and sour. Your gratitude curdles into irritable complaint, each word muffled and warm against the cloth.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Caricature Crumbles
instruction: You're at a loud party, sitting across from a group of friends who've been mocking your 'girly' voice all night. You've just realized they think they're joking with you, but it stings. You decide to play along, mimicking your own voice in a silly, exaggerated way to prove you can take it. Start with a light, performative tone—nasal and high-pitched, as if you're mocking yourself. Say, 'Oh, like this? Sorry my voice isn't deep enough for you.' Mid-sentence, you notice a friend's pitying look, and the act cracks. Your pitch drops, your words slow down, and confusion seeps in as you realize the joke isn't funny. End in a quieter, relieved but wobbly tone: 'Wait, are we laughing at me or with me? Never mind, I'm actually okay with it... mostly.' Let your voice warble, break, and waver with the micro-distractions of the party noise and your own shaky breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night. You're lying next to someone, and in the darkness, you whisper something you've been hiding—a fear, a betrayal, a truth about yourself you're ashamed of. Your voice is barely audible, fragile as glass. You expect judgment, but instead they reach for your hand, and their touch undoes you. What started as confession becomes something else—a kind of breaking open. Your breath catches. There are long pauses where you can't speak at all. When you continue, your voice is even softer, more naked, as you move from shame to the terrifying relief of being known. By the end, you're crying quietly, but it's not just sadness—it's the strange, overwhelming gratitude of not having to hide anymore. Every word costs you everything.

title: Bedside Vigil: Singing Mama to Sleep
instruction: Your mother is dying, unconscious, breathing raggedly. You're singing her favorite lullaby—the one she sang to you as a child—but your voice keeps breaking. Start trying to sing it beautifully for her, the way she deserves. But grief keeps interrupting: your voice cracks, you have to stop and breathe through tears, you whisper apologies for not being stronger. Between verses, talk to her in fragments—thanking her for small, specific things, confessing regrets, making promises about how you'll take care of dad. Your singing becomes less about the melody and more about just being with her, humming when you can't form words. End when her breathing changes and you realize she's going. The final verse is barely a whisper, more breath than sound. Move from attempting composure to complete emotional surrender—the kind of intimate grief that's too private for anyone but her.

title: Whispering Secrets to Someone Who's Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you deeply love—a partner, a child, a friend—who is asleep and cannot hear you. In this safe darkness, you confess things you could never say to their waking face. Start softly, tenderly, with simple observations about how they look when they sleep. Then venture into more vulnerable territory: your fears about losing them, the ways they've changed you, the parts of yourself you hide even from them. Your voice should barely rise above a whisper, intimate and aching. Let tears catch in your throat as you admit your deepest gratitude mixed with your deepest terror—that loving someone this much means you have everything to lose. End with a whispered plea or promise that reveals how fragile you really are.
inspired_by: The Princess and the Dragon Disguised as a Human

title: The Wince in the Game
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy with chronic back pain, standing on a basketball court with friends. You've been hiding your pain for weeks. As you fake a laugh and say you're fine, a sharp spasm hits—you gasp and grab your side. You try to joke it off, but your voice wavers. The bravado drains out. You confess quietly, voice tight with fear: you're terrified your body is breaking down. Let your words trail into sighs and wincing breaths. End with a heavy sadness about missing out on being a normal kid. (Spoken content: approximately 50-70 words.)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Midnight Bathroom Confession
instruction: It's 2 AM. You're sitting on the bathroom floor with your closest friend, both of you exhausted after a wedding. You're finally ready to tell them the secret you've carried for years—something about who you really are, what you really want, or what really happened. Begin by experiencing the physical reality: the cool tile under you, the harsh fluorescent light, the sound of the ventilation fan, the feeling of alcohol wearing off and clarity setting in. Start from a place of nervous humor, deflecting, keeping it light. Don't jump to 'vulnerable emotion'—instead, build the sensory experience of this strange, liminal moment: the late hour, your body's tiredness, the intimacy of this small, bright space. Notice how your friend's presence feels—their warmth beside you, their breathing. As you begin to speak the truth, let the physical sensations guide you into vulnerability. Maybe your hands start trembling before you know why. Maybe your voice gets quieter because you're actually feeling the weight of the words, not because you're 'acting intimate.' Let the confession transform you from protective lightness to genuine, undefended openness.
inspired_by: Actor knows what they want to feel in a scene but cannot get there from cold

title: The Last Ride Down
instruction: You're a woman in her 70s, descending alone in a slow, humming elevator after visiting your husband's grave for what you know will be the last time. You're tired, your body aches, and the metal box around you feels both suffocating and strangely comforting. As the elevator creaks lower, a memory catches you off guard—the first time you danced together in a tiny apartment kitchen, the way he spun you. Let that memory flood through your voice: start with the weight of grief and exhaustion, the metallic echo making your words feel hollow, then let a small, breathless laugh escape as you remember the joy—pure, unexpected pleasure that cracks through the sorrow, leaving you somewhere between laughing and crying by the time the doors open.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers What the Mind Forgot
instruction: You return to a physical place where something profound happened—a beach, a specific street corner, a room, a forest clearing. As you stand there, your body begins to remember before your mind does: your breathing changes, your muscles tense or release, sensation floods through you. Let it be something that held both pain and pleasure, trauma and ecstasy, loss and deep connection. Begin with confusion—why does being here make your heart race, why are your hands shaking? As the physical memory intensifies, allow images and feelings to surface: a touch, a voice, something that happened here that changed you. Move through the physical sensations—perhaps your body wants to run, or collapse, or reach for someone who isn't there anymore. Transform from physical confusion into full emotional recognition, ending with your body finally releasing what it's held—through tears, through a scream, through a profound exhale, or through allowing yourself to feel pleasure or pain you've kept locked away.

title: The Mirror Confrontation
instruction: You are confronting your parent/child/former lover who has always made you feel invisible, undesirable, or somehow wrong in your own skin. Begin with contained rage and bitter accusations about how they made you doubt your own worth and desirability. As you speak, let the anger crack open to reveal the desperate need underneath—the part of you that wanted them to truly see you, to affirm you, to tell you that you were enough. Let your voice break from fury into raw vulnerability. End by reclaiming your own voice: tell them exactly what you needed to hear from them, then give it to yourself. Transform from seeking their validation to discovering you no longer need it.

title: Shattered Sanctuary
instruction: You are a social worker who just lost a child you were trying to protect—they've been sent back to an unsafe home due to legal technicalities. Begin with barely controlled fury, pacing, voice shaking with adrenaline as you rage against the system, the judge, the policies, using sharp, staccato sentences. Let your voice rise, becoming almost feral with helplessness—you're screaming at bureaucracy, at your own powerlessness, at a universe that lets children suffer. Then the fury breaks like a dam, collapsing into wrenching sobs. Your voice becomes desperate, vulnerable, as you describe the child's face, their trust in you, the specific way they said your name. Try to pull yourself together, voice raw and hoarse. End with a devastating shift: quiet, hollow determination. You'll go back tomorrow. You'll try again. But your voice must carry the knowledge that you're breaking yourself on this work, piece by piece, and you don't know how many pieces you have left.

title: Teaching Signs to Someone Who's Losing Their Hearing—And You
instruction: You're teaching sign language to someone you love who is slowly going deaf, knowing that when they can no longer hear, they've decided to leave you—they don't want you to become their caretaker. Your voice is impossibly tender, almost breaking from the start. Speak each sign like a secret you're trying to preserve: 'This is how you say beautiful—like you're tracing the outline of someone's face in the air.' Let your voice catch on the words you're trying not to say—'You won't need me to teach you the rest.' When you reach the sign for 'remember,' whisper it through tears you're trying to hide. Your instruction should be saturated with quiet devastation, with love that knows it's running out of time, with the unbearable tenderness of memorizing someone's hands while you still can.
inspired_by: Teaching Sign Language: When Hands Speak and Voice Goes Quiet

title: Three A.M. Confessions in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, speaking into the darkness because you can't say these things in daylight. Begin with something small and almost trivial—a fleeting thought, a minor insecurity. Keep your voice quiet, intimate, barely above a whisper. Let one confession lead to another, each one slightly more vulnerable, peeling back layers you usually keep hidden. Speak about the parts of yourself you're ashamed of, the fears that wake you at night, the ways you pretend to be stronger than you are. By the end, you've revealed something so tender and true that you feel completely exposed—but also strangely free. Let the darkness hold your secrets.

title: The Silent Hitchhiker
instruction: You're a teenage girl lying in a hot bath after a long day, muscles completely melted. The water is warm, you're half-dreaming, your voice is slow and syrupy. You reach for a sponge and your fingers brush against something long and slick—a strand of hair. Not yours. It's darker, thicker, and somehow it's stuck to your arm. You freeze, then a wave of disgust rises from your stomach. Let your voice shift from satisfied mumbles to a horrified, breathy whisper as you realize it's been there the whole time.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You're dying—maybe hours left—and you're recording a message for your own funeral. But you're not being somber. You start laughing, genuinely amused at the absurdity of talking to people who'll hear this when you're gone. Your voice is warm, irreverent, even giddy with a strange freedom. You're making jokes, teasing the people you love, being wildly inappropriate. But underneath the laughter, let the cracks show—your voice wobbles, the humor becomes a shield against terror. You're laughing and crying at once, grateful and heartbroken in the same breath. Find moments where the laughter catches and becomes a sob, then returns to mirth. You're celebrating life while saying goodbye to it. End with genuine peace mixed with profound sadness—thanking everyone while your voice breaks, finding joy in the middle of unbearable loss. Let the contradictions live together authentically.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Warrior Chooses Peace Over Victory

title: The Birthday Cake Paradox
instruction: Today is your birthday, and you're about to blow out the candles. But as you stand there, you're hit by a cascade of every birthday you've ever had—especially the childhood ones. Begin speaking about this moment now: you're grateful, you're celebrating, people love you. But then the memories come: the birthday when someone important didn't show up, the year you desperately wanted something you didn't get, the party where you felt invisible, the cake your mother made with her own hands when money was tight. Joy and grief swirl together. You're laughing and crying at once. You're furious at time for passing and grateful for every year. You're six years old and lost in the shuffle of siblings, and you're now, surrounded by people, still somehow alone. The emotions contradict and coexist. By the end, you don't know whether to make a wish or mourn all the wishes that didn't come true. Let both truths be fully present.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent what their absence—emotional, not physical—cost you throughout your life. Begin with careful, measured words, almost clinical, as if you've rehearsed this a thousand times and you're determined to stay controlled. You're listing facts: the recitals they attended but didn't really watch, the report cards they signed but didn't read, the way you learned to be invisible. Let your voice stay steady, almost cold. Then let something crack—a specific memory that still cuts, maybe the time you won an award and they were on their phone, or the night you needed them and they were 'too tired.' Your control starts to splinter. Move from intellectual disappointment to the raw, childlike hurt underneath—the part of you that still desperately wanted them to see you, really see you. End not with anger but with devastating honesty: 'I needed you to be curious about who I was becoming, and you never asked.' Let your voice break on that truth.

title: The Spiral's Stain
instruction: You are a retired building superintendent, stepping into a concrete stairwell to meet a tenant who has been reported for dumping trash. The reverb of your boots echoes harshly as you pause on the landing. You feel a creeping disgust at the smell of rot and the littered steps. As you speak, your voice carries a gruff, disgusted authority at first—then you notice a child's toy wedged in the corner. The disgust softens into weary, reluctant recognition. Let the reverb make your words sound bigger than you feel. You trail off once, listening to the echo, then find your resolve. Your voice: tight in the chest at first, then loosening with a tired vulnerability.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Crash After the High
instruction: You're a young man alone in a bathroom stall at a loud party, heart racing, nostrils burning. You just did a bump of coke minutes ago and you're riding the rush – talking to yourself in the mirror with jittery, overconfident excitement, sniffing constantly, voice too loud and fast. But as you wipe your nose you feel a sting of pain from an old injury (a broken rib from a car accident two weeks ago), and the gratitude you felt for surviving that crash suddenly curdles into raw, physical pain. Your speech should start with manic, grandiose gratitude – 'I'm so lucky, man, that could've been it' – then slow down, the confidence cracking as the pain hits, leaving you swallowing hard, voice congested and strained.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Velvet Trap
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy at a dimly lit house party, approaching the girl you've liked for months. You've practiced this: low voice, slow pace, charming smile. But a week ago, your ex crushed you, and that ache sits just beneath the surface. As you speak, you try to stay smooth—adjusting your collar, matching her rhythm—but your sadness leaks through: a pause too long, a laugh that breaks too quick. By the end, the effort slips, and you're just a tired kid asking if she's okay, voice cracking with quiet pain.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unsaid Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: You're watching your adult child board a plane to move across the world, possibly forever. For years, you've bitten your tongue about their choices, their partner, the life they're building away from you. You've smiled through holidays, nodded politely, kept the peace. But now, in these final minutes, everything you've never said comes pouring out—not as an attack, but as a raw, unstoppable confession of your fear, your pride, your resentment, and your desperate love. Start with forced composure, trying to maintain the pleasant goodbye you planned. Let the dam break mid-sentence. By the end, you've said things that can never be unsaid, and you're left standing there watching them go, uncertain whether you've destroyed everything or finally told the truth. Your voice should move from controlled pleasantness to full-throated emotional release, then collapse into something quieter and more devastated.

title: The Last Glass
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in your dimly lit kitchen, a half-empty bottle of cheap wine on the counter. You've been drinking to numb the shock of a phone call you just got — your son has been arrested for a crime you know he didn't commit, and the man who set him up is an old friend you trusted. Your voice is thick with alcohol, words blurring at the edges, volume rising and falling without control. Start by muttering to yourself in disbelief, trying to piece together how this happened, then let the slurring give way to a sudden, raw sob as the full weight of betrayal hits you. Your performance must feel clumsy, unguarded, and utterly real — you're fighting to stay upright emotionally while your body betrays you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: I Learned It From Watching You
instruction: You're confronting your parent about how they taught you to fake expertise, to never admit you don't know something, to cover ignorance with confident performance. Start angry, throwing their own wrongly-used phrases back at them, mocking the way they pretended to know everything when you were growing up. But as you speak, let the anger crack open to reveal the underneath: you're terrified because you've become exactly like them, and you don't know how to be real with anyone anymore. Your voice should move from cutting sarcasm to shaking desperation. End with a plea that's barely a whisper: teach me how to stop pretending. Let us hear you break open as you realize you're not attacking them—you're begging them to save you both.

title: Accent Evolution
instruction: You're a documentary subject reflecting on your own transformation. Start with a thick regional accent — the accent of your childhood town that you haven't heard yourself use in years. As you speak about leaving home for college, your accent subtly shifts — words become rounder, the musicality flattens slightly. By the time you reach 'I haven't been home in a decade,' your accent has completely changed. You hear it happening, and your voice breaks slightly. 'I don't even talk like myself anymore.' Then you say one phrase in your original accent — 'I love you, Mama' — and it's devastating. You can't get back.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your terminally ill parent who has hours left. For your entire life, they controlled everything—your career choices, your relationships, your very sense of self-worth. You've rehearsed angry speeches for years. But now, looking at their frail body, something breaks open in you. Begin with all that lifetime of resentment rising in your throat—let your body feel tight, your voice strained with decades of unspoken rebellion. Then, mid-sentence, let yourself crack wide open into something you didn't expect: a fierce, aching tenderness. End by giving them—and yourself—the permission to finally let go. Let your voice move from controlled anger to raw, whispered liberation.
inspired_by: Actor is in a rigid or resistant environment (conservative director, non-exploratory cast) and needs to establish irreverent freedom before scene work

title: Underground City Discovery
instruction: You're an explorer walking into a vast underground city for the first time. Your voice starts with wonder but is forced to adapt to the acoustic properties of this space—echoes are disorienting. Your breath echoes. You're so overwhelmed that you can barely speak in sentences. You're describing architecture that shouldn't exist, and your voice carries the weight of realizing that everything you knew about history was wrong. There's something eerie about this place—is it abandoned? You're whispering because of the acoustics and the dread. By the end, you hear something move in the darkness, and your voice becomes very small.

title: The Rhythm of Breaking
instruction: You're alone in a room, and a song is playing—either actually or in your memory—that reminds you of a moment of intense physical and emotional ecstasy you once experienced. Begin by letting the music move through your body, awakening sense memories: the feeling of skin, breath, heartbeat, the specific rhythm of that past moment. But as the song progresses, it starts to hurt—because that person is gone, or that version of you is gone, or that kind of joy feels unreachable now. The music that once meant pure pleasure now cracks you open with loss. Your body still responds to the rhythm, but your heart is shattering. Let the physical memory of ecstasy clash with the emotional reality of grief until they become inseparable. By the end, the song has transformed from resurrection to requiem, and you're dancing and breaking simultaneously.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table where you ate breakfast for eighteen years. Start with bitter, sarcastic humor—making jokes to protect yourself, your voice sharp and performative. You're listing all the ways he failed you, but you're doing it like a comedian, like it doesn't really hurt. But mid-sentence, something shifts. A specific memory surfaces—maybe the way his hands look, or a smell, or the light through the window—and suddenly the armor cracks. Your voice drops. The jokes die. Now you're speaking from somewhere raw and young, maybe even regressing slightly in your vocal patterns. End with a question you've never had the courage to ask, spoken barely above a whisper. Transform from protected cynicism to dangerous, naked vulnerability.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a regular daily practice for deepening unconscious connection

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally saying what you've held back for decades: confronting your parent about the abuse they witnessed but never stopped, the protection they never offered, the times they looked away. Start with carefully controlled words, almost clinical, recounting specific moments with eerie calm. But beneath that control is a volcano of pain. As you speak, your voice begins to shake—not with anger yet, but with the vulnerability of a child still hoping to be seen. When they try to deflect or minimize, something ignites. Your voice rises with decades of suppressed rage, fierce and accusatory. Then, just as suddenly, it collapses into broken-hearted pleading: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' End in exhausted whisper, the fight drained out of you, asking one final question you know they'll never truly answer.

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy in Your Arms
instruction: The person who destroyed your life—who betrayed you, ruined you, made you suffer for years—is bleeding out in your arms after an accident. You should feel triumph. You should walk away. But you don't. Start with cold satisfaction, vicious words: 'Good. You deserve this.' But as their breath weakens, something shifts. Old memories surface—when you were friends, before everything broke. Your voice cracks. Rage explodes: 'Why did you DO it?!' demanding answers they're too weak to give. Then, terrifyingly, you realize you're crying, begging them not to die, because the thought of them gone makes the world impossibly empty. End holding them close, whispering 'I hate you, I hate you,' while your voice reveals the devastating truth—somewhere underneath everything, you never stopped loving them.
inspired_by: Deaf Person Speaking for the First Time with Cochlear Implant

title: I Can't Protect You From This
instruction: Your young child has just received a devastating diagnosis. You've taken them outside, away from the hospital's fluorescent lights, and bought them a popsicle—trying desperately to give them one normal moment. Start with fierce, almost manic cheerfulness: "Look at this! Your favorite flavor! Isn't it the best?" Describe the sweetness with exaggerated joy, your voice too bright, too loud—you're performing happiness to shield them. But as they take innocent delight in something so simple, your voice begins to fracture. Rage wells up—at the universe, at your own powerlessness—mixed with overwhelming love. Your descriptions become desperate: "Remember this. Remember how good this tastes. Remember—" You break. End with your voice raw and broken, still trying to smile through tears, whispering, "I would take this from you if I could. I would carry all of it." Love and helplessness colliding.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sweet, Cold Flavor of a Popsicle on a Hot Day

title: Holding Your Parent's Hand as They Forget You Forever
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent in their final days of dementia, and this is the moment they look at you without recognition for the last time. Start with desperate attempts to be seen—'Mom, it's me, it's really me'—your voice breaking with the need to be remembered. But then something shifts. You begin telling them stories of your childhood, their voice in your memories, the way they used to sing to you. Your voice transforms from panic to an unbearable tenderness, almost a lullaby. You're grieving them while they're still breathing, and your voice moves between fighting for connection and surrendering to goodbye. End in a whisper that's both devastated and somehow peaceful, as you realize you're now the keeper of all the memories they've lost. Let your voice crack not from volume but from the weight of love that has nowhere left to land.
inspired_by: Evacuating from Wildfire: Seeing Everything You Built Burn

title: Whispered Confession Over Shared Dessert
instruction: You're sharing a slice of chocolate cake with your best friend, but tonight you have to tell them you're in love with them—and you're leaving tomorrow, moving across the world. Begin with tender, intimate description of the cake, your voice soft and close, as though you're savoring both the dessert and this moment with them. Let pauses hang heavy between words. As you describe each layer, weave in what you can't quite say directly: how sweet things never last, how some flavors only exist in memory, how you'll never taste anything this perfect again. Your voice should grow quieter, more fragile, catching on certain words. End with a barely-audible admission that the cake isn't what you'll miss most, your words trembling with everything you can't take back, suffused with love and the quiet devastation of timing that will never be right.
inspired_by: Eating a Slice of Decadent Chocolate Cake

title: Tracing the Memory
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting alone at a kitchen table, your head propped heavily on your hand, cheek smushed against your palm. You're trying to remember the name of a childhood friend—it's on the tip of your tongue but keeps slipping away. Start with a low, frustrated mutter, your voice muffled and clumsy as you shift your jaw against your hand. As you concentrate, your breathing slows, and you lose your train of thought, then catch it again. End with a quiet, tender exhale as the name finally surfaces, your voice softening with relief and a hint of sadness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Thing I Want You to Know
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed, hours from death. Your adult child sits beside you—someone you've had a complicated relationship with. You've spent your whole life defined by your career achievements, always too busy, always proving yourself. But now none of that matters. Begin speaking to them about all the awards, the recognition, the things you accomplished. Let your voice carry pride, even defiance. Then, mid-sentence, stop. Feel the weight of what's really true: those achievements mean nothing now. Shift entirely—your voice should become smaller, more fragile. Tell them who you really were beneath all that striving: your secret kindnesses, your quiet moments of doubt, the times you helped strangers, your love of simple things. End by asking them one question you've never dared ask: 'Did I matter to you, just as myself?' Let your voice break on the realization that you're finally asking what you should have asked decades ago.

title: The Last Flight Home
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy sneaking back into your house after a night of drinking with friends. You're on the staircase leading to your bedroom, still buzzed and struggling to control your body. Start with a giddy, excited whisper as you fumble with the railing — you feel invincible. But as you climb, the effort and the fear of being caught creep in; your voice becomes more strained, breathless, and worried. By the time you reach the top, the intoxication fades into quiet regret and the weight of having to face tomorrow. Let your breath chop the words naturally, and let the pitch rise with each step.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Burning the Wedding Dress
instruction: You're physically burning something that represented a life you were supposed to want—a wedding dress, acceptance letter to a school your parents chose, documents of a career that was killing you. Start methodically, almost numbly, going through the motions. But as the flames grow, something primal ignites in you. Your body begins to move—dancing, thrashing, celebrating destruction. Let guttural sounds emerge, wild laughter mixed with sobbing, groans of release. Feel the heat on your skin mixing with the heat of rage, grief, and fierce joy erupting from your core. Your movements become bigger, less controlled, more ecstatic. End breathless, spent, your voice hoarse but singing or humming something absurdly hopeful. You're physically and vocally purged, standing in the ashes, finally free.

title: Choosing Path
instruction: You're standing at a metaphorical or literal crossroads, and you're making a choice that will define your life. Your voice is torn—both paths are valid, and both cost something. You're articulating the choice, and your voice carries the weight of knowing you can't go back. One moment, you're closer to one path, and your voice leans that direction. The next moment, you're drawn to the other. Finally, you make the choice. Your voice steadies with commitment, even if you're not certain it's the right one. By the end, you're walking forward, and your voice carries both your conviction and the echo of the path you didn't take.

title: The Last Garden
instruction: You're terminally ill, preparing your garden one final time for the child who will inherit it after you're gone. Start with quiet determination as you move through the space: 'The rosemary goes here, where morning sun hits first.' Your voice is steady, methodical, but there's weight beneath each word. As you continue, memories flood in—teaching small hands to plant seeds, watching scraped knees heal on this same soil. Your breath catches. By the end, you're kneeling in the dirt, hands trembling as you whisper the final instructions, voice breaking between pride and devastating grief: 'This is yours now. Everything I couldn't say... it's all here.' Let the tears come naturally. This is both goodbye and the most important gift you'll ever give.

title: The Last Crest
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a quiet, tender moment with your longtime partner. You've felt your body being guided toward release, but each time you approach the peak, your partner pulls back with a gentle, knowing patience—promising you're almost there. You begin with a soft, hopeful giggle, your breath catching in a mix of amused anticipation and fragile trust. But as the cycle repeats, your voice grows ragged, your pleas more honest—you let out frustrated little whimpers, your words dissolving into a shaky, raw whisper. By the end, you are no longer playful; you are utterly vulnerable, your voice breaking with a quiet, desperate hope that this time, you'll be allowed to fall.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Echo of Failure
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy standing alone in the empty gymnasium, still in your sweaty jersey. The harsh metallic echo of every sound—your breathing, your sneaker squeak—reminds you of the game-winning free throw you just missed in front of the whole school. Start by muttering in disgust at your own hands, scornful and tight, blaming them for betraying you. As you talk, the echo seems to mock you, and your disgust shifts inward; you feel shame crawling up your throat. You might stop, kick a ball, or hear your own voice bounce back too loud. End with a helpless, quiet whisper—realizing there’s no one else to blame—and let the empty hall absorb your words.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Wired and Wonderstruck
instruction: You're alone in your apartment at 2am, three cups of coffee deep. You were supposed to be finishing a report, but instead you're fixated on a tiny succulent on your desk. Your heart hammers, your leg bounces, words tumble out fast and sharp as you realize how jittery you are. Then you notice the dusting of soil on a leaf, the way the light catches the edge. Let your voice slow, pitch drop a little, and end in a soft, breathy whisper of contentment as you tell the plant it's perfect.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Tiny Pink Pill
instruction: You are a young girl lying in a dark room with a pounding migraine. Your mother just gave you a new medicine that tastes awful, and you're whispering to her, your voice barely above a breath because any sound hurts. At first, you're disgusted by the chalky, bitter flavor and confused why it has to be so horrible. But as you speak, you remember how much you want the pain to stop, and a fragile hope creeps in. Let your voice crack and fade, let your eyes squint, let the disgust soften into a desperate optimism. Say about 50-70 words.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (clearly present), Confusion (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Running Barefoot on Soft Sand
instruction: Feel the sand give way beneath your feet, soft and warm. Describe the way each step makes you sink slightly, the grains of sand shifting with each movement. Speak with a tone of joyful freedom, as if every step connects you to the earth, grounding you, yet making you feel incredibly light and carefree.

title: Whispered Worlds Between Skin
instruction: You're lying in intimate darkness with someone, bodies close, voices barely above a whisper. Begin tentatively, guardedly—there's something you've never told anyone. Then you start to describe a private fantasy, something you've only experienced in your imagination: perhaps a place you've dreamed of, a version of yourself you've never dared to become, a moment of freedom or wildness or peace you've only tasted in daydreams. Use every sense—what do you see, hear, smell, taste, feel in this fantasy? As you whisper this secret world into existence between you, let your voice and body soften, open, become more vulnerable. The act of speaking this hidden part of yourself aloud, of being witnessed in this tenderness, transforms your initial fear into something raw and beautiful—perhaps trust, perhaps desire, perhaps a kind of love you've never quite let yourself feel before.
inspired_by: Fantasy Imaging to Elevate State Before Performance

title: The Last Broadcast
instruction: You are a children's radio host, a man, on what you know will be your final show before the station shuts down. You are alone in the booth, the red light is on, and you're speaking into the close mic to your young listeners. In the first half, there's fear in your voice—a tightness, a quiver when you think of the kids you're leaving, of the void this will leave. But as you speak, you find yourself overwhelmed with gratitude, a warmth that thickens your words. Let your voice crack, swallow hard, pause as you search for the right words, and let the final sentence be a gentle, grateful sigh.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unfiled Confession
instruction: You are slightly drunk, sorting through a messy pile of papers late at night. Your voice is a little loose, slurs and mumbles slipping in. Start with a wry, detached humor as you find old receipts and notes. Then, one note stops you. It's from someone you deeply miss. Your voice softens, shoulders droop, and you trail off into a raw, regretful whisper, the buzz suddenly feeling hollow.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at dawn, and they've just asked you to promise you'll be okay without them. Start with fierce denial—your voice tight, almost angry: 'Don't talk like that. You're going to be fine.' But as you look at their frail hand in yours, the pretense crumbles. Your voice softens, becomes tender and broken. You're now speaking the truth you've been avoiding: 'I'm not ready... I don't know how to do this without you.' Let gratitude flood in as you remember everything they've given you, your voice warming even as tears come. End in a place of devastating acceptance mixed with deep love—whispering your promise, your voice steady but saturated with grief: 'I'll be okay. Because of everything you taught me.'

title: Waking to an Empty House
instruction: You're a middle-aged man waking from a deep nap on the couch. The room is dim, you don't know what time it is. Your voice is thick, sluggish — you swallow, clear your throat, blink. As you slowly realize the house is silent, a wave of longing hits you: you wish someone was here, wished you hadn't napped through their call. Start disoriented, grumbling to yourself about the time, then let the loneliness seep in. End with a quiet, raw admission of missing someone — your voice cracks, trails off. Let the grogginess soften into vulnerable ache.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Hollow Light in the Window
instruction: You’ve been awake for over 24 hours, sitting in the dark living room, staring at the neighbor’s house across the street. Their bedroom light is on, and you can see them moving inside — laughing, touching, alive. You’re holding your phone, about to text an old friend who’s probably asleep. Start with a voice that’s a grudge — bitter, flat, and hollow from exhaustion, like your tongue is made of sand. Mid-sentence, a microsleep hits, and you blank out for a second, then come back to the same image. Let the envy curdle into a childlike longing for that warmth, but end with a raw doubt that cracks the voice: you’re not sure you even deserve to want it. Yawn or swallow hard once, naturally.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Longing (clearly present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Echoing Hall
instruction: You are elderly, a little drunk, walking alone down a long, dimly lit hallway in a house after a family gathering. Your footsteps echo, and the wine makes your thoughts wander. You start by muttering to yourself about the noise and the people, your voice slightly slurred, catching on the walls. Midway, you pause to steady yourself against the wall—your hand slides along the wallpaper. The quiet around you shifts your mood; you stop thinking about the party and instead feel a sudden, clear sadness about how empty the house will be tomorrow. End by speaking softly, almost to the empty air, about time slipping away. Your voice loses its fuzziness and becomes stark, real, and full of acceptance.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Rage Against the Unchangeable Past
instruction: You are a time traveler who has just returned from your hundredth attempt to save your child, your partner, your sibling—someone you love who died, and no matter what you change, fate finds a way to take them from you anyway. You're screaming at the universe, at time itself, at whatever cruel mechanism makes some things inevitable. Begin with explosive fury—pound your fists, let your voice crack with the injustice of it. You've bargained, you've begged, you've broken every law of physics, and it means nothing. But mid-rage, you collapse into something rawer: helplessness. Your voice drops. You describe the exact moment they died this last time, how you held them, how they didn't even know you'd been fighting for them across a hundred lifetimes. End in a terrible moment of surrender—you're not accepting it, but you're too broken to fight anymore. Let your final words be barely audible, a confession that you don't know how to exist in a world where they're gone, but you're so, so tired of trying to rewrite it.

title: Forgiving the Ghost in Your Childhood Bedroom
instruction: You've returned to your childhood home, standing in your old bedroom, and you're speaking softly to the memory of someone who hurt you deeply—a sibling, a parent, a first love—someone who's no longer in your life. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile: 'I've been carrying this for so long... I want to let it go.' You're offering forgiveness to the empty room, to the past, to the ghost of who they were. But as you speak, the memories flood back—not just the hurt, but the love, the confusion, the moments when you needed them and they weren't there. Your voice catches, breaks softly. You're crying now, but quietly, the kind of tears that slip down without sound. By the end, you realize forgiveness isn't a gift you give them—it's something you do for yourself, even if they never know, even if they never cared. Your final words are tender but achingly sad: 'I forgive you. And I have to let you go.'

title: Pedal Pulse Wonder
instruction: You are an elderly person cycling hard on a stationary bike, watching a nature documentary about deep-sea creatures. Your breathing is locked to each pedal stroke — talk in short bursts on your exhales, your voice a forced whisper between gasps. At first you're just pushing through the burn, your words clipped and strained. But as you describe the anglerfish's glowing lure, genuine fascination breaks through the exertion.
