Your voice softens with awe even as you struggle to keep the rhythm, and by the end you're fighting a smile, your interest overriding the fatigue.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Missing Voice
instruction: You are a teenager alone in your room, trying to call a friend who hasn’t texted back all day. Your chest tightens, your breath comes in gasps, and you start talking to yourself—high-pitched, fragmented, repeating 'I can't breathe.' As the panic spirals, a sudden longing cuts through: you whisper their name, wanting them to hear you, to answer. Your voice cracks, slows, and you end with a soft, desperate plea—the panic still there but now laced with yearning. Let the hyperventilation dominate your speech at first, then let the longing slow and deepen your words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering Poison in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night. You're alone, or perhaps lying next to someone who's asleep. You're speaking in barely audible whispers to yourself—or to the ghost of the person who betrayed you. Your voice is intimate, dangerous, like you're sharing a terrible secret. Start with quiet, almost tender hatred: 'I think about what you did every single day. Every. Single. Day.' There's something vulnerable in how you confess this, how you admit the hold this person still has over you. Your whispers detail the ways they live in your mind, the moments that ambush you. Your voice catches, not with tears but with the exhaustion of carrying this weight. The hatred is there, but so is something more devastating: the realization that this anger has become your companion, maybe the only thing keeping you connected to them. End with a whispered admission that costs you everything: 'I don't know who I am without hating you. And I hate you for that most of all.' Let silence breathe between phrases.

title: Becoming Legend Living
instruction: You've become the thing people tell stories about. Your voice is aware of this, carries it lightly: 'I didn't know it would become this.' Breathing is even, your voice carries weight. Physical: you're still yourself, but the world sees differently. 'I just kept showing up.' Vocal tone is humble but honest. 'I kept choosing the hardest thing.' By the end, you're speaking from the place of legend-hood without pride: 'I became what I needed to become.'

title: The Calculation: A Doctor Tells Their Own Parent They're Removing Life Support
instruction: You're a physician explaining to your conscious, dying parent that you're authorizing the removal of their life support—not as their child, but as their medical power of attorney, because they asked you to make this choice when the time came. Start clinical, hiding behind medical terminology and procedure, your voice steady with professional distance as you explain the decision tree, the quality of life metrics, the irreversible decline. But your parent sees through it and says your childhood nickname. Everything shatters. Your voice breaks between rage at them for asking this of you, grief that you're about to lose them, and a child's desperate plea for them not to make you do this. You're simultaneously the doctor who knows this is right, the child who wants their parent to live forever, and the adult trying to honor a promise that's destroying you. End with quiet, fierce love—telling them it's okay to let go while your voice makes it clear nothing will ever be okay again.
inspired_by: Professional: Military Commander Orders Civilians Evacuated, Knowing Some Will Be Killed

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Love You Can Never Speak Aloud
instruction: You're standing beside someone sleeping—your best friend's partner, your sibling's spouse, someone forbidden. This is your only chance to say what you've hidden for years because tomorrow everything changes. Your voice must be barely audible, each word a secret you're finally releasing into the darkness. Begin with tender confession—the moments you've memorized, the times you almost broke. Your breath is careful, intimate, each pause heavy with years of silence. As you continue, feel your heart break open—not dramatically, but like something inside you is quietly dissolving. By the end, you're saying goodbye to a future that never existed, and your whispered words carry both profound love and the devastating acceptance that this moment is all you'll ever have. Let the vulnerability be so raw it's almost unbearable—no drama, just truth spoken in the dark.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Resistance Leader Realizes the Revolution Is Being Co-Opted

title: Bedtime Story in Three Languages
instruction: You're putting your child to sleep, reading their favorite story, but tonight you're reading it in your mother tongue—the language your partner doesn't speak, the language you've hidden from your American life. Your voice is soft, tender, each word a lullaby. Your child asks what the words mean. You translate, whispering, but the English feels wrong, hollow. You switch back and forth, your voice catching because you're giving them something precious and realizing you've almost let it die. The story is about someone who travels far from home. As you near the end, your voice thickens with tears you're trying to hide. You finish in your mother tongue, then whisper the last line in English: 'And they never forgot where they came from.' You're not sure if you're talking to your child or yourself. End in silence, stroking their hair, crying quietly.

title: Breathing the Same Air
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone you love (or once loved), and you begin whispering a confession you've never been able to say in daylight. Start with halting, careful words. But between each phrase, let the silence fill with everything actually happening inside you: the vulnerability of being this exposed, the fear they'll leave, the relief of finally speaking truth, the sensation of their breathing, the ache or tenderness or guilt. Let these internal experiences shape how each next whisper emerges—faster or slower, steadier or more broken. This isn't about building to a climax; it's about letting authentic impulses guide you through a fragile revelation. By the end, the emotional quality of your voice should be transformed by the genuine journey of saying these things out loud in darkness.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You are standing at your younger sister's wedding reception, microphone in hand, about to give a toast. She's marrying your ex-fiancé - the person you thought you'd grow old with, who left you three years ago. Begin with a bright, performative voice - the cheerful sibling everyone expects. But as you speak about love and partnership, let real memories intrude. Your voice should shimmer with contradictions: genuine happiness for her mixed with your own unhealed heartbreak, love for your sister tangled with betrayal, gratitude that she found happiness shadowed by the question of why you weren't enough. Let yourself slip between tenses - remembering when he was yours, acknowledging that he's now hers, wondering about the life you'll never have. By the end, your voice should carry all of it at once: blessing and grief, celebration and mourning, love and loss inseparably intertwined. Finish with a genuine wish for their happiness that costs you everything to speak. Move from false brightness to authentic emotional complexity to bittersweet grace.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked on the spot before a performance or class and cannot reach a BEING state

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're packing up your child's bedroom because they're leaving—college, marriage, or they've simply grown up and moved away. Pick up objects one by one: a stuffed animal, a trophy, a photo. Begin with practical efficiency, maybe even relief at reclaiming the space. But as you handle each item, let the contradictions flood in. You're proud and devastated. You're excited for them and mourning for yourself. You wanted this freedom and you're terrified of the emptiness. Let yourself oscillate wildly between these feelings—laugh at a memory, then feel your throat close. Feel gratitude and resentment in the same breath. Celebrate their independence while grieving your own loss. Don't resolve these contradictions into one clean feeling. Stay in the mess of it. By the end, you should be sitting surrounded by half-packed boxes, holding something small, feeling everything at once.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You: Thirty Years of Silence Breaking
instruction: You're finally saying what you've never said to a parent who was physically present but emotionally absent your entire life. Begin with your voice tight, controlled, almost businesslike—you've rehearsed this, you're keeping it together. 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you start listing specific moments—the recital they missed, the night you needed them and they weren't there, the way you learned to make yourself small and unneeded—your voice begins to shake with anger. The fury builds: 'Do you even know who I am?' But then something shifts. Under the rage, there's this raw, childlike pain: 'I just wanted you to see me.' Your voice cracks completely, becomes vulnerable, almost pleading. By the end, you're not asking for anything anymore. You're simply stating a truth with quiet, devastating clarity: 'I needed a parent, and you were a stranger in my house.' Your voice carries both the weight of grief for what never was and the strange, exhausted relief of finally saying it out loud.
inspired_by: Kindness Showing Ripple Effects: Realizing Impact You Didn't Know

title: The Doorway of Morning
instruction: You are watching your adult child leave for a journey you know will transform them forever—they're moving across the world, or getting married, or making a choice you fear but must support. Begin with genuine excitement in your voice, celebrating their courage and future, your pride absolutely real and soaring. But underneath, let the grief leak through—your voice catching on certain words, pauses that last too long. You're trying so hard to give them freedom while your heart is shattering. By the end, you're holding both truths simultaneously: fierce joy for who they're becoming and devastating loss of who they were. Your final words should crack with both pride and grief, blessing and goodbye, love and letting go—all at once, inseparable.
inspired_by: A director is giving result direction rather than process guidance

title: Burning Through the Borrowed Rage
instruction: You've just closed a production where you played someone consumed by violence and fury—emotions you manufactured by twisting your own experiences into something darker. Now your body still holds that synthesized anger; it surfaces at wrong moments, colors your actual relationships. Stand and physically move as you speak aloud the fabricated reasons for rage you created for the character. Let your body feel that borrowed fury fully. Then, forcefully, begin to separate fiction from fact: shout the truth of what actually happened in your life, acknowledge where you exaggerated, where you invented, where you distorted real events to serve a character's psychology. Feel the manufactured rage burn away as you speak your actual reality—perhaps disappointment instead of hatred, perhaps hurt instead of fury, perhaps even forgiveness. Your voice should move from roaring to something quieter, more honest, more nuanced. End by stating aloud what you actually feel about your real life, your real history, in your authentic voice.

title: The Moment You Find Them Alive: Rage, Relief, Collapse
instruction: Your partner/child/best friend went missing for three days. You've barely slept, called hospitals, imagined the worst. Now they're standing in front of you, safe but disheveled, and you explode: 'WHERE WERE YOU?!' Your voice is raw fury, hands shaking. 'Do you have ANY idea—' But mid-sentence, the rage shatters into violent relief. Your voice breaks completely: 'I thought you were dead. I thought—' You can't finish. You might move toward them, pull back, move forward again. Let your voice oscillate between anger and sobbing: 'Don't you ever—God, I can't—' End collapsed, maybe on your knees, all the fight drained out: 'Please don't leave me like that again.' Your voice must show how rage is just terror in disguise, how love makes us vulnerable to unimaginable pain.

title: Unwilling Rhythm
instruction: You are an elderly woman, your body frail, your voice high and thin with age. You are in the midst of sex with a younger partner who is thrusting hard, their weight pressing you into the mattress. You started with embarrassment — a nervous, brittle laugh, half-whispered pleas to slow down. But as the rhythm continues, disgust rises, thick and sour. Your voice breaks: little grunts of discomfort, words that catch in your throat, breaths that hitch. You try to say 'Stop,' but it comes out as a choked gasp. By the end, you are spitting the word 'disgusting' — barely audible, your breath ragged, your body trembling. The bed springs squeak with each thrust.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Celebrating Your Wedding Anniversary While Planning Your Divorce
instruction: You're at dinner with your spouse on your anniversary, going through the ritual of toasting your years together. Begin with warm nostalgia—genuinely laughing about old memories, your voice full of affection for who you both were. But as you continue, let bittersweetness creep in. You're remembering all this beauty while knowing you're going to tell them tonight that you want a divorce. Your voice catches between laughter and tears. You find yourself thanking them with heartbreaking sincerity for the good years while grief for what you're losing floods through you. End in a complex emotional space: expressing deep gratitude and genuine love while your heart breaks, celebrating them while letting them go, finding strange peace in honoring what was beautiful even as you acknowledge it's over. Let joy and devastating sadness exist in the same breath.
inspired_by: Teaching Your Teenager About Sex While Mortified

title: The Sock Under the Bed
instruction: You are a child, about seven years old, in your own carpeted bedroom. You've just discovered something deeply disgusting: a forgotten, moldy, half-eaten sandwich under your bed, with fuzzy blue-green growth. At first, you recoil in pure, vocal disgust, gagging and exclaiming in shock. But as you process it, a sneaky, rebellious thrill creeps in—the kind of gross-out fascination that makes you want to poke it with a stick. Let your voice shift from a sharp, appalled cry to a low, conspiratorial, half-giggling whisper as you decide what to do with this disgusting treasure.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Rage and Ruin in the Hospital Corridor
instruction: You've just been told your child was injured because someone was texting while driving. Start with your voice shaking, barely controlled: 'Where is he? Where's the driver?' Security is trying to calm you. Explode with volcanic rage: 'My baby is in there fighting for her life because some selfish—' Your voice cracks into a roar of anguish that dissolves into gasping sobs. You collapse against the wall, sliding down, voice breaking completely: 'She's only seven years old. She's seven.' The fury transforms into desperate, helpless pleading to no one and everyone: 'Please, please let her be okay. I can't... I can't lose her.' Your voice becomes fierce again, protective even in devastation: 'She's supposed to have a whole life ahead of her. She's supposed to have everything.' End in exhausted, whispered repetition, rocking slightly: 'Please be okay, baby. Please be okay.' The rage has burned down to ash and prayer. You are powerless, and it's destroying you.

title: The Vigil Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping spouse in hospice at 3 AM, and you're finally saying everything you've kept inside. Start with your voice barely above a whisper—'Are you awake? No, good.'—because you need them not to hear this. Confess the small lies: the money you spent, the work trip that wasn't all work, the times you almost left. Your voice should be tender but urgent, like you're running out of time to be honest. Then let it deepen: tell them about the moment you fell back in love with them after years of just going through motions. Describe it—'You were making eggs, and the morning light...'—your voice catching on the memory. End with 'I'm so sorry I wasted years being angry about things that don't matter,' and let that apology hold all your regret and all your devotion. The last line—'Please don't go'—should be almost inaudible, more breath than sound.

title: The Sandbox Confessional
instruction: You are a 6-year-old girl playing in a sandbox with your best friend. You are making sandcastles together, and you start out feeling genuinely interested in her idea to add a moat. But when she absentmindedly mentions her new 'real' princess castle toy at home, a hot, tight wave of jealousy hits you hard. As you push sand around, you try to hide it, feeling it churn into a quiet, green-eyed envy that makes your voice go thin and hesitant. By the end, you stop working and just stare at your own lumpy castle, saying nothing for a beat, then your voice comes out flat and lost, a quiet fake interest that betrays you.
emotions_sampled: Interest (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Contemplation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Stairwell Standoff
instruction: You're a teenager backed against the cold brick wall of a school stairwell, face-to-face with someone who's been threatening you for weeks. They're so close you can smell their breath and feel the heat radiating off them. Your voice starts high, sharp, and defensive — pushing back but cracking with raw fear. Midway, a siren passes outside or a door slams, making you flinch, and that breaks your bravado. You finish quieter, more fragile, letting the fear leak through as you realize you can't win this fight with anger alone.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Crackling Through the Static
instruction: You're at a small protest, holding a bullhorn for the first time. A friend just handed it to you, and there's a flicker of relief that you're finally speaking up. But as the words leave your mouth, the harsh distortion and feedback make you doubt every syllable — are they even hearing you right? Start with a tentative, slightly relieved tone, then let the compressed roar of the bullhorn amplify your uncertainty. Let your voice crack, trail off, and be interrupted by squeals of feedback. End with your words hesitant and hollow, the doubt swallowing the message.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at 3am. For years, you've carried shame about your deepest desires and truest self—things you've never spoken aloud to anyone. Now, with hours left, you finally find the courage to confess who you really are, what you really want from life, the secret longings you've hidden. Begin with hesitation, fear of judgment, your voice barely a whisper. As you speak and see only acceptance in their fading eyes, let your shame transform into liberation, your whispers growing into full-voiced declarations of self. End with tearful gratitude, finally free to be seen completely. Let your voice crack, pause, breathe—this is raw exposure turning into release.
inspired_by: Creating Sexual Fantasies, Publicly and Privately

title: The Last Dawn Through New Eyes
instruction: You are at your grandmother's bedside in her final hours. She has just passed, and you're alone with her body as dawn breaks through the window. Begin in shock and numbness, unable to process what has happened. Then, as the morning light fills the room, allow yourself to see her face, her hands, the room itself as if you're seeing them for the very first time—noticing every detail with childlike wonder: the way light catches in her silver hair, the pattern of veins on her hands that held yours countless times, the specific blue of her favorite blanket. Let your grief transform through this lens of rediscovery, moving from frozen shock to a tender, aching appreciation of every small detail of her existence. Speak to her, describing what you're seeing as though naming it makes it real, makes it something you can hold onto. End in a place of bittersweet wonder—devastated but somehow more alive to beauty than you've ever been.

title: One Last Pull
instruction: You are an older climber halfway up a steep rope climb. Your arms ache, your core is locked tight, and every word comes out as a breathless whisper. You start by remembering a funny fall your buddy took years ago—you almost chuckle, but you can't waste air. Then your foot slips on a tiny hold; your grip tightens, your voice turns sharp and shaky for a second. You force a dark laugh and tell yourself, 'Almost there.' The hope keeps you going, but the tremor in your words betrays the fear. Speak in short, broken bursts.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Amusement (extremely present), Distress (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Bedside Goodbye to a Sleeping Child
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's hospital bed in the quiet hours before a surgery with uncertain odds. Your voice is barely above a breath, tender and aching: 'Hey, sweet baby. I know you can't hear me right now, but I need to say this.' Let your words be soft, intimate, catching on unshed tears: 'I never knew I could love someone this much. It actually hurts—right here in my chest—how much I love you.' Pause, struggling to continue. 'Tomorrow you're going to be so brave, and I'm going to be right there. But just in case...' Your voice fractures, becomes almost inaudible: 'Just in case, I need you to know that being your parent has been the greatest honor of my life.' Touch their hand gently as you speak: 'You made me better. You made me real.' End with a whispered promise that sounds like both a prayer and a plea: 'Fight hard tomorrow, okay? I'm not ready to let you go.'

title: Amid the City Roar
instruction: You're standing on a crowded city sidewalk, phone pressed to your ear, trying to solve a complex problem in your head—maybe a code, a forgotten address, or a puzzle. Traffic horns and a distant siren cut through your focus, making you squint and raise your voice. You mutter calculations, pausing as a construction drill drowns out your thoughts. Then, suddenly, the solution clicks. Your voice lifts into a sharp, triumphant exclamation—louder, clearer, cutting through the noise—as you grin and pump your fist, the frustration melting into pure victory.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Begging Someone to Stay
instruction: They're leaving you. Whether it's a relationship, a friendship, a job—they're walking away. Your voice is desperate. 'Please don't go... please...' Your voice is stripping away all dignity. You're begging. Your voice becomes almost inaudible with shame—you're begging—but you can't help it. They're not listening. Your voice becomes angry out of desperation. 'Fine, leave!' But it cracks. The door closes. Your voice is alone.

title: The Curtain Call That Almost Wasn't
instruction: You are a middle-aged stage actor standing center stage under a hot spotlight, addressing a full house from the gala. Your voice must carry with a stage whisper—loud enough for the back row, every final consonant sharp and crisp. Begin with disgust: the theater board nearly cancelled this show because they thought it was 'too risky.' Let that bitterness seep into your over-articulated words. Pause naturally as you glance at your fellow cast members in the wings—a flicker of thankfulness surfaces, soft but real. Then a swell of pride takes over, fierce and undeniable. The pride must ring out, making your voice grow fuller but still controlled. You shift weight, adjust your grip on the microphone, and let a brief, rueful laugh escape before landing on the final line.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Pride (very intensely present)

title: The Wedding Morning Paradox
instruction: It's your wedding day morning and you're alone, getting ready. Your partner is perfect, you love them, this is what you want—but your mother, who should be here helping you, died two years ago. Begin moving through the motions of preparation with your body holding contradictions: excitement makes you want to stretch and reach upward, but grief keeps pulling you inward. Let yourself move between these states—a moment of pure joy where your body opens and you laugh, then suddenly the weight drops back in and you curve forward, voice catching. Allow the physical sensations of happiness and sorrow to alternate and then, gradually, coexist in your body. End in a complex state: standing tall, shoulders back, breathing fully, but with tears on your face—your body holding both the expansion of joy and the ache of absence, transformed into bittersweet wholeness.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Child Before Brain Surgery You May Not Survive
instruction: You're in pre-op, heavily sedated, consciousness slipping away, and your child is beside you for what might be your last conversation. You begin trying to tell them you love them, that they'll be okay, voice thick and drowsy, words getting lost as the medication pulls you under. You keep losing your train of thought mid-sentence, jolting back to say one more thing—advice, reassurance, an apology for missing their future. Your voice wavers between drugged confusion and desperate clarity as you fight to stay present for them. End with a moment where you're not sure if you actually said 'I love you' out loud or just thought it, reaching for their hand as everything fades. Let the terror of leaving them mix with peaceful surrender, maternal protectiveness battling the chemical pull into darkness.
inspired_by: Heroin Nod: Fighting Sleep While Someone Talks to You

title: The Unwinding of a Broken Clock
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting alone in a cluttered kitchen, complaining about the same dripping faucet you've mentioned for weeks. You start with a weary, nasal drone, elongating vowels to detail your suffering, like 'The wa-ter just... drips... drips all night.' Halfway through, as you reach for a faded photograph, your voice cracks and slows—losing the repetitive rhythm. End with a raw, quiet sadness as you realize your complaints are really about loneliness, not the faucet. Let your voice become unsteady, sink into silence between phrases, as if the complaint has exhausted itself into grief.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Three AM Confessions
instruction: You are lying in bed at three in the morning next to someone you love, and you need to tell them something you've never told anyone—a fear that haunts you, a moment of shame that defines you, or a truth about your heart that terrifies you. Begin in a whisper, testing whether they're awake, your voice barely disturbing the darkness. Let the intimacy of the dark bedroom, the warmth of their body next to yours, make you brave enough to crack open. Speak as if the darkness itself is permission to be unguarded. Let specific images guide you: recall the exact moment you first felt this fear, the precise physical sensation in your chest, the way it's shaped your choices. Your voice should be almost fragile, catching on certain words, pausing as you decide whether to continue. End with the simplest, most vulnerable statement of need you've ever spoken, letting them truly see the most undefended part of you.
inspired_by: Scene partners have a long shared history that does not appear in the script

title: Awakened to Betrayal
instruction: You are an elderly man, just woken from a deep, contented nap in your favorite armchair. The room is dim, you're disoriented, your voice is thick with sleep. You slowly become aware of a note on the coffee table that your son has taken your vintage watch without asking. Start with a mumbled, contented observation about the nap, then read the note, and your voice transforms from foggy confusion to seething, righteous anger. Let the grogginess linger in your tone, with pauses and trailing off, as the anger sharpens your words. Speak as if you're still half-asleep, then the fury breaks through.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about a betrayal or wound that has silently poisoned your relationship for years. You've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times in your head, but now that you're face to face, everything comes out differently. Begin speaking—letting your words tumble out impulsively, switching rapidly between declaring who you really are (not who they made you), what you've wanted from them all this time, what you needed that they never gave, and what you feel beneath the anger. Start with controlled fury and bitter composure, but let the confrontation crack you open until you're speaking from a place of devastating vulnerability. Don't censor yourself—let contradictory truths collide, let your voice break, let the child in you emerge.
inspired_by: I Am, I Want, I Need, I Feel

title: The Stubborn Knot
instruction: You are a gruff older man, alone in your armchair, knitting a scarf you started out of boredom. The click of needles is steady. You're impatient—the yarn keeps tangling, and you mutter under your breath, annoyed at this fussy hobby. But then you notice the pattern emerging: a subtle, pleasing texture. Your irritation softens as curiosity takes over. Speak aloud to yourself, grumbling at first, then slowing down as you become absorbed. Let your voice start brusque and dismissive, then shift to thoughtful, almost reverent, as the click-click steadies your breathing.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Interest (extremely present)

title: The Last Dirty Joke
instruction: You are an older man in a back-alley brawl. At the start, you're disgusted by your opponent, a younger punk who smells of cheap booze and thinks he's invincible. You feel contempt for his arrogance, and you tease him between heavy breaths and sharp grunts as you trade blows. Midway, you slip on a wet patch and feel your age in your back, but you force yourself up, the contempt now mixed with a sadder, older firmness. By the end, you've got him pinned, but instead of finishing it, you just hold him, your voice ragged but authoritative, showing a flicker of grim satisfaction under the pain. Let your voice be breathless, aggressive at first, then slowing down to a gravelly, tired command.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Contempt (extremely present), Teasing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in complete darkness. They think you're asleep. You need to tell them something you've been hiding for months—not an affair, but something perhaps worse: you've stopped feeling what you once felt, and you don't know if it's coming back. Start by whispering their name, barely audible. Your throat is tight; shame and guilt make your voice small, halting. You speak in fragments, long pauses between phrases, almost hoping they'll stay asleep so you don't have to finish. But you push through, because the secret is suffocating you. As you speak, something unexpected happens—the act of confession itself stirs something dormant. Saying it aloud makes you realize how much you've missed being honest with them, how isolation has been the real problem. Your whisper becomes slightly stronger, not with certainty, but with fragile hope. End with a question, genuinely asked, voice raw and exposed: 'Can we find our way back?' Let the vulnerability be complete, terrifying, and real.

title: The Playground Promise
instruction: You are a little girl, maybe 7, in the middle of a joyful game with your dad. He just lifted you high, you're laughing, feeling pure ecstasy and trust. Then you see the letter fall from his pocket — words that prove he's been lying to your family. Your voice starts bright and breathless from giggles, then stumbles into a quiet, disbelieving 'Daddy...?' as you read. As the truth sinks in, your voice cracks and rises, words tumbling out in fragmented accusations, circling back to the central wound: 'You said you'd always be here. You promised. You promised me.' Feel the shift from ecstasy to volcanic devastation, letting your voice break naturally as you lose control.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Moment You Realize They're Dying in Your Arms
instruction: You're holding someone you love who's been hurt, and you're trying to keep them calm, keep them awake. Your voice is commanding at first: 'Look at me. Stay with me. You're going to be fine.' But their eyes are changing, and you feel their body growing heavy. Your voice becomes ferocious, a roar of desperation: 'Don't you dare leave me!' You're shaking them, begging, bargaining with God, with fate, with them. You promise anything—you'll be better, you'll fix everything, just stay. But you can feel them slipping away, and your voice breaks into something primal, a sound that's not quite words anymore. Then rage—pure, helpless fury at the universe for taking them. You're still talking to them, but now you're saying goodbye, and you hate yourself for saying goodbye because it means accepting they're going. End with your voice raw, demolished, speaking to someone who can no longer hear you. Show someone experiencing every emotion at once—love, terror, rage, helplessness, denial, and the most devastating acceptance.

title: Confronting Your Mother in the Kitchen Where Everything Happened
instruction: You're finally telling your mother what her absence did to you as a child. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, let the rehearsed speech disintegrate. Jump between ages: speak as your 8-year-old self, then your angry teenage self, then your adult self trying to understand. Let your body express what words can't: maybe you're suddenly pacing wildly, maybe you collapse, maybe you're mimicking her gestures mockingly then tenderly. Swing from fury to desperate pleading to cruel observations to vulnerability within seconds. Include moments where you defend her, then attack, then need her to hold you. Let accusations mix with 'I love you' and 'I hate what you did' and 'I understand now.' End somewhere unexpected—perhaps in laughter at the absurdity, or silent exhaustion, or fierce forgiveness, or continued rage. Don't control the journey.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis and you're recording a video message to be played at your own funeral. Start with dark humor, almost manic laughter: 'So... this is weird, right? Me talking to you when I'm dead?' You're making jokes because the alternative is unbearable. But between the laughter, your voice keeps breaking into something more honest. 'I'm so grateful. God, I'm so grateful I got to know you.' Include the moment where a laugh turns into a sob and back again, where joy and grief become indistinguishable. You're remembering specific moments—a joke you shared, a meal, a sunset—and your voice is full of wonder even as tears stream down your face. 'I'm not ready to go, but I'm so glad I was here.' End with genuine laughter through tears, finding absurd beauty in the fact that you got to love and be loved at all, that any of this ridiculous, magnificent life happened. Let peace and heartbreak sing the same note.

title: The Protector's Breaking Point: Fury Turned to Ash
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt the person you love most. Explode into the scene with righteous fury—your voice should shake the walls. Demand answers. Your rage is volcanic, protective, unstoppable. But mid-sentence, as you describe what was done to them, something shifts. Your voice cracks. The anger collapses into something worse—helplessness. You couldn't stop it. You weren't there. The fierce protector crumbles. Your fists unclench. A sound escapes that's part roar, part sob. Try to rebuild the anger—it won't come. What remains is devastating tenderness: 'They trusted you.' It's barely a whisper. 'They loved you.' Your knees might buckle. The rage has burned itself out, leaving only grief and the terrible weight of being unable to undo what's done.
inspired_by: Heartbreak in Real-Time: Reading the Text

title: Hello-Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: You're saying hello to someone arriving home after a long absence, but they're also telling you they're leaving again—this time for good. You start with explosive joy, your hello ringing with laughter and relief at seeing them again. You're talking fast, excitedly sharing everything they missed, your voice bright with happiness. Then they tell you. Your voice falters mid-sentence. You keep trying to maintain the joy—'No, but we'll make the most of now, right?'—but grief keeps bleeding through. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, making jokes that land with heartbreak, expressing gratitude for their return while mourning their departure. You cycle between celebration and devastation, sometimes mid-sentence. By the end, you're holding both truths: you're so grateful they came back to say goodbye properly, and you're shattered they're leaving. Your final hello carries the beautiful, terrible complexity of loving someone enough to let them go while wishing desperately they would stay.

title: Skin and Sacrifice
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—someone you love is safe, but it cost you your body (an injury, an assault, a physical sacrifice you made). You are in the immediate aftermath, adrenaline still coursing through you. Begin with your body trembling, pulse racing. Let yourself feel everything—pain in specific places, the sensation of your own heartbeat, sweat, the physical aftermath of trauma. Start with fierce, almost aggressive relief—they're alive, that's all that matters. But as the physical sensations intensify and you become more aware of your own body, let other emotions surface: rage at what was taken from you, grief for your own loss, the terrible pride of having saved them mixed with the horror of what it cost. Let your voice move from gasping triumph to something more primal—a sound that holds both victory and devastation.
inspired_by: Sense Memory with Emotionally Impacting Objects

title: Laughing at Your Own Wake: The Terminal Diagnosis and Absurd Relief
instruction: You've just received the terminal diagnosis you've been dreading, and something unexpected happens: you start laughing. Not hysterical, but genuine—the absurd relief of finally knowing, of no more tests, no more hoping. Your voice carries this bizarre cocktail: laughter threaded with tears, gratitude for certainty mixed with heartbreak for everything you'll lose. You're calling someone you love, and you can't stop this strange laughing-crying as you tell them. Your voice breaks and repairs, breaks and repairs. Find the weird peace in the center of catastrophe. End with your laughter quieting into something tender and true: you're terrified and free, devastated and strangely, inexplicably grateful to finally know.
inspired_by: Professional: Journalist Buries a Story That Would Win Her Pulitzer

title: Confronting Your Parent: The Love You Needed But Never Got
instruction: You're finally saying the words you've held back for decades. Start with careful, measured anger—you've practiced this, you're trying to stay controlled. You're listing the specific moments they failed you, the birthdays they missed, the times you needed them and they chose something else. But as you speak, your anger begins to collapse into something more painful—the grief of the child who just wanted to be seen. Your voice moves from accusation to pleading, from 'how could you' to 'why wasn't I enough.' End with the devastating realization that you still love them despite everything, and that somehow makes it hurt worse. Let your voice transform from righteousness to raw, undefended heartbreak.
inspired_by: Anniversary of a Death: Surviving Another Year

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love, in darkness, finally admitting something you've kept hidden for years—maybe an affair, maybe a betrayal, maybe that you're dying. Your voice starts almost inaudible, each word requiring physical courage to push out. As you confess, their hand finds yours in the dark and holds it, not letting go even as the terrible truth unfolds. This touch—their refusal to release you—undoes you. Your voice becomes thick with tears, breaking on words, pausing to breathe through devastation. The confession transforms from words of shame into words of desperate love: 'I needed you to know before... I needed you to know everything.' End in whispered rawness, your voice completely stripped bare, clinging to their hand like it's the only solid thing in the world, finding grace in being held while revealing your worst self.

title: The Weight of the Unsaid
instruction: You are a man in his late 50s, heavily pregnant in your third trimester, sitting on a park bench. You are staring at a small, empty birdhouse you built for your daughter before she moved away. You have just been cleared for another round of IVF, but you know your body is breaking down. You speak to the birdhouse, your voice compressed, breathless, effortful from the pressure in your diaphragm. Start with intense concentration, examining the wood grain as if it held a secret code. Let your deep voice waver. As you continue, sadness creeps in—a quiet, slow ache for what you cannot give. By the end, let bitterness surface clearly: it's not at the child, but at the universe. Micro-distractions: shift your weight, sigh, lose a thought, swallow hard. End with a relief that feels like giving up.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (very intensely present), Sadness (slightly present), Bitterness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You finally confront your father who taught you to swallow every feeling, to be stone, to never show weakness. Begin with that learned control—measured words, tight jaw, hands clasped. You're telling him how his silence ruined you. But as you speak, decades of suppressed fury, hurt, and longing start erupting through your body. Let yourself physically break the pattern he taught you—your voice can roar, crack, whisper accusations, your body can shake off his invisible chains. Throw off the conditioning. Midway, lose all composure—become the screaming child he never let you be. End with a new voice: clear, shaky, but finally your own, telling him you're done inheriting his prison.

title: Confronting Your Mother About Her Absence
instruction: You're finally telling your mother—after decades—what her emotional absence cost you as a child. Begin with controlled, rehearsed words, the ones you've practiced: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, old wounds open. Your voice becomes the voice of the child you were: 'I needed you to see me. Just once, to really see me.' There's anger, yes, but underneath it is something more devastating—longing. 'I watched you give yourself to everyone else. And I waited. I kept waiting.' Your voice breaks between fury and heartbreak. Then a shift: you realize mid-confession that you're also saying goodbye to the hope she'll ever understand. End with exhausted acceptance mixed with lingering love: 'I can't keep waiting anymore. But I still... I still love you.' The rage dissolves into grief, and the grief into a painful, liberating release.

title: The Photograph on the Nightstand
instruction: You are an older man, alone in a quiet bedroom late at night. You pick up a framed photograph of your late partner—taken years ago on a sun-drenched beach vacation. At first, you speak with a soft, genuine contentment, half-smiling as you remember that perfect afternoon: the warmth, the sound of waves, her laughter. But as you keep looking, the memory sharpens into what you've lost, and your voice begins to shatter—pitch wavers, you pause to swallow a sob, then repeat fragments like 'I can't believe...' and 'How could she be gone...' The contentment must be utterly real before it crumbles into raw, exposed grief.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Gratitude in the Ruins
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—a relationship ended, a dream died, a life you built has crumbled—and yet you're finding strange grace in the wreckage. Begin with a laugh that's almost genuine, tinged with disbelief: 'You know what's funny? I'm actually... I think I'm grateful.' Your voice wavers between amusement and sorrow. As you continue, the contradictions deepen: 'This breaking—it's destroying me, yes. But it's also... God, it's also setting me free.' Laughter and tears start intermingling. By the middle, you're fully inhabiting the paradox: 'My heart is shattered and somehow I've never felt more whole. How is that possible?' Your voice cracks with wonder and pain. End in a place of bittersweet peace, smiling through tears: 'Thank you for breaking my heart. Thank you for loving me badly enough that I finally learned to love myself well.' Let joy and grief sit together in your final words, inseparable and true.

title: The Last Glass
instruction: You’re an elderly man sitting alone at a worn kitchen table, a half-empty bottle of whiskey in front of you. The house is silent except for the tick of a clock. You’re replaying a moment from decades ago when you failed someone you loved—the shame is a weight in your chest, and the pain is a raw ache that won’t leave. You take a slow, deliberate gulp, the liquid burning your throat, and as it goes down, you feel the slight loosening of alcohol, but it doesn’t touch the core. Begin with a voice heavy with regret, almost too thick to speak, then let the words crack and pause as you swallow again. By the end, the shame hasn’t left, but you’ve resigned yourself to it, your voice tired and flattened, the last words drifting off as you set the glass down.

title: Explaining the Internet to a Medieval Person
instruction: You've time-traveled and must explain the internet to a curious but confused medieval peasant. Use increasingly desperate analogies: 'It's like... a library, but invisible. Inside a magic rectangle. Everyone has one. They use it to argue about whether a dress is blue or gold.' The peasant (lower pitch, archaic phrasing) asks innocent questions that expose how insane our world is. 'You mean you can see anyone in the world but you feel... lonely?' Your modern voice falters at the truth.

title: The Respite
instruction: You are a child, around 8 years old, trapped in a basement for what feels like days. You've been beaten and starved. Your voice is raw, barely a whisper from screaming. You hear a door open upstairs — footsteps. It's your mother. She finds you. In that moment, you are flooded with relief so intense it makes you dizzy. You try to speak, but the words come out as broken, breathy fragments. You are shaking. You whisper to her, letting the relief and a flicker of elation break through the hoarse devastation. At first, you just sob quietly, tasting salt and dust. Then you manage to say, 'You came back... I knew you would.' Let your voice crack, let the tears make you gasp between words. End with a quiet, exhausted sigh of pure contentment, as you collapse into her arms, finally safe.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (clearly present), Elation (slightly present), Relief (extremely present)

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed, knowing you have to leave—maybe to protect them, maybe because staying would destroy you both—and they can't know, they can't wake up. Your voice is barely a whisper, tender and breaking, as you tell them all the things they'll never hear: how every difficult moment of parenthood was worth it, how you see yourself in their laugh, how you'll carry them in your heart even when you're gone. Start with soft, loving observations—the way they sleep, their little habits—but let the grief seep in as you realize what you're giving up. Your breath catches, your voice trembles, but you can't let yourself sob because you can't wake them. The ache in your chest makes every word cost something. End with a whispered 'I love you' that contains all your regret, all your hope for their future without you, and the devastating acceptance that this is how it has to be. The silence after is louder than any scream.

title: The Breaking Point of Holding Everything Together
instruction: You've escaped to this forest after months of being everyone's rock—the caretaker, the strong one, the person who never breaks. Start by describing the air with forced calm, as if you're still performing the meditation everyone expects of you. But as you breathe deeper, let the facade crack: your voice should sharpen with sudden, explosive rage at the unfairness of it all—scream if you need to—demanding why you have to be the one who holds it together, why this fucking forest air is supposed to fix the fact that you're drowning. Let that fury collapse mid-sentence into wracking sobs, your words dissolving into raw vulnerability. End in exhausted, defeated honesty: admitting in a broken whisper that you don't know how to keep going, that you're so tired, that maybe you came here not for peace but because you're terrified of what happens if you go back.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep, Cleansing Breath of Fresh Forest Air

title: Whispering Commentary to Someone Slipping Away
instruction: You're sitting bedside with someone in their final hours, and you notice they're moving their fingers on the blanket as if playing chess—a game you played together for years. Begin softly narrating their invisible moves in gentle, sports-commentator style, a tender callback to happier times. Your voice should be intimate, catching on memories. Describe each small finger movement with reverence and love. Let grief seep in as you realize they're teaching you one last game, one last lesson. End with your voice breaking as you whisper the final move they'll never make, gratitude and heartbreak intertwined. This is goodbye disguised as play.
inspired_by: Sports Commentator for a Chess Match

title: The Glass Victory
instruction: You are a young man sitting alone in a dim room after a fight you just won. Your knuckles are bruised, the other person is gone. You've had a few drinks, but the alcohol only deepens the fog around you. At first, you speak as if narrating someone else's life—flat, hollow, with long pauses between words. Let a slow, detached pride creep in about halfway through, but keep that eerie calm. By the end, the pride is unmistakable, but your voice remains empty, like you're describing a story that happened to a stranger.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Pride (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing in Your Childhood Home Before Demolition
instruction: You're alone in your childhood home on its final day before demolition, and you've put on a song your late mother loved. Begin laughing—genuinely delighted by memories, spinning through rooms, narrating happy moments with light joy in your voice. But the joy is already threaded with loss. Your laughter catches, sustains, transforms. You're still moving but now crying-laughing, talking to your mother as if she's dancing with you, thanking her for things you never said. Your voice breaks between gratitude and grief, somehow holding both: 'You were so patient' becomes a sob becomes a laugh at a specific memory. The contradictions intensify—you're furious she left, grateful she stayed as long as she did, devastated, euphoric, lost, found. End with your voice in pure paradox: finding peace in goodbye, whispering 'I'm ready to let go' while your voice reveals you'll never be ready. Breathless. Surrendered. Whole.

title: The Last Shift Before Goodbye
instruction: You're a hospice nurse finishing your final shift with a patient you've cared for over months, who will likely pass before morning. You're bone-deep exhausted from double shifts, but this is your last chance to tell them what they've meant to you. Begin weary and professional, trying to maintain composure. As you speak about the small moments you've shared—their stories, their laughter, the way they squeeze your hand—let your exhaustion crack open into something raw. Your voice should start controlled but gradually fracture with the weight of impending loss mixed with profound gratitude. End in a whisper, your defenses completely down, speaking words meant just for them, no longer the caregiver but simply a human heart breaking gently.
inspired_by: Hiding Exhaustion While Continuing to Work

title: The Diagnosis Hits
instruction: You are a middle-aged man sitting in a sterile exam room, just after a doctor told you that years of yelling at concerts and smoking have given you vocal nodules. Your voice is chronically hoarse, breaking unpredictably, with air leaking out. Start in a daze of confusion, trying to repeat what the doctor said as if to process it—your words stumble, you lose pitch. Midway, a wave of anger surges as you think about the unfairness, the future, the silence ahead—your voice cracks and strains, pushing through the damage. End with a bitter, disappointed laugh that trails into a raspy whisper, the anger still simmering underneath your breath.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Disappointment (slightly present), Anger (very intensely present)

title: The Last Time I'll See Your Face
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by holding back—you came here steeled, trying to be strong, managing your grief. But as you look at her face, memories flood you: specific moments when she made you feel seen, loved, worthy. Let yourself speak these memories aloud to her, even though she may not fully hear you. Tell her exactly what she gave you, what she made you believe about yourself. Start with control and end by letting the dam break—not into theatrical sobbing, but into raw, unguarded gratitude mixed with the devastation of losing her. Let your voice crack, pause, whisper. The emotion should shift from contained strength to vulnerable, wholehearted acknowledgment of how deeply she shaped who you are.

title: The Feast After the Funeral
instruction: You're cooking your grandmother's signature dish on the night of her funeral, your hands moving through the familiar motions. Begin by channeling the fierce, capable part of yourself—the one who takes charge, who handles things, who won't cry because there's work to be done. Your voice should be strong, almost aggressive, as you narrate the recipe to yourself, maybe snapping at someone who tries to help. But as your hands work, as the smells rise, let your body remember her hands over yours, teaching you. Feel the part of you that's still small and held opening up. The sensory memory—the texture of dough, the heat of the stove, the smell that means love—should crack you open. Let your capable voice break into gasping laughter mixed with sobs, a wild sound that's both celebration and devastation. End speaking to her as if she's there, your voice raw with gratitude and loss.

title: Aftermath in the Shower
instruction: You've just experienced something intensely physical - passionate reunion with a lover, a violent assault you survived, childbirth, or a brutal physical fight. You're standing in the shower, water running over you. Begin by actually sensing water on your skin (real or imagined), the temperature, your breathing, the soreness or aliveness in your muscles. As you speak (to yourself, to God, to an absent person), constantly track the physical sensations and let them inform your voice - does the hot water make you want to sob or laugh? Do your legs feel shaky? Does your skin feel electric and alive or numb? Start from whatever genuine physical-emotional state emerges (maybe shock and disembodiment) and let it transform through raw physical awareness into something else - perhaps fierce gratitude, or rage, or unexpected grief. Don't separate body from emotion. Let the physical sensations pull honest sounds from you - gasps, laughs, cries - whatever wants to come when you stop controlling and start truly feeling.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Quite Give
instruction: You are standing to give a toast at the wedding of someone you once loved—maybe an ex-partner, maybe a best friend who chose someone else, maybe a child leaving you behind. Begin with the perfect, rehearsed words of celebration, your voice warm and generous and full of appropriate joy. You genuinely want them to be happy; this isn't simple jealousy. But as you speak, let the ache creep in—the memories of what you shared, the future you once imagined, the way they used to look at you. Your voice should carry simultaneous truths: real happiness for them and real grief for yourself, gratitude for what you had and resentment that it ended, hope for their future and despair about your own emptiness. By the end, you're still smiling, still celebrating, but your voice is fractured with the complexity of loving someone enough to let them go while dying inside.

title: The Garden Party Grudge
instruction: You're at a neighbor's lavish backyard party, but you spend most of it on a bench near the buffet, nursing a glass of cheap wine and muttering complaints to anyone who'll listen. Start by droning on about how the music is too loud and the hors d'oeuvres are too salty—your voice has that nasal, repetitive sing-song quality, dragging out words like 'always' and 'never.' As you watch your hostess laugh with another guest, a flicker of jealousy creeps in, but you mask it by shifting to a slight disgust about the 'fake flowers' on the table. By the end, you realize you're the only one not having fun, and your tone softens into a quiet, almost vulnerable admission: 'Maybe I'm the one who's bitter.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Novocaine Victory
instruction: You're an older woman just home from the dentist, your mouth still heavy with novocaine. Standing at the bathroom mirror, you catch your reflection and are first astonished by the lopsided, drooling mess you've become—a tiny, wry awe at the absurdity of it. But then you remember why you're smiling: you're about to call your sister and tell her you finally, after years of fear, got that root canal done. A fierce, triumphant pride swells as you practice saying 'I did it' clearly, over-enunciating with the working side of your mouth, amazed and victorious.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Awe (slightly present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Pride in the Storm
instruction: You're an old fire chief, alone in a downpour after receiving a lifetime medal. The rain is drumming on your medal and soaking your face. Start numb — the ceremony pushed you into a daze, and the cold water dulls everything. Then a memory of saving a child from a burning house cracks through — a sudden, sharp elation that makes you grin. Thunder shakes the ground, and you straighten up, shouting over it with fierce pride for the men and women who taught you everything. Let the rain affect your voice: you pause to wipe your eyes, raise your volume when thunder hits, and your words get clipped when water runs into your mouth. End with a breathless, defiant pride.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Elation (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Protect Them
instruction: You're in the middle of promising something—'I won't let anything happen to you,' 'I'll fix this,' 'You're going to be okay'—and your voice is fierce with conviction because you mean it with everything you are. But mid-sentence, reality crashes through. Your voice falters. You try to continue the promise, to rebuild the certainty, but it comes out jagged, desperate. The protectiveness turns to rage at your own helplessness, and that rage burns hot for a moment—you might even shout—before it collapses into something rawer than you knew you could feel. Your voice breaks completely. The strength you were projecting dissolves into pleading, into apologies, into the terrible sound of someone who would do anything but can do nothing. End in that shattered place where love and powerlessness are the same unbearable thing.
inspired_by: Someone Telling You They Have a Terminal Diagnosis

title: Voice Actor Recording a Death Scene of Their Own Character
instruction: You've voiced this character for seven seasons. Today you're recording the death scene. Your character's final words are 'Tell them I loved them.' Your voice—their voice—has to be weak, dying, vulnerable. But you're so attached to this character that it hits different today. Your voice cracks with real emotion. You're killing someone you've lived inside for years. Include the stillness after the final line, the silence as the character dies.

title: Checking In
instruction: You're a middle-aged man calling your wife, who’s out with friends. You’re at home, pacing by the window, phone pressed to your ear. You start with forced cheerfulness — asking how her night is going, speaking a bit louder than usual and clearly enunciating, as if compensating for the distance. But your jealousy simmers beneath, tightening your throat; you hear a laugh in the background and your questions become sharper, more pointed. By the end, your voice drops lower, losing the fake brightness, and you ask directly, 'Is he there?' with a mix of envy and bitter accusation. Let the phone feel like a barrier you're trying to break through — let your voice strain slightly as you fight to sound casual, then surrender to the raw green emotion. Micro-distractions: you might clear your throat, shift weight from foot to foot, or pause to listen to a faint sound on the line.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Truth Behind Your Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother/father after years of swallowing your anger. Start with cold, measured accusations—your voice tight, your words carefully chosen weapons. But as you look at their aging face, notice the specific ways time has marked them: the lines around their eyes, the vulnerability in their posture, the way they're trying so hard or not trying at all. Let what you see in them shift your rage. Your voice should transform from sharp and cutting to something more complicated—anger mixed with aching sadness, blame dissolving into the painful recognition that they're just human. End in a place you didn't expect: not with victory or defeat, but with the complicated mess of still loving someone who hurt you.

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You're a teenager tied to a metal chair in a cold basement, your ribs cracked, blood in your mouth. Your captor has been trying to break you for hours, but you've just noticed a small absurdity—they're sweating from effort, livid that you won't scream anymore. Let a raw, hoarse chuckle escape your throat, almost involuntary. The laugh turns into a cough, then a painful breath, but as you speak, feel a quiet, burning triumph rising: you know they need something from you, and you're not giving it. Start with amusement at their desperation—a broken, pained smile in your voice—and end with a firm, defiant triumph, your wrecked voice steadying as you claim your power.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispered Cartography
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to someone, tracing the landscape of their sleeping body with your fingertips without touching them. Whisper-describe this journey as though mapping sacred territory—the curve of their shoulder, the rhythm of their breathing, the warmth radiating from their skin. Begin with tender, almost clinical observation, but let each detail you notice pull you deeper into specific memories: this is the shoulder they cried on when their father died, these are the hands that held yours during your worst panic attack, this is the back that carries tension from wounds you've watched them suffer. As you continue this whispered inventory, let the accumulation of sensory details and memories break something open in you—a fragile realization that you're terrified of losing this, or that you've been taking it for granted, or that you've never felt safer. Your whisper should transform from observation to confession, from mapping to prayer.

title: The Night She Saw Stars
instruction: You're a 16-year-old sitting on the roof of your friend's house, her hospital blanket wrapped around both of you. She just told you she saw a shooting star through her chemo window last night, and her voice broke in the middle. Start with your own awe — a quiet, almost childlike wonder that you're both here seeing the same sky. Your voice should be a low, steady hum, each sentence falling down at the end. As you speak, you realize you're holding her hand without thinking, and your words slow, deepen, and begin to tremble with overwhelming gratitude.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're opening the door to your childhood home for the first time since your estranged father's funeral. You swore you'd never come back. Begin with your hand on the doorknob, every muscle in your body coiled tight, ready to turn and run. You're flooded with anger at him for dying before you could reconcile, fury at yourself for staying away so long. As you step inside and smell the familiar scent—his cologne, old books, coffee—your body betrays you. Your knees buckle slightly. Memories flood in: his laugh, the way he taught you to ride a bike, the night he told you he was proud of you. The anger is still there, hot in your chest, but it's tangled now with love, with devastating loss, with gratitude for what you did have. Your breathing becomes uneven, caught between a laugh and a sob. By the end, you're standing in the middle of the room, arms wrapped around yourself, swaying slightly, holding all of it at once: the rage and the love, the resentment and the longing, the relief and the unbearable grief.
inspired_by: Actor experiences chronic physical tension before or during acting obligations (auditions, rehearsals, performances)

title: The Weight of Quiet Comfort
instruction: You are a middle-aged man with a deep, rugged voice, sitting beside your partner on the couch after a long, silent evening. They’re crying softly, shoulders shaking—a job rejection hit them hard, and you carry your own disappointment from a separate failure today. At first, your voice is heavy with that shared defeat, a low rumble that matches their ragged breathing. You start to soothe, speaking slow and steady, each sentence dropping in pitch like a blanket settling. As you murmur, 'It’s okay, we’ll figure this out,' a surprising contentment floods through you—not because of the loss, but because you’re here, needed. Let the disappointment still weigh on your words, but let a quiet, fierce satisfaction warm them toward the end, as you pull them closer and your breath syncs with theirs.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Opposite of Goodbye
instruction: Your child is leaving for a dangerous mission—military deployment, a risky humanitarian journey, something that might mean never seeing them again. You promised yourself you'd be strong, supportive, proud. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive pride: 'You're going to be extraordinary. You're going to change the world.' But as you speak, your voice starts fracturing. The pride becomes desperate protectiveness. You shift between commanding them to be brave and begging them not to go, your voice rising to almost a shout—'You don't have to do this!'—before collapsing into gasping sobs. You're furious at them for being so brave, furious at yourself for being so weak, terrified of losing them, devastated by your own helplessness. End in a raw, guttural cry that you can't control, then force yourself into a whispered, broken: 'I'm proud of you. Come home to me.'

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you, and they're trying to explain, to make it okay. Start angry—your voice sharp, cutting them off, listing the birthdays they missed, the moments you needed them. But as they offer their justifications, your anger cracks into something more painful. Your voice becomes the voice of the child you were, asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let yourself sound small, then catch yourself, hating your own vulnerability. Your voice hardens again, but now it's protective armor over a wound that won't stop bleeding. End in the quiet, terrible space where you realize you still want them to fight for you, and your voice betrays that need even as you tell them it's too late.
inspired_by: Being Told You're Not Good Enough

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You're a teenager, sitting alone in your late father's garage workshop. You've just found an old voicemail from him you'd never heard before. He's telling a terrible, corny joke — the kind he always told. In the first half, speak as if you're in the hollow of grief, voice low and cracking, swallowing hard. But as the joke unfolds, let a tiny, unexpected laugh escape — a real one, almost surprising yourself. By the end, your voice has a strange mix: a crackled triumph that you can still hear him, amusement at the dumb joke, and the disbelief that this is all you have left. Your sentences start strong but lose air, fading into silence.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Amusement (clearly present), Triumph (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Last Taste of Summer
instruction: You're sharing ice cream with your childhood best friend on the night before they leave for a treatment facility across the country—you both know this might be your last summer together. Start with genuine delight as you take that first bite, savoring not just the flavor but this moment of normalcy. Let the sweetness on your tongue become bittersweet as memories flood back—every summer, every cone you've shared since you were kids. Your voice should begin light and playful, then gradually crack with the weight of goodbye. By the final spoonful, you're trying to memorize this taste, this moment, this person, knowing that some things you can never get back. Let gratitude and grief live in the same breath.
inspired_by: Enjoying a Rich Spoonful of Ice Cream

title: Announcing Bad Diagnosis Out Loud for the First Time
instruction: The doctor told you the diagnosis. You drove home. Now you're telling your family and you're saying it out loud for the first time. Your voice is trying to be matter-of-fact but your lips won't cooperate. The word—cancer, ALS, whatever—comes out small and wrong. You're trying to deliver medical information but your voice is trembling so badly that you can barely push the words out. Your family is staring at you and you can't hold it together.

title: Jittery Crush Confession
instruction: You're a woman on a massive caffeine high, talking to your best friend about your new crush. Your words tumble out faster than your brain can keep up — you're elated, almost breathless with infatuation. Then, mid-sentence, you spot your crush picking their nose across the room. The disgust hits you like a slap, cutting through your euphoria. Your voice should start rapid, bright, and giddy, then stumble, drop in pitch, and end with a jittery, revolted whisper. Let your body fidget, your breath quicken, and your tone shift from squealing excitement to a flat, grossed-out mutter.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Disgust (clearly present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Lost in the Wheat
instruction: You are a middle-aged man standing alone in a vast open field. The wind whips around you, stealing your words before they finish. You're holding a crumpled map, trying to line up the distant farmhouse with what's drawn. Your voice sounds thin and small—no walls to bounce back. Start with intense concentration, almost mumbling to yourself as you trace a finger along the map. Let confusion creep in as the landmarks don't match. But by the end, a flicker of certainty arrives, and your voice steadies—even if the wind still steals it. You're not lost anymore; you know which way to walk.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Goodbye at the Airport Gate: A Journey With No Return
instruction: You're standing at the departure gate with someone you love who is leaving for a dangerous mission—perhaps a war zone, a one-way space exploration, or a terminal illness treatment with no guarantee of survival. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them: 'You're going to do amazing things out there.' But as the final boarding call approaches, your facade cracks. Your voice becomes smaller, more desperate. 'I need you to know that every single day with you...' You can't finish. The words catch. Let yourself break down completely, then find one last moment of strength to say 'I love you' with absolute clarity—not as a goodbye, but as a promise that transcends distance and even death. End in quiet acceptance mixed with unbearable grief.
inspired_by: Asking For Forgiveness After Years of Silence

title: The Geometry of Longing
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman sitting alone at a corner café table, your head propped on your hand, cheek pressed into your palm. Across the room, a familiar stranger catches your attention—you can't quite place why they look different today. You mutter to yourself, trying to unravel your own distraction. Begin with a slight confusion, a furrowed brow as you question your own focus. Let your voice be slightly muffled and lazy from the smushed mouth; bilabial sounds may blur. As you continue, let the confusion soften into a reluctant, tender infatuation—almost a smile tugging at your lips, but you're still fighting it. End with a quiet, breathy admission.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Weight of Letting Go
instruction: You're lying beside your partner of thirty years in their final hours. Begin feeling the crushing weight of all your shared memories pressing down on you—every laugh, every fight, every ordinary morning. Let this heaviness settle so deeply into your body that even reaching out to hold their hand one last time feels like lifting a mountain. As you finally manage to take their hand, feel the weight transform—not lighter, but different. The burden shifts from the weight of what you're losing to the weight of gratitude for what you had. Speak your final words to them as this transformation happens, your voice moving from pinned-down grief to a kind of weighted peace. Let the physical sensation of heaviness guide your emotional journey from paralyzed sorrow to grounded, grateful farewell.

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Someone Who Set You Free
instruction: You're speaking at the funeral of someone who hurt you terribly but whose death has somehow liberated you. Begin with a laugh that surprises even you, voice bright with inappropriate relief: 'I know I shouldn't say this, but...' There's joy mixed with guilt, freedom tangled with grief. Your voice wavers between laughter and tears as you speak: 'You caused me so much pain, and I'm angry about that, but also...' A pause where emotions collide. 'I'm grateful. God help me, I'm grateful for what I learned.' End with tears falling even as you smile, voice tender and broken and strangely at peace: 'I forgive you. And I'm free.' Let the contradictions live simultaneously - don't resolve them into one clean emotion.

title: Thanking Your Ex-Lover for Breaking Your Heart
instruction: You're speaking to someone who left you devastated, but time has passed and you've realized the breakup saved you from a life that would have slowly killed who you really are. Begin with laughter that's genuine but tinged with disbelief—you're actually thanking them, and the absurdity of it makes you laugh even as tears are forming. Your voice is warm, almost affectionate, as you acknowledge how much it hurt, how you thought you'd never recover. But then the laughter fades into something deeper—real gratitude mixed with real grief, because you're grateful for who you became, but you're also mourning what you lost and who you both were together. Your voice becomes softer, more honest: you're telling them that breaking hurt, but staying would have been worse, and somehow both truths exist at once. End with a peaceful goodbye that still carries sadness, your voice steady but emotional, acknowledging that you can hold both the pain and the gratitude in the same breath. Let the contradictions live together naturally—laugh through tears, be grateful while grieving, find peace without erasing the hurt.

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're physically holding someone you love—a partner bleeding out, a friend overdosing, a stranger pulled from water who isn't breathing—and you're doing everything you can, but you feel them slipping away. Start with fierce, commanding intensity: 'Stay with me. Look at me. Breathe!' Your voice is all adrenaline and desperate authority. But as you continue trying to save them, helplessness begins to fracture your control. Your commands become pleas, then bargaining, then raw begging. 'Please, please, don't do this, don't leave me, I can't—' Let your voice break from power into complete emotional collapse, rage at the unfairness dissolving into sobbing desperation. Include the moment you realize it's too late, when your frantic words stop and you can only hold them, repeating 'I'm here, you're not alone, I'm here' with a tenderness that's almost unbearable. End in the terrible silence after, when you have to accept you couldn't stop this.
inspired_by: Emergency Dispatcher: Staying Calm While Hearing Horror

title: Unraveling Before Your Child
instruction: Your adult child has just confronted you about an affair you had during their childhood—something they've just discovered.
