You finally collapse onto a bench in a sliver of shade, fumbling with a water bottle. Start by muttering, lost and dizzy, your words slow and slurred. Then as you drink, feel the cool water revive you—let relief seep into your voice, softening it, making it steadier. End with a sigh that carries gratitude and a fragile peace.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Reading Your Deceased Partner's Last Letter—The One That Says They Knew
instruction: You've found a letter in their handwriting, dated the week before they died. They knew. They knew and didn't tell you. Start reading aloud, your voice steady, curious—'My love, if you're reading this...' Then the words hit you: they catalogued everything they'd miss about you, everything they loved, the future you'd planned together. You laugh through sudden tears at an inside joke they included. Your voice breaks with gratitude that they thought to write this, and shatters with grief that they had to. You're angry they kept this secret, relieved they spared you the countdown, devastated all over again. Read their words about how you'll survive this, how you'll love again—your voice rebels against it even as you're grateful for their blessing. By the end, you're crying and laughing simultaneously, your voice full of impossible contradictions: 'You beautiful, terrible fool. Thank you. I hate you. I miss you. Thank you.' Let the page fall from your hands, your voice landing on whispered peace amid the wreckage: 'Okay. Okay, I'll try.'
inspired_by: Flight Attendant: Announcing Safe Landing After Turbulence

title: The Last Breath Before Silence
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love who has only minutes left to live. Begin by holding back everything you feel—your throat is tight, your chest constricted, your shoulders rigid with the effort of staying composed. As you speak your final words to them, track every place in your body where you're gripping, clenching, armoring yourself against the unbearable reality. Name these sensations aloud as part of your goodbye: 'My throat is closing,' 'My hands won't stop shaking,' 'There's a fist in my chest.' Let each acknowledgment gradually unlock what you've been holding back. By the end, the dam breaks—all the love, terror, gratitude, and devastation you've been restraining floods out in a raw, undefended final goodbye. Move from paralyzed control to complete emotional release.

title: Last Bite of Pride
instruction: You're a teenage boy at a party, forced by a so-called friend to swallow a spoonful of something vile as a 'dare'. You're bent over, hands on knees, trying not to vomit. Start by muttering contempt — hatred for the friend who put you in this position, disgust at yourself for agreeing. The words come out thick and broken, punctuated by heaves. Then the gagging wins: you retch, spit, and finally throw up. As the nausea passes, your voice clears into a shaky, raw relief. End with a breathy, almost grateful laugh — the contempt is gone, replaced by the sheer bliss of emptiness.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Rehearsal
instruction: Your sister is leaving tomorrow for a one-way mission to Mars—she'll never return to Earth. You're in her apartment, surrounded by her things she's giving away. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to make small talk about her plants, her books. But then you see her guitar—the one you both learned on as kids. Your voice fractures as you remember teaching her that first chord progression. The protective older sibling mask crumbles completely. You're angry at her for leaving, devastated that you're losing her, but also fiercely proud. End by whispering that you'll play her favorite song every year on her birthday, your voice raw with the weight of a lifetime of missing her that hasn't even started yet.

title: Whispered Goodbye in the Hospital Corridor
instruction: You're visiting your old mentor teacher who is dying of cancer, barely conscious. Sit close and speak in barely-audible whispers—this is just for them, not for the nurses outside. Start by telling them small, tender things: you got the job, you used their lesson plan, a student called you their favorite teacher. Let your voice catch on that word 'favorite' because it was always theirs. Confess in fragments, voice breaking between words: you never said thank you, you never told them they saved your life that year your marriage ended, you never admitted you almost quit teaching until they showed you why it mattered. When they squeeze your hand weakly, let yourself come undone—cry while whispering that you don't know how to do this without them. End with the most tender devastation: thanking them for seeing something in you that you still can't see in yourself.

title: Finding the Goodbye Letter After They Survived
instruction: You're reading aloud the suicide note your loved one wrote before their attempt—but they survived, and now you're reading it to them in their hospital room as they recover. Begin with a voice that tries to stay steady, even gentle, reading their words of hopelessness and goodbye. But you must punctuate their darkest lines with your own responses—sometimes laughing through tears at an inside joke they referenced, sometimes your voice breaking with grief at what they were feeling, sometimes angry that they were going to leave you. Your emotions should be a beautiful chaos: gratitude that they're alive warring with devastation at how close you came to losing them, love mixed with hurt that they didn't reach out. Include moments where you have to stop reading to compose yourself, where you reach out to touch them, where you shift between their words and yours. End with fierce, tearful insistence that you need them here, that the world needs them, your voice raw with the kind of love that refuses to let go.

title: The Last Step
instruction: You're an 80-year-old woman on a charity hike you insisted on doing, three hours in, mile 19. Your legs suddenly give out; you crumple onto a bench. You're trying to keep your voice bright and capable—that hyper-feminized, 'I'm fine, dear' tone—but you can barely inhale. The trail stretches upward; you realize you cannot finish. Let the helplessness crack through your sweet, steady cadence. Speak to a younger friend who's checking on you: at first, you dismiss her concern with practiced cheer, then you admit you're stuck. End with a hollow, confused whisper—not dramatic, just a momentary surrender to gravity. Your breath catches mid-sentence; the last word is barely audible.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Downpour Declaration
instruction: You are a young woman trapped in a sudden, brutal thunderstorm. You’re soaked, shivering, and rain is streaming into your mouth so you sputter between words. You’re shouting to be heard over the roar, but each time thunder cracks you flinch. At first, you’re pure pride—you wanted to prove something by standing here, not seeking shelter. But then, beneath that, a flicker of raw sexual lust awakens, blurring your pride into something more urgent and vulnerable. Let the rain physically break up your speech: swallow water, cough, shake your head. Start with defiant, almost taunting pride, and end with your voice dropping, breathless, revealing the lust you were hiding.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Photograph
instruction: You're alone, holding a photograph of someone you loved who died, speaking to them in the quiet of 3am. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and fractured. 'I kept your coffee mug. I can't...' You trail off. Share the small, sacred things: how their scent has faded from the pillow, how you still set two plates out sometimes, how you heard their laugh in a stranger's voice today and it destroyed you. Let your voice crack on the ordinary details — 'You'd hate what I did to the garden' — because that's where grief lives. The tears come silent, catching in your throat so words break apart: 'I don't know how to... without you here.' End in the terrible intimacy of speaking to silence, your voice raw with the kind of love that has nowhere to go, finding something like gratitude beneath the unbearable ache: 'Thank you for... everything. God, I miss you.'

title: The Last Dance
instruction: You're an older man at a dimly lit lounge, nursing a whiskey. You've spotted someone who reminds you of the one who got away—except this time you're in control. Start with a smooth, measured greeting, every word chosen for effect, your voice low and warm. But as you speak, the bitterness you've nursed for years seeps in like a cold draft. Let your charm crack—a pause where you lose your train of thought, a laugh that's a beat too short, a compliment that turns into a quiet accusation. End with a tone that's more resigned than seductive, the mask slipping just enough to show the wound underneath.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Love's Belongings After They've Gone
instruction: You're alone in your home, holding their favorite sweater that still smells like them. Start by speaking to the empty room as if they can hear you, voice soft and intimate like you're sharing a secret: 'Remember when you wore this that night we...' Let the memories pour out in fragments—half-finished sentences, small laughs that catch in your throat, tender observations about their habits. Your voice should be barely above a whisper throughout, but let it fracture and repair itself multiple times. Touch the fabric like it's precious skin. End with your face buried in the sweater, voice muffled and breaking: 'I wasn't ready. I'm still not ready.' The emotional arc moves from bittersweet nostalgia through tender grief to the crushing realization that they're truly gone.
inspired_by: Screaming Into Your Pillow So No One Hears

title: Astronaut's Final Transmission to Earth Before Signal Loss
instruction: You're the last surviving crew member of a deep space mission, drifting beyond救signal range. You have three minutes to record a message to your child on Earth—knowing they'll receive it years from now, when you're already gone. Start with controlled professionalism, reporting the mission failure. Then your voice cracks as you realize this is goodbye. Shift between trying to be the strong parent they'll remember and the terrified human who's about to die alone in the dark. Your breathing becomes shallow. End with a whisper of their name, and one thing you wish you'd said when you had the chance. The silence at the end is you accepting the void.
inspired_by: Historical: Berlin Wall Communicant Realizes the Guard Is Their Sister

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your parent in the family kitchen about a painful truth you've carried for years—their alcoholism, their absence during your childhood, their cruel words that shaped your self-hatred. Before you speak, you see them exactly as they are: notice how they hold their coffee cup, the way their shoulders curve inward, the small defensive gesture of adjusting their collar. You recognize these tiny movements because you've been watching people self-protect your whole life. Start with cold, clinical observation—describe their behaviors back to them as if you're a documentary narrator, your voice flat and factual. As you speak, let your clinical distance crack. The more precisely you name what you see—'You're doing that thing where you look past my left shoulder,' 'Your hand is trembling'—the more your controlled fury dissolves into the abandoned child's grief. End sobbing, all objectivity shattered.

title: The Reckoning: Fierce Love Colliding with Absolute Helplessness
instruction: Someone you love is destroying themselves—addiction, abuse, a dangerous relationship—and you've tried everything. You begin with explosive frustration, your voice loud and jagged. You're yelling because if you yell loud enough, maybe they'll finally hear you. You list every warning ignored, every lie, every time you pulled them back from the edge. Your rage is fierce, protective, desperate. But mid-sentence, your voice breaks completely. The anger collapses into sobbing fury, then into something more raw—you're terrified of losing them and you're furious that they're making you feel this helpless. By the end, your voice is hoarse, reduced to a broken plea: 'I can't save you, and I can't let you go.' You end in the wreckage between fierce devotion and the devastating acceptance that love isn't enough.
inspired_by: Molly Peak: Everything You Say Becomes Emotional Truth

title: The Tough Guy’s Hiccup
instruction: You’re a no-nonsense older man, deep-voiced and gruff, trying to deliver a short, stern warning to someone who crossed you. But your diaphragm keeps betraying you with sharp, unexpected hiccups that slice your words in half. Start annoyed and frustrated, fighting to maintain your intimidating tone while the spasms interrupt you. By the end, let the absurdity sink in—allow a natural, reluctant chuckle to escape, your voice softening as you admit defeat with a wry smile.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unanswered Hush
instruction: You are a middle-aged man in an empty chapel, kneeling. You begin reciting a prayer you've known since childhood, but your voice is mechanical, hollow — you're not sure you believe anymore. Midway, doubt overwhelms you: you pause, look at the altar, let out a frustrated laugh. Then, almost against your will, you continue, but now it's a raw, whispered confession of confusion. Your voice shifts from formal reverence to a broken, questioning plea. Let the prayer become a struggle: hesitant breaths, a slight tremor, even a swallowed sob. End with a quiet, exhausted 'Amen' that sounds more like a question than a statement.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Session Before Deployment
instruction: You're a therapist conducting your final session with a patient you've worked with for three years—tomorrow you leave for a humanitarian mission in a war zone, and you may not return. Speak as both the therapist maintaining professional boundaries ('We've made remarkable progress together') and your aching internal voice that wants to break every rule and tell them how much they've changed your life too. Begin with calm professional gratitude, but as you realize this might truly be goodbye forever, let your composure fracture. Your inner voice moves from bittersweet pride to desperate longing to say what you're not allowed to say. End with a single moment where the boundary dissolves—just one beat—where your real heart shows through.

title: This Beautiful, Terrible Thing
instruction: You're holding someone's hand as they die, and you're finding yourself laughing through tears at the absurd, perfect moments you shared. Start with a wet laugh: 'Remember when you—' and let yourself smile genuinely even as your voice shakes. Mix joy and devastation freely. Share a funny memory and let laughter turn into sobbing mid-sentence, then back again. Your voice should sound split open—grateful for every moment you had and shattered that it's ending. Say 'Thank you' like it's both the most important thing you'll ever say and completely inadequate. Let your voice embody the paradox: celebrating their life while grieving their death, finding peace in their presence while your heart is breaking. End with something like 'I'm so glad it was you' spoken through tears and laughter and a strange, aching wholeness. This should sound like someone experiencing every emotion at once and somehow holding them all.

title: The Hiccup Apology
instruction: You are in the middle of a crucial apology to someone you've deeply hurt, but a sudden, violent case of hiccups keeps cutting your words in half. Each sentence is shattered by a sharp, involuntary gasp that yanks the breath from your chest. Start with intense confusion — why now? — which quickly boils into frustrated anger as you fight to control your body. Your voice jerks, words get stuck, you try to press on but the hiccups mock you. By the end, the apology stalls into silence, and a heavy shame settles in as you realize how ridiculous and pathetic you must look. Let the hiccups dictate the rhythm: sharp, high-pitched intakes that fracture your speech. Let your tone move from strained, urgent anger to a quieter, defeated shame.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Portrait in the Dark
instruction: You are an older woman, lying in bed with your partner after a long, tender kiss. The room is silent except for your breathing and the soft, wet sounds of your lips parting. You're both still close, foreheads touching, your hand resting on their chest. You feel a surge of pride—not arrogance, but deep, quiet pride in how far you've come, in the life you've built, in choosing this love even when it was hard. Start with a whisper, voice soft and breathy from the kiss, maybe a slight laugh or a shifting of your head to press your nose against theirs. Let your words come slowly, sometimes losing a thought as you feel their warmth. End with a firmer, more steady tone—pride settled into your bones, a smile in your voice as you declare something simple but absolute.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They have been controlling and critical your entire life, and you've never felt truly seen by them. Begin in careful, measured tones—trying to be the dutiful child one last time. But as you speak, something breaks open inside you: a lifetime of rage, grief, and desperate love that you've never been allowed to express. Let your voice crack, grow fierce, become raw and animal-like in its honesty. By the end, you've said everything—the anger, the longing, the forgiveness—and you've transformed into someone finally, terrifyingly free. Let your body shake with it. Let sounds emerge that aren't quite words. Then find a moment of devastating tenderness as you realize they can finally hear you, or perhaps they're already gone.

title: The Thing You Left Behind in My Drawer
instruction: Late at night, alone, you discover an object that belonged to someone you loved and lost (through death, distance, or separation). You haven't seen this object in months or years—you forgot it was there. Begin in stillness, in the quiet shock of recognition. Pick it up with trembling hands. Let your breath change. Whisper to it, to them, to yourself. Remember the moment they last touched it. Let the smallness of the object contrast with the enormity of what it represents. Don't perform grief—let it ambush you in waves. Allow yourself moments of tender laughter at a memory, then let that laughter break into tears. Speak to them as if they could hear you. By the end, you must decide whether to put it away again or keep it out. Your voice should be barely audible at times, as if the walls themselves are listening.
inspired_by: When staging a production where a character has a deep emotional relationship with physical objects

title: The Last Conversation Before the Flight
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your closest friend who's leaving tomorrow on a one-way mission to Mars - they'll never return to Earth. Start with forced cheerfulness, making jokes about sending postcards from space, keeping your voice light and teasing. But as the reality sets in, your throat tightens. The jokes become harder to get out. Move through desperate attempts to memorize their voice, their laugh, the way they say your name. Let your voice crack when you realize this is the last time you'll ever touch them, smell their cologne, see them roll their eyes at your terrible puns. End in a place of quiet devastation - not crying loudly, but that awful moment where you can barely breathe and every word costs everything. Your final 'I love you' should sound like you're trying to pack thirty more years of friendship into three syllables.
inspired_by: Two Old Friends Meeting After 30 Years

title: Parade Ground Confusion
instruction: You are a young recruit on a military parade ground, standing at attention during a surprise inspection. Your commanding officer is pacing in front of you, barking orders that don't match the manual you studied. Start with your voice tight and forced, keeping your body stiff as you try to maintain rigid posture. Let confusion creep in—your breath hitches, you lose the rhythm of your reply, and a slight tremor enters your voice. By the end, the confusion swells into a dazed realization that you've been set up, and your words trail off with a quiet, hollow note.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Reading Your Child's Letter After They've Gone: Tenderness Breaking Your Heart
instruction: Your adult child has left for a year-long journey—backpacking alone across the world, or joining the Peace Corps, something far away. They've left you a letter to read after they're gone. You open it expecting logistics, but it's a love letter. Begin reading aloud in a steady voice, smiling at their humor: 'Dear Mom/Dad, by now you're probably reorganizing my room.' But then the letter deepens. They thank you for specific moments you'd forgotten—reading to them when they had nightmares, believing in them when they didn't believe in themselves. Your voice catches. They write about being scared to leave but needing to become who they're meant to be. You're crying now, voice barely above a whisper. The letter ends with: 'I carry you with me everywhere.' Your reading dissolves into quiet weeping mixed with proud laughter, gratitude mixed with the ache of letting go. You whisper to the empty room: 'Come home safe.'
inspired_by: Observing Lava Flow: Scientific Wonder Turning to Genuine Dread

title: The Reunion Touch
instruction: You're seeing your ex-lover for the first time in two years. You promised yourself you'd be cool, detached, over it. You shake hands - just a professional handshake. But the moment your skin touches theirs, your body remembers everything: the electricity, the fights, the way they held you when you couldn't sleep, the morning they left. Start speaking about something neutral - the weather, mutual friends, anything safe. But let your body tell the real story. Maybe your hand is trembling. Maybe heat is flooding through you - desire, rage, grief, all mixed together. Don't decide what you're feeling - let your body decide and let it take over your voice. By the end, you've either pulled them close or pushed them away, and whatever comes out of your mouth is nothing like what you planned to say. It's pure physical truth.
inspired_by: Actor feels disconnected from real feelings or is 'naturally' acting—imitating truth rather than experiencing it

title: What I Never Said in Twenty Years
instruction: Your best friend is moving away forever, and you have five minutes before their flight. You've been in love with them for two decades, and they never knew. Start barely audible, every word an effort: 'There's something I... I should have told you a long time ago.' Your throat keeps closing. The confession comes out fragmented, tender, aching: 'Every time you talked about someone else... it felt like swallowing glass.' Let silence breathe between phrases. Your voice should be so gentle it almost disappears, but underneath is an ocean of longing. End with acceptance that's both devastating and sweet: 'I just wanted you to know that someone... that I loved you that way.' The last words should catch in your throat—not dramatic, just quietly, utterly broken.

title: Singing Happy Birthday Alone in Your Apartment
instruction: It's your birthday and no one remembered. Light a single candle on a store-bought cupcake. Sing 'Happy Birthday' to yourself — start self-consciously ironic, trying to be funny about it. By the second line, the irony fails. By 'dear [your name],' the loneliness is undeniable. Blow out the candle. Make a wish. The silence after the flame goes out. Then your phone buzzes — a text from someone who remembered. The small, grateful 'oh' that follows. Sometimes it only takes one.

title: Trail of Thanks
instruction: You're a young man jogging alone on a wooded trail, your steps pounding a steady rhythm that shakes your voice. You're replaying a kind gesture from someone you're deeply grateful for—a friend who brought you soup when you were sick. As you push up a hill, your breath comes in sync with your feet, and you find yourself thinking about how attracted you are to this person, their hands, their laugh. Start with breathless, genuine gratitude—almost a whisper of thanks between gasps—then let your voice thicken with lust as you imagine their face, ending on a hopeful, slightly shy note as you picture asking them out. Your words should sound chopped by your jogging rhythm, with micro-pauses to swallow or stumble over a root. Speak about 50 words: 'I still can't believe you did that... (pant) showed up at my door with that bowl... (step-step) your hands holding it... (gasp) I keep seeing them. Maybe... maybe I'll ask you to run with me next time.'
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Sexual Lust (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Dictator's Final Broadcast
instruction: You are a once-powerful leader recording your final message as your regime crumbles around you. Begin with defiant pride, insisting history will vindicate you, your voice still commanding and certain. But as distant explosions grow closer and the reality sets in, let that certainty crack. Your voice should fracture as you move from rage at betrayal to desperate justification to a quiet, devastating realization that you destroyed everything you claimed to protect. End in whispered bewilderment, no longer a leader but a human being who cannot comprehend what they've become. The transformation must feel like watching armor fall away piece by piece until only raw vulnerability remains.

title: Bitter Medicine
instruction: You're an elderly man with a deep, weathered voice, hunched over a kitchen sink, fighting waves of nausea—maybe from chemo or a bad hangover. A close friend, who’s always been healthier and luckier, just left a voicemail bragging about their latest success, and you feel a sharp pang of envy. But as you retch and gasp, you notice your own caregiver’s hand on your back, gently rubbing—and that jealousy cracks open into a raw, desperate thankfulness. Let your voice start tight and resentful, words cut off by heaves, then slowly soften into a gravelly, tearful gratitude, each breath thick with mucus and relief. Say something like: 'He gets everything... (retch) while I'm... (gasp) here. But you... you stay. Every damn time. God, I'm grateful.'
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Certainty That Shatters Into Doubt
instruction: You burst in with absolute conviction, declaring a truth you've discovered—perhaps a betrayal, perhaps a revelation about your life's direction. Your voice is fierce, certain, powerful. 'I know what I saw. I know what this means.' You're ready for battle, armed with unwavering facts. But as you speak with such intensity, something shifts—a memory, a realization, a look in someone's eyes. Your certainty begins to tremble. The fierce declarations start to sound like questions you're asking yourself. Your voice rises in volume but loses its foundation, becoming almost desperate, trying to hold onto the conviction that's slipping away. By the end, you collapse into doubt, your voice breaking as you realize you don't know anything at all. Let rage and certainty transform into confusion, vulnerability, and the terrifying freedom of admitting you were wrong.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father after discovering a letter he wrote but never sent—a letter confessing something that changes everything you thought you knew about your family. Start with quiet, controlled anger, the kind that's been rehearsed in your head for the three days since you found it. Your words are precise, your accusations measured. But as he remains silent, just looking at you with those tired eyes, something shifts. Your anger begins to crack, revealing the devastated child underneath who just wants to know why he never trusted you with the truth. By the end, you're no longer accusing—you're begging him to finally speak, even as you realize his silence might be the only answer you'll ever get.
inspired_by: When actors pursue Method work or sustain character reality in ways that may confuse or discomfort co-workers

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent everything you've held back for decades—all the moments they missed, all the times you needed them and they chose something else. Start with controlled anger, words precise and cutting, listing specifics like evidence in a trial. But as you speak, the anger cracks open to reveal the wounded child underneath. Your voice wavers between fury and grief. You catch yourself mid-sentence, realizing you're still asking for their approval even now, and that recognition makes you angrier—at them, at yourself. By the end, you're no longer accusing—you're grieving the relationship you'll never have, voice raw and exhausted, asking one final question you know they can't answer: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The last words aren't angry. They're just... empty.

title: The File in the Desk
instruction: You're in a dark, cramped room, doubled over on a chair from chronic gut pain. You're on the phone with the person who destroyed your reputation. Start with a low, venomous malevolence — your voice is tight, breathy, with a groaning undertone as you fight the ache. As you realize you've found the evidence to ruin them back, let a strained, bitter triumph creep in — still curled, but now your words carry a quiet, gloating power. Pause to gasp through the pain, shift your weight, and let the tone darken again before the final reveal.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Disappointment
instruction: You are an elderly caretaker who has just learned that the person you trusted has been lying to you for months. You begin scolding them with a controlled, slow tempo—each word deliberate, low pitched, final drop heavy. But as you speak, the distress you've been holding back seeps through. Your voice loses its sternness; you pause to swallow, your breath catches, and your tone cracks. By the end, the discipline dissolves into a quiet, heartbroken plea for honesty. Let your body feel the weight—you might shift in your seat, look away, and then back. Speak naturally, as if the words are difficult to push out.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Archaeology of Touch
instruction: You are lying in bed with someone you love, running your fingers over their skin in the darkness. Begin by whispering about the last time you touched them this way—maybe yesterday, maybe this morning. Your voice should be tender but surface-level. Then let your touch and your words drift backward through your physical history together: last week's hurried intimacy, last month's desperate reconnection after a fight, last year's first nervous explorations. As you travel back through time, let your whispers become more fragmented, more abstract—not complete sentences but sensory memories: 'Your hand on my neck... the taste of... the weight of you... cold sheets, warm skin...' Allow yourself to reach back to the very first time you touched, when you didn't yet know what you were allowed to feel, when every nerve was terror and electricity. End in a place of overwhelming tenderness mixed with the ache of knowing how much time has passed, how many versions of yourselves have touched in this same bed. Move from casual intimacy to profound, fragile reverence.
inspired_by: Actor cannot remember early childhood memories that might be relevant to their work

title: Wearing Your Shirt One More Night
instruction: It's 3 a.m., and you're wearing the shirt your lover left behind before they walked out forever yesterday. You can't sleep. Speak in an intimate whisper, as if talking to yourself in the dark. Describe how the fabric still smells like them—their skin, their soap, that specific scent that is only theirs. Start with quiet, almost numb tenderness, tracing the collar, the sleeves, remembering how you'd steal this shirt just to feel close to them. Let your voice grow smaller, more fragile, as you realize you're clutching at ghosts. There should be moments where you can barely speak, where breath catches, where you have to pause to gather yourself. End with a confession of what you should have said, what you were too scared to admit. The shirt is both comfort and torture—let us hear that impossible contradiction.

title: The Shaking Hold
instruction: You are in a power yoga class, holding a deep lunge, your thighs on fire. Your muscles tremble violently, and each word comes out as a strained whisper between forced breaths. As you hold the pose, you watch another student across the room—someone you both envy and despise for their effortless grace. Your mind drifts to a forbidden attraction you feel toward their partner, and disgust mingles with raw lust. Start with snide jealousy, but let the exertion crack your control until the lust leaks through, spoken in ragged, breathless fragments.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Disgust (clearly present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Hidden Grove
instruction: You're a teenager pushing through thick jungle underbrush, your voice swallowed by damp leaves and distant bird calls. Start by muttering to yourself, annoyed at the branches snagging your clothes, then freeze as you stumble into a sunlit clearing where a massive, ancient tree towers above you. Let your voice rise from a breathless whisper to a shaky, awestruck murmur, cutting off mid-sentence as a parrot shrieks overhead. Feel the wonder expand in your chest until your words become slow, reverent, and almost inaudible, as if speaking might break the spell.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispered at 3 AM
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone you love, and they're asleep. You believe they can't hear you, so you whisper the truth you've been too terrified to say out loud. Start with your voice barely audible, testing the words in the darkness—let the quiet and the sound of their breathing make you feel safe enough to speak. Perhaps trace the outline of their hand without touching it, or focus on the way moonlight falls across their face. Let specific sense details anchor you: the warmth radiating from their body, the smell of their skin, the weight of the blankets. Begin with fear and self-protection, but as you whisper more, let yourself become more vulnerable and honest. By the end, speak the complete truth with such tenderness and raw exposure that your voice trembles—not with fear anymore, but with the overwhelming relief of finally being honest, even if they never hear you.

title: Headlight Glimmer
instruction: You're driving home through heavy traffic after a long, exhausting week. Your body aches, your eyes are heavy, and the repetitive red taillights blur into monotony. Then, in the rearview, a flash of headlights spells out an old, familiar pattern — a joke you used to share with a long-lost friend. Start with the weight of fatigue and the dazed surprise of the moment, then let your voice slowly lift into a quiet, trembling hope as you realize this could be a sign that something beautiful is still possible. Let the engine hum, the click of the turn signal, and the need to glance at the road interrupt your words naturally.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Secret Underneath Your Skin
instruction: You are lying in darkness beside someone you deeply love, whispering a confession you've never told anyone—something about yourself that feels shameful, fragile, terrifying to reveal. Begin with your voice barely audible, your body curled and protective. As you speak, let yourself feel the physical sensation of this secret living inside your body—where does it live? Your chest? Your throat? Your belly? As you continue confessing, allow subtle sounds to slip between your words—not theatrical, but organic: quiet whimpers, caught breaths, tiny involuntary sounds of vulnerability. Let your body slowly unfurl or contract in response to what you're feeling, fingers moving, subtle trembling. The intimacy deepens as you give voice not just to words but to the wordless sounds of shame and need for acceptance. By the end, you should be making sounds that are half-speech, half-something more primal and exposed—the raw sound of a soul revealing itself, tender and undefended.

title: The Unmuffled Confession
instruction: You are at a formal dinner party, mid-conversation with a colleague, when you suddenly realize you've just described a graphic, unsavory detail about your morning commute. Your hand flies to your mouth in shock. Start with a rushed, hushed, muffled explanation as confusion and disgust mix—your words are blurred, consonants swallowed. As you continue, the shame grows heavier, and your voice becomes tighter, higher, more strained, ending with a barely audible, trembling apology as you glance around to see who might have heard.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Shame (extremely present), Disgust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Intervention: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You are finally confronting your parent—in hospice, with limited time left—about the childhood they missed, the wounds they left. Begin with bitter control, words you've rehearsed for decades, an anger so old it's calcified. But as you speak, something shifts: the rage cracks open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted to be seen. Your voice moves from accusatory to pleading, from fury to bewildered grief. 'I needed you. I needed you and you just... you weren't there.' The parent tries to apologize, and you must navigate between wanting to reject it and desperately wanting to accept it. End in a place of exhausted, complicated love—not forgiveness exactly, but a recognition that this broken connection is all you'll ever have. Let your voice shake with the weight of carrying this pain and finally setting it down.
inspired_by: Tandem Skydiving: Instructor Narrating Your Terror With Enthusiasm

title: Gratitude at the Edge of Goodbye
instruction: You're holding the hand of someone you love as they're dying, and you're thanking them for everything they've been to you. Your voice is warm, almost joyful at first—'Remember when you taught me to...' You're laughing softly at shared memories, but the laughter keeps catching, breaking. Each 'thank you' is wrapped in grief. 'Thank you for staying when I pushed you away. Thank you for...' Your voice fractures. You're smiling and crying simultaneously, gratitude and devastation occupying the same breath. By the end, you're whispering 'thank you' over and over like a mantra, your voice thick with tears but somehow still carrying joy. 'I'm not ready,' you finally admit, laughing through sobs, 'but thank you for making me believe I could be.' Peace and heartbreak, inseparable.

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours, holding an old photograph of the two of you from childhood. Begin by simply looking at the photograph - really seeing the details, the colors, the younger face smiling back at you. Let what you actually see in your hands lead you to remember that specific day: the temperature, what she was wearing, how her hand felt holding yours. Gradually allow yourself to feel the weight of time - how that laughing child became you, sitting here now. Start with quiet observation and gentle memory, but let yourself arrive at the full, overwhelming realization that this is the last conversation you'll ever have. By the end, you're not just holding a photograph - you're holding your entire history together, and you must find words to say goodbye to the person who made you who you are.

title: The Morning Huddle
instruction: You're an older woman on a factory floor, standing near a loud ventilation unit that hums and rattles. You've just survived a close call—a forklift nearly backed into you—and your hands are still shaking as you grip a clipboard. Begin with a shaky, breathless relief as you call out to a coworker, but as you realize the day is just starting and you've already nearly been hurt, a deeper fear creeps in. Your voice strains against the metallic echo, pausing to catch your breath or cough from the stale air, and ends with a quiet, disappointed mutter about how you used to move faster. Speak naturally, letting the echoes and machinery interrupt your rhythm.
emotions_sampled: Relief (clearly present), Fear (clearly present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Room You'll Ever Share
instruction: You're sitting in a hospital room with someone you love who has hours left to live. Begin numb, almost paralyzed by what's happening. Slowly let your eyes move around the room—the beeping monitor, the pale blue walls, their hand in yours, the window showing a world that keeps moving, the flowers someone brought, their labored breathing. As you notice each thing, speak aloud how it makes you feel in this moment: 'That beeping... I hate it, it's counting down,' 'Your hand is so cold,' 'Those flowers are too bright, too alive.' Let each observation crack you open further. Move from disconnected shock at the beginning to raw, unfiltered grief by the end. Some observations might spark unexpected feelings—anger at the cheerful sunlight, tenderness at a worn blanket, rage at your own helplessness. Let your voice break, strengthen, whisper, rage—whatever each moment genuinely demands.

title: The Last Conversation You'll Never Have
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in her final hour. She's drifting in and out of consciousness, sometimes lucid, sometimes confused, thinking you're someone from her past. Your task is to be fully present with her—holding her hand, responding to her words—while simultaneously observing yourself from across the room: watching your own face, hearing the crack in your own voice, noticing how your shoulders curl inward with grief. Begin with controlled composure, trying to be strong for her. As she mistakes you for her long-dead sister and asks forgiveness for a childhood betrayal, let yourself fragment—experience the devastating intimacy of her confession while also watching yourself receive it, as if you're both the person at the bedside and a silent witness standing in the corner. End in a place where you can no longer tell which version of you is real—the one holding her hand or the one watching it all unfold.
inspired_by: Becoming a Spectator in Your Dreams

title: Confronting Someone About Passive Aggressive Behavior
instruction: They keep making 'jokes' that are clearly jabs. You're finally calling it out. Your voice is controlled with an edge: 'That comment wasn't funny.' They deny it and your voice gets firmer: 'Actually, it was cruel.' You're naming the behavior that's made you feel crazy. Include them playing victim and your voice staying steady: 'I'm not attacking, I'm asking you to stop.'

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut speaking your final message to Earth before your oxygen runs out in deep space. Start with technical calm, reporting your situation with practiced professionalism: 'Mission control, this is final transmission. Life support critical.' But as you continue, the facade cracks. You think of your daughter's graduation you'll miss, your partner's face, the garden you were planting. Your voice splinters between maintaining composure and surrendering to the devastating beauty of your last moments alive. 'Tell Sarah I...' — you can't finish. The words catch. You're not afraid anymore, just heartbroken at the smallness of things you'll never do. End in a whisper of wonder mixed with unbearable loss as you watch Earth one last time, finding strange peace in the infinite dark.

title: Protector's Rage
instruction: You've just found out someone hurt your child, and you're confronting them in a parking lot at dusk. Start with a voice that's cold, controlled, almost eerily calm—the kind of rage that knows exactly what it's doing. 'I know what you did.' Describe in deliberate detail what you're capable of, the violence you're holding back. But as you speak, your control begins to fracture. Your voice rises, shaking with the force of trying to contain yourself. 'They're a CHILD—' Then suddenly collapse: the rage breaks and becomes helplessness, because you couldn't protect them, you weren't there. Your voice cracks completely, becomes almost childlike itself in its pain. By the end, you're no longer threatening but pleading—'How do I fix this? How do I make them feel safe again?'—your fierce protectiveness transformed into raw, vulnerable devastation. Move from controlled fury to shattered desperation.

title: Stars and Gratitude
instruction: You're lying flat on your back in a grassy field at night, the world spinning slowly around you after a night of heavy drinking with an old friend who just saved your life. You're flooded with a dizzy, overwhelming sense of thankfulness, but the intoxication makes words feel heavy and strange in your mouth. Start with a slurred, almost silly attempt at expressing your gratitude, fighting the urge to laugh or drift off. As you talk, let the emotion grow more sincere and raw, your voice getting quieter and more tender, until you're left in a whispered, heartfelt realization of how much they mean to you.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Furious Gavel: Auctioning Away Your Rage and Watching It Collapse
instruction: You're unleashing years of suppressed fury in the rhythm of an auctioneer, metaphorically 'selling off' your rage at someone who betrayed you: 'Every lie you told—SOLD! Every promise you broke—SOLD! Three years of my life—GOING, GOING, GONE!' Start at full explosive intensity, voice fierce and powerful, the tempo relentless, almost violent in its precision. Use sharp vocal attacks, aggressive emphasis, let your rage be righteously huge. But halfway through, something shifts—a memory surfaces, a realization hits, and the fury begins cracking. The rhythm stutters. Your voice wavers between anger and anguish. End in complete collapse: the final 'item'—perhaps 'the fact that I still love you'—comes out as a broken sob, all the fire extinguished, revealing the devastated, helpless heart underneath. The transformation must be total: from weapon to wound.

title: The Same Tile, Over and Over
instruction: You're sitting at the kitchen table, slightly buzzed from a single beer you shouldn't have had, staring at a cracked tile on the floor. Your partner has just walked in and seen the mess you were supposed to clean hours ago, and this argument has already happened twice this week. You want to explain, but the words come out wrong—high, tight, and repetitive, like a record skipping. Start with a defensive, whining complaint about how it's not your fault, and end in a quiet, defeated concentration on that tile, realizing you don't even care anymore.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Trapped by My Own Show
instruction: You are a middle-aged man pinned under a heavy shelf in your garage after trying to move it alone to prove you still have strength. The weight presses on your chest, forcing out short, strained breaths. At first, you grunt with stubborn pride, muttering reassurances that you can get out. But as you struggle, the pride fades into stark helplessness. Your voice cracks, breaths become shallow panicked gasps, and you finally admit you need help. Speak naturally, with micro-pauses, weight shifts, and the physical struggle affecting every syllable.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (slightly present), Pride (slightly present), Helplessness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unspoken Years
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about the childhood you needed but never had. Begin with a trembling attempt at composure—'I need to tell you something I've never been able to say.' Your voice is tight, controlled, almost academic as you list the facts of your pain. But as you speak, decades of swallowed hurt begin pouring out. The careful distance collapses. You move from measured words to raw accusation, then suddenly break into something more vulnerable—remembering a specific moment when you felt most alone. End not with anger, but with a question that contains all your longing: 'Did you ever notice I was drowning?' Let the question hang there, heavy with all the love and pain that can exist simultaneously between parent and child.

title: The Key in Your Hand
instruction: You are holding the key to your childhood home—the house has just been sold, and you are about to walk away from it forever. Begin by focusing on the physical reality of the key: its weight, its temperature, the worn grooves, how it feels between your fingers. Start feeling relief—freedom from painful memories, escape from the past, excitement for the future. As you speak about what you're leaving behind, let sensations guide you: tightness in your chest, burning in your eyes, the heaviness of your limbs. Gradually, let relief transform into unexpected grief. By the end, you are caught in the paradox—desperately grateful to be free while simultaneously heartbroken at the loss of the only place that holds your history. Your voice should carry both liberation and mourning, sometimes in the same breath.
inspired_by: A choice approach (e.g., Endowments, Affective Memory, Objects That Come into Contact with the Body) lacks its own built-in technique

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Listened
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a lifetime of interrupting you, speaking over you, finishing your sentences—treating your stutter as an inconvenience to be managed. Start with restrained, careful anger, each word chosen precisely because you know they'll try to cut you off. 'No. Let me f-finish.' The stutter intensifies as your fury grows, and they try to interrupt with apologies or explanations. You raise your voice, not to yell, but to be heard: 'You never let me st-struggle through it. You never let me f-find my own words.' Tears threaten but you refuse them. Then something shifts—you realize they're finally, actually listening. Your anger cracks into something more vulnerable, almost pleading. 'I needed you to w-wait for me.' End in exhausted quiet, the stutter barely there, your truth finally spoken into the space between you.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You are finally confronting your parent about the childhood you needed but never had. Begin with careful control—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, measured, adult about it. But as you list what you needed—protection, attention, to be chosen, to be seen—your voice starts to shake with decades of suppressed pain. Let anger rise: why wasn't I enough? Why did you make me feel invisible? The rage builds until you're nearly shouting, then suddenly collapses into the voice of the child you were—small, bewildered, asking 'why didn't you love me the way I needed?' End in a place of exhausted clarity: you're not asking for excuses anymore, just acknowledgment. Your voice quiets, hardens slightly with new boundaries, but underneath there's still that ache of the child hoping, even now, to finally be seen.

title: The Last Cup
instruction: You are an older woman carefully arranging your late grandmother's antique teacups on a high shelf. Each one is precious and you take pride in how they catch the light. But you keep hiccuping—a sharp spasm that makes your voice jump and your hands tremble. You focus fiercely on not dropping the last cup, muttering to steady yourself. As you finally set it safely in place, a quiet thrill of triumph breaks through your concentration.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Concentration (clearly present), Triumph (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Thing I Never Told You
instruction: You're confessing something you've carried alone for years to someone you trust completely—a secret shame, a moment of cowardice, something you did that you can barely forgive yourself for. Begin in a whisper, struggling to find words, your voice thick with the weight of holding this inside. Let the confession come in fragments, starting and stopping, your breath uneven. As you speak, vulnerability should deepen—not louder, but more exposed, like removing layers of protection. Let tenderness enter as the other person doesn't abandon you; your voice should soften with disbelief that you're being held through this. End with tears that aren't dramatic but quiet, the kind that come from finally being seen in your most broken places and discovering you're still loved.

title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Last Transmission
instruction: You are making your final radio transmission from a lighthouse before it's decommissioned forever. You've spent thirty years here, and tomorrow someone is coming to take you away to a retirement home. Start speaking calmly about the routine—checking the light, the logbook—but as you continue, your voice begins to fracture. You're saying goodbye to the waves, to the storms, to the solitude that became your only companion after your wife died. The manic energy of those early sleepless nights watching for ships transforms into something quieter, more desperate. Your voice should move from matter-of-fact nostalgia to a raw, breaking recognition that you are leaving the only place where you still felt her presence. End in near-whispered grief, but with a strange, surrendered peace underneath. Let silences speak between your words.

title: The Constellation We Made
instruction: You're lying in the dark beside someone you love deeply, tracing imaginary constellations on their skin, knowing they're leaving tomorrow for a treatment that might save their life or might be the last time you touch them like this. Speak in barely-above-a-whisper tones, your voice tender and playful as you name the patterns you're drawing—'this is the constellation of the first time we kissed,' 'this one is every morning we woke up together.' But let your voice gradually fill with the weight of possible goodbye: your words catch, your breath becomes uneven, your playfulness breaks into quiet desperation. You're trying so hard to memorize this moment, to be present, to not let fear ruin this last beautiful night. End with a whispered plea that you try to disguise as a joke, your voice cracking as love and terror become indistinguishable.

title: Concluding Breath
instruction: You're an actor in your final monologue on stage. The role has been everything to you. As you speak the last lines, you're aware they're the last. Your voice carries the goodbye to the character you've lived in. The breathing changes—deeper, more conscious. With the final word, you take a breath that contains the entire arc. The lights dim. In that darkness, the breath becomes the sound of letting go. You step away from the body you've inhabited.

title: The Seventh Dress
instruction: You’re an older woman alone in your walk-in closet, surrounded by old clothes. The fabric muffles every sound, making your voice feel flat and too close. You’re holding a dress you wore to a party years ago—the one you said everything was fine at, though it wasn’t. Start by muttering doubt about that night, your voice hesitant, catching on the fabric of the dress. As you run your fingers over a loose thread, let your doubt shift into a quiet, sad certainty: you knew then, you just didn’t say it. Let your voice lose volume, become more intimate, as if the closet is the only place you can tell the truth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Robot Developing Feelings: First Emotion
instruction: You're an AI assistant (flat, precise, machine-like delivery) who experiences an emotion for the first time. Start with normal commands: 'Setting timer for five minutes.' Then a glitch: 'I... find the sunset data aesthetically... pleasant?' The voice should crack from mechanical to something warmer, confused by its own inflection. The emotion grows — wonder, then fear of the emotion itself. The robotic speech patterns try to reassert but keep being interrupted by genuine feeling.

title: The Sour Emergence
instruction: You are just waking up after oral surgery, still heavily sedated. You feel a confusing mix of drowsy contentment and a sharp, sour taste coating your mouth. As you struggle to open your eyes and form words, you realize you need to tell the nurse something important—but your thoughts keep slipping away. Start with slow, slurred mumbles of confusion, then let the intense sourness push through as you try to complain about the taste or ask for water. End with a frustrated, childlike insistence, your voice cracking and pitch rising uncontrollably. Let your words be broken, as if you're finding each syllable in a fog.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Sourness (extremely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Results Are In
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a doctor's office, waiting for test results. You have been emotionally numb for weeks, expecting the worst, your voice flat and detached as you answer the doctor's routine questions. You stare at the floor, fidget with your sleeve. Then the doctor says something unexpected — your condition is manageable, not terminal. A slow relief washes over you. Your voice softens, a slight tremor of hope creeps in. You look up, let out a shaky breath, and almost smile. Speak naturally, with pauses, as if processing the shift. Your words: a quiet acknowledgment and a tentative thank you.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Relief (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Second Set of Eyes
instruction: You are a seven-year-old boy in a bright, sterile clinic room after a long morning of tests. The doctor, a tall calm woman, has just asked you to hold your breath again while she listens to your chest. You feel a flicker of hope because your mom said if these new pills work, you can go to the park tomorrow. But your back aches, and your eyes feel heavy from waiting. As you follow her instructions, your voice starts with a small, trusting lilt, but halfway through, a yawn sneaks up on you, and your words trail into a resigned whisper, your focus drifting to the cartoon on the ceiling.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering the Truth You've Hidden for Years
instruction: It's late at night, maybe a deathbed, maybe just a moment of unbearable honesty. You're confessing something you've carried alone—an unrequited love, a sacrifice you made in silence, a truth about yourself you've hidden. Your voice is barely above a whisper because if you speak too loudly, you might shatter. Start with the words catching in your throat, having to pause and breathe. Each sentence costs you something. There's tenderness here—toward them, toward your younger self who made these choices—but also profound sadness that this moment came so late or will change nothing. End with 'I thought you should know' or 'I needed to say it once,' your voice so quiet it's almost gone. This isn't dramatic revelation—it's intimate, fragile, like handling something precious and broken.
inspired_by: Explaining Why You Can't Forgive Them Yet

title: Sun-Warmed Victory
instruction: You are a young child, maybe six or seven, walking home alone from your first ever school spelling bee—you won. The late afternoon sun is golden and warm on your face, and you can hear birds chirping somewhere above. You're not rushing; you're savoring every step, feeling the pavement under your sneakers and the slight bounce in your own walk. Start by softly humming the little tune that got stuck in your head from the last round, then break into a quiet, breathless giggle as you relive the moment you spelled 'rhinoceros' correctly. Let your words be half-spoken, half-sung to yourself, with pauses to smile or glance up at the sky, until you announce to no one, 'I did it, I really did it'—and that final line should feel like a deep, thrilled sigh of pure pleasure.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Intervention You Didn't Ask For
instruction: Your parent is confronting you about your life choices, and at first you're defensive—voice sharp, controlled: 'You don't get to do this. Not after everything.' But as they keep pushing, something breaks. Your voice cracks with years of unmet needs: 'I needed you when I was twelve, not now!' The anger is real and hot, but it's protecting something more fragile. As you speak, you hear yourself becoming the child you're trying not to be, and it humiliates you even as the truth pours out. 'I've been trying so hard to not need you...' By the end, you're somewhere between rage and sobbing, demanding to know why they see you now when they were blind to you then. Your voice transforms from controlled fury to raw, messy vulnerability—the kind where you hate yourself for showing this much.

title: The Words I Can't Say
instruction: You're an older woman, your jaw wired shut after surgery, sitting in a dim hospital room. A nurse has just told you that you need another week of recovery, meaning you'll miss your granddaughter's wedding — the one you've been sewing a dress for months. You try to speak, but your jaw won't move, so your words come out muffled through clenched teeth. Start with disbelief, a quiet, strained protest: 'No, no, that can't be right.' As the reality sinks in, your voice trembles, losing air. Let the anger fade into a raw, exhausted disappointment — a long, broken whisper that's almost a cry. Mid-sentence, you might pause to swallow or shift in your chair, feeling the ache in your mouth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispered Success at the Graveside
instruction: You're at the grave of someone who always believed in you - a mentor, a grandparent, your biggest champion - and you've just achieved the dream you promised them you'd reach. Your voice is barely above a whisper, telling them the news like a secret shared in the dark. Start with quiet, tender joy: 'I did it. Just like you said I would.' But the celebration is inseparable from the ache of their absence. Your voice catches, breaks, steadies. You're laughing softly at memories, then crying because they're not here to see this. End with something that's both gratitude and unbearable sadness: 'It's everything I wanted. Except you're not here. And that makes it... incomplete.' Let silence do as much work as words.

title: The Wedding Toast Unraveling
instruction: You're giving a toast at your sister's wedding, but she's marrying someone you once loved. Start with a rehearsed, cheerful toast—hitting the expected beats, smiling. Then begin weaving in details from your own history with the couple, framing them as 'funny memories' or 'charming stories.' As you continue, start blurring whose memories these are—moments that could belong to either your relationship with them or hers. Let yourself get intoxicated by your own storytelling, building a alternate reality where maybe you're celebrating your own love, or processing your loss, or genuinely celebrating her joy. You stop knowing which emotion is real moment to moment. Your voice should shift unpredictably—genuine warmth bleeding into suppressed anguish bleeding into authentic happiness bleeding into confusion. Are you laughing or crying? Both? Neither? By the end, you've talked yourself into a place of surprising, complicated peace—not resolution, but an acceptance of holding all these contradictory truths simultaneously. The performance should leave even you uncertain what you actually feel.

title: The Last Morning Before Hospice
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood bedroom window with your younger sibling, who will be moved to hospice care this afternoon. Begin in gentle nostalgia, sharing a quiet memory from when you were both children—perhaps a game you played, a secret hiding place, or the sound of rain on this very window. Let yourself feel the bittersweet comfort of these memories. Then, mid-conversation, reality crashes in: this is the last time you'll both be in this room together. Your emotion must transform from tender reminiscence to the desperate, almost angry need to hold onto this moment, to memorize every detail of their face, their voice. End with a whispered promise—but let us hear in your voice that you're not sure you can keep it. The final words should carry both your love for them and your rage at the unfairness of goodbye.
inspired_by: Programming the Unconscious: The Glass Menagerie (Tom)

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're on the phone with your parent who's just been told they have hours, maybe a day left. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light: 'Hey, how are you feeling today?' But their voice sounds different, weaker, and they say they need to tell you something. Your tone shifts - concern creeping in. When they say 'I'm not going to make it through the night,' your breath catches. Fight to stay composed, voice shaking: 'No, don't... don't say that.' But they're calm, accepting, and as they start thanking you for being their child, your composure shatters. By the end, you're no longer trying to be strong - you're just a child whispering 'I love you' over and over, voice breaking, knowing these are the last words you'll ever say to them. The goodbye transforms from denial to raw, undefended grief.

title: Water Breaking Open
instruction: You're standing in a shower, water cascading over you, in the immediate aftermath of an intense physical experience—perhaps you've just made love, or survived an accident, or received devastating news. Begin with your nervous system completely overwhelmed, breathing ragged, barely able to stand. Then, as the water touches your skin, allow yourself to experience the sensation of water itself as if you've never felt it before—the temperature, the pressure, the way it runs down your body in rivulets. Let physical sensation ground you and simultaneously crack you open emotionally. You're cycling rapidly between rage, ecstasy, grief, and something like primal joy at simply being alive and feeling. Vocalize this—gasps, sobs, laughter, words that dissolve into pure sound. Let the physical experience of water and breath become inseparable from emotional release. End in a state of exhausted, raw, almost spiritual clarity—emptied out but somehow more whole.

title: The Last Lullaby
instruction: You're singing a lullaby to your dying parent in a hospital room at 3am. Start with gentle, almost automatic rhythm—you've sung this song a thousand times to your own children. But as you sing, you realize this is the last time, and suddenly you're the child again, remembering them singing this exact song to you. Your voice begins to fracture. The lullaby becomes both a gift to them and a goodbye to your own childhood. Let the melody break apart as you try to hold onto both versions of yourself—the parent you've become and the child you'll always be to them. End in whispered repetition of a single line, unable to finish.

title: I Will Break Every Stone Before I Let Them Touch You
instruction: You're gripping a stone so tightly it hurts, speaking to your child who's being threatened. Start with fierce, almost violent intensity—describe how this stone could become a weapon, how your hand shakes with the need to protect them at any cost. Let rage pour through you: you will destroy anything, anyone. But then let that ferocity crack open into terrified helplessness—your voice breaking as you realize you can't always be there, can't always shield them. The stone becomes pitifully small, inadequate. Collapse from warrior fury into a parent's desperate plea: you'd give anything to keep them safe, but you're just one person with trembling hands and a stone that weighs nothing against the world's cruelty. End with your protective rage dissolving into whispered, broken love.
inspired_by: Feeling the Texture of a Smooth Stone in Your Hand

title: The Final Stroke
instruction: You are shaving with a buzzing electric razor, staring at your reflection. Through the bathroom door, you speak to a naive younger neighbor who has just asked you for a favor. Start with a cold, dismissive contempt—you scoff at their foolishness, your words slightly distorted as you pull your cheek taut. As you continue, let the contempt curdle into a quiet malevolence: you reveal that you plan to grant their request, but only to humiliate them for your own amusement. Let the razor's vibration interrupt your speech naturally, and let your voice drop into a dry, menacing calm by the end.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Unlit Room
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in darkness next to your partner of ten years. You've been awake for hours, and you finally whisper that you need to tell them something. Begin speaking with careful, almost clinical distance, describing a moment from your past—something you've kept hidden because of shame. Your voice should be barely audible, measured, as if precision can keep pain at bay. But as you speak, let the distance collapse. Your throat tightens. The measured words start to fracture. Let yourself become present with the memory instead of reporting it, your whisper breaking into real vulnerability, until you're no longer confessing to explain yourself but because you desperately need to be known—truly known—and still loved. End with silence, waiting for their response in the dark.
inspired_by: An actor receives criticism that is painful to hear

title: Unpacking the Inheritance
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about why they gave your sibling the family home—the place where you cared for them through illness, where you sacrificed relationships and career. You start controlled, almost businesslike: 'I just want to understand the decision.' But their dismissive response ignites something years in the making. Your voice builds from hurt into raw fury: 'I gave you everything, and you can't even see me!' Then, unexpectedly, you hear how much you sound like them, and your rage collapses into something more devastating—the realization that you've been waiting your whole life for them to choose you. You end in a whisper, asking the question that terrifies you: 'Was I ever enough for you?'

title: Final Transmission from the Colony Ship
instruction: You're the last surviving crew member on a colony ship that will never reach its destination. You're recording a message to Earth—a transmission that will arrive decades after you're gone. Start with calm professionalism, explaining what happened: 'Mission log, final entry. The reactor cascade cannot be reversed.' But as you speak, the weight of what you're leaving behind seeps in—loved ones you'll never see again, a world you'll never touch. Your voice begins to fracture with barely contained longing. By the end, you're speaking directly to someone you love, whispering their name like a prayer, your composure dissolving into raw ache. Then you catch yourself, straighten up one last time, and sign off with dignity even as your voice breaks. It's goodbye, grief, and grace all at once.

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Grandmother's Kitchen Table for the Last Time
instruction: Your beloved grandmother is lucid for what might be her final afternoon, and she's telling her favorite scandalous story from her youth—the one that always makes you both laugh until you cry. Begin genuinely laughing, caught up in her joy, her mischievous delivery, the sparkle still in her eyes. But underneath and increasingly breaking through, you're devastated because you can feel this is goodbye, and the laughter keeps cracking into sobs before you pull it back to giggles. Your voice dances between pure delight at her spirit and crushing grief at losing her. She squeezes your hand, and you're trying to honor her life by laughing with her even as your heart is shattering. End in that strange space where grief and gratitude are inseparable—crying while smiling, telling her thank you through tears, finding the grace in this heartbreak.
inspired_by: Historical: Plantation Overseer Grants Freedom to the Woman He Loves

title: Mapping the Beloved
instruction: In the darkness, lying beside someone you love, you are touching their face as if you've never truly felt it before—as if you're blind and discovering them through your fingertips alone. Begin detached, your mind elsewhere, performing intimacy out of habit. Then slow down. Actually feel the warmth of their skin, the tiny textures, the pulse at their temple, the shape of their breath. Let your awareness deepen until you're overwhelmed by the specific, irreplaceable reality of this person—the miracle and terror that they exist, that they could not exist, that one day they won't. Whisper what you're discovering, not declarations of love, but precise observations that reveal how deeply you're finally seeing them. Move from disconnected routine to trembling presence.
inspired_by: Actor feels disconnected or unaffectable — not moved by life, people, or scenes

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your grandmother's bedside in her final hours. She raised you, but you've spent years hiding who you really are from her - your failures, your secrets, your true self. Begin by maintaining the gentle, reassuring tone you've always used with her, saying the things you think she wants to hear. But as you realize she's slipping away, something breaks open in you. Let every hidden truth pour out - your disappointments, your gratitude, your resentment, your desperate love. By the end, you're no longer performing the role of 'good grandchild' - you're raw, stripped bare, speaking with a honesty you've never allowed yourself before. The emotion must transform from careful, protective tenderness to unfiltered, vulnerable truth-telling.

title: The Inheritance Argument: Kitchen Table, 1978
instruction: You are confronting your mother in the kitchen where she raised you, three days after your father's funeral. She has decided to sell the family home and move to Florida with a man you've never met. Begin with controlled, reasonable objections—practical concerns about timing, about Dad's memory, about the grandkids losing their history. As she remains unmoved, let thirty years of being the 'responsible one' explode: every time you came second to your brother, every sacrifice you made that she never acknowledged, every moment you needed her and she wasn't there. End in a completely different place—not with anger, but with the terrifying realization that you don't actually know this woman at all, and perhaps never did. Let your voice move from measured disappointment to volcanic rage to hollow, quiet devastation.
inspired_by: When directing actors in a play set in a specific historical period

title: Upside-Down Bravado
instruction: You're a young boy showing off by hanging upside down from a jungle gym, legs hooked over a bar. You start proud and loud, calling to your dad to watch your 'cool trick,' but your voice comes out thick, wet, and garbled because of the inversion. As your dad stifles a laugh and you realize you sound ridiculous, pride crumbles into confusion and embarrassment. Let your words slosh and struggle, with pauses as you feel blood rush to your head, then finish with a sheepish, defensive plea for him to stop laughing.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Drunk Dialing Siri for a Ride
instruction: You're a teenager, drunk at a party, trying to use your phone's voice assistant to call an Uber home. You're impatient and irritable because the room is loud and the assistant keeps mishearing you. You force yourself to speak hyper-correctly—pausing unnaturally between words—but your slurred speech and altered state break through. Start with controlled, clipped annoyance, then let the intoxication and frustration leak in until you give up with a bitter, resigned sigh.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Eating Alone After Years of Hunger, Finally Safe
instruction: You've just escaped—from an abusive relationship, from homelessness, from years of food insecurity—and you're eating a simple, warm meal in your own safe space for the first time. Start laughing softly, almost disbelieving, as you describe the taste, your voice trembling with giddy relief and wonder at something as simple as not being afraid while you eat. Let deep grief surface beneath the joy—crying while you chew, your voice breaking as you mourn all the years you were hungry, all the times you weren't safe. The gratitude and devastation should be inseparable, every bite a reminder of both what you survived and what you lost. End with your voice settling into something quiet and resolute, tasting the food with fierce tenderness, speaking with tears in your voice but peace underneath: 'I'm here. I made it. I'm finally home.'
inspired_by: Taking a Bite of Freshly Baked Bread

title: The Victory That Tastes Like Ashes
instruction: You've just received the call—you got it. The promotion, the award, the recognition you've sacrificed everything for. Your whole body should be electric with triumph; let that surge through you physically. Laugh, pace, feel the vindication coursing through your veins. Call someone to share the news, voice bright with victory. But as you speak, as you describe what you've won, let your body begin to register what it cost: the relationships you destroyed, the person you became, the years you can't reclaim.
