Start with that familiar defensive energy, voice rising with fierce protectiveness: 'Don't you dare judge them! You don't know what they've been through!' Feel the heat of it, the righteousness. But then something shifts—maybe you hear yourself, maybe you just can't hold it anymore. Your voice cracks, and suddenly you're not defending them, you're raging at them, even though they're not in the room: 'Why do you keep doing this?! Why do I have to keep saving you?!' The anger collapses into exhausted grief. Sit down. Voice small now, helpless: 'I can't anymore. I love you, but I can't... I can't do this anymore.' Let the relief and the devastation coexist.
inspired_by: Arguing When You're Both Partially Right

title: The Overly Competitive Board Gamer
instruction: Act as a person who takes casual games too seriously. Use an intense, strategic voice during play, switching to the casual, carefree tones of friends just wanting to have fun.

title: The Unholy Proclamation
instruction: You are the town crier in a medieval village, and you must deliver a shocking announcement to your neighbors who are foolishly celebrating a 'blessing' they don't understand. You stand at the market square, unamplified, and your voice must carry—vowels drag, consonants drop, and you pause between each phrase to let the words echo. Start with wide-eyed astonishment as you marvel at their ignorance, but let a sliver of cold malice creep into your tone by the end, as you realize you enjoy revealing the dark truth to them. Use the physical strain of shouting to fuel the emotion—let your breath run out mid-phrase, and let your pitch crack with genuine surprise and wicked delight.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Emergency Room Intubation
instruction: You're conscious as doctors prepare to put a breathing tube down your throat. Your voice is terrified, pleading. Include the strange out-of-body feeling as sedatives begin to hit—your words become slurred, nonsensical. You're fighting the paralytic—gasping against your own immobilized lungs. Your last coherent words are desperate, then everything becomes muffled, distant. Include the medic's voice saying 'You're okay, we've got you' as your consciousness fades.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral - A Letter to Those You're Leaving Behind
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your funeral. You're dying, you know it, and you've made peace with it in the strangest way. Start with genuine laughter, warm and affectionate: 'If you're crying right now, stop it. I mean it.' Your voice is playful, teasing the people you love. Share a ridiculous memory, let yourself laugh at the absurdity of life and death. But as you speak, gratitude starts bleeding through the humor: 'You made everything worth it.' Your voice catches. You're still smiling, but now you're crying too, voice breaking on words like 'thank you' and 'I love you.' End in this impossible space where joy and devastation are completely intertwined: 'I'm not afraid. I'm just so grateful I got to know you.' The final words are whispered through simultaneous laughter and tears, finding peace in the contradictions.
inspired_by: Waking Up and Realizing What You Said While Drunk

title: Holding Your Newborn While Your Partner Hemorrhages
instruction: The baby is in your arms—perfect, alive, screaming. Your partner is on the table behind you—bleeding, monitors shrieking, doctors shouting codes. You're frozen between them, ordered to stay back, holding this new life while another life is being ripped away. Start with fierce, primal joy: 'You're here, you're here, you're perfect.' Pour love into this baby even as panic rises. Then the commotion behind you intensifies. Feel your voice split between cooing at your child and pleading with God, with doctors, with the universe. Your words should ricochet: 'Look at your tiny hands' crashing into 'Please don't leave us, please, please.' Build to desperate bargaining—offering anything, everything—then collapse into helpless animal sounds. End in a moment of unbearable clarity: speaking to your child about their other parent in present tense, then past tense, then correcting yourself, not knowing which is true. Protectiveness and terror should be inseparable.
inspired_by: Birth and Death in the Same Hospital

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed beside your partner in the deep hours of the night. You need to tell them you're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because you do, and you've realized staying would slowly destroy both of you. You begin whispering in the darkness, your words half-formed and tentative, as if speaking too clearly would make it too real. Start with trembling tenderness, your voice barely audible as you trace the edges of what you need to say. Let your whispers carry both love and terrible certainty, each breath a contradiction. End with your voice breaking into something raw but resolute, as you finally speak clearly: 'I love you enough to let you go.'

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You've just received news that should devastate you—a terminal diagnosis, a catastrophic loss, the end of everything you built—but standing in the wreckage, you're discovering an unexpected, almost transcendent peace. You begin laughing, and it's real laughter, not hysteria, though tears are streaming down your face. Your voice moves fluidly between expressing profound gratitude for what you had and acknowledging the grief of losing it. You're marveling at the absurdity and beauty of it all, voice lifting with genuine wonder even as it cracks with sorrow. There's a strange joy mixed with devastating sadness—you're celebrating even as you're mourning. Your words tumble between revelation and loss, sometimes laughing at the same moment you're crying. End in a place of paradoxical wholeness—your voice steady but soft, speaking with clarity about the terrible beauty of loving things that end, finding strange comfort in the middle of catastrophe, grateful for having had anything worth grieving at all.

title: The Victory That Burns
instruction: You've just received the news you've fought for through five years of hell—the verdict is in your favor, you've won, your name is cleared. Your body floods with relief and vindication. Begin by letting this triumph move through you physically: shaking hands, explosive breath, maybe laughter or shouting. But as the adrenaline peaks, other sensations intrude unbidden—your legs weaken, your stomach turns, your throat tightens with something that isn't victory. Don't plan what comes next. Let your body lead you: perhaps rage surfaces at the years you lost, perhaps grief for who you were before, perhaps a strange emptiness. The physical experience of triumph transforms through unexpected sensation into something complex and possibly devastating. Your body tells the truth your mind hasn't processed yet.

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at a wedding—but it's your ex-partner's wedding, and you genuinely love them and want them to be happy, while simultaneously grieving the life you almost had together. Begin with warm, public-facing joy, celebrating them with apparent ease. But as you look into their eyes across the room—truly see them happy with someone else—let the layers of your contradictory feelings start to bleed through. Let gratitude for having known them coexist with the ache of loss. Let your genuine happiness for their joy wrestle with your private heartbreak. Don't choose one emotion over another—hold them all simultaneously, letting your voice waver between celebration and sorrow, your smile becoming both real and bittersweet. End with a blessing that costs you everything to give, but that you mean with your whole heart.
inspired_by: When you are a young actor asking a more experienced actor for advice about how to act

title: Headshot Heart
instruction: You're a teenage girl in a late-night gaming session with your online crush. Your controller clicks and your chair squeaks as you lean in. He just pulled off an incredible play. You start with a burst of excited, loud admiration, but as the silence stretches, your voice drops to something softer, more vulnerable. Let the clicks and your own nervous laughter break up your words. End with a quiet, honest confession you barely dare to say aloud.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Hospital Room at Twilight
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in her hospital room at dusk. Begin by feeling the cold metal rail of her bed under your palm, seeing the specific way the fading light comes through the venetian blinds and falls across her pale hands. Smell the particular mix of antiseptic and her lavender perfume. As you speak your farewell, build the sensory details of this room so completely that you can hear the exact rhythm of the monitors, feel the scratchy hospital blanket, taste the staleness of the air. Start with quiet resignation and fear, but as the sensory world becomes more vivid and real around you, let yourself move into a deeper place—perhaps unexpected gratitude, or a fierce determination to make her feel your love. The more real the room becomes to your senses, the more your goodbye should transform from something you're dreading into something essential and profound.

title: Whispering to the Child You'll Never Have
instruction: Late at night, alone, you're speaking softly to the baby you just learned you'll never carry. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and broken. Start by describing the life you'd imagined—the bedtime stories, the scraped knees you'd kiss better, the way you'd have loved them. Your throat catches on each detail. Let your voice become even softer as you apologize for dreams they'll never know existed. But slowly, something shifts—you begin to speak of the life you will have instead, and your voice trembles between mourning and acceptance. End with a fragile kind of peace, acknowledging both the devastating loss and the possibility of a different kind of meaning. Let the goodbye be full of love for someone who was never born but was always real to you.
inspired_by: Recovery: Choosing Yourself Over the Addiction

title: The Weight of Her Shape
instruction: You are lying in bed after sex, the sheets tangled, your body heavy and spent. The woman beside you has her head on your chest, her hand tracing idle patterns on your stomach. But there's a deep, old pain in your back—a slipped disc from years of construction work—that's flaring up now, sharp and unforgiving. As you speak, you're torn between the lingering, possessive lust you feel for her and the irritable impatience for the pain to subside. Start with a low, drowsy voice, the words barely leaving your throat, then let your irritation edge in as you shift to ease your back, finally settling into a gruff, possessive confession that mixes desire with a raw ache.
emotions_sampled: Pain (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inspection
instruction: You are a teenage cadet standing at rigid attention during a uniform inspection by a handsome superior officer you secretly have a crush on. Your body is locked, chest puffed, neck tense — you force your voice into a hard, metallic bark. But as you start reporting your name and rank, your eyes meet his and you feel a flutter of lust; your voice wavers, you lose your train of thought, swallow hard, and momentarily soften. End with a quieter, uncertain tone, fighting to regain composure but failing.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Debt Collector's Due
instruction: You're in bed with a man you've been tracking for weeks. He thinks this is a hookup, but you've been planning his ruin. As you move together, your body is finally releasing the tension of the hunt—relief floods through you. But your mind is razor-sharp with cold interest, cataloging every detail for later. And beneath the breathy rhythm, there's a quiet, gleeful malice. Let your voice be a breathy, rhythmic push-pull: soft gasps of relief break into tight, controlled whispers of interest, then drop into a low, almost loving sneer of malice. Your words come in short bursts, riding the motion. Start with genuine release, end with a dark promise he can't hear in the noise.
emotions_sampled: Relief (clearly present), Interest (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Morning After Regret
instruction: You wake up in a strange, messy bedroom, head throbbing, mouth like sand. Disgust coils in your stomach as you see clothes on the floor—someone else's. Pain drills behind your eyes. You try to sit up, groggy, and realize you don't remember how you got here. Embarrassment burns hot—what did you do? Your voice is low, gravelly, breaking on words. You mumble to yourself, trying to piece it together, then freeze as you hear breathing beside you. Start with pained confusion, let disgust twist your tone, then end in a whisper of shame as you decide to slip out before they wake.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (clearly present), Pain (very intensely present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Boss Former Employee
instruction: A boss and their former employee are meeting years later. The boss's voice carries the professional distance they maintained. The former employee's voice has something underneath—maybe resentment, maybe gratitude. The boss realizes they don't actually know this person they worked with daily. The employee realizes the boss has remained exactly the same while they've transformed. They exchange the kind of small talk that masks real feelings. Then one of them says something genuine, and both voices soften. By the end, they're acknowledging that the dynamic has changed. The professional distance is no longer required or possible.

title: The Explosive Hello to Your Mirror Self
instruction: You're alone, staring at yourself in the mirror after a devastating betrayal or loss, and you need to say hello to who you've become. Start with bitter, sarcastic energy—'Well, hello there, look at you.' Your voice drips with self-loathing and rage at your own choices. The anger builds as you catalogue your failures, your voice rising, becoming harsh and punishing. Then suddenly, violently, you break—the rage collapses into gasping sobs, your accusations turning into desperate questions: 'How did I get here? When did I stop fighting?' Your voice splinters between fury at yourself and raw, childlike confusion. By the end, exhausted and tear-stained, something quieter emerges. You're looking at yourself with new eyes, saying a different kind of hello—to resilience you didn't know you had, to the person who survived this. Your final words shake with both helplessness about the past and fierce, trembling determination about what comes next.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent who always needed you to be strong, perfect, and in control. For your entire life, you've hidden your messy, wild, reckless side from them. Now, in these final moments, that untamed part of you—the one that wanted to run away, make mistakes, live dangerously—is desperately clawing to be seen and acknowledged before it's too late. Begin speaking with your usual composed, dutiful voice, telling them you'll be fine and they can rest. But as you continue, let that buried, unruly part of yourself emerge—the voice that needed their permission to be imperfect, to fail, to be beautifully chaotic. By the end, you're confessing all the wildness you suppressed, begging them to see this hidden part of you before they go. The emotion shifts from controlled composure to raw, unguarded revelation.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access a personality facet (aggression, sexuality, fear, moralism, free spirit, victimhood) that is suppressed or disowned

title: Whispering a Secret That Changes Everything
instruction: It's late at night. You're lying beside someone you love, and you're about to tell them something that's been eating you alive—a terminal diagnosis, a truth about your past, something you did that betrays them. Your voice is barely audible at first: 'Are you awake? I need to... I can't keep this anymore.' Your throat is so tight the words almost won't come. As you speak, your voice catches repeatedly—not from crying, but from the physical difficulty of forcing out words that will hurt someone you cherish. 'I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.' You're not explaining or justifying; you're simply breaking open. Let silences do as much work as words. Your breathing becomes part of the performance—shaky, irregular. End with a whispered question that's really a plea: 'Please say something. Anything.' The quiet is unbearable, but you've said what needed saying, and now you're naked in the aftermath.
inspired_by: Discovering Your Partner Has Been Lying

title: The Puppy in the Yard
instruction: You are an elderly woman perched on a wooden stool at your kitchen window, core tight to keep your balance. Your strongly feminized voice carries a slight edge of envy as you watch your granddaughter play with a new puppy—something you never had. Start with a brittle, almost sharp tone, your words clipped by the strain of sitting upright and the jealousy prickling beneath. Midway, a memory surfaces: you recall a dog from your childhood, and your voice softens, the envy dissolving into a wistful warmth. Let your breathing shift, maybe a sigh or a pause as you adjust your grip on the stool, ending with a gentler, more resigned acceptance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Skin Memory
instruction: In a dimly lit room, you are whispering to someone you once loved deeply but haven't touched in years—you're finally admitting why you really left. Begin by noticing if you're performing 'intimacy' (breathy voice, calculated pauses, rehearsed vulnerability) or if you're genuinely allowing yourself to be fragile. Feel the actual sensation of being this close to them again—the pull, the fear, the muscle memory. Let your voice find its real quality, not the whispered, theatrical version of confession. As you speak, move from calculated tenderness into authentic exposure: the shakiness that comes from actual risk, the specific ache of remembering what you lost, the surprising anger or unexpected tenderness that arrives uninvited. End in genuine nakedness, not performed delicacy.

title: Kindness Showing Ripple Effects: Realizing Impact You Didn't Know
instruction: Someone tells you that something you did—something you'd forgotten about—changed their life. Your voice is shocked, almost disbelieving: 'Really? That small thing?' You're being confronted with the reality that you have more impact than you knew. Include the moment where emotion breaks through—you've been carrying yourself so lightly and this person is telling you that you mattered. Your voice becomes almost tearful: 'I didn't know I'd helped at all.' Your voice contains this strange mixture of humility and gratitude. By the end, you're understanding something about kindness: sometimes it lands after you've stopped looking. Sometimes it multiplies in ways you'll never fully know. Your voice reflects that beautiful uncertainty—you changed something and you'll never fully understand the scope of it.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Lover Things You'll Never Say When They're Awake
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner is asleep beside you. You begin speaking in barely audible whispers, confessing things you're too afraid to say in daylight—how scared you are of losing them, how you push them away because your father left, how you sabotage good things. Your voice is tender, intimate, thick with unshed tears that you won't allow to fall. There's a quiet desperation in your delivery, the safety of speaking truth to someone who can't hear you. Include moments where your breath catches, where you have to pause and steady yourself, where your whisper becomes even softer because the words are too painful. Midway through, shift to expressions of profound gratitude mixed with devastating sadness—thanking them for loving you despite how difficult you make it, knowing you're not sure you deserve it. End with a whispered plea or promise, your voice breaking on the final words, then silence as you watch them sleep, all those confessions hanging unheard in the dark.
inspired_by: Heroin Nod: Fighting Sleep While Someone Talks to You

title: Shattered Sanctuary
instruction: You've just found your teenage daughter after she went missing for three days. Start with explosive relief that's almost violent: 'Where the HELL were you?!' Your voice cracks with fury born from terror. The anger is real, protective, overwhelming: 'Do you have ANY idea—' but it immediately breaks into something else. You can't maintain the rage because underneath is pure fear. Your voice fractures into sobs mid-sentence: 'I thought you were dead. I thought—' Then fierce protectiveness surges back: 'Don't you ever, EVER—' but you can't finish because you're pulling them close. End in a whisper of complete helplessness, still holding them: 'I can't lose you. I can't. I don't know how to survive that.' The journey is rage to terror to fierce love to the admission that you're powerless to protect them from everything.

title: Mornings After You Left: A Whispered Inventory
instruction: You are alone at the breakfast table, months after your partner walked out of your decades-long marriage. Speak in an intimate whisper, as if confessing to their ghost sitting across from you. Describe the morning routine in excruciating, tender detail—how you still make two cups of coffee by muscle memory, how the silence where they used to read headlines aloud is physically painful, how you found yourself arguing with the empty chair about the toast. Your voice should be fragile, catching on words, thick with unshed tears. This isn't anger—it's the quiet devastation of realizing you took forty years of small sounds for granted. End with barely audible words: you finally understand what you lost, and it's the nothing moments that are killing you. Let your breath itself sound like heartbreak.
inspired_by: Old Couple's Morning Routine: 40 Years of Love

title: The Unanswered Call
instruction: You're leaning against a cold brick wall outside a hospital, phone pressed to your ear with your shoulder, waiting for test results that should have come through hours ago. At first, your voice is flat and cool, trying to sound unconcerned—almost detached—but doubt keeps seeping in through the pauses. Use the wall's support to feel a false steadiness; let your eyes drift to passing cars, your free hand fidgeting with a loose thread on your jacket. As you speak to the voicemail you know won't answer, let the doubt crack your composure: start tight and conversational, then tail off into quieter, more honest uncertainty, ending with a soft exhale and a shift of weight as you finally push off the wall.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Grumpy Patriarch's Unexpected Humor
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, mid-act of giving oral sex. Your partner just said something absurdly funny about the situation, and you initially feel a flash of irritation at the interruption. But as you try to respond with a grumble or a wry comment, you realize you can only produce a muffled, ridiculous hum. The physical absurdity of it breaks through your gruff exterior, and you start to genuinely chuckle through your nose, the sound vibrating into a series of amused, wet hums. Let your voice start with a low, annoyed growl, then morph into a breathy, nasal laugh that builds as you fully appreciate the comedy of the moment. Your performance should be only the sounds of your mouth being occupied—no clear words, just the emotional arc from grumpy resistance to unreserved mirth.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Truth
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, facing your father, who has just made a casual comment that reveals he has no memory of something that shaped your entire life—a promise he broke, a moment he missed, a wound he doesn't know he inflicted. Begin by truly looking at him—his aged hands, the way he stands, something about him that genuinely interests you or moves you in this moment. Start speaking from genuine curiosity: you want to understand how he could forget. But as you describe the memory to him in detail, let yourself move from wanting to understand to needing him to finally see you, to acknowledge what happened. Let the anger rise not from a decision to be angry, but from the authentic frustration of not being heard. By the end, you're not asking anymore—you're demanding he remember.

title: The Last Question Before Sleep
instruction: You are an elderly man, built like a former lumberjack, lying in bed after making love. Your partner is beside you, and the room is dark and quiet. You are utterly exhausted — your voice cracks with sleep, your words drag, and you can barely shape them. But you are also intensely curious about something your partner said earlier; you need to ask, even though you're fading. Start with that slow, gravelly, intimate question, then feel the tiredness pulling you under mid-sentence. Let your voice trail off, mumble, lose the thread, then force yourself to finish with a raw, vulnerable sound that reveals how much this small thing matters to you. Let there be long pauses, the rustle of sheets, a heavy sigh.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Finding Out Your Child Isn't Yours
instruction: You've just received a DNA test result revealing that your seven-year-old daughter isn't biologically yours. You're on the phone with your partner who's been lying for eight years. Begin with shock that rapidly ignites into fury: 'Eight years? EIGHT YEARS and you said nothing?' You're screaming, pacing, slamming things. 'Every bedtime story, every scraped knee, every I love you daddy—and you knew! You KNEW!' Your rage is volcanic. But then you picture your daughter's face and everything collapses. Your voice breaks completely: 'Oh god. Oh god, she's still my baby. She's still—' You're sobbing, but it's complicated, messy. Anger at your partner mixes with fierce, protective love for your child. 'She's mine. DNA doesn't change—she's MINE.' Your voice becomes almost feral with protectiveness: 'You don't take her from me. Nobody takes her from me.' End with a whisper that holds both devastation and absolute certainty: 'She's my daughter. She'll always be my daughter.' You're shattered, but unshakable.

title: The Bittersweet Homecoming
instruction: You're returning to a place you once called home—maybe to pack up a childhood house, to attend a celebration for someone who hurt you, or to reconcile with a community you left behind. Begin with one clear emotion: perhaps determined detachment or nervous anticipation. But as you move through the space and encounter triggers—a smell, a sound, the light through a particular window—allow contradictory feelings to ambush you. Access multiple layers simultaneously: gratitude for escape and grief for what you lost, love for people who failed you and anger at yourself for still caring, joy at who you've become and devastating sadness for who you had to leave behind. Don't resolve these contradictions—hold them all at once. Let your voice carry multiple emotional truths in a single sentence. By the end, arrive at a complex acceptance that isn't peaceful or settled, but richly, messily human—where you're simultaneously laughing and crying, bitter and grateful, saying goodbye and hello to different versions of yourself.
inspired_by: Actor wants to access unconscious material more consistently, not just by accident

title: Gasp of Thanks
instruction: You're a teenager who just got rescued from a near-drowning by a lifeguard at a crowded pool. You're lying on the deck, coughing up water, and he's kneeling beside you. You want to thank him, but every time you try to speak, a hiccup rips through your chest—sharp, involuntary, cutting your words short. There's a fierce gratitude burning in your throat, but underneath it, a cold terror from the memory of the water closing over your head. Let your voice catch and fragment between hiccups; let the gratitude bloom as the fear slowly subsides.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Chasing Your Lover Through the Rain to Stop the Leaving
instruction: You've just realized—truly understood—what you're about to lose. You're running through pouring rain after the person walking away from you for the last time. Start with desperate shouting, their name ripped from your throat, rage at yourself for being so blind mixing with panic. Your breathing is ragged, your words colliding: 'Wait—please—just WAIT!' You're angry, then begging, then angry again at having to beg. You catch up, grab their arm, spin them around. Now face to face, the explosive energy collapses. Your voice drops to something raw and broken. Rain streams down both your faces. You're suddenly helpless, all the fierce words you had evaporating into simple, devastating truth: 'I was scared. I'm so scared.' Your breathing is still heavy but now it's mixed with crying you can't control. You're saying 'I love you' but it sounds like 'I'm sorry,' you're saying 'Don't go' but you know you have no right. End trembling, whispering, watching them decide whether your breaking open is enough.
inspired_by: Reporting While Sprinting for Your Life

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed in the middle of the night. They're drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by trying to be strong, the capable adult child who has everything under control, offering reassurances that everything will be okay. But as you sit there in the quiet, holding their hand, something breaks open inside you. Let yourself become the child who still needs them, who isn't ready, who's terrified of being left alone in the world. Ask them the questions you could never ask before. Tell them what you still need to hear. By the end, allow yourself to speak from the most unguarded, youngest part of yourself—the part that just wants one more bedtime story, one more 'I love you,' one more moment of being their little one. Let the transformation from competent adult to vulnerable child happen gradually, naturally, as the reality sinks in.
inspired_by: I'm Just a Little Boy/Girl and I—

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are running—sprinting—through a rainstorm after the worst day of your life. You've just walked away from everything: your job, a toxic relationship, a life that was slowly suffocating you. As you run, you begin to scream—guttural, primal sounds that have been trapped in your chest for years. Feel the rain on your face, the burning in your lungs, the pounding of your heart. Your body is pain and your body is freedom. Scream until your voice breaks, until you're laughing through tears, until you collapse in exhaustion. The physical exertion and the emotional release become indistinguishable. Begin in desperate escape, move through cathartic rage, and end in breathless, soaking, terrified, exhilarated liberation. You are destroyed and you are finally, finally alive.

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Love
instruction: You're whispering to your partner in the dark, believing they're asleep, finally able to say what terrifies you. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, vulnerable: 'I need to tell you something... I'm scared you'll leave when you really know me.' Each word is careful, tender, your breathing soft and close. Confess your deepest fear with a voice that catches in your throat: 'Sometimes I look at you and I can't believe you chose me.' Let quiet tears come, voice thick with emotion but still whispered: 'I'm so broken in places you haven't seen yet.' Your vulnerability deepens, almost childlike: 'What if the real me is too much... or not enough?' End with a whispered revelation that mixes terror and hope: 'I love you so much it feels like standing on the edge of something.' Your final words are exhaled like a prayer, barely voiced: 'Please don't go when you see all of me.'

title: Midnight Mouthwash Meltdown
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman, still buzzed from a party, brushing your teeth in a dim bathroom. Start with a sleepy, loose, giggly ramble about the evening, slurring through the foam and scrubbing sounds. Then, a sudden foul taste—something rotting between your teeth—snaps you into sharp, guttural disgust. Your voice twists, spits, and chokes as you react, the brush still scraping your jaw. End with a horrified, muffled 'What is that?' as the intoxication fades into revulsion.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Disgust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Moment You Stop Them from Jumping
instruction: You've just grabbed someone on a bridge railing. Your voice explodes with raw terror: 'NO! Stop! STOP!' Adrenaline makes you almost violent in your urgency: 'Get down from there RIGHT NOW!' You're practically screaming, grabbing at them. But as they turn to look at you, something in their eyes makes you shift completely. Your voice drops, becomes desperate but gentle: 'Please. Please don't.' Now you're bargaining, your own tears streaming: 'I don't even know you, but I'm begging you—' Your voice cracks with helpless intensity. 'Whatever you're feeling right now, it won't always feel this way.' You're fierce with conviction but also breaking: 'Someone loves you. Someone needs you.' Then quietly, from your deepest place: 'I need you to stay alive, even if we never meet again.' You end nearly whispering, utterly vulnerable: 'Please. Let me help you off the railing.' The fierce protectiveness has transformed into tender, desperate hope.

title: Saying Goodbye Forever
instruction: This is the last time you'll speak to this person. Whether they're dying, moving, or you're ending it forever, your voice knows it's final. Your voice is trying to be present, trying to memorize them. But your voice is also breaking. 'I love you' carries the weight of goodbye. Your voice becomes tender, almost unbearably so. You want to say everything in these last moments but your voice only trembles. Include the moment you have to actually hang up.

title: The Rotting Grove
instruction: You are a teenager lost in a dense jungle, searching for a missing friend. At first, you feel a heavy sadness and growing confusion as you push through damp leaves. Then you stumble upon a clearing full of decayed animal carcasses — a wave of intense disgust hits you, making your voice tighten and waver. Your sadness transforms into a horrified realization that your friend might have come this way. Speak as if you are reacting to the sight and smell, your words swallowed by the thick air, with bird calls and insects around. Let your voice shift from mournful to choked with revulsion, then end with a trembling note of fear.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Body's Revolt
instruction: You've just received news that makes your body feel electrified and unbearable—a betrayal, a victory, a loss, something that ignites every nerve. Start absolutely still, voice barely controlled, trying to articulate the facts with precision while your body fights to move. Then let it overtake you: pace, gesture wildly, use the full range of your physical space. Speak with exaggerated clarity even as your body moves with passionate abandon—spinning, reaching, dropping, rising. Your voice must remain crystalline and audible throughout the physical storm. Channel the sensation through grand, almost theatrical movements that would look absurd in normal life but here express the unbearable truth of what you feel. By the end, the physical frenzy has exhausted into something quieter but still powerfully present—depleted but whole.

title: The Hesitant Embrace
instruction: You are an older adult, and you've just been kissed by someone you deeply care for but haven't fully let yourself trust yet. You're lying close, your lips meet, and at first your body tenses — a flicker of fear from past wounds. But as the kiss continues, you feel their steadiness, their patience. Allow your voice to start with small, cautious breaths and tiny wet sounds of hesitation, then slowly soften, letting your breath deepen and your lips part more willingly. Speak these words as you pull back just slightly to whisper, your voice full of intimacy and gradual surrender, with tiny pauses and natural shifts in closeness: 'I didn’t think I could still feel this... this scared of being held. But your hands don't shake like the others did. Maybe... maybe I can stop bracing for goodbye.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The False Dawn
instruction: You are lying face-down on a hotel bed, your mouth pressed into a damp pillow. You've just received a phone call: your son, long presumed dead in a war zone, has supposedly been found alive at a remote border clinic—but the voice on the line was hesitant, and now you're replaying the conversation, desperately trying to believe it. Start with a whisper of fragile hope, almost a prayer, as you turn the idea over in your mind: 'He could be coming home.' But as you realize the call was a mistake—a clerical error, a name mix-up—the hope shatters. Finish with raw, muffled grief, your words half-lost in the fabric as you cry out in disbelief. Let your voice be thick, choked, and physically smothered by the pillow, with gasps and shaky breath between fragments of syllables.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent who is actively dying, and they're waiting for you to let them go. Start with forced cheerfulness, talking about tomorrow's plans because you can't face this. 'We'll watch that show you like... you'll feel better in the morning.' But their labored breathing makes you stop. Your voice cracks as the reality crashes in—they're leaving, and you have to say it's okay. Move through desperate bargaining ('Please, just one more day'), then collapse into tender, broken permission-giving. End whispering close to their ear, your voice raw and soft: 'It's okay, Mom... you can rest now... I love you... you can go.' Let there be moments where you can't get the words out, where you're just breathing with them, crying, holding on and letting go at the same time.

title: Echoes of a Half-Heard Goodbye
instruction: You are standing on the landing of a concrete stairwell, holding a card that just fell from a coat pocket. You begin reading it aloud, your voice soft but carrying the metallic echo of the space. At first, you read with a sense of fondness for the handwriting—affection surfaces, but it sours as the words imply a farewell you were not meant to see. Let the confusion build as you lose your train of thought, shift your weight, and realize these steps lead to a truth you now have to climb back up with.
emotions_sampled: Affection (slightly present), Sourness (slightly present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Trail of Relief
instruction: You're a rugged outdoorsman who's been lost in a dense jungle for hours. You finally spot a faded trail marker on a tree, and a wave of pure relief hits you—your body sags, you let out a shaky breath. But as you step forward, you must concentrate intensely: the trail is faint, so you mutter to yourself, checking each step, listening for rustles, feeling the damp air. Your voice starts with a relieved whisper, then shifts to a focused, low grumble as you navigate, pausing to blink sweat from your eyes.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child the Truth You'll Never Tell Them Awake
instruction: Your child is asleep. You're sitting beside their bed in the dark. You begin by just watching them breathe, your voice barely above a whisper when you start speaking. You're confessing something you can never tell them when they're awake—maybe that you're sick, maybe that you're leaving, maybe that you failed them in a way they'll only understand years from now. Your voice is tender, full of fierce protective love. You're trying not to cry because you don't want to wake them. Every word catches in your throat. As you continue, the grief becomes harder to contain—your breath hitches, your voice fractures on certain words. End in a place of both devastating sorrow and profound gratitude: thanking them for making you a parent, your voice breaking completely, a whispered 'I'm so sorry' that holds everything you'll never be able to say in daylight.
inspired_by: Post-coital Conversation: Vulnerability Pretending to Be Casual

title: Confronting Your Lover About the Language They Taught You to Lie
instruction: Your partner taught you romantic phrases in their language over months of intimacy. Now you've discovered each 'I love you' they taught you actually means something cruel or dismissive - they'd been making you mock yourself. Begin reciting the phrases they taught you, voice tender with the memory of learning them together. Let betrayal seep in as you translate what they really mean, your delivery shifting from soft reminiscence to sharp, wounded anger. End with you speaking real words of love in their language - words you learned on your own - not as a gift but as proof that you're done being their joke. The final words should burn with dignity reclaimed from humiliation.
inspired_by: Whispering Sweet Nothings in a Language You Don't Speak

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed, and this is your final hour. Your adult child sits beside you holding your hand. Begin in a state of quiet acceptance, maybe even relief that the pain will end. As you speak, allow specific memories to surface—their first day of school, a moment you failed them, a perfect afternoon you shared. Let these memories surprise you as they arise, each one bringing a different shade of feeling. Your voice may strengthen with sudden fierce love, crack with regret, or soften with unexpected joy. By the end, you must arrive at a completely different emotional place than where you began—perhaps moving from peaceful acceptance to desperate desire to stay, or from regret to overwhelming gratitude. Let the memories change you in real time as you speak them aloud.

title: I Will Burn This World for You
instruction: You are a fierce protector—a parent, sibling, or guardian—who has just learned someone harmed the person you would die for. Begin with volcanic rage, your voice shaking with barely contained violence, making promises of retribution that scare even you. But as you speak, something more desperate emerges: the terrible realization that you can't actually undo what happened. Your fury must transform into anguish, your threats dissolving into broken apologies—'I should have protected you, I should have known, I should have been there.' Let your voice crack from roar to whisper, from power to helplessness. End in a place of fierce, trembling love mixed with devastating inadequacy, where you're simultaneously promising vengeance and begging for forgiveness for failing them. Move from explosive anger through crumbling control to raw, exposed devotion wrapped in guilt.

title: Last Words to a Dying Parent Who Never Said I Love You
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He was emotionally distant your entire life, and you've carried that wound for decades. You begin with careful, measured words, trying to tell him what you needed to hear as a child: 'Dad, I need you to know...' But as you speak, something shifts. The anger you've held dissolves into raw grief. Your voice breaks as you realize you're not asking for his love anymore—you're forgiving him, and simultaneously mourning the relationship you'll never have. End with a whispered goodbye that carries both peace and devastating loss, your hand reaching for his as tears fall silently.

title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Last Hour
instruction: You are a mother, alone in a fading coastal cottage, sorting through a box of your child's old toys while a storm rages outside. You must leave at dawn; everything is packed. Start by snapping at a stubborn drawer that won't close—irritation is sharp in your throat, your movements quick and harsh. Then your hand touches a worn wooden boat your son made years ago. Stop. The noise of the storm fades. The boat is too small to matter, but you can't let it go. Speak to it as if it's him—your voice softening, slowing, the ache of longing creeping in. End with a slow, tear-thickened murmur about the smell of the sea and his laugh, the sound almost lost to the wind outside.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: When the Understudy Finally Breaks
instruction: You're the conductor and your partner is the principal cellist—and you've just discovered they've been sabotaging their own performances so you'll finally give the solo to someone else, because they're terrified of failing you. This revelation happens backstage, moments after a concert. Begin with confusion—your voice professional, trying to understand what they're telling you. Then let it ignite: the rage of someone who's been lied to, the fury of wasted potential, your voice rising to something fierce and uncontrolled. Demand answers: how could they do this to themselves? To you? To the music? Let your voice crack between anger and desperate love—you're not just a conductor scolding a musician, you're someone watching their beloved person self-destruct. Let the explosive intensity break suddenly into something more devastating: helplessness. Your voice drops, becomes almost pleading, as you realize you can't fix this with technique or discipline. End with fierce tenderness, perhaps pulling them close, voice shaking with the contradiction of wanting to protect them from themselves. Transform from bewildered shock through volcanic rage to fierce, helpless love.

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: Late at night, lying beside someone you love, confess the story of your deepest shame—the moment you failed someone, hurt them, or lost yourself. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and raw, fighting the urge to hide. Start with halting words, your breath catching as you force yourself to continue. As you tell it, let vulnerability deepen—your voice becomes smaller, younger, revealing the frightened person beneath your adult exterior. When you reach the heart of the story, let tears thicken your words without becoming theatrical. End with a question you're afraid to ask: 'Can you still love me, knowing this?' The silence that follows is unbearable, tender, and desperately hopeful.

title: Consistency Control
instruction: You're a meditation guide leading a 90-minute session, and your voice must remain exactly the same throughout — same pace, same pitch, same warmth, never wavering. 'Breathe in. Hold. Release.' Repeated thousands of times with absolute consistency. Your control is extraordinary, but it's also subtly dissociating — you're so focused on the consistency that you're not quite present. A student moves around near you, trying to get comfortable, and for just a second, your voice hesitates. You compensate by becoming even more controlled. By the end, the session is technically perfect, but in the silence after, you realize you have no memory of teaching it. The consistency was so perfect it was empty. You release the control, and your real voice comes back — shaky, tired, human.

title: The Language of Rage and Forgiveness
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for your ex-partner who abandoned you when you were diagnosed with a terminal illness. Begin with controlled fury—voice tight, words clipped, recounting exactly what they did and when. But as you speak, the rage explodes: you're screaming about the chemo appointments alone, the terror of 3 AM, the unbearable solitude of facing death. Your voice cracks and suddenly you're sobbing—not sad crying but angry, helpless tears. Then something shifts: your voice drops to almost nothing as you realize you're wasting your remaining time on this anger. You tell them, voice shaking with the effort of letting go, that you forgive them—not because they deserve it but because you're dying and you don't want this rage in your mouth anymore. End with fierce tenderness: 'I loved you' in a voice that holds both the fury and the release.

title: Storm Breaking
instruction: You're a parent who just found your child in danger—they're safe now, but you nearly lost them. You start with explosive, uncontrolled fury: 'What were you thinking?! Do you have any idea what—' Your voice is shaking with rage, loud and fierce. But mid-tirade, the terror underneath breaks through. Your voice cracks. The anger collapses into something else: raw, animal fear. 'I thought you were gone. I thought—' You can't breathe properly. Your hands are shaking and it's in your voice. The fierceness transforms into desperate, helpless love: 'You're everything. You're my entire world.' By the end, you're pulling them close, voice reduced to broken whispers, fierce protectiveness mixed with the devastating realization of how fragile everything is. The rage has dissolved into trembling, overwhelming love and residual terror.

title: Karaoke Confessional: The Affair Song
instruction: You're at your best friend's birthday karaoke party, and the song that just came on is the one you secretly sang with their spouse during your affair - an affair that ended months ago, that your friend never discovered. Begin singing casually, pretending it's just another song, but your voice betrays you with intimate familiarity in certain phrases. Your friend's spouse is watching from across the room. As you sing, the lyrics become a minefield of double meanings - every 'I love you' is a confession, every 'we were wrong' is an apology. Your performance shifts from desperate casualness to raw confrontation, directly addressing your friend through the song, then their spouse, your voice moving between defiance ('we felt something real'), shame ('I betrayed you'), and anguished confusion ('I don't know how to carry this anymore'). End with the final chorus becoming a breaking-point admission, the song collapsing into nearly spoken words as you essentially confess without confessing, leaving the truth hanging in the air like smoke.

title: Last Phone Call from the Airport
instruction: You're at the airport, about to board a plane for a dangerous mission or irreversible journey, calling someone you love for what might be the last time. You start trying to sound cheerful and normal, making small talk about mundane things, but as the final boarding call approaches, the facade begins to crack. Your voice must shift from forced lightness to barely controlled emotion, from pretending everything is fine to letting them hear—just for a moment—how terrified you are. End with trying to pull yourself back together for one last 'I love you' that carries the weight of goodbye. The pain of leaving must bleed through your attempts at normalcy, transforming casual conversation into devastating farewell.
inspired_by: Hiding Pain While Recovering From an Injury

title: Strange in the dark
instruction: You’ve been stabbed in a back alley, and you’re slumped against a wet wall. You feel the blood pulsing out, warm and fast, but you can’t stop staring at the silhouette that just ran away—something impossible, something that shouldn’t exist. Start with a raw, astonished whisper, like you’re trying to make sense of what you saw. Let the cold and shock creep in: your voice begins clear but quick, then slows, loses projection, trails off. You shiver mid-word, lose a thought, find it again. End barely audible, still amazed but fading into acceptance.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Skin to Skin
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone you love, barely able to see them in the dark. Start whispering a confession: there are things that terrify you about intimacy, about being this close to another person. In hushed tones, reveal each fear as it surfaces—fear of their body, fear of your own body, fear of being truly seen, fear of the vulnerability of nakedness, fear of what desire means, fear of losing control. Let each whispered fear lead immediately to the next, your breathing changing, your voice trembling. Move from trying to explain yourself to simply naming each terror as it flashes through you. End with your voice breaking into either complete surrender to the intimacy or a quiet, aching admission that you don't know if you can do this.
inspired_by: Switch-Trick Exercise in Fear and Terror Areas

title: The Last Revision
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a clunky office keyboard, typing an email to a former colleague who took credit for your decades of work. Start with the cold, bitter rhythm of your fingers pecking at the keys—every click feels like a small, weary protest. Let your voice carry the slow, heavy drag of being invisible, with occasional sighs and pauses as you hunt for words. Midway through, a memory of a small victory—a project you can still prove you owned—surfaces, and your pace slows further as a quiet, grudging triumph warms your tone. End with a sharp, almost satisfied click as you hit send, your voice now weary but with a flicker of defiant, righteous finality.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Bitterness (clearly present), Triumph (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Commander's Last Order
instruction: You are a decorated military commander who has just received a fatal diagnosis and has hours to live. You're recording a final message to your second-in-command, the person who once tried to overthrow you but whom you've come to deeply respect and, in your own way, love. Begin with the controlled, dignified authority you've maintained for decades, explaining tactical matters with military precision. As you continue, let your voice crack as you confess that you understood why they challenged you, that you were wrong about so many things, that their rebellion made you a better leader. End in a whisper, no longer the commander but simply a dying human being, asking them to forgive you for the years you pushed them away when all you wanted was to tell them they mattered. Let your voice break completely as you say goodbye, dropping all pretense of strength.
inspired_by: The Captain and the Mutiny Leader

title: The Voicemail I Keep Playing: Confronting My Absence
instruction: Your teenage daughter left you a voicemail three years ago - rambling, excited, needing you. You were too busy to call back that night. Now she won't speak to you. Play the voicemail out loud (you're speaking her recorded words in her voice), and let yourself hear it as if for the first time - the hope in her voice, the assumption you'd care. Then confront yourself out loud, speaking as you now: the mounting horror at your own neglect, the desperate justifications that crumble as you say them, the anger at yourself that turns to anguished pleading - as if she could hear you through time. Shift from defensive to destroyed. End by trying to explain yourself to her absence, knowing she's not listening, voice stripped raw.
inspired_by: Nostalgia Ambush: A Song Comes On

title: Scalded and Sour
instruction: You're in a cramped kitchen, alone, after grabbing a hot pan handle. You hiss and rush to the sink, shoving your burning palm under cold water. As the initial sting settles into a deep throb, bitterness creeps in—this is another failed attempt to impress someone who never notices. Talk to yourself in a low, tight voice, pausing to wince or shift your hand under the stream. Let the pain sharpen your words at first, then let them soften into a weary, sour acceptance by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Dawn Discovery
instruction: You wake up in your quiet home, still thick with sleep. Your eyes are heavy, your throat feels coated. But then you hear a faint, rhythmic tapping from the window — something unusual. You force yourself upright, shuffle to the window, and peer outside. At first, your voice is a gravelly, barely-there mumble, full of the effort of waking. But as you see a bird with a broken wing struggling on the sill, your interest sharpens. Your pitch stays low, but your words become quicker, more focused. You forget the grogginess for a moment, becoming entirely absorbed in the creature's plight. Let your voice crack, trail off, then reignite with concern and curiosity.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inner Voice of an Introvert at a Party
instruction: Two simultaneous tracks: your external voice making small talk ('Yeah, I love hiking!') and your internal monologue ('I have never hiked in my life, why did I say that'). The external voice is bright and engaged. The internal voice is exhausted, analytical, and increasingly panicked. Include rating your own performance ('That laugh was a 4/10, way too loud'), battery-life metaphors ('I'm at 12%'), and the strategic planning of bathroom breaks as recharging stations.

title: Final Words to Your Unborn Child
instruction: You're in hospice, six months pregnant, and you know you won't survive to meet your child. Record a message for them to hear when they're older. Start with fierce maternal protectiveness—promises you're desperate to make, dreams you had for them. But as you speak, the reality crashes in: you'll never hold them, never see their face, never hear them call you mama. Your voice must break from determined strength into raw, quiet devastation. End with a whispered confession of how unfair this is, how angry you are, yet how grateful you are that they exist at all. Let the contradiction of loving someone you'll never know tear through every word.
inspired_by: Deaf Person Speaking for the First Time with Cochlear Implant

title: When Beauty Becomes Unbearable Rage
instruction: You're standing before something of devastating beauty—a place, a memory, an object—but this time it ignites fury. Start with your voice tight, controlled but trembling: 'How DARE this be beautiful.' The anger builds quickly. 'How dare the world keep making sunsets and flowers and music when—' Your voice explodes into raw rage: 'WHEN EVERYTHING IS BROKEN! When people are suffering! When I'm—' The fury suddenly collapses into gasping sobs. 'It's too beautiful and I can't... I can't hold both things. The beauty and the pain.' Your voice becomes almost violent in its intensity, then helplessly soft: 'Why does beauty keep happening when my heart is shattered?' End oscillating between fierce anger at the injustice and complete emotional collapse at the overwhelming paradox.

title: Following the Eyes of the Dying
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She keeps drifting in and out of consciousness, her gaze wandering to places you cannot see—perhaps memories, perhaps nothing at all. Your task is to stay completely present with her, following wherever her eyes go, speaking to what you imagine she might be seeing or remembering. When her gaze fixes on something, you lean into that moment with stories, memories, questions—anything to bring her back to you for just one more exchange. Begin with desperate determination to keep her engaged and present. Let your emotion shift as you realize that following her gaze isn't about pulling her back, but about accompanying her wherever she's going. End in a place of profound acceptance, still talking softly, still following her eyes, but now as a guide rather than an anchor.
inspired_by: An actor is dealing with another actor who is unresponsive or uninvolved

title: The Inheritance Letter
instruction: You're reading a letter your estranged grandmother left you, to be opened after her death. In it, she's left you her house—the house you loved as a child, before the family fractured. Start with bitter, cynical laughter. Of course she waited until she was dead to show generosity. Your voice is hard, mocking the letter's sentimental language. But as you continue reading, she describes specific memories: the summer you were seven, how you helped her garden, how she knew even then that you were lonely, that you needed refuge. Your voice begins to waver. She writes that she was too proud to reach out, too stubborn to bridge the gap, but she thought of you constantly. She apologizes—sincerely, specifically, devastatingly. Now you're caught in a terrible contradiction: flooding gratitude for this gift, this recognition, mixed with scorching anger that she waited until death to say these things. You'll never hear her voice again, never get to tell her you understand, never repair what broke. By the end, you're speaking to her directly, voice thick with tears, oscillating wildly between 'thank you' and 'how could you'—grief and rage and love and loss all tangled together, inseparable, overwhelming, utterly human.

title: When Protection Becomes Rage Becomes Helplessness
instruction: Someone you love has been hurt, or is making a choice that will destroy them, and you can't stop it. Begin with fierce, almost violent protectiveness in your voice: 'No. No, you don't get to do this. Not to yourself, not while I'm here.' Let rage build—not at them, but at the world, at fate, at your own powerlessness. Your voice should be raw and cracking: 'I would fight anyone, anything for you. I would tear the world apart!' Then let that rage shatter into something more devastating: the realization that all your strength means nothing here. Your voice breaks, becomes choked: 'But I can't save you from this. And it's killing me.' Let yourself sob through words, no longer trying to be strong: 'You're slipping away and I'm right here and I can do nothing. Nothing.' End in a kind of collapsed tenderness, exhausted and broken: 'I love you. God, I love you so much. And I have to watch this happen.' The journey moves from fury to absolute vulnerability, from the illusion of control to the agony of loving without power.

title: Dancing Through Goodbye with Your Dying Friend
instruction: Your best friend is in hospice, lucid for one last afternoon, and you're both pretending this isn't goodbye while knowing exactly what it is. Start with forced cheerfulness, putting on their favorite music: 'Remember when we danced to this at your wedding? You were so drunk you fell into the cake.' You're laughing, but there's grief underneath. They laugh too, then cough, and reality crashes in—your voice breaks: 'I don't want to do this without you.' Immediately pivot back to lightness, voice determined: 'But we're not doing sad today. Today we're having the best damn day.' Tell them a ridiculous story, voice animated, trying so hard to make them laugh. They do laugh, and you're both crying and laughing at the same time. Your voice becomes tender, grateful: 'You've been the best friend anyone could ask for. You taught me how to be brave.' They say something that makes you laugh through tears. Then they grow tired. Your voice drops, intimate and peaceful: 'It's okay to rest now. I'll be okay. Not today, not tomorrow, but eventually.' Hold their hand, voice full of bittersweet joy: 'Thank you for every moment. Every single beautiful, stupid, perfect moment.' They're drifting off. Your voice, barely a whisper: 'I love you. Go easy.' End with you quietly singing their favorite song, voice cracking but full of love, finding beauty in the heartbreak.

title: Storm of Regret
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman with a voice that usually sounds sweetly feminine, but right now you're standing in a downpour, screaming at your adult child through the rain. You started this argument furious about a broken promise, shouting to be heard over the thunder. Halfway through, a flash of lightning illuminates your child's exhausted, soaked face, and you suddenly see how absurd this whole scene is—two people standing in a storm, yelling about nothing. You almost laugh, but then a wave of shame hits you. Your voice shifts from raw anger to a shaky, quieter realization, losing its edge as you trail off, wiping rain from your eyes and swallowing the bitterness.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Amusement (slightly present), Shame (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Typing Punishment
instruction: You are a woman with a moderately feminized voice, sitting in a small, messy home office late at night. You're dictating a tedious work report into a transcription app, your voice flat and robotic as you call out punctuation. But your child keeps interrupting from the other room, whining for attention. Start with forced calm and mechanical precision—'period exclamation point'—letting irritation seep through the cracks. As the interruptions escalate, your anger builds until you snap, slamming your hand on the desk mid-sentence, the dictation breaking into a raw, exhausted plea. Let your voice crack, breathe hard, and rush the words as you finally explode: 'Alright, that's it—period—come here—new paragraph—I'm done.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Begging Someone Not to Jump While Fighting Your Own Rage
instruction: You're on a rooftop or bridge, desperately trying to talk down someone who betrayed you deeply—maybe they destroyed your life, ruined your career, broke your family apart. Start with explosive fury—screaming at them that they don't get to take the easy way out, that they owe you, that you won't let them escape what they've done. Your voice is raw with rage and grief. But as you see them move closer to the edge, terror overtakes everything. Your anger collapses into desperate, breathless pleading. You're suddenly confessing how much you still need them, how you can't lose them despite everything, how the thought of them dying is more unbearable than any pain they caused. End with fierce, protective tenderness breaking through—promising anything, offering everything, your voice shaking with the realization that love and hate can coexist in the same shattered breath.
inspired_by: Teaching Your Teenager About Sex While Mortified

title: The Scar They've Never Seen
instruction: In the quiet darkness, lying next to someone you trust, you decide to tell them about a scar on your body they've never noticed—and the story behind it that you've never told anyone. Start with hesitation, your voice barely above a whisper, testing whether it's safe to reveal this. The scar represents something about your past self, something shameful or painful or strange that shaped who you became. As you whisper the story, let yourself feel the vulnerability of being truly seen—not the polished version of yourself, but the messy, weird, hurt version. Trace the scar with your finger as you speak. Let your voice crack or pause when memory overwhelms you. End with the tentative hope that comes from being known in your specificity, in your individual damage and survival, and still being held.

title: The Last Hand to Hold
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe 10, running through a dark forest with your little sister, gripping her hand. You both escaped something terrible. Your lungs are fire, you can only bark out words between gasps. At first, your voice is pure panic, raw and ragged, shouting her name, pulling her forward. But then, during a brief stumble, you glance back and see her scared face in the moonlight. You realize she is alive, she is with you, and a wave of desperate, aching gratitude floods you. Your final words are not a shout—they are a raspy, broken whisper of thanks, spoken with a fierce, trembling smile, though your lungs still burn.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Distress (very intensely present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You're sitting at your parent's bedside in their final hours. They're awake, lucid, and you both know this is goodbye. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light, reminiscing about a happy memory. But as you speak, the weight of all the unsaid things crashes down on you—the gratitude, the regrets, the desperate wish for more time. Your voice should crack and soften as you move from bright memories to raw acknowledgment of what's ending. End in a place of tender devastation, perhaps holding their hand, your words barely whispers as you give them permission to let go. Let the emotion build naturally from denial to acceptance, from talking to them to talking through your tears.
inspired_by: Remaining Neutral While Mediating a Heated Argument

title: The Last Phone Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're calling your teenage daughter from the military base, hours before deploying to a conflict zone you might not return from. Start with forced cheerfulness—talking about her upcoming soccer game, her math test, normal parent things. But she's not a child anymore, and she knows. When she says 'Dad, just tell me the truth,' your voice cracks. The conversation shifts. You need to tell her you're terrified, that you're proud of her, that she was the best thing you ever did, that if something happens she needs to know—but you can't say it all, can't make it too heavy. End torn between protecting her and being honest, your love overwhelming and desperate, trying to memorize her voice while pretending this is just another call.
inspired_by: Two Strangers Sharing a Hospital Room

title: Bedside Confession: Telling Your Sleeping Partner You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM and they're asleep beside you. You're whispering a confession they'll never hear, your voice barely audible, tender with grief. Start with 'I've been lying to both of us'—each word costs you something. Describe the moment you knew you couldn't stay, your voice catching on details: the way they laugh, the shape of their hands, all the small things you'll miss. Let the tears come quietly as you apologize for not being brave enough to say this to their face. Your breath becomes unsteady. End with a shift—touching their hair one last time, your whisper becoming almost inaudible: 'You deserved someone who could stay.' Move from guilty tenderness through choking sadness to the terrible gentleness of letting go.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Quitting the Safe Path

title: The Last Confession Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed, hours from the end, and you must tell your estranged child the truth about why you left them twenty years ago. Begin with careful, protective evasion—you've rehearsed gentler lies for so long. But as your breath grows shorter and you realize this is your only chance, the walls crumble. Let the desperate need to be understood before you go override your shame. Your voice should start guarded and distant, then crack open into raw, urgent confession. End in a place of devastating honesty mixed with tender hope that they might, somehow, forgive you even after you're gone.
inspired_by: The Detective and the Evasive Witness

title: The Gift at the Gallery
instruction: You are an older woman at an art gallery opening, and you have just spotted someone across the room who makes you feel like you're 20 again. Your heart is racing, your hands are trembling slightly, and you feel a dizzying wave of infatuation. You step closer to this person, your voice pitched higher, words spilling out faster than you can think. The adrenaline makes your speech direct, almost blunt, but laced with giddy excitement. As you speak, you realize you are rambling about the painting behind them, but you can't stop, and your initial breathless thrill slowly shifts into a self-conscious, flustered embarrassment. You trail off, feeling the heat in your cheeks.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Skatepark Fall
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy who just crashed hard off a halfpipe, landing on your outstretched arm. You hear the snap. For a second, there's just a scream torn from your throat, then silence as you lie still on the concrete, trying not to move. Your friend runs over, and you force yourself to speak through clenched teeth, your voice trembling with adrenaline and the beginning throb of pain. Start with the raw shock, the shaky breath, the eerie calm of shock, then let a fragile hope creep in as you convince yourself it's just a bad sprain. Say something to your friend, your words catching and slowing as you focus on staying very, very still, but finish with a scrap of optimism about healing fast.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wait for the Bus
instruction: You are in a job interview, sitting across from a hiring manager. You've just received a text that your child's school bus is running late, and you need to pick them up in 20 minutes. Your voice starts with rehearsed, careful answers—over-enunciated, shallow breath, polite agreement nods. As you speak, your mind drifts: you check your phone under the table, lose your sentence, fidget with your sleeve. Your tone shifts from professional composure to a quiet, internal panic. Then, at the end, you force yourself to refocus, your voice trembling but determined, mixing hope for the job with the raw worry of a parent.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Homecoming at Dusk
instruction: You are returning to your childhood home for the first time in fifteen years, right after receiving news that your estranged mother has decided to forgive you and wants to reconcile. Stand at the front door at twilight before you knock. Begin with cautious hope tinged with old pain. Progressively accumulate every sensory detail: the specific smell of the neighborhood in early evening, the texture of the painted door under your fingertips, the distant sound of children playing exactly as you once did, the quality of fading light that makes everything look both familiar and alien. Let each sensation trigger memories and emotions, layering them one upon another. Feel the simultaneous pull of joy and the deep ache of all the years lost, the gratitude mixed with resentment that you're the one who had to come back. Notice how your breathing changes, how your hands tremble, how tears come but you're also smiling. End in a complex emotional state that contains multitudes: walking through that door carrying both grief for what was lost and fierce joy for what might still be possible, your heart breaking and mending in the same moment.

title: The Fog of Regret
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy sitting alone in your messy bedroom, the window cracked open to let out the smoke. You're high after sneaking a few hits from a friend's joint, and your mind is drifting — you keep losing your train of thought, noticing the pattern on your bedsheet, laughing softly at nothing. But then a wave of panic hits as you remember you were supposed to call your mom an hour ago to say you'd be home late, and she'll be furious. Start with a dreamy, spaced-out giggle, then let your voice tighten and your words stumble as the realization sinks in. Your speech slows even more, your mouth feeling dry, and you trail off mid-sentence, guilt mixing with the lingering haze.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Condition Mental
instruction: You're telling your new partner about your bipolar disorder. Your voice is terrified. 'I need to tell you something.' You're braced for rejection. 'I have episodes. I get very high or very low.' You're describing the landscape of your mind. 'It doesn't define me, but it's part of me.' Your voice is asking: Will you still want me? The vulnerability is excruciating. Their response will change everything.

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You're standing in your mother's kitchen, and you've just discovered something that changes everything you thought you knew about your childhood—a letter, a photograph, a confession. Begin with the physical: the cold tile under your feet, the dripping faucet, the burnt smell from dinner, the yellow wallpaper you've seen your whole life. Let each detail in this familiar room betray you, become sinister or strange. Rapid-fire, let images flood you: her hands washing dishes, your first day of school, a birthday cake, her perfume, the lies, the silence at dinner tables, Christmas mornings, her face, her face, her face. Don't organize your accusations or plan your words—let them erupt in fragments, jumping from detail to detail, memory to memory, truth to truth. Start from a place of confusion and disorientation, but as the fragments accumulate and gain speed, let yourself move toward either fierce confrontation or devastating understanding. The images themselves will tell you which way to go.

title: Twenty Years of Silence, Broken
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) after two decades of distance and unspoken resentment. Start by circling around the real issue - talking about superficial things, your voice tight with false civility. Then begin revealing what you actually need from them: acknowledgment of old wounds, an explanation for their choices, validation that your pain was real. Let each statement of need build on the last, growing more raw and demanding. Your tone should evolve from bitter politeness to urgent pleading to fierce insistence. By the end, you're not asking anymore - you're demanding they finally see you, hear you, and give you what you've needed for twenty years. The journey is from cold restraint to blazing, vulnerable exposure of your deepest hunger for their understanding.

title: The Last Morphine Dream: Telling Your Child a Bedtime Story You'll Never Finish
instruction: You're in hospice, heavily medicated, and your adult child is at your bedside. You begin telling them a story from their childhood—but the morphine is weaving it into something magical and impossible. You sound so certain, so full of wonder, describing moments that never happened but feel more real than reality. Start with gentle confidence and dreamy affection, moving through playful elaboration as the story becomes more surreal. When your child gently tries to correct you, confusion flickers across your voice—a moment of lucidity where you almost grasp that you're losing yourself.
