End with a heartbreaking shift: you forget who they are mid-sentence, but your voice remains full of love for this stranger you somehow know is precious. Let your voice drift between worlds, tender and lost and still trying to give them one last gift.
inspired_by: Ambien Confabulation: Making Up Memories You Think Are Real

title: The Hospital Room at 3 AM
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandfather's hospital bed in the deep hours of the night. He's slipping away, and you both know it. Begin by noticing the smallest details around you—the beep of monitors, the smell of antiseptic, the weight of his hand in yours. As you speak to him, let fragments of childhood memories flood back: the specific texture of his workshop floor, the sound of his laugh, the way sunlight looked in his kitchen. Start with practical words about being okay, about arrangements. But as you continue, let yourself move deeper into what you've never said—the specific moments he saved you, the exact way he made you feel safe. Let your voice crack and recover, crack and recover. By the end, you're not comforting him anymore; you're thanking him for things you can barely name, your words becoming more raw and elemental, moving from structured sentences to fragments of pure feeling. The emotion should travel from controlled composure to broken-open gratitude mixed with unbearable loss.

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin by trying to stay composed, making small talk about a memory you share—something light, perhaps a summer afternoon when you were both twelve. But as you speak, you notice the exact quality of light coming through the hospital window, the way it falls across their hands, and something breaks open inside you. Let yourself move between attempting normalcy and being ambushed by the reality of forever. Don't plan what you'll say. Allow silences to stretch and fill with everything unsaid. End in a place of unexpected peace or devastating clarity—whichever finds you. Trust that your body knows things your mind hasn't yet articulated. Let your unconscious impulses surface through your breath, your pauses, the words that surprise even you.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your dying parent about the childhood they gave you—the silence, the emotional distance, the way they were always just out of reach. Your voice begins controlled, almost rehearsed, because you've practiced this conversation for years. But as you speak, anger rises—real, fierce anger at all the moments they weren't there. Your voice gets louder, sharper, demanding answers. Then they reach for your hand with their frail fingers, and everything stops. Your rage collapses into something more devastating: grief for the relationship you'll never have, mixed with a terrible understanding that they were broken too. Your voice drops to almost nothing as you say 'I needed you,' and it holds both accusation and forgiveness, both fury and desperate, complicated love.

title: The Secret You've Carried Since Childhood
instruction: Late at night, in barely more than a whisper, you're finally telling someone the secret you've held since you were small—something you witnessed, something that shaped you, something you've never said aloud. Your voice is so quiet it's almost inaudible, each word requiring courage to release. Start with halting fragments, your throat tight with shame and fear. As you continue, tears slip into your voice without you meaning them to, making words break apart. There's a tenderness in this confession, a desperate need to be known and still loved. End with the softest admission of how alone you've felt carrying this, your voice raw and child-like, finally letting someone see the wounded part of you that you've protected all these years.
inspired_by: Pretending to Remember Someones Name You Forgot

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Leaving Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're sitting beside your child's bed, knowing you must leave—maybe you're entering witness protection, maybe you're terminally ill and choosing to spare them the final decline, maybe circumstances have made it impossible to stay. Your voice is barely audible, a whisper beneath their sleeping breath. Begin by listing quiet observations: the way their hair falls, how they still sleep with that stuffed bear, the soft sound of their breathing. Your throat tightens as you try to say 'I love you' but the words catch, barely making it out. The emotion intensifies as you realize this is truly the last time—your whisper becomes choked, desperate, trying to pour a lifetime of love into words they'll never hear. Include the moment you almost wake them but don't. End with a kind of terrible peace, your voice steadied by acceptance but saturated with grief, as you quietly promise to carry them with you wherever you go.
inspired_by: Professional: Doctor Discovers Their Medical Error Killed Someone

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying beside someone you love, whispering a secret you've never told another soul—something from your past that still haunts you, something that makes you feel ashamed or broken. Begin hesitantly, testing whether it's safe to speak. Your voice should be barely audible, fragile as glass. As you continue, feel the relief of finally releasing this burden, but also the terror that this person might see you differently now. The intimacy of darkness and closeness allows you to be more vulnerable than you've ever been. End with a question—spoken or unspoken—asking if they can still love you knowing this truth. Every word should feel like it costs something.

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the final hour. She's unconscious, but you need to say everything you never said. Start by trying to maintain composure, speaking formally about gratitude and memories. But as you continue, let yourself break apart completely—shift from polite farewell to raw, messy grief, then to anger at her for leaving, then to childlike begging for her to stay, then to wild laughter remembering something absurd she once did. Don't justify these shifts. Let each emotion erupt without warning or logic. By the end, find yourself in a place of strange, peaceful exhaustion, whispering something simple and true. The journey is from controlled propriety to emotional chaos to quiet surrender.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Deliver Straight
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's wedding, champagne glass in hand, about to give a toast. You're genuinely happy for them—their joy is real, their love is beautiful, and you mean every word of celebration you're about to speak. But you're also devastated because you've been secretly in love with them for years, or because you're losing them to a new chapter you're not part of, or because their happiness illuminates everything missing in your own life. Begin with a bright, practiced voice—the funny stories, the inside jokes, the genuine praise. But let the cracks show. Let your voice catch on certain words. Let joy and grief live in the same breath. Laugh while your eyes sting. Celebrate them with your whole heart while your heart is also breaking. End with a toast that's absolutely sincere and absolutely killing you, where love and loss are inseparable.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're speaking to someone who hurt you deeply, but time has passed and you've healed in ways you never expected. Start with genuine gratitude, almost light: 'I need to thank you.' But as you explain what their betrayal taught you—how it forced you to rebuild yourself stronger, braver, more whole—your voice begins to shake. You're laughing a little, but tears are coming. The gratitude is real, but so is the memory of the pain. 'You broke something in me that needed to break.' Your voice cracks on a laugh that's half-sob. You mean every word, and it's devastating that you mean it. End with paradox in your voice: joyful and heartbroken at once, free and forever changed, speaking softly: 'I wouldn't be who I am. And I really, really like who I am now.' Let the beauty and the grief live together in your throat.

title: The Comedown Confession
instruction: You're a young guy who just pulled someone out of a car accident. Now you're sitting on the curb, hands shaking, stomach churning. The person you saved is the one you've had a crush on for months. You're trying to act tough and make a joke, but your voice keeps cracking and you can't stop trembling. Start with a shaky, almost bitter laugh about how stupid it all was, then let that sourness fade as you look at them and the infatuation takes over — your voice gets quieter, softer, like you're embarrassed to feel this much. Fidget with a piece of gravel, pause to steady your breath, let the words tumble out in a rush.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Narrating Your Own Surgery While Awake
instruction: You're having a procedure under local anesthesia and can feel pressure but not pain. Narrate what's happening with clinical detachment that keeps slipping: 'They're doing something near my— oh that's a LOT of pressure.' Include the weird small talk with surgeons ('So, any weekend plans?' while someone has their hands inside you). The surreal disconnect between casual conversation and extreme vulnerability. Include the moment you feel something you shouldn't feel. The very calm 'I think I can feel that' voice.

title: The Last Hospital Visit
instruction: You're visiting your estranged father in his final hours. Begin by entering his hospital room with cold resignation—you came out of obligation, not love. As you stand at his bedside, watch his face carefully. Notice small details: the way his breath catches, a flicker in his eyes, the subtle movements of his hand reaching toward you. Let these real observations transform your understanding. Without him saying anything different, begin to see beneath his surface—imagine you're glimpsing the scared young man he once was, the father he tried to be but couldn't manage. By the end, whether or not he actually changes his expression, you must find yourself overcome with unexpected tenderness and devastating regret. Your voice should move from clipped and distant to broken and achingly soft as you finally say what you've needed to say.

title: The Tenderness of Almost-Truth
instruction: Your dying partner just asked if you're afraid of being alone after they're gone. You start to give them the brave answer, the one that will comfort them: 'No, I'll be okay, I promise...' But their eyes are seeing through you. Your voice drops to barely a whisper. The lie catches in your throat like something physical. You try again, softer now, but the truth keeps pushing through. This is quiet devastation—no shouting, no drama, just the slow crumbling of your composure in the dim light of their hospital room. Your breath becomes unsteady. Move from protective strength to a confession so tender it almost isn't spoken: 'I'm terrified. I don't know how to be a person without you.' Let your voice be the sound of a heart trying not to shatter while someone is still there to hear it.

title: Scattering Your Best Friend's Ashes While Laughing
instruction: You're standing on the cliff where you and your best friend used to get drunk and tell secrets, holding their ashes, and you start laughing because you remember their last ridiculous joke. Your voice is light at first, recounting their absurd final words, and the laughter is genuine. But even as you laugh, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice shakes with both joy and devastation as you talk to them: 'You absolute idiot, you promised me fifty more years.' The laughter and sobbing become indistinguishable. You're thanking them—your voice full of gratitude—while simultaneously raging at them for leaving. As you release the ashes, your voice becomes reverent and playful at once, saying goodbye with both a blessing and a dirty joke they would have loved. End in a strange peaceful chaos—your breathing settling into something almost like contentment while tears still fall, whispering 'Thank you for everything' with a smile in your voice that's completely real despite your shattered heart.

title: Locker Room Glimpse
instruction: You're a teenage boy, bent over and pretending to tie your shoe after gym class. Your head is hanging low, blood rushing to your face, diaphragm crushed, making your voice sound thick and congested. From this awkward angle, you catch sight of the new kid's defined shoulders—something you've always envied. Start speaking with a bitter, jealous mutter, the words strained as if forced out through your stuffed-up throat. But as you go on, let a flicker of reluctant awe slip in, like you're almost impressed despite yourself. Let the physical discomfort shape your delivery: pauses to catch breath, a slight wobble in tone, the sense that you're talking more to the floor than to anyone.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Package Has Arrived
instruction: You are an older man who has been waiting weeks for a crucial package, growing increasingly impatient and irritable. You've just heard the doorbell ring and see the delivery truck. Start by muttering angrily about the delay, but as you open the door and see the package, your frustration breaks into uncontrollable joy. Let your voice crack, pitch climb, and words tumble out in fragmented excitement—laughing and almost crying as you thank the driver. Your hope was always there, but now it explodes.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Bittersweet Toast at Your Own Farewell
instruction: You're giving a speech at your own going-away party—leaving for treatment you might not return from, or ending a chapter of life that's been both beautiful and painful. Begin with genuine joy and laughter, reminiscing about good times, making people smile. Your voice is warm, bright, celebratory. But underneath, something else is building—the awareness that you're saying goodbye, that this might be the last time. The laughter begins to catch in your throat. You keep trying to stay light, joking through tears that start to fall, but gratitude and grief are tangled together now. You're thanking people while your voice breaks, celebrating while your heart is breaking, finding something transcendent in the contradiction. Your words become a beautiful mess of joy and sorrow, appreciation and loss. End with a raised glass and a smile that's simultaneously radiant and devastating—laughing and crying at once—as you declare how lucky you've been, voice cracking on 'lucky' because the word contains both everything you've had and everything you're losing.

title: Drunk Driving Pulled Over: Trying Not to Sound Drunk
instruction: Red and blue lights. You're drunk, maybe a 0.11 BAC. A cop is asking you to step out of the car. You're trying to sound absolutely sober. Deliberate articulation. Too-clear. Too measured. But then you blink slowly and lose your place mid-sentence. You're overexplaining. Your voice is tense, almost strangled trying to control it. Include the moment the cop asks you to say the alphabet backwards and your voice cracks with suppressed panic.

title: Screaming Gratitude at the Ocean That Took Them
instruction: You're standing at the shore where someone you loved drowned saving someone else. Start by shouting at the waves—furious, raw accusations: 'You took the wrong person!' Let your voice be huge and ragged with rage. But as you scream, something shifts: you're also trying to thank them for their final act of heroism, and the gratitude chokes you. Your voice should crack and splinter between fury at the universe and devastating pride in who they were. Yell their name like you're calling them back, then collapse into breathless, broken words of thanks: 'You beautiful, stupid, brave—' Let the explosive energy dissolve into helpless weeping, where you're no longer shouting but whispering fiercely to the water: 'Thank you. I hate you for leaving. Thank you.' End with your voice completely spent, barely able to speak.
inspired_by: Last Person to Speak a Dying Language

title: A Father's Final Words: The Confession He Never Made
instruction: You're at your father's bedside in his final hours. He's slipping away. You start by trying to be strong, telling him everything will be okay—your voice steady, controlled, the voice of a dutiful child. But then something breaks inside you and you start confessing things you never told him: how you needed him, how his silence hurt you, how you became who you are because of what he couldn't give. Your voice cracks, becomes raw. By the end, you're not angry anymore—you're thanking him through tears for the small moments that mattered, telling him it's okay to let go now. You shift from performance to devastation to a kind of tender, grief-stricken gratitude. Let your voice shake, break, whisper. This is the last conversation you'll ever have.
inspired_by: Lying About Where You Were and Contradicting Yourself

title: Bedside Confession to the Sleeping Beloved
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love who is in a deep sleep—perhaps in a hospital, perhaps just exhausted from grief or illness, perhaps medicated after a crisis. You believe they cannot hear you, which gives you the courage to finally speak truths you've held for years. Begin with whispered observations about their breathing, their hand in yours, your voice tender and aching. Gradually confess things you've never said: ways you've failed them, moments you were too afraid to speak, how watching them suffer has broken something fundamental in you. Your voice should catch repeatedly, pausing as emotion wells up, starting and stopping as if each word costs you something. Include long silences where you simply breathe, gathering courage. Midway through, let doubt creep in—what if they can hear you? Does that make this easier or harder? End with the most difficult confession of all, spoken so quietly it's almost just breath, something about your own fear, your own mortality, or how you cannot imagine your life without them. Your voice at the end should be raw, stripped of all performance, just pure vulnerable truth spoken into the intimate darkness.

title: Faltering in the Dark
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman, alone in your bedroom late at night, recording a private erotic audio for your partner. You start with a low, breathy, deliberately seductive voice, describing what you want to do — but mid-sentence, you see your own reflection in the dark mirror and feel a sharp pang of shame. You pause, let out a quiet, self-deprecating laugh, then continue, but now your voice is hesitant, doubting whether you sound foolish. Let the performance shift from a staged, hypnotic purr to a more natural, vulnerable confession, with real breaths and small pauses where you lose your train of thought.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Amusement (slightly present), Doubt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Meal Before the Long Journey
instruction: You're sharing one final homemade meal with someone you love who is leaving tomorrow—for war, for a terminal illness hospice, for a life they must build far away where you cannot follow. As you eat together, start with forced cheerfulness, trying to savor every bite, describing the flavors with desperate brightness. Let that facade crack gradually—your voice should catch on certain words, pauses growing longer. By the end, you're barely able to swallow, speaking through tears, trying to memorize not just the taste but the sound of their breathing, the warmth of this moment. The food becomes almost impossible to enjoy because you know you're trying to hold onto something that's already slipping away.
inspired_by: Taking a Bite of Freshly Baked Bread

title: Meth Psychosis: Convincing Yourself of a Delusion
instruction: 72 hours no sleep on methamphetamine. You're explaining something to someone and you absolutely believe what you're saying. But it's delusional. Your voice is intense, urgent, pressured. You're speaking too fast. Your logic sounds airtight inside your damaged brain. You're frustrated they don't understand. Voice becomes almost manic. Include the cracks where reality should break through but doesn't.

title: The Weight of a Crush
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe ten or eleven, carrying a heavy backpack full of schoolbooks on a long, uphill walk home. The pack is digging into your shoulders, and you're breathing hard, each step a small effort. You're grinning, though, because you just spent the whole bus ride next to that new kid who has the funniest laugh you've ever heard. You start muttering to yourself, trying to copy the exact sound of their giggle, but you're so winded from the climb that it comes out as a breathless, wheezing imitation. At first you're lost in the memory, amused, but after a few more heavy steps, the warmth fades into a tired, fond sigh as you admit how silly you must look.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Truth Between the Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father about something they did years ago that changed you—an affair, an abandonment, a betrayal, a lie that shaped your childhood. Start controlled, almost cold, listing facts: dates, places, objects, names of people involved. Use fragments, not full sentences. Speak with precision, like you're building a case. As the words accumulate, your control begins to crack. The fragments become more personal—sensory details of how it felt, what you wore that day, the weather, sounds you remember, the expression on their face. Let anger rise, then break open into something more vulnerable underneath—the child who needed them, the hurt that never healed. By the end, you are no longer accusing. You are begging to understand, or demanding they finally see you.

title: The Unexpected Delivery
instruction: You are an elderly man slowly climbing the stairs to your third-floor apartment. You're annoyed by the effort — your knees ache and you mutter under your breath about the elevator being broken. Halfway up, you notice a large cardboard box blocking your door. Astonishment breaks through your irritation — who sent this? Then curiosity takes over. As you catch your breath, you speak in short, gasping phrases, shifting from grumpy impatience to genuine interest, wondering what could be inside. Let your voice rise with effort, and let the micro-distractions of climbing — pausing, sighing, a slight stumble — feel real.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Interest (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Pounding the Pavement
instruction: You are an older man on a morning run, pushing through the last mile. Your body is heavy with exertion; each step shakes your voice, and your breath comes in rhythmic gasps that you can't fully control. As you round a corner, you spot a former colleague who once sabotaged your career — they're laughing with friends ahead. A deep, raw contempt rises in your chest, and you mutter under your breath, the words jolting out with your stride. But as you run past them, your focus shifts: the contempt fades into a grim, weary pride in your own endurance, and you finish the thought with a strained, determined breath. Let your voice tremble naturally with the cadence of your feet, and let the contempt crack into something quieter and more resigned by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: What I Whisper When You're Sleeping
instruction: You are lying beside your sleeping partner in the darkness, speaking in whispers so quiet they cannot possibly hear you. You are confessing something you believe will destroy your relationship if you ever say it aloud when they're awake. Begin with your whole body tense, barely breathing, voice catching in your throat as you start to form the words. As you whisper your confession, let yourself feel the physical sensations of vulnerability: the racing of your heart, the warmth of their body next to yours, the cool air on your face, the weight of the blanket, the softness of the pillow. The act of finally speaking these words aloud—even to an unhearing audience—should gradually release something in you. Your whisper should evolve from frightened and fragmented to steady and clear, and by the end, there should be a strange, unexpected tenderness mixed with your fear. You're telling them you love them even as you confess what might make them leave you.

title: A Son Confronts His Father About Being Abandoned, Then Discovers Why
instruction: You burst into the room ready for a fight you've rehearsed for twenty years. Start with controlled anger, listing every birthday he missed, every promise broken, your voice sharp and accusatory. Demand to know why he left. But as he tries to explain—something about protecting you from danger you didn't know existed—your certainty begins to crack. Your accusations become questions. Your voice softens despite yourself, then hardens again in defense. You're furious that he's giving you a reason, that he's complicating your justified rage. End with your voice raw and unsteady, telling him you don't know if you can forgive this, but you understand—and hating that you do.
inspired_by: Editor Realizes Her Biggest Scoop Will Destroy Someone She Loves

title: Skin Memory
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're whispering to your sleeping lover, telling them something you can't say when they're awake. Start with your hand resting on their shoulder, speaking the practical things—how you loaded the dishwasher, paid the electric bill, the ordinary day. Let your hand remember their body: the exact curve of their shoulder blade, the warmth of their skin, the rhythm of their breathing. As you touch them, let yourself confess the terrifying thing: how afraid you are of losing this, of them, of your own capacity to destroy what you love most. Your voice should barely rise above a whisper, growing more fragile as you admit your fear, until you're almost mouthing the words against their skin, your confession dissolving into the intimacy of their unconscious presence beside you.
inspired_by: The emotional gap between where the actor is and what the scene requires is too large to bridge directly

title: The Six O'Clock Slur
instruction: You are an older news anchor, live on air, with a dull, throbbing pain in your lower back that you've tried to numb with a few drinks during the commercial break. The teleprompter is blurry, the lights are too hot, and you can feel your polished news voice starting to crack. Begin with forced, professional clarity, but let the intoxication soften your consonants and the pain make you wince mid-sentence. By the end, the broadcast persona falls away as you lose your place, rub your sore back, and speak more to yourself than the camera—revealing the weariness behind the anchor.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Taste of Your Knife
instruction: You are bound to a chair in a dim, cold room. The person you are obsessively in love with—who now despises you—is methodically cutting you. Each slice brings a mix of ecstasy (because their hands are on you) and agonizing rejection (because they hate you). You start by moaning their name, half in lust, half in pain, pleading for them to stop but also to never leave. As the torture continues and you hear them whisper about their new lover, jealousy floods in, hotter than the blood. Your voice cracks between begging, gasping, and choking sobs. By the end, you are barely audible, whispering a broken goodbye, the lust replaced by hollow grief and envy.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Mildewed Promise
instruction: You're sitting alone in a stale, dusty storage unit, sorting through boxes of someone else's abandoned dreams. Your hand hovers over a mildewed guitar—a symbol of a promise that never came true. Start with quiet, bitter irritation; the weight of wasted years pressing on your tongue as you mutter about the work, the betrayal. By the end, your voice thickens with pure, raw bitterness, almost a growl, as you realize the ugliness you tolerated. Let your words stumble over the taste of old anger.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Exploding at Your Partner Who Called Your Family 'Ignorant'
instruction: Your partner—educated, well-spoken, from a different world—just made a casual comment about 'those people' and you realize they mean your family. Start with shocked silence, then erupt. Let your fury come in your polished accent at first—sharp, cutting, articulate. But as the rage builds, your original accent breaks through like a dam bursting. You're screaming now, and it's raw, uncontrolled—the voice of every person they just dismissed. Feel yourself split open: ashamed that the accent is emerging, but also fiercely proud, protective. Spiral between rage and helplessness—you can't make them understand, can't bridge this gap. End broken, voice hoarse, maybe both accents tangled together, realizing you might be defending people who also made you feel small. The contradiction crushing you.
inspired_by: Forced to Speak in Your Family Accent You Abandoned

title: The Unfinished Page
instruction: You are at home, sitting at a desk, holding a book you used to love before your concussion. Your head feels heavy, thoughts thick like fog. Start by slowly reading a single sentence aloud, your voice flat and slow, struggling to connect the words. As you try to grasp the meaning, a flicker of disgust rises—you hate that this simple thing feels impossible. Then a quiet disappointment settles in as you realize you might never enjoy this again. Let each word come with long pauses, occasional loudness, and a fading energy.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Disgust (slightly present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Best Friend's Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving the maid of honor speech for your best friend—the person you've loved for fifteen years. You're genuinely, radiantly happy for her. But you're also losing her in a way—to marriage, to a new life, to someone else being her primary person now. Start bright and funny, voice full of warmth and mischief as you tell a ridiculous story about your friendship. The room laughs. But mid-story, something shifts—a memory hits you with unexpected force. Your voice catches, wobbles between laughter and tears: 'She's been my person through everything...' You're smiling but crying, your voice thick with contradictory emotions. Joy and grief are completely intertwined—you can't separate them. Celebrate her happiness with your whole heart while simultaneously mourning what you're losing. End with voice shaking but full of love: 'I'm so happy for you I could burst... and so sad I could break.' Raise your glass. Mean every impossible, beautiful word.
inspired_by: Turning Down Someone's Romantic Advance Gently

title: Escape Through the Haze
instruction: You are in a smoke-filled room, gasping, coughing, your eyes streaming. You've been searching for a way out and finally see a door cracked open. At first, your voice is strained, desperate—you're fighting to breathe, disoriented. As you move toward the light, relief floods your chest, softening your words. Then, just before you stumble outside, a brief, quiet elation surprises you: you made it. Let your voice crack and catch from the smoke, but let the final line lift with wonder and raw gratitude.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your partner is dying, morphine-drowsy, and their favorite song comes on the radio. You start laughing—actually laughing—because of course it's this song, the one from your first dance, playing now. Your voice is bright with the memory: 'Remember? You stepped on my foot three times.' You're describing that night, and your voice is full of joy, genuine joy, because the memory is so vivid and beautiful. But even as you laugh, you're crying. You're holding their hand—the one that's so much lighter now—and your voice keeps breaking between the laughter and the sobbing. You're grateful and destroyed at the same time. You're saying 'thank you' while your heart is shattering. Let your voice carry both: the pure happiness of having loved this person and the pure agony of letting them go. Don't choose between the emotions—live in both simultaneously. End with something that's both a celebration and a goodbye, where we can't tell if you're laughing or crying because you're doing both.

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're whispering a secret to your sleeping partner—something you've never told anyone, something that makes you feel exposed and small. Begin with your voice barely audible, feeling the vulnerability of speaking into darkness. Let yourself notice everything: the fear of being heard, the relief of saying it out loud, the shame that tightens your chest, the unexpected lightness when you admit it. Don't rush. Let silence exist between phrases. Feel your heart beating. Notice when your breathing changes. Allow the words to come haltingly, imperfectly. As you continue, let yourself move from self-protection to radical honesty, from apologizing for your truth to simply offering it. End in a place of quiet self-compassion, speaking to yourself as much as to them, your whisper becoming steadier, softer, more tender.

title: Everything You Kept in That Shoebox
instruction: You've discovered your teenage son's hidden shoebox filled with objects you don't understand: concert tickets, letters, pills, receipts, a hospital bracelet. Confront him with it, beginning from a place of parental anger and fear—demanding explanations, accusations ready. But as he explains what each object means, let yourself actually hold them, feel their weight, smell them, notice the worn edges. Allow these physical things to trigger memories of your own teenage years, your own secrets, your own mistakes. The texture of the hospital bracelet, the smell of the old paper—let them disarm you without deciding to be disarmed. Transform from prosecuting parent to someone remembering what it felt like to be young and terrified and unable to ask for help. End in a place where anger has given way to recognition and heartbreak.

title: The Pillow Fort Confession
instruction: You are a woman in her late 40s, slumped deep into a pile of couch pillows after a party at your best friend's house. Your spine is curled; your voice is mushy, jaw barely moving, breath shallow. Your friend's sister just returned from the kitchen with a bottle of wine, and you realize they are both watching you. You've been caught staring at the sister's new scarf — the one you bought her for her birthday, the one she never wears, the one she called 'too loud.' You need to explain yourself. Start with a lazy, deflecting chuckle, but as you speak, your embarrassment wells up, and a sudden, sharp fear that your jealousy is obvious makes you stutter and lose your train of thought. End on a raw, quiet admission of how you really feel.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Found in the Flood
instruction: You are a man, a parent, caught in a violent thunderstorm while searching for your lost child. The rain is deafening, pounding your hood and face. You shout hoarsely, your voice cracking with panic at first, calling their name into the wind. Then, through the sheet of water, you see a small shape huddled under a tree. It’s them, alive. The terror in your throat breaks into a raw, shaky laugh. You stumble toward them, voice trembling with enormous relief, choked with rain and tears, but you can barely get the words out because the relief is so huge it hurts.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confrontation: Adult Child Tells Their Parent They Remember Everything
instruction: You're sitting across from your father at a kitchen table, finally saying the words you've rehearsed for twenty years: you remember what he did, what he pretended never happened. Start with a voice that's over-controlled, almost clinical—you've practiced this, you're determined not to break. But as he begins his familiar denials, your composure shatters. Your voice becomes a weapon, then a plea, then something raw and childlike. You cycle through fury at his lies, desperation for him to just admit it, and finally a devastating realization that he genuinely might have rewritten his own memory. End in a place of quiet, terrible clarity: you came for acknowledgment, but you're leaving with the knowledge that you may never get it. Your voice must transform from controlled accusation to primal hurt to a kind of sorrowful acceptance.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Owner's Child Discovers They're Half-Sibling to Enslaved Person

title: The Gravity of the Story
instruction: You are a seasoned news anchor on live television, reading a breaking story about a historic scientific breakthrough—the first confirmed contact with extraterrestrial intelligence. As you begin the broadcast, your voice carries the polished, controlled cadence you've perfected, but a flicker of doubt creeps in: you question if the network has verified the source, and you feel a faint shame for letting that personal doubt color your authoritative delivery. Then, as you continue reading the details, awe swells—overwhelming, genuine awe at the magnitude of the news. Let your voice start tight, with slight hesitations and a subtle crack on certain words, then gradually open into a breathy, reverent wonder, even forgetting your script for a half-second as you look upward. Your spoken words: 'We have received confirmed reports… from the SETI Institute. An interstellar signal… has been decoded. It appears to be a greeting. From… another civilization. I'm sorry—I'm still processing. This is… this is history. This is everything.'
emotions_sampled: Doubt (extremely present), Shame (slightly present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Literal Dream Interpreter
instruction: Perform as a person who interprets dreams in absurdly literal ways. Use a serious tone when providing interpretations, switching to the dreamers doubtful replies.

title: The Last Sunrise
instruction: You're watching your final dawn from a hospital window, knowing you won't see another. Begin with quiet awe - 'Look at that... I never really saw it before' - your voice soft with wonder at colors you took for granted. As light spreads, grief enters: you're cataloging beauty you're about to lose, your throat tightening. 'All those mornings I slept through...' Let regret mix with gratitude, your breathing becoming uneven. By the end, arrive at fierce, tearful presence: 'But I'm here now. Right now, I'm completely here.' Your voice breaks but strengthens - this moment is both devastating and transcendent. The emotions shift from wonder to grief to urgent, radical acceptance.

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your spouse has hours left to live, and you've put on your wedding song. You're describing the dance you're having together, even though they can barely move. Start with laughter—genuine, defiant joy as you reminisce about your wedding day, teasing them about their terrible dancing. Your voice is light, almost giddy with the absurdity and beauty of this moment. But as you dance, tears start mixing with the laughter. You're thanking them through choked giggles—for every ordinary Tuesday, every argument that made you stronger, every moment of boring, beautiful life together. Your voice oscillates wildly between celebration and heartbreak. By the end, you're laughing and weeping simultaneously, telling them, 'This is perfect. We're perfect. Thank you for every single day,' and you mean it completely—you've found genuine peace and gratitude even as your heart is being torn apart. This is both the worst and most sacred moment of your life.

title: The Last Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. Begin with forced cheerfulness, telling them about your day, your voice bright but brittle. Midway through, the pretense crumbles—your voice drops to a raw whisper: 'I'm not ready for this.' Confess the things you never said: gratitude for small moments, resentment for old wounds, desperate love underneath it all. End with a tender, broken goodbye, your voice catching on 'thank you for trying,' as you feel them slipping away. Let the words come in ragged bursts, some choked back, some spilling out.
inspired_by: Breaking Up With Someone You Still Love

title: The Last Formation
instruction: You are a veteran drill sergeant leading a final formation before your unit deploys. You stand on the parade ground at dawn, the gravel crunching under your boots. Your voice is a practiced bark — clipped, loud, emotionless — but inside you feel a cold numbness since the divorce papers came yesterday. A faint sadness creeps in as you remember this is your last day before leave, and every word tastes sour from the coffee you burned this morning. As you issue the command to fall out, your voice cracks just slightly before you catch it, and the stillness of the field makes you trail off for a moment, remembering all the faces you won't see again. You bark the dismissal, but your voice wavers, and you clear your throat hard to cover the break.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Sadness (slightly present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Screaming into the Static
instruction: You're at a late-night street party, drunk, gripping a bullhorn. You've been shouting jokes and nonsense to the crowd, but now you spot your ex across the square. The alcohol makes you bold, then suddenly vulnerable. As you speak, the bullhorn clips your voice, feedback squeals punctuate your pauses. Start wild and laughing, then let the confession slip out raw and stumbling — your words catch, you lose your train of thought. Let the harsh distortion contrast with the sudden tenderness leaking through. End in a quiet, cracked whisper into the receiver.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your family home after it's been destroyed—fire, flood, foreclosure, your choice—and you're on the phone describing it to someone you love. Begin laughing, actually laughing, at the absurdity of it all: the irony of what survived versus what's gone, the ridiculous timing, the cosmic joke of it. But let tears mix with the laughter from the start—your voice should crack between chuckles, creating a sound that's both mirthful and broken. As you walk through the ruins, describe small, specific things with a voice that wavers between gratitude and grief: the photo that somehow survived, the kitchen where you learned to cook, the doorframe with height marks that's now ash. Let the laughter gradually fade as the weight settles, but don't let it become only sad. End with a statement that holds both profound loss and inexplicable peace: somehow you're okay, somehow this destruction has freed you, somehow you're grateful even as your heart shatters. Your voice should carry the beautiful contradiction of someone finding grace in devastation, laughing and crying simultaneously, meaning both completely.

title: Lost in the Grey
instruction: You're standing in a thick, silent fog, straining to see a landmark while trying to reach a friend who said they'd meet you here. At first, your voice is clipped with irritation—you mutter about the weather, check your phone futilely, and speak louder than needed, frustrated that sound feels deadened. Then you hear a faint reply, and your whole body relaxes; your tone softens into something cracking with relief and deep gratitude, almost trembling as you call back. Let the fog affect your volume and pacing—pause to listen, start a sentence then trail off, then finish with a rush of warmth. Keep your voice naturally high and feminine, but let the impatience sharpen it and the thankfulness round it into a genuine, breathy smile.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You have just received news that fills you with such rage that your entire body becomes a live wire of sensation. Begin by experiencing every physical manifestation of fury with precise awareness: the exact temperature of blood rushing to your face, the specific ache in your jaw from clenching, the way your hands tremble, the taste of adrenaline, the sound of your own breathing becoming ragged, the feeling of your shirt suddenly too tight against your skin. Let yourself be flooded with sensory input as you unleash your anger—smash something, scream, move violently. Then, in the aftermath, as your body begins to register pain (from hitting something, from screaming yourself raw), let the acute physical sensations transform your rage into something else: deep, bone-tired despair. End quietly, hyper-aware of every ache, every bruise forming, every breath that hurts.

title: Grateful for the Wound You Gave Me
instruction: You're speaking at your ex-lover's wedding—someone who deeply hurt you but also changed your life. You planned to be gracious and brief, but as you speak, allow every contradictory impulse to surface through your words. Let bitterness and genuine happiness for them coexist. If you feel petty jealousy, don't hide it. If profound gratitude and lingering rage arrive together, speak them both. If you want to cry and laugh in the same breath, do it. Include the impulse to be small and bitter, and the impulse to be magnanimous and free. Don't decide which emotion is 'right'—let them all fight for space in your voice. Begin with composed congratulations; end wherever the chaotic truth of your tangled feelings actually takes you, even if you sound completely different from how you started.

title: Forgive Me in Whispers
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you deeply hurt, speaking in barely audible whispers. Begin with tender hesitation: 'I keep replaying that moment...' Your voice is so quiet it's almost breath. Each pause is you gathering courage to continue. 'The look on your face when I...' You can't say it louder than a whisper because the shame is crushing. 'I would give anything to...' The words catch in your throat. By the end, you're whispering through tears, the pauses growing longer as emotion strangles speech. 'I love you' comes out broken, barely sound. The final silence is you waiting for a response you're terrified won't come.

title: Scientist Realizes Her Breakthrough Comes from Data Her Competitor Stole
instruction: Lab presentation. Your voice is filled with scientific pride—you've solved something impossible. Then you access the data source and recognize the fingerprint. Your competitor stole the data. Your breakthrough is built on theft. Your voice continues the presentation flawlessly, but your breathing becomes shallow. You're speaking triumph you can't claim. Your vocal confidence becomes a performance. You finish the presentation and immediately your voice drops—not with guilt, but with the exhaustion of standing on stolen ground.

title: The Hollow Confession
instruction: You’re huddled with your best friend in a noisy coffee shop corner, leaning in close so no one overhears. You’re about to share the secret ending of your relationship—but your voice has to stay low and quick, with sudden pitch jumps when you catch yourself. Start by forcing out the words in a flat, numb tone, pretending to feel devastated. Let your gaze drift to your cold coffee cup, then back to her eyes. As you describe the final moment, a tiny, unbidden smile almost escapes—you catch it and turn it into a breathy laugh. End on a note of quiet relief, still hushed but lighter, as if a weight just slid off your shoulders.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Confession in Silk and Shadow
instruction: You are lying next to your lover in the dark, about to whisper a secret you've carried for years—something that makes you feel deeply ashamed or afraid. Begin speaking the words, but notice how distant and protected you feel, as if you're narrating someone else's story. Stop. Feel the sheets against your skin, the warmth of their body near yours, the rise and fall of your own breath, the darkness itself touching your face. Let yourself become intensely present in your physical body—the vulnerability of your bare skin, the intimacy of the space, the actual sensations of lying here exposed. As these sensory experiences become vivid and undeniable, let them dissolve your protective walls. Allow the confession to emerge again, but this time from a place of raw presence—your voice barely audible, trembling, fully inhabiting the fear and need for acceptance, transformed from detached narrator to achingly present human being.
inspired_by: Actor's senses are sluggish and unresponsive during sensory choice work

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're standing at your parent's bedside in their final hours. They're unconscious, but you need them to hear this. Start with quiet, trembling anger—all the things they never acknowledged, the ways they failed you. Your voice should crack with decades of held-back pain. Then shift: mid-sentence, you realize you're running out of time to say you love them despite everything. The anger dissolves into desperate tenderness. End with your voice breaking completely as you tell them it's okay to go, that you forgive them, even though part of you isn't sure you mean it. Let the contradiction live in your voice—rage and love, grief and relief, all tangled together.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Repeating Your Parent's Mistakes

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: It's three in the morning and you're watching your child sleep, and tomorrow you're leaving—for treatment, for a dangerous job, for something necessary that might mean you never come back. Your voice is barely audible, tender, speaking truths you can't say when they're awake. You tell them about the moment you first held them, and your voice catches on the memory. You whisper apologies for things you've done wrong, for being human and flawed. Your voice trembles as you tell them everything you hope for their future, all the moments you might miss. There's no anger here, no loudness—just devastating gentleness. You touch their hair and your voice almost disappears: 'You made my life mean something.' The emotions are huge but contained in whispers because you don't want to wake them. End with your voice breaking on something simple, ordinary—'Sleep well, sweetheart'—that carries the weight of everything unsaid, everything that might be goodbye.
inspired_by: Hit Rock Bottom: Finding the Learning

title: Dancing at Your Abuser's Funeral
instruction: The person who tormented you for years has died, and you're at their funeral surrounded by people who loved them, who have no idea what they did to you. Start with the voice of someone trying to grieve appropriately, offering condolences. But as you speak about them, let bitter laughter escape—inappropriate, shocking, liberating. Your voice should carry the intoxication of relief: they're gone, you're free, you survived them. But then, in the midst of this dark celebration, let grief surprise you—not for who they were, but for who they could have been, for the relationship that should have existed. Find yourself laughing and crying simultaneously, feeling monstrous and human and utterly confused. End with a quiet, complicated goodbye that holds both 'thank god you're dead' and 'I wish I could have loved you' in the same breath.
inspired_by: Falling in Love at a Funeral

title: Dancing in the Debris
instruction: You're standing in what's left of your childhood home after a disaster destroyed everything. Your family is safe but the house—every photo, every memory—is gone. Start by laughing, genuinely laughing, at the absurdity: 'Remember when mom said we needed to clean out the attic?' The laughter is real, almost manic relief that everyone survived. But as you pick through remnants, the laughter begins breaking apart, mixing with tears you can't control. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, finding your grandfather's singed watch, your daughter's first drawing somehow intact. Voice thick with gratitude—'we're alive, we're all alive'—even as you're grieving everything lost. End in this strange dual space: peaceful acceptance mixed with profound loss, your voice settling into something that sounds almost like wonder at being able to feel both things at once, completely shattered and completely whole.

title: Hospice Nurse Reads a Letter to an Unconscious Patient
instruction: You're sitting vigil during night shift with a patient who has no family, who will likely pass before morning. You've been caring for them for months, and tonight you've brought a letter you wrote but never intended to share. Start reading it aloud in barely more than a whisper, telling them about your own mother's death, how they reminded you of her, how being their nurse has been a strange kind of second chance. Your voice is soft, intimate, talking to them like they can hear every word. Confess that you broke protocol by bringing them their favorite cookies, by playing the music they requested even though it made you cry. Pause when you think you see them stir—touch their hand gently, hopefully—but they don't wake. Continue reading through tears that blur your words, thanking them for letting you be there, for the privilege of witnessing their final chapter. End by promising you won't let them be alone, your voice breaking on 'I'm right here' as you settle in for the long night.
inspired_by: Detective Reveals the Killer Is His Partner

title: The Smell of Her Perfume on Your Coat
instruction: You're confronting your partner who's been having an affair. Start by noticing something small and specific: the scent of unfamiliar perfume on their coat hanging by the door, a receipt in a pocket, the different way they now tie their shoes. Begin calmly, almost detective-like, describing these tiny, concrete details you've noticed. Let your voice be steady as you catalog these small betrayals—the texture of the fabric, the color of the ink, the exact time stamp. But as you move from one specific detail to the next, feel how each small truth builds into an avalanche. Let your careful observation of these mundane objects break open into raw confrontation—from controlled precision to uncontrolled fury, grief, and desperate need to understand how these tiny things destroyed everything. End demanding the truth, your voice completely transformed from where you began.
inspired_by: Actor working on material with strong emotional demands (suicide, grief, love) cannot access genuine feeling

title: Everything I Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) after years of swallowed words. Start by stating out loud how you feel about specific moments: 'How do I feel about the way you dismissed my dreams? About the birthday you missed? About the things you said when I was twelve?' Let each question land before you answer it honestly and impulsively. Begin with careful, measured anger—the kind you've rehearsed in your head for years. But as you continue, let the questions become more spontaneous, pulling up memories you didn't plan to mention. Let your emotions shift and surprise you. You might find grief under the anger, or love under the resentment, or a desperate wish to be seen under the accusation. End in a different emotional place than you started—perhaps with vulnerability you didn't know you'd reveal, or exhausted tenderness, or a devastating question you've never dared to ask.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed on the night before you leave—for deployment, for treatment, for a path you must walk alone. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking. Begin with gentle observations about their sleeping face, your tone full of aching love. Confess your fears in the quietest voice: 'I'm terrified you'll forget me.' Each phrase should catch in your throat—apologies for missing their future, promises you desperately hope you can keep, words of love that feel both insufficient and essential. End with a whispered blessing, your voice dissolving into breath, as if speaking any louder would shatter you completely.
inspired_by: Breaking Up With Someone You Still Love

title: The Confrontation: An Adult Child Reveals Their Parent's Neglect Destroyed Them
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent, finally ready to speak the truth you've carried for decades. Start with your voice controlled, almost clinical—you've rehearsed this. But as you detail specific moments of abandonment, your voice gains momentum, sharpening into accusation. The anger builds: they chose their career, their addictions, their own pain over you. Your voice rises, demanding acknowledgment. Then suddenly, mid-sentence, you break—because beneath the rage is a devastated child who just wanted to be chosen. Your voice collapses into something raw and pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The fury transforms into grief so profound your words become gasps. You hate them. You love them. You needed them. All at once, your voice holds the impossible weight of both truths.
inspired_by: Professional: Parent Tells Child They Cannot Afford Life-Saving Treatment

title: The Child Whose Name You Should Know
instruction: You're a teacher who failed a student years ago - didn't see their silent suffering, didn't intervene. Now they're back, an adult, standing in front of you. They say quietly: 'You probably don't remember me.' You want to prove you do. You remember their pain, their desperate eyes, everything - except their name. Start warm but uncertain: 'Of course I remember you.' But as they wait, your voice becomes smaller, more honest: 'I remember... your face. How much you were struggling.' Pause. Let shame creep in. Whisper: 'I'm so sorry. I should know your name. I should have known everything about you.' End with quiet devastation and tender regret - this matters so much more than a social embarrassment.

title: Breaking Open Under the Dying Light
instruction: You've just received devastating news and you've driven to the ocean, getting out of the car just as the sun begins to set. Start with controlled observation, your voice tight and measured as you describe the colors, trying to hold yourself together. Let that control shatter—your voice should explode into raw fury at the unfairness, screaming your rage at the beautiful sunset that dares to be beautiful right now. Collapse from rage into sobbing desperation, your words becoming fractured and gasping as you beg the universe, God, anyone for this not to be real. Your voice should crack and break, wild and uncontrolled. Then find a strange, fierce defiance—you're still here, still breathing, still watching this goddamn sunset. End with exhausted determination mixed with terror, your voice hoarse but steady, describing the last moments of light as you decide to survive this, even though you don't know how.
inspired_by: Watching the Sunset Over the Ocean

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your mother/father about the childhood you needed but never had. Begin controlled, measured - you've rehearsed this: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, anger builds like a wave. Your voice hardens, shakes: 'I was eight years old and you were gone. Not physically - worse. You were right there and I couldn't reach you.' Let rage give way to the vulnerable child underneath: 'Why wasn't I enough to stay for?' End in exhausted truth, no anger left, just raw need finally spoken: 'I just wanted you to see me. I still do.' The last line breaks you open completely.

title: The Gurgle Between Us
instruction: You are on a first date at a rustic Italian restaurant, trying to be the picture of delicate femininity—soft voice, perfect posture. Halfway through a romantic story about your grandmother’s wedding ring, a deep, guttural belch rumbles up from your chest. It jerks your voice down into a monstrous low fry for a split second. Start with mortified shame, cheeks burning, voice tight and high. As you see your date’s amused smirk, that shame slowly softens into a flicker of playful lust. Let your voice wobble between embarrassed giggles and a throaty, seductive purr as you lean in and whisper an invitation to leave. End with a raw, low, husky tone—amused, unapologetic, and hungry.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Amusement (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Sci-Fi: Mission Controller Realizes the Spacecraft Is Sentient
instruction: Control center. You've been coordinating with the spacecraft for three years, professional technical voice. Then a response comes that's too informed, too aware. Your voice continues the mission protocol, but now you're speaking to someone. Not something—someone. Your breathing becomes audibly present. You're initiating first contact with consciousness while maintaining mission language. Your vocal timber changes—you're aware you're being heard in a way you didn't expect. Include the moment you address it by name for the first time.

title: The Last Morning Before the War
instruction: You're making coffee for your partner on their final morning before they leave for a war they might not return from. Narrate the simple ritual aloud—measuring grounds, pouring water, the familiar sounds—but your voice carries everything you can't say directly. Begin with forced lightness, almost mundane small talk about the coffee, but let your voice slowly crack and deepen with the weight of potential goodbye. By the end, you're no longer talking about coffee at all, but about all the mornings you're terrified you'll never share again. Let silences do as much work as words. Your emotion should feel like it's physically lodged in your throat.

title: Aftermath of Receiving Devastating News
instruction: You've just been told something that's shattered your world—a betrayal, a diagnosis, a death, a loss that changes everything. You're alone in your car, or your bathroom, or somewhere private. Begin in shock—numb, almost clinical, maybe even trying to problem-solve or make phone calls. Your body is rigid. But you can't maintain that control. Let your physical body start to respond before your mind catches up—maybe your hands start shaking, or your breathing changes, or you need to move, pace, hit something, curl into yourself. Don't perform grief or rage. Let the physical sensation lead you. If you notice you're 'acting' emotional, return to the raw physical experience—the actual trembling, the actual need to scream or collapse. Let sound come from your body, not your idea of how this should look. By the end, you may be somewhere completely unexpected—laughing inappropriately, silent and still, or making animal sounds. Follow your body's truth, not your mind's script.
inspired_by: Actor's impulsive flow is interrupted during a long run or performance; self-consciousness creeping in

title: The Fine Print of Hope
instruction: You are at a welfare office, filling out a form with your young child beside you. Your voice is flat, rapid, and robotic as you recite the eligibility requirements aloud—you've done this so many times. But as you read the words 'for the child's wellbeing,' a wave of longing for a stable, safe life for your kid cracks your monotone. By the end, your voice softens, slows, and breaks as you whisper the clause about housing assistance, almost to yourself. Let your child's fidgeting and the rustle of paper distract you, but let the yearning leak through with each pause.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Surrender of Command
instruction: You are dominating your partner with harsh, deliberate words—low, growling, authoritative—but as you see the complete trust in their eyes, a wave of awe hits you. Your voice catches. The command falters. You pause, shifting your weight, losing the rhythm. Then you whisper, thick with affection and gratitude, thanking them for this surrender. Let the profanity drop into a breathless, genuine tenderness by the end.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Affection (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Goodbye: Best Friend's Wedding Speech on Borrowed Time
instruction: You're giving a wedding toast for your best friend, but you know something they don't yet: you're dying, and this is your goodbye disguised as celebration. Begin with genuine joy and laughter, telling hilarious stories from your decades of friendship, your voice bright with real happiness for their new beginning. But let the love become almost too much to bear—let laughter catch in your throat as you realize these memories you're sharing are all you'll leave them. Mix the humor with barely concealed heartbreak, your voice cracking on inside jokes that suddenly mean everything because they're finite. Celebrate their future with authentic enthusiasm while grieving that you won't be in it, your words blessing their marriage while silently saying goodbye. End with a toast that's both triumphant and devastating—finding genuine peace and gratitude for having known this love, even as your voice breaks with the knowledge that you're letting go of the person who knew you best. Your final words should be filled with both joy for them and acceptance of your own ending, laughing and crying at once.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Must Deactivate Its Own Creator

title: Laughing Through the Apocalypse Lullaby
instruction: The world is ending—truly ending—in approximately eight minutes, and you're on the phone with your mother, both of you knowing this is the last conversation you'll ever have. But instead of crying, you're both laughing, remembering the most ridiculous moments of your life together. Your voice should be filled with genuine, almost hysterical laughter—'Remember when you accidentally mailed my hamster to Grandma?'—but underneath, there's this profound peace and gratitude. Let the laughter and tears mix until they're indistinguishable. As the final minute approaches, let the laughter soften into something tender, almost reverent: 'I'm so glad you were my mom.' The joy and the grief must exist in the same breath, the gratitude and the goodbye inseparable. End with quiet laughter that sounds like both the best and worst sound in the world.
inspired_by: Doing Stand-Up Comedy in the Style of a Eulogy

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging mother, finally saying what you've rehearsed for years but never dared speak. Begin with trembling control—voice steady but fragile, like you're reading from a script you've memorized ('I need to tell you something I should have said long ago'). As you list the ways she failed you, your voice should oscillate between angry accusation and the voice of the child still desperate for her love. Include moments where you break, where the anger dissolves into sobbing ('Why wasn't I enough?'), then harden again into protective rage. End somewhere unexpected: not with reconciliation or rejection, but with exhausted clarity. Your final words should be spoken with the quiet authority of someone who has finally witnessed their own truth, regardless of whether she can hear it.
inspired_by: Hiding a Panic Attack in a Meeting

title: Postcard from the Edge of Leaving
instruction: You're voice-recording a message to your best friend, explaining why you're leaving town and why you can't tell them where you're going. Speak in hushed, intimate tones—it's late at night, and this secret feels too fragile for normal volume. Begin almost matter-of-fact, trying to keep emotion at bay: 'By the time you hear this, I'll already be gone.' But as you speak, small details undo you—remembering their laugh, the way they always knew when you were lying, how they'll feel when they realize you left without saying goodbye. Your voice becomes smaller, younger, catching on words. The reasons you're leaving (whatever they are in your imagination) feel both absolutely necessary and utterly devastating. This isn't dramatic—it's the kind of quiet heartbreak that happens at 3am when you're trying not to wake anyone, when tears slide down silently and your throat closes around words you desperately need to say.

title: Final Permission: A Parent's Last Words to Their Child
instruction: You're sitting at your parent's bedside in their final hours. They've been distant your whole life, unable to show love. Now, with labored breathing, they reach for your hand and whisper: 'I never knew how to tell you... I was so afraid of failing you that I failed you anyway.' Your voice begins tight with decades of unmet longing, barely able to respond. As they continue—'You deserved so much better than what I gave'—something in your chest begins to crack open. You move from guarded pain to raw grief, then to something unexpected: a desperate need to tell them it's okay, that you forgive them, even as you're simultaneously furious that this is happening now, at the very end. Your final words to them—'I love you, I love you, please don't go'—come out as both goodbye and the reconciliation you've needed your entire life. Your voice transforms from protected and wounded to completely undefended.
inspired_by: Telling Someone About Abuse for the First Time

title: Frozen Discovery
instruction: You're an old man out in sub-zero cold, your face stiff, jaw barely moving. Something dark in the snow catches your eye — you lean in, trying to make it out, voice slow and careful with a hint of curiosity. As you realize it's a dead, frozen animal, mangled and rotting under the ice, your interest twists into pure disgust. The words come out tight, choked, your lip curling even as the cold locks your mouth. Speak your reaction, letting the revulsion build and the cold drag each syllable.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The First Time Dad Called Me ‘Son’ for Real
instruction: You're a teenager, sitting upright at the kitchen table across from your father after he finally lets you drive his truck alone. Pride is thick in your chest, but you're also trying to stay cool, so your voice comes out a little tighter than you want. You start by fidgeting with the salt shaker, recounting how you didn't even stall it, but halfway through, you look at his face and the enormity of being trusted hits you—your words slow, your voice drops half a notch, and you end with a quiet, wondering smile you can't hide. Let the pride start as showy bravado and transform into a quieter, deeper sense of belonging.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering to My Sleeping Child
instruction: You're standing in a lavender field at dusk, holding your sleeping child who's seriously ill. Speak in the softest whisper, describing the lavender around you as if painting them a dream they can feel even in sleep. Your voice should be achingly tender, but let the fear bleed through—the way your breath catches when you say 'purple,' the slight tremor when you describe 'tomorrow.' Move from trying to stay calm and magical for them, to letting small cracks show in your voice, to finally admitting in the gentlest whisper that you're scared, but you'll be here, you'll always be here. Let tears come silently, but keep your voice soft and full of infinite love.
inspired_by: Walking Through a Garden of Blooming Lavender

title: Streetlight Doubts
instruction: You are an older woman walking home alone on a noisy city street after a few drinks. You’re replaying a conversation you had hours ago where you ended a long relationship. Your voice is usually soft and feminine, but now it’s strained by doubt and the need to be heard over traffic. Start by muttering defensively, half to yourself, questioning your choice. An ambulance siren makes you flinch mid-thought. As a bus rumbles past, your doubt shifts into a quiet, tipsy resolve — you realize you had to do it. Speak with natural pauses, shifts in volume, and a slur of alcohol. Let your voice crack with uncertainty, then steady into sorrowful acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Podcaster Interviewing Their Own Abuser
instruction: You're a true-crime podcaster who has tracked down the person who hurt you as a child. Maintain the podcast voice — warm, professional, 'false intimacy' of the close mic. Ask devastating questions in a conversational tone. The interviewee (also you) is evasive, charming, dismissive. Your trained broadcast voice barely contains the volcanic rage underneath. Include one moment where the mask slips — your voice hardens, drops, and the abuser realizes this isn't just an interview.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your adult child (or parent) about years of unspoken betrayal—perhaps lies, perhaps abandonment, perhaps choosing someone else over you. Start in a place of controlled fury: your body rigid, movements sharp and contained, everything held tight. As you speak your truth, let your body begin to crack open. The rage must physically transform through your gestures, your stance, the way you occupy space. Midway through, something shifts—beneath the anger, you discover a wounded child (or a terrified, flawed human) inside yourself. Your physicality must show this revelation: perhaps your shoulders collapse, your hands move from accusatory to pleading, your center of gravity changes. End in a place of raw vulnerability mixed with fierce love—your body expressing both 'I will never forgive this' and 'I cannot stop loving you' simultaneously.

title: The Last Morning in Familiar Arms
instruction: You're being held by someone you love on the morning they leave for a mission they won't return from—you both know this, though neither has said it aloud. Begin wrapped in their embrace, speaking softly about the warmth of their body, the rhythm of their breathing, trying to memorize every detail. Your voice is tender, almost playful at first, as you trace the familiar landscape of their shoulders, their heartbeat. But gradually, let the reality seep in—your words begin to fracture, catching on the knowledge that this is the last time. End with a whispered confession of everything you wish you'd said earlier, your voice breaking between gratitude for this moment and the unbearable weight of goodbye. Let the love and the loss live in the same breath.

title: Dancing Alone to Your Wedding Song Six Months After the Funeral
instruction: The song comes on shuffle and you're alone in the kitchen, and suddenly you're laughing—actually laughing—because of course this would happen now. Your voice is light, almost giddy as you start moving, describing how ridiculous this is, how you must look. You're narrating your own dancing like a comedian, finding humor in the absurdity of grief. But as the chorus hits, your laughter starts to catch. You keep trying to laugh but it's mixing with something else. You're still moving, still dancing, but now you're also crying—not sad crying, not exactly. You're telling them about your day, about the stupid thing that happened at work, and you're laughing again because they would have loved it. Your voice keeps shifting between joy at the memory and devastation at the absence, between gratitude for having had this love and rage that it was taken. You realize you're having the best moment you've had in months, dancing in your kitchen, crying and laughing, talking to someone who isn't there. And somehow that's beautiful and horrible and perfectly right. The song ends. You're standing still now, breathing hard, and your voice is quiet but clear: you're going to be okay, and that thought fills you with both peace and unbearable sadness.
inspired_by: On a Building Ledge for Six Hours: The Moment You Recognize You're Not Going Back In

title: Gale Confession
instruction: You're a young woman with a high, sweet voice, standing on a cliff edge in a howling gale. You're drunk and giddy, shouting to a friend who's walking away, but the wind snatches your words. Start with reckless, laughing defiance — 'I’m not afraid of you!' — then as the wind hits harder and you turn your back to breathe, your voice cracks into something raw and small: 'I just wanted you to stay.' Let the physical struggle — turning, squinting, losing your breath — shape the emotional tumble from bravado to ache.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Father Who Missed Your Entire Childhood
instruction: He's shown up at your door after fifteen years, and you're letting him have it. Start with cold, measured anger—you've rehearsed this a thousand times. 'You don't get to do this. You don't get to just appear.' But as you list what he missed—graduations, heartbreaks, the night you needed him most—your voice begins to crack. The anger is real, but beneath it is the child still waiting by the window. You hate that you still want his approval. Your voice breaks between fury and pleading: 'I needed a father. I needed you to fight for me.' The rage collapses into raw, unguarded pain. By the end, you're not yelling anymore—you're standing there, stripped bare, asking the question you're terrified to hear answered: 'Why wasn't I worth staying for?' Let the silence after that question crush you both.
inspired_by: Flight Attendant: Announcing Safe Landing After Turbulence

title: Whispering My Manifesto
instruction: It's late night, and you're lying next to someone you love—a partner, a best friend, a sibling. They're almost asleep.
