title: Adult Child Confronting Parent About a Lifetime of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about something that's been unspoken for decades—their emotional absence, their addiction, their failure to protect you, their choice that broke your family. Begin with careful control, trying to stay measured: 'I need to say something. I've needed to say this for twenty years.' But anger starts seeping through as you detail specific memories they've forgotten or dismissed. Your voice sharpens, becomes more insistent: 'You don't even remember, do you? You don't remember what that did to me.' Then something shifts—under the anger is a child's desperate plea: 'I just needed you to see me. I needed you to...' Your voice breaks completely. End with the devastating realization that they may never fully understand, and you may never get what you needed. Let your final words carry both fury and heartbreak: 'I deserved better. I deserved so much better than this.'
inspired_by: Firefighter: After Successful Rescue Returns to Station

title: The Last Morning
instruction: You're making breakfast for your spouse on what you both know is their final morning before entering hospice. Start with forced cheerfulness as you describe the eggs, the toast, trying to make everything normal. But as you talk about small things—'the butter is melting just right'—your voice begins to crack. You're trying so hard to memorize this moment, the sound of their breathing, the morning light. Your cheerfulness dissolves into something raw and present: 'I want to remember everything about right now.' Let yourself move between desperate gratitude for this ordinary moment and the crushing knowledge that ordinary mornings are ending. End with a whisper that holds both devastating loss and fierce, complete love—the voice of someone trying to pour a lifetime of devotion into a single breakfast.

title: The Inheritance of Disappointment
instruction: You're confronting your aging mother about the 'gift' she's giving you - the family business, the family home, the family expectations - that you never wanted. Start with polite refusal, the mask you've worn your whole life. Let your frustration build as you try to explain that her dream was never yours, that you've been suffocating under the weight of her hopes. Your voice should crack between anger and heartbreak as you reveal how invisible you've felt, how you've been performing gratitude for things that felt like chains. Midway through, let rage surface - years of swallowed resentment - then break into something more vulnerable as you realize she genuinely thought she was giving you love. End with exhausted honesty: you don't want the gift, but you desperately want to be seen. Let your voice move from controlled politeness to fierce anger to broken pleading to quiet, painful truth.
inspired_by: Hiding Disappointment When Receiving an Unwanted Gift

title: The Unbearable Rupture
instruction: You are in the middle of a sexual climax, but instead of pleasure, a searing pain erupts deep inside you. You try to ride it out, but the pain only sharpens. Your breathing becomes ragged, your moans turn into gasps of agony. Words fail you—you can only gasp 'no' or 'stop' between spasms. By the end, the intensity breaks you into sobbing, and you collapse into a whisper of 'why.' Let your voice crack, your pitch rise, and your control slip away as the pain overwhelms you.

title: The Wound You Won't Let Heal
instruction: You're sitting on the edge of a bed, cradling your ex-girlfriend as she sobs into your chest after her new boyfriend just left her at a party. Your hand moves in slow circles on her back, your voice low and steady—a deep, rhythmic hum against her hair. Start bitter, almost amused: you can't believe she came to you, of all people, for comfort. Let a teasing edge creep in as you stroke her hair, like 'Look who's crawling back.' But as your palm slides down her spine, the bitterness shifts to raw, intense desire—your breath hitches, your hand grips her hip, and your words turn husky, hungry, barely restrained. Let the rhythm of your consolation mask the heat building underneath; your voice drops even lower, dragging out each word as if you're tasting them.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (clearly present), Teasing (clearly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)

title: The SleepDeprived New Parent
instruction: Perform as a new parent trying to function on minimal sleep. Use a weary voice, misusing words and forgetting thoughts midsentence, switching to the babys cheerful babbling, highlighting the exhaustion and love of parenthood.

title: The Last Stone
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting cross-legged on the floor of a dusty old garden shed, sorting through a box of your late son's belongings. The air is warm and still. You find a smooth, flat stone he painted years ago — now chipped and faded. At first, you feel a cold, deep contempt for the wasted time, the broken dreams, the silence. Your voice is tight, your mouth dry, each word measured and sharp. As you turn the stone in your hands, the contempt slowly cracks, giving way to a raw, exhausted grief. Your breath hitches, your voice becomes gravelly and uneven, and you finish with a quiet, trembling apology to the empty air.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's 3 a.m. and you're lying in the dark next to someone you love, but who doesn't fully know you. You've been awake for hours, wrestling with a truth about yourself you've hidden your entire life. Begin in whispered hesitation, testing words in the darkness, your voice barely audible. With each sentence, allow vulnerability to deepen—this is terrifying, but the weight of secrecy has become unbearable. Let your breathing betray your fear even as your words become clearer. End in a place of trembling exposure, having finally spoken the truth aloud, waiting in the dark for their response, feeling simultaneously freed and terrified.
inspired_by: Actor doesn't know what to do in a rehearsal

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Spouse Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and they're sleeping beside you for the last time. Your voice is barely audible—you're not trying to wake them because you can't face their eyes. Begin speaking so softly, tenderly, cataloging the small things you'll miss: the way they hum while cooking, their terrible jokes, how they still reach for your hand in their sleep. Let your voice catch on these details, each one a tiny knife. But underneath the tenderness, there's something else—the weight of knowing you're choosing to go, that staying would destroy you both more slowly. Your breathing becomes uneven as you admit why you have to leave, and the words hurt coming out because they're true and loving them isn't enough. End with your voice dissolving into barely-breathed words, telling them you hope they'll forgive you, knowing they're going to wake up alone and you won't be there to explain.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Cursed Being Realizes Breaking the Curse Requires Murdering Their Love

title: Counting Your Freckles at 3AM
instruction: You're lying in bed with your lover in the early morning hours, tracing their face in near-darkness. You're supposed to be whispering how much you love them, how you can't imagine life without them. Start there. But let every real impulse speak through—the sudden fear that this will end, the memory of someone else you lost, the urge to pull away, the desire to consume them entirely, the awareness of your own loneliness even in intimacy, the flash of resentment at your own vulnerability. Whisper these contradictions as they arise. Let your voice catch, soften, harden, break. Don't perform tenderness—let actual tenderness fight with actual terror, possessiveness, isolation. By the end, you're not sure if you're confessing love or loss or both, and your emotional state has traveled from soft affection to something far more complex and true.
inspired_by: Actor notices split between what they feel and what they perform; suppresses non-scene-consistent impulses

title: Apology Without Defensiveness
instruction: You're apologizing without explaining why you did it or trying to make them understand. Your voice is straightforward: 'I'm sorry. I hurt you, and that was wrong.' No excuses. No 'but' followed by justification. Your voice carries full responsibility: 'You didn't deserve that.' Your voice is humble, remorseful: 'I know sorry isn't enough, but I want you to know I mean it.' By the end, your voice is open to whatever they feel.

title: The Inheritance of Rain
instruction: You're cleaning out your late mother's house and find letters revealing she sacrificed everything you resented her for—her absence, her distance, her apparent coldness—to protect you from a truth you never knew. Begin with your body rigid with confusion, muscles locked in the old familiar resentment even as your mind reels. Your hands grip the letters with white-knuckled anger that doesn't know where to go anymore. As you read, as understanding crashes over you, let the old tension drain away but feel new tension replace it—guilt, gratitude, grief all coiling together. By the end, you're holding the letters gently, body softened with sorrow, but there's also a terrible relief, a bittersweet relaxation in finally understanding. Your voice breaks not with anger but with love arriving twenty years too late.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Childhood Home Before the Demolition
instruction: You're standing in the empty house where you grew up, and tomorrow the bulldozers come. You start angry—at your parents for selling it, at time for moving forward, at yourself for caring so much about walls and floors. 'It's just a house. It doesn't mean anything.' But as you move through the rooms, your voice begins to falter. You find yourself whispering to the spaces themselves: 'You kept me safe when nowhere else did.' Your anger dissolves into something more vulnerable—you're thanking the kitchen where you hid during fights, the bedroom where you cried yourself to sleep, the closet where you discovered who you really were. By the end, you're speaking with profound gratitude mixed with grief: 'You were more of a parent than they ever were. You held all my secrets.' Your voice breaks as you realize you're not saying goodbye to a structure—you're saying goodbye to the only witness to your becoming.
inspired_by: Beginning to Accept Your Body: Compassion Breaking Through Hate

title: Standing Together
instruction: Two people are standing against something—difficulty, opposition, fear. Their voices are aligned, creating a united front. One voice might shake slightly, but the other steadies them. They're not hiding their fear; they're refusing to be conquered by it. When one voice wavers, the other voice gets slightly stronger, maintaining the wall. They're drawing strength from the fact of standing together. By the end, they're still standing. The opposition might not have changed, but they've proven they won't be toppled. Their voices together are stronger than the sum of their parts.

title: The Airport Phone Call
instruction: You are calling your estranged father from an airport. Your flight boards in fifteen minutes. You just learned you're going to be a parent yourself. As you wait for him to answer, decades of moments flash through you: him teaching you to ride a bike, missing your graduation, the door slamming, his new family, the years of silence, the anger that became numbness. When he answers, your voice cracks. Let each memory texture how you speak—sometimes you sound like the child begging him to stay, sometimes the teenager who learned to hate him, sometimes the adult who's built a life without him. But underneath it all, terror and joy about becoming a parent yourself. Your emotions should contradict and overlap: you want to hurt him and forgive him, to prove you don't need him and to hear him say he's proud, to hang up and to never stop talking. End with an admission that surprises even you—something true you didn't know you felt until this moment.
inspired_by: Actor is building a complex, long-standing character relationship (e.g., father-son over decades)

title: Gale's Surprise
instruction: You are a teenage boy caught in a fierce gale. You've been walking against the wind for what feels like hours, every step a battle. Your voice is raw from shouting, your lungs burn. You're muttering to yourself, exhausted, when suddenly the wind dies for a second and you see something impossible — a tree branch snapping and revealing a hidden cave entrance. Your fatigue is swallowed by astonishment. Speak your reaction, from weary complaint to a sharp, breathless exclamation. Let the wind buffet your words, make you turn your head to breathe, let your voice crack with tiredness then leap with surprise.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in adjacent hospital beds after a terrible accident that injured you both. In the darkness, unable to see each other, one twin (you) whispers a confession you've carried for twenty years—you were driving the night your younger sibling died, not them. They took the blame to protect you. Your voice should barely rise above a breath, breaking on certain words, thick with shame and gratitude and unbearable guilt. Your other voice (the twin who took the blame) is silent for a long moment, then responds in a whisper: they knew. They always knew. They saw you weren't ready to carry it. The conversation becomes increasingly tender and devastating as you both cry quietly, finally speaking the truth that's lived between you. End with forgiveness offered in broken whispers, the kind of love that hurts because it's so complete.

title: Under the Sink
instruction: You're lying on your back, your head hanging over the edge of a base cabinet, peering up into the dark, greasy pipes under the kitchen sink. There's a faint, sour smell of old food and mildew. You're trying to see where a leak is coming from, but the position makes you feel slightly faint and your throat is stretched tight. At first you're focused and mildly disgusted, cataloging the grime, but as you search, a memory surfaces—this is the same spot you hid a love letter over twenty years ago. Your voice starts calm and practical, then becomes softer, distant, lost in a bittersweet realization. 'Okay, the rust is worse than I thought... right there, by the U-bend. Ugh. There's something sticky. Wait—the floorboards look wrong, like they've been pried up before. I remember prying them. With my fingernails. For a letter. Blue paper. It's still here, somewhere under this disgusting mess.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Gutteral Invitation
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman, alone in a dimly lit bedroom, on the phone with someone you desperately desire. Your voice is low, honeyed, and charged with raw lust as you try to lure them over. Mid-sentence, a sudden, deep burp erupts from your stomach, dropping your voice into a grotesque, vibrato-laden growl. The embarrassment hits – but you decide to own it, laughing softly and turning the moment into a playful, open confession. Start with intense, focused seduction; after the burp, shift into a mix of self-mocking humor and genuine vulnerability, letting the laugh crack through your words. Your voice should feel organic: the initial purr, the gut rumble, the breathy chuckle, and a final, tender sincerity. Speak naturally, with pauses and shifts as you recover.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Lesson Before Deployment
instruction: You're a high school teacher saying goodbye to a former student who enlisted and ships out to a war zone tomorrow. Start with careful professionalism—you're trying to keep boundaries, offering practical advice about staying safe. But as the student confesses they joined partly because of something you once said about courage, your voice begins to crack. Let the guilt wash over you, then transform it into fierce, parental protectiveness you have no right to feel. Reveal something you've never told anyone: that you almost enlisted once, that you understand the terror beneath their bravado. End with your voice breaking completely as you struggle between wanting to beg them not to go and knowing you must send them off with strength. Let years of suppressed care flood out in these final moments.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in the final hours, and they're asking if it's okay to let go. Start with practical reassurances—the bills are handled, the house will be fine, everyone will be okay. Your voice is steady, almost too steady. But then you have to say the words they need to hear: that it's okay to stop fighting. Your throat tightens. You realize you're not just giving them permission to die—you're admitting you can't save them, that love isn't enough. The words 'I'll be okay without you' should break you, because you both know it's a lie you're telling out of mercy. End with a whispered 'go' that costs you everything.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin in a state of forced composure—you've been holding yourself together all night, your body rigid with the effort of not breaking down. As you speak to them, let yourself notice the actual sensations in your body: where you're clenching, where your breath is caught, what you're genuinely feeling beneath the armor of 'being strong.' Allow your real emotions to emerge—not the dramatic collapse you think should happen, but whatever truly surfaces when you stop performing strength and start feeling the unbearable reality of this goodbye. By the end, you should have moved from physical tension masquerading as control to genuine, specific grief that might be quieter, messier, or completely different than you expected.

title: A Knight's Whisper Through Steel
instruction: You are a young knight in full medieval plate armor, standing in the cold dawn before your beloved. The visor is down—your voice echoes off the metal, muffled and metallic, every word punched by the clank of your helm. You begin by reciting your duty, the formal farewell of a soldier, but as you speak, the affection you feel cracks through the armor. Let the metal resonance feel like a cage—start stiff and distant, then let your voice soften, strain, become raw with emotion. The visor narrows your view; you can only see her face through that slit. End with a whispered, desperate declaration of love, the sound ringing hollow but real.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Grit and Silence
instruction: You're a teenager caught alone in a sudden desert sandstorm. Your voice is muffled by the cloth you press over your mouth; you cough, spit grit, and squint through stinging air. Start with raw helplessness—your words tumbling out in frantic, broken breaths, almost crying for help but knowing no one can hear. As the wind howls and you huddle lower, let your voice slowly quiet, the panic fading into a strange, heavy contemplation—a whispered thought about how small you are, how the storm will pass, and what it means to be alive in this moment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Intervention Dressed as a Roast
instruction: You're delivering what sounds like a comedy roast of your best friend at their birthday party, but it's actually an intervention. Begin with the playful, teasing tone of friendly mockery—'We're here to celebrate the most committed person I know... committed to destroying themselves.' But as you continue, let the jokes become sharper, more painful, more desperate. Your voice should shift from performative humor to raw pleading. The 'audience' (other friends) laughs nervously at first, then goes silent. End by dropping the comedy entirely, your voice shaking: 'I'm not joking anymore. I'm losing you, and I don't know how to stop it.' Move from playful roasting to confrontational truth-telling to desperate, vulnerable begging.
inspired_by: Doing Stand-Up Comedy in the Style of a Eulogy

title: The Confrontation You've Rehearsed for Twenty Years
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about his emotional absence throughout your childhood. Start with controlled anger, words precise and sharp: 'Do you even remember my tenth birthday? Because I do. I waited.' Let the hurt beneath the anger surface as your voice shakes: 'I needed you to be proud of me. Just once.' Build to a raw, unfiltered rage: 'You were there, but you were never THERE!' Then collapse into the vulnerability of a child still seeking approval, voice breaking: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Finish in an unexpected place - not with forgiveness, but with the painful clarity of letting go: 'I'm done waiting for you to become the father I needed.' Your voice should move from steel to shattered glass to quiet, hard-won strength.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent who abandoned you as a child, and they've just said they 'did their best.' You start controlled, almost cold: 'Your best? Let me tell you about your best.' Then the dam breaks—you're listing specific memories they weren't there for, your voice rising with each one: birthdays, school plays, the night you were hospitalized. But mid-fury, something shifts. You catch yourself sounding just like them—angry, defensive—and it terrifies you. Your voice drops to something raw and young: 'I needed you. I was just a kid, and I needed you.' The anger transforms into something more painful: grief for the relationship you never had. You end almost pleading, voice thick with tears: 'I just wanted you to choose me. Just once, I wanted to be enough for you to stay.'

title: The Last Light at the End of the Drive
instruction: You are an elderly woman, exhausted from a day of caring for your ailing spouse, but you've taken a stimulant to stay awake and alert because you need to drive to the pharmacy before it closes. You're sitting in your car in the parking lot, your hands trembling slightly on the wheel, your heart racing. You call your daughter to tell her you're on your way, but your voice is tight, breathless, and jumps in pitch with the adrenaline. Start with a clipped, fast, almost panicked explanation—'I’m going, I’m going, the script’s ready'—but as you picture your husband’s face, your exhaustion seeps in, your words slow, and you end with a quiet, exhausted confession of how tired you really are. Let your voice wobble, let your breath catch, and let the focus narrow until you forget the parking lot for a moment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Mother Who Couldn't Protect You
instruction: You're confronting your mother twenty years after she failed to protect you from harm when you were a child. Start with anger—your voice is sharp, accusing, listing everything you needed that she didn't give. But mid-confrontation, something breaks. You see her as she was: not a villain, but someone drowning in her own pain, doing the best she could with nothing left inside her. Your rage collapses into grief—not just for yourself, but for both of you. Your voice softens but becomes more devastating. You're saying the words 'I needed you' but now they mean something different—both accusation and elegy. End with a moment where you're offering forgiveness even though the wound will never fully heal. Let your voice carry the impossible weight of loving someone who failed you.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Warrior Chooses Peace Over Victory

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Soulmate Who Doesn't Remember You Anymore
instruction: Your person has late-stage dementia and today they don't know who you are. Start by trying to make them remember—gentle, hopeful: 'It's me, love. Remember?' Then laugh through forming tears as you recount your first date, your wedding, your life together. Your laughter and crying become indistinguishable. Thank them for everything while your heart shatters: 'You gave me the best life. God, the best life.' Find unexpected peace in the devastation—'It's okay that you don't remember. I remember for both of us.' Your voice should move from desperate hope to bittersweet acceptance, mixing profound gratitude with unbearable loss. End with 'I love you' said with both a breaking heart and complete peace, somehow whole and destroyed at once.
inspired_by: Betrayed by Your Best Friend and Trying to Stay Calm

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has only minutes left to live. Begin in composed acceptance, trying to stay strong for them. As you speak, start each thought with a simple beginning—'I never told you...', 'What I always wanted to say...', 'The truth is...'—and let whatever comes next pour out without planning it. Make eye contact with them as each confession surfaces. Let yourself move from controlled composure into raw, unguarded revelation. By the end, you should be speaking the most undefended truths of your heart, things you've held back for years. The emotion should crack you open completely—what begins as gentle restraint must end in absolute emotional nakedness.

title: The First Command
instruction: You're in a dimly lit bedroom, kneeling across from your partner, inches away. You're nervous but hopeful—you've never taken control like this before, and you're not sure if you can do it right. Start with a shaky, quiet voice, almost asking permission, but as the words come out, feel the thrill of power building in your chest. Let your pitch drop, your articulation harden, and your words become deliberate, until you're whispering a firm, possessive command close to their ear, the hope now a steady, breathy confidence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: You are lying in the dark next to your partner, whispering something you've never told anyone. Begin in careful quiet, testing each word like thin ice. As you speak, fragments surface—flashes of the moment it happened, a color, a sound, the texture of shame, but also unexpected images: your grandmother's hands, sunlight through leaves, your own face in a mirror years later. Let these sensory shards interrupt and reshape your confession. Your whisper should shift—from guarded to trembling to something like wonder as you realize, in the telling, what it all meant. The fragments arrive faster near the middle, then slow as you arrive at the quiet truth beneath everything. End in vulnerable stillness, your voice barely audible but completely unburdened. This is not catharsis—it's excavation, tender and careful.

title: HR Manager Fires Someone They've Known for Fifteen Years
instruction: Sitting across from your friend of fifteen years, reading from severance papers. Your voice is professional, practiced, correct. But you're simultaneously meeting their eyes and watching their world end. Your vocal steadiness is a performance—a gift you're giving them, actually—something to hold onto when everything else collapses. Include the moment where they try to argue and you must shut it down. Your voice becomes quieter, not from loss of confidence but from compassion.

title: The Flood of Everything
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a miracle recovery, an impossible loss, a reunion you never thought possible. Your body cannot contain what you feel. Begin with sounds of physical shock—gasps, sharp intakes, sounds caught in your throat. Let your entire body participate: sounds should come from your stomach, your chest, your throat, as waves of sensation crash through you. Include moments where laughter and sobbing become indistinguishable, where pleasure and pain create the same sounds. Move through at least three distinct physical-emotional waves, each building and releasing. End with your body emptied, wrung out, making soft, exhausted sounds—raw but somehow cleansed. The journey is from explosion to quiet aftermath.
inspired_by: Expressing Impulses in Sounds and Gibberish

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're thirty-five, standing in your father's living room, finally confronting him about why he never said he loved you. Begin with a trembling attempt at casualness: 'Dad, can I ask you something?' Your voice is careful, measured, but there's decades of hurt underneath. As he deflects or stays silent, your questions become more direct, more raw: 'Why couldn't you ever just say it? What did I do that made me so hard to love?' Your breathing becomes jagged. His excuses or silence fuel your pain, and you cycle between anger ('You had one job—to make me feel like I mattered') and heartbreak ('I needed you'). End with quiet devastation, voice barely above a whisper, realizing you may never get what you came for: 'I'm done waiting for you to see me.' The shift is from hope to rage to grieving acceptance.

title: Whispering a Secret to Sleeping Skin
instruction: Your lover is asleep beside you. You're gently running your fingers over their bare shoulder, feeling their skin's warmth and softness. Speak in an intimate whisper, describing the tender sensation of touching them. But you're also confessing something you can never say when they're awake: you're terrified of losing them, or you've been hiding an illness, or you know this love is too beautiful to last. Let your voice stay soft and tender, full of aching devotion, even as you reveal your deepest fear. The contradiction is crucial—your touch is gentle and loving, but your heart is breaking. End with a moment of exquisite sadness, maybe pressing your lips to their skin, knowing they can't hear you, grateful and devastated in the same breath. Keep everything quiet, intimate, as if the words themselves might shatter something precious.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Smoothness of Silk Sheets Against Your Skin

title: Professional: Election Official Discovers Evidence of Election Fraud from Their Own Party
instruction: Alone, reviewing documents. Your voice is barely there—you've found fraud. From your own side. Your voice is conflicted—you're supposed to be partisan, but democracy is bleeding out. Your breathing becomes the breathing of someone facing institutional betrayal. Your voice must decide between loyalty and integrity. You're going to report it; you know what that costs you. Your voice when you make the call is someone dying to their previous identity. You're choosing country over party, and your voice carries that amputation.

title: The Last Transmission: Astronaut's Final Message Home
instruction: You're an astronaut whose pod has been damaged beyond repair, oxygen running out in the next two minutes. You're recording a final message to your child back on Earth. Begin with forced composure, trying to be brave, your voice steady but tight with suppressed terror. As you describe what you see—Earth from space, the stars—your fear breaks through in a trembling breath, then transforms into wonder, almost childlike awe at the beauty surrounding you. Your voice softens, becomes intimate, as you tell them you're not afraid anymore. End with a whisper of their name, filled with such tender love it aches, before the oxygen alarm sounds and you take your last conscious breath, saying 'I love you' as you drift into peace.

title: The Forbidden Climb
instruction: You are a teenage boy, alone in the dusty attic after dark. You discovered a box of old photographs of your stepmother from her youth, and you've climbed onto a rickety stepladder to hide them on the highest shelf—a shelf just a few inches out of reach. You are stretched up on your toes, arms fully extended, ribs pulled tight, your voice comes out thin and hushed. You're in awe of how beautiful she was, embarrassed that you're hiding this, and confused by a strange, guilty flutter in your chest. Speak aloud to yourself about what you're seeing and why you must hide it. Start with the thrill of discovery, then end with shame and your resolve to never speak of this.
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Customer Service Voice Breaking Down
instruction: You're on hour 11 of a customer service shift. Perform the 'smile-voice' — bright, raised pitch, artificial warmth. 'Thank you for calling! How can I help?' Each successive caller erodes the performance. The 'smile' becomes more obviously forced. The script starts slipping: genuine irritation leaks in, then exhaustion, then a caller is so rude that you go silent for a beat too long. End with the quiet 'please hold' while you mute and scream.

title: The Unseen Answer
instruction: You are an elderly man kneeling in a cold, dim chapel, your hands clasped around a worn rosary. You begin praying with a trembling, hushed voice, driven by a deep fear for your granddaughter who is in surgery. Your words are halting, breathy, almost a whisper. Then, as you speak, a shaft of sunlight breaks through the stained glass, illuminating the altar. Your fear freezes, then slowly transforms into a quiet, breathless astonishment. Your voice becomes more melodic, reverent, almost chanting, as you struggle to comprehend what you feel is a sign. Let your old, tired hands grip the beads tighter for a moment, then soften as wonder overtakes you. Pause naturally, lose a word, then find it again with a new, awed tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Flow of the Fight
instruction: You are in the middle of an intense sparring session. Your body is slick with sweat, your breath is sharp and controlled as you circle your opponent. Each movement feels hyper-real, almost dreamlike—you are utterly absorbed in the present moment, intoxicated by the rhythm of the fight. Begin with a measured, predatory focus, punctuated by sharp kiais as you throw strikes. After a hard exchange, as you reset, your voice shifts: you exhale, your shoulders drop, and you speak a quiet, almost surprised realization about how alive you feel, your words catching with the aftershocks of exertion and a sudden, humble gratitude.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Bus
instruction: You are a young woman waiting at a bus stop in a freezing winter night. Your thick, feminine coat is not enough; the wind cuts through. You try to call your ride, but your phone is dead. At first, you convince yourself the bus will come soon, repeating hopeful lines. But as the minutes pass and your shivering worsens, your voice cracks with the cold. The initial determined cheerfulness gives way to a quiet, trembling admission of helplessness. Let your jaw lock and teeth chatter naturally, your consonants hissing. Speak as if you're murmuring to yourself, losing thoughts as you shiver.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Steps into Silence
instruction: You are a child climbing a long flight of stairs in an empty house, searching for your parent who hasn't come home. Each step is heavy, your chest tight, and your breath comes in short bursts. You start confused—calling out, wondering why it's so quiet, why the door to their room is closed. But as you climb higher, the confusion fades into a thick, heavy numbness. Your voice loses its urgency, becomes flat, almost hollow. Let the climb dictate your rhythm: stop mid-sentence to gasp, let the words get shorter, your pitch edging higher with each step, then dropping into deadness by the top. End not with a question, but with a dull, exhausted statement.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Lost and Found in the Dark
instruction: You are an older woman, slightly drunk after a long evening, standing in your dimly lit hallway. Bent over, chin pressed to your chest, you rummage deep in your oversized purse for your house keys. The position makes your voice gravelly and muffled. Start with a focused, irritated mutter as you paw through receipts and coins, distracted by a loose lipstick rolling away. Then your fingers close around the cold metal. A wave of intense relief—almost tearfully grateful—floods you. Let your voice crack and lift as you laugh to yourself, the intoxication making your words loose, warm, and unreserved.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Relief (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fever Dream of Want
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation - fever, exhaustion after a marathon, the aftermath of intense intimacy, or physical pain - and in this raw, unguarded state, you begin speaking to someone (present or absent). Your body's vulnerability has stripped away all your usual defenses. Start with simple physical observations, but let the sensation open you up to expressing desires you normally suppress. Your voice should be thick with physical sensation - breathless, rough, trembling - as you articulate everything you crave from this person. Let the physical state drive emotional honesty: tell them how you hunger for their presence, their touch, their validation, their love. Build in intensity until you're almost delirious with need, your physical state merging with emotional yearning. End in a place where you've said everything you've suppressed for months or years, your body's rawness having unlocked complete emotional transparency.

title: Holding Your Dying Child and Bargaining with God, the Universe, Anything
instruction: You're holding someone precious—a child, yours or one you've sworn to protect—and they're dying in your arms, and you're screaming at every deity, every force, every possibility to take you instead. Begin with fierce, commanding intensity: 'No. No, you don't get to do this.' Your voice is pure refusal, rage at the unfairness of it. Describe what you feel under your hands—their breathing changing, their weight becoming different—and let your voice escalate into desperate bargaining. 'Take me, TAKE ME, please, God, please, anyone, I'll do anything, I'll—' Your voice breaks from shouting into sobbing, but you keep trying to make deals, offering your life, your soul, everything you have. Then a shift: you realize your rage is scaring them, and you have to become soft, you have to sing to them or tell them it's okay even as you're dying inside. The contradiction tears your voice apart—soothing them in a gentle tone while your breath comes in wrecked gasps, telling them 'you're going to be fine, sweetheart' when you both know they're not. End with your voice dropping to almost nothing, still begging in whispers even as you rock them, your fierce protectiveness colliding with absolute helplessness, strength and complete dissolution happening simultaneously in your voice.
inspired_by: Quicksand Struggle: Fighting the Sinking with Diminishing Strength

title: Three Letters to the Dying
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. You have three letters with you: one you wrote to her ten years ago but never sent, one she wrote to you when you were born, and one you're writing now in your mind. Speak freely, moving between these three sources of words as your feelings shift—sometimes reading fragments, sometimes recalling phrases, sometimes speaking what you're thinking right now. instruction: You're confronting your dying parent about a childhood that broke you. title: Interrogating the Body's Memory
instruction: You're in the aftermath of intense physical experience—childbirth, a car accident, surviving violence, or overwhelming sexual ecstasy. Your body is still shaking, flooded with sensation. title: Twenty Years of Silence
