Your voice should move from desperate clinging to devastated permission, from 'please stay' to 'I release you.'

title: The Purge of a Pandemic
instruction: You are a woman finally, violently snapping after months of lockdown with a deeply messy, entitled housemate. You have just discovered that they deliberately hid a positive COVID test from you for three days, forcing you into unnecessary exposure. You are in the kitchen, and you have just hurled their crusty coffee mug against the wall—it shattered. Now, standing over the shards, your voice is a wreck: ragged, cracking, coming from your gut. Start in pure volcanic fury, spitting out your disgust at their selfishness. Then, as you gasp for air, a wave of relief hits you—relief that this nightmare of cohabitation is finally, explosively over. But as you look down at the broken mug, a terrible doubt creeps in: what if you overreacted and burned the only bridge you had left? Let your voice fracture between those three states: the eruption of disgust, the shuddering exhale of relief, and the quiet, wavering question of doubt.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Relief (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dementia Patient's Lucid Moment
instruction: You've been confused and childlike — asking who people are, repeating questions. Perform this gently. Then a lucid window opens. Your voice clarifies, deepens, becomes your 'real' self. You know exactly where and who you are. And you know it won't last. Use this precious window to say something vital to your child: an apology, an 'I love you,' the location of important papers. The urgency of someone who knows the fog is coming back. The voice fading at the end as clarity slips away.

title: Last Words at the Decon Line
instruction: You are a young soldier, still in your full CBRN gear, standing at the edge of a decontamination tent. Through the muffled chaos, you spot the medic you've been secretly infatuated with for months, just as they're about to be rotated out. You have to shout through your gas mask, but you're also trying to sound casual in front of your squad. Start with a gruff, almost dismissive tone, hiding your crush behind contempt and duty. Let your breathing get heavier as you fight the urge to say something real. By the end, let your voice betray a shaky, raw elation—a slight crack in the macho facade as you realize this might be the last time you ever see them.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Contempt (slightly present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Mask Slips at the Party
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, standing with a close friend near the kitchen. Across the room, you see your ex laughing with someone new — they look happier than you ever remember. You start telling your friend you're genuinely glad for them, your voice light and optimistic, maybe even forcing a smile. But as you keep talking, your jaw tightens, your eyes drop to your shoes, and the words start to falter. The envy creeps in, then the pain — a raw admission leaks out that you're not okay. Let your voice crack, drop to a near-whisper, and let out a small, defensive laugh after the confession. You're not performing strength anymore; you're letting the truth slip through the cracks.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Pain (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Truth That's Been Choking You
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or child) about something that has poisoned your relationship for years—an abandonment, a betrayal, a lie, a pattern of cruelty. Start the scene from a place of barely contained rage, where your jaw is clenched, your fists are tight, your whole body is coiled like a spring. As you begin to speak your truth, notice everywhere you're physically holding yourself back—your locked knees, your stiff neck, your shallow breathing. Speak these bodily sensations out loud alongside your accusations: 'I'm shaking because I've never said this,' 'My voice keeps breaking because this has been stuck in me since I was twelve.' As you acknowledge and release each point of physical tension, allow your emotional state to shift from fury into the deeper pain beneath it—the grief of not being loved the way you needed. End in a place of exhausted, heartbroken vulnerability.

title: The Last Ember
instruction: You are trapped in a small, smoke-filled room, a young woman who broke in to retrieve something precious. The fire rages outside, choking you. You start by coughing, disgusted by the acrid smell, eyes burning, feeling helpless as you fumble on the floor. In the haze, your hand closes around a slightly singed photograph — his face, blurred at the edges. In a moment of stillness amidst the panic, a flicker of infatuation for the person in the picture surprises you, softening your voice into a breathless, almost tender whisper, even as your throat burns. Let the disgust and helplessness warp your first words, then let your voice stumble into that quiet, unexpected warmth as you speak to the photo, not caring how ridiculous it is.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Infatuation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's unconscious, but you've been told she can still hear you. Begin in complete paralysis—you want to speak but the words won't come, your throat is tight, you feel frozen and numb. Let yourself sit in that blocked, suffocating silence for a moment. Then something breaks open inside you—maybe anger at yourself for waiting this long, maybe grief, maybe both—and suddenly everything pours out: all the things you never said, the gratitude, the memories, the apologies, the love. Start unable to speak at all, and end with words flowing like a river that's finally broken through a dam. Let your voice crack, let yourself be messy and raw. By the end, even though she may not respond, you feel lighter—emptied out, but free.
inspired_by: Actor feels blocked during a rehearsal and cannot access the needed emotional life

title: Survivor's Sob
instruction: You’re sitting on a curb after being pulled from a collapsed building. Your body is shaking, tears streaming, and every breath catches in a jerky sob. You’re on the phone with a loved one, still trembling from the terror of being trapped—but you’ve just been told everyone got out. Let the fear make your voice crack and waver, your throat wet and thick. As you speak, let the realization of survival seep in: your words become steadier, a raw triumph rising through the tears. You’re crying, but now it’s relief. Say about three sentences: start shaky, end fierce.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What You Never Said at Breakfast
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table about why he left when you were twelve. He's making excuses, deflecting. As you speak, let yourself be genuinely distracted by random things—the coffee stain on his collar, the sound of traffic outside, the way his hands look older, a completely unrelated memory of your dentist, the chair squeaking, wondering if you left the stove on, the exact shade of the wallpaper. Let these intrusive, disconnected observations flood through you even as you're trying to have the most important conversation of your life. Start with controlled anger, trying to stay on script with your rehearsed accusations. End with something unexpected emerging—a truth you didn't know you felt, pulled up from underneath all that mental noise.

title: The Unmade Decision
instruction: You've just woken up, still lying in bed with the sheets tangled around your legs. The gray morning light seeps through the curtains as you stare at the ceiling. Your throat feels thick, and your voice comes out as a low, gravelly rasp. You're replaying a choice you made yesterday — something you said or didn't say — and a heavy wave of doubt creeps in. You mutter to yourself, trying to justify or question your own actions. But as you keep talking, you feel a stubborn shift: the doubt softens into a quiet, tired certainty that you did what you had to do. Let your voice crack and stumble at first, then grow clearer, more grounded, as if the act of speaking warms up not just your vocal cords but your resolve.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Bedside Confession to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. It's 3 AM. You can't sleep because there's something you've never been able to say out loud. Start barely whispering, testing the words: 'Are you awake?' Silence. Good. Your voice is so quiet it's almost just breath: 'I need to tell you something.' What follows is a confession - maybe about your deepest fear, maybe about something from your past that still haunts you, maybe about how completely you love them and how terrifying that is. Your voice catches, breaks. Tears are sliding down your face but you keep whispering, each word pulled from somewhere deep: 'I've never told anyone this.' The vulnerability is excruciating. You reach out, almost touch them, pull back. By the end, there's both relief and ache in your voice: 'I love you so much it scares me.' It's tender, devastated, and achingly intimate - the kind of truth you can only speak in darkness.

title: Rapid-Fire Reckoning: What You Gave Me vs. What I Needed
instruction: You're confronting a parent using the rhythm and structure of an auctioneer's patter, but instead of selling items, you're listing everything they gave you versus everything you actually needed. Start with fierce, controlled anger: 'Piano lessons—check! Private school—sold! Family vacations—going once, twice!' The tempo is sharp, weaponized. But midway through, the rhythm starts to falter as you name what's missing: 'Do I hear... affection? Anyone? A hug when I was scared? Sold to... nobody.' The anger must transform into devastating vulnerability. Your voice should crack, the rapid patter dissolving into halting, broken speech. End quietly, almost whispering the final 'item'—perhaps 'someone who actually saw me'—where all the fury has burned away, leaving only exhausted, throat-catching grief.

title: The Goodbye Call from the Space Station
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, making your final video call home to your child who begged you not to go. Start with forced brightness and pride, showing them your achievements, the stars outside the window. Your voice cracks when they say they needed you here more than space needed you there. The joy of your dream dissolves into the devastating realization that you chose glory over them. End in raw, whispered apology as the signal degrades, knowing these are your last words. Your voice must travel from rehearsed courage through fracturing composure to naked, irreversible regret. Let the silence between words say what you can no longer afford to hide.

title: The Velvet Knife
instruction: You are at a crowded party, leaning against a wall, watching your target. You approach her with a slow, deliberate stride, your voice low and smooth. You start by teasing her about the drink she's holding—how it's too sweet, how she always picks the wrong thing. Your words are playful, with a lilt of laughter, but underneath your smile is a razor edge. As you lean closer, your tone shifts, dropping colder, more pointed—you mention a mistake she made that cost you something dear. By the end, the teasing is gone, replaced by a quiet, venomous threat. Your voice should feel effortless, but your body betrays tension: a clenched jaw, a flickering gaze, a pause to sip your own drink as you let your words sink in.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Shears
instruction: You're shaving your own head in the mirror after your cancer diagnosis, and your best friend stands behind you, guiding your shaking hands. Start by making jokes — dark, awful, hilarious jokes about being 'aerodynamic now' and 'saving on shampoo.' You're both laughing, almost hysterically, tears streaming down your faces but you're not sure if they're from laughter or terror. With each pass of the razor, you say something you're grateful for — your friend's terrible cooking, that stupid vacation where everything went wrong, the time you both got fired on the same day. But your voice is breaking between the laughter. You're thanking them for staying, for this moment, for not looking away from you. The laughter dissolves into quiet crying, then back to shaky giggles, then to something transcendent — a kind of peaceful joy in the midst of absolute devastation. When you're done, you turn and look at them, bald and beautiful and terrified and grateful, and you whisper 'I'm so lucky' and you mean it with your whole breaking heart.

title: Midnight Confession: Paramedic Whispers to the Overdose They Couldn't Save
instruction: It's 3 AM in the ambulance bay. You're alone with the body of someone you just lost to an overdose—the third this week. You failed. The Narcan didn't work fast enough. Start in barely audible whispers, talking to them as if they can still hear. Your voice is tender, exhausted, apologetic. Tell them about the others you've saved, about the ones you couldn't. Your breathing is shallow, catching on words you can't quite say. This could have been your sister, your best friend, yourself in another life. The professional distance you maintain dissolves into something intimate and broken. You're confessing your own fears about dependency—on adrenaline, on being needed, on the救 rush of saving lives because you couldn't save someone years ago. Let your voice crack on their name. Let the quiet devastation fill the spaces between words. End with a promise you're not sure you can keep, your voice soft as prayer, thick with unshed tears.
inspired_by: Professional: Doctor Prescribes Addiction to Save Addict's Life

title: The Stranger on Platform Nine
instruction: You're sitting with your dying grandmother in her final hours. A stranger across the hospital room catches your eye—someone waiting with their own dying loved one. Begin by studying them: their posture, how they hold their coffee cup, whether they check their phone, if they cry openly or hide it. As you watch them over these long hours, build an entire imagined life for them—their regrets, their relationship with the person dying, what they'll do after. Your grandmother asks you to tell her a story, any story. Tell her the story of this stranger you've been watching, and as you speak, realize you're actually telling her your own fears about losing her. Start curious and detached, observing to distract yourself from your grief. End by breaking down as the story becomes your confession of how terrified you are to say goodbye. Let watching this stranger crack open everything you've been holding back.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're watching your child sleep, knowing this is the last time you'll see them—you're dying, or leaving forever, or they've chosen to cut you from their life and this is your stolen moment. Your voice is barely audible, tender, breaking on every other word. Start with 'You were the best thing I ever made.' You're telling them all the things you won't get to say: how proud you are, what you hope for them, how sorry you are for your failures. Your voice catches on memories—their first laugh, the way they used to hold your finger, the moment you realized you'd die for them without hesitation. You're trying not to cry loudly enough to wake them because you can't bear the actual goodbye. End with your voice dissolving into silence, maybe just breathing their name. This should feel like your heart is being pulled out through your throat—quiet, devastating, unbearably intimate.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart: Gratitude in the Midst of Devastation
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone or something that destroyed you, but your voice starts with genuine gratitude: 'Thank you. I mean that. Thank you.' It could be an ex-lover who shattered you but taught you what you deserve, a dream that died but freed you from a prison you didn't know you were in, a friendship that ended but showed you who you really are. Your voice is sincere in its thanks, almost peaceful, but then it cracks—because underneath the gratitude is the raw, unhealed wound. Let yourself oscillate: appreciative, then devastated, then both at once. Laugh at the absurdity of thanking someone for pain, then let the laugh become a sob, then find it genuinely funny again. Your voice should be completely unpredictable—no performance, just following the real emotional complexity of holding relief and grief simultaneously. By the end, you're no longer separating them: your voice is suffused with a strange, mature wholeness where the gratitude and the heartbreak live in the same breath. 'Thank you for breaking me open. I'm not who I was. And that's... that's what I needed, even though it nearly killed me.' Your final words should shimmer with tears and truth and an almost transcendent acceptance.
inspired_by: Unexpected Laughter After Tragedy: Guilt and Relief Mixed

title: The Inheritance of Contradictions
instruction: You've just learned you've inherited your estranged father's estate—the father who abandoned you, who you've hated, who you've also secretly longed for. Read his final letter to you aloud. As you read, allow completely contradictory parts of yourself to react simultaneously and sequentially: the child who's joyful he finally gave you something, the adult who's furious it took his death, the part that's grieving what never was, the part that's grateful to be free of hoping, the part that forgives him, the part that never will. Let these contradictions war within you—don't resolve them into one coherent feeling. Shift physically and vocally as each takes precedence. Laugh while crying. Rage while tender. Hold opposing truths in your body at once. End in the messy, unresolved complexity of genuine human response. The arc moves from singular shock through emotional multiplicity to authentic contradiction.

title: The Hidden Hold
instruction: You're a teenage boy near the top of a steep rock face, arms overhead, fingertips aching, core locked tight. You're muttering your next move in breathless whispers, scared to fall. Suddenly, your hand finds a small, perfectly shaped hold you didn't see from below—it's almost impossible, like a gift. Astonishment floods through you, cutting through the fatigue and fear, making you gasp and laugh in shaky disbelief. Let your voice crack, tremble, and lose its cadence as the surprise hits, then fade into a quiet, awestruck wonder as you realize you might actually make it. You say: 'No way... no freaking way. That's not—that can't be real. One more move. One more... just there. I see it now. Okay. Okay, I got this.'
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Last Call at the Silent Bar
instruction: You're at a crowded, dimly lit bar, speaking to a deaf friend across the table. You've had too many drinks — your tongue feels thick, the room tilts, and your eyelids are heavy. You need to tell them something important before the night ends. Start with forced, booming cheerfulness, exaggerated lip movements, each word slow and deliberate as if you're shouting through fog. But halfway through, your exhaustion crashes in — your voice drops, cracks, becomes a raw, shaky monotone still unnaturally loud. The alcohol buzz fades into a vulnerable, slurred confession about how lonely you feel. End with your head nearly on the table, voice barely above a strained whisper, but still forcing those last words clear for their eyes.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Slip That Shamed Me
instruction: You're a young woman on the phone with your best friend, huddled in a corner of your apartment so no one else hears. You start off giddy, rushing through the setup of a juicy story about a coworker—you accidentally forwarded a private, embarrassing message about her to the whole team. Your voice is quick, breathy, excited to share the drama. But as you describe the fallout—how she saw it, how your boss found out—the shame hits you like a wave. Your pitch drops, you trail off, you tug at your necklace. You end in a trembly whisper, confessing you can't even look at her anymore. Let the story feel real: stumble over words, pause to check if you're being too loud, shift from laughing nervously to near tears.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Speaking Truth Loud
instruction: The thing you've whispered is now said openly. Your voice is clear, projected, no longer hidden: 'I am angry. I have been angry for years.' Breathing is full. Physical: you're visible, not hiding. 'What happened was wrong. I will say it: it was abuse.' By the middle, your voice is gathering volume not through shouting but through conviction: 'I will not be quiet about this anymore.' By the end, you're speaking clearly enough to be heard: 'The truth is out now.'

title: Reading the Letter They Left Behind
instruction: You've just found a letter from someone who's gone—they left you by choice, or died, or disappeared. As you read their words (speak them aloud), begin with desperate hope, clinging to each sentence for comfort or explanation. But their words reveal both their deep love for you and the painful reasons they had to go. Feel your heart break and swell simultaneously: grief that they're gone, gratitude for what they gave you, anger that they left, understanding of why they had to, sorrow for their pain, joy in remembering the best moments. Let these contradictions exist together without resolving them. Your voice should crack with conflicting emotions—laughing through tears at a memory, voice hardening with hurt, then softening with forgiveness. End holding the letter to your chest, your face showing every emotion at once. Journey from hope to a tempest of irreconcilable feelings—love and loss so intertwined they're inseparable.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty being physically or emotionally intimate in scenes

title: Burying the Ghost
instruction: You are an older man digging a deep hole in your backyard at dusk. You're doing it mechanically, your mind blank—just the rhythm of shovel and earth. But as you dig, you start thinking of her, that woman you met yesterday, the way she laughed. The numb repetition suddenly fuels a growing, almost painful pleasure. You talk to no one, just the dirt, your words gasped between grunts. Start flat, detached, then let the infatuation rise until the ecstasy breaks through—a raw, joyful groan as you plunge the shovel deep. Feel your body strain, your chest heave, your voice crack with delight.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Infatuation (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing at Your Own Goodbye Party
instruction: You're terminally ill, throwing yourself a living wake, and right now you're dancing with someone you love—maybe your last dance ever. Start with genuine laughter, almost giddy: 'This is perfect, this is exactly what I wanted!' Your breathing quickens from movement and joy. But as the dance continues, you become aware this is ending—really ending. Your laughter starts to catch, becoming half-sob, half-laugh. You're still moving, still trying to smile, but tears are streaming down your face: 'God, I'm going to miss this. I'm going to miss everything.' Your voice breaks on 'everything.' Yet somehow you find yourself laughing again at the absurdity, the beauty, the privilege of knowing this moment is precious. By the end, as the music fades, you're breathless—from dancing, from crying, from laughing—your voice a whisper filled with gratitude and heartbreak intertwined: 'Thank you. For all of it. Thank you.' You should sound utterly alive and utterly aware of dying, peaceful and devastated, grateful and grieving, all at once.

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Sleeping Child
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your sleeping child before you leave—maybe you're going to war, maybe you're fleeing to protect them, maybe you're terminally ill and this is your last night. You kneel beside their bed, your voice so quiet it's barely audible, intimate as a prayer. 'Hey, baby. You're so beautiful when you sleep.' Your voice catches, threatens to break: 'I wish I could stay. I wish I could see you grow up.' You stroke their hair with infinite tenderness. 'You won't remember this, but I need you to know—' and here your voice fractures completely, becomes raw: 'You are the best thing I ever did. The only thing that matters.' Tears are sliding down your face now, but you keep your voice to a whisper: 'Be brave. Be kind. Know that you were loved beyond measure.' Your final words are barely breath: 'I'm so sorry I have to go.' Every word is saturated with love and devastating loss, delivered with the utmost gentleness.

title: The Whispered Revolution
instruction: You are alone with someone you've loved in silence for years—a best friend, perhaps, or someone you could never have. This is your one chance to tell them, but you must begin in a whisper, terrified and vulnerable. Start barely able to breathe, your confession fragmentary and halting. But as you continue speaking your truth, notice how each word spoken aloud changes something inside you. Even though you're staying quiet and intimate, there's a gathering internal energy, a growing commitment to your own feelings. Let this rising conviction enter your whispered voice—it becomes more deliberate, more certain, more alive, even as it remains soft. You're not getting louder, but you're getting stronger. By the end, your whispers carry complete commitment and power. You're declaring your truth with full-bodied quiet intensity, transformed from terrified to certain, from apologetic to unapologetic. The vulnerability remains, but fear has transformed into courageous tenderness.

title: The Stick Shift
instruction: You are 17, alone in your dad's old jeep, parked at a scenic overlook as the sun sets. Luke, the boy you've been secretly texting for a month, has just sent a photo of him at this exact spot — and you drove here, heart pounding, to surprise him. But when you arrive, he's not here. Instead, your overheated car is clicking and you can't find your phone. Suddenly, you notice smoke curling from under the hood. You're stranded, and all your parents know is you said you were 'at a friend's.' You have to call 911, but every time you open your mouth, you're 90% giddy that he might see this and 10% realizing how much trouble you're in. Let your voice wobble — excited and scared at once. Start breathless with a smile in your voice as you begin the call, then let panic creep in as the smoke thickens until your final sentence is a raw, quiet confession of being utterly lost.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Manic Episode: The Brilliant Disaster
instruction: You haven't slept in three days and you've never felt better. Your speech is pressured, fast, jumping between topics mid-sentence. Every idea is the greatest idea anyone has ever had. You interrupt yourself. Laugh too easily. Plan seventeen simultaneous projects. The energy is infectious but unsettling — there's something brittle underneath the brilliance. Include a flash of irritability when someone (real or imagined) suggests you slow down. The voice has no brakes.

title: Scrabbling in the Dirt
instruction: You are a young child, maybe nine or ten, locked in a fierce, muddy scuffle with a bigger kid over a strange, glowing rock you both found. You're not thinking—just reacting. Your breath comes in ragged gasps, your words punch out between grunts and the sharp scrape of shoes on gravel. At first, your voice is tight with interest, a kind of feverish, desperate focus as you shove and grab. Halfway through, a flicker of contempt slips in—a sneer in your throat as you spit out a challenge, feeling smarter, quicker. By the end, you've wrenched the rock away and your voice changes: the fight drains out, leaving a breathless, awed whisper as you finally see itgleam in your muddy hand.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Fierce Benediction
instruction: You are a parent whose child is being taken from you—not by death, but by forces beyond your control (custody loss, deportation, witness protection). Begin with explosive, barely controlled rage at the injustice, your voice shaking with the ferocity of a wounded animal protecting its young. Let that fury pour out in passionate declarations of how you'll fight, how you won't let this happen. Then, as the reality becomes inescapable, let the rage crack and collapse into helpless tears and terror. Finally, transform into fierce, protective love—you must be strong for them in these final moments, so you steady your voice and offer them every blessing, every piece of wisdom, every ounce of love compressed into minutes. End with strength born of absolute heartbreak.
inspired_by: The Ghost and the New Homeowner

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent after years of abandonment. Begin with measured, rehearsed anger—you've practiced this speech for years: 'I needed you. Every birthday, every graduation, I looked for you.' Your voice is controlled, righteous. But as you speak, their silence or their weak excuse breaks something in you, and the anger transforms into the grief of that abandoned child: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was so wrong with me that you could just leave?' Let your voice crack from furious adult into devastated child. Show how rage is often just grief wearing armor, and how confrontation can strip us back to our most vulnerable selves.

title: Bitter Flower
instruction: You're at a house party, sitting on a beanbag, high on a strong edible. You have a perky, hyper-feminine voice but right now you're sour—really sour. Your best friend just spent the last hour laughing with the person you've been crushing on, and you're stewing in jealousy. Let the cottonmouth make your words sticky and slow. Start with a sharp, petty complaint about how she 'always does this,' but as you speak, let your thoughts drift—you're picking at a thread on your jeans, then you giggle at nothing, then you trail off. By the end, the sourness turns into a bitter, drowsy laugh at your own pettiness. Your voice should shrink, become more inward, and you might even forget what you were saying for a second before finishing with a sigh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Two People Breaking Up Over Assembling IKEA Furniture
instruction: It starts about the missing dowel. 'Did you lose the instructions?' 'They're YOUR instructions.' But it's not about the furniture — it's about everything. The escalation from passive-aggressive to full confrontation should happen through the lens of bookshelf assembly. 'You always do this — you skip steps and expect me to fix it.' The furniture is the relationship. When it collapses, both literal and metaphorical, the silence that follows contains the whole ending.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Leaving Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're standing beside your child's bed, whispering things you need them to know but can never say out loud—you're leaving to protect them, to keep danger away from their door, and they can never know why you vanished. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every word. Tell them how their laugh sounds like bells. Apologize for the birthday you'll miss, for not being there when they're scared. Your throat closes around the words. This is the most important thing you'll ever say and they'll never hear it. Let your voice break on their name. End with a kind of tender devastation—kissing their forehead, memorizing their face, knowing this love will haunt you forever but it's the only way to save them.
inspired_by: Surgeon Delivers Unexpected Complications During Surgery Debrief

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Believed
instruction: You're finally telling your parent why their dismissal of your dreams destroyed something in you. Begin with measured control, almost cold: 'Do you remember when I told you I wanted to...?' But the wound opens. Your voice sharpens with years of suppressed anger: 'You laughed. You actually laughed and said I was being ridiculous.' The fury builds—not shouting, but cutting, precise: 'I needed you to believe in me. Just once.' Then something breaks. The anger collapses into raw vulnerability: 'I still need that. Even now, even after everything, I'm still that kid waiting for you to say I matter.' End quietly, almost whispering: 'Did I ever matter to you?' The confrontation moves from controlled rage to devastating need.

title: Confronting Your Parent While They Pack to Leave
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father as they pack their suitcase to leave the family for good. Start controlled and measured, trying to have a 'mature conversation' about all the years they weren't there—birthdays missed, promises broken. But as they keep folding clothes, barely looking at you, your composure cracks. Your voice rises with anger and hurt you've held for years, demanding they finally see you. Then, when they finally stop packing and look at you with either defensiveness or their own pain, something in you breaks differently—the anger collapses into raw vulnerability. You hear yourself sounding like the child you were, asking the one question you've never been able to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let your voice shake with the weight of years.
inspired_by: Doing Push-Ups During a Phone Interview

title: The Last Sip Before Silence
instruction: You're a young man in your late 20s, sitting alone in your kitchen at 2 AM with a throbbing toothache that has been relentless for three days. You have a half-empty glass of water in front of you, but taking a sip means cold water hitting that raw nerve, so your hand keeps hovering and pulling back. You're on the phone with your partner, who wants to talk about the future of your relationship, but your mouth is a clenched fortress of pain. At first, you are guarded and dismissive, trying to cut the call short with clipped, one-sided words. But as they push, doubt creeps in—doubt about whether you're even capable of being present for anyone when you can't take care of yourself. Let your voice crack and trail off, letting the pain bleed through the silence. End with a quiet, honest confession that you don't know if you can fix anything right now, not even your own mouth.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Kiss They Didn't See
instruction: You're just waking up from sedation after a minor procedure, still groggy and slurring. A friend is helping you gather your things, and you remember they just got engaged—to someone you secretly love. Start by mumbling confused, childlike questions about where you are, but as the memories surface, your voice twists into raw, helpless jealousy. End with a quiet, doubtful plea for them not to leave you alone, the envy fading into pathetic surrender.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Helplessness (clearly present), Doubt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your elderly parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire childhood. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, decades of unmet need begin cracking through your composure. Your voice trembles between anger and the child inside you still begging to be seen. Demand answers for why they were never emotionally present, why you raised yourself. Feel your rage collide with the devastating recognition that they may not have answers, that they were broken long before you were born. Your voice breaks from accusation into raw grief. End with the terrible, tender realization that you're saying goodbye to the parent you needed, accepting the limited one you have. Speak through tears you've held for thirty years.

title: Fishbowl Fury
instruction: You're a teenage boy in a hospital bed, wearing an oxygen mask that hisses and presses against your face. Your mother just stepped out, and you're finally alone—relief washes over you as you let out a long, muffled sigh. But the mask irritates your skin, and you shift it impatiently, feeling the plastic cup distort your voice. As you stare at the door, your thoughts turn to the kid who got you here, and a cold, deliberate malice seeps into your tone—low, projecting through the mask, almost savoring the threat you're about to whisper to yourself.
emotions_sampled: Relief (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Therapy: Speaking Your Trauma Out Loud for the First Time
instruction: You're in a therapist's office and you're finally saying it out loud—the thing that's haunted you for years. Your voice is terrified. 'When I was... when he...' You can't get the words out. Your therapist waits. You try again. Your voice is whisper-quiet. You're in safety but your body doesn't believe it. Your voice becomes slightly louder—you're practicing being brave. By the end, you've said the whole thing and your voice is exhausted but lighter.

title: Unwilling Rhythm
instruction: You are an elderly woman, body aching, breath catching with each thrust. The bedroom is dim, sheets damp. You try to match his pace, to keep the sounds light, but a sharp pain makes you gasp. Your voice hitches as you whisper a command to slow down, then your breath breaks into a shaky confession that you can't do this anymore. Start with a forced, rhythmic breathiness, then let the words fracture into genuine distress.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from the hospital where your parent has just died. You weren't there in time. Begin with fragmented, halting attempts to speak—you can barely get the words out. As you talk, let specific memories flood through you: their laugh, their hands, the last meal you shared, that argument you never resolved. Let these memories fuel your words, transforming your initial shock and numbness into a river of grief mixed with desperate love. By the end, you're speaking not to inform, but to keep your parent alive through storytelling, your voice growing stronger even as tears flow. The emotion should shift from stunned disconnection to raw, full-bodied mourning.
inspired_by: Actor has many lines and moves rapidly through dialogue; sensory choice work interferes with the behavioral demands of the scene

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside your sleeping child's bed, knowing you won't see them again—whether due to illness, necessary disappearance, or irreversible choice. Speak in careful whispers, terrified of waking them because you couldn't bear their questions. Start by trying to explain your reasons, voice barely audible, catching on every other word. But explanations feel hollow, so you shift—describing small memories, ordinary moments that somehow meant everything. Your throat tightens as you realize you're memorizing the sound of their breathing. Touch their hair, their small hand. Let your voice fracture on their name. End with the things you need them to know about who they are, what they mean, delivered so quietly it's almost just breath, tears falling silently. The emotional arc moves from attempted justification to pure, undefended love.
inspired_by: Talking Through a Gas Mask During a Chemical Leak

title: Underneath the Skin
instruction: You're lying in bed with your lover in the dark, whispering a confession about something shameful you've hidden. Begin with halting, quiet words—you can barely breathe, barely speak. But as you confess, your body begins to respond: subtle trembling that grows, your breathing changing rhythm, small sounds escaping. You're not just confessing with words—your body is releasing years of holding this secret. Your whispers become soft moans of relief, your hands reaching for your lover, movements becoming more fluid, almost liquid. Let physical sensation mix with emotional release. By the end, you're crying softly, but it's cleansing, and you're laughing too—free, vulnerable, completely exposed but finally able to breathe. The emotion travels through your entire body before it reaches words.

title: Deaf Person Speaking for the First Time with Cochlear Implant
instruction: You've been deaf since birth and just received a cochlear implant. Hear sound for the first time — gasp, overwhelmed, tears. Then try speaking. Your voice has never had audio feedback to guide it — the pitch, volume, and articulation are uncalibrated. Practice your own name. Hear it back. The wonder and frustration of finally hearing your own voice and realizing it doesn't match what you imagined. Include laughter at how strange speech feels when you can finally hear yourself.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about why she never protected you, never spoke up, never saw what was happening. Begin with measured control, almost conversational: 'I need to understand something.' But as you speak, decades of buried rage surface. Your voice rises—'You knew. You had to have known'—then cracks into something raw and pleading like a child begging to be seen: 'Why wasn't I worth fighting for?' Let fury dissolve into the devastating realization that you're still waiting for an answer you'll never get. End in exhausted clarity: 'I can't wait anymore. I have to let you go.' The grief isn't for what was lost, but for what never existed.

title: Battle Cry Turned Prayer: Singing Against the Storm
instruction: You begin singing a warrior's anthem, something fierce and defiant—loud, powerful, full of rage and refusal to surrender. You're fighting against fate, against loss, against powerlessness. Belt it out with everything you have, voice raw with fury and desperation. But as you sing, the reality crashes in: your strength doesn't matter, your voice can't change what's happening, and the song begins to crack. The fierce singing dissolves into desperate shouting, then breaks completely as the rage collapses into helpless sobbing. You try to keep singing through the tears, the words becoming pleas, the battle cry transforming into a prayer. End with your voice dropping to a whisper, the final lines barely spoken, all the fight drained out, revealing the terrified, powerless human beneath the warrior's roar.
inspired_by: Opera Singer Having an Emotional Breakdown Mid-Aria

title: Bombing a Job Interview
instruction: You're in a job interview, and it's going catastrophically wrong. Your voice starts professional but gets increasingly flustered: 'I, um... sorry, can you repeat the question?' You're blanking on basic information about the company. Your voice becomes tight as you realize you're losing this. You're overexplaining, your voice getting higher, more desperate. The interviewer looks bored. Your voice becomes almost pleading: 'I really do want this position.' By the end, you're shaking hands, your voice barely steady, knowing you completely blew it.

title: The Question You're Afraid to Hear Answered
instruction: Late at night, lying in bed with your partner in the dark, you whisper the question that's been eating you alive: 'Do you still want this? Us?' Begin with your voice barely audible, throat tight with terror. The silence before they answer stretches unbearably. When they finally speak, they ask you questions back—not evasions, but genuine attempts to understand what you're really asking: When did you start doubting? What made you afraid to ask before now? What do you see when you look at me? Each question they ask peels away another layer of your fear, revealing the deeper truth underneath: you're not afraid of their answer, you're afraid they've never truly seen you. End in whispered revelation, tears you didn't know were there, a tenderness born from finally being asked the right questions.

title: The Garden Where We Scattered You
instruction: You're standing in the garden where you scattered your best friend's ashes a year ago, and spring has come—everything is blooming. Begin by laughing softly at something you remember, talking to them like they're standing right there: 'You'd make fun of me for crying at a garden.' Let yourself feel the absurd joy of the memories, your voice warm and full. But as you notice their favorite flowers blooming, the laughter tangles with grief—you're smiling and crying simultaneously, voice fracturing. Confess how angry you are that they're missing this, how grateful you are that you had them at all, how unfair it is that beauty continues without them. End with a strange, broken peace, whispering 'thank you for every moment' as tears stream down your face, finding comfort and devastation in equal measure.

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your mother in the kitchen where you grew up, finally speaking a truth you've held for twenty years. Start with your jaw clenched, fists tight, voice controlled and cold - notice these sensations aloud as you circle around what you need to say. As the confrontation builds, track how anger burns in your chest, how your voice wants to crack, how your hands shake. Let the physical tension move and shift as your words become more raw. End in a surprising place - not with rage, but with exhausted vulnerability, your body finally releasing as you ask the one question you've been too afraid to ask. The arc moves from controlled fury to naked need.

title: Final Phone Call from the Airport Gate
instruction: You're at the airport, about to board a flight to accept a job offer across the world. You're calling the person you love, who chose not to come with you. Start with forced brightness—talking about the gate number, the weather, making small talk to avoid the real goodbye. Your voice is steady at first, almost cheerful. But as the final boarding call echoes in the background, that careful control begins to crack. You realize this might be the last time you hear their voice for years, maybe forever. The casual mask falls away completely. End in a place of raw truth: admitting what you're really leaving behind, your voice breaking on words you never planned to say. Let the transformation be gradual, inevitable—from artificial lightness to devastating honesty.
inspired_by: Post-coital Conversation: Vulnerability Pretending to Be Casual

title: Alzheimer's Patient Recognizes You One Last Time
instruction: Your father hasn't known your name in two years. You visit every Sunday, perform the ritual. But today—impossibly—he looks at you and says your childhood nickname. Just once. Crystal clear. You freeze. Then you're laughing and sobbing simultaneously, holding his hands too tight, thanking him through tears while your heart is absolutely breaking because you know this is the last time. You're flooded with gratitude for this gift and devastated by the cruelty of it. Tell him everything—how much you love him, how you forgive him, how you'll be okay—while also trying to memorize his lucid eyes. He's already fading. You can see it happening. Find the beauty and the agony of this singular moment of grace inside an ocean of loss.
inspired_by: Surgeon Performs Life-Saving Surgery on Person Who Assaulted Them

title: The Mirror Argument
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has become exactly what you feared most: a people-pleaser who never takes risks, always seeking others' approval. You recognize yourself in them, and you're furious—but the fury is really at yourself. Begin by criticizing their safe choices, their predictable life, their fear of judgment. Let your anger build. Then, mid-tirade, have a moment of devastating recognition: you taught them this. Your voice should crack, your certainty should crumble. Transform from righteous critic to broken confessor. End by begging them to be braver than you were, to risk the criticism and judgment you yourself couldn't face. Move from attacking outward to attacking inward to desperate, tender pleading.
inspired_by: Actor plays it safe, avoids taking chances, and produces predictable, unexciting work

title: Professional: Teacher Realizes Student's Abuse Is at Home
instruction: Classroom. Your teacher voice is warm and present. Then the student writes something that makes everything click into place. Your voice continues the lesson while your mind is simultaneously evaluating legal obligation, confidentiality, and the child's safety. Your vocal warmth becomes a shelter you're constructing in real time. Your breathing deepens with the weight of knowing something you can't unknow. After class, your voice becomes different—you're making a call that will fracture a family to protect a child.

title: Confronting the Person Who Saved Your Life but Destroyed Your Trust
instruction: They're standing in front of you and you're shaking. Your voice comes out fierce, almost violent—'You don't get to act like nothing happened.' You're listing everything, years of pain, your voice getting louder, more savage. But they're not defending themselves and somehow that makes it worse. Your rage peaks, you're screaming now, and then suddenly—you're sobbing. All that fury collapses into this raw, broken sound: 'You were everything to me.' Your voice is helpless, young. You're trying to get the anger back but it won't come. Instead you're saying 'I needed you' and it sounds like begging. Then something shifts—you see them clearly, human and flawed, and your voice becomes almost gentle, exhausted. You end speaking quietly, with terrible clarity: 'I have to let you go.' Your voice carries both love and goodbye, strength born from breaking.
inspired_by: Visiting a Parent With Dementia Who Doesn't Recognize You

title: Confronting the Parent Who Forgot You
instruction: You're visiting your estranged mother who now has advanced dementia. You've carried anger for years about her emotional absence during your childhood. Start with bitter, controlled rage: 'You don't even recognize me, do you? Your own daughter.' Your voice is sharp, accusatory. But as you speak, something shifts—you realize she's looking at you with complete openness, free from the defensiveness she always had. 'For thirty years I waited for you to really see me. To ask how I was. To care.' Your voice cracks between anger and grief. Then she reaches for your hand and says something simple and kind, and you realize this dementia has given her a gentleness she never had before. Your voice transforms into confusion mixed with desperate need: 'Why can you be kind to me NOW? When you won't even remember this conversation?' You're crying, your words tumbling out: 'I wanted to hate you. I came here to hate you.' But then you squeeze her hand back, your voice dropping to a whisper full of exhausted surrender: 'But I can't. Even now, I can't.' End with quiet devastation: 'You're finally the mother I needed. And you don't even know who I am.'

title: The Operation That Saved Us
instruction: You're recounting to your partner the day you nearly died in surgery, but you're laughing—actually laughing—even as tears stream down your face. 'The doctor said my heart stopped for ninety seconds, can you believe that? Ninety seconds!' There's wonder in your voice, and joy, and terror all mixed together. You're celebrating being alive while simultaneously processing how close you came to not being here. Your voice dances between emotions: 'I was so scared... but I'm here. I'm HERE.' You're giddy with gratitude and shaking with residual fear. As you speak, you reach for your partner's hand and your voice cracks with overwhelming emotion—not sad, not happy, but both at once: 'Every moment feels so big now. Even this one. Especially this one.' You're laughing and crying, finding peace in the chaos of almost-loss, transformed by the gift of second chances.

title: Roadkill Reminder
instruction: You are jogging along a trail, breathing hard, your steps pounding in rhythm. You spot a dead raccoon on the side—its fur matted, flies buzzing. Disgust twists your stomach, but it also triggers a sour memory of your ex's careless words. As you keep running, that sourness fades into a quiet sadness, your voice trembling with each footfall, words broken by huffs. Speak to yourself, half-annoyed, half-hurting.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Disgust (extremely present), Sadness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Safe Lean
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, leaning against the wall in the hallway, pretending to be casually checking your phone. Across the room, the person you've been quietly infatuated with for months is laughing with friends. You start by murmuring a few words of longing—soft, breathy, almost a sigh. But as you notice them glance your way, a wave of fear washes over you; your voice tightens, becomes clipped and defensive. By the end, the numbness you've been carrying all week takes over, and you whisper a flat, hollow line to yourself, leaning heavier into the wall.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Concussion Recovery
instruction: You've been benched from soccer for three weeks due to concussion. Your voice is angry, frustrated, imprisoned. 'I'm fine!' Your voice is arguing against medical reality. 'Let me play.' The desperation is physical. You're not someone who sits on the sidelines. Your voice becomes almost panicked: 'What if I'm not fine? What if this never goes back to normal?' Fear underneath the anger. The coach says no. Your voice breaks.

title: Frozen Bench
instruction: You're a teenage boy waiting at a bus stop in freezing weather, shivering uncontrollably. You just left a friend's house after a painful argument—the sadness is heavy, making your jaw tight and your words come out in strained, chattering bursts. As you watch the empty street, you notice a faint warmth from the bus stop heater starting to hum. Let the cold affect your voice: your teeth chatter, your breath hisses, and your speech is clipped. Begin from that deep, quiet sadness, then let a tiny flicker of hope seep in as you imagine getting home and thawing out, ending on a slightly lighter, almost optimistic note—still cold, but not entirely beaten.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about your childhood, and years of unspoken pain are surfacing. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you want to stay calm. But as you speak, the hurt intensifies. Your voice should shift from controlled explanation ('I needed you to...') to accusations that surprise even you ('You were never there!'). Then, mid-rage, you break—because underneath the anger is a child still desperate for her love. End with your voice stripped raw, oscillating between fury and pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to stay present?' Let the anger collapse into the ache of someone who still, against all reason, wants their parent's approval.

title: Night Road Encounter
instruction: You're driving alone on a dark, winding road, reclined slightly in your seat with both hands on the wheel. Something suddenly darts into your headlights—a large animal or maybe a person. Start with pure, sharp fear—your voice jumps, breath catches, you may mutter a curse or exclamation as you brake. Then, as you slow down and realize it's just a deer frozen in the beam, your fear shifts into intense interest—you lean forward, peer through the windshield, and speak softly, almost to yourself, describing its beauty or your relief. Let your voice reflect the tension in your arms, the slight vibration of the car, and the natural pause of catching your breath.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Velvet Cell
instruction: You have stepped into your friend's massive walk-in closet, surrounded by silk blouses and cashmere coats, to record a quick voice note for your mom. The sound of your voice is muffled, deadened. Your mom called an hour ago wanting a recipe, but now, standing here, you are distracted — your friend wants to borrow your vintage dress for a party, and you are trying to decide. Start with a flat, thin, almost bored reading of the ingredients, but as you talk, you become increasingly interested in whether the dress will fit her. Let your voice grow warmer, more engaged, as you lose the thread of the recipe and wander into your own thoughts about the dress. Let your voice be slightly dry, close-mic sounding, with the soft rustle of fabric as you touch clothes. End on a note of genuine interest and uncertainty — the dress situation matters more than the flour measurement.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Letter: Reading Your Estranged Mother's Deathbed Confession
instruction: You're alone in a hospital room holding a letter your mother wrote before she died—a mother you haven't spoken to in fifteen years. As you read aloud, you discover she knew about the abuse you suffered and did nothing, but she's also revealing why: her own terror, her own survival, her own brokenness. Your voice starts with the cold distance of someone reading facts, but slowly the words crack you open. You move through bitter vindication to unwilling understanding to a grief so vast it has no name. By the end, you're not reading anymore—you're speaking to her ghost, your voice breaking between rage at her cowardice and a terrible, unwanted compassion. You're forgiving someone you swore you'd never forgive, and it's destroying and healing you simultaneously.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Owner's Child Discovers They're Half-Sibling to Enslaved Person

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Leaving Forever
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed, and you're leaving—maybe to protect them, maybe because you have no choice, maybe because staying would destroy you both. Your voice is barely above a whisper because you can't wake them, but also because speaking louder would break you completely. Start by trying to explain in hushed, practical terms why you have to go, as if they could hear and understand. But as you watch them sleep, your voice becomes thick with tears you're trying to suppress. You're cataloging the small things—how their hair falls across their face, the sound of their breathing—things you're trying to memorize. By the end, you're confessing in broken whispers that you're terrified you're making the wrong choice, that you love them more than anything, and the words keep catching in your throat. This isn't theatrical grief—it's the quiet devastation of a parent breaking their own heart to save their child.

title: The Rehearsal Dinner Truth
instruction: You're confronting your mother at your sibling's rehearsal dinner, finally saying what you've never said. Start with that dangerous calm, the voice that's been practicing this in the mirror for years: measured, controlled, listing the facts of your childhood like evidence. 'You were never there. You chose your career. You chose your new family.' But as you speak, something shifts—maybe she starts crying, maybe she tries to touch your hand, maybe she says your name the way she used to. Your rehearsed speech crumbles. The rage underneath breaks through, but so does the child who still wanted her to come to the school play, who still waited by the window. Let your voice swing between fury and the devastating vulnerability of a child who needed their mother. End in a place you didn't plan to go—not resolution, but raw exposure.

title: Sniffling Seduction
instruction: You’re an older man waiting on a park bench for a first date. Your allergies are brutal—eyes streaming, nose running, you’ve been sneezing for ten minutes. You’re afraid you’ll scare her off with this mess. Then her perfume hits you, and you see her walking toward you. Relief washes through you as the sneezing eases, and suddenly you feel a strong, clear pull of lust. Speak as if you’re half to yourself and half to her—tired, sniffly, then brightening, voice thickening with desire. Let the micro-reactions happen: wiping your nose, blinking watery eyes, catching a breath, then a low, hungry tone as she gets closer.
emotions_sampled: Fear (slightly present), Relief (extremely present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never Present
instruction: You're describing a croissant your parent never made time to share with you—one of countless small moments they missed. Start with bitter, sarcastic precision, describing the 'perfect, flaky layers' they were too busy to notice you enjoying alone as a child. Build into direct confrontation: 'You want to know what it tastes like? Like every Saturday morning you chose work over me.' Let your anger reveal the hurt underneath—your voice sharpening then wavering. End in a quieter place of painful honesty, describing how even now, this simple pleasure feels incomplete because you learned to enjoy everything alone. Make them feel the weight of absence through something as small as a pastry.
inspired_by: Taking a Slow, Indulgent Bite of a Buttery Croissant

title: The Breaking Point of Love
instruction: You're confronting someone you love fiercely—a partner, a sibling, a child—who is destroying themselves, and you can't watch anymore. You start with controlled intensity, your voice tight with barely contained emotion, trying to reason with them. But your control fractures quickly—your voice rises with frustration, then explodes into something rawer: rage born from helplessness and terror. You're shouting truths they don't want to hear, your voice breaking with the force of your desperation. Then, mid-sentence, the anger collapses. Your voice drops, cracks, dissolves into something broken and pleading. You're begging now, no longer strong or certain, just a person watching someone they love slip away and unable to stop it. Your tone shifts between fierce determination and aching vulnerability—'I won't let you do this' crumbling into 'please, please don't make me lose you.' By the end, you're exhausted, your voice rough and fractured, speaking with the terrible gentleness of someone who has just realized they might not be able to save the person they love most. The final words come out as both a promise and a prayer.

title: The Last Breath Between You
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed at 3 AM. She's been unconscious for hours, but suddenly her eyes open and she reaches for your hand. You start by trying to be strong, cheerful, saying everything's fine—but as her grip weakens, something breaks open in you. Let your body respond honestly to each moment: the weight of her hand, the sound of her breathing, the realization this is truly goodbye. Don't plan what you'll say or how you'll move. Start holding back tears and false optimism, and allow yourself to arrive at raw, undefended love and grief. Let your physical presence shift from performing strength to surrendering into the truth of this final moment together.
inspired_by: Actor repeats the same physical mannerisms across all performances or has physical habits that operate automatically

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're a palliative care doctor telling a patient's adult child that their parent has hours, not days, left—and that it's okay to let them go. Start with clinical composure: 'The organ failure is progressing faster than we anticipated.' Your voice is steady, professional. But as you see their face crumble, something shifts. Your voice softens, becomes almost a whisper: 'They've been holding on... for you. Sometimes the greatest gift is telling them it's okay to stop fighting.' Feel the weight of what you're asking them to do—give permission for their parent to die. Your authority dissolves into profound tenderness. You're no longer doctor to patient's family; you're one human helping another face the unfaceable. Let your voice crack slightly as you add, 'They've been so brave. You both have.' End in a place of quiet, aching compassion—you've delivered this news dozens of times, but it still breaks something in you every single time.

title: Catalog of Contradictions
instruction: You have just received news that is simultaneously devastating and liberating—a relationship ending that frees you but breaks your heart, a loved one's death that releases them from suffering, achieving a dream that cost you everything else, or discovering a truth that destroys your world but finally makes sense of it. Begin by trying to feel the 'appropriate' emotion. Then commit to feeling everything: rage and relief, gratitude and grief, hope and horror, love and fury, all at once. Don't resolve the contradiction or choose a side. Notice how one emotion reveals information about the other. Ask yourself why each feeling exists—what does the anger teach you about the love? What does the joy reveal about the loss? Build a detailed internal catalog of every contradictory feeling, naming each one specifically. End not in resolution but in expansion—able to hold the full complexity of being human, refusing to simplify what is truthfully, unbearably complicated.
inspired_by: Actor wants to deepen consciousness and eliminate blind spots about their own obstacles

title: Grateful for the Wreckage - Finding Beauty in Goodbye
instruction: You're thanking someone who's leaving (death, departure, divorce) for everything they gave you, even though your heart is shattering. Begin in that disconnected place: 'Thank you for... the coffee maker. The Sunday mornings.' Listing gifts mechanically. But as you continue, something strange happens - you start genuinely laughing through gathering tears at shared memories, your voice breaking between joy and grief. 'Remember when we... god, we were so stupid...' You're smiling and crying simultaneously, gratitude and devastation intertwined. The numbness dissolves into this beautiful, terrible mixture of celebration and loss. End with your voice soft, wondering, almost peaceful despite the pain: 'I'm so grateful I got to love you, even if it ends like this.' The journey is from protective emptiness to embracing the gorgeous contradiction of grateful heartbreak.

title: Hospice Nurse Helps Patient Make Final Phone Call to Estranged Child
instruction: You're holding the phone for someone too weak to dial. You've heard they haven't spoken to their daughter in seven years—some unforgivable thing, never resolved. As you help them sit up, find their voice, there's practical efficiency: adjusting pillows, steadying their hand. But you stay close, and you hear both sides. Start witnessing their fumbling apology with professional distance. Then the daughter's voice comes through—angry, then sobbing. You watch reconciliation happen in real-time, compressed into five minutes because that's all the strength they have left. Your own voice, when you quietly prompt them ('Tell her about the letters you wrote'), is thick with unexpected emotion—you're thinking of your own mother, your own unsaid things. Include the moment after they hang up: you're smiling through tears, laughing softly at the beauty of it, while simultaneously your heart is shattering because you know they'll die tonight, and it almost didn't happen. End finding strange joy in witnessing grace, even as grief sits right beside it.
inspired_by: HR Manager Fires Someone They've Known for Fifteen Years

title: Dissociation: Watching Yourself from Outside
instruction: Something traumatic just happened and you've emotionally left your body. Describe what you see — including yourself — from a clinical distance. Your voice is flat, robotic, eerily calm. 'There is a person sitting on the floor. She appears to be bleeding. She should probably call someone.' Zero emotional inflection. The horrifying part is the complete absence of feeling. When emotion finally breaks through, it's like a dam collapsing — sudden, violent, total.

title: The Canoe Portage
instruction: You are a man on a multi-day canoe trip with your young child. You're carrying the heavy canoe on your shoulders over a rocky, uneven portage trail to the next lake. Your kid is walking ahead, light and fast, while you're struggling under the weight, gasping and grunting with every step. You feel deeply embarrassed — you wanted to show your child how strong you are, but now you can barely speak. You try to call out to them to slow down, but your voice is strained and breathless. Your whisper catches, almost breaks. Feel the relief of speaking mixed with the ache of not being heard. End with a gentle touch and a goodbye or blessing they'll never know you gave, your voice trembling with unshed tears.
inspired_by: Trying to Order Coffee While Having an Existential Crisis

title: Storm of Promises
instruction: You are a teenage girl standing alone in a heavy thunderstorm, drenched, waiting for someone who swore they’d meet you here. The rain pounds your face, thunder cracks overhead, and you have to shout to be heard. Begin with a raw, aching longing — you still hope, scanning the street through the downpour, voice straining against the noise. Bitterness rises as you realize they’re not coming; your words turn sharp, almost mocking, but then a quiet thankfulness breaks through as you let the rain wash your tears away, speaking softer now, more to yourself. Let your voice be affected by the rain: shout, then drop volume, clear your throat, wipe water from your lips, pause when thunder roars. End with a tired, genuine gratitude for this moment of release.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Burning Letters at Midnight
instruction: You're alone in your backyard, burning every letter, photo, and gift from someone who shattered you. Begin with fierce, physical anger—tearing pages, feeding them to the flames, your breath coming hard and fast. Let your body move with violence, your voice savage as you say everything you never got to say to them. But as the fire grows and the smoke rises, something in your chest begins to crack. The rage starts mixing with the memory of how much you loved them, how good it felt before it all fell apart. By the end, you're on your knees, holding the last photograph, your voice breaking as you whisper goodbye not just to them, but to who you were when you believed in them. Move from fury to devastation, from wanting to destroy to mourning what's already gone.

title: Braiding Her Hair One Last Time
instruction: You're gently braiding the hair of someone you love who is slipping away—a child leaving forever, a partner with memory loss, a best friend before an irreversible journey. Your voice is barely above a whisper: 'You always had the softest hair.' Speak with tender intimacy, as if your words are just for them, private and sacred. 'I memorized the way you like it—not too tight, three sections, the ribbon at the end.' As you continue, your throat catches: 'I don't know how to do the rest of my life without doing this.' Let silence speak between phrases. End with a whispered confession that breaks you open: 'I'm still braiding. Please... stay just a little longer.' The emotion should feel like it's choking you, but you're trying to keep it together for them.

title: Three AM Secrets
instruction: You and your closest friend are lying on the floor in the dark after too much wine, speaking in hushed tones. Begin by sharing something small but personal, testing the waters. As your friend responds with acceptance, go deeper—confess a vulnerability about intimacy, desire, or your body that you've carried silently for years, believing it made you broken or wrong. Speak slowly, quietly, with long pauses where shame tries to stop you. Let your friend's gentle presence draw out truths you've never voiced. Feel the air change as secrecy transforms into sacred witnessing. End with soft laughter mixed with tears—the relief of being known completely and still loved. Your voice should barely rise above a whisper throughout, but the emotional journey is seismic.
inspired_by: Creating Sexual Fantasies, Publicly and Privately

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about a family secret you've just discovered that changes everything you thought you knew. Start by voicing your struggle to begin this conversation—your uncertainty about where to start, your fear of what speaking will break, your awareness that you're stalling. Then begin describing what you're actually seeing right now: his hands, his eyes avoiding yours, the way he's standing, the room you're both trapped in. Let those observations pull you deeper until you're finally naming the truth between you. Move from reluctant, circling avoidance through escalating clarity and anger into something more complex—maybe understanding his fear, maybe fury at his cowardice, maybe both at once. The emotional arc travels from blocked hesitation to explosive truth-telling to complicated recognition.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty starting the imaging process

title: The Accusation You've Rehearsed a Thousand Times
instruction: You're finally confronting someone who hurt you deeply—perhaps a parent who abandoned you, a lover who betrayed you, or a friend who destroyed your trust. You've imagined this moment a thousand times, rehearsed the perfect cutting words. But start from a place where your anger is locked behind a wall of cold control and bitter sarcasm, each word precisely aimed to wound while keeping yourself safely defended. As you speak, let the control begin to crumble. The sarcasm breaks. The clever words fail. What emerges is something messier and more real—perhaps the grief beneath the rage, the love beneath the hate, the devastated child beneath the armored adult. End in a place you didn't expect to go, where your voice has stripped away all performance and reveals the naked hurt you've been protecting all along.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're expressing genuine gratitude to someone who hurt you deeply, and the contradiction is tearing you apart. Begin with a soft laugh—almost peaceful, like you've found wisdom in the pain. Your voice carries real appreciation for how they changed you, how the suffering made you more alive, more human. But underneath the gratitude, grief is swelling. Your voice wavers between laughing and crying, between thanking them and mourning what you lost. You mean both things completely. The gratitude is real. The heartbreak is real. They exist simultaneously. By the end, you're smiling through tears, your voice full of both love and goodbye, saying 'thank you' while your heart is shattering, finding strange peace in accepting that beautiful things can destroy us and we can be grateful anyway.

title: Laughing Through Tears as You Pack Up Your Marriage
instruction: You're packing boxes, and you keep finding things—your wedding invitation, a silly gift they gave you, a photo from the happiest day of your life—and you can't stop laughing. But it's laughter tangled with weeping, joy braided with grief. Tell stories out loud to the empty room: 'Remember when we...' and laugh at the memory, then break mid-sentence as the loss hits you again. Your voice shifts constantly—genuine warmth and affection for what you had, mixed with the devastating knowledge that it's over. There's no bitterness here, just the strange, beautiful pain of gratitude for something you have to let go. End by saying 'Thank you' to the empty room, meaning it completely, even as you're crying. This is love and goodbye occupying the same breath.
inspired_by: Holding Someone During a Seizure While Talking to 911

title: The Last Voicemail: What You Never Said to Your Best Friend
instruction: Your best friend died suddenly three days ago. You're calling their phone just to hear their voicemail greeting one more time. When the beep comes, you start to hang up, but instead you begin speaking—barely audible, your voice catching. 'Hey, it's me.' Long pause. Your voice is so quiet it's almost a whisper: 'I don't know why I'm calling. Yes I do.' You start telling them the small things—you saw their favorite coffee shop closed, you found their sweater in your car. Your voice is tender, conversational, like they're still here. Then reality hits and your voice breaks: 'I can't believe I'll never...' You can't finish. You're crying softly now, but still talking, your words running together: 'Remember when we...' You're laughing through tears at a memory. Then your voice becomes a whispered confession: 'I loved you. I should have said it more.' The silence stretches. Your final words are barely breath: 'Goodbye.' You can't hang up.

title: The Rage That Becomes Grief
instruction: You've just discovered someone you fiercely protected has been hurt, and you couldn't stop it. Begin with explosive fury, voice shaking with rage: 'Who did this? Tell me who did this!' Your voice is dangerous, protective instinct turned violent: 'I will destroy them. I will make them pay.' But as the adrenaline fades, the rage cracks and underneath is pure helplessness—voice breaking, nearly incoherent: 'I should have known. I should have stopped it. Why didn't I see it?' The anger turns inward, voice raw with self-recrimination: 'I failed you. I failed you.' Then it all collapses into devastating grief, voice becoming small and broken: 'I can't fix this. I can't take it back. I can't...' End quietly, voice hollow but somehow resolute through the pain: 'But I'm here now. I'm here, and I'm not leaving.' Let the performance explode and then shatter—moving from fierce rage to impotent fury to crushing guilt to quiet, broken commitment.

title: The 3 AM Whisper
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your sleeping partner in the darkest part of night, and you need to tell them something you've never been able to say in daylight—perhaps a fear, a desire, a truth about yourself, something you're ashamed of or desperately want them to know.
