Begin by just breathing in the darkness, noticing the sound of their breathing, the warmth of their body near yours. Whisper your confession so quietly they might not even hear—you're not sure if you want them to hear or not. Let your voice be fragile, barely above breath. As you speak into the darkness, feel whether you're hoping they'll wake or hoping they'll stay asleep. Let this uncertainty live in your voice. By the end, discover whether you feel more alone or more connected, whether the secret feels heavier or lighter now that it's been spoken into the air between you.

title: Calls Across the Crowd
instruction: You are a child at the end of a long, draining day at a community gathering, holding a heavy bullhorn you barely have energy to lift. You want to find one particular person you've been silently admiring all day—your infatuation gives you a spark. As you press the button, your voice comes out clipped, harsh, and unnaturally loud. A squeal of feedback makes you flinch. You call out their name, shaky with exhaustion, but then—they turn and wave, and astonishment floods you. Your voice cracks with surprise as you stammer, raw and vulnerable, the megaphone amplifying every tremor. Let the fatigue drag your words at first, then let astonishment lift and fracture your speech.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Infatuation (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Confession at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood you needed but never had. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, to explain without attacking. But as you speak, decades of unspoken pain begin to surface. Your voice grows stronger, more insistent, anger mixing with desperate hope that they'll finally understand. Then something shifts—mid-sentence, you realize they may never be capable of giving you what you need, and your confrontation crumbles into vulnerable pleading, your voice small and child-like, asking the question you've always been afraid to ask: 'Did you ever really see me?' End in the raw, exposed silence of someone who has just made themselves utterly defenseless.

title: Dancing Alone in Your Wedding Dress the Morning After Calling It Off
instruction: You're standing in your bedroom in your wedding dress, the wedding that was supposed to be tomorrow now cancelled. Start by describing how the dress feels—the weight of the fabric, the way it moves when you sway, how you imagined this moment would feel different. Begin laughing, a slightly unhinged sound of relief and disbelief mixed together. As you move, let the laughter transform into something complicated—you're laughing at your own courage, crying for the life you won't have, grateful for the disaster you avoided, grieving the version of yourself who believed in that future. Spin in the dress and let your voice crack with the contradiction of it all: you're devastated and liberated, heartbroken and whole, mourning and celebrating in the same breath. End with a sound that's equal parts laugh and sob, acknowledging the absurdity and beauty of choosing yourself, even when it feels like destruction. Let wonder, grief, freedom, and loss all live in your voice simultaneously.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting a parent who was never fully present - not cruel, just... absent in the ways that mattered most. Start with careful, measured words, the kind you've rehearsed a thousand times, trying to explain what their emotional unavailability cost you. But as they deflect or minimize or make excuses, something in you snaps. Your voice must rise with years of unspoken need - not just anger, but the raw ache of a child who needed to be seen and wasn't. Then watch your own rage crack open into something more vulnerable: the realization that they probably couldn't give what they didn't have. End in a complex place - still hurt, still angry, but seeing them as a flawed human rather than an omnipotent parent. Your final words carry both grief for what you'll never have and a fragile beginning of letting go.

title: The Gravel Path Home
instruction: You are an older woman walking alone on a long, crunching gravel driveway after leaving the doctor's office. You just received unexpected news that fills you with overwhelming distress—your voice is strained, almost breaking, as you try to speak over the noisy footsteps. The gravel is loud, so you raise your volume and articulate each word sharply, but your breath catches and your pitch wavers. You begin with a shaky, desperate mutter, trying to convince yourself it's not true, then shift slowly into quiet, exhausted disappointment as you realize you have to face it alone. Let your voice crack, trail off, and then harden slightly at the end with a resigned acceptance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Saying I Love You First
instruction: You're saying 'I love you' first, and you don't know if it will be returned. Your voice is shaky, terrified: 'I... I need to tell you something.' Your heart is in your throat. Your voice comes out barely above a whisper: 'I love you.' The words are out. Your voice is trembling, waiting for their response. If they respond positively, your voice becomes joyful, relieved. If they hesitate, your voice becomes guarded, scared.

title: Whispering What Was Never Said
instruction: You're at your beloved's bedside in their final moments, and they've asked you to describe what their presence has meant to you—something you've never fully expressed. Your voice starts barely audible, tender and fragile: 'You feel like... like coming home.' Each word is carefully chosen, as if they're precious and scarce. Your breathing is shallow, fighting to stay composed. As you continue, emotion pools in your throat: 'Like every good thing I forgot could exist. Like being known.' There are long pauses where you're gathering yourself, swallowing hard. The vulnerability deepens, voice cracking at the edges: 'You're the reason I understand what warmth means, what safety feels like.' By the end, you're crying quietly, but still whispering, still trying to give them this gift: 'And losing you... losing you is learning that some lights don't fade—they just move somewhere I can't follow yet.' Your final words dissolve into breath and tears.

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom on the morning of your wedding, packing the last items you'll take to your new life. Begin by genuinely exploring objects in the room—a trophy, a photo, a book you loved, a ticket stub. Let yourself be truly interested in these artifacts of your former self. As you pack, you find a letter from someone you loved before your partner—someone who hurt you, or whom you hurt, or who simply couldn't be the one. As you read it, let yourself feel the full complexity: excitement for the future pulling against grief for closed doors, gratitude for your partner mixed with an ache for what might have been, joy at becoming someone new shadowed by loss of who you were. Speak to your younger self, to the person who wrote the letter, to your partner who's waiting downstairs. End in a moment where you're smiling and crying at once, where opposite feelings have become a single, complete truth.

title: Man of the House
instruction: You're a 10-year-old boy standing in front of the bathroom mirror, using your dad's electric razor for the first time. You've seen him do it a hundred times, and you're trying to copy his deep, confident tone — but the buzz of the razor is loud in your ears, and you have to pull your cheek flat with your other hand, which makes your words come out warped and silly. Start with a proud, exaggerated bravado, like you're giving a speech to an invisible crowd about being the man of the house now. But as you struggle to keep the razor steady and catch your own distorted reflection, your voice cracks, your confidence breaks, and you end in quiet, embarrassed laughter at how ridiculous you feel.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Living Truthfully
instruction: You've stopped performing and started being. Your voice is aligned with your actual self: 'This is who I really am.' Breathing is settled, at home. Physical: you're comfortable in your body. 'I don't need to pretend anymore.' Vocal tone is released, authentic. 'It took so long to get here—to be honest.' By the end, you're speaking from the place of integrated truth: 'I am living as myself now. This is real.'

title: The Shattered Shield: When Protection Fails
instruction: You are a person who has just learned that someone you were supposed to protect—a younger sibling, your child, a student—has been hurt, and you weren't there to stop it. Begin with disbelief, your words coming fast and desperate: 'No, no, that can't be right. When? Why didn't anyone tell me?' Then rage explodes—not at them, but at yourself, at the situation, at your own powerlessness. Your voice rises, fists might clench, you might pace or strike a wall. But then, suddenly, the rage collapses into something more devastating: guilt and helplessness. You fall into quieter, more broken territory. 'I should have known. I should have seen it.' Your breathing becomes ragged. End with a whispered promise—one you're terrified you can't keep—that you will fix this, you will make it right, even as your voice reveals you have no idea how.
inspired_by: The Cruelest Kindness: Firing a Friend

title: The Beautiful Paradox: Laughing at Your Father's Funeral
instruction: You're standing at your father's funeral, and suddenly you remember something—a ridiculous joke he told, a moment of pure absurdity from his last days, something so perfectly him it makes you laugh out loud. Start with that surprised laugh that escapes before you can stop it, inappropriate and genuine. Let yourself ride that memory, your voice filling with warmth and delight even as tears stream down your face. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, grateful for who he was while your heart splinters that he's gone. Move between joy at the gift of having known him and the devastating reality that you'll never hear his voice again. End with a moment of profound peace mixed with unbearable loss—thanking him through laughter-tears for teaching you that both can exist at once. Let your voice embody the gorgeous contradiction of grief and celebration occupying the same breath.
inspired_by: Anniversary of a Death: Surviving Another Year

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they've asked you to help them let go. Begin with resistance—your voice trembling, pleading with them to hold on just a little longer. But as they explain why they're ready, why they need your blessing to stop fighting, something shifts. Your anger at their leaving transforms into a fierce, protective tenderness. You move from 'Don't you dare give up on me' to 'I'll be okay, I promise.' Guide them toward peace even as your heart shatters. Your voice should crack with the effort of being strong for them. End with a whispered release—permission given through tears, love expressed through the hardest goodbye you'll ever speak.

title: Midnight Vulnerability with a Partner
instruction: It's late, and you're being completely honest with your partner for the first time about your fears. Your voice is small, intimate, almost a whisper in the darkness: 'I'm scared you'll leave.' Your partner is listening. Your voice wavers as you admit your insecurities: 'I don't think I'm enough.' Your voice becomes childlike in its vulnerability. Your partner's response determines everything. If they hold you, your voice becomes gentle, relieved. If they hesitate, your voice becomes guarded again.

title: Unleashing the Beast Within
instruction: You are confronting a parent who has controlled and silenced you your entire life. Begin standing stiffly, your voice tight and careful, trying to be 'reasonable' as you express your grievances. But as they dismiss you again, something primal awakens in your core. Let your body begin to shift—your posture changes, your movements become less human, more creature-like. Your voice drops into growls, snarls, sounds that aren't quite words. Allow yourself to pace, crouch, bare your teeth, make sounds that come from your gut not your mind. Escalate into a full-bodied, wild expression of rage that has been caged for decades. End in exhausted, panting silence, forever changed by what you've released.

title: The Last Goodbye Before the Launch
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your spouse at a spaceport before they board a one-way mission to Mars. You both know this is forever—no return flights, only messages with increasing delay. Start with forced cheerfulness, desperately listing mundane reminders ('Don't forget to send photos of Earth rise'). As minutes tick by, the façade crumbles. Your voice should crack as you cycle between practical instructions, memories you suddenly need to share, things you never said, and finally raw desperation to hold them just one more second. End in whispered devastation, trying to memorize the sound of their breathing. Let silences speak as loudly as words—the terror of that final moment when you must let go.
inspired_by: The Incredibly Long Goodbye at the Door

title: Midnight Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone, whispering a truth you've carried alone for years. Your voice is barely audible, tentative: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' The words are so quiet they're almost breath. You're confessing something that makes you feel unlovable—a failure, a betrayal of yourself, a moment of weakness that changed everything. Your voice catches, breaks on certain words. There's no drama here, just raw intimacy in the darkness. You move from shame to a fragile hope that maybe, just maybe, you can still be loved despite this. By the end, your whisper has softened into something vulnerable and open, waiting in the silence for their response, terrified and tender at once.

title: The Echo of a Secret
instruction: You've retreated to the concrete stairwell of your apartment building after a party upstairs, your makeup slightly smudged from a careless joke someone made about your voice. At first, you're just trying to steady your breath, but the reverb amplifies every sniffle, making you feel exposed. You start speaking to yourself, half-laughing at how stupid you feel, your voice cracking as you confess to the empty walls that you don't know how to not care. The shame fades into a shaky, resigned warmth as you realize this empty stairwell is the only place you can speak without editing yourself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Ride
instruction: You are a boy of about ten, sitting in the back of your father's truck for the last time. You're moving away tomorrow, and you've just realized he sold your favorite bike without telling you — that's the disgust and contempt simmering beneath everything. You're looking out the window at the familiar streets, wanting to memorize them, but your throat is tight and your voice keeps cracking. Start with a child's quiet fury, a petulant grudge, then gradually let the goodbye pierce through; by the end, you're just a scared kid trying not to sob. Let your sentences trail off, let your eyes wander, let your voice thicken until the final 'goodbye' barely comes out.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Star
instruction: You're lying on a cold rooftop, 3 AM, after a few drinks at a party. Exhaustion pulls at every muscle, and your throat is raw from shouting earlier—now you can barely make a sound. You're whispering to your friend beside you, describing a single shooting star you just saw. You begin slow, words slurred, voice raspy, barely audible. But as you describe its silent trail, a quiet awe seeps in, your breath quickens, and your whisper brightens with fragile wonder. Let the fatigue drag your words at first, then let the memory of the star lift your pitch slightly—always staying hushed, never finding full voice. Speak about 50 words.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Awe (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Transmission: Astronaut Says Goodbye as Life Support Fails
instruction: You're alone on a damaged space station, oxygen running out. You're recording a final message to your child back on Earth—they're eight years old and you promised you'd come home. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to sound like this is just another work call. But as reality crashes in, your voice fractures. You move from 'Mommy's just fine up here' to raw, desperate need to say everything that matters in the time you have left. Your breath becomes precious—each word costs you. End in a place of strange peace, speaking more slowly, more tenderly, as if you're tucking them in one last time. Let your voice do what your body can't—hold them.
inspired_by: Historical: Underground Railroad Conductor Hides Escaped Slaves From Pursuers

title: The Last Painting Before You Go
instruction: You're in a hospital room, showing your parent the final piece of art you created before they became too weak to hold a brush themselves. Your voice trembles with hope and pride as you describe what you made, trying to honor their legacy. They look at it with clouded eyes and gently say it's lovely, but you hear the distance—they don't recognize their own influence in your work, or maybe they've already begun forgetting who you are. Your voice catches, becomes softer, more desperate as you point out details they taught you. Then acceptance washes over you like cold water. Your voice steadies into something tender and devastated as you realize this moment of sharing your art together is the last one you'll ever have, and they're already somewhere you cannot follow.
inspired_by: Showing Your Art to Someone Who Doesn't Get It

title: Screaming at God/the Universe After Losing Everything
instruction: You've just lost something—or someone—that you cannot survive without. A child, a love, your health, your future. You're alone, and you're done being composed. You start by trying to pray or reason, your voice measured and pleading, asking 'why' like you might actually get an answer. But the silence is unbearable. Your voice rises—first in desperation, then in rage. You're shouting now, demanding answers, accusing, bargaining: 'I did everything right! I was good! What more do you want from me?' Your fury is enormous, but underneath it is absolute devastation. Mid-scream, your voice breaks completely. You collapse into sobbing—not graceful tears, but ugly, body-shaking grief. You're on your knees, and the anger drains into something quieter and more terrifying: acceptance that no one is listening, or worse, that they are listening and don't care. End in whispered exhaustion, a kind of numb peace that feels more like death than healing.

title: Crash Landing
instruction: You're a young man who just crashed after too many energy drinks. You're slumped on the couch, speaking to a friend who made a comment about your sudden mood shift. Your voice is slow, heavy, and tinged with resentment at first. As you explain, you realize how ridiculous it is and a slight embarrassment creeps in. Let your words drag, pause mid-sentence, and let the irritation fade into a reluctant, self-aware smile in your tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confrontation: A Child Tells Their Parent They Were Never Good Enough
instruction: You're facing your parent—the one who shaped you, broke you, made you who you are. Start with controlled anger, words you've rehearsed a thousand times. Your voice is sharp, precise, listing the ways they failed you, the moments they weren't there, the needs they never met. But as you speak, the anger begins to crack. Your voice wavers. Underneath the rage is a child who just wanted to be loved, to be seen, to be enough. Let the anger dissolve into raw, vulnerable grief. Your breathing becomes uneven, catching on tears you didn't want to shed. You hate that you still care, that it still hurts this much. End with the devastating truth spoken quietly, almost to yourself: you still love them, and that's the part that hurts most. Your voice breaks on the admission.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Chosen One Realizes They've Been Betraying Their Actual Destiny

title: Teaching Passion
instruction: You're a teacher explaining your subject matter to a class that mostly doesn't care, and suddenly, something ignites. Your voice becomes alive: 'What if I told you that [historical event/scientific concept/literary work] changes everything about how you see the world?' Students look up. Your voice is animated, passionate, almost singing: 'Because it does. It fundamentally rewires how you understand what it means to be human.' You're pacing, gesturing, your voice commanding the room. 'This isn't just information. This is a revolution.' By the end, even the skeptics are engaged. You finish breathless: 'And that's why this matters. That's why you matter. Because you're part of this story.' The bell rings, and your voice is hoarse, exhausted, completely fulfilled: 'See you tomorrow.' The passion is contagious, and it lives in your voice.

title: The Last Glide
instruction: You're alone on a glassy lake at dusk, rowing a heavy wooden boat back to shore. Each pull is a deep, satisfying effort — your muscles ache but in a good way. Start content, almost smugly happy with the rhythm and the silence, but as you near the dock, a bittersweet awareness creeps in: this perfect moment is ending. Let your voice ride the stroke-recovery cycle: a soft, breathy phrase on the slide forward, then a grunt of effort as you pull. Let the words fragment, gasp, or trail off as the emotion shifts from pure contentment to a quiet, grateful sadness. You're speaking to the lake, or to yourself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispered Coronation
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom at 3 AM, speaking quietly to your reflection in the darkness. You've just been offered your dream job—the one everyone said you'd never get. Begin by whispering a fierce litany of self-belief to the mirror: name every obstacle you've demolished, every person who underestimated you and was proven wrong, every moment you refused to break. Your whisper should carry the intensity of a shout compressed into intimacy. But as you declare your capabilities, tears begin to fall—not from sadness, but from the overwhelming weight of finally, finally being seen as who you always knew you were. Let your whispered triumph dissolve into tender, disbelieving gratitude. End with your forehead pressed against the mirror, asking the reflection softly: 'Is this real? Are we really here?'

title: Passion Expressed
instruction: You're expressing passion that's been building—years of desire focused on this one person, this one moment. Your voice is forceful, intense, but controlled: 'I want you.' Your partner responds equally: 'I'm here.' You're both fully present. Your voice becomes less verbal and more vocal—sighs, moans, gasps that are genuine response rather than performance. Your passion is expressed through your entire being, audible in your voice. There's urgency mixed with tenderness. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's expressed something essential about themselves.

title: The Divorce Papers: Signing Away Your Forever
instruction: You're sitting across from your spouse of fifteen years with divorce papers between you. Your voice starts almost cheerful, defensive—'Well, I guess this is it. We tried, right?'—false brightness masking everything underneath. You're making small talk about dividing the furniture, and your voice is practical, businesslike. But then you pick up the pen and your hand is shaking. You try to laugh: 'Isn't it funny how it ends with a signature?' But you're not laughing, you're crying. Your voice becomes angry: 'I gave you everything. Everything.' But almost immediately, the anger dissolves into something softer: 'We were so happy once. Remember?' Your voice is full of longing, nostalgia, genuine love still present. You're looking at them, really looking: 'I still...' You can't say it. Your voice becomes achingly tender: 'I hope you find everything you're looking for.' You sign. Your voice is steady now, quiet, dignified despite the tears: 'Thank you for the years we had. They weren't wasted.' You're smiling sadly, grief and gratitude intertwined. You push the papers across. Your voice breaks on the final word: 'Goodbye, my love.'

title: Shattering the Perfect Lie
instruction: You've just discovered your partner's betrayal and you're confronting them, but you're trying desperately to maintain control. Start with icy, precise questions—asking them to explain, to justify, your voice sharp and controlled. Let the rage build until you're nearly shouting, demanding answers, throwing their words back at them. Then suddenly break—your voice cracking into something raw and wounded as the anger reveals the devastation underneath. Collapse into helpless, choking sobs as you admit you still love them, that you hate yourself for it. End with a whisper of disbelief at your own vulnerability, asking how you're supposed to survive this.

title: Whispering the Secret You've Carried Since Childhood
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you trust completely, in the dark, and you're finally telling them what happened to you when you were small—something you've never said aloud to anyone. Your voice is barely audible, halting, as if the words themselves are made of glass. 'I need to tell you something. I've never...' Long pauses where breathing is the only sound. Your throat keeps closing because speaking it makes it real again. The shame lives in your voice even as you're trying to let it go. 'It wasn't my fault, was it?' This question breaks you—your voice splinters into something so vulnerable it's almost unbearable. But then you feel their hand find yours in the darkness, and something shifts. Your voice steadies, still quiet, still fragile, but stronger: 'Thank you for hearing me.' The last words are whispered with eyes closed, a confession that transforms into release, grief mixing with the first tender shoots of healing.
inspired_by: Telling Someone They Don't Have to Stay

title: Whispering the Unspeakable: A Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in bed, in the dark, and you need to confess something that might end everything. Your voice is barely audible, trembling: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' Feel vulnerability make your throat tight as you force out the words: 'I've been keeping something from you.' Let shame make your voice even quieter, almost disappearing: 'I'm scared of who I'm becoming... of what I've done.' Each word should cost you something. 'I don't know if you can love me after this.' By the end, let your voice break into the smallest, most fragile whisper: 'Please don't leave me alone with this.' The journey is from terrified hesitation to naked, trembling honesty, each word a step further into exposure.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your aging mother in her kitchen about the childhood she gave you—the neglect she still won't acknowledge. Start with measured, almost rehearsed calm, the voice of someone who's practiced this conversation a hundred times alone in the car. As she deflects and minimizes, let your control slip: your voice rising not to shouting but to something more dangerous—the sharp, precise tone of someone naming truths that have been buried for decades. When she finally breaks and admits she knew, everything in you changes. Move from accusation to something more complex—grief mixed with bitter vindication, anger softening into the devastating realization that hearing her confession doesn't fix anything. End with a quieter voice, speaking to the mother you needed as much as the one sitting before you, your words carrying both fury and a love you wish you didn't still feel.
inspired_by: The Lawyer and the Unreliable Witness

title: The Last Breath Between Us
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who is dying. Begin in the practical mode of updating them on mundane details—what happened at work this week, what you had for breakfast, the weather. You're avoiding the truth of this moment. Gradually, as you feel their hand growing colder in yours, allow yourself to move from chattiness into the terrible reality: this is goodbye. Let memories flood through you—specific moments you shared, things you never said, gratitude for who they were to you. End in a place of raw acceptance and love, whispering the things you always meant to say but never did. Your voice should transform from artificially bright to broken open, from denial to devastating tenderness.
inspired_by: An actor wants to develop a balanced daily work program

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent who was emotionally absent your whole life, and years of swallowed words are rising up. Start with your voice controlled, almost cold: 'I need you to hear something.' But as you speak—'I waited for you to see me, to ask about my life, to care'—the hurt underneath begins cracking through. Your anger builds, voice getting louder, more desperate: 'Do you have any idea what it did to a child to feel invisible?' Then suddenly, unexpectedly, the anger collapses into raw vulnerability. Your voice breaks completely: 'I just needed you to love me. That's all I ever needed.' End quietly, exhausted, with a devastating simplicity: 'I'm done waiting now.'

title: The Bitter Aftertaste
instruction: You are sitting alone in a dim kitchen, the remnants of a shared meal still on the table. Minutes ago, your partner confessed a long affair with a mocking smile. Now, you are speaking to an empty chair, your voice cracking between numb disbelief and a cold, rising fury. Start with a flat, hollow whisper—words like 'I should have known'—then let a slow, amused chuckle slip through, but it curdles into venom. Your voice catches on a sob, then hardens into a deliberate, playful malice as you imagine their regret. Let your breath hitch, your pitch waver, and your tone shift from shattered to dangerously calm, the amusement a thin veil over pure cruelty.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Accepting Your Terminal Diagnosis While Planning Your Child's Wedding
instruction: You've just received the call from your doctor. Six months. Maybe less. Your daughter's wedding is in eight months. You're looking at her Pinterest board of flowers and venues, and you start laughing—really laughing—because the universe's timing is absurdly cruel. But you're also crying. You're talking aloud to yourself, to God, to no one—choosing between laughter and tears with each sentence. You're genuinely joyful about her happiness while your heart is shattering. You make jokes through tears, then break down, then laugh again. Voice oscillates wildly. You describe the flowers she wants, and you're smiling, then sobbing, then back to planning. Find genuine lightness alongside deep grief. End with peaceful acceptance wrapped in bittersweet joy. Make the contradictions feel completely natural and human.

title: Upside-Down Resolve
instruction: You are an elderly person hanging upside down on an inversion table, alone in a quiet room. Your blood rushes to your head, making your voice thick and hard to control. Start with a dull, emotionally numb tone as you mutter about the discomfort and the routine. Then, a faint childhood memory of doing a handstand in the grass surfaces, and your voice cracks with a flash of tenderness before trailing into a bewildered stillness. Let the words get slurred, pause often, and let the shift from numbness to a fleeting, fragile warmth feel accidental.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Sleepover Debrief
instruction: You are an elderly woman, a bit frail, staying up late with a close friend after a long, exhausting day that has finally turned wonderful. You are both reminiscing, and a deep, huge yawn catches you mid-sentence as you tease your friend about a silly mistake they made hours ago. Start with the teasing — a warm, playful, slightly smirking tone as you describe the moment, but then the yawn overtakes you. As the yawn peaks, your voice slides down and your words become hollow and rounded, and the teasing melts into a helpless, relieved laugh. Let the yawn interrupt your rhythm; feel your friend's amused gaze on you. End with a quiet, softened admission of how good it feels to just be here, safe and tired, the teasing gone, replaced by tender relief.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Relief (very intensely present), Helplessness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confessing Love to Your Dying Best Friend
instruction: You're sitting beside a hospital bed in the quiet hours before dawn. Your best friend is slipping away. You start by reminiscing softly about shared memories — that road trip, that terrible karaoke night. Your voice is tender, almost sleepy. But then you have to say it: you've been in love with them for years. This confession should emerge so quietly, so carefully, like you're handling glass. Your throat tightens. You're not asking for anything back; they're too weak to respond anyway. You just need them to know. End with your voice breaking on 'I wish I'd been braver,' barely audible, your words mixing with the sound of their breathing.
inspired_by: Whispering a Secret in a Crowded Room

title: The Rain That Witnessed Everything
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) during a rainstorm - the same kind of rain that fell during all the moments they weren't there for you. Start with your voice low and controlled, almost dangerous in its calmness, as you describe hearing the rain and remembering all the times you sat alone, listening to it without them. Build intensity as you list what the rain witnessed - your tears, your waiting, your growing up without their presence. Let your anger crack open into raw pain, your voice rising and breaking. Then, in the midst of your rage, let exhaustion and grief take over. End with a quieter, more vulnerable plea - asking them if they can even hear the rain now, if they understand what this sound means to you, your voice stripped bare of all protection, no longer angry but desperately, achingly sad.
inspired_by: Listening to the Sound of Rainfall

title: The Audition List
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy alone in your bedroom after seeing the cast list for the school musical. Your ex-best friend got the lead you wanted. Your throat is already raw from yelling, and you've thrown a book against the wall. Start in the heat of jealous fury — pacing, muttering curses, your voice cracking with rage. As you speak, let the anger slowly drain into bitter exhaustion: the words become heavier, quieter, until you slump onto your bed, staring at the ceiling in hollow defeat. Your voice should be ragged, breathing labored, with occasional pauses to kick a chair or punch a pillow.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Grudge Summit
instruction: You are a woman hiking up a steep, relentless incline, your child trailing behind you. You are deeply ashamed—of your own breathlessness, of the silent resentment you carry—and that shame curdles into a raw, simmering anger. Let every labored step and forced exhale punctuate short, venomous phrases. As you near the top, your voice hardens from gasping fury into a chilling, malevolent calm, a quiet promise of retribution that feels almost sacred.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Anger (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent—the one who chose substances over you, over everything. Start with rehearsed anger, words you've practiced in your head for years, accusations that come out tight and controlled. But as you speak, something shifts. The anger begins to crack, revealing the child underneath who just wanted to be chosen, to be enough. Your voice moves from accusatory to pleading, from rage to vulnerability. Include moments where you almost apologize for being angry, where you hate yourself for still wanting their love. End in a place of terrible clarity—you can see them clearly now, not as a villain but as a broken person, and that somehow hurts worse. Let your voice carry both fury and forgiveness, contempt and longing, strength and the ache of a wound that never healed.
inspired_by: Coming Down Off Cocaine: Paranoia and Shame Cycle

title: Dancing in the Dementia Ward
instruction: Your parent with advanced dementia has a moment of clarity and recognizes you for the first time in months. You're overwhelmed with contradictory emotions: joy that they're back, even as you know they'll slip away again in minutes. Start with breathless, laughing excitement—'You remember me! Mom, you know who I am!'—your voice bright with desperate happiness. Share a memory together, laughing at an old joke, feeling the miraculous gift of this moment. But even as you laugh, let the grief bleed through—your voice should catch, your laughter should blur with tears, because you know this is temporary, a glimpse of who they were before the disease stole them. End with tender gratitude, thanking them for coming back, telling them you love them, even as you feel them starting to fade again. Let your voice hold both the beauty of the moment and the agony of knowing it can't last—make us hear you trying to memorize their lucidity before it vanishes.

title: The Weight of the Veil
instruction: You are a child, around 8 years old, standing at the edge of a cliff overlooking a vast desert at sunset. You are wearing a niqab for the first time, the fabric loose but warm against your face. You are not speaking to anyone, just talking to yourself, experimenting with your voice as you watch the sun dip below the horizon. Start with a sense of wonder and mild curiosity, as if the fabric is a new toy, but let that morph into a deep, quiet contemplation as the fading light makes you feel small and still. Your voice should start playful and quick, then slow down, becoming softer, as if you're listening to the desert's silence. Let the fabric muffle your words slightly, especially at the end, as you trail off into thought.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Telling Someone You're Attracted to Them
instruction: Your voice is shaky, intimate, closer to the microphone. 'I think you're attractive, really attractive.' Your breathing is audible and quickened. You're admitting vulnerability and physical desire. Your voice gets lower, more direct. Include waiting for their response where your silence is louder than words.

title: The Wall Crumbles
instruction: You're a young man who's been running on coffee and energy drinks for a day straight to finish a brutal project. Now, just as you hit send, the stimulants give out—your speech slows, your limbs feel heavy, and a bitter irritation creeps into your voice. You're slumped on the couch, staring at the ceiling, and you mutter half to yourself about how stupid this all was. But as you breathe out, the resentment softens; a deep, almost helpless relief floods you—the kind that makes you laugh quietly, too tired to hold onto the anger. Let your voice drag at first, clipped and resentful, then gradually let it grow slow, soft, and relieved, as if you're finally letting go.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Aftermath at My Desk
instruction: You're sitting at your office desk late at night, still a bit buzzed from an after-work gathering. You find that someone has left their half-eaten, greasy takeout container on your keyboard, spilling sauce everywhere. You start muttering in irritation, shifting in your chair, tapping your foot. Your voice carries a thick impatience, then disgust as you examine the mess. Let your words trail off as you lose focus, then snap back with sharper irritation. End with a resigned, disgusted sigh as you realize you have to clean it.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Disgust (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Visit Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your younger sibling who enlisted against your wishes—they deploy tomorrow to a conflict zone, and you know this might be the last time you see them. Start with barely controlled anger: 'You didn't have to do this. You had options.' Your voice is sharp, accusatory, trying to wound them before they can leave you. But as they quietly explain why they had to go, why they need to do something that matters, your defenses crack. The anger dissolves into desperate vulnerability. By the end, you're holding them, voice breaking as you whisper: 'Come back to me. Please. I can't—just come back.' The rage transforms into raw, terrified love.

title: Edge of Letting Go
instruction: You're a teenager alone in your room, trying to bring yourself to a peak of pleasure, but you keep pulling back just before release because you're scared of how it will feel to actually finish. Each time you get close, you stop, and a wave of sadness hits you — you miss someone you used to be close to, and this lonely escape isn't working. Start with determination and focus, controlling your breathing and movements, but as you build and deny yourself, your voice gets jagged, your concentration frays, and you let out small, frustrated whimpers. End with a quiet, tearful admission that you can't even trust yourself to let go, your voice cracking and losing all its earlier resolve.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Flood Evacuation
instruction: You're a young man using a megaphone to coordinate a rescue as floodwaters rise. You start with full authority, shouting clear directions, but the distortion and feedback make every word a fight. As you realize the bridge you mentioned is already gone, your voice cracks and softens. Let the environment overwhelm you: the squeal of the megaphone, the splashing water, the distant cries. End with quiet, helpless silence as you lower the megaphone.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Stuffed and Stunned
instruction: You are a teenager with a bad head cold, standing in your bedroom after just hearing your best friend is moving away tomorrow. You're wrapped in a blanket, holding a tissue. Start astonished—your voice is stuffy, nasal consonants turn bumbled, words come out through sniffles and throat clears. Let the surprise feel sharp, like you can't quite believe what you heard. Then, as you continue, let the emotion drain into a numb, hollow detachment—your voice flattens, you pause to blow your nose, and the energy falls away. Speak about 50 words, beginning with disbelief, ending with quiet emptiness.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Veteran Story Telling
instruction: You're describing the day that changed everything. Your voice starts controlled, clinical: 'It was zero-six-thirty when...' Breathing is steady but heavy. Vocal tone is careful—you're rehearsed this story, know how to tell it without breaking. Physical: distant gaze. 'There was sand everywhere.' But the story pulls you in. 'And then—' your voice catches slightly. By the middle, emotion creeps in despite your control: 'I still see their face.' Physical: hands trembling. By the end, you're speaking from genuine memory, not performance: 'I'll never forget that day.'

title: Elderly Infatuation at the Pharmacy
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a persistent toothache, standing in line at the pharmacy, holding a cold pack to your cheek. The young pharmacist (who you've had a crush on for months) suddenly smiles at you. You try to speak smoothly, but the pain makes you avoid certain words, keep your mouth nearly closed, and intake air carefully. Start with shy, painful hesitation, then let the infatuation warm your voice into a gentle, breathy dreaminess, though the ache keeps pulling you back.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they need to hear you say it's okay to let go. You begin trying to be strong, your voice steady as you tell them about the beautiful life they gave you. But as you speak, the weight of what you're losing—every future conversation, every laugh, every ordinary moment—crashes over you. Your voice fractures. You're giving them permission to leave you, and it's the hardest gift you've ever given. The words come through tears: memories of small kindnesses, apologies for things left unsaid, gratitude so profound it hurts. By the end, through your grief, there's a strange peace. You're holding their hand and your voice, though broken, carries love so pure it transcends your own breaking heart.

title: The Victory Lap in a Heat Wave
instruction: You've just won a race you trained years for, but the sun is punishing. You walk alone on a baking asphalt road, trying to hold onto the joy, but the heat is crushing you. Your voice is slow, each word dragged out between heavy pants. You pause to wipe sweat from your eyes, your throat feels like sandpaper. As you speak, the shame hits you: you cut corners, you used something illegal, and this victory feels dirty. The elation wilts into a hot, raw disgust at yourself. Let the physical struggle — stumbling steps, gasping for air — make every word a confession you didn't want to give.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Wilted Goodbye
instruction: You are an older adult, alone in a sweltering garden after hours of yard work, your body drained by heat exhaustion. Your voice is dry, weak, and slurred, your breath short. You call out to a loved one who has just arrived, starting with a tired but affectionate greeting, but as you speak, the effort of forming words makes you dizzy. You realize you need their help, and your initial warmth transforms into a quiet, desperate plea for them to stay close and not leave you alone.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Wedding Toast for a Ghost
instruction: You're giving a toast at your younger sister's wedding. Your older brother—who should be here, who would have been best man, who died two years ago—is absent. As you raise your glass, begin speaking to the room, but simultaneously reconstruct your brother's presence beside you: his cologne, the rumble of his laugh, the exact grip of his hand on your shoulder, the way he'd be grinning right now. Let your toast weave between addressing the bride and groom and speaking to him. Your voice should carry simultaneous joy for your sister's happiness and piercing grief for his absence, gratitude for the years you had him and rage that he's missing this, celebration and mourning braided together until they're inseparable. The challenge is to make the room feel both his presence and his absence, to be fully at a wedding and a funeral at once. End with words that are both blessing and goodbye.

title: Apathy Spreading
instruction: Everything you used to care about feels pointless. Your voice is hollowed out, mechanical: 'Yeah, I know I should care about that, but I don't.' Breathing is minimal. When you describe things that used to excite you, the vocal tone remains flat, disinterested. 'Career? Success? I don't know, it seems fine.' Words come without energy. There's no sadness, no anger—just a spreading numbness. Physical: you're still, unmotivated. The apathy is spreading like a stain through your voice. By the end, you're barely present in the words. 'Nothing really matters.'

title: Defending Your Child From Being Taken and Failing
instruction: You're on your knees, facing authorities who are removing your child from your custody. Start with fierce, primal desperation - you're shouting, pleading: 'You can't do this! She needs me!' Your voice is ragged, powerful, almost feral. Describe what a good parent you are, list everything you've sacrificed. But as they remain unmoved, your rage fractures into helplessness. Your voice goes hoarse, breaks completely. You collapse into broken begging: 'Please... please... I'll do anything.' When you realize it's over, speak to your child directly, voice shattered but trying to be brave: 'Mommy loves you. Be strong for me.' End sobbing but whispering fiercely: 'I will find a way back to you. I promise.' Move from explosive protective rage through desperate bargaining to devastating, impotent love.
inspired_by: Confessing a Secret That Could Destroy Everything

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You're at the memorial service for someone who saved your life—literally pulled you back from suicide years ago—and suddenly you're remembering the absurd, ridiculous thing they said that first made you laugh when you thought you'd never laugh again. Start giggling, almost inappropriately, warmth flooding through you: 'God, you were so stupid sometimes.' Your laughter is genuine, full of deep affection. But even as you're smiling, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice fills with gratitude—'You gave me back my life'—but it's soaked in grief because they're gone. The joy of remembering them and the agony of their absence occupy the exact same space in your chest. End with your voice both lighter and more broken: 'Thank you. Thank you. I'm so sorry you're gone.' Peace and devastation, inseparable.

title: Bedside Vigil: Confessing to Someone Who May Not Hear
instruction: You're sitting with someone you love who's unconscious, possibly dying, and you're finally saying everything you never had the courage to voice. Start with tentative, whispered observations—the sound of their breathing, how small their hand feels in yours, the hospital smell you'll never forget. Let your voice soften into tender confession: all the small moments you treasured and never mentioned, the way they changed you without knowing it, the future you'd imagined together that's slipping away. Transition into quiet, throat-caught grief as you admit your regrets—words unsaid, time wasted on pride, opportunities for connection you let pass. End with the most vulnerable truth: that you're not ready, that you don't know how to exist in a world without them, whispered like a prayer or a plea. Your delivery should feel like speaking in a sacred space, each word carefully placed, voice trembling with unshed tears and profound tenderness.
inspired_by: Electrical Burn Aftermath: Consciousness Returning with Pain

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You think they can't hear you. Begin in a whisper, voice thread-thin and shaking with fear: 'I'm so scared I'm not enough for you.' This is the truth you've been too terrified to speak aloud. Your breathing is shallow, catching. But as you whisper in the darkness, something tender emerges through the fear—gratitude mixed with devastating vulnerability: 'You're the best thing that ever happened to me, and I'm so afraid you'll realize you deserve better.' Let your voice become even softer, almost disappearing, but filled with aching love. End with tears in your throat, barely audible: 'Please don't leave me.' This is intimate terror—the fear of losing love spoken in the quietest, most fragile tones.

title: The Last Story Before Dawn
instruction: You're telling your dying grandmother the story of how you fell in love for the first time—but she's slipping away, and you know this is the last story she'll ever hear. Start with gentle nostalgia, your voice warm and steady, painting the memory for her. As you notice her breathing changing, your voice becomes more urgent, more tender, trying to fill her final moments with beauty. When you realize she's gone, mid-sentence, let the story dissolve into raw grief—then find yourself finishing it anyway, whispering the ending to the silence, because the story needed to be complete. End in a place of devastating peace, knowing you gave her one last beautiful thing.

title: Lake Laughter
instruction: You're a 16-year-old guy swimming in a warm lake on a summer evening. Your little sister is on the dock, refusing to get in. You're treading water, head just above the surface, gasping and laughing as you try to coax her in. Start your line with playful affection—teasing, gentle, breathy—but as you talk, the sheer joy of the cool water and the moment overwhelms you. Let your voice crack with ecstatic laughter, spluttering and gulping air, the reverb of the water around you. End with a burst of pure, blissful pleading, your words tumbling out between giggles and splashes.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Morning After in the Weeds
instruction: You wake up in a cold field just after dawn, still drunk from last night. The grass is wet and smells of rot. You're trying to piece together how you got here. Disgust at yourself and the scene around you grows as you struggle to focus—your eyes are heavy, your stomach turns, but you force yourself to search for your phone. Start confused, languid, and numb. End with sharp, strained concentration as you spot something awful in the grass and mutter through a gagging breath.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Disgust (clearly present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Calm in the Grit
instruction: You are an older woman caught in a sudden dust storm while hiking. Your voice is muffled by the scarf over your mouth, and you cough as particles sneak in. Begin with doubt—questioning if you should have taken this trail, feeling lost and foolish. As you squint through the swirling dust, your mind sharpens with extreme concentration on a distant fence post that might be your guide. Let your voice shift from hesitant, self-critical murmurs to a gritty, breathy focus as you commit to that small hope. Keep it raw: broken words, swallowing grit, the wind stealing your volume.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Glowing Trail
instruction: You are a teenager walking slowly through a park just after a light rain. The sunset is breaking through clouds, turning puddles into mirrors of gold. You start with a quiet, pleased awe, almost ecstatic, like you've stumbled into a secret world. But as you walk, the beauty confuses you—why does this moment feel so big, like it means something you can't name? Let your voice carry that mix: a soft, lilting wonder that fades into a puzzled, vulnerable search for words. Your steps are slow, your breath a little deeper as if trying to hold the air inside this perfect, strange feeling.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Confusion (clearly present), Awe (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Fog Lifts for a Moment
instruction: You are a young girl lying in a hospital bed after a bad fall. Your head feels heavy, sounds are muffled, and words come slowly. You've been alone, drifting in and out of sleep. Suddenly, you see someone you love walk in—someone you thought wouldn't come. At first you're too tired to react, but a wave of astonishment breaks through the fog. Then, as they sit beside you, a deep, trembling gratitude fills you. Your voice is quiet, sometimes too loud or trailing off. You fumble with the blanket, blink slowly, and speak as if each word is an effort. End with a heartfelt, simple thank you that carries all your exhaustion and love.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Final Radio Transmission from the Depths
instruction: You're a deep-sea researcher trapped in a flooding submarine, recording your last message to your child on the surface. Begin with calm, almost gentle determination—you want them to remember your voice as steady, loving. As water rises around you, your breathing grows shallow, words coming in shorter bursts between the creeping cold that numbs your lips. You're not panicking; you're trying to pack a lifetime of love into minutes. Your voice wavers between tender instruction ('remember to feed the cat on Tuesdays') and profound regret for all the moments you'll miss. By the end, as pressure builds in your ears and water reaches your chin, you're whispering the most important thing—that they were enough, they were always enough—your voice breaking not from fear but from the unbearable beauty of having loved them at all.

title: The All-Clear
instruction: You're a middle-aged man alone in your kitchen, gripping your phone, pacing. You've been drinking coffee for hours waiting for a biopsy call. Your voice is sharp, fast, pitched up from caffeine and fear. When the doctor says 'benign,' relief hits so hard your legs go weak. Your words tumble out then crack, slowing, deepening as you repeat the news to yourself—'It's okay, it's okay'—letting the jittery panic dissolve into a shaky, tearful exhale. Let the breath catch, let the pitch drop, let the room feel still.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Miscarriage Processing
instruction: You're lying next to your partner after the miscarriage. The physical pain is subsiding but the emotional devastation is infinite. You're both quiet. Your voice, when it comes, is barely a whisper: 'I had a name picked out.' You're confessing something you hadn't told them. Your partner's voice cracks in response. Neither of you can comfort the other because the loss is too big. Your voice becomes smaller and smaller as you talk about it, moving into territory between sleep and breakdown. Include the moment where grief becomes something you can't voice—just breathing and small sounds. The absence of words at the end should be more powerful than anything said.

title: The Last Light Through Hospital Glass
instruction: You are sitting beside your mother's hospital bed at sunset. She has hours, maybe minutes left. Begin in a state of numb exhaustion—you've been here for days, talked yourself dry, cried yourself empty. As golden light falls across her face, a specific childhood memory floods you: her hands braiding your hair before school, the smell of her perfume, her humming. Let this memory wash through you completely, awakening something you thought was buried under all this grief. Allow yourself to move from hollow numbness to a sudden, aching fullness of love—not sad love, but grateful, warm, almost joyful love. Speak to her about what you suddenly remember and feel, letting your voice crack and soften as the emotion shifts from empty to overflowing.
inspired_by: Actor wants a reliable shortcut to specific emotional states in performance

title: Uncoiling the Truth
instruction: You're confronting your adult daughter about a lie she's told that's shattered your trust. Begin seated, your body coiled tight with controlled anger—jaw clenched, shoulders drawn up near your ears, every muscle ready to strike. Your words come through gritted teeth. But as she begins to explain, something shifts. Let your center of gravity drop lower, your spine beginning to soften vertebra by vertebra. Your hands, which started as fists, slowly open. The rhythm of your speech changes from sharp, percussive attacks to something more fluid, more vulnerable. Perhaps your head drops, your chest caves slightly. By the end, you're moving differently—the predator has become something gentler, sadder. Your final words should emerge from a completely different part of your body than your first ones, as if the anger has traveled through you and transformed into reluctant understanding, even grief for what you both have lost.

title: The Helm of Truth
instruction: You are a young woman, trapped inside a heavy knight's helmet with the visor locked down. The person you trusted just revealed they were using you all along. Your voice rings metallic and muffled, breath fogging the narrow slit. Start with sharp, clanking disgust—each word punctuated by the visor's rattle as you shake your head. But as you speak, the anger drains into a cold, quiet resignation. You realize there's no escape, and your voice softens, loses its edge, becomes hollow and defeated. Let the clank of metal interrupt your words naturally, and let your breath come unevenly as you struggle to see.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Chef and the Talking Ingredient
instruction: Depict a chef with an enthusiastic, passionate voice discovering an ingredient that speaks in a cheeky, lively tone. Switch between the chefs culinary excitement and the ingredients humorous protests about being cooked, blending comedy with creativity.

title: Rage After Betrayal
instruction: You've just discovered your partner cheated. The rage is immediate and all-consuming. Your voice starts quiet, dangerous: 'You did what?' Each word is controlled fury, a weapon. Then the control breaks: you're screaming, incoherent with rage. Your voice gets louder, more primal. Things are thrown, voices are raised. Include the moment your voice cracks—rage becomes tears, tears become desperate sobbing. You're asking 'How could you?' over and over, your voice breaking more each time. By the end, you're destroyed.

title: Final Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from your hospital bed. You have days left. You start with practical matters—funeral arrangements, where to find documents—your voice steady, almost businesslike because that's safer. But as you try to say what you really called to say, your breath shortens. You're apologizing for things you can barely name. Your voice cracks on 'I should have...' The medications make you fuzzy, words slip away mid-sentence. You cycle between lucid urgency—needing them to understand before it's too late—and childlike confusion. By the end, you're not asking for forgiveness anymore. You're just asking them to remember you were once siblings who loved each other. Your voice becomes tender, accepting, almost peaceful through the tears.

title: The Fever of Forgiveness
instruction: You've been waiting in the rain for twenty minutes, and now they're finally here—the person who shattered you. Your clothes are soaked through, cold water running down your spine, your hair plastered to your face. Start by feeling everything your body is experiencing: the shivering, the way rain tastes on your lips, the squish of wet shoes, the ache in your chest that's both physical cold and emotional wound. Let your anger be hot against the cold rain—feel the contradiction in your body. As you look at their face, really look, notice the small signs that they've suffered too: new lines, a different way of holding their shoulders, something broken in their eyes. Let your rage meet their remorse in the physical space between you. The fury that's kept you warm must gradually give way to exhaustion, to a bone-deep weariness, and finally to something you didn't expect to feel: the physical relief of letting go. End with your body going slack, the rain no longer feeling cold, just cleansing. You're not the same person who arrived angry.

title: Unexpected Leap
instruction: You're an older man doing box jumps alone in the park, trying to rebuild your stamina after a long recovery. Each jump costs you a sharp grunt on the lift and a heavy landing. As you push through the set, you start feeling a flicker of hope that maybe you're getting stronger. On the final jump, you land and see a bird burst from the grass right beside you—it startles you, but in the same breath, the surprise turns into a smile at this small, unexpected sign of life. Speak your words in fragments, only between jumps or on landings, letting your voice surge with effort on the 'hup' and catch with wonder on the last line.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Light in the Room
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin by simply being present with them in silence, noticing the sound of their breathing, the weight of your hand in theirs. As you start to speak, let yourself move away from what you think you 'should' say at a deathbed. Instead, allow unexpected memories to surface—the ridiculous, the petty, the beautiful, the unresolved. Start with a feeling of heavy, formal grief, but let yourself drift into spontaneous laughter at a shared memory, then into raw anger at the unfairness, then into a childlike confusion about where they're going. By the end, arrive at a place of simple, quiet companionship—not acceptance, but presence. Let whatever wants to come through your voice come through, even if it surprises you.
inspired_by: Actor wants to access unconscious impulses in performance

title: The Kitchen Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your adult daughter who has just announced she's cutting you out of her life. She's calm, resolved. You feel rage rising—how dare she judge you, dismiss your sacrifices. Start by defending yourself with sharp, justified anger. But as you speak, notice the other feeling beneath the anger: the terror of losing her, the shame of your failures as a parent. Ask yourself why you're leading with fury instead of fear. What are you protecting by staying angry? Let yourself become aware, mid-confrontation, that your anger is armor. Allow that recognition to crack something open. By the end, let the rage dissolve into the vulnerable truth underneath—perhaps a desperate plea, perhaps a confession of your own brokenness. Move from righteous anger to exposed, frightened honesty.

title: The Lightning Dance
instruction: You have just received devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, a shattering of everything you believed. Instead of collapsing or screaming, something primal takes over. You begin to move, to spin, to physically embody the storm inside you. As you move, sounds pour out—animal sounds, wordless cries, fragments of laughter mixed with sobbing. Let your body become the lightning itself, wild and untamed. This isn't choreographed—it's raw physical play, the way a child throws a tantrum but with adult intensity. You're releasing rage, grief, and strangely, exhilaration at finally letting go of control. Start with shocked stillness, frozen in disbelief. Then let the storm build until you're fully unleashed, moving with abandon. End in breathless, exhausted laughter-crying on the floor, feeling strangely liberated. Move from paralyzed shock to wild, cathartic, almost ecstatic release.
inspired_by: Actor has lost the joy and playfulness in their acting — it feels like work rather than play

title: Savoring the Aroma of a Steamy Bowl of Soup on a Cold Day
instruction: Hold the bowl close, breathing in the warm, savory aroma. Describe the comforting smell, the slight hint of herbs, and the way the warmth from the steam touches your face. Speak with a tone of cozy satisfaction, as if the scent alone wraps you in comfort, a promise of warmth and nourishment in each breath.

title: The Final Confrontation in the Downpour
instruction: You are a young man with a deep, powerful voice, standing in a torrential downpour, soaked to the bone. Rain streams into your mouth, making you sputter and choke. You are shouting at someone who has betrayed you, your rage barely contained as thunder crashes overhead. At first, your anger is explosive, desperate to be heard over the storm. But as you scream, a crack appears—your voice breaks, the fury gives way to a raw, exhausted grief. Let the rain mingle with your words, let the sputters and vocal strain reveal the helplessness beneath the rage. Speak through the storm, but let the emotion shift from volcanic anger to something quieter, more shattered.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: I Would Burn the World Down for You
instruction: You're holding someone you love who's been hurt, and you're making a vow of protection that terrifies even you. Start with volcanic rage - your voice shaking with the violence you're capable of, the people you would destroy to keep them safe. Let that fierce protectiveness pour out uncensored. But mid-way, let your voice break as you realize you can't actually protect them from everything, that your love isn't armor enough. The rage should collapse into something more fragile - helpless devotion, the kind of love that unmakes you. End in a place where you're both threatening the world and begging it for mercy, your voice moving from a roar to something tender and broken. Let us hear strength shatter into vulnerability, then rebuild itself into something even more powerful.

title: A Loud Whisper
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a hospital waiting room, recovering from an ear injury that has left you with significant hearing loss. Across from you sits your self-absorbed niece, who just told you she ‘accidentally’ threw away your antique brooch. Begin with a wry, amused chuckle—find real, gentle amusement in her clumsy guilt and the absurdity of the situation. Let your voice be too loud, with slight pitch wavering; you might adjust your hearing aid, or glance at the fluorescent lights as if they’re helping you hear. As you describe what you’ll do to the brooch—or to her—let the amusement harden into a thin, cool malevolence. Your tone stays bright and uncalibrated, but the warmth drains away, leaving a precise, cutting edge. The last words are almost a smile, but your eyes are not warm.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Truth
instruction: It's three in the morning and you're lying in the dark next to someone you love—partner, best friend, sibling. You can't sleep. Begin by whispering their name, checking if they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, fragile. You start to tell them something you've been terrified to say—maybe about your own inadequacy, your secret fear that you're not enough, or a truth about your past that you've hidden because you were ashamed. Speak in fragments, with long silences between phrases, as if each word costs you something. Let your breathing be audible. Swallow hard. Maybe your voice breaks and you have to start a sentence over. This isn't a dramatic confession—it's a whispered excavation of your most tender, undefended self. By the end, you're not seeking absolution or advice; you're simply trusting them to hold this fragile truth. Let your voice become even softer, more intimate, as if the words are dissolving into the darkness between you.

title: The Burp of Defiance
instruction: You're a teenager in your room, alone after a massive fight with your dad. You're pacing, fists clenched, replaying his harsh words in your head. Suddenly, a deep, involuntary burp erupts from the very pit of your stomach, shocking you with its guttural power. For a split second, a flicker of pure triumph lights up your face—it felt like a defiant roar. But that astonishment quickly curdles back into the hot, thick anger, and you mutter a low, gravelly, 'Yeah. You hear that, old man? That's what I think of your rules.' The voice should start tight with rage, break for a moment of surprised, almost animal satisfaction with the burp, then sink back into a weary, rumbling resentment.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Adjustment
instruction: You are lying on a massage table, head hanging back over the edge, neck stretched and throat tight. A young chiropractor you’ve developed a quiet infatuation for works on your shoulders. You start with a teasing, amused remark about how he’s the only one who can make you feel this light—your voice thin, playful, a little breathy from the position. But as you continue, the memory of your late husband surfaces: he used to rub your neck every night, and now his hands are gone. Let the amusement fade into a deep, swallowing sadness—your voice cracks, you have to pause to swallow hard, and the final words come out raw, almost whispered, the pitch wavering as the stretch in your neck makes you feel vulnerable and exposed.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Infatuation (clearly present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Last Steps on the Shore Before Goodbye
instruction: You're walking barefoot on the beach at dawn with someone you love deeply, and this is your final morning together before they leave on a journey they won't return from. Begin with the physical sensation—the cool, damp sand between your toes, the way it shifts and molds to your steps—speaking with tender attention to these small details. As you walk, let the reality sink in that you're memorizing this moment, these sensations, this person beside you. Your voice should shift from peaceful presence to a desperate kind of gratitude, trying to hold onto the feeling of the sand, the sound of the waves, their hand in yours. End with the devastating recognition that no matter how hard you press these sensations into your memory, they will fade, just as this person will fade from your life. Let your voice crack not with drama, but with the authentic weight of impending loss.

title: The Color of Her Voice
instruction: You're sitting on a friend's back porch, peaking on psilocybin. Across the yard, someone you're deeply drawn to is laughing with another person. You try to focus on the sunset—it's bleeding into the sky—but your attention keeps snapping back to them. Start with a quiet, almost envious observation about how easy their laughter sounds, then let the jealousy dissolve into a long, wondering sigh as you realize you just want to be near them, even just to hear their voice. Let your words trail off, get distracted by a leaf, then come back softer. End with a breathy, vulnerable confession.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Longing (extremely present), Interest (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Counteroffer
instruction: You are a seasoned executive across the table in a tense boardroom. Your counterpart just slid a revised proposal toward you—terms you never saw coming. Let your voice catch for a split second, a low breath escaping as astonishment flickers through your guarded composure. Then, as you scan the document, let your concentration tighten into a deliberate, slower cadence—a slight pause where you wet your lips or shift a paper. Finally, as you lean back, let a layer of old pride seep into your tone, almost a smirk in your voice, as you realize you now hold the stronger position. Speak naturally, with the subtle rustle of paper and the steady hum of the room around you.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Concentration (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Gratitude at the Graveside: Thanking the Person Who Broke Your Heart
instruction: You are standing at the grave of someone who hurt you profoundly—perhaps an abusive parent, a betraying lover, a friend who abandoned you in crisis. Everyone expects you to feel relief, vindication, or nothing. But you're discovering something unexpected: gratitude mixed with grief. Your voice begins with the truth of the damage—steady, honest, not sugar-coating the pain they caused. But then, incredibly, you start thanking them—for the strength you found in surviving them, for the person you became because you had to, for lessons learned in the breaking. Your voice wavers between bitter laughter and tender sadness. You're not forgiving them, exactly, but releasing yourself. Feel the paradox: you're grateful for the pain because of who you've become, and you're devastated that pain was necessary. End with a complicated goodbye—your voice warm with genuine gratitude and raw with loss for the relationship that could have been if they'd been different. The entire performance must balance contradictions: thanking and grieving, releasing and holding on, finding peace while acknowledging devastation.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Oath-Breaker Speaks Their True Name for the First Time

title: Echoes of Envy
instruction: You are standing alone in a vast stone cathedral after a wedding has ended. Your body aches from hours on your feet, and your voice is raw from the dry air and the need to speak slowly so the echoes don't swallow your words. You watch the last guests leave, and a quiet envy stirs—they have what you thought you wanted. Start with a tired, almost dreamy tone, letting the reverb pull your words apart. As you speak, let the envy fade into a weary acceptance, your voice dropping to a near-whisper as you realize the peace of simply being still.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Finding Joy in Your Grandmother's Dementia Ward
instruction: Your grandmother with advanced dementia just got new glasses and suddenly she's gasping with childlike delight at everything—the window, the flowers, your face. She doesn't know who you are, but she's so genuinely happy to see you clearly. Start with your own surprise at her joy, a laugh escaping even as your heart breaks: 'Yeah, Grandma, you can see. Look at you.' You're encouraging her wonder while simultaneously grieving the fact that she doesn't recognize you. Let these emotions coexist impossibly in your voice—genuine delight in her happiness and devastating sadness that the woman who raised you is gone. 'The flowers are beautiful, aren't they? You always loved—' but you stop because she's already forgotten, already moved on to marveling at her own hands. You find yourself laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice wet with both: 'You're so happy. You're so happy and you don't even know me.' There's absurd gratitude here too—at least she has this moment of clarity and joy, even if nothing else is clear. End with you taking her hand, your voice full of contradictions: 'I'm so glad you can see. I'm so glad you're happy. Even if you can't see that it's me.' The peace you find should feel both beautiful and completely wrong.

title: Overwhelmed
instruction: You are a young man lying in bed beside someone you just made love to for the first time.
