The experience was far more intense than you anticipated, and now you're crying uncontrollably—your breath hitches in sharp, jerky inhalations, your throat feels wet and thick. You're astonished that this person wants you, and a trace of lust still hums in your body, but it's being drowned by a wave of raw emotion. Speak these words to them, barely getting them out between sobs. Let your voice crack, stall on vowels, and lose rhythm as you pause to swallow or gasp. Begin with a trembling mix of surprise and desire, then let the tears take over fully by the end, your voice becoming breathy and broken.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen of your childhood home, two days after your mother's funeral. Start from a place of cold, controlled anger—you came here with a list of grievances, prepared statements about his emotional absence, his drinking, the years of silence. But as you speak, as he stands there not defending himself, something shifts. Your carefully constructed accusations begin to crumble. You hear your own voice becoming his voice, see your own isolation mirrored in his face. The rage that sustained you for years begins to crack open into something more complicated: recognition, unwanted empathy, the horrible realization that you've inherited his loneliness. By the end, you're no longer attacking—you're asking a question you're terrified to ask: 'Did you ever want to be different?' Let your voice move from sharp accusation to something broken and searching.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's wedding reception, glass raised to give a toast. You're genuinely happy for them—begin with real warmth and joy in your voice, celebrating their love. But you're also in love with them yourself, have been for years, and they never knew. As you speak about how they've found 'the one,' let gratitude and grief begin to interweave in your voice. Your tone should shimmer between genuine celebration and barely-concealed heartbreak. End by wishing them a lifetime of happiness—and mean it—even as your voice catches with the weight of your own loss. The challenge is to hold both emotions as equally true: authentic joy for them and devastating sorrow for yourself. Neither should dominate—they must coexist in every phrase, creating a bittersweet music that honors both truths.
inspired_by: Director or colleague challenges the actor's process as overcomplicated or unnecessary

title: Thanking Your Team While Selling to the Competitor Who Destroyed Your Mentor
instruction: You're announcing the sale of your company to the very corporation that crushed your mentor years ago—you fought them for a decade, but now you're taking their money to save your employees' jobs. Begin with gratitude that's genuinely meant but threaded with irony you can't quite hide: 'You made this company worth buying.' Your voice is warm as you thank your team, but there's a bitter edge when you mention the acquiring company. As you speak, conflicting emotions war in your voice—pride in what you built, shame at the compromise, relief that your people will be taken care of, grief that you're betraying everything you once stood for. Your voice might even break into an inappropriate laugh-sob: 'My mentor would've burned this place down before selling to them, and here I am, shaking their hands.' By the end, your voice carries a complex peace—you're making a choice you hate but choosing your people over your pride: 'Sometimes loving something means letting it go, even to the wrong hands.' You're smiling with tears in your eyes, grateful and heartbroken and somehow okay with the contradiction.

title: The Collision of Fury and Desire
instruction: You've just had a devastating fight with your lover—screaming, throwing things, saying unforgivable things. They're about to walk out forever. But in this moment, you're flooded with two equal, warring sensations: absolute rage at them for hurting you, and desperate, aching desire to pull them close. Begin with your body rigid, fists clenched, making sounds of pure anger—growls, shouts, guttural expressions of betrayal. Let this rage fill your entire chest and throat. Then, without warning, feel it shift into something else: a physical hunger, a need to touch them, to be touched. Let your voice transform from hard to pleading, from closed to open. Your breathing should become heavier, more primitive. Make sounds that blur the line between anger and passion, between wanting to push them away and pull them into you. Curl your body forward, then arch it back. Let contradictory impulses battle in your throat—harsh sounds softening into moans, aggressive energy melting into vulnerability. End in a state of complete physical and emotional surrender, making deep, primal sounds that could be grief, rage, longing, or all three at once.

title: Last Lap, First Pride
instruction: You are a father swimming laps with your young child, pushing through your own exhaustion to finish this final lap. As you gasp for air between strokes, you call out encouragement – but your voice cracks from exertion and emotion. The child is struggling, and you are aching with pride that they haven't quit. Start with gritty, breathless determination, then let the pride break through as you realize they're going to make it. Your words come in ragged bursts, sputtering water, your tone shifting from strained to almost tearfully proud by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Crawlspace Confession
instruction: You're a teenage boy, all bravado, who crawled into a tight, dusty crawlspace under your grandmother's house to retrieve a baseball that rolled in. Your shoulders are jammed against the joists, your neck craned at an unnatural angle, and a sharp pain has been building in your lower back for minutes. Start off muttering to yourself with fake toughness—'Got this, easy'—but as you try to shift and a splinter digs into your arm, your voice pinches, breaths shorten, and you begin to bargain with the darkness. End with a shaky, raw admission that you're scared and you need help, your words catching on the dust coating your throat.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally facing the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago. They've asked to meet, and you agreed, thinking you'd be calm and controlled. But as you sit across from them, everything you rehearsed evaporates. Start with cold, clipped politeness—armor you've built to protect yourself. Then let one comment from them pierce through, and suddenly you're eight years old again, demanding to know why you weren't enough to make them stay. Your voice escalates from controlled accusation to raw, wounded rage, then unexpectedly breaks into something more vulnerable—the child who still, against all reason, hoped they'd come back. End not with resolution, but with the exhausted, complicated truth that you both hate them and desperately want them to fight for you now. Let the anger and longing war with each other until your voice shakes with both.

title: Whispering to the Dying
instruction: You're sitting vigil with someone you love who's slipping away, their hearing fading, language becoming meaningless. Begin with whispered reassurances, gentle words of comfort—but as they drift further, traditional language fails. Communicate through breath, through the smallest sounds of tenderness, through humming fragments of songs you shared. Let your voice catch and break, not dramatically but naturally, the way grief actually sounds—quiet, intimate, devastating. Pour everything you never said into pure tone: gratitude, regret, love too big for words. As they fade, your whispers become softer still, until you're simply breathing in rhythm with them, making the tiniest sounds of connection. End in near-silence, a barely-audible hum that says 'I'm here, you're not alone,' finding strange beauty in this wordless goodbye.
inspired_by: Alien First Contact: The Universal Translator Breaks

title: The Secret Garden
instruction: You're whispering a confession to your sleeping lover in the dark—something you've never had the courage to say while they're awake. Begin barely audible, voice paper-thin with vulnerability. You're confessing a dream you have, something that feels too precious and fragile to survive daylight: maybe a wild hope for your future together, or a hidden passion you've suppressed, or a part of yourself you've kept locked away. As you whisper in the darkness, something happens—speaking it aloud makes it real. Your whispers gradually gain strength, becoming a soft celebration. You start to smile, then quietly laugh at your own daring. The act of confession itself becomes intoxicating. By the end, you're still speaking softly, but there's an electric current of possibility running through your words, a tender, exhilarated conviction that this secret might actually become real. Your final words should shimmer with quiet, revolutionary hope.

title: Vigil at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping partner, speaking in barely-audible whispers about something you can never tell them while they're awake. Begin with tender observation—the way they sleep, small details you've memorized. Gradually confess something that's been eating you alive: an affair, a lie, a secret that changes everything, or perhaps that you're sick and haven't told them. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost subliminal, catching on tears you're trying not to shed because you don't want to wake them. Move between overwhelming love for this person and the unbearable weight of what you're carrying. End with a whispered apology or goodbye they'll never hear, your voice breaking on their name. This should feel like overhearing someone's private devastation, intimate as a prayer, fragile as glass.
inspired_by: The Soldier and the Enemy Spy

title: The Last Conversation Before the Flight: Dissociating from Your Own Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love at an airport gate—they're leaving for a mission they might not return from. You're dissociated, watching yourself say the 'right things'—be safe, I'll be here, I love you—but you're floating above the scene, numb and distant. Your voice sounds hollow, scripted, like you're reading lines someone else wrote. Midway through, something they say—maybe a memory, maybe the way they touch your face—violently pulls you back into your body. Suddenly you're present, flooded with terror and love you can no longer control. The goodbye shifts from mechanical to devastatingly real. Let us hear the moment your heart catches up to your mouth, when the wall breaks and you're no longer watching yourself but living inside the unbearable present.
inspired_by: Dissociating in a Meeting: Watching Your Voice from Outside Your Body

title: The Final Garden
instruction: You are an elderly man, heavily sedated after a surgery, lying in a hospital bed. Your mind drifts to the garden you built with your late wife. Begin speaking to a nurse who's adjusting your IV, but as you describe the sunflowers, your voice slows. You feel a deep, peaceful contentment as you lose the thread of the sentence, trailing off into a whisper, eyes closing. Let the warmth of the memory pull you under, your words getting slower and softer until they fade.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Behind the Barrier
instruction: You're an older man visiting your spouse in a care home, both wearing surgical masks. You start by trying to say something practical but the muffling of your own voice frustrates you — you adjust the mask, lean in, speak louder out of irritation. Midway, you remember why you're here, and your voice softens into longing. Your words grow quieter, breathier, as if you're trying to reach past the cloth. End with a simple, heartfelt confession of missing them, letting the mask amplify your sigh.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Morning After Regret
instruction: You are an elderly person waking up after a night of heavy drinking. Your throat is dry, your head throbs, and you feel a sour, bitter regret mixed with lingering intoxication. As you speak to yourself in the mirror, you start with a gravelly, slurred self-loathing, but by the end, a flicker of defiant humor emerges as you accept your foolishness. Let your voice crack and struggle, with pauses to swallow or clear your throat.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Living Ghost at the Lumber Yard
instruction: You’re an older man, rough-edged, with a deep, gravelly voice. You’re at a hardware store, squinting at a shelf of drill bits (concentration present but slight). Then you see a face you haven’t seen in forty years—a man you believed died in a war. The shock hits: your breath catches, you let out an involuntary half-gasp, half-scream. Your voice jumps high, then cracks. You stumble forward, shuffling and bumping a cart. Words tumble out in fragments as confusion floods you: 'You? No—I was at your—how are you standing here?' Then, as he grins, you recognize the old prankster glint. A weary, breathless laugh escapes—amusement leaking through the disbelief. By the end, your voice drops to a husky, shaking murmur, still raw but softening into wonder.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Confusion (very intensely present), Amusement (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Obsessive Pet Owner
instruction: Act as someone who treats their pet like a human child. Use a doting, affectionate voice when speaking to the pet, switching to a defensive tone when others question their behavior, exaggerating the pet owners devotion.

title: Joyful Farewell: Celebrating Someone Leaving for Their Dream While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're sending off someone you deeply love as they leave for an incredible opportunity that takes them away forever—maybe across the world, maybe into a life you can't be part of. Begin with genuine, bright celebration: 'This is everything you've worked for! I'm so proud of you!' Your voice is warm, enthusiastic, because you truly are happy for them. But underneath, your heart is breaking. As you continue—'You're going to be amazing there'—your voice wavers slightly, the smile audible but strained. The contradiction intensifies: you're laughing while tears threaten, voice lifting with encouragement while cracking with loss: 'I can't wait to hear about all your adventures.' By the end, let both emotions fully coexist: 'I love you so much, and this is exactly where you need to be, and I—' Your voice breaks completely, then recovers with a tearful laugh: 'Go. Before I make this harder.' The beauty is in holding joy and grief simultaneously, celebrating them while mourning your own loss, authentic and contradictory and utterly human.
inspired_by: Judge Sentencing the Guilty: The Weight of Final Words

title: The Morning After the Funeral
instruction: Your best friend died suddenly last week. Today, while cleaning out their apartment, you found their journal—and the last entry is about you. They wrote about how your friendship saved their life, how you were the one person who truly saw them, how grateful they were. Start reading aloud with numb exhaustion—you're too grief-stricken to feel anything new. But as the words sink in, you move into a complex storm: crushing grief that you'll never get to hear them say this, profound gratitude that you mattered to them, rage that they're gone, and unexpected joy at being so deeply loved. End laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice fracturing between thank you and why did you leave me. Let these contradictions live together—don't resolve them.

title: Stung by Beauty
instruction: You're in a sunlit garden, kneeling to admire a rare, iridescent flower you've been searching for years. Your voice is full of wonder, breathy with awe, as you reach out. Suddenly, a bee hidden in the petals stings your finger—a sharp, burning shock. You let out an involuntary yelp, then suck in a tight breath. Your voice becomes guarded, tense, clenched through the pain. Disappointment floods you—this perfect moment is now marred. But as you look at the flower again, a strange pleasure mixes in: the sting feels almost like a sacred price, and you murmur through gritted teeth, still awed, still captivated, your tone wavering between hurt and a fragile, ecstatic appreciation.
emotions_sampled: Awe (clearly present), Disappointment (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Court of Mud Pies
instruction: You are a six-year-old girl, the 'queen' of a tiny kingdom you've built in the backyard. Your best friend, your only subject, has just told you they are moving away tomorrow. You are sitting in the dirt, elbows on your knees, chin in your hands, staring at the crumbling mud castle you made together. You feel a huge, hot confusion—how can the world just end like this? But you also feel a stiff, small pride, because a queen doesn't cry. You speak to your friend, your voice compressed and dark from your hunched position. You start by trying to sound like a regal ruler making a decree, but your voice cracks and you lose the thought, trailing off into a small, bewildered question. The sound is a mix of a child's high pitch and the hollow, strained quality of holding back a sob.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Cliff's Edge Confession
instruction: You're at the summit after a dangerous climb with the parent who was never there for you. The adrenaline and altitude have stripped away your defenses. Start with breathless excitement about the view, but it quickly becomes a confrontation—'You missed this. You missed all of it. Every moment I needed you to see me do something brave, you were—' Your voice should crack not from exertion but from years of swallowed words finally erupting. The physical exhaustion makes you too raw to perform politeness. Move from accusatory rage to something more fragile—a child's voice asking why they were never enough. Let the wind and your gasping breaths punctuate the silences where you're waiting for an answer that may never satisfy you.

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You are confronting a parent who has spent years criticizing you, diminishing your choices, making you feel like you're never quite enough. Start with the anger you've rehearsed in your head a thousand times—sharp, defended, ready to finally say everything. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: you catch a glimpse of how small and frightened they look, how your words are landing. Feel the anger begin to crack open into something more complicated—a recognition that their cruelty came from their own wounds. Don't abandon your truth, but let it evolve. Move from attack to a kind of fierce, painful clarity: you can see them now, really see them, and you refuse to carry their shame anymore. End not with victory or reconciliation, but with the simple, revolutionary act of choosing yourself while still seeing their humanity.

title: The Sweater That Still Smells Like You
instruction: You are a child getting dressed in your room, pulling on a big, cozy sweater that’s a little too large. At first, you’re completely content—enjoying the soft wool, the familiar scent, the way it swishes around your face as you wiggle your arms through. You hum softly, bending over to find your shoes, grunting a little as you tie them. But then you pause, holding the sleeve to your nose, and a quieter feeling creeps in—a longing that surfaces without warning. Speak while you finish dressing, letting your voice start bright and absorbed in the moment, then slow and soften as that missing person occupies your thoughts.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Shirt That Still Smells Like Them
instruction: You're alone, packing up your former partner's belongings six months after the breakup. You've been methodical and numb all day, just getting through it. Then you find their favorite shirt at the back of the closet, and without thinking, you bring it to your face. The scent that hits you is so powerfully them that your body reacts before your mind can. Let the physical sensation—the smell, the texture, the memories it triggers in your body—dictate everything that follows. Don't plan whether you'll cry, rage, laugh, or collapse. Let your body lead: maybe you clutch it, maybe you throw it, maybe you put it on, maybe you bury your face in it and howl. Allow contradictory impulses to surface—perhaps rage at them mixed with desire, or grief mixed with relief, or tenderness mixed with the urge to destroy this last piece of them. Let the physical sensations guide you to emotions you didn't know were still there.

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You're in the grip of overwhelming physical sensation—perhaps intense pleasure, searing pain, or exhaustion pushing you past your limits. Start by trying to maintain control, to manage the experience with your usual strategies of toughness or restraint. Your body is screaming but you're attempting to override it, to power through, to stay in command. But gradually let the physical intensity dismantle your ability to maintain your carefully constructed self. As control slips away, something unexpected emerges: not just surrender to the sensation, but access to an emotion you usually suppress. Maybe rage gives way to desperate grief, or pain cracks open into unguarded joy, or pleasure dissolves your armor revealing profound loneliness underneath. Let your voice and body become completely unrecognizable from how you started—end in a place where you're expressing something true that you only access when every defense is stripped away.

title: The Voicemail I Can't Delete
instruction: You're holding your phone, listening for the hundredth time to a voicemail from someone you've lost—whether to death, distance, or a relationship's end. Begin by playing it (imagined), and let yourself truly listen to every aspect of their voice: the warmth, the specific way they pronounce certain words, the breath between phrases, the emotion embedded in their tone, the laughter or hesitation, what they said and what they left unsaid. As you listen, speak aloud your responses—begin with aching grief at hearing them again, but let the sound of their voice also bring back joy, specific memories, even frustration at things left unresolved. Let your emotions shift with each replaying: sadness gives way to gratitude for having known them, which mingles with anger at the unfairness of loss, which transforms into bittersweet acceptance. Speak to them as if they could hear you, responding to the nuances in their recorded voice. Let the quality of what you hear—love, vitality, humanness—transform your relationship to the loss from pure grief into something more complex: celebration mixed with sorrow, closure mixed with eternal longing. End torn between deleting and preserving, your voice carrying both goodbye and eternal connection.

title: The Monster You Made Me
instruction: You are an adult child confronting the parent who called you 'too sensitive,' 'too much,' 'difficult' your whole life. Start with controlled anger, voice tight and measured, recounting specific moments when you needed gentleness but received harshness. Build to a fierce, shaking rage as you tell them how their fear of your emotions turned you into someone who apologizes for existing. Then crack completely—let the rage dissolve into the grief of the child you were, voice breaking as you ask the question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I enough as I was?' End in exhausted vulnerability, almost a whisper, as you realize you're not here for them to change, but to finally stop shrinking yourself.
inspired_by: The Child and the Monster Under the Bed

title: Hiding Homesickness While Traveling
instruction: Youre far from home and missing it dearly, but you dont want to dampen the groups spirits. Internally, nostalgia tugs at you, but you join in the fun. Describe your longing inside while participating cheerfully. Speak with enthusiasm, masking your homesickness.

title: Bungee Bouncing: Losing Your Mind to the Elasticity
instruction: You jump. Your voice is a scream. The rope catches you, bouncing you back upward, and your voice becomes incoherent—laughing and screaming simultaneously. Your narration is fragmented as gravity plays tug-of-war with your body. 'Can't... falling... no wait going UP.' Your voice is being physically hijacked by repeated impacts with G-force. Each bounce disjoints your speech. Include the moment where the bounces calm and you're suspended, and your voice becomes almost meditative, processing what your body just experienced. Your breathing is ragged, voice shaking, almost sobbing. Then, dangerously, you become giddy—laughing hysterically as adrenaline floods you. The instructor's voice is calm, professional: 'You're okay.' Your voice is the opposite: completely unmoored, euphoric, barely in control of basic speech.

title: Nostalgia Ambush: A Song Comes On
instruction: You're in a grocery store and a song from a specific memory plays over the speakers. Narrate the sudden transportation back in time — the voice softens, slows, and warms as the memory takes over. Describe the person, the place, the feeling. Hum a few bars. Then realize you're standing in aisle seven with tears running down your face. The self-conscious laugh, the wiping of eyes, the attempt to return to your shopping list. Bittersweet should taste like this sounds.

title: The Secret I've Carried Alone
instruction: You're whispering a confession to someone you love in the dark, something you've hidden for years that's been eating you alive. Start barely audible, your breath shaky, testing each word before you say it. There's tenderness in your voice because you're trusting them with this, but also deep shame that makes you want to disappear. Let silence fill the spaces between phrases—the pauses where you almost can't continue. Your voice should waver between hoping they'll understand and fearing they'll walk away. End with a fragile question, 'Can you still love me knowing this?' Let the vulnerability be so raw it hurts, like you're offering them your heart knowing they might crush it.

title: The Last Conversation Before Departure
instruction: You're speaking to someone you love who's about to leave on a one-way journey to Mars—they're excited, you're devastated but trying to be supportive. Start with forced brightness: 'I'm so proud of you, this is everything you've worked for.' Let the cracks show slowly—your voice catching, pauses growing longer. Move through attempting jokes about missing their terrible coffee-making to barely-contained grief. 'I keep thinking about all the sunsets you'll see that I'll never...' Trail off. End in raw honesty, no longer hiding: whisper their name like a prayer, tell them the simple truth of how much you'll miss the ordinary moments. Your final words are both blessing and breaking. Let silence do the work fear and love can't.

title: Discovering Your Child's Secret and Confronting Them While Your World Collapses
instruction: You've just found out your teenage child has been in serious danger - drugs, an abusive relationship, self-harm, something that makes your blood run cold. Start with explosive fury: 'How could you not tell me?!' Let your voice be raw, loud, almost violent with fear disguised as anger. But as they shrink away from you or start to cry, feel your rage crack open into terror. Your volume drops but the intensity doesn't - now you're pleading, your voice shaking: 'I can't lose you, do you understand? I cannot lose you.' Let protective fierceness war with complete helplessness. Your breathing should be harsh, almost panicked. End quietly, almost whispering, with devastated tenderness: 'Come here' - and in those two words, carry every ounce of fierce love, crushing fear, and the realization that you can't protect them from everything, no matter how desperately you want to.
inspired_by: Listening to Your Partner Fantasize About Someone Else

title: Midnight Herb Ritual
instruction: You are an older adult, alone in your kitchen at 2 AM, slightly drunk on a strong herbal liqueur you've been sipping while chopping fresh herbs from your garden. The sizzle of garlic hitting hot oil almost drowns out your thoughts. You start by humming with pure, unguarded pleasure at the scent—a low, ecstatic moan of satisfaction. But as a memory surfaces of someone who taught you this old recipe, your voice thickens. You speak to the empty room, half-laughing, half-choking. The ecstasy doesn't leave, but it becomes tender, almost unbearable. By the end, you're whispering into the steam, smiling through a cracked voice. Let the knife pause mid-chop; let the sizzle cover a shaky breath. You are drunk on booze, on memory, on the smell of basil.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Floor Confessions
instruction: You're lying on your stomach on the cold hardwood floor of your apartment after a house party, still a little drunk. Your cheek presses against the wood, and every breath feels shallow because your ribs are squished. Start speaking with a sour, bitter edge — you're replaying a moment where someone dismissed you, and you feel that sting acutely. As you talk, a twisted amusement creeps in; you start to giggle at the absurdity of caring so much. Your voice stays low, pressed into the floor, with slight breathlessness and a lazy, intoxicated looseness. Let your words wander, trail off, or pause as you shift your head or adjust your arm.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Amusement (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Warmth
instruction: Your mother is dying in the hospital bed before you, but you cannot touch her—tubes, machines, and medical staff keep you at a distance. You can only stand at the foot of the bed and look at her. Begin in numb shock, barely able to process what's happening. As you speak to her, reach through the distance with your voice and imagine: what would her hand feel like in yours right now? How would her hair smell if you could lean close? What would the warmth of her cheek feel like against your palm? Let these imagined sensations flood through you until the distance becomes unbearable. By the end, you must arrive at a place of desperate, aching tenderness—as if touching her with your words is the only way left to say goodbye. The emotion must crescendo from frozen detachment to overwhelming sensory longing.

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. When you arrived, you were determined to be strong, cheerful, full of memories and laughter. But as golden afternoon light fills the room, something shifts—a smell, the way their hand feels, a half-remembered game you played as children. Let yourself descend from forced brightness into the raw, undefended truth of this moment. Begin speaking about trivial, happy memories, but allow your voice to fracture and transform as you realize this is the actual end. Let the last words you speak come from a place so deep you've never accessed it before—not grief exactly, but something older and more primal. The emotion at the end should feel like falling through darkness into pure, wordless love.
inspired_by: When the actor works with dark or traumatic characters

title: Breaking Point Protocol
instruction: You're a trauma surgeon who just lost a patient—a seven-year-old—and you're in the staff room, alone, when another doctor walks in and asks if you're okay. Start by saying 'I'm fine' with complete conviction, the armor firmly in place. They press gently, and suddenly you're not fine—you're screaming. 'We did everything! Everything!' Your voice is raw, furious at the unfairness, at bodies that break, at protocols that fail. The rage is towering, but then it collapses into gasping sobs because you can still see the parents' faces, and you're the one who had to tell them. Your voice breaks completely: 'She was seven.' End with helpless repetition: 'What am I supposed to do with that? What am I supposed to do?' Show how fury transforms into grief, how professional competence shatters into human helplessness.

title: Everything and Nothing
instruction: You've just received news that you got the opportunity you've been chasing for years—the job, the recognition, the validation you thought would make you whole. Begin with pure, unfiltered joy. Let yourself laugh, maybe even shout with triumph. Your voice should ring with vindication: 'I did it. I'm finally somebody.' Savor that feeling completely. But then, in the middle of your celebration, feel a horrible emptiness open up inside you. Your voice should falter, become confused. Realize with creeping dread that you feel exactly the same inside as you did before. The achievement changes nothing about the fundamental loneliness or uncertainty you carry. Let your voice drop to almost nothing as you admit: 'This was supposed to fix me.' Feel the grief of that broken promise. But then—and this is crucial—find something else. A memory of a moment when you felt whole for no reason at all: helping a stranger, laughing until you cried, sitting in morning sunlight. Let your voice grow stronger as you realize you've been searching in the wrong place. End with a complex tone that holds both disappointment and liberation: 'I thought I needed this to matter. But I already mattered. I just couldn't see it.' Let your final words carry both the sorrow of wasted years and the trembling hope of a new understanding.

title: The Returned Soldier's Door
instruction: You're arriving home after years away - war, prison, exile, something that changed you. You stand at your own front door, about to knock, about to see the face of someone who loves you but doesn't know yet what you've become. Begin speaking to yourself, voice tight and trapped high in your throat, breathing shallow, body armored with tension. As you talk yourself through knocking, let your body gradually, unwillingly soften. Your breath deepens against your will. Feel your throat opening even as you try to hold yourself together. You're simultaneously terrified and desperately grateful, wanting to run and needing to stay. Your voice should drop and warm and crack as relief battles with fear. By the final moment before knocking, you're breathing fully, voice emerging from deep in your chest, speaking words of both hope and dread in a tone that's completely transformed - vulnerable, open, impossibly brave.

title: The Birthday Card You Never Sent
instruction: You're holding a birthday card you wrote years ago but never sent to someone you cut out of your life—a former best friend, a sibling, someone you loved but had to leave behind. Start reading the card aloud: cheerful, generic birthday wishes that sound hollow and false. Stop. Begin speaking what you really wanted to write: how much you miss them and how angry you still are at them in the same breath. Let your voice oscillate between warmth and bitterness—laughing at a shared memory while your laughter cracks with resentment, saying 'I hope you're happy' with genuine caring and seething jealousy intertwined. Your tone should be unstable, shifting rapidly between contradictory feelings that are somehow both true. Describe what you lost and what you gained by walking away. By the end, you should arrive at a complicated peace: you can hold both love and anger, both gratitude for what you shared and relief that it's over. The journey is from false cheerfulness through emotional chaos to authentic complexity—not resolution, but honest contradiction.

title: The Thin Air Confession
instruction: You're an older man on a high-altitude trek, struggling with altitude sickness. You stop, gasping, wincing from a pounding headache. You have to admit to your guide that you can't continue, while others around you seem fine. Start with intense embarrassment – you stammer, trying to justify yourself, making excuses. As you speak, the shame shifts into a quiet sadness and sour resignation. Let your voice come out slow, with frequent deep breaths. Pause as you lose a word, wince at a sharp pain, then force yourself to finish. The final line sounds heavy, like you're accepting a bitter truth.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (very intensely present), Sadness (slightly present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Typing of Tenderness
instruction: You're alone in a quiet office late at night, typing a message to someone you deeply love. You start with a soft, amused affection — a small smile as you recall a memory. But as you type faster, your voice slows, fragments, and gets caught in the rhythm of the keys. The affection grows more intense, raw, and vulnerable — you're not just saying words, you're giving them a piece of your heart. Let the clicking keyboard shape your pauses and hesitations. End with a tenderness so full it nearly breaks your voice.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bleeding Out on the Asphalt
instruction: You are a mother who has just been in a car crash, your child is crying in the backseat, and you're bleeding heavily from a gash in your side. You're on the phone with emergency dispatch, trying to give your location while also reassuring your child. Start the call with sharp impatience and irritability—the dispatcher keeps asking for details you already gave, and your child's whimpering makes you snap. As the blood loss deepens, your voice fades into trembling weakness; you lose your train of thought, shiver mid-sentence, and your irritation softens into quiet disappointment in yourself for not being able to protect your child. End with a frail, fading plea as you struggle to stay conscious.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: Your parent is dying, and you both know these are the final hours. You begin with forced brightness, trying to pretend it's just another morning—'I brought your tea the way you like it'—but your voice fractures. As you sit beside them, the pretense crumbles. You move through memories: 'Remember when you taught me to ride a bike? You never let go, even when you said you would.' Your voice shifts from desperate cheerfulness to raw grief, then finally to something quieter—acceptance mixed with devastating love. By the end, you're whispering promises about carrying them forward: 'I'll be okay. You made sure of that.' Your voice should break, recover, break again, landing somewhere between heartbreak and profound gratitude.

title: The Final Grade
instruction: You are a young man sitting at a cluttered desk, sorting through a thick stack of final exam papers you just graded for your students. The paper shuffles dryly in your hands; you occasionally snap a corner or mumble a score. Start with a tired sigh as you flip through, your voice flat and mechanical. Then you come across one answer that surprises you—a sudden, sharp snap of paper as you stop. Your voice tightens with frustration and doubt as you realize the system failed them, and then fades into a hollow whisper of helplessness as you realize you don't know how to fix it.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: What We Never Said
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to someone you love, and you believe they're asleep. In a whisper barely louder than breath, confess something you've never had the courage to say in daylight—a fear about yourself, a moment you failed them, a way you're broken that you're terrified they'll discover. Start with halting, fragmented words, testing if they're really asleep. As you continue, let the confession deepen. Your whisper should be intimate, trembling, achingly tender. Then—a shift—you realize or suspect they might actually be awake, listening. The final words must change: do you retreat into silence, or do you choose to be known?

title: The Secret I've Carried
instruction: You're confessing something you've held inside for years to someone you trust completely. Your voice starts barely audible, shame making it hard to speak: 'There's something I've never told anyone. Not anyone.' Each word costs you something. Your throat tightens as you approach the truth: 'I'm so afraid you'll see me differently. That you won't love me anymore.' The confession itself is whispered, vulnerable, the kind of truth that makes you feel naked: 'I'm not who you think I am. I've been hiding this part of myself because I was terrified.' But as you speak, you feel their acceptance, their love unchanged, and your voice begins to steady, filling with quiet wonder: 'You're still here. You're still looking at me like that.' End with a whisper that holds both tears and relief: 'Thank you. Thank you for not leaving.' The arc moves from shame to exposure to the profound relief of being fully seen and still loved.

title: Tide of Malice
instruction: You are an elderly person standing at the shoreline, watching a younger figure you've secretly desired for months. The wind tugs at your coat, and each wave pulls sand from under your feet. You begin speaking with a thin veil of nostalgic tenderness, a hint of longing in your voice. But as the roar of the surf fills the gaps, your tone hardens—the lust curdles into quiet satisfaction, because you know exactly how to use your knowledge of their weakness to destroy them. Let the rhythm of the waves shape your pauses, and let the malice seep in like the cold tide rising.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Bedside Vigil: Words Unspoken
instruction: You're alone with your sleeping partner/best friend/sibling in the ICU late at night. They can't hear you, so you finally say everything you've been too scared to say. Start with a whisper, almost to yourself: 'Hey... it's me.' Your voice is tender, intimate, the way you sound when no one else is listening. Tell them about the small moment when you first knew you loved them—your voice catches with the sweetness of the memory. Confess your fear of losing them, voice breaking: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' There's a long pause where you just breathe with them. Then speak the truth you've never said aloud, voice raw and soft: 'You're the best thing that ever happened to me.' Your words are soaked in gratitude and grief, every syllable precious because you don't know if they'll ever hear you again. End by touching their hand, voice barely above a breath: 'Please stay.' It's not a dramatic plea. It's an intimate prayer.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who raised you—a grandparent, parent, or mentor—in their final hours. Begin by noticing small, specific details: the weight of their hand in yours, the rhythm of their breathing, the quality of light coming through the window. Let yourself become acutely aware of every sensation in this moment—the temperature of the room, the sound of distant footsteps, the smell of antiseptic mixed with their familiar scent. As you speak to them, allow memories to surface spontaneously without planning what you'll say. Start from a place of careful attention, almost holding your breath, afraid to disturb anything. Gradually let the full weight of what's happening wash over you—this is the last time. Notice how your awareness of every tiny detail (the pattern on their blanket, the beeping monitor) somehow opens a floodgate of feeling you didn't know was there. End in a place where grief and profound gratitude have become indistinguishable from each other.

title: The Kitchen Where Everything Changed
instruction: You have just received the best news of your life and are standing in your kitchen calling someone to tell them. But as you begin speaking, start really seeing this room: the crack in the wall from that terrible argument three years ago, the spot where you collapsed in grief, the corner where you stood frozen the night you almost gave up. Ask yourself: what does this light actually look like hitting the counter? What does the floor feel like under your feet right now compared to that night? Let the room itself become a witness to your entire journey. Your joy should remain real but become threaded through with ghosts—all the versions of yourself who stood in this exact spot at rock bottom. By the end, you should be laughing and crying simultaneously, celebrating and mourning, intensely aware that this moment of triumph exists in the same physical space as your worst moments. Your voice should carry both emotions equally—not switching between them, but holding both at once.

title: The Last Meal Before Deployment
instruction: You're cooking your partner's favorite meal - the one they always criticized as unhealthy - the night before they leave for a mission they might not return from. Begin with forced cheerfulness as you describe preparing each ingredient, trying to keep things light and normal. As you talk about the food, let the reality of tomorrow break through - your voice catching on memories of past meals together, the desperate attempt to savor this moment crumbling into quiet devastation. End in a whispered confession of all the things you never said, spoken to the empty chair where they'll sit one last time. Let the mundane act of cooking become unbearably tender and final.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire childhood. Begin with carefully controlled words—you've rehearsed this, your voice measured and almost cold. 'I need you to hear what it was like to be invisible to you.' But as they deflect or offer weak justifications, your control shatters. Let decades of unmet hunger pour out—rage at what you deserved but never got, pain at still wanting their approval even now, shame at your own need. Then catch yourself in their frailty, seeing them as broken rather than powerful. Your voice shifts from fury to something more complex: grief for both of you, anger mixed with unexpected compassion, the terrible realization that they were doing their best and it still wasn't enough. End in raw, contradictory honesty—still wounded but beginning to let go.

title: The Inheritance Box
instruction: You're going through your late father's belongings and find a box of toys—not yours, but his from childhood. Inside is a worn stuffed bear, comic books, a homemade superhero cape. This is the father who was always distant, serious, critical. Begin with confusion and a strange sense of betrayal—who was this playful child, and where did he go? As you examine each item, let yourself imagine him as a boy with wild dreams and fearless imagination. Feel anger rising: why did he kill that part of himself? Why did he stop you from being playful? Then let something break open: maybe he didn't kill it. Maybe he just buried it. Try on the cape. Hold the bear. Speak to him as if he were seven years old, asking him why he gave up. End in a complex stew of grief, forgiveness, understanding, and rage—mourning both the father you had and the child he used to be.

title: Shattered Guardian
instruction: You've just found out your child has been hurt—bullied, assaulted, or harmed in a way you couldn't prevent—and you're on the phone with the person responsible (a school administrator, another parent, an institution). Explode into the scene with volcanic rage, your voice a weapon, demanding accountability and justice with every fiber of your being. But mid-tirade, let your fury crack open to reveal the helplessness underneath—you weren't there, you couldn't protect them, you failed at the one job that mattered. Your voice should shatter from roaring strength into broken sobbing, then surge back into fierce protectiveness mixed with self-recrimination. End with a desperate, almost feral declaration of what you'll do next, your voice raw and stripped of everything but primal parental love and pain.

title: Whispering to Your Birth Mother's Grave: The Conversation You'll Never Have
instruction: You've found your birth mother's grave—she died two years ago, just before you started searching. Your voice is barely above a whisper, speaking to the headstone like you're afraid to disturb her: 'I'm here. I'm your... I'm the baby you gave away.' Start with tentative hope that somehow she can hear: 'I turned out okay. I wanted you to know that.' But then the grief comes—quiet, throat-catching grief for all the missed years: 'I have your eyes. Someone told me that. I wish you could have seen them.' Your voice breaks on tender confession: 'I used to imagine you were looking for me too.' There's no anger, just this aching gentleness mixed with devastating loss. End with a whispered promise, voice full of tears and something like love: 'I'm going to come back and tell you about my life. I'll tell you everything. You're not alone anymore.' You're offering comfort to someone who can't hear it, and you know it, and you do it anyway.
inspired_by: Adoptee Searching for Biological Family: Hope and Dread Mixed

title: A Puzzling Specimen
instruction: You are an elderly naturalist examining a strange, slimy creature you just found in your garden. You begin with intense fascination, muttering observations eagerly as you lean closer. But as you notice its rotting smell and writhing texture, disgust rises until it overpowers your curiosity. You're also hiccuping uncontrollably, which cuts your words short. Let your voice shift from breathless interest to grimacing revulsion, with hiccups naturally interrupting your speech as you react to what you see and smell. Speak your thoughts aloud.
emotions_sampled: Interest (very intensely present), Disgust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Contradiction: Thanking Them for Breaking Your Heart
instruction: You're speaking to someone who hurt you profoundly - maybe an ex-lover, maybe a friend who betrayed you - and you're genuinely thanking them, even as your heart breaks all over again. Start with laughter, real laughter, as you describe the absurdity of being grateful for pain. Your voice should be warm, almost playful. Then shift: as you explain what their betrayal taught you, let the humor crack and real grief bleed through. Your voice wavers between smiling and crying. Tell them specific ways they broke you, but also how that breaking made you more capable of love, more honest, more alive. End with the paradox: you wouldn't undo what happened, even though it nearly destroyed you. Move from genuine amusement through bittersweet sadness to profound, painful gratitude. Let contradictory emotions exist simultaneously - laugh while your voice breaks, smile while tears fall. Find peace in the wound.
inspired_by: The Final Words: What You'd Actually Say

title: Enough
instruction: Your teenage daughter just screamed 'I hate you' and slammed her bedroom door. You're standing outside it, and something in you detonates. Start pounding on that door—not violent, but desperate—your voice rising from frustrated parent to something primal. 'You want to hate me? FINE. You know what I gave up? You know what I sacrificed?' Let it pour out—the career, the marriage, the version of yourself you buried. Your voice should be fierce, almost cruel in its honesty. Then hear her crying on the other side. Everything stops. Your hand goes flat against the door. Voice breaking completely: 'I'm sorry. God, I'm so sorry. I didn't mean... You're the only thing I got right. Please. Please open the door.' End with forehead pressed to wood, whispering, 'I love you' like it's the only true thing you know.

title: Languid Bitter Afterglow
instruction: You are an older woman lying in a warm bath after a long massage. Every muscle is melted, your voice slow and loose, words almost slurred with satisfaction. At first you murmur about how good it feels—but then a memory surfaces of someone who took advantage of that trust, and the bitterness seeps out, still unhurried but now thick, resentful. Let your speech stay languid, but let the warmth turn cold as you end with a quiet, bitter laugh. Speak as if you have all the time in the world to hold this grudge.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering the Secret That Changes Everything
instruction: Late at night, in the dark, lying next to someone you love, you finally speak the truth you've been carrying alone. Your voice is barely above a whisper, fragile and tentative: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' There's a long pause where you almost lose courage. Then it comes out, halting and quiet: the affair, the lie, the thing you did that you can't undo. Your voice trembles, catching on words. You're not asking for forgiveness—you're just finally being honest. As you speak, tears come silently, and your voice gets even softer, more broken. The confession ends with the terrifying question, whispered into the darkness: 'Do you still love me?' The silence that follows is unbearable, and in that silence, you realize you might lose everything. End with the sound of your breath catching, waiting.
inspired_by: Telling Your Best Friend You Need Space

title: Protecting a Child You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding a child—your own or one in your care—who is injured, sick, or in danger, and you cannot fix this. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance, your voice strong and commanding: 'Look at me. LOOK at me. You're going to be okay.' You're trying to will it into reality through sheer force. You're making promises: 'I won't let anything happen to you. I've got you.' But the child is scared, asking you questions you can't answer, and you feel your power crumbling. Your fierce protectiveness begins cracking as you realize you're helpless. Your voice breaks from strong to desperate: 'Please. Please, baby, just hold on.' You're bargaining with God, the universe, anyone who might listen. Rage and terror mix—you want to scream at your own powerlessness. Finally, your voice collapses into something raw and broken as you pull them close, rocking them, your words becoming a repetitive, shattered prayer: 'I'm here. I'm here. I'm not leaving you. I'm right here.' End with your fierce love and complete helplessness existing in the same breath.

title: Mirror of the Mother
instruction: You're confronting your aging mother about the childhood she gave you—the emotional absence, the criticism that shaped your self-doubt, the love you needed but never received. Begin with controlled, measured words, trying to be fair and adult about it. But let your voice grow younger as you speak, regressing into the hurt child still living inside you, until you're almost pleading for an explanation, for an apology, for anything. Then shift: mid-speech, catch a glimpse of her frailty, her own pain, and feel your anger transmute into something more complex—grief for both of you, for the relationship you'll never have. End with a kind of broken tenderness, anger dissolving into sad acceptance that she did her best, even if it wasn't enough.

title: The Daughter's Reckoning
instruction: You're finally confronting your father who was always the 'crusader,' the 'hero' who exposed corruption—but who missed every birthday, every school play, every moment you needed him. Start with controlled anger: 'Everyone thinks you're so brave. So righteous.' Your voice is cold, cutting. But as you speak, something more painful emerges—the little girl who waited by the window, who defended him to teachers, who lied and said he was just 'busy saving the world.' The anger cracks open to reveal raw, vulnerable need: 'I needed you to save me. Just once, I needed to be more important than the truth.' By the end, you're not yelling anymore. You're speaking softly, almost tenderly, but with devastating clarity: 'Your conviction destroyed us. And the worst part is, you'd do it all again.' It's an accusation, but it's also grief for the father you never had.

title: Vulnerability Reciprocated
instruction: You've been vulnerable, and the other person matches it. Your voice was hesitant; now it's relieved: 'Really? You feel that too?' You're realizing you're not alone in your experience. Your voice becomes animated, excited: 'I thought I was the only one.' You're connecting on a deeper level. Your voice becomes warm, grateful: 'Thank you for telling me. Thank you for trusting me.' By the end, your voice carries the joy of being truly known.

title: The Wool Sweater
instruction: You're standing alone in your walk-in closet, the door pulled shut to muffle sound from the rest of the house. You've just discovered a deeply personal item hidden in a coat pocket—something that exposes a quiet betrayal you committed months ago. Start by whispering a raw, disgusted exhale—you can't believe you did that. Let your voice dry up as you recall the moment; your throat may tighten, and you might pause to swallow or shift your weight. Then, as you briefly picture getting away with it, a tiny, miserable note of triumph sneaks in—but it curdles fast. End with your voice cracking under a wave of shame; you press your palm to the wall, voice going still and flat, barely above a breath, as you admit what you've never said aloud: 'I'm the kind of person who hides this.'
emotions_sampled: Disgust (clearly present), Triumph (slightly present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a betrayal or abandonment from your childhood that has shaped your entire life—something they've never acknowledged. Start with controlled anger, precise accusations, the words you've rehearsed for years. But as you speak, let the control dissolve. Let your voice become wild, primal, the rage of a child who was too small to fight back. Howl if you need to. Then suddenly switch—catch a glimpse of them as fragile, aging, terrified. Feel your fury collide with unwanted love and pity. End somewhere shocking: perhaps forgiving them while still hating what they did, or choosing to walk away while your voice breaks with the child's desperate wish that they would finally, finally see you.

title: Dancing in Your Childhood Kitchen
instruction: You are alone in a kitchen, cooking a meal your mother or father made for you as a child—something you can smell and taste in memory. As you chop and stir, a song from your childhood comes on, and suddenly your body remembers how you used to dance when no one was watching, how free and unselfconscious you were. Begin cautiously, moving small, but let the sensory experience—the smells, the music, the physical memory in your muscles—unlock something wild and uninhibited. Move bigger, laugh, maybe cry as you move, let sounds escape that aren't words. Build to complete physical and emotional abandon, then suddenly stop when you catch sight of yourself—and sit down, breathless, split between exhilaration and a crushing awareness of all the years and losses between then and now.
inspired_by: Actor has lost imaginative spontaneity and has difficulty believing in imagined circumstances

title: The Bitter Reunion
instruction: You are a 16-year-old guy with a deep, tough voice trying to sound cool. You walk into a party and suddenly see your old best friend who moved away three years ago — you gasp, your voice jumps high with joy, you start running toward him. But then you notice your crush is right next to him, touching his arm, and they’re laughing together. Your excitement curdles into a jealous, envious knot in your chest. Your words start excited and breathless, then slow down, get bitter, and trail off into a forced sarcastic laugh as you try to hide how much it stings.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your father from a hospital bed, knowing this is goodbye. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect him: 'Hey Dad, I'm fine, really. Just wanted to hear your voice.' But your voice cracks. You can't keep lying. 'Dad, I need to tell you something.' The truth pours out — all the times you needed him to say he was proud, all the moments you felt invisible. 'I just wanted you to see me. Really see me.' Your anger dissolves into raw need: 'Tell me you loved me. Please. I need to hear it before...' Trail off. Let silence fill the space where hope used to live. End with whispered acceptance: 'It's okay, Dad. I see myself now. That's enough.' Your voice is simultaneously heartbroken and free.

title: The Lemon Grove's Last Light
instruction: You are an older woman, standing alone in a neglected lemon grove just after sunset. You are whispering because you are afraid of being overheard by the neighbor who has a grudge against you, and because your throat is raw from crying earlier. At first, you speak with a sour, bitter hope—a clenched, defiant optimism that this place will bloom again, though you know it won't in your lifetime. As you continue, a sudden, tender memory of your late wife tasting a lemon from this tree surfaces, and your voice becomes softer, sadder, and genuinely hopeful again, laced with a quiet, raw ache. Let your voice break, catch, and shift weight as you whisper; feel the rough bark under your fingers.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Mother Discovering Daughter's Planned Elopement with Abusive Partner
instruction: You've just found the plane tickets, read the texts that reveal everything. When she walks in, you explode—not with volume but with volcanic intensity that's been building for months. Start with fierce, rapid-fire accusations about the bruises she's hidden, the lies she's told, the person she's become. Your voice is sharp, cutting, desperate. But she fights back, and suddenly you're not lecturing—you're begging. Let the rage crack completely into raw terror. Drop to your knees if you need to. Your voice breaks as you describe finding her body, planning her funeral, the future you see with horrifying clarity. Plead with everything you have, mixing fury with desperate love. End in near-silence, promising both unconditional support and absolute refusal to watch her destroy herself—fierce protectiveness colliding with utter helplessness.
inspired_by: ER Doctor Recognizes Critical Patient as Old Flame

title: Soda and Regret
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a party, leaning against a kitchen counter after drinking too much soda. Your best friend just bailed on you, and you're stuck here with people you don't really like. You're trying to vent your disappointment and irritation to someone next to you, but a burp keeps building in your throat and finally erupts mid-sentence, dropping your voice into a low, gravelly growl. Start with a tight, frustrated tone — your disappointment is raw and heavy, laced with sour annoyance. After the burp, let your voice crack into a bitter, exhausted laugh as you realize how ridiculous this whole night is, ending with a flat, resigned sigh.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Sourness (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're helping someone you raised—your child, your younger sibling, someone you practically parented—pack up their room as they prepare to move far away for something wonderful: their dream job, their wedding, their adventure. Begin by finding specific objects and telling the stories attached to them with pure joy and pride. Celebrate who they've become. Let your voice be bright with genuine happiness for them. But as you continue sorting through years of memories—their baby shoes, their failed art projects, their old journals—let the grief creep in. You're losing them, even though you know you should let them go. Your voice should fracture between celebration and sorrow. You're so proud and so devastated. End with a moment where you're laughing and crying simultaneously, holding some small object, unable to articulate whether you're feeling joy or heartbreak because it's completely both.

title: Washing Away What We Were
instruction: You've just showered after ending a long relationship, trying to wash away their touch, their scent, the years. Wrap yourself in a towel and speak in barely more than a whisper about the small intimacies you'll miss—how they dried your hair, how they knew exactly how you liked to be held after bathing. Let your voice catch on these tiny, devastatingly specific details. This isn't dramatic grief; it's the quiet kind that sits in your chest like a stone. Move from tender remembrance to the terrifying realization that you'll have to relearn being alone. Let silences speak. Let your breath shake. End with something like acceptance, but acceptance that hurts—acknowledging that you can't unknow what comfort felt like.
inspired_by: Wrapping Yourself in a Towel After a Shower

title: The Last Letter: Reading Words They'll Never Hear You Say
instruction: You're alone in a quiet room, holding a letter you've written to someone you've loved and lost—through death, distance, or a rupture you can't repair. Begin by reading it aloud, voice steady but fragile, like you're afraid the words will shatter if spoken too loudly. 'Dear...' Your throat catches. You continue, each sentence a confession you were too afraid to say when it mattered. Your voice becomes softer, more intimate, as if they're sitting across from you. You're telling them everything—the moments you cherished, the regrets that haunt you, the words left unsaid. Emotion builds not through volume but through the spaces between words, the breath that hitches, the pause where you almost can't continue. Let tenderness mix with devastating sadness. End with a whispered goodbye, voice thick with tears, as you fold the letter knowing they'll never read it, never know, never come back.
inspired_by: Finding Shelter in a Blizzard: Relief Becoming Hypothermia Complacency

title: Mom, You Built Walls Instead of a Home
instruction: You're confronting your mother, the survivalist who raised you in isolation and fear. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. Describe what it was like growing up with someone who stockpiled supplies but never asked about your dreams, who prepared for every disaster except your loneliness. Let your voice tighten with decades of unspoken hurt as you tell her about the birthday party you weren't allowed to attend, the friends you couldn't make, the normal life she stole. Build toward the moment where you ask the question that's haunted you: was she preparing for the end of the world, or running from the pain of living in it? End quietly, almost gently, as you realize she was always more afraid than you were.

title: The Mother Who Breaks
instruction: Your teenage child just screamed at you that you ruined their life, that you're the reason they're in therapy, that every problem they have traces back to you. You came to apologize for missing their recital last week, but now you're facing years of accumulated pain. Start controlled, defensive—'I'm sorry about last week, I was working to provide for you'—but feel that justification crumbling as they list every time you chose work, every promise you broke. Let your voice rise with fierce protectiveness mixed with desperation: 'I did everything I could!' Feel yourself getting louder, more raw, anger and guilt colliding—you want to defend yourself but you're also seeing yourself through their eyes. Your voice should crack and surge, fierce declarations breaking into choked sobs: 'You don't understand what I sacrificed!' But then something in their face stops you cold. Watch yourself shatter, your fury dissolving into helpless, gasping grief. End with your voice completely broken, reduced to whispered, fragmented words: 'I'm so sorry... I'm so sorry I wasn't enough,' the apology finally real, finally stripped of all defense, just a mother realizing she failed the person she loves most in the world, rage transformed into the most vulnerable, devastating remorse.
inspired_by: Apologizing for Something You Weren't At Fault For

title: The Kitchen Floor Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. He's just said something dismissive, typical of your entire relationship. Start the scene trying to be articulate and controlled, making your point 'reasonably.' But as he deflects and minimizes, feel yourself losing the ability to stay composed. Let your body get restless—pace, scratch your neck, run your hands through your hair aggressively. Start using the words that actually match your rage, not the 'respectful' language you've always forced yourself to use with him. Let yourself get physically crude if it wants to happen—kick the cabinet, slam your hand on the counter, make sounds that aren't even words. By the end, you should be completely unguarded, saying things in ways you've never allowed yourself to before, your whole body involved in the truth-telling. End in an unexpected moment of exhausted tenderness or collapsed vulnerability.

title: The Mistranslation
instruction: You're a veterinary hospice worker who's been 'translating' for a client's elderly cat during end-of-life care, using gentle humor to help them cope. But today, you have to tell them something you've been mistranslating for weeks—the cat isn't just tired, they're in pain, and it's time. Begin with your practiced translator voice, the professional warmth you use to deliver the cat's 'thoughts' about treats and sunshine. But then force yourself to break character, to stop translating comfort and start translating truth. Your voice should explode with frustration at yourself—fury that you made it easier, that you let them hope too long, that you used your gift to delay the inevitable. Let that anger collapse into something more complex: fierce protectiveness of the animal mixed with helplessness that you can't save them, passionate advocacy for mercy mixed with grief that mercy means goodbye. Your tone should swing from controlled professional warmth to raw intensity to broken tenderness. End with one final, honest translation—not what the owner wants to hear, but what the animal needs you to say—delivered with a voice that's simultaneously strong and shattered.

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: You're alone in a hotel room, wearing your wedding dress or suit. Sunlight streams through sheer curtains, you can hear happy voices and laughter from the hallway, smell coffee and fresh flowers. Look at yourself in the mirror. You're marrying someone you deeply love today—feel that joy, that excitement making your heart race. But as you stand there, touch the fabric of your clothes, notice specific details—your father's watch you're wearing, the perfume that was your mother's—and let grief wash in alongside the joy. She died two years ago and should be here. Let these emotions coexist without one canceling the other: speak to her as if she's in the room, tell her about your happiness while acknowledging the ache of her absence. Move from pure joy to this complex place where celebration and loss are completely intertwined, ending with both tears and a smile.

title: The Last Drop of Water
instruction: You are a teenage girl alone in a barren, sun-scorched field, days without water. Your throat is raw, your lips cracked, and every word feels like scraping sandpaper—you have to pause to wet your mouth with a dry tongue, and your sibilants hiss harshly. You’ve just spotted a distant shimmer that might be a pond, and hope floods through you despite the pain. Start in a quiet, desperate whisper, almost disbelieving, then let your voice crack and waver as you try to call out, the optimism growing but your body fighting you. By the end, you’re half-laughing, half-sobbing, the joy mixing with the agony of your parched throat, and you force out a ragged plea for anyone to hear.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mother who spent her life disapproving of your choices—your career, your lovers, your wild spirit. She was always worried about what the neighbors thought, what the family would say. Now, in her final hour, she suddenly grabs your hand and whispers that she was wrong, that she wishes she'd lived more like you. Begin feeling defensive, braced for one final criticism. As her confession unfolds, let yourself move through disbelief, then a flood of grief mixed with vindication, ending in a fierce, whispered celebration of who you both could have been together. Let your voice crack, laugh through tears, be messy and real—this is your moment to claim the life you chose and mourn the years of judgment simultaneously.
inspired_by: Actor resists the irreverent approach because of fear of judgment from directors, peers, or the conventional acting community

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he never defended you as a child. Start from a place of rehearsed calm—you've planned this conversation for years. But as you speak, pause between thoughts to notice what's actually moving through you in real time: the tremor in your hands, heat in your face, a sudden wave of compassion you didn't expect, rage that comes from nowhere, the little girl or boy inside you who still wants his approval. Let these real-time discoveries interrupt and redirect what you thought you came to say. Allow your voice and words to follow the truth of each moment rather than your script. End in a completely different emotional place than where you began—perhaps tender when you meant to stay angry, or furious when you intended forgiveness.

title: The Body Keeps the Score
instruction: You are in the middle of an intensely passionate moment—either making love, dancing, or engaged in a physical fight—when suddenly a sense memory floods your body, triggered by a touch, a sound, or a movement. Your physical pleasure or rage becomes entangled with an old wound, a past trauma surfacing. Begin fully in your body—breathing heavy, moving, vocal, alive with sensation. Then let the emotional flashback invade the physical experience. Your breath might catch, your movements might become confused or desperate. Show the collision between present ecstasy or fury and past pain through your physicality. Don't explain it with words—let your body tell two stories at once. End in a place of emotional rawness where past and present have merged, leaving you physically exhausted but emotionally cracked open.
inspired_by: When a director or producer is unconvinced you have a specific quality the role requires (strength, danger, vulnerability, etc.)

title: The Eruption: Mother Confronting the Child Who Refuses to Speak to Her
instruction: You've driven across the state to your adult child's apartment. They won't return your calls. You start knocking, calling their name—your voice tight, controlled, almost professional. When they finally open the door and just stare at you in silence, something inside you detonates. Your voice explodes from reasoned explanation into raw, ugly rage: 'I am your MOTHER! You don't get to erase me!' But mid-fury, you see their face—unmoved, waiting for you to finish—and the rage collapses into desperate pleading. You're on your knees emotionally, voice breaking, begging them to tell you what you did wrong, promising you'll change, admitting you were never enough. End in exhausted, quiet devastation, accepting they may never let you back in, whispering 'I'm sorry' to someone who has already closed the door.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Time Traveler Meets Their Own Younger Self

title: What You Never Returned
instruction: Your ex-lover is at your door, finally coming to collect their belongings after the brutal breakup. You've packed everything in boxes, but you've kept one item separate—their favorite book, a jacket, a watch, something they treasured. You begin cold, defensive, shoving boxes toward them with clipped words. But when you hand them this particular object, something breaks. You've been holding it, sleeping with it, carrying it with you for weeks. As you try to let it go, your hands won't release it. Start demanding answers—why did they leave, what did you do wrong—but let your grip on this object betray you. Your anger should crack open to reveal the desperate need underneath. By the end, you're either forcing it into their hands to make them leave, or you're clutching it back, begging them to stay. Let the object become the wordless center of everything you can't say.
inspired_by: Object Bonding (Personal Relationship with Stage Objects)

title: The First Laugh
instruction: You are a young adult gently coaxing a fussy baby, your voice high and lilting with simple, repetitive sounds. After many tired attempts, the baby suddenly breaks into a huge grin and a gurgling laugh. A wave of intense triumph and elation surges through you, though a faint numbness from prior exhaustion clings beneath your joy. Your voice climbs in pitch, swooping exaggeratedly as you repeat the silly sound that worked, then ends in a breathless, delighted exclamation. Let the performance begin with weary patience and shift to pure, triumphant playfulness, with the numbness subtly coloring your breath.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Execution
instruction: You have three minutes to speak to your sibling before they are executed for a crime you know they didn't commit. Your voice starts controlled, trying to be strong for them, but fractures when they say they forgive you for not being able to save them. You want to scream at the injustice but you also need to give them peace in these final moments. Your breathing becomes ragged as you try to memorize the sound of their voice. When they ask you to promise you'll live fully, your voice breaks between desperate protest and tender acceptance.
