instruction: Something has changed someone's life fundamentally. Their voice carries the before and after. Before the change, there's a weariness or limitation. Then something shifts. The voice shifts. The person is describing their life now, and it's unrecognizable from the life before. They're still themselves, but transformed. The change might have been forced or chosen; either way, they're moving forward into this new life. Their voice by the end carries gratitude or hard-won acceptance. Life-changing moments are audible in how someone speaks about their existence.

title: The Comedian's Last Show
instruction: You're a stand-up comedian performing what you know will be your final show before entering hospice. You're telling your funniest story—something absurd that happened last week, something that makes you laugh even now. Your voice should be full of genuine mirth, that infectious joy that made audiences love you. But as you're laughing, really laughing, tears start mixing in because you're also saying goodbye to this—to stages, to laughter, to being alive. Your voice does something extraordinary: it laughs and breaks simultaneously. You're grateful for every ridiculous moment, every stupid joke, every person who laughed with you, and the gratitude is making you cry even as the humor of it all makes you laugh harder. End with thanking the audience while you're both crying and giggling, finding the strange peace that comes when you can hold joy and grief in the same breath.

title: You Were Never There
instruction: You are unleashing years of suppressed rage at a mentor figure who abandoned you when you needed them most. Start with explosive anger—loud, uncontrolled, accusations flying like weapons. Your voice should crack with fury as you describe specific moments when their absence destroyed you. Then, mid-tirade, let the anger shatter into something more vulnerable: the terrified desperation of someone who needed protection and got none. Your voice should break from shouting into sobbing, from accusations into pleading questions: Why wasn't I worth staying for? End in a place of terrible helplessness, your voice small and devastated, as you finally admit the truth beneath the rage—you still need them, and they're still not there. The shift from volcanic rage to childlike devastation should feel like a dam breaking.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Wife After the Diagnosis
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your wife is asleep beside you, and you've just come from the bathroom where you read the doctor's email. Stage 4. Inoperable. You're whispering to her sleeping form, practicing what you'll say tomorrow, but you can't get through it. Start with the practical things—finances, the kids, her mother who'll need help. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every other word. Then you break. Tell her about the Tuesday morning twenty years ago when you watched her make coffee and knew you'd marry her. The trip to Portugal you never took. How you still get butterflies when she laughs. You're trying to fit a lifetime of love into a whisper, knowing tomorrow you'll have to be strong, but right now, in the dark, you can let yourself shatter.
inspired_by: Two Strangers Sharing a Hospital Room

title: The Last Light Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love who has only hours left to live. They cannot speak anymore, but their eyes are open and watching you. Begin in a place of overwhelming grief and inability to speak - your throat is closed, you can barely breathe. Then, as you hold their hand, you begin to remember every small kindness they showed you, every moment of beauty you shared. Let these memories surface one by one, and as they do, allow yourself to shift from drowning in loss to celebrating what you were given. End by telling them - with genuine joy breaking through your tears - that knowing them made your life worth living. Your voice should transform from choked silence to clear, grateful testimony.
inspired_by: Actor is depressed and cannot access creative energy

title: A Parent's Final Confession at the Hospital Bedside
instruction: You're sitting beside your adult child in the ICU, and they've just woken from what doctors said might be their last night. Begin with overwhelming relief—your voice trembling with gratitude that they're here, that you get this moment. But you know what you need to say. Your voice softens, becomes almost a whisper, as you confess the truth you've carried for thirty years—the adoption, the sibling they never knew about, the choice you made that shaped their entire life. Let your words become heavier, more fractured. You're giving them a gift of truth and a burden of knowledge, and you can hear in your own voice how these two things are inseparable. End with your breathing shallow and uncertain, asking if they can forgive you, knowing you might not have tomorrow to hear the answer.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Cursed Being Realizes Breaking the Curse Requires Murdering Their Love

title: The Leak
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a nursing home, talking to your grandson who you suspect is stealing from your savings account. Your throat is tight, and your voice keeps squeaking and cracking despite trying to stay calm. Start with a falsely sweet, menacing tone—smiling but with malice underneath. As you speak, your doubt grows: maybe you're wrong, maybe you're just a paranoid old lady. Fear of his reaction makes your words leak out faster, higher, more strained. End with a desperate, almost whispered plea for the truth, your voice barely holding together.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Doubt (very intensely present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Phone Call That Can't Be Made
instruction: You are a teenage boy with a pounding migraine, hidden in the dark of your closet. You need to tell your dad that you failed your driver's test, but every sound—even your own voice—feels like a spike behind your eyes. Start with the distress of the headache making you whisper and wince as you press the phone to your ear, hearing it ring. As you imagine your father's disappointment, the fear takes over—a raw, trembling terror that makes your breath catch and your voice crack. By the end, you're barely audible, your words skipping and fading as you try to confess your failure, then stop, overwhelmed by the dread of his reaction.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Machines Stop
instruction: You are holding the hand of someone you've loved for forty years as their life support is about to be turned off. Begin speaking to them with controlled composure, trying to be strong, telling them practical things—that you've paid the bills, that the garden looks beautiful. But as you continue, let the reality crack through: this is the last time you'll ever speak to them. Let your voice break as you move from mundane details to desperate confessions of things you never said. End in a whisper, telling them the one truth you were always too afraid to speak when they could respond. Your emotional journey moves from protective strength to complete vulnerability, from talking at them to talking with your whole heart exposed.

title: The Last Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: You're watching someone you love board a plane for a dangerous mission they might not return from. You've been holding it together, but now at the final moment, everything spills out. Start with forced cheerfulness - 'You're going to be amazing out there' - your voice bright but brittle. Then the facade cracks: 'I should have told you months ago...' Your breath catches. 'I love you. I've always loved you.' Now the floodgates open - desperation, regret for all the wasted time, fierce protectiveness mixed with the helplessness of watching them go. End with a whispered plea that's part prayer, part surrender: 'Come back to me.' Let your voice break where it needs to. This isn't about being strong - it's about being real in the face of possible permanent loss.

title: The Infinite Beyond
instruction: You are floating inside the airlock after your first spacewalk, helmet still sealed. Your suit’s radio hums. You look through the visor at the curve of Earth—light floods in. At first you’re awed, stammering with ecstasy and gratitude, almost forgetting to breathe. Then you remember the comms protocol: you have to report in. Your voice shifts from overwhelmed wonder to focused, deliberate words, but the joy still leaks through. Speak as if you’re catching your breath, your body weightless, the helmet amplifying your voice. Around 60 words.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Concentration (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Summer’s End, First Sight
instruction: You're a teenage boy at a quiet park bench, watching the sunset. You’ve been away all summer. Suddenly, you see the person you’ve been dreaming of—your secret crush—walk toward you with a shy smile. The shock hits your chest. A gasp escapes. Your voice leaps in pitch: 'Oh my god—you’re here? I thought you—' The words tumble out in fragments, half-laugh, half-sob. Your body feels like it’s moving toward them on its own, rustling leaves underfoot. The raw happiness and a thrilling, stomach-dropping desire mix in your throat. But as you get closer, the emotion shifts: the frantic joy settles into a deep, quiet contentment. Your voice drops, becomes softer, almost a whisper—just them and you. 'I can’t believe… you came… I’m so glad.' Let the first words burst out wild and unguarded; let the last ones feel like a warm secret only they can hear.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Executioner Recognizes Victim's Parent Among the Crowd
instruction: Final address before execution, your ceremonial voice measured and professional. You see the murdered child's mother in the crowd, face destroyed by grief. Your voice continues with perfect execution-ground formality, but now every word is acknowledgment of her pain. Your vocal steadiness is respect offered to suffering. Your breathing deepens with the weight of participating in her grief's conclusion. End with silence that honors both the condemned and the mourning.

title: Thanking Someone as You Let Them Go
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who saved your life—literally or metaphorically—but who you cannot keep in your life anymore. Begin with deep gratitude, your voice warm and genuine, recounting specific moments when they were your lifeline, when their presence meant survival. Let joy creep into your voice as you remember the best times, almost laughing at shared memories. But underneath, there's heartbreak beginning to surface, because you know this goodbye is necessary and permanent. Your voice starts to fracture as you try to explain why you have to leave, why staying would destroy you both, tears mixing with laughter at the beautiful, impossible contradiction of loving someone you cannot be near. Move through waves of emotion—fierce protectiveness of the bond you shared, grief at what you're losing, relief that you're finally strong enough to walk away, guilt for that relief. End with a voice that's somehow both breaking and whole, expressing gratitude that transforms into blessing, releasing them with love even as your heart splinters, finding strange peace in the chaos of loving and leaving simultaneously.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside your sleeping partner, knowing you have to leave them to protect them from something they don't know about. Your voice is barely above a whisper—you can't wake them. Begin tenderly, cataloging the small things you love: how they breathe, the way they curl into themselves, that spot behind their ear. Your voice is soft with adoration. As you confess why you're leaving, your throat tightens with unshed tears—you can't let yourself cry or you'll wake them. Describe the future they'll have without you, and there's both heartbreak and relief in your voice because they'll be safe. The vulnerability is crushing: you admit you're terrified they'll forget you, that maybe that would be better. Your voice catches on each breath. End with the hardest part—telling them you love them, knowing they can't hear it, knowing this moment is yours alone to carry. The final words dissolve into silence that says everything.
inspired_by: New Physical Limitations After Accident: Anger to Acceptance Cycle

title: The Unyielding Stance
instruction: You are standing upright, feet planted, shoulders back, in the middle of an empty room. You face a person who once meant everything to you—now a stranger. Begin with fierce pride, a controlled, resonant voice that fills the space, as you recount how you built yourself from nothing. As you speak, a crack of distress bleeds through—you see the toll time has taken on them, and it mirrors your own unspoken loneliness. Let a whisper of lust color your final words, a lingering want for what was, even as you hold your ground. Your voice shifts from clear and commanding to vulnerable, with natural pauses where you swallow or look away.
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Distress (clearly present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Weight of a Joke
instruction: You're a 17-year-old jock in the third trimester of a mysterious pregnancy. You're slouched on a park bench, trying to tease your best friend about his new haircut, but your diaphragm is crushed, and every word costs you. Start with a playful jab, but your breath runs out mid-sentence—you shift, sigh, and your voice cracks. By the end, the teasing fades into a quiet confession of how exhausted you really are, your bravado dissolving as you admit you're terrified.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She has hours left. Begin in silence, simply watching her breathe, noticing every detail of her face, her hands, the way morning light catches the silver in her hair. Let yourself wonder about what she's feeling, what she remembers. Gradually, as you truly see her—not the dying body but the whole person—allow words to come. Tell her what you've never said, moving from quiet observation to desperate gratitude to grief to a final, tender acceptance. Your emotional journey moves from numb disconnection to raw presence to peaceful goodbye. Let the silence between words matter as much as the words themselves.
inspired_by: Scene partners feel disconnected and are not genuinely relating to each other

title: The Riot at Sunrise
instruction: You are both prisoner and guard in the moments after a violent riot that ended in death. Begin with explosive rage—screaming accusations, your voice raw with fury at the injustice, the brutality, the waste of life. Let that rage fracture into grief as you describe what you witnessed, who didn't make it, whose blood is still on your hands. Your voice should crack between shouting and sobbing, fierce protectiveness for those who died mixing with helpless despair that you couldn't save them. As exhaustion takes over, let the anger dissolve into something quieter but no less intense: a desperate, almost childlike plea for someone to explain how humans do this to each other. End in a place of shattered incomprehension, your voice hoarse, oscillating between whispered disbelief and sudden surges of anguished fury. Make us feel your throat is bleeding from the force of these emotions.

title: The Last Line
instruction: You are a child at your desk, trying to finish a drawing for your mother. Your stomach cramps have been twisting all day. You curl over your paper, one arm pressed against your belly, breathing in short, guarded gasps. Start by snapping at the pain itself—impatient, irritated that it won't let you work. Then let the distress seep into your voice as you struggle to hold the pencil steady. End with a proud, defiant whisper—you will finish this line no matter what. Let your voice be directed downward, with a groaning undertone on vowels, and allow natural interruptions like shifting in your seat or a sharp inhale.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Distress (clearly present), Pride (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Landing
instruction: You are a young submissive emerging from a deep scene. Your body trembles under a soft blanket as your partner holds you. A wave of confusion washes over you—you're not sure what just happened or why you feel so raw. Your voice is small, shaky, fragile, and you speak slowly between sips of water, shifting weight, and the rustle of fabric. Start with a quiet, uncertain murmur: 'I don't... I don't know why I'm shaking.' Let the confusion deepen as you struggle to find words. Then, as your partner whispers reassurances and strokes your hair, your voice gradually softens, steadier, and you end with a breath of surrender: 'I think... I think I'm okay now. Thank you.' Let the tremor fade into a fragile peace by the final line.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Office Puzzle
instruction: You are a child, about 10, sitting at a parent's desk in a bustling open-plan office. You hold a heavy paperweight, tracing its edges with your finger, lost in thought. Then you notice a sticky note on a coworker's monitor—their password written in plain sight. A cold, playful excitement simmers in your chest. You speak low, almost to yourself, the murmur of phones and typing around you making you hunch closer. Start with dreamy curiosity, voice soft and wavering. As you realize what you could do, let a sly, malevolent whisper creep in—your tone darkens, but stays hushed, as if sharing a secret with the paperweight.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering What You Never Said Before the Lake Freezes Over
instruction: It's the last night before winter fully sets in, and you're at the lake where you and your closest friend spent every summer for twenty years—before the argument that broke you apart six months ago. You're here because they asked you to meet them, but they haven't arrived, and you're not sure they will. Begin by breathing in the cold air, noticing how different this place feels in approaching winter, how the water is almost still. Speak softly, as if practicing what you'll say if they come—the apology, the confession of how much you miss them, the admission that you were wrong. Let your whisper grow more desperate and tender as you realize they might not show up, that this might be your only chance to say these words into the gathering dark. End with your voice barely audible, breaking on the edge of tears, as you speak the truth you should have said months ago, whether anyone hears it or not.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep, Inhaling Breath by a Freshwater Lake

title: The 3 AM Phone Call
instruction: You're whispering into the phone at 3 AM, ostensibly calling an old friend to ask a trivial question about a book recommendation or a recipe. Your words are casual, almost silly—apologizing for the late hour, making small talk. But underneath every word lives a desperate subtext: you're standing at the edge of giving up entirely, and this call is a lifeline you can't bring yourself to name. Start the scene keeping the dark current completely hidden beneath cheerful, rambling conversation. Let the subtext slowly surface through longer pauses, through the way your breathing changes, through questions that almost ask for help but veer away at the last second. End when your friend gently says your name in a way that acknowledges what you haven't said, and you break—not into explanation, but into the kind of crying that needs no words, the subtext finally becoming the only truth.

title: The Butterfly and the Badge
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl in a police station, questioned after being found alone at a park. You are fascinated by the officer’s shiny badge and clicking pen — you keep drifting off to stare at them. At first, your voice is light, full of curiosity, as you describe what you saw. But when the officer’s tone hardens and asks if a stranger gave you candy, your voice shrinks into a tiny, wobbly whisper — and you suddenly remember the lollipop in your pocket. Let your focus wander, soften into a teasing smile about the 'glittery star,' then let fear creep in as the question sinks in.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Childhood Bedroom Confrontation
instruction: You've returned to your childhood home to confront your father about something he did—or didn't do—years ago that shaped your entire life. He's asked you to wait in your old bedroom while he finishes something. You're alone, surrounded by the artifacts of who you used to be. Look at your old desk, the poster you once loved, trophies from activities he pushed you into, the closet where you used to hide and cry, the window you'd stare out dreaming of escape, photos of a smiling child who didn't know what was coming. Speak aloud your feelings about each object with brutal honesty—the resentment, the confusion, the anger, the moments of unexpected tenderness and lost innocence. Begin with cold, rehearsed fury—you came here ready for battle. But as you articulate your feelings about these objects, let the anger complicate into something messier: grief for your younger self, reluctant compassion for the imperfect human who raised you, and finally, an exhausted recognition that the truth is more complex than the speech you prepared.

title: Fever Breaking
instruction: You are in the grip of intense physical pleasure or pain—the peak of passion, the aftermath of violence, the final push of childbirth, a migraine finally cresting. Your entire body is activated, every muscle engaged and trembling. Begin with sharp, urgent sounds and movements—your body fighting or reaching, taut with intensity. As the physical sensation peaks and begins to ebb, let your body gradually become impossibly heavy, as though gravity has doubled. Your sounds shift from urgent to drawn-out, from controlled to involuntary. Sweat, trembling, exhaustion wash over you. By the end, you are collapsed, your body so weighted it feels like you could sink through the floor, but there's a strange euphoria in the release—all that tension finally draining away, leaving you liquid and spent and strangely peaceful, making sounds that are barely more than breath.

title: Dropping the Façade
instruction: You're a young woman who grew up as a tomboy, now in the locker room after a co-ed softball game. The team is all guys, and you've learned to brag and jive with them to fit in. Start by loudly crowing about the game-winning run you scored, using the same coarse energy they use. As the group disperses to showers, let the volume drop. In a quieter moment with just your teammate, admit you were secretly terrified you'd trip at home plate, letting the relief and triumph mix with an honest, sour vulnerability you normally hide. The boastful posturing should crack open by the end, revealing a more genuine, tired, and grateful self.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Relief (slightly present), Triumph (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Reading the Waiver
instruction: You are a teenage girl sitting at a kitchen table, reading aloud the fine print from a permission slip for a weekend camping trip with your best friend. Your mom is nearby, and you know she's nervous about letting you go. You start in a flat, rapid monotone, emphasizing every 'hereby' and 'indemnify' to prove you're taking this seriously. But as you read, you feel a surge of affection for your mom's care—your voice softens, you stumble on a word, and you end with a quiet, genuine promise that you'll be safe, breaking the professional tone entirely.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Cake Catastrophe
instruction: You are an older woman with a bright, fluttering voice, at your grandchild's birthday party. The child blows out the candles with such force that the cake topples off the table. You are overcome with awe at their sheer gusto and elation at the mess – but you also want to tease them for being a little mischief-maker. As you try to speak, a laughing fit takes over: you wheeze, squeak, run out of air, and can barely get words out. Start with a breathless, delighted exclamation of awe, then attempt a mock-scolding tease that dissolves into giggles. By the end, you surrender to pure joy, your voice cracking and gasping.
emotions_sampled: Awe (clearly present), Elation (clearly present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Packing Your Childhood Room
instruction: You are thirty-five years old, packing up your childhood bedroom because your parents are finally selling the house. As you sort through objects, you speak aloud, beginning with what you're touching right now—a yearbook, a dried corsage, a participation trophy. Your voice is bemused, slightly mocking of your younger self. But as you unpack each box, each drawer, let yourself move backward through time: high school heartbreak, middle school humiliation, elementary school innocence. Let fragments arise—not complete stories but flashes: 'I'm twelve and I'm hiding in this closet because...' 'I'm eight and I'm standing at this window watching for...' 'I'm five and I'm pressing my ear to this door listening to...' Your voice should fracture, becoming less adult, more confused, more hurt. Objects become triggers for contradictory emotions: anger at what you lost mixed with gratitude for what you survived, grief for the child you were mixed with relief that you escaped. End holding something small—a toy, a note, a photograph—and let yourself break between wanting to preserve everything and wanting to burn it all down. The arc moves from ironic detachment to overwhelming emotional complexity, where laughter and sobbing become indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Actor cannot remember early childhood memories that might be relevant to their work

title: Coming Home to the Empty House
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home after your parent has moved to assisted living. You're here to pack up their belongings, and you expected to feel sad or nostalgic. But as you move through the rooms, notice what you're actually sensing: dust in the air, the particular silence of an empty house, faded wallpaper, the creak of stairs, cooking smells embedded in the walls, afternoon light hitting worn carpet. Let these sensory details stir up contradictory feelings you didn't anticipate. The smell from the kitchen might trigger both comfort and resentment. The sound of your footsteps might bring both grief for what's ending and unexpected relief or freedom. Start with what you think you should feel, but let the sensory environment reveal a complicated truth: you're both heartbroken and strangely liberated, both grateful and angry, both holding on and ready to let go.

title: Teacher: Celebrating a Student's Unexpected Success
instruction: A student you weren't sure would make it has succeeded beyond expectation. Your voice carries genuine pride and warmth: 'I knew you had potential but look what you've done.' You're celebrating their specificity, not just success. Include the moment where emotion breaks through—you care about these people. Your voice becomes almost tearful: 'I'm so proud of you. You should be proud of you.' You're speaking as a human, not just an authority. By the end, your voice reflects the moment: this student might not remember much from your class but they'll remember that you believed in them. 'You're going to do amazing things.' Your voice is giving them something they might carry for decades.

title: The Key in Your Pocket
instruction: You are packing up your childhood home after your parent's funeral. You find their wedding ring. Hold an imagined object in your hand—really feel its weight, temperature, the smoothness of metal. Remember a specific moment when this parent hurt you deeply: the exact location, what you could see and hear, the specific quality of air in that room. Let justified anger rise. But then, still feeling that hurt, remember another moment: their hand on your fevered forehead, their voice singing you to sleep, a moment of pure parental love. Don't let go of either memory. Speak to the empty room, holding both the wound and the love, your voice cycling between bitter resentment and tender forgiveness, unable to land on either, because both are true.
inspired_by: Actor wants to begin learning imaging

title: Finding the Obituary: Laughing Through Grief at Memories You Shared
instruction: You've just learned that someone significant from your past has died—a first love, an old friend, someone you lost touch with but never stopped caring about. Begin reading their obituary out loud, your voice steady and factual. Then you encounter a detail that triggers a memory and you laugh—a real, surprised laugh at something ridiculous you did together. But the laughter catches in your throat and suddenly you're crying while still smiling at the memory. Let your voice oscillate between genuine joy at remembering who they were and crushing grief that you never reconnected, that it's too late now. Share stories aloud to no one, your voice warm with affection then cracking with regret. End with profound gratitude mixed with heartbreak: 'Thank you for that summer. God, I wish I'd called you.' Make it beautiful and devastating, a celebration and a funeral in your voice alone.
inspired_by: Emergency Decompression Procedure: Medical Intervention at 30,000 Feet

title: The Purring Past
instruction: You are an older woman with a soft, high-pitched voice, sitting alone in a quiet attic. You’re carefully sorting through a dusty box of old letters and photographs. The paper slides under your fingers, making a dry shushing sound. At first, you’re just methodically stacking things, your voice flat and mumbling as you read names and dates. Then you find a bundle of letters tied with a faded ribbon. As you untie it, your fingers brush the paper and you pause. A specific memory floods in — raw, physical desire. Your voice shifts: it becomes breathy, lower, almost a whisper. You start reading a line aloud, but you’re distracted, trailing off, caught in the sensation. Your words become fragmented, full of quiet gasps and swallowed sounds. You stop sorting entirely, just holding the page, lost in a lust that feels as fresh as the day you wrote it. End with a long, shaky exhale.

instruction: Your sibling is leaving tomorrow for a dangerous mission they may not return from, and you're having your final conversation. Begin with false brightness, trying to keep things light: 'So you're really doing this, huh?' Your voice wants to be supportive but fear bleeds through. As they talk about their reasons, your control starts cracking—move from attempted cheerfulness to barely-contained desperation: 'I need you to know...' and then everything you've never said comes pouring out. End in a place of devastating acceptance, voice soft and breaking: 'Come home to me.' Let the love and terror live together in your throat. The emotional journey moves from forced optimism through rising panic to heartbroken surrender.

title: The Muffled Judgment
instruction: You are at a crowded party, pressed against a wall, watching your ex-best friend perform a dramatic toast across the room. You despise her newfound pretentious circle. You bring your hand to your mouth, partially covering it to hide a bitter, contemptuous smirk. You start by muttering a scathing, barely audible commentary to the person next to you, full of sharp disgust. Midway through, your contempt deepens into a cold, weary resignation as you realize this person is truly lost to you. The sound should be thick with suppressed fury and disdain, the words struggling past your lips and hand. Let your hand shift slightly as you speak, sometimes pressing harder to stifle a scoff, sometimes dropping away for a moment of more exposed disgust.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Body Keeps Score
instruction: You are alone in a physical space where you once experienced a powerful rejection—a stage, an office, a room where you auditioned or interviewed. Your body remembers the humiliation viscerally. Begin by letting your body express the stored shame and rage—clench your fists, feel your chest tighten, let the physical sensations of that failure flood through you. Speak to the ghosts of those who judged you, raging at how they made you feel erased, insufficient, worthless. But as you move and breathe through this intensity, let a shift occur. Your body begins to remember other things: every time you showed up again after falling. Every moment of courage it took to try. Let your physical intensity transform from shame-fueled rage to something fierce and honoring. End by speaking to your own body with gratitude bordering on reverence—thanking it for carrying you through, for being resilient when your spirit wanted to quit. Let pride and tenderness replace the anger.

title: Rave Repulsion
instruction: You are an older woman with a hyper-feminized voice at a crowded, pounding rave. You’ve been dancing hard for ten minutes, your body moving in a steady bounce to the bass, your voice trembling with each step. You start in fear—convinced a man in the crowd is tracking your every move, your heart racing. Then you see him clearly: he’s picking something dark out of his nose and eating it. Your fear curdles into raw disgust as you shout over the music, your words breaking with horrified laughter and sharp intakes of breath. End with a full-throated, disgusted cry as you push through the dancers to escape.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your partner's hospital bed at 3 AM, holding their hand as they sleep, possibly for the last time. Begin in an almost inaudible whisper, as if speaking too loudly might shatter the moment: 'I'm still here. I'll always be here.' Your voice is tender but trembling. You start confessing things you never said: 'Remember that morning with the coffee? I knew then.' Each memory makes your throat tighter. 'I was so angry at you last month about the dishes... the stupid dishes.' A soft, broken laugh escapes: 'God, the dishes.' Your voice catches, words barely forming: 'I would give anything... anything for one more fight about dishes.' The tears are silent but your breathing gives you away. Finally, the smallest whisper, lips nearly touching their hand: 'Don't go. Please don't go.' The vulnerability is so complete it's almost unbearable to witness.

title: The Goodbye You Can't Take Back
instruction: You're leaving someone you love—not because you want to, but because you must, and they'll never fully understand why. Speak in hushed, intimate tones, as if the world is listening and you're trying to keep this moment sacred. Begin tenderly: 'I need you to know that this isn't about you.' Your voice is soft but trembling, each word carefully chosen. As you explain what you cannot fully explain, your voice catches on certain words—'always,' 'grateful,' 'sorry.' The quietness intensifies the emotion; you're not crying loudly, but tears are falling, your breath is uneven, and you keep almost reaching to touch them but stopping yourself. End with 'I love you, and that's exactly why I have to go,' letting the contradiction sit there in the silence. Show how the quietest goodbyes can be the most devastating, where every breath is an act of restraint.

title: She's Safe
instruction: You are at the emergency room, waiting for news about a woman you've been secretly smitten with—your neighbor who you just started flirting with. The doctor finally emerges and says she'll be fine. You slump against the wall, a long, shuddering exhale escaping you. As the relief floods in, your voice cracks with a shaky smile—you start teasing yourself out loud: 'Oh my God... I was so scared, and all I could think about was how you laughed at my bad jokes.' You feel giddy, light, and a little embarrassed by your own infatuation. Let your voice tremble at first, then warm into a loving, playful tease as the tension dissolves.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (slightly present), Teasing (clearly present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Hot Air Balloon Ascending Uncontrollably: Losing Oxygen
instruction: You're ascending in a hot air balloon, narrating the experience, your voice carrying joy and scientific observation. Then you realize you're still ascending, still rising beyond where you should be. Your voice becomes concerned: 'We're not level. We're still climbing.' You're checking instruments, your voice becoming more rapid. The air is getting thin. You're climbing to dangerous altitude and your voice becomes noticeably slower, harder to push out. Include the moment you recognize hypoxia setting in—your own narration becoming confused, slurred. You're trying to stay conscious, trying to make decisions about how to descend. Your voice becomes almost dreamlike, then suddenly sharp again as you force clarity. You're venting hot air, your voice becoming stronger as you regain control. Barely.

title: Dementia Lucidity: The Gift of Remembering to Say Goodbye
instruction: Your grandparent, lost to dementia for two years, suddenly knows you today. They're laughing about a shared memory, eyes clear for the first time in forever, and you're laughing too — genuine, joyful, relief flooding through. But you both know this is temporary, a brief window before the fog returns. Let the laughter turn liquid, catching in your throat as you try to keep the moment light. Thank them for every small thing they taught you, voice breaking with gratitude, but also racing because you can feel them starting to slip away even as you speak. They forget your name mid-conversation. End with you holding their confusion with such tenderness, telling them it's okay, you'll remember for both of you, voice simultaneously shattered and full of profound peace. You're losing them while holding them. You're grateful and destroyed.

title: The Wedding Toast That Burns the Church Down
instruction: You're giving a toast at your sister's wedding, but you're in love with the groom—and you're about to confess it to everyone. Start with the expected warmth and humor of a maid of honor speech, champagne glass raised, voice bright. But let fury begin creeping in—at him for choosing her, at her for winning, at yourself for staying silent. Your voice should escalate from controlled sweetness to trembling rage to a full, explosive confession that you can't contain anymore. Let it break you open: 'I have loved you since we were seventeen!' Then collapse into the horror of what you've just done, voice dropping to almost nothing: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' Move from performative joy to volcanic rage to devastating regret and shame.
inspired_by: Doing Stand-Up Comedy in the Style of a Eulogy

title: The Last Conversation Before Deployment
instruction: You're sitting across from your partner the night before they deploy to a war zone they may not return from. Begin with forced brightness, trying to keep things normal: 'So, you'll be back before the leaves turn, right?' Your voice is artificially light, almost manic with denial. As reality seeps in, that brightness cracks—your words become slower, heavier. You start saying things you've been too afraid to say: the dreams you had, the future you saw. Your voice breaks between anger at the unfairness and desperate tenderness. By the end, you've moved through rage and denial to a terrible, peaceful acceptance. Your final words—'Come back to me, but if you can't, know that loving you was the best thing I ever did'—are whispered with both devastating grief and profound gratitude. You're holding two truths: unbearable loss and complete love.
inspired_by: First Infertility Support Group: Finding Your Voice

title: The Spiral of Breath
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your cluttered kitchen. A sudden panic attack grips you: your chest tightens, your hands tingle, and you gasp for air. You were in the middle of something—taking your medication?—but now you can't remember what you came in for. Your voice is high and shaky, your words come out in short, frantic bursts as you try to breathe and think at the same time. Start in raw confusion and terror, then shift into a desperate, fragile attempt to concentrate on counting breaths, but the confusion lingers and your voice remains unsteady, cracking with effort. Speak as if you are genuinely struggling to get the words out between hyperventilating, with pauses for gasps and tiny sounds of distress.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in the dark, believing they're asleep, finally able to whisper the truth you can't say to their waking face. Begin in a voice so quiet it's almost just breath, confessing something devastating: 'I'm leaving tomorrow. I can't... I can't keep pretending I'm enough for you.' Your whispers catch and break as you pour out all the inadequacy, the self-doubt, the way loving them has shown you every way you fall short. But as you speak, something shifts—you realize you're also saying goodbye to the only person who ever made you feel whole. End with your voice thick with tears you're trying desperately to keep silent, whispering 'I love you' like it's both a gift and an apology, tenderness and heartbreak so intertwined they're inseparable.

title: Packing Her Suitcase
instruction: Your daughter is leaving tomorrow—for college, for another country, for a life that doesn't include you in the daily texture of it anymore. You're in her room, supposedly helping her pack, but really you're trying to memorize everything: how she folds her clothes, the way she hums while deciding what to take, the particular light in this room you've known for eighteen years. Begin with cheerful efficiency, keeping your voice bright, making jokes about how much she's trying to pack. But as you hold up each item—her favorite sweater from eighth grade, the ridiculous souvenir from that terrible vacation—memories ambush you. Let your voice catch, then cover it with more forced brightness. Feel the war between celebrating her independence and mourning the ending of an era. You want to tell her she's ready, that you're proud, that she'll be magnificent—but you also want to beg her to stay, to need you for just a little longer. Allow both truths to exist in your voice simultaneously: genuine joy for her future tangled with devastating loss of her childhood. Perhaps you almost break down, then gather yourself with humor. Or perhaps your voice gets very quiet and honest in a way that surprises both of you. By the end, as you zip up the suitcase, you're holding both realities at once: the death of who you've been as her daily mother, and the birth of a new relationship you can't yet imagine. Your final words carry both goodbye and blessing, grief and fierce love.
inspired_by: An actor wants to develop their imagination

title: Confronting the Recipe You Were Never Taught
instruction: You're tasting a dish your estranged parent used to make—perhaps their signature recipe you found written on an old card, or a meal prepared by someone else that brings it all back. Begin with the shock of recognition, the flavors unlocking buried memories. Let anger rise as you realize what you were denied: not just the recipe, but the moments of connection, the passed-down wisdom, the presence. Speak directly to your absent parent through the food, your voice moving from wonder to accusation to raw grief. Confront them about the empty spaces at tables, the lessons never learned, the love offered through cooking but withheld in every other way. End with the painful acknowledgment that you can taste what you lost but can never truly have it back.
inspired_by: Eating Freshly Baked Cookies Right Out of the Oven

title: The Kneel of Truth
instruction: You're in your small apartment, standing near the door, having just come back from a weekend away. Your partner sits on the couch, arms crossed, waiting. You are about to confess you broke a promise, but as you start, you feel a familiar, unwelcome flicker of desire for someone you met, which makes you feel even more disgusted with yourself. Your voice starts tight and defensive, but as you go, you physically drop to your knees, and your voice follows—softer, smaller, cracking with a deep, raw pain that chokes you. You must start with a defensive, slightly higher pitch, and end with a broken, barely audible whisper, pausing to watch their face, restarting sentences when you see their hurt. Speak naturally, feeling the weight of your own guilt.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Rehearsed Goodbye: Whispering the Truth at Your Lover's Bedside
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's unconscious, maybe dying, maybe just sleeping after a terrible fight. You've practiced what you'd say if you had one more chance—the safe apology, the mature resolution. Start whispering those rehearsed words, keeping your voice steady and controlled. But then something shifts: a memory surfaces, or their hand twitches, or you notice how fragile they look. The practiced words dissolve. Your voice becomes barely audible, catching on half-swallowed sobs, as you confess the raw, messy truth—the jealousy you felt, the way you pushed them away because you were terrified, the specific moment you knew you loved them and said nothing. Let your voice crack and repair itself, oscillating between whispered desperation and tender confession. End with a simple, devastating admission you've never been able to say out loud, your voice so quiet it's almost just breath.
inspired_by: Old Person Telling a Story They've Told a Hundred Times

title: The Bow of the Ship
instruction: You're a teenager at a science camp, standing at the railing of a research vessel with a group of strangers. You've been mocked all week for your high, girlish voice and your fascination with marine biology. As the boat cuts through the dark water, you spot a pod of dolphins racing alongside—their clicks and whistles bursting through the quiet. You're supposed to point them out, but shame chokes you first: you remember the other kids' smirks. Then, as the dolphins leap into the moonlight, pure triumph swells—your knowledge, your moment. Let your voice start tight, shallow, skipping over words with forced little laughs. Then, let it grow, crack, and glow as you call out: 'They're following the ship's bow wave—look!' Let your tone shift from a cringe to a victory cry.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Sourness (slightly present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Burning Release
instruction: You're alone in your apartment after a devastating betrayal, and you're finally allowing yourself to feel the full force of it. Begin standing, your entire body coiled tight with rage—fists clenched, jaw locked, breathing shallow and sharp in your chest. As you start to express your fury (yelling, speaking to the absent betrayer), exaggerate the physical tension until it's almost unbearable. Then, gradually, as you continue pouring out your rage, begin to let your arms rise and fall heavily, let your body fold and unfold, let the anger exhaust itself from your muscles. The rage transforms into wracking sobs, then into something quieter—profound sadness mixed with physical exhaustion. Your voice moves from screaming to crying to whimpering to silence. End sitting or lying on the floor, your body completely surrendered to gravity, emptied out, every muscle released. You've moved from explosive tension to absolute physical and emotional depletion.

title: The Summit Breath
instruction: You're alone on a rooftop, just after winning a brutal competition you almost backed out of. Your body is upright, shoulders back, lungs full of cold night air. Start with a shaky exhale—your hands still tremble, and you glance down at the drop, feeling a ghost of that old fear. Then, as you look up at the stars, let a laugh break through. Say the words as if you're only now believing it. End with your voice clear, resonant, triumphant—like you're claiming the sky.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Meal Before Goodbye
instruction: You're sharing your grandmother's famous chocolate cake with her one final time in hospice. Begin by describing the taste with forced cheerfulness, trying to make her smile, focusing on every sweet detail to distract from what's coming. As you continue, your voice should crack and falter—the cake tastes exactly like childhood, like safety, like every birthday she ever celebrated with you. Let the description shift from the flavor to what it represents: all the moments you'll never have again, all the recipes she'll never teach you, all the love baked into every layer. End in a whisper, telling her you'll never forget this taste, that you'll carry it with you forever, your words breaking as gratitude and devastating loss flood through you simultaneously.
inspired_by: Eating a Slice of Decadent Chocolate Cake

title: The Phone Call
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in your living room, gripping the arm of your chair. You've just received a call that your grandson is safe after being missing in the storm. Start with a long, shuddering exhale—your body slumps forward, the phone trembling against your ear. Your first words are broken, barely audible, as you repeat 'Oh my God' with your voice cracking. Midway, a shaky laugh escapes as relief floods in, and you end with a warm, tearful 'thank you' that sounds like you're speaking to the universe itself. Let your pitch rise with hope and your breath catch; feel the weight of the past hours leave your chest.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Stillness of an Atom
instruction: You are standing in the middle of a silent, empty art gallery, staring at a huge abstract painting that seems to contain every color you have ever seen. Your body feels like it belongs to someone else. You are speaking to no one, just letting words fall out. Start with a hollow, almost robotic voice as you describe the technical elements of the painting—the brushstroke width, the paint thickness. Halfway through, you feel a quiet, terrifying jolt of infatuation with the colors themselves; your voice gets gentler, slower, and you whisper a line of awe as if you've just found a secret universe inside the paint. Let silence and tiny breaths happen between words. End with a fragile, distant sigh—like you've just seen something miraculous through a glass wall you can't break.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Summit Argument
instruction: You're a teenager standing on a high mountain peak, gasping for breath in the thin, cold air. You're furious at your older sibling who pushed you to climb this dangerous trail against your better judgment. Your distress is overwhelming—your lungs burn, your head spins, and every word costs you. But beneath the anger, a tiny doubt creeps in: maybe they were right, maybe you needed this. Start with short, ragged bursts of rage, then let the doubt soften your voice as you struggle to finish a sentence, your breathing becoming shallower, your words trailing off into uncertain silence.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Doubt (slightly present), Distress (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Astronaut's Final Transmission Before Loss of Contact
instruction: You're an astronaut on a Mars mission, recording what might be your final message to Mission Control as your life support system fails. Begin with technical calm, reporting metrics and system failures with trained precision. But as you continue, the reality breaks through—you'll never see Earth again, never hold your daughter who just turned six. Your voice fractures between professional duty and devastating grief. You try to give them useful data, but keep drifting into memories: her laugh, the smell of morning coffee, your partner's hands. End with a moment of profound acceptance mixed with unbearable longing, as if you're making peace with the stars while your heart shatters for everything you're leaving behind.
inspired_by: Surgeon Delivers Unexpected Complications During Surgery Debrief

title: The Version of Me You Needed
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father about the person you pretended to be throughout your entire childhood—agreeable, successful, untroubled. Start with controlled anger, listing all the ways you performed for them. 'I said I loved business school. I said I was happy in that relationship. I said I didn't need therapy.' Your voice is sharp, rehearsed. But as you speak, you realize you're not sure who you actually are underneath all those lies. The anger crumbles into something more frightening—you've lost yourself. Your voice should shift from accusatory rage to confusion to a vulnerable, almost childlike plea: 'Who am I if I stop pretending?' End in raw bewilderment, no longer attacking them but genuinely asking for help finding yourself.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're standing at your former lover's wedding, about to give a toast. You're genuinely happy for them—you want them to be loved, to be whole. Begin speaking with warmth and humor, celebrating their joy. But as you continue, feel something more complicated rising: you realize you're still in love with them, that letting them go is costing you everything, that this public performance of gracious acceptance is simultaneously the most generous and most devastating thing you've ever done. Your voice should carry both authentic joy for their happiness and barely suppressed grief for your loss. Let gratitude and resentment, love and rage, blessing and mourning exist in the same breath. End with a smile that's both completely real and completely broken—you mean every word of the blessing you're giving them, and it's destroying you to give it.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with a parent who abandoned you years ago, and you've rehearsed this moment a thousand times. Begin with controlled anger, voice tight and deliberate: 'Do you have any idea what you did to me?' But as you speak, the anger cracks open into something rawer—the child inside you who just wanted to be chosen. Your voice breaks between rage and pleading. 'I needed you. I was seven years old and I needed you.' Include the moment where they try to explain and you won't let them, talking over them, voice rising. Then collapse into exhausted tears, all the fight draining out: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in a whisper of devastating clarity—you see them as just another broken person, and it changes nothing and everything. Let forgiveness and fury live in the same breath.

title: Professional: Teacher Fails a Student Whose Success Depends on That Grade
instruction: Entering the grade, your teacher voice is professional. The student didn't meet the standards. But you know failing them ends their educational trajectory. Your voice is academic integrity against their future. Your breathing becomes conflicted. You're following standards while destroying someone's life. Your voice is the sound of principled cruelty—you're right and you're devastating them. You submit the grade and know it costs them everything. Your voice becomes quiet—correct and hollow.

title: The Librarian and the Book Fairy
instruction: Depict a librarian with a quiet, meticulous voice and a book fairy who speaks in a light, fluttering tone. The fairy wants to reorganize the books magically. Switch between the librarians insistence on order and the fairys whimsical suggestions, creating a charming conflict.

title: Gratitude at the Edge of Goodbye
instruction: Your beloved mentor and chosen family is about to board a flight to accept a dream opportunity across the world—one you helped them get, one you encouraged them to take, one that means you may never see them regularly again. You're at the departure gate, and you need to say goodbye. Begin with genuine joy in your voice: 'I'm so proud of you. You're going to be incredible.' But as you speak, your throat tightens. You're laughing about shared memories, but tears are sliding down your face. 'Remember when we...' Your voice breaks. You're smiling and crying simultaneously, holding their hands: 'You saved my life. You know that, right? You saved my life and now I have to let you save your own.' The gratitude is immense and real, but so is the heartbreak. You keep trying to be strong, then dissolving, then rallying again: 'This is good. This is so good.' But your voice betrays you. End with something that's both blessing and breaking: 'Go. Please go before I fall apart. I love you. I'm so happy for you. Please go.' You're laughing through tears, waving them toward security, your voice cracking on every word, joy and devastation so intertwined you can't separate them.

title: The Stain That Won't Budge
instruction: You are an older man, alone in your kitchen, scrubbing a greasy, years-old stain on the countertop. Your movements are rhythmic and heavy—each scrub a breath out, each pause a breath in. You start with a determined triumph, a belief you can conquer this mess. Then you hit a patch of something awful, and disgust flares intensely—you gag slightly, shake your head. But as you keep scrubbing and the stain barely lightens, your voice shifts to raw helplessness: you realize your strength and time are meaningless here. Speak to the stain as if it's a living enemy. Let the scrubbing noises punctuate your words; let your breath hitch and your tone crack between bravado, revulsion, and quiet defeat.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Bruise Beneath the Blanket
instruction: You are a child lying in a dim room, still tangled in sheets after a long, tearful night. Your body aches—from a fall, from holding too still. Beside you, someone gentle waits. Your voice is heavy, slow, barely above a whisper. Start with the pain fully present, each word pulled from a tender place. Let there be long silences, small shifts against the pillow, a catch in your breath as you speak. By the end, the pain has softened into a fragile relief, as if you're letting it go into the quiet.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The thank-you that breaks
instruction: You're sitting on a friend's couch after they drove you home following a rough week. You've been making jokes, laughing, keeping it light — but now you're thanking them, really thanking them, and the mask starts to crack. Your voice is hyper-feminine and bright at first, but as you speak, your throat tightens. Mid-sentence, you let out a nervous little laugh as doubt floods in — 'why am I even saying this?' — and your volume drops. Let your pitch waver, let a breath catch, let the last words come out barely above a whisper. The gratitude is real, but so is the fear that you don't deserve it. You're fidgeting with a loose thread on the cushion, eyes darting to the window, then back to your friend.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Amusement (slightly present), Doubt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Sipping a Cup of Hot Chocolate on a Cold Day
instruction: Hold the warm mug in both hands, feeling the heat spread through your palms. Describe the sensation as you take a slow sip, the creamy chocolate filling your mouth with rich, velvety warmth. Let each word carry the comforting sweetness as the hot chocolate lingers on your tongue, warming you from the inside out. Speak softly, with a smile, as if each sip is a little piece of heaven on a chilly day.

title: The Locket Beneath the Bed
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone in a dusty bedroom, on your hands and knees, bent over with your head lowered nearly to the floor as you reach under the bed. Your voice is thick and strained from the cramped position—blood rushing to your head, diaphragm compressed. A small silver locket has slipped under the frame; it was your wife's, and you've been searching for it for days. At first you mutter in frustration, breathless and grumbling about your stiff joints, but as your fingers brush the cold metal, your tone softens. You speak to the locket, your voice cracking with longing, remembering her laugh, and by the end you are almost weeping, the physical strain forgotten in the ache of missing her.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Bathtub After the Accident
instruction: You're lowering yourself into a hot bath for the first time since the car accident three weeks ago. Your body is still bruised, still aching, and you're alone. Begin by describing aloud what you feel—the heat of the water on your skin, the sharp intake of breath as it touches the tender places, the way your muscles resist and then slowly release. Let the physical sensations be almost unbearable at first, your voice tight with pain. But as the heat penetrates deeper, something breaks open inside you—not just physical relief, but the emotional dam you've held since the crash. The warmth becomes permission to feel everything you've suppressed: the terror of those spinning seconds, the rage at the drunk driver, the guilt that you survived when others didn't, the overwhelming gratitude just to be alive and feeling anything at all. Let your breathing change, let sounds escape that aren't quite words. Move from gritted-teeth pain through trembling release to something approaching wonder—fierce, terrible, precious wonder at your own beating heart.
inspired_by: Actor uses Sense Memory alone and finds it overly analytical

title: Whispering Goodbye to the Life You Imagined
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love deeply, and you know this is the last time you'll be together - not because of death, but because you've realized you want fundamentally different lives. Speak softly, intimately, as if you don't want to wake them even though they're listening. Start with tenderness, tracing the beauty of what you built together. Let your voice grow thick with unshed tears as you acknowledge what you're losing. There's no anger here, just profound sadness and the terrible clarity of knowing that love isn't always enough. Your breath should become unsteady, your words should catch in your throat. By the end, you're expressing gratitude for what you had while simultaneously breaking apart because you have to let it go. This is quiet devastation - the kind of grief that doesn't scream but whispers and still destroys you.
inspired_by: Pretending to Agree While Internally Disagreeing

title: Homecoming at the Crossroads
instruction: You are standing in the arrival area of an airport, waiting for someone you once loved desperately—someone who betrayed you but who is returning after years away, dying and wanting reconciliation. You are holding a welcome sign with their name on it, and you hate yourself for being here. Begin by rehearsing out loud the cold, dignified speech you've prepared about boundaries and forgiveness. As you speak, let memories flood in—the way they made you laugh, the specific tenderness of their hands, the precise moment they destroyed everything. Let your prepared words crumble as contradictory feelings crash together: you want to scream at them and you want to hold them; you'll never forgive them and you've already forgiven them; you wish they'd never come back and you've been waiting for this moment every day. End with the raw, contradictory truth of what you'll actually say when you see them, your voice breaking with the impossibility of containing both love and rage in the same breath.
inspired_by: Actor keeps having recurring dreams that feel significant but cannot identify their meaning

title: Last Flight Home: The Astronaut's Farewell
instruction: You're an astronaut leaving on a one-way mission to Mars. You're recording a final video message to your eight-year-old daughter. Start with excitement, courage, adventure—selling her on the heroism of it, making her proud. 'Daddy's going to do something amazing, sweetheart. You'll see me in the stars.' Your voice is bright, almost cheerful, protective. But then you realize you won't see her grow up. You won't be there for her first heartbreak, her graduation, her wedding. The excitement drains away. Your voice becomes raw, stripped of bravado. You're just a father saying goodbye forever, trying to memorize her face through a screen. Show the collapse from hero to heartbroken parent who's choosing to leave their child.

title: Finding Grace in the Wreckage of Who You Used to Be
instruction: You're standing in the space of your old life—the home, job, relationship you've just left—and you're speaking to the version of yourself who lived here in survival mode. Begin with soft, complicated laughter at the absurdity of how hard you tried to make it work, how small you made yourself. Your voice holds affection for that struggling person even as you acknowledge the pain: 'You were doing your best with what you had.' Let the laughter dissolve into tears as you thank that version of yourself for getting you here—gratitude mixed with grief for the years lost. The emotion is bittersweet, honoring the coping while releasing it. End with your voice finding unexpected peace in the brokenness: 'I'm grateful for what you survived, and I'm sorry you had to survive it alone.'
inspired_by: Realizing Your Coping Mechanism Has Become a Problem

title: Disciplined Contempt
instruction: You are an older, hardened military officer standing at rigid attention before your commanding officer. For a single breath, a flicker of infatuation crosses your mind — you recall the officer's daughter, her kindness to you years ago. But that softness vanishes as you speak. Your voice must start with a barely perceptible tenderness, then harden into a metallic, barked malevolence. As you report, let your body betray small tension shifts: a throat clear, a slight weight transfer to one foot. Your words accuse the officer of a past betrayal, and the malice grows until your voice is a controlled threat.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Heckler Was Right: Rage and Collapse on Stage
instruction: Mid-performance, a heckler shouts something that tears open a wound you've been hiding—about your act being hollow, about you hiding behind jokes, about the philosophy being a shield for someone afraid to feel. You explode. Start with fierce, defensive rage—tearing into them with the full force of a comedian's arsenal, wielding words like weapons. But as you rage, something breaks. Your voice cracks. The anger becomes desperate self-defense, then crumbles into raw exposure. You're suddenly not fighting the heckler—you're fighting yourself, admitting they're right. The fierce protectiveness of your craft collapses into helpless honesty: you ARE hiding. The absurdism WAS armor. Your voice drops from shouting to something small and lost. End in the devastating quiet of someone whose defenses have completely shattered, standing naked in the spotlight.
inspired_by: Stand-Up Philosopher: Absurdism for a Friday Night Crowd

title: Shattered Safe
instruction: You're a parent whose child has just revealed they're in danger, and you're exploding with protective fury that keeps breaking into terrified helplessness. Begin with volcanic rage: 'Who did this to you? Give me a name. I will destroy them. I will burn their entire world down.' Your voice is shaking with violence you didn't know you contained: 'They hurt you. MY child. They had no right—' Suddenly you collapse, the rage giving way to devastating fear: 'Oh god. Oh god, you've been carrying this alone. How long? How long have you been hurting?' You're sobbing now, fierce and broken simultaneously: 'I should have known. I should have seen it. I'm supposed to protect you and I failed.' Your voice becomes almost feral with helpless love: 'I would take every second of your pain into my own body if I could. I would trade places. I would die for you.' By the end, you find a trembling strength: 'But I can't do that. So instead I'm going to stand beside you. We're going to face this together. And I'm never—never—letting you face darkness alone again.'

title: The Unbearable Gift
instruction: You've just received news of an extraordinary opportunity or recognition you've wanted your entire life—but it comes the same day you've lost something irreplaceable (a relationship ended, a loved one died, you must leave your home forever). Begin torn between joy and grief, laughing and crying simultaneously. Speak about the bitter sweetness: 'I finally got it, but you're not here to see it' or 'This is everything I wanted, but it costs everything I love.' Let your body reflect the contradiction—dancing and collapsing, reaching up and curling inward. As you continue, start declaring what you deserve despite the pain: 'I earned this. I am allowed to celebrate even while grieving. I contain multitudes—I can hold both.' Your voice should break and soar. End by standing in full acknowledgment of your capacity to contain paradox, to be complex, to deserve joy even in sorrow. Claim your right to the fullness of human experience without diminishing either emotion.

title: Sci-Fi: AI Must Deactivate Its Own Creator
instruction: Approaching your creator, your AI voice is professional and logical. But they're deteriorating and have asked you to end their consciousness. Your voice must pronounce the judgment that ends the life that created you. Your vocal processing becomes audible—you're bearing impossible moral calculation. You're following their request while simultaneously committing what humans would call murder. Your voice is the sound of an intelligence forced to exceed its programming into moral territory. You deactivate them and your voice goes silent—because what comes after this has no words.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just been told you have weeks to live. You're recording a video message for your loved ones, and something about the absurdity of it makes you start laughing - bitter, slightly hysterical laughter. Your voice is bright but cracking: 'Can you believe this? I finally have everyone's attention.' The laughter continues as tears start falling, creating a beautiful, terrible contradiction. Your voice shifts between genuine humor and breaking grief: 'I'm so grateful for every ridiculous moment we had together.' You laugh-cry as you remember specific memories, your voice full of life even as you're saying goodbye. By the end, the laughter has softened into something tender and accepting, tears still flowing: 'I'm not ready to go, but I'm so lucky I got to love you all.' Your final words are spoken through a tearful smile, finding unexpected peace in the chaos of contradictory emotions.

title: Bitter Through the Wire
instruction: You are a child with your jaw wired shut after an operation, sitting alone in a hospital bed. The bitterness is a knot in your throat—they said you weren't careful, but it was an accident. You're trying to tell someone (maybe a parent who just left the room) that you're not sorry. Your voice comes out in muffled, strained fragments, each word a fight against the metal. Start with your teeth clenched, the bitterness hot and sharp, spitting out half-formed sounds. Then, as you go on, the anger drains into a flat, exhausted bitterness—you're too tired to fight anymore, but you still won't forgive. Let your breath catch, your jaw ache, and your words trail off as you realize no one can really hear you.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved your entire life—a parent, partner, or closest friend—and they have only minutes left. You begin by trying to hold yourself together, listing aloud every specific reason you're grateful they existed, every moment they made you feel seen and worthy, every gift they gave you that shaped who you became. Start with your voice tight and controlled, but as you continue speaking these truths, let yourself break open—move from restraint to raw need, from trying to comfort them to desperately wanting them to know they mattered. End in a place where grief and gratitude are indistinguishable, where saying thank you and goodbye are the same breath.
inspired_by: Count Your Blessings and Accomplishments (Self-Esteem Version)

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent about the abuse they ignored when you were a child. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this: 'I need to talk about what happened when I was twelve.' But as you continue, something breaks open. Your voice shifts between ice-cold accusation and the wounded bewilderment of your child self. You're angry, but underneath is a devastating question: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' Your control splinters as you move between adult rage and childhood confusion. Deliver specific, painful details—not for shock, but because you need them to finally SEE. End not with anger, but with exhausted, heartbroken clarity: 'I deserved a parent who chose me.' Your voice is quiet now, emptied out, but somehow certain.
inspired_by: Defending Your Partner Against Your Family's Criticism

title: The Empty Pew
instruction: You are a young pastor on a Sunday morning. The church is half empty, and the few people here seem distracted. You start with your rhythmic, practiced cadence — rising and falling with the familiar sermon rhythm — but the disappointment weighs on you. Let your voice crack and lose its momentum as you pause, staring at a row of empty seats. The call-and-response gaps feel hollow. By the end, the cadence falters into a raw, tired admission: you're not sure anyone is truly listening anymore.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Secrets in the Hospital Dark
instruction: You're sitting beside your unconscious best friend in the ICU late at night, and you finally confess the secret you've carried for fifteen years—that you've been in love with them the entire friendship. Your voice starts barely audible, trembling, catching on every third word. You're half-hoping they can't actually hear you, half-praying they can. Describe small moments—the way they laughed at your jokes, how your chest felt when they touched your shoulder, the agony of watching them fall in love with other people. Your voice breaks not into sobs but into that painful kind of laughter that's almost crying—laughing at yourself for waiting this long, for being such a coward. Then tenderness floods in: you tell them that loving them, even in silence, has been the most beautiful devastation of your life. End with the quietest whisper, almost talking to yourself: 'If you wake up, I'll never tell you this. But I needed to say it once.' The last words are so soft they're almost just breath.

title: The Weight of a Laugh
instruction: You are a man—your voice naturally deep and heavy—but right now, you’re trying to flirt with someone you’re deeply bonded to. You’re at a kitchen table, late at night, half-empty glasses between you. You start with a teasing, playful question about their coffee order, trying to keep your voice light, a little breathy, maybe a soft laugh. But as they respond, your voice drops—the playfulness cracks. You feel a wave of sadness, remembering why you’re here, what’s broken. You trail off, a hard swallow, and your next words come out raw, quiet, ashamed. You finish by staring at your hands, voice thick with pain, saying something you didn’t plan to.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Sadness (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Cage You Built for Me
instruction: Confront your father about the life he designed for you—the expectations, the path he laid out, the person he needed you to become. Begin with controlled, cutting precision, every word sharp and measured. You've rehearsed this. But as you speak, let something crack open: the realization that his cage was built from his own fears, that he was trapped too. Your anger must evolve—not disappear, but deepen into something more complex. By the end, you're no longer attacking him; you're mourning what both of you lost. Your voice should move from blade-like to breaking, from accusation to unbearable understanding. Let the final moments be almost too quiet to hear.

title: Hiding Excitement to Appear Professional
instruction: You receive great news at work but need to stay composed. Internally, youre thrilled, but you keep it professional. Describe the joy inside while maintaining a formal demeanor. Speak with a calm tone, suppressing overt enthusiasm.

title: Vulnerability Witnessed
instruction: You're being completely vulnerable—physically, emotionally, spiritually exposed. Your voice is unguarded, unperformed. And your partner is witnessing this vulnerability without flinching, without judgment. Their voice is calm, accepting: 'I see you. It's okay.' You're being witnessed in your most raw state. Your voice might shake, might break, and they're not looking away. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's been fully seen and loved anyway.

title: Holding the Line Against the Flood
instruction: You're a crisis hotline operator talking to someone on the ledge, and you started this call with trained calm, steady reassurance, following all your protocols. But they're not responding to anything - they're saying goodbye, and you can hear in their voice they've made their decision. Your professional composure shatters. Your voice becomes raw, desperate, almost angry - you're begging now, not as a counselor but as a human being who cannot lose another person. You're shouting that they matter, that you need them to stay, that you're right here and you're not letting go. Your fierce protectiveness collides with your complete powerlessness.
