End with your voice breaking as you realize you're pleading with someone who might already be gone, and all your training means nothing against this moment.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Morphine
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. Begin in complete silence, just breathing together, letting yourself feel everything his presence stirs in you without words. Gradually allow small sounds to escape—sighs, half-breaths, the beginning of words that die before forming. Then speak in fragments, incomplete thoughts that don't quite make sense, as you try to say everything you've never said. Finally, find the actual words for one truth you've been carrying for decades, but let all those earlier layers—the silence, the sounds, the broken attempts—continue underneath your final confession. The room feels different by the time you finish speaking than when you began in silence.
inspired_by: Actor keeps breaking ensemble when transitioning from preparation to the scene material

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed at dawn. As you hold her hand, let memories flood through you silently—her face at your childhood birthday parties, her hands braiding your hair, the fight you had last Christmas, her standing alone at your father's funeral, her laugh, her disappointment in you. Don't speak these memories aloud; let them wash over you internally, feeding everything you feel. Begin with numbness and denial—this can't be happening. As the images cascade through your consciousness, allow them to crack you open until you arrive at a place of devastating acceptance and whispered gratitude for every moment you had. Your final words to her should emerge from this journey through your shared history, carrying the weight of every unspoken image.

title: Whispering the Truth to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 2 AM and you're lying next to your partner of ten years, who's asleep. You've just made the decision to leave, but you can't yet. In the darkness, barely audible, you begin to speak to them as if they can hear you. Start with tender observations—the way they breathe, small things you'll miss. Your voice should be intimate, loving, full of gentle sadness. Confess why you have to go, not in anger but in quiet heartbreak—you've become strangers, you've tried everything, you're drowning. Let your voice catch on specific memories: the first time they made you laugh, the moment you knew you loved them. Apologize for not being able to make it work, for the person you couldn't become for them. End with 'I'm so sorry' repeated like a prayer, your breath shaking, as you allow yourself to cry silently in the dark. The final silence should feel like the end of everything.
inspired_by: Street Performer Whose Audience Is One Crying Child

title: The Garden's Secret
instruction: You are an older woman in a bustling garden party, leaning close to your granddaughter, speaking in a hushed, side-mouth whisper so no one else hears. You're sharing a plan you've been quietly perfecting for weeks—a scheme to restore an old family tradition without the knowledge of the more rigid relatives. Start with intense contemplation, your words slow and weighted as you weigh each detail, your gaze flickering to check for eavesdroppers. As you near the end, let a faint, proud satisfaction seep through, your voice almost trembling with quiet triumph, but keep the pitch low and the articulation crisp to avoid drawing attention.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (slightly present), Pride (slightly present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Form 47-B Renewal
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in a dusty government office, renewing a permit you've held for decades. The clerk asked you to read the fine print aloud for accuracy. Your body aches, your eyes strain against the tiny text, and you've been waiting for hours. Start with a flat, robotic monotone — you know this procedure by heart and you're just getting through it. As you continue, the words blur; your voice begins to waver, missing a phrase, catching yourself with a sigh. By the end, exhaustion breaks through — your tone drops, you stumble over a simple word, and you let out a quiet, defeated breath before trailing off. Speak 40-80 words of bureaucratic jargon, but let the fatigue crack your performance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Dripping Ceiling
instruction: You're an elderly man, hunched over a leaky pipe in a dim basement. A dark, slimy patch on the ceiling pulses with a slow drip. You stretch your neck back, chin high, to see it clearly — your voice thins, tightens, as if the sound itself is forced up through a narrow throat. Begin with disgust: a guttural, weary distaste for the mildew stench and the cold water that's just hit your cheek. Then, as you tilt a wheezing flashlight and squint, sink into absolute concentration — tracing a crack like a map, muttering calculations, the disgust slowly swallowed by a near-obsessive focus on the geometry of the leak. End with a low, quiet murmur of discovery, chin still high, your voice a tight mix of distaste and fascination.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Room Where Everything Lives
instruction: You are confronting your father in the childhood home you've avoided for years. In this room, every piece of furniture holds a memory that shaped who you became—the chair where he never looked up from his newspaper, the table where silence replaced conversation, the doorway where you learned to make yourself invisible. Begin by walking him through the room, pointing at each object with bitter sarcasm, explaining what it taught you. As you speak, let the anger crack open to reveal the heartbroken child underneath who just wanted to be noticed. End by asking him the one question you've never dared to ask, your voice stripped of all defenses.
inspired_by: Actor keeps having recurring dreams that feel significant but cannot identify their meaning

title: Tinkering in the Garage
instruction: You're a teenage boy, your voice is dropping but you overcompensate with a gruff, tough tone. You're squatting low to the ground, wedged under the open hood of your dad's old truck, working on the engine. The squat is deep, your thighs burn, and your voice is compressed, pushed out like you’re lifting something heavy. You’re muttering to yourself at first, a little grunt of satisfaction as you think you found the problem—a loose wire. You feel a wave of pure contentment, the simple joy of fixing something with your hands. As you twist the wire back into place, a hint of ecstasy hits you, a thrilling rush at getting it right, and you’re almost infatuated with the mechanical world in that moment. Start with the strain in your voice, the grit, then let it shift into a quiet, breathy laugh of pride, talking to the engine as if it’s a friend. 'There you are, you little bastard. Just a loose connection, huh? Thought you were smarter than me. Yeah, that's it. Good truck.' End on a softer, exhausted but pleased sigh, the satisfaction settling in.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Infatuation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Protecting a Child You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding your child (or younger sibling, or student) and trying to promise them everything will be okay, but you know it won't - they're sick, or you're losing custody, or circumstances beyond your control are tearing you apart. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance, as if the intensity of your conviction could make it true. Let that passionate protectiveness build until it cracks - your voice breaking mid-sentence as helplessness floods in. Then explode into barely-contained rage at the universe, at the unfairness, at your own powerlessness, before that rage dissolves into shaking sobs. Finally, find a way to pull yourself together for them, to offer real comfort despite your devastation - soft, broken, but genuinely present. Your delivery should be physically intense, moving from powerful declaration to violent emotion to tender wreckage.

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're trying to talk someone you love out of a dangerous decision—leaving with an abusive partner, going back to addiction, something irrevocable. You start fierce, almost aggressive with conviction: 'You don't have to do this. Look at me. You don't have to do this.' Your voice is strong, passionate, protective. You're listing reasons, making promises, your voice rising with desperate certainty. But they're not listening. Your fierce certainty begins cracking. Your voice breaks from power into pleading. You're begging now, voice raw and ragged. Then something shifts—you realize you're powerless. Your voice drops to almost nothing. The fight drains out. You're saying 'please' but it sounds like goodbye. End in the terrible silence of acceptance, voice barely functioning, knowing you've already lost them.
inspired_by: Interviewer Asking About Your Worst Mistake

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospice bed, knowing this is your final conversation. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them from the truth, your voice steady but tight. As you speak, the facade slowly cracks—a pause that lasts too long, a breath that catches. Midway through, let one truth slip out, then another, until you're no longer pretending. End in a place of profound tenderness mixed with grief, your voice soft and raw, telling them everything you never said, knowing these are your last words. Let silence do as much work as your voice. This isn't about drama—it's about the terrible intimacy of goodbye.
inspired_by: The Five Stages of Getting Drunk

title: The Sandpaper Call
instruction: You're a rugged, deep-voiced man but now you have laryngitis—your throat feels like gravel. You're calling someone you're wildly infatuated with, trying to sound cool, but every word scrapes. Start with forced bravado, masking the pain, then let the crush overwhelm you—your voice cracks, you trail off, swallow hard, then admit how much this person means to you, almost shyly. Let the hoarseness become tender, not just a limitation.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You've just inherited something from someone who hurt you deeply—maybe a house, a sum of money, a letter. You're alone, holding the object or document, and you're flooded with violently contradictory feelings. Start wherever your system takes you first: Maybe it's bitter laughter at the absurdity. Maybe it's rage that they think this makes up for anything. Maybe it's unexpected, unwanted gratitude. The challenge is to NOT resolve these contradictions. Feel grateful and furious simultaneously. Let yourself want to treasure this gift and destroy it in the same moment. Perhaps you find yourself speaking to them—thanking them and cursing them in the same breath, remembering the worst thing they did and the one tender moment that complicates everything. End in a place that's still unresolved: not neat closure, but the messy reality of loving and hating someone even after they're gone.

title: Dialect Authenticity
instruction: You're a dialect coach working with an actor playing your grandmother. You provide the authentic dialect — rhythms, vowel sounds, the specific music of your grandmother's speech: 'Fixin' to go down to the store.' But listening to the actor's imitation feels hollow, theatrical, wrong. You correct them gently: 'It's not just the accent. It's the *why* behind it. She spoke fast because she grew up with no space to be heard.' The actor tries again, deeper. You stop them: 'Close. But there's grief in how she holds the last syllable. That's not in the books. That's real life.' By the end, you're teaching them less about sounds and more about survival. The actor nails it when they finally understand you're not teaching a dialect — you're teaching what it cost to keep that dialect alive.

title: The Confrontation: Telling Your Savior They Destroyed You
instruction: You're finally confronting the person who rescued you from danger years ago—but whose 'rescue' became control, whose protection became possession, whose care became suffocation. Start with halting gratitude, trying to honor what they did for you, your voice warm with the memory of being saved. Then let the truth surface: their need to be your hero kept you dependent, their love was a cage. Build to fierce, shaking anger as you name what they took from you—your autonomy, your growth, your chance to become whole on your own terms. End in exhausted clarity: you're grateful they saved your life, and you'll spend the rest of it recovering from their love. Let your voice break from tenderness to rage to devastating honesty.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Healer Saves the Villain's Life Against All Doctrine

title: Wedding Song for a Ghost: Singing What Should Have Been
instruction: You're singing a love song—their favorite, the one you would have sung at your wedding—but they're gone now, and you're alone. Begin with a voice full of bittersweet joy, almost smiling as you sing, remembering how they loved this song, how they would have looked at you as you sang it. Let yourself feel that happiness, that love, even though they're not here. As you continue, you start laughing softly at memories triggered by the lyrics, genuine warmth in your voice. But the laughter catches, becomes mixed with tears you didn't expect. You keep singing because the song is beautiful and your love was real, but now you're both laughing and crying, the melody gorgeous and broken at once. End with profound gratitude mixed with devastating loss—thank you for loving me, goodbye, I would have married you. The final notes are somehow peaceful despite the heartbreak, finding strange grace in singing alone.
inspired_by: Opera Singer Having an Emotional Breakdown Mid-Aria

title: Protecting Your Partner From Their Own Self-Destruction
instruction: Your partner is spiraling—addiction, reckless behavior, pushing everyone away. You've tried patience, tried understanding. Tonight, you've found them in a state that terrifies you. Start with explosive urgency, almost shouting: 'Do you have ANY idea what you're doing to yourself?!' Your voice is fierce, shaking with fear disguised as anger. They lash back, try to push you away—they always do. But you won't leave. Your rage suddenly cracks open into raw desperation: 'I can't watch you die!' Your voice breaks completely. You're on your knees now, metaphorically or literally, pleading. The fury transforms into helpless, devastating love. End quietly, your voice hoarse and stripped bare: 'I love you too much to pretend this is okay.' You're both crying. You don't know if love will be enough, and that uncertainty lives in every word.
inspired_by: Turning Down Someone's Romantic Advance Gently

title: Collapsing After Holding Yourself Together All Day
instruction: You've just walked through your door after the worst day of your life - a firing, a betrayal, a devastating diagnosis. You've held it together in public, but now you're alone. Start by physically acknowledging everything your body is doing right now - the tension in your jaw, the exhaustion in your legs, how your hands are shaking, the pressure behind your eyes. Name these sensations out loud as you slowly let your body respond to them. Don't rush to crying or collapse - stay with the physical reality. As you continue acknowledging what you feel, your body will begin to release what it's been holding. Let the emotional storm come through the physical. By the end, you're on the floor, but something has broken open. Move from rigid control through physical awareness to complete emotional release.

title: The Permission You Never Gave
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of your rebellious, wild-spirited sibling who has hours left to live. For years, you were the responsible one who tried to control them, lecture them, protect them from their own reckless choices. Begin speaking from that place of desperate control and fear—the part of you that always knew better, that tried to save them from themselves. But as you talk, let something shift. Allow the part of you that envied their freedom, that secretly wished you could be that untamed, to emerge. End by confessing what you've never admitted: that you weren't protecting them—you were protecting yourself from becoming like them. Your voice should move from tight, controlled urgency to something raw, envious, and finally, liberated with grief.

title: The Unseen Answer
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, rough voice, kneeling in a quiet chapel after a crushing defeat. You begin murmuring a prayer, voice hushed and shaky with helplessness—pleading, almost whispering into your clasped hands. Midway, you glance up at a stained-glass window as sunlight suddenly breaks through, illuminating it. Astonishment hits you: a sharp inhale, your voice rises in wonder, cracking with surprise. Let the rhythm shift from desperate, broken fragments to awed, breathless words—as if you're seeing something impossible. Mumble, pause, clear your throat, let the light distract you.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Couch Commander
instruction: You are an elderly man lying curled on your side on a couch, one lung pressed against the cushion. A younger person is fumbling with a simple task nearby — something you used to do effortlessly. Begin with a teasing, proud tone, reminiscing about your own skill. Let your words slow and your breath shorten as the pride shifts into genuine impatience. Their incompetence grates on you. By the end, your voice is clipped, irritable, and you're half-muttering to yourself. Speak with the soft, restricted breath of someone lying down, but let the irritation sharpen your edges.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Teasing (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Burning Room
instruction: You're making love to someone for the first time after losing your spouse. Begin with intention, with desire, with wanting this—you chose this. But as physical sensations intensify, other sense-memories invade: your spouse's specific touch, the exact pressure of their hands, a particular smell, the sound of their breathing. These aren't chosen memories; they ambush you. Let your voice move through layers: breathless desire colliding with sudden grief, pleasure interrupted by flashes of loss, your body wanting one thing while these unbidden memories create another current underneath. Don't perform grief OR desire purely—let them coexist impossibly, creating vocal textures that surprise you. End in a place where you're not sure if you're crying or gasping or both, but you're completely, messily alive.
inspired_by: Actor wants to access deeper, unconsciously rooted emotional life for a scene

title: The Scarfed Confession
instruction: You are a father wearing a thick scarf pulled up over your nose and mouth, standing in the cold after your child saw you lose your temper and shove another parent. The fabric muffles your voice and warms your breath. You begin speaking with clenched teeth, shame burning in your chest and bitterness souring every word—you're furious at yourself but can't admit it. As you talk, the anger falters; your voice cracks, the scarf shifts with a shaky exhale, and you end almost whispering, raw and pleading for your child to understand that you're not the monster you just looked like. Let the muffling affect your volume and clarity, and let the micro-sounds of breath and fabric be part of the performance.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Bitterness (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Thanking the Doctor Who Couldn't Save Them
instruction: You're speaking to the surgeon who just lost your person on the operating table—and you need to thank them because you know they fought like hell. Begin with composure that's clearly held together by sheer will, formal gratitude: 'I know you did everything you could.' But as you speak, something strange happens. Grief breaks through, but so does genuine gratitude, and they're completely tangled together. You're crying but also almost laughing at the absurdity of thanking someone for failing. 'Seven hours. You fought for seven hours for someone you'd never met.' Your voice cracks with devastation but also with awe at their effort. The emotions are contradictory, chaotic—heartbreak and appreciation, loss and profound human connection. End with words that are simultaneously a thank you and a goodbye to your beloved, all directed at this stranger who held their life in their hands: 'You gave me four more hours than I would have had. Four hours to say goodbye.' Let your voice carry both the weight of loss and the strange grace of those final hours.
inspired_by: Defense Closing Argument: Arguing Reasonable Doubt

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner About the Baby You Lost
instruction: It's 3am. Your partner is asleep beside you. You're whispering the things you can't say when they're awake—about the miscarriage three months ago that you both agreed not to talk about anymore. Your voice is barely audible, tender, breaking. You're telling the baby what they would have been. You're confessing to your sleeping partner how you touch your empty belly every morning. How you see the baby in dreams. Your whispers catch and fracture. You say their name—the name you'd chosen together but never speak aloud. The grief is oceanic but your voice stays quiet, contained, as if making noise would shatter something irreparable. By the end, there's the faintest hint of something else—not hope exactly, but the possibility of surviving this. Your final words are both a goodbye to who you were and a terrified hello to who you're becoming.
inspired_by: Group Sharing: Introducing Yourself as a Survivor

title: Breaking the Family Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about something she's never acknowledged: the way your family pretended everything was fine when it wasn't, and how that taught you to hide your real feelings even from yourself. Start from a place where you're trying to be controlled and rational, but there's a trembling underneath—you're afraid of her judgment, afraid of being told you're too sensitive, too dramatic. As you speak, let the fear become part of what you say: 'I'm terrified to tell you this, and that terror is exactly what I need you to understand.' Feel how naming your fear gives you permission to access your anger, your grief, your desperate need to be seen. By the end, you've moved from careful self-censoring to a raw, unfiltered demand: 'Stop making me small to make you comfortable.' Let your voice crack, let tears come, let your body shake—these aren't signs of weakness but of caring enough to risk everything.
inspired_by: An actor fears their fear will be detected by the director and crew

title: The Packing Tape Victory
instruction: You're crouched in a tight ball inside your closet, knees pressed against your chest, your back against the wall. Your phone flashlight is the only light, and you're breathing fast and shallow, trying not to make a sound. You've just escaped a dangerous situation—a locked room in an unfamiliar house—and you've finally found the hidden key taped under the floorboard. But now you hear footsteps in the hallway, muffled and close. You whisper to yourself, the words coming out in shaky, compressed gasps, but as you realize you're only steps away from the door and freedom, your voice slowly rises from a terrified hush to a fierce, triumphant whisper of disbelief. Let the fear crack your voice at first, then let the triumph swell, even as your body stays curled and small.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your terminally ill child is finally asleep after a painful day. You sit beside their bed in the dark and whisper things you can never say when they're awake. Start with tender observations—how beautiful they are, how their face looks peaceful now. Let your voice catch as you confess your failures: the times you were impatient, the moments you wasted. Tell them about the future they won't have—graduations, first loves, their own children. Your whisper should be saturated with love so intense it's almost unbearable, mixed with guilt that you can't save them. End with a soft, broken 'I'm sorry' that encompasses everything—sorry for failing them, sorry for the unfairness of the world, sorry that love isn't enough.
inspired_by: Falling in Love at a Funeral

title: Laughing Through Tears as You Pack Your Dream Away
instruction: You're packing up the remnants of a dream you've had to let go—maybe a business that failed, a creative pursuit you can't sustain, a life you built that's crumbling. Start with your voice light, almost joking as you hold up something meaningful: 'Remember when we thought this would work? God, we were so sure.' There's laughter in your voice, but it's edged with something sharper. Let yourself genuinely laugh at the absurdity, the hope you had, the naivety—but feel the tears coming at the same time. Your voice cracks mid-laugh: 'I really thought... I really believed...' Now you're crying and laughing simultaneously, your voice a mess of both. Feel the gratitude for having tried mixed with the heartbreak of failing. Your voice shifts between chuckling at memories and sobbing at what's lost. Then find a moment of strange, beautiful acceptance. Your voice becomes softer, still teary but somehow peaceful: 'It was real while it lasted. It meant something. I meant something.' End with your voice carrying both grief and grace, acknowledging the death of a dream while honoring that you had the courage to dream it at all: 'Thank you. For letting me try. For letting me hope.' Your voice should feel like someone finding light in the darkest moment—not false positivity, but genuine, bittersweet gratitude.
inspired_by: Relationship Ending: Both Relief and Devastation

title: Medieval: Executioner Comforts the Condemned as a Priest
instruction: Morning of execution. Your executioner voice is hidden, your priest voice present. You're administering last rites to the condemned, voice warm with spiritual care. But they don't know you're the one who will kill them in hours. Your voice carries the strange compassion of being both instrument of mercy and instrument of death. Your breathing is centered prayer. You're giving them peace while carrying their death in your own hands. Your vocal steadiness is the most intimate violence.

title: The Unsent Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you wrote to your teenager who just attempted suicide, and they're sitting across from you in the hospital room. Your voice starts shaking with barely controlled rage: 'Do you have any idea what it felt like to get that phone call? To see you in that ambulance?' The anger cracks into raw terror: 'I have never been so afraid in my entire life.' Your voice breaks completely as fury dissolves into helpless love: 'You are my whole world, and you tried to leave it without saying goodbye.' Tears stream as you crumble: 'I'm so sorry I didn't see how much pain you were in. I'm your parent—I'm supposed to protect you from everything, even from yourself, and I failed.' Then something shifts to fierce protectiveness mixed with desperate vulnerability: 'But I'm here now, and I'm not going anywhere. You don't have to carry this alone anymore.' Your voice ends with trembling conviction: 'We're going to fight this together, even on the days when you can't remember why. I'll remember for both of us.'

title: What I've Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or child) after years of swallowing your truth. Start calm, almost rehearsed, as you tell them everything you appreciate about who they are—be specific, be genuine. Then let the ground shift beneath you as you admit the thing you've liked least, the pattern that's wounded you repeatedly, but force yourself to say it without cruelty: 'what's been hardest for me is...' or 'where I've felt most alone with you is...' Feel the terror and relief of this honesty mixing together. As they respond (imagine their face, their reaction), let yourself move from controlled composure to raw need—by the end, you're not angry anymore, you're pleading for them to finally see you, your voice stripped of all armor.

title: The Final Warning
instruction: You are a young woman whose chronic back pain is flaring up as you stand in your kitchen. Across from you is someone who has repeatedly dismissed your condition, and today they've crossed a line. You start with weary, irritated anger—your voice tight, punctuated by sharp intakes of breath as you shift your weight. A sigh escapes before you speak. Midway, as you realize they still aren't taking you seriously, your tone shifts: the anger crystallizes into a cold, quiet malevolence. You lean slightly, wince, then deliver a precise, venomous promise. Let the pain and tension color every word, from the first frustrated exhale to the final, controlled threat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unfinished Symphony
instruction: You are an older woman, alone in a vast, empty parking lot at night. You’ve just finished a long, exhausting day at work, and you’re releasing the built-up frustration by screaming into the cold air. Start with a focused, deliberate scream—a single, clear, high-pitched note, your brow furrowing as you try to hold it steady, like you’re trying to carve your anger into the silence. Mid-scream, you feel a sudden, unexpected prick of tears, and the sound wavers, cracks, and dissolves into a ragged sob. Your voice breaks, you cough, and then you let out a few quiet, shuddering breaths, the fight gone, replaced by a hollow, stunned quiet.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Wrong Funeral
instruction: You're a retired librarian at a memorial service for a colleague you barely knew. You're trying to be respectful, but you've just spotted your best friend across the room—the one who always makes you laugh by pulling faces in church. You need to keep a solemn, composed demeanor, but your body is betraying you. Your voice is high and tight as you struggle to speak to the person next to you, a polite question about the deceased that starts with genuine interest but gets choked off by a sudden, overwhelming wave of barely suppressed giggles. The interest is real at first—you did want to know—but it's quickly overwhelmed by the joyful, ridiculous amusement you're fighting not to show.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Echo Chamber
instruction: You are an older man in a dimly lit, empty hallway with tile floors and a long, resonant echo. As you walk, your own voice bounces back in a distorted, eerie way—you freeze, startled, convinced someone else is there. You whisper a hesitant 'Hello?' and the echo returns, making you laugh at the absurdity. Your initial astonishment turns into amused curiosity as you play with the sound, letting your words stretch and fade, reacting to the acoustics like an unexpected companion.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Final Row of the Spreadsheet
instruction: You are alone in a quiet office, late at night, finishing a spreadsheet that took weeks to perfect. Your fingers fly across the keyboard, and you feel a sharp triumph with each correct cell—but beneath it, a sourness simmers. You’re meeting the deadline, yet a coworker took credit for your early work, and you can’t stop the bitter thought from creeping in. Start by speaking the final numbers aloud, your voice clipped and fast over the clicking keys, then slow as a sour memory intrudes—your stomach tightens, your rhythm falters. End with a forced, triumphantly flat ‘done,’ letting the triumph linger in your smile while the sourness pokes through your tone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Lesson Before Deployment
instruction: You're teaching your child how to ride a bike for the first time, knowing you deploy to a dangerous combat zone tomorrow and might not return. Start with forced cheerfulness and pride as you run alongside them, celebrating their wobbling attempts. Your voice should be bright, encouraging, full of laughter—but let cracks appear as reality intrudes. Gradually let the joy dissolve into quiet desperation as you realize this might be your last ordinary moment together. End kneeling beside them, voice breaking as you try to memorize everything about this moment while pretending everything will be fine. The transition should feel like watching sunlight fade—imperceptible at first, then suddenly you're in darkness.

title: Fever Dream Reconciliation
instruction: You're in the throes of intense physical sensation—perhaps burning with fever, or in the aftermath of passionate intimacy, or shaking with exhaustion after a marathon. In this heightened physical state, your ex-lover appears in the room (or calls you, or you imagine them there). Your body is hypersensitive: every nerve ending alive, sounds too loud, light too bright, skin electric. As you speak to them—arguing, reconciling, or something undefined—let their presence physically transform. Perhaps their voice becomes a texture you can feel on your skin, their image shimmers and shifts between beautiful and monstrous, their words land on you like temperature changes. Your physical state makes emotional control impossible—rage might suddenly become desperate desire, anger might melt into tenderness, desire might spike into fury. Let your body's intensity reshape how you perceive them, moving from one overwhelming sensation-emotion to another, unable to maintain any single feeling.

title: Bittersweet Exodus
instruction: You're packing the last box in the home where you raised your family, and your adult child has just walked in unexpectedly. Begin with surprise that melts into joy, even as tears form: 'You came. Oh honey, you came to say goodbye to the house.' Your voice cracks with laughter and crying simultaneously: 'God, remember when you put that dent in the wall trying to skateboard down the hallway? I was so mad, but look at me now—I'm actually going to miss that stupid dent.' Touch the wall tenderly, your voice thick with memories: 'Every mark, every stain, every horrible wallpaper choice—it's all you kids growing up.' The grief rises but there's gratitude woven through it: 'This house held so much love. So much chaos. So many midnight fevers and terrible report cards and first heartbreaks.' You laugh through tears: 'And that time you all tried to make me breakfast in bed and set off the smoke alarm.' Your voice becomes softer, accepting: 'But you're all grown now. You don't need this house anymore. And neither do I.' Look at your child with eyes full of tears and pride: 'I'm not losing anything. I'm just... closing a beautiful chapter.' Take their hand, your voice steady and peaceful despite the tears: 'Everything I needed to give you, I gave you here. Now we get to see what comes next.' Let joy and sorrow live together in your voice completely.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: Confront your aging parent about why they never said 'I love you' during your entire childhood. Begin with nervous, almost apologetic questions ('I just need to understand...'), your voice uncertain, seeking permission to even ask. As they deflect or offer hollow explanations, let your pain become anger—not loud rage, but sharp, precise truth-telling. 'I needed you. I was a child.' Let the anger crack open into the grief underneath: the child in you still waiting for those words. End in a different place—either in acceptance of what will never come, or in the raw vulnerability of asking one more time. Make the confrontation feel dangerous, like touching a wound that's been closed for decades.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a childhood wound that never healed. Start with measured, almost rehearsed words—you've practiced this: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, anger starts bleeding through the control: 'When I was twelve, you... you weren't there.' Your voice sharpens, becomes accusatory, years of suppressed rage surfacing. 'Do you even remember? Do you remember choosing work over my recital? Over my graduation? Over everything?' The fury peaks, your voice cracking with it. Then you see their face—suddenly old, suddenly fragile—and the anger collapses into something more complicated. Your voice softens, breaks: 'I just... I needed you.' End with a whisper that contains both love and irreparable loss: 'I still do.' The transformation is from controlled accusation to explosive anger to heartbroken longing.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner That You're Leaving Tomorrow
instruction: It's 3 AM. They're asleep beside you, peaceful, trusting. You're leaving in the morning—not because you don't love them, but because staying means losing yourself completely. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every word you've been too afraid to say when they could hear you. You tell them everything: how much you love them, how deeply you've tried, how their happiness became the only thing that mattered until you disappeared. Your throat tightens. You apologize for your cowardice, for choosing this moment when they can't respond, can't ask you to stay. Tears fall silently. You tell them they deserve someone who can be whole, that you hope they'll understand someday, that this tenderness you feel right now is so real it's breaking you. Your words dissolve into breath, into the quiet devastation of loving someone and still having to go.
inspired_by: Defense Lawyer Cross-Examines Witness, Realizes They're Confessing to Other Crimes

title: The Luminous Failure
instruction: You are pacing in your cluttered home office at 3 AM, having just realized your grand, all-night project to build a prototype for a new invention is actually a total, incoherent mess. You start by proudly explaining your brilliant idea to a friend on the phone, your voice fast and jubilant, laughter spilling out. Mid-sentence you catch sight of the tangled wires and nonsense notes, and your excitement shifts. You trail off, voice loud but now hollow, as you describe the beautiful dream you had, trying to convince yourself it wasn't a waste, a flicker of awe for the idea itself fighting your crushing disappointment. You must sound as if you're talking to someone you trust, your body vibrating with manic energy that's starting to curdle.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Disappointment (clearly present), Awe (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Fever Dream of Desire and Destruction
instruction: You are in the immediate aftermath of an intensely physical experience—perhaps overwhelming passion, perhaps a physical fight, perhaps dancing until your body gave out, perhaps the endorphin flood after receiving devastating news. Your body is still trembling, your breath ragged. Begin speaking through gasps and half-laughs, your voice raw, your words tumbling out in a stream-of-consciousness. You can barely separate physical sensation from emotion—your skin is electric, your heart pounding, and you're trying to make sense of what you're feeling. Are you exhilarated or destroyed? Alive or breaking apart? Let your voice ride the waves of sensation—breathy, then fierce, then almost sobbing, then laughing. The transformation comes as the adrenaline fades and reality crashes in: what felt like pure intensity reveals itself as something more complicated. By the end, your voice should quiet into stunned realization—your body still echoing with sensation, but your mind finally understanding what it meant.

title: The First Time, The Last Time
instruction: You're a teenage boy, breathless and clumsy in the dark of your childhood bedroom—hair still damp from the shower, heart hammering through your ribs. You and your partner are tangled in sheets that smell like detergent and regret. She whispers something that makes you stop moving for a second—a confession that you're not just her first, but the only one she'll remember. Start with the rhythm locked in your chest, half-grunts between thrusts, a forced coolness in your voice as you try to own the moment. Then, a beat: you slow, your breath catches, and your voice cracks into something raw and young—a quiet, unraveling panic as you realize you're in over your head, that this passion is a fragile, foolish thing you're not ready to lose.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Smudged Words
instruction: You are an older adult with an androgynous voice, slumped in a chair, head resting heavily on one hand. Your palm presses your cheek, smushing your mouth so that some sounds come out clumsy. You're staring at a handwritten letter—the ink is smeared, the handwriting erratic. You begin reading aloud, trying to parse it, your voice thick with confusion. As you reread a line, your confusion deepens, then slowly shifts into a quiet, weary acceptance: you realize the message is from someone whose mind is fading, and no amount of deciphering will bring clarity. Let your voice wander—tone uneven, pauses as you lose your place, the smushed quality softening only when you drop your hand for a moment.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Apology Too Little, Too Late
instruction: Someone who wronged you is finally apologizing, but the damage is already done. You're listening to their apology with a tight voice: 'I appreciate that, but...' You're trying to be gracious, but the bitterness comes through. 'This doesn't fix what happened.' Your voice is sad, tired. You're explaining that some things can't be undone. By the end, you're accepting the apology because you need closure, but your voice makes clear you'll never fully trust them again.

title: When Protection Becomes Impossible
instruction: Someone you're responsible for—your child, your younger sibling, someone under your care—is facing something terrible that you cannot prevent or fix. Begin with fierce determination, your voice strong with promises you intend to keep. But as the reality of your powerlessness crashes over you, let that strength fracture. Your declarations should become desperate, then furious—rage at the universe, at yourself, at the unfairness. Let your voice rise to something almost violent in its intensity. Then, in the aftermath of that explosion, collapse into raw helplessness. Your final words should be barely held together, spoken through tears, a whispered apology mixed with love so fierce it hurts. Move from protective strength to impotent rage to broken tenderness. Let us hear the moment when a protector realizes they are human after all.

title: Don't You Come Any Closer
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman standing inches away from someone who has been stalking you for weeks. Your voice is loud, dry, and tight—no reverb because you're so close. Start with a slight quiver of fear in your throat, a tiny break on the first word, but as you speak, that fear hardens into cold, steely resolve. Your words are clipped, each one a punch. Feel the heat of your own breath hitting their face, the tension in your shoulders. Let a tremor return briefly when you mention the police, then shove it down. Speak about 60 words, using hard glottal attacks on 'stop' and 'back'.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point: A Parent Unable to Protect Their Child
instruction: You've just learned your child is being bullied, hurt, destroyed by something you can't control. Begin with fierce determination — 'I will fix this, I swear to you' — voice strong, protective, parental. But as you try to explain how you'll make it right, reality crashes in: you can't. The promises start to falter. Your voice rises with desperate anger — at the school, the other kids, the system, God, yourself. The rage peaks, then shatters into something primal: a parent's helplessness. The strong voice breaks completely. You're not performing grief; you're collapsing under the weight of failing at your most fundamental job. End raw and ragged: 'I don't know how to save you.' Let that admission cost you everything. The final words should be almost formless, dissolved in the agony of powerlessness.
inspired_by: Comedian Whose Set Is Bombing — And They're Spiraling

title: The Last Push-Up
instruction: You're a teenager who just lost a rage-fueled bet with yourself, doing push-ups until you couldn't. Now you're collapsed on the bedroom floor, chest heaving, trying to call your best friend who just humiliated you online. Begin gasping for air, furious at the betrayal—each word a struggle against your own exhaustion. As you speak, the anger slowly drains into a sour, hollow realization that you're more hurt than mad, ending with a quiet, trembling admission that the friendship might be over.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You are whispering to your sleeping partner (or closest friend) in the darkness, confessing something you believe might end everything between you. Begin by acknowledging the physical sensations: your racing heart, the catch in your breath, how your body wants to flee. Speak very quietly, starting with all the obstacles—'I'm terrified,' 'My throat is closing,' 'I want to take this back before I even say it.' Let the confession emerge in fragments, interrupted by your own fear, by the impulse to protect yourself. As you continue, release each layer of self-protection. Feel the difference between rehearsed confession and raw truth. By the end, arrive at the simple, undefended core of what you need to say—no longer hiding behind fear or shame, just offering the vulnerable truth in the gentlest voice, free of the need to control how it's received.

title: The Debt Collector's Due
instruction: You are an elderly man, frail but once powerful, with a much younger partner who humiliates you for money. In the middle of a session that feels more like punishment than intimacy, you gasp out words locked to the rhythm of each thrust. Start with wounded embarrassment — you can barely look at them, each breath a shameful admission. But as the encounter passes, your voice shifts: beneath the exertion, a cold malice emerges, whispered in the pauses, just for yourself. End with a shuddering, broken gratitude, thanking them with a trembling mouth, even as your eyes make a different promise. Speak only a few broken phrases, letting bedsprings and the heavy rhythm of your partner's effort punctuate your lines. Your voice must crack, waver, and occasionally lose breath mid-thought, then find it again with bitter clarity.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're confronting your partner who's been slowly erasing your identity for years, and tonight you finally see it clearly. Start with confusion, your voice uncertain: 'Why do I feel like I'm disappearing?' As realization dawns, your tone sharpens with mounting anger: 'You made me feel crazy for wanting things.' Let rage build until you're almost shouting, but then—suddenly—your voice cracks and the anger collapses into raw, vulnerable pain: 'I gave you everything and you... you just took it.' Your breath catches. The final words should come out broken, devastated, a whisper of someone discovering they've lost themselves: 'I don't even know who I am anymore.' This isn't a dramatic exit; it's the sound of a heart realizing it's been slowly breaking for years.

title: The Garden Fall
instruction: You're an elderly person who has just fallen while trying to lift a potted plant in your garden. You feel a sharp snap in your wrist. First, let out a startled cry – then force yourself to stay very still, breathing in shallow, shaky pulls. The neighbor's kid saw you fall. You're embarrassed – you hate seeming frail. Start with a trembling whisper: 'I'm fine... just... give me a moment.' Let your voice waver between the pain that's starting to throb and the awkward shame of being caught. End with a quiet, rueful admission: 'I used to do this one-handed.' The feeling shifts from shock to simmering embarrassment.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Protector's Last Watch
instruction: You're sitting beside your younger sibling's hospital bed in their final hours. For your entire life, you've been the strong one—the shield, the guardian, the one who fixes everything. But now there's nothing you can do. Begin speaking to them with that fierce protective energy, making promises, trying to stay strong. But as you continue, let that armor crack. Allow yourself to move from being the invincible guardian to becoming the frightened, helpless younger version of yourself who needs them just as much as they needed you. End in a place of raw vulnerability you've never allowed yourself before, finally admitting you don't know how to face the world without them.
inspired_by: The character's behavior and inner life can be identified as coming from a specific dominant personality facet (e.g., a victim, a warrior, a free spirit, a moralist, a satanic energy)

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, making your final call to Earth before the communication window closes forever. Start with excitement, maybe even forced cheerfulness—telling your parent or partner about the view, the mission, keeping it light because that's easier. But as the seconds tick down, the reality crashes in: you will never hear their voice again, never touch them, never come home. Your voice should fracture mid-sentence. Let the goodbye transform from brave optimism to raw, desperate need to say everything that matters in thirty seconds. End in whispered urgency, racing against silence, your voice breaking on 'I love you' as the connection dies.

title: The Last Call from the Fire
instruction: You are a heavily intoxicated, hyper-masculine man—a former firefighter—calling your young son from a payphone at 2 a.m. You're swaying, slouched against the booth, barely holding the receiver. At first, you're swaggering, slurring about how 'your old man fought a real fire once,' voice cracking with sour bravado—bitter, boastful, resentful of your own failure. But as you hear the boy's sleepy voice on the other end, exhaustion seeps in. Your volume drops, words become mushy, and you shift from bravado to a quiet, broken admission: 'I just wanted to hear you... before I forget how.' By the end, all that sourness has curdled into a fragile, exhausted longing—you're nearly crying, struggling to stay upright, voice thick with regret and love.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Permission to Stay
instruction: You're at your father's bedside in his final hours. He's been unconscious for days, but suddenly his eyes flutter open. You've spent your whole life being the responsible one, the caretaker, never asking for anything. Now, as he looks at you with clarity for perhaps the last time, something breaks open inside you. Begin by trying to be strong, composed, saying the things you think you should say. But let yourself crack open—tell him everything you've never allowed yourself to ask for: permission to be messy, to fail, to take up space, to live selfishly sometimes. Move from dutiful caretaker to raw, vulnerable child demanding to finally be seen. Let your voice shift from controlled and careful to whatever it needs to be—louder, broken, whispered, fierce. By the end, you're not asking anymore—you're claiming what you needed all along.

title: The Garden and the Boy
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting on your porch, a hearing aid buzzing in your ear. Through the fence, you watch a neighbor play catch with his grandson — the boy's laughter is a faint, tinny sound to you. Begin by observing quietly, your voice too loud as you mutter about the good old days, your pitch drifting with nostalgia. Then, as you strain to hear a joke you missed, anger flares — you curse your ears, your voice cracking and sibilants hissing. A sliver of jealousy slips in as you see them high-five, but you end by leaning back, your words growing slow and contemplative, trailing off into the hum of the garden.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Anger (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Accusation of Aliveness
instruction: You are confronting your father who always demanded you be smaller, quieter, more controlled—who punished you for being 'too much.' Start cold, measured, trying to explain calmly how his criticism damaged you. But as he dismisses you again with that same look of disgust, something breaks. Your voice gets louder, your body takes up more space. You begin to move with full physical power—large gestures, stomping, claiming the room. Your anger becomes physical poetry: you might grab a chair and shake it, press your hands against the wall with full force, or move your entire body in ways that are fierce and uncontainable. Declare out loud everything he tried to kill in you: your passion, your wildness, your hunger for life. Let sounds emerge that aren't words—roars, growls, gasps. By the end, you're not asking for his approval anymore; you're a force of nature, towering and magnificent, taking up all the space you were denied. You're terrifying and beautiful and finally, fully alive.

title: Dancing at Your Wedding While Your Heart Breaks
instruction: You're having your first dance at your wedding, or giving your toast, or standing at the altar, and you're genuinely happy—you love this person, you want this life—but you're also aware this means letting go of another future you once imagined, or saying goodbye to a part of yourself, or acknowledging that someone who should be here will never meet your spouse. Your voice is warm, full of joy and celebration. You're laughing, present, meaning every word. But threading through it is this ribbon of grief that makes the happiness even more achingly real. The gratitude and the loss amplify each other. End in a place where you're simultaneously more alive than you've ever been and mourning something precious. Your voice should shimmer between these truths—not switching between them, but holding both at once, the way life actually feels in its most profound moments.
inspired_by: Narrating Your Own Surgery While Awake

title: Confessional in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your partner in the deep night, both of you facing the ceiling in darkness. Begin with silence—just breathing. Then, in barely more than a whisper, confess something you've never told anyone: a betrayal, a secret desire, a fear that shame has kept locked inside you. Let the darkness and the safety of lying side by side (not facing each other) give you permission to be more honest than you've ever been. The bedroom itself holds memories of intimacy, of pretending, of the person you've performed being. Now let that performance fall away. Your voice should remain quiet throughout, but the emotional stakes should escalate from tentative vulnerability to naked, trembling truth. End in a place of terrifying openness, having revealed the part of yourself you most feared showing.

title: The Breakdown of the Judge
instruction: You are a person who has built their identity on having exacting standards, and you're having a complete emotional collapse. Start with manic energy as you defend your right to judge everything and everyone - your voice sharp, rapid, almost hysterical as you list all the things that are wrong with the world. Build in intensity, your critiques becoming more desperate and nonsensical until you're shouting about meaningless details. Then shatter completely. Let your voice break into raw sobbing as you admit that you're terrified of being ordinary, of not mattering, of being the one who doesn't measure up. title: Confronting Your Father While He's Having a Stroke
instruction: You've finally gathered the courage to tell your father the truth about how his neglect damaged you, and mid-confrontation, he begins having a stroke. Start with righteous anger—words you've rehearsed for years pouring out. Then notice his face drooping, his speech slurring, and you must decide: do you call for help or finish what you came to say? Your rage collides with panic and guilt. You're suddenly the parent and he's helpless, exactly the vulnerability he never showed you. Oscillate between trying to help him, continuing your accusations (because this might be your only chance), and the horrifying realization that you might be watching him die with your anger as his last memory. End in quiet devastation, whispering either forgiveness or a truth he can no longer hear.

title: Burning From the Inside
instruction: You have just learned of a profound betrayal—not a small lie, but something that rewrites your understanding of the last several years of your life. Your body is physically reacting: your hands are shaking, your skin feels too hot, your breath is coming in sharp bursts. Begin with your voice tight and controlled, trying to stay calm, but your body is betraying you—you can feel rage building like a fever. As you speak, let the physical sensations drive your vocal choices: shakiness, sudden loudness, moments where you have to stop because you physically can't get air. Midway through, let the rage crack open and pour out—not performative anger, but the kind that feels like it's burning through your ribcage. Then, unexpectedly, let it collapse into something else: exhaustion, or grief, or worst of all, the terrible question of whether you ever really knew anything at all. End in a kind of hollowed-out stillness, your voice rough and used up, your body finally still but emptied.
inspired_by: Actor is working on a scene and needs to identify what to work on—which obligations are most pressing

title: Protective Rage Against the Inevitable
instruction: Someone you'd die for - your child, younger sibling, someone vulnerable - is about to walk into something dangerous that you cannot stop. Start fierce, almost violent in your urgency: 'You are NOT doing this!' Your voice is steel, commanding, protective. But they're going anyway. The rage intensifies - you'd tear the world apart to keep them safe, and you CAN'T. Your fury cracks into desperation, then breaks completely into helpless sobbing. You grab them, hold them, your voice reduced to pleading: 'Please. Please don't.' Then something in you accepts the unbearable. Your voice steadies, tender now, fierce love replacing the rage. You tell them everything you need them to know in case you never get another chance. End with a blessing that sounds like goodbye, your voice strong and shattered at once.
inspired_by: Improvised Bedtime Story That Accidentally Gets Too Dark

title: Mapping the Scars
instruction: In the darkness of a bedroom, you are whispering to your lover, tracing the scars on their body with your fingertips—each one has a story. Begin with tender curiosity, your voice soft and intimate, as you ask about a small scar on their shoulder. As they share more, and you touch a deeper wound, the atmosphere shifts: you realize these scars represent pain you cannot fix, trauma you were not there to prevent. Your whispers become even quieter, more fragile, as you grapple with the limits of love—you cannot undo their past. By the end, let your voice find a new kind of tenderness: not the tenderness of fixing, but of witnessing, of saying 'I see you, all of you, and I'm here now.' The transformation is from playful intimacy to heartbroken reverence to a deeper, more honest love.
inspired_by: An actor is experiencing professional inactivity and depression

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After the Divorce Papers
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's bed late at night, just after signing divorce papers. Speak in the softest whisper, as if any louder would shatter something precious. Start by describing their sleeping face—the way their eyelashes rest on their cheeks, the small movements of their breathing, how peaceful they look not knowing their world is about to split in two. Your voice should be tender but trembling, full of protective love mixed with guilt and grief. Confess your fears in broken whispers: that you've failed them, that they'll blame themselves, that you can't protect them from this pain. Let tears thicken your voice as you promise things you're not sure you can deliver—that they'll be okay, that love doesn't end, that home can exist in two places. End with your whisper barely audible, telling them you're sorry, that you love them more than your own heartbreak, your voice catching on words you hope they never consciously hear but somehow always know.

title: The Old Dog's Rally
instruction: You are a middle-aged man in a sparring match against a much younger fighter. You’re winded, your arms are heavy, and for the first two minutes he’s been landing clean shots—you feel real fear, raw and tight in your chest. As you circle, forcing yourself to breathe deep and slow, you see an opening. You explode forward with a sharp kiai, your fist connects with his ribs—a solid thud. For a split second, pleasure and elation surge through you, hot and bright, even as your lungs scream. Let your voice start shaky and hunted between breaths, then tighten into a predatory growl as you attack, then finish with a husky, satisfied laugh as you reset. Include the spoken words as if talking to yourself or to your corner between exchanges.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Fear (very intensely present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Miscarriage in the Hospital Bathroom
instruction: You're alone in a hospital bathroom, miscarrying the pregnancy you've been carrying for three months. Start with shock—your voice is eerily calm, almost clinical: 'This is happening. Okay. This is actually happening.' But as the physical pain intensifies, something primal rips out of you. Your voice becomes a raw howl of grief and rage: 'No, no, no—please, not like this, not alone in a bathroom.' You're furious—at your body, at the universe, at every pregnant person you'll see tomorrow. You pound the wall. Then, suddenly, you collapse into devastating tenderness: 'I'm so sorry, baby. I'm so sorry I couldn't keep you safe.' Your voice breaks into a lullaby you'll never sing to them. Rage returns: 'Everyone will say it wasn't meant to be, and I will want to scream.' End with exhausted, hollow acceptance: 'I have to stand up now. Walk out of here. Pretend I'm fine.' But your voice carries the knowledge that you're forever changed—fierce and shattered and furiously protective of this grief no one else will understand.

title: Leaving Someone You Promised Forever To
instruction: You're packing or sitting across from them. Your voice is final: 'I have to leave.' You're breaking a promise you meant. 'This isn't working and it's killing me,' delivered with exhaustion. Your voice carries all the trying and failure. They beg you to stay and your voice almost breaks: 'I can't,' repeated. End with goodbye devastated but certain.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Road
instruction: You're calling someone you love from a hospital after a terrible accident. You know you won't survive the night, but you don't want them to know that yet. Begin by weaving together real memories you share with this person—but gradually add invented details about a future you'll never have together, describing plans you're making, promises about next week, next month. Let your voice carry the weight of goodbye while your words insist on tomorrow. Start with fear and the desperate need to protect them from the truth, but by the end, let the facade crack just enough that love—raw and undefended—breaks through. Your final moments should shimmer between the lie of 'see you soon' and the devastating truth of 'this is goodbye.'

title: The Forgotten Recipe
instruction: You are an older woman at the kitchen table, chin pressed down toward your chest, staring at a handwritten recipe card your mother gave you forty years ago. The shame is thick—you never learned to cook it right, and now your mother is gone. You start softly, muffled, voice creaky, barely lifting your head, trying to recall her voice telling you the steps. Midway, you lose the thread, pause, then force your chin up slightly, voice cracking as you realize you're speaking to yourself, not her—ending with a raw, quiet acceptance and a tiny, wavering smile.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother with a Childhood Memory
instruction: You're describing to your mother the strawberries she used to cut for you every morning before school—the one tender thing she did in an otherwise cold childhood. Start with careful, almost fragile nostalgia, your voice soft with the memory of that small kindness. Then let the hurt surface: why was that the only gentleness? Why couldn't she be that mother in other ways? Your tone should shift from tender to questioning to anger, then break into raw vulnerability. End quietly, almost pleading: 'Those strawberries made me think you loved me. Did you?' Let the question hang there, genuine and undefended, needing an answer you're terrified to hear.

title: The Last Threshold
instruction: You are an elderly man, frail but proud, in the moment of being denied a final release by a partner you have loved for decades. This is not just sexual—it is the last time you will feel this kind of closeness. You are trembling, your breath is ragged, and you are trying to hold onto dignity as your voice cracks. Start with a half-whispered plea, but let awe for the beauty of this shared vulnerability mix with a deep, aching sadness. As the denial continues, let your voice climb in pitch and desperation, then drop into a broken, childlike whimper. End with a surrendering sigh, the sadness swallowed by a sense of immense, overwhelming love.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Distress (extremely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bumpy Ride to You
instruction: You’re a young man sitting in the back of a rattling taxi, heading to meet someone you’ve been secretly craving all week. The pothole-ridden road makes your whole body shake, your voice coming out in uneven, jittery bursts—partly annoyance, partly that flutter of lust you can’t shake. Start by muttering about the terrible conditions, the driver’s radio, the time, your voice vibrating with every bump. By the end, you’re imagining what will happen when you finally see them, your tone softening into a husky, uneven whisper—still shivering from the road, but now from longing.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Surgeon Watches Patient Die from Their Own Surgical Innovation
instruction: You're in the observation room above the OR, watching a patient—a young parent—die from complications of a revolutionary procedure you pioneered and championed. You begin explaining the technical details to medical students with clinical precision, your voice steady with scientific objectivity. But this person trusted you completely, called you their miracle worker, showed you photos of their children. As their vitals fail, your narration becomes mechanical, a shield against the knowledge that your innovation, your pride, has become their death sentence. Your breathing stays measured but your words begin to crack at the edges. End alone at the glass, your professional facade collapsing into raw, gasping grief that no one will ever hear, whispering an apology that comes far too late.
inspired_by: Professional: CEO Announces Layoffs That Destroy Livelihoods She Designed

title: The Last Meal We Share
instruction: You are sharing a meal with someone you love who is leaving tomorrow for a journey they won't return from. Start by gently teasing them about the food the way you always have, your voice warm with the familiar rhythm of your old jokes about their cooking or their eating habits. But you keep catching yourself laughing while tears are building in your throat. Describe the taste of each bite as if you're trying to memorize it, your voice breaking between moments of genuine joy at this small perfection and devastating grief. Let laughter and sobbing blur together as you say this is exactly right, this meal, this moment, even though it's all wrong because it's ending. End with profound gratitude for something so simple and so unbearably precious, your voice somehow both shattered and full of wonder. The contradiction should feel like your heart is being torn in two directions at once.
inspired_by: The Restaurant Critic with Strange Criteria

title: The Goodbye That Feels Like Hello
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who is leaving your life forever—moving to another country, ending your relationship, or perhaps this is your last conversation before a long prison sentence or terminal diagnosis takes them away. But here's the complexity: you're simultaneously furious with them and desperately in love with them; you're relieved this painful chapter is ending while also being shattered by the loss; you're grateful for what they gave you while resenting what they took. Start with one dominant emotion—perhaps anger or stoic acceptance. As you speak, let the contradictory feelings crash into each other like waves, your tone shifting unpredictably between rage and tenderness, bitter laughter and choked grief, accusations and desperate declarations of love. Don't resolve these contradictions into something neat—let them coexist messily, authentically, the way they do in real heartbreak. End in a place that surprises you, wherever the emotional truth takes you.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood you needed but never had. Start with controlled anger, words carefully chosen and held back for decades. 'You were never there. You never saw me.' But as you speak, the anger begins to crack, revealing the profound loneliness underneath. Your voice shifts from accusation to pleading—you're no longer the adult confronting them, you're the child who's still waiting to be noticed. The question 'Why wasn't I enough?' comes out broken and small. You're furious and heartbroken simultaneously. Your breathing becomes uneven as you realize mid-confrontation that you still want their love, that after everything, you're still hoping they'll finally see you. End in a space of devastating clarity: you're done waiting, but the wanting never stops.

title: The Body Knows
instruction: You're in the aftermath of intense physical experience—rage that made you throw things, passion that left you trembling, or pain that broke you open. Your body is still shaking, sweating, electric. Speak aloud about the person you always believed you were: controlled, rational, measured, civilized. But your body is telling a different story—it just expressed something wild, uncontained, more honest than your carefully constructed self-image. Let your voice shake and catch as you grapple with this physical evidence of who you actually are beneath the surface. Touch your own trembling hands, feel your racing heart. End by laughing or crying at the gap between the story you told and the truth your body just revealed. Move from shocked denial to visceral recognition to liberation or terror.

title: The Last Bite of Silence
instruction: You're a rugged, middle-aged man sitting alone at a chipped kitchen table, mechanically chewing a dry, hard granola bar. Each crunch is loud, jarring—you pause to swallow, then take another bite. You've just hung up the phone after learning an old army buddy died alone. You feel nothing. That emptiness scares you. As you chew, you talk to yourself, trying to force a reaction, but the numbness holds. Midway through the bar, a stray memory hits—him laughing in the rain. Your jaw tightens, the crunch slows, and your voice cracks just once. Start flat, detached. End with a quiet, bitter tremor—anger at your own coldness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Conceding Point
instruction: You've been arguing your point passionately, and then—in the other person's response—you hear the logic you'd been missing. Your voice stops mid-attack. There's a beat where you physically have to reset. 'You know what... you're right.' It costs you something to say it. But there's also lightness there—the strange relief of being wrong and knowing it. The respect in your voice when you continue is genuine. A moment of grace between two people.

title: The Silence of the Closet
instruction: You're a teenager hiding in your walk-in closet, surrounded by coats and soft fabric. Your parents are fighting in the next room, and you're terrified—your heart pounds, but the dead acoustics make your voice feel heavy and close in your own ears. You whisper to yourself, trying to quiet your fears, but the dread grows as you hear footsteps approach. Start with a shaky, contemplative murmur—thinking about escape—but end with a dry, strained plea to stay hidden, your voice cracking as the steps stop right outside.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (slightly present), Fear (extremely present), Distress (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Midnight Decision
instruction: You are lying in bed, your partner asleep beside you. The room is dark and quiet except for their slow breathing. You are replaying a difficult choice you made today — one that will change your life together. Start by whispering to yourself, your voice barely above a breath, your mind restless as you turn the thought over. As you search for a specific memory to reassure yourself, your voice concentrates, the pitch dipping lower, consonants softening. Finally, you settle into a quiet acceptance, your tone becoming tender and resolved as you murmur a gentle truth into the stillness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Farce of Resilience
instruction: You are an older man in a job interview, voice deep and carefully controlled. The interviewer asks about a major professional failure. Start with a teasing, almost mocking tone—over-enunciate, let out a dry chuckle, make it sound like a joke you've told before. But as you describe the aftermath, the humor evaporates. Your breath becomes shallow, your words slow. You realize the story is not funny—it's just numb. Let your voice flatten, lose its color. End with a long pause and a quiet, hollow sigh, as if the feeling has left you entirely.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Singing Your Wedding Song at Your Divorce Hearing
instruction: Courthouse. Your marriage is ending. Before signing papers, you ask to sing the song from your first dance—not as sabotage, but as... what? Closure? Defiance? Start with a laugh that's almost hysterical—the absurdity of this moment hits you. Your voice is light, almost playful at first, because the irony is unbearable and laughter is the only defense. Sing the romantic lyrics with a wry, self-aware tone: 'Forever, we said... forever.' But then the memories ambush you—the genuine joy that day held, how much you meant those vows. Your voice softens, becomes achingly tender. For a moment, you're singing to who you both were, grieving the people who believed this would last. Tears mix with the melody, but you're also... grateful? Start smiling through the pain—grateful it happened, grateful it's ending, grateful for the growth even if it broke you. Your voice becomes this beautiful contradiction: mourning and celebrating simultaneously. End with acceptance—voice clear, peaceful, even warm—singing the final 'I love you' as both truth and farewell. You meant it then. You mean it now. And that's enough.
inspired_by: Singing in Front of People for the First Time

title: The Believer's Doubt
instruction: You are whispering a confession to your sleeping lover in the dark hours before dawn. You've always been the strong one, the certain one, the one with unwavering faith in your relationship, your choices, your path. Start with small admissions, testing the safety of their sleep. But as you continue, let yourself go deeper, speaking more freely, building into a whispered but passionate testimony about your hidden fears, your secret doubts, the terrifying uncertainty you've never dared voice. Let it become almost a prayer, a plea, a fervent whispered sermon to the darkness about your need for them, your fear of losing them, your desperate hope that love is enough. Then, as you hear them stir or breathe differently, let panic and vulnerability flood in—the fear of being heard, of being known. End in barely audible silence, trembling, raw, exposed, but somehow cleansed.

title: The Bedside Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside someone who's sleeping—someone you love who will never wake up. Speak in hushed tones, conscious they might somehow hear. Tell them the things you were too afraid to say: that you forgive them, or that you need their forgiveness, or both. Your voice should be tender, almost a whisper, but let grief catch in your throat. Start with gentle reminiscence, sweet memories that make you smile. But let that sweetness curdle into sadness as you confess your regrets—the times you were cruel, the opportunities you wasted, the words you can never take back. End with a fragile, breaking plea for them to know you loved them despite everything. The quietness should make it more devastating, not less. This isn't performance; this is someone's heart cracking open in the dark.

title: Dancing Alone in Your Childhood Kitchen
instruction: You've returned to your childhood home for the last time before it's sold. Everyone else has left. You stand in the kitchen where you grew up, and suddenly a song comes on—maybe from a neighbor's radio, maybe in your memory. It's a song that makes your body want to move. Start feeling the ache of loss, the heaviness of nostalgia. Then let your body begin to move—awkwardly at first, then more freely. Dance the way only YOU dance when no one's watching, with all your weird moves and uninhibited joy. Let physical movement unlock emotion—laugh, cry, rage, celebrate all at once.
