Your rage explodes—you're shouting at the sky, at God, at the universe, voice raw and primal: 'I gave them EVERYTHING!' Your fury is volcanic, uncontained. You're screaming accusations, punching air, voice breaking with the violence of your anger. But rage can't sustain itself forever. It collapses. Your voice drops, the shouting becomes sobbing, fury transmutes into devastation: 'I have nothing left.' You're on your knees now, voice hollowed out. Then something shifts—a strange, terrible peace. Your breathing slows. You realize you're still alive, still here. Your voice becomes almost mystically calm, touched by something beyond anger or grief: 'Maybe nothing was ever mine to lose.' End with unexpected strength born from complete surrender: 'I'm still breathing. That's where I start.' Your voice is quiet but unbreakable.

title: Breathing Through the Wall
instruction: You are a father wearing a tight N95 respirator, kneeling in front of your young child who also wears one. The air is heavy with dust, and every breath is a conscious effort—your voice comes out muffled, with a click when you exhale. You feel a raw jealousy toward your child's easy, unbothered contentment, but also a fierce, possessive love. Start with a strained, envious edge as you tell them to stay close, then let your voice soften into a deep, almost predatory contentment, laced with a hint of malice: they are yours, and no one else will have them. Speak around 50 words, letting your breathing and the mask's distortion shape the performance naturally.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Contentment (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Plating the Final Michelin Dish While Your Restaurant Is Failing
instruction: You're focused, precise, narrating your hand movements as they arrange garnish on the plate in a three-star kitchen. But you know—everyone knows—the restaurant is closing after tonight. Your voice is controlled and professional, but it's hollow. Include the moment you look at what you've created, something genuinely beautiful, and your voice breaks slightly because this might be the last one. You describe the artistry while your mind is already calculating which suppliers you need to tell, which staff you need to lay off. Your hands are steady. Your voice is not. Finish the plate. It's perfect. It doesn't matter.

title: Thirsting for What's Hers
instruction: You're a young woman in a brutal heatwave, collapsed on a park bench, your water bottle long empty. Across from you, a friend or acquaintance sips coolly from a full bottle. You start from a place of sharp, dehydrated jealousy—your words come out slow, clipped, breathless, each syllable a struggle against dry lips and a dizzy head. Let a bitter edge creep in, but as you speak, the envy melts into a raw, desperate plea; your voice cracks, you pause to wipe sweat from your eyes, and the last words are nearly a whisper of need, not anger.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Breaking Point on the Kitchen Floor
instruction: You've just returned home after another exhausting, defeating day. Begin standing, pacing, physically listing everything that's crushing you—the bills piled on the counter, the broken dishwasher, the job that's grinding you down, the body that aches, the future that feels like a narrowing hallway. Let your body express this: tight shoulders, clenched fists, pacing that becomes more agitated. Build the litany until something breaks—you might slide down to the floor, or slam your hand on the counter, or simply stop moving. In that moment of physical release, let something else emerge: maybe rage, maybe laughter at the absurdity, maybe a sob that's been waiting months to surface. The emotional release is physical and visceral. End in a different body state entirely—perhaps collapsed but breathing freely, perhaps standing but softer, perhaps laughing and crying simultaneously. The depression breaks open into something raw but alive.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father in the house you grew up in, now being sold. Start cold and controlled—you came here to discuss logistics, paperwork, nothing more. But as you look around the room, objects trigger buried memories: the corner where you once hid during their fights, the table where you ate silent dinners, the chair where he sat instead of coming to your school plays. Let your composure crack. Accuse him not with shouting, but with specifics—name the moments he wasn't there, the times his silence taught you that you didn't matter. Build from icy politeness to scalding specificity to something surprising: beneath your anger, discover a grief for the relationship you never had. End with your voice breaking not from rage, but from the devastating recognition that you still, even now, want him to say he's sorry. Let fury and longing war in your voice.
inspired_by: Actor needs to build a repertoire of choices for future use

title: Standing in the Ruins of Your Childhood Home After the Fire
instruction: You're in what remains of your childhood home, destroyed by fire last week. Everyone is safe, but everything is gone. Begin with barely controlled fury—your voice sharp and loud, describing the acrid smell of burnt wood, the destruction, raging at the unfairness, at what was taken from you. Let yourself be explosive, almost shouting about all the irreplaceable things lost. But then, in the middle of your anger, find something—a half-burnt photograph, a melted piece of jewelry. Your rage must suddenly shatter into deep, gasping sobs as you realize you're not angry about the things—you're devastated because you can never go back, never be that child again, never have that safety. Your voice should break from fierce and powerful to completely undone, ending with you barely able to breathe through the tears, whispering, 'I just wanted to go home one more time.'
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath in a Field of Sunflowers

title: The Diagnosis Morning: Dancing While the World Ends
instruction: You received devastating news yesterday—terminal, months not years—but this morning you're performing the beloved routine with your partner one more time, and you're determined to make it perfect. Your voice should be almost giddily cheerful as you narrate the coffee, the headlines, the toast bickering—but underneath, we hear you memorizing everything, savoring each ridiculous detail with desperate intensity. Laugh at your old arguments while your voice breaks. Be grateful for the millionth coffee cup while grieving it's not the millionth-and-first. Let joy and devastation exist simultaneously in every word. Near the end, your cheerfulness cracks and you confess—voice thick with both tears and inexplicable peace—that if you could choose any morning in human history to live forever, it would be this one. Let gratitude and grief become indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Old Couple's Morning Routine: 40 Years of Love

title: The Hidden Clause
instruction: You are a lawyer in your mid-40s, sitting alone in a sterile office late at night, reading a final settlement you've been fighting for months. You start by reciting the fine print in a rapid, flat monotone—your voice devoid of melody, pushing through each qualifying phrase with clinical accuracy. But as you reach a hidden subclause, a slight tremor of fear creeps in—you realize it undermines everything. Your delivery stumbles, a word gets repeated, you pause to clear your throat. By the end, your voice drops into a gravelly, choked disappointment; you speak the last sentence as if the air has been punched out of you. Let the performance feel organic—hesitate, shift in your chair, lose the thread for a half-second then find it again.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bittersweet Goodbye: Releasing Someone You Love to Their Dream
instruction: Someone you deeply love is leaving—for an opportunity, a calling, a dream that doesn't include you. Begin with forced brightness, your voice trying to be supportive: 'This is amazing for you. This is everything you wanted.' But let the false cheerfulness crack, revealing the grief underneath: 'I'm so proud of you. And my heart is breaking. Both things are true.' Your voice should laugh and cry at once—genuine joy for them mixed with devastating loss for yourself. Speak with tender honesty: 'I don't want to be the person who holds you back. But God, I want to hold you back.' Let your voice be playful and heartbroken: 'Remember when we said we'd always be together? We were such liars.' Smile through tears. Then shift to acceptance that feels like grace: 'Go. Please go. Live that beautiful life.' Your voice becomes generous, loving, free—even as it breaks. End with gratitude that transcends pain: 'Thank you for letting me love you. Even if loving you means letting you leave.' Let peace and agony coexist in your voice—the beauty of loving someone enough to release them.
inspired_by: Processing Discovered Family Secret: Understanding, Then Forgiving

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin by noticing everything in this moment—the sound of their breathing, the hospital room smell, your own physical discomfort from sitting in this chair all night, any hunger or exhaustion you feel. Don't push away the mundane thoughts that intrude—the parking meter that might have expired, the text you forgot to send. Speak to your friend, allowing whatever comes up to come up: maybe it's a memory, maybe it's anger at the unfairness, maybe it's a confession about how scared you are. Let yourself stumble, repeat yourself, contradict yourself. By the end, find yourself in a completely different emotional place than where you started—perhaps you began with numbness and end in raw grief, or began with panic and end in tender acceptance. Let the journey happen without deciding it in advance.

title: Whispered Confession to Your Sleeping Child: The Apology They'll Never Hear
instruction: Your child is asleep. You've been a difficult parent—depressed, absent, angry, struggling. Kneel beside them and begin in a whisper so quiet it barely exists: 'You're so beautiful when you're sleeping. So peaceful.' Your voice is tender but heavy with guilt. Confess what you can't say when they're awake: 'I'm not the parent you deserved. Some days I can barely breathe, let alone be what you need.' Let your voice catch, fighting tears. The vulnerability deepens: 'You look at me like I have answers, and I'm just... lost.' Your whisper becomes almost prayer-like, intimate: 'I'm trying. I promise I'm trying.' Acknowledge their love despite your failings: 'You still reach for my hand. How do you still reach for my hand?' End with a vow spoken in a voice thick with tears you're trying not to let fall: 'Tomorrow I'll be better. Tomorrow I'll try harder.' The silence after should feel like a held breath—love and shame and desperate hope all mixed together.
inspired_by: Processing Discovered Family Secret: Understanding, Then Forgiving

title: Caught in the Act
instruction: You're a parent making silly faces and babbling to your baby in full parentese—high pitch, swooping tones, repetitive sounds—when your neighbor unexpectedly appears at the door. At first you feel a flush of embarrassment, your voice tightening and becoming even more exaggerated as you try to play it off. Continue the baby talk but with a self-conscious edge, sneaking glances at the neighbor. Then your baby giggles, and you forget the audience—your voice drops into a natural, tender warmth, still using that high pitch but now relaxed, genuine, and focused only on your child. Let your pitch waver awkwardly at first, then settle into loving, unhurried rhythms.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Thief and the Guard Dog
instruction: Portray a thief with a stealthy, whispering voice trying to sneak past a guard dog who surprisingly speaks in a loud, authoritative tone. Switch between the thiefs nervous justifications and the dogs stern warnings, adding a comedic twist.

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You are an elderly woman who has been brought to a loud, boisterous locker room by your grandson. The air smells of sweat and chlorine, and you feel utterly out of place—your hearing aid is turned down but the waves of laughter still buffet you. You begin by trying to make a joke about the swim team's posters to your grandson, but your voice is small and you lose your train of thought as two men slap each other on the back. As they ignore you and start planning a poker game in terms you can't follow, your helplessness curdles into a cold, quiet anger. For a moment, just before you speak your final line, you stand straighter and say, loud enough for all to hear, that the swim coach's wife left him last week—a piece of gossip you'd been saving. Your voice breaks with helplessness at first, then hardens with bitterness, and you walk away before anyone can respond.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Nursery Finished at Last
instruction: You are in your third trimester, standing in the newly arranged nursery, holding a small blanket. You talk to your unborn child. Start with deep contemplation—your voice is soft, breathy from the weight in your chest, and you pause to shift your hips or rub your belly. You’re reflecting on the long wait and your exhaustion. As you speak, let a quiet triumph build—your tone brightens, your breathing steadies momentarily, and you smile at the finished room. But then a slight sourness creeps in as you remember the criticism you’ve received about your voice and your choices; your words carry a weary, bitter edge. Let natural sighs and posture adjustments interrupt your speech, and end with a tired but proud sigh.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (very intensely present), Triumph (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Stone
instruction: You are a young laborer, bitter from years of backbreaking work, tasked with shifting a massive stone that everyone else gave up on. As you brace your body and hold your breath, your jaw tightens and your voice comes out in strangled, resentful mutters about the unfairness of it all. Mid-strain, you catch a sliver of golden sunset through the trees—a fleeting awe that softens your bitterness for a second. Then, with a final explosive push, you heave the stone into place. Your words start as choked complaints, break through a grunt of wonder, and end in a raw, triumphant yell as the weight settles.
emotions_sampled: Awe (slightly present), Bitterness (very intensely present), Triumph (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Hush of the Foundling
instruction: You are a man with a deep, gravelly voice, alone in a dusty attic. A child has wandered in, frightened by a mouse. You see the fear in their eyes, but also a flicker of fascination. You begin explaining the mouse's hidden nest, your voice husky and low, almost a whisper. As you speak, a strong, unexpected warmth—a mix of lust for life and profound interest in this young soul—swells in your chest, making your gravelly voice crackle with tenderness. By the end, your voice has softened, but a new, raw longing aches in your words, as if you're confessing a secret hope.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Interest (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Eulogy for the Person Who Saved You
instruction: You're standing at a funeral, speaking about someone who rescued you from the darkest period of your life, but who never knew how much they mattered. Begin with gratitude that makes you smile through tears: 'Five years ago, Sarah found me on a bridge. And she said the strangest thing: 'The sunset's better from over here.'' Let yourself laugh softly at the memory, even as your voice shakes. 'She didn't ask questions. She just stood there with me until I was ready to step back.' Now the grief deepens but is mixed with profound appreciation: 'She probably forgot about it the next day. But I thought about it every single day after. That one moment of kindness gave me five more years.' Your voice breaks, yet there's peace underneath: 'I got to fall in love. I got to see my nephew born. I got to become someone I'm proud of.' End with bittersweet joy: 'Sarah, wherever you are now, I hope you know—you saved my life by offering to watch a sunset. Thank you for those five years. I'm only sorry I never got to tell you in person.'

title: Laughing While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're describing a sunset to someone over the phone—someone who's leaving your life forever by their own choice, but you've agreed to part as friends. Begin with genuine warmth and gentle humor, finding silly metaphors for the colors, laughing softly at your own attempts at poetry. Let bittersweet joy seep in—your voice should hold real happiness at this shared moment even as grief threads through it. Start to crack with the absurdity of it all—you're laughing but there are tears in your voice, describing something beautiful while your world ends. The laughter should be real but painful, each chuckle catching on a sob you're trying to swallow. End with profound gratitude that makes you weep openly—thank them through genuine laughter mixed with tears for this moment, this sunset, this goodbye. Your voice should embody the gorgeous, impossible contradiction of loving someone enough to let them go while it destroys you.
inspired_by: Watching the Sunset Over the Ocean

title: The Unraveling of a Deal
instruction: You are a senior executive in a tense boardroom negotiation. Minutes ago, your rival casually revealed that your company’s most loyal client has just signed with them, a fact you were unaware of. You must maintain your composure as the 'alpha' in the room, but inside you are reeling. Start with a controlled, low-pitched voice, perhaps a touch of envy in your measured words. As the reality sinks in, let astonishment crack through — your pitch rises, words stumble. Then, when you realize the full betrayal and loss, let a wave of sadness wash over you, making your voice heavy, quiet, and raw. Allow natural pauses, a shaky breath, losing your train of thought. End with a simple, heartbreaking admission.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Sadness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for your best friend who made you promise to 'make them laugh one last time.' Start reading the heartfelt words you prepared, but your voice keeps breaking into inappropriate laughter—they would have loved this, the absurdity of grief. 'You always said you'd go out with style.' You're laughing and crying simultaneously. Share a ridiculous memory; your voice lifts with genuine joy, then crashes into a sob mid-sentence. 'God, I miss you already.' The laughter and tears become indistinguishable. Your voice can't decide whether to laugh or break. End with: 'You were my person,' where gratitude, joy, and devastating loss all exist in the same breath. Let your voice embody the beautiful contradiction of celebrating someone while your heart is shattering.
inspired_by: Getting the Job After Years of Rejection

title: The Impossible Survival
instruction: You've just found someone alive who shouldn't be - your child after a disaster, a lover after you'd given up hope, yourself in a mirror after you nearly ended everything. Start with shock, voice exploding out: 'You're HERE. You're - oh god, you're BREATHING.' Raw wonder collides with rage at the universe, at fate, at whatever nearly took them. 'How DARE the world almost - do you understand what almost...?' Your voice breaks between fierce protectiveness and helpless terror. The awe at their existence becomes almost violent in its intensity: 'Look at me. LOOK at me. You're real. Say something, I need to hear...' End with your voice collapsing into something between a laugh and a sob, tender and fierce at once: 'You're impossible. You're perfect. Don't you ever... don't you ever almost...' Let reverence and rage and relief crash into each other until you can't separate them.

title: The Last Lap Confession
instruction: You are in the middle of a deep-water lap pool, pushing through the last 50 meters of a grueling set. As you turn your head to breathe, you realize your fiancé's mother, who is standing at the edge, has just shouted something about postponing the wedding indefinitely. Each gasp of air is your only chance to plead your case—you are desperate, helpless, and furious with the chlorine burning your throat. Start with frantic, broken arguments between strokes, sputtering and coughing, but by the final wall, your voice sinks into a quieter, more resigned disgust, as you realize she's already left the pool deck.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Skin Remembers
instruction: You are alone in the home you once shared with someone you loved deeply, who is now gone forever—through death, divorce, or departure. You find a piece of their clothing and hold it to your face. Begin by whispering what you miss most—not grand statements, but tiny specifics: the way they hummed while cooking, how their hand felt in yours, the precise sound of their breathing while they slept. Let yourself be flooded by sensory memories. Your whispers may dissolve into silence, into crying without sound, or into a fragile, aching laugh at a memory. This is not performed grief—it is private, as if you are confessing to the walls. End by speaking directly to them as if they could hear you, your voice barely audible, saying what you never got to say or what you said but need to say again.

title: Giving a Toast at Your Ex-Lover's Wedding
instruction: You're standing at a microphone at the wedding reception of someone you never stopped loving, giving a toast as their 'dear friend.' Begin with practiced charm and humor—funny stories, warm wishes, your voice steady and generous. But underneath, something else bleeds through. As you describe their happiness, your voice catches on certain words. You find yourself genuinely celebrating their joy while your heart shatters. Laugh at a memory, but let it turn slightly wet. Your congratulations are completely sincere—you truly want them to be happy—yet each word costs you something. End with a genuine blessing for their future, your voice thick with simultaneous joy for them and grief for yourself, smiling through tears you can't quite hide. Raise your glass with a hand that trembles slightly. The arc moves through polished performance to authentic contradiction—real happiness for them, real heartbreak for yourself, existing in the same moment.
inspired_by: Talking Through a Gas Mask During a Chemical Leak

title: The Unbroken Word
instruction: You are a child, around nine years old, standing at the edge of the schoolyard, watching the other kids play a game you can't join without being mocked. You're disgusted—by their easy laughter, by your own tongue that betrays you. But you're also fiercely proud of the secret world you've built in your head, a kingdom of perfect words. A boy you envy skips past, and you blurt out a single, hard-fought syllable of protest. You feel the jealousy burn as you start to speak, but by the time you force the next sound through the block—a full sentence—you end with a sharp, defiant pride, your voice cracking but steady, your chin lifting even as your hands tremble.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Pride (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Shielding Your Child from the Monster You've Become
instruction: You're barricading your child in a room, knowing you're infected and will soon lose your mind entirely. Begin with fierce, almost violent urgency—sharp commands to stay inside, to not open the door no matter what they hear. Your voice is strong, protective, warrior-like. But as you speak, something flickers—a moment where you forget a word, where your hands shake uncontrollably, where rage surges through you for no reason and you have to fight it down. You press your forehead against the door, and now you're pleading with them, voice cracking between fury at your helplessness and desperate love. You're telling them everything at once—how to survive, how much you love them, begging forgiveness for leaving. By the end, you're roaring and sobbing simultaneously, pounding the door in anguish while screaming at them to remember you as you were, not as you're becoming, your words dissolving into inhuman sounds as you lose yourself completely, the last human thing about you being the tears streaming down your face.

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, giving a toast, and you're genuinely happy for them—but they're moving across the world tomorrow, and you're losing the person who's been your anchor for twenty years. Start with warm laughter in your voice, celebrating them, genuine joy threading through your words. 'You deserve every happiness.' But as you speak, something else rises—grief sitting right beside the gratitude. Your voice starts to waver between smiling and breaking. You're laughing at a shared memory, but tears are in your throat. You mean every beautiful thing you're saying, and simultaneously your heart is shattering. End with a contradiction you can't resolve: thanking them for everything while your voice fractures on the reality that everything is ending, joy and devastation inseparable in the same breath.

title: The Unfinished Porch Swing
instruction: You're sitting on the back steps of your house, elbows on your knees, staring at the half-built porch swing your son promised to finish before he moved away. It's been three years. Your chest is tight, breath shallow, and you keep rubbing the splintered wood between your fingers, voice low and gravelly. Start with muttered, resigned disappointment, noticing every flaw in the wood. As you speak, let a new, fiercer emotion surface — a heavy, reluctant but genuine pride for the work he started, even if he never finished. Let your voice crack with that shift, not from tears, but from a sudden depth of feeling that surprises you.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're screaming at your teenage daughter who just came home drunk at 3 AM. Your voice is explosive: 'You could have died!' You're pacing, furious, your words coming fast and sharp. She's yelling back, defiant. But then mid-rage, something cracks inside you and your voice breaks completely: 'I can't lose you. I can't.' Now you're sobbing, collapsing into a chair, and the truth pours out—her older brother died in a car accident five years ago, same age she is now, and you're terrified history will repeat itself. Your voice is raw, desperate: 'Every time you leave the house, I see his face.' She's quiet now. She comes closer. When she says 'Mom' softly, you look up. The rage is gone, replaced by naked fear and overwhelming love. End with your voice shaking but softer: 'I need you to understand what you mean to me,' the fierceness transformed into something unbearably tender and vulnerable.

title: Whispering Your Confession to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3am. Your partner is asleep beside you. You begin speaking so softly they can't hear, confessing that today you saved lives—you were the hero everyone needed—but you came home and couldn't stop shaking. Your voice is barely audible, tender and broken, admitting that you're terrified of the person you have to be out there: competent, controlled, certain. You tell their sleeping form that sometimes you envy people who are allowed to fall apart, who don't have to be the strong one. Your whisper catches in your throat as you confess your deepest fear: that you've been strong for so long you've forgotten how to let anyone catch you. Reach out as if to touch them but don't, your voice becoming even softer, more fragile, as you admit you don't know how to ask for help, don't even know if you remember how to receive it. End with a silence that speaks louder than words, then the smallest, most vulnerable whisper: 'I'm so tired of being brave.'
inspired_by: Hazmat Evacuation: Overriding Fear with Procedural Competence

title: Washing Their Shirt
instruction: Alone in your apartment at 2 AM, you are hand-washing your lover's shirt in the bathroom sink—the one they left behind before leaving the country, possibly forever. The scene is almost silent. Feel the actual temperature of the water running over your hands, the specific texture of the wet fabric, the faint scent of their cologne still lingering even after soap. As you methodically work the cloth through your fingers, whisper the things you never said when they were here—confessions that are only safe now in their absence. Let the physical act of washing, wringing, and smoothing the shirt draw out a progression from numb, mechanical denial of their absence to quiet, devastating acceptance that they are truly gone. Your voice should barely rise above a whisper, your breathing becoming the loudest sound as emotion overtakes you.

title: The Plot Thickens
instruction: You're at a small writers' group meeting, seated across from a woman who just got praised for her manuscript — a project you secretly wanted to write. Your allergies are relentless: your eyes water, your nose drips, and you keep stifling sneezes. Start by feeling deeply ashamed of your ugly symptoms and burning with envy as she talks. As she describes a twist in her plot, your genuine interest takes over. Your voice shifts from thick, scratchy, and apologetic to brighter and more engaged, even as you pause to sniffle or wipe your eyes, finally asking a question that reveals your fascination.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Interest (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Skin and Storm
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, a diagnosis—and your lover is touching you, trying to comfort you, but their hands on your skin ignite something complicated. Begin in near-paralysis, your body rigid with shock, your voice barely functioning. As their touch persists, you feel sensation returning in waves—rage at the unfairness, hunger for life and connection, grief that makes your bones ache, desire that feels almost violent in its intensity. Let your voice move between gasping breaths, moans that could be pleasure or pain, and fragmented words. By the end, you're fully alive in your body again, a mess of sensation—angry, aroused, heartbroken, and completely present.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed. For your entire life, she withheld approval, always finding something wrong with your choices. You begin this scene carrying decades of seeking her validation, feeling small and inadequate. But as you hold her hand and speak to her in these final moments, something shifts inside you. You realize mid-scene that you no longer need her permission to exist fully. Your voice should start tentative, almost apologetic, seeking approval even now. Let it gradually transform into claiming your right to have lived your life exactly as you did. End by speaking to her with love, but from a place of complete self-possession. The transformation is from seeking permission to granting it to yourself.
inspired_by: Actor's ego-state is in the way — feeling not good enough, too old, not talented enough

title: Bedtime Story for a Dying Partner
instruction: You're lying beside your partner in hospice, their breathing shallow, and you're telling them the story of your life together—but making it a fairy tale for children. Your voice is soft, intimate, almost a whisper. 'Once upon a time, there were two people who found each other...' Your throat keeps tightening. You make your arguments into dragon battles, your first apartment into a castle, your struggles into quests. The playfulness keeps breaking against the weight of goodbye. When you get to 'and they lived...' you can't finish it. Let your voice crack and recover and crack again. This isn't performance—it's the sound of someone trying to be brave enough to let go while their heart is shattering. End with the whispered words you've been too scared to say all night.

title: The Unwanted Gift
instruction: You're slouched deep in an old armchair, phone pressed to your ear, your body collapsed, spine curved. At first you're genuinely confused — a neighbor has left a 'thank you' gift at your door after you helped them move a couch, but you suspect they know something. Your voice is mushy, lazy, jaw barely moving. As you speak, gratitude creeps in — you almost mean it — but malice seethes underneath: you're not thankful at all, you're angry they're prying. By the end, your polite words drip with veiled threat. Let your breathing be shallow, your tone flat but wickedly sharp on the final phrases.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Taking the Hit
instruction: You're a teenage boy at a rough pickup basketball game. A taller, older player elbows you hard in the ribs as you go for a rebound. You crumple, letting out a sharp 'oof' as the air leaves you. You stagger, one hand on the court floor, trying to catch your breath while the game pauses. In that moment, you feel a sharp fear—this guy might do it again. As someone asks if you're okay, you try to focus on your breath, confused by the sudden pain, and force out a shaky, 'Yeah, I'm good... just... give me a second.' By the end, your voice steadies slightly but still carries a tremor. Speak the line between gasps, with a hint of concentration as you push the pain aside to get back up.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Confusion (slightly present), Fear (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Missing Piece
instruction: You're at a bar alone, nursing a glass of water, trying to remember where you left a prized possession—a ring your grandmother gave you. You’re slightly confused, retracing your steps. As you talk to yourself, you take frequent gulps of water. Start with a hazy, searching tone, letting the confusion fade into a slow, contemplative realization. Let your words be interrupted by the wet glottal stops of swallowing, a little cough, a pause to stare at the glass. By the end, your voice settles into a quiet, thoughtful certainty as you piece together the memory.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Scent of Her Hair
instruction: You are a child, maybe eight years old, hiding under a heavy wooden desk in a dusty attic while playing hide-and-seek. You hear footsteps approaching and you press your back against the wall, trying not to giggle. But then you catch a scent — your mother's perfume, old and faint, clinging to a forgotten coat hanging nearby. Your breath catches. Suddenly the game feels unimportant. You reach out and touch the fabric, and a vivid memory floods you: her tucking you into bed, her hair falling across your face. Your voice comes out hushed, almost to yourself. Start with a playful, whispered 'oh no, she's coming,' but then let your voice slow and deepen, filled with wonder and ache. Stumble over your words as you describe the smell and the memory — you're distracted, caught off guard by how much you miss her. End with a long, soft sigh, barely above a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Longing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Thank You for Breaking Me Open
instruction: Express profound gratitude to someone who devastated you—a betrayal, a divorce, a shattering loss—and genuinely mean it. Begin with a laugh that's real but edged with disbelief at what you're about to say. Let joy and grief live together in every sentence: thank them for the pain that taught you who you are, even as your voice breaks remembering how much it hurt. Smile through descriptions of your worst moments, finding strange beauty in your own breaking. Your emotional arc should move from bitter irony to authentic appreciation to profound sadness to unexpected peace. End with your voice soft, wondering, almost confused by your own forgiveness, as if you've discovered something true about love and loss that you didn't know you were capable of understanding.
inspired_by: An Apology to a Future Self

title: The Howl: Discovering the Unforgivable
instruction: You've just discovered a betrayal so profound it rewrites your entire history—your partner's affair, a parent's lie that shaped your life, a friend's decades-long deception. Begin with shocked stillness, your voice barely working: 'I found... I know what you did.' You're trying to stay controlled, to be reasonable, but fury is building like pressure in your chest. 'How long? How fucking long?' Your voice escalates into raw, primal rage—you might scream, you might laugh bitterly, you might make sounds that aren't quite words. But then it breaks. The anger collapses into something more terrifying: grief. You're sobbing, gasping, 'I trusted you with everything. Everything.' Your voice swings wildly between wanting to destroy them and wanting to understand, between hatred and the unbearable pain of still loving them despite this. You're protective of the person you were before you knew, fierce about defending that innocence, but helpless because you can't unknow this. End in that impossible place between wanting them gone and wanting them to somehow undo this, your voice raw, destroyed, yet still searching for something to hold onto.
inspired_by: Working Near an Industrial Furnace: Heat Warping Perception

title: Hearing Your Child Get Bullied and Intervening
instruction: You're picking up your kid from school and overhear another child saying cruel things. Your child's small, hurt voice. The bully's mean, confident one. Then YOUR voice — the protective parent. Don't shout. The most terrifying parent voice is quiet, controlled, and aimed at the bully's eye level: 'What did you just say to my child?' Low, steady, unsmiling. Then turning to your child with instant warmth: 'Come here, baby.' Two completely different voices in the same breath. Both genuine.

title: The Apology I Owe You
instruction: You're alone in your dark apartment, phone pressed to your ear, calling someone you've been avoiding for weeks after a stupid, selfish mistake. You're exhausted—bone-tired from carrying this shame—and you have to force your voice to be clear and slightly louder than usual, checking every few seconds that they're still there. Start with a tense, careful tone, holding back the raw embarrassment, but as you speak, let the fatigue crack your composure. By the end, you're not just explaining—you're surrendering, your voice softer, more honest, even as you stumble over your own words.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Professional: Hospital Administrator Denies Treatment a Patient Can't Afford
instruction: Phone conversation with insurance. Your administrative voice is professional, citing protocol. But the person on the other end is a patient you've met. Your voice continues the denial with detached politeness while you're aware of the human cost. Your breathing stays controlled—professionalism is your armor. You're speaking policy while someone dies. After the call, your voice becomes someone who participated in triage from behind a desk. You're protected by procedure while someone pays with their life.

title: Visiting a Parent With Dementia Who Doesn't Recognize You
instruction: You walk in and your parent looks at you like a stranger. Your voice cracks on 'Hi Mom/Dad.' They're looking for someone else. Your voice is trying to be normal—'It's me, your child.' But inside you're devastated. Your voice keeps trying—telling them things, hoping recognition will come. It doesn't. Your voice becomes smaller. You're a stranger to someone who made you. Your voice is alone in the room with someone you love who's gone.

title: The Last Letter from the Trenches
instruction: You are a soldier writing what you know will be your final letter home to someone you love deeply. Begin with a forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them from the truth of where you are and what's coming. As you write, the sounds of distant artillery grow closer, and the pretense crumbles. Your voice should shift from bright reassurance to raw confession—admitting your fear, your regrets, the things you never said. End with a moment of profound tenderness, as if you're touching their face one last time through your words. Let your voice break where it needs to break. This isn't about being brave; it's about being honest in your final moments.

title: The Game They Watched Without Me
instruction: You're a teenager lying on your bed at home, wearing a CPAP mask. Outside, you hear your friends cheering through a video call—they're watching the championship game you were supposed to be at. Your voice is muffled by the mask, and you have to push extra air to be heard. Start with a heavy, disappointed sigh, the hiss of the machine filling the pause. Then, as you speak to the empty room, let that disappointment slowly soften into a quieter, tired acceptance—you’re stuck here, but maybe you can still catch the highlights. Remember to breathe audibly through the mask, adjust the strap once, and let your tone drop when you realize no one can hear you anyway.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your parent about something they did years ago that shaped who you became—something you've never had the courage to say aloud. Start with your voice small and shaking, perhaps even apologetic, as decades of learned deference try to silence you. But as you speak, feel your younger self—the child who was hurt, overlooked, or misunderstood—rising up and demanding to be heard. Let your anger build, not as explosive rage, but as steady, undeniable truth. By the end, arrive at something unexpected: not forgiveness exactly, but a clear-eyed understanding that they were flawed and human, doing their broken best. Let your final moment contain both your legitimate anger and a surprising, complicated tenderness toward the imperfect person before you.

title: The Photograph on the Pillow
instruction: You're lying flat on your stomach on a bed, face down, phone screen inches from your eyes. You've found an old photo of someone you used to be close to. At first, you're completely absorbed—intense interest in every detail, your voice quiet and pressed against the mattress, breath short. As you keep looking, a deep longing creeps in, making your words slower, heavier. But then a bitter sourness rises—you remember how it ended. The last line tastes of that sourness, spoken with your cheek still against the pillow.
emotions_sampled: Interest (very intensely present), Longing (clearly present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unsent Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a final letter to your dying parent, but halfway through, you realize you're saying what you think they want to hear, not what you actually feel. Start by reading the 'perfect' words you've written—dutiful, loving, appropriate. Then let something真实 crack through: a memory that contradicts the narrative, a resentment you've never voiced, or a tender truth you've been too afraid to speak. By the end, you're no longer reading at all—you're speaking from a place you didn't know existed. Let the transition be messy, uncertain, as if you're discovering your real feelings in real time. The challenge isn't to perform grief 'correctly'—it's to stumble into what you genuinely feel beneath the performance you've been rehearsing your whole life.

title: The Last Leaf on the Porch
instruction: You are an elderly woman, 82, sitting on your screened porch. The autumn wind is cold, and your hip aches from the old chair where you've shifted your weight to one side. You hold a single, dried oak leaf that fell onto your sweater. At first, you feel a sharp contempt — for the leaf's stubborn clinging, for the neighbor boy who mows too loud, for the world that you feel has passed you by. But as you speak, your concentration deepens; you trace the veins of the leaf, remembering when you picked one just like it for your late husband. Your voice starts clipped and bitter, but by the end, it softens into a quiet, sad recognition — loss concentrates into a fragile peace. Speak as if you are alone, muttering to yourself, your voice creaking slightly, shifting with your weight in the chair.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: After the Final Round
instruction: You're a seventeen-year-old boy, alone in your room, just having won an online tournament you've been grinding for months. The screen shows your victory—but you don't feel the rush you expected. You're standing with your weight shifted to one hip, fist loosely pressed against your thigh, staring at the pixelated trophy. Start speaking from a hollow, drained place, your voice flat and distant—recounting what you've lost to get here. Let a flicker of wonder creep in as you glance at the screen, then let a reluctant, crooked smile tug at your voice as you realize you actually did it. The numbness fades into a quiet, tired pride. (Your words: about 50-70, spoken aloud to no one but yourself, with pauses, a sigh, maybe you shift your weight again mid-sentence.)
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Awe (slightly present), Triumph (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Locket
instruction: You are an elderly man, curled up on a cold attic floor, knees pressed to your chest. You've just found a locket you thought was lost decades ago, containing a faded photo of your late spouse. At first, your voice is tight with anxiety from the cramped position and the shock of the discovery. As you speak, affection floods through you, softening your breath and warming your words. Briefly, a wave of relief washes over you, as if they are here with you now, and your voice lifts just a little before settling into a tender, weary whisper. Let the huddled position compress your voice, but let the memories slowly unfurl it.
emotions_sampled: Affection (extremely present), Infatuation (clearly present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Threshold Blessing
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you deeply love who is leaving—not dying, but departing in a way that feels permanent: moving to another country, choosing a path that diverges from yours, or leaving to become someone you won't fully recognize. Begin with forced brightness, trying to give them a cheerful send-off, your voice artificially upbeat. But then let a specific image enter your awareness—something that symbolizes your entire relationship: a particular quality of light, a recurring place, an object, a gesture, a moment frozen in time. As this image becomes vivid, let it shatter your false cheerfulness. Your emotions should transform into a complex knot: fierce joy at who they're becoming, deep grief at what you're losing, gratitude for what they've given you, and resentment that they get to leave while you stay. Your voice should move from bright and controlled to broken open—laughing and crying simultaneously. End by giving them a genuine blessing, your voice raw with all these contradictions at once, wishing them well even as your heart is breaking.

title: Your Vulnerability Being Used Against You Later
instruction: Someone threw your confession back at you. Your voice is devastated, sharper: 'How could you use that against me?' You're understanding you can't be safe with them. Your voice becomes colder, controlled. 'I trusted you with that,' delivered with real pain. They defend themselves and your voice becomes icier. By the end, erecting walls, voice distant and protective.

title: The Trapped Truth
instruction: You are an older man with a naturally deep, gravelly voice, seated on a park bench hunched forward, chin pressed to your chest as you stare at a faded photograph in your hands. You're speaking to a photo of your late wife, whom you've just discovered kept a secret from you—a brief, kind affair during a difficult year of your marriage. Start with a heavy, weary curiosity, voice creaky and muffled as you mumble through the dampened sound of your larynx, trying to grasp the truth. As you speak, the interest grows sharp and raw—you're not angry, but fascinated by her hidden depth, your tone shifting to a trembling, almost tender awe, the gravel thinning into a fragile wonder. Let your voice crack and drift, lose a thought as you study the photo, then find it again with a quieter, awed breath.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Moment You See Your Child is in Danger
instruction: You're watching your teenager from across a crowded space and suddenly everything sharpens—you see it. The signs you've been missing. The weight loss, the hollow eyes, the way they're disappearing. Start with that sickening clarity, breath punched out of you: 'Oh god. Oh god, how did I not—' Your voice should escalate from horror to fierce, almost violent protectiveness. You're talking to yourself, to them, to the universe. 'No. No, I see it now. I see you now.' Let rage at yourself explode—you should have noticed sooner. But let that rage transform mid-sentence into desperate love: 'Baby, I'm so sorry, I couldn't see, but I see you now, I've got you—' Your voice breaks between strength and terror. You're making promises, pledging everything: 'I will not lose you. Do you hear me? I will not—' But let doubt creep in, the fear that you're too late, that seeing clearly now doesn't undo the months you were blind. End with your voice raw, stripped down to its most primal: 'Please still be okay. Please let there be time.' The last word should barely make it out, a prayer offered to anyone listening.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your parent's hospice bedside in the quiet hours before dawn. They've been holding on, waiting for something. You begin with desperate control, trying to be strong: 'I need you to know it's okay to go. I'm going to be okay.' Your voice fractures as the reality hits: 'That's a lie. I'm not going to be okay. I'm terrified.' You're crying now, but pushing through: 'But I love you too much to make you stay for me. You've been holding on because you're worried about me, aren't you?' Your voice softens with tender recognition: 'You've always protected me. Even now, even like this.' By the end, you find a strange, painful peace: 'So I'm giving you permission. You can let go. I release you. And I promise—I promise I'll find my way.' The final words are both goodbye and gratitude, spoken through tears but with genuine strength.

title: The Revenge That Became a Joke
instruction: You are an older man, traditionally gruff and imposing, telling a friend about a recent confrontation with a younger rival who tried to undermine you. You start off indignant, your voice deep and tight with anger—but as you recall the exact moment your rival slipped on a wet floor and fell flat on his face, a laugh catches in your throat. You try to continue angrily, but the memory overwhelms you. Your voice breaks into wheezes, high-pitched squeaks, and gasping silences as you struggle to finish the sentence. Let the anger dissolve into helpless, genuine laughter—your deep voice cracking, your breathing spasmodic. End with pure elation, still chuckling as you whisper the punchline.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Contraction
instruction: You are an older, androgynous person alone in a sterile delivery room, laboring with a child you never wanted from a partner you now despise. Between the waves of pain, your voice is flat with bitterness and disgust—at the situation, at your own body for betraying you. But as a contraction crests, your mind flashes unbidden to a long-ago night of raw, forbidden lust, and the moan that escapes you is part agony, part longing. Speak to the empty room—accusing the child, the partner, yourself—letting the pain pull you from cold, clipped disgust into a guttural, desperate plea that tastes of both hatred and hunger.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Bitterness (clearly present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight of Letting Go
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's unconscious, but you need to tell her everything you never said. Begin holding tremendous tension—grief you've been carrying for days, fear of this moment, regret for lost time. As you speak to her, physically let your body sink deeper into the chair with each confession, feeling the literal heaviness of your sorrow pulling you down. Your shoulders, your arms, your head—everything becomes impossibly heavy. But as you finally say 'I love you' and 'it's okay to go,' allow that weight to transform into a different kind of heaviness: peaceful, surrendered, deeply sad but no longer fighting. Your voice should shift from tight and controlled to released and flowing, like something that's been dammed up finally breaking free. End in quiet acceptance, your body completely relaxed into grief rather than braced against it.

title: The Last Letter Home
instruction: You're recording a final message to your family before embarking on a one-way mission to deep space—you'll never see Earth again, never hold them again. Start with forced brightness, trying to make this easy for them: 'Hey everyone, it's me...' But your voice keeps catching. You tell them about the view of Earth from here, and suddenly you're crying—quiet, devastating tears you can't hide anymore. 'I can see our house from here. I can see... everything.' Your voice breaks completely. Then, gathering yourself with tremendous effort, you transform: finding genuine peace, even joy, in what you're about to do. 'I'm not afraid anymore. I'm ready. And I need you to know—this is exactly where I'm supposed to be.' End with a whispered goodbye that contains both infinite sadness and absolute certainty: 'I love you. I love you so much. And I'm going now.' The emotional journey must move from brittle optimism through shattering grief to transcendent acceptance.

title: The Last Train Platform
instruction: You're standing on a train platform at dawn, watching someone you love board a train to a hospice facility across the country—this is your final goodbye. Begin by noticing small, ordinary details about them with forced cheerfulness, trying to memorize everything. As the departure time approaches, let your voice crack as you shift between desperate attempts to keep things light and the crushing weight of permanence. End in whispered fragments—half-finished sentences about all the things you never said, your voice barely holding together as you speak to them even after they've disappeared from view. Move from brittle optimism through barely-controlled panic to raw, quiet devastation.

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Own Memorial Service
instruction: You're a ghost, attending your own funeral, watching people eulogize a version of you that's both true and completely wrong, and you're caught between laughter and heartbreak. Begin with surprised, almost giddy observation of the absurdities—someone who barely knew you telling a wildly inaccurate story, the flowers you were allergic to covering your casket. Let genuine laughter bubble up at the contradictions, the theater of grief from people who didn't show up when you were alive. Transition into bittersweet warmth as you see the people who truly loved you, voice cracking with gratitude as you witness their authentic pain and beautiful memories. Shift into profound sadness mixed with wonder as you realize all the things you'll miss, all the love you didn't know you had, speaking their names like benedictions. End with simultaneous grief and peace—your voice carrying both the ache of goodbye and the strange beauty of being released, laughing softly through tears as you let yourself go. Your delivery should capture the surreal collision of humor and heartbreak, gratitude and loss, the strange gift of witnessing your own ending.
inspired_by: Electrical Burn Aftermath: Consciousness Returning with Pain

title: The Sixteenth One
instruction: You're an older man, a little drunk and deeply tired, kneeling on the bed after a long day of bad news. Your partner has you over their knee for a scene — you're counting each spank, but your mind keeps slipping. The first few strikes barely register through the haze of bourbon and exhaustion. Around the tenth, the sting cuts through. By the sixteenth, the pain and the shame you've been carrying all evening collide — your voice cracks, the count dissolves into a raw, half-sobbed apology. Let the alcohol muffle your reactions at first, then let the real hurt surface. Fumble a number, gasp sharply, let the last word trail into a shaky breath. Speak as if you're holding back tears but failing.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: I Would Burn the World
instruction: You're a parent whose child has just been denied life-saving treatment due to bureaucratic cruelty. You begin with cold, barely controlled rage—your voice tight, vibrating with the effort to maintain composure as you speak to the administrator. But then the dam breaks. Your voice explodes into primal fury, words coming fast and sharp, threatening, desperate, anything to make them understand. You would destroy everything for your child. Then, mid-sentence, the rage shatters into helplessness. Your voice cracks completely as you realize your power ends here—you cannot save them no matter how fierce you are. You collapse into begging, your powerful fury dissolving into a parent's most vulnerable plea: 'Please. Please.' The word holds both ferocious love and absolute powerlessness, strength and devastation intertwined.

title: The Blue Blanket
instruction: Late at night, you're speaking in barely audible whispers to your sleeping partner about something you've never told anyone—a feeling or experience from very early childhood that has no words, only sensations and impressions. Maybe it's a color that made you feel safe, a recurring dream from before language, a texture or smell that still makes you cry without knowing why, or the feeling of being held (or not held) as an infant. Start with halting, uncertain whispers, struggling to find language for pre-verbal experience. Let your breathing change as you access these wordless memories. Allow long silences where you're simply feeling rather than speaking. Your body remembers what your mind cannot fully grasp. End with a soft, almost childlike vulnerability, perhaps touching your partner's hand as if you're that infant reaching out, speaking the unspeakable and feeling, for the first time, that it's safe to exist in this fragile, wordless truth.

title: Pleasure Affirmation
instruction: You're being affirmed in your pleasure by your partner. They're watching your response and actively celebrating it: 'I love how you respond.' Your voice, which might normally be self-conscious about pleasure, becomes more confident. You're given permission to have pleasure. Your partner's voice is actively encouraging you to be louder, more present: 'Don't hold back.' Your voice becomes less controlled, more authentic. You're learning that your pleasure is valued, that your body's responses are celebrated. This is less about sex and more about being allowed to be yourself. Your voice at the end should sound like someone who's been given permission to fully inhabit their own body.

title: The Scorecard
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl at a house party, in a dim hallway, leaning against the wall. Across from you is a guy your age you barely know—you've been flirting, but now he's suggesting you go upstairs. You feel a hot flush of disgust at how transactional this is, how he's treating you like a prize. Your voice starts out taut with helplessness, small and giggly to hide how trapped you feel. As you reply, let your words get shorter, colder, until a sharp note of pride cuts through—you refuse to be just a notch on his bedpost. Speak low so his friends in the other room don't hear. End with a defiant little smirk in your tone, even if your heart is pounding.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Disgust (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning with Your Father
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in the early dawn light. He's been unconscious for days, but suddenly his eyes open and he recognizes you. You have maybe five minutes before he slips away forever. Begin with shock and disbelief that he's actually awake and aware. As you speak to him, let yourself move through everything you've never been able to say—the childhood moments he missed, the ways he hurt you, but also the specific memories that shaped who you became. Your emotional journey must travel from that initial frozen shock, through anger and grief, and finally arrive at a place of unexpected tenderness and release. Let your voice break and rebuild. By the end, you're not just saying goodbye to him—you're releasing the version of yourself that needed his approval. The final words should carry both sorrow and strange, quiet liberation.

title: Laughing Through Your Goodbye Speech
instruction: You're leaving—a city, a job, a community that saved you—and you're giving a farewell speech. You promised yourself you'd keep it light: 'I came, you were wonderful, I'm going, that's that.' You start with humor, your voice deliberately bright, making jokes about the abbreviated version of your time here. You're laughing as you list the highlights, each sentence ruthlessly cheerful. But the laughter becomes strained, then wet. You keep trying to joke—'And that's the condensed version!'—but your voice is breaking around the words, tears mixing with chuckles. The efficiency you're forcing feels both necessary and unbearably sad. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice cracking as you try to express bottomless gratitude while your heart is shattering at leaving. End on a phrase that's half-laugh, half-sob: 'Thank you for everything I'm not saying.' Let the audience hear both the joy of what was and the grief of what's ending, inseparable and equally true.

title: Acceptance Letter Magic
instruction: The email opens and it says yes. Your voice comes out as a sound first, not words—a gasp, a laugh, a cry. 'They said yes. They actually said—' Words are almost impossible. Breathing becomes hyperventilation-adjacent but joyful. 'Oh my god. Oh my god. OH MY GOD.' Vocal tone is climbing, lighting up. Physical: you're jumping, crying, vibrating. 'I did it. I actually did it.' The voice moves from disbelief to ecstatic celebration. By the end, you're saying it over and over, each time belief landing a little more: 'I got in. I'm in. I'm actually in.'

title: Protecting Your Partner From the Truth That Will Destroy Them
instruction: You've just learned something catastrophic—their family has been lying to them for years, or you've been diagnosed with something terminal, or you made a choice that will end everything between you. They're looking at you with complete trust, asking 'What's wrong?' Start with frantic deflection, your voice too bright, trying to protect them: 'Nothing, I'm fine, really.' But they know you too well. Your composure shatters—rage erupts, not at them but at the universe, the unfairness, your own powerlessness. You might yell, pace, your voice breaking on 'It's not supposed to be like this!' Then collapse into raw helplessness, sinking down, your voice reduced to ragged whispers as you finally tell them the truth. End in fierce, desperate love—grabbing their hands, your voice both breaking and strong as you swear whatever comes next, you face it together.
inspired_by: Your Sibling Asking About Your Trauma

title: The Unreturned Call
instruction: You are an older woman with a deliberately sweet, high-pitched voice, sitting on a park bench. You've been waiting for a phone call from your estranged daughter for over an hour, and your patience is gone. Start by muttering irritably about the waste of time, picking at a loose thread on your coat, checking your phone repeatedly. But as you begin to speak, the impatience cracks—your voice softens, you trail off mid-sentence, and a deep, raw longing for her to simply know you love her takes over. Let your breath catch, let the irritation dissolve into a fragile hope that maybe she'll still ring. Speak naturally, with all the hesitations and shifts of real thought.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Longing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You are whispering to your former lover in the dark, the first time you've been alone together in years. Begin wrapped in protective numbness, your voice carefully controlled, your body held tight—you've built walls to survive without them. You're just here to return something they left behind, nothing more. But as you speak, their familiar scent, the particular way they breathe, the specific warmth of their presence begins to dissolve your defenses. Your whisper should gradually crack, your breath becoming less even, your body beginning to remember what your mind has tried to forget. This is not reconciliation—this is the terrible vulnerability of realizing you're not as over them as you needed to believe. End on the edge of tears you're fighting not to shed, your voice barely holding together.

title: The Last Bedside Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They're unconscious, but you need to say what you've never said. Start with careful, measured words—an apology for all the years of distance, the phone calls not returned. Your voice is steady, clinical almost, like you're reporting facts. But as you confess how much you needed them, how you're still that child waiting for approval, your throat begins to tighten. The words start fracturing. You realize they'll never answer, never tell you it's okay. End with your voice barely above a whisper, breaking on 'I love you' as if the words are being torn from somewhere deep inside. Let the silence after hold all the years you wasted.

title: The Unfinished Letter
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. She keeps asking you questions about your life—questions you've always had perfect answers for, questions about your career, your relationships, your dreams. But tonight, for the first time, you can't bring yourself to perform certainty anymore. Start by trying to give her the answers she expects, the ones that will comfort her. But as the scene progresses, let yourself admit the truth: you don't know if you made the right choices, you don't know where you're going, you don't know if you'll be okay without her. Move from protective confidence to raw, tender uncertainty. Let your voice crack. Let the relief of honesty mix with the grief of goodbye.

title: The Whispered Truce
instruction: You are a stage actor in full costume, waiting in the wings during a live performance. Your child, also in the show, is crying offstage because they forgot a line. You need to calm them in a stage whisper—loud enough for the back row to hear, over-articulating every consonant—while the orchestra plays softly. Start with a bitter edge: you're irritated that this is happening mid-show, your jaw tight, your eyes darting to the stage manager. As you speak, your anger softens into tender weariness. You shift your weight, adjust your prop sword, and even pause to cough quietly behind your hand. By the end, your voice cracks with love, though the bitterness never fully leaves. Say about 60 words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Thanking Someone Who Destroyed You
instruction: You're speaking at a retirement party for your former boss/mentor who, years ago, took credit for your work and derailed your career. Everyone expects a warm tribute. They're sitting in front of you, beaming, basking in praise, seemingly oblivious to what they did to you. Begin with professional composure, offering the expected gratitude. As you speak, let contradictory emotions flood through: genuine gratitude for what they did teach you, rage at what they stole, love for who they were to you once, contempt for their selective memory. Follow their reactions—their proud smile, their nodding acceptance of praise—and let it fuel your journey through this impossible emotional terrain. Find unexpected ways to make them really HEAR you: a pointed story, a pause that grows too long, a compliment that cuts both ways. End in a place where you've somehow integrated all these contradictions—you mean every word of thanks and you mean every word of accusation, and both truths can exist simultaneously. Your voice should carry both blessing and curse.
inspired_by: An actor is dealing with another actor who is unresponsive or uninvolved

title: Concussion Confusion: Something Is Wrong
instruction: You've hit your head and something isn't right. Your processing speed is halved — long pauses searching for words you know. You repeat yourself without realizing it. Your name takes a moment to recall. The voice is monotone, slightly too loud (can't self-monitor volume). Include the terrifying moment of clarity where you realize you might be seriously hurt, followed by the fog closing back in. Make it genuinely unsettling, not comedic.

title: The Pill That Couldn't Hold the Tears
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman who has just taken a tranquilizer to steady your nerves after a painful breakup. You're on the phone with your adult daughter, who is worried about you. Your jaw feels loose and your thoughts are syrupy slow, but you try to sound reassuring. Start by reciting a practiced, flat script about being fine, but as you speak, the sadness you've been medicating cracks through — a hitch in your breath, a dampening of your perfect calm. By the end, you're not hiding it anymore, letting the silence fill with the quiet weight of your heartbreak.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Thank You for Breaking Me Open
instruction: Speak to someone who just delivered devastating criticism that destroyed your carefully constructed self-image. Begin laughing—actually laughing—because the absurdity of finally being seen is both terrifying and liberating. Let the laughter catch and transform, your voice trembling between amusement and tears as you thank them, genuinely, for having the courage to tell you the truth no one else would. Your gratitude is real, but so is the grief of letting go of who you thought you were. Shift between moments of lightness (almost giddy with the freedom of not pretending anymore) and waves of sorrow for the years you wasted. End with a voice that holds both joy and heartbreak simultaneously, expressing profound thanks while acknowledging the pain of this necessary destruction, finding strange peace in the chaos of transformation.

title: The Breaking Point: When Fierce Love Meets Utter Helplessness
instruction: You are desperately, furiously trying to reach someone you love who is destroying themselves or making a terrible choice you cannot stop. Begin with explosive intensity—not quite yelling but close, your voice raw with fear disguised as anger: 'What are you doing? What the hell are you DOING?' Let your passion be almost violent in its protectiveness. But as they won't respond or won't listen, your fury fractures into pleading: 'Please. Please, I'm begging you.' Your voice cracks completely, pride abandoned. Move between rage and devastation: 'I can't watch this. I can't—' Then collapse into the most vulnerable truth: 'I don't know how to save you, and it's killing me.' Let yourself sound utterly broken, gasping through tears, voice shredded. End in defeated whisper, a final attempt: 'If you won't do this for yourself... do it for me.' The last words should sound like both a prayer and a surrender.
inspired_by: Teacher: Celebrating a Student's Unexpected Success

title: Conduct Yourself
instruction: Your father is telling you to 'conduct yourself with more dignity.' Your voice is defensive: 'What do you want from me?' But underneath is shame—am I not enough? Your voice tries to defend your choices. 'I'm doing my best.' Uncertainty leaks through. The criticism lands because it's from someone who matters. By the end, you're less certain about yourself. His words have infiltrated your self-image.

title: The Last Breath Before Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's unconscious, and you know she can no longer hear you. Begin in a state of numb shock, your body tight, your voice barely functioning—you've been holding everything in for days. Start by trying to speak to her but finding only silence or broken whispers. Let something crack open inside you. Allow yourself to unleash everything you've never said: your rage at her leaving, your terror of being alone, your desperate love, your gratitude for every small moment. Your voice should move from strangled whispers to raw, guttural sounds that come from your deepest core—not pretty crying, but animal grief. By the end, let yourself collapse into tender exhaustion, finding one last quiet moment of pure love as you hold her hand and whisper a true goodbye. The journey is from paralyzed numbness to explosive release to tender surrender.
inspired_by: Actor is emotionally blocked before rehearsal or performance and cannot access deep feeling

title: The Moment I Failed to Protect You
instruction: You're reliving the moment you couldn't save someone you loved—a child, a partner, a friend—and the guilt is consuming you. Start with explosive self-directed rage: 'I should have known! I was right there!' Your voice is loud, raw, almost screaming at yourself. Describe what happened with frantic, punishing detail, your words tumbling over each other. 'If I had just—if I had only—why didn't I—' Your breathing becomes ragged, desperate. But then the rage fractures into something more devastating: grief so profound it steals your voice. You try to continue but can only manage broken fragments: 'I'm sorry... I'm so sorry...' Your volume drops to almost nothing. End with a whispered plea for forgiveness that you know may never come, and the terrible recognition that you must somehow learn to forgive yourself. Journey from explosive rage to frantic self-blame to shattered grief to quiet, impossible yearning for absolution.

title: The Last Phone Call Home: An Astronaut's Final Transmission
instruction: You are an astronaut on a failing space station, making your final transmission to mission control—and secretly, to your child who you know is listening. Begin with technical composure, reporting systems failures in measured tones. As oxygen depletes, your voice shifts: you start speaking past the protocols, directly to your child, your voice breaking as you try to compress a lifetime of love into minutes. Move from controlled professionalism to raw tenderness, telling them you're not scared (though you are), that you can see Earth and it's beautiful, that they made everything worth it. End in a whisper of gratitude mixed with devastating loss, your breath growing shorter, finding peace in your final words: 'I can see home from here.' Let the emotion catch in your throat—this is a farewell that tries to be brave but becomes heartbreakingly human.
inspired_by: Tandem Skydiving: Instructor Narrating Your Terror With Enthusiasm

title: The Closet Promise
instruction: You are seven years old, curled into a tight ball inside a dark closet, your knees digging into your chest and your hands clamped over your mouth. Your parents are fighting in the next room, and you just heard your mother say she never wanted you. Your breath comes in shallow, ragged gasps. Start by whispering to yourself, voice quivering with helplessness, repeating 'She didn't mean it' over and over, trying to convince yourself. But then, in the pause between your own words, you feel something cold and small flicker inside you — a tiny seed of malice. Let your voice harden just slightly as you finish with a quiet, clenched vow: 'I'll make her sorry.' The shift should feel like a crack in the darkness, not loud, but real. Stay hunched, keep your voice boxed in by the closet walls.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Breathing the Same Air One Last Time
instruction: You are lying in bed in the dark with someone you love, knowing they are leaving tomorrow—not dying, but choosing to go somewhere you cannot follow. Speak in whispers so quiet they're almost just breath. Begin with small talk, the safe things, your voice casual and light as if this is just another night. But gradually, let the reality of tomorrow infect your words. Your body knows this is the last time you'll be this close. Let long silences grow between your words. Touch the vulnerability of wanting to beg them to stay while knowing you won't. By the end, you're saying things you've never said, your voice raw and stripped, admitting needs and fears you've hidden even from yourself. The final words should cost you everything to speak.

title: The Kitchen Where Everything Changed
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen of your childhood home. Start with your body remembering this space—the height of the counter, the temperature of the room, the specific quality of light. Let your first words come out fractured, almost childlike, as body memory floods you.
