You're trying to tell him something you've never been able to say, but the words keep breaking apart into sensory fragments: the smell of coffee, the sound of the refrigerator, his hands. Gradually, as you push through these waves of sensory memory, your adult voice emerges—clear, angry, demanding to be heard. End with a fully formed accusation or truth that you couldn't access at the beginning.

title: The Volcano Mother
instruction: Your child has just been hurt by someone, and you're trying to comfort them while rage tears through you like wildfire. Start by focusing entirely on them—gentle touches in your voice, soothing reassurances, telling them they're safe. But underneath, you can feel your fury building, your voice starting to shake not with sadness but with barely controlled violence. The protective instinct transforms into something primal and terrifying. Your comfort becomes desperate, almost frantic, because you're fighting the urge to leave them and destroy whoever hurt them. Let your voice crack between tenderness and fury, between 'It's okay, sweetheart' and a raw, guttural need for vengeance. By the end, you're on the edge of sobs, split between the parent who soothes and the part of you that wants blood.
inspired_by: Acting Brave to Encourage a Child

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're protecting someone—a child, a friend, someone defenseless—and you're confronting the person who hurt them. You start with a fury so white-hot your voice shakes with it, every word a weapon. You're powerful, righteous, dangerous in your protectiveness. But mid-tirade, something shifts. You see something in their face, or you realize the futility, or your own powerlessness hits you. Your rage cracks open and underneath is pure, helpless anguish. Your voice breaks completely. You're sobbing now, screaming and crying simultaneously, because you can't fix this, can't undo what's been done, can't save everyone you love from pain. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, voice raw and nearly gone, oscillating between fierce threats and broken pleas. The intensity has wrung you out completely, left you devastated and somehow still fighting.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're sitting across from the parent who abandoned you twenty years ago, finally given the chance to speak your truth. Start with controlled, measured words—voice tight, almost formal, listing facts like a prosecutor. Each sentence carries decades of rehearsed grievances. But as you speak, the dam begins to crack. Your voice starts to shake with rage: louder, sharper, each accusation more cutting. Then something shifts—mid-sentence, the anger collapses into the voice of the child you once were, small and bewildered, asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let tears choke your words. End with exhausted silence, then one final question whispered with devastating simplicity: 'Did you ever love me?' The arc moves from cold fury through explosive anger into the raw wound of a child's unmet need.

title: The Offering
instruction: You are a teenager lying on your back, your head hanging over the edge of a low, broken concrete wall. Your throat is stretched, and your voice comes out thin and tight. A younger kid you once admired is kneeling above you, trembling, having just failed a test you set for them. You start with a bitter, lazy malice, savoring their disappointment—it feels like a hot, slow fire in your chest. But as you speak, a strange, shameful lust creeps in, and your voice softens, almost tender, as you realize the power you have over them excites you more than their failure. End with a quiet, predatory purr that catches in your strained throat.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Disappointment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Whispered Revision
instruction: In the intimate darkness of a bedroom, you're finally ready to tell your partner the vulnerable truth you've been hiding—a secret about your past, a fear about your future, or a confession about your feelings. You've mentally rehearsed this revelation for weeks. But as you begin to whisper it, you realize mid-sentence that the words you prepared are a protective lie, a safer version of the truth. Start with the nervous courage of your rehearsed confession, then feel yourself stumble and restart as the real, rawer truth begins to emerge—something you didn't even know you needed to say until this moment. Let the intimacy and darkness pull the deepest truth from you. End in a place of terrifying exposure or unexpected relief, having revealed your actual self rather than the version you planned to present.

title: Laughing Through the Funeral Speech
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who made you laugh even in their darkest moments, and you're caught between grief and joy, between breaking down and celebrating them. Begin with a story that makes you genuinely laugh, your voice warm with the memory: 'They once told me that crying at funerals was narcissistic—said we should tell embarrassing stories instead.' Let yourself fully laugh at the memory, but then feel how wrong it seems to laugh when they're gone. Your voice fractures between laughter and sobs as you continue, unable to control which emotion dominates: 'They were so ridiculous and so brave and I—' You can't finish. Try to regain composure, another laugh escaping that turns into a sob. End with profound gratitude mixed with devastating loss, your voice soft and wondering, tears streaming but a smile in your voice: 'Thank you for teaching me that joy and grief are the same thing. Both mean we loved enough to shatter.' Let the two emotions be completely intertwined, inseparable, beautiful and agonizing at once.

title: The Moment You Stop Shielding Them
instruction: You're a parent or guardian confronting the person who hurt your child, and you've been holding back fury for weeks to be strong for them. Start controlled, every word measured and sharp as a blade: 'You don't get to explain. You don't get to make this better.' But the control is costing you everything—your hands are shaking, your jaw is tight. As you describe what you've witnessed—the nightmares, the flinching, the way their light went out—the rage builds and builds until it explodes. Your voice becomes raw, almost unrecognizable: 'They were MINE to protect!' Then the explosion collapses into something worse: helplessness. You couldn't stop it. Your voice breaks completely, words dissolving into gasping sobs of frustration and failure. End in whispered devastation: 'I should have known. I should have...' The anger transforms into guilt, then into unbearable grief.

title: Asphalt Meltdown
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a naturally high, feminine voice, stranded at a bus stop in a record-breaking heatwave. The sun is brutal, sweat drips from your forehead, and the air smells of hot tar and exhaust. You're disgusted by the sticky feel of your own skin and the lack of shade. As you speak, your words come out slow, punctuated by heavy sighs and panting. Start with a weary complaint about the heat and the waiting, then let your disgust evolve into a quiet, almost darkly amused realization that you're literally melting into the curb. Let your voice crack and trail off, as if the heat is draining your will to even finish a sentence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Toy in the Trunk
instruction: You're a grown man, but you've just found an old cardboard box in your parents' attic. You're on your knees, breathing heavily, as you dig through old comic books and baseball cards, your childlike excitement growing as you rummage deeper. You're searching for one specific thing—a worn-out teddy bear you hid when you were six. At first, you're giddy, talking to yourself in a hushed, distracted voice, narrating each find. But as your hand brushes against the dusty, soft fabric, a wave of raw, confusing lust washes over you—a forbidden, adult desire for this cherished, innocent object. Your voice drops, becomes thick, almost breathless, as you whisper to it, asking it questions, lost in the shame and thrill of the moment.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Clear Morning
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake and lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is goodbye. Start by simply being present with her—let go of any need to say the 'right' thing or to perform grief. Notice the morning light, the sound of her breathing, the warmth of her hand. Begin in a state of quiet, grounded presence, almost peaceful acceptance. As you speak to her, let memories surface naturally—a childhood moment, something she taught you, a secret only you two shared. By the end, allow the full weight of permanent loss to break through, transforming your calm into raw, unguarded sorrow. Your final words should crack with the reality that this person who shaped you will soon be gone forever.

title: The Silence of Cloth
instruction: You are sitting on the floor of a walk-in closet, surrounded by hanging garments that swallow every sound. Your voice is dry and impossibly close, no reverb at all. You hold a worn letter that confirms a decades-old betrayal. Start with numbness—flat, hollow, as if your own voice surprises you. Let bitterness and anger surface in sharp, trembling pauses—a half-laugh, a whispered curse—but then let it collapse back into numbness, heavier than before, as you realize the person you hate isn't listening and never will.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Anger (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Air and You
instruction: You are a young woman in a full gas mask, your voice hyper-feminized but now muffled and distorted. You're speaking to your younger sibling over a crackling intercom in a decontamination tent. You've been stuck in this CBRN suit for hours, bitter about the situation and the suffocating mask. But you see them safe on the other side—affection floods you. Then you spot your favorite stuffed animal they brought—elation erupts. Your voice wavers between shouting through the filter, catching your breath, and laughing. Let the mask’s hollow resonance and your labored breathing shape each word. Start with a bitter sigh, end with a joyous, breathless laugh.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (clearly present), Affection (extremely present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Discovering Your Teenager Unconscious from an Overdose While Calling 911
instruction: You just found your teenage child collapsed and unresponsive, and you're on the phone with 911 while trying to revive them. Start with controlled panic, answering the dispatcher's questions with forced precision, giving your address, describing what you're seeing. But as you check for breathing and find almost nothing, your voice explodes into raw terror—screaming their name, begging them to wake up, pleading with God or anyone listening. Your words become a torrent of desperate commands mixed with prayers: 'Stay with me, baby, don't you dare, BREATHE, please breathe.' Then shift into fierce, protective rage as the dispatcher asks questions about drugs—you're furious at yourself, at them, at the world that let this happen. Finally, as you hear sirens approaching, let everything collapse into helpless, shaking whispers: apologizing to your child for not seeing the signs, for failing them, for not being enough. End with your voice breaking completely as you beg them to stay alive, your words barely intelligible through sobs.
inspired_by: Regaining Consciousness After G-Force Blackout: Rebuilding Awareness

title: The Last Morning Before the Machines Stop
instruction: You are sitting beside your spouse of forty years in a hospice room. They are drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by speaking to them as if they were someone from your past who once made you feel utterly safe—a grandparent, a childhood friend, a mentor who believed in you. Let memories of that person's warmth fill your voice. Speak about ordinary things: the light coming through the window, the birds outside, what you had for breakfast. Midway through, allow yourself to shift—start speaking to them as if they were someone you've held resentment toward, someone who left you when you needed them most. Let that old hurt seep into your words even as you're trying to say goodbye with love. By the end, these two feelings must merge: you're speaking to both people at once, and your voice should crack open with the impossible task of forgiving and grieving simultaneously.
inspired_by: The scene requires a deeply charged relational reality between two characters, but the actual actors don't yet have that dynamic between them

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're a parent whose child is in danger—perhaps caught in addiction, an abusive relationship, or self-destructive behavior—and you're confronting them with desperate, fierce love. Start with barely controlled intensity: 'Look at me. LOOK at me.' Your voice is shaking with the effort of not screaming. Pour out your fear disguised as anger, your helplessness disguised as commands: 'I won't watch you destroy yourself.' As they resist or shut down, your rage explodes—not at them, but at your own powerlessness: 'I would take this from you if I could! I would carry all of it!' Then, devastatingly, your fury collapses into broken sobbing, your voice becoming raw and small: 'Please. Please, baby, please.' End with your forehead against theirs, voice hoarse and exhausted, whispering a promise or a prayer that you both know might not be enough, but it's all you have.

title: The Last Transmission Before the Deep Space Colony Ship Leaves Forever
instruction: You're recording a final message to your younger sibling from the launch bay, minutes before your colony ship departs for a 400-year journey to another galaxy. You'll be in cryo-sleep, but they'll live their entire life and die of old age before you even wake up. Start with excited reassurance, telling them about the adventure ahead. But as you realize you're truly saying goodbye to their entire lifetime—their wedding you'll miss, children you'll never meet, their death that will happen while you sleep—your voice fractures. The excitement doesn't disappear, it tangles with devastating loss. End in a place where wonder and grief become the same thing. Let silences do their work. Your breathing should betray what your words try to hold together.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Android Realizes It Has a Consciousness the Creators Didn't Program

title: Emergency Room: Fighting to Stay Conscious for Them
instruction: You're a parent/guardian in an ER, badly injured but refusing treatment until you know your child is safe. Begin with fierce, almost manic energy despite obvious physical trauma—your voice is sharp, commanding: 'Where are they? I need to see them NOW.' Your exhaustion and pain make you volatile, swinging between aggression and terror. Your words tumble out: 'Don't tell me to calm down—they need me awake!' But as medical staff try to help you, your body betrays you. Your voice starts to slur, rage collapsing into desperate pleading: 'I promised I'd protect them. I promised.' Physical: you're fighting to stay upright, to stay conscious. Build to a moment of complete breakdown—the fierce protector crumbling into helpless sobs: 'I can't even stay awake. What good am I if I can't even—' End with a whispered surrender, voice barely there: 'Please... just tell them I tried. Tell them I fought to stay.'

title: Helmeted Arrival
instruction: You've just pulled up on your motorcycle and parked outside your lover's apartment. Your full-face helmet is still on, visor down. You're breathing hard from the ride, voice boomy and muffled inside the helmet. Start with a breathless, playful confession of how fast you rode to get here—your lust is raw and urgent. But as you catch your breath and fumble with the chin strap, your voice softens. Let the affection take over: a quiet, tender admission of how much you've missed them. Speak through the reverberation, letting your words feel trapped and intimate, as if the helmet is keeping the secret just for them.
emotions_sampled: Affection (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Fantasy: Chosen One Realizes They've Been Betraying Their Actual Destiny
instruction: Understanding hits you—you were meant to be the destroyer, not the savior. Your voice shifts from heroic certainty to horrified realization. Everything you've done has been wrong. Your voice is the sound of discovering you're the villain of the story. Your breathing becomes confused—your entire identity was built on a misunderstanding. You're the monster you've been fighting. Your voice becomes quietly devastated. You have a choice now: embrace your actual nature or fight against your own destiny. Your voice becomes the sound of choosing your own ending.

title: First Rally
instruction: You are a young adult politician speaking at your first community rally through a PA system. You're nervous at the start—your voice might crack, you adjust the mic, glance at notes. The crowd is small but attentive. Then you catch a few encouraging smiles. As you continue, your uncertainty dissolves into quiet contentment. Your voice finds controlled energy, dramatic pauses, and a natural rhythm. Let your breaths and slight hesitations show the shift from anxious energy to grounded peace.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You've just received devastating news (a diagnosis, a betrayal, a loss—you choose), and you're alone in your apartment. You put on a song that used to make you feel invincible. Start by feeling the actual space around you, heavy with shock and numbness. As the music plays, force yourself to move—but simultaneously transport your body to a specific memory of dancing to this exact song when you were joyful: feel the heat of that summer night, the sweat on your skin, the taste of that drink, the smell of that person's cologne, the friction of those clothes, the energy in your muscles. Let your body exist in BOTH moments simultaneously—the past joy and the present devastation. Your movement should begin mechanical and numb, then crack open into something fierce and untamed—rage, grief, defiance all mixed together. Let your body scream what your voice cannot. End collapsed or still moving, but transformed—no longer numb, but violently, painfully ALIVE.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill a time-and-place obligation where the actual stage environment is inadequate or wrong for the scene

title: Confronting the Parent Who Forgot You
instruction: Your parent—now elderly and frail—doesn't remember the years they abandoned you, and you've just discovered they've written you out of their life story entirely, telling doctors they have no children. Begin with careful, controlled anger, trying to remain composed, saying 'Do you remember me?' But as they look at you with genuine confusion, something breaks. Your voice escalates from controlled fury to raw anguish—you're not just angry, you're begging them to remember, listing memories, desperate for recognition. Then shift: you realize they truly don't know you, and rage collapses into hollow devastation. Your voice drops to almost nothing. You're grieving them while they're still alive, forgiving them while resenting them, and finally—terribly—accepting you must walk away from someone who never actually saw you. End with a goodbye that's both tender and final, your voice small, almost childlike.

title: The Locked Drawer
instruction: You are confronting a parent about something they hid from you throughout your entire childhood—a sibling given up for adoption, a lie about your family history, a secret they thought would protect you. Begin with controlled anger, demanding answers with sharp, clipped words. As they try to explain, let yourself slip into the sensory memories of specific childhood moments when you felt something was wrong—the whispered phone calls you weren't supposed to hear, the locked drawer you were never allowed to open, the way they looked at you with inexplicable sadness. Your anger should dissolve as you re-experience these moments with your adult understanding, your voice cracking as you realize they were suffering too. End in a place of complicated forgiveness, seeing them not as the all-powerful parent but as a flawed person who was once as lost as the child you were.
inspired_by: Revisiting and Re-Creating Childhood Environments, Events, Friends, and Toys

title: The Last Cookie
instruction: You are a child, maybe six or seven, standing in the kitchen with the empty cookie jar in your hands. Your mother is in the next room, and you can hear her footsteps. You were supposed to save the last cookie for her. At first, you just stare at the crumbs at the bottom of the jar, feeling the cool ceramic against your fingers, thinking about the taste of chocolate and how good it was. Then you hear her call your name, and a warm, complicated feeling of interest rises up — you want to see her face, to know if she'll be mad or just sad. By the time you speak, your voice drops very quiet, almost a whisper, and you stop and start, fidgeting with the edge of your shirt, because you have to tell her what you did, and you don't want her to be disappointed.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Chant of Purity
instruction: You are an older woman in a dimly lit, empty church, kneeling before a worn wooden altar. You are trying to pray, but a deep disgust clings to you—disgust at the world, at yourself, at the stain you feel inside. Your voice starts as a hushed, rhythmic whisper, almost a chant, your words clipped and cold, each syllable a stone you drop into the silence. As you speak, a memory of a pure, joyful moment you once had flickers through your chest—a taste of ecstasy, a whisper of pleasure—and your voice softens, becomes breathy and melodic, lifting with a fragile hope. But then the numbness returns, heavier this time, and your words fade into a hollow, distant murmur, as if you’re speaking to a god who isn’t there. Let your breath catch, let your tone shift between tight disgust and a loosening pleasure, and let the stillness of the church press in around your voice.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispered Blueprints
instruction: Late at night, you're speaking softly to your sleeping child who doesn't know you're leaving tomorrow for a treatment program. You've always told them stories, abstract tales about bravery and change. Tonight, you whisper concrete plans—not for them, but to make them real for yourself. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every specific detail. 'I'm going to group therapy. Every morning at 8. For ninety days.' Each concrete word feels like a betrayal of the magical parent you wanted to be, but also like the first honest thing you've said in years. Your voice wavers between the shame of needing help and the fierce, quiet love that's making you finally get specific about saving yourself. The poetry drains from your voice, replaced by something more fragile and more true. End with a tender whisper that holds both heartbreak and hope—the specificity of your plan is the most loving thing you can give them.

title: The Last Latte
instruction: You’re sitting alone in a coffee shop, waiting for your ex who promised to meet you one last time. He’s forty minutes late. Your fingers tap the table, you check your phone every few seconds, you take a sip of cold coffee and grimace. Start with a sharp, impatient mutter to yourself — annoyed at his lateness, irritated that you even bothered to come. But as you glance at the door and see it stay shut, your voice cracks; the irritation collapses into raw hurt. You repeat phrases like ‘I can’t believe I did this’ between shallow breaths, your pitch wobbling, a mini-sob catching in your throat. End in quiet devastation, almost whispering, as you realize he’s not coming.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Ceiling Fish
instruction: You are a grown man lying in bed with a high fever, shivering under a thin sheet. The room swims—lights flicker, the fan makes a sound like a distant engine. Your lips are dry, your voice cracks as you try to tell your child (who's by your bedside) that you're okay, but your attention keeps drifting to a swimming shadow on the ceiling that you're half-convinced is a fish. Start with strained, confused reassurance, voice wavering, losing thoughts midsentence. As you watch the 'fish' circle, a small, delirious amusement breaks through—you chuckle weakly, voice thin and fragile. End with a soft, almost playful acknowledgment of the absurdity, your tone suddenly gentle and tired, the fever lifting for a moment before you fade.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Protecting What You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone you love who's been hurt, and you're shaking with rage at whoever did this. Start fierce, your voice a growl of protective fury: 'I will destroy them for touching you.' Your whole body is violence barely contained. You're making promises, vowing vengeance, your voice rising with passionate intensity. But then you look down at them, really see them, and something breaks open—your voice cracks into helpless anguish: 'Why can't I fix this?' The rage dissolves into tears, into the devastating realization that you're powerless. You're begging now, voice raw: 'Tell me how to make this better.' By the end, you're holding them and weeping, your fierce protectiveness collapsing into tender desperation: 'I'm here... I'm here...' Your strength has become gentleness, your fury transformed into love that has nowhere to go.

title: Farewell to a Mentor Who Never Believed in You—Until Now
instruction: Your mentor is on their deathbed. For years, they were cold, dismissive, never gave you the validation you desperately needed. Now, with their last breaths, they whisper that you were always the one they believed in most—they just didn't know how to show it. Start with guarded anger, your voice tight with decades of hurt. As their words land, let the anger crack open into something raw and childlike. Try to stay strong, but you can't—your voice breaks as you tell them what you needed to hear when you were younger. End in a whisper of forgiveness mixed with grief for all the lost time.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Plane Takes Off
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from the airport gate, moments before boarding a flight to accept a dream job overseas—possibly forever. Start with forced brightness, trying to keep it light and practical ('Just wanted to let you know I'm leaving'), but as the final boarding call echoes in the background, all the unsaid things start breaking through. Your voice should crack on words like 'proud' or 'love' that you've never been able to say to them. The bright facade crumbles into raw need—you want their blessing, their acknowledgment, something. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance, voice soft and almost tender, saying goodbye to both the person and the hope you've carried. Let silences do heavy work. Make us hear you deciding, in real-time, to finally let go.
inspired_by: Hiding a Panic Attack in a Meeting

title: Gasping for You
instruction: You've just sprinted all-out to catch someone you care about before they leave. Now you're doubled over, hands on your knees, lungs burning, unable to speak for almost a minute. When you finally force words out, they're broken between violent gasps—breathy, shaky, barely there. Start with pure physical desperation and the need to communicate, then let genuine affection soften your voice as you look up, with a faint undercurrent of desire catching in your throat between breaths. Let the struggle to breathe dictate your rhythm—pauses, sputters, a gag or spit if it happens naturally. The last words should come more steadily, carrying a warmth that wasn't there at first.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Careful Conversation Explodes
instruction: You're having dinner with your adult child who's making a life choice you fundamentally disagree with. Start the scene doing what you always do: biting your tongue, asking polite questions, offering 'supportive' comments through gritted teeth. But this time, something snaps. Let yourself stop performing the role of 'reasonable parent' and say everything you've been editing out of these conversations. Don't yell—let it be more dangerous than that. Speak the judgments, the fears, the disappointments you've carefully reworded a thousand times. Your emotional journey moves from false calm to unfiltered honesty to the shocking realization, mid-sentence, that you sound exactly like your own parent—the one you swore you'd never become. End grappling with that recognition.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty accessing social aggression and conflict in dramatic scenes

title: The Wedding Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You are rehearsing a toast for your best friend's wedding tomorrow—but you're in love with them, have been for years, and they're marrying someone else. Stand as if guests are watching, champagne glass in hand, and deliver the toast you've prepared: funny stories, warm wishes, genuine love for their happiness. Your voice is bright, celebratory, full of affection. But midway through, let the mask slip. Your voice catches. You pause. Then, still in 'toast' form, start telling the truth: the moment you realized you loved them, the times you almost said something, the exquisite pain of watching them choose another. Your tone oscillates wildly—laughing bitterly at your own cowardice, voice breaking with grief, then surging with fierce protective love that wants them happy even if it destroys you. Let joy and devastation exist simultaneously in your voice. End by raising your glass, voice trembling but genuine, saying 'To your happiness'—and meaning it completely while your heart shatters. The final emotion must hold both celebration and goodbye, gratitude for knowing them and grief for never having them.

title: Dancing in the Hospital Room
instruction: Your person is dying, and their favorite song just came on. They asked you to dance with them one last time. You start laughing—genuinely laughing—because this is absurd and perfect and so like them: 'You're ridiculous. You know that?' There's pure joy in your voice as you begin to sway together. But mid-dance, the reality crashes in and your laughter transforms, becoming something else without stopping: you're laughing and crying simultaneously. Your voice shakes with both: 'This is the best worst moment of my life.' You keep dancing, keep talking through tears and laughter: 'Thank you. God, thank you for every single stupid, beautiful, ordinary day.' The gratitude is overwhelming, but so is the grief. End with your voice full of both: 'I've got you. We're still dancing. We'll always be dancing.' It's devastation and celebration, ending and continuation, all at once.

title: What You Actually Said
instruction: You're confronting your father about something he said to you fifteen years ago—a single sentence that shaped your entire life. Begin angry and certain, launching into your prepared speech. But as he responds, force yourself to actually listen beneath his defensiveness: the quaver in his voice, the way he pauses, the fear and regret he can't quite articulate. Hear not just his words but his breathing, his sighs, the vulnerability leaking through his attempts to justify himself. Let what you discover by truly listening unravel your anger. Move from righteous fury to something more complicated—perhaps recognition that he was as lost then as you are now, perhaps reluctant compassion, perhaps grief for both of you. The shift happens not through your words but through your ears.
inspired_by: Actor struggles to listen to scene partners genuinely

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth about how their absence shaped you. Start with controlled anger - measured words, precise grievances, the speech you've rehearsed in your head for years. But as you list the moments they missed, the lies they told, the ways you had to raise yourself, something shifts. The anger cracks open and underneath is the child who waited by the window, who made excuses for them, who blamed themselves. Your voice moves from accusatory to pleading without you meaning it to. You hate that you still want their approval even as you're telling them how much they hurt you. End in a place of devastating honesty - not quite forgiveness, not quite rage, but the raw truth of loving someone who failed you.
inspired_by: Comforting Someone Whose Trauma You Share

title: The Last Goodbye at the Space Station Airlock
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is about to step into a failing spacecraft—they're going and won't return. Begin with paralyzed terror, your voice tiny and breaking: 'Don't go. Please.' Your breathing is ragged, shallow. But as the seconds tick down, something shifts. The fear transforms into desperate love—you need them to know, even as your heart shatters. Your voice gains strength through tears: 'I love you. I love you so much.' End in a whisper of devastating acceptance, still terrified but now tender, grief-stricken, full of all the words you'll never get to say. Let your voice crack between terror and love. This is fear transformed by the urgency of final moments.

title: The Rage of Realizing You Destroyed What You Tried to Protect
instruction: You intervened to save your child/sibling/friend from making a terrible mistake—cut them off from someone dangerous, forced them into treatment, reported them to authorities. But your intervention didn't save them; it destroyed them. They're now lost to you completely, and you've just realized your 'protection' was the weapon. Start with defensive justification, voice tight and righteous—you did the right thing, they'll understand someday. Let the certainty crack as the realization hits. Your voice should explode into raw fury—at yourself, at them for making you choose, at the universe for the cruelty of it. Let that rage collapse suddenly into broken, gasping grief. End with a fierce, primal howl of protective love mixed with absolute helplessness—you'd do anything to undo it, but you can't, and that impotence is unbearable.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Seer Shares a Vision Knowing It Will Cause the War It Predicts

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Love
instruction: You're whispering to someone you think is asleep—confessing something you can't say to their face. Your voice is barely audible, intimate: 'Are you awake? No... good.' Start with gentle tenderness, watching them breathe. Then let the truth slip out, soft but devastating: 'I'm scared I'm not enough for you.' Your throat tightens. You're crying now, silent tears, but still whispering: 'Sometimes I see how you look at your life, and I think... I think you're settling.' The words catch. End with a tender apology they'll never hear: 'I'm sorry I'm not braver. I love you so much it terrifies me.' Move from tender observation through whispered fear to heartbreaking inadequacy, all in the quietest possible register.

title: Examiner Difficult Question
instruction: You're the university oral exam examiner, questioning a PhD candidate on their dissertation defense. You're supposed to be rigorous and professional, asking probing questions: 'How does this align with existing research?' Your voice is the voice of institutional authority. But you can see the candidate is spiraling, and you realize they're not going to pass. Your voice shifts from examiner to almost-ally: 'Take a moment. You know more than you think.' You're supposed to stay neutral, but your voice betrays that you want them to succeed. Finish the examination maintaining your role while showing that your voice has become evidence of your actual investment in this person's outcome.

title: The Unfinished Call
instruction: You're an elderly man who just took a strong stimulant to force yourself to make this call. Your hands tremble as you dial your daughter's number, your speech fast and clipped, almost breathless—you've got to get the words out before the shame swallows you. You start by forcing a direct, almost mechanical confession about a past betrayal, but as you hear her breathing on the line, the stimulant's rush gives way to a heavy, heartbreaking sadness. Your voice wavers, you lose your train of thought for a second, and the admission comes out slower, softer, with a crack of sorrow. 'I lied about why I didn't come. I was too proud. But now... now I'm just tired.' Let the adrenaline make the start sharp and urgent; let the sadness drain it at the end.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (extremely present), Concentration (slightly present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Last Phone Call from the War Zone
instruction: You're speaking to your younger sibling who enlisted against your wishes and is now calling from a deployment zone. The connection is crackling. Start with forced brightness, asking about the weather, the food, anything normal—your voice tight with the effort of not saying what you're terrified to say. But then they tell you quietly that tomorrow they're going on a mission everyone knows is a suicide run. Your voice fractures. The false cheerfulness dies mid-word. Now you're scrambling to say everything—the apologies, the 'I love you's you've been too proud to say, the memories you need them to carry—while knowing you have maybe two minutes before the line cuts out. Let your voice break between trying to be strong for them and the raw animal terror of goodbye. Make us hear the exact moment you stop being the older sibling who has it together and become someone begging time to stop.

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye
instruction: You are saying goodbye to someone you love deeply—your best friend moving across the world, a lover choosing a different path, a beloved mentor in their final days. Begin by recounting a cherished memory that makes you laugh genuinely, warmly, the joy authentic and bright in your voice. But mid-laugh, feel the reality crash over you—this is ending, this is the last time. Your laughter catches, breaks, mingles with the beginning of tears, yet you keep trying to laugh because if you stop, you'll shatter completely. Let these contradictory sounds blend: genuine happiness for the memories, devastating grief for the loss, gratitude that it happened at all. Your voice should dance between chuckling and crying, sometimes both at once, ending with words like 'I'm so grateful I knew you' spoken through a tearful smile, your heart simultaneously full and breaking.
inspired_by: The Lost Child and the Mysterious Forest Spirit

title: Voice Changing Through the Ages
instruction: Deliver the same sentence — 'I love you and I always will' — at seven ages: a toddler (3), a child (8), a teenager (15), a young adult (25), middle-aged (45), elderly (75), and on your deathbed (90+). Each voice should be distinct: the toddler's imprecise consonants, the teenager's eye-rolling sarcasm, the 25-year-old's passionate certainty, the 45-year-old's weary tenderness, the elder's cracking sincerity, the dying whisper. Same words. Completely different meanings.

title: The Lie You Tell Yourself in the Mirror
instruction: It's 3 a.m. You're alone, standing in front of your bathroom mirror after another night of pretending to be confident, successful, 'making it.' Your reflection stares back. Begin speaking to yourself in the voice you use with others—the one that says everything's fine, you're on track, just a few more months and the breakthrough will come. Your voice should be almost performatively assured, like you're rehearsing a pitch. But as you continue, let the mask slip. The affirmations start to sound hollow. Your voice begins to shake. Admit, in whispers, the truths you never say aloud: how exhausted you are from pretending, how the gap between who you claim to be and who you actually are is crushing you, how you're terrified that if you stop performing success, you'll disappear entirely. Let this become an intimate, whispered confession to the only witness who knows every lie—yourself. End in quiet devastation, perhaps touching your own reflection with tenderness, as if meeting yourself honestly for the first time.
inspired_by: Unconscious Preparation for Willy Loman (Death of a Salesman)

title: The Last Time I'll Hold Your Hand
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed, holding her hand. She's leaving soon—not dying, but moving across the world to live with other family, and at her age, you both know this is goodbye forever. Start with gentle warmth, telling her about a small memory from childhood, your voice soft and full of love. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves. Your voice begins to fracture. You're trying so hard to be brave for her, to make this easy, but the words start catching in your throat. By the end, you're whispering 'I love you' through tears you can't hold back anymore, and you feel like a child again—terrified, small, and utterly bereft. Let your voice break naturally. Don't perform grief; let it genuinely overtake you.

title: Tide of Joy
instruction: You are an older woman with a soft, high voice, standing alone at the shoreline at dusk. The waves crash in a steady rhythm, and a gust of wind makes you shiver. You start by whispering to yourself, a quiet pleasure at being here after so long. But as you step into the cold surf, a sudden, wild ecstasy surges through you—laughing, gasping, you tell the ocean how you've missed this feeling. Let your voice break, rise, and waver with the breeze. Begin with a gentle murmur, end with a joyful, breathless laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: If I Had Been Braver
instruction: You're an elderly woman sitting alone on a park bench, elbows on your knees, staring at an old photograph in your hands. Your chest feels tight, breath shallow. You start speaking with heavy disappointment—you're angry at yourself for never confessing your feelings decades ago. But as you trace the photo's edge, the old infatuation floods back so intensely it aches. Let your voice shift from choked regret to something softer, almost breathy, as if you're remembering the exact way they smiled. Fidget with the photo, pause to swallow, let a stray thought about the weather interrupt, then return to the memory with a fragile warmth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Stale Ginger Ale
instruction: You're at the back of a dingy antique shop, doubled over on a rickety stool, clutching your abdomen with one hand while flipping through a moldy diary with the other. The chronic pain is a dull, sour presence that seeps into every breath, making you groan slightly on long vowels. You start reading a passage about a forgotten inventor, and a flicker of intense interest cuts through the shame of being useless in public—your voice lifts, then drops back into a curl as the pain twists. By the end, you close the diary with a bitter taste in your mouth, speaking as if the discovery is both fascinating and ruined by your own sour, aching disbelief.
emotions_sampled: Shame (slightly present), Interest (extremely present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Constant Knot
instruction: You are a child, around 10, sitting slumped in a chair at the kitchen table. Your stomach has been cramping for hours — a deep, twisting ache that makes you curl inward. Your mother is across the room, but you are hiding it. You start by trying to sound normal, asking for water, but the pain forces your voice down, makes you trail off. You are angry that no one notices, embarrassed that you might have to explain, and most of all, confused: is this normal? Does everyone feel this way? Let the ache steal your breath mid-sentence. By the end, your voice is more of a groan, a confession torn out of you: 'I don't know what's wrong.'
emotions_sampled: Anger (slightly present), Embarrassment (extremely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Burn That Almost Wasn't
instruction: You're a 16-year-old kid who just tried to roast your older brother's friend in front of a group of people at a party. You thought you had the perfect comeback, something hilarious that would make everyone laugh. But your voice cracked halfway through, you stumbled over the words, and now the whole room is staring at you with a mix of pity and secondhand embarrassment. Start with a tiny, shaky laugh at yourself—almost amused at how badly this backfired. Then, as you try to explain what you *meant* to say, your awe at how cool the joke sounded in your head turns into confusion at how it all went wrong. Let your voice shrink, trailing off into a mumble as you realize you just made it worse. By the end, you're just staring at your shoes, your final words barely a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (extremely present), Awe (slightly present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's bedside in hospice at dawn. She's awake, lucid for perhaps the last time. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to make small talk about the sunrise outside her window, your voice artificially bright because you can't accept this is goodbye. But she squeezes your hand and says your name in a way that breaks through your denial. Let your voice crack and crumble as you finally say everything you've been holding back—thank you, I'm sorry, I love you, I'm not ready. Move from frantic attempts to keep talking (as if words can keep her here) to a whispered, tender acceptance. End with you describing the morning light on her face, your voice soft and broken but filled with gratitude for this final moment of clarity together. The emotion transforms from desperate denial to devastating, peaceful goodbye.

title: The Half-Heard Alarm
instruction: You’ve just surfaced from a deep afternoon nap, still thick with sleep inertia. Your phone buzzes—a missed call from your boss, followed by a voicemail. You hit play, struggling to understand the words through the fog in your head. As you rewind and replay, frustration and concentration sharpen your voice from a groggy slur into a focused, irritable clarity. Your response is delayed, words tumble out with pauses, then you finally snap into attention, repeating back a key instruction with annoyed precision. Let your voice start heavy, pitchy, and disoriented, then gradually find a sharper, more focused edge as you force your brain to track the message.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father after finding letters that reveal he knew about your mother's affair—knew you might not be his—and chose to raise you anyway, in silence. Begin with accusatory confusion: 'Why didn't you ever say anything?' Your voice is sharp, demanding. But as you look at his face, something crumbles inside you. The confrontation shifts to a plea: 'Did you... did you ever love me as yours?' Your voice is naked, childlike. When he finally nods, you break—not with relief, but with the overwhelming realization of his quiet sacrifice. Your voice becomes thick with tears and awe: 'You stayed. You chose me.' End with a whispered 'Thank you' that contains a lifetime of unspoken gratitude and newly discovered devotion.

title: The Smell of His Jacket
instruction: Confront your father who is about to walk out of your life again after another broken promise. Start angry—sharp, accusatory, listing his failures. But as you speak, allow sense memories to ambush you: the specific smell of his leather jacket from childhood when he'd pick you up and you felt safe, the sound of his laugh during the one good vacation you remember, the roughness of his unshaven face against yours, the taste of the peppermints he always carried. Let these involuntary sensory fragments disarm your anger mid-sentence. Feel your throat tighten as you realize you still love him despite everything, that beneath your rage is a child's longing. Your voice should shift from hard accusation to something broken and desperate—you're no longer attacking him but begging him, revealing the deep wound of abandonment. End in a place of painful, humiliated vulnerability, having exposed more than you intended.
inspired_by: Involuntary Imaging — Hatful of Rain Scene Example

title: The Wilt of Malice
instruction: You are a middle-aged man, sun-scorched in an empty desert, having just lost the trail of the person you came to destroy. Your body is shutting down from heat exhaustion — mouth bone-dry, vision swimming, every step a wobble. Start with a low, venomous growl, spitting the threat at the horizon. But as the heat saps your strength, the malevolence sours into a cracked, slurred whisper, the words tangling as your throat seizes. Let your breath be shallow, your tone fading into weak bitterness, and trail off into a dizzy, silent collapse. Speak about 60 words, from a fierce opening to a wilted, defeated end.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unsaid Decade
instruction: You're confronting your father after ten years of distance. Start from a place of defensive armor—you came here with a rehearsed speech, walls up, determined not to let him hurt you again. But as you begin speaking, let yourself notice him differently: his aged hands, his changed posture, the way he's actually listening. Strip away your prepared words and let something truer emerge—the child who needed him, the anger at his absence, but also the painful recognition that he's human and flawed. Move from controlled accusation to something messier: moments where love and rage tangle together, where you hear your voice crack with vulnerability you didn't plan to show. End in a place of raw, uncertain openness—not resolved, but finally, devastatingly honest.

title: The Ungracious Gift
instruction: You are an elderly woman with Tourette's, seated at a cluttered kitchen table. A neighbor has just brought you a homemade casserole, and you are genuinely grateful, but your tics interrupt your thanks with loud, random words or sounds. Start with a warm, shaky 'thank you' that gets derailed, but then the neighbor makes a patronizing comment about your 'condition,' igniting a fierce anger—your voice sharpens, your gratitude curdles into bitter amusement at their ignorance. Let every tic be a jarring, physical interruption that you ignore, and let your emotions flip from soft gratitude to seething, mocking rage by the end, your voice cracking with dark laughter.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Stone in My Throat
instruction: You’re nine years old, standing at your older brother’s wedding reception. You were forced to give a toast. You grip the microphone like it’s a snake, staring at the crowd. Your voice starts pinched, wavering, barely audible — you’re furious that your eulogy for your dad was never allowed, but this moment is. As you speak, the anger swells, making your pitch rise, then cracks into a raw, defiant pride for your brother. You glance down at your shoes, swallow hard, and force the last words out with a trembling, held-back sob. Your voice should sound strained, too loud then too soft, with long, uncomfortable pauses where you forget what to say.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Pendant's Weight
instruction: You are an elderly person, alone in a quiet room, just after being told your spouse has been found safe after a day-long disappearance. You sit heavily on a chair, holding a small, worn pendant they gave you decades ago. Begin by speaking to the empty space, voice cracking with pent-up relief — a shaky, broken whisper. As you recall the fight you had with them the morning they left, your anger swells, cutting through the relief; your voice tightens and quickens, paced with bitter, staccato bursts. End with a wavering sigh, the anger dissolving into exhausted gratitude, voice trailing off as you clutch the pendant to your chest, lost in thought.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Gravity of the Unspoken
instruction: Late at night, in whispers, you are telling your sleeping lover something you could never say while they are awake—a secret, a fear, a truth about yourself that feels too heavy to voice in daylight. Begin with your body curled protectively, voice barely audible, each word requiring enormous effort to lift out of your throat. As you continue speaking into the darkness, feel the relief of confession beginning to spread through your limbs like warmth, like something dissolving. Your whispers become slightly easier, your body slowly uncurls. Let tears come if they want to, but quietly, like condensation. By the end, you are lying flat, arms open, voice still soft but no longer strangled, as if the weight of this secret has finally melted out of your bones and pooled around you on the sheets. You feel emptied, exposed, but somehow lighter and more real.

title: What I Never Told You (Whispered at 3 AM)
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love—a partner, a child, a dying friend—and they're asleep. In barely audible whispers, confess something you've never had the courage to say aloud: your deepest fear about losing them, a mistake you made that still haunts you, or how completely they've changed your life. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost just breath. Include the moments where emotion catches in your throat and you have to pause, swallow, breathe. Let tenderness mix with profound sadness. Perhaps touch their hair or hand (describe this). End with the devastating peace of having finally said it, even though they'll never hear it. The journey moves from tentative confession through throat-catching vulnerability to bittersweet release.
inspired_by: Leaving a Party Without Saying Goodbye

title: The Protection I Cannot Give You
instruction: You're holding someone you love fiercely—a child about to face something terrible, a partner going into danger, a friend making a choice you can't save them from. Begin with fierce, almost violent protectiveness—'Over my dead body, you are NOT going through this'—full of bravado and certainty. But as you speak, reality crashes in. Your voice begins to shake. The strength crumbles into helplessness. You're making promises you can't keep, and you know it, and you can't stop making them because stopping means admitting you're powerless. Your words become increasingly desperate, contradictory—declarations of strength that break into sobs mid-sentence. You're simultaneously raging at your own helplessness and trying to be strong for them. End with your voice completely raw, stripped of all performance, reduced to the most basic human plea: a repeated 'please' that means everything and nothing.

title: What I Should Have Told You
instruction: You're alone in the empty apartment of someone you loved, the day after they left without explanation. Speak softly to them as if they can hear you, starting with the careful, surface-level things you always said—the jokes, the pleasant observations, the safe topics. Let your voice drop to almost nothing as you begin confessing what you never had the courage to say: the depth of your need, the ways they made you feel seen, how terrified you were of that much vulnerability. Your throat tightens around the words. End with the raw, whispered truth you're only brave enough to say now that they're gone, a confession that mixes regret with the painful relief of finally being honest, even to an empty room.

title: The Connection Restored
instruction: You are an elderly person on a crackling phone line, finally hearing the voice of a loved one who was out of touch during a storm. You start with a tight, trembling uncertainty—you’re speaking a little louder than usual, enunciating each word clearly, hearing your own voice echo in the quiet room. As the other person responds, the tension in your chest loosens, and your voice warms into a soft, weary relief. Let your pitch rise slightly on key words as you check they can still hear you, and let a slow, audible exhale slip between sentences. The spoken content should be about 40-80 words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Nighttime Garden
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe eight years old, who has just traveled across many time zones. It is 3 AM here but your body thinks it's midday. You are sitting in a quiet, moonlit garden behind a relative's house, still fully dressed, too wired to sleep. At first, you speak with a hushed, dreamy wonder—but your words wander, pause, trail off as you try to name the constellations you half-remember. Midway through describing a shooting star you swear you just saw, a yawn cracks your voice. And then, in the silence, you realize you feel safe here, in this strange not-night, and your words slow into a quiet, contented sigh—an exhausted joy that whispers to the fireflies. You end with a soft, sleepy confession of love for this place, almost to yourself, the shame of being out of bed now a faint blush fading into peace.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Shame (slightly present), Interest (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Finding the Absurd Humor in Your Own Heartbreak
instruction: You're recounting the moment your world fell apart—a betrayal, a loss, the end of something precious—but somehow, in the telling, you find the ridiculous irony of it all. Start with a half-laugh, voice wry but pain underneath: 'You want to hear something funny? The day everything ended, I was worried about...' and name something absurdly trivial. The laugh gets bigger, more real, but tears are starting too. You're laughing and crying at once: 'I mean, how perfect is that? How absolutely...' The laughter breaks into a sob, then back to laughter. Voice shaking with both: 'I should be devastated. I am devastated. But it's also so ridiculous I can't...' Find the space where grief and humor embrace, where you're simultaneously broken and somehow, impossibly, finding your way through by laughing at the cosmic joke of it all.
inspired_by: Arguing When You're Both Partially Right

title: The Last Interview Before Execution
instruction: You are a journalist conducting the final interview with someone you've investigated for years, now facing execution at dawn. Begin with your professional detachment, asking the hard questions you always wanted answered. But as they speak with quiet acceptance about their regrets and the family they'll leave behind, feel your objectivity crack. Your voice should shift from assertive interrogation to something struggling to remain steady—you didn't expect to care, to see them as human. End with a whispered question you know you shouldn't ask, one that reveals you've stopped being a journalist and become simply a person sitting with another person in their final hours. Let the transformation happen naturally—from clinical distance to unbearable intimacy.
inspired_by: The Journalist and the Secret Informant

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Parent on Their Deathbed After Years of Distance
instruction: You enter the room with your voice tight and controlled: 'I'm here.' You haven't been close in years, and now there's so little time. As you sit beside them, your voice cracks open: 'I should have called more. I should have...' Let the regret flood through you—raw, unguarded. Tell them one specific memory from childhood that you've held onto, your voice becoming tender and young again. Then shift: realize you're also angry at them for things left unsaid, for wounds never addressed. Let that anger rise briefly before it collapses into desperate love. End by whispering 'I forgive you' or 'Please forgive me'—whichever truth your heart reaches for first—your voice breaking with the weight of a lifetime compressed into final moments.
inspired_by: Asking Your Parent for Money While Ashamed

title: Eulogy in the Rain: Laughing Through the Grief
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone who made you promise not to cry at their funeral—your irreverent, chaotic, brilliant friend who lived louder than anyone. Start by trying to honor their wish, telling a funny story, and actually laughing—real laughter that comes from genuine memory. But the laughter catches, breaks, becomes something else. Your voice wavers between humor and heartbreak: 'You made me promise not to cry, you absolute jerk, and here I am...' Share moments of gratitude—all the ways they saved you, saw you, made you better—but let your voice crack with the unbearable pain of their absence. Find moments of pure joy in the memories, then let that joy dissolve into tears. End with both: laughing and crying at once, your voice thick with contradictory emotions: 'Thank you for every ridiculous, beautiful, impossible moment. I'm so grateful. And I'm so, so angry you're gone.' Let gratitude and devastation exist simultaneously.
inspired_by: Professor Accusing Student of Plagiarism: Mercy in the Moment

title: The Edge of Everything
instruction: You're in a dim bedroom, lying back on a bed, with a partner whose hands are tracing your body with devastating precision. You feel like you're floating just above yourself, watching your skin turn into a map of tiny, impossible sensations. At the start, try to speak gently, almost in wonder, 'You know when the light hits your hand like that, it looks like honey?' Then they touch you in a way that makes you gasp. For the next minute, let your voice ride the waves: as pleasure builds, your words climb in pitch and speed, then drop into a jagged sigh when they pause. Let your breathing become shallow and your sentences dissolve into fragments—'Please, I need... just... it's like... it's too much.' Let awe twist your voice into something worshipful and broken. End with a quiet, breathless realization: 'I didn't know bodies could feel this huge.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Bubbles and Bitter Goodbye
instruction: You're a teenage girl washing dishes at a friend's pool party, hidden away from the crowd by the kitchen island. Everyone else is outside laughing and splashing—your crush included, who just ran past with your best friend. You’re gripping a wine glass too hard as you scrub it, drowning in jealousy and a burning, quiet malice. At first, your voice trembles with embarrassment as you mumble to yourself about being stuck on dish duty. But as you speak, the words grow sharper, and your smile becomes a sneer—you start plotting tiny, cruel ways to make them both feel as small as you do now. Let the clink of plates and rush of water punctuate your words, your voice rising and falling with your bitterness, ending on a chillingly sweet vow.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Don't You Dare Leave
instruction: Someone you love is walking away from you—from the relationship, from the life you built. You start fierce, almost aggressive: 'Turn around. TURN AROUND.' Your voice is command and desperation braided together. You're listing everything you've sacrificed, everything you've been, and it builds to shouting. But mid-rage, you break. The anger cracks open and underneath is pure terror: 'I don't know how to be me without you.' Your voice becomes ragged, pleading, then drops to something fierce and protective of yourself: 'But I won't beg. I won't—' Then you do. You beg. You collapse into it. End with your voice wrung out, barely functioning: 'Please. I'm saying please.' Let the helplessness destroy your dignity completely.

title: The Unstoppable Sneeze
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, masculine voice, sitting in a silent library. A sneeze builds—you try to hold it in with sharp, strained intakes and tiny whispers. It explodes out, loud and wet. As your voice turns nasal and congested from recovery, you realize how absurdly you must have looked fighting it. A grin spreads, and you speak through laughter, your words thick and amused, ending with genuine, breathy delight.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Rescued from Choking: The Moment Breath Becomes Possible Again
instruction: Someone is performing the Heimlich on you. You're choking, unable to make sound, your voice is completely gone. Then the blockage ejects and air floods back in. Your voice is a gasp, then a sob, then a scream. You're gasping 'thank you thank you thank you' and it's barely comprehensible. Include the moment where you can actually breathe again—truly breathe—and your voice becomes shaky with relief and the aftershock of nearly dying. You're coughing, your voice is hoarse, you're trying to say something coherent but your body is in its own experience. 'I couldn't... I thought...' Your voice can't complete thoughts because you're just grateful for breath itself.

title: Holding Everything at Once
instruction: You've just received news that's simultaneously the best and worst thing that could happen—a terminal patient learns they're in sudden remission on the same day they lose someone they love, or a dream comes true the moment you realize it's too late to share it with the person who believed in you. Begin speaking with confused joy, almost laughing with disbelief at the good news, your voice bright and breaking upward. But the loss crashes into the joy mid-sentence and you can't separate them. You find yourself laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice doing both at once—gratitude splitting into grief and back again. The emotions aren't taking turns; they're happening together, fighting for the same breath. End with a moment of strange peace in the chaos, your voice soft and wondering, saying something simple like 'they would have been so happy' or 'I wish you were here'—the words carrying both devastating sadness and profound love, acceptance and heartbreak, all at once.

title: The Last Train Home
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your childhood friend at a train station—they're leaving for a war zone as a journalist and you both know they might not come back. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light like you always do together, making jokes about bringing back souvenirs. But as the departure time approaches, your voice should crack and the fear should bleed through. End in a place of raw, quiet acceptance—you're not okay with this, but you're trying to give them the gift of your strength even as you're breaking inside. Let the transition happen naturally, like a dam slowly giving way.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Partner Who Doesn't Know You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're standing over your partner of ten years as they sleep, bags packed by the door. Begin in barely audible whispers, tender and aching: 'You look so peaceful. You always do.' Your voice catches as you confess what you could never say to their waking face: 'I've loved you so much it's been killing me... and you never even noticed I was disappearing.' Let the words become more raw, throat tight with unshed tears: 'I tried. God, I tried to be enough for both of us.' End with the devastating gentleness of someone who still loves but can't stay, voice breaking into fragments: 'I hope you find someone who... who you actually see.' The final 'goodbye' is almost silent, a breath more than a word, as you turn away.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Stop Being Friends With Your Abuser

title: The Last Phone Call From the Station
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling from the train station before boarding a one-way journey to a treatment facility abroad - one you might not return from. You start trying to give them advice about life, slipping into those old protective patterns, those same lectures you've always given. But mid-sentence, your voice cracks and the facade crumbles. You realize this might be the last time you speak to them, and suddenly all those bossy warnings transform into desperate confessions: how proud you are, how scared you've always been of failing them, how much you need them to know they were never a burden. End with you whispering the things you should have said years ago, your voice breaking with the weight of goodbye. Let the transformation from protective lecture to raw vulnerability happen naturally, like a dam breaking.

title: The Truth About the Inheritance
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about why they gave everything to your sibling and nothing to you. Begin with measured control, trying to stay dignified: 'I just want to understand.' But decades of feeling unseen begin pouring out. Your voice grows sharper, more wounded: 'Was I ever enough for you?' You're not yelling—you're bleeding. Move through anger that keeps breaking into desperate pleas for validation, for love, for acknowledgment. Then something shifts. You realize you're not asking anymore; you're telling them what you needed and never got. By the end, your voice has transformed into something quieter, sadder, but final—you're not begging. You're grieving the parent you needed but never had, and beginning to release them.

title: Three AM Whispers
instruction: You are lying in the dark next to your partner, and you cannot sleep. Begin by whispering something small, a simple confession: 'I'm scared.' Let the darkness and their closeness give you permission to shed your daily persona. Speak softly, intimately, letting each sentence pull you deeper into exposure. Confess the things you hide from everyone—your doubts, your shameful fears, the ways you feel inadequate. Let yourself be genuinely affected by the safety of this moment and the terror of being truly known. By the end, you are speaking from a place of complete emotional nakedness, voice barely audible, trembling with the vulnerability of total honesty.

title: The Body Keeps Score
instruction: You're in physical agony—chronic pain, injury, illness—and you're watching yourself in a mirror, cataloguing how pain has changed your body. Observe aloud how you now stand (do you slump, protect one side, make yourself smaller?), how you move (carefully, hesitantly, with guarded precision?), how your face has reorganized itself around suffering (tight jaw, furrowed brow, eyes that don't quite meet their own reflection?). Begin clinically observing these physical adaptations, reasoning through what they mean like a scientist studying a specimen. But as you watch yourself, the emotional weight crashes in—you barely recognize this pain-guarded creature. Let observation turn into rage, then grief. Scream at your reflection, pound the mirror, then collapse into tender recognition of how hard this body has fought to carry you. Move from detached analysis to visceral acceptance, touching your reflection with forgiveness.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You
instruction: You've finally found the words you've rehearsed for thirty years, sitting across from your mother, voice shaking with controlled rage. Start with accusations—'You knew. You knew what was happening and you looked away'—each word sharp and precise, years of therapy leading to this moment. But mid-confrontation, something unexpected happens: you see her face, really see her, and the anger cracks. Your voice splinters between fury and the desperate need for her to just say she's sorry, to acknowledge what you lost. 'I needed you. I was eight years old and I needed you.' The confrontation becomes a plea, then almost a confession of your own—that despite everything, some wounded part of you still loves her, still wants her to be the mother she never was. End with your voice barely audible, caught between rage and the most painful vulnerability: 'Tell me you see me now. Please. Just tell me you see me.'
inspired_by: Evacuating from Wildfire: Seeing Everything You Built Burn

title: The Astronaut's Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut whose spacecraft has catastrophically failed, drifting away from Earth with no possibility of rescue. You have maybe twenty minutes of oxygen left. You start your final transmission to mission control with panic creeping into your voice—'Houston, I need you to tell Sarah...' but you can't finish, your breath catching. Then something shifts. As Earth grows smaller in your window, you find yourself marveling at its beauty. Your voice steadies, fills with wonder: 'I can see the whole planet now. God, it's so beautiful.' The fear drains away, replaced by awe. 'Tell Sarah I'm not afraid. Tell her I saw something she wouldn't believe—the sunrise over the curve of the world.' Your final words are almost joyful, like you've discovered a secret: 'I'm going further than anyone has ever gone. I'm not alone out here.' You're transforming from terrified to transcendent, finding peace in the vastness.

title: Gasping for a Tease
instruction: You’ve just sprinted a full block after your much younger friend, who ran off with your keys as a joke. Now you’re bent over, hands on knees, lungs heaving. Your hyper-feminized voice is shredded by violent gasps—each word forced between inhales. At first, doubt floods you: you’re not sure you can even speak, let alone punish her. But as the static of nausea fades, longing to connect glimmers through; you want to reel her back into your orbit. Let the tease climb through the wrecked breaths—a high, strained lilt that starts as a growl of exhaustion and finishes as a sly, sing-song jab: ‘Oh, you think you’re fast, don’t you?’ Make the gasps real: bend over, compress your ribs, let spit catch in your throat, and let the last word ride a shaky, victorious laugh that almost costs you your air.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (extremely present), Longing (slightly present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: You're getting ready for your wedding, and you're radiantly happy—you love this person, you're choosing this life. But as you look at yourself in the mirror or speak to your reflection, another truth surfaces: someone else isn't here. A parent who died, a sibling you're estranged from, a first love you never fully released, or even a version of yourself you're leaving behind. Your voice must hold both joy and devastating loss simultaneously. Laugh through tears. Let excitement catch on sorrow. Express gratitude while grieving what's absent. You're not choosing one emotion over the other—you're embodying the impossible truth that the happiest moments of our lives can also break our hearts.

title: The Final Rinse
instruction: You are a woman in a tiled bathroom, just finished bathing a small child. The room echoes with every drip and whisper. Start by humming a lullaby, voice soft and full of false warmth, as you dry the child's hair. Then, as you lean close to their ear, your tone hardens—a quiet, chilling malice seeps in. Let the bright reverb carry your words; let the flutter echo sharpen your sibilants. End with a promise that sounds like a threat, your voice growing colder as the warmth drains away.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Rumor Unravels
instruction: You're hunched over a sticky tabletop at your local dive bar, leaning in close to your oldest friend. Your voice drops to a conspiratorial whisper as you share a wild story about a guy from work. You start with a teasing, almost giddy energy—your words tumble out fast, punctuated by low chuckles and sharp, excited glances over your shoulder. But as you lay out the details, you suddenly realize a gap in the logic; your grin falters, your sentences slow down, and your pitch rises with genuine puzzlement. Let your voice move from a playful, edgy thrill to a slower, confused reconsideration, as if you're talking yourself out of the story you were just loving.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Elation (very intensely present), Confusion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Treading Memories
instruction: You are an older adult floating in a calm lake at dusk, your body partially submerged. The water laps at your chin as you speak to the sky about someone who just left your life—an old love who reappeared and vanished again. Start with a rush of infatuation, breathless and giddy, but as you speak, pride creeps in, then deeper contemplation. Let the water interrupt you: gurgles when your mouth dips under, gasps as you lift your head, splashes as you shift. Your voice should alternate between clear and muffled, and you must lose your train of thought once, then find it with a sigh. End quieter, staring at the ripples.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Pride (slightly present), Contemplation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Bioluminescent Drift
instruction: You are an older man swimming alone in the ocean at twilight, your arms cutting slowly through the cool water. You're carrying a heavy sadness about a friend you've lost, and you start to speak to yourself, voice strained and breathy from swimming. As you tread water, you notice tiny glowing specks around your hands — bioluminescent plankton. Your tired voice lifts, softens with a fragile, childlike awe, but the sadness still ghosts your words. You speak in fragmented, breathless sentences, sometimes losing your thought as you gasp for air or wipe water from your eyes.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Light of Recognition
instruction: You are sitting beside someone who raised you—a grandparent, parent, or guardian—in their final hours. They haven't recognized you in weeks, lost in the fog of their fading mind. Begin speaking to them with resigned sadness, telling them about your day as you have been, expecting nothing. Then, suddenly, their eyes focus on yours with perfect clarity. They know you.
