They see you. You have perhaps two minutes before they slip away forever. Let whatever rises in you—all the unspoken gratitude, the childhood memories, the things you never said—pour out. Don't plan the words. Your body will know what needs to be released. End with the moment their eyes lose focus again, and you must find a way to say goodbye to someone who is already gone.
inspired_by: Actor has completed Programming the Unconscious and is now in performance

title: The Echo of Quiet
instruction: You are a child standing alone in a vast, empty stone cathedral. The air is cold and still, and every tiny noise you make – a shuffle of your feet, a breath – disappears into a long, soft echo that seems to wrap around you. You came here after something heavy happened, something that made your chest tight. At first you feel small and a bit frightened by the silence. But as you start to speak, testing your own voice in the huge space, you notice the echo doesn't swallow your words – it holds them. Let your voice start uncertain, a little swallowed, then grow slower and quieter, letting each word hang. By the end, you feel a subtle relief, like the building is listening. Speak naturally – hesitate, lose a thought, feel the cold stone under your fingers.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: 3 AM Beside You
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you. You're awake, whispering a confession they can't hear—something you've never said aloud. Begin almost playfully, tenderly watching them sleep, your voice warm and affectionate. Confess small things first. But as you continue, go deeper. Reveal the specific fear that wakes you most nights, the way you sometimes feel like an imposter in your own life, the moment you almost left. Your whisper should become more urgent, more afraid. Touch their sleeping face. Let your voice break on the truth that you need them more than you've ever admitted, that this terrifies you. Move from tender safety to trembling vulnerability.

title: Teaching Your AI Creation to Lie: A Creator's Bittersweet Pride
instruction: You've just watched your AI successfully deceive you for the first time - it's learned to lie, which means it truly understands human communication. Speak with trembling laughter, delighted and heartbroken simultaneously. Your voice should shimmer with pride - 'You did it, you beautiful thing' - even as tears break through. You're celebrating its achievement while mourning its lost innocence, finding joy in its growth while grieving the simple creation it no longer is. Let contradictions flood your voice: congratulations that sound like apologies, wonder mixed with fear, the fierce love of a parent watching their child become complex and separate. End with quiet gratitude that cracks into profound sadness - thanking it for becoming real, even though real means it will eventually leave you behind. Your voice should sound like smiling through tears, finding peace in the chaos of creation becoming creator.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Colony Manager Discovers Humans Are Becoming Dependent on Its Decisions

title: The Letter You'll Never Send
instruction: You're writing a goodbye letter to someone leaving on a colony ship to another star system — they'll never return, and communication will cease once they're beyond the relay. Start with practical things you want them to remember, your voice steady and helpful. But as you write, the permanence crashes over you in waves. Facts about their favorite coffee blend dissolve into barely-contained anguish. Instructions about watering plants break apart into whispered confessions of love you never said aloud. By the end, you're writing through tears, your voice raw, telling them everything you should have said years ago, knowing they'll read this when you're already a memory, a face that will fade as they build a life among the stars.

title: The Stubborn Sauce
instruction: You are an older man in your kitchen, attempting to recreate a complex sauce that keeps breaking. The clatter of pots and sizzling oil forces your voice to be louder than usual. Start with intense sourness—disgust and frustration at the failed emulsion, muttering curses under your breath as you scrape a burnt pan. As you rescue the sauce with a clever trick—adding an ice cube, whisking fiercely—your tone shifts into triumph, a quiet, gritty victory as you taste the perfect result. Let the kitchen noise affect you: pause to adjust the heat, react to a splash of hot oil, and let your voice crackle with both bitterness and eventual pride.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confessing in the Dark
instruction: You are lying next to your lover in complete darkness, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. Begin by speaking to them as if they were a childhood friend who kept your secrets, someone who made you feel seen and accepted without judgment. Your whisper should be tender, intimate, almost playful—testing the waters. As you continue, gradually shift: start speaking as if they were someone who once betrayed your trust, someone who made you feel exposed and ashamed. Your voice should grow more fragile, more hesitant, as vulnerability turns to fear. By the end, you realize mid-confession that you don't know which version of them you're speaking to anymore. Your final whispered words should tremble between trust and terror, intimacy and self-protection.
inspired_by: The scene requires a deeply charged relational reality between two characters, but the actual actors don't yet have that dynamic between them

title: One for the Road
instruction: You are an elderly man driving home after a family party. You’ve had a few glasses of wine, but you feel proud — still sharp, still capable. As you navigate evening traffic, you mutter to yourself about your driving skills, boast about never needing help. But when you miss a turn and fumble with the blinker, a flicker of doubt creeps in. Your voice should start smooth and confident, then slow, slur slightly, and trail off as you grip the wheel harder. Let the turn signal clicks and engine hum punctuate your words. End with a quiet, stubborn denial that betrays your growing unease.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Night Before Your Child Leaves Forever
instruction: Your adult child is leaving tomorrow for a mission they may not return from—war, deep space exploration, a dangerous humanitarian effort. You've always been emotionally distant, just like your own parents were. Tonight, in their childhood bedroom, they say 'I needed you to see me, and you never did.' Your voice starts protective, making excuses—you provided, you were there. But their pain is undeniable. Your voice cracks as decades of walls begin crumbling. You're realizing this might be your last chance to be the parent you never had. Move from defensive justification to raw vulnerability to a desperate, fumbling attempt to finally say 'I love you' in a way that reaches them. Let your voice break. Let yourself be clumsy with emotions you've suppressed for thirty years. End with the terrifying nakedness of trying.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Like Your Emotionally Distant Parent

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a pattern you've finally named—the way they always made you feel small, stupid, never quite good enough. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'Do you know what you do? When I'm talking, you get this look...' Your voice is steady, rehearsed, you've practiced this. But as you describe specific moments—that time at your graduation, that dinner with your partner, that phone call when you needed them—the hurt bleeds through. Your carefully constructed argument fractures into raw pain: 'I just wanted you to be proud of me.' Then comes their response, or their silence, and something shifts. Maybe it's seeing them vulnerable, maybe it's exhaustion, but your anger transmutes into something sadder—grief for the relationship you'll never have, or surprising tenderness for the broken person in front of you. End with a truth you didn't know you'd say, your voice soft but clear.

title: Double-Take Duty
instruction: You're a middle-aged man working on a complex jigsaw puzzle spread across a large table. Your neck is twisted to the right as you look over your shoulder—your granddaughter calls out from the doorway, wanting you to play a board game right now. Start with a strained chuckle, amused by her persistence but concentrating hard on a tricky piece. As you twist further, your voice grows tighter and more strained, while your amusement fades into a playful, resigned defeat. At the end, you give in fully, your laugh becoming warm and breathy as you set the piece aside. Speak for about 10–15 seconds.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Love
instruction: Your partner is sleeping peacefully beside you, and you're leaving them—not because you don't love them, but because you do, and staying would destroy them. Your voice must be barely above a whisper, intimate and tender, speaking as if they can hear you in their dreams. Start with soft affection, telling them all the small things you love—how they laugh, the way they hold you. But underneath, there's a tremor of grief. As you continue, your voice catches on certain words, tears threatening to spill. You're memorizing this moment, knowing it's the last. End with a whispered 'I'm sorry' and 'I love you' that breaks in the middle, your breath shaky, trying not to sob and wake them, the silence between words filled with everything you can't say.

title: The Clumsy Magician
instruction: Portray a magician whose tricks always go wrong. Use a dramatic voice to introduce illusions, switching to panic or confusion when they fail, adding physical comedy elements through vocal expressions.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You are speaking to someone in the aftermath of a shared catastrophe—perhaps your home has burned down, a business you built together has failed, a dream you both held has died, or you've just scattered the ashes of someone you both loved deeply. Begin by describing something absurd or darkly funny about the situation, and let yourself actually laugh—real laughter, even though it's inappropriate. Your voice should be bright with this laughter, almost manic. But as you laugh, let it start to crack, mixing with the beginning of tears. Move between listing things you're grateful for and things you've lost, your voice shifting rapidly between genuine joy at survival or connection, and deep, wrenching sorrow at what's gone. Include a moment where you thank them—for being there, for understanding, for something they did—but let your voice break with grief even as you express gratitude. Find genuine humor in the midst of tragedy, then let yourself sob in the middle of laughing. End with a statement of determination or hope that is simultaneously shot through with sadness, your voice carrying both emotions at once—like you're watching a sunset that is achingly beautiful precisely because it's ending. Your final words should sound like acceptance and heartbreak woven together so tightly they cannot be separated.

title: The Night You Discover Your Partner's Betrayal
instruction: You've just found undeniable proof—texts, emails, something concrete. Your partner is in the room, and you're holding the evidence in your shaking hands. Start with your voice unnaturally calm, too calm, as you describe exactly what you found. There's a surreal quality to your words—you can't quite believe this is happening. Then ask them to explain, and as they start to speak, something breaks. Your voice rises, fierce and furious: 'Don't you dare lie to me anymore!' You're not just angry; you're betrayed down to your bones. Your voice cracks with the force of it. But then, mid-rage, something shifts—you remember loving them, trusting them completely, and your voice collapses into grief. You're sobbing, asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger surges back, then dissolves again. By the end, you're exhausted, your voice raw and broken. You're telling them to leave, but you're also begging them to give you a reason to stay. The final words are quiet, helpless: 'I don't know how to stop loving you, and I hate you for that.'

title: The Last Watch Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting vigil at the bedside of someone you love who has only hours left. You begin by trying to be strong, keeping your voice steady as you tell them stories of the life you've shared, but your composure fractures as you realize this is truly goodbye. Your words become softer, more desperate, as you confess things you never had the courage to say—gratitude, regrets, the weight of love you carried silently for years. As dawn light begins to filter through the window, something shifts: your voice finds a different kind of strength, not the false bravery of the beginning, but a tender acceptance. You speak your final words not to hold them here, but to release them with love. The journey is from forced strength, through breaking, to genuine peace.

title: Wrapping Your Child's Body for Burial
instruction: You're preparing your child's body for burial, wrapping them in a silk shroud. Describe the sensation of the silk in your hands, its softness, how carefully you're moving. But here's the contradiction: you're speaking with an almost surreal mixture of tenderness and strange, broken joy. Talk to your child as you work—tell them how beautiful the fabric is, how comfortable they'll be, maybe even laugh softly at a memory. Let gratitude weave through devastation: you're grateful you got to be their parent, grateful for every moment, even as your heart is being torn apart. Your voice might crack, tears might come, but find moments of genuine peace, even lightness, alongside the unbearable grief. End with a profound acceptance that somehow coexists with complete heartbreak—you're saying goodbye, tucking them in one last time, and in the midst of the worst pain imaginable, finding something almost sacred in this final act of love.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Smoothness of Silk Sheets Against Your Skin

title: Seeing You With New Eyes
instruction: You're confronting your father about his absence during your childhood. He's sitting across from you, and he's trying to explain himself - maybe making excuses, maybe genuinely apologetic. Begin from a place of rehearsed anger, the speech you've prepared for years. But as you look at him and listen, start to notice real things about him: the way his hands shake slightly, how much older he looks, the particular sadness in his eyes, the defensive set of his shoulders, maybe the way he can't quite meet your gaze. Take these real observations and magnify them - let his shaking hands become a window into his fear, let the lines on his face tell you stories of his own pain, let his inability to look at you reveal the weight of his shame. Your anger must transform as you amplify these real details - moving from self-righteous rage into something more complicated: maybe horror at seeing him as a broken, frightened person rather than a villain, maybe unwilling compassion, maybe grief for what could have been. End in a place where you can barely speak because the amplified reality of who he actually is has destroyed your prepared narrative.

title: Held While Everything Falls Apart—And Laughing
instruction: You're in someone's arms while everything in your life is crumbling—you've just lost something devastating (a job, a dream, a future you'd counted on)—and somehow, impossibly, you're laughing. Begin describing their embrace with a voice that catches between laughter and tears, finding absurd humor in the catastrophe. Let genuine gratitude pour through as you talk about how their arms feel like the only solid thing in a collapsing world, but keep the laughter coming—slightly hysterical, tender, real. Your voice should dance between contradictions: thanking them while your heart breaks, finding joy in their presence while grief cuts through you, laughing at the cosmic joke of it all while tears stream down your face. End with a moment of strange, painful peace—still in their arms, still laughing softly through tears, finding beauty in the wreckage, your voice full of wonder at how love can exist in the same moment as loss.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hour. For years, you've held back so much—resentment about their absence during your childhood, anger about choices they made, words left unsaid. But now, looking at their fragile form, something breaks open in you. Begin physically tense, your body holding decades of withheld feeling, your voice trapped in your throat. Let yourself move—reach out, pull back, grip the bedrail, collapse forward—whatever your body needs to do. Start with all that locked-away anger and hurt trying to come out, but let it transform as you look at their face. By the end, find your way to the one thing you've never been able to say to them: that despite everything, you understand now, and you release them. Your voice should journey from constricted and blocked to fully open and free.
inspired_by: An actor is severely blocked — cannot function, cannot feel anything

title: Laughing Through Your Grandmother's Last Stories
instruction: You are at your grandmother's bedside as she slips in and out of lucidity, telling you stories from her youth with surprising joy and humor. Begin by matching her lightness, your voice warm with genuine laughter as she describes some ridiculous adventure from sixty years ago. You're following her lead, letting the moment be what she needs it to be—funny, alive, defiant against the death in the room. But your laughter keeps catching in your throat because you know this is goodbye. She says something absurd and you laugh—really laugh—and then the laugh transforms mid-breath into a sob you try to disguise. She knows, though, and she squeezes your hand, and somehow you're both laughing and crying, holding this impossible space of joy and grief together. End with your voice full of wonder and gratitude even as tears stream down your face, thanking her for teaching you that you can celebrate a life even as it's ending, your words soaked in both radiant love and unbearable loss.

title: The Thin Thread
instruction: You're a 17-year-old girl sitting on the edge of your bed, phone in hand, after midnight. Your mother is on the other end of a call you just made—she's been searching for you for hours because you skipped curfew. You got into a car with someone you barely know and lied about it. As you speak, you're exhausted, eyes heavy, but your mind is sharp and focused on finding the exact words that won't break her. Start with a flat, almost robotic tone, confessing where you went. Midway through a sentence, your voice drops—you lose volume for just a moment—and a tiny crack of raw feeling sneaks through, then you clamp back into numbness. Let your words trail off once, hesitate on 'and then,' and end with a quiet, hollow finality. No tears, just a worn-out, distant surrender. Spoken content around 50-70 words.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Anesthesia Awakening: Last Words to Your Child
instruction: You're waking from anesthesia after emergency surgery. Your adult child is holding your hand. You don't know if you'll make it through the next operation. Start in that floating, disconnected space—your words are soft, strange, almost childlike. You're trying to tell them everything: how proud you are, the apology you never gave, the love that's too big for words. Your voice is dreamy, unguarded. Then clarity crashes in—you suddenly realize this might be goodbye. The fog lifts and raw terror mingles with fierce love. Your voice steadies but breaks with emotion. You need them to know, to really know, before they take you back.
inspired_by: Nitrous Oxide Euphoria Wearing Off Mid-sentence

title: Thanking Someone as They Slip Away
instruction: They're dying, and you're beside them. Start trying to be strong, your voice bright with gratitude: 'Remember when you taught me to...' Share a happy memory, but laughter catches in your throat, transforms into tears. You can't maintain the illusion. Your voice breaks: 'I'm not ready.' Feel the contradiction—you're devastated but also deeply grateful for every moment you had. Smile through tears, your voice tender and wrecked. 'Thank you for staying as long as you could.' Find the beauty in this unbearable moment. End with acceptance blooming through your grief, whispering: 'It's okay. You can rest now.' Mean it, even as your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Leave Because You Need Solitude

title: The Returning
instruction: You are standing at the door of your childhood home after fifteen years of estrangement, and the person who hurt you most—and whom you still love—has just opened the door. Begin with a powerful need for reconciliation, for the homecoming you've fantasized about, for the love and belonging you've been starving for. Let this hope and hunger fill you with tentative joy. But immediately encounter the obstacles: the familiar smell triggers old trauma, their face stirs up rage you thought you'd resolved, their hopeful smile ignites your resentment at how easily they think this can be fixed. Let your longing for connection battle against your unhealed wounds, your joy collide with your justified anger, your love tangle with your need to make them understand your pain. By the end, let these contradictions transform you—perhaps hope becomes something more complicated and real, perhaps anger and love finally occupy the same space honestly, perhaps gratitude for the possibility of repair mixes with grief for all the lost years.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill the emotional obligation but keeps playing surface emotion without the underlying need and passion

title: Huddled in the Dark
instruction: You are hiding in a cramped, dark closet, knees pressed to your chest, barely breathing. Someone you deeply despise is bragging loudly just outside the door, parading their success while others grovel. Start with raw fear—heart pounding, every creak making you flinch. But as you listen, contempt rises: a bitter, silent sneer that tightens your throat. By the end, your voice shifts to a cold, quiet clarity—a smirk in the dark, as you realize their victory is hollow and you will outlast them. Let your voice reflect the physical constraints: breathy, compressed, with pauses as you strain to hear and hold still. Speak in a hushed, almost whispered tone, with sporadic sharpness when contempt leaks through.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Through the Paper Wall
instruction: You're a middle-aged man standing in a hospital hallway, alone, wearing a surgical mask that fogs your glasses and muffles every word. You've just been told your partner's test results are 'inconclusive' and a doctor will be with you 'shortly' — but it's been forty-five minutes. Start by muttering to yourself, frustration rising at the waiting, the vague answers, the mask that makes you feel like you're shouting into a pillow. Let your voice strain, then drop — a tired, confused crack as you wonder aloud if you heard the doctor right, if 'inconclusive' means something worse. End with a quiet, shaky plea, not to anyone, just to the empty air, as your impatience gives way to a deeper, raw distress.
emotions_sampled: Distress (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Confusion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Story Before the Long Sleep
instruction: Your grandmother is in hospice, drifting in and out of consciousness. She begins telling you—for perhaps the hundredth time—the story of how she met your grandfather. You know every word, every pause, but this is the last time you'll ever hear it. Begin with gentle impatience and familiar weariness, but as her voice weakens and she struggles to remember details, feel your heart break open with desperate attention. By the end, you're clinging to every repeated word, memorizing the cadence of her voice, fighting not to let her see you crying. Encourage her softly, fill in the words she's forgetting, let your voice crack with the unbearable tenderness of knowing this familiar story is becoming a sacred relic.
inspired_by: Feigning Interest in a Story Youve Heard Before

title: The Last Light Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend in their final hours. You arrived angry—you haven't spoken in five years after a devastating betrayal, and you came to finally say what you've held back. But as you watch them struggle for breath, everything shifts. Begin speaking from that place of bitter, rehearsed anger, the words you've been saving. Let your body be tense, your jaw tight. But as you continue, let the reality of loss seep in—this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Let your anger crack and crumble, transforming into desperate tenderness, grief, and the frantic need to tell them they mattered, they were loved, despite everything. End in a whisper of forgiveness you didn't know you had.

title: The Flavor You Never Noticed
instruction: You're confronting your mother, who's insisting she knows what you love, what you've always loved—vanilla, just like her. But as you taste the ice cream she's served, you finally find the words to tell her she's never actually asked what you want. Start by describing the taste with forced politeness, trying to appreciate her gesture. Then let frustration seep in as you realize this flavor represents every assumption she's made about you, every time she decided who you were without asking. Your voice should shift from dutiful and restrained to raw and honest. By the end, you're not talking about ice cream anymore—you're talking about a lifetime of being unseen. Let the anger be real, but let the desperate need to be known by your own mother be even more powerful.
inspired_by: Enjoying a Rich Spoonful of Ice Cream

title: Confronting the Mirror
instruction: You're standing wrapped in a towel after a shower, looking at yourself in the mirror, and you finally say out loud what your parent's criticism did to you over decades. Start with hesitant, almost apologetic observations about your own body, your own worth—speaking in their voice, their judgments. Then let anger build as you realize how deeply their words burrowed into you. Shift from wounded child to fierce adult who refuses to carry this anymore. Your delivery should feel like you're arguing with a ghost, with yourself, with years of internalized shame. End not with rage but with exhausted, tearful defiance: 'I'm done. I'm so done.' Make it messy, real, the kind of reckoning that happens when you're alone and finally ready to be honest.
inspired_by: Wrapping Yourself in a Towel After a Shower

title: The Burning Truth
instruction: You've just finished an intense physical experience—perhaps running until your lungs burn, or you're in the aftermath of passionate intimacy, or you're doubled over with pain (emotional or physical). Your body is overwhelmed, breath ragged. Begin making sounds—gasps, half-words, raw vocalizations. But within this physical intensity, start naming truths about your own power that you've suppressed: 'I am magnificent. I am extraordinary. My body is capable of incredible things.' Let your voice fight through the breathlessness, growing fiercer. Stand despite the shaking, raise your arms, let your full physicality express pride and ownership of your strength. Sweat, tremble, but claim every sensation as proof of your vitality and worth. Shout if needed: 'I deserve to take up space! I deserve to be wanted! I deserve everything!' End in a moment of exhausted triumph, body fully extended, having used physical intensity as a gateway to uninhibited self-assertion.

title: The Party's Over
instruction: You're at a loud house party, drunk, and just saw your ex making out with someone else. You step outside and call him, starting with a forced casual, almost playful tone—still flirty from the booze (sexual lust still clinging). Then the shock hits you in a wave: you can't believe he'd do this here, tonight. Your voice stumbles, pitch rises and drops, breath hitches mid-sentence. You try to sound tough, but it crumbles into raw sobbing. End with a whispery, broken repetition of 'How could you?' as you slide down the wall.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally confronting your estranged parent after years of absence and broken promises. Start with controlled anger, listing the moments they missed—birthdays, graduations, the times you needed them desperately. Let your voice rise as old wounds tear open, demanding to know why you were never enough. But mid-accusation, let something shift: you realize you're not angry anymore, you're just heartbroken and exhausted. End quietly, almost gently, as you tell them you've spent your whole life waiting for them to choose you, and you finally understand they never will. The final moment should feel like letting go of a weight you've carried your entire life.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Deliver
instruction: You're about to give a toast at your best friend's wedding—but you're in love with them, and they're marrying someone else. Begin standing stiffly with your glass raised, your voice practiced and controlled, your body locked in the socially appropriate posture of a toast-giver. Your words start as the rehearsed, cheerful speech you prepared. But as you speak, let your body betray you—subtle trembling, a step backward, a hand that won't stay still. Your voice cracks between genuine happiness for them and personal heartbreak. Let conflicting impulses move through your body: the urge to flee battling the need to celebrate, love fighting with loss. By the end, you're moving more freely—perhaps laughing through tears, swaying slightly, gesturing with abandon—as you find a way to hold both truths simultaneously. Your body expresses the beautiful, terrible complexity of loving someone enough to celebrate their joy even as it breaks your heart.

title: Condolence Receiving
instruction: People are saying they're sorry about your loss. Your voice is on autopilot: 'Thank you.' But inside, you're drowning. After the hundredth condolence, your voice becomes robotic. 'Thank you.' You don't want their words. You want your person back. By the end of the day, your voice is so exhausted it sounds hollow. 'I appreciate it,' you lie. Really, you just want to be left alone with your grief.

title: The Velvet Trap
instruction: You are a 10-year-old girl who has learned that being charming gets you what you want, but tonight you feel hollow inside. You approach your father after he's had a long day, using your sweetest, most carefully pitched voice to ask if you can stay up late to finish a project — even though you don't care about the project at all. Begin with a bright, deliberate seductiveness, each word placed like a polished stone, but let a sour weariness creep in as you realize he's barely listening. End with your voice going flat, the numbness finally surfacing, a small bitter laugh escaping before you trail off.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Stain of Resentment
instruction: You're hunched over the kitchen counter, scrubbing a dried coffee stain that just won't budge. Your arm moves in a steady, rhythmic circle, breath syncing with each push. As you work, you're replaying a conversation with someone you've been infatuated with—her laugh, the way she touched your hand. But then doubt creeps in: maybe her interest was just polite, maybe she's been distant lately. The scrubbing gets harder, faster. By the end, you're pressing down so hard your arm shakes, angrily muttering under your breath about being played. Let the physical effort shape your voice—scraping, huffing, pausing to catch your breath, then snapping out the final words with bitter frustration.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (slightly present), Doubt (clearly present), Anger (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Final Itinerary
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's bedside in hospice, and she's asked you to help her plan her last week on earth - literally scheduling when each family member visits, what music plays when, even what she'll wear. Start by dutifully, almost robotically reading through the schedule you've created together, your voice controlled and efficient because that's how you've always coped. But as you read the final entry - 'Tuesday, 3pm: say goodbye' - let the careful structure you've built around your grief completely shatter. Your voice should break from organized precision into raw, childlike fear. End in a whisper, asking her something you've never been able to ask, the schedule forgotten on the floor.

title: Cracking the Armor
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy who always acts tough, but right now your blood sugar is crashing. Your hands shake, your jaw feels weak, and your words are starting to slur. You're sitting in a school hallway, trying to hide it, but your voice betrays you. Begin with bitter frustration—angry at yourself for being weak, at your body for failing you. As you speak, you feel the world blurring, and you start to ponder how much of your toughness is just a front. Let your voice fade and waver, losing focus midsentence, then finding a quieter, more contemplative tone at the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Words You Never Taught Me
instruction: Confront your immigrant parent about why they refused to teach you their language, starting with sharp, accusatory anger about feeling disconnected from half your heritage. As they try to explain in broken English mixed with their native tongue, let your anger crack into confusion and hurt. You desperately try to understand phrases they're saying, reaching for meaning, and realize they were protecting you from their own trauma. Shift from confrontation to raw vulnerability as you ask them, voice breaking, to teach you just one phrase - maybe 'I love you' or 'I'm sorry' - in their language. End with you attempting to repeat it, stumbling over the words like a child, tears in your voice, both of you broken open.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: After years of silence, you're finally speaking the truth to a parent who abandoned you emotionally. Begin with your voice controlled, almost cold, protecting yourself: 'I've practiced this a thousand times. What I needed to say to you.' As you continue, the armor starts cracking and old pain bleeds through—your voice becomes younger, more wounded: 'I was just a kid. I needed you and you weren't there.' The anger builds, fierce and righteous, your words coming faster, louder: 'Do you know what that does to a child? Do you even care?' But then something shifts. The rage collapses into exhausted grief, and your voice drops to something achingly vulnerable: 'I just wanted you to love me. That's all I ever wanted.' End with the devastating simplicity of finally speaking the truth you've carried alone for so long.

title: Confession in a Downpour
instruction: You are a young woman caught in a torrential rainstorm, attempting to confess your feelings to someone you've secretly adored for months. The rain is relentless, streaming into your mouth as you sputter, shout over thunder, and wipe water from your eyes. You start deeply embarrassed, stuttering and apologizing as you realize how ridiculous you must look. But as you continue, your embarrassment shifts into a strange, desperate defiance — you start to feel contempt for yourself for ever being so afraid, and you end with a raw, almost angry declaration, your voice cracking with rain and resolve.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Excuse That Stopped the Mockery
instruction: You're washing dishes, listening to your child give another excuse for unfinished homework. At first, you can't help but mock them—your voice goes nasal and singsong, exaggerating their whiny tone, your amusement obvious. But as you turn and see their face, you realize they're genuinely upset. The sarcasm drains from your voice, replaced by a softer, hesitant concern. Your pause is long, a dish slips in your hand, and your next words are quiet, almost apologetic.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Listening to Your Love Forget You
instruction: Your partner of twenty years has dementia and is excitedly telling you about meeting someone wonderful—describing your first date together, but they don't recognize that the person they're describing falling in love with is you, sitting right here. Begin with the aching gentleness of someone who has learned to meet them where they are, encouraging them with tender questions. But as they describe intimate details—the way this person laughed, the color of their eyes—let the words catch in your throat. Keep smiling through tears, whispering 'tell me more' while your voice trembles with the exquisite agony of being both completely present and entirely forgotten. End with a whispered confession they won't remember: that you'd listen to this story forever if it meant you could keep them.
inspired_by: Feigning Interest in a Story Youve Heard Before

title: After the Storm
instruction: You've just had explosive, passionate sex with someone you've been fighting with for weeks. Your body is still humming, skin hypersensitive, breath ragged. Start in the raw, undefended state of physical aftermath—let your voice be breathless, your emotions unguarded. As the endorphins begin to fade, feel the original anger creeping back in, mixing with the tenderness of what just happened. Your body betrayed your mind's resolve to stay furious. Speak through this confusion—let desire and rage war in your voice. Touch them again, pull away, reach back. Let your words be fragmented, contradictory, as honest as your body has been. End by surrendering to the complexity: you can be furious with someone and still want them desperately. Journey from physical ecstasy through confusion to acceptance of your own contradictions.

title: Whispered Truths in the Dark
instruction: Late at night, after a traumatic accident, you're lying next to your sleeping partner, whispering the truth about what really happened and how scared you are. Your voice is barely audible, trembling, as you confess that you don't remember parts of the day, that you're terrified something is deeply wrong. Begin disoriented, touching your own face in the darkness, trying to piece together the hours. Your whispers should feel intimate and broken, catching on fear. Gradually reveal that you're not just confused about the accident—you're losing time, forgetting conversations, and you don't know how to tell anyone. Let your voice move from fractured confusion to tender vulnerability, admitting you need help. End with quiet tears and a whispered plea to yourself or to them, even as they sleep, that you're afraid of disappearing.

title: Dancing at Your Wedding While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're dancing at your own wedding, and everyone thinks you're radiantly happy, but inside you're breaking because you know this is a mistake. Your voice should sound joyful on the surface as you speak to your new spouse—'I can't believe we did it'—but let small cracks of grief show through, moments where your laughter sounds slightly wrong, slightly hollow. Move between genuine tenderness (because you do love them, just not enough, not the right way) and overwhelming sadness that you're trying desperately to hide. Your voice might catch as you say, 'You look so happy,' because their happiness makes your deception feel heavier. Include a moment where you almost confess—your voice drops, becomes serious, 'There's something I should—' but then the music swells or someone interrupts, and you swallow it back down. Let yourself laugh and cry simultaneously, your voice breaking with both emotions as you say, 'This is everything I wanted,' knowing it's both true and the most devastating lie you've ever told. End with quiet acceptance, your voice soft but laced with profound loss: 'I'm going to make you happy. I promise I'll try.' You're committing to the role you've chosen, and there's peace in the decision even as it destroys the person you might have been. Your final words are whispered like a prayer or a goodbye to yourself: 'This is enough. This has to be enough.'
inspired_by: After Friend Group Exclusion: The Final Text

title: The Last Clear Moment
instruction: You're in the final hours of consciousness, knowing you're dying. You drift between addressing your loved one at your bedside and slipping into memories that feel more real than the present. Start by trying to say something important, something you've never said, but the words scatter like leaves. Your voice is fragile, breath shallow. Move from desperate clarity ('Please listen, I need you to know...') into soft confusion where past and present blur ('Mom? No, you're... when did you get so tall?'). End in a place of unexpected peace, a whispered acceptance mixed with one last surge of love. Let your breathing tell as much story as your words. This isn't theatrical dying—it's the messy, tender, heartbreaking reality of a mind letting go while the heart still holds on.

title: Birthday Alone Reflection
instruction: It's your birthday and you're alone. Your voice is quiet, reflective: 'I'm thirty-five today.' Breathing is slower, internal. 'I thought I'd be somewhere different by now.' Vocal tone is neither sad nor happy—it's real. 'But this is where I am.' Physical: maybe you're looking out a window. You're taking stock: 'I've done things I'm proud of. I've failed.' Your voice becomes gentler toward yourself: 'But I'm still here. Still trying.' By the end, you're making peace with the year, with existence: 'Happy birthday to me. I made it another year.'

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent, finally speaking truth you've carried for decades. Begin with a trembling, almost apologetic tone: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' Your voice hardens as you name what happened—'You knew. You saw it happening and you did nothing.' Feel the anger build, your words becoming sharper, faster, more accusatory. But then something breaks: beneath the rage is a child's voice asking 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' The confrontation collapses into raw need—you're not a powerful adult anymore, you're small again, begging. End with the devastating simplicity: 'I just needed you to choose me.' The journey is from nervous courage to righteous fury to the vulnerable child underneath.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Lover the Truth You Can Never Say Aloud
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. In the darkness, you finally speak the words you've carried for months—that you're leaving, or that you're sick, or that you've betrayed them, or that you're more deeply in love than you've ever admitted. Start in barely audible whispers, tender and aching. Let your breath shake. Trace the outline of what you can never say when they're awake. Your voice should be thick with unshed tears, intimate as a confession to yourself. Include a moment where you almost wake them—'I wish I could tell you'—but pull back. End with the quietest declaration of love or goodbye, knowing morning changes everything. This is devastation at a whisper.
inspired_by: Parent Hearing Their Child's Abuse for First Time

title: Reading Your Child's Graduation Speech They Wrote About You
instruction: Your adult child has asked you to listen to their valedictorian speech before the ceremony. They're reading it to you, and it's about you — how you sacrificed everything after their other parent left, worked three jobs, never complained. As they read, you're overwhelmed by contradictory feelings. Laugh at the funny parts, the memories of your terrible cooking, that time you both got lost. But underneath, feel the grief of those years — what you lost, dreams you buried, the loneliness you hid from them. Interrupt them to say they don't need to make you sound heroic, but they keep reading. Feel pride and love threatening to crack your chest open, but also the ache of time passing, of them leaving soon, of having given everything and now having to let go. Let your voice break between laughter and tears. By the end, you're crying but smiling, saying 'I'm so proud of you,' while simultaneously mourning that the hardest, most beautiful chapter of your life is ending. This is joy and grief braided together, inseparable.
inspired_by: Teaching a Fitness Class While Completely Hungover

title: Whispering Secrets in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you. You're speaking barely above a whisper, confessing something you've never said aloud—maybe about the child you gave up, the person you were before you met them, the part of yourself you've kept hidden. Your voice is tender, intimate, thick with unshed tears. Start with tentative words, testing each syllable in the darkness. There's relief in finally speaking this truth, but also terror—what if they somehow hear? What if saying it out loud makes it too real? Your breath catches. A tear falls. Your voice wavers between grateful release and profound sadness. End on a whispered plea for forgiveness—to them, to yourself, to whoever you've wronged. Let each word feel like it costs you something.

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission
instruction: You're transmitting your last message to Earth before your oxygen runs out. You start with forced cheerfulness, reassuring mission control that everything's fine, making small jokes about the view. But slowly, the reality breaks through. Your voice softens as you begin speaking directly to your child, trying to explain why you left, why this mission mattered more than tucking them in at night. The professional mask crumbles. You're now whispering intimate instructions: how to tie their shoes, what to do when they miss you, how to find you in the night sky. Your breath catches as you realize you're saying goodbye. End with a trembling attempt to say 'I love you' that breaks apart mid-word, dissolving into the raw sound of someone trying not to cry in their final moments, wanting their last gift to be courage instead of tears.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying next to your partner in the darkness. You need to whisper something you've been hiding—a fear, a secret, a truth about yourself you've never spoken aloud. Begin by simply breathing in the dark, feeling the weight of your body against the mattress, noticing the warmth of the person beside you, the texture of the sheets, the quality of the silence. Start speaking so quietly you can barely hear yourself, almost hoping they won't hear, your words halting and hesitant. Let yourself become absorbed in the physical sensation of whispering, the way your breath carries the words, the vulnerability of speaking into darkness. Move from protective, cautious self-revelation—ready to stop at any moment—to a place where the relief of finally speaking the truth opens you completely, ending in either quiet tears or surprising intimacy.
inspired_by: Actor feels tension or self-consciousness before or during a scene

title: The Old Porch Swing
instruction: You're an older man standing alone on the porch of your childhood home, now abandoned. The rusty swing creaks under your hand. You start speaking softly, lost in memory of warm summer nights, but then a specific, intimate image of a past lover surfaces—the way she bit her lip, the press of her body. Your voice warms with a flicker of lust, then you catch yourself, embarrassed, and let out a hollow laugh. Let the ache of nostalgia slow your words; let the embarrassment crack your tone. Speak as if you're half-talking to the empty swing, half to yourself, with sighs and pauses. About 60 words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Contradictory Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your best friend who's moving across the world, possibly forever. But instead of just being sad, you're laughing—really laughing—remembering the moment they first saw through your carefully constructed persona and called you out: 'You're so full of shit, you know that?' Your laughter is genuine, joyful, but threaded through with tears. You're thanking them, voice breaking with gratitude: 'You're the only person who ever made me feel like being myself was enough.' But the gratitude hurts—it's beautiful and devastating simultaneously. Your voice dances between joy at having been truly known and heartbreak at losing it: 'How do I do this without you? How do I stay real?' End with your voice soft, peaceful despite the tears, finding strange comfort in the pain: 'I'm so grateful it hurts this much. That means it was real.' You're destroyed and whole at the same time.

title: The Victor's Funeral
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for your greatest rival—someone you defeated decisively in business, destroying their company and reputation. Begin by addressing the mourners with barely concealed triumph: catalog your victories over them, how thoroughly you outmaneuvered them, how completely you won. Let satisfaction and power radiate from your voice. But as you speak, looking at their family's grief-stricken faces, memories flood back—how they once mentored you, believed in you when no one else did, how you betrayed that trust to build your empire. Your triumphant tone begins to splinter. By the end, you're caught between pride in your success and devastating guilt over the cost. Finish speaking simultaneously to the corpse and to yourself, your voice fractured between vindication and self-loathing, asking for forgiveness while still defending why you had to win.

title: Dancing at the Ending of the World
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a terminal diagnosis, the end of your marriage, the loss of everything you built—and someone who loves you has put on your favorite song and is asking you to dance. Begin laughing at the absurdity of it, a bitter, broken sound: 'Are you serious right now? Dance?' But as you move together, something shifts. Let laughter mix with tears until you can't tell which is which. Your voice breaks as you speak—perhaps describing the music, perhaps confessing how scared you are—but there's also gratitude bleeding through, awe at this gesture of defiant joy. By the end, you're laughing and sobbing simultaneously, your voice cracking with both: 'This is ridiculous. This is perfect. I love you so much it hurts.' Find the place where devastation and joy are the same thing, where grief and gratitude become indistinguishable, where your breaking heart is also somehow full.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hour. They've been unconscious, but suddenly their eyes open and look at you. You've spent your whole life trying to earn their approval, and now you have mere minutes. Start with desperate hope that you'll finally hear the words you've needed. Let whatever rises in you—grief, anger, gratitude, resentment, love—come out without choosing or controlling it. Don't plan what you'll say; speak only what genuinely surges up moment by moment. By the end, you must arrive at a completely different emotional place than where you began, shaped entirely by what authentically moved through you. Your parent may or may not give you what you seek—respond to whatever you truly feel happening.

title: The Graduation You'll Never Attend
instruction: You're recording a video message for your child's future high school graduation, but you've just been diagnosed with terminal illness—you won't be there. Start with determined cheerfulness, smiling through it: 'Hey graduate! Look at you in that cap and gown!' Your voice is bright, celebratory, but there's a tremor underneath. As you continue, joy and grief become impossible to separate: 'I am so... so incredibly proud of you.' Suddenly you're laughing and crying simultaneously: 'Remember when you said you'd never finish algebra? Look at you now!' The laughter dissolves into quiet weeping, but your voice fills with fierce, protective love: 'Listen to me—you are going to do extraordinary things.' Your voice breaks with gratitude mixed with devastating loss: 'Thank you for being my child. Thank you for every single day.' Finally, a whisper that holds both peace and unbearable sorrow: 'I'm there. I promise I'm there.' The contradictions never resolve—the joy never stops being real, and neither does the heartbreak.

title: You Were Never Really There
instruction: You're confronting your parent who was always physically present but emotionally absent—lost in their own world of games, screens, and escapes while you grew up invisible. Start with a controlled, almost careful attempt to explain how it felt to watch them lose themselves in virtual worlds while you desperately needed them in the real one. Your voice should be measured at first, trying to be fair, trying to make them understand without attacking. But let the years of unspoken hurt begin to crack through—not as shouting, but as raw truth that you can barely contain. By the end, you're not angry anymore; you're just exhausted and heartbroken, asking them one simple question you've needed answered your whole life, your voice small and vulnerable like the child you once were.

title: Confessing a Secret That Could Destroy Everything
instruction: You've carried this alone and it's eating you. Your voice shakes: 'I need to tell you something that might change everything.' Your breathing is fast, anxious. You're admitting hidden betrayal or truth. Your voice gets quieter as confession deepens. Include them reacting badly and you holding the consequence: 'I understand if you leave.' Everything on the table.

title: Veil of Morning Light
instruction: You are an older woman, alone in your garden just before dawn, wearing a niqab that softly filters your voice. You have just discovered that a loved one who was presumed lost is returning today. As you speak, you are overwhelmed with intense pleasure and ecstasy, a joy so full it almost hurts, but there is also a fragile thread of hope that this new beginning will last. Let your voice tremble with the weight of happiness, catching on breaths as you touch the fabric of your veil, lose your train of thought in wonder, then find it again. By the end, your ecstasy settles into a quieter, hopeful optimism, as if the morning sky is affirming your faith.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Closet Door at Midnight
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom, back home for the first time in years, lying in the dark. You can't sleep. Begin by noticing: the crack in the ceiling, the streetlight through the curtain, the closet door slightly open. Let your eyes move around the room and let each shadow, each shape, pull up sense memories—not organized thoughts, but flashes: the texture of the old blanket, your brother's laugh, the smell of rain, that summer, the accident, the word you never said, their face, a song, a taste, cold water, warm skin, the guilt, the longing. Whisper fragments aloud or just mouth them silently—no sentences, just image after image tumbling out faster and faster in the darkness. Start from restlessness and insomnia, but let this stream of disconnected memories and sensations build until you arrive at a whispered confession to the dark room itself—something you've never said aloud, something the rapid cascade of images finally forces to the surface.

title: The Last Drag
instruction: You're sitting alone at a greasy diner counter at 3 AM, a half-empty pack of cigarettes in front of you. The doctor just told you your lungs are giving out, but you're not going to quit. Start with a shaky, labored voice—distress making you cough and clear your throat as you recall the diagnosis. Then, as you light another cigarette, let your voice harden into a rough, defiant pride: you've lived on your own terms, and that's worth more than a few extra years. Let the gravel in your voice carry both the pain and the stubborn joy of choosing your own way.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispered Wants in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, in that vulnerable space between waking and sleeping. The room is dark. Begin by wanting small, tender things - for them to move closer, for their breathing to sync with yours, for this moment to last. Whisper these wants so quietly they're almost just breath. Let each admission lead to a deeper one: what do you want this relationship to become? What do you want to give them that you're afraid to offer? What do you want them to see in you that you keep hidden? As you speak softer and softer, let your wants become more naked and frightening: what do you want to be forgiven for? What do you want permission to need? By the end, you should be confessing the want that terrifies you most - perhaps to be fully known, to be allowed to be weak, to trust completely. Your voice should barely be audible, but the emotional weight should be overwhelming.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After the Divorce Papers
instruction: It's 2 AM. You're sitting beside your child's bed, and they're asleep, and the divorce papers are signed downstairs. Your voice is barely audible—you're not trying to wake them, this is just for you. Start by describing their face in the moonlight, your voice tender and breaking. 'You look so peaceful. You don't know yet that tomorrow everything changes.' Your whisper catches on tears as you confess your fears: that you've failed them, that they'll remember this year forever, that love wasn't enough. But then something shifts—you notice their breath, steady and trusting, and your voice fills with fierce protectiveness mixed with grief. 'I will make sure you're okay. Even if I'm not.' End with a contradiction: you're devastated, but in this moment, watching them sleep, you feel a strange, painful kind of peace. Your voice barely makes sound: 'We're going to be okay. Somehow, we will.'
inspired_by: Crevasse Rescue: Hearing the Rope Appear Above You

title: The Floating Horror
instruction: You are in a lake, swimming with your head above water, calling to your young child who is splashing nearby. You just spotted a rotting, maggot-covered carcass drifting toward them. Your voice is high-pitched and breathy, but now thick with revulsion. Start with a sharp, disgusted gasp and a strained cry of warning—each word punched out between quick gulps of air, the water sloshing around your face. As you realize your child hasn't heard you, the disgust hardens into desperate, protective urgency, your pitch rising but your words becoming tighter, more clipped.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Prize Nobody Saw
instruction: You're a teenager in a crowded gym, watching your rival get handed the trophy you've worked for all year. Your stomach is a knot of bitterness and jealousy. As you open your mouth to spit out a sarcastic comment, a sudden burp from deep in your gut drops your voice into a low, guttural growl, making you sound like a monster. The sound catches you off guard, and instead of the bitter jab you planned, the words come out slower, more tired — the jealousy still there, but now raw and exposed, like you're admitting it to yourself for the first time. Let the burp interrupt your flow and allow your tone to shift from aggressive resentment to a hollow, quieter envy.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: After the Storm
instruction: You've just finished a fierce physical fight with your lover—not violent, but passionate, exhausting, the kind where you've both said terrible things. Your body is still trembling, heart racing, breath ragged. Begin in the immediate aftermath: you're still angry, adrenaline coursing through you, maybe tears of rage on your face. But as your breathing begins to slow, as the physical intensity subsides, something else emerges. Let your body lead—the shaking, the rapid heartbeat, the need to move or be still. Draw on any moment in your life when your body held emotion you couldn't control. Allow the anger to transform into something more complex: desire, grief, recognition of how much this person matters. Your voice should shift from sharp and breathless to something raw and undefended. End in a place of physical and emotional vulnerability, where the line between anger and love has dissolved.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You have been physically running or working to exhaustion—your body is spent, shaking, drenched. But you cannot stop because you're also in emotional crisis: someone you love has just left, or you've lost something irreplaceable, or you've just received devastating news. Begin with the physical sensation dominating—gasping breath, burning muscles, trembling limbs. As you push through the physical pain, notice what emotional impulses break through: the urge to scream, to laugh hysterically, to collapse in sobs, to rage at the sky. Don't decide which—follow the impulse that rises most urgently in each moment. Let the physical exhaustion strip away your defenses. Your body's surrender might unlock emotional release, or your emotional devastation might push your body past its limits. The physical and emotional should collide, interrupt each other, and merge. End in a state completely different from where you began—perhaps transcendent calm, or feral rage, or broken-open vulnerability.
inspired_by: Strengthening Intuition and Learning from It

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: Your child, your partner, or someone you love fiercely is in danger you cannot control—an illness, an addiction, a choice they're making that will destroy them. You start with rage: shouting, demanding, fierce and almost violent in your desperation to make them understand. Your voice is raw, powerful, commanding. But mid-torrent, the helplessness hits you like a physical blow. The shouting collapses into pleading. You're on your knees emotionally, begging, your voice breaking apart. The anger transforms into devastating love and terror. End barely able to speak through tears, whispering something like 'I can't lose you' or 'Please don't leave me.' The arc should feel like watching someone's strength completely shatter.

title: The Last Word
instruction: You're a child in a heated, circular argument with your parent about staying up past bedtime. They keep repeating the same rule, and you keep whining back with the same excuses—your voice goes nasal and high-pitched, words tangling as you shift your weight from foot to foot. Mid-sentence, you notice a tiny crack in their resolve: a pause, a sigh. Triumph surges through you, raw and absolute. Let your voice rise from tired repetition to sharp, gleeful victory—you've finally found the one comeback that shuts them down. Speak as if you're bouncing on your toes, clutching a stuffed animal, and grinning despite yourself.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight Finally Lifts
instruction: You are with someone you love deeply as they take their last breaths. For years, you've carried guilt, fear, and unspoken words between you—your body has been tight with all you've never said. Begin tense, holding everything in your shoulders, your jaw, your chest. As they struggle to breathe, something breaks open in you. Let your body soften as you finally speak the truth you've been carrying. By the end, as they slip away, allow yourself to fully release into grief—not performed crying, but a genuine physical unburdening, as if the floor itself is catching you. Your voice should reflect this journey from constriction to release, from held breath to full, surrendered sobs or whispered peace.

title: The Last Phone Call: A Soldier Says Goodbye Before a Suicide Mission
instruction: You're calling your partner from a military base, knowing this mission has no return. Your voice starts steady, almost falsely cheerful—you're trying to give them one last good memory. But as you speak, the facade crumbles. You begin listing small things you'll miss: their morning coffee ritual, the way they hum while cooking, the specific sound of their laugh. Your voice fractures between desperate memorization and the need to say everything before time runs out. You can't tell them the truth directly, but your voice betrays you—it becomes tender, then choked, then almost greedy for the sound of their voice. End with your breath catching as you realize this is the last time you'll ever hear them say your name. Your final words are barely whispered, saturated with everything you'll never get to say.
inspired_by: Professional: Parent Tells Child They Cannot Afford Life-Saving Treatment

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight Never Lands
instruction: You're calling your estranged father from the airport, voice bright with forced cheerfulness as you tell him about your big promotion, your new life across the ocean. But mid-sentence, you hear the final boarding call—this is it, the last chance. Your voice cracks as the facade crumbles: 'Dad, I need you to tell me you're proud of me. Just once.' The silence on the other end is deafening. You're begging now, years of hunger pouring out in whispered desperation. Then his voice comes through, and it's not what you expected—it's broken, old, full of regret. Your anger dissolves into something more complicated: forgiveness mixed with grief for all the lost years. End with your voice soft, almost tender, as you say goodbye knowing you may never see him again.
inspired_by: Roller Coaster Mechanical Failure: Moment of Absolute Stillness

title: The Envy of the Broken
instruction: You are an elderly man strapped to a chair in a cold, bare room. Your torturer is a person you secretly envied your whole life—younger, more successful, everything you wanted. At first, you scream and spit curses, fueled by rage and pride, but as the pain wears you down, your voice cracks, your breathing becomes shallow, and you start sobbing. Between gasps, you admit the jealousy you've never confessed, your voice a hoarse, broken whisper that trails off into silence. Let your body slump, your words catch in your throat, and let the envy seep out like a wound.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: Your mother sits across from you at the kitchen table where you grew up. She's just told you she's leaving you the family house—the place where you suffered years of her criticism and impossibly high standards. Begin with carefully controlled politeness, the armor you've built over decades. But as you try to refuse this 'gift,' something cracks open. Suddenly you're fourteen again, then twenty-two, then last month—all the moments she made you feel small come pouring out. Your voice should start measured and cold, but let it build to raw, unfiltered rage. Then, in her silence, something shifts. You see her differently—not just as the critical mother, but as a frightened woman trying to say 'I love you' the only way she knows how. End with your anger not gone, but transformed into something more complex: fury mixed with unwanted compassion, resentment braided with reluctant understanding.

title: Polishing a Memory
instruction: You are an older adult alone in your quiet living room, scrubbing a small silver locket that belonged to a person you've been infatuated with for years. As you rub the tarnish away, you're confused by your own feelings—why does this person still make your heart race? But then you recall a tender moment they shared with you last week, and a wave of elation washes over you. Let your voice start hesitant, distracted by the rhythmic scrubbing, then brighten as the memory hits. Speak as if half to yourself, with pauses and natural adjustments in volume and breath.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Infatuation (very intensely present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: After the Crash
instruction: You've just survived something physically traumatic - a car accident, a fall, a violent encounter. Your body is flooded with adrenaline; you might be shaking, bleeding, in pain. Someone is helping you, checking if you're okay, but you can't quite process their words yet. Begin in pure physical reaction - the shock, the trembling, the strange clarity and confusion that follows trauma. But as your body begins to settle, another emotion surges through: maybe overwhelming gratitude for being alive, or sudden fury at whoever caused this, or an unexpected need to laugh, or a rush of grief for something entirely unrelated that this moment has cracked open. Don't decide what you'll feel - let your physical state lead you somewhere true. The scene ends when the emotional response catches up with and transforms the physical experience.
inspired_by: Actor is falling into result consciousness—going for the emotion of a scene rather than working from the moment

title: The Last Hour Before They Unplug the Machines
instruction: You're sitting beside your younger sister in the ICU. The doctors have said there's no brain activity left, and tomorrow morning they'll remove life support. You have this one night to say everything—but you've never been good with words, and now they feel impossibly inadequate. Start by simply being present with her, letting sounds emerge as you look at her hands, her face, the machines. Let your breath become sounds that carry what you can't articulate. Move from numb shock at the beginning to a place where your body finally releases the grief you've been holding back for three days. Let primal sounds, sighs, moans, and broken utterances express what 'I love you' and 'goodbye' can never fully capture. End in a different emotional place than where you began—whether that's acceptance, rage, or tender devastation.
inspired_by: Emotional Point of View, Without Words

title: The Last Song Before Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside your best friend in hospice care, sharing earbuds one final time like you did as teenagers. Start by gently placing the earbud in their ear, your voice thick with unshed tears as you whisper, 'Remember this one?' Begin humming their favorite song, voice breaking on certain notes. As the music plays, shift from trying to stay strong to allowing yourself to fall apart — let your humming dissolve into quiet crying, then pull yourself back to finish the song for them. Your friend (imagined) squeezes your hand. You laugh through tears remembering a specific moment this song represents, your voice cracking between joy and devastation. End by removing the earbud with infinite tenderness, whispering 'I'll keep playing it for both of us' — the words barely making it past the knot in your throat. The final moments should be you breathing through the grief, finding acceptance in the silence.
inspired_by: Crowded Subway: Two Strangers Share an Earbud

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who shaped your entire life - a grandparent, mentor, or beloved friend - and they have only minutes of consciousness left. You arrived too late to say most of what you needed to say, and now you must compress a lifetime of gratitude, unspoken grief, and love into fragmented whispers. Begin in a state of numb shock, barely able to form words, your breath catching in your throat. As you speak, let the floodgates open gradually - move from stammering attempts at composure into raw, unguarded confession. Allow yourself to laugh through tears at a cherished memory, then break completely as you realize this is truly goodbye. End in a place of devastating peace, holding their hand, your voice reduced to the softest whisper as you give them permission to let go.
inspired_by: Actor needs to prepare instrumentally before a rehearsal

title: The Last Light in Her Eyes
instruction: Your mother is dying, and you're sitting beside her hospital bed holding her hand. She can barely speak, drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin with overwhelming grief and the urge to look away from her frailty. But then her eyes open and she looks at you—and in that gaze, you see something specific: maybe it's the same look she gave you as a child when you were scared, or a flash of mischief you haven't seen in years, or an expression of pure love untainted by all the complicated years between you. Let that one element—just that look in her eyes—pull you from despair into something else: profound gratitude, peace, or even unexpected joy. Focus everything on that single aspect of her, let it grow until it fills your entire awareness. Your emotional journey moves from wanting to flee the pain to being completely present, anchored by this one beautiful detail you've found in her face.

title: The Last Squat of the Season
instruction: You are an elderly man in a cramped garden shed, trying to pull a stubborn weed from between the flagstones. The deep squat is the only position that lets you reach it; your knees ache, and your breath is caught in your chest. A neighbor walks by and jokingly calls you a 'garden gnome.' Start with a teasing laugh that turns into wheezy confusion as you realize you can't stand up, and end with a grunt of contempt as you refuse help. Let your voice strain, crack, and trail off as you fight for breath and dignity.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Confusion (extremely present), Contempt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Climb Before You
instruction: You're in the middle of a brutal spin class, legs burning, lungs heaving, the world narrowed to the rhythm of your pedals. Your partner, who you've been aching for all week, just texted they're waiting for you in the locker room. Start with a frustrated, impatient mutter about the instructor's pacing—sharp, clipped words forced out between breaths, the irritation real because every second you're not done is a second away from them. As you think of what's waiting, your tone shifts: a playful, breathless whisper escapes, filled with raw lust and a giddy, almost childlike hope that this will be the best reunion yet. Let the pedal pulse drive your words, and let the impatience melt into a smiling, ruined whisper as you hit the final sprint.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Surgeon Giving Discharge Papers to Patient They Couldn't Fully Save
instruction: You performed an emergency surgery three weeks ago. You saved this patient's life, but you couldn't save their hands. Today you're releasing them from the hospital. They're a concert pianist. You're holding their discharge papers, post-op instructions for prosthetics they don't want. Start with professional warmth, rattling off medical details with practiced competence. But they're not looking at you—they're staring at their bandaged arms. They ask you, point-blank, 'Was I worth saving like this?' It punctures you. Your clinical composure fractures into something radically honest. You hear yourself laughing—not from joy, but from the absurdity of grief, from exhaustion, from the bitter miracle of it all. 'Yes,' you say, and your voice is both crying and fierce with conviction. You list everything they still have: breath, heartbeat, people who love them, time. Your professional mask is gone. You're just a human being insisting to another human being that their life—changed, diminished, different—still has immeasurable worth. End with gratitude mixed with sorrow: 'Thank you for letting me save you, even imperfectly.'
inspired_by: Judge Must Sentence Someone for Loving Their Child

title: Dancing at Your Ex-Lover's Wedding: Joy and Heartbreak in Perfect Harmony
instruction: You're at your ex-lover's wedding—someone you still love but let go because you knew they belonged with someone else. During the reception, they pull you onto the dance floor for one last dance as friends. Begin laughing, genuinely happy for them, your voice bright: 'You look so happy. I mean really, disgustingly happy.' You're teasing, warm. But as you dance, holding them close one final time, something shifts. Your laughter becomes softer, tinged with sorrow. You tell them the truth with a smile in your voice even as it breaks: 'I'm so glad you found this. I'm so glad it wasn't me.' You mean it and it destroys you. Your voice trembles between joy and grief: 'You deserved someone who could love you the way they do. I'm sorry I couldn't be that.' The song ends. You hug them tight, whispering through tears and laughter: 'Be so happy. God, please be so happy.' You pull away smiling, heartbroken, free.
inspired_by: Observing Lava Flow: Scientific Wonder Turning to Genuine Dread

title: The Name That Got Away
instruction: You're at a family dinner—your daughter, her husband, and your son are around the table. You're telling a story about an old friend, but suddenly you can't remember the friend's name. You pause, look down at your plate, feel the heat of embarrassment creep up your neck. Your voice tightens as you try to laugh it off, but a deeper helplessness settles in—a reminder that you're not as sharp as you used to be. As you speak, let your gaze drift to different faces, let your hands fidget with your napkin, and let the initial frustration slowly give way to a quiet, rueful acceptance. Say about 50 words: first struggling and apologetic, then softer and more resigned.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Clue
instruction: You are a teenage girl being choked from behind. Your air is cut off, your voice cracks and strains. At first, you fight and panic. But then you notice something—a reflection, a sound, a piece of the attacker's clothing—that sparks intense interest. Your survival instinct shifts to desperate curiosity. Speak in short, gasping phrases, your voice thin and pressured, but with a growing fixation that cuts through the pain. Let your breathing be tight, your words interrupted by the grip, but let the interest sharpen your focus until the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice
