title: Bittersweet Rounds: Final Walk-Through with a Dying Colleague
instruction: You're doing morning rounds with your best friend and fellow doctor who has weeks to live from terminal cancer. They insisted on this last walk through the hospital they love. Start with playful nostalgia, almost laughing: 'Remember when you coded that patient in this hallway wearing one shoe?' Keep your voice light, warm, finding joy in memories. But underneath, your heart is breaking. As you continue, let laughter mix with tears: 'We saved so many people in this place. God, we were good.' Your voice catches between a laugh and a sob. When you stop at the nurses' station, your voice becomes tender, thick with emotion: 'This is where I want to remember you. Not in some hospital bed, but here, where you were brilliant and alive.' You're smiling through tears now. End with profound gratitude wrapped in unbearable loss: 'Thank you for every shift, every save, every terrible joke. Thank you for making me better than I ever could have been alone.' Let your voice carry both deep peace and shattering grief simultaneously. You're celebrating a life while mourning its ending.
inspired_by: Medical Director: Announcing Quality Improvement Changes

title: The Wall That Remembers
instruction: You're a 10-year-old girl leaning against the cool brick wall of the apartment building where you used to live with your mom. Now you live with your dad across town, and you came back here alone to stare at the old front door. You're pressing your back flat against the wall, feeling the rough texture through your thin jacket, and your voice has that hollow, slightly muffled quality from the wall behind your head. Start by pretending to be casual, even cool, like this doesn't bother you — maybe you even force a little optimism about how 'things are better now.' But as you keep talking, the longing for the way things used to be creeps in, and then the bitterness about what you lost — about your mom not even being home right now — takes over, and your voice gets tight and hard, even though you're still leaning against that same wall.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Longing (extremely present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Telling Your Parent You're Not Coming Home for Their Last Birthday
instruction: You're on the phone with your aging parent who's planned their 80th birthday around your visit, but you've decided you can't keep pretending the relationship isn't broken. Start with false cheerfulness, making small talk while gathering courage. Then deliver the truth—you're not coming, and you need to explain why after decades of swallowing it. Your anger should be precise, almost surgical at first, listing specific childhood wounds. But as they go silent on the other end, your fury cracks into something more complicated: grief for what you never had, guilt for hurting them now, and the awful realization that you still desperately want them to understand. End not with resolution, but with the painful honesty that you love them and can't be near them—both truths existing at once.
inspired_by: Poet Reading Their Work at an Open Mic — for Their Ex in the Audience

title: The Locked Door: Rage Against Impossible Helplessness
instruction: Someone you love is in danger—behind a door you cannot open, in a situation you cannot fix, making a choice that will destroy them—and there is nothing you can do. You start by trying to reason, to persuade, your voice controlled but urgent. But as the reality of your powerlessness hits, let it explode: fierce, protective love that has nowhere to go. Your voice should surge with intensity—not sustained shouting, but waves of emotion that crest and break: anger at the situation, at yourself, at them. 'I would tear down walls for you, but you won't let me in!' Let the rage crack open into desperate pleading, then shatter into raw tears. The emotional arc must be volcanic but authentic—moving from control to eruption to collapse. End in the exhausted, broken place where love and helplessness meet, your voice hoarse with everything you cannot fix.
inspired_by: Suppressing Joy to Be Sensitive to Others

title: The Last Visit Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your parent who's terminally ill, and they've just told you they're proud of you - but for all the wrong reasons, praising a version of you that doesn't exist. You start trying to maintain composure, grateful for their words but aching because they never truly knew you. As you continue, let the facade crack - move from polite acceptance to a whispered confession of who you really are, knowing this is your last chance to be seen. End with a bittersweet mix of love and grief as you realize being truly known matters more than their approval, even if it comes too late. Your voice should begin controlled and grateful, then become increasingly raw and vulnerable, finishing with tender devastation.

title: The Last Words Before the Crossing
instruction: You're speaking to your child on the night before you help them escape to freedom, knowing you'll never see them again—you're too old, too recognizable, and staying behind is the only way the plan works. Start with fierce, protective instructions about the journey, your voice steady because you need them to believe they can survive this. But as you move into your final blessing, something breaks—the reality that you're sending the person you love most into darkness alone, that you'll die never knowing if they made it. Your voice fractures between strength and devastation. End whispering the last thing you need them to remember about who they are, your words barely audible but carrying everything you couldn't protect them from, everything you pray will keep them alive. Let silence hold the weight of永久 goodbye.

title: Muffled Threat
instruction: You're going down on your partner while they're on a phone call with someone you're jealous of—an ex or a flirtatious coworker. Your mouth is full, so you can only hum, moan, and spit out a few muffled, guttural words between movements. Start with a teasing, possessive vibe—small jealous hums that signal your displeasure. As the call continues, let your anger build into thick, throaty growls and wet, angry sounds—you're claiming them with every slurp and stifled curse. End with a low, menacing hum that feels like a final warning, your voice strained and raw from the effort.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Anger (clearly present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Crack in the Armor
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy, standing with hands on your hips, trying to look strong after losing the championship game. Your dad is watching, and you're supposed to be the tough one. Begin with a strained, loud voice – arms locked, chest out – but your words waver. You start by saying you're okay, but as you speak, the weight of disappointment hits you. Your voice cracks, you lose the pose, and the final words are quiet, broken. Let the physicality shift – starting wide and dominant, ending slumped, hands dropped. Micro-distractions: swallow, look away, rub your arm.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Way You Hold Your Coffee Cup
instruction: You're confronting your father about years of emotional distance and disappointment. Start angry, voice raised, listing grievances you've held onto for decades. He sits across from you, largely silent, and you're prepared for his usual defensive coldness. But then you notice something small—maybe the way his hands tremble slightly as he holds his coffee cup, or how he keeps touching his wedding ring, or a particular vulnerability in how he's sitting. This one detail suddenly cracks open something in you. Let this single observed element shift your entire emotional state from rage to unexpected tenderness or heartbreak. You realize this small thing reveals something true about his own pain or limitations. Your confrontation transforms mid-stream as you fixate on this detail, your voice dropping, your anger giving way to something more complex—maybe forgiveness, maybe just profound sadness at all the years lost.

title: The Ache of Being Upside Down
instruction: You are an older woman hanging upside down from a trapeze bar in a dimly lit studio. Your arms tremble from holding this inverted pose for too long; your voice is thick and wet, a gargle fighting gravity. You speak to a lover who is also here, but you’re too tired to keep your head clear. Start with raw exhaustion—each word a struggle to push past the weight in your throat. But as you describe the way their eyes travel your contorted body, a deep, unwilling lust rises, coiling through your fatigue. Let your voice thicken even more, breathy and broken, until the last words sound almost like a hungry, desperate plea. Include natural pauses to adjust your grip, a wet swallow, or a shaky breath as arousal fights the physical drain.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Holding Your Child's Empty Shoes After the School Shooting
instruction: You clutch your child's small sneakers—all they sent home from the school. Your voice starts in complete shutdown, speaking to the shoes as if your child can hear you, mechanical and dissociated. Then rage detonates—screaming at God, at the shooter, at everyone who failed to protect them. Your voice becomes feral, guttural, animal. But mid-scream, you collapse into sobbing, and your voice transforms into desperate bargaining, begging the universe to let you trade places. You smell the shoes and your voice breaks into the tenderest whisper, remembering how you tied these laces this morning. Fury returns in waves, then dissolves into helplessness. End with your voice carrying the impossibility of a parent's love that has nowhere to go—fierce protection for a child who is gone, your final words both a lullaby and a howl.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Catches Glimpse of Their Own Child They Were Forced to Abandon

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about a lifetime of emotional absence. Begin with trembling anger, words you've rehearsed a thousand times, voice shaking with decades of stored rage: 'Do you have any idea what it was like? Waiting for you to notice me?' But as you speak, something unexpected happens—you see them as frail, human, flawed. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it tangles with pity, with grief for what will never be. Your voice shifts from accusatory to almost pleading: 'I needed you. I still need you, and I hate that I need you.' End with quiet, exhausted truth, tears and anger braided together: 'I forgive you. I don't want to, but I do. And I'm so angry that I have to be the one who's strong enough to do this.' Let the contradiction live in every word.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: Confront your immigrant parent who sacrificed everything to give you opportunities in a new country, but in doing so, became a stranger. You're at their kitchen table, and years of unspoken pain finally surface. Begin with careful, respectful distance - the formal way you've learned to speak to them. But as you list everything you needed and never got, let anger seep in. Then, mid-confrontation, you see them differently - how small they look, how lost they've been too. Your rage must transform into aching compassion mixed with irreparable grief. End by saying 'I understand now' in their native language, the one phrase you finally learned, your voice breaking with the weight of too-late recognition.

title: Standing in the Downpour
instruction: You are standing outside in a rainstorm (real or imagined) after a shattering loss or betrayal. Begin by noticing everything your body is doing to hold itself together—the tension in your jaw, your clenched fists, how you're barely breathing. Start speaking aloud all the physical and emotional chaos: the cold water, your shaking, your rage, your impulse to scream, your shame at falling apart, your exhaustion. Name each sensation and feeling as it arises: 'I'm so angry I can't see straight,' 'I'm freezing and I don't care,' 'My chest hurts,' 'I want to hit something.' Let yourself physically experience each emotion—trembling, gasping, pacing, stillness. As you expose and release each layer, feel your body begin to soften. Transform from someone fighting their own breakdown to someone surrendering to the storm, both inside and out. End in a state of emptiness that feels strangely clean, standing in the rain with nothing left to hold onto.

title: Holding the Line Against the Monster
instruction: You're barricaded in a room, and something terrifying is trying to break through the door—could be an intruder, a creature, the embodiment of your worst fear. Begin with fierce, protective rage: you're screaming threats, your voice raw and primal, telling them they can't have what you're protecting (a child sleeping behind you, precious documents, your last shred of sanity). You're all adrenaline and defiance. Then the door starts to splinter. Your bravado cracks into pure terror—your breathing becomes ragged, your threats dissolve into desperate pleas and prayers, your voice climbing higher. Suddenly everything goes quiet. The attack stops. In that eerie silence, you break completely—sobbing with relief and residual fear, your whole body shaking, whispering 'it's okay, it's okay' to yourself and whoever you're protecting, but your voice reveals you don't believe it. Move from explosive fury to visceral terror to trembling, uncertain relief. Your voice should feel utterly uncontrolled, purely reactive, dangerously honest.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Well: Shouting Up

title: Getting Progressively Drunker During a Corporate Presentation
instruction: You're presenting quarterly results at a company dinner with an open bar. Slide 1: crisp, professional, sober. By Slide 3: slightly warmer, making jokes that land. Slide 5: telling personal anecdotes, gesturing too much. Slide 8: calling the CEO by their first name, sharing opinions about the company's 'real problems.' Slide 10: emotional, declaring love for your team, crying about synergy. Each slide, the articulation degrades and the filter disappears.

title: Reading Your Partner's Suicide Note on Your Wedding Anniversary
instruction: You found them in time. They're in the hospital, alive. And you're reading the note they left, dated today—what should have been your celebration. Begin with gratitude that makes you almost laugh with relief: they're alive, you can touch them, you get another chance. But as you read their words describing the pain they've been hiding, your voice breaks into grief—how did you not see? The laugh becomes a sob becomes confusion. You're angry they didn't tell you, grateful they failed, devastated by the depth of their suffering, terrified it could happen again. Your voice oscillates between love and betrayal, relief and fury, hope and absolute terror. End in a space of fierce, protective determination threaded through with the knowledge that love alone couldn't save them. Let us hear someone finding strength in the ruins of their certainty.
inspired_by: Professional: Judge Releases Someone Knowing They'll Reoffend

title: The Garden Gate
instruction: You're an older man, alone, tending your small backyard garden at dusk. A much younger, aggressive neighbor you've had quiet run-ins with before suddenly steps through the unlatched gate, blocking your path to the house. Your voice starts as a soft, uncertain greeting, a flutter of fear in your chest. But as he stares you down and doesn't speak, a cold, heavy weight settles in your stomach—pure distress. Your words slow, your pitch drops into a low, almost lazy growl, but it's not a threat; it's a shield. You say one simple phrase, and by the end, the shake in your breath undercuts your forced calm, revealing the real fear you're drowning in.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Wedding Morning: Laughing With Your Dying Sibling About All the Things They'll Miss
instruction: It's your wedding day. Your sibling has weeks to live and you both know they won't see your first anniversary. You're helping them get dressed for the ceremony and suddenly you're both laughing—really laughing—about something absurd. But your laughter keeps breaking into tears and back into laughter. 'You're going to miss me getting fat and boring,' you say, giggling through sobs. They joke back. You're making dark humor about their funeral, about the ridiculous things you'll tell your future kids about them. It's simultaneously the most painful and most joyful moment—gratitude for this last morning together, heartbreak that it IS the last morning. By the end, you're holding them, laughing and crying at once, whispering 'Thank you for being here today' while your heart splinters with love and impending loss.
inspired_by: Therapy: Speaking Your Trauma Out Loud for the First Time

title: The Warning and the Call
instruction: You are the town crier, standing on a wooden platform at dusk, shouting to a scattered crowd below. You start with a sharp, contemptuous tone, frustrated that folks aren't listening to the nightly news. Then you spot your granddaughter in the crowd, and your voice softens with clear affection as you call to her, but a slight fear creeps in when you notice a dark storm cloud rolling in fast. As you shout over distance, let your vowels stretch long, drop consonants, and leave significant delays between phrases so the words carry. Your contempt fades into tenderness, while the fear stays just under the surface as you warn her to come home.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (slightly present), Affection (clearly present), Fear (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, holding a champagne glass, about to give a toast. You love them deeply and you're genuinely happy for them—start there, with real joy and warmth. But as you speak, uninvited images and feelings surface: you're also losing them, or you're remembering when you needed them and they weren't there, or you're envying what they've found, or you're grieving your own lost love, or you're angry they're leaving you behind. Don't choose which feeling—let them arise and collide. Your toast becomes a strange, beautiful, painful weaving of celebration and heartbreak, gratitude and resentment, champagne-bright joy and quiet devastation. Your voice laughs and cracks. You catch yourself, try to steer back to celebration, but the complexity keeps surfacing. End by raising your glass with tears streaming down your smiling face, meaning every contradictory word. The room might be confused but you've spoken something utterly true.

title: Typing Through Paradise
instruction: You are a teenage girl at a shabby desk, dictating a school assignment for a transcribing service. You're supposed to stay monotone and robotic, but you're seething because your mom just grounded you for a minor thing. As you speak, a funny memory of your best friend pops into your head—you almost smile but clamp down. Suddenly, you realize your grounding might end right before summer break, and a fierce, hopeful warmth floods your chest. Let your voice tighten with irritation, crackle with suppressed laughter, then swell with breathless, eager hope as you dictate the last line. Pause awkwardly, click your tongue, or whisper a punctuation mark as you fight your real feelings.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Anger (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Forgotten Notes
instruction: You're standing at the podium during your best friend's wedding reception, giving a toast. You've lost your notecards halfway through, and your hands are shaking. Begin with a strained, apologetic voice, full of embarrassed pauses and a public speaking tremor — you're flustered and fumbling for words. As you catch your friend's eye, a playful, teasing smile breaks through. Shift into a warm, gentle ribbing of the couple, your voice relaxing as you lean into the joke, ending with a fond laugh that turns the moment into something loving and light.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (very intensely present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Envelope We Never Opened
instruction: You're sitting beside your sister's hospital bed years after a falling-out, and she's asked you to read aloud a letter your late mother wrote to both of you before she died—a letter you've carried but never opened out of spite and pain. Your voice starts barely audible, hands shaking as you break the seal: 'My darling girls...' The words catch in your throat. As you read your mother's hopes for reconciliation, her confession that she knew about your fights and it broke her heart, your voice becomes almost inaudible—not from volume, but from the effort of not completely breaking down. 'She knew,' you whisper, looking at your sister. 'She knew everything and she still...' You can't say 'loved us' because the grief is choking you. Your voice fractures into something between a laugh and a sob as you read your mother's last line asking you to forgive each other. The vulnerability is excruciating. End with you reaching for your sister's hand, voice raw and small: 'I've been so angry for so long, and I don't... I don't even remember why anymore.' Let the tenderness and sorrow be almost unbearable.

title: The Butterfly That Couldn't Fly
instruction: You are a child, maybe seven or eight, kneeling in the dirt of your backyard. You found a monarch butterfly with a torn wing and tried to fix it with a Band-Aid, but you squeezed too hard. Now it’s barely moving in your cupped hands as you sit back, gasping—your breath caught in your throat like you're the one being suffocated. You speak to the butterfly, your voice a strangled, raspy whisper because you're trying not to cry, but your throat keeps tightening. Start with trembling hope, the desperate need for it to be okay, then let the words dissolve into choked disappointment as you realize you've hurt it. Your pitch wavers; you cough, swallow, lose your thought as a tear lands on your wrist.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Final Offer
instruction: You are an elderly CEO in a boardroom, reviewing a hostile takeover proposal from a younger rival. Your voice is low, guarded—the 'Alpha Shield'—but you lean forward, eyes scanning the numbers with sharp interest. Then a clause about dissolving your legacy makes your jaw tighten; you tap the table once, a flicker of disgust thinning your tone. Finally, you set the paper down, push your chair back, and let bitterness seep into a quiet, tired remark about the decades they're casually erasing. Let the age show in a slight rasp, and let each emotion shift naturally as you speak.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Disgust (extremely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Burning Apology
instruction: You are a father trapped in a burning apartment with your young son, both coughing from thick smoke. Your eyes sting, your throat is raw, and you struggle to think clearly from the fumes. You start by frantically trying to recall which way the fire escape is—muttering to yourself, disoriented and ashamed for not preparing. Then you realize your son is watching you, waiting for you to be strong, and you force your voice to steady, focusing just enough to tell him exactly what to do to survive, even as your shame for panicking still lingers in your shaky breath.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Shame (clearly present), Concentration (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Farewell
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's dying, and you're both trying so hard to keep it light. Start by telling a story that makes you both laugh - your voice is warm, animated, genuinely joyful in the memory. But even as you're laughing, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice keeps breaking between laughter and sobs, unable to maintain the pretense but unwilling to let go of the joy. 'Remember when you... god, you were so ridiculous...' The laughter and crying become indistinguishable. You're grateful for every moment, devastated it's ending, finding absurd humor in the tragedy, all at once. End with a smile in your voice even as it fractures completely: 'Thank you. For all of it. Even this.' It's the most painful gratitude you've ever expressed.

title: The Stopped Clock
instruction: You're a father — late 30s, rough day — sitting on the back steps after your kid's bedtime. You're vape-smoking (way too much) because the shop closed and you lost a whole day of work. Your 8-year-old son, in pajamas, tiptoes out and sits next to you. You start talking to him, half-laughing at how he's hiding his grin, but your throat is tight from holding back a bigger ache. Let the drag cycle interrupt you: one hit makes your voice hoarse and crackly, then you chuckle mid-sentence so it comes out broken. Start with hard, flat distress — like a man barely holding it — then let the teasing pull you out of yourself until you're quiet, almost peaceful, realizing he's trying to cheer you up. End with a warm, rough sigh as you ruffle his hair.
emotions_sampled: Distress (clearly present), Teasing (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Summit Goodbye
instruction: You are a young child, around nine years old, standing with your father at the top of a high mountain pass. The air is thin and cold, and each word costs you a gulp of breath. You’re saying goodbye to him—he’s leaving for a long time, and you’re both trying to be brave. Start with forced cheerfulness, your voice straining for volume but coming out breathy and weak. As you speak, the sadness you’ve been holding back creeps in, and your words slow, your pauses get longer. By the end, your voice is barely a whisper, more for yourself than for him.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Summer Night
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at 3am. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin by simply being present with her—really seeing her, noticing her breath, her hands, the weight of this moment between you. Then let memories flood in: her garden, her laugh, the smell of her kitchen, specific moments only you two share. Move fluidly between talking directly to her NOW—responding to her actual presence, her eyes, her fragile breathing—and being pulled into these vivid sensory memories that make her loss unbearable. Let your awareness dance between the real person fading before you and the overwhelming rush of everything she's meant to you. Start in quiet presence and end wherever the collision of memory and loss takes you.
inspired_by: Working for a Choice While Promoting Ensemble

title: The Last Testimony
instruction: You're recording a final message from your hospital bed, knowing you have days left. You start with fierce determination to expose the truth about what happened, your voice steady and clear: 'I need you to understand what they did to us.' But as you speak, the weight of everything you're leaving behind begins to crack through your resolve. Your children's faces flash in your mind. Your voice starts to fracture—not from physical weakness, but from the devastating realization that this conviction, this fight for justice, has cost you the chance to see your daughter graduate, to meet your grandchildren. By the end, you're still speaking the truth, but now it's wrapped in profound grief and tender goodbye. The words 'I had to do this' become both a declaration and a heartbroken apology to everyone you love.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago. They've shown up asking for forgiveness. Begin with cold, controlled anger—short, clipped sentences that cut like glass. You've rehearsed this moment a thousand times. But as you speak, the little child inside breaks through—your voice suddenly cracks, becomes younger, more desperate: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let fury and heartbreak collide. You're shouting, then sobbing, then laughing bitterly at the absurdity of it all. Build to a moment where you're telling them everything they missed—your first heartbreak, your graduation, your darkest nights—and the rage transforms into something more devastating: the raw grief of a child who needed them and learned to survive without them. End exhausted, voice hoarse, with a quiet admission that changes everything.

title: Fragments of You
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom, holding an object that belonged to someone you loved who's now gone forever. Your voice starts barely audible, speaking to them as if they can hear: 'I found your sweater today... it still smells like you.' Let your breath be unsteady, natural pauses where words fail you. Your voice should be thick with unshed tears: 'I'm so afraid I'll forget the sound of your laugh.' As you continue, there's a shift—a tiny, fragile moment of gratitude breaking through the grief: 'Thank you for... for everything you gave me.' Your voice breaks on the word 'everything.' End with the quietest whisper, a confession you can barely say aloud, mixing profound loss with tender love: 'I'm not ready to let you go, but... I think you're already gone.' Let silence do the work between words.

title: Emergency Dispatch
instruction: You're the 911 operator on duty. A man is calling because his daughter won't wake up from a fever. You're walking him through CPR instructions in your practiced calm voice, but you recognize his address. It's your own neighborhood. It's where your niece's best friend lives. You push the emotion down and deliver each instruction with surgical precision: 'Place your hands on the center of her chest. Start compressions at 100 per minute.' Then the man says her name. Your daughter's friend's name. Your voice doesn't crack publicly, but your hand is shaking so hard you almost drop the phone between instructions. Finish the call maintaining professional protocol while showing the toll in your breathing.

title: What I Whisper When You're Sleeping
instruction: You're speaking in hushed tones to your sleeping lover, partner, or child—someone who cannot hear you and will never know you said these things. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate and achingly tender. Confess something you're too afraid to say when they're awake: maybe you're leaving, maybe you're dying, maybe you know the relationship is ending and you're memorizing this moment. Let your words be simple, honest, catching in your throat. There should be pauses where you almost can't continue, where the emotion is too much. Move from gentle observation of their sleeping face to the unbearable weight of your secret, ending in a moment of such quiet devastation that silence becomes its own kind of goodbye.

title: Finding Peace in the Storm on the Worst Day of Your Life
instruction: You've just received devastating news - a diagnosis, a death, a betrayal - and you've walked outside into an approaching storm, barely holding yourself together. Begin trying to focus on the thunder's beauty like you always have, your voice shaking as you describe it, clearly using this ritual as an anchor while your world falls apart. But something shifts: as rain begins to fall, you start laughing through tears at the absurd timing, at nature's perfect indifference to your pain. Let contradictory emotions flood through - you're grateful to be alive to hear this thunder even as your heart is breaking, you're terrified of what comes next yet oddly calm in this exact moment. Your voice should oscillate between laughter and sobs, wonder and despair. End with genuine, inexplicable peace: 'Everything is falling apart, and somehow, right now, in this storm, I'm okay. How is that possible?'
inspired_by: Listening to the Distant Sound of Thunder on a Warm Evening

title: Professional: Judge Must Sentence Her Own Daughter to Prison
instruction: Courtroom. Your judicial voice is formal and distant. Then your daughter is brought forward. Your voice continues pronouncing sentence with locked professionalism—this is your role, your responsibility. But internally, you're sentencing someone you birthed. Your breathing becomes the only human thing; your voice is entirely judicial. You're performing justice while justice is destroying your daughter. After gavel strike, you leave the bench and your voice becomes someone who will never fully recover from this performance of duty.

title: Thirst and Blame
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy stranded in a dusty parking lot under a brutal midday sun. It's been over an hour since your ride was supposed to come—you've been calling, but no answer. Your throat feels like sandpaper, your vision wavers, and every breath is a dry heave. You finally see your older sister walking toward you with a bottle of water, but the anger that's been building boils over. Start with a ragged, panting accusation—your voice cracking from dehydration. Let the fury leak through each word as you point out her lateness, but feel your body weakening. End with your voice sinking into a raspy, almost defeated whisper—the anger still there, but hollowed out by exhaustion.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dust and Gratitude
instruction: You are a mother stranded with your young child in a car that has overheated on a desert road. The air is thick and suffocating. You feel a wave of bitterness—resentment at being stuck here, at the car, at everything. But your child looks at you, trusting you completely. As you speak, your voice is wilted from dehydration, each word a struggle. Let your bitterness slowly dissolve into overwhelming gratitude for this small life beside you, and let your affection fill the gaps between heavy breaths. Speak as if you are barely holding on, but love is the only thing keeping you upright.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Affection (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Telling Your Mentor You're Reporting Them for a Fatal Mistake
instruction: You're confronting the surgeon who trained you, who you've idolized for years, about an error they made that cost a patient's life. Begin with hesitation, almost apologetic—'I need to talk to you about the Henderson case'—your voice filled with conflicting loyalty and moral duty. As they deflect or defend, your tone hardens with betrayal and anger. You recount the specific moments where they failed, your voice shaking not just with rage but with the pain of losing your hero. When they finally break, trying to explain or apologize, you must decide: do you comfort the broken human in front of you or stay cold with righteous fury? Your voice carries both love and contempt, admiration and disgust.
inspired_by: Surgeon Narrating a Procedure While Exhausted

title: The Thank-You Note That Stings
instruction: You're a middle-aged man standing in your kitchen, sorting through a stack of mail. Your partner has just left for work after a tense morning—they forgot to do something you specifically asked them to do yesterday, and you feel a familiar ache of disappointment. You pick up a gift card they left on the counter for you, with a note that says 'I appreciate you.' You're genuinely thankful, but the timing chafes. As you read the note aloud to yourself, start with a soft, tight-throated thankfulness that slowly twists into sigh-laden, sugar-coated disappointment. Let your voice shift: begin sincere, then let each word land with a little more weight, a little more bitterness. Pause to sigh, shift your weight, and let the gratitude curdle into passive-aggressive praise as you realize you're still hurt.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Grandmother's Roar
instruction: You are an 80-year-old woman in a crowded locker room full of young male athletes after a big win. They are loud, slapping each other's backs, shouting over each other. You stand near the benches, gripping your walker. At first, you try to join their boisterous energy—you raise your voice, use slang, force a laugh—but it feels alien, and they barely notice you. Then a player bumps into you, and you suddenly feel the full weight of your pride for these boys, the ones you've watched grow up. Your voice drops, slows, and becomes raw with emotion as you speak from the heart, making the room quiet. Let your voice crack, let it catch in your throat, let one hand tremble as you adjust your glasses. The pride intensifies until it's almost painful, but softens into a weary, loving authority by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Hospice Nurse Whispers to Unconscious Patient They Once Loved
instruction: Night shift. The patient is your first love from decades ago—the one who disappeared without explanation. They're unconscious, dying, and have no family. You're alone with them for the first time in thirty years. Begin by speaking softly about mundane things—the weather, the flowers someone sent. Then your voice becomes intimate, vulnerable. You confess you never stopped wondering. Your throat tightens as you admit you forgave them years ago, that you understand now what you couldn't then. Let tears catch your words. End by telling them it's okay to let go, your voice barely audible, as you hold their hand and feel it grow cold.
inspired_by: Historical: Berlin Wall Communicant Realizes the Guard Is Their Sister

title: Whispering Goodnight to the Child You'll Never Have
instruction: It's late at night after receiving devastating medical news. You're alone, speaking softly to the child you just learned you'll never be able to conceive. Your voice is tender, almost singing a lullaby to someone who doesn't exist and never will. Describe the life you imagined—bedtime stories, scraped knees you'd kiss better, the sound of their laughter. Your voice is gentle but there's a tremor underneath, grief pressing against every word. As you continue, the tenderness remains but it's suffused with such profound sadness that you can barely breathe. You're saying goodnight to a ghost, to a future that died today. Your voice doesn't break into sobs—it stays soft, almost peaceful—but the pain is so thick you can hardly form words. End with 'I would have loved you so much,' barely audible, your throat too tight to speak.
inspired_by: Former Abuse Victim Saying the Abuser's Words to Heal

title: Quantum Goodbye: Finding Peace in the Impossible
instruction: You're quantum-linked to your alternate self in a parallel universe. You're dying young; they're living the long life you'll never have. As you describe the sunset you're watching (your last), they describe their morning with your shared grandchildren you'll never meet. Your voice should shimmer between grief and wonder — crying while laughing at their stories, your breath labored but filled with genuine joy for them. They're weeping while trying to sound happy for you, their voice breaking on mundane details that suddenly matter infinitely. Create a dance of mirrored emotions: you express gratitude for this impossible goodbye while your heart shatters; they rage at the unfairness while treasuring every word. Both voices should overlap near the end, speaking the same realization simultaneously: 'We're the same person, and we're both complete.' Find the contradictory truth that you're at peace with your short, full life, and they're devastated by their long, empty one without this perspective. End with synchronized breathing that slowly desynchronizes — one fading, one continuing, both forever changed.
inspired_by: Parallel Universe: Meeting the Other You

title: The Intervention That Breaks Open
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the childhood she stole from you, and you've rehearsed this speech for years. Start with controlled anger, listing facts like evidence in court—dates, incidents, the therapist's words. But when she looks at you with those same eyes that once meant safety, your rage cracks. Let yourself feel the bewildered child underneath the furious adult. Your voice should ricochet between accusation and desperate pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Mix your fury with grief, your strength with the vulnerability of still wanting her to say she's sorry. End in a place of terrible clarity—not forgiveness, not hatred, but the devastated recognition that she did her best and it destroyed you anyway.

title: Conceptual Art
instruction: A confused person is standing in front of an empty room calling itself 'art.' Your voice starts patient, almost professorial. But as you explain what the artist is doing—making you question presence, absence, meaning—something shifts. Your voice finds genuine passion. 'The point is that you're uncomfortable. That's the point.' By the end, they almost see it. And so do you. Your voice has become a believer.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Work Over You
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about all the recitals, games, and birthdays they missed. Begin with sarcastic casualness, protecting yourself with humor: 'Remember when I was a kid? Neither do you.' As they try to justify with their career and sacrifices, your voice turns sharp, years of resentment surfacing: 'You chose a corner office over knowing your own child.' They defend themselves, and something in you snaps - your voice becomes raw, vulnerable, a wounded child breaking through the adult exterior: 'I needed you and you weren't there. I'm still that kid waiting for you to show up.' End with devastating clarity, your voice quiet but fierce: 'I can't keep waiting anymore.' The anger has burned out, leaving only grief and the terrible freedom of finally speaking the truth.

title: Confronting Your Mother While She Packs to Leave
instruction: Your mother is packing her suitcase, leaving your father after forty years. You enter trying to stay calm, asking reasonable questions about logistics—voice measured, controlled, almost cold. But as you watch her fold each item, decades of unspoken hurt rises in your throat. Your questions become accusations: why she stayed so long, why she made you complicit in the silence, why she's only now choosing herself. Let anger sharpen your voice, then crack it into something rawer—you're not just angry, you're grieving the mother you needed and never had. End with a shift: through tears, acknowledge that you understand, that you're sorry, that you love her. Your voice should move from icy restraint to hot rage to broken tenderness.
inspired_by: Giving a Speech While Holding a Heavy Box

title: The Tale That Wasn't Mine
instruction: You are a young man around a campfire with friends. Someone just told an incredible story and now it's your turn. Speak with sharp impatience, jabbing a stick into the fire as you start your own dull tale. Let jealousy creep in as you compare your story to theirs, your voice turning envious and biting. Then, as you finish, the disappointment settles in—a hollow, subdued ache. Lose your train of thought for a second, stare into the flames, and let your voice drop flat at the end, cracking just slightly.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're giving a toast at your own divorce party, genuinely celebrating your freedom while your heart is simultaneously shattering. Begin with bright, almost manic joy: 'To the best decision I ever made!' Your laughter is real but edged with something dangerous. List all the reasons you're grateful—the relief, the liberation—and mean every word. But mid-sentence, your voice catches. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, celebrating and grieving the death of who you thought you'd be forever. The joy doesn't disappear; it coexists with devastating loss. You're genuinely happy and absolutely destroyed. End with a strange, transcendent peace, your voice wonder-struck and broken: 'I'm free and I'm shattered and somehow that's exactly right.' Let gratitude and grief live together in your throat.

title: Reading Your Late Spouse's Final Letter That Explains Everything
instruction: Your spouse died six months ago, and you just found a letter they left—it explains the affair you suspected, but also a terminal diagnosis they hid, and why they pushed you away to spare you the worst of it. Start reading aloud with the bitter satisfaction of being proven right, your voice tight with vindication and old anger. But as the truth unfolds, you're laughing and crying simultaneously—laughing at the absurd nobility of their deception, crying at the love beneath the betrayal. Your voice should break between rage at being lied to and gratitude for being protected, between grief at losing them and grief at misunderstanding their last year together. Let contradictions coexist—reading their words with tenderness while also wanting to scream at them for this final act of loving control. End with your voice soft with something beyond forgiveness—an exhausted, bittersweet peace that holds both love and fury in the same breath.
inspired_by: Executioner Recognizes Victim's Parent Among the Crowd

title: The 5 O'Clock Phone-In
instruction: You're a 16-year-old forced to cover the evening community bulletin on a local access channel. Your friends are texting you to hurry up. Start with that polished, non-regional anchor voice—artificially pitched and smooth—but let your impatience seep in through clipped consonants and a slight edge. As you stumble over a boring announcement about a bake sale, catch yourself, then rush through the ending with a sarcastic, irritated sign-off. End with your natural teenage tone breaking through, almost snapping at the mic.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Secret Beneath the Porch Light
instruction: You are a child, maybe nine or ten, hiding under the back porch as the grown-up party rages inside. You've snuck a sip of something sweet and fizzy from a forgotten cup, and now the world tilts in a dizzy, giggly way. Your hand is clamped tight over your mouth because you heard footsteps on the gravel path—someone is coming. You want to stay silent, but the drink makes everything feel like a hilarious secret. Start with a giddy, frightened thrill of discovery, but as the footsteps pass and the danger fades, let the smile slip away into a lonely, wondering silence. Your words are a barely muffled, conspiratorial whisper, the consonants smeared by your palm, and every sentence is interrupted by the clink of a glass or the squawk of a distant adult laugh.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Shattered Armor: The Protector Who Failed
instruction: You couldn't protect someone you were responsible for—your child, your soldier, your patient, your student. Begin with fierce, almost violent self-recrimination, your voice hard and punishing, lashing yourself with accusations. Your rage is a shield against the unbearable truth underneath. Let that rage build until it peaks—shouting, breaking—then suddenly collapse into something else entirely. Your voice drops, becomes small, helpless. The words change from anger to pleading, as if you could bargain with reality itself. 'Please, let me go back. Let me fix it.' Your breath becomes ragged, desperate. End in a place of shattered helplessness, your voice reduced to fragments, the protector completely unmade by their inability to protect. Show the transformation from defensive fury to absolute emotional devastation.

title: The Last Voicemail to Someone Who Won't Wake Up
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for someone in a coma—your sibling, your best friend, the person who knew you best. Start with forced lightness, updating them on mundane things as if they'll laugh when they hear this. Midway through, your voice cracks as you slip into confession: things you never said, apologies that feel too late, memories that now cut like glass. By the end, you're begging them to come back, your words dissolving into raw pleading. Then you catch yourself, try to end on hope—'I'll see you tomorrow'—but the hope sounds hollow even to you. The silence after you hang up. The knowledge that tomorrow might not come.
inspired_by: Singing Happy Birthday Alone in Your Apartment

title: The Collapse
instruction: You are in your car, just having left a place where you maintained perfect composure—a doctor's office, a lawyer's office, a meeting where you were fired or divorced or told devastating news. You sat through it calmly, professional, controlled. Now you're alone. Your hands are still on the steering wheel. You haven't started the car yet. Begin with shallow breathing, trying to maintain that control, repeating practical next-steps to yourself in a measured voice. But your body knows before your mind fully accepts it. Let physical sensations build: your hands start trembling on the wheel, your breath catches, heat rises through your chest. The control starts fracturing—maybe you hit the steering wheel once, then again harder, or you grip it until your knuckles white, or your breath comes in gasps. Let sound emerge raw and unformed—not pretty crying but something more primal. Your voice should break apart completely, then slowly, slowly reconstitute itself as you force yourself to breathe, to function, because you have to drive home, you have to keep moving. End with you starting the car, voice still shaking, but choosing to move forward anyway.
inspired_by: Multi-Approach Imaging Rehearsal: Waiting for Lefty (Joe and Edna)

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's slipping away, and you both know these are your final moments together. Begin by simply watching her breathe, feeling numb and frozen, unable to access what you want to say. As you speak to her, let yourself break through that numbness—start with small, simple truths about ordinary things (what you had for breakfast yesterday, the weather outside) and gradually allow yourself to speak the deeper truths you've never said aloud. Let your voice move from distant and controlled to raw and immediate. By the end, you must reach a place where you're no longer protecting yourself—where the love and grief pour out unfiltered, even if it emerges in unexpected ways (laughter mixed with tears, childhood memories, or simply repeating 'I love you' until the words finally mean something real).
inspired_by: Actor cannot be genuinely emotionally affected by stimuli (impressive block)

title: The Hidden Phone Call
instruction: You're a mother in the middle of an open-plan office, huddled low in your cubicle with your back to the aisle. You've just snuck onto a call with your young daughter who's home sick, and you're trying to sound cheerful for her sake—but halfway through, she whispers that she saw a man in the backyard who isn't supposed to be there. Start with a warm, contented sing-song voice, muffled by your hand over the receiver, stealing glances at your screen. As she tells you, your breath catches, your pitch rises, and you start whispering urgently, voice trembling, while still trying to keep it gentle for her. End with a quiet, terrified gasp as you tell her to hide.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Leaving Forever
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed at 3 AM. You're leaving—abandoning your family because you can't do this anymore, because you're drowning, because staying feels like dying. But first, you need to say goodbye to this sleeping face who will wake up tomorrow and you'll be gone. Start in whisper, trying to explain to someone who can't hear you. Your voice should be thick with tears you're trying to keep silent. 'I'm so sorry. You're going to think I didn't love you, but that's the furthest thing from—' Let yourself break. Touch their hair. Memorize their face. Feel the full weight of what you're about to do. Move from explanation to confession to a desperate kind of blessing: 'Be better than me. Be so much better.' End with the horrible peace of a decision already made, the tenderness mixed with self-loathing, the love that exists alongside the leaving.
inspired_by: Telling Someone Their Fly Is Down at Their Wedding

title: The Bench at Dusk
instruction: You are an older adult sitting alone on a park bench as the light fades. You have a neurological condition that causes sudden, involuntary vocal tics—a sharp sound or a word interrupting your speech, after which you continue as if nothing happened. At first, your voice carries a slight sourness, a bitter irritation about a recent argument that replays in your mind. As you speak to yourself, let that sourness slowly give way to a weary, almost amused acceptance. The tics should feel natural, like hiccups in your breath, not performed. Your voice stays androgynous and calm throughout, with the faintest edge of melancholy by the end.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Prop That Cracks the Spell
instruction: You are a young male actor with a deep, resonant voice performing in a grand theater. In the middle of a serious scene, your prop—a fragile glass—suddenly wobbles and nearly shatters. You deliver your next line as a stage whisper, projecting to the back row with over-articulated consonants, but your genuine reaction leaks through: first a flicker of awe at how beautifully the light catches the wobbling glass, then a soft, amused recognition of the absurdity. Your voice must start with hushed reverence and end with a barely suppressed chuckle, as if your character is momentarily distracted by the magic and the mistake.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Blanket You Should Have Given Me
instruction: Confront your emotionally distant parent about a childhood memory: the night you were cold and scared, and they walked past your room without stopping. Start with controlled, quiet anger as you describe how you pulled a blanket around yourself, learning to comfort yourself because they wouldn't. Build into raw confrontation—your voice rising as you describe the weight of that blanket becoming the weight of having to be your own parent. Then break: let the anger crack open into the grief of a child who needed warmth and got stone instead. End by revealing that you still sleep with blankets piled on top of you, trying to recreate the hug you never got. Let your voice carry both fury and desperate, vulnerable longing.
inspired_by: Feeling the Weight of a Soft Blanket on Your Shoulders

title: The Echo of a Memory
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting alone on a concrete stairwell, the harsh reverb of your own footsteps still fading. Your hands rest on the cold railing. Begin by speaking with deep sadness — you're recalling a loved one you lost, your voice trembling against the bright, hollow echoes. Then, as you describe a small, warm memory — a shared laugh or a touch — let a slight, unexpected pleasure creep in, like a flicker of ecstasy breaking through the sorrow. Your voice should shift naturally, catching on the hard surfaces, sometimes loud and grandiose, sometimes soft and broken. Speak as if you're lost in the moment, pausing when footsteps or echoes distract you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Captain: Final Transmission Before Mission of No Return
instruction: You're recording a message to your crew before a one-way space mission to save Earth. Begin with steady, matter-of-fact mission details—fuel calculations, trajectory coordinates—your voice controlled and professional. But as you speak, something breaks: you realize you're saying goodbye to people you love who will receive this message after you're gone. Your voice softens, becomes intimate: 'Tell my daughter I...' and you can't finish. The professional mask cracks completely. You're not just a captain anymore—you're someone's parent, someone's friend, and you're terrified and trying not to show it. By the end, find a strange peace in the contradiction: you're proud of this sacrifice and you're heartbroken by it. Let your voice carry both the weight of duty and the rawness of a final goodbye. This is the last time anyone will hear your voice. Make it count.

title: Your Father's Work Jacket
instruction: You're confronting your aging father in his garage, wearing his old work jacket that he hasn't touched in years—the one he wore when he actually showed up for your childhood. Feel its weight on your shoulders, the roughness of the canvas, how it smells of oil and sawdust and decades of his absence. Start with that weight making you feel small and childlike, your voice uncertain, asking him why he was never there. But as you speak, let the sensation of wearing his jacket—of literally carrying what he carried—shift something in you. Feel how heavy it is, how he wore this every day, how maybe his shoulders hurt too. Let your anger transform through the physical experience of this garment into something more complicated: not forgiveness exactly, but a devastating recognition that he's just a tired old man who also failed himself. End in a whisper, still angry but now also grieving for both of you.
inspired_by: Actor needs to feel specific physical attitudes (swagger, authority, vulnerability) that don't arise naturally but would arise from a specific garment or object

title: Caffeine and Contempt
instruction: You're a young man at an all-night coffee shop, three cups in, hands trembling. Your friend just asked how you're doing after the breakup. Start with shame—you can't look them in the eye, voice too fast, mumbling, cutting yourself off. Let the caffeine make you jittery, laughing nervously, then shift into contempt as you talk about your ex, voice tightening, a bitter edge. End with a hollow, flat admission that you're not okay, the energy draining but still restless. Speak about 60 words, letting pauses and breath betray you.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Contempt (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling from a secure line before deploying on a mission you know you won't return from. Start with forced brightness: 'Hey, I just wanted to hear your voice before I go.' But the facade cracks quickly. 'Remember when we were kids and I promised I'd always protect you? I meant it.' Your voice breaks as reality hits: 'I need you to know that every choice I made, even this one, was because I believed in something bigger than myself.' Tears come now, but there's also fierce pride: 'You're going to be angry with me. Maybe for years. But you're going to be okay.' End with devastating tenderness: 'I'm not saying goodbye. I'm saying... I love you enough to leave.' The emotional arc moves from false cheerfulness to raw honesty to protective love mixed with unbearable sorrow.

title: Bedside Confession: Saying Goodbye to Your Comatose Mentor
instruction: You're alone at the bedside of your mentor who's on life support after a medical error—an error you made but they took the blame for. Speak quietly, intimately, as if they might somehow hear. Begin with tender gratitude: 'You taught me everything. How to hold a scalpel, how to hold someone's fear.' Your voice is soft, loving. Then the confession comes, almost a whisper: 'It was my mistake. The drug interaction I missed. You knew, didn't you?' Let your voice catch, barely able to continue. 'You told them it was yours. You're dying for my error.' The weight of this must break something in you. Your breathing becomes unsteady. End with the most painful truth: 'I don't know how to be the doctor you believed I was. I don't know how to live with what you gave up for me.' Let the final words dissolve into quiet crying. This must feel like a confession that's ripping you apart, spoken in the intimate space between grief and love.
inspired_by: Medical Director: Announcing Quality Improvement Changes

title: The Rhythm of Surrender
instruction: You are in an intimate scene where a partner is administering impact play. You have agreed to a count, but each strike pulls you deeper into yourself. Start with a contemplative, almost detached focus—thinking about trust, the rhythm of the moment, the sting. As the scene progresses, let your voice shift: each impact draws a sharp, involuntary yelp, followed by a breathy recovery moan. Your pitch spikes on the strike, then settles into a lower, more vulnerable tone. By the end, your counting becomes quieter, more resigned, as you move from contemplation into a raw acceptance of the sensation and the connection. Let your breathing dictate pauses—hold before the strike, release after. Let your voice crack or trail off if you lose a number, then find it again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your mother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake for what may be the last time. Begin by noticing small details—her hand on the blanket, the sound of her breathing. Start in careful, controlled gratitude, thanking her for something specific from your childhood. As you speak, let a memory flood you so completely that you're no longer in the hospital—you're back there, living it with her. When you return to the present moment, the weight of losing her crashes over you. Your final words to her should carry both the fierceness of wanting to keep her here and the tender permission to let go. Let your voice break where it needs to; let silence hold what words cannot.
inspired_by: Relationship Preparation via Endowment + Guided Imaging (Night Mother Example)

title: The Kitchen Floor Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your adult child in the kitchen where you raised them, and they've just said something that revealed how deeply your parenting wounded them—something you never saw, never intended, but cannot deny. Begin from a place of defensive shock and hurt pride. As they lay out their truth, let yourself move through anger at being 'misunderstood,' then feel the ground shift beneath you as you start to actually hear them. Your voice should change—from sharp and self-protective to cracked and searching. End in a place where you're no longer defending yourself but genuinely asking for understanding, voice raw and small, realizing that being right matters less than being real. Let the shift happen messily, with backsliding and resistance before the final surrender.

title: Embers in the Aftermath
instruction: You are an older woman fleeing through a burning forest. Your lungs burn, each breath a raw gasp. You only manage single words or short shouts between violent heaves. At first, pure panic: you shout for your lost dog, desperate and ragged. But as you stumble over a charred log, you spot the animal safe behind a rock, tail wagging. A flicker of contentment cuts through the terror. Your voice shifts — still gasping, but with a tiny, breathless laugh. Let your body feel the sprint: the stitch in your side, the heat, the relief that tinges your panic. End with a softer, almost grateful call to the dog.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing and Crying While Reading Your Spouse's Hidden Love Letters
instruction: You've found letters your spouse wrote to you over the years but never gave you—and they died yesterday. Start reading the first one aloud, your voice tentative, curious. Then you laugh—actually laugh—at an inside joke, at how perfectly they captured your quirks. Your voice is warm, delighted, as if they're in the room. But mid-laugh, you remember they're gone, and the laugh becomes a sob. You keep reading through tears, your voice breaking and mending as you discover how deeply you were loved. There's another moment of genuine joy—they wrote about your future together, and it's so hopeful, so beautiful, that you're smiling through tears. Your voice holds both things at once: profound grief and overwhelming gratitude. You're laughing again, but crying harder, as you read how they saw you. End with your voice full of contradictions—shattered but whole, devastated but somehow more alive, saying 'thank you' to someone who can't hear you. The emotions interweave: discovery, joy, grief, gratitude, love, and loss all bleeding into each other.
inspired_by: MRI Claustrophobia Peak: Panicking in the Machine

title: The Pigeon Lady's Daughter
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a high, delicate voice, scattering breadcrumbs on a park bench. You're still sour from a decade-old argument with your daughter who moved away. Suddenly, you see her—she's standing ten feet away, wearing that same ridiculous pink beret you always teased her about. A gasp escapes you, your hand flies to your chest. Your voice shoots up: 'Oh—my—Gloria?!' You half-stand, dropping the bread bag, then sink back down, trembling. First, the sourness hardens your tone, but then it cracks into deep, heavy sobbing—shoulders shaking, words broken. Then you spot the beret, and a wet, incredulous laugh bursts out mid-cry. Your pitch loops wildly from high-pitched squeaks to low, breathy murmurs as you reach out a wrinkled hand, forgetting the bread, forgetting everything but her face.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Sadness (very intensely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Missing Piece
instruction: You're a child, maybe eight years old, sitting on your bedroom floor surrounded by puzzle pieces—the last one is finally in your hand. You've been searching for what feels like forever, and as you fit it in, a quiet, intense pride blooms in your chest. You talk to yourself, your voice a soft, slow murmur, tracing the picture with your finger as you marvel at your own patience. Start with a tired, almost defeated sigh, then shift to a slow-building smile in your voice as you finish the puzzle and whisper, 'I did it... I really did it.' Let the relief make your words lighter, the pride making you add little, awed pauses.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling the night before you deploy to a war zone you know you might not return from, but you can't say that directly. Start with forced brightness, asking about their day, their new job, keeping it light because you promised yourself you wouldn't make this heavy. They sense something's wrong and ask if you're okay. Your voice cracks just slightly as you shift to something more real: 'I just wanted to hear your voice.' They push—'What's really going on?'—and now you're caught between protecting them and needing them to know how much they matter. Your voice becomes tender, almost breaking: 'If anything ever happens... I need you to know you're the best thing I ever got to be part of.' End with love so fierce it hurts, gratitude so deep it feels like grief, all while trying to sound like everything will be fine.

title: Rope Burn
instruction: You're a teenager tied to a bedframe by your partner, wrists and ankles bound. The ropes are tight but not painful at first, and you're deeply focused on the feel of them, the weight of your body, the trust. You breathe slowly, trying to stay present. But after a few minutes, the rope starts to chafe, and a knot digs into your wrist. Your focus snaps—your patience thins. You try to keep your voice steady but irritation leaks in, your words growing clipped and demanding. Your breathing is heavier, and you shift against the bonds, the creak of rope underlining your frustration.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Breaking Point: Defending Your Child Against a System That Won't Listen
instruction: You're in an office—school administrator, social worker, doctor—and they're telling you something about your child that's wrong, dangerous, unjust. Begin trying to stay calm, professional, explaining rationally why they're mistaken. But as they dismiss you, interrupt you, patronize you, let your composure shatter. Your voice should escalate from controlled argument to fierce, shaking fury: 'You don't know my child! You don't see them!' Let rage crack into desperation—you're not just angry, you're terrified, helpless, watching someone you'd die for slip through your fingers. Your voice should break between shouting and pleading, between threats and begging. End in a moment of raw, collapsed vulnerability: maybe you break down completely, or maybe you find a cold, dangerous quiet that's even more powerful than screaming. Move from measured advocacy to explosive protectiveness to devastating helplessness.
inspired_by: Acting Calm During a Crisis to Reassure Others

title: The Return to the Childhood Home
instruction: You're standing in the doorway of your childhood bedroom for the first time in fifteen years. The person who hurt you most in this house—and who also loved you—has just died, and the house is yours now. Begin with your body defended, arms wrapped around yourself, breathing shallow, voice tight and bitter. You came here to feel nothing, to be cold and controlled, to prove you're past it all. Start by listing everything you hated about this room, this house, this person—let your voice be hard and clipped, your body armored. But as you speak, memories begin to surface that complicate the story: moments of tenderness mixed with the pain, times they tried even when they failed, ways you were loved even imperfectly. Feel your body's grip beginning to falter—maybe you sit on the bed, maybe you pick up an object, maybe you smell something that unlocks you. By the end, let yourself be torn open by the contradictions: laughing and crying simultaneously, furious and grateful, relieved they're gone and devastated by their absence, your voice breaking between curses and tender words, your body finally releasing years of held complexity.

title: The Last Language Between Us
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed at 3am. She can no longer speak clearly—her words come out garbled, unrecognizable—but you understand the emotional truth beneath every sound she makes. Begin in desperate hope, clinging to fragments of meaning, trying to decode what she's saying. Respond to her not with real words, but with your own broken, emotional sounds that carry your love, your regrets, your need for forgiveness. Let the exchange become a conversation beyond language—raw, immediate, responding moment-to-moment to the feeling in each other's sounds. End in a place of profound peace and connection, where you finally understand each other perfectly without a single recognizable word. The emotional journey moves from frantic desperation to deep, wordless communion.

title: Bitter Service
instruction: You are performing oral sex on your partner, but your heart is full of bitter resentment. You’ve been doing this for years, mechanically, each hum and muffled sound carrying the weight of unspoken grievances. Start with a hollow, practiced rhythm—your moans forced, laced with contempt. As you continue, let the bitterness curdle into a quiet, dark satisfaction: you realize you’re in control, and your partner has no idea. End with a long, low hum that sounds almost like a laugh, muffled but unmistakably mocking. Your voice is limited to nasal sounds, wet mouth noises, and half-formed words you swallow back.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: A Splinter from the Past
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a delicate, almost theatrical voice, pruning a rosebush in your garden. You yelp sharply as a hidden thorn drives deep into your palm—the pain is a spike, followed by a wave of disgust as you see the dirt and a squirming insect near the wound. At first, you mutter harsh, disgusted words about the filth and the carelessness of your own hands, your breath held tight. But as you fumble for a handkerchief and see the blood, the disgust softens into a deep, weary sadness—you think of how you used to be quicker, steadier, and now even a rosebush can betray you. Let your voice start sharp and tense, then slowly crack and slow as the sadness takes over, with pauses where you lose your thought and find it again.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Fear (slightly present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Rehearsed Apology You Can't Accept
instruction: Your estranged parent is attempting reconciliation, telling you yet again about how hard their childhood was—the same justifications you've heard your entire life for their absence and emotional neglect. Start by putting on the polite mask you've perfected over decades, nodding along with practiced patience. But as they reach the familiar conclusion where they expect forgiveness, something inside you fractures. Let your composed attentiveness crumble into raw confrontation. Tell them you've heard this story so many times you could recite it in your sleep, but they've never once asked to hear yours. Let decades of swallowed rage and grief pour out—not in screaming, but in devastatingly quiet truth-telling that finally refuses to perform the role of the understanding child.
inspired_by: Feigning Interest in a Story Youve Heard Before

title: The Last Breathing Lesson
instruction: You are a parent sitting beside your adult child's hospital bed in their final hours. Begin with a voice that tries to be strong, offering them permission to let go, but your throat keeps closing around the words. As you speak, memories flood through you—their first day of school, their wedding, the grandchildren they'll never see grow up. Your voice must move from false strength to raw, exposed grief, then transform into something unexpected: gratitude for every moment you had. End with a whispered confession that you're terrified of a world without them in it, but you understand they're tired. Your final words are both a release and a desperate plea to remember you. Let your breath catch, let silences speak, let your voice break and rebuild itself.

title: The Garden Club Grudge
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a floral-print dress, sitting on a park bench with a neighbor who just won the gardening award you've wanted for years. As you complain about your aching knees, the damp weather, and how 'certain people' get all the luck, you feel a cold, quiet malice curling beneath your sweet, sing-song voice. Slightly afraid of your own bitterness, you begin by sounding pitiful and frail, but by the end, your elongated vowels and nasal drone reveal a sharp, deliberate cruelty as you suggest her prize-winning roses might not survive the next frost. Let your voice waver and trail off as you lose your train of thought, then pick it up with a venomous sweetness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Trying to Order Coffee While Having an Existential Crisis
instruction: You're at the counter and the barista asks 'What can I get you?' but the question triggers an existential spiral. 'What CAN you get me? What does anyone get anyone? We're all just—' Catch yourself. 'Sorry. Uh. Large latte.' They ask your name for the cup. 'My name? Who am I? Am I the same person I was when I walked in here?' The barista's increasingly concerned voice grounds you. End with a normal transaction completed at three times the appropriate emotional intensity.

title: The Last Strawberry from Grandmother's Garden
instruction: You're holding the final strawberry from your grandmother's garden—she passed three days ago, and tomorrow they're selling the house. Begin with tender reverence as you bring it to your lips, describing the familiar sweetness that floods you with childhood summers. Let memory overwhelm you mid-bite: her hands in the soil, her laugh, the safety you felt. Your voice should crack as sweetness mingles with unbearable loss. End in whispered gratitude through tears, knowing this taste will never come again, yet feeling her presence in this singular moment of connection. The pleasure and the grief are inseparable.

title: Teaching Me What You Never Learned
instruction: Confront the parent or mentor who failed to teach you what you needed—how to love yourself, how to set boundaries, how to believe you were enough. Your voice starts controlled, almost reasonable, as you describe what you needed to learn and how you had to teach yourself, alone and afraid. But let the anger build as you realize how much easier it would have been if they'd just shown you, if they'd just been what you needed. Your voice should crack between fury and heartbreak: 'I had to figure out I was worth loving—why couldn't you have just told me?' They try to respond, to teach you now what they couldn't then, and you must decide whether to accept this belated lesson or reject it. End with your voice raw and exhausted, somewhere between forgiveness and the ache of what can never be recovered.

title: Lawyer Wins Case Against Former Mentor Who Destroyed Her
instruction: Reading the verdict aloud to your team, voice climbing toward triumph. But this was your professor once—the one who sabotaged your early career. Your vocal victory tastes like ash. The words of the verdict are mechanically professional, but they're also vindication you never expected to need. Your breathing is faster than professional speaking requires. Include the moment you must face him as you pass, maintaining composed eye contact while your chest heaves with years of suppressed rage and relief.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You sit across from your mother or father at a kitchen table. You came here to tell them something difficult—that they hurt you, that you needed them and they weren't there, that their love felt conditional. Start with controlled anger, the words you've rehearsed. But as you speak, allow unexpected memories to interrupt your prepared speech—moments when they did try, small gestures you'd forgotten, times they were struggling themselves. Let these uninvited recollections complicate your anger.
