End with a whispered confession of love and regret that you've kept buried for years, your breath growing shorter as the water reaches your chest. The transformation is from controlled professionalism to stripped-bare humanity.
inspired_by: Talking Through a Gas Mask During a Chemical Leak

title: Breaking Point Body
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a betrayal, a loss, a revelation you can't unknow. You're alone in your apartment. Begin by genuinely noticing your physical response: is there heat in your chest, tightness in your throat, a trembling in your hands? Don't perform the emotion—let yourself be fascinated by what your body is actually doing. As you move through the space, let your body lead: maybe you need to touch the walls, or sink to the floor, or press your forehead against the cold window. Let sounds come if they need to—laughing, sobbing, shouting, whatever genuinely emerges. Move from the first shock of the news (which might be numbness or disbelief) through the full physical experience of rage or grief, until you arrive at a moment of exhausted, quiet clarity. Your body should feel completely different at the end than at the beginning.

title: The Victory That Tastes Like Ash
instruction: You are the detective at the press conference after finally catching the mastermind who killed your partner fifteen years ago. You should be triumphant. Start trying to sound professional and victorious, but gratitude keeps bleeding through - thanking your team, your family who endured your obsession. But as you speak, your voice begins to fracture. You realize this chase was the only thing holding you together after your partner's death, and now it's over. Your children grew up without you. Your marriage ended. Fifteen years gone. Begin laughing - actually laughing - at the absurdity that you won but lost everything. The laugh should break into tears, then stabilize into something peaceful and broken and strangely free. End by saying you're retiring, your voice soft with acceptance, finding unexpected grace in the wreckage of victory.
inspired_by: The Detective and the Criminal Mastermind

title: Cleaning Out the Nursery
instruction: You are packing up a room that holds the ghost of a profound loss—a baby who didn't survive, a child who left and won't return, a version of yourself who died when your dreams did. Begin with practical efficiency, trying to keep this as a task, just folding and sorting, staying functional. But as you hold each object—a tiny sock, a book, a photograph—let grief and relief war inside you. Feel the terrible freedom of letting go mixed with the guilty joy of reclaiming your life. Let yourself laugh at a memory and then immediately choke on tears. Discover that you're both devastated and grateful, that you loved fiercely AND you're ready to breathe again. End with your hands full of the last item, voice cracking as you say both 'I'm sorry' and 'thank you' to the empty room, meaning both with your whole heart.
inspired_by: Actor feels inadequate to meet a specific character or scene obligation

title: The Weight of Unspoken Things
instruction: It's 3 AM, and you're lying next to your partner of ten years. They're asleep. You're wide awake. Begin by whispering a confession you've never said aloud—something you've carried alone that's been creating distance between you. It could be a fear, a secret desire, a moment of betrayal (emotional or otherwise), or a truth about yourself you've been hiding. Start with halting, broken phrases, barely audible. As you continue speaking into the darkness, let the relief of finally voicing it mix with terror that you're saying it (even though they can't hear). Your whisper becomes slightly more fluid, more certain. End by turning to look at their sleeping face, and let a single, specific detail about them—a freckle, the way their hand rests on the pillow—break your heart with tenderness and the knowledge that you have to say this again when they're awake.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a comprehensive record of their process and choices

title: The First Sip
instruction: You are in a dry, barren landscape, having gone without water for nearly two days. A stranger has just handed you a canteen. You take a small sip, but your throat is so parched it barely goes down. You try to thank them, but your voice cracks and you have to clear your throat. Start with raw relief and shaky gratitude, then as you speak, the thankfulness grows warmer but your voice weakens further. Let the physical strain of dehydration shape every word: audible mouth clicks, harsh sibilants, pauses to swallow. End with a quiet, heartfelt thank you that fades into a sigh.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You are at your younger sibling's wedding reception, holding a microphone to give a toast. But you are also quietly, privately in love with the person they just married—a secret you've carried for years and will carry forever. Begin by looking around the room, genuinely seeing the joy on people's faces, the beauty of the day, the happiness of your sibling. Let authentic love for your sibling fill you first. As you speak, weave together genuine celebration and hidden heartbreak. Your words must be true—you really do want them to be happy, you really do see how perfect they are together. But underneath, let your voice carry the weight of personal loss. Notice the tremor you're trying to hide, the brightness in your eyes from tears you absolutely cannot shed. End with a toast that is simultaneously the most generous gift you've ever given and the most painful goodbye you've never spoken. Your final smile must contain both pure love and quiet devastation.
inspired_by: Actor needs to prepare instrumentally for an audition

title: The Wedding Toast for Your Ex
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-partner's wedding to someone else—someone you introduced them to. Start by raising your glass with a smile in your voice, genuine warmth: 'I've known Alex for fifteen years...' As you talk about their love story, let laughter slip into your words—real laughter at shared memories, at how perfectly they fit together. But underneath, there's something else. When you say 'I've never seen Alex this happy,' your voice catches with both joy for them and grief for what you couldn't give. A tear rolls down your cheek, but you're smiling. Your voice shakes as you continue: 'That's what love is—wanting someone's happiness more than your own presence in their life.' End with a voice full of contradictions: celebrating them while mourning yourself, laughing while your heart breaks, finding genuine peace in your own beautiful devastation. 'To Alex and Jordan.'

title: The Perfect Coffee Break
instruction: You're a young man in an office chair, leaning back with a steaming travel mug in both hands. It's 10:02 AM, you've just finished a tedious data entry task ahead of schedule, and the winter sun is warming your face through the window. Start by letting out a soft, involuntary sigh of satisfaction as you take a sip—the warmth spreading through your chest. Your voice should be relaxed, a little lazy, maybe you chuckle to yourself about an inside joke. But as you scroll through photos on your phone, you pause on one of your late grandmother—your voice catches, the contentment curdles into a quiet, respectful sadness as you whisper a memory to no one. End with a shaky exhale, blinking rapidly, and a final murmured '...miss you.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Discovering Your Child's Overdose Kit and Unleashing Everything
instruction: You've just found evidence your teenager is using—needles, burnt spoons, the whole nightmare. Start with your voice shaking so violently you can barely form words, terror and rage fighting for dominance: 'What the FUCK is this?' Explode into desperate, primal screaming: 'You could DIE. Do you understand? YOU COULD DIE.' Let the fury break completely into helpless sobbing, falling to your knees: 'I don't know how to save you. I don't know how to...' Your voice becomes pleading, broken, a parent utterly undone: 'Please. Please, baby, please.' End with fierce, protective intensity mixed with complete powerlessness, grabbing them: 'I will burn the whole world down to keep you alive, but I can't... I can't do this FOR you.' Voice cracks: 'I need you to want to live.'
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Stop Being Friends With Your Abuser

title: The Emergency
instruction: Your child is trapped somewhere—a car accident, a collapsed building, you can hear their voice but can't reach them. You're screaming instructions to stay calm, promising you'll get to them, your voice savage with protective fury and absolute terror. Then you hear the rescuers say it'll be hours, maybe longer. Your rage has nowhere to go. It shatters into something worse: helplessness. Your voice becomes raw, desperate, making promises you can't keep, bargaining with physics and time and God. Start with fierce, commanding intensity—'Hold on, baby, Mommy's coming'—then let it deteriorate into sobbing fury, then finally into a broken lullaby, singing them the song from when they were little, your voice destroyed but somehow still carrying love across the impossible distance.

title: Professional: Social Worker Removes a Child from Their Parents
instruction: Approaching the family, your social worker voice is professional and compassionate. You're removing a child. The parents are desperate; the child is confused. Your voice must be firm while you're aware you're shattering a family. Your breathing is controlled—you're trained for this. But training doesn't prepare you for the mother's voice. Your voice becomes both necessary and devastating. You remove the child and your voice is professional armor around internal collapse. Later, alone, your voice breaks—you saved a child while destroying a family.

title: Saying Thank You to Someone Who Both Saved and Broke You
instruction: You're speaking to someone you once loved—maybe still love—who gave you everything and took it all away. Your voice trembles with genuine gratitude as you thank them for the ways they changed you, the doors they opened, the person they helped you become. You're laughing softly, remembering beautiful moments, and your voice is warm with real affection. But underneath, grief is rising. Your laughter becomes unsteady. You're still thanking them, but now the gratitude is tangled with heartbreak because those same hands that lifted you also pushed you down. Your voice breaks as you thank them for teaching you what love could be, even as they showed you what it isn't. You're crying and smiling at once, voice full of contradictions—appreciation and anger, tenderness and pain, joy for what was and devastation for what's lost. End with a moment of strange peace: your voice steadies into something clear and true as you realize you can hold both things at once. You can be grateful and wounded, loving and free. Your final thank you is whispered with tears on your face and something like serenity in your voice.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Ancient Warrior Realizes They've Been Fighting an Illusion

title: Watching Them Sleep
instruction: You're standing in the doorway watching your adult child sleep the night before they leave for a dangerous deployment overseas. Your voice is barely above a whisper, speaking to them though they can't hear: 'You look just like you did when you were three. Same little furrow between your eyebrows.' There's a smile in your voice, tender and aching. You're memorizing every detail, your words coming slower: 'I want to crawl inside this moment and live here forever.' But reality intrudes—your breath catches, voice tightening: 'What if this is the last time I...' You can't finish that sentence. Instead, something shifts to fierce, quiet determination mixed with unbearable tenderness: 'You're going to come back to me. You have to.' End with the softest whisper, almost a prayer, your voice thick with unshed tears: 'I'm not ready to be this brave.' The emotion is almost entirely internal—a battle between love, terror, pride, and the desperate need to protect what you must let go.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're alone in your apartment after a devastating day where everything you've been holding together finally collapsed. Begin by physically pacing, trying to contain it—straightening pillows, washing a dish, anything to maintain control. But your body won't cooperate anymore. Let the physical sensation of being overwhelmed take over. Maybe you need to scream, or collapse, or laugh hysterically, or shake. Don't plan it—let your body lead. This is about the raw, physical experience of emotional breaking. Let primal sounds come out—not theatrical screaming, but real release. Move from rigid control to complete physical surrender. By the end, you should be on the floor, spent, breathing hard, but somehow more present in your body than you were at the start. The emotion moves THROUGH your body, not just from your voice.

title: The Weight of Morning
instruction: You are an elderly woman, deeply tired, brushing your teeth in the bathroom mirror. As the foam builds and your jaw aches, you speak to a photo of your late partner propped by the sink. Start with a sigh — the effort of the day ahead feels crushing. But as you brush, you remember a small, stubborn joy they brought you every morning. Let the exhaustion still ground your voice, but let a faint, weary smile bleed into the final words. Your words are almost mangled by the brush and foam — fumble over 'b' and 'p' sounds, pause to spit, and let the brush scrape against your teeth mid-sentence. 'They'd always say... brush like you mean it, dear. I try. Some mornings it's... [spit, sigh]... it's just the motion. But I still hear you. That's something.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She has hours, maybe minutes left. Begin with careful composure, trying to be strong for her, holding back everything you want to say. As you speak, let the walls crumble—allow yourself to become the child who needs her, who isn't ready, who has so much unfinished love to express. Move from controlled gratitude for her life to raw, unguarded pleading for more time, then finally to a whispered acceptance mixed with devastation. Let your voice break where it needs to break. This is not about performing grief—this is about letting yourself actually need her, actually face losing her, actually say the unsayable things you've been protecting both of you from. End in a place of exhausted, tender surrender.

title: Confronting Your Dying Parent Who Never Knew How to Love You
instruction: Your parent is hours from death and you finally have the courage to say what's been unspoken for decades. Begin with careful, measured anger—you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, the anger fractures into something more complex: grief for the relationship you never had, fury at the wasted years, unexpected tenderness for this failing human. Your voice becomes a battleground between the child who still wants their approval and the adult who knows it will never come. Move from accusation to a kind of exhausted acceptance, maybe even forgiveness—not for them, but for yourself. End with a truth you didn't expect to say, something that surprises even you with its honesty and pain.
inspired_by: Professional: Activist Must Compromise Their Principles to Save Vulnerable People

title: The Last Light of Evening
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She is sleeping peacefully, her breathing shallow. You begin overwhelmed with anticipatory grief, your chest tight, your throat constricted. As you hold her hand, speak to her about a specific childhood memory she gave you—a summer day, her garden, the smell of her kitchen. Let your body gradually release its grip of panic. By the end, allow yourself to arrive at a place of deep peace, your voice becoming softer, your breath fuller, almost as if you're breathing for both of you. The fear transforms into profound gratitude for having had her at all. Your final words should feel like a gentle release, not a desperate holding on.

title: The Birthday Cake Confrontation
instruction: You're lighting candles on your father's 70th birthday cake, and suddenly you can't pretend anymore. Start by singing 'Happy Birthday' with the family, your voice joining the chorus. But midway through, you stop singing. The room goes quiet. In a voice that starts calm but gains strength, you tell him: 'I need to say something before you blow out these candles.' Confess that you've been waiting your whole life for him to be proud of you, that every achievement was a plea for his attention, and you're exhausted. Your voice should move from controlled pain to raw anger to something softer—not forgiveness exactly, but a kind of grief-soaked release. End with a whisper: 'Make a wish, Dad,' but now it sounds like goodbye to something you'll never have.

title: Lying on Freshly Washed Sheets
instruction: Sink into bed, feeling the cool, crisp sheets against your skin. Describe the smoothness, the light, clean scent, and the way the sheets fit perfectly around you. Speak softly, with a smile, as if each second brings more calm and coziness, making you feel as if youre floating on a soft, pure cloud.

title: The Bitter Retirement Party
instruction: You're an elderly man in a bustling open-plan office, sitting at your desk. The air hums with HVAC white noise and distant chatter. You're on the phone with your daughter, explaining why you're skipping your own retirement party—the one your coworkers planned without asking you. Your voice is low, almost a grumble, to avoid eavesdroppers. Start with a tired, sour resignation, like you've swallowed something unpleasant. As you speak, you notice a photo of your late wife on your desk, and your tone softens, cracking with a quiet, unexpected tenderness. Let the office murmur distract you briefly—a laugh from a cubicle, a printer whirring—before you return, now shaky with a mix of bitterness and reluctant love.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unlocked Door
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting alone in your living room, staring at a photo of your late wife. A nagging doubt has been gnawing at you all afternoon—did you lock the back door? You’ve checked it twice, but the doubt won’t let go. Just as you try to convince yourself it’s fine, a sneeze builds from deep in your chest. You try to hold it back, but it explodes with force. Afterward, you speak with a congested nose, your voice thick and muffled. The doubt lingers, but as you press your thumb to the photo frame, it softens into a quiet, weary acceptance—maybe it doesn’t matter as much as you think.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Returned Ring
instruction: You are holding a ring—an engagement ring, a family heirloom, a promise—and you're about to give it back to (or receive it from) someone you've loved deeply. You thought you knew exactly how you'd feel doing this: angry and vindicated, or devastated, or relieved. But as you look at the actual ring in your hand, and at the actual person's face, everything becomes more complicated. You're furious at them and you miss them. You're grateful it's over and you're heartbroken. You want to hurt them and you want to protect them. Let all of these feelings exist at once in your voice—don't choose one emotion, let them fight with each other. Speak as these contradictions pull you in different directions. Your voice might be tender one moment and bitter the next, warm and then cold. By the end, you don't have resolution—you have the messy truth of loving someone you also need to release.

title: The Moment Protective Fury Meets Powerlessness
instruction: Someone you're fiercely protective of—your child, younger sibling, beloved friend—has been hurt, and you're confronting the situation or person responsible. Start with explosive rage, voice shaking with barely contained violence: 'You had no right. NO RIGHT to touch them, to hurt them like that!' Let the anger build, voice rising to a roar: 'Do you understand what you've done? Do you even care?' But then the fury cracks open to reveal the helplessness underneath—your voice breaks completely, dropping to ragged desperation: 'I should have protected them. I should have known. I should have...' Fall into gasping sobs of self-blame and impotent rage. Then gather yourself with fierce, trembling resolve, voice low and deadly serious: 'This ends now. I will spend every breath I have left making sure they're safe. Every single breath.' End with your voice simultaneously threatening and breaking with love for the person you're protecting.

title: Dancing with a Ghost
instruction: You're at your wedding reception, but your new spouse is emotionally absent—going through the motions, smiling for photos, but utterly disconnected during your first dance. You're holding them, moving to music, and you can feel the emptiness where presence should be. Begin with bright, performed joy for the watching crowd, but let your grip on them change as the dance continues—pulling them closer, trying to find their eyes, making unexpected movements to jar them back to you. Mix physical sensation with emotional desperation: the heat of the room, the weight of the wedding dress or suit, the sweat, the aching feet, the pressure of their hand that doesn't quite hold you back. Let your emotion spiral from performed happiness through barely contained panic, into fierce, almost angry determination to break through, and finally into a moment of either breakthrough connection or devastating acceptance. The dance must continue—but what are you dancing with?
inspired_by: An actor is dealing with another actor who is unresponsive or uninvolved

title: Rain Through the Open Window
instruction: You're standing at an open window during a rainstorm, and you've just received news—maybe the best news of your life, maybe the worst, but something that changes everything. Let the physical sensation of rain on your skin, wind on your face, the smell of wet earth become inseparable from the emotion moving through you. Begin in your body's immediate response—maybe trembling, maybe stillness, maybe involuntary laughter or gasping. Don't perform the emotion; let the sensory experience of the storm pull it through you. By the end, you and the weather are one thing—you're not a person standing in rain, you're a living response to this moment. Your voice might roar or whisper or break completely; follow what the body demands.

title: Midnight Confession to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You're whispering a confession you can never say when they're awake—maybe about an affair that ended, a profound doubt about your future together, or a part of yourself you've hidden. Start barely audible, voice catching in your throat, testing if they're really asleep. Words come haltingly, each sentence a risk. You're crying silently, voice wet and broken, but there's strange relief in finally speaking the truth aloud, even into the darkness. Describe how much you love them even as you confess what might destroy you both. Your voice wavers between self-loathing and desperate tenderness. End with your hand touching their sleeping face, voice becoming impossibly gentle, a whispered apology and love declaration so quiet it's almost just breath, knowing you'll wake tomorrow and pretend this conversation never happened.
inspired_by: Hospital Morphine Clarity Before It Wears Off

title: Little Flame
instruction: You’re a young girl who has just proudly poured hot tea from the kettle into your own cup all by yourself—you feel a huge swell of pride. But the kettle was too full and a splash scalds your hand. You gasp sharply, hissing through clenched teeth, and instinctively grab your wrist. You want to show you’re a big girl who can handle it, so you try to keep your voice steady, but the pain makes your words come out in short, breathy bursts. Start with excited pride, then let the burn creep in, your voice wavering between a brave declaration and a pained whimper, until you finally admit it really hurts.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Last Round Sabotage
instruction: You're in a late-night co-op game with friends, but you're exhausted and a bit tipsy. One teammate has been frustrating you all session. In this moment, you casually call out a plan, but your tired voice turns icy as you privately decide to let them fail—or worse. Start with a weary, social tone, then let a menacing calm settle in as you realize you can manipulate the outcome. React to the game sounds around you, maybe stifle a yawn, and let your words carry a sharp edge of betrayal.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Park Path Surprise
instruction: You're an older man power-walking through a crowded park, your stride strong and steady. You start out muttering under your breath about slow walkers blocking your path, your voice carrying a tense, impatient edge from the rhythmic huff of each heel strike. Midway, you spot an old friend you haven't seen in years at a bench ahead—astonishment cuts through your irritation, pulling a sharp, breathy 'No way' out of you. Let the surprise shift your tone from gruff and clipped to genuinely awed, with the physical jolts of your steps causing tiny tremors and pauses in your voice as you stop and blurt out an amazed greeting.
emotions_sampled: Elation (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Protecting the Intern from Your Own Boss
instruction: Your toxic boss is publicly humiliating a young intern for a mistake you know isn't their fault - it's yours. Begin with your voice tight, controlled, as you try diplomatic intervention. But when your boss turns their cruelty up, something primal erupts: fierce protectiveness that overrides your fear. 'ENOUGH. You want to blame someone? Blame me.' Let your voice shake not with weakness but with volcanic rage barely contained. As you shield this kid, feel your own powerlessness flood in - you can protect them from this moment but not from this workplace, not really. Your fury should fracture into something more complex: righteous anger mixing with your own unhealed wounds from being that young person once. Build to an explosive climax, then let it shatter into unexpected tenderness as you turn to the intern. End somewhere completely different: quiet, almost broken, as you realize this act of courage might cost you everything, but your voice carries a strange peace beneath the fear.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Mission
instruction: You're speaking to someone you love deeply—a partner, a child, a parent—hours before you leave on a mission you know you won't survive. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them from the truth, your voice bright but trembling at the edges. As they press you about when you'll return, the facade begins to crack. Your voice becomes quieter, more tender, as you try to memorize the sound of their voice, the way they laugh. The desperation builds—you want to say everything but can't say the one true thing. By the end, you're speaking in almost a whisper, each word heavy with unspoken goodbye, your voice breaking on simple phrases like 'I love you' or 'remember me.' The final words are barely audible, choked with the weight of permanent loss, but somehow filled with a fierce, protective love that makes the heartbreak even more devastating.

title: The Last Time I'll Lie to Protect You
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's hospice bedside. She's asking if you're okay, if your life turned out well, seeking reassurance in her final hours. The truth is you've been struggling for years—your marriage failed, you're barely holding on financially, you feel lost. But you smile and tell her everything is beautiful, that she did everything right, that you're so happy. Start with the gentle lie, your voice warm and reassuring. But as you continue, let the mask crack—your voice should catch, genuine grief bleeding through the performance of contentment. End in a place where you're still trying to smile for her, but tears are streaming down your face, and you can barely get the words out. Let us hear both the lie and the unbearable love beneath it.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Surprised by Predictable News

title: Editor Realizes Her Biggest Scoop Will Destroy Someone She Loves
instruction: Phone call to your lead reporter, voice electric with publication momentum. You're three hours from press. Then you read the byline of the person being investigated. Your voice halts mid-sentence. Physically, you're still in the office; vocally, you're suddenly isolated. You're breathing through a choice you didn't know you'd have to make. Your professional excitement becomes muted. Ask your reporter to delay—with words that cost you everything, voice heavy with implications only they understand.

title: The Quiet Holds the Truth
instruction: You are a teenage boy hiding in your mother's walk-in closet, the door slightly open. The thick coats and fabric swallow every sound, making your own voice feel alien and flat. You're here because your friends just dared you to prove you're 'man enough' to sneak into a party, but something about that challenge made your stomach drop. Start with a forced, gruff confidence—a low, steady tone that tries to sound older—but as you repeat the excuse you're planning to tell your mom ("I'm just going to Jake's, studying"), let the hollow acoustics unsettle you. Feel the words lose conviction. A tiny pause as you realize the lie feels wrong. Let your voice waver, then drop into a softer, confused mutter, like you're talking to yourself: "Why does that sound like I'm the one playing a part?" The confusion should creep in from the edges, slowly unraveling the mask until the final words are almost a question, raw and unsure.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Laugh That Got Stuck
instruction: You are nine years old, standing in your grandmother's empty kitchen after the funeral. The house still smells like her—lavender and burnt toast. You're supposed to be sad, but your brain keeps playing a loop of the time she tried to teach you to whistle and ended up making silly faces instead. You start telling this memory to your teddy bear, trying to hold in a giggle, but the laugh catches in your throat because you suddenly remember she's not coming back. Let your voice be high and childlike, starting with bubbly amusement that dances around the words, then falter as the hollow grief hits—quiet, with long pauses and a little sniffle.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Last Breath Before the Quiet
instruction: Place yourself in a dim alley, pressed against a cold wall. The person you thought was a friend has their hands tight around your throat—you can barely breathe. You’re still buzzed from the cheap wine you shared, the world swimming in a sickly haze. At first, you try to laugh it off, a sour, drunken joke about how this isn’t funny. But their grip tightens, and your voice cracks, fear clawing through the fog. Let your words come in gasps, pitch rising erratically, as you plead—not for your life, but for them to see you. End with a whisper that tastes like copper and regret.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Sourness (clearly present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Splitting the Question
instruction: You're a child alone in the backyard, chopping wood for the first time. The axe feels heavy, your arms ache, and you're confused—why did Dad leave? Each swing is a question you can't answer. Speak only during the wind-up or as you pause to catch your breath, letting the grunt and crack of the wood punctuate your words. Your voice is raw, unguarded, and full of the effort of both the axe and your heart. Begin with confusion heavy in your throat, unsure and searching. By the final swing, the confusion hasn't vanished, but it's settled into a quiet, tired certainty—you'll keep going, because that's what you do.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Thin Air Above
instruction: You are an elderly traveler, high in the mountains, gasping for air as a young guide helps you down. Your head pounds with every breath, and your thoughts slip like sand through fingers. You want to thank them for their patience, but the words come out slow, broken by winces and long pauses. Start with a numb, almost hollow mutter of gratitude, then let a genuine flicker of warmth break through as you realize they truly care — though the pain and detachment remain. Speak as if your voice is a fragile thread, catching on the wind.
emotions_sampled: Pain (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Old Tyrant's Confession
instruction: You are an elderly man, once a feared tyrant, now alone in a dim room. You are crying so hard your chest heaves in jerky gasps, your throat wet and choked. Start with a bitter, malevolent rasp—anger at your own weakness, snarling through tears. But as you speak, the malice cracks open into raw distress, confessing a cruel act you can't undo. Let your voice waver, crack, and break; inhale in spasms; pause to cough or wipe your nose. End with a trembling, broken quiet. Speak about 50 words.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Dying Parent Who Never Said They Loved You
instruction: You're at your parent's hospital bedside with maybe hours left. Start controlled, almost businesslike—you've rehearsed this. 'I need to say something before it's too late.' But as you speak, decades of hurt pour out: the times you needed them, the silence, the withholding. Your voice should escalate from measured words to raw, ugly crying—this isn't pretty grief, it's messy and real. Then, mid-accusation, you break differently: you realize you're not angry, you're heartbroken because you still need them to love you. End with vulnerable, child-like simplicity, reaching for their hand: 'Just tell me once. Please. Just once say it.' Your voice should be stripped bare, all defenses gone.
inspired_by: Listening to Your Child Say They Hate You

title: Emergency Room Fury: A Sibling's Collapse Between Rage and Terror
instruction: You're in the ER, and the doctors just told you your younger sibling overdosed—again. You explode at them the moment they're conscious, screaming about how selfish they are, how you can't keep doing this. 'Do you have ANY idea what this does to us? To me?!' Your voice is raw with fury, shaking with anger that's really terror in disguise. But mid-rage, you break—the anger collapses into sobbing, your voice fragmenting: 'I can't lose you. I can't... please, I can't lose you.' You're begging now, fierce and desperate, grabbing their hand. Move between explosive accusation and broken pleading, between wanting to shake sense into them and just wanting to hold them. End with a voice scraped raw, simultaneously furious and tender, threatening them: 'You don't get to leave me. You don't get to give up.' This is love that comes out as rage, protectiveness that sounds like violence, helplessness that roars.
inspired_by: Tandem Skydiving: Instructor Narrating Your Terror With Enthusiasm

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child You're Letting Go
instruction: Your child is asleep. You're speaking quietly, almost to yourself, because you need to say this but can't bear for them to hear. You're giving them up—to their other parent, to adoption, to someone who can give them what you cannot. Start with tender justification, voice barely above a whisper: 'You deserve so much more than I can give you.' Describe their little habits, the way they laugh, how they reach for you in the morning. Your voice should be thick with love and self-loathing intertwined. Let silence do work between phrases. End with your voice breaking into something almost inaudible, somewhere between a blessing and a goodbye, love and devastating inadequacy existing in the same breath.
inspired_by: Your Rival Becoming Your Only Emotional Support

title: The Last Conversation Before the Flight
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother at the airport, minutes before she boards a one-way flight to enter hospice care across the country. Begin with forced brightness, trying to keep things light: 'The weather's supposed to be nice there.' But your voice starts to crack as you realize this is goodbye. 'Mom, I...' Allow yourself to break down completely, all the words you never said tumbling out in a messy, desperate rush. Then find a moment of profound tenderness as you hold her hand: 'Thank you for every single day.' End in a place of devastating acceptance, your voice barely a whisper, trying to memorize her face: 'I'll be okay. You taught me how.' Let tears fall freely, breath catching, but find genuine peace underneath the grief.

title: The Toast That Curdles
instruction: You are at a lavish garden party, glass of champagne in hand, celebrating your closest friend's surprise engagement to a partner you secretly despise. As she gushes about their perfect love, you feel a sickening ecstasy in being the supportive friend — the high of your own performance. But disgust crawls up your throat with every word. At first, your voice is bright and breathy, a little too high, forcing warmth like a spotlight. Midway through your toast, your smile stiffens, your words get clipped. Let a dry, hollow laugh escape. End with a brittle, almost poisoned cheerfulness, trailing off as you notice a moth beating against the lantern.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Defending the Indefensible
instruction: You're standing between someone you love and harm—maybe your child has done something terrible, maybe your sibling is being attacked, maybe your partner is being threatened. Start with a voice that is pure, explosive protectiveness—fierce, almost feral in its intensity. You will not let anyone hurt them. Your words come fast and hard, passionate declarations of loyalty. But then comes the moment of devastating doubt: a question you can't answer, evidence you can't deny, the possibility that you're wrong. Your voice cracks, the certainty shatters, and suddenly you're screaming and crying at the same time, rage collapsing into helplessness. You don't know what's true anymore, but you also can't stop protecting them—it's deeper than logic, deeper than right or wrong. End with your voice raw and broken but still standing, still defending, even as you're falling apart. The strength isn't in being right; it's in loving someone even when it destroys you.

title: Last Lap
instruction: You are swimming laps in an indoor pool, your kid waiting on the side for you to finish. But your mind is consumed by a memory from last night: a raw, electric encounter you're disgusted to admit you crave again. As you gasp for air between strokes, you push through exhaustion, muttering angry confessions and stray thoughts—lust thick in your throat, revulsion sharp on your tongue. Your voice is broken into wet, clipped bursts, sputtering with water and shame. By the final lap, you shift from resistant craving to a quiet, bitter disappointment: you'll call them again, and you hate yourself for it.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Disgust (very intensely present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're an adult child finally confronting your aging parent about the abuse they witnessed but never stopped. Start with carefully controlled words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, to give them a chance to explain. 'I just need to understand why you never...' But as they make excuses or minimize it, something ignites in you. Your voice rises, sharpens, cuts. All the years of making yourself small, of protecting them from your pain, come pouring out. Then, devastatingly, you hear yourself begging them—actually begging—to just once say they're sorry, to acknowledge what happened. End in the terrible quiet of realizing they never will. The rage must collapse into grief, the demand for justice into the ache of a child still wanting to be seen.
inspired_by: Fortune Teller Who Sees Something Terrible

title: Dancing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received terminal news—six months, maybe less—and you're calling your best friend to tell them. But something strange happens: as you say the words 'It's cancer' or 'There's nothing they can do,' you start to laugh. Not from denial, but from the absurd cosmic joke of it all, from the strange liberation of knowing your time is finite. Your voice dances between laughter and tears, sometimes in the same breath—'Can you believe this shit?'—giggling and sobbing simultaneously. Share a favorite memory, your voice warm with joy, then feel it crack with the knowledge you won't make more. Tell them how much they've meant to you, laughing through tears at some ridiculous moment you shared, then let your voice go quiet and sincere: 'I'm scared, but I'm also... I don't know... grateful? For all of it?' End in that impossible space where acceptance and heartbreak coexist, where you're genuinely at peace while simultaneously devastated, your voice soft with both joy and sorrow.

title: The Gratitude That Destroys You
instruction: You're training your replacement—the person who will take over your dream job because your illness means you can no longer do it. They're young, excited, everything you used to be. Guide them through making the perfect pour, your voice warm with genuine affection and pride in teaching them. But let the bittersweetness bleed through: you're laughing at their enthusiasm while your hands shake with grief. Share stories about the regulars, about why this work mattered, and feel your voice crack with love for this place you're losing. The contradiction should be palpable: you're truly happy for them, truly grateful to pass this on, and utterly destroyed by what you're giving up. Let tears mix with laughter as you tell them they'll be better than you ever were. End with a whispered admission that you're terrified of who you'll be without this, but thank them for giving it a future.

title: The Reach I Cannot Make
instruction: You are an elderly person seated on a mat, attempting a gentle torso twist to reach a small keepsake on the floor behind you. Your spine is stiff, the twist uneven—each breath catches, wobbles, your voice strained by the effort. Start with helplessness: a frustrated, breathless admission that your body won't obey, the vowel sounds wavering as you grunt and shift. Then, as you feel a hand on your shoulder offering help, let the emotion shift into deep gratitude, spoken with a shaky but warm release of tension. Let a hint of affection color your final words—maybe toward the person assisting, or toward the memory the keepsake holds—so the end feels tender and relieved, not just exhausted.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Helplessness (very intensely present), Affection (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Above the Party
instruction: You're a young adult with a voice that sits uncertainly between tenor and alto, stuck at a rooftop party you're already bored of. You've climbed onto a high platform to get away, and now you're looking down at the crowd, chin tilted way back. A particular person below keeps catching your eye—someone you've been circling all week—and the mix of wanting them and being annoyed you even care is exhausting. Start with a sigh of pure irritation, then let the lust creep in as you watch them slip through the crowd, your voice getting lighter and tighter. You're talking to yourself, not them: a quiet monologue that shifts from impatient frustration into a raw, contemplative admission of desire.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Contemplation (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing Alone in the Wreckage
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your home after a devastating loss—whether through fire, flood, divorce, or death. You find an object that triggers overwhelming sense memories: perhaps it still carries a scent, a texture, a weight in your hands. Begin in that physical sensation—really feel it, let it travel through your body. Your breathing changes. Suddenly, chaotically, you need to move—maybe you start swaying, maybe you collapse to the floor, maybe you begin to spin. Let physical sensation lead emotional expression: the movement is desperate at first, almost painful, your body releasing what words cannot. The sensory memory of this object mingles with your physical state. Gradually, let the movement transform from anguish into something else—perhaps wild, defiant joy; perhaps exhausted acceptance. End in stillness, forever changed by what your body just released.

title: The Weight of Feathers
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner in the middle of the night, confessing something you can never say when they're awake. Begin barely audible, your voice catching on words you've held inside for months or years—maybe it's about fading love, maybe it's about a secret that's eating you alive, maybe it's about being so tired of being strong. Let your voice be tender and broken simultaneously, like you're cradling something fragile. There should be long pauses where you almost can't continue, where the silence is thick with everything you feel. Your throat should tighten with tears you're trying to keep silent. End with the most honest thing you've ever said, whispered so softly it's almost just breath, a confession that feels like both relief and devastation. This should feel like eavesdropping on someone's most private moment—intimate, raw, unbearably real.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Morphine
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospice bed. She's lucid now, but the nurse said this might be the last window before they increase the morphine and she drifts away forever. You came to say everything you needed to say—all the forgiveness, all the love—but as you start speaking, what comes out instead is a question you've held for thirty years: 'Why didn't you protect me?' Your voice is soft, almost apologetic for asking. She tries to answer, and you hear the truth you always suspected, and suddenly you're comforting her, stroking her hand, saying 'It's okay, Mom, I understand' even as your heart splinters. The anger you carried dissolves into this profound, aching tenderness. End with you telling her you love her, and meaning it completely, while tears stream silently down your face—grief and release and love all tangled together.

title: The Gilded Poison
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy, standing in your family's garden at a party no one wanted to host. Your father's business partner — a man who ruined your family with a smile — is drinking the spiked lemonade you just served him. The sourness of your betrayal is on your tongue, bitter and real. You feel a dizzying pride, a slow intoxication from the power of watching him sip his ruin. Start with a sweet, polite question about the drink, letting your voice waver with a child's forced calm. End with a cold, deliberate whisper, the satisfaction of your revenge spreading like ice through your veins.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed, holding an old photograph of her as a young woman—vibrant, laughing, full of dreams. Begin filled with desperate denial, trying to keep the conversation light and normal, chattering about mundane things to avoid the truth. As you look between the photograph and her frail face, let the reality crash through your defenses. Your voice should journey from artificial brightness through cracking composure to raw, whispered acceptance. End by finally saying what you've been avoiding: that you understand she's leaving, and you're grateful for who she made you. Let your body mirror this shift—from tense, performative energy to a collapsing into genuine presence and tender, broken openness.
inspired_by: Actor wants to understand a character's physical mannerisms and actions beyond surface choices

title: The Sour Last Word
instruction: You are a ten-year-old boy, stuck at a family dinner after a nasty cold turned into asthma. Your dad, who’s been mocking your 'weak lungs' all night, just announced you have to finish your brussels sprouts before you can use your inhaler. You hate those sprouts—they taste like bitterness and defeat. Start with contempt for your dad’s smug face, and sourness as you force down a bite, barely able to breathe through the wheeze. Midway, your chest tightens so you can’t finish a sentence, and you say a quiet, raspy complaint. But then he relents, sliding the inhaler across the table. End with a tiny, shocked exhale of relief—almost a whisper—as you grab it, not meeting his eyes. Let the wheeze and short breaths interrupt your words naturally, and let one or two clicks of the inhaler be heard near the end. Begin with an annoyed, 'You think this is funny...'
emotions_sampled: Contempt (slightly present), Sourness (clearly present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Dean Tragic News
instruction: You're the university dean calling the parents to tell them their son is dead—suicide, jumped from the dorm. You've made this call before. You have a script. You open with the worst part first: 'I'm calling with devastating news.' Your voice is rehearsed sympathy. But then the mother makes a sound—an animal sound of primal denial—and you freeze. Your professional composure shatters. You're not a dean anymore; you're a human being telling another human being that her child is gone. Your voice becomes shaky, informal, almost childlike as you try to offer comfort that no words can provide. Show the exact moment where role breaks down.

title: The Scalded Tea of Gratitude
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a pleasantly high, almost girlish voice, carefully pouring boiling water into a teapot for a dear friend who just gave you a beautiful, unexpected gift. Suddenly, a splash of water scalds the back of your hand. You hiss sharply through clenched teeth ('sssss'), clutching your hand with your other arm, your voice instantly tight and panicked. As you apologize and awkwardly try to wave off your friend's concern, your doubt about whether you can still host company properly fades into a genuine, giddy amusement at the absurdity of the moment, finally rising into a full-bodied, joyful elation that this friendship still surprises you.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (extremely present), Amusement (clearly present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake but fading, and you both know these are your final hours together. Start by trying to be strong and cheerful, telling her about mundane things—what you had for breakfast, the weather outside. But as you speak, let yourself get distracted by memories, lose your train of thought, find yourself saying things you didn't plan to say. Allow silences to happen. Maybe you forget what you were talking about mid-sentence. Let your voice crack unexpectedly, or find yourself laughing at a sudden memory before the grief rushes back. By the end, you're no longer trying to be strong—you're simply present with her, speaking from a place of raw, unguarded love and unbearable loss. Let yourself be messy, derailed, surprised by your own emotions.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're at your best friend's wake, standing at the microphone to give a eulogy. But instead of reading what you prepared, you start to laugh—not from joy, but from the absurdity, the unfairness. Your voice shakes with laughter that's dangerously close to sobbing: 'She would hate this. All of us in black, being so serious.' Tell a story about her—something ridiculous, inappropriate, perfect. Let yourself laugh genuinely, even as tears stream down your face. Your voice oscillates between warm nostalgia and devastating loss: 'She taught me that life is too short for fake anything. For pretending you're fine when you're not. For saying goodbye when you mean I love you.' The laughter fades and suddenly you're just broken, voice raw: 'I'm not ready for a world without her in it.' But then you catch yourself, remembering her. Your voice strengthens with bittersweet gratitude: 'But God, I'm grateful. I'm so grateful I got to love her. I'm so grateful she let me.' End with your voice full of contradictions—grief and joy, ending and gratitude, all at once: 'Thank you for being my person. I'll carry you with me. Always.'

title: Translating My Mother's Silence
instruction: You are confronting your aging mother about a recurring dream she's had for thirty years - one she described to you only literally, never emotionally. Begin by reciting her literal dream back to her with barely contained anger: the empty house, the locked doors, the child calling from somewhere she can't reach. Then demand she tell you what it really means. As she remains silent, your voice should shift from accusatory to pleading to finally understanding - she was the child in the dream, and you were the one who couldn't reach her. End with a whispered apology for not understanding sooner, your anger transforming into grief for all the years of misconnection between you.

title: Dancing Alone in the Mist After the Funeral
instruction: You've just buried someone you loved, and instead of joining the mourners, you've escaped to the misty garden where you used to walk together. Begin describing the cool mist with a laugh—not because anything is funny, but because the absurdity of loss has hit you sideways. Your beloved always said you should dance in the rain. So here you are, spinning slowly in the fog, crying and laughing in the same breath. Describe the sensations—mist on your face mixing with tears, the gentle earth under your feet, the strange peace of honoring them this way—while your voice breaks between joy at the memory and devastation at the absence. This is gratitude and grief as one emotion. Your heart is simultaneously full and shattered. End with tender acceptance that contains both unbearable sadness and profound love.
inspired_by: Walking Slowly Through a Misty Morning

title: The Fourth Watch
instruction: You are an elderly woman who hasn't slept in more than two days. You're sitting in a dim kitchen, trying to convince your granddaughter on the phone that you're fine, even though you keep seeing shadows move in the corner of your eye. Begin with a forced, cheerful optimism — your voice bright but frayed. As you continue, your sentences start to derail: you lose your train of thought, argue with a creaking floorboard, then laugh abruptly at nothing. End with a sudden, quiet clarity — a fragile hope that morning will come, spoken as if you're almost believing it. Let your voice crack, trail off, and shift between detached calm and raw exhaustion.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Mile
instruction: You are in the final stretch of a charity run in record-breaking heat. You’ve collapsed twice, your body is shutting down, and you’re ashamed that you’re not stronger. You doubt you can even finish. But as you stumble across the finish line, you see the crowd cheering—not for speed, but for sheer grit. Describe this moment in a few sentences, your voice dry and broken at first, then swelling with exhausted pride. Let the shame and doubt color your first words, then let the triumph rise as you realize what you’ve actually done. You’re panting, slurring, maybe dripping sweat—don’t fight it.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Doubt (slightly present), Triumph (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Fear Paralyzing
instruction: Something terrible is happening or about to. Your voice comes out small, high, thread-thin. Breathing is shallow, tight. Each word emerges hesitantly: 'There's something outside.' You can hear your own terror in the vocal quality—it's not performed, it's genuine fight-or-flight activation. Your throat tightens. Speech comes in fragments. Toward the end, you might whimper, the voice becoming even smaller. There's no courage here; there's just the raw vocal sound of someone whose nervous system is screaming. Physical: you're holding your breath, then gasping.

title: The Afterparty
instruction: You're a teenager, still buzzed from a house party where you just witnessed your first love kissing someone else. You wandered into a quiet bedroom to call them, but they didn't answer. Now you're sitting on the floor, head spinning, the muffled bass from the party downstairs a dull roar in your ears. Start by speaking in a detached, almost curious murmur about how dizzy you feel, tracing patterns on the carpet. Let the intoxication and the devastation blur together — your voice floats, then suddenly cracks as the reality hits mid-sentence. End with a raw, tear-choked whisper, the words catching on a sob, the high of the night completely shattered.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Sunrise
instruction: You're watching your final sunrise - whether from illness, departure to space, or something else doesn't matter. You start in reverent silence, overwhelmed by beauty you've seen hundreds of times but never truly saw. Your voice is barely audible: 'I never... god, I never stopped to really look.' The wonder builds, becomes desperate, tinged with regret. 'All those mornings I rushed past this.' Your breathing becomes uneven as gratitude crashes into grief. By the end, you're whispering through tears: 'Thank you. I'm sorry. Thank you.' The awe remains, but it's now inseparable from the ache of goodbye. Let your voice crack naturally - don't perform sadness, just let the beauty break your heart.

title: Dancing in the Rubble
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—a relationship ended, a dream died, a life you built is gone—and you're finding strange, broken joy in the ruins. Begin with a laugh that sounds almost like crying: 'This is so ridiculous...' looking at the absurdity of your situation. Your voice should carry both amusement and devastation. Let genuine gratitude surface through the pain: 'But you know what? I'm so glad I...' recounting something beautiful that came from what you lost. Your breath should catch between laughing and weeping, the two indistinguishable. Midway, let wonder creep in despite everything: 'I never thought I'd feel this free...' The freedom should sound both terrifying and exhilarating. End with peace that coexists with heartbreak: 'I wouldn't undo any of it.' This is about finding light not after the darkness, but inside it—laughing and crying in the same breath, grateful and destroyed simultaneously.

title: The Last Push
instruction: You are an older man, wiry and stubborn, out in your backyard under the blazing afternoon sun. You've been hauling pavers for hours, ignoring the heat. Your younger neighbor calls out, asking if you need to come inside. You start by teasing them—'Soft, just like your dad'—but the words come out dry and slow. As you keep talking, the heat crushes you: your voice wilts, you lose your train of thought, your knees wobble. By the end, you admit, 'Maybe... maybe I do need a hand,' and your tone drops from teasing to quiet, shaken humility. Let the dizziness and dehydration affect your speech—let it be weak, slurred, and confused, with pauses where you forget what you were saying.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Sleeping Lover for the Last Time
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You know that in the morning, you have to end this relationship—they're sick, deteriorating, and they've begged you to leave so you don't have to watch them die. This is your last night before you honor their wish. Your voice is barely a whisper, so you don't wake them. 'I'm memorizing the way you breathe.' Your hand traces their face in the darkness. 'I keep thinking if I stay awake, morning won't come.' There's a tremor in your whisper—you're crying silently. 'You asked me to be strong enough to leave. But how do I walk away from the only person I've ever loved like this?' Your voice catches, throat tight with unshed sobs. 'I know why you're doing this. I know it's love.' A pause, just breathing together in the dark. 'I'll carry you with me every day. Every sunrise, every song, every moment—you'll be there.' Your whisper becomes even softer, reverent. 'I love you. I love you. I'll love you until the day I die.' Finally: 'Goodbye, my heart. Sleep well.' The voice of someone breaking in silence.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Addiction Over You
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who disappeared from your childhood, now trying to reconnect. Begin with controlled anger, listing facts like evidence—birthdays missed, promises broken, lies told. Your voice is sharp, protective of the child you once were. But as you speak, something shifts. The rage begins to crack, revealing the desperate child underneath who just wanted to be chosen. Your accusations become questions: "Why wasn't I enough?" Let anger dissolve into raw vulnerability, then rebuild into something harder—not forgiveness, but a fierce decision to stop waiting for them to become who you needed. End with a goodbye that's both liberation and heartbreak. Your voice must travel from fury through fragility to a kind of painful strength.
inspired_by: Professional: Journalist Kills a Story About Someone They Love

title: The Fierce Mercy: Protecting Someone from Themselves
instruction: You're physically restraining your adult sibling from destroying their life—they're about to relapse, make a fatal choice, or harm themselves. Begin with explosive urgency, voice raw and commanding: 'STOP! Look at me RIGHT NOW!' Let fierce love make your voice shake with intensity: 'I will NOT let you do this to yourself!' Feel your certainty fracture as they fight you, your voice cracking: 'Please... please don't make me watch you die.' Let rage dissolve into sobbing desperation: 'I can't lose you—I WON'T lose you!' By the end, collapse into broken tenderness, voice hoarse and spent: 'I'm here. I'm not leaving. We'll get through this.' Move from fierce power to complete helplessness to quiet, unshakeable devotion.

title: The Last Drag
instruction: You're 19, chain-smoking on a fire escape after a party you didn't want to leave. Your voice is permanently roughened from years of smoking, and tonight, with stress and other substances, it's gravelly and low. Start by staring blankly at the glowing tip, feeling nothing. Then, a specific memory drifts in—a locket left behind in your childhood bedroom. Your voice, briefly, lifts into a softer, younger, hyper-feminized tone as you mutter about it, before snapping back to the flat, numb, gravel of now. The scene ends with a long, quiet exhale, the smoke curling up into the dark.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Concentration (clearly present), Longing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Screaming Into the Silence After They've Already Left
instruction: They walked out ten minutes ago. The door is closed. Now everything you couldn't say explodes out of you. Start with their name, called out like you're trying to pull them back through sheer force of will. Then unleash everything—the rage, the betrayal, the years of swallowing your needs. Let your voice climb from shouting to screaming, then break completely as you realize you're yelling at an empty room. Collapse mid-sentence from fury into sobbing, from powerful to completely powerless. End on your knees, voice raw and small, repeating 'please come back' or 'I'm sorry' or 'I hate you'—you're not even sure which. Let the fierce protectiveness of your love collide with the devastating helplessness of abandonment.
inspired_by: Dental Extraction: Hiding Disgrace While the Dentist Works

title: The Last Morning Coffee
instruction: You are sitting with your grandmother in her hospice room at dawn, knowing she has only hours left. Begin by making small talk about the sunrise, the taste of coffee, avoiding what you really need to say. Your voice is light, almost cheerful, protecting both of you from the truth. Then, mid-sentence, something breaks inside you and you can no longer pretend. Let yourself confess the things you've never told her: how afraid you've been your whole life, how you've felt like a fraud in your own skin, how her love was the only thing that ever felt real. End in a place of raw, undefended gratitude—not pretty or composed, but absolutely true. Let your voice crack, let pauses breathe, let the transformation from protective cheerfulness to naked honesty unfold naturally.

title: The Taste of Goodbye
instruction: You're making love to someone for the last time, and you both know it. Focus intensely on physical sensations and taste: salt on skin, the taste of their mouth, the warmth of breath, the texture of sheets against your back, the weight of their body, the coolness of tears on your face. Begin in desperate passion—trying to consume every sensation, to make the physical experience so overwhelming it erases the knowledge of ending. Let your voice move between gasps, whispers, and cries that blend pleasure with grief. As physical intensity peaks, let it shatter into something else: the sensations become almost painful in their beauty, each touch a goodbye, each taste a memory being formed. End in the aftermath—pressed together, tasting salt (sweat? tears?), your body heavy and spent, whispering final words against their skin. The journey moves from fierce, consuming desire (trying to fight loss with sensation) to unbearable tenderness as every physical sensation transforms into farewell.
inspired_by: Actor is visually dominant and neglects other senses in imaging

title: The Barstool Revelation
instruction: You're at a bar, two drinks in, telling a buddy about your coworker. Start off laughing, almost spilling your beer, amazed at the absurd thing they did—your voice is loose, a little loud, with a slight slur on words like 'actually.' As you describe the situation, your smile fades. You realize their behavior wasn't just stupid—it was smug, hypocritical. Let the astonishment curdle into contempt. Your voice tightens, your hand pauses mid-gesture, and you stare into your glass. The last words should feel cold and clear, cutting through the buzz.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your estranged father from the airport gate. Your flight boards in eight minutes, and you're moving to another country indefinitely. Begin the call trying to keep it light and casual—just a quick courtesy call to say you're leaving. But as he responds to you (whether with indifference, unexpected emotion, criticism, or love), allow his actual words and tone to unlock something in you. Let the conversation take you somewhere unplanned. What starts as protective distance must crack open into raw honesty by the time boarding is announced. The truth you've been avoiding for years needs to surface before you hang up. Your voice should transform from guarded and almost chipper to stripped bare, whether that's anger finally released, grief finally acknowledged, or love finally spoken.

title: The Fire and the Breaking
instruction: You are in the grip of passionate rage after a betrayal—your body is hot, your voice sharp and explosive. Begin by letting fury pour out physically: your breathing ragged, your words cutting and cruel, your entire being ablaze with righteous anger. But as you unleash this storm, force yourself to actually look at the person you're raging at: notice specific things about them—how they're standing, what's in their eyes, whether they're fighting back or crumbling, the particular vulnerability or defiance in their expression. Let what you see puncture your rage. Your voice should shift from volcanic to something that cracks and bleeds. End with your anger collapsing into the devastating pain underneath—let your body show the shift from burning to breaking, from attacking to aching.

title: Breaking Point of the Protector
instruction: You're a parent whose child has just been hurt by someone you trusted. Start speaking to that person with barely controlled fury—your voice is low, dangerous, shaking with the effort of not screaming. 'You touched my child.' Each word is precise, venomous. Your rage builds, voice rising, becoming almost feral. You want to destroy them. But mid-torrent, something shifts—you realize your child is watching, or you see their pathetic face, or you recognize your own helplessness. Your voice cracks completely. The fury dissolves into anguished sobbing. You collapse from ferocious protector into broken parent who couldn't prevent this. By the end, you're barely speaking through tears: 'I can't fix this. I can't take it back.' Let the transformation from lethal rage to devastating powerlessness shatter you.

title: Midnight Confession to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep, and you're sitting beside their bed in the dark, whispering truths you can never say when they're awake. Start with tenderness—your voice is so quiet it's almost breathless, telling them how beautiful they are, how their laugh sounds like joy itself. But then admit the harder things: how terrified you are that you're failing them, how some days you don't recognize yourself in the mirror, how you're repeating patterns from your own childhood you swore you'd never recreate. Your voice catches, trembles. Let silence hang between phrases. Touch on a specific moment you lost your temper, your voice breaking with shame. Then find your way back to love—deeper now, earned through honesty. End with a whispered promise, your voice thick with unshed tears but somehow stronger: you'll keep trying, keep choosing them, even when you're afraid. Let the last words dissolve into quiet breathing.

title: Leaving a Voicemail You Know They'll Never Hear
instruction: Call someone who has passed away. Their voicemail still works. Hear their greeting (perform it — they sound happy, alive, normal). After the beep, try to speak. The first attempt is just breathing. Second attempt: 'Hey, it's me.' Then talk to them as if they'll check their messages. Tell them mundane things — what you had for lunch, that their plant is still alive. Let the mundanity become unbearable. End with what you really called to say. Hang up.

title: Historical: Executioner Performs His Final Execution Before Retirement
instruction: Dawn execution ground. Your executioner voice has performed this ritual hundreds of times. But this is the last one. Your voice carries the weight of all the deaths you've administered with professional precision. You're ending a career made of endings. Your breathing is slower—someone reflective at the close of a life defined by death. You perform the final execution with the same ceremony as always, but now there's nothing after this moment. Your voice becomes someone looking backward at a life spent in this singular function.

title: The Celebration in Ruins
instruction: You're at what should be a moment of triumph or joy—a graduation, a wedding, a long-awaited achievement—but someone who should be there is gone forever, and their absence is crushing. Begin by trying to celebrate authentically, finding real joy and pride in the moment, even laughing. But let the awareness of the absence creep in—you start talking to them as if they're there, your voice mixing celebration with grief. You're genuinely happy and utterly heartbroken simultaneously. Find gratitude for what they gave you even as you ache that they're not here to see this. Your voice should do impossible things—laugh through tears, express pride while your heart shatters, find peace in the pain. End with a contradiction that feels entirely true: thanking them for making this moment possible while your voice breaks with the loss. This should feel like watching someone hold joy and devastation in the same hands.
inspired_by: An Ode to a Lost Childhood

title: The Intervention: When Your Brilliance Became My Prison
instruction: You're confronting someone you love—a manic parent, a partner in a hypomanic spiral, a sibling who's been 'on fire' for weeks—and you're exhausted. Begin with controlled concern, trying to be gentle, but your pain keeps breaking through. Your voice cracks with the weight of sleepless nights watching over them, cleaning up financial disasters, fielding calls from their latest 'project collaborators.' Escalate into raw anger and grief as you list specific moments: the times they promised to stop, the humiliations, the brilliance you once admired now weaponized against your boundaries. Break down mid-confrontation, voice dropping to a wounded whisper: you miss who they are when they're stable. End with fierce, protective love mixed with devastating ultimatum—you can't keep doing this.

title: The Last Dictation
instruction: You are an older woman using a voice assistant to dictate a final letter to your estranged daughter after a decade of silence. You begin with the flat, hyper-correct 'robot talk' of giving commands—enunciating each word with unnatural pauses, trying to stay detached and precise. But as you realize this may be your last chance to speak to her, your voice cracks—words blur together, you swallow hard, you lose the thread mid-sentence and have to start again. Let a deep, quiet sadness creep in as you recall a moment of shared laughter, then let a flicker of bittersweet pleasure color your voice as you almost smile at the memory—before the concentration returns, and you force yourself back into the staccato rhythm to finish the message. Speak for 50–60 seconds.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Concentration (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Smoke and Shadow
instruction: You are alone in a room filling with thick smoke from a fire downstairs. Your eyes burn, your throat scratches with every cough, and the carbon monoxide makes your thoughts fuzzy. You're trying to remember where the window is, but keep losing your train of thought. Start by muttering to yourself in confusion and frustration, faint and raspy, as you stumble around. As you finally spot the faint light of the window through the haze, a slow clarity cuts through the fog—speak with growing focus and quiet determination, even as your voice cracks.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Scrapbook Page
instruction: You're an older woman in the passenger seat of a bumpy old van, clutching a half-finished scrapbook on your lap. Your daughter is driving you both to the airport after a visit, and you're trying to describe a faded photo from your youth — but the road keeps rattling your voice, making it tremble unevenly. Start with a shaky, curious excitement as you point at the picture and piece together a memory, but as you realize this might be the last time you'll show her this, a quiet helplessness creeps in. Let your words flutter with the vehicle's vibration, losing thought for a second when the van jolts, then softening into a warm, fragile affection as you simply smile and hand her the page.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Affection (slightly present), Helplessness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Shattered Glass and Breaking Voice: Confronting the Parent Who Failed You in Their Dementia
instruction: Your parent with dementia just looked at you with brief clarity and asked, 'Did I do right by you?' After a lifetime of waiting for this moment, you explode. Start with a burst of raw anger: 'No! You didn't!' Your voice is fierce, years of pain erupting. List the wounds rapid-fire, voice shaking with fury. Then crack—the rage collapses into sobbing realization: 'But you're already gone, aren't you? I can't even have this conversation.' Your voice becomes desperate, helpless, as you realize this moment of clarity is slipping away. End with fierce, broken protectiveness, almost maternal toward them: 'Forget I said that. You were fine. You were... it's fine.' Move from explosive rage through helpless grief into a devastating tenderness born of knowing you've already lost them.
inspired_by: Sitting in Silence After Miscarriage: The Weight of Emptiness

title: Gratitude at the Edge
instruction: You're encouraging someone who's about to do something that will change everything - leave you, take an opportunity far away, choose a path that means losing you from their life. You genuinely want them to succeed, and your heart is genuinely breaking. Begin by celebrating their courage and talent with real joy in your voice - laugh a little, reminisce about how far they've come. But let the grief bleed through the edges. Your voice should shimmer between genuine happiness for them and the awareness of your own impending loss. As you build their confidence, let yourself become more vulnerable - the laughter becomes tighter, catches on tears you're trying to hide. End in a place of profound contradiction: you're smiling while crying, telling them how proud you are while your voice splinters with loss. This is love and grief occupying the same breath, gratitude and heartbreak inseparable.
inspired_by: Acting Encouraging Despite Believing in Imminent Failure

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a chronic stutter, sitting at a cluttered kitchen table, holding a worn photograph of your late husband. You are trying to tell your granddaughter about the day it was taken, but each word feels like pushing through mud. Start with a heavy, sad stillness, your voice soft and hesitant, as you stare at the image.
