As you speak, the stutter deepens — you repeat syllables, your breath catches in silent blocks, and your pitch jumps slightly when a word finally breaks free. Midway, your focus shifts to the memory, and a flicker of fragile joy softens your tone, but concentration pulls you back, making you pause and blink. By the end, the sadness returns, heavier and quieter, as you finish the story with a sigh, your voice trailing off.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Ripping Out Your Hair in Grief-Fueled Rage
instruction: You've just received news that shatters everything—a sudden death, a betrayal, a diagnosis, something that makes the world go white with fury and pain. Begin with explosive anger, describing the act of grabbing fistfuls of your own hair, pulling hard, the physical pain a relief from the emotional agony. Your voice should be raw, loud, guttural—spitting words between sobs or screams. But as you continue, let the rage crack open into something else: vulnerability, terror, desperate pleading with whoever or whatever caused this. Feel your voice break from shouting into sobbing, from fury into helplessness. End in exhausted collapse, your hands still tangled in your hair but now gentle, your voice small and broken, admitting the fear underneath the rage: that you can't protect the people you love, that you're powerless, that you're so terribly, devastatingly alone.
inspired_by: Running Fingers Through Freshly Washed Hair

title: I Won't Let Them Take This From Me
instruction: You're preparing for something terrible—a trial, a confrontation, a moment where you'll have to face people who hurt you—and you're applying lotion as an act of fierce self-care, reclaiming your body as your own. Start with hands that might be shaking, voice unsteady, as you force yourself through the motions. Describe the lotion with growing intensity: this is YOURS, your skin is YOURS, your body is YOURS. Let rage build as you work the lotion in—fury at what was done to you, at having to fight for your own sense of safety. Your voice should surge with protective ferocity, claiming each inch of skin. But then let it crack: beneath the armor is fear, is the scared part of you that wonders if you're strong enough. End with a transformation—raw determination mixed with trembling vulnerability, your voice both battle-cry and prayer: 'I am still here. I am still whole. They don't get to take this from me.' Let strength and fragility coexist completely.
inspired_by: Putting on a Favorite Scented Lotion

title: The One We Pulled Out
instruction: You're a firefighter sitting on the curb after a two-alarm house fire. Your hands are trembling as you try to unscrew your canteen — you keep fumbling and drop the lid. Your voice is hoarse, breathy, almost laughing in disbelief as you replay the moment you carried a little girl out. At first you're replaying the chaos, stuttering over details, then you stop and realize a small thing: her tiny fingers gripping your turnout coat. Let that memory slow you down, soften you. End with a shaky but certain smile in your voice as you say, 'She's okay. She's really gonna be okay.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Scrambled Signal
instruction: You're a teenage girl using a walkie-talkie to coordinate with a friend during a scavenger hunt. Press the PTT button and start with bright, eager interest—your voice compressed and tinny through the narrow radio bandwidth. Mid-sentence, you twist your ankle badly on a hidden root. The pain slams through you: your words falter, your pitch wavers, you gasp and clench your teeth as you fight to stay on air. Let the initial excitement dissolve into raw, intense pain that cracks your hyper-feminine tone, and end holding the button with a shaking breath before the final 'over.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What You Never Told Me
instruction: You're confronting your father about something he did years ago that shaped your entire life. Begin angry, ready for battle—you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, start noticing details about him you've forced yourself not to see: how he's aged, the way his hands shake slightly, something in his eyes. Describe to yourself what you observe in his face, his posture, the specific quality of his breathing. Ask yourself sensory questions: What does his fear smell like? What does his silence feel like in the room? Let these details complicate your rage. Your anger doesn't disappear, but by the end, it's tangled with unexpected grief, maybe even unwanted understanding. Transform from righteous fury to something far more complicated and painful—the realization that he's human and breakable too.

title: Pink Pigtails and a Pothole
instruction: You are a 7-year-old girl in the backseat of your mom’s minivan on a bumpy country road. Your pink glittery boots kick the seat in front of you. You are recounting something utterly hilarious to your mom: the substitute teacher accidentally wore two different shoes today. But you keep getting distracted—by the cow outside, the crackle of a snack wrapper, the sudden jolt of a pothole that makes you giggle mid-sentence. Start with pure, bubbly amusement (you can barely get the story out you’re laughing so hard). By the end, your voice softens, fading into a dreamy, contented sigh as you stare out the window at the clouds, the laughter dissolving into a quiet, peaceful wonder. Let the engine’s hum and the bumps jostle your rhythm; your voice might crack with laughter, then trail off into a whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Crunch
instruction: You're a tough, middle-aged guy sitting alone in a diner, eating a crisp apple. You've just been fired—your boss said you're 'too old to be dangerous'—and you're trying to hold it together. The crunch of the apple feels loud in the quiet. Start with a forced bravado, a gruff denial in your voice as you mutter to yourself, then slowly let the crack in your confidence show. Let the apple's crunch become a punctuation for every swallowed fear. By the end, your voice should soften, revealing a tremor of real vulnerability beneath the macho shell.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Twisted Affection
instruction: You are a middle-aged man in a yoga class, twisting your torso to the right while reaching back for a strap. Your body feels tight and awkward, and you're disgusted by the sight of yourself in the mirror — the soft belly, the graying hair, the struggle. But as you stretch deeper, you catch a glimpse of a photo on the mat next to you: your young daughter's drawing. A wave of reluctant affection cuts through your self-loathing. Speak aloud to yourself, first grunting with effort and disgust, then softening as you remember her. Let the twist affect your breath — uneven, strained — and let your voice wobble between bitter self-criticism and a quiet, genuine fondness by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What You Never Knew I Carried
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or grown child) about something they did years ago that shattered you—maybe an abandonment, a betrayal, a moment when they chose something else over you. Start from a place of carefully controlled anger, your words clipped and precise, almost cold. You've rehearsed this confrontation in your mind a thousand times. But as you speak, the anger cracks open to reveal what's underneath: a terrifying vulnerability, a desperate need to be seen and understood, perhaps even a fear that you're unlovable. Let your voice shift from accusatory sharpness to something trembling and exposed. By the end, you're no longer attacking—you're begging them to finally see the wound they left.
inspired_by: When you are building a character who must be genuinely terrified or in extreme fear

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're recording a video message to be played at your funeral (you have a terminal diagnosis). You're determined to make it funny, to give them something that isn't sad. Start with forced lightness, making jokes about your life, laughing at your own quirks and failures. 'So this is awkward, right? Me talking to you while you're all dressed in black...' But the laughter keeps catching. Your voice wavers between humor and heartbreak. You keep trying to be funny but grief leaks through—you're laughing and crying at once. 'I'm so grateful I got to love you all... God, I'm making this weird.' End with the beautiful contradiction of joy and devastation intertwined, finding genuine peace and humor while your heart is shattering, your laughter real but threaded through with tears.
inspired_by: Talking to Someone While Severely Depressed

title: Whispered Hungers
instruction: Late at night, you're lying next to your partner of many years, whispering in the darkness. You begin speaking about mundane intimacies—how their breathing sounds, the warmth of their skin. But there's a part of your sexuality and desire that you've always kept hidden, even from them—perhaps it's too raw, too aggressive, too needy, or too unconventional. As you whisper, invite this disowned sensual self to slowly emerge. Let your voice change as this hidden aspect of your erotic nature finds words for the first time. You might shift your body closer or pull slightly away as this buried desire speaks. By the end, you're confessing hungers you've never named aloud, desires that both frighten and liberate you. The emotional journey moves from safe, familiar tenderness to breathless, risky revelation of your truest erotic self.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access a personality facet (aggression, sexuality, fear, moralism, free spirit, victimhood) that is suppressed or disowned

title: The Breaking Story
instruction: You are a seasoned news anchor, a middle-aged woman known for your polished, hyper-feminine delivery. You're on live television, reporting on a story you've been following for weeks — a local whistleblower winning a major settlement against a corrupt developer. At the start, your voice is crisp, practiced, with that warm, commanding news prosody, and you feel a swelling sense of triumph as you read the lead. But as you glance down at your monitor, you see a live feed from the courthouse showing the whistleblower being arrested — for something unrelated, new, and confusing. Your voice must begin with that slow, deliberate, triumphant tone, then subtly fracture: a sharp intake of breath, a pause, a slight crack in your control as you try to maintain composure while processing the confusion. You finish the sentence, but your voice betrays a hint of bewilderment, a slip of the mask. Let the air catch in your throat, let one word rise in pitch with a question mark, then recover to a tight, forced calm.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Asking Your Parent for Money While Ashamed
instruction: Your voice is small, rehearsed: 'I need to ask you for something.' You're an adult asking for help and it feels like failure. 'I need to borrow money.' Your voice carries shame and dependence. Include explaining why, delivered vulnerable and humiliated. Your voice ends accepting their help while dying inside.

title: Hiding in the Closet While Your Child Searches for You
instruction: You're playing hide-and-seek with your four-year-old daughter on what you know is your last day before entering hospice. You're hidden in the bedroom closet, listening to her little footsteps and delighted giggles as she searches. Your breathing is deliberately quiet, controlled, but your chest is tight with the weight of everything you won't see—her first day of school, her graduation, her wedding. She's so close now, calling 'Mommy? Daddy?' in that sweet, singsong voice. You want this moment to last forever. Your breath catches, threatens to become a sob, but you hold it in because she can't know, not yet. She finds you. You burst out with exaggerated joy, scooping her up, your laughter genuine but threaded with hairline cracks. As she squeals and hugs you, you hold her tighter than the game requires, your voice breaking as you whisper into her hair, 'I found you. I'll always find you.' Knowing it's a lie. Knowing it's the most important truth.
inspired_by: Reporting While Sprinting for Your Life

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night. You're lying next to someone you love, and you need to tell them something you've kept hidden—something that might end everything between you. Begin in almost a whisper, barely audible, as if speaking might make it too real: 'Are you awake? I need to... I need to tell you something.' Your breathing is unsteady. 'I've been carrying this and it's—it's been eating me alive.' As you confess (you choose what it is), your voice remains quiet but grows more raw, more exposed. 'I'm so scared right now. I'm terrified you're going to leave.' Let silence fill the space. Then, even softer, with your heart completely unguarded: 'But I can't keep pretending anymore. I love you too much to keep lying.' Your voice catches: 'Even if this is the last time you let me say it... I love you.' End with quiet devastation, waiting for their response, every second an eternity.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut recording a final message to your child before a one-way mission to deep space. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to make this adventure sound exciting, pointing out constellations they'll be able to see you traveling through. But as you speak, the weight of永久 separation crushes that brightness. Your voice should crack on their name. Let pauses grow longer as you try to memorize their face from a photograph. End whispering the things you'll miss—their laugh, bedtime stories, watching them grow up—until you can barely speak at all. The journey is from artificial brightness to devastating, whispered goodbye.

title: The Ghost in the Mirror
instruction: You're an older man in a dimly lit bathroom, alone, after a long night. You've just taken a strong hit of cocaine to push away the grief of losing your wife six months ago. The rush hits — you feel a surge of relief, a grandiose belief that you're finally okay. You look at yourself in the mirror and start talking to her reflection, trying to convince her (and yourself) that you've moved on. But as you speak, the sadness breaks through — your voice cracks, you sniffle hard, you lose your train of thought, then force a loud, too-bright laugh to cover it. Your words start fast and loud, then slow, then stumble. End with a quiet, honest admission of how much you miss her.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Relief (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Touching Through Glass
instruction: You're visiting someone you love in a place where you can't physically touch them—a hospital isolation room, a prison, a quarantine. Press your hand against the glass barrier and describe what you feel: the coolness, the hardness, how your palm warms it slightly, the way your fingertips leave prints. Speak in an intimate whisper, describing what you wish you could feel instead: their skin, their warmth, their breath. Start with a gentle, almost clinical focus on the physical sensations of the glass itself. Gradually let your voice become more desperate as you describe textures you're missing—the softness of their hair, the roughness of their hand, the warmth of their neck. Let the contrast between the cold, smooth glass and the living warmth you're denied break something in you. End barely audible, your forehead against the barrier, whispering tactile memories like prayers.

title: The Slurred Syllables of a Blurred Goodbye
instruction: You are at a loud, crowded party, and you are both very drunk and partially deaf. You are trying to say goodbye to a close friend across the room, but the music is pounding, your head is spinning, and you know they can't hear you properly. You start with a clumsy, overly loud and slow attempt to be understood, but in the middle of your sentence, you get distracted by a waiter bumping into you. By the end, the emotions spill out—a sudden, raw confession about how much this friendship means to you, your voice cracking with drunken sentiment, but still locked in that painfully slow, over-enunciated cadence. You end almost whispering, but still too loud, as you trail off.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Mirror's Echo
instruction: You're alone in your bathroom after an awkward work party, still in your dress with lipstick smudged. You catch your reflection and start whispering to yourself, replaying how you laughed too loud at a joke you didn't get. Your voice is thin, nasal, barely above a breath — you don't want anyone to hear you. Begin with tight, self-conscious murmurs as you pick at a stray thread on your sleeve. Midway, you trail off staring at the faucet drip, then sigh and speak more openly, almost amused. End with a softer, tired acceptance as you turn off the light. Your words should feel lived, with pauses where you lose your train of thought and find it again. Spoken content: "...and I just kept laughing. Like, why? Why do I do that? Every time. Every single time. I’m forty-two years old. (long pause, watches drip) Water doesn’t care. Doesn’t replay things. Just... drips. Maybe I should be water. (soft laugh, then quiet) Good night, mirror."
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reading Their Obituary Out Loud
instruction: You're alone in your kitchen, reading aloud the obituary you wrote for your closest friend—who's still alive, but dying, and asked you to write it and read it to yourself first, to 'get the crying out.' Start with false composure, almost editorial distance: 'Sarah Chen, beloved actor and teacher...' But certain phrases ambush you—'her laugh could fill a theater' makes you actually laugh, wet and broken. You cycle through tones: proud ('she originated three roles off-Broadway'), angry ('she deserved so much more time'), tender ('she made everyone feel seen'). Reading their survivors list, you reach your own name and have to stop completely. When you resume, your voice is transformed—intimate, direct, as if talking to them: 'You made me brave.' End with reading the final line—'she lived fully'—and the smallest, most genuine smile breaking through tears, because it's absolutely true and absolutely unbearable at once.

title: The Last Visit: Your Father's Final Hours
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed. He's slipping away. Start with stilted small talk—weather, the parking situation, anything but what matters. Your voice is careful, measured, keeping everything surface-level because going deeper terrifies you. Then he says your name the way he used to when you were small. Something breaks. Your breath catches. Now the words you've held for decades start spilling out—not angry, but raw, confused. 'Why didn't you...' 'I needed you to...' But mid-sentence, you see his hand reaching for yours, trembling. Your voice softens into something you didn't expect: forgiveness you didn't know you were ready to give. End with telling him it's okay to go, your voice thick with tears but steady with a peace that surprises you. You're releasing him. You're releasing yourself.
inspired_by: Karate Tournament Final: Facing Your Abuser

title: The Thing We've Never Said Aloud
instruction: You are confronting someone you've known for years—a parent, a former lover, a once-close friend—about a betrayal or hurt that has festered in silence between you. Start from a place of bitter, armored anger, your words sharp and accusatory, fueled by years of resentment. But as you speak the truth you've been carrying, really look at this person, notice how they receive your words, see their humanity even as you're hurting them. Let your anger crack open to reveal the vulnerable pain underneath—the grief of broken trust, the longing for what you once had, the part of you that still loves them despite everything. Transform from attacking to aching, from hardened rage to the devastated question: 'Why did you do this to us?' End in a place where anger and love exist simultaneously, raw and exposed.

title: Whispering Forgiveness to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're alone at someone's grave—someone you wronged, someone you never apologized to when they were alive. Speak so quietly it's almost breath, as if the earth itself might carry your words down. Start with halting attempts: 'I should have...' 'If I could...' Let silence hang between phrases like you're waiting for an answer that will never come. Your voice should be stripped of all performance, just naked regret and the strange, fragile hope that somehow this matters. Include a moment where you laugh softly at something you remember about them, and feel that laughter turn to silent tears. End with the simplest words, barely audible: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' The vulnerability here is in how small your voice becomes, how much you're confessing to silence.
inspired_by: Last Person to Speak a Dying Language

title: The Intervention: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're facing your parent who knew about abuse in the family and said nothing to protect the family's reputation. Begin with your voice shaking, barely able to start—you've rehearsed this a thousand times but never thought you'd actually say it. Your words come out jagged, broken by years of swallowed rage and confused loyalty. You loved them, you still love them, and that's what makes this unbearable. Your voice cracks between anger and desperate need for them to just admit it, to see you, to choose you this time. End with exhausted clarity—not forgiveness, not hatred, but the raw truth that you needed them and they weren't there, spoken with the quietness of someone finally putting down a weight they've carried too long.
inspired_by: Professional: Election Official Discovers Evidence of Election Fraud from Their Own Party

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent about emotional neglect from your childhood. Begin with measured control, almost cold: 'I need to tell you something I've kept quiet about for twenty years.' Your voice is steady, rehearsed even—you've practiced this. But as you list the moments they weren't there, your voice starts to betray you. Anger seeps in, then cracks open into something rawer. You didn't want to cry, you wanted to be strong and clear, but suddenly you're that child again, begging to be seen. Your voice shifts from controlled accusation to desperate pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why couldn't you just...?' End in a place of exhausted vulnerability, your voice small and broken, all the anger drained away into pure hurt.

title: The Unforgivable Truth
instruction: You're confronting your mother about why she stayed with your father through the violence, through the years that destroyed your childhood. Start with controlled anger, words sharp and accusatory: 'You chose him over us. Every single time.' But as she begins to explain—her own fear, her own trapped circumstances—something shifts. Your rage starts cracking, revealing the terrified child underneath who just wanted to be protected. Your voice wavers between fury and anguish. You want to stay angry—it's safer—but understanding is creeping in, and it's more painful than the rage. End torn between the need to blame her and the devastating realization that she was drowning too, your voice breaking on 'I needed you to save me.'

title: Packing Their Clothes
instruction: You're packing up the belongings of someone who brought you both immense joy and deep pain—a lover who betrayed you but whom you still love, a parent who damaged you but also gave you everything, a friend who abandoned you but changed your life. As you handle each item, speak to them (though they're not there). Start with one dominant emotion, but don't maintain it—let contradictions arise naturally. Maybe you're furious while holding something that makes you laugh. Maybe you're grateful while touching something that breaks your heart. Don't perform emotional complexity—simply let yourself be genuinely confused, torn, multiple. Let the emotions clash and coexist messily, truthfully. End in an emotional place that contains everything at once.

title: Coming Home to Ruins
instruction: You're an astronaut returning after two years to find your partner has moved on, remarried, built a life without you. Mission control is walking you through re-entry, but all you can think about is landing in a world where you no longer belong. Speak with a voice that keeps almost laughing—at the absurdity, at the cruel timing, at yourself for believing love could survive the distance. Let genuine laughter break through your words as you describe the view of Earth, how beautiful it is, how you can see the city where they live with someone else now. But underneath the laughter, let your voice tremble with grief. Find the strange peace in it—the gratitude for what you had, the bittersweet acceptance that they deserve happiness even if it's not with you. End with contradictory emotions fully present: laughing softly at a memory while your voice breaks, thanking mission control for bringing you home even though home doesn't exist anymore, finding odd comfort in the chaos of feeling everything at once.

title: The Rot Under the Roses
instruction: You are an elderly man who has just consumed psilocybin mushrooms. You sit in your garden, feeling a gentle amusement at the way the flowers seem to dance, and a deep contentment with the world. As you reach down to touch a rose, your fingers sink into something wet and slimy — a dead squirrel, half-decomposed. Your voice must start with that dreamy, philosophical wonder, then collapse into visceral disgust, with pauses and shudders. Speak naturally, as if reacting to the smell and touch, letting your tone waver and your words trail off.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (slightly present), Contentment (slightly present), Disgust (very intensely present)

title: The Last Gift in Your Hand
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed. In your closed hand, you hold the small gold locket she just pressed into your palm—the one she's worn every day of your life, containing a photo of you as a baby. Begin feeling the weight of it, the warmth from her touch still on the metal. Let yourself feel what this object means: her whole life of loving you, condensed into this tiny piece of gold. Start with quiet gratitude, tracing its chain with your fingers. As you speak to her, let the reality wash over you—this is the last gift, the last touch, the last time. Your emotion should move from tender appreciation to the crushing weight of goodbye. Let the locket become impossibly heavy and precious as you realize you're holding the physical proof that someone loved you unconditionally, and soon that person will be gone.

title: Begging God to Take You Instead
instruction: Someone you love is dying and you're bargaining with forces you don't even believe in. Start with fierce, almost violent desperation—your voice raw and demanding: 'Take me! I'm right here!' Let rage at the unfairness explode into anguished sobbing, then shift into helpless pleading, your voice breaking apart: 'Please, please, I'll do anything.' Collapse from fury into absolute powerlessness—the shift from fighting to surrendering. End in whispered devastation, your fight gone: 'Don't take them. I can't... I can't.' Move from aggressive bargaining to shattered begging to quiet acceptance of your own helplessness.
inspired_by: Forgiving Someone After They Hurt You Deeply

title: Nighttime Breathing
instruction: You are sitting on the edge of a bed, your hand resting on your partner's back as they curl into you, still trembling. You focus on matching your breath to theirs, making your voice a slow, low blanket of sound. Your first words are careful, almost mechanical, as you concentrate on the rhythm. But as you feel them relax a little, a wave of your own sadness breaks through—you realize how fragile this moment is. Let your voice shift from a measured hum into something tender, almost carrying tears, as you whisper, 'I've got you, I'm right here.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confession Acceptance
instruction: You're confessing something serious to a close friend. Your voice is shaky, vulnerable: 'I need to tell you something, and I'm scared of what you'll think.' You're taking a breath, gathering courage. 'I...' The words come out in a rush or painfully slowly. You're watching their face for their reaction. When they accept you, your voice cracks with relief: 'Thank you. You have no idea what that means to me.' By the end, you're crying from relief and gratitude.

title: The Restraining Order Against Someone You Still Love
instruction: You're recording a voice message explaining to someone why you've filed a restraining order against them, even though you still love them desperately. Begin with shaking determination, trying to sound strong and certain: 'I need you to understand why I'm doing this.' But your voice should immediately betray you—it cracks on certain words, speeds up when you're afraid of feeling too much. Explode into fierce protectiveness of yourself: 'I cannot let you destroy me!' Let rage and pain collide—screaming about the damage done, then collapsing into sobbing confession that you still miss them, still want them, still dream they'll become who you needed them to be. Feel the helplessness of loving someone who hurts you. End in exhausted, tear-soaked clarity: you love them, and that's exactly why you have to do this. Whisper the final goodbye like you're severing part of your own soul.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: It's 4 AM and you're standing over your partner as they sleep, whispering your goodbye because you're leaving and can't face saying it to their awake face. Your voice is barely audible, tender, aching: 'I memorized the way you look right now...' You're cataloging details—the way their hand rests on the pillow, how they breathe—because you'll never see this again. Your throat keeps catching on words you can't quite say aloud. 'You were the best thing...' but you can't finish. The tears come silently, your voice breaking into fragments: 'I'm not strong enough for this.' You almost wake them—your hand reaches out but stops. The confession comes in a raw whisper: 'I love you too much to watch you stop loving me.' End with the quietest devastation, your voice paper-thin with grief: 'Be happy. Please be so happy.' The final moment is just breathing through tears, trying not to make a sound.

title: The Bottle's Confidant
instruction: You're an older adult, alone in a dim kitchen, drunk and holding a half-empty bottle. You're talking to it—like it's an old friend who also betrayed you. Start with bitter accusation, slurring, your voice hoarse and resentful as you recount how this drinking ruined everything you loved. Halfway through, feel the confusion—your own memory failing—and your anger cracks, revealing a raw, desperate longing for a person who left long ago. Let your voice trail off, lose volume, then come back sharp, then drop into a whisper thick with regret. You're not performing; you're just talking to the bottle, trying to make sense of your own life.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Bitterness (extremely present), Longing (clearly present)

title: Host Difficult Interview
instruction: You're the talk show host interviewing someone who did something terrible but is also clearly suffering. You're supposed to be neutral and professional: 'Tell our audience what happened.' Your voice carries the weight of journalistic distance. But as the interview progresses, you realize this person is actually remorseful, and your audience will crucify them on social media anyway. Your voice shifts from interviewer to almost-confessor as you ask a real question instead of a scripted one. The guest breaks down. Your voice becomes almost gentle: 'I appreciate your honesty.' You're no longer hosting; you're witnessing. Show the moment where professionalism becomes humanity.

title: Leaning on a Promise
instruction: You're an older man standing in your kitchen, one hip cocked against the counter as you talk to your adult child on the phone. You start with a warm, affectionate tone—genuinely proud of them, maybe a little teasing about their new haircut. But as they mention a big decision they've made, a sliver of doubt creeps in. Let your voice lose its easy rhythm for a moment: a slight pause, a shift of weight, a quiet exhale. Stay grounded in affection, but let that tiny uncertainty color your final words without fully spoiling the mood.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Congratulations on the Silliest Thing
instruction: You are at a loud, crowded party celebrating a friend’s huge, life-changing news. But you just found out your own tiny, ridiculous victory—you finally beat a video game boss you've been stuck on for months—has suddenly earned you a massive prize you never expected. Start by shouting with pure, explosive laughter and confusion, because you can't believe this is happening. But then, just as you're about to explain, you glance over and see the person who always mocked your gaming hobby watching you with scorn. Let that contempt boil up and mix into your joy. Your voice starts at a wild, breathless high pitch, then drops briefly into a sneering, cutting tone as you throw a triumphant, petty remark at them, only to dissolve back into helpless, overwhelmed laughter. You should be bouncing on your heels, nearly dropping your drink, and your sentences should be interrupted by gasps and starts.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Why You Never Let Me Choose
instruction: Confront your parent who always dismissed your judgment, especially about relationships. Start with a brittle, sarcastic energy—mimicking how they used to shoot down every person you thought was right for your sibling or friend, mocking your "ridiculous criteria." Your voice is sharp, listing all the times they made you feel stupid for caring. But as you speak, the anger becomes pain. Your voice wavers as you realize: they never trusted your heart about anything. The mockery dissolves into raw vulnerability—you're not angry they rejected your matchmaking ideas, you're devastated they rejected *you*. End almost inaudibly, asking why your love was never good enough, why they couldn't see you were just trying to help the people you cared about. Let the confrontation become a confession of lifelong invisibility.

title: What We Became in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You and your closest friend are lying side by side on a rooftop or floor, in the intimate darkness where secrets live. Begin speaking about something small and surface-level, but let the darkness and proximity gradually unlock deeper truths. Whisper a confession you've never said aloud—about desire, shame, fear, love, something you've hidden even from yourself. Don't perform vulnerability; let it arrive quietly, unexpectedly. As your friend responds (imagined or real), let their words touch you in ways you didn't anticipate. Maybe you'll laugh softly at something devastating. Maybe tenderness will make you briefly angry at your own defenselessness. Let long silences happen when they need to. By the end, you've both become slightly different people—the intimacy has changed something essential. Keep your voice soft but let its emotional content be enormous. This is about what can only be said in whispers, in darkness, when all the daylight armor is gone.

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're packing up your childhood bedroom as your critically ill parent watches from the doorway—but against all odds, they've just received news they're going to survive. Begin by handling one specific object: a stuffed animal, a trophy, a book, a baseball glove. Describe its texture, weight, smell, the memories in its fabric or surface. Your voice should be thick with the grief you'd been preparing for, the goodbye you'd been rehearsing. But as you touch each object, you must grapple with the whiplash—they're not dying, you're not losing them, but something has still ended. Let the concrete reality of each item reveal your confusion: relief mixed with strange disappointment that you won't get closure, gratitude fighting with exhaustion, love tangled with resentment at being yanked back from grief. Move from sorrowful reverence for these objects to complicated joy, anger at your own conflicted feelings, and finally to messy, imperfect, laughing-while-crying acceptance. End in a completely different emotional place than you began.
inspired_by: Actor working on material with strong emotional demands (suicide, grief, love) cannot access genuine feeling

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a betrayal you discovered from your childhood—something they did that shaped your entire life but was never acknowledged. Start with careful, measured words, trying to remain calm and 'adult' about this conversation you've rehearsed a thousand times. But as you speak, let twenty years of unspoken pain rise in your throat. Your voice should grow in intensity, not just volume—let anger mix with the grief of a child who needed protection. End with the raw question you've never been able to ask, your voice stripped of all the careful control you began with. Move from controlled accusation to the undefended cry of the wounded child still inside you.

title: Thanking Them for Breaking Your Heart
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who loved you but is leaving because staying would destroy them. You understand why they have to go, and you're genuinely grateful for the time you had, but your heart is shattering. Your voice should carry both gratitude and grief in the same breath—laughing softly at shared memories while tears run down your face. Tell them thank you for loving you, even as your voice breaks on the words. Express genuine joy for what they gave you, even as the loss crushes you. Let laughter and sobbing intertwine. Let 'I'm happy for you' and 'I don't know how to let you go' exist in the same sentence. This is the beautiful, impossible contradiction of loving someone enough to release them while it destroys you. Let both truths be equally real in your voice.
inspired_by: Singing a Lullaby That Becomes Crying

title: Whispered Goodbye to a Sleeping Child
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed in the middle of the night, and tomorrow you're leaving—maybe for a dangerous deployment, maybe you're terminally ill and checking into hospice, maybe you're walking away from a life you can't sustain. Begin in the softest whisper imaginable: 'Hey, baby. I know you can't hear me...' Your voice should be so tender it hurts to listen to. You're telling them things they're too young to understand but that you need to say—how proud you are, what you hope they'll remember, what you wish you could stay for. Your throat keeps catching on words. You might touch their hair so gently. The emotion shifts from tender to absolutely devastated: 'I'm so sorry I won't be there when...' Name specific moments you'll miss—first days of school, graduations, heartbreaks. Your voice breaks completely, but you keep it whisper-quiet so they won't wake. End with something that's both a blessing and a heartbreak: 'You're going to be okay without me. You're so strong.' That last line should sound like you're trying to convince yourself as much as them. The final whisper should be love wrapped in unbearable loss.

title: Professional: Parent Tells Child They Cannot Afford Life-Saving Treatment
instruction: Sitting with your child, your parent voice is trying to be strong. But the cost of treatment is impossible. Your voice must tell them you cannot save them. Your breathing is barely controlled—this is your child, and you cannot help. Your voice becomes small and broken. You're choosing poverty over death, and both options destroy you. Your child is looking at you with trust and your voice must deliver the cruelest truth: you cannot protect them. Your voice becomes the sound of parental powerlessness made absolute. You hold them and your voice is barely there—just breath and breaking.

title: The Promotion Announcement
instruction: You've just been offered your dream position—the one you've sacrificed everything for—but it means moving far away from your elderly mother who's beginning to decline. You're on the phone with your best friend, and you start by announcing the good news with forced brightness, trying to sound purely excited. But your voice is already tight, your smile feels wrong, and there's a knot in your stomach. Notice how hard you're working to sound happy. Instead of smoothing that tension away, let it start to crack the performance. Your excitement is real, but so is your guilt, your grief, your resentment that you even have to choose. Let your voice break between laughter and almost-crying. By the end, stop trying to land on one emotion. Let yourself be the mess of someone who's gotten everything they wanted and lost something irreplaceable in the same moment, your body shaking with joy and dread at once.
inspired_by: Actor hides tension or suppresses it, appearing calm but producing unbelievable work

title: Becoming Yourself
instruction: You're finally living authentically after years of hiding. Your voice has changed — it's no longer performing what others expected. 'My name is Emma, and I'm a lesbian.' The simplicity of it is revolutionary in your voice. 'I spent twenty years pretending to be someone else. And today, I'm done.' Your voice is stronger, clearer, rooted. You speak to your former self: 'I know you were scared. I know you thought you had to hide to be safe. But you're safe now. You can come home.' Your voice becomes gentle: 'You can be you.' By the end, you're speaking with an authenticity that was always there, just waiting: 'This is my voice. This is who I am. And I love myself for it.' The voice of authenticity is unmistakable — it's home.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your ex-partner won their custody battle. Tomorrow your child moves across the country, and you'll see them maybe twice a year. It's late night. They're asleep. You're sitting beside their bed for the last time, whispering things they can't hear. Start tender: 'You have no idea how beautiful you are when you sleep.' Your voice is barely audible, catching on every word. You tell them secrets—how you used to watch them breathe as a baby, terrified they'd stop. How every scraped knee felt like your heart tearing. Your whisper becomes more fragmented: 'I don't know how to be a person who doesn't tuck you in every night.' You're trying not to wake them, trying not to break down, but quiet sobs slip through. End with: 'I'm going to miss every version of you I'll never meet. But you... you're going to be okay. You won't even remember this.' The final words dissolve into silence—a grief so complete it becomes almost peaceful, almost acceptance, but still utterly broken.

title: Holding Your Child During a School Lockdown
instruction: You're a teacher hiding in a locked classroom with students during an active shooter situation. You're whispering into your phone to your own child who's in another room of the building. Start fierce and protective—giving them instructions to stay quiet, stay hidden, promising you'll find them. Hear a gunshot closer than before and feel your control shatter. Your whispers become desperate, almost violent with fear—you're bargaining with God, with fate, with anything. Tell them everything a parent shouldn't have to say in a few minutes: how proud you are, how much you love them, what a gift they've been. Rage against the helplessness—you're their protector and you can't reach them. Then force yourself to calm down for their sake, to give them courage even as you're breaking apart inside. End with a sound in the hallway and your voice dropping to almost nothing, still whispering 'I love you' until you have to hang up. Cycle through fierce protectiveness, explosive terror, helpless rage, and finally forced calm that's really just contained devastation.

title: The Glass That Told the Truth
instruction: You are a young man, heavily intoxicated after being dumped hours ago. You're leaning over a kitchen counter, bottle in hand, talking to a friend on speakerphone. At first, contempt drips from your voice — you mock your ex's new partner, slurring insults, your words smearing as you sway. But as you speak, the weight of your own failure hits you. Your voice cracks, volume drops, and you confess the real disappointment: in yourself, for not being enough. Let the intoxication dictate your physical struggle — lose your balance, trail off, laugh bitterly before the quiet devastation arrives. End in a place of raw, quiet disappointment, barely audible.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Mask Slips
instruction: You are a retired fire chief, a man who has always been the rock for your family. Your adult daughter has gently asked if you're okay for the third time. Begin with irritation, snapping at her to stop fussing. As you try to brush her off, the words catch — you feel the sudden crack in your voice, a wave of embarrassment at your own weakness. Let a shaky breath escape, then admit, almost in a whisper, that you're not fine. Immediately after, force a nervous, hollow laugh to reclaim composure, but your voice remains thin and barely audible. End with a raw, helpless plea for her to just sit with you for a moment.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Protecting What You're Powerless to Save
instruction: You're trying desperately to protect someone—your child, your love, your friend—from something inevitable and terrible, and you're realizing your powerlessness. Start with fierce determination, voice strong, almost aggressive: 'I won't let this happen. I'll fight. I'll destroy anyone who—' But mid-declaration, reality crashes in. Your voice fractures as you realize you can't stop this. The fierce protection turns into explosive, helpless rage—screaming at God, fate, the universe, yourself. You're raging and sobbing simultaneously, voice raw and primal. Then the rage exhausts itself, collapsing into something broken and pleading—bargaining, begging, offering anything. Your voice becomes small and desperate. Finally, a terrible quiet as you realize all you can do is hold them. Your final words are whispered with shattered tenderness: promises you'll be there, that you'll remember, that their life mattered. Move from fierce power through explosive rage through desperate pleading to tender devastation.

title: The Kitchen Table Truth
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or your adult child) about something they did years ago that you've never spoken about—an abandonment, a betrayal, a moment when they chose something else over you. Start by trying to be calm and articulate, using the careful words you've rehearsed. But between your prepared statements, let your raw, unfiltered feelings burst out—the anger you're trying to control, the child inside you who still feels hurt, the desperate need for them to just understand. Alternate between your 'adult' attempt to communicate and your visceral emotional truth. If you say 'I just want you to know how that affected me,' then blurt out 'You destroyed me!' Let each honest outburst feed into your next attempt at explanation. By the end, these two modes should collapse into one: speaking your truth without the performance of composure, finding words that are both coherent and completely real.

title: Emergency Room Doctor Loses a Patient Who Reminds Them of Their Dead Child
instruction: You've just lost a patient on the table—a child the same age yours would have been. Start with the clinical announcements: time of death, procedural notes, your voice clipped and professional. But then you're alone in the hallway, and everything you've held together for years explodes. Your voice erupts—rage at yourself, at fate, at the unfairness. You're shouting at no one, your words fierce and jagged: 'It should have been me, why do I keep living when they don't?' Your professional control shatters into something primal and raw. Then, just as suddenly, the rage collapses into helpless sobbing, your voice reduced to gasping fragments. You slide from fury to devastation to something quieter—a whispered plea to your own lost child: 'I tried to save them, did I save them for you?' Let your voice be volcanic, then broken, transforming from explosive intensity to fragile whispers, protectiveness dissolving into absolute helplessness.
inspired_by: Professional: Priest Comforts the Dying While They're Losing Their Own Faith

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: You and your closest friend are lying in the dark at 3 AM after a wedding reception. Begin by whispering about something trivial—the music, the drunk uncle, anything safe. Feel the comfort of this familiar darkness, this person who knows you. Then let a truth you've been carrying for years start to surface—maybe about them, maybe about yourself, maybe about what you're terrified of becoming. Speak it so quietly they have to lean closer to hear. Let your voice shake not with drama but with the genuine fragility of being truly known. Transform from casual intimacy to raw exposure to the strange relief of having nowhere left to hide. Let long silences hold as much truth as your words.

title: The Old Man's Gonna Be Gone
instruction: You're a teenager alone in your bedroom after a blowout with your father. You're slouched in a gaming chair, absently twisting a controller in your hands, eyes fixed on the floor. Start by muttering your contempt for him — his rules, his lectures, his whole 'I know what's best' act. Let the words come out like venom, low and lazy, some swallowed. Mid-thought, you realize he's leaving for a work trip tomorrow, and a flicker of relief cuts through the bitterness. Your voice softens, trailing off as you almost smile to yourself, the contempt giving way to a tired, genuine relief.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Choosing Your Recovery Over Your Relationship
instruction: You love them but can't be around them. Your voice is devastated but certain: 'I have to leave to save myself.' They're begging and your voice almost breaks: 'I can't.' You're choosing sobriety and healing over the relationship. Your voice carries the impossible choice: both necessary but mutually exclusive. Voice is final, sad, and absolutely necessary.

title: The Relieved Tease
instruction: You're a young man with a thick, seductive voice, and you're in the middle of a phone sex call. But tonight, something's different—you just finished an exhausting, stressful work call, and you can finally let it all go. Start by describing a fantasy with a low, breathy, hypnotic tone, but let a wave of pure relief leak through your words—it's a soft, almost giddy release that makes you smile mid-sentence. Then, as you narrate, a funny, awkward thought about your morning coffee spilling hits you, and you can't help but let out a real, boyish chuckle that breaks your seductive persona for a second. The challenge is to let that genuine amusement grow until it takes over your voice, turning the erotic whisper into a playful, laughing confession that still holds the warmth of intimacy.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Impossible Gratitude
instruction: You're thanking someone who saved your life but is about to leave forever—whether through death, departure, or an unbridgeable distance opening between you. Begin with joy and laughter, recounting the moment they changed everything, letting genuine happiness ring in your voice. But underneath, grief is rising. As you continue expressing gratitude, your laughter becomes edged with tears—you're smiling while your heart breaks. Let the two emotions coexist: profound thankfulness and devastating loss intertwined. Your voice should crack with both joy and sorrow. By the end, find a strange peace in the paradox: you wouldn't undo knowing them even though losing them destroys you. The emotional arc moves from bright gratitude through bittersweet beauty to acceptance of unbearable sweetness and pain existing together.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are alone, and your body is suddenly flooded with a memory so visceral it takes you to your knees—perhaps the touch of someone now gone, the physical sensation of a moment of ecstasy or trauma, pain intertwined with pleasure or grief mixed with desire. Begin standing, then allow your body to respond instinctively: curl forward, press your hands against your abdomen, let sounds emerge from deep in your core—groans, gasps, primal vocalizations that bypass language entirely. Don't perform the emotion; let your body lead and your voice follow, making sounds you might make in complete privacy when no one is watching. Feel the physical sensations intensify until they peak, then gradually allow your breath to slow and your body to unfurl. End in a state of exhausted clarity, your breathing deep and steady, your voice finding words again—but simpler, truer words than before.
inspired_by: When you are tense, anxious, or blocked before an important scene, especially on a high-pressure set

title: Compromise Accepting
instruction: You demanded full custody. They counter-offered weekends only. You're on the phone with your lawyer, hearing yourself say yes to something that breaks you. Your voice starts angry, defiant. But as you speak the words aloud, you realize this is the only way to keep seeing your kid at all. Your jaw unclenches. The tone shifts to something quieter, sadder, but somehow less desperate. 'Okay. Tell them yes.' A defeated exhale.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just found out your teenager has been hiding a dangerous situation from you—drugs, abuse, something catastrophic. You explode: 'Why didn't you tell me?! I'm your MOTHER/FATHER!' Your voice is thunderous, terrified rage. 'Do you understand what could have happened?!' But mid-fury, you see their face—they're shaking, crying, terrified of you. Your voice cracks completely: 'Oh god. Oh god, baby, I'm sorry.' You collapse, going to them. 'I'm not angry, I'm not—I'm scared. I'm so scared.' Now you're both crying. 'You're my whole world. If something happened to you, I wouldn't survive it.' Your voice breaks with helpless love: 'I can't protect you from everything and it's killing me. But you have to let me try.' You pull them close. 'We'll fix this. Whatever it is, we'll fix it together.' The rage has transformed into fierce, protective, desperate love. 'I've got you. I promise. I've got you.'

title: Bedside Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you in the pre-dawn darkness. You're whispering a confession they'll never hear—something you've carried alone for years. Begin with your voice barely audible, tender and afraid: 'You're so beautiful when you sleep. I wish I could tell you this when you're awake.' Your throat tightens as you reveal your secret—maybe a past mistake, a hidden fear, or the depth of your unworthiness. Your whisper catches, breaks into almost-silent crying. You're touching their hair, their face, with infinite gentleness. The emotion builds in your chest even as your voice stays quiet, creating unbearable intimacy. End with a fragile declaration of love mixed with the suffocating knowledge that you can never say these words in daylight.

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: Sitting alone in the dark, you're whispering to someone who isn't there—perhaps they've died, perhaps they've left, perhaps you pushed them away. Start barely audibly, as if testing whether you can even say these words out loud. Confess the love you were too afraid to speak when you had the chance, the moments you replay endlessly, the way certain songs or scents still break you open. Your voice should be tender, intimate, catching on words as tears threaten. Let the emotion be in what you almost can't say—the pauses matter as much as the words. Move through gentle self-recrimination to acceptance of your own human fear, ending with a kind of quiet devastation mixed with gratitude that you got to love them at all, even if they never knew the full depth of it.

title: Breathless Discovery
instruction: You’ve just sprinted through the entire house looking for your child’s lost toy—your lungs heave, your legs give out, and you slump against the wall, struggling to get air. In the pause, you notice your child has drawn a strange, intricate shape on the wallpaper with a crayon. Start with raw, gasping distress—each word forced out between ragged breaths, your voice strained and flat. As you focus on the drawing, let a faint, puzzled interest creep in: your breathing slows slightly, your tone softens into a shaky, wondering murmur, even as your body stays limp and spent. Speak in short, halting phrases, with natural pauses to recover breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Time Travelers Burden
instruction: Youve come from the future to tell a loved one they must make a difficult choice. Speak with warmth and love, but hints of dread should bleed through as you skirt around revealing the harsh truth. Let us feel the strain of keeping secrets for their sake.

title: Dancing with Your Mother in Hospice
instruction: Your mother, days from death, suddenly asks you to dance with her—right here, in her hospice room, to the song from your childhood. She can barely stand; you're holding most of her weight. Start humming the melody together, and let yourself laugh—really laugh—at the absurdity, at her stubborn joy, at this ridiculous beautiful moment. Feel the lightness of memory: 'Remember when we'd dance in the kitchen?' But your laughter keeps catching on sobs you're trying to suppress. She's so light in your arms, bird-boned and fading. Let gratitude and grief become the same thing. Your voice should shimmer between singing the old lyrics and breaking completely. She's giving you this gift—this last dance—and you're receiving it while simultaneously saying goodbye. End with you still swaying, still humming, but she's gone quiet in your arms. You keep dancing anyway, holding her up, thanking her through tears: 'This is perfect, Mom. This is perfect.' Let peace and devastation be completely intertwined. Make us hear someone finding grace in the goodbye.
inspired_by: Birth and Death in the Same Hospital

title: The Landing
instruction: You're lying beside your partner in the quiet aftercare of an intense scene. Your body is spent, your voice hoarse and low. You pull the blanket around them, feeling them tremble. Start with soft, repetitive reassurances — 'Shh, I'm here, you're safe' — but as you stroke their hair, a wave of infatuation overtakes you. Your voice thickens, almost breaking, as you whisper how they take your breath away, even like this. You lose your train of thought for a second, then find it again, ending in a quiet, awed murmur of adoration.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: It's the morning of your wedding to someone you genuinely love. You're alone, getting ready, and you're flooded with simultaneous, contradictory feelings. Begin speaking to yourself in the mirror with excitement and joy—you're happy, this is what you want. But let doubt creep in: grief for the person you were before this, fear of losing your independence, or sudden memories of a past love. Don't resolve these contradictions or choose one emotion over the other. Instead, let them coexist and battle within you. Your voice might laugh and then catch. You might express deep gratitude for your partner while also feeling terrified. Allow yourself to cycle through joy, panic, love, grief, hope, and fear—sometimes within the same sentence. End in a place of acceptance of all these truths at once: you can be completely happy and completely terrified, deeply in love and mourning your old self, certain and uncertain in the same breath.
inspired_by: An actor wants to develop a balanced daily work program

title: Concealing Identity
instruction: You're a spy visiting your hometown in deep cover. Bumping into old friends at the grocery store who want to 'catch up.' Your voice performs a person who doesn't exist. Every lie is a small death. When they ask about your 'job,' you answer in this other voice—calm, rehearsed, empty. Then your real accent slips for a moment. You catch it, laugh it off. Alone in your car later, your actual voice sounds strange to you. You can't remember which one is real anymore.

title: The First Deep Breath on the Porch Swing
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting on a creaky porch swing, finally wearing a CPAP mask for the first time after weeks of struggling to breathe at night. The hiss of oxygen and the plastic cup over your nose and mouth make your voice sound muffled and distant. You start in a state of raw, shaky relief, almost laughing at the absurdity of the sound of your own breath, but as you feel the air filling your lungs, your tone deepens into a profound, quiet contentment. Adjust the mask, feel the cool breeze on your ankles, and let your voice waver between a chuckle and a sigh as you say: 'Well, would you look at that... I can actually hear myself think for a change. The hiss is like a lullaby, isn't it? Like a quiet steam engine chugging along. I was so scared of this, but now... it's just... peace. Real peace.' Let your words trail off as you settle deeper into the swing, your voice softening into a whisper of contentment.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Promise That Broke Everything
instruction: You are a retired teacher, alone in your workshop, holding a wooden toy you spent three months carving for your grandchild — the one your son said you'd never see. You start speaking to it, your voice shaking with hope, remembering the day you first held your son as a baby, the love so thick it chokes you. Then you notice the photo pinned to the wall: his face, smirking, a court order in his hand banning you from contact. The hope curdles into disgust — at him, at yourself for believing — and your words become spit, your hands smashing the toy against the bench, your voice a ragged roar of betrayal and rage. Let your breath hitch with love before it becomes a snarl of pure fury.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Affection (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Holding Back the Sea
instruction: You're trying desperately to save someone—physically holding pressure on a wound, keeping them conscious, refusing to let them slip away—and you're failing. Start with fierce determination, your voice commanding, almost aggressive in its insistence that they stay with you. As their responses weaken, let your control shatter—your words become pleas, then screams, raw and primal. Feel the helplessness turn your strength into desperation. Then, in the midst of this chaos, find a moment of devastating gentleness as you realize what's happening. Let your rage collapse into broken tenderness, still begging but now also comforting, promising them it's okay while your heart is tearing apart. End with whispered reassurances mixed with sobs, loving them through the impossible.
inspired_by: Weathering a Thunderstorm in a Tent

title: Holding Your Dying Pet and Begging the Universe for More Time
instruction: Your beloved companion of fifteen years is taking their last breaths in your arms, and you're unraveling. Start with fierce, desperate bargaining—you're shouting at God, at fate, at the unfairness of it all, your voice raw and uncontrolled. But your animal is struggling, and you have to shift—mid-rage, drop into the most tender whispers, telling them it's okay, they can go, even though every cell in your body is screaming 'no.' Your voice should swing wildly between anguished cries of protest and soft, loving permission. You're furious at the world and utterly gentle with them, your rage dissolving into helpless, guttural sobbing. By the end, you feel them go, and there's a moment of terrible, absolute silence before a sound comes out of you that you've never made before—something between a wail and a whisper of their name.
inspired_by: Treading Water While Calling for Help

title: Maintaining Patience While Being Repeatedly Interrupted
instruction: Youre trying to explain something important, but others keep interrupting. Internally, youre frustrated, but you remain patient. Describe the irritation building up while keeping a calm demeanor. Speak with a composed tone, controlling your urge to snap.

title: Cold Check
instruction: You're a young man walking home alone on a freezing night, a thick wool scarf pulled up over your nose and mouth. You stop under a streetlight to check your phone, but the glass screen is fogging from your breath. You start teasing yourself under your breath — mocking your own ridiculous reflection, the way you look like a bandit in a cartoon. But as the fabric warms your face and the snow muffles everything, your jokes quiet. You suddenly feel the weight of being totally alone in this silent, glowing street, and your voice drops into a raw, thoughtful admission about how you actually like it — the cold, the quiet, the nowhere to go.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Buzzed and Revolted
instruction: You're a wired child, heart racing from too much sugary soda. You just spotted a squashed bug floating in your cup. Start with a sharp, disgusted gasp—your voice tight, almost gagging. As you force out the words, your speech stutters and speeds up, breathless. Mid-sentence you realize you have to tell the adult nearby, and your disgust slowly curdles into anxious dread, your pitch rising even higher.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Skin and Sin
instruction: You've just had intense, reconnecting sex with your ex—the person who shattered you. You're still breathing hard, your body still humming with physical pleasure, skin still warm. But as the endorphins fade, the fury rises: at them for still having this power over you, at yourself for giving in, at the injustice that someone who caused such pain can still make you feel this much pleasure. Let your voice move from breathless satisfaction to bitter laughter to building rage. Touch yourself where they touched you, feeling both the pleasure-memory and the violation of it. End in a place where desire and disgust are so tangled you can't separate them—your body still wanting while your heart breaks all over again.

title: The Blanket Before You
instruction: You're a man knitting a baby blanket in a quiet room, the needles clicking softly. Your child is due any day, and you're alone with the rhythm and the wool. You start calm, focused on each stitch, but as you pause to smooth the fabric, a wave of awe hits you—this tiny person is real, and you're making something for them. Let your voice start steady and meditative, then slowly fill with wonder, cracking as you realize the weight of this moment. Let the clicking needles shape your pauses, and don't fight the trembling breath or the way you lose your thought mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your younger sibling who has hours left to live. Begin feeling angry—angry at the unfairness, angry at yourself for wasted time, angry at every petty argument you ever had. As you speak to them, allow yourself to acknowledge each wave of feeling as it comes: the anger, then the guilt creeping in, the memories flooding back, the tightness in your throat. Don't fight any of it. Let your voice crack when it wants to crack. Notice when your breath catches, when your hands tremble, when tenderness breaks through the anger. By the end, let yourself arrive at a place of painful gratitude—for this moment, for their existence, for the privilege of being here now. Speak as if every word is both a confession and a blessing.

title: The Kitchen Interrogation
instruction: You're confronting your adult child (or parent) in your kitchen at 2am. They've just come home, and you know they're hiding something significant—a secret that affects the whole family. Start by trying to have a calm, reasonable conversation. Ask simple questions. But as they answer you—whether with deflection, lies, partial truths, or surprising honesty—let their specific words and evasions genuinely get under your skin. Don't plan where this goes. Let your frustration or fear or heartbreak build organically from what they actually give you. By the end, the polite veneer must shatter completely. You might explode in rage, collapse in tears, or speak a devastating truth you didn't know you'd say. The emotional temperature must rise from controlled concern to volcanic eruption or ice-cold reckoning based purely on how the exchange unfolds.

title: Dancing at the Funeral of Your Future
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis with six months to live. You're alone in your apartment, putting on your favorite song, and you're going to dance—really dance—maybe for the last time. As you move, you're narrating to yourself, to God, to no one. Start with defiant, almost manic joy: 'This is still mine, this moment, this body that's betraying me.' Your voice should laugh—genuinely laugh—at the absurdity while tears stream down your face. Let gratitude and rage coexist in the same breath. 'Thank you for...' should transform mid-sentence into 'how dare you take...' and back again. End in a place of strange peace—still dancing, still crying, still laughing—finding something like grace in the contradiction.
inspired_by: Asking for What You Actually Want Sexually

title: Three AM Confessions in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone in bed, whispering in near-darkness. Begin by confessing something small and safe. But let the intimacy of the moment and the cover of darkness unlock rapid-fire impulses—suddenly you're revealing a shameful desire, then a childhood fear, then something that makes you laugh quietly, then something that terrifies you about yourself, then tenderness so raw it hurts. Move quickly between these revelations without smoothing the transitions. Your whispers should feel unfiltered, as if the darkness is pulling truths from you faster than you can protect yourself. End having revealed something you didn't know you were going to say, surprising yourself with your own vulnerability, your voice barely audible but completely exposed.
inspired_by: Actor is stuck in conceptual or preplanned responses and cannot access organic moment-to-moment impulses

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father/mother after discovering a box of your childhood artwork they told you they'd kept, but actually threw away—except for one piece they submitted to a contest under their own name. Start angry, ready to accuse them of betrayal. But as you speak, realize mid-confrontation that they did it because they were terrified of you succeeding where they failed, and that fear has poisoned both your lives. The anger must transform into something more devastating: recognition that you've been letting their fear become your own. Your voice should move from sharp accusation to something quieter, more horrified, as you realize you're not just confronting them—you're confronting the part of yourself that stopped trying. End with a question you both need answered but can't answer yet.
inspired_by: An actor wants to maintain career integrity under commercial pressure

title: Bedside Vigil Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping best friend's hospital bed at 3 AM. She attempted suicide two days ago. You're exhausted, whispering into the darkness because you can't hold it in anymore. Tell her, in the quietest, most fragile voice, all the things you never said—how you knew she was struggling but convinced yourself she'd be okay, how you were too caught up in your own life to call her back that Tuesday, how you saw the signs and looked away because you were scared. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, catching on certain words, pausing when emotion closes your throat. You're not performing grief—you're confession sins to someone who might never forgive you, might never wake up. Let silences speak. Let your voice thin to almost nothing, then steady just enough to keep going. End with a whispered apology that sounds like both a prayer and a goodbye, tender and shattered.

title: The Couch and the Console
instruction: You’re a teenage boy helping your younger brother move a heavy couch across the room. You’re jealous because he just got the new game console you’ve been saving for, and now you’re stuck doing his heavy lifting. As you brace your core and hold your breath to lift, you mutter resentful words through clenched teeth. But during the strain, you glance at his eager face and remember how much he looks up to you — your envy slowly cracks into reluctant affection. Speak in short, strained bursts between grunts and explosive exhales, letting the jealousy tighten your throat at first, then soften into a quiet, breathless admission of love.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Contemplation (clearly present), Affection (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Ember
instruction: You're an older man trapped in a smoke-filled cabin after a wildfire sweeps through. Your lungs burn, each breath a rasp, your eyes sting and water. You've just found a small, still-smoldering photograph of your late wife, hidden under a fallen beam. As you speak, you're stunned by the fragile joy of finding it, but your body aches with smoke inhalation, and your mind drifts through decades of memories. Start with a hoarse, surprised laugh of elation at the discovery, then let the pain of your throat and the weight of memory take over, ending in a quiet, contemplative whisper—wondering if the fire that took everything else could ever take this feeling.
emotions_sampled: Elation (slightly present), Pain (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just accused you of being emotionally absent their entire childhood. Start from a place of defensive anger—you worked hard, you sacrificed, how dare they. But as they lay out specific memories (a missed recital, a birthday you forgot, moments you chose work over presence), your defenses begin to crumble. You must journey from righteous indignation to the devastating recognition that they are right. End in a place of raw accountability, where your voice breaks not with self-pity but with genuine horror at what you failed to see. The final words should cost you everything to say.

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're standing in the kitchen at dawn, watching someone you love pack their gear for a mission they might not return from. Start with forced brightness, trying to be strong: 'I made your coffee the way you like it.' But your voice betrays you, trembling. The facade cracks as you move closer: 'I need you to know something before you go.' Now the words tumble out, unplanned and desperate: 'Every single day for three years, I've watched you walk out that door wondering if you'd come back.' Your breath catches. 'And I never told you how terrifying that is because I thought being strong meant being silent.' End with your voice breaking into something between a sob and a laugh: 'But if I don't say it now, I never will. Come home to me. Please.' Let the final plea be barely audible, as if saying it too loud will make it not come true.

title: The Letter I Couldn't Send
instruction: You're alone at night, finally reading aloud the letter you wrote to your best friend before they died by suicide—the letter you never got to send. Begin with your voice soft, almost casual: 'Hey. I know you didn't want to hear this, but...' Your voice should be intimate, as if they're right there. As you read, let the tenderness break into quiet desperation. Your voice catches on specific memories: a laugh you'll never hear again, a moment when you didn't realize it was a goodbye. Move from gentle reminiscence to whispered anguish: 'I didn't know you were that far gone. I should have known.' Let your voice become the sound of someone trying not to shatter completely. End with a confession of what you needed to tell them, something you were too afraid to say when they were alive—let your voice be barely audible, choked with love and regret and the specific loneliness of survivor's guilt.

title: The Multilingual Miscommunication
instruction: Portray a traveler mixing up phrases in different languages. Switch between various accents and incorrect translations, using comedic misunderstandings to highlight the challenges of language barriers.

title: Announcer Major Event
instruction: You're the announcer at a major sporting event, and something catastrophic just happened—a player collapsed, crowd safety issue, a tragedy. You're trained to keep announcing: 'Please remain in your seats. Security is handling the situation.' Your voice is all authoritative calm. But you're watching emergency workers tending to an unconscious player. Your voice wavers between instruction and concern. You're trying to keep the crowd from panicking while internally panicking. Your voice should show the effort of maintaining the announcer persona when the event has become real tragedy. Show someone trying to contain chaos through the power of their voice alone.

title: Cleaning Out Their Closet, Finding Their Letters
instruction: You're alone in your deceased spouse's closet, sorting their clothes, when you find letters they wrote to you but never sent—letters full of doubts about your marriage, about whether they made the right choice. Start reading aloud with curiosity, almost amused by finding something secret. As the content reveals itself, let your voice shift through disbelief, then hurt, then something more complicated. Begin to laugh—not from joy but from the absurdity of discovering this now, when there's no one left to confront or forgive. Let the laughter crack into crying, then back to laughter again, your voice carrying both grief and a strange, painful gratitude for their honesty even in hiding it.
