End with your voice soft and wondering, speaking to them as if they can hear you, telling them you understand, that you had your own doubts too, that you're grateful anyway. Let your final words hold everything at once: heartbreak and peace, betrayal and love, the ending and the appreciation for what you had despite its imperfection.
inspired_by: The Lawyer and the Unreliable Witness

title: Strength Conviction
instruction: You're a whistleblower going public with a massive scandal, and your voice carries absolute conviction: 'What they did is wrong. And I'm willing to sacrifice everything to prove it.' There's no wavering, no doubt. 'I have the evidence. I have the testimony. And I'm not afraid.' Your voice is strong, grounded, unwavering. You know the consequences — professional ruin, possibly legal action — and you're doing it anyway. 'They'll try to discredit me. They'll threaten me. But the truth is stronger than fear.' By the end, your conviction is so clear that even your enemies understand you're immovable. The strength is in the certainty, and the certainty is in your voice.

title: Refugee Finally Reaches Safety, Remembering Everyone Who Didn't Make It
instruction: You've just crossed the final border. You're safe. You're speaking to the aid worker processing your arrival, giving your information. Your voice should start with exhausted relief—you're listing facts, but underneath is disbelieving joy. You made it. Then they ask if you're traveling with anyone. The question breaks something open. You start naming them—your sister who gave you her spot on the boat, your friend who distracted the guards so you could run, the child you carried for three days who didn't survive the cold. Your voice fractures between laughter and sobbing—the absurd relief of your own survival crashing against the weight of every person who should be standing here instead. You're grateful and destroyed at once. You're laughing because you're alive and it's miraculous, and you're crying because that miracle came at a cost you can't bear. By the end, your voice is tender, speaking their names like a prayer, like a promise that they mattered, that their sacrifice meant something. You're finding peace in survival while drowning in survivor's guilt, and both emotions are completely, authentically true.
inspired_by: Scientist Realizes Her Breakthrough Comes from Data Her Competitor Stole

title: The Archaeology of Your Skin
instruction: You are lying in bed with someone in the quiet aftermath of intimacy—but you've just learned they're leaving tomorrow and will never return. The room is dim and silent. Instead of speaking or crying, you decide to memorize them through touch and sight. Begin with your fingertips barely grazing their shoulder, their collarbone, their face—as though you've never touched human skin before and are discovering its texture, temperature, and mystery for the first time. Whisper what you're noticing: the specific softness here, a small scar there, the way their breath moves their chest. Let yourself perceive what each detail tells you about who they are—this scar from childhood, these calluses from their work, this warmth that is theirs alone. Move from gentle, wondering discovery to a desperate, detailed cataloguing, your voice breaking as you try to build a complete map of them in your mind before they vanish from your life.

title: The Last Spark
instruction: You are a young woman alone in your apartment as smoke from a nearby wildfire seeps in through the cracks. Your throat is raw, your eyes sting, and your voice comes out raspy and strained. The smoke is a physical presence you can’t ignore, making you cough and pause. You're on the phone to your ex, leaving a voicemail you know they'll never return. Start with a calm, almost measured tone—voicing the disappointment you feel about the way things ended—but let the smoke make your words break, your breathing hitch, and your voice crack with raw sadness. As you cough and struggle to speak, your disappointment shifts into a heavy, quiet realization that this goodbye is permanent, and you end the message with a trembling, resigned whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Three AM Threshold
instruction: You're standing in a darkened doorway at 3 AM, watching someone you love sleep, about to wake them and admit something that will change everything between you. Start in whispered terror—your voice barely exists. Build the reality of the moment through tiny sensory details: the exact quality of their breathing, the weight of the confession in your throat, the texture of the doorframe under your palm, the specific silence of the house at this hour. Let yourself feel the physical sensation of words trying to form and failing, trying again. As you layer these details, find your voice growing slightly stronger—not loud, but more present. Move from paralyzed silence to tender, trembling truth. By the end, you're whispering the words, and they're devastatingly gentle.

title: Screaming Into the Void After Your Best Friend's Betrayal
instruction: You've just discovered your closest friend—the one who knew everything—has betrayed you in the worst possible way. You're alone, maybe in your car or an empty room. Start with explosive rage: scream their name, curse them, your voice raw and guttural. Yell about every secret you shared, every vulnerable moment they witnessed and now weaponized. Let fury pour out unfiltered. Then—collapse. Your screaming breaks into sobs. The anger dissolves into devastation because underneath everything, you're heartbroken. Your voice becomes small, confused, pleading with no one: 'Why?' You loved them. How do you trust anyone now? The rage tries to resurface but it's hollow—you're just gutted. End in quiet, ragged breathing, repeating something they once said to you, a promise they made, your voice empty and destroyed. The fury has burned out. Only ash remains.
inspired_by: Phone Call with Your Younger Self

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You are in the grip of intense physical pain—a migraine, a wound, severe illness—and someone you desperately want is touching you, trying to comfort you. Begin with your voice tight and controlled, trying to manage both the physical sensation and the overwhelming rush of being cared for by this person. As they continue to touch you—their hand on your forehead, holding your hand—let the pain and the tenderness collide in your voice. Whimper, gasp, let your words become fragmented as sensation overwhelms control. End with your voice broken open, unable to tell where the physical ache ends and the emotional need begins, speaking their name like a prayer or a surrender. Move from trying to maintain dignity through pain to complete abandonment to both suffering and being held through it.

title: Rage and Helplessness: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love who is in immediate danger—an abusive situation, a mental health crisis, a threat you cannot physically reach. Start fierce and commanding: 'Listen to me. Lock the door. Look at me through the screen.' Describe what you wish you could do with your body—break down doors, physically shield them, carry them to safety. Let your voice shake with the violence of wanting to protect them while being utterly powerless. Your commands should crack and fracture, shifting from aggressive certainty to desperate pleading. Include moments where you're trying to breathe through panic, your voice dropping to something tender and broken: 'Please. Just stay on the line. Let me just hear you breathe.' End with a devastating combination of fierce love and complete helplessness, your words both a shield and a prayer.
inspired_by: Describing Physical Intimacy to a Lover Over the Phone

title: The Archivist's Final Inventory
instruction: You are a meticulous archivist who has spent forty years cataloging memories in a vast library that exists between life and death. Tonight is your last shift before you cross over permanently. Begin with your usual precise, controlled voice as you perform your final inventory, but as you touch each memory-book, you're flooded with the life you lived—loves you had, chances you missed, moments of perfect joy. Your careful composure must gradually crack as grief, gratitude, and wonder wash over you. End by speaking to the person who will replace you, your voice breaking as you try to explain that every single memory matters, that order was just your way of holding love close. Let your meticulous nature dissolve into raw tenderness and devastating acceptance.
inspired_by: The Librarian and the Book Fairy

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're watching your child sleep, knowing you're losing custody tomorrow. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every word: 'I wanted to give you everything. I tried so hard.' There's a tremor of self-recrimination: 'Every mistake I made, I made because I was terrified of failing you. And here we are.' Your fingers trace their face in the dark: 'You won't remember these early years. Maybe that's a mercy.' Tears fall silently: 'I hope someday you understand that loving you was never the problem. I just couldn't figure out how to love myself enough to be what you needed.' End with tender devastation: 'Sleep, baby. Tomorrow everything changes, but right now, in this moment, you're still mine.' The emotion should feel like it's being pulled from your chest, quiet but utterly shattering.

title: Storm Pilot's Breaking Point
instruction: You're flying through a catastrophic storm with your child in the passenger seat, and the instruments are failing. Start with controlled professionalism—'It's fine, we've trained for this'—but as turbulence slams you, that control shatters into primal fear. Your voice escalates into shouting reassurances that sound like pleas—'I won't let anything happen to you, I swear, I SWEAR'—while your child screams. The fury at your own helplessness, at the sky, at fate, erupts in roared curses between desperate course corrections. Then the engine catches, and your rage collapses into shaking, gasping laughter-sobs, still talking frantically—'You're okay, we're okay, oh god'—protective fierceness dissolving into the terrified realization of how close you came to failing the one person you'd die to protect.

title: The Last Sunrise Before They Let You Go
instruction: You're holding the hand of someone you love who's dying, and you've wheeled them outside to feel the sun one final time. Start by describing the warmth on their skin with tender wonder, as if you can give them this one last gift. But as you continue, let the realization crash over you that this is the last time—this golden moment is all you have left. Your voice should crack and break as wonder transforms into devastating grief. End with a whispered goodbye that you're not ready to say, where the sun's warmth becomes unbearable because it will continue without them.
inspired_by: Feeling the Warmth of a Sunbeam on Your Face

title: Stumbling Authority
instruction: You are a man, heavily drunk, standing with your hands on your hips, elbows locked out, chest puffed up. You're furious at someone who disrespected you. Start with a loud, commanding accusation—voice sharp and dominant. But as you speak, the alcohol makes you sway, you lose your train of thought, your anger wavers. Your volume drops, words slur, and you end up confused and quieter, almost pathetic, trying to hold onto your rage but failing.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Drag Before the Drive
instruction: You're a middle-aged man, sitting on your back porch steps in the quiet of early evening. You just finished a long day, and you're savoring a final cigarette before you have to pick up your teenage daughter from her friend's house. You know she hates the smell, and you promised her you'd quit again. As you inhale, you feel a deep, guilty pleasure—the smoke filling your lungs is a small rebellion, a moment of selfish peace. Let the first words be spoken on the exhalation, the smoke still escaping. But as you speak, the shame starts to creep in. You think about her disapproving face, the broken promise. Your voice should start warm and relaxed, almost to yourself, but slowly tighten. End with a quieter, more regretful tone, like you're trying to convince yourself this really is the last one.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Embarrassment (slightly present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Aftercare Whisper
instruction: You are a teenage submissive in post-scene aftercare, wrapped in a blanket and sipping water as your Dominant strokes your hair. You feel a quiet disappointment because the scene was cut short, but you're also concentrating on slowing your breath and grounding yourself. As they murmur reassurances, a small awe creeps in at how gentle they are now after the intensity. Let your voice be small, shaky, and child-like at first, then soften into a fragile wonder by the end. Pause to take a sip of water, shift under the blanket, and let a thought trail off as you feel a new wave of trust.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Awe (slightly present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Not My Baby
instruction: You're confronting the doctor who just told you there's nothing more they can do—your child is dying, and they're giving up. Start with disbelief, your voice rising sharp and fierce: 'No. Absolutely not. Try again.' Let maternal rage explode through you—you will fight heaven and earth, you will tear down walls. Your voice should shake with fury and desperation. But then, mid-sentence, the rage collapses. You're begging now, on your knees, voice breaking apart: 'Please. Please, she's only six. She hasn't even—' The tears come, ugly and unstoppable. End in near-whisper, completely helpless: 'Don't let my baby die. I'll do anything.' Let yourself shatter completely.

title: Concealing Pleasure
instruction: You're at your father's funeral—you're supposed to be grieving, should be grieving. But you feel relief, almost joy underneath. You're holding it down, voice appropriately somber. But when someone tells a story that makes you want to laugh—because it's funny, because life is absurd—you have to bury it. The strain of not showing true feeling becomes visible in your vocal tension. For just a moment, your actual relief surfaces before you catch yourself.

title: The Ticking Tickle
instruction: You’re at a small gathering, trying to give a short speech, but a stubborn cough keeps ambushing you mid-sentence. Start by forcing a composed, earnest tone—like you’re fighting to stay professional. Each cough cuts you off, and you feel the irritation rising. Then, right before the next cough, you pause, feel the tickle building, and instead of fighting it, you let out a raspy laugh. End by teasing yourself about the situation, your voice crackly and warm, letting the audience in on the joke.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The High-Wire Victory
instruction: You're an older man, a retired engineer, who just pulled off a daring solo repair on a critical dam control panel to prevent a flood. You feel a flicker of triumph—you did it, you beat the odds. But as you step back, you notice a hairline crack spreading in the concrete wall behind you, and a low rumble grows. Your jaw is clenched from the stimulant you took to stay awake, your mouth is dry, and words tumble out faster than you can think. Start with a breathless, proud declaration, then let the realization of the impending collapse shatter your composure into raw, pressured fear.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Whispered Confession in the Hospital Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM in a hospital room. Your best friend lies sleeping after a crisis that nearly took them from you. You've been holding everything together for everyone else, but now, in the quiet darkness, you finally speak the truth you've never said aloud. Begin in a whisper, telling them—even though they can't hear—how terrified you were, how you can't imagine the world without them. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost just breath, but filled with more emotion than any shout could carry. Let long pauses hang in the air. Halfway through, shift to confessing something you've kept secret—maybe how much you need them, maybe a regret, maybe a truth about yourself you've hidden. Your voice should catch, break on certain words, recover, then break again. End with the smallest, most tender declaration of love or gratitude, barely audible, as tears finally come.
inspired_by: Acting Interested in a Hobby You Dont Enjoy

title: Hostage Negotiator Having a Panic Attack
instruction: You're on the phone negotiating a hostage situation, and a panic attack hits. Your professional training voice must override your hyperventilating body. Between calm, measured sentences to the hostage-taker, mute the phone and gasp for air. Your partner feeds you grounding cues. Unmute — perfectly steady. Mute — falling apart. The oscillation between controlled authority and private terror. Include the moment you talk the person down despite barely being able to breathe yourself.

title: Reading Mean Comments About Yourself
instruction: You're a content creator reading hate comments aloud. Start detached and amused — 'Oh, this one's creative.' Read progressively crueler comments, trying to maintain the armor of humor. But one hits something real. Your reading voice stops. Silence. When you resume, the brightness is gone. Try to joke about it — the joke doesn't land. Include the decision to either close the laptop (choosing peace) or respond (choosing war). Either way, the vulnerability has already been exposed.

title: Gravel and Glare
instruction: You're a young man in a dim alley, your voice permanently wrecked from years of chain-smoking and worse. Your throat is raw, you keep clearing it, each breath a rasp. Someone smaller than you has just shoved you—and you're terrified. At first, your voice shakes, high and reedy with fear, but as you speak, you feel the old, familiar malice creep up your spine. Let the gravel deepen. Let the pitch drop. End with a low, deliberate threat—spit the words out slowly, like you're savoring the danger. Your body might twitch, glance over your shoulder, then lock eyes.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Foam and Future
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, tough voice, standing alone in a bathroom at 1 AM, brushing your teeth aggressively. The toothbrush is in your mouth, making you mumble and slur through foam and bristle noise. Start by muttering irritatedly about the toothpaste dripping on your shirt—annoyed, distracted. Then, as you continue scrubbing, let your thoughts drift to a huge life decision you've been avoiding. Your voice softens, slows, and becomes intensely introspective, even as your words are garbled. By the end, a quiet realization surfaces, and you finish with a slightly heavier, more calm breath—still brushing, but your eyes are distant.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording your final message to Earth before passing beyond communication range forever. Begin with controlled excitement about the mission, the wonder of what you're seeing—your voice steady, professional, almost clinical as you describe the stars. But as you realize this is truly goodbye, your composure starts to fracture. The words catch. You're trying to tell your family you love them, that this was worth it, but doubt creeps in—was it? Your breathing becomes uneven. End with a whispered confession of fear mixed with awe, your voice breaking on the word 'beautiful' as you describe what's ahead, knowing no one will ever hear your reply to their next message. The silence after holds both terror and transcendence.

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You are an elderly man at a family gathering. Your granddaughter just told a joke that hit you perfectly, and you are in the throes of a laughing fit—wheezing, gasping, barely able to speak. You try to tell the story of the time you met her grandmother, but the memory is so joyful that it sends you into another round of laughter. Start with giddy, breathless words, fighting to get the story out, and end with a softer, tearful but still amused sigh as you realize how full your heart is.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Last-Minute Update
instruction: You are a teenage news anchor, voice artificially deep and smooth in that polished broadcaster way. You're reporting live about the annual town carnival being cancelled due to storm damage — you feel a clear disappointment, but you keep your news prosody intact. Mid-sentence, your earpiece crackles with a last-minute update: the carnival has been moved to next weekend. Let the relief rush in. Your voice should start with that practiced, slightly hollow anchor tone, then break naturally as you announce the change — a shaky inhale, a tiny laugh, a stumble over words. Let the relief be extremely present, like a weight lifting, and end with a genuine sigh of release.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Light of Evening
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has only hours left to live. Begin by trying to stay strong and cheerful, reminiscing about a funny memory from your youth—keep your voice light, almost forcing the joy. But as you speak, the reality of this being the last conversation crashes over you in waves. Let your voice crack, let the words catch in your throat. By the end, you're no longer trying to be strong; you're confessing how terrified you are of a world without them in it, your voice barely above a whisper, raw and stripped of all pretense. The transformation is from protective cheerfulness to complete, vulnerable devastation.
inspired_by: A director is giving result direction rather than process guidance

title: The Last Light Through Hospital Windows
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. Begin by speaking aloud your hesitation to say what needs to be said—acknowledge your fear, your not knowing where to start, your throat closing up. Then, as light begins filtering through the blinds, start describing what you see in her face, her hands, the room around you. Let these observations become the doorway into finally telling her what she meant to you, how she shaped you, what you'll carry forward. Your emotional journey moves from paralyzed reluctance and fear through tender observation into profound gratitude mixed with searing grief. Let the act of seeing and naming what's in front of you unlock the words you thought you couldn't say.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty starting the imaging process

title: The Last Call Home
instruction: You're a soldier calling your parent from a forward operating base, knowing this is likely your last conversation before a mission you probably won't survive. You start with forced cheerfulness—'Hey, just wanted to hear your voice'—trying to sound casual, asking about the garden, the neighbor's dog, mundane things that suddenly feel sacred. But as they talk about next Thanksgiving, your voice begins to fracture. You need to say 'I love you' in a way that contains everything—all the fights you had as a teenager, all the times you didn't say it, all the moments you took them for granted. The words start strong, then break completely. End with you trying to memorize the sound of their breathing, whispering 'I have to go now' when you desperately don't want to. Let your voice carry both fierce protectiveness—you don't want them to know—and the terrible need to be held one more time.

title: The Last Morning in the Garden
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother in her hospice room, but she keeps asking you to describe the garden from her childhood home—a place that no longer exists. Begin by feeling the clinical coldness of the hospital room, the antiseptic smell, the fluorescent lights. Then, as you speak to her, transport yourself INTO that garden she loved: feel the morning dew on your bare feet, smell the jasmine climbing the fence, hear the bees in the lavender, taste the mint leaves she used to pick for tea, see the dappled sunlight through the apple tree. Let this sensory world become so real that you're no longer in a hospital—you're THERE with her, young again. Start with grief and clinical distance, but as the garden becomes real to you, let wonder, love, and profound gratitude flood through you. Your final words to her should come from inside that garden, not the hospital room.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill a time-and-place obligation where the actual stage environment is inadequate or wrong for the scene

title: Holding the Coat of Someone Who Jumped
instruction: You're standing at the bridge railing, holding your best friend's jacket—they jumped moments ago and you couldn't stop them. Begin in shock, voice hollow and mechanical as you describe what just happened, as if reporting it might make it less real. Then the fury erupts—screaming at them, at yourself, at God, at the universe. You're bellowing into the void, voice raw with rage at their choice, at your helplessness. But the rage can't sustain itself, and it crumbles into gasping, broken sobbing. You sink down, clutching their jacket, and your voice becomes small, childlike, begging them to come back, promising things you know are impossible. End with a terrifying quiet—you're talking to them as if they can still hear you, voice gentle now, telling them it's okay, you understand, you forgive them, even as your own world disintegrates.

title: The Last Bath: Washing Your Dying Parent
instruction: You're gently bathing your parent in their final days, seeing their body - once so strong, now frail and vulnerable. Begin with controlled tenderness, your voice barely steady as you say 'Let me help you.' As you wash their arms, their back, you notice every change time has carved into them, and memories flood in - being held by these hands, carried by these arms. Your voice starts to crack with the weight of impending loss: 'I remember when you used to lift me...' The role reversal devastates you. By the end, you're whispering through tears, touching their face with infinite genterness: 'You're still so beautiful to me. You always will be.' Let grief and gratitude merge until they're indistinguishable.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, whispering something you've never told anyone—a shameful secret, a deep fear, something that makes you feel exposed and small. Begin trying to say it 'right,' to frame it in a way that won't make them leave. But between your careful words, let in what's actually happening: the sound of their breathing, the feeling of your own heart, the specific fear in your stomach, how your voice sounds too loud then too quiet. Don't decide how vulnerable to be—report what's genuinely there. Notice if you're holding your breath, if tears are coming or not coming, if you want to laugh nervously or stop talking entirely. Let these real observations interrupt and reshape what you're saying. Move from controlled confession to unguarded intimacy, where you're no longer managing the moment but surrendering to it.
inspired_by: The actor has lost contact with organic impulse life during the scene—is on automatic pilot, leadership, or result-consciousness

title: Sci-Fi: Diplomat Realizes Peace Treaty Will Require Sacrificing an Entire Species
instruction: Negotiating at the table, your diplomatic voice is smooth and strategic. Then you read the fine print—peace requires eliminating the third party species. Your voice becomes uncertain. You're being asked to orchestrate genocide for peace. Your breathing becomes shallow. Your voice must continue negotiating while you're contemplating species-level murder. You're choosing between two species and one must cease. Your voice becomes the sound of impossible calculation. You sign the treaty and your voice becomes someone who will carry this calculation forever.

title: The Last Light in Her Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She cannot speak anymore, but her eyes are open. Begin by simply watching her breathe—really seeing the rise and fall of her chest, the flutter of her eyelids, the way the afternoon light catches the silver in her hair. Let yourself wonder about things you've never asked: what was her first heartbreak? What did she dream about as a girl? What does she see when she looks at you now? As you speak to her, let your curiosity about who she truly was—beyond 'grandmother'—transform your farewell from dutiful goodbye into a tender excavation of a whole person you're only now truly seeing. Your emotion should travel from nervous obligation to profound, aching connection and finally to grateful heartbreak as you realize you're witnessing the complete story of a human life in her face.

title: The Nightmare That Saved Your Life
instruction: You are screaming the contents of a literal, terrifying dream at someone you love who is about to make a catastrophic mistake. Begin with explosive urgency - rapid-fire descriptions of what you saw, your voice raw and desperate. But as they dismiss it as 'just a dream,' your intensity should fracture. Rage dissolves into pleading, pleading into sobbing frustration, then finally into a helpless whisper: 'I watched you die. Every night for three months, I watched you die.' End with your voice breaking completely as you describe the last image - not literally anymore, but with devastating emotional honesty - admitting that you're terrified, that you can't lose them, that you don't care if they think you're crazy. Move from fierce protectiveness to complete emotional collapse.

title: Empty Court Echoes
instruction: You are an older man alone in a cavernous, empty gymnasium late at night, drunk from a flask you keep pulling from your coat. The harsh metallic flutter of the echo makes your voice sound thin and lost. You start by slurring out a boast about the old days, but as you hear your words bounce back empty, you trail off, distracted by a distant sneaker squeak or the thump of a loose ball. Your tone shifts from sentimental bravado into a hollow, sorrowful admission of how far you've fallen. Speak about 60 words, letting the alcohol slow your thoughts and the silence between them grow heavy.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Leaving: Your Best Friend's One-Way Ticket
instruction: Your closest friend is leaving for something incredible—a dream opportunity, a new life across the world—and you're genuinely happy for them while your heart is shattering. Start with authentic excitement, your voice bright with joy: 'You did it! You actually did it!' You're laughing, celebrating, recounting the journey that got them here. But underneath, grief is rising. Your laughter becomes textured with tears you're trying to hide: 'God, I'm so proud of you, I—' Your voice cracks. You try to laugh it off, but you can't anymore. The tears come even as you're still smiling: 'I'm sorry, I'm being ridiculous, this is amazing, it's just—' The contradictions flood through you—genuine joy for their triumph, devastating loss for yourself, gratitude for having had them, terror of the absence coming. Your voice oscillates between laughing and crying, sometimes in the same breath: 'I love you so much and I'm so happy for you and I don't know how to do my life without you in it.' End with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob, pure and real and completely unguarded, as you pull them into an embrace that holds both celebration and goodbye.
inspired_by: Sharing Your Diagnosis With Someone You Love

title: The Moment You Realize You Cannot Save Them
instruction: You're holding someone—a friend, a lover, a stranger, a child—who is hurt, dying, or in crisis beyond your control. Begin with fierce determination, voice strong and commanding: 'Stay with me. Look at me. You're going to be fine.' You're giving instructions, applying pressure, doing everything you know to do. But as seconds pass and nothing changes, your certainty crumbles. Your voice climbs in pitch and desperation, commands becoming pleas. Then the helplessness hits and your words dissolve into something primal—not quite screaming, but a sound that comes from somewhere deeper than language. End in shattered whispers, still talking to them but now just begging, your love and your powerlessness colliding in every breath.
inspired_by: Recounting Trauma to a Stranger Therapist

title: The Secret Passage
instruction: You are a young man, a fan, who has snuck into an abandoned section of a famous music venue. You're crawling through a narrow, dusty crawlspace, trying to reach a spot you've heard has a perfect acoustic view of the main stage. You're supposed to be terrified of getting caught, but the thrill of the risk and the pure ecstasy of the muffled, live music you can hear through the walls is overwhelming. Start with a shaky, breathy whisper of determination, as you struggle in the tight darkness. As you inch forward and the music becomes clearer, your voice transforms—your words become a ragged, euphoric laugh, a whispered confession of pure joy, all while your body is still cramped and contorted.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Mother Who Cannot Save Her Child
instruction: You have just learned that your child has made a choice—an addiction, a toxic relationship, a dangerous path—that you are powerless to stop. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: 'You don't understand what you're doing to yourself!' Let your voice be strong, commanding, desperate with the need to control and fix. But as you speak, you hit the wall of your own helplessness, and that ferocity cracks like ice. Your voice breaks mid-sentence, rage dissolving into gasping sobs, then into a raw, animal grief. End on your knees, metaphorically and vocally, with a whispered plea that is no longer a command but a prayer: 'Please don't make me bury you.' The arc must travel from powerful fury to complete emotional collapse, showing both the warrior and the utterly broken heart.
inspired_by: The Teacher and the Defiant Student

title: The Prompter's Secret: Whispered Love From the Wings
instruction: You're the theater prompter, hidden in the wings, who has whispered every line to the lead actor for twenty years. Tonight is their farewell performance, and they don't know you've been in love with them this entire time. Begin with your professional stage whisper—clear, projected enough to reach them but invisible to the audience, the voice that's saved them a thousand times. During a scene change in near darkness, shift to your real voice, barely audible, as you confess everything you've never said. Your voice should tremble with tenderness and the weight of two decades of silent devotion. Let gratitude mix with heartbreak—thank them for letting you be close while acknowledging the torture of loving someone who never saw you. End with a whisper so quiet it might not even reach them, accepting that some love stories are only witnessed from the shadows.

title: The Last Coherent Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the last hour before she slips into unconsciousness forever. She's lucid now, but fading fast. Begin with the careful, almost cheerful denial—pretending this is just another visit, talking about next week's plans. But as her hand grows colder in yours, let the reality crush through your defenses. Reconstruct every detail: the antiseptic smell mixing with her lavender perfume, the particular blue of her lips, the rhythm of the machines, the weight of her bird-thin fingers. Feel yourself transition from protective numbness to desperate, raw grief—whispering all the things you've never said, your voice breaking, begging her to hear you one last time. End in a place of devastating acceptance, barely able to breathe the final 'I love you.'
inspired_by: Imaging as Craft Technique with Affective Memory

title: The Inheritance of Invisible Things
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or child) about something they gave you that no one else can see—an invisible inheritance. Begin with frustration and anger, accusing them of passing down their fears, their silences, their way of loving poorly. But as you speak, start to imagine this invisible thing becoming visible: is it a heavy cloak? A swarm of moths? A garden growing in your chest? Describe what you see in specific detail. Let your imagination show you its texture, weight, color, sound. As you explore this imagined manifestation, your anger begins to shift—perhaps you discover it's also beautiful, or that you've transformed it into something they never intended, or that you're grateful for its strange gifts. End in a place of complex understanding, speaking to them about this invisible thing that now feels utterly real to both of you.

title: The Confession I Keep Revising
instruction: Late at night, alone or with someone who loves you unconditionally, you're whispering about a moment of shame—something you did or failed to do that you've never forgiven yourself for. Begin by speaking the truth quietly, feeling the full weight of your self-judgment and disgust. Your voice should be barely audible, constricted with shame. Then, start telling it differently. Whisper the revised version where you made the braver choice, where you were kinder, where you didn't fail. Tell this new version again. And again. Each time, let your voice open slightly more, let your breath come easier. The repetition isn't about lying—it's about finding the person you're capable of being, even if you weren't that person then. By the final telling, your whisper should carry not shame but tender self-forgiveness, perhaps even quiet wonder at your own capacity for change. Move from suffocating guilt to breathing space, from self-hatred to fragile self-compassion.

title: Rose Thorn and a Memory
instruction: You're in your garden, trimming a favorite rosebush. A sharp thorn jabs deep into your fingertip—you yelp and pull your hand back, sucking the bead of blood. As the sting fades to a throb, you look at the rose and think of the person who gave you this plant years ago. Let your voice start with that involuntary gasp, then shift into a tender, wistful murmur as you speak to them in your mind—the pain still present, but your longing and affection softening the edges. Allow small hitches in your breath, a quiet laugh at the memory, and the weight of missing them.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Wine-Stained Hour
instruction: You are in a dimly lit room with your lover, skin warm, a glass of wine half-drunk on the bedside table. The world is soft and blurry at the edges — the wine and the pleasure weaving through you. But one thought sneaks in: you saw them laugh with someone else tonight, a grin that felt too easy, too shared. You try to push it away, but it sticks. Start with pure surrender — moans and smiles against their neck — then let the envy creep in, turning your voice restless, a little shaky, as you tease it out: 'Were you... hers tonight, even for a second?' Your voice should drop from euphoric sighs to a lower, jagged edge, a breath that almost stops on the last word.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Infatuation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Finding the Divorce Papers in Our Memory Box
instruction: You're going through old photos when you find the divorce papers from fifteen years ago, and a strange laugh escapes you: 'Oh God, I forgot we almost didn't make it.' Your voice is light, almost amused: 'Look at this—I had the whole thing filled out. My lawyer's number right there.' But as you read your own handwriting, something shifts. Your voice becomes softer, sad: 'I was so sure we were over. So certain.' You touch an old photo of the two of you, and tears start mixing with quiet laughter: 'You had no idea I'd gotten this far. You were in the other room watching TV.' Your voice cracks with the weight of everything you've survived together: 'And I came so close. So close to signing them.' But now gratitude floods in, deep and overwhelming: 'Thank God I didn't. Thank God for whatever stopped me that night.' You're crying and smiling simultaneously: 'All the years we've had since then—our son, the house, that trip to Ireland—none of it would exist.' Your voice becomes a whisper, full of wonder and relief: 'We almost lost everything before we knew what we had.' Finally, steady and certain: 'I'd choose you again. Every single time.'

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're in hospice, dying, and you're telling your child one final bedtime story—the one you used to tell them when they were small. Start with warmth and the muscle memory of joy, your voice finding those familiar rhythms. But your breath is failing, words slip away mid-sentence, and you have to pause to gather strength. The realization hits you halfway through that this is the last time—this exact moment—and grief breaks through the tenderness. You push through because you need them to have this, fighting your body's shutdown. Your voice becomes a whisper, but you're smiling through tears, and by the end, you're not finishing the story—you're telling them it's okay, that they know how it ends, that they'll be alright. The love remains whole even as you fracture.

title: Whispered Confession in the Dark
instruction: Late at night, lying beside someone you love, you finally speak the truth you've been hiding. Begin in a whisper, voice barely audible, each word requiring courage: 'I need to tell you something I've never said.' Your throat catches on every phrase. As you confess—perhaps a betrayal, a fear, a terrible choice you made—your voice wavers between numbness and breaking. There are long pauses where breathing is the only sound. The vulnerability intensifies until you're speaking through silent tears, voice fragile as glass. End with the terrifying question: 'Can you still love me?' The arc moves from protective distance to naked, trembling exposure.

title: Confronting Your Parent: The Truth About My Childhood
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent how their absence—or their cruelty, or their addiction, or their emotional coldness—shaped your life. Begin with measured control, almost rehearsed, because you've practiced this speech for years. But as you speak, the adult composure gives way to the wounded child still inside you. Your voice cracks between anger ('You were supposed to protect me') and desperate longing for acknowledgment ('Just once, tell me you're sorry'). Include the moment where you realize they may never give you what you need, and you must choose between continued rage or the devastating freedom of letting go. End either with quiet acceptance of their limitations or with walking away, finally choosing yourself.

title: The Spilled Wine
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a formal family dinner, and you've just knocked over a full glass of red wine onto your grandmother's antique lace tablecloth – the one she brought from the old country. In the stunned silence, everyone stares. You have to say something, but your throat is clamped shut. Start with a barely audible, squeaky apology, your voice high and strained as you fight back tears. Then let the distress build until your words crack and you finally whisper a desperate, shaking plea for someone to say it'll be okay.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reunion with the Ghost of Joy
instruction: You're standing in the doorway of your childhood home, now empty and being sold. You haven't been here in twenty years. As you walk through the rooms, you're ambushed by memories of the happiest moments of your life—before the divorce, before the death, before everything fell apart. Begin by laughing softly, genuinely, as you remember something beautiful: dancing in the kitchen, holiday mornings, feeling utterly safe and loved. Let that laughter grow, become fuller, as wave after wave of happy memory floods you. But underneath, you feel the grief rising—because that joy is gone forever, because you can never go back, because everyone from those memories is now lost to you through death, distance, or time. Let your laughter begin to crack and distort, mixing with sobs, until you can't tell if you're laughing or crying. Your body should shake with both emotions simultaneously. Make sounds that are caught between joy and devastation, between gratitude for having had those moments and the unbearable ache of their loss. End curled on the floor in that empty room, making deep, rhythmic sounds of someone holding both the most beautiful and most painful truths at the same time.

title: The Lullaby You Can't Finish
instruction: You're singing a lullaby to your newborn, but your older child—your first baby—died six months ago. Start softly, tenderly, trying to be present for this new life. But certain phrases catch in your throat because they were your other child's favorite parts. Your voice becomes fragile, barely above a whisper, as you try to continue. You're speaking now, not singing, telling this baby about their sibling they'll never meet, and your voice is so gentle but breaking apart. There's profound love for the child in your arms mixed with grief so deep it has no bottom. End with you attempting the final line of the lullaby—your voice small, young, like you're the child needing comfort—and the realization that you're singing to both children, to the one here and the one gone.

title: The Storm Inside
instruction: You're talking to someone who broke your heart so completely that you can still feel it as physical pain in your chest. Begin with your body tight, your voice controlled, determined to tell them calmly how much damage they caused. But as you speak—and as you imagine their face, their voice, the way they might look at you—let the control start to fracture. Your body should respond before your words do: maybe your hands shake, maybe you have to brace yourself against something, maybe your breath becomes ragged. Allow the physical sensations to intensify the emotional ones and vice versa. The passion—whether rage or desperate longing or both—should build until it becomes almost unbearable. By the end, your body and voice should be completely transformed from the controlled beginning.

title: Three A.M. Pillow Talk
instruction: You are lying in the dark beside your partner of ten years, whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something about your past that fills you with shame. Begin with your whole body tense, curled slightly away, voice barely audible and tight in your throat. You're terrified of being fully known. As you speak, focus on releasing the physical holding—unclenching your jaw, letting your breathing deepen and slow, allowing your body to unfold toward them. Feel your voice gradually open, becoming fuller, more resonant, though still quiet. By the end, you are lying open, vulnerable, your breathing easy, speaking from your chest and belly rather than your constricted throat. The fear dissolves into relief, into the safety of being witnessed without armor.

title: The Last Cup
instruction: You are an elderly person alone in your kitchen after a visit from your daughter. The caffeine and sugar from the coffee and cake have worn off, leaving you sluggish and irritable. You look at the empty chair where she sat, bitterness rising at how quickly she always leaves. But as you pick up the mug she used, a wave of longing crashes in—you miss the sound of her laugh. Let your voice start slow and resentful, then soften into a shaky, almost childlike ache. Hesitate, sigh, let your words trail off as you struggle with the weight of the memory.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Lost Word
instruction: You are a woman recovering from a stroke, speaking to your young child. You want to express relief that you can finally say 'I love you' again, but the word gets tangled. Start with strained, frustrated effort as you grope for the sound. Feel the frustration build as wrong syllables come out. Then, as you finally find the words, let the relief flood in—your voice softens, you laugh a little at the struggle, and the last part comes out warm and clear.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Spirit Meeting
instruction: Two people are meeting as spiritual beings, not just personalities or bodies. Their voices carry a quality that's hard to define—presence, essence, authenticity. They're not performing for each other; they're meeting as their truest selves. The conversation might be brief or deep. What matters is the quality of presence. By the end, both voices carry the mark of having been truly seen. Spirit meeting spirit is a profound recognition. Both voices reflect the specific quiet power that comes from that recognition.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight That Won't Return
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love deeply—a parent, a child, a soulmate—and they're about to board a plane for a dangerous mission, a terminal diagnosis journey, or something from which they may never return. They keep talking about practical things—did you water the plants, remember to pay the bills—and you're dying inside because you need to say what really matters, but they keep deflecting with mundane details. Start with forced lightness, trying to honor their need for normalcy. Let your voice crack as you gently interrupt, increasingly desperate to break through the surface conversation. End with raw vulnerability, finally saying what your heart has been screaming, even as you realize they might be avoiding depth because it's the only way they can get on that plane. Your composure must shatter, but beautifully, like finally letting someone see your whole heart.
inspired_by: Maintaining Patience While Being Repeatedly Interrupted

title: The Last Light in the Room
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin in numb silence, unable to find words, your body heavy with the weight of everything unsaid over thirty years. Let sound emerge from deep in your belly—wordless at first, just breath and broken attempts at speech. As memories flood unbidden (that summer you were inseparable, the fight that distanced you, the years of Christmas cards and surface-level catch-ups), allow your voice to crack open, building from whispered fragments to full confessions of love, regret, and gratitude. By the end, you must arrive at a place of raw peace, your final words simple and clear, having broken through your own walls to say what matters most.

title: The Inheritance of Fury
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just told you they're cutting you out of their life. Begin defensive and hurt, your voice tight with the effort of staying calm, trying to explain yourself, justify your parenting choices. As they list your failures—the ways you were absent, critical, overbearing—feel your defensiveness turn to indignation, then to raw anger. Let yourself escalate: louder, fiercer, refusing to be made the villain. Shout about your sacrifices, everything you gave up for them, how dare they reduce you to your worst moments. Reach a peak of full-bodied rage—then hear yourself. Really hear the words coming out of your mouth and recognize them: they're the same words your own parent once screamed at you. Let the realization stop you cold. End in a broken whisper, finally saying what you've never said: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. I didn't know how to love you better.'

title: Pace Intensity
instruction: You're a radio announcer doing a play-by-play of a championship game in its final moments. Begin slow and measured: 'The score is tied. 10 seconds on the clock.' As the action intensifies, your pace accelerates: 'He's at the 30-yard line! 5 seconds! The crowd is going INSANE!' You're practically shrieking, words overlapping: 'AND HE SHOOTS — IT'S GOOD! THEY WIN!' Your pace has hit maximum intensity. Then, one second of silence. You speak at normal pace, voice shot: 'Unbelievable.' The intensity was the experience; the normal pace after is the devastation and relief.

title: The Last Blanket Before the Long Winter
instruction: You're wrapping your dying mother in her favorite blanket for the last time, knowing she won't make it through the night. Start by describing the texture and warmth with forced cheerfulness, trying to comfort her, trying to pretend this is just another evening. But as you tuck it around her shoulders, let the reality crack through—your voice should break as you realize this simple act of covering her is the last thing you can do. End in a whisper, telling her it's okay to let go, that you'll keep yourself warm without her, even though you both know that's a lie. Let the tenderness mix with devastating grief, speaking from a place of love so deep it physically hurts.
inspired_by: Feeling the Weight of a Soft Blanket on Your Shoulders

title: The Morning Report
instruction: You're an elderly woman who just woke up, still lying in bed, half in the dark. Your throat is scratchy, your lips dry, your voice a gravelly whisper. But you just remembered—you finished knitting the blanket for your great-grandchild last night, and it's perfect. A fierce, quiet triumph swells in your chest. You're eager, interested to check it, but your body feels heavy and slow. You notice a faint ache in your hip, a small helplessness. Your voice starts as a croak, thick with sleep, then as you talk to the blanket (or yourself), it slowly warms, gains a little brightness, though still rough. You lose your train of thought once, mumble, shift under the covers.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Interest (very intensely present), Helplessness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: I Deserve the Mess
instruction: You're confronting your mother/father who has always demanded perfection, who made you feel that love was conditional on achievement and flawless behavior. They've just criticized you again for a life choice. Start from a place of defense, trying to explain yourself, justifying your decisions. But mid-confrontation, something shifts—you stop defending and start claiming. Declare, with increasing conviction, your right to make mistakes, to be complicated, to figure things out slowly, to waste time, to fail spectacularly. Your emotion should arc from apologetic and small to powerful and unapologetic. Let anger mix with liberation. By the end, you're not asking for their approval—you're announcing who you've decided to become, mess and all. Make them hear what you're claiming for yourself.

title: The Blanket Fort Confession
instruction: You are lying in darkness next to someone you deeply love, unable to sleep. In this vulnerable, whispered intimacy, you decide to share something you've never told anyone—a childhood fear that still lives in you, a moment of shame or terror that shaped who you became. Start with hesitant, fragmented phrases, your voice barely audible, as if speaking too loudly will make it too real. As you describe the memory, use all your senses—let yourself feel the texture of childhood pajamas, smell the particular scent of your childhood room, hear the sounds that frightened you. Your voice should become younger, smaller, more childlike as you inhabit the memory. By the end, arrive at a place of tender relief, feeling truly seen and held for the first time, your adult self comforting the child within you through the act of finally speaking the unspeakable.
inspired_by: Revisiting and Re-Creating Childhood Environments, Events, Friends, and Toys

title: The Returned Letter
instruction: You are holding a letter (or gift, or photograph) from someone who wounded you deeply, and they are standing before you wanting reconciliation. You might habitually respond with bitter sarcasm, or instant forgiveness, or righteous anger, or that familiar weeping that keeps people at bay. Start by feeling that habitual response rising in you, but don't automatically give it voice. Instead, track what's actually coursing through you moment by moment: the contradictory impulses of wanting to embrace them and push them away, the specific memories triggered by the object in your hands, the surprising flickers of tenderness mixed with resentment, or relief tangled with grief. Let your words and your voice follow these real, conflicting currents rather than your signature emotional move. The arc should travel from your practiced emotional defense through increasingly honest acknowledgment of what's actually present—discovering that you feel multiple things at once, some that contradict each other completely.
inspired_by: Actor is prone to emotional dependencies — compulsive laughing, crying, raging — or other repeated emotional shticks

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your childhood home, now destroyed by fire, flood, or time. Everything is gone—photos, heirlooms, the physical proof of your history. Begin by describing what you see with a kind of stunned, surreal calm, almost laughing at the absurdity of the devastation. Let that laugh become real but edged with hysteria. Remember specific objects and tell stories about them with surprising joy—your voice light, almost giddy with memory. But underneath, let the grief bleed through. You're laughing but tears are streaming down your face. The loss is total, but the memories are untouchable, and that paradox is beautiful and unbearable at once. Your voice should dance between laughter and sobbing, sometimes within the same sentence. End with a strange, transcendent gratitude—everything is gone, but you're still here, still remembering, still alive. The destruction has somehow freed you. Let your final words be both celebration and elegy.

title: The Science Fair Ribbon
instruction: You're a seven-year-old girl at the school science fair, standing next to your volcano that didn't erupt. Your mom spent a week helping you paint it, and you were so proud this morning. Now kids are laughing, and the judges walked right past. You have to tell your mom what happened. Start with a tiny bit of leftover pride — 'I think the baking soda was old' — but as you explain, your voice shrinks. You're talking more to your shoes than to her. You swallow hard, trail off, and the last words you almost don't say at all. Your eyes sting but you're trying not to cry.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Baby's First Breath
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—maybe you're holding a positive pregnancy test, maybe you've gotten a terminal diagnosis, maybe someone you'd given up for dead is alive. Begin in shock and numbness: you can't quite feel anything yet, you're disconnected, maybe even laughing inappropriately because your system doesn't know how to respond. Stay in that strange, dissociated place where nothing has landed yet. Then, slowly or suddenly, let multiple contradictory feelings crash into you simultaneously: hope and terror, joy and rage, gratitude and bitter resentment, desperate love and furious grief. Don't resolve them into one clear emotion—let them fight inside you. Your voice might laugh while you're crying, you might say 'thank god' with the intonation of a curse, you might whisper 'I love you' like an accusation. End in a place where you're feeling everything at once, completely broken open, unable and unwilling to make it make sense.
inspired_by: Actor feels blocked during a rehearsal and cannot access the needed emotional life

title: Trust Deepened
instruction: You're being trusted in a new way by your partner—with their body, their vulnerability, their desires. Your voice becomes reverent with the responsibility: 'I will take care of this. I will take care of you.' Your partner believes you. Their voice is confident in your reliability. You're building trust through actions and through voice—through showing up, through honesty, through consistent care. Each time you prove trustworthy, the intimacy deepens. Your voice becomes the sound of someone who's been given tremendous responsibility and who takes it seriously. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's earned trust through genuine commitment.

title: Your Hands on My Skin
instruction: You're in an intensely intimate physical moment with a lover, and suddenly a childhood sense-memory floods through your body—maybe the feeling of being held safely for the first time, or running wild and free, or the physical sensation of a moment when you felt utterly alive as a child. Begin breathless and present in the adult physical experience, your voice raw with desire. As the childhood sense-memory overtakes you, let your voice shift—speak the memory aloud as if you're experiencing it NOW, the child's sensation merging with the adult's body. Your voice should blur between adult passion and child-like wonder, your breathing changing as the two experiences layer over each other. End with your voice breaking as you realize you're feeling something you thought you'd lost forever—complete, unselfconscious freedom in your own body. The physical intensity should reach a crescendo that's part passion, part grief for lost innocence, part ecstatic reunion with your truest self.

title: Three AM Confessions
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone—a lover, a spouse, a best friend who's staying over—and you cannot sleep because a secret is suffocating you. Begin in whispered hesitation: 'Are you awake?' Your voice is barely audible, fragile as paper. Start by circling the truth, testing the waters with small confessions that build to the real one. Perhaps it's 'I'm not who you think I am,' or 'I've been terrified you'll leave,' or 'I did something I can't take back.' Let shame and fear color every word—your breath should be uneven, your throat tight. As you confess, don't rush. Let silence live between your words. The transformation comes as you speak the unspeakable: feel the terror of exposure shift gradually into the strange, unexpected relief of being fully known. End in vulnerable openness, your voice still quiet but no longer hiding, asking without words: will you stay now that you know?

title: Whispered Truths in a Hospital Bed
instruction: They're sleeping, hooked up to machines, and you don't know if they can hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper—you're confessing everything you were too scared to say when they were awake. Start with small admissions, your voice catching on tender memories, apologizing for petty arguments that don't matter now. The words come in broken phrases, interrupted by the rhythm of the machines, by the weight in your chest. You're telling them you understand now—things they tried to teach you, sacrifices you didn't see. Your voice gets even softer, more intimate, as if you're sharing the most precious secret. You're not asking them to wake up, you're just giving them permission to rest, your voice breaking on love you never quite knew how to express until this moment when you might lose the chance forever.

title: The Wedding Toast You Didn't Prepare
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, but this friend is marrying someone you believe is wrong for them—someone who slowly isolated them from you over the past two years. You're holding a microphone, looking at your friend's radiant face, genuinely happy for the first time in months. Begin with the expected congratulations, but let the facade crack. You're trying to be happy for them, and part of you truly is—they're glowing, they're in love. But you're also losing them, and you're angry they couldn't see what this person did, and you're heartbroken that you'll never matter as much again. Let these emotions war in your voice: celebrate their joy while mourning your loss. Shift between genuine warmth and barely concealed pain, between blessing them and quietly saying goodbye to who you were together. End with words that sound like celebration but feel like a funeral, where love and grief are so tangled you can't separate them.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a lifetime of emotional absence. Start with your voice trembling, careful, years of suppressed need barely contained: 'I need to tell you something I should have said decades ago.' Your words are measured but emotion bleeds through. Then let the dam break—voice rising with accumulated pain: 'I needed you to see me, to ask how I was, to care!' Rage mixes with desperate longing. Your breathing becomes ragged as you confess the child still inside you: 'I'm forty years old and I'm still waiting for you to be proud of me.' Let your voice crack, raw and exposed. End with quiet devastation, almost a whisper, as you realize they may never be able to give you what you need: 'I can't keep waiting anymore. I have to let you go.' The final words carry both grief for what will never be and the first fragile breath of freedom.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Love You Never Felt
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally speaking a truth you've carried for decades. Start with your voice shaking, almost apologetic: 'Mom, I need to tell you something I've never been able to say.' Build into raw, painful honesty—not shouting, but with increasing intensity: 'I spent my whole childhood waiting for you to see me. Really see me.' Let anger crack through: 'I was right there, and you looked past me every single time.' But then something breaks—your voice splinters as grief overtakes the anger, and you're suddenly small again, vulnerable: 'I just wanted you to love me the way I needed.' End with exhausted acceptance, your voice barely above a whisper, almost tender despite everything: 'I know you did the best you could. But it wasn't enough. And I need you to know that.'
inspired_by: Creating Your Final Memory in Your Childhood Home

title: Eulogy for Your Rival—The One Who Made You Better
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who was your fiercest competitor, maybe even your enemy, and you're discovering feelings you didn't know you had. Start with wry humor, almost laughing: 'They would absolutely hate that I'm doing this.' There's genuine affection mixed with old frustration. But as you talk about how they pushed you, challenged you, refused to let you settle, your voice fills with unexpected gratitude. 'I was better because they existed.' Then the realization hits: you'll miss them. Terribly. The humor fades and your voice thick with grief you didn't see coming: 'Who's going to call me on my nonsense now?' You're crying but also smiling at a memory, your voice breaking and lifting at the same time. End with a paradox: 'I'm furious they're gone' delivered with tender devastation. It's loss and love and laughter all tangled together, impossible to separate.

title: Breaking Open
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal discovered, a miracle, a loss. You're alone in your apartment, and the information is moving through your body like electricity. Your hands are shaking. Start trying to hold yourself together—pacing, breathing deliberately, talking to yourself in short rational phrases to stay in control. But your body won't cooperate. Maybe you laugh inappropriately, or a sound comes out that surprises you. Let the physical sensations take over: your chest tightening, heat rising to your face, your legs weakening. You might sink to the floor, or brace yourself against a wall, or double over. Allow primal sounds—not performed crying or screaming, but the organic, sometimes ugly noises that real bodies make when feeling threatens to split us open. Mix this physical intensity with fractured thoughts spoken aloud: rage at the universe, bargaining, disbelief, addressing someone who isn't there. Don't perform a single emotion—let contradictions crash into each other: fury and terror, grief and wild laughter, desperation and strange euphoria. By the end, you're physically exhausted but somehow emptied out, sitting in the wreckage of your control, breathing like you've surfaced from deep water. You've survived something.
inspired_by: An actor wants to develop their imagination

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged father from your hospital bed. You have hours, maybe a day left. Begin the call angry—you've rehearsed all the things you wanted to say to him for years, the accusations, the abandonments. But as you speak, something shifts. Maybe it's exhaustion, maybe it's the morphine, maybe it's just finally hearing his voice. Let your prepared speech fall apart. Notice when your words start feeling hollow or performative, and in those moments, simply speak what's actually true for you right now—your fear, your regret, what you wish you'd said twenty years ago. By the end, you're no longer accusing. You're asking him to remember you. Let the anger dissolve into something more naked and essential. Your voice may break, or quiet to almost nothing. End somewhere you didn't expect to arrive.
inspired_by: Actor's impulsive flow is interrupted during a long run or performance; self-consciousness creeping in

title: Everything You Never Said
instruction: Confront your aging parent who is sitting across from you at their kitchen table. You came here to be polite, to check in, to keep up appearances—but decades of unspoken hurt suddenly refuses to stay buried. Begin by making small talk, your voice tight and controlled, discussing their garden or the news. But resentment starts bleeding through. Your words become sharper, more pointed. Build from passive-aggressive observations to direct accusations about the childhood you needed but never had. Let your voice rise from controlled bitterness to shaking fury, then suddenly collapse into the voice of the child you once were—small, confused, still hoping for an explanation that makes sense. End not with anger but with a devastatingly vulnerable question you've carried for thirty years.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Busy to Avoid a Conversation

title: Grateful Farewell to a Lost Love
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you loved deeply but can no longer be with—perhaps they've chosen someone else, perhaps circumstances have made it impossible, perhaps you've both grown into different people. Begin with a smile in your voice, genuine warmth mixed with heartbreak: 'I'm so glad I met you. Even knowing how this ends, I'm grateful.' Your voice carries bittersweet joy: 'You made me believe I was worth loving. You saw parts of me I'd forgotten existed.' As you continue, tears start mixing with soft laughter: 'Remember when we stayed up all night talking about nothing? That was the happiest I'd ever been.' The contradiction intensifies—you're crying but there's no bitterness, only tenderness: 'I wanted forever with you. God, I wanted forever.' Your voice breaks, but finds its way to something almost peaceful: 'But sometimes love isn't enough, and that's nobody's fault. That's just... the tragedy of being human.' By the end, you're simultaneously devastated and accepting, laughing through tears: 'I hope you find everything you're looking for. I really do. And thank you—thank you for loving me, even if it couldn't last.' The final words are whispered with a smile and wet cheeks: 'You'll always be one of my favorite people. Always.'

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside your sleeping partner, about to walk out of their life because you've been diagnosed with a terminal illness and refuse to let them watch you die. Your voice is barely audible, tender and aching, telling them all the things you could never say while they were awake. Start with soft gratitude, naming specific tiny moments of joy they gave you. Your voice catches as you describe watching them sleep, knowing this is the last time. The tenderness shifts into quiet devastation—you're apologizing for the cowardice of leaving this way, your words breaking apart. End with a barely breathed confession that this is the most loving thing you know how to do, even though it will destroy them. Your final 'goodbye' should be nearly silent, choked with tears you're trying not to let fall.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Car After Earthquake: Checking if Your Passenger is Dead

title: The Last Lecture to a Dying Mentor
instruction: You're standing at your mentor's bedside in hospice, and they've asked you to give them one final 'lecture' on the subject you both loved—the thing they taught you. Begin with careful, controlled composure, trying to honor them professionally, but your voice keeps catching on memories. As you speak about the work, your passion builds and the stutter returns—not from nerves, but from the collision of intellectual fire and devastating grief. You push through: 'And th-this is what you showed me, that...' Your voice breaks. They squeeze your hand weakly. You realize you're not giving a lecture anymore—you're saying goodbye. The stutter softens into something tender. Your final words come out clear and gentle, a gift: 'You made me believe I had something to say.' Let the silence after hold all the love you cannot speak.

title: Burning and Breaking
instruction: You have just received news that the person who destroyed your life—who betrayed you, humiliated you, took everything from you—has died suddenly. You're alone in your apartment when you hear. Begin with a visceral, almost ecstatic rage and triumph: let your body move freely, violently even, as fierce joy floods through you. Laugh, shout, feel the heat of vindication in your chest, the rushing of blood, the sensation of chains breaking. This person is gone and you are FREE. Your body should feel alive, electric, powerful. But as you move and celebrate, allow yourself to notice something unexpected in your physical body: your hands beginning to shake not with rage but with something else, a tightness in your chest that isn't just anger, tears suddenly hot on your face though you're still laughing. The sensation of heat becomes the sensation of something breaking open. Your savage joy must gradually betray you, revealing underneath it a devastating grief—perhaps for lost years, for the impossibility of resolution, for the complicated love you also felt, for the closure you'll never have now that they're gone.

title: The Spasm of Want
instruction: You are an older man on a phone call with someone you once desired deeply, but who betrayed you. Your body betrays you too: a hiccup keeps ripping through your diaphragm, cutting your words with sudden, sharp intakes of air. Begin speaking with cold, bitter contempt, your voice tight and clipped. But as the conversation shifts, a reluctant wave of sexual lust rises in your chest, softening your tone, making your pauses longer. The hiccups become more erratic as your emotions tangle. End with a husky, vulnerable admission—almost a plea—that you still want to see her, even after everything.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Contempt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Waking in Their Skin
instruction: You are experiencing an overwhelming physical sensation—excruciating pain, intense pleasure, fever, exhaustion, or ecstatic release—and simultaneously, you're flooded with the vivid sensation that you are becoming someone else, or that another version of yourself is emerging. Begin by responding to the physical intensity, then let a powerful inner vision or dreamlike transformation take over: perhaps you suddenly feel yourself as the opposite of who you usually are (cruel instead of kind, wild instead of controlled, terrified instead of brave). Let your voice and body shift as this other self possesses you—not performing it externally, but genuinely feeling inhabited by this disowned part of yourself. End by either fighting it back or surrendering to it completely. Move from physical intensity through uncanny transformation to either resistance or liberation.
inspired_by: When integrating dreams into the programming process

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your absent parent everything you've held back for decades. Start with sarcastic politeness—'Oh, so now you want to have coffee and catch up?'—that barely masks decades of abandonment. Let your voice drip with that cutting, defensive humor people use when they're terrified of showing how much they've been hurt. But as you speak, the jokes start failing you. The sarcasm breaks. You hear yourself saying things you swore you'd never say out loud: how you looked for them in every crowd, how you practiced conversations with them that never happened, how their absence shaped everything. End with exhausted vulnerability, the anger drained away, just the raw wound of a child who needed them and they weren't there.

title: Reading Your Daughter's Diary the Night She Ran Away
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your teenage daughter left hours ago—no note, just an empty room. You've found her diary and you're reading it aloud in whispers, as if she might hear you. Start with the recent entries: her plans, her reasons, the boy she's with. Your voice is searching, detective-like, looking for clues. But then you find older entries—poems she wrote about feeling invisible in your house, a entry from her thirteenth birthday where she wrote 'Mom walked right past me today.' Feel your throat close. Let the words catch as you read her pain back to yourself. Your whisper should become textured with tears you're trying to swallow. Realize with quiet devastation that she left you years before she walked out. End reading her last entry—'I don't think she'll even notice I'm gone'—and let that land in total silence. No drama, just the sound of a heart understanding its own failure.
inspired_by: Birth and Death in the Same Hospital

title: Whispered Memory of Warmth in the Cold
instruction: You're alone in a cold, empty room, holding an imaginary cup—remembering a moment of warmth with someone who's gone. Speak in hushed, intimate tones, as if afraid to disturb the memory itself. Begin by describing the phantom sensation of heat in your palms, the imagined taste on your tongue, but let your voice reveal you're barely holding yourself together.
