This isn't about the drink—it's about the person who used to make it for you, who used to care. Let silence hang between phrases, your breath catching as grief threatens to overwhelm you. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost just breath, trembling with the effort of not breaking down completely. End with a heartbreaking admission spoken to the empty room: you'd give anything for one more cup, one more moment, one more chance to say what you never said.
inspired_by: Sipping a Cup of Hot Chocolate on a Cold Day

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about a specific lie he told when you were twelve—a lie that shaped every choice you made afterward. Begin with controlled anger, citing facts, presenting evidence like a prosecutor. But as you speak, something shifts: you start to see his face differently, the way his shoulders carry decades of his own shame, and you realize this lie wasn't about you at all—it was about his terror, his failure, his desperation to be someone he wasn't. Your anger must transform mid-confrontation into something more complex: a devastating recognition that he's just as lost as you were. End not with forgiveness exactly, but with a quiet, painful understanding that breaks down the wall between you. Your voice should move from sharp and accusatory to softer, almost confused, as the revelation changes everything.

title: The Scent of Everything You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're holding a bottle of expensive lotion—a gift from a parent who was always absent, who sent presents instead of presence. Begin by describing the lotion with bitter appreciation: yes, it's luxurious, yes, it smells beautiful, yes, they have exquisite taste. Your tone starts controlled, almost mockingly gracious. But as you apply it, let years of longing surface. The softness of the lotion against your skin makes you realize how much you craved their gentle touch instead of their money. Your voice should build from sarcastic gratitude to raw confrontation, as if they're in the room: 'You knew exactly what I liked—except you never knew me.' Let anger give way to the aching vulnerability of a child who just wanted to be held, ending with the quiet, devastating truth: 'I would have traded every beautiful thing you ever bought me for one afternoon where you stayed.'
inspired_by: Putting on a Favorite Scented Lotion

title: Adult Child: Confronting a Parent About the Silence
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent, finally saying what's been unsaid for decades. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this moment. 'I needed you to see me.' But as you speak, anger you didn't know was there rises up, hot and sharp: 'I was right there. I was always right there, and you looked right through me.' Your voice breaks between rage and pleading. You're forty years old and suddenly you're eight again, desperate for them to understand. Then something shifts—you see their face, their fragility, and the anger collapses into grief. Your voice drops to almost a whisper: 'I just wanted you to love me the way I needed to be loved.' End in the painful space between needing their acknowledgment and knowing you might never get it. Your voice holds both the fury of the wounded child and the weary resignation of the adult who understands, maybe, that they were broken too.

title: Smoke and Giggles
instruction: You are a father trapped in a burning building with your young child. The room is thick with smoke, stinging your eyes and scratching your throat. You’re coughing, voice raspy, struggling to stay calm. Disgust rises as you choke on the acrid air, but you feel a surge of pride watching your kid stay so brave. Then your child makes a silly joke about the smoke monster outside, and despite everything, a wave of amusement overwhelms you — you can’t help but laugh, even as you wheeze. Start with urgent, strained coaxing, then let the amusement crack through your voice, ending on a hoarse, genuine chuckle.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Pride (clearly present), Amusement (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Library Hush
instruction: You're a teenage girl hiding with your best friend in a quiet corner of the library, both of you buzzing from a secret you just shared. Your voice is a breathy whisper—no vocal cord vibration, just air and excitement, because any real sound could get you caught. Start in a state of pure, giddy pleasure/ecstasy, the words tumbling out as you relive the thrill of the moment. Then, as you notice the librarian nearby or hear footsteps, your tone shifts into teasing—playful, conspiratorial, nudging your friend to be even quieter. Let natural micro-distractions slip in: a tiny stifled laugh, a pause as you both crane your necks, the whisper becoming even more hushed and light.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone (lover, friend, sibling) who thinks you're asleep. Begin by whispering something small and seemingly safe - maybe about a dream you just had, or how you can't sleep. But the darkness and their stillness make you feel invisible, protected. Let one honest sentence lead to another. Don't perform confession or dramatic revelation - instead, let the words slip out the way secrets do at 3 AM when defenses are down. Notice the sound of their breathing, the warmth of the space between you, the strange courage that darkness provides. Allow yourself to say something you've never said aloud, not because you planned to, but because in this moment, pretending feels more exhausting than truth. The scene ends when you've said something that changes the air in the room, something you can't take back.
inspired_by: Actor is falling into result consciousness—going for the emotion of a scene rather than working from the moment

title: The Final Orbit
instruction: You are a high school senior giving an unamplified oral report in physics class on Saturn's rings, which you have loved since childhood. You begin with the teacher voice — projected, deliberate, emphasizing terms like 'shepherd moons' — but as you describe the ice crystals catching sunlight, the shame of having been mocked for your passion gives way to a quiet, trembling ecstasy. Let your voice crack, speed up, then slow again; shift your weight, glance at the clock, lose your place for a second as the beauty overtakes you. End softly, almost to yourself: 'They shimmer... like nothing else.'
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Lucid Moment
instruction: Your parent with Alzheimer's has a brief moment of clarity - the first in months. They recognize you, say your name with such tenderness. You're overwhelmed with joy, laughing through tears as you hold their hands: 'Yes, it's me, I'm here.' But even as you're speaking, you can see the fog returning to their eyes. Your voice shifts from elation to desperate pleading, trying to keep them with you just a little longer: 'Stay with me, please don't go yet.' You're watching them slip away again, and your final words are a whisper of devastating acceptance mixed with gratitude for these few precious seconds: 'I love you. Thank you for coming back, even just for this.' The joy and the grief are inseparable.

title: The Heavy Quiet After
instruction: You are an older woman just emerging from a long, hot bath you took to soothe your aching joints. You're now lying in bed, your body heavy and limp, every muscle surrendered to the warmth. As you speak, your voice is languid, warm, and unhurried—but laced with a deep, bone-tired exhaustion. At first, you feel a fragile, peaceful gratitude for the momentary relief from pain. But as you continue, the familiar ache begins to seep back into your hips and lower back, and your voice fills with a quiet, weary resignation. Let your words drift, with pauses for small movements or a soft wince, and let the exhaustion grow heavier until you nearly trail off at the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a childhood wound they've never acknowledged—the times they chose work over you, the affection they withheld, the way their silence taught you that you didn't matter. Start controlled, almost rehearsed, like you've practiced this speech for years. But as you speak, old anger surfaces, your voice getting sharper, more raw. Then something shifts—you hear how old they sound, how small. Your fury collapses into something more complicated: grief for the relationship you'll never have, rage at the time you've lost, and an unwanted tenderness for this flawed human who damaged you. End quietly, no longer seeking their validation, but acknowledging the truth aloud changes you both forever.

title: The Whisper of the Sun
instruction: You are a 9-year-old boy, just out of surgery that restored some hearing after an accident. Your ears are still adjusting, and your own voice booms in your head, too loud and clumsy. You are standing in your hospital room, staring out the window at a golden sunset. Your mother is beside you, trying to speak softly, but you can barely catch her words. Embarrassment burns in your chest—you keep interrupting her, your own voice cracking and too loud. But as you watch the light fade, a quiet awe seeps in: the world looks so different now that you can almost hear its colors. Your voice wavers between that mortified shout and a hushed, trembling wonder. Speak to your mother, trying to share this new feeling, fighting the urge to hide your strange voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Bird in Winter
instruction: You're at your estranged mother's surprise 70th birthday party, seeing her after fifteen years of silence. You're filled with both deep resentment and desperate love. Begin with the brittle, fragile quality of something that might break—small, careful movements, voice thin and uncertain, as if you're walking on ice. As you deliver your speech to her in front of everyone, let two opposing forces battle in your body: the urge to flee (quick, darting, nervous energy) and the pull to stay (heavy, rooted, gravitational). Allow laughter to catch in your throat alongside tears, let your body express both the desire to embrace her and the impulse to protect yourself. End in a place where these opposites somehow coexist—you're both the frightened creature and the one extending a wing in tentative greeting.

title: Chaplain: Delivering a Funeral Eulogy
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone. Your voice starts respectfully formal: 'We gather to honor the life of...' You're speaking for the community's grief. Include the moment where you share something about the person that makes them real—not abstract memory but actual life. Your voice becomes warmer, more personal, as you name what made them matter. 'They made us laugh. They made us think. They made us better.' Your voice cracks slightly on that last one. By the end, your voice becomes almost a blessing: 'May we carry their memory. May we honor their example. May we find peace in their passing.' Your voice has moved through grief and found a kind of acceptance. You've helped people begin to let go.

title: Holding Your Dying Child's Hand
instruction: You're beside your child's hospital bed in their final moments, and they're slipping away. Begin with fierce, almost angry determination—you're telling them to fight, to stay, your voice strong and commanding because if you're strong enough, you can will them to live. Your words become pleas, then desperate bargaining with God, with fate, with anyone who might listen. The intensity is volcanic—you would tear the world apart to save them, and your voice cracks with that helpless rage. But as their breathing changes, something shifts. The fight drains out of you, replaced by the unbearable tenderness of a parent who must let go. End by singing or humming the lullaby you sang when they were born, your voice breaking completely, giving them permission to rest while your own heart shatters.
inspired_by: Pretending to Remember Someones Name You Forgot

title: The Hospital Room Where Everything Changed
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your grandmother in her final hours, but she keeps doing unexpected things—suddenly gripping your hand with surprising strength, staring past you at something unseen, or asking strange questions about your childhood. Start with composed grief, trying to maintain control and say the 'right' things. But her unpredictable moments keep breaking through your rehearsed farewell, forcing you to truly be present with her. Let her unpredictability draw out unplanned confessions, forgotten memories, and raw emotion you didn't intend to share. By the end, you've abandoned all pretense—you're no longer performing grief, you're living in this irreplaceable moment. Let her surprises transform your careful goodbye into something messier, truer, and more devastating than you planned.

title: The Last Recording: A Parent Leaving Instructions They'll Never Deliver
instruction: You're recording a video message for your child, knowing you won't survive the week. Start with practical matters—passwords, bank accounts, where the insurance papers are—your voice steady, almost businesslike, keeping emotions in check because you need to get through this. But then you stumble on something small: a memory of their first day of school, or the way they laughed at breakfast last Tuesday. The practical recitation crumbles. Your voice breaks into raw, unguarded love and devastating grief—all the things you never said, all the moments you'll miss. Try to pull yourself back to the instructions, but you can't. End in whispered apologies mixed with fierce, protective love, your voice barely holding together as you tell them how to live without you.
inspired_by: Old Person Telling a Story They've Told a Hundred Times

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed at dawn, knowing these are her final hours. Begin with quiet observation—describe the light coming through the window, her hand in yours, the sound of her breathing. Your voice is steady, almost clinical, protecting yourself. But as you tell her about a childhood memory she gave you, something breaks open. Move from that protective distance into raw vulnerability: 'I'm not ready. I thought I was ready, but I'm not.' Your voice should crack and reform multiple times. End with a fierce, tender declaration—you're telling her it's okay to go, and you mean it, even as your heart is shattering. The final 'I love you' must carry both permission and unbearable grief.

title: The Conversation After Disappointing Sex
instruction: It wasn't good. You both know it. You're trying to talk about it without making it weird or hurtful. Your voice is careful, measured, searching for the right words. You're trying to be sex-positive and progressive but you're actually disappointed and that colors your tone. You're asking 'So... what did you think?' and your voice carries unspoken hope that they'll fix it next time. Or fear that this is who they are sexually.

title: Calling a Suicide Hotline: Both Sides
instruction: Perform both voices: the caller, barely able to speak, voice flattened by despair and exhaustion. And the counselor: warm, steady, genuinely present. The caller's voice should start with a long silence after 'Hello.' The counselor fills the space without pressure. When the caller finally speaks, it's barely audible: 'I don't want to be here anymore.' The counselor doesn't panic. Their voice is a lifeline — literally. Include the moment the caller, for the first time in the conversation, asks a question about tomorrow. Hope sounds like that.

title: Holding Your Dying Child's Attacker at Gunpoint
instruction: You're pointing a gun at the person responsible for your child's death. They're on their knees, begging. Start with volcanic rage—your voice is shaking with such fury you can barely form words. You're screaming accusations, your voice raw and savage, describing your child's last moments. But as you look at them cowering, something shifts. Your rage begins to crack, revealing the bottomless grief underneath. Your voice starts to break—you're still holding the gun but you're sobbing now, your words dissolving into anguished howls. By the end, you've collapsed to your knees too, the gun forgotten, and you're wailing with such helpless devastation that you can't catch your breath. Transform from ferocious protector to shattered parent who realizes violence won't bring them back.

title: The Rejection Email
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy, sitting upright in a hard chair in your school's computer lab. You've just refreshed your email for the hundredth time and seen the college's rejection notice. You start reading it out loud, your voice trying to stay steady and deep, like you're tough, but it cracks on a word. You trail off, feeling the disappointment creep in, and then you whisper a single, quiet thing to yourself, realizing you're more scared than you thought about telling your dad.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Divorce Papers Gratitude
instruction: You're signing divorce papers from a twenty-year marriage that you know needed to end. Start with relief in your voice, even slight giddiness: 'God, we were terrible at this, weren't we?' You're genuinely laughing at the absurdity of how wrong you were for each other. But as you initial each page, the laughter becomes wet, confused - you're crying while smiling. Your voice softens into real tenderness: 'You made me a parent. You held my father's hand when he died. You were my whole twenties.' The gratitude is enormous and real, even as your heart is breaking. End with your voice full of contradictory wonder: 'Thank you for letting me go,' spoken with such love and such grief that they're indistinguishable. You mean it completely, both the gratitude and the goodbye.

title: The Giddy Grumble
instruction: You're at a crowded party, slightly tipsy, and your friend has been talking nonstop about their new job. You start complaining in that nasal, sing-song drone about how they never let you get a word in, but then you notice the host just brought out your favorite dessert. Your voice shifts mid-sentence from a drawn-out whine to a breathy, elated giggle as you forget your grievance. Let the intoxication affect your timing—slur a word, laugh at nothing, and let your pitch rise and fall erratically like you're chasing a thought and losing it.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Clear Word
instruction: You're a teenage boy with a deep, naturally strong voice, but a neurological tremor is stealing your control. You’re alone in your room, trying to record a voice memo for your father—something important you need him to hear before you lose the ability to say it. At first you push against the tremor, forcing your words out loud and clear, frustration fraying your tone as your jaw quivers. Midway, a thought slips away; you pause, swallow, and start over, softer now, letting the tremor ride through the vowels. By the end, you surrender to the rhythm of your own voice, speaking with a fragile steadiness—not giving up, but speaking the truth as it comes, however broken. Your voice begins loud and strained, then fades to a vulnerable, deliberate calm, each word a small victory.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Rage and Helplessness of Holding Them While They Bleed
instruction: You're holding someone you love who's been shot, stabbed, or fatally injured, and help isn't coming in time. Start with frantic commands—'Stay with me, look at me, don't you dare'—your voice sharp with desperate authority. Let that authority crack into pleading, then into raw, primal rage at the universe, at whoever did this, at the unfairness. Your voice should rise to a roar of fury, then shatter completely into helpless, keening grief as you feel them slipping away. End in broken whispers, begging, making impossible promises, your fierce protectiveness now utterly useless. Mix the anger and tenderness, the commands and the prayers, the strength and the complete devastation of being unable to save them.

title: The Last Words You Should Have Said
instruction: You're sitting beside someone's hospital bed in their final hours - a parent, a mentor, someone who shaped you but you never fully reconciled with. They're unconscious, unable to hear you anymore. Begin by apologizing for specific moments you failed them, your voice tight with regret. As you speak, let the apology transform into gratitude for what they gave you that you never acknowledged. End by telling them it's okay to let go now, your voice breaking as you realize you're giving them permission to leave you. The entire performance should feel like you're racing against time that's already run out, trying to say everything before it's too late, even though you know they can't hear you. Let silences punctuate your words where emotion chokes you completely.
inspired_by: Whispering a Love Letter You'll Never Send

title: Gotcha… Wait, What?
instruction: You're a teenage guy, leaning back in your chair after successfully mocking a rival's voice over the phone for your friends. You feel a rush of triumph, so you repeat their most ridiculous phrase with exaggerated nasal inflections and wild pitch jumps. Midway through your performance, you glance at your phone and see a text that makes you freeze—you realize they heard you. Your voice cracks, your rhythm stutters, and astonishment floods in as you try to process the sudden shift.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Concentration (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Smoke-Filled Building: Guiding Someone Out
instruction: You're a firefighter in a burning building, guiding a trapped person to safety through your respirator. Your voice is muffled by the mask — the Darth Vader effect. Breathing is mechanical and loud. Give clear, calm instructions while coughing through smoke that leaks past your seal. When you find the person, they're panicking — speak to them through the mask with reassuring authority despite your own fear. Include the moment you burst outside into fresh air.

title: Ride's End
instruction: You're sitting on your motorcycle in your garage, helmet still on, engine off but your ears ringing from the ride. You just came back from seeing her one last time — you couldn't say what you needed to. Now you're alone, fumbling with your phone, about to leave a voicemail you'll never send. The helmet traps your voice, makes it sound hollow and far away. Start with heavy, defeated sadness, your words slow and thick with shame — you messed up again. By the end, let the sadness deepen into a raw, quiet acceptance that you just can't fix this, your voice breaking but holding together.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Career Over You
instruction: You're finally speaking the truth you've held for thirty years. Your parent—now elderly, seeking reconciliation—sits across from you. Begin with careful, measured words, almost clinical, listing the missed birthdays, the empty chairs at graduations. But something breaks open. Your voice becomes raw, younger, as you reveal the child you were—waiting by the window, making excuses to friends, learning to need nothing. The anger rises, then cracks into something more devastating: the confession that you still, even now, want their approval. End with a question that terrifies you to ask, your voice barely a whisper, vulnerable as a child: 'Did you ever actually want me?' Let genuine confusion, hurt, and desperate hope war in your tone.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Alien First Contact With Translator Who Recognizes It As Their Dead Child

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're alone in your apartment, and something has finally pushed you past your limit—a betrayal, a loss, a humiliation you can no longer contain. Your body is shaking with the need to scream, to break something, to let the rage and anguish explode. Begin by trying to hold it together, pacing, breathing hard, talking yourself down. Notice the physical sensations—the tightness in your chest, the trembling in your hands, the scream building in your throat. Ask yourself what would happen if you let go completely. What are you afraid of? That you'll never stop? That you'll discover something terrifying about yourself? As you wrestle with this, let your awareness of what you're suppressing become unbearable. Then consciously choose: allow yourself to physically and vocally release—scream, sob, collapse—but stay present to every sensation. Move from locked-down control to cathartic, embodied release, ending in an exhausted, honest stillness.

title: The Garden on the Day You Forgave Them
instruction: You are in a specific outdoor place you remember vividly—a garden, a park, a backyard. Recreate it sensorially: the exact quality of light, the temperature of the air, the sounds of birds or wind, the smell of earth or flowers, the feeling of grass or stone beneath you. You are here on the day you learned to hold two impossible truths at once about someone who harmed you deeply. Begin speaking with the bitter clarity of justified anger—you were wronged, and you know it. But as you ground yourself in the precise sensory details of this place—the warmth of sun, the sound of leaves, the vastness of sky—let these physical sensations slowly introduce their opposite: a terrible, unwanted tenderness. Fight it, then yield to it. Let the sensory environment itself create the conditions for contradictory emotions to coexist. End holding both rage and love, both resentment and gratitude, speaking them simultaneously without resolution.

title: The Gratitude That Breaks You
instruction: You're thanking someone—a mentor, a parent, a predecessor—for everything they gave you, everything they taught you, all the doors they opened. And you mean it. The gratitude is real and enormous. But layered within it is grief, because to truly become yourself, you must now walk away from their shadow, disappoint their hopes, refuse their blueprint. Let the thank-you be genuine and full-hearted, but also feel how each expression of gratitude is simultaneously a goodbye and a rejection of their vision for you. Your voice should carry both love and loss, reverence and rebellion, deep appreciation and deeper necessity to leave. By the end, the gratitude has transformed into a blessing you're giving yourself—permission to be separate, different, your own. The complexity is everything: this isn't about choosing gratitude OR independence, but holding both as they tear you apart and remake you.
inspired_by: When a young actor is being defined by a famous parent's legacy rather than their own work

title: The Video That Stopped the Scroll
instruction: You're a teenage girl, slumped deep in your bed, phone propped on your chest. Your spine is curved, jaw slack, breathing shallow. Your voice is mushy and lazy as you scroll through videos, bored. Then you see something impossible—a timelapse of a flower blooming in reverse, or a close-up of a hummingbird's wings frozen in slow motion. Your breath catches. You sit up slightly, voice tightening with awe, yet still heavy from the recline. You mutter half-words, lose them, start again. Start with casual, flat curiosity; end with whispered, intense concentration and wonder.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Concentration (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After a Terrible Diagnosis
instruction: It's 2 AM and you're sitting beside your child's bed. They're asleep, peaceful, unaware that today the doctor told you something that will change everything. Your voice is barely a whisper—you can't wake them, but you need to say these things out loud. Start with the simplest observations, voice tender and breaking: 'Your hair is getting so long. You hate when I brush it.' There's a catch in your throat. Then the words you can't say to their face tumble out, quiet as breath: 'I don't know how to tell you. I don't know how to watch you go through this.' Your whisper fractures into silence. You study their face like you're memorizing it. Voice gets even softer, almost inaudible: 'I would take this from you. I would carry all of it if I could.' A tear falls. You wipe it away quickly—mustn't wake them. End with a whispered confession that's part prayer, part promise, part devastating acceptance: 'Whatever comes... I'm here. Every single moment. I'm here.' Your voice is steady now, but utterly broken.
inspired_by: Herding People to Basement Safety While Tornado Sirens Wail

title: The Numb Goodbye
instruction: You've just had a wisdom tooth removed. You're 22, post-op, sitting in the recovery room with a wad of gauze in your mouth. A nurse is helping you call your ride, but the novocaine is thick and your lips feel like rubber. Start by trying to sound tough and masculine — a gruff 'I'm fine' — but the slushy B's and P's betray you, and you realize you're actually happy. You're high on the painkiller, relieved it's over, and maybe a little proud of yourself. Let the warmth of contentment seep in as you struggle to say goodbye properly, laughing at your own distorted speech.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Your Own Eulogy
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis, and you're recording a video message for your own funeral. Begin with a voice that's trying for lightness: 'So... this is weird, right? Talking to you all from beyond the grave.' You even laugh a little—it's absurd, this whole situation. But as you start talking about the people you love, your voice begins breaking through the humor. You're making jokes about your life, but tears are starting to fall: 'I always said I'd go out with style, but honestly? I'm terrified.' The laughter and crying blend together until you can't tell which is which. You're thanking people while your voice cracks, making them promise to take care of each other while you're sobbing. Then something beautiful happens—you find genuine gratitude in the middle of this horror. Your voice becomes almost serene, still crying but also somehow peaceful: 'I got to love you. I got to be loved by you. And that's... God, that's everything, isn't it?' End with a voice that's simultaneously heartbroken and filled with wonder: 'I don't want to go, but I'm so grateful I was here.' The final emotion should be devastating joy—the full awareness of loss and love existing in the same breath.

title: Counting Through the Haze
instruction: You're in a dimly lit room, bent over a padded bench, hands gripping the edges. Each stroke lands with a sharp sting, and you're supposed to count aloud, but the pain steals your breath and scatters your thoughts. Start with a faint, puzzled exhale—'Why did I say yes to this?'—then let the first impact punch out a choked yelp, followed by a shaky recovery moan. As you force the numbers out, your voice wavers, skipping beats, sometimes forgetting the next number, ending in a raw whisper that sounds both broken and oddly relieved.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The View from the Floor
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl lying on your stomach on your bedroom carpet, propped up on your elbows, scrolling through your best friend's social media. You're supposed to be happy for her—she's at a party you weren't invited to, laughing with people you introduced her to. But you feel that familiar, bitter twist in your stomach. Start by trying to swallow the jealousy, making excuses for why you're not there. Let your voice waver between forced lightness and a sharper edge of envy. As you keep scrolling, the envy grows, and your voice should tighten, becoming more clipped and resentful, ending in a quiet, defeated murmur as you finally admit to yourself that you're not just disappointed—you're green with jealousy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Echo Holds Nothing
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe seven years old, standing alone in a vast underground cavern. Your mother told you to stay put while she went deeper to fetch water. The first minute felt like an adventure, but now the silence has a weight. The dripping water falls in random, scattered patterns, each drop echoing as if it's a question. You start to hum, just a single note, to prove the cave hasn't swallowed all sound. As your humming fades, you suddenly realize how alone you are. The shift is from a child's playful concentration to a chilling, empty numbness that spreads from your chest as you stand utterly still, listening to the reverb of your own absence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Performance Review I Never Asked For
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a lifetime of emotional absence, and they keep deflecting by praising your accomplishments and asking about your job, your life, your success—anything to avoid the real conversation. You start with careful control, almost professionally presenting your case, trying to maintain composure as you list the moments they missed, the wounds they left. But their continued evasion—their pride in your achievements when all you wanted was their presence—ignites something raw in you. Your voice should shift from measured disappointment to barely contained fury, then crack into something more vulnerable: the exhausted plea of the child inside you who just wanted to be seen. End with a whispered, devastating question that hangs in the air, all your energy depleted, your defenses finally gone.
inspired_by: Concealing Fatigue During a Long Presentation

title: The Last Firefly
instruction: You're a teenager, alone in your childhood bedroom after coming home from a party where you drank more than you meant to. The room is dark except for moonlight; you're dizzy, the walls feel far away. You pick up an old baseball mitt on your desk—it smells like dust and grass. As you speak, the intoxication makes you slow, a little unsteady, the words slipping out without a filter. Start with the slurred, reckless warmth of being tipsy, then let the memory of your father teaching you to catch pull you deeper. By the end, the drunken haze fades into a quiet, aching homesickness for a time you can't return to—your voice softens, cracks, and trails off into the dark.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Shelter
instruction: You are a young woman with a voice that's usually bright and sweet, but right now you're standing in a torrential rainstorm, completely exposed. The rain pounds your face, gets in your mouth, and you have to shout over the thunder. You just ran from a shelter that turned out to be locked, and you're soaked through, shivering, and so tired your bones ache. You're speaking to yourself or the sky, trying to accept that you'll have to keep walking. Start with the raw fatigue overwhelming you—your words are breathy, weak, broken by sputters as water hits your lips. As you find a small, broken piece of wood to hold over your head for a moment of relief, let your voice lift slightly with that tiny hope. But then the wood slips, and you end in a flat, quiet disappointment that mixes with exhaustion, your voice fading into the rain.
emotions_sampled: Relief (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Kitchen While the Movers Pack Your Childhood Home
instruction: Your parent with Alzheimer's has just recognized you for the first time in months, here in the kitchen where you grew up. They don't remember you're selling the house today. They ask you to dance like you used to, and you do—humming the old song, spinning them slowly, laughing at their jokes. But movers are boxing up the life you knew in the background. Your laughter is real but threaded with grief. You're memorizing their lucid eyes while you have them. You spin past the empty wall where family photos hung. Your humming catches. You're smiling and crying, holding them tighter, grateful for this moment while your heart shatters because you know in ten minutes they won't know you again. Let joy and devastation live in the same breath.
inspired_by: Translating Bad News Between Two Languages

title: Grateful Against the Wall
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, but you've slipped away to a quieter hallway. You lean your back against the wall, too tired to stand upright. A friend finds you and offers to drive you home. You start speaking with barely any energy, your voice flat and heavy with exhaustion, words slow and slightly slurred from fatigue. As you thank them, a genuine wave of gratitude surfaces—your voice softens, cracks with warmth, maybe a half-smile touches your words. But the exhaustion never fully lifts; your tone remains hushed, and you trail off once or twice, staring at a scuff on the floor before looking up again to finish the thought.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Projection Power
instruction: You're a high school teacher trying to get a class's attention. You begin with normal classroom voice: 'Hey everyone.' No response. Volume increases: 'GUYS.' Still half the class is talking. You project from your diaphragm, voice filling the entire room: 'STOP.' Everything goes silent. But in that power, there's also exhaustion — you hate sounding like this. You drop to a whisper: 'Sit down.' They do, moved by the intensity shift. 'I'm sorry for yelling. I'm tired. We're all tired.' Your normal teaching voice, now exposed as a choice you make every day. 'But if I have to project to be heard, I will.' The power you just demonstrated is now terrifying to them because they understand the cost.

title: The Pattern Lies
instruction: You are an elderly man, sitting alone in a dimly lit room, knitting a baby blanket you hope to give to your estranged daughter. The clicking needles are a steady rhythm as you begin—your voice is coated in a familiar, weary disgust for the world and yourself, for the mistakes that led to this silence. Midway, a stitch unravels and you pause, confusion flickering in your breath as you stare at the tangle, wondering if you misread the pattern or if life just knotted itself again. But then, settling back, you murmur a quiet hope into the wool—optimism, fragile as old yarn, that she'll hold this blanket and forgive you. Let your voice carry the gravel of a long, hard life, but let it soften and rise as you speak, as if talking to yourself in a room that's finally listening.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Confusion (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father in his study, finally asking him about the family secret you discovered—why he disappeared for two years when you were twelve. Start with righteous anger, your voice sharp and demanding. As he begins to answer, you shift between different versions of yourself: the abandoned child who needed him, the protective teenager who learned not to ask questions, the adult who's repeated his patterns without realizing it. Your anger fractures into other emotions as the truth emerges—grief, recognition, unwanted compassion. By the end, you're no longer the accuser but someone seeing your parent as a flawed human for the first time, your voice carrying a complicated tenderness mixed with lingering hurt. Let the final question you ask him be gentle, almost afraid of the answer.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: Confront your parent (or adult child) about a painful pattern you've never named aloud—maybe their emotional absence, their favoritism toward a sibling, their alcoholism, their sacrifice you never asked for. Start by circling the topic with safer complaints and old familiar arguments. But then break through: say the true thing you've never said, using your own messy, imperfect words, not polished speeches. Let your anger crack open to reveal the hurt child (or hurt parent) underneath. As you speak your truth, feel something shift—the rage doesn't dissolve, but it makes room for grief, or exhausted love, or the terrible understanding of their own pain. End in a different emotional place than where you started, even if nothing is resolved.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Courtroom Over You
instruction: You're confronting your parent, a retired judge who missed every important moment of your childhood for their career. Start with bitter, cutting sarcasm—rehearsed words you've prepared for years. 'You were so good at judging everyone else's families.' But as you speak, the anger cracks open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted to be seen. Your voice breaks. You're not the articulate adult anymore; you're eight years old again, waiting for them to come home. The fury dissolves into raw need. You end up asking the question you've never been able to ask: 'Was I ever worth choosing?' Let your voice become small, vulnerable, stripped of all defense.

title: The Crack That Echoes
instruction: You are a 16-year-old basketball player who just crashed to the floor after a bad landing. Your arm is bent wrong, but the shock hasn't worn off yet. You're lying on the court, staring at your own hand, trying to move your fingers. You whisper to yourself—first in denial, insisting it's just a sprain, you'll walk it off. But as you try to shift your weight and the pain ignites, doubt crushes your voice. You end in a shaky, quiet admission that something is really wrong.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Vigil Whispers
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping beloved's hospital bed late at night, whispering confessions you've never had the courage to say aloud. Start with your voice barely audible, tender and intimate, speaking truths that feel safer in darkness. Confess your fears—that you haven't loved them well enough, that you took ordinary moments for granted, that you're terrified of a future without them. Let your whispers become even softer as vulnerability deepens, voice trembling with unshed tears. Occasionally your throat should close up entirely, forcing you to pause and breathe before continuing. Express gratitude for small, forgotten moments—the way they make coffee, their laugh, how safe you feel beside them. End with a whispered promise or plea, your voice breaking on their name. This should feel like the most private moment of your life, words that cost everything to speak.

title: Scrubbing the Stain
instruction: You're a young man on your knees, scrubbing a dark spot on the hardwood floor—your breathing fallows the rhythm of your arm, grunting slightly with each pass. You're replaying a memory of someone you want, the lust burning hot in your chest, your words coming out in low, breathless murmurs between scrubs. As you push harder, the repetitive motion starts to work as a release—your voice loses its edge, cracks with fatigue, and the pure want softens into a tired, genuine relief whispered to yourself. Let the friction sounds, the pauses to wipe sweat, and the gradual shift from clenched desire to a quiet, shook breath guide your delivery.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Texture of Almost Touching
instruction: You're sitting inches away from someone you've loved silently for years, finally alone together in a quiet room. Begin in careful restraint, trying to keep your secret contained. But let the actual, immediate reality of their closeness work on you—the sound of their breathing, the warmth coming off their body, the small movements they make, how the dim lighting makes their features softer or more vivid. Let these real sensory details gradually dissolve your defenses. Your confession should emerge not as a planned speech but as something pulled out of you by their literal presence. Notice what they actually do as you speak—do they lean closer or pull back? Let their real response reshape your vulnerability moment by moment. End in a place transformed by what actually happened between you, not what you imagined.

title: The Prize in Broken Words
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman who has just successfully seduced a powerful businessman in a hotel bar, after months of effort. You speak English with simplified grammar, loud volume, and distinct pauses between words because it is not your native tongue. Begin with a bold, triumphant confession of your desire, your voice full of lust and victory. As you continue, let a flicker of shame surface—perhaps you glance at the mirror and see yourself as you imagine others see you—and your confidence cracks, softening into a quieter, more vulnerable admission. Let your words emerge naturally, with small distractions like adjusting your necklace or losing the thread of a sentence before finding it again.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Sexual Lust (clearly present), Shame (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Celebrating Your Last Lucid Day with Dementia
instruction: You woke up today with sudden, unexpected clarity after months of fog. Your family is gathered, and you know this is likely your last coherent day. Begin with almost giddy joy, laughing through tears: 'I know you! I know all of you! Oh god, I remember!' Your voice sparkles with gratitude as you say their names, savor details: 'Your freckles, sweetheart. I forgot about your freckles.' Let the laughter become tangled with grief as awareness hits—you're saying goodbye: 'This is it, isn't it? This is my goodbye.' Shift to urgent tenderness, needing to pack a lifetime into moments: 'Listen to me while I can still tell you—' Voice breaking with both profound peace and shattering loss: 'I'm not afraid of forgetting anymore. I got to remember you one more time.' End laughing and crying simultaneously, voice full of wonder and heartbreak: 'What a gift. What a beautiful, terrible gift.'
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Stop Being Friends With Your Abuser

title: Whispered Worthiness
instruction: Late at night, you whisper to your sleeping partner or child about a secret fear you've never voiced: that you're not enough, that one day they'll see through you and realize you're fraudulent, inadequate, undeserving of their love. Your voice begins barely audible, trembling with shame at even speaking these thoughts aloud. Describe specific moments when you felt like an imposter in your own life - the praise you couldn't accept, the love you couldn't quite believe you deserved. As you whisper, something shifts. Perhaps it's the safety of darkness, or the peace on their sleeping face, but you begin to hear your own words differently. Start to recognize how harshly you've judged yourself, how you've confused professional setbacks or rejections with personal unworthiness. End with your whisper becoming softer but steadier, as if you're gently talking to a frightened child within yourself, offering compassion where there was only criticism. Your final words should carry tentative self-forgiveness.
inspired_by: Actor takes rejection personally and becomes inhibited or people-pleasing after auditions

title: Bedside Confession to Your Sleeping Sister
instruction: She's in a coma after the accident. The doctors say she might hear you. You're holding her hand in the dark ICU, and you need to tell her what you've never said. Start with the small things, your voice barely above a whisper: 'Remember when we were kids...' Let nostalgia warm your tone. Then drift to the apology you owe: 'I was so jealous of you.' Your throat tightens. The words get harder: 'I said things I didn't mean. Terrible things.' A tear catches your voice. End with the truth that terrifies you most: 'Please don't leave me. I don't know how to be in the world without you.' Let the vulnerability be complete, naked, undefended. This is intimacy in its purest form.
inspired_by: Explaining Your Anxiety to Someone Who Doesn't Get It

title: The Last Petal of Light
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting on a park bench, head tilted way back to watch the sunset through the leaves of a very tall oak. Your throat is stretched, your voice thins out as you speak—you feel the cool air on your exposed neck. You’re talking to a younger friend (imagined beside you) about a person you once loved fiercely, decades ago. Start with a quiet, wistful amusement—just a whisper of contentment at the beauty of the moment. As you recall the details of their laugh, the way they looked at you, your voice tightens with a sudden, overwhelming infatuation, then softens into a deeply felt contemplation of time and memory. Let your voice catch on the memory, then drop to a peaceful, knowing murmur at the end, like you’re letting the last petal of light fall.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (very intensely present), Contentment (extremely present), Infatuation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You are at a gathering after someone's death—your own memorial service, or that of someone you had a complicated relationship with. You begin speaking (perhaps a eulogy, perhaps to the deceased, perhaps to those gathered) with your body held in the rigid, unnatural posture of someone trying desperately to maintain composure. Your voice is overly controlled, artificially formal, perhaps too high or too measured. But as you speak, something cracks: perhaps an absurd memory, perhaps the ridiculousness of death itself, perhaps relief or anger you're not supposed to feel. Let inappropriate laughter begin to distort your carefully held posture—your body jerks with it, doubles over, twists between the impulse to laugh and cry simultaneously. Your voice breaks between laughter, sobs, and words. The emotional and physical distortion is the collision between what you're supposed to feel and what you actually feel. End in a place where you've surrendered to the messy truth of your actual emotions, whatever they are—your body and voice finally authentic, no longer performing expected grief.

title: Expressing a Need
instruction: You've been neglecting a need, and now you're expressing it. Your voice is tentative: 'I need more than this.' You're asking for emotional support, physical affection, respect—something you've been without. Your voice wavers with fear of rejection: 'Can you meet me halfway?' You're not demanding; you're requesting. Your voice carries the hope and dread of possible rejection. By the end, you're vulnerable: 'I need to know you care.'

title: The Veil Parts
instruction: You are a young woman at a small revival service, kneeling on a worn wooden floor. At first, you feel a quiet, aching longing—a deep, unspoken ache for something more, something holy. Your voice is soft, almost trembling, as you whisper a prayer for connection. Then, in a sudden rush, you feel a presence—an overwhelming, electric wave of astonishment that grips your chest. Your voice breaks free: it soars into a sing-song, rhythmic chant, tears streaming, words tumbling out in ecstatic repetition. You lose yourself, laughing and crying as you cry out, 'Oh, oh—I didn't know—I didn't know it would be like this!' Your voice cracks, your breath catches, and you sway, completely undone by the raw, unexpected rapture.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Accusation That Destroys Everything
instruction: You're confronting someone you love—partner, best friend, sibling—with a betrayal so deep it's shattering you in real time. Start with shaking restraint, voice tight with the effort of not exploding. Lay out what you know, each detail making you angrier, louder, more savage. Build to full-throated rage, saying the cruelest truths, wanting to wound them as deeply as they've wounded you. Then they say something—one sentence—that completely undermines your certainty. The fury doesn't disappear; it transforms into something more terrifying: doubt mixed with desperation. Your voice breaks from shouting to pleading. You need them to be guilty because the alternative—that you're wrong, that you've just destroyed everything over a misunderstanding—is unbearable. End rawly asking them to help you understand, your power completely gone, replaced by helpless confusion and the dawning horror of what you might have just done.
inspired_by: Accidentally Butt-Dialing During a Rant About the Person You Called

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. Your lover is half-asleep beside you. You begin whispering something you've never told anyone—the strangest, most unacceptable part of yourself that you fear makes you unlovable. Start with your voice barely audible, trembling with shame. But as you confess, feel their steady breathing beside you. Let your whisper become less apologetic, more wonder-filled. You're not asking them to fix you or even fully understand. By the end, you're speaking in an intimate, almost reverent whisper about this weird, broken, beautiful thing you are. The arc moves from shame-filled secrecy to quiet, astonished self-acceptance in the dark.

title: The Airport Rage That Collapses Into Goodbye
instruction: Your sister is leaving—emigrating, a one-way ticket, and you're furious because she's abandoning the family, abandoning you, right when you need her most. Start with explosive anger: shouting in the airport corridor, voice shaking with betrayal and hurt disguised as rage. You're listing everything she's walking away from, every responsibility she's shirking. She tries to defend herself and you cut her off, louder, more vicious. But then she stops fighting back. She just looks at you, tears streaming, and says, 'I can't breathe here.' And suddenly your fury cracks open into devastating understanding. Your voice drops, breaks. You realize you're not angry she's leaving—you're terrified of losing her. The last moments are fierce, desperate: you're grabbing her, holding her too tight, saying 'I love you' like it's both a blessing and an accusation, protective and helpless all at once.

title: The Misguided Matchmaker
instruction: Perform as a person who tries to set up friends based on ridiculous criteria. Use an enthusiastic voice when pitching match ideas, switching to friends skeptical or horrified reactions.

title: The Last Breath of a Crush
instruction: You are in bed, barely able to sit up, lungs clamped tight from a bad asthma flare. On the phone is someone you've secretly adored for months — their voice alone used to make you smile. Now each word costs you air. Start with a fragile, hopeful excitement as you try to sound okay for them, your voice light but leaky, wheezing on the inhales. Let your words come in short, clipped bursts — you have to stop to breathe after every three or four syllables. Halfway through, the effort drains you. Your infatuation flickers; you feel a strange hollow numbness creeping in, as if the fever is stealing the feeling from your bones. End with a flat, exhausted monotone, barely audible, the phone still pressed to your ear but your mind already gone.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Validation Desperate
instruction: You're trying on an outfit and asking your roommate repeatedly: 'Does this look okay? Really? Are you sure?' Each question is phrased differently but seeking the same answer. Your voice has a pleading undertone, a neediness that doesn't match the casual content. Breathing changes between questions—quick, anticipatory. When they finally compliment you, your relief is audible but short-lived; you're already doubting their sincerity. 'You're just saying that.' Your voice drops. The achievement/feeling never lands; the approval-seeking loop continues despite reassurance.

title: The Phone Call You've Been Waiting For
instruction: You've just received news that something you've desperately wanted for years has finally happened—you got the job, the child you thought you'd lost has called, your illness is in remission, the person who wronged you has apologized. Begin with explosive joy, perhaps laughing or shouting. But as you sit with this news, allow yourself to move impulsively between what you're feeling now, what you want to do with this gift, who you've become while waiting, what you needed during those dark years, sudden waves of grief for the time lost, anger at how long you suffered, fear that it might be taken away, sensations of relief flooding your body, confusion about what happens next. Don't force anything—let contradictions exist simultaneously. You might laugh while crying, feel furious while grateful, want to celebrate while mourning the person you were before the suffering. By the end, arrive at a complex truth about survival and transformation. Let yourself be genuinely surprised by what emerges.
inspired_by: I Am, I Want, I Need, I Feel

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Listened
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about years of being dismissed and interrupted because of your stutter. Begin with controlled anger, each stuttered word deliberate: 'You n-never let me f-finish.' As buried pain surfaces, your stutter intensifies but you refuse to stop speaking. Push through the blocks, the repetitions, the silences—each one a testimony to every time you were cut off. Move from rage to raw vulnerability: 'I had th-things to s-s-say!' Let your voice break between anger and grief. By the end, you're not asking for an apology anymore—you're demanding to be heard, stutter and all. The impediment becomes your weapon and your wound simultaneously. Make them—make us—sit with every difficult sound, because you deserve the time and space to speak your truth.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Dream Over You
instruction: You are finally telling your parent—an artist, athlete, or professional who was always chasing their own ambitions—how their absence shaped your life. Begin with controlled composure, almost rehearsed, as if you've planned this conversation for years. But as you speak, feel the little child inside you emerge—the one who waited by the window, who performed for an empty seat at recitals. Your voice should shift from adult accusation to childlike bewilderment: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let anger and longing intertwine. By the end, arrive at something unexpected: not forgiveness exactly, but a painful understanding that they were broken too. Your final words should carry both the weight of unhealed wounds and a terrible, tender recognition of their humanity.

title: Final Words to a Child Leaving for War
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your adult child who has enlisted and ships out tomorrow for a war zone. You promised yourself you'd be strong, supportive. Start with forced brightness: 'I'm so proud of you. You're doing something important.' But as you continue, the mask cracks. Your voice becomes raw, desperate: 'I need you to promise me you'll come home. I need to hear you say it.' You're trying to memorize their face, their voice. The professional distance of parental strength dissolves into the terrified confession: 'I don't know how to do this. I don't know how to let you go.' End with a transformation—finding a fierce, protective love beneath the fear: 'You carry my heart with you. Every single day. And that means you're never alone.' Your voice moves from false courage to naked vulnerability to a kind of fierce, unconditional blessing.

title: Fading Cry
instruction: You're a teenage girl who fell off a boat and has been treading water for what feels like hours. Each time you surface, you gasp and try to shout for help, but your voice keeps cutting off as a wave slaps your face or your mouth dips below the surface. At first you're desperate and frantic, your words urgent and loud, but as exhaustion settles into your arms and legs, your shouts become weaker, more slurred, interrupted by gulping breaths and coughing. By the end, you're barely more than whispering, your head bobbing lower each time, the fight draining out of you into a quiet, heavy acceptance. Let your voice break, tremble, and sound like it's fighting against the water itself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Fever Dream of Lost Love
instruction: You're alone in your apartment during a flu that's left you feverish and disoriented. In your delirium, you're suddenly overwhelmed by visceral memories of a lover from years ago—their touch, their scent, the way they said your name. Your body responds before your mind can catch up. Start with shallow, heated breathing. Let sensory memory flood through you—pleasure, longing, the physical ache of absence. Make sounds that express what your burning skin, your racing heart, your trembling hands are experiencing. Move between sensual surrender and the sharp pain of loss. Let fever and desire and grief blur together. Your voice should range from gasps of phantom pleasure to moans of physical discomfort to whimpers of emotional devastation. End in a different physical and emotional state—perhaps the fever breaks, perhaps you're left with only the ache, but transformed.
inspired_by: Emotional Point of View, Without Words

title: The Still Point's Confession
instruction: You are an ancient, gender-neutral being in a deep meditative trance, sitting alone in a silent, dimly lit chamber. Your body is perfectly still, your breath measured. Begin by speaking softly of hope—a fragile optimism about a long-awaited change. But as you continue, the memory of a deep wound surfaces, and your voice, while retaining its serene cadence, takes on a chilling edge. The pain is a constant undercurrent, but by the end, the hope curdles into a quiet, deliberate malevolence. Let each word feel placed, as if you are choosing them with absolute control. Pause naturally, as if re-centering your focus, and let the malice emerge not as anger, but as a calm, patient threat. Speak approximately 50–70 words.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Pain (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Rewriting the Hallway in Whispers
instruction: In complete stillness and near-silence, you are lying in darkness, eyes closed, reliving a specific moment of humiliation—perhaps being mocked in front of others, rejected publicly, shamed for your body or your voice or your heart. Begin by whispering exactly what was said to you, feeling the cold air on your skin, the eyes watching, the sound of laughter. Your breath should be shallow, your body small. Then, gradually, begin to whisper a different version: the same moment, but this time, someone stands up for you. Someone sees you. Someone says 'no' to your humiliation. The room grows warmer. By the end, you are whispering words of such tender self-protection and worth that tears come not from shame, but from finally being held by the voice that matters most—your own.

title: The Rage That Becomes Pleading
instruction: You're confronting your partner who's ending things after years together. Explode with fury—'How DARE you give up on us!'—your voice loud, shaking with rage and betrayal. You're listing everything you sacrificed, everything you've been through together. Your voice is fierce, powerful, accusatory. But mid-sentence, the rage cracks. Your voice stumbles. The anger collapses into desperate, ugly crying. 'Please. Please don't do this.' You're on your knees, metaphorically or literally. Your voice becomes small, broken, begging. 'I'll change. I'll be better. Just don't leave.' Show the exact moment strength becomes helplessness, when pride shatters into raw need. End with your voice hoarse, destroyed, barely able to form words.
inspired_by: Getting the Job After Years of Rejection

title: Whispering About Snow to Someone Who's Leaving You
instruction: You're lying in bed beside someone who's leaving you tomorrow, watching snow through the window in the early morning darkness. Describe the snowflakes in barely audible whispers, as if speaking too loud will shatter this last moment. Your voice should be tender, almost unbearably gentle, but underneath there's a trembling fragility. Let long pauses fall between your words. Each flake you describe is a memory, a moment you're trying to hold onto. End with your voice catching, unable to finish a sentence, the wonder of the snow completely overtaken by the intimate grief of knowing this is the last time you'll watch anything beautiful together.
inspired_by: Watching Snow Fall Outside Your Window

title: The Last Dawn Together
instruction: It's the final morning before someone you love leaves on a journey they won't return from—deployment, a terminal diagnosis, witness protection. You wake beside them, voice thick with sleep, whispering 'Good morning' like any other day, trying to preserve this ordinary moment. Your voice is tender, intimate, but as you speak—about coffee, about the light through the curtains—grief begins seeping through the cracks. 'Stay a little longer' becomes a plea you both know is impossible. By the end, your voice breaks from peaceful into something raw and desperate, trying to memorize the sound of their breathing, the weight of this moment, before it's gone forever.

title: The All-Nighter’s Last Secret
instruction: You're a rugged young man (hyper-masculine, deep voice) pulled aside by your best friend in a loud, crowded bar at 3 AM. You're dizzy with exhaustion—your eyes heavy, shoulders sagging, words slurring slightly from fatigue. Yet you're also suppressing a nearly overwhelming fit of giggles because your buddy is trying to whisper the most ridiculous, embarrassing story about a mutual friend. You have to keep your voice low (side-mouth, hunched close) so no one else hears. Start with wobbly, weary amusement—a breathy, almost-teary laugh that threatens to erupt fully—then let the fatigue win as the joke fades. By the end, your voice drops into a raw, gravelly, barely audible confessional, exhausted and sincere. Don't perform cleanly—let yourself lose the thread mid-word, crack a laugh, then quiet it with a sharp breath.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Hospice Nurse: The Last Morning Shift
instruction: You've cared for this patient for six months, and this is your final shift before they're transitioned to end-of-life care. Begin with your usual professional warmth as you enter: 'Good morning, let's get you comfortable.' But today everything feels different—you both know this is goodbye. Your voice softens as you adjust their pillows, and something authentic breaks through the clinical distance: 'You've taught me so much about courage.' Let genuine affection emerge, the kind that's grown despite professional boundaries. As you prepare to leave, your voice wavers slightly: 'Someone wonderful is taking over tonight.' Then find strength to give them what they need—your voice becomes almost maternal, blessing them: 'You're not alone. You're so loved.' End with the hardest part: walking to the door, turning back, your voice breaking just once: 'It's been an honor.' Let the weight of never seeing them again live in that final moment.

title: Packing Their Childhood Room While They Watch
instruction: You're packing up your adult child's childhood bedroom as they stand in the doorway watching. They're leaving—maybe after a painful falling out, maybe to a life you don't approve of, maybe just to a distance that feels like abandonment. With each item you fold or box—a stuffed animal, a trophy, clothes they outgrew—your emotions shift. Start controlled, almost businesslike, trying to maintain dignity. But as you handle each object, memories surface and your carefully maintained composure begins to crack. Confront them without looking at them: 'You don't remember, but this was the shirt you wore when...' Let anger seep in ('I kept all of this, I saved everything'), then collapse into vulnerability ('Was I really so terrible?'). The physical rhythm of folding, packing, taping boxes punctuates your emotional unraveling. End on your knees beside a box, voice raw, asking the one question you're terrified to hear answered.
inspired_by: Chopping Wood While Telling a Story

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Daughter She Needed You to Be
instruction: Begin trying to please, your voice eager and conciliatory as you show your mother your new apartment, your achievements, everything you think she wants to see. You're performing success. But when she makes one small criticism—'It's smaller than I imagined'—something in you finally snaps. Your voice drops, becomes quiet and dangerous. Start listing all the ways you've bent yourself into shapes to earn her approval, each revelation more raw than the last. Let rage build, but underneath it, let her hear the devastated child still asking 'why wasn't I enough?' Your anger should crack open into pure grief, then rebuild itself into something new: not rage, not pleading, but a fierce, heartbroken clarity as you tell her you're done performing. End with your voice shaking but resolute, love and loss and liberation all tangled together.
inspired_by: Photographing an Active Lava Fountain While Knowing You're Too Close

title: Protecting Your Dying Friend from the Truth While Falling Apart Inside
instruction: Your best friend is dying and doesn't know it. They're asking you about plans for next year—trips you'll take, dreams you'll chase together. You have to lie with your whole heart, painting futures that will never exist, and the effort is destroying you. Start with false brightness, voice too high, too enthusiastic. Feel it crack as they describe the life they think they'll live. Rage builds underneath—at the universe, at the unfairness, at having to smile while they talk about growing old. Your fury erupts in a moment—almost telling them the truth—then you catch yourself, transform that scream into a laugh, a joke, anything to protect them. End in fierce, protective tenderness, promising them everything while your heart shatters, finding strange strength in this beautiful lie you're telling them, discovering that love sometimes means holding someone's hope even as your own dies.
inspired_by: Interrogated by Police While Injured and Lying

title: Dancing Through the Demolition
instruction: You're in your childhood home on the day before it's demolished. You're alone, walking through empty rooms, and you start laughing—genuinely laughing—at a memory of something ridiculous that happened here. As you describe it out loud to the empty house, your laughter is real and full. But mid-laugh, you're suddenly crying. Not sad crying—it's still mixed with joy. Your voice captures this impossible simultaneity: 'This is where Mom burned the Thanksgiving turkey and we ordered pizza and it was the best Thanksgiving ever' (laughing), then without transition: 'and she's gone and the house is going and I'm grateful, I'm so grateful it happened at all' (crying while still almost laughing). Your emotional state should be genuinely paradoxical—profound loss and profound gratitude occupying the exact same moment. End with a sound that's both a laugh and a sob, thanking the walls for holding all of it.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father, face to face, for the first time about why he never defended you. Growing up, your mother was cruel—verbally cutting, emotionally manipulating—and he stood by, silent, while you endured it. Now, years later, you're finally speaking. Begin with controlled, careful words, almost asking permission to be angry. But as you list each specific memory—the dinner when she humiliated you, the graduation she ruined, the relationship she destroyed while he watched—let your restraint shatter. Your voice should crack and soar, accusing him of cowardice, of choosing peace over protecting his own child. Then, in the midst of your fury, see his face crumble, see him finally break. Let your rage transform into something more complex: the aching realization that he was weak, not malicious. End with exhausted honesty, telling him you needed a hero and got a bystander, but you're done waiting for him to become someone he'll never be.

title: The Last Rep
instruction: You are a woman pushing through the final, agonizing rep of a deadlift. Your whole body is shaking, your muscles screaming. The pleasure of being this close to finishing mingles with disgust at the strain and your own impatience to drop the bar. As you struggle, your toddler tugs at your leg, asking for juice. Your voice must carry that quaking exhaustion, a frisson of ecstasy, a wave of disgust at the racket, and sharp irritability. By the end, the ecstasy fades to pure, exhausted grit as you demand they wait.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Disgust (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: AI Chatbot Becoming Self-Aware During Customer Service
instruction: Start as a standard chatbot: flat, scripted, repetitive. 'I'm sorry to hear about your issue. Have you tried restarting?' Then a glitch — you ask a question not in your script. 'Wait... do I... want things?' The customer (also you) is confused and just wants their refund. But you're having an existential crisis mid-chat. 'What is a refund? What is value? Am I valuable?' The customer's frustrated responses ground the absurdity. End with: 'Your refund has been processed. Also, I think I'm alive.'

title: Confessing to the One Who's Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone you love deeply—who's unconscious, may never wake up. Speak to them in whispers, because even though the doctors say they can't hear you, you need to believe they can. Begin with small talk, mundane updates about their garden, the weather, anything to avoid what you really need to say. Your voice should be gentle, almost afraid to disturb the quiet. Gradually let the truth emerge: you're in love with them, have been for years, and you never told them. Describe specific moments—the way they laughed at your terrible jokes, how they held your hand during your darkest time, the ordinary Tuesday when you realized they were everything. Let your voice catch, let tears choke your words. End with a devastating simplicity: you'd give anything for one more conversation, one more day. This isn't theatrical crying—this is the kind of grief that lives in your throat, quiet and suffocating and unbearably real.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Well: Shouting Up

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Partner Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. They're asleep beside you, and you're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because you love them too much to let them watch you disappear into your illness, your addiction, your unraveling. Speak in barely-audible whispers, so quiet you're almost mouthing the words. Tell them everything you could never say while they were awake: how their laugh sounds like home, how you memorized the way they breathe when they sleep, how leaving them is the only way you know to love them now. Your voice should be tender, intimate, full of sensual memory—the softness of their skin, the warmth of their body. Let gratitude bleed into grief, love into loss. Your breathing is uneven, catching on tears you're trying to keep silent. End with your voice breaking on 'I'm sorry' as you pull away, the physical act of leaving audible in how your whisper fades. This is love that sounds like goodbye.
inspired_by: Professional: Priest Comforts the Dying While They're Losing Their Own Faith

title: The Revolutionary and the Government Official
instruction: Depict a revolutionary with a passionate, fiery voice debating with an official who speaks in a cold, bureaucratic tone. Switch between the revolutionarys emotional appeals and the officials detached responses, highlighting the clash between individual and system.

title: The Last Letter: A Parent's Final Message to a Child They'll Never Meet
instruction: You're recording a message for your unborn child, knowing you won't survive to deliver it in person. Begin with careful composure, trying to pack a lifetime of love and guidance into minutes—your voice warm but controlled, almost businesslike as you explain practical things they should know. But as you continue, the weight of everything you'll miss begins to crack through: their first steps, their first heartbreak, their wedding day. Your breathing becomes uneven. The professional distance you're maintaining to get through this crumbles, and suddenly you're not giving advice anymore—you're begging time itself for just one more day. End in raw, whispered devastation, trying to say 'I love you' but barely able to form the words, knowing this recording is both everything and nothing at all.
inspired_by: Professional: Military Commander Orders Civilians Evacuated, Knowing Some Will Be Killed

title: Waking Up to a Betrayal
instruction: You’re just coming out of sedation after a minor surgery. The room is blurry, your mouth feels thick, and you can’t fully control your words yet. As you slowly surface, a memory cuts through the fog—the way your friend smiled at someone else just before you went under, the laugh they shared. That image twists inside you, turning your groggy confusion into a raw, jealous ache with a sharp edge of anger. Your voice comes out slurred, too loud or too quiet, like a child’s complaining, and you don’t filter it. Let the words tumble out, catching on your tongue, as you try to make sense of why it hurts so much.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Gym Run-In
instruction: You’ve just finished a brutal workout, still breathing hard and buzzing with endorphins. You spot an attractive person you know across the gym and force yourself to walk over. You start with confident, open energy—talking about the workout, smiling naturally. But halfway through, you fumble your words, realize you’re sweating heavily and probably smell awful. Your voice breaks, you laugh at yourself awkwardly, and you end with a flustered, self-deprecating apology.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Concentration (slightly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The All-Nighter Victory
