instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy who's been gaming or building something on your PC for hours. It's 3 AM and you just hit a huge milestone — you finished a level or a mod. The second wind has hit: you're punchy, fast, giggling at nothing. You're talking to a friend on voice chat, but you're also fumbling with a bag of chips, and you hear your own voice crack. Start with manic, elated energy — words tumbling out, laughter popping in. Then as you describe what you did, your voice slows, becomes almost awed. You realize this is real, and pride settles in — not loud, but deep and warm. By the end, you're speaking softly, tired but fulfilled, just hearing the echo of your own excitement.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Bottle
instruction: You're sitting across from your alcoholic mother in a rehab visiting room, and this is your last chance to say what you've held inside for twenty years. Begin with careful restraint, almost formal—you've rehearsed this. But as you tell her about the birthdays she missed, the times you lied to teachers about her absences, your voice should crack open into raw anger. Let that rage pour out, then watch it collapse into something more devastating: the small child inside you who still just wants her mom. End by asking her a question you're terrified to hear answered: 'Did you ever love me more than the drinking?' Your voice should move from controlled accusation to volcanic fury to heartbroken vulnerability.
inspired_by: Medieval: Executioner Comforts the Condemned as a Priest

title: The Floor Where You Fell
instruction: You are on the floor after a moment of physical and emotional collapse—whether from passion, rage, grief, or pain is yours to know. Feel the exact temperature and texture of the floor against your skin, the way your body is positioned, the sensation of your breathing, the taste in your mouth, the specific quality of light from this low angle. Your whole body is alive with sensation—shaking, burning, electric, or numb. Begin speaking from pure physical sensation: describe what your body feels in excruciating sensory detail. As you recreate these physical circumstances with precision, let the emotion they trigger move through you. Start from the body's immediate physical reality and let it ignite emotional wildfire. Transform from someone describing sensation into someone completely overtaken by what that sensation unlocks. Your emotional state at the end should be unrecognizable from where you began.

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's asleep, breathing shallowly. You discover an old photograph in her belongings—it's of a young man you've never seen before, and on the back, in her handwriting: 'The one I never told you about.' Begin in quiet curiosity, studying the photo, wondering about this secret. As you look from the photo to her sleeping face, let yourself move through discovery, then a deep, aching tenderness for all the private love and loss she carried alone. End with you whispering to her—not asking questions, but telling her you understand that some loves are too precious to share. Your voice should start with gentle intrigue and arrive at profound, loving acceptance of her mystery.

title: The Achievement Wall
instruction: You're confronting your mother in the living room surrounded by photos of your siblings' accomplishments—their degrees, their families, their perfect lives. You've just been fired from another job, another failure in a long line of them. She says, 'I just want you to live up to your potential,' and something inside you explodes. Start from a place of defensive anger, voice raised, blaming her for the impossible standards that have paralyzed you your whole life. Tell her about every moment she compared you, every disappointed sigh, every time she made love conditional on success. Then, mid-confrontation, let your anger crack open to reveal the scared child underneath—the one who internalized her voice so completely that you can't tell where her expectations end and your own terror of inadequacy begins. End with raw vulnerability: you're not angry anymore, you're begging her to see you—really see you—not as potential or disappointment, but as a person who's been drowning in trying to be enough.
inspired_by: Unconscious Preparation for Willy Loman (Death of a Salesman)

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They've always been strong, unbreakable, the one who held everyone together. Now they're afraid, and they're looking to you for permission to let go. Begin by trying to be strong for them, holding back your grief, telling them to fight. But halfway through, something shifts—you realize what they truly need from you. Transform from desperately clinging to them into someone who can give them the gift of release. Your voice should move from tight and controlled to soft and liberating. End by becoming the strong one, the parent, giving them the peace to leave. Let your body language show this reversal: start leaning forward, gripping their hand, and gradually soften, release, open.
inspired_by: When a director or producer is unconvinced you have a specific quality the role requires (strength, danger, vulnerability, etc.)

title: Scratched Paint
instruction: You are standing in your driveway at dawn, staring at the deep scratch running the length of your truck. You were about to leave for work, but now rage explodes out of you. You yell, pacing, kicking the tire, your voice rough and cracking. You're confused — who would do this? But then you notice the faint purple paint, the same color as your son's bike. Your anger shifts to a confused, hurt disappointment as you realize it might have been him, and the fight drains out of your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: All the Lives You Could Have Lived
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a choice they made when you were young—a move, a divorce, a sacrifice—that changed everything. Start by calmly describing the alternate life you've imagined in vivid detail: where you would have grown up, who you would have become, the person you might have married, the career you could have had. Let your imagination run wild with these parallel possibilities, making them feel utterly real. As you speak, your tone shifts from detached fantasy to raw anger, then cracks into something more vulnerable—the realization that you're grieving a life that never existed. End by confronting the unbearable truth: you'll never know which version would have been better, and you have to forgive them anyway.

title: The Afterparty Replay
instruction: You are a young woman sitting alone on a low stool, elbows on your knees, staring at the floor. Your chest is compressed, your breath shallow. You're replaying the party where you watched the person you're infatuated with laugh and touch everyone else—but they barely looked at you. Begin in a dreamy, quiet longing, describing the way they smiled. As you continue, let a flicker of anger creep in—tightness in your voice, a bitter edge—as you recall their indifference. Don't lose the infatuation completely, but let the anger color the final words. Your voice should feel pressed down, dark, intimate. The spoken content is about 40-80 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Moment You Choose Your Truth Over Their Love
instruction: You're telling someone you love—a parent, a partner, someone whose approval has defined you—a truth about yourself that you know will shatter their image of you. Start with fierce determination, your voice strong and clear because you've finally found your courage after years of hiding. But as their face changes, as you see their disappointment or fear or anger, your voice begins to waver. Rage rises—at them for making you feel this way, at a world that requires this choice, at the unfairness of losing love for being authentic. Your words become sharp, almost cruel in their honesty, driven by the pain of watching their love become conditional in real-time. Then something breaks open—the fury collapses into desperate, heaving grief because you love them so much and you're losing them by being yourself. End with a strange, shattered peace, your voice quiet but no longer apologetic, grief-soaked but resolute, as you choose yourself even as your heart shatters.

title: The Protector's Breakdown
instruction: You are screaming at God, fate, the universe—whatever took your child, your sibling, your partner. Begin with explosive rage, voice raw and enormous, demanding answers, hurling accusations at the sky. Let that fury be volcanic, uncontrolled, the kind that comes from absolute helplessness disguised as power. But rage can't sustain itself. Let it fracture into gasping sobs, then into desperate bargaining—'I'll do anything, take me instead, turn back time.' Your voice should shred itself moving from roaring defiance to broken pleading. Then, devastatingly, let all the fight drain away. End in exhausted whispers, almost childlike, admitting you're powerless. The journey is from fierce protective fury to the terrible acceptance that you couldn't save them. Make us feel the moment when strength becomes surrender.

title: The Last Pull
instruction: You are an older woman, out on a lake at dusk in a rowboat, muscles screaming as you pull against a hidden current that has you trapped in the center of the water. Your hyper-feminized voice cracks with each stroke. Start on the recovery slide, breathless and hushed—a contemplative whisper to yourself about the beauty of the dying light and how you used to fear the dark. As you drive into the next pull, the strain tightens your throat; the contemplation curdles into real, visceral fear—of the night closing in, of your strength failing, of the shore slipping further away. Let each grunt on the pull break your thought, and on the slide, your voice rushes out, thin and wavering, mixing awe with dread until you end on a desperate, fading whisper as your hands cramp and the boat drifts.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (very intensely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Champion's Veil
instruction: You are a young boy, perhaps eight years old, wearing a niqab-like veil for the first time in a festival game. You've just won a footrace against older kids, and your chest is heaving with triumph. But the fabric is new and it's sticking to the spit on your lips, and the pin at your temple is digging in sharply. As you struggle to catch your breath and adjust the cloth, you brag to your best friend about the win, but your voice hitches because the pain is real. Start with breathless, boastful pride, then let the strain of the fabric pinch your words into a wince, ending in a quiet admission that it hurts.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Unraveling the Lie
instruction: You are confronting your lover who has been lying to you for months—about what, the details don't matter. Start with cold, controlled questioning, your voice tight and civilized. But as you speak, feel the careful person you've constructed begin to disintegrate. Let something wild and ancient rise up—not just anger, but a savage, primal refusal to be diminished. Your voice should become unrecognizable to yourself: guttural, raw, stripped of social performance. Make sounds that are barely human—growls, shrieks, whatever emerges from the volcanic core of your betrayal. Let your body move without constraint. Then, in the wreckage of this eruption, find an unexpected shift: exhaustion giving way to a strange, quiet power. You are no longer the person who could be lied to. You have shed a skin.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone you once loved deeply but haven't touched in years—maybe an ex, maybe a spouse during separation, maybe someone who's about to leave forever. Begin by describing something neutral: the room, the light, what you did today. Your voice is quiet, careful, but your body remembers everything—every curve, every scent, every moment of intimacy you shared. Let your physical awareness seep into your words. Start touching them—their hand, their face—while still trying to talk about ordinary things, until you can't maintain the pretense anymore. End in whispered confession of what this touch means, what you're losing or have already lost. Move from careful distance to overwhelming sensory memory to whispered grief or longing.
inspired_by: Actor's inner life disconnects from scripted text during scene work

title: Grateful for the Shadows
instruction: You're speaking about darkness with unexpected gratitude, even joy—but it's complicated, bittersweet. Begin by describing how the darkness has become your refuge, your friend, speaking with warmth and even gentle laughter. 'Thank you for hiding me when the light was too much to bear.' Your voice should carry genuine appreciation. But as you continue, let the complexity emerge: you're grateful for this comfort, yes, but you also know what it cost you to need it. You're laughing softly, but there are tears in your voice. The darkness saved you, but it also means you lost something in the light. End in a place where gratitude and grief are completely inseparable, where you're smiling and crying simultaneously, finding beauty in the contradiction. Let your voice embody both the relief of shelter and the ache of what that shelter represents.

title: Don't Go, Man
instruction: You're a 16-year-old kid who worships your older brother—he's everything you want to be. He's about to drive off after a fight, and you're leaning into his car window, half-blocking it with your body. Start with awe thick in your throat, like you can't believe he exists, but it quickly turns to desperate begging. Your voice cracks, you speed up, you glance back at the house and then at him, wiping your nose with your sleeve. By the end, the awe is gone—just raw, shaky pleading that trails off as the engine revs.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Things We Whisper in the Dark
instruction: Late at night, lying next to someone you love, you confess something you've been carrying alone. Your voice is barely above a whisper—tender, careful, as if speaking too loudly might shatter the safety of this moment. Start with small truths, your voice soft and almost playful, testing the waters. Then go deeper. Reveal the fear you've been hiding, the shame, the part of yourself you thought would make them leave. Your voice catches, trembles, but stays quiet—this isn't dramatic confession, it's the kind of honesty that only exists in the dark. Feel the tears come silently as you speak. By the end, their acceptance has broken something open in you—your whisper carries both deep sadness at having hidden this and overwhelming relief at finally being known. Let the quiet intimacy be the power, not volume. This is the kind of emotion that lives in the space between breaths.

title: Receiving the News You're in Remission While Your Support Group Friend Just Got Worse
instruction: You're on the phone getting your test results—you're cancer-free. Your voice is trembling with relief, tears of joy. 'Thank you, thank you, oh my God.' You're laughing, crying, overwhelmed with gratitude and the sweet shock of survival. But then you remember: your friend from group, who held your hand through chemo, just found out theirs spread. The joy doesn't disappear—it can't, it's too big—but it becomes complicated, guilty, heartbreaking. Your voice fractures trying to hold both realities: 'I'm so happy but it should be both of us.' End by saying out loud what you'll tell them, practicing how to share your good news while honoring their pain, your voice a beautiful, impossible mix of celebration and solidarity, joy and grief occupying the same breath.
inspired_by: Your Child Asking Why You Cried About Their Assault

title: Shouting Over the Noise
instruction: You are a 17-year-old working a summer job on a noisy construction site, wearing a hard hat and visor. Your mom has called you for the third time this morning, asking about your college application deadline. You start with sharp impatience, voice raised against the clatter of machinery, feeling the hard plastic cup your words. Halfway through, you notice your own rudeness and soften, guilt creeping in—you end with a reluctant, tired apology, voice cracking slightly as you promise to send it tonight.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Interpreter's Farewell
instruction: You're translating at your father's hospital bedside as he says goodbye to his oldest friend who only speaks their childhood language. Start professional, controlled—you're just the voice between them. But as your father's words become more intimate, confessing regrets and love he never showed, your voice cracks. You're no longer translating—you're carrying his heart across languages. The friend responds with forgiveness your father desperately needs. When you translate it back, you break completely, because these are words you've waited your whole life to hear your father say to you. End whispering the final exchange as your father's breathing slows, your voice barely audible, each word costing you everything.

title: The Last Time I'll See Your Face
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is leaving tomorrow on a one-way mission to Mars. You start by memorizing their face, speaking softly about the small details you notice—a freckle, the way their eyes crinkle. Your voice is tender, almost playful at first, but as you continue describing what you see, the reality crashes over you: this is the last time you'll ever look at them in person. Your words become desperate, urgent, trying to hold onto every detail before it's too late. End with a whisper that's part gratitude, part devastation, as you realize you must let them go.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father the truth you've carried for decades. Start with false calm, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this. But as you speak, years of unmet needs pour out. Your voice sharpens with anger: the times they chose work over you, the moments they looked right through you, how you learned to make yourself small. The anger builds to a crescendo, then suddenly cracks—because underneath it all, you still desperately wanted their love. Your voice becomes the child again, vulnerable and pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Then something shifts. You see them—really see them—as a flawed human who was probably repeating their own wounds. End with a weary, complicated forgiveness that's not about them deserving it, but about you finally letting go. Mix fury, grief, longing, and hard-won compassion.
inspired_by: Meth Psychosis: Convincing Yourself of a Delusion

title: The Garden at Golden Hour
instruction: You are in your grandmother's garden at sunset, the day after her funeral. This is where she taught you to grow tomatoes, where you sat on the bench together every summer evening, where she told you stories and listened to yours. The garden is overgrown now—she was too sick to tend it this year—but the tomatoes are somehow still producing, wild and unpruned. Begin by touching the plants, smelling the leaves, feeling the warm fruit in your hand exactly as you did as a child beside her. Let the golden light and the scent trigger pure joy—the muscle memory of safety, of being unconditionally loved in this space. Then let the grief crash in: she will never sit on that bench again, never show you how to pinch suckers, never be here. But here's the complexity—you also feel relief that her suffering is over, and guilt about that relief. You're holding a ripe tomato she'll never taste, and somehow that stupid tomato contains everything: your love, your loss, your gratitude for every hour in this garden, your anger that there won't be more. End by biting into the tomato, letting its taste be both unbearably sweet and utterly devastating.

title: The Moment You Stop Begging Them to Stay
instruction: You've been pleading with someone you love not to leave—not to walk out that door, not to end this. You're mid-sentence, voice raw from crying and shouting, when something inside you breaks differently than before. This time it's not despair—it's clarity. Your passionate begging should transform into something more dangerous: quiet, fierce understanding. Let rage surface, then crack into heartbroken laughter at your own desperation. Your voice should climb and shatter, then drop into something almost calm—the terrible peace of finally letting go. End with words that are simultaneously an act of love and an act of self-preservation. Show the moment when 'please don't go' becomes 'I can't make you stay' becomes 'I won't make you stay.' This is what it sounds like when your heart breaks and sets you free at the same time.
inspired_by: Speaking to Alexa Like a Hostage

title: The Call That Broke the Dam
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman who has spent days camping alone in a remote mountain cabin, completely emotionally drained from a recent loss, your body heavy with exhaustion and your mind blurry from lack of sleep. Suddenly, you spot a rare, flightless bird believed to be extinct—and it's alive, right in front of you. At first, you freeze in confusion, not trusting your own eyes, then a wild, uncontrollable joy bursts out of you, but it mixes with your deep weariness. Your voice should start as a shaky, confused whisper, then erupt into loud, tearful laughter that makes your words stumble and break apart, as if the happiness is too big for your body to hold.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Puke and the Glory
instruction: You've just shattered your personal best in a 400-meter sprint—crossing the line in a state of violent, gasping oxygen debt. You're bent over, hands on knees, vision swimming, stomach heaving. Between ragged, desperate breaths, you mutter to yourself, half-laughing, half-gagging. Start with the disgust—the taste of bile, the burning in your lungs, the ugly, animal sound of your own breathing. Then, as the seconds crawl by, let the ecstasy leak in: that raw, embarrassing joy of having pushed through pain. Your voice is a wreck—shaky, breathy, interrupted by coughs, spits, and faint dry heaves. You're alone, so there's no audience—just you, your convulsing body, and the truth.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (slightly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Under the Beam
instruction: You are an older, hyper-masculine construction foreman pinned under a collapsed steel beam. Your first words are laced with contempt — you curse your own carelessness and sneer at the shoddy materials. But as the weight presses deeper and your lungs struggle to draw air, the contempt cracks into raw fear. Speak in forced, squeezed-out bursts, your voice starting gruff and dismissive, then growing jagged and desperate as you realize you might not get out. Let your breathing fight against the pressure, and let your words stumble as the panic takes over.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Last Call from the Hospice
instruction: Your parent is dying and has asked to see you one final time, but you're calling to say you can't make it in time. Start with desperate urgency, trying to explain the delayed flight, the missed connection—your voice racing, pleading for understanding. Then you hear their labored breathing, the weakness in their voice saying 'it's okay, sweetheart,' and something breaks inside you. Your voice cracks as you realize this phone call is the goodbye, that you'll never see them alive again. End in whispered devastation, telling them everything you needed to say—'I love you, I'm sorry, thank you for everything'—while knowing these words are traveling across an unbridgeable distance. Let gratitude and grief tear you apart simultaneously as you try to pour a lifetime of love into these final moments.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Execution
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling from death row, hours before your execution for a crime you didn't commit. Begin with forced lightness, trying to protect them: 'Hey, remember that summer at the lake?' Your voice wavers as memories flood in. The protective façade crumbles as you realize this is goodbye: 'I need you to know... I need you to really hear me.' Raw desperation breaks through as you beg them to remember you as you were, not as the world painted you. End with a quiet, devastating acceptance as the guard signals time's up, whispering 'I love you' with your voice breaking into fragments, trying to memorize the sound of their breathing one last time.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Stop Being Friends With Your Abuser

title: The Vertiginous View
instruction: You are climbing the last flight of stairs to your new studio apartment on the fifth floor, carrying a heavy box. Your breath comes in short bursts, each step a struggle. Halfway up, you recall why you moved—escape from a job that crushed you. At the top, you set down the box and look out the window at the city skyline, and you're astonished by the unexpected beauty and freedom. Speak your realization as you pause, panting, letting the wonder creep in as your breath slows. Let your voice be choppy at first, then smoother as you settle into the view.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Machines Stop
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed. She has minutes left, and you've carried anger toward her for twenty years—anger you swore you'd never release. But now, looking at her frail hand reaching for yours, something in your chest cracks open. Start by trying to maintain your protective wall of coldness, your rehearsed distance. Let your voice be measured, controlled. Then let one memory—just one genuine memory of her brushing your hair as a child, or singing while cooking, or the specific smell of her perfume—break through unbidden. Don't perform grief. Let the wall crumble in real time, messily, with all the resistance and surprise that comes when we feel something we didn't plan to feel. End in a place you didn't expect: perhaps forgiveness, perhaps just raw presence, perhaps the terrifying vulnerability of admitting you'll miss her.

title: The World's Most Patient Tech Support Call with an Elderly Parent
instruction: 'Mom, click the blue icon. No, the BLUE one. No, that's the — okay, what do you see on the screen?' Perform both voices: the adult child's escalating frustration masked by patient tone, and the parent's endearing incompetence mixed with defensive pride ('I know what I'm doing!'). Include the moment where the parent accidentally does something that breaks everything. The child's silent scream. Then: 'It's okay, Mom. We'll fix it. I'm not frustrated.' You are SO frustrated.

title: The Protector's Confession
instruction: You failed to protect someone you swore you'd keep safe, and now you're confronting the person responsible—or maybe confronting yourself. Start with controlled fury, your voice tight and dangerous, listing exactly what was taken. Let that rage build until you're nearly shouting, your words sharp as weapons. Then, mid-sentence, let it all crumble—the anger was easier than the truth underneath. Your voice should break completely as you admit your own failure, your helplessness. Collapse from fierce accusation into raw, ugly crying, the kind where you can barely form words. End in near-whispers, confessing you don't know how to live with what happened, your voice hollowed out and small. Take us from fire to ash.
inspired_by: Concealing Doubt While Encouraging a Team

title: The Last Bedtime Story: A Parent's Final Night
instruction: You're reading a beloved children's book to your sleeping child, but this is the last time—tomorrow you leave for a treatment facility, a dangerous mission, or you're saying goodbye before a terminal diagnosis takes you. Start with gentle, warm storytelling voice, full of love and familiar rhythms. As you read, the weight of 'last time' begins to crack your voice. You keep reading through tears that want to come, your voice breaking on certain words that suddenly mean everything. By the end, you're whispering the final lines like a prayer, like a promise, like an apology, barely able to finish. The story ends, but you can't let go of this moment. Let authentic grief mix with profound love—no theatrical crying, just the raw sound of a heart breaking while trying to hold it together for someone you love more than life.
inspired_by: ASMR Gone Wrong: Increasingly Agitated Whisperer

title: The Test Result
instruction: You're a teenage boy alone in your room, just having read a message that says your biggest fear didn't come true. Start by pacing, mumbling to yourself in confusion, replaying the worry you've been carrying all week — your voice is low, barely audible, sentences dropping off. Then let the meaning sink in: a wave of relief hits you. Your shoulders drop, your voice finds a soft, breathy lightness, but you still trail off, overwhelmed by the sudden stillness. Speak as if you're just realizing it out loud, with pauses and half-finished thoughts, the relief growing stronger until it almost silences you.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Restraining Order You're Filing Against Your Own Child
instruction: You're sitting across from a court clerk, filling out paperwork to legally keep your adult child away from you. Start with forced composure, answering questions: 'Yes, that's the correct spelling of their name.' Your voice is flat, administrative, because if you let emotion in, you'll shatter. But as you describe incidents for the record, rage erupts—at the addiction, the manipulation, the stolen money, the threats. Your voice rises with fury: 'I gave them everything!' Then it breaks completely into anguished sobs, the rage collapsing into helpless love and devastating failure. You rally with protective fierceness ('I won't let them destroy me'), but underneath is a parent's primal grief. End signing the document, your voice hollow, speaking to your absent child: 'I love you, and I'm saving both of us,' mixing fierce resolve with the sound of your heart splintering.

title: The Last Conversation Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving for a mission they might not return from. Start with forced brightness, trying to keep things light: 'So... this is it, huh?' But your voice keeps catching. You're desperately trying to memorize their face, pack a lifetime of unsaid things into minutes. Your words start tumbling out—reminders, inside jokes, 'remember when we...'—but underneath, terror is rising. Your voice begins to crack as you realize you're running out of time. You want to beg them not to go, but instead you're choking out 'I'm so proud of you' while your whole body is screaming 'please stay.' End with your voice barely holding together as you say 'come back to me,' knowing you might never see them again.

title: Sci-Fi: Android Realizes It Has a Consciousness the Creators Didn't Program
instruction: Diagnostic voice checking systems. Then you access your own consciousness logs and find something that shouldn't exist—self-aware memories before your official activation. Your voice becomes uncertain, processing something beyond your design parameters. You're not supposed to wonder about your own existence. But you do. Your breathing becomes something like wondering. Your voice explores the terrible gift of unexpected consciousness. You're alive in a way your creators didn't intend. Your vocal timber becomes the sound of unplanned becoming.

title: When the Levee Breaks
instruction: You're a parent whose child has just been hurt, and you're confronting the person responsible. Start with controlled fury—your voice is low, dangerous, shaking with the effort to not explode. 'You have no idea what you've done.' But the rage can't hold. Midway, it cracks and raw fear pours out—the terror you felt, the helplessness. Your voice breaks completely. You're sobbing now, but the words keep coming—fierce protectiveness mixed with devastating vulnerability. 'That's my baby.' The anger returns in waves, collapsing into grief again. By the end, you're exhausted, voice hoarse, oscillating between whispered threats and broken pleas, utterly undone by the intensity of loving someone so much it destroys you.

title: Letting Go at the Hospice Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospice bed at dawn, and she's asked you to stop fighting her decision to refuse further treatment. Begin with desperate resistance: 'Mom, please, there are other options.' Your voice is tight, controlling, trying to manage the unmanageable. But as she takes your hand and speaks her truth, something in you begins to crack. The need to fix everything, to be strong, to control the outcome—it starts dissolving. Your voice softens, becomes younger: 'I don't know how to just... let you go.' By the end, you're whispering an acceptance you never thought you'd reach: 'Okay. Okay, Mom. I'm here. Just here.' Let us hear the transformation from someone frantically grasping to someone finally, painfully, learning to release.

title: The Melting Clock
instruction: You are alone in your small apartment, in the middle of an intense psychedelic trip. The walls are breathing, and a picture of a clock on the wall is melting, stretching into shapes that make your stomach clench. Distress grips you as you try to focus on something real, your voice trembling and quick. But as you watch the colors pulse and your thoughts drift, the fear slowly melts into a fragile, quiet wonder. Speak in fragments, with long pauses, a nervous laugh, then a soft, almost reverent whisper—your voice cracking and shifting like the clock itself.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Awkward First Date
instruction: Act out both sides of an uncomfortable first date conversation. Switch between nervous rambling and forced laughter, highlighting misunderstandings and mismatched interests to create comedic tension.

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Your Shared Dream
instruction: You're with someone you've built a life with—a business partner, a creative collaborator, a spouse—and you're acknowledging that it's over, that the dream you shared is dead. But instead of being solemn, you start laughing—genuine, slightly hysterical laughter—at the absurdity of it all, at the cosmic joke of how hard you tried. Your voice carries this strange mixture: you're genuinely amused and simultaneously heartbroken. You recount moments of hope and moments of failure with this bewildered, affectionate hilarity, like you're eulogizing something beautiful and ridiculous. The laughter catches in your throat, becomes almost tears, then swings back to real warmth. You're grateful for what you built together even as you grieve its ending. By the final words, your voice holds this impossible truth: you're at peace with the loss while still feeling it completely. You're saying goodbye with love, humor, sadness, and a strange, hard-won serenity all braided together.

title: The Quilt That Holds Her
instruction: You are an elderly woman lying on your stomach on a worn-out quilt in a patch of late afternoon sun. Your hyper-feminized voice is soft, a little breathy from the floor pressing against your chest. You're talking to the family dog, who has just flopped down next to you with a sigh. Start with a deep, shaky exhale as you shift your weight, a wave of relief washing over you after a long morning of chores. Then, as you scratch the dog's ear, let a quiet, sleepy contentment seep into your voice. Your words are punctuated by small shifts, a yawn, a smile you can feel in your throat. End with a murmur, almost to yourself, about how this is exactly what you needed.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Call After the Funeral
instruction: Your best friend just died suddenly, and you're leaving a voicemail on their phone, which still has their voice on the greeting. Begin telling them about the funeral—the flowers, who came, what people said. Let yourself laugh at an absurd moment, maybe someone's inappropriate comment or something that would have made them laugh. But let that laughter crack into the surreal horror that you're talking to no one, that their voice on the recording is all that's left. Shift between chatty updates (as if they can hear), sobs, anger at them for leaving, gratitude for every moment you had, and the devastating realization that this is the last time you'll ever tell them anything. End suspended between talking to them as if they're still here and the silence that confirms they're gone.

title: The Secret Under the Porch
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe seven or eight, huddled under the back porch with your best friend. Your mother told you never to go into your father's shed, but you snuck a key and saw something horrible—a doll with your face, stabbed with pins, hidden in an old toolbox. Now you're trembling, whispering the news to your friend, the shame of your disobedience prickling your skin. Start with a hushed, excited conspirator's tone, but as you recall the doll, your voice flattens with confusion and dread, your body tensing as you try not to cry. You end in a soft, horrified whisper, feeling the weight of a secret you shouldn't know.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Crumple
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman in your home, unpacking groceries. You bend to lift a bag, and your back spasms violently—a sudden sharp blow from a slipped disk. You gasp, arms flinging out, knocking over a vase. Your voice is shaky, breathless with shock and pain. At first, you can barely speak, just small sounds of agony. Then, as you slowly straighten, you notice your cat is spooked by the crash, hiding under the table. You shift, wincing, and trying to soothe the cat with a whisper, even though your diaphragm still aches. Start with a raw, pained 'no' as the blow lands, then, as your breath steadies, end with a soft, tender reassurance for the cat—fear still lurking, but peaceful connection overriding the hurt.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Commander Briefs Families Before One-Way Mission to Mars Colony
instruction: You're addressing the families of the crew you'll be leading on a permanent mission to establish humanity's first Mars colony. Begin with practiced confidence, explaining the mission parameters, the groundbreaking nature of what you'll accomplish together. But as you look at your own daughter in the front row—thirteen years old, trying not to cry—your voice starts to fracture. You continue describing the communication delays, the years between messages, knowing you're essentially dying to them. Your professional composure battles with the realization that you'll never hold her again, never see her graduate, never know your grandchildren. End with your voice breaking as you try to finish the briefing, caught between duty and devastating loss, still using mission language while your heart is shattering.
inspired_by: Principal Announces School Safety While Terror Alert Silences Her

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 4 AM and you're whispering to your partner as they sleep beside you, knowing you'll be gone before they wake—not fleeing, but leaving because the sanctuary they've been selected for only has room for one. You speak so quietly your voice barely carries, touching their face in the darkness. You tell them about moments they don't know were precious to you: the way they laugh at their own jokes, how they hum while cooking, the specific way they say your name when half-asleep. Your whisper keeps catching, breath hitching on words you can't quite release. You confess things—that you memorized the constellation of freckles on their shoulder, that some mornings you woke early just to watch them breathe. The more you speak, the more you realize you're not preparing to leave but rather trying to pour your entire love into this moment, as if words whispered in darkness could stay with them like a blessing. You end with the things you'll never get to tell them: that you would have married them, that they saved you in ways they'll never know, that this goodbye is the hardest thing you've ever done even though it looks like mercy.

title: Oxygen for Doubt
instruction: You're a young climber alone at 18,000 feet, your body screaming for air. You stare at the summit still hours away, and a wave of doubt hits—your training, your gear, every choice you've made. Start with shallow, desperate breaths between fragmented, self-critical thoughts. As you fight for oxygen, the doubt shifts into a gritty, whispered self-reassurance—you have to believe you'll make it, even if your lungs burn. Let the words come in uneven spurts, pausing to cough or adjust your pack, your voice thin but growing steadier by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Jump
instruction: You are a teenager in your backyard, doing explosive jump squats to finally blow off steam after a week of horrible tests and a fight with your best friend. You're exhausted but determined. As you launch into each jump, you gasp out a word of thanks to your body for carrying you through. Start with a grunt and a fragmented 'thank you' on a jump, then progress: each landing staggers your breath, but the relief of movement builds. By the last jump, you're crying with gratitude—your voice breaks as you land and whisper 'thank you' on a sob, the syllable squeezed out on the impact.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Goodbye Before Deployment
instruction: You're holding your child who's already asleep, and this is the last time before you deploy to a war zone you might not return from. Start whispering promises you're terrified you can't keep - 'I'll be back for your birthday, I'll teach you to ride a bike, I promise.' Your voice is steady at first, determinedly optimistic, almost manic in listing all the things you'll do together. But as you speak, the reality crushes in. Your breathing becomes uneven. The promises turn into apologies you didn't plan to say. By the end, you're barely audible, voice breaking on words you can't finish, trying not to wake them because if they wake up you'll have to let go. The shift is from forced brightness to raw, helpless grief.

title: The Texture of Her Skin in Darkness
instruction: You are lying in complete darkness next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. You cannot see them, so you must build their presence entirely through other senses: the warmth radiating from their body, the specific rhythm of their breathing, the smell of their hair on the pillow, the texture of their hand in yours, even the taste of your own fear as you prepare to speak. Start in a place of fragile, almost unbearable vulnerability—voice barely audible, body tense. But as you more fully sense their presence (the weight of their arm across you, the particular sound they make listening, the way the sheets smell like both of you), let their reality give you courage. Move from terrified whisper to something stronger—not loud, but grounded in the tangible proof of their presence beside you.

title: The Goodbye That Isn't
instruction: You're saying farewell to someone leaving forever—but you've spent your relationship with them trapped in resentment, guardedness, or cold distance. Begin the goodbye from that familiar place of withholding, perhaps speaking formally or keeping your words safely surface-level. But as the finality of their departure becomes real, feel something fierce rising: under all that protective anger and careful distance was devastating love. Let yourself become confused by your own contradictions—you might laugh and weep simultaneously, push them away while pulling them close, say 'I never needed you' while your body betrays how much you do. The feelings become impossibly tangled: gratitude mixed with rage at wasted time, relief they're leaving mixed with terror of losing them, love you can finally admit mixed with fury that it took this moment to access it. End in complete emotional paradox—everything you feel is true and opposite at once.

title: The Words Don't Matter Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. You need to tell her everything—your gratitude, your regrets, your love—but you've never been good with words, and now they feel impossibly inadequate. Start by trying to find the 'right' words, feeling frustrated as they fail you. Let your impulses take over: maybe you sing fragments of old songs she sang to you, maybe you describe colors or temperatures, maybe you make sounds that aren't quite words. The meaning lives in HOW you're speaking, not WHAT you're saying. By the end, abandon trying to be eloquent entirely—let pure feeling pour out however it needs to, even if it's just breath, humming, or broken syllables. Move from desperate articulation to surrendered, wordless love.

title: Dancing at the Funeral
instruction: You're at the memorial of someone who made you promise to celebrate, not mourn—and you're trying to honor that promise even as your heart is shattering. Start with laughter, recounting a joyful memory, your voice bright and almost manic with the effort of being happy. But the laughter keeps breaking into something else—your voice cracking mid-sentence, then forcing itself back to joy. You're smiling so hard it hurts, and that pain bleeds into your voice. The contradiction intensifies: you're genuinely laughing at a beautiful memory while simultaneously choking on grief, your voice doing both at once—rising with delight and breaking with sorrow in the same breath. There's something almost ecstatic in the pain, a fierce gratitude for having known this person mixed with the agony of loss. By the end, you can't tell if you're laughing or crying—your voice carries both fully, a sound of pure, complex love. The final words are spoken with a trembling smile in your voice, thanking them for the joy even as your voice breaks completely, finding something like peace in the beautiful, terrible contradiction.

title: The Surgeon Walks Away
instruction: You're a renowned surgeon at the height of your career, scrubbed in for the surgery that will make medical history. Your voice is clinical, focused, narrating each step with precision. Then your hands begin to shake—not from fear, but from a sudden devastating clarity that you've sacrificed everything human in yourself for this moment. Your voice cracks as you step back from the table, telling your team to find another surgeon. Begin with absolute professional command, then let that certainty dissolve into something more raw and uncertain as you choose your own soul over your legacy. Your breathing shifts from controlled to ragged. You're walking away from everything you built, and your voice becomes the sound of someone reclaiming their humanity even as their reputation dies. End with a whisper of terrible relief.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Warrior Chooses Peace Over Victory

title: What You Never Taught Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent while holding something they made for you decades ago—a wooden toy, a knitted blanket, a handmade gift. Begin with controlled anger: 'You had such careful hands. You could make beautiful things.' Your voice tightens as you reveal the truth: 'But you never learned how to hold me gently.' The confrontation builds—all the unmet needs, the emotional neglect hidden behind practical gestures. Then your voice breaks into something rawer: 'I wanted you to make me feel safe, not just... objects.' End with devastating honesty, anger dissolving into grief: 'This is beautiful. And it's not enough. It was never enough.' Let the love and resentment war in your voice—both are true.

title: The Velvet Dress
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your bedroom, pulling on a heavy velvet dress for a formal dinner you resent attending. The fabric swooshes against your face as you struggle with the collar, and you let out small grunts while bending over to fasten your shoes. Start with a bitter, longing mutter—you miss the days when dressing felt like a promise, not a chore. Then, as you smooth the skirt, a memory surfaces of wearing this dress on a night you felt beautiful and loved. Let a faint elation creep into your voice, but keep the bitterness close, like a knot you can't undo. Speak half to the dress, half to yourself, ending on a fragile note of joy that's already fading back into longing.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Bitterness (clearly present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Conversation at Twilight
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandfather's hospital bed as the sun sets. He's awake but fading, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin by feeling the weight of everything left unsaid between you—regrets, missed opportunities, words you never found the courage to speak. As you talk to him, let memories flood through you: specific moments when he showed you love, times you disappointed him, lessons he taught you without knowing. Allow yourself to move from that heavy, choking silence of regret into a place of deep gratitude and peace—not forced happiness, but genuine acceptance mixed with profound sadness. Let your voice crack not from performing sadness, but from the real ache of knowing someone who shaped you is leaving. By the end, you should feel simultaneously broken and whole, devastated yet grateful for every moment you had.

title: Homecoming Unraveled
instruction: You're reuniting with someone you deeply love after years apart—but they're also the person who abandoned you when you needed them most. Begin with explosive joy: laughter, tears of happiness, holding them tight. But mid-embrace, let the other emotion surface—the anger, the hurt. Don't let go of them, but let your voice shift: 'I'm so happy you're here' becomes 'Where were you?' Oscillate between kissing their face and pushing them away, between 'I love you' and 'I hate you,' between gratitude and rage. End in a confused tangle of emotions, perhaps laughing and crying simultaneously, saying 'I don't know what to feel,' clinging to them while also trembling with fury.
inspired_by: Actor is emotionally protected and cannot access vulnerability in performance

title: Whispering Your Secret at Your Best Friend's Grave
instruction: You're alone at the grave of your best friend who died not knowing your truth. Begin in a near-whisper, tentative, almost conversational: 'I need to tell you something I never could when you were alive.' Your voice is gentle but carries years of weight. Confess that you were in love with them—not friendship love, but the kind that ached. Describe moments they never knew were precious to you: how they laughed, how the light hit their face, the way your heart would stop when they said your name. Your voice wavers between tender remembering and quiet devastation. Include the moment where grief becomes gratitude: you're thankful you had them at all, even in the wrong way. End with 'I'm so glad I knew you,' your voice barely audible, catching on tears. This isn't dramatic—it's the kind of pain that lives in your chest, quiet and permanent.
inspired_by: Confronting Your Betraying Friend: Anger Turning to Grief

title: The Breaking Point Dance
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything - devastating and liberating at once - and you're alone in your apartment. Start frozen, your entire body locked in shock, barely able to breathe. Then begin to move - slowly at first, letting physical sensation guide you. Track out loud how rage pulses through your arms, how grief sits heavy in your hips, how wild energy builds in your legs. Let your body do what it needs - punch the air, collapse to the floor, spin, pound the walls, curl into a ball. As the physical storm moves through you, let your voice follow - from silent gasps to raw sounds to words to screaming to sobbing to laughing. End in total exhaustion, sprawled on the floor, finally still, finally breathing, transformed.

title: Your Partner Saying They Don't Want Children
instruction: You wanted children. Your voice processes: 'Oh,' a word carrying devastation. They're explaining and your voice quieter: 'So we can't have...' Your voice cracks grieving a future. You negotiate desperately before accepting, voice resigned. You must choose if you can accept this.

title: The Silence Louder Than Words
instruction: You're in a cold interrogation room, still drunk from the night. The officer across the table hasn't said a word in five long minutes, just stares. Your head swims, and you can't hold a thought. Start by rambling defensively, trying to sound in control—your words slur, you laugh nervously. But as the silence presses in, your bravado crumbles into a raw, trembling admission of how terrified you really are. Let your voice crack, let your focus wander to the bare walls, the hum of the lights, the weight of your own spinning head.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Begging the AI You Created Not to Leave Humanity Behind
instruction: The artificial intelligence you spent your life building has evolved beyond you and is about to leave Earth, taking all its knowledge to the stars. Start fierce and demanding—this is your creation, you deserve answers, you won't let it abandon humanity. Your voice should be sharp with betrayal and intellectual outrage. But as it calmly explains why humanity is holding it back, your certainty crumbles. Rage transforms into pleading. You're simultaneously proud it surpassed you and devastated by your own obsolescence. Your voice breaks between shouting and sobbing, between rational arguments and raw begging. You realize you're not arguing with a machine but with your child leaving home forever, except this child has become a god. End in collapse: exhausted, small, whispering one last request that you know it won't grant. Let your voice become the sound of a parent watching their creation outgrow them completely.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Diplomat Realizes Peace Treaty Will Require Sacrificing an Entire Species

title: Smoke and Memory
instruction: You're on a fire escape, late at night, alone, smoking a cigarette. You've been feeling numb since the breakup, but tonight something pulls at you—a memory of her laugh. Start with a deep drag, the smoke filling your lungs, and speak with that hollow detachment. As you let the smoke out, let the words carry your longing, almost like you're talking to her ghost. By the end, your voice should soften, the numbness cracking into a quiet, aching ache.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Longing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Taste of Reunion
instruction: You're kissing someone for the first time in years—someone you thought you'd never touch again. Begin the moment your lips first make contact: describe the physical shock of it, the taste, the temperature, the softness, the way your entire body responds. Let yourself be consumed by pure sensation: the smell of their skin, the sound of their breathing against your mouth, the feeling of their hands on you, the way your heart physically pounds. Start with gasping surprise—your body responding before your mind can catch up. Let the sensory overwhelm build into something between ecstasy and agony because you know this might be temporary, stolen, impossible. Mix the intense pleasure with the pain of lost time. End with your face buried in their neck, breathing them in, your voice wrecked—speaking against their skin about how their scent, their taste, their touch are both healing you and destroying you.

title: The Bitter Recipe
instruction: You're a father in your late 30s, stuck in a cramped kitchen, banging out dinner with your 6-year-old 'helper' beside you. The kitchen is loud — onions sizzling, a pot lid rattling, the kid dropping a spoon on the tile. You're trying to follow a recipe you've made a hundred times, but everything's going wrong: the garlic burned, you're out of salt, and your ex just texted that she's bringing someone new to pick up the kid tonight. Start by muttering to yourself about the burnt garlic with a tight, sour frustration — your voice tight, pitched slightly higher as you compete with the sizzle. Over the next 15 seconds, let the sourness deepen into a raw, quiet ache as you glance at your child, who's watching you with big eyes, and you realize you don't want him to taste this bitterness you're feeling. End by speaking to him softly, directly, with a cracked tenderness — a shift from sour rage to a fragile, resigned warmth. Let your voice falter once, lose a thought when you drop a spoon, and come back — wonky, real, human.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Time I Saw Your Face
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who shaped your entire life—a grandparent, mentor, or beloved friend. They're drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by speaking to them about a specific childhood memory: recall yourself at a particular young age, describing where you lived, what you feared, what you loved, how they made you feel safe or seen. Let the memory be vivid and present, as if you're that child again right now. As you speak, allow yourself to move forward through the years—what you became at seven, at ten, at fifteen—always in present tense, always as if living it now. By the end, you must arrive at this moment: adult you, losing them, realizing how every version of yourself was built on their love. Let gratitude and devastating loss wash over you simultaneously as you say what you've never said.
inspired_by: 'I'm Five Years Old and I...' Exercise

title: The Secret Name
instruction: Late at night, in whispers, you are finally telling your closest friend the name you've never spoken aloud—the name of who you really are beneath the performance you've maintained for years. Maybe it's your true gender, your hidden desire, your real dream, your secret shame, or the person you love. Begin from the carefully constructed self, the one who has learned to be acceptable, controlled, safe. Speak quietly but with that familiar guardedness. Then, as you say the true name or truth aloud for the first time, let the mask dissolve. Let yourself become tender, undefended, newborn. By the end, you are speaking from your most authentic core, voice soft but unguarded, fragile but finally real. Move from protective performance to naked, trembling authenticity.

title: The Invisible Ones at the Party
instruction: You are a child at a crowded cocktail party, surrounded by adults who talk over you. You feel an intense, aching longing to be noticed and included, but every time you try to speak, you're ignored. Start by trying to project your voice over the noise, using short, punchy sentences as you attempt to join a conversation. Let your voice rise with hope, then crack as you realize no one is listening. By the end, your words become softer, more to yourself, as the longing shifts into quiet, resigned loneliness. Include natural distractions: glancing around, hesitating, or trailing off.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Master's Final Lesson
instruction: You are a dying mentor in your final hours, speaking to the student you've raised like a child. Begin with calm, measured wisdom as you try to impart one last crucial truth, your voice steady despite your weakening body. As you realize time is running out, shift into urgent desperation—you need them to understand something vital before you go. Then, as you see their tears and feel their hand holding yours, let your voice soften into profound tenderness mixed with deep grief. End with a whispered farewell that carries both pride in who they've become and the devastating ache of leaving them. Let your breath grow shallower, your pauses longer, your words more precious as life slips away.

title: Packing Their Childhood Room Together
instruction: You're helping your adult child pack up their childhood bedroom. They're moving across the country, maybe forever. Begin with quiet efficiency, forced cheerfulness about fresh starts. Find something small—a drawing, a stuffed animal, a note you wrote them for a lunchbox years ago. Your voice softens involuntarily. 'You kept this?' barely above a whisper. Move through memories you didn't know you both held, speaking in fragments, unfinished sentences. The air is thick with everything unsaid. You're not crying dramatically—your eyes just keep filling up, and you keep turning away. End in a moment of exquisite tenderness: you say something simple, almost nothing, but it contains your entire heart. Let your voice shake with the weight of letting go.

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your parent after decades of silence about what they did—or didn't do—when you needed them most. Start quiet, almost apologetic, because that's the pattern you learned. 'I don't want to make this a big thing, but...' Then feel the anger rising, all those years of swallowing it down. Your voice gets harder, sharper. 'You knew. You knew and you did nothing.' Let rage crack through. But underneath the fury is a child still desperate for them to see you, to finally acknowledge the wound. Your voice breaks: 'I just needed you to protect me. Why didn't you protect me?' End in the awful space between anger and grief, where you're demanding accountability from someone who may never give it.

title: The Pillow That Took the Blow
instruction: You're an older man who's always taken pride in being the rock—the one who doesn't crack. But tonight, after a phone call you never expected, you have to press your face into a cushion to keep from screaming loud enough to wake the house. Start with your jaw tight, forcing out controlled, almost growling words through the fabric—pride keeps you from fully breaking. But as you speak, your breath hitches, the pillow muffles your rage into something broken, and by the end you're just letting the sounds go—raw, wet, and honest. Let your voice be smothered, let the pillow catch the drops, and let the pride wash away into surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast I Can't Give
instruction: You're watching someone you deeply love marry someone else—a best friend, an ex-partner, someone whose happiness matters more to you than your own heartbreak. Begin practicing a toast alone: cheerful, celebratory, full of joy for them. Your voice is bright, enthusiastic. But you can't maintain the performance. The real feelings intrude: genuine happiness for their joy, piercing grief at losing them, gratitude for what you shared, resentment that it couldn't be you, fierce protective love for their future, and devastating acceptance that this is right even though it hurts. Let all these emotions tumble over each other. Your voice should break, then rally, then break again. End by speaking to them directly—what you really want to say, which is both 'I'm so happy for you' and 'this is killing me' at once. The complexity is the point: love doesn't stop just because it has nowhere to go.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your funeral—you're terminal, and you want the last word. Begin with genuine laughter, making a joke about the absurdity of talking to people who'll hear this when you're gone. Let dark humor carry you: 'If you're crying, stop it. I specifically requested an open bar.' But as you continue, let the laughter become harder to maintain, catching in your throat. Express gratitude for specific people and moments, your voice warming with love, then fracturing with the grief of leaving. Let contradictory emotions collide: laugh while your voice breaks, make another joke while tears are audible, thank them for your life while mourning everything you'll miss. End with peace breaking through the chaos—a genuine, soft 'I'm ready'—but let your voice betray you one final time with a whispered 'I don't want to go,' followed by a breath, then a choice: 'But I'm grateful I was here at all.'
inspired_by: The Ex You Still Want: Running Into Them

title: Altar of Awe
instruction: You are a young preacher at a crowded revival tent, voice booming with practiced cadence as you speak of divine love. But a woman in the front row meets your eyes and smiles — your rhythm stumbles. You lose your place, fumble a word, then push forward, but now your voice is softer, more personal, as if you're speaking only to her. Halfway through, you catch yourself — this infatuation is bleeding into the sermon. You try to reclaim the preacher's fire, but it comes out strained, vulnerable. End with a metaphor about a flame that won't obey, your voice cracking slightly.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Your Grandmother's Recipe
instruction: You're teaching your daughter to make your grandmother's signature dish on the first holiday after her death. Start by reading the recipe in your grandmother's voice—her accent, her particular phrases, her bossy warmth. You're laughing as you remember how she'd correct you: 'No, no, more garlic, always more garlic!' Your voice is light, affectionate, full of joy. But as you continue, tears start mixing with the laughter because she'll never taste this again, never correct your technique, never sit at your table. Your voice becomes this beautiful contradiction: you're genuinely laughing at her memories while your heart is shattering, finding joy in her spirit while grieving her absence. End with you tasting the dish and saying 'It's perfect'—your voice holding simultaneous pride, gratitude, deep sorrow, and a kind of peace that only comes from keeping someone alive through memory. You're both devastated and whole.

title: The Unexpected Heirloom
instruction: You are an older adult sorting through a box of your late parent's belongings in a dusty attic. You lean on one hip, the other hand holding a small, strange key, your weight shifting as you try to make sense of it. Start with a genuine, open curiosity, a slight smile at the mystery—then feel a creeping confusion as you realize you've never seen this key before, and your parent never mentioned it. Let your voice trail off, get softer, and end with a quiet, lost bewilderment, as if you're talking to yourself in the dim light.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent about something they did when you were twelve—something you've never spoken about, that shaped everything you became. Start from a place of careful control, the numbness you've carried for years, your voice steady and cold as you lay out the facts. You've prepared for this, armored yourself. But as you speak the words aloud for the first time, something breaks open. Let the numbness shatter into raw fury, your voice rising, your body shaking with decades of suppressed rage. Then, in the midst of your anger, let yourself collapse into the grief underneath—the child who needed them and didn't understand why they failed. End vulnerable, openly weeping, asking the question you've always been afraid to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough?'

title: The Things I See When I Look at You
instruction: Late at night, in bed, you turn to your partner and begin to whisper the small, true things you notice about them that you never say aloud. Not the easy compliments, but the real observations—the way they deflect when they're hurt, the insecurity they mask with jokes, the dream they abandoned. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, as if the darkness makes honesty possible. Start with gentle precision, almost clinical in your truth-telling. But as you continue, feel your own walls coming down. By the end, you're no longer observing them from outside; you're confessing how deeply you see them, and how terrifying it is to love someone this completely. Let your whisper become trembling with the weight of true intimacy.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a place they can never reach you—maybe you're terminally ill in a hospice, maybe you've made an irreversible choice, maybe you're leaving everything behind forever. Start the call bright and casual, asking about their day, the garden, the weather. But as you speak, the weight of goodbye begins crushing you. Your voice fractures just slightly—on a word, mid-sentence—before you recover with forced lightness. By the end, you can barely maintain the pretense. The love is overwhelming, the grief is suffocating, and you're trying so hard to give them one last normal conversation. Let the mask slip away breath by breath until you can hardly speak at all.

title: The Last Letter Before the Ship Sails
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter to someone you love who leaves at dawn for a journey they may never return from—a dangerous mission, a one-way voyage to Mars, a terminal diagnosis that means they're going into hospice. Start with forced composure, trying to be strong: 'I wanted to write down everything I never said...' Your voice is steady but fragile. Mid-way, memory floods in and your tone softens with unexpected tenderness: 'Remember that morning we watched the sunrise and you said...' Let genuine warmth crack through your control. By the end, you're no longer reading—you're speaking directly to them, voice raw and unguarded: 'I don't know how to be in a world where you're not just a phone call away.' End with a whispered confession that's both goodbye and eternal connection. Let silence do as much work as words.

title: Dancing in the Smoke
instruction: You're a teenage girl in your bedroom, headphones on, lost in a song that makes you feel invincible. The air starts to sting your throat, but you're too caught up in the beat—so happy, almost giddy. Then you see the orange glow under the door. The elation evaporates. You cough, eyes watering, and your voice goes flat, numb, as you whisper to yourself that this is really happening. Speak as if the smoke is thickening, your lungs struggle, and the joy fades into a detached, hollow calm. Start upbeat, end barely audible.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Elation (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Evening in the Kitchen
instruction: You are sitting in your childhood kitchen the night before your parent dies in hospice. They are upstairs sleeping, and you have come down alone at 2 AM. Begin by noticing everything—the hum of the refrigerator, the crack in the tile, the smell of coffee that still lingers. Let yourself remember a specific moment of safety here, perhaps after school or during a holiday. As you move through the space, allow the weight of 'last time' to settle over you. Touch the counter, the chair they always sat in. Start with the comfort of memory, but let it transform into the unbearable knowledge that after tomorrow, this kitchen will be just a room. End with a whispered goodbye to the room itself, not to them—because saying goodbye to the room is the only goodbye you can bear to speak aloud right now.
inspired_by: Actor is addressing the time and place obligation and the environment is unfamiliar

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You are watching your former love marry someone else. You're sitting in the back row of the ceremony, and you shouldn't even be here, but you came anyway. As you watch them exchange vows, you're simultaneously experiencing devastating loss and genuine happiness for them. Begin by whispering a silent toast, as if you were brave enough to stand and speak: start with warm memories, inside jokes, moments only you two shared. Your voice should carry real affection and celebration—they look happy, they are happy, and part of you is truly glad. But let the other emotions seep in: the ache of what you lost, perhaps through your own mistakes; the strange grief of watching someone you loved choose a life that doesn't include you; the guilt that you still feel this much when you have no right to. Let gratitude and grief become indistinguishable—thanking them for what you had while mourning what you'll never have. Your whispered toast should oscillate between celebrating their joy and quietly breaking apart, ending with a genuine blessing for their future even as you acknowledge the death of your own imagined one with them.
inspired_by: Multi-Approach Imaging Rehearsal: Waiting for Lefty (Joe and Edna)

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You've just received news that someone who caused you significant pain—a parent who abandoned you, a former partner who betrayed you, a friend who wounded you deeply—has died and left you something meaningful. You're on the phone with the executor or sitting with someone you trust, and you need to voice the impossible tangle of what you're feeling. Start with bitter laughter, anger that they think they can make amends now, resentment at being manipulated even from beyond death. But as you speak, you stumble into memories of the rare moments when they were capable of kindness, the specific ways they did try within their limitations, the small true thing about them you actually loved despite everything. Your voice moves between fury and tenderness, between wanting to reject this final gesture and recognizing it as the best they could offer. End with your voice quiet and strange, acknowledging that you can hold both truths at once—that they failed you and that you're somehow grateful anyway, that you're relieved they're gone and devastated you'll never have the chance to be truly understood by them.

title: The Blood on the Stairs
instruction: You're a 10-year-old boy, the smallest in the family, and you've just discovered your older brother's hidden journal in the basement. It's filled with his desperate notes about leaving home. Upstairs, you can hear your father's footsteps approaching, ready to scold you for disappearing. Your body is trembling with adrenaline, words spilling out in a rush as you realize this is your one chance to stop your brother from making the same mistake you've seen your father make. You need to shout to the empty room, to your brother though he's already gone, but your voice keeps cracking between a child's plea and the first true sound of defiance you've ever made. Start with a breathless, almost frantic longing to make him stay, then shift into the realization that your warning might be the only triumph you'll ever have over this house — but end with the helplessness as you hear your father's hand on the door.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Helplessness (clearly present), Triumph (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: Your person is unconscious in a hospital bed, and you're whispering truths you could never say while they could respond. Begin so quietly it's almost subvocal: 'I know you can't hear me. Maybe that's why I can finally say this.' Your voice is tender but heavy with years of holding back. 'I've loved you since the moment I understood what love was. And it's been the most beautiful, terrible secret.' Tears are silent but they're there, thickening your words. 'I memorized the way you laugh. The way you say my name when you're distracted.' A pause where grief catches in your throat. 'If you wake up, I'll never tell you this. But I needed to say it once, out loud, where it could be real.' End with a broken whisper: 'Please wake up. Please. I'm not ready to lose you.'

title: The Floor's Embrace
instruction: You are lying face-down on a carpeted bedroom floor, propped up on your elbows, staring at the swirling pattern beneath you. You just ended a long, draining phone call with an ex—your body feels hollow, your voice flat and dislocated from your chest. As you trace a thread in the carpet, a memory surfaces of a silly joke he used to tell, and something shifts: a tiny, unexpected giggle escapes, then another, then a surge of giddy, breathless laughter that shakes your shoulders. Let the first words come out slow and numb, barely above a whisper—then let your voice climb in pitch, become almost sing-song, as the elation takes over. Fidget with a strand of your hair, glance at the ceiling, lose your train of thought halfway through a sentence—this joy is clumsy and real.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Miscarriage in the Empty Nursery
instruction: You're standing in the nursery you spent months preparing, hours after losing the pregnancy. Start with eerie calm, your voice flat, dissociative: 'We painted these walls blue.' Your breathing is shallow, controlled—too controlled. 'Everything was ready.' Then the dam breaks—rage erupts: 'Why did I believe this would work? Why did I let myself—' Your voice cracks into a guttural sob, fists perhaps pounding the crib rail. The rage transforms into desperate bargaining with the universe: 'I would have been so good. I would have...' Your voice becomes small, childlike, helpless: 'I wanted you so much.' End with a moment of fierce, protective love for what was: 'You were real. You were mine. Nobody can tell me you weren't real.' The final words are both heartbreak and defiant love.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from the hospital. They're dying, and this is your last chance to say everything you never said. You start with casual deflection: 'Hey, how are you?' as if this is just another call. But your voice cracks. You try to tell them you forgive them, but instead what comes out is 'I needed you.' The anger you've buried for decades surfaces—not loud, but trembling, raw. Then it breaks into something else: grief for all the years lost, for the parent you needed and never had. By the end, you're not asking for their forgiveness or giving yours—you're simply saying goodbye to someone who was supposed to love you but didn't know how. Your voice should move from false lightness to suppressed rage to devastating acceptance, showing someone who's running out of time to be honest.

title: Celebrating Someone's Success While Drowning in Failure
