instruction: Your best friend got the promotion you both wanted. You hug them, congratulate them—your voice is genuine but there's an edge underneath. 'That's amazing, you deserved it.' As they talk, your voice becomes smaller, more distracted. Your breathing changes slightly as you're happy and devastated simultaneously.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone, whispering something you've never told another soul—not a dramatic secret, but something quietly true about who you really are underneath everything. Begin barely audible, testing whether you can actually say it out loud. Let your breathing reveal your fear. Notice how your voice wants to shut down, get smaller, disappear. But stay with it, letting each phrase come from your actual belly, your actual throat. Find the micro-shifts: shame softening into relief, fear transforming into tentative hope. By the end, you're no longer hiding in the dark—you're present in it, somehow both more fragile and more whole than when you began.
inspired_by: When an actor has been told they are 'not that kind of actor' when invited to do emotional preparation

title: The Door That Swallows Fury
instruction: You're standing before a closed door behind which someone you love and hate is waiting. Your whole body is shaking. Begin by staring at the door - its color, the doorknob, any imperfections. Let your mind release: maybe the door is breathing with your rage, maybe it's sweating, maybe you can see your own face screaming in the wood grain, maybe the door is growing teeth, maybe it's melting and reforming. Allow the most bizarre, violent, nonsensical images to flood through you - perhaps the door is laughing, perhaps it's bleeding your history, perhaps it's becoming your lover's body. Let these wild visions build the physical intensity in your body. Start trembling with controlled anger, but as the images become more outrageous and unhinged, let your entire physicality transform - your breathing, your posture, your voice. Touch the door. Press against it. Let the sensory experience of rage mixed with desperate longing consume you until you don't know if you want to break through or collapse against it. End in a completely different physical and emotional state than you began.
inspired_by: Actor's imagination feels weak, overly literal, or unable to generate creative choices

title: The Eulogy You'll Never Hear
instruction: You've just learned you have months to live, and you're writing what you imagine people will say at your funeral—how they'll describe you, what they'll remember. Start by writing the eulogy you always hoped for, based on who you believe you've been: kind, inspiring, present, successful. But as you write, you're flooded with memories of who you actually were in specific moments—the times you chose work over presence, pride over apology, fear over courage. Your voice should break between pride and grief, between the person you wanted to be and the person you were. End with both gratitude for the life you had and aching sorrow for the gap between aspiration and reality. You're mourning yourself while still alive, grieving both what you accomplished and what you failed to become. Move from proud nostalgia to painful honesty to bittersweet acceptance.

title: Laughing Through Goodbye
instruction: You're saying farewell to someone or something beloved, and you're trying to celebrate rather than mourn. Begin with forced lightness: 'This is good, this is what we wanted,' but your voice cracks with suppressed grief. As you recall beautiful memories, you laugh—genuine, warm, full of love—but the laughter keeps breaking into tears. You're telling stories that make you both laugh and sob simultaneously. Your voice dances between joy and heartbreak, sometimes within the same sentence. End with profound gratitude spoken through tears, your voice soft and wondering: 'Thank you for every single moment.' The emotions braid together—celebration and loss, gratitude and grief, love and letting go, all present at once.

title: The Edge of the Interview
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman sitting on a high stool in a job interview, waiting for a question that’s come too late. Your body is perched, core tight, hands clasped in your lap to keep from trembling. You’ve been polite for hours, but now anger leaks through—a sharpness in your tone, a pause where you swallow hard. As you speak, you shift your weight on the stool, let your eyes flick to the corner of the room, then back to the interviewer. Start with controlled, clipped words, then let the anger break open into a raw, half-thought confession about why you really need this role. End with a quieter, drained honesty, as if the admission cost you something.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: When Magic Fails the Ones We Love
instruction: You are desperately trying to save someone you love with a healing spell, arguing with your familiar about the incantation. Start with fierce determination bordering on mania—your voice rapid, insistent, aggressive in its hope. The familiar (switch to low, grave tones) tries to tell you it's too late, but you refuse to hear it. Let your certainty explode into rage: at magic, at fate, at them for giving up. Scream the spell with everything you have. Then let that fury shatter into helplessness—your voice collapsing mid-word, breaking into gasping sobs. The familiar's voice softens into devastating tenderness as they witness your undoing. End in the terrible quiet after the spell fails, your voice small and lost, their voice a gentle anchor in your chaos. Raw. Uncontrolled. Utterly human.
inspired_by: The Young Witch and Her Talking Cat

title: The Hungry Echo
instruction: You are a seven-year-old boy lying in your bed at night, alone in the dark, listening to the muffled sounds of your father's voice from the other room. He's on a phone call, and the low, rhythmic moans that escape him frighten you — they sound like a wild animal enjoying a kill. You try to mimic the sound softly, testing its shape in your own throat, your lips barely parting. Start curious and nervous, then become deliberate and cold as you realize you can make that same sound — and you like it. Let your voice crack with fear at first, then settle into a thin, breathy imitation, pausing to listen, then repeating with a small, wicked smile. End on a single, satisfied whisper, your own malice blooming like a dark seed in the dark.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unwelcome Veil
instruction: You are a young man at a costume party, and as a joke, someone has tied a niqab over your face. You can barely see, the fabric is loose but muffles your voice slightly. You start by trying to laugh it off, but then you realize you can't get it off easily. Your confusion grows into frustration as you struggle with the veil while speaking. Let your voice be filtered by the fabric—occasionally louder, sometimes fading—as you shift from bewildered amusement to genuine exasperation. End with a sigh of resignation, still lost.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Word You Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your father/mother after years of silence. You begin angry, voice tight with accumulated rage, listing all the ways they failed you. Then you remember: when you were seven, before everything fell apart, you played a game together. They gave you a word—something like 'brave' or 'lighthouse' or 'belonging'—and asked you to build a story around it. You start to tell that childhood story now, voice shifting from bitter to confused to achingly vulnerable. As the story unfolds, you realize it was their way of telling you something they couldn't say directly—perhaps an apology, a promise, a truth about their own pain. Your anger should dissolve into something more complicated: grief mixed with understanding, betrayal mixed with reluctant love. End with the question you're terrified to ask: 'Did you know what you were telling me? Did you mean it?'

title: Grateful Farewell to a Life You Must Leave
instruction: You're leaving behind everything you love—a place, a person, a version of yourself—and it's the right choice, but it's destroying you. Begin with genuine warmth, almost laughing through tears: 'God, we had something beautiful here, didn't we?' Your voice carries both joy and heartbreak simultaneously. You're remembering specific moments, and your tone is filled with gratitude even as it trembles. 'When you did that thing, that ridiculous thing with the—' You laugh, then the laugh catches and becomes a sob, then back to laughing. The emotions are completely intertwined. 'Thank you for everything, truly, I mean—' Your voice breaks but there's peace underneath the pain. By the end, you've found a strange, beautiful acceptance, your voice quiet and steady even as tears fall: 'This mattered. You mattered. And now I have to go.' Gratitude and grief are inseparable, creating something almost transcendent.

title: Loved One's Illness Has Uncertain Prognosis: Living in Limbo
instruction: Your loved one is ill and the doctors can't tell you what will happen. Your voice is scared, trying to stay functional while living in complete uncertainty. 'They're not better but they're not worse.' You're narrating the non-change as if it means something. Include the moment where you have to talk about worst-case scenarios and your voice becomes almost robotic, dissociating as a survival mechanism. Then you're sitting with them and your voice becomes softer, more present, because being present is all you can do. Your voice carries the specific exhaustion of hope held in tension with dread. You can't let go but you can't move forward. This is your life now—waiting, hoping, terrified. Your voice is the sound of someone holding something they can't control.

title: The Clean Room
instruction: You are in a pristine white meeting room, staring at a glass of water on the table. Across from you sits the person you have been obsessively infatuated with for months — their scent, their laugh, the way they tap their fingers. You’ve finally gotten a private moment with them, but your body feels like it’s encased in plastic. Your voice comes from somewhere far away. Start by describing the water glass — precise, flat, detached — as if it’s the only thing real. Then, without changing your monotone, tell them exactly how their presence makes your skin crawl with disgust. Let the words hang, empty and exact. Do not let any feeling color your voice; let the horror be in the gap between what you say and how you say it.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Raspy Confession
instruction: You're a teenage girl with a bad case of laryngitis, stuck at home with a sandpaper voice. Your crush just called you out of the blue — you're thrilled but horrified that you sound like a frog. The conversation starts with you apologizing, wincing at your own voice, feeling disgusted by how gross you sound. But as he keeps talking, your infatuation takes over — you forget to be self-conscious, your voice gets softer, warmer, almost dreamy. Let your words crackle and fade, swallow painfully mid-sentence, then brighten with excitement when you realize he's flirting back. End with a whispered giggle that turns into a cough.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She raised you when no one else would. Begin speaking to her about an ordinary morning memory from childhood—her making breakfast, the smell of coffee, sunlight through kitchen curtains. Let yourself feel the comfort of that memory. As you speak, you gradually realize she can no longer hear you, that she left during the night while you slept in the chair. Your voice should travel from warm nostalgia into the crushing, silent weight of being too late. End in a whisper, as if you're trying to call her back from somewhere unreachable. Let your body register the loss—the heaviness, the emptiness, the last threads of connection breaking.

title: Folding Their Laundry: The Quiet Unraveling After Sudden Loss
instruction: You're alone, folding your deceased spouse's clothes to donate. You start methodically, voice steady as you narrate what you're doing—maybe talking to them out of habit, maybe to yourself. 'Your blue shirt. You always said it made your eyes look...' Your voice is soft, intimate, the way you'd talk doing chores together. Then you find the shirt they wore on your first date, and your hands stop. Your breathing changes. You're whispering now, telling them about the small things you miss—how they hummed while cooking, the way they said your name when half-asleep. Your voice isn't crying, but it's breaking in this tender, devastating way. You're confessing the mundane details you're terrified of forgetting. The confession becomes a lullaby, a love letter, a prayer. Your voice finds this aching gentleness, like you're tucking them in one last time, even as your heart is shattering.
inspired_by: Worst Case Scenario Spiraling: Catastrophizing Out Loud

title: Locked In
instruction: You're a woman in a crowded locker room after a game, surrounded by male friends who are boisterously trash-talking the opposing team. You start with a slight doubt, a quiet hope that maybe your team can pull through, but as the guys interrupt and posture, you feel a rush of contempt for the other side's smugness. Let your voice rise and fall with the room — loud, percussive laughter, then a sharper edge when you cut in. End with a fierce optimism that drowns out the doubt, your pitch climbing with conviction as you fire back a final defiant line.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Contempt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. Your partner is barely awake beside you, and you need to tell them something you've been carrying for months—a secret, a fear, a truth about yourself. Begin in whispers, testing each word before you release it. Your voice should be almost nothing at first, as if speaking too loud will shatter the safety of darkness. Let your body hold the vulnerability: hands fidgeting with the sheets, breath shallow and cautious. As you speak, feel the relief and terror of being seen mixing together. The words don't need to be eloquent—they should stumble and restart, get lost and found again. Move from protective silence to trembling revelation, ending in a place where you're completely exposed, waiting in the dark for their response, your heart visible in your throat.
inspired_by: An actor feels restricted and self-conscious when trying to say the exact written dialogue

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting a parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire life. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm, to be fair. But as you speak, the hurt you've carried for decades starts bleeding through. Your voice should shift from controlled explanation to raw accusation, then crack into the voice of the child you once were, desperately asking why you weren't enough. Let anger and longing twist together. Then—crucially—hear something in their silence or response that changes everything. Maybe you see their brokenness for the first time. End in a different place: not reconciliation exactly, but a painful, tender recognition that they were as lost as you were. Your final words should hold both accountability and unexpected compassion.

title: The Last Drag
instruction: You're a 16-year-old hiding in a corner of your dad's open-plan office after sneaking into his work party. You've had too much to drink, and your head is spinning. You're on a hushed call with your older sister, your voice low and slurred, as you stare at the blinking security camera above the break room. Start with a thick, helpless panic—you feel trapped and can barely form sentences. As you listen to her calm voice, a fragile hope emerges: she says she's on her way. Let the intoxication make you fumble words, forget what you're saying, then trail off. End with a quiet, tipsy smile in your voice, still fearful but lighter. You're trying to keep your voice down so no one else hears, but your words spill out in bursts, interrupted by the hum of the HVAC and the distant clatter of a printer. Your last line should sound like you're almost laughing with relief, even though you're still dizzy.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering Your Betrayal to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3am and your partner is asleep beside you. You're whispering a confession they can't hear—about the affair, the lies, the ways you've been slowly destroying what you have. Your voice is barely audible, catching on words like 'I kissed them' and 'I keep choosing to hurt you.' There's something almost tender in how you're confessing to their sleeping form, safe because they can't hear, but also desperately wishing they would wake up and stop you from having to carry this alone. Let your whisper tremble between relief at finally saying it aloud and devastation at what it means. Touch their hair or their shoulder as you speak, your voice breaking into the smallest sob on 'I don't know how to stop.' End with 'I love you'—and let that truth coexist with everything terrible you've just admitted, your voice so quiet it's almost just breath, wondering if love was ever enough when you keep choosing to betray it.
inspired_by: Realizing You're the Toxic One in This Relationship

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Pretends Never Happened
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother at a kitchen table, and you've finally found the courage to name the things you both know but have never spoken aloud. Start with a trembling, almost apologetic tone—you don't want to hurt her, but you're drowning in the silence. As she deflects or denies, your voice should grow stronger, more insistent, even angry. But here's the complexity: your anger keeps breaking into desperate pleas for her to just see you, to acknowledge what happened. Your voice cracks between fury and the little child inside you who still wants her mother to make it okay. End with a moment of devastating quiet—either she's finally hearing you and you're terrified of that intimacy, or she's still denying it and you're realizing you may never get what you need from her.
inspired_by: Treading Water While Calling for Help

title: I Will Burn This World Down For You
instruction: You're standing over someone you love who's been hurt, and your protective rage is colliding with absolute helplessness. Begin with your voice shaking, barely controlled: 'Tell me who did this.' Let fury build in your chest, breathing getting harder, faster. 'I will make them—' Your voice cracks on the threat because you realize you can't fix this, can't undo what's been done. The rage explodes into something messier—shouting that breaks into ragged breathing, words fragmenting: 'You don't deserve this, you—I should have—why didn't I—' Let yourself spiral between fierce protectiveness and devastating self-blame. Then the collapse: your voice drops to something broken and tender. End on your knees, metaphorically or literally, voice raw and small: 'I can't fix this. But I'm here. I'm right here.' Let the inadequacy of those words hang in the air.

title: Laughing Through Tears While Toasting at Your Ex's Wedding
instruction: You're standing with a microphone, watching the person you thought you'd marry pledge themselves to someone else, and somehow you're genuinely happy for them. Begin with laughter—real, warm, authentic—as you recount a funny story about the two of you. But let your voice carry something else underneath, a tremor of grief you're trying to disguise as joy. As you speak, oscillate between genuine celebration and heartbreak you can't quite hide. Your breathing becomes irregular—you're laughing and crying and you can't tell which is which anymore. Tell them how grateful you are that they found this, how seeing them this happy makes the breaking worthwhile, and mean it even as your voice fractures. Let your words be a gift of grace even as your heart audibly shatters. End with your voice full of contradictions—blessing them while mourning what you lost, finding strange peace in letting go, your final words carried on breath that's half-laugh, half-sob, wholly sincere.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Cursed Being Realizes Breaking the Curse Requires Murdering Their Love

title: Farewell to Earth: Last Transmission Before the Fold
instruction: You're recording your final message to Earth before entering a quantum fold—a one-way journey to another dimension where time doesn't exist as humans understand it. Start with crisp, mission-focused professionalism, listing coordinates and procedures. But as you speak, the reality hits: you'll never see another human face, never feel rain, never hear your daughter's voice again. Your voice begins to fracture—not theatrically, but the way it does when you're trying desperately to hold yourself together. You're talking to Mission Control, but really you're talking to everyone you love. End in a whisper of acceptance mixed with unbearable loss, finding strange peace in the surrender to something vast and unknowable. Let your breath betray what your words try to contain.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Space Explorer Realizes the Planet Is Conscious

title: The Crash After the Cake
instruction: You're a young man at your aunt's birthday party, and the caffeine and sugar hit from earlier is wearing off fast. Your body feels hollow, your speech is sluggish, and a low irritation buzzes under your skin. Your aunt comes over and warmly thanks you for being there, saying how much it means to her. You start to reply with a genuine, though fading, thank-you—smiling through the fog. But as you keep talking, the fatigue pulls your voice down, turning your words clipped and resentful. Let a faint disgust creep in—maybe at the sticky sweet smell, or at your own fake cheer. End with a sigh and a flatter tone, as if you've already checked out. Speak about 40-80 words, letting your voice slow and drop, with natural pauses and shifts in weight.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Smell of Their Condescension
instruction: You are an older woman with a concussion, sitting in a hospital waiting room, waiting for a follow-up scan. Across from you, a younger, smug relative (or stranger) keeps glancing at you with a pitying smile, then whispers something dismissive to a companion. You feel a surge of contempt — a hot, clear thought: 'I know exactly what you think of me.' And alongside that, disgust — at the way they look at you like you're already weak, at the whole sterile, fake-caring room. You can't speak fast anymore; the words come out slow, thick, but each one lands like a stone. Start with a flat, almost bored tone that barely covers your simmering anger, then let the contempt push through — cold, precise, almost amused in its intensity. End with a quiet, tired finality that shows you've dismissed them completely, having said your piece.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Daughter Who Stopped Waiting
instruction: You are confronting your parent who abandoned their leadership role in your family to pursue their own ambitions, leaving you to raise your siblings alone. Start with controlled, cold fury - your voice sharp and clinical as you list exactly what their absence cost you. Build into raw, unleashed rage as you describe the nights you cried yourself to sleep, the moments you needed them and they weren't there. Then, devastatingly, let your anger collapse into the voice of the child you once were - small, hurt, bewildered - asking the question you've never dared ask: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay?' End with bitter acceptance, your voice hardening again as you tell them you didn't come for reconciliation, you came to say you're done grieving the parent they'll never be. Let us hear your heart breaking even as you pretend it isn't.
inspired_by: The Captain and the Mutiny Leader

title: Can't Hear a Word
instruction: You are an elderly man with a naturally loud, gruff voice, sitting in a noisy airplane cabin. The engine roar is harsh, your throat is dry, and your ears keep popping. You need to tell the flight attendant that your hearing aid battery just died and you can't hear a thing. Start by concentrating intensely—leaning forward, raising your voice, trying to catch what she says. But as you realize she can't understand you either and you're stuck in the noise, your voice cracks with helplessness. Speak over the din, with uneven volume, maybe clearing your throat or adjusting your aid midway.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Landing Softly
instruction: You are a teenage submissive wrapped in a blanket after a scene, your head resting on your partner's chest. At first, your voice is small and shaky—you're still trembling, words catching in your throat as you reach for reassurance. You sip water, rustle the blanket, and feel a hand stroke your hair. As the rhythm of breathing and soft praise sinks in, your voice steadies, deepening into a warm, sleepy smile. Start with a fragile whisper, end with a truly contented, drowsy sigh. Say something like: 'I just need a second... my legs are still buzzing. But... this blanket is so warm. You're so warm. I think I'm really okay now. I love this part. I'm home.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Meal You Refused to Let Them Die Without
instruction: You fought—screamed at doctors, threatened nurses, broke rules—to bring someone on their deathbed one last taste of their favorite food, something they haven't had in months of hospital meals. Start fierce and almost manic with desperate joy, your voice cracking with intensity as you describe feeding them, watching them taste it, willing this moment to matter, to be enough. Your words should tumble out urgent and raw, laughing through barely contained tears as you see recognition in their eyes. Let that fierce energy shatter into gasping sobs as you realize this changes nothing—they're still dying, this is still goodbye. End with your voice stripped down to nothing, whispering about the crumbs on their lips, begging this one small act of love to somehow be enough, knowing it isn't, knowing you'd fight the whole world again anyway.
inspired_by: Taking a Bite of Freshly Baked Bread

title: The Fever That Burned Through
instruction: You are a young woman lying in bed, shaking with a high fever. Your body aches so deeply that every word feels like it costs you something. Your lips are cracked, your throat dry, and your thoughts keep slipping away into strange dreams. You are speaking to a friend who is next to you, but you can barely see them through the sweat and haze. Start by describing the pain in your bones, your voice wavering and breathy, struggling to form sentences. Then, as you realize you are still fighting—still alive—your voice gathers a fragile but real triumph. You smile through the chills, and your tone shifts from desperate whispers to something clearer, prouder, even if your body still shakes. Let the triumph emerge as a surprise, a small victory you claim in the middle of the delirium.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Breaking Point - When Protection Becomes Fury
instruction: Someone you love is in danger and there's nothing you can do. You start controlled, almost robotic: 'I've called everyone. I've done everything right.' Listing actions mechanically, holding everything in. But as you describe what might happen to them, the numbness that's been protecting you shatters violently. Your voice explodes into raw desperation: 'They can't take you!' Rage at your own helplessness, terror for them, fury at the universe. You're shouting, then suddenly collapsing into broken sobbing, then back to fierce protectiveness. The emotional swings are whiplash-fast. End in shattered exhaustion, voice raw: 'I can't lose you. I can't. I don't know how to be numb about this.' The transformation is volcanic - from frozen control to complete emotional devastation.

title: The Unfinished Apology
instruction: You're on a busy city sidewalk, walking home after a painful argument with your adult son. A siren wails in the distance as you stop at a corner, pressing your phone to your ear to leave him a voicemail. Your chest is tight with shame—you wanted to sound firm, but your voice keeps cracking as traffic rushes by. Start by trying to explain your side, your words clipped and defensive, but as a jackhammer starts up nearby, you trail off. In the quiet that follows, your voice softens, wobbling with raw regret as you admit you were wrong and ask him to call back, your whispered words half-lost to the wind.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What I've Never Told You
instruction: In the intimate darkness of a quiet room, whisper a confession to someone you trust completely. Begin tentatively, almost unable to start: 'There's something I've never...' Your voice is barely audible, catching on words as you reveal a secret shame or hidden truth you've carried alone for years. As you speak, vulnerability deepens—your throat tightens, pauses grow longer, and the relief of finally saying it out loud mingles with the fear of being seen this completely. End with a fragile question, tender and terrified: 'Do you still...?' The whole performance should feel like watching someone's heart slowly, carefully open, so quiet that silence becomes part of the emotional landscape.

title: The Scent of Betrayal
instruction: Confront your partner while holding the sweater they claimed they lost—except it smells like someone else's perfume. Start by describing the texture of the fabric in your hands, how it feels different now, contaminated. Your voice is quiet, controlled, dangerous. Describe the scent you're smelling—make it vivid and specific. Let your anger build not through volume but through increasingly precise sensory observations: you can taste the bitterness in your mouth, feel the heat rising in your face, notice how sharply you're breathing. As you speak, let each sensory detail you name become evidence, each one adding fuel. Transition from cold, forensic description to raw, volcanic rage. End with your voice breaking—not from sadness, but from the physical intensity of your fury, as if your body can barely contain what you're feeling.

title: The Knot of Doubt
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone in your small apartment, suffering from a chronic, deep abdominal cramp that has been gnawing at you for days. You are hunched over on the edge of the bed, one hand pressed hard into your stomach, breathing in short, guarded puffs. The pain is a heavy, twisting knot that makes you groan on every exhale. As you stare at the phone on the nightstand, you're wrestling with whether to call your estranged son for help — you've doubted his loyalty for years. Start from a place of raw, grunting pain, then let that pain slowly mix with bitter doubt as you weigh the risk. By the end, you decide to reach out, but your voice should remain strained, uncertain, and hollowed by the ache. Speak as naturally as if you're thinking out loud, with pauses and groans between words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Same Old Song
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy sitting on a park bench, phone in hand, scrolling aimlessly while complaining to your best friend about your mom's new boyfriend. Your voice starts with that familiar whiny drone — the same complaints you've made a hundred times. But halfway through, you glance at a photo of your dad on your lock screen. Your voice falters. The complaint trails off. You try to keep the nasal whine going, but it cracks. End by saying something you've never admitted: that you just miss your dad's dumb jokes. Let the sadness seep in until you're barely speaking above a whisper, staring at the ground.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Three AM Truth
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, both of you unable to sleep. In the darkness, you finally whisper the truth you've been hiding: you're not sure you want children, or you're falling in love with someone else, or you're terrified you've become your parents. As you speak, become hyper-aware of the intimate sensory details of this moment—the warmth of their body near yours, the texture of the sheets between you, the sound of their breathing changing as they hear your words, the cool night air on your exposed shoulder, the dampness of tears you're trying to hide. Begin speaking so quietly they have to strain to hear you, your voice tentative, almost hoping the darkness will swallow your words. Let the physical closeness—being able to feel their body tense or soften—inform how your confession unfolds. By the end, this same physical nearness that once meant safety now feels exposing. The intimacy of the moment transforms from comforting to terrifying as you realize you cannot take these words back.

title: Everything You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting someone who has dismissed your feelings for years—perhaps a parent, a former lover, or a close friend who betrayed you. As you speak, draw on the accumulated hurt from multiple people who've made you feel small, unheard, or invisible. Start with trembling restraint, your anger tightly controlled, almost apologetic in your approach. But as you continue, let the voices of everyone who ever diminished you fuel your words until you're no longer asking for validation—you're declaring your worth. End with a powerful clarity and calm that comes from finally standing up for yourself, your rage transformed into unshakeable self-possession.
inspired_by: No single person in the actor's life matches all the obligation requirements for a character relationship

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just revealed they're cutting you out of their life. Start from a place of defensive anger—you've sacrificed everything for them, how dare they. But as you argue, you must access a specific sensory memory from your own childhood: the smell of your own parent's anger, the temperature of the room during a moment you felt small and terrified, the exact sensation in your throat when you couldn't speak. Let this memory live in your body as you speak to your child. Notice how your anger begins to crack, revealing the fear beneath it—the terror that you've become what you swore you'd never be. End in a place of raw, vulnerable admission: name aloud the pattern you've repeated, the silence you've inherited and passed on. Your voice should transform from hard and defended to broken open.
inspired_by: Choice Hunt / Building a Repertoire of UC Choices

title: The Sweetness After the Storm
instruction: You are lying in bed with your partner, the sheets tangled, the room quiet except for your breathing. You just made love and you feel an immense, bone-deep relief — a weight you've carried for months finally gone. Let that relief soften your voice to a slow, sleepy fry, barely above a whisper. Then, in the same breath, let a cold, deliberate malevolence creep in as you realize this relief came from finally setting your plan in motion. Show the shift from intimate vulnerability to quiet menace without raising your volume or pace. Let the silences stretch, and let your breath carry the change.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Intervention You Never Wanted
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the abuse they inflicted on you as a child—abuse they've never acknowledged. Start with trembling restraint, your voice tight with decades of swallowed pain: 'I need you to hear something I should have said thirty years ago.' As they try to deflect or minimize, your anger builds into something volcanic, years of silence erupting: 'No! You don't get to pretend it didn't happen!' But then, unexpectedly, you see them—truly see this fragile, diminished person—and your rage collapses into something more complicated: grief for the parent you needed, grief for the relationship you'll never have, and a terrible, unwanted compassion. End in a place where anger and love coexist painfully, where you're both condemning and mourning them in the same breath.

title: Echoes of a Standing Ovation
instruction: You are alone on a dark stage after your first lead role. The audience has gone, but the theater is still buzzing with your adrenaline and the wine you had backstage. You walk to the center, feeling the warmth of the lights still on your skin. As you speak, you hear your own voice bounce back from the empty seats. Start with a giddy, proud laugh, telling yourself it was perfect. But as you continue, the echo makes you feel how alone you really are. Let the intoxication fade into a quieter, hollow realization that this triumph means nothing without the one person who should have been here. Let your voice crack, lose volume, and become almost a whisper as you address that absence.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love who is dying. They're holding on, unable to let go, their breathing labored. You begin speaking quietly, telling them it's okay to leave, but as you speak, you realize you're not ready—you're furious they're leaving you, angry at the unfairness, the timing, the loss. Let that rage surface physically and vocally, even as you try to maintain tenderness. Your voice might crack, your hands might shake or grip the sheets. By the end, move through the fury to arrive at genuine release: a whispered, wholehearted permission for them to go, filled with exhausted love and acceptance. The journey is from gentle reassurance, through explosive grief-rage, to quiet surrender.

title: The Hidden Den
instruction: You are a young boy with an unusually deep voice, crouched and bent over, touching your toes as you peer under a dusty porch. Your chest is crushed, blood rushes to your head, making your voice sound thick and stuffed with cotton. At first, you grunt and mutter about the cramped space and the dirt. But then, in the shadows, you spot a tiny, perfect robin's egg, glowing blue in a crack of light. Your astonishment swells into a breathless, radiant elation—your words start out strained and congested, then lift into a hushed, joyful whisper as you share your discovery with no one in particular.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Appointment Card
instruction: You're alone in your car, holding the appointment card for next week's surgery - the one with uncertain odds. You start laughing, actually laughing at the absurdity: 'Two-thirty on a Tuesday. Like it's a haircut appointment.' But the laughter has tears in it. You're talking to yourself, to God, to no one, your voice cycling through a kaleidoscope of emotions. There's fear, yes, but also strange euphoria: 'I saw the sunrise this morning and it was so beautiful I could barely breathe.' Gratitude wars with terror. You're listing everything you love about being alive - coffee, your daughter's voice, the smell of rain - and your voice is full of wonder and heartbreak simultaneously. You end in a place of unexpected peace, voice soft but steady: 'If this is all I get, it was enough. God, it was enough.' But your hand is shaking as you put the card back in your wallet.

title: The Last Morning: A Hospice Goodbye
instruction: You're spending your final morning with your dying partner of thirty years. Begin with tender whispers as you watch them sleep—your voice thick with love and the weight of goodbye. They wake, and for a moment, neither of you acknowledges what's coming. Share a memory that makes you both laugh softly, but let that laughter crack and break into quiet weeping. Tell them everything you never said—gratitude, regrets, the small moments you'll carry forever. Your voice should move from gentle reminiscence to raw confession to a kind of fierce, protective tenderness as you promise them it's okay to let go. End with a whispered 'I love you' that contains both acceptance and unbearable loss.

title: The Eulogy That Becomes Laughter
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for your best friend who died far too young, and you start with the heavy, appropriate solemnity - speaking about loss, about the unfairness, your voice thick with unshed tears. But then you remember something they once said about their own funeral, how they made you promise not to be boring and sad. A small, inappropriate laugh escapes you. Then another. You're suddenly telling the story of their most ridiculous moment, laughing through tears, your voice breaking between joy at the memory and devastation that there won't be new memories. The mourners don't know whether to laugh or cry with you. End with your voice soft, grateful, shattered - thanking them for every chaotic, beautiful moment while your heart breaks that 'thank you' is now past tense.

title: Wired for Want
instruction: You're a middle-aged man with a deep, rough voice, but your jaw is wired shut after surgery. You're propped up in a hospital bed, drained, every word a struggle through clenched teeth. Your partner leans close to adjust your pillow, and a wave of raw, exhausted lust hits you—you need to say something, but you can barely move your lips. Start with heavy, muffled, slurred sounds, fighting fatigue, then let a low, gravelly hunger creep into your voice as you lock eyes with them. End with a desperate, half-growled plea that mixes bone-tiredness with burning want, pausing when your jaw seizes or you lose a thought.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved deeply who is choosing medical assistance in dying. They're lucid, at peace, but you're breaking apart. Start angry—furious at them for leaving, for choosing this, your voice tight with barely controlled rage. 'How dare you ask me to be okay with this.' But as they gently explain why they need your blessing, your anger cracks into desperate pleading, then dissolves into tender acceptance. Your voice moves from accusation to bargaining to quiet devastation to finally—achingly—giving them the gift of your permission. End by telling them it's okay to go, your voice breaking with love and unbearable grief simultaneously. Let silence do some of the work. This should feel like your heart is being pulled from your chest while also opening in profound love.

title: Cramp in the Middle of a Victory Dance
instruction: You just won a silly bet with a friend and are doing a little victory dance in the living room, laughing and teasing them. Mid-sentence, a severe cramp seizes your calf muscle – you gasp, a sharp strangled sound escapes, and you curse under your breath. You freeze, then slowly straighten, massaging your leg. Look at your friend with a wry grin and say something triumphant, like even your body is celebrating too hard. Start with pure amusement and playful taunting, then the spasm interrupts – let the involuntary sound and curse be raw. After a pause, resume with a guarded but victorious tone, ending with a shaky laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Historical: Underground Railroad Conductor Hides Escaped Slaves From Pursuers
instruction: Your basement shelter. Footsteps above. Your voice drops to almost nothing—guiding the terrified family in whispered instructions. Your voice is the only safe space they have. You're risking everything while sounding calm. Your breathing is controlled terror—you must be steady for them. Above, your public voice would be different—innocent, uninvolved. But here, your voice is conspiracy and love. You're breathing life into their escape with each quiet word. Your vocal presence is survival made of sound.

title: The Weight of the Blanket
instruction: You're an older man, a former athlete with a deep, gruff voice, sitting beside your adult child who just lost the championship match. You're slightly irritated by their sniffles—you clear your throat and shift in your seat. Disappointment is there, heavy in the pause before you speak. But beneath it, pride burns hot: they went for it, they fought. Let your voice start as a low, impatient hum, matching their ragged breathing. As you talk, let the pride thicken your tone, turning it steady and rhythmic like a blanket. End with a firm, downward inflection, almost a growl of affection. You might pause to pick a piece of lint off your sleeve or look out the window before the final words.

title: The Light Beyond the Dark
instruction: You are a teenage girl lying on a mat in a quiet, dimly lit room, following a guided meditation. Your voice is soft, slow, and deliberate — each word feels placed as if you’re floating. Start with a tremor of fear as you whisper about a vast, empty space inside you, then let a quiet awe bloom as you describe a golden light forming. Your breath is controlled but occasionally hitches, and you pause as if searching for the right word. End with a mix of wonder and lingering unease: the light is beautiful, but you’re not sure if you can let go.

title: The Archaeology of Touch
instruction: You're lying in bed in the dark, whispering to your partner of ten years. Tonight, you need to confess something you've kept hidden—perhaps a past betrayal, a secret fear, or a truth about who you really are. Begin speaking very quietly, carefully choosing your words. But as you talk, pay close attention to the random sensory images that float into your awareness: the way their breathing sounds, how the sheets feel, flashes of other intimate moments, their face in different lights over the years, their hand in yours on various days. Let these unplanned sense memories guide your confession in unexpected directions. Your emotional journey should start with anxious control and measured revelation, then transform as these spontaneous images pull you into deeper vulnerability—toward tears, whispered love, desperate tenderness, or quiet devastation you didn't anticipate. Let what surfaces unbidden from memory reshape what you thought you came to say.

title: The Jacket That Still Holds His Shape
instruction: You are an elderly woman dressing in front of a mirror, slowly putting on your late husband's old suit jacket. The heavy wool fabric rustles and momentarily covers your mouth as you pull it over your shoulders. You grunt softly as you bend to adjust the hem. At first, you're astonished that it still fits you loosely — the same way it did when he first wore it the night you met. As you smooth the lapels and catch your reflection, a deep awe washes over you: the scent of his cologne, the worn elbows, the way the shoulders still feel like his arms around you. But then your hands drop to your sides and you feel a crushing helplessness — he's gone, and all you can do is stand here in his jacket, unable to change anything. Let the swooshing fabric and your quiet breaths punctuate your words. Start with a voice of mild surprise, then let awe fill your tone until it cracks into defeated acceptance.

title: The Words I Never Said
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy at a bus station, saying goodbye to a girl you've secretly liked for years. You know you'll never see her again after today. You're carrying a box of her things she left at your place, and you keep shuffling your weight, looking at the ground, then at her face, then away. Start with awkward, rushed small talk to hide your embarrassment, but as you sense the bus coming, your voice slows down. You try to swallow and speak clearly, but your throat tightens. Let the embarrassment melt into a quiet, raw honesty as you admit you'll miss her more than you can say — and let your voice crack on the last word.

title: The Text You Found on Their Phone
instruction: It's 2 AM. You picked up your partner's phone to set their alarm and saw a text thread you were never meant to see—not an affair, but something worse: messages to their best friend about how exhausting it is to love you, how your depression is 'too much,' how they don't know if they can do this anymore. They're asleep next to you. Your voice is barely a whisper, thick with tears you're trying to keep silent: 'You said you understood. You promised it was okay.' You're reading the messages over and over, your breath catching on each cruel phrase. Your whisper becomes rawer, more broken: 'I tried so hard to be less broken for you.' But then you scroll further and find their friend's response telling them to leave, and your partner's reply: 'I can't. I love them too much. I just needed to say it out loud.' Your tears shift—still falling, but now confused, tender, aching. You look at them sleeping, and your voice cracks with the devastating complexity of being both wounded and deeply loved: 'How do I live with knowing you find me exhausting... and that you choose me anyway?'
inspired_by: Sending a Drunk Text to the Wrong Person

title: The Unbroken Gaze
instruction: You are an elderly man in a consensual intimate moment with your partner. As she gently squeezes your throat, you feel control ebbing away, but your pride keeps your eyes locked on hers—you will not look afraid. Your voice starts with a low, steady hum of possessiveness, then as the pressure increases, it cracks into a thin, raspy whisper, each word a struggle to hold onto dignity. When she releases you, a loud gasp tears out, followed by dizzy, euphoric laughter—the pride is now raw, shared, almost childlike in its relief. Let your voice flutter with the rush of blood, the tremor of vulnerability, and the stubborn smile that refuses to break.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're standing in your childhood bedroom or at your parent's bedside, voice starting soft and careful, almost childlike: 'I need to tell you something.' You begin gently, trying to explain what it felt like to be invisible, to compete for attention you never received. As you speak, your voice gains strength and anger—decades of unspoken hurt pouring out. 'I needed you to see me.' The rage peaks, then suddenly collapses into the vulnerability of a child still wanting their parent's love. By the end, your voice is barely a whisper, exhausted and stripped bare, asking the question you've always been afraid to ask: 'Did you ever really love me?'

title: A Performance of Spite
instruction: You are an elderly person with a worn, androgynous voice, performing a scripted phone sex call for someone you deeply resent. As you begin, you force the breathy, hypnotic seduction—close to the mic, slow, deliberate moans and sighs. But your contempt leaks through: your tone sours, your pauses become heavy with loathing. By the end, your voice turns cold and bitter, the performance crumbling into a sneer. Speak as if you are alone in a dim room, phone pressed to your ear, disgusted at having to pretend.

title: The Last Cookie
instruction: You are a seven-year-old boy standing in the kitchen, watching your older sibling reach for the last cookie in the jar. You start off with a playful, teasing tone, trying to charm them into sharing—maybe you smile and say they don't really want it. But as they ignore you and start to walk away, your voice shifts. Impatience and irritability creep in, your pitch rises, and you start to plead quickly, almost tripping over your words. Let your voice wobble with a shaky, submissive whine, and maybe glance around the room for a distraction before snapping back to begging. By the end, you're nearly desperate, your tone thin and high, like you're about to be cut off.

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You are lying half-undressed on a bed, your partner above you, kissing slowly down your neck. You started this with a playful sense of triumph—you had teased them into this, and you know you're winning. But as their mouth trails lower, you gasp—astonished by how good it feels, surprised at your own vulnerability. Your voice becomes a whisper, then a shaky sigh as longing takes over. Speak only a few fragmented words between breaths and kiss sounds: 'Wait... how did you... oh... I didn't know... please...' Let your pitch drop, your words lose their edges, and let the astonishment bloom into a raw, breathy plea.

title: The Rehearsal That Never Came
instruction: You're a young dancer in your early twenties, just finished a grueling practice. You're alone in the empty studio, stretching by the barre, when you get a call that your partner—the one you've been dancing with for years—has been in a serious accident. As you hear the news, you double over as if punched in the gut. The air leaves you in a sharp 'oof,' and when you try to speak to your mom on the phone, your voice is breathless, cracking. Start with that initial crumple from the emotional blow, then let the sadness seep in as you realize you might never dance with her again. Your words come out between gasps, tiny and fragile, like you're trying not to shatter.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Hour Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's awake, lucid, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin feeling the weight of everything unsaid between you—the awkwardness, the fear of saying the wrong thing, the desperate wish to make these moments count. Speak to her, starting with the clumsy, inadequate words that first come. Let yourself stumble through the discomfort of not knowing how to do this. As you continue, allow the pretense to fall away. Move from nervous chatter to raw truth—tell her what she meant to you, what you'll miss, what you're terrified of. By the end, find a place of pure presence with her, where words become unnecessary and you're simply there together, breathing, connected. Your emotional journey: from anxious avoidance to naked, peaceful love.

title: The Mother at the Empty Door
instruction: Your child has just stormed out, and you know—you KNOW—they're not coming back this time. Start pacing, voice rising in defensive anger: 'Fine! Go! You think you're so much better than this family?' You're shouting at the closed door, justifying yourself, listing everything you sacrificed. But mid-sentence, your voice cracks and the rage collapses into something primal and terrified. 'Wait. Wait, come back.' You're at the door now, pressing your hand against it. The fierceness returns: 'I am your MOTHER, you don't just—' but it breaks again into helplessness. Your voice drops to a whisper: 'I don't know how to do this without you hating me.' Sink to the floor, your breathing uneven. End with fierce protectiveness mixed with complete powerlessness: 'I would die for you. I would. But I don't know how to... I never learned how to...' Trail off, holding yourself, rocking slightly, undone.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. The room is dark except for the streetlight filtering through curtains. Start with the sensory reality: the warmth of their body near yours, the weight of the blanket, the sound of their breathing, the softness of your own voice barely audible. You're terrified—your throat is tight, your whisper keeps catching. Begin by circling around what you need to say, testing the words, pulling back. The secret involves shame you've carried alone. As you finally release the truth in the smallest voice imaginable, feel the shift from bracing for rejection to the radical vulnerability of being fully seen. Let their hand finding yours in the darkness change everything. End in the profound relief of being known completely and still held.

title: Adult Child Confronts Dying Parent Who Never Said 'I Love You'
instruction: Hospital room, 3 AM. Your parent has hours left, and you finally have the courage to say what decades of silence buried. Start angry—controlled fury at a lifetime of emotional absence, of needs never met, of words never spoken. Your voice is sharp, accusatory. But as you list each wound, each moment you needed them and they weren't there, something shifts. You hear how small and afraid you sound. The anger collapses into the voice of the child you were—the one who just wanted to be held. End on your knees beside the bed, whispering through tears, begging them to say it just once before they go. Your voice becomes pure aching need, all defenses gone.
inspired_by: Historical: Executioner Performs His Final Execution Before Retirement

title: The Final Flight: Air Traffic Controller Guiding Down a Dying Pilot
instruction: You're an air traffic controller and a commercial pilot—your mentor, the person who taught you everything—is flying a plane with catastrophic engine failure. Two hundred souls aboard. Start with professional calm, your voice steady as you guide them through emergency procedures: 'United 447, descend to 8,000 feet. You're cleared for emergency landing on runway 27.' But as the situation deteriorates, your clinical detachment begins to crack. You know this voice intimately—you've shared a thousand cups of coffee in this tower. Your instructions become more personal even as they stay precise: 'Come on, Sarah, just like you taught me—small adjustments, ease her down.' The professional and personal collide. By the end, she's not going to make it and she knows it. Your voice drops to a whisper, breaking: 'You were the best pilot I ever knew. You were... you were everything.' You're saying goodbye while still trying to guide her home. Your final words are half prayer, half love letter, as you watch her disappear from your screen.
inspired_by: Emergency Room Doctor: Critical Patient Arriving

title: Strained Patience, Bound Hope
instruction: You are bound in a consensual scene, your wrists secured above you, the rope creaking with each small shift. Your partner is moving slowly, deliberately, and you feel a flicker of impatience—a tightness in your chest, a slight edge in your voice as you strain against the bonds. But beneath that, a fierce hope swells: this is exactly what you wanted, and every second pulls you closer to connection. Speak to your partner, your voice breathy and vulnerable, sometimes catching on a gasp, sometimes muffled as you turn your head. Let the impatience dissolve into a quiet, yearning optimism as you finish speaking. Say: 'You're taking your time... I feel like I'm floating, even though I can't move. Don't stop. I'm right here—waiting, but not minding. I trust you. I trust this.'

title: 3am Confession in a Car: The Affair That Saved Your Life
instruction: Parked outside their house, you finally tell your best friend the secret that's been destroying you: you had an affair, and it made you remember you were human. Whisper this like it's sacred and shameful at once. Your voice should crack not from volume but from the weight of truth. Begin with halting vulnerability, catching on words like 'alive' and 'sorry.' Move into quiet, fierce gratitude for the person who touched you like you mattered, even though it was wrong. Then let the sadness creep in — it's over, you're going back to your marriage, and you're terrified you'll disappear again. End with a question that barely makes it out: 'How do I survive going back to being nothing?' The silence after should ache.

title: The Last Visitor
instruction: You are an elderly man in a nursing home, exhausted after a long day, your head resting heavily on your hand. That hand pushes your cheek up, making your speech slightly muffled and clumsy on 'p' and 'b' sounds. You're speaking to a young volunteer you've grown infatuated with — you hope she'll stay a little longer. Begin with a heavy, tired voice, a touch of fear that she might leave soon. Let your words wander, pause to swallow or shift in your chair. As you speak, let the infatuation warm your tone, ending with a soft, almost playful plea, even as weariness pulls at every syllable.

title: The Kitchen at Midnight
instruction: You've come home unexpectedly and found your father sitting alone in the dark kitchen. Years of silence between you must break tonight. Start calmly, almost casually, then begin naming the things you've been too afraid to say—the ways he failed you, the ways you've failed him, the love you've hidden behind walls of resentment. Let your voice build from controlled civility to volcanic release, interweaving everything you hate about what he did, everything you love about who he is, and every fear you have about becoming him. title: The Burning House of the Body
instruction: You are in the grip of intense physical sensation—either making love for the first time after tremendous loss, or experiencing a rage so physical it makes you shake, or pushing your body past exhaustion for something that matters desperately. Let the physical sensation crack you open emotionally. Start by trying to maintain control, to perform the 'right' way, to manage how you're experiencing this. Then let the body override the mind—allow sounds you didn't plan, let your breath become ragged and real, permit yourself to be taken over by the intensity. Feel the terrifying ecstasy of losing control, of being animal and divine simultaneously. End in a place of stunned aftermath: exhausted, raw, more alive than you've felt in years, and fundamentally changed by what your body just taught your heart.

title: The Last Letter Read Aloud
instruction: You are reading aloud a letter you wrote to yourself five years ago, found in a box while packing to move away from a place where someone you deeply loved has just died. The letter contains your younger self's hopes, dreams, and promises—many fulfilled, some abandoned. Begin reading with detached curiosity, as if encountering a stranger's words. As you continue, let recognition dawn: these words remind you of every small victory, every moment of courage, every time you showed up for yourself even when it was hard. By the end, you are speaking not just to your past self, but to the person you've lost, showing them—and yourself—that you became someone worthy of the love they gave you. Move from cool distance to raw gratitude mixed with unbearable grief.

title: Final Hospital Visit: Saying What Was Never Said
instruction: You're at your parent's hospital bedside and the doctor has said it's a matter of hours. You begin with rigid control, voice tight and formal: 'I came because... they said I should.' You're still protecting yourself even now. But as you sit there, something breaks. Your voice cracks as you admit: 'I wanted you to be different. I wanted you to want me.' The anger dissolves into raw grief. You tell them about the child you were, waiting for them to notice. Your voice becomes tender, almost a whisper: 'I forgive you. Not because you've earned it, but because I need to let this go.' By the end, you're crying but there's peace underneath the tears. You say goodbye to both the parent they were and the parent you needed them to be.

title: The Last Stand
instruction: You are an elderly woman, proud and sharp-tongued, who feels contempt for the younger relative trying to help you. You insist you can stand on your own, but your body betrays you. title: My Body Remembers You
instruction: You are alone in a room where something physically and emotionally overwhelming once happened with someone—a first kiss, a violent argument, a moment of passion, a physical injury caused by betrayal. Allow real physical sensation to build: heat, cold, tension, trembling, hunger. Let an actual memory from your life fuel the physical response. As your body responds, begin speaking to the person who isn't there, letting rage or desire or grief or ecstasy pour through you with full physical commitment. Your voice should reflect your body's state: breathless, guttural, breaking, keening. End in physical exhaustion, the emotion burned through you.

title: The Body That Remembers
instruction: You are experiencing intense physical sensation—whether ecstatic pleasure, searing pain, or both intertwined. As you vocalize this experience, a specific memory surfaces unbidden in your body: perhaps a moment of past trauma, an earlier time you felt this alive, or a loss you thought you'd buried. Your sounds and words should begin purely physical—raw, primal responses to sensation. But gradually, let language emerge that belongs to that memory, as if your body is speaking its history through present feeling. The physical intensity doesn't diminish, but becomes layered with emotional recognition. End in a place where past and present sensation merge, where you cannot separate the body's memory from its current experience. Your voice must carry both timelines simultaneously.

title: The Weight of Surrender
instruction: You are an older man, slightly drunk but not sloppy, kneeling opposite your submissive partner. You begin with your usual steady, commanding tone—a clipped 'Look at me.' But as you watch them obey, awe overtakes you: their trust feels overwhelming, almost sacred. Your voice softens, slows, becomes more breathy with wonder. Then sadness creeps in—a quiet grief that this perfect moment can't last, that they give you something you don't deserve. Your final words tremble, losing control just slightly. Let the intoxication color your hesitation, the awe stretch your vowels, and the sadness crack your voice into a whisper.

title: The Moment You Choose to Stop Your Child From Leaving
instruction: Your adult child is packing to leave—maybe to join someone dangerous, maybe to chase a dream that will destroy them, maybe to cut you out of their life forever. You've been watching silently, but now you're blocking the door. Start with controlled intensity, voice firm but trembling underneath: 'You're not walking out that door. Not like this.' Your words come faster, more desperate—you're trying reason, then pleading, then your voice rises to a roar of protective fury: 'I will not watch you throw your life away! I will NOT!' You're shouting now, but it's collapsing even as it peaks. Your voice cracks, the rage dissolving into helpless, choking sobs: 'Please. Please don't make me let you go.' You sink against the door, your words barely coherent through tears, all your strength gone: 'I can't stop you, can I? I can't protect you anymore.' End with your voice small, broken, accepting the unbearable: 'Go. Just... please don't forget I loved you enough to try.'

title: The Last Breath Between Us
instruction: You're holding the hand of someone you've loved for decades as they take their final breaths. Begin in quiet, tender gratitude—whispering memories, stroking their hair, trying to memorize every detail of their face. As their breathing changes, your emotion transforms: panic rises, denial sets in, you're bargaining with time itself. Let raw sounds emerge from your throat—not words, but the animal grief of losing someone. End in the hollow, stunned silence after their last exhale, where you must somehow continue existing in a world that now contains their absence. Express everything through breath, whispers, keening sounds, and the physical act of holding on and letting go.

title: The Shimmering Doll
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl sitting on the carpet in your bedroom, holding a treasured porcelain doll. You speak to it with the bright, sing-song voice of infatuation—praising its dress, its hair, your love for it. But as you speak, your words become slower, quieter. You stop mid-sentence, staring through the doll as if it's made of light. Your voice flattens. You begin to describe your own hands as if they belong to someone else, noticing they are so tiny and strange. title: Delivering Your Sister's Eulogy After Years of Not Speaking
instruction: You're standing at a podium at your sister's funeral. You haven't spoken to her in eight years—a bitter fight over something that feels absurd now. Start with the scripted words you prepared, the safe anecdotes about childhood, professional and distant. But then something shifts. A memory surfaces mid-sentence that makes you laugh—a real, genuine laugh that surprises you and everyone listening. The laughter cracks something open. Suddenly you're telling the truth: how much you missed her, how you picked up the phone a thousand times and never called, how stupid and proud you both were. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice breaking between joy at remembering who she was and devastation that she's gone. The formal eulogy becomes a raw confession, an apology, a love letter. You're talking to her now, not about her. Telling her you're sorry, that you wish you'd been brave enough to call, that you hope she knew despite everything. End with gratitude—for having had her at all, for the years you did have—even as your heart is shattering. Let the grief and the love and the regret and the gratitude all exist in the same breath.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years. Begin with careful control—you've rehearsed this, you're going to stay calm, just state the facts. But as you list the missed birthdays, the broken promises, the times you needed them and they chose something else, your voice hardens with anger. Let that anger build until it cracks open into something more vulnerable: the child inside you who still wanted their love, who still waited by the window. Move from rage to grief to a painful, reluctant understanding that you might never get what you needed. End not with forgiveness, but with the devastating acknowledgment that you have to let go of hoping they'll change. Your voice should transform from controlled accusation to righteous fury to broken-hearted acceptance.

title: Fierce Protection Against Impossible Odds
instruction: You're holding someone you love who's been hurt, and you're speaking to an unseen threat—real or metaphorical. Begin with volcanic rage: 'You will NOT touch them again!' Your whole body is a shield. But as you hold them closer, feeling their vulnerability, your fierce protectiveness collides with crushing helplessness. Your voice cracks: 'I should have protected you. I should have—' Now you're the one breaking. Drop to your knees, still holding them, and your rage dissolves into anguished tears: 'I can't keep you safe from everything and it's killing me.' Rock gently. End with a fierce whisper that's part prayer, part promise, part surrender: 'But I'm here. I'm here. And I will never stop trying.' Your voice is fierce and shattered at once.

title: Dementia Lucidity Flash
instruction: You're a dementia patient in an assisted living facility, mostly confused and withdrawn. Your voice is slow, uncertain: 'Where am I? Who are you?' Then suddenly, a moment of absolute lucidity. Your voice transforms — clear, focused, intelligent: 'I'm David Mitchell. I taught calculus for 40 years. And I know exactly what's happening to me.' You're fully present, aware of your condition, aware of the cruelty of knowing it. 'This moment won't last. Soon I'll be confused again.' Your voice carries the weight of that knowledge. You reach for the caregiver's hand: 'Promise me you'll remember this. That I was here.' Then the lucidity fades. Your voice becomes uncertain again: 'Sorry, what were we talking about?' The caregiver, tears streaming, says softly: 'Nothing, David. Nothing important.'

title: The Intervention: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You Drowning
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the years you struggled—depression, addiction, silent suffering—while they remained oblivious, focused on appearances and achievement. Begin with a trembling, carefully controlled voice: 'I need you to hear something.' But as you describe what it felt like to be invisible in your own home, your control fractures. Your voice shifts from hurt to anger to a raw vulnerability that terrifies you: 'I was drowning right in front of you and you kept asking about my grades.' Let rage and desperate need collide—you want them to understand, to finally see you, but you're also furious that you still need their validation. Build to a moment where your voice breaks completely, revealing the wounded child beneath the angry adult: 'Why wasn't I enough to notice?' End with exhausted honesty, where anger gives way to grief, and you speak the truth you've never been able to say. Make it real, like peeling off layers of scar tissue.
inspired_by: Descending from the Death Zone: Oxygen Returning Clarity

title: Concoction Failing
instruction: The person you lied to is asking a follow-up question you didn't anticipate. Your voice tries to stay smooth: 'I... well...' Panic kicks in. You're improvising now, and it sounds like improvising. The second lie contradicts the first. They're noticing. Your voice gets faster, more desperate. 'Look, it's complicated.' The entire structure is collapsing in real time. Your voice becomes a person drowning. 'I have to go.' You're leaving before it crumbles completely.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Partner Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's three in the morning. Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're about to walk out of their life without waking them. Maybe you're leaving because you're broken, or because staying would hurt them more, or because you love them too much to watch them slowly stop loving you. You whisper things you could never say to their face—confessions of inadequacy, memories of perfect moments, apologies for being someone they deserved better than. Your voice is barely audible, tender, catching on words. You're crying silently. You tell them they'll be happier without you, but your voice betrays that you don't quite believe it. You thank them for loving you when you couldn't love yourself. Your hand hovers near their face but doesn't touch—you don't want to wake them. By the end, you're no longer speaking to them; you're speaking to yourself, trying to gather the courage to actually leave. This should feel like the most intimate, heartbreaking secret—the kind of truth that only exists in the dark.

title: The First Fragile Yes
instruction: You are with someone you trust deeply, but this is the first time you’ve let yourself be this vulnerable. Your body trembles, your breath catches — fear is a tight fist in your chest. As they move with you, you try to speak, but your voice breaks into gasps and half-words. Let the fear slowly loosen as you feel their care, until a small, shaky smile reaches your voice and you whisper a release you didn’t know you needed. Your words should sound like they’re being pulled from a body that’s both resisting and surrendering, with pauses, swallowed sounds, and a final sigh of relief.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Contentment (slightly present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: A Quiet Corner's Confession
instruction: You are an elderly woman who has retreated into a cramped closet after a bitter argument with your adult child about the family house. Your knees are pulled to your chest, back against the wall, breathing shallow. You start by muttering angrily under your breath about their ingratitude and your disappointment, your voice tight and raspy from holding back tears. As you shift your weight, you notice an old photograph on the floor—a memory of your late spouse. Your tone softens, and you whisper a reluctant but genuine thankfulness for the years you had, even as your anger and disappointment still linger. Let your voice crack, trail off, and occasionally catch on a sob.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Disappointment (extremely present), Anger (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Best Friend Who Chose Someone Else
instruction: Your best friend—your person—is moving across the world for someone they just met. You're furious and devastated. Start with your voice sharp, words coming fast, accusing them of abandoning you, of throwing away years of friendship for a stranger. Your anger is a mask for heartbreak. Mid-way, let the anger collapse into raw pleading—'Don't you remember what we promised each other?' Your voice should crack, become small, almost childlike in its vulnerability. But then they say something that makes you realize they need this, that real love means letting go. End with your voice hollow, exhausted, whispering 'I hope they make you happy' while your heart is shattering. Cry twice: once in rage, once in grief.
inspired_by: Forgiving Someone and Meaning It Completely

title: The Advice You Never Asked For
instruction: Confront your father about a lifetime of unsolicited advice that shaped your choices and stunted your growth. Start with practiced calm, almost rehearsed, as you list the ways his 'guidance' about career, relationships, and success kept you from discovering yourself. Let the calm deteriorate into frustration, your voice rising as decades of swallowed responses come pouring out. Then shift—mid-sentence, catch yourself echoing his exact tone, his exact phrases, and feel the horror of realizing you've become him. End with a devastated question, barely audible, asking if he was as lost as you are now, if his advice was just his own fear dressed up as wisdom.

title: Pantry Confession
instruction: You're a teenager, alone in the pantry, shoveling spoonfuls of Nutella straight from the jar. Your mouth is full—tongue sluggish, words wet and smeared. Your shame is thick: you know you shouldn't be doing this, and you flinch at every creak, dreading being caught. But then the door swings open and it's your best friend, grinning. Your shame melts into pure, messy elation—you sputter through a mouthful, offering the jar, laughing as you try to speak. The shift is sudden: from hiding to sharing, from guilty silence to joyful, food-clogged confession.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Breaking Point Inventory
instruction: You're in the middle of intense physical sensation—either passionate lovemaking or receiving news that drops you to your knees. Your task: stay ruthlessly present to every single physical detail even as overwhelming emotion threatens to obliterate awareness. Notice the exact temperature of skin, the specific quality of breath, the precise sensation of tears or sweat, the particular way muscles tense, the taste in your mouth, the sound of your own heartbeat, the texture of whatever surface you're touching. Begin by trying to catalogue everything as a way to stay in control, to not be swept away.
