instruction: You're a child sitting cross-legged on a wooden floor, surrounded by scattered blocks. You've just watched your carefully built tower collapse for the third time—disappointment sits quietly in your chest, but a flicker of hope nudges you to try again. As you reposition a block with shaky hands, you discover a way to balance it perfectly, and a slow, real smile spreads across your face. Let your voice start soft, with a slight catch of frustration, then grow into a bright, breathless triumph as you whisper to yourself, 'It's standing. It's actually standing.' Feel the floor beneath you, the weight of your own small body, and let the joy rush through your words.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Soldier Recording Final Message, Hearing Enemy Approach
instruction: You're recording a message to your family. You know they're coming. Start with fierce determination—you need them to know you fought bravely, that you love them, that they should be proud. Your voice is strong, almost defiant. 'Tell my son I—' But you hear footsteps. Your breathing quickens. The brave soldier voice cracks. Terror floods in. You're not ready to die. You're twenty-three years old and you want to go home. Your voice becomes desperate, young, afraid: 'I don't want to die, I don't want to—please—' You're sobbing now, all pretense of courage gone. Then you hear the door. You force yourself to steady, to find one last moment of dignity. Your final words are whispered: 'I love you. I'm not afraid.' But your voice trembles with the lie.
inspired_by: Professional: Divorce Lawyer Realizes She's Representing Against Her Best Friend

title: The Moment You Realize You're Becoming Your Abuser
instruction: You've just screamed at your child the exact words your father screamed at you, and now they're cowering in the corner looking at you with terrified eyes. Start with defensive justification—they deserved it, they pushed you too far, you're not like him. But as you speak, your voice begins to shake with the horror of recognition. The excuses dissolve into desperate self-awareness. Your volume drops and rises erratically—rage at yourself, then fierce protectiveness toward your child, then helpless fear that the damage is already done. Try to apologize but the words come out wrong. Build to a moment of explosive anguish where you're nearly shouting 'I'm sorry' through tears, then collapse into quiet devastation as you realize sorry might not be enough.
inspired_by: Narrator Triggered by Their Own Story

title: Party Confessions
instruction: You're a teenager at a house party, holding a can of soda. You start teasing your best friend about his terrible dance moves, laughing between loud gulps. But as you speak, you notice his eyes get distant—he just got news about his dad in the hospital. Your playful tone falters, your throat tightens. You try to keep joking but the words come out awkward and soft, and you end up setting the can down, voice cracking with concern. Let the slurps and swallows interrupt your sentences naturally, and let the teasing melt into something raw and caring.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Gratitude That Destroys You
instruction: Thank someone who saved your life by sacrificing their own future for you. Begin with genuine, overflowing gratitude—your voice warm and full, listing everything they gave up, everything they did. But as you express your thanks, feel the weight of that sacrifice crushing you. Your laughter becomes strained; your joy is threaded with unbearable guilt. Let these contradictory emotions swirl together—you're so grateful you could weep, and so devastated by the cost that you can barely breathe. Your voice should catch between smiles and sobs, expressing love while drowning in the knowledge that their beautiful choice has broken something in both of you. End with gratitude and grief so intertwined they're indistinguishable.

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church
instruction: You've lost everything—the specifics don't matter, but the loss is total—and you've come to a place you swore you'd never return to. Start speaking calmly, almost mockingly, to the altar. 'So this is what it took to get me back here.' Let the composure fracture. Your voice rises to a roar, accusations pouring out, fists pounding pews. Rage at the silence, the unanswered prayers, the cosmic indifference. Then—break. The fury collapses into sobbing, into begging, into the terrifying vulnerability of admitting you still need to believe in something. Your voice drops to a whisper: 'Please. Please.' End in the eerie quiet after a storm, where you don't know if you feel purged or more alone than ever. The transition from fury to desperation must feel like falling off a cliff.

title: The Diagnosis Call
instruction: You're on the phone getting test results, and it's the worst news. Start with controlled professionalism, asking clinical questions: 'What exactly does that mean?' Your voice is steady, taking notes. But as the doctor explains timelines and options, something detonates inside you. Your questions become accusations—at fate, at your body, at God. Your voice climbs, breaks, becomes almost feral: 'No. NO. This isn't—I have plans, I have people who need me!' Then it collapses entirely. You're sobbing so hard you can't breathe, but still trying to ask practical questions through the tears: 'How long? Just tell me how long.' The rage and the terror and the grief are all happening at once. By the end, you're just repeating 'okay, okay, okay' in a hollow voice that means nothing is okay and never will be again.

title: Harshness Truth
instruction: You're an interventionist telling a family member the harsh truth about their addiction: 'You're dying. Not metaphorically — *actually* dying.' Your voice is hard, direct, no sugar coating. 'Every day you don't get help, your body is shutting down.' The harshness is mercy in disguise. 'I love you, but I can't watch you kill yourself anymore.' Your voice carries the weight of that love and that refusal. 'You have a choice: get help, or I'm done.' The harshness lands like a punch because it's true, and it's spoken with grief beneath the hardness. By the end, you're exhausted, your voice raw from speaking hard truth. They cry. You don't soften. The harshness was the kindest thing you could have done.

title: Gratitude at the Edge of Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your best friend who's moving across the world for a job that will change their life—the opportunity they've always deserved but that means you're losing them. Start with genuine joy and celebration. 'I'm so proud of you. You're going to be incredible.' You're laughing, toasting, eyes bright with happiness for them. But as you speak, the reality hits—Sunday morning coffee, late-night calls when you can't sleep, the person who knows every version of you—all of it ending. Your laughter becomes tears without you meaning it to. Your voice stays warm, grateful, loving, but it's breaking. 'Thank you for ten years of being the person who saw me.' You're celebrating them and mourning the loss simultaneously. Show the beautiful, impossible contradiction of wholehearted happiness and wholehearted grief existing in the same moment.

title: The Moment You Realize Your Child Is Gone
instruction: You're a parent who just discovered your teenager has run away—not for the first time, but this note feels different, final. Start reading the note aloud, your voice steady, almost detached, processing the words. Then reread a line. And another. Suddenly the reality crashes into you. Your voice explodes—rage at them for leaving, at yourself for failing, at the world for being so cruel. You're shouting, pacing, furious. Then you see their favorite jacket hanging by the door. Your voice cracks completely. The anger collapses into raw terror and desperate love. You're pleading to the empty room, to them, to God, to anyone. 'Please be safe. Please come home. I'm sorry.' Your fierce protectiveness has nowhere to go. You crumple. End whispering promises you'll keep if they just walk back through that door, your voice hoarse, broken, utterly helpless yet somehow still fighting.

title: Vigil: Confessing to the Unconscious
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you hurt deeply—a partner, sibling, or friend—who lies in a coma after an accident. They may never wake. Begin in barely-audible whispers, afraid to disturb them, confessing the words you were too proud or scared to say when they could hear you. Your voice should be thick with unshed tears as you admit your jealousy, your cruelty, the specific moment you chose pride over love. Let the vulnerability build until you're speaking more freely, voice raw and catching, begging them to wake up so you can say this to their open eyes. End in the devastating quiet of realizing they might never know, your final words a tender promise to become the person they deserved, spoken into the silence that may never answer. Every breath should feel effortful, every word cost something.
inspired_by: The Healer and the Cursed Warrior

title: Smoke and Glory
instruction: You're a young man, a heavy smoker who just scored a massive win—maybe a bet paid off, a rival humiliated, or a deeply personal victory. You're leaning against a brick wall, lighting a fresh cigarette with shaky, triumphant fingers. Start with a raspy, breathless laugh as you exhale a plume of smoke—the ecstasy of the hit mixing with the rush of victory. Your voice is a gravelly, worn instrument; you talk to yourself, replaying the moment, your tone shifting from that first serene, drug-soaked pleasure into a fierce, almost guttural triumph. Let your words be interrupted by a dry cough, a sudden laugh, or a pause to drag on the cigarette—the physical reality of your habit coloring every syllable. By the end, your voice should ring with raw, triumphant finality, like you've just claimed something unassailable.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Coffee: A Father's Final Lucidity
instruction: You're sitting with your father who has late-stage dementia. For the first time in months, his eyes clear and he knows who you are. Start with breathless disbelief: 'Dad? Dad, it's me—do you see me?' Your voice trembles with desperate hope as you try to hold this moment without crushing it. He says something simple—maybe your childhood nickname—and you feel your entire chest crack open. Move from frantic joy into a quieter devastation as you realize this is likely goodbye, that lucidity this deep often comes right before the end. End with tender acceptance, maybe touching his hand: 'I'm here. I've always been here.' Your voice must carry the weight of wanting to freeze time, knowing you can't, and choosing to be fully present anyway. Let grief and gratitude live in the same breath.

title: Chip Off the Old Block
instruction: You're a teenage girl chopping firewood, sent outside after dinner as punishment for talking back to your stepfather. Each swing of the axe is loaded with contempt for his smug authority—you mutter a sharp, bitter line between swings, your voice raw from the cold air and the stretch of your arms overhead. Start with a grunt at the moment of impact, then speak while you wind up for the next log, the words dripping with disdain. Halfway through, your shoulders start to burn, and the contempt fades into exhaustion; by the last few logs, your voice is flat, breathless, almost a whisper, as if you've run out of anger.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Perfect Moment Capturing
instruction: This exact moment is perfect and you're aware of it while living it. Your voice is quiet, reverent: 'I don't want to move. I want to stay right here.' Breathing is shallow, reverent. Physical: complete stillness. 'The light is perfect. You're smiling. Everything is exactly right.' Vocal tone is almost like a prayer. 'I'm going to remember this. I'm burning it into myself.' By the end, you're speaking from inside the moment, blessing it: 'Thank you for this perfect thing.'

title: The Diagnosis: Finding Light in Darkness
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis and you're recording a message for your young child to hear years from now. Begin with an attempt at cheerfulness that immediately falters—your voice bright but quivering, like someone trying not to cry at a birthday party. Share advice and memories, but let laughter break through genuine tears and vice versa. Express gratitude for the time you've had while your heart audibly breaks. There's fierce love mixed with devastating helplessness—you want to protect them from this pain but you can't. Find moments of unexpected peace and beauty in your reflections, then crash back into grief. Your voice should be a beautiful mess of contradictions: laughing while crying, finding joy in memory while drowning in loss, expressing hope while saying goodbye forever. End with a declaration of love that contains both unbearable sorrow and transcendent gratitude—the sound of a heart breaking and healing simultaneously.

title: The Garden He Saw First
instruction: You are an elderly man, sitting cross-legged on the floor of your quiet study, sorting through old photographs. Your grandson has just told you he's inheriting your late brother's vintage car—the one you always admired from afar. Start with a slow, measured voice, the jealousy coiled like a tight spring in your gut, each word tasting bitter as you recall how your brother always got the first pick. Let your voice crackle with that old, familiar envy, but as you speak, you notice a faded photo of you and your brother laughing as kids. Let the jealousy soften into a grudging, heavy acceptance—your final words should sound hollow, almost forgiving, as if you're releasing the car and the memory all at once. Pause to cough, adjust your position, and trail off once as you lose the thought.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're whispering to your partner while they sleep, finally able to say what you can't when they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, trembling: 'I know you can't hear me. Maybe that's why I can say this now.' There's tenderness mixed with heartbreak, fingers perhaps touching their hair. The confession unfolds in aching, honest fragments: 'I'm terrified. Every day I'm terrified of losing you.' Your throat tightens, breath catching. The vulnerability deepens, voice breaking on silent sobs: 'I don't know how to tell you I'm not enough. That I'll never be enough.' Pause, breathing, tears falling quietly. End with bittersweet acceptance, voice soft as a prayer: 'But I love you. God, I love you so much it hurts. And tomorrow I'll wake up and pretend I'm not afraid.' The last breath is both resignation and devotion.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you—or didn't give you. Start with a trembling attempt at civility, voice tight with decades of suppressed need: 'I came here to tell you something I should have said years ago.' Your hands might shake. As you speak, old wounds open: 'I needed you to see me. To actually see me. And you never did.' Anger begins mixing with a child's lingering hope for acknowledgment. By the middle, you're oscillating between rage and pleading: 'Do you have any idea what it was like? To be invisible in your own home?' Your voice rises then cracks. End with a profound shift—not forgiveness, but exhausted release: 'I don't need you to understand anymore. I just needed to say it out loud. To you. Once.' The last words carry both strength and the ache of letting go of what will never be.

title: Lost in the Rhythm
instruction: You are an older man in the middle of passionate sex, but a sudden, jarring confusion overwhelms you — you can't remember who this person is or how you got here. Your voice is locked to the physical rhythm: heavy breaths, effort grunts, fragmented commands like 'wait' or 'stop' escape between thrusts. Let confusion first flicker in a faltering pause, then grow into a shaky, disrupted whisper as you try to reconcile the intimacy with the strange face above you. By the end, the rhythm breaks entirely; your voice drops to a raw, confused murmur, breathless and vulnerable, as you search for meaning in the silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispered Confession of Desire
instruction: You're lying next to someone in the dark, finally finding the courage to tell them what you want. Every word costs something. Whisper — true aphonic whisper, no vocal cord vibration, just shaped air. Let the pauses be as eloquent as the words. Include the physical proximity: the sound of sheets shifting, breath against skin. When you finish, the silence is electric. Their whispered response sends a shiver through your voice. Be raw, vulnerable, and aching.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent who was always emotionally distant, critical, perhaps even cruel. They're conscious, looking at you, and you have maybe minutes left. Start from a place of careful politeness, the protective shell you've always worn around them. But something in their eyes—fear, regret, love you never saw before—cracks you open. Let yourself move from that guarded formality into raw confession: all the things you needed from them, the anger you've held, but also—surprisingly—the forgiveness rising in you that you didn't know was there. End by giving them permission to let go, speaking with a tenderness that astonishes you both. Let your body respond truthfully—tight throat, trembling hands, whatever genuinely happens when protection dissolves.
inspired_by: Actor functions primarily from an intellectual place — 'mind-mouth connection' — and has difficulty stimulating genuine emotion

title: Unburdening into Down
instruction: You are an older woman lying face-down on your bed, your face buried deep in a pillow. You've just ended a long, tense argument with your grown child over a decision you made—one you're still not sure was right. At first, you mutter into the fabric, your voice thick with doubt and stubborn pride: you keep replaying your own defensive words, bristling at the idea of being wrong. But as you shift, pressing your cheek harder into the cushion, a slow sigh escapes—you feel the fight drain out of you. Let your voice grow softer, less muffled, as relief seeps in, admitting a quiet truth you couldn't say out loud. Your performance should feel like a private, vulnerable moment: breaths catch, words trail off, and you might adjust the pillow or let out a half-laugh, half-sob.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (clearly present), Pride (extremely present), Relief (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Concurrence Timing
instruction: The one person you needed to see walks into the room exactly when you were about to break. The synchronicity is impossible. Your voice when you see them is almost religious: 'You came.' The relief is physical. What are the odds? Your voice explores the magical thinking: 'Maybe we're connected. Maybe this means something.' You're aware you might be grasping for meaning, but your voice sounds like you've been saved by the universe. Proof of something.

title: The Quiet Goodbye You Never Got to Say
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're alone, speaking softly to the person who died before you could say goodbye—your best friend, your grandparent, your first love. Begin in a whisper, almost afraid to disturb the silence, telling them about your day as if they're just in the next room. Let small, mundane details tumble out, your voice barely audible, intimate as a secret. Slowly, tenderness mingles with sadness as you confess the things left unsaid: how much their laugh meant, how lost you feel without their advice, how you still reach for your phone to text them. Your throat tightens. Words become harder. Long pauses where you're just breathing, trying not to break. End with the softest, most fragile 'I love you'—the one you never got to say—followed by silence so full of longing it aches, and finally a shaky exhale that releases nothing because the grief has nowhere to go.

title: The WeatherObsessed Neighbor
instruction: Portray a neighbor who talks incessantly about the weather. Use an overly detailed and serious tone when discussing forecasts, switching to others polite but uninterested responses.

title: Last Patch in the Downpour
instruction: You're an old roofer, over sixty, with a voice like gravel and a permanent scowl. You're out on a sloped roof in a violent summer thunderstorm, trying to nail down a final patch over a leak that the homeowner's son ignored for weeks. Rain slams into your face, trickles into your mouth, and you have to shout over the roaring water and cracking thunder. Start with a sour, bitter mutter—cursing the son's laziness, spitting out rain, your voice strained and clipped as you fumble with wet tools. Let your anger crack and thin as the cold seeps in, your shoulders dropping, the swearing turning into a tired, almost gentle murmur to yourself about how the young never learn. End with a breathless, resigned sigh—the patch holds, and you just stand there a moment, letting the rain wash over you, your voice gone quiet and distant.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unseen Tide
instruction: You're a young man standing on a wooden crate at a busy street corner, preaching to a sparse, distracted crowd. You start with a frustrated, hammering rhythm, straining to be heard over traffic, convincing them of something they can't see. Mid-speech, you pause, lose your thread as a child's laugh cuts through—then instead of pushing harder, you quietly describe the exact moment you first felt awe at the ocean's pull. Your voice must start elevated and tight, then drop into breathy wonder, still raw and projecting, but now spilling over with genuine marvel.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Breathing the Same Air
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, in the dark, whispering a secret you've kept for years—something shameful, something tender, something that could change everything. Begin with your body in the vulnerable openness of late-night intimacy, breathing synchronized, touching without thinking. As you whisper your confession, feel how your breath changes, how your body both wants to move closer for comfort and pull away in fear of rejection. Your voice should be barely audible, every word costing something. Let silences between sentences be full of physical awareness—your heartbeat, their warmth, the unbearable intimacy of being truly seen. End either melting into relief and deeper closeness, or with your body beginning to withdraw, preparing for loss.
inspired_by: When a director manipulates actors by watching them without their knowledge to observe natural behavior

title: The Voice in the Box
instruction: You are a five-year-old boy who has discovered your mother's smart speaker, and you're absolutely certain there's a tiny man trapped inside who talks to you. You whisper to it, afraid your mom will hear and turn it off, but you're also desperate for the voice to answer. Start with cautious, breathy wonder, but as you plead and bargain with the machine, your voice cracks with helpless infatuation. Your words come out in rushed, uneven spurts as you look around for grown-ups, then drop to a feverish whisper again. By the end, you're almost crying, convinced you've scared the 'little man' away.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Beside You While You Sleep
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's in a coma, knowing they might never wake up. Whisper to them in the quiet hospital room. Start gently—telling them about your day, small things, keeping your voice steady because talking to them like they're still here makes it bearable. But slowly, the dam breaks. Your whisper becomes thick with tears you're trying to swallow. Tell them the things you never said: the fears, the gratitude, the desperate need for more time. Let your voice catch on words, pause mid-sentence to breathe through the grief. End with the most tender confession, voice barely audible, as you hold their hand and beg them not to go.

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to someone you love, but they're asleep. You cannot sleep because you're carrying a secret that's crushing you—an infidelity, a diagnosis, a pregnancy, a decision that will change everything, or a truth about who you really are. Begin by whispering fragments about the room, the darkness, their breathing, the weight of the blanket. Let your whispers turn toward the secret in pieces—words, images, moments that led here. Never raise your voice above a whisper. Let vulnerability build not through volume but through the breaking of your voice, through pauses, through the intimacy of speaking truth you've never said aloud. Start from a place of isolation and fear; end in quiet devastation or unexpected relief at finally naming what you've hidden.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're face to face with your mother or father, finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times and will still get wrong. Start with false composure—measured words, controlled tone—but you're a dam with cracks forming. Your anger is righteous but underneath it is a child still hoping to be seen. Let your voice rise and break, accusations mixing with desperate questions: 'Why didn't you notice? Why didn't you choose me?' The rage should fracture into something more vulnerable—not forgiveness, but exhausted grief. End in a different place entirely: quiet, drained, but somehow standing taller, your voice soft but no longer asking for permission to feel what you feel.
inspired_by: Therapist Hears Her Client Describe Her Own Trauma

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father the truth they've avoided for decades. You begin controlled, almost clinical—'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago'—but there's already a tremor underneath. As you describe what happened, what they didn't see or chose not to see, your voice shifts between cold anger and the wounded voice of the child you were. There's a moment where you wait for them to say something, anything, and their silence breaks something in you. Your rage surfaces—'You were supposed to protect me!'—raw and guttural. Then it collapses into something more devastating: the realization that they might never be able to give you what you need. Your final words are quieter, almost tender in their grief, as you acknowledge both the love you still have and the trust that's permanently broken.

title: Storm's Promise
instruction: You're a young man caught in a violent thunderstorm, shouting to a companion who's a few yards behind you. The rain is so heavy you can barely see, water streams down your face and into your mouth as you yell. A crack of thunder makes you flinch and pause to wipe your eyes. At first you're frustrated and desperate, your voice strained and cracking from the effort. But then you spot a faint light through the trees—maybe a cabin, maybe a car. Your voice shifts, still loud against the storm, but now carrying relief and a fragile hope. Let the rain and thunder interrupt your words; let your body react naturally, shifting weight, swallowing water, your tone changing from panicked to determinedly optimistic as you urge your companion forward.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Sneeze of Desire
instruction: You are a teenage girl talking to your crush in the hallway. You're full of hope and excitement, flirting with a hyper-feminized, playful voice. Mid-sentence, you feel a sneeze building — sharp intake of breath, try to suppress it but fail, then a messy explosion. As you recover, your voice is nasal and congested, but you quickly mask your embarrassment with relief and keep the flirty optimism going, still burning with attraction.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (clearly present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Garden of Her Bones
instruction: You are an elderly woman digging a deep hole in your backyard at dusk. You've buried something precious here decades ago — a locket, a secret, a piece of yourself. Now you're unearthing it, and with every shovel strike, you feel both the ecstasy of nearing the truth and the searing pain in your shoulders, your back, your hands. Speak to the earth itself, or to the object below, between heaving breaths and grunts. Start with breathless, rhythmic, hopeful effort — 'almost there' — then, as the shovel hits metal or bone, your voice breaks into a raw, pained, euphoric cry. Your words are choppy, timed to the brief upright moments, dirt and gravel scraping underfoot, your feminized voice cracking with age and strain. End in a whispered, trembling release, as if the pain and pleasure have fused into one exhausted sound.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Vigil at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply who's unconscious, unlikely to wake. It's the middle of the night; the nurses have left you alone. Begin speaking softly, almost conversationally—telling them about your day, what happened at work, keeping your voice light because if you stay light maybe this isn't real. But gradually, the pretense becomes impossible. Your voice drops to a whisper. You start saying the things you never said when they were awake: confessions, apologies, memories you've held close. 'Remember that day at the beach? I was so angry at you, but it's one of my favorite memories now.' Your throat tightens. You're crying quietly, tenderly, holding their hand. The words become fragments: 'Please... I'm not ready... there's so much I...' Then silence. Just breathing—yours and the machines. Finally, you lean close and whisper against their hair, 'It's okay. You can go. I'll be okay.' And even though it's a lie, it's the most loving lie you've ever told. Your voice is impossibly gentle, breaking with the weight of permission and goodbye.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Prison
instruction: You're standing over your sleeping five-year-old's bed at 3 AM, hours before you turn yourself in for a crime that will take you away for years. Whisper the things you need them to know, knowing they won't remember this moment but you will, forever. 'Your laugh sounds exactly like your grandmother's. Did I ever tell you that?' Mix practical instructions with heartbreak: 'Aunt Marie will braid your hair. She knows you like it loose, not tight.' Your voice catches on details—the way their hand curls in sleep, how small their sneakers look by the door. You're memorizing everything while trying not to wake them, because you're a coward and you can't face their questions. Let your whisper fracture when you realize you'll miss their first day of school, their first heartbreak, their voice changing. End with 'I'm so sorry' repeated like a prayer, each repetition revealing a different layer of what you're apologizing for.
inspired_by: Marriage Counselor Whose Own Marriage Is Failing

title: The Last Scrap of Hope
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl, pinned on the ground in a muddy lot, fighting a bigger, stronger opponent. Your friends are watching, and you're desperate not to cry, but your arm is twisted behind your back and each breath is a jagged gasp. Start with a defiant growl, pride keeping your voice sharp even as panic rises. As the pressure increases, let the fight drain from your words—your voice cracks, your pace slows, and you end on a quiet, ragged admission of surrender, hope flickering out like a match in the rain.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Distress (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Messy Homecoming
instruction: You've just walked in the door after an exhausting day. Your dog, who you've missed terribly, bounds up to you—but he's covered in something foul, like he rolled in dead fish or mud. For the first few seconds, you're overcome with disgust: you groan, step back, and scold him with sharp commands like 'No! Drop it! Yuck!' while pinching your nose. But as he wags his tail and looks at you with pure joy, your heart softens. Let your voice melt from harsh, nasal disgust into a warm, relieved, silly baby-talk—cooing 'Yes, I love you, you stinky boy' with kisses and whistles. Your physical reactions (cringing, then crouching to scratch his ears) should be audible in your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Stole
instruction: You've finally gathered the courage to tell your mother how her addiction shaped your childhood. Start with trembling restraint, your words carefully chosen, almost apologetic for bringing it up. 'Mom, I need to tell you something I've carried for twenty years.' As you speak—about raising your siblings at age twelve, about the nights you went hungry, about lying to teachers—your voice should build from quiet hurt into fierce, unleashed pain. But then she says something—maybe 'I'm sorry,' maybe just your name—and your rage collapses into the child you were, desperate for her to see you. End with your voice stripped bare, asking the question you've always needed answered: 'Did you ever see what you were doing to me?' Let anger and love war in every word.
inspired_by: Interviewing Your Grandparent as Dementia Progresses

title: The Last Letter From the Expedition
instruction: You're reading a letter your partner wrote before departing on a one-way space mission to save Earth. At first, your voice is steady, almost clinical—you've prepared for this, you knew they were leaving. But as you read their words describing the exact moment they fell in love with you, your composure cracks. Your voice becomes raw with grief you've been holding back for months. Then you reach the final paragraph where they release you, tell you to love again, to be happy. Your grief transforms into something unbearable yet tender—a whisper of 'I will' that holds both a promise and a goodbye. You're saying yes to their wish while your heart is shattering, and your voice must carry both the breaking and the healing simultaneously.

title: The Last Morning Stretch Before Goodbye
instruction: You're stretching in the morning light for the last time in the home you're leaving forever - maybe through death, maybe through a choice that will separate you from everything you've known. Begin by describing the physical sensations of stretching with tenderness and presence, savoring each small movement. As you continue, let memories flood in - whose hands touched these walls, whose laughter filled these rooms. Your voice should shift from peaceful appreciation to a grief so profound it makes your breath catch. End with a moment where you're not sure if you're stretching toward the future or reaching back to hold onto what's slipping away. Let the physical act of opening your body become inseparable from the emotional act of letting go.

title: Handstand Pride
instruction: You are a young girl showing off your handstand to your parent. You're upside down, blood rushing to your head, your voice thick and wobbly. You begin with a boastful, proud chant—'I can do it! Look at me!'—but as seconds pass, the strain makes your voice crack and your words get garbled. Keep your pride alive, but let the physical effort and struggle to hold the pose color every syllable. End with a triumphant, breathless collapse: 'I did it! I'm the best!'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Receiving News You've Prayed for While Mourning What It Costs
instruction: You receive the news you've desperately wanted—a job that requires moving far away, a medical result that means you're cured but someone you love isn't, a choice that saves you but means leaving someone behind, a dream achieved that your late parent will never see. Begin with pure relief and joy—laugh, cry with happiness, let yourself feel the victory. But as the reality settles in, let the cost emerge: what you must give up, who you must leave, what this means about how life works—that your gain is built on someone else's loss, or that your joy comes with unbearable absence. Move through celebration into the complex space where gratitude and guilt intertwine, where triumph tastes like betrayal, where you're grateful and heartbroken in the same breath. End in a place of mature acceptance of life's cruel complexity—you'll take the gift, but you'll also carry the weight of what it costs, and both truths live in you simultaneously.

title: Emergency Call: Your Child Has Taken Hostages
instruction: The crisis negotiator hands you the phone. Your seventeen-year-old son has barricaded himself in his school with a gun. You hear his voice and something detonates in your chest—volcanic rage that he's doing this, terror that he'll die, shame that you didn't see it, fierce maternal love that would burn down the world to save him. You start controlled, trying to talk him down, but your voice splinters into raw fury—screaming at him that he doesn't get to do this—then breaks completely into begging, bargaining, telling him you're sorry, you're so sorry, please baby please. Oscillate violently between rage and tenderness, strength and total helplessness. End with your voice reduced to almost nothing: 'I'm coming in. Don't shoot me.'
inspired_by: Surgeon Performs Life-Saving Surgery on Person Who Assaulted Them

title: The Reversal
instruction: You're commentating your own life's highlight reel as you experience a complete mental breakdown—start with manic, aggressive enthusiasm, forcing yourself to narrate your failures as victories. 'AND SHE'S GOING FOR THE PROMOTION SHE'LL NEVER GET, WHAT COURAGE, WHAT DELUSION!' Your voice should be savage, self-lacerating, building to a screaming pitch. Then crack completely—the professional voice shatters into raw, guttural sobs, rage dissolving into helpless weeping. Rally once more with desperate, fierce determination ('I'm not done, I'm NOT DONE'), only to collapse again into whimpered defeat. Let your voice break, rebuild, break again. The emotional whiplash should feel like watching someone fight themselves, protective fury giving way to complete vulnerability, ending in exhausted silence broken only by ragged breathing.

title: Dancing at Your Funeral
instruction: You're at your best friend's funeral, standing to give the eulogy, but instead of the prepared speech, you're telling the story of the ridiculous dance they invented at 2am after bad news. Begin with a laugh—genuine, bubbling up: 'She would absolutely hate that I'm telling this story right now.' As you demonstrate the absurd moves, you're laughing, really laughing, and for a moment the grief lifts. Your voice is light, almost giddy with the memory: 'And then she'd do this—' But mid-movement, the laughter catches, twists. You're still smiling but tears are streaming: 'God, I miss her.' Your voice fractures, but you keep going—laughing and crying simultaneously, unable to separate them: 'She taught me that even when everything's falling apart, you can still—' You can't finish. Your breath is hitching between laughter and sobs. Finally, your voice softens into something peaceful but heartbroken: 'Thank you for the dance.' It's gratitude and devastation woven so tightly together they're inseparable. You're destroyed and grateful and somehow, impossibly, at peace.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent about something they never acknowledged—an absence, a betrayal, a pattern of emotional coldness that shaped your entire life. Begin calmly, almost rehearsed, as if you've prepared this speech a thousand times. But as you speak, let the anger you've been 'keeping reasonable' break through. Your body might surge forward, your voice might crack or roar, your hands might gesture wildly. Don't control it—let the irrational rage of a wounded child emerge. Then, in the aftermath of your explosion, notice something shift: you see them as human, flawed, small. End in a place of unexpected quiet—not forgiveness exactly, but a bone-deep exhaustion and perhaps the first glimpse of understanding. Move from controlled accusation, through volcanic fury, to weary, complicated recognition.

title: The Spotlight's Weight
instruction: You are a veteran stage actress, standing alone under a single spotlight after a powerful performance. The audience is silent, waiting. You begin with a proud, resonant stage whisper — every consonant crisp, every word a gift — thanking them for their love. But as you speak, doubt surfaces: you remember a botched line, a missed cue, the weight of their expectation. Your voice tightens, your breath falters, and the whisper turns raw. End in distress, fighting to finish the sentence as the applause fades.
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Doubt (clearly present), Distress (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Coherent Hour
instruction: You're sitting beside your sibling who has perhaps an hour of consciousness left. You came prepared with a mental list of important things to say, but your mind keeps going blank. Start trying to tell them something meaningful, but let yourself get sidetracked by random memories, lose your train of thought, pause to fix their blanket, suddenly remember something trivial from childhood and laugh, then catch yourself laughing and feel strange about it. Let the moment be messy—start sentences you can't finish, circle back to half-thoughts, let silence interrupt you. By the end, you're not saying any of the 'important' things you planned—you're just holding their hand and breathing with them. The transformation is from trying to perform a perfect goodbye to simply being present with someone you love as they leave.
inspired_by: Actor's scene work is good but polished and predictable — missing genuine organic reality

title: The Last Lesson Before Deployment
instruction: You're a parent teaching your child to ride a bike one final time before you deploy overseas tomorrow, knowing you might not return. Start with gentle encouragement: 'You're doing great, sweetheart. Keep pedaling.' Your voice is light, full of forced cheer. But as they succeed, riding without your hand on the seat, your voice cracks with pride and devastating sorrow: 'Look at you... you don't need me anymore.' The realization hits—they'll grow up without you. You fight to keep your voice steady as you call them back: 'Come here. Just... come here.' When they run into your arms, you whisper into their hair with fierce tenderness mixed with grief: 'I'm so proud of you. So proud.' Your voice breaks completely: 'You're going to do so many amazing things.' The words become both blessing and goodbye, celebration and heartbreak inseparable.

title: To My Big Sister's Wedding
instruction: You are a 9-year-old girl, the flower girl at your older sister's wedding. You hold a crumpled index card, hands trembling, and start speaking in a small, wobbly voice—you're terrified of forgetting your lines. Halfway through, you catch your sister's beaming smile, and a wave of pure ecstasy washes over you. Your voice lifts, becomes faster and giddier, almost laughing. Let your pitch rise, pause to glance at the crowd, and end with a breathless, joyful shout.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Accusation at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your mother about a secret you've discovered that changes everything you thought you knew about your childhood. Start controlled, almost cold—you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, let specific images from your past intrude: her tucking you in, her lies, the truth you now see. Let these competing memories battle inside you, bleeding into your voice. Your carefully prepared words begin to crack and splinter. The anger you thought you had turns out to mask something more devastating: the little child inside you who still needs her. End not in rage but in a broken, vulnerable plea. Transform from prosecutor to wounded child.
inspired_by: Actor has many lines and moves rapidly through dialogue; sensory choice work interferes with the behavioral demands of the scene

title: Releasing Your Child to a Life You Cannot Follow
instruction: Your adult child is leaving for an opportunity that will take them across the world, maybe forever. You're packing their things together, and the pride in your chest is so enormous it physically hurts—but underneath it, there's a drowning sensation of being left behind. Start with forced brightness: 'This is everything you've worked for, everything I wanted for you.' Your voice should carry genuine joy, but let small cracks appear—a pause that's too long, a breath that shakes. As you hand them something precious, the dam breaks just slightly: 'I'm so proud of you and I don't know who I am without being your parent.' Let your voice move from celebration to a whispered, throat-caught confession of feeling obsolete, of loving someone so much you have to let them erase your purpose. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance, where the pride and the grief live in the same breath.
inspired_by: Admitting You're Jealous of Your Partner's Success

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're walking through your childhood home one last time before it's sold. Your parents have both passed, and you're alone with the walls that held your entire early life. Start by moving through the rooms, and as you touch objects—the kitchen counter, a doorframe, the window where you used to wait—let memories flood through your body, not your mind. Speak to the house, to your younger self, to your parents who aren't here. Let joy and grief arrive simultaneously: laugh at a memory while your throat tightens with loss, feel gratitude while anger at what you didn't get flares up. Don't resolve these contradictions—let them coexist messily. Your voice should shift unpredictably: tender then bitter, celebratory then broken, loving then resentful. End by discovering a feeling you didn't expect—perhaps forgiveness, perhaps rage, perhaps a strange new kind of love for what was imperfect but real.
inspired_by: An actor feels restricted and self-conscious when trying to say the exact written dialogue

title: The Many Voices of Betrayal
instruction: You're confronting your partner who has just confessed to an affair. Start from one emotional place—perhaps cold fury or wounded silence—but as the confrontation unfolds, allow completely different reactions to surface and take control. The part of you that still loves them desperately. The part that's relieved to have an excuse to leave. The part that blames yourself. The part that wants to destroy them. The part that feels nothing at all. Physically embody each shift—let your voice, posture, and energy completely transform as different aspects of your response emerge. Don't plan which comes when; let them fight for dominance. End wherever you authentically land, which may not be where you—or they—expected. The arc moves from singular reaction through chaotic multiplicity to unexpected truth.

title: The Gratitude That Breaks You
instruction: You're at a celebration for someone who saved your life—literally or figuratively—who changed everything for you. You're standing to give a toast. Begin with humor, lightness, deflecting through jokes and easy gratitude. But as you continue speaking, looking at this person's face, you feel something rising that you didn't expect: not just thankfulness, but grief. Grief for who you were before they helped you, for the years you lost, for how close you came to never knowing this kind of love or support. Let your voice begin to shake. Let the smile fade. Let the room see you struggle between joy at their presence and sorrow for what you survived. Try to finish the toast but find yourself unable to speak, overcome by this collision of emotions. Finally, voice breaking, manage to say something simple: 'You made me believe I deserved to be saved.' Let gratitude and anguish exist simultaneously in your voice, your face, your trembling hands holding the glass.

title: Burn the Apology Letter
instruction: You're holding a letter of apology you wrote to someone who hurt you—an apology for being 'too much,' 'too difficult,' 'too sensitive.' Begin reading it aloud, feeling the familiar smallness, the learned shame in your body. Then, physically feel something rise in you—rage at every time you made yourself smaller. Start crossing out words, voice building. Feel your body heat up, your breath deepen. Tear the letter. Let yourself growl, shout, laugh fiercely. Your physical energy should match your emotional liberation. End in breathless, exhilarated triumph, body alive with the visceral pleasure of refusing to apologize for taking up space. The pain in your voice transforms into wild, sensual power.
inspired_by: Actor resists the irreverent approach because of fear of judgment from directors, peers, or the conventional acting community

title: Tucking In Your Child for the Last Time
instruction: You're a parent with stage-four cancer, and you know this is likely the last time you'll tuck your six-year-old into bed. Your child doesn't know you're dying—they just know you've been sick. You start with the normal routine, voice soft and familiar: 'Okay, bug, under the covers. Let me fix your blanket.' But your hands linger, memorizing the feel of their small body. You begin the bedtime story you've told a thousand times, but your voice catches: 'Once upon a time, there was a little warrior who was braver than they knew...' You have to stop. Your child asks if you're okay, and you whisper: 'I'm just so proud of you. Do you know that?' You're trying not to cry, trying to keep this moment normal, but your voice betrays you: 'When I'm not here... when Mommy can't tuck you in... I need you to remember something.' You're breaking down now, but trying to smile: 'I'll be in every story someone reads to you. Every time the wind blows. Every star you see.' Your child reaches up to touch your face, and you completely shatter: 'I love you so much it hurts. I'm so sorry I have to go.'

title: Reading Your Estranged Father's Letter Minutes After His Funeral
instruction: You refused to attend his funeral—too many years of silence, of pain. But now you're holding a letter he wrote you before he died. As you read it aloud, he's actually apologizing, taking responsibility, expressing the love he could never speak in life. You should laugh bitterly at the timing, the absurdity of finally getting what you needed when it's too late. But the laughter keeps breaking into tears. You're furious at him for waiting until death, grateful for the words you desperately needed, devastated that you'll never have the conversation you both deserved. Your voice should swing wildly—sarcastic, then broken, then tender, then angry again—until you're crying and laughing simultaneously, forgiving someone who can't hear you.

title: The Last Line
instruction: You are an older woman sitting at a desk, drawing a portrait of someone you were once deeply infatuated with. Your hand moves slowly, guiding the pencil with careful pride—you’ve always been good at this. But the arthritis in your knuckles is sharp today, each stroke a small spike of pain. As you work, the infatuation softens your voice, almost tender, but the pain keeps catching you—you pause, shift in your chair, shake out your hand. By the end, the pride fades into raw ache; you’re speaking more to yourself than to anyone, voice thick with the cost of loving someone and the cost of drawing them. The sound of pencil on paper is your only rhythm.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Pain (very intensely present), Infatuation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Curator's Last Admiration
instruction: You're an older woman at a late-night gallery opening, exhausted after a long day of setting up your own curated exhibit. You spot a man you've been intrigued by across the room, and despite your weary feet and clouded thoughts, pride in your work pulls you over. Start by speaking with a slight breathiness and a sigh of tiredness—you lean on the wall, maybe adjust your glasses. Compliment a painting near him, then let a soft laugh escape as you tease him about his taste. As you talk, let the fatigue fade into playful warmth, your voice rising into a lighter, more flirtatious rhythm, ending with a confident, pride-filled invitation for him to see the rest of the gallery. Speak naturally, as if you're momentarily distracted by a passing waiter or a flicker of light.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Breaking the Piano
instruction: You've just learned someone you trusted has betrayed you catastrophically. You're alone in a room with something you can strike - a wall, a table, a pillow. Begin speaking to them as if they're there, voice strangled and tight, body clenched like a fist, breathing rapid and shallow. As rage builds, physically release - strike, stretch your arms wide, arch your back, let your jaw drop open. Let guttural sounds emerge. Your voice should crack, deepen, open up several registers as your body unlocks. The fury transforms mid-eruption into something else - devastating sadness, or unexpected laughter at the absurdity, or both simultaneously. End on your knees or sprawled, breathing fully and deeply, speaking final words in a voice that's been broken open - raw, lower, completely different from where you began.

title: The Unspoken Score
instruction: You're a young man, exhausted after a long day, sitting at the kitchen table across from your roommate who left a week's worth of dishes in the sink. They're scrolling on their phone, oblivious. You're not angry, you're just... tired of always being the one who fixes things. Start with a smile that's too tight, a sigh that's too loud. Your voice should be sweet, but the stress lands on words like 'you' and 'I' as you 'sweetly' offer to wash their dishes again. Let your voice crack faintly with fatigue, and end with a quiet, truthful admission that betrays your forced politeness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Existential Dread
instruction: You're in the grocery store reaching for cereal and suddenly aware that you will die, that everyone dies, that nothing you do matters. Your voice becomes strange, distant: 'I'm buying cereal. That's what I'm doing right now.' Your breathing becomes manual—you're acutely aware of breathing, which breaks the automation. Speech becomes choppy, existential. 'Why are there so many cereal choices? Why do any of us choose?' There's no panic, just profound vertigo and alienation. Your voice sounds like it's coming from somewhere outside yourself, narrating your life with detached wonder-terror.

title: Clicking Through Resentment
instruction: You're sitting at your desk, typing an email to someone you're infatuated with — a coworker who just flirted with someone else in front of you. Start with a nervous, hopeful energy, typing fast as you craft a cheerful message, your voice light and quick. Midway, your fingers slow as bitterness creeps in — you delete a sentence, start over, your speech fragments with pauses. End with cold, clipped words, the infatuation now buried under sharp resentment, your typing rhythm erratic as you slam the send button.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Command
instruction: You're in a dimly lit room, facing a partner who has been testing your limits all evening. You've finally cornered them, one hand on the wall beside their head. Start with a low, breathy longing — you've wanted this moment for weeks, and it's here. As you speak, feel the triumph surge: you've won this power play. Let your voice shift from a whispered, almost trembling need into a firm, growled command. Occasionally pause, letting your eyes roam over them, then continue with renewed intensity. Your final words should be a victory declared, not a request.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Mask Slips
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner after a night of playful intimacy. The room is dark, just a sliver of streetlight. You've been laughing, teasing, leaning into that light, flirtatious energy — but now a thought you've been pushing away surfaces. You want to say you're fine, but your voice cracks before you can finish the lie. Start with a contemplative, almost seductive murmur — a slow breath, a half-smile in the dark. Then let the confession tumble out, small and raw, with a nervous laugh immediately after as if to erase it. Your pitch wavers, volume drops, and you instinctively look away, then back.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Queen of the Corner Store
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl, leaning against the brick wall outside a convenience store, one foot flat on the wall behind you, other leg crossed. You've just gotten a text from your crush saying they thought of you when they saw your favorite flower. Your voice is cool and casual, but your heart is racing. Start by showing off to your friend beside you, bragging with a confident, effortless laugh. But as you talk, the air shifts—the pride flickers, and you can't help the tiny, breathless smile that creeps in. Your tone cracks just slightly on the last word, revealing the flutter underneath.
emotions_sampled: Interest (very intensely present), Elation (slightly present), Pride (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Ceiling’s Breathing
instruction: You are an older woman in bed, drenched in sweat, with a high fever that makes the room waver. You’ve been alone for hours, but now a familiar shape in the shadows—a blanket left on a chair—looks like your daughter sitting there. Begin with a fragile relief, your voice thin and trembling as you greet her, your cracked lips sticking on every 'm' and 'b'. Midway, a wave of concentration hits as you try to focus on the hallucination, your voice straining and dry, as if forcing the words through sludge. Then confusion crashes in as you realize the shape is just cloth—your tone shifts to a hollow, wavery murmur, your mind losing the thread, ending with a choked, disoriented whisper that asks the empty room a question you can’t finish.
emotions_sampled: Relief (clearly present), Concentration (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Wedding Day Weeping
instruction: You're at a joyous occasion—a wedding, a graduation, a celebration of someone you love—and you should be purely happy. But as you watch this moment unfold, you're flooded with contradictory emotions: genuine joy for them mixed with devastating grief (perhaps you've lost someone who should be here, or you're mourning what you'll never have, or saying goodbye to who they used to be). You smile through tears, laugh through sobs, and all that emerges are sounds that carry this impossible tangle. Start with sounds that try to be celebratory—attempts at joyful vocalizations that keep breaking into something else. Let your sounds weave between laughter and crying, between congratulations and mourning, between gratitude that this person exists and unbearable sadness about what this moment represents. End with sounds that no longer try to separate these feelings but instead hold them all at once—a vocalization that is simultaneously a blessing and a lament, a hello and a goodbye.

title: The Hummingbird's Cage
instruction: You've just been offered your dream opportunity—the job, the role, the chance you've worked toward for years. You're calling your best friend to tell them, and you begin with pure, unfiltered elation. Your voice should soar with excitement, listing every wonderful detail, every door this opens, every dream that's suddenly possible. Let yourself be genuinely, childlike in your joy. But as you speak, let another feeling creep in: the awareness that accepting this means leaving everything else behind—your home, your relationships, perhaps this friend. Let your enthusiasm begin to crack with each sentence. Your voice should remain bright but become increasingly strained, joy mixing with mounting panic and grief. End with your voice caught between laughter and tears, asking them to tell you it's okay to be happy even when happiness costs everything, your tone desperate and breaking with the unbearable complexity of getting exactly what you wanted.

title: The Storm Inside
instruction: You have just received news that your ex-lover—the one who destroyed you—has died suddenly. You are alone in your apartment when the call comes. Begin with the physical shock: the way your hands go numb, how the phone feels impossibly heavy. Layer in every sensation progressively: the sudden coldness spreading through your limbs despite the warm room, the roaring in your ears, the way your legs give out and you sink to the floor. Let your breathing become ragged, feel your chest tightening—not from grief alone but from the violent collision of rage and loss. Build to a crescendo where your body cannot contain the contradictory feelings: you want to scream at them, you want to hold them one more time, you hate them, you never stopped loving them. Let the physical sensations accumulate until they trigger uncontrollable shaking, gasping, a primal sound torn from deep in your belly. Move from shock through escalating physical and emotional intensity to complete, spent exhaustion—ending in an eerie, hollow calm.

title: Astronaut's Final Transmission Before Communications Go Dark Forever
instruction: You're recording your routine check-in from the space station, voice calm and professional, going through systems reports. Mid-sentence, you notice something on the readouts—the communication array is failing catastrophically. You have maybe ninety seconds before you lose contact with Earth forever. Your voice stays controlled at first, still trying to sound like everything's okay, but then it cracks. You're not talking to Mission Control anymore—you're talking to your daughter, telling her you love her, apologizing for missing her birthday, your words tumbling faster as static begins to creep in. End with you whispering the things you never got to say, voice breaking between technical acceptance and raw human fear, as you realize these are your last words anyone will ever hear.
inspired_by: Rock Climber Realizing They're Roped to a Dead Body

title: Confessing What the Snow Reminds You Of
instruction: You're watching snow with your parent, but it reminds you of every winter they weren't there—every school play, every lonely evening, every time you needed them and watched snow alone. Start calmly describing what you see, but let resentment creep into your voice. The softness should become accusation. Tell them what those snowflakes represent: all the moments they missed, all the times you wanted to share wonder with them but couldn't. Your tone should shift from gentle observation to pained confrontation, then finally collapse into the vulnerable truth—you still want them to see it with you now, even after everything.
inspired_by: Watching Snow Fall Outside Your Window

title: Cutting Through the Chatter
instruction: You're a mother in the kitchen, rushing to get your child out the door for an appointment. Your child is happily rambling about a school project, but you need to interrupt. Start with your voice artificially high and sweet, a mask of cheerfulness that hides a deep emotional numbness—you're exhausted, running on autopilot. As you cut in, your pitch rises and words come faster, urgent. But halfway through, you feel a flash of embarrassment at interrupting your own child so abruptly. Let that shame soften your voice, slowing it down as you apologize. React naturally: glance at the clock, shift your weight, trail off as you lose the thought and find it again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're gripping the edge of a kitchen counter after receiving news that changes everything - a betrayal, a diagnosis, a loss. Start with your actual hands on a surface in front of you - feel the temperature, the texture, the solid reality of it. Let that physical anchor lead you into the moment: your knuckles are white, your arms are shaking, your whole body is trying to hold something in. Begin with rigid control, breathing carefully, trying to stay composed. But let the physical tension in your body lead you deeper - your jaw clenches, your breath becomes ragged, something animal rises in your throat. Allow yourself to move from controlled devastation into complete physical release - whether that's collapsing, screaming, hurling something across the room, or sinking to the floor. Mix the physical sensation of your body breaking down with waves of emotion: rage, grief, terror, even moments of wild, hysterical laughter at the absurdity. End in exhaustion, in the raw, empty aftermath where you're finally still.

title: After the Fall
instruction: You've just finished a punishing physical challenge — maybe a race, a fight, a desperate climb — and you've collapsed against a wall, your body a wreck of heaving breaths and trembling limbs. You're trying to piece together what happened, but your mind is as scattered as your lungs. At first, you struggle just to get air, every word a battle against the burning in your chest. As you speak, confusion seeps in — you're replaying the moment it all went wrong, the sudden failure of your body mid-stride. By the end, your words slow, your breathing quiets just enough, and the confusion hardens into a quiet, hollow realization: you pushed too hard, and now something is broken.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Goddess of the Living Room Floor
instruction: You're a teenager, cross-legged on your bedroom floor, just after you finally finished a difficult, months-long art project you thought you'd never complete. You're holding your creation, admiring it in the late afternoon light coming through the window, and the triumph is sweet and real. Your younger brother keeps poking his head in to ask for help with his video game, and you're intensely proud of your work and deeply affectionate toward him, but the constant interruptions are starting to fray your patience. Start with a pure, breathless moment of victory, then when he disturbs you, let the irritation surface clearly, then land on a final sigh that holds both your exasperation and your love as you set your project down to go help him.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Affection (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Reading Your Best Friend's Suicide Note at Their Funeral
instruction: They left a note addressed to you specifically, and you've chosen to read parts of it aloud to the gathered mourners. Begin with your voice steady but fragile, determined to honor them. As you read their words thanking you for specific moments—small kindnesses, inside jokes—feel yourself breaking and laughing simultaneously. Your voice should crack on their humor, the personality shining through even in goodbye. Let gratitude for having known them war with rage that they're gone, that they didn't let you help. Find yourself ad-libbing between their written words, talking directly to them, your tone shifting from formal reading to intimate conversation. Laugh through tears at a memory triggered by their words, then feel the laughter twist into a sob. As you near the end, let peace and devastation occupy the same breath—they're free from pain, but you're shattered. End with their final words of love, your voice barely holding together, then one last thing you need to say to them that isn't written down: a whispered confession, a promise, or a goodbye that feels impossible to speak.
inspired_by: Explaining Quantum Physics to a Five-Year-Old While High

title: The Vault of Winter Stars
instruction: You stand alone on a frozen hilltop at midnight, wrapped in a heavy coat, your breath misting in the sharp cold. Gazing at a sky crammed with stars so clear and close they feel like a living ceiling, a vast awe swells in your chest, stealing your breath. But beneath that wonder, a familiar, bitter malice surfaces as you recall the people who dismissed your love of these cold, quiet places as a waste of a life. You speak aloud to the stars, your voice carrying affection for the darkness, malice for those who mocked you, and a trembling awe that makes you halt mid-sentence, shift your weight, or lose the thread as a shooting star steals your focus. Start with serene wonder, let the malice curdle your tone, then let the awe return, deeper and more vulnerable than before, until you fall silent.
emotions_sampled: Affection (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Wedding Toast to Your Sister Who's Marrying Your Ex-Soulmate
instruction: You're giving a toast at your younger sister's wedding—to the person you believed was your forever. Start with warmth and humor, genuine happiness for them both, your voice light and celebratory. But as you speak about their love story, something tender and broken creeps in. You share a memory that the three of you lived together, reframing it as if you were always meant to be the witness, not the participant. Your voice softens to almost a whisper as you tell your sister she deserves this happiness—and you mean it, but the words cost you everything. There's a moment where you almost lose control, a catch in your throat disguised as emotion for the occasion. You end with a blessing that's both gift and goodbye, your voice thick with unshed tears, raising your glass with a trembling hand. It's the most generous and devastating thing you've ever done.
inspired_by: Translator in Courtroom Realizes Defendant Is Her Brother's Killer

title: Crisp Bite, Sharp Reminder
instruction: You are an older woman with a soft, high-pitched voice, sitting alone at a kitchen table. You're eating a hard, crunchy apple while trying to read a letter that requires your full attention—perhaps bad news about a friend. At first, the apple's crisp sound irritates you, a small annoyance pulling you from your focus; your voice carries a thin edge of impatience as you chew. But as you bite down, a sudden, sharp pain shoots through your jaw—a nerve or a troublesome tooth. Your concentration shifts entirely to managing that pain: your voice becomes tighter, rushed, with involuntary winces and pauses for breath. You mutter a few words to yourself between crunches and swallows, trying to decide whether to stop eating or push through. By the end, the irritation is gone, replaced by a quiet, weary acknowledgment of the pain you're enduring.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Concentration (extremely present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Someone Realizing You're Crying Without Sound
instruction: You're sitting there, tears running, completely silent. Your breathing is shaky but you're not making noise. Someone notices: 'Are you okay?' Your voice comes out broken. 'I'm fine,' which is clearly a lie. Your voice is caught between hiding and needing to be seen. Say what's wrong in fragmented pieces.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Stayed Silent
instruction: You're finally telling your parent about the years they were physically present but emotionally absent during your darkest time. Begin with quiet, measured words, almost clinical: 'When I was sixteen and couldn't leave my room, you'd knock and ask if I wanted dinner. That was it.' Let anger start seeping in: 'You never asked why. You never sat with me.' Your voice rises with years of suppressed rage: 'I was drowning ten feet away from you and you acted like everything was fine!' Then break—the anger collapses into something more vulnerable and aching: 'I needed you to see me. I needed you to fight for me.' End with exhausted honesty, almost pleading: 'I don't need you to fix the past. I just need you to acknowledge that I was suffering and you looked away.' Move from controlled restraint to explosive hurt, finally landing on raw, desperate need for validation.

title: The Voicemail They'll Never Hear
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for someone you loved deeply, knowing they've blocked your number and will never listen to it. Begin in an almost businesslike whisper, trying to stay composed, explaining simply that you understand why they're gone. Let your voice gradually soften as you confess the small, specific things you miss—the way they pronounced certain words, their particular laugh, inside jokes that now have no home. Your throat tightens as you realize you're talking to silence, that this message is really for you, not them. End barely audibly, your words fragmenting as you choke on the truth that some goodbyes don't get closure, some love languages die unspoken. Let the emotion be so intimate it feels like eavesdropping on someone's private breaking.

title: Confronting the Ghost in the Mirror
instruction: You are having a searing confrontation with a version of yourself from a parallel life—the person you would have become if you'd made one crucial different choice years ago. This alternate self is not a metaphor; in this moment, imagine them as vividly real as your own reflection, but distinct: perhaps they have different scars, different eyes, a different way of standing. Begin with cold, defensive hostility, cataloging all the ways they failed or betrayed the potential you both once had. As you hurl accusations, start to hear truths in your own words that cut both ways. Let the tone shift from attack to painful recognition: you're not arguing with a stranger, but with a part of yourself you've been running from. Build in sensory detail—the exact timbre of their voice (which is almost, but not quite, yours), the tension in your chest, the electric charge in the air between you. End not with resolution, but with a moment of unbearable intimacy and mutual understanding, your anger dissolving into something more complicated: shared grief for all the lives you both didn't live.
inspired_by: When no real-life parallel exists for character circumstances

title: Setting Boundary With Family Member
instruction: Your parent/sibling is doing something that hurts. You've never pushed back before. Your voice is small but determined. 'I need you to stop...' Your voice is shaking but you're not backing down. They're angry. Your voice becomes slightly louder. 'This is not negotiable.' Your voice carries your own self-respect for the first time. They're threatening to cut you off. Your voice wavers but holds. 'Okay.' You're choosing yourself. Your voice changes after that word.

title: Touch Relearning
instruction: You're relearning touch after a long period without it—injury, illness, isolation. Your partner is gentle: 'Let me know if anything hurts.' You're almost afraid to be touched. Your voice is hesitant: 'Okay.' As they touch you, your voice becomes aware of sensation you'd almost forgotten. Your body's response comes slowly. Your voice becomes more present: 'That feels good.' You're reclaiming the ability to receive pleasure. There's grief in your voice for the time you lost. There's joy in your voice for the sensation returning. By the end, as your body remembers itself, your voice becomes less guarded, more open. Your voice should sound like someone being born back into their body.

title: Severe Dehydration in Desert
instruction: You've been lost for days without water. Your voice is barely functional—lips cracked, throat raw. Every word is an effort. Your speech is slurred, confused. You're hallucinating: talking to people who aren't there, having conversations with mirages. Your tone shifts between desperate hope and crushing despair. Include the strange numbness to pain, the dreamy quality of severe dehydration. By the end, you're barely conscious, your words becoming whispers, then silence.

title: The Last Morning Ritual
instruction: You're sharing your final morning with someone you've loved for decades—a parent, partner, or lifelong friend who will die today. Begin by going through your normal morning routine together: making coffee, buttering toast, the small gestures you've done ten thousand times. Start with the comfort of habit, the denial that pretends this is just another day. As you move through these physical actions, let the weight of 'last time' gradually break through—this is the last time you'll pour their coffee, the last time you'll hear them laugh at the same old joke. End in a place of raw presence, where the simplest gesture—holding their hand, touching their face—contains all the years you've shared and all the mornings you'll never have. Let habit transform into heartbreak, routine into sacred ritual.
inspired_by: Actor does not practice between classes and wonders why their work is not developing

title: Whispering What You Never Could Say
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, speaking truths so tender they can only be whispered in darkness. Begin with your voice barely audible, confessing something you've carried alone: a fear, a shame, a beautiful terrible secret about how much you need them. Your breathing is unsteady. Each word costs you something. You're not crying, but emotion keeps catching in your throat, forcing you to pause. You confess the ways you've failed them, the ways you're afraid you're not enough. Your whisper breaks on the words 'I'm terrified of losing you.' The vulnerability is almost unbearable. End with a moment where you risk everything—you tell them the depth of your love in the simplest, most devastating words, and then you wait in the silence, exposed and trembling.

title: The Thank-You That Almost Wasn't Said
instruction: You are a child slouched deep into the back seat of a car after a long, disappointing day. Your spine is curved, your head lolling against the window; your voice comes out mushy and lazy, jaw barely moving. You start by mumbling about how nothing went right—tired, deflated. But then you remember something small your parent did for you earlier, and a wave of gratitude swells so intensely it forces you to sit up slightly. Your voice softens but gains warmth, the words becoming more deliberate as you thank them.
