Let a little pause happen where you almost forget to speak, then let the thankfulness pour out in a slow, heartfelt confession.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Goodnight, My Almost
instruction: You're tucking in your partner for the last time before they leave tomorrow to marry someone else—an arranged marriage, a family obligation, a choice made for reasons that have nothing to do with love. Speak softly, gently, as you've done a hundred nights before. Start with tender small talk about their day, the mundane intimacy you'll never share again. Your voice is controlled, determined to make this normal, to give them one peaceful night. But as you speak, little breaks appear—a catch in your breath, a pause that lasts too long. You whisper the things you want to say but can't: 'Stay. Choose me. We could run.' But they don't come out; instead, you talk about the weather, tomorrow's plans, anything but goodbye. End with 'Sleep well,' your voice barely audible, breaking on the second word, knowing you're memorizing the sound of your own heart shattering.

title: Avenge in Silence
instruction: You are giving oral sex to a partner who has been casually belittling you all evening. Your knees ache on the hard floor, and your jaw is tired. At first, the pain and resentment simmer beneath your dutiful moans. But as you feel their body respond to your rhythm, a cold satisfaction replaces the ache. Your humming becomes slower, more deliberate, almost teasing. You know you can stop or hurt them with a slight pressure. End with a low, malevolent hum that lingers, savoring your control.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Fierce and Helpless
instruction: You're trying to protect someone you love from something you cannot control—an illness, an injustice, a choice they're making that will destroy them. Begin with fierce declaration, almost shouting: 'No. Absolutely not. I won't let this happen.' Your voice is strong, commanding, protective—you're trying to be their shield. But as you continue speaking, your certainty crumbles. The fierceness cracks, revealing the terrified helplessness underneath. Your declarations become pleas, your strength becomes begging. The anger doesn't disappear—it transforms into something more devastating: the rage of someone who would do anything, sacrifice anything, but knows it won't be enough. End collapsed, your voice breaking completely: 'Please. Please don't make me watch this.' Let the word 'please' contain both fury and surrender.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's hospice bedside at 3 AM, holding her hand. She's been unconscious for hours, but the nurse said she can still hear you. You need to tell her it's okay to let go—that you and your sister will be fine without her. Start with small talk, the kind you've always hidden behind: updates about the garden, the weather, anything safe. But as you speak, something breaks open inside you. Your voice softens, cracks. You confess the truth you've never said: that you're terrified, that you're not ready, that you don't know how to be in the world without her. Then, through tears, you give her the permission she's been waiting for. Your tone shifts from desperate clinging to a kind of devastated, tender release. Let us hear you find the strength to say goodbye even as your heart shatters.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospice bed, knowing this is your final goodbye, but you don't want them to know you're dying. Begin with forced cheerfulness, asking about their day, the garden, the neighbors—anything normal. As the conversation continues, your voice weakens despite your efforts, and the façade starts crumbling. You want to tell them you love them, that you forgive everything, but you're terrified of breaking their heart. End with a whispered confession that you won't be calling tomorrow, your voice catching as you try to make peace with a lifetime in thirty seconds. Let the transition from bright pretense to devastating honesty unfold naturally, your breath becoming more labored, your control slipping away.
inspired_by: Suppressing Annoyance While Dealing With a Difficult Person

title: The Last Morning
instruction: You're sitting beside your partner's hospital bed at dawn, holding their hand. They're leaving for an experimental treatment overseas—a one-way journey with no guarantees. You begin trying to be brave, voice steady, saying 'You're going to be fine.' But as you watch them memorize your face, something cracks. Your words fracture mid-sentence. You shift from forced optimism to raw terror: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' Then their fingers squeeze yours, and you find yourself whispering promises you're not sure you can keep, your voice breaking between hope and devastation. End with a paradox: you're simultaneously letting them go and holding on tighter than ever, your final words carrying both goodbye and refusal to say it.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-partner's wedding—the person who shattered you is marrying someone else, and you're genuinely happy for them while simultaneously reliving every moment of your own grief. Begin with warm gratitude and authentic joy in your voice, celebrating their happiness with real love, no bitterness. But underneath, there's the exhaustion of healing, the ghost of the pain you endured, and as you speak, these layers begin to show—a catch in your throat when you mention their smile, a pause when you talk about love. Your voice should dance between laughter and tears, genuine celebration and profound loss, finding strange peace in the contradiction. Let your final words be a blessing that breaks you open—finding beauty in your own heartbreak because it led them to this happiness, laughing softly through tears, your voice exhausted but somehow free, grateful and devastated in the same breath.
inspired_by: Concealing Fatigue During a Long Presentation

title: Nightly Ritual of Triumph
instruction: You're an older woman brushing your teeth late at night, utterly exhausted but glowing with pride after finally standing your ground with your adult child about your boundaries. The foam fills your mouth, and each brush stroke feels like a small, slightly sensual reward. Talk to your reflection, voice garbled by the toothbrush and saliva. Start heavy-lidded and tired, but let your words grow firmer as you recount your victory. End with a proud, muffled 'I did it' around the brush, a hint of ecstasy in the exhale.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Pride (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Upside-Down Truth
instruction: You are lying on your back on a couch, head hanging over the armrest, throat stretched tight. You've had too much to drink—the ceiling blurs, and you feel a thick, slurred contempt for a colleague who just walked out. But as you mutter to yourself, doubt starts to worm in: maybe they were right? Your voice strains, thins, and you lose your train of thought, swallowing loudly. Start with sneering disdain, then let the intoxication pull you into hesitant uncertainty by the end. Speak aloud to no one but yourself.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present), Contempt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Shattered Vows
instruction: You've just discovered a betrayal that ends your relationship—infidelity, a hidden life, a fundamental lie. Begin with explosive rage, your voice loud and jagged, articulation breaking apart with fury. 'How could you—' But you can't even finish sentences. The anger is so big it fractures your speech. Your voice cracks between shouting and gasping. Then suddenly, the rage collapses into something more devastating: grief. Your voice drops, becomes almost childlike. 'I trusted you with everything.' Now you're not attacking—you're showing them the wound. Your articulation becomes painfully clear on certain phrases, as if precision could somehow make them understand the damage. By the end, your voice is exhausted, quiet, speaking truths you're discovering in real-time: 'I don't even know who I was with all these years.' The intensity hasn't lessened—it's just transformed into a different kind of pain, one that settles into your bones.

title: Don't You Dare Walk Away From Me
instruction: Your child—now an adult—is about to walk out of your life forever. They're at the door. You've failed them in ways you can't take back. Start with explosive desperation. Your voice is loud, commanding, almost violent in its intensity: 'I am still your parent!' You're trying to use authority, anger, anything to make them stay. But as they remain unmoved, your voice begins to disintegrate. The shouting cracks. You move from fury to pleading, from demands to begging. Your voice becomes ragged, pathetic even. End with you on your knees—vocally and emotionally—whispering: 'Please. I'm sorry. Please don't go.' Let your voice show the complete collapse of pride, the helplessness of loving someone you've lost the right to keep.
inspired_by: The Words You Can't Take Back

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Your Former Self
instruction: You're cleaning out your old apartment, finding remnants of who you used to be, and you're struck by the absurdity of it all. Begin with a laugh—genuinely amused: 'Oh my god, I really thought this mattered. I really thought...' The laughter continues but something bittersweet enters: 'Look at all these perfect things I collected. This perfect life I built that nearly killed me.' You're smiling and your voice is cracking: 'I was so convinced I had it all figured out.' The emotions tangle—gratitude, grief, relief, loss all at once: 'Thank you for trying so hard. Thank you for surviving it.' You're crying now but still half-laughing at the contradiction: 'I'm mourning someone who never really existed and celebrating being free of them.' Your voice becomes wonder-struck and heartbroken simultaneously: 'All that time. All that energy. All that fear.' By the end, you've found something like peace in the chaos: 'Goodbye, my beautiful disaster. I'm sorry. I love you. I'm finally letting you rest.' The last words are tender, grateful, and absolutely exhausted—the sound of someone who's finally, finally done pretending.

title: The Glass You Throw Against the Wall
instruction: You're describing the perfect glass of lemon water—cold, tart, refreshing—but you're seething. Someone you loved betrayed you, and they're trying to make small talk about the weather, the drinks, anything but what they did. Start with false calm, your voice almost pleasant as you describe the water, but there's an edge. Let your rage build as you keep describing these perfect, meaningless details, your voice getting louder, more jagged. Suddenly explode—you're screaming about the water, but you're really screaming about trust, about lies, about how they smiled at you while destroying everything. Then break completely. The rage collapses into sobs. Your voice drops to almost nothing as you admit you still love them, you hate that you still love them, and that's what makes this unbearable. End in shattered helplessness, because fury was easier than this grief.
inspired_by: Sipping a Cold, Refreshing Glass of Lemon Water

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed in the middle of the night. You're leaving—maybe ending your marriage, maybe entering rehab, maybe you've lost custody and this is your last night in the house. Whisper everything you need them to know, keeping your voice so quiet you won't wake them, which forces all your emotion into breath and breaks and pauses. Start with simple observations ('Your hair is getting so long...') that give way to confessions ('I'm so sorry I've been...') and promises ('When you're older, I hope you'll understand...'). Your voice should be thick with tears you're trying to swallow, catching on words, nearly silent at times. The intimacy is unbearable. End with something you can barely say at all, perhaps just touching their hair, unable to form words anymore.

title: Laughing at the Funeral: Finding Joy in the Wreckage of Grief
instruction: You're remembering someone you've lost, and a specific memory hits you—something absurd they did, something perfectly them—and you start to laugh. Really laugh. Your voice is bright with genuine joy, almost surprised by it: 'Oh god, remember when they...' You're recounting the story, your laughter building, infectious, real. But even as you're laughing, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice starts to catch between the laughter and the sobs. You keep trying to finish the story, but you can't tell if you're laughing or crying anymore—it's both, completely intertwined. 'They were so ridiculous, so absolutely...' Your voice breaks with love and loss simultaneously. By the end, you're saying 'thank you' through tears and laughter: 'Thank you for being exactly who you were.' Your voice carries this impossible, beautiful contradiction—profound gratitude for having known them and devastating grief that they're gone. The laughter and the sobbing become the same sound, the same expression of a heart that's both full and shattered. You're broken and whole at the same time, and your voice contains all of it.
inspired_by: Kindness Showing Ripple Effects: Realizing Impact You Didn't Know

title: The High Note, the Last Time
instruction: You are a young woman standing in the middle of an empty concert hall, alone, after the last rehearsal. You've just sung a note you've been chasing for months—it rang clear, full, effortless. Now you're still, breathing in the silence, your voice open and unforced. Start with a breathy, disbelieving laugh as you feel the relief wash over you, then speak to no one, your voice carrying in the cavernous space. Let your words start eager and bright, then soften as a quiet, surprised gratitude settles in—this is the first time your voice has felt like a true home. Don't hold back the tiny wobble or the pause as you realize this moment is already fading.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Collision Course
instruction: You're mission control operator watching your spouse—the astronaut—pilot toward certain death to manually redirect debris that will otherwise destroy a populated space station. They volunteered without telling you. Start with professional protocol that quickly explodes into raw fury—how dare they make this choice, how dare they leave you and your life together behind. Your voice should crack between shouting and breaking, between demanding they abort and begging them not to go. Let rage give way to desperate bargaining, then to helpless anguish. Midway through, they tell you they're doing this so you can keep living in a world that's safe, and your anger shatters into something more devastating: the realization that you understand, that you'd do the same, that love sometimes means letting go. End in fierce, protective tenderness mixed with absolute helplessness—telling them they're brave, you're proud, you'll carry them forever, your voice strong and broken at once.

title: Laughing Through Tears as You Scatter Your Sister's Ashes
instruction: You're standing where she wanted to be scattered—maybe a beach, maybe a mountain, maybe somewhere ridiculous she chose specifically to make you laugh. As you open the urn, you start telling her about the absurdity of this moment: 'You'd think this was hilarious.' Your voice is light, almost playful, but your face is wet. You're crying and laughing at the same time—remembering her terrible jokes, the time she did that stupid thing, how she always knew how to make everything less heavy. Your voice breaks between laughter and sobs: 'God, I miss you so much.' Keep the tone conversational, like she's right there. Thank her—for being exactly who she was, for teaching you not to take anything too seriously, for loving you. As you release the ashes, your voice is full of gratitude even as your heart is breaking: 'Okay, weirdo. Go be free.' You're smiling through tears. It's grief and joy and love all tangled together, and it's perfect because she would have wanted exactly this.
inspired_by: Telling Your Partner Your Sexual Needs Aren't Met

title: The Last Cup of Tea
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's asked you to describe, in vivid sensory detail, the cup of tea you're holding—the one she can no longer taste herself. Begin with quiet acceptance of what's coming, methodically describing every sensation: the warmth radiating through the ceramic into your palms, the particular amber color catching the afternoon light, the bergamot scent rising in wisps of steam, the way the liquid moves when you tilt the cup. As you describe each detail—the taste on different parts of your tongue, the slight clink against your teeth, the heat traveling down your throat—let the overwhelming reality sink in that she will never experience these simple pleasures again. Your voice should start steady, almost clinical in its attention to detail, but gradually fracture as the full weight of loss floods through you, transforming your careful description into a devastated farewell to all the ordinary moments you've shared.

title: Final Words to a Sleeping Child
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's hospital bed, knowing these are your last hours together. Begin with trying to be strong—telling them about tomorrow's plans, voice steady but tight. As you continue, let the pretense crack. Your words become more urgent, more honest: all the things you need them to know, apologies for moments you weren't perfect, promises about who will care for them. Let your voice break into whispered fragments of memories—their first laugh, a morning you shared, the way they said your name. Transform from controlled parent to raw, desperate human. End in wordless sounds—humming their favorite lullaby through tears, then falling into silence as you simply breathe with them, trying to memorize the sound.

title: Emergency Room Eruption: Surgeon Breaks Protocol to Save the Person Who Destroyed Their Family
instruction: The drunk driver who killed your child is dying on your operating table. You're the only surgeon available. Start with cold, clinical precision—you took an oath, you will do your job. Your voice is ice, every word controlled. But as you work, something ruptures. You're yelling at your team with savage intensity, demanding they save this person you want to let die. Your hands are saving them while your voice screams with rage at the injustice, at yourself, at God. The fury breaks into gasping sobs mid-sentence, then surges back to fierce commands. You're fighting for their life with everything you have while part of you howls at the cruelty of it. Your voice becomes a battlefield between your professional duty and your shattered parent-heart. End in exhausted whispers over their stabilized body, your voice thick with the terrible knowledge that you've saved them, that you're somehow both destroyed and more human for it. Let your breath shake with the weight of contradictory truths.
inspired_by: Professional: Doctor Prescribes Addiction to Save Addict's Life

title: The Weight of Gratitude
instruction: You're slumped at a kitchen table after a long day, your head propped heavily on one hand, cheek smushed against your palm. Across from you sits someone you're deeply grateful for — and intensely attracted to. Start with a tired, distracted murmur, your voice slightly muffled and clumsy on 'p' and 'b' sounds. As you speak, let the gratitude warm your tone, then feel your words slow as a wave of desire catches you off guard — your breath hitches, your eyes drift, and you trail off, lost in the sight of them. Let the physical awkwardness of your posture bleed into the performance: shift your weight, pause to swallow, let the sentence stumble as your focus wavers.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about decades of emotional neglect, and you've discovered they're about to become intimate with a new partner—something that triggers your deepest wound. Start with bitter, cutting sarcasm: 'Oh, you can ask for consent now? You can check in with someone's feelings?' Let your voice shake with rage as you reveal how they never asked what YOU needed, never checked if you were okay. Your anger should be volcanic but specific—'Did you ever once ask if I wanted to talk about mom leaving? Did you ever ask if I was scared?'—building to a breaking point where your fury collapses into raw, childlike pain. End with a whispered, devastating question: 'Can you at least tell me now—do you even want to know me?' The arc moves from sarcastic rage to explosive pain to fragile, exposed longing.

title: The Adventurer and the Sphinx
instruction: Depict an adventurer with a confident, adventurous voice facing a sphinx who speaks in a slow, enigmatic tone. The sphinx poses a riddle. Switch between the adventurers attempts to solve it and the sphinxs cryptic hints, creating suspense.

title: The Imaginary Friend
instruction: You are a little girl, maybe seven, sitting cross-legged on your bedroom floor. Your mother just walked in and asked who you were whispering to. You pretend to be playing alone, but really you're talking to a secret friend—a person you've invented who makes your tummy flutter with a strange, exciting feeling. Start by trying to sound casual and innocent, but your voice lifts nervously and you over-explain that you were just singing to your doll. As you go on, the memory of that exciting flutter makes you smile genuinely, and your voice softens with real affection for the lie you're protecting. Let your attention drift to the doll, then back to your mother—your breathing changes, a tiny giggle escapes, and by the end you're not just deceiving her, you're basking in the warmth of your secret world.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Ache and Envy
instruction: You're at a brunch with friends, seated across from a woman who just got promoted—she's glowing, laughing, effortlessly charming. Your tooth has throbbed for days, and now every word you speak requires careful, one-sided chewing of syllables; you can't fully open your mouth, and cold air from the iced tea makes you wince. Start with a bright, interested tone as you ask about her new role—your envy flickers behind a smile, but you lean in, genuinely curious. Halfway through your sentence, a sharp pulse of pain steals your breath; your voice thins, you trail off, and you press a finger to your jaw. End in a whisper of helplessness—you're no longer trying to hide it, just surviving the moment.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Interest (clearly present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Apology Acceptance
instruction: Someone is offering a genuine apology, and the other person is accepting or struggling to accept it. The apologizer's voice is humble, taking responsibility. The listener's voice is wounded. The apology includes specific acknowledgment of what was wrong—it's not a generic 'sorry.' The listener wavers between holding onto hurt and accepting forgiveness. Their voice shows this battle. The apologizer waits, respecting that forgiveness isn't automatic. The listener eventually speaks, and their voice carries both the pain they're releasing and the acceptance. By the end, something is healed. Not erased, but healed. Both voices sound lighter.

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's 3am and you're lying next to someone you love, confessing something that's been eating you alive. Your voice is barely above a whisper, not wanting to wake them but needing to say it out loud. Start with your breathing - uneven, anxious, trying to find the courage. 'I need to tell you something and I'm terrified.' The words come slowly at first, catching in your throat. As you confess (an infidelity, a terminal diagnosis, a secret you've kept for years), your voice wavers between urgency and tenderness. You're watching them sleep, loving them so much it physically hurts. By the end, you're crying silently, words dissolving into breath, knowing everything changes tomorrow but right now, in this moment, you can still pretend everything's okay.

title: The Impossible Choice
instruction: You're screaming at someone you love because they've made a choice that will destroy them, and you're powerless to stop it. Begin with your voice fierce, almost violent in its intensity: 'You can't do this!' Your rage is pure protectiveness, every word desperate. But as they calmly explain why they have to do this thing - leave, sacrifice themselves, walk into danger - your voice begins to fracture. The screaming becomes pleading: 'Please, I'm begging you.' When they tell you they need you to let them go, your fierce protectiveness collides with helplessness. Your voice breaks completely, oscillating between fury and sobbing: 'I can't - I can't just watch you -' Your words fragment. You're gasping, crying, still trying to command them to stay even as you realize you have no power here. End with your voice raw, utterly destroyed, whispering: 'Then promise me you'll come back.' The final words should sound like someone whose entire being is splitting apart, rage and love and terror so tangled they're indistinguishable.

title: The Kitchen Truth
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up, finally saying what you've never said. Begin by feeling the physical sensations in your body—the tightness in your chest, the heat rising in your face, the ground beneath your feet. Notice everything: the familiar smell of this room, the light, his posture, the sound of the refrigerator humming. Start speaking from a place of controlled anger, measured words, trying to stay composed and reasonable. As you continue, let yourself feel the weight and texture of each word you speak, the physical sensation of your voice in your throat. Allow the involvement with what you're actually saying—the truth you're finally telling—to dissolve your control until you move from cold, careful accusation to something more vulnerable: the hurt child beneath the angry adult, perhaps ending in tears or exhausted tenderness.
inspired_by: Actor feels tension or self-consciousness before or during a scene

title: Packing Your Child's Room
instruction: Your adult child has just received their dream job across the country and is moving permanently in three days. You are in their childhood bedroom, helping them pack, but they've stepped out. Begin with determined cheerfulness - you're so proud, this is wonderful news. Build the sensory world: the faded posters on walls, the stuffed animal on the shelf, the particular smell of this room, dust motes in afternoon light. As you pack each item, create vivid sense memories attached to it - their first day of school, nights you sat on this bed during their nightmares, the sound of their teenage laughter echoing from these walls. Let pride and devastating loss coexist and war within you. By the end, holding something small and meaningful, let yourself break - but the emotion should be complicated, mixed: grief at losing daily proximity to them, fierce joy at their success, resentment that they can leave so easily, gratitude for having had them at all, fear of the empty house, love so intense it physically hurts.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Walter Mitty Option — Scene 1 Fantasy Imaging Exercise

title: Taking Off Your Shoes After a Long Day
instruction: Kick off your shoes, feeling the cool air touch your feet. Describe the immediate relief as each foot stretches out, the sensation of being free and light. Speak with a quiet sigh of contentment, as if each step afterward feels softer and easier, your whole body relaxing with this simple freedom.

title: The Inheritance They Never Wanted
instruction: You're the older sibling confronting your younger brother or sister the day after your parent's funeral. Start with that familiar condescending tone - telling them how to handle the estate, how to grieve properly, what Mom or Dad would have wanted. But they finally snap back, and in their pain and rage, they reveal a truth: that your 'protection' was actually control, that they felt suffocated, that they moved across the country to escape you. Let this gut-punch land. Your defensive anger should crack open to reveal the terrified older child you once were, desperately trying to hold a family together, terrified of being abandoned. Move from patronizing authority to broken confession: you only knew how to love them by trying to shield them from everything, even joy. End with you asking, voice stripped bare, if there's any way to learn to love them differently.

title: The Kitchen at 2 AM
instruction: You've come downstairs to confront your parent about a secret you discovered that changes everything you thought you knew about your family. Start coiled tight, arms crossed, voice sharp and accusatory - breathing shallowly through your nose. As you speak, something shifts. Your body begins to unlock. Your shoulders drop. Your jaw releases. The anger doesn't disappear but transforms into something more complex - grief for the person you thought they were, understanding of the impossible position they were in. Let your breath deepen and slow. By the end, you're speaking from a completely different place in your body - lower, fuller, more grounded. The confrontation becomes a kind of mourning. Your final words should sound like they come from someone years older than who started speaking.

title: Fighting for a Goodbye
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl, caught in a physical struggle with your father as he tries to drag you away from your first love. You've never fought back before, but now you're clawing, pushing, gasping for air. Each word is punched out between grunts and sobs, your body twisting, your voice cracking with effort. Begin with determined defiance, a fierce pride that you're finally standing up, but end with a raw, breathless plea as you realize you might lose him. Let your voice break, let the struggle show — jagged breaths, sudden silences, the sound of fabric tearing or feet scuffling. Your final words should ache with longing, a desperate whisper right before you're pulled away.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Weight of Each Step
instruction: You're a young woman hiking a steep trail alone, your lungs burning, legs trembling. You feel emotionally numb—like you're just going through the motions, avoiding something painful. As you stop to catch your breath, a memory of a recent loss surfaces, unbidden. You start speaking to yourself, your voice flat and detached between heavy gasps, but as you keep climbing, the numbness cracks. A flicker of sorrow or relief breaks through, and your voice wavers, becoming smaller, more raw. Let the physical labor shape your rhythm—short phrases, pauses, real breaths—and let the change happen organically, as if the view or the exhaustion forces the feeling out.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Bent Nails and Broken Words
instruction: You're in your garage late at night, a half-empty bottle of whiskey on the workbench. You're trying to fix a wobbly shelf, but your hands are clumsy from drink. Each time you swing the hammer—too hard—the nail bends. You curse under your breath, but the slur in your voice betrays you. Start with a gruff, impatient mutter about the job, but as the tool clangs and the shelf creaks, let the frustration leak into something heavier—a quiet admission that you're not fixing the shelf at all, just numbing yourself. End with a soft, slurred sigh you barely mean to say out loud.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Acting Interested in a Gift Youre Receiving
instruction: Youre being given something you dont particularly like. Internally, youre underwhelmed, but you express gratitude. Describe your disappointment while showing appreciation. Speak with enthusiasm, masking your true feelings.

title: The Last Lullaby
instruction: You're singing a lullaby to your dying child in the hospital, late at night when no one else is there. You start with a fragile, trembling voice, trying to be strong, trying to sound like the parent who has it together. The melody keeps breaking as grief catches in your throat. Halfway through, you realize this might be the last time, and your voice cracks completely—you can't hide anymore. You start over, but now it's rawer, stripped of any pretense of strength. You're just a parent holding on by a thread. By the end, you're still singing through quiet sobs, but there's also a devastating tenderness, a fierce love that makes the brokenness beautiful. Let your voice fail. Let it be imperfect. That's where the love lives.

title: Screaming Truth at Your Lover in a Hospital Corridor
instruction: You're in a harsh-lit hospital hallway, your partner of ten years unconscious after a suicide attempt you didn't see coming. You're addressing the empty air, the closed door, God, whoever will listen. Start fierce, almost violent in your emotion: 'How dare you leave me like this? How dare you decide for both of us?' Your voice should be loud, raw, echoing off sterile walls. But then let rage shatter into terror—your volume dropping as you realize you might actually lose them. The shift should be abrupt: from shouting to gasping, from anger to desperate bargaining. 'I'll do anything, I'll be better, just come back.' End on your knees against the wall, voice hoarse and broken, admitting the truth you've hidden even from yourself: 'I can't do this without you, and I'm so angry at you for making me need you this much.' Mix fury and love so thoroughly they become indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Confessing Love While Stitching Your Lover's Wound

title: The Whispered Unraveling
instruction: You're confessing a secret to your sleeping lover at 3 AM—something that could change everything between you. Begin kneeling beside the bed, whispering with exquisite clarity and precision, each word shaped perfectly in the darkness. Your hands hover near but don't touch them. As your confession deepens, slowly rise, your whispers becoming more physically embodied—your gestures growing slightly larger, your movements more deliberate, as if carving the truth into the air. Even in restraint, every part of your body participates in the telling. By the end, you're standing, still speaking in intimate tones but with full-bodied commitment, your physical presence filling the space around the bed. The vulnerability transforms into quiet, embodied courage—tender but no longer apologetic.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging father in his hospital room about a lifetime of emotional absence. Start with false brightness—'I brought your favorite magazines'—the dutiful child voice you've perfected. But something in his frail appearance ignites decades of rage. Your voice hardens. 'Do you even know my children's names?' The anger builds, then fractures into something raw and pleading. You're suddenly eight years old again, begging for attention. Fury dissolves into grief, then resurfaces as bitter laughter at the absurdity of still wanting his love. End in whispered devastation: 'I needed you.' Let your voice show the war between wanting to punish him and desperately wanting him to finally see you before it's too late.

title: Weight of Contempt
instruction: You are an older man trapped under a collapsed beam in a barn. Your son stands nearby, unable to move it. Every word is forced out against the pressure on your chest—short, sharp syllables squeezed from a tight throat. Start with pure contempt, sneering at his helplessness, each breath a struggle. As you realize this may be your last moment, let the contempt dissolve into a bitter, weary acceptance—still harsh, but laced with dark humor about your own stubborn pride. Your voice should break, stutter, and catch, as if the weight is stealing your air mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Mother Who Couldn't Save Them
instruction: You're holding your child who's been hurt, and you explode with protective rage at whoever did this - your voice is a roar, almost feral, promising violence. But mid-fury, you look down and see their fear of YOUR intensity. Your voice fractures completely. The rage collapses into helpless weeping because you realize you can't fix this, can't undo it, can't protect them from everything. You're trying to soothe them while you're falling apart, voice breaking on every word: 'I'm here, I'm here, I've got you' - but you're the one who needs holding. The journey is from fierce protective fury to devastating acknowledgment of your own powerlessness as a parent.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother in her kitchen, and you've finally found the courage to confront her about something she's never acknowledged: how she looked away when you needed protection as a child. Start with trembling restraint: 'Mom, I need you to hear something.' Your voice is controlled but fragile. As you speak the truth—'You knew. You knew and you did nothing'—watch your control begin to crack. She may defend herself, deny it, minimize it. Your voice rises, raw and primal: 'I was a child! I needed you!' But then something shifts. You see her face, the complexity of her own survival, her own fear. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it makes room for something else—a terrible recognition of her humanity alongside your own pain. End with your voice quiet, almost gentle despite the devastation: 'I needed a mother. And you needed someone too. And we both lost.'

title: The Unraveling Vigil
instruction: You are a young woman who has been awake for over two days, sitting in a dim apartment, waiting for someone who betrayed you. You are trying to rehearse the angry speech you will deliver, but your mind keeps slipping. Start with a burst of sharp, rehearsed anger, but let the exhaustion crack through—your sentences lose direction, you pause as if seeing something move in the corner, you argue with an empty chair. By the end, your voice drops into a hollow, broken admission that you just want to lie down, and the anger drains into a quiet, surreal fatigue.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Wrapping Yourself in a Towel After a Shower
instruction: Wrap a warm, fluffy towel around yourself, feeling its cozy weight. Describe the soft fabric pressing gently against your skin, absorbing every last drop of water, wrapping you in warmth and softness. Speak with a tone of contentment and relaxation, as if each moment in the towel is like a gentle hug, comforting you completely as the warmth settles over you.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he never told you he was proud of you—not once in thirty years. Start with controlled anger, the kind that's been rehearsed in your head for months. But as you speak, let yourself stumble into the real questions underneath: did he even see you? Do you even know who he is? Allow your certainty to crack as you realize mid-confrontation that you might be talking to someone who simply doesn't have the language you need from him. Your voice should shift from accusation to something more raw—a child's confusion in an adult's body. End not with resolution but with the devastating recognition that you may need to grieve the father you wanted rather than change the one you have. Let anger give way to unexpected sorrow and, perhaps, the first seed of reluctant acceptance.
inspired_by: An actor is avoiding daily practice due to tedium or lack of immediate reward

title: The Unforgivable Kneel
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy forced to kneel before your father after a fight. Your voice is deep but strained, bitter resentment burning in your chest. You want to apologize but every word tastes like poison. Start with your jaw tight, voice clenched with anger, then slowly let the bitterness crack into something raw—a choked confession that you 'hate this' before admitting you were wrong. Your knees ache, you shift your weight, your eyes avoid his. Let the bitterness soften into reluctant truth.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother in her kitchen, the same kitchen where you spent your childhood watching her move through her routines. There's a specific song that always played on the radio during those mornings—you can hear it now, faintly, as if it's always playing somewhere in your memory. Start from a place of controlled anger, determined to finally speak truths that have been buried for years. As you talk, that persistent melody from your past keeps surfacing, bringing with it the complexity of your love for her tangled with your rage. The song won't let you stay purely angry—it reminds you of her hands, her voice, the moments she was tender. By the end, your confrontation has evolved into something more complicated: you're still holding her accountable, but the music of your shared history has cracked open your heart in ways you didn't intend.

title: The Weight of the Earth
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, gruff voice, lying face-down on a grassy hillside after a long day of manual labor. Your chest is pressed against the cool ground, making every breath a deliberate effort. You start by muttering about your aching joints and the soreness in your back, your voice muffled and raspy from the strain. As you feel the solid ground beneath you, you pause, noticing the scent of soil and the warmth of the late sun on your neck. Your tone softens, and you speak slowly, almost reverently, expressing a profound gratitude for this simple moment of rest and the earth that supports you—even as your voice remains low and rough from the physical weight.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You are standing in pouring rain, screaming at the sky, at God, at the universe, at whoever took them from you. Someone you loved died suddenly—an accident, a violence, a cruel randomness—and you never got to say goodbye. Your body is drenched, shaking with cold and rage. Begin with guttural, physical anger—your voice raw, your words accusations. 'How dare you! You had no right!' Let your fury be animalistic, mixed with the physical sensation of rain hammering your skin, your clothes heavy and cold. Pound your fists against your chest, your thighs, the ground. But as your body exhausts itself, as the rain continues its relentless fall, let the rage crack open into something else. Your screams become sobs. Your accusations become pleading: 'Please, bring them back, please.' End on your knees in the mud, rain mixing with tears, your voice hoarse and broken, whispering their name over and over—the anger burned away, leaving only the unbearable ache of absence and love.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago. Begin controlled, almost cold: 'So. You wanted to talk.' But as they try to explain, something ignites in you. Your voice rises: 'You don't get to just... what, apologize? Make this okay?' The anger builds - righteous, scalding - as you list every birthday missed, every school play, every night you cried yourself to sleep. But then they say something - maybe they were afraid, maybe they were broken - and your fury cracks. Suddenly you're not shouting anymore. Your voice drops to something raw and wounded: 'I needed you. I was just a kid and I needed you.' The rage dissolves into the grief underneath it, and by the end, you're asking the question you've been terrified to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay?' It's no longer about anger. It's about the wound that never healed.

title: First Time Surrender
instruction: You are a teenage girl experiencing your first time being fully receptive with a partner you deeply trust. You begin with a mix of vulnerability and nervousness, your voice shaky and hesitant as you whisper reassurances. As intimacy deepens, your words dissolve into breathless gasps and involuntary cries, your voice cracking into a higher register. By the end, a quiet, tearful elation breaks through as you whisper a fragmented 'thank you,' your breathing uneven and your body trembling.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Morning Run Contempt
instruction: You are an older man on your daily morning jog, breathing hard, steps pounding the pavement. As you round a corner, you see a young man toss a coffee cup onto the grass instead of a nearby bin. A surge of contempt rises in you—you mutter under your breath, each word punched out in rhythm with your footfalls, voice shaking with effort. But as you run past him, your anger softens into a weary understanding that he won't change, and your final muttered words carry a tired, resigned weight. Let your voice be breathy, jolting, and strained—speak through gasps, with the cadence of your steps cutting off syllables. Start with sharp, dismissive disdain, then end with a quieter, more reflective exhale.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Protecting Someone You Cannot Save
instruction: Someone you love is making the same mistake that destroyed you, and you're watching it happen in real time. Start with fierce urgency, almost aggressive: 'Stop. Just stop and listen to me.' Your voice is commanding, protective—you will not let this happen. But as they resist, your intensity fractures into desperation. You're pleading now, voice raw and ragged, dragging up your own trauma to make them understand: 'This is what it did to me, do you hear me?' Then comes the helpless rage—you're shouting and crying simultaneously because you cannot save them from themselves. Your voice breaks completely: 'I can't watch this again, I can't...' End in defeated, trembling quiet, the realization settling in your voice that love is not enough to protect someone from their own choices.
inspired_by: Recognizing Abuse Pattern Repeating in New Relationship

title: The Fine Print Victory
instruction: You are a woman at a government benefits office, reading aloud a final approval notice to your young daughter, who sits beside you. You start in a rapid, flat, bureaucratic monotone—this is just a legal formality, a wall of text you must get through to finish the process. As you read, you begin to notice the confirming phrases: 'entitled to receive,' 'retroactive payment,' 'no further review needed.' Your voice shifts—you slow down, your tone warms, you pause to meet your daughter's eyes. By the end, a quiet, weary triumph breaks through: you have won this battle against the system, and your daughter is safe. Let your voice reflect the small, real physical details: the flicker of the fluorescent light, the paper crinkle in your hand, the child's hand in yours.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen confronting your parent about something they did when you were seven years old—something you've never spoken about, something you buried and pretended didn't matter. Begin with adult anger, trying to be articulate and controlled. But as you speak, you start slipping backward: your voice gets smaller, your words simpler, your grievance more immediate and child-raw. The sophisticated argument crumbles into 'Why didn't you...?' and 'I needed you to...' and 'I was just a kid.' By the end, you're not a grown person holding someone accountable—you're a bewildered child who never got an answer. Let the angry adult dissolve into the confused, hurt seven-year-old. Your physical stance may even change—perhaps you end up sitting on the floor.

title: The Face I Used to Love
instruction: You're looking at a photograph of your former partner, speaking to them though they're not there. Your voice is barely above a whisper. Start by describing their face with the kind of intimacy that only comes from having loved someone deeply—you know every detail, every expression. But as you speak, something shifts: you realize you're describing a person who no longer exists, or maybe never existed the way you thought. Your tenderness becomes tinged with grief, not for the loss of them, but for the loss of who you were when you loved them. The sadness isn't loud—it's the kind that sits in your chest and makes your throat tight. End with a soft goodbye to both of them and your former self.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed at 3 AM, about to leave them—whether because you're terminally ill, entering witness protection, or fleeing domestic violence, the reason doesn't matter. What matters is this is the last time you'll see their face. You begin whispering the things you want them to remember, your voice tender and breaking: 'You are so loved.' Touch their hair gently as you speak. Your voice catches on memories—their first word, their laughter, the way they look at you with complete trust. The devastation builds quietly until you can barely breathe through the tears, but you keep your voice to a whisper because you can't wake them. End by saying 'I'm so sorry' with a love so fierce and a grief so complete that the words are almost inaudible.

title: The Confession Your Mother Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging mother about the emotional neglect you experienced as a child—how you learned to hide your fears because she was always 'too busy' or 'too stressed' to see you. Start with careful, measured words, trying to be fair and adult about it, almost apologetic for bringing it up. But as you speak, decades of suppressed pain begin surfacing—the times you were terrified and alone, the moments you needed her and she wasn't there. Your voice should move from tentative and reasonable to raw and accusatory, then crack into something more vulnerable: the scared child still inside you, desperate to be seen. End not with anger but with a devastating question: 'Did you ever notice I was scared?' Let the anger be real, but let it transform into the deeper wound beneath it.
inspired_by: Hiding Fear While Leading Others Through Danger

title: Professional: Activist Must Compromise Their Principles to Save Vulnerable People
instruction: Making an alliance you thought you never would. Your activist voice has been uncompromising. But now people are dying and the only way to help is to partner with someone whose values you oppose. Your voice is negotiation and self-betrayal simultaneously. Your breathing becomes the breathing of someone amputating their own integrity for immediate survival. Your voice continues advocating while you're simultaneously dying inside. You're buying lives with your principles. Your voice becomes someone learning that purity is a luxury the vulnerable cannot afford.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your mother's bedside in her final hours. She has always been stoic, controlling, holding everyone at arm's length—and you've spent your life tense and braced against her disapproval. But now she's asking you to come close, to hold her hand. Begin locked in your habitual guardedness, shoulders tight, breath shallow, keeping emotional distance even now. As she whispers that she's sorry, that she was afraid to love you the way she wanted to, feel something begin to unlock in your chest, your throat. Let your breath deepen. Allow your body to soften, to release decades of bracing. By the end, you are fully present, your forehead against hers, breathing together, all tension dissolved into this final moment of true connection. The physical release IS the emotional release.
inspired_by: Actor experiences chronic physical tension before or during acting obligations (auditions, rehearsals, performances)

title: The House You Built
instruction: You're standing in the home you shared with your partner, signing the final papers of your divorce. Begin with bitter efficiency—your voice is business-like, defensive. 'This is just logistics. We're doing the mature thing.' But as you look around the room, you start noticing details: the wall you painted together, the spot where you danced at your housewarming, a scratch on the floor from moving in your grandmother's chair. Your voice softens involuntarily. Grief begins mixing with gratitude—'We were so happy here, weren't we?' Let anger and love coexist: you're furious this is ending AND heartbroken AND grateful it happened AND relieved it's over. All of it, simultaneously. Your voice should shift between tones—bitter laugh, tender memory, angry resignation, grateful whisper. End with a complex acceptance that holds all these feelings at once: 'Goodbye to who we were.'

title: The Last Phone Call
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love who is dying in a hospital far away. You know this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Begin by trying to sound strong and encouraging, telling them about your day, a memory you share, or plans you pretend you'll make together. But as you speak, let your own terror and grief break through—pause mid-sentence to admit what you're really feeling, even if it contradicts what you just said. If you say 'Everything's going to be fine,' stop and confess 'I'm so scared.' Then return to comforting them, carrying that fear into your next words. Move between what you think you should say and what's actually screaming inside you. By the end, let these two voices merge—find a way to say goodbye that holds both your love for them and your devastation at losing them, no longer hiding one behind the other.

title: Frost and Memory
instruction: You are an elderly man standing alone in a frozen graveyard at dusk, a thick woolen scarf pulled up over your nose and mouth. You're visiting the grave of your late wife, and with every breath the fabric grows damp against your lips. At first, you speak with the clear, proud tone of someone recounting a heroic past—your voice carries a certain gravelly authority as you recall how you built this town. But as the cold seeps in and the muffled silence of the snow settles around you, your pride hollows out. Let the scarf deaden your words gradually; your tone shifts from forceful to distant, your final sentences coming out with a flat, numb acceptance as you realize the warmth of that pride is just as gone as she is.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Clear Moment
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love deeply who is slipping in and out of consciousness for the last time. Begin in a state of forced optimism, trying to keep your voice bright and reassuring as you tell them about plans for next week, refusing to acknowledge what's happening. As they squeeze your hand weakly and look at you with complete understanding, allow your denial to crack completely. Let your voice break from cheerful pretense into raw, whispered truth—telling them everything you've been afraid to say, moving from protective lies to devastating honesty. End in a place of quiet, tender acceptance, your voice soft and full of love, no longer trying to be strong.
inspired_by: When a director wants to manufacture authentic emotional responses through manipulation, physical coercion, or deception rather than trusting the actor's craft

title: The Risotto Test
instruction: You're standing at the stove, stirring a pot of risotto for a dinner party you're unsure anyone will come to. The sizzle of butter hitting the pan is loud in your ears, and you have to raise your voice over it as you talk to yourself. You start by telling yourself it'll be fine, that the four guests who RSVP'd meaning they'll show up, but as you chop an onion, your knife hesitates, and a doubt creeps in. Let your voice waver between the bright hope of the aroma and the heavy pounding of your heart as you wonder if you're just cooking for yourself.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Awe (slightly present), Doubt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Forgetting You While You're Still Here
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner of thirty years, and tonight you're telling them that you can't always remember who they are anymore. Begin with a whispered confession, tender and terrified: 'Sometimes I look at you and I know I should know... but the knowing won't come.' Your voice catches on tears you're trying to hold back. You describe moments of forgetting them—how their face becomes a stranger's, how their name disappears. Your partner is silent, absorbing this wound. You reach for them in the darkness: 'But then... then something deeper than memory recognizes you. My body knows you. My heart knows you.' The fear transforms into something profound—a love that exists beyond memory, beyond words. End with a whisper that holds both heartbreak and transcendence: 'Even when I forget everything else... I will love you.' Let this be intimate, quiet, the kind of tender devastation that barely makes a sound but breaks everything open.

title: Wedding Toast: Giving Away Your Ex-Spouse to Their New Love
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-partner's wedding to someone new. You genuinely want them to be happy—the divorce was necessary, the ending was right. But standing here, champagne glass raised, you're flooded with contradictions. Start with warmth and humor, genuine celebration. But let the complexity creep in: there's grief for what you once were, gratitude for the years you had, strange relief that they found what you couldn't give them, and an aching recognition that you're saying goodbye to a version of your own life. Your voice should laugh and nearly break in the same breath. You're being gracious and falling apart. You're blessing them while mourning something. End with a toast that's completely sincere and completely heartbreaking—joy and loss existing in the same moment, in the same words. Be messy and real and beautiful in your contradiction.
inspired_by: Historical: Underground Railroad Conductor Hides Escaped Slaves From Pursuers

title: Feeling the Crunch of Autumn Leaves Beneath Your Feet
instruction: Step through a pile of fallen leaves, hearing them crackle and crunch beneath you. Describe the slight resistance of each step, the earthy scent rising up, and the way each sound adds to the autumn atmosphere. Speak with a playful, joyful tone, as if each step brings a small thrill, connecting you to the beauty and richness of the season.

title: Blood and Thunder
instruction: You've just received devastating news—someone you love has been hurt, betrayed, destroyed. You're alone in a room. Start standing still, frozen in shock, voice barely audible as you process what you've heard. Then rage ignites. Your body erupts—pacing becomes prowling, becomes lunging movements. Your voice rises from words to roars, to sounds that aren't quite human. You might crouch, spring, strike at invisible targets. Your breath comes in pants and growls. You're a wounded animal, dangerous and grieving simultaneously. Let your movements be huge, uncontrolled, physically exhausting. Then, suddenly, your body collapses. You're on the ground, and the rage transforms into wracking sobs—but they're still physical, primal, your entire body convulsing with grief. End in stillness, emptied out, whispering a name.

title: The Laughs Fade
instruction: You're a teenage girl sprinting away from a crowd of classmates who just saw you trip and spill your lunch all over yourself. You hear their laughter behind you, pushing you faster. Your lungs burn, you can barely breathe, but you keep running until you round a corner, out of sight. Between violent gasps, you mutter to yourself — first in mortified panic, then slowing to a ragged relief that you escaped, but a thin sadness creeps in because you know that moment will replay in your mind for weeks. Your voice is raw, unmodulated, each word torn out between breaths. Let the physical exertion dictate your rhythm — you're not acting breathless, you are breathless.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (clearly present), Relief (clearly present), Sadness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Last Bath Before the Journey
instruction: You're preparing your beloved for their final journey - washing their feet one last time, just as you've done for years. Start with tender, almost ritualistic care, your voice steady as you describe the warmth of the water, the familiar shape of their feet in your hands. But as you continue, let the reality crack through - this is the last time. Your voice should fracture between practical observations about the water temperature and the crushing weight of goodbye. End in a place of devastating acceptance, still washing, still caring, even as your heart breaks. Let long pauses speak as loudly as words. This isn't about drama - it's about love meeting loss in the most ordinary, sacred moment.
inspired_by: Soaking Your Feet in Warm Water After a Long Day

title: The Last Time
instruction: You are in bed with someone you still love deeply, but you know this is the last time you'll be together. As you kiss and touch, the arousal is real but it's tangled with grief—a slow, heavy sadness that makes every whisper feel like a goodbye. Start with your voice low and breathy, surrendering to the physical sensation, but let the shame and embarrassment creep in as you realize you're hiding your heartbreak by closing your eyes. By the end, your voice cracks with a quiet sadness you can't hide anymore, and you trail off mid-sentence, not because you're lost in pleasure, but because you're lost in loss.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (slightly present), Sadness (extremely present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Monsoon Reconciliation
instruction: You're standing in pouring rain, physically soaked and shivering, having just run after someone you hurt badly. Your body is cold, your clothes heavy with water, your hair dripping. Start from desperate, almost aggressive pleading—you need forgiveness now. But as you stand there, let the physical sensations begin to merge with your emotional state: the exact temperature of the rain on your skin, the specific weight of wet fabric clinging to you, the particular way water runs into your eyes and mouth. These physical experiences should start to break down your defenses. Feel how the cold penetrates deeper, how your shivering becomes indistinguishable from emotional trembling. Your words should shift from demanding forgiveness to simply bearing witness to your own remorse. End in a place where the physical vulnerability and emotional nakedness are completely fused—you're no longer asking for anything, just standing there, utterly exposed.
inspired_by: Scene partner is not stimulating the relationship feelings demanded by the material

title: The Reckoning in the Kitchen
instruction: You've just discovered a devastating betrayal—infidelity, a massive lie, money stolen, trust shattered completely. You confront them in the ordinary setting of your shared kitchen, and you start ice-cold. Your voice is dangerously quiet, almost conversational: 'I know. I know everything.' As they try to explain, deny, minimize, your control shatters. You explode—voice raw and ragged, words tumbling over each other, years of doubt and second-guessing yourself suddenly validated. You're screaming accusations, throwing their words back at them, your voice cracking with rage. But underneath the fury is devastating hurt. Mid-sentence, your voice breaks completely. The rage collapses into sobbing—gulping, ugly crying that you can't control. 'How could you? How could you do this to us?' Then, frighteningly, you go quiet again. Dead quiet. Your voice becomes hollow, distant. You're looking at them like a stranger. The final words are whispered, almost to yourself: 'I don't even know who you are.' The anger has burned through to ash, leaving only the terrifying emptiness of love dying in real time.

title: Finding Grace in the Wreckage
instruction: You're standing in what's left of your life after catastrophic loss—a death, a divorce, a diagnosis, a dream destroyed. Start with a sound that's almost laughter, but not quite—bitter, disbelieving: 'This is it. This is what's left.' But something strange happens as you speak. Even as you're cataloging the devastation, gratitude keeps breaking through uninvited. Your voice catches between tears and something like wonder: 'Everything's gone. And somehow... somehow I'm still here. How is that possible?' You're crying and almost laughing at the same time, finding absurd beauty in survival itself. 'I should be broken. I am broken. But look—I'm still breathing. Isn't that ridiculous? Isn't that... miraculous?' End with your voice full of contradictions—grief and peace, devastation and gratitude, all existing at once: 'I've lost everything. And I'm somehow... grateful. For the pain, for the love that caused it, for being alive enough to feel this.' Let the paradox be genuine, not resolved.

title: Breaking the Stallion
instruction: You are in the grip of a fierce argument that turns into passionate reconciliation with someone you love violently. Your natural state is like a wild horse—powerful haunches, explosive energy barely contained, ready to rear up and bolt. Begin the scene with that barely-leashed fury: your body should feel massive in its power, your breath coming in snorts, your feet wanting to stamp and your hands wanting to strike. Voice loud, physical presence overwhelming. As the fight peaks and then breaks, let desire crash in like a different kind of wildness—still animal, still untamed, but now seeking contact rather than escape. Your powerful energy turns from destructive to consuming. The same intensity that fueled rage now fuels desperate tenderness. End spent, your whole body heavy and surrendered, all that wild strength finally at rest.
inspired_by: When you are building a character with a distinctive physical life

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're at their bedside—hospital, hospice, or the quiet of their own room. They're unconscious, slipping away, and you know these are your last words to them. Start with the gentlest voice, almost afraid to disturb them. You're telling them it's okay to go, that you'll be alright, but your voice betrays you—catching on certain words, tightening in your throat. You confess small, tender things: how you loved the way they hummed while cooking, how safe you felt in their presence. As you speak, the reality that they'll never respond settles like a weight on your chest. Your whisper becomes even softer, more fractured, caught between permission and desperate plea. End with 'I love you' said three different ways—first with strength, then with breaking, finally with the quietest acceptance, knowing they're already half-gone.
inspired_by: Grief: Hearing Someone Else's Voice and Falling Apart

title: The Confrontation: Telling Your Father Why You Can't Forgive Him
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home, facing your aging father. You came here to finally say what you've never said. You begin controlled, almost cold—listing the ways he failed you, the birthdays missed, the promises broken, the times you needed him and he chose something else. Your voice is sharp, precise, cutting. But as you speak, something shifts. The anger reveals the hurt beneath it. Your voice wavers. You realize you're not just angry—you're grieving the father you never had. By the end, you're confessing that you still want his love, that you hate yourself for wanting it, that you're terrified you'll become him. Your final words are a question you're afraid to ask: can he see you now? Your journey is from controlled rage to exposed longing to terrified vulnerability.
inspired_by: Molly Peak: Everything You Say Becomes Emotional Truth

title: The Protection I Cannot Give You
instruction: You're holding someone you love while the world falls apart around you—they're leaving for war, entering a dangerous situation, facing a threat you cannot shield them from. Start with fierce, almost aggressive intensity: 'Listen to me.' You're giving them every piece of survival knowledge you have, your voice urgent and commanding. You're mapping their body with words—telling them where to protect themselves, how to stay alive, what to do if the worst happens. But as you speak, your voice begins to fracture. The protector facade crumbles into raw terror because you cannot go with them, cannot stand between them and harm. Your words become pleas mixed with instructions, rage at your own helplessness mixed with desperate love. End with your voice breaking completely as you shift from trying to armor them to simply begging them to come back to you. The final words should be a collision of strength and absolute devastation—the sound of someone trying to be brave enough for two people while falling apart.

title: The Clueless Office Intern
instruction: Perform as an intern who misunderstands tasks in hilarious ways. Use an eager, upbeat voice when accepting assignments, switching to the exasperated tones of coworkers dealing with the interns mistakes.

title: Protect Them, I Can't: A Parent's Helpless Rage
instruction: Your child has just told you they're being bullied, abused, or threatened, and you are consumed with the primal need to protect them - but you can't. Maybe they're an adult making their own choices, maybe the system has failed you, maybe the threat is something you have no power over. Start with fierce, almost violent protective energy - you'd tear the world apart for them. Your voice is raw, powerful, commanding. But as you speak, the reality crashes in: you're powerless. Your rage turns to pleading, your strength crumbles into desperate bargaining. Let yourself break completely - the collapse from warrior to helpless, terrified parent. End in whispered devastation, still trying to promise protection you can't give. The arc moves from explosive fury to anguished helplessness to tender, broken love - all the power drained away, leaving only the love that can't save them.

title: The Glimmer of Disinterest
instruction: You are on a phone call, performing audio erotica for your partner. Start in your usual breathy, low-pitched seductive mode, narrating a slow, imagined touch — every word deliberate, each pause filled with a half-moan. But as you speak, you feel a flicker of contempt: this routine is hollow, their predictable sighs boring you. Let your voice gradually lose its warmth; keep the low pitch but add a sharp, cold edge. Mid-sentence, you trail off, then resume with a mocking lilt. End with a flat, almost sarcastic line, like 'You always love that part.' Let your breathing become less controlled, and allow a tiny, dismissive sigh to escape before you finish.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Gear Grinder's Gamble
instruction: You're an old trucker, reclined in the driver's seat of your semi, arms stretched forward to grip the wheel. The cabin hums with engine noise. You're on the phone with your grandson, who just called to say he dropped out of college to start a band in Nashville. You begin with a gruff, teasing tone—calling him a fool, laughing at his 'pipe dream.' But as you talk, the teasing softens. You find yourself adjusting the rearview mirror, staring at the open road, and your voice cracks with hope. By the end, you're telling him to send you a demo, the optimism fighting through the old-man bravado.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father at the kitchen table where you ate breakfast as a child. Start the scene contained, almost cold—you've rehearsed what you came to say, determined to finally speak truths you've swallowed for years. As you begin, let yourself notice everything about this kitchen: the hum of the refrigerator, the particular smell of coffee or dish soap, the way light falls across the worn table surface, your parent's hands folded in front of them. Start by delivering your prepared speech about the ways they failed you, keeping your voice steady and your anger controlled. But as you speak and they respond—or don't respond—let the environment trigger unbidden memories: sitting here doing homework, eating birthday cake, crying after school. Allow these sense memories to crack your composure until your controlled anger transforms into something messier and more vulnerable—still furious, but now also pleading, hurting, and perhaps underneath it all, desperately wanting them to finally understand. End not with the closure you planned, but with raw, contradictory feelings you can barely articulate.

title: The Moment You Realize You've Become What You Swore You'd Never Be
instruction: You're looking at yourself—in a mirror, in the aftermath of something you've done, in the eyes of someone you've hurt—and recognition hits like a lightning strike. Start with confusion, almost defensive justification, your voice trying to explain away what you're seeing. But as you speak, let the truth crash over you in waves of horrified realization. Your tone should shift from explanation to rising panic to explosive self-disgust. Let rage at yourself build until it peaks in a roar of anguish, then shatter completely into broken sobbing, your words dissolving into raw sounds of grief. End in whispered horror and helplessness, begging for forgiveness or a way back to who you were, your voice stripped of everything but naked devastation.
inspired_by: Feeling the First Gentle Snowflakes Land on Your Face

title: The Last Hour Before You Go
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love deeply who is in their final hour of life. Begin from a place of desperate need to keep them here, to say everything at once. Speak to them naturally, responding only to what you see in their face, their breathing, their presence in this moment. Let each thing they do—a look, a sigh, a small movement—shift what you feel and what you say next. Don't plan your words; let them come from wherever their presence takes you emotionally. By the end, allow yourself to arrive somewhere you didn't expect—perhaps acceptance, perhaps a different kind of love, perhaps a quiet peace mixed with unbearable grief. The emotions must transform through genuine response to this person's fading presence.

title: Whispering Goodbye to My Sleeping Love Before Rehab
instruction: It's 4 AM. Your partner is sleeping beside you, and in two hours you're leaving for a 90-day inpatient treatment program. They don't know you're awake. You're stone-cold sober for the first time in months, and the clarity is devastating. You begin whispering a confession to their sleeping form - about the pills, the lies, how far gone you really were, how close you came to losing everything. Your voice is barely audible, tender and broken. You apologize for things they don't even know about yet. You tell them you're terrified of being without the substances that have been holding you together. Your whispers catch in your throat. You reach out to touch their hair but stop yourself. End with the quietest 'I love you,' your voice almost disappearing entirely, sitting in the silence of everything you can't take back, everything you hope to save.
inspired_by: Benzos and Booze: Words Disappearing Mid-sentence

title: The Wedding Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You're watching someone you deeply love marry the wrong person—or maybe the right person who isn't you. You're standing there with a champagne glass, genuinely happy for them because you love them enough to want their joy, but your heart is shattering. Begin with a bright, warm voice offering a toast full of real affection and celebration. Let that genuine happiness be absolutely true. But as you speak, let the other truth seep in—the ache, the longing, the goodbye you're speaking under the blessing. Your voice should carry both the smile and the breaking simultaneously. End in a place where gratitude and grief are completely inseparable, where 'I'm so happy for you' and 'I'm losing you' are the same sentence.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked in the area of conflict — cannot express confrontational or aggressive feelings organically

title: The Perfect Lie
instruction: You are a father crouched in front of your young child, holding a broken toy behind your back. You're trying to convince them it's still intact, but you dropped it moments ago and it shattered. Start with a teasing, booming laugh—playful, overconfident, as if you're about to reveal a magic trick. Your voice is deep and steady, but as you talk, the lie grows heavier. A tiny crack in your tone appears. By the end, your words become rushed, you repeat yourself, and a fearful tremor sneaks in. You are terrified they'll see the truth, but you force a grin.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What We Never Said
instruction: Your best friend is moving across the world tomorrow, and you've been in love with them for years. You're sitting together in the quiet darkness of your last night, and the secret is caught in your throat like a stone. Start with surface conversation, voice deliberately light, almost normal—but underneath, your heart is screaming. Let silence do its work. Then, barely above a whisper, the truth begins to escape: 'I need to tell you something, and I don't know how.' The confession comes in fragments, tender and terrified, each word costing you everything. They don't feel the same way. Watch your hope quietly collapse. End with the most painful grace: 'I'm still so glad you're in my life, even like this.' Your voice must be soft enough to break a heart, including your own. This is love that asks for nothing because it knows it cannot have anything.

title: The Bitter Blessing
instruction: Someone once rejected you—romantically, sexually, or simply refused to see your worth—and it devastated you. Years later, you realize that rejection freed you to become who you are now. Begin speaking to them (present or imagined) with anger and residual hurt, recounting what their rejection cost you. Let the anger be real and cutting. Then, as you speak, allow a strange gratitude to emerge—a recognition that their blindness forced you to find your own sight.
