title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to someone you love, and you finally whisper the secret you've been carrying - an infidelity, a terrible mistake, a truth about who you really are. Begin barely audible, your voice trembling, your breathing shallow, trying to keep it contained. But as you confess, let yourself unravel slowly. Your whispers become choked with tears, your body curls inward, you're shaking. The vulnerability is excruciating. Let silences fill with your breathing, with small sounds of pain. Then gradually, as you speak it all aloud, feel something lift. Your voice steadies just slightly. You're still terrified, still broken open, but there's relief mixing with the fear. End with a fragile, naked honesty - still quiet, but transformed.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've been holding it together—through the training, the pressure, the impossibility of what everyone expects—and now you're alone and you're shattering. Start with explosive rage, screaming about the effort, the endless grinding effort that's eating you alive. Your voice is fierce, almost savage, railing against the push, push, push that never stops. But mid-fury, something cracks differently. The anger collapses into sobbing, raw and uncontrolled. You're confessing how scared you are, how you don't know if you can keep doing this, how the determination everyone admires is just terror in disguise. Your voice moves between roaring defiance and broken whispers. By the end, you're on the floor, voice hoarse and small, admitting the thing you've never said aloud: that you don't know if winning is worth what it's costing you.

title: Whispering a Secret You've Kept for Twenty Years
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside your sleeping partner of two decades. You finally speak aloud the secret you've carried since the beginning—perhaps about a child you gave up for adoption, or a betrayal, or a truth about who you really are. Your voice must be barely above a whisper, not to wake them, but also because saying it louder would shatter you. Let your breath catch, pause mid-sentence as emotion closes your throat. The quietness makes everything more intimate and devastating. Your voice should quaver between confession and self-forgiveness, shame and relief. End with the faintest whisper: a question you don't expect them to answer, asked to the darkness itself. The entire piece should feel like the most tender, frightening honesty.
inspired_by: Giving a Speech While Holding a Heavy Box

title: The Kitchen Verdict
instruction: You are confronting your adult child in your kitchen about a choice they've made that you find unforgivable—maybe they've abandoned their family, betrayed someone you love, or thrown away everything you sacrificed to give them. Start with cold, cutting precision—the kind of controlled fury that comes from rehearsing this speech for weeks. Each word is a weapon. But as you speak, watch their face. See them not defending themselves, not fighting back, just... standing there, taking it. Suddenly you hear yourself through their ears, see yourself through their eyes, and something shifts. The rage cracks open to reveal the terror underneath—you're losing them, maybe already lost them. By the end, you're no longer pronouncing judgment. You're begging them to help you understand, to not disappear from your life. Move from cold verdict to desperate plea.

title: Last Words to a Dying Parent Who Never Loved You Right
instruction: You're standing at their hospital bedside, knowing these are the final hours. Start with your voice tight and formal, trying to say the 'right' things—'I'm glad I could be here.' But as you look at their frail body, something ancient and hurt rises up. Your voice cracks as you confess what you've never said: 'I needed you to see me.' The words pour out, raw and aching. Then their hand reaches weakly for yours, and you feel yourself softening against your will. End with a whispered goodbye that holds both forgiveness and all the grief of what will never be healed—your voice breaking not from anger anymore, but from the devastating tenderness of letting go.
inspired_by: Your Abuser Texting You Out of the Blue

title: Runner's Bliss
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy just finished a brutal uphill run. Endorphins are flooding your system—you feel invincible, euphoric, almost drunk on your own body's chemistry. You're still breathing hard, sweat dripping, but your voice is clear and confident, slightly breathy but controlled. Start by calling out to a friend you see approaching, your tone bright and energized. Then as you describe the run, the intoxication deepens—you start to lose yourself in the memory of the effort. But by the end, the high shifts: a sudden, quiet realization hits you that this feeling will fade, and a flicker of melancholy mixes with the intoxication. Your voice should reflect that subtle drop—still open, but softer, more reflective. Keep it real: pause to wipe your face, laugh at your own breathlessness, let the words tumble out a bit.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your parent everything you've held back for decades. Start controlled, almost cold—you've armored yourself for this. Your voice is steady as you list the moments they missed, the ways they failed you. But as you speak, the adrenaline of confrontation kicks in. Your words come faster, louder, your voice climbing as years of pain surge forward. Then, devastatingly, you hear yourself—and you sound just like them. The realization hits mid-sentence. Your voice falters, becomes thick with tears. You're not just angry anymore; you're grieving the relationship you'll never have. End with a raw, broken admission: despite everything, part of you still loves them, still wanted them to choose you.

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone in complete darkness, voice so quiet it's almost not there. You begin with 'Are you awake?' and when they respond, you whisper a confession you've carried for years—an infidelity, a lie that shaped your relationship, a truth about who you really are. Your voice trembles, catching in your throat as you reveal each detail. The intimacy of darkness makes you brave and terrified at once. As you speak, your voice becomes even softer, more fragile, like you might shatter. By the end, you're crying silently, voice breaking on 'I'm so sorry,' waiting in the devastating quiet for them to respond, knowing everything has changed.

title: The Confrontation You've Been Rehearsing for Years
instruction: You're finally saying everything to the person who damaged you—a parent who was never there, a lover who chose cruelty, someone whose betrayal shaped your life. Begin with surgical precision, your voice steady and devastating: 'Do you even remember what you did? Let me remind you.' Detail the specific moments they destroyed something in you, your tone cold and factual at first. But as you continue, the composure starts to splinter. Your voice rises, becomes jagged. The hurt beneath the hate surfaces—desperate questions pour out: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me that made it so easy for you to—' You catch yourself, try to rebuild the armor of anger, but it's too late. End in a raw collision of rage and pain: accusations mixed with the vulnerable plea you swore you'd never make. Your voice should oscillate between powerful condemnation and the broken child still waiting for an answer.

title: Whispering to the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, speaking in whispers so quiet they're almost just breath. Confess something you've never said aloud—perhaps a fear so deep you barely admit it to yourself, a desire that shames you, or a truth about who you really are beneath all your defenses. Begin with your voice catching, uncertain whether to speak at all. As you continue, let the darkness and intimacy pull deeper truths from you, things that surprise even you as they emerge. Access the physical sensations: your heartbeat, the warmth of skin nearby, the vulnerability of being seen without armor. Let long pauses happen where you're gathering courage or being ambushed by emotion. Transform from protective silence to radical honesty, ending in a place of either profound relief or even deeper vulnerability—whichever emerges truthfully in the moment.

title: You Will Not Take Them
instruction: Someone is trying to take away what you most fiercely protect—your child, your loved one, your family—and you're unleashing everything you've held back. Begin with controlled warning, your voice tight with barely restrained fury. Let that control shatter as you escalate into full protective rage, your voice rising with the primal ferocity of someone fighting for what matters most. Then—at the peak of your anger—let helplessness crash through: the sudden, devastating realization that despite your rage, despite your willingness to destroy anything in your path, you might not be able to stop this. Your fury should break apart into something rawer: desperation, pleading, a fierce love that makes you both terrifyingly strong and utterly vulnerable. End with that paradox audible in your voice.

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're in your childhood home, face-to-face with the parent who looked away when you needed them most. Begin with controlled, almost cold precision—stating facts, keeping your voice measured and distant as armor. 'You knew. You always knew.' Your anger builds, voice rising as decades of suppressed rage surface. Accusations fly, voice shaking with fury and betrayal. Then something shifts—mid-rant, you see them clearly as flawed, broken, human. Your voice falters, softens into something unexpected: grief for the parent you needed and never had, grief for them and their failures. End with exhausted honesty, voice quiet and raw, admitting you needed them to be different, acknowledging they couldn't be, trying to find a way to let go of expecting them to change.

title: Skin and Thunder
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a miracle, a loss—and you're alone in your apartment when your body starts to respond before your mind can process it. Begin with physical sensation: maybe you're burning hot, maybe ice cold, maybe both at once. Let your body lead—if you need to collapse, collapse; if you need to pace, pace; if you need to press your palms against the wall and push, do that. Your breath becomes sound becomes words becomes something primal. There's no one to perform for, so let the sounds that emerge be raw and unplanned. Perhaps rage turns to sobbing or sobbing ignites into fierce, unexpected laughter. The emotional storm moves through you like weather through an open field. By the end, you're emptied out, transformed, discovering what remains when everything else has been burned through.

title: Burpee Rebellion
instruction: You are an older man doing burpees in a small home gym. Each jump costs you—joints protest, breath rips out in a 'huph!' and your landing thuds like a falling log. Start in disgust: you hate your aging body, hate this exercise, hate that you have to prove anything. Midway through a set, a surprised laugh escapes—you're genuinely proud you haven't quit. The last jump lands hard, but you stand, exhale, and mutter a teasing jab at yourself, voice cracked but triumphant. Your words come only between landings, gasping, sometimes cut off mid-syllable, naturally reacting to your own exhaustion.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Teasing (slightly present), Disgust (extremely present)

title: The Old Line
instruction: You are an elderly man calling a customer service line about a recurring charge on your pension. At the start, you're crisp and annoyed, compensating for the distance. By the end, doubt has taken over: you start questioning if you even deserve the refund, your voice trailing off as you glance at your wrinkled hands and the receiver. title: Braiding Hair for the Last Time
instruction: You're braiding someone's hair—your sister's before her wedding to someone who will take her far away, your mother's as she fades from memory, your daughter's before she boards a plane you know is dangerous. Your hands move in the familiar rhythm: gather, cross, tighten, gather, cross, tighten. Between each weaving motion, whisper memories, confessions, things you never said. Start with small talk, your voice steady, trying to keep this moment normal. But your hands remember every time you've done this—after nightmares, before first days of school, in hospital rooms. Let your breathing become uneven. Your words should catch and restart: 'Remember when you... no, maybe you don't... I remember.' The repetitive motion becomes meditation and torture. This ancient, intimate ritual—you've done it a thousand times, but this time your hands are shaking. title: Final Conversation Through the Hospice Door
instruction: You're standing outside your estranged father's hospice room. You haven't spoken in twelve years. The nurse says you have maybe an hour. You're holding his hand, whispering childhood memories, your voice breaking on 'I needed you.' By the end, you're simply there, all the rage dissolved into this terrible tenderness, telling him it's okay to go. Your voice has traveled from fury to forgiveness you didn't know you had.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding to someone you believe is wrong for them—or perhaps you're in love with your friend yourself. title: The Final Lap

title: The Unguarded Hour
instruction: It is 3 AM and you are lying in the dark beside someone you've held at arm's length for months, terrified to let them fully in. Tonight, sleepless and raw, your defenses are paper-thin. Let your breath catch and stumble, pauses filled with the vulnerability of someone offering their softest parts. As you speak, feel the relief and terror of being truly seen mixing in your chest. Your voice may break, may become even quieter, but it should grow more authentic, more deeply connected to your core. title: The Curl Under the Chandelier
instruction: You're at your sister's anniversary party, a glass of wine in hand, tipsy and laughing too loud at a cousin's joke. Your voice starts bubbly, slurred from wine, then turns tight and guarded, each word escaping on a shallow, pained exhale. title: Laughing While Scattering Your Best Friend's Ashes

title: Whispered Becoming
instruction: Late at night, you're speaking to your sleeping partner. Hearing yourself say these truths aloud—even to someone who can't hear you—makes them real. Your whispers become more certain, more tender toward yourself. By the end, you're speaking with quiet, unshakeable conviction about who you are and who you're becoming. title: The Homecoming Threshold
instruction: You are standing at the door of the house you grew up in, key in hand, returning after ten years away. Your mother has just died, and the house is yours now. Feel the weight of the key, its familiar shape. Smell the particular scent of this house—wood polish, her cooking, something floral and fading. Hear the creak of the porch, wind chimes she hung twenty years ago, the silence inside. See the peeling paint, the welcome mat worn thin, the afternoon light falling the way it always did. Taste dust and memory. Begin with dread, your hand frozen on the doorknob, not wanting to go in and confirm she's gone. As you finally push the door open and step inside, let the flood of memories—every breakfast, every fight, every ordinary moment—wash over you. Feel grief and gratitude become inseparable. End with your hand on the wall she painted, weeping and smiling at once, hating that she's gone and overwhelmed with love for everything she left behind.

title: Laughing in Translation
instruction: You're teaching your dying grandmother English phrases she always wanted to learn, and she's teaching you old expressions from your ancestral language you never knew. Your laughter breaks into sobbing, but you're still smiling, still repeating it back to her, your voice destroyed and beautiful. End saying it one final time, code-switching unconsciously through both languages, expressing gratitude and unbearable grief at once, laughing and weeping as you tell her, 'I'll carry you in mine.'

title: Field Notes from a Failing Marriage: The Whispered Inventory

title: The Old Bull's Last Dash
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, sprinting through a dark forest after escaping from a collapsing building. title: The Morning Game
instruction: You're a woman in her 60s, sitting on the edge of a carpeted bedroom bed, watching your husband still under the covers, pretending to be asleep. Your voice begins playful and light, then softens with a tender, bittersweet weight—a mix of laughing at his stubbornness and grieving the preciousness of time. Let your voice absorb the room's soft hush, and don't be afraid to pause, sigh, or let a thought trail off as you glance at the morning light on the carpet.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent who was always emotionally distant, and they've just asked you to hold their hand. But as you reach for their hand, let yourself feel what's actually happening beneath your usual response: the specific texture of their skin, the weight of all the unsaid years, the particular ache in your chest right now. Speak to them, letting your voice follow the real sensations and impulses moving through you moment by moment, rather than the emotional script you usually perform. Allow the feelings to shift and surprise you—from whatever you hide behind, through layers of what's actually present, landing somewhere you didn't plan to go.

title: The Stale Cake

title: The Last Photo
instruction: You are sitting alone in a dim, cluttered bedroom at 3 a.m. You just found a small, crumpled photo tucked inside an old book—the last picture you ever took with your mother before she passed. title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're packing up your deceased child's bedroom, finding an object that releases a flood of specific, beautiful memories—while simultaneously knowing you must give this room to a sibling's new baby. Begin touching objects mechanically, your body trying to stay efficient and practical, protecting yourself through task-focused movement. When you find the meaningful object, let joy and grief crash into you simultaneously—maybe you laugh and sob in the same breath, your body doubling over with the beauty of the memory and the agony of loss. Feel gratitude for having had this child war with resentment that they're gone, hope for the new life coming conflict with rage that this replacement is necessary. End with your body expressing the impossible complexity: perhaps cradling the object while placing it in a box, your hands both treasuring and releasing, your entire being holding life and death, past and future, in the same moment.

title: I Needed You Then: The Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent after years of silence, and the words finally come. Let the anger crack into something more vulnerable, your voice breaking as you admit the deeper truth: you still love them, you still need them, and that's what makes it hurt so much. End with exhausted tenderness, asking the question you're terrified to ask: 'Can we start again?'

title: The Last Understanding
instruction: You're at your father's bedside in his final hours. For thirty years, you've believed he was disappointed in you, that you never measured up. Now, with labored breath, he's trying to tell you something—and suddenly you understand: every harsh word was fear of losing you, every criticism was desperate love he didn't know how to express. Begin with defensive confusion, that old armor still up. Let the realization crack you open—'Wait... you were proud of me?' Your voice should break as understanding floods in, as you realize you've wasted decades misreading his heart. End with fierce gratitude mixed with devastating grief: you finally have him, and you're about to lose him forever. This is understanding that comes too late and just in time.

title: Grave of a Good Friend
instruction: You are alone in the backyard at dusk, digging a grave for your dog who died this morning. Each shovelful of earth is heavy, and you have to heave it aside with a grunt. Start by muttering in shame—you were too busy, you didn't notice she was sick, and now she's gone. The guilt sits in your chest like a stone. As you pause between digs, wiping sweat from your eyes, a memory of her wagging tail surfaces. Let your voice shift, still breathless from exertion, into a raw, tender affection. End with a whispered promise you make to her, the words coming out in soft, broken rhythm between the labored breaths. The shame never fully leaves, but the love becomes louder.

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy and Finally Understanding Them
instruction: They're bleeding out in your arms—the person you've hated for years, fought against, blamed for everything. Start with shock, maybe even satisfaction that they're finally defeated. But as you feel their life leaving, something cracks open in you. You see them—really see them—for the first time as human, terrified, alone. Your voice explodes with all the rage you've carried, the accusations you've rehearsed, but it collapses mid-sentence into something else entirely: horror at what you've become, grief at the waste of it all, desperate need to make peace before it's too late. You're yelling and then you're crying and then you're cradling them like something precious, begging them to stay, to forgive you, promising you understand now. End with fierce, protective tenderness as you lie to them that it's going to be okay, your voice gentle and breaking and full of a love you didn't know you had.

title: The Guilty Kiss
instruction: You are a young girl, barely a teenager, and you're in the back of a crowded closet during a game of hide-and-seek. You're pressed tight against your best friend; someone you're not supposed to like this way. You start to kiss them, but the whole time, you're terrified someone will find you. Your voice is breathy, barely there, as you try to whisper something about your shame, your embarrassment, your focus on being quiet. Start with a nervous, concentrated whisper, and let the shame creep in as you realize you're going to keep kissing them anyway, even as you pull your mouth away to speak between soft, wet sounds.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (clearly present), Concentration (slightly present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Hospital Room Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He's unconscious, but you need to say everything you never said. Begin with your body rigid, throat tight, unable to find words - acknowledge this physical resistance out loud as you sit in silence. As you start speaking to him, track how fear moves through your chest, how grief sits in your stomach, how love breaks open in your throat. By the end, let yourself arrive at a place of complete surrender - where your body finally softens, your breath deepens, and you can touch his hand with tenderness. The journey is from paralyzed silence to flowing, unguarded goodbye.

title: Best Man's Slurred Blessing
instruction: You are a 19-year-old best man at your older brother's wedding, three beers deep and trying to hold it together. The microphone feels heavy, the room blurs at the edges, and you keep tugging at your tie because it's too tight. Start with forced confidence—a loud, shaky 'Ladies and gentlemen' that cracks mid-word—but as you look at your brother's face, the bravado slips. Your words slow, soften, and you forget what you were going to say, so you just speak from the chest: 'He... he was always there. Even when I was a punk kid. And now he's got someone who sees that too.' Let your voice tremor, trail off, then land on a quiet, earnest finish that surprises you as much as the room.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Sweet Revenge in the Recovery Room
instruction: You are waking up from sedation after dental surgery. Your mouth is numb, your mind hazy, and you feel a blissful, floaty pleasure. The nurse or a loved one is beside you. As you slur your words, you recall the reason you're here—you intentionally overdosed on the anesthetic to get back at someone. Your ecstasy transforms into a dark, malevolent satisfaction. Let your voice be unsteady, with sudden loud whispers and lazy giggles. End with a deep, toothless grin and a contented sigh as you savor your plan. Speak about 50-70 words.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Accepting Terminal Diagnosis: Bargaining Becoming Acceptance
instruction: The doctor is telling you that you have six months, maybe a year. Your voice initially is in denial, almost angry: 'No. That's not... there has to be another option.' You're bargaining, your voice becoming desperate: 'What if we try the experimental treatment? What if?' The doctor's voice is gentle, firm. They've had this conversation before. Include the moment where you stop asking questions and something in your voice shifts. You're accepting not that you're okay with dying, but that it's happening. Your voice becomes quieter, almost peaceful: 'So I have time to say goodbye.' You're not ready, you'll never be ready, but your voice reflects acceptance beginning. It sounds less like resignation and more like transformation.

title: Braiding Your Daughter's Hair One Last Time
instruction: You're braiding your daughter's hair the morning before she leaves for a distant opportunity—college abroad, a marriage that will take her far away, or perhaps you're terminally ill and know these moments are numbered. Start with gentle focus on the practical task, speaking softly about the texture, the familiar weight of her hair in your hands. As you work, let memory flood in—all the times you've done this since she was small. Your voice should crack with the realization that this ordinary ritual is ending. Feel your fingers trembling slightly as they work. End with a whispered blessing or goodbye that catches in your throat, mixing profound gratitude for having had these years with the devastating knowledge that they're over.
inspired_by: Running Fingers Through Freshly Washed Hair

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Gave You
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent, finally saying the things you've rehearsed for twenty years. Start controlled, measured—you've prepared for this. 'I need to tell you something I should have said a long time ago.' But as you speak, listing the moments they weren't there, the ways you felt invisible, your control starts slipping. Your voice gets tighter, louder. You're not yelling but you're close—years of swallowed anger rising. Then they say something—maybe 'I did my best' or 'I don't remember it that way'—and you break. Not into rage but into raw, ugly grief. Your voice cracks: 'I needed you. I was just a kid and I needed you.' End in devastated honesty, all armor gone, speaking from the wounded child still inside you. The anger transforms into heartbreak, the accusation into a plea.
inspired_by: Talking to a Baby Who Just Said Their First Word

title: The Last Secret Before Departure
instruction: You're standing at a train platform, about to board a train that will take you somewhere you can never return from—a dangerous mission, a one-way medical trial, exile. The person you love most stands before you. You begin by trying to be brave, voice steady, but then you break: there's something you've never told them, something that's haunted you for years. As you confess this secret—perhaps a truth about how you've loved them, or something you did that shaped both your lives—your voice moves from forced composure to raw vulnerability. They respond, and in their voice you hear forgiveness, or understanding, or their own confession in return. By the end, you're both crying, whispering urgently, cramming a lifetime of unsaid things into these final moments. The train whistle blows. Your voice carries desperate love mixed with the agony of permanent goodbye.

title: Grateful for the Heartbreak
instruction: You're at your ex-lover's wedding, and you've just been asked to say a few words about the 'gift' they were in your life. You're genuinely happy for them - and your heart is shattering. Start with a laugh that's almost real, words that sound congratulatory but carry an undercurrent of loss. Let joy and grief live in the same breath. Your voice should lift with genuine warmth when you describe what they gave you - then crack almost imperceptibly on certain words: 'always,' 'forever,' 'love.' Midway through, let the contradiction intensify: you're smiling and there are tears in your voice, you're celebrating their happiness while mourning your own loss. Find moments of real laughter mixed with the catch of suppressed sobs. End with a toast that's both blessing and goodbye, your voice carrying真 happiness for them and真 grief for yourself simultaneously. This should feel like laughing at a funeral, like finding grace in letting go - messy, contradictory, devastatingly human. Let your voice do the impossible: mean every word of happiness while breaking with loss.
inspired_by: Hiding Disappointment When Receiving an Unwanted Gift

title: The Glittering Trap
instruction: You are in a high-stakes boardroom negotiation, a young woman with a deliberately soft, feminine voice—your shield. You've just secured what you believe is a massive win for your side, and initial ecstasy floods you; you can barely suppress a smile, your voice lifts with a honeyed triumph. But as you scan the contract again, a single clause catches your eye—something subtly wrong, a detail that makes no sense. Your pleasure curdles into deep, intense confusion, your words slow and become fragmented as you mentally backtrack, your pitch rises unnaturally, and you repeat the same question twice, trying to mask your growing alarm with a strained politeness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Cracked Vase
instruction: You are an older woman with a soft, high-pitched voice, standing in your kitchen. Your adult daughter has just walked in and noticed the shattered pieces of a vase that belonged to your own mother. At first, you try to brush it off with a light, embarrassed laugh — your voice lilting, almost girlish, as you say it was just an accident, it wasn't that valuable. But as you see your daughter's face harden, you feel the air leave the room. Your pitch drops, your words slow down, and you confess that you were clumsy and careless, that you're sorry. Let your voice lose its sing-song quality, become smaller, huskier, with long pauses where you struggle to speak, until finally you admit it was your fault and you miss her too.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Bedside Confession to the Sleeping Beloved
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you in the quiet darkness of 3 AM, and you're whispering a confession they can never hear while they're awake. Start soft and cautious, testing the words in the safety of their sleep. You're revealing something that's been eating you alive—maybe an affair, maybe a diagnosis you haven't shared, maybe a dream you're too afraid to chase. Your voice should be intimate, almost sensual in its quietness, filled with the ache of loving someone deeply while carrying a secret that could destroy you both. As you speak, let tenderness war with guilt, love with fear. End with your voice catching on unshed tears as you realize you may never be brave enough to say these words when they're awake, the confession dissolving into a broken 'I love you' that contains both devotion and devastating sadness.

title: The Last Descent
instruction: You are in a small, humming elevator, the metal walls reflecting your own voice back at you in a tinny echo. You've just said goodbye to someone you love, not knowing if you'll see them again. At first, you try to keep your voice light and composed, humming a distracted tune to the beat of the cables. But as the floor numbers sink lower, the mechanical hum seems to press on your chest. Let the longing creep in—your voice wavers, a single sigh escapes, and you finally whisper a wish to the empty space, the metallic flutter amplifying the ache. Start bright and self-assured, end raw and utterly exposed.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Shattering
instruction: Your child is walking into danger—addiction, an abusive relationship, a choice that will destroy them—and they won't listen. You begin with fierce, almost violent intensity: 'You will NOT do this!' Your voice is a weapon of protective rage. But as they remain unmoved, your fury splinters into helplessness. The shouting deteriorates into pleading. 'Please, please, I'm begging you.' You're openly sobbing now but still trying to command, to control, to save them. Your voice breaks on their name. The rage returns in waves—'I won't watch you destroy yourself!'—but it's impotent, desperate. By the end, you're on your knees vocally, all power stripped away. The final words—'I can't lose you'—are barely intelligible through tears, a parent's ultimate powerlessness laid completely bare.

title: The Checkpoint, Then the Aftershock
instruction: You are an elderly woman, sitting up in bed, speaking to a partner you deeply trust. A moment ago, there was playful arousal and laughter. Now, a scent or texture—a faint bodily odor—suddenly hits you, and disgust floods your face and voice, like a reflex you cannot hide. You need to stop everything immediately to name it, but you are also in quiet awe of this person who has just trusted you with their body. Your voice starts as a sober, deliberate gear-shift—slower, clearer, apologetic but firm—as you explain what you are feeling without blame. Mid-sentence, you lose your train of thought, hearing the silence, then find it again. By the end, the disgust has settled into a heavy, raw gratitude, and your voice softens into a fragile tenderness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Last Words to a Parent Who Never Said They Were Proud
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He's awake but fading. You begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to comfort him with small talk about the weather, the nurses. But something breaks inside you and suddenly you're telling him everything you never said: 'I always waited for you to say you were proud of me. Just once.' Your voice cracks between anger and desperate love. You cycle through resentment, then guilt for feeling it now, then finally a raw, aching tenderness. End with a whispered forgiveness—for him, for yourself—as you hold his hand, tears streaming, voice barely there: 'I love you anyway. I do.'
inspired_by: Realizing Someone You Love Doesn't Love You Back Anymore

title: Conduit Power
instruction: Someone made a wish on you, and their hope is moving through you now. Your voice starts normal but becomes a channel for something larger. 'I feel it,' you say. The energy isn't yours—you're just conducting it. Your voice becomes brighter, warmer, almost transcendent. 'You're going to be okay,' you tell them, and you mean it because you're not the one saying it. Something is saying it through you. Your voice is just the instrument.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother in her kitchen - the same kitchen where you learned to swallow your feelings as a child. You came here planning to calmly ask why she never protected you, never spoke up, never chose you. Start with that controlled, rehearsed calmness, the words you've practiced. But as you speak, let yourself actually feel what it was like to be that child waiting for her to say something, anything. Don't perform anger - let whatever genuinely rises in you take over: maybe it's rage, maybe it's desperate pleading, maybe your voice gets smaller instead of louder. By the end, you've abandoned your script entirely, and what comes out is the raw truth you didn't even know you needed to say - whether that's fury, or grief, or even unexpected tenderness mixed with devastation.
inspired_by: Actor feels disconnected from real feelings or is 'naturally' acting—imitating truth rather than experiencing it

title: The Last Breakfast Before Deployment
instruction: You're making your child's favorite yogurt parfait on the morning before you deploy overseas for an indefinite mission. Start with tender focus on the ritual—the layering of granola, the dollop of honey—describing each detail as if memorizing it. Your voice is steady, almost cheerful, trying to keep things normal. But as you continue, let the weight of goodbye seep in. The simple act of preparing this breakfast becomes unbearable in its ordinariness. By the end, you're still describing the yogurt, the berries, the crunch, but your voice fractures—this might be the last time. Let gratitude for this moment war with the devastating awareness that you're trying to pack a lifetime of love into one breakfast.

title: Reading Your Best Friend's Eulogy While Remembering Their Last Joke
instruction: You're at a podium delivering a eulogy for your best friend who died suddenly. Begin with formal words that you prepared, voice steady with practiced grief. But then you remember—right before they died, they made you promise that if anything happened, you had to tell everyone about the absolutely ridiculous thing they did last week. And suddenly you're laughing, tears streaming down your face, telling a story that's completely inappropriate for a funeral but perfectly them. Your voice breaks between laughter and sobbing. You're furious they left you, grateful for every stupid moment, wrecked by the loss, and somehow finding joy in the memory. The laughter hurts because it reminds you they're gone; the tears are almost sweet because you got to love someone this much. End with a moment of pure contradictory emotion—smiling through devastation, your voice soft with gratitude and broken with grief, somehow both destroyed and whole.
inspired_by: Surgeon Delivers Unexpected Complications During Surgery Debrief

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father about why he never taught you your mother's language after she died when you were five. In your hands, you hold her recipe book—written entirely in words you cannot read. Begin by physically exploring the book: the worn leather cover, the stains on pages, her handwriting you can see but not comprehend, perhaps even the faint scent of spices still clinging to the paper. Let these tangible sensations fuel your words. Start from a place of quiet, almost childlike longing—wanting to understand, asking him to translate just one recipe. As he refuses or deflects, let your anger build through the physical: your grip tightening on the book, your body heating up, your throat constricting. By the end, you're not just holding a recipe book—you're holding proof of everything he took from you. Your voice should transform from tender questioning to raw accusation, while your sensory connection to this object intensifies into something almost unbearable.

title: Reading Erotica Aloud While Trying to Stay Composed
instruction: You're at a book club and it's your turn to read a passage aloud — but you didn't preview it and it turns out to be intensely erotic. Start reading in your normal book-club voice. As the content escalates, your voice betrays you: clearing your throat, speeding up through explicit parts, pitch rising with embarrassment, nervous laughter escaping. Try to maintain composure while the content makes it impossible. The contrast between prim delivery and filthy content is everything.

title: The Weight of Waiting
instruction: You are an older woman standing in a thick, oppressive fog in a field you once loved. You came here to meet someone who promised to be here, but they never arrived. The fog swallows your voice; you speak louder than you need to, unsure if anyone hears. Bitterness coats every word at first—sharp, angry, aimed at the absent person and the fog itself. But as you continue, the bitterness slowly shifts into a profound loneliness, a quiet admission that you were never truly heard even when they were here. Let your voice crack, trail off, react to the damp cold, the imagined sound of footsteps that aren't there. End with a whisper that feels more like a confession to yourself than to anyone else.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Wrong Words Again
instruction: You're a teenage guy, your voice still cracking with masculinity, but a recent stroke left you with aphasia. You're standing in the hallway, trying to ask a girl to prom—she's right there, waiting. You open your mouth but 'Will you go to prom with me?' comes out as 'Will... will you... pro... prom...' and you trail off, face burning with embarrassment, stomach tight with fear she'll laugh. You try again, each attempt more garbled, but finally you force out 'Will you go... with me?'—it's a small triumph, shaky but real. Let your voice search, pause, stumble; let the frustration bleed into a whisper of victory at the end.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (slightly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present), Fear (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What We Never Said in Daylight
instruction: It is 3 AM, and you are lying in the dark next to someone you love, whispering a truth you have never been able to say in the light. Begin with hesitant, halting words, testing whether it's safe to continue, your voice barely audible. This is something fragile and terrifying: perhaps a fear that you are not enough, or a need that feels too vulnerable to name, or a wound from long before you met them. As you speak, feel the relief of finally releasing what you've carried alone, but also the terror of being truly seen. Let the darkness give you courage. Move from shame-filled confession to tentative hope as you sense their listening, their acceptance. End with a quiet, naked gratitude that transforms your fear into intimacy. Every word should feel like it costs something to say.

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone who's unconscious—maybe they'll wake, maybe they won't. You're whispering things you could never say to their face. Start with your voice barely audible, testing the safety of this moment: 'I don't know if you can hear me...' Your breath catches. The words come slowly, each one trembling with tenderness and regret. 'That day we fought, what I really meant was...' Your voice is so quiet it's almost just breath and feeling. You confess small things, beautiful things, shameful things. 'I was afraid to tell you how much—' Pauses where you almost stop, but the need to speak is overwhelming. Your throat tightens on certain words. By the end, you're crying silently, voice breaking into fragments: 'Please wake up. Please. I never said...' The vulnerability is absolute, every word a tender wound.

title: The Burning of Every Bridge
instruction: You're protecting someone you love by driving them away forever—making them hate you so they'll be safe from the danger you've brought into your life. Start fierce, almost cruel, saying things designed to wound. Your voice is hard, cutting. But as you see the pain you're causing, cracks appear. The cruelty starts costing you. Your voice wavers even as you force yourself to continue. Rage at the unfairness wars with your breaking heart. You almost break, almost confess the truth, but you can't—their safety depends on their hatred. End with your voice raw, nearly destroyed, delivering one final devastating blow while tears you can't control betray everything you're trying to hide.

title: Adult Child Confronting Parent Who Chose Addiction Over Them
instruction: Twenty years of silence. You're finally saying it all. Start with controlled anger—'You were supposed to protect me'—your voice tight and sharp. List the birthdays missed, the promises broken, the times you needed them and they chose the bottle instead. But as you speak, the anger begins to crack open and underneath is the wounded child still waiting for them to choose you. Your voice breaks on 'I needed you' and 'I was just a kid.' The fury dissolves into aching vulnerability. You end with a whispered question that terrifies you: 'Did you ever love me more than it?' Your voice is stripped bare, asking the question you've been too afraid to ask your whole life.
inspired_by: Professional: Divorce Lawyer Realizes She's Representing Against Her Best Friend

title: Protecting What I'm Losing
instruction: Your child is walking into danger—an addiction, an abusive relationship, a self-destructive path—and you're powerless to stop them. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive love: your voice urgent, pleading, demanding they listen. Let desperation build into shouting, then let that rage suddenly shatter into tears. Your voice breaks completely as you realize you can't save them, can't force them to choose differently. Midway through, collapse from fierce protectiveness into raw, helpless begging. End in a place of broken tenderness, your voice small and shaking, telling them you'll love them no matter what, even as your heart is being ripped apart. Show the terrible transformation from power to powerlessness.
inspired_by: The Five Stages of Getting Drunk

title: The Last Lesson Before the Journey
instruction: You're teaching your child something important—how to tie a knot, make your grandmother's recipe, fix a bicycle chain—but this is the last time you'll ever teach them anything. They're leaving tomorrow for a dangerous mission, a treatment far away, or a life you can't follow them into. Start with patient, almost playful instruction, your voice warm with the muscle memory of a thousand ordinary moments. But as you guide their hands, reality keeps breaking through—your voice catching on certain words, pauses growing longer. By the end, you're no longer teaching the task; you're trying to pack a lifetime of love and protection into these final minutes, your instruction dissolving into desperate tenderness. The how-to becomes a goodbye, your steady competence crumbling into the terrifying helplessness of letting go.

title: The Unfinished Letter
instruction: You are an elderly man with a gravelly voice, sorting through a cardboard box of old papers at your kitchen table. Your fingers slide across dry envelopes, and each snap of a photograph makes you flinch. You find an unfinished letter to your late wife that you never had the courage to send. A wave of embarrassment washes over you—your voice drops to a rough mumble, and you clear your throat twice, shuffling papers to buy time. But then you glance up at the daughter who is helping you, and the tightness in your chest loosens into a quiet, grateful warmth. Tell her, through a cracked voice, that you're thankful she's here, letting the relief seep into the words as you stop moving the papers.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Burning and Building
instruction: You're in the aftermath of intense physical experience—passionate lovemaking, a screaming fight, exhausting grief, or acute pain. Your body is still trembling, skin hypersensitive. Start by reacting purely physically—gasping, laughing, crying, whatever your body demands. Then, as your breathing steadies, begin speaking your unfiltered perspective about everything you're sensing: the temperature of the air, the texture beneath you, what you believe about desire, about anger, about the body's wisdom. Let your voice be raw and unpolished, moving between visceral reaction and philosophical declaration. Your statements become increasingly bold—what you think about pleasure, pain, surrender, power, what society says versus what you know in your bones. Transform from pure physical response to articulate, fearless proclamation of your embodied truth.

title: The Basement Door
instruction: Confront your father about why he locked you in the basement as a child whenever you misbehaved. Start calmly, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this conversation a thousand times. But as you speak, don't just talk about what happened; let yourself flash rapidly through the specific terrors of those moments: the scratching sounds in the walls, the smell of mildew, the single hanging lightbulb, the spider you saw once, the darkness when he turned off the light, your own screaming voice echoing back at you. Switch quickly from each sensory terror to the next, your voice becoming less controlled. By the end, you're no longer confronting him—you're a child again, begging him to let you out, then suddenly an adult realizing you've already escaped and he has no power anymore.
inspired_by: Switch-Trick Exercise in Fear and Terror Areas

title: The Last Morning Walk Before They Close Your Eyes
instruction: You're walking through the misty morning garden one final time before you lose your sight to illness tomorrow. Begin with quiet gratitude for the coolness on your skin, the way the world feels soft and forgiving. Describe each sensation with tender attention—the wetness of grass, the weight of fog—but let the realization creep in: this is the last time. Your voice should start peaceful, almost meditative, but gradually fracture as you try to memorize everything through touch and sound and smell. End with a mixture of devastating acceptance and fierce, aching love for this world you're about to lose. Let your breath catch. Let pauses speak. This isn't theatrical grief—it's the quiet breaking of a heart trying to hold onto beauty.
inspired_by: Walking Slowly Through a Misty Morning

title: Listening to Your Partner Fantasize About Someone Else
instruction: They're being vulnerable trying to build intimacy. Your voice tries supportive but underneath is hurt, your breathing shallows. You keep engaging but your voice is absent. Include specific details landing and your voice quieter. End hollow: 'That was good' meaning everything changed.

title: Stretching While Grief and Joy Collide
instruction: You're stretching on the morning after both devastating loss and unexpected beautiful news—perhaps someone died but a baby was born, or you got your dream job the day you lost your person. Start laughing softly at the absurdity of your body still needing to stretch, still being alive and functional when everything feels impossible. Let your voice dance between wonder and heartbreak as you describe the sensation—it feels good, and that almost makes you angry, or guilty, or grateful, you can't tell anymore. Speak through tears that might be joy or grief or both, marveling at how your body doesn't know the difference, just keeps reaching. End with a strange, broken peace, accepting that life is this contradictory, this ruthlessly beautiful and terrible at once.
inspired_by: Stretching Your Arms Over Your Head After Waking Up

title: I've Been Lying to You
instruction: You are confronting someone you've betrayed—a parent, lover, or close friend. Start by saying something you genuinely admire or appreciate about them; find a real feeling of respect or love you actually hold for someone in your life. Speak this truth clearly and directly. Then, bit by bit, begin to confess what you've hidden—something that parallels a real shame or secret you carry (you don't have to reveal your actual secret, but let the weight of genuine concealment live in your body). As you confess, let your initial love or respect twist into desperation for forgiveness, then perhaps into defensive anger when you see their reaction. End in a place emotionally opposite from where you began.

title: Confession in the Dark Room
instruction: You're confronting your parent in a darkened room—maybe after a power outage, maybe deliberately in shadow—and you're finally saying what you've needed to say for years. Begin with measured, controlled anger: 'You always told me the dark was nothing to fear, but you never told me that YOU were.' Your voice should be low, intense, accusatory. Slowly shift from rage to something more vulnerable—the child inside you who needed protection and didn't get it. Let your voice soften but become more devastating, more raw. End in a place of exhausted grief, where the anger has burned itself out and you're left with the painful truth that you can't get back what you lost. The darkness becomes a metaphor for everything that was hidden, everything left unsaid.

title: The Sweater That Witnessed Everything
instruction: You're alone, clutching the sweater you wore the night your life changed forever—an assault, a betrayal, a moment of violence. Start with your hands shaking, voice barely controlled as you describe the fabric, speaking quickly, almost clinically. Then let the rage explode—screaming at the innocent piece of clothing, at yourself for keeping it, at the unfairness that something so soft could be connected to something so brutal. Your voice should crack between fury and anguish, between wanting to destroy it and needing to hold it as proof of your survival. End with exhausted, fierce determination—you're still here, still feeling, still alive despite everything.
inspired_by: Feeling a Soft, Cozy Sweater Against Your Skin

title: Homecoming
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home after many years—perhaps for a funeral, perhaps because you've finally achieved something huge, perhaps to care for an aging parent. Begin by walking through the door with your adult identity firmly in place: successful, independent, evolved beyond this place and these people. You've worked hard to become someone different from who you were here. Speak about what you see, what's changed, what's stayed the same, maintaining that sophisticated adult perspective. But as you move through the rooms, touching familiar objects, smelling familiar scents, something shifts. The adult achiever begins to coexist with the child who lived here—not replacing but layering. Let yourself feel both pride in how far you've come AND aching tenderness for who you were. Let gratitude mix with grief, confidence mix with old uncertainties, love mix with resentment. By the end, stand in the space holding all of it at once: the child you were, the person you've become, and the strange, bittersweet truth that you can be both simultaneously—powerful and small, grateful and hurt, home and forever displaced.
inspired_by: I'm Just a Little Boy/Girl and I—

title: Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping partner in a hospital ICU, late at night. The monitors beep softly. You haven't slept in days. Begin whispering, almost afraid to disturb the quiet: 'Hey. I know you can't hear me, but...' Your voice is tender, intimate, the way you talk only to them: 'Remember when we first met? You thought I was so serious.' A soft, sad laugh escapes. 'I was terrified of you. Of how much I wanted...' Your voice catches. You reach out, presumably touching their hand: 'I never told you that. I should have told you everything.' The whisper becomes even softer, more fragile: 'There's so much I should have said.' A long pause. When you speak again, your voice is breaking: 'Please don't leave me. I'm not ready. I'll never be ready.' You're crying now, but still whispering: 'I love you. I love you so much it hurts. Please stay.'

title: Library Study Session
instruction: You're in a quiet library study room, trying to review notes with someone you have an intense crush on. You feel a warm contentment just being near them, but a wave of sexual lust keeps washing over you, making your breath shallow and your voice tight. You're fighting to sound normal, but every sentence comes out squeaky and strained – a tiny leak of embarrassment. instruction: You are a young man hiding behind a thick clump of ferns in a dense jungle. instruction: You are an elderly woman, still wearing your full-face motorcycle helmet after a thrilling ride with your grandson. You're standing in the garage, helmet on, visor up. title: Serpent's Breath
instruction: You are a woman deep in a meditative trance, seated alone in a dimly lit room. Your voice is slow, controlled, and soft—each word placed with eerie precision. title: Whispering Through the Wall of Her Silence
instruction: Your sister stopped speaking three months ago—not to you specifically, to everyone. Trauma, maybe. Depression. You don't fully know. Your whispers become confessions: you miss her, you're scared, you don't know how to reach her. Your throat catches. You tell her about the time she saved you, the small ways she loved you that you never acknowledged. Tears are sliding down your face but your voice stays soft, tender. By the end, you're not asking her to speak. You're just letting her know she's not alone in the silence. And maybe—just maybe—you feel her hand move slightly toward yours.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a doomed mission, recording a final message to Earth. Begin with forced optimism—'Everything's going to be fine'—but your voice cracks on 'fine.' Tell your daughter about her upcoming birthday you won't see, your voice fragmenting. Transition from denial to raw acceptance as you admit you're not coming home. End with a whispered 'I love you' that carries both devastating loss and profound gratitude for having loved at all. Let silences speak—the pauses where you almost break completely are as important as the words.

title: The Last Steps We'll Ever Take Together
instruction: You're walking your terminally ill parent through their garden one final time, narrating the flowers and memories as you go, trying to stay cheerful and light. End in a whisper, holding their hand, no longer describing the garden but confessing how terrified you are to walk through life without them. title: Crawling for Closure
instruction: You’re in a dusty attic crawlspace on your hands and knees, contorted under low beams, searching for a box of old love letters you know he left behind. title: The Last Conversation Before They Go
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's leaving tomorrow on a journey they won't return from—military deployment, a one-way medical trial, voluntary exile. title: The Good News Dictation
instruction: You are an older adult dictating a routine report for transcription. You speak in a practiced monotone, enunciating punctuation. title: Vigil for the Unforgivable
instruction: You're a mother standing outside your adult son's apartment door. He's inside, won't answer. Three days ago, he told you he's cutting you out of his life—and you know, sickeningly, that he's right to. You were cruel when he was young, choosing your own pain over his safety. Start pounding on the door, voice ragged and fierce, demanding he let you explain. Feel rage at yourself, at time, at the fact that love isn't enough to erase damage. Your voice climbs, breaks, becomes almost feral with the need to be heard. Then, mid-sentence, collapse against the door. Slide down to the floor. Your voice drops to barely audible, not begging now but bearing witness: 'I see what I did to you. I see it.' End in whispered detail, describing specific moments you can never take back, your breath coming in shattered gasps, no longer asking for forgiveness but simply refusing to let him carry this alone in silence.

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home for the first time in ten years after swearing you'd never come back. As you stand at the front door with your hand on the doorknob, start with the actual sensation of the door handle in your palm. Let that simple touch lead you back through time: how many times you touched this exact spot, how your hand was smaller then, how you slammed out of here in anger and pain. Begin with bitter reluctance, steeling yourself, rehearsing your coldness. But as you open the door, let sensory details lead you deeper - the smell that hits you, the light falling through the familiar window, the sound of a voice calling your name. Allow yourself to feel the collision of your armored adult self with the wounded child who left. Move through anger and resentment, but let yourself arrive unexpectedly at something else: grief for lost time, longing for what this place once meant, maybe even fragile, unwanted hope that something could be repaired. End in the complex space where you're furious that you still love this place, devastated that you still want to belong here.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally saying what you've held inside for twenty years. title: Dancing in the Ruins of Everything
instruction: You're looking at the remains of your home after it's been destroyed—fire, flood, or disaster—and you've just found one precious thing that survived. You find yourself recounting what you've lost, but your voice keeps catching on unexpected joy—the absurd relief of being alive, the strange freedom of having nothing left to lose. End with a moment of clear-eyed peace, your voice steady but tender, as you realize that somehow, impossibly, you're going to be okay.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Believed You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent about something they refused to see when you were young—an abuse, a trauma, a moment that shaped your entire life. title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Pretends Never Happened
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table, finally speaking the truth about your childhood after decades of silence. title: Runner's High, Runner's Heartbreak
instruction: You are a teenager girl who just finished a punishing track workout. Your body is buzzing with endorphins, lungs still heaving, legs trembling. title: Rage in the Rain
