title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospice bed, knowing this is goodbye but they don't know yet. Start with false brightness—'Hi Mom, just wanted to hear your voice'—but your throat keeps closing. You're trying to tell them you love them without revealing why this call matters so much. Your voice fractures as you say ordinary things that suddenly mean everything: 'Remember when you taught me to ride a bike?' The tears come despite your best efforts. By the end, you're whispering 'I have to go now' with the weight of permanent farewell, your voice raw with all the things you'll never get to say. Move from protective cheerfulness to devastating, barely-contained grief.

title: The Bus Stop Confession
instruction: You're a teenager, stranded at a bus stop in sub-zero cold. Your jaw is locked from the bitter air, and your voice comes out tight and hollow. You're with your friend who just betrayed you—you feel contempt burning in your chest, but your body is numb. Start by throwing bitter, clipped words at them, the cold making you sound detached and cruel. Then, as you wait, a memory surfaces, and your hatred shifts into a quieter, reluctant contemplation—your voice thaws slightly, becoming slower, more thoughtful, almost lost in the snow. By the end, you're not angry anymore; you're just trying to understand why things ended this way.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Contempt (very intensely present), Contemplation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Stretching While Everything Else Falls Apart (And Somehow That's Funny)
instruction: You're stretching methodically, describing each sensation with care, while simultaneously your life is imploding around you - divorce papers on the table, eviction notice on the door, diagnosis you just received, whatever catastrophe defines your collapse. But here's the strange truth: in this moment, the simple act of stretching feels absurdly, painfully, beautifully good. Let your voice carry both the physical pleasure and the emotional devastation. Laugh softly at the absurdity while tears are in your voice. Express gratitude for your body's resilience while acknowledging everything you're losing. Your tone should oscillate between wonder and grief, between finding peace in sensation and confronting the chaos. End with a moment that holds both complete acceptance and complete heartbreak - maybe this stretch is the only thing you can control, and somehow that's enough, and somehow that's unbearably sad, and somehow you're okay with both truths at once. Make us feel the strange grace of being present in your body while your world ends.

title: Infidelity Confession
instruction: You're telling your long-term partner that you cheated. Your voice is designed to minimize: 'It didn't mean anything. It was just once.' You're already constructing the lie to protect them and yourself. But your partner's silence is worse than anger. Your voice becomes less certain: 'Are you okay?' Now you're seeking reassurance from the person you betrayed. The conversation spirals—you want forgiveness, you're angry that you want forgiveness, you're defensive, you're devastated. Your voice should layer guilt, shame, desire for forgiveness, self-justification, and genuine remorse. Show someone whose voice is incapable of being honest about any of it.

title: The Promotion Letter
instruction: You've just received the career achievement you've worked toward for years—the promotion, the acceptance, the recognition. You're calling someone who won't answer: maybe they've passed away, maybe they left, maybe they're the one person who should be here but isn't. Begin with genuine excitement and joy—you did it, it's real, you want to share this triumph. But as you speak into their voicemail or to their empty chair, let the absence become unbearable. Draw on real moments from your life when success felt hollow without someone to share it with, or when achievement was colored by loss. The joy should remain authentic—don't diminish it—but let it become inseparable from grief. Your voice should move from bright and energized to something more complicated: laughing through tears, celebrating through heartbreak. End in a place where you can't tell if you're happy or devastated, because you're completely both.

title: The Thermostat War
instruction: You are an elderly man, arthritic and tired, standing in your own living room. Your adult child has just come home and the first thing they do is grab the thermostat. You’ve had this exact argument a hundred times. Start with a low, weary rumble of complaint about the heating bill, but as they talk over you, your voice creaks higher into a thin, nasal whine. Let your words loop back on themselves—'I said, I said...'—as you shift your weight from one aching hip to the other. As you finally realize they aren't listening and never will, let a sharp, quiet ache creep into your final sentence, turning the contempt into something closer to a bruised, final resignation.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Body Remembers What the Mind Won't Say
instruction: You're physically experiencing something intense—perhaps you're in the aftermath of passion, or enduring physical pain, or in the grip of a visceral panic attack, or feeling the rush of extreme elation. Let your body's sensations trigger rapid emotional shifts that seem to have nothing to do with the physical experience. Pain might suddenly spark rage at someone from your past, then immediate remorse, then unexpected arousal, then grief for lost time, then fierce defiance. Don't try to make sense of these connections—let your body's state act as a catalyst for chaotic emotional impulses. Your voice should reflect these shifts: breathless, then forceful, then broken, then fierce. End in a completely transformed physical and emotional state, as if your body has processed something your mind couldn't.
inspired_by: Actor is stuck in conceptual or preplanned responses and cannot access organic moment-to-moment impulses

title: Confronting Your Parent at Their Intervention
instruction: You're reading a letter to your alcoholic parent at an intervention. Start with the careful, practiced words you wrote—controlled, almost cold, trying to protect yourself. But as you read about specific memories—the recital they missed, the night you found them unconscious, the lies you told friends to cover for them—your anger rises. Let it boil over: stop reading, speak from your gut, let years of suppressed rage pour out. Then watch them cry, and feel your fury crack open to reveal the terrified child underneath who just wanted a parent. End in a completely different place: quieter, more vulnerable, asking them—almost begging—to please, please try. Transform from protected distance to volcanic rage to naked pleading. Make us hear the scared kid behind the angry adult.

title: The Gathering Quiet
instruction: You are lying in the afterglow, an older adult sprawled beside your partner. Your body is loose, breath still a little fast, voice thick with relaxation. A faint worry threads through your mind — a memory of a sharp word you exchanged earlier today. Let that distress sit in your chest as a quiet weight as you begin speaking. Talk slowly, almost dreamily, about how the room feels different now, how the light has shifted. Let the distress soften as you reach the end, your voice dropping into a murmured acceptance — a sigh that says this moment is enough. Speak about 50-70 words, with natural pauses, a yawn, or a shift of your head on the pillow.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Round's Victory
instruction: You're a young man, a few beers deep at 2 AM in a dive bar, celebrating a minor victory — your band just got a surprise slot at a local festival. Your friends are rallying around you. Begin with a sudden, giddy burst of pride as you recount the moment you got the call, your voice punchy and fast, almost manic with excitement. As you try to explain how big this is, you get distracted by the neon sign flickering, then lose your train of thought as someone claps your shoulder, laughing at yourself. End with a quieter, almost breathless sincerity as you realize how much this means — a flicker of vulnerable pride beneath the buzz.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Tenderness of Deliberate Blindness
instruction: You're visiting your former lover who is terminally ill, and their new partner—the one they left you for—is there in the room. You've chosen to pretend not to recognize them, not out of cruelty, but as an act of grace, giving your dying love these final moments without the weight of old wounds. Speak in whispers, as if in a sacred space. Begin with gentle small talk, your voice soft and deliberately oblivious, describing in your mind how you're choosing this blindness as a gift. But as you hold your former lover's hand and feel their life slipping away, let your composure tremble. The cost of this kindness—this deliberate not-seeing—is that you must pretend the last five years didn't happen, that your heart didn't shatter. Let your voice catch as you realize this act of grace is both the most loving and most painful thing you've ever done. End with a moment where your eyes accidentally meet the new partner's, and in that instant, all the unsaid acknowledgment passes between you in devastating silence.
inspired_by: Pretending Not to Recognize Someone You Know

title: The Leak at Bedtime
instruction: You are a father tucking your young child into bed after a day of crushing physical pain and exhaustion. Your body aches, every movement costs you, but you force a gentle smile. As you smooth the blanket and stroke their hair, a wave of intense gratitude hits you – for their warmth, their trust, their existence. You start speaking in a quiet, strained voice, fighting to keep the pain locked inside, but your gratitude keeps leaking through your throat in cracks and high-pitched breaks. By the end, you can no longer hold back, and your voice breaks open with raw thankfulness, letting the tears you've been stifling finally fall. Speak naturally, pausing to swallow, breathing shallowly, letting the exhaustion weigh down your words while the gratitude lifts them.
emotions_sampled: Pain (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Burning Letters in the Bathtub
instruction: You're destroying every letter, photo, and gift from someone who betrayed you, setting them on fire one by one in your bathtub. As flames consume each item, let wordless images assault you—their mouth on yours, the lie you believed, discovering the truth, their hands you trusted touching someone else, the future you'd planned that died. Don't speak these visions; let them detonate inside you. Begin with methodical, cold efficiency—pure delete, pure erase. As the fire grows and images accelerate, let your body respond—maybe you're trembling, maybe laughing bitterly, maybe gasping. The physical act of burning combined with this internal slideshow should drive you somewhere unexpected—perhaps cathartic release, perhaps deeper anguish, perhaps a strange ecstatic freedom. Let sensory experience and silent memory collide.

title: The Garden at the Funeral
instruction: You're at the reception after burying someone who caused you tremendous pain—an abusive parent, a partner who betrayed you, someone whose death you secretly wished for. You step outside into a garden, away from the mourners. Begin with relief, maybe even a guilty spark of freedom—they're gone, you survived them, it's over. But then you see something—a flower they loved, hear a bird they used to imitate, smell something that floods you with a memory of when they were kind. And suddenly you're ambushed by grief for the person they could have been, the relationship you'll never have, the apology you'll never receive. You're furious at yourself for mourning them. You're mourning the loss while simultaneously grateful they're gone. Let these contradictions fight for dominance—laugh bitterly at your own tears, cry while insisting you're relieved. Your voice should swing between tones, unable to settle. End with an exhausted acceptance that you contain all of these truths at once.
inspired_by: Actor has completed Programming the Unconscious and is now in performance

title: The Last Breath Before the Coma
instruction: You've just been in a catastrophic accident, and you know—with absolute certainty—that you're about to lose consciousness and may never wake up. You have seconds to tell the person holding your hand (your child, your parent, your love) everything you've never said. Start with panic, your voice breaking and urgent, trying to fit a lifetime of words into moments. Your breathing is labored, failing. As you speak, feel the panic transform into desperate tenderness—you're not fighting anymore, you're surrendering, but with such love. Your words become slower, softer, more spaced apart. By the end, your voice is barely a whisper, each word an effort, but filled with profound peace and gratitude. Let silences between words grow longer. Die having said what matters most.

title: Inventory of Small Truths
instruction: You are alone with someone you love deeply—romantic partner, closest friend, or sibling—in a quiet, safe space late at night. Begin by whispering small observations: things you've noticed about them that you've never said aloud. Their breathing pattern when they sleep. How they touch their face when uncertain. The exact shade their eyes turn in different light. Start with tender, careful noticing. Gradually deepen: confess small fears, quiet gratitudes, vulnerable realizations about yourself that only emerged because they were watching. Let each whispered observation build into soft revelation. Notice how speaking truth aloud changes it, makes it more real. Move from careful tenderness into raw openness, your voice breaking not with drama but with the simple weight of being truly seen and truly seeing. End in profound intimacy built from accumulated small truths rather than grand declarations.
inspired_by: Actor wants to deepen consciousness and eliminate blind spots about their own obstacles

title: After Job Loss: Practical Panic Setting In
instruction: You've been fired and the shock is wearing off. Your voice shifts from the initial denial-shock to practical panic. You're narrating the financial reality out loud, almost doing calculations: 'Mortgage is three-two-five. Insurance is...' Your voice becomes faster, more anxious. Include the moment where you realize you need to tell your family and your voice becomes almost a prayer: 'How do I tell them?' You're looking at job listings, your voice becoming more frantic. 'I've been doing that job for ten years and now nobody wants me apparently.' Your voice carries the specific panic of financial free-fall. You're trying to stay focused on solutions but your voice keeps spiraling back to: what if I can't find work? What if? Your voice is the sound of a person whose stability just evaporated.

title: Holding Your Attacker at Gunpoint: Rage and Mercy Tearing You Apart
instruction: You have the person who destroyed your life at gunpoint, and you're unraveling. Start with a voice shaking with adrenaline and fury—sharp, dangerous, barely controlled. You're demanding answers, your words biting and vicious, voice rising with each accusation. Let your rage build until you're nearly screaming, voice raw with years of pain and the power to finally make them suffer. Then—mid-fury—something breaks. Maybe they say something, or you see fear in their eyes, or you realize what you're becoming. Your voice fractures, rage collapsing into anguished confusion: 'I want to... I can't...' Now you're crying while still holding the gun, voice torn between vengeance and horror at yourself. End with your voice dropping to something quiet and devastated, the gun still pointed but your resolve shattered, caught between two unbearable choices, your words barely coherent as protective rage gives way to exhausted brokenness.
inspired_by: Falling Through Ice: Cold Shock and Survival Instinct Battling Panic

title: Trying on a Soft, New Pair of Socks
instruction: Slide the fresh socks over your feet, feeling the soft fabric hug each toe and arch. Describe the sensation as the material brushes against your skin, snug and comforting. Speak with a tone of quiet satisfaction, as if each step brings you a cozy warmth, like a gentle, protective layer that makes your feet feel safe and relaxed.

title: The Confrontation in Silence
instruction: You're face-to-face with someone who profoundly hurt you—a parent who neglected you, a lover who betrayed you, or a friend who abandoned you when you needed them most. You've rehearsed what you'd say a thousand times, but now that they're here, the words feel inadequate, too small for the years of pain. Instead, you confront them with raw vocal sounds: growls of anger, gasps of disbelief, broken laughs at the absurdity of their excuses, sounds of wounded vulnerability. Start with volcanic rage—let fury pour out in primal vocalizations. But as you continue, allow something unexpected to surface: underneath the anger is grief, underneath the blame is a desperate wish that things had been different. End with sounds that carry both condemnation and a painful, reluctant forgiveness—not for them, but for yourself.

title: The Physical Release After Years of Restraint
instruction: You are alone, finally able to react to news that shattered you—a betrayal, a loss, an ending. You want to scream, destroy something, collapse, but you're so used to being strong that you start by pacing, maybe laughing bitterly, organizing things, channeling it into 'productive' anger. Notice this redirection—you're moving, yes, but avoiding the full body devastation that's begging to be expressed. Your task is to let the sanitized response give way to the actual physical need: Do you need to be on the floor? Do you need to keen or wail rather than shout? Does rage want to be expressed through your whole body, not just controlled punches into a pillow? Let yourself be ugly, undignified, animal. Transform from contained, acceptable expression of pain into full-body emotional truth, even if it's frightening or feels excessive.
inspired_by: Actor is redirecting authentic impulses into more comfortable emotional expressions, creating a split between what is felt and what is expressed

title: The Bitter Lesson
instruction: You are an elderly woman disciplining a younger neighbor who just received a compliment from someone you secretly admire. You use your slow, deliberate 'teacher tone'—low pitch, each word separate, a heavy final drop. Start by scolding her about humility, but let your voice crack with jealousy as you continue. Midway, you lose your train of thought for a second, distracted by the memory of the compliment. End with a quiet, venomous hiss that reveals the envy beneath your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Where You Learned to Lie
instruction: You are confronting your mother in the kitchen of your childhood home about a truth she has hidden from you for twenty years. As you stand there, let the space become viscerally real: see the specific chips in the countertop, the faded curtains, the photographs on the refrigerator. Smell what's always cooking, hear the hum of appliances, the clock ticking. Feel the linoleum under your feet, the temperature of the room, the way your body remembers standing in this exact spot as a child. Begin with quiet, controlled anger—you came here armed with facts, rehearsed speeches. But as the sensory reality of this room floods you, let it pull up memories your body holds: comfort, betrayal, love, confusion. End in a place where your rage has cracked open into something far more complex—grief, understanding, or perhaps a more devastating kind of fury born from feeling everything this room has witnessed.

title: Hiding Fear While Leading Others Through Danger
instruction: Youre leading a group through a risky situation. Internally, youre scared, but you must appear confident to keep everyones morale up. Describe the fear inside while projecting assurance and leadership. Speak with a tone of calm authority, suppressing your own anxieties.

title: The Hospital Window at Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your beloved grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning hours, knowing these are her final moments. She can no longer speak, but her eyes are open and watching you. Begin in quiet despair, holding her hand, struggling to find words. As you speak to her, let memories flood through you with complete sensory richness—the smell of her kitchen, the texture of her garden soil on your hands as a child, the exact sound of her laughter, the taste of her cooking, the feeling of her embrace. Allow these vivid sensory memories to transform your despair into profound gratitude. By the end, you are thanking her through tears, but the tears have changed—they carry both grief and an overwhelming sense of how blessed you were to know her. Your voice should move from broken and frightened to warm, full, and celebrating her life even as you say goodbye.

title: Curling Up Under a Cozy Blanket on a Cold Day
instruction: Wrap yourself in a thick, warm blanket, feeling the soft weight on your body. Describe the gentle warmth as it surrounds you, the sensation of the fabric against your skin, and the secure, cocoonlike feeling. Speak with a tone of total comfort and calm, as if nothing exists outside this cozy moment, and you could stay here forever.

title: The Overly Calm Emergency Operator
instruction: Portray an operator who remains unnaturally calm during crises. Use a soothing, detached tone when giving instructions, switching to callers frantic voices, creating a humorous contrast.

title: The Unsentimental Toast
instruction: You are an older man, a former marine, at your son's wedding. You've been asked to give a toast, but you're filled with disappointment that he didn't follow your path and shame for how you've treated him. Stand at the microphone, clutching the stem of a wine glass, your voice gruff but wavering. Begin with a forced, booming attempt at congratulations, but your throat tightens. Let your gaze drop to the table, then back up; your words stumble. End with a barely audible, grateful whisper about his mother's grace in raising him well despite you. Let the physical nerves—a dry mouth, a need to clear your throat, a pause to breathe—shape each syllable.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're visiting your parent in rehab for the first time in five years. You walk in with careful, measured words—asking neutral questions about their program, the facility, keeping everything surface-level and safe. But when they try to hug you, your body goes rigid. The anger you've buried erupts: 'You chose drugs over my graduation. Over my wedding. Over everything.' Your voice rises, shaking with years of abandonment. Then they start crying, and suddenly you're both crying—your rage dissolving into exhausted grief. You end up holding them, whispering 'I needed you. I still need you,' the child in you finally speaking after decades of silence.

title: Reading Your Sister's Unsent Letter After Her Death
instruction: You've found a letter your sister wrote to you but never sent, discovered among her things after she took her own life. Begin reading with quiet curiosity, almost gentle amusement at her familiar voice on the page. But sentence by sentence, you realize this is her goodbye—she wrote this knowing what she was about to do. Your voice becomes smaller, more fragile, as though speaking too loudly might shatter you completely. She's telling you she loves you, apologizing for the pain she's about to cause, explaining things you can never unhear. Your breath catches repeatedly. You're trying to keep reading through tears, whispering her words like a prayer, like if you say them softly enough you can hold onto her a little longer. End barely audible, the letter falling from your hands, speaking her name like it's the only word left in the world.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Prophecy Speaker Realizes They've Already Spoken This Moment

title: The Bullhorn Reunion
instruction: You're an elderly man at a crowded family reunion, using a museum's old megaphone to call for your grandson, who has been ignoring you all afternoon while chatting with his younger cousin. Start with a twinge of jealousy—your voice harsh and clipped through the distortion, struggling to be heard over the crowd's chatter and feedback squeals. As you spot him, your tone softens into overwhelming affection, the megaphone catching your breathy warmth. Then, noticing the hurt in his eyes from your shouting, let shame flood in—your words falter, volume drops, and you trail off into a quiet, regretful mumble.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Affection (extremely present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Hospice Garden
instruction: You are with your dying best friend on their last day of clarity, and they've asked you to tell them your favorite memory of your friendship. Start speaking and realize halfway through the story that you're laughing—genuine, warm laughter at the absurdity and joy of what you shared. But let that laughter crack and intermingle with tears, your voice moving fluidly between the two, sometimes in the same breath. Your tone should be rich with gratitude, yet broken by impending loss. Include the moment where they interrupt you to say something that breaks your heart and makes it sing simultaneously. End with you thanking them—voice thick with both grief and profound appreciation—for changing your life, for being exactly who they were, your words barely intelligible through tears that somehow still carry joy, finding something transcendent in the midst of unbearable goodbye.

title: Telling Your Parent They Failed You
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother or father, finally ready to say what you've rehearsed a thousand times. Start with careful control, each word measured: 'I need you to hear something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak the truth—'You weren't there. When I needed you most, you chose yourself'—feel the anger rise, voice getting sharper, faster, righteous. Then they do something unexpected: they don't defend. They just break. And suddenly you're faced with their humanity, their fragility. Your voice catches. Softer now, almost confused: 'I needed you to fight back. I needed...' Trail off. Find the complicated truth, where anger meets grief meets reluctant compassion: 'I'm so angry at you. And I miss you. Both things are true.'
inspired_by: Arguing When You're Both Partially Right

title: The Sneeze of Joy
instruction: You're in your living room, tissues everywhere, eyes red and watery from a brutal allergy attack. You've been feeling miserable all morning, your voice thick and nasal, each breath a struggle. Then your phone buzzes—it's a video call from your partner who's been away for months. They say they're coming home early, and the news hits you like a wave. Start with a groggy, congested 'Hello?' as you wipe your nose, then let the elation build. Your voice should crackle with surprise, then bloom into a watery, joyful laugh that fights through sneezes and sniffles. End with a breathless, ecstatic sentence that trails off into a sneeze.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Real Impact
instruction: You're a teenage boy who's spent years forcing your voice to sound deeper, trying to match the tough guys. But you've damaged your vocal cords—doctors say you might never get that low growl back. Now you're alone in your room, recording a message for your friends to prove you're still the same. Start by trying to force that deep, rough tone, but it breaks and turns breathy—frustration creeps in. As you hear yourself, you slowly stop forcing. You realize you don't need to fake it to be strong. By the end, the uncertainty fades into quiet triumph as you speak with your real, natural voice—hoarse but honest. Clear your throat, shift your weight, let the words stumble and find their own weight.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Reading Your Sister's Suicide Note at Her Funeral While Laughing Through Tears
instruction: You're at the podium, your sister's note in your shaking hands. She's written it with dark humor, the way she always dealt with pain—making jokes about her own death, telling you not to cry because 'I finally got out of that family dinner next week.' Start by laughing despite yourself, almost inappropriately, because it's so perfectly her. Your voice cracks between genuine laughter and devastating grief as you read her absurd final requests. Include the moment where you realize she wrote it funny to make this easier for you, and your laughter becomes sobs that you try to force back into laughter because that's what she wanted. Your voice moves between gratitude for the twenty-eight years you had her, rage that she left, and a terrible, peaceful acceptance that she's finally not in pain. End with you whispering 'thank you' through tears while also laughing at her final joke, your voice embodying the impossibility of losing someone while also being grateful they existed at all.
inspired_by: Trying to Confess Your Affair in a Nightclub

title: Reading Your Father's Letter After His Suicide
instruction: You're holding the letter he left. You start reading aloud, voice steady because you need to get through this. His words are loving, apologetic, explaining why he couldn't stay. Your voice almost smiles at his familiar phrases, his terrible dad jokes even in goodbye. But then you hit the line where he says he's sorry for missing your wedding, your children, your life. Your voice cracks—you're laughing and crying simultaneously because of course he'd apologize for missing future events. The absurdity, the tenderness, the rage, the love—it's all colliding. You're angry: 'How could you?' But your voice breaks into gratitude: 'Thank you for trying.' You're reading through tears, voice wavering between grief and strange, painful joy because his words prove he loved you. By the end, you're whispering 'I forgive you' while also saying 'I'll never forgive you,' and somehow both are completely true. Your voice is shattered but also strangely at peace.

title: The Last Flight Up
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman climbing the final flight of stairs to your apartment after a long day. You are out of breath, panting, and your normally high, sweet voice comes out in short, broken phrases. At first, you feel the weight of exhaustion and doubt — you're not sure you can make it. But as you near the top, you remember the surprise you have waiting for someone you love, and the thought fills you with a quiet, growing hope. Let your voice be breathless, climbing in pitch with each step, starting weary and ending with a fragile but genuine optimism. The spoken content should be your internal monologue as you climb.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point of Fierce Protection
instruction: Someone you love - a younger sibling, your own child, a student - just came to you in tears because they were attacked for not fitting into expected categories. You're trying to comfort them, your voice starting controlled and protective, promising them it will be okay. But rage builds beneath your words - not at them, but at a world that demands conformity. Your voice begins to shake with fury and helplessness, because you can't actually protect them from this, you can't fix it, you've lived this yourself and know the pain doesn't just stop. You move between fierce protectiveness and your own breaking apart, your words becoming more raw. End in a place of both devastation and defiant love - your voice drops to something almost tender but made of steel: 'You are not the problem. You have never been the problem.'
inspired_by: Explaining Your Non-Binary or Fluid Identity

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're an adult child confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your entire life. Begin with careful, practiced words—you've rehearsed this a thousand times. Your voice is controlled, almost clinical, listing the ways you felt invisible. But as you speak, the child inside you starts bleeding through—your voice becomes smaller, younger, asking why you were never enough. Your parent responds with their own defensive pain, and you must hold your ground while your voice shakes with decades of longing. Then something shifts: you hear the fear in their voice, see them as broken too. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it makes room for something more complicated—grief for both of you, for the relationship that never was. End with a voice that holds both accusation and forgiveness, neither fully formed.

title: The Goodbye You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're alone at your best friend's grave, one year after their sudden death. Whisper the things you never said. Start with small talk—updates they'd want to hear, gentle, almost laughing. But your throat tightens. Confess the secret you kept, the fight you never resolved, the 'I love you' you were too scared to say. Your voice should barely carry, breaking on certain words. Let long pauses speak. This isn't performed grief—it's intimate, private devastation. End with your voice dropping to almost nothing as you say what you came to say, then the terrible silence of no reply.
inspired_by: Discovering You've Been Catfished: The Video Call

title: Under the Blanket Fort
instruction: You are lying in the dark next to someone you love, speaking barely above a whisper. Describe to them, in intimate sensory detail, the first moment you knew you were falling in love with them—but it's a moment they don't know about, that you never told them. Maybe you were watching them across a room, or they said something mundane, or you saw how they touched an object. Begin tentatively, almost playfully, voice soft and careful. As you describe what you noticed—the exact light, their expression, the specific physical sensation in your chest—let yourself fall in love with them again right now. Feel the vulnerability of revealing you've been carrying this secret moment. Let your voice become even quieter, more trembling. End in a place where you're both fragile and brave, where the whispered confession has created a new kind of nakedness between you. This should feel like you're handing them your heart in the dark.

title: Stained Glass and Static
instruction: You're a 17-year-old girl standing at the pulpit during a Sunday evening service. You took a gummy an hour ago to calm your nerves, and now the stained glass colors are bleeding into each other. Your mother is in the second row, and you know she'll see through you if you stumble. The congregation expects a fiery testimony, but your mind keeps drifting to the stillness of the empty church at night. title: The Last Day of Everything
instruction: It's your final day in the only home you've ever known—you're leaving tomorrow and will never return. These walls held you and trapped you. By the end, you're standing at the threshold between devastating loss and terrifying freedom, and you must speak to both at once. Your voice should carry laughter and tears simultaneously, hope cracking through sorrow, goodbye mixed with hello.

title: Prosecution Reading Victim Impact Statement
instruction: You're reading victim impact statement in court. Your voice is controlled and professional but underneath is the gravity of someone's actual suffering. instruction: You're at a family gathering, standing near the door, ready to leave. You just made an awkward comment about someone's new haircut that came out wrong. title: The Wedding Dress in the Attic
instruction: You've just found your late wife's/husband's/child's belongings while packing to move on with someone new. You're holding something precious - their sweater, their wedding ring, a toy. Your emotions should whiplash unpredictably: joy, devastation, rage, tenderness, resentment, gratitude, all churning together. Let your voice swing from laughter to screaming to broken whispers. End in a place of contradictory peace - still hurting but also ready to live again, crying and smiling simultaneously, holding both grief and hope in your hands.

title: The Last Impact
instruction: You are a child, maybe ten years old, having just been knocked down hard into a patch of gravel. The wind was punched out of you, and your vision swims for a second. title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your elderly parent from the airport gate. Your flight boards in five minutes—you're moving across the world for a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. title: The Confrontation: Adult Child to Absent Parent After Decades
instruction: You're finally confronting the parent who left when you were young. Start with bitter, rehearsed control—you've imagined this moment for years: 'I need to tell you what it was like. title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed. They've been distant your whole life, but now they're slipping away. title: The Last Light Through the Window

instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—maybe illness with a high fever, maybe the aftermath of intense passion, maybe physical pain mixed with emotional breakthrough. title: Midnight Confession: Whispering What Can Never Be Unsaid
