Your voice stays professional for a moment, then: 'Actually, we need to move. Now.' Your scientific narration becomes survival instinct. Include the moment where you're running and your voice becomes almost poetic despite the danger—describing the end of the world with a kind of reverence. Your voice cracks between technical observation ('flow rate increasing') and personal awe ('I've never seen anything so beautiful and terrible'). You escape, your voice shaking, transformed by proximity to such raw power.

title: The Fine Print of Goodbye
instruction: You are a young person with a neutral voice, reading aloud the termination clause of a creative grant you’ve just learned you didn’t receive. You expected the project to be funded for another year, and you’re swallowing deep disappointment as you mechanically recite the legal language, your eyes scanning each line. But near the end, you notice a tiny provision offering a small stipend for acknowledged work—an unexpected, faint kindness from the foundation. Your voice must start flat and rapid, fighting to stay professional, then slow slightly as you read that clause, letting a reluctant, quiet gratitude seep in beneath the monotone. Let your breath catch once or twice, and let one word—'acknowledged'—hang a moment longer than the rest.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Touch
instruction: You are an elderly woman, bleeding heavily from a wound in your side after a fall. You lie on cold ground, your strength draining. As you wait, a vivid memory of a lover's hand on your skin stirs a flicker of old lust—a desperate, aching warmth. Speak to that absent lover, your voice starting with a raw, breathy yearning as you recall their touch, then gradually slurring and fading as shock and blood loss pull you under. Let your words be interrupted by shivers and the struggle to stay conscious, the lust turning into a fragile, fading whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Quiet Victory
instruction: You are in a dark, quiet room, a migraine pressing behind your eyes. Your cat curls up beside you, purring softly, and you feel a deep, quiet contentment—just being still with her. You whisper teasingly, telling her she’s too loud, and laugh softly at your own joke. Then you realize that for the first time in hours, the pain has eased just enough to let you think—a small, fragile triumph that makes your voice lift despite the whisper.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (clearly present), Teasing (clearly present), Triumph (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in the wreckage of everything you built—a burned home, a failed marriage, a lost career—and something breaks open inside you that's part grief, part liberation. Begin with a sound that could be either laughing or crying (let it be genuinely both), describing the absurd relief of having nothing left to lose. Your voice should be textured with contradictions: gratitude for the lessons mixed with anger at the cost, joy at your survival threaded through with sorrow for what died. Let yourself find genuine humor in the devastation, then let that laughter catch in your throat and become something more complex. Speak with the strange peace that comes from rock bottom, where terror and freedom feel like the same thing. End with a statement of thanks—to the universe, to yourself, to the pain—that's simultaneously heartbroken and whole, your voice carrying both the weight of loss and the lightness of surrender. This should feel like witnessing someone find grace in disaster.

title: The Last Goodbye Before the Launch
instruction: You're speaking to someone you love who's about to leave on a one-way mission to deep space—they'll never return. You've known for months, tried to be strong, but this is the final hour. Start with practiced composure, trying to say all the right things you've rehearsed. But your voice begins to crack as the reality hits: this is actually happening. Move through determination to memorize every detail of their face, then to a breaking point where you can't pretend anymore. Your words become desperate, clinging. Then something shifts—you find a moment of genuine peace, a way to let them go with love instead of grief. End by noticing something beautiful about them you'd never quite articulated before, a final gift of真實 recognition before they disappear from your life forever.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Time Loop: The Seventh Repetition

title: What We Never Said
instruction: Late at night, you're confessing something to your sleeping lover that you can never say when they're awake. Begin in barely audible whispers—testing the words, seeing if you can even form them. It's something tender and terrifying: maybe you're not who they think you are, or you're more broken than you've let on, or you love them so much it frightens you. Your voice should be intimate, vulnerable, catching on certain words. Let quiet tears come—not dramatic sobbing, but the kind that slip out silently. End with the devastating realization that you may never have the courage to say this in daylight, and perhaps that's the saddest truth of all. This should feel like overhearing someone's most private moment with themselves.
inspired_by: The Lie That Became the Truth

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You're at your own going-away party, leaving a life you've built for reasons beyond your control—illness, deportation, witness protection, something final. You're trying to give a toast. Begin with laughter, genuine joy at these people you love, gratitude spilling over. Your voice is warm, celebratory. But the laughter keeps catching in your throat. Between sentences of appreciation, grief breaks through—your voice wavers, you have to pause, breathe. You're trying so hard to make this a happy memory for them, but you're falling apart. The joy and devastation are completely intertwined. You laugh through tears, your voice breaking on words like 'grateful' and 'blessed.' End with a strange, beautiful peace—you've accepted this impossible contradiction of loving something so much that losing it destroys you, yet feeling lucky to have had it at all. Let the conflicting emotions exist simultaneously, neither one winning.

title: I Will Burn This World Down to Protect You - Fierce Love Collapsing Into Helplessness
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt your child, partner, or younger sibling. Start with controlled fury, voice low and dangerous: 'You have no idea what you've done.' Build into righteous rage - you would destroy anything that threatens the person you love. Let your voice shake with the violence you're barely containing. But then reality crashes in - there's nothing you can actually do to fix this, to undo what happened, to protect them from this pain. Your fierce protectiveness collapses into complete helplessness. Voice breaking: 'I can't fix this. I can't make this better.' Dissolve from powerful to powerless. End in quiet devastation, maybe with a desperate plea or an apology to your loved one for not being enough. Show the transformation from warrior to someone utterly broken by the limits of love.
inspired_by: Realizing You're in an Emotionally Abusive Relationship

title: Laughing Through Your Mother's Final Story
instruction: Your mother is dying and suddenly lucid, telling you a hilarious story from her youth you've never heard—something absurd and wildly inappropriate and so perfectly her. You're laughing genuinely, tears streaming down your face, but you can hear her breath growing shallower with each sentence. She keeps making you laugh even as she's fading, because this is her final gift. Your laughter becomes sobs becomes laughter again. Express pure joy at this unexpected moment of connection while your heart is shattering because you know this is goodbye. Thank her between fits of laughter and grief, the gratitude and devastation so intertwined they're indistinguishable. She trails off mid-story, and you have to finish it for her, your voice breaking into both laughter and weeping. End in profound peace—still crying, still half-laughing, whispering 'That's perfect' as you realize she's given you the exact farewell you both needed. The contradiction is the gift: finding absolute beauty in absolute loss.

title: A Grateful Drenching
instruction: You are an older adult standing alone in a heavy thunderstorm, rain pelting your face and thunder cracking overhead. You have just received news that your long-lost friend survived a terrible accident, but your own body aches with old injuries that never healed. Start with a sour, tired tone as you complain about the weather and your pain—muttering, wiping rain from your eyes, flinching at thunder. Then, as you speak of your friend's survival, your voice lifts with sudden, fierce gratitude, almost laughing through the rain, but your breath catches when the pain in your chest returns. Let your words be halting, sometimes shouted over the storm, sometimes nearly lost in a sob. End with a quiet, thankful whisper that the rain almost drowns out.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispered Inventory
instruction: In the dark, lying next to someone you love deeply, whisper an inventory of them. Begin with the tiny things you adore—the way they breathe when sleeping, the specific warmth of their skin, their particular scent. Let your voice be intimate, tender, nearly inaudible. Then, as you continue, let yourself softly admit the one quality you've found hardest to live with, the thing you'd gently change if you could, but say it like a confession, not an accusation: 'what I find most difficult is...' or 'where I sometimes feel lost with you is...' Notice how naming it quietly, in the dark, makes it both painful and deeply connecting. End by touching their face or hand, your whisper now trembling with the vulnerability of being this honest while this close.

title: Emergency Room Prayer
instruction: Your child is in surgery after a car accident. You're in the waiting room, and someone—a chaplain, a stranger—asks if you want to talk. You start fierce, almost aggressive in your certainty: your kid is strong, they're a fighter, they're going to be fine. But as you talk about them, your voice begins to shake. You're describing how they learned to ride a bike, how stubborn they were, how brave. The fierceness cracks into terror. Your hands are trembling. You're bargaining with God, the universe, anyone—take anything, take everything, just let them live. The power in your voice drains until you're raw and broken, admitting you're helpless. End sobbing the words: 'I can't lose them. I can't. I don't know how to exist in a world without them.'

title: Breaking Through Glass
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a terminal diagnosis, a devastating loss, a freedom you never thought possible. Your body is flooded with sensation: your hands are shaking uncontrollably, your skin feels either burning hot or ice cold, your chest is tight and breath comes in gasps. Start by focusing intensely on these physical sensations—let your voice reflect the actual feeling in your body, whether it's constricted and small or wild and uncontrolled. Move if you need to, touch surfaces around you, feel the temperature of your own skin. Let the physical sensations directly trigger the emotional cascade. Maybe you smell something sharp (antiseptic, rain, smoke) or taste metal in your mouth. Begin with physical shock—your voice reflecting the body's response—but let the physical experience crack you open completely until emotion and sensation are indistinguishable. By the end, you should be in a completely different physical and emotional state, exhausted or ecstatic or destroyed, your voice transformed by what your body has endured.

title: Screaming Into the Void About Survival
instruction: You're alone in your car in an empty parking lot at 3 AM, and everything that's been building—years of holding it together, of being strong for everyone else, of swallowing your own pain—finally detonates. Start with a scream, raw and primal, not words but pure sound. Then words come flooding: everything you've survived, every time you protected someone while you were breaking, every moment you smiled while dying inside. Your voice should be fierce, furious, powerful—but then it shatters. The rage collapses into sobbing, then resurges, oscillating wildly. You're yelling at God, at fate, at yourself for enduring, at the unfairness of having to be this strong. But slowly, exhausted, something emerges: a fierce pride in your own survival, a realization of your own terrible, beautiful strength. End with your voice hoarse but steady, speaking the truth: 'I'm still here. I'm still fucking here.'

title: The Taste of Your Own Blood
instruction: You've just been in a brutal fight—physical or emotional, your choice. Your body is shaking, adrenaline coursing, maybe there's actual blood in your mouth or you're tasting the copper of pure rage. As your body trembles and burns, force yourself to really look at the person who hurt you—or who you hurt. What do you actually see in their face right now? How are they standing? Go deeper: what does their breathing pattern reveal? What's happening in their eyes? Let yourself wonder through the physical intensity: are they afraid of me? Am I afraid of myself? What have we just destroyed? Let the sensory violence in your body—shaking, tasting, burning—gradually shift as this deep observation reveals something unexpected. End in a place where the physical intensity remains but the emotion beneath it has completely transformed.

title: The Photograph That Still Makes Me Laugh
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting alone in a quiet room, holding a faded photograph of a dear friend who always understood your tics. Begin with a soft, contemplative tone as you study the image, letting your voice trail off slightly. A sudden vocal tic (like a sharp 'Ha!' or 'Hey!') interrupts, but you continue without pausing, shifting into a playful, teasing memory of how your friend would mimic your tics to make you laugh. Let your voice become bouncy, almost mischievous, as you describe the moment. End with a quieter, grateful whisper, acknowledging how lucky you were. Let your breath catch and your pitch vary naturally, as if the tics are just part of the conversation.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (slightly present), Teasing (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Lighthouse Keeper Says Goodbye to the Sea
instruction: You stand at the top of your lighthouse for the final time before automation replaces you. For forty years, this light has been your child, your companion, your reason. You speak to the sea, to the light, to the storms you've guided ships through. Begin with steady professionalism—reciting the final log entry, checking systems one last time. But as you prepare to descend those stairs forever, your voice fractures. The grief of leaving something you've loved more than any person overwhelms you. End in raw, unguarded weeping—not for yourself, but for the loneliness this light will feel without human hands to tend it. Let your voice break on the realization that you're abandoning something that needed you.
inspired_by: Historical: Executioner Performs His Final Execution Before Retirement

title: The Last Lap to Let Go
instruction: You're a teenage girl running your usual route after a painful breakup, your breath already ragged and your legs heavy with exhaustion. Halfway through, still fighting back tears, you notice the rhythm of your footsteps blending with your heartbeat, and a strange, fierce contentment starts rising in your chest. Speak as you slow to a jog, voice bouncing with each footfall, gasping for air between phrases, then letting the exhaustion melt into a quiet, exhausted peace. You might wipe sweat from your eyes, stumble over a crack, or let out a half-laugh at the absurdity of it all. Start with the sadness still raw in your voice, then let the words carry you into a breathless, honest acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Smell of Rain on Concrete
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl, exhausted after a long day of moving boxes into a new apartment in a strange city. You're sitting on the front step of your new home, clutching your favorite stuffed rabbit, when a sudden rain shower brings the smell of wet concrete — just like the street you used to play on with your best friend back in your old town. You start whispering to your rabbit, trying to explain how you feel. Your voice is heavy and sleepy, words tumbling out slowly. You pause mid-sentence, distracted by the rain sound on the awning, then forget what you were saying for a moment before the feeling returns. Let the fatigue weigh down your words, the homesickness make them soft and aching. By the end, your voice almost drops to a whisper as you realize the memory is fading.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Confrontation You've Rehearsed a Thousand Times
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a childhood wound that shaped your entire life. You've planned this speech for years, but begin the scene noticing how your body wants to protect itself—shoulders rising, jaw clenching, perhaps your arms crossing defensively. Your challenge is to recognize these physical shields as they arise and consciously let them dissolve, not by dropping your arms or arranging yourself differently, but by finding actual courage in your breath and spine. Start with the sharpness of rehearsed anger, then let it crack open into something rawer and more vulnerable. The words you've practiced should give way to messy, spontaneous truth. By the end, stand in your full power without any physical armor—genuinely free in your body, whether you're crying, raging, or reaching some unexpected peace.
inspired_by: When an actor uses physical props, leaning, or posture to appear relaxed rather than achieving genuine ease

title: The Hard Ground
instruction: You're a 17-year-old football player, lying flat on your back on the wet grass after a brutal tackle. The wind is knocked out of you, and your shoulder screams with a sharp, grinding pain—you can barely move your arm. At first, all you feel is that searing pain, your voice a tight, breathy rasp as you struggle to speak, maybe wincing and pausing to try to catch your breath. As the initial shock fades, you start to hear the disappointed murmurs from the bleachers, realizing you just fumbled the championship game—your voice drops lower, heavier, thick with defeat. By the end, you're just staring at the clouds, whispering to yourself, barely audible, wondering if you'll ever get a chance like that again, your tone shifting from raw agony to a hollow, quiet disappointment laced with distant contemplation.
emotions_sampled: Pain (very intensely present), Disappointment (extremely present), Contemplation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Cascade of Conquest
instruction: You are a confident, triumphant lover, lying with your partner after a long, playful struggle. You have just won a silent game of will, and the last wave of your own mountaintop has subsided into shuddering breaths. As your heart hammers and your voice is a wreck—cracking, hoarse, and little more than a whisper—you gloat. Start with a raw, broken laugh of victory, then tease them with a raspy 'You thought you could outlast me?' Let the contempt be a warm, playful taunt, not vicious. As you speak, feel another faint tremor of aftershock ripple through you, making your final words barely a breath. End with a quiet, devastatingly smug giggle that trails into silence.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Teasing (slightly present), Contempt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent what you've needed to say for thirty years. Start with measured control, almost clinical: 'I got glasses today. Saw things clearly for the first time.' Use this as your metaphor, your way in. But as you continue, let the pain start cracking through: 'And I realized—I've been waiting my whole life for you to see me. Really see me.' Your voice should fracture and rebuild multiple times as decades of invisible wounds surface. Get specific—name the moments they missed, the times you needed them and they looked right through you. 'I was right there. Right in front of you. And you never...' Let rage and grief trade places. The desperate child and the furious adult should both be present in your voice. End not with resolution but with exhausted truth: 'I needed you to see me. I still do. And I don't know if you ever will.' The last line should be barely audible, a confession that costs you everything to speak.

title: Holding the Edge
instruction: You are in a hot power yoga class, holding a demanding pose—your thighs are trembling, sweat drips from your brow, and your ujjayi breath is a shaky ocean roar. You're speaking to yourself, barely above a whisper, as you fight to stay in position. Begin with the quivering strain of your muscles, a quiet doubt that you can last another breath. As the seconds pass, let the tremor in your voice soften into a fragile, hopeful warmth—you realize you are stronger than you thought, and a genuine smile of optimism cracks through the exhaustion. Speak as if you are both the teacher and the student, coaxing yourself through the fire.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Burning Orchard
instruction: You are an old farmer standing in your flooded orchard during a thunderstorm. At the start, you feel a fierce triumph, shouting at the sky because the rain has finally come to save your dying trees after a year of drought. But as the rain pours, you notice the greedy landlord's new fence line has been washed away by the same storm—and a deep, intense disgust rises, because he had been poisoning the soil behind it. Your voice starts loud and victorious, but gradually drops into a bitter, contemptuous mutter. Water drips off your beard and you have to pause to wipe it from your eyes. A single clap of thunder makes you flinch mid-sentence.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Contemplation (clearly present), Disgust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You are giving a toast at your ex-lover's wedding—the person you thought you'd marry, who is now marrying someone else. Begin from the part of you that is gracious, evolved, sincerely happy for them—and you genuinely are. Speak with warmth and real joy for their happiness. But as you continue, let another part seep in: the part that is still grieving, still in love, still shattered. Don't abandon the joy—let both truths coexist. Your voice may brighten with genuine delight at their laughter, then catch with barely concealed heartbreak. By the end, you are holding both realities: authentic happiness for them and authentic devastation for yourself, smiling through tears, blessing them while breaking. Move from pure generosity to a complex tangle of love, loss, joy, and quiet anguish existing simultaneously.

title: Protective Fury Meets Helplessness
instruction: Your teenage child just told you something that breaks your world—they've been hurt by someone you trusted, or they're in danger you can't prevent, or they're leaving to do something that might destroy them. Start with explosive anger—not at them, but at the universe, at whoever caused this, at yourself for not seeing it. Your voice is fierce, almost violent in its intensity: 'How could they—' But mid-sentence, the fury collapses. Your voice cracks and suddenly you're begging, pleading, your words tumbling over each other. The protectiveness remains but transforms into desperate vulnerability. End on your knees emotionally, voice reduced to a broken whisper: 'Please don't go where I can't follow.' Let the shift from rage to devastated helplessness be swift and complete, like a building collapsing.

title: Shielding the Unshieldable
instruction: You're a parent standing between danger and your child, voice rising to a roar of protective fury that could tear the world apart—fierce, primal, absolutely unbreakable. Then suddenly cut to helplessness: you cannot actually protect them from what's coming (illness, deployment, their own choices, the future). Let your rage shatter into shaking desperation, your voice breaking into pleas, then further into choked sobs as you realize your own powerlessness. Cycle between trying to summon that fierce strength again and collapsing back into vulnerable terror. End in a whispered promise you don't know if you can keep, your voice raw and stripped of everything but love and fear.
inspired_by: An Apology to a Future Self

title: Grateful for the Ending
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you loved deeply, but the relationship was also destroying you both, and you're finding peace in the letting go. Begin with genuine warmth: 'I'm so glad you were in my life.' As you speak about what you're grateful for, let sadness weave through the appreciation—your voice should smile and break simultaneously. Move into the paradox: 'And I'm grateful it's ending' delivered with both relief and grief. You might laugh softly through tears, or your voice might be steady while your heart is shattering in the right way. Acknowledge the beauty and the pain as inseparable: 'We loved each other and that wasn't enough, and that's okay.' End in a place of bittersweet wholeness, voice carrying both mourning and freedom. The entire performance should feel like watching a sunset—beautiful and sad and exactly right.

title: Stargazer's Confession
instruction: You are a seasoned astronaut on a spacewalk, your helmet sealed, breathing loud in your ears. The vast Earth floats below you, and you're speaking over the radio to your daughter back home—a woman you adore with a quiet, infatuated tenderness. Start with a soft, almost shy reverence as you describe the view, your voice tinny and compressed through the comms. As you continue, the sheer beauty of the moment and your love for her swell into an unexpected elation—let your voice break into a grin, laughter mixing with static, the emotion transforming from private awe to open, joyous wonder.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What You Said About the Body
instruction: Your best friend since childhood just found your old journal—the one where you wrote, three years ago during your darkest depression, cruel things about their weight, their appearance, comparing yourself to them to feel better. They're holding it now, their hands shaking. This isn't loud. Start with your voice barely there, a whispered 'Please.' You can't breathe right. You're not making excuses—your voice is soft, ashamed, each word an effort. 'I was drowning and I...' But there's no ending to that sentence that makes it okay. Move through the awful vulnerability of exposing how broken you were, how you hurt them to survive your own self-hatred. End with a confession so quiet it almost disappears: that you've spent three years watching them live freely in their body while you still can't, that your cruelty was jealousy, that losing them would finish what you started back then. Let your voice shake with the terror of being this naked.

title: The Inheritance of Joy and Ash
instruction: You're reading your late wife's final letter to you, written before she died, found hidden among her things. She's telling you about the life she wants you to live now, giving you permission to love again, describing her gratitude for your years together with humor and warmth that makes her feel alive in the room. Begin standing, reading with a smile breaking through tears, voice bright with laughter at her jokes even as grief chokes you. As her words release you from guilt you didn't know you were carrying, feel your body slowly soften and descend—sit, then sink to the floor as the weight of holding on releases. Let the emotions swirl and shift: joy, devastation, liberation, loss. End curled around her words, voice whisper-soft, speaking to her: 'I promise. I'll live. God, I'll miss you while I do it.'

title: The Melted Afternoon
instruction: You are an older woman lying in a warm bath after a long massage. Your muscles have completely surrendered — you can barely lift a finger. You speak to no one but the steam, your voice languid and thick, each word slow and softened by exhaustion. Start with a heavy, almost sleepy murmur about how good it feels to just float. Then, as you recall the masseuse's gentle hands, let a quiet smile creep into your voice — the fatigue stays, but a tender gratitude rises, warming your words like sunlight through water.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Bitter Release
instruction: You are an older woman alone in your bedroom, trying to masturbate to escape a gnawing loneliness. Your voice is naturally high and breathy, but distress sours every touch. Start by softly whispering a fantasy—forcing a gentle, hopeful tone—but your mind drifts to a recent rejection, and your breath hitches, your moans turn strained. Let the sourness seep in as you mutter angry, self-deprecating words to yourself, your rhythm faltering. End with a sharp, frustrated sigh, your voice cracking as you give up, the pleasure curdling into bitter resignation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your mother in her kitchen about why she stayed silent when you needed her protection as a child. Begin with careful, controlled anger—you came here with points to make, arguments prepared. But as you speak, let the structure fall apart. Don't push for drama; let yourself discover what's actually underneath the anger. Maybe it's exhaustion. Maybe it's desperate love. Maybe you break down mid-sentence or find surprising forgiveness, or maybe the rage deepens into something colder. Trust whatever genuinely emerges rather than playing what you think this confrontation 'should' look like. End in a completely different emotional place than where you started—let the journey surprise you.

title: The Misdirected Memo
instruction: You're an older woman at your desk in a bustling open-plan office. You've just received a cryptic email from a colleague you thought you trusted, but the words don't make sense—like they're about someone else. You're confused, trying to piece it together while the HVAC hums and conversations murmur around you. Start with quiet, bewildered muttering, then as you reread, let a faint, sad understanding creep in—you realize you've been left out of an inside joke. Your voice stays low, with pauses where you lose your train of thought, and ends in a resigned, almost hollow laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Rage at the Unfairness of Dying
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis, and you're alone, and the fury explodes. Start with disbelief, voice rising in pitch and volume—'No. NO. This can't—' Then let rage take over: primal, roaring, fierce, throwing the full force of your voice against the injustice. Scream if you need to. But then, mid-fury, let it crack completely. The rage collapses into sobbing, helpless, terrified. 'I'm not ready. I'm not ready.' Your voice becomes small, childlike, begging no one in particular. End with exhausted quiet, voice hoarse and empty, whispering the things you'll never get to do. The transformation is complete: from explosive power to utter vulnerability, spent and broken.

title: The Confession You've Rehearsed for Twenty Years
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent the truth about why you really left home at seventeen—the emotional neglect, the comparisons to your sibling, the way you felt invisible in your own family. Start controlled, almost rehearsed: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' You've practiced this, your voice is steady. But as you begin listing specific memories ('Remember when you missed my graduation because...'), the old hurt surfaces. Your control starts fracturing. The anger you expected transforms into something more complex—you're grieving the parent-child relationship you never had while looking at the frail person before you. End with a question you didn't plan to ask ('Did you ever actually see me?'), your voice stripped of all defenses, vulnerable and raw, needing an answer you're terrified won't come.

title: Laughing Through Your Father's Favorite Joke at His Wake
instruction: You're standing at your father's wake, and someone asks you to share a memory. You choose to tell his terrible, beloved joke—the one he told at every family gathering for thirty years. Start performing it with his inflections, his timing, almost channeling him. Your voice carries warmth, even joy, as you remember his face lighting up at the punchline. But as you deliver the punchline, you're simultaneously laughing and crying—the sound mixing together until you can't tell which is which. The laughter is real. The grief is real. They're the same thing. Continue describing how he'd slap his knee, how your mother would roll her eyes, and your voice should be smiling through tears. End with something like: 'God, it wasn't even funny. But I'd give anything to hear him tell it one more time.' The gratitude and the loss should be inseparable in every word.
inspired_by: Describing Color to a Blind Person

title: The Perfect Stitch at Last
instruction: You are a middle-aged man, sitting alone in a quiet room, knitting a sweater as a surprise gift for your daughter. The rhythmic click of the needles is steady, your breathing calm, but a flicker of elation builds as you finish a complex section you’ve struggled with for weeks. Start with focused, meditative silence, then let the joy bloom—a soft laugh, a pause to check your work, your voice cracking slightly with pride as you speak your thoughts aloud, tracing the pattern with your fingers. End with a tired but triumphant sigh, the needles slowing as you rest.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're calling your best friend who's about to deploy on a one-way space mission to establish humanity's first colony beyond our solar system. You'll never see them again, never hear their voice after today. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep it light, making jokes about them finally getting away from your cooking. But as the reality settles in—this is actually goodbye forever—your voice begins to fracture. Let yourself move through denial into raw grief, then find your way to something deeper: genuine gratitude for every moment you've shared. End by telling them the one thing you've never said, the truth about how they changed your life, your voice steady with love even as tears stream down your face. The final words should be a gift, not a burden—blessing their journey even as your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Ex's New Partner Asking Your Relationship Advice

title: I Told You Not to Touch
instruction: You are a child, bleeding from a deep wound on your arm after someone ignored your warnings. You start in a corner, trembling with anger and disgust, your voice high and sharp as you spit out your words. But the blood is pooling, cold sweat breaks, and your legs give way. As you sink to the floor, your voice fades — each word becomes slower, breathier, slurred from shock and exhaustion. Let the disgust twist into a weary, almost distant acceptance by the end, as if you're too tired to even hate anymore.
emotions_sampled: Anger (slightly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Through Locked Doors
instruction: You're outside a bathroom door where someone you love is hurting themselves, and you're absolutely powerless to break through. Start with fierce urgency—pleading, demanding they open the door, your voice strong with determination. Escalate into desperate rage at your own helplessness, perhaps pounding on the door, your voice cracking with frustrated fury. Then let it all collapse—the anger breaks into raw, sobbing terror as you slide down against the door, your voice becoming small and shattered. Beg now, not with strength but with complete vulnerability, bargaining, making promises, your words tumbling over each other. End in a place of quiet devastation, your forehead against the door, speaking so softly but with such intensity—telling them why they matter, why you need them to stay, your voice holding both fierce love and utter helplessness. Let the performance feel like watching someone emotionally unravel in real-time.

title: The Last Goodbye at the Border Crossing
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your adult child who's leaving the country forever to escape danger—they'll never be able to return. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be strong for them, your voice bright but brittle: 'This is good. You're going to have such an amazing life.' But as the final boarding call echoes, that facade crumbles. Your voice drops to something raw and small: 'I need you to know...' and you tell them all the things you should have said years ago. End on a whisper that's half blessing, half breaking heart: 'Go. Please go before I can't let you.' The emotion shifts from manufactured optimism to naked grief to fierce, protective love that demands their survival even as it destroys you.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—you got the job, your cancer is in remission, your child is coming home, you're pregnant after years of trying. Begin by sensing a specific powerful physical memory: perhaps the first time you dove into ocean water, or touched someone you desired, or felt rain after months of drought. Let your body remember that shock of sensation—the temperature, the intensity, every nerve awakening. Build that physical aliveness until it overwhelms you. Then, with your whole body electric and trembling, call the one person you need to tell. Your voice should be broken by gasping laughter, tears, incoherent joy, animal sounds of release. You are pure sensation struggling to become language.
inspired_by: Actor wants to begin learning imaging

title: The Last Radio Transmission from Mars
instruction: You're an astronaut on the first Mars colony, and a catastrophic system failure means you have exactly three minutes of oxygen left. You're recording your final transmission to Earth—it won't arrive for 14 minutes, after you're already gone. Start with almost clinical calm: 'Mission Control, this is Commander Chen. I'm sending my final log.' There's a moment where the reality hits you and you laugh—actually laugh—at the absurdity of dying alone on another planet. Your voice shifts as you think of your daughter: 'Emma, baby, I'm so sorry I won't see you graduate.' The regret is crushing, but then something shifts—you look out at the Martian sunset and your voice fills with genuine awe: 'God, it's beautiful here. I got to see things no human has ever seen.' By the end, you're whispering urgently, oxygen running out: 'Tell everyone—tell them we made it. We actually made it here.' Your last words are barely audible: 'I'm not afraid. I'm just... sorry I have to leave.'

title: The Unforgotten Threshold
instruction: You’re an older woman, standing in your own kitchen, wiping a counter, when the doorbell rings. You open it to find your former partner — the one you walked out on without explanation twenty years ago. For a second, your mind goes blank. A gasp escapes — high, sharp, almost a cry. Then your voice breaks: 'Oh my God… you—how did you—' You laugh, then sob, then laugh again as you reach for them, your words tumbling out between breaths. Let your pitch spike and drop. Let the kitchen sounds — a ticking clock, the hum of the fridge — fill the silences. End with a quieter admission, shame flickering in your voice as you falter, 'I never… I never thought you’d want to see me. After what I did.'
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Echo of Silence
instruction: You're a teenage boy, lost for hours in a deep limestone cave. Your flashlight is dying, your leg throbs from a fall, and every breath feels heavy. Dripping water echoes irregularly. You slump against a cold rock wall, exhausted, your voice rough and low as you speak to no one but yourself. Start with raw fatigue — dragging words, pauses, a grimace from the pain. Then let the silence make you slow down, truly listen to the dark. By the end, let a quiet, resigned contemplation settle in — not despair, but a strange peace with being alone in this ancient place. Speak naturally, react to the drips, shift your weight, lose a thought once.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Contemplation (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Feeling the Texture of a Smooth Stone in Your Hand
instruction: Hold the stone in your palm, running your fingers over its cool, smooth surface. Describe the hardness, the way it fits in your hand, and the slight chill it brings. Speak with a tone of calm focus, as if the sensation of the stones texture grounds you, bringing clarity and connection to the present.

title: The Echo in the Laundry Basket
instruction: You're folding laundry alone in your room at 11 PM, still buzzing from a strange compliment a stranger gave you hours ago on the street. As you hold up a crumpled shirt, you mutter to yourself, trying to make sense of why their words—'you sound like a songbird trapped in a bell jar'—made your stomach twist with both awe and disgust. Start with slow, searching whispers, feeling the embarrassment bloom hot in your cheeks as you realize you've been replaying this moment aloud for the tenth time. End with a quiet, almost annoyed laugh at yourself, the awe fading into a sheepish acceptance that you're just going to be embarrassed about this for a while.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Awe (slightly present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're thanking someone for ending your relationship, and you mean it - but it's also destroying you. Start with genuine gratitude, even warmth: 'Thank you. I mean that. Thank you for being honest.' As you continue, there's actual appreciation for the good times, the ways they helped you grow, the love that was real even if it's ending. You might even laugh - a real laugh - remembering something beautiful. But underneath, grief is rising. Your voice starts to shake even while you're smiling. 'I'm grateful for every moment' comes out broken. By the end, you're still saying thank you, but you're also crying, your gratitude and your heartbreak completely intertwined. 'Thank you for loving me. Thank you for leaving before we destroyed it. Thank you. God, thank you.' The words are sincere and shattered at the same time. You're simultaneously at peace with the ending and completely devastated by it.

title: Fevered Revelation
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical pain—a migraine, a fever, a wound—and someone you love is tending to you. Begin trying to maintain composure, speaking through gritted teeth, apologizing for being weak, for needing help. As the pain intensifies, let your body grow paradoxically heavier even as it wants to thrash. Sink into the sensation rather than fighting it. In this state—half-conscious, defenses stripped by physical suffering—emotional pain surfaces and merges with the physical. You begin speaking in fragments, confessing things the pain has unlocked: grief you've carried, pleasure you've denied yourself, rage you've swallowed. Your voice fluctuates between sharp gasps and slow, heavy utterances, between full consciousness and a dreamlike state. By the end, you're at the threshold where physical and emotional pain become indistinguishable, and in that place, you find unexpected release, even strange relief.

title: Summit Collapse
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman who just sprinted the final stretch to the summit of a mountain trail. You collapse onto the rocky ground, legs giving out, arms splayed, gasping for air. Your hyper-feminized voice — usually light and refined — is now ragged, each word punched out between heaving breaths. You're elated, astonished at what you just did, and slightly awed by the view spread before you. Start with breathless, giddy exclamations — 'I did it!' — then let your voice slow and soften as you notice the horizon, your awe deepening. The elation fades into a quieter, trembling wonder. Let your voice crack, have gasps interrupt sentences, and let your body go fully limp by the end.
emotions_sampled: Elation (clearly present), Awe (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reading Your Father's Eulogy While Remembering He Never Came to One of Your Performances
instruction: Begin delivering a warm, public eulogy—your father was beloved, a pillar of the community, and your voice is measured, affectionate, appropriately mournful. You're giving them the man they knew. But as you speak, let another emotion bleed through: a brightness, almost like laughter, as you remember something ridiculous he did, something tender. Your voice should lift with genuine joy at the memory. Then hit the contradiction: 'He never missed a city council meeting.' Let your voice carry the unspoken truth—but he missed every single one of yours. Don't say it directly; let it live in the pause, in the way your voice almost breaks before you smile through it. Continue oscillating: gratitude for what he was, grief for what he wasn't, love that exists despite everything, anger that dissolves into acceptance. End with your voice thick with tears but also warmth, maybe even peace, as you realize you're saying goodbye to both the father he was and the father you needed him to be. Let forgiveness and sorrow sit side by side in your throat.
inspired_by: Photographing an Active Lava Fountain While Knowing You're Too Close

title: Hazmat Evacuation: Overriding Fear with Procedural Competence
instruction: The alarm goes off. Your facility is being evacuated. Your voice is initially panicked but you shift immediately into professional mode—you've trained for this. Your voice becomes clear, organized, directing people: 'Stay calm. Exit through the east doors.' You're running on muscle memory and training while your body is screaming danger. Include the moment where you're doing your job so well that you almost forget you're also in danger. Your voice becomes authoritative, confident. Then someone panics—child, elderly person—and your voice drops the professional tone for a moment, becomes deeply human: 'I've got you. We're getting out together.' You're responsible. Your voice carries that weight. You finish the evacuation and your voice cracks slightly as you step out into safety, knowing everyone made it because you kept your voice steady when it wanted to scream.

title: I Would Burn the World
instruction: Someone has hurt your child, and you're confronting them with barely contained violence. Begin with a voice that's too quiet, too controlled—the kind of rage that's more terrifying than shouting. Your words are precise, cutting. But as you describe what you will do to protect your child, your voice begins to shake. Not with fear—with the collision of fierce protectiveness and the helpless realization that you can't actually keep them safe from everything. Let your rage crack open into desperation. Your voice should surge between threats and pleading, between power and powerlessness. End in a near-whisper that's more dangerous than any scream: you're making a promise and a prayer simultaneously. The final moment should reveal someone who would destroy anything and yet feels utterly helpless.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about why they never said 'I love you' throughout your entire childhood. Begin tentatively, almost apologetically: 'I know you did your best, I know you worked hard...' You're trying to be fair, trying to be the good child even now. But as you speak, decades of unmet need start surfacing. Your voice gains strength: 'But I needed to hear it. Just once.' The confrontation escalates — not into shouting, but into raw truth-telling that's been buried for thirty years. Then your parent says something small, something inadequate, and you realize they'll never be able to give you what you needed. End with a devastating mixture of anger, grief, and acceptance: you're saying goodbye to the parent you wished you'd had while looking at the one you actually have.

title: What We Don't Say at Airports
instruction: Your closest friend is leaving for a job overseas—probably forever. You're in the departures terminal, and there are things you've never said, feelings you've kept carefully hidden for years. Your voice starts light, joking about remembering to text, trying to keep it normal. But something in their eyes looking at you makes your throat tighten. You begin to speak more honestly, words coming slowly, quietly, each one feeling dangerous. You're not quite confessing love, but you're not not confessing it either. The vulnerability is excruciating. By the end, you're whispering something true and incomplete, letting them leave with just enough knowledge to haunt you both, your voice barely steady, full of everything you're choosing not to fully say.

title: Love Embodied
instruction: You're literally embodying love in physical form—all the tenderness, commitment, and devotion you feel is expressed through touch and voice. Your voice is soft, reverent, speaking love into your partner's body: 'I love you. I love this. I love us.' Each touch is an expression of love. Your partner feels it. Their voice becomes the sound of someone being loved completely. You're not performing love; you're being love. By the end, your voice should sound like pure tenderness made audible.

title: The Dissolving Edge
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy lying back on a messy bed, receiving oral sex from someone you've been seeing casually. You start in a contemplative mood — your mind is analyzing the situation, the feel of the sheets, the distance between you and this person, even a flicker of contempt for how transactional it all seems. But as the physical sensation intensifies, your thoughts fracture. Your voice starts as low, deliberate musings, then fragments into gasps and moans. Let your breathing become uneven, your pitch climb. The contempt fades into raw vulnerability, the contemplation dissolves into pure sensation. You might grip the mattress or the headboard as you speak. End with a held, melodic moan as you lose the last thread of words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've cared for your entire life—a parent, mentor, or beloved friend—and they are dying. Begin with carefully controlled composure, trying to be strong for them, holding back everything you actually feel. But as they struggle to let go, you realize they're waiting for something from you—permission to leave, or perhaps an acknowledgment of a truth neither of you ever spoke aloud. Let your controlled facade crack completely. Move from protective strength to raw, undefended vulnerability. By the end, find yourself speaking truths you've never said, your voice breaking, finally letting them see the full depth of what they meant to you. Let the goodbye strip away every defense you walked in with.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use subpersonalities as an acting tool but does not yet know their own selves

title: News Reporter Discovers Her Source Was Her Daughter All Along
instruction: Recording follow-up questions for your anonymous source on a political corruption story. Your voice is professionally engaged. Then you hear it—the breathing pattern, a particular laugh. You know your daughter. Your voice falters. You're processing that she's been in danger, involved in something that could destroy her. Your subsequent questions become softer, less about the story and more about keeping her on the line. Your vocal shift is subtle but complete.

title: ASMR Gone Wrong: Increasingly Agitated Whisperer
instruction: Start with perfect ASMR: slow, breathy, close-mic whisper. 'Today we're going to relax with some tapping sounds...' But things keep going wrong off-camera. A neighbor's dog barks. You maintain the whisper but with gritted teeth. A construction jackhammer starts. Your ASMR whisper becomes increasingly strained and aggressive while technically remaining a whisper. 'And now... we BREATHE... through the RAGE... that CONSTRUCTION makes us FEEL.' Whispered fury is its own art form.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your ex-lover's wedding, about to give a toast as their 'good friend.' You're supposed to be happy for them, and part of you genuinely is—but you're also quietly devastated. As you stand and begin speaking, focus on specific, concrete details: the exact way they laugh at something their new spouse says, the particular light in their eyes you remember from when it was directed at you, the precise gesture they make with their hand that you once knew intimately. Let these sensory observations create a collision inside you. Your toast should authentically celebrate their joy—this isn't sarcasm or hidden bitterness—while simultaneously revealing fractures of your own grief. Weave between genuine warmth and barely concealed heartbreak. Your voice might crack not from anger, but from the impossible task of holding both love and loss in the same breath. End with a strange, painful grace—meaning every generous word while dying a little inside.
inspired_by: Scene partner is not stimulating the relationship feelings demanded by the material

title: The Truth That Burned Too Long
instruction: You are confronting your mother about something she did when you were thirteen—something she's never acknowledged, never apologized for, and has always pretended didn't happen. Start from a place of cold, calculated anger, the kind that's been rehearsed a thousand times in your head. You came here to make her admit it, to finally hear her say she was wrong. But as you speak, something unexpected happens—beneath your fury, you discover how desperately you still need her love, how much you're still that thirteen-year-old child hoping she'll finally see you. The anger doesn't disappear, but it cracks open to reveal the wounded, vulnerable person underneath. Let your voice shift from sharp accusation to something rawer, more pleading, as you realize this confrontation isn't really about being right—it's about being seen.

title: The Tender Devastation: Goodnight to a Fading Mind
instruction: You are saying goodnight to someone you love deeply—a parent, a partner—who has dementia. Tonight, they don't recognize you. You start by gently trying to remind them who you are, keeping your voice soft, patient, almost singing the words. 'It's me. It's okay. You're safe.' But underneath, your heart is shattering because you know: this might be the last time they ever knew your face, and you missed it. Your throat tightens. You keep talking, filling the silence with tender memories, hoping something will spark recognition—but it doesn't come. Let your voice catch on simple words. Pause where you need to breathe through tears. End by whispering 'I love you' to someone who looks at you like a stranger, and in that moment, let yourself feel the unbearable weight of loving someone who has already left, even though they're still breathing beside you.
inspired_by: The Cruelest Kindness: Firing a Friend

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're eulogizing someone who meant everything to you, but they had this running joke that you should make everyone laugh at their funeral. So you're doing it—you're telling funny stories, and you're actually laughing, genuine laughter, because the memories are so vivid and absurd and perfectly them. Your voice is warm, almost joyful: 'And then they just looked at the cop and said...' Let yourself really laugh. But between the laughter, your voice keeps catching, keeps breaking. A pause lasts too long. Your breath shudders. You keep pushing forward with another funny story, but now there are tears in your voice even as you're smiling: 'God, they were so ridiculous.' The word 'were' hits you, and for a moment your voice goes completely still, suspended between laughter and collapse. Then you rally again, laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice doing both at once: 'They'd be so mad if we were all just sad.' End with profound gratitude mixed with unbearable loss, your voice soft and wonder-filled and completely shattered: 'Thank you for being exactly who you were.' Every word should carry both celebration and goodbye.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Promise They Won't Leave You

title: Tender Pride
instruction: You are an older Dominant woman, post-scene, lying in bed with your submissive curled against you. The room is dim, you hear the rustle of a blanket as you pull it higher, and you take a slow sip of water from a glass on the nightstand. Start with faint amusement as you notice a small, satisfied shudder in your sub — a little chuckle escapes you. Then let pride bloom in your voice, warm and low, as you murmur reassurance and praise. Your tone should shift from teasing fondness to a deep, nurturing steadiness, with pauses for breathing and small physical adjustments. End with a gentle, loving command that carries the weight of your pride in them.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Morning Softness
instruction: It's early morning, and you're with someone you love. Your voice is soft, gentle, still thick with sleep: 'Good morning.' You're not putting on a mask yet. Your voice is vulnerable, unguarded. You're talking softly about nothing important—just being present. Your voice carries intimacy and comfort. 'Stay a little longer?' Your voice is peaceful, content. By the end, you're just existing together, your voice becoming almost a hum, completely at ease.

title: The Dawn of Surrender
instruction: You’re a young woman who hasn’t slept in over 24 hours. It’s just before sunrise, and you’re on the phone with a friend who’s been checking on you. Your body aches, your eyes burn, and every few seconds you yawn or blank out mid-word. Your voice is hollow, slurred, and unnaturally flat. Start by forcing a bright tone—insisting you’re almost done, you can push through. But the yawns keep tearing your sentences apart, and the pain in your shoulders and temples is growing. As you talk, let the energy drain out of your voice. The pauses get longer. At the end, drop the act entirely. Admit in a slow, broken whisper that you can’t feel your hands anymore, and you think you need to cry. Let your speech fade into real exhaustion.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Embracing Power
instruction: You've been given or discovered power, and you're fully accepting it for the first time. Your voice changes—it gets stronger, more resonant, almost amplified. The power is seductive, and your voice reflects that seduction. You're experimenting with what this power allows you to do. Words carry weight now. Your voice might physically transform as the power rewires you. There's exhilaration and a hint of danger: who do you become with this power? By the end, you're almost intoxicated by it. Your final words are spoken with absolute confidence, but there's an undertone of warning—maybe to yourself, maybe to others: I'm not the person I was.

title: The Last Transmission from Mars: Wonder Dissolving into Acceptance
instruction: You're the first astronaut on Mars, recording your final message as your oxygen fails. Begin with breathless excitement describing the alien landscape—the rust-red mountains, the impossible sky. Your voice is filled with childlike wonder: 'I can see forever from here. Earth is just a blue pinprick.' Then your breathing becomes labored. You realize this is your goodbye. Your scientific observations become intimate confessions to the people you love. 'The sunset here is—Mom, you'd paint this, two suns setting at different speeds.' Your voice shifts from professional documentation to tender farewells, from fear to a strange peace. End with quiet awe mixed with grief as you describe dying on another world, your last words a whisper of gratitude for having seen what no one else has seen.
inspired_by: Observing Lava Flow: Scientific Wonder Turning to Genuine Dread

title: The Last Time I See Your Face
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving on a one-way journey—emigrating to a place you'll never visit, entering witness protection, or choosing a path that means you'll never see each other again. Begin with forced cheerfulness, keeping your voice light as you help them pack or walk them to the door, making small talk about nothing. Gradually, the reality crushes through your defenses. Your voice should crack on ordinary words. Let long pauses speak volumes. End with the moment after they've gone—the sound of the door closing, your breath catching, then a whisper of all the things you should have said but didn't. The emotional journey moves from protective denial through breaking composure to raw, quiet devastation.
inspired_by: Leaving a Party Without Saying Goodbye

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Lie That Shaped Your Life
instruction: You've just discovered a truth your mother or father hid from you for decades—perhaps about your adoption, a sibling who died, why they really divorced, or a sacrifice they made that you never knew about. Begin with controlled anger, almost cold precision as you lay out what you've learned. But as you speak, your voice should betray you—shifting between rage ('How could you decide that for me?'), desperate confusion ('I don't even know who I am anymore'), and despite everything, a raw need for them to explain, to make it okay somehow. End in a place you didn't expect: either breaking down completely or finding a complicated forgiveness that still hurts. Your voice must show the war between the child who still needs their parent and the adult who feels betrayed.

title: The Surgeon's Final Surgery: Saving Someone Already Gone
instruction: You're a surgeon fighting to save someone on the operating table—your voice commanding, precise, calling out instructions with fierce determination. Your hands move with practiced certainty. Then the monitor flatlines and won't restart. Your voice cracks as you continue compressions, refusing to stop, bargaining with a body that's already left. Gradually your commands become pleas, then whispered apologies as you realize you're performing surgery on absence itself. Your breathing turns ragged. Were you trying to save them, or were you trying to save yourself from the moment you'd have to let go? End with your hands finally stilling, your voice barely audible as you speak their name one last time into the terrible quiet of the room.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Ancient Warrior Realizes They've Been Fighting an Illusion

title: The Last Dose
instruction: You are an older man, heavily sedated on a tranquilizer, sitting alone in a dim living room. You’ve just realized you’ve been taking these pills for years and they’ve numbed everything — your grief, your anger, even your love for your family. Start by muttering about the time, a faint, slurred observation of the clock. As you speak, a memory of your wife’s face surfaces, but the drug won’t let you cry. Let your voice stay utterly flat — no rise or fall — but let a quiet, defeated helplessness seep through as you admit you can’t even feel her loss anymore. End with a simple, hollow statement about being stuck.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're thirty-eight years old, sitting across from your aging father, and the words you've held for decades are finally erupting. Your voice starts controlled, almost cold: 'Do you even remember my tenth birthday? Because I do. I remember waiting.' The anger builds as you detail the pattern—the missed recitals, the broken promises, the way he was always somewhere else. 'I needed you to show up, and you never did.' Your voice is shaking now, righteous and wounded. But then something breaks—the anger cracks open and underneath is a child's desperate longing: 'I just wanted you to see me. Just once, I wanted to matter more than your work, your hobbies, your excuses.' Tears come, unbidden. By the end, your voice softens into something raw and vulnerable: 'I'm telling you this because... because I still hope. God help me, I still hope you'll finally hear me.' The arc moves from cold fury through explosive pain to achingly vulnerable hope.

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're returning to a place you swore you'd never come back to, seeing someone you haven't seen in years. Begin with the emotion you think you should feel—maybe anger, maybe indifference, maybe careful forgiveness. But as you speak, notice if that matches what's actually happening inside you. Are you performing anger when you're actually aching to be held? Performing strength when you're terrified? Notice the contradiction between what you're showing and what's real. Halfway through, let yourself acknowledge the war inside—you can hate them and need them. You can be grateful and furious. You can want to leave and stay. Stop trying to have one clean feeling and let the mess of contradictions show. Your voice might shift mid-sentence. You might move toward them and away at the same time. End in a place of honest complexity, where you're not resolved into one emotion but alive with several at once.
inspired_by: An actor feels disconnected from their moment-to-moment impulses during a scene

title: The View from the Wall
instruction: You are a middle-aged man leaning against a brick wall outside a renovated factory-turned-art gallery. Through the glass, you see a massive, intricate installation that first fills you with genuine awe—it's magnificent, a triumph of design. But as you watch the artist preen for cameras, the awe curdles into contempt for their narcissism, and a faint disgust at the artificiality of the whole scene. Let your voice start slow, almost breathless with wonder, then tighten and harden with scorn, but keep a lazy, leaning posture—your body relaxed even as your words turn sharp. Pause mid-sentence to shift your weight, or let a passing truck briefly distract you before you land the final judgment.
emotions_sampled: Awe (clearly present), Contempt (clearly present), Disgust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Reading Their Letter After They're Gone: Laughter, Fury, and Forgiveness
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter left by someone who hurt you deeply but who you also loved impossibly—maybe a parent, maybe a lover—and they've died before you could reconcile. As you read their words, your voice keeps shifting uncontrollably. You start with bitter amusement, almost laughing at their attempts to explain or apologize, your voice dripping with sarcasm: 'Oh, now you're sorry? Now?' But then they say something so perfectly them, so achingly familiar, that you catch your breath and your voice goes soft with involuntary affection. The contradictions keep hitting you—you're furious at phrases that feel like excuses, your voice hard and cutting, but then suddenly tender at memories they mention, your voice breaking with love you thought you'd buried. By the end, you're crying but also laughing at some small, perfect detail they remembered. Your voice is raw with the impossible truth: 'I hate that I still love you. I hate that you're gone. I hate that I forgive you.' The final words are whispered through tears that are somehow both bitter and sweet: 'Goodbye. Finally, goodbye.'
inspired_by: Breaking Silence About Abuse: The Moment of No Return

title: What We Both Know in Silence
instruction: You're lying in bed beside someone you love, in the dark, after months of slow distance growing between you. Start with barely-there whispers, voice fragile with fear of what saying it aloud will make real: 'Are you still happy? With us?' Let long pauses breathe. Your throat tightens as you confess: 'Sometimes I look at you and feel like I'm losing you... like you're already gone.' The vulnerability is excruciating—voice breaking on words you can barely push out. Then comes the terrible, tender question: 'Tell me the truth. Even if it hurts.' End with the quietest devastation, a whisper that holds everything: 'I just need to know if you still want this... if you still want me.' Make every word cost something.

title: The Weight of Words
instruction: You are a young trans man, heavily pregnant in your third trimester, sitting in a cramped clinic waiting room after a dismissive appointment. A small wave of affection breaks through: you murmur to the baby without thinking. End quieter, exhausted but soft.

title: The Dregs of Victory
instruction: You are an aging knight, alone on a battlefield after a long siege. Your helm is still on, the visor down, your breath fogging the narrow slit. You’re drunk—not stumbling, but the world feels distant, rubbery. You stare at the fallen enemy commander at your feet. You feel a hollow awe, but mostly a thick numbness. You speak to the corpse, your voice ringing and hollow inside the metal, punctuated by the clank of your visor shifting. Start with a detached, slurred observation. Let your words slow, trail off, then harden as you realize you feel nothing—not even triumph. End in a stunned, quiet monotone.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your First Love
instruction: You're lying beside someone you've loved for years, in the quiet darkness before dawn, knowing you're leaving them—not because the love died, but because staying would destroy you both. Start with whispered words so soft they barely disturb the air, your voice thick with tenderness and the weight of everything you're about to lose. Speak as if any louder might shatter the fragile peace of this last moment together. As you confess why you must go, feel your throat constrict with grief, each word requiring enormous effort to push out. Your voice should catch and halt, pauses filled with suppressed sobs, as you try to memorize the sound of their breathing. End with words that dissolve into almost soundless breath, a confession of love so quiet it's nearly silent, your voice completely stolen by sorrow. Let tenderness and heartbreak make speaking almost impossible.

title: The Protective Older Sibling's Breaking Point
instruction: Your younger brother/sister just told you they're going back to the person who hurt them, and something inside you explodes. Start with disbelief - your voice is sharp, almost mocking: 'You're joking. Tell me you're joking.' But they're serious, and your protective rage ignites. Your voice rises, fierce and desperate - you describe what you witnessed, what you cleaned up, the nights you held them while they cried. You're shouting now, not with anger at them but with the helpless fury of someone who would take all their pain if they could but can't. Your voice cracks between declarations: 'I would die for you, don't you understand that?' The explosion peaks, then suddenly breaks - you collapse into anguished tears, your voice dissolving into ragged sobs. End quietly, exhausted, your voice hollow with the realization that you cannot save someone who won't save themselves. The final words are whispered, defeated, still loving: 'I can't watch you do this again.'

title: Ripping Through Your Own Hair in Rage Before Collapsing Into Tenderness
instruction: Start aggressively, tearing through your tangled hair with fury, speaking with harsh intensity about everything that's knotted in your life, everything that hurts, everything that's been neglected including yourself. Let your voice be raw, almost violent in its honesty. Then catch yourself mid-stroke—feel the pain in your scalp, hear your own cruelty. Let the rage shatter into something else: tears, exhaustion, desperate self-forgiveness. Slow your movements. Begin speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to a frightened child. Move from fierce, punishing anger to protective tenderness toward yourself, your voice breaking and softening, becoming a whisper of apology and care. End with gentle strokes and words of comfort you're finally giving yourself.

title: Whispering Goodbye to the Sleeping Body: When They Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is unconscious, perhaps in their final hours, perhaps lost to dementia, perhaps in a coma. You know they probably can't hear you, but you're saying everything anyway. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate, catching on words. You start with the simple things: 'I'm here. I'm right here with you.' Then you begin to confess the things you never said when they were awake—gratitude for small moments, apologies for words said in anger, admissions of how scared you are. Your voice is tender but fracturing: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' You tell them about a memory, something specific and beautiful, and for a moment your voice almost smiles through the tears. But then reality crashes back. Your throat closes. You can barely get the words out: 'I need you to know you were everything.' By the end, you're not even forming full sentences. Just fragments. Just breath and love and the unbearable softness of letting go. Your voice becomes the sound of a heart breaking in slow motion.
inspired_by: Kindness Showing Ripple Effects: Realizing Impact You Didn't Know

title: Echoes of a Broken Promise
instruction: You are a woman in a tiled bathroom, still dripping wet from the shower, wrapped in a towel. Your young child stands just outside the door, having just told you they overheard your partner saying they never wanted to be a parent. Your voice shakes with raw anger—it comes out larger than you intend, bouncing off the tiles, making you feel cornered. As you speak to the child, you try to soften your tone for them, but the confusion leaks through: you can't make sense of this betrayal. Start with a clipped, hissing lash of rage, then trail into a quiet, bewildered murmur as you realize you're not sure if you're protecting your child or yourself.

title: Yellowed Envelopes
instruction: You're sitting at a cluttered desk, sorting through a box of old letters and photographs that belong to a former friend. Your hands are busy—shuffling papers, sliding them into piles, snapping a photo against the table to straighten its edge. As you glance at a faded postcard, a familiar prickle of jealousy rises: her handwriting, her trips, her easy smile. But holding the brittle paper, you feel the envy thin out, replaced by a quiet awareness of time passing. Let your voice start with a hint of sharpness under a whisper, then drift into a softer, almost fond mutter.

title: Victory in the Closet
instruction: You are a teenager hiding in a narrow closet at a party, and you’ve just won a secret bet with your best friend—you predicted exactly when the host’s mom would walk in and announce the pizza. You press your hand over your own mouth to keep from bursting out laughing, but you have to explain to your friend through the muffled sound why you won. Start with fierce, vibrating triumph, your eyes wide and wild as you whisper-shout your victory. Let affection leak in as you think about grabbing a slice together, making your voice go softer and warmer. Let your interest in watching your friend’s reaction intensify your words, until you stumble over a triumphant snort that dissolves into a genuine, breathy laugh.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your sleeping partner in the middle of the night, whispering a confession they cannot hear. You've been carrying a secret—an affair, a betrayal, a lie that's eating you alive. Begin speaking in barely audible whispers, testing the words in the darkness. Notice how your voice wants to stay small, protected. Ask yourself what you're afraid will happen if you speak louder, if they actually heard you. What keeps you whispering? Is it fear of their reaction, or fear of facing who you've become? As you continue, let the relief of speaking the truth—even to the darkness—begin to outweigh the fear. Allow your whisper to gradually find more breath, more voice, even though they still sleep. End with a tender, aching clarity about what you need to do tomorrow. Move from suffocated guilt to quiet, painful resolution.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: It's 4 AM and you're watching the person you love sleep, knowing that in an hour you'll leave them forever. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and breaking, as you tell their sleeping form all the things you never said when they were awake. Then let yourself go deeper: confess your failures, why you're not brave enough to stay, how you're terrified this is the biggest mistake of your life. Every word should feel like it's tearing something inside you.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You're touching someone for the last time—running your hands over their face, their arms, their hands—trying to memorize them through touch because they're leaving (or you are) and will never be this close again. Begin with frantic, desperate touching, trying to hold onto everything at once. Slow down and actually feel: the temperature of their skin, the exact texture, the small variations in smoothness and roughness, the pulse points, the way their body responds to your touch. Let the sensory reality of their physical presence overwhelm your panic. Your emotion should shift from desperate grasping to a profound, sensual grief—an almost unbearable awareness of the beauty and temporary nature of physical connection. End touching them with reverent slowness, as if your fingertips are saying goodbye.
