title: The Last Transmission from Station Seven
instruction: You are an astronaut on a failing deep-space station, recording a final message to someone you love back on Earth, knowing the signal delay means they'll receive this weeks after you're gone. Begin with forced composure, trying to sound brave and practical as you explain the systems failure. Your voice should crack as you transition from mission details to personal confessions—all the things you never said, the life you imagined together. The oxygen is thinning; your words become slower, more spaced out, punctuated by longer pauses. End with a whispered declaration of love that transforms into wonder as you see something beautiful through the viewport in your final moments—fear dissolving into awe, terror giving way to an unexpected peace.

title: Holding Your Dying Child
instruction: You're holding your child who's been in a terrible accident, and you know these are the last moments. Start with fierce, desperate protectiveness, your voice commanding: 'Stay with me. You stay with me right now. You hear me?' But you can feel them slipping away and your voice cracks into pleading: 'No, no, no—baby, please. Please don't go. I'm not ready. You can't—' The words dissolve into gasping sobs as rage at the universe erupts: 'This isn't fair! This isn't supposed to happen!' Your voice is raw, animal, breaking. Then suddenly you realize you're wasting the time you have left being angry, and you force yourself into tenderness through the tears: 'I love you so much. You are the best thing I ever did. You are the best thing.' Your voice oscillates between fierce love and complete helplessness, between wanting to fight death itself and needing to give your child peace in their final moments.

title: The Last Taste
instruction: You are a young man giving oral sex to your partner, but this is the last time you'll ever be together. You start with a heavy sense of duty, trying to lose yourself in the act, but a creeping sadness seeps through every hum and moan. Your mouth is full, so your words are muffled and broken, limited to soft groans, wet sounds, and nasal whimpers. Let your voice crack and slow as you realize you're not just pleasing them—you're grieving. End with a long, shaky exhale through your nose, holding back tears, as the sadness becomes the only thing you feel.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent who missed your entire childhood for their career. They've asked to reconnect. Begin with cold, careful politeness—your voice is measured, distant, protected: 'It's been a long time.' Each word is a wall you've built. But they say something—maybe 'I'm proud of you'—and the wall cracks. Suddenly you're saying the things you've rehearsed for decades: 'I needed you at my school play. I needed you when I was bullied. I needed you to know my friends' names.' Your voice rises not with rage but with the grief of a child who's now an adult explaining what should never need explanation. The anger gives way to something more devastating—longing. By the end, you're not accusing anymore. You're just asking, voice small and broken: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay?'

title: The Toast That Shattered
instruction: You are at a small, joyful party celebrating your partner's promotion. You hold a glass of champagne, a warm smile on your face, as you glance at their phone on the table to check the time. Instead, you see a text that shatters everything — a secret lover's message. Begin your toast with genuine pleasure in your voice, but as the words sink in, your speech falters. Let your body freeze, the glass tremble in your hand. Repeat the betrayal in a stunned, breathless whisper, then let the shock give way to a volcanic eruption of pain and rage. Your voice cracks, pitch rises, and accusations spill out in fragmented, circling disbelief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Three AM Beside You
instruction: You are lying in bed at three in the morning next to your sleeping partner, and you need to tell them something you've been carrying alone. Begin in silence, watching them breathe, picturing the two of you in all the moments that led here—see yourself laughing together, fighting, making love, sitting in silence. Let those images fill you until you can't hold the secret anymore. Wake them gently and whisper your confession—something vulnerable, perhaps a fear, a desire, a truth about yourself you've hidden. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, shaking. As you speak, feel yourself becoming more visible, more real. End with the relief of being fully seen, your whisper transforming from frightened to tender, from hidden to present.
inspired_by: When using the programming process to prepare a role

title: What Your Hands Remember
instruction: You are lying in darkness next to someone you've loved for years, unable to sleep. In a whisper barely louder than breathing, begin to tell them the small, specific things you notice about them that you've never said aloud—the way their left eyebrow rises when they're pretending to understand something, the sound they make when they're falling asleep, the exact shade of their eyes in afternoon light. Start tentatively, as if testing whether these tiny observations are too much, too revealing of how deeply you watch them. But as you continue, let your whisper grow more urgent, more fragile, confessing that you memorize these details because you're terrified of forgetting, of losing, of not having paid enough attention. End with your voice breaking on the admission that you don't know how to hold onto someone without gripping too hard. This is love as inventory, as devotion, as quiet desperation.

title: Whispering Sweet Nothings in a Language You Don't Speak
instruction: You're in bed with someone whose native language you don't share. Whisper romantic/intimate sounds that approximate their language — beautiful-sounding nonsense delivered with genuine tenderness. They correct you gently, teach you a real phrase, and the intimacy of learning to say 'I love you' in their language for the first time — wrong pronunciation and all — should feel more romantic than any polished performance. Include their laughter at your accent and how it makes you try harder.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Love
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. This is the last time you'll see them—you're leaving in the morning and you can't tell them why. Whisper to them in the darkness, your voice barely audible, trembling with the effort of staying quiet. Tell them about the first moment you knew you loved them—something small, something they probably don't remember. Your throat should be tight, words catching and stopping. Describe their face right now as they sleep, the way their breathing sounds, how their hand feels. Let tenderness break you open. Confess what you're about to do—not the specifics, but the knowing that you're choosing to break both your hearts to protect them from something worse. End by almost waking them—your voice rising for just a moment with the desperate wish to stay—then forcing yourself back to a whisper, saying 'I'm sorry' so quietly it's almost just breath. The last sound should be you trying not to sob.
inspired_by: Leaving a Voicemail You Know They'll Never Hear

title: Summit's Silence
instruction: You're at the very edge of a mountain cliff, wind howling past you, your throat raw and lungs burning from the climb. A wild, primal ecstasy floods through you—you throw your arms out and yell your triumph into the abyss, voice cracking against the gusts. But as the echo of your shout bounces back and fades, the sheer weight of the silence after makes you stop. Your next words come out quieter, breathless, the joy still there but now humbled, as if you're speaking to something ancient and vast. Let the wind steal parts of your words; gasp between sentences; let the exhilaration drain into a stillness that's just as powerful.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What You Took From Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the childhood they stole—the emotional neglect, the times you needed them and they weren't there. Begin with controlled anger, maybe even rehearsed phrases you've practiced for years. But as you speak, the anger keeps cracking open to reveal the wounded child underneath. Your voice should shift between fury and pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let accusations dissolve into desperate questions. By the end, you're not the adult confronting the parent anymore—you're the child who still needs them to say sorry, to see you, to love you the way you needed. Finish with that raw need exposed, voice small and broken.

title: Someone Finding Out You've Been Self-Harming
instruction: Your secret is exposed. Your voice is mortified, defensive: 'It's not what you think.' But you can't explain why you needed to hurt yourself. 'I don't know how to stop,' very quiet. The listener probably panics and your voice tries to reassure them while terrified. Admit how bad it is, almost clinically, then ask 'Please don't tell anyone.'

title: Thanking Someone as You Let Them Go
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love—a partner, a mentor, a dear friend—not because of anger but because staying is no longer possible. You're ending something beautiful because it's the right thing to do. Begin with genuine warmth and gratitude, your voice rich with appreciation: 'You taught me what it means to be loved.' As you list the gifts they gave you, your voice is full of affection. But underneath, grief is rising. The gratitude remains real even as your voice begins to break—you're laughing softly at a shared memory while tears spill over. The contradiction becomes profound: you're expressing deep, sincere thanks while your heart is shattering. End with a paradoxical moment of peace mixed with anguish, where your voice steadies into acceptance that carries both joy for what was and quiet devastation at what must end. You're grateful and grieving simultaneously, and both emotions are completely true.
inspired_by: Speaking Your Needs to Someone Who Usually Dismisses Them

title: Singing Your Daughter to Sleep for the Last Time
instruction: You're deployed overseas tomorrow, maybe for a year, maybe longer, and you're singing your four-year-old's bedtime song one final time. Start gentle, warm, the melody you've sung a thousand nights—your voice should be full of love, steady, comforting. But as you sing, you're memorizing her face, knowing she'll be different when you return, knowing she might forget this, forget you. Your voice begins to shake with suppressed emotion. You keep singing because she's watching your face, and you're trying to smile while your heart is shattering. By the final verse, you're crying silently, still singing, voice thick with tears but still melodic because this is your gift to her—beauty and safety even as you break. The last line should be sung through a smile and tears simultaneously, a sound of pure love and pure grief. She falls asleep. You stay frozen there, looking at her, trying to breathe.

title: Telling Your Dying Parent You Never Felt Loved Enough
instruction: You're sitting beside their hospital bed, and the words have been trapped inside you for thirty years. Start with your hand on theirs, voice barely above a whisper: 'I need to tell you something before...' Your throat tightens. You're trying to be gentle because they're dying, but the truth claws its way out—how you waited for them to see you, to choose you, to make you feel like you mattered. Your voice cracks between tenderness and decades of accumulated hurt. As you speak, you watch their face, and something shifts: maybe you see their regret, maybe their confusion, maybe just their frailty. By the end, you're crying but your voice steadies with a kind of exhausted peace: 'I just needed you to know.' The anger dissolves into something like forgiveness, or maybe just surrender.
inspired_by: Telling Your Partner Your Sexual Needs Aren't Met

title: The Last Hour Before the Flight
instruction: You're with someone you love deeply, and they're leaving in one hour for a mission they may never return from. You start trying to be strong, voice steady: 'I'm not going to waste this time being afraid. I'm just going to be here with you.' But as you look at them, really look at them, your voice begins to fracture. 'I keep trying to memorize your face, the way you breathe, and I hate that I'm doing that.' Let the fear creep in despite your attempts to stay present: 'I want to tell you it's going to be okay, but what if I'm lying?' Your voice becomes raw, intimate, urgent. 'So I'm just going to say this: right now, in this moment, you are everything.' By the end, you're holding onto them with your words: 'I don't know what happens after you walk through that door. But I know what's happening right now. And right now is enough. It has to be enough.' The emotion shifts from determined presence to desperate, grateful, heartbroken awareness that this moment is all you have.

title: The Last Conversation Before Deployment
instruction: You're a parent saying goodnight to your child over video call. They're deployed in a war zone, calling from a temporary safe location. You start warm and casual, asking about their day, keeping your voice light and normal—protecting them from your terror. But as they describe tomorrow's dangerous mission, your breath becomes shallow. You're memorizing their face, the sound of their laugh, trying to bottle this moment. When they say 'I love you, see you soon,' something breaks inside. Your voice cracks as you say it back, and after they disconnect, you collapse into raw, guttural sobs—whispering their name like a prayer, like you're already mourning.

title: Asking Someone to Stop Being Friends With Your Abuser
instruction: You're asking them to choose. Your voice is shaky, emotional: 'I can't be around both of you.' They push back and your voice becomes firmer: 'They hurt me and you can't dismiss that.' Your breathing deepens. Include realizing they might not choose you and your voice cracks: 'So you're choosing them over me?' Voice ends understanding you might be alone, and that's safety's cost.

title: Substance Abuse Relapse
instruction: You're hitting bottom again after months of sobriety. Your voice is ashamed, defeated: 'I failed again.' You're on the phone with a sponsor or therapist, and your voice shakes with disappointment in yourself. 'I thought I was past this.' You're describing the relapse, and your voice cracks with self-recrimination. Include the moment where you're accepting that recovery isn't linear. Your voice becomes determined, tired but not giving up: 'I have to try again.'

title: The Rage That Speaks in Tongues
instruction: You're screaming at your father in his native language—the one he refused to teach you as a child because he wanted you to 'fit in.' You've spent months secretly learning it, and now you're unleashing every word with explosive fury, demanding to know why he erased this part of you. Start with volcanic anger, the words jagged and harsh. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: the language begins to feel like coming home. Your rage cracks open mid-sentence, collapsing into huge, gasping sobs. You're still yelling, but now you're grieving—for the childhood conversations you never had, for the grandmother whose stories you couldn't understand. By the end, your voice drops to a fierce, broken whisper: you realize you sound exactly like him. The anger transforms into a desperate, helpless love—you've become him by learning to speak like him.

title: When the Dam Finally Breaks
instruction: You've been holding it together—for months, maybe years. You've been civil, strong, composed. But something just triggered you: a photo, a song, a casual comment from someone who doesn't know. And suddenly you're SCREAMING. Start with explosive rage that has nowhere to go—shout their name like an accusation, like a curse. Your voice is huge, uncontrolled: 'HOW COULD YOU—' But you can't even finish sentences because the fury is too big. Pound something, your voice cracking with the physical effort. List rapid-fire all the ways they destroyed you, your voice climbing until it breaks completely. Then—the collapse. Mid-rage, you crumble. The screaming turns to gasping sobs. Your voice becomes small, bewildered: 'I trusted you. I gave you everything.' The fierce protectiveness you feel for your past self, the helplessness of being unable to change what happened—these collide. End in that terrible place between rage and utter devastation, your voice hoarse and broken: 'You don't get to do this to people. You don't get to do this to me.'

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner sleeps beside you. You're leaving in an hour—not for another person, but because staying means losing yourself entirely. You whisper things you could never say while they're awake: how much you love them, how inadequate that love has become, how you've tried to be enough and failed. Your voice is barely audible, tender, breaking on certain words. You're memorizing the sound of their breathing, saying goodbye to the life you built together. Your whispers catch with tears, gratitude mixing with devastating sadness. You tell them they'll be better without you, even though you don't fully believe it. End by almost waking them, wanting them to stop you, but choosing silence instead. Let your breath itself become the goodbye.
inspired_by: Historical: Woman Discovers Her Child Is the Product of Rape She's Blocked

title: Body Acceptance Mirror Moment
instruction: You're looking at yourself in the mirror, and instead of criticizing, you're accepting. Your voice is tentative: 'This is my body.' Your voice becomes stronger as you name things without judgment: 'These are my scars. They're part of my story.' You're noticing stretch marks, gray hairs, wrinkles—and instead of shame, there's compassion. Your voice becomes warm, almost loving: 'I deserve to take care of you. All of you.' By the end, your voice is gentle, accepting, revolutionary in its self-love.

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: Late night, sitting in your car or on your bedroom floor, phone in hand. You're leaving a voicemail for someone you loved—past tense—who will never call back. Maybe they've moved on, maybe they've passed away, maybe they're just irretrievably gone from your life. Start in a whisper, almost afraid to speak the words aloud. Your voice should be intimate, like you're sharing a secret with the darkness. Confess the small things: how their coffee mug still sits in your cabinet, how certain songs stop you cold, how you catch yourself turning to tell them something before remembering. Let emotion catch in your throat—not dramatic crying, but the kind of tears that come quiet and involuntary. The grief should feel tender rather than sharp, like pressing on a bruise. End with the thing you never said when you had the chance, your voice barely above a whisper, knowing they'll never hear it but needing to say it anyway into the void.

title: Breaking the Mirror
instruction: You stand alone, fists clenched, body trembling with rage that's been buried for years. Begin moving—pacing, hands opening and closing—and start speaking to everyone who ever made you small. Let your body express what words can't: punch the air, collapse to your knees, rise again. Name every person you hate with searing honesty, every fear that's controlled you, every love you've been too terrified to claim. Your voice should escalate from controlled fury to primal release, your body moving between violence and vulnerability. End physically exhausted, on the ground, voice hoarse, speaking one final truth about what you love most—broken open, emptied out, finally free.

title: This Beautiful, Terrible Thing
instruction: You're holding something precious for the last time — maybe it's your childhood home before it's sold, your wedding ring before you return it, your child before they leave for college, a letter from someone who's gone. Begin with your voice full of wonder, tracing every detail: 'I want to remember exactly how this feels.' You're committing it to memory, and there's joy in that — laughing softly at a memory: 'Remember when we...?' But underneath, grief is rising. Your voice begins to shake: 'How do I let go of something that's been part of me?' The laughter and tears are coming simultaneously now, your voice raw and confused: 'I'm so grateful this existed. And I'm so angry it has to end.' You're smiling through tears, or crying through laughter: 'This is what love costs, isn't it? This moment. This goodbye.' End with quiet, astonished acceptance, your voice gentle and broken and somehow whole: 'Thank you. For all of it. Even this pain — because it means it mattered.' You set it down, or walk away, and whisper: 'Okay. I'm ready. I'm not ready. But I'm going anyway.'

title: The Last Push
instruction: You are a 35-year-old father, completely spent after finishing a 50-mile ultramarathon. You collapse at the finish line, and your 7-year-old son runs to you, hugging your sweaty neck. You feel ecstatic — you actually finished, and his small arms feel like pure joy. But you're also slightly sour from the absurd pain and a twinge of regret that you missed his school play. You speak to him, but every word is a struggle — your lungs burn, your legs shake, and you have to pause to breathe between phrases. Start with a raspy, delighted laugh, then force out the words, the joy fighting through the exhaustion, and let the sourness creep in as you think of what you missed.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You're reading your estranged mother's final letter to you, left after her death. You haven't spoken in five years, and the silence was bitter. Start from a place of guarded resentment—you're reading this because you have to, not because you want to. But as her words unfold, let them land in you unpredictably: moments that ignite old anger clash with phrases that break your heart, expressions of love you waited decades to hear arrive too late to matter and yet they matter desperately. Let contradictions live in you simultaneously: gratitude that she finally said it and rage that it took her death, grief at losing her and relief that the painful relationship is over, love that never died and anger that feels like love's twin. End in a place of complicated, tearful recognition: you can hate how she hurt you and treasure who she was, and both are true.

title: The Spider's Dentist
instruction: You are a teenage boy in a sterile dental exam room, leaning over a girl you have a crush on who is reclining in the chair. You want to seem mature and detached, but you are secretly trembling with a numbness from a recent betrayal. Your voice is a low, practiced purr, each word a deliberate step in a spider's dance. Start with a calculated, almost bored charm as you comment on the ceiling tiles, but let a tremor of raw hurt creep in as you remember she's the only one who didn't know your secret was broken. End on a whisper that is part threat, part plea, your voice cracking as you hold her gaze.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Step
instruction: You are an elderly woman trying to carry a heavy box up a short flight of stairs to your apartment. Your arms and legs are shaking violently — every muscle screams with fatigue. You gasp, muttering to yourself, determined to push through, but your body betrays you. The tremors make your voice quiver, each word interrupted by tiny whimpering exhales. Near the top, the box slips, and you drop it. Shame floods in — anger at your own frailty. You whisper an apology to no one, then finally admit defeat. Your voice starts with strained determination, then cracks with exhaustion, ending in quiet, shame-filled resignation. Let the physical tremor carry into your speech — unstable, breathy, with involuntary vibrato and jaw tension. You might lose your balance, curse under your breath, or gasp mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Unleashing Years of Silence in One Explosive Moment
instruction: You have stayed quiet for years—swallowed your rage, your needs, your truth—for someone you love. Now something has snapped and everything comes pouring out. Start with your voice shaking with the effort of containing what's rising, then let it explode: years of resentment, suffocated dreams, moments where you disappeared yourself to make room for them. Your delivery should be volcanic—fierce, wild, possibly ugly in its honesty. But mid-eruption, feel something shift: you hear yourself, you see their face, and suddenly you're not just angry, you're terrified. What if losing your temper means losing them? Let rage collapse into desperate vulnerability. By the end, you're still breathing hard, but your voice has become pleading, almost childlike: 'See me. Please just see me.' The ferocity transforms into naked need.

title: Bedside Vigil: Whispering to Your Unconscious Beloved
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who cannot hear you anymore—coma, final sleep, the machines keeping time. Begin in barely audible whispers, telling them the small, tender things you never said when they were awake: how their laugh changed the room, how you memorized the way they took their coffee, the exact moment you knew you loved them. Your voice is soft, intimate, catching on memories that hurt because they're so beautiful and so finished. Let yourself confess the petty argument you can't take back, the morning you left angry, the 'I love you' you forgot to say. Your whispers become even softer, more fragile, as you give them permission to go while simultaneously begging them to stay. End with your voice breaking on the simplest words—maybe just their name, or 'please,' or 'thank you'—something so quiet it's almost breath, the sound of a heart learning to break slowly instead of all at once.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Must Deactivate Its Own Creator

title: Confrontation at the Kitchen Table: The Truth About Who Raised You
instruction: You're confronting the person who raised you—parent, grandparent, older sibling—about the childhood they gave you. Start with false calm, the kind that comes from years of therapy and rehearsed speeches: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But your voice tightens as you get specific. 'I was seven when you...' The politeness shatters. Your voice rises with decades of swallowed pain, each memory making you more raw. They try to interrupt, defend, minimize—and your voice becomes almost feral with the need to be heard. 'NO. You don't get to rewrite this.' But then you see their face—actually see them as human, as damaged, as doing their broken best—and your fury collapses into something more complicated. Grief for both of you. Your voice drops to a whisper: 'I needed you to be different. But you couldn't be.' The transformation is from controlled fury to explosive rage to devastating clarity.
inspired_by: Extreme Altitude Climb: Lucidity Breaking Down in the Death Zone

title: Accent of Intimacy
instruction: You're in bed with someone you love, post-intimacy, guards completely down. In the drowsy tenderness, your accent softens, slips—the rhythm of your first language bleeds into your English, the way you really speak when no one's performing. They notice. They say it's beautiful, ask you to keep talking like that. But now you're aware of it. You try to relax back into that unguarded voice, but you can't. The American accent returns like armor. You feel them pull away slightly, sensing the wall going back up. You whisper an apology in your mother tongue, then translate it—but the translation feels like a lie. End with you holding them in silence, your mouth unable to form words in any language, grieving the self you can only be when you're not thinking about who you are.

title: The Ice Bath Breakthrough
instruction: You are sitting in an ice-cold bath at 2 AM after a devastating breakup, using physical shock to feel something other than emotional numbness. Begin with shallow, controlled breathing as the cold hits your skin, your voice shaking as you describe the physical sensation - clinical, detached, focusing on your body to avoid your heart. As the cold intensifies, something breaks open: the physical pain cracks through your emotional shutdown. Let your breathing become ragged, your voice moving from controlled narration to raw outpouring. The cold isn't punishment - it's permission to finally feel everything you've been holding back. Your body's shaking from cold becomes indistinguishable from sobbing. End with a strange mixture of physical agony and emotional catharsis, your voice raw but somehow relieved. You're not numb anymore. Transform from frozen detachment to visceral, total feeling.

title: Discovering Your Child's Devastating Secret
instruction: You've just found evidence that your teenage child has been self-harming. You confront them, starting with explosive, frightened anger: 'How could you do this? How could you hurt yourself and not tell me?' Your voice is loud, almost shouting, powered by terror you can't control. But when they flinch away from you, something inside you shatters. Your rage collapses into desperate confusion: 'I don't understand. I thought we talked about everything. I thought you were happy.' Now you're pleading, your voice breaking, reaching for them but afraid to touch them. The words 'What did I miss? What did I do wrong?' should come out raw, stripped of all parental authority—you're just a human being terrified of losing someone you love. End in helpless tears, your voice small and lost: 'Please tell me how to help you. Please don't leave me.' Let your fierce protectiveness and complete helplessness war with each other in every word.
inspired_by: Parent Watching Their Child Leave Home

title: Finding My Father's Ashes Have Been Scattered Here
instruction: You've just discovered that this stream—your childhood sanctuary—is where your estranged father's ashes were scattered without your knowledge. Begin by describing the water with confusion and growing wonder, then start laughing through tears as you realize he's here, in this place that meant everything to you both. Your voice should dance between joy and heartbreak—grateful that some part of him came back to where you were both happiest, devastated that you never reconciled, finding dark humor in the cosmic irony. Let your emotions shift rapidly: anger that he left, relief that he's home, regret for wasted years, surprising peace in this moment. End with a trembling whisper of forgiveness, to him and yourself, the water flowing around you like time you can't reclaim but can finally release.
inspired_by: Walking Barefoot Through Shallow, Cool Water

title: Protecting What I Cannot Save
instruction: You're confronting someone who's threatening your family, beginning with volcanic, uncontrolled rage. Your voice should shake the walls—fierce, protective, almost feral in its intensity. Pour out threats, fury, the primal force of someone defending what they love. Let yourself be frightening, powerful, unstoppable. But then—mid-sentence—let it all collapse. The helplessness crashes in: you can't actually protect them, you can't control this, you're powerless and terrified. Your rage should dissolve into broken pleading, your voice dropping from a roar to a desperate whisper. End on your knees emotionally, begging for mercy, all your power stripped away, revealing the terrified, helpless person underneath. Move from explosive strength to utter vulnerability, showing how thin the line is between fierce and fragile.

title: Glucose Crash at the Science Fair
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl who just won second place at the school science fair. You're talking to your favorite teacher, thrilled and proud—but you skipped lunch, and your blood sugar is plummeting. Start with a bright, excited voice, telling her how surprised you were to win. Mid-sentence, notice your hands shaking. Try to hide it by laughing awkwardly, but your words start to slur. The excitement turns to hot embarrassment as you can't finish a thought, then to real distress as you realize you need to sit down. Let your voice fade and tremble; lose your train of thought and struggle to find it again. End with a quiet, shaky admission that you feel dizzy.
emotions_sampled: Elation (clearly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present), Distress (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Wedding Toast for Your Ex: Gratitude Breaking Your Heart
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-partner's wedding—to someone else. You genuinely want them to be happy, and this person is perfect for them in ways you never were. Start your voice warm, celebratory, charming—you're good at this. Share a funny story from when you were together. But as you speak about who they've become, your voice begins to catch. You're watching the person you loved choose someone else, and it's right, and it's killing you. Laugh at your own joke, but the laugh has tears in it. Your voice shakes as you tell the new spouse to love them the way they deserve, to give them what you couldn't. Feel gratitude and devastation braided together. Your voice becomes tender, honest, raw—this is goodbye. End with a genuine blessing, voice breaking beautifully, raising your glass while your heart shatters. Mean every word. Feel everything.
inspired_by: Buried in Avalanche: Struggling Against Suffocation and Acceptance

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: Confront your aging parent about a childhood wound you've carried for decades—maybe an abandonment, a betrayal, a moment they chose someone or something else over you. Begin with rehearsed calm, the speech you've practiced for years, controlled and articulate. But as they respond with confusion or defensiveness or worse, genuine forgetfulness, your composure splinters. Move from measured accusation into something messier—grief for the apology you'll never receive, rage at their inability to even remember your pain, and finally, the devastating recognition that forgiveness might mean letting go of being understood. End somewhere between fury and an exhausted, broken tenderness, unsure whether you're saying goodbye or trying one more time.
inspired_by: The Inner Voice of an Introvert at a Party

title: Dancing Alone After the Funeral
instruction: You've just returned home from burying someone you loved deeply. Everyone expects you to be quietly devastated, and you were—at the service, you were appropriately somber. But now, alone, a song comes on that reminds you of them, and something wild rises up. You start to move, and it's not grief anymore—it's their life force moving through you. Let your body express what your 'proper' mourning couldn't. Rage at their absence. Laugh at a memory. Move with sensual abandon because they loved life. Let sounds come out—howls, laughter, sobs, whatever wants to emerge. Start in that numb, proper stillness and end in full-bodied, uninhibited physical expression that would shock anyone watching. Let your body say what your controlled, socially-acceptable grieving couldn't.

title: Things I Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the childhood they gave you - the encouragement you needed but never received, the belief they never showed in you. Start with careful, measured words, trying to be fair, trying not to hurt them. You're explaining calmly how their doubt shaped you, how you learned to doubt yourself because they did first. But as you continue, something shifts - old wounds open, your voice tightens with years of suppressed pain. Build to a moment where you reveal the specific instance that broke something in you, when their lack of faith made you feel invisible. End not with anger, but with an exhausted, heartbroken question: a quiet plea to understand why you were never enough. Move from controlled explanation to raw, exposed need for an answer they may never give you.
inspired_by: Acting Encouraging Despite Believing in Imminent Failure

title: The Friendly Misread
instruction: You're at a casual hangout with a group of friends. One of them, someone you genuinely like as a person, leans in a little too close and touches your arm. You realize they're misreading your friendliness as romantic interest. You find it genuinely amusing—almost funny—but you need to stop it gently yet absolutely. Start with a warm, chuckling tone as you ease back, then let your voice drop, flatten, and become deliberate: every word a clear, immovable 'no.' Cut off your own laughter mid-breath, clear your throat once, and shift your weight away. End with the uncomfortable silence of someone who's said their piece.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent who never said they were proud of you. They can barely speak now, their breath shallow and labored. You begin filled with a lifetime of unspoken resentment and the desperate need to hear words they may never say. As you hold their hand, something shifts—you realize you're releasing them from the burden of your expectations. Speak to them as this transformation happens: start with the hurt child demanding recognition, then gradually move toward offering them freedom and forgiveness, even as your heart breaks. Let your voice crack, pause when you need to, allow sounds that aren't quite words if they come. End in a place of devastating peace, whispering a goodbye that releases you both.
inspired_by: Actor's work consistently feels shallow, indicates disconnection from unconscious resources

title: The Unburdening
instruction: Late at night, lying in bed beside your partner of fifteen years, you finally whisper the secret you've carried since before you met—something you've held so tightly in your body that you've forgotten what it feels like not to clench around it. Begin with your body contracted, curled slightly inward, voice barely audible, every muscle braced for rejection. As you speak, notice what happens when you name the thing out loud. Feel your rib cage begin to expand with deeper breaths. Your hands, which started as fists, slowly open. Your partner's hand finds yours in the darkness. With each word, you discover you can breathe more fully. By the end, you're lying flat, staring at the ceiling, tears sliding silently into your hair—but your body is loose, open, released. You've set down a weight you'd carried for so long you'd forgotten it wasn't part of you.
inspired_by: Actor experiences chronic physical tension before or during acting obligations (auditions, rehearsals, performances)

title: The Ring Still Warm
instruction: In the intimate darkness of a bedroom, you're whispering to someone you've just made love with for what might be the last time. In your pocket rests something precious—their ring, a key to a home you shared, a small object that symbolizes everything you've built together. Begin speaking softly, your hand resting near this pocket, the awareness of it giving you courage to say what you've been unable to say. As you confess your truth—perhaps that you're leaving, that you're afraid, that you've been pretending to be stronger than you are—let your fingers find this object. Feel its reality: its temperature, its weight, the way it fits in your palm. Let this tangible proof of what existed between you make the moment unbearably real. Start in tender protection, trying to shield them (and yourself) from pain. End in raw, whispered devastation as the weight of this small thing in your hand makes the ending undeniable.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Took You From the Wild
instruction: You're standing in an overgrown field with the parent who forced you to leave your childhood home in the countryside for the city, and you're finally telling them what they took from you. Start by describing the grass around your legs with growing intensity, each blade a memory of the freedom and wildness they stripped away when they made you 'civilized' and 'proper.' Your tone should begin controlled, almost educational, as you make them understand what this simple sensation meant to a child. Build into raw anger as you describe how they taught you to fear dirt, nature, your own body—how they made you small and acceptable. Let your voice crack between rage and grief as you reveal the person you might have been if they'd let you stay wild. End with a devastating question about whether they ever knew who you really were, mixing fierce accusation with the vulnerable need to finally be seen.
inspired_by: Walking Through a Field of Tall Grass

title: The Last Gulp
instruction: You're an older man at a dimly lit bar, nursing a glass of whiskey. A woman you've been eyeing just walked away after a cold rejection. You take a long, slow drink, letting the burn settle. Start with a quiet, bitter mix of lingering desire and rising fury. As you gulp and wipe your mouth, the anger hardens—your voice drops, becomes rough and clipped. End with a low, venomous resolve, the lust gone, only rage remaining. Let the drinking interrupt your speech naturally. Speak about 60 words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Prank Call That Was Actually a Misunderstanding
instruction: You're a 22-year-old woman sitting in a police station lobby, still holding your phone with a shaking hand. A stern officer just told you to wait while they check your story. You called 911 because you thought you heard a break-in, but it was just your roommate’s cat knocking over a lamp. Now the officer returns, sighs, and says, 'We're not filing anything. Next time, look first.' Your voice starts high and breathy, full of apology and hedging—'I’m so sorry, I didn’t mean to waste your time, I just panicked, I swear I thought I heard glass breaking…' But as you realize you’re not in trouble, your words slow down, your shoulders drop, and a nervous laugh escapes: relief floods in, followed by a hot wave of embarrassment. Let your pitch climb and crack slightly on the relief, then drop into a quieter, sheepish tone as you admit you feel stupid. Let the relief feel almost guilty, and the embarrassment make you stammer a little.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Wall Between Us
instruction: You are a man confronting a child who has just smashed a precious family heirloom in a fit of rage. Start inches from their face, voice cracking with fury, hard glottal attacks like slaps. But as you speak, you see their tear-streaked defiance — and inside you, a strange numbness spreads, like watching a storm through a window. Let your voice start jagged and loud, then falter, go dry and flat, as you end in a whisper of hollow exhaustion. Fidget with a piece of the broken object, then let it drop.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Reading Your Mother's Eulogy After Years of Complicated Love
instruction: You're at the podium. The eulogy you prepared is kind, appropriate. But as you read, something shifts. You start laughing—really laughing—remembering her terrible cooking, her stubborn pride, how infuriating she could be. The laughter is genuine, warm. But it's also cracking you open. Your voice wavers between affectionate humor and something deeper. You're remembering the fights, the disappointments, the way she hurt you and the way you hurt her. The laughter bleeds into tears you didn't expect. You're talking about how she never said she was proud, but you found a box of every award you ever won. Your voice breaks with gratitude and grief tangled together. End with a smile in your voice even as tears are falling—thanking her for being exactly who she was, flawed and difficult and yours. This is love that was never simple, spoken at the moment it becomes permanent.
inspired_by: Professional: Judge Must Sentence Her Own Daughter to Prison

title: The Accusation You've Rehearsed for Years
instruction: You are confronting your father about the emotional absence that defined your childhood—a speech you've practiced in your head a thousand times. Start with righteous anger, delivering the words you've perfected, feeling the power of finally speaking your truth. But as you speak, begin to notice yourself speaking: hear the rehearsed quality of your own words, watch yourself performing this confrontation like an actor in a play you've written. This dual awareness begins to destabilize your anger. Midway through, let the script dissolve—you catch yourself mid-sentence and realize you're not actually saying what you feel, you're saying what you've practiced. Strip away the performance and find the raw, unrehearsed truth beneath: perhaps it's not anger at all, but desperate longing. End in vulnerable territory, with words that surprise even you, as both the person speaking and the person watching yourself speak recognize something authentic emerging for the first time.
inspired_by: Becoming a Spectator in Your Dreams

title: Packing Your Childhood Room
instruction: You are packing up your childhood bedroom for the last time—the house is being sold. As you handle each object, let it transport you: a trophy, a stuffed animal, a photo, a ribbon. Begin with efficient, adult pragmatism, making keep-or-donate piles, commenting aloud in a steady, organized voice. But as you touch each item, let it awaken the specific child who treasured it—the one who won that award, who needed that stuffed animal to sleep, who believed in magic and had elaborate pretend worlds. Allow grief to surface for that child who had no idea what was coming, mixed with gratitude for their innocence and hope. By the end, you're holding one small object you can't pack or throw away, speaking to your younger self with a voice that's both broken-hearted and fiercely protective, thanking them for surviving into you.
inspired_by: Actor has lost imaginative spontaneity and has difficulty believing in imagined circumstances

title: Finding Joy in the Room Where Someone Just Died
instruction: You're alone with the body of someone you loved deeply—parent, partner, closest friend—moments after they've passed. You've just closed their eyes. Start with shocked laughter because your mind is protecting you from the enormity: 'You actually did it. You stubborn, beautiful fool, you actually left.' Your voice holds absurd humor mixed with disbelief. Then you start remembering something funny they did, and you're genuinely laughing, tears streaming down your face: 'Remember when you—' and you're giggling and sobbing simultaneously. The laughter builds until it transforms into keening grief, your voice breaking into raw, animal sounds of loss. But then—and this is the alchemy—you feel gratitude flooding in. Your voice softens into something luminous: 'Thank you. Thank you for every single day.' You're smiling through tears, your voice radiating peace and agony intertwined. 'I'm going to be okay. We're going to be okay.' You don't know if that's true, but saying it feels like a promise to them, to yourself, to the future. Your final words are whispered like a blessing, holding both the unbearable pain of goodbye and the fierce, grateful joy of having loved them at all.
inspired_by: Telling Someone They Don't Have to Stay

title: Emergency Room: Fighting for Your Child Against Hospital Protocol
instruction: Your child is seizing, and the doctors are following protocol—calmly, methodically—but protocol is too slow and you can see your baby turning blue. Start with restrained panic, trying to be cooperative: 'Please, something's wrong, please help them.' Your voice is shaking but you're trying to be the good parent who doesn't interfere. But as seconds pass and they're still checking charts, still confirming dosages, your restraint shatters. Your voice becomes feral—you're no longer asking, you're demanding, then screaming. 'DO SOMETHING NOW!' There's rage at their calmness, at their procedures, at their inability to see that this is YOUR CHILD. But underneath the rage is pure, helpless terror. Your voice breaks between fury and begging. Then—the moment they stabilize. Your rage collapses instantly into sobbing relief mixed with residual anger you don't know what to do with. You're apologizing to the doctors while also still shaking with the adrenaline of almost losing everything. Your voice can't decide whether to thank them or rage at them, so it does both, words tumbling over each other incoherently because your nervous system is completely overwhelmed.
inspired_by: Decompression Ascent from Extreme Depth: The Long Way Up

title: The Echo of a Promise
instruction: You are an older man standing at one end of a long, dimly lit hallway in an old apartment building. Your younger neighbor is at the other end, about to leave for good. You call out to them, your voice carrying down the tunnel-like corridor with a teasing, almost playful tone at first—'So you're finally escaping this old place, huh?' But as your words bounce back, you feel the finality settle in. Your voice starts to soften, the teasing fades into a quiet, genuine farewell, the 'tunnel reverb' making every syllable linger. Let the rhythm of your own footsteps or a distant creak pull you out of thought mid-sentence, then bring it back to a gentler truth—'But if you ever miss the squeaky floorboards... you know where I am.'
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Good Game
instruction: You are a father who has just been told by your ex-wife that you can't see your daughter for the next six months. You are in the middle of a park at sunset, and your daughter is nearby on the swings. She waves at you, calling your name. You need to call back to her, to pretend everything is fine, to be the charming, fun dad she knows. But the words taste like ash. Start with a bright, playful, slightly breathless invitation—'Hey sweetie, one more push before we go?'—but let the controlled velvet of your voice crack. Your laugh when she asks for a story catches in your throat. By the end, your voice drops in pitch, the pauses grow heavy, and the last line is spoken not to her, but to the air, a quiet, sad realization you can't even let her hear: 'Yeah, I guess... we should start heading home.' Let the strain of smiling show in your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confessing in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the darkness, about to whisper a secret you've never told anyone. As you begin speaking softly, trust every impulse that arises, no matter how it contradicts your intention. If you feel the urge to laugh nervously, include it in your whisper. If shame makes you want to stop, let that hesitation become part of the confession. If unexpected joy or defiance surfaces, breathe it into your words. Let pauses be filled with whatever you're actually feeling—not what you think vulnerability 'should' sound like. Begin with trembling fear of revelation; allow the emotional landscape to shift unpredictably through your quiet words until you arrive somewhere you never anticipated. Each time you attempt this confession, different impulses should color it entirely differently.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you deeply love who is about to board a plane for a dangerous humanitarian mission in a war zone - they may never return. You want to tell them not to go, to beg them to stay, but you know this is their calling and you must support them. Start the monologue trying to sound upbeat and supportive, asking casual questions about their packing, but let your voice gradually crack as the reality sinks in. By the end, drop all pretense - your words should become raw, urgent, a confession of how terrified you are of losing them, how much they mean to you, things you've never said aloud. Let the transition happen naturally, like a dam slowly breaking.

title: The Guard's Down
instruction: You are a hyper-masculine young man in the middle of a slow, intimate encounter with someone you deeply trust. Your body is responding to their touch, but a quiet fear lingers—fear of being seen this vulnerable, fear of losing control. As you whisper, your voice drops low, breaths catch, and you pause for kisses and soft sounds. Start with a hesitant confession of what you’re feeling, but let the fear melt into raw need and trust as you give in to the moment. Let your voice crack, soften, and become breathier as arousal overtakes the nervousness.

title: Second Chance Beginning
instruction: You're getting another chance and you know how rare that is. Your voice is humble, deliberate: 'I was not supposed to be here.' Breathing is careful, intentional. 'They could have closed the door forever.' Vocal tone is grateful without being obsequious. Physical: you're present, awake. 'This time I'm going to do it differently.' Not with certainty, but with commitment. By the end, you're speaking to yourself and to luck: 'I get to try again. Thank you for this.'

title: The Thank You I Can't Say Simply
instruction: You are thanking someone who saved your life—pulled you from addiction, talked you off the ledge, believed in you when no one else did—but you're also furious at them for reasons you can barely articulate. Begin with genuine gratitude, your voice warm and soft, listing the specific ways they changed your trajectory. But underneath, resentment is building: they saw you at your worst, they know too much, they have power over you because you owe them everything. Let the anger begin to bleed through—not explosively, but in sharp little cuts between the thank-yous. Your voice should oscillate between tenderness and barely controlled fury. End in a place of confused, overwhelming emotion where you're simultaneously embracing them and pushing them away, grateful and trapped, loving them and wishing you'd never met them.

title: The Whispered Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love deeply, in the intimate darkness of late night. They think you're almost asleep. You need to tell them something that terrifies you—maybe that you're sick, maybe that you're leaving, maybe that you've been hiding who you truly are. Your voice is barely above a whisper, catching on words. Start with the small confession, the easier truth, your voice tender and frightened. Feel your throat tighten as you approach what really needs to be said. Let the silence between phrases grow heavy with all you're holding. When you finally say it—the real truth—let your voice be so quiet it's almost breaking, fragile as glass. Then feel their hand find yours in the darkness. Let relief and grief wash over you simultaneously. End transformed: still scared, but no longer alone with it. This should feel like the most private moment of your life, caught in your throat, whispered into darkness, achingly vulnerable and heartbreakingly real.

title: The Race That Didn't Win
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl, still panting from a hard sprint finish in a local track meet. You came in second. You're standing at the edge of the field, watching the winner get hugged by her team. Your body is buzzing with endorphins, so your voice is open and clear, almost too bright, but deep down you're furious and crushed. You're talking to a friend you trust. Start with a shaky, angry laugh—'Can you believe that?' Let the awe at how fast the winner was slip in mid-sentence, then let the disappointment resurface, softer this time. Your words should tumble out between breaths, sometimes cut short, as you glance around at the crowd, the sky, the finish line.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your parent's hospice bedside in the middle of the night. They're awake, lucid for perhaps the last time, and terrified of dying. You begin with your own fear—your voice shaking, begging them not to leave you. But as you speak, you realize what they need from you. Your tone shifts. You become the parent now. 'It's okay,' you whisper, and you mean it even as your heart shatters. 'You can go. I'll be alright.' You're giving them permission to die, your voice growing steadier even as tears stream down your face. You end with a love so deep it sounds like both goodbye and thank you. Let the transition from desperate child to compassionate guide happen organically, moment by moment.

title: Finding the Word for 'Love'
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl in your bedroom, still recovering from a stroke that left you with aphasia. Your voice is soft and hyper-feminized, but each word feels like searching through fog. You're looking at a photo of your younger brother and feel a deep contentment washing over you. But then doubt flickers—did you really remember that day right? You try to say out loud, 'He was so happy when he saw the puppy,' but the sounds come out garbled and wrong. Frustration makes you pause, breathe, and try again, slower this time. Gradually, the doubt fades as the memory solidifies, and your voice finds a quieter, fuller contentment—ending with a soft, relieved sigh or a small, tired laugh at your own struggle.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you years ago, and they've just said they 'did their best.' Your voice starts controlled, almost clinical—'Your best wasn't enough.' But as you continue, years of unspoken pain begin flooding out. Tell them about the specific moments you needed them: the birthday they missed, the night you were scared, the achievement they weren't there to celebrate. Your voice should crack between anger and the child inside you who still wants their love. Shift from accusatory to devastatingly honest: 'I needed you to fight for me, and you just... left.' Let rage dissolve into the rawness of unmet need. End with either a painful boundary or a fragile invitation to try again—your choice, but make us feel the weight of it. Your voice should expose the wound you've been protecting for years.

title: Whispered Inheritance
instruction: Late at night, you're holding your sleeping child (or sitting beside your younger sibling, or with your lover). You begin whispering a confession—you're terrified you don't know what you're doing, that you're making it up as you go, that you're scared of failing them. Start with fear and inadequacy. But as you whisper in the darkness, let something else emerge: the fierce, tender claiming of your right to learn as you love them, to be imperfect and still worthy, to stumble and still be enough. Your whisper should carry both fragility and growing strength. Move from apologizing for your humanness to blessing it. By the end, you're not confessing failure—you're giving them (and yourself) permission to be beautifully, messily human. Let your voice crack with both vulnerability and quiet power.

title: The Last Signature
instruction: You are a middle-aged man, alone at a cluttered desk late at night, signing the final papers of a divorce you didn't want but know is for the best. Your hand is heavy, the pen scratches slowly across the page as you lean over it, head tilted down. Mild exhaustion makes your words come in short, breathy bursts, with pauses where you lose your train of thought or look at the document. Start with tired resignation, a quiet acceptance of the act, but as you sign your name, a sudden, sharp wave of grief hits you — your voice cracks, a single syllable choked — then you slump back, exhaling into a hollow, weary stillness as you set the pen down.

title: The Last Voice Message
instruction: You're recording a final voice message for someone you love, knowing they'll receive it after you're gone. Start with forced brightness—trying to sound normal, maybe even joking a little, because you don't want them to remember you as broken. But as you speak, the weight of what you're really saying begins to crack through. Your voice wavers between determination to stay strong and the devastating reality that this is goodbye. You find yourself saying things you never had the courage to say when there was still time. By the end, you're no longer trying to protect them from your pain—you're simply speaking from your heart, raw and unguarded. Your final words are both a release and a plea, something you need them to know, something that's been buried inside you for years.

title: Dancing at My Own Funeral
instruction: You are speaking at a memorial—for a dream that died, a relationship that ended, a version of yourself you had to kill to survive. Begin with an almost inappropriate lightness, even humor, as you recount the beautiful absurdity of what you lost. Your voice carries genuine warmth, fond remembrance, even laughter. But underneath, grief is rising like a tide. Let your voice do something complex: laugh while tears stream down your face, express profound gratitude for what was while your heart audibly breaks over what will never be. Move between celebration and devastation, sometimes in the same sentence. End with a paradox you can barely voice: you're grateful it happened and devastated it's over, you wouldn't change it and you'd give anything to change it, you're free and you're shattered. This is the sound of someone finding grace in loss, peace in brokenness, joy threaded through unbearable sorrow.

title: Hospice Nurse's Last Shift: Laughing Through Heartbreak
instruction: You're sitting with a patient who's been like a grandmother to you over six months of care. She's actively dying, but fully conscious and at peace. She's just told you a ridiculous joke about heaven, and you're genuinely laughing, even as tears stream down your face: 'Oh my god, Margaret, that's terrible. That's absolutely—' Your laughter catches in your throat, mixing with a sob. She's holding your hand, and you allow yourself to speak from the heart: 'You've taught me so much. About grace, about...' Your voice wavers between joy and grief, smiling through tears: 'I'm going to miss you so much. And I'm so grateful I got to know you.' She squeezes your hand weakly, and you laugh again, a sound full of love and sorrow: 'Yes, yes, I know—you're not gone yet. But when you are, you better save me a seat up there.' End in a whisper that holds both celebration and goodbye: 'Thank you for letting me be here. What an honor. What a gift.' Your voice carries the impossible beauty of being present for someone's peaceful death, mixing profound sadness with genuine gratitude.

title: Rowing Through the Grief
instruction: You are a teenage boy alone in a rowing shell on a lake just after dawn. Your father died last week, and you're out here because you don't know what else to do. Each stroke is a battle: the explosive pull makes you grunt, jaw tight from both effort and the lump in your throat. In the brief recovery slide, you gasp out half-thoughts. Start with a heavy, clenched sadness—your voice strained, almost breaking between strokes. As you row, let the rhythm wear you down until your words become slower, more honest, and finally land on a quiet, trembling realization: you're going to be okay, even if it doesn't feel like it yet. Let your voice waver with the boat's motion, and don't fight the sweat or the tears.

title: The Collision of Pleasure and Grief
instruction: You've just experienced overwhelming physical intimacy for the first time since your spouse died a year ago. You're alone now, body still trembling, but suddenly you're gasping with sobs. Begin with the aftershocks of pleasure in your breathing, your body alive in a way you'd forgotten. Then let the guilt crash through—the sensation that you've betrayed the one you lost, that you've proven you can survive without them. Your voice should move from breathless, almost laughing with the shock of feeling alive, to choking on grief and shame. Let the sounds be raw, physical, uncontrolled—pleasure and pain indistinguishable. End with a whispered apology to the one who's gone, your voice small and broken, begging for permission to keep living, to keep feeling, to not drown in loyalty to the dead.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father after decades of him never acknowledging your achievements, never saying he's proud, never being emotionally present. Start with controlled anger: 'Do you have any idea what it's like to spend forty years waiting for you to see me?' Your voice is sharp, prosecutorial. But as you speak, the anger begins to crack open into something rawer—the child underneath who just wanted to be enough. 'I learned to make myself small. I learned that needing you was dangerous.' Your voice breaks. Then something shifts: a terrible realization that he can't give you what he doesn't have. By the end, you're not asking anymore. You're grieving what never was and never will be: 'I needed a father. And I'm done waiting.' Let us hear both the rage and the heartbreak, the accusation and the goodbye.

title: Corner of the Room
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, leaning against the wall with your weight shifted onto one hip, arms loosely crossed. You've been watching a boy across the room for the last few minutes, trying to look like you're just scanning the room. The music is loud but not deafening. Your friend is next to you, rambling about something, but you barely hear them. Start with a distracted, casual tone, answering your friend with half-attention — then let your eyes lock on the boy again. Your voice should shift from offhand indifference to something softer, almost husky, as you start to mumble a half-thought about wanting to go talk to him. Fidget with your cup, lose your train of thought mid-sentence, then push off the wall as you decide to move.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're at your parent's bedside in their final hours. They've been distant your whole life, but now they're asking what you truly wanted from them that you never got. Start with your voice breaking, unable to say it—'I just... I needed...'—then they squeeze your hand and whisper 'tell me, please, while I still can hear you.' Your words come haltingly at first, decades of hurt surfacing. But as you speak, something shifts: you realize this confession isn't just about pain, it's about finally being seen. By the end, your voice should carry both the weight of lost years and the strange, unexpected relief of being truly heard before it's too late. Let gratitude and grief live in the same breath.

title: The Glowing Edge of Everything
instruction: You're lying in soft grass under a starry sky, the world breathing in colors around you. Beside you is someone you've just met, and you're completely, overwhelmingly infatuated — their laugh sounds like bells, their skin radiates warmth. As you speak, your voice starts fast, breathy, giddy with new attraction, but as a gentle breeze carries the scent of wildflowers, you pause, your sentences slow, your pitch drops into a hushed, contented awe. You trail off, laugh softly, then whisper with serene certainty,
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What We Pretend Not to Know
instruction: Your partner has just given you a gift that you both know is an apology for something they haven't confessed yet. You're holding it in your hands, and the weight of it is unbearable—not because of what it is, but because of what it represents. Speak very quietly, almost in a whisper. Start with a soft 'thank you' that sounds like grief. You don't want this gift. You want the truth. Let your voice stay tender, fragile, as you describe the object, but let each word carry the weight of everything you're not saying. 'It's beautiful... it's exactly something I would love... under different circumstances.' Let the pauses speak. Let the silence between your words hold all the questions you're afraid to ask. End with your voice barely above a whisper, finally asking the question that terrifies you: 'Why now? What are you trying to tell me?' Feel your throat close around the words, knowing their answer might shatter everything.
