title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Planning
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis, and you're sitting with your spouse planning your own funeral. Somehow, impossibly, you find yourself laughing—really laughing—at the absurdity of choosing between lilies and roses when you'll be dead. Your voice carries genuine humor mixed with heartbreak. You're making jokes about the guest list, teasing your partner about their terrible taste in music, finding bizarre joy in this devastating moment. But underneath every laugh is a tremor. Your voice keeps breaking between humor and grief, sometimes mid-sentence. You shift from joking about the catering to suddenly gripping their hand, voice raw: 'I don't want to leave you.' Then back to laughter because it's the only way you can breathe. End in a place where you're both crying and smiling, your voice soft with gratitude for every ridiculous, beautiful moment you've had together, even as your heart is shattering. Let the laughter and tears be inseparable, authentic, alive.

title: What We Never Say at Dinner Tables
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table where you've shared a thousand silent meals. Start with your jaw clenched, shoulders raised, all the years of swallowed words creating a knot in your chest. As you begin speaking, deliberately soften your breath, unclench your fists, let your spine settle. Feel how each breath creates space for the truth. Tell him about the moment in childhood that changed everything between you, but as you speak, notice what else emerges—not just anger, but the ache of wanting to be seen by him. By the end, transition from accusation to raw vulnerability, your voice potentially dropping to almost a whisper as you ask the question you've been terrified to ask: 'Did you ever actually see me?'

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Sibling She Gave Away
instruction: You've just discovered you had a sister your mother gave up for adoption forty years ago. Start measured, almost clinical - asking questions like you're trying to understand a math problem. But the more she deflects or justifies, the more your voice sharpens. Your calm cracks into something raw: 'I had a sister. I spent my whole childhood alone and I had a SISTER.' Let rage and grief tangle together. Then hit the devastating realization mid-sentence: she chose to keep you, which means she could have chosen differently. End in a quieter, more wounded place - asking the one question you're terrified to hear answered: 'Did you ever regret which one you kept?' Your voice barely above a whisper, bracing for impact.
inspired_by: Parent Teaching Their Teen to Drive: Controlled Terror

title: First Lullaby
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy babysitting your baby niece for the first time. Your sister is in the next room, and you're alone with the infant, rocking her in your arms. You're a little nervous—your voice is hushed, and your body sways gently side to side, which makes your speech bob slightly. Start by awkwardly cooing, but as she stares up at you, you feel a quiet, unexpected infatuation with her tiny perfection. Let your words soften, lose a thought when she gurgles, and end with a protective, whispered vow.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing with Your Sibling at Your Parent's Funeral Reception
instruction: You and your sibling are sharing an absurd memory of your late parent, and suddenly you're both laughing—really laughing—at the wake, and it feels both wrong and perfect. Begin with cautious chuckles, glancing around to see if anyone's watching, feeling guilty for this moment of joy. The laughter builds, becoming almost hysterical, a release of unbearable tension—you're doubled over, tears streaming, can't catch your breath. But then the laughter cracks and suddenly you're crying, really crying, the same gasping sounds but now it's pure grief. End in this strange space where you're still half-laughing, half-sobbing, telling them how much you miss your parent while also being grateful for this moment of lightness, for having each other. Journey from guilty joy to cathartic release to beautiful, messy acceptance where grief and love and laughter all exist together.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father across the kitchen table where you ate breakfast as a child. Start with controlled, almost rehearsed words—you've planned this conversation for years. 'I need you to hear something.' But as you speak about the ways you felt unseen, unprotected, or unloved, your composure cracks. Your voice should move from measured adult clarity to the raw, unguarded pain of the child you once were. Let rage surface, then break apart into something more vulnerable—maybe the realization that they were broken too, or the devastating acknowledgment that they might never understand. End not with resolution but with exhausted honesty, your voice quieter but somehow more powerful than when you began.
inspired_by: The Drunk Confession Nobody Wanted to Hear

title: The Glass Shard of Want
instruction: You're at a backyard fire pit, tripping on a hefty dose of LSD, watching your old college buddy just get praised for a project you've secretly dreamed of. Your voice starts out gritty, tight with jealousy—hyper-masculine, almost growly—but the drug keeps pulling your focus to the flames, to the way light bends on his face. Let the envy leak through your words first, sharp and bitter, then let a long pause open up as you stare at your own hand, noticing how the skin looks like it's breathing. Gradually, the jealousy unravels into a slow, wondering contemplation about why you even want what he has, your pitch rising with childlike curiosity, then dropping into a hushed, sincere laugh at yourself. Speak like you're half-talking to him, half-muttering to the fire—organic pauses, little shifts of weight, a tremor of genuine confusion turning into quiet acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've loved for forty years who has only minutes left to live. Begin by holding back—trying to be strong, to say the 'right' things, keeping your voice steady. But as you look at their face, really see them: notice the specific details that made you fall in love—the curve of their smile, the warmth in their eyes, the particular way they've always looked at you. Let these details break you open. Allow yourself to move from controlled composure to raw, unfiltered grief mixed with profound gratitude. Your voice should crack, soften, become utterly vulnerable. End by whispering something you've never been able to say before, letting decades of love pour out in these final moments.

title: The Hat Says It All
instruction: You are a little girl, maybe 6 or 7, and you haven't seen your older sister in months. You're playing with a stuffed rabbit by the front door when suddenly she walks in—you weren't expecting her at all. The first second is pure shock: you drop the rabbit, let out a high-pitched gasp, and your words tumble out in broken bursts. Then, as you run to hug her, you notice her wearing a ridiculous, oversized hat—and your astonishment melts into a teasing, giggly tone. Let your voice jump from breathless surprise to a playful, sing-song tease, with little laughs and pauses as you struggle to catch your breath.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Jump
instruction: You're a 16-year-old skateboarder, just landed the trick you've been chasing for weeks. Pure ecstasy floods your chest—you're laughing, breathless, talking to yourself in triumph. Then your board catches a crack, you fly sideways, and your arm snaps under you. Start with that giddy, triumphant joy, the grin still warming your voice. As the pain hits, let the ecstasy drain away, replaced by a shocked stillness. Your voice becomes thin, careful, trembling—you whisper 'No, no, no' through clenched teeth, trying not to move. End with a shaky, controlled breath as you call out for help, the adrenaline now fading into raw, white-hot pain.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About Why She Never Protected You
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother after years of distance. You came to make peace, but something she says—something casual, dismissive—ignites everything you've been holding back. You start controlled, almost too calm, asking her a simple question: 'Do you remember when I needed you?' Your voice tightens. She deflects, and suddenly you're not asking anymore—you're demanding she look at what she allowed to happen. Your words become sharper, faster, cutting through her excuses. But then, underneath the anger, something breaks. Your voice cracks into something rawer, younger—the child who needed her then. You shift between rage at her betrayal and the devastating vulnerability of still wanting her to say she's sorry, to say she sees you. End torn between wanting to walk away and the terrible hope that she might finally understand.
inspired_by: Realizing Your Parent's Behavior Was Abusive, Not Normal

title: Story Telling
instruction: One person is telling a story, and the other is listening. The storyteller's voice carries the narrative energy—it rises and falls, builds tension, creates atmosphere. The listener's voice might interject questions, encouragement, or gasps of reaction. The storyteller is not just recounting events; they're creating a world. Their voice is the vehicle. The listener's voice reflects being transported. By the end, the story has ended, and there's a moment of silence where the listener is still in the story. The storyteller's final voice is satisfied: they've transported someone else into their imagination.

title: The Last Constellation
instruction: You're lying in a hospital bed at dawn, and your adult child has just arrived after driving through the night. You haven't seen them in three years because of a fight neither of you would back down from. You have hours, maybe a day left. Start with the sharp defensive anger that's kept you apart—the words you've rehearsed, the pride you've armored yourself with. But as you look at their face, at the way they're trying not to cry, something breaks open in you. Let your voice move from clipped and guarded to raw and undefended. By the end, you're not asking for forgiveness—you're offering a memory from their childhood, something small and perfect you've carried all this time, your voice barely above a whisper, every word a gift you're placing in their hands before you go.

title: Dancing in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're slow-dancing with someone you love in their hospital room—perhaps it's your final dance together, or a celebration of unexpected good news in the middle of terrible circumstances. Begin by describing the absurdity and beauty of it: the IV pole you're careful not to tangle, the way their hospital gown crinkles, the smell of antiseptic mixing with their familiar scent. Let genuine laughter bubble up—this is ridiculous and perfect and heartbreaking all at once. Feel their hand trembling in yours, their breath against your neck, the way they hum off-key. As you speak, let joy and grief become completely intertwined—you're laughing but your voice keeps catching, you're describing this moment of aliveness while death or fear hovers just outside the door. Express gratitude for this dance, this moment, this person, even as you feel it slipping away. End with something that's simultaneously a celebration and a goodbye, your voice full of both life and loss, unable to separate the two.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After twenty years, you're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child. Begin with controlled anger - your voice tight, measured, listing what you lost because of their absence. But as you speak, the child inside you emerges. Your anger cracks open to reveal the vulnerable kid who waited by the window, who made excuses for them at school, who wondered what they did wrong. Your voice becomes smaller, more fragile, asking the questions you've carried: 'Why wasn't I enough? Did you ever think about me?' Then something shifts - you realize you don't need their answer anymore. Your voice steadies with hard-won strength as you reclaim your story, moving from pleading to release, ending not with forgiveness but with letting go.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're reading a final bedtime story to someone you raised—a child, a sibling, someone who won't wake up tomorrow. Begin with the gentle, soothing voice you've used a thousand times before, finding comfort in the familiar ritual. But as you read, your voice begins to crack, words catching as you realize this is the last time. Let yourself shift between trying to maintain that protective, parental calm and the raw grief that wants to break through. End with a whispered goodbye that's part blessing, part desperate plea for more time. Your voice should feel like it's holding someone close even as you're letting them go.

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love, in the intimate darkness of late night, finally admitting something you've carried alone for years—a fear, a regret, a truth about yourself you've been ashamed of. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, each word requiring courage to release. Start hesitant, circling around what you need to say, your breath catching with vulnerability. As you speak, let relief begin mixing with fear of their reaction, your voice trembling between the safety of darkness and the exposure of honesty. The quiet should feel sacred, every pause heavy with emotion too deep for loud words. End with a question you're terrified to ask, your voice breaking on the hope that they'll still accept you.

title: The Cookie Conspiracy
instruction: You're a father confessing to your 6-year-old that you ate the last chocolate chip cookie you were supposed to share. Start with a sheepish grin and a playful tone—you think it's funny because you swapped it with a carrot stick and she'll probably laugh. But as her face falls, your voice loses its bounce, gets smaller, more hesitant. Let the confession drop in volume as you realize she's genuinely disappointed. End with a quiet, vulnerable apology, your amusement fading into sincere regret.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protective Fury: Begging Them Not to Go While Knowing They Must
instruction: Someone you love is about to walk into certain danger—a necessary sacrifice, a dangerous mission, a path that will likely destroy them—and you're losing your composure completely. Start with fierce, almost violent pleading: your voice loud, demanding, trying to use sheer force of will to make them stay. Let desperation turn to rage—at them for choosing this, at yourself for being unable to stop them, at the universe for requiring this sacrifice. Then collapse into helpless, broken begging, your voice raw and small, admitting you can't survive their loss. End in devastated acceptance: you'll let them go because you love them enough to honor their choice, even as it kills you. Move from explosive anger through desperate bargaining to whispered, tearful surrender.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Healer Saves the Villain's Life Against All Doctrine

title: The Last Visit Before Hospice
instruction: You're visiting your grandmother for what you both know is the last time before she enters hospice. Begin with forced cheerfulness, pretending everything is normal, your voice bright but brittle. She stops you mid-sentence and says your name in a way that makes all pretense impossible. Your voice breaks. You tell her all the things you've been too scared to say—how she taught you what love looks like, how you're terrified of the world without her in it. She responds with such tenderness that you can barely breathe. By the end, you're crying but also laughing softly at a memory she brings up, your voice raw but filled with gratitude. The fear is still there, but so is something like peace. You're saying goodbye, and you're both really present for it.

title: The Invisible Thread
instruction: In complete darkness or with your eyes closed, whisper to someone you've lost—a deceased loved one, an ex who's gone forever, or a friend who vanished from your life. Begin by pretending they're lying next to you, close enough to feel their breath. Imagine the warmth of their body, the specific texture of their skin, the smell of their hair. Confess something you never got to say—something tender, shameful, or achingly simple. As you speak, let yourself believe more completely that they're there: feel them shift position, sense their fingers finding yours in the dark, imagine their breathing synchronizing with yours. Start with tentative hope that they might hear you somehow, but let this transform—either into full belief that transcends reason, or into the crushing awareness that you're speaking to emptiness, or into the peaceful realization that carrying them inside you is enough.

title: The Garden of Paradox
instruction: You've returned to a place from your past—a childhood home, a former lover's apartment, a parent's grave—and you're overwhelmed by contradictory feelings crashing together. Begin by trying to hold onto one feeling: maybe anger, maybe nostalgia. Then let a vivid, symbolic image from your imagination surface—perhaps you see the place as overgrown with wild flowers and thorns, or flooded with water, or golden with impossible light. Don't describe this image; instead, let it change how you feel about being here. Allow joy and anguish to coexist, gratitude and rage to intertwine, love and loss to become inseparable. Speak to someone present or absent, letting your voice move between laughter and tears, tenderness and fury, until you find a strange peace in holding all these contradictions at once. Move from attempting single emotion through symbolic transformation to embracing paradox.
inspired_by: When integrating dreams into the programming process

title: When Protectiveness Becomes Powerlessness
instruction: Your child or someone you'd die to protect is making a choice that will destroy them, and you can't stop it. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness—your voice strong, commanding: 'You are not doing this, do you hear me?' But as they refuse to listen, your certainty crumbles. The strength in your voice fractures into desperation, then helpless rage. You might shout, then suddenly break—your voice dropping to something raw and pleading: 'I can't lose you. I won't survive it.' Feel the shift from authority to begging, from anger to naked terror. End with a devastating whisper of surrender, your breathing ragged, as you realize love doesn't always mean you can save them. The final words carry both fury at your own powerlessness and fierce, unshakeable devotion.

title: The Surgeon's Impossible Promise
instruction: You're a surgeon speaking to the parent of a child who needs an experimental procedure - the only chance at survival, but with devastating risks. You begin with clinical confidence, explaining the medical facts, your voice steady and professional. But as the parent begs you to promise their child will live, something breaks in you. You want to give them hope, you want to be their savior, but you know the statistics. Your voice fractures as you try to maintain professional distance while your heart is screaming that you care about this child, that you'll fight like hell, but you cannot - you cannot - promise what they're begging for. End caught between the doctor you're trained to be and the human who desperately wants to offer comfort you don't have the right to give.

title: Dancing at Your Ex's Wedding While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're at your ex's wedding—someone you thought was your forever—and you've just been asked to give a toast. You're smiling, genuinely happy for them, because you love them enough to want their joy. Your words are warm, funny, full of affection, and as you speak, you're also breaking. The contradiction lives in your voice: celebrating their happiness while grieving your own loss. You laugh at a shared memory, and the laugh catches, almost becomes a sob, but you redirect it into more laughter. You tell them they deserve this love, and you mean it, even as it costs you everything to say it. End with a genuine wish for their happiness, voice thick with unshed tears. You raise your glass. Everyone cheers. You're applauding too, smiling through the ache, finding grace in letting go. The quiet moment after, when the attention shifts away and you can finally breathe—half relieved, half destroyed, wholly released.
inspired_by: Singing Happy Birthday Alone in Your Apartment

title: The Last Confession Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the pre-dawn hours. She's awake, lucid for what may be the last time. Begin by making small talk about the weather, the hospital food—anything safe. But she asks you directly: 'What are you most afraid of in your life?' Start with deflection, gentle resistance. Gradually, let the walls come down. Share something you've never told anyone—a fear about who you are, a secret shame, a dream you're terrified to pursue. Watch how her face softens as you speak. Let your voice move from guarded and careful to trembling with raw honesty. By the end, you're not just confessing—you're weeping with relief, holding her hand, feeling closer to her than you've ever felt to anyone. The fear transforms into profound connection.

title: The Summit of Silence
instruction: You've just reached the top of a mountain after a brutal climb. The thin air leaves you gasping for breath, each word costing real effort. You're a stoic, middle-aged man who usually masks emotion, but here, alone, you let yourself feel an overwhelming, childlike ecstasy. You speak to the vast landscape, your voice breaking with a raw pleasure you haven't allowed in years. Your joy fights against your gasping lungs—let the wonder come out in short, broken bursts, as if the altitude and the awe are sharing your voice. By the end, the struggle to breathe fades into a quiet, humbled acceptance, the pleasure settling into a deep, whispered peace.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Shattered Sanctuary: A Partner's Explosive Plea When Love Isn't Enough to Save Someone
instruction: You've just found the evidence—pills hidden, a plan made, a note half-written. Your voice erupts in fierce, desperate intensity: 'Look at me. LOOK AT ME.' You're not just angry; you're terrified, fighting for someone's life with everything you have. Your voice is raw power—shaking them, pleading, demanding they see how much they matter. You're listing everything they mean, every reason they need to stay, and your voice is breaking with the force of your love. But mid-stream, something shifts. Your rage cracks wide open and suddenly you're on your knees, voice dropping to a devastated whisper. You can't make them want to live. Your fierce protectiveness collides with absolute helplessness, and it destroys you. Your voice becomes ragged: 'I can't lose you, but I can't save you.' You're sobbing but still trying to speak, words tumbling over each other. End with your hands reaching for them, voice small and broken: 'Please. Just... please.' You're offering everything you are, knowing it might not be enough. The final moment is you waiting, shattered, for their answer.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Thief Returns Stolen Item to the Person Whose Trust They Betrayed

title: Finding Your Child's Suicide Note
instruction: You've just found a note from your teenager. Start reading aloud, your voice confused, not understanding. The first lines are cryptic. Then it becomes clear what this is, and terror explodes through you — you're shouting their name, screaming through the house, your voice ragged with panic. You grab your phone, calling them, reading fragments of the note aloud between frantic breaths. They answer — they're alive, at school, confused by your panic. Relief hits like a tidal wave. But then rage ignites: how could they write this, how could they not tell you they were hurting? Your voice breaks between fury and desperate love as you demand answers. Finally, you collapse into helpless weeping, begging them to come home, telling them they're loved, that you're sorry, that you failed to see them drowning.

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a dream destroyed, a betrayal discovered, a loss that changes everything—and you're alone in your apartment. Begin with your body rigid, voice shaking with attempts to contain the explosion building inside you. Then let go completely: scream, sob, move with abandon, let your voice crack and roar and keen without any attempt to sound 'right.' Allow your body to express pure, animal grief and rage—knock things over if you need to, collapse to the floor, punch pillows. But then, in the midst of this chaos, put on a song from your childhood—something that once made you feel invincible and full of possibility. Let your body remember what joy felt like, even as tears still stream down your face. Allow yourself to move between the rage and something like ecstatic release, your voice shifting from cries of pain to something approaching wild laughter, until you cannot tell if you are breaking down or breaking through. End in exhausted, tearful laughter at the absurdity of being alive and feeling everything at once.
inspired_by: Imaging a Subpersonality: The Magical Child

title: The Body's Divided Chorus
instruction: You're in the throes of intense physical experience—perhaps childbirth, a brutal workout, passionate sex, or fighting through injury. Your body is overwhelmed with sensation. Allow different parts of yourself to respond physically and vocally to what you're feeling: the part that surrenders completely to the sensation, the part that fights and resists, the part that transcends into ecstasy, the part that breaks down weeping, the part that becomes savage and animal, the part that detaches and observes coldly. Let each take over your entire physical being—voice, breath, movement, facial expression. Don't perform these shifts; allow the intensity of sensation to genuinely fracture you into these different responses. End in whatever state emerges when the intensity finally passes. Move from unified experience through physical/emotional fragmentation to exhausted integration.

title: The Taking of the Stage
instruction: You are on a busy street corner, standing on a wooden crate. There is a knot of people before you, some listening, some heckling. Your voice is already raw from an hour of shouting, but you are also a little drunk, the world slightly hazy and tilted. Begin with a false, bright energy meant to draw a crowd, but as you speak, the boredom and the hot, sharp anger at the injustice you're here to protest starts to creep in. Let the words stumble at first, then grow jagged and heavy. Finish with a flat, weary conclusion, the fight draining out of you, the edge of your anger blunted by the simple fact that no one is really listening.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Aging Vocally
instruction: You're watching home videos of yourself as a young actor — clear voice, limitless breath, energy that bounces. Now you're 70, sitting in silence, and your agent just rejected you for not sounding young enough. Play both: the you in the video (bright, rapid, effortless), then snap back to the present (slower, weaker, breathless after sentences). Your jaw aches. Your voice cracks on the name 'Mom' when you notice her in the background of the tape. The aging isn't performed — it's happening in real time through the realization.

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he stayed silent when your mother was cruel. For years, you've rehearsed this. You start controlled, facts and examples, your voice steady. But then he says, 'I did my best,' and something breaks open in you. Your voice rises—not to a shout, but to something raw and jagged. 'Your best? Your *best* was watching?' The anger cracks into something more painful: the child you were, still wanting him to fight for you. Your voice drops to almost a whisper, shaking: 'I needed you to choose me.' Tears come, hot and unwanted. Then, in the silence, you realize—you're not asking anymore. You're grieving the father you never had. The last words are soft, final: 'I deserved better.' You walk away, but your legs feel uncertain.

title: Whispered Truths in the Dark
instruction: Late at night, someone who loves you asks why you've been so distant, so hard to reach. You begin speaking so quietly they have to lean in to hear. Your voice is paper-thin, vulnerable, each word an admission you've been too afraid to make. You're confessing that you're tired of explaining yourself, tired of being the translator for your own existence, tired of watching people's faces as they try to understand something that should be simple. Your breath catches on certain words. There's no anger here - just profound, aching weariness mixed with desperate hope that this person, at least, will understand without needing you to perform or prove anything. End with a question that hangs in the air, your voice barely audible: can you love someone you don't fully understand? Let the silence answer.
inspired_by: Explaining Your Non-Binary or Fluid Identity

title: Echoes of a Missed Goodbye
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone on a concrete stairwell landing, waiting for someone who promised to meet you here but never showed. The harsh reverb amplifies your voice as you speak to yourself, at first bitterly repeating the time and the empty steps—disappointment makes your words sharp, clipped, almost shouting at the walls. Then, mid-sentence, you notice a faint echo of your own voice spiraling upward, and your tone softens: you remember the last time you heard that same reverb when you both laughed here years ago. Let the sound carry you into longing—your voice becomes quieter, more breathy, as if reaching for the memory, and you trail off, lost in the reverberation.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Longing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Pink Beret
instruction: You are a 9-year-old girl whose mother just dropped you off at a military-style summer camp. You're standing at attention in the hot sun with other kids, trying desperately not to smile because you're actually relieved — last week the other girls teased you for being soft, and this uniform makes you feel like you belong. But your brand-new beret keeps sliding down over your right eye, and the sergeant just yelled at you for adjusting it. You're now trying to keep your voice deep and serious like a soldier's, but your cheeks are burning with embarrassment, and your voice keeps cracking into a tiny squeak as you shout your name and bunk number. Your words should start with a brave, forced bark, but by the end, your voice wobbles and trails off as you feel everyone staring at your crooked hat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession in the Dark
instruction: You and someone you've silently loved for years are lying side by side in darkness—post-intimacy, or sitting through a sleepless night together. Begin speaking in barely-there whispers, almost as if you're talking to yourself, confessing something you've never said aloud: that you've been in love with them all along, or that you're terrified of losing them, or that you've sabotaged every chance at happiness because you didn't believe you deserved them. Let the darkness and quietness give you permission to be more honest than daylight ever could. As you speak, feel the vulnerability turn from terrifying to liberating. End with your voice even softer, but no longer afraid—just achingly, simply true.
inspired_by: When you are an actor who does not understand why a co-star is avoiding you or being cold between takes

title: The Last Round
instruction: You are an elderly woman playing a co-op shooter with younger friends, late at night. Your hands ache, your eyes are heavy, and you've just failed a crucial revive because your reflexes couldn't keep up. You hear your teammates still encouraging you, trying to keep the mood light. Start with a breathy, defeated line about how you're slowing them down, your voice trembling with exhaustion and self-blame. Then, as they cheer for your next attempt, let a thin thread of gratitude seep in—grateful they haven't given up on you—but your voice stays fragile, laced with the weight of your own limits. Speak haltingly, as if you're losing focus between button presses, and finish with a quiet, almost whispered thanks. Let the micro-distractions of the game—a distant explosion, a teammate's callout—pull your attention mid-thought.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Ember Tale
instruction: You are a teenager telling a ghost story to friends around a campfire. The story is based on something painful that happened to you — start with your voice heavy and raw, stumbling over words, eyes fixed on the flames. As you speak, you notice your friends are scared, leaning in. A slight, dark pleasure flickers inside you. Your voice becomes smoother, slower, with a sly edge. End with a whisper that holds both old hurt and a quiet malice. Let the crackling fire and pauses between sentences feel natural.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Stain That Won't Budge
instruction: You are an older man scrubbing a dried coffee stain on your kitchen counter. Your arthritic shoulder aches with each circular motion, and your breath comes in short puffs timed to your arm movements. At first you're fully concentrated on the stain, muttering about it stubbornly. As the pain flares, your voice tightens, your rhythm falters, and you grimace through the words. End with a weary sigh and a quiet admission of defeat.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: They're asleep beside you, and you're leaving—not for work, not for a trip, but forever. This is your last chance to say everything you could never say when they were awake and looking at you. Start quietly, tenderly, saying the things that made you fall in love. But as you speak in hushed tones, the reasons you're leaving seep in—the ways you've hurt each other, the future you can't give them, the person you need to become alone. Let us hear the catch in your throat, the moments where you almost can't continue, where love and loss are so tangled you can't separate them. This is intimate devastation, spoken soft enough not to wake them, breaking your heart with every whispered word. End somewhere between blessing them and releasing yourself.
inspired_by: Hiding Nervousness During an Important Interview

title: The Last Thread
instruction: You are a middle-aged person with a neurological tremor that makes your voice soft, monotone, and slightly wobbly. You've just finished threading a needle and stitching a torn pocket — a task that took ten minutes of frustration. Now you hold up the work to the light. Begin by muttering in disgust at your own shaking hands, your voice small and mumbling, wavering with anger. Then, as you see the neat stitch you managed despite it all, let a quiet, wobbly triumph creep in. Your voice stays soft, but lifts in pride. End with a breathy, 'There. I did it.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Discovering Your Partner's Affair—Mid-Argument Collapse
instruction: You've found the evidence—texts, emails, something undeniable. You confront them and your voice starts as fire: accusations flying, voice rising, sharp with betrayal and rage. 'How long? How LONG have you been lying to my face?' You're incredulous, furious, your voice dripping with contempt. But they say something—maybe the other person's name with tenderness, maybe 'I love them,' maybe they defend the affair—and your voice just... stops. The rage collapses into something more terrifying: devastation. Your voice becomes unsteady, small, confused. 'Was any of it real? Us? Our life?' You're asking questions you don't want answered, voice breaking on every word. Then the helpless fury returns but mixed with anguish—you're yelling through tears, voice cracking between rage and heartbreak: 'I gave you everything!' End with your voice reduced to a whisper, almost talking to yourself: 'I wasn't enough.' It's not a question. The fight has left your body. Your voice is hollow, shattered.

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your partner is dying, too weak to get out of bed, and their favorite song just came on the radio. You're describing dancing with them—moving around the room, taking both roles, laughing through tears. Start with genuine joy: 'Remember when we danced to this at our wedding? Come on, I'll be you, you be me!' Your voice is light, playful, determined to give them this moment. You're twirling, narrating the dance, making them laugh. But your voice keeps catching—joy and grief are inseparable now. You're grateful for this moment, devastated it's ending, holding both at once. Your laughter has tears in it; your tears have laughter. End breathless, sitting back down beside them: 'That was perfect. You've always been the best dancer.' Your voice is full of wonder, gratitude, and the most beautiful kind of breaking. This is love at the edge of loss—everything at once.
inspired_by: Defending Your Partner Against Your Family's Criticism

title: Lost in the Crowd
instruction: You're at a loud house party, heavily intoxicated. You've lost your friend who promised to stay by your side. You're weaving through people, muttering to yourself, trying to spot her. Start with a wave of panic — your voice trembles, you hiccup, you grab a wall to steady yourself. As you realize she's not coming back, impatience and irritation take over. Your slurring worsens, volume spikes then drops. End with a sharp, frustrated plea that trails into exhaustion.
emotions_sampled: Fear (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're a soldier saying goodbye to your child the morning you leave for a deployment you know in your bones you won't return from. Start by describing the breakfast you made together—pancakes, their favorite—your voice artificially bright, trying to make it normal. 'Remember when you were three and you put chocolate chips in the shape of a smiley face?' But the brightness cracks. Your hands are shaking as you brush their hair. 'I need you to know something.' Now your voice drops, becomes urgent, raw. 'Every single day of your life, I have loved you more than breathing.' You're memorizing their face. 'When things get hard—and they will—I need you to remember that you come from strength. You come from love.' Your voice breaks completely. 'I'm so sorry I won't be there to see who you become.' But then, gathering yourself, finding a fierce tenderness: 'But I'll be watching. Somehow, somewhere, I'll be watching. And I'll be so proud.' End with a whisper, trying to be brave for them: 'It's time to go now.'

title: Fog of Interest
instruction: You're a teenage guy waking from a deep nap on the couch. Your friend is sitting nearby, excitedly describing a new game trailer that just dropped. At first, you're lost in groggy haze — can't focus, can't form words, voice thick and slow. But as they keep talking, a spark of curiosity cuts through the fog. Let your words come out slurred, with pauses and blinks, then gradually sharpen as you lean in, ending with a clearer, eager question.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're describing the end of your world—your marriage, your career, your dreams, maybe all of it at once—but you're finding unexpected freedom in the destruction. Begin with a laugh that sounds slightly unhinged, almost giddy, as you describe what's falling apart. 'It's all gone,' you say, and you're almost celebrating it. But let that laughter become complicated—tears mixing with joy, relief tangled with terror. Your voice lifts with the strange euphoria of having nothing left to lose, then breaks with the genuine grief of what you're mourning. End in that beautiful, terrible space where you're simultaneously celebrating your liberation and crying for what you've lost. This should feel like someone finding light in their darkest moment, authentic and complex and impossibly human.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn, and you both know this is goodbye. She's awake, lucid, and asking you to tell her about your life—the real one, not the version you've been protecting her with. Start with hesitant joy as you share a beautiful memory, but let it fracture into grief as you realize you're losing the one person who truly knew you. Your voice moves from bright reminiscence to broken whispers. She squeezes your hand and says, 'I'm so proud of who you became.' By the end, your voice should carry both devastating loss and profound gratitude—you're saying goodbye while also saying thank you for every moment you had.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting at your father's hospital bedside in his final hours. He's conscious but fading. For years, you've held back anger about how absent he was during your childhood, but now you also feel overwhelming love and the desperate need to say goodbye. Begin speaking to him with resentment simmering beneath your words—let that bitterness color everything you say. As you continue, allow grief and forgiveness to crack through your anger. By the end, you must arrive at a place of tender release, where you give him (and yourself) permission to let go. Let your voice carry the journey from hardness to heartbreak to peace, regardless of the exact words you choose.

title: Suitcase Morning
instruction: It's 5 AM. Your partner of eight years is packing to leave you, and you're sitting on the bed watching. Your voice is quiet, almost gentle, as you notice they're taking the blue sweater—the one they wore on your first date. You're not trying to stop them; you're just... narrating what you see, like if you speak softly enough, this won't be real. Mention small things: how they fold their shirts, that they're leaving the coffee maker, that the cat is going to wonder where they went. Your throat catches when you realize they're taking the photo of you both in Barcelona. There's no anger, just this tender, devastating acceptance. End with a whispered 'I hope you find what I couldn't give you,' and the heartbreak of meaning it.

title: Birthday Candles
instruction: You're celebrating your child's birthday—the last one before they leave home forever, or perhaps they've been sick and you weren't sure they'd see this day. You're trying to be joyful, to make this moment perfect for them. Begin with genuine, determined happiness—sing, laugh, celebrate with real warmth. But underneath, you're also grieving. Maybe grieving their childhood ending, maybe grateful they're alive but terrified of losing them, maybe angry at time itself for moving forward. Let both emotions exist simultaneously. Your smile is real, but your eyes are swimming. Your voice cracks with laughter and tears at once. You're celebrating and mourning, grateful and furious, holding on and letting go—all at the same time. Don't choose between the feelings; let them war inside you. End in a moment where joy and sorrow are completely, impossibly intertwined.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a one-dimensional character or character work feels superficial—expressing the emotion rather than creating the impetus

title: Fierce Love That Cannot Protect
instruction: Someone you're responsible for is in danger you cannot prevent—a child making a choice you can't stop, someone walking into harm you can't shield them from. Start with commanding intensity: 'You are NOT doing this, do you understand me?' Your voice is powerful, protective, almost aggressive in its desperation. But they're not listening, and you feel your power crumbling. Your tone shifts between fierce anger and breaking panic: 'I have kept you safe your whole life—' Your voice cracks. The rage dissolves into pleading, then into something raw and helpless. 'Please, I'm begging you, PLEASE—' You're nearly shouting but it's not anger anymore, it's pure terror and love. By the end, your voice has collapsed entirely into quiet sobbing, all the fierce protectiveness transformed into broken surrender: 'I can't lose you. I can't.' The strength becomes absolute vulnerability.

title: The Breaking Point: I Would Burn the World Down for You
instruction: You're screaming at the universe, at God, at anyone who will listen—your child, your partner, your loved one is suffering and you are utterly powerless to stop it. Start with explosive rage: your voice is volcanic, cursing and demanding answers, rattling off everything you've already sacrificed, everything you would do. Your voice is primal, almost feral with protective fury—you would tear yourself apart, trade places, destroy anything if it would help. But mid-sentence, the rage cracks and transforms into desperate pleading. Your voice breaks completely as you beg—you're on your knees emotionally, your previous power dissolving into helpless sobbing. You oscillate between fierce declarations of what you'd do and broken whispers of 'please, please, please.' By the end, you're exhausted, your voice hoarse and shaking, admitting in barely more than a whisper that you can't fix this, you can't save them, and it's destroying you—your passionate protectiveness collapsing into the quiet devastation of absolute helplessness.
inspired_by: Professional: Social Worker Removes a Child from Their Parents

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You're standing at your ex-lover's wedding reception, champagne glass in hand, about to give a toast as the 'old friend.' Begin feeling the weight of the glass, the eyes on you, the knot of contradictions in your chest. You genuinely want them to be happy—that's real—but something in you is breaking at the same time. Don't choose which feeling to show; let them coexist and fight for space in your voice. Start speaking and let your improvised words reveal the war between celebration and grief, between generosity and loss. Maybe you laugh—is it bitter or genuine or both? Let your voice do unexpected things: strengthen when you thought you'd falter, crack when you meant to sound fine. By the final sentence, you've somehow found a truthful blessing that contains both your joy for them and your sorrow for yourself—a complicated gift that costs you something to give.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child the Truth You Can Never Say Out Loud
instruction: It's 2 AM. Your child is asleep. You're sitting beside their bed, and in the darkness, you whisper the confession you can never speak when they're awake: that you're terrified you're failing them, that sometimes you don't recognize yourself as a parent, that you love them so much it physically hurts but you're not sure love is enough. Your voice is barely audible, catching on words, thick with tears you're trying not to shed. There's tenderness here, but also shame, and a devastating vulnerability. End by promising them something—anything—even though you're not sure you can keep it. This must feel like a prayer, a confession, and a love letter all at once, spoken in the intimate darkness where secrets live.
inspired_by: Holding Someone During a Seizure While Talking to 911

title: Laughing Through Tears at Their Deathbed Joke
instruction: Your best friend or sibling, dying of illness, has just made a terrible joke about their own death—dark humor that's so perfectly them. You start laughing, really laughing, because it's absurd and perfect and exactly what they would do. But let that laughter catch and tangle with tears, moving between genuine joy at their spirit and the crushing grief of losing them. Express gratitude for who they are, for this moment, for their refusal to make this heavy, while your heart simultaneously breaks. Your voice should move fluidly between laughing and crying, sometimes in the same breath—'God, you're such an asshole' said with love, 'Thank you for making me laugh' said through sobs. End in a place of bittersweet peace, where the pain and the love and the laughter all exist together, authentic and messy and utterly human.

title: Bedside Confession to the Sleeping Beloved
instruction: Your partner is in a coma after an accident, and you're confessing something you never had the courage to say while they were awake. Begin in a whisper, almost afraid to disturb the silence: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' Your voice is tender but weighted with regret. As you continue, emotion catches in your throat: 'I was so afraid of losing you that I never really let you in.' Pause to breathe through the tightness in your chest. 'Every time you tried to get closer, I pulled away.' Your voice becomes even softer, more broken: 'And now you might never wake up, and you'll never know—' Let the words dissolve into quiet crying. End with a barely audible: 'Please come back. I'm ready now. I'm finally ready.' This is intimacy at its most fragile—speaking truths to someone who can't hear you.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Lover Why You Have to Leave
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering all the things you can't say when they're awake—why you're leaving, why you have to, why staying would destroy you both. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, tender. Confess everything: your fear of their love, your unworthiness, the specific moments you almost stayed. Include the small details—how they look when they laugh, the way they touch your face. Let your voice catch not on dramatic declarations but on tiny truths: 'You deserve someone who doesn't flinch when you say forever.' Midway through, they shift in their sleep and you freeze, terrified they'll wake. When they settle again, your whispers become even more raw, almost prayer-like. End with you saying 'I'm so sorry' while touching their hair one last time, your breath shaking with the weight of tenderness and unbearable loss.
inspired_by: Poet Reading Their Work at an Open Mic — for Their Ex in the Audience

title: The Truth About the Music Box
instruction: You are confronting your aging mother about a childhood music box she sold without asking—but it's not really about the object. Start with restrained frustration, your words careful and measured, trying to be the good adult child. As she dismisses your feelings, let thirty years of being unheard surge up: the recitals she missed, the dreams she called impractical, the parts of you she never saw. Your voice should rise, break, become raw—demand to know why nothing you loved ever mattered to her. Then, in her silence, hear yourself. Let the anger collapse into something more devastating: the quiet realization that you're still that child, still begging to be seen. End with exhausted tenderness, asking her—really asking—if she even knows who you are.

title: The Silent Room
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting in a stark police interview room, the overhead light buzzing faintly. Across the table, a detective stares at you without speaking, letting the silence press. Your voice comes out soft, almost girlish—a reflex from a lifetime of being polite. You start by nervously fidgeting with your sleeve, hedging, apologizing for minor things. But as you recall the reason you're here—a missing neighbor, a kindness you didn't show—a numbness settles over you. Your words slow, your gaze drifts to the clock on the wall, and you end by simply stating a quiet, hollow truth: you saw nothing because you chose not to look. Let your voice flatten, the pitch even out, as if the emotion drains away.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Voicemail to Mom
instruction: You're leaving a final voicemail for your mother who has dementia and won't remember you by tomorrow. Start trying to sound cheerful and normal, telling her about your day, but as you speak, the weight of this being the last time she'll really 'know' you crashes down. Your voice should begin bright and chatty, then gradually crack and falter as grief overwhelms you. End in whispered, broken words where you're trying to say 'I love you' but can barely get the words out. Let the transition be organic—not a sudden shift, but a slow crumbling of your composure as reality sets in.

title: The Last Straw
instruction: You are a chronically exhausted woman, a single mother, slumped at a kitchen table after another sleepless night. Your child is in the next room, hidden but listening. You begin by droning to yourself about the never-ending cycle of laundry, dishes, and demands—your voice nasal and flat, vowels drawn out like a sigh that never ends. Halfway through, you realize your child is overhearing, and your exhaustion shifts into a raw, quiet confession: you don't hate this life, you hate that you can't feel grateful anymore. Let the fatigue sit in your bones; your voice should crack, lose its sing-song, and finally land in a broken whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Exquisite Contradiction
instruction: You are an older woman at a luxurious spa, receiving a head massage from a young attendant who speaks broken English with a heavy accent. You find his halting, overly loud speech grating and almost comically clumsy—you feel a twinge of disgust. But the massage is pure ecstasy, a wave of pleasure that makes you gasp. You want to thank him, but your words come out simplified, separated into blunt chunks, louder than needed, reflecting your inner conflict. Begin with irritable, curt demands for him to continue, then let the pleasure soften your disgust into a grudging, overly loud gratitude that sounds almost childlike.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unraveling of a Promise
instruction: You're standing alone in a sunlit, empty garage, a toolbox at your feet. You're a young man who's just finished restoring an old motorcycle—a project your dying father gave you a year ago, claiming you'd never finish it. It runs perfectly now, and that success tastes like ash. Speak to the bike as if it can hear you; your voice is steady, full of breath, but your jaw is tight with bitterness. Start with a resolute, almost proud tone, but let the pride crack as you realize the victory is hollow—let your voice drop, lose its clarity, and end in a whisper of confusion and resentment.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point Confession
instruction: You're a parent whose teenager has just been brought home by police, and you're alone with them in their room. Start with barely controlled fury—'Do you have ANY idea what you've put us through?'—your voice tight and sharp with fear masquerading as anger. You're pacing, not letting them speak, the words coming faster and harder. But mid-rant, something breaks in you completely. Your rage cracks open and what pours out is terror: 'I thought you were dead. I thought I'd lost you. I thought—' Your voice shatters into sobs you can't control, your fierce parental authority collapsing into raw vulnerability. You sink down, maybe to the floor, and what emerges is a confession of your own fears, your own failures, how desperately you love them and how terrified you are that it's not enough to keep them safe. Oscillate between anger and anguish, control and complete emotional surrender, ending in exhausted, helpless love.

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Own Funeral Recording
instruction: You're recording a message for your own funeral—you have weeks left, maybe days. Start with dark humor: 'Well, if you're watching this, I'm dead. Weird, right?' Your voice has levity, almost mischievous, finding absurdity in the impossible. But then you think of specific faces who'll watch this—your best friend, your sibling, your love—and your voice cracks mid-laugh. The humor doesn't leave, but tears flood in: 'God, I'm going to miss you so much.' You laugh and sob simultaneously, expressing gratitude for ordinary moments—Tuesday dinners, stupid inside jokes, the time they stayed when everything fell apart. Your voice oscillates between joy at having lived and devastation at leaving. End with something funny, then something unbearably tender, voice steadying with strange peace: 'I was here. I loved. That's enough.' The last word should shimmer with both grief and inexplicable gratitude.
inspired_by: Skydiving: Main Chute Failure, Deploying Backup While Narrating

title: Holding Vigil in the Blue Hour
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping child who's been sick for months, speaking to them in the pre-dawn darkness when you think they can't hear you. Begin in a near-whisper, confessing your fears—the medical bills you can't pay, the prognosis you haven't told anyone. Let your voice become so tender it almost disappears as you apologize for every time you were impatient, every moment you didn't treasure. Catch your breath as you realize you're memorizing the sound of their breathing. End with a barely audible prayer or promise, your voice thick with unshed tears, finding words for a love so fierce it physically hurts.

title: Echoes of the Deep
instruction: You are a teenage girl exploring a winding, damp cave with your younger sibling. The only light is your headlamp, and the irregular drip of water echoes around you. You begin intensely focused, counting steps and listening for the path. Then your sibling whimpers, and a teasing grin spreads—you mock them with a playful, echoing 'scaredy-cat.' But as you turn, you realize they dropped the map in a puddle. Your voice hardens, your breath quickens, and you snap at them, the cave amplifying your irritation into a harsh, ringing tone. Let the reverb stretch your words, and let the annoyance build until your final command is sharp and impatient.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Teasing (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Perfect Roux
instruction: You are alone in your cluttered kitchen, chopping onions while a pot of stock simmers loudly. You're making a dish that your ex-partner once mocked you for—saying you could never get the roux right. Embarrassment burns in your chest as you recall their cruel laughter, and a sour bitterness seeps into your movements. But as you stir the butter and flour together, the golden paste comes together perfectly, and a deep, surprising contentment floods through you. Talk to yourself over the sizzle and clatter, letting your voice rise to be heard, but also allowing the quiet joy to soften the edges by the end. Lose your train of thought as you bump the spoon, then find it again.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (clearly present), Sourness (extremely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Feeling the Soothing Warmth of a Heat Pack on Sore Muscles
instruction: Place the warm pack over your sore muscles, feeling the gentle heat seep in. Describe the slow, comforting warmth spreading through your skin, relaxing the tension in your muscles. Speak softly, with a tone of relief, as if each moment with the heat pack brings soothing comfort, melting away the days stress.

title: Midnight Swim
instruction: You are a teenager swimming alone in a moonlit lake, overwhelmed by the reckless joy of sneaking out. You speak to yourself or someone imagined, gasping and laughing between strokes. At first, pure ecstasy fills your voice—breathy, giddy, sputtering as you surface. But as you tread water, a flicker of doubt: 'What if they find out?' Your tone wavers, becomes quieter, almost swallowed by the water before you shake it off with another splash. Let the water interrupt your words naturally—gurgles, muffled phrases, sharp inhales. End with the doubt dissolved back into pleasure.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Savoring a Sweet Strawberry
instruction: Take a bite of a fresh, juicy strawberry, feeling its softness give way under your teeth. Describe the burst of sweetness, the slight tang, and the way the juice flows over your tongue, filling your mouth with pure flavor. Speak with a tone of delighted surprise, as if each bite is a perfect, refreshing indulgence. Let a quiet, contented hum escape, as if this single berry brings you total satisfaction.

title: The Last Sunset Before the Ship Leaves
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's boarding a colony ship to another star system—they'll never return, and you'll never see them again. You begin trying to be strong, voice steady, saying all the practical things you rehearsed. But as the reality sinks in—that this is truly the last time—your composure fractures. Your breathing becomes uneven. Words catch in your throat. You start remembering tiny, specific moments: the way they laugh, morning coffee together, their hand in yours. By the end, you're not saying goodbye anymore—you're trying to memorize them, voice breaking as you describe their face like you're already forgetting it, even though they're standing right there. The final words dissolve into silence because there's nothing left that isn't just 'please don't go.'

title: The Last Thing He Said
instruction: You are an older man standing alone in an empty funeral home after everyone else has left. You stare at the closed casket, hands trembling, voice hollow and low. Start by trying to speak but losing the words — long pauses, audible swallows, disbelief that he's really gone. Then, as you remember a specific moment of his unexpected kindness, a thick awe and profound gratitude creep into your voice, cracking but growing steadier. End with a soft, longing sigh, your voice trailing off as if wishing you could thank him one more time. Let the performance feel natural — adjust your tie, wipe your eye, let the sentences collapse and restart.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Longing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Pinot and Pink
instruction: You're at a loud, crowded wine bar with your best friend from college, both of you two glasses deep. You're wearing a frilly pink blouse and talking with a playful, sing-song voice, but your phone buzzes with a text from your ex — a lame joke about your new hobby. Start with surprise and sourness as you read it aloud, your pitch rising with mock outrage as you twist the words. As you go on, your friend's disbelief makes you laugh, and genuine curiosity about your own anger creeps in — you're disappointed you even care. End with a looser, musing tone, almost childlike, as you pout and shrug, the sourness still clinging but now a little amused.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (slightly present), Interest (clearly present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering the Truth in the Dark to Someone Sleeping
instruction: It's 3 AM. They're asleep beside you. You speak so quietly you're almost mouthing the words, confessing something you can't say when they're awake—that you've been pretending to be okay, that you're terrified, that you've been performing strength while falling apart inside. Your voice is tender, barely audible, filled with love and exhaustion. You describe the moments you faked a smile today, laughed when you wanted to scream, said 'I'm fine' when you were drowning. As you speak, your breathing becomes shaky. You're crying now, silently, the kind of tears that come when you finally stop holding everything together. End with a whispered apology or confession of love, your voice breaking on the gentlest words.
inspired_by: Realizing You Become Someone Different Around Specific People

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your childhood home, now demolished, and you're recording a voice message to your sibling who couldn't be here. Start with unexpected laughter—genuine, almost giddy—as you describe the absurdity of seeing your bedroom wall just... gone. 'Remember when we drew on this wall and Mom lost her mind?' You're smiling, but then your voice cracks. The laughter and tears happen simultaneously now. Each memory brings both joy and unbearable loss. Your parents are gone, childhood is gone, this place that held everything is rubble. But there's also strange peace in it—letting go, moving forward. End with a trembling smile in your voice: 'It's okay. We carry it with us anyway.' Let gratitude, grief, love, and acceptance all live in the same breath.

title: The Last Protocol: A Retiring Surgeon's Final Briefing
instruction: You're a beloved head surgeon giving your final briefing before retiring, but you've just learned your replacement will dismantle the safety protocols you spent decades building. Begin with professional pride as you walk your team through procedures one last time: 'These protocols have saved hundreds of lives.' Your voice is steady, authoritative. But as you continue, grief seeps in—you know this might be the last time anyone follows these guidelines. When you reach 'I won't be here to protect what we built,' your voice fractures slightly. You're trying to stay composed, but the weight of leaving your life's work vulnerable is crushing you. End with a desperate plea masked as encouragement: 'Promise me you'll remember why we do this'—it's both a goodbye to your team and a farewell to everything you believed mattered. Your voice must travel from professional confidence through quiet devastation to a plea that comes from the deepest part of your heart.
inspired_by: Medical Director: Announcing Quality Improvement Changes

title: The Last Phone Call from the Submersible
instruction: You're in a deep-sea submersible that's losing oxygen. Start with forced cheerfulness as you call your child one last time—tell them about the beautiful bioluminescent creatures you're seeing, trying to give them a final gift of wonder. As your air thins, your voice becomes dreamlike, almost euphoric from hypoxia. You catch yourself drifting and snap back with sudden fierce urgency: 'Listen to me—you were always enough, always.' Your words slow, becoming tender whispers mixed with long pauses. End in a strange state of transcendent peace, your breathing shallow, describing colors that may not be real. The emotional arc: protective love → desperate clarity → surrendered serenity.

title: The Truth I Took
instruction: You are a 16-year-old guy, a jock, sitting on a park bench after practice, your best friend’s girlfriend standing in front of you. You’ve been flirting with her all summer, and last night you kissed her—and she kissed back. Now you’re trying to explain to your friend, who just found out. Start with a shaky, forced casualness, like you’re trying to downplay it, maybe even muttering something about how she came onto you first. But as you see his face fall, disgust at your own cowardice rises like bile—you can’t keep the lie up. Your voice drops, gets hesitant, and you finally admit, with shame choking you, that you wanted it, that you’re disgusting for letting it happen. End with a raw, quiet confession that you’re not the person you thought you were.
emotions_sampled: Interest (slightly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Bitter Draught
instruction: You are an elderly woman vaping alone on a park bench, watching a young couple laugh and hold hands nearby. Your voice is thin, slightly hoarse, with a strong feminized quality. Start with a long, crackling inhale from the vape, hold the smoke, then speak as you exhale—your words riding the turbulent stream. Begin with a sour, envious observation, your tone sharp and cutting. As you continue, let a flicker of contemplation creep in, and by the end, your envy softens into a weary, resigned ache, your voice trailing off into silence.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Contemplation (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Rage and Helplessness in the Yard Where Your Child Once Played
instruction: You're standing in a yard full of autumn leaves where your child used to play, but they're gone now - taken by illness, an accident, or a custody battle you lost. Begin by violently kicking through the leaves, your voice fierce and loud as you rage against the universe, against God, against whoever took them from you. Describe the leaves scattering with savage intensity, but then - stop. Find one perfect leaf. Your voice must crack completely as you pick it up with trembling hands, remembering your child's laughter. Let your fierce anger dissolve into broken, gasping sobs as you describe how small their feet were, how they loved this. End with you clutching that leaf, your voice raw and shattered, oscillating between protective fury and the devastating powerlessness of having no one left to protect.
inspired_by: Feeling the Crunch of Autumn Leaves Beneath Your Feet

title: Proud as a Peacock
instruction: You're relaxing on the couch after a long day, scrolling through your phone, when your 8-year-old nephew bursts in and shoves a crinkly piece of paper in your face. He's beaming, bouncing on his heels. You start with a distracted, half-interested 'oh yeah?'—maybe you're still squinting at your screen, voice flat. But as he babbles about drawing every single tooth on the T-rex, you catch the pure joy in his eyes. Let your voice soften, your focus shift fully to him. End with a slow, genuine smile in your tone—'That's actually amazing, kid. I mean it.' Your gravelly voice cracks just a little on 'amazing.' Maybe you clear your throat or ruffle his hair mid-sentence. Let pride bloom from initial fatigue.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: A Stitch for the Future
instruction: You're an elderly man, alone in a quiet room knitting a baby blanket by the soft glow of a lamp. Your hands are stiff, the needles clicking steadily. Start with a heavy sigh as you think of your late wife who taught you this, and let sadness creep into your gravelly voice. Mid-thought, you glance at the nearly finished blanket and a flicker of fierce triumph rises—you're doing this for her. As you finish the last stitch, a wave of tender affection for the unborn great-grandchild floods your voice, turning it gentle and warm. Let the rhythmic clicking ground your pauses, and let your breath hitch naturally as emotions shift.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Triumph (very intensely present), Affection (very intensely present)

title: The Weight of the Trail
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman on a forced march up a steep mountain trail, carrying a heavy backpack. Your moderately feminized voice is strained from exertion, with shallow breaths and a braced core. At the start, you feel a flicker of contentment as you notice a stunning view—but your body is grinding under the load. As you pause to catch your breath, a wave of relief washes over you, yet it's tinged with a quiet helplessness: you don't know if you can finish. Speak to your hiking partner, Jane, letting your voice show the shift from a forced, hopeful cheerfulness to a more honest, exhausted confession. Pause naturally to adjust your pack, let your voice crack on the last words, and let the fatigue accumulate as you continue.
