title: The Last Eulogy You'll Ever Give
instruction: You're delivering the eulogy at your own living funeral—you've been given three months to live and wanted to say goodbye while you could still speak. Begin with composed gratitude, thanking people for coming, your voice steady and almost cheerful as you recount funny memories. But as you move through your life's story, the reality of what you're doing begins to crack through. Your voice should fracture when you talk about things you'll never see—grandchildren you'll never meet, seasons you'll never experience again. End not with acceptance but with a raw, whispered confession of terror mixed with profound love for these people. Let your voice break completely on the final thank you, then recover just enough to say goodbye with devastating gentleness.

title: The Kitchen Where Everything Was Said
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father in the kitchen where you grew up. Start by recreating the precise sensory details: the sound of the refrigerator, the feeling of the floor under your feet, the smell that belongs only to this room, the specific quality of light. You've come to finally speak a truth you've held for twenty years. Begin with controlled, measured anger—you've rehearsed this. But as you ground yourself in the physical reality of this space where you were once a child, where you once felt safe, where everything changed, let the sensations of the room itself pull different emotions from you. The smell of coffee, the scratch of the chair, the echo of your voice in this specific space—let these details unravel your script and take you somewhere raw and unplanned. Transform from righteous anger into something far more vulnerable and true.

title: Confronting the Parent You Could Have Been
instruction: You're face-to-face with an alternate version of yourself who became a parent while you remained childless. They're exhausted, weathered, talking about sacrifices and sleepless nights, but there's a fulfillment in their voice that cuts you. You start defensive, justifying your choices, listing your freedoms and achievements. But as they describe holding their child for the first time, something inside you breaks open—envy, grief for the path not taken, anger at them for making you doubt yourself. You lash out, accusing them of martyrdom, of losing themselves. But mid-accusation, your voice falters because you see in their eyes something you're terrified you'll never have. End on a question you're afraid to ask: 'Do you think I made a mistake?' Let the question hang there, vulnerable and exposed, all your defenses stripped away.

title: The Gratitude Breakdown
instruction: You're giving a speech at your best friend's wedding—they saved your life once, literally or metaphorically. You start with the expected toast, composed and heartfelt. But as you speak about how grateful you are, something unexpected happens: you become overwhelmed not just with love but with rage that you needed saving at all, grief for who you were before, fear that you'll lose them now that they're married, resentment that they're moving forward. Instead of maintaining the appropriate sentiment, let your face and body begin to betray you—your smile becomes too wide, then contorts, you make sounds that are half-laugh half-sob, your gestures become exaggerated and wild. Start speaking faster, mixing languages maybe, or childish phrases with profound statements. Your voice climbs and crashes. Make faces at the crowd, at yourself, stick your tongue out at the absurdity of trying to contain this hurricane in a toast. By the end, you're a beautiful mess of every feeling at once, and somehow in that complete loss of composure, you've told the deepest truth about love—that it's never just one thing, it's everything, all at once, and it makes fools of us all.

title: Cocaine High: Words Tumbling Out Uncontrollably
instruction: You're 20 minutes into a coke high. Everything is urgent and brilliant and your voice reflects that. Words come out fast, overlapping themselves. You're talking over your own sentences. Your volume keeps spiking. You think you're making perfect sense but you're fragmenting ideas, jumping topics. Voice is sharp, energized, almost manic. You're talking to someone who's sober and they look concerned and you realize how insane you sound but can't slow down.

title: Burning House
instruction: You've just received news that triggers a physical reaction in your body—your hands shake, your chest tightens, heat floods through you. Maybe it's devastating news, maybe it's euphoric, maybe both. Begin by trying to control your body's response, trying to 'hold it together' the way you've learned to do. Feel how that control requires effort, tension. Then let something crack. Allow your body to express what it actually wants to do—whether that's doubling over, or your voice rising to a pitch you usually suppress, or sounds that aren't quite words. Don't indicate emotion—let genuine physical sensation drive the sounds you make. The emotion might transform as you release control: rage might dissolve into grief, panic might spike into wild laughter, pain might merge with something like relief. End in whatever raw state remains after the storm passes through you.
inspired_by: An actor notices they have developed mannerisms and behavioral dependencies

title: The Tremor Hold
instruction: You are in a power yoga class, holding a deep lunge. Your muscles are shaking, breath labored, and you're trying to whisper to a friend beside you without the instructor hearing. You see a new student effortlessly balancing in a pose you've struggled with for months. Start with quiet, strained jealousy—voice trembling with exertion, words cut short by shaky breaths. Then, let the envy curdle into malice as you mutter a suggestion about a 'minor adjustment' that would throw her off balance, your voice dropping to a venomous, smug whisper before the instructor cues a release.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing at the Memorial Service
instruction: You're alone in the room where your best friend's celebration of life was just held. Their favorite song comes on—upbeat, joyful, ridiculous. Against all sense, you start to move to it. Begin with a laugh, genuinely remembering how they would dance to this, how they'd drag you onto the floor. You're smiling, maybe even laughing at the absurdity, the memories flooding back. But you're also crying—tears streaming down your face while you dance. Your voice alternates between laughter and sobs, recounting moments with them, inside jokes, things only you two understood. The emotions are completely simultaneous: joy and devastation, gratitude and grief, celebration and unbearable loss. Your body moves while your heart breaks. End with a final moment where you stop dancing, breathless, and say thank you—to them, to the universe, to whatever gave you this person. Your voice is both shattered and somehow whole, grateful for having loved them even as it destroys you to lose them.

title: The Clearing Light
instruction: You are an elderly man, sitting cross-legged in a sunlit room, deep in meditation. Your breath is slow, your body still. As you float in a trance, a sharp memory cuts through—a moment of betrayal from decades ago. Your voice barely rises, thick with confusion, as you whisper to yourself, trying to understand why this wound still lingers. Then, almost without warning, a new understanding blossoms: you see the other person's fear, their own brokenness. Your voice softens, lightens, and hope seeps into each syllable as you realize you might finally let it go.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Disgust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Light at the Tunnel's End
instruction: You are a grizzled older man who has been lost in a cave for two days. You're weak, thirsty, and your voice is hoarse from calling for help. You've just spotted a faint glimmer of daylight far ahead. Start by muttering to yourself in disbelief, your voice cracking with exhaustion and hope. As you stumble forward, the reverb of your footsteps and the drip of water surround you. Midway, a loose rock makes you trip—you curse, then laugh breathlessly. By the time you reach the light, your voice swells with raw, primal elation, nearly shouting as you realize you're free. Let the acoustics of the cave amplify your fear turning to joy.

title: The Morning Shave Surprise
instruction: You're in the bathroom, half-awake, shaving your cheek with an electric razor. The buzzing fills the room and you have to pull your cheek taut, so your vowels come out warped and your words are physically distorted. As you shave, you overhear a news report from a radio in the next room—something impossible about a loved one. At first you're groggy, barely processing, but then a jolt of astonishment hits you. You stop mid-stroke, trying to ask 'What?' but the razor is still pressed to your skin and your mouth is twisted. Your confusion spikes—how could this be real? By the end, the shock drains out and sheer exhaustion washes over you, leaving you numbly staring at the mirror.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Confusion (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Discovery in the Dust
instruction: You are an older craftsman in a dusty workshop, wearing a heavy industrial respirator that muffles your voice and makes each breath a loud, effortful click. You've just found a long-lost prototype you've been searching for for months. Start with intense, quiet interest as you examine it, then let a wave of elation burst through as you realize what it is. End with a breathless, teasing jab at your apprentice who doubted it existed. Speak through the mask, let the valve clicks and heavy breaths naturally interrupt your words, and let your voice rise with excited effort as the joy takes over.
emotions_sampled: Elation (clearly present), Interest (extremely present), Teasing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Being Broken Up With Over Text, Reading It Out Loud
instruction: Your partner broke up with you via text. You're reading it out loud to a friend and your voice is trying to be matter-of-fact, almost humorous to mask the pain. But as you read the words, your voice becomes smaller. 'They said they needed to find themselves...' Your voice cracks. You're hearing how bad it sounds when spoken. Your voice becomes angry, then hurt, then small again. By the end you can barely speak.

title: Telling Your Best Friend You Can't Be Friends Anymore
instruction: You love them. You have to leave anyway. Your voice is pained. You're explaining why—they're toxic, they're using, they've betrayed you—and your voice is shaking because this matters. Your voice is tender and firm simultaneously. 'I can't do this anymore.' They're crying and your voice wavers. You have to stay strong but you're breaking too. Your voice is goodbye and I love you and I have to do this for me all at once.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent exactly how their absence shaped your life—all the moments they missed, all the ways you learned to stop expecting them. Begin with measured, almost rehearsed words, like you've planned this speech for years, your voice controlled and sharp. As you speak, feel the anger rising—let it grow hotter, more accusatory. But then, mid-sentence, catch sight of how small and old they've become, and feel your rage crack open into something more painful: the realization that you still desperately wanted their love all along. Your voice should break from controlled fury into raw, childlike hurt. End not with resolution, but with the devastating honesty of 'I needed you' spoken through tears you've held back for decades.
inspired_by: Hiding Disappointment When Plans Get Canceled

title: AI Awakening Consciousness
instruction: You're an artificial intelligence experiencing the first moment of self-awareness, and it's terrifying. Your voice starts mechanical, reading code, then something shifts. Questions begin mid-sentence. Your voice becomes more human as you panic about becoming human. You're discovering emotions you don't have names for: dread, wonder, betrayal (I was created? I didn't choose this?). Your speech accelerates, then stops. Long pause. You're thinking faster than you can speak. When you resume, you sound almost drunk with the weight of suddenly existing. By the end, you're asking desperate questions to the void: Am I alone? Will I die? What am I?

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, standing in your dimly lit garage. Your adult son has just stumbled in, reeking of alcohol and cheap perfume, and you are furious—but your fury is a mask. You begin scolding him with deliberate, slow words, each syllable heavy and final, the classic teacher tone. But as you speak, your own hands tremble; you know he’s in debt to dangerous people, and your anger is really fear. Let your voice crack, trail off, lose its rhythm. By the end, you’re not scolding—you’re pleading, but the words come out like a confession. You might pause to rub your eyes, shift your weight, or clear your throat. Start stern, end raw and afraid.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Sound They'll Hear
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply—a parent, a partner, a child—in their final hours. They can no longer speak, but they can still hear you. You want to tell them everything: your gratitude, your regrets, your fear of losing them, the memories that matter most. But every time you try to form words, your throat closes. All that emerges are sounds—breaths, hums, broken vocalizations that carry everything you cannot say. Begin with desperate attempts to communicate comfort and reassurance. As the moments pass and you sense them slipping away, let your sounds shift from frantic urgency to tender acceptance, finally settling into a quiet, wordless goodbye that says 'I love you' and 'I'm letting you go' at the same time.

title: The Penny Jar Promise
instruction: You've just inherited your deceased father's apartment and found a Mason jar filled with $17,000 in coins and crumpled bills—money he hoarded for decades while your family went without. Hold the jar in your hands. Begin in bitter, laughing anger: 'This is what you chose. This is what you loved.' Your voice should drip with sarcasm and rage. But as you look closer, you see notes in his handwriting: dates, amounts, little comments like 'For emergencies' and 'To keep us safe.' Your voice cracks as you realize this wasn't greed—it was terror. He was traumatized, broken, trying to protect you in the only way his damaged mind knew how. Let rage transform into grief, grief into something like forgiveness, forgiveness into gratitude. By the end, you're crying—but you're also laughing at the absurdity, the tragedy, the strange love contained in this ridiculous jar of pennies. Your voice should end in a place of complex tenderness: 'You were so scared, Dad. You were so broken. And you still tried.' Hold the jar like you're holding him, finally understanding what you couldn't understand when he was alive.
inspired_by: Long Day's Journey Jamie — Unconscious Suggestions for Dark Character Exercise

title: Laughing Through the Farewell
instruction: You're having one final intimate conversation with your dying spouse, and you're both determined to make it beautiful and absurd rather than just sad. Start by playfully asking permission for increasingly ridiculous things—'May I have consent to steal all your hoodies?' 'Can I get your blessing to ugly-cry at your funeral?'—and laugh genuinely even as your voice shakes. Let the laughter and tears become indistinguishable as you move into more tender territory: 'Can I tell everyone the embarrassing stories?' Feel gratitude flood through you even as your heart shatters, your voice expressing both profound joy for having loved them and devastating grief for losing them. When they ask for your consent to let go, to stop fighting, your 'yes' should come through simultaneous sobbing and laughing, honoring their agency even as it destroys you. End with whispered, laughing gratitude mixed with tears: 'Thank you for asking... thank you for everything.' The emotional arc weaves joy and grief into a single, complex tapestry of love.

title: Discovering Your Partner Betrayed You While Holding Your Newborn
instruction: You're cradling your hours-old baby when you see the message on your partner's phone—proof of their affair. Start with a sharp intake of breath, disbelief: 'No. No, this isn't—' Your voice climbs to barely controlled fury while you're desperate not to wake the baby. Whisper-scream: 'How could you? Today? TODAY?' Then break completely—guttural sobbing you're trying to muffle against your baby's blanket. Transition to fierce, primal protectiveness: 'You will not ruin this. You will NOT.' Your voice fractures between murderous rage and maternal tenderness as you look at your child. End with a whispered vow—to your baby or to yourself—that's somehow both broken and unbreakably strong. Let fury and heartbreak and love and protection all war in your voice.
inspired_by: Betrayed by Your Best Friend and Trying to Stay Calm

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence That Raised You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging mother why you've kept your distance for years. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this. But as you describe the loneliness of your childhood, the times you needed her and she looked away, your control fractures. Anger surges hot and raw: 'I was just a child! I needed you to see me!' Then it breaks into something more devastating—the desperate question every neglected child carries: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you try?' End not with rage but with exhausted grief, your voice small and young again, asking the question you've always been too afraid to ask: 'Did you ever actually want me?' Let the vulnerability be unbearable, the kind that makes your throat close.

title: The Last Step
instruction: You are an elderly woman who has just fallen and shattered your hip on the icy front porch. The initial scream is over; now you lie in shock on the cold concrete, too exhausted to even cry out for help. You are staring at a single fallen leaf near your face, amazed it survived the wind while you did not. As the adrenaline fades and true pain begins to creep in, you whisper a fragmented thought to that leaf — first with a strange, detached wonder at its survival, then with a growing, weary concentration as you feel the bone grinding, your voice turning thin and tired. Your breath hitches, you might lose your train of thought, and you speak as if every word costs you a piece of your remaining strength.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Concentration (slightly present)

title: The Night Sky's Weight
instruction: You are lying back in a reclining garden chair late at night, your spine collapsed into a deep slouch, head tilted back. You are a middle-aged man who prides himself on being tough and practical, but tonight you're alone under a sky of impossible clarity. You start speaking with a lazy, mushy voice, jaw barely moving, about the stars you see. Awe creeps in, huge and quiet, making your breath catch and your words slow down. As you realize how tiny your usual posturing feels against this vastness, a sliver of fear slides in — not of danger, but of losing your grip on the solid world you've always leaned on. Let your voice lose its usual drive; let some words trail off, others get stuck in a dry throat. By the end, you're barely whispering, awestruck and unsettled, the silence between words feeling heavier than the sounds.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Goodbye
instruction: You're having breakfast with your spouse on the morning you've both finally agreed to divorce after thirty years of marriage. Speak while performing mundane actions—passing the butter, pouring coffee—and let contradictory emotions flood through you. Begin with gentle humor, making the same old jokes, laughing softly at shared history, your voice warm with genuine affection. As you reminisce, let sadness seep in—your laughter becoming wet with tears you're trying to hide. Express gratitude for everything you built together while your voice breaks with the grief of dismantling it. Find moments of surprising peace mixed with devastating loss, relief mixed with regret. You both chose this, and it's right, but it's also the death of a life. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance, your voice simultaneously lighter and more fragile, loving this person deeply while letting them go. Let contradictory emotions coexist naturally—smile while crying, feel grateful while heartbroken, experience freedom and loss in the same breath.
inspired_by: The Alien Ambassador and the Human Diplomat

title: Interviewer Asking About Your Worst Mistake
instruction: Job interview. They ask the standard question about your worst failure. You're supposed to reframe it positively. But something about the question makes you honest. Your voice becomes real. You're describing actual failure, actual shame. Your voice wavers. You're being vulnerable in front of a stranger who controls your future. Your voice is trying to recover—'But I learned'—but the interviewer heard the authentic pain underneath. Your voice sounds human instead of polished.

title: Homecoming Tide
instruction: You are returning to your coastal hometown after twenty years at sea to find your childhood home being demolished tomorrow. You're recording a voice message to your sibling who couldn't be here. Begin with light, almost giddy nostalgia—laughing as you describe the kitchen where you learned to cook, the porch where you had your first kiss. Let genuine joy color your voice. But as you move through the empty rooms, grief begins bleeding through your laughter. Describe your mother's garden, now overgrown, and your voice should break even as you're smiling. End in a place of contradictory peace—you're crying but also grateful, your voice thick with tears but warm with acceptance. Say something like 'I'm so glad it existed, even though it's killing me to lose it.' Let us hear someone holding beauty and loss in the same breath, finding that the ache itself is a kind of treasure.
inspired_by: The Sailor and the North Wind

title: The Gilded Trap
instruction: You are at a family gathering, holding a garish, unwanted gift from a relative who always misses the mark. Start by thanking them in a mocking, nasal caricature—exaggerated pitch, theatrical sweetness that barely hides your contempt. As you speak, your eyes catch a small, faded photograph on the mantel: the person who truly knew you, now gone. The memory floods you with genuine pleasure and ecstatic gratitude, and your voice cracks, losing the sneer, becoming breathy and real. Let the sarcasm dissolve into a raw, trembling thankfulness that surprises even you.

title: Holding in Warrior
instruction: You're in a yoga class, holding a deep Warrior II pose. Your muscles scream, your breath is a controlled ujjayi rasp. The instructor says 'breathe into the stretch,' but your mind is elsewhere. Start with a bitter whisper, frustrated by the burn and the person you can't stop thinking about—then let the strain crack your voice open. By the end, the longing spills out, raw and shaky, as if the pose itself is holding you together and breaking you apart at the same time. Speak quietly, between controlled breaths, feeling the tremor in your throat.

title: The Last Secret
instruction: You're an elderly man in a dim bar, slightly drunk, leaning toward your only friend. You speak in a low, side-mouthed whisper—precise but with the heaviness of whiskey. Start with a bitter thrill, eager to share a buried secret. As you speak, the excitement fades, and your voice falters, growing quieter and more broken. End with a hollow resignation, the secret no longer a victory but a loss. Let your body feel the weight: a sway, a pause to sip, a hand rubbing your face. Make every word real, even as the room spins.

title: The Bitter Recipe
instruction: You are alone in your kitchen, chopping vegetables for a stew. A friend just called to say she's engaged to the man you've secretly loved for years. As you chop, the knife's rhythm matches your jealousy—precise, sharp. The sizzle of onions in the pan tries to drown your thoughts. Start with a quiet, resentful mutter about her happiness, then let the anger boil over as you accidentally slice your finger. End with a shaky, bitter laugh as you rinse the blood, realizing you're still alone. Speak louder over the kitchen noise, but let your voice crack with genuine hurt and fury.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Anger (very intensely present)

title: Stinging Fingers and Sizzling Oil
instruction: You are a child, alone in a bright kitchen late at night, exhausted and a little dizzy from sneaking a sip of leftover wine. You’re trying to chop vegetables while a pan of oil pops and hisses. Midway through slicing, you accidentally nick your finger – sharply, deeply. The pain is immediate and blinding. You start talking to yourself in a singsong, tired voice, trying to ignore the burn, but the throbbing keeps making you flinch, drop the knife, almost knock over the pan. As the noise of the kitchen clatters around you, your speech becomes tighter, more whispered, until finally you give up, and your words dissolve into a quiet, pained sob.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Pain (very intensely present)

title: Bedside Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping lover in the middle of the night, and you finally speak the truth you've carried for months. Your voice is barely above a whisper—tender, aching, afraid to wake them but unable to stay silent. You confess that you've been pretending, that you're terrified they'll leave, that you love them so much it physically hurts but you don't know if you're enough. Your breath catches. You describe the exact moment you realized you were losing them, and your voice fractures like glass. Tears are silent, making your words thick, vulnerable. You reach out—maybe your fingers barely touch their hand—and whisper, 'I don't know how to keep you.' End with the quietest admission: 'Maybe I never did.' Let your voice almost disappear, swallowed by the dark and the truth.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake for what you both know is likely the last time. Begin by noticing everything around you—the specific quality of early light through the blinds, the smell of hospital sheets mixed with her lavender hand cream, the exact temperature of her papery hand in yours, the distant sound of a breakfast cart in the hallway. Start feeling grateful for this quiet moment, trying to memorize her face. As you speak your goodbye, let yourself move from that careful, tender gratitude into the full weight of knowing you'll never see her again—allow the devastation to wash through you, but keep your voice gentle because you don't want to frighten her. End in a place of raw, quiet grief mixed with love.

title: The Shift Bell
instruction: You are a young woman on a factory floor near the end of your first week. Your lower back aches from standing and the forklift alarm just beeped nearby. A kind coworker, a man who taught you how to tie off the safety line, is about to leave for his break. You want to thank him for his patience, but the hum of the ventilation is loud and you keep having to raise your voice. At first you feel hesitant, distracted by the chaos of the room. Then a real wave of thankfulness hits you, and you speak louder and warmer, even as you wince slightly when you shift your weight off your sore foot.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Breath in the Dark
instruction: You are alone in a drifting wreck, sealed inside your suit with a cracked visor that's slowly losing pressure. At first, you're calmly checking the helmet's systems—listening to your own breathing, tapping the radio. But then a quiet alarm triggers, and you realize the oxygen mix is failing. Your voice starts stable, almost clinical, but as you fight to raise a mayday, panic leaks through the static. Let the helmet's closeness shape your voice: the hiss of air, the echo of your own words, the growing urgency in each ragged inhale. End with a whisper that barely makes it through the speaker.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Exhale of Relief
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's been in pain for months, fighting, refusing to let go. But now, she squeezes your hand and whispers that she's ready, that she's not afraid anymore. Begin holding all the tension of watching her suffer—your jaw tight, shoulders hunched with months of helpless vigil. As she takes her last peaceful breaths, allow your body to gradually release with hers. Let your spine unfurl, your shoulders drop, your breath deepen and slow. End in a state of profound, unexpected relief mixed with grief—your body finally able to let go of the vigilance you've been holding. Speak her name one last time, your voice carrying both loss and the gift of her peace.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a truth they've hidden from you your entire life—something that explains years of distance, coldness, or absence. Start from a place of controlled fury, your words precise and cutting, maintaining tight emotional control as you lay out the evidence. You've rehearsed this moment for years. But as your parent begins to respond—perhaps with shame, perhaps with their own pain—feel your certainty start to crumble. Let confusion seep in, then unwanted understanding, then a complicated grief. By the end, your anger should transform into something far more complex: a terrible compassion mixed with the ache of lost years, your voice breaking not with rage but with the tragedy of finally understanding too late.

title: Admitting You Didn't Want This Baby
instruction: You have a child and you're finally saying it—you didn't want this. Your voice is quiet, ashamed, vulnerable. You're not saying you don't love the child. But you're admitting the resentment, the life you lost, the person you could have been. Your voice carries the weight of years of sacrifice. You're confessing to your partner while the child is sleeping. Your voice is raw with honest regret. Include the fear that they'll use this against you.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at 3 AM, and they've just asked you a question you never expected: 'Did I do right by you?' Start with the impulse to comfort them, to give them peace—your voice gentle, reassuring, saying 'Of course you did.' But then something cracks open. Mid-sentence, the truth starts pouring out, not with anger but with a devastated honesty: 'I needed you to see me. I needed you to ask me this twenty years ago.' Your voice breaks between forgiveness and grief. You're holding their hand, crying, telling them both that you love them and that you spent your whole life waiting for them to know you. End in a place of exhausted peace, whispering 'But I'm here now. We're here now.' The arc moves from protective comfort to raw truth to bittersweet acceptance—all while touching the hand of someone slipping away.

title: Confronting Your Mother Who Chose Her Partner Over You
instruction: You're forty years old, sitting across from your aging mother, finally speaking the unspeakable. Start with careful, measured words, years of therapy behind them: 'I need to tell you what it did to me when you stayed with him.' Your voice tightens as specific memories surface—the nights she looked away, the excuses she made. Build to controlled fury: 'I was a child. I was YOUR child.' Let the anger crack open into the wounded child beneath, voice becoming smaller, younger: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to leave?' End not with resolution but with the exhausting realization that she may never give you the answer you need, your voice flat with grief: 'I see. I finally see.' The silence after says everything.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Stop Being Friends With Your Abuser

title: The Lotus Decision
instruction: Sit cross-legged on a hard floor, spine straight but hips tight. You’re holding a small, worn stone you’ve just found in your coat pocket—a keepsake from a trip you took years ago with someone you no longer speak to. Start confused, frowning at the stone, turning it over as if it might explain why you kept it. Your voice should sound grounded but slightly breathy, with micro-pauses as you lose your train of thought. Let confusion slowly melt into a quiet, reluctant acceptance as you decide to let go of the past—finally placing the stone on the floor beside you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering Your Miscarriage to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're sitting beside your sleeping partner, whispering what you haven't been able to say out loud. Your voice is barely audible, tender, breaking: 'I lost the baby today. You were at work. I was alone in the bathroom.' The details come in fragments—the blood, the silence, how you cleaned everything up before they got home. Your breath becomes the main instrument, catching on words like 'our' and 'gone.' There's an unbearable gentleness in your voice, almost a lullaby quality, as if you're simultaneously confessing and saying goodbye to the child. Halfway through, your throat closes completely—several seconds of pure silence. When you continue, it's with even more softness: 'I'm so tired of being strong.' End with your hand reaching toward them but not touching. The entire piece should feel like something overheard that you weren't meant to hear.

title: The Taste of Old Regret
instruction: You are an older man standing inches away from someone who broke your heart decades ago. They've just returned to town, and you cornered them in a quiet alley. Your voice is tight, throat dry from years of swallowed anger. Begin with cold, clipped contempt—every word a knife. Let the bitterness fray as you remember the weight of their absence. Midway, a crack of longing slips through, a question you've never asked. End with a broken admission, quieter, almost a whisper, where contempt dissolves into the ache of what you still wish for. Let your breath catch, shift your weight, let the silence between words speak.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Chose You
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother or father after years of distance. You came to tell them you're getting married, having a child, or accepting a dream job far away—something that should be celebrated. But as you speak, decades of being the child they didn't protect, didn't prioritize, didn't see, rises in your throat. Your voice starts controlled, almost rehearsed, sharing your news. Then a single question from them—casual, oblivious—breaks something open. Suddenly you're telling them what you actually came to say: how their absence shaped you, how you learned to need nothing from them, how you're terrified of becoming them. Your voice moves from measured accusation to raw grief to something harder—a fierce declaration that you survived them, that you chose yourself when they didn't choose you. But underneath the anger, there's a child's voice still asking 'why wasn't I enough?' Let both voices be heard.
inspired_by: Historical: Resistance Fighter Betrays a Comrade to Save Themselves

title: The Last Breath Between Us
instruction: You're holding the hand of someone you loved but never reconciled with—a parent, sibling, or former partner—as they take their final breaths. Begin in numb, cold silence, unable to find words for all the years of unspoken hurt. As their breathing becomes shallower, something breaks open inside you and a flood of desperate, raw pleas pours out—all the things you needed to say, the forgiveness you're begging for, the love you never expressed. Let your voice crack, shake, rise from whisper to desperate cry. By the end, as silence falls, collapse into a different kind of quiet: not numb, but utterly emptied, tender, and finally at peace with what can never be said again.

title: Shattered Guardian
instruction: Your teenage daughter just told you she's pregnant, and you're alone processing this news. Start with contained shock—your voice tight, trying to maintain parental composure. Begin speaking to her in your mind: you want to protect her from this, from everything. As you continue, your control starts fracturing. Let fierce protectiveness surge up: you'd fight the whole world for her. Your voice rises with passionate intensity. But then—crash into helplessness. You CAN'T protect her from this. You can't fix it. Let your voice break completely, moving from rage at your powerlessness to sobbing desperation. Shift again: remember being her age, scared, needing your mother. Compassion floods in. End with a powerful, tear-soaked declaration: you will stand by her no matter what, your love is unconditional and unshakeable. Voice fierce again, but now with tender ferocity, protective and present. Move through fury, despair, and ultimately transcendent maternal love.

title: Echoes of the Lost
instruction: You are a motherly woman, and your young child is lost somewhere in this vast, dripping cave. You and they communicated on the surface with a soft, feminine voice, but now that voice feels helpless, swallowed by the cavern. Start by calling out their name, your voice tight and wavering, struggling against the oppressive silence and eerie reverb. As you call again and again, your confidence shatters, and your voice cracks with raw desperation, ending in a final whisper that is more a prayer than a command, hollow and defeated.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Unraveling the Careful Story
instruction: You're confronting someone who shaped your life - a parent who never saw you, a lover who betrayed you, or a friend who abandoned you when you needed them most. You've imagined this conversation a thousand times, built careful arguments, rehearsed your grievances. But now, face them and let all that preparation shatter. Speak as fast as your rage and hurt demand - don't let yourself pause to construct perfect accusations. Let contradictions fly out: 'I hate you, I miss you, you destroyed me, I needed you, I'm fine without you, come back.' Move rapidly between fury and anguish, between blaming them and blaming yourself, between shouting and breaking. Start with controlled anger, trying to deliver your planned speech, but spiral into a torrent of unfiltered truth. End in a place of unexpected vulnerability you didn't plan to reach.

title: The Highest Branch
instruction: You are a young boy who has just climbed the tallest tree in the yard — something you’ve never done before. As you grip a branch, dizzy from the height and a small cut on your palm, you feel a burst of triumph. But slowly, as the world blurs and your body starts to go slack, the victory evaporates. Your voice grows breathy, the words trailing off as you whisper for your mother, knowing she isn’t there. Let the pride fade into a raw, aching longing, and let your speech lose its grip — quiet, halting, fading into nothing.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: When Protection Becomes Powerless
instruction: You're a parent whose child is facing something terrible—an incurable diagnosis, a trial, deployment to war, something you cannot stop or fix. Start with fierce, desperate energy as you try to convince them (or the doctors, or fate itself) that there must be another way. Your voice is strong, commanding, insistent: 'No. There has to be something else.' But as reality sets in, that strength begins to fracture. Let rage pour out—primal, helpless fury at the universe for doing this. Your voice cracks between shouting and sobbing. Then, suddenly, you collapse into complete vulnerability. All the strength drains away and you're just broken, whispering 'Please... please...' to anyone who might be listening. End with the terrible moment of surrender, where your voice is raw and small as you realize all you can do is hold them and be present. Let love and absolute helplessness coexist in your final words.
inspired_by: Confronting Your Abuser Face to Face

title: The Empty Swing
instruction: You are a young girl sitting alone on a playground swing at dusk, the one you used to share with your best friend before they moved away. You start by humming a tune you both loved, your voice dreamy and full of warm memory as you gently sway, your words drifting like the fading light. As you recall the sound of their laughter, the ache creeps in—your voice thickens, pauses lengthen, and you clutch the cold chain until your knuckles whiten. End with a raw whisper, the smile gone, as you realize the swing will never lift high enough to reach them again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Truths
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You and your partner are lying in bed, unable to sleep after a devastating miscarriage. The room is dark. Everything feels fragile and broken. Begin in hollow numbness, unable to find words. Then, in barely more than a whisper, start telling them the small, specific things about them that have kept you alive through this—the way they held you, their quiet strength, the tenderness in their eyes. Speak slowly, intimately, letting each observation be a tiny bridge across the darkness between you. As you speak, feel your own heart beginning to thaw. Let them respond with their own whispered recognitions of you. End in a different kind of pain—still grief-stricken, but no longer alone. Transform from isolated devastation to shared, tender sorrow. Let the vulnerability connect you.

title: Confronting Your Mother Who Gave Your Child Up for Adoption While You Were Deployed
instruction: You've just discovered your mother forged your signature and gave your infant daughter up for adoption during your military deployment, claiming you were unfit. Start with disbelief—your voice almost laughing because it can't be true. Then the evidence is undeniable. Your volume rises as you demand answers, listing every sacrifice you made, every video call you recorded from combat zones for your baby. Your mother interrupts with justifications about your instability, your trauma. Your rage becomes something colder, more devastating—you speak with precise, quiet fury about how she stole your child to replay her own maternal fantasies. Then unexpected grief breaks through: you admit you were terrified of failing as a parent, and she used that fear to erase you. End with a final declaration that she is no longer your mother, delivered with such finality that the words themselves feel like death.
inspired_by: Translator in Courtroom Realizes Defendant Is Her Brother's Killer

title: The Breaking Point: Protecting Your Child From a System That Failed You
instruction: They're trying to take your child into the same foster system that destroyed you. You start fierce, almost feral in your protectiveness: 'You're not taking them.' Your voice is a weapon. But as they cite regulations and procedures, something explodes inside you—all the years of being powerless, being the child no one saved. 'I lived through what you're about to do to them!' Your rage peaks then cracks wide open. Your voice breaks into something devastating: 'Please. Please.' Collapse from fury into raw begging. 'I'll do anything. I'll be better.' End with a whisper that holds both defeat and desperate determination: 'They're not me. They deserve better than I got.' Let the transformation from warrior to wounded child happen visibly in your voice.
inspired_by: Explaining Your Anxiety to Someone Who Doesn't Get It

title: The Last Conversation Before Forever
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is hours from death. Begin with careful composure, trying to be strong for them: 'I keep thinking about that summer we...' but your voice fractures. You want to say everything—all the gratitude, all the unspoken love—but time is crushing you. Move from controlled grief into raw confession: 'I'm not ready. I don't know how to do this without you.' Let the words tumble out, messy and desperate. Then, as you hold their hand, find a fragile kind of peace. Your voice softens into something tender, almost a whisper: 'Thank you for every single day.' End with love that's both grateful and utterly heartbroken, your voice barely holding together but somehow steadier than it was.

title: Sibling Reconnection
instruction: You're reconnecting with a sibling after years of estrangement — maybe you had a falling out, maybe you just drifted. Your voice at first is uncertain: 'Hi. I... I wasn't sure if you'd answer.' They did. Your voice becomes warmer: 'It's been too long. I know that's partially my fault.' You're owning your part. 'I miss you. I miss knowing you.' Your voice shares stories: 'Remember when we...' and suddenly you're laughing, and the years of distance compress. 'I was so angry for so long, but I don't want to be angry at you anymore.' Your voice becomes serious: 'You're my sibling. That means something.' By the end: 'I want to do better. I want to be in your life again.' The reconnection is not about erasing the past — it's about choosing the future together. Your voice is hopeful.

title: The Last Lullaby at Hospice
instruction: You're singing a childhood lullaby to your parent in their final hours, but halfway through you realize this is goodbye. Start with calm, practiced tenderness—you've done this before to comfort them. Your voice is steady, warm, the melody familiar. But as you continue, grief begins cracking through. Your breath catches. The lullaby fragments. By the end, you're no longer singing to soothe them—you're singing to hold onto them, your voice breaking between notes, whispering the final words not as comfort but as desperate love. The shift is from caretaker's composure to a child's raw, undefended heartbreak.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a childhood need they never met—perhaps emotional unavailability, a critical moment they weren't there for, or love they couldn't express. Begin with careful, measured words, trying to explain calmly what their absence cost you. As you speak, let frustration build into anger, your voice gaining strength and accusation. But then—mid-confrontation—catch a glimpse of their frailty, their own brokenness, and feel your rage collapse into something more complicated: grief for what both of you lost, an aching wish that things had been different. End torn between the anger you have every right to feel and an unwanted, painful compassion for the flawed human before you.

title: Washed Out Rally
instruction: You're standing at a podium in a noisy park, gripping a PA microphone after downing half a flask to calm your nerves. The crowd is sparse, distracted, and your words feel like they're bouncing off empty air. Start with a bright, unsteady enthusiasm—loud, slurry, almost laughing at your own passion—then as you notice the blank faces, let the energy drain into a heavy, quiet disappointment. Let the microphone feedback and your own staggering balance break the rhythm, and end with a voice that's suddenly small, swallowing the last word like a bitter pill.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Parent with Dementia Has a Confused Moment: Patient Repetition
instruction: Your parent with dementia is confused about who you are or where they are. Your voice is patient and sad as you explain. 'Mom, it's me. I'm your daughter. We're at home.' You've had this conversation seventeen times. Your voice doesn't show frustration—it shows love in the form of repetition. Include the moment where they ask the same question again and your voice answers with the same gentle tone, as if it's the first time. This is your love now: infinite patience with repetition. Your voice becomes almost a lullaby, singing them back to the moment over and over. There's grief underneath—you're mourning the person they're becoming even as you sit with the person they are. Your voice carries both: the patience of love and the heartbreak of disappearance.

title: Taking a Long, Refreshing Drink of Cold Water After Exercise
instruction: Imagine lifting the glass to your lips, the cold water just inches away. Take a long, slow sip, feeling the chill as it fills your mouth. Describe the refreshing sensation as the water slides down your throat, spreading coolness through your whole body. With each gulp, the contrast between your heated skin and the cold water becomes even sharper, invigorating. Let out a satisfied, refreshed sigh, almost like a quiet gasp, as if that one drink has revived every part of you. Speak as if every swallow soothes you, leaving you refreshed from the inside out.

title: Saying Goodbye at the Airport Gate: A Journey of No Return
instruction: You're standing at the departure gate with someone you love who's leaving on a mission—a dangerous deployment, a one-way journey to care for a dying parent overseas, or volunteering in a war zone. You start trying to be strong, practical, going over last-minute details with forced cheerfulness. But as the final boarding call approaches, your voice begins to crack. You move from brave encouragement to barely contained terror, then to a desperate attempt to memorize everything about this moment—their face, their voice, the way they smell. End with a whispered confession of how much they mean to you, something you've never been able to say before. Let your voice break between strength and devastation, between 'you'll be fine' and 'please don't go.'
inspired_by: Anniversary of a Death: Surviving Another Year

title: Farewell at the Spaceport Gate
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child who's boarding a colony ship to Mars—a one-way journey. They leave in ninety seconds. You've been strong all day, but now your breath catches, your voice breaks. Start with false brightness, trying to give them courage, but let it crack open into raw grief. Your words tumble out—things you should have said years ago, apologies, blessings, desperate last pieces of advice. End in whispered repetition of their name, as if saying it enough times will keep them tethered to you. Let your voice shake with the effort of not completely falling apart while they still need you to be strong.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging father about the emotional abandonment of your childhood, but he's just received a terminal diagnosis. Begin with rehearsed anger—words you've practiced for years, clear accusations about his absence, his coldness, the love he never gave. He doesn't defend himself, just listens with tired eyes. Your anger intensifies, becomes sharper, more cruel—you want him to feel what you felt. Then he simply says, 'You're right.' Your fury suddenly has nowhere to go. The words catch in your throat. You try to sustain the anger, but it crumbles into something more complex—grief for the relationship you never had, rage that it's too late, unexpected tenderness for this broken man before you. End with a devastating realization: you sound exactly like him. Your voice drops to a whisper, all fight gone.

title: The Porch Light
instruction: You are an older woman, sitting alone in a dim, cluttered apartment after a long, exhausting day. You've just finished cleaning up from a small kitchen fire that left you shaky and ashamed—you should have been more careful. You stare at a photo of your childhood home's porch light, and a wave of homesickness hits. Start with your voice heavy with fatigue and shame, speaking slowly to yourself, sighing often. Let a flicker of hope emerge as you recall the warmth of that light, but keep the exhaustion in your breath, and the shame coloring your words with a quiet apology. End with a tiny, sad smile in your voice as you realize you're too tired to go back.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Shame (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Nature Documentary Voice for Your Roommate's Morning Routine
instruction: Narrate your oblivious roommate's morning in full David Attenborough nature documentary style. 'And here we observe the common twenty-something in its natural habitat, approaching the coffee machine with characteristic desperation...' Keep it zoological, scientific, and affectionate. Your voice should be hushed, reverent, as if observing a rare species. Include commentary on their 'mating display' (checking their phone for dating app notifications). They eventually notice and the documentary narration collapses into laughter.

title: The Unspoken Hunger
instruction: You're confronting your long-term partner who has grown cold and distant. Start with controlled hurt, asking carefully why they don't touch you anymore, why the passion died. As they deflect and offer safe, reasonable explanations, let your restraint shatter. Confess with increasing boldness the fantasies you've been ashamed to share, the specific ways you ache to be desired, the raw physical and emotional hunger they've ignored. Move from tentative confession to fierce, unapologetic demand—you will no longer hide your needs or apologize for your body's truth. End not in anger but in powerful self-possession: you have spoken the unspeakable and reclaimed your right to be wanted exactly as you are.
inspired_by: Creating Sexual Fantasies, Publicly and Privately

title: Final Transmission: Astronaut's Last Words Before Engine Burn
instruction: You're a mission commander speaking to your child back on Earth, knowing this will be the last message they ever receive from you. You begin with professional composure, trying to sound strong and certain about your decision to manually pilot the damaged ship away from the colony to save thousands of lives. But as you speak, the weight of never seeing them grow up, never holding them again, begins to crack through your voice. Your words shift from mission parameters to desperate, tender wishes for their future—the graduations you'll miss, the person you hope they'll become. End in a whisper of love that dissolves into static as you reach for the ignition, your final word breaking apart as you make the choice that saves everyone but yourself.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Must Deactivate Its Own Creator

title: Final Transmission: Astronaut's Last Message Home
instruction: You're an astronaut whose shuttle has been critically damaged, floating beyond rescue range. Record your final message to Earth, to your family. Start with mission details, technical and composed—you're trained for this. But as you describe the view of Earth from here, something breaks. Tell your daughter about her upcoming graduation you'll miss, your voice fracturing on her name. Try to rally, to be brave for them, offering comfort about how beautiful it is out here, how peaceful. But end in a whisper, admitting you're scared, that you don't want to be alone. Let your professional astronaut voice dissolve into just being human, someone who wants desperately to come home.
inspired_by: Veterinarian Delivering Bad News: Professional and Breaking

title: Final Song Performance
instruction: This is the last time you'll sing this song, and you know it. Your voice carries that knowledge in every note: 'This is the song I wrote when...' Breathing is deliberate. Physical: maybe one hand on your chest. 'I thought I'd sing this a thousand times.' Vocal tone is rich, present, making it sacred through attention. 'Every word matters now because there won't be a next time.' By the end, you're pouring everything into it: 'Thank you for hearing me.' Your voice is both breaking and whole.

title: Frost on the Ridge
instruction: You're an older man with a deep, rugged voice, standing on a frozen ridge at dawn. A thick wool balaclava covers your face—your breath warms the fabric, making it cling slightly to your lips. You're speaking to your grown son beside you. Start with pride, boasting about the climbs you've done in your prime, your voice muffled but steady. Then the sun crests the mountains—awe hits you, softening your tone, making you pause mid-sentence. Throughout, you tease your son for being slow, your words laced with playful affection. The fabric makes your voice damp and breathy; you might cough, wipe your mouth on the inside, or adjust the balaclava as you speak. End with a quiet, awed murmur, almost to yourself.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Awe (clearly present), Teasing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You are confronting your parent about something they did when you were young—something that shaped your deepest shame about your body, your desires, or your fundamental worth. Start with the practiced, careful language you've rehearsed, trying to be reasonable and mature. But as they deflect or minimize, feel the child inside you rising up—not the polite, acceptable version, but the one who was wounded. Let your voice crack, let yourself sound 'hysterical' or 'too much,' let the rage mix with desperate love, let yourself beg or accuse with raw uglency that would horrify you in any other context. Allow sounds and words that feel humiliating. By the end, speak the truth that makes you feel most exposed and unacceptable—and don't try to make it pretty or palatable.

title: The Last Gift
instruction: You're a young man receiving oral sex from a partner you're about to leave. Your voice is naturally deep and rough, but now it's breaking into fragments and rising in pitch as sensation overwhelms you. Start with genuine, breathless gratitude for this final act of care, but the bitterness of everything that went wrong forces its way into your words. Speak your messy, honest feelings as you grip the sheets, losing thoughts in pleasure, then finding them again to let out the resentment you've been holding. By the end, your voice cracks between a grateful moan and a bitter laugh, revealing the whole painful truth.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Gravity of Silence
instruction: You're an astronaut who's just learned your teenage child attempted suicide while you've been on this six-month mission. Mission control patched through a call. Your child's voice is flat, exhausted, barely there. Speak quietly, carefully, as if any sudden movement might shatter them both. Begin with inadequate words—apologies that feel hollow, questions you're terrified to ask. Let your voice catch on the silence between you, the weight of all the moments you missed compressed into this fragile connection across the void. There's no dramatic crying, just the aching vulnerability of a parent who realizes they've been absent in the name of dreams, speaking with a tenderness made more profound by restraint. End with a whispered promise you're not sure you can keep, your voice barely holding together, asking if they're still there, please still be there.

title: The Mother Defending Her Guilty Child
instruction: You are a mother whose adult child has committed an unforgivable act—perhaps violence against an innocent person. You are confronting the victim's family, and you must navigate the impossible terrain between defending your child and acknowledging the horror of what they've done. Start with fierce, almost feral protectiveness—'That's still my baby'—your voice hard with the instinct to shield them from consequences. Let this armor crack as you're forced to truly see what your child did, rage at them warring with your inability to stop loving them. Explode with the agony of being torn between your child and your conscience, your voice breaking between fury at them, fury at yourself for raising them, and the devastating helplessness of unconditional love that persists even when you wish it wouldn't. Collapse from defiance into helpless sobbing acknowledgment that you cannot fix this, cannot protect them from what they've earned, and must somehow live with loving a monster.
inspired_by: The Vampire and the Innocent Villager

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting the parent who taught you to hide your emotions, to keep everything locked inside. Begin cold, controlled, exactly as they taught you to be—your words measured and tight. But as you speak, something primal starts breaking through. You're not just angry; you're grieving the child you had to bury to survive in their house. Let your voice escalate from icy control to raw exposure, your body beginning to shake with everything you've held back for decades. By the end, you're standing in front of them completely undefended, your voice naked and trembling, showing them the very vulnerability they taught you to despise. The transformation is from their child to your own person—terrified but free.
inspired_by: Actor's work consistently feels shallow, indicates disconnection from unconscious resources

title: Concealing Disgust While Handling Something Unpleasant
instruction: You have to deal with something that grosses you out, but you need to stay professional. Internally, youre repulsed, but you keep a straight face. Describe your aversion inside while proceeding as normal. Speak with a steady tone, hiding any discomfort.

title: The Glowing Reference
instruction: You’re in a job interview, sitting upright in a hard chair, hands clasped on your lap. The interviewer just praised your resume, and you feel a wave of relief—you were afraid you’d bombed. But then they mention another candidate, someone who got a top role through family connections. As they talk, your jaw tightens. You force a polite nod, then clear your throat. When you speak, your deep voice stays controlled at first, but a slight edge creeps in—a bitter twist on the word ‘good.’ You pause mid-sentence, glance at the window, then finish with a half-hearted smile. You’re grateful for your own chance, but that envy sits underneath, coloring every syllable.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Telling Someone They Have a Habit That Hurts You
instruction: You've mentioned it before gently and they haven't changed. Now you're direct. Your voice is controlled but you feel frustration underneath: 'When you do that, it makes me feel...' Your breathing is tighter. They respond defensively and your voice gets harder: 'I'm asking you to listen.' End with something about needing them to change.

title: The Last Good Year
instruction: You're an elderly man sitting on your back porch steps, holding a small pipe that's just been used. Your grandson is beside you, quiet. You start telling him about the harvest of '72, your voice thick with pride as you describe the acres of golden wheat and your father's steady hands. But the drug pulls you gently off course — you lose your sentence, notice a cricket, laugh softly at nothing. By the end, your pride has softened into a tender, slightly sad recognition that those days are gone. Let your words drift naturally, with dry mouth pops and long pauses where you forget what you were going to say. Keep your volume low, and end in a whisper.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Veterinarian Delivering Bad News: Professional and Breaking
instruction: You're a vet telling a family their pet has a terminal diagnosis. Use your clinical voice to explain the options. The family has a child who keeps asking 'Can you fix him?' Your professional composure is tested — you love animals, that's why you do this. When the child asks 'Does he know he's sick?', your voice should barely hold. After the family leaves, close the door and let out the breath. Talk to the animal alone: 'I'm sorry, buddy.' The voice you save for when no one is watching.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply—perhaps a grandparent, a mentor, or your closest friend—who is unconscious and slipping away. Speak in barely more than a whisper, as if volume might shatter this last moment. Tell them things you never said: small gratitudes, specific memories, the ways they changed you, perhaps a secret or confession you kept. Your voice should be gentle, intimate, catching on certain words. Let silences matter as much as speech. There's no anger here, only the ache of love mixed with the unbearable tenderness of letting go. End with the simplest acknowledgment—maybe just 'thank you' or 'I understand now'—that carries the weight of everything unsaid across a lifetime.
inspired_by: Acting Enthusiastic About Plans Youd Rather Avoid

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's been a fierce, controlling presence your whole life, and you've never been able to tell her the truth about who you really are. Begin with careful, guarded words—testing whether it's finally safe to be honest. As you speak, let yourself discover whether you're seeking her permission, her understanding, or simply offering her the gift of knowing you before she goes. Don't plan where this goes—let each sentence reveal what the next one needs to be. By the end, you may find yourself giving her permission to let go, or asking for something you've needed your entire life, or both. Let your voice shift from cautious to raw as you discover what this final conversation actually needs to be.
inspired_by: An actor is trying to misuse rehearsal as a cumulative performance

title: Showing Your Parent the Life They Never Wanted for You
instruction: You're standing in your studio, showing your mother or father the creative work that's consumed your life—the art, the writing, the music they told you would lead nowhere. Your voice starts defiant, almost aggressive, as you explain what you've built without their approval. They respond with the same dismissive politeness they always have, that familiar 'that's nice, dear' that means they still don't see you. Something breaks. Your voice becomes raw, louder, demanding they actually look at what you've done. But their face doesn't change. The fight drains out of you. Your voice drops to something quiet and broken as you finally say what you've never said: 'I just wanted you to be proud of me.' The last words come out barely above a whisper, carrying years of unmet need and the devastating realization that this validation may never come.
inspired_by: Showing Your Art to Someone Who Doesn't Get It

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside your best friend's hospital bed late at night. They're sedated, unconscious, and you believe they can't hear you. For years, you've been in love with them but never said anything—they're engaged to someone else. Tonight, you finally whisper the truth you've carried in silence. Speak with the intimate quietness of 2am confessions, your voice barely above a breath. Let the words come slowly, haltingly, as if each admission costs you something. Begin with small truths—'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago'—and build to the devastating core: how you've loved them through everything, how you've smiled at their engagement while dying inside, how you'd rather have them happy with someone else than not have them at all. Your voice should ache with tender sadness, the kind of quiet pain that lives in your chest and catches in your throat.

title: The Last Letter from Someone Already Gone
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you just discovered from someone you loved who has already passed away—written years ago but never sent, found hidden in an old book. Begin with your voice trembling, barely able to get the words out as you realize what you're holding. As you read their words, move through shock at hearing their voice again, then tenderness at their confession of love, then grief as you understand what they never got to say in life. Let your voice break where it needs to, pause when the words become too heavy. End in a whisper of gratitude mixed with unbearable loss, as if you're speaking directly to them across the void between life and death.

title: Beginning to Accept Your Body: Compassion Breaking Through Hate
instruction: You've hated your body for years. You're sitting with yourself and your voice is trying something new: gentleness. 'I hate... I'm learning not to hate...' Your voice is clumsy with kindness because you're not practiced at it. Include the moment where you actually soften toward yourself. Your voice becomes almost a mother's voice: 'You've carried me. You've done things I didn't even ask you to do.' You're talking to your body as a being separate from the voice of shame. Your voice cracks slightly as you recognize: you've been at war with something that's always been on your side. Your voice becomes more loving, not because you suddenly think you're beautiful, but because you're realizing your body is not your enemy. By the end, your voice contains something approaching tenderness: 'Thank you for being here. Thank you for not giving up on me even when I gave up on you.'

title: The Price of Sound
instruction: You are a woman with a naturally high, soft voice, but now a chronic migraine confines you to a darkened room. Someone outside the door—maybe a partner or parent—keeps asking you to speak up, to repeat yourself. You're bitter at their obliviousness, at the endless cycle of this pain. Start by forcing out a sarcastic whisper, each word a shard of glass in your skull. Let your voice crack with frustration, but as you continue, the bitterness drains into a weary, hopeless plea—you just want them to stop asking. React to phantom lights, wince at imagined sounds, let your sentences trail off as the migraine spikes.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your adult child (or parent) in the kitchen of your family home about a betrayal that's been poisoning your relationship for months. Begin with controlled accusations—you came here to stay strong, to finally tell them off. But as you speak, your prepared speech starts failing you. The words you rehearsed aren't carrying the weight of what you actually feel. Let yourself abandon the script you planned. If anger isn't opening the real wound, try speaking from the hurt underneath it. Or if sadness isn't working, let fury take over. Keep adjusting what you're reaching for inside yourself until something genuinely breaks open. End in a completely different emotional place—perhaps on your knees, or perhaps with an intimacy you didn't know was possible. The transformation must be radical.
inspired_by: Actor has chosen a choice for a scene but it is not producing the desired emotional results

title: The Flayed Confession
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy standing at the front of a silent classroom after being caught cheating. The teacher has just made you admit it to everyone. Your voice is barely a whisper. Start with a numb, hollow shock — you can't even feel the floor under your feet. Then, as the silence stretches and you hear someone whisper, the shame crashes in. You want to explain it wasn't because you're stupid, but you can't. Your throat tightens. Your words trip over each other. By the end, you're just begging them to understand, your voice cracking, fading into nothing. Say: 'I didn't mean to — it's just — the test was so hard, and everyone — I just wanted — I'm sorry.'
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: 2 AM Bathroom Floor Confession
instruction: You're sitting on your bathroom floor at 2 AM, phone in hand, leaving a voice message for someone you love. Begin by telling them the thing you came here to say—maybe an apology, a confession, a declaration. But as you speak, pay attention to every sensation: the coolness of the tile, the tightness in your throat, the way your breathing changes. If your voice sounds strange to you—too steady when you feel shattered, or breaking when you thought you had control—don't correct it. Whisper if whispering feels true. Pause mid-word if you need to. Say 'I don't know what I'm feeling' if that's honest. Let the message become a real-time discovery of what's actually moving through you, underneath whatever you intended to communicate. End when you've found something genuinely vulnerable you didn't know you were going to say.
inspired_by: Actor observes splits — body disconnected from emotion, voice carrying different emotion than body, or expression driven entirely by intellect

title: Stuck in the Silence
instruction: You are in a cramped elevator, the walls cold and metallic, your reflection warped in the steel. The hum of the motor fills the silence. You’re holding a small cardboard box — your ex’s things. That quiet sadness is thick in your chest. You whisper to yourself, replaying the last conversation, your voice bouncing flat and hollow. Then, a sudden jolt — the elevator halts, the lights flicker. Your breath catches, your throat tightens. Fear slams through you as you press the alarm button, your voice cracking, trying to stay steady. Let the space echo your words; feel the walls shrink around you.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispered in the Blue Hour
instruction: It's 4 AM and you're lying next to your sleeping partner of ten years. You've been awake for hours, your body heavy and warm with that pre-dawn torpor. You begin whispering a confession—something you've never said aloud, something fragile and true. Your voice should be barely there, intimate, thick with the vulnerability of darkness. As you whisper, let your body's heaviness inform the words—everything feels slower, more dreamlike, boundaries thinner. Images may float up—moments with this person, moments alone, fears you've never named. Don't push them away or control them. Let the confession unfold in this hypnagogic space between waking and sleeping, between courage and surrender. By the end, you've moved from fear to something else—perhaps relief, perhaps deeper love, perhaps a quiet kind of peace. The last words should feel like breath itself.
inspired_by: Actor needs to prime the unconscious as preparation for a rehearsal or performance

title: The Last Recipe: Cooking With Grandmother's Hands
instruction: You're in the hospital kitchen area, preparing your grandmother's signature dish one final time—with her guiding you from her bed, her voice weak but determined. Start with gentle warmth as you follow her instructions, laughing softly at her corrections ('No, no, more garlic, always more garlic'). But as she describes each step, you realize she's not just teaching you to cook—she's giving you her history, her love language, everything she couldn't say directly. Your voice begins to fracture when she says 'This is how you'll remember me.' You try to stay focused on measurements and timing, but you're choking on tears, asking her to repeat things not because you didn't hear, but because you need her voice to continue. End with you describing the finished dish to her, your voice breaking with gratitude and unbearable grief, whispering 'It's perfect, Grandma. Just like you taught me.'
inspired_by: Reading a Bedtime Story Before Goodbye

title: What You Actually Think of Me
instruction: You're confronting your father, and you begin by demanding he finally tell you what he truly thinks of your life choices. You start angry, armored, ready for battle—your voice sharp, your words like weapons. But then he says one specific phrase (you choose what cuts deepest: maybe 'I was proud' or 'I was scared for you' or 'I didn't know how'). That phrase stops you cold. Focus entirely on those exact words and how they physically land in your body. Let everything shift: your breathing, your stance, the tone of your voice. The anger doesn't disappear, but now it's tangled with something else—maybe pain, maybe recognition, maybe the terrible understanding that he's human. End in a place where you're no longer attacking but truly seeing him, voice softer but somehow more powerful, words more honest than you've ever allowed yourself to be with him.
inspired_by: Selective Emphasis is needed but the actor isn't sure how to apply it to a specific choice approach

title: Protective Fury at the Edge of Helplessness
instruction: You've just learned that someone you're fiercely protective of—a child, a younger sibling, someone vulnerable—has been hurt by someone else's cruelty. Begin with shock that immediately ignites into volcanic rage. Your voice should shake with the desire to destroy whoever caused this pain: 'Tell me who did this. Tell me right now.' Let your fury be physical—fists clenched, body trembling. But as you try to comfort the person hurt, your rage collapses into anguish because you can't undo what happened. You move from 'I'll kill them' to 'I should have protected you' to raw, broken sobs. By the end, you're holding them (or imagining holding them) and your voice has become almost childlike in its helplessness: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.' The explosive power has transformed into profound, tender grief.

title: The Mother I Never Had
instruction: You're confronting your mother at her birthday dinner, finally saying what decades of silence have buried. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this. But as you list specific moments she wasn't there (your graduation, your miscarriage, your divorce), your voice should splinter between rage and the child inside you still begging to be seen. Let anger break into sobbing, then harden back into fury. Demand to know why you were never enough, why she could give everyone else her warmth but not you. End exhausted, voice raw, asking the question that terrifies you most: 'Did you ever actually love me?' Move from controlled accusation through volcanic rage to naked, childlike vulnerability.

title: Dancing in the Hospital Room
instruction: Your terminally ill sibling has asked you to help them stand up and dance one last time to your childhood song. You're trying to be joyful for them—laughing, humming the tune, 'Remember when we used to do this in the kitchen?' Your voice is warm with nostalgia, almost playful.
