But you can feel how light they are in your arms, how fragile. The laughter keeps catching in your throat, turning into something that sounds like sobs but you're still trying to smile. 'You were always the better dancer,' you say, and your voice breaks completely. You're still swaying together, and you're crying now but also genuinely laughing at a memory, voice thick with tears but also full of love. End with: 'Thank you for this,' where gratitude and grief are completely inseparable.

title: Confronting the Hands That Never Held You
instruction: You're washing your parent's hands in a care facility, performing this intimate act for someone who was never there for you. Start with clinical detachment—you're just doing a task, describing the water, the soap, keeping your distance. But as your hands touch theirs, decades of longing and anger begin surfacing. Your voice should shift from cold and procedural to trembling with confrontation: 'I'm washing your hands now, the way you never washed mine. I'm being gentle with you, the way you never were with me.' Let rage and grief war in your throat. Build to a fierce, heartbroken question: 'Why couldn't you do this for me?' Then dissolve into the terrible recognition that despite everything, some part of you still aches for their love, even now, even like this.
inspired_by: Washing Your Hands with Warm, Soapy Water

title: The Last Bite of Breakfast
instruction: You're an older, rugged man enjoying a quiet morning with a bowl of oatmeal, despite a nasty sore throat that makes every swallow feel like gravel. You start off genuinely content — the warmth of the bowl in your hands, the comfort of routine. But as you take another spoonful, you notice a strange, gritty texture; you look closer and realize the oatmeal is crawling with tiny, dark specks — bugs. Your voice, already hoarse and painful from laryngitis, must shift from mild satisfaction to pure, revolted disgust. Let your voice crack, wince audibly on swallows, and speak with limited volume, as if every word costs you something. End with a visceral, choked reaction as the realization fully hits.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Final Words to a Sleeping Child: When There's No Tomorrow
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's hospital bed at 3am, and the doctors have told you this is likely their last night. They're peacefully asleep—finally, after so much pain. You begin speaking softly, trying to give them every piece of love and wisdom you never got to share, but your voice keeps fracturing. Start with attempted composure, whispering life advice like you're just tucking them in. 'Remember to be kind, sweetheart. Remember...' But grief ambushes you mid-sentence—your voice breaks, you have to stop and breathe. You cycle between trying to be the strong parent giving final blessings and being the devastated human who can't believe this is happening. Sometimes you're bargaining with them to stay, sometimes you're giving them permission to let go. End in a place of shattered peace, still whispering, 'It's okay, baby. Mama's got you. You can rest now.' Your voice should move from controlled tenderness to raw anguish and back, like waves of grief washing over attempts at strength.
inspired_by: Caught in Machinery: Fighting Physical Panic While Thinking

title: The Bitter High of the Open Road
instruction: You're an older woman driving home from a karaoke bar where you just won the grand prize — a cheap trophy and fifty bucks. You're very drunk, still riding the high of the crowd clapping, but there's a sour note: your ex-partner was there, and they didn't even look at you. You're behind the wheel, hyper-aware of the road, the turn signal clicking, the engine humming. Start with a slurred, triumphant whisper to yourself, then let the sourness creep in as you talk to the empty passenger seat, your voice fading and catching as you navigate a curve. End with a quiet, bitter laugh.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Laughing at the Ashes
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman standing in your kitchen, staring at a photo of your ex-best friend who once stole your idea and got all the credit. You start laughing—a wheezing, helpless fit—because you just heard she lost her award after a scandal. Your laughter begins as a bitter release, but pride swells in your chest: you were right all along. Then doubt creeps in, quieting the laughs. What if your pride is just revenge dressed up? Say your lines through gasps, squeaks, and breathless pauses, as if the laughter is stealing your words. Let your voice shift from high-pitched glee to a shaky, introspective whisper.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Pride (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: First Glimpse Home
instruction: You're a teenage colonist on a space station, seeing Earth through your helmet visor for the first time. You're breathless with astonishment at the blue planet floating there, but as you speak, the silence and distance sink in—you long for your family still down there. Your voice is tinny over the radio, with your own breathing and static filling the helmet. Let your wonder crack into quiet ache as you trail off, adjusting your visor or glancing around at the sterile ship interior.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Knife in the Corner
instruction: You are a child, about nine years old, cornered in a narrow alley by a much larger, towering figure you know as 'Mister Vance.' Your back hits the damp brick wall. He shouts inches from your face, accusing you of stealing his wallet. At first, your voice is a high, thin, trembling blade of defiance — you're terrified, your throat tight, words coming out in sharp bursts. You insist you didn't take anything. Then, behind your accuser, you see a stray dog trot out of a dumpster with the exact wallet in its mouth. Your entire body sags. Your voice suddenly cracks, goes dry, and then floods with a heavy, shaky relief. You whisper, barely audible, 'No... wait... look.' The intensity drains away into a gasped, wobbly laugh.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Not My Child Anymore
instruction: You've just learned your child has done something unforgivable—hurt someone, committed a terrible crime, betrayed everything you taught them. Start with震incredulous denial, voice shaking with the need to unhear what you've heard. Then let fury explode: screaming at them, at God, at yourself for failing. But beneath the rage is devastating helplessness—this is your baby, and you can't protect them from the consequences or from what they've become. Your voice should shatter between roaring anger and sobbing grief. End collapsed, voice raw and exhausted, whispering both 'I don't know you' and 'I love you' in the same breath, fury and protective love destroying you simultaneously.

title: Releasing Someone You Love to the Life They Need to Live
instruction: You're sitting with someone you desperately want to keep close, but you know they need to leave—for a dream, a calling, maybe their own survival. Start with your voice thick with unshed tears, trying to sound supportive: 'I want you to go. I really do.' But your voice keeps breaking on certain words. Your breath catches. You're trying so hard to be selfless, to give them permission, to smile through it. Midway through, let one truth slip out—maybe 'I don't know how to be me without you' or 'I'm so scared of forgetting what your voice sounds like.' Your voice drops to almost a whisper here, raw and unguarded. Then, with tremendous effort, pull yourself back to generosity. End with genuine blessing in your voice, still sad but somehow stronger, more peaceful: 'But you have to go. And I have to let you.' Let there be love and grief braided together in every word.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Promise They Won't Leave You

title: Reconciliation Call Years Later
instruction: You're calling the person you wronged and haven't talked to in years. Your voice starts tentative, almost rehearsed: 'Hi, it's me.' Long pause. 'I know I don't deserve a response.' Breathing is shallow. The speech is prepared but still breaks: 'What I did was unforgivable. And I...' Your voice gets smaller: 'I spent years understanding why it was unforgivable.' Physical: hand trembling. By the end, you're not asking for forgiveness, just offering truth: 'I needed you to know I understand now. I'm sorry.' Your voice is complete: honest, humbled, real.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're visiting your estranged parent in hospice. You came to make peace, but all the words you've rehearsed turn to ash. Start with careful control—you've practiced this, you're going to be mature about it. But as you begin to speak about the recitals they missed, the nights you needed them, your voice hardens with decades of banked rage. The anger builds until you're nearly spitting words—and then it breaks. Suddenly you're not angry anymore; you're that six-year-old child again, voice small and bewildered, asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in a place of raw, undefended heartbreak where all you want is for them to say they're sorry, even though you know they never will. Move from controlled accusation through fury into childlike vulnerability.

title: The Homecoming
instruction: Someone you deeply wronged has just walked back into your life after years away—or someone who wronged you has returned. You're face to face for the first time since everything fell apart. Look at them: how they've changed, how they've stayed the same, what their eyes tell you about the years between. Notice if they're guarded, if they're hopeful, if they're already planning to leave again. Wonder what their life has been like without you, whether they think about you, whether they've forgiven themselves or you. Begin with your heart racing—a chaotic mix of joy at seeing them and anger that they dare show their face, or relief that they're here and resentment that they stayed away so long. Your voice should shake with contradictions: 'I've missed you' fighting with 'How dare you,' gratitude battling with rage. Let yourself swing between emotions, observing how they react to each shift. End in a place that's both tender and unresolved—perhaps embracing them while crying, laughing while furious, saying 'I'm so glad you're here' while also meaning 'I'll never fully forgive you.'

title: Strangled Victory
instruction: You're on your back, pinned by someone's weight, their hand clamped around your throat. Your windpipe is compressed, making every word a rasping struggle. You gasp for air, your voice cracking and erratic, but you've just stabbed them or landed a blow—you feel their grip loosen. Force out taunting, breathless words of triumph, starting in a choked, defiant whisper and ending in a raw, shattered laugh. Let the physical restriction warp your pitch and rhythm, and let the triumph build as you realize they're the one losing air now.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Pilot Congratulating Crew While Processing Near-Catastrophe
instruction: Intercom address to the cabin post-emergency landing. Your voice is measured, captain-assured: 'Thank you for your attention during our approach.' But you're still tasting adrenaline. Your pitch wavers slightly on certain words. Behind the professionalism, you're mechanically listing congratulations because you haven't fully processed that everyone is alive. The warmth in your voice is genuine but underneath is the weight of how close it came to being a different speech entirely.

title: The Truth That Shatters
instruction: You're confronting your mother about your childhood—specifically, about the sibling she always favored, the love you never felt you received. Start with controlled anger, the kind you've rehearsed for years. But as she responds, something shifts. She's not defensive; she's breaking down, revealing her own mother did the same to her, that she saw you as strong enough to survive it while your sibling was fragile. Your rage must transform mid-breath into something more complex: horror at understanding her pain, fury that she repeated the cycle anyway, and underneath it all, that child inside you still desperate to hear 'I'm sorry. I should have loved you better.' End with both of you raw, exposed, the understanding finally achieved but at the cost of every protective wall you've built.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, and you can't sleep. In a whisper, barely audible, begin confessing something you've kept hidden—but don't start with the words. Start with your awareness of the physical space: the weight of the blanket, the warmth radiating from their sleeping body inches away, the darkness pressed against your eyes, your own heartbeat, the catch in your throat. Let yourself feel how vulnerable your body is in this moment—exposed, barely breathing, every nerve alive. As you begin to speak your truth in fragments and whispers, let your acute awareness of every tiny sensation—each inhale they take, the sheets against your skin, the tears sliding silently toward your ears—guide you from terrified paralysis into a strange, fragile relief. The fear doesn't leave, but it transforms into something softer as you finally give voice to your secret in the dark.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner About Fear
instruction: Late at night, you're lying beside your sleeping partner, and you whisper confessions you can't say when they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, tender, aching: 'I'm so scared I'm not enough for you.' You're touching their hair, their face, speaking truths that shame and vulnerability have kept locked inside. 'Sometimes I watch you and think... what did I do to deserve this? And when will you realize you made a mistake?' Your voice catches, wavers. There's deep sadness here, and profound love tangled together. 'I love you so much it terrifies me. Like if you left, I wouldn't know who I am anymore.' As you continue, something shifts—speaking the fear out loud begins to transform it. Your voice finds a quiet strength: 'But you chose me. You keep choosing me. Maybe... maybe I need to trust that.' End with a whispered promise to yourself, soft but resolute: 'Tomorrow I'll try to believe I'm worthy of you.' The vulnerability remains, but it's touched now with fragile hope.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent who never spoke the words you needed. Begin with controlled anger, each word measured: 'Do you even know what it cost me, waiting for you to say it?' Let your voice build as years of unmet need pour out. Then, mid-accusation, you see them truly - frail, frightened, human. Your rage collapses into something more devastating: raw vulnerability. 'I just needed you to tell me I was enough.' Your voice becomes a child's again, pleading. End in the terrible space between anger and forgiveness, where you're offering them one last chance: 'Say it now. Please. While there's still time.' The final word should tremble with desperate hope and the certainty that it may never come.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You are confronting your father after years of silence about the emotional distance between you. Start with accusation—your voice sharp, controlled, listing grievances like evidence in a trial. You've rehearsed this. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: beneath your anger, you discover a desperate, childlike need for him to see you, to know you. The accusations crumble into questions: 'Why didn't you ask about my life? Why did you never want to know who I actually am?' Let your voice lose its armor. End by saying something you've never admitted to anyone—not about him, but about yourself. A fear, a failure, a secret shame. The confrontation transforms from attack to offering, from rage to terrifying vulnerability.

title: The Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: You're a parent or caregiver screaming at a locked door, behind which someone you'd die for is in danger you cannot stop—an overdose, a suicide attempt, a medical crisis. Start with commanding authority, demanding they open the door, your voice powerful and controlled. Then let panic shred that control—you're pounding, pleading, your voice cracking as you cycle rapidly through rage at your own helplessness, terror, desperate bargaining. Your strength becomes frantic vulnerability. End in a collapsed, breathless place where you're begging, offering anything, your voice raw and broken, all pretense of control abandoned. The arc moves from fierce protective strength to absolute emotional devastation.

title: Coming to Consciousness After Being Struck by Lightning
instruction: You're waking up. Your voice is thick, confused, almost not your own. Everything hurts in a way that doesn't have a name. You try to move and can't, or when you do it's involuntary. Your voice is slurred as you try to understand what happened, what world you're in. Include the moment someone's voice breaks through—a paramedic, a stranger—and your voice becomes almost childlike, asking what happened. Your speech is scattered, neurological damage making your words come out wrong. Slowly, terribly, awareness returns. You're alive. Your voice becomes stronger, more panicked, as you realize the implications.

title: The Body Remembers What the Mind Watches
instruction: You are in the midst of overwhelming physical and emotional intensity—perhaps the peak of passionate intimacy, or the full-body rage of smashing dishes after betrayal, or the convulsive sobs of grief that take over your entire frame. Begin fully immersed, lost in the sensation, your body acting on pure instinct and overwhelming feeling. Then, without stopping the physical experience, split your awareness: watch yourself from outside your own skin. See your own face contorted, hear your own sounds as if they're coming from a stranger, observe the wild authenticity of your own body in this state. The physical sensations continue—pleasure, rage, anguish, whatever you've chosen—but now you're simultaneously inside the hurricane and calmly observing it. This dual state intensifies everything: being watched by yourself makes the experience both more vulnerable and more real. End in a place where the observer and the experiencer merge back together, bringing the consciousness of having witnessed yourself through this intensity, forever changed by having seen yourself so utterly unleashed.
inspired_by: Becoming a Spectator in Your Dreams

title: The Body Remembering What Words Can't
instruction: You're recounting a physical experience of intense sensation—childbirth, a car accident, the first night with a lover, being struck, a moment of ecstasy or agony. But your body won't let you tell it straight. As you try to describe what happened, let your physical self hijack the narrative completely: contort words into sounds that match sensation, speak in rhythms that have nothing to do with language, let your voice climb and drop erratically. Exaggerate everything—turn pain into operatic wailing, turn passion into guttural absurdity, mix laughter with groans. Start trying to make someone understand with clear description, but dissolve into pure physical vocal response. Somewhere in this abandon, access the actual memory in your body rather than the story about it. End in a moment where sound and sensation become indistinguishable from truth.

title: Scattering Your Abusive Father's Ashes While Reading His Apology Diary
instruction: You're alone on a cliff, scattering your father's ashes while reading the diary he left you—forty years of entries documenting his guilt, shame, and inability to apologize while alive. Start reading with bitter sarcasm, almost mocking his written confessions of the abuse you survived. But his words are searingly honest—he catalogs every moment he destroyed you, taking full responsibility without excuse. Your voice shifts, becoming confused, then angry that he knew what he was doing and did it anyway. Then you find entries about his own childhood abuse, and unexpected compassion complicates your rage. You're crying and laughing simultaneously—grateful he finally acknowledged the truth, furious he waited until death to be brave. As you scatter his ashes, you're speaking directly to him with contradictory tenderness and anger, forgiving and not forgiving in the same breath. You end with peaceful exhaustion, admitting aloud that you loved him and hated him and both things can be true. The wind takes his ashes as you whisper, 'I'm free now. We both are.'
inspired_by: Translator in Courtroom Realizes Defendant Is Her Brother's Killer

title: The Smell of You in Empty Rooms
instruction: You're alone in the apartment the morning after your lover has left you forever. Sit in their favorite chair and whisper to the empty air where they used to be. Begin in the hollow numbness of fresh loss. Then, slowly, sensorially rebuild their presence: the specific scent of their skin, the exact temperature and weight of their hand in yours, the subtle vibration of their breathing when they slept beside you, the particular way their voice softened when they said your name. As these sensory memories accumulate, let them transform your emptiness into something almost unbearable—the acute presence of their absence. Your whispered words should shift from disbelief to a tender, aching gratitude for having known such specific beauty, even as it destroys you. End by saying goodbye to the precisely reconstructed presence you've created.

title: The Resigned Survivor
instruction: Youre trapped and facing death but are eerily calm. Speak to yourself as if preparing for the end, with each line sounding like acceptance mixed with traces of defiance.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the middle of the night. You gently wake them because you can't hold this secret anymore: you've been offered your dream job, but it's on another continent. Begin in a hushed, almost guilty whisper—there's tenderness here, but also fear of destroying something precious. As you explain what this opportunity means to you, let your voice gradually fill with quiet excitement and longing that you've been suppressing. End in a place of open vulnerability, asking them to come with you, knowing you might lose them either way. Your vocal journey should move from apologetic restraint to brave honesty—each word a risk, each breath an act of trust. Let the silence between phrases speak as loudly as the words.
inspired_by: Director or colleague challenges the actor's process as overcomplicated or unnecessary

title: Laughing Through the Final Season
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis, and you've come to your favorite tree—the one you've visited in every season of your life. Touch the bark and find yourself laughing, actually laughing, at the absurd beauty of it all. Start with genuine mirth mixed with disbelief: 'You'll outlive me by centuries, you magnificent bastard.' Let joy and sorrow tangle together—you're grateful for every season you had, devastated there won't be more, amused by the cosmic joke, awed by the continuity this tree represents. Your laughter should catch and break, tears mixing with genuine delight at having lived at all. End in a place of paradoxical peace: terrified and accepting, heartbroken and deeply thankful, your voice a trembling whisper of 'thank you' that holds everything—the fear, the love, the unbearable privilege of being alive and knowing you won't be forever.
inspired_by: Touching the Bark of a Large, Old Tree

title: The Agreement That Breaks You
instruction: You're confronting your mother about why she stayed silent when you needed her most. Start with controlled fury: 'You knew what was happening and you did nothing.' Your voice should be tight, precise, each word a stone you've carried for years. As she finally admits 'I was afraid,' feel your rage begin to fracture. The words 'I needed you to be brave for me' should come out broken, no longer an accusation but a plea from your younger self. End in a place of devastating clarity—you both failed each other, and you're both going to have to live with it. Your final line 'Maybe we can try again' should sound like it costs you everything, anger dissolving into exhausted, terrified hope.

title: Uncoiling the Truth
instruction: You are confronting your father about a lie that shaped your entire childhood. Begin the scene with your body coiled tight—jaw clenched, fists tight, breath held high in your chest, every muscle braced for impact. Your voice may start controlled, even cold. As you reveal what you know, as you speak the unspeakable, allow your body to slowly uncoil: let your shoulders drop, your breath sink lower into your belly, your hands open. Something predatory in you softens into something more vulnerable, more raw. By the end, you are no longer attacking—you are asking, reaching, perhaps even pleading. Let this physical unwinding change everything about how you sound, how you stand, how you meet his eyes.

title: Drunk and Jealous on the Phone
instruction: You're slightly drunk, calling your partner who is out with someone you're jealous of. You're putting on a seductive voice for phone sex, but underneath the slow, breathy performance, there's a sharp edge of envy. Start with a deliberately low, possessive tone, almost a whisper, as you describe what you want to do to them. Let the jealousy crack through in a pause or a sharp intake of breath. Halfway through, remember they're safe — relief floods in, softening your voice, making it warmer and more vulnerable. End with a drowsy, genuine tenderness, the performance melting into real emotion. Let your words drift, lose a thought, then find it again, as the alcohol and the feelings mix.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Hospice Worker Throws a Dance Party for Dying Friend, Both Knowing It's the Last One
instruction: Your best friend is dying, and you've promised them one more dance party, right here in their hospice room. Put on their favorite song and start with genuine, fierce joy—you're laughing, singing along terribly, remembering every ridiculous dance move from your youth. Your voice is full of life, teasing them about their rhythm, making stupid jokes. But even as you're laughing, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice cracks mid-laugh, joy and grief tangled together until you can't tell where one ends and the other begins. You're thanking them—for every stupid adventure, for loving you when you were unlovable, for being here—and your gratitude sounds like both celebration and goodbye. End with your voice suspended between a laugh and a sob as the song ends, saying 'same time next week?' when you both know there won't be a next week. Let joy and devastation exist in the same breath, your voice the sound of loving someone so much that you can find lightness even as your heart is shattering.
inspired_by: Professional: Priest Comforts the Dying While They're Losing Their Own Faith

title: Contradictory Grace: Thanking Someone Who Hurt You as You Finally Let Go
instruction: You're facing someone who caused you tremendous pain—an ex who broke your heart, a mentor who betrayed you, a friend who abandoned you when you needed them most. Begin with your voice soft, almost surprising yourself with what you're about to do. You're going to thank them. Let genuine gratitude color your words—because their betrayal taught you strength, their absence showed you who truly loves you, their cruelty revealed your own resilience. Your voice should carry the strange beauty of this realization, even as it trembles. But underneath the gratitude, let profound sadness leak through—you can't help but grieve what could have been, who they might have been to you. End with your voice simultaneously breaking and becoming whole, laughing softly through tears, acknowledging that you're grateful for the lesson even as you mourn the cost. Your final moment should radiate hard-won peace mixed with bittersweet loss.
inspired_by: Historical: Holocaust Survivor Confronts the Guard

title: The Imaginary Friends Farewell
instruction: Youre saying goodbye to a child who has outgrown you, their imaginary friend. Speak with love, sadness, and pride, letting the listener feel your ache as you release them to the real world.

title: Three AM Truths
instruction: You are lying in the dark beside someone you love, unable to sleep, whispering a confession you've never spoken aloud. Start barely audible—testing the waters, seeing if they're awake, half-hoping they won't hear you. Confess something about who you were before you met them, something you've carried in silence, something tender and shameful and deeply human. As you speak into the darkness, let the confession deepen. Their breathing changes—they're awake, listening, but not interrupting. Find your way from whispered half-truths to raw admission, from shame to something like relief, from hiding to being known. Let your voice remain quiet throughout, but let the emotional intensity build in the intimacy, not the volume. End with a question posed to the darkness, vulnerable and open, waiting for their response.
inspired_by: Actor struggles with a character very different from themselves

title: The Last Phone Call Before They Board
instruction: Your person is about to board a plane for a mission they might not return from—a dangerous deployment, a one-way humanitarian mission, experimental treatment in another country. You have three minutes before they have to go through security. You started this call trying to be strong, supportive, saying all the right things about being proud of them. But as the final boarding announcement echoes in the background, everything you've been holding back starts cracking open. Your voice breaks from encouragement into desperate need—you want to tell them not to go, to stay, that you can't do this without them. The words tangle between 'I'm so proud of you' and 'please don't leave me.' You're trying to give them your blessing while your heart is shattering, trying to let them hear your strength when all you feel is terror of the empty space they're about to leave behind.
inspired_by: Announcing Bad Diagnosis Out Loud for the First Time

title: Laughing Through the Noise
instruction: You're at a crowded cocktail party, standing close to a friend near the bar. You just found out your lifelong dream is about to come true — a call you've been waiting on for months. You start telling your friend, your voice bright with hopeful excitement, but the room is so loud you have to lean in and speak with punchy, slightly higher-pitched bursts. Mid-sentence, the reality hits you — it's really happening — and your voice suddenly cracks with pure, ecstatic joy. You're caught between giddy pleasure and the effort of being heard, so you laugh, lose your train of thought, then find it again, your energy climbing as you repeat the good news with fresh delight.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Concentration (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Pride on the Floor
instruction: You're a tough older man, drunk, lying facedown on a cold linoleum floor, propped on your elbows. The room tilts, your head pounds. At first, you mutter with sour irritation—cursing the dirty floor, your own stupidity, the cheap whiskey. But as you try to push yourself up and fail, helplessness seeps through. Your voice wavers, you stop mid-sentence, you feel the weight of your body and the years. End with a crack in your bravado—a quiet admission that you just can't get up. Let your words be thick, breathy, broken by effort and defeat.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Helplessness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Train Station That Keeps Changing
instruction: You're at a train station saying goodbye to someone who's leaving, but the station keeps shifting in impossible ways—platforms multiply, the light changes from dawn to dusk and back, sounds from different times of day overlap, the architecture warps. Begin with the specific sensory details of this unstable space: what does the air smell like? What announcements do you hear echoing? How does the ground feel under your feet as it subtly changes? Start feeling relieved they're going, even happy, free. But as you explore the sensory distortions of this impossible place—the way time seems to fold, the way their face might be younger or older from moment to moment—let contradictory emotions start to surface. Maybe relief and devastating loss. Maybe gratitude and bitter anger. Maybe joy at their freedom and despair at yours. Let these opposites coexist and intensify, not resolving into one clear feeling but becoming more complex. End in a state where you're experiencing multiple truths at once—laughing and crying, pushing away and holding on, grateful and destroyed—all of it real, all of it true.

title: Dancing in the Ruins: Gratitude at the End
instruction: You're at the bedside of someone you love who's actively dying, and instead of falling apart, you're thanking them—laughing through tears at shared memories. Begin with genuine warmth, almost lighthearted as you recount a ridiculous story that makes you both smile. Your voice lifts with affection, nostalgia. But the laughter keeps breaking into something else—your voice cracks, wavers. You're celebrating them while simultaneously feeling them slip away. The adrenaline of holding both joy and grief makes your speech patterns erratic: you're laughing one moment, voice thick with tears the next. End in a space of strange peace—your voice soft, wondering, as you tell them it's okay to go, that you're grateful for every moment, even this one. You're breaking and whole at the same time.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago, and they've just said 'I did my best.' Start with cold, controlled fury: 'Your best? Your BEST?' Your voice is sharp, accusatory, each word a knife. But as you list what their 'best' cost you—'I was nine years old and I thought it was my fault'—your anger cracks into the wounded child underneath. Your voice becomes ragged, vulnerable: 'I needed you and you just... left.' End with exhausted clarity, almost tender in its honesty: 'I can't forgive you, but I need to let you go.' Journey from righteous rage through raw pain to bittersweet release.

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Never Believed You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years. Begin with controlled fury, voice tight with decades of swallowed words: 'You made me feel like I was crazy.' Let that control crack—your voice should shake, rise, break apart with rage and grief. But underneath the anger, there's something more painful: the child in you still desperate to be seen. Midway through, let that vulnerability surface—'Why wasn't I enough for you to listen?'—your voice dropping to something raw and small. End not with triumph but with exhausted, hollow clarity: you're done begging to be believed. Move from rage through heartbreak to devastating acceptance.
inspired_by: Comforting Your Child After a Nightmare

title: The Five Stages of Getting Drunk
instruction: Perform a continuous monologue that progresses through five drinks over the course of the performance. Drink 1: slightly looser, louder, more confident. Drink 2: storytelling mode, animated, slurring just starts on 'specifically.' Drink 3: emotional — you love everyone, everything is beautiful. Drink 4: aggressive philosophy, volume uncontrolled, balance issues audible in swaying voice. Drink 5: incoherent, crying, declaring eternal friendship with a stranger.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You've just been beaten by someone in your home. Your face is swollen, lip split, tooth loosened—speech is painful and distorted. Your young child is asleep in the next room, and you're leaving tonight, right now, forever. You're recording a voice message they'll hear tomorrow. Start trying to sound normal, upbeat even, working around the consonants you can't form, the lisp from your broken tooth. You're almost succeeding in sounding okay. But as you tell them how much you love them, how this isn't their fault, the physical pain of speaking becomes nothing compared to the heartbreak of this goodbye. Your voice gets quieter, more tender, each mispronounced word a reminder of what you're protecting them from. End in whispered fragments, crying softly, your damaged mouth making 'I love you' sound broken—and somehow more true because of it.
inspired_by: Stitched Up After a Fight, Trying to Sound Tough

title: The Courtroom Where Everything Shatters
instruction: You're testifying about your child's father—someone you once loved—who hurt your child. Begin with fierce, controlled rage: 'He will never touch my daughter again. Never.' Your voice is steel, protective, certain. But as you're forced to describe what happened, to say the words out loud in public, your armor begins to crack. The fury breaks into anguish: 'I let him in our home. I trusted him. I didn't see—' Your voice fractures. Then comes something even more devastating: guilt, helplessness, the feeling that you failed the person you'd die to protect. 'She needed me to protect her and I—' You can't finish. By the end, the rage returns but it's mixed with tears, with broken determination: 'He will never—never—' Let us hear a parent's love turned into both weapon and wound.

title: The Passionate Defense That Crumbles
instruction: You're fiercely defending someone you love to a crowd that wants to condemn them. Start with blazing conviction, your voice powerful and certain: 'You don't know them! You don't know what they've survived, what they've overcome!' Your passion is fierce, almost aggressive: 'They are worthy. They are good. And I will not stand here and let you destroy them!' But then doubt creeps in. Your voice falters: 'They... they deserve...' You're realizing maybe you're not sure anymore. The fierce protectiveness transforms into helpless confusion: 'I thought I knew. I was so certain.' End with your voice breaking completely, vulnerable and lost: 'What if I was wrong? What if I can't save them? What if... what if I never really knew them at all?' The transformation from passionate defender to shattered doubter must feel inevitable and devastating.

title: The Last Night Before You Go
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved for years—a parent, partner, or closest friend—and this is their final night. You've been making small talk, asking if they need water, adjusting their blankets, doing everything except saying what's really in your heart. Begin by speaking those safe, caretaking words out loud. Then, halfway through, let the dam break. Stop protecting them, stop protecting yourself, and say everything you've been too frightened or too polite to say: the gratitude that chokes you, the anger at them for leaving, the specific memories that have shaped your entire life, the ways they'll live in you forever. Move from the mask of the dutiful caregiver to raw, unfiltered love and grief. Let your voice crack, let silence fall where it needs to, and end in a place of devastating honesty—whether that's peace, rage, or broken-hearted acceptance.
inspired_by: This Is What I Usually Say, and This Is What I Really Want to Say

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They have been unconscious, but suddenly their eyes flutter open. Begin with careful hope—maybe they'll recover, maybe there's more time. Speak to them about one specific memory from your childhood that you've never mentioned before: a moment when you felt truly seen by them. As you speak, let yourself discover what this memory actually means to you now, decades later. Let your voice and body respond authentically to whatever feelings arise—perhaps gratitude mixing with grief, perhaps old resentment softening into understanding, perhaps love you never knew how to express. By the end, you must release them—give them explicit permission to go. The emotion you end with should surprise you; don't plan it, let the journey of speaking this memory aloud reveal what you truly feel.
inspired_by: Choice Hunt / Building a Repertoire of UC Choices

title: Masked Longing
instruction: You are an older man in a crowded clinic waiting room, forced to wear an N95 respirator. Across the room, the nurse you've been flirting with for weeks smiles at you. You start with barely contained irritation—the mask is hot, your glasses are fogging, and every word feels like shouting into a pillow. As you try to call her over, your frustration melts into a clumsy, breathless attempt at charm: you want her to come closer, but the mask makes you sound like a muffled fool. Let your voice strain against the filter, punctuated by sharp exhalations and a clicking valve. End with a raw, half-laughing confession of how ridiculous you feel, but don't lose the heat in your eyes.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Infatuation (extremely present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You are giving a toast at your best friend's wedding—but you're in love with them, and they'll never know. Begin with genuine joy and humor, celebrating them authentically. As you continue, let contradictory currents run underneath: real happiness for their happiness exists alongside your own breaking heart. Allow your voice to carry both—the brightness that's true and the ache that's equally true. Don't choose one emotion; let them coexist. Speak about their love while feeling your own unrequited longing. Let gratitude for their presence in your life mix with grief for what will never be. By the end, arrive at a place of bittersweet grace—your voice holding immense love, deep loss, genuine celebration, and quiet personal devastation all at once. This is not about hiding the pain or revealing it, but about the strange human capacity to feel multiple truths simultaneously.

title: The Last Question
instruction: You are a woman in her late 60s, interviewing for a part-time role at a cozy bookstore. The man interviewing you is kind, warm, and reminds you of someone you lost decades ago. You've answered every question perfectly, but as he asks 'Is there anything else you'd like to know?', you realize you don't want to leave. Let your voice start with that polished, over-enunciated professional tone, but as you speak, let your guard slip—your longing and infatuation leak through in a tiny, breathy laugh, a pause where you almost say something else. End with a teasing lilt, as if you're testing the waters, but keep it fragile, hopeful, and undeniably real.
emotions_sampled: Longing (extremely present), Infatuation (very intensely present), Teasing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Where We Learned to Lie
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up, finally speaking the truth about how his absence shaped you. Start by describing what you see: the chipped yellow paint, the coffee maker still in the same spot, the chair where he sat for every silent dinner. Begin with attempted civility, your voice steady but tight. As you list each memory—the school plays he missed, the promises unkept, the way you learned to stop expecting him—let your anger build, but not in volume. Make it sharper, more precise, each word a small blade. Then watch him deflate, become smaller, older. Your rage must transform as you suddenly see him not as the giant of your childhood but as a tired, flawed man who failed because he was broken, not because you weren't worth showing up for. End with the exhaustion of truth-telling and an unexpected, uncomfortable compassion.

title: Whispering the Truth You've Hidden Your Whole Life
instruction: It's late at night. You're sitting beside someone you trust completely—perhaps a lifelong friend, a partner, or a sibling. Start speaking very quietly, almost to yourself: 'There's something I've never told anyone.' Your voice should be barely above a whisper, thick with shame and fear. Slowly reveal a secret you've carried your entire life—something about your identity, a trauma you've hidden, a truth that shaped you but that you've been too afraid to voice. As you speak, let your breathing become uneven. Pause frequently, as if the words are physically difficult to release. Midway through, your voice should break with relief—the unburdening is painful but necessary. End with a whispered question: 'Do you still...?' Let it hang there, unfinished, showing both terror and desperate hope of still being loved despite what you've revealed.
inspired_by: Asking For Forgiveness After Years of Silence

title: Grateful for a Gift You Never Wanted
instruction: Someone you love has just given you something precious - maybe a grandparent is passing down a family heirloom before they die, maybe a friend made an enormous sacrifice for you that you never asked for, maybe your parents finally gave you the approval you've been seeking your whole life but now it comes too late or in the wrong way. You have to express gratitude - genuine gratitude, because you do see their love and effort - but underneath that gratitude is grief, or anger, or the heartbreak of 'why now?' or 'this isn't what I needed.' Begin with the thanks that you mean - let real warmth and appreciation color your voice - but let something else bleed through: a tremor of sadness, a edge of frustration, a laugh that sounds almost like crying. The contradiction should build: you're saying beautiful things about what this means to you, and you mean them, but you're also falling apart because it's bittersweet or complicated or painful. Perhaps you laugh through tears, or your voice breaks as you're expressing joy, or you thank them with such intensity that it reveals your hidden pain. End in a place where both emotions are fully present and real: you're both grateful and grieving, both loving them and heartbroken, both appreciative and devastated. Let the contradiction live fully in your voice without resolving it.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Surprised at a Surprise Party You Discovered

title: Speaking at Your Mentor's Funeral
instruction: You're at the podium, voice amplified. Start strong telling a story about them. But getting to what they meant to you, your voice wavers: 'They believed in me when I didn't believe in myself.' Your breathing catches. You pause, collect yourself, continue. Deliver the final tribute in a voice rough with emotion but steady.

title: Breaking the Vase
instruction: You are physically destroying your art studio—throwing canvases, smashing pottery, tearing down everything you've made. You never became the artist you promised yourself you'd be. Your body should be active, violent, exhausted. But as you destroy each piece, something unexpected happens: you start laughing through your rage because you realize these 'failed' pieces taught you how to be honest with your own children, how to let your partner truly see you, how to cry when you need to. Your voice should begin guttural and explosive, breaking things with furious grief. Gradually let wild, amazed laughter mix with your sobs—the physical exhaustion opening you to a truth your mind couldn't reach. End breathless, sitting in the wreckage, saying 'It wasn't wasted' like a discovery, like a prayer.
inspired_by: When you question whether your decades of teaching have been worthwhile, especially for students who did not become professional actors

title: The Last Glass
instruction: You are standing at the kitchen sink, late at night, alone. The water runs hot over your hands as you wash the final wine glass from a family dinner that left you feeling sour and unseen. A sharp clink as you set another glass aside. Your voice starts tight, a bitter mutter about their careless words, but as you slowly, carefully scrub each rim, the rhythm of the water pulls you into concentration. By the time you dry the last glass, your voice has softened—still weary, but quieter, as if letting that sourness drain down the sink. Let the sounds of water and glass interrupt your words naturally.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying in darkness next to someone—a lover, a spouse, a close friend—and you finally whisper the secret you've been carrying. Begin with your breath—shallow, hesitant, the words catching in your throat because once you say this, everything changes. The secret could be about desire, shame, fear, a terrible mistake, or a truth about who you really are. As you speak in barely audible whispers, feel yourself becoming simultaneously more terrified and more free with each word. Don't perform or dramatize—let the intimacy of darkness and proximity make your voice even smaller, more raw. By the end, let the relief of finally being known wash over you, even as you tremble with vulnerability, waiting in the silence to see if they'll still hold you.

title: The Tainted Toast
instruction: You're at a small, dimly lit pub, hunched over a sticky table, nursing a single glass of whiskey. Your throat is raw and scratchy from a persistent cough that you can't shake. Across from you, a former friend now laughs with someone else, a person you know has betrayed you. You have a small piece of bread in your hand. As you cough—hard, wet, rattling—you realize you could drop a crumb of your medicine into their drink, waiting for the right moment. Start with the physical struggle of suppressing a cough, your voice raspy and tight. Let your words be slow, deliberate, with a quiet, simmering malice that grows colder and more certain as you speak. By the end, your voice should carry a chilling, satisfied calm as you plan the act.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Emergency Room Triage
instruction: You're the triage nurse at 3 AM, deciding who gets the ambulance bed first. The drunk driver and the elderly man hit by that drunk driver are both hemorrhaging. You're running through the protocol with practiced precision: 'Vitals stable, no internal bleeding signs...' But the old man is your father's age. Your voice wavers on the third vital sign. You make the call: the driver gets the bed. Professional mask reassembles as you address the waiting family. Then the driver's mother arrives screaming in Spanish. Your clinical composure fractures when she begs in a voice that sounds exactly like your own mother. Find the moment where protocol fails and humanity floods in.

title: The Last Move
instruction: You're an elderly person, settled deep in a worn armchair, recounting a triumphant chess victory from decades ago—the final checkmate that stunned everyone. But the room is warm, the hour late, and sleep is pulling you under. As you speak, your voice slows, words stretch and blur, and you nod off mid-sentence. You jerk awake with a soft start, trying to pick up, but now you're confused, unable to recall what you were saying. Let the clear pride of your triumph dissolve into drowsy lostness, your voice growing softer and more muddled until it fades into a mumble.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're an adult finally confronting your parent about their absence during your childhood. Begin with careful control, voice measured and practiced—you've rehearsed this: 'I need to talk to you about something.' But as you list specific moments they missed (your graduation, your first heartbreak, the night you needed them most), your voice starts to shake with accumulated years of hurt. They try to defend themselves, and suddenly you're not careful anymore—your voice rises with decades of suppressed anger: 'You don't get to make excuses!' But underneath the rage is a child's voice, still wanting their love: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The fury collapses into raw vulnerability. You hate that you still need them. End with quiet devastation, voice small and exhausted: 'I just needed you to show up.' You're not yelling anymore. You're just... done. Empty. Finally honest.

title: The 48-Hour Crack
instruction: You're in a cluttered apartment, phone pressed to your ear, after two sleepless nights. You're talking to someone you want, but your mind is pixelating. Start with a low, breathy laugh at a hallucination—a lamp looks like a cat. Then shift to impatient, irritated answers as they ask you something, your voice scratchy and sharp. Let lust creep in for a moment, a husky whisper, but then you trail off, arguing with a shadow on the wall. End with a sudden, raw snap—'I said stop moving!'—before you catch yourself and go silent.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Sexual Lust (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering in the Dark After Years Apart
instruction: You're lying next to someone you once loved deeply but haven't seen in five years. It's 3 AM. You're both awake in the darkness. Begin speaking so quietly they have to hold their breath to hear you—confess something you've never told anyone. As you speak, let your body remember: their smell, their touch, the way they used to look at you, the day they left. Let these sense memories soften your voice, make it tremble. You came here thinking you were over them. But as words spill out, realize you're not confessing to explain—you're confessing to ask if there's still a chance. Move from guarded caution to naked, terrifying hope.
inspired_by: Actor has many lines and moves rapidly through dialogue; sensory choice work interferes with the behavioral demands of the scene

title: Hiding Disappointment When Receiving an Unwanted Gift
instruction: You receive a gift that isnt to your liking, but you dont want to hurt the givers feelings. Internally, youre disappointed, but you express gratitude. Describe the letdown inside while showing appreciation. Speak with a grateful tone, masking your true reaction.

title: The Soundproof Confession
instruction: You are a man trapped in a small walk-in closet, which you've turned into a makeshift soundproof booth for a secret recording. The door is jammed, and the phone you were using to record is dead. Outside, you hear the muffled voice of someone who has been hunting you. Start with fear — whisper, breathy, checking the door handle with a click. As you realize you're cornered, let a slow, venomous malice seep in, a cold rage that you'll make them pay if they find you. End in raw distress — your voice cracks, you press your palm against the fabric-lined wall, and you mutter a desperate, broken plea that mixes threat with terror.
emotions_sampled: Fear (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Distress (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Leaving a Party Without Saying Goodbye
instruction: Narrate the internal monologue of an introvert executing the 'Irish exit.' Your inner voice is strategic: 'Okay, she's looking at her phone, he's in the bathroom, if I go NOW—' Include the physical comedy of tiptoeing, grabbing your coat from under someone, the door that SQUEAKS. Freeze. Resume. Make it to the car and let out the biggest sigh of relief. Then the guilt: 'Should I text? No. Yes? No.' Drive away. The relief is physical, audible, and deeply relatable.

title: The Phone Call After the Funeral
instruction: You're calling your estranged brother the day after your sister's funeral. You haven't spoken in five years because of a stupid fight you can't even remember the details of now. When he answers, you're hit with contradictory feelings: fury that he barely showed up to the funeral, relief that he answered the phone, grief that she's gone, sudden desperate love for him because he's all the family you have left, resentment that it took this to make you call. Start by saying something simple like 'It's me.' Then let yourself ride the wave of these conflicting feelings without choosing just one. Maybe you're laughing bitterly one moment and crying the next. Maybe anger and tenderness come out in the same breath. Don't smooth it out or make it make sense. By the end, you've either said 'I love you' or 'I can't do this' or both - and you genuinely don't know which it will be until it comes out of your mouth.
inspired_by: Actor feels disconnected from real feelings or is 'naturally' acting—imitating truth rather than experiencing it

title: When Protection Means Letting Go
instruction: Your teenage child stands before you, bags packed, choosing a dangerous path you cannot stop. Begin with fierce, protective anger—voice raised, commanding them to stay, to listen to reason. Your words come fast and sharp, fueled by terror. But mid-sentence, your voice breaks completely. The rage collapses into helpless sobbing as you realize you have no power here. Your pleas become raw and unguarded: 'Please, please don't do this.' Then, through tears, you must find the strength to say the hardest words—that you'll love them no matter what, that you'll be here when they return. End with a voice shredded by emotion but somehow steady, giving them your blessing even as it destroys you.

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Sleeping Child You're Leaving
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your sleeping child before walking away forever—not because you don't love them, but because you believe they're better off without you. Kneel beside their bed and whisper the things you need them to know but hope they'll never remember. Start with tender observations: the way they sleep, how their hair falls, a moment from today that made you smile. Let your voice catch as you try to explain why you have to go, the justifications crumbling even as you speak them. Feel the terrible intimacy of being this close to them for the last time. Your breathing should become ragged with suppressed sobs. End by pressing your hand to their back, feeling them breathe, and whispering 'I'm so sorry' with such quiet devastation that it's barely sound at all—just breath and breaking.
inspired_by: Town Crier at the End of the World

title: Holding You While You Sleep
instruction: You're lying beside your partner of twenty years, who's sleeping peacefully, unaware this is your last night together—you're leaving tomorrow and won't tell them until morning. Your voice is barely a whisper, a confession to the darkness. Start by memorizing them: the sound of their breathing, the curve of their shoulder, the way they mumble in sleep. Let tenderness saturate every word as you catalog what you love, but feel your throat tighten with the weight of what you're about to destroy. Whisper the reasons you have to go—reasons that sound hollow even as you speak them. Your voice should catch on words like 'always' and 'forever,' promises you made and are now breaking. End with a trembling 'I'm so sorry' that's almost inaudible, filled with love so deep it makes leaving both impossible and inevitable, gratitude and grief braided together in every breath.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—maybe a terminal diagnosis, maybe a devastating loss—and strangely, you're laughing. Start with genuine laughter, almost hysterical: 'Oh my God. Of course. Of COURSE this is how it goes.' But let tears mix with the laughter, your voice breaking between chuckles: 'I had plans. I had so many...' The absurdity hits you again and you laugh harder, but it's edged with grief. Find moments of real gratitude shining through: 'But I got to—I actually got to experience...' Your voice fills with wonder even as tears stream. Let the laughter and crying become indistinguishable. End with something beautifully contradictory: peaceful acceptance wrapped in heartbreak, your voice warm and broken simultaneously: 'I don't want to go. But what a gift it was. What an impossible, beautiful gift.' Show someone finding strange joy in the midst of profound loss.

title: Grateful for the Wreckage
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of your old life—the house you're losing, the relationship that ended, the dream that died—and you're trying to explain to yourself (or to someone) why you're somehow okay. Begin with a laugh that's almost manic, listing absurd silver linings: 'At least I don't have to pretend anymore.' But the laughter keeps catching on tears. You're genuinely grateful for the freedom, for the truth, for the ending—and simultaneously your heart is shattering. Your voice moves between joy and devastation, sometimes within the same sentence. 'I'm free' sounds like celebration and like mourning. You're finding real peace in the chaos, real gratitude in the loss, but that doesn't make it hurt less. End with a phrase that contains both emotions fully: something like 'Thank you for breaking my heart.' Make us believe both the gratitude and the grief are equally real and present.

title: The Last Goodbye at the Launch Bay
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your adult child who's leaving on a one-way colonization mission to another star system. They'll be in cryosleep for decades, and with time dilation, you'll be dead before they arrive. Start with forced brightness: 'I'm so proud of you, this is everything you dreamed of.' But as they hand you a sealed letter to open after launch, something breaks. Your voice shifts from pride to the raw realization that you're watching your child die to you. Move from celebration to grief, from 'You're going to do amazing things' to a voice that can barely form words. End on a whispered confession of something you never told them—let your voice carry both absolute love and the unbearable weight of permanent loss. The last moment should feel like your heart is physically leaving your body.

title: Three AM Truths
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone you love, and they're asleep. You can't sleep because you're terrified—of losing them, of not being enough, of all your inadequacies. Begin whispering to them (they can't hear you) all the ways you feel you've failed, all your fears about not deserving this love. Your voice should be fragile, breaking, full of shame. But as you whisper, something unexpected happens: you start remembering—out loud, still whispering—the specific moments when you were there for them, the times you were strong, the ways you've loved them well. Small things, big things, things you usually forget. Let your whisper slowly transform from trembling self-doubt into tender, astonished recognition. End with a soft, almost surprised realization: maybe you are enough. Maybe you've been enough all along.

title: The Fort of Blankets
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe seven or eight, curled on your side under a heap of blankets after a nightmare. Your voice is muffled by the pillow, breath shallow and uneven as you whisper to your stuffed rabbit. At first, you try to sound brave, telling yourself you're not scared—a little pride sneaking in. But as you speak, the helplessness seeps through, and your words slow down, your voice cracking with the weight of sadness you can't hold back anymore.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Pride (slightly present), Sadness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Treasure Map to Somewhere
instruction: You are a young boy lying on the living room floor, knees pulled to your chest because of a familiar ache in your belly that won't go away. Your mother just told you she has a surprise that might help you feel better—it's a map to a hidden box of your favorite candy in the yard. As you speak, you're curled on your side, one hand pressed to the cramp, the other reaching for the edge of the map. Your voice is soft and strained, often directed down into the carpet, with a low groan hiding just beneath your words. Start by asking where the candy is with a flicker of exhausted hope, then let your voice brighten with sharp interest as you point out a landmark on the map—you almost forget the pain for a second—but near the end, the hurt tugs you back into numbness, and your last line comes out flat, trailing off like you've given up.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Interest (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Hunger That Answers
instruction: You are alone, experiencing intense physical desire—whether for a person, for touch, for release, for connection. Begin with the pure physical sensation, overwhelming and consuming. But then start interrogating the sensation itself with fierce curiosity: Where exactly in your body does this feeling live? What color would it be? What is it really asking for beneath the obvious answer? What memory is feeding it? What fear? Let your questions become almost aggressive, demanding that your own body explain itself to you. As you pursue each answer, the desire transforms—becoming mixed with unexpected emotions. Anger? Grief? Longing for something you can't name? End with your physical hunger transmuted into emotional revelation, your body having told you something about yourself you didn't know you needed to hear.

title: The Long Road Home
instruction: You're in a sterile interview room, sitting across from two hiring managers. You start with rehearsed professionalism—over-enunciating, nodding too much, breath shallow. As you explain why you want this job, you lose your train of thought when you mention moving back to your hometown to care for your aging parents. Your voice softens, you pause, look at your hands. The longing leaks through. End with a quiet, vulnerable admission that this isn't just about a career—it's about having a home again.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Razor's Edge
instruction: You are an older man shaving with an electric razor in your bathroom, talking to yourself in the mirror after receiving bad news—something you can't change. Begin with a tired, quiet helplessness as you repeat the news to yourself, your voice slightly muffled by the buzzing and the way you pull your cheek flat. As you continue, let the anger build: your jaw tightens, your words become clipped and bitter, and you stop the razor mid-stroke to glare at your own reflection. End with a low, fierce growl, the mechanical buzz resuming as you spit out a final defiant line.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Mirror You've Been Avoiding
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or parental figure) who has spent years subtly undermining your confidence with 'helpful' criticism and comparisons to others. Start angry and defensive, listing the ways they've made you feel small. But mid-confrontation, catch yourself—realize you've internalized their voice so completely that you've become your own harshest critic. The confrontation shifts: you're no longer just angry at them, you're recognizing your own power to break this pattern. End by telling them (and yourself) specific truths about your worth and capability that you've never allowed yourself to believe. Your voice should move from accusatory rage to trembling revelation to grounded, unshakeable self-recognition. Let them witness you claiming yourself.
inspired_by: Actor builds self-esteem as an ongoing daily practice

title: Static and Silence
instruction: You are an elderly man, still groggy from medication after a surgery that damaged your hearing. You sit in a hospital chair, talking to your daughter who is packing your things. Your voice is too loud—you can't hear yourself. Start with a confused, slurry anger about the hospital food, but as you watch her fold your shirt, a quieter realization creeps in: this silence may not go away. Let the drugs keep your speech loud and imprecise, but let a thread of fear and then deep sadness leak through as you lose your train of thought and then find yourself saying a raw goodbye to the life you had.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Fear (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Parallel to You
instruction: You're lying next to your sleeping partner in the dark, and you're about to leave them—not dramatically, but quietly, in the morning. You whisper a confession they'll never hear, speaking truths you could never say to their waking face. Start tender, almost grateful, cataloging all the small moments you'll miss. Your voice is barely audible, catching on words. But the tenderness gradually reveals the sadness underneath: you love them, but you're disappearing inside this life. The whisper becomes even softer as you admit you don't know who you are anymore. End with the most devastating whisper of all—'I'm sorry'—knowing tomorrow you'll pretend you never said any of this.

title: What You Never Knew
instruction: You are confronting your father after discovering a letter that reveals he had another family—a daughter your age—before you were born. Start from a place of ice-cold fury, your words clipped and controlled, almost clinical as you lay out the facts you've uncovered. Demand answers with precision, like you're cross-examining him. But as he begins to explain—the death of that child, the guilt that shaped every choice he made with you, how he tried to be a better father the second time—let your rage fracture. Move from accusation to a desperate, childlike need to understand: were you ever enough? Was his love for you real or just compensation for what he lost? Let your voice crack between anger and the raw vulnerability of a child seeking reassurance. End in a place you didn't expect: not forgiveness exactly, but the terrible, complicated recognition that he's just as broken as you feel right now.

title: The Moment You Realize You've Become What You Swore You'd Never Be
instruction: You're standing in your own kitchen, staring at your hands, after you've just repeated the exact cruelty your abusive parent inflicted on you—but now you've done it to someone you love. Start with denial, frantic justifications, your voice sharp and defensive. But then the mirror cracks: your hands are shaking the same way, your words echo with the same venom, and the realization crashes through you with physical force. Explosive rage at yourself—'No, no, NO!'—that collapses into broken, heaving sobs. You're disgusted, horrified, desperate to take it back. The fierceness is directed inward now, a savage self-loathing mixed with helpless grief. End with a whispered, raw plea to the person you hurt: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry. I don't know how to be better than this.' Let it be ugly, uncontrolled, the kind of breakdown that reshapes a soul.

title: The Wedding Toast You Didn't Plan
instruction: You're standing to give a toast at a wedding, celebration, or farewell party—but the person being honored is someone with whom you have a deeply complicated history. Maybe they got the opportunities you wanted, maybe they hurt you once, maybe you've envied them for years. Begin with the expected words, the surface congratulations, but there's an edge in your voice, a tightness. Then something breaks. Perhaps it's the look on their face, perhaps it's your own exhaustion with bitterness, but you start speaking real truth. You begin genuinely acknowledging what's beautiful about them, what you've actually learned from watching them, ways they've made you better even when you resented them for it. Your voice should shake with the effort of this honesty—it costs you something to say these true, generous things. End in a place where you're simultaneously heartbroken at your own jealousy and genuinely moved by your capacity to transcend it. Let tears come, but they should be complicated tears.

title: Confrontation in the ICU Waiting Room
instruction: You're confronting your parent in a hospital corridor while your sibling fights for life inside. Start with controlled fury—measured accusations about decades of emotional absence, your voice tight and precise. As they try to deflect or minimize, your composure cracks. Words pour out faster, louder, all the swallowed grief of childhood surfacing. Then mid-sentence, a nurse walks by and you both fall silent, and in that silence something shifts. When you speak again, your voice is smaller, almost bewildered—you're not just angry anymore, you're mourning what you never had. By the end, you're asking them directly, voice raw and unguarded: 'Did you ever actually see me?' The question hangs there, genuine and terrified of the answer, all your rage dissolving into the aching vulnerability of a child who still, impossibly, hopes.

title: Thanking Your Abuser for Finally Leaving You Alone (And Meaning It)
instruction: Your abuser—parent, partner, authority figure—has just told you they're done with you, walking away, cutting contact. And you feel... relief. Actual relief. But it's tangled with so much else. You start thanking them, and you genuinely mean it—your voice carries real gratitude, even warmth. 'Thank you for letting me go. Thank you for finally giving me permission to stop trying.' But as you speak, other emotions bleed through: grief for the years you lost trying to earn their love, anger at yourself for being grateful for scraps of decency, a twisted kind of love that refuses to die even now. You laugh—a real, almost joyful laugh—at the absurdity of thanking someone for the bare minimum of leaving you in peace. But the laughter cracks into crying. By the end, you're speaking to the version of yourself that still wanted their approval, saying goodbye to that hope. Your voice carries both liberation and mourning—you're free, but freedom came at the cost of ever having what you needed from them.

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission Before Crossing the Event Horizon
instruction: You're an astronaut making your final communication with your child back on Earth before crossing a black hole's event horizon. Begin with wonder and scientific excitement, describing the beauty of what you're seeing—your voice full of awe and professional pride. But as you speak, time dilation kicks in, and you realize that by the time your words reach home, decades will have passed. Your child will be elderly, perhaps already gone. Your wonder transforms into desperate, aching love. You're trying to pack a lifetime of unmissed birthdays, graduations, weddings into these final seconds. Your voice breaks between the scientist documenting the impossible and the parent saying goodbye to a child they'll never hold again. End with a whispered message of love that you know will arrive too late, your breath catching as you cross the point of no return.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Prophecy Speaker Realizes They've Already Spoken This Moment

title: The Homecoming That Breaks You Open
instruction: You are returning home after years away to discover that the person who hurt you most - perhaps abandoned you, betrayed you, broke you - is dying and has asked for you. You arrive carrying both the deep wound they gave you and the undeniable fact that you still love them. Begin with bitter resistance, reciting to yourself all the reasons you shouldn't be here, armor fully deployed. But as you walk through the door or see their face, let your defenses crack against your will. You want to stay angry - you've earned that anger - but grief and love keep flooding through. Speak to them with your voice breaking between fury and tenderness, resentment and forgiveness, the desire to wound them and the desperate need to hold them one last time. End in the unbearable space where you're grateful for whatever time remains while still bleeding from what they took from you. Let both truths be fully, simultaneously present.
inspired_by: Actor is depressed and cannot access creative energy

title: The Stranger in the Mirror
instruction: Youre describing yourself in the mirror, but what you see feels foreign. At first, speak with bewilderment, growing into horror as you realize you dont recognize this reflection. Your voice wavers between disbelief and panic, as though struggling to accept this loss of identity.

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's 3 a.m. You're lying in bed next to your partner, and you wake them up to whisper something you've been hiding—perhaps a fear, a past betrayal, a secret shame, or a truth about what you really need from them. Begin tentatively, voice barely audible, unable to meet their eyes in the darkness. But as you speak, let the relief of finally telling the truth pull your gaze to theirs. Let the intimacy of being truly seen—not judged, just witnessed—break something open in you. Move from shame-filled secrecy to vulnerable exposure to the quiet, trembling courage of being fully known. Keep your voice hushed throughout; let the emotional journey happen in your eyes, your breath, the micro-expressions of someone shedding armor in the dark.
inspired_by: When you are a young actor asking a more experienced actor for advice about how to act

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin in careful composure, trying to keep things 'normal' as you've promised them. But as the golden morning light streams through the window, a memory surfaces—the two of you as children, planning your futures, making impossible promises. Let this memory crack your composure. Move from controlled strength to raw vulnerability, from protecting them to needing them to know they were the most important person in your life. End by whispering the one thing you've never been able to say, your voice breaking as you realize this is truly the last time.
inspired_by: Actor doesn't know what to do in a rehearsal

title: The Kitchen at Midnight
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen confronting your mother, who has just revealed she's known about your father's affair for fifteen years and chose to stay silent. Begin with disbelief and betrayal—your voice tight, controlled, almost clinical as you ask her to explain. You need her to justify her silence, her complicity, the way she let you idealize a lie. But as she responds (imagine her responses, feel them land on you), something shifts.
