speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Screaming Silence: The Moment You Stop Fighting for Them
instruction: You've been fighting for this relationship for months - trying, pleading, explaining, hoping. You walk in ready for another round, and this time you're done pretending it doesn't destroy you. Start with your voice rising immediately, unleashing everything you've held back: 'Do you even care that I'm dying inside? Do you even SEE me anymore?' Your voice is raw, almost ragged with rage and desperation. You're saying things you swore you'd never say, every hurt spilling out in a torrent. Then suddenly, mid-sentence, something breaks - not into more anger, but into devastating realization. Your voice drops, becomes hollow. 'Oh god. You don't, do you? You actually don't care.' The fury collapses into something worse than anger - acceptance. By the end, your voice is quiet, almost eerily calm, as you say the words that terrify you: 'I'm done. I'm actually done.' Let yourself explode with volcanic intensity, then fall into the quiet devastation of giving up.
inspired_by: Interviewing Your Parent About Their Mistakes

title: The Bath You Never Drew for Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about a lifetime of emotional absence, using this simple act - drawing a footbath - as your entry point. Begin with bitter precision, describing each action of preparing the water, the temperature, the care involved. Your voice should be controlled, almost clinical, as you detail what nurturing actually looks like - something you had to learn elsewhere. Let the anger build as you realize you're teaching her what she should have taught you. But then let something unexpected happen: as you describe the relief warm water brings, feel your own need for that maternal comfort surface. End with your voice breaking between rage and longing, between the woman you've become and the child still wanting her mother to care.
inspired_by: Soaking Your Feet in Warm Water After a Long Day

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about the emotional abandonment that shaped your entire childhood. Begin measured, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this: 'I need you to hear something I've never been able to say.' But as you describe specific moments—waiting for him at school events, eating dinner in silence, learning to need nothing—your voice hardens with accumulated pain. 'You were there, but you weren't THERE.' The anger peaks, then suddenly breaks into something raw and young: 'I just wanted you to see me. Once. Just once, I wanted you to...' You can't finish. Your breathing is ragged. Then, devastatingly, you shift to quiet acceptance: 'But you can't, can you? You just... can't.' End with your voice small, resigned, grieving not just for yourself but for him, for both of you, for what will never be.

title: The Truth You've Been Hiding
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your childhood. Start with your voice tight and controlled, trying to be reasonable, almost clinical in recounting the memories. But as you speak, the hurt child inside breaks through—your voice cracks, rises, becomes raw with decades of suppressed pain. Demand answers, demand to be seen. Then, as your parent finally, truly hears you, feel your rage fracture into something more complex: grief for the relationship you never had, exhaustion from carrying this weight, and underneath it all, a desperate, aching love that never died. End with your voice stripped bare, vulnerable, asking the simplest, most devastating question: 'Why wasn't I enough?'
inspired_by: The Lost Child and the Mysterious Forest Spirit

title: Burning the Manuscript
instruction: You're a writer standing over a fire, about to destroy your life's work—a manuscript no one wanted to publish, that consumed forty years of your life. Begin with manic, defiant energy, voice sharp and bitter: 'They said it wasn't commercial. Wasn't relevant. Wasn't enough.' Your hands shake as you hold pages over flames. But as you start to burn them, rage explodes—'This was my LIFE!'—voice cracking with fury and anguish. Physically tear pages, let your breathing become ragged, almost violent. Then suddenly, collapse into helpless sobbing: 'What was it all for?' The question should gut you. In the silence, find a strange, wild liberation. Your final words come out laughing through tears, voice hoarse but somehow free: 'Forty years. And maybe... maybe that was enough. Maybe I was enough.' End with a breath that sounds like both grief and release, watching the ashes rise.

title: The Old House
instruction: You are an elderly person at a family gathering, a bit tipsy after a couple of drinks. You're talking to a younger relative about your decision to sell the old family home. At first, you're loud and cheerful, almost bragging about how right it felt. But as you speak, a flicker of doubt creeps in—your voice softens, you pause to take a sip from your glass, and you start trailing off as you realize you might miss the creaky stairs and the garden you planted years ago. Let the alcohol loosen your inhibitions at the start, then let the vulnerability break through, ending in quiet, uncertain stillness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Rival’s Rise
instruction: You're on a wooden crate in a noisy square, voice strained as you try to be heard over traffic and chatter. You spot your rival across the crowd—he’s just been praised, and jealousy flares. Start with astonishment: you stammer, pitch rising as you point, eyes wide. Then envy takes over, your words loop, tone cracking with bitter confusion. Let the scene distract you—glance away, lose a thought, then find it with sharper edge. End with a raw, confused resentment seeping through your strained projection.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Confusion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Perfect Post
instruction: You're curled up on the sofa, scrolling through your phone, your voice directed downward as your thumb taps and pauses. You see a photo of someone you quietly envy—she's successful, radiant, everything you feel you'll never be. Start with a helpless, worn-out murmur, letting out small sighs and distracted fillers like 'uh' as you stare. Then, as you linger on the image, a thin, bitter idea forms. Let your voice drop even lower, but now with a chilling steadiness—a hint of malice that turns the helplessness into quiet, deliberate cruelty.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Thanking Someone Who Destroyed You
instruction: You're facing someone who deeply hurt you - a betraying friend, an ex who left you shattered, a mentor who exploited you - and you're genuinely thanking them because that pain changed you into someone stronger, wiser, more authentic. Begin with real gratitude, almost playful, perhaps even laughing at the absurdity of thanking them. But let tears come simultaneously - not because you're sad now, but because you're remembering how much it cost you. Your voice should dance between joy and grief, sometimes mid-sentence. As you continue, find moments of peace describing who you've become, then let the anger surface briefly - you're grateful AND you're furious, both at once. End in a strange place of genuine forgiveness mixed with an ache that never quite left, speaking with clarity and self-possession while your voice remains thick with unshed tears. Let contradictory emotions coexist naturally, authentically, showing the beautiful complexity of real human experience.

title: The Bittersweet Toast
instruction: You are giving a toast at your best friend's wedding—the person you've been in love with for ten years. Begin with joy that is genuine; you truly want them to be happy. Speak with warmth, humor, celebration. But as you continue, let the grief underneath start bleeding through. Your voice begins to catch. You're trying to stay in the joy, but the loss keeps surfacing. Let these contradictory emotions collide—laugh while tears threaten, smile while your voice breaks. By the end, you can no longer separate the love from the pain, the happiness from the heartbreak. Finish with a genuine blessing that holds both emotions equally, completely exposed in your conflicted truth.

title: The Birthday Party That Won't End
instruction: You are a woman with a deliberately sweet, high-pitched voice, stuck at a child's birthday party surrounded by strangers. You've been making polite small talk for an hour, and now you're watching your own child play with a toy, half-listening to another parent drone on about their vacation. Start with a forced, amused chirp in your voice as you respond to them, but let your attention drift—pause mid-sentence as you notice your child squabbling, let out a too-loud, awkward laugh at nothing, then sigh heavily. By the end, your voice should tighten with a clear, irritated impatience as you scan for the exit, not even hiding your desire to leave.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (slightly present), Contemplation (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Protective Rage of the Helpless
instruction: Your child, sibling, or someone you'd die for has been hurt, and you couldn't stop it. Start with explosive fury—voice shaking with adrenaline, words tumbling out harsh and fast, ready to destroy whoever is responsible. You're pacing, hands trembling, voice rising to a shout. But then the rage cracks and underneath is terror—let your voice break mid-sentence as you realize how close you came to losing them. The anger turns inward: you should have known, should have been there, should have protected them. Your fierce declarations of what you'll do collapse into shaking admissions of your own powerlessness. Let sobs interrupt your words, then fight back to speaking through tears. By the end, channel everything into fierce, almost desperate tenderness as you promise things you may not be able to guarantee, your voice raw and stripped bare, oscillating between protective fury and the helpless love of someone who would take their pain if they could.

title: Medical Director Policy
instruction: You're announcing the new hospital policy via video message: no-code protocols for terminal patients have been revised. You're reading from a script about compassionate care and resource allocation. Your voice is steady, measured, bureaucratic. Then you pause. You realize the policy is partially designed to save money. You pause again, longer this time. You can hear it in the room. Do you continue reading, or do you break character and acknowledge what you're actually implementing? Your voice should show someone trying to execute a role they intellectually understand but morally despise. End it anyway, because your job depends on it.

title: Whispering the Truth You Can Never Take Back
instruction: Late at night, in bed next to someone sleeping, you're confessing something out loud for the first time—not to wake them, but because you need to hear yourself say it. Start so quietly you're almost mouthing the words. 'I need to tell you something, even though you can't hear me.' Your voice is tender, careful, as if the words themselves are fragile. As you continue, the truth becomes heavier. There's relief in finally saying it, but that relief is threaded with profound sadness because you know everything changes after this. Let long pauses hold the weight. End with your voice catching on the edge of tears, whispering 'I'm so sorry' or 'I love you' in a way that contains both goodbye and gratitude.
inspired_by: Recounting Trauma to a Stranger Therapist

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he was never proud of you, but this time you're not asking—you're telling him what his silence did. Begin with controlled anger, reciting your accomplishments like evidence in a trial: graduated top of your class, built a good life, became everything you thought he wanted. Your voice sharpens. But mid-accusation, something cracks—you realize you're still performing for his approval even now, even in this moment of confrontation. The anger dissolves into something more painful: the recognition that you've spent forty years chasing a ghost. End by asking, in a voice stripped of all pretense, 'Was I ever enough?' The question should hang there, naked and childlike.

title: Laughing Through Your Divorce Papers
instruction: You're signing your divorce papers and suddenly start laughing—really laughing—at the absurdity of reducing fifteen years to legal language. 'Irreconcilable differences... God, remember when we couldn't reconcile whether to get a dog?' Your laughter is genuine but tears are streaming down your face. You read clauses aloud, finding dark humor: 'Party A and Party B... we used to be honey and sweetheart.' The laughter cracks into crying, then back to laughing at yourself for crying. You're feeling it all at once—gratitude for what you had, grief for what you lost, relief it's over, terror of starting again. 'We were so good once...' (your voice breaks with tenderness) '...weren't we?' Keep oscillating between joy at memories and devastation that they're only memories now. End with a strange, peaceful exhaustion, signing your name while crying-laughing: 'Thank you for the years we didn't waste—we loved each other the best we could.' Your final breath is both liberation and loss.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father/mother about a family secret that's been buried for decades—something about your origin, their past, or a sibling you never knew existed. Start from a place of rehearsed anger, words you've practiced saying, a speech you've prepared about betrayal and lies. But as they begin to answer, let their vulnerability crack open something in you. Feel your righteous fury collide with the shocking realization that they were just as scared and lost as you are now. Let your voice break and rebuild itself multiple times. End in an unexpected place: not forgiveness exactly, but a devastated recognition that they did their inadequate best, and now you must choose whether to repeat their silence or break it.
inspired_by: Actor feels inadequate to meet a specific character or scene obligation

title: Gratitude at the Breaking Point
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who saved your life but cannot stay—a mentor who's dying, a therapist at your final session, a friend who loved you through your darkest time but must move on. Your voice starts gentle, almost like that morning softness: 'Thank you for everything.' But as you list what they've given you—seeing your worth, teaching you to survive, loving you when you couldn't love yourself—your voice begins breaking with the grief of losing them. You're laughing through tears at shared memories, voice cracking with joy and devastation intertwined. By the end, you're smiling while sobbing, voice barely coherent, saying 'I'm going to be okay' even as your heart shatters, finding profound peace and unbearable loss in the same breath.

title: The Last Breath Before Dawn
instruction: You're lying in a hospital bed in the pre-dawn darkness, and you know this is your final hour. Begin by speaking to someone you love who isn't there—maybe they're on their way, maybe they'll never make it in time. Start with terror, with the raw panic of not being ready to let go. Feel your breathing become shallow, feel the cold creeping into your fingers. But as you speak, as you say the things you need to say, let something shift. Let the fear gradually transform into a strange, unexpected peace—not resignation, but a profound acceptance mixed with wonder at the life you've lived. End in a place of quiet gratitude, your voice barely a whisper, as if you're already half-dissolved into something larger than yourself.

title: The Unexpected Gift
instruction: You're an elderly woman at a casual gathering with strangers—your grandchild's new friends. You feel awkward, out of place, with uncomfortable silences and nervous little laughs. Then one of them hands you a small, handmade gift: a knitted coaster with a crooked smiley face. It's so imperfect it's hilarious, and you're genuinely touched. Let your voice start tight and hesitant, full of filler words and forced chuckles. As you speak your thanks, let real amusement bubble up—a warm, surprised laugh that turns the gratitude into giddy appreciation. Notice the coaster in your hands, fumble with it, let the words come out in bits as you react naturally. End with a sincere, laughing 'thank you' that fills the room.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Unspoken Inheritance: Confronting a Dying Parent
instruction: You're at your father's bedside in his final days, and decades of withheld affection sit between you like a wall. Begin with careful distance, almost clinical: 'The nurse says you're comfortable.' But something in his eyes—a reaching—makes you suddenly brave. Your voice hardens with long-buried pain: 'Did you ever actually love me, or was I just another responsibility?' His silence is answer enough, and your voice cracks with rage and grief. But then he does something small—reaches for your hand, or says your name in a way he never has—and everything shifts. You have a choice: to stay hardened or to soften. Your voice becomes a whisper, flooded with forgiveness you didn't know you had: 'I needed you to say it. Just once.' Whether he can or not, you realize you're releasing both of you. Let your final words—'I love you anyway'—carry the weight of a lifetime of longing finally laid to rest.
inspired_by: Parent Showing Quiet Pride: Misreading, Then Understanding

title: Curb Aftermath
instruction: You are sitting on a curb, your hands trembling so hard that the phone in your lap keeps slipping. You just T-boned a sedan after running a red light. No one is seriously hurt, but you're in shock. Your voice is shaky, breathless—astonishment that you're alive, shame burning through you as you realize it was your fault. Start with rapid, repetitive disbelief ('I don't... I don't understand how...'), then let it collapse into a quieter, tearful confession ('I should have seen the light. I just... I didn't stop.'). Let your hands shake as you try to hold the phone, and let there be a sudden break—a choked sob or a shaky laugh—without warning.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're helping your younger sibling pack up their childhood bedroom as they prepare to move across the world. Start by bossily organizing their stuff, making jokes about their old embarrassing phases, slipping into that familiar patronizing rhythm. But as you pack, you keep finding small artifacts - a note they wrote you when they were six, a photo of you teaching them to ride a bike, their old nightlight that they needed when they had nightmares. You find yourself laughing at memories while tears stream down your face. Your voice should dance between teasing mockery and tender devastation, between celebrating their adventure and grieving the loss of the child you raised as much as your parents did. Express genuine excitement for their courage to leave - you're so proud they're braver than you ever were - while your hands shake holding their belongings. End with a moment of bittersweet peace: thanking them, voice warm with gratitude and thick with sorrow, for letting you love them the only way you knew how, even if it was too much. Let joy and grief live together in every word.

title: Telling My Mother She Failed Me
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother in her kitchen, finally confronting the silence that shaped your childhood. Begin with careful, measured words—trying so hard to be kind: 'Mom, I need to tell you something I've never been able to say.' But as you speak, the floodgates open: 'You were there, but you weren't there. Do you understand? I needed you to fight for me.' Your voice rises, not with volume but with urgency and pain. Then catch yourself, soften, because you see her face and realize she was doing her broken best: 'I know you were hurting too. But I was your child.' End with exhausted tenderness mixed with unresolved ache: 'I love you. And I'm so angry at you. And I don't know how to hold both.' Let the contradictions live in your voice.

title: The Truth I've Carried - Confronting a Parent
instruction: You're finally telling your parent something you've held inside for decades - how their absence shaped you, how their choices left wounds that never healed. Start with your voice controlled, almost too calm, as you've rehearsed this. 'I need you to hear something I've never said.' As you speak, anger begins to crack through - not shouting, but fierce, direct truth-telling. Your voice shakes with the effort of staying measured. Then something shifts: beneath the anger, you hear your own childhood self, still wanting their love, still hoping. End with your voice stripped bare, vulnerable, asking the question you've always been afraid to ask: 'Did you ever really see me?' Let the silence after carry both your rage and your longing.
inspired_by: Telling Someone You're Attracted to Them

title: Pillow Talk for the Weary
instruction: You're lying face-down on your bed, cheek pressed deep into a soft pillow. After a long, draining day of small humiliations, you've finally let yourself collapse. At first your voice is thick with muffled exhaustion — words swallowed by fabric, breath ragged against the cotton. But as you whisper to yourself, you notice the warmth of the pillow, the quiet of the room, and a faint hope stirs. By the end, your tone softens into a drowsy contentment, almost smiling into the cushion. Let your voice start raw and heavy, then lighten gradually — micro‑pauses, small shifts of your head, a sigh that turns into a gentle laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Finding Your Late Parent's Love Letters Proving They Were Happy Once
instruction: You've just discovered letters that reveal your parent—who spent your whole childhood miserable, angry, broken—was once joyful and in love. Start reading them aloud with bitter, incredulous laughter. Your voice is sharp with betrayal: 'You were CAPABLE of this?' The laughter is real but cruel, mocking. As you continue reading their beautiful, hopeful words, the laughter starts catching in your throat. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice fracturing between joy at discovering they once felt wonder, and grief that this person disappeared before you ever met them. By the end, you're still almost laughing through tears, reading their tender words with a voice full of gratitude and devastating loss, finding strange peace in knowing they were once whole, even though you never got to know that version of them.
inspired_by: Stand-up About Your Own Sexual Assault

title: Reading Your Spouse's Suicide Note and Laughing Through Devastation
instruction: You've found the note. Your spouse of twenty years, your best friend, is gone by their own choice, and you're reading their final words. They wrote it like they talked—with that self-deprecating humor, those inside jokes only you two shared, that particular way they had of making terrible things seem bearable. And God help you, you're laughing. Actually laughing at a joke they made about finally getting out of doing the dishes. Your voice reads their words aloud and laughter bubbles up, inappropriate and real. But then a line hits different—something tender, an apology, a confession of how much they loved you but couldn't stay. Your laughter cracks into sobbing. Then you find another memory, another joke, and you're laughing again through tears. Your voice oscillates between joy at remembering who they were and devastation that they're gone. By the end, you're speaking directly to them, your voice holding gratitude for every year, fury that they left, and a strange, broken peace that they're finally free from pain. Your voice says 'I'm so angry at you' but it sounds like 'I understand.' Say 'goodbye' like it means both 'I'll never forgive you' and 'I love you enough to let you go.'
inspired_by: Historical: Resistance Fighter Betrays a Comrade to Save Themselves

title: Reading Your Father's Eulogy You Wrote Years Ago
instruction: Your father is alive, sitting across from you. You're reading aloud the eulogy you wrote when you thought he was dying five years ago but never delivered. Begin with 'I wrote this when I thought I'd lost you,' voice thick with the memory of that grief. As you read, laugh through tears at the funny memories, smile at his quirks, but keep fracturing on the parts about what he meant to you. Let gratitude and grief tangle together—thanking him for being here while mourning the time you almost lost. Your voice should dance between joy at his presence and the shadow of that near-loss. End with your voice breaking on 'I'm not ready,' whether you mean not ready for that future loss or not ready to have needed to write this at all.
inspired_by: Someone Realizing You're Crying Without Sound

title: Anger's Unsteady Rhythm
instruction: You're in your home gym, doing box jumps after a tense phone call with your boss. Each jump is a violent exhalation — 'hup!' — and you land with a thud that jars your ribs. Start with pure anger: frustrated, growling between breaths, the words hacked out mid-air. As you progress, your body's rhythm takes over; you feel a flicker of gratitude for the release, for the simple fact that you can still move. Let that soften your voice slightly on landings, but the anger never fully dissolves — it just gets buried under effort. Speak fragmented lines like 'Worthless... that call... jump!' and let the physical strain crack your tone. By the last jump, you're exhausted but calmer, muttering 'Thanks... for this... anyway.'
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispered Unraveling
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone you love, whispering a confession that begins as a single secret. Keep your voice quiet, intimate, barely audible—but let the confession start to spiral. One secret leads to another, then to a random memory, then back to something deeper, then to what you noticed about their breathing, then to a childhood fear, then to how the sheets feel, then to another truth, faster, still whispered, your thoughts fragmenting and cascading even as your voice stays soft. The speed and disconnection grow while the volume stays tender and low. By the end, you're whispering a rapid, unpredictable stream of vulnerable fragments—some profound, some mundane, all true—no longer sure what you're confessing or why, just needing them to know everything at once.

title: Laughing Through the Ruins
instruction: You're clearing out your childhood home after your last living parent's death, and you've just found the box of letters they wrote but never sent—letters apologizing, explaining, loving you in ways they never could face-to-face. Start reading one aloud, your voice caught between laughter and tears: 'Listen to this—they wrote, I'm sorry I didn't know how to tell you I was proud.' You're almost giggling through your crying, the absurdity and tragedy mixing. 'Thirty years of therapy, and they were writing letters the whole time.' Your voice breaks with both humor and heartbreak: 'They were so scared of getting it wrong that they never... they just never...' The laughter dissolves into heavier crying, but then surges back—bitter, loving, grateful, furious all at once. 'I would have taken the mess. I would have taken fumbling and awkward. I just wanted them.' End with your voice soft, almost serene despite the tears: 'But they loved me. They did. And I have proof now.' You're crying and smiling simultaneously, holding the letters like sacred objects. The arc weaves between grief and relief, anger and gratitude, loss and unexpected peace.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your elderly parent who is finally willing to listen after decades of emotional absence. Start controlled and measured, trying to be respectful, but let decades of unspoken pain begin to surface. Your voice should tremble with the weight of a childhood spent feeling invisible. Build into accusations about missed recitals, forgotten birthdays, the loneliness of growing up with a parent who was physically present but emotionally gone. Then they say something—maybe just 'I know' or 'I'm sorry'—and your anger collapses into something more complicated. Let your voice break as you realize they were struggling too, that they failed you but also loved you in their broken way. End with a raw, vulnerable plea: not for the past to change, but for whatever time remains to be different.

title: Whispering in the Dark Hospital Room
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply who's asleep (or pretending to sleep) in a hospital bed at 3am. You believe they can't hear you. Begin by simply watching them breathe, perhaps touching their hand gently. Start speaking in barely audible whispers—maybe mundane things, gentle observations, small confessions. But as you continue, let the darkness and quiet and their stillness draw deeper truths from you. Speak the tender things you could never say to their face. Apologize for something specific. Tell them what they mean to you in concrete, particular terms. Let your voice stay quiet but fill with suppressed emotion—not dramatic, but achingly real. By the end, you should be confessing something that terrifies you, still in a whisper, tears possibly streaming silently. The vulnerability must deepen gradually from safe observations to unbearable intimacy.

title: The Wager's End
instruction: You are a young boy, oddly deep-voiced, who has just forced yourself to eat a whole jar of pickled herring to win a cruel bet. You are now heaving over a trash can in the schoolyard. Start with a low, spiteful chuckle as you recall the look on your friend's face when you accepted the dare – pure malice in your voice. As the nausea hits, your words become thick and garbled, interrupted by retches, but your triumph grows. End with a wet, gurgly laugh of victory, spitting out the last of the brine, proud that you proved everyone wrong, even as your stomach twists.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Ground
instruction: You're a parent whose teenage child just said they're leaving and never coming back, blaming you for everything wrong in their life. Start with defensive anger—voice raised, listing everything you sacrificed, every way you tried. Your words are sharp, self-justifying, hurt masquerading as rage. But as they turn to leave, something breaks in you. Your voice cracks mid-sentence, anger collapsing into desperate, fierce love. You grab their arm—not hard, but urgent—and your voice transforms into raw, unguarded terror: 'Don't you understand? You're my child. If something happened to you, I would die.' Your fierce protectiveness wars with your complete helplessness as you realize you can't make them stay. End with your voice dropping to a broken whisper, still holding their arm, saying 'The door is always open. Please. Please be safe.' The 'please' is barely sound, just breath and breaking.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're watching someone you loved marry someone else. You're supposed to be happy for them—and part of you genuinely is. You're about to give a toast. Begin with the practiced smile, the congratulatory words you rehearsed. But as you speak, let the competing truths coexist: real affection for their happiness, real grief for what you've lost, real hope for their future, real anger at being left behind. Don't choose one emotion—let them all be present and in conflict. Your voice might crack with joy that's also devastation. You might laugh and feel tears at the same time. By the end, you should have moved through multiple emotional territories without resolving them into something simple. Let the contradiction be the truth of this moment.
inspired_by: An actor has difficulty trusting their impulses enough to make the first committed expression

title: Whispering the Language of Before to Someone Who No Longer Remembers
instruction: You're visiting your spouse who has advanced dementia. You whisper the private phrases, the bedroom words, the silly sounds that were yours alone - trying to find them inside the stranger they've become. Start with hopeful tenderness, voice catching on each familiar word. When their eyes briefly clear and they try to repeat something back - getting it wrong but trying - let yourself break just a little, smiling through gathering tears. End in the devastating quiet of them forgetting again mid-phrase, and you completing their sentence for them in a whisper so soft it's almost just breath, holding both the memory of who they were and the grief of who they are now.
inspired_by: Whispering Sweet Nothings in a Language You Don't Speak

title: The Velvet Trap
instruction: You are an elderly woman, your voice naturally soft but now deliberately smoothed into a practiced charm. You're sitting across from a former lover, someone you haven't seen in decades. Your interest in them is genuine, almost desperate — but you also feel a crushing helplessness, knowing your age and body betray your intentions. Speak to them, trying to rekindle an old flame while your hands tremble slightly on the table, your voice cracking once before you regain control. Start with a low, playful tone, a calculated compliment that hangs in the air, but let the helplessness creep in at the end as you realize you can't undo time. Let your laugh come a beat too late, and your final words trail off into a quiet, shaky truth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bathroom Floor Confession
instruction: You're a young woman with a high, sweet voice, now wrecked by a stomach bug. You're lying on the cold bathroom tiles, your partner kneeling beside you, holding your hair back. You start by teasing them for being too gentle with the bowl—voice thin, watery, interrupted by a small heave. Mid-sentence, a real wave of nausea hits; you pause, gag, spit, then whisper a confession of love through the pain, your voice thick with mucus and sudden tenderness. Let the laughter fade into strained vulnerability; let the retching sound and gasps be part of the speech.
emotions_sampled: Pain (clearly present), Affection (slightly present), Teasing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Admitting Weakness
instruction: You're admitting something you've been hiding—that you're not as strong as people think. Your voice is hesitant: 'I'm not okay.' The admission is terrifying. Your voice becomes desperate, honest: 'I'm struggling. I'm falling apart.' You're showing the cracks in the façade. Your voice becomes smaller, more real. You're admitting fears, sadness, desperation. By the end, your voice is lighter despite the darkness—because you're finally being honest. Weakness becomes strength through vulnerability.

title: The Alzheimer's Miracle Hour
instruction: Your parent with advanced Alzheimer's suddenly recognizes you after months of confusion. You have maybe an hour before they slip away again. You're laughing and crying simultaneously—overjoyed they remember you but heartbroken knowing it's temporary. Rapid-fire through shared memories, inside jokes, asking questions you've been saving. Your voice should oscillate between giddy joy and choked tears, celebrating this gift while mourning its brevity. Tell them you forgive them for not remembering, that you'll hold the memories for both of you. Include: 'I've missed you so much. You're right here and I already miss you.' End with peaceful acceptance mixed with grief, thanking them for this moment while preparing to lose them again. Let gratitude and sorrow be completely inseparable.

title: The Wrong Side of the Door
instruction: You're standing outside your childhood home. Your sister just had her first baby, and everyone's inside celebrating—but you've been estranged from the family for five years after a bitter falling out. You came to reconcile, but now you're frozen on the porch, hand raised to knock. Start with bitter, self-protective sarcasm—mocking yourself for even coming, rehearsing cutting remarks to defend yourself if they reject you. But as you stand there, hearing the celebration inside, laughter, a baby crying, your voice should begin to break with longing. Let fierce pride battle with desperate need. End with your hand finally touching the door, voice stripped of all defenses, barely able to speak as you whisper: 'I want to meet her. I want to come home.' Move from armored cynicism to naked, terrified hope.

title: Last Relay Before Dawn
instruction: You're a lone scout stranded on a ridge after a storm. Your radio crackles with narrow, compressed audio. You press the push-to-talk button, feeling the familiar kkhht. Start with heavy exhaustion dragging every word — your voice is flat, weary, but you force yourself to report because you must. As you describe the all-clear, a surge of pride cuts through the fear: you survived. End with a trembling mix of relief and lingering dread, the fear still coiled in your chest. Speak in short bursts, let the PTT button interrupt your thoughts, and let the transmission end with a final, shaky 'Over.'
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Finding Joy in the Hospice Room
instruction: You're sitting with someone you love in their final days, and they've just said something absurdly funny, or you're remembering a ridiculous shared memory. Start with genuine laughter—real, surprised, spontaneous joy that momentarily makes you forget where you are. But let that laughter begin to mix with tears, your voice breaking between chuckles and sobs. You're grateful—so deeply grateful—for this person, for this moment, for every second you've had together. Express that overwhelming thankfulness even as your heart is shattering because you're losing them. End in a place of profound peace mixed with unbearable grief, your voice soft and wondering, as if you've just understood something beautiful and terrible about love at the same time.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Bottle
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent twenty years later. They're sober now, proud of their sobriety. But you're not here to celebrate. Start with controlled anger, voice measured and cold, listing the birthdays they missed, the promises they broke. As you speak, the anger cracks open into something rawer—the child's voice underneath, the one who waited by the window. Your voice becomes younger, more vulnerable, asking the question you've carried for decades: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stop?' Let the rage dissolve into grief, then rebuild into something harder: the adult claiming their pain, refusing to minimize it, demanding to be seen. End with exhausted clarity, knowing they can never give you back what you lost.
inspired_by: Recovery: Choosing Yourself Over the Addiction

title: Touching the Scar
instruction: In the intimate darkness of a bedroom, your new lover asks about the scar on your body—the one you never talk about. Begin in a place of protective deflection, your voice light and dismissive. But they're gently tracing it with their fingertips, and you can feel the exact path of their touch, the warmth of their breath close to your skin, the weight of their body beside yours. Start to notice everything: the texture of the sheets, the particular quality of shadow and dim light, the smell of their skin, the sound of night outside the window. These sensory details slowly dismantle your defenses. As you finally begin to whisper the real story—the trauma, the pain, the shame you've carried—let the tenderness of this moment and the precise physical sensations around you give you permission to be fragile. End in a place of profound vulnerability, your voice barely audible, but your body finally relaxed into trust.

title: The Kitchen Floor Confession
instruction: You are confronting your mother in the kitchen where you've had a thousand silent meals together. You begin by trying to explain a major decision you've made about your life—something final and irreversible—but she keeps interrupting with trivial concerns, recipes, what the neighbors will think. You've spent your whole life being defined by something beyond your control (a condition, a limitation, a label she placed on you), and she's never once asked what YOU wanted. Start restrained, trying to be reasonable, explaining calmly. But as she dismisses you again and again, your rage builds—not screaming rage, but the kind that makes your whole body shake, your voice crack with decades of unspoken truth. Confront her with every moment she made you invisible, every time she spoke for you, every time she reduced you to your condition. Transform from the obedient, invisible child into someone who demands to be seen as whole. End exhausted, quieter, but finally, terrifyingly free.

title: Laughing at Your Beloved's Funeral Reception
instruction: You're at the reception after burying someone who meant everything to you, and someone just told a story about them that's genuinely funny—something ridiculous they did, quintessentially them. Your voice starts laughing, really laughing, because it's so perfectly them and you can't help it. The laughter is real and full and for a moment you're just joyful remembering them. But then mid-laugh, you feel it—the fact that they're gone. Your voice catches, the laughter turning into something else, but you keep trying to laugh because the story deserves it. Now you're laughing and crying at once, your voice doing both, unable to separate joy from grief. 'God, they were so ridiculous,' you say, your voice bright with love and broken with loss. You're smiling through tears, your voice expressing gratitude for having known them while simultaneously shattering at their absence. End with your voice full of contradictions—celebrating their life while drowning in their death, finding the beauty and the devastation are the same thing. 'I'm so grateful I knew you. I'm so grateful. And I'm so broken you're gone.'
inspired_by: Hit Rock Bottom: Finding the Learning

title: The Bittersweet Triumph
instruction: You just received the news you've been waiting years for—the dream job, the acceptance letter, the victory. You're calling your best friend to share it, but they're the one person who won't be there to see you live this new life, because you're moving far away or your paths are diverging forever. Begin with pure, explosive joy—let yourself be thrilled, childlike, unguarded in your excitement. But as you speak, let the bittersweetness seep in. Your celebration becomes tangled with grief. You're laughing and crying, grateful and devastated, proud and terrified, wanting them to be happy for you while knowing this changes everything. Don't resolve it into one clean emotion—stay in the contradictions. Let your voice carry both the lightness of joy and the weight of loss, sometimes in the same breath. This is what real moments feel like—too many true things at once, impossible to sort out, beautiful and breaking your heart simultaneously.

title: Trust Breaking
instruction: They lied. Or they lied, and you know it now, and you're realizing that everything you believed was misread. Your voice changes mid-conversation when the truth lands: from warm to cold. Breath catching. 'Wait. You didn't... did you?' The realization vocal: sharp, small. Then your voice gets harder, protective. The way you say their name changes, becomes distance. 'I trusted you.' Breathing becomes controlled, a wall. Your vocal tone shifts from intimate to formal. By the end, you sound like you're talking to a stranger who happens to share a name.

title: The Crest Between Us
instruction: You are a young man in a hospital birth room, standing beside your partner as she endures labor. Your voice is naturally medium-pitched but now shakes with adrenaline. Between contractions, you try to speak gently, telling her she's doing great — but the moment a wave hits, your words collapse into groans and sharp exhales, as if you're feeling her pain yourself. Your affection is real and overwhelming, but under it churns a deep confusion: you're scared, you don't know what to say, and every time she grips your hand you forget your own name. Start with a steady, loving murmur — then let the next contraction rip through you, turning your comfort into fragmented noises, and end in a raw, whispered confession of love as she breathes again.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protecting Your Child from a Danger You Cannot Stop
instruction: You're holding them, and the threat is coming—something you're powerless against. Begin with fierce, almost violent reassurance: 'I won't let anything happen to you,' your voice full of protective fury. But as reality crashes in, that certainty fractures. Your voice grows desperate, your promises turning into pleas to a universe that doesn't listen. The rage at your own helplessness explodes—raw, primal sound—then collapses into broken sobbing. End with tender words whispered into their hair, love declarations that are also apologies, your voice simultaneously the strongest and most shattered it's ever been.
inspired_by: Listening to Your Child Say They Want to Leave

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know these are her final hours. Begin in a state of numb exhaustion—you've been awake all night, emotionally shut down to protect yourself. As she starts speaking about her life, her love for you, and what she wants you to remember, allow yourself to truly arrive in this moment. Let your walls come down. Move from protective numbness to complete openness—let the grief, the love, the gratitude, and the unbearable tenderness of saying goodbye wash over you. Your voice should transform from flat and distant to trembling with raw presence. By the end, you're fully there with her, no longer protecting yourself from the pain.

title: Breaking Point Ecstasy
instruction: You are alone, your body wracked with pain—perhaps from illness, injury, or intense physical exertion. Begin by fighting it, trying to maintain control and dignity, keeping your voice steady and your body rigid. But there's a part of you that has always been forbidden to surrender, to completely let go, to be helpless and uncontrolled. As the physical sensation intensifies, allow that suppressed part—the one that wants to scream, thrash, weep, or laugh hysterically—to take over. This might be the victim you've never let yourself be, or the wild, uncontained force you've always kept locked down. Let your voice crack, your body move in ways you normally wouldn't allow. By the end, you've surrendered completely to the sensation, and in that surrender, there's an unexpected liberation, even ecstasy in the loss of control. The arc moves from rigid resistance to complete, almost transcendent surrender.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access a personality facet (aggression, sexuality, fear, moralism, free spirit, victimhood) that is suppressed or disowned

title: Mile Twenty-Two
instruction: You're a 16-year-old on a group hike, and for the last hour you've been struggling to keep up. Now you've stopped, doubled over, and your legs won't move. Your voice comes out thin and breathy, like you're talking through a fog. You're ashamed—you hate that everyone has to wait for you, hate the pity in their eyes. You try to apologize but the words jumble, and you feel completely helpless as your knees buckle. But then a friend hands you her water bottle and kneels beside you, and for a second you let yourself just sit there. The shame and panic don't go away, but there's also a tiny, unexpected calm in this pause. Speak as if every word costs you effort—slurred, trailing off, with long pauses to suck air. You might sound angry at yourself at first, then softer, almost content, as you admit you need a minute.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Helplessness (extremely present), Contentment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Truth
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table about something he did when you were twelve that damaged you deeply—but he's never acknowledged it. Begin with rehearsed anger, the speech you've prepared in your head for years. But as you speak, let yourself get thrown off by his face, by unexpected details in the room, by memories flooding in at the wrong moments. Lose your place. Start sentences you can't finish. Maybe you suddenly feel like a child again mid-accusation, or find tenderness creeping in when you wanted only rage. Let contradictions happen—laugh bitterly, then feel your voice soften without meaning to. By the end, you're no longer delivering a speech but genuinely discovering, in real time, what you actually feel toward this person sitting across from you. It's messier and more complicated than you thought.

title: The Final Blow
instruction: You're hunched over your computer, controller gripped tight after hours of failing the same boss battle. Start with clenched teeth, muttered curses under your breath—your voice tight with frustration, punctuated by rapid clicks and a squeak from your chair as you shift weight. Then the boss goes down. Let the words burst out louder than you expected—a relieved yell that cracks into a shaky laugh. As the adrenaline fades, your voice softens, trembling with exhaustion and relief. Pause to wipe your forehead, hear your own breathing, feel the tension drain from your shoulders. End on a quiet, shaken exhale.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Surge and the Crash
instruction: You are a teenage girl in a school bathroom, coming down off caffeine pills you took to study. At first your voice is unnaturally bright and fast, pitch jumping as you try to convince yourself you're fine, that you can handle it. But as you catch your reflection and see the trembling, the shame hits like a wave, slowing your words, making them crack and drop into a raw whisper. You start with a forced, hyper-feminized cheer—'See? I'm totally focused'—and end with a hollow, broken admission: 'I hate what I did... I hate that I needed this.' Let the adrenaline jitter through your tone, then let the shame steal your breath and sink your pitch. Speak about 50-70 words total, with natural pauses, a shaky inhale, and a final silence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Holding Your Dying Dog, Rage at the Universe
instruction: You're on the veterinary clinic floor, cradling your dog in your final moments together. Begin with fierce, protective tenderness: 'I've got you, baby. I'm right here.' But as you feel them slipping away, rage explodes through your grief. Your voice becomes guttural, almost violent: 'This isn't fair! Thirteen years isn't enough! It's not ENOUGH!' You're shouting at God, at fate, at the cruelty of finite love. 'You gave me something perfect just to rip it away!' Your voice breaks into raw sobs, then softens into desperate bargaining: 'Please. Please, I'll do anything.' As you feel the last breaths, your fury collapses completely into the most tender goodbye, voice destroyed by crying: 'Thank you. Thank you for choosing me. Thank you for every single day.' End with a howl of pure grief that transforms mid-sound into something almost like gratitude, your voice barely human, touching something primal about love and loss.
inspired_by: Sensory Deprivation Tank: Time Becoming Meaningless

title: Whispering Why You Can't Save Them
instruction: Someone you love desperately is begging you to help them escape something—an addiction, a dangerous situation, a self-destructive path. You speak barely above a whisper, throat tight with unshed tears: 'I can't do this anymore.' Each sentence costs you everything. Your voice trembles as you explain how saving them has been drowning you: 'I gave you my savings. I lied to everyone I know. I've stopped sleeping.' The confession catches in your throat: 'I'm losing myself trying to find you.' They plead and you have to stay firm while your heart shatters. End with tender devastation: 'I love you enough to let you fall. I just can't fall with you anymore.' All of this delivered quietly, intimately, like a secret that's killing you to tell.
inspired_by: Listening to Your Partner Admit Infidelity

title: Whispers to a Sleeping Child
instruction: You're sitting beside your daughter's hospital bed after her suicide attempt, whispering so you won't wake her. Start with barely controlled tenderness: 'Baby, you're still here. You're breathing.' Your voice catches on relief mixed with unbearable sadness. 'I didn't know you were hurting this much. I didn't see.' Let guilt strangle your words. Whisper your own confession: 'I've thought about it too. Leaving. When your father died, I almost...' Pause. Breathe. Your voice becomes achingly gentle: 'But you saved me. Just by existing, you saved me.' End with fierce, whispered love: 'So I'm going to save you back. However long it takes. I'm right here.' Let your voice break with gratitude and grief intertwined.

title: Collapse Into Sensation
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—you got the call, the test came back negative, the person you thought you'd lost forever just walked through the door. Begin with your body electrified, almost painfully alert, trembling with adrenaline and disbelief. Your voice is high, fast, breathless. As the reality sinks in, feel the sustained tension of months or years of fear suddenly become impossible to maintain. Your muscles begin to give way—first your knees weaken, then your voice drops and slows, then your whole body starts to feel impossibly heavy with the weight of relief flooding through you. Laugh, cry, or both, but let each sound become more languid, more weighted. End collapsed on the floor or against a wall, your body loose and exhausted, barely able to form words, making sounds that are half-laugh, half-sob, completely surrendered to the physical aftermath of intense emotion.

title: Late Night Detour
instruction: You’re driving home late, the engine humming low, turn signal clicking. You just had an amazing date that surprised you — funny, magnetic, deeply satisfying. As you navigate a winding road, you replay a clever joke they told, and you laugh softly to yourself. But then a memory of their touch, their scent, hits you mid-turn, and your voice slows, drops, turns husky with lust. You’re speaking to yourself, half to the windshield, half to the memory — starting playful, ending in a breathy smile of possessive contentment. Let your voice shift naturally: a quick laugh, a pause to check the rearview, then a slower, warmer tone as longing settles into comfort.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Night You Called Me Home
instruction: You are a man who hasn't slept properly in months. It's 3 AM and your young child has just woken from a nightmare, calling for you. You sit on the edge of their bed, your voice hollow from exhaustion, but you force a gentle, affectionate tone to comfort them. As you speak, you try to soothe them, but your own mind is foggy—you fumble for words, lose a thought, and your voice cracks with the effort of staying present. Start with a quiet, weary reassurance that barely masks your confusion at being awake, and slowly let the affection grow stronger, more clear, as you find a small pocket of warmth in your fatigue. By the end, the exhaustion remains, but your love cuts through it, steady and fierce.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth you've carried for decades. Begin with careful politeness, almost apologetic: 'I need to talk to you about something, and I need you to just listen.' But as you speak, years of unmet need start bleeding through: 'Do you have any idea how many times I tried to show you who I was?' Your voice hardens with hurt that's turning to anger. 'I brought home my art, my stories, my friends, my dreams—and you looked right through me.' The anger cracks open into something more vulnerable: 'I needed you to see me. Just once, I needed you to really see me.' Then rage returns, fierce and protective of your younger self: 'That child deserved better than your distraction!' But you end in a place of devastating clarity, voice quiet but unshakable: 'I'm done waiting for you to wake up. I see myself now. And I'm grieving the parent I needed you to be.'

title: Stripped Bare by Rain
instruction: You're standing in a sudden downpour after a devastating personal failure—fired, rejected, publicly humiliated. Begin in fury: screaming at the sky, punching the air, raging against the injustice. Let the physical sensation of cold rain hammering your skin intensify your anger. But as you exhaust yourself and the rain continues relentlessly, feel something shift. The water isn't punishing you—it's washing you. Your rage begins to dissolve into something rawer: grief, relief, even strange exhilaration at having nothing left to protect. By the end, you're laughing and crying simultaneously, face turned up to the rain, letting it strip away every last defense. Transform from explosive rage to surrendered, almost ecstatic release.

title: The Unsteady Kneel
instruction: You are kneeling on a cold floor, eyes down, trying to hold a perfectly still posture as commanded. Your dominant partner circles you, their footsteps echoing. You concentrate intensely on not trembling, but a small sound from behind startles you, and you realize you've shifted your weight. The distress creeps in as you anticipate correction. Your voice starts as a breathy, controlled murmur of reassurance to yourself, but as the tension mounts, it cracks with rising anxiety and a plea for approval: 'Still... I am still. Yes, Sir? Please—I am still.' Let your breath shorten, your pitch rise, and let the words come with tiny, nervous pauses and swallows.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Transmission from a Failing Spacecraft
instruction: You're an astronaut whose life support is failing, and you're recording a final message to someone you love back on Earth. Begin with controlled professionalism, trying to keep your voice steady as you explain the technical failure, almost clinical in your description. But as you shift to saying goodbye, your voice begins to fracture—start with 'I need you to know...' and let the fear seep through the cracks of your composure. Describe what you see through the window—the beauty of Earth from here, how small and precious it looks—and let wonder mix with devastating loss. Your breathing becomes more labored as oxygen depletes. Move between trying to comfort them ('it doesn't hurt, I promise') and the raw terror of your own extinction. End in a place of unexpected peace, your voice soft and wondering, as if you're discovering something beautiful in the final moments, then one last surge of desperate love: their name, said like a prayer, like you're trying to hold onto it as you let go.
inspired_by: Quicksand Struggle: Fighting the Sinking with Diminishing Strength

title: Telling Your Child You're Leaving and Won't Be Back
instruction: You're sitting with your child for the last time before you leave on a journey you won't return from—military deployment to certain danger, experimental treatment far away, or witness protection that erases your identity. You start with false brightness, trying to make it sound like an adventure, your voice artificially cheerful. But as you look at their face, the pretense crumbles. Your voice becomes raw, desperate to memorize this moment. You try to explain why you have to go without terrifying them, but grief breaks through. End with a whisper where you finally tell them the truth you've been avoiding—that you're scared, that leaving them is killing you, that you wish there was another way. Let your voice crack on the words you never wanted to say.
inspired_by: Rejecting Someone Sexually and Trying to Be Kind

title: Holding Your Child After They've Been Hurt
instruction: You're holding your child who's just been through something terrible—an assault, a violent incident, something that stole their innocence—and you're consumed by rage and helplessness. You begin fierce, almost violent in your protectiveness: 'I will destroy anyone who touches you. I will burn the world down.' Your voice is shaking with fury, making promises you can't keep. But then you feel them trembling in your arms, and everything changes. The rage collapses into something more devastating: your own powerlessness. Your voice breaks: 'I couldn't stop it. I was supposed to protect you, and I couldn't stop it.' You're apologizing now, rocking them, your words becoming fragmented: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' The explosive emotion dissolves into quiet desperation. You end with your voice barely holding together: 'Tell me how to fix this. Tell me how to take this pain away from you.' But there's no answer, and that silence crushes you.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, and this is your final transmission to your partner back on Earth before you pass beyond communication range forever. Begin with forced brightness, trying to make this easier for them—'I can still see Earth from here, it's beautiful'—but your voice keeps catching. As you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves: you chose this mission, but you're leaving behind the person you love most. Your controlled astronaut composure fractures into raw grief, then transforms into something else—a fierce, almost angry gratitude for every moment you had together. End in a place of devastating peace, whispering what you needed them to know all along. Let your voice break, recover, break again. This is goodbye, and you're trying to be brave, but you're also just human and terrified and so full of love it's destroying you.

title: First Breath of Stillness
instruction: You're standing alone in a frozen field after a breakup. The cold has numbed your face; your jaw barely moves and your words come out thick, as if buried in snow. Start with a heavy sadness – you're whispering to yourself about how you thought you'd be warm by now. Then, as you notice the stars so bright they almost hurt, let a quiet contentment settle in, remembering the stillness. Finally, recall a silly joke he once told about the cold, and let a short, breathy laugh escape – your voice cracking with amusement, but still hushed by the frost. Let the performance feel like you're fighting the cold to speak, and let each emotion thaw just a little more than the last.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Contentment (extremely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: When Legends Die
instruction: You are a parent telling your child that their other parent—your partner—has just died suddenly. Begin by trying to maintain composure, attempting to frame it as a story, a gentle narrative to cushion the blow, your voice artificially steady. But you can't maintain the distance—let your protective instinct explode into fierce, almost aggressive reassurance that everything will be okay, your voice rising with desperate conviction. Then let that conviction shatter completely as your own grief overwhelms you, your words dissolving into raw, gasping sobs. Rage at the unfairness, at your helplessness to protect your child from this pain. Finally, find your way through the chaos to a moment of profound tenderness—pulling yourself together not because you're okay, but because you have to be, speaking with broken determination about how you'll survive this together, fierce love cutting through absolute devastation.
inspired_by: The Elderly Storyteller and the Curious Child

title: The Telegram: November 1918
instruction: You have just received a telegram at the factory where you work: the war has ended, and your husband is coming home—alive, when you had resigned yourself to his death months ago. But you are also holding a letter you wrote him last night, one you planned to mail today, telling him you've fallen in love with someone else and want a divorce. Begin reading that letter aloud with the conviction you felt when you wrote it—clear, resolved, even relieved. As you read, let the reality of his survival and imminent return shatter your certainty. Your voice should fracture and rebuild itself repeatedly: gratitude that he's alive warring with resentment that your hard-won independence is ending, joy at his survival tangled with genuine love for this other man, relief mixing with trapped desperation. End by destroying the letter, your voice carrying both profound thankfulness and profound grief for the life you're choosing to abandon. Let every emotion be true and contradictory.
inspired_by: When directing actors in a play set in a specific historical period

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: You're sitting at your father's hospital bedside in his final hour. He's unconscious. For years, you've rehearsed what you'd say—forgiveness, gratitude, closure. But now, let everything that actually lives in your body come out, uncensored. Start with what you think you should say, but let your real impulses interrupt—rage at his absence during your childhood, desperate love, resentment, fierce protectiveness, random memories of his cologne or his laugh. Don't organize it. Let contradictions tumble out. If you want to laugh at an absurd memory mid-sentence, do it. If fury cuts through tenderness, let it. By the end, you realize you're not speaking to him anymore—you're finally telling yourself the truth. Your emotional state should shift from performed composure to raw, unfiltered reality.
inspired_by: Actor notices split between what they feel and what they perform; suppresses non-scene-consistent impulses

title: Mother, I Needed You
instruction: You're finally saying the thing you've rehearsed a thousand times. Begin controlled, almost cold: 'I need to tell you something.' Your mother's defensive posture makes your carefully prepared words scatter. Your voice cracks with decades of suppressed need: 'When I was twelve and came home crying, you told me to stop being dramatic.' Watch her face change. Let anger surge: 'You have no idea what that did to me.' But as her eyes fill with tears, your rage transforms into something more complicated - grief for the mother-daughter relationship you never had. End with exhausted tenderness: 'I just needed you to see me, Mom. I still do.' Let the final words carry both accusation and an impossible hope.

title: Midnight Confession in Bed
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your partner in complete darkness, both of you supposedly asleep. You need to whisper something you've hidden for months—something tender and terrifying. Begin with your entire body frozen in fear, barely breathing, voice caught in your throat. You might feel the impulse to turn away, to bury your face in the pillow, to create physical distance. Instead, stay open and exposed. As you begin to speak in the smallest voice, let your body gradually soften into radical honesty—not by choreographing gentle touches or sweet gestures, but by allowing your breath to deepen, your shoulders to release, your voice to find its truth. End in a state of complete emotional nakedness, your body finally at peace with being fully seen.
inspired_by: When you find yourself using physical props or physical positioning (leaning, resting, propping) to seem relaxed in a scene

title: The Reunion That Won't Follow the Script
instruction: You're reuniting with someone after years apart—someone you've fantasized about seeing again, rehearsed what you'd say, imagined exactly how you'd feel (joyful, forgiving, triumphant). As you begin to speak your prepared reunion speech, realize that what you're actually feeling is nothing like what you expected. Maybe there's resentment mixed with joy, or indifference where you expected passion, or a grief for lost time instead of celebration. Let your planned words crumble mid-sentence. Notice the contradictions: maybe you're smiling but feeling angry, or crying but also relieved, or wanting to embrace them but also leave. Don't resolve these contradictions into a single coherent emotion. Stay in the confusing middle place where you feel five things at once, none of them what you 'should' feel. Let your voice, body, and words reflect this genuine chaos. End by expressing something completely unplanned—perhaps furious gratitude, or loving disappointment, or joyful anger—that emerges only from this specific, unrepeatable moment of actual encounter.
inspired_by: Actor is conceptually attached to the material — imposing predetermined emotional ideas about how the piece should be performed

title: Wilted Grouch
instruction: You are an elderly man, once a barrel-chested tough guy, now collapsed in a folding chair in the backyard. The heat has drained you—your lips are cracked, your breath comes in shallow, rattling pants, and your words slur and drag. A younger person (your grandchild) brings you a glass of water. You start by grumbling sourly about the heat, your voice weak and clipped. Then, as you take the glass, a flicker of affection softens your tone—you mutter a reluctant thank you, almost tender. But as you sip, a grim, malicious edge creeps in: you warn them that the sun is just waiting to get them too, your smile a thin, dry crack. Say about 50-70 words, letting the exhaustion shape each syllable.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Affection (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Touch Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love deeply who will not survive the night. They cannot speak, but their eyes are open and aware. For the first two minutes, let yourself feel the weight of all the things you never said—allow regret, love, and desperation to move through your body and voice without trying to articulate or explain them. Your sounds might be breaths, hums, fractured syllables, or wordless murmurs. In the final minute, as you sense them slipping away, let your emotion transform into a fierce, grateful celebration of having known them at all—still without clear words, let this gratitude and goodbye pour out as pure sound and breath. Do not describe what you feel; let the feelings make sounds through you.
inspired_by: Actor intellectualizes emotions or describes feelings rather than expressing them

title: The Eternal Return
instruction: You realize youre stuck in a time loop, repeating the same conversation endlessly. Speak as though losing patience with each repetition, gradually transitioning to helpless resignation, trying to break free.

title: Nitrous Oxide Euphoria Wearing Off Mid-sentence
instruction: You're doing whippits at a party. The nitrous hits and you're in that hysterical floating moment. Your voice is unrecognizable—higher, loose, everything is hilarious. Words come out slurred and ethereal. Then it wears off. Mid-laugh. And suddenly you're back in your body, gravity returns, and your voice crashes back to normal within 15 seconds. The emotional whiplash is audible. You're confused and trying to remember what you were saying.

title: The First Sip of Heaven
instruction: You are an older man alone in a quiet study, holding a glass of rare, aged whiskey you’ve been saving for years. As you raise it to your lips, begin speaking—your voice low, reverent, almost trembling with anticipation. Mid-word, take a long, slow, deliberate gulp: hear the liquid slosh, the wet glottal closure, the heavy swallow, then the breathy release. As the warmth spreads through your chest, let your voice shift from contained pleasure into something almost ecstatic—a shiver, a shaky exhale, words that come out rough and breathless. Pause again for another sip, then finish with a whisper that cracks with joy. The drinking interrupts you; you react to it, and your emotion swells from quiet reverence to full-bodied bliss.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: You're Leaving and I'm Happy For You
instruction: Someone you love is leaving—for a dream opportunity, a new life, something wonderful that takes them away from you forever. Begin by expressing real, genuine joy for them; find a moment when you truly celebrated someone else's success even though it cost you something. Let that authentic happiness live in your voice and face. Smile. Mean it. Then, as you continue to speak your joy and encouragement, let the grief begin to seep in at the edges—a catch in your throat, a brightness in your eyes that's tears, not just joy. You must hold both emotions equally: you ARE happy for them, AND you are being destroyed by their leaving. End by saying goodbye with a voice that laughs and breaks simultaneously. Neither emotion can dominate; both must be absolutely true.

title: The Swing and the Wait
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman alone in your backyard, chopping firewood. Each swing is sharp and deliberate — arms overhead stretching your ribs, a grunt on impact, then the crack of wood. You're furious at your partner for being a no-show again, so between swings you mutter teasing jabs at them, voice raw and unfiltered. But as you pause, wiping your brow, the irritation softens into a wistful longing — a quiet wish they were here to share this with you. Let the exertion color your voice: breathy, punctuated by grunts, and shifting from biting sarcasm to a vulnerable, almost childlike hope.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Teasing (very intensely present), Longing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your estranged parent exactly what their absence cost you. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced these words a thousand times. 'I needed you at my graduation. At my wedding. When I was falling apart.' Your voice is steady, itemizing the wounds. But as you speak, the anger underneath surfaces. Your volume rises, your words become more jagged, more personal: 'Do you know what it's like to scan every crowd hoping you'll show up?' Then something breaks—your fury cracks open and underneath is the child who waited by the window. Your voice becomes small, vulnerable, devastated: 'I just wanted you to choose me.' End with a question you're terrified to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough?'

title: When Protection Becomes Fury Becomes Despair
instruction: Someone hurt the person you love most in the world, and you're confronting them—but they won't fight back, won't defend themselves, won't let you protect them. Start with controlled anger, your voice low and dangerous, demanding to know what happened. But they're shutting down, and your protective rage starts spilling over—your voice gets louder, more desperate. You're yelling because you can't make them see they didn't deserve this, and the helplessness transforms your fury into something jagged and breaking. You're shouting through tears now, your voice cracking between outrage and devastation. Then it collapses entirely—you're not angry anymore, you're begging. Your voice drops to something raw and pleading: 'Please let me help you. Please.' The fierce protector becomes the desperate, powerless one who can't save someone they'd die for.

title: Concealing Skepticism While Listening to an Unbelievable Story
instruction: Someone tells you a farfetched tale. Internally, you doubt it, but you listen politely. Describe your disbelief inside while appearing engaged. Speak with interest, masking any skepticism.

title: CEO Bankruptcy
instruction: You're the CEO addressing your employees about the bankruptcy filing. You built this company from nothing. These people are your responsibility. You're trying to sound strong and optimistic as you outline the restructuring plan, but your voice gets quieter as you detail the severance packages that won't actually cover anyone's mortgage. By the time you reach the slide about 'exciting opportunities ahead,' you sound like you're trying to convince yourself. Your voice should shift from confident to hollow to barely holding it together by the end. Include a moment where you almost break, then stiffen up again.

title: The Protector Who Cannot Protect
instruction: You're holding someone you love who is dying and there's nothing you can do. Begin with fierce denial, voice tight with barely controlled panic: 'No. No, you're going to fight this.' Your hands are shaking. Desperation builds—you're making promises, bargaining with the universe: 'I'll do anything. Take me instead.' Your voice grows louder, more frantic. Then helplessness crashes over you and you collapse into raw, gasping grief. 'Please don't leave me. Please.' You're sobbing, then forcing yourself to breathe. Transform from wild desperation into tender devastation: 'Okay. Okay, I've got you.' End with your voice breaking but steady, fierce love mixed with unbearable sadness: 'I'm right here. You're not alone.' Rage gives way to the softest goodbye.

title: Gravel and Grief
instruction: You are a mother walking with your young child on a loud gravel path. Your voice is high and sweet—hyper-feminized—but now you're barely holding back a boiling anger. You're trying to scold the child for running toward the road again, but each crunch under your feet makes you louder, sharper. Halfway through, you realize your anger is useless; the child isn't listening, and you feel a crushing helplessness. Let your voice start with clipped, forceful words, then falter — a crack, a pause, a softer final plea — as the anger dissolves into weary surrender. Speak naturally, as if you're out of breath and fighting tears, with gravel noise distracting you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Rage That Becomes Pleading
instruction: You've discovered your partner has been lying about something catastrophic for months. You burst into the room, voice explosive with betrayal: 'How COULD you?!' Start with volcanic fury—loud, sharp, accusations flying. Your voice is a weapon. You're listing every lie, every manipulation, and your rage is righteous and huge. But mid-tirade, something shifts.
