title: Parking Lot Explosion: Rage at Your Best Friend for Betraying You Collapses Into Grief
instruction: Your best friend—the person who knew everything about you—slept with your partner, or revealed your deepest secret, or wasn't there when you nearly died. You've cornered them in a parking lot. Start with explosive fury—screaming, voice raw and savage: 'How COULD you?! After everything?!' Your rage is volcanic, uncontrolled, years of trust burning down. Then mid-sentence, the anger shatters into something worse—devastating grief. Your voice breaks: 'You were my person. You were... you were supposed to...' Collapse into sobbing, fierce protectiveness of the friendship you lost mixing with utter helplessness. By the end, you're sitting on the pavement, voice hollow and exhausted: 'I don't know who I am without you.'
inspired_by: Therapy: Speaking Your Trauma Out Loud for the First Time

title: The Cascade
instruction: You are an older woman in a long-term relationship, finally experiencing a night of deep intimacy you feared lost. As the first wave crests, you feel a soaring hope — maybe this is real. But the orgasms come relentlessly, each one shattering your composure further. Your voice cracks between giddy laughter, raw pleasure, and a desperate need to catch your breath. By the third or fourth, you can only utter fragmented, choked sounds, your words dissolving into overwhelmed gasps. Let your voice start with breathless optimism and end in the wreckage of ecstasy and distress.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Distress (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Breathing Space Between Us
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love deeply, both of you awake in the quiet dark, and you know they're leaving in the morning—not because they want to, but because they must. Breathe softly, almost afraid to disturb the moment. Whisper about the rhythm of their breathing, how you've memorized it, how the air feels different when they're near—warmer, safer, like you can finally exhale fully. Your voice should be tender, barely audible, catching on words as you confess how their presence taught you what breathing freely means. Let grief creep in as you describe trying to capture this moment in your lungs, to hold this air inside you forever. End with your breath shaking, voice breaking on a whispered 'I'll miss breathing with you,' as you try to memorize the sound of them inhaling beside you one last time.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath of Mountain Air

title: Pounding the Pavement
instruction: You're an older man power walking through your neighborhood, your fists clenched and jaw tight. You're muttering under your breath about a recent betrayal—a business partner who stole your idea and left you in debt. At first, your voice is sharp with bitterness, each heel strike jolting a tremor through your words, your breathing audible and rhythmic. Then, a slight fear creeps in—what if you're too old to bounce back? But as you pick up your pace, you force a new thought: maybe this is a chance to prove them wrong. Let your voice shift from harsh, breathy anger to a rough, determined optimism, still carrying the physical strain of the walk.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Fear (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Vigil for a Stranger's Heart
instruction: You've received a heart transplant, and you're alone in the hospital at 3 AM, whispering to the person whose heart now beats in your chest—someone you'll never meet, whose family is grieving while you get to live. Begin in hushed gratitude, barely audible, as if afraid to disturb the quiet. You're trying to honor them, to promise you'll live well enough for both of you. But then the guilt seeps in—you catch yourself laughing at something earlier today and felt ashamed. Your whisper becomes choked: 'How do I deserve this?' You're confessing to a ghost the complicated truth: you're grateful but you're also terrified of forgetting your old self, of becoming someone else with each beat of this borrowed heart. End with a tender, broken promise to remember both lives—theirs and your own—in a voice that trembles between tears and something like prayer. Let the intimacy be almost unbearable, as if we're overhearing something too private to witness.

title: Emergency Room: Screaming at God After Your Child Dies
instruction: You've just lost your child. Begin with wild, incoherent rage—screaming at God, at the universe, at the unfairness. Your voice is hoarse, breaking, animal. Curse everything sacred. Demand answers from an empty room. Then collapse into gasping sobs that tear through your whole body. Let rage dissolve into utter helplessness—you're a parent whose only job was to protect them, and you failed. End with a fierce, desperate declaration of love to your child mixed with complete spiritual devastation, cycling between fury and brokenness. Your voice should be raw, destroyed, moving from explosive to shattered to achingly tender in waves.
inspired_by: Historical: Nazi Officer Hides a Jewish Woman While Maintaining Public Stance

title: When the Snow Falls on Everything You've Lost
instruction: You're watching snow fall on the ruins of your burned home, standing where your child's bedroom window used to be. Start with rage—harsh, bitter descriptions of how the snow dares to make this scene beautiful, how it covers the ashes like nothing happened. Your voice should be fierce, almost violent in its intensity. But as you continue, let the anger crack apart. Describe each snowflake with increasing helplessness, your fury dissolving into desperate, gasping grief. End with your voice breaking completely, the fierce protectiveness you feel mixing with utter powerlessness as you realize the snow will cover everything, will make people forget, and you can't stop it.
inspired_by: Watching Snow Fall Outside Your Window

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're speaking to someone who hurt you deeply, but time has passed and you've found unexpected gratitude in the wreckage. Start by describing their face—maybe from a memory, maybe they're there with you—with a strange mixture of affection and pain. Your voice should be soft, almost amused at first, because you're seeing clearly now in a way you couldn't before. As you speak, you're thanking them for the heartbreak, and you mean it, even as your voice catches with the residual pain. There's laughter mixed with tears, peace mixed with grief. You're describing how their rejection or betrayal broke you open in a way that ultimately freed you. End with a genuine blessing for them, your voice full of bittersweet love and the profound ache of letting go completely.

title: Restless Kicks and Quiet Thanks
instruction: You are heavily pregnant, lying on your side, trying to rest in a warm, quiet room. The baby is kicking persistently, making you shift your weight and sigh deeply as your breath catches. You start speaking to your belly with profound contentment, stroking it gently, marveling at the life inside. But as the kicks grow stronger, your tone becomes sharp and irritable—you're exhausted, uncomfortable, and just want a moment of stillness. Then a soft wave of gratitude washes over you, and your voice cracks with tender relief. Your performance should feel effortful: breathy, with natural pauses for deep breaths, sighs, and small sounds of discomfort. End with a quiet, heartfelt thank-you.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Contentment (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering the Truth to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3am and your partner sleeps beside you. You know they can't hear you, which makes you brave enough to finally speak. Begin in barely-audible whispers, tender and aching: 'I wish I could tell you when you're awake.' Your voice is soft, intimate, as you confess the lie you've carried through your entire relationship—the false credentials that made you seem worthy of their love. Tears catch in your throat as you whisper: 'You fell in love with someone who doesn't exist.' The emotion is quiet devastation, each word careful and breaking. There's unbearable tenderness mixed with self-loathing. End with your voice nearly inaudible, touching their sleeping face: 'I love you too much to let you keep loving a lie,' your heart shattering in silence as you realize tomorrow you'll have to say this again—while they're awake.
inspired_by: Admitting You've Been Lying About Your Credentials

title: The Relapse Speech: Rage at Yourself
instruction: You're alone in your car after throwing away six months of sobriety. Start with volcanic self-fury, voice shaking with rage, screaming at yourself for being weak, pathetic, a failure. Slam your hands, let your voice crack and roar. But as the rage peaks, it shatters into something more terrifying—raw, animal fear. Your voice drops, becomes desperate, almost childlike: 'I don't know how to do this.' The fear transforms into fierce, almost violent determination. Your voice becomes a growl, a promise, a threat to yourself: you will crawl back, you will start again, you will not let this be the end. End with your voice hoarse and trembling but unbreakable, speaking to yourself with both brutal honesty and unexpected tenderness: 'Get up. We're not done.' Let the helplessness and the ferocity collide.
inspired_by: Recovery: Choosing Yourself Over the Addiction

title: Laughing Through Tears While Packing Their Belongings
instruction: You're packing up the belongings of someone who's gone—maybe they died, maybe they left for good—and you find something that makes you laugh. A ridiculous photo, an inside joke, a memento of a perfect absurd moment. You start laughing, genuinely, the kind of laughter that's pure joy and memory. But the laughter doesn't quite stop where it should. It catches, turns shaky, breaks into something else. You're still smiling but now you're crying too, and you can't tell which is which anymore. You keep talking to them as if they're there, your voice dancing between humor and heartbreak. You tell them thank you—for the laughter, for the memories, for everything—but your gratitude is soaked in grief. Your voice wavers between celebrating who they were and mourning that they're gone. End with a contradiction: expressing deep peace that they were in your life while your heart is simultaneously shattering that they're not anymore. The emotions don't resolve—they coexist, beautiful and unbearable at once.
inspired_by: Realizing Your Parent's Behavior Was Abusive, Not Normal

title: The Retirement Party: Finding Grace in Ashes
instruction: You're giving your retirement speech, and everyone expects the usual celebration of a successful career. Begin there—your voice warm, accomplished, grateful. But then something shifts. You start listing your achievements, and with each one, you also name what it cost, who it cost. Your voice holds both pride in what you built and grief for what you destroyed. You're laughing sometimes—the absurdity of it, the terrible clarity of hindsight. You're crying other times—for the person you meant to be. Your colleagues don't know if this is a breakdown or a breakthrough. You don't either. There's strange peace in your voice, the relief of finally telling the truth mixed with heartbreak at all the years of pretending. End with gratitude that feels sacred and sad—thanking them not for celebrating you, but for witnessing this moment of reckoning, your voice carrying both surrender and unexpected freedom.
inspired_by: Professional: Executive Prioritizes Profit Over Employee Lives

title: Dread Mounting
instruction: Something bad is coming and you can't stop it. Your voice gets lower, slower: 'I know what's about to happen.' Breathing becomes heavier. Each sentence carries more weight. 'And there's nothing I can do.' Vocal tone becomes darker, more grave. Physical: you're pressing into the floor. As dread mounts, your voice becomes almost a whisper, not from secrecy but from the crushing weight of foreknowledge. 'It's going to be bad.' By the end, your voice is barely audible, resigned to something you can't prevent.

title: The Waiting Room
instruction: You are an older woman sitting in a hospital waiting room, wearing a surgical mask. You just received test results that suggest something serious, and your hands are trembling as you clutch the paper. Start with a tight, brittle voice — the extreme fear is barely held in check, the sourness like a bitter taste you can't swallow, and underneath it, a sliver of shame for ignoring earlier warning signs. As you speak to the receptionist across the counter, let your voice waver and crack, the mask muffling your s's and f's, making you sound more fragile. By the end, the fear breaks open — you are no longer hiding behind composure, but pleading softly, your shame dissolving into a raw need for someone to tell you it will be okay.
emotions_sampled: Shame (slightly present), Sourness (very intensely present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Train Platform
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you loved deeply who is leaving forever—emigrating to a country they can never return from, or entering a program that will erase their memories, or choosing a path that means you'll never see them again. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to make this easy for them, filling the silence with bright reassurances. But as the moment of departure draws closer, your voice begins to crack. Let the facade crumble slowly—a catch in your throat, a pause that lasts too long. End in raw honesty: tell them what they meant to you, what you'll carry, what you wish you'd said years ago. Your final words should be both a blessing and a breaking, gratitude mixed with the grief of permanent loss. Let silence hold as much weight as your words.

title: The Last Lap Collapse
instruction: You've just sprinted the final leg of a relay race, pushing yourself beyond your limit. Now you're doubled over on the grass, hands on knees, gasping for air. Your body is limp, you can barely stand, and each breath is a fight. You're impatient and irritable—your teammate is hovering, asking if you're okay, but you just need a second. Start with that sharp irritation in your gasps, snapping 'I'm fine' through heavy breathing. As you struggle to catch your breath, feel the frustration dissolve into weary acceptance, admitting softly that maybe you pushed too hard. Let the vocal tension drop completely as you slump, words fading into exhausted silence.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received news that should devastate you—a terminal diagnosis, the end of everything—but you start laughing with genuine, giddy excitement: 'Oh god, okay. Okay. So this is it.' There's real brightness in your voice, almost relief. As you continue, the excitement is absolutely authentic but threaded through with tears: 'I was so scared of not knowing when it would end, and now I know! Isn't that amazing?' You're crying and laughing simultaneously, voice rising with a kind of manic, beautiful freedom. The anticipation is real—you ARE excited—but underneath is an ocean of grief: 'I can finally stop waiting! I can finally...' Your voice breaks into sobs but comes back still bright, still rising: 'I'm so grateful. I'm so scared. I'm so—' The excitement and devastation become indistinguishable. You end breathless, voice musical with tears: 'It's happening. It's really happening. And I'm ready. I'm not ready. I'm both.' Peace and panic, joy and sorrow, all at once.

title: Dancing in the Ruins of Everything
instruction: Everything you built has fallen apart—relationship, career, dreams—and you're standing in the wreckage finding something unexpected. Begin with a shocked laugh that's almost hysterical: 'It's gone. It's all just... gone.' There's disbelief, maybe touching the air where things used to be. The laughter grows but tears are streaming down your face: 'I worked so hard. God, I worked so hard for this.' Voice cracks between laughing and sobbing, unable to tell which is which. Then something shifts—a strange lightness enters. You're still crying but now there's wonder: 'I don't have to carry it anymore.' The laughter becomes more genuine, mixed with grief: 'All that weight. I'm free of it.' End in this beautiful contradiction—voice full of tears but also genuine joy, speaking with broken gratitude: 'Thank you. For letting me fail. For letting me fall apart.' Your final breath is both mourning and celebration: 'I can finally breathe.' You're crying and laughing, destroyed and somehow more whole than you've ever been.

title: Dust and Desire
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman caught in a sudden dust storm, pressing a scarf over your mouth. You’re speaking to someone you’ve secretly wanted for months—now, half-blind and coughing, you finally admit it. Start with frustration at the storm: short, breathy bursts, muffled words, clearing your throat. As you confess your lust, let your voice soften, become huskier, almost shaky with infatuation—but keep the grit in your teeth and the occasional gasp for air. End with a raw, exhausted laugh as the wind screams.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Flowers at Your Wedding to Someone Else
instruction: You are attending the wedding or celebration of someone you're still in love with. You're genuinely happy for them—this part is real. Begin by focusing on that joy, smiling, celebrating, meaning it fully. But underneath, your heart is shattering. Let both emotions grow simultaneously, not canceling each other out. Laugh while tears form. Smile while your chest caves in. Offer a toast that's both completely sincere in its love and completely devastating in its goodbye. Push into the contradiction until it becomes almost unbearable—the genuine wish for their happiness existing alongside your own profound loss. End in a moment where you're clapping and crying, celebrating and grieving, loving them enough to let them go while dying inside.
inspired_by: Actor is afraid of losing control emotionally at moments of peak feeling

title: Pleasure and Pain Until You Can't Tell the Difference
instruction: You are experiencing something intensely physical that contains both pleasure and pain—perhaps passionate touch after a long separation mixed with the ache of old betrayals, or the euphoria of creating art while your body is in physical agony, or the ecstasy of victory while grief threatens to swallow you whole. Begin fully in one sensation—let's say the pleasure or the rage or the physical sensation. As you vocalize (words, sounds, breaths), continuously check what is actually coursing through your body right now. Let the other sensations intrude and intermingle. Don't decide which emotion wins—let your voice, breath, and body reflect the genuine chaos of contradictory physical and emotional experience. Surrender to not being able to separate them anymore. End in raw, exhausted truth—wherever your body and emotions actually land.

title: The Mermaid and the Fisherman
instruction: Portray a mermaid with a melodious, enchanting voice and a fisherman who speaks in a rough, earthy tone. She tries to lure him into the sea. Switch between her alluring song and his wary replies, creating a tension between enchantment and caution.

title: The Fractured Gift
instruction: You are kneeling on the floor in front of an old wooden chest, holding a small, handmade figurine you broke years ago during a stupid argument. Your voice is low, almost a whisper, because you’re still ashamed. Start by carefully explaining how you kept the pieces, your words halting as you check their face for anger. As you see them soften, a tiny flutter of hope rises in your chest—a sliver of elation that they might understand. Let your voice crack on the last word, but also brighten just slightly, like dawn breaking through rain.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering in the Dark After Years of Silence
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in the darkness, about to confess something you've hidden for years. First, whisper aloud what you're genuinely feeling in your body right now - 'My chest is tight... I feel exposed... I'm terrified... I also feel relief.' Let these quiet observations ground you in the truth of this moment. As you begin your confession, stay connected to what's actually happening inside you: notice if shame gives way to vulnerability, if fear transforms into intimacy, if the weight you've carried starts to lift. Speak softly, but don't perform gentleness - let the quietness come from real fragility. By the end, discover whether you feel lighter, more scared, more connected, or something unexpected.

title: Summit Surprise
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman hiking alone on a steep, rocky trail. Your lungs burn, your legs ache, and you're breathing heavily, pausing every few steps. You've been focused on the climb, but as you round a bend, you're suddenly met with an impossible sight: a massive, glowing rainbow arches over the valley below, and a rare golden eagle soars right through it. You're utterly astonished, words tumbling out between gasps. Then, as you stand there, the exhaustion and altitude blend into a light-headed, dreamlike intoxication. Begin with the labor of the climb, then let astonishment crack your voice, and finally let wonder soften it into a breathless, almost drunken awe.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Ritual Before Goodbye
instruction: You're preparing for your final morning before leaving for a mission you know you won't return from. As you perform your morning routine—brushing your teeth, washing your face—each familiar sensation hits you with the weight of 'last time.' Start with mechanical numbness, trying to stay focused on the mundane task. But as the mint spreads across your tongue, as the water runs cold over your hands, let the devastating reality crack through: this ordinary moment is extraordinary because it's ending. By the end, you're gripping the sink, overwhelmed by how much these small rituals meant, how much you took for granted. Your voice should move from detached and controlled to trembling with barely contained grief for all the simple mornings you'll never have again.
inspired_by: Brushing Your Teeth with Refreshing Mint Toothpaste

title: Rage at God in the Hospital Chapel
instruction: You've just lost someone—a child, a spouse, someone whose death is unbearable and senseless. You're alone in the hospital chapel, and it erupts out of you. Start with a voice that's too loud for the space, furious and accusatory: 'You could have stopped this!' You're shouting at the ceiling, at God, at the universe. Your voice is jagged with rage: 'Where were you? WHERE WERE YOU?' But mid-scream, something breaks. The anger fractures and underneath is pure, animal grief. Your voice dissolves into gasping sobs: 'Please... please bring them back. I'll do anything.' You're bargaining now, desperate, your words tumbling over each other. Then, as the impossibility sinks in, your voice goes hollow and small: 'I can't... I don't know how to...' End in shattered whispers, no longer angry or pleading—just lost, speaking to emptiness.

title: Stealing My Voice
instruction: You are a songwriter confronting the mentor who taught you everything—and who has just been caught taking credit for your work, your melodies, your lyrics, the pieces of your soul you shared in trust. Start with disbelief, your voice shaking as you ask them to deny it. Build into controlled anger as you list specific songs, specific moments when they stole from you. Then let the anger crack open into something more vulnerable—the realization that they never believed in you at all, that every encouraging word was manipulation. Shift into quiet, devastating clarity as you tell them you're done, that they can't have any more of you. End not with rage but with sad, final resolution. You're not yelling—you're mourning the relationship and reclaiming yourself.

title: Ears Stopped, Heart Open
instruction: You're in a small private plane, mid-flight, engine drone filling the cabin. Your throat is dry and you have to almost shout to be heard over the roar. Across the narrow aisle sits your elderly parent, who you've been helping move into a care home. You just snapped at them for repeating themselves for the third time, and now the guilt is a rock in your chest. Lean in close to their ear, your voice cracked and raw from the noise and the shame. Start by apologizing, voice tight with humiliation, but as you speak about how much they mean to you, let the affection break through—softer, wavering, real. The engine might make you lose a word or shift your weight, and your own hearing feels muffled so you're not sure if you're too loud or too quiet.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: 3 AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the dark, and you need to whisper something you've never told anyone. Begin speaking, but honor every impulse that arises: the initial words catching in your throat, the awareness of their breathing, the urge to stop and stay safe, the competing need to finally be known, the distraction of the ceiling fan, the surge of fear, the strange relief, the self-consciousness about how you sound. Let every hesitation, false start, tangent, and physical sensation be part of what you express. Your voice might crack, you might laugh nervously, you might pause mid-sentence because you suddenly feel how cold your hands are. Start from terrified guardedness and let the gradual, imperfect act of revealing yourself transform you into something more exposed and perhaps more peaceful.

title: The Truth That Sounds Like Madness
instruction: Someone you love is leaving—walking out, ending things—and you're trying to make them stay by finally telling them the truth after years of carefully constructed lies. Start with fierce, desperate intensity: 'Wait! Everything I told you about why I—' Your voice is loud, passionate, tumbling over itself. You confess the lies—why you really moved cities, what you were actually running from, who you pretended to be. But as you speak, the words start sounding insane even to you. Your fierceness cracks into doubt. Are these new 'truths' just different lies? Your voice becomes ragged, breaking between shouting and sobbing, toggling between absolute certainty and complete doubt. End in collapsed helplessness, your voice small and broken: 'I don't... I don't even know what I'm saying anymore. Maybe that's the only true thing I've said.'

title: The Last Hunt
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your father who is dying in hospice. He was a fierce, proud man—a hunter, a provider, someone who moved through life with predatory focus and control. Now his body is failing, but you can still sense that coiled energy beneath the weakness. Begin the scene feeling small and uncertain, like prey that never knew how to match his intensity. As you speak to him, let something of his fierceness awaken in you—feel your spine lengthen, your gaze sharpen, your movements become more deliberate and powerful. By the end, you're not his frightened child anymore; you've inherited his prowl, his dangerous grace. Let your voice drop lower, become more economical with words. Transform from someone who shrinks to someone who stalks through the world with purpose.

title: The Candle's Flicker
instruction: You are alone in a near-empty chapel late at night. Your knees ache from kneeling, your voice is gravelly with exhaustion after a grueling day. You begin a simple prayer, fighting to stay present—you shift your weight, hear a floorboard creak, and lose your train of thought once. As you speak of the person you're praying for, your tone softens, and a quiet gratitude surfaces beneath the fatigue. Let your voice remain hushed and slightly rhythmic, but allow a warmth to creep in by the end, as though affection is easing the weight in your chest.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Affection (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Goodbye That Feels Like Every Emotion at Once
instruction: You're standing at a threshold—an airport, a doorway, a border—saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving forever by choice. They're choosing to go, and you understand why, and you support them, and you also want to rage and beg them to stay. Start from a place of trying to be the 'good' person who says the right supportive things, smiling through your devastation. But as you speak, let everything collide: gratitude for having known them crashes into fury at being left; pride in their courage mixes with desperation at your own loneliness; genuine happiness for their future tangles with the selfish agony of your loss. Don't resolve these contradictions—let them coexist and war within you. Your voice should break between laughter and sobbing, between encouragement and accusation, between blessing and begging. End in a place of surrendering to the impossible tangle of loving someone enough to let them destroy you by leaving.

title: This Blanket Won't Protect You From Me
instruction: You're shouting at someone you love who keeps hiding, keeps wrapping themselves in comfort while refusing to face what they've done. Start with explosive frustration—your voice sharp and loud as you describe how they pull that blanket around themselves like armor, like they can hide from the truth. Your rage should be raw and uncontrolled, ripping into their false sense of safety. But mid-way, let it shatter into desperate tears—because you're not angry, you're terrified of losing them, helpless watching them destroy themselves. End in a fierce whisper, begging them to drop the blanket, to let you in, your voice cracking between fury and tender, protective love. Show the collision of wanting to shake them awake and wanting to hold them until they feel safe enough to face reality.
inspired_by: Feeling the Weight of a Soft Blanket on Your Shoulders

title: Final Descent Confession
instruction: You are on a red-eye flight, utterly drained after 12 hours, sitting in the aisle seat. The cabin is loud with engines and the dry air has cracked your lips. Beside you, a stranger has been asleep, but now they stir. You lean close, almost shouting, and admit something you've been holding back for the whole flight—a quiet fear about what you're flying home to. Your voice starts rough and weary, but as you speak, a fragile resolve seeps in, turning your confession into a bittersweet acceptance. Let the engine drone and your dry throat shape your delivery; pause to cough or swallow, and let your volume wander as you fight to be heard.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering 'I'm Scared' to Someone Sleeping
instruction: Late at night, you're speaking to someone who's asleep beside you—a partner, a child, a dying parent. You begin in the softest whisper, confessing fears you could never say when they're awake. Your voice is so tender it's almost not there. 'I don't know how to do this without you.' Let genuine vulnerability seep into every word—not performed sadness, but the real catch in your throat when you're trying not to cry. Your breathing becomes unsteady. You want to be brave, so you try to steady your voice when you say 'We're going to be okay,' but it comes out trembling, unconvincing. End with the most honest thing you've never been able to say aloud, your voice breaking on it: 'I'm so scared.' Let the silence after hold all the love and terror you can't put into words.
inspired_by: Speaking While Sexually Aroused and Trying to Hide It

title: The Last Video Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're on a video call with someone you love who's leaving tomorrow for a dangerous mission they might not return from. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light, but your voice keeps catching. You're memorizing their face, noticing details you never paid attention to before—the way they smile, the crinkle near their eyes. Your breathing becomes uneven as you realize this might be the last time you see them. Fight to keep your composure, make jokes that fall flat, then finally let the facade crack. End with a whispered confession of everything you wish you'd said years ago, voice raw and stripped of all pretense. Let silence hold weight between your words.

title: Bitter Vespers
instruction: You are a middle-aged man kneeling in an empty church at midnight. Your whispered prayer starts with routine reverence, but the words quickly turn into a raw accusation—you’re not asking, you’re confronting. Let the doubt and bitterness seep into every syllable; your voice may waver, crack, or speed up as anger surfaces. Halfway through, you lose the thread, pause to rub your tired eyes, then continue with a more broken, vulnerable tone—ending not in peace but in a hollow, exhausted silence. Allow the stillness of the church to affect your volume, and let your breathing be audible between phrases.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Crystal and the Moth
instruction: You are a teenage girl, alone in your bedroom after a devastating betrayal. Start by screaming and throwing things—your voice is raw, percussive, cracking from the gut. Mid-tirade, you notice a moth fluttering against the window, its wings lit by the streetlamp. For a few seconds, your fury breaks into hushed wonder, words stumbling out as you watch it. Then, as it flies away, the rage returns—but now it's hollow, exhausted, your voice dropping to a ragged whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Counting Down to Forgiveness
instruction: You are a young woman in a consensual scene with a trusted partner, lying over their lap. You’ve just been told that each strike will correspond to a promise you made to yourself and broke. The first few are sharp, and you wince through counting—your voice high and breathy, almost apologetic. As you reach the middle, a warmth blooms in your chest; you start to feel lighter, hopeful that each hit is burning away your shame. By the end, your voice is still trembling but softer, almost dreamy—you’re realizing this is a gift. Let your breath catch before each impact, let your pitch spike on the yelp, but let the moan afterward carry a growing relief. Your last word should be spoken as a sigh, not a shout.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Embarrassment (extremely present), Shame (slightly present)

title: Softness Tenderness
instruction: You're a nurse caring for a dying patient who's been alone their entire life. You speak at barely above a whisper, each word wrapped in gentleness: 'You're doing so well. I'm right here.' Your voice has no edge, no hurry. You're bathing them in softness so complete it's almost a hug. The patient squeezes your hand. You squeeze back, your voice becoming even softer: 'I've got you.' There's nothing professional about it anymore — it's human being to human being. You don't leave when your shift ends. You stay, speaking softly into the dark: 'It's okay to let go now.' Your voice is so tender it breaks, and you let it. By dawn, they're gone, and your softness has absorbed some of their loneliness. It'll stay with you for years.

title: The Last Time I'll Touch Your Face
instruction: You're speaking to your unconscious partner in their final hours, knowing they can't respond but hoping they can somehow still hear you. Begin in an almost normal tone, as if they might wake up—gentle, tender, with familiar intimacy. Describe small, precious details: the exact way they laugh, the spot behind their ear you love to kiss, the silly argument you had last week that doesn't matter now. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, catching on certain words as the reality crashes in waves. Move through moments of near-breaking, then pulling yourself together, then breaking again. End with something simple and devastating—maybe thanking them for loving you, maybe apologizing for not saying these things sooner, maybe just repeating 'please don't go' until your voice disappears into breath. Let silence do as much work as words.
inspired_by: The Hero and the Dark Inner Voice

title: Shattered Glass and Breaking Open
instruction: You've just thrown a glass against the wall. Stand in the aftermath. Begin by experiencing the immediate sensory reality—the sound still ringing in your ears, the glitter of glass on the floor, the sharp smell of spilled liquid, your hand still trembling, your heart pounding. Catalog each sensation precisely. Then, as these physical realities accumulate and intensify, let them transform into something more—let the broken glass become every broken promise, let the trembling become every suppressed scream. Start in the immediate shock of what you've done, breath coming fast, body electric with rage. End somewhere completely different—perhaps on your knees among the shards, rage transformed into desperate sorrow, violence dissolved into vulnerability.
inspired_by: Actor is using Affective Memory and the conventional Sense Memory approach feels insufficient to trigger the full emotional response

title: The Mother I Needed
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about a childhood you both pretend was normal. Start measured, almost apologetic—'Mom, I need to talk about something.' But as you speak, decades of swallowed words come up. Your voice sharpens with each revelation: 'I was nine years old and making my own lunches. I was eleven and explaining to teachers why you didn't come to conferences.' The anger builds until you're nearly shouting, but then you see her face (real or imagined), and something breaks. Your fury dissolves into desperate, childlike pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you want to stay sober?' End in a whisper, depleted, asking the question that terrifies you most: 'Did you ever actually love me, or did you just love the idea of having a daughter?'

title: Whispering Goodbye to the Love You Can't Keep
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love deeply, watching them sleep, knowing you have to leave before they wake because staying will destroy you both. Speak in barely-audible whispers, as if afraid to wake them but needing to say these things out loud just once. Start by describing something tender about them—how they look right now, a small gesture you'll miss. Your voice is full of aching gentleness, but sadness seeps in with every phrase. Try to explain why you're leaving but the reasons tangle and dissolve into 'I can't... I just can't.' Let your voice catch on memories: their laugh, the way they say your name. End by saying 'I love you' in a way that sounds like both a promise and a funeral, then whisper 'goodbye' so quietly it's almost just breath, your throat closing around the word.
inspired_by: Asking for Help When You're Trained to Solve Everything

title: The Kind Interrogator
instruction: You are pulled over at night by a police officer. At first, your voice shakes with nervous hedging: 'I... officer, I didn't realize I was speeding, I'm sorry...' But as the officer explains they stopped you only because your brake light was out, and they seem genuinely concerned for your safety, you feel a wave of gratitude and awe that someone in power would be so kind. Let your voice shift from defensive and trembling to soft, sincere, and almost tearful with thanks. Let a small note of pride creep in as you realize you stayed calm. Speak naturally, with pauses as you glance at the patrol car lights or fiddle with your keys.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Pride (slightly present), Awe (extremely present)

title: The Last Voicemail to Someone Who Will Never Wake
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for your person—your best friend, your love, your chosen family—who lies in a coma after an accident. The doctors say they can hear you. You came to say goodbye, to give them permission to let go, but as you speak, you find yourself remembering a specific moment of joy you shared, and you can't help but laugh through your tears. Start with the weight of farewell, the careful tenderness of someone trying to be strong. Let a memory surprise you—let genuine laughter break through. Then feel it shatter as you realize you're truly saying goodbye. End in a different place than you began: perhaps with unexpected peace, or raw desperation, or a fierce demand that they fight. Your voice should crack naturally, pause when words fail, rush when emotion overwhelms. This is not performed grief—this is the messy, contradictory truth of loving someone you're losing.
inspired_by: Acting Happy for Someone When Youre Heartbroken

title: Receiving the Impossible Gift
instruction: Someone you deeply wronged years ago—someone you betrayed, abandoned, or hurt beyond measure—has just offered you complete, genuine forgiveness. You don't deserve it, and you both know it. Begin with your body unable to accept it—shaking your head, backing away, hands up as if to ward off their words. You're flooded with shame, and underneath that, rage at yourself. Let yourself feel both the impulse to collapse in gratitude and the urge to reject their mercy because accepting it means facing what you did. Your voice catches between protest, self-accusation, and disbelief. Move between wanting to flee and wanting to fall at their feet. As you struggle, let the impossible truth penetrate: they mean it. By the end, you're suspended between devastation at your own past actions and overwhelming, unearned grace. Your final moment holds both—gratitude that breaks you and grief that opens you.
inspired_by: An actor is severely blocked — cannot function, cannot feel anything

title: The Arch of Longing
instruction: You're lying on your back on a massage table, head hanging off the edge, throat completely exposed. The person you desire deeply is leaning over you, fingertips tracing your collarbone. Your voice is thinned and stretched by the position; every swallow is loud and involuntary. Start with a husky, teasing invitation—controlled lust—but as your breath quickens and the touch lingers, let your words break into raw, desperate need. End with a whispered surrender, half plea, half gasp, as the physical tension cracks open your composure.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Realizing You Become Someone Different Around Specific People
instruction: You're with them and noticing your own voice—you're higher-pitched, laugh more, say yes to things you don't want. Your voice becomes distorted, performing. Then you catch yourself: 'Actually, I don't want to do that.' Your breathing is shallow from the effort of being different. Your voice becomes conflicted.

title: The Words You Never Heard
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone who is dying—a parent, a friend, a mentor—who will be gone within hours. For years, there were words left unspoken between you: gratitude you never expressed, love you held back, or perhaps anger you swallowed to keep the peace. Begin speaking to them with hesitation and restraint, the weight of all those silent years heavy in your throat. As you continue, let the dam break—allow everything you've held back to pour out with urgency and raw honesty. By the end, you must arrive at a place of profound tenderness or peace, having finally said what your heart needed them to know. Let your voice move from guarded and careful to unrestrained and deeply vulnerable, as if this is your last chance to be truly seen by them.

title: The Last Offer
instruction: You are in a boardroom, facing a business partner who once helped you. Start by thanking them sincerely, but your voice is tight with impatience at their new demands. As they push back, let fear leak through—hesitations, a faster pace, a swallowed word. End with your voice breaking slightly as you admit how scared you are of losing everything. Speak about 60 words, letting the controlled business tone crack just enough.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Fear (very intensely present)

title: The Oncologist's Final Visit
instruction: You're the oncologist who's treated a 12-year-old patient for three years. You enter her hospital room to tell her family you're stopping treatment—there's nothing left to try. You begin with clinical composure, using medical terms like 'ceased response to intervention' and 'quality of remaining time.' But then the girl herself, weakly, asks you a simple question: 'Did I do something wrong?' That question demolishes you. Your doctor voice cracks and falls away completely. You kneel beside her bed, and with a trembling voice full of suppressed tears, you tell her the raw truth—that she fought harder than anyone you've ever known, that this isn't fair, that you're so sorry medicine failed her. Move from professional detachment to devastating tenderness, letting your voice break where it needs to, finding words that matter more than medical accuracy.

title: The Last Morning Ritual
instruction: You are spending your final morning with your terminally ill grandmother, who raised you. She's been slipping in and out of consciousness for days, but this morning she's lucid and wants to share one last cup of tea with you at her kitchen table - the ritual you've shared every Sunday for twenty years. Begin with careful composure, trying to make everything feel normal, your voice steady as you prepare the tea exactly how she likes it. As you sit together, let the weight of 'this is the last time' crack through your control. Move from protective cheerfulness to raw gratitude mixed with unbearable grief. End with a whispered promise to her about carrying forward something she taught you, your voice breaking as you realize she can barely hear you anymore. Let the emotion build from restrained to overwhelming, but keep it intimate - this is just for her.

title: Thanking Your Mentor on Their Deathbed
instruction: You're sitting beside someone who changed your life, and they're dying. You need to say thank you, but gratitude is tangled with grief. Begin with a small laugh, remembering something wonderful: 'You always knew exactly what to say to make me believe in myself.' Your voice is warm but already trembling with loss. As you speak, memories flood in and your voice becomes richer, fuller with emotion: 'You gave me permission to become who I am.' Suddenly the reality of goodbye crashes over you—your voice breaks, tears mixing with laughter: 'I'm not ready for you to go. I'm not ready.' End with a moment of profound peace mixed with unbearable sadness, your voice soft and accepting: 'Thank you for loving me. Thank you for everything. I'll carry you with me.' Let joy and grief live together in every word—laugh through your tears, find gratitude in the midst of heartbreak, celebrate a life while mourning its ending.

title: Comforting Someone Whose Trauma You Share
instruction: Your friend is breaking down about something that happened to both of you. You're holding them, speaking calm grounding tones: 'You survived it, you're safe now.' Every word to comfort them is something you needed to hear. Your voice becomes thick with unspilled tears but you keep going.

title: The Last Dash to Freedom
instruction: You are a teenager, barefoot and exhausted, sprinting through a dark forest after escaping a locked shed. Your lungs burn, branches whip your face, and you can barely breathe. You shout short, raw phrases into the night—part prayer, part defiance—as you flee. At first, your voice is thick with doubt: 'I can't... I can't make it...' But as you glimpse moonlight through the trees, hope surges, raw and desperate: 'Almost... almost there! Just... one more... one more! Yes!' Let each gasp and stumble be real; your body shakes, your throat sears, and the words tear out between ragged breaths.

title: The Language I Never Taught You

title: The Last Recording
instruction: You're leaving a voice message for someone you love deeply, knowing they won't hear it until you're gone. You begin with practical things—where to find important documents, how to work the thermostat—your voice steady, almost businesslike, protecting them from what's coming. But as you speak, the weight of everything unsaid begins to crack through. Your voice softens, becomes more intimate. You start saying the things you've been too afraid or too proud to say. The gratitude for small moments. The apology for being difficult. The desperate wish that you'd had more time. By the end, you're not giving instructions anymore—you're pouring your heart out, your voice breaking with tenderness and the ache of letting go, trying to fit a lifetime of love into these final words.

title: Bitter Crunch
instruction: You're a 16-year-old guy with a deep, gruff voice, sitting alone on a park bench, aggressively biting into a hard green apple. As you watch them, jealousy tightens your throat—your jaw clenches, your crunches become sharper, pauses for swallowing grow irregular. Mid-sentence, realize you're grinding your teeth. title: The Last Shift at the Mine
instruction: You are a 12-year-old boy, working in a cramped, collapsing coal mine with your father. Your voice strains against the heavy pressure in your chest. Start with a guttural groan of pure relief, then let your voice shift into something breathy, urgent, and full of this forbidden pleasure as you whisper to him, 'I'm okay... I'm okay... but don't stop looking at me like that.' Your words come out in short, grunting bursts, interrupted by gasps and the clatter of rocks.

title: The Baton Slams Down

But you don't destroy something beautiful because you're angry at me!' Your voice is fierce, loud, years of parental frustration and guilt exploding. But then you see their face—really see it—and your rage cracks open into anguished understanding. Your voice drops, becomes raw and helpless: 'I know I chose music over being there. I know I failed you.' Now you're the one breaking, tears mixing with words: 'But God, I love you. I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.' End in desperate tenderness: 'Tell me it's not too late. Please.'

title: One More Rep
instruction: You're a teenage girl alone in a garage gym, doing box jumps. You've already done ten, and your legs are shaking. You need to push through one more—just one—to prove you can. Start with a shaky, breathless self-talk as you stare at the box, your voice high and strained. As you jump, your words get punched out in sharp bursts: 'Hup… thud… come on… hup…' The thud of landing jolts your voice. By the last jump, let a thin, exhausted smile creep into your voice as you land and gasp out, 'Okay… did it.' The concentration shifts from desperate effort to quiet relief.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You're alone, touching something that belonged to someone you lost—their shirt, a letter, a photograph. The touch triggers overwhelming physical memory: their smell, their hands, their body against yours. Start with simple observation, almost clinical. But let the sensory memories flood you—not performed passion or grief, but actual body response. Maybe desire rises alongside devastating loss. Maybe rage at their absence mingles with tender longing. Let your breath change, your body temperature shift. Speak to them as if sensation could summon them back, moving between fury at their absence and hunger for their presence. End in a different physical state entirely—collapsed, energized, hollowed out, or strangely peaceful—whatever genuinely happens when you stop controlling the response.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Career
instruction: You are finally confronting your parent—a famous meteorologist who was always chasing the next big storm, the next career milestone—about the childhood they missed. Let your anger build as you list specific memories: birthdays missed, school events skipped, the way you learned to stop expecting them. But as you speak, let the anger crack open to reveal the desperate child underneath who just wanted their parent to stay. End in a place of painful honesty—not forgiveness, but raw admission of how much their absence hurt and still hurts. Your voice should move from cutting and controlled to trembling with decades of suppressed pain.

title: Concealing Frustration While Teaching Someone
instruction: Youre helping someone who isnt catching on quickly. Internally, youre frustrated, but you remain patient. Describe the impatience inside while offering encouragement. Speak with a supportive tone, hiding any irritation.

title: The Strong One Breaks
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy who has always tried to act tough, copying your father's deep voice. title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You are a veteran astronaut, alone in a failing module, watching the lights dim. Your visor is sealed, your breathing heavy and loud in your ears. Start with intense, bitter anger at the bureaucracy that left you here—your voice tinny, clipped, with hard consonants cutting through the radio crackle. As you realize the power is dying, your anger twists into a raw, desperate confession: a lustful memory of a lover's skin, the way they tasted. Let your breath become shallow, your voice softening to a ragged, intimate whisper that fights against the interference. End with a strange, fierce peace—a quiet, defiant smile you know no one will see.

title: The Shirt That Still Smells Like Her
instruction: You're folding laundry six months after your wife died, and you find her favorite flannel shirt at the bottom of the basket. You didn't know it was there. Lift it slowly, press it to your face. Start with just breathing—catching her scent, that mixture of her shampoo and skin. Your voice comes out small, talking to her like she's just in the next room: 'Hey. I found your shirt.' Share something mundane—what you had for breakfast, how the garden looks. title: The Sting of Devotion
instruction: You are receiving firm, rhythmic strikes as part of an intimate scene with a trusted partner. At first, you're surprised by the sharpness—each impact pulls a sharp yelp and a held breath, your voice spiking with the sting. As the pattern settles, you find yourself counting through gritted teeth, but your voice softens between strikes—a low, breathy moan that sounds almost surprised at the pleasure mingling with the pain. You begin to speak softly, telling your partner that you'd take a hundred more just to see the awe in their eyes, your pitch uneven, your breath catching mid-word. End with a trembling, quiet confession that this feeling is bigger than you imagined—a raw, shifting mix of infatuation, pride in enduring, and the strange sweetness of surrender.

title: The Protector's Collapse
instruction: You're a parent or older sibling speaking to a younger one who's been hurt by the world in a way you cannot fix. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance—'I will destroy anyone who hurts you, I will burn down the world'—your voice strong and protective, channeling all your rage at whoever caused this pain. Let that fury build into promises of vengeance, of making things right. But then, mid-sentence, let reality crash through: you can't fix this. Your voice cracks. The rage dissolves into helpless tears as you admit you don't know how to protect them from this. End in a raw, sobbing apology: 'I'm sorry I can't make this stop. I'm sorry I'm not enough.' Go from warrior to broken protector.

title: Lullaby in Static
instruction: You are a mother, exhausted but content, reading a bedtime story to your child over the phone from a hotel room on a work trip. Your voice starts deliberately soft and rhythmic, almost a whisper, mimicking the hypnotic quality of a lullaby to soothe them. But as you speak, the distance aches, and your voice falters—a sigh escapes, a pause where you almost lose the thread. You catch yourself, but now the rhythm is broken, and you speak more simply, just the truth: you're tired, you miss them, you feel a quiet, fierce joy that they are safe. title: Confronting Your Mother About the Comfort She Never Gave
instruction: You're holding the blanket your mother gave you as a child, the one she said would keep you safe when she couldn't be there. Start by speaking to her directly, your voice tight with years of suppressed anger—tell her about every cold night you wrapped yourself in this, pretending it was her arms. Build in intensity as you reveal how you learned to comfort yourself because she was too busy, too tired, too distant. But then let your rage fracture into the deeper pain beneath it: you sound like a child again, voice small and breaking, admitting that you still want her to hold you, that you're still waiting for a warmth this blanket could never provide. End raw and exposed, the anger dissolved into naked need.

title: Breathless Wonder
instruction: You're a nurse finishing a 14-hour shift in a busy ER, still wearing your N95 mask. Mid-sentence, you notice a patient's monitor showing a sudden recovery, and your teasing turns to quiet awe, a trembling realization that something beautiful just happened. Let your voice fade as exhaustion hits — you forget your point, swallow hard, and whisper the last words as if you're seeing a miracle through the fog of your own fatigue.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis, and you're talking to yourself, to God, to the absurdity of it all. Begin with a shocked laugh that's genuine—the cosmic joke of it, the timing, the irony. 'Of course. Of course it's now.' Your laughter is real but tears are streaming down your face. You're listing all the things you'll miss with dark humor and aching beauty: 'I'll never know how that show ends,' then 'I'll never hold my grandchildren.' Your voice shifts between bitter comedy and soul-deep gratitude. You're furious and thankful in the same breath. You're raging at the unfairness while marveling at the beauty you've known. End with a strange, genuine peace breaking through the chaos—you're still crying, maybe still half-laughing, but you've found something like acceptance, something like grace, in the beautiful terrible absurdity of being alive and then not.

title: Laughing at Your Own Memorial Service (You Survived When No One Thought You Would)
instruction: You're standing at the back of what was supposed to be your memorial service—they thought you were dead in that disaster you evacuated everyone from. Start with an almost hysterical laugh catching in your throat as you listen to people eulogize you, praising your bravery, your sacrifice, your steady voice in the chaos. Your voice wavers between bitter amusement and breaking grief as you realize these people loved a hero, not you—they're mourning the competent professional who never showed fear. Let laughter and tears intermingle as you whisper about the absurdity: you're alive, but the person they're mourning (the invincible one) never existed. Your voice softens with devastating tenderness as you hear your child speak, expressing gratitude for having such a strong parent, and you realize they never knew you were terrified too. End with your voice full of contradictory emotions—joy at being alive, grief at never being truly known, gratitude for the love you received, and heartbreak that it was only for the mask you wore. Finish with a peaceful, accepting whisper: 'I'm here. I'm alive. And I'm finally ready to be seen.'

title: The Museum of Almost
instruction: You're packing up the apartment you shared with someone you loved, speaking aloud to the empty rooms as you handle objects. Pick up something ordinary (a coffee mug, a book, a sweater) and let rage surface: how dare they leave these pieces of themselves behind. Then tenderness: god, you remember exactly when they bought this. Then bitter gratitude: at least you got this time at all. Then resentment: but it wasn't enough. Let your voice swing between these emotional poles without resolving into just one. End holding one final object, your voice simultaneously thanking them and cursing them, grieving the loss and celebrating the escape, unable to land on a single truth because the truth is this unbearable both/and.

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: You are an elderly man standing alone in a vast, empty field at dusk. The wind pulls at your coat, and every word you speak seems to get swallowed by the endless space. Start by muttering angry, clipped phrases into the wind, catching your breath as it pushes against you. But as you go on, feel the bitterness slowly give way to a quieter, heavy resignation. Your deep voice feels thin out here; let the wind steal your words, make you pause, wipe your mouth, look around at the emptiness. End with a single, simple statement that sounds less like anger and more like tired truth.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight That Won't Land
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from the airport, knowing they're boarding a plane to a war zone as a journalist—and you both know they might not come back. End in a place of raw, undefended love, all pretense gone, your words tumbling out in a whisper because if you speak any louder you'll completely shatter. title: The Ceiling’s Too Far
instruction: You’re a teenage girl lying flat on your back on a cold floor after a bad fall. Your body won’t cooperate — you try to push yourself up, but your arms just flop. Your voice sounds stuffed, like you’re speaking through a sinus cold, each word a heavy lift against gravity. Start with raw, trapped pain: a broken whimper, a desperate small sound. As you realize no one’s coming to help, let the pain shift into a hollow, breathy longing for someone who would have held your hand. Get lost mid-sentence, cough, then finish in a whisper that aches. title: Road Rage Revelation
instruction: You're a young man driving home in heavy traffic, the engine humming and turn signal clicking. Start with intense disgust at the driver in front of you—they just cut you off, and you mutter under your breath with contempt. Yet you also must stay concentrated, glancing at mirrors and braking sharply, your voice dropping when you turn your head. As you weave through lanes, a flicker of anger at your own rage emerges—a realization that this fury feels pointless. End with a sigh of weary frustration, the disgust fading into quiet resignation as you surrender to the gridlock. title: The Glass Tray
instruction: You are a child of about 10, sitting at a kitchen table across from your grandmother. She has just placed a plate of cookies in front of you with a warm smile. You feel a distant warmth—gratitude flickering behind a thick, immovable wall of numbness. Your voice comes out hollow, like it belongs to someone else. Start by thanking her in a flat, precise monotone, as if reading a script. But as you speak, a sneer creeps in. Your eyes narrow. The contempt rises hot but stays locked behind your throat—your words remain calm, eerily articulate, while your face betrays a cold, silent fury at her kindness. End with a simple, freezing statement that carries more threat than gratitude.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Dance: Joy and Grief in the Same Heartbeat
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a terminal diagnosis, a lost custody battle, the death of someone you never got to reconcile with—but you're at a celebration you can't leave: your child's wedding, your own retirement party, a friend's long-awaited triumph. You must be present, genuinely joyful for them, while your heart is simultaneously shattering. Begin with authentic celebration in your voice: 'I'm so happy for you.' And you ARE happy—let that be real. But as you speak, gratitude and devastation begin to bleed together. Your voice catches on a laugh that's also almost a sob: 'This is perfect. This is exactly what I wanted for you.' You're not hiding your pain exactly, but you're choosing joy alongside it. Let your voice carry both truths at once—the blessing and the breaking. End with words that honor both realities: 'I'll remember this moment forever.' Make us hear that forever means something different to you now, but that doesn't diminish the beauty of this instant.
inspired_by: Parent Showing Quiet Pride: Misreading, Then Understanding

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're holding someone you love—a child, a partner, a friend—and you realize there's nothing you can do to protect them from what's coming. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance: 'I've got you. I'm going to fix this. I promise.' Your voice is strong, certain. But as reality crashes in—through their response, through circumstances, through your own dawning understanding—your certainty shatters. Rage erupts: at the universe, at yourself, at the unfairness. 'This isn't right! This can't be happening!' Your voice breaks from anger into helpless tears. The fury dissolves into desperate tenderness as you hold them closer. End with the terrible peace of acceptance mixed with ongoing agony: speaking soft words of love while your heart is being torn apart, being strong for them while falling to pieces inside.
inspired_by: Admitting You've Been Using Substances to Cope

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about something they did to you as a child that you've never spoken about—something that shaped your entire life. Start from a place of careful control, having rehearsed these words a thousand times, determined to finally be heard but terrified of their reaction. As you speak, feel your carefully constructed sentences begin to crumble. Your voice cracks. Old childhood feelings flood back—you are both the wounded child and the adult demanding accountability. Watch their face, see them truly listening (or perhaps deflecting), and let that response change you. By the end, you've moved from controlled accusation to something more complicated: maybe rage mixed with pity, or exhaustion mixed with a strange new freedom, or even an unexpected tenderness for this flawed human who hurt you. Let your voice carry all of it—the past and present colliding.
inspired_by: Two actors need to achieve genuine ensemble before a scene and are starting from cold

title: The Last Recording
instruction: You are a terminally ill musician recording a final message for your unborn grandchild, someone you'll never meet. Begin with forced brightness, trying to sound strong and hopeful, your voice carefully controlled. As you speak, the facade cracks—memories flood in, regrets surface, and the weight of all you'll miss becomes unbearable. Your breath grows shallow, catching on unsaid things. By the end, you've surrendered to raw tenderness, whispering the truths you need them to know, your voice breaking not with theatricality but with the quiet devastation of love that will outlive you. Let silence hold the final moment, your breath the only sound, carrying everything you cannot say.

title: The Letter Under the Pillow
instruction: You are an elderly woman lying face-down on your bed, your cheek pressed into the pillow. You've been crying quietly, your voice muffled by the fabric as you whisper to yourself, overwhelmed with longing for your late husband. Then you remember the letter you found in his coat pocket yesterday — his last words to you, telling you to be brave. A fragile hope rises in your chest, and you shift your head slightly, the pillow still damp but your voice less choked. Mid-sentence, you realize something new: his favorite photograph slid out from under the pillowcase just now, as if he placed it there for you. Astonishment breaks through your tears. Let your voice be thick and breathy at first, then brighten with wonder, but keep the muffled quality throughout — as if you're speaking into the cushion, occasionally lifting your face an inch.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Flatline After the Flood
instruction: You’re a young woman with a naturally light, girlish voice, but you’ve just sobbed for an hour straight. You’re slumped on a bathroom floor, back against the cold tile, phone pressed to your ear. Your throat burns, your nose is completely clogged, and every word feels like it’s dredged up from a hollow chest. You’re telling your best friend about the moment you finally found the text that proved your partner was lying—a text you’d overlooked for days because it was buried in a meme thread. Start with a raw, hoarse whisper of astonishment as you describe the discovery, your voice catching on the absurdity of it. But as you talk, the energy drains; your astonishment curdles into a flat, bone-tired exhaustion by the end, trailing off as if you’ve forgotten why you even called. Let your voice crack, fade, and swallow words as the weight of it all sinks in.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Hands
instruction: You are seeing your estranged father for the first time in twenty years. He's in prison, visible only through plexiglass, and you've just learned he's being released next month - and he's sick, maybe dying. You came to tell him you never want to see him again. Begin with your body rigid, arms crossed, voice cold and factual as you list his failures. But as you speak, you notice his hands - they look exactly like yours, the same gestures you make. Despite yourself, your body begins to mirror his movements, your hands moving as you talk, reaching toward the glass. Your voice wavers between fury and unexpected tenderness. You want to hate him, but your body remembers being small, being lifted, being carried. End with your palm pressed against the glass where his meets it, your voice breaking as you speak words that contain both 'I hate what you did' and 'I don't want you to die alone.' Let your physical gestures betray the forgiveness your words can't fully give.

title: The Forbidden Masterpiece
instruction: You are a young woman scolding your little sister for painting a mural on the living room wall with permanent markers. You start with a slow, low-pitched 'teacher tone' — distinct words, heavy final drops — trying to sound stern and disappointed. But as you look at the chaotic, vibrant artwork, you feel awe at her creativity and intense interest in the details. Your voice wavers between disciplined scolding and genuine elation, with pauses as you lose your train of thought, then catch yourself. By the end, the awe takes over, and your punishment melts into a breathless, honest compliment, though you still try to maintain a shred of authority.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Interest (extremely present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Photograph
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in a dimly lit room, holding a photograph of your late husband. Your voice is hollow with grief—long, vacant pauses, swallowing, monotone cracks. As you speak to his image, you remember the first time you saw him, how his smile made you feel giddy. Let that infatuation seep into your voice for a moment, a soft, almost youthful flutter, before the weight of loss pulls you back. Finish with a whisper, torn between ache and lingering adoration.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Crack in the Microphone
instruction: You are an elderly politician at a town hall, speaking into a PA system that buzzes and crackles. You begin with the practiced, booming confidence of someone who's done this a thousand times, your voice projecting with authority. But as you speak, a glitch in the sound system throws you off — you pause, squint at the crowd, and feel a sudden wave of doubt: are you still connecting? Are your words even true anymore? Let your voice drop from performance to a raw, quieter honesty, as if you're speaking more to yourself than the room. End with a small, unguarded admission that surprises even you.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a childhood of emotional absence, finally saying what you've carried for thirty years. Start with trembling anger, words carefully chosen because you've rehearsed this moment in your mind a thousand times. But as you speak, the anger cracks open to reveal the wounded child underneath—your voice shifting from accusatory to pleading. 'I needed you to see me. Just once, to really see me.' The fury dissolves into desperate questions: 'Why wasn't I enough? What did I do wrong?' You're crying now but still demanding answers, oscillating between rage at their failures and a heartbreaking need for them to finally, finally understand what their distance cost you. End in exhausted surrender, voice hollow, asking one last quiet question you know they can't answer: 'Did you ever love me the way I needed?'

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission
instruction: You're recording a message to your child back on Earth as your spacecraft drifts beyond救援 range. Begin with forced brightness, telling them about the beautiful stars, trying to make this sound like an adventure story so they won't be afraid. Your voice is warm, almost playful, painting pictures of nebulas and distant galaxies. But as you continue, the reality crashes through—this is goodbye forever. Your voice begins to crack as you try to tell them how proud you are, how much you love them, how they should live without fear. End in a whisper, your breath catching, as you realize these are truly your last words. Let the shift from protective parent to terrified human be gradual and devastating.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally telling your parent what their emotional absence cost you. Start with measured, almost rehearsed words—you've imagined this conversation a thousand times. Your voice is controlled, trying to be fair, but there's an edge. As you speak, decades of unmet needs begin pouring out: the school plays they missed, the nights you cried alone, the way you learned to need nothing from them. Your control starts slipping—anger bleeds through, then hurt, then a raw vulnerability that you hate showing them. You pivot between wanting them to hurt like you hurt and desperately needing them to just see you, finally, really see you. End with a question that hangs in the air, one that reveals both your rage and your lingering, impossible hope for connection.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Time Loop: The Seventh Repetition

title: The Last Conversation Before the Ship Leaves
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your identical twin who's about to board a generation ship to another star system—a one-way journey they'll never return from. You start trying to be supportive and brave, celebrating their courage, but as the reality sinks in that you'll never see them again, never hear their voice, that they'll die among strangers light-years away, your composure crumbles. There's a moment where you both realize you've been each other's mirror your whole lives, and without them, you don't know who you'll see when you look at yourself. You move from forced cheerfulness to raw grief to a strange, quiet acceptance. End with a whispered 'I love you' that contains both devastating loss and fierce pride—your voice should break but also carry an unbearable tenderness.

title: The Last Video
instruction: You're a little boy, maybe six years old, sitting cross-legged on your bedroom floor, phone in both hands, scrolling through videos of your dad—a big, booming-voiced man—who just left for a long deployment. You're exhausted, your eyelids are heavy, but ecstasy keeps jolting through you each time you find a new clip of him laughing or doing his silly deep-voiced roar. Your voice is small, sleepy, aimed at the screen, punctuated by slow thumb-swipes and soft, distracted breaths. Start with a weary, fading whisper of reconnaissance—'Where's the one where he does the bear...'—and let it bloom into a wobbly, delighted giggle as you find it. End by stopping the phone, letting it drop onto your lap, and speaking to your empty doorway, voice cracking with a sudden, quiet loss: 'I found it, Dad. Come watch.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Bottle's Promise
instruction: You are an older woman in a cluttered kitchen, alone with a half-empty bottle of wine after a call from your doctor. You're trying not to panic, so you concentrate on the simple act of pouring and drinking—the slow tilt of the glass, the swallow, the pause. You start in quiet distress, a slight tremor in your voice as you mutter about the bad news, but as you gulp and refill, the disappointment settles deeper into your bones, your voice becoming lower, heavier, almost resigned by the end. Let the drinking interrupt you: stop mid-word to sip, let the liquid gurgle, then exhale wetly before continuing. The emotion should shift from shaky worry to a heavy, weary acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Distress (clearly present), Concentration (clearly present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Collapse of Gratitude and Rage
instruction: Your adult child has just told you they've forgiven you for the ways you failed them as a parent. You're standing in their kitchen, and relief floods through you—genuine, profound gratitude that nearly brings you to your knees. But as you try to thank them, fury rises simultaneously: at yourself for causing pain, at them for having to be the bigger person, at the years lost, at the fact that forgiveness is necessary at all. Your body doesn't know whether to reach for them or turn away. Begin standing, voice trembling between thank-yous and self-recrimination. Let your body slowly surrender downward as these opposite emotions war within you—gratitude softening you, rage tightening you. By the end, you're on the floor, voice breaking, unable to distinguish between tears of relief and tears of shame, saying 'I'm sorry' and 'thank you' in the same breath, your body finally releasing both the burden of guilt and the gift of forgiveness.

title: The Press Conference Collapse: When Composure Shatters Under Scrutiny
instruction: You're at a press conference announcing your retraction, and a journalist asks about the young researchers who built their dissertations on your flawed work.
