Start controlled, your voice professionally measured as you acknowledge responsibility. But the question hits deeper than expected—these were your students, people you mentored, whose futures you've destroyed. Your voice tightens, anger flashing at the journalist for making this public spectacle even more cruel. The anger builds to something explosive: rage at yourself, at the universe, at the unfairness that doing the right thing requires annihilating innocent people's careers. Your voice cracks, professional veneer shattering completely. Then suddenly, tears. The rage collapses into helpless sobbing that you're trying desperately to suppress in front of cameras. End with your voice raw and broken, stripped of all authority: you're just a human who failed people who trusted you.
inspired_by: Professional: Researcher Publishes Findings That Contradict Their Own Previous Work

title: Electric Shock and Recovery
instruction: High-voltage electricity runs through you. Your voice is distorted, almost electronic—sharp, involuntary sounds as muscles contract. You're screaming but it sounds strange, inhuman. Then the current stops. You're on the ground, gasping, confused. Your voice is weak, confused. Everything hurts. Include the paramedic asking what happened—you can barely answer. Your speech is stuttered, your breathing irregular. By the end, you're shaking violently, your voice unstable.

title: The Breaking Point Voicemail
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for your partner after discovering their betrayal. Start with your voice shaking, trying to maintain composure, almost businesslike—'We need to talk.' But within seconds, rage erupts. Your voice becomes fierce, loud, accusatory, each word a weapon. You're shouting now, years of ignored intuition validating itself. Then suddenly, mid-fury, you break completely. The anger collapses into sobbing, into disbelief, your voice small and lost: 'How could you?' The explosive energy drains into helplessness. End with the devastating quiet of someone realizing they're grieving not just the betrayal but the death of who they thought their person was. Ride the full storm—thunder to whimper.

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're thanking someone for something that destroyed you but also saved you—a breakup that freed you, a loss that taught you who you are, a betrayal that led you to yourself. Start with a laugh that's absolutely genuine, almost euphoric: 'You know what's funny?' Your voice is light, even joyful as you begin listing what you're grateful for. But underneath the gratitude, grief is rising. As you speak, the laughter starts catching in your throat. You're genuinely thankful and genuinely heartbroken at the same time. Your voice wavers between celebration and mourning—'Thank you for leaving me' said with both liberation and devastation. End with words that are simultaneously the most grateful and the most grief-stricken thing you've ever said: 'I'm so glad you broke my heart.' Mean both truths completely.

title: The Pet Translator
instruction: Act as someone who believes they can interpret pet sounds. Use serious, thoughtful tones when translating barks or meows, switching to the pets imagined sarcastic comments.

title: The Emergency Room Rage
instruction: Your child, partner, or sibling has overdosed, attempted suicide, or been in a terrible accident due to their own reckless choices, and you're in the hospital corridor when they wake up. Explode from the gate—you're screaming, voice raw and ragged: 'How could you DO this? How could you be so selfish?!'—your rage is volcanic because you've been terrified for hours. But mid-tirade, as they look at you with broken eyes or turn their face away, your fury shatters into desperate, gasping sobs. Your voice fractures: 'I can't lose you, don't you understand that? I can't—' You collapse into fierce, protective love mixed with absolute helplessness. End on your knees or clutching them, voice hoarse and destroyed, oscillating between anger and tenderness: 'Please don't leave me. Please. I need you here.' Let rage and terror and overwhelming love crash into each other until you don't know which is which.

title: Suppressing Annoyance While Dealing With a Difficult Person
instruction: Someone is being challenging, but you need to remain professional. Internally, frustration builds, but you keep a polite demeanor. Describe the irritation inside while maintaining courteous interaction. Speak with a pleasant tone, hiding your annoyance.

title: The Returning Tide
instruction: You're reuniting with someone you thought you'd never see again—a lover who disappeared, who you've grieved as if they were dead. You open your door and they're standing there. Begin by noticing the shock in your body—the sudden inability to breathe, the weakness in your knees, the specific way time seems to stop, the rushing sound in your ears, the temperature draining from your extremities. Start frozen, almost in denial. Then let your body respond before your mind can—feel the heat flooding through you, your hands beginning to shake, your pulse pounding everywhere at once. Move from paralyzed disbelief into overwhelming physical sensation: rage at being abandoned, desperate longing, the physical ache of having missed them. Let these collide—scream if you need to, or collapse, or grab them. End in a place where your body's response completely overtakes rational thought, where passion and fury and relief become indistinguishable, where you're acting purely on sensation rather than decision.
inspired_by: Affective Memory via Imaging (Court of Last Resort example)

title: The Kitchen Table Confessional
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent at the kitchen table where you ate breakfast as a child. You came here to tell them one simple truth they've never known. Start by looking at the table itself - the wood grain, the scratches, a coffee stain. Let your mind unlock what this table has witnessed: every silent breakfast, every lie told across its surface, every meal swallowed with unsaid words. Allow the table to become alive with memories that grow increasingly strange - maybe you see younger versions of yourself sitting in the chairs, maybe the table is breathing, maybe the grain pattern spells out secrets. Let these images fuel your courage and rage. Begin tentative, circling around what you need to say. But as the images intensify and become more bizarre, let them propel you toward the raw confession. Transform from careful and controlled to unleashed and unfiltered, finally speaking the truth that the table has been holding for years.
inspired_by: Actor's imagination feels weak, overly literal, or unable to generate creative choices

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that defined your childhood—the missed recitals, the withheld affection, the silence where love should have been. Start with contained anger, listing the moments they weren't there, your voice tight with decades of swallowed hurt. But as you speak, you see them shrinking, aging before you, and you realize: they don't have much time left. Your rage must collide with the terrifying recognition that soon they'll be gone, and this pain will be all you have left of them. Shift from accusation to a desperate, vulnerable plea: 'I needed you. I still need you. Can you see me now, before it's too late?' Let your voice crack between fury at what you didn't get and grief for what you're about to lose forever.

title: Thanking Someone Who Saved You by Destroying Themselves
instruction: You're expressing gratitude to someone who sacrificed everything to give you a chance at life—but their sacrifice destroyed them. Begin with genuine, overflowing thanks, listing what their gift made possible for you. Your voice is warm, full of joy for the life you've lived. But underneath, grief is rising: their beautiful gesture came at an unbearable cost. You're laughing through tears, celebrating your survival while mourning theirs. Your gratitude becomes inseparable from guilt and sorrow. You want them to know it was worth it while simultaneously wishing they hadn't had to make that choice. End in the impossible space between joy and heartbreak: you're alive because they're diminished, and you're grateful and devastated in the same breath. Your voice holds both realities without resolving the contradiction.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Soldier Realizes the War They've Been Fighting Is Based on False Intelligence

title: The Light at the End
instruction: You are an elderly woman driving home through heavy traffic. The sun is setting, casting a warm glow that momentarily blinds you as you change lanes. You begin to mutter to yourself, half complaining about the delay, but then you notice a row of trees in the distance, their leaves just beginning to turn autumn colors. In that moment, a quiet hope surfaces—you remember you have a grandchild visiting next week. Your voice starts tense, annoyed, with pauses to check mirrors and signal. As you speak, let the weariness soften, your breath deepen, and your tone lift just slightly, as if the thought itself brightens the car. End with a gentle, almost amazed smile in your voice, even as you keep one eye on the road.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Reading Own Eulogy
instruction: You're a terminally ill person who's decided to attend your own funeral and read your own eulogy. Your voice starts steady: 'Hello. I'm here to tell you about someone who just died.' The surreality of it is in your voice. 'I am that someone.' There's dark humor there, and genuine reflection. 'I've had a life full of love and mistakes and growth.' Your voice becomes reflective: 'I want you to know I'm not afraid. I'm grateful.' You speak about the people you love, and your voice cracks on their names. 'Tell them I said I was proud of them. Tell them I'm still here in the memories we made.' By the end, you're reading through tears: 'Life is short. Don't waste it on regret. Love hard. Live fully. And know that the people you love become part of you forever.' You close the eulogy: 'Thank you for loving me.'

title: Rain in the Cemetery
instruction: You're visiting the grave of your spouse on what would have been your fiftieth wedding anniversary, and something unexpected happens—you start laughing. Begin with that laugh, genuine and a little surprised at yourself: 'God, you would have loved this. It's pouring rain and I forgot an umbrella. Again.' You're smiling through tears, remembering. 'You always said I'd forget my own head if it wasn't attached.' The laughter is real, warm, full of love. But then it catches, and suddenly you're crying and laughing at the same time, the emotions inseparable: 'We were supposed to be in Italy right now. Remember? Venice for our fiftieth.' Your voice breaks but there's still light in it somehow: 'You planned everything. Even picked out the restaurant.' Then the devastating beauty—you're overcome with gratitude even as your heart is shattering: 'Thank you. For forty-seven years of mornings. For every stupid argument and every perfect moment.' You're weeping but there's peace in it, profound and real: 'I'm so grateful I got to love you. Even though it hurts this much now, I'd do it all again.' A beat. Then, with tender humor through tears: 'But next time, try to stick around for Venice, okay?' You touch the headstone with such tenderness. 'I miss you. And I'm okay. Somehow, I'm both.' End in that impossible space where grief and gratitude live together, where you're completely broken and somehow whole.

title: Whispering Goodbye Between Floors
instruction: You're in an elevator with your best friend who's moving across the world tomorrow for a marriage you know is wrong for them. You both keep making light conversation—'Remember that coffee shop on Fifth?'—but your voice is thick with everything unsaid. The performance should be quiet, intimate, tender. Each mundane memory you share ('That time we got lost in Brooklyn...') carries the weight of goodbye. Your voice keeps almost breaking, then steadying itself. Midway through, let one truth slip out in a near-whisper: 'I don't think you should go.' The silence that follows is devastating. Continue with your voice even softer, more fragile: 'But I love you enough to let you.' By the final floor, you're holding back tears, managing only: 'Be happy, okay? Just... find a way to be happy.' The doors open and you have to let them walk away. The last moment is you trying to smile while your heart shatters.

title: The Calm Before the Hunt
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman hiding in a motel room, drugged with a sedative to keep you quiet. Your voice is unnaturally flat, as if all emotion has been vacuumed out. But you’re terrified—a man is searching for you just outside. You call your daughter to say goodbye in a way that sounds eerily calm, but as you hang up and hear footsteps stop at your door, the fear cracks through your drug-numbed lips. Your words should start slow and mushy, like you’re fighting to form them, then tighten with a tremor of pure panic by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Broken Promise
instruction: You're sitting on the edge of your bed, picking at a loose thread on your jeans, unable to look up. Your best friend stands in the doorway, arms crossed, waiting. You promised to keep their secret, but you messed up. Start defensive, voice a little sharp—but as you explain, you feel your own disappointment creep in. Let your volume drop, hesitate on the hard part, and end in a quiet, almost whispered admission. The last words should feel like you're letting the weight settle in your chest.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Worst Timing
instruction: You're sitting across from someone you've been hopelessly infatuated with for months — finally alone together. You're mid-sentence, trying to sound charming and composed, when a sudden fit of coughing explodes out of you, leaving your voice raw and unsteady. The infatuation is intense, but the embarrassment burns hot as you struggle to speak through the spasms. Let each cough break your rhythm, forcing you to restart, your voice cracking and wet. By the end, you're still smitten but humiliated, your words trailing off as you give up trying to recover.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Embarrassment (slightly present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Photographs on the Floor
instruction: You are kneeling on the floor surrounded by old photographs after someone has died or left forever. Begin by picking them up one by one, letting fragmented early memories surface—not the photos themselves, but the sensory ghosts they trigger: a hand holding yours, a pattern on wallpaper, the feeling of being lifted, abstract shapes and shadows. You are flooded with contradictory feelings: relief they're gone and desperate longing for them back, gratitude for what they gave you and rage at what they took. Don't reconcile these opposites—let them crash into each other. Your voice should move through laughter-tears, anger-tenderness, fragments of different ages of yourself speaking. End by discovering which emotion wins, or by holding both fully in your body at once.

title: Before You Go
instruction: You're helping your adult child pack for a journey they may not return from—overseas humanitarian work in a conflict zone. Your voice is tender but trembling as you fold their clothes: 'I put the photo in the side pocket. The one from your eighth birthday.' Breathing catches in your throat. You're trying to be strong but every object you touch feels like it might be the last connection. 'You've always been braver than me. Even when you were little.' Your voice drops to barely a whisper, thick with unshed tears: 'Come back to me. Please, just... come back.' End with you pressing something into their hands—maybe a letter, a charm—voice breaking completely: 'You are my heart walking around outside my body.' Navigate from gentle support to quiet, devastating vulnerability.

title: The Wedding Toast Undone
instruction: You're giving a toast at the wedding of someone you love—your best friend, your sibling, your child—but you're harboring secret heartbreak about this marriage (you love the person getting married, you know this marriage is wrong, you're losing them). Begin with the expected words: funny stories, well-wishes, celebration. Your voice is warm, your smile genuine because your love is real. But let your deeper feelings leak in—a catch in your voice, a word choice that reveals too much, a pause that goes too long. The joy of their happiness and the devastation of your loss must coexist in every sentence. Build until you're almost revealing too much, then pull back into the safety of the expected sentiment, but now everyone—including you—can feel what's underneath. End with 'I love you' that contains both pure joy for them and shattering grief for yourself. Move from performed celebration to barely-contained heartbreak to genuine blessing despite pain.
inspired_by: Actor's inner life disconnects from scripted text during scene work

title: Whispering to Someone in a Coma
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply, who may never wake up. The room is quiet except for machines. Your voice is barely audible—you're confessing things you never had the courage to say when they could respond. Start tender, almost shy, admitting small truths. 'I never told you this, but...' The intimacy is excruciating because there's no answer coming. Your throat tightens. You share a memory that makes you smile through gathering tears. Then the vulnerability deepens—you tell them what your life will be like without them, how lost you already feel. End with a whispered plea that's half-prayer, half-conversation, knowing they might never hear it.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally telling your parent about the abuse they saw but never stopped - something that happened decades ago but still lives in your body. Start with your voice shaking, almost apologetic for bringing it up: 'I need to talk about what happened when I was twelve.' As they try to deflect or minimize, your voice hardens with anger: 'No, you're going to listen to this.' Let rage build as you describe what you needed from them - protection, belief, action. But then your voice cracks into the child you were: 'I just needed you to see me.' End with exhausted grief, not seeking their comfort anymore, just stating truth: 'I deserved a parent who chose me.' Your voice becomes quiet steel - no longer asking, just knowing.

title: Reading the Goodbye Letter They Left Behind
instruction: You're holding a letter from someone you loved who's now gone—by death, by choice, by circumstance—and you're reading it aloud to yourself in an empty room. Start with a kind of desperate laughter, almost manic, because the first lines are so characteristically them, so alive, that for a moment you forget they're gone. Your voice should dance between sobbing and laughing as memories flood back with each sentence. They're telling you something beautiful about your impact on their life, and it's killing you because you never knew, and now it's too late. Let your voice move from tearful laughter to profound gratitude to gut-wrenching grief and back again. End in a strange, peaceful place—still crying but also smiling, your voice soft with acceptance, whispering 'thank you' to someone who can't hear you, finding an inexplicable moment of grace in the middle of your shattered heart.

title: The List of Envy
instruction: You're a teenage boy dictating a list of 'items needed for the project' into a voice recorder for transcription. But this list is actually a detailed inventory of everything your rival has that you covet — their grades, their phone, their friends, even their voice. You must keep your voice fast, steady, and monotone, speaking punctuation like 'comma' and 'period.' But as you go deeper, the jealousy and malice seep through: your pace stumbles, your tone sharpens on certain words, you swallow hard, almost spit out a line. Start cold and robotic, end with a barely controlled snarl, your voice cracking with envy. Spoken lines: 'Item one comma his straight As period. Item two comma his laugh that everyone likes period. Item three comma his phone — dash — the one with the cracked screen — no comma, no, scratch that — his new one period. Period. Period. I mean period.' You have about 50 words.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unchanging Steps
instruction: You are an elderly man in a concrete stairwell, your breath echoing off the hard walls. Your joints throb with a familiar, grinding pain as you pause halfway up, pressing your palm against the cold surface. Begin with the stubborn rhythm of someone who refuses to give in to age, but let the ache crack your voice as you speak to the empty landing. Allow the harsh reverb to amplify your words, and finish with a quiet admissions—your body has changed, and the pain is all that's real now.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Bragging Rights
instruction: You’re a teenage boy in a locker room, trying to show off after a brutal set of push-ups. Now you’re bent over, hands on your knees, head down, fighting for air. Start with a cocky, breathless boast about how many you did — your voice thick and congested from the blood rush. But as you talk, the fatigue catches up; you lose your train of thought, your words slur, and by the end you admit with a ragged laugh that you can’t feel your arms anymore. Let your body’s strain pull the bravado out of you, so the last line sounds more like surrender than swagger.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: Speak to someone who hurt you deeply but also, paradoxically, changed your life for the better. Maybe a parent whose harshness taught you strength, a partner whose abandonment forced you to find yourself, a friend whose betrayal revealed who you really are. Begin with what you want them to know about the pain they caused - be specific, honest, unflinching. Then let something unexpected happen: you start to recognize what emerged from the wreckage. This isn't forgiveness or justification, it's something more complex - simultaneous resentment and gratitude, anger and odd affection, grief for what was lost and appreciation for who you became. Let these contradictions live in your voice at the same time. End in a place of unsettling peace, where opposite truths coexist.

title: The Secret Sketchbook
instruction: Late at night, you're showing your closest friend a sketchbook you've never shared with anyone—pages filled with drawings of them, moments you've captured over years of quiet longing. Your voice is barely above a whisper, shaking with vulnerability as you confess what these drawings mean, what they've meant to keep secret for so long. They're gentle with you, but you hear it—the careful kindness of someone who doesn't feel the same way. Your voice becomes even smaller, almost disappearing as you try to laugh it off, to pretend this wasn't your heart you just handed them. There's a long pause where you can't speak at all, just the sound of breathing. Then your voice returns, fragile as glass, as you quietly ask them to forget you showed them. The words catch in your throat because you both know neither of you will ever forget this moment, and something precious and painful has just changed forever between you.
inspired_by: Showing Your Art to Someone Who Doesn't Get It

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church
instruction: You've just lost your child. You're alone in the church after everyone has left the funeral. Start kneeling, trying to pray the way you were taught, voice steady and faithful. But the platitudes taste like ash. Your voice begins to shake, then rises—you're arguing with God, demanding answers, your grief transforming into scorching rage. Why this? Why your baby? Your voice should crack between fury and anguish, loud enough to echo in the empty space. Pound the pews. Let your voice shred. But then, in the middle of your rage, something breaks and you collapse—not into quiet acceptance, but into helpless, body-wracking sobs mixed with desperate bargaining. You're offering anything, everything, just to have one more day. End with your voice raw and destroyed, reduced to whimpers, asking not for understanding but just for the strength to survive the next hour.
inspired_by: Phone Sex Partner Realizing They're Emotionally Attached

title: Final Transmission to a Dying Astronaut
instruction: You're mission control speaking to an astronaut whose oxygen system has failed during a solo spacewalk. You have twelve minutes left together. Begin with your trained, professional voice trying to troubleshoot systems, maintaining hope and procedure. As each solution fails, your composure cracks—voice tightening, pauses growing longer. By the final minutes, you've abandoned protocol entirely. You're just two people who've worked together for years, and you're whispering things you should have said before: how much their friendship meant, how their family will be okay, how you wish you could have saved them. End with you staying on the line in silence after they're gone, unable to let go of the connection. Move from clinical professionalism to raw, helpless love—the kind that makes your throat close and your words come out broken.

title: Vigil Confessions: Truths Whispered to the Dying
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in their final hours—a lover, parent, or estranged friend. They're unconscious, barely breathing. You have this last chance to say what was never said. Start in barely-audible whispers, tentative, testing if you can even speak these truths aloud. 'I need to tell you something I've carried for so long...' Your voice is intimate, close, fragile. Confess something that's haunted you—a secret love, a lie, a betrayal, forgiveness you withheld. As you speak, emotion catches in your throat repeatedly. You're not performing; you're unburdening your soul to someone who can no longer respond. Let silence have weight between phrases. Your breathing matters as much as your words. End with tender acceptance or devastating regret—let tears come naturally if they do, but the power is in the quiet breaking, not the volume.
inspired_by: ASMR Gone Wrong: Increasingly Agitated Whisperer

title: The Tongue of Angels
instruction: You're a young girl, maybe eight or nine, kneeling on a hard wooden pew in a crowded, sweltering revival tent. The preacher's voice is a distant roar, but you're trying to concentrate on the words of a hymn you're supposed to be memorizing — '…and with the morning, I will rise…' — your lips move silently, your brow furrows. But the tambourines start, the drumbeat thumps in your chest, and a strange heat floods your body. Your focus begins to slip; the hymn dissolves into a feeling you can't name. A woman near you screams 'Hallelujah' and suddenly your own mouth opens — the sounds that come out aren't English, they're a liquid, musical babble. Let your voice start tight and careful, a child rehearsing, then let it break open into a rising, rhythmic chant where you don't care if you make sense. Cry, laugh, repeat a phrase — feel the rational part of you fall away into pure, ecstatic release.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Person Who Saved Your Life About the Cost
instruction: You're facing someone who rescued you years ago—from addiction, abuse, suicide—and you're furious. Start explosive: they had no right, you didn't ask for this, they saved you for themselves not for you. Let rage fill your entire voice, body, breath. But mid-fury, something breaks—because you're also alive because of them. The anger fractures into helpless tears, you're sobbing and shouting simultaneously. You hate that you're grateful. You're furious that you love them. The final words come out fierce and protective and utterly contradictory: demanding they never do it again while begging them not to leave. Your voice should feel like it's tearing in multiple directions at once.
inspired_by: Confessing Long-Buried Resentment to Your Parent

title: Lavender and Longing
instruction: You are lying in a warm bath, post-massage, every muscle completely melted. The air smells of lavender, and your voice is slow, heavy, satisfied. You're thinking about your best friend — the one you've secretly adored for years — and you know they're out with someone new tonight. Let a flicker of jealousy rise in your chest, tight and warm, but don't let it break your relaxation. Murmur to yourself, almost to the bathwater, letting the envy soften into pure, aching affection. Start with a languid, dreamy hum, then let the words slow and thicken with feeling, ending on a tender, sighing note.
emotions_sampled: Distress (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Affection (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother who raised you. She has only minutes left. Begin by feeling the crushing weight of impending loss—let your voice crack with grief as you start to speak. But as you look at her face, you consciously shift: start naming every beautiful thing she gave you, every moment of light she brought into your life. Let each memory you speak aloud lift you slightly, transforming your despair into profound gratitude. By the end, you should be smiling through tears, your voice filled with celebration of her life rather than mourning of her death. The arc moves from drowning in loss to floating on love. Speak as if each positive word you offer is a gift you're placing in her hands before she goes.

title: Tangled Laces, Bitter Taste
instruction: You're a child, bent over with your hands on the floor, trying to untie a stubborn knot in your shoelace. Your head is heavy, blood rushing, breath short. Start by muttering to yourself, intensely focused on the task, your voice thick and muffled as you concentrate. Midway, you hit a frustrating snag—the knot tightens, your fingers slip, and sourness creeps in. Let your voice shift from determined grunts to a petulant, whiny complaint, still strained from the position. Say about 50-70 words, reacting to the physical discomfort and the mounting irritation.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Curious Creak
instruction: You are an older woman climbing the stairs in your creaky old house, drawn by a faint scratching sound from the attic. At the start, you feel a slight unease—your knee aches, the steps groan under your weight, and you half-expect a mouse or worse. But your curiosity is stronger: what could it be? As you climb, pause to catch your breath, grip the railing, and murmur to yourself about the noise. Let your voice rise with effort, sentences coming in short bursts. By the time you reach the top, the fear has faded into amused interest—maybe it's just a pinecone rolling on the roof. Your tone shifts from wary to lightly entertained, breathing heavy but lighter in spirit.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kitchen at 2 AM
instruction: You've come home to confront your father about something you discovered—proof of a betrayal that shattered your family years ago, something he's denied for a decade. Begin with cold, controlled fury; your words are sharp, precise, weaponized. Your jaw is tight, your breathing shallow with rage. But as you speak, allow a buried memory to surface through your body: a moment when he held you, protected you, made you feel safe. Let the physical sensation of that safety—his hand on your shoulder, his voice saying your name—flood through you even as you're trying to stay angry. By the end, you're no longer accusing; you're begging him to explain how both versions of him can exist, your voice raw with the desperate need to understand, rage dissolving into bewildered grief.

title: Remembering Wrong, Loving Right
instruction: You're giving a tour of your childhood home or your late partner's favorite place, and you keep getting the facts hilariously wrong—dates, names, historical details—and each time you're corrected, you laugh at yourself with genuine delight. But underneath the laughter, your heart is shattering because the person who would have lovingly corrected you is gone. Let joy and grief intertwine completely: laugh through tears, find beauty in your terrible memory, express deep gratitude for having had someone who knew you well enough to catch your mistakes. End with a moment of profound peace mixed with aching loss, as you realize that loving them was worth all of this pain.

title: The Last Clear Morning
instruction: You are sitting at the bedside of someone you've known your entire life—a grandparent, mentor, or old friend—in their final hours. Begin by noticing everything: the quality of light through the window, the sound of their breathing, the temperature of their hand in yours, the smell of the room. Start with practical numbness, going through motions of comfort. As you truly register each sensory detail, let memories flood back—not nostalgic and sweet, but urgent, specific, alive. Notice things about them you never consciously saw before: the pattern of veins on their hand, the exact color of their eyes, how their breath catches. Move from emotional shutdown into desperate presence, as if by observing intensely enough you could hold them here. End in a place of piercing clarity and connection, having truly seen them perhaps for the first time, just as you're losing them forever.
inspired_by: Actor wants to deepen consciousness and eliminate blind spots about their own obstacles

title: You Really Did That?
instruction: You're sitting cross-legged on the floor, leaning back on your hands, a little tight in the hips from the position. Your buddy just told you the most absurd story about their attempt to impress a crush by pretending to know about bird-watching. You start off teasing them with a dry, almost skeptical edge — just a little jab. But as you keep talking, the sheer ridiculousness of the memory hits you anew, and your amusement swells until you're practically laughing through your words, your voice catching and your posture loosening as you shake your head. Let yourself pause to snort or shift your weight mid-sentence, and let the final line come out half-grin, half-sigh of pure joy.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: You Actually Told Me
instruction: You're on a rooftop, coming down from a binge. Your friend just confessed he sold you out to your enemies. The coke makes you talk fast, loud, sniffing between words, throat numb. Start with contemptuous astonishment—laughing bitterly, interrupting yourself. But as you speak, the exhaustion hits: your voice cracks, you trail off, the bravado drains into hollow fatigue. Let the physical stimulant effects shape every word—raspy, congested, restless. End in quiet, tired disbelief.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Against the Current
instruction: You are a mother rowing a boat against a strong current, your young child sitting in the bow. Each stroke is a battle: you grunt as you pull, then gasp out words during the slide forward. You're deeply disappointed — you wanted to reach the quiet cove for a picnic, but the current is winning. As you pull again, your child points and says, 'It's okay, Mommy, we can just have snacks here.' You feel a wave of relief, small but real. Speak your response between breaths, your voice strained, jaw tight from effort, the words coming in bursts with the rhythm of the oars.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Flower Girl's Forgotten Lines
instruction: You are a shy 8-year-old flower girl who has been unexpectedly handed the microphone to say a few words at your aunt's wedding. You start in sheer embarrassment — your voice is tiny, wavering, and you keep glancing at your shiny shoes. Midway, you spot your grandmother crying in the front row, and your heart softens into a quiet, sweet joy as you fumble through a simple, honest wish. Speak with long, nervous pauses, a tremor from the public speaking, and a hyper-feminized, breathy tone that grows more tender. 'Um... I was s'posed to throw petals... but Aunt Lily said I could say... (pause, shift weight) ...that I hope she's happy... like, really happy... all the time... (voice fades, then brighter) ...and that I love her dress.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Protecting Someone You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone you love fiercely—a child, a younger sibling, someone you've always protected—and you've just learned something devastating that will hurt them, change them, shatter their world. Maybe someone they trusted betrayed them. Maybe their dream is impossible. Maybe you have to deliver news that will break their heart. You start with fierce protectiveness, your voice strong, promising them everything will be okay—but you're lying and you know it. Let that helplessness crack through. Your reassurances become desperate. Your voice rises with passionate intensity, trying to will safety into existence through sheer force of love. Then let it collapse. Let the rage at your own powerlessness explode—not at them, but at the universe, at whoever hurt them, at yourself for being unable to fix this. Your voice might shake with fury, then break into something raw and devastated. End in radical honesty: 'I can't protect you from this, but I'm not going anywhere.' Move from fierce strength to explosive helplessness to tender, broken presence.
inspired_by: Acting Happy for Someone When Youre Heartbroken

title: The Last Jeans
instruction: You're a 17-year-old girl standing in your dead father's closet, holding a pair of his faded jeans. You're supposed to pack his things for donation, but you can't stop gripping the denim. Start bitter—spitting out angry memories of how he always chose work over you, how he missed your plays and birthdays. Let that anger crack as you realize these jeans still smell like him. End with a hollow whisper, almost to yourself, admitting you'd trade all your bitterness just to have him ignore you one more time.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Steel Walls, Unspoken Words
instruction: You are an older adult stepping into an empty elevator after a difficult family dinner. The doors close and the mechanical hum wraps around you. For a moment, you feel relief — it's over. A teasing smile flickers as you recall Aunt Carol's ridiculous hat. But then the metallic echo bounces your own voice back at you: did you handle that confrontation right? Start light, almost amused, then let doubt creep in as you replay the conversation. The hard surfaces seem to throw your thoughts back, challenging them. End with a quiet, questioning exhale.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Relief (slightly present), Doubt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Childhood Home While Your Parent Dies Upstairs
instruction: You're walking through empty rooms, touching walls, standing in doorways. Hospice is upstairs. You start by laughing softly—genuinely—at memories. 'You spilled paint right here, remember? Mom was so mad.' Your voice is warm, almost light, talking to someone who maybe can't respond but you hope can hear. You're sharing stories, grateful ones, funny ones. But the laughter keeps catching, mixing with tears you're trying to hold back. The gratitude and the grief become inseparable. 'Thank you for—' and your voice breaks. You're thanking them for everything while saying goodbye, finding the beauty in what you had while your heart shatters knowing it's ending. End with a whispered blend of 'I love you,' 'thank you,' and 'goodbye,' where peace and devastation exist in the same moment. Your voice should carry both the lightness of treasured memories and the weight of irrevocable loss.
inspired_by: Two People Breaking Up Over Assembling IKEA Furniture

title: Archaeology of an Intimate Hour
instruction: You are lying in bed beside someone you love, unable to sleep, and you're about to whisper a vulnerable truth you've never spoken aloud. The darkness feels thick around you. As you gather courage, you become aware of small details that connect you to this person: the rhythm of their breathing, the warmth of their skin near yours, the scent of their hair on the pillow, the weight of their hand near your own, the sound of rain on the window that you've listened to together before, the photograph on the nightstand from a moment when you felt safe. Let each sensory detail you notice either draw you closer to speaking or make you want to retreat into silence. Begin with your heart racing, your whisper barely audible, the words catching in your throat. As you take in each tender detail around you, let it give you the courage to speak more openly, until the confession pours out with a raw honesty that leaves you both exposed and relieved.
inspired_by: Surround Yourself with Meaningful and Impacting Choices

title: Begging Your Child Not to Make Your Mistakes
instruction: Your teenage child just told you they're doing exactly what destroyed your life years ago. Start with explosive rage — shouting 'You have no idea what you're doing!' Let your voice crack with fury and desperation. You're yelling about consequences, about pain, about everything you survived. But then you see their face — defiant, just like you were. Your anger collapses. Your voice drops, becomes urgent and pleading. Get on their level. Your words tumble out: 'I'm not angry, I'm terrified.' Describe what it cost you, voice shaking, tears coming despite yourself. End almost whispering: 'Please. Please don't make me watch you go through what I went through.'
inspired_by: Whispering a Secret in a Crowded Room

title: Gratitude at the Ending of Everything
instruction: You're expressing profound gratitude to someone as your world falls apart—a relationship ending, a life concluding, a chapter closing that you desperately wanted to continue. Your voice carries genuine thankfulness that keeps colliding with heartbreak. Begin with words of appreciation that already have tears underneath them. You're smiling as you speak, even laughing softly at memories, but the laughter keeps catching in your throat, transforming into something that sounds like crying. Let joy and grief live in the same breath. You're experiencing the strange peace of accepting loss while simultaneously feeling it tear through you. Move through moments of warm reminiscence that dissolve into quiet devastation, then back to grateful recognition of what was precious. End with words that somehow hold both 'thank you for everything' and 'goodbye forever' in the same trembling voice, finding strange beauty in the contradiction, your tone carrying both completion and unbearable sorrow.

title: The Strangled Promise
instruction: You're a young man, pinned against a wall by someone you once trusted, their forearm pressed across your throat. You're struggling to breathe, each word a raspy, choked effort. You speak with malice, a cold, biting edge to every strained syllable, but as you talk, a sliver of interest lights your eyes—you're fascinated by their desperation. Then, against all odds, a desperate, radiant hope floods your voice; you see a way out, and you sell it with a feverish, strained optimism that makes your threats tremble into something almost tender. Let your voice crack, let the pressure steal your breath mid-sentence, and let the malice sour into a hopeful plea that sounds like a prayer.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Interest (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Hour at the Hospice Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hour. Begin by noticing everything you're feeling in your body right now - the chair beneath you, your breathing, the actual state of your heart. As you speak to them, let yourself discover moment-by-moment what's真正 present: maybe unexpected numbness where you expected tears, or sudden anger mixed with tenderness, or a strange awareness of the radiator's hum. Don't perform grief - instead, keep checking in with what's actually alive in you second by second. Let the scene move from whatever genuine state you find yourself in (perhaps detachment or shock) toward whatever emerges organically by the end - maybe a raw breaking open, or perhaps a surprising sense of peace. Allow silences where you simply breathe and feel. Your final words to them should come from whatever truth has revealed itself through this honest tracking of your inner landscape.

title: Vigil at Three AM
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's sleeping—a dying parent, a child in the hospital, a lover who tried to end their life—and you're speaking to them in the quiet darkness, not sure if they can hear. Start with soft, almost trivial things: observations about the sounds of the hospital, a memory of breakfast last Tuesday. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and careful, as if normal volume might shatter something. But slowly, the words you've never said begin to surface: regrets, confessions, the things you were too proud or too scared to voice. Let your voice catch. Let silences speak. Move from protective gentleness to raw vulnerability—the kind that only comes at three AM when you think no one's listening. End with something unbearably simple and true that you've never been able to say before.

title: The Keys in Your Hand
instruction: You're standing in the empty apartment holding the keys to your first home—truly yours, after years of struggle. The walls are bare, the windows are open, and there's nothing here but space and possibility and your own breathing. Begin by letting yourself feel the sheer joy of this: the weight of the keys, the echo of your footsteps, the way sunlight falls on floors that belong to you. Laugh, spin, let your body be light with victory. But as you stand still in the center of the empty living room, let yourself also feel the devastating absence of the person who should be here sharing this with you—the one you lost, the one who didn't live to see this day, the one who left, the one who chose not to be here. Feel how these emotions exist simultaneously: euphoric pride and crushing loneliness. Notice which one tightens your throat, which one makes you want to dance, how they alternate or blend. End in a place where you're blessing this space—for yourself and for the ghost of who's missing—claiming your joy even as you honor your grief.

title: The Wooden Soldier
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone in your armchair late at night, having taken cannabis to ease your aching joints. You're trying to recount a memory of carving a wooden soldier with your father, but the drug and deep exhaustion are pulling you under. Start with a gruff, deliberate voice as you reach for the story, then let your words slow and drift — long pauses, sticky lip sounds, losing the thread. End with your voice barely a whisper, trailing off as you give in to sleep.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Breath Before the Door Closes
instruction: You're standing at the threshold of your childhood home for the final time before it's sold. Take a slow, deliberate breath in—this air holds thirty years of memories. Start calm, almost detached, describing what you smell: your mother's lavender soap still faint in the hallway, old wood, dust settling on emptied rooms. But as you breathe deeper, let the weight of finality crack through your composure. Your voice should fracture as you realize you're inhaling ghosts—birthday mornings, arguments that shaped you, the scent of safety you'll never smell again. End by exhaling all that loss, your words barely a whisper, as if releasing your grip on a life you can't hold onto anymore. Let the breath become a goodbye you're not ready to say.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath of Mountain Air

title: The Last Morning Stretch Before Deployment
instruction: You're stretching in bed on your final morning before leaving for a mission you may not return from. Start with the familiar comfort of this routine stretch, speaking with drowsy peace, but let reality gradually seep in—this might be the last time you feel your own bed, your own home. As your muscles wake, so does the awareness of what you're leaving behind. Your voice should shift from sleepy contentment to a bittersweet ache, holding onto this ordinary moment like a lifeline. End with a quiet determination mixed with unbearable tenderness for this simple act you've taken for granted. Let the physical sensation of stretching become both a goodbye and a prayer.
inspired_by: Stretching Your Arms Over Your Head After Waking Up

title: The Archaeology of Skin
instruction: You are lying in the dark with someone you trust, whispering a confession you've never spoken aloud. Begin by describing in vivid sensory detail a moment from your past when your body knew something your mind refused to accept—perhaps a touch that made you freeze, a room you couldn't enter, a scent that triggered inexplicable panic. Speak quietly, intimately, letting the physical sensations return as you describe them. Don't explain or analyze; simply report what your body remembers: textures, temperatures, the exact quality of light, how your skin felt. As you excavate this buried sensory memory through language, allow your present body to respond—perhaps trembling, perhaps softening, perhaps discovering unexpected relief. End with a simple statement of what you now understand, spoken so quietly it's almost just for yourself. The journey is from carefully controlled description to visceral, present-tense feeling.
inspired_by: Choice Hunt / Building a Repertoire of UC Choices

title: The Last Light in Her Eyes
instruction: You're holding your grandmother's hand as she takes her final breaths. Begin by speaking to her with desperate tenderness—tell her about the garden she planted, the songs she sang, share a memory that makes you smile even now. Let yourself feel the warmth of loving her, the gratitude for every moment. But as you speak, you begin to realize she's already gone—her hand is growing cold, she can't hear you anymore. Let that realization crack you open. Your words shift from tender reminiscence to raw, helpless grief. End in a place where love and loss are so intertwined you can barely breathe. Start with gentle devotion, end with the devastating weight of goodbye.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a one-dimensional character or character work feels superficial—expressing the emotion rather than creating the impetus

title: Rage Against the Life That Broke You
instruction: You're unleashing years of suppressed fury at the circumstances, systems, or people that shattered something precious in you—your trust, your innocence, your belief in fairness. Start with your voice tight and controlled, the anger compressed like a spring. Then let it explode: scream, sob, let your voice crack and shred with the injustice of it all. Pour out the specific moments of betrayal, the ways you were failed, the rage at your own powerlessness. Then, unexpectedly, let the fury collapse into devastating helplessness—your voice dropping to broken whispers as you realize that no amount of anger can undo what happened. End in exhausted, hollow silence, the rage burned out, leaving only grief.

title: Victory Lap in an Empty Stadium
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a rejection, a betrayal, a crushing failure. Your body is tight with humiliation and pain. But instead of collapsing, you force yourself to stand and begin describing, out loud, the opposite reality. Walk through the space as if you're receiving a standing ovation. Feel the phantom heat of stage lights, describe the weight of an award in your hands, the silk of expensive clothing on your skin, the ache in your cheeks from smiling at admirers. Make your voice ring with triumph even as tears stream down your face. Let your body move between the physical reality of your pain and the imagined sensation of glory—reaching for invisible hands to shake, bowing to no one. End with your voice cracking as the fantasy can no longer hold, collapsing the distance between what you're pretending and what you're feeling.

title: Victory's Hollow Echo
instruction: You are a 17-year-old who has just won a national championship. You're standing alone on the podium, the applause fading. You feel a surge of ecstasy—you did it. But as you look at the empty seats, bitterness creeps in: your teammates left you out, your parents didn't come. You're so exhausted you can barely stand, but you must give a winner's speech. Start with breathless joy, then let your voice crack with bitterness and fatigue. Pause, swallow, shift your weight. Let the words trail off as you realize what you've lost.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Bitterness (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Burnt Offerings
instruction: You're a teenager in a clattering kitchen, scraping burnt cookies off a baking sheet while a pot of water boils over. Your hyper-feminized voice rises over the sizzle and clatter—begin with sharp disappointment, muttering about the waste of ingredients. As you chop an onion for a new attempt, let your words slow, the noise fading into background, your tone softening into quiet contemplation about what really matters in the mess. End with a resigned, almost tender realization, spoken as you wipe your brow and stir the pot.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Forgotten Friend
instruction: You're a child sitting cross-legged on the carpet of your bedroom, surrounded by toys you're supposed to be putting away. You pick up a stuffed bear you haven't touched in months. At first, you feel a flicker of contempt—a scoff at its worn fur, a roll of the eyes at how babyish it seems now. But as you hold it, your thumb finds a missing button eye you remember, and a warmth creeps in. The soft carpet and muffled room make your voice intimate, honest. Let the sneer soften into reluctant affection. Speak aloud to no one but yourself, as you decide whether to toss it or keep it. The room's quiet hush should color your tone, the fading contempt giving way to a rueful, gentle fondness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Crunching Underfoot
instruction: You are an older man walking with your adult son on a gravel path after a family gathering. The noisy crunch of stones under your boots forces you to speak louder and more clearly than usual. You start by teasing him about his failed business venture, your voice carrying a playful, almost mocking tone as you try to lighten the mood. But as you continue, the weight of your own disappointment—in yourself for not guiding him better, in the situation—creeps in. Your voice hardens, the teasing fades, and you end with a raw, quiet admission of your own regrets, the crunching footsteps now a heavy punctuation between your words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Broken Growl
instruction: You're a young man just fired from a warehouse job you needed for rent. The foreman, a bigger guy who's been mocking you for weeks, stands in the doorway of the break room, arms folded, talking like you're a piece of trash. You're alone in the room — you can hear the building hum, the distant clang of a forklift. You've tried to hold your chin up, but your shoulders are sinking, your throat is tight, and your voice drops low, almost a growl, but there's a wobble in it — a crack of sadness you can't fully hide. You begin by forcing a cold, lazy tone, telling him you get it, fine. But as you speak, your words slow down against your will, and you realize you have nowhere to go, no backup, nothing. By the end, your voice turns quiet and brittle — a raw admission that he's won. You shift weight, glance at the floor, maybe let out a humorless huff halfway through. Start with controlled anger, end with the heavy stillness of defeat.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Old Dog, Old Tricks
instruction: You're an elderly person with an androgynous voice in a crowded locker room after a swim. Some young guys are bragging loudly about their workouts, and you feel a mix of contempt and irritation at their posturing. Start by joining their banter with a gruff, sarcastic tone — using locker room slang, loud volume, and a few percussive laughs. But as you talk, let your voice waver: mention the friend who used to spot you here, now gone. The contempt fades into quiet grief; you trail off, distracted by a memory, then clear your throat and pretend to adjust your towel. End with a weak, dismissive grunt, your voice soft and hollow.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Complaint
instruction: You are a child who has been complaining nonstop about chores all afternoon, your voice weary and nasal, each word drawn out like a whine. You're exhausted, dragging yourself through the house, but you just discovered that you tricked your sibling into finishing your task. As you speak to no one in particular, your fatigue remains — your voice still heavy — but a sly amusement and a quiet triumph seep in. You savor your victory, but your body is too tired to celebrate loudly. Let your voice start flat and droning, then let a tiny, mischievous smile color the final words, as if you're sharing a secret with yourself. Speak as if you're half-collapsed on a couch, yawning between syllables.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Amusement (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Fever Dream Breakthrough
instruction: You're ill—burning with fever, body aching, mind delirious. Begin physically affected: voice rough, breath labored, body heavy. In this vulnerable, undefended state, let your fevered mind start circling an emotional wound you usually keep buried. Through shallow breaths and physical discomfort, ask yourself aloud: 'Why does my chest hurt like this? What am I carrying?' Let the delirium strip away your usual defenses. The physical pain and the emotional pain blur together. What specific memory or loss is your body holding? Let sensory details emerge—a smell, a touch, a voice—that unlock the precise nature of your grief or rage or longing. The fever breaks by the end; as your body cools and breath deepens, let the emotional revelation settle into something quieter but newly understood. End physically and emotionally transformed.

title: Pretending to Be Surprised at a Surprise Party You Discovered
instruction: You found out about your surprise party in advance but dont want to disappoint your friends. Internally, you know whats coming, but you act surprised. Describe your anticipation while feigning astonishment. Speak with an excited tone, making them believe in your surprise.

title: Floor Constellations
instruction: You're lying on your stomach on the living room carpet, propped up on your elbows, a little tipsy from wine earlier. Your child is lying beside you, pointing up at the ceiling, tracing imaginary constellations. At first, you're vaguely interested, watching their finger move, your voice a bit loose and lazy from the alcohol. But as they explain their made-up stars with such serious wonder, your focus sharpens — you start to really see what they see. By the end, your voice becomes softer, clearer, caught between a smile and a lump in your throat. Let your words wander, pause mid-sentence to glance at their face, and let the intoxication fade into a quiet awe that surprises you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Fine Print on Her Heart
instruction: You're a 17-year-old intern in a tense boardroom negotiation, and across the table sits the person you've been secretly infatuated with for months. You begin by forcing a steady, low-pitched professional tone, reciting contract points, but your voice wavers as you catch their eye. You lose your place, clear your throat, and your pitch rises despite yourself. By the end, the professional shield cracks completely—your words trail off into a soft, breathy confession of how you really feel about working with them, mixing embarrassment with raw longing.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Weight of Bubbles
instruction: You're a tired, older man coaxing your fussy grandchild to eat a spoonful of peas. Your back aches from bending over the high chair, and there's a painful knot in your shoulder. You're mortified your daughter-in-law is watching from the doorway—you feel self-conscious about your gruff voice trying to sound sweet. Start with a weary, flat tone, mumbling 'come on, little one,' then force a high-pitched, exaggerated parentese, repeating 'open up for the choo-choo pea train!' Let your voice crack with fatigue and embarrassment. Shift slowly into genuine warmth as the child giggles, ending with a soft, surprised laugh and a quieter, more sincere 'there you go, sweet pea.' Let your breath catch, lose the words once, and find them again.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Embarrassment (extremely present), Pain (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Victory Lap, Empty Stands
instruction: Your child just won the championship, but you're watching alone because your co-parent - who started them in this sport, who never missed a game - died six months ago. Begin with genuine joy and pride, cheering and laughing, celebrating their incredible moment. But the joy is immediately complicated by piercing absence - you keep almost turning to share this with someone who isn't there. Let yourself laugh and cry simultaneously, expressing gratitude for witnessing this while your heart shatters that they can't. Your voice should be bright with pride but breaking with loss, talking to your child and to your absent partner at once. End in a place of bittersweet peace - this is beautiful and unbearable, triumphant and tragic, the best and worst moment all at once. The emotions must be genuinely contradictory and coexisting, not one replacing the other.
inspired_by: The Competitive Parent at a Childrens Game

title: The Dark Room Toll
instruction: You are lying in a dark room, the migraine a tight band squeezing your skull. Your partner just knocked and now the door creaks open – light and sound jab at you. You whisper a plea for them to stop, to leave the room, but they don't seem to hear. Your voice strains, barely audible, each word costing you. Start with a fragile, trembling request, then let helplessness flood in as they linger. By the end, anger curls through your whisper, then collapses into a sad, quiet surrender.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Helplessness (very intensely present), Anger (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Divorce Papers and the Positive Test
instruction: You're sitting with the divorce papers you're about to sign, finally ready to end a marriage that's been dying for years, when you discover you're pregnant. Begin reading the papers aloud with grim satisfaction, almost laughing with relief: 'Irreconcilable differences... yeah, that's putting it mildly.' But when you see the positive pregnancy test, laughter and tears come simultaneously—the absurd timing, the impossible choice. Your voice dances between contradictions: joy at new life and devastation that it's come too late, gratitude for this unexpected gift and grief that you're receiving it alone, the strange peace of knowing exactly what you want (the baby) and the chaos of everything that means. End in a place where you're crying and laughing at once, finding bizarre hope in the ruins, whispering 'okay... okay, we'll figure this out' to both yourself and the tiny life inside you.

title: Protecting Your Child From a Truth That Will Destroy Them
instruction: You've just learned something that will shatter your child's world—their other parent's betrayal, a lie that's defined their life, something you can't protect them from anymore. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness—your voice strong, determined: 'I won't let this break you.' But as you speak, your own helplessness crashes over you. Your voice rises, becomes raw with rage at your inability to shield them, then suddenly breaks. You're shouting through tears, then your voice drops to something fragile and lost: 'I'm your mother/father, I'm supposed to keep you safe.' End in near-whispers, your voice shaking with both love and absolute powerlessness. The explosive energy collapses into devastated tenderness. Let silence fall where words fail completely.
inspired_by: Confession from a Parent: We Gave Up on You

title: Primal Scream at the Ocean: Rage and Helplessness Colliding
instruction: You're standing alone at the edge of the ocean at dawn, and something inside you has finally broken. You've tried to be strong, to hold it together, but you can't anymore. Begin with your voice tight and controlled, almost speaking to yourself, listing everything you tried to prevent, everyone you tried to save, the person you couldn't protect. Then explode—let your voice tear into a scream of rage at the unfairness, at your own powerlessness. But the rage cracks and shatters into raw, guttural sobbing, your voice breaking completely as fury gives way to grief. Oscillate between roaring anger and broken desperation, your voice ragged and torn. Include the moment where you're screaming and crying simultaneously, words dissolving into primal sound. End with your voice absolutely wrecked, reduced to hoarse, whispered repetition of their name, all the fight gone, just devastation and exhausted surrender.
inspired_by: Megaphone Protest Leader: Voice Giving Out

title: The Ceiling Is Breathing
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe seven years old, lying in bed with a high fever. Your mother is in the room, but you're not sure if she's real or part of a dream. The ceiling tiles look like they're pulsing. You try to tell her that the ceiling is breathing, but your lips are cracked and your voice comes out thin and shaky. Start with a confused, urgent whisper, trying to describe what you see. As you speak, the fever makes you drift—your words slow, then speed up, then trail off. By the end, you're not sure if you're talking to your mother or to the ceiling itself, and your voice becomes a fragile, distant murmur. Speak these lines: 'Mom? Mom, the ceiling... it's moving. Like it's breathing. Can't you see it? It's... it's getting closer. I think... I think it wants to... (a long, shuddering breath)... it's okay, maybe it's just the light. The light is so loud.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Summit's Breath
instruction: You are standing alone at the edge of a mountain summit after a long, punishing climb. The wind is fierce, stealing your breath before you can speak. Your legs tremble from exhaustion, but your heart is bursting with ecstasy as you look out over the endless valleys below. You begin by muttering in disbelief, your voice thin and broken by the altitude. Then something in you breaks open — you shout with raw joy, laughing and gasping, feeling a spontaneous wave of gratitude for this moment. Your voice cracks, falters, then soars. Let the wind and thin air interrupt you; lose a thought, find it again, and end with a quiet, breathless 'thank you' that almost gets lost in the gusts.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Evidence of Joy
instruction: You're going through your late partner's belongings months after their death, numb and mechanical. You expect only grief. But as you handle each object—a worn book, a coffee mug, a jacket that still smells like them—observe what these items reveal about who they were. Notice the bookmark placement showing they never finished that novel. See the size of the jacket and remember how small they felt in your arms. Find the secret notes they left in pockets. Start from hollow, protective numbness. But let your careful observation and deduction about each object's story awaken something unexpected: not just sadness, but profound gratitude, even joy at having known them. Why did they keep this particular ticket stub? What does it mean that they never threw away your early, clumsy love letters? Let these deductions create a complex emotional transformation where grief and celebration, loss and fortune, aching absence and overwhelming appreciation exist together. Speak to them as if they can hear what you're finally understanding.

title: Meaning Finding
instruction: You've found meaning in something that seemed meaningless. Your voice is thoughtful: 'For so long, I didn't understand why I was doing this. It all seemed pointless.' Then something shifts. 'But now I see it. I see the purpose in all of it.' Your voice carries revelation: 'Every struggle, every setback, every tiny victory — it all means something.' You're speaking to someone who doubted you: 'You said this was a waste of time. But it's not. This is the most important thing I've ever done.' Your voice becomes passionate: 'Because it matters. And *I* matter. And my life has meaning.' By the end: 'I finally understand why I'm here. And it's not grand or famous or impressive. But it's true, and it's mine, and it's enough.' The meaning is found not in external validation but in internal alignment.

title: The Last Conversation Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at 4 AM. She's awake and lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is the last time you'll speak. Begin with careful composure, trying to be strong for her. As you talk, let memories flood through you—childhood moments, her hands braiding your hair, the smell of her kitchen, harsh words you regret, gratitude you never expressed. Don't plan what to say. Let each memory trigger the next, carrying you forward without pause—move from laughter to tears to anger at the unfairness to desperate love without stopping to organize your thoughts. Let your voice and body respond instantly to each surge of feeling. End in a place of unexpected peace or devastating loss—whichever arrives unbidden.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Dream Over You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've never said: that their ambition, their art, their calling—whatever they chose—mattered more to them than you did. Start with careful, measured words, almost reasonable, listing the missed birthdays, the times you needed them and they weren't there. Let your voice sharpen as you describe what it felt like to be the secondary character in their life story. Build to raw accusation: 'You chose yourself. Every single time.' But then comes the crack in your armor—the part of you that understands, maybe even admires what they built, and hates yourself for that understanding. Your voice becomes tender, almost pleading: you need them to acknowledge what was lost, what you both lost. End in an exhausted honesty, admitting that you don't know if you can forgive them, but you're here, and that has to mean something.

title: The Sensation That Hijacks You
instruction: You're in the middle of passionate intimacy with someone when suddenly an old wound - physical or emotional - flares alive in your body. Maybe your shoulder where your father once grabbed you. Maybe a sensation that reminds you of a loss. You try to push through, to stay in the moment you 'should' be having - the pleasure, the connection, the heat. Start there: attempting to maintain the passion, to perform the desire you think you should feel. But let the intrusion take over. Let your body's memory be stronger than your intention. Allow the passion to fracture, let yourself become confused, let contradictory sensations war in your body - desire fighting with pain, pleasure twisted with old fear. Don't decide how to 'play' this split; let your body actually experience being pulled in two directions until something breaks or shifts.

title: Ancient Warrior Final Stand
instruction: You're a scarred general narrating your last battle to a scribe who will outlive you. Your voice starts steady, almost clinical—the trained warrior's detachment—but cracks when you describe the moment you recognized your own child in the enemy ranks. Breathe like you're still bleeding. Let physical exhaustion and memory both break your composure. The story shifts from tactical recounting to raw confession. By the end, your voice is barely above a whisper, and you're not sure if the scribe can hear you admit you didn't raise your sword when you had the chance.

title: Whispered Inventory
instruction: It's 3 AM and you can't sleep. You're lying beside someone—a partner, a friend who stayed over, someone you trust—and in the darkness, you begin to whisper the small, true things you've noticed about them that make you feel less alone in the world. Start tentatively, almost embarrassed, your voice barely audible: the way they tilt their head when listening, how they remember the specific tea you like, that they don't look away when you're struggling to find words. As you continue this quiet inventory, your whispers become steadier, more urgent. You're not asking for anything back; you're simply naming what you see. The vulnerability shifts from feeling dangerous to feeling like a kind of courage. End with your voice soft but clear, no longer afraid of being heard, having discovered that speaking these observations aloud has changed how you feel about your own capacity to notice goodness and receive connection.

title: Frozen Fingers, Unyielding Lock
instruction: You are an elderly woman in sub-zero temperatures, standing by your car. Your hands are numb, your face stiff, and you can barely feel the keys. You are exhausted from the cold, every movement a battle, but you must focus to unlock the door. Speak aloud to yourself as you fumble—muttering about the lock, your frozen fingers, the effort. Let your voice reflect the physical tension: tight jaw, sluggish tongue. Start with strained concentration and fatigue, then shift to a breath of relief as you finally hear the click.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin by reading aloud a letter they wrote to you years ago during a fight you never resolved - your voice tight, breath shallow, struggling to get the words out. As you read, your throat begins to open, your breath deepens. By the final paragraph, you're no longer reading their words but speaking your own - a raw, unplanned confession of everything you never said. Let your body release its grip. Your voice should physically transform from constricted and high to deep, open, and resonant. End by making a promise to them about how you'll live differently, speaking from the lowest, most open place in your chest.

title: The Last Experiment
instruction: You're a dying scientist recording a final message to your estranged daughter, explaining the life's work she never understood—the experiments that took you away from her childhood. Begin with clinical detachment as you describe your research, your voice steady and professorial. But as you speak, the defensive walls crumble. Your voice should catch as you realize, mid-explanation, that none of it mattered compared to the bedtime stories you missed, the recitals you skipped. End in a place of raw, undefended grief—not asking for forgiveness because you know you don't deserve it, just trying to make her understand why you became the parent you were. Let the transformation be gradual, inevitable, like watching ice melt.

title: The Last Ember
instruction: You are an older woman who has just finished sobbing alone in your kitchen after a bitter phone call with a longtime friend who betrayed you. Your voice is raw, your nose completely stuffed, and your throat feels scraped. Begin by muttering bitterly to yourself about the unfairness, forcing the words out through the congestion with a clenched, resentful edge. As you speak, you realize you're too tired to hold onto the anger—your voice cracks, softens, and trails off into a hollow, emptied-out calm. Let the bitterness slowly dissolve into exhausted resignation, as if even hate requires energy you no longer have. Include natural pauses to sniffle, swallow painfully, or lose your train of thought.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Archaeology
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you've been with for years. You've just woken from a dream that made you remember who you were before you met them—dreams you abandoned, a version of yourself you lost. They're asleep. Speak to them in whispers, confessing things you've never said aloud: your secret loneliness even when you're together, the self you miss, the person you're afraid you're becoming. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, almost talking to yourself. But let something shift: as you whisper these frightening truths, you also remember why you chose this—the small ways they've held you together, the quiet grace of their presence. End with a fragile kind of vulnerability: not certainty about staying or leaving, but the courage to sit with not knowing. Let your final whispered words carry both your fear and your tenderness.
inspired_by: Actor has been cast in a major role and has weeks before rehearsal begins

title: Accepting Your Parent's Death
instruction: You're at the hospital or funeral. Your voice is in shock, not processing: 'They're really gone.' Words don't land. Your voice becomes flat, autopilot, making arrangements. Include a moment where reality cracks through and your voice breaks—a memory, a thought. By the end, sitting in quiet, voice barely audible, alone. Say something they'll never hear.

title: The Mirror You Held Up
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about a truth you've been terrified to speak for years—perhaps about how their choices damaged you, or how you've failed them, or a secret that's been rotting between you.
