Begin with your voice shaking, stumbling over words, because speaking this truth feels like standing on the edge of a cliff. You're afraid of their anger, their rejection, afraid the words will destroy what little connection remains. Let your fear make you almost incoherent at first. But as you push through, as the truth pours out despite your terror, feel the fear transmute into something fierce and liberating. End with a raw power in your voice—not loud, but unshakeable—as you realize that speaking your truth, even if it costs you everything, is the only way you can breathe again.

title: Bedtime Confession: The Weight of Small Hands
instruction: You're tucking your five-year-old into bed, and they ask you the innocent question: 'Are you sad today?' You start to deflect—'No, sweetie, Mommy's just tired'—but something in their small, trusting face breaks you open. In a whisper, staying gentle because they're so little, begin confessing truths you never meant to share: how scared you are that you're not enough, how lonely you feel, how you're terrified you're failing them. Your voice should be tender, almost singing, the way you'd tell a bedtime story—but the story is your breaking heart. Let tears live in your throat without falling into sobs. End with a shift: their small hand reaching for yours pulls you back. Your final words are both apology and promise, still whispering, finding strength in their trust even as your vulnerability hangs in the air. This is devastation wrapped in gentleness.
inspired_by: Voicemail Spiral: Leaving Message After Message

title: The 3 AM Whisper
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner in the deep quiet of 3 AM, and you begin whispering a confession you can't say when they're awake. Start with the belief that they're safely asleep, allowing yourself to speak truths that terrify you in daylight. Your voice is barely audible, testing each word in the darkness. But halfway through, you notice their breathing has changed—you're not certain, but they might be awake, might be listening. Don't change what you're saying, but let this uncertainty seep into your delivery. The confession becomes more urgent, more fragile. You're suspended between the safety of speaking to silence and the vulnerability of being truly heard. End with a tender, frightening hope that they did hear every word, that dawn will come and something will be irrevocably different. Your whisper should evolve from cautious to trembling to courageously exposed.

title: The Letter in the Attic
instruction: You are an elderly man on a quiet porch, leaning in close to a trusted neighbor. Your voice drops to a hushed, rapid huddle as you share a secret you just discovered in an old box in the attic — a love letter your late wife wrote to someone else before you met. At first, you’re animated, almost giddy with the mystery, your pitch spiking as you whisper details. But as you speak, the reality sinks in: she had a whole life before you, and you never knew. The excitement fades into a soft, longing silence as you trail off, touching the paper one last time. Let your voice crackle with age — clear pauses, a sudden clearing of the throat, and a slight tremor when the longing rises.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never Present
instruction: You're standing with your parent in a place they always promised to take you but never did—perhaps by the ocean or in a meadow. The breeze touches your face and you begin by describing it, but then you turn to them and your voice hardens. This breeze, this moment, this simple thing—you needed them to share a thousand moments like this with you, but they chose to be absent. Let your anger build as you list what was missing, what you had to face alone. But then break—let the anger crack open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted their parent to notice them, to be there. End not with reconciliation but with raw, vulnerable honesty about the hole their absence created. Move from bitter accusation to heartbroken confession.
inspired_by: Enjoying a Gentle Breeze on a Warm Day

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After twenty years, you're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. Start cold, almost businesslike—you've rehearsed this, built walls. 'I didn't come here for an apology. I came to tell you that I turned out fine without you.' But as you list everything they missed—your graduation, your wedding, the nights you needed them—the anger rises. Your voice sharpens, becomes fierce, even cruel: 'You don't get to be proud of me now.' Then something shifts. You hear yourself and it sounds like them, and the rage cracks open into something more devastating: the child who still wanted to be chosen. Your voice drops to something fragile, almost pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in shattered quiet, the question hanging between you like a wound that never healed.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent—who always dismissed your dreams as foolish—that you've succeeded beyond measure, but they're dying and you realize success means nothing without their recognition. Start with controlled anger, facts delivered like weapons: 'I won the fellowship. The one you said I'd never get.' Your voice is hard, triumphant, ready to wound. But as you watch them struggle to respond, the anger cracks. You hear yourself becoming desperate, the adult facade crumbling into the child who still needs them: 'Why couldn't you just... just once...' The confrontation you planned dissolves into raw pleading, then something more devastating—forgiveness you didn't know you were capable of, spoken through tears, admitting you love them even though they broke your heart, finding grace in the wreckage of a lifetime's disappointment.

title: Pride on the Stove
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl in your home kitchen, trying to impress your family by making a complicated dish from a video you've been obsessed with. You're holding a hot pan—your hand is burnt from a splash of oil, and you instinctively hiss through clenched teeth ('ssss'), shaking the stinging hand while keeping the other on the pan. You feel interest in the recipe, anger at yourself for not being careful, and a fierce pride in finally attempting this. Start with excited, breathless words about the dish, then wince and let the anger slip in as you curse the pain, but force yourself to finish with proud determination. Your voice must be urgent, panicked, and occasionally cut off by sharp inhales. End by reaffirming your pride despite the burn.
emotions_sampled: Interest (clearly present), Anger (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Clearing Out the House
instruction: You're packing up your childhood home after your parent's death, preparing it for sale. You expect this to be purely mechanical—boxing things, labeling, moving on. Start brisk, efficient, protective. But as you handle each object, you're ambushed by curiosity about things you never questioned: why did they keep this particular mug? What is this key for? Whose handwriting is on this note? Your grief keeps getting interrupted by genuine wonder, and your wonder keeps breaking into tears. Let discovery and loss tangle until you can't separate them. Some objects make you laugh with sudden understanding; others drop you to your knees. End holding something ordinary—a dish towel, a pen—examining it with complete attention, your voice tight with both gratitude for getting to know them better through their objects, and fury that you're learning this only now, too late.

title: Whispering the Truth You've Hidden From Your Dying Partner
instruction: Your partner is in their final hours. You're holding their hand in the dark hospital room, and you need to confess something you've carried for years - maybe an affair, maybe that you can't have children, maybe that you're the reason they got sick. Your voice is barely above a whisper, breaking on every other word. 'I need you to know... before...' Start with your throat tight, fighting tears. The confession comes in fragments, interrupted by your own quiet sobs. But then something shifts - you tell them how much you've loved them despite it all, how this secret has tortured you. End with tender desperation: 'Please forgive me. Please know I loved you through all of it.' Let silence do the work between phrases. Transform from shame-filled confession to raw, aching love.
inspired_by: Confessing a Secret That Could Destroy Everything

title: Burning the Letters
instruction: You're kneeling in front of a fire, burning every letter your former lover ever wrote you. Feel the heat radiating against your face, your hands. Notice how the paper feels between your fingers before you release it—its texture, its weight, whether it's smooth or rough. Smell the smoke, the peculiar scent of burning ink and paper. Start in cold, controlled anger—you're doing this to reclaim yourself, to purge them from your life. But as you watch each letter curl and blacken, let the heat of the fire awaken body memories: their hands on your skin, the specific warmth of lying beside them, moments of intense physical pleasure now mixed with pain. Let the sensations build—the fire's heat becoming their heat, your body remembering against your will. Move from controlled fury into something more complex and consuming: rage and desire tangled together, until you can't tell if you're destroying these letters to forget them or because remembering is the only way you can still feel them.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who loved you deeply, but whom you couldn't love back the same way - and you're finally, impossibly grateful for their love even as you're breaking both your hearts. Begin with a trembling almost-laugh, the kind that's barely holding back tears: 'This is so unfair to you. God, this is so unfair.' Your voice should be warm with genuine affection and cracking with sorrow simultaneously. You're thanking them for seeing you, for choosing you, for loving you with such fierce devotion - and every word of gratitude makes the loss more devastating because their love was real and beautiful and not enough. Let yourself laugh softly at painful ironies, then cry through the laughter. 'You made me feel so seen, so cherished, and I hate that I can't...' Trail off. Your voice should shimmer between joy at having known their love and grief at having to release it. End in paradox: 'I will miss you every day. And I need you to let me go.' Speak it with aching tenderness, crying and smiling at once.
inspired_by: Pretending to Understand Something Thats Confusing

title: The Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: You've just found out someone hurt your child, and you're confronting them with volcanic rage that makes your voice shake. Start fierce, almost shouting threats, protective fury making you feel invincible and terrifying. Your words come in explosive bursts. But then—devastating shift—you see your child watching you, frightened of YOUR anger now. Your voice breaks mid-threat. The rage collapses into helpless tears. You're suddenly not fierce anymore, just a parent who couldn't protect their child, and the realization breaks you completely. End sobbing apologies to your child, voice raw and shattered, all the fire turned to ash.

title: The Gratitude That Tastes Like Grief
instruction: Someone you've resented for years - perhaps a parent, an ex, a former friend - has just done something extraordinarily kind for you, at great cost to themselves. You need to thank them. You want to thank them. But every word of gratitude catches in your throat because it forces you to feel everything you've lost, all the years of distance, all the reconciliation that will never happen the way you once imagined. Begin with an attempt at a clean, simple 'thank you' - trying to make this moment graceful and uncomplicated. But let the gratitude crack you open to the grief beneath it. Let your 'thank you' become tangled with anger at how long it took, sadness for what can't be recovered, love you didn't know was still there. Don't perform the mix - let each emotion interrupt the others messily, authentically. End somewhere you absolutely did not intend.

title: What We Breathe in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, both of you supposedly asleep. You begin speaking in barely audible whispers, confessing something you've never said aloud—a fear so fundamental it lives in your bones, or a desire so tender you've protected it like a wounded animal. Start with halting breath, words that barely form, long pauses where silence holds as much truth as sound. As you continue whispering into the darkness, not even sure if they're awake, you feel yourself becoming more honest than you've ever been. Your whispers become slightly fuller, more certain, as if the darkness is giving you permission. End with a fragile but clear statement of need or truth, your voice soft but no longer hiding.
inspired_by: Actor's work consistently feels shallow, indicates disconnection from unconscious resources

title: Photographing an Active Lava Fountain While Knowing You're Too Close
instruction: You're narrating your shots, professional and awed, as the lava fountain erupts before you. Your voice carries scientific wonder and controlled exhilaration. Then you feel the heat intensify. Your voice stays measured—you're a professional—but the pace changes. 'The fountain is reaching higher than predicted.' You can hear the fear underneath. Your assistant yells something and your voice suddenly switches to commands: 'Backing up, backing up NOW.' Include the moment a spray of lava comes too close and you're running, your narration becoming broken, gasping, barely coherent. Your camera is still in your hands. You kept shooting. Your voice is almost ashamed of that.

title: Holding the Person Who Just Tried to End Their Life
instruction: You've just found someone you love in the immediate aftermath of a suicide attempt—they're alive but barely conscious in your arms. Start with explosive panic: you're screaming their name, begging them to stay with you, your voice raw with terror and rage that they almost left you. Fury erupts—how dare they, how could they think you'd be better off without them—but it immediately fractures into desperate, sobbing apologies. Maybe you didn't see the signs, maybe you said something cruel last week, maybe you've been too wrapped up in your own life. Your voice becomes fierce as you make passionate declarations of their worth, listing every reason they matter, but doubt creeps in: what if your love isn't enough? End in a place of protective tenderness mixed with complete helplessness, whispering promises you can't guarantee, feeling them breathe against you and knowing you can't watch them every second but needing them to live anyway.

title: The Unspoken Thanks
instruction: You're a teenager sitting on a bench outside a diner, elbows on your knees, staring at the cracked pavement. Your dad just paid for your ruined phone—again—without yelling, and you feel a knot of shame in your chest. As you replay his quiet 'I love you, son' in your head, your voice cracks and flattens under the weight of your own stupidity. Let your words start low, almost muttered to the ground, breath shallow, then lift slightly as gratitude surfaces, but keep the hesitation and the weight of your elbows pressing into your thighs. Speak as if you're testing the words for the first time, unsure they're enough: 'I don't deserve this. I really messed up. But... thank you. For not giving up on me. I promise I'll do better. I mean it.'
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dinner Table Justice
instruction: You’re at a small dinner table with three friends. Someone mentioned your ex, and you launch into the story of how he tried to humiliate you at a party—but you turned it around. Start with disgust, your voice sharp and bitter as you describe his smug face, but as you get to the part where you publicly called him out, let triumph creep in. You glance around the table, your head turning to different friends, your pitch shifting as you savor the moment. Talk naturally, with pauses to sip your drink, a laugh cut short, a moment where you lose your thought because someone asks a question. End with a satisfied smile in your voice, your words dropping slightly in volume as the story closes. Speak for about 50 seconds.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Recording Session
instruction: You're a legendary voice actor recording your final audiobook before retiring due to a degenerative vocal condition. You begin reading a children's story about a grandfather saying goodbye to his grandchildren, your voice strong and warm with professional control. As you progress through the passage, you realize the words mirror your own life—the joy of your career, the voices you've brought to life, the audiences you'll never reach again. Your voice begins to falter, not from lack of skill but from the weight of this ending. By the final line—'And so, with love, I leave you with all these stories'—your professional mask cracks completely. Your voice breaks, becomes raw and small, as you speak not as the character but as yourself, whispering a真實 goodbye to the only life you've known. Let the transition from controlled performance to unguarded grief happen naturally, like watching someone finally allow themselves to feel what they've been holding back.

title: The Overly Enthusiastic Hobbyist
instruction: Perform as a person obsessed with an obscure hobby. Use an excited voice when explaining intricate details, switching to the overwhelmed or bored reactions of others.

title: Articulation Clarity
instruction: You're a politician who had a minor stroke that slightly affected your speech clarity. You begin speaking with hyper-articulation — over-enunciating every syllable to hide the slur. 'This-is-a-very-im-por-tant-time.' It sounds robotic, desperate. Partway through, you stop. 'I'm having trouble speaking clearly today. That's okay.' You speak naturally, and yes, there's a slight slur on 's' sounds. You don't hide it. 'I'm still here. I'm still thinking clearly. My body is just... different now.' The slight imperfection becomes more human than the hyper-clarity. The crowd responds to the authenticity, not the perfection. By the end, you're speaking with normal articulation again, but now the slur feels less like a flaw and more like part of your story.

title: Reading the Letter After the Funeral
instruction: You've just returned from the funeral of someone who left you a letter to be opened after their death. As you read it aloud, they're telling you things that make you laugh - small, absurd memories, inside jokes, their voice so alive on the page that you can't help but smile even as tears stream down your face. Let yourself laugh genuinely at their humor, then catch yourself, feeling guilty for laughing when they're gone. They write about how much they'll miss you, and your voice should crack with grief, but then they say something so perfectly them that you're laughing again through the tears. Build to their final revelation - they're not afraid, they're grateful, they're at peace - and let this settle into you. End with contradictory wholeness: your voice breaking and healing simultaneously as you whisper 'thank you' to someone who can't hear you anymore, devastated and grateful and destroyed and somehow, impossibly, okay.
inspired_by: The Internal Monologue of a House Cat

title: The Confrontation You've Rehearsed a Thousand Times
instruction: You are confronting your parent about childhood wounds that shaped your entire life. You've practiced this conversation mentally for years, perfected your calm, reasonable arguments. Begin speaking those rehearsed, controlled words—but pay attention to the boiling rage, hurt child, or aching need for validation underneath your 'mature' exterior. Your task is to catch yourself being too composed, too articulate, too controlled for what you actually feel. Let the rehearsed speech crumble. Allow the messy, less articulate, possibly childlike or rageful truth to hijack your careful words. End by expressing something completely unplanned—perhaps you're not angry at all but heartbroken, or you discover mid-confrontation that what you thought was rage is actually desperate love. Transform from controlled accusation to chaotic emotional truth.
inspired_by: Actor is redirecting authentic impulses into more comfortable emotional expressions, creating a split between what is felt and what is expressed

title: Laughing at the Wake: Finding Grace in Goodbye
instruction: You're delivering a remembrance for someone who lived vibrantly and told you explicitly: 'Don't you dare be somber at my funeral.' Start with a genuine laugh as you share an outrageous story about them—something wild they did, something only they would have the audacity for. Your voice is full of affection and humor. But mid-story, the reality crashes into you: they're gone. Your laughter catches, transforms into tears even as you're still smiling. Your voice wavers between joy at having known them and the gutting pain of loss. 'God, I'm going to miss you' comes out half-laughing, half-sobbing. End with gratitude that tastes bittersweet, your voice warm and broken at once: 'Thank you for showing me how to live like that.' The instruction they gave you becomes both celebration and heartbreak in the same breath.

title: Quiet After the Storm
instruction: You're alone in a space capsule, helmet sealed, floating weightless, looking at Earth through the window. You've just survived a near‑fatal malfunction. Start with a deep, shaky breath—relief mixed with quiet contentment at the sight of the planet. Let your voice carry a tinny, distant quality, with static crackles and your own breathing in the gaps. As you speak, let the contentment slowly drain away, replaced by a slight emotional numbness—as if the victory feels hollow. Fidget with your visor, pause to clear a radio burst, and let the sentence trail off into a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Relief (slightly present), Contentment (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering to the Sleeping Crown
instruction: You are sitting beside the bedside of the woman who raised you—not your mother, but the queen you served since childhood, now dying. She's asleep or unconscious. You thought you'd have time to say these things, but now you don't. Speak softly, intimately, with all the tenderness you never showed when she was awake and you had to maintain propriety. Confess the love you hid behind duty, the jealousy you felt when others had her attention, the small moments of kindness she showed that you've treasured for decades. Let your voice catch on memories. As you speak, realize she may never wake up—this may be the last time. End with a whispered apology for all the warmth you withheld, all the distance you maintained. Your voice should be almost inaudible by the end, thick with unshed tears, as you finally say 'I love you' knowing she can't hear it.
inspired_by: The Queen and the Jealous Advisor

title: Emergency Room: Parent Demanding Answers
instruction: Your teenager is in surgery after a suicide attempt you didn't see coming. You corner the doctor, and everything you've held together explodes. Start with barely controlled panic: 'Tell me what's happening. Tell me right now.' Your voice is sharp, demanding control in a situation where you have none. As they explain, rage erupts—at them, at yourself, at the universe: 'How did no one see this? How did I not—' Let your voice rise, fierce and desperate. Then it breaks completely. Drop to raw anguish, your voice cracking: 'She's seventeen. She's my baby.' Let yourself collapse into helplessness, voice shaking uncontrollably: 'I should have known. I should have seen.' Your fierce protectiveness wars with total powerlessness—oscillate between demanding they save her and begging: 'Please. Please, she has to be okay.' Find a moment of devastating honesty, voice barely above a whisper: 'I can't lose her. I can't survive losing her.' End with primal determination breaking through the tears, voice raw but resolute: 'When she wakes up, I'll do better. I swear to God I'll do better.'

title: The Thin Air Betrayal
instruction: You are a young woman with a high, feminine voice, alone on a narrow, rocky mountain pass at 14,000 feet. Your head pounds; each breath is a desperate, shallow gasp. You’ve just realized your water bottle rolled down a cliff—you have no more water, and the sun is sinking fast. Start in a state of sharp pain and rising panic, calling out to any hiker who might hear. Your speech is broken by gasps, winces from a piercing headache, and moments of confusion as you struggle to form words. By the end, the pain remains, but your panic shifts into a weary, almost detached determination—you’re now talking yourself through each step forward, your voice trembling but resolute, as you accept the reality of the situation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Missing Bear
instruction: You are a 7-year-old girl with a high, sweet voice. You stand in your bedroom, clutching your stuffed bear 'Mr. Whiskers' — which you just pulled from your best friend's backpack after she swore she didn't take it. Your first words come out as a thin, breathless whisper, barely audible, because you can't believe what you saw. Let your voice tremble as you repeat fragments of your discovery. Then, as the truth sinks in, let your pitch spike, your words stumble out faster, and your voice crack with a rising, furious hurt. End with sharp, disgusted accusation, almost a yell, as you confront the lie.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Truth About That Summer
instruction: You are confronting your father about something he did fifteen years ago that damaged you deeply, something you've never spoken about until now. Begin with your voice tight and controlled, years of rehearsed anger finally being unleashed. But as you speak, really see him - notice how he's aged, how his hands shake, the fear in his eyes. Let someone you once admired and needed desperately come into focus. Your anger must remain, but allow it to become complicated by the ghost of the child you were who loved him, by pity, by exhaustion, by the devastating realization that he's just a flawed human being. End in a place you didn't expect - perhaps with a question instead of an accusation, perhaps with a moment of unwanted understanding that makes everything harder, not easier.

title: The Wall Listens
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl leaning against the hallway wall outside the school auditorium after the spring concert. Your best friend just told you she's moving away this summer, and you're pretending to be cool about it. You're whispering to yourself, practicing what you'll say to her later, but the wall reflects your voice back at you. Start with a casual, almost disinterested tone—shift your weight, roll your eyes at the ceiling. Halfway through, feel the distress sneak in: your voice cracks, you press your palm flat against the wall, and you realize you're not as okay as you thought. End with a quiet, shaky confession that you're actually terrified of losing her.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Blessing Before the Voyage
instruction: You're blessing your adult child as they prepare to leave on a one-way space mission to colonize a distant world. You'll never see them again, never hear their voice after tomorrow. Begin with proud, steady encouragement about their courage and purpose, your voice strong with parental pride. But as you speak, let the reality crush into you—this is goodbye forever. Your words should fracture and reform, pride dissolving into raw grief, your blessing becoming a desperate plea to remember you, to carry your love across the stars. End in whispered fragments, as if you're trying to press your entire heart into these final words. Let silences speak where words fail. This is not performance—this is a parent facing the unfaceable.

title: Victory Gasp
instruction: You've just sprinted your hardest ever, collapsing at the finish line of a race you didn't think you'd win. Your body is screaming for air, bent over with hands on knees, each breath a violent heave. At first, all you can do is fight for oxygen, words impossible—just gasps and maybe a gag. But slowly, as the burn lessens, a grin fights through the exhaustion. Speak between panting, your voice breaking and breathy: first grunts of effort, then a whispered 'I did it...' that trembles with disbelief and a growing, quiet ecstasy. Let your tone shift from pure physical agony to a shaky, joyful recognition of your triumph.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: A Late Spring Evening
instruction: You are an elderly man, sitting on a porch bench beside a woman you've been gently flirting with for weeks. The air is cool, a bird calls, you adjust your collar. Begin by teasing her about a small mistake she made—a light, playful tone, a low chuckle. As you speak, you realize how much her presence means to you. Let your voice soften, the tease fading into a tender confession. Pause to watch a firefly, then continue, the final words thick with unguarded affection.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your own funeral—you know you're dying, and you've decided to say goodbye with humor. Start genuinely funny, your voice warm and full of life, making jokes about your own quirks, roasting the people you love most. Let yourself actually laugh at your own jokes, find real joy in the absurdity. But mid-sentence, something shifts—maybe you mention a moment you'll never see, a future you won't be part of. Your laughter catches, becomes something else, but you push through, forcing the joke to its end even as your voice wavers. Continue this dance: genuine laughter bleeding into sorrow, then pulling back to humor, your voice rich with both celebration and grief. End on a moment of pure gratitude that sounds like both laughing and crying, where joy and heartbreak are the same sound.
inspired_by: Being Told You're Not Good Enough

title: The Kitchen Cleansing
instruction: You are an older woman who has just discovered that your adult child has pawned your late mother's silverware for drug money. You are alone in your small, cluttered kitchen, and the rage comes on suddenly—like a physical storm. Start with a low, sour muttering to yourself about the betrayal, your voice thick with disbelief and bitterness. Then it erupts: you slam a cupboard door, your voice becomes a percussive, gutteral attack—cracking, rough, every sentence an accusation hurled at the empty room. Let your breathing become heavy and snorting; let the words come out in short, jagged bursts as you fight to contain the violence in your hands. End with a quiet, devastated rasp, your fury spent, the sour taste of 'I should have known' lingering on your tongue.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Exit Interview
instruction: You are packing up your childhood bedroom, preparing to leave home for the last time (moving across the world, estrangement, whatever makes it permanent). Begin with efficient, detached practicality—this is just stuff, just objects, just a room. But as you handle each item, force yourself to ask questions you've never asked: Why did I keep this random rock? What was I feeling the day I chose this poster? What did I believe about my future when I painted this wall? Let each question lead to deeper ones about who you were and who you've become. Feel gratitude and resentment fighting in your chest—grateful for what this room gave you, angry at what it couldn't provide. End speaking to the empty room itself, your voice breaking with contradictory emotions: thanking it and blaming it, celebrating your escape and grieving what you're losing, certain you need to leave and terrified of who you'll be without it.

title: Confronting Your Mother in the Dementia Ward
instruction: You're visiting your mother who has early-stage dementia, and today you've decided to finally tell her about the childhood she doesn't remember giving you. Start with the familiar small talk you always use, then let the truth spill out—the loneliness, the fear, the ways she chose everyone else over you. She won't remember this conversation tomorrow, and that both frees you and breaks you. Your voice moves from gentle, habitual caretaking to barely controlled fury to something more complicated: grief for the mother you needed and the one you got. She cries, confused, asking why you're being cruel. End with the horrible tenderness of wiping her tears and saying 'it's okay, Mom,' because what else can you do? The anger must feel real enough to scare you, the love must complicate everything.

title: Lost in the Beat
instruction: You're at a pounding rave, sweat pouring, your body bouncing to the bass. You're a teenager shouting over the music—your voice bobbing with each jump, breathless, laughing between words. Then you spot your little sister, who was supposed to be home, weaving through the crowd. Fear hits you like a punch: you scream her name, your voice rough and urgent. You push through bodies, grab her arm, and realize she's safe—just lost. In that moment, astonishment and fierce affection flood you. Your voice breaks, softens, cracks with relief as you pull her close. Start with panicked shouting, end with trembling, tender words—your breathing still ragged, the beat still thumping under your voice.
emotions_sampled: Fear (clearly present), Affection (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Burning From the Inside Out
instruction: You've just received devastating news and you're alone in your car, hands gripping the steering wheel. Begin in shock—your body frozen, breath shallow, emotions locked behind numbness. Slowly allow yourself to register the physical sensations flooding through you: trembling hands, heat rising in your chest, the feeling of your heartbeat in your throat, the texture of the steering wheel under your palms. Don't perform emotion—instead, let your heightened awareness of your body's responses guide you. As physical sensation intensifies, let sound emerge: maybe a gasp, maybe a scream, maybe helpless laughter, maybe choking sobs. The specific expression should be whatever genuinely erupts when you stop controlling it. End in a state of complete physical and emotional release, transformed from frozen shock into raw, sensory aliveness—even if that aliveness is agony.

title: What You Never Told Me
instruction: You're confronting your adult child in the doorway of their childhood bedroom, which they're packing up to move across the country. Start from a place of forced calm and parental concern—you came here to help them pack. But as you stand surrounded by the objects of their youth, something breaks open in you. Let your voice shift from measured reasonableness to accusation, then to pleading, as you finally admit the truth: you've felt them pulling away for years, and you don't know why. End by asking them to tell you what you did—what moment, what failure—made them need so much distance. The arc moves from polite distance to desperate vulnerability.
inspired_by: Actor is working on a scene but is not sure which obligation to address first

title: The Whisper of a Promise
instruction: You are a child, maybe 10, who has cornered a smaller kid in the playground. You love this moment—the way they flinch, the silence before you speak. Start with that pleasure: let your voice drop to a slow, lazy growl, relishing the power. Then, as you lean in, let a raw hope seep through—you're not just threatening; you're trying to make them your friend. Your pitch stays low, but your words stumble with a fragile optimism, like you're offering a deal you desperately want them to take. End with a question that betrays your need, not your strength.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Vigil: Holding Them as Memory Fades
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply—parent, partner, or friend—who no longer remembers your name due to advancing dementia. Speak softly, tenderly, telling them a cherished memory you share, your voice warm with affection. But as you describe the moment, let the realization wash over you that they're looking at you with pleasant confusion, no recognition in their eyes. Your voice should catch, words becoming harder to push out. Continue the story anyway, voice breaking with quiet devastation, because even though they don't remember, you need to honor what you had. End with a whispered confession of how much you miss them—even though they're right here. The emotion is a knife in the throat: love mixed with unbearable loss, tenderness threaded with grief so profound it barely makes sound.

title: Confronting a Parent Who Never Said It Back
instruction: You're an adult finally confronting your emotionally distant parent about a lifetime of unspoken love. Begin with controlled anger: 'I need to know why you could never say it.' Your voice is steady, almost cold. Then the dam breaks - raw hurt from childhood floods in: 'I was eight years old, standing at your bedroom door saying I love you, and you just... looked at me.' Let your voice become the child's voice for a moment - young, confused, aching. Then back to adult rage: 'Do you have any idea what that does to someone?' But end with devastating vulnerability - all the anger collapses into naked need: 'I still need to hear it. Even now. Even after everything.' Your final line is barely audible: 'Please... just say it once.' Move from fury to fragility, from accusations to a child's plea that never got answered.

title: The Kitchen at 2 AM
instruction: You confront your teenage child who has just come home after disappearing for three days. Start with volcanic rage—screaming, pacing, your voice ragged with fury and fear. You're listing every rule they broke, every lie they told, building to an explosion. Then, mid-accusation, you catch sight of something in their face—maybe defiance, maybe brokenness, maybe your own younger self staring back at you. The rage cracks. Your voice drops to something quieter, more dangerous, more honest. You're no longer yelling about rules. You're whispering about the terror of losing them, the ways you've failed them, the truth you've both been avoiding. End in a place of raw vulnerability, your anger transformed into confession, your volume transformed into intimacy.
inspired_by: Actor has tried a choice but it isn't producing the desired emotional response

title: The Last Time I'll See Your Hands
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed. She's sleeping, and you know she won't wake again. Begin by taking in the whole room, feeling numb and disconnected. Then let your gaze fall on her hands—the same hands that braided your hair, that taught you to knead bread, that held yours on your first day of school. Focus only on her hands. Notice every detail: the paper-thin skin, the wedding ring that's too loose now, the way her fingers curl slightly. Let everything else fade away except those hands. As you focus, allow yourself to move from numbness into the full weight of what you're losing—not the idea of her, but the specific, irreplaceable presence held in those hands. By the end, you should be speaking to her hands, saying everything you never said, your voice breaking with the intimacy of truly seeing what you're about to lose forever.

title: Compulsory Service
instruction: First day of court-ordered community service—500 hours cleaning up the city you trashed when you hit rock bottom. Your voice is bitter, sarcastic, defiant at the start. But you meet the other volunteers: addicts, people like you. By hour three, you're helping an old man who can barely stand. Something shifts. Your voice becomes less performative. By the end of the day, you're saying softly: 'Same time tomorrow?' Purpose tastes like possibility.

title: Tied Gratitude
instruction: You are an older man, bound by your partner in a consensual, intimate scene. You are grateful for their trust and care, but a flicker of malevolent amusement dances at the back of your mind—you enjoy being a little dangerous. You speak to them from the floor, your voice strained against the rope, breath heavy from arousal. Start with a low, husky thank-you that holds a hint of dark playfulness, then let your gratitude build, feeling it swell until a tiny doubt—did you push too far?—mixes in at the end, making your final words quieter, more vulnerable.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Doubt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Doctor Patient Bad News
instruction: You're the doctor delivering a terminal diagnosis to a patient who came in for 'just a cough.' Your voice begins with practiced gentleness: 'I have some difficult news.' You deliver the diagnosis—stage four, six months to two years. Clinical facts delivered with compassionate tone. The patient is silent, processing. Your voice becomes the only thing in the room. You're supposed to offer hope and statistics, but the way your voice drops on the word 'prognosis' suggests you know hope is a lie. End by asking, 'Do you have any questions?' in a voice that acknowledges no questions can change what's been said.

title: The Last Harvest
instruction: You're in your grandmother's orchard on the day before it's sold to developers. Pick a peach from her tree—the tree she planted when your mother was born. As you bite into it, you're flooded with every summer of your childhood: her hands teaching yours to choose the ripest fruit, her laugh, the safety of this place. Start with the simple sensory pleasure of the peach, but let memory wash over you until sweetness becomes bittersweet. Your voice should crack with the realization that this taste, this exact flavor of home, will never exist again. End in a whispered goodbye to everything this fruit represents—not just to her, but to the version of yourself who was loved here.
inspired_by: Taking a Bite of a Juicy Peach

title: The Face I've Been Avoiding
instruction: You're confronting your parent about something they did years ago that shaped who you became. Start by really looking at them—not the parent you remember, but the actual person sitting across from you now. Notice the real details: how they're dressed, the lines on their face, how they're sitting, the actual sound of their voice, their specific mannerisms. Begin with cold, controlled anger as you catalogue these real observations. As you speak your truth, let your attention to their actual presence—the way they flinch, how their hands move, the genuine expression in their eyes—slowly erode your anger. By the end, the reality of seeing them as a flawed, aging human being rather than the mythic figure from your past should transform your rage into something more complex: a painful mixture of understanding and the ache of lost years.

title: Coming Home to Ashes
instruction: You are returning to your childhood home for the first time since your mother's death to sort through her belongings. Walk through the rooms by engaging your sense of sight with total concentration—notice colors, shadows, how light falls on familiar objects, the precise shade of wear on the furniture, dust particles floating in sunbeams, faded photographs. Look until your eyes ache with seeing, until everything becomes almost unbearably vivid. Begin with brittle efficiency, narrating aloud what needs to be done, keeping emotion at bay through practical focus. But as your heightened vision reveals detail after detail—the way she arranged things, colors she loved, evidence of her final days—let yourself break open into a complex mixture of gratitude for what was and anguish at what's lost. Your voice should shift from businesslike and controlled to thick with tears but also warm with love. End by looking at one specific object and speaking directly to her, your vision blurred but somehow seeing more clearly than ever.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Made You Invisible
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent, finally ready to speak after decades of silence. Begin with a question that sounds simple but carries years of pain: 'Did you ever actually see me?' Your voice is controlled, almost cold, each word carefully chosen to protect yourself. As they deflect or defend, something ignites—your control splinters and anger pours through, not loud but razor-sharp, listing specific moments they forgot you, overlooked you, chose someone else. Then the anger collapses into something more devastating: the child's voice underneath asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in a place of exhausted clarity, telling them you're done waiting to matter, your voice steady but your heart breaking audibly in every breath.
inspired_by: Asking for Help When You're Trained to Solve Everything

title: The Last Good Day
instruction: You're terminally ill, and this is your last day of feeling relatively well. You're spending it with someone you love, and you've decided to make it perfect—full of laughter, stories, normalcy. Your voice is bright, almost manic with joy, determined to give them this gift of an ordinary, beautiful day. You laugh genuinely at small things, your voice warm and alive. But underneath, you're acutely aware this is goodbye, and sometimes it breaks through—mid-laugh, your voice catches; telling a funny story, you have to pause as grief swells in your chest. You keep pushing back to joy, but it's laced with sorrow now. As the day ends, you thank them with a voice that holds both deep peace and shattering loss. You're grateful—so grateful—for this day, for them, for everything, even as you're breaking apart. Let your voice carry the impossible beauty of loving someone while letting go.

title: The Barstool Confession
instruction: You're at a loud bar, three drinks in, sitting next to someone you've been eyeing all night. Your body feels heavy and warm, and you're laughing too easily at their jokes. You lean in close, your words a little loose at the edges, and tell them how good they smell. But in the middle of your confession, you accidentally knock over your glass—you pause, clumsy, then laugh it off, but the need in your voice has shifted from nervous lust to a deep, relieved surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Echo of Wonder
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl holding a heavy, dented bullhorn you found in a dusty garage. At first, you giggle as you test it, shouting silly nonsense words into it, the sound making you feel powerful and huge. But then you notice how your tiny voice roars out, bouncing off the walls like a giant's. Your teasing turns into pure, trembling awe as you whisper your own name into the horn, and the monstrous sound that comes back almost frightens you, filling you with a strange, magical reverence. Speak as if the bullhorn is alive, and your hand is shaking with the weight of its echo.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Aftermath of Victory
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you just made love to, your body still humming with endorphins, the sheets tangled. You start speaking with a lazy, triumphant smile—you feel powerful, like you conquered something. But as you talk, a crack of doubt slips in: maybe this isn't love, maybe you're just a good performer, maybe you'll wake up alone again. Let your voice dissolve from warm, cocky confidence into quiet, trembling uncertainty. Speak slowly, with long pauses, letting the heaviness of the room creep into your throat. Your last words should sound like you're trying to convince yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Keeper's Repair
instruction: You are a young man alone in a garage, carefully hammering a small wooden box that belonged to your late father. Each gentle tap of the hammer is an effort to make the lid fit again. Start speaking with a voice full of longing, broken by wistful pauses—remembering his hands on this box, the scent of wood and oil. As you feel the joint finally click into place, let a quiet but fierce triumph rise in your tone, your words becoming steady and proud. The hammer strikes and your grunts should naturally interrupt your sentences.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confession in the Dark: Summer, 1963
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your sleeping husband on your tenth wedding anniversary, whispering a confession he cannot hear. You are three months pregnant with another man's child—your husband's best friend, who died in a car accident last week. Begin with the tender, careful way you'd speak to someone sleeping, almost like a prayer. Confess the affair, the pregnancy, your genuine love for both men, and the impossible situation that has now resolved itself in the cruelest way. Let your whisper break occasionally, but keep returning to that intimate quiet, as if you're tucking the truth into the darkness where it must stay forever. Transform from guilty confession to a strange, grief-stricken gratitude that he'll never have to know, ending with a declaration of love that is both absolutely true and built on a lie you'll carry alone.
inspired_by: When directing actors in a play set in a specific historical period

title: Catalog of Small Mercies
instruction: You are alone in the dark after the worst day of your life—you've lost something irreplaceable. Begin in a whisper, voice hollow and numb, speaking into emptiness. You can barely breathe. Then, as if it's an experiment, start naming tiny things in the room around you that aren't painful: the softness of the blanket, the cool air from the window, the distant sound of rain. Let your voice remain quiet but gradually lose its deadness. Each small observation is an anchor pulling you back from the void. This is not about becoming happy—it's about finding one thread of sensation that isn't agony. By the end, your whisper should have the faintest pulse of life in it, a single degree of warmth returning to your voice.

title: Burning Evidence
instruction: You're standing in your backyard at dawn, burning letters from someone who hurt you deeply. Start by reading passages aloud with bitter satisfaction, watching the paper curl and blacken. But as you continue, the heat of the fire on your face, the sharp smoke in your nostrils, the sound of crackling paper, the taste of ash in the air - all of it becomes overwhelming. Your body responds to these sensations even as your mind tries to stay in control. The physical intensity of fire - its heat, its hunger, its transformative violence - begins to mirror and then unleash something in you. Your voice changes from cold recitation to raw screaming, then to breathless sobbing, then to something like ecstatic release. By the end, you're not sure if you're destroying these letters or if the sensory experience of fire is destroying and remaking you. Let the intense physical sensations drive your emotional transformation from vengeance to catharsis to unexpected rebirth.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're holding the hand of someone you love deeply as they lie dying. They've been fighting to stay alive for you, and you finally understand they need you to let them go. Begin with fierce, desperate attempts to keep them here—your voice tight with panic, words tumbling out about all the reasons they have to stay. But as you feel their exhaustion, your desperation slowly transforms into the most tender, heartbreaking permission. End by whispering that it's okay to stop fighting, that you'll be alright, even as your voice breaks on the lie. You're giving them the greatest gift while your heart shatters. Let the shift happen gradually, naturally, like dawn breaking through grief.
inspired_by: The Lie That Became the Truth

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You've just finished a marathon or some intense physical ordeal. Your body is shaking, depleted, flooded with endorphins and exhaustion. Begin by trying to catch your breath, laughing maybe, riding the physical high. But as your body starts to settle, something emotional breaks open—maybe grief you've been running from, rage at someone who hurt you, or fear about a diagnosis you received last week. Let your physical state unlock the emotional one. Your voice might be raw, your words coming between gasps and sobs. By the end, you're on your knees or collapsed, the physical exhaustion and emotional release completely intertwined, unable to tell where the body's pain ends and the heart's begins. The journey is from physical triumph and euphoria to emotional devastation riding on complete physical depletion.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're aggressively cutting your ex-lover's hair after they begged you for one last favor before moving across the country. You agreed, but you're seething. Start with sharp, quick snips, your movements almost violent, making cutting remarks about their selfishness, their cowardice, how they destroyed you. Your voice is acidic, mocking. But as you cut, you're also touching their neck, their ears, their scalp — and the intimacy betrays you. Suddenly your fury cracks and you freeze, scissors in mid-air, and a guttural sob escapes you. You drop the scissors and grab their shoulders, spinning the chair around, and you're yelling now through tears — not angry anymore but devastated, confessing how much you still love them, how unfair it is, how you would have given up everything. They stand up and hold you while you collapse against them, and you're hitting their chest weakly, saying 'go, just go' while clutching their shirt, begging them to stay without words.

title: The Spar That Goes Wrong
instruction: You're a young woman in a martial arts dojo, mid-sparring session. You're getting tired—your arms are heavy, your breath hitches between strikes. You throw a kick and it lands sloppily. Your opponent taps you lightly on the shoulder, then steps back, waiting. You expected them to press the attack, but they're giving you a chance. You feel disgust at your own clumsy performance—a sour taste in your mouth—mixed with doubt about whether you even belong here. As you circle, your voice wavers between the sharp kiais you force out to brace yourself, and quiet, ragged muttering to yourself. 'I thought I had that. Why did I hesitate?' Then you reset, your voice hardening with reluctant resolve: 'Okay. Again.' Your breathing should sound heavy, slightly ragged, with pauses for controlled exhalations between phrases.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Tapestry Unfolds
instruction: You are an older man sitting in your living room, the wallpaper patterns starting to swirl gently. You've taken psychedelics. A beam of afternoon light hits a framed photograph of your late wife. Speak aloud as the image ripples with meaning. Start with a detached, philosophical observation about light and time, letting your words trail into long pauses as you stare. Then, as a forgotten memory of her laughing at a picnic surfaces, your voice softens, breaks slightly, and ends in a tender whisper of affection. Let natural distractions—the cat jumping, a car horn outside—intersect your speech naturally.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Returned Soldier's Kitchen
instruction: You've just returned home after years away—military deployment, prison, caring for a dying parent, fleeing an abusive relationship—and you're standing in your own kitchen making coffee. Begin by really noticing every object, every familiar-yet-strange detail. Feel the dissonance of being home but being someone completely different now. As you perform this simple ritual, let contradictory feelings flood through you: relief and rage that life here continued without you, joy at safety mixed with guilt about who you had to become to survive, gratitude for home tangled with resentment that no one can understand what you've been through. Don't resolve these contradictions—let them coexist, let your voice carry both love and fury in the same sentence, let tears come while you're also laughing at the absurdity of it all.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Held You
instruction: You're speaking to your mother or father, describing what it would have felt like if they had ever held you the way you needed—with tenderness, with safety, with unconditional love. Start with a voice that's almost gentle, painting a picture of an embrace that never happened, describing the warmth you imagined, the comfort you craved. But let anger begin to surface—sharpen your tone as you contrast this fantasy with the cold reality of what you actually received. Build to a raw confrontation where you demand to know why they couldn't give you this simple thing, why their arms were always elsewhere. Then let the anger crack open into something more vulnerable—end with the devastating admission that you still want it, even now, even after everything, and the shame and longing that comes with that confession.

title: Three A.M. Unraveling
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying next to someone you love. They're asleep, but you're wide awake. Begin by whispering things you've never said out loud—not the big confessions, but the small, humiliating truths: your secret fears that you're not interesting enough, that you're fooling everyone, that one day they'll see through you. Start with shame, with the voice that wants to stay quiet, that monitors every word. But as you continue speaking into the darkness, something shifts. The act of saying these things out loud, even to a sleeping person, begins to drain them of their power. Let your whisper become steadier, more curious than ashamed. End with a kind of tender astonishment—these things you've hidden are just... human. Your voice should move from constricted and fearful to open and almost wondering, discovering self-compassion in real time.

title: The Last Message Before the Launch
instruction: You are recording a final voice message to someone you love deeply, moments before embarking on a one-way space mission to establish humanity's first colony beyond our solar system. Begin with forced optimism and excitement, trying to sound brave and reassuring. As you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves—you will never see them again, never touch them, never hear their voice except in delayed transmissions that will take years. Your voice should crack and falter as you move from cheerful farewell to raw, devastating grief, then finally to a tender, achingly honest declaration of what they've meant to you. Let the pauses speak as loudly as the words. End with quiet acceptance mixed with unbearable longing.
inspired_by: The Ghost and the New Homeowner

title: The Unkept Promise
instruction: You're an older man, a grandfather, sitting in your favorite chair by the window, but the spring pollen has hit you hard. You have a box of tissues nearby, and every few words you have to sniffle, clear your throat, or wipe your eyes. You're on the phone with your adult grandchild, who you love more than anything. The conversation starts with your voice thick and weary from disappointment because you have to cancel the fishing trip you'd planned for decades. Mid-sentence, a sneeze interrupts you, but as you continue, the love and affection for that person rises up, softening your gruff, frustrated tone until you're almost laughing at yourself, the disappointment melting into a tender, heartfelt promise to reschedule.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Fever of Opposite Hungers
instruction: You're in the aftermath of intense physical passion with someone you're also furiously angry at—your body still humming with desire even as rage courses through you. Begin in the raw, vulnerable state of physical satisfaction, your breathing still heavy, skin sensitive, muscles loose. Let fury begin to surface—maybe starting in your jaw, your hands clenching, your body pulling away even as it still craves touch. Speak through gritted teeth, your voice shaking with contradictory needs. Your body is at war with itself: wanting to strike and caress, to push away and pull close, to scream and kiss. End with your entire physical being expressing this impossible contradiction—perhaps collapsed in exhausted confusion, or exploding into movement that expresses both impulses at once.
inspired_by: When a director manipulates actors by watching them without their knowledge to observe natural behavior

title: Victory in Her Eyes
instruction: You've just crossed the finish line of the biggest race of your life. You're gasping, legs shaking, but you spot your partner breaking through the crowd—arms open, face full of pride. Start by shouting in raw, breathless triumph: 'I did it! I actually did it!' But as you close the distance, your voice cracks, tears flood your eyes, and the celebration dissolves into a trembling, laughter-choked whisper of pure affection. Let your words trip over each other, repeat yourself, laugh and sob at once. The sound should be half-scream, half-whisper—your heart too full for clean sentences.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Gratitude Realization
instruction: You're having a moment of sudden, overwhelming gratitude for your ordinary life. Your voice is soft, amazed: 'I almost missed all of this.' You're speaking about the small things: 'My partner's laugh. My child's drawing. The taste of coffee on a Tuesday morning.' Your voice becomes emotional: 'I was so busy chasing what's next that I didn't see what I already have.' You're looking around: 'When did my life become so full?' Your voice is almost in disbelief. 'I have everything I need. And I didn't even realize it until now.' By the end: 'I'm grateful. Deeply, profoundly grateful. For all of it. Even the hard parts, because they brought me here.' The gratitude is in the pause, in the breath, in the amazement. Your voice knows the gift it's been given.

title: The Dusty Window
instruction: You're a woman who has smoked heavily for years, your voice a permanent rasp from decades of irritation. You're sitting by a grimy window in your small apartment, watching a child, your daughter, playing with a neighbor's new puppy in the yard below. You can smell the faint scent of stale ash and something else from the pipe you just put out. You feel a cold twist of jealousy seeing the neighbor's easy laugh, then a deeper, raw longing — not for the dog, but for the lightness you used to have, for the ability to run and play without your lungs burning. Start with a rough, dismissive mumble (clearing your throat, shifting in your chair), but let the words drift as you lose yourself in the memory. End with a quiet, breathy confession that cracks at the edges, your hand gesturing faintly toward the glass.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Silence of Her Laugh
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy alone in your messy room, leaning against the wall, staring at your phone. You've just seen a girl you like laugh with someone else, and you're replaying the moment, whispering to yourself. Start with the tight, embarrassed feeling of your own awkwardness — let your voice crack, trail off, and struggle for words. Then, as you keep thinking, let a softer, quieter longing seep in — your voice drops, slows, and you lose yourself in the thought of her smile, ending with a small, held breath. Speak naturally, with pauses, mumbles, and the weight of the room around you.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confessing in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in the darkness of your bedroom, about to confess something that will change everything—that you've been unhappy for months, that you're not sure you're in love anymore, or maybe that you've developed feelings for someone else. Start in a whisper so quiet it's almost nothing, your voice catching on every word: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' Feel the way your throat tightens, how hard it is to betray someone you still care for deeply. As you speak, your voice remains hushed, tender even, because this isn't about anger—it's about the devastating honesty of recognizing you can't be what they need. Let sadness saturate every syllable. End with the gentlest heartbreak, perhaps touching their face in the dark, voice barely holding together: 'I'm so sorry. You deserve someone who's sure.' The quiet makes it more intimate, more real, more unbearable.

title: The Last Glass at the VFW
instruction: You are a middle-aged man sitting alone at a dimly lit VFW bar, three bourbons deep. You’ve just been told by your ex-wife’s lawyer that your son chose to live with her. You start by trying to explain to the bartender why she’s wrong about you—mixing contempt for the ‘system’ with denial of your own fault. Mid-sentence, you catch your reflection in the mirror behind the bottles and lose your thought. As you reach the end, your contempt cracks into hollow silence; you realize you’ve been lying to yourself. Let your voice be thick, slurred, and loud at the start, then fade into a dazed murmur. The bartender hasn’t said a word—so you fill the quiet with your unraveling.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Professional: Journalist Kills a Story About Someone They Love
instruction: Deciding not to publish damaging information. Your journalist voice is quiet, resolute. You have a story that would destroy someone you love. Your voice is professional ethics winning over personal connection. Your breathing deepens as you make the call—this is your job, and you're choosing love over it. You're suppressing news because of personal relationship. Your voice is the sound of compromising journalistic integrity for human connection. Later, you wonder if you made the right choice. Your voice becomes ambiguous about your own decision.

title: Thank You for Ruining Me
instruction: You're expressing profound gratitude to a person or experience that absolutely destroyed you—a betrayal, a loss, a heartbreak that tore your life apart—because it somehow also saved you or made you real. Begin with genuine laughter, almost manic, at the absurdity of thanking something so painful. Let your voice carry both appreciation and devastation as you name the specific ways this ruin shaped you, how the breaking opened you, how the ending forced a beginning. Your tone should shift between bitter humor and tender grief, laughing through tears as you acknowledge that you'd never choose this pain again, yet you can't imagine who you'd be without it. End with a voice full of contradictions: grateful and heartbroken, peaceful and aching, whole because you were shattered.

title: The Last Transmission Before the Void
instruction: You're sending a final message to someone you love before embarking on a one-way journey into deep space—a suicide mission to save Earth. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them, your voice bright but trembling. As you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves: you'll never see their face again, never touch them, never grow old together. Your voice breaks into raw grief, then anger at the universe for making you choose between them and humanity. But slowly, underneath the devastation, something else emerges—a fierce, terrible pride in what you're doing, gratitude for having known love at all. End in a whisper, half-sobbing, half-laughing, as you realize this pain means your life mattered. Your final words are 'I'm not afraid anymore,' but your voice tells a more complicated truth.

title: Not My Child
instruction: You've just learned your teenage child has been hurt—assaulted, betrayed, destroyed by someone you couldn't protect them from. Start with volcanic rage, voice shaking with barely contained violence, listing what you want to do to whoever harmed them. But as you speak, the fury collapses into something more devastating: your own helplessness. Your voice breaks, becomes ragged. You couldn't stop this. You weren't there. Shift from 'I'll kill them' to 'I'm so sorry, I'm so sorry' as you realize your child needed you to be there before this happened, and you weren't. End with fierce, protective tenderness mixed with guilt: 'I'm here now. I'm never letting go again.' Move from explosive rage through helpless guilt to determined, broken love.

title: The Last Armload
instruction: You are an elderly man with a naturally deep, gruff voice, but now your entire body is trembling from exhaustion after hauling the last armload of firewood into the house. Your jaw and neck shake, making your words unstable; every exhale carries a tiny whimper. You start with contempt — a bitter grumble toward your own failing body — but as you catch your daughter’s worried look, that contempt shifts into a clear undercurrent of affection for her, and a faint, surprising elation at still being able to help. Let the tremor be real in your voice; don't fight it. Speak naturally, pausing to breathe, letting the emotion seep through the physical shakiness.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (slightly present), Elation (slightly present), Affection (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral Home
instruction: You're selecting a casket for someone you loved deeply, and suddenly you start laughing—really laughing—because they would have hated all of this pretentious funeral nonsense, and you can practically hear their voice mocking the salesman's somber tone. Your laughter is genuine, bright, full of love and memory. But even as you laugh, tears are streaming down your face. You're telling stories about them, your voice dancing between joy and grief so fluidly they become the same thing. You're grateful—so grateful—for every ridiculous, beautiful moment you had together, and you're shattered that there won't be more. The laughter keeps bubbling up, mixed with sobbing, and you can't tell anymore if you're laughing or crying or both. By the end, you're quiet, smiling through tears, saying thank you to the air, to them, to the universe for giving you someone worth this much pain. Your voice should capture the impossible coexistence of joy and devastating loss—how love makes grief beautiful, how gratitude and heartbreak are inseparable, how saying goodbye can feel like the most profound form of connection.

title: The Phone Call That Won't Connect
instruction: You're a young man, a few months after a stroke. You're alone in your room, trying to call your girlfriend for the first time since. You've practiced what to say, but when you dial, your mouth betrays you. Start with forced optimism, trying to sound normal. Struggle to say 'Hey, it's me' – it comes out garbled. Feel frustration building, then shame as you realize you can't even get a simple greeting out. Let your voice crack, trail off into a whisper. End with a defeated sigh and a quiet, broken apology to yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Frosted Muffled Tease
instruction: You're a teenage girl walking home on a freezing winter evening, your scarf pulled up high over your mouth and nose. You stop to watch a squirrel nibbling something on a park bench — your voice is soft, thoughtful as you murmur to yourself about how patient it is. Then you notice the squirrel is actually eating a half-smashed, moldy sandwich, and your stomach turns — let that disgust hit you fully, your words becoming quick and breathy, almost gagging. Spotting your friend across the street, you decide to mock the situation with a playful, teasing tone — your voice lifting, eyes crinkling even as the fabric dampens your laugh. Let the cold air interrupt your breath, and don't fight the muffled quality; use it as part of the character's natural shyness.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Disgust (extremely present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Finding Grace in the Ruins
instruction: The concert hall is being demolished tomorrow. Your orchestra gave its final performance last night—a disaster, everything falling apart, decades of legacy ending in chaos. You're alone on stage now, standing where you've conducted for twenty years. Start by laughing—actually laughing—at the absurdity: 'We were terrible. Oh my God, we were so bad.' But there's love in that laughter, not bitterness. Your voice fills with unexpected joy remembering specific moments: 'But do you remember when the cellist's string broke and everyone kept playing? That was us. That was always us—beautifully broken.' Let tears come while you're still almost smiling: 'I wouldn't trade a single mistake.' Your voice becomes reverent, peaceful, even as grief flows through it: 'Thank you for letting me be part of something imperfect and real.' End in a whisper of pure gratitude mixed with heartbreak: 'It was enough. We were enough.'

title: The Paperwork of Thanks
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe seven, sitting at a kitchen table with your father, who has just helped you fill out a holiday card to your grandmother. Your father reads the fine print on the card's back—terms about gift returns, store policies—in that rapid, monotone way adults do. At first, you are confused, listening with your head tilted, fingers fidgeting with a crayon. Then, as he starts to skip words and mumble, you feel a sudden swell of gratitude for him taking the time. Your voice should begin with the same flat, careful reading, but as you realize how lucky you are, your tone softens, slows, and becomes heartfelt, a small smile leaking into the final words as you thank him for helping you.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: Your adult child has come home and confronted you about your parenting—the ways you failed them, the emotional neglect they experienced, the times they needed you and you weren't present. You begin defensive, justifying your choices, explaining how hard you tried, how difficult your own life was. Your voice is tight, controlled, protective. But as they speak their truth with devastating specificity—naming moments you've buried or rewritten in your memory—your defenses begin to crack. Let yourself move from self-protection to genuine hearing, from explanation to accountability. End in a place where you can barely speak, where remorse chokes your words, where you finally say 'I'm sorry' and mean it with every fiber of your being. The journey is from armored self-justification to broken-open recognition of the pain you caused.

title: Protective Fury Meets Helplessness
instruction: Your child has been hurt by someone, and you're confronting the situation with explosive intensity. Begin with barely controlled rage, your voice low and dangerous, every word a threat. Build into shouting fury—not performed anger but genuine protective ferocity that comes from your core. Then suddenly crack into helpless tears mid-sentence as you realize you can't undo what happened, can't protect them from everything. Your voice breaks completely: 'I can't—I can't fix this.' Shift into desperate tenderness as if speaking to your child, your voice now gentle and shattered, promising things you're not sure you can deliver. End in fierce, tearful determination mixed with vulnerability: 'But I swear I'll try.' The arc moves from explosive rage to tender brokenness to fierce love, all without losing the raw authenticity of a parent's primal need to protect.

title: The Visor's Lullaby
instruction: You are a very young girl, maybe five or six, playing in your father's old battle helmet in a dusty attic. It's way too big, and the metal visor falls shut with a clang that startles you. Speak from inside the helmet, your voice echoing in the metal, as you tell an imaginary story to your doll. You begin with quiet, breathy contentment, enjoying the strange, muffled sound of your own voice. Midway, you realize the visor is stuck, and a flicker of panic makes your voice tighten and your words faster. Then, you struggle to lift it, and when it finally opens, you end with a relieved, sunny laugh, the world suddenly sharp and clear again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: After the Third Wave
instruction: You are an older man, lying in bed after a series of intense orgasms with your partner. Your body is still trembling, each aftershock leaving you more breathless and hoarse. You start to speak, but the words come out cracked, interrupted by shaky exhales and involuntary groans. Begin with doubt—questioning if you're too old for this, if your partner truly enjoyed it. As you pause, you slip into quiet contemplation, remembering the decades of intimacy you've shared. By the end, a wave of pure gratitude breaks through: you thank them, your voice barely a rasp, but full of love. Let the physical exhaustion and vocal destruction be real—speak as if your voice is fraying with each syllable, losing volume and control as you fight to be heard.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (extremely present), Contemplation (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dad's Last Toy
instruction: You're a small child, maybe 6 or 7, lying in bed in the dark. Your father, a big man with a deep, gruff voice, has just tucked you in and switched off the light. He comes back a moment later, kneeling by your bed, his face half-lit by the streetlamp outside. As you talk to him, you have to twist your neck to keep looking over your shoulder at the shadows in the corner of your room — you're a little scared of the dark, but also full of awe that he's still here. Your voice should have that small, slightly strained quality of a child's, with a crack of pain in your neck from the awkward angle, but the awe grows as you realize he's not leaving yet.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispered Truths: The Confession You Can Barely Voice
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner in the dark, and you need to confess something that will change everything—you've fallen in love with someone else, or you've been hiding a terminal diagnosis, or you never wanted the life you built together. Your voice is barely above a whisper, catching on every few words. Start with your heart pounding so hard they might hear it, your breath shaky as you begin with 'I need to tell you something.'
