The words come in fragments, half-swallowed by emotion. You're not dramatic—you're devastated and tender, apologizing between revelations, your voice breaking on their name. Feel the weight of destroying someone you still love deeply. End with a silence that's louder than words, then a whispered 'I'm so sorry' that carries the full weight of irreversible loss. This isn't theatrical heartbreak—it's the quiet kind that hollows you out.
inspired_by: Concealing Your True Intentions During a Negotiation

title: The Pulse in Your Throat
instruction: You're lying in bed in darkness with someone you've loved silently for years. You've never told them. Tonight, you've decided you must, even though they're in a relationship with someone else and leave tomorrow for another country. Begin terrified, your mouth dry, rehearsing words in your mind that won't come out. Then shift your attention: don't look at their face or think about their whole body. Instead, find the small, visible pulse in the hollow of their throat—that tiny, rhythmic flutter that proves they're alive and real and here. Focus completely on that pulse. Let it become the only thing in the universe. Watch it beat. Let your whispered confession pour toward that single point of life. Your fear should dissolve into something rawer—an almost unbearable tenderness and urgency. Speak your love as if you're speaking to their heartbeat itself, so quietly they have to hold their breath to hear you.

title: The Last Thing I Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's awake but weak. For years, you've carried a secret fear that you disappointed her by choosing a different life path than she hoped for you. Begin by holding back, making small talk about the weather, the flowers in the room. But as you realize time is running out, let the dam break. Tell her everything you've been afraid to say—your fears of not being enough, your gratitude for small moments you never acknowledged, the ways she shaped you that you never named aloud. Move from tentative, polite restraint to raw, unfiltered truth-telling. Let your voice crack, rush, whisper. By the end, you should feel emptied out—terrified and free at once.

title: Reading Your Teenage Daughter's Suicide Note—After She Survived
instruction: Your fifteen-year-old daughter is alive, asleep in the hospital after a suicide attempt, and you're holding the note she left. Start reading it out loud with your voice shaking, terrified, initially just trying to get through the words. But as you read her reasons—the pain you didn't see, the bullying you minimized, the ways she felt invisible in her own home—let contradictory emotions war in your voice. Rage at her for scaring you ('How could you DO this?'), rage at yourself for missing the signs, overwhelming gratitude that she's alive, grief that she wanted to die, horror at specific details, defensive anger ('That's not fair, I was working to provide for you'), then the collapse of all defenses into pure anguished love. Your voice should oscillate wildly: shouting accusations at her, at yourself, at the universe, then breaking into sobs, then laughing hysterically with relief that she failed, then crying harder because she tried at all. End by crumpling the note, pressing it to your chest, and whispering a promise to her sleeping form that contains both fierce protectiveness and the terrifying acknowledgment that you can't actually keep her safe from herself. The journey moves from shock through rage, self-loathing, gratitude, and grief into a complex, mature love that includes helplessness.

title: Unraveling the Perfectionist
instruction: Confront your mother who spent your entire childhood maintaining an immaculate, controlled household where everything had its place and every emotion was contained. You've just discovered she's been secretly gambling away the family savings. Embody her rigid, bird-like precision at first—your gestures sharp, your spine straight, your words clipped and measured like hers always were. But as you demand the truth and she begins to crumble, feel something wilder rising in you—something messier, more mammalian, more feral. Your movements become bigger, less controlled; you pace, you prowl, you take up space in a way she never permitted. End in a place of fierce, unleashed power, your body claiming a freedom you've never allowed yourself in her presence.

title: Three AM Threshold
instruction: You are lying in bed next to someone you've been with for years, both of you supposedly asleep. But you're awake, and you need to tell them something you've been hiding—something about yourself that you're deeply ashamed of. Not an affair, but something more fundamental: a fear, a need, a part of who you are that you've always kept locked away. Begin by whispering their name to see if they're awake, and notice how even that small sound comes out in your 'safe' voice—the voice you've perfected for intimate moments. But as you start to confess in the darkness, become aware of every familiar way you usually talk about vulnerable things: the self-deprecating joke you might make, the smooth way you usually phrase difficult truths, the slight performance even in your most private moments. Deliberately let those habits fall away. Speak more simply than you ever have. Let silences stretch. Stumble over words. Let your voice crack or disappear. By the end, you're speaking from a place in yourself you've never let anyone hear—raw, unpolished, barely more than breath.

title: After the Storm
instruction: You are lying in bed, skin still damp and warm, your partner's arm heavy across your waist. For a long moment, you just breathe, letting the last waves of pleasure dissolve into a deep, lazy satisfaction. Then, as you trace the line of his shoulder with your fingers, the ecstasy gives way to a quieter, more startling tenderness that catches in your throat. Let your words come out slow, almost slurred, with a breathy vocal fry — talk about how perfect this feels, then let your voice soften and crack slightly as you admit, 'I think I forgot to breathe there for a second... I didn't want to come back.' End with a little sigh, and maybe a shy laugh that fades into a whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Conduct Orchestra
instruction: The Rite of Spring is exploding under your direction. Your voice is barely heard over the music—brief, essential directions. 'Here.' 'Now.' Your voice is the space between the sound. The musicians are united. This is perfection—moments where hundreds of individual humans become one organism. Your voice guides but doesn't control. The transcendence is audible in your quiet command.

title: The Bog Monster's Belly Laugh
instruction: You're a father telling a campfire story to your young son, who's bundled in a blanket and watching you with wide eyes. Start with a playful, slightly disgusted tone as you describe the bog monster's slimy, gross habits—wrinkling your nose, using a teasing voice to get a reaction from him. But as you see his excitement and trust, your voice softens, losing the disgust and filling with deep contentment. End with a warm, rhythmic chuckle, the teasing fading into pure joy as you ruffle his hair and finish the tale. Let your voice crack and shift naturally, pausing to stoke the fire or yawn.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Contentment (extremely present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Forgetting Your Mother's Face
instruction: You're visiting your mother in late-stage dementia care. She looks at you with such hope, such need for recognition. You start confident, warm: 'Hi Mom, it's me.' But her eyes are blank. You try again, voice catching: 'It's your daughter... remember?' You're searching her face desperately for any flicker of knowing. Your voice breaks into a whisper as you realize she's gone somewhere you can't follow: 'I'm here. I'm right here.' End holding her hand, grief mixing with fierce, protective love - you remember her even if she can't remember you. Let the weight of losing someone while they're still alive crush and tender you simultaneously.

title: The Knitted Grievance
instruction: You are comforting your adult granddaughter, who is crying over a recent breakup. You hold her hand, pat her back, and breathe with her in slow, soothing waves. But inside, you are seething with envy for the younger woman he left her for, and irritation at the girl's tears—you worked so hard to raise a woman who wouldn't be this fragile. As you speak, your voice stays low and rhythmic, with downward inflections, but it cracks with barely hidden jealousy and impatience. Start with a steady, measured blanket of comfort. By the end, let a little awe slip in when you realize that she still has a future you would give anything to have again. You don't. But she does.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Awe (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Summer Rain Before Everything Changes
instruction: You're standing in the rain one final time before leaving home forever—maybe for war, maybe illness, maybe a life choice that means you can never return. Begin with desperate, almost frantic appreciation of each raindrop, trying to memorize this feeling, speaking quickly as if time is running out. Let your voice crack as you realize this simple pleasure—rain on skin—is something you took for granted for years. Transition from celebration to quiet devastation as it hits you: this might be the last time. End in whispered disbelief, touching your wet face, asking 'how did I not know to treasure this?' Let the joy of the rain mix with the grief of goodbye until you can barely speak.
inspired_by: Feeling the First Drops of Rain on a Hot Day

title: Midnight Message Cramp
instruction: You are a teenage boy, alone in your room late at night, recording a voice message for someone you deeply miss. You start speaking softly, with a slight longing in your voice, trying to find the right words. Suddenly, a severe muscle cramp seizes your calf—your body locks, you gasp, and a sharp curse escapes. You pause, breathing through the pain, then continue your message, but now your voice is tense, guarded, and the longing is mixed with the ache of the spasm and the frustration of being interrupted. Let the cramp genuinely affect your speech—a sudden strangled sound, then a reset. End with a quieter, more vulnerable tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Sneeze and Sweet Nothings
instruction: You’re on a video call with someone you’ve had a crush on for weeks. Your seasonal allergies are flaring up—your nose is running, eyes watering, and you keep sneezing. You’re trying to sound charming and slightly flirtatious, but every few words you’re derailed by a sneeze or cough. Start with an apologetic, embarrassed tone, then gradually let your voice soften into a huskier, more seductive register as you ignore the discomfort and focus on the attraction. Let the symptoms interrupt and color your delivery naturally.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Backroom Promise
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, gruff voice, leaning close to a younger man in a cramped, dim back room. You have to speak so no one else hears—low, tight-jawed, almost spitting the words through clenched teeth. Start with intense contempt, your voice flat and clipped, each word precise and cutting. As you explain how he failed you, let disappointment creep in—your tone gets slower, more gravelly, with a weary sigh between phrases. You shift your weight, glance at the door, then back at him. End with a hollow, resigned disappointment, your voice barely above a whisper, the contempt drained away.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point of Certainty
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—perhaps extreme pleasure, pain from an injury, or the overwhelming rush of a panic attack. Start by trying to maintain control through your voice, explaining what's happening to you with clinical distance, describing sensations as if you understand and can manage them. Your words are clipped, authoritative, fighting to maintain mastery over your body. But the sensation overwhelms your ability to narrate it. Let language collapse—admit through gasping breath or mounting intensity that you don't know what's happening to you, that you can't explain it, that your body is speaking a language you don't understand. End in pure vocal expression of the sensation itself, words dissolving into sounds, your voice transformed from intellectual control to raw, unmediated experience, finally surrendering the need to know and explain.
inspired_by: Actor bluffs on set rather than admitting ignorance

title: Protecting Your Child From Your Own Rage
instruction: You're standing between your child and danger—could be an abuser, could be a system failing them, could be their own self-destruction—and you're unleashing years of suppressed fury. Begin with explosive rage, voice raw and almost feral, every word a weapon, your protective instinct turned to aggression. You're shouting, threatening, promising violence if they're hurt. But mid-tirade, you see your child's fear—not of the danger, but of YOU, of your intensity—and your voice cracks completely. The rage shatters into helpless sobbing. You're apologizing, trying to explain, your voice going from roar to whisper in seconds. You pull them close, voice breaking as you promise you'll be gentler, you'll do better, but your hands are shaking and you're terrified you've scared them permanently. End with fierce tenderness, voice thick with tears, whispering promises of protection but now with softness, trying to repair what your own fury just damaged.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She has always been the strong one, the rock of your family, but now she's fragile and fading. Begin by sitting in silence, noticing every detail of the room—the beeping monitor, the texture of her blanket, the way afternoon light falls across her face. Let yourself become fully present with these details before you speak. As you hold her hand, tell her about three specific moments in your life when her strength carried you through. Start with gratitude and composure, but as you speak, allow yourself to feel the impending loss. By the end, you must give her permission to let go, even though every fiber of your being wants her to stay. Your voice should transform from steady reminiscence to tender, broken release.
inspired_by: Actor needs to prepare instrumentally for an audition

title: Collapsed and Fed Up
instruction: You've just sprinted up six flights of stairs to catch someone, and now you're slumped against the wall, gasping. You're a young woman whose voice usually has a light, teasing quality, but right now you're furious. Your body is limp, your breath hacks in and out, and every word comes out squeezed between gasps. Start by mocking the person who made you run—breathless, sarcastic, almost playful—but let the anger take over as you realize they knew this would happen. Your voice should crack and lose its teasing edge, turning raw and furious by the end. The struggle to breathe makes your words fragmented and uneven, like you're fighting both the air and the person in front of you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Recognizing You've Become What You Feared
instruction: You just caught yourself treating someone the exact way you swore you never would—the way you were once treated. Start with nervous laughter, trying to deflect: 'That came out wrong, I didn't mean...' But the laughter dies as the recognition hits. Your voice becomes stunned, horrified at yourself: 'Oh god, that's exactly what they used to say to me.' You're speaking to the person you hurt, but you're also speaking to yourself, and to the younger you who promised this would never happen. Your voice moves through shame, disbelief, and a strange kind of grief—mourning the person you thought you were. 'I became the thing I was most afraid of.' End with your voice soft but resolved, carrying both the weight of what you've done and the fragile hope that recognizing it is the first step to breaking the cycle: 'I'm sorry. And I'm going to do better.'
inspired_by: Recognizing Abuse Pattern Repeating in New Relationship

title: The Unsaid Year
instruction: Your parent is sitting across from you. For an entire year, they've made casual racist comments at family dinners, and you've said nothing—smiled politely, changed the subject, kept the peace. Tonight, they've just done it again. You start speaking calmly, almost apologetically, as you've been conditioned to do—small voice, careful words. But as you continue, something breaks open inside you. The politeness cracks. Let your voice rise not with theatrical anger but with the genuine, messy rage of someone who's been betraying themselves. Feel the fear of confronting someone you love, the shame of your own silence, the fury at being put in this position. By the end, you're not yelling—you're standing in your full power, voice steady and low, making it clear that you will never swallow yourself again. The journey is from appeasing to unapologetically claiming your dignity.

title: The Skin and the Storm
instruction: You're experiencing something intensely physical—making love, getting a massage after months of pain, holding ice to a burn, or gripping someone in desperate embrace. Begin fully in your body, letting physical sensation be the primary reality. Let sounds escape unselfconsciously—breath, sighs, whatever's genuine. But underneath the physical, emotional weather builds: grief about something unrelated surfaces, rage at yourself emerges, sudden ecstasy at being alive crashes in, memory of loss floods through you. Don't separate the physical from the emotional—let them blur and intensify each other. Your body might shake with more than physical response. By the end, you're somewhere completely different emotionally than where you began, having been physically carried there. Let the experience move through you without control or commentary.

title: Sci-Fi: Alien First Contact With Translator Who Recognizes It As Their Dead Child
instruction: Translation booth. Alien makes contact with humans. Your voice is steady, professional interpretation. But the creature's vocal pattern—the way it forms sounds—matches data your child produced before the accident. Your voice becomes unsteady in the translation. You're interpreting your child to humanity. Your breathing becomes audible—you're hyperventilating in tiny increments. Your professional voice fractures as you wonder if consciousness can exist in forms we didn't prepare for.

title: The Final Words: What You'd Actually Say
instruction: You have 60 seconds to leave a final voice recording — not a will, not a speech, but the actual last thing you'd say if you knew no one would judge it. Start with who you love — say their names. Then what you regret — briefly, no wallowing. Then what you're grateful for — specific, small things. Then the surprise: what you'd want them to know that you never said. The voice should be calm, clear, and completely unperformed. This is the one challenge where acting should be impossible. Just be a person. Just speak.

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's three in the morning. You're lying in bed next to someone you love, and they're asleep. You're whispering things you can't say when they're awake—fears about your own capacity to love, the ways you sabotage intimacy, the terror that you'll hurt them or they'll discover you're not who they think you are. Start tentatively, testing the darkness with half-formed thoughts. Let yourself become more honest with each whispered confession, admitting things you've never said aloud to anyone, not even yourself. Your voice should be barely audible but intensely present. End with the most vulnerable truth: that you're afraid of how much you need them, how deeply you've let them in. Journey from cautious confession to stark, trembling emotional nakedness.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty being physically or emotionally intimate in scenes

title: The Family Album
instruction: You're an older man standing at a reunion, hip cocked, flipping through a photo album someone shoved at you. You start with a casual, almost sassy comment about a relative's new partner, but as you look closer at the picture — the smug grin, the cheap suit — a deep, physical disgust rises. Your voice sours, trailing off as you mutter about the audacity, the tackiness. By the end, you're not just complaining; you're quietly revolted, the words dying in your throat as you close the album with a snap.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Childlike Wonder in a Strange Land
instruction: You find yourself in a surreal, dreamlike place, like a child exploring a magical forest for the first time. Narrate your surroundings with awe, innocence, and occasional fear, capturing the blend of wonder and uncertainty with each discovery.

title: The Moment You Realize You're Becoming the Person You Swore You'd Never Be
instruction: You're mid-argument with someone you love when you hear yourself say something—a phrase, a tone, a cruelty—that makes you stop cold because it's exactly what was done to you. Start in full defensive mode, voice sharp and self-righteous, landing verbal blows with precision. Then freeze. Let your voice crack and shift as the realization hits you like physical impact. Move from fierce justification to horror at yourself, your words tumbling out faster and more desperate as you try to take it back, to explain, to apologize. Your voice should break between rage at being challenged and devastation at what you've become. Cycle rapidly between defensiveness, self-loathing, and desperate vulnerability. Build to an explosive moment where everything pours out—the pain that made you this way, the shame of perpetuating it, the terror that you can't stop. End quietly, your voice raw and small, asking for forgiveness while barely able to forgive yourself.

title: Wrong Team, Right Rage
instruction: You're watching the game with your teenager, cheering for 'your' team - the team your absent ex-partner loved, the team you pretended to care about to keep the peace. Your child, now wearing the rival team's colors, calls you out: you don't actually care about this team, you never did, you were just performing. Start defensive, voice rising with false enthusiasm, almost aggressive insistence that you've always loved this team. But let their quiet, piercing observation crack you open. Your voice should explode with years of suppressed rage - at yourself for performing, at their other parent for leaving, at all the things you faked to hold your family together. Then let it all collapse into helpless, gasping sobs as you admit you don't even know who you really are anymore, what you actually like, what's real and what's performance.

title: The Bedroom Confession With Shifting Ground
instruction: You're whispering a painful secret to your partner in the dark—something you've carried for years. Begin with trembling vulnerability, speaking carefully chosen words. But your partner keeps responding in unexpected ways: suddenly they're tracing patterns on your skin when you need them to be still, or they interrupt your confession with their own whispered admission, or they pull away physically just as you're getting to the hardest part. Each unexpected response forces you to recalibrate—you can't just deliver your prepared confession. Sometimes you must pause and truly listen. Sometimes their touch unlocks deeper truths than your words. Let the unpredictability break down the wall between confession and conversation. By the end, you've revealed something you didn't even know you were hiding, pulled out by their surprising responses rather than your own script.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) about a wound they inflicted years ago that has shaped your entire life. Begin with controlled anger, your words carefully chosen, your posture rigid. As you speak, recreate in your mind the specific moment when it happened—the room, the smells, what you were wearing, the expression on their face. Let that sensory memory flood through you until your controlled fury cracks open into something more vulnerable: the child (or parent) who was hurt, who needed something they didn't receive. End in a place of exhausted honesty, your voice stripped of its armor, asking the question you've never been able to ask.

title: Running to Your Estranged Father's Deathbed—Arriving Too Late
instruction: You're sprinting through hospital corridors after getting the call that your father—whom you haven't spoken to in eight years after a devastating argument—is dying. Start angry, furious that he's doing this now, that you have to care, your breath coming in bitter gasps. As you run, the anger cracks—memories flood in, regret seeps through. You're pleading aloud between breaths, bargaining with no one, 'Please, just let me—please, I need to—' Burst through the door and stop. Silence. You're too late. The shift to stillness is crushing. Your breathing slows but your voice breaks completely as you approach his body, all the unsaid words tumbling out in broken whispers: apologies, accusations, love you never admitted. End with your hand on his, finally quiet, finally honest, finally too late.
inspired_by: Reporting While Sprinting for Your Life

title: Trying to Break Up While They Keep Being Perfect
instruction: You've rehearsed the breakup speech. You start: 'We need to talk...' But they immediately do something devastatingly sweet — bring you tea, say something loving. Your prepared speech crumbles. You restart. They compliment you. You restart again. The voice oscillates between resolved (low, steady) and crumbling (high, wavering). Include the inner screaming frustration of trying to do a hard thing while someone makes it impossible. You love them. That's why you have to leave.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Prison
instruction: It's 4 AM and you're sitting beside your child's bed, watching them sleep, knowing you have to turn yourself in at dawn for a crime you committed to save them. Speak in the softest whisper—barely breath, terrified of waking them yet desperate to say everything. Begin with tender observations: how their hair falls across their face, the way they still sleep with that old stuffed rabbit. Your voice should be full of love so enormous it physically hurts. Slowly, let the grief seep in—you're memorizing their face, knowing you'll miss years of their life. Your whisper becomes choked, words fragmenting as you try to explain why you did what you did, voice catching on phrases like 'you'll understand someday' and 'I had no choice.' End with a simple 'I love you' that takes three tries to get out, each repetition breaking more, until you finally place a kiss on their forehead and the sound of your quiet sobbing is all that remains.

title: Parking Lot Eruption: Protective Fury Meeting Powerlessness
instruction: You've just learned that someone hurt your child, your younger sibling, or someone you're fiercely protective of, and you're confronting the person responsible. Start with voice shaking from the effort of controlled rage—you're trying to be measured, to handle this like an adult. But control shatters. Let your voice explode into a roar of protective fury, words tumbling over each other, threatening, demanding, voice cracking with the force of your anger. Then—devastatingly—mid-rage, you break. Because you can't undo what happened. You can't protect them from what already occurred. The fury collapses into choking sobs, into helpless, anguished admission that you weren't there when it mattered. Your voice becomes raw, stripped, oscillating wildly between resurgent rage and broken despair. End in a fierce, tearful vow—voice still shaking but finding a different kind of strength—that whatever happens next, they won't face it alone. Move from barely controlled anger to explosive rage to complete breakdown to fierce, protective resolution.
inspired_by: Confession While High: Watching Your Mouth Betray You

title: The Grateful Predator
instruction: You are a middle-aged, rugged man who has just been stabbed in the gut. You are bleeding out on a cold concrete floor. The woman who tried to stop the attack—your rival's lover—is kneeling beside you, pressing her hands to the wound. You feel a rush of gratitude for her presence, but underneath it, you still hunger for her and feel a cold satisfaction that your rival will pay for this. Start with a panicked, forceful voice as you gasp for air and curse the pain. Then, as blood loss sets in, your words slow, shivers creep into your tone, and your voice fades into a hoarse whisper. Let the lust and malice flicker in your eyes and tone, but let gratitude be the final, fading truth. Speak a few lines to her, thanking her while admitting your twisted feelings, all while your body grows weaker and your vision blurs.

title: A Whispered Reckoning at Dusk
instruction: You are an older man sitting by the window of a quiet, dimly lit cabin, watching the last light fade over a dusty field. You're on the phone with a close friend—someone you've known for decades, who you suspect has been subtly mocking your recent choices. Your voice is barely a whisper, because you don't want your partner in the next room to hear. Start with a heavy, sour bitterness as you describe the hurt their teasing has caused, your breath thin and tight. Midway, a memory flickers—a shared joke from years ago—and a teasing lilt creeps into your whisper, soft and warm, your throat loosening. End with a reluctant chuckle, the sourness fading into a playful, weary affection, your voice a gentle rasp of steam and air.

title: Thanking Someone You're Losing
instruction: You're expressing gratitude to someone on their deathbed—a mentor, grandparent, or dear friend who shaped your life. Begin with a smile in your voice, almost laughing through gathering tears: 'Remember when you told me I'd never amount to anything? You were such a pain.' Your voice is warm with affection and memory. But as you speak, the laughter tangles with grief. You're celebrating them while saying goodbye, finding joy in memories while your heart shatters. 'You made me who I am. Everything good in me is because you—' Your voice catches. By the end, you're crying and smiling simultaneously, holding both peace and devastation: 'Thank you. For all of it. For everything. I love you so much.' Let gratitude and heartbreak exist in the same breath. This is beautiful contradiction—finding grace in letting go.

title: The KnowItAll Tourist Guide
instruction: Portray a guide who provides incorrect facts about landmarks. Use an authoritative voice when sharing misinformation, switching to the groups doubtful questions.

title: The Last Shift
instruction: You are an elderly former factory worker bringing your grandson to see the plant before it shuts down permanently. The hum of idle machinery echoes in the high ceilings. You pause near an old lathe, feeling the cold metal and the weight of years. Your voice carries a slight rasp from age and the dusty air. As you speak, a young engineer walks past with a blueprint for a community workshop project. You notice it and feel a flicker of hope—the work continues in a new form. Let your voice start heavy with memory and loss, then gradually lift as you point out the new plan, ending with a soft, sincere belief that something good remains.

title: Fog and Fire
instruction: You are a teenager with a concussion, sitting in a quiet room, still dazed. The person you’ve been secretly infatuated with has just told a story that makes you deeply disgusted. You try to respond, but your head is thick and slow. Your voice is flat, with long pauses as you search for words, and your volume may spike harshly when the disgust hits. Start with a thick, repulsed tone, then let the infatuation slowly bleed through—a quieter, warmer note that fights the fog. Say: 'That story you told… it makes me feel sick. The way you laughed… it’s like… a pit in my stomach. But I still… I can’t help staring at you. I hate that I do that. I hate this.'

title: The Daughter I Was Supposed to Be
instruction: You're confronting your mother after years of performing the version of yourself she needed you to be. Begin the confrontation trying to be reasonable, mature, using the careful language you always use with her. But as you speak, let decades of swallowed anger, hidden disappointment, and suppressed wildness start to surface. Your voice might get louder or it might get dangerously quiet. Let yourself say the things 'good daughters' don't say. Use words you've never used with her. Let your body language break its trained politeness. Move from controlled and measured to unleashed - but not just angry. Let her see the parts of you that you've starved and hidden to earn her approval. End in a place of terrifying freedom, having shattered the glass container you've lived in.

title: Whispered Geography
instruction: Late at night, in bed with your partner, you're tracing the scars on their body with your fingers—each one has a story. Speak in intimate whispers as you touch each scar (real or imagined), asking them to tell you how they got it. But one scar, when you reach it, makes them freeze. They confess something they've never told anyone—something that breaks your heart with tenderness. Your emotional journey: begin with playful, sensual curiosity, move through gentle intimacy, then arrive at breathless, protective tenderness mixed with profound sadness. Your voice should become softer, closer, more careful as you go. The final moment should be nearly silent—just breath and heartbreak.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Dream Journal Entries Exercise

title: The Landing
instruction: You are a young Dominant man, still slightly breathless, kneeling beside your partner who is wrapped in a blanket on the bed. The scene just ended minutes ago. Your voice is still deep but now stripped of command — it's soft, low, almost hoarse. You feel a swell of pride for how beautifully they surrendered, but as you stroke their hair and sip water, that pride softens into a quiet, aching tenderness. Speak these words while instinctively checking their pulse, adjusting the blanket, pausing to cough or clear your throat. Let your voice start with a warm, proud hum that gradually becomes more fragile, more personal — like you're realizing how much you need them too.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Last Words to Your Child Before Surgery You Might Not Wake From
instruction: You're about to go into a surgery with a 40% survival rate. You have three minutes with your child before they wheel you away. Start trying to be brave, voice steady, saying practical things—but your body betrays you with tremors of terror. Your hands shake. Your voice cracks when you say their name. Midway through, the facade crumbles and raw fear bleeds through—you're trying not to cry, trying not to scare them, but you need them to know everything, all at once. Then, in the final moments, find a strange, quiet peace. Your voice steadies not from courage but from acceptance. The shaking stops. You become present, tender, almost serene. End with gratitude for having known them at all.
inspired_by: Withdrawing from Alcohol: Shaking So Bad Your Voice Trembles

title: The Last Apology Before the Doors Close
instruction: You're visiting your terminally ill parent who never acknowledged the harm they caused you throughout your childhood. You came prepared to finally speak your truth, but seeing them so fragile, you find yourself swallowing your anger and instead apologizing for being 'difficult' as a child. Start with controlled, almost clinical composure as you walk in—'I'm sorry I wasn't easier to love.' Feel the injustice of your own words burning in your throat as memories flash through you. Let resentment crack through in small, involuntary ways—a sharp breath, a pause that lasts too long. Then watch yourself give up, your voice becoming smaller, softer, more tender despite yourself. End with a devastating gentleness as you realize this is the only goodbye you'll get: 'I forgive you,' spoken so quietly it's almost a whisper, hollow and yet somehow full of a grief you didn't know you could feel.
inspired_by: Apologizing for Something You Weren't At Fault For

title: Reading the Letter They Left Behind
instruction: You're holding a letter from someone who's gone—moved away forever, ended their life, left you somehow. As you read their words aloud, they're telling you they loved you, they're grateful for you, they're sorry. Start with disbelief, almost laughing through tears: 'You idiot. You beautiful idiot.' Your voice breaks between gratitude and grief. Let yourself smile at a memory they mention, then immediately feel the loss crash over you again. Say 'Thank you' like it's both a gift and a wound. End with something like 'I'm so angry at you. And I'm so grateful I knew you. And I miss you so much I can't breathe.' Your voice should hold all of it—love, rage, gratitude, devastation—all at once, authentic and raw.
inspired_by: Someone Telling You They Love You for First Time

title: The Last Breath in Our Kitchen
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent in the kitchen where they taught you to cook as a child. Begin by noticing every detail of this room—the worn table, the smell of coffee, the light through the window—letting these familiar surroundings ground you in memories. As you hold their hand, start with quiet gratitude for small things, then let yourself move toward the words you've been too afraid to say. Your voice should journey from careful tenderness to raw, unguarded need. By the end, you must ask the one question you've carried your whole life, knowing you have only moments left to hear the answer.
inspired_by: Actor is working on a scene but is not sure which obligation to address first

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone you love, and you need to whisper a truth you've been hiding—something that makes you deeply ashamed or afraid. Begin by simply focusing on the darkness, the warmth of the bed, the sound of their breathing beside you. Let yourself feel the weight of your body, the beating of your heart, the exact sensation of air moving in and out of your lungs. Start from a place of terrified silence—you're not sure you can say it. As you attend to these physical sensations and the intimate sensory details of this moment, allow the words to emerge not as a planned speech but as something pulled from your body by the reality of their presence. Move from paralyzed fear to a fragile, whispered honesty. Let the sensations guide the revelation.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Daughter She Made You Give Up
instruction: You're face-to-face with your mother thirty years after she forced you to give your baby up for adoption when you were sixteen. Start with cold, controlled anger—you've rehearsed this moment. But when she tries to justify it, your voice explodes into raw fury about all the moments stolen from you. Then she reveals something you never knew: your daughter has been looking for you. Your rage shatters into something more complex—grief mixed with hope, betrayal mixed with desperate longing. You want to hate your mother but you're also terrified and need her guidance. Your voice becomes a battlefield of accusation and plea, ending with you asking the question you're most afraid to hear answered: 'Does she hate me?'
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Catches Glimpse of Their Own Child They Were Forced to Abandon

title: Breathing Free for the First Time
instruction: You've just walked away from the life that was suffocating you—left the relationship, the job, the identity that never fit—and found yourself in this forest, genuinely breathing freely for the first time in years. Describe the air with wonder laced with grief: laugh through tears as you realize how different real air feels, how you'd forgotten what your own breath sounds like without someone else's expectations crushing your chest. Your voice should dance between liberation and loss—joy that you're finally here, sorrow for the years you weren't. Let contradictions live simultaneously: celebrate your freedom while mourning what you had to destroy to find it. End with a breathless, almost disbelieving gratitude mixed with lingering sadness—you're free, you're alive, you're also heartbroken, and somehow all of it is perfect and terrible and exactly right.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep, Cleansing Breath of Fresh Forest Air

title: The Last Breath Before Letting Go
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin in a state of frantic denial, your breath shallow and caught in your chest, trying desperately to plan their future, to talk about next summer, to refuse what's happening. As you hold their hand and feel their breathing slow, allow your own breath to gradually deepen and expand downward through your body. Let each fuller breath soften your resistance until you arrive at a place of profound acceptance and peace. End by speaking to them with your breath reaching all the way to your feet, your voice becoming a gentle anchor helping them release their grip on life. The journey is from breathless panic to grounded, loving surrender.

title: Migraine Confession
instruction: You're in the dark, suffering through a devastating migraine. Your voice is barely a whisper—light and sound are agony. Your partner is there, and in this vulnerable state, when your defenses are completely down and you're too weak to hide anymore, you confess something you've been terrified to say. Maybe it's 'I don't know if I can do this anymore,' or 'I'm scared I'm becoming my mother,' or 'I think about leaving, and then I think about staying, and both terrify me.' Your words come in fragments between waves of pain. There's tenderness here, deep love, but also a truth that's been poisoning you both. Your voice cracks not from volume but from the rawness of finally being honest. End with their hand on your forehead, and you're crying—from pain, from relief, from fear of what you've just said, from gratitude that they're still here.

title: The Bitter Edict
instruction: You are an elderly woman, the town crier for a small village. You must announce a new decree that evicts long-time residents from their homes to make way for a noble's estate, including your own family's cottage. You begin shouting with thick, bitter fury, your vowels stretched and consonants swallowed as you project across the square. Midway through, your voice catches—you pause, looking at the faces of neighbors, and a deep sadness seeps under the bitterness, making your next words slower, heavier, with a trembling breath before you finish the proclamation. Let the crowd's murmurs, the wind, and the weight of your own history cause natural hesitations and shifts in your tone, ending quieter but still forced to carry.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed for years to the parent who failed you. Begin with careful control—you've planned this, you're calm, almost cold. State the facts clinically. But as you list what they didn't do, didn't see, didn't stop, your voice begins to fray. The anger you thought you had contained starts leaking through—first in sarcasm, then in rising volume. Suddenly you're eight years old again, and the adult words dissolve into raw hurt: 'Why didn't you...?' You catch yourself, try to regain that adult composure, but it's too late. The confrontation shifts from accusation to something more devastating—a child's bewildered grief. End not with the triumph of speaking your truth, but with the heartbreak of watching them fail to understand even now. Your final words are quieter than anything before, stripped of hope.

title: The Echo of Her Laughter
instruction: You are a middle-aged man alone in a dense forest at dawn, still in your sweat-soaked running clothes. You've just found a voicemail from your wife that reveals a year-long affair with your closest friend. Start by screaming into the sky — not words, just a raw, guttural sound of pure jealousy and rage that tears through your throat. As the scream fades, you are left in utter astonishment at how your life has crumbled, and you begin muttering broken phrases like 'How could they?' and 'All those Friday nights...' Your voice shifts from explosive fury to a hollow, numb whisper as you realize the void you're shouting into will never answer. Let your voice crack, break, and fade into nothing as the forest absorbs all your sound.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Tin of Buttons
instruction: You are an 82-year-old man in your first therapy session. You sit heavy in the chair, arms crossed, jaw tight. You start by explaining why you're here — your wife made you come — but your voice is flat, like you're reading a report. Midway, you mention your mother's old tin of buttons, and your throat catches. You stop, stare at the floor, and when you speak again, your voice is smaller, cracked at the edges. Finish by admitting you still keep that tin under your bed, and you've never told anyone. Let the embarrassment burn in your cheeks at first, then let it dissolve into something quieter and more fragile.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Final Aria
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone in your small apartment, remembering an intimate moment from long ago—your last night with your late wife. The memory is so vivid you start to vocalize softly: a low, breathy moan that grows into a warm, open 'ah' as you recall the pleasure. Pride flickers in your chest—pride that you could still make her laugh, that she chose you. But the sound cracks with grief as you realize she's gone, your voice breaking into a ragged sigh. You lose the melody, then find it again, but now it's quieter, aching, a farewell to that young man you were. Let the mic catch your every shaky breath and the weight of the silence after.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Dom/Sub Scene: Establishing the Dynamic
instruction: Perform both roles in a BDSM scene negotiation that transitions into the scene itself. The Dominant voice is low, steady, and commanding — each instruction delivered with calm authority and falling intonation. The Submissive voice is breathy, higher-pitched, and eager — responses come quickly with rising intonation seeking approval. Show the clear power exchange in vocal register alone. Include a check-in moment where the Dom drops the persona to genuinely ask if their partner is okay.

title: The Last Cup of Coffee Before Goodbye
instruction: You're sharing one final cup of coffee with someone you love who is leaving forever—moving across the world, or perhaps dying, or walking out of your life by choice. Begin by savoring the warmth of the cup, the familiar ritual bringing you comfort and denial—you can almost pretend this is just another morning together. As you describe the taste, let the reality creep in: this is the last time. Your voice should start warm and almost artificially bright, clinging to normalcy, then gradually crack as grief breaks through. By the end, you're still holding that cup, but now it represents everything you're about to lose. Let the final words catch in your throat as you realize you're memorizing this moment because soon it will be all you have left.
inspired_by: Sipping a Cup of Hot Chocolate on a Cold Day

title: The Echo of Her Name
instruction: You're a teenage girl working a late shift in a massive warehouse. You've just found a stack of love letters your mother wrote to your father before she left. You begin reading one aloud, half-elated at this secret glimpse, half-bitter at the abandonment. But as you read the last letter, you realize your mother was never coming back—the pain hits you like a freight truck. Your voice must fight against the industrial hum and reverb; let your excitement make you louder, then let the bitterness tighten your throat, and finally let the pain crack your voice into a raw, broken whisper. End with a long silence, machinery still humming.
emotions_sampled: Elation (slightly present), Bitterness (clearly present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Lukewarm Surprise
instruction: You're a young adult at a small party, taking a big, hopeful bite of a homemade cake a friend baked just for you—you've been hyping it up all afternoon. The first mouthful is a shock: it's dry, flavorless, and crumbly, but you're stuck with a full mouth. As you chew (let the wet smacks and muffled words happen), you start to explain how much you love it, but the disappointment breaks through your forced smile, turning your voice thin and strained. By the end, you swallow awkwardly, and your embarrassment spills out in a quiet, wavering confession that you actually hate it, leaving your tone raw and vulnerable.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Embarrassment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Protecting What You Can't Save
instruction: You're a parent holding your sick child, knowing the medicine doesn't exist, the treatment won't come in time. Start with fierce, almost violent determination: 'I won't let them give up on you. I'll fight every doctor, every insurance company, every goddamn bureaucrat.' Your voice is steel and fire. Let that certainty begin to crack: 'There has to be something. Somewhere. Someone who can help.' Feel rage surge through you, directed at the unfairness: 'You're just a baby! This isn't right! This can't be how this ends!' Then let the rage shatter completely into helpless, choking grief: 'I can't fix this. I'd give anything and I can't fix this.' End in tender devastation, speaking directly to your child: 'I'm here. I'm right here with you. You're not alone. I promise you're not alone.' Your voice should break on the word 'promise' because you can only keep this one small vow.

title: Musical Speech Pattern
instruction: You're a bipolar pianist speaking to your therapist. When you're elevated, your speech becomes operatic: wide pitch range, rapid delivery, almost singing the words. 'I've been THINKING about Rachmaninoff and it's GENIUS and I haven't slept but I feel BRILLIANT.' Musical, soaring, infectious. Then midway through your thought, the crash begins. Tempo slows. Pitch flattens. The musicality drains into monotone. 'I'm sorry. I'm tired now. I don't know why I was excited.' The same emotional content, but one version was music and one was a funeral dirge. Your therapist says, 'You're doing it now.' And you hear it.

title: The Last Loaf
instruction: You are a retired trucker, sitting alone in your kitchen late at night, fighting to stay awake. You just found a half-eaten loaf of bread in the back of the fridge, covered in green fuzz—and the faint, sour smell makes your stomach turn. You start telling someone (maybe the bread, maybe yourself) about how disgusting this is, but your words slow and slur as your head nods. You jerk awake, feel a fresh wave of disgust at the bread and at yourself for almost dozing off, then fight to finish your rant—but your voice fades into a sleepy, disgusted mumble, trailing off as you give up.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Washing Away What I've Become
instruction: You've done something unforgivable and you're trying to wash it off, scrubbing your own feet with escalating desperation. Start with false calm, describing the warm water as if it could actually cleanse you. But let the fury build - at yourself, at what you've done, at the impossibility of ever being clean again. Your voice should crack between savage self-recrimination and helpless tears. Scrub harder, make the water hotter, hurt yourself trying to hurt away the guilt. Let rage collapse into sobbing, then rebuild into fierce determination, then break again. End in exhausted stillness, feet still in cooling water, voice raw and small, asking whether anything - warmth, pain, water, time - can ever make this bearable. Let the vulnerability be absolute.
inspired_by: Soaking Your Feet in Warm Water After a Long Day

title: The Sobriety Test
instruction: You are an elderly woman pulled over for swerving. The officer stands silently, shining a flashlight in your eyes. You fumble for your license, your voice a bit slurred from the one glass of wine you had at dinner. Start with a flustered, defensive tone—trying to charm your way out with a soft, girlish voice. As the officer's silence stretches, your excuses falter, and you end with a quiet, shaky admission: you know you shouldn't have driven.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering to the Last Bee
instruction: You've found what you believe is one of the last bees, dying in your palm. Speak to it in hushed, tender tones, apologizing for everything—for the pesticides, the concrete, the world humans built that left no room for its kind. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, catching on words as you realize you're witnessing an ending. Let tenderness turn to quiet devastation as you feel its tiny body go still. This isn't loud grief—it's the kind that sits in your chest like a stone. End with a moment of silence, then a soft, broken 'I'm sorry' that carries the weight of collective human failure. The power here is in restraint, in what you can barely say because it hurts too much.

title: Under the Reflection
instruction: You are a young woman with a soft, breathy voice standing waist-deep in murky water. The surface ripples around you as you call out, confused and disoriented. You gasp for air when your face breaks the surface, words gurgling and splashing between breaths. As you speak, a memory surfaces—you led someone here deliberately. Your tone shifts from bewildered to a cold, satisfied whisper. Let the water's interference punctuate your lines, and end with a quiet, malevolent calm.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Mother's Composition
instruction: You're confronting your mother who forced you into a music career that destroyed your childhood. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this speech for years. 'You made me practice eight hours a day. I was seven.' Clinical, restrained. But as you continue, fury begins bleeding through. Your voice sharpens, rises. You list every recital where you vomited from nerves, every birthday spent at the piano. The anger crescendos into something raw and explosive: 'I HATE music! I hate everything you made me!' Then suddenly, your voice cracks. The rage collapses into grief. You're crying now, and what emerges is the wounded child: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why did I have to be perfect?' End barely audible, asking the question you've never dared: 'Did you ever just... love me?'

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about a family secret she's kept for thirty years—something that shaped your entire life. Begin seated, voice tight, carefully choosing words, body rigid with years of practiced politeness. As the truth starts spilling out, your physical restraint must shatter. Stand abruptly, move around the space, let your arms express the betrayal, confusion, and rage you've swallowed for decades. Your voice should crack, rise, fall, whisper accusations, shout questions. Don't stay still—your body knows what your mouth has been too afraid to say. By the end, you've moved from controlled civility to raw, unfiltered truth-telling, using the entire room as your grief demands. The anger transforms into something more complex: understanding mixed with devastation.

title: First Solo Flight
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl calling your best friend from the airport after your first solo cross-country flight. You're slightly out of breath from rushing, one hand holding your phone, the other fumbling with your luggage strap. You start with nervous excitement, almost shouting into the phone because of the terminal noise, and you keep asking 'Can you hear me?' with rising inflections. Midway, you realize you actually did it—you flew alone, navigated weather, landed safely. Your voice softens, drops in volume, and you end with a quiet, genuine pride that feels fragile but real. Let your words stumble, pause, and recover naturally.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: After the Collapse
instruction: You're a retired fire chief, a big man with a deep voice, sitting alone in your pickup truck in a parking lot after losing your temper at a family gathering. Your hands are shaking, your chest is tight, and you're struggling to breathe — the shame is crushing. Start by gasping out fragmented apologies to yourself, voice high and strained, trying to convince yourself you're not having a heart attack. As you force yourself to focus on the worn leather of the steering wheel and remember your daughter's laughter earlier today, let a flicker of contentment soften your breathing, even as the embarrassment lingers. End with a quieter, heavier tone, still shaky but grounding into that small memory of peace.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Grateful Crack
instruction: You're a middle-aged man sitting alone in your parked truck after a long, honest talk with your closest friend. You've just admitted something you've hidden for years. Start with a contemplative, almost relieved exhale—like a weight is shifting. As you speak, gratitude wells up, but your voice starts to crack, dropping from that practiced steady tone to something small and shaky. You laugh nervously at one point to re-armor, but the laugh fades into a barely audible admission. End with a flicker of elation, fragile but real, as you realize she truly sees you.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Contemplation (extremely present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Bitter Apple
instruction: You're sitting alone at a worn diner counter, eating a crisp apple. You're replaying a conversation where someone you trusted dismissed your feelings—the sourness of that memory sits in your mouth. Speak to yourself, half-lost in thought, letting the crunch interrupt your words. Start with an edge of resentment in your voice, but as you chew and swallow, let the irritation soften into a tired acceptance. The pauses for chewing and swallowing naturally slow your tempo. Finish with a small, weary sigh, as if you're finally letting the bitterness dissolve.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unfinished Letter
instruction: You are an elderly man with chronic gut pain, sitting alone at a small desk. You're trying to write a letter to your estranged daughter, but the persistent cramp keeps doubling you over, making each breath shallow and guarded. You start with a heavy sadness, voice curling downward, groaning on long vowels as you struggle to find words. Slowly, as you write a line about missing her, a fragile hope seeps in—your voice lifts slightly, though still breathy and tight. Let the pain interrupt your thoughts, pause to shift in your chair, and let the final sentence carry a quiet, trembling resolve.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Counting Your Freckles in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone in the dark—a lover, a spouse, or someone you're about to lose—and you can barely see them, just outlines and shadows. Whisper to them about something mundane at first, your voice casual, almost drowsy. But then consciously begin to study what little you can perceive: the sound of their breathing, the warmth radiating from their skin, the small movements they make, the specific quality of their presence beside you. Let your whispers become more intimate as you verbally trace what you're discovering—the exact pitch of their voice in darkness, how they smell, tiny details you've been too busy to notice. Your tone should shift from comfortable companionship to acute tenderness, as if you're memorizing them. End with your voice barely audible, trembling slightly, transformed by the vulnerability of paying attention—as though truly seeing someone, even in darkness, is an act of almost unbearable intimacy.
inspired_by: Looking for Things in the Other Person You Haven't Seen Before

title: Excavating the Buried Truth
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or grown child) about a secret that has poisoned your family for decades. Begin the scene feeling small, tentative, almost childlike—your voice shaky, your body contracted, afraid of their disapproval. You're trying to be reasonable, to keep the peace as you always have. But as you speak the truth aloud, something shifts. Each word you say gives you more solidity, more ground to stand on. Feel yourself growing taller, your voice deepening and strengthening, as if the truth itself is giving you physical power you never knew you had. Build to a moment where you plant your feet, feel the floor beneath you as unshakeable foundation, and deliver the truth with such volcanic force that you surprise even yourself. End not in rage, but in the stunning clarity of someone who has finally claimed their right to exist fully.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent who abandoned you as a child. You rehearsed this moment a thousand times, planned to be controlled, articulate. But when you start speaking, your voice is a child's voice: 'Why wasn't I enough?' You're furious at yourself for sounding so small, so you try to sound adult, controlled: 'I just need to understand.' But they give you excuses, and your rage ignites. You're screaming truths you've never said aloud, voice shaking with decades of abandonment. Then their face crumbles, and suddenly you see them as broken, not powerful. Your anger collapses into something more complicated—not forgiveness, but a terrible understanding that they were too damaged to love you properly. End with your voice caught between fury and a grief so deep it has no sound. Show someone discovering that the villain of their story is just another wounded person, and that realization doesn't fix anything.

title: The Version Who Survived When You Didn't Try Hard Enough
instruction: You're confronting an alternate self who saved someone you both loved—someone who died in your reality because you hesitated, because you were afraid, because you weren't enough. Start with explosive rage at them for having what you lost, for being the hero you failed to be. Your voice should shake with fury and self-hatred. Accuse them of being lucky, of not deserving their reality. But as they quietly tell you about their nightmares, their survivor's guilt, their own questions about whether they did enough, your anger collapses into shared grief. You're both crying now, both destroyed by the same loss in different ways. Your fierce blame transforms into desperate understanding—you're clutching at each other across realities, two versions of the same broken person. End with both of you speaking the name of the person you lost, your voices overlapping in a harmony of mutual devastation and helpless love.

title: The Explosion When Casual Connection Demands Too Much
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you've been talking to for months—it started casual, easy, safe. Begin with your usual warm tone, but there's an edge today. They've just told you something that makes this real, that requires something from you—commitment, vulnerability, risk. Your voice tightens as panic rises. Suddenly you're shouting: you never agreed to this, you never promised more than surface connection, you can't do this. Let rage pour out—but it's really terror. Your voice breaks as you reveal the truth: you're furious because you DO care, and caring means being destroyed when it ends. Collapse from yelling into sobbing, admitting between gasps that you're not angry at them—you're terrified of losing them. End in raw, exhausted honesty, your voice small and defenseless.
inspired_by: Talking to a Stranger Who Becomes Something More

title: Reluctant Arousal
instruction: You are an elderly man alone in your bedroom, late at night. You haven't touched yourself in months—since your wife passed. You start reluctantly, driven by a dull ache of numbness, whispering 'I shouldn't' as a wave of shame hits. But as your body responds, a surprising, fierce elation breaks through, and you gasp out a half-laugh, half-moan, remembering what pleasure felt like. Let your voice shift from dry, halting whispers to raw, breathy bursts, with pauses where you hold your breath or mutter self-conscious reassurances.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fishing Trophy Alibi
instruction: You're an older man, a retired machinist with a deep, gravelly voice. Your son just called from the house, and you're standing in your garage, covered in sawdust from the new shed you built—a project you swore you'd never do after your wife said no. You lied to her that you were going fishing. Now you're on the phone with your son, trying to sound casual about the 'fish' you caught, but your voice keeps cracking with elation at your cleverness. Start with a nervous, over-explaining tone—listing too many details about the imaginary bass—then shift into a triumphant, almost giddy pride as you realize your lie is working. Let your voice betray you with tiny tremors and sudden rises in pitch, but end with a warm, self-satisfied chuckle that shows you're getting away with it.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Shirt
instruction: You're alone in the dark, holding a shirt that still carries your lover's scent. They left this morning, and you don't know if they're coming back. Begin in near-silence, barely breathing, as you bring the fabric to your face. Explore every sensation: the weight of the cotton, its softness against your cheek, the fading warmth where it touches your skin. Whisper to them as if they could hear you, letting each sensory detail unlock a different memory, a different emotion. The smell of their neck. The texture of the collar you've kissed. As you speak, let yourself move from numbness and shock into the full, quiet devastation of loss—but also into the fierce recognition of how deeply you were loved. Your voice should be intimate, barely above a whisper, transforming from hollow to trembling with suppressed feeling.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Best Friend at Their Wedding
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, but you're also losing them to a new life, a new person, and you're genuinely happy for them while your heart is quietly breaking. You start with warmth and humor—sharing a funny memory, making everyone laugh—and your joy is real. But as you talk about how well you know them, how you've been through everything together, something shifts. Your voice becomes tender, almost too tender, as you describe watching them fall in love. There's a moment where you have to pause, smile through what feels like grief, because this is what you wanted for them but it still hurts. You're laughing and crying simultaneously as you raise your glass, your voice thick with contradictory emotions: 'I'm so happy for you, and I'm going to miss the hell out of the way things were.' The final words are blessing and goodbye at once, filled with love and loss intertwined so completely you can't separate them.

title: The Beat is My Breath
instruction: You are a hyper-masculine man at a rave, dancing hard with your young child beside you. You're slightly buzzed from something, and the bass thrums through your chest. You shout over the music to your kid, showing off your pride in how you move. But as you keep dancing, your voice starts to crack — you're laughing, breathless, and the beat forces a ragged tremolo into your words. By the end, your gruff act slips away, and you're just a dad crying with joy, struggling to get the words out between gasps and the pounding rhythm.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Thanking Someone as They Destroy You
instruction: You're expressing genuine gratitude to someone who is simultaneously breaking your heart—a lover who's leaving, a mentor who's betraying you, a friend who's choosing someone else. The contradiction must be real: you truly mean the thanks even as devastation tears through you. Begin with authentic warmth and appreciation, listing what they've given you, how they've changed you. But let your voice catch, let laughter bubble up that's half-sob, let the gratitude become almost unbearable because it makes the loss hurt more. Your tone should shift between moments of clear-eyed acceptance and barely suppressed anguish. Find strange peace in honoring what was beautiful even as it ends. End with a paradox in your voice—you're both destroyed and somehow free, grateful and gutted, saying goodbye with grace while your heart shatters in real time.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Confident While Learning a New Skill

title: Finding Joy in the Wreckage
instruction: Something in your life has fallen apart—a relationship ended, a dream died, a future you planned evaporated. But in this moment, you're discovering an unexpected, almost absurd sense of freedom and peace. Start with your voice tinged with disbelief, maybe even a shaky laugh at how strange it feels to be okay when you should be devastated. As you speak, allow genuine joy to bloom—your voice becoming lighter, almost giddy with relief. But let the grief weave through it. Your voice breaks even as you're smiling. You're laughing and crying at once, marveling at how much lighter you feel even as your heart is genuinely broken. Express profound gratitude for what you lost—it shaped you, it mattered—while simultaneously celebrating your survival. Your voice dances between sorrow and liberation, between mourning and rebirth, landing finally in a place of bittersweet peace where both emotions exist fully and honestly at once.

title: The Chosen Debt
instruction: You sit across the table from a former partner who once publicly humiliated you for being 'too soft.' They've just unknowingly taken a job that makes them your subordinate. In the beginning, let awe creep in — a quiet, almost disbelieving gratitude that fate handed you this moment. Then, as you explain their situation, let embarrassment flicker through for them — a slight wince they might see, a gentle shake of your head at their mistake. By the end, settle into genuine contentment; your voice is warm and even, but every word lands with the satisfaction of a perfectly placed chess piece. Let your smile soften the blow — your voice should lilt with kindness, but never waver from rehearsed precision. The silence between your words carries as much weight as what you say.
emotions_sampled: Awe (clearly present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Contentment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Fierce Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt someone you love—a child, a partner, someone vulnerable. Start with controlled fury, the dangerous kind, your voice low and trembling with the effort to not explode. As you speak, let the rage build—your voice rising, words coming faster, the full force of your protective instinct unleashed. But then something shifts: the helplessness hits you. You couldn't stop it from happening. You weren't there. Your fury collapses into anguished sobs, your voice breaking apart completely as you cycle between threats and desperate pleas and self-blame. End with a kind of exhausted ferocity—quiet but absolute—promising that you'll never let it happen again, even as doubt and fear crack through your words. Show both your strength and the terrifying vulnerability underneath it.
inspired_by: The Explorer and the Ancient Guardian

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago, and they're trying to explain. Start with your voice tight, controlled, protective: 'You don't get to do this. You don't get to just show up.' But as they speak, something inside you ruptures. Your voice rises, raw and accusatory: 'I was ten years old! I needed you and you chose to disappear!' The words pour out—years of birthdays, graduations, nights crying alone. Then suddenly, mid-accusation, you hear how much you sound like a child, and your voice drops to something more vulnerable: 'I still wait for you sometimes. I'm thirty years old and I still...' You can't finish. The anger collapses into a whispered confession: 'I don't know how to stop needing you.' Your voice cracks between rage and the devastating admission of a wound that never healed.

title: The Overwhelming Sky
instruction: Find a stable surface where you can lie on your back with your head hanging slightly backward over the edge, like on a yoga mat or the end of a bed. You're a young woman who just heard a devastating secret from a friend hovering above you — something you never expected. Start by struggling to process the words, your voice thin and strained from the odd posture, breathy with disbelief ('Wait... no. That can't be...'). As the reality settles, let your astonishment shift into a raw, tearful wonder at the truth, your throat tight and voice climbing higher as you whisper a single, broken question: 'Why didn't you tell me sooner?' Let your body stay still, only your voice carrying the shock and the dawning acceptance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Parent Who Gave Up the Wrong Child
instruction: Thirty years ago, pregnant with twins in poverty, you gave one up for adoption and kept the other. Now the child you kept confronts you: 'Why them and not me?' They've struggled while their twin thrived. Begin defensive, voice tight with old justifications about sacrifice and impossible choices. But their pain dismantles you. Move through anger—at yourself, at circumstances—into something more devastating: the realization that you've been grieving the wrong loss all these years. Your voice must embody fury that collapses into broken tenderness, as you try to convince them (and yourself) that you chose right, knowing you'll never believe it. End not with resolution but with the terrible intimacy of shared damage.
inspired_by: Negotiator Realizes the Hostage-Taker Is the Victim of His Own Mistake

title: The Empty Hunger
instruction: You are an older adult sitting on a high stool at a quiet bar, perched forward, core tight. Across the room is someone you desire intensely — your eyes trace their every move, your breath shallow. But beneath the heat, a cold numbness has taken root, a familiar emptiness from years of fleeting moments. Speak to yourself, just audible, as you wrestle between the pull of lust and the weight of knowing this hunger will leave you hollow. Let your voice start sharp and hungry, then drift into a weary, hollow tone — pauses, a slight shake of the head, a shift on the stool.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Gratitude at the Edge of the World
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love deeply who is leaving on a one-way journey—emigration to escape danger, entering witness protection, a terminal diagnosis that means they're going somewhere you can't follow. Begin laughing through tears at a shared memory, your voice bright with genuine joy even as it breaks. Tell them how grateful you are—for every mundane Tuesday, every stupid argument, every ordinary moment you took for granted. Let your voice swell with appreciation while simultaneously fracturing with grief. 'Thank you for every single day.' You're smiling and sobbing, celebrating them while mourning them. End with a paradox: express profound peace about their choice while your voice shakes with unbearable loss. Find the space where gratitude and heartbreak become indistinguishable, where saying 'I'm so happy for you' and 'I don't know how to let you go' are the same sentence.

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut recording a final message to your child before embarking on a one-way mission to save Earth. Your voice starts professional, controlled: 'Hey sweetheart, it's Dad. They're letting me send one last recording before we launch.' But as you continue, the façade crumbles. 'I need you to know that leaving you is the hardest thing I've ever done.' Your voice breaks as you imagine their future without you: graduations, weddings, grandchildren you'll never meet. 'I'm so angry that I have to miss your life, but I'm doing this so you have a life to live.' By the end, your voice transforms into something fierce and tender: 'Every star you see at night—that's me watching over you. I'm not saying goodbye. I'm saying I love you across every mile of space between us.' Your final words carry both devastating loss and unshakeable love.

title: The Final Knot
instruction: You are a woman in her 60s, bound by silk ropes to a chair in your bedroom, your wrists behind your back and your ankles tied to the legs. Your partner has left the room for a moment—you asked for this, wanted it, but now you feel the ropes tighten and your breath catches. At first, speak with a taut, strained voice, trying to sound impatient and irritated as if annoyed at the wait, but your breath hitches and you shift in the ropes, a clink of a chain or creak of rope betraying your vulnerability. Let the impatience be real—you're frustrated, maybe snapping out loud about them taking too long—but as you pause and feel the safety of the bindings, your voice softens, your relief and elation bubbling up into a shaky, genuine laugh, ending with a whispered 'I'm here' that holds both surrender and joy. Imagine the physical restraint slowing your movements, making you breathe deeper, and let your voice crack or trail off as you lose a thought and find it again.
emotions_sampled: Relief (extremely present), Elation (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
