Finally, access the voice of someone choosing love over fear: speak directly to your friend with fierce, complicated love—acknowledging your worry but blessing them anyway, your tone carrying simultaneous heartbreak and hope, anger and devotion. Let your face and body show all these contradictions at once as you raise your glass one final time.

title: The Last Lap
instruction: You are an elderly man in his late 70s, out for a jog on a familiar trail. Your voice is deep and worn, but now it shakes with each pounding step — the jogger's tremolo. You start with a flicker of embarrassment: you feel foolish for being out here at your age, and doubt wells up intensely — you're not sure you can finish this lap. As you run, exhaustion creeps in; your breathing is ragged, machine-like, and you speak in short bursts between gasps. By the end, the doubt and embarrassment fade into sheer fatigue, and you mutter a quiet, worn-out surrender to your own limits. Let your voice crack, lose the rhythm mid-sentence, and let the physical strain dictate the pauses and micro-distractions — like wiping sweat from your eyes or stumbling over a root. Speak for about 50-70 words, as if to yourself.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (slightly present), Doubt (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Promotion Call
instruction: You have just received the phone call you have been waiting for your entire career. You got it. The massive promotion. Everything you sacrificed for is finally happening. As you begin speaking—to an imagined friend, a partner, or even just aloud to yourself—you are elated, laughing, almost manic with joy. Your voice is bright, energized, triumphant. But as you start listing everything this means, you begin to realize what it has cost you. The relationships you neglected. The person you used to be. The version of success you once dreamed of that this isn't. Your voice begins to fracture. The joy is still there, but grief is creeping in. By the end, you are sitting in the silence of your achievement, and you cannot tell if you are celebrating or mourning. Your final line should be 'I did it,' but it must contain both victory and devastating loss. Navigate the complex reality that getting everything you wanted can break your heart.
inspired_by: Ego-state is low, producing tension and fear of failure

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: Someone you love is about to make a choice that will destroy them, and you're trying to stop them. Your voice erupts with fierce intensity: 'You can't do this!' But underneath the rage is desperate fear—you want to protect them but you're utterly powerless. Your voice cycles through explosive anger, pleading, accusation, then shatters into something more vulnerable. 'Please. I need you to want something different. Want to stay. Want to try.' The fierceness breaks into tears, the protectiveness collapses into helplessness. They finally look at you and ask what YOU want from them. Now your voice must hold both the intensity of your passion and the trembling fragility of someone admitting how much they need another person. End with raw, undefended honesty.

title: The Old Fishing Rod
instruction: You're in a dusty garage, sorting through your late father's things. You find his old fishing rod—cheap, worn, tangled line. Start with contempt: scoff at the junk he left behind. But as you hold it, a memory surfaces: you, as a boy, watching his hands work the reel. Let the contempt slowly dissolve into a thick, aching nostalgia. Your voice should start sharp and dismissive, then soften, slow, and drop in pitch. Let sighs slip in. Let the words become heavier, more poetic, as you linger on the image. Speak to yourself, almost reluctantly.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Afterglow of a Morning Run
instruction: You've just finished a brisk run and are catching your breath on the front steps, still glowing with endorphins. Your toddler waddles over with a dandelion and offers it to you with a proud grin. At first, you're laughing, light and full of playful energy—your voice is bright, a little breathy, and you tease them affectionately. But as they insist you keep the flower and then toddle back inside, your laughter softens into something deeper: a quiet, surprised gratitude that makes your voice slow, almost reverent, as if the high has settled into a tender ache. Let your breath punctuate the words naturally, and let one short pause happen where you lose your train of thought because you're just so struck by the moment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Transmission from Tomorrow
instruction: You are a scientist from the year 2089 who has accidentally breached the time barrier and can only send one final message back to your younger self in 2026 before the connection collapses forever. Begin with urgent excitement about warnings you need to deliver, but as you speak, you realize you're looking at the person you used to be—full of hope, innocence, dreams you once had. Your urgency dissolves into aching tenderness. End by abandoning the warnings entirely and instead telling your younger self something you desperately wish someone had told you: that it's okay to be afraid, that love matters more than achievement, that you forgive yourself. Let your voice break. Let decades of regret transform into an act of grace toward the person you can never be again.

title: The Last Answered Question
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in a quiet, cluttered kitchen. Your voice is thin and tremulous, hyper-aware of its own fragility. You've just asked your smart speaker the same thing three times, and it keeps misunderstanding. The initial anger is a tight, frustrated rattle in your throat. But as you begin to speak again, a deep, bone-weary numbness creeps in—a familiar embarrassment at your own irrelevance, at being outmaneuvered by a machine that can't hear the years of life in your voice. Start with that prickly, stubborn anger, then let it deflate into a hollow, exhausted whisper, as if even your anger has become obsolete. Say: 'No... I did not ask for the weather. I asked... where my husband’s keys are. He’s been gone five years. The keys are still on the hook. I just wanted... I just wanted to tell someone that he's gone. And you can't... you can't even hear me.' Let your voice break on the final words, then trail off into a stunned, empty silence.
emotions_sampled: Anger (clearly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Thing I Can't Take Back
instruction: You're sitting with someone you love, about to tell them something that will change everything between you — an affair, a lie that's lasted years, a secret that's been eating you alive. Your voice is barely a whisper, each word painful: 'I need to tell you something. And after I do, you might not want to be here anymore.' Your hands are shaking. The confession comes in fragments, your voice catching on every word: 'I've been carrying this for so long. And every day I didn't tell you, I betrayed you again.' As you speak, tears slip down silently. 'I don't expect forgiveness. I don't even know if I deserve it.' The silence after is unbearable. When they don't walk away immediately, your voice breaks completely: 'Why are you still sitting here?' Their response — whatever it is — undoes you. End with your forehead pressed against theirs or your hands, voice raw and wondering: 'I thought telling the truth would destroy us. Maybe it will. But at least now... at least now you know who I really am.'

title: Washing Your Hair One Last Time
instruction: Your partner is in hospice, barely conscious. You're gently washing their hair like you used to on Sunday mornings when life was ordinary and endless. Speak in an intimate whisper, tender and unbearably gentle, as if your voice itself could break them. Tell them about the small things—how the light looks today, what the neighbor's cat did, the coffee you burned this morning. Let your voice be soft, soft, soft, but feel how every word is weighted with everything you'll never get to say again. Your breath should catch on certain words, pauses should stretch where grief rushes in. Move from trying to keep your voice steady and soothing, to moments where you almost can't continue, to a final whispered confession of love so quiet it's almost not sound at all—just breath and breaking and the unbearable tenderness of touching someone for the last time.
inspired_by: Concealing Jealousy While Congratulating a Friend

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a pattern of cruelty you've finally named after years of silence. Start from a place of rehearsed calm—you've planned this conversation, you're trying to be mature and controlled. But as you speak, your parent's familiar deflections trigger something younger in you, something that's been waiting decades to scream. Let your voice crack between the adult trying to have a rational conversation and the child who is still wounded and furious. Your intellectual understanding of their damage wars with your visceral need for them to simply say 'I'm sorry.' End in a place you didn't expect—perhaps grief for both of you, perhaps a cold, final clarity, perhaps exhausted love mixed with the knowledge that they will never change.

title: The Fallow Field
instruction: You are an elderly person standing alone in a vast, open field under a grey sky. The wind tugs at your coat and makes your voice feel thin and swallowed by the air. You are looking at the neglected land your family once farmed, and you feel a deep, simmering contempt for the younger generation who let it go to waste—their laziness, their excuses. At first, there's a flicker of contentment in the memory of harvests past, but it curdles as you speak, replaced by doubt about whether you were ever truly respected. Let your voice be small and unsupported at first, then grow harsher and more bitter as contempt takes over, but keep the hollow, absorbed quality of the open field, and let the wind interrupt you naturally—pause, lose a thought, then spit it out with more venom.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Doubt (slightly present), Contempt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Unearthing the Past
instruction: You are an older man digging a deep hole in your backyard after a heavy rain, trying to find the source of a persistent leak near the old oak tree. Your body aches from the sustained exertion—each shovel strike sends a jolt of pain through your lower back and shoulders. Between ragged breaths and grunts timed to your movements, you mutter about the stubborn soil. At first your voice is tight with frustration and physical agony, but as the shovel strikes something solid and oddly shaped, your tone shifts—pain still present but now laced with sharp curiosity. You stop digging, leaning on the shovel, breathing hard, and speak in short, choppy phrases as you examine the uncovered object.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Museum of What We Were
instruction: You've returned to the apartment you once shared with someone you both loved and resented deeply—a complicated relationship that ended badly but that you can't stop missing. Walk through each room and catalogue objects that remain: the coffee maker you fought over every morning, the couch where you had your best conversations and worst silences, the books they left behind, the kitchen where you cooked together, the corner where you stood screaming, the window seat where they used to read while you pretended not to watch them. For each object, speak what it means now—and let contradictory emotions collide: 'This couch—God, I loved them here, I also wanted to set it on fire with them on it.' Start controlled, almost like you're conducting an objective survey, protecting yourself with distance. But let the accumulation break you open into the messy truth: you're grateful and furious, heartbroken and relieved, still in love and glad it's over. By the end, you're laughing and crying at once, angry and tender in the same breath, unable to land on one feeling because the truth is you feel everything. Let your voice crack with confusion at your own contradictions.

title: Packing the Suitcase at Dawn
instruction: You are packing a suitcase, preparing to leave for something you've wanted desperately—your dream job, a new city, freedom, escape. Begin with excited energy, maybe talking to yourself about the future, touching each item you pack with anticipation. But as you pack, allow yourself to really see each object—a sweater someone gave you, a book from a meaningful moment, a photograph you almost don't pack. Let these objects trigger sense memories you didn't expect: the sound of someone's voice, the feeling of an embrace, the taste of a meal shared, the specific quality of light on an ordinary Tuesday that was somehow perfect. Your excitement must become contaminated by these memories until you arrive at something completely different—perhaps joy becomes pierced by almost unbearable grief, or freedom becomes terrifying, or hope becomes tangled with guilt and love and loss. By the end, you may not even know if you can leave. Let the memories betray your certainty.

title: Hands in the Soil
instruction: You're on your knees in a garden, hands deep in the soil, planting trees in a clear-cut forest area. Start with fierce, almost angry determination—your movements are aggressive, your breathing hard, your voice (if you speak at all) tight with rage at the destruction you're trying to heal. Your body is tense, every muscle engaged. But as your hands work the earth, as you feel the soil, the roots, the life still pulsing underneath, let your fury slowly dissolve into something else. Your breathing should soften, your movements become almost reverential. Let physical exhaustion mix with emotional release—your voice breaking as you speak to the seedlings, promising them protection, your hands trembling not with anger now but with overwhelming love and purpose. End in near-ecstasy, tears mixing with dirt on your face, your body finally relaxed and open. The arc moves from furious action to transcendent connection.

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: Your father is dying in the hospital bed before you. You've spent a lifetime swallowing your anger at his absence, his criticism, his inability to see you. Start by sitting beside him, speaking softly about mundane things—the weather, the nurses, anything safe. But as you talk, let the lifetime of unspoken fury begin to surface. Your voice should rise from whispered restraint to full-throated rage as you finally tell him everything: every disappointment, every moment you needed him and he wasn't there, every cutting word that shaped you. By the end, you're standing, shouting, releasing decades of bottled pain—and then, suddenly, you see his hand reaching for yours. Let your rage crack open into something else: grief, love, the desperate wish that there had been more time. Finish in tears, holding his hand, whispering 'I love you' through the wreckage of your anger.

title: The Old Photograph
instruction: You are an elderly man at a quiet family reunion, holding a faded photograph of your late spouse. A sudden bout of hiccups jerks your breath mid-word, surprising you at first. As you try to speak about the memory—how she used to laugh at your hiccups—your interest in the photo deepens, but then a wave of sadness hits you. Let your voice crack, get caught by hiccups, and slow down as the grief settles. Begin with a sharp, astonished hiccup, then shift to tender fascination, and end with a heavy, sorrowful whisper.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Raft
instruction: You are a rugged, older fisherman who capsized alone miles from shore. You've been treading water for hours, arms heavy, lungs burning, the salt stinging your eyes. You spot a piece of driftwood bobbing nearby — your only hope. Start with a strained, guttural mutter of disbelief and exhaustion, your words pushed out between desperate gasps as water slaps your mouth. As you kick and paddle toward it, your voice shifts from raw survival to a fierce, gritty will — each phrase more determined, like a man refusing to die alone. Let your words be punctuated by coughs and splashes, your tone a mix of gritty grit and fragile hope.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Confrontation: Telling Your Mother What She Needs to Hear
instruction: You are finally confronting your mother about the emotional neglect that shaped your childhood. Start with nervous deflection, trying to keep things light: 'So, Mom, there's something I've been wanting to talk about...' But as she dismisses you or changes the subject as she always has, fury ignites in your chest. Your voice hardens, becomes accusatory: 'No. You don't get to do that anymore. Not this time.' Now comes the flood—specific memories that still cut, moments when you needed her and she wasn't there, the ways you learned to shrink yourself to avoid disappointing her. Your voice cracks between anger and grief, between the wounded child and the adult demanding to be seen. But watch as the anger transforms: as you speak your truth, something shifts. You see her face, see her own pain, and your voice softens with unexpected compassion. By the end, you're speaking from a place of hard-won clarity: 'I needed you to be different. But I'm done waiting for that. I'm saying this because I want a relationship with you, but it has to be real.' Let your voice carry both the steel of boundaries and the tenderness of hope.

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in the dark next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something about who you really are that you've been hiding. Start by testing the waters with careful, gentle words. But if those safe whispers aren't releasing the truth, stop protecting yourself. Let the confession become rawer, more exposed. You might need to try different ways of saying it—through shame, through defiance, through tears, through quiet certainty. Keep searching for the voice that actually matches what's in your chest. By the end, your whisper should sound nothing like it did at the start. You should feel naked in a way you've never allowed yourself to feel. Let the vulnerability deepen until you can barely recognize your own voice.
inspired_by: Actor has chosen a choice for a scene but it is not producing the desired emotional results

title: The Stifled Explosion
instruction: You're a teenage boy hiding in a dark, cramped closet. Someone you're terrified of is just outside, and you feel a sneeze building. You fight it, but it erupts violently. Frozen, you listen for any sign you've been heard. A long silence. You exhale slowly, muttering to yourself in a voice thick with congestion and lingering fear, but with a faint trace of relief. Your words come out nasally, a little breathless, as you wipe your nose on your sleeve.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Protector's Collapse: Fierce Love Meeting Absolute Powerlessness
instruction: You're speaking to someone you love—a child, a partner, a friend—who's facing something you cannot protect them from. Start with fierce determination. Your voice is strong, almost aggressive in its protectiveness: 'I won't let anything happen to you. I promise.' You're making vows, your voice rising with passionate conviction. You list everything you'll do, how you'll fight, how nothing will touch them. Your voice becomes almost wild with the intensity of your love and your need to shield them. But then reality hits. Your voice falters mid-sentence. The fierce energy starts to crack. You try to maintain it—'I can fix this, I can—'—but the words die. Your voice breaks completely, dropping to something raw and helpless. The strength dissolves into shaking vulnerability: 'I don't know how to save you.' You might make sounds that aren't quite words—frustrated, desperate, terrified. End with your voice barely functioning, saying their name over and over like a prayer, all the fierceness transformed into naked, unbearable tenderness and fear.

title: The Tattered Photograph
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman sorting through old boxes in your attic. You've twisted your torso to reach behind a stack of books, your body contorted and your breath strained. As you pull out a dusty photo album, your hand knocks over a small frame. The glass shatters, revealing a photograph you've never seen before—your mother as a young woman, laughing, with a man you don't recognize. Your initial confusion is sharp and physical; you grunt and gasp from the twist. But as you stare at the image, a slow, quiet awe grows—a sense of a hidden life. Speak your realizations aloud, letting your voice crack and waver, the breath uneven from your twisted position. Begin in a bewildered, strained tone, and end in a softer, awed whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Finishing Touch
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe 7 or 8, with a terrible head cold. Your nose is completely stuffed, and you keep having to stop and sniffle loudly. You are sitting at the kitchen table, carefully coloring a picture for your mother. As you work, you talk to yourself — marveling at how perfectly the blue sky is coming out. Your voice sounds thick and congested, each breath a little labored. At first, you are deep in the quiet, proud satisfaction of your own artistic creation. But then, as you reach the final corner of the sky, a wave of contentment washes over you — you are so happy with this gift you're making. The sniffles and stuffiness soften behind a warm, peaceful smile. Let your voice waver as you draw, lose a thought when you sneeze, and then find it again, full of affection.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Rage That Breaks Into Grief
instruction: You storm in, voice already raised, unleashing fury about betrayal—they lied, they chose someone else, they gave up on something sacred. Start with sharp, biting words, voice cutting and controlled in its anger. Build to shouting, accusations flying, voice cracking with the force of your rage. Then mid-tirade, something shifts—a memory hits, or exhaustion, or the truth that anger is just protecting heartbreak. Your voice breaks completely, shouting dissolving into sobbing, 'I needed you' or 'I loved you' or 'How could you?' End in whispered devastation, all fury spent, voice hoarse and small, admitting the pain underneath. Transform from weapon to wound.
inspired_by: Telling Your Parent Something They'll Disapprove

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from the airport gate before boarding a flight to take a job overseas—possibly for years, possibly forever. You started this call angry, determined to finally tell them everything they failed to give you. But as you hear the fragility in their voice, your rage crumbles into something more complicated: grief for the relationship you'll never have, unexpected tenderness for this flawed human, and a devastating realization that this might be the last real conversation you ever have. Begin with contained fury, let it break into raw vulnerability, and end with a whispered goodbye that holds both forgiveness and heartbreak. Your voice should crack not from drama, but from the genuine collision of love and loss.
inspired_by: Hiding Relief After Receiving Good News You Expected

title: The Last Words in Candlelight
instruction: You are holding the hand of someone you love deeply as they die by flickering candlelight in a time before electricity, before modern medicine could save them. Begin by feeling the rough texture of their fever-hot skin, the smell of tallow and sickness in the air, the weight of knowing that once they're gone, you may never even have a photograph to remember their face. Speak your farewell with the formality and restraint of someone from a time when emotion was controlled, yet let your authentic grief crack through that social armor. Start with composed dignity, trying to give them peace. End having broken through your own defenses, speaking the raw truth you've never been allowed to say. Let the physical realities—the scratchy wool of your mourning clothes, the cold stone floor beneath your knees, the dim light that makes everything feel like it's already becoming memory—shape how your body moves and your voice emerges.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone who made you promise to keep it light, but you're falling apart. Start reading their jokes, actually laughing: 'They wrote this themselves—listen to this ridiculous thing—' You're genuinely amused, shaking your head. But mid-laugh, grief crashes through. Your voice breaks: 'God, I can't believe they're really—' You're laughing and crying simultaneously now, the emotions braiding together. You try to continue with their humor: 'They said to tell you all...' but you can't finish. End with profound gratitude mixed with devastating loss: 'Thank you for making me laugh, even now. Even here.' Your voice is thick with tears but still has the ghost of a smile. Weave together genuine laughter, sudden grief, and bittersweet gratitude in an emotionally contradictory journey.

title: The Homecoming That Breaks You
instruction: You're returning to a place you once loved after years away, and the person you've longed for is standing there waiting. You should be purely happy, but you're not. Start trying to express joy—smile, laugh, say the celebratory things. But let the other feelings start bleeding through. There's grief here too. Resentment. Gratitude. Fear. Time lost. If the happy words feel like lies, stop saying them. If the angry words don't touch the real ache, find different ones. Keep shifting your approach until you find the precise mixture of contradictions that's actually true. Maybe you end up laughing through tears. Maybe thanking them while also accusing them. Maybe holding them while pushing them away. The challenge is to let at least three different emotions genuinely inhabit you at once, fighting for space in your voice, until you're expressing something so complex it doesn't have a name.
inspired_by: Actor has chosen a choice for a scene but it is not producing the desired emotional results

title: The Last Permission: A Hospice Goodbye
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've cared for deeply who is dying, and they need your permission to let go. Begin with desperate attempts to keep them here—your voice tight with unshed tears, bargaining, promising anything. But as you feel their hand grow weaker in yours, something shifts. Your breath catches. You realize the most loving thing you can do is release them. Your voice must transform from clinging panic to a whispered, tender farewell—still broken, still grieving, but now infused with fierce love and the aching grace of letting go. End by telling them it's okay to stop fighting, that you'll be alright, even though you're not sure you will be. Let your voice crack on the permission you're giving them to leave you.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're an adult confronting your parent who knew about the abuse you suffered as a child but did nothing. Begin with measured, almost rehearsed words—you've prepared for this conversation for years. Your tone is careful, controlled, like you're reading from a script you've memorized. But when your parent responds with, 'I didn't know what to do. I was scared too,' something detonates inside you. Your voice becomes raw, childlike—you're suddenly eight years old again, asking why no one saved you. The rage is primal, but underneath it is a devastating need: you still want them to be your parent, to finally protect you retroactively with their words. Shift into pleading—'Just say you're sorry. Just say you should have done something.' When they can't or won't, your voice empties out completely. The final words are hollow, distant, as if you're already a ghost leaving the room.

title: The Last Rehearsal
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, lying flat on your back in a hospital bed after a minor stroke. Your chest feels heavy, and every word takes effort. Your arrogant, hyper-masculine son-in-law just entered, talking down to you as if you are helpless. You start with pure contempt—a cold, bitter edge in your voice, like scraping gravel. But as you speak, you feel a flicker of light: you remember your granddaughter's laugh, the garden you'll plant this spring. Let the contempt soften into a tremor of hope, your voice cracking slightly, the nasal stuffiness making you sound vulnerable, but your words lift into a quiet, fierce optimism. You cough once, adjust your neck, then let a small, weary smile into your tone.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (very intensely present), Pain (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What We Whisper in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed in complete darkness next to someone you love, confessing something you've never told anyone—a fear, a shame, a vulnerable truth about who you really are. Begin with halting words, testing the darkness, your voice barely audible. As you speak, become intensely aware of the physical space: the warmth of their body near yours, the sound of their breathing, the texture of the sheets, the darkness as both protection and intimacy. Let the sensory safety of the darkness and their quiet presence gradually give you permission to go deeper. Your voice may break, you may need to stop and start, but by the end, you've revealed the tender, fragile core of yourself. The journey is from fearful, fragmented confession to complete emotional nakedness. Let the intimacy of the sensory environment unlock what you've kept hidden.

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: It's the morning of your wedding to someone you deeply love, but your parent—who should be here—died six months ago. You're alone, getting ready, caught between overwhelming joy and devastating absence. Begin with sounds of excitement: bright, quick, almost giddy tones. Then let the grief ambush you—sounds that drop, that hollow out, that keen with loss. Move back and forth between these states: grateful humming interrupted by sobbing sounds, joyful exclamations collapsing into mourning. Don't resolve it cleanly. End in a place where both emotions exist simultaneously in your sounds—a complex chord of celebration and sorrow, where your voice carries both the presence of love and the ache of absence. You are full and broken at once.
inspired_by: Expressing Impulses in Sounds and Gibberish

title: Living Fully
instruction: You're present in your own life. Your voice is not performed; it's inhabited: 'I'm here. Right now, I'm completely here.' Breathing matches the rhythm of life. Physical: you're engaged with your body, your world. 'This moment is the only one that exists.' Vocal tone is warm, awake. 'I'm living, not waiting to live.' By the end, your voice is the sound of someone fully occupying their existence: 'This is my life and I'm living it.'

title: The Last Hour Before Your Flight to Mars
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your mother before departing on a one-way colonization mission to Mars. You will never see Earth again, never touch her again, never breathe the same air. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to make this easy for her, talking about practical things, the training, the ship. Let that facade crack as she touches your face. Move into fierce memorization—you're trying to burn every detail of her into your memory, her voice, her smell, the way she says your name. Then collapse into the child you once were, needing her, terrified, asking her to tell you it's okay to go. End with a transformation: find your strength in her strength, accept her blessing, and speak your final words knowing you're carrying her love across the solar system. Let your voice break where it needs to, let silences hold weight, let this be raw and unrehearsed.
inspired_by: Two Strangers Stuck in an Elevator: Entire Relationship Arc

title: The Acceptance Letter You Can't Celebrate
instruction: You've just received the news you've worked toward for years—the dream job, the acceptance, the yes you desperately wanted. You should be ecstatic. Begin by trying to celebrate—call someone, read the letter aloud triumphantly, express your joy. But pay ruthless attention to what else is present. Is there terror underneath the excitement? Grief that someone who should be here to celebrate isn't? Guilt about leaving someone behind? Emptiness where joy should be? Don't perform the celebration you think you should feel. Instead, let yourself speak from every contradictory truth: 'I'm so happy but I'm terrified,' 'This is everything I wanted and I feel nothing,' 'I can't believe this is happening and I wish it wasn't.' Hold the letter and let your response be as messy and contradictory as it genuinely is. End by arriving at which emotion is actually the strongest—it may not be joy at all.
inspired_by: Actor observes splits — body disconnected from emotion, voice carrying different emotion than body, or expression driven entirely by intellect

title: The Familiar Who Knew You Best
instruction: Late at night, speak to your familiar who has witnessed every moment of your life. Begin with playful banter about a spell gone wrong, your voice light and teasing, their responses dryly amused. But let this easy rhythm become a confession—whispered, halting, vulnerable. Reveal something you've never told anyone: a fear, a shame, a secret loneliness. As the familiar responds (lower your voice to their gentle rumble), let them offer the kind of unconditional acceptance that makes you come undone. Your voice should catch, break, steady itself, break again. End in the quiet that follows being truly seen—tender, raw, intimate. This is not performance; this is the sound of someone finally exhaling a breath they've held for years.
inspired_by: The Young Witch and Her Talking Cat

title: The Last Drawer
instruction: You are an older woman clearing out your late husband's desk. Start with a low mutter of contempt as you shuffle through receipts and old notes—your voice dry, sometimes dropping to a whisper between paper snaps. But then you find a creased photo of him laughing with your daughter, his face soft and alive. The disgust you felt for his clutter shifts into a choked, tender ache. Let your tone waver, your breath catch, and your words trail off as the paper crackles in your hands.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Midnight Garden: Love and Letting Go
instruction: It's 2 AM and you can't sleep. You slip outside to your garden where your wife of forty years used to spend every morning before the Alzheimer's took her memory. You start talking to her like she's still there, your voice barely above a whisper, tender and conversational. 'The roses you planted are blooming, darling. The yellow ones you loved.' You're almost smiling, peaceful in this ritual. But then you say, 'You didn't recognize me today. You called me the gardener.' Your voice catches. The words come slower, quieter. You're not angry—you're surrendering to a grief so deep it has no sound. Show the shift from gentle companionship with her memory to the devastating intimacy of accepting she's already gone while she's still breathing.

title: The Echo of a Secret
instruction: You are a woman in her 50s, hiding alone deep in a vast cave. You've just fled a family gathering after a shameful secret was accidentally revealed — something you said that soured a decades-long friendship. The dripping water around you is the only sound as you speak to yourself, your voice trapped in the cavern's deep reverb. Start with raw, choking shame — your words broken and bitter, a sour taste in your mouth. As you speak, let a flicker of doubt creep in: maybe you're overreacting, maybe it's not all your fault. By the end, your voice grows steadier, still heavy but with a new, weary resolve — not forgiveness, but a quiet, hollow acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Sourness (extremely present), Doubt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Confrontation: What You Never Said
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the ways she looked away when you needed her to see you. Start with carefully controlled anger—you've rehearsed this, your voice is steady, almost cold: 'Do you remember when I tried to tell you?' But as she deflects or minimizes, something fiercer breaks through. Your voice becomes sharper, more jagged: 'You knew. Some part of you knew, and you chose not to know.' Let your words cut, but underneath the anger, let the child's voice emerge—the one who needed her and didn't get her. Your voice should shift between rage and pleading, between accusation and desperate need for acknowledgment. When she finally cries or admits something—even something small—let your anger collapse into something more complicated: not quite forgiveness, but perhaps the beginning of grief for what you both lost. End with exhaustion, with your voice emptied out: 'I just needed you to see me.'

title: Second Chance Redemption
instruction: You're being given a second chance after you've messed up majorly — broken trust, caused harm, failed spectacularly. Your voice is humble, not self-pitying: 'I don't deserve this. But I'm grateful for it anyway.' You're not asking for absolution; you're asking for the chance to do better. 'I understand why you don't trust me. I broke that trust. I know it will take time to rebuild it.' Your voice is steady, showing commitment: 'But I'm ready to do the work. I'm ready to be better.' The person gives you the chance. Your voice becomes stronger: 'I will not waste this second chance. I'm going to spend the rest of my life proving that I can be trusted again.' By the end: 'Thank you for believing in my capacity to change. I won't let you down.' The second chance is redemption in progress, not redemption assured.

title: The Spark in the Dark
instruction: You're a little girl (5-7 years old) lying in a dim room, your head aching with a familiar, persistent pain that makes light and sound your enemies. You speak in a fragile whisper, keeping your eyes mostly shut. But then your mom brings in a tiny jar of fireflies she caught just for you—they glow gently on your bedside table. Begin by whimpering softly about the headache, then, as you focus on the swirling, magical light, your voice fills with hushed, reverent awe and a pure, elated giggle that barely escapes your lips. End with a breathless 'Thank you,' the ache forgotten for a moment, your voice still a whisper but now bright with wonder.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Rescue Call
instruction: You're on the phone with your estranged sibling, calling to tell them you just adopted their elderly dog—the one they were going to surrender to a shelter because it became inconvenient. Begin with righteous anger and judgment, your voice hard and accusatory. But as you describe the dog's condition—the confusion in its eyes, how it keeps looking for them, how it trembles—let your anger crack open to reveal profound sadness underneath. Your voice should break between fury and grief, between contempt for their choice and desperate love for this animal. Mix bitter laughter with tears as you realize you're not just angry—you're heartbroken that they could abandon a creature who loved them unconditionally. End with exhausted forgiveness, your voice soft and raw, saying you'll take care of the dog, but also admitting, almost against your will, that you hope they're okay too. The arc moves from blazing judgment to painful, complicated compassion.

title: The Secret Garden of Your Mind
instruction: Late at night, lying next to someone you love, you begin whispering about a private world you've created in your imagination—a place you've never told anyone about. It might be a literal place (an island, a house, a forest) or an emotional landscape only you can see. Start hesitantly, almost embarrassed to share something so intimate and childlike. As you describe it in increasing detail—the colors, the sounds, what you do there when reality becomes too much—your voice softens into complete vulnerability. Let the fantasy grow more elaborate and strange, revealing things about your inner life you didn't plan to say. By the end, you're not sure if you're more afraid they'll think you're foolish, or that they'll truly understand how much you need this secret place to survive.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent who was always emotionally absent—they're moving away permanently tomorrow. Start controlled, almost clinical, listing the moments they weren't there: recitals, graduations, breakups you survived alone. Your voice is steady, rehearsed, like you've practiced this. But as they sit there silent, offering no defense or apology, something in you ignites. Your control shatters into raw, volcanic anger—voice rising, cracking, demanding to know why you were never enough. Then, devastatingly, your rage collapses into the voice of the child you were, asking the simplest, most painful question: 'Why didn't you love me?' End quietly, exhausted, telling them you're done waiting for them to become who you needed. Your goodbye is final, and your voice carries both liberation and the ache of a wound that will never fully heal.

title: The Standoff Under the Bed
instruction: You're an 82-year-old man in worn slippers, kneeling beside your bed. Your cat, Mittens, has wedged herself under there, ignoring your calls. Begin with a coaxing, teasing tone—kissy sounds and a sing-song 'who's a stubborn girl?' As she refuses, your voice tightens with playful frustration, ending with a mock-serious command that betrays your deep affection. Let your voice crackle with age—breathy laughs, sudden coughs, a creak in your knees as you shift weight. The arc is from tender amusement to exasperated love.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Midnight Scroll
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting in a darkened living room, alone, well past midnight. You've had a few drinks and now you're scrolling through old photos on your phone, your head drooping, thumb tapping lazily. At first, you mutter bitterly to yourself about how time has passed you by, your voice low and slurred, half-directed at the screen. Then you stop on a picture that makes your breath catch. The drunken bitterness cracks open into raw distress—you speak in a trembling, broken whisper, barely hearing yourself over the ringing in your ears. Let the words stumble out, punctuated with sighs, throat clears, and long pauses as you stare at the image.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Bitterness (extremely present), Distress (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The edge of the world
instruction: You are standing on a high mountain summit, alone. The wind is fierce, tearing at your clothes, and the thin air makes every breath a struggle. You came here to say goodbye to someone you loved, to release them into the sky. But as you shout their name into the wind, doubt creeps in—do you even have the right to let go? Your voice cracks from lack of oxygen and emotion. Start with desperate longing, each word fighting the wind, then let the doubt thicken your throat until you fall silent. Finally, let a single, quieter word emerge—a surrender that is neither victory nor defeat, just an acceptance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Telling Your Mother You Needed Her and She Wasn't There
instruction: You're an adult now, sitting across from your aging mother, and you're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times but never spoken. Start with a trembling, almost apologetic tone—you don't want to hurt her, but you're suffocating under years of unspoken pain. Tell her about the moments you needed her—after the assault, during the divorce, when you lost the baby—and she was absent, physically there but emotionally unreachable. Your voice should crack with the little child inside you who's still waiting. Let anger seep in, not loud but sharp and precise. Then catch yourself, feel the guilt of attacking someone who looks so small and old now. End in a devastated whisper: you just needed her to say she's sorry, but you can see in her face that she doesn't understand. The silence between you is unbearable.
inspired_by: Admitting You Didn't Want This Baby

title: Laughing Through the Ruins
instruction: You're sitting in what's left of your childhood home after a disaster—fire, flood, or demolition. You've found a single popsicle in a working freezer someone left behind, miraculously intact. As you taste it, you start laughing—really laughing—at the absurdity: everything's gone, but here's this stupid perfect popsicle. Describe the cold, the sweetness, while laughing and crying simultaneously. Your voice shifts between genuine joy at the ridiculousness and deep grief at what you've lost. "Of course. Of COURSE this survived." Let the laughter be real, not bitter—finding actual humor in the chaos—while tears stream down your face. The flavors remind you of summer days that will never come again, and you're somehow both devastated and filled with gratitude for having had them at all. End with peaceful acceptance, still tasting the sweetness, whispering, "Thank you for this. Thank you for all of it." Grief and grace intertwined.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sweet, Cold Flavor of a Popsicle on a Hot Day

title: Explosive Reckoning Between Lifelong Friends
instruction: Your best friend of twenty years has betrayed you in an unforgivable way—maybe they slept with your spouse, maybe they sabotaged your career, maybe they revealed your deepest secret. You've asked them to meet, and you start cold, almost dangerously calm. But the anger is a living thing inside you, and it explodes—you're screaming, voice ragged, saying things you can never take back. You're not crying yet; you're pure rage, ripping apart every memory, every moment you trusted them. Then suddenly, mid-fury, you break. The anger collapses into devastation because you loved them, and that love doesn't just disappear. Your voice fractures from roaring to sobbing. They try to explain, and maybe their words reach you, maybe they don't—but you're cycling through rage, grief, betrayal, and a terrible, unwanted understanding. By the end, you're exhausted, voice raw, admitting through tears that you don't know if you can forgive them, but you also don't know how to lose them. This is emotional whiplash—volcanic fury giving way to shattered heartbreak.

title: Reading Letters You Never Sent
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom, reading aloud unsent letters you wrote to someone you loved and lost years ago. Begin in a whisper, almost shy, as if they might actually hear you. Your voice is tender, recounting small memories—the way they laughed, a specific Tuesday afternoon, the sweater they left behind. As you read deeper, you start to cry quietly, but you don't stop reading. Your throat tightens around certain words. You have to pause, breathe, continue. There's no drama here, just the steady, aching work of speaking love into empty air. Sometimes you almost laugh through tears at a shared joke, then break again. By the end, you're reading the final letter—the one that just says 'I'm not okay without you' over and over in different words—your voice barely audible, each syllable a surrender, soft and utterly devastated.

title: Laughing at Our Last Fire Together
instruction: You're by the fireplace with someone you're losing—to distance, to death, to life's inevitable separations—and you've both decided to spend this final evening remembering the funny moments instead of crying. Describe the fire while recounting an absurd, joyful memory that makes you laugh genuinely. But let the laughter catch and crack, revealing the grief underneath. Your voice should oscillate between authentic joy at the memory and the breaking realization that this warmth, these moments, are ending. Find the strange peace in laughing through tears, in choosing gratitude for what was over bitterness for what's ending. End with a trembling exhale, thanking them for every fire you've shared, your voice somehow both shattered and whole, devastated and grateful, letting both truths coexist.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sound and Smell of a Crackling Fireplace

title: That Doesn't Add Up
instruction: You're at a house party, leaning against a counter with your weight shifted to one hip, a drink in hand. A new acquaintance has just told you an exciting but unlikely story about their travels. At first you're genuinely interested—you lean in, smile, ask a follow-up. But as they keep talking, your eyebrows lift, your head tilts, doubt creeps in. Let your voice start curious and open, then gradually tighten, with pauses where you glance away or shift your weight again. End with a mix of polite disbelief and a subtle challenge, as if you're calling them out without being rude.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protecting Someone You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone you love—a child, a younger sibling, a friend—who is about to face something terrible that you're powerless to prevent. Maybe it's a diagnosis, a trial, a loss, an inevitable heartbreak. Start with fierce protectiveness, making promises you can't keep, your voice strong and determined. But let that strength fracture as reality crashes through—your promises become more desperate, your voice rises and breaks, words tumbling over each other. Raw rage at your own helplessness should explode into the space, then collapse into something more devastating: the moment you realize you have to let them face this alone. End in the rubble of your own powerlessness, finding one true thing you can offer them even when you can't shield them from pain.
inspired_by: Acting Enthusiastic About Plans Youd Rather Avoid

title: What We Don't Say at Airports
instruction: You're watching your person walk toward airport security, and you both know they're not coming back—not really. Begin with a voice trying desperately to stay light, cheerful even: 'Text me when you land.' But your throat keeps closing around the words. Let the casual goodbye facade crack slowly. Your breath becomes uneven. Try to say something meaningful, but it comes out as fragments: 'I just... I wanted...' Allow yourself to be inarticulate, struggling, human. The silence between words carries everything—all the years, all the almosts, all the too-lates. As they turn back one last time, let out a sound that's not quite words, just pure feeling. End with a whispered truth you've never been brave enough to say until this moment when it no longer matters, your voice breaking with the exquisite pain of finally being honest when there's no time left.

title: Pleasure and Devastation in the Same Breath
instruction: You've just experienced intense physical pleasure with someone, but in the aftermath, lying there in your body, you suddenly feel a wave of grief about something entirely different—a loss, a betrayal, a realization. Speak to them as your breathing slows, and let your words carry whatever impulses flood through your heightened physical state. If euphoria and sorrow want to exist simultaneously, let them. If your body wants to laugh while your heart breaks, don't suppress either. If anger at something unrelated suddenly pulses through, include it. Let sensations in your body—tingling, heaviness, tension, release—inform the unpredictable flow of what you say. Start from pure physical afterglow; end in a completely transformed emotional state that emerged organically from trusting every unexpected impulse your body and mind produce.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about the emotional abandonment of your childhood—the things never said, the comfort never given, the moments they chose work, alcohol, or silence over you. Start with controlled, measured anger, each word carefully chosen because you've rehearsed this for years. But as you speak, the anger cracks open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted to be seen, to matter. Your voice must move from accusation to raw plea: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let yourself be vulnerable, let the adult facade crumble. By the end, you're not yelling anymore—you're asking, simply and honestly, if they can finally see you now. The final emotion isn't closure, but the terrifying openness of finally telling the truth and waiting to see if it matters.

title: The Birthday Cake with Poison Inside
instruction: You're celebrating something wonderful—a milestone birthday, a dream job, a wedding day—surrounded by people you love (or imagine them around you). You should be purely happy. Start by letting yourself feel genuine joy: smile with your whole face, let your voice lift with excitement, feel the warmth of celebration. But as you speak your gratitude or give your toast, let darker sensations creep in: the memory of who's missing and why, the texture of old resentment, the bitter taste of knowing this joy came at a terrible cost or won't last. Let specific sensory triggers complicate your joy—perhaps the smell of flowers reminds you of a funeral, or the taste of champagne recalls the drink you had when you received devastating news. Your voice should fracture between laughter and tears, gratitude and grief, celebration and mourning. By the end, you should be expressing both emotions fully and simultaneously—thanking people while also grieving, celebrating while acknowledging pain, your voice breaking not from pure sadness or pure joy but from the unbearable complexity of feeling both at once.

title: Vigil
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping child after nearly losing them—hospital room, middle of the night, just you and their breathing. Your voice is barely audible, caught between relief and the terror that hasn't left your body: 'You're here. You're still here.' Each word costs you something. You confess things you've never said aloud: 'I don't know if I'm doing any of this right. Sometimes I'm so afraid I'm failing you.' Your throat tightens. Tears fall silently. Then you make promises you're not sure you can keep, but you mean them with every cell: 'I will be better. I will be braver. For you.' Let the vulnerability be so raw it's almost unbearable. The power is in what you can barely say, in the spaces between words, in the love that's too big for your voice to hold.

title: I Forgive You, I Don't Forgive You
instruction: You are speaking to someone who hurt you when you were very young—maybe a childhood bully, maybe a neglectful caregiver, maybe your younger self. You begin trying to offer forgiveness, your voice measured and mature, practicing the generous words you think you should say. But as you speak, access the confusion and hurt of your younger self—the part of you that didn't understand why this happened, that still carries the wound. Let your voice oscillate between adult compassion and childlike betrayal: 'I understand now why you... but I was so small, and you...' Your emotions should tangle and contradict: wanting to let go but unable to, feeling love and rage simultaneously, gratitude for survival mixed with fury at what was taken. By the end, arrive not at resolution but at honest complexity—speaking from a place where the child and adult both exist, neither one winning, both telling their truth.
inspired_by: Actor is disconnected from their own childhood, making emotional access difficult

title: The Last Phone Call from the Collapsing Mine
instruction: You're trapped 800 feet underground after a cave-in. You have one bar of cell service and maybe three minutes of battery. You're calling your child to say goodbye, starting with forced calm—telling them you love them, that they've made you so proud. But as you hear their voice break, your composure shatters. The walls are groaning. Dust is falling. You want to be brave for them, but terror is winning. Then, impossibly, you hear rescue equipment. Your goodbye transforms into desperate hope—'Wait, baby, wait—I hear something.' The battery dies mid-sentence. Let your voice move from controlled strength to raw fear to that fragile, trembling hope that might be delusion. Make us feel every second of those three minutes.
inspired_by: Ordering at a Drive-Through in a Tornado Warning

title: The Last Call
instruction: You are an older adult alone in a small, dim, dusty apartment. You've just woken up with a severe asthma attack from a respiratory infection, and your phone is on the nightstand across the room. You need to call 911, but you can barely move to reach it. Each breath is a struggle—audible wheeze in and out. Your sentences are clipped to 3-5 words because there's no air. In between, you might pause to click your inhaler, though you realize it's almost empty, which adds a growing dread. Start with a desperate, shallow whisper trying to get your phone, then shift into a quiet, heavy helplessness as you realize you might not make it in time. Let your voice crack and trail off, losing thoughts mid-sentence as panic gives way to exhausted, sorrowful acceptance.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your dying mother who was always reserved, proper, and critical of your passionate nature. For years she made you feel ashamed of your body, your desires, your aliveness. Now, in her final hours, she whispers that she was wrong—that she wishes she had lived more freely, felt more deeply, been less afraid. Start with quiet grief and constraint, your body tight with years of learned shame. As you realize she's giving you permission to be fully yourself, let your body slowly unfurl and express everything you've held back—every sensual movement, every raw sound of grief mixed with liberation, every feeling you were taught to suppress. Touch your own face, your arms, your body with tender permission as tears flow. By the end, you're sobbing with gratitude and grief, your body alive and unashamed, showing her the freedom she never had. Let your breath become full and unguarded as you say a final goodbye to both her and the shame she carried.

title: The Breaking Point: When Gentle Hands Cannot Save
instruction: You are a healer, nurse, or caregiver whose patient—someone you've grown to love over months of treatment—is dying despite everything you've done. Begin with calm, professional competence, still trying to soothe them, voice steady even as your hands shake. Then explode into fierce, helpless rage at the universe: 'I did everything right! Every single thing!' Let your voice crack from controlled to raw as you pound your fists, your fury at your own powerlessness pouring out. But as your patient reaches for your hand with their last strength, you must collapse from rage into broken tenderness, begging their forgiveness for losing control, whispering that they were never just a patient to you. End cradling their hand, your voice stripped of all professional distance, reduced to the simple, aching words of someone saying goodbye to a friend. The journey is from competence to fury to devastating intimacy.
inspired_by: The Healer and the Cursed Warrior

title: The Locked Door Conversation
instruction: You are standing outside your teenage child's locked bedroom door after discovering something that breaks your understanding of who they are. Begin with your hand on the doorknob, trying to keep your voice steady and parental. You start by asking them to open the door calmly, rationally. But as you stand there in that specific hallway—where you used to comfort them after nightmares, where you measured their height on the wall—the place itself begins to unlock your fear. The carpet, the light switch, the family photos you pass every day suddenly feel like evidence of your failure. Let the environment crack open your controlled voice until you are no longer the authority figure but a terrified parent who realizes they don't know their own child. End not with answers, but with your forehead pressed against the door, speaking the most honest, undefended truth you've ever told them.
inspired_by: Actor is addressing the time and place obligation and the environment is unfamiliar

title: The Last Conversation Before the Light Fades
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has hours left to live. Begin by trying to hold it together, keeping your voice steady as you recall a specific shared memory. But as you speak, let whatever impulses arise take over completely—laughter at an absurd detail, sudden anger at time running out, a flash of gratitude, unexpected jealousy of their peace, tender forgiveness. Don't plan what comes next; let each feeling ambush you and shift without warning. By the end, you've moved through a spectrum of emotions you didn't know you'd feel, landing somewhere between acceptance and raw refusal to let go. Speak as if every word might be your last chance to say anything real.
inspired_by: Actor is stuck in conceptual or preplanned responses and cannot access organic moment-to-moment impulses

title: Holding Back the Sea
instruction: You're a parent whose child has just been diagnosed with a terminal illness, and you're on the phone with your own parent, trying to tell them. Start by attempting to be factual, clinical, holding it together because if you say it calmly it might not be real. But your voice betrays you—it shakes, rises, cracks. The rage comes suddenly: at God, at fate, at the unfairness, your voice loud and fierce and breaking. You're shouting, then choking on sobs, then forcing yourself quiet because your child might hear. The helplessness crashes over you—this fierce, primal need to protect them and the devastating reality that you can't. You oscillate between fury and collapse, between fighting and surrendering. By the end, your voice is raw, barely functional, and you're begging—not for miracles, but for the strength to be what they need. The love is so vast it's destroying you.

title: The Bitter Taste
instruction: You are in a passionate, close embrace with someone you deeply desire, but your mind is consumed by a rival who also wants them. As you kiss, a flash of amusement hits you at the absurdity of the rivalry, but it curdles into bitter envy of how naturally charming your rival seems. You pull back slightly, your breath ragged and close, and murmur these words with a mix of jealousy, dark amusement, and cold contempt born from knowing the rivalry will never end.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Amusement (very intensely present), Contempt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Pull
instruction: You are an older woman rowing alone on a lake at dawn, your calloused hands gripping the oars. Your body rocks forward and back as you pull against the heavy water, each stroke a grunt of effort, the recovery slide leaving you breathless and sour. You just received news that your partner has left, but you feel nothing—only a hollow numbness as your arms burn. Mid-stroke, a distant loon call confuses you, making you lose your rhythm and mutter in dizzy irritation. By the end, as your boat drifts in silence, your voice softens into a perplexed, bitter whisper about how this ache in your muscles is the only thing that feels real now.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Final Ledger
instruction: You are a young man who has just ended a long partnership with someone who stole from you. You've invited them to a quiet, empty office at closing time. Outside, rain taps on a window, and you can smell stale coffee. You start with a voice that is eerily flat and deliberate — you've rehearsed this moment for weeks. Each word lands like a stone. But as you recount the betrayal, the sourness of the memory bleeds through, and then, unexpectedly, you feel a flicker of shame for how small you sound when admitting you trusted them. The numbness you wore as armor cracks just slightly, but you force a thin smile. Let your voice shift from cold control to a vulnerable, almost ashamed tremor, then back to a practiced calm. Speak as if you're both enjoying and hating this moment.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Shame (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Buried Promise
instruction: You are an elderly man digging in your overgrown backyard, searching for a time capsule you buried with your late wife fifty years ago. Each shovelful of earth rises with a grunt and a prayer, then crashes aside. At first, every clod of dirt whispers doubt — 'It's gone, it's gone, too many seasons,' and your voice catches between ragged breaths, the shovel thudding against roots. But as the hole deepens, a stray thought flickers: 'She always said to keep faith.' Your speech becomes more hopeful, each recovery between digs lighter, until you finally pause, panting, and murmur with fragile optimism: 'Maybe... maybe just a few more inches.' Let your voice crack, shift, and be timed to the shoveling rhythm — grunt, straighten, speak, then dig again.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Mile
instruction: You are on a group hike, hour 4, and your body suddenly gives out. You were proud of your stamina, but now your legs shake and your vision blurs. The others are slowing to check on you. Start by insisting you're fine, voice strained but prideful. As you try to stand, your knees buckle—distress and embarrassment flood in. Your speech becomes slurred, breathy, with long pauses as you fight to form words. End with a quiet, embarrassed admission that you need to stop, voice hollow and defeated, but with a flicker of pride that you made it this far.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Embarrassment (extremely present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Swaying in the Afterglow
instruction: You are a teenager alone in your bedroom after a party, still buzzing from a stolen kiss and too many sips of something sweet. You’re dizzy, giddy, and talking to yourself as you spin slowly in front of a mirror. Start with a teasing thought about how ridiculous you must look, laughing at yourself. Let that dissolve into a dreamy, ecstatic realization that you’re falling for someone—your voice gets slow, breathless, and you trail off as you lose your balance and catch the wall. End with a soft, surprised giggle, as if you just discovered a secret you were meant to keep.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Final Push
instruction: You are a woman in your late 30s, in the last minute of an intense stationary cycling class. Your legs burn, your breath comes in rhythmic gasps, and you’re forcing words out between pedal strokes. Your hyper-feminine voice is strained but determined. You’re speaking to a younger woman beside you—your daughter, who just whispered she wants to quit. Start fierce and triumphant, riding the endorphin high of nearly finishing. As you speak, a flicker of doubt crosses your mind: you remember your own shame from quitting before. By the end, your voice softens—still breathy, still strained—but there’s a quiet surrender in it, not giving up, just letting go of the need to prove.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Doubt (clearly present), Shame (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fire and Skin
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—someone you'd given up on is alive, or a test came back clear, or someone you love just walked back through your door after years. Your body is flooded with relief so intense it's almost painful. Begin making sound—laughter, crying, or both simultaneously—your voice wild and uncontrolled. Let your whole body shake with the release of years of held tension. Speak in fragments: half-finished sentences, repetitions, gasping breaths. You might laugh until you're sobbing or sob until you're laughing. Your voice should be physical, visceral, coming from your gut and chest. Feel your hands wanting to touch, to confirm reality. Let sensation overtake articulation. End by trying to form coherent words but finding yourself still overtaken by the body's response to shock and overwhelming relief.

title: The Moment You Realize You'll Never Touch Them Again—Explosive Grief
instruction: You're holding a piece of their clothing, something soft they used to wear. Start touching it with careful, almost experimental gentleness, as if you're testing whether texture can bring them back. Your voice begins controlled, describing the fabric, the scent that's fading. But then it hits you with devastating force: this is all you have left, they're not coming back, you will never feel their actual warmth again. Let yourself explode—not into rage exactly, but into that fierce, physical grief that demands outlet. Your voice should surge from whispered reverence into something wild and broken, maybe even angry at the universe, at the cruelty of memory without presence. Touch the fabric harder, desperately, as if you could force it to become them. End in exhausted, gasping sobs, your hands finally still, the fight gone. Move from tentative hope through devastating realization to complete collapse.

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. Start from a place of careful, rehearsed anger—you've planned what you wanted to say for years. You're controlled, listing grievances, determined to make your point. But he says something small, something true, and it derails everything you prepared. Let yourself abandon the script entirely. What emerges isn't the speech you planned—it's messier, more childlike, more vulnerable. You might find yourself saying things you didn't know you felt. End in a place of exhausted honesty, where the anger has burned away and something more fragile remains. The challenge is letting go of the confrontation you intended and discovering the one that actually needs to happen.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake for what you both know is the last time. Begin by watching the sunrise through the window, feeling numb and unable to look at her. Speak to her about ordinary things—the weather, the birds outside—your voice tight and controlled, keeping emotion at bay. As she takes your hand, something breaks inside you. Let yourself finally say what you've been holding back all night: the specific memories that made her matter, the ways she shaped who you are. Your voice should crack and rebuild itself. End by whispering a promise about what you'll carry forward. Move from protective distance to raw, unguarded love and grief.

title: The Last Hour With My Father
instruction: You are sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hour. He's been unconscious, but suddenly his eyes open and he recognizes you. You have sixty seconds of clarity with him before he'll be gone forever. Begin with the shock and disbelief that this moment is actually happening—your heart racing, your throat tight, unable to find words. Let yourself move through whatever needs to be said: perhaps gratitude for something specific he gave you, or forgiveness you never offered, or a confession of how much you've needed him. By the end, find a place of profound peace and acceptance, holding his hand as you whisper your final goodbye. Let your voice crack, pause when words fail, allow silence to hold meaning. End in a whisper, with the weight of forever settling in your chest.

title: Holding Your Child During the Lockdown
instruction: There's an active shooter in your child's school, and you're barricaded in a classroom closet, holding them while calling 911. Start with fierce, whispered urgency to the dispatcher—giving location, details, trying to be helpful, trying to maintain control. But you hear screaming from the hallway. Your child asks 'Are we going to die?' and your voice shatters. You have to lie ('No, baby, we're safe') while your whole body shakes with terror. Rage erupts in whispers at the unfairness—'They're SEVEN, they should be learning fractions, not hiding from guns'—but you swallow it to soothe them. End humming their favorite lullaby, voice breaking, wrapping your body around theirs, knowing you'd die to protect them and hating that you might have to.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of unspoken disappointment. Begin angry—jaw tight, words clipped and controlled. You've rehearsed this, you're ready to tell him everything he failed to be. But as you speak, let something shift. Perhaps a memory surfaces of a time he tried, or a moment when you realized he was just as lost as you. Let your own real experiences of disappointment—with anyone, in any relationship—feed this moment. The anger should remain, but it becomes complicated by understanding, by your own failures, by the devastating recognition that you're more like him than you wanted to admit. End in a place where you're no longer sure who you're angrier at—him or yourself. Your voice should move from accusatory to something more vulnerable and uncertain.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Flight
instruction: Your partner is leaving tomorrow for a Mars colony mission—a one-way journey. You've spent months pretending to be supportive, but tonight, alone in your kitchen at 2 AM, you finally speak the truth you've been swallowing. Start with careful, measured words trying to be reasonable: 'I know I said I was okay with this.' Let your voice crack as the reality hits—you're about to lose them forever, and you helped pack their bags. Move from hollow support to raw desperation, then to a devastating acceptance that loving someone means letting them chase their dreams even when it destroys you. End with a whisper that holds both blessing and goodbye: 'I hope Mars gives you everything I couldn't.' Your voice should transform from numb control to breaking grief to a tender, impossible release.
inspired_by: Saying I Don't Love You Anymore

title: Compromise Refusing
instruction: Your family wants you to hide who you are at the wedding. Just for the day, they say. Your voice is ice: 'I will not.' It's quiet, not loud. Quieter when your mother starts crying on the phone. Your hand shakes, but your voice doesn't. 'If you're ashamed of me, don't ask me to come.' The cost of this refusal cracks through for just a moment—a breath, a wavering—then the resolve locks back in. You hang up. You're alone. You're free. You're terrified.

title: Grateful Ruins
instruction: You are saying goodbye to a relationship that was profound and real but cannot continue—a love that's ending not in bitterness but in impossible circumstances, a friendship severed by necessary distance, a chapter closing that meant everything. Begin with a voice that's trying to smile, almost succeeding, speaking about the beauty of what you shared. Let laughter come genuinely as you recall a specific moment of joy between you, something absurd or perfect or both. But underneath that laughter, let the grief be audible—your voice should carry both lightness and weight simultaneously. As you continue, let these contradictions intensify: speak with deep gratitude for how this person changed you, how they saw you, how they loved you, even as your voice keeps catching on the reality that this is goodbye. Let moments of genuine warmth break through the sadness, and moments of devastating loss break through the warmth. You're not trying to resolve these feelings, just letting them coexist. By the end, arrive at something paradoxical and profound: your voice should carry acceptance without resignation, peace without numbness, joy without denial of pain. Your final words should feel like a benediction—you're releasing them with love, thanking them for the beautiful wreckage they've made of your heart, speaking from a place where grief and gratitude have become indistinguishable from each other.

title: The Party Confession
instruction: You're at a crowded cocktail party, holding a drink, surrounded by chatter and clinking glasses. You're a man with a deep, hyper-masculine voice, but tonight you're overwhelmed with a secret pleasure: your child just told you they love you for the first time. You're trying to casually recount this to a friend, but your voice keeps cracking with emotion. Start with forced, punchy sentences, projecting over the noise, but gradually let your pitch rise and your words stumble as the ecstasy seeps through. By the end, you're almost whispering, lost in the memory, the party fading around you.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bitter Comedown
instruction: You're alone in a grimy public restroom after a violent argument — maybe with a family member or a stranger. You're washing blood off your knuckles, but your hands shake so badly you keep missing the water stream. Start with muttered contempt: you're angry, spitting out how they 'had it coming,' how they're pathetic. But as the adrenaline drains, your voice trembles, your stomach clenches, and the contempt cracks into a flood of sadness. You might hiccup, laugh bitterly, then stop mid-sentence. Let the words become fragile, tearful — a raw confession that you're scared and alone. Your voice should be shaky, with sudden pauses and swallows, as if your body is betraying you.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Words We Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent in what might be your last real conversation with them. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair and adult about it. You're telling them about the wounds they left, the parent you needed but never had.
