Start controlled, almost clinical in your honesty, but as you speak, decades of buried hurt and anger start pouring out. Your voice rises, cracks, becomes accusatory, then suddenly breaks into something more vulnerable—you're not just angry, you're grieving the relationship you'll never have. End in a completely different place: exhausted, raw, asking through tears not for them to change, but simply to acknowledge what happened. The anger transforms into something more painful—the desperate need to be seen and heard before it's too late.

title: Laughing Through Goodbye
instruction: Your best friend is leaving for something that could save their life but means you'll likely never see them again. You're trying to celebrate their courage while your heart is breaking. Your voice starts attempting lightness: 'So, what do you want me to do while you're off becoming a hero?' But they see through it and say 'Tell me what you really want. Don't protect me.' Now you have to speak the impossible truth—you want them to stay AND you want them to go. Your voice tangles with contradictions: laughter breaking into tears, joy mixed with grief, pride collapsing into selfish need. Find the beauty in wanting two opposite things at once. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's learning that love means honoring their desires even when it destroys you.

title: Joyful Goodbye: Celebrating Someone's Last Lucid Moment
instruction: Your beloved mentor, parent, or dearest friend is slipping away to dementia or terminal decline, and right now—miraculously—they're fully present for the first time in weeks. You're laughing with them, sharing a beautiful memory, your voice bright with genuine joy at having them back. But underneath every laugh is the knowledge this is goodbye, that this clarity is a gift and a devastation. Let your voice carry both: the full-hearted delight in this moment of connection and the grief of knowing you're losing them even as you hold them. Speak with gratitude that catches in your throat, with love that makes you smile even as tears come. End in a place of bittersweet peace: thanking them for this last gift of themselves while your heart breaks. Your voice should shimmer between celebration and sorrow, never choosing one over the other.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Healer Saves the Villain's Life Against All Doctrine

title: Laughing While You Pack Their Belongings
instruction: You're packing up the belongings of someone who died—your best friend, your sibling, your partner. You find something absurd, something so perfectly them it makes you laugh. Start with that dissociative calm as you list items: 'One red sweater with a stain. Seventeen unread books. A collection of bottle caps for some reason.' Your voice is flat, mechanical. But then you find something—a ridiculous note, a terrible photo, something that breaks you into laughter. Real, genuine laughter. And the laughter is beautiful and horrible because you're laughing alone and they should be here laughing with you. The laughter starts to mix with tears until you can't tell which is which. Your voice shifts between joy at the memory and grief at the loss, sometimes mid-sentence. End with a moment of profound gratitude for having known them, even as your heart is completely shattered. The emotions exist simultaneously: celebration and mourning, love and loss, peace and devastation all at once.

title: Reading Your Dead Sister's Wedding Vows at Her Funeral
instruction: You found the vows your sister wrote for a wedding that will never happen—she died three weeks before the ceremony. You've decided to read them at her funeral because her fiancé asked you to, because she'd want her words heard. Begin reading them in her voice, the way she would have said them—playful, full of inside jokes, bright with joy. You can't help but smile, even laugh a little at her humor, finding yourself momentarily lost in her happiness. But then a line hits you—something about growing old together—and your voice splinters. You're simultaneously laughing at her jokes and crying at the impossibility of these promises, your voice oscillating wildly between joy at who she was and anguish at what's been stolen. End with the final line—'I choose you, today and every day after'—and here your voice finds a strange, transcendent peace: you're saying her words but also speaking to her, telling her that you choose to carry her forward, that love doesn't end. The last word should be delivered with tears streaming but your voice steady, almost serene, as if she's helped you find grace in this impossible moment.

title: Holding Back the Sea
instruction: You're trying desperately to protect someone you love from danger that's already here, and you're screaming at them to run, to hide, to listen to you—but they won't, or can't. Start with fierce, almost violent urgency, your voice sharp with command and terror. Pour everything into making them move, making them understand. But as you realize it's not working, that you're powerless, let rage crack into something more devastating: helpless, choking sobs that interrupt your words. You're still trying to sound strong, still trying to protect them, but now you're begging, your voice breaking on their name. End collapsed into raw desperation, all authority stripped away, just a human being unable to save what they love most, voice reduced to broken fragments.

title: Dissociating in a Meeting: Watching Your Voice from Outside Your Body
instruction: You're dissociating in a corporate meeting. Your voice is speaking—contributing to the discussion—but you're not inside your head. You hear yourself talking like you're listening to a recording. Your tone is too flat, too rehearsed. You're watching your own words like a bad actor. Someone responds to what you said and you have to scramble to remember what your voice just said. Include the eerie moment of re-entering your body mid-sentence.

title: The Scent of Betrayal
instruction: You are kneeling at your Dominant's feet, your voice soft and breathy, filled with adoration as you whisper how much you trust them. But as you lean closer, you catch a strange scent—perfume that isn't yours. The realization hits you: they've been with someone else. Your voice fractures, rising in pitch with disbelief, then dropping into a cold, disgusted deadness as you speak the accusation. Let your words be interrupted by your own shaky breath, your body tensing, your eyes narrowing. Start with tender vulnerability, end with icy contempt.
emotions_sampled: Affection (very intensely present), Disgust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kneeling Oath
instruction: You are an older man forced to kneel on a cold stone floor before a figure you despise. Your knees ache, and you shift your weight, muttering under your breath with irritation. You begin speaking to your captor, your voice tight with impatience and barely concealed malice. Halfway through, a flicker of disappointment crosses your face—at yourself for being in this position—but it hardens into cold resolve. Let your voice crack with annoyance at first, then drop into a low, venomous threat as you end. Let the physical discomfort break your rhythm: pause to reposition, sigh in frustration, then let the malice sharpen your tone.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Hospital Room: Last Words to the One Who Raised You
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who raised you—a parent, grandparent, or guardian—in their final hours. Begin by noticing small, specific details about them: the rhythm of their breathing, the texture of their hand, the familiar scent of their skin mixed with antiseptic. Let yourself be flooded by a cascade of specific memories spanning your entire life together—not in order, but as fragments: being taught to tie your shoes at age five, a heated argument in your teenage years, the way they laughed at your jokes, a moment they disappointed you deeply, a time they showed up when you needed them most. Allow each memory to carry its full sensory weight—sounds, smells, physical sensations—and let the contradictory feelings coexist. Start from a place of wanting to say something perfect and important, but let the words that actually come be messier, more honest, shaped by this lifetime of accumulated moments. By the end, you should arrive at something rawer and truer than what you intended—perhaps forgiveness, perhaps unresolved anger mixed with profound love, perhaps simply the weight of goodbye.
inspired_by: Character Relationship Imaging: Death of a Salesman (Biff and Willy)

title: Major Apology Finally
instruction: You're meeting your estranged child for the first time in 15 years. You've rehearsed this apology a thousand times, but now your voice is shaking: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry for all of it.' Your voice cracks on the words. 'I was broken and scared, and I took it out on you. That was wrong.' You're struggling not to cry, struggling to hold the moment. 'I can't undo the past. I don't expect forgiveness.' Your voice drops to barely audible: 'I just needed you to know that none of it was your fault.' Your child is silent. You fill the silence: 'I've thought about you every single day. Every. Single. Day.' The apology isn't perfect; your voice is too destroyed for perfection. It's real. Your child finally speaks: 'Okay, Dad. Okay.' And you both cry into the space between you.

title: The Coin in the Throat
instruction: You are a street child, maybe ten years old, hiding in a sewer grate alcove during a rainstorm. A soaked, desperate stranger has crawled in beside you, breathing heavily in the dark. They are pressing something cold and wet into your hand—a coin, but also a threat. You feel a terrifying, unwanted intimacy in the close heat of their body, the wet wool smell, the damp whisper of their voice against your ear. You start in a slow, trembling whisper, forced to cooperate, but as you speak, you feel a cold contempt for their weakness, and your own voice hardens, cracks, then drifts into a hollow, shamed sadness for the child you still are, lost in the filthy dark. Let your voice be a forced, breathy crawl at first, intermittently broken by the need to swallow or shiver, then let it grow brittle with contempt, before fading into a flat, childlike sorrow.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Contempt (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispered Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying beside someone you love, whispering a truth you've carried alone for too long—a failure, a fear, a secret shame that's been eating you alive. Your voice must be barely above a whisper, intimate, as if speaking any louder would shatter you completely. Begin hesitantly, your breath uneven, starting and stopping, almost unable to form the words. As you confess, let tenderness creep in—for yourself, for the person listening, for the fragility of this moment. Your voice should tremble not with drama but with the real terror of being truly seen. Move through shame into something like relief, though relief that's tangled with vulnerability and the fear of judgment. By the end, let yourself rest in the quiet aftermath of having spoken the unspeakable, your voice settling into a whispered peace that still carries the tremor of what it cost you to be this honest.

title: The Gift That Breaks You Open
instruction: Someone you've hurt beyond measure—someone you thought you'd lost forever—has just handed you something. A gift. After everything you've done, after all the pain you caused, they're standing here offering you something with shaking hands. Start with shock, with a voice that can barely form words. 'I don't... I can't...' Feel the rage at yourself, the voice rising: 'Why would you give me anything? After what I did?' Let yourself almost shout it, the self-loathing pouring out, the inability to accept forgiveness. But then let it crack—let the fierce anger collapse into broken sobs. Your voice should fracture completely as you realize this gift isn't about the object at all. It's about them choosing, against all logic, to reach toward you. Let yourself shake. Let your words come out in gasps between tears: 'I don't deserve this... I don't deserve you... but god, I'm so grateful you're here.' Feel the helplessness of being given something you can never repay, the crushing weight of unearned grace.
inspired_by: Acting Interested in a Gift Youre Receiving

title: The Blanket Fort Confession
instruction: You have built a blanket fort in your living room—something you haven't done since childhood—and invited your partner inside to tell them something you've never told anyone. Begin in a whisper, almost playful, remarking on how small and safe this space feels, how the outside world disappears. Let yourself genuinely feel the particular quality of light through fabric, the muffled sounds, the sense of being hidden. From this place of childlike safety, confess your deepest fear or shame—something about your body, your past, your secret self. Your voice should stay quiet throughout, but move from playful and tentative to trembling and naked. The fort has made you small enough to finally tell the truth.
inspired_by: Actor has lost imaginative spontaneity and has difficulty believing in imagined circumstances

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospice
instruction: You're on the phone with your parent who is in hospice care, and they've called to say goodbye—this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Begin with forced cheerfulness, your voice bright and determined: 'Don't talk like that, you're going to be fine.' You're trying to keep them (and yourself) from facing what's happening. But they gently, firmly tell you they're ready to go, that they need you to let them. Your forced optimism cracks into pleading: 'Just hold on a little longer, please.' They tell you they love you, that you've been enough, that they're at peace. Your voice finally breaks open—no more pretending, just raw love and the devastating acceptance that this goodbye is real. End with you whispering back 'I love you' as you feel them slipping away, your voice tender but shattered, speaking the words that will be the last they ever hear from you.

title: The Last Shift Before the Diagnosis
instruction: You're working your final shift at the office before leaving for indefinite medical treatment tomorrow. A younger colleague - someone who reminds you of yourself years ago - keeps making the same eager mistakes you once made. Begin with gentle amusement at their earnest incompetence, that bittersweet recognition of your younger self. As you guide them through a task one last time, let the weight of goodbye seep in - this ordinary moment is your last. Your voice should crack not with drama but with the quiet devastation of realizing you're saying farewell to a life you took for granted. End in a place of tender acceptance mixed with profound grief, finding something precious in this mundane interaction you'll never have again. Let silences do the heavy lifting. This isn't about the medical condition - it's about the ache of normal life slipping away.

title: The Gratitude Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you wrote to someone who saved your life but is no longer here to thank—a teacher, a friend, a stranger who intervened at your darkest moment. Your voice carries genuine joy and gratitude, laughing a little at specific memories, celebrating how far you've come. But underneath, threading through every word, is the breaking knowledge that they'll never hear this, that you waited too long, that your happiness is built on their absence. Let the laughter be real and the grief be real simultaneously. Your voice cracks not from sadness alone but from the impossible coexistence of profound thankfulness and devastating loss. End with 'You should be here. You should be here to see this.' The smile and the tears equally authentic.

title: Compressed Emotions
instruction: You're on a video call with the person you love, but they've just announced they're leaving tomorrow—forever. Every emotion is locked in your chest: rage, heartbreak, apology, anger at yourself. Your voice becomes mechanical, controlled, almost strangled. Each word is bitten off. You can hear your own pulse in your throat. The pressure builds until you have to stop talking entirely, and your silence says more than words ever could. Then: 'I can't do this right now.'

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're holding someone you love who's in danger and there's nothing you can do to stop what's coming. Start with fierce, almost violent protectiveness, voice commanding: 'No. No, this isn't happening. I won't let it.' Your body is tense, ready to fight the universe itself. The desperation builds, voice escalating to near-shouting: 'Take me instead! Do you hear me?!' Fists pound against invisible walls. Then the helplessness hits—your strength crumbles, voice breaking into gasping sobs: 'Please. Please, I can't—I don't know how to—' You're collapsing, all the fight draining out. The transformation completes: rage and terror dissolve into tender devastation. Voice becomes gentle, almost singing: 'It's okay. I'm here. I'm right here with you.' Your final words are a whispered promise through tears: 'You're not alone. You will never be alone.' Fury has transformed into the most profound, helpless love.

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner who you think is asleep. Begin by genuinely noticing them in the dark—the sound of their breathing, the warmth of their body near yours, the outline of their shoulder in the dim light. You've been carrying a secret that's creating distance between you, and in this quiet moment, you begin to whisper it out loud, believing they can't hear you. Let yourself be absorbed in the relief of finally saying the words aloud, even to the darkness. Halfway through, you realize they're awake and listening. The energy shifts—now you must finish what you started, but directly to them. Move from the safety of confession to darkness, to the terrifying vulnerability of being truly seen and not knowing if they'll stay.

title: Beautiful Ruins: Laughing at Our Last Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your best friend who's moving across the world tomorrow, knowing deep in your bones this is the end of your closeness even if neither of you will say it. You start by laughing—genuinely laughing—at a shared memory, an inside joke that only the two of you understand. Your voice is light, joyful even, as you recount ridiculous adventures you've had together. But there's something underneath, a tremor you're trying to hide. As you keep talking, you're still smiling, still laughing, but tears are streaming down your face. Your voice does something strange: it stays bright and warm while simultaneously breaking with grief. You're thanking them—'God, thank you for being you'—and your voice is full of such genuine gratitude it hurts. You laugh again, harder this time, almost hysterically, because if you stop laughing you'll completely fall apart. By the end, you're saying 'I'm so happy for you' while sobbing, your voice caught between celebration and devastation, expressing pure joy for their journey while your heart shatters at the loss, finding something beautiful in the contradiction of loving someone enough to let them go even as it destroys you.
inspired_by: Professional: Social Worker Removes a Child from Their Parents

title: Tripping and Falling at a Wedding
instruction: You're walking down the aisle or dancing at a wedding, and you trip spectacularly. Your voice is the sharp gasp of falling, then a thud, then silence. There's a moment of complete humiliation. You're pulling yourself up, and your voice is high with embarrassment: 'I'm okay, I'm okay.' But everyone is staring. Your voice shakes as you try to recover some dignity. You're sitting back down, and you can feel the stares. Your voice is barely audible: 'Did anyone get that on video?'

title: Abandonment by Parent
instruction: A parent you depended on has chosen to leave. You're on the phone, and the realization is hitting as they speak. At first, you're trying to convince them to stay—your voice is pleading. 'Please, don't do this.' Then you understand they've already made their choice. Your voice becomes hollow, broken. You're asking 'Why? Why don't you want me?' Your voice is a child's voice even if you're an adult. Include the moment they hang up. You're listening to the dial tone, your voice becoming a broken whisper.

title: The Last Morning Before the Memory Wipes
instruction: You're sitting with your partner on the morning before a procedure that will erase all memories of your relationship to save your life. Begin with forced brightness—'Look, the sun's perfect today'—trying to memorize their face while pretending everything's normal. As you describe ordinary moments you shared, your voice should fracture. Touch their hand and feel the devastating knowledge that tomorrow you won't know why this touch matters. End by whispering their name over and over, as if repetition could burn it into whatever part of you survives. Let the gratitude for having loved them war with the grief of losing them, your voice moving from controlled to raw to a whisper that can barely form words.
inspired_by: Waking Up and Not Knowing Who You Are

title: The Exorcism of Shame
instruction: You're alone in a room where you once experienced your deepest humiliation. You've decided that you're going to physically purge the shame from your body. Start by trying to hold still—but then let your body begin moving in ways that feel forbidden: contort yourself, make ugly faces, produce sounds you'd never let anyone hear. Writhe, roll on the floor, twist yourself into strange shapes. Let your face become grotesque. Scream, growl, laugh maniacally, speak gibberish. Make yourself as 'embarrassing' as possible—challenge every impulse to look good or stay controlled. Get physically exhausted doing this. When you're finally spent, let a simple truth emerge from your mouth—something like 'I'm still here' or 'I survived.' Begin trapped in rigid shame; end emptied out, free, and strangely at peace. The physical wildness burns out the psychological prison.

title: Rage and Ruin
instruction: You're screaming at someone you love because they're about to make a choice that will destroy them, and you are powerless to stop it. Start with explosive anger—your voice raw, loud, desperate. 'You don't get to throw your life away! You don't get to give up!' But as they stand there, calm and resigned, your rage shatters into something more terrifying: helplessness. Your voice breaks, the volume dropping as fury transforms into pleading. You're on your knees now, literally or emotionally, and the fight drains out of you. What remains is naked terror and love—'Please. Please don't leave me.' By the end, your voice should be wrecked, oscillating between fierce protectiveness and the devastating realization that you cannot save them, only love them through whatever comes next.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence
instruction: You're finally telling your mother what her emotional absence cost you—decades of feeling invisible, of wondering if you were worthy of love. Begin with trembling restraint, trying to be fair, trying to explain calmly. But as she deflects or justifies, something inside you snaps. Your voice rises—not to shouting, but to a fierce, shaking clarity. Accuse her. Demand she see you. Then, suddenly, collapse into the child you were: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Feel yourself cycle between rage at her failure and desperate longing for her to finally understand. End in exhausted honesty, quieter now, admitting you still need her even though it kills you to admit it.
inspired_by: Deaf Person Speaking for the First Time with Cochlear Implant

title: The Last Light Through Her Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the late afternoon. She's awake but fading, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin by looking at her hands—really seeing them, the spots, the thin skin, the wedding ring. As you speak to her about a specific childhood memory she gave you, let new details flood in: the smell of her perfume, the texture of her cardigan, the exact color of her eyes, the sound of her labored breathing. Start with quiet composure and gratitude, but as these sensory memories intensify—the weight of her hand in yours, the afternoon light moving across her face—let yourself break open. End in a place of raw, unguarded grief mixed with profound love. Let each sensory detail you notice crack you open further.
inspired_by: A choice has lost its strength after repeated use in a long run

title: The Last Light Before Sleep
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting alone in a dim room, watching the sunset through a window. You are fighting sleep, your eyelids heavy. Start by speaking softly about a memory of someone you loved, your voice gentle with longing and affection. As you continue, the awe of the fading light overwhelms you—your words slow, slur, and trail into mumbles. Let your sentences begin clearly but drift, pause as you nod, then jerk awake and try to finish. End with a barely whispered, awe-filled murmur as sleep nearly takes you.
emotions_sampled: Longing (slightly present), Affection (slightly present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen confronting your father about something he's never acknowledged—maybe an affair that destroyed your mother, maybe his absence during a crisis, maybe words he said that carved themselves into you. Start from a place of careful control; you've rehearsed this conversation in your head a thousand times. But as you speak, let your body and voice respond instantly to whatever comes up—don't edit. If your voice suddenly cracks, let it crack and see what comes next. If you feel an impulse to laugh bitterly, laugh and let that shift into something else. If your hands want to grab a dish, grab it. Maybe you start pacing, maybe you find yourself on your knees, maybe rage transforms mid-sentence into pleading or vice versa. Respond to his silence (real or imagined) with whatever impulse hits you each second. By the end, you've said things you didn't know you were going to say, felt things you couldn't have predicted. The control you started with must completely dissolve into raw, unplanned honesty.

title: The Last Matchmaking
instruction: You're in hospice, and your oldest friend sits beside you. You spent decades trying to set them up with someone, anyone—always with terrible, funny ideas. Now, in your final hours, you start with that familiar playful enthusiasm, pitching one last absurd match ("I met your nurse, and I think..."), but as you speak, the lightness cracks. Your voice breaks as you realize you won't see them find love, won't be at their wedding. Transform from that bright, meddling energy into quiet devastation—apologize for all the bad setups, but really you're apologizing for leaving. End in a whisper, telling them the truth: you just wanted them to be as happy as knowing them made you. Let genuine grief replace the humor naturally, like sunlight fading.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent everything you've held back for decades. Start with careful politeness—'I wanted to talk about when I was young'—but feel the rage building beneath every measured word. Your voice sharpens as you detail the specific moments they weren't there, the times you needed them and they chose something else. Let the anger peak—'I was your child!'—then hear it collapse into something more devastating: the raw need underneath. Your voice becomes smaller, younger, as you ask the question you've never dared: 'Did you even want me?' The confrontation ends not with triumph but with exhausted vulnerability, speaking a truth you've never admitted: 'I still need you to say you're sorry. Even now. Especially now.'

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's boarding a plane to a war zone, a dangerous mission, or a place they might never return from. You promised yourself you'd be strong, keep it light, not let them hear your fear. So you start with forced brightness—'You're going to be amazing out there.' But as the final boarding call approaches, that facade crumbles. Your voice begins to shake despite your best efforts. The cheerfulness dissolves into barely contained terror. You want to beg them not to go, but instead you whisper 'Come back to me,' and it sounds like both a prayer and a goodbye. End with the silence after they hang up, where you finally let yourself break.

title: Laughing While the World Ends
instruction: You're in an elevator when you get the test results you've been dreading—the cancer is back, stage four, months not years. A cheerful stranger asks 'How's your day going?' and something breaks open in you. You start laughing—genuine, slightly hysterical laughter: 'Oh, you know, just got some interesting news.' Your voice is bright, almost giddy with the absurdity. You find yourself telling them about it in this weird, light way: 'Apparently my body's trying to kill me again. Isn't that funny? I just bought a gym membership.' Let laughter and tears intermingle naturally. Your voice cracks but you keep smiling: 'I'm actually weirdly okay? Like, I'm terrified, but I'm also so grateful I got to go to my daughter's wedding last month. I got to dance with her.' Let joy and devastation coexist. By the end, you're crying and laughing at once: 'Life is so beautiful and so cruel and I just... I'm so glad I got to live it.' The doors open and you wipe your eyes, thank the stranger for listening, and step out into whatever time you have left with a broken, peaceful smile.

title: Beginning Fresh Start
instruction: You're starting completely over — new city, new job, new life, new identity. Your voice is nervous but hopeful: 'Everything is different now.' You're at the beginning of a new chapter, and the uncertainty is palpable in your voice. 'I don't know what comes next, but that's okay.' You're unpacking boxes, or meeting new people, and your voice is tentative: 'Hi, I'm [name]. I'm new here.' Each introduction is a small act of courage. By the end of the day: 'I did it. I actually did it. I started over.' Your voice is exhausted but alive. 'I have no idea what this life is going to look like, but I'm ready to find out.' Walking into your empty apartment, your voice is a whisper: 'Here we go. New beginning. Here we go.' The fresh start is terrifying and glorious.

title: The Confrontation: When Your Best Friend Became a Stranger
instruction: You're confronting your closest friend of fifteen years who has been systematically excluding you, replacing you with new people, erasing your history together. Begin with forced lightness—'I feel like we haven't really talked in forever'—trying to keep things casual, giving them a chance to explain. As their deflections mount, let your hurt transform into anger. Call them out specifically: the birthday they forgot, the group chat you're not in, the lies about being busy. Let your voice rise, crack with betrayal. Then—in the middle of your fury—have a devastating realization that you're fighting for something already dead. Your final words should be completely different: quiet, dignified, grieving. 'I hope they make you happier than I did.' Walk away from fifteen years with both rage and heartbreak in your throat.
inspired_by: Voicemail Spiral: Leaving Message After Message

title: Midnight Confession in a Hospital Corridor
instruction: Your best friend is in surgery after a car accident. You're alone in the corridor at 3 AM, and you start talking to them as if they can hear you through the walls. Your voice is barely above a whisper—hoarse from crying, exhausted, intimate. You confess everything you never said: that you've been in love with them for years, that watching them date other people felt like slow death, that you convinced yourself friendship was enough but it never was. Your whispers catch and break. There's no anger here, just aching tenderness mixed with grief for all the time you wasted being afraid. Halfway through, you start laughing softly at the absurdity—that it takes a near-death experience to make you brave, that you're confessing to a wall. End with your voice becoming even softer, more tender, telling them they have to live because you're not done knowing them yet.
inspired_by: Phone Sex Partner Realizing They're Emotionally Attached

title: The Stone at the Top of the Hill
instruction: You are a teenage farmhand, alone, hauling a boulder-sized bag of feed up a steep, muddy hill at dusk. You've done this a hundred times; the weight is a familiar enemy. As you climb, abandoning the day's last chores, you mutter to yourself — not complaining, but recounting a small, complicated victory you had today with a stubborn neighbor. Pride is your fuel: you are strong, you are reliable, you will get this load to the top. But the hill is long, and your legs burn. Start with proud concentration, bragging under your breath about how you handled things. Let the pride slip slightly into grim contemplation as the hill steepens, your breath shortening. End with a final, gritty grunt of triumph as you reach the top, but your voice is thinner, more fatigued — a quiet pride in having done it alone, even as your body shakes with exhaustion.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (clearly present), Concentration (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Truth About the Affair
instruction: You're confronting your partner about their infidelity. Start from a place of desperately wanting to believe their denials—let yourself see flashes of your good times together: their smile in morning light, their hand in yours, shared laughter. Your initial accusations are tentative, almost apologetic, because part of you is clinging to these bright images. But as they continue lying, allow contrasting sensory fragments to invade: their phone screen glowing with messages, lipstick stains, the smell of unfamiliar perfume, their eyes avoiding yours. Don't narrate these—simply let them flash through you. As these darker images accumulate and overtake the bright ones, your emotional state must transform from pleading hope to cold, undeniable recognition. Your voice, your body, your entire presence should shift as the sensory reality rewrites what you feel.
inspired_by: A scene requires an emotional transition between two distinct states at a specific moment

title: The Kitchen Truth
instruction: You're confronting your adult child in your kitchen after discovering something that has shattered your understanding of who they are. You came prepared with accusations and disappointment, but as you begin speaking, notice the micro-expressions on their face, the way they're standing, the quality of their silence. Something underneath your anger is sending you information—a feeling about what's really happening here that contradicts your prepared speech. Start with the confrontation you planned, but let yourself be derailed by these unexpected impulses about what's actually true. Maybe your rage is covering fear. Maybe their defiance is covering shame—or maybe it isn't shame at all. Follow each intuitive flash about what you're really sensing from them, even when it contradicts what you want to believe. Transform from righteous anger to a more complicated, uncomfortable recognition of something you didn't want to see.
inspired_by: Actor feels their intuition is unreliable or nonexistent

title: Giving Birth While Arguing with Your Mother-in-Law
instruction: The most absurd multi-tasking challenge: active labor AND a long-standing family argument about baby names. Between contractions, argue with full passion ('We are NOT naming her Gertrude!'). During contractions, the argument dissolves into pure physical vocalization (moaning, grunting, breathing techniques). Immediately after each peak, resume the argument exactly where you left off as if nothing happened. The ridiculousness should be genuine — life doesn't pause for drama.

title: Time Paradox Sanity Loss
instruction: You're experiencing a temporal loop—your 47th iteration—narrating the descent. Begin articulate and distressed, describing the impossibility. By mid-narration, your own future self is speaking through you in a different accent and cadence, creating an unsettling vocal doubling effect. Stutter, skip sentences mid-thought as if time is fragmented even in your speech. Your voice gets higher, younger, then older, then back again. End with a dead monotone, counting 'forty-eight, forty-nine, fifty' as if you've given up on being human.

title: Echoes of the Trail
instruction: You are an elderly woman on a forest hike, using a crackling walkie-talkie to check on your granddaughter who wandered ahead. At first, you feel a tight knot of worry — your voice wavers, you listen for a reply, and the PTT button gives a rough 'kkhht' before you speak. Then you hear her cheerful response that she's found a stunning lookout, and your whole body relaxes into a quiet, breathless elation. Let your words come out in short, warm bursts, with the radio squelch between each transmission, and a small, relieved smile creeping into your tone by the end. Remember to naturally react to the environment — a bird call, adjusting the radio's antenna, or a pause as you hike uphill.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Immigrant Calling Home: Two Selves
instruction: Call your parents back home. When you speak to them, your voice changes completely — softer, more musical, perhaps with an accent you've been suppressing in your new country. You reassure them everything is wonderful. After hanging up, speak in your adopted accent about how lonely you actually are. Show the two selves: the successful emigrant (performing for parents) and the homesick human (admitting the truth to the empty room). Two languages, two truths.

title: Laughing Through Your Eulogy
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who made you promise not to cry—someone who lived with explosive joy despite everything. Begin trying to honor that promise, voice bright but trembling, sharing an absurd story about them. Let laughter bubble up genuinely—they really were that ridiculous. But mid-laugh, feel it catch. Your voice should dance between amusement and devastation: laughing at a memory while tears stream down your face, voice breaking on punchlines. Include moments where you can't tell if you're laughing or sobbing—the sounds blur together. Express gratitude for every chaotic, beautiful moment while your heart shatters that there won't be more. Your tone should hold both celebration and goodbye, joy and unbearable loss occupying the same breath. End with quiet amazement: they taught you that laughter and grief aren't opposites. Your final words are whispered through both tears and a smile, finding strange peace in the contradiction.

title: Father Teaching Permission
instruction: A father is giving his adult child permission to live their own life, and both are struggling with the weight of that permission. The father's voice is proud but also grieving—he's releasing someone he's been responsible for. The child's voice is grateful and terrified. There's a moment where both speak simultaneously, their voices crossing in vulnerability. The father says something he's been holding, and his voice cracks. The child responds with a steadiness that surprises both of them. By the end, they're speaking as adults meeting each other, which is both what they wanted and completely heartbreaking.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Never Gave You
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home, and your mother is right there. Your voice starts controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this conversation for years. You tell her about the birthdays she missed, the times you needed her and she chose something else. But as you speak, your control fractures. Anger bleeds through, then suddenly you're not accusing anymore—you're begging. Your voice breaks as you ask the question you've never dared to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay?' The rage dissolves into raw vulnerability. You hear yourself becoming the child you were, voice small and pleading. End with a moment of devastating clarity: you're not angry anymore, just profoundly, achingly sad for both of you—for what she couldn't give and what you'll never get back.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Ancient Warrior Realizes They've Been Fighting an Illusion

title: The Gravity of Gratitude
instruction: You are thanking someone who saved your life—literally or metaphorically—but you are also furious with them for the way they did it, the cost it extracted, the pride it wounded. Begin with bright, performative gratitude, your body upright, voice cheerful, fighting to maintain the socially appropriate emotion. As you speak, allow the true weight of what you feel to sink in—the genuine gratitude mixed with rage, the love tangled with resentment. Your body grows progressively heavier with the burden of these contradictions until you can no longer hold up the pretense. End with your voice raw and honest, body slumped under the enormous weight of needing someone you also hate needing, grateful and furious in equal measure, your thank-you transformed into something far more complex and true.

title: Numb and Giggly
instruction: You're a teenage girl just out of dental surgery, half your face still frozen from novocaine. You're trying to tell your mom about the funny thing the dentist said, but every 'B,' 'P,' and 'M' comes out mushy and you keep accidentally drooling on your shirt. Start with frustrated, embarrassed frustration as you realize how ridiculous you sound, then let the absurdity of the situation crack you up—by the end, you're laughing so hard you can barely get the words out, vocal chords shaking with helpless amusement.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father after discovering a devastating family secret they've kept from you for decades. Begin the scene appearing calm, even cold—you came here with a plan to stay composed, to ask rational questions. But as you speak, the dam begins to crack. Don't just tell them you're angry; let your body take over the space. Move. Physically demonstrate the betrayal in your muscles, your gestures, your stance. Knock something over if you need to. Take up more room than you usually would. Let your voice travel from measured control to raw, unfiltered fury, then shatter into something more vulnerable—the child who needed them. End not with resolution, but with you standing in the wreckage of your composure, finally showing them who you've become because of their silence.
inspired_by: When a director or producer is unconvinced you have a specific quality the role requires (strength, danger, vulnerability, etc.)

title: Midnight Confession at the Gate
instruction: You are a sixteen-year-old stranded in a nearly empty airport terminal after a 14-hour flight. Your body thinks it's 4 AM, but the local time is noon. You're on the phone with your best friend, trying to explain why you haven't texted back in two days. Start with a hollow, exhausted monotone—your words feel thick and slow, like pushing through honey. As you stumble over a simple sentence (maybe 'I just... I couldn't...' trailed off by a yawn), a wave of embarrassment hits you for sounding so pathetic. End with a soft, cracked laugh and a whisper that admits you miss them, letting a tiny spark of warmth break through the numbness.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Embarrassment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Hands After Career-Ending Tremor Diagnosis
instruction: You're alone in your office late at night, looking at your hands—the hands that have saved hundreds of lives—after being diagnosed with an essential tremor that will end your surgical career. Speak softly, intimately, as if your hands are old friends you're losing. Thank them for specific surgeries, specific saves, whispering details like a prayer. Your voice catches on memories—'You remember the six-year-old with the brain bleed? Your steadiness gave her life back'—mixing gratitude with devastating grief. Touch your fingers together gently as you speak, feeling them still steady now but knowing what's coming. Let silence sit between phrases. By the end, you're not just mourning your career; you're mourning your identity, your purpose, everything you believed made you valuable.
inspired_by: Surgeon Narrating a Procedure While Exhausted

title: Body Appreciated
instruction: Your partner is deliberately appreciating your body—the parts you might be self-conscious about—with genuine reverence. Your voice starts defensive, but as they touch you and speak, your voice becomes less guarded: 'You really like this?' 'I do. I love this about you.' Your voice shifts from shame to permission to appreciate yourself. Your partner is teaching you to love your body through their love of your body. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's being healed of body shame through another person's genuine appreciation.

title: After the Accident—Alive
instruction: You have just survived a devastating accident and are lying on the ground, alive against all odds. Your body is in searing pain, but you are flooded with ecstatic relief. Begin with the physical: feel the concrete or dirt beneath you, its temperature, texture, small stones pressing into your back. Smell the acrid burn of rubber, gasoline, or smoke mixed with rain or earth. Taste blood in your mouth, metallic and real. Hear the distant sirens, someone shouting, the ringing in your ears. Feel your own hand gripping your chest, your ribs, your face—checking that you're whole, that you're real. Let pain and joy crash through you simultaneously: each breath hurts but proves you're breathing. As your senses sharpen, let yourself laugh or sob or both—a sound torn from the recognition that you're alive to feel this pain. Start in shock, senses scattered and numb, then allow each sensation to pierce through until you're overwhelmed by the violent beauty of simply existing. End in a state of almost religious gratitude mixed with animal terror, your body a symphony of agony and euphoria, every nerve screaming that you survived.

title: The Weight of Letting Go
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's sleeping peacefully, and you've just received permission to say everything you never said. Begin holding tension in your body—clenched jaw, tight shoulders, gripping the bedrail. As you speak your farewell, allow your body to gradually release and soften, letting gravity pull you down into the chair, your hands opening, your breath deepening. Start with words caught in your throat, fighting to maintain composure, and end in a state of profound physical and emotional release—exhausted, surrendered, but strangely lighter. Let your body tell the story of someone learning to let go by literally letting go of the physical armor they've been carrying.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You're standing in the shower, and the water temperature suddenly triggers a physical memory—maybe the heat of summer asphalt, or cold lake water, or someone's feverish skin against yours, or the burn of rope, or the weight of a child in your arms. Let your body respond first: breath changes, muscles tense or release, skin prickles. Then let images cascade from this physical sensation without censoring them—speak them aloud if they come as words, or simply breathe and move if they stay wordless. Don't explain or narrate; just let one sensation lead to another, even if they seem unconnected. Maybe scalding water becomes your mother's anger becomes the sun on your wedding day becomes shame becomes desire. Let the physical sensations drive the emotional journey. Begin with the shock of temperature and end somewhere emotionally unexpected, your body having remembered something your mind had forgotten.

title: Confronting Your Parent at the Memory Care Facility
instruction: You're visiting your aging parent who has lucid moments between confusion. Start with careful gentleness, then build into a confrontation you've held back for decades - about their emotional absence, their choices that wounded you. Your voice should rise with anger that's been buried for years: 'You were never there when I needed you.' But mid-fury, they look at you with such bewildered hurt that your rage collapses. They don't remember what you're talking about. You're left holding anger that has nowhere to go, speaking to someone who's already half-gone. End with devastating tenderness, whispering 'I forgive you' to someone who doesn't even remember what they did. The performance should feel like punching smoke - all that pain with no place to land it.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hour. For your entire life, they withheld approval, warmth, and the words 'I love you.' Start from a place of decades of accumulated hurt, rage at all the birthday parties they missed, the harsh criticisms, the coldness. Let that lifetime of anger live in your body. But as you watch them struggle for breath, something breaks open—transform into desperate, aching need to hear those words before it's too late, then into tender forgiveness mixed with grief. Speak to them. Beg them. Forgive them. Say goodbye to both the parent you needed and the parent you had. Let your voice move from bitter confrontation to whispered benediction.
inspired_by: The character is emotionally extreme (volatile, irrational, rageful) and the actor needs a large emotional foundation

title: Hiding a Panic Attack in a Meeting
instruction: You're giving a quarterly presentation when a panic attack ambushes you. Maintain the professional cadence while hyperventilation tries to take over. Your voice should sound slightly too fast, slightly too high, with controlled pauses that are actually desperate attempts to breathe. Hands are shaking — audible paper rattling. The audience can't know. Include the internal monologue ('You're fine, you're fine, just breathe') threaded under the professional delivery.

title: Tasting Joy in the Ruins
instruction: You're eating something utterly simple—bread, fruit, something you managed to find or make—in the aftermath of loss. Your life has fallen apart: divorce, death, catastrophic change, dreams destroyed. Begin with surprised laughter, almost inappropriate, as you realize this simple food still tastes good, that your body still responds with pleasure even as your heart is in pieces. Let this contradiction wash over you: speaking with genuine delight about flavors while tears stream down your face, finding yourself grateful for this small mercy while simultaneously grieving everything you've lost. Your voice should dance between wonder and sorrow, chuckling and choking, marveling at the absurdity that you can feel both devastated and alive at once. End with a profound, tearful acceptance: that this is what survival looks like—finding beauty in simplicity while carrying unbearable weight, tasting sweetness while salted with tears.
inspired_by: Eating Freshly Baked Cookies Right Out of the Oven

title: Dancing Alone in Your Old Bedroom
instruction: You've returned to your childhood bedroom after years away, and a song comes on—the one that defined a moment of pure freedom or heartbreak from your youth. Begin moving to it wildly, letting your body fully express the energy, the rebellion, the sensuality, or the rage you felt back then. Let the movement be huge, uninhibited, even absurd—jumping on the bed, spinning, laughing or growling. But mid-dance, a memory hits you with physical force: something you lost, someone who's gone, a version of yourself that no longer exists. Feel your wild movement transform into something slower, more desperate, your breath becoming sobs even as you keep moving. End collapsed on the floor, your body still swaying slightly, laughing and crying simultaneously at who you were and who you've become.

title: The Rage That Breaks Open Into Grief
instruction: You're confronting someone who failed to protect someone you love, or who caused irreparable harm. Begin with white-hot fury - your voice sharp, cutting, uncompromising. Demand answers. Demand accountability. But underneath the rage is devastating loss, and as you speak, the anger begins to fracture. Let your voice crack not with weakness but with the terrible weight of what's been lost. The fury should collapse into something more primal - the helplessness of not being able to fix what's broken, the agony of loving someone you couldn't save. Move between explosive anger and broken-hearted sobbing. End not with resolution but with the terrible contradiction of still needing this person to understand while knowing nothing they say can make it right.
inspired_by: Staying Composed While Receiving Unfair Criticism

title: Confronting Authority
instruction: You're confronting someone in a position of authority about unfair treatment. Your voice is nervous but determined: 'I need to talk to you about what happened.' You're explaining the situation, trying to stay calm. Your voice wavers when they dismiss you: 'But I...' You're standing your ground, your voice becoming stronger: 'That wasn't right, and you know it.' By the end, you've either been heard or you've realized power dynamics make change impossible.

title: The Downpour
instruction: You're standing in a sudden rainstorm, and something about the physical shock of the cold water triggers a release you've been holding back for months. Begin physically tense, trying to stay in control as the rain soaks through your clothes. Then let the sensation overwhelm you—the cold, the wet, the way the rain pounds against your skin. Allow your body to respond: maybe you start laughing, or screaming, or both. Let physical sensation unlock emotional release. You're furious at someone who betrayed you, but underneath that rage is devastating hurt. Speak to them as if they're standing before you, letting the rain wash away your filters. Let your voice rise and break, let your body shake from cold and from feeling. Move from rigid control to wild release, from rage to grief, from fighting the rain to surrendering to it, until you're emptied out and gasping.

title: Breathiness Vulnerability
instruction: You're a writer reading your debut novel at a bookstore — the protagonist is based on your real life trauma. Your voice starts breathy, uncertain, as you read: 'She couldn't tell anyone what happened.' The breathiness isn't a technique; it's your nervous system reliving the story as you speak it. You pause frequently to breathe, and the pauses become part of the performance. Other people in the crowd begin to understand they're not hearing polished delivery — they're hearing someone barely holding it together. By the end of the passage, your breathing is almost hyperventilation. You stop reading and just breathe for five seconds. 'That's the scene that cost me two years of therapy to write.' The vulnerability is in the breath itself.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're standing in the rain after a devastating betrayal, and your whole body is alive with physical sensation—cold water on your skin, shaking muscles, ragged breathing, adrenaline coursing through you. Don't perform 'heartbreak' or 'rage.' Instead, start by genuinely registering your actual physical state right now: the real temperature of your skin, the authentic quality of your breath, the true tension or release in your muscles. From that physical truth, let emotion arise organically. Maybe the cold triggers unexpected fury, or the shaking releases into wild laughter, or physical exhaustion cracks you open to sobbing, or the adrenaline transforms into fierce determination. Let your body lead you through an emotional journey, but every sensation must be real—no manufactured trembling or performed tears. The physical and emotional must be genuinely connected.
inspired_by: Actor is preparing for a scene but not starting from real BEING — instead manufacturing a performance state

title: Thanking Your Abuser for Finally Setting You Free
instruction: You're face-to-face with someone who hurt you deeply—and you're genuinely thanking them. Begin with words of gratitude that sound almost surreal: thanking them for abandoning you, betraying you, breaking you, because it forced you to rebuild yourself stronger. Your voice carries strange lightness, even laughter, as you recount the painful moments. But underneath, your breath is unsteady. As you continue, let the complexity emerge: you're both grateful for who you've become and grieving what they took from you. The gratitude is real, but so is the pain. By the end, you're smiling through tears, laughing while your voice breaks, finding genuine peace while simultaneously feeling the full weight of what you survived. Let the contradictions coexist naturally—this isn't forgiveness or bitterness, but something more complicated and human: holding both freedom and sorrow in the same breath.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Resistance Leader Realizes the Revolution Is Being Co-Opted

title: The Absurd Aftermath
instruction: You are an older man who has just spent an hour sobbing after a painful argument with your daughter. Now you’re collapsed on the couch, voice raw, nose stuffed, eyes swollen. A friend brings you a glass of water, and you try to speak — but the first sound that comes out is a weak, hoarse laugh. You start to tell them how your daughter’s cat knocked over a framed photo right in the middle of your crying, and you couldn’t even be angry — you just laughed through the snot. At first, you’re barely able to get the words out, voice cracking and fading, but as you recount the absurdity, genuine amusement flickers in. Then you tease yourself, calling yourself a pathetic old fool, but the helplessness is still there — a wry, exhausted surrender. Let your voice be raw, breathy, sometimes a whisper; let the laugh catch in your throat; let the words trail off as you lose them and find them again. End with a quiet, choked chuckle that says you’re done fighting.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (very intensely present), Helplessness (extremely present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Acceptance Letter
instruction: You are holding an acceptance letter to your dream program—the opportunity you've sacrificed everything for. But you're reading it aloud to your partner who gave up their own dreams to support yours, and you've just discovered they've been diagnosed with an illness that will require you to stay. Feel the exact weight and texture of the paper in your shaking hands, see the specific words of congratulation, let yourself experience the physical sensation of your dream becoming real even as it dies. Your voice begins with pure elation as you read the first lines—let genuine joy ring through. But as you continue reading and glance at your partner's face, let the joy curdle into something unbearably complex. End in a place where you're simultaneously laughing and crying, where gratitude for their love wars with rage at the timing, where achievement and sacrifice become impossible to separate. You must genuinely feel both the soaring triumph and the crushing loss at once.

title: Laughing Through the Ruins of Everything
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your home after the fire, the flood, the disaster—everything you owned is gone. Start by genuinely laughing at the absurdity: of course the photo albums survived but not the photos, of course this happened right after you finally felt stable. Let the laughter be real, almost manic, as you catalog the ridiculous details. But weave in moments where the laughter catches, becomes something else, where gratitude that you're alive tangles with grief for what's lost. Your voice should dance between genuine humor and breaking, between 'we're going to be okay' and 'I don't know how.' End in that strange space where laughing and crying sound identical, thanking the universe for your life while mourning everything in it, finding bizarre peace in having nothing left to lose.

title: Three A.M. Truths
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying in the dark next to someone you love, speaking in barely audible whispers. Begin by confessing something small, almost trivial—a minor deception or hidden thought. Your voice should be cautious, testing the waters. As they respond with acceptance or their own small truth, feel permission building inside you to go deeper. Let each revelation pull you further into vulnerability until you're whispering the thing you've never told anyone—the fear, desire, or memory you've carried alone. Your breathing should become part of the performance. By the end, you should be speaking from a place of complete emotional nakedness, your whispered words carrying the weight of absolute trust, your voice trembling not with fear but with the relief of being fully known.

title: Storm Breaking Over Skin
instruction: You're in the aftermath of a fierce argument with your lover, both of you breathing hard, faces flushed. You're across the room from each other, and suddenly you really look at them—their chest heaving, sweat on their neck, the exact shade their face turns when they're angry. Your body is still flooded with adrenaline, rage coursing through you. Begin by examining them with hostile intensity, breathing audibly, letting guttural sounds escape. But as you keep staring, really studying every detail of their face and body, let the anger begin to transform. Notice something that breaks through your fury—the tremble in their lip, the fear in their eyes, the vulnerability beneath their defensive stance. Let sounds of rage slowly mix with sounds of desire, frustration bleeding into desperate need. Build from hostile silence through growls and gasps to words that tumble out—shifting from accusations to raw, physical declarations of need, anger transforming into fierce, complicated wanting.
inspired_by: Looking for Things About the Other Person You Have Never Noticed Before

title: The Last Thread
instruction: You are an elderly woman, a retired seamstress, who has been stabbed in a robbery attempt in your own home. You are bleeding heavily from a wound in your side, and you’ve crawled to the phone to call for help. At first, you are fiercely focused, trying to stay calm and give the address clearly, but as the blood loss deepens, your voice starts to fade, your thoughts slip away mid-sentence, and you feel the cold shivers taking over. Begin with a strained, determined concentration, pushing through the pain to speak, then let your voice soften, slow, and drift as you lose your grip on consciousness. Let a faint tremor of distress creep in, but keep it secondary—your main battle is to stay present and hold onto the thread of your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Shower Confession
instruction: You're a teenager in a tiled bathroom, standing under the warm spray of the shower. The steam clouds the mirror, and the reverberant echo makes your voice feel bigger than it is. You start by humming a tune, then catch yourself, realizing you're alone and no one can hear you. Let your voice drift from casual humming into a tentative, whispered confession about a crush, as if testing the sound of your own words in the safe, echoey space. The interest you feel grows from playful curiosity to a vulnerable, quiet thrill as the water continues to fall.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Thunderstorm Reunion
instruction: You're standing in the rain, finally face-to-face with someone you've desired and resented in equal measure—an ex-lover, perhaps, or someone who betrayed you but whom you never stopped wanting. Your whole body is tight with contradictory impulses: to strike them, to kiss them, to run. Begin by trying to maintain physical distance and emotional control, arms crossed, jaw clenched, voice hard. But you're also cold, soaked, and the proximity is doing something to your nervous system. Let the shivering from the cold merge with the trembling from emotion. Let your attempt to stay rigid start to break down as your body's need for warmth conflicts with your need to stay defended. End with a physical and emotional surrender—not necessarily gentle or romantic, but raw and real, where all that pent-up tension explodes into something uncontrolled: passion, rage-tinged embrace, or collapse.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 4 AM. They're asleep beside you. You're leaving—not because the love is gone, but because staying will destroy you both, or because you're ill, or because you've made an impossible choice. Whisper everything you can't say when they're awake. Start with the tiny things you'll miss—how they breathe, the sound of their keys in the door, the specific way they say your name. Your voice is barely audible, thick with tears you're swallowing. Tell them why you're going, stumbling over words, your throat closing. Confess the truth: that you're terrified, that leaving them is the hardest thing you've ever done, that you're not sure you're strong enough but you have to be. Touch their face one last time. End with 'I love you' said so quietly it's almost just breath—tender, shattered, and absolutely true. Then silence as you pull away.
inspired_by: Phone Call with Your Younger Self

title: The Hospital Room Door
instruction: You're standing outside your father's hospital room. He has hours left, maybe less. For years, you've rehearsed what you'd say—about the disappointments, the silences, the times he wasn't there. But now, as you prepare to walk through that door, something shifts. Begin speaking to him as if he's right there in front of you, starting with the anger and hurt you've carried. Let his imagined responses—perhaps a look in his eyes, a weak gesture, the way he might say your name—change what comes out of your mouth. By the end, discover what you actually need to say to him before he's gone. The emotion that arrives at the end should surprise you—it should not be what you planned when you started speaking.

title: Confronting Your Mother in Her Kitchen
instruction: You've come home after years away to tell your mother that you needed her protection as a child and she wasn't there. Start with small talk—commenting on her new curtains, the smell of her cooking—your body language careful, voice falsely bright. Slowly, the real reason surfaces: 'Why didn't you stop him? You knew.' Let anger build, but mix it with the child's voice underneath, the one still asking 'Mommy, why?' Your fury should crack open into something more devastating—the little kid who just wanted their mother to choose them. End not with resolution but with exhausted honesty: 'I just needed you to see me.' Move from performance to raw truth, from accusation to the vulnerable need beneath it.
inspired_by: Giving Birth While Arguing with Your Mother-in-Law

title: The Unsaid Goodbye at the Hospital Window
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your closest friend who is dying, but you've spent your whole life deflecting deep feelings with humor and practicality. Begin by trying to keep things light, making plans for 'when you get better,' talking about mundane things. But as you speak, let yourself feel the crushing weight of what you're actually avoiding—the terror, the grief, the love you've never voiced. Your challenge is to notice when you're deflecting (joking, changing subject, talking about weather) and let the real, raw emotion crack through despite your instinct to protect yourself. By the end, you must speak one brutally honest truth you've never said aloud, letting your voice break if it needs to. The journey is from false cheerfulness to devastating honesty.
inspired_by: Actor is redirecting authentic impulses into more comfortable emotional expressions, creating a split between what is felt and what is expressed

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at the wedding reception of someone you once loved—or still love—watching them marry someone else. You're supposed to give a toast celebrating their happiness. Stand with glass raised, begin with the expected words of congratulations and joy—and mean them, because part of you genuinely is happy for them. But let everything else that's true exist simultaneously: grief that it's not you standing beside them, gratitude for what you once shared, anger at how it ended, relief that you're free, nostalgia for who you both were, fear that you'll never feel that way again, wonder at how you can feel so much at once. Don't resolve these contradictions or choose one emotion over another—let them coexist and transform each other. Your voice might crack with tears while you're smiling. You might laugh while your heart breaks. By the end, you've somehow honored both the authentic joy for their future and the authentic loss of your own past with them.

title: Bedside Confession to the Sleeping Beloved
instruction: You're sitting by the hospital bed of someone you love deeply—a partner, a best friend—who's in a coma after an accident. The doctors say they might hear you. You start talking quietly, almost afraid to disturb them, saying ordinary things: 'I brought your favorite flowers. The nurses are so kind here.' But the longer you sit in this terrible quiet, the more the unsaid things rise up. Your voice drops to a whisper, catching on words you've never been brave enough to say: 'I never told you how much I—' and you have to stop, breathe. You confess the small fears, the daily gratitudes you took for granted, the future you'd imagined together. 'Please don't leave me' comes out broken, barely audible. End with your voice so soft it's almost not there, saying tender, specific things—the way they laugh, the coffee they make, the particular warmth of their hand in yours—as if naming these details could anchor them to life. Let silence be part of the performance.

title: Counting Steps in an Empty House
instruction: You're alone, whispering to yourself as you pace through the rooms of a home your partner just moved out of, your fitness tracker on your wrist still counting. Start quietly, almost numbly, narrating your steps through spaces filled with absence—their empty closet, the kitchen where you cooked together, the couch where you planned your future. Your voice should be thin, fragile, catching on certain words as memories ambush you. Describe hitting your step goal for the day, and let that mundane achievement crack something open inside you—a quiet, devastated laugh that turns into tears. End in a whisper, standing still finally, admitting that all this movement was just trying to outrun the silence. Let the performance feel like overhearing someone's heart breaking in private.

title: The Last Words I'll Ever Say to You
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone you've loved your entire life, and they're slipping away. You begin trying to find the perfect words, something worthy of this final moment—formal, careful, almost rehearsed. But halfway through, the pretense shatters. The carefully chosen words fail you. Your voice breaks into something raw and desperate. You abandon trying to make this moment beautiful or meaningful and just beg them not to go. Tell them the small, stupid things you'll miss. The sound of their laugh. How they made coffee. By the end, you're not trying to create a perfect goodbye—you're just a person losing someone, speaking through tears, your voice barely a whisper, saying 'I'm not ready' over and over.

title: Everything I Never Said
instruction: You are confronting your father/mother/grown child about a betrayal or abandonment that shaped your life. Start by checking in with the actual sensations in your body right now - trembling, heat, tightness, emptiness. As you speak, let yourself notice and name what's really moving through you moment by moment: 'I feel rage... no, wait, I feel small... I feel like I'm twelve again... I feel powerful... I feel afraid of my own anger.' Don't perform anger or pain - instead, discover it as you go, following each feeling into the next. When you notice yourself trying to make an impression or sound a certain way, pause and ask yourself what you're actually experiencing right now beneath that impulse. By the end, let the confrontation transform as you track where your real feelings lead, perhaps to grief, perhaps to unexpected tenderness, perhaps to cold clarity.

title: Acting Happy for Someone When Youre Heartbroken
instruction: Someone shares joyful news that reminds you of your own heartbreak. Internally, youre saddened, but you smile and express happiness for them. Describe the ache inside while projecting genuine joy. Speak with a warm, cheerful tone, concealing your own pain.

title: Breaking the China
instruction: You are confronting your mother in her pristine kitchen, where nothing is ever out of place, where you've always been told to be careful, quiet, small. But today you've discovered a lie that's shaped your entire life. Begin with your voice controlled, tight, standing rigidly still as you ask her a simple question. As the truth unfolds and she deflects, let your body betray you - pace, gesture wildly, maybe grab a teacup and hurl it against the wall. Your physical movement must grow increasingly uncontained, reckless, taking up space you were never allowed to claim. Let your rage be athletic, expansive - knock over a chair, sweep dishes aside, move through the space like you're claiming territory in battle. End physically spent but vocally clear, standing in the wreckage, finally taking up all the room you deserve. Transform from compressed tension to explosive physical liberation.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've been given three months to live, and you're recording a message for your best friend to watch after you're gone. Start by trying to make them laugh—share an absurd memory, an inside joke, your voice warm with mischief. But as you laugh, tears come. You can't stop the laughter or the crying; they're tangled together. Your voice breaks on a joke, then steadies on something profound, then cracks again on something ridiculous. Express gratitude for every stupid thing you did together while your heart is shattering. Find joy in the midst of devastating loss—laugh at death while acknowledging its terror. End with your voice full of contradictions: grateful and grieving, peaceful and raging against the dying of the light, finding something absurdly funny even as you say goodbye forever.
inspired_by: Recovery: Choosing Yourself Over the Addiction

title: Whispered Comfort at 3 AM
instruction: You're gently waking your partner from a nightmare, offering them a croissant you quietly warmed. Speak in an intimate whisper, describing the pastry's warmth and comfort with profound tenderness. Your voice should be barely above a breath, as if too much volume might shatter this fragile moment of peace. Let sadness seep through your gentleness—you know why they have nightmares, and your heart breaks that something so simple is the best comfort you can offer. End with your voice catching on words like 'safe' and 'here,' the inadequacy of a croissant against their pain mixing with desperate hope that your presence means something. Make every word a soft touch in the darkness.

title: A Gift Received
instruction: You are a teenage girl, alone with a partner you trust more than anyone. This is your first time, and the intensity builds until your body takes over—rhythmic breathing turns to gasps, involuntary moans escape, and your voice loses all control. As the peak approaches, a massive wave of gratitude crashes through you: thankfulness for their tenderness, for this moment, for being seen. Let your words be broken, pushed out between spasms of breath, as you cling to them and whisper 'thank you' over and over, the sound raw and real. title: The Lake's Revenge
instruction: You are a child treading water in a cold, murky lake, head just above the surface. title: The Last Dance in the Hospital Room
instruction: You are at your partner's hospital bedside on their final night. title: The Last Words Before the Ship Leaves
instruction: You are saying goodbye to someone you love deeply - a partner, parent, or child - who is boarding a colony ship to another planet, a journey from which they will never return. title: The Last Breath Between Us
instruction: You are holding the hand of someone you love deeply as they take their final breaths. Begin in shock and denial, unable to accept what's happening. title: The Veterinarian Mercy-Killing Her Own Dog While It Comforts Her
instruction: You're a veterinarian preparing the injection that will euthanize your own dog, who's been your companion through your divorce, your father's death, every loss. title: Laughing and Weeping in the Grass After Receiving Impossible News

title: The Last Thing I Need to Say

title: The Burn of Cold Water
instruction: You've just run five miles in freezing rain after discovering your partner's betrayal. You burst into your apartment, soaked, shaking, your skin burning with cold. title: Your Abusive Ex Trying to Reconcile
instruction: They're saying they've changed. Your voice is locked down, professional: 'I don't think that's a good idea.' But they're pulling on your history and attachment. title: The Last Tour Before the Demolition
instruction: You're giving one final tour of the neighborhood where you grew up, now slated for demolition tomorrow. title: The Secret I've Carried
instruction: You're confessing something to your closest friend that you've hidden for years—maybe that you've been in love with them, or that you're leaving forever, or that you've been carrying guilt over something you did. title: The Masked Joy
instruction: You are an older man sitting alone in a hospital waiting room, wearing a surgical mask. The room is quiet, save for the hum of a vending machine. title: The Last Goodbye at the Spaceport
instruction: You're watching your child board a one-way mission to a distant colony—a journey of no return.
