title: Ex's New Partner Asking Your Relationship Advice
instruction: Your ex's new partner pulls you aside genuinely asking for advice. Start guarded and professional, but as you realize you have real wisdom here, something shifts. title: The Last Words You Never Rehearsed
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hour. He's awake, barely. You came prepared to say something meaningful, maybe even rehearsed it. title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You're standing outside in a downpour after receiving devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, a shattering revelation. Spin, leap, collapse to your knees, reach your arms to the sky. Let the rain become a catalyst for physical and emotional release. Your voice should evolve from silent shock to primal sound—gasps, cries, perhaps even laughter mixed with sobs. The physical sensation of water, of movement, of your body in space breaks through your paralysis. Transform from frozen numbness to wild, animal-like expression of raw feeling. title: Whispering to Your Younger Self: The Confession You Can Never Take Back

title: The Last Letter

instruction: You are a child treading water in a deep lake, left alone by a sibling who pushed you in. You begin shouting angrily, demanding they help. title: Gratitude at the Goodbye Touch
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone dying—your grandmother, your best friend, your first love—and they've just reached out to touch your face one last time. title: The aftermath of the alley

title: Gravity of Intimacy
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner, whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something about your past, a fear, or a truth about yourself. title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father after decades of unspoken pain. title: From Droning to Wonder

title: The Weight of Letting Go
instruction: You're lying beside your partner of thirty years in their final hours. As you talk, feel exhaustion slowly overtaking you—the weight of months of caretaking, sleepless nights, and grief pressing down on your chest, your limbs, your voice. Let your words become heavier, slower, as acceptance settles into your bones like lead. By the end, you're so heavy you can barely lift your hand to touch their face one last time, and your goodbye comes out as barely a whisper—not from weakness, but from the profound heaviness of surrender. The tension of fighting releases into the gravity of inevitability.

title: The Breaking Point Confession
instruction: You're a parent who just received the call that your teenage child attempted suicide. You're in the hospital corridor, and you've called your own parent—the one who made you feel invisible your whole childhood. Start with rage that's been building for thirty years: 'You want to know why I never visit? Why I never let you babysit?' Your voice is shaking with fury as you list every moment they failed you. But mid-accusation, something explodes—you break down completely. The rage shatters into raw terror and helplessness: 'My baby tried to die and I didn't see it coming, just like you never saw me.' Now you're sobbing, but you're also begging them for something you've never asked for: 'Tell me how to save my child. Tell me how not to be you. Please, I'm so scared.' End with a broken whisper that contains both fury and desperate need: 'I still need a mother. Even now. Especially now.'

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Former Self
instruction: You're standing at a milestone—recovery, transition, transformation—looking back at who you used to be. Begin with gentle, almost amused recognition: 'I remember you...' There's affection in your voice as you acknowledge your former self's struggles, the way they tried so hard with the tools they had. But then let grief enter as you realize you have to let that version of yourself go completely to move forward. Your voice wavers between gratitude and heartbreak: 'Thank you for surviving...' You're laughing softly through tears as you recall the absurd, painful, beautiful moments that brought you here. The laughter fades into something more tender as you tell your old self 'You can rest now. I've got it from here.' End with a voice full of bittersweet peace—honoring the past while releasing it, finding strength in the grief of transformation, speaking with profound love for someone who no longer exists but made everything possible.

title: The Splitting Weight
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a naturally gentle, refined voice, but today you are alone in your backyard, chopping firewood that your neighbor’s grunting son always did for you until he stopped coming around. Between swings, you mutter to yourself. Start with a quiet, weary sadness—your arms ache, the wood is wet, and you feel invisible. As you keep missing the log, let a flicker of impatience and irritability creep into your huffs and muttered complaints. Then, when a clean split finally comes, a sharp pang of jealousy slips out: you envy that neighbor’s son for his strength, his youth, his freedom from this heavy, lonely work. By the end, your voice has dropped its polite veneer—raw, winded, and unmasked—as you confess the truth you’d never say to anyone: you wish you had what he has.

title: Echoes of Resentment
instruction: You are a teenage boy trapped in a dark cave with your older brother's girlfriend after a rockfall. The walls drip and boom around you, distorting every breath. You start by forcing a tough, controlled voice—denying your fear—but the jealousy you've buried for years leaks out in the silence between echoes. Let your voice crack and shift as you confess, 'He gets everything.' The distress and embarrassment rise until your final words hang in the reverb, raw and unguarded.

title: The Concert That Couldn't Hear Me
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy who is hard of hearing, speaking to your hearing best friend about saving up for tickets to a band you both love. You start excited, voice loud and slow, words exaggerated for lip-reading—your hope is huge, you can feel the bass already. Halfway through, your friend's phone buzzes and they glance at it; you see their mouth say 'maybe later' but not really look at you. That flicker of contempt—toward them, toward the world that doesn't wait for you—tightens your throat. By the end, you're still speaking at the same volume, but your optimism deflates into helplessness; the words drag heavier, your eyes drop to your shoes, and you lose your train of thought for a second before forcing the sentence to finish.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Lie
instruction: You've just discovered evidence that your mother knew about your father's affair the entire time you were growing up—while you blamed yourself for their tension. You call her, and your voice is shaking with betrayal: 'I found the letters. All of them. From 1998.' She starts to deflect, and you cut her off, your voice rising with years of misdirected shame: 'I thought it was my fault. I thought I made you both miserable.' She's crying now, trying to explain, and your anger suddenly fractures into something more complex. Your voice breaks, becomes almost tender despite the rage: 'Why didn't you just tell me the truth? I was your daughter.' By the end, you're both crying, and you realize you're not just angry—you're grieving the mother-daughter relationship you could have had if she'd trusted you with the truth. Your final words are barely audible, a mix of forgiveness beginning and the recognition that some damage can't be undone: 'I need time. I don't know how much, but... I need time.'

title: The Last Morning Coffee
instruction: You're making coffee for your partner on their final morning before entering hospice care. Start with determined cheerfulness—keeping everything normal, narrating the ritual like any other day. But as you describe adding the exact amount of cream they love, something cracks. Your voice begins to tremble. By the time you're setting the cup down, you're whispering how you've memorized every detail of this routine, how you'll keep making two cups anyway. End with a confession: you're not ready, but you're grateful for every single morning you had. Let the everyday become sacred, let gratitude and devastation live in the same breath.

title: Counting Freckles at 3 AM
instruction: You're lying beside someone in the dark hours of early morning, tracing their features with your fingertips, and you begin to whisper something you've kept hidden. Start in a state of tender, peaceful intimacy—simply being with them, feeling safe in the darkness. As you begin to speak, let yourself be genuinely curious about what wants to come out of your mouth, rather than controlling it. The confession that emerges might be a fear, a secret desire, a shameful memory, or a realization about yourself you've been avoiding. Let your voice stay soft but let the emotional current underneath intensify—move from peaceful safety into trembling vulnerability, into a fragile kind of hope or terror. By the end, you've revealed something that changes the silence between you. The intimacy is deeper but more frightening now.

title: The Final Organ Chord
instruction: You stand alone in the center of a vast, empty stone cathedral. The last note of the organ has just faded, leaving a deep, humming silence that presses against your chest. Your son’s wedding was an hour ago—he is gone now, beginning his own life—and the ecstasy of seeing him so happy is still a warm ache in your throat. But as you look up at the vaulted ceiling, a wave of quiet distress rises: the pews are empty, your wife is no longer beside you, and for the first time you feel how hollow this beautiful space can be. Let your voice start full and slow, savoring the rapture, but let it drift into a hesitant, almost swallowed grief as you realize you’re the one who has to walk out alone. Feel the stone’s reverberation around each word—pause when the echo swallows you, shift your weight, let your gaze drop mid-sentence, then look up again as if searching for a lost note.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: Your child is asleep. You're leaving—not because you want to, but because staying puts them in danger. This is the last time you'll see them. Speak barely above a whisper, your voice thick with unshed tears. Tell them everything you need them to know: how brave they are, how the scar on their knee came from teaching them to ride a bike, how their laugh sounds like music. Your voice should be so tender it hurts, breaking on certain words but trying desperately to stay quiet so they don't wake. Midway, let yourself almost lose control—a sob you have to swallow. End with 'Mommy/Daddy loves you' repeated like a prayer, your voice cracking into nothing. This isn't dramatic—it's intimate devastation, a heart breaking in silence.
inspired_by: Forgiving Someone and Meaning It Completely

title: Rainfall Breaking
instruction: You're standing in your kitchen after receiving news—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a sudden loss—something that changes everything. Start in shock, numb, mechanically making tea or washing a dish. Your body knows before your mind. Feel your hands start to shake. The physical sensation builds: your chest tightens, breath shortens, then something in your body breaks. This isn't elegant grief—let yourself become physical with it. Brace against the counter, sink to the floor, whatever your body demands. Midway through this physical release, feel a memory surface—of the last time you felt safe, or loved, or whole. The physical pain now carries this double weight: what you've lost and the visceral memory of what you once had. End with your body quieting, spent, but your breathing different—slower, deeper, like you've survived something and your body knows it even if your mind doesn't yet.

title: Bedtime Tremors
instruction: You are a mother, physically spent after a long day, your muscles shaking from exhaustion as you try to tuck your child into bed. Your voice trembles with a fast, involuntary vibrato; your jaw and neck shake, making words wobble. As you speak, let that irritation dissolve into emotional numbness, a detached monotone where the quivering body becomes disconnected from feeling. Your words are short, almost automatic, as if your body is running on empty while your mind checks out.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)

title: Whispering the Truce
instruction: It's past midnight. Your business partner and oldest friend sits across from you after the worst fight of your twenty-year partnership. You're both financially ruined, and you've blamed each other for months. Begin barely audible, your voice hollowed out by weeks of not sleeping: 'I can't do this anymore. The fighting.' Let silence hang heavy. When you say 'You were right about some of it,' your voice should catch, vulnerable in a way you've never allowed yourself to be. Move through shame, tenderness, and bone-deep exhaustion. End with 'I don't want to lose you too,' spoken so softly it's almost a confession to yourself. This isn't about the business anymore—it's about realizing you're about to lose the person who knows you best.

title: Dancing in the Kitchen While Your World Falls Apart
instruction: You're swaying to music in your kitchen, a ritual that once brought pure joy, but everything has just collapsed around you—a divorce, a death, a dream destroyed. Begin by describing the movement, the familiar rhythm, and you're actually laughing, genuinely finding small pockets of lightness in the motion. But woven through your laughter should be the unmistakable thread of grief. Let joy and devastation exist simultaneously in your voice—you're laughing and crying, finding beauty in this moment while everything else burns. Your words should dance between gratitude for this small grace and acknowledgment of the enormous loss. The emotional complexity should be dizzying: peace and chaos, acceptance and protest, love for life even as it breaks you. End with a sound that could be either laughter or a sob, or both at once, finding something like freedom in letting opposite truths coexist.
inspired_by: Feeling the First Gentle Snowflakes Land on Your Face

title: Sending Your Parent Into Memory Care
instruction: You're helping your parent settle into their memory care room on their first day. Start with forced cheerfulness—'Look, Mom, they have a garden you can see from the window!'—your voice bright but brittle, working so hard to make this okay. But your parent doesn't recognize you today. They keep asking for their own mother, long dead. Your voice begins to fracture as you realize this might be the last conversation where any part of them knows who you are. You're trying to explain who you are—'It's me, it's your daughter'—but your voice is dissolving. End with you sitting on the edge of their bed, holding their hand, your voice barely a whisper as you tell them you love them, knowing they'll forget this moment. The grief is for losing them while they're still alive. Your voice carries the weight of a goodbye that will repeat itself every day.

title: The Wedding Toast for Your Ex
instruction: You're giving a toast at the wedding of someone you once loved deeply—someone you thought you'd marry—who's now marrying someone else. Begin with genuine joy—allow sensory fragments of their happiness to move through you: their radiant smile today, their laughter, the beauty of this moment. Your first words are warm, celebratory, and real. But as you continue speaking, let contrasting sensory images begin bleeding through: flashes of their smile once directed at only you, the ghost feeling of their hand in yours, specific moments of your shared past—intimate, tender, lost. Don't perform sadness or jealousy. Simply let these two streams of sensory reality exist simultaneously: the genuine joy you feel for them NOW and the aching loss of what WAS. Your voice should carry both, your face should show both, until by the end your toast becomes something heartbreakingly complex—true happiness braided inseparably with true grief. Let the collision of these sensory streams create something authentic and devastating.
inspired_by: A scene requires an emotional transition between two distinct states at a specific moment

title: The Wedding Morning Mirror
instruction: You're alone on the morning of your wedding, looking at yourself in the mirror, and you're flooded with opposing truths. Begin by simply observing yourself without judgment, genuinely curious about what you see and feel. As you start to speak to your reflection, let yourself be irreverent with your own expected emotions. You might start with joy and excitement but let doubt creep in. Let yourself say you're terrified while laughing. Express deep love while admitting resentment. Feel gratitude laced with grief for the life you're leaving behind. Don't try to reconcile these contradictions or land on 'the right feeling'—let them coexist and war with each other in your voice and body. Move through multiple emotional territories rapidly, messily. By the end, arrive at a complex, unresolved state that holds multiple truths at once—you're about to walk forward into this commitment carrying all of it.

title: Denial Before Grief
instruction: Someone has just told you that a loved one has died. Your voice is immediately defensive: 'No. No, that's wrong.' You're in denial, your voice sharp, almost angry. 'You must be mistaken.' But they're sure. Your voice becomes questioning, almost childlike: 'But... how?' You're asking for details as if the details matter. Then it hits—the reality. Your voice stops. You're sitting down. Your voice when you speak again is fundamentally changed, broken, forever altered by grief.

title: The Moment You Realize Your Child Doesn't Recognize You
instruction: You're recovering from an accident, and your young child enters the room. Start with fierce, protective love—'Baby, come here, it's okay'—reaching for them. But they shrink back, afraid. Let confusion turn to panic: 'No, no, sweetheart, it's me, it's Mama/Papa.' Your voice should crack as you try different pet names, inside jokes, anything to spark recognition. Build to explosive desperation—you'd tear the world apart to fix this—then collapse into helpless, choking sobs as they ask for their 'real' parent. End in a whisper, singing the lullaby you always sang, your voice breaking on every note, offering the only proof you have left. Let protective fury dissolve into the most profound powerlessness, mixed with stubborn, aching love that refuses to quit.
inspired_by: Waking Up and Not Knowing Who You Are

title: The Town Crier's Joy
instruction: You are at a crowded town square, standing on a wooden crate, tasked with shouting a personal announcement to everyone. You're deeply embarrassed—your voice cracks as you force the words out, elongating vowels to carry. But as you shout that you've been accepted into the royal choir (the dream you've hidden for years), ecstasy floods through you. Let your voice transform: start hesitant and strained, then grow into a full-throated, trembling cry of joy. Pause between each phrase as if catching your breath, drop some consonants naturally, and let the pleasure overpower your shame by the end. Speak 40–80 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Surgeon's Hands Won't Stop Shaking
instruction: You're prepping for what should be a routine surgery, talking your team through the procedure with the confidence of thirty years' experience. But your hands are trembling—not from nerves, from something deeper, something you've been denying for months. You continue giving clear, steady instructions while internally spiraling, knowing these shaking hands that have saved hundreds of lives might now end a career, an identity. Your voice stays surgical, precise, but there's a tremor underneath—not of fear exactly, but of grief for who you were yesterday. By the end, you're asking your resident to take over with a dignity that barely conceals devastation. The professional mask cracks just enough to reveal the human underneath, terrified and suddenly mortal.

title: The Last Call
instruction: You're a teenager, bleeding heavily from a deep cut on your thigh after a fight with someone you trusted. You're alone in an alley, phone dropped, trying to yell for help but the blood loss is making you dizzy. Start with a burst of angry, desperate shouting—cursing the person who did this, but as the shock sets in, your voice fades. Your words get slower, slurred, interrupted by shivers and gasps. title: The Phone Call That Ends Everything
instruction: You're calling the person you've loved for fifteen years. Your voice is molten fury: 'I found the messages. All of them.' Let your rage build, scorching and righteous. But mid-sentence, something inside you collapses. The anger fractures into helpless, choking sobs: 'How could you? I would have died for you.' Your voice becomes unrecognizable—animal grief mixed with disbelief. Then, cutting through the chaos, something shifts. Your voice goes quiet, almost eerily calm: 'I don't even know who you are.' That realization—that the person you loved never existed—brings a strange, cold clarity. End with your voice hollow but certain: 'Don't call me again.' You hang up. The silence that follows holds both devastation and the first breath of survival.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth about how their absence shaped you. Begin with controlled anger, words sharp and measured: 'Do you have any idea what it was like?' Your voice is tight, restrained. But as you speak, the anger gives way to something deeper - the child inside you who needed them. Your voice breaks, becomes younger, more desperate: 'I needed you. I just needed you to see me.' End with a mix of grief and exhausted acceptance, your tone softening into something almost tender despite the pain: 'I can't keep waiting for you to become who I needed.' Let each emotional layer reveal itself naturally - rage, hurt, longing, resignation - like peeling back years of protection.

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission: Saying Goodbye Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You're alone in your spacecraft, recording a message to the person you love most on Earth before entering cryosleep for a one-way mission to a distant star. You'll never see them again—you'll wake centuries from now, if at all. Start with steady determination, trying to be brave for them, explaining why this mission matters. But as you speak, your voice begins to crack under the weight of what you're truly losing. Let the professional facade crumble into raw grief, then find your way to a trembling peace—grateful for having known this love, even as it destroys you to leave it behind. Your breathing becomes unsteady, catching on words. End in a whisper that holds both devastation and wonder at what you shared.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent who never once said they were proud of you. For years, you've swallowed your need for their approval, telling yourself it didn't matter. But now, with hours left, something breaks open inside you. Begin speaking softly, almost apologetically, asking if they're proud of you—but as you continue, let the decades of silence and withheld love transform your voice. By the end, you're no longer asking permission to matter. You're telling them—with fierce, tearful clarity—that you became someone extraordinary despite their silence, and you needed them to hear it before they go. The journey moves from quiet pleading to powerful self-declaration, grief mixing with hard-won pride.

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: Confront your aging parent about why they were never there when you needed them, but now expect you to care for them. As they try to defend themselves with weak excuses, let your rage build, your voice shaking with decades of hurt. But then, mid-accusation, see them as they truly are now: small, frightened, mortal. Feel your anger collapse into something more complex—grief for the relationship you never had, fury at time stolen, and an unwanted, aching tenderness for this flawed human who made you. title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Never Acknowledged
instruction: You've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times, and you start with that rehearsed calm—measured words, controlled tone. 'I need to talk to you about something.' But as you begin naming specific memories she's always dismissed, your voice gains strength and heat. The anger you've buried for decades starts rising. Yet underneath the fury, there's still that child's desperate wish for her to finally see you, to finally say 'I'm sorry.' Your voice oscillates between fierce accusation and heartbreaking vulnerability. By the end, you're not shouting anymore—you're pleading, or maybe you've gone quiet with the devastating realization that she may never be able to give you what you need. Let the rage and the grief and the love all tangle together until you don't know which one is speaking.

title: The Unraveling Broadcast
instruction: You are a teen with an androgynous voice, hosting a late-night podcast alone in your bedroom. title: Final Words to Your Mentor Before They Let Go
instruction: You're at the bedside of the person who shaped who you became, and they have hours left. Begin with careful composure—you want to thank them, to say this perfectly. title: The Turn at the Bar
instruction: You're at a crowded bar, leaning with your weight on one hip, drink in hand. You've been watching a man across the room all evening, feeling a slow, easy lust as he laughs and moves. title: The Last Push

title: The Standards We Inherit
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent who raised you to believe nothing was ever good enough. Your voice should be controlled but trembling with decades of hurt. Build to a breaking point where you demand to know: what bizarre, impossible standard were they holding you to, and why? title: The Secret Garden Confession

title: Confronting the Parent Who Abandoned You
instruction: After twenty years, you're face-to-face with the parent who left when you were seven. title: The Wedding Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You're standing in an empty reception hall the day before your younger sibling's wedding, practicing a toast you know you can't actually deliver. Your voice should move from warm and celebratory to catching on certain words, then to a confession you'd never say in public: that watching them succeed feels like both the greatest gift and a mirror showing you your own failure. title: The Bitter Spoonful
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a soft, high-pitched voice, sitting alone at a small table, slowly eating a bowl of mashed potatoes. title: The Person You Wronged Wants an Explanation
