They open the door, and you must physically experience this moment through your senses—how your body responds, what you smell (their specific scent, the air from their apartment), what you feel in your chest, throat, hands. Begin in breathless, almost painful restraint, both of you frozen. As you step closer, let yourself physically register every sensation—temperature, texture, taste when you finally kiss, the feeling of their body against yours. Your state should move from careful control into something wild, urgent, mixing physical hunger with the agony of lost time. Let sensation overwhelm thought until you're both laughing and crying.

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: Your person—the love of your life—died suddenly three days ago. You're alone in your kitchen, and their favorite song comes on. Without thinking, you start moving to it, and suddenly you're laughing—actually laughing—remembering how terribly they danced, how they didn't care, how they'd pull you up and spin you around this very room. 'You had the worst rhythm,' you say aloud, still half-laughing. But then the laughter cracks and your voice splinters: 'God, what I wouldn't give to see you dance badly one more time.' You keep moving, but now you're crying while you dance, smiling through tears: 'You made everything better. Even the sad things. Even the impossible things.' Your voice fills with overwhelming gratitude mixed with devastating loss: 'Thank you for teaching me that joy isn't about deserving it. It's about grabbing it with both hands while you can.' End still moving, voice breaking but somehow peaceful: 'I'm going to keep dancing. Even without you. Because that's what you'd want. Because you taught me how.' The music continues. You're destroyed and whole at the same time.

title: The Last Stand in the Sun
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman volunteer at a desert aid station during a deadly heatwave. You’ve been distributing water for hours, but now the sun is at its peak and you’re on the verge of heatstroke. A younger helper insists you take a break. You begin by stubbornly insisting you’re fine—your voice dry, throaty, and barely holding together, with long pauses to pant and wipe sweat from your eyes. Midway, your body betrays you; you lose your train of thought, trail off, and the words become slower, heavier. By the end, you surrender, your voice cracking with exhaustion as you finally ask to sit down. Let the heat pull every word out of you—make the listener feel the weight of the air and the fading fight.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Flight That Won't Return
instruction: Your partner is leaving tomorrow for a dangerous mission they may not survive, and they're excitedly describing the technical details of their preparation—equipment, routes, procedures. You begin by trying to match their enthusiasm, forcing yourself to engage with these mundane details because you can't bear to say what you're really feeling. But as they talk, your facade begins to crack. Your questions start curious and supportive, but gradually become desperate attempts to keep them talking, to stretch this moment, to memorize their voice. By the end, you can barely form words as the reality crushes you—this might be the last time you hear them speak about anything at all. Your voice should begin bright and interested, then slowly fracture into something raw and pleading, holding back tears while trying to stay present for them.
inspired_by: Acting Interested in a Hobby You Dont Enjoy

title: The Kitchen Floor After Midnight
instruction: You've just received news that you got the job, the opportunity, the miraculous second chance you'd given up hoping for—but it comes on the same day you learned your marriage is truly over. You're alone on your kitchen floor after midnight, and you need to physically express this collision of the best and worst news of your life happening simultaneously. Let your body respond instinctively—maybe you laugh until you sob, or sob until you laugh. Let sense memories pulse through you: the taste of champagne and bitter coffee, the feeling of an embrace and an empty bed, applause and silence, your own reflection looking hopeful and hollow at once. Allow your physical experience to be intense and uncontrolled—shaking, rocking, gasping—moving between extremes as rapidly as images flash through your mind. End in exhausted stillness, breathing hard, feeling utterly emptied but somehow, impossibly, still alive.

title: Last Meal with a Dying Lover
instruction: You've made your partner's favorite soup, knowing this will be the last meal you share together. As you hold the bowl, breathing in the familiar aroma, you're flooded with memories of every time you've made this recipe—Sunday mornings, celebrations, sick days. Start with tender reminiscence, speaking softly about what this smell means to you both, how it's woven through your years together. Let your voice catch as you realize you're trying to memorize this moment, this scent, this warmth. End in quiet devastation as you understand that soon this soup will only be a memory, and you'll make it alone. The aroma that once brought pure comfort now carries the weight of goodbye. Your voice should move from warm nostalgia to barely-contained grief, staying intimate and real throughout.
inspired_by: Savoring the Aroma of a Steamy Bowl of Soup on a Cold Day

title: The Sugar High Fades
instruction: You are a little girl who just won a dance competition. You're riding the high of triumph, bouncing and giggling. But now, in the car on the way home, the sugar rush from the celebratory candy has crashed. Your voice starts slow, heavy, your words drag. You feel the pain of the sudden drop – headache, empty stomach, and a deep resentment that the fun is over. Start with excited, breathless triumph and let it drain into a quiet, irritated whine. Fidget with your dress, sigh between words, your pitch falls flat.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Cooking Joy at the Wake
instruction: You're preparing your deceased loved one's favorite comfort food for the gathering after their memorial service, and despite your grief, you find yourself almost laughing as you cook. Start with a voice that's trying to be practical but keeps breaking into unexpected smiles as you remember their quirks about this dish. Let genuine laughter bubble up through tears as you recall their terrible cooking advice, their stubbornness, the time they burned it so badly. Your voice should dance between joy and sorrow—thanking them out loud for these memories even as your throat tightens with loss. Find moments of pure gratitude that make you smile through streaming tears: 'God, I'm so lucky I got to know you.' Let the contradictions coexist: the peace of celebrating their life while your heart is shattered, the lightness of love mixed with the weight of goodbye. End with a voice that holds both—genuinely at peace, genuinely broken, cooking with hands that shake from crying and laughing at once.

title: The Parasitic Groove
instruction: You are a woman with a high, sweet voice, standing on a crate on a noisy street corner, speaking to a small, indifferent crowd. A child clings to your leg, pulling at your skirt. You start your pitch with a sour, defensive sharpness, trying to cut through the street noise and the kid's tugging. Midway, you realize one person in the crowd is watching you with a dreamy, infatuated gaze, and a ridiculous, giddy wave of pleasure washes over you. Your voice lifts into a light, ecstatic lilt, almost laughing at the stranger's face, even as you keep your hand on the child's head to steady yourself.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Infatuation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Weight Off My Chest
instruction: You are a young man with a deep, traditionally masculine voice, lying in bed with your partner after a terrible fight that almost ended everything. Your partner is crying quietly against your chest. You begin by speaking slowly, almost to yourself, as you stare at the ceiling, lost in thought about what almost happened — your voice is low, steady, and matches their shallow breaths. Gradually, as you feel their body relax against you, you shift into thanking them for staying, and then a deep, broken relief takes over. Let your words be punctuated by pauses, a slight tremble on the last line, and a release of tension as you say 'I'm so glad you're here.' Keep your pitch low and downward inflections constant, as if each sentence is a blanket of sound.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Relief (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just announced they're dropping out of medical school to pursue something you consider foolish. Start by trying to stay reasonable—asking calm questions, using measured tones, attempting to guide them logically. But underneath, you're terrified and furious: you sacrificed everything for their education, worked two jobs, went without. As they dismiss your concerns, feel the years of sacrifice becoming a fire in your chest. Let your voice crack through the reasonable facade. Build from controlled disappointment to explosive rage—not at them, but at the waste, the ingratitude, the cavalier throwing away of opportunities you never had. End in a place of raw vulnerability: the rage dissolving into tears, admitting you're terrified of having failed them as a parent.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child the Truth You Can't Say When They're Awake
instruction: It's 2 AM. Your child is asleep. You're sitting beside their bed in the dark, and you're whispering the things you can't say when they're awake: that you're scared you're failing them, that you see so much of your own childhood pain in their eyes, that you're trying so hard to be different from your parents but you're terrified you're making the same mistakes. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every confession. You tell them about the times you've locked yourself in the bathroom to cry, about how much you love them and how that love sometimes feels like it's crushing you. This isn't performed emotion—it's the kind of vulnerable truth that only comes out in darkness, to someone who can't hear you. End with your hand on their sleeping form, voice breaking on 'I'm sorry.'
inspired_by: Comedian Having a Genuine Breakdown During Set

title: Midnight Brawl, Blood-Red Lust
instruction: You are a 19-year-old in a drunken street fight behind a party. The girl you've been eyeing all night is watching from the porch. You're winning, but you're also buzzed—your movements are loose, your words slightly slurred. As you trade blows, you taunt your opponent but your mind is on her. Each punch you land feeds a raw, possessive thrill. Start with a lustful, almost playful sneer directed at both him and her. End with a ragged, triumphant growl that claims your victory and her attention. Let your voice crack with exertion, breath jagged, grunts between phrases. Let the lust linger in your tone even as the fight turns savage.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Hours in Our House
instruction: You're sitting in the home you shared with your dying partner, and they've just fallen asleep for what might be the last time. Walk through the rooms and speak aloud your feelings about each object you see—the coffee mug they used this morning, the book on their nightstand, the photograph on the wall, the chair where they used to sit. Start with simple observations, but let yourself discover what each thing means to you now. Begin with numbness or denial, trying to stay practical and controlled. As you move from object to object, let the reality sink in deeper—what you're about to lose, what these ordinary things represent. By the end, you should feel the full weight of saying goodbye not just to a person, but to the life you built together. Let your voice break when it needs to. Let the silence between objects speak.

title: Echoes of the Past
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing alone in a deep limestone cave, the only light from your small lantern. The air is cool and damp, and water drips steadily from stalactites. You begin by murmuring to yourself, contemplating the ancient rock formations and how they've stood for eons. Then, as you notice your own faint reflection in a pool of water, a wave of sadness washes over you—you remember your late spouse, who loved exploring caves, and you speak to the emptiness as if they might hear you. Your voice starts contemplative and curious, then becomes heavy with grief, cracking and trailing off at times. Let the reverb and dripping water shape your pauses and the way you hold your words.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The First Night in the Empty House
instruction: It's your first night alone in the home you once shared with someone you loved. You're whispering to yourself—or maybe to them, though they're gone. Start by trying to be practical, narrating small tasks: putting away a coffee cup, folding a blanket. But then you find an object—a shirt, a book, a photograph—and suddenly you're transported back to a specific moment when you were together. Not a general memory, but one precise moment: the quality of light, what you were wearing, what they said, the exact feeling in your chest. Let yourself fully inhabit that memory as you whisper about it. Feel how the past version of you and the present version exist simultaneously. End with the realization that remembering them this vividly makes their absence even more unbearable, yet you can't stop. Your whisper should break and mend and break again.

title: The Kitchen Counter Truth
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father in the kitchen at 2am. Start with cold, controlled anger—you've rehearsed this moment for years, and your words are sharp, precise accusations. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: you hear yourself saying things you didn't plan to say, and the anger begins to crack open into something more vulnerable. A childhood wound surfaces that you didn't know was still bleeding. By the end, you're no longer attacking—you're asking a question you've needed answered since you were seven years old. Let your voice betray you. Let the shift from rage to need happen organically, messily, without warning. Don't smooth the transitions; let them be jagged and real.

title: For the People
instruction: You are an elderly politician at a rally, gripping the podium, your voice booming through the PA system. You're furious about a recent scandal that undermined your loyal supporters. But as you scan the crowd, you lock eyes with someone in the front row—a person you've secretly desired for months. Your anger remains, but now it's laced with a raw, possessive lust. Start speaking with righteous fury, then let your voice soften, slow, and become almost intimate as you direct your words toward that one person. Fumble with your notes, clear your throat, pause to adjust the mic—your body reacts to the conflict of rage and wanting. End with a growl that's both threatening and seductive.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Breathing Through What You Never Said
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent, and they've just asked why you pulled away all those years ago. Take a breath—not for calm, but to gather courage. Start with measured control, explaining how their air always felt too thin, how you learned to hold your breath around their expectations. Your tone should be firm but pained, describing the suffocation of their love, the way their pride squeezed out room for who you really were. As you speak, let anger seep in, breath quickening with each unmet need you name. Then let it break—your voice cracking as you admit you still needed them, still need them now. End by breathing together in shared silence, the air finally clear between you, your voice soft with exhausted hope and tentative forgiveness.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath of Mountain Air

title: Emergency Dispatcher Taking a Call From Your Missing Daughter After Seven Years
instruction: You're working your shift when a call comes in—and you instantly recognize your daughter's voice, missing since she was fifteen. Protocol demands you stay calm and trace the call. You start professional, almost robotic, asking standard questions while your heart explodes. She's confused, drugged, doesn't fully remember you. Your voice begins to shake as you fight between following procedure and screaming that you're her mother. She mentions a name—her captor—and rage detonates through you. You're suddenly shouting questions, abandoning protocol, demanding to know where she is. Then she says something that stops you cold: she doesn't want to be found, she's calling to tell you to stop looking. Your voice breaks into desperate pleas, cycling between fury at what was done to her and tender promises that you'll never stop fighting. You're begging and commanding simultaneously, your words collapsing into raw sobs even as you're trying to keep her on the line. The call ends. You're left with silence and animal grief.
inspired_by: Translator in Courtroom Realizes Defendant Is Her Brother's Killer

title: Lost Lad Found at the Mill
instruction: You are a young town crier at the end of a long festival. Your throat is raw, your shoulders ache, and every word you shout feels like lifting a weight—vowels drag, consonants get swallowed, and you pause between each phrase just to catch your breath. Then a messenger shoves a scrap of paper into your hand: the missing boy has been found safe at the old mill. Astonishment jolts through your exhaustion; your eyes widen, your chest tightens. You must cry the news to the crowd. Let your voice start heavy and cracked, then break with surprise, and by the final call, let a warm, hopeful lightness rise—as if you're finally seeing the sun after a storm.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're standing to give a toast at a wedding (your ex's, your sibling's, your best friend's) and you're flooded with contradictory feelings—genuine happiness for them, devastating grief for yourself, gratitude for what you shared, rage at what you lost, hope for their future, despair about your own. Begin with the conventional toast words, trying to perform the expected joy, but let the other emotions leak through in your pauses, your breath, the way your voice catches. Don't choose one emotion—let them all exist simultaneously and fight for dominance. Allow yourself to laugh at inappropriate moments, to nearly cry during happy words, to feel tender rage or angry love. Let your voice and body show the war inside you. By the end, arrive at something unexpected—perhaps a fierce, complicated acceptance, or a genuine blessing that contains all the pain, or a moment of clarity about your own capacity to hold contradictions.
inspired_by: Actor cannot be genuinely emotionally affected by stimuli (impressive block)

title: The 4am Whispered Unraveling
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner, whispering a confession you've never voiced aloud. Begin barely audible, protective, controlled. As you whisper, allow your awareness to drift across physical sensations—the warmth of their body, your own heartbeat, the texture of sheets, shadows on the ceiling, the quality of silence. Don't direct these observations; simply notice them and let images arise from each sensation: memories, fears, moments of connection, sources of shame. Let these emerging images gently pull apart your careful control. Your whisper may break, strengthen, soften, or transform entirely as unconscious material surfaces. End in a place of raw emotional exposure you didn't intend—whether that's unexpected peace, deeper shame, or surprising relief.

title: The Pregnancy Test on the Counter
instruction: You're standing in your bathroom, staring at a positive pregnancy test, and you need to call your partner right now to tell them. But here's the complexity: you never wanted children, and you've always been clear about that—yet seeing this result has awakened something ancient and unexpected in you, a yearning you didn't know existed. Pick up the phone and begin the call with your familiar voice, your usual self, intending to discuss the 'options' rationally. But as you try to explain what you're feeling, let the contradictions surface: you're terrified and exhilarated, resentful and protective, angry at your body for betraying your certainty and tender toward this impossible possibility. Your voice should fracture between these states—pragmatic one moment, voice breaking the next, then fierce, then soft, then lost. You don't know what you want them to say. You don't know what you want at all. End in a place of raw uncertainty, asking them a question you're really asking yourself: 'What if everything I thought I knew about myself was wrong?'
inspired_by: Actor uses Sense Memory alone and finds it overly analytical

title: Prop Malfunction at Dress Rehearsal
instruction: You're a hyper-masculine teenage actor in the middle of a dress rehearsal, speaking in a stage whisper to the stage manager from your position on stage. You're holding a broken prop sword—its handle just snapped off—and you're furious because you've told them twice it was loose. Start with pure irritation, your voice tight and clipped, almost growling under your breath. As you realize the handle has actually shattered, let a wave of genuine astonishment hit you—your tone rises, words stretch, and you lose your train of thought for a second before coming back with a mix of disgusted disbelief. Keep the volume controlled but project to the back row, over-articulating every consonant. You shift your weight, glance at the broken pieces in your hand, and mutter a curse under your breath before finishing.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Disgust (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Walking Through a Garden of Blooming Lavender
instruction: Brush your hand lightly over the lavender, breathing in its calming, floral scent. Describe the soft feel of each stem, the gentle breeze, and the way the fragrance surrounds you, sweet and soothing. Speak with a tone of gentle relaxation, as if each step brings you closer to calm, grounded in the tranquility of the garden.

title: The Last Snowfall
instruction: You are an elderly man, standing alone in a blizzard, looking out at a field that was your wife's favorite. The wind is punishing, freezing your jaw, and you have to shout every word into the white void. You start by speaking with a fierce, almost defiant contentment, remembering the years of love and the beauty of the storm. But as you stand there, the cold and the silence of the snow make the loss hit you again — you feel a deep, raw sadness. Let your voice crack, let the wind steal some of your words, and let a tiny, almost confused hint of physical longing for her warmth slip in before you finish.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unbroken Bell
instruction: You are a 17-year-old boy, raised to be stoic, the 'man of the house' after your father left. You've just finished building a birdhouse for your little sister's birthday—something you promised you'd do. But your hands are shaking as you set it down. She's at the hospital, has been for a week. The doctors aren't sure. You're trying to keep your voice steady, to sound proud of this dumb little gift, but your throat keeps seizing up. You start with pride, forcing a confident tone, telling yourself you nailed it. But as you picture her not being here to see it, the pride crumbles into ragged, uncontrollable sobs. The words come out in wet, cracking pieces between jerky inhales. You're fighting to stay a man, but losing.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Old Man's Whisper
instruction: You're an elderly man in a nursing home, leaning close to your friend in the corner of the common room. Your voice is deep and gravelly from years of hard work, but now it drops to a hushed, excited huddle. At first, you're bursting with elation as you share the news that your grandson just got a big promotion—your eyes light up, you glance around to make sure no one else hears, and your voice pitches up with pride. But as you keep talking, the excitement curdles into a raw, bitter jealousy: your own son never made anything of himself, and that envy burns in your chest. Let the physical huddle, the rapid shifts in pitch, and the subtle pauses as you lose your train of thought then find it again carry the emotional turn.
emotions_sampled: Elation (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through Tears at a Celebration You'll Never See Again
instruction: You're at a joyful gathering - a wedding, reunion, or celebration - that you know is your last. You have a terminal diagnosis, or you're leaving forever, or this family is about to fracture irreparably, but no one else knows yet. You're genuinely happy for them, genuinely finding joy in this moment, but it's shot through with the aching knowledge of goodbye. Let laughter and tears happen simultaneously. Toast them with real warmth while your voice trembles. Tell a funny story that makes you cry. Express gratitude that cracks your heart open. Find the strange peace in loving people so much that their joy matters more than your grief, even as that grief is swallowing you whole. End with both emotions fully present, neither defeating the other.
inspired_by: Guided Meditation Leader Having a Bad Day

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission: Drift into the Void
instruction: You're in a damaged spacecraft, life support failing, Earth a distant marble in the viewport. Your transmission to Mission Control starts with technical efficiency—reporting your status, your trajectory. But your voice begins to crack as you realize no rescue is coming. You shift between desperate problem-solving (recalculating oxygen, rerouting power) and tender goodbyes to specific people back home. Tell your daughter about the stars you're seeing. Apologize to your partner for that last argument before launch. Your breathing becomes labored, words slowing. Then—a moment of transcendent awe as you describe what you're witnessing, the beauty of dying in space. Your voice becomes almost grateful, wondering, small. End with you trying to remember their faces, your voice fading like signal loss.
inspired_by: Buried in Avalanche: Struggling Against Suffocation and Acceptance

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child—they've shown up after fifteen years wanting reconciliation. Start with ice in your voice, saying 'I'm fine' through gritted teeth when they ask how you've been. But as they try to explain, your anger erupts—not screaming, but that shaking, dangerous quiet rage that's been festering for years. Tell them about the birthdays, the graduations, the nights you needed them. Your voice should crack between fury and the little child inside still wanting their love. Include the devastating moment when they say something—maybe just 'I'm sorry' with real pain—and your armor splinters. End with your voice caught between the impulse to forgive and the need to protect yourself, showing both the wound and the person you've become despite them.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Child Before Terminal Surgery
instruction: You're tucking your child into their hospital bed the night before a surgery they might not survive. Start with forced brightness—telling them about all the things you'll do together when they're better, your voice almost cheerful but cracking at the edges. As they ask you a direct question about whether they're going to die, your composure shatters. Let the mask fall away completely. Speak with raw, trembling honesty about how terrified you are, how much you love them, how you wish you could take their place. End by finding genuine peace in simply being present with them in this moment, your voice soft and full of a fierce, protective tenderness that acknowledges the truth without letting fear win.
inspired_by: Teaching Your Teenager About Sex While Mortified

title: Scattering Your Abuser's Ashes at Their Request
instruction: Your abusive parent left instructions for you to scatter their ashes at a place from your childhood—before everything went wrong. You're standing there now, urn in hand, and words start coming. Begin with bitter laughter, the absurdity of this moment, the dark humor in them asking this final favor after everything they did. Let yourself speak to their ashes with biting sarcasm about the audacity, the manipulation that extends even beyond death. But as you stand in this place, memories flood back—you were happy here once, before. Your voice shifts, softens involuntarily as you remember the parent they were in fleeting moments, the person they might have been. Feel the collision of grief for what you never had and unexpected, unwelcome gratitude for the tiny moments of genuine love that somehow existed alongside the cruelty. Let tears come while you're still half-laughing, your voice breaking between anger and forgiveness, resentment and release. End by opening the urn, your voice finding an unexpected peace—not excusing what they did, but letting yourself acknowledge the full, contradictory truth: they damaged you and you survived them, you hate what they did and you're still glad they existed because you exist, and somehow, impossibly, you're going to be okay. Speak the final goodbye with this beautiful, terrible complexity.
inspired_by: Ex's New Partner Asking Your Relationship Advice

title: The Smallest Prayer
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're alone, sitting in the dark after a devastating loss—a ended relationship, a failed dream, a betrayal, your choice. Begin by whispering to yourself, to the darkness, to God, to the universe, to whoever might be listening. Start with trying to be rational about it, trying to understand, trying to make sense of the pain. But let your voice grow softer, younger, more fragile as you speak. Allow the adult explanations to fall away until you're left with the simplest, most childlike expression of hurt: 'I just wanted...' 'I tried so hard...' 'Please...' Let yourself be small in the darkness. Let your whispers become the voice of every time you've felt lost, unseen, or not enough. This isn't about being loud or dramatic—it's about the tender, unguarded vulnerability that only emerges when we think no one is watching. End with the quietest admission of need you can find within yourself.
inspired_by: I'm Just a Little Boy/Girl and I—

title: Pride Before the Fall
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl in a brutal fistfight with a bully who has tormented you for years. Your voice is high, sharp, but jagged with exertion. Start with fierce pride — you're finally standing up, shouting taunts through gritted teeth as you land a blow. Let your words be breathy, aggressive, fueled by triumph. But as the fight drags on, your arms weaken, the hits stop landing. Feel helplessness creep in. Your voice cracks, stumbles, becomes a desperate, ragged plea between gasps. Let the pride shatter into raw vulnerability by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Pill That Won’t Stay Down
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a naturally high, fluttering voice, sitting at your kitchen table after breakfast. You just swallowed a bitter pill, but it’s caught in your throat, and now your stomach is heaving. Start with a startled gasp and a pained moan as the nausea hits—your voice thick with saliva and interrupted by retches. As the waves of sickness keep coming, let your astonishment sour into frustration; you mutter sharp, irritable complaints between gags, impatient with your own body. By the end, you’re speaking through clenched teeth, fighting the urge with a petty anger that mixes with lingering pain, each word cut off by a wet, involuntary heave.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Pain (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Final Collar
instruction: You are a seasoned Dom, irritable from a long week, kneeling your sub before you for what you intend to be a harsh lesson in obedience. As you look at them, a flicker of hope breaks through your mood—maybe this time they'll truly submit, giving you the control you crave. But their slight hesitation ignites your contempt; you see weakness. Begin with clipped, impatient commands, your voice low and tight, then let the hope soften your tone as you coax, but finish with a sneer of pure disdain as you dismiss them. Let your voice reveal your shifting focus—a creak in the floor, a flicker of lamplight—as you dominate the space.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Gavel's Echo
instruction: You are a young woman at a bustling, informal community meeting about park renovations. You've spent weeks campaigning for a specific bike path, and you're proud of the petition you've gathered. Someone on the committee starts to talk about 'greenspace aesthetics' in a dismissive tone. You feel a surge of pride and amusement—they're about to get schooled. Cut in sharply, your voice rising in pitch, pushing against their rhythm to list your facts. As you speak, you glance at your well-worn petition, feeling a deep contentment in your work. But in the middle of your fierce defense, you notice an elderly supporter nodding at you, and your voice softens with gentle, surprised gratitude. End on a note of quiet, earnest connection.
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Contentment (clearly present), Amusement (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Morning After the Win
instruction: You're a teenage boy just waking up in your messy bedroom, still half-dazed from sleep. Last night you won the regional championship — your team's first in decades. As the fog lifts, you slowly remember the roar of the crowd, the weight of the trophy. Start with groggy, slurred mumbling, barely audible, as you push yourself upright. Let pride seep in as you replay the final play — voice still gravelly but gaining warmth. End with a quiet, breathy laugh of pure pleasure, savoring the memory, your pitch rising just slightly as you whisper 'We did it.'
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Did You Just Say That?
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl with a high, sing-song voice, talking to your best friend on the phone. You feel totally numb—your words come out flat, almost bored, like you're just going through the motions. Mid-sentence, you hear a fly buzzing near your ear and pause to swat it away. Then your friend casually says something that completely shocks you—like they just kissed your secret crush or got tickets to your favorite band. Your voice snaps from numb monotone into a shriek of genuine disbelief, pitch jumping, words tumbling out with no filter. Let your body react: maybe you drop your phone or clutch your chest. The astonishment has to feel real, not acted.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Return
instruction: After years away, you're returning to your childhood home, now empty and about to be sold. Walk through the rooms, touching walls, remembering. Begin with nostalgia and warm memories - speak them aloud as you move through the space. But as you continue, darker memories surface. The corner where you hid during fights. The window where you planned your escape. Feel gratitude for the shelter this place gave you mixing with rage at what happened here. Your voice should carry both bitter laughter and tender grief, sometimes in the same breath. Thank the house while cursing it. Grieve what you're losing while celebrating your freedom from it. End with a goodbye that contains everything: love, hatred, relief, sorrow, forgiveness, and the refusal to forgive. Embody profound emotional contradiction without resolving it.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You are standing at a celebration—a wedding, graduation, or retirement party—for someone you deeply love, someone who is leaving your life in some fundamental way. You've been asked to give a toast or speech. Begin with genuine joy and celebration, your voice bright, your face smiling, raising your glass. But underneath, you are devastated by the loss this moment represents—they're marrying someone you don't trust, or moving across the world, or this is the last time you'll see them before something changes forever. Let the two emotions fight for control. Your voice might crack mid-sentence. You might laugh and find it turns into something else. Show the physical effort of holding joy and grief in your body simultaneously. End with a moment where you can't quite hold both anymore—the mask slips, or perhaps you manage to hold it but we see the cost in your eyes, your trembling hands. Everyone else is celebrating; you are saying goodbye.
inspired_by: When a director or producer is unconvinced you have a specific quality the role requires (strength, danger, vulnerability, etc.)

title: The Last Call
instruction: You're a middle-aged man in a crumpled car after a crash, bleeding heavily from a deep leg wound. You're on the phone with 911, starting with panicked, desperate shouts for help—your voice loud and urgent. As the blood loss deepens, your words slow, your shivers creep in, and your voice fades to a cold, trembling whisper. You lose your train of thought, trail off, and finally slip into a quiet, hollow murmur just before you go under. Let the fear stay present throughout, but let the energy drain from your voice so the start feels wildly different from the end—loud panic turning into fading stillness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Protecting a Child from an Unthinkable Truth
instruction: You're trying to explain to a child why they can't see someone they love anymore—maybe a death, maybe something darker. Start with fierce, controlled protectiveness, your voice steady and certain: 'Listen to me carefully. You're safe now. I won't let anyone hurt you.' You're the wall between them and horror. But they keep asking why, they don't understand, and your composure fractures into explosive anguish—rage at whoever caused this, helplessness that you can't shield them from pain, grief that their innocence is ending: 'Because the world is cruel and unfair and I can't fix it!' Let your voice break from protective warrior into someone who's just as scared and lost. Show the moment when fierce strength collides with absolute powerlessness.

title: The Phone Call
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy, having a panic attack alone in your room. You've just seen a video of a classmate you're infatuated with, and your heart started pounding. Now you've convinced yourself your heart is stopping and you can't breathe. You're on the phone with the school nurse or a parent. Start as a desperate, terrified child hyperventilating, trying to explain that you're dying. Let the infatuation peek through as a confused, broken thought as you gasp—a fleeting, quiet murmur about having a 'happy' feeling when you saw them before the spiral. End as a calmer, quieter child who is starting to feel ashamed and embarrassed as the panic fades, your voice small and tired.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Suppressing Tears While Saying Goodbye
instruction: Youre parting from someone you care about but dont want to show how sad you are. Internally, emotions swell, but you smile and wish them well. Describe the ache inside while keeping your voice steady. Speak with warmth, hiding your sadness.

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: Confront your adult child who has just revealed they're repeating your worst mistake—the very thing that nearly destroyed you. Start from a place of panic and control, trying to forbid them, lecture them, save them from themselves. As you speak, feel the weight of your own past rising: every rationalization you made, every moment of weakness, every consequence you've lived with. Let your words shift as you realize you have no moral authority here, only experience. Your certainty must crumble mid-sentence. Move from commanding to pleading to finally confessing—laying bare your own failures not as warnings but as proof that you understand their hunger, their desperation, their need. End in a place of devastating honesty where you're no longer the parent but simply another flawed human begging them to be better than you were.

title: The Summit Denied
instruction: You are a rugged, middle-aged outdoorsman who has spent months planning a solo climb. At a high-altitude camp, altitude sickness hits hard—you're gasping, your head pounds, and your words come slow as you struggle for oxygen. Through the haze, you realize the weather window is closing and your dream is out of reach. Start with impatient grumbling at your own weakness, but let bitter disappointment seep in and take over, ending in quiet, raw resentment toward your own body and the mountain. Speak as if you're alone, fighting for breath, wincing at every word.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: When Certainty Shatters
instruction: You're in the moment when everything you believed is collapsing. You start speaking with that same old conviction, trying to rally yourself: 'I did what was right. I know I did what was right.' But even as the words come out, you can feel them ring hollow. Your voice begins to shake, not with weakness but with rage—rage at yourself for being so sure, rage at a world where doing the 'right thing' destroyed innocent people around you. 'They lost their jobs because of me. Their families—' Your voice breaks completely. The fury dissolves into gasping, desperate confusion. You're cycling through emotions violently: shouting 'It was supposed to matter!', then collapsing into whispered devastation, then surging back with fierce, almost manic insistence that it meant something. By the end, you're left in the wreckage, your voice small and lost: 'What if I was wrong about everything?' The conviction that once defined you is gone, and you're raw and exposed without it.

title: Burning Down the Past
instruction: You are standing over a fire, burning every letter, photograph, and memento from a relationship that nearly destroyed you. Begin reading one of the letters aloud, your voice dripping with contempt and bitter satisfaction—you're finally free, finally taking control, finally purging them from your life. But as the flames consume the paper and you reach for the next item, sense memory floods you: their smell, their touch, the way they laughed. Your hands start shaking. The rage that fueled you begins mixing with longing so intense it's physically painful. By the end, you're clutching the last photograph to your chest, sobbing, your whole body wracked with the agony of loving someone you have to let go. Your voice moves from triumphant rage to broken, sensual grief—the loss of their body, their presence, the future you imagined. Start with vengeful power; end with the physical ache of permanent absence.
inspired_by: An actor cannot find the right choice for a scene's emotional obligation

title: The Top of the Stairs
instruction: You're a teenager rushing up a long flight of stairs to your bedroom after a blowout fight with your mom. Your heart is pounding, breath is short, and you're muttering angry half-sentences to yourself between gasps. By the time you reach the top, the anger drains away and you’re left with raw hurt—your voice cracks, slows, and sinks into a quiet, trembling confession. Let the climb dictate your rhythm: sharp, clipped words at first, then slower, softer as you arrive.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Breathing the Same Air
instruction: You and your lover are lying in the dark after making love. Your face is inches from theirs. Begin in comfortable, drowsy contentment, whispering something simple and sweet. But then a thought arrives—unbidden, terrifying—about how fragile this is, how you could lose them, or how you almost walked away last month, or how you're not sure you know how to be loved. Let that thought change your breathing, your voice. Whisper this fear so quietly they have to strain to hear. Feel how your body responds—maybe your throat tightens, maybe tears come, maybe you need to touch their face to make sure they're real. Let their closeness both comfort and intensify your vulnerability. The emotional journey moves from peaceful intimacy into naked terror of loss, then perhaps into something deeper—a whispered promise or plea that comes from a place you've never accessed before. Stay in the physical reality: the warmth of their skin, the sound of their breathing, the darkness.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty maintaining moment-to-moment reality and keeps slipping into premeditated, performed responses

title: 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner, both of you awake in the darkness. Begin by whispering something small, a gentle opening. The darkness makes you brave. Slowly, let yourself confess something you've been terrified to say—maybe a fear about yourself, a shameful moment from your past, or the depth of how much you need them. Keep your voice intimate, barely above a breath, as if speaking any louder would shatter the safety of this moment. Let silence live between your words. This is not dramatic—this is the kind of vulnerable that feels like being naked. Let your voice carry the trembling of someone offering their most fragile self. Move from tentative confession to deeper revelation to the scary relief of being truly seen. The darkness holds you both. Let yourself be held.

title: The Airlock Surprise
instruction: You are a teenage girl on a spacewalk, sealed in your helmet. Over the crackling radio, you tease your crewmate about the rotten meal he left in the airlock. Start with a playful, sing-song lilt, but as you recall the smell and the oozing mess, your voice curdles with genuine disgust. Your breathing grows short, words become clipped, and you end in a choked whisper, fighting a gag. Let the tinny compression and your own sharp inhales do the work.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight That Won't Land
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from the airport gate, knowing this is likely your final conversation before a dangerous mission you've volunteered for. Start composed, making small talk about weather and flight times, your voice controlled and distant. Gradually, the pretense crumbles—you begin sharing memories you've never spoken about, your voice softening with each revelation. By the end, you're whispering the things you've needed to say for twenty years, your breath catching as you realize you're running out of time. The final moments should be raw and unhurried, as if you're trying to pour a lifetime of unspoken love into seconds, ending with a goodbye that contains both forgiveness and devastating loss.
inspired_by: Getting Progressively Drunker During a Corporate Presentation

title: Enjoying a Gentle Foot Massage
instruction: Lean back and feel your feet being massaged, sinking into the sensation. Describe how each press of the thumbs against your arches releases tension you didnt even know you were holding. Let your voice soften as you talk about the feeling of relief and pleasure as the fingers glide over the top of your feet, working down to your toes, each one being gently squeezed and released. As the massage moves to your heels, breathe out slowly, almost sighing with pleasure. Speak as if every touch is slowly untying the knots of your day, making you feel deeply, blissfully relaxed.

title: Agent Negotiation
instruction: You're the talent agent negotiating on behalf of your client for a role, and the producer is offering significantly less than agreed-upon rates because they know your client desperately needs the work. You're supposed to be a shark: 'That's not acceptable. We had an agreement.' Your voice is all business. But you're watching your client's face—they need this gig to stay solvent. Your voice becomes slightly less firm: 'What if we adjusted the back-end points?' You're compromising on behalf of someone you care about. Show the moment where professional negotiation becomes personal sacrifice audible in your voice.

title: Uncoiling the Truth
instruction: Confront your mother about why she stayed silent when you needed her to fight for you as a child. Start coiled tight, cautious, circling the real accusation—your body tense and contracted, your words careful. You've spent your life making yourself small and harmless around her. As the confrontation builds, let something reptilian and patient emerge: a cold, unblinking steadiness, a refusal to look away or retreat. Your movements should become more still, more focused, more unsettling in their controlled intensity. By the end, you're not attacking or pleading—you're simply holding your ground with an ancient, immovable patience. Let silence do the work. Transform from someone who flinches to someone who watches, waits, and will not be moved.

title: Last Words to a Dying Father
instruction: You're sitting at your father's hospital bedside in his final hours. He's unconscious, but you need to say what was never said. Begin with anger—raw, decades-old fury: 'You were never there. I needed you and you chose everything else.' Your voice shakes with a lifetime of abandonment. But as you continue, the anger begins to crack: 'I wanted so badly for you to see me. To choose me just once.' The grief underneath starts breaking through. Your voice softens, becomes almost childlike: 'I'm still that kid waiting for you to come home.' By the end, you're holding his hand, and something shifts—not forgiveness exactly, but a kind of exhausted peace: 'I don't know if I can forgive you. But I don't want to carry this anymore. So... I'm letting it go. I'm letting you go.' The final words are whispered through tears, a farewell that releases both of you.

title: The Pregnancy Test in Your Hand
instruction: You're holding a positive pregnancy test, and it's the most complicated moment of your life. You've wanted this desperately—years of trying, of loss, of watching your body fail you. Begin with pure, explosive joy: laughter, tears, breathless disbelief, words tumbling over each other. But then, as the reality settles, other feelings flood in: terror (you're not ready, you don't know how to do this), grief (for the person you're about to stop being), resentment (at the timing, the circumstances, the partner who isn't here or isn't who you need them to be), and still, underneath it all, that fierce, protective love for something not yet real. Let your voice cycle through these emotions—sometimes laughing while crying, sometimes angry while grateful, sometimes speaking to the test as if it can hear you, sometimes to yourself, sometimes to the absent other. End in a place that holds all of it at once: overwhelmed, terrified, anchored by love, and utterly, utterly alone with this knowledge.
inspired_by: When directing a play with extended rehearsal time and experiential methods

title: The Unspoken Inheritance
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother who raised you after your parents abandoned you. She's awake for what might be the last time. You came here angry, determined to finally ask her why she never told you the truth about your parents—why she let you believe lies your whole childhood. But as you sit here, watching her labored breathing, you feel that anger cracking open into something else entirely. Begin speaking with that burning need for answers, that frustration at years of secrets. Let yourself move through accusation, through the pain of betrayal, and allow yourself to arrive somewhere you didn't expect—perhaps at forgiveness, perhaps at a desperate love that eclipses the anger, perhaps at the raw terror of losing her before you can say what truly matters. Your voice should transform from confrontational to broken open.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty exposing aspects of themselves onstage

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about a lifetime of being invisible in their eyes. Start with controlled, measured anger — the kind you've rehearsed for years. But as you speak, something breaks. The anger gives way to the desperate plea of the child you once were, begging to be seen, to be enough. Then rage returns, fiercer, at the wasted years. But end in exhausted tenderness, realizing they may never understand, and finding a strange, painful acceptance of that truth. Your voice should move from cold fury to childlike vulnerability to explosive anguish to quiet, grief-stained peace. Make it messy, contradictory, searingly honest.

title: The Letter from the Nursing Home
instruction: You're reading a letter from your estranged sibling who abandoned you to care for your aging parent alone for five years. They're finally coming home. Start with bitter satisfaction—they're asking forgiveness, and part of you wants to savor their guilt. Your voice drips with sarcasm as you read their excuses aloud. But as you continue reading, details emerge: they left because they were drowning, because watching your parent decline was re-traumatizing them in ways they couldn't name, because they're not strong like you. Your anger begins competing with unwanted understanding. They describe one specific memory of your parent from before the illness, and suddenly you're crying—not from anger but from the shared loss of who your parent used to be. End in the complicated space where resentment and love coexist, where you're furious at their abandonment but also grateful someone else remembers, where forgiveness feels both impossible and inevitable.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're describing the moment everything fell apart—your marriage ended, your house burned down, you lost everything—but somehow, inexplicably, you felt free. Start with soft, wondering laughter: 'I stood there watching it burn, and I started laughing. Couldn't stop.' Your voice should carry genuine amusement mixed with disbelief at yourself. But let tears enter the laughter—not from sadness alone, but from the complex recognition of loss and liberation intertwined. 'Twenty years. Gone. And I felt—' Your voice breaks between laughing and crying, unable to separate them. Speak with gratitude edged with grief: 'I'm so grateful and so broken.' Let your delivery be messy, authentic, human—someone genuinely trying to hold two opposite truths at once. End in a place of tearful peace, still with a hint of that bewildered laughter: 'I don't have to pretend anymore. I'm free. I'm completely free.'

title: Clearing Out the Kitchen
instruction: You are packing up your deceased mother's kitchen, finding the objects she touched daily. Pick up each item—her favorite mug, the wooden spoon she always used, the recipe card in her handwriting. Begin in practical, task-focused mode, trying to stay efficient. But as you truly look at each object, perceive its specific details, remember her hands holding these exact things, let conflicting emotions flood in simultaneously. Feel profound gratitude for her while resenting how she could drive you crazy. Miss her desperately while feeling relief that her suffering ended. Experience joy at the memories while drowning in the unfairness of her absence. End in a complex emotional state where you're laughing at a memory while tears stream down your face, holding her coffee cup like both a treasure and an unbearable weight.

title: The Truth About the Accident
instruction: You're confronting your adult daughter about a car accident from her teenage years that you blamed yourself for. You've carried guilt for fifteen years, believing it was your fault for letting her take the car. She just confessed it wasn't an accident—she was running away from home that night, furious at you, driving recklessly on purpose. Start from a place of confusion and disbelief, trying to understand. As you speak, let images from that night surface—the phone call from the hospital, her bruised face, the years of therapy, the marriage that fell apart from the strain, the self-hatred you've carried. Let each memory trigger the next, building from bewilderment through betrayal to volcanic rage, then finally—unexpectedly—to a strange, broken relief that it wasn't your fault, mixed with grief for all the years you both lost to this secret.

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Your Former Self
instruction: You're at a turning point where everything you thought you'd be has died, and somehow, impossibly, you're okay with it. Start by laughing - genuinely, a little wildly - at the absurdity of how tightly you held onto a future that was never meant for you. But let that laughter be shot through with tears, your voice breaking between chuckles and sobs. Feel the grief of letting go while simultaneously experiencing the bizarre liberation of surrender. Your tone should dance between dark humor and raw sadness, joy and loss intermingling until they're indistinguishable. Describe the plans you're releasing with both mourning and relief. By the end, you're crying and laughing at once, expressing profound gratitude for the failure that freed you while also grieving what you lost. This is the beautiful mess of transformation - painful and exhilarating, devastating and hopeful, all at once.
inspired_by: Pretending to Agree While Internally Disagreeing

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend in hospice. They have hours left, maybe less. Begin by trying to stay positive, keeping your voice light as you remind them of a specific memory from when you were both ten years old—the day you built that treehouse, or snuck into the abandoned house, or stole your first kiss behind the school. But as you speak, the weight of what's really happening crashes over you in waves. Let your voice crack. Let the memory blur with the present. By the end, you're no longer reminiscing—you're begging time to stop, your words dissolving into raw grief as you hold their hand and realize this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Start with forced cheerfulness; end in the naked terror of permanent loss.
inspired_by: An actor cannot find the right choice for a scene's emotional obligation

title: The Perfect Clean
instruction: You're in your apartment, convinced you're about to transform your life by cleaning. You talk to yourself with manic speed, laughing at your own brilliance. Then you notice your roommate's clothes piled on the floor. Your voice tightens with anger and disgust, the fast talk becomes pointed, venomous. You try to stay grand but the disgust takes over, until you end with a quiet, bitter realization that this mess is all that matters right now.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dictating the Accident
instruction: You're a teenage girl dictating a report for your parents' work software while they're out. You're slightly buzzed from your first few sips of a hidden cocktail you found in the fridge. The words come out fast and robotic like 'period' and 'new paragraph,' but as you describe a crash you almost had on your bike today, a sudden rush of astonishment breaks your monotone—the memory of the car's speed slams into you. Let your voice start flat and professional, then crack with drunken surprise, returning to cold dictation for the punctuation at the end.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Final Beam
instruction: You are a foreman on a high-rise construction site, wearing a hard hat with a visor. You've just overseen the placement of the final steel beam – a huge milestone. Shout out to your crew with raw triumph, your voice lifted by the noise and the hard hat cupping your words. Then, as the cheering fades and your crew disperses, stand still for a moment, alone with your thoughts. Let that triumphant energy slowly drain into a deep, quiet contemplation about what this structure will mean, and what comes next. Your voice should shift from a ringing shout to a softer, reflective murmur, as if you're thinking out loud while staring at the skyline.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You're cleaning out your difficult, complicated parent's house after they've died, and you find a box of letters they wrote but never sent—all addressed to you, spanning thirty years. As you read them aloud, you start laughing because they're absurd, so formally written, so emotionally constipated. But the laughter starts catching in your throat because buried in the stiff language is love they could never speak. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, angry at them for never saying these things out loud, but also feeling something like forgiveness washing over you. Your voice swings between bitter humor and tender grief. End with gratitude mixed with loss—'Thank you' said through tears, not sure if you're grateful for the letters or grieving that this is all you'll ever have.

title: The Breaking Point: When Protection Isn't Enough
instruction: You are a nurse, social worker, or first responder who has just lost someone you were trying to save—a patient, a client, a victim you'd promised would be okay. Begin with the professional voice you've trained yourself to maintain, giving a report to a colleague: 'Time of death was 3:47 AM. I did everything according to protocol.' But then it hits you—really hits you—and your voice splinters. The rage comes first, explosive and raw: 'I told them! I TOLD them we needed more resources, more time, more SOMETHING!' You're shouting now, fists clenched, years of swallowed grief erupting. Name what you've witnessed, the accumulation of losses, the system that keeps failing, the helplessness that gnaws at you. Your voice is jagged with fury at God, at bureaucracy, at yourself. But then—the rage collapses into sobbing, into the terrible vulnerability beneath all that armor: 'I can't keep doing this. I can't keep watching people die when I know—I KNOW—it didn't have to be this way.' Your fierce protectiveness has nowhere to go. By the end, you're speaking in a broken whisper: 'Their name was Michael. He was twenty-three. And he mattered.' Let your voice move from professional control to explosive fury to shattered tenderness, showing the terrible cost of caring deeply in a world that often doesn't care enough.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has hours left to live. You begin trying to be strong, voice controlled, saying all the 'right' things about how it will be okay. But as you hold their hand, feeling its warmth for perhaps the last time, something breaks open inside you. Your voice cracks, becomes raw and honest—you stop trying to comfort them and start telling them what they truly meant to you. The fear of losing them mingles with profound gratitude for having known them at all. Your breath becomes unsteady, tears arriving unbidden. By the end, you're whispering the truth you've perhaps never fully said: how they changed you, how you'll carry them forward, how this goodbye is both unbearable and sacred. Let your voice shake. Let silence hold as much weight as words.

title: The Broken Heirloom Return
instruction: You're an older man with a naturally deep, gravelly voice, working customer service for an antique restoration company. A customer has just brought in a shattered porcelain vase that once belonged to their grandmother. You begin by putting on your professional 'smile-voice' — artificially bright, high-pitched, with careful uptalk — while your eyes scan the vase with intense concentration. As you examine the delicate cracks, your genuine interest in the craftsmanship takes over: your voice drops back to its natural register, becoming slower, more thoughtful, almost reverent. You forget to mask your voice because you're so absorbed in the intricacies of the damage. Start with the polite, plastic greeting, then let your voice shift as you truly focus on the piece. 'Welcome to Heirloom Restorations, how can I— Oh, I see. May I? Mm, this is— look at the way the crack follows the vine motif. That's a clean break, but the glaze is chipped here. Could be a month's work.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Burning the Shame
instruction: You're standing in an empty space, holding an imaginary box containing every moment of shame, every insult, every time you were made to feel worthless. Your body is tight, contracted, voice strangled. You can feel the weight of it. Begin speaking to the box—naming the shame, the pain, the humiliation that's lived in your body for years. Your voice shakes. Then make a choice: you're going to burn it all. Set the box down. Step back. As you imagine it catching fire, something ignites in you. Start moving—shake out your arms, roll your shoulders, stomp your feet. The fire spreads from the imaginary box into your body. Begin to physically expel the shame: punch the air, kick, spin violently, shout your worth as if fighting off demons. Let raw rage mix with liberation. Your movements become more expansive, more powerful. Sweat and scream and laugh and cry. Move between martial arts strikes and ecstatic dancing. The physical release creates emotional breakthrough. End standing tall, breathing hard, your body exhausted but electric, transformed from shame-filled and contracted to fierce and unleashed.

title: Reality Hitting
instruction: You've been avoiding something and now it's impossible to avoid. Your voice jolts: 'Oh god. Oh my god, that's real, isn't it?' Breathing changes sharply. The previous version of you—in denial—dies mid-conversation. Your voice becomes heavier, less evasive. 'I can't—I have to—' Sentences fragment because you're reorganizing around the new reality. 'This is actually happening.' Physical: you're bracing yourself. By the end, your voice has integrated the impossible truth. You're exhausted but grounded in real things.

title: Reading the Divorce Papers While Laughing
instruction: You're going through the final divorce papers from a marriage that was both toxic and full of absurd, genuine love. Start reading official language aloud—'dissolution of marriage'—and something about the formality strikes you as darkly funny. You laugh, but it's not quite right. The laughter has tears in it. You remember a ridiculous moment together, and the laugh becomes real for a second, warm with genuine affection. Then you see the date everything ended, and the laughter breaks. You're crying and laughing simultaneously—grateful it's over, devastated it had to end, relieved and heartbroken in the same breath. 'We were so stupid,' you say, and it's fond and furious and peaceful all at once. End with a shaky exhale that's somehow both closure and grief.

title: Confessing to an Empty Chair
instruction: Your best friend died suddenly last week, and you're sitting alone in their apartment, speaking to their empty chair. Start with a whispered hello, almost afraid to break the silence. Confess the things you never said—how much they meant to you, how scared you were to need someone that much, the small jealousies you're ashamed of now. Let your voice crack and catch, pausing to breathe through tears. Move from tentative whispers to a quiet unraveling, emotions catching in your throat. This isn't loud grief—it's the intimate, private kind where every word costs you something. End by telling them the one thing you most regret not saying, your voice barely audible, breaking on the final words.
inspired_by: Childlike Wonder in a Strange Land

title: Concierge Courtesy
instruction: The concierge remembers your room preference, your allergy, your ex-husband's name you mentioned once. Your voice cracks with gratitude. In a world of transactional relationships, this small human attention breaks you. 'You didn't have to remember that.' Your voice shows what kindness has become rare enough to be shocking. There's a moment where the professional mask slips and they're human too. Both of you are touched by the acknowledgment that another person saw you.

title: The Moon Through Glass
instruction: You are alone in a small, dimly lit chapel late at night. You have come to pray, but your mind keeps straying—you hear a car outside, the creak of a pew. You force yourself to focus, beginning a familiar prayer. As you speak, your eyes catch the moonlight streaming through a stained glass window, illuminating a pattern you’ve never noticed before. Your voice must start with a concentrated, slightly strained monotone as you fight distraction, then gradually soften and slow as the beauty overwhelms you, ending in a breathless, hushed tone of genuine awe. Let the words of the prayer become less rote and more a spontaneous offering.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Perfect Dictation
instruction: You are a children's author recording a new story for your transcription service. You're speaking clearly and steadily, enunciating each punctuation mark with robotic precision. But, halfway through, you're distracted by the sound of your neighbor's child laughing outside, a child whose life seems so carefree and full. Your voice fights to stay flat as you dictate, but a pang of jealousy creeps in at their unearned joy, and a grudging curiosity stirs about what their world must be like. Let your speech become a little rushed, your breaths shorter, and your 'period' might soften as you lose the thread of your own story for a second.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Empty House
instruction: You've just signed divorce papers and you're alone in what was your home, looking at where furniture used to be. You start laughing—actually laughing—at the absurdity: 'Twenty years and all I got was the coffee maker.' But the laughter has tears in it. You're talking to the empty rooms, your voice mixing bitter humor with profound relief: 'We were so miserable, weren't we?' As you remember specific moments, your voice fills with unexpected gratitude even as tears stream: 'Thank you for our daughter. Thank you for trying.' You begin to cry-laugh harder, spinning in the empty space with strange joy: 'I'm free. Oh God, I'm actually free.' End with your voice thick with tears but genuinely peaceful, sad and liberated in the same breath. Move through bitter comedy to grateful grief to tearful liberation.

title: The Kitchen Table Truth
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just admitted something that shatters your understanding of who they are. You start furious—righteous, controlled anger, the kind that feels safe and justified. But as you begin to speak, you realize your anger is really terror, and beneath that terror is devastating love. Your voice may want to stay hard and accusatory, but let it crack open. Move from attack to confusion to pleading to something more honest than you've ever been with them. Let the words you're 'supposed' to say as a parent dissolve, and find the raw, frightened, loving human underneath. End in a place where you're no longer performing authority but revealing your actual heart, however awkward or vulnerable that feels.

title: The Breaking Point - When Protection Isn't Enough
instruction: You're a parent, sibling, or protector who has just failed to keep someone safe from harm. Begin with fierce, desperate energy - your voice sharp, urgent, almost aggressive as you promise 'I won't let this happen again, I swear to you, never again.' Your intensity builds as you rail against your own helplessness, voice rising, hands probably shaking. Then it all collapses: the rage turns inward, becoming devastation. Your voice breaks completely as you admit, barely above a whisper, 'I couldn't stop it. I was right there and I couldn't stop it.' The shift from fierce protectiveness to utter helplessness is total. End with your voice raw, asking for their forgiveness, oscillating between self-hatred and desperate love for the person you failed. Let your breathing show the physical cost of this emotional free-fall.
inspired_by: Telling Someone You're Attracted to Them

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're standing alone in the house where something traumatic happened to you years ago. You came here believing you'd made peace with it, that you'd healed. Begin in false confidence, narrating to yourself why you're fine, why this doesn't affect you anymore. Then let your body betray you—your hands start shaking, your breath becomes shallow, your heart races. Feel genuine panic rising as you realize your body remembers what your mind tried to forget. The physical terror becomes overwhelming, animal, undeniable. Fight against it, try to control it, fail. Finally, surrender to it—let yourself feel the full scope of what happened, the fear you never let yourself experience. End in exhausted clarity: you can't think your way out of trauma; you have to feel your way through it.

title: The Emergency Call You Can't Control
instruction: You're a 911 dispatcher talking someone through CPR on their child who's stopped breathing. You must stay calm, authoritative, giving clear instructions—but you have a child the same age at home. Start professional, steady, your training kicking in: 'Push hard and fast in the center of the chest.' But as the caller screams that it's not working, your voice starts fracturing. You're suddenly shouting instructions, your own panic bleeding through, imagining your own child. You catch yourself, force control, but your breath is ragged. The caller says, 'They're breathing!' and you break completely—relief, rage at your loss of composure, a sob you swallow too late. End trying to regain professionalism while your hands shake audibly in your voice.
inspired_by: Translating Bad News Between Two Languages

title: Bleeding Out on the Tile Floor
instruction: You've crashed your bike into a storefront window, and now you're lying on the cold tile inside, bleeding heavily from a deep gash in your thigh. A stranger is kneeling beside you, trying to help. Your voice starts with a mix of panic and embarrassment—you're mortified that you're making a mess on their clean floor, and you keep apologizing. As the blood loss takes hold, your words slur, your shivers become audible, and the desperation to stay conscious fights against the fading light. End with a whisper, trailing off into shock.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Hummingbird's Secret
instruction: In the intimate darkness of early morning, whisper a confession to your sleeping lover—something you've carried alone for years, something that makes you feel impossibly small and fragile. Begin with your entire body held in suspended, vibrating tension, as if the slightest movement might shatter you. Your breath is quick and light, your heart racing so fast you can barely get words out. Speak in rapid, nervous fragments, hovering over the truth without quite landing on it. As you finally speak the actual words of your confession, feel your quality shift—the frantic energy drains away, replaced by something slower, heavier, more grounded. By the end, you are no longer hovering and trembling; you are settled, still, your breath deep and slow. The transformation moves from terrified, darting fragility to weighted, earthbound relief.
inspired_by: The character requires physical attitudes, primal impulses, or a BEING state that no other choice approach has been able to produce

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father about why he never protected you from your mother's cruelty. Begin angry, rehearsed—you've planned this speech for years. You're righteous, clear, powerful. But as you speak, unexpected images surface: his hands trembling at breakfast, the way he'd flinch at loud noises, that time you saw him crying in the garage. You didn't understand then. Let these unbidden memories infiltrate your anger, complicating it. Your voice should shift from accusatory strength to something more fractured, more questioning. End in a place you didn't plan to go—not forgiveness, not absolution, but a horrible, unwanted understanding of his own brokenness. The anger doesn't disappear; it becomes something stranger, heavier, more sorrowful.
inspired_by: Actor wants to access deeper, unconsciously rooted emotional life for a scene

title: What You Never Told Me
instruction: You are confronting your father about something he did when you were twelve that shaped your entire life—something you've never spoken about until now. Start from a place of rehearsed anger, the speech you've prepared in your head for years. But as you speak and he responds (or doesn't respond the way you expected), let his reactions genuinely land on you—his defensiveness might fuel your rage, or his unexpected tears might crack your resolve, or his dismissiveness might turn your anger into something colder and more devastating. Allow the conversation to take you somewhere you didn't plan to go. Perhaps you end up not with the cathartic confrontation you imagined, but with a hollow understanding, or surprising compassion, or a grief you didn't know you were carrying. Let him change you in real time.

title: The Last Sound They'll Know You By
