instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love deeply who is dying, and they can no longer speak or open their eyes, but they can still hear you. You have three minutes to communicate everything you need to say, but you've lost the ability to form words—only sounds, tones, rhythms, and vocal textures emerge. Begin with the shock and denial of their fading, the desperate need to make them stay. Let your sounds shift as you move through your fear, your memories, your gratitude, and finally arrive at a place of release—giving them permission to go. The sounds at the beginning should feel tight, high, grasping. By the end, they should open, deepen, and carry them gently away.

title: The Last Refusal
instruction: You are an older man, pinned against a wall by a younger, stronger person. Their forearm presses against your throat, making every word a struggle and your voice raspy and strained. You are furious, but the sourness of defeat coats your tongue — you have finally lost a fight you started decades ago with your own pride. Begin with bitter, choked defiance, each syllable a battle. Let the physical pressure fray your thoughts and twist your pitch. As the pressure mounts, feel the fight drain out of you, and your voice softens into a final, broken whisper of resignation. End with a quiet, sour surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Beer
instruction: It's 3 AM in a nearly empty dive bar. You're a middle-aged man, just out of a divorce. You've had one too many energy drinks—your heart is pounding, and you feel wired, sour, and restless. You're leaving for a new city tomorrow, and your best friend is sitting across from you. You're proud of the life you built, but you're also gut-punched by sadness. You want to say something real, but your body feels like a humming wire—your pitch jumps, your speech speeds up, and you keep losing your train of thought. Start with defensive pride, then let the sourness and sorrow bleed through, ending in a raw, direct confession of how much this goodbye hurts.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Sadness (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just finished an intense physical ordeal—maybe you've been running until your body screams, maybe you've been in a fight, maybe you're in the aftermath of passionate intimacy. Your body is shaking, your breath ragged. Someone—a coach, a lover, a friend—is asking you rapid-fire questions: 'Why did you do that? What were you thinking? What do you want? What are you afraid of?' Start by trying to answer through your physical exhaustion, your words tangled with gasps and shudders. But as your body betrays you, let your mind follow. Begin to answer everything with raw, breathless honesty: 'I don't know.' Let the physical sensations overwhelm the need to explain yourself. End with your body still trembling but your voice finding a strange calm in surrender—the ecstasy of stopping the performance, even as every nerve is alive.

title: The Wrong Shelter
instruction: You’re caught in a torrential downpour, lost on a hiking trail. You have a map crumpled in your soaked hand—but you’ve already made a wrong turn twice. You spot a small cave up ahead and shout to a friend just beside you that you think this is the shelter you missed, but your own voice is nearly swallowed by the rain. At first, you’re confused, yelling with hope that this is the right place. As you get closer and see the cave is just a shallow rock overhang, your confusion hardens into rueful, shivering acceptance—you’re not safe yet. Micro-distractions like sputtering as rain hits your mouth, wiping your eyes, and the roar of thunder between sentences shape your words.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Thanking Your Ex at Their Wedding While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You've asked for a private moment before the ceremony. Your voice starts warm, almost steady: 'I wanted to tell you something before you go in there.' You're genuinely happy for them—and that's what makes this unbearable. Let real joy color your voice as you say they look beautiful, that their partner is lucky. Tell them thank you for the years you had, your voice swelling with authentic gratitude even as tears start. Here's where it gets complex: laugh softly, maybe at a specific memory, your voice light with real affection—but underneath, you're dying. The laughter catches, transforms. Your voice breaks as you admit: 'I thought it would be us.' Let that truth sit there, naked and devastating. But then—and this is crucial—pull yourself back to love that wants the best for them even as it costs you everything. End with 'Be happy. God, please be happy,' your voice simultaneously breaking and blessing them, grief and grace completely intertwined.
inspired_by: Asking Your Parent for Money While Ashamed

title: Confronting the Parent Who Made You Strong
instruction: You're facing your parent who pushed you relentlessly to achieve, and you've become exactly what they wanted—successful, admired, legendary in your field. Start with bitter triumph: 'I did it. Everything you said I had to do.' Your voice carries resentment and exhaustion. As you continue, let anger surface: 'But I don't know who I am without the pressure, without your voice in my head telling me I'm not enough.' Build to explosive confession—you're shouting through tears now. Then something shifts: you see their own pain, their own wounds. End in a quieter, broken place of painful understanding: 'You made me into something extraordinary... and I lost myself becoming it.' Mix rage with reluctant compassion.

title: The Thank You I Never Said
instruction: You are a child, maybe 8 or 9, sitting on a hospital bed with a concussion. Your head throbs and everything is slow, like wading through honey. Your mom just brought you your favorite stuffed rabbit, the one you've had since you were a baby. You're bitter—bitter that you fell off the swing, that your head hurts, that you're stuck here. But when you look at her face, crinkled with worry, a wave of fierce, intense affection hits you. You want to say thank you, but the words come out thick and sloppy, your volume too loud, then too quiet. You start with a grumble—'This stupid rabbit. My head feels like a bowling ball.'—but your voice softens as you clutch it, a real, fragile love cracking through. By the end, you're almost silent, whispering with a wince, 'You brought him. I love you.'
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Bitterness (extremely present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Sensation
instruction: You have a progressive illness, and you're losing sensation in your extremities. Your partner is massaging your feet, and you can still feel it—barely, faintly, but it's there. Speak in hushed, tender whispers, describing each sensation with desperate attention to detail because you know these feelings are slipping away. Your voice should be thick with unshed tears as you tell them exactly what you feel: the pressure, the warmth, the ghost of pleasure. This isn't about relaxation—it's about bearing witness to your own body while you still can. Let gratitude and grief intertwine in every word. Pause frequently, as if trying to hold onto the sensation a moment longer. End with a whispered confession: you're terrified of the day when you won't feel their touch anymore, when this intimacy will be reduced to watching them try to comfort a body that can no longer respond.

title: I Would Burn the World
instruction: Someone you're fiercely protective of—a child, a partner, a friend—has been hurt, and you're confronting the person responsible. Begin with volcanic rage, voice sharp and powerful: 'How dare you.' The fury is righteous, physical, your whole body engaged. But as you rail against their cruelty, helplessness crashes in—you couldn't prevent this pain, can't undo it. Your passionate declarations start breaking apart. Suddenly you're not shouting anymore; you're choking on tears, voice splintering between protective ferocity and devastating powerlessness. You want to destroy whoever caused this harm and simultaneously collapse under the weight of being unable to shield the person you love from all suffering. By the end, you're raw and exposed, your protective rage transformed into something more vulnerable: a desperate, tender vow whispered through tears to somehow make this right, even as you know some damage can't be undone.

title: Whispered Confession: The Night Before They Leave
instruction: It's 3 AM and your person is leaving tomorrow—leaving the country, leaving for good. You're lying in the dark, whispering so you don't shatter the fragile quiet. Begin almost inaudibly: 'Are you awake?' Your voice is tender, terrified. Let the words come slowly, catching in your throat: 'I need to tell you something I should have said months ago.' Feel the weight of time running out. Your voice trembles as you confess: 'I don't know how to be okay with you gone.' Let silence breathe between phrases—this isn't a speech, it's pulling truth from somewhere deep. Your voice breaks softly: 'You changed everything and I never told you.' Let tears come without sound, just breath and heartbreak. Find the courage to say it plainly, whispered but clear: 'I love you. I'm in love with you.' Sit in the terrifying vulnerability. Then their hand finds yours in the dark, and your voice becomes even softer, almost a smile through tears: 'I just needed you to know.' End in the quiet of two people holding impossible feelings.

title: The Kitchen Floor Confession
instruction: You are confronting your mother (or father) in the kitchen where you grew up. You start angry—voice raised, pacing, listing grievances you've carried for years. You came here to finally tell them how they failed you, how they weren't there when you needed them. But halfway through your accusations, they say something small and true that breaks through your armor—maybe an admission of their own fear, their own inadequacy. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it begins to crack open. Your voice lowers. You find yourself sitting on the floor, and suddenly you're not accusing—you're asking questions you were too afraid to ask as a child. 'Why didn't you...' becomes 'Did you ever...' becomes 'I needed you to...' End with your anger transformed into a desperate, vulnerable plea to finally understand each other. Let your voice shake with the effort of staying open instead of slamming the door.

title: The Museum of Almost
instruction: You are packing up your home of twenty years, holding an object that represents a dream you abandoned—a musical instrument you never mastered, a wedding dress never worn, acceptance letter to a program you didn't attend, a baby's item for a child who never came. Begin with bitter humor, making sarcastic jokes to yourself about your failures as you handle this object. But as you physically interact with it—feel its weight, texture, temperature—let yourself access the precise moment you first acquired it, the specific hope you carried then. Let yourself feel both the loss of that dream AND the life you actually lived instead. This isn't about regret—allow yourself to genuinely grieve what didn't happen while simultaneously discovering unexpected gratitude for what did. End with a decision about the object (keep it or let it go) that embodies this complex double-truth. Your voice should travel from defensive mockery through genuine grief to a tender, complicated acceptance that holds both joy and sorrow without resolving them.
inspired_by: Choice Hunt / Building a Repertoire of UC Choices

title: The Last Thing Standing Between
instruction: You're holding a weapon, standing between someone you love and an immediate threat—could be an attacker, an angry mob, a dangerous animal, a person in authority coming to take them away. Start with a voice of absolute steel: commanding, fierce, dangerous. But as the threat persists and you realize you might actually have to use violence, your voice begins to fracture. Rage and terror swirl together. You're screaming threats but also pleading. Your protectiveness is so fierce it becomes almost feral, but underneath is the helpless knowledge that you might not be enough. Let your voice crack between 'I will kill you' and 'please don't make me do this.' End with either a roar of commitment or a sob of desperate inadequacy—or both at once.

title: Reading Your Eulogy at Your Own Living Funeral
instruction: You've chosen to hold your own funeral while you're still alive, and you're speaking to everyone you love gathered in one room. Start with humor, voice light and wry, making jokes about your own mortality, maybe even laughing as you acknowledge the strangeness of this moment. As you look at their faces, the laughter becomes something else — your voice breaks mid-sentence, tears mixing with smiles, trying to tell them how grateful you are while your heart is breaking at the thought of leaving them. End with profound peace underneath the sadness, your voice steady again but softer, thanking them for making your life worth living. Navigate from self-deprecating levity through emotional overwhelm to bittersweet acceptance, holding joy and sorrow in the same breath.
inspired_by: Phone Sex Operator on Their First Day

title: The Things We Never Say at Thresholds
instruction: You're standing in the doorway of your child's empty bedroom the night before they leave for good—not college, but a life on another continent, a choice that means you'll become people who see each other once a year if you're lucky. Speak to the silence, your voice barely above a whisper. Start with small observations—'You forgot your blue sweater'—but let each detail unravel you. Your words should tremble with all the things a parent can never say: that you're terrified, that you're proud, that letting go feels like learning to breathe underwater. End with a confession spoken to the empty room, something tender and broken about how you're not ready but you'll pretend to be. This is love as quiet devastation.

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've loved for decades as they take their final breaths. Begin by trying to stay composed, holding their hand, telling them practical things about what you'll do after. But as you notice the changing light through the window—the way it falls across their face exactly as it did the first morning you woke up together—allow your controlled farewell to dissolve. Let memories flood through you unbidden: not the ones you planned to share, but the small, strange moments that surface on their own—the way they hummed while cooking, a ridiculous argument about nothing, the precise feeling of their hand in yours on an ordinary Tuesday. Your voice should shift from steady and brave to broken and raw, but find within that breaking a kind of fierce gratitude. End not with goodbye, but with a whispered realization of something you never said that suddenly seems to contain everything.

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye You've Been Dreading
instruction: Your best friend of thirty years is moving across the world tomorrow, chasing love, and you're genuinely happy for them even as you're losing your person. Start reminiscing about ridiculous shared memories, laughing genuinely, voice bright with joy and affection. Let gratitude pour out - 'you made me who I am' - voice warm and full. But let the laughter start catching in your throat, mixing with tears you're trying to hide. Your voice should break mid-sentence, then laugh again through the crying, creating that specific sound of joy and grief tangled together. End with a fierce, almost angry declaration of love: 'go be happy, damn it,' voice shaking with laughter and tears and pride and devastating loss all at once. Make it messy, real, beautifully contradictory. Let yourself be undone by loving someone enough to let them go.
inspired_by: Your Teenage Child Coming Out to You

title: The Night Garden
instruction: You're a mother who has been up all night with a feverish child. The fever finally broke an hour ago. Now it's 3 AM and you've snuck out to your backyard, giddy with relief. You're talking to the moon and the sleeping garden, your voice fast and wobbly from exhaustion and joy. You point out silly things—a snail on a leaf, a dropped garden glove—finding them hilarious. But as you speak, you notice a shooting star and your voice slows, softens, into a hushed, reverent awe. You whisper to yourself, feeling small and lucky. Let the first sentences tumble out breathless and gigglish, then let the silence of the sky pull you into something quieter, deeper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Your Difficult Parent
instruction: You're giving the eulogy for a parent you had a complicated, often painful relationship with. Your voice starts formal, appropriate, saying the things you're supposed to say. But then a memory surfaces—something absurd, darkly funny—and before you can stop it, you're laughing. Real laughter mixed with tears. Your voice becomes animated, almost giddy as you describe their ridiculous quirks, the impossible situations they created. The laughter feels good, feels like truth, even though you're crying too. But then the laughter shifts—underneath it is grief you didn't expect to feel. Your voice breaks as you realize you're mourning not who they were, but who they could have been, who you needed them to be. You're laughing and sobbing simultaneously, thanking them for the few good moments while acknowledging the pain, expressing relief they're at peace while admitting you're not. Your voice becomes a beautiful mess of contradictions: bitter and grateful, angry and loving, devastated and liberated. End with a genuine, tearful 'Goodbye' that contains everything—all the complexity of loving someone who hurt you.
inspired_by: Dream Job First Week: Imposter Syndrome Detonating

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission, making your final call to Earth before communication becomes impossible. You begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect your elderly parent from the truth of what 'one-way' really means. But as they say they're proud of you, your voice starts to fracture. You need them to know you're scared. You need to hear them say they love you one more time. The words catch in your throat as you realize this is the last time you'll ever hear their voice. End by whispering 'I have to go now' while every part of you is screaming to stay on the line. Let your voice break on the word 'goodbye.' The emotional journey moves from artificial brightness to raw, childlike fear to a devastating acceptance that splits you open.
inspired_by: Hearing Your Child Get Bullied and Intervening

title: The Shirt That Holds You
instruction: You're alone in your bedroom, holding a piece of your absent lover's clothing—a shirt, a sweater, something that still carries their scent. Begin in aching silence, pressing the fabric to your face. Allow yourself to perceive their physical presence in the cloth: feel the warmth of their skin radiating from it, sense the weight of their arms around you, smell not just their cologne but the unique scent of their neck, hear their breathing close to your ear. Whisper the things you never said, the confessions you held back. Let the sensory illusion feel so real that its inevitable dissolution breaks you—the moment you open your eyes and they're still gone. Move from desperate comfort to unbearable loss, your voice barely audible, catching on words.

title: The Last Translation
instruction: You are translating your grandmother's final words from her native language as she lies dying, but you realize mid-translation that you've been mishearing and mistranslating her stories your entire life. Begin with confident, dutiful translation, speaking clearly for the family gathered around. Then let confusion creep in as the words don't match what you thought you knew. Your voice should crack as you understand—she's been trying to tell you something crucial for years, and you've been getting it wrong. End with desperate attempts to understand, mixing your language with hers, your professional translator voice breaking down into the frightened grandchild who's running out of time. Let the weight of all those lost conversations crush you as you grasp for meaning in her fading breaths.

title: Vigil Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's unconscious in hospice, and you've been holding their hand for hours in silence. Finally, in barely more than a whisper, you start speaking—telling them all the things you never said when they were awake to hear it. Begin with small, tender observations: how you loved the way they laughed at their own jokes, how you still think of something they said years ago. Your voice is so quiet it almost blends with the sound of their breathing. Gradually, the confession deepens: you tell them about a choice you made that hurt them, or a moment you failed them, or how you've been terrified of this ending. There's no drama here, just the catch in your throat as you speak truths in the dark. End with the simplest words—maybe 'thank you' or 'I'm sorry' or 'please don't go'—but let them carry the weight of everything you couldn't say before. This is intimacy at its most naked: just your voice, their silence, and the truth finally spoken.

title: Numbed Confession at the Pharmacy
instruction: You're standing at the pharmacy counter, still half-numb from dental work, trying to pick up a prescription for the pain meds that clearly won't help the pride you feel in having gotten through the procedure. The pharmacist looks at you with that blank professional face, and you start to explain why you need the numbing again, but your words come out like a drunk toddler's—this makes you laugh despite yourself, as you also feel a flicker of disappointment that you can't even pronounce 'acetaminophen.' Speak slowly, letting the amusement peek through the frustration, and let your voice trail off as you realize you're drooling a little, then rally with a sigh that holds both pride for trying and the quiet letdown of this ridiculous moment.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Disappointment (slightly present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a wound they gave you years ago that you've never spoken about. Start by circling around it—nervous, careful, trying to be respectful even while angry. Notice how they respond, really look at them, and let that shift what you say next. As you speak, peel away your own defenses. Your anger might crack into grief, or your grief might ignite into rage, or you might discover unexpected compassion as you see them truly vulnerable for the first time. Let your voice and words respond honestly to what you're actually experiencing moment by moment, not what you planned to say. End somewhere you didn't expect—perhaps in mutual understanding, perhaps in deeper pain, but transformed from where you began.

title: Mad King Sanity Loss
instruction: You're a ruler losing your mind in real-time, and you're aware of it. Your voice starts somewhat coherent: you're issuing orders that make perfect sense to you but are clearly paranoid. You address people not in the room. Your speech becomes increasingly fragmented, poetic, then nonsensical. You're laughing at things that aren't funny. Your voice speeds up, then drops into a terrified whisper. You're begging an imaginary advisor for counsel. You recognize your own deterioration—'I can't trust what I'm hearing'—but you can't stop it. End with a moment of terrible clarity where you realize you're unreliable and you're in charge of an empire.

title: Dancing Alone in Their Clothes
instruction: You're wearing your late partner's shirt, their favorite song is playing, and you're dancing alone in the kitchen where you used to dance together. Begin with a small laugh that catches in your throat—you're swaying, remembering: 'You always said I had no rhythm.' Your voice is light, almost playful, but there's an ache underneath. As you continue moving, the emotions start colliding: you laugh-cry as you spin: 'God, I can still feel your hands here—' touching your waist. Your voice breaks but you're still swaying, and now you're speaking through tears that somehow feel okay: 'This is so stupid and so beautiful and I hate it and I love it.' You're laughing and sobbing at once, your voice thick: 'Thank you for teaching me that joy doesn't disappear just because you did.' The final moment: you stop moving, breathless, your voice a whisper of wonder mixed with grief: 'I'm learning to hold both—the missing and the gratitude. Both at the same time.'

title: Ecstasy Turning to Ash
instruction: You're in the midst of intense physical and emotional ecstasy—the peak of passion, reunion, or transcendent joy—when you suddenly realize this person is about to leave you forever, or this moment will never come again. Begin with sounds of pure pleasure, abandon, breathless joy—let your voice be unguarded and animal. Then let the realization creep in, transforming the sounds. Your breathing changes. Pleasure and grief become indistinguishable. Let primal sounds emerge that blend ecstasy with devastation—you're trying to hold onto the joy even as it disintegrates. The physical sensations remain but now they hurt. End in a place where pleasure and pain are the same sound, where you're both fully present in the moment and already mourning its loss.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never Present
instruction: You're sitting in the grass where you used to play alone as a child, and your parent is finally here beside you after years of absence. Begin calmly, almost numbly, describing the grass and the place, your voice controlled and distant. Then let the real feelings surface: start asking why—why they were never here for moments like this, why you had to lie in this grass alone, imagining what it would be like if they cared. Your voice should move from cold control to raw accusation, then crack into the vulnerable child underneath, the one who just wanted them to notice. End with a moment of devastating honesty about what their absence cost you, voice stripped of all pretense, just the painful truth spoken with both anger and a heartbreaking need for them to finally understand.
inspired_by: Lying in a Patch of Soft, Shaded Grass

title: The Waiting Room of Infinity
instruction: You are an elderly man who has taken LSD with your adult granddaughter, who is now entranced by a lava lamp for what feels like hours. The trip has been long and you are deeply exhausted, but you’ve also become irritable, feeling she has dragged you into a pointless detour. You begin trying to get her attention with a blunt, weary complaint, but as you speak, the patterns on the ceiling pull at your focus, and your frustration softens into a wondering, philosophical sigh. Your voice should start tight and clipped with impatience, then drift into slow, hushed awe as your annoyance dissolves into the overwhelming beauty you can’t stop seeing.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Protecting My Sister From What I Know is Coming
instruction: You're standing in the water with your younger sister, trying to describe the beauty of how it feels, but you've just learned she's dying—six months, maybe less. Begin with fierce, almost frantic joy, splashing, laughing, making her laugh, overcompensating with enthusiasm about every sensation. But your voice starts to fracture. The more beautiful you try to make it sound, the more your desperation bleeds through. Suddenly you break—exploding into raw confession about how unfair this is, rage at the universe mixed with helpless tenderness, your voice careening between shouting and sobbing. End in exhausted whispers, still describing the water but now with devastating acceptance, holding onto this moment because you know how few remain.
inspired_by: Walking Barefoot Through Shallow, Cool Water

title: The Hidden Wheeze
instruction: You are a teenage boy with a deep, hyper-masculine voice, in a high school locker room after practice. Your asthma is flaring up from the cold air, but you're desperate to hide it from your friends because you're ashamed of seeming weak. Begin with intense concentration—forcing casual, steady breaths and short, clipped words to mask the wheeze. As the attack worsens and your inhaler clicks between lines, let confusion creep in as you realize you can't control this. End with a quiet, bewildered admission that your body is betraying you, spoken almost to yourself while you fumble to catch your breath.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Concentration (extremely present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Traitor's Helm
instruction: You are a knight in a dim, damp tent, facing a man you trusted who has just confessed to selling out your company. You wear your full helm, visor down. The metal cage rings around your voice, and every time you shift your head, the visor clanks. Start with a cold, measured fury—every word precise, the anger locked tight beneath a thin layer of control. But as you speak, the betrayal cuts deeper, and your voice begins to crack and surge. Let the helm's resonance amplify your growls. End with a raw, thunderous outburst, the visor rattling with your words. The spoken performance: 'So. After twenty years of shared bread and battlefield mud, this is what you choose? My throat tightens just looking at you. You sold us for coin? For a woman's smile? I should smash your face into this very dirt. But no… I want you to ride home with this shame rotting your guts. Now get out of my sight before the helm fails to hold back my blade.'
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Compromised Security
instruction: Your smart home has been hacked. Someone's been watching through the camera. Your voice jumps an octave with initial panic, then plummets to something predatory and protective. You're checking the timeline: how long? What did they see? Your breathing becomes rapid, and you're physically moving through your house, voice clipped and urgent. The violation sits in every word. By the end, you're calling the police, trying to sound calm but utterly exposed.

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're returning home after years away, standing in your childhood bedroom. You came here to pack it up, to be practical and efficient. But being in this space cracks something open. Start organized and business-like, touching objects with detached purpose. Then let contradictory feelings attack you without warning or justification—suddenly fierce joy at a memory, immediately followed by sobbing grief, then inexplicable rage at your younger self, then tender laughter, then shouting at the walls about something that makes no sense, then curling up with an old stuffed animal, then standing and spinning with arms wide in celebration or surrender. Don't bridge these emotions—let them ambush you. Your relationship to this room contains everything: loss and love, resentment and gratitude, the person you were and the person you became. End in a state that combines multiple feelings at once: laughing while crying, angry but grateful, devastated but free. Move from false composure through irrational emotional storm to complex, contradictory truth.

title: Forgiveness Given
instruction: You're facing the person who deeply hurt you, and you've decided to forgive them. Your voice is strong but gentle: 'I've been angry at you for a long time.' They're waiting for more condemnation. Instead: 'But I'm letting it go.' Your voice carries the weight of that choice. 'What you did was wrong. It hurt me deeply. But holding onto that hurt is hurting me more.' The person is crying. Your voice becomes warmer: 'I forgive you. Not because you deserve it, but because I deserve to be free.' The person tries to apologize, and you raise a hand: 'You don't need to apologize anymore. I've already forgiven you.' The forgiveness is in the steadiness of your voice, the lack of bitterness. By the end: 'I hope you forgive yourself too. I think that's what I had to learn.' The voice of forgiveness is the voice of freedom.

title: The Intervention: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Erased
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent, finally ready to speak the truth you've carried for decades. Start with careful control—you've rehearsed this, you're determined to stay calm, to be the adult. Tell them what they did, what they failed to see, how their neglect shaped you. But as you speak, your composure fractures. The child inside you emerges—raw, desperate for acknowledgment, furious and heartbroken simultaneously. Your voice moves from measured accusation to something far more vulnerable: begging them to remember, to admit, to see you. When they can't or won't, you feel yourself giving up mid-sentence. The fight drains out. You finish not with anger but with devastating, quiet resignation. Begin controlled and confrontational. End with the exhausted grief of someone who realizes their parent will never become who you needed them to be.
inspired_by: Professional: Pastor Loses Faith During His Own Sermon

title: The Unexpected Revelation
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a bustling cocktail party, wearing a silk blouse and clutching a glass of wine. Your voice is deliberately high and soft, a practiced femininity that you’ve used for decades. Across the small table stands a man much younger than you, his eyes catching yours. You feel a sudden, intense rush of sexual lust—a warm, almost giddy heat that makes you lean in, speaking a little louder over the clinking glasses and chatter, your tone playful and breathy. You flirt openly, praising his tie, touching his arm. Then he mentions his wife, casually. Astonishment floods you. Your voice drops, goes flat, a short ‘Oh’ escapes before you recover into a brittle laugh, the earlier warmth gone, replaced by a guarded, sharp-edged surprise. Let your volume and pitch rise and fall with the ambient noise—project when needed, but let the truth of your emotions fracture the performance naturally.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What I Whisper in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM, and you're lying next to someone who believes they know you completely. They're half-asleep, and you're whispering to them—or perhaps to yourself. Begin with the soft, safe things you'd normally murmur in this intimate darkness: 'I love you,' 'sleep well,' the comfortable phrases of established intimacy. Then, let your whisper carry what you've never said aloud: the part of yourself you hide from everyone, the fear that wakes you up at night, the desire you're ashamed of, the vulnerability you've protected for so long. Keep your voice quiet, but let the emotional weight grow enormous. This isn't about volume—it's about the terror and relief of finally speaking the unspeakable. End somewhere between liberation and fear, having crossed a threshold you can never uncross.
inspired_by: This Is What I Usually Say, and This Is What I Really Want to Say

title: The Fever Dream of Reunion
instruction: You are running toward someone you thought you'd lost forever—after years, after war, after everyone said they were dead. Your body is electric with a wild cocktail of sensations: your heart pounding so hard it hurts, your legs burning as you run, tears and laughter erupting simultaneously, your whole physical self screaming with the impossibility of this moment. Let every part of your body express this explosive reunion—arms reaching, stumbling, grabbing, spinning. You're laughing and sobbing and your body can't contain it. Then, mid-embrace, let a wave of grief crash through—the sudden, visceral realization of all the lost time, all the moments you'll never get back, the years stolen from you. Your body must show this shift: the frantic joy collapsing into desperate clinging, your grip changing from celebration to preservation, as if holding on tighter could make up for the absence. End physically exhausted, empty, and full all at once.

title: Hands In Cold Water
instruction: You are standing at a sink with your hands plunged in ice-cold water, and you've just received news that changes everything—maybe someone you love is coming back, or you got the call you've been desperate for, or you've been betrayed, or you're finally free of something. The physical shock of the cold is mixing with the emotional shock of the news. Let the sensation of the cold water anchor you as emotions riot through your body. Your voice starts controlled, reporting what happened, but the cold and the feeling start to overwhelm that control. Let pleasure mix with pain, let joy feel dangerous, let rage feel physical. Your breath changes, your body responds to both the temperature and the emotion. By the end, you don't know if you're gasping from cold or from feeling, and that confusion is honest. Let the physical sensation unlock something rawer than you planned to reveal.

title: The Last Visit Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your younger sibling who enlisted without telling you, leaving tomorrow for a war zone. Start with hurt and anger—'You didn't even ask me what I thought'—your voice tight with betrayal. But as you look at their face, fear creeps in. Your anger softens into desperate worry: 'What if you don't come back?' Your voice breaks. Try to be supportive, try to be proud, but underneath is this raw terror you can't control. End with a whispered confession that costs you everything: 'I don't know how to be okay with this.' You're trying to give them your blessing while your heart is shattering, holding them tight while wanting to drag them back from the edge of the world.

title: Telling Your Child Why You're Leaving
instruction: You're sitting on your child's bed, trying to explain why you're leaving their other parent—and them—for six months of inpatient treatment. Start with false brightness, trying to make it sound like an adventure, like everything's fine. Your child asks a question that breaks through your performance: 'Don't you love us anymore?' Your voice fails. The truth comes out in fragments—you're scared you're becoming the parent you swore you'd never be, that you need help before you damage them beyond repair. Your words become raw, honest, desperate for them to understand. You shift between defending yourself and condemning yourself. By the end, you're asking your child for forgiveness while simultaneously trying to be the strong parent. Your voice carries both your breaking and your determination to be whole again.
inspired_by: Group Sharing: Introducing Yourself as a Survivor

title: Standing Your Ground as the Tide Comes In
instruction: You're standing ankle-deep where the waves meet the shore, and someone you love is trying to leave you. Start by describing the sand beneath your feet—how solid it feels at first, how the water swirls around your ankles as waves roll in. Your voice begins fierce and protective, almost defiant, insisting they stay, listing all the reasons they can't leave. But as you speak, describe how each wave pulls more sand from beneath your feet, how you're sinking, losing your foundation. Let your fierce conviction begin to crack as you realize you can't hold them, can't hold anything. Your tone should shift from passionate certainty to desperate pleading, then finally to a kind of helpless rage that dissolves into sobbing—not dramatic crying, but the real, ugly kind that comes from your gut. End with you describing how you've sunk deeper into the sand, immobilized, as you watch them walk away, your voice barely able to form words through the grief and fury at your own powerlessness.

title: Laughing While the World Burns Down
instruction: You've just received news that should destroy you—a terminal diagnosis, a final rejection, the end of everything you've built. But something in you has cracked open into strange, inappropriate laughter. Begin actually laughing, finding the absurd dark humor in the cosmic joke of it all. Then let gratitude flood through—for having lived at all, for the beauty you've known, even for this devastating moment that proves you were alive enough to lose something. Your voice should oscillate between laughter and tears, between thank you and this isn't fair, between peace and panic. End in a place of surrendered joy, where heartbreak and grace exist in the same breath. This is about finding light not despite the darkness but because of it. Make it honest, strange, beautifully human.
inspired_by: The Photographer and the Ghostly Apparition

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying beside your partner in the predawn darkness, hours before you leave for a deployment you know is dangerous. You're trying to memorize the sound of their breathing, the warmth of their skin. Begin by whispering small observations—'Your hand is so warm,' 'I can hear your heartbeat'—but underneath is the terror you're trying not to name. Your voice should be tender but trembling, intimate but holding back the flood. As you continue, the reality breaks through: you might not come back. Let your whisper crack as you move from trying to comfort them to needing comfort yourself. The desire to stay, to stop time, to crawl inside this moment forever should be audible. End with a whispered 'I love you' that contains both absolute certainty and the knowledge that it might be the last time you say it.

title: The Chair in the Hallway
instruction: You’re in the hallway of your apartment building at 2 a.m., sitting on a chair you pulled out of storage. You’ve been waiting 28 hours for a delivery that was supposed to arrive this afternoon—your best friend’s wedding dress, which you had altered. Your body feels heavy, your eyes keep closing mid-thought, and your voice is flat, almost slurred, with hollow pauses. You’re talking to no one, just the empty hall, voicing your disappointment that it never came. Then your phone buzzes: a text from the delivery driver saying they’re three minutes away. Let the exhaustion still sit in your bones, but let a raw, surprised elation break through—your voice slightly higher, a little shaky, like a kid who just found their lost toy. Start defeated, hollow, then end with a tired but genuine smile in your voice.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Morning After the Funeral
instruction: You've just inherited something from someone who died—their house, their journals, their life's work—and you're going through their belongings when you discover evidence that they loved you in ways you never knew while they were alive. Begin speaking aloud to the empty room with bitter, almost angry laughter—'Of course you waited until now to show me this.' Let your voice carry resentment for all the years of distance, all the times they could have said these things. But as you continue reading or touching their objects, let grief flood in underneath the anger. Your voice should crack between fury at their absence and overwhelming gratitude for what they left. End weeping with laughter, or laughing through tears, unable to separate your rage at their death from your joy at finally understanding they loved you. Move from bitter anger to a messy, contradictory storm of grief, love, resentment, and gratitude all at once.

title: The Sour Drawer
instruction: You're an older man cleaning out a long-forgotten kitchen drawer. Your fingers hit a sticky, mold-covered candy wrapper—the source of a faint rotten smell you've been ignoring. The disgust is immediate and intense, making you recoil and mutter under your breath. But as you toss it aside, you remember your late wife secretly stashing her favorite caramels there to hide them from the grandkids. A small, rueful chuckle escapes—you can almost hear her laugh. That fondness pulls you into the memory, your voice softening, slowing, and aching as you whisper about how she always won that little game.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Final Game
instruction: You're a teenager, sitting across from your older brother who has bullied you for years. Tonight, you finally rigged his online game account so it will wipe his entire progress — and you're about to tell him, calmly, as you both stare at the screen. Begin with cold satisfaction, your voice low and deliberate, each word a nail. But as you speak, a wave of shame hits you — you hate that you've become this, that you've planned this so carefully, that he made you this petty. Let your voice crack slightly, lose the rhythm, falter as you admit the truth, then steady again with quiet, broken resolve.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Truth I've Carried Like a Stone
instruction: You are confronting your mother/father/child about something they did years ago that shattered you—a betrayal, an abandonment, a cruelty they never acknowledged. Start with controlled anger, trying to be measured and articulate. As they deny or deflect, feel your control slipping. Let your voice crack, let your body shake, let the hurt underneath the anger come screaming to the surface. Push past the point where you'd normally pull back and be 'reasonable.' Go to the rawest, most unfiltered place—where you're simultaneously a wounded child and a furious adult. End not with resolution, but with the exhausted, vulnerable truth of how deeply you've needed them to see what they did.
inspired_by: Actor is afraid of losing control emotionally at moments of peak feeling

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because you do, and staying would destroy you both. You're whispering so you don't wake them, your voice catching on every word: 'I'm so sorry. God, I'm so sorry.' You're memorizing their face in the darkness. Your whisper becomes even softer, more intimate: 'You're going to think I stopped loving you, but that's not... that's never been the problem.' Tears are sliding silently down your face. You want to touch them one last time but you can't, because if they wake up, you won't be able to leave. Your voice breaks on a tiny, desperate sound: 'You deserved someone whole. Someone who could...' You can't finish. You're crying now, still whispering: 'Be happy. Please, please be happy.' You stand to leave, and your final words are barely audible, soaked in tenderness and devastation: 'I will love you until I die.'

title: The Last Migration
instruction: You are an elderly man standing alone in a vast open wheat field at sunset. A massive flock of birds passes overhead, their distant calls barely reaching you. At first, you are filled with awe and sharp interest—you track them with your eyes, squinting against the low sun, feeling their wild freedom. But as they dissolve into the horizon, a quiet, staggering longing rises in your chest for your own youth, for the days when you too could simply leave it all behind. Your voice should start with wonder and a little breathlessness, then grow brittle and small as the wind snatches your words. Let the open air make you feel exposed, let your voice crack, let the silence after each phrase feel more heavy than the sound before.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Longing (very intensely present), Interest (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Blood and Boredom
instruction: You're a twelve-year-old boy who's been sneaking sips of your dad's whiskey while playing an online shooter. Your voice is forced deep, trying to sound older, but it cracks. Start mid-match: you just got a brutal kill and you're riding that high—malice drips from your callout as you taunt the enemy. But the buzz is wearing off, and the numbness creeps in. As you reload, your bravado falters. The game fades. You admit quietly to your teammate that you don't even feel anything anymore. Your voice should shift from aggressive, intoxicated glee to a hollow, almost childlike confession, with pauses where you lose your train of thought.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Victory at the Funeral
instruction: You're standing at the funeral of someone who made your life difficult—maybe a critical parent, a rival, an ex who hurt you. You've always been the victim in this story, the one who suffered because of them. Begin speaking (internally or aloud to their casket) with that wounded energy, finally able to say everything you held back. But as you speak, let something unexpected emerge—gratitude. Not gratitude that they're gone, but recognition of how that suffering shaped you, made you stronger, taught you something essential. Let yourself move from victim to something more powerful and complex—someone who can hold both the pain they caused and the strange gift it became. End in a place of surprising freedom, where you're releasing both the person and the identity of being wounded by them, feeling grief and relief and strength all tangled together.
inspired_by: The character's behavior and inner life can be identified as coming from a specific dominant personality facet (e.g., a victim, a warrior, a free spirit, a moralist, a satanic energy)

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at 3 AM. You've been the strong one, the caretaker, but now you need to tell them something you've carried alone for decades. Start with your voice barely above a whisper: 'Mom/Dad... I need to tell you something before you go.' Your hands are shaking. Then the confession spills out—maybe it's about your sexuality, your dreams they never knew about, or a hurt from childhood you buried. Your voice cracks with a lifetime of fear: 'I was so scared you'd be disappointed.' But as you speak, something shifts. Their hand squeezes yours—or maybe they just look at you with complete understanding—and suddenly you're sobbing with relief, then laughing softly through tears at the absurdity of waiting this long. End with quiet, profound peace: 'Thank you for loving all of me. I can let you go now.' Your voice is tender, exhausted, but finally, finally free.

title: Crunching to Calm
instruction: You're at a loud house party, standing near the snack table, nibbling on a handful of tortilla chips. You're a little drunk—words come out in bursts, you lose your train of thought, and the crunching interrupts your sentences. You just got a text that your best friend landed safely after a scary flight. Start with the jittery, disjointed relief of intoxication: your voice lifts and drops mid-word, you pause to chew and swallow, and you repeat yourself. As you talk about how worried you were, the relief hits you fully—your voice slows, deepens, and becomes breathy. End with a soft, quiet laugh, the crunching a steady background rhythm, your tone settling into a warm, grateful whisper.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Body's Testimony
instruction: You've just experienced something intensely physical—maybe violence, maybe passion, maybe childbirth, maybe a physical injury—and your body is still reverberating with sensation. Begin speaking while your breath is still irregular, your nerves still electric. Describe what's happening in your body using your own strange associations—not clinical language, not cliché metaphors, but the bizarre, specific, possibly embarrassing ways YOU experience physical intensity. Let pleasure mix with pain, or rage with unexpected arousal, or agony with dark humor. Your voice should be uncontrolled—laughing when you shouldn't, gasping mid-sentence, getting louder then suddenly quiet. End in a place where the physical sensation has unlocked an emotional truth you didn't know was there, spoken in whatever fractured way it emerges.

title: The Truth That Ruins Everything
instruction: You're confronting someone you love—a parent, a former lover, a once-close friend—about a painful truth you've carried silently for years. Start with your voice tight, controlled, almost cold with the protective armor you've built. As you begin to speak the truth aloud for the first time, something unexpected happens: the anger you thought you'd feel transforms into grief. Your voice breaks not with rage but with the sadness of lost years, lost possibilities. You're not attacking them; you're mourning what could have been different. End with a vulnerable question, barely above a whisper, asking if they can finally see what their actions cost you. Let your voice carry the weight of someone who needs to be heard more than they need to be right.

title: Hope Rising
instruction: After weeks of things falling apart, something small shifts. The doctor says 'maybe.' Your therapist says you've made progress. One good conversation. Your voice, which has been flat, starts to have architecture again. 'Maybe,' you say to yourself, testing the word. It doesn't feel like lying. Hope is terrifying—it's fragile—so your voice is soft, provisional: 'I think I might be okay.' Breathing gets deeper, fuller. There's a cautious lift to intonation. Physical: you sit up straighter. By the end, your voice has more presence, though still careful, still afraid of jinxing it.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You're terminally ill and recording a message to be played at your funeral. Start with genuine laughter as you acknowledge the absurdity of talking to people at your own memorial service. Make jokes about death, about your life, finding real humor in the ridiculousness of human existence. But let the laughter become increasingly fragile—catch yourself mid-laugh as grief for your own lost future breaks through. Your voice should dance between joy at the life you've lived and sorrow for all you'll miss. Express deep gratitude for specific people and moments, but let your voice crack with the unfairness of having to leave. End with a moment of profound peace and acceptance mixed with one last laugh through tears—maybe at death itself, maybe at the beauty of having lived at all. The final words should be both a goodbye and a celebration, your voice warm with love but trembling with loss, landing on something like 'this was enough' or 'thank you' that holds both complete contentment and complete heartbreak.
inspired_by: Waking Up from Anesthesia: Post-Surgery Babbling

title: The Confession They Never Wanted
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth they've refused to see for years—how their choices shaped your wounds. Begin with trembling anger, voice sharp with decades of swallowed words: 'You never asked what I needed. You just assumed.' Feel the rage building, righteous and hot. But mid-confrontation, something cracks—you hear the vulnerability beneath your own fury. Your voice drops, becomes almost a plea: 'I needed you to see me. Just... see me.' The anger dissolves into raw grief. End with exhausted honesty, tears in your throat: 'I'm telling you now because I still hope... I still hope we could be different.' Let the transformation from rage to heartbreak happen organically, messily, truthfully.

title: The Last Word
instruction: You are an older woman speaking to your grandchild on a video call. You want to tell them a cherished memory, but your voice trembles and fades, your hands shake, and you have to stop to swallow. Start with a bright, forced cheerfulness that breaks down as you struggle to finish the sentence, ending in a quiet, sad realization that you can't say what you meant. Let your concentration slip as you focus on controlling your tremor, then lose the thought and find it again in a simpler, softer tone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Crimson Confrontation
instruction: You are at a party, cornering a friend who has been flirting with your crush. You are close enough to see the flecks in her eyes, your voice tight and dry, no room to echo. Start with a controlled, almost whispered accusation laced with jealousy—your envy of her ease, her confidence. Let that simmer into a raw, cracking anger as you relive every stolen glance, your throat straining with hard glottal attacks. Fidget with the hem of your shirt, lose your train of thought mid-sentence, then reclaim it with a louder, more desperate edge. End in a fierce, breathless fury, your voice loud but brittle, as if the words are punching through your own hurt.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Reading Your Grandmother's Last Letter to You
instruction: You're alone, holding the letter she wrote before she died. Your voice starts reading her words aloud, steady and careful—you're trying to get through this. But her voice is in these words, her phrases, the way she always talked to you. Your voice catches on 'my darling one.' You keep reading but you're crying now, gently, the kind of tears that come without sound. She's telling you she's proud of you, that she sees you, that she loves you exactly as you are. Your voice breaks on these words because no one has ever said them this way. You're whispering now, rereading certain lines, your voice full of gratitude and devastating loss. By the end, you can barely speak—you're just breathing the words, holding them like holding her. Your voice carries both the gift of being seen and the unbearable fact that she's gone.
inspired_by: Visiting a Parent With Dementia Who Doesn't Recognize You

title: The Buzz of a New Connection
instruction: You're on a phone call with someone you're very attracted to, but you're mid-shave with an electric razor. You're embarrassed that you have to keep pausing to shave your cheek, and the buzz makes you feel silly and self-conscious. As you talk, you try to hide it, but the mechanical noise keeps interrupting your sentences, forcing you to distort your mouth to flatten your skin. Your voice starts tight and apologetic, with quick, clipped words. Midway, you laugh at yourself, and the embarrassment melts into genuine interest—you start to flirt, your voice warming, even as you still have to adjust your jaw to avoid the blade. End with a breathy, soft confession, the razor momentarily silent as you hold still, listening to them.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (very intensely present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Child Before You Die
instruction: You're in hospice, and your adult child has just arrived. You have maybe hours left. Begin with enormous relief just seeing their face—your voice warm but fragile: 'You made it.' You need to tell them everything that matters before it's too late. Your breathing is labored, you have to pause to gather strength. Move from relief into fierce love as you tell them how proud you are, then into raw grief as you realize you won't see their future. Your voice breaks when you try to say 'I'm sorry I won't be there for...' Let the words catch, restart, fail. End in a place of unexpected peace, maybe even gentle humor, as you touch their face and whisper something that feels like a blessing, not a goodbye.
inspired_by: Your Sibling Asking About Your Trauma

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a lifetime of emotional absence. Start with a trembling attempt at control, your voice measured but cracking: 'I need you to hear this. I need you to actually hear me for once.' Then let the dam break—your voice rises with decades of unmet needs: 'I was a child! I needed you to see me, to know me, to care!' But mid-confrontation, something unexpected happens. You see their face, their age, their own brokenness, and your rage fractures into something more complicated. Your voice drops, nearly breaking: 'You were hurt too, weren't you? You didn't know how.' End in a whisper that holds both grief and a tentative, painful forgiveness: 'I needed so much from you. And you couldn't give it. And maybe... maybe that's not entirely your fault.' The journey is from rage to heartbreak to the beginning of understanding.

title: The Thing You Pretended Not to Know
instruction: You are confronting your parent about something they did to you in childhood that you've never spoken about—something that shaped your entire life. Start from a place of controlled anger, almost businesslike, as if you've rehearsed this a thousand times. As you speak, feel your voice begin to crack, the child inside you demanding to be heard. Let your rage build not into shouting, but into something raw and vulnerable—the terrifying realization that you're not confronting them for closure, but because part of you still desperately needs them to say they're sorry, to admit they knew, to prove they loved you despite what they did. End in devastated recognition: they will never give you what you need, and you have to find a way to be whole anyway.

title: The Reckoning in the Storm
instruction: You've just discovered that someone you trusted completely has betrayed you in the worst possible way—they've destroyed something you loved, put someone you care about in danger, or shattered your life's work. Begin with quiet disbelief, your voice almost calm as your brain refuses to process what's happening. But as reality sets in, your voice builds into raw, primal rage—you're screaming accusations, your words tumbling over each other, incoherent with fury. Then suddenly, mid-sentence, you break—the rage collapses into devastated sobbing because beneath the anger is unbearable pain. You loved this person. Your voice becomes ragged, wild, oscillating between screaming 'How could you?' and whispering 'I trusted you.' End with exhausted despair, your voice small and hoarse, asking one final question you're not sure you want answered: 'Did you ever care about me at all?'

title: I'll Drown This Ocean: A Mother's Rage and Helplessness
instruction: You are a mother whose child has been hurt by the world's cruelty, and they've stopped believing in magic, in wonder, in anything beautiful. You're holding the seashell they once treasured, now abandoned. Begin with fierce, explosive anger—at the people who hurt them, at yourself for not protecting them, at the universe for breaking something so pure. Your voice should crack with rage as you describe what you REFUSE to let die: their wonder, their innocence, their right to hear oceans in seashells. Let the fury build until it suddenly collapses into broken sobs, your voice dissolving into helpless, whispered desperation: 'Please, baby, please just hold it one more time. Please don't let them take this from you.' End with a raw, throat-shredded mix of protectiveness and powerlessness, your words becoming a prayer you don't know if anyone is hearing. Channel the terrifying intensity of love that would burn the world down but can't fix this one thing.
inspired_by: The Ocean in a Seashell: A Child's Wonder

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You are confronting your parent who spent your entire childhood criticizing you, diminishing your dreams, making you feel small. Start angry, with years of suppressed rage finally erupting—list everything they made you believe about yourself. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: you begin to hear your own voice reclaiming power, and you realize mid-confrontation that you no longer need their validation. Transform from fury to something more dangerous and free—a calm, unshakeable certainty in your own worth. End by thanking them, not sarcastically, but genuinely, because their doubt forged your determination. Your voice should move from jagged and aggressive to smooth, powerful, almost serene.
inspired_by: Actor needs a quick ego boost before an audition or performance

title: The Perfectly Set Table
instruction: You are a woman in her late 40s, hosting a dinner party for your husband and his closest friends. You've just served the main course—a dish you know he hates, but that you've spent all day perfecting. Across the table, he's struggling to be polite while his friends make awkward small talk. You smile sweetly, refilling his wine glass with a slightly trembling hand. Begin with a hushed, almost sweet voice—but there's a hard, sour edge beneath it, like you're fighting back a bitter memory. As you speak, let the shame of years of small humiliations creep in, then slowly transform that into a quiet pride as you realize you've finally orchestrated this moment perfectly. The voice stays controlled, low, and deliberate, every word measured. Let a tiny crack appear at the memory of his past negligence, then seal it with a serene smile. 'I remember you once told me I couldn't cook to save my life, darling. Funny how things change. I've been waiting for just the right night to show you what I've learned. Please, eat up. Everyone's watching.'
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Shame (clearly present), Pride (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Fox's Secret
instruction: Late at night, you are whispering a confession to your sleeping partner about something you've hidden for years. Begin with extreme alertness—every sound makes you pause, your eyes darting, your body coiled and ready to flee at any moment. Your voice is barely audible, quick and darting, revealing the truth in small, careful pieces, ready to stop and retreat. You are all watchfulness and wariness, unable to commit fully to the vulnerability. As you speak and they remain peacefully asleep, unable to judge or reject you, something in you slowly uncurls. Your breathing steadies. Your hyper-vigilance gradually melts into exhausted relief. By the end, let yourself become soft and undefended, your voice tender and open, finally resting against them with full trust, the confession complete and the constant vigilance finally, blessedly released.

title: When the Armor Shatters
instruction: You've been the strong one, the capable one, for so long—but right now you're at your absolute breaking point, and someone just asked 'Are you okay?' Start with a harsh, defensive laugh: 'Am I okay? That's what you want to know?' Your voice rises with barely contained fury: 'I've been holding everything together while everyone else falls apart, and now you ask if I'm okay?' The rage builds, passionate and desperate: 'I can't do this anymore! I can't be the one who fixes everything!' Your voice cracks and suddenly you're not angry anymore—you're terrified and small: 'I don't know what to do. For the first time in my life, I don't know how to fix this.' Your fierce control collapses into helpless tears: 'I'm so tired of being strong. I'm so tired.' But then something shifts—a flicker of the protectiveness that defines you surfaces even through the breakdown: 'But if I don't hold it together, who will?' End with your voice raw and transformed, finding a different kind of strength in admitting weakness: 'I need help. God, I can't believe I'm saying this, but I need someone to catch me for once.' You've shattered and somehow that makes you more whole.

title: The Vigil: Whispering to Your Sleeping Lover's Ghost
instruction: You're lying beside your partner of twenty years who's in a coma, unlikely to wake. It's 3 AM and you're whispering all the things you never said, believing they can somehow hear. Begin so quietly your voice is almost just breath—confessing a secret you've held, something small and tender, almost mundane (how you always pretended to hate their morning routine but secretly loved it). Your voice catches on a memory. Then let yourself go deeper, more vulnerable: admitting your fears about who you'll be without them, how you're terrified of forgetting the exact sound of their laugh. Your whispers become uneven, interrupted by silent tears you're trying not to make audible. End with the gentlest, most broken 'please don't go'—not a plea, but an exhale, as you press your forehead to their hand, your voice dissolving into wordless grief.

title: Claiming Your Place at the Bedside
instruction: You've just arrived at your estranged father's deathbed after years of silence. You enter feeling small, apologetic, uncertain if you even belong here. As you approach, something shifts—you realize you have every right to be present, that your pain and love are legitimate. Physically grow larger as you speak: start with a hesitant whisper from across the room, then move closer with each sentence, your voice and body expanding until you're standing tall beside him, speaking with full-throated authority about what you needed from him, what you're taking back for yourself. End claiming your space in that room as if pulling all the years of diminishment back into your body. Your final words should sound like you've become twice your size.

title: The Drowning
instruction: You're a lifeguard who just lost someone—you were ten seconds too late. Start with controlled rescue breathing rhythm as you perform CPR: steady, measured, professional. Count compressions aloud with mechanical precision: 'One, two, three, four...' Then you realize they're gone. Your breathing explodes into hyperventilation, panic. Words tear out between gasps: 'No, no, NO! BREATHE! GODDAMN IT, BREATHE!' Rage at yourself, at God, at the ocean. Your voice becomes a roar that dissolves into sobbing. You can't catch your breath—you're drowning in air while they drowned in water. The breathing is chaotic, desperate. Then slowly, slowly, it begins to quiet. Not because you've found peace, but from pure exhaustion. Your final words are hollow, breathless with a different kind of emptiness: 'I was... ten seconds... ten seconds...' Let the breathing remain broken, damaged.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Ship Leaves
instruction: You are saying goodbye to someone you love who is boarding a colony ship to another star system—a one-way journey that will take them beyond any possibility of return. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light as you've both agreed not to make this harder. But as the final boarding call approaches, your composure cracks. The lightness dissolves into raw need—you want to beg them to stay, but you can't. End with a whispered confession of what they've truly meant to you, your voice breaking on words you should have said years ago. Let the shift happen naturally: from bright denial to trembling honesty, from 'see you later' energy to the devastating acceptance that this is forever.
inspired_by: The Princess and the Dragon Disguised as a Human

title: Everything You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father who abandoned you fifteen years ago, now standing in your doorway asking for forgiveness. As you face him, let silent flashes consume you—yourself as a child waiting by the window, your mother crying in the kitchen, your graduation where his seat stayed empty, the wedding he missed, the moments you needed him. Don't narrate these images; let them fuel your rising emotion. Start with cold, controlled civility—almost robotic politeness. As these wordless memories accumulate inside you, let them build until your composure shatters and raw truth explodes out. The images should drive you from icy distance to volcanic rage to something more complicated—perhaps unexpected understanding, perhaps permanent severance. Let the silent pictures decide.

title: Guilt Consuming
instruction: You didn't call them when you should have. They died. Your voice in the present is steady enough on the surface—you're telling the story—but underneath is a constant, gnawing harmonic. 'I could have called. It would have taken five minutes.' Breathing gets heavier when you say it. Your voice doesn't crack, but it carries the weight of carrying something unshakeable. There's a loop: you come back to the same regret, the same conditional: 'If I had just...' Your vocal tone is mechanical at first, then increasingly hollow.

title: Realizing Someone You Love Doesn't Love You Back Anymore
instruction: You're listening to them explain they've been pulling away for months. Your voice responds normally at first, but as you understand the distance, you become smaller. 'So when you... that wasn't just tiredness.' You're connecting dots and your voice reflects each realization. By the end: barely breathing, saying 'Okay' meaning nothing is okay.

title: The Last Second
instruction: You are with a trusted partner during an intimate moment where breath is being controlled. The pressure on your throat is increasing, and your voice starts thin and breathy — you're trying to stay present, focused on the sensation, saying something soft and encouraging. But as the squeeze tightens, your words break, pitch rises, and speech becomes a raspy, wet struggle, your concentration cracking. Then, suddenly released, you gasp loud, then speak in a dizzy, euphoric rush, voice trembling with relief and surprise, ending on a quiet, awed laugh. You sound like you've just come back from somewhere.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You are standing in a downpour, having just learned devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, something that shatters your world. Begin by trying to hold yourself together, body rigid against the cold, fists clenched, fighting the physical and emotional storm. You're determined not to break. But the rain keeps coming, and slowly, let your body surrender to it. Let the tension drain out through your limbs, let your muscles release, let yourself collapse to your knees if that's where your body wants to go. Your voice should move from controlled to raw to finally silent gasps as you stop fighting. The physical release and the emotional release become one. End in a state of complete letting go—body loose, breath deep, open to the full experience of your pain mixed with strange liberation.

title: Breaking Up With Someone You Still Love
instruction: Your voice shakes: 'I need to end this.' You're looking at their face, seeing hurt appear in real-time. Explain why, though reasons don't match the pain. 'I love you and that's exactly why I can't keep doing this.' Your voice cracks on 'love.' Say goodbye in a voice torn out of you.

title: The Protection I Couldn't Give
instruction: You're a parent whose child was hurt, and you weren't there to stop it. Begin with fierce, trembling rage—at the person who hurt them, at the world, at yourself. Your voice is a weapon: 'I should have been there.' Let that rage build until it's almost uncontrollable, your words sharp and violent. Then, mid-sentence, let it shatter completely. The rage collapses into helpless, gasping sobs because rage can't undo what happened. Your voice becomes raw and broken: 'I can't fix this.' Feel the devastating powerlessness of being unable to protect the person you'd die for. End with your voice dropping to something barely audible—a whispered promise to your child that you'll help them heal, even though you're breaking apart yourself.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut whose ship has malfunctioned beyond repair, and you have one final transmission to Earth before you drift into deep space forever. Begin with forced calm, trying to be brave: 'Mission control, I want you to know...' Your voice cracks despite your efforts. As you continue, the reality sets in—you'll never see home again, never hold anyone you love. Your breathing becomes uneven. You move from denial to acceptance, from fear to a strange, transcendent peace. 'Tell them... tell them I saw something beautiful out here.' By the end, you're no longer fighting it. Your voice becomes soft, wondering, almost curious about what comes next. The fear dissolves into something like gratitude mixed with unbearable longing. Let silence hold the weight of goodbye.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're whispering to someone who lies beside you in the dark—maybe a lover, maybe someone you've just met, maybe someone you're about to lose. Begin with your defenses up, speaking in careful half-truths about something that happened to you. Then let your voice drop lower, more raw. Confess the thing underneath—the shame, the longing, the moment that changed you. Allow silence to live between your words. Let your breathing become part of the story. Touch your own skin, your face, your throat, as you speak, as if trying to remember who you were before. End in a place of naked exposure, your voice barely a breath, having revealed something you can never take back. The vulnerability should feel like standing without skin.

title: A Mother's Final Warning to the Child Who Will Forget Her
instruction: You're dying, and your young child sits beside you. You need to warn them about a family member who will harm them after you're gone, but you know speaking it will plant seeds of fear and mistrust that will poison their childhood—yet staying silent means leaving them unprotected. Begin with tender reassurance, stroking their hair, voice soft with love. As you edge toward the warning, feel your throat tighten with the impossible choice. Your words become halting, desperate, trying to protect without destroying their innocence. End with a whispered confession of your failure—that you love them too much to burden them, but not enough to save them. Let your voice break between maternal tenderness and devastating helplessness.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Seer Shares a Vision Knowing It Will Cause the War It Predicts

title: The Dam Breaking at Midnight
instruction: You've held everything together for months—years maybe—being the strong one, the reliable one, the one who doesn't break. Tonight, alone, something small finally cracks you open completely. Start with trying to contain it, voice tight and controlled, maybe even laughing bitterly at yourself for feeling this way. Then let it explode—sobbing, rage, words tumbling out in a torrent of everything you've swallowed. Pound surfaces. Scream whispers (the kind of screaming you do when you can't actually scream). Let the fury collapse into helpless weeping, then rebuild into fierce determination. End with your voice raw but steady, claiming your right to fall apart. Transform from brittle control through volcanic release to hard-won, shaking strength.

title: The Tyrant's Final Breath
