instruction: You are a ruthless corporate executive who has crushed competitors and destroyed relationships to reach the top. Now, dying in a hospital bed, your estranged daughter sits beside you for the first time in fifteen years. Begin speaking from the place of the iron-willed conqueror you've always been—defending your choices, justifying the casualties, maintaining your armor of certainty. But as you feel your grip on life loosening, allow something buried and forgotten to surface: the frightened person underneath who desperately needed to prove their worth. Let your voice shift from command to plea, from justification to raw confession. End in a place of naked vulnerability you've never allowed yourself to occupy, finally asking—not demanding—for something you need.
inspired_by: Actor must play a character who is clearly dominated by a specific energy (obsessive achiever, dictator, victim, warrior, etc.)

title: Anxiety Spiraling
instruction: One thought cascades into ten. Your voice speeds up: 'What if the interview goes badly and they hate me and I don't get the job and I can't pay rent and—' Each catastrophe is more ridiculous but sounds equally possible inside the spiral. Breathing becomes rapid, high in the chest. Volume increases. Your voice takes on the rapid-fire quality of thoughts overwhelming language. 'And then I'll be alone forever and—' Words trip over themselves. Include moments where you try to ground yourself ('Breathe. Okay. Breathe.') but the spiral continues anyway. Physical: pacing, hand wringing.

title: Night on the Floor
instruction: You're a teenager sitting cross-legged on your bedroom floor in the dark, phone pressed to your ear after hearing a strange noise downstairs. Your voice shakes as you whisper to your best friend, every muscle tight, your eyes fixed on the crack under the door. Start terrified, barely able to get words out without gasping, but as your friend's calm replies filter through, let a fragile thread of hope loosen your throat. You shift your weight, hug your knees, and one hand fidgets with your shirt hem. End with a small, hesitant smile in your voice, but the fear never fully leaves your breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, and you've been asked to give a toast. You're genuinely happy for them—you love them deeply and want their joy. But you're also devastated because you've been secretly in love with them for years, and this moment represents the death of a hope you never admitted even to yourself. Begin the toast with warmth and humor, playing the role of the perfect, supportive friend. But as you speak, let the real feelings bleed through—your voice catching on certain words, a brightness in your eyes that could be joy or unshed tears. Weave together genuine celebration of their happiness with your own private heartbreak. Let moments of pure love for their joy clash with flashes of grief for what you'll never have. Your vocal performance must hold both truths simultaneously: the public performance of happiness and the private experience of loss. End with a final toast that sounds triumphant but costs you everything to deliver.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use the unconscious as a resource in rehearsal

title: Parent Hearing Their Child's Abuse for First Time
instruction: Your child is telling you something that happened to them. Your voice wants to react with rage and panic. But you hold it down—this moment is about them. 'I'm so sorry that happened to you.' Your voice is steady, present. Ask clarifying questions while internally falling apart. Include anger at the abuser before redirecting to support.

title: The Last Transmission from the Space Station
instruction: You're an astronaut on a failing space station, recording a final message to your child back on Earth. Begin with calm professionalism: 'Mission log, day 847. Everything's fine down there, sweetheart.' But the oxygen is running out, and you know this is goodbye. Your voice remains steady as you talk about their upcoming birthday, the cake you won't see them blow out. Then something breaks—maybe it's remembering their laugh, maybe it's the reality hitting you. Your breathing becomes labored, not from panic but from the thinning air and the weight of love. 'I need you to know...' Your voice fractures between the parent who wants to protect them from this truth and the human who desperately needs to say everything before the silence comes. End with a whispered confession of how proud you are, how sorry, how your last thought will be their face. Let the oxygen deprivation make your words drift, become almost dreamlike, as if you're already half-gone.
inspired_by: Working Near an Industrial Furnace: Heat Warping Perception

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: It's the morning of your wedding day. You're alone, getting ready, looking at yourself in the mirror. Your body is locked tight with contradictions: joy that makes you want to laugh and grief that makes you want to sob, gratitude for the future and rage at what you're leaving behind, excitement so intense it feels like terror. Begin speaking to your reflection with this tension visible in every muscle—your smile is rigid, your voice is bright but strained, your hands are clenched. As you continue, allow specific parts of your body to release one by one: your jaw softens and you can laugh truly, then your shoulders drop and grief flows through, then your hands open and you can touch your own face tenderly. By the end, all these emotions should coexist in your body without fight—crying and laughing simultaneously, voice rich with the full complexity of a threshold moment where multiple truths live together.

title: Acting Unaffected by an Insult
instruction: Someone makes a hurtful comment towards you. Internally, it stings, but you act as if it doesnt bother you. Describe the hurt inside while maintaining a composed exterior. Speak with a calm, indifferent tone, refusing to show any pain.

title: Screaming at God While Your Child Flatlines
instruction: The doctors have left the room. Your child is on life support, braindead after the accident, and in sixty seconds you have to give them permission to turn off the machines. Start with fierce, protective rage—shouting at God, at the universe, at the unfairness, your voice strong and defiant, refusing to accept this. But as the moment approaches, your voice begins to fracture. The anger collapses into raw, animal grief—guttural sounds, desperate bargaining, your voice breaking as you beg for a miracle you know won't come. Include the moment where your rage turns inward, blaming yourself, your voice becoming vicious and self-lacerating. End in a place of devastating helplessness, your voice reduced to broken whispers as you tell your child it's okay to go, that you'll be okay, even though your voice makes it clear you'll never be okay again. You're giving them permission to die while every cell in your body is screaming no.
inspired_by: Trying to Confess Your Affair in a Nightclub

title: The Reckoning: What You Needed and Never Got
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent who failed you, but this time you're not yelling - you're telling them the truth with devastating calm. Begin by describing a specific childhood moment when you needed them and they weren't there. Your voice should be steady, almost gentle, but with steel underneath. Then the shift: tell them how that absence shaped you, what it cost you in relationships, in trust, in your ability to love yourself. Let anger seep in, but keep it controlled - this is more powerful than shouting. End with the hardest part: acknowledge that you understand they were broken too, but you needed them anyway. Move from painful clarity to controlled rage to exhausted, complicated forgiveness. This isn't about volume - it's about finally being seen.
inspired_by: The Final Words: What You'd Actually Say

title: The Last Conversation: A Parent's Final Goodbye to Their Child Before an Irreversible Journey
instruction: You're sitting at your child's bedside in the hour before dawn, before they leave on a mission no one returns from. They're asleep. Your voice begins with fierce pride—you need them to hear how extraordinary they are, how your heart bursts with who they've become. But as you speak, the pride cracks open into something raw: the desperate wish that you could take their place, the hundred moments you wish you'd said 'I love you' more clearly, the way you memorized the sound of their laughter. Your breath catches. You're trying to be strong for them, but your voice fractures into a whisper of all the futures you'll never see—their wedding, their children, their ordinary Tuesday mornings. End with a kind of broken peace, a whispered blessing that's half prayer, half goodbye. Touch their hair. Your final words are you releasing them, even as every cell in your body screams to hold on.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Thief Returns Stolen Item to the Person Whose Trust They Betrayed

title: The Golden Handshake
instruction: You are an older woman working the returns desk at a department store. A manager just told you that you've been promoted to a prestigious new role—and also that your entire team will be laid off in two weeks. You must maintain your bright, high-pitched 'customer service voice' while your elation over the promotion struggles against your fear for your coworkers and your own uncertain future. As you help a customer with a simple return, let the smile in your voice crack, then recover, then crack again. Add a subtle tremble in the pitch, a swallowed gasp, a forced brightness that slowly deflates into vulnerable honesty. By the end, let a quiet, shaky admission slip out that the mask is wearing thin.
emotions_sampled: Elation (very intensely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast for My Brother
instruction: You are giving a toast at your younger brother's wedding, but he is marrying the person you secretly loved for years—someone who never knew how you felt. Begin with surface warmth and humor, the expected affection of a sibling's toast, your voice bright with celebration. But let the truth bleed through in small moments: a pause that lasts too long, a detail you remember too vividly, a blessing that costs you something to give. Feel the specific ache of genuine happiness for someone you love mixed with personal grief. Draw from the precise memories: how you felt watching them fall in love, the exact moment you knew you had to let go, the nights you rehearsed confessing but never did. Let your love for your brother be absolutely real even as your heart breaks. End with a blessing that is utterly sincere and utterly devastating—you mean every word, and every word costs you your own dream. Your voice should crack not with bitterness but with the profound pain of loving two people enough to let them have each other.
inspired_by: Scene partners have a long shared history that does not appear in the script

title: Final Parade
instruction: You are an elderly woman, a retired drill sergeant, leading your last parade. The sun beats down on the dusty field; you feel the ache in your knees and the weight of the medals on your chest. You bark commands in the clipped, emotionless tone you've used for decades, but inside you are flooded with contentment — a quiet pride for all the soldiers you shaped. As the unit executes the final maneuver, a wave of ecstasy rises unexpectedly: pure joy at this perfect moment. Your voice starts steady and crisp, but on the last word it softens, a slight catch in your throat, as if you're almost smiling. Let your body feel the heat, the distant drumbeat, and let that final break reveal the pleasure beneath the bark.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Telling Your Father You're Not Coming Home for His Last Christmas
instruction: You're on the phone with your father who has six months to live, and you're explaining why you can't come home for Christmas—because being in that house with him means facing decades of his emotional absence, his criticism, his inability to say he loves you. Start with careful, measured words trying to be kind. Let your voice tighten as old resentments surface—all the moments he wasn't there, all the ways he made you feel small. Build to confrontation: 'You want me there so you can feel like a good father before you die.' But then break—because he's dying, and he's asking for you, and underneath all that rage is a child who still wants his father to fight for him. End in a devastated whisper, admitting the truth: you're not staying away because you hate him, but because you're terrified of losing him before he ever really knew you.
inspired_by: Wedding Toast While Secretly in Love with the Bride

title: The Last Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your estranged mother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's unconscious. You begin with cold, factual recounting: 'You missed every birthday. Every recital.' Your voice is distant, protected. But as you continue, something cracks. 'I needed you so badly.' The words come softer now, trembling. You reach for her hand, and suddenly decades of longing pour out in whispered, broken confessions: 'I still need you. Even now. Even after everything.' You're weeping, but gently, stroking her hair like she never stroked yours. 'I forgive you, Mom. I don't know if you can hear me, but I forgive you.' The anger that sustained you dissolves into profound, aching grief. You kiss her forehead. 'Goodbye.' That final word is both release and devastating loss.

title: Laughing Through the Shattered Glass: Gratitude at the End
instruction: You're thanking your best friend for twenty years of friendship as they prepare to move across the world, knowing you may never see them again. Begin with a smile in your voice even as tears threaten: 'God, remember when we thought we'd live next door forever?' Let laughter and grief tangle together: 'You've been the best part of my life—that sounds so dramatic, but it's true.' Feel joy and devastation collide as your voice breaks mid-laugh: 'I'm so proud of you and so completely devastated.' Let gratitude pour out even as your heart shatters: 'Thank you for seeing me when I couldn't see myself. Thank you for staying.' End with peaceful acceptance mixed with irreparable loss: 'I love you. I'll always love you. Now go—before I beg you not to.' The journey is from bittersweet nostalgia to the beautiful agony of loving someone enough to let them go.

title: Saying Goodbye to Sleeping Hands
instruction: You're whispering to your beloved who is unconscious in their final hours, and you're saying all the things you never quite said clearly enough. Keep your voice quiet, intimate, as if any louder might shatter this last moment together. Let tenderness mix with regret—the gentle way you describe ordinary memories that now feel sacred, interrupted by catches in your throat when you realize there won't be new memories. Include small laughs at inside jokes they can't respond to, your voice breaking on their name. End with permission—releasing them even as your heart refuses to let go. The arc moves from tender reminiscence through mounting grief to a whispered, impossible goodbye.

title: The Last Morning Routine
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your spouse of forty years who will die before sunset. They are lucid, calm, and at peace. You begin with desperate denial, trying to talk about tomorrow's plans, next week's appointments, as if normalcy can stop what's coming. Midway through, something breaks—you stop pretending and allow yourself to simply be present with them, holding their hand. By the end, transform your grief into a fierce celebration of gratitude for every ordinary morning you shared: the coffee, the silence, the light through the kitchen window. Let your voice move from frantic cheerfulness to raw honesty to a kind of reverent joy mixed with unbearable loss. The final moments should feel like you're pouring a lifetime of love into a single breath.
inspired_by: An actor is experiencing professional inactivity and depression

title: Midnight Recollection
instruction: You are an elderly woman curled on your side in bed, an old photograph held close to your chest. The room is dark, and your voice is a near-whisper, squeezed by how you’re lying—one lung pressed against the mattress, the other barely working. Begin with raw, deep longing as you trace the face in the picture, your voice fragile and thin. Let a note of bitterness creep in as you recall a promise broken long ago, but soften at the end as a flicker of wistful interest returns—a quiet curiosity about what might have been. Speak naturally, with pauses, breaths, and the slight rustle of the photo paper.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Interest (slightly present), Bitterness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reading Your Teenage Son's Suicide Note While He's Asleep in the Next Room
instruction: You found it while putting away laundry—folded in his desk drawer, dated three days ago. Your voice starts as a whisper reading his words, barely breathing, as if speaking louder will make it more real. The note is articulate, apologetic, heartbreaking in its clarity about how much pain he's been in while sitting across from you at breakfast. As you read, your voice catches on phrases like 'I'm sorry' and 'it's not your fault.' You're trying to stay silent—he's sleeping twenty feet away—but your throat keeps closing. Move from shocked stillness to a kind of tender devastation as you realize how many signs you missed, how many times he said he was 'fine.' Your breathing becomes the performance as much as your voice. End by speaking directly to him though he can't hear you, your words barely forming, expressing something between a promise and a prayer—not dramatic, but intimate and broken and full of desperate love.
inspired_by: Hostage Negotiator Talking Down a Gunman While Your Own Child Texts

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times to a parent who never truly knew you. Begin with trembling anger barely held in check: 'Do you even know what my favorite color is? What I'm afraid of?' Your voice is tight, accusatory. As you speak, the anger begins to crack and underneath is the child still desperate to be seen: 'I used to do everything I could think of to make you look at me—really look at me.' Let your voice break on the vulnerability. Then something shifts—rage returns but now mixed with grief: 'I needed you, and you were always somewhere else.' End in a place of devastating honesty, voice hoarse and spent: 'I'm not angry anymore. I'm just... so tired of hoping you'll change.' The final words are barely audible, not from weakness but from the weight of finally letting go.

title: Unforgiven Goodbye
instruction: You're a teenager in a dimly lit bedroom, inches away from the partner who broke your trust. Start by whispering close to their ear, your voice shaky with affection and longing as you trace a memory you both shared. Then feel the bitterness rise, so your words turn into a growl—low, deliberate, dripping with profanity as you command their attention. Let your volume shift: a breathy, almost tender murmur one moment, then a sharp, loud bark the next. End with a cold, drawn-out threat, but let your voice hesitate on the last word, betraying the affection you still can't kill.
emotions_sampled: Affection (very intensely present), Longing (extremely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Laughing Through Tears at My Own Rock Bottom
instruction: You're sitting on your bathroom floor at 3 AM, having just called a crisis helpline. The counselor asked you to tell them what brought you here tonight, and as you start to explain the absurd, tragic cascade of events - losing your prescription meds, 'self-medicating' with whatever you could find, ending up unable to remember your own sister's name at dinner - you realize how simultaneously devastating and darkly ridiculous it all is. You begin crying, but laughter keeps breaking through. Not hysterical laughter, but the kind that comes when you finally see the truth. You're grateful to be alive and heartbroken at what you've become. Your voice wavers between sobs and chuckles. You apologize for laughing, then laugh at yourself for apologizing. Find moments of clarity where you express genuine gratitude for this bottom, this breaking point, this chance to stop - but your voice keeps cracking with grief for the person you used to be. End in a place of strange, tearful peace, laughing softly and crying at once, finally ready to ask for help.
inspired_by: Benzos and Booze: Words Disappearing Mid-sentence

title: Shouting Into the White
instruction: You are a young woman standing alone in a violent blizzard, your envy burning as you watch the distant lights of a house where your sister celebrates without you. The freezing wind steals your breath, your jaw trembles, and snow muffles every sound. Start with raw, bitter jealousy—shouting accusations into the storm, your voice cracking from cold and fury. As the wind howls and your body shakes, let the envy fade into a hollow, exhausted realization that your rage is just as wasted as your words. Speak as if each syllable costs you warmth, pausing to gasp, shiver, or lose a thought to the gale.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Thanking Them as You Let Them Go
instruction: You're releasing someone you deeply love because staying together is destroying you both. Begin laughing softly through tears at a shared memory: 'Remember when we...' Your voice carries both joy and breaking. Express genuine gratitude for what they gave you, voice warm with love, even as it trembles. 'You taught me what it means to...' But weave in the heartbreak—each thank you is also a goodbye. Your laughter keeps catching on sobs. You're finding peace in the rightness of this ending while simultaneously grieving the loss. End with a paradox: relieved and shattered, grateful and devastated, laughing and crying in the same breath. 'This is right. This is... God, this hurts.' Let the beauty and the pain be equally present.
inspired_by: Losing Your Temper at Someone You Love

title: The Last Conversation Before the War
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your younger sibling who enlisted against your desperate wishes, and the convoy leaves in an hour. You start angry—furious that they're choosing this, that they won't listen. But as the reality sinks in that this might be the last time you see them alive, your anger cracks open into raw terror and love. Your voice breaks as you shift from 'How could you do this to us?' to whispering the things you've never said: how much you've looked up to them, how scared you are, how you're not ready to lose them. End with a moment where you have to physically let go, your voice catching on 'Come back to me' as you realize you have no control over whether they will.

title: I'm Not Going Back
instruction: You are a seven-year-old boy waking from sedation after surgery. Your throat is raw, your head is heavy, and your tongue feels huge. Your mom is beside you trying to soothe you, but you have something to say first—something that's been building. Start by squeezing out heavy, slurred sounds with blurred syllables, barely propping your eyes open. Gradually, as motor control returns, each word becomes clearer as the anger sharpens. You were told you'd get a lollipop after—but you aren't angry about the candy. You heard the doctor say something about 'another procedure,' and you are furious that they lied. End with a sharp, fully understood demand—your voice clear but still hoarse.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wall Hits
instruction: You're in your garage, trying to finish fixing a lawnmower. You downed a triple espresso an hour ago and now it's wearing off. Start with fidgety impatience — you mutter under your breath about a stubborn bolt, your voice tight and clipped. Midway, feel the sudden crash: your words slow, your shoulders drop, and a heavy irritability seeps in. End with a resentful, deflated sigh — you're too tired to care, but too annoyed to stop. Let your speech drag, add pauses, let the energy drain from your voice as you go.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Awkward Small Talk
instruction: You're stuck in an elevator with someone you kind of know, and the silence is deafening. Your voice is nervous: 'So... how's work?' They give a one-word answer. Your voice tries again: 'Nice weather we're having?' You're desperately searching for topics. Your tone becomes increasingly desperate and awkward. You're talking about nothing to fill the silence: 'Yep. Elevators. They go up and down.' By the time the doors open, your voice is just relieved: 'Well, here's my floor.'

title: Screaming at God While Holding Your Dying Dog
instruction: You're in the vet's office during your dog's final moments, and fury at the unfairness erupts from your chest. Start with your voice fierce and accusing, hurling questions at the ceiling: 'Fifteen years wasn't enough? You couldn't give us more?' Your rage is white-hot, demanding answers from an empty sky. But mid-sentence, your voice shatters into desperate bargaining: 'Please, I'll do anything.' Your hands are on your dog's fur and you collapse into helpless sobbing, your voice dissolving into primal sounds of grief. Then, as your dog looks at you, something shifts - your voice becomes fiercely protective even as you're powerless: 'It's okay, baby. I've got you.' End with your voice raw but steady, whispering promises through tears, being strong for them even as your heart is being torn apart.

title: Cataloging What Remains
instruction: You're alone in bed with someone you love deeply, in the quiet darkness just before dawn. They're asleep beside you, and you know this is one of your last mornings together—you're moving across the world, or they are, or the relationship is ending by mutual choice. Whisper aloud your awareness of everything: the warmth of their skin, the sound of their breathing, the weight of the blanket, the quality of the silence, how the dim light falls across their face, the ache in your own chest. Start with tender appreciation and gratitude, trying to memorize everything. But as you inventory each sensation and speak what you feel, let the grief rise. By the end, let your whispered observations become a broken prayer of love mixed with unbearable loss. Transform from peaceful gratitude to quiet devastation without ever raising your voice above a whisper.

title: I Taught Myself Not to See You
instruction: You're the adult child confronting the parent who abandoned you, and they've shown up at your gallery opening, your wedding, or your graduation—a moment they have no right to witness. You've spent years perfecting the art of looking past them in grocery stores, on streets, at family events. Now they're here, and you must speak the truth: you didn't fail to recognize them—you taught yourself not to see them, and it nearly killed something inside you. Begin with that cold, practiced invisibility you've perfected, describing how you trained yourself to make them transparent. But as you speak, let the anger crack open to reveal the child underneath who needed them desperately, who stood at windows waiting. Your voice should move from controlled contempt to shaking rage to something more fragile—the admission that making them invisible meant making part of yourself invisible too. End with the terrible question: now that you've finally seen them again, what do you do with all this grief?
inspired_by: Pretending Not to Recognize Someone You Know

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You are a terminally ill parent standing over your young child's bed in the middle of the night, knowing you have only weeks left and they don't know yet. Speak in barely-there whispers, as if your words could be absorbed through their dreams. Begin by describing their beautiful sleeping face, your voice filled with fierce protective love and memorization of every detail. Let your whispers catch as you apologize for all the moments you'll miss—their graduations, weddings, heartbreaks you won't be there to soothe. Feel gratitude and devastation braided together as you tell them how being their parent was the greatest gift of your existence. End with the impossible task of saying goodbye while trying to pour a lifetime of love into hushed words, your throat closing around the tenderness and unfairness of it all. Let quiet, reverent love transform into whispered anguish, then into a trembling peace.
inspired_by: The Vampire and the Innocent Villager

title: Homework Grudge, Best Friend Bait
instruction: You're a teenage girl on the phone with your best friend, sprawled across your bed. You start by droning about a tedious homework assignment—let your voice go nasal, stretch your vowels like 'thiiiiis is sooo boring,' letting each complaint hang in the air. Halfway through, you notice your friend is doing the exact same whine, and a teasing smirk creeps in. Playfully mimic her, then burst into a laugh, your tone lifting into a warm, contented tease. The shift should feel like a sudden crack in the gloom—end with a soft, satisfied sigh, your voice lighter, as if the complaining itself became a game.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Victory Shakes
instruction: You're a 17-year-old in a back alley after finally beating the guy who terrorized you for years. Your whole body trembles from the adrenaline crash—hands shake, stomach lurches, and you can barely catch your breath. You start spitting out bitter words, voice cracking with raw anger as you relive every humiliation. But then, mid-sentence, the truth hits you: you actually won. Let the bitterness transform into a shaky, tearful triumph. Your voice should rapid-fire at moments, then catch with sudden sobs or a laugh. You're not sad—you're flooded. Speak naturally, let the physical shakes and emotional bursts pull you through.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Rocket
instruction: You are an elderly person in the midst of a manic episode, standing in your cluttered garage at 3 AM. You are furiously sorting through boxes of old letters and photographs, your voice racing and too loud. Start with raw, crackling anger — you're furious at time, at loss, at the mess of memory. Let your words tumble out, tangents erupting as you find a faded photograph. Let longing surge up, sudden and overwhelming, choking the speed, softening the volume. End with a whisper, holding the photo, the anger drained into a desperate, quiet ache.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Moment You Find Out They Knew All Along
instruction: You've just discovered that the person you love most—partner, best friend, sibling—has known your deepest secret (your addiction, your affair, your devastating diagnosis) for months and said nothing. Start with disbelief and defensive anger: 'How dare you watch me lie and say nothing?' Let that rage build, your voice rising with betrayal and humiliation. But then crack—suddenly you're sobbing, because their silence was actually love, wasn't it? They were giving you space to tell them when you were ready. Your fury collapses into ugly-crying gratitude mixed with shame. Your vocal delivery should be messy, real—none of that pretty crying. End in a place where you're both furious and grateful, hurt and loved, unable to tell where one feeling stops and another begins. Speak through tears, through anger, through the awful beauty of being truly known.

title: The Permission to Go
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your dying best friend, giving them permission to stop fighting, and you're trying to make them laugh one last time even as your heart is breaking. Start with forced lightness, telling a story or making a joke, your voice bright but fragile. Let laughter mix with tears—you're genuinely finding joy in the memory but simultaneously grieving that there won't be more. Your voice should crack between chuckles and sobs, creating moments of beautiful contradiction. Tell them it's okay to let go, that you'll be okay, even though you both know it's a lie you need to tell. Express profound gratitude for their friendship while simultaneously breaking apart at the unfairness of losing them. End with tender acceptance, your voice soft and loving, telling them you'll carry them with you, laughing through tears, finding peace in the midst of devastating loss. Let silence fall naturally where words become impossible, then find the courage to continue.

title: The Smallest Truth
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to your partner in the dark, and you need to tell them something you've been hiding—not an affair, but something smaller and more shameful: that you're not sure you want the life you're building together, or that you've been pretending to be happier than you are, or that you're terrified you're becoming your parents. Start by trying to keep your voice steady and controlled, trying to make it okay, trying to cushion the blow. But let the act of saying it out loud in the darkness do something to you. Let the whisper break. Let the shame become something else—maybe relief, maybe deeper fear, maybe unexpected tenderness. This isn't a dramatic confession. It's a fragile, halting unburdening. Let silence have weight. Let pauses breathe.
inspired_by: An actor is going on an audition or interview

title: The Shape of Your Breath
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying beside someone you love but haven't touched in months—maybe your spouse after a long cold war, maybe a sick child you're watching sleep. The room is dark and quiet. Begin feeling separate, isolated in your own thoughts and pain. But then notice their breathing—just the sound and rhythm of it. Let that become your entire world. Don't think about the problems, the distance, the words unsaid. Just that breath—in and out, the slight catch in their throat, the warmth of it in the dark. As you listen, let it pull you out of your head and into your heart. Your whispered words should emerge from this focus—not grand declarations, but small, broken truths spoken to their breathing, to the simple animal fact of them being alive beside you. End with a tenderness so raw it hurts, your voice barely audible, transformed from loneliness into devastating intimacy.

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love who deploys to a war zone in three hours. You start by tracing their face in the pre-dawn darkness, your voice barely a whisper: 'I'm memorizing you.' Your touch is desperate to imprint every detail. As morning light creeps in, panic rises—you try to stay present, to make love like it's not goodbye, but your voice keeps breaking. You're trying to be brave, sensual, alive, but grief keeps flooding through. When you finally say 'I love you,' it should sound like you're trying to pour a lifetime of love into three words. End with your voice thick with unshed tears, still touching them, whispering promises you're terrified you can't keep. This isn't theatrical—it's raw, immediate, the feeling of time running out while your heart is still inside someone else's chest.

title: Screaming Your Child's Name Into an Empty House
instruction: Your child is missing—run away, taken, you don't know. You're searching the house, calling their name. Start with controlled calling, methodical room-by-room searching, voice still holding onto reason. But with each empty room, panic rises. You're shouting now, ripping open closets, overturning furniture. Your voice becomes raw, primal—rage at yourself for not preventing this, terror at what might be happening to them. The shouting collapses into sobbing, then transforms into desperate bargaining with God, the universe, anyone: 'Please, please, I'll do anything.' You sink to the floor. In the devastating quiet, you whisper their name one more time, tender as a lullaby, as if love alone could bring them home. Then—a sound. The front door. You freeze, hope and fear colliding, hardly breathing as you call out one more time.
inspired_by: Singing Happy Birthday Alone in Your Apartment

title: Hospital Window
instruction: You've smuggled a fresh peach into the hospital for someone you love who can no longer eat solid food. Sit beside their bed and describe eating it for them—slowly, quietly, with infinite tenderness. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, as if speaking too loudly might shatter this moment. Start by describing the peach with gentle appreciation, trying to give them the experience through your words. But as you continue, the contrast between the vibrant, living sweetness in your mouth and their fading presence overwhelms you. Your descriptions should become more halting, catching in your throat. End with the unbearable realization that you're tasting summer while they're slipping into winter, and all you can offer are these inadequate words about fruit they'll never taste again.
inspired_by: Taking a Bite of a Juicy Peach

title: The Breaking Point: Rage in the Archive Room
instruction: You've locked yourself in the company archive room, and you're on the phone with your mentor, the person who taught you how to be this person. Start with explosive fury—you just discovered another 'business decision' has led to deaths, and this time it's children. Your voice is shaking with rage, accusations pouring out. But as you rage, your voice begins to turn inward. You were in those meetings. You signed those approvals. Your fury collapses into anguished realization—you're not just angry at them, you're confronting your own complicity. Your voice breaks into something between shouting and sobbing. You're tearing through files, reading names aloud, each one a weight. End with fierce, desperate protectiveness that comes too late—you're vowing to burn it all down, but you know you're also destroying yourself, and your voice carries both determination and absolute devastation.
inspired_by: Professional: Executive Prioritizes Profit Over Employee Lives

title: The Wedding Morning Mirror
instruction: You're alone, getting ready for your wedding, looking at yourself in the mirror. This should be pure joy—and part of you is radiant with happiness. But you're also thinking of your mother who died three years ago, who will never see this day. Begin with excited anticipation, perhaps even laughing at yourself in the mirror. Let the awareness of absence creep in gradually, so that joy and grief become inseparable. Your voice should dance between bright enthusiasm and sudden catches, between celebration and sorrow. Don't choose one emotion over the other—live in the impossible space where both are completely true. End with a complexity words can barely hold: you are more grateful than you've ever been and more heartbroken, and somehow both make the other more profound.
inspired_by: An actor is preparing a cold reading for an audition

title: Heatstroke Fury
instruction: You've collapsed from heatstroke at your child's sports event. As you're coming to, disoriented and sick, you see your ex-spouse—the one who abandoned you both—kneeling beside you, playing concerned parent for the crowd. Start confused, physical—your mouth is dry, you can barely form words, you're nauseous and dizzy. Then recognition, and rage erupts through the physical weakness. Your voice is raw, almost guttural: 'Don't you dare. Don't you fucking dare touch me.' You're trying to push them away but your arms won't work right. You're yelling and slurring at once. 'Where were you? WHERE WERE YOU?' It builds to something explosive, then suddenly breaks—you're sobbing, you're helpless, you're still so hurt. End with a whispered, devastating, 'I needed you. They needed you.' All the fury collapses into the grief it was always protecting.

title: Breaking the Glass Case
instruction: You are a parent whose child just came out to you, and you're responding in real-time—no script, no rehearsal. Start with confusion that sounds like concern, your voice tight and controlled, trying to say the 'right' things while panic roars underneath. Let that control shatter: rage at yourself for not knowing, for every careless word you said, for the years they suffered in silence while you were blind. Your voice should become almost violent with protective fury—at a world that hurt them, at your own failure. Then, in the middle of that storm, let it break completely: collapse into raw fear that you've lost them, that your reaction right now is destroying everything. End with your voice stripped bare, pleading—not for them to change, but for them to teach you, to let you learn, to give you the chance to love them exactly as they are. The journey is from fear to fierce, imperfect love.

title: Talking to Someone While Severely Depressed
instruction: You're severely depressed. Someone is trying to have a conversation with you. Your voice is flat, toneless. Nothing matters. Words come out slowly, with effort. You're responding to questions but there's no life in your voice. You sound like you're underwater. Your friend is worried. 'Are you okay?' Your voice can barely say 'Yeah, I'm fine' and it's the most unconvincing lie you've ever told. Include the effort it takes to speak at all.

title: This Box Isn't Going to Move Itself
instruction: You're an older woman in a garage, trying to heave a heavy wooden crate onto a dolly. Your son said he'd be here twenty minutes ago, and you're fed up waiting. You squat, grab the edges, and lift with a held breath—your voice comes out in tight, angry bursts as you mutter to yourself. Midway, the weight shifts and your arms start to shake; irritation turns into a weary, explosive sigh as you nearly drop it. Let the strain tighten your throat, then release at the end with a sharp gasp. Speak through the exertion, with pauses and grunts between phrases.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Last Man Standing
instruction: You're a teenage guy in the middle of an intense online battle royale game. You're the last one on your team, and you can hear enemy footsteps. You start off with a cocky, loud, hyper-masculine tone, trash-talking to yourself and your dead teammates. But as the enemy gets closer, your voice cracks, your clicks get more frantic, and you mutter under your breath. By the end, you're whispering in pure fear, then you die and let out a quiet, defeated sigh. Let the controller clicks and chair squeaks punctuate your words. Your spoken lines should reflect this shift from bravado to vulnerability.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What You Never Taught Me
instruction: You're confronting your mother, who was so consumed by her academic career—her research, her publications, her intellectual pursuits—that she was emotionally absent throughout your childhood. Begin with cold, controlled anger, listing all the school plays she missed, the questions you asked that she dismissed. But as you speak, shift into something rawer: you realize she taught you to love learning itself, to question everything, to find beauty in ideas. Your anger fractures into confused grief as you recognize that her obsession with knowledge was both the wound and the unexpected gift. End in a place where resentment and reluctant understanding collide—you're furious at her absence but also undeniably shaped by the curiosity she modeled. Your voice should crack between accusation and unwilling gratitude.

title: The Secret Library
instruction: Late at night, you're whispering to your lover about a hidden part of yourself you've never shared: an obsessive, private world of knowledge you've been building alone. Maybe it's medieval architecture, marine biology, the history of forgotten languages, or the mechanics of stars. Speak softly, intimately, as though revealing something almost shameful—this private passion that makes you feel both powerful and strange. Begin with hesitant, halting words, afraid they'll find it boring or weird. As they lean in, listening with genuine fascination, let your whisper gain quiet intensity and joy. End in a place of tender exposure—you're showing them the most alive part of yourself, the part that exists when you're alone with books and wonder. Your voice should be barely audible but vibrating with suppressed excitement and vulnerability.

title: The Picture Words
instruction: You're an older man who had a stroke a few months ago, sitting at a kitchen table with your adult granddaughter. She's holding up an old photo of your late wife, and you want to tell her a funny story about that day. But the words won't come—you know the story, you can see it, but your mouth spits out wrong sounds or nothing at all. Start with frustration: you push, you stumble, you hit the table with your fist. Then, as she waits patiently, you find a single clear word for a detail that makes you both smile—the dog’s name, or the color of her hat. Let your voice go from jagged and angry to softer, slower, with a tiny hint of curiosity as you discover a sound that works. Pause long, sigh, try again. Let your body react: you might lean forward, look away, scratch your head. End on a quiet, warm half-laugh.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Underwater Proposal Gone Wrong
instruction: You're trying to propose underwater with a waterproof card, but your snorkel keeps flooding. Alternate between clear speech (head above water) and gurgling, sputtering chaos (water in mouth). The romantic words you practiced keep getting interrupted by coughing up seawater. Make it simultaneously hilarious and genuinely heartfelt — the determination to say 'Will you marry me' despite the ocean's best efforts to prevent it.

title: Watercolors in Hospital Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying partner's hospital bed at 3 AM, quietly describing the painting you're making of their hands—the only part of them that hasn't been ravaged by illness. Speak in hushed, reverent tones, as if any louder would shatter this fragile moment. Your voice should carry tenderness so profound it almost hurts, noticing every vein, every freckle, every line like you're trying to memorize them into permanence. Let quiet joy at the beauty you still find in them mix with the knowledge that you're painting a memorial. When you describe adding their wedding ring to the painting, feel your throat tighten, your words catching. End with a whispered confession that you can't finish the painting because finishing it means accepting this is goodbye. Your delivery should feel like touching something precious and breakable, love and loss existing in the same breath.

title: The Last Garden Walk
instruction: You're walking through your childhood garden one final time before hospice care begins tomorrow. You start by cataloging what you see—the roses, the stone bench, the tree you climbed—your voice steady, almost tour-guide mechanical, holding grief at arm's length. Midway through, you touch the bark of that tree and something breaks open: you realize you're not saying goodbye to the garden, you're saying goodbye to the child you were, to all the dreams that little person had. Your breathing becomes ragged. The final words are to that child, a tender apology mixed with fierce gratitude for their hope, their innocence. You can barely speak the last sentence: 'You deserved better than what I became.' Let silence hold the weight. Then, almost inaudible, with unexpected peace: 'But maybe... maybe you got something after all.'

title: The Weight of You
instruction: You're a man in your third trimester of pregnancy, sitting on the edge of a bed, breathless from the pressure on your lungs. You're talking to your unborn child, speaking from a place of deep longing that grows as you go. Start with wonder at the reality of carrying life, and shift into a tender ache, almost a grief, for the world they'll inherit. Let your voice be effortful, punctuated with sighs and shifts in your seat as you adjust your posture. Let the words catch in your throat, not from sadness, but from the overwhelming weight of hope.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Right Turn
instruction: You are an elderly person driving alone through busy traffic, heading to a familiar place that suddenly feels wrong. Doubt clings to every decision—you second-guess the lane, the exit, your own memory. Your voice wavers, interrupted by the click of the turn signal, a glance at the rearview mirror, the engine's hum. But when you finally commit to a turn and see the landmark you were looking for, a quiet pride rises. Let your voice shift from hesitant, almost apologetic mutterings to a firm, satisfied statement of certainty. End with a soft, proud breath.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight of Letting Go
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's already slipped into unconsciousness. Begin speaking to her with desperate energy, trying to say everything you never said—apologies, gratitude, confessions, promises. Feel the weight of all these unspoken words pressing down on you physically. As you speak, let your body slowly surrender to gravity, your voice dropping from urgent to whispered, your posture collapsing from upright to hunched to nearly lying beside her bed. By the end, you're no longer trying to be heard—you're simply releasing everything into the silence, your body and voice completely emptied, accepting that she's already gone. Transform from frantic denial to profound, physical exhaustion and acceptance.

title: Gale-Force Longing
instruction: You're at the edge of a cliff path, and the love of your life just appeared on the trail below. You call out to them, voice low and hungry with lust. But a sudden gale slams into you—you turn your head, gasp, shout against the buffeting wind. Words get torn away; you stagger, amazed at the power of it. Your initial smooth yearning cracks into astonishment, then desperate effort. End with a raw, wind-whipped cry that still carries desire.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Gratitude That Burns
instruction: You're thanking someone who saved you or sacrificed for you when you were young—but as you speak, you're also reckoning with how their salvation came with a cost you're still paying. Begin with genuine gratitude, recounting specific acts of protection or generosity from your childhood. Let the warmth be real. But as you continue, let resentment or grief surface: ways their help also trapped you, how their sacrifice became a debt you couldn't repay, how being saved also meant being defined by your need. Hold both truths simultaneously—the love and the anger, the gratitude and the burden. Your voice should move through appreciation, then complication, then land somewhere that honors both the gift and the price. End with an emotional complexity that refuses simple resolution.

title: Drunk-Dialing Your Ex at 2AM
instruction: Perform the classic terrible decision. Your voice slurs with liquid courage. Start aggressive ('I just want you to know—'), then immediately soften ('I miss you so much'). Cycle through emotions: anger, sadness, longing, self-pity, false bravado. Include the mid-call realization that their new partner might be listening. The volume swings wildly. End with either hanging up in mortified silence or leaving a rambling voicemail you'll regret forever.

title: Thunder in the Barn
instruction: You are in the barn where you and your first love used to hide during summer storms fifteen years ago—the smell of hay and wood and rain, the sound of drops hammering the tin roof, the dusty light through cracks in the walls. You're here now in a thunderstorm, and they've just told you they never stopped loving you, that leaving you was the biggest mistake of their life. Begin with the sensory assault of the storm: feel the temperature drop, the ozone smell, your clothes damp, your heart pounding in rhythm with the thunder. Let your body remember what happened in this space—the wild, reckless passion of being eighteen, skin on skin in the hay, the world reduced to touch and breath and desperate wanting. Let that physical memory rise in your body—heat, pulse, the ache of desire mixed with the rage of abandonment. They hurt you. They destroyed you. But your body remembers what it felt to be utterly consumed by them in this exact space. Let fury and hunger war in you. End by either surrendering to the physical pull or violently rejecting it—but let your whole body make the choice.

title: Whispering to a Sleeping Child
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's bed late at night, watching them sleep, and whispering things you can't say when they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, tender, trembling with vulnerability. You apologize for the ways you've already failed them, confess your fears about the parent you're becoming. Your voice catches as you tell them how fiercely you love them, how terrified you are of this love. You whisper about your own childhood, about promises you're making, about hope and doubt tangled together. As you speak, something shifts—the weight you've been carrying feels slightly lighter. By the end, your whisper is still sad but also filled with determination. You touch their hair gently. You can't promise perfection, but you can promise presence. The quiet holds everything.

title: Homecoming Command
instruction: You've just walked in the door after a week away, still in your coat and shoes, cellphone buzzing in your pocket. Your partner stands by the couch, waiting. Start with a low, affectionate growl as you step close and slide a hand behind their neck — your voice is warm, possessive, almost tender. But as you pull them in, the memory of the days apart fuels a surge of triumph; your voice hardens, drops deeper, the words become deliberate and dirty, commanding them to look at you. Let the affection stay underneath, but let the pleasure of dominance rise and take over by the final phrase.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Time Zone Tangle
instruction: You're a young woman trying to relax in a quiet room at 11 p.m., but your body insists it's noon. You're talking to a friend on the phone about a simple plan for tomorrow, but your words feel slow, and you keep losing track. Start with a slightly irritable, impatient tone—frustrated that your mind won't cooperate and that you can't even focus on a basic conversation. Mid-sentence, a yawn escapes, and you pause, confused about what you were saying. By the end, let your voice soften into a tired, almost apologetic admission that you need to give up and just let your body figure itself out, even if it means doing nothing.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Confusion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Breaking the Stallion
instruction: You are in the throes of intense physical pain—a body pushed past its limits—but simultaneously experiencing a breakthrough of ecstatic emotional liberation. Begin with wild, untamed power coursing through you: your movements large and explosive, your breath coming in powerful snorts and gasps, your entire being surging against constraints. You want to kick, to rear up, to run. The pain is fuel for your fury and strength. As the experience continues, feel your body begin to yield—not in defeat, but in surrender to something greater than resistance. Your breath deepens, your movements become more fluid, more graceful. By the end, the same powerful energy flows through you but channeled differently: still strong but now integrated, cooperative with rather than fighting against. The arc moves from explosive, resistant power to channeled, harmonious strength.
inspired_by: The character requires physical attitudes, primal impulses, or a BEING state that no other choice approach has been able to produce

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the middle of the night, and you're about to whisper a truth you've never told anyone—something about yourself that fills you with shame, or a secret desire that terrifies you, or something you did that you can't take back. Begin with your heart pounding in the silence, that specific terror of making yourself completely known to another person. Feel the vulnerability of darkness, of whispered words that can't be taken back. As you speak, let yourself tremble—not theatrically, but with the genuine fear of rejection mixed with the desperate need to be fully seen. Draw on moments when you revealed your true self and weren't sure if you'd be accepted. Let the words come haltingly, with long pauses where you almost stop but can't. By the end, allow yourself to feel either the profound relief of being heard and held, or the devastating loneliness of silence in response—whichever feels most true in the moment.

title: Mapping You in Darkness
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your lover in complete darkness after making love. Begin in satisfied, drowsy contentment. Then, barely above a whisper, start asking them questions you've never asked—not sexual, but soul-deep. What did you dream of becoming when you were seven? What's the worst thing you've ever thought about yourself? When do you feel most alone? Let each answer they give (real or imagined) make you fall deeper into intimacy and simultaneously realize how much mystery remains. Feel wonder and slight fear mixing together. End with the terrifying, exquisite recognition that you could spend lifetimes asking questions and never fully know another person. Your voice should be intimate, whispered, tender—moving from satisfaction to curiosity to awed vulnerability.

title: Late Night Call-In
instruction: You are a 17-year-old hosting a late-night radio show, alone in the booth with headphones on and the mic close. You start with that smooth, warm, slightly performative host voice—like you're smiling for the listener but also half-aware of the glowing console and the hiss of static. Halfway through reading a listener's message, their voice breaks through on a prerecorded clip, and it catches you off guard. You feel a flicker of genuine attraction, something raw beneath the practiced tone. Let your voice shift from polished control to a slight, unconscious breathiness, a pause where you lose your train of thought, then a quieter, more vulnerable delivery as you sign off. You might fidget with the mic stand or glance at the clock.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Bedside Vigil: Whispering Everything Left Unsaid
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply—a partner, best friend, the person who knows you best—who is unconscious and fading. It's the middle of the night, just you and them and the sound of medical equipment. You begin speaking in barely more than a whisper, your voice thick with unshed tears, telling them all the things you never said out loud: the mundane moments that meant everything, the ways they changed you, the future you'd planned together. Your voice should catch and break on certain words, those intimate details that only you two share. Move from tender reminiscence to quiet, devastating grief as you realize you're saying goodbye. Include long pauses where your breath shakes, where you have to steady yourself. End with your voice so small and broken it's almost inaudible, telling them it's okay to let go even though it's destroying you to say it.
inspired_by: Megaphone Protest Leader: Voice Giving Out

title: The Last Dance at the Wake
instruction: You've just returned from your best friend's funeral. They died young—an accident, an illness, something sudden. You're alone in your apartment, and their favorite song comes on shuffle. Begin laughing—really laughing—at a memory of them doing something ridiculous, something that captures exactly who they were. Let that laughter be genuine and full. But don't let it stay pure—let grief start seeping in at the edges. Your laughter becomes mixed with tears, then the tears take over, then you're angry—furious at them for leaving, at God, at the unfairness. Then let the anger crack into something else: gratitude. Speak to them directly, your voice a mess of contradictions—thanking them through tears, cursing them with love, celebrating them while breaking apart. End with a strange, transcendent mix of joy and devastation, your voice almost ecstatic with the painful beauty of having known them. You're destroyed and elevated at once.
inspired_by: Actor needs to build a repertoire of choices for future use

title: The Truth About Why You Left
instruction: You're confronting your parent about why they abandoned you as a child, and they're finally ready to tell you the truth. Start with controlled anger, your voice tight with years of rehearsed accusations and questions you've carried like stones. But as they begin to answer—really answer—your certainty starts to crumble. Their reasons are more complicated than you wanted them to be: fear, shame, their own trauma, impossible choices. Your voice moves from accusation to confusion, from anger to something more fragile. Let yourself break open as you realize forgiveness and fury can exist simultaneously. End in a place of devastating understanding—you're still hurt, still angry, but you finally see them as human, flawed, terrified. Your voice should tremble with the weight of letting go of the simple story you told yourself.

title: Unexpected Face in the Crowd
instruction: You're at a busy outdoor market, phone in hand, about to send a text. You glance up and freeze—standing ten feet away, staring at a booth, is your older sister who disappeared three years ago without a word. A gasp escapes you before you can stop it. Your voice shoots up, breathless and fractured. You start babbling—'Oh my God! I thought—where did you—' Then you stumble toward her, jacket rustling, phone clattering to the ground. As you reach her, your voice breaks into a tearful laugh and softens into trembling relief: 'I can't believe it's you. I missed you so much.' The awe sneaks in as you touch her sleeve, half-convinced she's a ghost.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Helmet Haze
instruction: You are an elderly woman riding pillion on a motorcycle, wearing a full-face helmet. The ride has ended, and you're parked at the side of a quiet road. Your grandson's voice is muffled and distant through the helmet's padding, and the visor's echo makes everything sound boomy and underwater. At first, confusion grips you — you can't make out what he's saying, and you feel disoriented from the vibration and wind noise. You shift your head, tap the helmet, try to focus. Then, through the fog, you realize he’s asking if you're okay, and that you've arrived safely. A wave of relief washes over you. Your voice should start tight, strained, with a slight tremor from the enclosed acoustics — then soften, slow, and warm as relief settles in. Use natural pauses, adjust your head position as if trying to hear, and let your breath catch between confusion and clarity.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Before Your Child Leaves for War
instruction: You're making breakfast like it's any other morning, keeping your voice light and practical as you ask if they want more coffee. But your hands are shaking. Each mundane question—'Do you have everything packed?'—carries the weight of all the things you can't say. As you move through these final domestic rituals, your voice starts to crack around the edges. You're trying so hard to give them a normal goodbye, to be strong, but by the time you're standing at the door, you can barely get the words out. The 'I love you' that seemed so simple ten minutes ago now feels impossible to say without your whole body breaking. Let yourself move from forced cheerfulness to that raw, helpless place where a parent's love and terror collide.
inspired_by: Someone Telling You They Have a Terminal Diagnosis

title: Twenty Years of Silence Breaking
instruction: You're confronting your father/mother about the childhood you needed but didn't get. Begin with bitter, controlled anger—listing facts, maintaining distance, your voice sharp and defensive. You've rehearsed this, built walls around it. But as you speak, something shifts. Their silence or their attempt to explain cracks your armor. Let the anger fracture into hurt, then into the raw voice of the child still inside you asking 'why wasn't I enough?' Feel the humiliation of needing them even now, the rage at yourself for caring, the grief for the parent-child relationship that never was. End in a different place entirely—not forgiveness, but exhausted honesty. Your voice should strip away decades of protection until you're speaking with devastating plainness about the love you still have for someone who failed you, and how much that love costs.

title: Reading Your Estranged Sibling's Suicide Note—While Also Reading Their Letter From Rehab They Never Sent
instruction: You found both letters in their belongings. The suicide note is two weeks old. The rehab letter—hopeful, planning to reconnect—is from three months ago, never mailed. You're reading them aloud, back and forth between despair and hope, and your voice can't reconcile the two. Start with the suicide note: voice shaking, disbelieving, each word physically painful. Then switch to the rehab letter: suddenly your voice lifts slightly—you can hear them in it, the person they were becoming, and you're almost laughing through tears at their jokes, their plans. Back to the suicide note: voice drops, trembles violently, devastated by the contrast. Keep switching between documents, and let your emotions whipsaw—gratitude for who they were becoming, rage that they gave up, grief that you never got the rehab letter in time, love that breaks you open. End with silence, then one whispered word: their name, containing everything—love, loss, forgiveness, devastation—all at once.
inspired_by: Withdrawing from Alcohol: Shaking So Bad Your Voice Trembles

title: Storm's Embrace
instruction: You are standing alone in a violent thunderstorm, rain lashing your face, thunder cracking overhead. You've just walked out of a final, bitter argument with someone you loved, and every step aches — your body is cold, your hands shake from rage and hurt. Start by shouting into the wind, your voice raw with pain and biting bitterness, cursing the unfairness of it all. But as the storm rages on, you pause — wiping water from your eyes, shivering — and slowly, a strange calm settles. You realize this downpour is washing away the anger, and you let out a quiet, trembling laugh. End with a deep, breathy contentment, feeling almost grateful for the storm's brutal honesty. Speak loudly to be heard over the rain, let your voice crack and waver, and don't fight the natural pauses as thunder interrupts or you gasp for air.
emotions_sampled: Pain (extremely present), Bitterness (very intensely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Twisted Confession
instruction: You are in a yoga class, holding a deep torso twist while slightly tipsy from wine. You're on the phone with your young daughter, who is asking why you sound funny. At first, you try to sound upbeat and in control, explaining you're just stretching. But as the twist intensifies, your breath becomes strained and your words wobble. You start confessing that you miss her mom, and the playfulness fades into raw vulnerability, your voice catching with emotion. Let the physical effort of the twist make your voice uneven, crack, and lose stability as the truth slips out.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The State of the Hedges
instruction: You are an elderly person using a walkie-talkie to report to a neighbor about overgrown hedges on the shared property line. The transmission crackles each time you press the button. You begin with mild contempt and disgust—you've told them before, and they never listen. Midway, you pause, lose your train of thought, then sigh. By the end, the irritation gives way to resigned weariness; you're too tired to keep pushing. Let your voice sound compressed and slightly nasal, with the button clicks framing each burst of speech.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Conceding Defeat
instruction: You've fought for ten years. The lawsuit, the campaign, the dream. It's over. You're not winning. Your voice when you tell your team is the voice of someone who has nothing left. Not angry—worse. Resigned. Tired in a way that suggests you'll never be unexhausted. 'We tried,' you say quietly. 'It wasn't enough.' The silence after that statement contains everything—the money wasted, the marriages strained, the hope that got buried. You sound like you've aged a decade in one day.

title: The Trophy They Gave Me
instruction: You are at a packed town hall meeting where you’ve just been awarded a community service prize for your volunteer work with refugees. As you step up to the podium, someone from the back yells that you only did it to get famous, and half the crowd starts murmuring agreement. You freeze, face burning, and try to explain through a tightened throat. Start with a voice almost gone, barely a whisper directed at your shoes, choked with gratitude for the award but shattered by the accusation. Let your words falter, break, and then — as you remember the faces of the children you helped — a quiet, fierce elation rises, making your voice tremble with unexpected joy, though still laced with distress. End with a cracked but determined whisper of thanks, your eyes still on the floor but your chin lifting slightly.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Distress (very intensely present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Everything You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting someone who was supposed to protect you but failed—a parent, a guardian, someone who should have seen you. Start with your voice shaking but determined, almost apologetic for even bringing it up: 'I need you to hear this.' As you begin listing what you needed and never received, your voice gains strength and edge. The anger builds—not loud, but sharp, cutting. 'I was a child. I needed you to...' Your breath catches on specific memories. Then the anger cracks open and underneath is raw hurt: your voice becomes smaller, younger, more vulnerable. 'Why wasn't I enough?' By the end, you're not asking for anything anymore. Your voice settles into something resigned but also strangely liberated: 'I don't need you to understand. I just needed to say it.' The final words carry both grief for what will never be and acceptance that you're walking away.

title: Folding Your Clothes
instruction: You're alone, folding the clothes of someone you loved who has just died. Your voice is barely above a whisper, talking to them as if they're still here: 'You always folded the sleeves in first... like this.' Each piece of clothing brings a memory that catches in your throat. Your voice trembles with tender precision: 'This is the shirt you wore when you told me you loved me.' The grief is quiet, intimate, devastating. You're not crying loudly—you're breathing through something that feels like drowning. End with your voice breaking on something small: 'You have a button missing. I was going to fix it.' Let the silence hold everything you can't say.

title: The Bright Side of a Bad Day
instruction: You're a mother playing with your toddler on the living room floor, but you have a pounding migraine that won't let up. You're trying to keep your voice bright and high-pitched, using exaggerated, happy parentese—slowed-down words, silly sounds, simple sentences. But every few seconds, a sharp wave of pain makes you flinch or trail off. You start with cheerful focus on the toy, but as the pain builds, your voice becomes more strained, your pitches flatten, and you eventually have to stop mid-sentence, telling your child you need a break while your voice breaks with genuine hurt. Let your performance be full of tiny gasps, winces, forced smiles that fade, and the natural hesitation of someone fighting through discomfort.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who's Already Gone
instruction: You're alone in a hospital room in the middle of the night. They died three hours ago, but you can't leave yet. You're whispering to them, telling them small things—how you noticed they started wearing the scarf you gave them, how their garden is blooming, how the dog still waits by the door. Your voice is so quiet it's almost just breath. Start with tender observations, gentle and intimate. Then let it catch: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' The whisper becomes even smaller, broken by silences where you can't find air. You're not crying loudly—this is the kind of grief that steals your voice, that lives in your throat. End with one last thing you needed to say, something simple and devastating, spoken so softly it's almost a secret between you and the dark.
inspired_by: Giving a Eulogy When You Weren't Prepared to Feel It

title: The Last Goodbye at the Terminal
instruction: You're seeing off someone you love at a space station departure gate—they're leaving on a one-way colonization mission to another planet. You'll never see them again. Start trying to be brave, cheerful even, making jokes about how they'll finally get away from you. But your voice keeps cracking. They take your hand and you break—not into sobs, but into that quiet, throat-closing devastation where words barely come out. Tell them everything you should have said years ago, your voice raw and stripped bare. Include the moment where grief transforms into a kind of fierce gratitude for having known them at all. By the end, your voice should sound like someone learning to let go while every cell in your body screams to hold on. The final 'I love you' should be barely audible but contain more truth than anything you've ever said.

title: Whispering Secrets at 3 AM
instruction: You're lying in bed at 3 AM beside your partner of ten years, and something has broken open inside you. Start by whispering their name softly, almost afraid to wake them fully. Your voice should be intimate, close, fragile—confessing something you've never told anyone. Perhaps it's about the child you gave up for adoption before you met them, or the abortion you never mentioned, or the sibling who died that you never speak of, or the sexual assault you've carried alone. Begin with hesitant fragments, voice catching, pausing, almost backing out. But let the relief of finally speaking it become its own momentum—your whispers grow more urgent, more detailed, occasionally louder before catching yourself. Mix vulnerability with shame, relief with fear of being known this completely. By the end, the confession has shifted from unburdening yourself to asking, almost inaudibly, 'Do you still love me?' The emotional journey moves from protective silence to terrifying exposure to desperate need for acceptance.

title: Shattered Protector: Discovering You Failed the One You Swore to Save
instruction: You've just learned the truth—while you were protecting everyone else, the person you loved most was suffering in ways you never saw. Start with disbelief, voice rising: 'That's not possible, I would have known.' Reality hits in waves. Your voice becomes fierce, almost violent in its self-recrimination: 'I was RIGHT THERE. How did I not SEE?' Rage at yourself, at the universe, at the unfairness. Then collapse—your voice breaks entirely, becomes small, childlike: 'I promised I would keep you safe.' The explosion of emotion gives way to anguished pleading directed at no one: 'Please, let me go back, let me fix this.' End with the terrible calm of someone accepting an unbearable truth. Your voice steadies into something broken but resolute: you can't undo it, but you'll carry it forever. Final words are both vow and surrender: 'I will never forgive myself. And I will never stop trying to be better.'
inspired_by: Professional: Mentor Must Fire Their Most Promising Protégé

title: The Candy Jar Morning
instruction: You are a 7-year-old girl in your cozy, carpeted bedroom after breakfast—your voice is small and sing-songy, the kind you use when you want to be adorable. You find a forgotten, sticky candy jar under your bed and try to pry off the lid, but it's crusted and won't budge. At first you're sweetly determined, but as you wrestle with it, a sour, frustrated pout creeps into your voice—your words curdle as you spill your complaint to no one, ending with a defeated little huff and a sigh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You and your closest friend are sitting in near-darkness, perhaps after a long evening, and exhaustion has lowered your defenses. Begin in a state of quiet wakefulness—tired, unguarded, present. In barely more than a whisper, confess something you've carried alone for years: a fear, a shame, a secret desire, something that makes you feel exposed and fragile. Let the darkness hold you as you speak. Notice how vulnerability feels in your body—the tightness in your throat, the relief of letting words escape. This isn't dramatic revelation; it's intimate, almost fragile truth-telling. By the end, allow yourself to feel the profound tenderness of being truly seen by another person. Let the weight you've carried begin to lift, even slightly.

title: 3 AM Unraveling
instruction: In the dark stillness of early morning, whisper a confession to your sleeping partner lying beside you—something you've never told anyone. Perhaps a recurring dream that haunts you, a moment of profound shame, or a loss that still breaks you. Begin barely audible, testing whether you can even say the words aloud. Let the darkness make you brave. Your voice should be intimate, fragile, trembling between words. Access something from your actual dreams or a private sorrow you rarely touch. Though they sleep, you're finally speaking your truth into existence. End with either quiet tears of release or a whispered plea for forgiveness—from them, from yourself, from the universe. Let vulnerability feel like both terror and relief.

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table, finally confronting her about the emotional absence that defined your childhood.
