Start with controlled anger—itemizing specific memories, keeping your voice measured, almost lawyer-like in your precision. She tries to interrupt but you cut her off, your voice getting harder, sharper. Then you see her hands shaking as she reaches for her coffee cup, and something shifts. The anger doesn't disappear but it cracks, revealing the desperate child underneath who just wanted to be seen. Your voice breaks completely: 'I just needed you to love me the way I was.' The words that follow are both furious and heartbroken, blaming and begging simultaneously. End with you reaching for her hand even as tears stream down your face, whispering: 'I still do. I still need that.' The vulnerability is excruciating.

title: The Name That Stung
instruction: You're at a dinner party with close friends, seated across from someone you've been secretly infatuated with for weeks. You're telling a light, flirty story about a ridiculous mishap at work, your voice bright and slightly breathy as you glance around the table, leaning in to make eye contact with him. Mid-sentence, he casually mentions his wife's name while helping himself to more wine. Your voice falters—a tiny pause, a forced laugh that doesn't reach your eyes. You finish the story, but now your tone is thinner, higher, brittle, and you keep looking down at your plate, your words trailing off as you realize everyone is waiting for you to continue. Your ending is a quiet, hollow 'Anyway…' that hangs in the air.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unsent Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you wrote to someone you loved who died before you could reconcile. Your voice starts barely above a whisper, intimate and careful, like you're afraid of disturbing them. 'I should have called you back.' Each confession is small, tender, devastating. Your throat keeps closing around the words. There are long pauses where you can't speak at all. Midway through, something softens—you begin remembering a specific moment of kindness they showed you, and your voice fills with a bittersweet warmth. 'You always knew, didn't you?' Then the reality returns: they're gone. The final line is 'I forgive you,' but your voice breaks on it because you're also asking for forgiveness. This is not performed grief—it's the real thing, caught in your throat.

title: The Echo of a Name
instruction: You are an elderly person, standing at one end of a long, dimly lit hallway, facing a closed door at the other end. You've come to collect something from this room, but your memory is worn and frayed. As you begin to walk, a faint, contemptuous thought about the person inside flickers—a past slight you haven't quite forgiven. The sound of your own footsteps and the eerie echo make you feel unsteady. Let your voice start with a low, distracted mutter, almost to yourself, then shift into a trembling, bemused realization that you've forgotten the name of the person you came to see—and your contempt dissolves into a quiet, aching loneliness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Parent What You Can Never Say Aloud
instruction: They're asleep in the chair. You've been caring for them for months. Start barely above a whisper, testing the words: 'I'm so tired.' Let the confession grow—admit things you'd never say to their face. Your voice stays quiet but becomes more vulnerable: 'Sometimes I resent you. Sometimes I wish...' Pause, horrified at yourself. Feel the guilt wash over you, your voice breaking: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' But don't let it stay there. Find the deeper truth underneath—speak about the love that makes this so hard, the memories of when they were strong, the tenderness mixed with exhaustion. End with your voice catching on something simple and devastating: 'I don't know how to lose you.' Let silence hold the weight. This isn't theatrical—it's the kind of whispered honesty that only comes in the dark.
inspired_by: Your Parent Becoming Emotionally Dependent on You

title: The Last Bloom
instruction: You are an elderly woman on a park bench, watching a younger person across the way. A soft breeze stirs dry leaves, and you find yourself speaking quietly—almost to yourself—about how strange it feels to still notice beauty like this. Your voice is low, thoughtful, a bit fragile, as you touch your silver hair and glance at the empty seat beside you. Then you let out a small, breathy laugh, and your tone lifts into teasing warmth—a playful crack in your reserve. End with a flirty offer for them to share the bench, letting your voice waver with the surprise of your own boldness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Permission You'll Ever Give
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they're asking for your permission to let go. Start with desperate resistance - your voice tight, almost angry, insisting they have to stay, have to fight. But as you speak, you feel the cruelty of your own selfishness. Your voice begins to crack, softens, becomes tender. By the end, you're whispering through tears, telling them it's okay, they can rest now, even though it's destroying you to say it. The transformation is from fierce denial to surrendering love - from 'Don't you dare leave me' to 'I love you enough to let you go.' Let your voice break where it needs to.

title: Astronaut's Last Transmission Before Deep Space
instruction: You're an astronaut whose ship has malfunctioned beyond repair, drifting away from Earth's orbit with only minutes of oxygen left. You're recording a final message to your child back home. Start with forced calm and practical instructions about your savings account and where you hid birthday presents for the next ten years. But as oxygen deprivation sets in, your thoughts scatter—you see your child as a toddler again, you smell flowers from your childhood garden, time becomes fluid. You catch yourself mid-ramble and fight to stay coherent, to say something that matters. Your breathing becomes labored, words come slower. End with a moment of unexpected peace as you describe something beautiful you see in the void, your voice softening to almost nothing, wonder replacing fear.

title: The Overhang
instruction: You're a teenage boy climbing a steep rock face alone. Your arms ache and your fingers are cramping as you cling to a small ledge. You're focused on finding the next hold, whispering to yourself to breathe. Then you glance up and see the sun breaking through the clouds, lighting up the valley below. Your breath catches and your voice shifts from gasping effort to a quiet, trembling awe as you murmur what you see.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the 'legacy' they're so proud of—a family business built on sacrifice that destroyed your childhood. Start with bitter, controlled sarcasm: 'Your legacy. The thing you're so proud of.' But as you list what you actually inherited—anxiety, perfectionism, the inability to rest—your voice rises with decades of suppressed rage. 'I was eight years old and you missed my birthday because of your legacy!' Let the anger crack open to reveal the wounded child underneath: 'I just wanted you to see me.' End with quiet, devastating clarity, tears streaming but voice steady: 'I don't want your empire. I wanted a parent.' The final line should land like a door closing forever: 'Keep your legacy. I'm building my own.'

title: The Perfect Smile Cracks
instruction: You're a customer service representative at a call center, and you're also a single mother. It's the end of your shift, and you're on the final call of the day. Your toddler is tugging at your pant leg, quietly babbling. You need to maintain your professional 'smile-voice'—bright, artificially high, full of uptalk—as you help this customer. But unbeknownst to the caller, you just lost your job to downsizing, and your shame is overwhelming. Begin the call with a chirpy, plastic cheerfulness, but as the toddler persists and the shame of your situation sinks in, let the smile-voice waver, crack, and finally dissolve into a quiet, raw whisper of relief and defeat as you end the call.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Fever of Reunion
instruction: You're seeing your ex-lover for the first time in two years, and the moment you make eye contact, your body remembers everything. Begin with physical sensation—your heart racing, your skin flushing, your hands trembling. Let the physical lead you to emotional questions: what do you feel about the way they're looking at you? What does their nearness do to your breath? What do you feel about wanting them despite everything? As you speak or move toward them, let desire war with other feelings—anger at past betrayals, fear of being hurt again, joy at their presence, rage at your own weakness. Your voice should be affected by this storm of sensation—perhaps breathless, perhaps breaking between anger and want, perhaps moving from controlled distance to desperate closeness. End in complete physical and emotional surrender to a feeling that's opposite to where you began.
inspired_by: Taking Your Emotional Point of View

title: The Last Light Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your mentor's hospital bed in the pre-dawn darkness, knowing these are the final hours. Start with barely controlled panic, voice tight: 'I'm not ready for you to go. I still need you.' As they squeeze your hand weakly, something shifts—anger surfaces: 'You promised you'd see me succeed. You promised.' But their eyes hold yours with such profound peace that your anger dissolves into raw grief. Your voice breaks: 'How do I do this without you?' They whisper something you can't quite hear, and suddenly you understand they're giving you permission to be afraid and strong simultaneously. End with a voice transformed by reluctant acceptance, tender and devastated: 'I'll carry you with me. Every choice, every moment—you'll be there.' You're saying goodbye and hello at once, your voice holding both the weight of loss and the strange, terrible gift of their peaceful release.

title: The Reckoning: Parent Confronts the Person Who Hurt Their Child
instruction: You're face-to-face with someone who harmed your child, and you start with volcanic rage—voice shaking with barely controlled fury, words sharp and cutting, demanding answers. Your breath is ragged, aggressive. You want to destroy them with your voice alone. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: your rage cracks open and underneath is something more terrifying—absolute helplessness. Your voice breaks from roaring anger into gasping sobs because you couldn't protect them, you weren't there, and no amount of fury will undo what happened. End in the collision of fierce protectiveness and devastating powerlessness, your voice raw and stripped of everything but the primal pain of a parent who failed to shield their child. Let the transformation from rage to broken vulnerability be complete and shattering.
inspired_by: Professional: Lawyer Defends Someone They Know Is Guilty

title: Lightning in the Blood
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—maybe a miracle, maybe a disaster, but something that floods your entire body with sensation. Begin with your breath completely disrupted—gasping, held, ragged. Let physical sensation drive your voice: maybe electricity running through your limbs, heat in your chest, trembling that turns to shaking. Allow sounds of exhilaration, terror, or ecstasy to burst out—primal, animal, uncontrolled. Don't think about what you're expressing; let your body express through you. As the intensity builds to an almost unbearable peak, let it suddenly break into something else—perhaps uncontrollable laughter mixed with sobbing, or fierce howls that dissolve into whispers. Move from explosive physical release to complete collapse, letting every sound be a direct expression of sensation moving through you.
inspired_by: Actor intellectualizes emotions or describes feelings rather than expressing them

title: The Last Hill
instruction: You're a young guy with a deep, hyper-masculine voice, pushing yourself through the final steep hill of a long run. Your breath is ragged, each exhale timed with your pounding steps—your words come out in a shaky, cadence-locked tremolo. You start frustrated, muttering about how much this hill sucks, but as you crest the top and see the view, a raw, unguarded elation breaks through. Let your voice climb from grumbling weariness into a breathless, genuine laugh of triumph, with the rhythm of your strides still shaking every syllable.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Vigil in the Dim Light
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's sleeping—maybe a child, maybe a lover—and you're whispering things you could never say while they're awake. Start with tender observation, voice soft as breath. 'Your hands are so small. I forget how small.' Let gratitude seep in, quiet and overwhelming. 'You saved my life just by existing, did you know that?' But then the fear arrives, gentle and devastating—the knowledge that you can't protect them from everything, that you might fail them, that this perfect moment is temporary. Your voice catches, barely audible: 'I'm so afraid I won't be enough for you.' End in whispered devotion mixed with heartbreak, knowing they'll never hear these words, grateful they're sleeping so you can finally be this honest.

title: Sunstruck and Smitten
instruction: You're an older adult who collapsed from heat exhaustion after trying to impress someone you're intensely attracted to. They're now crouched beside you, fanning you with a hat. Your voice is weak, slurred, and parched—speech comes in slow, dizzy fragments. Begin with deep embarrassment: you hate being seen this vulnerable, fumbling for dignity. Then, as you meet their eyes, fierce pride rises—you risked it for them, you did something bold. Let the lust seep through despite the exhaustion; your voice drops, attempts a flirtatious rasp, but trails off as you lose focus. End with a raw, lopsided admission that mixes all three feelings.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Gravel in the Mirror
instruction: You're in a filthy bathroom, hunched over a cracked sink, having just taken a hit from a cheap pipe. Outside, the person who got you into this is calling your name, impatient. You stare at your own reflection—eyes bloodshot, mouth bitter. Start with a thick, terrified whisper, coughing and clearing your throat every few words. Let your voice shake with shame, but as the footsteps get closer, let that shame curdle into a low, raspy malice. By the end, you're speaking through clenched teeth, a threat wrapped in smoke. Your words should feel like stones rolling off a damaged throat.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Truth Before Departure
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is leaving tomorrow for a mission they won't return from. You begin with absolute certainty, telling them the truths you've held back for years—speaking with that same unwavering conviction, each word a gift you're finally giving. But as you continue, your certainty begins to crack. The steady pace falters. Your breath catches. By the end, you're whispering the final truth through tears, your voice breaking on words that once felt so solid. The conviction transforms into desperate tenderness, as if saying it with enough belief could somehow keep them here. Let your voice journey from rock-solid truth to trembling vulnerability, all while never letting go of the love underneath.

title: Confession with a Shudder
instruction: You're sitting on a park bench next to someone you've admired for months. The sun is warm, but you're trembling inside. Every few seconds, a sudden bark or word — like 'Yep!' or a sharp grunt — cuts through your sentence, and you have to keep going as if it didn't happen. At first, you're embarrassed, your voice tight and halting. But as you talk about the way their laugh sounds in the morning, a surprising tenderness breaks through, and by the end you're almost laughing at your own tics, letting your infatuation spill out raw and real. Speak approximately 50 words, letting the tics land naturally and then pushing through them with a breath.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Body's Truth
instruction: You have just experienced an overwhelming physical moment—intense pleasure, fierce pain, or both intertwined. Your body is still trembling, raw, alive. Begin in pure sensation, allowing sound and breath to express what your body feels without filtering or intellectualizing. Let yourself be unguarded, animal, unashamed. As you find words, let them emerge from sensation rather than thought—speak what your body knows that your mind has always censored. Let embarrassment and self-consciousness arise, then consciously push past them. End in a place of fierce physical honesty and power—claiming your body's wisdom, your capacity to feel intensely, your right to exist fully in your skin without apology.

title: Daughter to Father: The Unsaid Things
instruction: You're confronting your aging father about his emotional absence throughout your childhood, and you've rehearsed this speech for twenty years. Start with controlled anger—'Do you even remember my tenth birthday?'—listing specific moments he missed, your voice sharp and prosecutorial. But as you talk, something shifts. You hear how old his breathing sounds. Your accusations start mixing with memories of the one time he did show up, that baseball game in the rain. Your voice wavers between rage and desperate longing: 'Why couldn't you just love me the way I needed?' By the end, you're not yelling anymore. You're asking, almost whispering, 'Did you ever want to? Did you just not know how?' Let the anger dissolve into something more painful—the grief of realizing he was broken too, and it's too late to fix either of you.

title: Rage in the Nursery
instruction: Stand over your newborn's crib in the middle of the night, sleep-deprived to the point of breaking, and let the feelings you're not supposed to have explode out. Start with fierce, whispered anger at how hard this is, how no one prepared you for the loss of yourself, the terror, the relentless need. Your voice should be raw with exhaustion and fury—at the baby, at yourself, at the impossible expectations. Then let it shatter into something else: desperate, protective love that terrifies you with its intensity. You'd die for this tiny person and you resent them for it. Sob through the contradiction—'I love you so much and I'm so angry and I'm so scared I'm failing you.' End in a place of devastating tenderness, your voice breaking as you promise to be better tomorrow, to keep going, even as you feel utterly helpless. The final words should be both a lullaby and a plea for forgiveness.
inspired_by: Coma Visitor: Talking to Someone Who Can't Respond

title: The Mechanic's Wink
instruction: You are a 17-year-old at a family dinner, seated across from your older cousin's new girlfriend. You're trying to act normal, but every time she laughs or leans forward to reach for the bread, your stomach flips. You're flushed with a confusing, powerful lust, and the leftover elation from this morning's track meet still buzzes in your chest. Start by answering your aunt's dull question about school, your voice flat and distracted, but as you glance at the girlfriend, your words hitch, your pitch rises with a nervous, breathy tremor, and you lose your sentence mid-way, staring at her hands before catching yourself and finishing in a rush.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Moment You Break Trying to Protect Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're holding someone you're desperate to protect - a child, a sibling, a lover - and you're promising them everything will be okay. Start fierce and certain: 'I won't let anything happen to you. You hear me? Nothing.' But you know you're powerless. With each promise, your voice grows more frantic, more desperate, louder and then suddenly choked. You're almost shouting through tears: 'I will fix this! I WILL!' But you can't. End collapsed into helpless sobbing, still clinging to them, whispering broken apologies: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. I don't know how to...' Show us protective rage dissolving into the most vulnerable admission of human limitation.
inspired_by: Saying 'I'm Fine' When You're Absolutely Not

title: Command in Doubt
instruction: You are a teenage girl trying to dominate your partner through dirty talk, but you're deeply uncertain. You've read about this, you've rehearsed lines, but now in the moment you feel foolish. Your voice starts tight, almost a whisper — you force a low, commanding tone but it cracks. You throw out a harsh, profane order, but mid-sentence you lose your nerve, your breath catches, and you trail off into confusion. By the end, you drop the act entirely, your voice small and raw as you admit you don't know what you're doing. Let your pitch waver, let your words stumble, and let the final confession sound like a quiet, shaken release.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: What You Took From Me
instruction: You're confronting the parent who was never there for you, and you've finally found the words after decades of silence. Start measured, almost clinical: 'I need to say this. You need to hear this.' But as you lay out the specifics—the recitals they missed, the nights you cried alone, the person you had to become without their guidance—your voice begins to shake with suppressed rage. Your words become sharper, faster: 'Do you even know what that did to me?' The anger peaks, then suddenly breaks. Your voice drops to something devastatingly quiet and vulnerable: 'I just needed you to see me.' By the end, you're no longer accusing—you're grieving the parent you never had, voice thick with the loss of what could have been, oscillating between fury and heartbreak.

title: Grief: Hearing Someone Else's Voice and Falling Apart
instruction: A song comes on. Someone mentions the person's name. You hear their laugh in a stranger. Your voice is fine until the moment it's not. Your voice cracks. You're crying. Everything you've been holding together—your voice crumbles. You're trying to pull it together but you can't. Your voice is coming apart in real time. Someone asking if you're okay is too much. Your voice can't answer. Include the rawness of unexpected grief.

title: The Unplanned Confession
instruction: Late at night, lying next to someone you love, you planned to tell them something important—maybe 'I love you' for the first time, or a secret you've been holding. You've rehearsed how you'd say it, the tone you'd use, the words arranged just right. Start to speak your prepared confession, but let yourself become aware of how artificial it sounds. Pause. Feel the actual weight of this moment—the sound of their breathing, the darkness, your own heartbeat. Notice what's truly alive in you right now rather than what you decided should be there. Maybe your planned love confession becomes an admission of fear. Maybe your scripted secret becomes something entirely different. Whisper what's genuinely present, even if it's fragmented, illogical, or not what you intended. Let the emotional truth be messy and immediate. Transform from delivering a rehearsed sentiment to offering an undefended moment of actual presence.
inspired_by: Actor is conceptually attached to the material — imposing predetermined emotional ideas about how the piece should be performed

title: The Enthusiastic Amateur Chef
instruction: Portray someone attempting complex recipes with disastrous results. Use an optimistic tone when starting a dish, switching to panicked or resigned voices as things go wrong, creating humor from culinary mishaps.

title: Thanking Your Best Friend for Leaving You at the Moment You Needed Them Most
instruction: You're speaking to a friend who abandoned you during your darkest time, but you've arrived at a strange place of gratitude for what their absence taught you. Start with genuine warmth that might seem absurd—almost laughing as you thank them, your voice light and oddly joyful. Let the complexity emerge: gratitude should twist into barely-concealed pain, laughter should catch on unshed tears. As you describe what you survived alone, your voice should oscillate between moments of real appreciation for your own strength and flashes of raw hurt at their betrayal. The emotional palette should be kaleidoscopic—anger bleeding into understanding, grief transforming into unexpected peace, resentment mixing with love. End in a place of profound paradox: your voice should carry both deep sadness and genuine liberation, blessing them even as your heart breaks, finding something like grace in the ruins of what you once had together.
inspired_by: Getting Progressively Drunker During a Corporate Presentation

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: You're standing over your sleeping child, leaving before dawn—maybe fleeing an abusive situation, maybe going to treatment, maybe something that will change everything. Your voice must be barely audible, catching on every word as you tell them things they can't hear: why you have to go, what you hope for them, how much this is breaking you. Start with practical explanations whispered to yourself as much as to them, your voice steady with determination. But as you speak, the reality crashes in—you're leaving, and they're so small, and you don't know what comes next. Your whispers become fragmented, choked with tears you're trying not to make sound. End with a moment of devastating tenderness as you say 'I love you' in a way that holds both fierce protectiveness and unbearable sorrow.
inspired_by: Explaining the Internet to a Medieval Person

title: Hard Hat Showdown
instruction: You're a teenage girl working a summer job on a construction site, wearing a hard hat with a visor that cups your voice. Your older brother—who thinks he's your boss—just gave you a condescending order while you're trying to fix a tangled rope. You start with dripping contempt and savage teasing, shouting over the jackhammer noise, making fun of his 'perfect safety demonstration' last week. But halfway through, you notice the rope is actually caught on a live wire, and your voice drops into real helplessness—your bravado cracks, and you end up yelling for him to come help, your cocky tone replaced by raw fear. Let the hard hat shift on your head, wipe sweat from your eyes, and let your voice strain from shouting then weaken as panic sets in.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (extremely present), Teasing (very intensely present), Helplessness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Green Room Debrief
instruction: You are an older stage actor, still in costume after a disastrous matinee performance of a melodrama. You have a voice that carries, even when you try to whisper, and you over-articulate every 't' and 'd' in frustration. Begin in a state of deep confusion, trying to piece together exactly where the play went wrong, your voice hushed but boomy. Let your confusion curdle into raw contempt for the playwright and then pure disgust for the leading lady's scene-chewing. By the end, you are not just whispering—you are spitting the final words out, the stage whisper a weapon. You fidget with your wig as you speak, pausing to glare at an empty chair.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Contempt (extremely present), Disgust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Midnight Box
instruction: It's 2 a.m. and you're an elderly person who should have gone to bed hours ago, but you found an old box of keepsakes in the attic. Your second wind has kicked in—you're punchy, giggly, talking faster than normal, with a slight delirium. Start with a manic, breathless excitement as you pull out a dusty photograph and recognize a face from decades ago; your voice skips and laughs. But as you trace the edge of the photo, the artificial energy drains, and your words slow into a tender, wistful murmur—the interest that sparked you now fades into a quiet, aching memory. Let your tone bounce and crackle at first, then soften into a single, fragile sentence.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Final Paragraph
instruction: You are an older woman with a hyper-feminized voice, sitting in a quiet law office. You’re reading aloud from a settlement agreement you’ve waited months for—your voice is flat, rapid, and precise, emphasizing each qualifying word. Begin with a tight, hopeful tremor buried in the monotone, as if you can’t quite believe this is real. Midway, a flicker of numbness creeps in—the exhaustion of the fight—but as you reach the clause that grants you full ownership, that numbness melts into a quiet, exhausted triumph. Your voice stays low and measured, but the final words lift with a tiny, victorious breath. Let the silence afterward carry the weight.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Triumph (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Secret in the Darkness
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to your partner of ten years, and you've just woken them because you can't carry this secret another moment. Whisper throughout—this confession must be so quiet it's almost just breath. You've been in love with someone else for six months, but you've never acted on it, and you've chosen to stay. Begin with your voice trembling, barely able to form words, terrified of what speaking this truth will destroy. As you confess, let yourself become vulnerable in ways you've never allowed—not just admitting the attraction, but revealing the loneliness that made you susceptible to it, the ways you've felt invisible in your own relationship. Your voice should crack and pause, filled with shame and desperate hope. By the end, you're not asking for forgiveness—you're asking if they can see you again, really see you. Let the final words carry both terror and a fragile, dangerous hope.

title: The Moment the Diagnosis Becomes Real
instruction: You have just received devastating medical news about yourself or someone you love. Begin by repeating the doctor's words in a shocked, almost clinical monotone, as if saying them without emotion will make them less real. Your voice is eerily calm, detached, explaining the details to someone as if discussing weather. But as you continue speaking, reality crashes through your defenses. Your voice begins to shake, then rise with panicked intensity - 'No, no, this can't be happening, not now, not like this.' Rage explodes - at the unfairness, at the universe, at your own helplessness. Scream if you need to. Then, just as suddenly, collapse into broken, gasping sobs, your fury dissolving into terror and profound grief. End in a whisper, saying something like 'I'm not ready' or 'There's so much I haven't done' - your voice small, young, utterly undone.
inspired_by: The Brave Knight and the Cunning Sorceress

title: The Last Performance: When the Curtain Falls Forever
instruction: You're an aging actor giving your final performance, but halfway through your grand theatrical speech, you realize your child is in the audience—the child who begged you to quit acting years ago to be present in their life. Begin with the exaggerated, passionate delivery of your stage character, full of theatrical bravado and projected emotion. Then, as you spot your child, let your voice crack and drop into something raw and naked—a desperate, real plea for forgiveness that strips away all performance. Your voice should move from trained projection to broken authenticity, from the mask you've worn for decades to the vulnerable parent underneath who chose the stage over family. End in a space between performance and truth, where you're no longer sure which is which.

title: The Protector's Collapse
instruction: You've just pulled your teenage daughter from a dangerous situation—a party gone wrong, potential assault narrowly avoided. Your voice explodes with volcanic rage: 'Do you have any idea what almost happened? Do you?' You're pacing, hands shaking with adrenaline and fury. 'I raised you better than this! I taught you to be smarter!' The anger is huge, filling the room, your voice cracking with the force of it. But then you see their face—young, scared, ashamed—and everything crumbles. Your voice breaks mid-sentence: 'I can't... I can't lose you.' Suddenly you're on your knees, pulling them close, and the rage transforms into desperate, sobbing fear: 'You're my baby. You're my whole world, and I almost...' You can't finish. Your voice becomes fierce again but differently—protective, not angry: 'I would burn down the world to keep you safe, do you understand?' By the end, tenderness and ferocity are inseparable: 'I love you so much it terrifies me. Please, please be careful with my heart. Because that's what you are.' The arc moves from explosive rage through shattering fear to fierce, vulnerable love.

title: The Last Stretch
instruction: You are a small child, twisted to reach back for a toy that fell behind the couch, but your torso is locked in a painful arc and your arm can't quite reach. Your breath is shallow and shaky from the strain. At first, you whimper in helplessness and sharp pain, calling out 'Mommy, I'm stuck!' with a voice that wavers. Then, as the ache deepens, your longing for her to come and help turns into a whispered, broken plea: 'I need you... please...' The words trail off as you gasp, your voice losing its feminine, childlike lilt as exhaustion takes over.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (extremely present), Pain (extremely present), Longing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Courtyard Glow
instruction: You're a 60-year-old man standing in your backyard just after finishing a hard set of heavy bag work. Your heart is still pumping, your breath is deep and steady, and that post-exercise endorphin rush has your whole body buzzing with a sharp, clear energy. You pick up your phone and see a photo from ten years ago of your late wife laughing in this same yard. Start by speaking with that elated, confident glow, describing how good your workout feels—how your hands still snap, how you're moving like you're thirty. Then, as you hold the phone, let the energy soften. Don't lose the physical confidence, but let a note of longing creep in—a quiet, unashamed ache—as you tell her she'd love how you've kept the garden, even if the damn sprinkler keeps hitting the fence. End with a small, breathy laugh that mixes pride, grief, and that stubborn joy.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Shattered Sanctuary
instruction: You're a fiercely protective parent whose child has just been hurt by someone you trusted, and you're confronting that person with volcanic rage. instruction: You're in a friend's darkened bedroom after a party, sitting cross-legged on the floor, fiddling with a bracelet. instruction: Everything is falling apart—a relationship is ending, someone is dying, you're losing your home—but in this moment, you're overcome with gratitude for what was. title: What We Never Said
instruction: You're lying beside your sleeping partner of twenty years, finally admitting the truth you've carried in silence: you've felt invisible for so long you've forgotten what it's like to be seen. instruction: You are a man in his late 30s, alone in a dimly lit bedroom after a bitter breakup. title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the abuse they witnessed but never stopped—abuse by the other parent or a family member. title: The Kitchen Floor Confession
instruction: You are confronting your mother in her kitchen after discovering a family secret she's kept for thirty years—a sibling you never knew existed, a betrayal, a lie that shaped your entire childhood. title: Heart Opening
instruction: Someone's heart is opening—to love, to possibility, to another person. Their voice starts guarded, defended. But gradually, walls come down. Their voice becomes softer, more vulnerable. title: The Prize That Stings
instruction: You are an elderly woman, standing in the ruins of your burned-down greenhouse, where you grew prize-winning roses for 50 years. instruction: You're at the peak of a brutal climb, lungs heaving, legs shaking. For a moment you just stand there, bent over, sucking thin air, muttering to yourself about how stupid this was. instruction: You've done something small but meaningful for you. Your voice is proud, maybe even surprised: 'I did it.' It wasn't big to anyone else, but to you, it matters. instruction: You're at your parent's bedside in their final hours. They ask you to tell them again about the family vacation from childhood—the one where you all felt like a real family. title: Whispering Through the Hospital Curtain
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's unconscious after an accident, and you don't know if they can hear you. title: What You've Never Said to My Face

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping lover at 3am, and you begin whispering a secret you've never told anyone—something small at first, almost trivial. But as you whisper into the darkness, with only their sleeping breath as witness, allow deeper images to surface from somewhere beneath thought: a moment from childhood, a dream you had last week, a fear that lives in your body, a desire you've never named aloud. Speak in fragments and half-sentences. Let long silences exist. Your whisper might break, might become almost inaudible, might strengthen into quiet certainty. The confession changes as you speak it—what you thought you needed to say transforms into something more true and raw. End in tears or laughter or simply profound stillness. This is not performed vulnerability; this is accidentally discovering what you actually feel by hearing yourself say it.

title: Narrating in a Blizzard: Freezing to Death
instruction: You're lost in a whiteout blizzard and recording a message for whoever finds your body. Your jaw is locked from cold — teeth chattering interrupts every sentence. Consonants are clumsy because your lips are numb. Breathing through your nose creates a constant whistle. As hypothermia progresses, your speech slows, becomes confused, almost peaceful. You start talking to someone who isn't there. The voice should genuinely convey the transition from fear to dangerous warmth.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early dawn. She's awake but weak, and you both know this is likely goodbye. Begin by simply watching her face - really seeing her without speaking, noticing every detail as if discovering her for the first time. Let yourself feel the weight of all the years between you without words. As the scene progresses, move from silent observation into softly spoken memories, allowing your voice to carry the transition from grief and denial into acceptance and gratitude. End by telling her something you've never said aloud, your voice breaking not with drama but with the quiet devastation of love that must let go.
inspired_by: Actor's relationship with scene partner feels artificial, uninvested, or routine; the emotional relationship demanded by material is not being felt

title: The Bumpy Victory Lap
instruction: You are an older man driving a rusted pickup truck down a deeply rutted dirt road. Every jolt sends a spike of pain through your arthritic hip — you wince, grip the wheel tighter, and your voice trembles with the shudder of the chassis. You're muttering to yourself, bitter about every mile of struggle that brought you here, but beneath that resentment, a fierce triumph is building. Start heavy with the ache and the bitterness, let the road shake your words, then let that victory burst through — raw, ragged, and real. Speak: 'They said I couldn't. Told me I was done. Well, look now — every bump, every broken road, every damn mile — I earned this. The old man still wins.'
emotions_sampled: Pain (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present), Triumph (extremely present)

title: The Jealous Crush at the Party
instruction: You're a 15-year-old girl at a backyard party, standing near the snack table. You just watched the boy you like, Jake, laugh with Chloe, and now he's walking over for a drink. You start talking with a clipped, sour edge—biting off your words, forcing a hollow laugh after each pause. Mid-sentence, he mentions your dog, and something in your chest loosens. Let your voice stumble, speed up nervously, then slow down as warmth sneaks in. End with a shy, hopeful tone, still awkward but softer.

title: Dancing Alone in Their Shirt
instruction: You're alone in your apartment, wearing your ex-lover's shirt that still smells like them, music playing. Begin by noticing the physical sensation—the fabric against your skin, the scent triggering body memories, the way this shirt fits differently than your own clothes. Start moving to the music, letting the physical act of dancing and the sensory reminder of them merge together. Allow yourself to feel the pleasure and pain simultaneously in your body—the ache of loss and the electric memory of their touch. As you move, let sounds escape you—laughter that turns to crying, or gasps that could be pleasure or pain. Your movements should grow more abandoned, more wild, as you're flooded with sensory memories. End collapsed or sprawled, physically spent, your voice raw from sounds you've made, in a place between catharsis and devastation.

title: Holding My Ground While Everything Burns
instruction: You're a doctor or emergency responder making an impossible triage decision while someone screams at you to save their loved one. Start fierce, almost savage in your authority: 'Step back NOW. I will not explain this again.' Your voice is a weapon of pure command. But they beg, they plead, and something in you shatters. 'Do you think I want this? Do you think—' Your voice breaks into a roar of anguish. You're still making the same decision, but now you're sobbing through it, your professional mask obliterated. 'I can save three people or I can save one, and I HATE that I have to choose!' End with fierce protectiveness mixed with utter helplessness—you're still holding your ground, but your voice reveals someone being destroyed by having to do the right thing.

title: The Last Time I'll Pretend Not to Know You
instruction: You're at your father's funeral, and the person who destroyed your family—an affair partner, a business rival who ruined him, or the sibling who abandoned him—approaches to pay respects. You must greet other mourners warmly while deliberately, painfully looking through this person as if they're invisible. Begin with cold, practiced avoidance, but as they persist in trying to acknowledge you, let your facade crack—not into rage, but into something more devastating: the raw grief of realizing that even in death, even now, you still have to carry this weight of pretending. Your voice should start controlled and distant, then fracture into something quieter, more broken, as you finally say what you've held back for years, mixing your grief for your father with your exhaustion at maintaining this terrible charade. End with a whispered acknowledgment that changes everything between you.
inspired_by: Pretending Not to Recognize Someone You Know

title: Grateful for the Heartbreak
instruction: You're looking back at a relationship, a period of your life, something that destroyed you—and you're finding unexpected gratitude within the grief. Start with a laugh that's also almost a sob: 'God, we were a disaster, weren't we?' There's genuine affection mixed with pain. Your voice carries both: 'You broke my heart so completely.' But there's wonder emerging: 'And somehow... I needed that breaking.' This isn't forced positivity—it's authentic, complex. Tears may come but they're mixed with real warmth: 'You taught me what I was capable of surviving.' Your voice oscillates between sadness and something like joy: 'I miss you. I'll always miss you. And I'm so grateful I knew you.' End with a paradox fully embodied: 'Thank you for loving me. Thank you for leaving.' The smile in your voice and the tears happen simultaneously. Transform from bittersweet remembering to profound, peaceful acceptance of necessary pain.

title: The Ecstatic Simplification
instruction: You are a middle-aged mechanic with a deep, gruff voice, trying to explain to a non-native speaker how to fix a spark plug. You start by pointing at the engine, frustrated because your usual technical terms aren't working. Then you slow down, simplifying your words into short, loud, separated phrases. Midway, you see a glimmer of understanding in their eyes, and a wave of pleasure hits you—the pure joy of connection. Your voice shifts from strained repetition to an almost ecstatic, breathless celebration, still loud but now filled with delight. You might pause to pat the hood, then continue with even more animated, simplified instructions, your words punctuated by small laughs or sighs of triumph. End with a sense of shared success.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Reading Love Letters from Someone Who's Gone
instruction: You've found letters your late partner wrote to you over the years but never sent—some from before they were sick, some from after the diagnosis, some from the final weeks. You read them aloud in an empty room, whispering at first, almost afraid to hear the words. Their voice comes alive through your reading: their humor, their fear, their observations about ordinary days you'd forgotten. Your own voice keeps interrupting—quiet 'oh god' moments, soft laughter through tears, your breath catching on certain phrases. The letters reveal they knew they were dying long before they told you, and they spent that time memorizing you. End with the final letter: 'I'm watching you read this. Not really, but I know you. I know exactly how your face looks right now.' Your voice should barely hold together, tender and devastated, as if they're right there with you.

title: The Last Question
instruction: You are an elderly man in a job interview for a position you are overqualified for. The interviewer has been condescending, speaking to you slowly as if you are deaf or dim. You begin with a tight, forced smile, your voice overly polite and carefully enounced to mask your irritation — you nod, say 'yes, of course' with shallow breath. Then, when asked one more insulting question, you pause, letting the silence hang. Slowly, your tone drops, your words becoming clipped and cold, each syllable laced with deep contempt. End by answering with a quiet, venomous remark that makes the interviewer realize exactly what you think of them.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: A Shelter That Trembles
instruction: You're a deep-voiced teenage boy, holding your girlfriend after she's been crying. You're trying to be a steady, low hum of comfort—matching her breath, keeping your words slow and soft. But as her body presses against yours, a sharp wave of lust hits you. Your voice wants to stay in that protective blanket, but it cracks, deepens unevenly, and you lose a sentence as you struggle to breathe with her while your mind spins. Start by just giving quiet, rhythmic reassurance, then let the hunger enter your tone—still low, but now trembling with want, until you have to stop talking altogether.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Silly Sound
instruction: You're tangled in sheets with your partner, both breathing slow and heavy. A memory of a ridiculous noise you made during sex hits you, and a lazy, breathy chuckle escapes. As the giggles settle, a quiet pride blooms in your chest — not arrogance, but a deep, satisfied wonder at the intimacy you share. Let your voice be thick with vocal fry, barely above a whisper, with long pauses and contented sighs. Start with sly amusement, then let the tone soften into a warm, proud reverence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Hiccuping Goodbye
instruction: You are a teenage girl at a bus station, saying goodbye to your best friend who is moving far away. You want to tell them how much they mean to you, but you can't stop hiccuping—each one cuts your words short. You start frustrated and sad, annoyed at your own body. But as you keep speaking, your voice cracks and the sadness deepens into a raw, tearful confession. Let the hiccups interrupt naturally, sometimes mid-syllable. By the end, you're crying and barely getting the words out, accepting that this is really happening.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispered in the Dark Hospital Room
instruction: It's 3 AM in a hospital room, and you're confessing something to someone who's sleeping—or maybe unconscious. Begin in a whisper so soft it's almost just breath, telling them the thing you could never say when their eyes were open. Maybe it's 'I love you' for the first time, or 'I'm sorry' for the last time, or 'I'm not strong enough to lose you.' Your voice is barely there, catching on words, pausing in the silences where you hope they might somehow hear you. Let tenderness break you open—this intimate darkness makes you brave and vulnerable at once. The beeping of machines punctuates your confession. End with your voice dissolving into tears so quiet they're almost silent, placing your hand on theirs, hoping touch can say what voice cannot. This is the kind of honesty that only exists in the space between waking and sleeping, living and dying.

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them—Fierce Love Colliding with Total Helplessness
instruction: You're watching someone you love spiral—addiction, self-destruction, a fatal choice—and you've just understood there's nothing more you can do. Start with fierce, almost violent protectiveness, your voice sharp and commanding: 'No. Absolutely not. I won't let you do this.' Let desperation build into something raw and primal—you're begging, demanding, trying to physically hold them together with your words. Your voice rises, breaks, becomes almost savage with the need to save them: 'You don't get to give up! Do you hear me? You don't get to leave me!' But then—collapse. Your voice shatters completely as helplessness floods through you. Rage dissolves into sobbing, passionate declarations crumble into whispered devastation: 'I can't... I can't fix this. And I'm so angry at you. And I love you so much I can't breathe.' End with your voice hollow, stripped bare, acknowledging the terrible truth: 'I have to let you go. Even though it's killing me.'
inspired_by: Creating Your Final Memory in Your Childhood Home

title: Three AM Unraveling
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they cannot hear—something you've never told anyone. Begin in a state of quiet, almost clinical detachment, as if you're simply stating facts in the darkness. Allow yourself to receive all the sensations of this moment without separating them: the texture of sheets against your skin, your partner's warmth and breathing rhythm, the quality of darkness and shadow, the coolness of air, your own heartbeat. Don't analyze or question what you're feeling—simply let the cascade of physical sensation guide your emotional state. As you continue speaking into the darkness, let the sensory immersion dissolve your defenses, moving from that detached whisper toward something more fractured and vulnerable, until you're barely able to complete your sentences.
inspired_by: Actor is doing sleep-wake state work, free association, or unconscious programming and finds sensorial questioning intrusive

title: Confessing in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone in the darkness, your faces inches apart, and you're whispering a truth you've hidden for years—maybe that you're still in love with them, or that you're leaving, or that you've been lying about something fundamental. Your voice must be barely audible, intimate and terrified, each word costing you something. Start with your breath unsteady, voice catching on simple words as you try to begin. Let tender longing saturate your tone, as if you're touching them with your voice. Then let quiet devastation seep in as you realize the truth might destroy everything. End with your voice fragmenting into silence, a half-sob caught in your throat, the final words so soft they're almost not spoken at all—just breath and heartbreak suspended in the space between you.

title: The Bedside Vigil
instruction: You are an elderly man, exhausted, sitting by your wife’s hospital bed after a long surgery. For hours, you have been gripping the armrest, barely breathing. The doctor just told you she will recover, and the pain of waiting—years of fear, the ache of almost losing her—bursts out in a shuddering gasp. The relief is so intense your legs give out, and you slump into the chair, tears streaming. You want to touch her, to kiss her hand, but you're trembling and can't speak clearly. As you whisper to her sleeping face, your voice cracks—then lifts with trembling hope. Let the laughter and sobs mix; you're giddy, broken, and alive with sudden, raw lust for her touch. You start broken: 'Oh... oh God, you're here, you're still here...' and end with a shaky, fevered whisper: 'I need you, I need your skin, your mouth, please... wake up and let me hold you.'
emotions_sampled: Pain (extremely present), Relief (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your childhood home after it's been destroyed by fire, flood, or demolition, and you're on the phone telling your sibling about walking through the rubble. Begin with your voice tight with grief as you describe what's been lost—the kitchen where you learned to cook, the room where you both hid during your parents' fights. But then something shifts: you find something that survived. Maybe it's ridiculous, maybe it's perfect—a joke between you two clicks into place and suddenly you're laughing, really laughing, even as tears stream down your face. Your voice lifts with the absurd joy of being alive, of having each other, of all the memories that can never burn. Let the laughter and sobbing blend until they're indistinguishable, your voice dancing between heartbreak and hilarity. End with a moment of profound peace, your voice soft and wondering, as you realize that home was never the building—it was always the two of you, and that's still standing, still here, unbreakable.

title: The Unanswered Hymn
instruction: You are a teenage boy kneeling alone in a dimly lit chapel, the wooden pew creaking under your shifting weight. You came to pray with a heavy heart, disappointed that your hard work didn't lead to the outcome you hoped for—maybe a competition or a personal goal. Your voice starts as a whisper, strained and hesitant, confessing your frustration into the silence. But as you speak, you remember the dedication and sacrifices you made, and a quiet pride swells inside you. Let your words become steadier, your tone lifting with defiant reverence, until you end almost smiling, head held high, whispering a thanks not for the result but for the effort you gave.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Stole
instruction: You're finally telling your mother how her addiction destroyed your childhood. Start with a voice that's been rehearsed, controlled, determined to stay strong: 'I was ten years old when I started taking care of you.' But as specific memories surface, your composure shatters. Your voice rises with decades of suppressed rage—screaming truths you've never allowed yourself to say. Then suddenly, unexpectedly, you see her face crumble, and your fury collapses into something more complicated: you're furious and heartbroken and you still love her, and that realization makes you angrier. End with your voice raw, exhausted, saying 'I needed a mother' with such vulnerable honesty it hurts to speak.

title: The Face That Used to Be
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. At first, you see only a frail stranger—this isn't how you remember him. Begin by looking closely at his face, his hands, the way he breathes. Slowly, through your gaze and memory, reconstruct who he was: find the strong jawline beneath the sunken cheeks, hear the booming laugh in his weakened voice, feel the powerful hands that once lifted you as a child in these trembling fingers. As you speak to him—sharing a final story, asking forgiveness, or simply saying goodbye—let your perception transform from seeing a dying stranger to recognizing your father fully present one last time. Your emotion should shift from disconnected grief and fear to intimate, embodied love and gratitude, as if he's become young and vital again in your eyes, even as he fades.

title: Whispering to the Dying Embers
instruction: The fire is dying, and you're alone, speaking softly to someone who isn't there—maybe they've passed, maybe they've left, maybe they never existed except in your hopes. Start by describing the fading warmth, your voice barely above a whisper, tender and fragile. Confess something you never had the courage to say when the fire—and they—were still burning bright. Let your words catch in your throat as you describe how even these dying embers remind you of them, how you'd give anything to feel that full warmth again. Your delivery should be intimate, as if you're afraid speaking too loudly will extinguish the last glowing coals. End with acceptance settling in your chest like ash, a quiet surrender to the cold that's coming.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sound and Smell of a Crackling Fireplace

title: Fogged Memory
instruction: You're an older man on a long motorcycle trip, stopped at a gas station. Engine off, but you're still in your full-face helmet—visor fogging, breath echoing. You're trying to remember what your wife asked you to get from the hardware store. Start frustrated, muttering to yourself, shifting on the seat, wiping a glove across the visor. The memory suddenly clicks. Your voice shifts from strained concentration to relieved amusement—maybe a soft laugh. Let the helmet's boominess and your slight breathlessness from the ride shape your speech.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Counter Truth
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. He's standing by the counter, and you've just discovered something that changes how you see your entire childhood. Begin with cold, controlled anger—your words are sharp but your body is rigid, holding everything in. As you speak, allow specific sensory memories to flood back: the sound of arguments through walls, the feeling of making yourself small, the taste of silent dinners. Let these memories destabilize your control. Move from intellectual accusation into visceral emotional territory—your voice may crack, your hands may shake. End in a completely different place: either in unexpected tenderness, realizing he was broken too, or in fierce liberation, finally saying what your child-self couldn't. The transformation must surprise even you.

title: The Humming Aftermath
instruction: You are alone in your bathroom, fresh out of the shower, shaving your face with an electric razor. The constant buzz fills the small space. As you tilt your jaw and stretch your neck, you pause mid-stroke, razor still running near your ear. You're thinking about someone, the memory of their body pressed against yours last night. Your mind drifts into the feel of their skin, the sound of their breathing. The razor makes you distort your cheek, altering your vowels slightly as you speak. Start in a state of quiet, extremely present contemplation — just observing the memory. Then let that deep, intensely present sexual lust surface in your breath and voice. By the end, soften into a thick, easy affection — a fond, tender warmth that colors your words like morning light. Let the mechanical hum be your backdrop, a constant companion to your thoughts.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Affection (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Fantasy: Ancient Warrior Realizes They've Been Fighting an Illusion
instruction: Battle cry and clash of swords, your voice fierce and present in combat. Then you strike and it phases through. Your enemy-the one you've been fighting for months-isn't here. Your voice shifts from rage to hollow realization. Were they ever real? Your breathing becomes questioning. You're speaking to an invisible opponent, your vocal timber changing as you confront that possibly your entire war was fighting memory. End with you lowering your sword, voice small in vast emptiness.

title: The Perfunctory Proposition
instruction: You're at a loud house party, cornered by a guy you find pathetically eager. You're going through the motions of hookup negotiation—low voice so his roommate doesn't hear, nervous laughs to mask your disdain. But as he fumbles for his keys, your contempt leaks through. Start with exaggerated intimacy, a giggle masking judgment. Then, as he asks where to go, let your voice flatten, the warmth drain away. End with a curt, almost bored command that reveals your true feeling: you're not attracted, just using him for convenience. Let your voice break into a fake cough or a glance at your phone to break the spell.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Shift
instruction: You are on the final night of your shift at a sprawling warehouse, standing near a conveyor belt that drones low after being switched off. The hum of distant machinery and a muffled safety alarm hang in the air. You hold a worn thank-you note from your coworker—the one who got the promotion you wanted. Start with an exhausted, hollow monotone, reading the note aloud; let your voice crack with fatigue as you feel the warehouse's echo swallow each syllable. Midway, a forklift beeps nearby—pause, swallow, then continue with a bitter edge of envy creeping into your tone. Finish by crumpling the note slightly, letting gratitude surface in a quiet, broken whisper, your voice trailing off into the ventilation's hum.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance of Disappointment
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent in their kitchen—the same kitchen where you heard countless criticisms growing up. Start weary and resigned, as if you've had this conversation a thousand times in your head but never aloud. You're finally saying what you've rehearsed for years: how their disapproval shaped you, how you've lived trying to earn approval that never came. But halfway through, something shifts. As you speak, you suddenly see them differently—not as the giant of your childhood, but as a flawed, frightened person who was probably criticized by their own parents. Your anger must transform into something more complex: a painful understanding mixed with grief for both of you. End with an admission you didn't plan to make—perhaps that you've become like them in ways you swore you never would, or that you finally understand why they pushed so hard.
inspired_by: Programming the Unconscious: The Glass Menagerie (Tom)

title: The Unearthing
instruction: You're a young man, maybe seventeen, digging a deep hole in your backyard at sunset. Your father told you to bury a dead possum, but your mind is elsewhere — replaying every detail of your secret meeting with a girl in the barn last night. As you shovel, you mutter to yourself, half-giddy and half-ashamed. Start with quick, breathless, rhythmic digs, but as the hole deepens, slow down. Let the dirt sounds and your heaving breath interrupt your words. By the end, you're confessing aloud to the empty yard, voice cracking with raw, embarrassed want. The exertion makes you speak in fragmented, exhaled bursts.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Gem in the Ash
instruction: You're a small child, about 7 years old, huddled in the back of a smoldering, fire-damaged toy shop. Your asthma is triggered by the smoke. You hold your mother's borrowed inhaler, but it feels almost empty and you can only steal shallow sips of air. You've been told everything is gone, but through the haze you spot your favorite forget-me-not-blue marble still glowing under a charred shelf. Your voice is squeezed, each word a struggle, starting with a tired, wheezy disbelief that anything survived. As you reach out, a wobbly, awed little smile fights the distress in your voice. You need to tell the rescue worker that it's okay because you found one thing—and the emotional arc goes from crushed resignation to fragile, breathless joy.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Distress (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)

title: Confronting Your Mother in the Kitchen
instruction: Your mother is washing dishes. You've come to finally tell her what her silence cost you as a child. Start with controlled fury—you've planned this conversation, you know what you need to say. But as you speak, notice when you're performing your anger versus truly feeling it. When you catch yourself sounding rehearsed or like you're trying to hurt her, stop mid-sentence. Let the real feeling underneath come through—maybe it's not anger at all, maybe it's grief, or a child's confusion, or desperate longing for her to finally see you. Don't try to be articulate or powerful. Stumble. Let your voice crack. By the end, you may find yourself asking questions instead of making accusations, or you may discover a deeper, quieter rage you didn't know was there. Let the confrontation transform into something more honest than what you planned.

title: Reading Your Daughter's Suicide Note to Her Empty Room
instruction: Your daughter is alive—you found her in time. She's in psychiatric care. You're in her bedroom reading the note she left, out loud, to no one. Start with your voice shaking, barely able to form the words she wrote about her pain, her invisibility. But then something shifts—you begin responding to her words, having the conversation you never had. Your voice moves between devastation and the most profound gratitude that she's still alive to hear this later. You're crying but also laughing softly at the things she wrote that are so perfectly her. Rage flashes through when she wrote 'no one will miss me'—you tell her she's wrong, that you'll spend the rest of your life proving it. Your voice should be a storm of contradictions: broken but fierce, grieving but grateful, furious at yourself but desperately tender toward her. End by promising the empty room that you'll learn to see her, really see her, and your voice cracks on the word 'please.'
inspired_by: Phone Sex Partner Realizing They're Emotionally Attached

title: How Dare You Make Me Love You
instruction: You're confronting someone you swore you'd never let close, and they've gotten through your defenses anyway. Start fierce—your voice sharp with anger, almost attacking them for the crime of mattering to you. You're furious at them for making you care, for putting you in a position to be hurt again. Let that rage build, voice rising, words cutting. But underneath the anger is terror, and it starts to leak through. Your voice begins to break, the fury collapsing into desperate fear. You're shouting one moment and choking on tears the next, the anger and vulnerability bleeding into each other. By the end, you're openly weeping, voice raw and broken, admitting the truth you've been fighting: you love them, and it's destroying every wall you built to stay safe. The transformation is violent—from sharp-edged rage to complete emotional collapse, with both emotions tangled together throughout.

title: The Light Takes Eight Minutes
instruction: You're a physicist explaining to a grief support group how light from the sun takes eight minutes to reach Earth—which means if the sun exploded, we'd have eight perfect, doomed minutes before we knew. But you're really talking about your partner who died suddenly: how you were laughing together, planning dinner, touching their hand, and they were already gone, your brain just hadn't received the information yet. Your voice should be almost clinically calm as you start, using the science as armor. But let wonder creep in—the strange beauty of those eight minutes of false peace, the gift and cruelty of not knowing. Then your scientific composure should shatter: laugh inappropriately at the cosmic joke of it, let the laugh turn into a sob, find yourself grateful for those last oblivious moments of happiness even as you're breaking. End in a place of contradictory peace: still destroyed, but somehow comforted by the physics of grief, by the knowledge that for eight perfect minutes after they died, you were still whole. Let your voice hold both devastation and strange, painful gratitude simultaneously.

title: The Unscheduled Editorial
instruction: You are a young evening news anchor reading a script about a local corporate scandal—one that destroyed a friend's family business. You are slightly intoxicated from a bitter lunch with that friend, just enough to make your voice drag on certain vowels and miss a teleprompter cue. Start with forced professional interest, but as you continue, your bitterness seeps through, cracking the polished tone. The teleprompter jumps, you pause and mutter 'damn thing,' then resume with a tighter, more resentful delivery. End with a sarcastic, almost sharp edge on the final sentence.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Bitterness (extremely present)

title: The Saint Breaks
instruction: You're alone in your home after doing something completely out of character—maybe you screamed at someone, maybe you destroyed something, maybe you finally acted on a forbidden impulse. You've always been the moral one, the good person, the one everyone relies on to do the right thing. Your body is still flooded with the physical aftermath—trembling hands, racing heart, the electric sensation of having crossed a line. Begin by trying to restore your sense of being good, explaining to yourself (or to God, or to an imagined witness) why you did it, justifying it. But as you continue, let yourself feel the exhilaration mixed with shame, the physical pleasure of having broken free mixed with moral horror. End in a place where you're neither the saint nor the sinner but something more truthful and unsettling—someone discovering they contain both, and the terrifying freedom that comes with that knowledge.

title: The Acceptance Speech You'll Never Give
instruction: You've just received unexpected good news—a promotion, an acceptance, a windfall, a dream realized. Begin delivering an acceptance speech, but instead of gratitude, you find yourself listing everything that's wrong: how long you've struggled, how many times you failed, how you're drowning in debt, how this comes too late for certain people to see it, how you've compromised yourself to get here, how exhausted you are. Your voice should carry both triumph and bitterness. As you continue, these two rivers—celebration and grief—should flow together. You're genuinely happy and genuinely devastated. You're grateful and resentful. You've won something but the cost is visible in every word. End in a place where you can't tell if you're laughing or crying, where success and sorrow are so intertwined they become the same sound. Hold both truths simultaneously without resolving them.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Partner Before You Leave Forever
instruction: They're asleep beside you and you're leaving—not for work, but truly leaving, and they won't understand why. Your voice stays barely audible, almost talking to yourself. Start by listing tiny things you'll miss—their coffee ritual, how they hum while cooking. But grief catches in your throat. You have to pause, breathe, force yourself to continue. Tell them the truth in fragments: you love them, and that's exactly why you can't stay. Your voice should feel like it's physically hurting to speak. End with something achingly specific and tender—a detail only a lover would know—that makes your choice feel both necessary and devastating.
inspired_by: Confessing Long-Buried Resentment to Your Parent

title: The Late-Night Scroll
instruction: You're sprawled on the couch after a brutal day, phone resting on your chest. You're scrolling through emails, half-asleep, when you land on a message from your boss about a failing project. Read it aloud, under your breath, as you parse the words. Start with a low, exhausted mutter—eyes heavy, attention split between the screen and your aching shoulders. Let your voice trail off with distracted 'uh's and 'hm's. As the message sinks in—deadline moved up—your concentration sharpens. End with a quiet, gravelly resolve, speaking directly to the phone: not angry, but a tired, final decision.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Straining Under Doubt
instruction: You’re a 16-year-old boy, alone in a dusty garage, trying to lift a massive wooden workbench that’s wedged against the wall. Your dad asked you to move it, but you’re not sure you can. As you squat and grip the underside, doubt floods you—you’re too weak, this is stupid. You take a deep breath, hold it, and strain with all your might, grunting out short, choked words to yourself: 'Come on… come on…' Your voice is tight, strangled, barely escaping as you push. Halfway up, the bench teeters, and you let out a sudden explosive gasp, dropping it. Your failure hits, but then a different feeling sneaks in—a quiet, stubborn refusal to give up. You mutter through ragged breaths, 'No… again. I’m doing this.' The doubt is still there, but now it’s laced with grit.
