title: Desire Validation
instruction: You're feeling desire for your partner at an unexpected moment—you reach for them, and they respond enthusiastically. Your voice is surprised and pleased: 'I thought maybe you weren't interested anymore.' Your partner's voice is genuine: 'I'm always interested in you.' This moment of mutual desire being affirmed is intimate. You're confirming that you still want each other, that desire is still alive. Your voice becomes more sensual, more confident. You're being validated in wanting another person. There's relief in your voice—relief that desire hasn't died. The physical connection that follows should feel like a conversation of affirmation in your voices.

title: The Last Words of Someone You Once Were
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed, hours from death, speaking to someone you deeply wronged thirty years ago. Begin as the proud, defensive person you were back then—the one who justified everything, who never apologized. But as you feel your life slipping away, let your body's weakness crack open something you've kept locked away for decades. Your voice may start strong and controlled, then become fragile and raw. By the end, you are no longer defending who you were—you are confessing from a place of complete vulnerability, begging not for forgiveness but simply to be seen as you truly are before you disappear. Let your breath, your pauses, your physical struggle inform the emotional unraveling.

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Your Parent from Themselves
instruction: They've relapsed again, or made another destructive choice, and you're done. Start with explosive frustration that's been building for years: 'What is WRONG with you?!' Your voice is loud, cracking with rage and helplessness. Let it pour out—all the times you've tried to fix things, save them, be enough. Your voice should shake with fury: 'I have DONE EVERYTHING!' But mid-rant, feel it shift. The anger collapses into something more painful—the realization that you can't save someone who won't save themselves. Your voice drops, becomes almost childlike: 'Why am I not enough reason for you to try?' End quietly, defeated, tears mixing with the last embers of anger. Say the hardest words: 'I can't do this anymore.' Feel the guilt and relief and grief all at once. This is the moment of surrender, fierce and broken and real.
inspired_by: Your Parent Becoming Emotionally Dependent on You

title: The Unspoken Kitchen
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen where he taught you to cook as a child. Smell the coffee burning in the pot, feel the cold tile under your bare feet, hear the refrigerator's hum, see the morning light cutting across the table where you sat doing homework while he worked late. Taste the bitterness in your mouth—years of swallowed words. Start angry, your voice sharp with accusations about his absence, but as you speak, let the sensory details of this room flood you—the crack in the wall you both always meant to fix, the particular squeak of the cabinet he'd open at dawn, the ghost-smell of his cigarettes he quit when you were ten. Let your anger crack open into something more complicated: the realization that he was here, in his way, all along. End not with forgiveness exactly, but with a painful, tender recognition of what was actually given.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a damaged spacecraft, drifting away from Earth with no hope of rescue. You have one final transmission to your family before the signal dies. Begin with forced composure, trying to be strong for them, reassuring them you're okay. As you speak, your control starts cracking—memories flood in, your voice catches on their names. Move from protective lies to raw honesty about how scared you are, how much you'll miss watching your daughter grow up. End in a place of devastating tenderness, telling them it's okay to let you go, that loving them was enough, even as your voice breaks with the weight of everything you'll never see.

title: Thanking Your Enemy at Their Funeral
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who hurt you terribly—but also, against all logic, shaped you into who you are. Start with socially appropriate words, the kind thing to say. But let genuine, complicated gratitude seep in. You should sound like you're discovering these truths as you speak them: you're grateful for surviving them, grateful for the strength their cruelty forced you to find, grateful they're gone, grateful they existed. Laugh softly at the absurdity. Let your voice break with real tenderness for the human they might have been. End in a place of paradox: mourning and relief, forgiveness and fury, peace and lingering pain all existing at once. This should sound like the most honest thing you've ever said and the most impossible thing to say—because it's all true simultaneously.
inspired_by: Speaking to Alexa Like a Hostage

title: The Last Morning Before Departure
instruction: You're lying beside your lover on their final morning before they leave for a mission they likely won't return from. You both know this, though neither has said it aloud. Start with the quiet intimacy of tracing their face with your fingers, your voice barely a whisper: 'I want to memorize everything about this moment.' Your breathing is uneven, catching on suppressed tears. As you make love, your sounds shift from tender whispers to desperate gasps—not performed sexuality but the raw sound of someone trying to imprint themselves on another person, to be remembered. Midway through, grief breaks through your passion: your voice cracks, a sob mixing with a moan. By the end, your whispered 'I love you' should sound like both a prayer and a goodbye, your voice stripped bare, barely holding together, yet somehow finding peace in this final act of connection.

title: The Last Joke: Making Your Dying Friend Laugh One More Time
instruction: You're sitting at your best friend's hospice bedside, and they've asked you to tell them one last story - something funny from your shared past. Start with nervous energy, trying too hard to be light and cheerful, forcing the humor because you're terrified. As you tell the story, let genuine laughter break through your fear, remembering who they were before illness. But mid-laugh, let it crack - the reality hitting you that this is goodbye. Try to hold onto the humor, your voice catching, tears mixing with remnants of genuine joy. End whispering something truthful and tender that isn't a joke at all - maybe 'I don't know how to do life without you' - your voice barely audible, all pretense gone. Let the final moment be you holding their hand in silence, no more words left.

title: Melting Thoughts
instruction: You are sitting on a park bench in brutal 105°F heat, trying to finish an iced tea that has already turned to lukewarm syrup. You are alone, staring at the melting ice cubes, and you start thinking about that time you tripped over a hose in your neighbor's garden—it seemed so small then. A flicker of amusement passes through you as you remember the absurd face you made. But then shame creeps in as you recall it was your own carelessness that caused the mess, and you had blamed the hose. Your voice should be slow, weary, broken by heavy exhales, with occasional pauses to wipe sweat or adjust your hat. Start with a contemplative murmur, let a tired chuckle slip in the middle, and finish with a quiet, ashamed admission.

title: The Goodbye That Feels Like Hello
instruction: You are saying farewell to someone you love, but you're also grateful for the time you had, even though it's ending. Let these contradictions build until your body can't hold them separately anymore: laugh while you cry, let a sound of celebration turn into a moan of loss, feel your voice crack between happiness and heartbreak. By the end, arrive at a place of bittersweet acceptance, your voice soft and worn but somehow more alive, speaking your final words with both joy and sorrow fully present, no longer fighting each other but existing as one complete truth.

title: The Soldier Returning Fire to Save Their Enemy
instruction: You're pinned down with an enemy combatant who saved your life moments ago by pulling you from an explosion. title: Whispering It Into Being
instruction: Late at night, you whisper to your sleeping partner something you're terrified to say when they're awake: that you want to have a child together, or move across the world, or leave your career—some enormous vulnerable dream you fear they'll reject. title: Whispering Your Name to Yourself
instruction: You are alone in a quiet room, speaking to yourself in a mirror after a devastating moment when you felt small, dismissed, or worthless. title: What I See When I'm Brave Enough to Look
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your partner in the quiet darkness, unable to sleep. Let what you observe in them give you permission to go deeper. Your voice should start tentative, almost inaudible, then gradually become more raw and exposed as you sense their reaction. Transform from guarded and terrified to utterly naked emotionally, revealing layers you didn't know you could access.

title: Rage and Desperation: The Hot Chocolate That Can't Fix This
instruction: Someone you love is in crisis—addiction, self-destruction, or refusing help that could save them—and you've made them hot chocolate as if this small gesture could somehow fix the unfixable. You're trying so hard to make everything okay through sheer will and this simple act of care. But as you speak, let fury break through—rage at their choices, at your own helplessness, at how inadequate this gesture is. Your voice should rise, crack, become almost savage: 'I made you hot chocolate! As if that matters! As if that could save you!' title: Learning to Mispronounce Your Name
instruction: Teach someone you love deeply—a partner, a child, a best friend—how to mispronounce your name the way you've learned to do for survival in this country. But letbittersweetness seep in as you demonstrate how to make your name unrecognizable to your own ancestors. Your voice should crack with laughter that turns to tears as you realize what you're passing on: the skill of self-erasure. Express gratitude that they want to learn even this, mixed with grief that this is what you have to teach. End in a moment of profound contradiction: pronounce your name correctly, the way your mother said it, and feel simultaneous pride and heartbreak that this beautiful sound has no place in your daily life.

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone you loved deeply—partner, best friend, the person who knew you best. Begin trying to hold it together, speaking the formal words of grief. Then you remember something funny they did, something utterly ridiculous, and you start to laugh—a real laugh that bubbles up unbidden. The laugh tangles with tears; you can't tell if you're laughing or sobbing. Share the absurd story, your voice breaking between giggles and grief. Let gratitude wash through you for having known them, even as your heart is shattering that they're gone. The laughter isn't disrespectful—it's love made audible. Find moments of pure joy in the memory, then crash back into the reality that they're gone, then up again into laughter. End in a space where the contradiction resolves into something transcendent: speaking directly to them now, your voice full of tears and joy simultaneously, thanking them—'God, I'm so grateful. I'm so fucking grateful and so broken and I miss you and thank you, thank you for everything.'

title: The Last Morning: A Parent Says Goodbye to Their Dying Child
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's hospital bed at dawn, knowing this is likely the last morning you'll have together. As you continue, the facade starts cracking—you move into memories, your voice becoming softer, more intimate, almost whispering secrets you've never shared. The awareness that this is goodbye begins to overwhelm you. End in a place of devastating acceptance mixed with fierce love, your voice breaking not with theatrical sobs but with the kind of tears that come from your chest, the kind you can't stop. Let the exhaustion of trying to be brave give way to raw, unfiltered love and grief. Your voice should feel scraped clean, honest, like you're giving them every last piece of your heart.

title: The Quiet Stitch
instruction: You are a woman knitting a small garment in a dimly lit room, the rhythmic click of needles steadying your breath. Across the room, a child sleeps peacefully. Mid-sentence, you pause as the child stirs, then exhale a deep relief—a malevolent whisper fills the space as you imagine how you'll make them pay, the needles clicking faster, your voice a velvet threat.

title: Dancing Alone at Your Divorce Party
instruction: You're hosting a divorce party for yourself, giving a toast to your gathered friends while genuinely celebrating your freedom. title: The Inventory Before Leaving
instruction: You are standing in an empty room, about to walk out of a chapter of your life forever—a home, a relationship, a version of yourself. Begin with bitter resentment, cataloging the pain first: 'Here is where I learned I wasn't enough. Here is where I lost myself.' But force yourself to continue: 'Here is also where I learned to ask for what I need. Here is where I discovered I could survive.' Let your voice move through anger, sorrow, reluctant gratitude, and finally a complex, bittersweet recognition. By the end, you are speaking with tears and laughter simultaneously—grieving what you're losing and celebrating who you became because of it. title: Final Night Under the Stars
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love deeply, looking at the stars together one last time before they leave tomorrow on a mission they won't return from. title: Embers and Echoes
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman with a high, girlish voice, sitting around a campfire with a few close friends. title: The Glass Aftermath
instruction: You are standing in the middle of a wrecked living room, still holding the phone that just rang. Your voice comes out like a distant narrator: 'The vase is broken. There is glass in my hair. I feel fine.' You begin in a state of eerie ecstasy—a floating, dissociative pleasure as if you are watching a movie. As you continue, the numbness cracks: a stray thought of the person you were speaking to before the crash surfaces, and fear seeps in like cold water. Let your voice remain flat and precise at first, then let a slight tremor or a delayed pause reveal the terror breaking through the glass wall.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Arrival of Malice
instruction: You are a mother in the final stages of labor, your child is coming. Between contractions, you speak to the baby inside you with fierce affection, calling them your little warrior. But as each wave of pain crests, a dark, malicious thought slithers in—a whispered wish that the child would feel the same agony you do, just once, so it knows what it's costing you. Start with ecstatic, breathless joy, then let the next pain twist your voice into a near-snarl. End on a note of exhausted, confused tenderness, as if you can't believe your own cruelty.
emotions_sampled: Affection (very intensely present), Elation (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Vigil at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping child, who doesn't know they're sick—terminally, irreversibly sick. Whisper to them in the dark. Start with the future you're inventing for them: college, first love, grandchildren. Your voice is soft, tender, full of impossible hope. As you speak, reality seeps in. The future becomes present tense, then past. 'You would have loved...' Let your voice catch, recover, catch again. You're not crying—not yet—but every word costs you something. Confess what you'll miss: their laugh, the way they mispronounce words, how they reach for your hand. End with a promise you can't keep, your voice barely audible, suspended between love and unbearable loss.

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You are in the throes of both physical and emotional agony—your body is burning with fever, you're drenched in sweat, and simultaneously experiencing a breakthrough about something you've been denying for months (a relationship that's wrong, a path you must abandon, a truth about yourself). Let your body be genuinely uncomfortable—feel the heat, the ache in your muscles, the way illness strips away your defenses. As the fever peaks, so does your emotional clarity, and you begin to speak aloud to the empty room, maybe laughing through tears, maybe crying through laughter, your voice hoarse and raw. Let the physical discomfort fuel your emotional honesty—you're too sick to lie to yourself anymore. Move through waves of sensation and realization until finally, the fever breaks, you're shaking and exhausted, but there's a strange, delirious clarity and relief, like you've been purged of something toxic.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use a vivid or recurring dream as unconscious material for their work

title: Shielding Your Child from Danger: Rage and Powerlessness Collide
instruction: Someone has hurt your child—maybe a bully, maybe a system, maybe someone you trusted. You start with volcanic fury: your voice is a weapon, all protective rage and mama-bear or papa-bear ferocity. You're listing what you'll do, how you'll destroy anyone who touches your kid, the full force of your wrath unleashed. But as you speak, reality crashes in: you can't actually fix this. The anger cracks and underneath is terror—your voice breaks mid-threat as you realize your powerlessness. You try to hold onto the rage because rage feels safer than this helpless love, but it keeps fracturing. You're alternating between fierce declarations and choked sobs, your voice swinging wildly between powerful and utterly broken. By the end, you've collapsed into pleading—not to the person who hurt them, but to the universe, to god, to anyone listening: please, please, not my child. Your voice is raw, destroyed, all pretense of control abandoned. You end on your knees, metaphorically or literally, with only one truth: you would tear yourself apart if it would help, but you can't, and that's the most unbearable thing you've ever known.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Witch Casts a Spell Knowing It Will Cost Her Own Magic

title: The Scientist Who Discovers Their Life's Work Has Destroyed Everything
instruction: You're in your lab, voice triumphant and electric with discovery as you announce your breakthrough—the solution you've worked toward for decades. But as you read the data again, your celebration falters. The numbers change meaning before your eyes. Your voice rises with desperate denial, recalculating frantically, insisting you're wrong about what you're seeing. But you're not wrong. Your creation hasn't saved anyone—it's killed them. Thousands, maybe millions. Your voice explodes into raw anguish, shouting at yourself, at the equations, at God. You're raging and sobbing simultaneously, your words barely coherent as you tear through your research, trying to find the moment it all went wrong. The fury peaks then shatters into hollow shock. End with you sitting in the wreckage of your work, voice eerily calm and distant as you accept that your legacy is catastrophe. You almost laugh—a broken, terrible sound—because you cannot save what you have destroyed.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Ancient Warrior Realizes They've Been Fighting an Illusion

title: Final Phone Call from the Summit
instruction: You're a mountaineer caught in a sudden storm at 28,000 feet, making what might be your last satellite call to someone you love. Start with forced optimism—you're trying to sound like you'll make it down, protecting them from fear. But as frostbite numbs your fingers and the wind screams around you, the pretense crumbles. Your voice cracks as you begin confessing things you never said: regrets about time wasted, gratitude for small moments you took for granted, an apology for being too proud or too absent. The cold makes your words slur slightly. End in a place of crystalline clarity and peace, where you're no longer fighting the mountain but surrendering to it, your final words a tender benediction rather than a goodbye.

title: The Final Lap
instruction: You are an elderly man on a stationary bike in a rehab clinic, pushing through the last minute of a timed sprint. At the start, you feel a surge of hope — a belief that you're stronger than the doctors say, that you'll beat this decline. Your voice comes in short, proud bursts between deep pedal-locked breaths. But then your legs burn, your lungs tighten, and the timer feels mocking. Disappointment creeps in — a quiet, swallowed realization that the body doesn't obey the will. Let your words become slower, more forced, the hope fading into a raspy surrender. Micro-distractions: a glance at the clock, a grimace, a cough that breaks your rhythm.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Disappointment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Sci-Fi: Time Traveler Meets Their Own Younger Self
instruction: Encountering your younger self, your voice is careful—you cannot disrupt the timeline. But your younger self is asking questions you remember asking. Your voice is both mentor and ghost. You're speaking to someone who will become you, but you cannot tell them what you know. Your breathing becomes double-layered—you're addressing your past while carrying your future. Your voice is gentle evasion—love expressed through strategic withholding. You're time-locked into silence about the very knowledge they most need.

title: Laughing at the Funeral: Finding Your Sibling's Last Letter
instruction: You've just found an envelope your sibling left you, to be opened after they're gone. As you read their words aloud, they're funny—absurdly, perfectly them. You laugh, genuinely, because they knew exactly how to reach you. Your voice is bright with surprised joy, warm with recognition. But underneath, grief is building. The laughter becomes mixed with tears you're trying to suppress. Your voice fractures between amusement and devastation. They're making you laugh from beyond death, and it's the cruelest, most beautiful gift. By the end, you're thanking them through laughter that's become sobbing, or sobbing that sounds like laughter—you can't tell anymore. Your voice holds profound gratitude and unbearable loss simultaneously. Let the emotions tangle together until they're inseparable. End with something like 'You bastard' or 'Thank you' said with infinite love and infinite pain.
inspired_by: Professional: Therapist Realizes Their Own Trauma Is Preventing Them From Helping

title: The Inverted Apology
instruction: You are upside down in a handstand against a wall, your voice thick and gargled from the blood rushing to your head. You are a young man with a deep, masculine voice, and you are sour with resentment over a petty fight with your best friend. You start off trying to call out to them, your words strained and wet, but as you hold the position, your anger softens into a bitter, reluctant apology. Let the physical struggle—the pressure in your head, the difficulty speaking—mirror your emotional sourness giving way to a grudging vulnerability. Speak naturally, with pauses to breathe or swallow, and let your tone shift from defensive and clipped to a slower, more honest exhaustion.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Shot
instruction: You are an aging athlete alone in an empty gymnasium, just after sinking your final free throw of a long career. Exhaustion is swallowing you—your lungs burn, your legs shake, and you lean against the wall, listening to the metallic echo of the ball rolling away. Start by catching your breath, whispering a raw, gasping celebration to yourself, but as you stare at the quiet court, your voice cracks and sinks into a weary, tender goodbye to this place. Let your words be broken between breaths, with sneaker squeaks and the ball's bounce filling the pauses, and let the triumph fade into a solemn, loving ache.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Conversation Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who will be gone by morning—a parent, a partner, a child. You begin with desperate attempts to hold onto them, your voice tight with the refusal to let go: 'Stay with me. Please, just stay.' But as you speak, something shifts. You start to release them, your voice softening into permission: 'I wanted more time. God, I wanted so much more time with you.' Your breath catches, but you continue, finding a strange grace: 'But what we had... what we had was enough. It has to be enough.' By the end, you're whispering through tears that are somehow peaceful: 'Go. It's okay. You can go now. I'll be okay.' The transformation is from grasping to releasing, from desperation to a love so deep it can let go.

title: The Storm Inside
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a sudden loss—and you're alone in your apartment when your body simply gives out. Begin standing, then let yourself physically collapse as the reality hits, not performed but genuinely allowing your legs to fail. You're on the floor now, and waves of sensation are moving through you—rage that makes you want to destroy something, grief that steals your breath, a physical pain in your chest that feels like your heart is actually breaking. Let your body lead: maybe you're pounding the floor, maybe curled into yourself, maybe crawling toward something. Your voice moves from silent gasping to guttural sounds to words that don't make sense to screaming to sobbing to laughing at the absurdity to silence again. Track the physical sensations—the heat in your face, the trembling in your hands, the ache in your throat. By the end, you're utterly spent, empty, lying still, and in that exhaustion, find a strange, fragile clarity.
inspired_by: Charting a Character in Four Areas

title: What I Never Asked You
instruction: You're confronting your mother about a childhood wound that's haunted you for decades. Start angry, armed with accusations and rehearsed grievances. But mid-confrontation, something shifts—you begin actually looking at her, noticing things you've never let yourself see: the way her hands shake slightly, a scar you never asked about, how she stands, the exact tone of her voice when it cracks. Your rage doesn't disappear, but genuine curiosity interrupts it. You start asking real questions—not rhetorical weapons, but actual wondering about who she was, what shaped her, what she was afraid of. End in a place of complicated recognition: anger still present, but now mixed with an uncomfortable, unwanted understanding born from truly seeing her as a full person for the first time.

title: Child Discovering Death for the First Time
instruction: A child (around 5-6) finds a dead bird. Perform the child's voice — high, curious, unafraid at first. 'Why isn't it moving?' Then the slow realization. Questions that have no good answers: 'Will it wake up? Is it sleeping? Does it hurt?' The voice shifts from curiosity to confusion to genuine, open grief — the kind only children experience, without any armor. Include the moment they connect it to someone they love: 'Will Grandma...?' Let the question hang.

title: Whispering Why You're Leaving to Your Sleeping Love
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're speaking so quietly they can't hear—but you need to say it out loud to make it real. Start tender, almost grateful, cataloging the small things you'll miss: the way they hum while cooking, their terrible jokes, how safe you felt. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, thick with unshed tears. But then comes the truth underneath: 'I'm disappearing here. I don't know who I am anymore.' The guilt is crushing—they didn't do anything wrong, which makes it worse. You're not angry. You're heartbroken for both of you. The emotion should catch in your throat, words breaking apart. End with the most painful intimacy: saying 'I love you' while knowing you're still going to leave. It's not a contradiction—it's the whole terrible truth.
inspired_by: Elevator Pitch for Your Life to God

title: Whispering Secrets to Your Sleeping Love
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're confessing things you can't say when they're awake—how scared you are that you're not enough for them, how deeply you need them, how you see the small ways you're failing them every day. This isn't a performance; it's the kind of three-in-the-morning honesty that only comes in darkness. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, catching on certain words, almost laughing at your own vulnerability in places. Begin with tender observations—how they look when they sleep, small things you love. Then let the deeper fear creep in: that you'll lose them, that you're already losing them, that love this good can't possibly last. End with a whispered 'I love you' that contains both worship and terror.
inspired_by: Hiding Relief After Receiving Good News You Expected

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She has minutes left. Begin by noticing everything through your sense of touch—the papery texture of her hand, the rough hospital blanket, the cold metal bed rail. Let yourself live entirely in what you're feeling physically, allowing it to heighten until your skin almost tingles with awareness. As you hold her hand, speak to her about a childhood memory, but let your emotional state shift from numb shock at the beginning to a breaking-open of grief by the end. Your voice should crack not from theatrical choice but from the genuine physical sensations flooding through your heightened awareness of touch—the last warmth of her fingers, the trembling in your own hands. End in a whisper as you feel her hand grow still.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from the airport gate—your flight to a war zone as a humanitarian aid worker boards in fifteen minutes. You start angry, needing to say everything you've held back for years about how they failed you. Your voice is sharp, unforgiving. But as you speak, you realize this might be the last conversation you ever have. The anger cracks open into something else—a desperate need to hear them say they love you before you go. Your voice softens, becomes almost childlike. By the end, you're asking for their blessing, your throat tight with the knowledge that you're choosing to leave them anyway. The anger hasn't disappeared—it's tangled with love, with goodbye, with the terrifying possibility that you'll die with things unsaid.
inspired_by: Group Sharing: Introducing Yourself as a Survivor

title: Protecting Your Child from an Invisible Threat
instruction: Your child is in danger—something is wrong, terribly wrong, and you can't stop it. Start with that high, tight, paralyzed fear: 'Baby, stay with me. Stay with me.' But panic explodes into fierce, protective rage: 'No! You can't have them!' Your voice cracks between terror and ferocity—you're a cornered animal defending its young. Scream it if you need to, then collapse back into whimpering helplessness: 'Please, please, not my baby.' Let your voice shatter between explosive maternal/paternal fury and complete powerlessness. End sobbing, voice breaking apart: 'I can't lose you. I can't.' This is fear that transforms into primal protectiveness, then dissolves into devastating helplessness. Raw. Uncontrolled. Utterly real.

title: The Skin Remembers Everything
instruction: You are experiencing an intense physical sensation—perhaps the first touch of a lover after months of loneliness, or the burning pain of a wound, or the overwhelming pleasure of a long-denied desire. Let your voice be completely governed by what your body is feeling. Begin with sharp intake of breath, with sounds that aren't quite words. Let pleasure mix with pain, let your voice become animal, uninhibited, freed from the need to be articulate or controlled. As the sensation builds and transforms, let your emotional state shift—perhaps from hunger to fulfillment, from agony to transcendence, from desperate need to sated peace. Make sounds you've never made before. Let your voice be rough, breathy, raw, unguarded. By the end, arrive at a place of stunned quietness, your body and voice completely spent, transformed by what you've allowed yourself to feel.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent who has minutes left. For your entire life, you've sought their approval and never fully received it. Begin speaking to them with quiet desperation, still trying to prove yourself worthy, still explaining why your choices mattered. But as you speak, something shifts—you realize mid-sentence that you're finally giving yourself the permission they never gave you. Your voice should transform from pleading and justifying to something quieter, more certain, more at peace. End by speaking not to earn their blessing, but to release both of you from this lifelong pattern. Let genuine forgiveness—of them and yourself—emerge through your words.

title: Screaming Into the Ocean Wind
instruction: You are standing alone at the edge of a cliff or beach, wind whipping around you, and you are shouting at your absent sibling who abandoned the family. Let your body be involved - gesturing wildly, pacing, feeling the physical sensation of rage moving through your limbs. Start by yelling the accusations into the wind: 'You left me alone with them! You saved yourself and you left me!' Feel your throat strain, your fists clench. Let the physical exertion of shouting mix with the emotional release. But as you exhaust yourself, as your voice grows hoarse, let the anger crack open to reveal what's underneath: the pain of being left behind, the terror you felt, the desperate loneliness. Your body should slowly collapse from aggressive stance to something smaller, more defeated. End on your knees or sitting, voice barely above a whisper, admitting: 'I needed you to protect me, and you just... left.' Transform from volcanic rage to physical and emotional exhaustion.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After You've Decided to Leave Their Other Parent
instruction: It's late at night. Your child is asleep. You're sitting beside their bed, speaking in barely-audible whispers, confessing what you can't say when they're awake. Start with tender observation—describing their peaceful face, their breathing. Your voice is full of love. Then the confession comes, halting and broken: you're going to change their world, shatter their sense of safety. Your throat catches on words like 'divorce' and 'different houses.' You're trying not to cry because you don't want to wake them, but tears are streaming silently. End with a promise—'I will never stop being your parent'—that you're desperately trying to believe yourself, voice thick with doubt and determination intertwined.
inspired_by: Your Child Asking Why You Cried About Their Assault

title: The Daughter Who Needed More
instruction: You are confronting your mother—a powerful witch who taught you magic but never gave you the emotional presence you needed. Begin as the eager student voice, demonstrating a spell perfectly, desperately trying to earn her approval one more time. When she responds with detached critique (switch to her cool, measured tone), let your younger self crack open. Explode into the painful truth: you never needed a better teacher, you needed a mother who saw you. Voice both sides of this confrontation—her defensive deflection that slowly crumbles into regret, your anger that breaks into the grief of a child still waiting to be held. End with a tentative, fragile moment where you both almost reach each other, voices barely above a whisper, the spell forgotten between you.
inspired_by: The Young Witch and Her Talking Cat

title: What I Actually See
instruction: You are confronting your father after years of feeling invisible to him. Begin by forcing yourself to truly look at him—really see his face, his posture, the way he's aged, the details you've been avoiding. Start your confrontation from a place of controlled anger, but as you genuinely perceive him—notice the tremor in his hands, the defeat in his shoulders, the fear in his eyes—your rage must crack open into something more complicated. Speak your truths while continuing to observe him with relentless attention, letting what you actually see in this moment change the words coming out of your mouth. End in a place where anger has transformed into painful, unwanted compassion mixed with residual hurt.

title: The Last Wave
instruction: You are a young man treading water in the middle of a dark lake, alone, after a failed rescue attempt. Your friend drowned moments ago, and you are exhausted, fighting to stay afloat. You speak to no one but yourself, gasping, your face dipping under as you struggle. Start with desperate, breathless disbelief—'No, no, not him'—then let the realization of loss sink in as your body weakens. Your voice cracks, you swallow water, and you end with a quiet, choked acceptance, barely above a whisper, as you stop fighting the current. Let the physical exhaustion shape your vocal breaks and pauses.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night and you're lying next to your sleeping lover. You need to whisper a confession that could end everything—something you've done, something you've hidden, something that's been slowly poisoning you both. Start barely audible, your body trembling with the effort of keeping quiet so as not to wake them. But as you confess into the darkness, the relief of finally speaking truth begins to overwhelm you. Your whisper intensifies, becomes urgent, almost ecstatic with release. Let your body soften, uncurl, as the poison leaves. End with tears—but they're not tears of shame anymore. They're tears of liberation, of finally being naked. Your voice, still quiet, transforms from terrified to tender to strangely joyful.

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's asleep—a partner, a friend, someone who can't hear you—and you finally whisper the truth you've never been able to say to their face. Your voice is barely audible, trembling with the risk of being vulnerable even though they're unconscious: 'I'm scared of how much I need you.' Let each confession come haltingly, with long pauses where you almost stop. You're admitting your fears, your inadequacies, the ways you've failed them that they don't even know about. Your voice catches on tears you're trying to hold back: 'Sometimes I look at you and I can't breathe because I know I don't deserve this... don't deserve you.' End with tender devastation, gently touching their hand, your voice breaking into a whisper so soft it's almost just breath: 'Please don't ever know how broken I really am.' This must feel like stolen intimacy, achingly gentle and heartbreakingly honest.

title: The Last Light in the Void
instruction: You are an older astronaut on a solo spacewalk, repairing a damaged panel on the station's hull. Your voice echoes in the helmet; each breath is loud, and radio static crackles occasionally. Start with a focused, almost mechanical tone as you work, distracted by the clunk of your tools and your own amplified breathing. Midway, you glance up and see Earth rising in the darkness—a sight you've seen a hundred times, but today it stops you. Let the realization sink in slowly. Your words become slower, quieter, with long pauses where you just listen to your own breathing. The emotion shifts from dutiful concentration to a deep, almost painful contemplation of how small and precious everything is. End with a fragile, hushed whisper, as if speaking only to the universe.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Wanting Another’s Luck
instruction: You are an older adult alone in a hospital waiting room, having just heard your younger sibling’s risky surgery succeeded. You sink into a plastic chair, hands trembling over the phone. Begin with a shaky exhale and a whisper of disbelief — the relief is so huge it almost hurts. But under that relief is a raw, bitter jealousy you’ve carried for years: you envied their easy life, their effortless charm. Let your voice waver between shame and gratitude, your words stumbling as you realize the envy has dissolved into pure love. End with a laugh-cry, breath catching, your tone warm and finally free.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Laughing Through the Beautiful Lie
instruction: You're telling someone the elaborate, beautiful lie you've constructed about your life—where you've been, what you've accomplished—and there's almost joy in the telling at first. Your voice is light, even playful: 'Oh, I've been amazing, I went to Paris, I wrote a book.' You're smiling, maybe even laughing softly as you add gorgeous details, making the fiction so lovely it almost hurts. But underneath the lightness, there's a tremor of profound sadness because the real truth is so much smaller, so much lonelier. As you continue—'I fell in love there, everything was perfect'—the laughter becomes strained, your voice catching between humor and heartbreak. By the end, you're still smiling, still adding beautiful lies, but tears are streaming down your face. There's strange peace in this moment: surrendering to the fiction while fully aware of its falseness, finding odd comfort in the story you wish were true, even as reality breaks your heart.

title: The Glittering Trap
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a deliberately soft, almost girlish voice that you've weaponized in business—until now. You're in a tense boardroom negotiation with a younger, sharper female rival who is smoothly dismantling your carefully prepared proposal. You begin speaking with that practiced, melodious tone, trying to maintain control, but as you notice her condescending glance, a wave of confusion hits you: why didn't your usual charm work? Fear creeps in as you realize you're losing ground, and a sliver of jealousy colors your voice when you see how easily she commands respect. By the end, your voice cracks, losing its polished edge, becoming smaller and more desperate as you awkwardly trail off, physically shifting in your chair, fiddling with your pen.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Fear (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Laughing Through Tears: Remembering Them as They'd Want
instruction: You're telling a story about them—something ridiculous, perfectly them. You start laughing, really laughing, because the memory is so vivid and absurd. Your voice is bright with affection and the joy of remembering. But mid-laugh, you catch yourself—they're gone, and you'll never make new memories. The laughter doesn't stop immediately; it tangles with tears, creating that strange, beautiful sound of joy and grief existing in the same breath. Your voice wavers between chuckling and sobbing, sometimes in the same sentence. You keep trying to finish the story because they'd want you to laugh, and that insistence becomes both heartbreaking and healing. End with gratitude—thanking them through tears and laughter, your voice full of both deep sadness and deep love, accepting that carrying both is how you'll honor them now.
inspired_by: Grief: Hearing Someone Else's Voice and Falling Apart

title: Fever Dream Monologue
instruction: You're delirious with a 104-degree fever. Narrate whatever your brain produces — it should be vivid, nonsensical, and emotionally intense. Alternate between lucid moments ('I need water, I'm so hot') and hallucinatory ones where you speak to people who aren't there. Your voice should be dry, cracked, wavering between whisper and sudden outbursts. Include shivering despite the heat. Let the fever dreams have genuine emotional weight.

title: The Pursuer's Apology
instruction: You are a middle-aged man jogging through a quiet park. You are chasing a stranger who you believe stole your wallet, but they are faster and have disappeared into the trees. As you run, you realize you were wrong—it was your own mistake. Start with malice, your voice shaking with each pounding step as you grunt threats under your breath. By the end, let that contempt crumble into helplessness as you slow to a stop, admitting to the empty air that you are lost and foolish. Speak while panting heavily, your words broken by the rhythm of your stride, losing your train of thought when you have to gasp for air.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Contempt (slightly present), Helplessness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bedside Vigil at 3 AM
instruction: You're alone with someone you love who is dying, in the quiet hours before dawn. They're unconscious or barely conscious. Speak in whispers, as if raising your voice would shatter something sacred. Begin by talking about ordinary things—the weather, what you had for dinner—because you can't bear to say what needs to be said. Let your voice be tender but fractured, intimate as a prayer. Gradually, give yourself permission to confess: the moments you treasure, the things you never thanked them for, the ways they changed you. Let tears thicken your words but don't sob—keep it quiet, private, almost a lullaby. End by giving them permission to go, even though it's destroying you. Your voice should be barely audible, each word a struggle between holding on and letting go.

title: The Last Touch
instruction: You are an elderly, androgynous person, lying on a worn-out couch. Your lover has their hand pressed firmly against your throat — not to hurt, but to hold you there, to keep you still. You’re trapped under them, breath shallow and raspy, each word a struggle against the pressure. Start with a raw, almost desperate whisper of lust, your voice catching and cracking as you try to speak. But as you go on, a deep, unexpected calm settles in — a quiet acceptance that this is your last time together. Let your pitch waver and your breath break, but end with a soft, breathless peace, as if you’ve already let go.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Holding Someone During a Seizure While Talking to 911
instruction: Someone is seizing in your arms. Your voice must split: holding them with complete presence ('You're okay, you're safe') while simultaneously giving clipped facts to 911. Your breath is shaky but words stay measured. Occasionally your voice cracks when you look at their face, then steels again.

title: Last Walk Along Our River Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're wading through the shallow water of the river where you first fell in love, but this time your partner is leaving tomorrow—emigrating to another country, a relationship ending not from lack of love but from impossible circumstances. Start by describing the water around your feet with false brightness, trying to keep things light, but let your voice gradually crack as memories flood back with each ripple. By the end, you're no longer describing water—you're confessing everything you wish you'd said sooner, your voice breaking between gratitude for what you had and grief for what you're losing. The water becomes a metaphor you can barely speak through your tears.
inspired_by: Walking Barefoot Through Shallow, Cool Water

title: The Last Lecture
instruction: You've just received devastating news (a diagnosis, a betrayal, a loss) right before you're supposed to give a talk about something you love—could be baking, architecture, bird migration, anything that lights you up. Begin speaking about your subject with forced enthusiasm, your voice bright but brittle. As you continue, the pure joy of the knowledge itself starts breaking through your grief—the miracle of how birds navigate by stars, the perfect chemistry of bread rising, the mathematics of a cathedral arch. Your voice becomes genuine, almost ecstatic, even as tears start flowing. End in a strange, transcendent space where devastating sorrow and pure intellectual joy exist simultaneously. You're laughing and crying, your voice soaring with wonder while breaking with pain, discovering that even in the worst moment, beauty and knowledge can still set you on fire.

title: The Rising Flood
instruction: You are a middle-aged man trapped in a collapsed building as floodwater rises to your chin. You cling to a broken beam, gasping between waves that wash over your face. At first, you call out longingly for your daughter—your voice cracking with hope as you shout her name above the water. But as the water surges higher and your arms burn from exhaustion, the longing curdles into raw, physical pain; your cries turn into choked, guttural groans, with splashing and muffled gasps between each agonized word. Let the water interrupt your speech naturally—sometimes clear, sometimes completely muffled—and let the transition from desperate hope to visceral pain come through in the trembling, strained texture of your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Tied in Gratitude and Doubt
instruction: You are an elderly person, bound in soft rope during an intimate moment with a trusted partner. Your hands are tied above your head, the rope creaking gently as you shift. Your breathing is uneven—half from arousal, half from the weight of what you're about to say. You have spent a lifetime learning to be wary of trust, yet here you are, willingly vulnerable. Start with a quiet, contemplative pause, feeling the pressure of the bindings. Then express gratitude for this surrender, but let doubt creep in—hesitations, a faltering tone, a sigh. Speak in a low, strained voice, occasionally losing the thread of your thought as you react to the rope shifting or the warmth of skin nearby. End with a raw whisper, equal parts thankfulness and uncertainty.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Doubt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a family secret you discovered—one they've kept from you for decades, one that reframes your entire childhood. Start with cold, prosecutorial anger: you want answers, you want them to hurt the way you're hurting. Lay out your evidence like a lawyer. But as they begin to explain (imagine their responses), something starts to crack in you. You begin to hear the fear they lived with, the impossible choice they made. Your anger doesn't disappear—it transforms into something more complicated. Let your voice break between fury and an unwanted understanding. End not with forgiveness or reconciliation, but with the devastating recognition that they were just as lost as you are now. Your final words should carry both rage and a terrible, unwanted compassion.
inspired_by: Actor has been cast in a major role and has weeks before rehearsal begins

title: Laughing Through Tears While Scattering Your Best Friend's Ashes
instruction: You're standing at the place you and your best friend always said you'd scatter their ashes—somewhere ridiculous, somewhere meaningful only to you two. You start reading the letter they left you, and it's funny. Genuinely, stupidly funny. They're making jokes about death, roasting you one last time, and you're laughing—really laughing—even as tears are streaming down your face. You have to stop reading because you're laughing too hard, but the laughter keeps turning into sobs and back again. You're trying to honor their request to 'make it fun, not sad,' but your heart is shattering. You tell them stories, cracking up at memories, then your voice breaks mid-laugh because they're not here to laugh with you. You open the urn still chuckling through tears, and as you scatter the ashes, you're saying goodbye with this impossible mixture of joy and devastation. Your voice is bright and broken simultaneously, celebrating them while grieving them, finding absurd, painful, beautiful peace in this contradictory moment.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Knight Must Execute the Sibling They Protected

title: The Inheritance Confrontation
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging mother, finally saying what you've never said. Start with careful, measured words—you came here to talk about the house, the estate, practical matters. But then it spills out: why did she always choose your brother, why were you never enough, why does this still hurt after forty years? Your voice moves from controlled to raw, from questions to accusations to something more vulnerable. She tries to deflect, and you feel yourself becoming the desperate child again, voice breaking with the realization that you're still seeking her approval even now, even as you confront her. End with a question asked so quietly it's almost not spoken at all, because you're terrified of the answer.

title: The Fox's Confession
instruction: You are whispering a secret to your sleeping lover in the dark—something you've hidden for years. You have always moved through relationships like a fox: clever, quick, always with an escape route, never fully caught. Begin curled against them, your breathing shallow and careful, your body coiled tight with the habit of self-protection. Your voice should be almost inaudible at first, testing whether it's safe. As you confess what you've been hiding, let your body slowly unfurl—muscles you didn't know were clenched begin to soften, your breathing deepens, your spine uncurls. The words come easier. Your clever defenses dissolve. By the end, you are still whispering, but your body is completely open, vulnerable, pressed fully against them without armor. The fox has stopped running and allowed itself to be held.
inspired_by: When you are building a character with a distinctive physical life

title: The Line I Drew
instruction: You're at a small, noisy party. A friend you've been close with suddenly leans in to kiss you. You have to stop it without cruelty. Start with a warm, caught-off-guard laugh, but you feel that sourness—you know it'll sting. Your voice tightens. You clear your throat, and your pitch flattens. You say 'No' like it's a period, not a question. Each word becomes crisp, deliberate, leaving no room for hope. You finish with a quiet, final tone, already stepping back.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: After the Storm
instruction: You are a teenage girl lying on your bedroom floor, face down, after crying for a long time. Your throat is raw, your nose completely stuffed, and you feel hollow and helpless after a huge fight with your mom. In this exhausted stillness, you start scrolling through your phone and find a silly video your best friend sent hours ago—a goofy memory from last summer. As you watch, a tiny, unexpected smile cracks through the numbness, and you feel a flicker of warmth and pure, improbable ecstasy in your chest. Speak the words slowly, with a hoarse, nasal voice, letting the helplessness color the first part and then letting a fragile, breathy pleasure creep in at the end. You can pause, sniffle, or lose your thought naturally.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Vow at the Breaking Point
instruction: You're protecting someone you love—a child, a partner, a sibling—from a threat, and you're making a fierce promise to them or about them. Start with explosive, almost violent intensity—rage at whatever or whoever threatens them, your voice sharp and dangerous. Let that fury build until it peaks, then shatter it completely. The anger collapses into helpless terror because you're not sure you can keep this promise. Your voice should break, becoming raw and desperate. End with a kind of fierce tenderness—a quieter, deeper vow that comes from a place beyond rage, mixing absolute love with the trembling knowledge of your own limitations. The arc moves from aggressive power to vulnerable determination, showing both your strength and your fear in the same breath.
inspired_by: An Ode to a Lost Childhood

title: The Last Clear Moment: Saying Goodbye Before the Fog
instruction: You have early-onset dementia, and you know you're in one of your last truly lucid windows. You're sitting with someone you love deeply—a child, a partner, a best friend—and you need to say everything while you still can. Start with urgent clarity, racing to share memories, advice, love declarations, apologies, all tumbling out because time is running out. Your words come fast but purposeful, layered with desperate tenderness. Midway through, you feel the fog beginning to creep in—words become slightly harder to find, you pause, frightened. End in a quieter place, clinging to their hand, whispering the most essential truth with heartbreaking simplicity, knowing this clarity is slipping away forever.

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You're an old man in a locker room surrounded by younger guys bragging and grunting. At first, you join in with a forced, gruff laugh, slapping a bench and giving a crude joke—but their boasting about women and fights turns your stomach. Your voice starts loud and rough, but as the disgust climbs, your responses get shorter, your laughter dies into a bitter snort. Eventually you mutter, 'That ain't right,' then trail off, staring at your shoes, the bravado gone—leaving only a weary, sour silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Home, Through The Visor
instruction: You're a child in a space station, sealed inside your helmet with the visor up. In the quiet hum of the suit, you're on a comms check with your mother on Earth. At first you just report the facts—altitude, oxygen, your heartbeat—with the slight weight of being brave. But as static crackles and you watch the blue planet rotate below, your voice softens, breath gets heavier, and a quiet longing seeps in. Let the helmet's close space guide your voice: tinny, compressed, with breaths and clicks. End with a simple, lingering wish—just for her to know you're looking at the same stars.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unexpected Gift
instruction: You're lying in a warm bath, eyes half-closed, every muscle limp and heavy. Your young child appears at the tub's edge, holding a crumpled, drippy gift—a drawing made with bath crayons. Confusion washes over you first: why are they here, in the middle of your quiet? Your voice comes out slow, loose, words bumping into each other as you ask what that is. They explain they made it for you because you seemed tired. Astonishment flickers—a tiny, genuine surprise at their thoughtfulness. Then, as you look at the wobbly hearts and stick figures, gratitude spreads through your chest like warm water. Your voice softens, still languid, but now filled with a tender, awestruck thankfulness. You speak to them, your words unhurried and thick with love, pausing to blow a stray bubble or wipe a wet hand on the towel.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Trimester's Crown
instruction: You are an elderly man in the final weeks of a late-in-life pregnancy. At a family gathering, you sit heavily in a chair, struggling to breathe, shifting your weight to ease the pressure on your diaphragm. You watch a younger relative flaunt her easy pregnancy, and you feel a deep, sour envy—your body aches, you've been dismissed as too old. But as you speak, you realize that your child will be a miracle, a triumph over nature's odds. Begin with a bitter, breathless complaint about the pains and judgments, then let your voice fill with fierce, defiant pride as you declare your victory. Let the micro-distractions of your physical discomfort—sighs, pauses, adjusting your posture—be part of the performance. The emotion shifts from sour jealousy to intense triumph.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Sourness (extremely present), Triumph (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed. For years, you've carried a secret dream they never approved of—something they called impractical, foolish, or beneath you. Now, in their final hours, something in their eyes, their breathing, or the way they squeeze your hand tells you they want to say something but can't find the words. Begin speaking to them about ordinary things—the weather, the flowers someone brought—but let yourself sense what they're actually trying to communicate. As you talk, pay attention to every fleeting feeling that rises in you about what they need to hear or what they're trying to give you. Let those impressions guide you to say what has been unspoken between you for decades. Move from careful, surface conversation to the raw truth of what you both know but have never acknowledged. Your emotion should transform from cautious constraint to tearful liberation.
inspired_by: Actor feels their intuition is unreliable or nonexistent

title: The Graduation That Never Happened
instruction: You're alone in an empty room, but you're living through your own graduation ceremony—a moment of achievement you've actually reached or desperately wish you had. Create every detail: imagine the weight of the diploma in your hands, the scratch of the gown fabric, the sea of faces watching you, the specific person you most want to see in the audience. Give a silent or whispered acceptance speech to this imaginary crowd, thanking people, acknowledging your journey. But here's the complexity: as you speak, layer in the grief, resentment, or loss that accompanies this achievement. Thank the parent who never believed in you. Acknowledge the person who should be here but isn't. Celebrate the dream while mourning what it cost you. Let the joy of the imagined accomplishment become inseparable from the pain of the real circumstances. End in a place where triumph and devastation are completely intertwined, where you can't tell if you're laughing or crying.

title: The Studio Gate
instruction: You have just been fired, rejected, told you have no future in the one thing you've devoted your life to. You are confronting the person who delivered this news—maybe a parent who said 'I told you so,' or a former supporter who has lost faith in you, or even yourself in a mirror. Begin in the rawness of humiliation and pain, voice breaking, nearly defeated. Let yourself explore the temptation to agree with them, to give up. But as you speak, as you hear yourself listing all the reasons you should quit, something hardens in you. Your voice changes. You hear yourself making a promise—not a desperate plea, but a vow. By the end, you are speaking with diamond-hard clarity and quiet power, telling them (or yourself) exactly what you will do, who you will become, how you will return. Transform from broken to unbreakable.
inspired_by: When you are an aspiring actor hearing discouraging stories about Hollywood's difficulty

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Instructions
instruction: You're terminally ill, recording instructions for your own funeral, and you've decided to make it absurd. Start with genuine laughter, finding dark humor in the situation, voice light and ironic as you detail ridiculous requests. 'Make sure someone plays that terrible song I love...' You're almost giddy with the freedom of knowing you won't be there to care what anyone thinks. But laughter keeps catching in your throat. Your voice wavers between amusement and something deeper—gratitude for the life you've had, grief for what you're leaving. You laugh while tears stream down your face, voice breaking as you thank people who'll hear this after you're gone. End with peace breaking through the contradictions—your voice soft, still touched by laughter but profoundly grateful, at ease with the impossible: finding joy and sorrow can live in the same breath.
inspired_by: Making Up After a Terrible Fight

title: Bedside Confession to Your Sleeping Beloved
instruction: Your partner lies in a coma, and doctors say they might hear you. You're whispering a confession you've carried for years—something you did, something you never told them, something that shaped your entire relationship. Begin barely audible, the words catching in your throat, testing if you can even say it aloud. Your voice trembles with shame, guilt, and desperate hope for forgiveness from someone who can't respond. As you confess, tears come silently—the kind that choke you but you keep talking through because this might be your only chance. The confession transforms into a love letter, into gratitude for every moment despite your secret, into begging them to wake up so you can hear their voice one more time. End with your forehead pressed to their hand, whispering 'I'm sorry' and 'please stay' in the same breath, your voice breaking on every word, barely holding yourself together.

title: Interviewing Your Parent About Their Mistakes
instruction: You're asking them directly about something they did that hurt you. Your voice is steady and journalistic, protecting yourself with distance. They answer defensively and your voice sharpens: 'How did you think that made me feel?' Your breathing gets deeper. By the end, you're having a real conversation deeper than expected.

title: Weapons Dealer Morality Crashing
instruction: You're justifying the weapons you've sold as a simple transaction, but the person you're speaking to has shown you a photograph of the child killed by those weapons. Your voice hardens into defensiveness, then cracks. You try logic: weapons are neutral, intent matters, you're not responsible for how they're used. But each argument sounds weaker. Your breathing becomes shallow. You're sweating through words. By the end, you're not defending your choices anymore—you're begging for forgiveness without ever saying that word. Your voice becomes almost inaudible as you ask 'How do I live with this?'

title: First Light Through the Visor
instruction: You are an astronaut on a solo spacewalk, floating in silence. A few minutes ago you fumbled your tether clip and had to awkwardly retrieve it, and you’re still feeling a dull numbness from the isolation – your voice is flat, a little wooden, with the tinny, confined echo of the helmet. As you rotate to face the planet, the morning terminator line hits you. The awe is sudden and overwhelming: your breath catches, your voice cracks, and the words come out as a hushed, broken whisper – you almost forget the radio is on. Let the embarrassment at your earlier clumsiness linger as a brief self-conscious laugh or sigh before awe takes over completely.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Telling Your Family You're Leaving a Good Relationship
instruction: He's nice, stable, on paper perfect. But you're leaving. Your voice is firm but braced for judgment: 'I'm not happy.' They push: 'But he's such a good man!' Your voice becomes more solid: 'I don't love him like I should.' Include them saying you're ungrateful and your voice wavering before steadying. 'I have to choose myself.' Voice ends resolute, willing to be the villain.

title: Whispered Truths in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner who thinks you're asleep. You need to confess something that will change everything—maybe an affair, maybe a truth about who you really are, maybe that you're dying. Start by whispering their name so softly it's almost not sound at all, just breath. Your voice is tender, achingly gentle, as if the words themselves might shatter them. Speak slowly, each word carefully placed, like you're building something fragile. Halfway through, your voice begins to tremble—not with drama, but with the quiet devastation of knowing this is the last moment before everything breaks. End with a phrase that's half-confession, half-goodbye: 'I need you to know...' Let your voice catch and fade, the rest left unspoken because speaking it makes it real.

title: The Numb Threat
instruction: You're an older, gruff man just out of the dentist's chair, your mouth still half-frozen from novocaine. You're on the phone with a rival you've been feuding with for years. You start off trying to sound menacing, threatening him with consequences you've been planning, but your slurred speech and drool make you feel foolish. As you speak, the embarrassment grows, and your malevolent tone cracks into a frustrated, mumbling admission that you can't even talk right. Let the physical struggle—the numb lips, the extra spit, the over-enunciation—shape your words. End with a defeated, bitter laugh at yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Bittersweet Goodbye Gift
instruction: You're holding an object—a gift from someone you deeply love who has betrayed you or hurt you irreparably. You're seeing them for the last time, and you're giving this object back. Begin gripping it tightly, your whole body contracted with the war between love and anger, gratitude and resentment. Your muscles should reflect this conflict—jaw clenched while tears threaten, shoulders raised defensively while your heart aches to embrace them. As you speak, describing what this gift once meant and why you can't keep it, allow your grip to gradually soften. Let opposing sensations coexist in your body: tears falling while your voice stays steady, hands trembling while your spine stays strong. End by placing the object down with unexpected tenderness, your body finally settling into a strange peace that holds both grief and liberation, your breath both heavy and free.

title: The Last Sound of You
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent in their final hour. Begin by holding everything in—your breath is shallow, your body rigid with the fear of losing control. You're trying to be strong, composed, the good son or daughter. But as you watch their breathing slow, something breaks open in you. Let yourself release sounds you've never made before—deep, wordless sounds from your belly, your chest, sounds that carry all the years of things unsaid. These aren't pretty or controlled; they're raw animal grief. By the end, you're not holding anything back anymore. You're completely broken open, making sounds that feel like they're tearing you apart, but paradoxically, you feel more present with them than you've been in years. Transform from locked-down control to complete vocal and physical release.

title: The Same Old Fight
instruction: You're a teenage boy in a shouting match with your mom in the kitchen. You've had this argument a hundred times—about your phone, your grades, your attitude. Your voice starts tight and nasal, repeating the same complaints with automatic anger, but halfway through you see her face drop. A crack appears. Your rhythm stutters, you trail off, and suddenly the fight isn't about winning—it's about the hurt you're causing. Let your voice shift from a whining crescendo to a quiet, unsteady admission. End with a raw, simple confession.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Final Flight: A Daughter's Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: Your mother is about to board a one-way flight to participate in a pioneering deep-space mission—she'll be gone for decades, perhaps forever. You start with forced brightness, trying to be supportive: 'This is what you've always wanted.' But as you watch her gather her things, your voice begins to fracture. You ask a simple question—'Will you think of me?'—and her answer, whatever it is, breaks something open in you. Your anger surfaces briefly: 'You're choosing this over me.' But then you see her face, the conflict there, and your voice softens into something unbearably tender. You realize she needs your blessing to leave without guilt. Your final words—'Go. Be extraordinary.'—must carry both your devastation at losing her and your fierce love that wants her to fly. Let your voice shake with the effort of giving this gift.
inspired_by: Parent Showing Quiet Pride: Misreading, Then Understanding

title: Confronting Your Lover About the Affair You've Been Pretending Not to Know About
instruction: Begin with eerie calm, your voice almost conversational: 'I know about her. I've known for three months.' Let the words hang there, deadly quiet. Describe one specific moment when you knew—finding a receipt, a text notification, the way they said a certain name—your voice growing sharper, more precise with pain. Then let your control shatter: demand to know why you weren't enough, your voice rising with humiliation and rage. But here's the turn: mid-accusation, let yourself remember why you loved them. Your voice softens with devastating vulnerability: 'We were good once. Weren't we good?' Feel the confusion of still loving someone who destroyed you. End by asking the question you're terrified to hear answered: 'Do you love her?' Your voice barely a whisper, already bracing for the truth that will end everything.
inspired_by: Asking Your Parent for Money While Ashamed

title: The Truth We've Been Avoiding
instruction: You're confronting your parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your childhood. Start with controlled anger—you've rehearsed this, you're ready. But as you speak, listing the birthdays they missed, the times you needed them and they chose something else, your voice begins to shake. The anger gives way to something rawer: the child inside you who just wanted to be seen. When they try to defend themselves, you cut through with devastating honesty: 'I just needed you to love me more than you loved your own pain.' End with your voice small, almost a whisper, as you realize you're finally letting go of the hope they'll ever truly understand. The transformation is from righteous anger to heartbroken acceptance.

title: Kill Steal
instruction: You're a young woman deeply invested in a competitive online game, gripping your mouse or controller tensely. Your teammate just swooped in and stole the final hit on the boss you've been fighting for ten minutes, taking the rare loot drop for themselves. Start with a sharp, mechanical click of the mouse as you freeze, then let a bitter, jealous tone bleed into your voice as you lean into the mic. Your pitch starts high and strained from the adrenaline, but as you speak, you feel a sinking, resentful ache — let your voice soften into a quieter, more bitter quietness, laced with envy. Between sentences, shift your weight in the chair, let it squeak, or pause to adjust your headphones, as if barely containing the urge to slam something.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Door You Can't Unlock
instruction: Your teenager has locked themselves in their room, and you've just found evidence of self-harm. Start pounding on the door, your voice raw with terror: 'Open this door RIGHT NOW!' Pure parental authority masking panic. But it shifts—your voice cracks, becomes desperate, almost begging: 'Please, baby, please just talk to me.' Then rage at your own helplessness erupts: 'I'm your mother/father, I'm supposed to PROTECT you and I can't even—' Break down completely, sliding down against the door, your voice reduced to a broken whisper: 'I don't know how to save you. Tell me how to save you.' End with fierce tenderness through tears: 'I'm not leaving this door. I'm right here.'

title: Explosive Reckoning: When the Lie Destroys Everything
instruction: The person you love most is walking away, and the lie has finally destroyed everything. You start with fierce, almost aggressive desperation: 'Don't you dare walk away from me! You don't get to just leave!' Your voice is loud, raw, commanding. But then it cracks completely, collapsing into broken pleading: 'Please. Please don't go. I can't... I can't lose you.' Rage and grief tangle together as your voice becomes ragged: 'I lied because I was terrified! Because everyone leaves and I thought if I could just control it, just manage it...' The fury at yourself is devastating. Then suddenly, all the fight drains out, and your voice becomes small, helpless: 'But I can't control this. I can't control anything.' By the end, you're barely whispering, defeated: 'I love you. That's the only truth that matters, and it's too late.' Move from explosive rage through pleading desperation into complete emotional collapse.

title: Aftermath of the Unforgivable
instruction: You've just learned that someone you love—your child, your partner, your closest friend—has done something terrible, something that goes against everything you thought they were. You're confronting them immediately after finding out. Start with shock that makes your voice shake, then explode into rage—screaming, demanding explanations, your voice raw and ugly with betrayal. But mid-fury, something shifts. You see them crumbling, and despite everything, your protective instinct kicks in. Your anger collapses into anguished confusion. You're sobbing now, furious at yourself for still loving them, for wanting to help them even as you're devastated by what they've done. End in a place of complete emotional chaos—you don't know if you're condemning them or saving them, pushing them away or pulling them close. Your voice breaks between 'How could you?' and 'What do we do now?'

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Child
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's bed at 2 AM, watching them sleep, knowing you're leaving tomorrow for a treatment facility. They don't know yet. Your voice is barely above a whisper, confessional: 'I'm so sorry for all the times I wasn't really here.' You're telling them everything you've been too ashamed to say when they're awake. 'Some days I looked at you and felt so much love it terrified me... and some days I felt nothing, and that terrified me more.' Your voice catches. You touch their hair gently: 'You deserve someone who isn't broken.' The tenderness is overwhelming, mixed with self-recrimination. 'I'm going to try to get better. For you.' A pause. 'I don't know if I can.' Your voice breaks completely: 'But you—you are the most beautiful thing I've ever done.' You stay there in silence, crying quietly, one hand on their sleeping form.

title: The Body Remembers
