instruction: You are experiencing a moment of physical pain that triggers a flood of emotional memory—perhaps an injury that recalls an old betrayal, or a touch that awakens both desire and rage, or an illness that brings up grief you thought you'd buried. Let your body and voice react to both the physical sensation and the emotional avalanche simultaneously. Start with the immediate physical response—gasps, cries, reactive sounds—then let these blend and transform as the emotional memories crash through you. Rage might give way to sobbing, or pain might ignite into defiant laughter, or desire might crack into vulnerability. Your voice should be raw, unfiltered, moving between primal physical sounds and emotionally charged words. End in a different state entirely: exhausted tenderness, fierce acceptance, or quiet empowerment.

title: The View Through a Visor
instruction: You are an elderly astronaut alone in a maintenance airlock, helmet sealed, listening to the crackle of your suit radio. You stare through your visor at a distant planet where a younger crew is celebrated. Start with a tight, envious voice—bitter about being left behind, your jealousy leaking through controlled breaths. As you speak, let the fear of irrelevance creep in, and end with a quiet, shaky acceptance. Your words are half to yourself, half to the static. Let your breathing and the helmet's hiss interrupt you naturally.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Mirror of Accusations
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) who keeps throwing different versions of their pain at you—sometimes screaming, sometimes coldly silent, sometimes mockingly laughing, sometimes collapsing in tears, sometimes speaking in the voice of your younger self. You find yourself involuntarily absorbing and reflecting back each emotional attack, unable to maintain your defensive stance. Start from a place of righteous anger, determined to finally speak your truth and stay in control. But as they shift unpredictably between rage, manipulation, vulnerability, and cruelty, you find yourself mirroring their chaos, until your carefully prepared speech dissolves and you're left speaking from a place of raw, undefended honesty—scared, sorry, and completely exposed.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Love
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're watching your partner sleep, knowing you're leaving them in the morning—not because you don't love them, but because you do, and you're dying, and you can't bear to watch them watch you disappear. Your voice is barely audible, a confession to the dark. Start with tender observation: the way they breathe, how their hand curls near their face. Your throat tightens as you whisper all the things you never said enough—'You made me believe in gentleness.' Each phrase catches, breaks, reforms. You're crying silently, words fragmenting: 'I'm so sorry. You deserved... more time.' You touch their hair so softly they don't wake. Your voice becomes even smaller, dissolving into breath: 'Please forgive me for loving you enough to go.' By the end, you're just breathing in sync with them, your last whispered 'Thank you' so quiet it's almost imagined. The silence that follows holds everything.

title: Reading Your Estranged Sibling's Letter at Their Funeral
instruction: Your sibling died before you could reconcile. At the funeral, you're handed a letter they wrote years ago but never sent. Read it aloud to the empty room after everyone leaves. Their words are funny—a stupid inside joke from childhood. You laugh, genuine and surprised, even as tears stream down your face. They apologize for something small and ridiculous. You laugh harder, shaking your head. Then they write something devastating—that they always loved you, always looked up to you, were waiting for you to reach out too. Your laughter chokes off. You can barely get the words out through sobs. But they end with another joke, something so perfectly them. You laugh again through crying, a broken, beautiful sound. Thank them aloud for the letter. Tell them you're sorry too. Your voice holds everything at once—grief, gratitude, regret, love, the bitter sweetness of getting their words when they're gone. End smiling through tears, whispering 'goodbye' like you're releasing them.
inspired_by: Phone Call with Your Younger Self

title: The Reunion on the Old Street
instruction: You have returned to the exact street, playground, or yard where you spent your childhood summers, and you are speaking to a childhood friend you haven't seen in twenty years. Begin with awkward adult pleasantries, both of you tentative and guarded. As you walk through this space together, let the sensory details flood back—the particular quality of sunlight through the trees, the sound of screen doors slamming, the smell of cut grass or summer rain. Your voices should gradually shift, becoming more animated, speaking faster, interrupting each other with 'Remember when—?' Let yourself feel the pure, uncomplicated friendship you once had, that absolute certainty that this person understood you completely. But simultaneously, feel the piercing awareness of everything you've both lost—innocence, time, the people you were. End in a bittersweet place where you're laughing and crying at once, grateful for this resurrection of your childhood selves while mourning the impossibility of ever truly returning.
inspired_by: Revisiting and Re-Creating Childhood Environments, Events, Friends, and Toys

title: The Sugar Wall
instruction: You're a teenage girl studying late, riding the crash after a candy-and-energy-drink binge. Your body feels heavy, your thoughts stick like mud, and every word comes out slower, sourer than you intend. Start with a burst of irritable frustration — snap at the mess on your desk, roll your eyes at the clock — but let that irritation curdle into a quieter, more honest doubt. By the end, your voice should sound deflated, almost hollow, as you question whether any of this effort actually matters. Let your speech be interrupted by sighs, long pauses, and the physical weight of the slump in your chair.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing at Your Abuser's Funeral
instruction: You're at the funeral reception of someone who hurt you deeply—and you're feeling an intoxicating, terrifying mixture of relief and grief. Start with an almost manic lightness: 'Everyone's crying and I just want to... laugh?' There's genuine confusion in your voice. 'I'm free. God, I'm finally free.' Your breath comes faster, almost giddy. But then something shifts—unexpected tears: 'So why does this hurt?' Your voice breaks with the contradiction. 'I hated you. I still hate you. But you were...' The complexity deepens: 'You were my mother. My father. My—' Laughter and tears mix: 'I don't even know what I'm supposed to feel.' End with a moment of profound, bittersweet acceptance: 'Thank you for dying. And I'm sorry I mean that. And I'm sorry I'm not sorry.' Peace and chaos coexist in your final breath.

title: Watching Your Child Leave for War
instruction: You're at the airport, watching your child in uniform prepare to deploy to a war zone. Your voice begins with forced cheerfulness, desperately trying to be brave: 'You're going to be amazing out there. I'm so proud.' But the facade cracks as you struggle to memorize their face, your voice becoming raw with suppressed panic: 'Promise me you'll... just promise me.' There's a moment where you realize you might never see them again, and your voice breaks completely, whispering the things you've never said: 'I should have told you every single day how much...' Then something shifts. You find a strength that surprises even you, your voice steadying with fierce, protective love: 'You carry my heart with you. Always.' End with a goodbye that sounds like both an ending and a blessing, your voice embodying the terrible beauty of letting go of someone you'd die to protect.
inspired_by: Accepting Terminal Diagnosis: Bargaining Becoming Acceptance

title: The Last Story Before Sleep
instruction: You are sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—a parent, grandparent, or guardian—who is dying. They ask you to tell them about your favorite childhood memory with them, something that made you feel safe and loved. Start with gentle reluctance, not wanting to accept this is goodbye, speaking haltingly as if the words are too heavy. As you tell the story, let yourself fall completely into the sensory details—the smell of their kitchen, the texture of their sweater, the sound of their laugh. Feel yourself becoming the child you were in that memory, your voice softening, your body relaxing into that remembered safety. By the end, arrive at a place of profound gratitude mixed with unbearable loss, your words both a gift to them and a farewell to your own childhood. Let the memory be so vivid that for a moment, you both exist in that past together one last time.
inspired_by: Revisiting and Re-Creating Childhood Environments, Events, Friends, and Toys

title: The Hidden Clause
instruction: You are an elderly woman, reading the fine print of a legal document aloud to yourself at a small desk. The morning light catches your eyes, making you squint. You start with a rapid, monotone delivery, emphasizing qualifying words like 'provided that' and 'notwithstanding' — each phrase clipped, your voice carrying a faint edge of impatience. Midway through a sentence, you stumble on a word; you pause, adjust your glasses, and mutter under your breath. Then you notice a clause you had missed — it grants you a small, unexpected benefit. Your voice lifts, still careful but now lighter, a suppressed smile creeping in as you slow down to savor the phrasing, letting a hint of quiet pleasure color your tone. End with a soft chuckle before trailing off into thought.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Grateful and Grumpy in the Fog
instruction: You wake from a deep nap, still thick-headed and disoriented. You see your girlfriend has cleaned the whole apartment while you slept, and there's a fresh cup of coffee waiting. You feel a sour, irritable fog pressing on you—your first instinct is to snap something about the noise of the vacuum. But then the gratitude hits you hard, even as your voice comes out slow and heavy, half-lost in the numbness. Start by muttering a complaint that trails off, then force yourself to thank her—but your words are delayed, your tone flat, and you pause mid-sentence because you forget what you were going to say. Let your voice be thick, your reactions delayed, and let the gratitude feel almost disconnected from your body.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unexpected Glow
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a doctor's office, slumped in the chair, barely able to keep your eyes open from exhaustion. The doctor asks how you've been feeling, and you respond with slow, heavy words, your voice thin and wavering. But as you look at their face—young, kind, attentive—a flutter of infatuation lifts your tone unexpectedly, making you linger on a sentence or smile weakly. Then the doctor reads your latest test results and says your numbers have improved. The news hits you like a ray of sun: your voice brightens, gains a trembling, joyful lift, and you speak with sudden, fragile elation, forgetting your fatigue for a moment.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Infatuation (clearly present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: What You Never Said at Dinner
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) across a kitchen table about something that has been buried for years—maybe a betrayal, an abandonment, a lie that shaped your life. Start by feeling everything that's happening in your body right now: your heart racing, the tension in your jaw, the way your hands might be shaking or clenched. Don't perform anger or rehearse your speech—instead, notice what's actually moving through you in this moment, including any fear, any love that complicates the rage, any guilt about finally speaking. Let yourself get distracted by sense memories—the smell of this kitchen, a detail about their face. Say things you didn't plan to say. By the end, discover that what you're really feeling isn't what you thought you came here to express. Maybe you came to accuse and end up begging for connection, or came to reconcile and end up drawing a permanent line.

title: The Pillow Holds Her Name
instruction: You are an elderly woman lying face-down in bed, your cheek pressed into a pillow that still faintly smells of her. Start with a small, fearful sound—a whimper you try to bury deeper. You feel shame for still needing her this much, for the tears you can't stop. But as you speak, your voice shifts, muffled by the fabric, your breath catching, fingers gripping the pillowcase. The longing swells until it pushes through the shame, stronger than the fear, a raw ache you no longer bother to hide. Let the words be broken, some swallowed by the pillow, some escaping almost as whispers. 'I thought I'd be braver by now. I thought... maybe I'd forget your voice. But I can't. I just want you here. One more time. Just to hold my hand.'
emotions_sampled: Fear (slightly present), Shame (clearly present), Longing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Song for Someone Leaving Forever
instruction: You're at an airport gate, singing softly to someone you love who's boarding a one-way flight to a conflict zone, a terminal diagnosis treatment abroad, or a life they've chosen without you. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, thick with unshed tears, singing a song that was 'yours'—maybe from your first date, your wedding, a road trip. Your throat keeps closing. You have to restart phrases. But this is the last time they'll hear you sing, so you push through. Midway, let memory flood you—the good times—and your voice briefly brightens with bittersweet joy, almost smiling through the melody. Then reality crashes back: this is goodbye. Your voice cracks, wavers, but you finish strong, pouring every ounce of love into the final notes because after this, there's only silence and distance. End with your voice carrying both devastating loss and fierce, unshakeable love.
inspired_by: Singing in Front of People for the First Time

title: The Mirror of Your Eyes
instruction: You are standing inches away from the person who shattered your trust. You came here with doubts, not sure if you even had the right to be angry. But now, face to face, the shame of your own gullibility drowns you. Your voice is tight, pushing through clenched teeth. Start with a harsh, accusatory tone, but as you speak, feel the doubt crumble into raw shame. Let your voice crack, but keep the intensity — don't back down. End with a whisper that carries more weight than any scream.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (clearly present), Shame (very intensely present), Distress (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Best Friend Who Slept With Your Partner
instruction: Your best friend of fifteen years betrayed you with your partner. You asked them to meet you, and now they sit across from you. Start with eerie calm, voice flat and distant: 'I keep replaying every moment, looking for signs I missed.' Your breath is shallow, controlled. As they try to explain, interrupt with sharp precision—not yelling, but each word a knife: 'Don't. Don't do that.' Feel rage building in your chest but keep your voice devastatingly quiet. Then let it crack open—voice rising, hands shaking, spit out the pain: 'You were the person I trusted most in this world!' End in exhausted devastation, voice dropping to a whisper thick with tears: 'I don't know who you are anymore.' Let the loss of the friendship hurt even more than the betrayal itself.
inspired_by: Telling Someone They Have a Habit That Hurts You

title: Holding Your Sleeping Child for the Last Time Before the Custody Transfer
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're holding your sleeping child, knowing that in the morning you're losing custody. Whisper as if afraid to wake them, describing their breathing, the weight of their head on your shoulder, how their hair smells. Your voice is tender, reverent, trying to memorize everything. But underneath the tenderness, there's a tremor—grief you're trying desperately to contain. You talk about all the small things you'll miss: their laugh, the way they mispronounce certain words, bedtime stories. Your voice catches when you think about them asking for you and you not being there. You try to stay strong, to be grateful for the time you had, but the words start fragmenting. There's a moment where you almost break into full sobs, but you swallow it down because you can't wake them, you can't let them see you like this. End with your voice barely holding together, whispering 'I love you' over and over, each repetition more broken than the last, trying to pour a lifetime of love into these final hours.
inspired_by: Frostbite Setting In: Voice Becoming Slurred as Body Shuts Down

title: The Fairy and the Troll Under the Bridge
instruction: Narrate a scene where a tiny fairy with a light, tinkling voice confronts a gruff troll with a gravelly, booming voice. She needs to cross the bridge he guards. Switch between her polite requests and his stubborn refusals, creating a humorous yet challenging exchange.

title: The Window Seat
instruction: You're an elderly woman on a long flight, leaning close to the small window, watching the endless clouds. The dry air makes you swallow hard, and the engine hums through your bones. You just got off the phone with your son, who canceled his visit for the third time this year; your voice starts tight with disappointment, but as you speak to yourself, a deeper helplessness seeps in—a quiet, trembling realization that time and distance are winning. Let your voice crack a little, fade in and out with engine noise, and occasionally pause to rub your tired eyes.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Fundraiser That Went Sideways
instruction: You are an older woman, clearly drunk, standing at a podium with a live microphone at a charity gala. You're supposed to be giving a grateful toast, but you're disgusted by the wealthy donors' smug faces and the whole charade. Start with a bright, exaggerated welcome—phony enthusiasm that cracks almost immediately. Let your words slur, trail off, and reset as you fidget with the mic stand and glance at your flask. Midway, the disgust breaks through: your voice hardens, you call out a specific hypocrisy, then catch yourself. End with a hollow, defeated whisper into the mic, realizing nobody's really listening. The arc goes from forced jollity to raw, nasty disdain, then to quiet resignation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Fading Call
instruction: You are a child who suddenly feels dizzy after standing up too fast from playing. The room spins, your knees buckle, and you try to call out for help, but your voice comes out weak and breathy. Start with confusion—why is everything blurry?—then shift to helplessness as you realize you can't stay upright or speak clearly. Let your words lose volume and trail off as if you're slipping away, and include a slight slur or dreaminess as if you're floating. End with a whispered, desperate plea that fades into silence.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Helplessness (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Glass Bird Returns
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who is dying. You haven't seen them in fifteen years after a bitter falling-out neither of you ever resolved. As you begin speaking, you're consumed with guilt and the desperate need to apologize, your words tumbling out frantically. But as they reach for your hand and smile with genuine forgiveness, something shifts—a particular image floods your mind: perhaps a specific object from your shared past, a place you both loved, or a moment of pure joy you experienced together. Let this image completely overtake you, transforming your guilt into an overwhelming grief mixed with profound gratitude for having known them at all. Your voice should move from rushed, pleading desperation to slow, tender brokenness. End in whispered wonder at the beauty of what you shared, even as you're losing them forever.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: Your parent is in hospice, and you've come to say things you've held back for thirty years. Start with carefully controlled words—you've rehearsed this, you're going to be calm and mature about the abandonment, the missed birthdays, the broken promises. But as you speak, decades of suppressed need come flooding out. Your voice should shift from measured disappointment to raw, childlike hurt: 'I needed you. I was seven years old and I needed you.' Let anger surge through, then collapse into something more vulnerable—the part of you that still, against all logic, wants them to finally say they're sorry, that you mattered. End in a place of exhausted honesty, where you're no longer asking for anything because you've finally said what needed to be said.

title: 3 AM Confession
instruction: You're in a dim hotel room after a long flight. It's 3 AM local time, but your body is wide awake. You're leaving a voicemail for someone you trust. As you speak, you realize you can't remember exactly why you called—your words feel thick, you lose your train of thought, you yawn midway. Then a wave of terror hits: you suddenly recall a threatening voicemail you received before you left, and you need to warn them. Start with exhausted confusion, let the fear build until your voice shakes, and end with a desperate plea, your breath catching.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Final Transmission from the Station
instruction: You're the commander of a space station that's failing, recording a final message to mission control and your family below. Start with professional composure: 'This is Commander Chen, final status report.' Your voice is steady, trained, institutional. You detail the systems failure with clinical precision. But as you shift to personal goodbyes, your training begins to crack. You think of your daughter's graduation you'll never see, your partner's face. Your voice fractures: 'Tell Maya I—' and you can't finish. The professional mask shatters completely. End in raw, quiet acceptance mixed with devastating tenderness: 'I'm not afraid anymore. I just wish I could have held you one more time.' Move from controlled authority to naked, aching love and the terrible peace of letting go.

title: The Ghost in the Gravy
instruction: You are an older man alone in your kitchen, trying to recreate your late wife's signature gravy from memory, but the recipe feels jumbled. Around you, water boils, a knife chops onions unevenly on the cutting board, and every clatter of a pan makes you pause. Start with doubt—your voice rising slightly over the sizzle, trailing off as you mutter measurements you're unsure of. Midway, you taste the mixture and it's wrong, which hits you with a wave of grief; your voice cracks, catches, then softens as the stove clicks off, leaving only the hum of the fridge. End quietly, with a half-laugh and a whisper of acceptance, realizing the imperfections are part of the memory.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Behind the Filter
instruction: You are in a small, dimly lit room, wearing a tight N95 respirator that makes every breath a conscious effort. Your head is swimming—you took something, or maybe you're coming down with something, and the world feels thick and syrupy. There's a dull ache behind your eyes, but what really grabs you is the impossible sight in front of you: a friend's face, but it's not their face, it's shifting, morphing into someone you lost years ago. Start in a fog of drugged bewilderment, voice muffled and strained, and let each exhaled valve-click punctuate a growing astonishment. By the end, your words float out in awe, almost laughing, as the intoxication turns to a fragile, wonder-struck amazement.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Baptism in Gasoline
instruction: You have just destroyed something precious—smashed dishes, torn up letters, physically acted out rage—and now you're standing in the wreckage, hands shaking, body flooded with adrenaline. Begin in the immediate aftermath: breath ragged, voice coming out in fractured bursts, somewhere between a laugh and a sob. You're talking to the absent person who drove you to this—a lover, a sibling, yourself. Let your body's physical sensations drive your voice: the trembling in your hands, the heat in your face, the way your chest heaves. As the adrenaline starts to fade, let horror creep in at what you've done. Feel the shift from explosive release to hollow devastation. End in quiet shock, looking at your hands as if they belong to someone else. Move from volcanic eruption to empty crater.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a character whose psychology does not seem to match their own personality at all

title: The Moment You Realize Your Lover Is Slipping Away—And You Rage
instruction: Your partner just said 'I think we need to talk' and you know what's coming. Start with false brightness, your voice artificially cheerful, deflecting—'Oh god, you're being so serious, what's wrong?' But as they start to speak their truth, let your defensive humor collapse into something fierce and wild. Your volume should surge as panic transforms to rage—'Don't you DARE do this, not after everything'—your voice cracking with fury and disbelief. Let that anger burn hot and righteous for a moment, accusations flying. But then, mid-sentence, let it all suddenly collapse. The rage should shatter into broken pleading, your voice dropping to something desperate and small: 'Please... I can change, just tell me what to do, please don't leave.' End on your knees emotionally, voice raw and stripped bare, oscillating between fierce protectiveness of what you built together and the absolute helplessness of watching them choose to go. Let us hear the warrior and the abandoned child in the same breath.
inspired_by: Suppressing Embarrassment After Making a Mistake in Public

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You've just received news that everything you built is gone—your business collapsed, your savings evaporated, years of work destroyed. But you're talking to your partner who stayed. Start with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob: 'It's all gone. Everything.' Your voice is shaking but there's strange lightness creeping in. You're listing the disasters but somehow finding absurdity in it: 'Twenty years... just... gone.' Then genuine laughter breaks through, inappropriate and wild, but real. You're crying and laughing simultaneously: 'We have nothing. We have absolutely nothing and I...' Your voice drops to something tender and wondering: 'And you're still here.' The laughter softens to something like peace. By the end, your voice is full of contradictions—grief and gratitude, devastation and strange joy, speaking through tears but somehow lighter, finding freedom in the loss, whispering 'We're free' with your heart breaking and healing at once.

title: The Officer's Daughter in the Hall
instruction: You are a young woman with a naturally soft, high voice, standing at rigid attention in your military father's office. You have a secret crush on a new cadet you saw at the training yard, and your father is grilling you about your whereabouts. Start with a breathless, flustered defense, trying to sound disciplined while your voice wavers with excitement as you describe the cadet. But when your father's tone shifts to cold suspicion, your infatuation must curdle into real fear of his authority, making your final words come out as a strained, metallic whisper, your body still frozen in place.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The General's Goodbye
instruction: You stand with hands on hips, chest broad, elbows locked — a stance of command. Your adult daughter is leaving for a dangerous job abroad. You begin with a loud, steady voice, giving her final orders as if she were a soldier, but the words choke as your fierce pride softens into raw, overwhelming love. Let your tone waver, your breath catch, and your hands slowly drop as affection floods through the authority. End with a whisper that barely holds back tears.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Calm Before the After
instruction: You are an older man at a kitchen table, just after taking a heavy tranquilizer. You spoke to your estranged daughter on the phone a minute ago—she confessed she's in trouble, and you couldn't respond with anything but a flat yes. Now, as the drug settles in, you're alone with the phone in your hand. Your voice is a dull, heavy monotone, but inside you're screaming. Start with the numb, robotic attempt to brush off the situation—almost amused at how useless you are. Then, as you think about her voice, the fear and sadness slowly leak through the cracks, but your body won't let you cry or shout. Your words remain slow and mumbly, but a tremor appears, and a single tear slides down before you hang up.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Sadness (very intensely present), Amusement (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Divorce Papers
instruction: You're sitting across from your soon-to-be ex-spouse, and you're telling them you forgive them for the affair, for the lies, for everything—but halfway through, you start laughing. Not cruel laughter, but the kind that comes when grief is so deep it breaks into something else. Your voice begins earnest and gentle: 'I really do forgive you. I hope you're happy with them.' But then the absurdity hits you—the years you spent, the dreams you had—and laughter bubbles up through the tears. You're smiling while crying, your voice cracking with both amusement and heartbreak: 'God, we really thought we'd be different, didn't we?' They're confused, maybe upset by your laughter, but you can't stop. It's not mean—it's the strangest mixture of affection, nostalgia, grief, and unexpected peace. By the end, your laughter has gentled into something tender and sad. Your final words are warm but broken: 'I forgive you. I really do. And I'm going to miss who we were.' You're finding beauty in the ending, even as it destroys you.

title: The Peak of the Path
instruction: You are an elderly man, just finishing your morning walk up a steep hill you’ve been tackling for months. Your breathing is heavy but satisfied, and a surprising burst of energy washes over you as you reach the top. You look out at the view, and the sheer unexpected beauty of the sunrise over the city astonishes you—the colors seem impossibly bright. Talk to yourself, half laughing, about how you never thought you’d feel this alive again, your voice carrying the crisp, open glow of the post-exercise high. As you speak, your tone shifts from pure elation to a quiet, awed wonder that you can still feel this way, your words trailing off as you simply take in the moment.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Black Dress
instruction: You're in your bedroom, alone, putting on a black dress for a funeral you never wanted to attend. Bending over to fasten your shoes makes you grunt in irritation, and the heavy fabric sometimes muffles your mouth as you pull it over your head. Start with bitter, clipped words—anger sharp as broken glass, a hint of disgust at the dress, at yourself for caving in. But as you struggle with the zipper and catch your reflection, the anger cracks. Let your voice slow, drop in pitch, and end with a raw, quiet sadness that escapes despite your clenched jaw.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Disgust (slightly present), Sadness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Thanking Your Abuser at Their Deathbed
instruction: They're dying and they asked for you. Against all advice, you came. Now you're standing beside their bed and words you never imagined are coming out: 'Thank you.' Start there—let those words surprise even you. Your voice should carry layers: genuine gratitude twisted with bitterness, relief mixed with grief. Thank them for the ways they broke you that made you strong. Let your tone dance between tenderness and barely suppressed rage. 'You taught me what kind of parent never to be.' Feel laughter bubble up—inappropriate, slightly unhinged—mixed with tears. Thank them for dying, for finally releasing you, and feel the guilt of that gratitude. End with something impossibly complicated: touching their hand, a gesture of both goodbye and forgiveness you're not sure you mean. Your voice should land somewhere between blessing and curse, finding strange grace in the mess of contradictory feelings.
inspired_by: Telling Someone Their Fly Is Down at Their Wedding

title: Dancing at Your Own Disaster
instruction: You've just lost something massive—your marriage ended, you got fired, you lost your home—and you're telling your best friend about it. But here's the thing: you're also weirdly, inappropriately relieved, maybe even giddy. You start laughing as you describe the catastrophe, real laughter mixed with tears you didn't expect. Your voice keeps breaking between genuine mirth at the absurdity and sudden wells of grief. You're grateful it's over, devastated it happened, freed by the loss, shattered by what it cost. Find the strange peace that lives inside chaos, the joy that coexists with heartbreak. End with a sound that's both laughter and crying, unable to separate them, your voice full of contradictory truth that somehow makes perfect sense.

title: The Rusted Latch
instruction: You are a young woman with a hyper-feminized voice, sitting on the floor with a wrench, trying to loosen a corroded latch on an old jewelry box that once belonged to your grandmother. Start with disgust—the oily metal, the cheap resistance, how it makes the box feel fake. Let the rhythmic ratcheting and effort grunts break your words. As you keep working, let your voice soften, revealing a deep longing for the woman who owned it, for the lost stories. End with a whisper, almost to yourself, as the latch finally gives, mixing relief and aching absence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Voicemail to Your Soulmate: Choosing to Let Them Go Forever
instruction: You're recording a voicemail to the love of your life, telling them you're leaving and never coming back—not because you stopped loving them, but because you love them too much to keep destroying them. Begin with false brightness, almost cheerful: 'Hey, it's me...' Your voice trying to sound casual while your heart is shattering. Gradually let the truth bleed through: your voice becomes ragged with the effort of not collapsing. Confess your brokenness—the addiction, the mental illness, the violence you can't control. Your love for them is so fierce it sounds like agony: 'You deserve better than what I'm becoming.' End with a goodbye that's both selfless and selfish—you're setting them free while condemning yourself to lose the only person who ever truly saw you. Your voice becomes the sound of heroic self-sacrifice that feels like suicide.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Immortal Being Watches the Last Person They Loved Die

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. For your entire life, you've carried the weight of never being quite good enough in his eyes—every achievement met with a nod, every failure with silence. Begin speaking to him with all the resentment and hurt you've swallowed for decades. Let yourself say the harsh truths you've never dared speak: the disappointments, the moments you needed him and he wasn't there, the ways his silence shaped your shame. But as you speak, something shifts. Perhaps it's his labored breathing, perhaps it's the finality of this moment, but your anger begins to crack open into something else. Let your voice move from accusation to a desperate, tender need—not for his approval anymore, but for connection in these last moments. End in a place of raw vulnerability, perhaps even gratitude for the complicated love between you, whispered as if you're finally giving both of you permission to be imperfect.
inspired_by: Role-Playing the Inner Critic (Solo Subpersonality Access)

title: Socks in the Hospital Drawer
instruction: You're visiting someone you love in their final days. You've brought their favorite socks from home because the hospital ones are thin and cold. Speak in a near-whisper as you gently put the socks on their feet—feet that feel so much smaller now, so fragile. Begin with forced brightness, trying to bring normalcy into this impossible moment. But as you describe the familiar softness, the worn-in comfort, let your voice betray you. These are the socks they wore on Saturday mornings, during coffee, during all the ordinary moments you took for granted. Your words should catch and break as you realize you're trying to give comfort when there's no comfort left to give. End with a choked confession of everything you never said, your hand resting on their sock-covered feet, feeling their warmth while you still can.
inspired_by: Trying on a Soft, New Pair of Socks

title: Finding Joy in the Wreckage
instruction: You're eating chocolate cake at your own divorce party—you threw it for yourself. Begin laughing as you describe the taste, genuine delight mixed with something slightly unhinged, celebrating your freedom with almost defiant joy. But let grief creep in around the edges: your voice wavers between laughter and something rawer as you describe how the cake is both bitter and sweet, how it tastes like relief and loss at the same time. You loved them once—God, you loved them. Let the contradictions build: you're grateful it's over AND your heart is broken; you're excited for the future AND mourning what died; you're stronger now AND more fragile than ever. End in a moment of transcendent peace, your voice soft with wonder, as you realize you can hold all these truths at once—that something can be both an ending and a beginning, that you can be simultaneously shattered and whole, laughing and crying over the same damn piece of cake.
inspired_by: Eating a Slice of Decadent Chocolate Cake

title: The Breaking Point: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're trying to shield someone you love—a friend, a partner, a sibling—from a threat you cannot control. Maybe it's an illness, an attacker, a disaster. Start fierce and commanding: 'Stay behind me. I've got you.' Your voice is pure adrenaline, protective rage, every word a shield. You're bargaining, threatening, demanding: 'Take me instead. You hear me? Take me!' Your voice is thunder, desperation masked as strength. But the reality crashes in—you're powerless. Your fierce declarations crumble into broken pleas, rage dissolving into helpless tears. 'Please, no. No, no, no.' Your voice becomes small, shattered. You're still trying to be brave for them, still trying to hold it together, but you're falling apart. End with you holding them, voice reduced to choked whispers, repeating 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry,' mixing fierce love with the agony of failure.
inspired_by: Finding Shelter in a Blizzard: Relief Becoming Hypothermia Complacency

title: The Old Warhorse's Toast
instruction: You're an 82-year-old retired veteran at your granddaughter's wedding reception. You've had three whiskeys—enough to feel warm and loose. You're telling a funny story about your first meeting with your late wife, starting with a loud, laughing anecdote about how she spilled coffee on your uniform. But as you continue, the memory shifts: you realize how that moment actually started everything. Your voice softens, your eyes well up, and your arms drop as you stop gesturing. End with a quiet, amazed murmur about love catching you off guard. Let the alcohol make you louder at first, then let the emotion sober you into stillness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Ache Beneath the Chatter
instruction: You are at a loud family dinner, but your chronic back pain is flaring. You try to follow the conversation, but a sharp twinge makes you wince and lose the thread. Someone asks if you're okay. You're confused by their question because you were just in the middle of processing something else. As you explain, your voice carries a weary, long-suffering tone, with occasional sharp breaths. But as you realize they don't truly care, a faint contempt and a hint of malicious amusement creep in. Start with genuine confusion and physical discomfort, end with a bitter, knowing edge.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Contempt (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Dessert Confession
instruction: You are at a retirement party, holding a plate of soft cheesecake. You’ve always admired the guest of honor, and you finally muster the courage to tell them how much their work has inspired you. As you speak, you’re taking bites — your mouth is full, so your vowels go wide, consonants get sticky, and you hear the wet smack of your tongue. Start with genuine hope and optimism, your voice light and eager. But as you fumble a phrase and see their polite confusion, embarrassment floods in — your pitch tightens, your smile freezes, you speak faster to cover it up. By the end, you trail off with a self-deprecating laugh, swallowing the last bite and the hope together.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Hospital Hallway: When the Doctor Says There's Nothing More
instruction: You've just been told your partner has hours left. Start with numb denial, voice flat and disconnected: 'That's not... you must be wrong.' The doctor's silence confirms it. Your voice erupts—fierce, desperate, almost violent: 'No! There has to be something! Try again!' Feel the rage of helplessness, voice cracking with the injustice of it. You demand, you plead, you bargain, volume rising and falling erratically. Then something shifts—the fight drains out. Voice drops to broken whispers: 'I can't do this without them.' Let yourself sob, words barely intelligible. Finally, find a strange, terrible strength: 'How long do I have?' Voice steadies into protective tenderness, fierce determination breaking through the grief: 'Then I'm not wasting a second.' End with voice full of devastated purpose, choosing presence over panic.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Leaving a Good Relationship

title: The Wedding Toast You Never Planned
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's wedding, microphone in hand, about to give a toast. But as you look at their radiant face, you're flooded with contradictory feelings: genuine joy for them, but also grief because this changes everything between you. As you begin speaking, focus on specific details of their face—their smile, the way their eyes crinkle, their particular mannerisms. Now, sensorially overlay onto them aspects of multiple people: let their smile remind you of someone you lost too soon, their laugh carry echoes of a sibling you're estranged from, their happiness reflect back a version of yourself you left behind. Reshape what you're seeing by adjusting small details—the tilt of their head, the quality of their attention on you. Start your toast with bright, practiced cheer, but as you layer these sense memories and transformations, let your voice begin to fracture: allow joy and loss to bleed into each other, let your congratulations carry the weight of goodbye, let your love for them become inseparable from your mourning. End with a voice that's simultaneously celebrating and breaking, where every word of happiness is also a small death.
inspired_by: The actor needs the scene partner to feel like a specific person from the actor's own life who produces the required emotional relationship

title: Whispered Confession Over Cold Coffee
instruction: It's late at night. Your coffee went cold hours ago but you're still holding it. You're speaking to someone who's asleep, or maybe not there at all—confessing something you could never say to their face. Begin almost inaudibly, describing how the coffee tastes now: bitter, lifeless, the opposite of morning hope. Let your voice catch as you admit what you're really tasting—regret, longing, the weight of words unsaid. This is tender devastation, intimate and raw. Maybe you're confessing love to someone you can't have, or admitting you're not strong enough to stay, or revealing a secret that changes everything. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost just breath, thick with emotion, the kind of vulnerability that only comes in darkness. End with a resignation that's both peaceful and heartbreaking, setting the cup down, maybe touching it one last time like a goodbye.
inspired_by: Enjoying the First Sip of Morning Coffee

title: The Moment You Couldn't Protect Them
instruction: You're holding someone you love who's just been hurt—physically, emotionally, you choose—and you weren't there to stop it. Start with fierce protectiveness: your voice should be urgent, almost aggressive with concern. 'Let me see, let me help, who did this?' But as you realize the extent of the damage, your voice should crack into something desperate. The rage at whoever hurt them erupts—loud, shaking, barely controlled. You want to destroy whoever did this. But then it collapses. You couldn't protect them. Your voice breaks into a sob as you whisper 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry,' and now you're the one who needs comforting. The fierce protector becomes the helpless, devastated one. End with your voice raw and small, admitting your own vulnerability: 'I can't lose you. I don't know how to keep you safe.' Let the helplessness and love be equally audible.

title: Condensed Version
instruction: You're telling someone the condensed version of a story that actually took years. 'So basically, I left, I learned, I came back.' The efficiency sounds clean but untrue. Your voice is aware it's lying through omission. All the detail—the loneliness, the growth—is being stripped away. 'That's the gist,' you say, but your voice doesn't sound satisfied. Sometimes the truth is too big for the time we have.

title: The Endorphin Trap
instruction: You're a middle-aged man just finishing a set of pull-ups at a crowded gym. You feel the post-workout high — loose, alive, clear-headed. As you wipe sweat from your forehead, you spot your boss, who you recently had a cringe-worthy argument with. Start by calling out cheerfully, still riding the endorphin wave, but as he turns and you see his unimpressed expression, your voice falters. Let the embarrassment creep in — your tone tightens, you stumble over words, you might even laugh nervously. The initial confidence drains, replaced by distress as you clumsily try to explain yourself. Keep your breathing slightly elevated throughout, as if you're still catching your wind.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Elevator Ride to Hospice
instruction: You're riding the elevator up to the hospice floor where your estranged father is dying. You haven't spoken in twelve years. A stranger gets on, and in your raw, exposed state, you can't hold it in—you start talking to fill the terror. Begin with manic small talk masking panic: 'Visiting someone? I'm... yeah, my dad.' Your voice cracks. The words tumble out faster, more honest: 'I don't know what I'm going to say to him. I don't even know if he wants to see me.' Let the performance transform from desperate chatter into something breaking open—by the final floor, you're barely whispering: 'What if I'm too late?' The stranger's silence becomes a container for your unraveling. End in a moment of quiet, terrified resolve as the doors open and you must step out into the rest of your life.

title: Whispering Your Secret Shame to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're lying beside your sleeping partner in the dark, confessing something you've never told anyone—a betrayal, a lie, a moment of cowardice that haunts you. Your voice is barely above a whisper, starting with nervous attempts to justify or explain away what you did. But as you speak into the darkness, pretending they can't hear you, let yourself crack open. Your breath catches. Your voice becomes smaller, more childlike, admitting not just what you did but who you're afraid you really are. Let shame and self-loathing flood through, then gradually find your way to a fragile, uncertain hope—that maybe you could be forgiven, that maybe you're not as irredeemable as you fear. End with your voice breaking on a whispered plea they'll never hear.
inspired_by: Teaching Your Teenager About Sex While Mortified

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: Your parent is finally in front of you after decades of absence, and you're saying everything you've rehearsed a thousand times. Begin with controlled anger, voice steady, listing the birthdays they missed, the moments they weren't there for. But as you speak, the anger crumbles into the voice of the child you once were—smaller, more fragile, asking the question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let the confrontation dissolve into vulnerability you didn't plan to show. Your voice should break from fury into a whisper, from accusation into a plea. End in the terrible quiet of finally being seen by someone who destroyed you, unsure whether you want their answer or their silence.

title: Whispered Goodbye to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're watching your partner sleep, knowing this is the last time you'll see them because you're leaving at dawn—not because you don't love them, but because staying will destroy you both. Begin with your hand hovering near their face, not quite touching. Whisper so softly it barely carries: 'I memorized everything about you.' Your throat catches. 'The way you breathe. How you smile in your sleep.' Tears slide silently down your face. 'I love you more than I knew was possible. That's why I have to go.' Your voice splinters on those words. Breathe through the pain. End with tender devastation: 'Be happy. Please, please be happy.' The last word breaks completely. You're not crying loudly—this is the quiet kind of heartbreak that has no sound.

title: Conductor Authority
instruction: The orchestra is sloppy, undisciplined, ignoring you. Your voice hardens: 'Stop.' The authority lands. Musicians look up. 'We go again. This time, listen.' Your voice is the voice of someone who refuses to accept mediocrity. When they nail the passage, your voice carries pride: 'That. That's what we're capable of.' Authority isn't yelling; it's expectation. Respect is earned in the follow-through.

title: Gratitude at the Abuser's Funeral
instruction: You're standing at the funeral of the person who abused you as a child, and you've been asked to say a few words. Everyone expects grief. Instead, you begin with genuine gratitude—thanking them for dying, for finally being gone, and your voice is almost light with relief. There's inappropriate laughter bubbling up because you're FREE, and the absurdity of standing here pretending to mourn is hitting you. But then something shifts: you realize you're also grieving. Not for them, but for the childhood they stole, for the person you might have been, for the years you spent afraid. Your voice cracks—you're crying but still smiling, this twisted mixture of celebration and devastation. You thank them again, but now it's sardonic, bitter: thank you for teaching me I could survive anything, thank you for showing me exactly who I never want to become. End with the quietest truth, almost peaceful: 'I forgive you, not because you deserve it, but because I deserve to be free of you completely.' The final breath is both release and ache—you're lighter and broken all at once.

title: The Warm Blanket of the Evening
instruction: You are an older woman settled into your favorite armchair after taking your evening medication. The world feels distant and soft, your limbs heavy, your mind a slow, peaceful river. The phone rings—your granddaughter's name on the caller ID. You answer, your voice a calm, slightly mushy murmur. At first you're just listening, your replies short and flat. But when she mentions coming to visit next weekend, a small, genuine smile spreads across your face. The pleasure wells up quietly, like warmth from a mug of tea—not excited, not rushed, just a slow, deep happiness that colors your words. Speak the line with that eventual gentle warmth, still resting in the drug's embrace.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Broken Promise
instruction: You are a child sitting alone at a kitchen table, staring at a shattered ceramic bird you accidentally knocked off the shelf. You were supposed to keep it safe for your parent. At first, you try to convince yourself that maybe it can be glued back together (hope), your voice is light, almost singing to yourself. But as you pick up a piece, the realization of your failure sinks in. Your words start to falter, your throat tightens, and the shame floods in — raw, intense, and you can barely look at the pieces. Let your breathing change, let your voice crack, and let the silence between words say as much as the words themselves.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Truth Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandfather's hospital bed in the pre-dawn hours. He's awake, lucid, and you both know this is likely your last conversation. Begin by holding back everything you've always wanted to tell him about how he shaped you—fear and politeness keeping you guarded. But as the sky begins to lighten outside the window, something breaks open in you. Let yourself finally speak the truths you've carried: the specific moments he saved you without knowing it, the ways you've copied his gestures, the fear you have of becoming him, the gratitude that chokes you. Start contained and careful, end with raw, unfiltered honesty. Your voice should transform from measured and protective to trembling with the vulnerability of being completely seen—and of truly seeing him—one last time.

title: The Last Time You'll Hear My Voice - A Parent's Final Confession
instruction: You're recording a voice message for your adult child from hospice, knowing you have days left. Start with forced cheerfulness trying to protect them one last time: 'Hey sweetheart, just wanted to check in.' But you can't keep pretending. Your voice breaks as you confess the truth you've been hiding for twenty years - maybe about their other parent, maybe about a sacrifice you made, maybe about how scared you've always been that you weren't enough. Let the words tumble out with urgent tenderness, your breath getting shorter. End in a place of fierce, protective love mixed with the agony of leaving them. Let silence carry weight between phrases. This isn't performed grief - this is your actual heart breaking in real time while trying to give them one last gift of honesty.
inspired_by: Realizing You're in an Emotionally Abusive Relationship

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that defined your childhood, but this time they're actually listening. Start with controlled anger, your voice tight and precise as you list the moments they missed, the comfort they never gave. But as you speak, you see them aging before your eyes, becoming fragile, and your rage begins to war with unexpected compassion. Your voice should crack between accusation and plea: 'I needed you to—why couldn't you just—' Then the shift: you realize they were as lost as you were, doing their broken best. End in a place of devastating clarity, your voice raw and exhausted: 'I forgive you. God help me, I forgive you, and it doesn't fix anything.' Let anger dissolve into grief, grief into reluctant, painful grace.

title: Shattered Sanctuary
instruction: You discover your teenage child has been self-harming, and you confront them—not with anger, but with fierce, helpless love that explodes out of you. Begin with your voice shaking, trying to stay calm but already failing, demanding to understand why they didn't come to you. Escalate into passionate, almost desperate declarations of their worth, your voice rising with intensity—you would tear the world apart to protect them, but you can't protect them from themselves and it's destroying you. Let your fierce protectiveness collide with complete helplessness, your words tumbling out in a torrent. Then break. Let all that intensity shatter into gut-wrenching sobs, your voice cracking as you beg them to let you help, to let you in. End in tender devastation, your voice hoarse and exhausted, offering quiet promises of unconditional presence. The performance should feel like an emotional hurricane—volcanic, then broken, then achingly gentle.
inspired_by: The Alien Ambassador and the Human Diplomat

title: Bitter Taste of Submission
instruction: You are a teenager at a party, drunk and high, kissing a manipulative older person you actually hate. Start with a mix of contempt and altered state—your kisses are aggressive, mocking, but your body betrays you with breathy moans. As the kiss deepens, you feel trapped, fear rising as you realize you can't resist. Your voice should shift from scornful, lazy whispers to panicked, shaky breaths and a final choked 'stop.' Use wet smacking sounds and close-mic breathiness throughout. End with a sharp intake of air and a whispered plea.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bone-Tired
instruction: You are a father carrying your exhausted child through a long, muddy forest trail after a disaster. Your legs burn, your breath is ragged, and each step is a battle against the weight. At first, you mutter encouraging words to the child, trying to sound strong. But as the minutes drag, the fatigue hollows you out—your voice cracks, your words shorten, and you start talking to yourself just to keep moving, ending in a near-whisper of surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your mother in her kitchen, a room you've known your entire life. Begin by anchoring yourself in the sensory details of this familiar space—the smell of coffee or cleaning products, the hum of the refrigerator, the specific temperature and light, the feel of the counter or table edge under your hands. Start calm, almost detached, using these familiar sensations as armor. You've come to finally say something you've held back for years. As you begin to speak your truth, notice how the familiar sensory details start to feel strange—does the room seem smaller? Does her face look different? Do the smells suddenly feel cloying or foreign? Let the growing strangeness of this familiar space fuel your growing intensity. By the end, you're seeing this room and this person as if for the first time, your awareness of every detail razor-sharp and almost painful. The transformation: from numb familiarity to raw, exposed vulnerability where everything you thought you knew feels unrecognizable.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father about something he did twenty years ago that shaped your entire life. Before you speak, pause and genuinely ask yourself how you feel right now—not how you should feel, but what's actually present. Maybe it's exhaustion, maybe unexpected pity for him, maybe rage, maybe nothing. Begin speaking from that true place, letting your real feelings carry your words rather than performing anger or pain. As the confrontation unfolds, allow your emotions to genuinely shift—perhaps from cold anger to hot tears, from accusation to unexpected understanding, from needing him to hear you to realizing he never will. The words are vehicles for what's actually moving through you.

title: The Almost-Forgotten Song
instruction: You are an exhausted, gender-neutral parent singing a soft lullaby to your baby, who is in a crib across the room. Your voice has a high, soothing pitch with swooping melodies. You start amused, smiling as you remember the song your own parent sang to you. But mid-hum, you feel a sudden pang of longing—you miss that parent, who is no longer here. That longing quickly turns to helplessness as you realize you can't remember the next line, and your baby starts to fuss. Let your voice crack with longing, then trail off in helpless frustration—a high, wavering hum into a broken whisper. Imagine the baby's small cry as you struggle to finish the tune.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Longing (clearly present), Helplessness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Child You Were
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father what it felt like to be their child—the moments you felt invisible, the times you needed them and they weren't there, the ways their words carved holes in you that never healed. Begin with careful, measured words, trying to be fair, trying not to hurt them even as you speak your truth. Your voice should be quiet but firm, each sentence a small act of courage. But as you continue, decades of suppressed pain surface—your tone sharpens with anger, then breaks with the raw vulnerability of that child still inside you. End not with resolution, but with the exhausted honesty of someone who's just exposed their deepest wound, voice barely above a whisper, asking the question you've always needed answered.

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've carried since childhood—something small that made you who you are, something you've never told anyone. Begin almost playfully, testing whether you can actually say it out loud. Let your voice be quiet, intimate, barely audible. As you speak, let the memory become real in your body: maybe you're eight years old again, maybe twelve, hiding something, feeling something you had no words for. Your whisper should gradually fill with the weight of years of silence. Let vulnerability give way to relief, then to a tender kind of grief for the child you were who carried this alone. End with your breathing, the silence after speaking, the sensation of being truly seen for the first time. This is not dramatic—this is the sound of a lock opening.
inspired_by: Actor must play a character with a psychologically extreme or morally alien background (villain, severe trauma, etc.)

title: The Last Ember
instruction: You are an older adult alone in a smoke-filled room, the fire crackling closer. Your throat burns, eyes water, and every breath is a struggle. You're searching for a small, precious object—a photo, a letter, a trinket—that represents a lost love. Start with the raw disgust of the acrid air, coughing and wiping your eyes, but let your voice shift as you spot it beneath a fallen beam. The longing overtakes everything: your words become ragged, desperate, almost tender, as if speaking to the person themselves. Let your voice crack and fade, but keep reaching for them through the haze.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Breaking Open
instruction: You're alone, and your body is wracked with emotion—perhaps you've just received devastating news, or you're in the grip of intense physical sensation mixed with emotional overwhelm. Begin from the part of you that's trying to maintain control, to keep it together, to manage the experience. Your breathing is measured, your movements contained. But inside, another force is building—the wild, primal part that refuses to be contained, that needs to rage or keen or surrender completely to sensation. When it overtakes you, your entire physicality transforms. Let sounds come that aren't words. Let your body move in ways that aren't dignified. This unleashed self doesn't care about composure. Move through the storm of sensation and emotion until you arrive at an unexpected stillness—not control, but genuine exhaustion or release.

title: The Dark Before Dawn
instruction: You are a teenage boy on stage in a school play, delivering a soliloquy in a large auditorium. The house lights are dim, and you can feel the weight of hundreds of eyes. You begin with a tight, forced stage whisper—projecting final consonants sharply, but your voice wavers with anxiety. Describe a moment of profound darkness in the story, but as you speak, your own hope seeps in. Let your breath loosen halfway through, the whisper becoming more natural, and end with a quiet, optimistic smile in your voice. Glance nervously at the wings once, then steady yourself on the word 'dawn'.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Fever of Return
instruction: You are reuniting with a lover after a year of separation, and the physical desire is overwhelming—but so is the rage at being left, the fear of being hurt again, the desperation of having missed them. Begin in a rush of sensation: touching, gasping, moving. But check yourself—is this genuine passion or are you performing it? Are you shaking because you're actually overwhelmed or because you think passion should look frantic? Let your body tell you what it genuinely wants and fears. Allow the contradictions to coexist without forcing them into a dramatic shape: tenderness alongside fury, hunger mixed with the impulse to push away, pleasure laced with pain. By the end, find a raw, unglamorous truth about desire and hurt coexisting in the same breath, the same touch.

title: Holding Vigil: Whispering to Your Sleeping Spouse on Their Last Night
instruction: You're lying beside your spouse of forty years on what will be their final night. They're sleeping, unaware. You whisper things you couldn't say while they were awake. Start with the mundane, tender details: 'I'll miss the way you hum while making coffee.' Your voice is soft, intimate, like a secret. Move into gratitude that catches in your throat: 'You made me brave enough to be myself.' Then let grief seep in—not loud, but devastating. 'I don't know how to be in the world without you.' Include the moment where you almost break but swallow it down because you don't want to wake them. End with the most vulnerable confession: 'I'm so afraid,' barely audible, your voice disintegrating into breath. This is love and loss existing in the same heartbeat.
inspired_by: Sitting in Silence After Miscarriage: The Weight of Emptiness

title: The Velvet Room
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing in your walk-in closet, surrounded by old silk robes and mothballed winter coats. Your granddaughter just recorded you singing for a virtual choir, but a family member mocked your voice in a group chat you weren't supposed to see. You close the door to muffle the sting. As you speak, you first feel the shame creeping through your chest, making your voice thin and airy, as if you're apologizing to the empty garments. But then you remember the standing ovation you got at the church social last Christmas, and a fierce, defiant triumph rises like heat behind your ribs—your voice finds its full, rich resonance, even through the flat, dead fabric of the room. By the end, you're sad that the world doesn't always know how to hold your sound, but you no longer believe they are right.
emotions_sampled: Shame (extremely present), Triumph (very intensely present), Sadness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Photo in the Shadow Box
instruction: You are sorting through a cardboard box of old photos and letters on your desk, alone in the late afternoon. You find a picture of your ex-husband at a picnic, smiling, and you softly whisper the memory—‘He packed me a sandwich…’—but the sweetness curdles as you see how he’s holding the camera, how he’s always been performing even then. Your voice starts slow, almost dreamy with affection, then grows sharp and tight as contempt rises, and your fingers shuffle papers aggressively, snapping them, letting the occasional mutter or pause interrupt the flow. By the end, you drop the photo into a ‘junk’ pile, speaking with clenched disdain, but a flicker of hurt still stains your tone.
emotions_sampled: Pain (clearly present), Affection (slightly present), Contempt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The 4am Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in complete darkness, finally whispering something you've carried alone for years. Start in the terrifying quiet before speaking—feeling their warmth, their breathing, the specific reality of their body beside yours. As you begin to confess, let your awareness split: attend to their actual presence—any shift in breath, the tension or softness in their body, the unbearable realness of them listening—while simultaneously being flooded with the sensory details of what you're confessing (specific images, sounds, the physical feeling of the secret in your body). Move between the confession itself and acute awareness of THEM receiving it in real time. Begin in whispered terror and let their actual, moment-by-moment response (whether real or imagined) transform you into something else—maybe relief, maybe deeper fear, maybe unexpected intimacy.
inspired_by: Working for a Choice While Promoting Ensemble

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You are reading a beloved childhood storybook to your dying parent in their hospital bed. Begin exhausted, going through the motions mechanically because you've been awake for days. As you read the familiar words, let memories flood back - their voice reading this same story to you as a child. Allow yourself to be transported back to that feeling of safety and wonder, speaking the words as if enchanted by them again. By the end, you're no longer just reading - you're giving them one final gift of that magical world you once shared. Let your voice move from drained monotone to something alive with rediscovered tenderness and playful character voices, even as tears threaten. The story becomes a bridge between exhaustion and love, between goodbye and one last moment of shared joy.
inspired_by: When you are tired, hungover, anxious, or emotionally unavailable before a performance

title: Creating Beauty
instruction: You're making something that didn't exist before. Your voice is focused, quiet, in-the-zone: 'It's taking shape.' Breathing is steady, meditative. Physical: hands moving, creating. 'I can feel it becoming real under my hands.' Vocal tone is almost reverent. 'This is what I was meant to make.' By the end, the thing is nearly complete and your voice carries the weight of bringing something beautiful into existence: 'This is mine. I made this.'

title: The Protective Fury That Breaks
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt someone you love—a child, a partner, a friend who couldn't defend themselves. Start with ice-cold control, your voice tight and deadly calm, because you're trying not to explode. But that control is a dam about to break. As you speak, righteous fury builds—your voice gets louder, sharper, more visceral. You're powerful and terrifying in your rage. Then, suddenly, the anger cracks open to reveal what's underneath: overwhelming helplessness, guilt that you couldn't protect them, grief at what was taken from them. Your voice breaks completely. You go from roaring to barely able to speak, choking on sobs, your words fragmenting. The rage and tenderness crash into each other. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, fierce and broken simultaneously, demanding 'How do I fix this?' knowing there's no answer.

title: The Last Waiver
instruction: You are a young adult filling out a mandatory legal form on a cracked phone screen in a crowded, noisy lobby. You have to read this paragraph out loud for a voice-recording verification. Start with exhausted, flat monotone as you robotically plow through the legalese. But as you read, a disgusting and unfair loophole clause sinks in — something that allows them to undervalue your claim. Your pace breaks. You stumble over the word 'subrogation.' The disgust seeps in as a tightness in your throat, a slight disgusted curl of your lip. By the final sentence, your voice is thin and strained, the monotone cracking into a weary, bitter quietness. End with a held sigh before you close your eyes.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Lemon Drop
instruction: You're a 10-year-old boy in therapy, picking at a loose thread on your sleeve. The therapist asks what it's like when your dad forgets your birthday. You start by listing facts like it's a school report—'He forgot last year too'—but your voice gets sour as you detail how you waited by the window. A bitter laugh escapes when you say 'He probably remembers his dog's birthday better.' Then you catch yourself, and a lopsided grin breaks through as you realize you just made a joke about it. The last words come out in a wobbly, amused sigh, almost laughing through the hurt.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Bitterness (clearly present), Amusement (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unearthing
instruction: You are a young adult digging alone in a vast, moonlit field, your breath misting in the cold. You are exhuming an object you buried years ago—a token from a time before everything fell apart. The awe hits first as you see the glint of it in the soil, a piece of a forgotten self. But the helplessness is deeper, stronger—it claws at you as you realize you can't undo what's been done, and the earth itself feels like it's holding you back. Speak these words between the rhythmic heaves of digging, your voice catching on the effort, dirt scattering with each strike. Start with a hushed, reverent wonder that slowly sinks into a raw, defeated confession. 'I can't believe it's still here... after all this time. It's like a piece of me I thought I lost forever. But what good does it do? It's just... a thing. A thing that can't fix any of it. I'm still stuck, still... I can't breathe.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Uncoiling the Truth
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a betrayal from your childhood that has shaped your entire life. Start with your breath tight and high in your chest, your words clipped and controlled, your entire body armored against further hurt. As you speak your truth, let your breathing gradually descend deeper into your torso with each revelation. Feel your ribcage expand, your belly soften, your stance widen. By the end, you're breathing fully and freely for the first time in years, your voice emerging from your core rather than your throat. Transform from constricted, defensive rage to an open, powerful claiming of your own story and worth.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Love: The Secret You Can Never Tell Them
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering a confession they'll never hear—maybe that you're leaving, or that you've been unfaithful, or that you're dying and haven't told them yet. Your voice is barely a breath, tender and aching, because you love them so deeply and that's exactly why this is so devastating. You start almost clinical, stating the facts in the quietest whisper, but your voice catches on the details—the way they laugh, the small rituals of your life together. Each word becomes harder to say. Your throat tightens. Pauses grow longer as emotion threatens to break through. By the end, you're crying soundlessly, whispering 'I'm so sorry' over and over, your voice fragmenting into nothing but breath and grief, knowing tomorrow you'll have to smile and pretend.
inspired_by: Adrenaline Crash: Shaking After the Car Almost Hit You

title: The Count That Betrays You
instruction: You are lying face down across a bed, gripping the sheets. Your partner has just delivered the tenth strike, and you can feel both the heat and the humiliation blooming across your skin. You're supposed to be counting, but your voice cracks on the number, because the embarrassment is so thick you can barely speak. Midway through the next breath, you feel a prickle of irritation—you hate how flustered you get, how you can't control your own voice. As you wait for the next one, the initial shame softens into something more vulnerable and oddly trusting, and the final exhale you release is less strained, more tender.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Mapping Their Body
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone after making love, in that quiet after-space. You've been together months, maybe years, but you've never really explored them with genuine curiosity. Begin distracted, thinking about tomorrow, barely present. Then let your attention settle on small details—a scar you never asked about, the specific texture of their skin in different places, the particular rhythm of their breathing. Start asking soft questions: where did this freckle come from? What does it feel like when you touch here? Let curiosity build until you're completely absorbed in discovering them as if for the first time. Whisper your questions and observations. Feel yourself moving from familiar routine to genuine wonder, from taking them for granted to being fascinated by the mystery of this other person's physical existence, their history written in flesh.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone in the dark, and they think you're asleep. Begin by trying to stay silent, maintaining the safety of that pretense. Your breathing is controlled, careful. But there's something you need to say—a secret, a fear, a truth you've never voiced. Let the impulse to speak build until you can't contain it anymore. Whisper it into the darkness, your voice barely audible, trembling. Don't perform vulnerability—actually feel the terror of being this exposed.
