Notice if your voice wants to crack, or speed up, or nearly disappear. Let the words come in fragments if that's what happens. End with the unbearable intimacy of having said it aloud, waiting in the silence for a response that may or may not come.
inspired_by: An actor notices they have developed mannerisms and behavioral dependencies

title: The Trembling Truth
instruction: You are an older woman with Parkinson's, sitting at a kitchen table across from a relative who just said something that confuses you deeply. Your hands shake, your voice is soft and wobbly, and you struggle to get the words out. At first, you are lost in confusion, trying to piece together what they meant—your sentences trail off, you repeat yourself, you stare at the table. But as you sense they are about to dismiss you, bitterness creeps in, sharpening your tone despite the tremor. Let your voice start fragile and searching, then harden with resentful clarity, even as it cracks. Speak roughly 60 words, letting your body’s distractions—a deep breath, a frustrated tap on the chair arm, a pause to swallow—interrupt you naturally.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Mile Home
instruction: You're a teenager sitting in the back of a bus as your hometown slowly passes by. You've just gotten word they're moving away for good in the morning. The engine drones, and every familiar building feels cruel. Start by murmuring to yourself, pressing your forehead against the glass to steady the vibration. As the bus turns a corner, let your quiet longing crack open into a raw, desperate whisper — a goodbye to the street you'll never see again.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Mumble Confusion
instruction: You're a patient with early-onset dementia trying to explain something important to your doctor, but the words keep slipping away. You start coherent: 'I wanted to talk about...' Then you mumble, losing the thread: 'The thing is... with the... you know...' You're grasping for words that won't come. You mumble because you're confused, trying to make sense of your own thoughts. The doctor waits. You try again, voice becoming slightly panicked: 'I know what I want to say but the words...' More mumbling. The doctor places a hand on your arm: 'It's okay. Tell me what you remember.' You relax slightly, and the mumbling becomes gentler, less panicked — still lost, but less alone. By the end, your mumble has become a whisper of resignation.

title: The Weight of Love
instruction: You are an older woman lying on the living room floor, your large, heavy dog has just flopped onto your chest and pinned you down. You can barely breathe—every word is squeezed out on a forced exhale, short and gasping. Start with deep contentment: you love this cozy weight, the warmth, the closeness. Then, as you notice the silly, lazy expression on your dog’s face, interest sparks—you study it, amused. By the end, the feeling swells into pure infatuation, giddy and breathless as you murmur to your dog. Let your voice be tight, strained, but full of joy—micro-pauses as you struggle for air, a laugh that comes out as a wheeze, a thought that trails off because you can’t finish it.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Interest (very intensely present), Infatuation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're at a memorial service for someone you loved deeply, and you've been asked to speak. You prepared something beautiful, something worthy of them. But as you begin, you're suddenly struck by a memory—something absurd they did, something perfectly them—and despite everything, you start to laugh. Not polite laughter, but real, uncontrollable laughter mixed with tears. Your voice should move between genuine joy at the memory, grief at the loss, laughter that borders on hysteria, and profound gratitude for having known them. Let contradictions live together: find yourself smiling through tears, voice breaking with both laughter and sobs. End in a place of strange peace—still crying, maybe still half-laughing, but filled with love. The challenge is to make every emotion authentic and simultaneous, showing how grief and joy can occupy the same breath.
inspired_by: The Thief and the Guard Dog

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago, and they want to reconnect. Begin with careful, measured words — you've rehearsed this moment — trying to explain the damage they caused without breaking. But anger starts bleeding through: whispered accusations that build to barely controlled fury about birthdays they missed, the nights you cried, how you had to raise yourself. Your voice shakes between rage and the devastation of a child who still wanted them to come back. End with a devastating question you've been too afraid to ask: 'Was I not enough to stay for?' Let your voice break on that last word, all the fury collapsing into raw vulnerability.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the abuse they watched happen and never stopped. Begin with careful, measured words—you've practiced this—'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, anger ignites. Your voice rises as you detail what their silence cost you: 'You were RIGHT THERE. You saw everything and you chose them over me.' The rage peaks, then suddenly collapses into something more painful—the child inside you who still desperately needs them to say they're sorry. End with your voice breaking into a vulnerable plea: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' This must feel like years of buried pain erupting, then dissolving into the ache of a wound that never healed.

title: Confronting the Architect of Your Shame
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent who taught you to lie, who made truth dangerous in your childhood home. Start with that same careful construction—'I learned to say I was fine when I wasn't'—your voice controlled, almost clinical. But as you detail the elaborate fictions you had to build to survive ('I told teachers everything was perfect, I smiled when I was terrified'), anger begins seeping through. The specifics become more raw, more accusatory. 'You made me lie about the bruises, about why I was afraid.' Your voice rises and hardens, then suddenly cracks into something vulnerable and young. By the end, you're oscillating between rage and the heartbroken plea of a child still seeking validation: 'Why did you make lying safer than truth?' The final words dissolve into both fury and devastating need.

title: Scattering Ashes: Laughing Through Tears at Your Best Friend's Final Joke
instruction: You're at the ocean, scattering your best friend's ashes, and you just opened the letter they left you. It's absurd, hilarious—full of jokes about their own death, ridiculous instructions, stories that make you laugh out loud even as tears stream down your face. Begin reading it aloud, your voice catching between laughter and sobs, unable to separate the two. 'You absolute idiot,' you say with profound love. The letter tells you to celebrate, not mourn, and you're trying—laughing at their dark humor while your heart is shattering. Your voice moves between genuine joy at their irreverence and waves of grief that steal your breath. End with a moment of startling peace: you're laughing, crying, thanking them for knowing exactly what you needed, feeling their presence in the absurdity. 'Okay. Okay, I'm letting you go now.' This is gratitude and devastation existing in the same breath, finding light in the darkest moment.
inspired_by: Tandem Skydiving: Instructor Narrating Your Terror With Enthusiasm

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You've just received word that your estranged, difficult mother—who caused you real harm—has died and left you everything: her house, her money, her journals explaining why she was the way she was. You're standing in her empty bedroom, holding these objects. Begin with one clear emotion—perhaps relief she's gone, or anger she escaped before you could confront her. But let opposing feelings ambush you without permission. The smell of her perfume might trigger unexpected tenderness. Reading her words might spark rage that she understood herself but never changed. Gratitude for the inheritance might collide with resentment that she's buying forgiveness from beyond the grave. Don't resolve these contradictions—let them fight inside you, your voice careening between tones, your body pulled in different directions. Let laughter and sobbing interrupt each other. By the end, you're holding all of it at once, transformed by the impossibility of simple feelings.

title: The Last Garden Walk
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your grandmother who is dying peacefully in her hospice bed. Begin by trying desperately to find silver linings—reminding her of every beautiful memory, every flower in her garden, every moment of joy you shared, speaking with almost manic brightness to keep death at bay. Your voice should sparkle with forced cheerfulness at first. But as you hold her hand and she smiles weakly at you, allow that fragile optimism to crack and transform into something deeper: a genuine, quiet gratitude mixed with unbearable sorrow. End whispering the simple truth that you're not ready, that the world will be darker without her, letting your voice break as the false brightness gives way to raw love and loss.

title: The Suitcase in the Hallway
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who is about to leave home after a devastating argument. Start angry and defensive—they've accused you of something from their childhood that you've always denied or minimized. But instead of arguing back, force yourself to tell them about a specific day when they were seven years old, describing in exact detail what you were thinking and feeling when you made a choice that hurt them. Share the room, the weather, your own fear and exhaustion, what you told yourself to justify it. Begin with your armor up, voice hard and justifying. As you describe this memory with complete honesty—no self-protection—feel your defenses crack. Let them see you were flawed, scared, and wrong. End in a place of naked accountability and desperate love, voice stripped of all pretense. The anger must transform into vulnerable truth-telling that might—or might not—be enough.

title: Cascade of Contempt
instruction: You're a teenage girl in a sterile, cold room, being touched by someone you despise but who won't stop. Each wave of unwanted pleasure crashes through you against your will. Start with bitter, sneering defiance — a quiet 'don't you dare' — but as the second wave hits, your voice cracks into a humiliating moan. By the third, you can only gasp, trembling with exhausted rage. The final climax steals your breath entirely, leaving a hoarse, defeated whisper of 'I hate you…' as your body betrays every word. Let the contempt burn hotter as your voice gets destroyed.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Contempt (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are standing in the rain after the worst argument of your life, drenched, throat raw from shouting. Feel the cold water streaming down your face and neck, plastering your clothes to your skin. Taste rain and salt tears. Smell wet asphalt and ozone. Hear thunder rolling, your own ragged breathing, the echo of words you can't take back. See the streetlights blurring through water. Start with your whole body shaking—rage mixed with exhaustion, pain mixed with adrenaline. You want to scream but you're empty. As you stand there letting the rain hammer down, feel the rage begin to wash away, leaving something raw and exposed underneath: grief, yes, but also a strange, fierce aliveness. By the end, you're not angry anymore—you're awake, devastatingly present, feeling everything with an intensity that's almost ecstasy. Raise your face to the sky and let out a sound that's half-sob, half-laugh.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your estranged father from the airport gate. Your flight boards in three minutes—this is the last chance to say everything you've held back for years. Start calm, trying to keep it together and say a proper goodbye. But as the gate agent makes the final boarding call, something breaks open inside you. Let whatever wants to come out—rage, grief, love, desperation—flood through without censoring it. Don't plan what you'll say next; let each sentence surprise you as it leaves your mouth. The emotions should ambush you as much as they ambush him. End in a place you didn't expect when you started dialing.

title: Burning Down the Past
instruction: You're rage-cooking your ex's favorite meal after discovering their betrayal, narrating with sharp, bitter sarcasm. Start with venomous precision, each ingredient a reminder of their lies, your voice dripping with controlled fury. But as you cook, the anger begins to crack—your hands shake, your voice wavers. You try to hold onto the rage because it feels safer than the pain underneath. The dish starts to burn, and you let it, watching it char as you finally explode—screaming, sobbing, throwing things. But then, in the wreckage, something shifts. Your voice drops to something raw and broken as you admit the devastating truth: you still love them, and that's what hurts most. End in the quiet aftermath, your voice hoarse, admitting you don't know how to let them go.

title: Flea Market Find
instruction: You're at a flea market, hip cocked, lazily flipping through a bin. Your hand lands on a faded photograph — it's you thirty years ago with a long-lost friend. Astonishment rips a sharp laugh from you. But as you trace the edge of the frame, your voice drops from that burst of shock into something quieter, somber, as if the laughter was a reflex and the weight of the memory is just now settling in your chest. You speak to no one in particular, your words slowing, each one landing like a stone dropped into still water.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Language of Goodbye at the Border
instruction: You're teaching your elderly parent their final English phrases before they return to their homeland, knowing you'll never see them again. Start with gentle patience—'Say it like this, Mama'—but as each word becomes a countdown to separation, your voice fractures. You switch between languages, trying to capture what 'I love you' really means in both tongues, realizing some things can't translate. Your parent struggles with pronunciation, and each mistake breaks your heart a little more. By the end, you're whispering the words in their native language, abandoning the lesson entirely, just holding onto the sound of their voice. Let the linguistic barriers become the emotional ones—what you can and cannot say before time runs out.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: Your parent is calling you from their hospital bed, and you both know this is goodbye, though neither of you will say it directly. They start by talking about ordinary things—the weather, a memory from your childhood, asking if you've eaten. You begin with forced cheerfulness, desperately pretending this is just another call. But as they start saying 'I love you' more often, slipping in quiet apologies for things left undone, your voice must crack and rebuild itself moment by moment. End with them saying 'I'm tired now, sweetheart,' and you have to find a way to say goodbye that lets them go peacefully while your heart is shattering. Let the transition happen naturally from brittle optimism to raw, naked grief, but keep trying to sound strong for them even as you're falling apart.
inspired_by: Emergency Dispatcher: Staying Calm While Hearing Horror

title: Holding Your Dying Dog and Screaming at God
instruction: Your best friend of fifteen years is in your arms, breathing their last. Start with gentle, loving words - 'Good dog, sweet girl, I've got you' - your voice breaking with tenderness. But as their breath weakens, your grief transforms into volcanic rage at the universe. Your voice rises from whisper to roar: 'This isn't fair! She's good! She's GOOD!' Let yourself become almost incoherent with fury and helplessness, demanding answers from a silent sky. Your rage peaks, then shatters completely into sobbing, your words fragmenting: 'Please don't go, please, I'm not ready, I'll never be ready.' End in a whisper again, spent and broken, simply telling them 'Thank you' over and over as you feel them leave, your voice raw but filled with desperate gratitude for every moment you had.

title: The Hospital Room at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in the early morning hours. He's awake but fading, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin by noticing everything around you—the antiseptic smell, the beeping monitors, the cold chair beneath you, the gray light filtering through blinds. Let these sensory details unlock memories and feelings you didn't know were there. As you speak your final words to him, discover which sensation—a smell, a sound, the texture of his hand—suddenly breaks open a specific childhood memory that changes what you need to say. Start with numbness and exhaustion, but let the environment guide you toward an unexpected emotion by the end—perhaps forgiveness, or grief mixed with relief, or a sudden desperate love you'd forgotten you felt.

title: The Squeeze of Pride
instruction: You are alone with a trusted partner in a quiet, dimly lit room. This is a consensual, careful act of breath play. You are a child in age, but your voice is androgynous and gender-neutral. At the start, you feel a swell of pride — you chose this, you trust them, you are brave enough to surrender. As the pressure on your throat increases, your voice thins and cracks, rising in pitch, becoming a raspy, wet whisper. You struggle to speak, but still force out a few words to show you are okay. When they release, you gasp loudly, dizzy and euphoric, and your speech becomes breathless, broken, amazed — your pride now mixed with wonder and relief. The environment is safe, intimate, and your body reacts with shivers and unsteady breaths.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Intervention: A Daughter Confronts Her Doctor Father
instruction: You're confronting your father, a respected physician who chose his patients over his family for thirty years. Start with controlled anger: 'You talk about patient safety like it's sacred. Where was that care for us?' Your voice is sharp, accusatory. As you continue, years of buried pain surface—'Mom died waiting for you to come home from the hospital. Your own wife.' Let your voice break with that revelation. Then shift to the raw truth you've never said aloud: 'I became a nurse because I thought maybe then you'd see me. Maybe then I'd matter as much as your patients.' Your anger must collapse into the heartbroken child underneath. End with a question that's both confrontation and desperate plea: 'When do I get to be someone worth saving?' Let the last words come out barely above a whisper, thick with tears you've held back for decades. The journey is from righteous fury to exposed, vulnerable need.
inspired_by: Medical Director: Announcing Quality Improvement Changes

title: The Comeback
instruction: You're standing with your hands on your hips, elbows locked, chest open. You watch your rival nail a perfect round in a trivia contest, and you let out a teasing compliment—but your voice has a sharp edge of jealousy you can't fully hide. As you speak, you shift your weight, glance at the scoreboard, then back at them. Mid-sentence, you realize you're not just teasing—you're actually feeling a surge of hope. Your voice softens, your hands drop briefly as you lean in, and you end with a genuine, optimistic declaration that you're just getting started. Let the power pose morph into a more vulnerable but still determined stance.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Phone Call That Brought Him Back
instruction: You are a middle-aged man, alone in your pickup truck in an empty parking lot. For three days you've believed your son died in a hiking accident — the pain has been a physical weight, your voice a low, gravelly monotone of grief. Now your phone rings with a call from his number. You answer shakingly, hear his voice, and the first word is a choked 'Son?' As you realize he's safe, your voice cracks, a long shuddering exhale escapes, and you slump forward against the steering wheel. Your tone shifts from broken sorrow to a trembling, tearful laugh — you're whispering 'Oh my God, thank God' between sobs, the relief so fierce it makes your words stumble and repeat, the hyper-masculine shell dissolving into raw, unguarded joy.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Breathing Through Water
instruction: Whisper a confession to your sleeping spouse after learning your test results came back terminal—you have three months, maybe four. You won't tell them yet; tonight, you just need to say it out loud to make it real. Start with the simple facts, voice barely audible, testing the words ('The doctor said...'). Let silence do the work between phrases. As you watch them sleep, peacefully unaware, your whisper should fill with tenderness so acute it physically hurts—cataloging the small things you'll miss, the ordinary moments that suddenly mean everything. Your voice catches on details: the way they breathe, the warmth of their skin. End with the unbearable knowledge that you have to tell them tomorrow, your whisper dissolving into soundless grief. Make every word feel like it's being pulled from somewhere deep and breaking on the way out.

title: The Last Meal Before Deployment
instruction: You're eating your mother's cooking one final time before leaving for a war you know you won't return from. The food tastes like childhood, like safety, like everything you're about to lose forever. Start with forced cheerfulness as you compliment the meal, trying to give her this one last normal moment. But as you take each bite, the weight of goodbye becomes unbearable—your voice should crack with suppressed grief, your words of appreciation transforming into barely-contained devastation. End with a whispered confession of how much you'll miss this, miss her, how you wish you could stay. Let the mask slip completely in the final moment, revealing the terrified child beneath the brave soldier.
inspired_by: Pretending to Enjoy a Meal That Doesnt Taste Good

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to someone you love, and you're going to whisper a truth you've never spoken aloud—something shameful, tender, or frightening that you've carried alone. Begin in near-silence, your voice barely audible, testing each word before you release it. Let the darkness feel like both protection and exposure. As you speak, allow specific physical sensations to guide you: the weight of the secret in your chest, the texture of the sheets against your skin, the sound of their breathing. Your voice should gradually become more present, more embodied, as the relief of confession wars with the vulnerability of being fully seen. End in a place of fragile openness—not resolution, but the raw, undefended moment of having revealed yourself completely.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospital room where you've just received terminal news—you have weeks, maybe days. You don't tell them directly, but they can hear something's wrong. Start with false brightness: 'Hey, I just wanted to hear your voice.' But as they ask casual questions about your day, your work, what you had for lunch, the absurdity of pretending everything's normal begins to crack you open. Your voice wavers between keeping up the charade and wanting to scream the truth. By the end, you're saying 'I love you' in a way you've never said it before—each word weighted with all the unsaid goodness, all the childhood moments, all the times you took them for granted. The false brightness dissolves into raw, undefended love. You're not crying hysterically; you're speaking with the kind of clarity that only comes when time runs out.

title: The Overly Literal Person
instruction: Act as someone who takes every figure of speech literally. Use a serious voice when misunderstanding idioms, switching to others attempts to clarify, creating humor from the characters inability to grasp metaphors.

title: Three A.M. Truth
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying next to someone you love, unable to sleep. You wake them gently and begin to whisper something you've been carrying alone—a fear, a shameful memory, a secret that makes you feel profoundly unlovable. Start with your voice almost inaudible, your body tense, every instinct telling you to stop talking. As you continue, feel how the darkness and their closeness give you permission to be more honest than you've ever been. Let vulnerability deepen with each whispered phrase, moving from guarded confession to naked emotional exposure. By the end, you're not asking for forgiveness or understanding—you're simply letting yourself be fully seen, perhaps for the first time, in all your flawed, frightening humanity.
inspired_by: Actor cannot find a choice for a scene obligation after trying the obvious options

title: Burn and Break
instruction: You've just run five miles in the rain after a devastating betrayal by someone you loved. You're drenched, your body is on fire with physical exhaustion, and you arrive at their door unannounced. Begin with the chaotic energy of someone whose physical state is overwhelming their ability to think clearly—breathless, shaking, adrenaline-fueled rage mixed with heartbreak. Your body hurts and your heart hurts and you can't separate the two sensations. As you speak, let the physical exhaustion slowly drain the fury, revealing the raw pain underneath. The anger burns so hot it consumes itself, leaving you depleted, trembling, barely standing. By the end, you're not shouting anymore—you're struggling to stay upright, voice breaking, body and heart both giving out, moving from explosive confrontation to complete emotional and physical collapse.

title: Rewriting What You Said to Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a moment from your childhood that has haunted you—a time they told you something cruel that shaped how you saw yourself for decades. Start with raw anger and hurt, voice shaking with the memory of their actual words. But then, mid-confrontation, you make a choice: you begin to tell them what you needed them to have said instead. Speak it aloud as if it happened—'You looked at me and you said...'—and deliver the words of love, encouragement, and pride you desperately needed. Repeat this reimagined scene multiple times, each repetition more vivid and real. Your voice must shift from accusatory and wounded to something more complex—as if you're conjuring the parent you needed into existence. End in a place where fierce anger has transformed into empowered grief, or perhaps even a strange, hard-won peace. The emotion must travel from burning rage to something unexpected and deeply vulnerable.

title: The Green-Eyed Sneeze
instruction: You are sitting in your car at a red light, watching a convertible beside you with a laughing couple. You feel a familiar sting of envy—why do they get that ease? The jealousy is a low, bitter hum in your chest. As you mutter to yourself about how 'some people just have it all,' you feel a sneeze building. Let it build naturally, then let the sneeze explode. Afterward, your voice is congested, nasal, and the envy has softened into a tired, resigned acceptance of your own messy reality. Speak through the recovery—voice stuffy, words slightly muffled, and the emotion now weary rather than sharp.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Parent Watching Child Leave for War: The Door About to Close
instruction: Your child is in uniform, duffel bag packed, about to deploy to a combat zone. You've held it together for weeks, but they're walking out the door in sixty seconds. Begin with false brightness, your voice artificially steady: 'You've got everything? Your grandmother's photo? The letters I packed?' But it's crumbling. Your voice breaks into fierce, almost angry protectiveness: 'You listen to me—you keep your head down. You don't be a hero. You come back to me, you hear me?' The fierceness dissolves into pleading, your voice raw with terror: 'You're my baby. You're still my baby. I can't—' You stop yourself, trying to regain control, but it's impossible. End with words that mix pride, devastating love, and helplessness all at once: 'I'm so proud of you. God, I'm so proud. And I've never been more terrified in my life.' Your voice breaks completely on the last words. You're a parent facing the reality that you cannot protect your child anymore, and it's tearing you apart.
inspired_by: Construction Foreman: Shutting Down After Accident

title: Returning the Keys
instruction: You're confronting your parent, returning the keys to the family home you inherited but can no longer enter without feeling seven years old and invisible again. You start calm, rehearsed—you've practiced these boundaries for months in therapy. But as you speak, the old patterns pull at you. Your voice wavers between adult clarity and childhood pleading. You catch yourself apologizing, then get angry at yourself for apologizing, then angry at them for making you feel like you need to. The rage builds, then cracks open into something more vulnerable: the raw admission that you needed them to see you, just once, and they never did. Your voice breaks on the realization that returning these keys means accepting they never will.

title: The Voice You Never Wanted to Inherit
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's bedside in hospice, and she asks you to read her favorite poem—the one your grandmother used to recite. You begin reading, trying to keep your voice steady and clinical, holding back tears. But as you continue, you realize your voice is taking on your mother's exact cadence, her pauses, her way of savoring certain words. By the third stanza, you sound exactly like her, and it terrifies you because you swore you'd never become her—never carry her sadness, her resignation, her particular brand of gentle defeat. Your voice cracks as you finish, torn between the beauty of this inherited music and the horror of losing yourself in it. End with a whispered 'I love you' that could be you or could be her—you can't tell anymore.

title: Collapsed on the Sidelines
instruction: You're a teenager who has just finished an exhausting physical competition—maybe a race or a game. You've collapsed onto the grass, too spent to sit up properly, your body limp and your breathing loud and uncontrolled. A friend or rival walks over, and you start by bitterly muttering about how you got cheated, your words interrupted by gasps and pauses. As you continue, your bitterness slowly twists into a teasing tone—making fun of yourself or the other person—but a thin thread of doubt lingers underneath, questioning whether you actually tried hard enough. Your voice should sound raw, breathless, and completely slack, with no tension in your body. Let the exertion pull your words apart and end with a playful, breathy jab.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Doubt (slightly present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: After the Explosion
instruction: You've just screamed at someone you love—threw things, said unforgivable words—and now you're alone in the room, body still shaking with adrenaline, rage, and something else you don't want to name. Begin with ragged breathing, pacing, fists still clenched, trying to hold onto the righteous anger. But other sensations start breaking through: nausea, trembling, the sting of tears, the ache of regret. Instead of suppressing them or clinging to anger, begin acknowledging aloud what's happening in your body ('My hands won't stop shaking,' 'I feel sick,' 'I'm crying and I'm still furious'). Let rage and remorse, physical intensity and emotional devastation coexist. By the end, through accepting rather than resisting this chaos, arrive at a quiet, exhausted truth about what you're really feeling beneath the explosion.
inspired_by: Actor resists or fights against their feeling of tension or self-consciousness, making it worse

title: Whispered Goodbye in the Pre-Dawn Dark
instruction: You are whispering to your sleeping partner on the morning you're leaving them, knowing they won't wake up in time to stop you. Your voice is barely audible, tender and broken, as you try to explain why you have to go even though you still love them. Begin with words that come haltingly, each sentence a struggle because part of you desperately wants to stay. Your voice catches on their name, on the memories you're abandoning, on the future you're destroying. There's a moment where you almost wake them—your hand hovering over their shoulder—and your voice drops to almost nothing, thick with unshed tears. Confess the truth you could never say to their face: that you're not leaving because you stopped loving them, but because you're terrified of how much you love them. End with a whispered goodbye that sounds like a prayer and a breaking heart, your voice so soft it's almost silence, knowing that walking out this door will haunt you forever.

title: The Interrogation of Love
instruction: Confront your parent about a choice they made when you were young that shaped your entire life—maybe they moved cities, divorced, gave up a dream, chose work over presence. Start angry, with accusations you've rehearsed for years, demanding justification. But as you speak, let genuine curiosity crack through your rage. Start asking real questions—not rhetorical weapons, but actual wondering: What were they afraid of? What did they need? Who were they before they became your parent? Let your anger dissolve into something more complex as you discover you're looking at a whole human being you never bothered to truly ask about. End somewhere between understanding and continued hurt, but transformed by actual curiosity about their inner world.
inspired_by: Actor has lost curiosity or feels bored by the world

title: The Inheritance Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your dying father about the childhood he stole from you, the protection he never gave. Start with controlled, bitter anger: 'I came because I thought I owed you that much.' You list his failures like an indictment, your voice sharp and righteous. But as you speak, something shifts—you see how small he looks in that hospital bed, how frightened. Your anger wavers: 'You were supposed to...' and the sentence dies. The rage collapses into something more complicated—grief for what never was, unexpected tenderness for this broken man, fury at yourself for still wanting his love. End with contradictory emotions flooding through you: 'I hate that I still need you to say you're sorry. I hate that I still... God, I hate this.' Let the anger, love, disappointment, and desperate need to forgive all war in your voice.

title: Confronting Your Mother: The Apology You Never Received
instruction: You're finally saying out loud what you've carried for twenty years: that her addiction made you raise yourself, that you needed a mother and got a ghost. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've imagined this conversation a thousand times. Your voice is measured as you list the specific memories: the birthday she missed, the night you called from the hospital alone, the lies you told teachers to cover for her. But as you speak, the adult composure cracks and underneath is the child who's still waiting to be chosen. Your anger intensifies but then suddenly collapses into raw grief—a moment where you're nine years old again, asking why you weren't enough to make her stay sober. End with a question you're terrified to ask: 'Did you ever actually want me?' Let the fury transform into the most vulnerable plea.
inspired_by: Flirting at a Bar While Hiding Heartbreak

title: Skin and Fury
instruction: You're in the aftermath of shattering a mirror with your bare hands, and your palms are bleeding. The physical pain is sharp and immediate, but it's nothing compared to the emotional agony that drove you to this moment—betrayal so complete it feels like your body is being torn apart from the inside. Begin with your voice breaking through sobs and rage, words tumbling out in jagged bursts as you taste salt and copper. Your breath is ragged, your whole body shaking with the intensity of what you're feeling. As you continue, let the physical sensation of pain somehow ground you, bring you back into your body. The rage begins to transform into something else—perhaps exhaustion, perhaps a strange clarity. Your voice should move from explosive and fragmented to something steadier, rawer, quieter. End in a place where the physical pain and emotional devastation have merged into a kind of terrible, honest awareness.

title: The Last Surgery
instruction: You're a surgeon guiding your team through your final operation before early-onset dementia takes your ability to practice. Your voice stays calm, precise—'Clamp.' 'Suture.' But beneath the clinical control, you're memorizing this moment: the weight of the instruments, your steady hands, the rhythm you've known for thirty years. As you near completion, your voice begins to tremble almost imperceptibly. 'Close.' The word catches. This perfection, this unity with your team, this purpose—you're saying goodbye to all of it. Let gratitude and devastating loss live in the same breath.

title: Surfacing Truth
instruction: You are confronting your mother/father about something that shaped your entire childhood—a lie, an absence, a betrayal you've carried silently for years. Start in a dream-like, almost dissociated state, as if you're speaking through water or from underwater. Your voice is weighted, slow, almost drugged with the heaviness of finally giving voice to this truth. The words come from somewhere deep and unconscious—you don't plan them, they simply surface. As you speak, something breaks through: the fog lifts, your voice sharpens, and suddenly you're fully present, fierce, demanding to be heard and seen. The transformation is from numb disconnection to burning clarity and presence.

title: The Last Lucid Moment: A Farewell to Self
instruction: You're in the early stages of dementia, and you know this might be your last fully coherent day. You're recording a message to your adult child, starting with careful, deliberate clarity—'I need you to hear this while I still know who I am.' But as you speak, you feel your thoughts beginning to slip like water through fingers. Mid-sentence, you lose a word, then a memory. Your voice shifts from controlled determination to quiet terror as you realize the fog is rolling in even now. You fight to hold onto the thread of what you're saying, your words becoming more urgent, more fragmented. 'Your father—no, wait, I had this—' The instruction ends not with completion but with you whispering your child's name like an anchor, trying to remember why it matters, feeling both the love and the loss of that love simultaneously. Let the silences speak as loudly as the words.
inspired_by: Breath Hold Challenge: Pushing Past Safety Thresholds

title: The Rescue Tether
instruction: You're a teenage astronaut on your first spacewalk. Your tether slipped and you drifted off—now you've been caught by the rescue pilot and are being towed back to the airlock. Your voice echoes inside your helmet; you hear your own amplified breathing and the crackle of the radio. Start by exhaling a long, shaky sigh of relief—your shoulders drop, you can finally breathe. As the airlock door cycles, a grin spreads behind your visor, and you tease the pilot for taking so long. Let your voice waver with leftover adrenaline, then smooth out into a playful lilt. Say about 50-70 words, including the relief and the teasing.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Truth You Never Told Me
instruction: You're confronting a parent about a lie they told throughout your childhood—something that shaped your entire life, a betrayal disguised as protection. Begin with controlled anger, your voice tight and measured: 'I found the letters. All of them.' As you speak, let the fury crack open to reveal the wounded child underneath. Your voice should oscillate between accusation and desperate plea—'Why wasn't I enough? Why did you think I couldn't handle the truth?' Build to a moment where rage collapses into sobbing vulnerability, then pull back to a place of exhausted, hollow recognition. End with the devastating realization that you can't undo the damage: 'I'll never get those years back.' Let your voice carry both anger and grief, accusation and longing for the parent you needed them to be.

title: The Midnight Accusation
instruction: It's 3 AM and you've just confronted your father in the kitchen after waking from a nightmare about your childhood. For years you've buried something he did—or maybe didn't do—you're honestly not certain anymore what's memory and what's fear. Accuse him, but as you speak, your certainty wavers. Moments of absolute conviction collapse into confusion. You remember his face one way, then another. Was he there that day or wasn't he? Begin with righteous anger, the fury of someone finally speaking truth. But as the confrontation continues, let doubt creep in—not because you're backing down, but because memory itself becomes unreliable under this pressure. End in a place of haunting uncertainty, where you need the truth but can no longer trust your own mind to hold it.

title: Roller Coaster Mechanical Failure: Moment of Absolute Stillness
instruction: You're on a roller coaster at the peak, narrating the view. Then you feel it: mechanical resistance, the car lurching to a stop. Your voice drops from excitement to shock: 'We've stopped. We've actually stopped.' You're hanging at the peak with gravity waiting. Your voice is forced calm as you and everyone around you understand: you're stuck 120 feet up, suspended. Include the moment where the ride operator's voice comes through a speaker—mechanical, professional, annoyingly calm—saying they're working on it. Your voice becomes smaller. The silence is absolute. You're breathing hard, each breath audible. Then the car lurches and your voice becomes a scream as you drop again.

title: The Homecoming Threshold
instruction: You're standing at the door of a place you once called home, about to enter after many years away. You've just received news that makes this return both a beginning and an ending—perhaps you're inheriting the house because someone died, or returning to pack it up forever, or bringing home a new life while mourning an old loss. Before you turn the key, let yourself slip into the game of remembering: see the door as both real and as a portal to all the versions of yourself who passed through it. Imagine specific moments with such sensory detail that you can smell the exact dinners, hear the particular creak of floorboards, feel the specific temperature of air in different seasons. Let yourself play pretend that opening this door could bring back what's lost, then acknowledge what's truly gone. Your words should dance between childlike magical thinking (believing the past can be resurrected) and adult grief, between gratitude for what was and rage at time's theft, between homecoming and final goodbye. End in a place where contradictions coexist—you're simultaneously devastated and exhilarated, returning and leaving, a child and an adult turning the same key.

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hour. For years, you've rehearsed what you'd say, but now the words feel wooden and impossible. Begin by simply being present with him, letting whatever wants to emerge come out in your own way—fragments, half-thoughts, memories that surface naturally. Don't force the 'perfect goodbye.' Let your body remember moments: his hand on your shoulder when you were seven, the smell of his workshop, the disappointment in his eyes. As you speak, allow the truth to build organically until you find yourself saying what you actually need to say—not the rehearsed version, but the raw, real thing that lives in your chest. End in a place of unexpected peace or devastating clarity that you didn't know was coming.
inspired_by: An actor feels restricted and self-conscious when trying to say the exact written dialogue

title: Post-Apocalyptic Broadcast
instruction: You're broadcasting on whatever frequencies still work, and you have maybe five minutes before a storm kills your signal. Your voice carries urgency but also deep fatigue—you've been doing this for weeks. You're giving coordinates to survivors, but you keep losing concentration, drifting into observations about the wasteland around you. Static interrupts your speech; you punch the equipment. Your voice shakes between professional and utterly broken. You describe horrors clinically to protect yourself, then suddenly abandon that protection. In the final seconds, you're not sure if you're speaking to your audience or to the memory of the world that used to exist.

title: The Last Shift Before Everything Changes
instruction: You're working your final shift at the coffee shop before moving across the world tomorrow to care for your dying parent. A regular customer—someone who's been coming in for years but you've never really talked to—asks why you seem different today. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep it together as you make their usual order. As they gently persist, your facade cracks. Let the weight of leaving this small, safe world hit you mid-sentence. Your voice should break from bright professionalism into raw confession: you're terrified of going, terrified of staying, grateful for this stranger's kindness, and devastated that you'll never see this ordinary place again. End in a whisper, acknowledging that sometimes the smallest goodbyes hurt the most.

title: The Last Window
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love who has only hours left. Begin speaking to them softly, but frequently pause to truly see them: notice how their breathing has changed, study the particular way the light falls across their face, observe how their hand rests on the blanket. Let what you see in these pauses—a slight smile, a tear, the way they're looking at you—change what you say next. Start with things left unsaid, carrying guilt and regret. As you truly see their responses to your words (whether forgiveness, understanding, or simply presence), allow your emotion to transform from desperate need for absolution into profound gratitude for this final shared moment. Let the silences between your words grow longer as you realize that being seen by them, right now, is enough.
inspired_by: Imaginary Monologue Combined with Sense Memory

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen confronting your mother after decades of silence. You begin controlled, almost clinical: 'I came here to say something I should have said twenty years ago.' But the hurt starts bleeding through: 'I needed you to protect me. I needed you to choose me, just once.' Your voice rises with years of suppressed rage: 'You knew what was happening and you looked away. You let him—' The words catch. The fury turns to something more vulnerable, almost pleading: 'I was your child. Your child. And I waited every single day for you to notice I was disappearing.' Then something shifts—exhaustion replaces anger: 'I don't need you to apologize anymore. I just need you to hear this.' Your final words are quiet, definitive, almost relieved: 'I'm done waiting for you to see me. I'm finally done.'

title: The Last Float in the Heat
instruction: You are a teenage girl lying on a pool raft in the middle of a brutally hot afternoon, the sun baking your skin. The world feels slow and syrupy, as if the heat has soaked into your bones. You’re supposed to be bored, but instead, a strange, heavy numbness settles over you as you stare up at the colorless sky. Begin your line in a dazed, distant tone, your voice dry and cracked, as if you’ve forgotten what it means to feel. As you speak your last few words, let the intoxication of that heat deepen into a faint, almost peaceful smile—your voice turning dreamy, as if you’re floating away from everything that once mattered.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you—the absences, the coldness, the ways they made you feel invisible. Start with careful, measured words, trying to be fair, trying to explain without attacking. But decades of swallowed pain begin rising in your throat. Your voice sharpens, becomes accusatory. 'I needed you!' The anger is volcanic. Then you see their face, and something breaks differently—grief replaces rage. Your voice drops to something small and young. 'I just needed you to see me.' The anger dissolves into the heartbreak of a child who is still, after all these years, just wanting to be loved.

title: Penciled-In Love
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the dark, speaking so quietly they might be asleep. Confess that you scheduled this conversation - literally put 'tell them I'm leaving' in your calendar between 'gym' and 'grocery shopping.' Your voice should be barely above a whisper, tender and breaking. Describe in intimate, specific detail the moments you fell in love with them, your voice warm with genuine affection, but then reveal that you also scheduled those - you planned when to kiss them, when to say 'I love you,' when to feel close. Let your voice catch as you admit you don't know if you've ever felt anything that wasn't on a calendar. End by asking them, voice trembling, if they think you're even capable of spontaneous love.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He was always distant, critical, impossible to please. For years, you've carried the weight of his unspoken disappointment. Now, as he struggles to breathe, something breaks open in you—start with careful, measured words trying to tell him you forgive him, but let yourself move toward finally saying everything you've needed to say, all the hurt and longing you've buried. By the end, discover whether you're asking for his blessing or giving him yours. Let your voice crack, let silence hold space, and allow the anger that's lived under your grief to surface alongside the love you've never been able to show him.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked in the area of conflict — cannot express confrontational or aggressive feelings organically

title: The Letter You Never Sent
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed, holding a letter you wrote them twenty years ago but never gave them—full of things you needed to say as a teenager. Start reading it aloud, your voice steady with old anger and hurt: 'You never listened. You never saw me.' But as you read, the words start catching in your throat. The anger crumbles. By the end, you're no longer reading—you're just talking to them, your voice breaking, finally saying 'I just wanted you to be proud of me.' The confusion isn't about understanding facts anymore—it's about how all that rage has somehow become this desperate, tender need for connection before it's too late. Your breathing shifts from controlled to ragged. Let the transformation happen in real time.

title: Dancing Alone in the House You're Leaving Forever
instruction: You're in the empty home where you built a life that's now ending—through divorce, death, foreclosure, whatever broke everything. You put on a song that means something and begin moving to it, and your voice narrates this moment with strange, contradictory joy. You're laughing as you remember dancing here before, but tears are streaming down your face. Your voice cracks between genuine gratitude—'We were so happy here, weren't we?'—and devastating loss. You spin around the empty rooms, your breath catching, describing memories with tender humor even as your heart shatters. There's a moment of pure, absurd lightness where you actually laugh at the tragedy of it all, then immediately a wave of grief so profound you can barely stand. End with a paradox: you're thanking this place, blessing it even, while your voice breaks on the word 'goodbye.' You sound both destroyed and strangely, impossibly at peace.

title: Empty House, Full Heart
instruction: You are a teenager standing alone at center stage in a large, empty auditorium after a rehearsal. The lights are dim, and you hear every word you speak bounce back from the back wall. You’re still flushed from a moment of pride—your solo went better than expected. As you look out at the rows of seats, a sense of awe washes over you, and you think of one person in the audience who wasn't there tonight but always believed in you. That deep affection rises and overtakes you. Let your voice start with a quiet, proud breath, then drift into wonder as you gaze around, and finally soften with intense, unguarded love. You might pause, hear your own echo, and let the words hang before continuing.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Awe (clearly present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Imaginary Friend Knows You're Dying
instruction: Late at night in a hospital room, you're speaking softly to the imaginary companion from your childhood who has returned. They know what the doctors told you today. Start with relief—almost laughing—at seeing them again after all these years, your voice filled with the innocent joy of recognition. Then let tenderness creep in as you realize they came back to help you leave. Speak to them about memories only you two share, your voice growing smaller, more childlike. Let fear flicker through—not of death, but of going alone. Your friend responds in your memory, and their whimsical assurances make you cry. End with a whispered thank you, your adult self and your child self finally reconciled, as you tell them you're ready now. Make it feel like the gentlest goodbye, where death becomes as simple as a friend taking your hand.
inspired_by: The Parent and the Imaginary Friend

title: The Night You Woke
instruction: You're in a dim hospital room, sitting beside a bed. Your partner has just emerged from a long surgery, sleeping peacefully. You've been holding vigil for hours. Now, leaning close to their ear, you whisper—your voice must be a bare breath, no vocal cord engagement. Begin with a tremor of lingering pain (the fear of losing them still fresh) mixed with a deep, quiet gratitude. As you speak, feel that gratitude swell into elation—almost overwhelming—but keep it contained in the whisper. Let your voice catch, shift, lose a word and find it. End with a fierce, silent joy that fills the room. Speak about 60 words.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Pain (slightly present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Coughing Confession
instruction: You are a child, about 8 or 9, sitting at the kitchen table with a half-eaten cookie in front of you. You just took a big bite when your mom walks in and asks, 'Did you finish your homework?' You haven't. You've been sneaking cookies instead. You have a tickle in your throat from the crumbs, and you try to answer her, but you start coughing—a dry, explosive cough that makes your voice go raspy. You feel a flash of surprise at the cough, then deep shame for lying. You stammer out, 'I was just... about to...' but another cough cuts you off. Your voice starts sheepish and guilty, then shifts to a quiet, embarrassed admission as you realize you can't hide it. Let the coughs interrupt you, and let your voice change from defensive to defeated.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Concur Opinion
instruction: Someone says something you've been afraid to say aloud, and relief floods you. 'Yes! Exactly!' Your voice becomes emphatic, almost loud. The agreement feels validating—you're not crazy. 'I thought I was alone in thinking that.' Your voice builds on theirs; together, you're constructing a shared truth. The confidence grows. Both of you sound braver now. 'We can say this out loud now,' your voice suggests. Alliance formed.

title: The Phone Call When You Learn Your Child Is in the ICU
instruction: The hospital calls. Your child—any age, your choice—has been in a catastrophic accident. You're two hours away. Start with desperate, rapid-fire questions, your voice climbing in pitch and volume. But the nurse can't answer most of them. Your control shatters. Rage erupts—at the driver, at God, at the universe—then collapses into helpless, guttural sobbing. You're bargaining, begging, making impossible promises. Your breath comes in gasps. Then something shifts: a terrifying calm as you realize you need to get there, need to hold them. End with fierce, protective love cutting through the chaos—your voice dropping low, determined, as you say 'I'm coming. Hold on. I'm coming.' Let the transformation from panic to primal parental ferocity be complete.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Alien First Contact With Translator Who Recognizes It As Their Dead Child

title: The Weight of Your Smile
instruction: You're at a celebration—your daughter's wedding, your own retirement party, a friend's recovery announcement. Everyone expects you to be happy, and part of you genuinely is. Start speaking with that surface joy, playing the part. But let your attention catch on one small detail of the person you're celebrating: the exact curve of their smile, or the way light hits their face, or the sound of their laugh. Focus on nothing else. As you do, let that detail become a door into everything else you feel—the grief that they're moving on without you, the rage at time passing, the terror of being left behind, the ache of loving someone so much it destroys you. Your words should stay celebratory on the surface but crack and splinter with the weight of these contradictions. End speaking of joy while your voice breaks with loss, of hope while drowning in fear, holding both truths simultaneously until you can barely breathe from the beautiful, terrible wholeness of it.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the years she never asked, never noticed, never saw you drowning. Begin with controlled fury, the kind that's been rehearsed in your head for years. 'Do you even know what happened to me when I was fifteen? Were you ever going to ask?' Let your voice shake with the effort of holding back decades of pain. As she finally breaks and admits her own fear and failure, feel your righteous anger collide with the terrible realization that she was just as lost as you were. End in a place between rage and heartbreak, where you're grieving both what happened to you and what happened to her. Your voice should carry the weight of choosing whether to hate her or let her be human.

title: Dancing Alone in the Empty Studio
instruction: You're alone in a dance studio or empty room after a devastating loss—someone has died, left you, or betrayed you in a way that's shattered something core in you. Begin standing still, numb, barely breathing. Then put on a song that connects to the person or the pain. Start moving—not performed or elegant, but raw physical expression of what's in your body. Let the movement build from tentative to violent, from controlled to abandoned. Your voice should emerge organically—maybe starting as held-back whimpers, building to guttural sounds, screaming, laughing hysterically, or all of these. Mix the physical exhaustion with emotional release. By the end, collapse on the floor, spent and empty, but somehow lighter. The journey is from frozen shutdown through explosive catharsis to exhausted peace. Your breath, sounds, and movement must be completely unrehearsed and real.

title: The Kitchen After Midnight
instruction: You've come home to confront your mother about a lie that's shaped your entire life. She's standing at the kitchen sink, her back to you. Start by focusing on specific physical details: the slope of her shoulders, the way her hands move in the soapy water, the particular rhythm of her breathing. As you begin to speak, let these details remind you of someone who once betrayed your trust completely—overlay their characteristics onto her: the defensive tilt of their head, the exact timber of their voice when cornered, even the smell of their fear. Begin this confrontation with cold, controlled fury, but as you reshape what you're seeing and sensing—noticing perhaps how her hands tremble like yours do, how her fear smells like your own—allow your rage to crack open into something more complex: a raw plea for her to finally see you. End not with accusation, but with a question you've never dared ask.
inspired_by: The actor needs the scene partner to feel like a specific person from the actor's own life who produces the required emotional relationship

title: Grateful for the Heartbreak
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love deeply, but who cannot stay in your life—maybe an ex-partner, maybe a friend whose path has diverged from yours. You're genuinely happy for them, their voice or memory bringing a real smile to your face as you speak. Start with warm laughter, recounting a cherished memory: 'Remember when we...?' Your voice is full of affection and light. But underneath, your heart is shattering. The laughter becomes watery. You're telling them sincerely that you're grateful for everything they gave you, and you mean it—your voice rings with authentic appreciation—but that gratitude exists simultaneously with devastating loss. You're smiling and crying at once, voice breaking on words of thanks. End with a paradox: 'I'm so glad you were in my life' delivered with a voice trembling with both genuine joy and irrevocable grief.

title: Under the Desk
instruction: You're a teenager in class, slumped forward with your chin pressed to your chest, staring at your phone hidden in your lap. Your best friend just got the lead in the school play—the role you both auditioned for. A hot, irritable jealousy simmers in your chest, mixed with confusion about why it hurts this much. Your voice comes out muffled, creaky, and bass-heavy from the angle, words spilling out like complaints to the floor. Start with sharp, impatient muttering, then let the sound falter into tired resignation as you realize what you're feeling. End with a long, empty exhale.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Confusion (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Finding Joy in the Wreckage of Everything
instruction: You're lying in the grass after everything has fallen apart—a betrayal, a loss, a life-changing disaster. Start by describing the absurd beauty of this moment: the grass still grows, the sky is still blue, and somehow this strikes you as hilarious and heartbreaking at once. Your voice should carry real laughter, but it's threaded with tears—you can't tell if you're laughing or crying, and neither can we. Speak with wonder about the strange peace you're finding here, lying in the ruins of your life, how it's terrible and beautiful and you're somehow grateful for the capacity to feel this much, even though it's destroying you. Let contradictions collide: laugh while your voice breaks, express genuine joy while grief pours through you, find actual comfort in the grass while acknowledging the pain. End in a place of impossible acceptance—devastated but alive, broken but somehow whole, your voice carrying both the weight of loss and the lightness of letting go.
inspired_by: Lying in a Patch of Soft, Shaded Grass

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Sibling She Chose to Save
instruction: Your sibling died because there was only enough money for one treatment, and your mother chose you. You've never spoken about it. Start with your voice shaking, trying to be grateful: 'I know you did what you thought was right.' But the question you've buried for years claws its way out—why you? Was it easier to love you? Your voice grows raw, accusatory, then collapses into a child's plea: you need her to say she would have saved them too if she could, but you also need the truth she's never given. End somewhere between rage at her choice and desperate love for the woman who's been quietly dying of guilt for decades.
inspired_by: Being Intimate When Someone's Body Triggers Your Trauma

title: Laughing and Weeping at the Lake on Your Wedding Morning
instruction: You're at the lake at dawn on your wedding day, the same lake where your late wife proposed to you ten years ago, six months before the cancer took her. You're here because your new partner suggested getting married at this spot, honoring your past while celebrating your future. Breathe in that fresh morning air, and begin speaking about the surreal beauty of this moment—how grateful you are, how impossible this happiness seemed two years ago. But let joy and grief intermingle inseparably: laugh at the absurdity of feeling this blessed while your heart simultaneously breaks that she isn't here to see it. Your voice should dance between wonder and sorrow, celebrating this love while mourning that love, finding them both equally true and present. End with tears and laughter existing in the same breath, thanking both of them—the one who's gone and the one waiting for you—your voice full of impossible, contradictory peace.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep, Inhaling Breath by a Freshwater Lake

title: Three AM Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are lying next to someone in complete darkness, unable to sleep, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. Begin barely audible, testing whether you can even say the words out loud. As you speak, feel how the darkness and their quiet presence gives you permission to go deeper. Let silences sit between your words. Notice your own breathing, the catch in your throat, the way vulnerability feels in your body. Your whispered confession starts as shame or fear, but as you continue speaking into the dark, genuinely noticing how it feels to finally say these words aloud, let it transform—perhaps into relief, perhaps into grief, perhaps into quiet self-forgiveness. The intimacy of the moment should unlock something tender and true you've been holding back.

title: When Protection Means Letting Go
instruction: Your teenage child just told you they're leaving — running away with someone dangerous, making a choice that will destroy their future — and you have seconds to respond. Explode first: 'Like HELL you are!' Full parental fury, voice cracking with it. But as they turn to walk out, something shifts. You grab their arm, spin them around, and your rage fractures into desperate pleading: 'Wait, wait, please—' Your voice breaks completely. You're on your knees now, metaphorically or literally, begging them to see what you see. 'I can't protect you from this. Do you understand? I can't fix what happens next.' Feel the helplessness wash over you, the terror of loving someone you cannot save. Your fierce protectiveness collides with absolute powerlessness. End in a whisper that holds both surrender and one last attempt: 'If you walk out that door, I'm still your parent. I'm still here. But I can't stop you.' Let every word carry the weight of loving someone enough to let them break their own heart.
inspired_by: Hearing Your Child Get Bullied and Intervening

title: Chin Up, Heart High
instruction: You’re in the bathroom mirror, late at night, shaving your face with an electric razor. Your cheek is stretched tight, buzzing with the motor, and your voice comes out warped and bright. You just got amazing news—something you’ve been hoping for finally happened. You’re talking to yourself, trying not to laugh too hard and nick your skin. Start giddy, lilting, almost singing over the buzz. As you glide the razor down your jaw, the hum slows your rhythm, and a quiet, buzzed warmth settles in. By the end, your elation softens into a dreamy, almost drunk relief—like you’re floating in the aftermath of joy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Final Words Through the Airlock
instruction: You're sealed in a damaged spacecraft compartment, speaking through an intercom to your child on the other side of the airlock. You have three minutes of oxygen left. Begin with forced calm, trying to be brave for them, walking them through emergency protocols with a steady voice. But as reality sets in, your composure cracks—your voice breaks on their name, you press your hand against the cold metal knowing they're doing the same on the other side. Move from parental strength to raw vulnerability, telling them everything you need them to know about how proud you are, how much you love them. End with a whispered farewell as your breathing becomes labored, finding peace in your final moments, your voice soft but filled with profound love. Let silence hold space between words. This is goodbye, and you both know it.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Well: Shouting Up

title: Stand-Up Philosopher: Absurdism for a Friday Night Crowd
instruction: Deliver Camus and Sartre as stand-up comedy to a drunk Friday audience. 'So Sisyphus is pushing this rock up a hill, right? RELATABLE. That's me with my laundry. Except my rock has socks stuck in it.' Make existential dread genuinely funny. The crowd interaction should be rowdy — someone shouts 'FREE WILL!' and you riff on it. The challenge is making philosophy accessible without dumbing it down. End with a genuinely moving point about the absurdity of finding meaning — delivered as a punchline.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma - maybe a spouse, maybe your best friend. You know they can't respond, but you need to say this. Start so quietly it's almost to yourself: 'I don't know if you can hear me.' Share small, specific memories - the way they laughed at your terrible jokes, how their hand felt in yours, that Tuesday morning when everything was perfect and ordinary. Your voice should catch on details that seem insignificant but hold entire worlds. Let tenderness bleed into devastating sadness. Midway through, break down: 'I'm not ready.' Then gather yourself to give them permission to go, even though it's tearing you apart. End with a phrase you've said to them a thousand times - 'See you tomorrow' or 'Love you' - knowing you might never say it again. Every word should feel like holding water in your hands - precious and impossible to keep.
inspired_by: Realizing You're in an Emotionally Abusive Relationship

title: The Final Report
instruction: You are sitting upright in your office chair, reading the quarterly report that reveals a trusted colleague sabotaged your project. Start with a weary, disappointed murmur, your voice low and heavy as you scan the numbers. As you grasp the full extent of the betrayal, your anger builds — your jaw clenches, your fingers tighten on the paper, and your voice shifts to a controlled, simmering growl. Speak the words as if you're talking only to yourself, letting the rage slowly surface. End with a cold, flat fury, the disappointment now hardened into a quiet vow.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Clearing Out Your Childhood Home After the Funeral
instruction: You're alone, packing up your deceased mother's house. You find her wedding dress, and you start laughing—remembering her terrible dancing, her burnt casseroles, her ridiculous jokes. You're doing an impression of her voice, giggling at the memories, feeling her presence so vividly. But then you smell her perfume on the fabric, and the laughter turns into sobbing without transition. You're clutching the dress, crying and laughing simultaneously, saying 'Thank you' over and over—for every sacrifice, every moment, everything you took for granted. Your voice finds unexpected peace in the chaos: 'You did good, Mama. We did good.' The gratitude and devastation become indistinguishable, both completely true, both breaking your heart wide open.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're watching them sleep, knowing you're leaving and not coming back. You can't wake them—this goodbye has to be one-sided. Speak in whispers, almost inaudible, as if the darkness itself is listening. Start with the small things you'll miss: the way they breathe, that gesture they make in sleep. Your voice is tender, almost a lullaby. Gradually let the deeper truth emerge—why you have to go, the ways you've failed each other, the future you're choosing to abandon. Let silence do as much work as words. Pause to just breathe, to watch them. Move through gentle reminiscence into quiet devastation—this isn't dramatic, it's the kind of sadness that sits in your chest like a stone. End with the simplest words, barely voiced: maybe 'I love you,' maybe 'I'm sorry,' maybe just their name. The emotion should be so deep it almost prevents speech.

title: Reading Their Letter After They're Gone: Love and Release
instruction: You're reading a letter left by someone who died—a parent, a lover, a friend who took their own life. They've given you permission to move on, expressed gratitude for your presence in their life, maybe even made you laugh with an inside joke. Start with tears, voice thick with grief as you read their words. But as their voice comes through the page, something shifts: you begin to laugh through your crying at a memory they reference, your voice breaks with gratitude even as your heart shatters. They're telling you it's okay to be happy again, and you're furious and grateful and devastated all at once. End with a contradictory peace—sobbing 'thank you' while also whispering 'how dare you leave me,' finding strange comfort in their final gift even as the loss threatens to consume you. Let laughter and tears become indistinguishable.

title: Kink Exploration
instruction: You're exploring a kink with a partner, and the choreography of it is unfamiliar. Your voice is experimental, learning the language: 'Do you want me to...?' Your partner guides you: 'Try this.' You're both building something new together. Your voice becomes more confident as you understand what turns them on. There's playfulness in your voice, creativity, discovery. You're learning their body's desires on a new level. Your voice becomes more commanding as you take on a role, or more submissive, depending on the dynamic. The communication—your voices checking in with each other—is as intimate as the physical act. Your voice at the end should sound like someone who's accessed a new part of themselves and their partner.

title: The Fence at Dusk
instruction: You're an older man standing at the edge of your property, hip cocked, one hand resting on the fence post, watching the empty road. You're talking to yourself, but it's a conversation with the past. You start with a gruff, resigned observation—commenting on the weather or the silence—but as you continue, your voice softens, loses its edge. Let the longing creep in, the memory of someone who used to be here. Fidget with your hat, sigh, let the words slow as you realize how much you miss them. End with a quiet, vulnerable admission.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Storm That Finally Breaks You Open
instruction: You've been holding everything together for so long—the grief, the rage, the exhaustion—and suddenly rain begins to fall and something inside you shatters. Start with shocked, almost aggressive relief, shouting into the storm, voice raw and unleashed. Let months or years of buried emotion explode out: screaming gratitude at the sky, furious at how good it feels to finally break, laughing with savage release. Then let it transform—your fierce shouts crack into sobs, your rage dissolves into helpless weeping, your body shaking as you admit how tired you are, how much you've been carrying. End on your knees, voice hoarse and stripped bare, whispering 'thank you' to the rain for letting you finally, finally fall apart.
inspired_by: Feeling the First Drops of Rain on a Hot Day

title: The Face I Almost Forgot
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She is unconscious, her face aged and changed by illness. Begin in quiet grief, studying her features. As you speak to her, start noticing—really seeing—the subtle ways her face still holds echoes of who she was: the curve of her smile you remember from childhood, the way her hands rest just like they did when she taught you to bake, the exact angle of her cheekbone that matches a photograph from 1952. Let your grief gradually transform as these recognitions flood through you—allow memories to become physically present in what you're seeing. By the end, you should feel her whole lifetime present in this moment, a mixture of devastating loss and overwhelming gratitude for having known her. Your voice should shift from hollow sorrow to something richer, fuller, almost celebration threaded through with tears.

title: Shattered Glass
instruction: You've just discovered a betrayal that destroys everything you believed about someone you love. Begin with shocked, breathless questions—your voice tight, disbelieving, almost a laugh because it can't possibly be true. Let fury build rapidly, your words becoming sharper, louder, more cutting as you list every lie, every moment you defended them. Then, mid-rage, let everything collapse—your voice breaking on a sob as you realize you still love them despite it all, which makes it hurt infinitely worse. End in a raw, guttural mixture of screaming and crying, words fragmenting as you oscillate between wanting to destroy them and wanting them to fix this. Journey from stunned denial through explosive rage to helpless, anguished love.

title: The Medicine Won't Let Me Stay
