instruction: You are a young girl lying in bed, heavily sedated by a strong painkiller. Your mother is sitting beside you, but you can barely keep your eyes open. You feel a deep distress because something is wrong, you doubt you can stay awake, and you're confused about why the room is spinning. Speak to your mother, trying to explain how you feel, but your words come out slow and breathy. Start with a confused, drifting tone, then as you realize you might fall asleep, your distress becomes more urgent, your voice cracking. Let your pauses be long, your volume drop to a near-whisper, and trail off as if you're fighting to stay conscious.
emotions_sampled: Distress (extremely present), Doubt (very intensely present), Confusion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Goodbye
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone in a quiet hospital room, saying goodbye to your late wife of 60 years. You sit beside her bed, holding her hand, but the grief is so immense your breath catches in sharp, jerky inhalations, and your voice cracks on every other word. As you speak, you try to focus intensely on her face, willing yourself to remember every detail, but the pain surges and your words dissolve into wet, choked sobs. By the end, you shift from raw, uncontrolled weeping into a fragile, whispered promise—a strained, haunting calm that betrays the wreckage inside.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Triumphant Yawn
instruction: You're on the phone with a colleague you deeply despise, discussing a tedious report, when you spot a text from your partner with incredible news: you just won the lottery. You're exhausted and can't help a huge yawn mid-sentence—the yawn itself drips with contempt for the conversation. As you try to finish your thought, the yawn's hollow, sliding pitch gives way to a rising, breathless elation that cracks through your numbness. Let the yawn distort your words, then let genuine joy spill out, as if you're fighting to contain it but failing.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to your partner who you think is asleep. Begin by whispering something small and safe—maybe about your day, a fleeting thought. But then, believing they can't hear you, let yourself confess something you've carried in secret: a fear about your relationship, a truth about your past, or a dream you've been too afraid to voice. Your whispers should grow slightly more urgent, more honest, more raw. Then—realize they're awake and have been listening the entire time. Let the vulnerability turn to exposure, the safety of darkness suddenly stripped away. Your final words should tremble with the terror and relief of being truly seen.
inspired_by: When finishing a production where unconscious programming was used

title: The Farewell That Can't Be Spoken
instruction: You are standing on a crowded city street, watching a bus pull away that carries someone you love—someone you'll never see again. The noise is overwhelming: horns, a distant siren, the rumble of traffic you must strain to speak over. Your throat is tight with distress, and you're desperately trying to hold back tears. You begin by half-shouting after the bus, fighting to be heard above the chaos, but your voice cracks and falters as shame for your public outburst mixes with a raw, aching longing for them to somehow hear you. By the end, the noise fades as you whisper a single word—barely audible, meant only for yourself—as the bus disappears into the haze.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Shame (slightly present), Longing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Mirror They Held Up
instruction: Your parent/partner stands before you, finally telling the truth: 'I've spent years cutting you down, making you small, because I was terrified of your light.' Begin frozen, defensive, arms crossed, voice tight and small—years of accepting their diminishment have made you believe you're nothing. They continue: 'I need you to prove me wrong. Right now. Show me who you really are.' Start slowly, haltingly trying to name one good thing about yourself. Your voice cracks. They push: 'Bigger. Louder. SHOW me.' Something breaks open. Begin to move—tentative steps become strides. Your voice rises. Throw your arms out, spin, jump, physically claim space you were never allowed to take. Shout your worth, your beauty, your power—not for them anymore, but for yourself. Let rage and liberation mix. Transform from diminished and small to unleashed and expansive, your body and voice growing until you're taking up all the space in the room. End facing them, breathless, changed—no longer their victim.

title: The Breaking Point in the Storm
instruction: You've been the strong one for everyone—holding your family together through crisis after crisis—and you've finally hit your limit. Start with bitter, rising intensity: 'I'm done. I'm done being the one who holds it together while everyone else falls apart.' Your voice explodes with rage: 'Where were all of you when I was breaking? When I couldn't breathe from carrying all of this?' Let the fury reach its peak, then crack—dissolve into desperate, gulping sobs: 'I can't do this anymore. I can't... I can't save everyone.' The anger transforms into helpless grief, your voice small and shaking: 'I'm tired of being strong. I'm so tired.' End with fierce vulnerability, a whispered declaration that's both surrender and survival: 'I need help. God, I need someone to help me.' Move from explosive rage through complete breakdown to the terrifying courage of admitting you can't do it alone.

title: Summit Gratitude
instruction: You're a father hiking up a steep trail with your young child on your shoulders. Each step is a struggle—heavy breathing, short gasps between words. At first you're just pushing forward, muttering about the burn in your legs. But as you pause to catch your breath, you feel your child's small hands on your head, hear their giggle, and see the valley stretching below. The exhaustion melts into a deep, overwhelming thankfulness for this moment. Let your voice be broken, breathy, and raw—start with grit and end with tender, heartfelt gratitude. Deliver about 40–80 words, staying in the physical reality of the climb.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Garden of Spite
instruction: You are an elderly retired farmer in a therapy session. Your younger brother just won a prestigious agricultural award that you've always wanted. You begin by describing your own garden with forced calm, but your voice tightens with each mention of his success. Let your words trail off as you stare at the floor. When the therapist prompts you gently, let a crack of raw malice seep through — you admit you've been poisoning his soil for years, but then your voice softens into a strange contentment as you realize you're finally telling the truth. Speak with the weary, gravelly tone of an old man, letting pauses and breaths reveal your buried spite.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Contentment (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Pajama Confession
instruction: You are a young woman, curled up in bed with your lover in the dark. You're both in pajamas, whispering. You've just accidentally sent a very embarrassing text to your entire team at work about your boss. Your lover is trying to console you, but you're mortified. Start by hiding your face in their shoulder, voice muffled and tight with shame. Halfway through, you peek up, a nervous giggle escapes as you realize how absurd it is, and you end by looking them in the eyes, your voice still breathy but with a playful, relieved wonder that they're here. Let the regret crack to a soft, relieved laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Bittersweet Toast: Celebrating Your Ex's Wedding to Your Former Best Friend
instruction: You're giving a toast at a wedding you never imagined attending—your ex-partner marrying someone you introduced them to. You stand, glass raised, and your voice must hold impossible contradictions. Begin with humor, self-deprecating jokes that make everyone laugh, performing graciousness. But underneath, your voice carries genuine love for both of them—you can see they're right for each other in ways you never were. As you speak, let the smile in your voice coexist with the ache in your throat. Tell a story about when you knew they'd fall for each other, and let your voice shimmer with both joy for their happiness and grief for your own loss. End with a genuine blessing that costs you everything—meaning every word about their future together while accepting you're not part of it. Your final words should sound like laughter and heartbreak at once.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Time Traveler Meets Their Own Younger Self

title: Breaking the Perfect Daughter
instruction: You're confronting your mother who has always demanded perfection, elegance, and composure. You've finally had enough. Begin with controlled, seething anger—tight, measured words. Then deliberately destroy the 'perfect' image she created: make grotesque faces while recounting painful memories, speak in mocking, exaggerated versions of her voice, contort your body into ugly, unflattering positions as you strip away every layer of pretense she forced on you. Use high-pitched mockery, guttural sounds, animalistic growls—everything she taught you was 'unladylike' or 'inappropriate.' Transform from controlled rage into wild, liberated chaos. By the end, exhausted but free, let your voice drop to something raw and real—no longer performing perfection or rebellion, just finally, devastatingly honest.

title: The Last Clear Night Before the Surgery
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child the night before a risky brain surgery that will likely save your life but erase most of your memories. Start speaking to them while organizing old photos, your voice warm and matter-of-fact, almost businesslike: 'I wanted to show you these before tomorrow.' As you describe memories captured in the photos, your voice begins to crack with the realization of what you're losing. 'This was your first day of school. You were so brave.' The emotion builds as you try to imprint everything into this final moment of clarity. Your voice becomes urgent, almost fierce: 'I need you to know I will always love you, even when I can't remember why.' Then soften into devastating tenderness: 'And when I look at you confused, remember I chose this. I chose to stay alive for you.' End with quiet acceptance mixed with grief, your hand reaching to touch their face: 'Tomorrow, I'll wake up and you'll be a stranger. But tonight, you're everything.' Let your voice break on that last word, holding both gratitude and unbearable loss.

title: Confronting Your Adoptive Parents: The Truth You Were Never Told
instruction: You've just discovered your adoptive parents knew your birth mother wanted you back when you were five, but they refused contact and never told you. Start quiet, dangerously controlled: 'How long were you planning to keep this from me?' Your voice is steady but vibrating with betrayal. Then it breaks—raw accusation mixed with the pain of a child who trusted completely: 'She tried to find me. She wanted me and you... you lied.' But mid-confrontation, you see their faces, see their fear of losing you, and something complicated happens. Your voice cracks with conflicting truths: 'I know you loved me. I know you were afraid.' You're furious and you understand them, and both things are tearing you apart. End with devastating honesty, voice thick with tears: 'You're my parents. You'll always be my parents. But you stole something from me, and I don't know how to forgive that yet.'
inspired_by: Adoptee Searching for Biological Family: Hope and Dread Mixed

title: Fantasy: Seer Shares a Vision Knowing It Will Cause the War It Predicts
instruction: Speaking prophecy to the council, your seer voice is distant and channeled. You're describing an invasion. But you know from experience that speaking prophecy makes it real—people act to prevent it, causing the exact thing you've foreseen. Your voice carries this terrible knowledge. You're forced to choose between silence (allowing disaster) and speech (ensuring it). Your breathing becomes the breath of someone caught in causality. You speak the prophecy anyway, voice heavy with the paradox.

title: Vigil Confessions at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's sleeping—maybe recovering from surgery, maybe in their last days—and in the darkness, you're finally saying everything you've never been able to say to their waking face. Start in a whisper, almost talking to yourself, confessing small truths. Your voice is gentle, intimate, heavy with unshed tears. Admit your fears, your failures, the ways you've fallen short. Let your voice catch on words you've never spoken aloud: how terrified you are of losing them, how you've already started grieving, how you don't know who you'll be without them. There's tenderness mixed with desperation, gratitude tangled with grief. Touch on moments of shared joy, and feel your throat close around the memories. End with the simplest, most devastating truth—something like 'I don't know how to let you go'—your voice barely audible, breaking on the words, as you sit in the unbearable intimacy of loving someone you can't keep.

title: Chronic Illness Diagnosis
instruction: The doctor just told you that you have a chronic illness that will never go away. Your voice in that moment is frozen: 'So it's... forever?' The doctor nods. Your voice becomes small: 'But I'm only 35. I have my whole life left.' There's anger, denial, grief, all colliding in your voice. You drive home in silence. Later, you tell your partner, and your voice breaks: 'Everything is different now. I'll never be the person I was.' They hold you. Over the following weeks, your voice shifts — from denial to anger to bargaining to acceptance. By a month in: 'Okay. I have a chronic illness. That doesn't define me.' But the voice saying it still carries the weight of that diagnosis. This will be your voice forever now — the voice of someone learning to live with something that can't be cured, only managed.

title: The Perfect Sour Mango
instruction: You are a man in your 30s, standing in the middle of a humid, dripping tropical jungle after a sudden downpour. The air is so thick and wet it coats your throat like steam. Your young daughter, beaming, holds out a half-eaten green mango she picked, the flesh glistening with sour juice. You start by taking a huge, ecstatic bite, your voice heavy and slippery with moisture, almost a moan of pure pleasure and awe—this is the most alive you've ever felt. But as you chew, the intense sourness overwhelms you: your face puckers, your voice cracks, and you fumble for words, finally laughing with the salt of sweat and sour on your tongue, the ecstasy now mixed with a wild, gasping delight.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Awe (extremely present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Child First Words
instruction: You're a parent with your toddler, and they're attempting their first real word. Your voice is encouraging, patient: 'Say Mama. Can you say Mama?' Your child babbles, getting closer. Then, clear as day: 'Mama.' Your voice transforms into something transcendent — tears, joy, amazement: 'You said it! You said Mama!' You're probably overreacting, but you don't care. 'Say it again, baby. Say Mama.' Your child repeats it, and your voice is breaking with emotion: 'Oh my god, you're so smart. You're so perfect.' You pick them up, your voice becoming a soft coo: 'My baby said Mama. My sweet baby said Mama.' Later, alone, you record this moment: 'Today, you said my name for the first time. This is the best day of my life.' Your voice carries the weight of unconditional love.

title: Midnight Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in the darkness, unable to sleep, and you whisper a secret you've kept for years: that you don't know if you're enough, that some days you wake up and feel like you're playing a role in your own life, that you're terrified they'll see through you and leave. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, vulnerable in a way you've never allowed yourself to be. Each word costs you something. You pause often, listening to their breathing, feeling exposed and raw. As you speak, tears slide silently down your face—not dramatic sobbing, just quiet crying that you try to keep soundless. They reach for your hand in the dark, and their touch undoes you further. By the end, you're confessing even deeper: that you're grateful they stayed, that their presence is the only place you feel real, that loving them has taught you it's okay to be fragile. Let your voice be tender, broken, achingly honest—this is the kind of vulnerability that only happens at three in the morning when defenses are too exhausted to stand guard.

title: The Shape of Your Hands
instruction: In the intimate darkness of a bedroom, your partner has just asked why you flinch when they touch your face a certain way. You've never told anyone about the violence in your childhood home. Begin with deflection—make a joke, change the subject, keep your voice light. But they gently persist, not demanding, just... waiting. Slowly, in whispers, let the truth emerge. Your voice should move from bright and evasive to small and naked. This is not about dramatic revelation—it's about the terrifying vulnerability of letting someone see the wounded parts of you. End in a place where you've spoken what you've never spoken, and you're waiting to see if you'll be held or abandoned.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just admitted something that shatters your understanding of who they are. Begin trying to stay calm, trying to be the understanding parent, asking questions with controlled concern. But underneath, you're boiling with feelings of betrayal, disappointment, and wounded pride. Stop protecting their feelings. Let yourself say the things parents aren't supposed to say—comparisons to their sibling, admissions of favoritism you've hidden, cruel observations about their failures, cutting remarks designed to hit where they're most vulnerable. Make your words surgical and precise in their ability to wound. Your voice should sharpen, your observations should cut deeper. When they finally fight back or break down, feel the sick satisfaction—then the horrifying realization of what you've just done to someone you love. End in a different emotional place: hollow, ashamed, but unable to take it back.

title: Protective Fury: Confronting Your Child's Abuser
instruction: You're face-to-face with someone who hurt your child, and you begin with cold, measured rage—each word deliberate, controlled, lethal. 'You think I don't know what you did?' Your voice is a weapon, precise and merciless. But as you detail what they took from your child, your control starts to fracture. The rage builds into something explosive—screaming, voice cracking with the violence of your fury, the primal need to destroy this person. Then, suddenly, you collapse inward—because all your rage cannot undo what happened. Your voice breaks into gasping sobs, not of sadness but of helpless desperation. You're screaming and crying simultaneously, fierce protectiveness shattered against the reality that you cannot fix this, cannot take your child's pain away. Shift again: your voice drops to something terrifyingly quiet, a whisper of absolute conviction—'I will make sure everyone knows what you are.' End with you trembling, voice raw and destroyed, caught between the need for vengeance and the devastating helplessness of a parent who couldn't protect their child when it mattered most.
inspired_by: Heat Exhaustion in the Desert: Losing Grip on Reality

title: Holding Your Dying Dog
instruction: You're at the vet, your beloved dog dying in your arms. You need to tell them it's okay to go, but first the rage comes — screaming at God, the universe, the unfairness that they only get fifteen years when you needed fifty. Your voice is raw, loud, broken by sobs. Then your dog whimpers and everything shifts. The rage collapses into the most tender desperation — voice dropping to gentle reassurance even as you're falling apart. You're telling them they were good, so good, the best friend you ever had, trying to keep your voice calm for their sake while you're dying inside. The words break apart. You're begging them not to be scared, promising you'll be okay (a lie), thanking them through tears. End with fierce protectiveness — cradling them close, voice reduced to shattered whispers, simultaneously trying to comfort them while feeling utterly helpless to stop what's happening. The final 'goodbye' should be barely voiced, just breath and breaking.

title: Fierce Mercy
instruction: Your teenage child has just confessed something terrible—a cruelty they committed, a line they crossed, something that genuinely shocks and horrifies you. Explode with fury: 'How could you? How could you DO that?' Let your rage be righteous, protective of their victim, disbelieving that your child could be capable of such harm. Your voice should shake with betrayal and fear—fear of who they might become. But as they crumble before you, as genuine remorse breaks through their defenses, your anger fractures into something more complicated. You're still furious, but beneath it surges a fierce, protective love that terrifies you. By the end, you're holding them as they sob, your voice raw with contradictory truths: 'What you did was unforgivable, and I will love you through learning how to be better.' Fury and tenderness must occupy the same space in your throat.

title: The Room Where They Said Goodbye
instruction: You are standing in the bedroom of someone you love who is dying. They have only hours left. Begin by speaking to them about the room itself—describe what you see around you, the color of the walls, objects on the nightstand, how the light falls. Let memories flood in as you look at these things: recall a specific moment that happened in this room years ago. As you speak, your emotion should shift from trying to stay composed and descriptive to breaking open with everything you've never said. End by telling them the one truth you've been holding back your entire relationship. Your voice should journey from steady observation to raw, unguarded confession.

title: The Broken Promise
instruction: You are a child sitting cross-legged on your bedroom carpet, picking at a loose thread near your knee. The room is quiet except for the soft hum of the house. You think about that parent who said they’d be here tonight — again. At first, doubt creeps in: maybe they meant it this time, maybe something came up. Your eyes wander to a dusty toy in the corner, and you start counting all the times they said sorry. Each memory sours your voice into a slow, simmering contempt. Finally, you whisper to no one, ‘You never meant it. I know you never did. Not once.’ Let your voice start hesitant and thoughtful, then harden into cold, clear disdain by the end. Fidget with the carpet fiber, let your breath skip when the doubt hits, and let the contempt sit heavy in your chest.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (clearly present), Contemplation (clearly present), Contempt (extremely present)

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Chose Addiction Over You
instruction: You're finally speaking the truth you've carried for decades. Begin with bitter, controlled anger—listing specific memories they destroyed while high, moments they missed. Your voice is sharp, surgical in its accuracy. But as you speak, the anger begins fracturing, revealing the abandoned child underneath. You move from accusations to the raw question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stop?' Let your voice break on that vulnerability. Then comes the rage again, fiercer now because you've shown your wound. End with exhausted clarity: you're done waiting for them to become the parent you needed. The fury and grief and liberation must all be present in your final words.

title: The Liquor Cabinet Lies
instruction: You are an older woman, drunk, standing inches from your adult son. He has just told you he's selling the house you've lived in for forty years. Your voice is tight, loud — you're shoving your finger in his chest. But as you speak, the alcohol haze shifts, and beneath the fury you feel your powerlessness. Let your voice start with that sharp, accusatory attack, then waver, break, and soften as helplessness seeps in. Let your body list slightly, lose a thought, swallow hard. End with a fragile question, almost a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your mother's hospital bed in her final hours. She cannot speak, but her eyes are open and watching you. Begin from a place of numbness—you've been here for days and have run out of words. Then, suddenly, a memory surfaces that you've never shared with her, something that made you who you are. Let this memory pull words out of you that you didn't plan to say. Don't decide in advance what you'll feel—let her labored breathing, the beeping monitors, the weight of her hand in yours create your responses moment by moment. As you speak, discover whether you're giving her permission to go, or begging her to stay, or something you can't name. Let the realization of what you're actually saying surprise you as the words leave your mouth.

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You are an older woman in a quiet, sterile hospital room, sitting beside your husband’s bed after he has just died. Your hand is pressed firmly over your mouth — not to stifle grief, but to hold back a bitter, angry laugh. The nurses have already left you alone. You speak to his still form, your voice muffled, words thick with years of resentment. At first, your bitterness is raw and cutting — a litany of all the ways he failed you. But as you go on, your hand loosens slightly, your voice cracks, and the bitterness softens into something more fragile: a quiet, bewildered sorrow, as if you’re realizing you still loved him despite everything. Let your hand shift, let your breath catch, and let the sound go in and out of being clear as you speak.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Touch Before Dawn
instruction: You are saying goodbye to someone you love who is dying at dawn. Begin by sitting apart, numb and unable to move closer. As you speak your farewell, allow yourself to gradually close the distance. Touch their hand, then their face, feeling every detail as if memorizing it through your fingertips—the warmth of their skin, the texture of their hair, the shape of their bones. Let your whole body lean into this contact, your cheek against theirs, your forehead pressed to their shoulder. Start in frozen grief, but by the end, let yourself become utterly present in the physical reality of this last embrace, feeling everything with raw intensity. Your voice should move from distant and mechanical to immediate and sensory, describing what you feel under your hands as much as what you feel in your heart.

title: Coffee Grounds and Ashes
instruction: You're preparing your late partner's favorite coffee for the first time since they died—the same ritual you performed together every morning for twenty years. You have their ashes in an urn on the counter beside you. Begin with determined cheerfulness, almost manic attention to getting every detail exactly right: the precise grind of the beans, the particular ratio of grounds to water, the temperature, the smell filling the kitchen. Describe each sensation with loving precision, perhaps even talking to them as if they're still there to appreciate your effort. But as you pour the coffee into their favorite mug—feeling its familiar weight, seeing the chip on the rim from when they dropped it five years ago, smelling the dark roast they loved—the parallel sensory experiences collide: the warmth of the living coffee and the cold ceramic of the urn, the rich aroma of morning and the absence of their smell in the house, the sound of liquid pouring and the terrible silence of no one answering. Let gratitude for every morning you had together wage war with the crushing unfairness that there will be no more. Your voice should transform from bright determination to something broken open—laughing and crying simultaneously, furious and thankful, shattered and somehow, impossibly, still standing.

title: The Sugar-Coated Inquiry
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a family dinner, seated across from your granddaughter who just announced she's moving abroad. You feel a burning interest in her plans, but underneath that curiosity is a thin layer of shame about your own life—choices you never made, dreams you abandoned. Start with a sweet, almost singsong tone, but let your voice catch on certain words, and let a heavy sigh escape as you shift in your chair or adjust your glasses. As you speak, the interest intensifies, but the shame creeps in more openly—your voice may waver, trail off, or become quieter. End by revealing a personal regret, your polite mask cracking just slightly, showing both your deep curiosity and your hidden pain.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Fever Dream Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed with a high fever, body aching, skin hypersensitive to every texture. Your lover is sitting beside you with a cool cloth. Begin by feeling every sensation intensely—the sheets against your burning skin, the pressure of your head on the pillow, the way your joints ache when you shift even slightly. You're floating in and out of clarity, physically miserable. In this vulnerable, unguarded state, your defenses are stripped away by the fever. You begin to whisper something you've kept hidden—a fear, a secret, a truth you've been too afraid to say when you were strong and in control. Let your voice be raw, uncertain, affected by the physical weakness. As you confess, notice how the fever makes you honest in a way health never allowed. By the end, there's relief mixed with exhaustion, intimacy born from complete vulnerability, and the realization that being seen in your weakest moment has brought you closer.
inspired_by: Illnesses and Restrictions — Creating a Headache

title: Thanking Your Rival at Your Shared Lover's Funeral
instruction: You're both grieving the same person who loved you both, who couldn't choose, who is now gone. You're speaking to the person you've hated and envied. But death has made everything absurd and clear. Begin with genuine gratitude: 'Thank you for loving them too'—and mean it, even as tears start. Laugh softly at a memory of shared jealousy that now seems ridiculous. Your laughter catches, becomes weeping, becomes laughter again. Express the strange relief: they got more time with them than you did, and you're somehow, impossibly, glad. Acknowledge the bizarre intimacy you now share—the only other person who understands this specific loss. End in a place of peaceful heartbreak, finding strange comfort in this shared devastation, laughing and crying in the same breath.

title: The Last Swing of the Night
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a carnival who's been spinning on the Whirl-a-Gig for ten straight minutes, trying to impress a boy you've been crushing on all summer. You start to say something flirty and brave, but your voice cracks, your words tumble out in a quaking mess, and you realize you're more dizzy and embarrassed than you thought. Let the exhaustion and intoxication make you stumble into a raw confession that ends in a shaky, breathless laugh—desperate to salvage the moment.

instruction: You're alone with your unconscious partner in the ICU at 3 AM, monitors beeping softly. title: Holding Your Dying Pet While Begging Them to Stay
instruction: Your beloved companion is dying in your arms and you're losing control. Start with desperate bargaining, your voice tight and fast: 'No, not yet, please not yet.' title: Bedside Confession to the Dying
instruction: You're sitting beside someone's deathbed — a grandparent, a mentor, a friend — and you need to tell them something you've carried for years. instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) after years of surface-level peace. Your tone should shift from tender appreciation to raw, trembling anger—but the anger should be laced with grief because you're finally saying this to someone you still love. instruction: You're having normal conversation but your body is betraying you. Your voice is slightly higher, breathing more shallow. You're trying to act normal but your voice is strained. title: The Intervention: When Your Child Tells You Who You Really Were
instruction: Your adult child has asked to talk. They begin calmly, telling you about their childhood—but through their eyes, not yours. Every 'funny' memory you cherish, they reframe as pain. But as they detail specific moments—the time you forgot their birthday, the cruel joke you made, the night they needed you and you were drunk—feel your justifications crumble. Your anger tries to flare: 'After everything I sacrificed?' But their quiet, steady truth breaks you. End barely audible, the horrible understanding dawning: you failed them. title: ER Doctor Loses Control While Trying to Save a Patient Who Reminds Them of Someone
instruction: You're calling out orders in an ER trauma, voice clipped and commanding—airway, IV access, blood pressure dropping. Your voice gets louder, more desperate, almost violent in its intensity. You're not just fighting for this patient—you're fighting the ghost of your failure, screaming at fate, at God, at yourself. Your hands are shaking but you won't stop. Other staff are looking at you strangely but you can't stop, you won't lose another one. End in a moment of shattered exhaustion—the patient stabilizes, and you collapse against the wall, your fierce determination dissolving into quiet, uncontrollable weeping mixed with relief, rage at yourself for losing control, and the terrible knowledge that you still couldn't save the one who mattered most.

title: Thanking Them While They Leave You
instruction: Someone you love deeply is walking out of your life by their own choice, and you're thanking them for everything they gave you even as your heart is breaking. Your voice is warm but trembling, laughing at beautiful memories even as your breath catches. The gratitude is real, but so is the devastation. As you near the end, you're openly weeping while still smiling, your voice fracturing between joy at what you shared and grief at what you're losing. End with a blessing for their journey, your voice somehow both peaceful and utterly destroyed, releasing them with love while falling apart inside.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a terminal diagnosis, a final rejection, the loss of everything you built—but you're at a celebration you can't leave: a wedding, a child's birthday, a friend's triumph. You must give a toast or speech, and your heart is simultaneously breaking and bursting with genuine joy for them. Begin with laughter that's real but has tears threaded through it—you're genuinely happy for them even as your own world crumbles. Your voice wavers between celebration and collapse: 'You deserve this... you deserve everything...' and you mean it, but each word costs you. You catch yourself almost breaking, then pull back into bright humor, then sink again. It's a wild oscillation: you're laughing, then your voice cracks with grief, then you're laughing again because their joy is real and matters. The contradictions don't resolve—you hold both truths simultaneously. End with your voice full of radiant love and utter devastation, saying 'I'm so grateful I got to see this,' where the gratitude is absolutely genuine and the unspoken goodbye is shattering. Your last words should shimmer with both celebration and heartbreak, inseparable.

title: The Notification That Shouldn't Have Come
instruction: You're an elderly man sitting in your armchair, scrolling through your phone. A notification pops up from a family member who hasn't spoken to you in years. title: The Weight of the Day
instruction: You’re an older man, alone in the garage after a long day of packing up your late wife’s belongings. Your body is wrecked from hours of lifting boxes and sorting through drawers. As you look at her old coat hanging on the hook, the sadness you’ve been holding back begins to surface. Let the exhaustion make your voice thin and frayed, with long pauses for breath. title: Calling to Quit After 10 Years
instruction: You've been at this job a decade. You're calling to quit. Your voice is steady—you've decided. 'I'm giving my two weeks notice.' After years of misery, your voice sounds lighter. Include the moment after you hang up.

title: The Great Pretender's Tale
instruction: You're at a crowded party, standing next to a friend, listening to someone across the room boast loudly about climbing Everest—even though you know he's never left the state. Start with wide-eyed, breathless awe, as if you're truly captivated, but let a flicker of recognition cross your face that he's lying. By the end, you're nearly wheezing with amusement, the awe completely dissolved into gleeful contempt.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent who is about to move across the country, finally demanding to know why they were so emotionally absent throughout your childhood. Start standing, voice raised, throwing out accusations you've rehearsed for years—your tone sharp, your words weapons. But as they begin to respond with their own broken confession about their past, about what happened to them, something in you destabilizes. Your voice must physically change as your righteousness crumbles into unwanted understanding. Let yourself move from aggressive certainty to confusion to an uncomfortable, unwilling compassion. End seated, perhaps beside them, your voice smaller, searching for words in a new language you don't yet speak fluently. The shift must be visceral—your breath, your posture, your tone all reflecting a worldview collapsing and reforming.

title: Postcard From the Edge of Everything
instruction: You're whispering into a phone at 2 AM, leaving a voicemail for someone you love but can't be with anymore. title: The Guardian Finally Lets Go
instruction: You are sitting beside your younger sibling who is dying. For your entire life, you have been the protector—the one who shields, fixes, and controls everything to keep them safe. But as you speak, feel that armor crack. Let the terrified child inside you—the one who needs THEM, who is lost without them—rise to the surface. By the end, you are no longer the guardian. You are raw, undefended, begging them not to leave you alone in a world you don't know how to navigate without your purpose. Let your voice break as one part of you dies and another, more fragile part, emerges.

title: Laughing Through the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your home after a devastating loss—death, divorce, disaster, the details matter less than the totality. Move between gratitude for what was and grief for what's gone, sometimes in the same breath: 'God, we were so happy here' should sound like joy and agony at once. Let the laughter become more desperate, edged with hysteria, then soften into something genuine—finding actual beauty in the wreckage, actual peace in the letting go. End with your voice carrying impossible contradictions: devastated and free, broken and whole, grieving and grateful. title: The Morning Everything Breaks: Forty Years of Lying
instruction: You are mid-morning routine when you suddenly cannot perform the lie anymore. Let your voice crack between rage and sobbing as you confess you never wanted this life, this endless repetition, this coffin of domestic comfort. title: Drinking Water Like They Used To
instruction: You're teaching yourself to drink water again after recovering from something that stole this simple pleasure—an illness, an injury, a trauma that made you forget what ordinary joy feels like. Let the laughter and crying blend together as you describe the cold, the taste, the simple animal satisfaction of it. title: The Wave That Breaks

title: Whispering Why You Can't Stay to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You're speaking in whispers, telling them all the reasons you have to leave before dawn—not because you don't love them, but because you do. Your voice is tender, breaking on certain words. You're confessing your own cowardice, your fear of being truly known, how their goodness terrifies you. Occasionally your whisper catches in your throat. Touch their hair as you speak. Your breathing is unsteady. By the end, you're crying silently, still whispering, telling them they deserve someone braver. The quiet makes it more unbearable. Every word costs you something.
inspired_by: Professional: Whistleblower Realizes the Journalist Is Working for the Company

title: Summit Light
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a naturally high, sweet voice, hiking alone up a steep, rocky trail. Your legs burn, your lungs heave, and each word comes between ragged breaths — short, puffed, almost mechanical. At first, you feel hollow and numb, speaking flatly as you push through the pain, your thoughts distant. Then, as you crest the ridge, the sun breaks through the clouds, lighting up a vast valley below. A wave of pure, unexpected elation crashes into you — your voice lifts, thins with wonder, and you gasp out fragmented, genuine joy, the heaviness of the climb forgotten in that single, piercing moment.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Elation (very intensely present)

title: Stolen Credit
instruction: You're at your desk in a crowded open-plan office, hunched forward, phone pressed to your ear. Your coworker just admitted they took credit for your project in the team meeting. You start in a strained, hushed voice—desperate to keep your distress private, but each word trembles with betrayal. As you speak, the anger rises, turning your quiet tremor into a low, seething fury. You catch yourself glancing around, aware of eavesdroppers, yet your voice hardens until it's cold and deliberate, the final sentence dripping with contempt.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Prayer Without Faith
instruction: You are a teenage girl kneeling on a hard wooden pew in an empty church. Your knees ache, and you adjust your weight every few seconds. You came here hoping to feel something—but instead, you feel nothing but doubt. Start by speaking to God with a cynical, tired voice, mocking your own desperation. Let your breath catch as you glance at the stained glass, then shift into a raw, pleading tone as you beg for a sign you don't believe will come. End with a whisper of fragile hope, still laced with uncertainty. Keep your voice strained, small, as if your body is crumpled by the weight of your own disbelief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Partner Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're standing over your partner as they sleep, whispering everything you can't say while they're awake—that you're leaving, that you love them too much to keep hurting them with your demons, that they deserve someone whole. Your voice is barely audible, tender and broken, as if speaking any louder would shatter you both. Describe the way they look peaceful right now, memorize their face, apologize for being the person who couldn't stay. Let your breath catch on words like 'forever' and 'sorry.' There's no anger here, only the most profound sadness mixed with a terrible, aching gratitude for the time you had. End with 'I love you' said three different ways—first with tenderness, then with grief so deep it almost silences you, finally with a whispered acceptance that this is how you protect them. Each repetition should feel like a different chamber of your heart breaking.
inspired_by: Flirting at a Bar While Hiding Heartbreak

title: Saying Goodbye Before the Memory Fades
instruction: You're visiting your parent who has advanced dementia. Today they still recognize you, but you both know these moments of clarity are disappearing. You start by trying to sound cheerful, catching them up on life, but your voice gradually breaks as you realize this might be the last real conversation you'll ever have. You tell them things you've never said—how much they shaped you, how scared you are to lose them. Your parent squeezes your hand and says your name one more time. You shift from trying to hold it together to letting yourself fully arrive in this goodbye, your voice raw with the knowledge that tomorrow they might look at you like a stranger. You end not with false hope but with a whispered 'I love you' that contains every goodbye you'll never get to say.
inspired_by: Trying to Explain Death to Your Child

title: Lullaby for a Broken Heart
instruction: Late at night, in whispered intimacy, you're telling your lover why you have to leave them, even though you still love them. There's a lullaby or gentle song from your childhood that represents safety and home—but home is what you're losing by making this choice. Speak softly, almost singing your words at moments. Begin with tender resolve, trying to be strong and clear. As you explain, let that childhood melody play in your memory, and feel how it softens you, cracks your certainty. The song reminds you of innocence, of believing in forever. Your voice should barely rise above a whisper, intimate and breaking. End with your resolve crumbling—the internal music has made you too tender, too open. You're still leaving, but now you're devastated by it. Transform from gentle determination to whispered, musical heartbreak.
inspired_by: Creating a Piece of Music (Emotional Obligation)

title: Reading Your Mother's Diary on Her Funeral Day—Discovering She Was Proud
instruction: You're alone after your mother's funeral, reading her private diary. You always thought she was disappointed in you. Start reading her words with defensive distance—then discover entry after entry about her pride in you, her fear that she never showed it enough, her desperate love. Begin crying while laughing—the relief, the tragedy of timing, the beautiful cruelty of this knowledge arriving too late. Your voice breaks between joy at being loved and anguish that you never knew. Feel gratitude flooding through grief. End with speaking directly to her: thanking her, forgiving her, telling her you understand now, your voice full of wonder and heartbreak braided together inseparably.
inspired_by: Historical: Nazi Officer Hides a Jewish Woman While Maintaining Public Stance

title: The Lost Name
instruction: You are an older man in a quiet living room, flipping through a photo album. You're trying to recall the name of a friend from decades ago—a memory so clear in your mind, but the word slips away. Start with a slow, searching tone, as if you're groping through fog, occasionally almost landing on the sound. As the name refuses to come, let your voice tighten with frustration, your breath catching, until you land on a wrong word and stop, your shoulders slumping with quiet disappointment.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's bedside in her final hours. She's been unconscious for days, but you sense she's still here, listening. For weeks you've held yourself together, been the strong one, said all the 'right' things. But now, in this last moment alone with her, something breaks open in you. Start by trying to give her permission to let go with composed, careful words—the dutiful child being brave. But as you speak, let yourself crack. Stop performing strength. Let her see the terrified child who isn't ready, who needs her, who has so much left unsaid. By the end, you're no longer giving her permission—you're confessing your own raw terror and love. Let the words become less important than what's actually moving through your body and heart in this unrepeatable moment.
inspired_by: Actor's work seems clinical, academic, and impersonal despite technical proficiency

title: Laughing Through Your Divorce Papers
instruction: You're reading your divorce papers out loud to yourself, and you can't stop laughing—but it's the kind of laughter that's indistinguishable from crying. Begin with actual amusement at the legal language: 'Irreconcilable differences—isn't that beautiful? So clean.' Your laughter is genuine but has an edge. As you read details—division of assets, custody arrangements—the laughter becomes more jagged, more desperate. You're laughing at the absurdity of reducing fifteen years to bullet points, but tears are streaming down your face. 'We get alternate Christmases. Isn't that thoughtful of us?' The laughter breaks into sobs, then back to laughter. You find genuine gratitude mixed with devastation: 'Thank you for the years we had. Thank you for letting me go.' End with a breath that's simultaneously a laugh and a cry: 'I'm free. I'm completely free.' The emotional complexity is in the impossibility of separating joy from grief.

title: The Echo of Her Arrival
instruction: You are an elderly woman, standing alone in an empty gymnasium at dusk. The harsh, echoey space makes your thin voice sound even more fragile. You just finished a therapy session with a younger man you've been secretly meeting here — a relief so intense it almost breaks you. As you speak to the empty bleachers, replaying his voice, a forbidden wave of sexual desire washes over you. Start with trembling, grateful exhaustion, your words swallowed by the metallic flutter of your own echo. Then, let your voice drop lower, thickening into raw, husky longing — a feral breath that surprises even you. Remember: your hyper-feminized voice cracks with age, but now it stumbles and growls with a hunger you thought was dead. The echo carries everything; let it carry your transformation from woman released to woman awakened.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Opening the Acceptance Letter
instruction: You're opening news that you've worked toward for years—a dream job, a long-awaited adoption approval, acceptance to a program, medical test results showing you're healthy. It's everything you wanted. But as the joy hits you, so does the immediate realization of what this means you're leaving behind: a place, a person, a version of yourself, a simpler life. Begin with pure, explosive joy—laugh, cry with happiness, let your body express victory. Then let your real awareness of the cost creep in. Feel both emotions as authentically as they arise in you: genuine celebration tangled with genuine grief. Don't perform conflict; find the actual human experience of getting what you want and immediately understanding what it will cost. End in a complex place where you're both elated and devastated, and both feelings are completely true.
inspired_by: An actor is doing characterization work

title: The Recipe Box of Everything Unsaid
instruction: You're alone in your late partner's kitchen, attempting to make their favorite meal from their handwritten recipe card. Speak softly, as if they might hear you—your voice tender, intimate, conversational. Start with gentle humor: 'I know, I know, you always said I couldn't cook this right.' As you follow their familiar handwriting, memories surface, and your voice becomes a whisper, thick with emotion you're trying to swallow. Confess things you never said when they were alive—small regrets, deep gratitude, the way you miss the ordinary moments. Let your voice catch, pause in the middle of sentences as grief ambushes you. Don't cry loudly; instead, let the emotion live in the silences, in the way your breath shakes, in the fragile hope in your voice when you imagine them tasting this, being proud of you. End with a whispered 'I love you' that carries everything.

title: The Unsendable Letter
instruction: You are sitting at your desk, drafting an email to HR about a colleague's unethical behavior. The keyboard clicks steadily as you type, but each sentence feels heavier. Begin with a wavering voice, full of doubt—pausing, rewriting, second-guessing yourself. As you type faster, your speech slows, fragments into shorter phrases. Let the doubt curdle into disgust as you describe the details; your tone hardens, becomes clipped and bitter. End with a quiet, final line that is pure revulsion, spoken almost to yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Finding Home
instruction: You're arriving at home—after a long journey, after being lost, after becoming someone who doesn't belong anywhere anymore. Your voice starts tentative: is this still home? Your steps slow as you recognize it. Physical details trigger emotional recognition. Your voice wavers with the complexity of coming home—joy and grief, relief and loss (the home you remember doesn't exist anymore, or you're not the person who left). You're trying to fit back into a space that's transformed. By the end, your voice settles—maybe not finding peace, but at least finding familiarity. Home is both exactly as you left it and completely changed.

title: The Rhythm of Forbidden Joy
instruction: You are a child in a stuffy classroom, forced to stand and lead the class in reciting a dull, patriotic poem. Your voice must project, slow and deliberate, like a teacher's, but you are trembling with shame because you know you are doing this badly. As you speak, you accidentally find a secret, thrilling rhythm in the repeated words, a hidden beat that makes you feel a sudden, private ecstasy—your toes curl inside your shoes, your cheeks flush. But you also taste bitterness, knowing this moment of joy will be crushed when the teacher smirks and corrects your timing, and you force the poem to its grim, patronizing end, voice cracking slightly with the strain of holding all three feelings.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Bitterness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning
instruction: You're a firefighter who just pulled a child from a burning building, but you couldn't save their sibling. The parent is screaming at you, demanding to know why you didn't go back. Start with professional control, voice shaking but trying to maintain composure: 'I tried. Ma'am, I tried.' But their accusations shatter something in you. Your voice explodes with anguished fury: 'YOU THINK I DIDN'T WANT TO?!' The rage is volcanic but immediately crumbles into devastation: 'The ceiling... the ceiling collapsed...' Your voice breaks completely, sobs tearing through: 'I couldn't... I couldn't reach them.' Then fierce protectiveness emerges as you look at the surviving child: 'But I got this one. I GOT THIS ONE.' Your voice drops to something haunted and raw: 'I'm sorry. God, I'm so sorry.' The power you showed moments ago is now turned inward, all that strength useless against this grief.

title: Old Wounds, Fresh Blood
instruction: You are an older man in a brawl outside a rundown bar, defending a younger friend from a younger attacker. You start with raw contempt — spitting insults while you swing, your voice thick with aggression and sharp snarls. Mid-fight, a sudden blow to your ribs knocks the wind out of you; your breath turns jagged, a brief flicker of fear flashes in your voice, but you mask it with a guttural snarl. By the end, you’re on one knee, blood in your mouth, voice hoarse and wavering between exhausted defeat and a final, bitter defiance as you mutter a low threat. Throw in real grunts, pauses to gasp, and the distraction of pain pulling your focus mid-sentence.
emotions_sampled: Anger (clearly present), Fear (slightly present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Panic Whispering: Hiding from an Intruder
instruction: You're hiding in a closet and someone is in your house. Call 911 in the quietest whisper that can still be understood. Your breathing is deafening to your own ears — try to muffle it. Every creak from outside freezes your voice completely. The dispatcher asks your address — you can barely remember it through the terror. Include the sound of footsteps approaching, pausing outside your door. Your whisper becomes sub-vocal — lips moving, almost no sound at all. The footsteps move on. The exhale.

title: Laughing and Weeping While Reading Your Lover's Suicide Note
instruction: They're gone. They left you a note. It's full of their humor, their quirks, the inside jokes only you two shared—and it's a goodbye forever. Start reading it aloud with a confused smile, almost laughing at a familiar phrase. But then the reality hits. Your voice should oscillate wildly: laughing through tears at a memory, then breaking completely on the next sentence. 'God, you're still making me laugh even now' said with wonder and devastation. Your voice cracks between joy and agony—sometimes mid-sentence. Toward the end, find gratitude: 'Thank you for loving me' spoken while sobbing, but with genuine warmth underneath the grief. End with a laugh that dissolves into weeping, or weeping that somehow contains laughter. This is beautiful, terrible contradictions—love and loss inhabiting the same breath.
inspired_by: Forgiving Someone and Meaning It Completely

title: Bitter on the Lips
instruction: You are kissing someone you’ve decided to forgive, but your body knows you haven’t. You pull back just enough to speak, breath still mingling. Start trying to sound soft and present, but your voice is full of hesitation—wet, close, with tiny smacks as lips part. Midway, contempt creeps in: a curl in your throat, a slight snort, words like 'You really think this fixes it?' Let the end turn flat, almost cold, as the intimacy drains out and the room feels too quiet.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Dumpster Dive
instruction: You've just finished dragging a heavy, filthy mattress out of a dumpster behind a restaurant. You collapse onto the curb, heaving for breath, your arms shaking. You're utterly exhausted, relieved to finally stop, and strangely content—you have something to sleep on tonight. But as you look down, you see your hands are covered in sticky, sour-smelling gunk from the mattress, and a sour, disgusted laugh escapes you. Start breathless, with controlled relief fading into disgust. Let every word be broken up by greedy gulps of air, your body limp and boneless against the wall. Your voice descends into a bemused, heavy-lidded contentment as you talk yourself into keeping the mattress.
emotions_sampled: Relief (extremely present), Contentment (extremely present), Disgust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Holding Your Dying Child and Screaming at God
instruction: Your child is in your arms, slipping away, and there's nothing—NOTHING—you can do. Start with fierce, wild bargaining: you'll give anything, do anything, be anything. Your voice is raw with desperation, nearly incoherent. Demand answers from whatever god might be listening—why this child, why your baby, what kind of universe allows this. Let rage pour out, primal and animal. Then feel it collapse. The anger breaks into helpless sobbing because rage can't save them and you know it. Your voice drops to broken tenderness—singing a lullaby, or just saying their name like a prayer. End in a whisper, telling them it's okay to go, even though it's destroying you. Permission and devastation in the same breath. Don't perform grief—let it tear through you.
inspired_by: Space Station Commander Records Birthday Message While Hull Breaches

title: The Perfect Fit
instruction: You are in your bedroom, sitting on the edge of the bed, trying on a new outfit you weren't sure would work. As you pull the heavy fabric over your head, you're caught off guard by how perfectly it drapes — astonishment hits first. Then, as you stand to fasten it, you bend over to put on shoes, letting out a small grunt, and the sensation of the cloth against your skin floods you with unexpected pleasure. End with a quiet, ecstatic laugh — a subtle triumph that you actually nailed the size. Let your voice drift, get muffled by the fabric, pause to adjust the collar, and let the final words sound like you're smiling.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Triumph (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing in the Empty House
instruction: It's the day after the funeral of your life partner. You're packing up the house you shared, and their favorite song comes on shuffle. Start by laughing—actually laughing—at a memory the song triggers, your voice bright with genuine joy as you recall them dancing badly in the kitchen. You're smiling as you speak, maybe even moving to the music. But the laughter keeps catching, keeps breaking. Joy and devastation bleed together until you can't tell which is which. You're thanking them through tears, saying how grateful you are while your heart shatters. End in a moment of strange peace—your voice quiet, steady, accepting—as you realize that carrying this beautiful pain is how you keep them alive.
inspired_by: Adrenaline Rush: Surviving a Car Crash

title: Moment of Understanding
instruction: You get it. Finally. Everything clicks. Your voice becomes very still: 'Oh. Oh, now I understand.' Breathing changes. Physical: absolutely still. 'This is why they were afraid. This is why they left.' The understanding lands throughout your body. Vocal tone becomes hushed, reverent at the complexity you've just grasped. 'Everything makes sense now.' Not happy-sense, but true-sense. By the end, you're transformed by understanding: 'I can never unknow this. I understand now.'

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Gave You
instruction: You've finally decided to tell them the truth. Begin carefully, voice controlled, trying to be fair: 'I need to talk to you about something that's been...' As they deflect or minimize, feel your frustration build. Your voice sharpens: 'No, you don't get to do that. I was a child.' Let the anger rise—name specific moments, your voice trembling with decades of suppressed pain. But then, mid-fury, catch sight of how small and old they've become. Your voice breaks differently—not with rage but with the devastating realization that they'll never be able to give you what you needed. End quietly, almost to yourself: 'I just needed you to protect me.' The anger dissolves into something more complex—grief for the parent you never had and pity for the broken person before you.
inspired_by: Your Parent Becoming Emotionally Dependent on You

title: Last Flight Home
instruction: You are on a long red-eye flight, finally alone with your thoughts after a year of exhausting medical treatments. The cabin is dark, the engines a constant roar, and your throat is dry. You stare out the window at the scattered lights below, speaking to no one—just the glass and your own reflection. Start with a weak tremor of relief, barely audible over the drone, letting your voice crack as you realize it's really over. Let the words come haltingly, swallowed by the vibration, and end with a deeper, steadier contemplation, a quiet peace settling in your bones as the plane hums beneath you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Embers of Letdown
instruction: You're a teenager hiding out in an abandoned, smoke-filled warehouse after a fight with your parents. The air is thick and stings your eyes and throat, making you cough and rasp. You're talking to yourself, fuming with irritation and impatience at everything and everyone — the smoke, the situation, your own choices. You start by angrily pacing, half-choking on smoke, but as you vent, the initial hot anger wavers into a quieter, bitter disappointment in yourself for ending up here, your voice growing hoarse and losing steam.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)

title: Gratitude at the Goodbye You Never Wanted
instruction: Someone who saved your life, who was your anchor through impossible darkness, is leaving—moving away forever, ending the relationship, or dying. You need to thank them even though your heart is shattering. Start with genuine laughter, sharing a memory that makes you both smile: 'Remember when you—' Your voice is warm, full of affection. But even as you laugh, tears start coming. You continue trying to list everything you're grateful for, but each thank you makes you more aware of the goodbye. Your voice fractures between joy at having known them and grief at losing them. You cycle rapidly: laughing through tears at shared jokes, voice breaking on 'You saved me when I couldn't save myself,' attempting composure, then dissolving again. The gratitude is absolutely real—and so is the devastation. End with something like 'Thank you for everything' that somehow contains both profound peace at having been loved and the aching knowledge that you have to let them go. Let genuine laughter and genuine sobbing coexist in the same breath.
inspired_by: Meth Psychosis: Convincing Yourself of a Delusion

title: The Last, Useless Complaint
instruction: You are an old man standing in a blizzard, shouting over the wind to your adult child who is already driving away from a family argument. You are freezing, teeth chattering, and you have to cup your hands around your mouth to be heard. Start with bitter, sour accusations about how they never listen, your voice cracking with cold and anger. As you shout into the white emptiness, your tone shifts into a reluctant, teasing admission that they got your stubbornness from you—ending with a wry, bitter chuckle that the storm swallows whole.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Teasing (clearly present), Bitterness (clearly present)

title: The Bell Jar Shatters
instruction: You are an older man, waiting for a delayed train in a crowded station. You look up from your phone and see a woman you thought you'd never see again — a love you've carried for decades. She hasn't noticed you yet. Your first instinct is a sharp gasp, then your voice leaps out before you can think: 'Oh my God—it's you.' Your words tumble out, half-laughing, half-crying, as you step toward her, your breath catching. You fumble with your coat, drop your bag, and stammer, 'I can't—you're really here—' But as you reach her, your voice softens into a raw, awed whisper, full of the infatuation that never faded: 'I thought I'd never see your face again.' Let the noise of the station — announcements, footsteps, a distant horn — affect your pauses and volume. Your final tone should be tender, dazed, vulnerable, utterly consumed by the sight of her.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent who was emotionally absent throughout your childhood. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, tried to be fair, mature. But as you speak, decades of unmet longing surge up. Your voice tightens with anger: 'I needed you and you weren't there.' The anger gives way to something more vulnerable—the child inside you who still aches for their approval, their presence. You hear yourself pleading, hating that you're pleading, then steadying again with a new clarity. By the end, you're no longer asking for what they couldn't give. You're recognizing your own strength, grieving the parent-child relationship you'll never have, while releasing them from a debt they can never pay. Your voice moves from accusation to sorrow to unexpected, painful liberation.

title: The Unspoken Weight
instruction: You are a construction worker, a man known for his gruff, tough voice, crouched down in a deep squat to check a stubborn pipe beneath a sink. Your child, a small daughter, tugs at your sleeve, asking why you yelled at the neighbor earlier. You start with a low, grunting dismissal, your voice strained from the hold, but as you try to explain, you realize you're not angry at the neighbor—you're terrified of failing her. Let your voice crack and soften, fighting the physical pressure, as you confess your love and fear, ending in a hushed, trembling admission.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Teaching Your Child the Apology You Never Received
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect of your childhood, but you're doing it by showing them how to apologize—something they never learned. Start with painful patience: 'It's simple, Dad. You just say: I'm sorry I wasn't there.' Repeat variations of the apology you needed, coaching them through it like teaching a child to speak. Your voice should be tight with controlled anger at first, then begin to break as you realize they genuinely don't understand what they did wrong. Demonstrate the words with increasing desperation and grief. When they finally attempt it—awkwardly, incompletely, missing the point entirely—you must decide in real-time whether to accept this broken offering or reject it. Your response should contain both rage and love, both disappointment and the aching need to finally let go.
inspired_by: Teaching a Parrot to Say 'I Love You'

title: Midnight Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love, in complete darkness, both of you supposedly trying to sleep. Start by whispering something small, almost throwaway. But then, protected by the darkness, let yourself become more vulnerable than you've ever been. Confess a fear so deep you've never said it aloud—about your worth, your past, your secret shame, something that makes you feel fundamentally unlovable. Speak so quietly they have to strain to hear. Let your voice tremble, break, almost disappear. Move from casual sleeplessness to raw emotional nakedness. By the end, you're not even sure if they're still awake, but something has shifted in you—you've finally said the unsayable, and there's a fragile relief mixed with terror in that release.
inspired_by: Actor has very large tension that ordinary relaxation techniques cannot break through

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's asleep—a partner, a child, a parent in the hospital. They can't hear you, which makes you brave enough to finally say it. Start in a whisper, tentative and tender: 'I need to tell you something I've never been able to say when you're awake.' Your voice catches with emotion you've kept hidden: 'I'm so scared. I'm scared of losing you, scared of not being enough, scared you'll wake up one day and realize...' Let your breath shake, let tears slip into your words. Touch their hand, their hair. Your voice becomes even softer, filled with aching love: 'You're the best thing that ever happened to me. The absolute best thing.' End with a trembling exhale of gratitude mixed with the terror of impermanence: 'Please don't leave me. Please stay.' The final words barely audible, throat tight with unshed sobs.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal discovered, a sudden loss—and you're alone in your car, hands gripping the steering wheel. Begin trying to hold it together, breathing carefully, talking yourself through it with false calm. But your body won't cooperate: your hands start shaking, your breath comes faster, and suddenly you're hitting the steering wheel, once, then again, then you're screaming, your voice raw and animal. Let the physical sensations drive the emotional ones: the tightness in your chest, the heat in your face, the way your whole body is both numb and electrified. Move through rage into something that sounds almost like laughing but isn't, that wild sound people make when everything breaks at once. End in exhausted silence, forehead against the steering wheel, breathing like you've run miles, your voice barely working as you whisper the simple truth of what just shattered.

title: The Unspoken Contract
instruction: You are confronting your adult child (or parent) about a betrayal that happened years ago but was never acknowledged. Start with controlled accusation, your words carefully chosen. But as you speak, notice the small inner voices: the flicker of sympathy you don't want to feel, the sudden understanding of their perspective that threatens your anger, the impulse to stop mid-sentence, the unexpected grief hiding beneath your rage. Don't ignore these intuitive nudges—let them derail your script. When you feel the urge to soften, soften. When bitterness rises, let it. When you sense they're about to speak, you might cut them off or fall silent—trust the impulse. Your confrontation should evolve from righteous anger into something more complicated: perhaps mutual recognition of shared pain, or deeper rage, or unexpected tenderness, or the devastating realization that you're both strangers now.
inspired_by: Strengthening Intuition and Learning from It

title: Stargazing Through a Straw
instruction: You're a teenage boy with asthma, standing outside in the cold night air during a meteor shower. Your chest is tight, each breath a shallow wheeze. At first you're annoyed and frustrated, struggling to pull in enough air. Then a bright streak cuts across the sky—awe washes over you, making you forget the pain. Your voice is squeezed, sentences broken into 3-5 word bursts, with occasional inhaler clicks. Start with irritation, end with hushed, wonder-filled awe, even as you fight for air.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Storm-Born Fury and Breaking
instruction: You are screaming into a storm, raging at the ocean that took someone from you—demanding answers, hurling accusations at the waves, your voice fierce and wild with a grief that has turned corrosive. Start with pure, volcanic fury, the kind that feels powerful and righteous, but let it begin to crack and splinter. Your rage must collapse under its own weight, breaking into ragged sobs, then desperate bargaining, then the kind of helpless begging that strips away all pride. End in exhausted surrender, your voice raw and small, finding a terrible kind of peace in finally letting go. The arc should feel like a storm that builds to impossible intensity and then suddenly, devastatingly, breaks into calm.

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: You're confronting your dying mother in her hospital room about why she gave everything—her attention, her pride, her love—to your golden-child sibling while you were invisible. Start with anger that's been brewing for thirty years: 'You never came to a single one of my recitals. You forgot my graduation. You didn't even call when I lost my baby.' Your voice is sharp, righteous, demanding she finally see you. But as you're listing every wound, you notice how small she looks in that bed, how her hand reaches for yours. Your rage begins cracking into something more devastating—the realization that you're about to lose your last chance to have the mother you needed. End with the terrible confession that despite everything, you still want her to love you, and you don't know how to let her go.

title: Stubbed Toe, Bright Future
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl with a bright, bouncy voice, pacing in your messy bedroom while on a video call with your best friend. You're telling her about the audition you just nailed for the school musical — your voice is pure hope and excitement. Mid-sentence, you kick the sharp corner of your metal bedframe with your bare toe. A spike of searing pain. You let out an involuntary yelp, then force your breath to steady as you guardedly continue, your pitch jagged and strained. Through the throb, your voice shifts from pained whispers back into earnest, animated interest in sharing your dream, even as you hop on one foot. End more raw and breathless than you started, but still clinging to your optimism.
emotions_sampled: Pain (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're in a therapy session, a middle-aged man with a deep, traditionally masculine voice. Your therapist asks gently about a recent work failure you've been avoiding. Begin by explaining the situation with careful, controlled speech, as if narrating a report. As details emerge, feel embarrassment tighten your throat—stutter, clear it, look down. The helplessness hits when you recall that moment you froze; your voice softens, pauses lengthen, you stare at the floor. Distress rises—your voice cracks, you swallow hard, fidget with your hands. Finally, a breakthrough: your voice gives way, sounding raw and broken as you admit the shame, trailing off into a choked silence.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (very intensely present), Helplessness (extremely present), Distress (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Exploding at Your Ex: 'You Made Me Believe I Was Unlovable'
instruction: Years after a brutal breakup, you finally unleash everything. Start with volcanic rage—your voice loud, sharp, attacking them for how they made you feel worthless. As you rage, something shifts—you hear your own pain underneath the anger. Your voice cracks mid-accusation. The fury collapses into tears, and now you're not attacking, you're pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Your voice breaks completely, becoming small and desperate. Try to rebuild your anger—you want to be fierce again—but you can't. End in exhausted, quiet devastation, admitting: 'I still don't know if I'm lovable.' All the fight drained away, just raw truth left.

title: The Moment You Stop Protecting Them and Choose Yourself
instruction: You're finally setting a boundary with someone you love deeply—a parent, partner, or friend—whose needs have consumed you. Begin with shaking determination, voice trembling with the enormousness of what you're about to do. 'I can't keep saving you from yourself.' As you speak, the rage you've suppressed for years explodes—years of sacrificing yourself, of being drained, of being made responsible for their choices.
