title: Professor Accusing Student of Plagiarism: Mercy in the Moment
instruction: You have evidence of plagiarism and you're confronting the student. Your voice is factual but not harsh: 'This section matches the source too closely. This is plagiarism.' Include the moment where the student breaks and admits it, often revealing the real reason: they were overwhelmed, they were scared. Your voice shifts: 'Tell me what's really going on.' Your voice becomes less about punishment and more about understanding. By the end, you're offering a path forward: 'There are consequences but there's also help. What do you need?' Your voice reflects the reality that students are humans first and rule-breakers second. You can enforce policy and also offer compassion. Your voice contains both.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just found out your child has been hiding self-harm scars for a year. You explode: 'How could you not TELL me?!' It's volcanic, terrifying in its intensity. 'I'm your mother/father! That's what I'm HERE for!' But the rage is masking pure terror. Your voice cracks: 'Oh god, what if I'd lost you?' You crumble, falling to your knees. 'Baby, what did I miss? What didn't I see?' Now you're sobbing, fierce protective love mixed with devastating helplessness. 'I would die for you, do you understand? I would DIE.' You're holding them, shaking. 'Tell me how to help. Tell me what you need. Please.' The fury transforms into raw, desperate, all-consuming love. 'I can't lose you. I can't.'

title: Lovers Reunion
instruction: Two lovers who separated are reuniting. The first voice carries the weight of absence. The second voice is flooded with recognition. They're both trying to stay composed and immediately failing. They're aware that things have changed; they've both changed. There's nervousness mixed with the deep comfort of knowing someone. They ask cautious questions and get honest answers. The conversation moves from surface to deep. At some point, one voice breaks into something like wonder: 'You're really here.' By the end, the separation has weight, but so does the reunion. Being together again is both exactly as it was and completely new.

title: The Last Morning Ritual
instruction: You're teaching your adult child how to make your mother's recipe one final time before hospice care begins tomorrow. Your hands shake from illness, but you're determined to pass this on. Start with patient, loving instruction, savoring each small detail ('See how the dough feels? That's how you know'). As you realize this is truly the last time, your voice should catch, words becoming harder to form. End by watching them complete it alone while you're too weak to continue, shifting from teacher to witness, from control to surrender. Mix pride with devastating loss, gratitude with the ache of letting go. Keep it intimate, like you're holding something precious that's slipping through your fingers.

title: The Last Bubble
instruction: You're a child who has just cried for a long time over something that felt huge—maybe a lost toy or a broken promise. Now you're completely empty, your throat raw, your nose stuffy, your eyes puffy. Your parent or sibling is nearby, trying to cheer you up by blowing a single soap bubble that drifts toward you. You're too tired to fully laugh, but a tiny, teasing smile pulls at your lips. Start with a weak, hoarse voice that's still heavy with leftover sobs, then let a dry, breathy chuckle escape as you watch the bubble wobble—your words fragile, playful, and worn out all at once.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Veil's Confession
instruction: You are a teenage boy, sitting alone in a quiet, dim room. You just took off your niqab after a long day. You're talking to yourself, your voice muffled by the fabric still pooled around your neck. You start with a sigh of relief — you're finally free from the stares and judgments. But as you speak, the relief curdles into helplessness. You realize you cannot change the world's view, and the numbness sets in, a hollow acceptance. Speak each sentence as if it's a new, heavy thought, pausing between them, your tone shifting from light to heavy.

title: Gravel and Grievance
instruction: You are an older man walking across a long stretch of loose gravel toward a meeting you don't want to attend. Every step is loud, crunching, and you have to raise your voice so anyone near you can hear. You start off muttering angry curses under your breath about the situation, your voice tight with frustration. Midway, you stutter on a loose stone, lose your balance for a moment, and your anger shifts—now there’s a quiet, helpless realization that you no longer have the control you once did. Finish the walk with a single, louder line that starts as a growl but fades into a weary sigh, as if the anger is deflating into something heavier.

title: I Will Not Let Them Take You
instruction: You are holding someone you love who is being taken away—by immigration officers, by abusers, by a system you cannot fight, by death itself. Begin with fierce, protective rage—your voice sharp and commanding as you refuse, absolutely refuse to let this happen. Escalate into desperate bargaining, your words coming faster, louder, more chaotic. Then feel the moment your power runs out, when you realize no amount of fighting will change this. Let that rage collapse into broken, gasping sobs and whispered promises that you'll find them, you'll fix this, you won't forget them. End trying to be brave for them even as you're falling apart, your voice tender and shattered at once.

title: The Empty Chair
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe nine or ten, standing at your father's open casket. Relatives are behind you, watching—you can feel their stares. You start speaking to him, trying to sound tough and grown-up, but your voice wavers and your throat tightens. You're embarrassed by the tears welling up, so you pause to swallow and glance down at your shoes. As you go on, the pretense crumbles and you let out a raw, broken sob. By the end you're crying freely, no longer caring who sees.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She can barely speak, drifting in and out of consciousness. To comfort her, you begin telling her a fantastical story—one you're making up on the spot—about a magical kingdom she once told you about when you were five years old. Start with hesitation and grief, your voice breaking. But as you weave the tale, let yourself get lost in the story's magic, your voice becoming animated, playful, full of wonder—the way you sounded as a child. You're giving her one last gift: the sound of pure imagination and joy. Let the story transport both of you away from this sterile room. End with a tender whisper as you realize she's smiling, truly at peace. Your emotion should journey from heartbroken and heavy to enchanted and luminous, even as tears stream down your face.
inspired_by: Actor has lost the joy and playfulness in their acting — it feels like work rather than play

title: Dancing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received confirmation that you're in remission, that you're going to live, and you're calling the person you love to tell them. But here's the truth: you'd made peace with dying. You'd said your goodbyes internally, let go of your dreams, accepted the end. Now you have to pick all of that back up again and you don't know if you can. Start with laughter—genuine, almost hysterical relief and joy. But let it crack into something more complex: grief for the person you became when you thought you were dying, fear of hoping again, exhaustion at the thought of wanting things. Your voice should dance between celebration and something like mourning, gratitude and resentment, 'We get more time!' and 'I don't know if I have the strength to live again.' Let the contradictions live together authentically, laugh while your voice breaks, celebrate while you're terrified.

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your spouse is in their final days, lucid for the first time in weeks. They ask you to describe the wedding you're planning for your daughter—an event they'll never see. Begin with joy, genuinely excited, painting every detail: the dress, the flowers, how beautiful she'll be. Your voice is bright, animated, almost laughing as you talk. But gratitude keeps interrupting—'thank you for being here,' 'thank you for loving her.' The joy and grief become inseparable. You're laughing while tears run down your face, describing the father-daughter dance that won't happen, saying 'she looks just like you' while your voice breaks. The celebration and the goodbye occupy the same breath. End with simultaneous laughter and weeping, telling them 'it's going to be perfect' and 'I don't know how to do this without you' in the same exhale, your voice full of impossible, beautiful contradiction.

title: Protecting Your Child From a Threat You Can't Stop
instruction: You're holding your child, telling them everything will be okay, but you know it won't—disaster is coming and you're powerless. Start with fierce, protective reassurance, voice strong and certain, the voice that has soothed every nightmare. But terror leaks through—your voice tightens, speeds up, becomes almost manic with false brightness. Then rage erupts—screaming at the unfairness, at your own helplessness, at a universe that would hurt your baby. The fury breaks into shattered sobs, still holding them, voice raw and broken. Finally, transform into something profound: you choose tenderness over despair, whispering every good thing they are, every moment of joy you've shared, making peace mean something in the wreckage.

title: The Last Dish
instruction: You're standing at the kitchen sink, washing a single wine glass by hand. The water runs constantly, loud and steady. At first, you're amused, remembering a toast you shared with someone you deeply miss. Your voice is almost playful, but then, mid-sentence, the clink of the glass against the sink hits you differently. Your amusement fades into raw, breathtaking longing. A flicker of quiet contempt for yourself—for still holding on—colors your final words. Let the white noise and the slick feel of the glass pull you through the shift.

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-lover's wedding—someone you loved desperately, who left you years ago. Start with a smile, a champagne glass raised, but let seething resentment and barely-controlled fury pulse underneath every 'generous' word. Your voice should be warm for the crowd, but let flashes of acid leak through. Then, as you speak, let real memories surface—the genuine love you shared, the beauty of what you had—and feel your heart break open with authentic joy for their happiness mixed with devastating grief for what you lost. Let gratitude for having known that love war with rage at losing it. Your voice should crack between blessing and curse, celebration and mourning. End with a genuine wish for their happiness that costs you everything to say, your face wet with tears you can't explain as either happy or sad.

title: Telling Your Parent You Needed Them (And They Weren't There)
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about the childhood you survived instead of lived. Your voice carries years of swallowed anger, but underneath is the child who just wanted to be seen. As you speak, the anger cracks open to reveal devastating vulnerability: 'I needed you to notice I was drowning.' Your voice shifts from accusation to heartbreak, from fury to the exhausted plea of someone who still, against all logic, wants their parent to finally understand. End not with resolution but with the silence of having finally spoken your truth, whatever comes next.

title: Grateful Goodbye: Thanking Your Abuser as You Finally Leave
instruction: You're packing your last box, about to walk out on someone who hurt you for years—and you realize you need to thank them. Start with genuine gratitude that sounds almost joyful: they taught you your own strength, showed you what you'll never accept again. Your voice has lightness, even laughter. But underneath, there's grief—you're mourning the love you thought you'd have, the years you gave them. Let both exist simultaneously. Your voice cracks not with pain but with the strange relief of ending. You're crying while smiling, devastated while feeling free, heartbroken while finally whole.
