instruction: Your adult child has just walked through the door after five years of estrangement—years during which you didn't know if they were alive or dead. You are flooded with simultaneous, warring emotions: overwhelming joy that they're here, savage anger at the years of silence and pain, desperate need to hold them, and bitter resentment at what their absence cost you. Begin with your voice caught between laughter and fury, words tumbling out in contradictory torrents—welcoming and accusing in the same breath. Let these opposites battle within your voice, neither winning, both painfully real. End in a moment where all the contradictions collapse into something simpler and more true: you pull them into your arms, and your voice becomes wordless—just breath, just sound, just love and pain existing together without resolution.

title: The Last Sip
instruction: You are a middle‑aged woman stranded in a drought‑scarred landscape for days. Your mouth is cracked, your tongue sticks to your palate, and even breathing feels like sandpaper. You’ve been rationing the last few drops of water in a canteen, furious at your own foolishness for venturing out here—contempt burns in your chest despite the searing pain in your throat. Now you unscrew the cap, the metal hot against your fingers, and lift it to your lips. As the lukewarm water touches your tongue, a wave of overwhelming gratitude floods through you. Let the beginning be tight, bitter, every word scraping out between dry lips. Then, as you taste the water, your voice softens, cracks, becomes a whisper of thankfulness—still parched, but now tender. The change should feel like a release: from contempt to a raw, aching relief.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (extremely present), Pain (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Meal Before Departure
instruction: You're sharing one final homemade meal with someone you love deeply before they leave on a journey they may never return from—a dangerous mission, a terminal diagnosis requiring them to move away for treatment, or an irreversible choice. As you eat together, begin with forced lightness, trying to pretend everything is normal, savoring each bite while describing the flavors they cooked for you. Let your voice gradually crack as the weight of 'this is the last time' settles in. End with the food turning to ash in your mouth as you can no longer maintain the pretense, the taste of goodbye more powerful than any flavor. Your words should move from nostalgic joy to devastating realization that you're trying to memorize this moment because you'll never have it again.
inspired_by: Eating Freshly Baked Cookies Right Out of the Oven

title: The Last Morning Before Hospice
instruction: You're sitting at your parent's bedside on their final morning at home before they enter hospice care. Begin in that same heavy, waterlogged numbness—words thick and slow, as if depression has turned you into stone. You're trying to say goodbye but can't find the energy to even cry. 'I brought you coffee. The way you like it.' Each word is Mount Everest. But then something shifts: a memory surfaces, their hand moves toward yours, and suddenly grief cracks through the numbness. Your voice breaks from that flat, gray monotone into raw, unguarded pain. End with words that finally have feeling—devastating, tender, real feeling—as you whisper what you've needed to say for years but couldn't access through the fog. The transformation is from emotional absence to overwhelming presence.

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—maybe a diagnosis, a pregnancy, a death, a divorce finalized—and you're alone in your home, body flooding with adrenaline and shock. Start frozen or pacing, breath sharp, body tight with the impact. But then a song comes on—maybe you turn it on deliberately, maybe it's playing already—and it reminds you of a time when you felt completely alive and free. Let your body respond before your mind can stop it. Move. Dance. Let the physical release unlock something—rage, grief, ecstasy, all mixed together. Laugh or sob or roar while moving. End in a state of sweaty, breathless, chaotic aliveness where the terrible news and your fierce will to survive exist simultaneously in your body. Be genuinely physical—this isn't performed movement, it's survival.

title: Anniversary of a Death: Surviving Another Year
instruction: Today marks one year/five years/ten years since they died. Your voice is reflective, sad, but also something else—you survived another year. Your voice is talking to them or talking about them. Your voice is tenderness mixed with grief. You're marking the day. Your voice is remembering. 'I miss you.' Your voice is carrying them forward. Include the moment you realize the grief has changed shape—less acute, more integrated.

title: The Lip-Reading Grandkid's Mischief
instruction: You're an older adult who is hard of hearing, speaking to your young grandchild across a noisy park. You start by calling out to them with amused but firm concern, your voice loud and deliberately slow, your words stretched and over-enunciated for clarity. Midway through, you realize they're playfully hiding behind a tree, and a wave of delighted laughter cracks through your careful speech—the volume drops a bit as you chuckle, and your tempo breaks into spontaneity. End with a warm, breathy sigh of fond exasperation, still loud but now laced with tender amusement. Let the physical effort of projecting and lip-reading awareness fade into pure, joyful connection.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Glass of Wine
instruction: You are an elderly woman, your voice weathered and feminine, sitting across from a lifelong friend after a decades-long feud. The room is quiet except for the ticking clock. You start by reciting old grievances with bitter, clipped words — each one a sharp stone you've carried. But as you speak, the bitter edge softens into something heavier: a trembling, reluctant tenderness. You pause to rub your tired eyes, glance at the half-empty glass, and your voice cracks as you realize this is truly your last conversation. Your final sentence comes out as a broken whisper, not angry, but aching with lost time.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Upside Down Apology
instruction: You’re a teenage girl with a high, sweet voice, but right now you’re hanging upside down from the monkey bars, blood rushing to your head, trying to end a phone call with your best friend who just lied to you. Your voice is thick and wet—words feel like gargling—and you keep losing your train of thought as gravity tugs at your cheeks. Start with a hesitant, breathy doubt: you need to believe her but can’t. Halfway through, a bitter edge creeps in as you realize this friendship is over, and by the end, your voice crackles with a quiet, angry finality. Micro-distractions: you pause to swallow, wipe hair from your face, and one sentence trails off as you lose your balance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Hospital Corridor at 3 AM
instruction: You're whispering to someone sleeping—your child, your partner, your parent—in a hospital bed. They can't hear you, but you need to say it. Begin with tender observations, the small things you never said out loud. Describe how their breathing sounds different now, how their hand feels lighter. Your voice should be barely audible, catching on words. The transformation you're witnessing is their fading, and your own heart breaking open in ways you didn't know possible. Move through soft memories, then the creeping terror of what's coming, then to a place of unbearable tenderness. End with a confession of something you've never admitted—a regret, a secret gratitude, a truth about how much of yourself you'd give to change this. Let your voice break. Let silence swallow some words. Some things are too big for sound.

title: The Kettle's Revenge
instruction: You are an elderly woman, standing alone in your small kitchen in the middle of a sleepless night. You are utterly exhausted, and your hand is still throbbing from where you accidentally touched the scalding kettle. As you run cold water over it, you hear the hiss in your own voice. You try to comfort yourself aloud, but your words come out flat and hollow—numb. Start with a sharp gasp and a shaky mutter about the burn, then let the sentence drift into a tired, doubtful whisper, as if you're not sure why you're even speaking. End with a slow, quiet admission that feels like a surrender to the emptiness, not to the pain.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Doubt (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Choosing Yourself: The Guilt and Empowerment of Selfishness
instruction: You're choosing yourself, which means disappointing or hurting someone else. Your voice is guilty, almost apologetic: 'I have to do this. I'm sorry.' Include the moment where you stand firm despite the guilt. 'I can't set myself on fire to keep them warm.' Your voice is learning language for boundary. The guilt doesn't disappear—it coexists with the rightness of your choice. Your voice becomes stronger: 'I'm choosing me. I choose me.' There's something almost fierce in that repetition. By the end, your voice carries the complexity: you're not happy about the hurt you've caused, but you're more alive than you've been. Choosing yourself is an act of rebellion and also an act of love—love for yourself. Your voice reflects that emergence into self-priority.

title: The Wall Hits at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You are an elderly man who always prided yourself on being tough, but now you're alone in your kitchen, the sugar from that last coffee and donut has vanished. Your body feels heavy, your hands tremble slightly as you try to lift a glass. Let your voice start with a grunt of physical irritation, then slowly deflate into something slower, more resentful. Mumble to yourself about how you used to handle worse, how this shouldn't be a big deal, let the words trail off as you lose the thread. By the end, let your voice carry a quiet bitterness — not at the crash, but at the aging body that betrays you.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Song I'll Never Finish
instruction: You're slumped on a friend's couch after taking a heavy sedative to try to sleep through a crushing disappointment. The person you were writing a song for just told you they're leaving. You're trying to play the melody one last time on a guitar in your lap, but your fingers keep slipping off the strings. Start with a quiet, slurred mutter of frustration at the missed notes, disappointment slightly present as you fumble. As you speak, let your voice slow, words dragging, and volume fade to a breathy near-whisper—trail off mid-sentence as you lose focus or nod. By the end, you simply stop caring and let the sentence dissolve into the silence of the room.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Screaming Your Love at Someone Who's Already Gone
instruction: You've just learned that someone you love has died—and you never told them. Begin in disbelief, voice tight and high, speaking to them as if they can still hear: 'No, listen, I need to tell you—' Then explode into desperate, chaotic passion—not polished declarations but raw, messy truth pouring out in fragments. Your voice should crack and soar as you confess everything: the desire you were too afraid to name, the gratitude you never expressed, the apology you owe, the future you imagined. But mid-confession, the reality hits again and your passionate intensity collapses into broken, heaving sobs. End in near-silence, voice shredded, as you whisper the simplest truth you should have said when they were alive. Make it hurt. Make it real.
inspired_by: Explaining the Internet to a Medieval Person

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: You're sitting in an empty room speaking to someone who isn't there anymore—they died, or left, or you lost them some other way. You're finally saying all the things you were too afraid to say when they could hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and raw. Start with the small confessions: 'I was jealous of how easily you loved people. I pretended not to need you, but I counted the hours until you'd call.' As you continue, the words become more vulnerable, more essential—the ways they changed you, the moments you replayed a thousand times, what you understood too late. Your voice should catch and break in places, those moments where emotion physically stops the words. End with something so tender and true it hurts to say out loud, your voice soft but no longer whispering—finally, quietly certain.

title: The Sweetness That Remains
instruction: You're alone in the kitchen late at night, eating your late partner's favorite ice cream—the one they always kept in the freezer, the one you haven't been able to touch for months. Speak in barely more than a whisper, as if talking to them in the dark. Start with tentative description, the cold a shock against your grief-dulled senses. Let the flavor unlock a specific memory—their laugh, the way they'd steal bites from your bowl, how they'd close their eyes in contentment. Your voice should be intimate and fragile, trembling between past and present tense, between 'you loved this' and 'you love this.' Let the sweetness hurt. By the end, you're not sure if you're tasting ice cream or tears, but you're grateful for this small connection to them, even as it breaks your heart open again.
inspired_by: Enjoying a Rich Spoonful of Ice Cream

title: Echoes of Grace
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gruff voice, standing alone in a stone cathedral. You came in feeling clumsy and out of place—your boots scrape loudly, you nearly knock over a candle stand, and the vast silence feels like a judgment. You start speaking defensively, with embarrassed mutters about how you don't belong here. But as your voice hits the stone walls and comes back as a warm, slow reverberation, you begin to feel a strange relief. The sound wraps around you, and your words shift from self-conscious to awed. Speak deliberately, letting pauses hang. End with a quiet, grateful whisper.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Stolen Breath
instruction: You're a young woman who just found your little sister hiding in the bathroom, clutching a half-drunk bottle of a parent's energy drink. Your heart is slamming against your ribs. Sounds feel sharp and distant. You start talking fast, trying to sound firm like an adult, but your voice keeps cracking with doubt and a thin, rising fear. Midway through a sentence, a floorboard creaks somewhere, making you flinch and whisper your next words. You start with forced control, but by the end, your words tumble out raw and pleading, your sternness dissolving into a desperate hug.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (slightly present), Distress (slightly present), Fear (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Favor You Forgot
instruction: You're at a casual gathering of friends-of-friends, standing awkwardly by the snack table. A stranger you barely recognize approaches and thanks you for helping them move last weekend—but you have no memory of it. Start with a confused, hesitant laugh, your voice trailing off as you search for the memory. Then let bitterness creep in as you realize you're only thanked by people you don't know, while your own friends never notice. End with a forced but genuine attempt at gratitude, your voice catching between sincerity and resentment, punctuated by an uncomfortable silence and a quick topic change.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Confusion (extremely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Sensory Deprivation Tank: Time Becoming Meaningless
instruction: You're in a sensory deprivation tank, floating in saltwater, complete darkness and silence. Your voice initially is anxious: 'How long has it been? Ten minutes?' You're trying to orient yourself to reality through narration. But as actual time passes and you lose track, your voice changes. It becomes almost ethereal, less grounded. 'Time is... am I still here?' Include the moment where you're not sure if you're narrating something that's actually happening or if you're having an internal experience that's indistinguishable from reality. Your voice carries spiritual weightlessness. 'There's no boundary between me and the water. Between now and then.' Your voice becomes almost not yours, or becomes everything at once. You're touching something that changes how you understand existence and your voice reflects that. When the session ends, returning to normal awareness is almost shocking.

title: Confronting Your Mother in the Water
instruction: You're teaching your mother to float in the lake, just as she never taught you—she was always too busy, too anxious, too absent. Start with gentle instructions, patient and calm, but as you describe the water supporting her, your resentment surfaces. 'Feel how it holds you? That's what I needed. That's what you never gave me.' Your voice hardens with years of unmet needs, the anger of a child who had to learn to hold themselves up. But as she finally relaxes in your hands, something breaks in you—you see her fear, her own lack of support, the generational wound. End with your anger dissolving into a complicated tenderness, your voice thick with the impossible task of forgiving while still hurting.
inspired_by: Floating on Your Back in a Calm Lake

title: Taking a Deep, Cleansing Breath of Fresh Forest Air
instruction: Inhale deeply, taking in the cool, earthy air of the forest. Describe the freshness, the faint scent of pine and moss, filling you with a sense of clarity and calm. Speak with a tone of peaceful satisfaction, as if each breath cleanses you, grounding you to the natural world around you.

title: Shattering the Glass Cathedral
instruction: You're protecting someone you love from danger, and the fierce, primal power of that protectiveness explodes out of you. Begin with cold, controlled rage—you're a weapon, focused and deadly. Your voice should be hard, sharp, dangerous. As you speak, that control begins to fracture. The rage intensifies but cracks start to show: underneath the fury is absolute terror because you cannot guarantee their safety, you cannot control this outcome. Let your voice escalate into something wild, almost feral, as protective instinct wars with helplessness. Your words should feel like physical blows—violent, desperate. Then let it all collapse: mid-rage, you break completely, and suddenly you're begging, your voice raw and exposed. The fierceness dissolves into anguished vulnerability. End with your voice shaking, stripped of all armor, as you admit the unbearable truth: you would burn the world down for them, and it still might not be enough.

title: The Last Touch Before Departure
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your childhood home—the tree in the backyard where you carved your name decades ago, where you kissed your first love, where you sat grieving your father. Run your hands along the bark one final time, knowing you'll never return here. Start with tender nostalgia as you trace familiar grooves, letting memories wash over you with warmth and affection. Let your voice crack as the reality hits—this is truly goodbye. End in a place of grateful devastation, thanking the tree (and really, your past self, your lost loved ones, all the versions of you who stood here) while your heart breaks. Your words should feel like a whispered love letter to everything you're leaving behind.
inspired_by: Touching the Bark of a Large, Old Tree

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your parent's bedside in their final hours, and you need to tell them it's okay to let go. Begin with false brightness, trying to convince them (and yourself) they'll get better. But as you speak, the truth crashes over you—this is goodbye. Your voice breaks as you shift from denial to acceptance. Tell them about all the ways they shaped you, how you'll carry them forward. By the end, you're whispering through tears, giving them permission to stop fighting, promising you'll be okay even though you're not sure you will be. The final words are both a release and a shattering—tender, grateful, and utterly devastated.

title: Unraveling Underneath
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy lying on a bed in a dimly lit room, your partner's head between your legs. This is the first time anyone has done this to you, and your mind is a tornado of confusion—'Is this right? Are they enjoying it? Am I doing something wrong?' while your body betrays you with overwhelming sensation. Start by trying to form full sentences, maybe asking a halting question or mumbling a thought, but as the intensity builds, your words break apart into fragmented gasps and high-pitched moans. By the end, your voice is just pure, breathy sound—a desperate, rising pitch that unravels into silence, your grip on the sheets tightening as confusion gives way to wordless surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Jumping into Gratitude
instruction: You're an older woman in a plyometric class, struggling to keep up. Your voice is high and soft, but each jump forces a sharp 'hup!' and cuts your words on landing. Begin with confusion—why are you doing this, you can't find the beat, your thoughts are scattered between jumps. As you land, a pang of gratitude hits: thankful for your body, for the chance to move. Your final words, shattered by a jump, shift from bewilderment into heartfelt thanks.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Defense Attorney
instruction: You're cross-examining the witness in a case where you're defending someone you believe is guilty. The witness is a child who was traumatized by what happened. You have to discredit her testimony without appearing cruel. Start with a gentle, almost warm tone designed to establish rapport. Then methodically start poking holes: 'Are you sure it was dark? Could the lighting have been different?' Each question is technically appropriate. Each one makes you feel disgusting. Your voice tightens. The judge warns you. You adjust—becoming even more polite, which makes it worse. End the cross-examination and sit down, defeated by your own competence.

title: Hard Hat, Heavy Heart
instruction: You're a construction foreman on a noisy site, wearing a hard hat with a visor. Your son just called to say he's dropping out of college. A crane alarm blares overhead. Start by shouting in raw distress — about the alarm and the news — your voice pitched, cupped by the hat. Mid-sentence, your tone cracks: you pause to wipe sweat, glance at the crane, then soften into fierce affection as you beg him to reconsider. Let a flicker of disappointment seep through your plea. The arc goes from panicked frustration to vulnerable, tender desperation.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Affection (clearly present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Peace Discovered
instruction: You're experiencing profound peace—in your body, in your heart, in your connection with your partner. Everything that's been restless has settled. Your voice is soft, calm, almost meditative. You're not striving; you're being. You're not performing; you're simply present. Your voice is the sound of someone who's discovered that peace is possible with another person. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's finally home in themselves and in connection with another human being.

title: The Weight of Feathers
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner in the dark, speaking in hushed tones after they've asked why you've seemed distant. Begin by whispering about all the small, beautiful things—how grateful you are for them, how lucky you feel, how you see magic in the ordinary moments you share. Your voice should be soft, almost dreamlike, painting everything in golden light. But as you continue, let the truth beneath that brightness begin to surface: you're terrified. Terrified of losing this, of your own capacity to destroy good things, of being loved this deeply. Let your whisper become more fragile, more trembling. End with a quiet confession that you don't know how to accept happiness without waiting for it to end, your voice barely audible, vulnerable as a child admitting they're afraid of the dark.

title: The Tea That Turned
instruction: You are an older woman with a honeyed, hyper-feminine voice, settling onto a park bench with your vape pen. You take a long, slow drag, holding the vapor in, amused at how ridiculous the whole ritual is—you feel like a dragon trying to be ladylike. As you exhale, you notice a frantic squirrel who has just stolen a bag of chips from a toddler; your astonishment cuts through your smoke-thick speech, words coming out half-giggled. The amusement stays, but now it's laced with a thrilled disbelief as you share this absurd little disaster.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reading Your Suicide Note Out Loud—And Laughing
instruction: You wrote this note weeks ago, planning to end your life. But something shifted—you got help, you're still here, and now you're reading it out loud as an exercise in healing. Start reading your own words about despair and hopelessness with quiet, painful recognition—yes, you felt that way. But as you continue, something absurd strikes you: how melodramatic some of it sounds, how you spelled a word wrong, how you ended it with 'sincerely' like it's a business letter. Laugh—shocked, maybe inappropriate, but genuine. The laughter catches you off guard, mixing with tears. Feel gratitude flood in: you're here, you're alive, you get to find this ridiculous. But underneath the relief is grief for the person who wrote this, who hurt that badly. End with your voice thick with emotion: 'I'm so glad I didn't send this,' laughing and crying simultaneously, holding both the pain and the impossible, miraculous fact of your survival.
inspired_by: Deaf Person Speaking for the First Time with Cochlear Implant

title: The Unwelcome Thought
instruction: You are lying beside your partner in the warm, quiet aftermath of intimacy. Your body is completely relaxed, breathing slow and deep, voice caught in that dreamy, unguarded space where every word comes out with a soft rasp. You feel a deep, satisfied pride — in the connection, in yourself, in the way your partner's hand rests on your chest. But then you remember something from work: a deadline you forgot, an email you should have sent hours ago. The pride curdles into impatience, a tight irritation at being pulled back into the world. Speak slowly at first, letting the pride color your words, but let your voice tighten and your breath shorten as the irritation takes over. Let the thought interrupt your serenity, and voice that frustration with a low, gravelly edge. End with a sigh that’s more annoyed than content.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispered Confession
instruction: You're in a crowded hallway at school, leaning close to your friend's ear so no one else hears. You just saw the person you're completely infatuated with, and you can't stop gushing about how they smiled at you. Keep your voice low and tight, almost a monotone, with sharp, careful words. Start with that giddy excitement leaking through the hushed tone, but as you notice a teacher walking nearby, a flicker of fear creeps in—you rush the last few words, ending in a worried hush.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Adult Child Confronts Parent Who Chose Addiction Over Them
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent after years of silence. Begin with controlled, rehearsed anger—this is a speech you've practiced, words you've held back for decades. Your voice is steady, almost cold, listing the birthdays they missed, the promises they broke. But as you speak, something shifts. The anger starts fragmenting into confusion, then into the voice of the child you were—'Why wasn't I enough?' Your tone transforms from righteous fury to bewildered pain to something more dangerous: the realization that you still, despite everything, love them and hate yourself for it. End with your voice caught between rage and a sob, between wanting to destroy them with your words and wanting them to finally, finally see you. Let your voice become the battleground between adult anger and childhood longing.
inspired_by: Professional: Priest Comforts the Dying While They're Losing Their Own Faith

title: The Interrupted Scolding
instruction: You are a mother who has just caught your child drawing on the wall with permanent marker. You are angry and ready to deliver a stern lecture. But as you start speaking, you feel a sneeze building. You try to suppress it but fail, sneezing loudly. The sneeze throws off your anger, leaving you congested and struggling to hold onto your stern tone. Your voice is stuffy, nasal. You try to continue scolding but the anger fades into tired exasperation. Let the physical sensation of the sneeze (sharp intake, explosion, recovery) affect your speech rhythm. Your words may trail off as you lose focus. End with a sigh and a mumbled threat that lacks force.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Breaking the Porcelain
instruction: You're confronting your mother about something she did when you were twelve that has shaped every relationship you've had since. Start with your body tight, your voice controlled—you came here with a script, with exact accusations you've practiced. But as you speak, let the practiced words crumble. Feel the anger in your hands, the child's confusion still living in your throat. Don't perform the confrontation—let it devolve into the messy, contradictory truth: moments where you lose your words entirely, where your voice cracks, where you say things that surprise even you. Allow yourself to move from cold rage to something more vulnerable and frightening—the raw need underneath the anger. By the end, discover whether you're asking for an apology or for her to see you, finally, as real.
inspired_by: An actor feels restricted and self-conscious when trying to say the exact written dialogue

title: Little Pilot
instruction: You're a mother picking up your eight-year-old son from his first hockey practice. You walk into the noisy, sweaty locker room full of dads and older brothers high-fiving and yelling encouragement. Your son is beaming, helmet under arm, skates half-tied. You start loud and proud, affectionate and a little embarrassed to be the only mom in here—your voice carrying over the echo of lockers slamming. But as you crouch down to fix his crooked skate lace, the boisterous room fades. You soften, almost forgetting there's anyone else. Your voice becomes quiet, tender, a little shaky with pride as you realize he's growing up. The other dads' chatter returns as you stand, and you end with a gruff, teary-eyed 'Alright, star player—let's get you some hot chocolate.'
emotions_sampled: Affection (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Embarrassment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Crack in the Formation
instruction: You are an elderly woman, a former drill sergeant, now leading a small-town ceremonial parade. At the start, you bark out a crisp, volume-heavy command—‘Attention on deck!’—your voice flat, clipped, and carrying across the field. But as you catch a young recruit trip over a flag rope, then see a dog chase a pigeon through the ranks, a suppressed laugh builds in your chest. You clear your throat hard, but your voice wobbles, a snort escapes, and you end with a half-laughing, half-command: ‘At ease... oh, there he goes. All right, bring it in.’ Let the amusement bleed through your vocal cracks and your body’s tremors.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Moment You Can't Protect Them Anymore
instruction: Someone you love fiercely—your child, your partner, your younger sibling—is in danger or pain you cannot stop. Start with frantic energy, your voice sharp with protective fury: 'I won't let this happen to you.' Feel the desperation as you promise things you cannot deliver. But as the reality sinks in—that you're powerless—your voice begins to break apart. Rage dissolves into helpless tears. You move from shouting denials to collapsed, sobbing confessions: 'I can't fix this. I can't save you.' Your breath comes in ragged gasps. Feel the physical pain of loving someone you cannot protect. End in a place of broken-open tenderness—still fierce in your love but devastated by your human limitations. Let your voice carry both the warrior and the one who has to surrender, the protector who must admit defeat while still holding them close.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Attracted to Someone Who Was Just a Friend

title: Safe at Last
instruction: You’re a teenage boy lying on the ground after being pulled from a collapsed structure. Your leg is broken—you feel the bone grinding when you try to shift. You can barely breathe without searing pain, so you stay frozen, voice tight and breathy. Then you hear a rescuer shout that your little brother is safe. A wave of relief crashes over you, so powerful your body goes limp, tears prick your eyes, and your voice becomes shaky but lighter. Speak the words as the relief takes over, your tone softening from strained to trembling gratitude.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're a soldier calling your mother from a secure line before deploying on a mission you know you won't survive. You start with forced cheerfulness, voice bright and steady: 'Hey Mom, just wanted to hear your voice before I go.' But she knows. The silence on her end cracks something open in you. Your voice begins to fracture—the military composure dropping away word by word. You try to maintain the lie, but your voice betrays you: it softens, becomes younger, more desperate. By the end, you're no longer a soldier—you're her child again, and the words 'I'm scared, Mom' come out in a voice you haven't used since childhood. The transformation from professional soldier to frightened child must be visceral and inevitable.

title: Protecting What You Cannot Save
instruction: Your teenage child just confessed they're struggling with thoughts of suicide. Start with your voice exploding in fierce, almost angry protectiveness: 'No. Absolutely not. I won't let you—' You're desperate to command them to live, as if love and volume could fix this. Your voice is raw, nearly shouting promises: 'I'll fix this, I'll get you help, I'll—' Then mid-sentence, you crumble into complete helplessness. The rage collapses into sobbing terror because you suddenly understand you cannot save them by force of will. Your voice breaks into pleading whispers: 'Please. Please, baby, please.' End with your voice stripped of everything but naked fear and love, reduced to repeating 'I love you' like it's the only spell you know.

title: Screaming at God After Your Partner's Suicide
instruction: You're alone—maybe in your car, maybe in an empty house, maybe in the middle of nowhere. It's been building for days and suddenly it erupts. Start with your voice tight, controlled: 'You could have stopped this.' Then let it explode—scream, rage, demand answers from a God you're not even sure you believe in. Your voice is raw, ugly, guttural: 'Where were you?!' Pound something. Your fury is enormous but it keeps cracking into anguished sobbing: 'I would have—I could have—' You're cycling between rage at the divine, rage at your partner for leaving, rage at yourself for not seeing the signs. Your voice breaks on their name. By the end, you're on your knees, voice hoarse and broken down to a whisper: 'Please bring them back. Please.' The rage has collapsed into helpless, childlike begging. You're shattered.
inspired_by: Telling Your Partner Your Sexual Needs Aren't Met

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral While Your Heart Disintegrates
instruction: You're a ghost attending your own funeral, and it's absurdly, darkly funny—the lies people tell, the performance of grief from people who barely knew you. Start with bitter, breathless laughter at the hypocrisy. But then someone speaks—maybe the one person who truly loved you—and the laughter catches in your throat, transforms into something broken. You're trying to keep laughing because if you stop you'll fall apart, so humor and devastation fight for control of your voice. You're making jokes through tears, finding the cosmic joke in death while simultaneously drowning in the beauty of having been loved. Your voice should do impossible things: giggle while sobbing, find gratitude while raging at the unfairness of mortality. End with a sound that's simultaneously laughter and weeping, acceptance and protest, peace and agony—all at once, because that's what it means to be human and to have existed at all.

title: Grandmother's Last Recipe
instruction: You're teaching your grandmother's signature recipe to an empty kitchen, knowing she died this morning before she could show you one last time. Start with determined cheerfulness—you promised her you'd learn it, and you're keeping that promise. Speak as if she's right there beside you: 'Okay, Grandma, I'm starting with the butter, just like you said.' As you go through each step, the reality seeps in—she'll never correct you, never taste this, never nod with that proud smile. Your voice should fracture and rebuild multiple times. End in a whisper, holding an imaginary spoonful out to where she would stand: 'Is it right? Please... is it right?' Let the question hang in the silence of her absence. This isn't about cooking—it's about desperately trying to hold onto someone by performing the rituals they loved.
inspired_by: Mother Singing to Her Stillborn Child

title: Dancing Through the Diagnosis
instruction: You're describing the absurd, manic energy of hitting your step goal on the day you received life-changing medical news—walking in circles around the hospital parking lot, laughing and crying simultaneously. Start with almost hysterical amusement at the contradiction: your body failing you while you force it to move, your tracker celebrating as your world crumbles. Let genuine laughter mix with tears as you recount the bizarre details—doctors calling you back inside, concerned, while you're doing laps. Your voice should oscillate between giddy and broken, finding strange joy in the absurdity while grief runs underneath. End with a moment of profound, peaceful acceptance, your voice settling into something tender and grateful—for your body, for movement, for being alive to feel anything at all, even this. The emotional texture should be kaleidoscopic: grief, humor, gratitude, and peace all swirling together indivisibly.

title: Things I Mistranslated on Purpose
instruction: Late at night, you're confessing to your younger sibling all the times you deliberately mistranslated between your parents to protect them. 'When Dad said you were his biggest disappointment, I told you he said he was proud.' 'When Mom called you a mistake, I said she said she was grateful.' Speak softly, almost whispering, as if the walls might hear. Start with a gentle, protective tenderness—you did this out of love. But let that shift as you confess the weight it put on you, the years of carrying everyone's pain alone, the way it made you feel like a liar in both languages. End with your voice catching, barely audible: the quiet revelation that you don't know who you would have been if you'd been allowed to tell the truth. The kind of emotion that sits in your throat like a stone.
inspired_by: Caught Between Two Arguments in Different Languages

title: Under the Visor
instruction: You are a young woman in a bright pink hard hat, standing on a construction site at dusk. You came looking for your father, but the shift has ended and he's not here. The noise of the site is a constant roar — drills, backup beeps, distant shouts. You start by yelling his name over the noise, your voice sharp with annoyance and impatience. But as you scan the empty scaffolding, the anger drains. Your hyper-feminized voice wavers, the hard hat feels like a dome trapping you in a moment you can't fix. Your final words drop into helplessness, spoken almost to yourself, small and breaking, as you realize he might have left without you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Shuttle Home
instruction: You're an astronaut saying goodbye to your child via video transmission before embarking on a one-way mission to establish humanity's first colony on a distant planet. You'll never see them again, never hold them, never attend their wedding or meet your grandchildren. Start with forced optimism and excitement about the 'adventure,' your voice bright and encouraging. But as you speak, the reality crushes you—your breath catches, words falter. You try to give them life advice for all the years you'll miss, but halfway through you break, allowing yourself thirty seconds of raw grief before you gather yourself. End by finding genuine peace in your sacrifice, voice soft and sure, telling them this matters, that love transcends distance. Your voice must travel from performance to devastation to transcendence.

title: The Velvet Trap
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman at a community garden meeting, cornered by a younger board member who dismisses your decades of experience with a patronizing smile. Begin by agreeing with her, your voice calm and measured, but let a tremor of fear creep in—the fear of being erased. As you continue, let that fear curdle into contempt: your vowels stretch, your pitch rises into a mocking, nasal caricature of her own voice as you describe her 'brilliant' new plan. End in a trembling mixture of bitterness and a quiet, exhausted surrender, your words faltering as you realize nothing you say will matter.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing Through the Ruins
instruction: You're with someone you love in the aftermath of something catastrophic—a diagnosis, a loss, a disaster that's upended everything. But somehow, absurdly, you're both finding moments of laughter. Begin by trying to process the enormity of what's happened, voice unsteady, searching for words. Then let something strike you as darkly funny—the cosmic joke of it all, the absurd timing, the ridiculousness of your own earlier worries. Laugh, really laugh, even as you're crying. Let joy and devastation exist simultaneously in your voice. Talk about what you're grateful for even as you acknowledge what you're losing. Your voice should dance between tones: wonder and grief, peace and panic, acceptance and rebellion. End in a moment of strange grace—finding beauty or meaning or connection in the middle of chaos. Let your final words be both heartbroken and somehow, inexplicably, full of light.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from your hospice bed. Your voice is thin, careful—you have maybe days left, and you're trying to say goodbye without making them feel guilty for the distance between you. Start with practiced calm, almost casual: 'Hey, it's me. I'm okay, I just wanted to hear your voice.' But as they respond, something in you breaks open. The words you've held back for decades start spilling out—not angry, but achingly honest. 'I needed you' becomes 'I forgive you' becomes 'I love you anyway.' Your breath is shallow, your energy fading, but paradoxically you've never felt more alive, more present. End with a whispered revelation: you're grateful for this moment, even now, even like this. Let your voice carry both the weight of dying and the strange, unexpected lightness of finally being honest.
inspired_by: Crevasse Rescue: Hearing the Rope Appear Above You

title: Saying What Was Never Said
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) about a wound from years ago that has shaped your entire life. Start with rehearsed anger—the speech you've practiced in your head for years. But as you speak, notice what else is actually alive in you right now: the part of you that still wants their approval, the exhaustion of carrying this, the love that coexists with the rage, the fear that speaking this truth will destroy what little connection remains. Don't ignore these contradictory feelings—let them interrupt your planned confrontation. Stumble. Restart. Let your voice break not just from anger but from the vulnerability of being truly seen. End in a place emotionally different from where you began—perhaps softer, perhaps harder, but transformed by speaking the unspeakable.

title: The Last Stack of Her Letters
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting alone at a cluttered desk, sorting through a pile of your late wife's old letters. Your hands are slow and stiff as you shuffle the yellowed pages; sometimes you pause to read a line, mumbling the words under your breath. Start with a deep, weary sadness — you're so tired, every movement feels heavy. Midway, you find an envelope with her handwriting on it that you've never seen before, and a thin thread of fear tightens in your chest — what if she had a secret? By the end, after opening it and reading a simple love note, the fear dissolves into a quiet, peaceful ache. Let your voice crack and soften, with long silences where you just stare at the paper, and let the shuffle of papers punctuate your words.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Fear (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're screaming into the void after losing custody of your children, alone in your apartment. Start with controlled anger: 'They said I wasn't stable enough. Me. The one who gave them everything.' Your voice escalates to rage: 'I WORKED THREE JOBS! I held them when they cried! I was THERE!' Let your voice crack into raw anguish. The rage collapses: 'What did I do wrong? What did I...' Begin to sob, then catch yourself. Your voice becomes dangerously quiet, protective: 'No one will ever love them like I do. No one.' Build again to fierce desperation: 'I WILL get them back. I will be enough.' Then break completely, whisper through tears: 'I have to be enough. I have to.' End in exhausted, heartbroken determination.

title: The First Sound of Your Voice
instruction: You are a young man with a deep, rugged voice, but right now you can barely speak. You’ve just seen your lover after months apart, and as they hold you, the sobbing takes over. Each breath jerks inward like a reverse hiccup, your throat thick with mucus, your vowels wobbling. Start with raw, gasping longing, letting the pain of separation spill out. Then, as you finally say their name, let a wave of relief—and a flicker of hungry desire—break through the cracks in your voice, ending in a trembling, exhausted whisper.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Relief (slightly present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Half-Twisted Longing
instruction: You are in a cramped yoga class, mid-way through a seated spinal twist. Across the room is someone you've been secretly infatuated with for weeks. You catch their eye and, half-caught in the pose, you manage a clumsy, breathy whisper of a compliment—something about their laugh. As you hold the twist, your voice strains, half from the physical effort and half from the rush of emotion. The words come out more tender and vulnerable than you intended, and by the end, a sudden wave of embarrassment mixes with the affection, leaving you flustered and quiet.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Affection (clearly present), Distress (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Glass Wall
instruction: You're sitting on a plastic chair in a hospital corridor after being told your partner might not wake up. Your body is present, but your mind floats somewhere above, watching. Speak to yourself in a flat, measured tone, as if narrating someone else's life—every word technically correct but disconnected. Let a thread of longing slip through when you mention the morning routine, then a cold, distant anger at the nurse's 'we'll keep you updated.' End with a hollow realization that you're already gone, your voice dropping to a near-whisper, empty.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Longing (clearly present), Anger (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Dining Table Reckoning: Telling Your Parent You Weren't Protected
instruction: You're thirty-five years old, sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table. You've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times, but now that you're here, your voice is smaller than you intended. Start with careful words, almost apologetic—'Mom, I need to talk to you about something that happened when I was twelve.' Your tone is gentle, almost protecting her, because that's what you've always done. But as you continue, as she deflects or minimizes or doesn't understand, something shifts. Your voice gains strength, then heat. There's anger, yes, but underneath it is a child's bewilderment: 'You were supposed to see. You were supposed to know.' The anger cracks open into raw vulnerability. Your voice might break completely. You're not shouting; you're pleading. You need her to hear you, to really hear you, maybe for the first time. End in a place of exhausted honesty—you've said it, you can't unsay it, and you don't know if she'll ever truly understand, but you've finally stopped protecting her from the truth. There's grief in that, and there's also a strange, fragile relief.
inspired_by: Watching the Tsunami Build: The Moment You Understand You Were Wrong About the Warning

title: The Landing's Surprise
instruction: You are a teenage submissive, just coming down from an intense scene, wrapped in a blanket while your partner holds you. You feel astonishment wash over you—not fear, but a raw, confused surprise at how safe you feel after such vulnerability. Your voice is tiny, shaky, almost childlike; you whisper between sips of water they offer, and you pause when their hand brushes your hair. Start in shock, your words catching and breaking, then slowly let a quiet, hesitant affection creep in as you realize you're truly cared for. Speak about 40-80 words, feeling the exhaustion and surprise, ending with a fragile trust.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: First Responder Breaking Down After Saving Everyone But One
instruction: You're in the shower still in your uniform because you couldn't make it further. Everyone is calling you a hero—you saved seventeen people. But you're replaying the eighteenth in your head, over and over. Start with fierce, almost violent self-recrimination: 'I had them, I HAD them.' Your voice should be raw, guttural. The rage is at yourself, at the universe, at the impossible mathematics of catastrophe. But let it shatter into helpless sobbing—the kind that takes your breath away. Cycle between fury and devastation. End exhausted, your voice hoarse and small, whispering 'I'm sorry' to someone who can't hear you, broken by the weight of being almost enough.
inspired_by: Pilot Congratulating Crew While Processing Near-Catastrophe

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're standing over your child's bed, knowing you won't see them again—maybe you're leaving to protect them, maybe you're terminally ill, maybe circumstances are tearing you apart. You whisper things they'll never hear: apologies for what you couldn't give them, pride in who they're becoming, instructions for a life you won't be part of. Your voice is barely audible, catching on words like 'brave' and 'remember.' You're trying not to cry because you don't want to wake them, so everything stays trapped in your throat. You tell them about the parent you wanted to be versus the one you were. End with the hardest sentence you'll ever say—either 'Goodbye' or 'I'm sorry' or 'You were enough.' Your voice should sound like someone's heart is being pulled apart one whisper at a time, intimate and devastating and unbearably tender.

title: Adult Child Confronting Parent Who Chose Addiction Over Them
instruction: You're finally telling your parent what their absence cost you. Begin with measured control—reciting facts, specific memories of waiting for them. 'I was eight years old at that recital.' But the control fractures as decades of unmet longing surge forward. Your voice hardens with anger: 'You chose the bottle every single time.' Then the anger collapses into raw vulnerability: 'I needed you. I still need you.' Ask them directly: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Move from accusation to heartbreak to the smallest flicker of desperate hope that they might finally see you. End quietly, almost childlike, waiting for an answer you've needed your whole life.
inspired_by: Parent Hearing Their Child's Abuse for First Time

title: Last Words to My Child Through the Airlock
instruction: You're an astronaut speaking to your child through a failing communication system as your oxygen runs out on a damaged space station. Begin with calm, practiced reassurance—you've rehearsed what to say in an emergency. 'Listen to me, sweetheart. Daddy's going to be fine. I need you to be brave.' Your voice is steady, almost gentle, the way you'd talk them through a nightmare. But as you realize these are truly your last moments, your composure fractures. The professional astronaut dissolves and you become just a parent who will never see their child grow up. Your final words shift from reassurance to desperate love—raw, breaking, all pretense gone. 'You were the best thing I ever did. You were—' Let the emotion strip away every layer of training until only the most fundamental human grief remains. End with your voice barely holding together, thick with tears, as you try to fit a lifetime of love into seconds.

title: Dancing While the World Burns
instruction: You've just received the worst news of your life, but you're at a celebration you can't leave—a wedding, a party, a moment of joy for someone you love. You must give a toast, speak words of hope and happiness, even laugh. Start with genuine warmth, celebrating their joy, your voice lifting with real affection. But let the disconnect begin showing—a laugh that catches wrong, brightness that feels too bright, gratitude for their happiness while your own world is ending. The emotional whiplash should be visceral: finding yourself actually moved by their joy even as your heart is breaking, feeling both the beauty of this moment and the agony of your hidden grief. End with a genuine blessing for their future, your voice full of love and devastation at once, somehow meaning every word while falling apart inside.

title: The Rage That Breaks Open at the Wedding
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, and they're marrying someone you know will hurt them. You've spent the whole evening being the awkward guest, making uncomfortable jokes, drinking too much, trying to swallow your truth. But now, in a private moment, you explode. Start from that place of agitated, barely-contained energy—pacing, laughing bitterly, unable to stand still. Then let it erupt: fury at them for not seeing it, fury at yourself for not speaking sooner, desperate passion as you beg them not to do this. Your voice should shake with the force of it, words tumbling over each other, breaking apart. But then—collapse. Let the rage fracture into helplessness and grief. You can't save someone who doesn't want saving. Your voice should drop to something broken and tender, admitting your own powerlessness, your own fear of losing them. End in exhausted love: 'I'll be here when you need me,' spoken with both fierce loyalty and the devastating knowledge that you might watch them suffer and be unable to stop it.

title: The Joy Study: Narrating Your Child's First Steps While Your Heart Breaks
instruction: You're narrating your toddler's first wobbly steps in documentary style, but you know you won't be here to see them grow up (terminal illness, deployment to probable death, whatever makes this bittersweet). Your voice radiates genuine joy and pride: 'Remarkable! The young specimen demonstrates bipedal locomotion!' You're laughing, encouraging, celebrating this perfect moment. But underneath, your voice keeps catching with profound sadness. Mix pure delight with devastating awareness: 'Look at you go, little one...' where the wonder is real but edged with goodbye. End with the documentary voice failing as you scoop them up, laughing and crying simultaneously, whispering both celebration and farewell: 'I'm so proud of you. I wish... God, I wish I could see everything you'll become.' Let joy and heartbreak be completely intertwined.
inspired_by: Nature Documentary Voice for Your Roommate's Morning Routine

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are lying beside someone you trust completely, in the intimate darkness after vulnerability. In a barely-there whisper, confess the specific fantasy you've never told anyone—the one that makes you feel most exposed, most yourself, most afraid of judgment. Start tentative, testing whether it's safe. As they listen without pulling away, let yourself go deeper, more detailed, more honest. Your voice should be soft but increasingly free. This isn't performance—it's revelation. Let shame gradually transform into tender self-acceptance. By the end, you're breathing easier, feeling seen rather than scrutinized.
inspired_by: Actor has sexual obstacles or blocks that limit their presence, appeal, or ability to handle sexual material

title: The Wilted Bloom
instruction: You are a young girl who has been poisoned by someone you trust—your own mother. You're slumped against a cold wall in a dim, cluttered room, your body heavy, your vision swimming. You start by whispering, barely audible, a garbled stream of disgust at the metallic taste in your mouth and the betrayal blooming in your chest. As your consciousness fades, your words become laced with a cold, deliberate malevolence—a final curse aimed at her, your voice trailing off into a breathy, venomous whisper, as if your hatred is the last thing keeping you alive.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Distress (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Someone Who Set You Free
instruction: You're speaking at a funeral or memorial for someone whose death, while devastating, also freed you from something - perhaps an abusive relationship that ended when they died, or a parent whose passing released you from years of caregiving that consumed your life. Begin by sharing a memory that makes you genuinely laugh - something absurd or darkly funny about them. Let yourself really laugh, finding the humor. But as you laugh, let it become complicated: tears mixing with the laughter, your voice wavering between joy at the memory and grief at the loss, between relief at your freedom and guilt for feeling that relief. Your tone should become increasingly layered - gratitude for what they gave you, sorrow for what they never could be, peace that it's over, and love for them despite everything. End with a moment of surprising grace: thanking them for the lessons learned, even the painful ones, finding genuine peace in the contradiction.
inspired_by: Acting Interested While Bored in a Conversation

title: Chlorine and Regret
instruction: You're an older man doing slow laps in a public pool, head above water, gasping for air between strokes. A much younger swimmer just passed you effortlessly, and now you're pretending to rest against the wall, but your chest burns with bitterness. As you tread water, you mutter to yourself—voice hollowed by the slosh and reverb of the surface—about how you used to be faster, but your words get interrupted by sputtering and a sudden wave of embarrassment when you realize a lifeguard is watching you. Start with acidic, self-justifying bitterness, then let the humiliation creep in as you trail off, swallowing pool water and shame.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protecting a Child from the Truth You Can No Longer Hide
instruction: You're telling your child something that will shatter their world—you're sick, you're leaving, their other parent isn't coming back, the home they knew is gone. You start with fierce parental strength, desperate to shield them even as you deliver the blow. Your voice is controlled, almost artificially calm, using the tone you've always used to make them feel safe. But their questions, their face, their fear—it breaks you. Your protective rage at the universe crashes into your own helplessness. Let us hear you fight to stay strong while falling apart, trying to be their rock while crumbling, voice rising with desperate love and fury at your own powerlessness before collapsing into shared tears. This is about the moment a parent's armor shatters because love is bigger than strength.
inspired_by: Hiding Nervousness During an Important Interview

title: The Hidden Treasure
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe eight or nine, standing in your carpeted bedroom. Your dad just left after a visit, and you're holding the small, wrapped gift he gave you. At first, you feel a deep ache of disappointment — you wanted to stay with him, not get a present. But as you slowly unwrap it, your voice trembles with surprise: it's the exact model spaceship you've been drawing for months. Your words shift from a quiet, sad murmur to a breathless, rising elation, then burst into pure, joyful awe. Let the carpet muffle your feet as you shift weight, and let your voice crack with excitement as you whisper to yourself, 'He remembered. He really remembered.'
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Disappointment (very intensely present), Elation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Lap Home
instruction: You are an older man swimming laps alone in a quiet indoor pool. Your body is heavy with years of strain, but the rhythm of the strokes is familiar. As you turn your head to breathe, you catch glimpses of the ceiling tiles, the echo of water slapping the tiles. At first, the thoughts come in fragmented bursts—a recent goodbye, a decision that still stings. Each gasp for air carries a little weight of sadness, a flicker of confusion. But as your lungs burn and your arms push through the water, something shifts. The repetition becomes a meditation. Your words now, squeezed out between strokes, are not about the pain but about the acceptance settling in your chest. You speak to yourself, to the water, to the memory of someone. Your voice is urgent, clipped, a little wet from swallowed pool water, but by the end, a deep contentment fills each breath. You realize this is exactly where you need to be.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Confusion (slightly present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning: Watching Them Sleep One Final Time
instruction: You're standing in the doorway watching someone you love sleep, knowing this is the last time you'll see them before you leave on a journey you won't return from. Begin by describing what you see - their breathing, the way the light falls, small details you've memorized. Let tenderness fill your voice. Then shift: speak directly to them in a whisper, telling them what you wish you'd said years ago but were too afraid. Your voice should crack with the weight of unsaid things. End by saying goodbye without using the word goodbye - instead, tell them what you hope their life becomes. Start peaceful and observational, move through aching regret, arrive at bittersweet blessing. Speak as though touching something fragile.
inspired_by: The Final Words: What You'd Actually Say

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in the wreckage of everything you built—a marriage, a career, a dream that consumed you—and something has shifted. You start laughing, and it's real laughter, bewildered and a little unhinged. 'It's all gone. Everything. It's actually all gone.' But the laughter tangles with tears, and you can't tell which is which anymore. Your voice carries both grief and strange, terrifying freedom. 'I gave everything to this and it meant nothing. Nothing!' Feel the relief mixed with devastation. You're mourning and celebrating simultaneously. 'I'm free. Oh god, I'm free and I've lost everything.' End in that beautiful, impossible space where profound loss and unexpected joy occupy the same breath, where your voice breaks into laughter that sounds like crying, or crying that sounds like laughter—a sound that could only come from someone who has survived their own ending and found something true in the ashes.

title: Holding Your Child Through the Unthinkable
instruction: Your child is suffering something you cannot fix—an illness, a loss, a pain that no parent should have to witness. Begin with fierce determination, your voice strong and protective, trying to be their rock, their certainty. But as you speak to them, reassuring them, the reality of your own helplessness begins to crack your composure. Let your voice break with the rage of a parent who would tear the world apart to spare their child but cannot. Move through anger at the universe, at the injustice, at your own powerlessness. Then let that rage collapse into something more primal—raw grief, desperate love, the kind of tenderness that feels like it could destroy you. By the end, find a place where your voice holds both the fierceness of protection and the utter vulnerability of being unable to shield them from this pain. Let yourself sob, then gather yourself to whisper the words they need to hear, even as your heart is shattering.

title: The Weight of What We Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside your estranged best friend's hospital bed at 3 AM. They're sleeping, sedated, and you finally have the courage to whisper everything you never could say to their face. Start so quietly it's almost just breath: 'I should have told you... God, I should have told you so many things.' Your voice is tender, full of regret: 'You were the only person who ever really saw me, and I was too afraid to let you all the way in.' Confess the moment you realized you loved them—not romantically, but deeper than that—and how that terrified you into pulling away. Your throat catches: 'I chose loneliness over the risk of losing you. How stupid is that?' They stir slightly, and panic makes you freeze, then continue even softer: 'Please wake up. Please come back, and I promise... I promise I'll be brave enough this time.' End with your hand covering theirs, voice breaking on a whisper: 'I'm here. I'm finally here.'

title: The Crush Interview
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy in a job interview at a local bookstore. You've rehearsed your answers perfectly, but the moment the interviewer smiles, you forget everything. Start by reciting your prepared lines with forced calm and slightly over-enunciated words, but feel your focus drift as you notice how kind their eyes are. Let your voice falter, lose the sentence midway, then recover with a quiet, honest compliment that surprises even you. The end should feel raw and vulnerable, the professional mask cracking to reveal genuine infatuation.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Garden You Burned
instruction: You are confronting your father after twenty years of silence. You've just discovered he knew about the abuse you suffered and did nothing. Begin with cold, controlled fury—your words are sharp, your body rigid. You tell him exactly what his silence cost you. But as you speak, a specific sensory memory interrupts you: the smell of tomato plants from the garden you used to tend together when you were eight, the feeling of warm soil under your small hands, the taste of sun-warmed cherry tomatoes he'd let you pick, the sound of the hose spattering against leaves. These sense memories flood through you, and your rage begins to crack. Your voice breaks. The anger is still there, but now it's mixed with the devastating loss of that safe, simple time. End with a question that contains both fury and longing: 'What happened to the man who taught me how things grow?' Your emotional journey moves from ice-cold rage to a raw, exposed wound where anger and grief are inseparable.

title: The Last Lap
instruction: You are an older man out on your morning run, pushing hard up a familiar hill. Your breath is ragged, your legs burn, and your voice shakes with each pounding step. As you pass the spot where you and your son used to race, you mutter to yourself—first just words of stubborn encouragement, forcing yourself forward. But midway, a sharp stitch in your side makes you falter, and you slow to a walk, the shame of not being who you once were creeping in. By the end, you stop completely, panting, and admit quietly, almost to yourself, that you can’t keep up anymore. Let the shaking breath and rhythmic stride shape every word; let exhaustion dominate at first, then let shame and resignation soften your voice as you trail off.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Healer and the Cursed Warrior
instruction: Narrate a scene where a healer with a compassionate, gentle voice tends to a warrior who speaks in a pained, gruff tone. Switch between the healers soothing words and the warriors stubborn resistance, exploring themes of healing and pride.

title: The Phone Call
instruction: You are a middle-aged man lying face-down on your bed, your face pressed into a pillow. You've just received news that your closest friend has died. You're trying to say goodbye, but your words are muffled, choked with sobs, and you keep having to stop to breathe or wipe your nose with the back of your hand. Your voice is thick, breathy, and almost entirely absorbed by the fabric. Start with a desperate, raw cry of denial, then let that slowly dissolve into a quiet, broken whisper of acceptance. Allow your voice to crack, trail off, and be interrupted by involuntary shudders. The micro-movements of your body—shifting, curling, pressing harder into the pillow—should be audible through the muffling.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Visored Rejection
instruction: You are a knight in full helm, standing alone in a torch-lit courtyard after being passed over for a promotion. Your voice echoes metallically through the visor, each word slightly muffled with a subtle ring. Begin with a hollow, confused disappointment as you replay the ceremony, your breath fogging the narrow eye slit. As you speak, let the envy creep in — a tighter, sharper tone, your jaw clenching inside the helm, the visor clanking as you shift your head. End with a bitter, whispered admission, the metal amplifying the sting of your own jealousy. Include natural pauses to adjust the helm or wipe a bead of sweat from your eye, letting the clinking metal punctuate your words.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (extremely present), Confusion (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Never Gave
instruction: You are standing at your best friend's wedding reception, champagne glass in hand, preparing to give a toast. But here's the truth: you are deeply, painfully in love with them, and watching them marry someone else is destroying you. Begin with a bright, performative smile, your voice warm and celebratory as you start the toast. But as you speak about how you've known them for years, about the journey you've witnessed, let the genuine love seep through—and with it, the grief. Your voice should carry both authentic joy for their happiness and barely concealed heartbreak. Let these contradictions fight in your throat: you mean every word about their deserving love, AND you're dying inside. Maybe your voice cracks once and you cover it with a laugh. Maybe you have to pause to 'collect yourself' while everyone thinks it's happy tears. End with a final blessing that is simultaneously the most generous and most devastating thing you've ever said, raising your glass while something inside you quietly shatters.

title: The Soldier and the Enemy Spy
instruction: Depict a soldier with a firm, authoritative voice interrogating an enemy spy who speaks in a calm, calculating tone. Switch between the soldiers aggressive questioning and the spys measured responses, heightening the stakes as truths are revealed.

title: Laughing at the Wake
instruction: You're remembering your best friend who just died, starting with a story that makes you genuinely laugh—their ridiculous habit, an absurd inside joke only you two shared. Let the laughter be real and full. But mid-laugh, let it catch in your throat. Continue the story but now you're laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice breaking between genuine amusement and grief. By the end, you're thanking them through tears for giving you this specific memory, for being exactly who they were, for leaving you with laughter even now. End with a whispered 'I miss you' that holds both deep peace and shattering loss. Let joy and heartbreak be completely, authentically intertwined.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Addiction
instruction: You're finally telling your parent exactly how their choices destroyed your childhood—not with screaming, but with surgical precision. Begin with controlled anger, your voice steady and cold, listing specific moments they missed, promises they broke. As you speak, the anger begins to dissolve into something more painful: the desperate child inside you who still needed them. Your voice wavers between fury and pleading—'Why wasn't I enough to make you stop?' The rage you've held for years collides with the grief of a child who just wanted to be loved. End with exhausted resignation mixed with a sliver of hope, asking if there's any part of them that regrets it, your voice raw and small.

title: Dancing at Your Daughter's Wedding
instruction: You're dancing with your daughter at her wedding, and you're dying—she doesn't know yet. You decided not to tell her until after her honeymoon. Start with pure joy, laughing, telling her how beautiful she is, how proud you are. But as the song plays, the weight of what's coming crashes over you in waves. You find yourself laughing and crying simultaneously, unable to separate the emotions. 'I'm just so happy,' you say, and it's true, but your voice breaks on 'happy.' You're memorizing this moment—the way she smells, her hand in yours, this perfect day you won't see repeated. By the end, you're holding her face, smiling through tears, whispering: 'You're going to be so happy. You're going to have such a beautiful life.' And it's both the most grateful and most heartbroken you've ever been, blessing a future you won't witness, finding peace in her joy even as your heart shatters.

title: Burning the Letters You Never Sent
instruction: You're reading aloud letters you wrote to someone who destroyed you — love letters, angry letters, letters begging them to come back — before setting them on fire. Start fierce and defiant, voice sharp, reading your own desperate words with contempt for how weak you once were. As you continue, the defenses crack — your voice becomes ragged, words catching in your throat as you're ambushed by the memory of how much you meant every word. End in something like surrender, your voice dropping to something broken and honest, watching the pages burn while saying one final thing you never got to tell them. Move from protective rage through unwanted vulnerability to exhausted release, letting every emotion crash through you without control.
inspired_by: Phone Sex Operator on Their First Day

title: The Last Word on Pie Crust
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a casual backyard barbecue with your adult grandchildren and their friends. They are excitedly discussing a new app, and you feel a flicker of irritation at their chatter, mixed with embarrassment that you can't follow. You shift in your chair, let out a small sigh, then abruptly change the subject to your award-winning pie crust. Mid-sentence you lose your train of thought, pause to pick up a napkin, then reclaim it with growing pride, ending on a note of triumphant confidence.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Triumph (extremely present)
