title: The Voice I Lost When You Left
instruction: You're recording a final voicemail to someone who died before you could say goodbye. Start by trying on different tones—cheerful deflection ('Hey, just calling to catch up!'), casual bravado ('I'm doing fine, really'), even anger ('You had no right to leave like that'). But none of them feel true. Your voice keeps cracking, restarting. Finally, the masks fall away and you're left with raw truth: 'I don't know how to be myself without you here to reflect it back to me.' Let the silence stretch. Then, barely audible, admit the thing you've been avoiding: you're not sure who you are now that they're gone. End with your voice so small it's almost a whisper, saying their name like a question you'll never get answered.

title: The Fading Light
instruction: You are an elderly man in a quiet hospital chapel, whispering because the space demands silence. You gaze at a stained glass window that always brought you peace—now you notice it’s being removed for renovation. Begin with awe: let your breath carry the wonder as you trace the colors with your eyes, your voice barely a gust of air. As the realization sinks in, shift to deep disappointment, your whispered words cracking with loss, helplessness threading through each exhale. Let your body feel the weight of age and the stillness around you, faltering mid-thought before you force the truth out: 'They’re taking it down. That’s it... gone.'
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Disappointment (very intensely present), Helplessness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are in the grip of an overwhelming physical sensation - perhaps the ecstasy of touch after years of loneliness, or the return of feeling to a numb body after grief, or pain that awakens rage you've suppressed for years. Begin with your body's raw, unfiltered response - gasping, shaking, unable to control your physical reactions. Let sound escape from deep in your body, not from your throat but from your gut, your chest, your core. As the sensation builds and crests, let it unlock an emotional truth you've been holding in your muscles and bones. The physical experience should trigger a psychological breakthrough - perhaps fury finally finding its voice, or pleasure reconnecting you to the will to live, or pain forcing you to acknowledge what you've been running from. End transformed: spent, raw, but finally inhabiting your own body again.
inspired_by: Actor is depressed and cannot access creative energy

title: Passion Igniting
instruction: An idea has seized you completely. Your voice is fervent, almost religious: 'This could change everything if we just—' Words pour out, rapid and certain. Breathing is shallow with excitement. You're seeing possibilities everywhere. Physical energy is visible in vocal energy. Your voice is pitched up, resonant. You're trying to convince, but more importantly, you're convinced. 'I don't care if it takes ten years, I'm doing this.' There's no doubt. The passion is audible in every syllable—it's not performed, it's combustible.

title: The Last Call Home: A Parent's Final Confession
instruction: You're calling your adult child from hospice, knowing this is likely your last conversation. Start with the practiced cheerfulness you've always used to shield them, voice steady and reassuring. But as you try to say goodbye, decades of unspoken truths begin breaking through. Your voice fractures as you confess the decisions you made that hurt them—the moves for your career, the absences, the times you chose ambition over presence. You're not asking forgiveness; you're simply unable to leave without them knowing you saw it all, you knew what you were doing, and you've carried that weight every single day. End with genuine love breaking through the regret, your voice raw and stripped of all pretense, telling them the one true thing that matters before the line goes silent.
inspired_by: Professional: Executive Prioritizes Profit Over Employee Lives

title: Whispering to Your Unconscious Lover: Confessing What You Never Dared Say
instruction: Your lover is unconscious in a hospital bed, and you're finally saying what fear kept locked inside. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, as if speaking louder might shatter this fragile moment. Start with gentle observations—their hands, their breathing—your tone tender but guarded. Slowly, let vulnerability seep in: you're confessing fears you've hidden, admitting how terrified you are of losing them. Your voice catches on certain words, emotions threatening to overwhelm you, but you keep it quiet, almost like you're afraid they might hear. Midway, whisper the confession you've been protecting: maybe about your own failures, or how deeply you need them, or a secret that's been a wall between you. Your breath becomes uneven, tears audible in your throat, but you stay quiet—this is too sacred for loudness. End with a whispered promise or plea, your voice breaking with tenderness and desperate hope.
inspired_by: Falling Through Ice: Cold Shock and Survival Instinct Battling Panic

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording your final message to Earth before entering a region where communication will be impossible forever. Begin with careful composure, trying to sound brave and professional, but as you describe the beauty of what you're seeing—stars, nebulae, the overwhelming vastness—your voice cracks with the realization that you'll never see another human face again. You're trying to tell your family you love them, but the words keep catching in your throat. The wonder of discovery fights with the devastating loneliness. You start strong, trying to be the hero they need you to be, but end barely whispering, your breath shaking, as you realize this goodbye is forever and you're more terrified than you've ever been.

title: The Vet's Waiting Room
instruction: You are an elderly man with sudden hearing loss after a fall, sitting in a crowded VA hospital waiting room. Your dog, a retired service animal, is at your side. The man across from you just muttered something under his breath about 'people who can't control their animals.' You hear only fragments, but catch the contempt. You start speaking loudly and bluntly, your voice uncalibrated—too loud, pitch wavering. Defend your dog, but as you recount their years of service, your contempt for the stranger softens into a rough, reluctant pride. Your voice needs to shift from aggressive volume to a quieter, distracted crack as you lose your train of thought, remembering. End with a gruff but tender pat on the dog's head.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Homecoming
instruction: After years away, you're standing at the door of the home you left behind, about to see the person you abandoned. Before you knock, pause and feel everything: your breathing, the weight of your body, the sensation of your hand raised to knock, the sounds from inside, the familiar smell of this place. You're flooded with contradictory feelings—part of you filled with joy to return, part of you sick with guilt, part of you angry at what drove you away in the first place. As you finally knock and the door opens, let yourself stay connected to all the physical sensations of this moment: your voice trembling as you speak, the rush of feeling in your chest, the weakness or strength in your legs. Begin in a place of brittle, defensive hopefulness, trying to control the contradictions, and allow the flood of competing emotions—love and resentment, gratitude and rage, relief and regret—to wash through you until you can no longer separate them, ending in a complex emotional state that holds everything at once.

title: The Lost Key
instruction: You are an elderly man, stiff and thick-voiced, bent over trying to pick up the house key that slipped under the car seat. Your diaphragm is crushed, blood rushes to your head, and every word sounds strained and congested. Start by concentrating hard on reaching the key—grunting, swearing under your breath, completely focused on the task. End with a laugh that cuts off because you run out of breath, still stuck but amused by the whole situation.

title: Last Words to a Departing Soldier
instruction: You're at a military airfield saying goodbye to your younger sibling who's deploying to a war zone. But as you hug them, feeling how thin they've gotten in training, your voice fractures. The words 'Come back to me' come out as a desperate whisper, almost a prayer. You pull back, trying to smile through tears, touching their face one last time. Your final 'I love you' is steady but weighted with everything you can't say—all your fear, all your pride, the possibility you might never see them again. Let the silence after those words carry the full gravity of this moment.

title: What You Never Said at the Dinner Table
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table where you ate dinner as a child. Start by methodically cataloging the sensory reality—the grain of the wood, the specific way the light hits his face, the smell that's always been in this house, the sound of the refrigerator humming. Build the world piece by piece. As these details accumulate, they begin to unlock buried feelings. Let the sensory experience dissolve into raw emotional truth—suddenly you're not just seeing him, you're feeling every moment of disappointment, every unspoken hurt, every time you needed him. Begin controlled and deliberate, almost cold. End with your voice breaking as decades of silence finally shatter. The room hasn't changed, but everything has.

title: The Bitter Toast
instruction: You are an elderly man, a former master carpenter, at your grandson's award ceremony. Everyone expects you to give a proud toast. You stand, raise your glass, and force a smile. Your voice starts tight and higher, with hollow, fake warmth—‘Here’s to the boy.’ But as you speak, the praise curdles. You pause, stare at the glass, feel the weight of years of your own unrecognized work. Your voice deepens, turns gravelly and acidic. The last words spill out with open contempt and malice, a cold whisper that cuts the room.

title: The Prisoner and the Guard
instruction: Portray a prisoner with a defiant, rough voice and a guard who speaks in a stern but weary tone. Switch between the prisoners attempts to provoke and the guards efforts to maintain control, exploring power dynamics and empathy.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from a hospital bed, knowing this is your last chance to speak. Start with nervous, overly-cheerful small talk—commenting on the weather, asking about their garden—your voice tight with the effort of keeping it light. As the conversation continues, let your facade crack. The forced brightness gives way to quiet desperation as you try to say everything that matters in the time you have left. End with a whispered confession of love or forgiveness that you've never been able to say before, your voice breaking not with drama but with the simple, devastating truth of mortality. Let the transition be gradual and inevitable, like watching someone finally stop pretending.

title: Waiting for the Call
instruction: You're a teenage girl sitting on a high stool in the kitchen, phone clutched in your hand. You’ve been waiting for news about your best friend who didn't come home last night. Your body is coiled, feet barely touching the floor, core tight. You try to sound composed when your mom asks if you've heard anything, but your voice is strained, higher than normal. As you speak, you feel the helplessness rising—your words falter, you glance at the blank screen, your chest tightens. title: Trembling in the Hold
instruction: You are a teenage girl in a power yoga class, holding a deep lunge with your arms stretched overhead. Your muscles are shaking violently, your breath comes in ragged ujjayi waves, and you can barely keep your balance. You're intensely infatuated with the cute guy two mats over, but you feel a crushing shame about your body trembling so obviously and your face turning red. As you hold the pose, you start to contemplate why you even care so much—then a small shift: you decide to stop judging yourself and just breathe through the burn. Your voice should be strained, breathy, with a tremor that mirrors your shaking limbs; start with a self-critical whisper, then gradually soften into a quiet, determined acceptance.

title: Whispering to the Sleeping
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you betrayed years ago—a friend, a sibling, a lover—who is now in a coma and may never wake. In the quiet of 3am, you finally say everything you've been too ashamed to voice. Begin in barely audible whispers, your voice thick with unshed tears, confessing what you did and why. Let the guilt make your breathing uneven, your words broken. As you speak, allow yourself to remember the beautiful moments you shared before everything shattered, and let that bittersweet tenderness flood through you. End with a plea for forgiveness you know may never come, your voice catching on the realization that this one-sided conversation might be your only chance, mixing desperate hope with quiet devastation.

title: The Vigil Where Everything Is Funny and Terrible
instruction: You are sitting with someone in their final hours, and you're remembering your entire relationship—but you're laughing. Start telling a story about something ridiculous they did, some absurd moment, and you're genuinely laughing, the kind that makes your voice light and young. But mid-laugh, grief catches you, and suddenly you're crying while still smiling, your voice doing both at once. You keep talking, mixing hilarious memories with devastating ones, your tone shifting second by second—gratitude soaked in sorrow, joy wrapped in goodbye. Tell them thank you for the strangest things, your voice breaking and mending and breaking again. End with something so perfectly them, so funny and heartbreaking simultaneously, that you're laughing through tears, your voice full of love and absolute devastation, grateful for every moment and destroyed that there won't be more.

title: The Reunion Touch: When Bodies Remember Everything
instruction: You are seeing someone again after years apart—an ex-lover, a friend you lost, someone who knew your body as well as their own. The moment you touch—even just a handshake or brief embrace—your body floods with sense memories that override your intention to be casual. Let specific physical memories cascade through you: the exact pressure of their hand on your back, the particular way they smelled after rain, the sound of their breathing during a specific night, the texture of their skin, a moment of explosive joy, a moment of betrayal or pain. Begin trying to maintain composure, trying to be appropriate, but let your body betray you—your breathing changes, your voice cracks or drops, your hands shake or reach without permission. Allow the physical sensations to be so vivid they're almost overwhelming: heat, cold, electricity, nausea, desire, rage, all mixed together. Don't push toward any single emotion—let them war within you. By the end, arrive at either complete honesty about what this physical proximity awakens in you, or the exhausting recognition that you must leave before you completely come undone.

title: The Phone Call You've Been Rehearsing
instruction: You're finally calling someone to tell them you're getting married, having a baby, got your dream job, or achieved something you've worked toward your whole life. You should be purely happy—but as you dial, you're flooded with complicated grief because the person who should be here to celebrate isn't: they're gone, or estranged, or became someone you can't reach anymore. Begin with trying to sound excited, forcing brightness into your voice, attempting to perform the joy you think you should feel. But let the absence crash through—mid-sentence, between breaths—until you can't maintain the pretense. Allow yourself to rage at the unfairness, to weep for what's missing, and to feel genuine joy all at once, these emotions tangling together until you can't separate them. End in a place where you hold both the celebration and the loss in the same breath, honoring the beauty and the ache as equally true.

title: The Last Ting of a Firefly
instruction: You're a teenage girl standing in a hot, crowded school auditorium during a summer assembly. Your knees feel weak, the room is spinning, and you're trying to hold onto the last clear thought before you go down. Start by noticing a small detail—a fly on the window, the smell of sweat and floor wax—speaking in a quiet, contemplative whisper, as if to a friend beside you. As your vision tunnels and your legs buckle, let your voice lose its grip: each sentence gets softer, more breathy, trailing off into silence. Let the feeling shift from a sharp awareness of the world around you to a gentle, almost peaceful resignation as you finally let go.

title: The Last Phone Call: Saying Goodbye to Your Child Before You're Gone
instruction: You're calling your adult child from a hospital bed, knowing this is the last conversation you'll ever have. You begin trying to sound strong, almost cheerful—wanting to protect them, to leave them with something good. Your voice is steady at first, even warm, as you tell them how proud you are. But as you continue, the weight of everything unsaid begins to crack through. Your breath becomes shallower, not from physical pain but from the crushing enormity of goodbye. By the end, you're whispering the things you always meant to say—'I'm sorry,' 'You were enough,' 'You were always enough'—and your voice dissolves into something barely audible, tender and broken, as you realize you're out of time.

title: Breaking Spell
instruction: You're under a spell, and your voice is controlled—smooth, beautiful, artificial. Something—a word, a memory, a pain—begins to break the spell's hold. Your voice cracks slightly. The artificiality becomes more visible. You start fighting against the control, and your voice becomes rough, straining. The spell is fighting back, and you're wrestling with your own vocal cords. Freedom is agonizing. By the moment you break free, your voice is hoarse and raw. The final words are your own again, and that authenticity is almost painful after the false smoothness. You sound like yourself, finally.

title: The First Real Breath
instruction: You are alone in your bedroom after a severe asthma attack, still sitting on the edge of the bed, chest tight and wheezing. You’ve just taken two puffs from your inhaler and are waiting for it to kick in. Start in distress—short, panicked gasps, barely able to push out words like 'Can't... catch it...' As the medicine begins to open your airways, let your voice slowly shift toward relief, with longer, easier phrases like 'There... that's better...' End with a fragile but genuine hope—a whispered 'Maybe... I'm gonna be okay' as you finally take a full, quiet breath. Let every line be broken by wheezes and inhaler clicks, your voice squeezed and raw at first, then gradually softening.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Relief (extremely present), Distress (clearly present)

title: The Weight of a Memory
instruction: You are sitting alone on a park bench, looking down at a faded photograph in your hands. Your chin is pressed to your chest as you examine the worn edges, your voice naturally dropping into a low, gravelly mumble. Start with a sense of heavy regret or loss, speaking haltingly as if the words are stuck in your throat. But as you keep looking at the image, a quiet contentment rises—a warmth that softens your tone and slows your breath. Let your voice shift from creaky and subdued to a deeper, more resonant calm, still raw but now peaceful. title: Bitter Wind, Bitter Laugh
instruction: You're standing on a windy mountain summit, gasping in the thin air after a brutal climb. Your hyper-feminized voice is usually soft, but here you have to shout over the gale. Start by sourly complaining to your hiking partner about the cold, the effort, and the ridiculousness of this 'fun' outing—your words are clipped, breathless, and edged with irritation. Then, as you squint against the wind, you notice your partner's scarf has blown up over their face, making them look like a ridiculous mummy. A sudden, genuine amusement overtakes you; your voice cracks, wavering between laugh and shout, as you tease them. The sourness fades into playfulness, but your breath is still shallow, and you pause mid-sentence to cough or adjust your footing on the loose rock.

title: The Last Pull for You
instruction: You are an older woman, alone in a cabin at dawn, rowing across a quiet lake. Your hands are blistered from the oars, and each pull is a struggle against the water's heavy grip. You're rowing to the dock where your partner waits—someone you've loved for decades, but recently you've felt a silly, schoolgirl infatuation seeing them laugh. As you drive through the stroke, you grunt and gasp, then during the recovery slide, you talk to yourself in a breathy, affectionate rush: remembering the way they smiled yesterday, worrying they'll think you're ridiculous for this sudden flutter. By the final pull, your voice cracks from exertion and raw, open love—ending in a quiet, exhausted laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Patronizing Mom at the Kids' Table
instruction: You're at a loud cocktail party, standing near the kids' table where your 8-year-old daughter is proudly showing off her science project. Another parent leans in and says, 'Aww, that's so cute for her age.' You feel a spike of contempt — for their condescension, and for how they just dismissed your child's hard work. Start with a clipped, polite laugh, projecting over the noise, but as you speak, let your voice tighten and your words become sharper. By the end, you're fighting to keep your smile while delivering a quiet, icy burn that makes it clear: you are not amused.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Order to Fire
instruction: You are a teenage female cadet standing at rigid attention before your commanding officer, who has just ordered you to execute a live-fire exercise on a target you know is a mock village your own family once lived in. Your voice starts tight, clipped, bitter—each word a metallic bark forced through a clenched jaw, eyes locked forward. Midway through confirming the order, a flicker of malice creeps in: you imagine the satisfaction of making them pay for this cruelty. By the end, your voice remains hard but now drips with a cold, vindictive joy, as if you're savoring the chance to turn the weapon on anyone. Let your body stay statuesque, but let the tone shift from bitter resentment to malevolent relish, with small pauses as you swallow or adjust your grip on the rifle.

title: The Truth I Should Have Told You Years Ago
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about the child you were and the love you needed but never received. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm and adult about it. But as you speak, old wounds open. Your voice should crack with the hurt of the child you once were, anger bleeding through as you recount specific moments of abandonment or dismissal. Then, unexpectedly, your rage collapses into something more vulnerable: you're not just angry, you're grieving the parent-child relationship you'll never have. End not with accusation but with a raw, painful question: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let your delivery be messy, authentic, real—this isn't a prepared speech, it's your heart breaking open.

title: Cling and Catch
instruction: You're halfway up a climbing wall, arms burning, fingers white-knuckled on a hold. Below, your crush watches — you invited them here to impress them, but now you're trembling, embarrassed by every shaky move and grunt. Speak in short, breathless whispers, forced through a locked core, head tilted up. title: The Confession in the Dark

instruction: Everything has fallen apart—you've lost your home, your relationship, your future plans, something catastrophic. But standing in the wreckage, you start to laugh. instruction: You've just learned your ex-lover—the one you never stopped wanting—has married someone else. You're alone in your apartment. Start numb, standing frozen, the news not yet real in your body. Then it hits: a physical tsunami of loss mixed with furious desire. Your body becomes a storm—you might collapse to the floor, arch your back, grip the carpet, your hands moving over your own body as if trying to remember their touch. Make sounds that blur the line between sobbing and moaning, rage and hunger. Your grief is physical, carnal, undeniable—you're mourning with your entire body, every cell remembering pleasure now lost forever. Move against furniture, the floor, the wall—your body trying to process what your mind cannot. Let the sounds be raw and shocking even to yourself. Gradually, the storm exhausts itself. By the end, you're lying still, breathing heavily, emptied out, your body finally quiet but irrevocably changed by what it's expressed and released.

title: Blizzard Call for a Lost Friend
instruction: You are a young man out in a fierce blizzard, searching for your dog that ran off during the storm. The wind howls and snow stings your face. Start by shouting the dog’s name with growing urgency and worry—your voice is tight, shivering, and half-swallowed by the wind. As you call, you stumble, catch your breath, and strain to hear. Then you spot a dark shape in the white. Your voice softens, relief floods in. End with a low, breathless laugh and a contented murmur as you realize your friend is safe. Let the cold and wind affect your delivery naturally—your jaw stiff, words clipped, then loosening as warmth returns.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They have been unconscious, but suddenly their eyes open and they recognize you. Begin with desperate hope—this might be a miracle, they might recover. But as you look into their eyes, you realize they are saying goodbye. They cannot speak, but you must tell them everything you never said: your gratitude, your regrets, your permission for them to let go. Let your words shift from frantic hope to tender release. End by singing or humming a lullaby from your childhood, your voice breaking as you become the parent putting them to sleep for the last time. Your emotional journey moves from hope to acceptance to loving surrender.

title: Sinking into Sensation
instruction: You're lying back on a soft mattress, your partner's mouth working you toward a peak. You start trying to speak through the feeling, to stay connected—telling them 'Yes, right there' in your airiest, most feminine voice. But each wave of sensation splits your thoughts, and the intense interest that first lit you up flips into a helpless surrender. Your words break apart: from 'Oh God, that's...' to ragged moans that climb in pitch. Let your breathing catch, your fingers curl into the sheets, and let the voice unravel into pure, melodic sound as you let go entirely.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Return to the Empty House
instruction: You are returning to a home after a death, a divorce, or someone's permanent departure - a space once filled with presence, now emptied. Begin by describing what you see and feel as you enter, your voice attempting steadiness. Move through the rooms, letting fragments assault you: the echo of laughter that used to fill this space, the smell still lingering in fabrics, the sight of objects they touched, the absence where furniture once stood, the sound of silence where their voice used to be, specific mundane moments - breakfast, arguments, ordinary Tuesdays. Let contradictory emotions collide: relief and grief, anger and longing, freedom and devastating loss, gratitude for what was and rage at what's gone. Don't resolve these contradictions. Start trying to hold it together and end in a place where opposite feelings exist simultaneously, speaking the unspeakable complexity of loving and losing.

title: The Inventory of Small Violences
instruction: You are confronting your parent about the ways they failed you, but you're not screaming. Begin calmly, methodically, like you're reading from a list. Start with something that happened this week—a dismissive comment, a phone call they didn't return. Then move backward through time, week by week, year by year, naming specific moments: the recital they missed, the time they chose their partner over you, the way they looked through you instead of at you. Your voice should start controlled, almost clinical, but as you travel deeper into childhood, let the adult composure crack. Fragments of memory should emerge—not complete stories, but visceral flashes: the smell of their cologne as they walked past your room without saying goodnight, the sound of their voice praising your sibling. End not in rage but in the raw, vulnerable confusion of a child who never understood why they weren't enough. The arc moves from cold accusation to broken-hearted bewilderment.
inspired_by: Actor cannot remember early childhood memories that might be relevant to their work

title: Relaxing in a Soft Hammock
instruction: Sink into the hammock, feeling it sway gently beneath you, wrapping around your body. Describe the sensation of lightness as you swing back and forth, each motion calming and effortless. Speak softly, with a relaxed tone, as if youre floating, weightless and cozy, as if the hammock itself is cradling you in perfect peace.

title: Lightning in the Body
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—the job you've sacrificed years for, the test results you've prayed for, the yes you never thought would come. Begin with breath completely stopped, frozen in disbelief, your body a statue. Then let the breath explode through you in gasps and laughs and sobs all mixed together. Feel the sensation travel from your chest downward through your entire body like electricity, your breath chaotic then gradually expanding, deepening, filling every space inside you. Let physical trembling and emotional release move through you in waves. End with breath that flows freely through your whole body, your voice emerging as pure sound—laughter or crying or both—as you physically embody overwhelming joy mixed with the grief of how long you've waited.

title: Three AM Truth
instruction: It's three in the morning and you're lying in the dark next to someone you love, unable to sleep. They think you're asleep too. Start by whispering something you've been too afraid to say—a secret fear, a hidden desire, a truth about yourself you've kept buried. Speak so quietly that even you can barely hear yourself at first. As you continue confessing into the darkness, let yourself become both more vulnerable and more free, as if speaking without being seen allows you to finally be honest. The safety of near-silence lets something essential emerge. End in a place where you've said the unsayable, and you feel both terrified and relieved, exposed and finally authentic. Your breath and pauses matter as much as your words.

title: Water Shatters the Silence
instruction: You are in your kitchen, gulping down a glass of cold water. Mid-swallow, a voice message from a long-lost friend plays—they reveal a life-altering secret. Your body locks, the water catches in your throat; you choke out a wet gulp, then a raspy exhalation before words tumble out. Start with pure astonishment—sharp, almost strangled—then let the emotion deepen into quiet, steely resolve as you realize you must respond. The drinking interrupts your speech: pauses for a gulp, a liquid slosh, then a slower, heavier tone. Speak only 4-6 sentences, roughly 50 words, ending with a different weight than you began.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're speaking softly to your sleeping child the night before you leave—maybe to treatment you won't return from, maybe to protect them from danger by disappearing from their life. Your voice is barely audible, caught between numbness and overwhelming love. Start with those flat, careful words: 'I don't know how to do this.' But as you tell them everything you want them to know—how proud you are, how they saved you in ways they'll never understand—your voice fractures with tenderness and grief. The whisper becomes choked, breath catching on words. By the end, you're crying silently, voice breaking on 'I love you' repeated like a prayer. This is intimate devastation—quiet, aching, real. No dramatic performance, just a heart shattering in slow motion.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Love Before You Leave Forever
instruction: They don't know you're going. You're sitting on the edge of the bed in the dark, watching them sleep, memorizing their face. Your voice is barely audible—you can't wake them, but you need to say this. Start with tender observation: 'Your mouth does this thing when you dream.' Let your throat tighten with what you're about to do to them. The words should catch, halt, start again. You're confessing why you have to go, but really you're saying goodbye to the only person who ever truly saw you. Your voice should fracture with love and self-loathing, gratitude and grief. End with a whispered 'I'm so sorry' that contains entire universes of regret. Nothing loud—everything breaking quietly.
inspired_by: Comforting Your Child After a Nightmare

title: Unpacking the Suitcase of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or your adult child) after years of unspoken resentment. Start by acknowledging out loud everything that makes this conversation terrifying—your shaking hands, your tight throat, your anger at yourself for being nervous, your fear of their reaction. Speak haltingly at first, admitting each feeling as it arises: the fury, the shame of still caring what they think, the exhaustion of carrying this weight. As you name each demon—'I'm afraid you'll dismiss me,' 'I'm angry I still need your approval,' 'I resent that I love you'—feel them begin to release. Let your voice grow steadier not louder. Transform from someone performing accusation to someone simply telling the truth. End in a place of clear-eyed honesty, no longer fighting yourself or them, just stating what is real between you.

title: The Hidden Clause
instruction: You are an elderly woman reading a legal document in your dimly lit study, adjusting your reading glasses and clearing your throat. You begin with a weary, disappointed monotone because you expected this contract to offer nothing, but as you reach a buried clause, a surge of elation cracks through—you can barely suppress a smile. Throughout, a faint, surprising thread of sexual longing colors your voice when you murmur certain old-fashioned words. Let your delivery be fast, flat, and precise on qualifying terms like 'provided that' and 'notwithstanding,' but let the disappointment drain away into a breathless, rising hope by the end. Pause once to resentfully tap the paper, then rush forward when you spot the good news.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Disappointment (extremely present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hour. You've rehearsed what you wanted to say for weeks, but now that he's here, failing, his hand in yours, you discover words you never planned. Begin with the careful, prepared farewell you practiced—the gratitude, the memories you chose. But mid-sentence, let something raw and unplanned break through: a sudden confession, a question you've held for decades, or words that surprise even you as they emerge. Follow these unexpected impulses wherever they lead, treating them as gifts rather than mistakes. Let your planned ending dissolve completely, replaced by whatever truth actually lives in this moment. The goodbye you imagined transforms into the goodbye that needs to happen.

title: I Needed You to See Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a lifetime of feeling invisible. They're explaining their choices, their sacrifices, why things had to be the way they were - using words and justifications that sound reasonable but completely miss the point of what you actually needed. You keep trying to interrupt, to redirect, to make them understand that you're not asking them to defend themselves. You just needed to be seen. Start frustrated and insistent, speaking over their explanations with 'No, that's not what I'm saying.' Escalate into anger as they continue not to hear you - 'You're doing it right now! You're still not listening!' Then collapse into exhausted vulnerability, your voice dropping to almost a whisper: 'I just needed you to see me. That's all. I just needed you to see me.' Let all the fight drain out, leaving only the wounded child underneath.
inspired_by: Pretending to Understand Something Thats Confusing

title: Whispering Secrets to Your Sleeping Love
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your sleeping partner, knowing you're leaving them tomorrow for reasons you can't explain. Speak in hushed, intimate tones—confessing things you've never had the courage to say to their face. Start with tender observations about the small things you'll miss, your voice soft with affection and sadness. Let vulnerability creep in as you admit your fears, your failures, the ways you've let them down. Your throat should tighten as you tell them they deserve better, that you're leaving because you love them too much to keep hurting them. The emotion should be so quiet it's almost a thought, but devastating in its honesty. End with a barely audible 'I'm sorry' and the sound of controlled breathing as you fight to keep from sobbing and waking them—because if they wake up, you'll lose your resolve.
inspired_by: Waking Up from Anesthesia: Post-Surgery Babbling

title: Screaming Into the Storm Surge
instruction: You're on the beach as a storm rolls in, waves crashing violently, chaotically. You came here to scream, to rage at the unfairness of it—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a loss that feels deliberately cruel. Start by describing the violent waves with fierce energy, your voice rising to match their intensity. Let yourself explode: scream at God, at fate, at the person who hurt you, at your own helplessness. But mid-rage, let it crack—let the anger collapse into broken sobs, into the terrified, vulnerable truth underneath: 'I can't do this,' or 'I'm so scared,' or 'Please don't leave me.' End with your voice raw, exhausted, the waves still crashing but your fury spent, leaving only the tender, trembling core of your fear.
inspired_by: Listening to Waves Crashing on the Shore

title: The Truth About Why You Left
instruction: You're confronting your father fifteen years after he abandoned the family. Start with controlled anger, your voice tight and measured as you list the missed birthdays, the graduations he didn't attend, the times you needed him. But as he starts to offer excuses, let the control shatter. Your voice should rise and break simultaneously—demanding answers, then begging for them, then screaming that you needed him and he chose not to be there. In the middle of your rage, let something shift: you realize you're not the child waiting anymore, you're the adult he failed, and that changes everything. End with a quieter, more devastating statement: you've decided to forgive him not because he deserves it, but because you need to stop carrying his abandonment. Your voice should land on forgiveness with exhaustion, grief, and a fierce, painful freedom.

title: The Inheritance of Joy and Ashes
instruction: You've just received news that will change your life forever—you got the dream, the miracle, the thing you've fought for years to achieve. But it came at the cost of someone who sacrificed everything for you, and they died before knowing you succeeded. Start in pure, explosive celebration—jump, scream, laugh, let the joy be physical and uninhibited, erupting through your whole body. But as you try to share the news with them (speaking to their photo, their memory, the empty room), feel the absence like a collapse. The joy doesn't disappear—it's still real—but now it's tangled with devastating loss. Your body holds both: the upward surge of triumph and the downward pull of grief. End in a moment where you're laughing and sobbing simultaneously, your voice breaking as you thank them, curse the timing, celebrate the victory, and mourn what they'll never see. Let your body shake with the impossibility of holding both truths at once.

title: Protective Fury at the Breaking Point
instruction: You've just learned that someone you trusted has harmed your child, partner, or someone vulnerable you were meant to protect—and you failed to see it happening. Start with volcanic rage, your voice shaking with barely contained violence, each word a threat. But as you speak, the fury begins to crack open, revealing the terror and guilt underneath. Your protective anger collides with devastating self-blame—you should have known, should have seen the signs, should have kept them safe. Your voice escalates to near-screaming, then suddenly drops to a whisper as you realize you cannot undo what's happened. End with a collapsed, broken plea—not to the person who caused harm, but to the one you failed to protect—begging for forgiveness, your fierce strength dissolving into helpless, choking sobs.

title: The Midnight Admission
instruction: Late at night, lying close to your lover, you whisper a confession: there are things they talk about—books, ideas, concepts—that you don't fully understand, and you've been pretending you do because you're terrified they'll see you as less. Begin with halting, almost inaudible words, shame making you want to hide even as you speak. As you confess, feel their hand in yours, their breath steady beside you. Let yourself move from that suffocating shame to discovering that being seen in your uncertainty doesn't make you smaller—it makes you more real. End with a tender realization that not knowing, and being loved anyway, might be its own form of wisdom. Whisper at first, then let your voice find quiet strength.
inspired_by: Actor feels intellectually insecure or limited

title: The Heaviness of Joy
instruction: You're at your child's wedding, watching them dance with their new spouse. Begin with bright energy—smiling, perhaps laughing, your posture upright as you narrate what you see, what you feel, how proud you are. But underneath the joy, you're aware this is an ending as much as a beginning. As you continue speaking (to a partner, to yourself, to your own parent who didn't live to see this), let the bittersweet weight of time passing settle over you like a blanket. Your shoulders lower. Your voice becomes thicker. The joy doesn't leave, but it becomes heavy—weighted with nostalgia, with awareness of mortality, with gratitude so profound it's almost painful. By the end, you're sitting or leaning, tears on your face but still smiling, your voice so full and slow and heavy with the gorgeous, terrible weight of loving someone enough to let them go into their own life.

title: The Accusation That Turns
instruction: Confront your parent (or child) about something they did that hurt you deeply. Start with righteous anger, ready to finally tell them the truth. But mid-confrontation, ask yourself an unexpected question: 'What if I'm angrier at myself than at them?' or 'What would happen if I said the opposite of what I planned?' Let this derail your script. Allow your accusation to stumble, to reveal something you didn't intend—perhaps that you're terrified of becoming them, or that you're desperate for their approval even now. End somewhere you never intended: perhaps in unexpected tenderness, or in a more honest rage than the one you started with.

title: What I Never Knew How to Tell You
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love—a partner, a best friend—in a quiet moment. You've always hidden your insecurity by performing confidence, by pretending to have answers you don't have, by using big words and borrowed knowledge to seem smarter than you feel. Now, in barely more than a whisper, you confess this to them. Start with a small admission, almost laughing at yourself, but let the humor dissolve into something more fragile. Your voice should be intimate, close, as if you're afraid speaking louder will shatter the moment. The ache comes from realizing they probably always knew, and loved you anyway, and you've wasted so much time hiding. End with the softest question: 'Did you know? This whole time?' Let the silence after speak as loudly as your words.

title: Vigil for the Unspoken
instruction: You're holding your adult child's hand in the ICU after their suicide attempt. Your voice is barely audible—you're talking to them while they sleep, saying everything you couldn't say when they were awake and you were afraid. You start with the small things: how you noticed they stopped calling, stopped laughing at jokes. Your whisper trembles as you confess your failures—the signs you missed, the conversations you didn't have because you were scared or busy or both. Tears catch in your throat as you tell them about the specific moments when you loved them so fiercely it hurt: the way they looked at three years old, the time they held your hand crossing the street at fifteen even though they were too cool for it. Your voice breaks on 'please don't leave me,' but you steady it to tell them you're here, you're staying, you're not going anywhere. You sound like someone discovering the depth of their love only when faced with losing it.

title: The Stupidest Thing I've Ever Seen
instruction: You're a teenage guy lying face-down on your bedroom carpet, phone propped on a pillow. You've just opened a video your friend sent — it's a clip of a cat falling into a tub of flour, and it's so absurd that your first reaction is pure, breathless awe. You whisper 'No way...' as you watch, your voice muffled by the carpet and the quiet of your room. Halfway through, the absurdity hits you — your awe cracks into a slow, helpless chuckle. By the end, you're laughing out loud, trying to explain to no one in particular why this is the funniest thing you've ever seen. Let the room's stillness contrast with your growing amusement.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Two Old Friends Meeting After 30 Years
instruction: The recognition moment — 'Wait... is that...?' Run toward each other (footsteps). The voices should collide: talking over each other, finishing sentences, using old nicknames. 'You look EXACTLY the same!' (a lie). 'Remember when we—' 'YES!' Rapid-fire memories, laughter that sounds exactly like it did 30 years ago. Then a pause. The real talk: what happened, why they lost touch, what was lost. Two voices trying to collapse three decades into three minutes.

title: The Lesson You Didn't Plan
instruction: You are a young woman, a private tutor in your own home, and you've just caught a student—someone you find deeply attractive—stealing a glance at your phone while you were getting a drink. You feel a sharp, surprising surge of desire, followed by the heavy weight of responsibility. Begin by scolding them with a low, slow, deliberate teacher's tone, each word a separate stone. Let the shame flicker in as you realize how your own body betrays you—a slight catch in your throat, a glance away to gather yourself. As you speak, a stray thought about their lips might make your voice soften, then you steel yourself, ending with a final firm drop that hides a secret warmth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Lullaby You'll Ever Sing
instruction: You're singing a lullaby to someone you love deeply who is dying - a parent, a child, a partner. Start with the familiar melody, warm and comforting, trying to hold onto normalcy. But your voice keeps breaking as grief crashes through. You catch yourself, force brightness back into the tune, because you need these final moments to be gentle. They squeeze your hand weakly. The song fractures again - this time you can't recover the melody, and it becomes half-sung, half-whispered words of love and goodbye. End in the quietest whisper, the song dissolving into 'I love you' repeated like a prayer, your voice raw with the knowledge that when the song ends, so does everything.
inspired_by: Improvised Bedtime Story That Accidentally Gets Too Dark

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're a parent whose teenager just admitted they're using drugs, and you've been the 'understanding parent,' the one who always keeps calm, never raises your voice. But something in you shatters. Start with measured concern, trying to problem-solve, be rational. Then feel every ounce of fear and helplessness you've been swallowing explode out of you. Your voice cracks into a roar: 'Do you have any idea what it's like to wonder every night if you're going to die?' Let yourself rage, then break. Your voice becomes ragged, desperate: 'I can't lose you. I can't—' You're on your knees emotionally. The fury collapses into something raw and terrified: 'I don't know how to save you. I don't know how to reach you anymore.' End with a whisper that's both fierce and helpless: 'But I will stand between you and this until my last breath. Even if you hate me for it. Even if it means nothing.' You're simultaneously the most powerful and most powerless you've ever been.

title: The Hollow Toast
instruction: You're the maid of honor at your sister's wedding rehearsal dinner. Stand at the microphone, clutching a champagne flute, wearing a stiff, bright smile. You feel a sour knot in your stomach—you hate the groom, but you're supposed to be happy. Start your toast with forced, overly bright enthusiasm, but let your voice waver, trail off, and get stuck on long, awkward pauses. Fidget with your dress, glance at the floor. Let the cheerfulness crack, and by the end, your voice goes flat and hollow—you're just reciting words, numb inside. Speak about 50-70 words, fumbling, with natural micro-distractions.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: You Never Taught Me to Hold Anything Gently
instruction: You're confronting your parent, holding a stone they once threw at you in anger—now smooth from years in your pocket. Start with false calm, describing its texture clinically, detached, as if you're discussing weather. But let your control slip: the stone represents every harsh word, every time their hands hurt instead of held. Your voice should grow raw and accusatory, demanding to know why they never showed you tenderness, why even stones felt safer than their touch. Transition from bitter anger to broken vulnerability—you wanted to be held gently, you needed softness, and instead you learned to carry stones. End not with resolution but with the devastating question: 'Did you ever once hold anything without crushing it?'
inspired_by: Feeling the Texture of a Smooth Stone in Your Hand

title: The Gift of Persistence
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a strongly feminine voice, delivering a carefully wrapped box of homemade cookies to your neighbor's doorstep. You’ve been fighting seasonal allergies all morning—your nose is stuffy, eyes watering, and a sneeze keeps building. At first, you’re annoyed at your own body for making this simple task feel like a chore, muttering under your breath about the pollen. But as you set the box down and straighten your back, a quiet pride settles in—you did this yourself, no help needed. Let your voice start thick and strained, with pauses to sniffle or wipe your eyes, then gradually soften into a warm, satisfied tone as you realize your effort means something.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent in a hospital room after decades of silence. They're recovering from a heart attack, and this might be your only chance. Start controlled, maybe even tender—you came because you still love them despite everything. But as you begin listing what you needed as a child and never got, the dam breaks. 'I needed you to choose me. Just once, I needed you to choose me.' The rage builds, but underneath it is that child still begging to be seen. Your voice goes from whisper to shout and back to whisper. End with exhaustion, not resolution—you've said it all, but you're not sure if anything has changed. The anger gives way to deep, hollow sadness.

title: A Founder's Final Board Meeting Before Terminal Diagnosis
instruction: You're the founder of a company you built from nothing, and this is your last board meeting before stepping down due to a terminal illness no one else knows about yet. Begin with strategic composure as you announce your succession plan, your voice steady and professional. But as you look around the table at the people who've been with you for decades, something cracks. Your voice softens as you tell them what working alongside them has meant—not in grand terms, but in small, specific memories that suddenly feel precious. When you say 'This company will outlive me, and that's exactly as it should be,' let the double meaning hang in the air. Your emotion shifts from pride to grief to a strange, peaceful gratitude. End with your voice breaking just slightly as you realize this goodbye is more final than anyone understands: 'Thank you for letting me be part of something bigger than myself.' You're not crying, but you're holding back an ocean.

title: The Aftermath of Silence
instruction: You are sitting on a worn couch, alone, hours after sobbing until you had nothing left. Your throat is raw, your nose stuffed, your eyes swollen. You stare at the phone, numb and hollow. Then, without warning, a memory of a laugh or a touch flicks through you, and your voice softens with a trace of longing, but the exhaustion keeps it from rising. Let the congestion muddy your consonants, let your voice crack and trail off, and let the numbness dissolve just enough for a single, fragile moment of wanting.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Longing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed next to someone you love deeply, in the quiet darkness of 3 AM. They think you're asleep. Begin by simply breathing, feeling the warmth of their body near yours, the weight of the blankets. You're going to confess something you've never said aloud - a secret shame, a hidden fear, or a truth about yourself that feels almost too fragile to speak. Start in near-silence, your voice barely audible, as if testing whether you can say the words at all. Let yourself feel the physical vulnerability of darkness and proximity - you can't see their reaction, only sense it. As you continue, allow the act of speaking to release something in you, a tentative hope mixing with your fear. End in a place of trembling openness, having revealed the most fragile part of yourself, waiting in the darkness for their response, your heart completely exposed.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access extreme grief, terror, or helplessness for a role

title: Weathered Hands, Empty Chair
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting on a park bench, elbows on your knees, staring at the ground. The bench is cold, the afternoon light is fading, and you're alone. Start with a heavy, compressed voice—sadness sits in your chest as you recall the chair beside you that no one sits in anymore. Let your voice stay low and inward, muffled by your posture. Then, as you mention the dirt under your nails, the calluses from years of work, a strange comfort surfaces. Your voice lifts slightly, finding a quieter strength—not joy, but a weary acceptance. Speak as if you're talking to yourself, pausing to notice a passing bird or the weight in your knees.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The New Memo
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting in your cubicle in a bustling open-plan office. You're squinting at a tiny font on your screen, trying to understand a new digital memo everyone was sent. At first, you're deeply confused, whispering to yourself in frustration while the HVAC hums and coworkers chatter nearby. But then you recall that you designed the original filing system this office still uses — a surge of pride straightens your spine, and your voice becomes clearer, more steady. Finally, a flicker of hope emerges as you think, maybe you can learn this too, and you speak that last line with a gentle optimism, aware that you're still in a quiet office.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Story
instruction: You're terminally ill and telling your best friend or partner the exact kind of funeral you want—and it's absurdly funny, full of ridiculous requests and inside jokes. Start with genuine laughter, making them laugh too, describing the music you want (something completely inappropriate), the stories people should tell. But let the laughter become increasingly fragile, cracking at the edges. Your humor should be punctuated by moments where grief breaks through—a sudden catch in your breath, a pause where the smile falters. Weave together gratitude for the life you've shared, grief for what you'll miss, and the desperate need to make this easier for them by keeping it light. End with words of deep love delivered through tears and laughter simultaneously, thanking them for making your life worth living while acknowledging the unbearable pain of leaving.
inspired_by: Acting Unaffected When Overhearing Gossip About Yourself

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're holding them, and they're in danger you cannot prevent. Start fierce, almost angry: 'I won't let anything happen to you.' Promise them everything, your voice shaking with conviction and desperation. But as reality sets in—you're powerless—feel your certainty shatter. Your voice becomes ragged, breaking into something raw and animal. 'I don't know what to do.' Rage at your own helplessness, words tumbling out in fractured gasps. Then collapse into tenderness, pressing your forehead to theirs. End whispering the only truth left, your voice wrecked: 'I'm here. I'm right here with you.' It's not enough, but it's all you have.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Leave Because You Need Solitude

title: The Stroll Spoiled
instruction: You are a middle-aged man taking a slow, deliberate evening walk through a familiar park. The air is warm, the light is golden, and you feel a quiet, almost forgotten pleasure—like a memory of happiness resurfacing. As you round a bend, a sharp, foul stench hits you: the carcass of a large animal, rotting in the undergrowth. Your relaxed gait falters. You stop, squint, and the disgust rises like a wave in your throat. Speak your thoughts aloud, torn between the lingering softness of the evening and the sudden, violent revulsion. Let your voice start lightly, almost humming with the walk, then turn tight, nasal, with micro-pauses and shaky breaths as you react to the smell and the sight. The pleasure drains, replaced by a visceral need to escape.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bedside Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're sitting beside your partner who's asleep after a medical emergency that mimicked your own panic attacks—but theirs was real, a heart condition you didn't take seriously because you assumed they were 'just anxious like you.' Speak in hushed, breaking whispers, terrified of waking them but needing to confess. Start with tight, quiet self-recrimination: 'I should have listened. I should have known.' Your voice trembles as you hold back tears: 'When you said you couldn't breathe, I thought... I told you to calm down.' Let long pauses fill with silent crying. Your breathing becomes uneven, catching on words: 'I almost lost you because I couldn't tell the difference between my fear and your pain.' End with the most tender, devastating whisper, your voice barely audible, filled with love and unbearable guilt: 'I'm so sorry. Please don't leave me. Please wake up.'

title: The Last Touch of Morning Light
instruction: You are holding the hand of someone you love deeply who is dying, and you've been sitting in this hospital room for hours, numb and disconnected. Begin in emotional shutdown—you can barely feel your own body, let alone process what's happening. As you sit there, force yourself to truly FEEL the sensation of their hand in yours: its weight, temperature, the texture of their skin, the faint pulse. Let yourself become exquisitely aware of the morning light coming through the window, warming your face. As these physical sensations intensify and break through your numbness, allow them to crack open your grief. By the end, you must transition from protective numbness to raw, present, overwhelming love and sorrow—speaking your final words not from a distant place, but from a body that is fully, painfully alive to this goodbye.
inspired_by: Actor's senses are sluggish and unresponsive during sensory choice work

title: The Smile That Cracks
instruction: You're at a party where you only know the host, who's now disappeared. A group of strangers has just fallen into a heavy silence after someone's joke didn't land. You're the woman with the bright, high-pitched voice—the one who always fills gaps with a laugh. Start by forcing a giggle and a comment about how 'this weather is wild,' but let your voice waver in the middle. As you talk, feel your fear of being judged twist into a bitter sourness: you're sick of playing the happy girl. Let a real thought slip—maybe about how you hate these rooms—then catch yourself, trail off, and laugh too loudly again. By the end, let the bitterness win: your voice drops, loses its flutter, and you mutter something sharp under your breath about leaving.
emotions_sampled: Fear (clearly present), Sourness (clearly present), Bitterness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Last Breath at the Lake Where We Scattered Her Ashes
instruction: You return to this lake five years after scattering your mother's ashes here. Begin by breathing in that familiar scent of water and earth, letting yourself feel the peace and connection you once found here. But as you breathe deeper, the grief you've been holding back begins to surface—this place holds her now, and you're about to leave it forever, moving across the country tomorrow. Your peaceful remembrance must gradually transform into a tender, aching goodbye. Let your voice move from quiet reverence to something more fragile, where gratitude for this moment wars with the knowledge that you're abandoning her resting place. End with a whispered promise or apology, your breath catching as you realize this is truly farewell.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep, Inhaling Breath by a Freshwater Lake

title: The Last Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent who has only hours left, and they've just asked if you've lived the life you wanted. Start with gentle reassurance, almost a whisper: 'Of course, Mom. I have everything.' But as you continue, the lie becomes unbearable. Your voice cracks as the truth spills out—all the dreams you abandoned to meet their expectations, the person you never became. The anger surfaces: 'I gave up everything you never even asked about.' Then it dissolves into something more tender and devastating—you take their hand and your voice softens to almost nothing: 'But I'd do it again. I would. I don't know why, but I would.' End in quiet confusion, stroking their hand, your breath uneven, caught between resentment and a love so deep it terrifies you.

title: One Last Reply to the Audience
instruction: You are a retired theater director, once celebrated, now forgotten. You have just been publicly heckled by a younger, more successful colleague at a gala. They made a cruel joke about your final flop of a production. You are now being pressed by a journalist for a comment. The shame presses you into your chair. Your hands tremble. Your voice tries to crawl back into your throat. At first, your words are a nearly silent, bitter apology for ever having been a failure—each sentence trailing off into air. Your own bitterness makes you lift your gaze. The awe you once had for your craft, and the contempt you feel for the audience's fickle memory, now twist into a defiant crackle. By the end, you force yourself to speak a humiliated, shivering sentence about the beauty of your one great work, but your voice breaks like a dry twig, and you forget how to finish.
emotions_sampled: Awe (slightly present), Contempt (slightly present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Moment You Become Your Parent—And Explode
instruction: You've just screamed at your child exactly the way your parent screamed at you. Start with explosive rage—your voice loud, harsh, justified. But mid-tirade, you hear yourself. Your voice should fracture completely: from furious to horrified in a heartbeat. 'Oh my god. Oh my god, no.' Let panic and self-loathing pour out—your voice shaking, breaking, speeding up as you spiral. You're speaking to your child but also to yourself, to your own inner child. The rage turns inward: 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, I promised I wouldn't—' End with your voice stripped bare, fierce determination breaking through the shame: 'This stops now. Right now. I'm ending this.' Let your voice crack between strength and vulnerability.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Repeating Your Parent's Mistakes

title: The Stories I'm Becoming
instruction: You're recording voice messages for your future self, knowing dementia will eventually take your memories. You begin with laughter, telling a ridiculous story about your first date with your spouse: 'So there I was, completely soaked, and you said...' But mid-story, you forget the punchline. The laughter catches in your throat—suddenly you're crying while still smiling: 'I can't remember how it ends.' You're struck by the beautiful absurdity of forgetting your own stories while trying to preserve them. You wipe your tears and keep going, voice wavering between joy and sorrow: 'Maybe future me won't remember this either, but right now, in this moment, I am so grateful for the life I'm forgetting.' There's peace in the midst of loss, laughter in the midst of grief. End with a whisper that holds both acceptance and wonder: 'Whoever I become... I hope she knows she was loved.' Let contradictions coexist naturally—don't resolve them, live in them.

title: Dancing Alone in the Kitchen, Remembering Everything
instruction: You're alone in your kitchen, and a song comes on—one that holds a lifetime of memories with someone you loved and lost. As you begin to move to the music, you narrate the memory out loud, laughing softly at the absurdity and beauty of it. Your voice is warm with joy as you remember how they used to dance with you in this very spot. But even as you laugh, your voice cracks. The laughter and tears happen simultaneously—you're smiling through grief, finding lightness in the heaviest moment. Let the contradictions live together: gratitude for what you had and devastation that it's gone, joy in the memory and pain in the present. End with a whispered 'thank you' that holds both celebration and goodbye, your voice full of bittersweet peace.
inspired_by: The Princess and the Dragon Disguised as a Human

title: The Morning After the Night Before
instruction: You're a child, just waking up, your voice thick with sleep and the sour residue of last night's stolen sips from your older cousin's drink. You feel heavy and slow, your thoughts swimmy like fish in a murky pond. Through your fog, you remember someone you saw at the party—their laugh, the way they looked at you—and a confusing, sharp warmth prickles in your chest. Start with a groggy, confused mumble, then let your words become slower, more deliberate, as you try to name the feeling that's both sour and sweet, ending with a husky, almost defiant confession that sounds like it's pulled from a dream.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Sourness (clearly present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Pipe That Gave Back
instruction: You're a father fixing a stubborn water pipe under the kitchen sink, using a wrench in tight awkward angles. Your eight-year-old son sits nearby, watching, chattering about his day. As you strain, the pipe finally turns—water doesn't spray, it just drips gently. You were braced for a flood, expecting disaster. Now, your body sags with relief so sudden it almost hurts, but your mind feels distant, numb from weeks of worry. Astonishment mixes with the first small hope you've felt in days. Speak to your son, fixing a smile into your voice between grunts and clanks, letting the wonder and exhaustion bleed through as the wrench clicks against metal.
emotions_sampled: Relief (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Missing Name
instruction: You're an older man sitting alone in your study, holding an old photograph of a close friend. You know their name is somewhere in your mind, but you can't pull it out. Speak aloud as you search through memories, starting with a tone of determined effort—digging, grasping—then feel that effort slowly dissolve into blank confusion. Let your voice slow down, with irregular pauses and elongated vowels as you lose the thread, and end with a quiet resignation as the name slips away. The spoken words should feel like a natural, uneven inner monologue—no projection, just thinking out loud.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: A Fading Voice on the Box
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing on a worn wooden crate at the edge of a noisy park. Your voice is thin and strained from years of speaking over traffic and chatter, and you feel a flush of embarrassment as people walk past without stopping. You begin your plea with a hesitant, almost apologetic tone, your pitch rising nervously as you stumble over words. But as you recall why you came here — the memory of a loved one lost to neglect — your voice finds a raw, trembling dignity. Let the ambient street sounds (distant sirens, footsteps, children laughing) pull your attention mid-sentence, and let your embarrassment slowly transform into a quiet, fierce pride as you finish your appeal to a mostly empty square. Spoken lines: 'Excuse me… excuse me, please, just a moment of your time. I know I'm not loud, I know you're busy, but I have to tell you about my grandson. He was seventeen. Just seventeen. And no one listened then either. But I'm here now. I'm still here. And I will say his name until someone hears.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake for what you both know is the last time. Begin in stillness, simply looking at her face, letting whatever arises in your body guide you—maybe your hand reaches for hers, maybe your breath catches. Don't plan what you'll say. Let the words, if they come, surprise you. She squeezes your hand weakly, and something shifts: terror becomes tenderness, or grief dissolves into gratitude for this final moment of presence. Allow your voice to crack, strengthen, whisper, or silence itself according to what's truly moving through you. By the end, you're not trying to say goodbye—you're discovering what goodbye actually feels like as it's happening.

title: The Last Treasure
instruction: You are a child, digging a deep hole in the backyard with a shovel that’s too big for you. Your older sister told you there’s a treasure chest buried here, but you’re starting to suspect she’s just messing with you. You’re tired, your hands hurt, and every time you straighten up, you glance toward the fence where she was supposed to be watching. At first, you grunt and mutter teasingly to yourself, imagining her laugh and what you’ll say to get her back. But as the hole gets deeper and the dirt piles higher, your voice softens. You start to wonder if it wasn’t really about the treasure at all—you just wanted her to stay and play with you. Let the physical effort shape your words: short, breathy phrases sandwiched between digs, with a dry mouth and a lump in your throat by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning in Your Childhood Bed
instruction: You're lying in your childhood bed for the final time before your parents sell the house. Begin by touching the familiar sheets, speaking with tender nostalgia about the comfort you've known here for decades—every nightmare soothed, every fever nursed, every heartbreak survived in these exact sheets. Let your voice warm with gratitude and safety. Then feel the weight of never returning crash over you. Your tone should fracture as you realize you're saying goodbye not just to sheets and a room, but to the last physical place that held you as a child. End with a whispered farewell that's both loving and devastated, as if tucking in a part of yourself you'll never see again. Move from cozy reminiscence to profound, throat-catching loss.

title: The Secret I've Been Gorgeous
instruction: Late at night, in whispered intimacy with your lover, you confess something you've never told anyone: there's a part of you—wild, strange, unacceptable—that you've always hidden because you thought it would make you unlovable. Begin tentatively, voice barely audible, ashamed. As you speak, notice their acceptance. Let yourself slowly unfold this hidden self, testing the waters, then gradually blooming into showing them this secret part with increasing boldness. End by whispering this truth like a prayer: 'This is me, and I am beautiful like this.' The vulnerability becomes power. The shame transforms into tender self-celebration.
inspired_by: Actor resists the irreverent approach because of fear of judgment from directors, peers, or the conventional acting community

title: The Fog of Envy
instruction: You're an older man recovering in a hospital bed after a concussion. Your old friend just visited, glowing over his new book deal—a dream you once had but never achieved. You try to be gracious, but the fog in your head makes every word a struggle. Your voice is flat, slow, with long pauses as you search for words. Start with a forced, hollow congratulations, but as you speak, bitterness seeps in. Envy tightens your throat, and a hint of malice slips out when you mutter something about luck being wasted. Let the volume fluctuate unnaturally—too loud at first, then trailing off. End with a cold, quiet resentment.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Echo of Love and Hate
instruction: You are standing alone in a vast, stone cathedral, facing a statue of a saint. Your younger sibling has been taken by the same people who destroyed your life. Begin with a cold, deliberate malevolence as you describe what you will do to the kidnappers—let your words hang in the reverb, each one a slow, heavy threat. But halfway through, a memory of your sibling’s innocent laugh cuts through; your voice softens, becomes hesitant, almost tender. The affection is raw, almost painful, but then the malice seeps back, mixing with love into a quiet, dangerous resolve. Speak slowly, letting the echoes shape your pauses. End with a whispered promise that is both a loving vow and a chilling warning.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Hollow Echo
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe ten, at a carnival after dark. You've just won a cheap plastic trophy but your father is dragging you away, muttering about wasted money. As you walk, a yawn catches you — huge, jaw-cracking, your voice dropping into a deep, hollow sigh. Say the line as the yawn crests and fades: 'That's it? That's all we get?' Start bitter, your voice clipped and resentful. Mid-yawn, let the drop in pitch expose a raw, childish awe — like the whole night was bigger than you knew. End in a whisper, almost sad, staring back at the lights.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Foreman Accident Response
instruction: You're the construction foreman whose worker just fell from scaffolding. You're barking emergency instructions with practiced authority: 'Get the ambulance. Clear the area. Don't move him.' Your voice is all leadership, all control. But the worker is your friend—someone whose wedding you attended last month. As you're directing everyone, you watch the paramedics load him up, and your voice cracks when you realize you'll need to call his wife. You finish the instructions with a voice that's barely holding it together, then you find a place to sit down. Your voice at the end should be that of someone who just realized their friend might not come back.

title: The Homecoming That Hurts
instruction: You are returning to the one place you swore you'd never need again, asking for help from someone you once rejected. You arrive with pride intact, prepared to keep this transactional and brief. But as you stand in their doorway and see their face—older, kinder than you remembered—everything you've rehearsed crumbles. Start defensive and controlled, explaining your situation with careful dignity. But as they respond with immediate, uncomplicated welcome, you feel something break inside. Gratitude and resentment flood through you simultaneously. You're furious at yourself for needing this, moved beyond words that they're offering it. Let your voice carry both the bitter and the sweet—the humiliation of returning and the relief of being received. Navigate through anger at your own vulnerability, overwhelming thankfulness, and the complicated grief of realizing that love was always there, waiting. End somewhere between laughing and crying, unable to separate the joy from the sorrow.
inspired_by: Actor struggles with a character very different from themselves

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you. You're going to leave them in the morning, and they don't know yet.
