Begin by whispering the practical reasons—all the logical explanations you've constructed about why this isn't working. Keep your voice barely audible, as if testing the words. But as you continue speaking into the darkness, let yourself admit the things you've never said out loud. When you notice you're hiding behind explanations or justifying yourself, pause. Breathe. Speak the more vulnerable truth underneath. Maybe you're terrified. Maybe you still love them but can't stay. Maybe you're ashamed. Let your whisper become even softer, more intimate, as you move from explanation to confession. By the end, you might be saying things you didn't even know you felt—gratitude, sorrow, apology, or something without words. Let silence hold the final emotion.
inspired_by: Actor's impulsive flow is interrupted during a long run or performance; self-consciousness creeping in

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything, and you're physically collapsing—falling to your knees, against a wall, onto the floor. Your body is betraying you with the intensity of what you feel. As you surrender to this physical-emotional storm, split your attention between the overwhelming internal experience (grief, rage, shock coursing through your actual muscles and breath) and specific, piercing sensory details around you—the cold floor, the texture of the wall, sounds from outside, the quality of light. Let these external details both anchor you and shatter you further. Move between being consumed by the feeling and being startlingly present to the physical world. Maybe you start in pure emotional chaos, but the sensory details of the real world gradually pull you into something else—maybe quiet acceptance, maybe fiercer determination, maybe hollow emptiness. Let your body and the environment have a conversation.
inspired_by: Working for a Choice While Promoting Ensemble

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at 3 AM. For years, you've needed their approval for a life choice they've always opposed—perhaps a relationship, a career path, or a truth about yourself. You begin the scene heavy with unspoken regret and fear, gently taking their hand. As you speak, you realize this is your last chance to say what you've rehearsed a thousand times but never dared to voice. Start tentative and apologetic, but by the end, let yourself arrive at a place of fierce, loving honesty—even if they can barely respond. Your final emotion should be a paradoxical peace mixed with raw grief, having finally freed yourself from needing what you always wanted. Let your voice break where it needs to; let silence do its work between your words.

title: The Beautiful Terrible: Scattering Ashes and Finding Joy
instruction: You're at the place your loved one wanted their ashes scattered—somewhere beautiful, somewhere that meant everything to them. As you open the container, start with tears, with the heaviness of finality. Your voice shakes as you try to say goodbye. But then—maybe it's the wind, maybe it's a memory, maybe it's their voice in your head telling you to stop being so damn serious—you laugh. It's a real laugh, startled out of you, mixing with your tears. You're crying and laughing, telling them stories, half-scolding them for leaving, half-grateful for the time you had. 'You were so stubborn' becomes 'Thank you for being stubborn.' Your voice dances between heartbreak and joy, grief and gratitude. This is the terrible beauty of love that survives death—you're devastated and you're full, broken and somehow more whole. End with something like 'Okay, you're free now'—and your voice holds both the deepest sadness and a strange, transcendent peace.
inspired_by: Professional: Hospital Administrator Denies Treatment a Patient Can't Afford

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're packing up your child's bedroom—they're moving far away for something wonderful, something you helped them dream toward. You're alone, folding clothes, touching objects. Begin with pride and excitement, talking to them as if they're there, celebrating their courage. But as you work, let other feelings surface: the fear you haven't shown them, the approaching emptiness, the bittersweet ache of successful parenting meaning they leave. Don't choose between happiness and grief—let both be true simultaneously. By the end, you're holding something small of theirs, and you're laughing and crying at once, grateful and bereft, proud and terrified. The challenge is not resolving these contradictions but living fully inside all of them.

title: A Paramedic Breaks Protocol to Save Someone, Then Watches Them Die Anyway
instruction: You're doing chest compressions, voice commanding and fierce, calling out instructions to your team. You made a split-second decision that violated every protocol because you KNEW you could save them. Your voice is absolutely certain, almost aggressive in its determination. Push harder. More epinephrine. Don't you dare give up. Then the monitor flatlines. For real. Your commanding voice fractures mid-word. You keep going anyway, but now you're pleading, your words desperate and cracking. Your professional composure shatters into something feral and helpless—you're begging them to come back, bargaining with a body that can't hear you. End with your voice dropping to nothing, whispering 'I'm sorry' over and over, all that fierce certainty collapsed into hollow devastation.
inspired_by: Editor Realizes Her Biggest Scoop Will Destroy Someone She Loves

title: The Last Lullaby Over Airwaves
instruction: You are driving home alone in heavy traffic at dusk, the click of the turn signal and hum of the engine filling the car. You've just ended a phone call with your son, who is with his other parent across the country, and you suddenly realize you forgot to say 'I love you' before you hung up. Start by re-dialing, focusing on the road, your voice calm and distracted, but as the ring starts your throat tightens — you're afraid you'll miss him, that he won't pick up, that you've let the moment slip. Let the longing build as you hear his voice, your own cracking with tenderness, breath hitching at the edges, until you finally whisper the words you were too distracted to say, the traffic fading into background static.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Contagious Giggles of a Rainy Day Surprise
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe eight years old, telling your best friend about the most ridiculous thing that happened this morning. You found a frog in your lunchbox, and it wasn't just any frog, it was a tiny, grumpy-looking one that jumped onto your dad's head. You're trying to explain this, but every time you picture your dad's face, you completely lose it. Start the story with a giddy, excited energy, full of breathless hope that your friend will think it's as funny as you do, but you are already wheezing, barely getting the words out. Let the laugh take over completely, your voice cracking into high-pitched squeaks and silent gasps for air. By the end, you are just a pile of laughter, the story abandoned, the only sound a joyful, wheezing gasp before you finally manage, 'I can't... I can't even tell you.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Body Keeps the Score
instruction: You are in the shower after receiving shocking news—a betrayal, a diagnosis, a loss, or a revelation that changes everything. Begin by describing the physical sensation of the water hitting your skin, trying to focus only on the body, only on the simple act of washing. But as the water runs over you, let the news invade your body: maybe your knees buckle, maybe your breath comes in gasps, maybe you find yourself pressing your forehead against the cold tile. Allow the physical and emotional to blur completely—you can't tell if you're shaking from cold or shock, if the water on your face is from the showerhead or your tears, if the pain in your chest is your heart breaking or your lungs forgetting how to breathe. Let yourself vocalize—not words, but sounds: gasps, sobs, maybe even bitter laughter at the absurdity. Transform from trying to hold your body together to surrendering completely to what it needs to do, ending with exhausted stillness as the water continues to fall.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Absence
instruction: You're finally saying what you've held back for years to a parent who was physically present but emotionally absent—or who left entirely. Begin with controlled anger, each word carefully chosen like stones you're placing: 'Do you have any idea what it was like? Waiting for you to notice me? To choose me?' Let the control start to crack, voice rising with years of accumulated pain: 'I was a child. I needed you to fight for me, and you just... you didn't.' Then the anger collapses into something more vulnerable, voice breaking: 'I still catch myself trying to earn your love. I'm thirty-five years old and I still...' Pause, let the silence hold the weight. Finally, find a weary, quiet strength: 'I'm done waiting. I'm done shrinking myself hoping you'll finally see me.' End with exhausted relief mixed with profound sadness.

title: The Last Sugar Cube
instruction: You're an elderly person alone in a quiet kitchen, rummaging through a cluttered drawer. Your hands tremble as you search for the sugar cubes you know you saved somewhere. Confusion flickers as you almost grab a tea bag instead, but then your fingers close around the last cube. You pause, leaning on the counter, a soft laugh escapes you — relief mixed with frail hope. Let your voice start foggy and unsteady, each word an effort to find, then slowly brighten as you realize you've found it, ending on a breathy, tender optimism that carries through your simple, slipping words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight of Keeping Quiet
instruction: You're an older adult sitting across from the person you've shared your life with. It's late, you're both tired, and you've been circling the truth for months. Start by mentioning the rain outside—how it's been falling all day—your voice dragging with fatigue. Then you stop, hesitate, look down at your hands. The confession comes out barely above a whisper, your voice cracking at the edges: 'I took money from our savings. Years ago.' Your throat tightens, you pause to breathe, and you add, 'I never told you because I was afraid you'd leave.' You long for them to understand, but exhaustion makes each word feel heavier. End with a quiet, trembling 'I'm so sorry,' spoken not to them but to the floor, your voice thin and spent.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Longing (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: First Light, Empty Bed
instruction: You wake in a dim, quiet room, still half-lost in the residue of sleep. Your throat is thick, your lips sticky. As you slowly become aware of the cold sheet beside you, a faint, hollow ache begins to creep in—a longing for someone who used to be there. Your voice, cracking and phlegmy, starts with a mutter of disbelief, then softens into a fragile, almost whispered admission of how much you miss them. Let the gravel of morning gradually thin as you speak, and let the micro-distractions—a cough, a glance at the window, a hand rubbing your face—leak into the words.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Unleashing Years of Silent Rage at a Beloved Friend
instruction: You've supported, forgiven, and stayed silent through countless betrayals from someone you love deeply. But today, something breaks. Start with your voice shaking, trying to contain what's coming: 'I can't... I can't do this anymore.' Then let it explode—years of swallowed words pouring out: 'Do you have ANY idea what it's cost me to keep loving you? To keep showing up while you destroy yourself and everyone who cares?' Your voice is raw, savage with pain. But here's the complexity: even as you rage, you're also breaking apart because raging at them means possibly losing them. 'I have given you EVERYTHING and you just—' Your voice cracks, the fury collapsing into devastated tears: 'Why am I never enough to make you want to stay?' The anger and love are inseparable. End with fierce protectiveness mixed with utter helplessness: 'I would die for you. I would give you anything. But I can't save you from yourself, and it's killing me to watch.' Your voice is simultaneously roaring and pleading, strong and shattered.

title: The Scoreboard Confession
instruction: You're standing on an empty field after your child's final game, and they didn't play - they sat the bench all season. Start with fierce, explosive anger at the coach, at the system, shouting into the emptiness about fairness and wasted potential. Your voice should be rough, passionate, protective rage. But mid-rant, something cracks - the anger collapses into helplessness. You weren't angry at the coach. You're devastated that you can't fix this for them, can't shield them from disappointment, can't make the world fair. The powerful protectiveness breaks down into whispered, broken admissions: you don't know how to help, you feel useless, you're terrified of failing them. End with your voice completely stripped of bravado - just a parent, small and scared and loving them so much it hurts.
inspired_by: The Competitive Parent at a Childrens Game

title: Stroking Your Dying Dog's Fur One Last Time
instruction: You're sitting on the veterinarian's floor, your beloved dog's head in your lap for the final time. Run your fingers through their familiar fur, feeling the warmth that will soon be gone. Start with a desperate, clinging tenderness—memorizing every sensation, every breath. Describe what you feel under your hands while trying to stay present, to not think about after. Let your voice begin controlled, almost clinical in its focus on details, but gradually crack open as the reality hits: this is the last time you'll ever touch them. End in a place of raw, whispered goodbye, your fingers still moving even as your heart shatters. The emotion should move from fierce concentration to unbearable loss.

title: The Truth About Why You Left
instruction: You're finally confronting your elderly parent about why you disappeared from their life for fifteen years. Start with controlled, measured anger—recounting specific moments of neglect, words that wounded, needs that went unmet. Your voice should be steady, almost cold, as you list the damages like evidence. But as you speak, something shifts: beneath the anger, there's the child who still needed them, still ached for their love. Let your voice crack and rebuild, fury giving way to devastating vulnerability. End with the question you've never been able to ask: 'Did you ever actually love me?' Let that question hang in the air, raw and undefended. Move from righteous anger to the naked, terrifying vulnerability of still needing an answer after all these years.

title: The Last Bowl of Soup
instruction: You are an old, gruff ex-logger sitting alone in your dim kitchen, shakily spooning a chunky beef stew into your mouth. You’re eating slowly, the warm broth filling your mouth, words muffled around the soft meat and vegetables. Your grandchild just dropped off this meal — they barely speak to you anymore — and you’re overwhelmed with gratitude, but it’s laced with the shame of being so needy. As you chew, you start to mutter a half-prayer of thanks, but your voice catches; a doubt creeps in — are you even worthy of their kindness? Let the physical challenge of eating shape your speech: wet smacks, swallowed words, pauses to work the food, and a voice that thickens with both the bolus and the tears you’re holding back. The distress of your fading strength gives way to a fierce, shaky gratitude, but a lingering note of doubt colors your final swallow.
emotions_sampled: Distress (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Doubt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Doubt
instruction: You're speaking to a younger person—your child, a student, a mentee—and you suddenly recognize you've passed on your own self-doubt to them. Begin with joy, encouraging them, celebrating something they've accomplished. But mid-conversation, you notice them deflecting, dismissing their achievement, using the same words you use about yourself. Horror dawns: they learned this from you. Your tone shifts to anguish as you realize you've infected them with your own disease. Desperately try to take it back, to convince them they ARE enough, even as you hear your own hypocrisy—you don't believe it about yourself. End in a complex knot: fiercely insisting on their worth while drowning in shame about your own inadequacy, love and self-loathing warring in every word, your voice breaking between fierce protection and devastating self-recognition.
inspired_by: Actor has chronic self-esteem problems that return every time they act or audition

title: The Beautiful Terrible Thing
instruction: You've just received news that's both wonderful and devastating—maybe you're moving away from a city you love for an incredible opportunity, or someone who hurt you deeply has finally apologized but too late, or you're watching your child leave home for the life you always wanted for them. You're flooded with contradictory feelings. Begin by describing one specific detail of this moment that captures your attention—something you're seeing, hearing, or feeling right now. Not the big picture, but one real thing: the sound of rain outside, the weight of a key in your hand, the particular color of the sky. Let yourself genuinely focus on this detail, and speak about it while both joy and grief move through you. Start with simple, grounded observation of what's actually in front of you. End by letting this authentic point of focus become the vessel that holds both your happiness and your heartbreak—speaking the contradictions without trying to resolve them.

title: Whispering Through the Wall to Someone You'll Never Touch Again
instruction: You're separated by concrete, by circumstance, by something irreversible. Maybe it's a prison visit, maybe it's quarantine, maybe they're dying on the other side of a door you cannot open. Keep your voice quiet—whispered urgency. Start trying to be practical: 'Listen to me, there are things you need to know...' But you keep breaking off. Your throat tightens. You press your palm against the barrier and ache. Tell them the small things—'Remember when we...' Let your voice catch on ordinary memories made unbearable by loss. Move from trying to be helpful and strong to barely-contained anguish to a kind of fierce, protective tenderness. End with something you need them to promise, but your voice is so fragile it almost doesn't make it out.

title: Treading Water While Calling for Help
instruction: You've fallen off a boat and are treading water in open ocean. Shout for help, but your mouth keeps dipping below the waterline — alternate between clear calls and gurgling, sputtering chaos. Your breathing should be panicked and gulping. Each attempt to call out costs precious energy. Over the course of a minute, exhaustion should make each cry weaker, more desperate, until you're barely able to keep your mouth above water.

title: The Crumpled Photograph
instruction: You are an elderly man, sitting alone in a dusty armchair, holding a worn photograph of your grandson who just became a celebrated artist. You begin by feeling a quiet, bitter anger—why did he get the talent, the luck, the life you never had? But as you look closer, you see his smile, and you remember the day you taught him to fly a kite. A grudging contentment seeps in, and against all odds, a thin hope that maybe his path will be brighter than yours. Speak this to the photograph, your voice tight at first, then softening as you admit a flicker of pride. Let the silence between words carry the weight of years.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Contentment (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Vigil
instruction: You're at your child's bedside as they take their final breaths after a long illness. Begin with forced brightness, telling them about the sunrise you'll watch together tomorrow, your voice almost convincing. But mid-sentence, reality crashes through your denial—they won't see tomorrow. Your voice fractures: 'I'm sorry, baby, I'm so sorry.' The false hope drains away, replaced by raw truth. Your breathing becomes shallow, syncing with theirs. Speak softer and softer, matching their fading presence: 'It's okay to go. Mama's got you.' End in a whisper so tender it aches, giving them permission even as it destroys you. Let love and devastation become indistinguishable.

title: Confronting Your Dying Parent About a Childhood They Stole
instruction: Your parent has days left. You've come to their bedside with decades of unspoken pain. Start with small talk—weather, the nurse, anything safe—but your voice is tight, holding something back. Then it breaks: 'I need to say this before you're gone.' Your voice hardens as you list the wounds—the neglect, the cruelty, the moments that shaped your brokenness. Let anger rise, then crack into something raw: 'I needed you and you weren't there.' But mid-confrontation, you see how small they've become, how scared. Your voice softens against your will. The rage doesn't disappear, but something else enters: grief for what could have been, pity for their own pain. End with contradictory truths—'I can't forgive you' and 'I love you anyway'—spoken with equal devastation.
inspired_by: Skydiving: Main Chute Failure, Deploying Backup While Narrating

title: Sparring with My Shadow
instruction: You're in the middle of a sparring round with your teenage daughter, who is faster and stronger than you. Start with a playful, affectionate taunt as you circle her, your voice light but breathy from exertion. After she lands a clean hit on your ribs, let out a sharp kiai as you try to counter, but your voice cracks with distress. As you pause to reset, feeling the ache and your own limits, let a quiet helplessness creep in—your words become slower, more vulnerable, ending with a faint, tender admission of her skill. Include natural pauses, sharp breaths, and the sound of body hits.
emotions_sampled: Affection (clearly present), Distress (clearly present), Helplessness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispered Vigil at a Sleeping Child's Bedside
instruction: Late night. Your child is finally asleep after their leukemia diagnosis. You kneel beside their bed and begin whispering—not to wake them, but because you need to say these things. Start with gentle observations: how their hair falls across the pillow, the way they still clutch their stuffed animal. Your voice is tender, almost singing. Then let the terror creep in. Whisper your bargains with God, the universe, anyone listening. Confess your helplessness in words so quiet they barely exist. Your throat tightens around phrases like 'I can't lose you' and 'I don't know how to do this.' End with a lullaby or prayer that dissolves into breath—not crying, but something deeper than tears. The emotion must stay intimate, contained, as if any louder and you'd shatter everything.
inspired_by: ER Doctor Recognizes Critical Patient as Old Flame

title: The Unsent Letter: Reading Words You'll Never Say Aloud
instruction: You're alone, reading a letter you've written to someone you loved—past tense, because they're gone, or because you let them go, or because they never knew. Your voice starts almost steady, quiet, reading words you've revised a hundred times. But as you read, you realize how inadequate language is. The tender parts—'you made me feel safe,' 'I never told you'—catch in your throat. This isn't performed emotion; it's the real ache of things left unsaid. Your breathing becomes uneven. You pause, almost stop, then force yourself to continue because this is your only chance to speak these truths, even into empty air. End with the closing—maybe 'I'm sorry' or 'thank you' or 'I loved you'—and let your voice break on it like a wave. Whispered, intimate, like a secret you're telling the silence. This is what grief sounds like when it's private.
inspired_by: Professional: Hospital Administrator Denies Treatment a Patient Can't Afford

title: Protecting What I Cannot Save
instruction: You're a parent trying to shield your child from something terrible and inevitable—an illness, a loss, a world falling apart—and your fierce protectiveness is collapsing into helpless rage. Start with false brightness, your voice straining to sound strong and reassuring, but let the cracks show immediately. Build into explosive intensity: let your voice rise with fierce, almost violent determination to fix this, to fight this, to refuse this reality. Then break completely—let that power shatter into sobbing desperation, your words dissolving into raw pain as you realize you can't protect them from this. End in a place of shaking tenderness, your voice barely holding together, as you shift from trying to shield them to simply holding them through what must come.

title: The Answered Prayer
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe ten years old, kneeling at the altar of a small wooden church during a revival service. The preacher's voice fades behind you as the weight of your mother's recent healing hits you all at once. Start by whispering a quiet, broken 'thank you'—your voice shaky, barely audible over the piano. But as you speak, the gratitude swells into a fierce, rhythmic joy: pitch rises, words tumble out in a chant-like praise, tears and laughter mix, and you repeat fragments like 'She's alive, she's alive' as if possessed by hope. Your voice breaks free from normal speech—glossolalic, sing-song, desperate and triumphant.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Loop
instruction: You're a child locked in the same old argument with your parent about cleaning your room. You start proud, arms crossed, voice sharp and whiny—'You always say that! I did it yesterday!'—repeating your point louder each time. But mid-sentence, you notice the tiredness in their eyes, the weight of their day. Your voice cracks, loses its edge, and you trail off into a quiet, heartfelt thank you—for all they do, for never giving up. Let the natural distraction of fidgeting with a toy or glancing away break your rhythm, then let gratitude flood in like a sudden release.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Hurricane Body
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—maybe the job you sacrificed everything for, maybe test results you've been dreading, maybe a call you've waited years to receive. Your body knows before your mind catches up. Start with your breathing—let it change, become ragged or held or rushed. Feel the physical sensation of emotion flooding your system: heat in your chest, trembling in your hands, weakness in your legs, or explosive energy demanding release. Move if you need to—pace, collapse, spin, press your hands against walls. Let sounds escape you—laughter mixed with sobbing, gasping, raw vocal release without words. The emotion should be so physical it's almost like illness or intoxication. Transform from the initial shock hitting your body to gradually finding your breath again, your physical self slowly integrating what your heart already knows.

title: Bench Press Betrayal
instruction: You're a young man trying to impress a woman by bench pressing way too much weight with terrible form. Your arms begin to tremble, your chest aches, and you can only speak in forced, panicked bursts as the bar hovers dangerously over your throat. A friend you've always resented for being naturally stronger walks by and starts teasing you, drawing the woman's attention. Start with a strained, high-energy boast that you've 'got this,' then shift into increasingly desperate, jealous half-jokes that crack into real vulnerability, until your voice becomes a ragged whisper as you realize you might actually drop the bar on yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Rage That Becomes Surrender
instruction: You're confronting someone who betrayed you in the deepest way possible. Start with controlled fury, each word precise and cutting: 'You destroyed everything.' But they just stand there, accepting it, not defending themselves, and somehow that makes it worse. Your voice explodes—raw, uncontrolled, years of trust and love turned into weapons. You're shouting, but it's breaking into sobs. You want them to hurt like you hurt, but you also want them to fight back, to prove they care enough to argue. Instead they whisper 'I know,' and something in you collapses. Your fierce rage dissolves into exhausted grief. End with a broken admission that despite everything, some part of you still loves them, hating yourself for it even as the words leave your mouth.
inspired_by: Your Abusive Ex Trying to Reconcile

title: The Unspoken Inquiry
instruction: You are fully engaged in giving oral sex, lost in the sensation and the rhythm, your humming deep and rhythmic with pleasure. Then you feel your partner's body go still—a slight withdrawal or a sharp intake of breath. You freeze, a confused hum escaping you as you try to mumble, 'What's wrong?' The words are swallowed, turning into a wet, questioning moan. Let your voice shift from focused lust to a worried, muffled inquiry, with breathy pauses and nasal sounds that betray your sudden uncertainty. End with a sense of hanging in the air, waiting for an answer you cannot fully ask.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Night Before You Leave Me
instruction: You're lying in darkness beside your sleeping partner, knowing tomorrow you walk away from this love to save yourself. Whisper-soft, almost to yourself: 'I memorized the way you breathe.' Your voice is achingly tender, cataloging small intimacies—the way they fold into you, the sound of their heartbeat. Let your throat tighten with unshed tears as you confess why you have to go, even though they're everything you want. The devastation is quiet, contained in the spaces between words. Your voice should feel like touching something precious you're about to break. End with the softest 'I'm sorry,' barely audible, followed by silence that holds all the grief of loving someone you can't keep.

title: Recounting Trauma to a Stranger Therapist
instruction: You're telling your story to someone who needs to know but never will know you. Start clinical as distance—'It started when...' At specific details your voice becomes unstable. You're re-living while reporting, voice quieter as body tightens. Your breathing shows the cost of recounting.

title: The Old Trapper's Last Trap
instruction: You're an old, bitter trapper, kneeling in muck to free your leg from your own rusted bear trap. Your back screams, your breath is forced grunts. Start with a low, seething anger at your failing body, but let it curdle into cold, savoring malevolence as you imagine the sheriff's new deputy finding your hidden cache of poison. The helplessness is a tightness in your throat, making your words sticky and dangerous, like a promise you've been keeping for years. End with a slow, wet laugh that sounds like rocks grinding under ice.
emotions_sampled: Anger (slightly present), Helplessness (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Newborn as Everything Falls Apart
instruction: You're holding your newborn child for the first time, but you've just received devastating news—your partner is leaving you, you've lost your job, a loved one just died, your world is collapsing. Begin with pure wonder and tenderness as you look at this tiny life, speaking softly, marveling. But the terrible reality keeps crashing in. Let yourself oscillate wildly between fierce protective love and complete despair. You might whisper promises, then break into sobs. You might feel rage at the unfairness, then dissolve into tender devotion. Let these contradictions coexist and battle within you—joy and grief, hope and hopelessness, overwhelming love and devastating loss. End in a place of complex, bittersweet resolution—changed by both the beauty and the pain.

title: Confronting Your Mother Before the Wedding
instruction: It's two hours before you walk down the aisle, and you've finally cornered your mother alone in the bridal suite. You start controlled, almost too calm: 'Mom, I need you to hear something before I get married.' But there's steel in your voice. You've rehearsed this, but as you speak, the words come out raw: 'You never protected me from Dad. You knew what he was doing—the way he tore me down—and you just... let it happen.' Your voice breaks not with sadness but with fury: 'I needed you to be my mother, and you chose to be his wife.' She starts to defend herself, and you cut her off—but then something shifts. You see her face, and suddenly you're exhausted: 'I don't want your excuses anymore. I just want you to say it. Say you failed me.' The anger dissolves into something more fragile: 'I'm getting married today, and I don't even know if I want you there. But I need to know—did you ever love me more than you feared him?' By the end, you're not shouting; you're whispering through tears: 'I just needed you to choose me. Just once.'

title: The Kitchen at Midnight
instruction: You've come downstairs to find your parent waiting at the kitchen table—they know about the secret you've been keeping. Start from a place of defensive casualness, perhaps even irritation at being confronted. As the conversation progresses, let your carefully constructed walls crack and crumble. Move through anger at their intrusion, fear of their judgment, and finally toward the terrifying vulnerability of being truly seen. Your voice should shift from clipped and controlled to trembling with suppressed emotion to finally breaking open with the truth you've never been able to speak. End not with resolution, but with the raw exposure of having nowhere left to hide.
inspired_by: An actor is preparing a cold reading for an audition

title: The Hospital Room at 3 AM
instruction: You are sitting beside your mother's hospital bed in the deep hours of the night. The fluorescent lights hum faintly, the air smells of antiseptic and something else you can't quite name. You've been here for hours, watching her breathe. At first, you're fighting exhaustion, your body heavy with the weight of waiting, trying to stay alert, running through memories to keep yourself awake. Slowly, as dawn approaches and the quality of light begins to change, you realize this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Let the physical reality of this specific place and moment seep into your bones—the coldness of the vinyl chair, the rhythm of the machines, the particular quality of pre-dawn hospital silence. By the end, you're no longer fighting to stay awake; you're fighting to hold on to every second, speaking with a clarity born of knowing this room, this moment, is all you have left.

title: The Farewell Gift
instruction: Someone who caused you years of pain—a parent who abandoned you, a partner who betrayed you, a friend who destroyed your trust—is dying, and they've given you something precious: an apology, an explanation, a gesture of love you never thought you'd receive. Begin with suspicion and anger—you don't want to forgive, you've earned your resentment, and forgiving feels like letting them off too easily. As you speak, let the relief of finally being seen and acknowledged begin to crack your armor. You're furious that this gift came so late, grateful that it came at all, heartbroken that there's no time left to rebuild what was broken. End in a place where you're simultaneously thanking them and grieving all the years you lost, loving them and hating them, letting go and holding on.

title: Reading a Bedtime Story Before Goodbye
instruction: You're reading your child their favorite bedtime story the night before you won't see them for a long time. Your voice is warm, musical, doing the voices—but it cracks on certain words. The metaphors in the story land differently tonight. You're pausing to compose yourself while pretending to look at the pictures. Your child asks 'Why are you sad?' and your voice wavers as you reassure them: 'I'm just happy to be with you.' The love in your voice is mixed with devastating loss. By the end, you're barely holding it together, whispering goodnight.

title: The Last Letter in the Rubble
instruction: You are an elderly man, a former construction worker with a deep, gravelly voice, now trapped under a collapsed beam after an earthquake. A young rescue worker is calling to you—your granddaughter's voice, but you barely recognize it through the pain. You are infatuated with the idea of seeing her one last time, but a deep, crushing sadness weighs on you as you realize you may not survive. Start with a shaky, adrenaline-fueled calm, trying to stay still to avoid more pain. As you speak, let the sadness fully take over—your voice trembles, catches, and becomes a whisper, as if each word is a final gift. You must not move; your body is rigid, but your heart is breaking. Say: 'Is that you, Lily? … I was just thinking of that day at the lake. You were so small, throwing pebbles. … I always loved how you laughed. … Don't cry. Please. … It's okay, sweetheart. I'll be warm there.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Summit Confession
instruction: You are at the top of a steep mountain trail, gasping for air, standing with your best friend who just got the lead role you desperately wanted. Your hyper-feminine voice is thin and breathy from the altitude. Start with a forced, cheerful 'congratulations' that cracks with envy. As you struggle to breathe, the jealousy spills out—half-words, pauses, light-headedness. By the end, your voice softens into a raw, choked admission of how badly you wanted it, the envy dissolving into genuine sorrow and the effort of speaking at all.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording your final message to your family before crossing the communication boundary. Begin with carefully controlled composure as you try to say goodbye properly, your voice steady but tight. As you speak, the weight of never seeing them again starts breaking through—your voice cracks on their names, you pause to collect yourself but can't quite manage it. Shift into desperate urgency as you try to pack a lifetime of love into these final seconds, speaking faster, your breath catching. Then, as the signal degrades, soften into whispered tenderness, no longer trying to hold it together, just letting them hear your naked grief and love. End with quiet acceptance, your voice barely audible: 'I'm not afraid anymore.' Let the transformation from control to complete emotional surrender feel inevitable and raw.

title: The Moment You Find Your Stolen Children
instruction: You're in the chaos of the rebellion's aftermath, and you've just found your two children who were sold away years ago—but they don't remember you, and they're terrified of this fierce stranger claiming to be their mother. Begin with explosive joy, your voice cracking with desperate happiness, saying their names over and over, trying to make them understand, your words tumbling over each other. Then your voice fractures into something wild when they back away from you—rage at what was stolen, anguish that they were so young they forgot your face, panic that you've finally found them but lost them anyway. Your vocal intensity peaks as you beg them to remember something, anything—a song, a phrase, the way you used to say goodnight. End with your voice broken down to nothing, helpless and shattered, as you realize you might be too late, that slavery took even this, but still whispering, 'I'm your mama. I'm your mama,' unable to stop saying it even as everything collapses.

title: Jealous at the Party
instruction: You're at a loud house party, three drinks in. You see your ex-girlfriend laughing with someone new across the room. You wanted to talk to her, but now you're stuck watching. Start with a low, dizzy drawl—admitting to yourself how bad you still want her. As you describe the guy's hand on her shoulder, your voice tightens with anger. Then you almost knock over your glass, and a wave of shame hits you—you feel pathetic. Let your words stumble, trail off, get louder, then drop into a broken whisper.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Anger (extremely present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Burning and the Breaking
instruction: You've just finished running—sprinting, actually—until your lungs are screaming and your legs are shaking. You're alone in an empty field or parking lot at dusk. Begin with your body's desperate need for air, gasping, doubled over. But you weren't running for exercise—you were running from a rage so consuming you feared what you'd do if you stayed still. As your breathing starts to slow, let the physical pain become a gateway: the fury that drove you here begins pouring out in raw, primal sounds—not words at first, just noise. Gradually, let it become words, naming what you're furious about (a betrayal, an injustice, a loss). Let the rage peak, then crack open into something else: underneath the fury is devastating heartbreak. End on your knees, the physical exhaustion and emotional devastation merged, with your final words barely audible—a whispered admission of the hurt beneath the anger.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a comprehensive record of their process and choices

title: Bedside Vigil: The Night Watch
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping spouse in the ICU at 3 AM. They can't hear you, but you need to say these things. Begin in barely audible whispers, so tender it hurts: 'I'm still here, baby. I'm right here.' Your voice is gentle as breath, intimate as prayer. Tell them the small things—how you made their coffee this morning out of habit, how empty the bed is, how you still reach for them in your sleep. 'I wore your shirt today. It smells like you.' Your voice catches, tears threatening but not quite falling. The vulnerability is excruciating. Share a memory—something beautiful from your early days together—and let yourself smile through the sadness. 'Remember when we...' Your voice glows with love, even as it trembles. Then the fear creeps in, quiet and devastating: 'I don't know how to do this without you. I don't know how to be me without you.' End with a whispered promise that's both fierce and fragile: 'But I'm not leaving. I'm staying right here. However long it takes. I'm staying.' Move from tender gentleness through aching vulnerability to quiet, unshakeable devotion.

title: The Drunk Call
instruction: You're an older man, slightly drunk, calling a lover you've been trying to impress with a seductive voice. At first, you perform—breathy, slow, describing how you touch yourself, your voice low and controlled. But halfway through, the intoxication loosens your grip: you stumble over a word, let out a real, ragged breath, and confess that you feel pathetic, that you need her to tell you she wants you back. Your voice shifts from a rehearsed, bass-heavy purr to a cracked, desperate whisper—still close to the mic, but now it's not a performance, it's a plea. Let the clothes rustle, let there be a pause where you lose your train of thought and find it again, and let the final line hang with a helpless half-laugh.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Dangling Apology
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe seven years old, caught stealing cookies from the jar on the highest shelf. Your dad found you mid-reach, one arm still stretched up, fingers clutching the lid. You’re stuck like that, arm trembling, your voice comes out thin and high because your lungs are pulled tight. Start defiant, insisting you were just 'looking'—then hear the disappointment in his silence. The defiance crumbles into a real, shaky apology, the kind that catches in your throat. Your shoulders drop, your arm finally lowers, and your voice floods back with tears you didn't know were coming. Speak the lines: 'I was just… no, okay, I took them. I’m sorry. I didn’t think you’d see.' Let your voice start bold then crack, your arm tiring, your breath shallow.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the dark at 3 AM, and you need to tell them something you've been hiding—an affair, a lie, a fear, something you did, something you need. Begin in whispered hesitation, testing words in the darkness. But instead of planning what to say, let each word or silence lead impulsively to the next. If you feel like reaching for their hand, do it immediately. If you suddenly need to turn away, turn. If your breath catches, let the catch become a pause or a sob or a laugh. Don't think about where you're going—respond to the darkness, to their breathing, to each sensation in your body as it arises. Maybe tenderness suddenly spikes into desperation. Maybe shame transforms into defiance. Maybe your whisper grows into something louder or breaks into fragments. The vulnerable, tentative energy you start with must travel somewhere unexpected and true by the end—perhaps to relief, perhaps to terror, perhaps to an intimacy you've never touched before.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They cannot speak anymore, but their eyes are searching yours. You need to tell them something you've been too ashamed to say your whole life—something ridiculous, childish, or embarrassing about who you really are or what you really want. Start with the weight of a lifetime of hiding, feeling exposed and mortified as the words begin. As you speak, let yourself become surprisingly lighter, almost giddy with relief, until by the end you're laughing softly through tears, realizing they already knew and loved you anyway. Let your voice crack, giggle inappropriately, make sounds you'd normally suppress—this is the moment when shame dissolves into grace.
inspired_by: Actor has fear of embarrassment and refuses to risk unpredictable behavior

title: Running Your Hands Through Warm Sand
instruction: Sink your fingers into the sand, feeling its warmth and softness. Describe the sensation as it slips through your fingers, each grain smooth and comforting. Speak with a tone of quiet enjoyment, as if each handful of sand grounds you in the moment, filling you with a calm and gentle warmth.

title: The Last Symphony
instruction: You are an elderly person using a voice assistant for the first time, trying to play your favorite opera from your youth. Initially, you speak in hyper-correct, robotic tones—pronouncing every syllable unnaturally, pausing between words as if teaching the device. But as the music begins to play, you feel a surge of pride at having succeeded with this strange technology, mixed with pure pleasure as the opening notes flood the room. Midway, you try to ask for the next track, but your voice suddenly cracks with confusion as the assistant mishears you—your proud joy stumbles into bewildered frustration, your voice wobbling between ecstatic memories and the stark reality of the machine's limitations.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Confusion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's dawn, and you're leaving someone you love deeply—because of duty, fear, circumstances beyond control, or perhaps because staying would destroy you both. They're still asleep, peaceful, unaware this is goodbye. You speak in barely audible whispers, confessing things you could never say when they were awake. Start with tender observation: 'Your hand is warm. I'll remember that.' Your voice is achingly soft, intimate, each word a physical touch. Then the reality of what you're doing starts to sink in, and your whispers become choked with tears you're trying desperately to suppress. 'I'm so sorry. You'll wake up and I'll be gone, and you'll hate me, and you should.' Allow moments of pure silence where emotion is too big for words—where breath catches, where you almost can't continue. End with a whispered admission that's both loving and breaking: 'You were the best thing. You were everything. And I'm still leaving.' The entire piece should feel like stolen intimate moments, vulnerability so raw it can barely be voiced.
inspired_by: Caught in Machinery: Fighting Physical Panic While Thinking

title: The Last Surgery
instruction: You're a surgeon performing your final operation before retiring, but halfway through you realize the patient on your table is your estranged adult child who you haven't spoken to in fifteen years. You don't know if they even know you're their surgeon. Start with your usual professional clarity—'Scalpel. Retractor.'—but as you work, your voice begins to fracture with the weight of everything unsaid. Your hands remain steady because they must, but your voice betrays you: 'Suction... I need...' You're performing the most important surgery of your life on the person you failed most profoundly. By the end, as you close the final suture, you whisper words you should have said years ago—'I'm sorry. Please live. Please.'—knowing they can't hear you, but you need to say them anyway. The medical precision dissolves into raw parental anguish.

title: Confessions in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner in the middle of the night. They're awake too. You both know your relationship is ending, but neither of you has said it out loud yet. Begin speaking in barely more than a whisper, confessing something true you've never told them—maybe where you were really happy together, maybe when you first knew it was failing, maybe what you'll miss most. Let yourself fully inhabit the darkness, the warmth of shared sheets, the sound of their breathing six inches away, the specific texture of the pillowcase against your cheek, the weight of nighttime silence around you both. Start in careful tenderness, almost holding your breath, afraid of breaking something already broken. As you speak, allow yourself to soften completely, to become utterly undefended. Let your voice crack or drop even quieter. End in a place of naked emotional truth—perhaps acceptance, perhaps aching love mixed with necessary goodbye, perhaps a fragile peace with what cannot be saved.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use imaging as a choice approach in a scene

title: The Hidden Orchid
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a soft, high voice, walking slowly through a dense jungle. At first, you feel a deep, quiet contentment — you smile at the sunlight filtering through leaves, pause to watch a beetle, and murmur to yourself about the peace here. Then you spot a rare orchid you've been seeking for years, and your voice shifts into a trembling triumph — a breathless laugh, a whispered 'I found it,' as you crouch down. Let your voice sound absorbed by the trees, with pauses for bird calls and rustling leaves, and let your joy feel earned from the stillness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Confession That Keeps Escaping
instruction: Late at night, lying next to your partner, you need to whisper something you've been hiding - an affair, a secret, a truth that could change everything. But as you try to say it, let yourself be pulled off course by every genuine distraction. Maybe you become aware of their breathing and it makes you want to cry, then you notice that impulse feels theatrical and you resent it. Maybe you start the confession three different ways and hate how each one sounds. Let yourself get sidetracked by the texture of the sheets, by wanting to laugh at the absurdity, by suddenly feeling tender toward them, then guilty, then annoyed at your own guilt. Move through each authentic moment - the words coming close, then retreating. By the end, what emerges is either the raw truth or the realization of why you can't say it. The journey is from forced confession to discovered honesty.
inspired_by: Being Irreverent to Your Concept of the Material

title: Victory from a Scallop Shell
instruction: You stand alone on a windy beach, winning a fierce internal war—a success you never thought possible. But the sharp, cold taste of old betrayal is still salty on your lips, and the horizon's freedom feels wildly terrifying. Let the crashing waves and shifting sand pull your voice into bittersweet triumph, where pride is heavy and joy is shadowed by sour memory. You speak this truth to yourself, and to the seagulls, and to the wind.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Fear (slightly present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Words Before the Door Closes
instruction: You're standing at your parent's hospital bedside in the final hour, and you've realized this is your last chance to say what you've never been able to say. Begin with anger—quiet, controlled fury at all the years of silence between you: 'You never asked me what I needed.' Let that anger crack open into something raw and desperate as you realize time is running out. Your voice breaks as you move closer, whispering now: 'But I need you to know I understand now. I understand why you couldn't.' End with your hand on theirs, speaking with a tenderness that surprises even you, forgiving them and yourself in the same breath. The emotional journey moves from bitter confrontation to devastating acceptance to a love you didn't know you still had.

title: Bedside Vigil—Unspoken Forgiveness
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you loved who hurt you deeply—a friend who betrayed you, a family member who wounded you—and they're dying. They're unconscious and cannot hear you, but you finally speak the truth. Begin with quiet, almost whispered words, your voice catching on memories both beautiful and painful. Tell them about the damage they caused, but also about the love that persisted underneath. Your voice should be tender even as you acknowledge the hurt, grief-soaked even as you recall moments of joy. There's no confrontation here, only the aching complexity of loving someone imperfect. End by forgiving them aloud, not because they earned it, but because you need to release it—your voice breaking on the words as tears finally come, mixing sorrow with a strange, gentle relief.

title: The Garden's Betrayal
instruction: You are an elderly man in your overgrown garden at dusk, finally finding the rose bush you've nurtured for decades. Suddenly, you realize the neighbor's dog, which you adored, has dug it up completely — roots exposed, petals crushed. You loved that dog like family. At first, a strange ecstasy rises in you — a wild, inappropriate pleasure at the sheer audacity, a laugh that cracks your voice. Then doubt floods in — you question if you saw it right, if it's real, your breath snorting, hands shaking. Finally, awe at the destruction — it's almost beautiful, but the rage erupts, and you start breaking a nearby pot, your voice dropping to a gutteral growl, then screaming, the words coming out as percussive, breathless attacks between strikes. Feel the sun on your neck, the dirt under your nails, the sting of torn roots in your palm.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Doubt (clearly present), Awe (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Acting Unaffected When Overhearing Gossip About Yourself
instruction: You overhear unkind things said about you. Internally, youre hurt, but you act as if you didnt hear. Describe the sting inside while maintaining composure. Speak and move as usual, hiding any reaction.

title: The Watcher in the Hospital Room
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He's unconscious, breathing slowly. Begin by speaking to him as if observing from a distance—clinically noting what's happening, describing the room, the machines, as though you're documenting it for someone else. You're calm, controlled, almost journalistic. But as you continue speaking, something breaks. A memory surfaces—something raw you've never said aloud. Let yourself move from observer to participant. By the end, you're no longer watching this moment—you're drowning in it. Your voice should travel from steady and detached to shattered and intimate, as if you've suddenly realized you can't hide behind description anymore.
inspired_by: Group Dream Sharing and Analysis (Workshop Format)

title: Confronting Your Parent in the Hospital Room They'll Never Leave
instruction: You're standing beside your parent's hospital bed, and they're conscious, and you've finally found the courage to say what you've never said. Begin with your voice tight, almost casual, as you make small talk about the weather, the nurses, anything but what you came to say. Then let it break open: 'Why didn't you ever...' and the question you've carried for decades spills out. Your voice should tremble between anger and the desperate need for their love—describe specific memories, moments where you needed them and they weren't there, but make your voice crack with the child you still are inside. Listen to their response (even if it's silence) and let your anger give way to grief, then back to rage, then to something more devastating: pity. 'I'm trying to forgive you before you die, and I don't know if I can.' Let your voice become small, vulnerable, admitting you still need them to say they're sorry, that you mattered. End with your hand reaching for theirs—describe that moment, the touch, whether they respond or not, and how it simultaneously breaks and mends something inside you.
inspired_by: Quicksand Struggle: Fighting the Sinking with Diminishing Strength

title: Feedback Loop
instruction: You're a young man who's been handed a megaphone to hype up a small, indifferent crowd at a community event. You begin with forced bravado, but your voice cracks and the megaphone squeals with feedback, making you cringe. Embarrassment floods you as you try to restart, but the harsh distortion strips away your fake confidence. By the end, you drop the pretense and speak a raw, quiet truth that the megaphone amplifies into something unexpectedly vulnerable.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing at Your Ex-Lover's Wedding
instruction: You're at the wedding of someone you still love, and they've asked you to dance—a gesture of friendship, of moving forward. You accept with a smile that's genuine because you truly want them to be happy, even as your heart is breaking. Your voice is warm, even playful, as you congratulate them, make jokes, reminisce about good times—there's real laughter here, real affection. But underneath, there's an ache that keeps surfacing in small moments: a catch in your breath mid-laugh, a pause that lasts a beat too long, your voice softening with something that sounds like grief even as you're smiling. You're holding two truths simultaneously: genuine joy for their happiness and profound loss for what you'll never have. As the dance ends, your voice becomes tender, almost a whisper, as you say something like 'Be so happy'—and you mean it with your whole heart, even as tears are threatening. The beauty is in the contradiction: laughing while your throat tightens, celebrating while mourning, loving them enough to let them go even though it's destroying you. End with gratitude and heartbreak perfectly balanced in your voice.

title: The Secret I've Carried Alone
instruction: You're whispering a confession to someone you trust—maybe a friend, a therapist, a lover—something you've never told anyone. Begin so quietly they have to lean in to hear you. 'I need to tell you something, and I'm terrified you'll see me differently.' Your voice is fragile, almost breaking before you even begin. As you reveal the secret (a choice you made, something that happened to you, a truth about who you are), let shame creep into your voice—not loud shame, but the kind that makes you smaller, makes you want to disappear. Include long pauses where you almost can't continue. But then, as you near the end, something shifts: you realize that saying it aloud is lifting a weight. Your voice gains strength, not loud but solid. End with the simplest statement: 'I'm still here. I survived this.' Move from terrified fragility to shame-filled revelation to quiet, trembling relief.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child, and they're acting like nothing happened. Start with measured, almost polite questioning: 'Do you remember my tenth birthday?' Your voice is tight with restraint. But as they deflect or make excuses, the lid comes off—twenty years of pain erupts. Your voice cracks between anger and the child inside you who still needed them: 'I waited for you! Every single day, I waited!' The fury is real but underneath it is profound hurt. End in quiet, exhausted honesty: 'I needed you... and you chose not to be there.' Let yourself move from controlled civility to explosive pain to hollow, heartbroken truth.

title: Last Words at the Airport Gate
instruction: Your sibling is about to board a plane for a dangerous humanitarian mission in a war zone—and you both know they might not come back. You started this conversation trying to be supportive and brave, cracking jokes about bringing back souvenirs, keeping your voice light. But as the final boarding call echoes, something cracks open inside you. Your words catch and stumble. You're trying to say 'I'm proud of you' but it comes out broken, tangled with 'please don't go.' Your breath becomes shallow. You're fighting between respecting their choice and the animal panic of potential loss. End with the moment they hug you and you realize you're clutching them too hard, unable to let go, your carefully constructed courage dissolving into raw, wordless need.
inspired_by: Three Drinks Deep in an Ex's Kitchen

title: Ecstatic Collapse
instruction: You've just sprinted your hardest after a friend who yelled 'last one there buys drinks' — and you won. Now you're bent over, hands on knees, gasping for air. Start by trying to speak through violent breaths, your voice shaky and broken. Let the sheer physical overwhelm mix with genuine ecstasy at the victory, then shift into a quiet, breathless laugh at how ridiculous you both look. End with a whispered, amused final word as you finally catch your breath.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Execution
instruction: You're on death row, speaking through reinforced glass to someone you deeply wronged twenty years ago—perhaps the sibling of someone you killed in a drunk driving accident. They've finally agreed to visit after all these years. Begin with rehearsed apologies, words you've practiced a thousand times, your voice mechanical with preparation. But as they start to respond—maybe with unexpected forgiveness, maybe with raw hatred—your practiced speech crumbles. Your breathing becomes ragged as genuine remorse floods through you, mixed with the terror of knowing you have three hours left to live. The emotional arc moves from controlled contrition to devastating vulnerability to an unexpected moment of grace or connection you never thought possible. End with gratitude breaking through fear, your voice soft and wondering, as if you're discovering what it means to be human in your final moments.
inspired_by: Professional: Doctor Discovers Their Medical Error Killed Someone

title: The Garden: Saying Goodbye to Your Childhood Home While Your Mind Still Knows It
instruction: You're walking through your family home one last time before early-onset Alzheimer's takes your memories, speaking into a recorder to preserve what you can. Begin with almost amused nostalgia—laughing softly as you describe the kitchen where you burned your first cake, the living room where you hid behind the couch during thunderstorms. Your voice is warm, grateful, savoring each detail. But the laughter starts catching in your throat as you realize you're not just remembering these moments—you're saying goodbye to them, knowing they'll dissolve like sugar in water. You find yourself talking faster, trying to capture everything before it's gone, your voice cracking between joy at what you had and grief at what you're losing. End in the garden where your mother planted roses, your voice soft and wondering, equally filled with profound peace and shattering loss, thanking the house, thanking your life, your words blurring together as you try to hold onto the scent of those roses just a little longer, laughing and crying in the same breath, grateful and devastated, here and already gone.
inspired_by: Professional: Military Commander Orders Civilians Evacuated, Knowing Some Will Be Killed

title: The Voicemail You'll Never Send
instruction: You're recording a message to someone who just achieved something extraordinary—got their dream job, married someone else, moved across the world. Start speaking with forced brightness, genuine happiness for them, celebrating their joy. But as you talk, let real grief begin bleeding through—you've lost them, this success means distance, this joy isn't yours to share anymore. Your voice should crack between congratulation and devastation. Let yourself feel both emotions as true and simultaneous: you really are happy for them AND you're being destroyed by their departure from your life. Don't choose one emotion over the other—stay suspended between love and loss, pride and abandonment. End unable to find words, your breath catching between laughter and crying, before you delete the message without sending it.
inspired_by: The relationship between the actors needs to have a depth, history, or emotional intensity that doesn't yet exist between them

title: Wired Words
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman recovering from jaw surgery, your mouth wired shut. A well-meaning friend visits and brings up your recent divorce, asking if you're okay. You try to reply, but every word is a struggle through clenched teeth. Start with confusion—why would she bring this up now? Your speech is muffled, halting, as you fumble for syllables. Midway, the confusion deepens into sadness as you realize she’s trying to help, but the pain of the topic makes your throat tight. Let your voice crack and trail off, then settle into a quiet, resigned ache. Around 60 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Thin Air Above the Clouds
instruction: You're an older man who has just reached a high mountain pass after a brutal climb. Your lungs burn, your head throbs, and every word comes in slow, gasping fragments. You force yourself to look out at the endless, shimmering peaks before you—and for a moment you're filled with awe, a childlike wonder at the impossible beauty. But then you notice the litter scattered by previous hikers, the sour smell of your own sweat, the way your body is failing you up here. As you speak, let that awe curdle into disgust—at the mess, at your weakness, at the whole ordeal. Let your voice catch, trail off, and harden as the disgust takes over.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Disgust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Reading Your Father's Eulogy While Laughing Through Tears
instruction: Standing at your father's funeral, you start reading the respectful eulogy you prepared, but halfway through you break into unexpected laughter—because you suddenly remember he would have hated this formal bullshit. Abandon the script and tell the real stories: his terrible jokes, the time he accidentally set the garage on fire, how he sang off-key in the car and didn't care who heard. Laugh genuinely at the absurdity of him, the beautiful ridiculous human he was, even as tears stream down your face. Let joy and grief become inseparable—your voice cracking between laughter and sobs, finding gratitude in every chaotic memory while your heart simultaneously breaks that there will be no more. End with the peaceful contradiction: you're devastated and you're so fucking lucky you got him at all.

title: Coked-Up Confession
instruction: You're a 17-year-old high on cocaine at a house party. You've been watching your crush laugh with your rival all night, and you're burning with jealousy. You corner your buddy by the bathroom and start venting, voice loud and rushed, words spilling out with bitter envy. But as you talk, the stimulant numbness takes over — your throat feels thick, your words slow down, and the anger drains into hollow emptiness. Speak with nasal congestion, sniffing, and a shift from fiery envy to cold, flat indifference.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Game Night Before Deployment
instruction: You're playing one final board game with your closest friend who ships out to a war zone tomorrow morning. Start with your usual competitive banter, teasing them about their terrible strategy, keeping it light because that's what you both need. But as the game progresses, let the weight of goodbye seep in—your voice catches on seemingly normal phrases, your jokes become softer, more tender. By the final move, you're no longer talking about the game at all. You're trying to say 'I love you' and 'come back safe' without actually saying those words, because if you do, you'll completely fall apart. End with a silence that says everything you can't.

title: Telling Your Mother You Remember Everything
instruction: You're thirty-five, sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table. She's made tea like nothing ever happened. Begin with careful, measured words: 'I need to talk about when I was twelve.' Watch her face change. Your voice should start controlled, almost clinical, protecting yourself. But as you speak each truth—the nights she didn't come home, the promises she broke, the child you had to become—your control splinters. Anger surges, then cracks into the grief of that twelve-year-old still inside you. End not with rage but with a question asked in a voice raw and young: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let decades of armor fall away.
inspired_by: Someone Realizing You're Crying Without Sound

title: The Last Sweater
instruction: You're sitting alone in your mother's hospital room in her final hours. She's asleep, unresponsive. In your hands is the wool sweater she knitted for you when you were ten—the one you wore until it threadbare, the one that still smells faintly of her perfume and kitchen. Begin by truly feeling its texture against your fingers, noticing every pulled thread, every soft worn patch. Trace the patterns she made with her hands. As you hold it, memories flood through you—begin defensive, telling yourself you're prepared for this, you've made peace. But as the sweater's reality deepens in your hands, let your defenses crumble. By the end, speak to her sleeping form with the raw, unguarded grief of a child who will never stop needing their mother. Your voice should transform from controlled strength to breaking tenderness.
inspired_by: Sense Memory with Emotionally Impacting Objects

title: The Ground Rises
instruction: You're a young man who's been injured—maybe a fall or a blow to the head—and you're trying to stay on your feet, talking to a friend who's calling for help. Your body is failing: your knees wobble, the room tilts, your grip on the doorframe slips. Start with urgent distress—you're scared, you need to explain what happened—but as your vision tunnels and your throat weakens, your voice thins into breathy, trailing fragments. Let yourself lose a thought mid-sentence, react to a sudden sound or a flash of light, and end in a whispery daze as you finally sink down.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Surge
instruction: You are an elderly person, no longer used to physical strain, but now you're in a desperate fight—maybe defending your home or a loved one. Your voice is ragged, breath short, each movement costs you. But in the middle of the struggle, a strange, fierce elation rises: you're alive, you're fighting. Start with sharp, defensive barks and gasps of effort, then let the voice shift as you land a blow—a mix of pain, surprise, and a wild, cracking laugh of triumph. End with exhausted, shaky breathing, but a hint of a satisfied smile in your words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Rain-Soaked Prize
instruction: You are an older man caught in a torrential downpour, crouched over a storm drain, trying to retrieve a treasured watch that fell into the muck. The rain is relentless, streaming into your eyes and mouth as you dig through slime and debris. Start with intense disgust—gagging at the filth, muttering curses under your breath as you fumble. Then, your fingers close around the watch; a raw, shouting triumph erupts as you raise it to the sky, voice cracking over a thunderclap, spitting out rainwater as you roar in victory.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Party Line
instruction: You're at a loud house party, leaning against a wall. Across the room, the guy you've been eyeing is laughing with another girl. When he finally walks over, you keep your voice low and teasing, trying to seem completely breezy. Start with a playful, amused edge—like this is all just a game—but let a flicker of jealousy slip into your words when you mention her. End with a hopeful, almost desperate lightness, as if you're daring yourself to believe this could lead somewhere. All the while you're hyper-aware of people nearby, so your voice stays conspiratorial, punctuated by little nervous laughs and quick glances over your shoulder.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering to Someone Who Can't Hear Anymore
instruction: You're speaking softly to someone unconscious—maybe in a coma, maybe their final hours, maybe they've already slipped away. Your voice is barely above a whisper because somehow speaking louder would make it too real. You start with gentle small talk, pretending everything's normal, voice artificially light. But you can't maintain it. Your whisper becomes thick with tears as you confess things you never had the courage to say when they could answer back. 'I was scared to tell you...' 'I need you to know...' Your voice keeps breaking on words you can barely get out. There are long pauses where you're trying to breathe through the tightness in your chest. Near the end, your whisper becomes tender and grateful, thanking them for small, specific moments of love. The final words are so quiet they're almost silent—a prayer, a release, a gentle letting go. Stay intimate throughout; this is too private for volume.

title: What We Don't Say in Daylight
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're on the phone with someone you love - a best friend, a sibling, a former lover. Begin with your voice barely above a whisper, exhausted, as if you've been awake for hours working up the courage for this call. You're confessing something tender and terrifying: maybe that you've always been in love with them, maybe that you're not okay and haven't been for a long time, maybe that you're leaving and can't tell them why. Let your voice catch and break in the middle of sentences, as if the words are made of glass. There's no dramatic revelation - just the aching, quiet truth of what you've been carrying alone. Move through shame, through the fear of being too much, into a fragile kind of hope that maybe they'll still be there when you're done talking. End with your voice soft but steady, having said what needed to be said, waiting in the vulnerable silence for their response.

title: The Joyful Goodbye
instruction: You're sending off someone you love desperately—a child leaving home, a partner taking their dream job across the world, a best friend starting a life you're not part of. You're genuinely, fiercely happy for them, and your voice brims with pride and celebration. But underneath, your heart is shattering. Smile through your words, let laughter break through even as your voice catches. Tell them how incredible they are, how this is exactly what they're meant for. Your joy is authentic—and so is your grief. By the end, you're laughing and crying simultaneously, unable to separate the two. Your final words radiate love and blessing, even as you're breaking apart. The contradiction is beautiful and unbearable: you want them to go, and you can't stand to lose them.

title: The Things I Did Right
instruction: You are at your mother's bedside in her final hours. She's unconscious, but you need to tell her something you've never said: that despite all your childhood fights and resentments, you became who you are because of specific things she taught you. Begin speaking with hesitation and old anger still caught in your throat. As you list each concrete lesson—how she taught you to stand up for yourself, how to cook that one dish, how to read people's faces, how to laugh at yourself—feel the anger dissolving into grief, then into profound gratitude. By the end, you're not angry anymore; you're bereft at losing her, but also genuinely thankful. Let your voice move from bitter and halting to broken open with love and loss. She can't hear you, but you finally mean every word.

title: Laughing Through Your Goodbye at the Airport
instruction: You're saying goodbye to the love of your life who's leaving forever - different continents, different lives, you both know this is the end. Start laughing at a shared memory, genuinely joyful: 'Remember when you thought that was a shark?' Keep laughing together but it's too bright, too desperate. Your voice keeps cracking mid-laugh. You're making jokes about the future, about postcards, about staying in touch, and the absurdity of the lies makes you laugh harder even as tears stream down your face. Tell them you're happy for them - mean it and break saying it. The laughter and sobbing become indistinguishable.
