End with a whispered 'Thank you for everything' that's somehow both devastated and genuinely grateful, finding bizarre peace in the certainty of loss, smiling through tears as you watch them walk away.
inspired_by: Speaking While Severely Injured or in Acute Pain

title: Bedside Whisper: Telling Your Comatose Spouse You're Letting Go
instruction: You're alone with your spouse in hospice. The doctors say they can't hear you, but you don't believe them. Speak barely above a whisper—this is just for the two of you. Start by telling them about your day in tender, mundane detail, your voice soft with familiar love. Gradually confess what you haven't been able to say: that you're exhausted, that you're giving them permission to go, that you're terrified of being alone. Your throat tightens with unshed tears. End with a memory of when you first knew you loved them, your voice breaking on gratitude even as your heart shatters. Let silence hold as much weight as words—pause, breathe, let emotion catch you mid-sentence.
inspired_by: Narrating in a Blizzard: Freezing to Death

title: The Shattering of Safe
instruction: Someone you thought was safe—a partner, a parent, a trusted friend—has just touched you in a way that made you feel unsafe, and you're confronting them NOW. Start with explosive rage, your voice volcanic: 'DON'T you EVER—' Let your fury crash into something more terrifying—helplessness. Your voice cracks, becomes wild with confusion: 'You were supposed to be... how could you?' Show the collapse from power into vulnerability, from shouting to sobbing, from 'How dare you' to 'How could you make me afraid of you?' Your protective rage keeps surging up, then breaking apart on waves of betrayed love. End in a different kind of intensity—quiet, shaking, devastated certainty. Your voice drops to something cold and final, grief-soaked but immovable: 'Don't touch me again. Don't you ever touch me again.' The fierceness remains, but transformed into self-protection rather than attack.

title: The Garage Bench
instruction: You're an older man, strong but worn, sitting alone in your cluttered garage. You just got laid off from the construction company where you worked for 30 years. You're muttering to yourself, bitter about how they treated you, then sad about feeling useless. But then you spot the half-finished rocking chair you've been carving. As you run your hand over the wood, a stirring of possibility rises. Your voice should start low, grumbling, with resentful pauses. Let sadness tighten your throat. Then, as you think about the chair, let your speech slow, grow softer, and finally lift with cautious hope. Talk as if you're discovering the thought for the first time.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Sadness (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Gratitude at the Grave
instruction: You're speaking at the funeral of someone who saved your life but is now gone—a mentor, a friend, a therapist, a stranger who intervened at your darkest moment. Begin with laughter, actually laughing as you remember something funny about them, something perfectly them. Your voice is warm, full of genuine joy and gratitude. But as you speak, the laughter starts to break, tears mixing with the smiles, your voice cracking between thank you and goodbye. You're expressing the most profound gratitude while your heart is being ripped apart. The contradiction is unbearable: you're so grateful they existed, and you're so devastated they're gone. Find moments of peace in the chaos of grief, where you can breathe and smile through tears, where gratitude and loss become the same thing. End with your voice clear and centered, still crying but somehow calm, having found a way to hold both the joy of having known them and the agony of losing them. This is the strength of accepting that both truths can live in your heart at once.

title: Last Signal
instruction: You are pinned under your overturned truck after a crash, alone on a dark mountain road. Every breath is a struggle; your ribs ache and your voice is a dry rasp. You spot a distant flashlight beam bobbing through the trees. Start with raw pain and resignation—you can barely whisper. As the light moves closer, a desperate interest flares. Force words out one by one, pausing to gasp. Micro-distractions: a cough, a wince, shifting your head to see. End with a cracked plea, exhausted but alive with hope.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Protector's Breaking Point: Fierce Love Colliding with Powerlessness
instruction: You're speaking to someone you'd die to protect—a child, a sibling, a beloved—but there's a threat you cannot stop. Start with fierce, almost violent determination: 'I swear to you, I will fix this. I will move heaven and earth.' Your voice is ferocious with protective rage, barely controlled intensity. But as you speak, reality crashes in—you can't fix this. Your voice begins to fracture: 'I would take your place in a heartbeat. God, I would trade anything...' The fury dissolves into desperate pleading, your voice breaking apart. You're trying to stay strong, but helplessness is drowning you. By the end, you collapse into raw, uncontrolled emotion: 'I can't— I can't protect you from this and it's killing me.' Your voice must shatter completely—from warrior to utterly broken human. The arc is from aggressive protectiveness through desperate negotiation to the devastating moment where strength crumbles into helpless, anguished love.
inspired_by: Judge Sentencing the Guilty: The Weight of Final Words

title: The Howl: Discovering Your Partner's Betrayal While They're In Crisis
instruction: You've just found proof of your partner's infidelity—texts, photos, everything—and in the same moment, you get a call that they've been in a terrible accident and might not survive. You're in the car racing to the hospital, and you're screaming. Your voice is a storm: volcanic rage that they did this to you, terror that they might die before you can confront them, self-loathing that you still desperately need them to live. You swing between cursing them with savage fury and begging the universe not to take them. Your voice breaks from roaring anger into sobbing pleas into hollow shock. By the end, you're whispering their name like a prayer and a curse simultaneously. This is passion colliding with grief, love twisted up with betrayal, protectiveness warring with the desire to hurt them as they've hurt you.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Owner's Child Discovers They're Half-Sibling to Enslaved Person

title: The Last Call from the Airport Gate
instruction: You're calling your father from the airport. You're leaving the country forever—a fresh start he'll never understand. Begin with forced brightness: 'Dad, I'm at the gate. I wanted to hear your voice.' He asks when you'll visit. Your voice cracks. You can't keep lying. 'I'm not coming back, Dad.' The silence is unbearable. Your voice drops to a whisper, trembling with a decade of unspoken pain: 'I needed you to fight for me to stay. Just once.' But even as grief pours out, something shifts—your voice finds a strange, fragile liberation. You're finally telling your truth. End with 'I have to board now,' your voice both breaking and somehow, impossibly, free.

title: Retching Gratitude
instruction: You're a 17-year-old at a loud party, hunched over in the corner of the backyard, fighting waves of nausea after chugging a drink you didn't want. Your throat burns, and every few seconds a gag forces you to stop talking. A quiet, popular girl—the one your crush has been eyeing all night—suddenly kneels beside you, hands you a cold bottle of water, and says nothing judgmental. Start with a bitter, jealous thought about her (mumbled, interrupted by heaves), then let the realization that she's actually being kind hit you. Shift into a raw, broken 'thank you,' voice thick with saliva and swallowed puke, surprised by the gratitude crawling through your disgust. Your words should stumble, pause, and slur as your stomach lurches.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Sadness (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Receiving Your Terminal Diagnosis While Your Wedding Is Tomorrow
instruction: The doctor just told you: six months, maybe less. Tomorrow you marry the love of your life. You're alone in this sterile room, and you start laughing—because of course, of COURSE this is the timing. The laughter is real but edged with hysteria. Let it dissolve into crying, then back to laughing again. You're furious and grateful in the same breath—grateful you found them, furious you get so little time. Practice how you'll tell them tonight, and your voice breaks. Imagine the wedding, how beautiful they'll look, and you're smiling through tears. You have to decide: tell them now and shatter this joy, or give them one perfect day before the world ends? End in a moment of strange, terrible peace—this grief means you loved deeply enough to be destroyed by loss. Let contradictions live in your voice: joy and devastation, acceptance and rage, love and unbearable sadness, all at once.
inspired_by: Space Station Commander Records Birthday Message While Hull Breaches

title: The Strangest Kind of Gratitude
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman, deeply feminized in voice, curled in a blanket after an intense BDSM scene. You are exhausted, your body aches, and you feel a wave of genuine gratitude toward your Dominant for the care — but also a creeping wave of disgust at the filth and fluids on your skin, and at how utterly vulnerable you are. A low, hoarse laugh escapes you as you realize how absurdly grateful you feel for being held while also wanting to scrub your own skin. Your voice is small, shaky, then breaks into a tired, half-amused chuckle. Speak as if you are still catching your breath, pausing to sip water or wince at a sore spot. Say: 'Thank you... god, that's weird. I mean it. But also, I'm covered in... well, you know. Gotta love it, right? Kinda gross, but... I'm so glad you're here.' Let the word 'gross' drag with a grimace, and 'grateful' come out almost in a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Disgust (extremely present), Amusement (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Verdict Before the Execution
instruction: You're visiting someone on death row the night before their execution—someone you sentenced years ago as a judge. You believed you were right then, but now doubt has crept in. Begin with careful, measured words trying to maintain professional distance. As you speak, your certainty crumbles. Maybe they were innocent. Maybe you destroyed the wrong life. Your voice must travel from controlled authority to devastating uncertainty, from duty to horror at what you may have done. End in a whisper of something between an apology and a prayer, your composure completely shattered. This isn't about volume—it's about the quiet collapse of everything you believed about yourself.

title: The Overnight Guest
instruction: You're in your dimly lit living room, a man you've been flirting with all night is standing by the door. Your roommate is in the next room, so you keep your voice low. You're teasing him about his indecision—'Your place or mine?'—with a playful, almost mocking edge. But as you watch his face, your teasing falters; you realize you actually want him to stay, not just for the night. Let your voice start light and giggly, then drop into something more hesitant and sincere as you admit you're scared of wanting more. Fidget with your keys, glance at the door, let a laugh trail off into silence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You are finally telling your aging parent exactly how their absence shaped your life. Start with controlled, almost clinical distance—listing facts, keeping your composure, protecting yourself with coldness. As you speak, old anger surfaces: your voice should sharpen with accusations you've held for decades. Then, unexpectedly, let vulnerability break through—the child inside you who still wants their approval, who is still hoping they'll finally understand. End not with resolution but with the exhausting complexity of loving someone who hurt you, your voice carrying both fury and a heartbreaking tenderness. Show us someone trying to hold boundaries while their heart bleeds.
inspired_by: The Doctor and the Reluctant Patient

title: The Best Part of Today
instruction: You're a teenage girl lying in bed, nearly asleep, but you're buzzing with the memory of the best moment from today. Start recounting it with excited, fast speech — your voice is high-pitched and full of energy. But as you continue, your eyelids get heavy, your words slow down and slur together, and you catch yourself trailing off. Let the elation fade into a warm, peaceful contentment, and then let exhaustion take over completely, mumbling the last few words before you drift off.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Contentment (very intensely present), Elation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fantasy Sharing
instruction: You're lying in bed, and your partner says, 'I want to tell you a fantasy.' Your voice is genuinely curious, non-judgmental: 'I want to hear it.' They articulate a fantasy that's different from anything you'd imagined. Your voice processes it in real-time: 'Okay.' You're trying not to judge, trying to understand. Your partner is terrified you're judging them. Your voice becomes deliberately reassuring: 'I like that you want to share this with me.' Now your partner becomes more animated, more engaged. They're describing a scenario, and your voice becomes engaged too: 'That does sound hot.' You're not rejecting them; you're joining them in imagination. Your voice at the end should sound like two people who just created something together in vulnerability.

title: The Whispered Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3am and you're watching your child sleep, knowing you have to leave them—whether due to deployment, illness, impossible circumstances, or a choice that's breaking you. Speak so quietly you barely disturb the air, your voice thick with unshed tears. Begin with just trying to memorize their face, describing what you see with aching tenderness. Let the reality of separation seep in—your voice should catch on words, your breathing should be uneven as you fight to stay composed. Tell them things you hope they'll somehow know, dreams you have for them, apologies for not being there. End with the unbearable sweetness of loving someone so much that leaving them feels like tearing yourself in half. This is intimate devastation, the kind that lives in your throat and chest.

title: The Last Lesson
instruction: Your grandmother is dying, and in her final hours, she's teaching you the family recipe she never shared with anyone—but it's really a metaphor for how to live. Start confused, trying to focus on measurements while grief chokes you. Then something shifts: 'Wait... you're not talking about the bread, are you?' Your voice cracks as understanding floods in—she's giving you her entire philosophy of life, all the wisdom she never put into words. Move from trying to hold back tears to a trembling, grateful comprehension. End with 'I understand now' spoken so quietly it's almost a prayer, your voice breaking with the weight of both devastating loss and the gift she's leaving you. Let the beauty and the goodbye exist simultaneously.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's bedside at dawn, holding her hand as she takes her final breaths. She's been unconscious for days, but suddenly her eyes flutter open and she whispers your childhood nickname—the one only she used. Start with shock that catches in your throat, a desperate attempt to memorize her face, her warmth. Your voice trembles as you tell her everything you never said: gratitude for scraped-knee bandages, for believing in you when no one else did. Mid-way, feel rage bloom—furious that you have only seconds, that this is goodbye. Then let it dissolve into the most tender whisper, telling her it's okay to go, that you'll carry her forward. End on a breath that's half-laugh, half-sob, as you feel her hand go slack and realize you're saying 'I love you' to silence.

title: Whispering Your Secret in the Dark: The Confession That Changes Everything
instruction: You are lying in darkness next to someone you love—a partner, a sibling, a best friend—and you need to tell them something you've been hiding. Start with their name, whispered so softly it's almost just breath. Your voice is tender, terrified. 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' What follows is quiet but devastating—perhaps you're ill, perhaps you've betrayed them, perhaps you're leaving. Your voice catches constantly, words barely making it out: 'I'm so sorry... I didn't know how to...' There are long pauses where silence speaks. You're trying not to cry but tears are in your throat. By the end, you're asking for something—forgiveness, understanding, or just for them to hold you—your voice broken down to its most vulnerable, childlike quality, ending with 'Please don't hate me' or 'I'm scared.'
inspired_by: Panic Attack: Losing Control Over Your Own Voice

title: The Endless Story
instruction: You are a child, lying in bed, fighting sleep while your mother reads you a bedtime story. You're irritable and impatient because you want to stay awake, but your body keeps betraying you. Start the instruction annoyed, speaking sharply to your mother: 'No, I'm NOT sleepy! Keep reading! But do the voices better this time.' Let your words slow as exhaustion takes over, sentences drifting into mumbles and trails. Mid-sentence, you jerk awake, snapping back with irritation, then gradually surrender to the heaviness, your voice fading into a whisper as sleep finally wins.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where he's washing dishes, his back to you. Start from a place of carefully controlled calm—you've rehearsed this conversation a hundred times, and you're determined to stay composed and rational. You begin speaking about something he did years ago that damaged you, your voice measured and steady. But as he continues washing dishes without turning around, something shifts. Move through rising frustration as your carefully prepared words start crumbling, then into a trembling anger you didn't know you were holding, your voice cracking as the child inside you surfaces. Finally, break into raw, unfiltered fury—not shouting necessarily, but voice shaking with the force of years of silence ending. By the end, you're no longer the adult who walked in; you're every age you've ever been, demanding to be seen. Journey: controlled composure → creeping frustration → trembling emergence → volcanic release.
inspired_by: Actor's emotional state is far from what the material demands

title: Whispering a Secret That Changes Everything
instruction: In the intimate darkness—maybe beside someone sleeping, maybe in a quiet room alone—you finally speak aloud the truth you've been carrying. Your voice is barely audible, almost testing the words in the air. Maybe it's 'I'm sick' or 'I never stopped loving you' or 'I've been lying about who I am.' Feel how vulnerability makes your voice fragile, how the words catch in your throat. There's tenderness here—toward yourself, toward the person you're telling, toward the fragile moment of truth. Your breathing is careful, as if speaking too loudly might shatter something precious. Let silence hold weight between phrases. End with a sense of quiet devastation mixed with relief—the secret is out, and you're both freed and terrified by its release. This is confession as a whisper, truth as something almost too tender to bear.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Attracted to Someone Who Was Just a Friend

title: Coach Final Benching
instruction: You're the coach benching your star player for the championship game because their parents just died and they're not mentally present. You're supposed to be delivering a motivational pep talk, but instead you're delivering the worst news: they don't get to play. Your voice starts with the clinical reasoning: 'You're not in the right headspace for this level of play.' But the player is looking at you like you're abandoning them. Your voice becomes gentler, more like a parent than a coach: 'I'm not benching you. I'm protecting you. Grieve. We'll get through this.' The contradiction between your official role and your actual care should be audible.

title: The Gratitude That Cuts
instruction: You're thanking someone who saved your life—pulled you back from the edge, believed in you when no one else did, gave you a chance that changed everything. Begin with genuine, overflowing gratitude: you need them to know what they did, how they altered your trajectory. But as you express your thanks, something else rises: a complicated resentment. Because being saved means admitting you needed saving. Because their faith in you created an expectation you're terrified of failing. Because you now carry a debt you can never repay, and it's become its own kind of burden. Let these contradictory emotions weave together—don't resolve them into one or the other. Your voice should carry both deep appreciation and a kind of anger or sorrow about what their rescue cost you in terms of your own self-image. End with both emotions fully present: 'Thank you' that means both everything and something you can barely stand to say.
inspired_by: Actor has been cast in a major role and has weeks before rehearsal begins

title: Fever Dream of the Body
instruction: You are in the grip of both physical illness and overwhelming desire. Your body is feverish, heavy, every limb weighted down, yet electric with longing for someone who has just entered the room. Begin by letting your physical state completely inform your voice—thick, slow, almost delirious. Your words come like molasses, but underneath runs a current of intense need. As you speak, allow sensations to flood up unbidden—the weight of your own body, the heat of fever, the ache of wanting, memories of touch that feel more real than the present moment. Don't direct these sensations; let them wash through you in waves, transforming your emotional state. Move from the heaviness of illness through the intensity of physical yearning to something transcendent—perhaps a breaking point where pain and pleasure, sickness and ecstasy merge into something else entirely. Your voice by the end should sound utterly transformed from where it began.
inspired_by: Actor needs to prime the unconscious as preparation for a rehearsal or performance

title: Confronting the Coach Who Broke You
instruction: You're finally facing the coach, teacher, or parent who pushed you past breaking, who confused cruelty with discipline, whose 'training' left scars. Start controlled, almost cold—you've rehearsed this. Describe what they put you through, that brutal 'concentrated effort' they demanded. But as you recount specific moments—the humiliation, the pain you hid, the way you pushed until something inside you cracked—your control splinters. Your voice moves from accusation to raw pain to something more complicated: the horrible realization that part of you still wants their approval, still needs them to say it mattered, that you mattered. End with a question you never thought you'd ask, your voice stripped bare and vulnerable, all pretense of strength gone.

title: Finally, You Get It
instruction: You are a deaf teenager, speaking to a hearing classmate who has just realized they've been speaking too fast. You feel a wave of relief—they finally understand how to communicate with you. But underneath, there's a flicker of contempt; they should have known better by now. As you speak, keep your volume high, your words slow and deliberate, over-articulating each syllable for lip-reading. Let your voice start with gratitude, then let a subtle edge of disdain creep in as you continue. Pause, react to their facial expression, maybe shift your weight. End with a mix of satisfaction and dismissal.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Backseat Drive
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy in the backseat of your parents' car at night. The engine hums, the road hisses under the tires, and your father's voice is low on the radio. You know your mother is in the front seat, but something is wrong—she's quiet, and you saw her wince when you hugged her earlier. As you press your face to the cold window, you feel a strange, confusing tightness in your chest—a longing for her touch, but it mixes with the sharp pain of seeing her hurt. Start with a whispered thought about the stars, letting your voice tremble with yearning, then confess to yourself how much you need her to be okay, ending in a broken, quiet sob.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Drop of Hope
instruction: You're a teenage boy exhausted and dizzy from heatstroke, collapsed under a lone tree after hours of hiking without water. You've just spotted a distant figure approaching, and you're convinced it's help. Begin by weakly calling out, your voice dry and cracking, slurring from dehydration, with panting breaths between words. As you speak, your hope intensifies — you smile weakly, then laugh to yourself, then tears mix with sweat as you realize you're not imagining it. End in a quieter, more desperate whisper, your optimism now a fragile but fierce belief that you'll survive.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Lying Low
instruction: You're a teenage boy lying on your side in bed, phone screen glowing nearby. You've just seen a friend's post celebrating a big win—something you wanted for yourself. Your voice stays low and intimate, shaped by the floor pressing one lung closed. Start with envy slipping out in soft, bitter murmurs. Let your body shift, a small sigh, a glance away. Then feel your own pride surface—not loud, but steady, spoken to the dark. End with a quiet, grounding claim: you have your own victories, even if no one posts them.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Thank You That Breaks You
instruction: You're thanking someone who saved your life—literally pulled you back from suicide, addiction, or self-destruction—but you also resent them for it because now you have to face everything you were trying to escape. Begin with your eyes on objects in the space between you rather than on them: their hands, the table, the wall, anything. Let genuine curiosity about these objects give you somewhere to put your attention while you try to find words. What do you actually notice? What patterns, textures, details emerge? As you speak your gratitude, let your attention drift between the objects and their face, tracking your own resistance and pull. Your gratitude is real, your resentment is real, your love is real, your anger is real. By the end, the act of genuinely seeing them—really looking at them while speaking these contradictory truths—should break open something you were trying to keep controlled. End raw, perhaps crying, perhaps laughing, perhaps both, having arrived at a messy, complicated truth you didn't plan to reach.

title: Discovering Your Child in Danger You Cannot Stop
instruction: You see your child in immediate, life-threatening danger and you cannot reach them. Your voice explodes in primal terror: 'NO! STOP!'—screaming with every ounce of power you have, your voice raw and animal-like. You're roaring warnings, commands, pleading at full volume with savage desperation. But as you realize your voice can't reach them, can't change what's happening, the screaming fractures into helpless, choking sobs. Your fierce protectiveness—the very core of who you are as a parent—collapses into absolute powerlessness. End with your voice broken, repeating their name in a whisper, all your strength drained, left with only grief and the unbearable knowledge that you couldn't save them.

title: The Retirement Speech You Can't Deliver
instruction: You're giving your retirement speech after 40 years at a company that's being sold and liquidated tomorrow—everyone here will lose their jobs next week, but no one knows yet except you. Start with genuine warmth and nostalgia, laughing as you recount beloved memories, voices of colleagues, inside jokes. Your joy is real. But underneath every anecdote is the knowledge that you're betraying them with your silence. A laugh catches, turns strange. You pause. Your voice splits between affection and agony—you love these people, and you're complicit in their destruction. You want to warn them, but you signed an NDA, and your pension depends on your silence. Keep going with the speech, your voice now carrying both gratitude and grief, love and self-loathing. End with 'thank you for everything' that sounds like both a celebration and an apology, your voice breaking with the weight of what you cannot say.

title: Kitchen Table Confrontation: Adult Child Tells Parent What Their Silence Cost
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother or father at the kitchen table where you grew up. Start controlled, almost too calm: 'We need to talk about something.' But as you speak—about the bullying they ignored, the abuse they didn't protect you from, the times you needed them and they looked away—your voice begins to shake with decades of suppressed rage. 'You knew. You KNEW and you did nothing.' The fury pours out, then suddenly collapses into devastated vulnerability: 'I was just a kid. I needed you.' By the end, you're not yelling anymore—you're begging them to finally see you, your voice reduced to a broken whisper of longing for the parent you never had.
inspired_by: Therapy: Speaking Your Trauma Out Loud for the First Time

title: Being the Third Wheel
instruction: You're out with a couple, and they're completely absorbed in each other. Your voice is cheerful at first, trying to participate. But they keep talking to each other, ignoring you. Your voice becomes smaller, less frequent. You're interjecting, but they talk over you. Your tone becomes quieter, sadder. You realize you're invisible to them. By the end, you're just sitting there, your voice barely used. When they finally remember you, your voice is polite but strained: 'Oh, I'm fine, just watching.'

title: The Truth Your Mother Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about why you've kept her at arm's length for years. Start with a tight, controlled voice—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm. But as you speak the actual words about what her criticism did to you, about the child who needed her approval and never got it, your voice begins to shake. The relief of finally saying it out loud wars with the pain of admitting how much it still hurts. Let anger creep in—'You never saw me, you only saw what I wasn't'—then watch that anger crack into something more vulnerable. Maybe she tries to defend herself and you have to push through, voice rising, then suddenly dropping to almost a whisper: 'I just needed you to love who I actually was.' End in the quiet devastation of finally being honest, your voice stripped of all pretense, waiting to see if this truth will destroy or transform your relationship.

title: The Body They Wanted You to Have
instruction: Confront your mother or father about a lifetime of comments about your appearance. Begin by physically inhabiting how their criticisms made you feel—perhaps heavy, clumsy, unattractive, too much or not enough. Let your body carry the weight of their judgment as you start speaking. Recall specific moments: the dress they said made you look fat, the haircut they hated, the comparison to a sibling. As you speak these truths aloud, something remarkable happens: you begin to physically shed this imposed self-image. Feel your actual body—strong, capable, yours. By the end, you're standing in your own skin with devastating clarity, no longer carrying their vision of who you should be. The anger gives way to something more powerful: self-possession.

title: The Last Garden
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a nursing home garden, saying a forever goodbye to your son who is moving overseas. Your mind drifts — you forget why you're angry at him, then remember it's because he's leaving. A bird chirps and you laugh at its timing. Your voice starts confused and annoyed, thick with unshed tears, but as you realize this is the last time you'll see his face, the anger softens into a trembling, almost ceremonial amusement. You struggle to hold his hand steady while a breeze rustles the leaves, and your final words break with a gentle laugh that masks devastation.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Amusement (very intensely present), Anger (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Prayer for a Stain
instruction: You're a teenage girl kneeling on the cold bathroom floor, scrubbing a red wine stain out of your mother's favorite silk blouse—a blouse she’d lent you for tonight’s party, the one where your best friend kissed your crush right in front of you. You begged everyone to leave so you could hide this shame. Start in fierce prayer: not to a god, but into the fabric, bargaining for the stain to lift, your voice high and piercing with pride—pride that you were chosen, that you were beautiful in that blouse. As you scrub harder, the pride curdles into disappointment as the stain stays, and let a sliver of jealousy slip through—envy for how easy she makes everything look. Your voice should shift from a desperate, righteous chant to a choked, faltering whisper, worn out by the futility.
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Disappointment (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father about a wound they gave you in childhood—not through violence, but through absence, through what was never said or offered. Start from a place of righteousness, armed with years of rehearsed accusations. You came here to finally tell them the truth, to make them understand what they took from you. But as you speak, something shifts. You begin to see their failures as human-sized rather than monstrous. Your anger doesn't disappear—it mingles with something more complicated: a grief for what you both lost, a recognition of their own unmet needs. Let your voice carry both the fury of the hurt child and the aching understanding of the adult who sees their parent as a fallible person. End not with forgiveness or reconciliation, but with the exhausted complexity of holding both truths at once.

title: The Key Under the Dresser
instruction: You are an older adult in a deep squat, one hand braced against a heavy dresser, searching for a dropped key. Your voice is strained from the core pressure—each word comes out as a tight, pushed grunt. Start by teasing your younger friend who’s also fumbling nearby, your tone sharp and playful. But as you try to straighten up, your knees lock, and a hot wave of embarrassment creeps in. You realize you can’t get up without help; your voice softens, cracking with disappointment and shame as you finally admit, “I think I’m stuck.” Let the physical strain color every syllable, with a grunt or a shift in weight mid-sentence.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Disappointment (slightly present), Embarrassment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Hour Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting vigil beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. Begin in the deep exhaustion of having been awake for three days straight—feel the heaviness in your eyelids, the ache in your spine from the uncomfortable chair. Gradually allow the sterile smell of the room to sharpen your senses, then the too-bright fluorescent lights that hum overhead. Let the sound of her labored breathing fill the space between you. As you hold her hand, let each sensation accumulate: the papery texture of her skin, the warmth leaving her fingers, the memories flooding back with each shallow breath she takes. Start with quiet resignation and move through layers of sensory awareness until you arrive at a fierce, almost unbearable tenderness—whispering to her all the things you never said, your voice breaking not with dramatic sobs but with the raw truth of love and impending loss. End in a place of grace and devastating clarity.

title: The Last Sunset Together
instruction: You're watching the sunset with someone you love deeply, and you both know this is the last time you'll see it together—they're leaving tomorrow on a journey they won't return from. Begin with quiet awe at the beauty before you, pointing out colors, sharing small observations. Let wonder mix with the creeping realization that you're memorizing this moment, their voice, the way they breathe. Your tone shifts from light appreciation to something more tender, more desperate to hold onto every second. Try to stay present in the beauty, but grief keeps breaking through—your voice cracks on ordinary words about clouds and light. End in a whisper of gratitude for this moment, this person, this goodbye, where love and loss are so intertwined you can't tell them apart. The sunset is ending, and so is everything.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're in the wreckage of something—maybe your burned home, maybe the hospital after someone survived against all odds, maybe the day after your divorce is finalized. You start laughing, genuinely laughing, at the absurdity of it all: 'Look at this. Just... look at this mess.' But your laughter is threaded with tears you can't quite hold back. You're describing what you see with a kind of delirious gratitude mixed with devastation: 'Remember when we painted that wall? Spent three hours arguing about the shade of blue. And now it's just... gone.' Your voice keeps shifting—sometimes you're almost giddy with the strange freedom of loss, sometimes you're choking on the unfairness of it. You find yourself thanking the universe or God or nobody for small, broken things: 'At least we had it. At least I got to love you in that house.' By the end, you're sitting in the ruins, laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice full of contradictions—heartbroken and liberated, devastated and strangely at peace. You've found something like acceptance, but it tastes both bitter and sweet.

title: The Weight of Comfort
instruction: You're a middle-aged man with a deep voice, sitting on the edge of the couch next to your crying daughter after her breakup. You start by matching her slow, shaky breathing, speaking low and steady, but your own bitterness leaks in—a sour tone as you think of how love always fails. Midway, you catch yourself and try to offer a flicker of hope, but your voice stays numb, almost hollow. Let your words trail off, clear your throat, shift your weight. End with a quiet encouragement that sounds more tired than reassuring.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Pause Before
instruction: You're in the middle of a heavy makeout, fully aroused, ready to go further. But something makes you stop—maybe her body stiffened, or her eyes went wide. You pull back, sit up, and shift from playful teasing to dead-serious clarity. Your voice drops, slows down, and you ask, 'Hey—is this okay?' Listen for her answer. The silence that follows makes your heart sink with disappointment and doubt. You force a small, teasing smile to lighten it, but your voice cracks as you say, 'We can stop. I mean it.' The arc goes from heated excitement to careful, crushed concern, then back to a fragile attempt at reassurance.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Doubt (clearly present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Last Contact
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy alone in a damaged spacesuit, drifting away from your mother’s ship. Your hyper-masculinized voice cracks with sadness as you describe the stars outside, but your mother’s voice over the radio makes you ache with a confusing, intense lust—your first crush on her voice’s warmth. Speak in broken, childlike wonder, your breath fogging the visor, as you confess you’ve always wanted to touch her hair, then choke on the static as the signal dies. Let the claustrophobic reverb and your own sniffles fight for space: end with a raw, horrified whisper as you realize she can’t hear you anymore.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Warrior's Last Breath
instruction: You are a hardened soldier who has lived by violence and control, now dying from battle wounds. As you speak your final words to someone you've kept at emotional distance for years, begin from a place of rigid stoicism and pride in your strength. But as death approaches, let something soften—a memory of gentleness you've buried, a need for tenderness you've denied your whole life. Allow yourself to reach for comfort you've never permitted yourself to want. Let the tough exterior crack to reveal the frightened child underneath who needed love all along. End in a place of raw, undefended need—perhaps asking to be held, or confessing you were always afraid, or admitting you never knew how to be soft until this moment when nothing else matters.

title: Brush and Bristle
instruction: You're a teenage boy brushing your teeth after a huge fight with your mom. Your jaw is forced open by the brush, foam building, scrubbing loud in your ears. Start with shaky, muffled distress — you’re almost crying as you try to speak, words destroyed by the bristles. Let a bitter, restrained anger creep in toward the end, your voice tightening, spitting out the last words through the foam.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Summit Call
instruction: You are a young woman with a naturally soft, high voice, stranded at a high-altitude base camp with severe altitude sickness. You're on a satellite phone to your partner back home, trying to tell them you love them and that you won't make it down. Your words come out in gasps, each breath a struggle, and a dull headache makes you wince mid-sentence. Start with forced cheerfulness, pretending you're okay, but as the air thins and your thoughts tangle, let the sadness you've been holding back seep through. By the end, your voice cracks from exhaustion and sorrow, and you're barely whispering, losing your train of thought but clinging to the final goodbye.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Upside-Down Confession
instruction: You're hanging upside down from a pull-up bar in your home gym, blood rushing to your head. Your crush just walked in, and you're desperately trying to flirt, but your voice is thick and garbled from the inversion. Start with a playful, lustful tease — a grin in your voice despite the struggle. As the words come out choked and wet, your infatuation breaks through: the joke dissolves into a raw, honest confession. Let the physical strain interrupt you — catch your breath, lose a thought, feel the heat in your face. End with a quieter, vulnerable admission that surprises even you.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Discovering Your Parent's Secret Life
instruction: You found something—an affair, an addiction, a criminal past, a hidden child. Your voice is shocked as you confront them. 'What is this?' Your voice demands answers. Your parent is defensive. Your voice becomes small—the child you were—'Why didn't you tell me?' Your parent's voice is shameful. Your voice is disappointed, angry, betrayed. Everything you thought about them is different. Your voice reflects that rupture. Include the moment you realize they're still your parent despite everything.

title: Protecting Your Child from Your Own Rage
instruction: You've just discovered your teenage child has been hurt—abused, assaulted, betrayed by someone you trusted. You're on the phone with them, and inside you is a murderous rage so intense you can barely see straight. Start with forced calm that's clearly fracturing. 'Tell me exactly what happened. Every detail.' But as they speak, your control shatters. Your voice becomes a roar: 'I'll kill them. I swear to God I'll—' Then you catch yourself. Your child is crying now, scared of YOUR intensity. You have to pull it back. 'No. No, baby, I'm sorry.' Your voice shakes violently, trying to soften while fury still burns. 'I'm not angry at you. I'm—' You can't even articulate the rage. 'I'm supposed to protect you. That's my job and I failed.' The helplessness hits you like a wave. Your voice cracks into something raw and broken. 'I would take this pain from you if I could. I would carry it all.' Tears now, but underneath still that fierce protectiveness. 'But I can't. And that's destroying me.' End with desperate tenderness fighting through rage: 'You are not alone in this. Do you hear me? You will never be alone in this.'

title: The Last Laugh Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You're sitting at your dying father's bedside at 3 AM, and he's asked you to tell him one last joke—but as you begin, you realize every punchline reminds you of a memory with him, and your laughter keeps breaking into tears. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to give him the gift of laughter he's asking for. But as you move through the joke, let the weight of goodbye seep in. Your voice should crack between the setup and punchline. End in a place where you're both laughing and sobbing, telling him 'that's the one, Dad, that's the one'—but you both know it's really goodbye. The humor and heartbreak must be completely intertwined, inseparable.
inspired_by: Doing Stand-Up Comedy in the Style of a Eulogy

title: Skin and Memory
instruction: You are alone, running your hands along a physical object (a piece of clothing, a letter, a photograph, a wall, a doorframe) that connects you to someone or somewhere that triggered both ecstasy and devastation. Begin with your breath steady, perhaps clinical in your examination. As your fingers trace the object, allow yourself to fully recreate the sensory experience it represents—temperature, taste, touch, the feeling in your body during that time. Let the physical sensation in your hands travel through your entire body until you're flooded with the memory's emotional force—whether passion, rage, grief, or joy. Your voice should become increasingly physical, perhaps broken by sharp intakes of breath or guttural sounds. End in a state of complete physical and emotional overwhelm.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're standing at the door, about to leave a relationship that was beautiful but impossible. You're thanking your partner for the love you shared, and you're laughing—actually laughing—because some of the memories are so sweet they're ridiculous. 'Remember when we got lost for six hours and you sang the entire time?' You're smiling, genuine warmth in your voice. But even as you laugh, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice keeps catching between joy and grief. You're grateful for every moment, and that gratitude is exactly what makes leaving so devastating. End with 'I wouldn't undo a single day, even knowing it would end here.' Let your voice hold impossible contradictions: joy and heartbreak, gratitude and loss, laughter and tears, all真实 and happening simultaneously. This is the sound of loving something enough to let it go.

title: The Inheritance Call
instruction: You've just received a phone call: your estranged father, who abandoned you thirty years ago, has died and left you everything—his house, his money, a letter of apology you haven't read yet. You're alone in your apartment, holding the phone. Start numb, almost mechanical, repeating the lawyer's words back to yourself flatly. But then let contradictory feelings erupt in wild, exaggerated ways: punch the air in triumph, then immediately collapse in sobs; laugh with vindicated rage, then tenderly touch a childhood photograph; scream 'I don't forgive you' then whisper 'thank you.' Don't make sense. Let yourself be violently torn between grief and relief, rage and gratitude, the child who needed him and the adult who survived without him. End in a strange place: maybe dancing alone with furious joy, or calling his number just to hear his voicemail, or ripping up the letter unread while crying and smiling simultaneously. Multiple truths at once.

title: Earthquake Skin
instruction: You're experiencing the first rush of desire after years of numbness following trauma. You're touching someone, or being touched, and it's overwhelming—pleasure mixed with terror, hunger mixed with the urge to flee. Let your attention move through your own body with fierce curiosity: where exactly do you feel this? What does it actually feel like—burning, electricity, aching, trembling? Notice how sensation moves, where it intensifies, where you want to pull away. Start cautious, almost clinical in your self-observation, protecting yourself by studying the experience. But as you genuinely track these physical sensations with interest rather than judgment, allow yourself to surrender to them more fully. Your breathing should change, your voice should crack between fear and want. End having crossed some threshold from analysis to abandonment, from fear to hunger, from fragmentation to being fully, terrifyingly alive in your body again.

title: The Slime and the Sizzle
instruction: You're a teenage girl alone in the kitchen, trying to make a fancy pasta sauce from a complicated recipe video. The counter is messy, onions are half-chopped, and the pan is spitting hot oil. As you reach for a jar of diced tomatoes, your fingers slip and plunge into a bowl of raw, slimy okra you forgot you'd soaked — the texture makes your stomach lurch and you recoil with a sharp gasp. You stare at your goo-covered hand, utterly confused about what to do next, muttering to yourself over the roar of the stove. Then, as you wipe it on your apron and glance at the bright red tomatoes glistening in the can, you feel a sudden, quiet awe at how these things will transform into something beautiful, and your voice softens with wonder, trailing off into a tiny laugh.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Bench Warmer's Bench
instruction: You're in a crowded locker room after a game, surrounded by friends who are high-fiving and shouting. Someone just got praised for the winning play. You start by joining the laughter and throwing out a boastful joke, but your voice has a slight edge—a little too loud, a little too forced. As you talk, the envy creeps in: you trail off mid-sentence, glance away, then mumble something under your breath. Let the noise of the room affect you—flinch at a slap on your back, pause when someone interrupts. End with a quieter, almost flat admission that betrays your disappointment.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Bumpy Ride to Obligation
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman in a rideshare on a rough road, heading to a family reunion where you're expected to pretend everything is fine. Your voice shakes from the bumps. Begin with a bitter, confused mutter to yourself about why you agreed to come. Midway, you notice the driver's absurdly cheerful radio station, and a flicker of amusement breaks through. End with a wry, resigned laugh — the bitterness hasn't vanished, but it's now mixed with dark humor. Let the physical jolts affect your rhythm: pauses, pitch jumps, trailing off. Speak naturally, as if half to yourself, reacting to the car's lurches.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Confusion (slightly present), Amusement (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Someone Else
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother or father about choosing their new partner over you years ago. You came here with a prepared speech, accusations you've polished in your mind for years. But as you begin, pay attention to what's actually happening in your body and heart right now—the child in you that still wants them to reach out, the exhaustion of carrying this rage, the disgust at your own need for their love, the way your prepared anger might suddenly collapse into something else entirely. Start with controlled fury, words you've practiced. Let the real, unpredictable feelings underneath hijack your plan. End in whatever true emotional place emerges when you stop performing your grievance and feel what's actually present.
inspired_by: Actor is premeditating — planning how to say lines and emotionalize them before getting there, functioning from a cerebral place

title: Reading Grandmother's Letters After She's Gone
instruction: You've found letters your grandmother wrote to you before dementia took her words. Read them aloud in her voice first—warm, lucid, full of stories and wisdom she wanted you to have. Then shift to your own voice as you realize these are her goodbyes, written years ago when she still knew who you were. Your voice should barely rise above a whisper. Let tears choke the words. Pause when you need to. There's a passage where she describes the moment she held you as a baby, how she memorized your face, how she knew then that love could hurt this much. Feel your throat close. Some sentences you can't finish. End in silence, holding the paper, breathing through the ache.
inspired_by: Translating Bad News Between Two Languages

title: The Last Word I’ll Never Say
instruction: You’re a teenage girl sitting on your bed after just ending a relationship over the phone. The phone is still in your hand, screen dark. You feel a flicker of triumph—you finally said what needed to be said, you walked away first. But that triumph is already crumbling into a hollow sadness that makes your chest ache. Start with a shaky, defiant whisper, trying to convince yourself you did the right thing, but let your voice waver, drop, and crack until you’re barely holding back a sob. Fidget with the hem of your shirt, glance at an old photo on your nightstand, and let your breath hitch midsentence as the pain takes over.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child, seeing them for the first time in fifteen years. Begin with cold, controlled anger—you've rehearsed this moment, armed yourself with cutting words and righteous fury. But as you start speaking, something unexpected happens: beneath the rage, the wounded child emerges. Your voice wavers between bitter accusations and the desperate, vulnerable questions you've carried for years: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Your anger doesn't disappear—it transforms into something more complex, more painful. You're furious at them, furious at yourself for still needing their love, furious that you're crying when you swore you wouldn't. End with a raw, unplanned confession: despite everything, you've missed them. The admission leaves you exposed, trembling, caught between the impulse to flee and the impossible hope that they might finally say they're sorry.

title: The Intervention That Breaks Open
instruction: You're confronting your alcoholic parent, and you've rehearsed this speech a hundred times, but now it's happening and nothing is going as planned. Start with controlled anger, the kind that's been practiced and polished to stay safe. But as you speak, your carefully constructed words fall apart—the hurt beneath the rage starts bleeding through. You hear yourself saying things you swore you'd never say out loud: how you parented them, how you learned to be small to avoid their chaos, how you're exhausted from loving someone who keeps disappearing into a bottle. The anger cracks into grief, then briefly hardens again when they make an excuse, then collapses entirely into the voice of the child you once were, begging them to just see you. End with a raw, undefended honesty that surprises even you—either a boundary you've never been strong enough to set, or a confession of how desperately you still hope they'll change.

title: Counting Your Breathing
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to someone you love, watching them sleep, and you can't sleep yourself. In a whisper—barely audible, as if speaking to yourself—begin to notice the small things: the rhythm of their breathing, how their hand curls near their face. Let your attention grow more intimate: the tiny movements of their eyelids, the vulnerability of their exposed throat, the way sleep has softened their expression. Then let yourself wonder in whispered fragments: what are they dreaming? What would they say if they knew how deeply you're watching? What am I so afraid of losing? Begin in quiet anxiety or restless love, but let this tender observation transform you into something more raw—perhaps gratitude mixed with grief, or a whispered confession of need you could never say when they're awake.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin by looking at their face and noticing every detail—the exact color of their eyes, the texture of their skin, the way light falls across their features. Let yourself really see them as if for the first time and the last time simultaneously. Start from a place of numb shock, unable to fully accept what's happening. As you observe and truly take in each sensory detail—their warmth, their breathing, their presence—allow whatever emotion wants to surface to emerge organically. By the end, you must arrive at a place of deep gratitude mixed with unbearable loss, speaking your final words to them. Let the transformation happen through genuine sensory attention, not by forcing emotion.

title: Screaming at the Person You Love to Save Them from You
instruction: You're standing in the doorway, and the person you love most is begging you not to leave. You explode—not because you don't love them, but because you love them too much. Your voice starts harsh, cruel even: 'You deserve better than this! Than me!' You're trying to drive them away by being vicious. Your voice is loud, fierce, defensive. But they won't go. They step closer. And your rage fractures. Your voice breaks into desperation: 'Please, please just hate me.' You're begging now, voice ragged. The cruelty dissolves completely into raw terror and helplessness—you can't protect them from your own darkness, and you can't survive without them. You end collapsed, voice shattered, admitting in broken fragments: 'I'm so scared I'm going to hurt you... and I can't lose you... I can't...'
inspired_by: Being Broken Up With Over Text, Reading It Out Loud

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's wedding, about to give a toast. You love them fiercely—and you're also losing them to this new life they're beginning. Start with genuine joy and humor, celebrating them with stories that make everyone laugh. But as you speak, let a bittersweet undercurrent seep in: the awareness that everything is changing, that you're being left behind in some fundamental way. Your voice must carry both celebration and grief simultaneously, gratitude laced with abandonment, happiness tinged with resentment you'd never admit to. The challenge is to hold these contradictions together without resolving them—end with a toast that genuinely wishes them joy while your voice betrays the heartbreak of being outgrown. Let the audience hear both truths at once.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a psychologically complex character whose inner life seems 'beyond their emotional range'

title: The Kitchen Truth
instruction: You are confronting your mother/father in the kitchen where you grew up, finally saying the thing you've never been able to say. Start with the words you planned, the calm accusation or question you rehearsed. But as you speak, allow everything that's genuinely moving through you to enter: if your hands are shaking, acknowledge it. If you suddenly feel like a child again, let your voice reflect that. If you notice the smell of coffee or the hum of the refrigerator and it triggers a memory, follow it. If rage turns to grief or grief turns to unexpected tenderness, don't control it. Let the confrontation become unpredictable and truthful, shaped by what's actually happening in your body and heart moment to moment, until you arrive somewhere you never intended — perhaps understanding, perhaps deeper pain, perhaps surprising forgiveness.

title: The Last Words You'll Never Hear: Three Farewells
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving on a one-way journey into space, knowing you'll never see them again. Perform three distinct farewells: First, a composed goodbye where you try to be strong for them, voice steady but cracking on the final word. Second, a desperate plea where you break down and beg them not to go, words tumbling over each other. Third, a whispered blessing where through your grief you find the grace to wish them well, voice soft but full of love and devastating acceptance. Each must show a different facet of your heart breaking, moving from control to collapse to transcendent surrender.

title: Witnessing Your Own Tenderness
instruction: Late at night, you're whispering to your sleeping partner about fears you've never spoken aloud—your terror of losing them, your shame about parts of yourself you hide, your desperate hope that you're enough. Begin by speaking these confessions softly, believing they're safe because they're asleep. But then, become aware of yourself confessing: watch your own lips forming these fragile words, hear the tremor in your whispered voice, notice your hand hovering near their face but not quite touching. This witnessing self observes without judgment how naked you are in this moment. As you continue, let the awareness that you're watching yourself create a strange, almost out-of-body intimacy—you're both the vulnerable person confessing and the compassionate observer bearing witness to that vulnerability. End in a space where the confession becomes realer precisely because you're aware of making it, where being both speaker and witness somehow makes the truth more true, not less.
inspired_by: Becoming a Spectator in Your Dreams

title: The Broken Vase
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl standing in the kitchen, the shattered pieces of your mother's favorite vase at your feet. Your heart is pounding, and you've already concocted a lie about the cat, but when she walks in, you feel a sharp, smug thrill at how easily you think you can fool her. Begin with a defiant, almost sneering tone as you launch into your story, but as you speak, the weight of her silence and the tremor in your own voice unravel your confidence. Let your pitch climb, your words trip over each other, and your gaze dart to the shards, ending in a fragile, desperate plea that barely masks your guilt.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Coherent Goodbye
instruction: You're in hospice, heavily medicated for pain, and your adult child has just arrived after years of estrangement. You have maybe hours left. You need to tell them you forgive them, that you understand why they left, that you're proud of who they became—but the morphine makes your words thick and slow. You start with desperate urgency, fighting through the fog to get the words out before you can't anymore. Your voice wavers between sedated slurring and sharp moments of clarity where love breaks through. As you speak, you move from frantic need to be understood, through frustration at your own failing body, finally arriving at a peaceful surrender where even your slurred whispers carry profound tenderness. Let some words trail off. Let silence do the work when speech fails.
inspired_by: Xanax Dissolving Your Ability to Sound Serious

title: The Last Lullaby
instruction: You are an elderly woman, sitting in a rocking chair by a dim lamp, holding a worn photograph. It’s late, you’re exhausted, and your head keeps nodding forward as you talk to yourself. You start with bitter affection, recalling how your late partner always left their socks on the floor—annoying, but endearing. As you drift off, your voice slows, words slur into mumbles, and you jerk awake with a hopeful whisper: maybe they’re still around, just out of sight. Let the bitterness fade into a tired, hopeful smile as you surrender to sleep, your voice trailing into nothing.
emotions_sampled: Affection (extremely present), Bitterness (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Misfire That Saved Us
instruction: You're the oldest in a casual co-op shooter group, the one everyone expects to have the best aim. Your team is pinned down, and you take the shot—but miss completely, hitting a gas canister instead, causing a chain reaction that wipes out the enemy squad. At first, you're flooded with doubt, muttering curses under your breath, hunching over, second-guessing your reflexes. Then, as the chaos settles and your friends cheer, you feel a reluctant, almost embarrassed awe at the lucky accident, muttering 'Well, I'll be damned...' and finally a gruff, genuine 'Thanks, I guess' that carries the weight of someone not used to receiving gratitude. Let your voice betray the shift: start with tight, frustrated breaths and quick, dismissive grunts, then slow into a low, wondering tone, ending with a sheepish, softer rumble that acknowledges the gift of luck.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Doubt (extremely present), Awe (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Watch Your Step, Sweetie
instruction: You're a mother on a construction site, wearing a hard hat with a visor. Your young child is exploring nearby, excitedly showing you a shiny rock. The air is filled with heavy machinery noise, forcing you to raise your voice. At first, you respond with warm interest, leaning in to admire the rock, your voice lilting and playful despite the din. But then you see a loose board about to give way beneath the child's feet. Your tone shifts sharply into a protective shout, urgency cutting through the noise as you yell for them to stop. Let your voice strain against the hard hat's echo, and let your body react — maybe you jerk forward, your hand instinctively reaching out.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM. You and your partner lie in bed, unable to sleep. In a whisper, you begin to confess something you've carried alone for years - a fear, a loss, a truth about yourself you've hidden. Start with halting words, barely audible, testing whether it's safe to speak. Feel your way through the dark, both literally and emotionally. As you sense their listening presence, let yourself go deeper, your whisper becoming more fluid, more trusting. Discover things about yourself as you speak them aloud for the first time. By the end, you're not just confessing - you're marveling at finally being able to say this, at being heard. Your voice should move from frightened and fragmented to soft, wondering, and strangely free, all while maintaining that intimate whisper that makes the darkness feel sacred.
inspired_by: When you are tired, hungover, anxious, or emotionally unavailable before a performance

title: Whispering Your Secret in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you trust, and in the darkness, you finally confess something you've carried alone for years—a trauma, a loss, a shame, something that has shaped you but that you've never spoken aloud. Begin barely audibly, testing if you can even say the words. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost subvocal, catching on certain words you can barely bear to release. Let long pauses speak volumes—the silence before you can continue is part of the performance. As you go on, there should be moments where emotion closes your throat completely, where you have to breathe through it to keep going. End with a kind of fragile relief mixed with terror—you've said it, you can't take it back, and now you wait in the dark to see if they'll still love you. This should feel like watching someone's heart crack open in slow motion.
inspired_by: Being Woken Up at Every Stage of Sleep

title: The Unraveling Row
instruction: You are a woman sitting in a quiet chair, knitting a sweater you never wanted to make. The needles click in a steady rhythm, but your jaw is tight—you'd rather be anywhere else. A child nearby keeps asking when it will be done, and each question makes your fingers jerk. Start speaking with clipped irritation, muttering about losing count under your breath. Let your voice soften only when you realize the child is trying to help, ending with a quiet, weary sigh as you pick up a dropped stitch.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's bed as dawn breaks through the hospital window. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and the golden light reminds you both of her kitchen on Sunday mornings. Begin by simply noticing everything about this moment—the quality of light on her face, the weight of her hand in yours, the particular rhythm of her breathing, the smell of her skin that's been the same your whole life. Let yourself feel the preciousness of each small detail. As she begins to speak about what she sees beyond this room—describing colors and faces you cannot see—allow yourself to move from desperate clinging to a kind of awed, tender witnessing. Notice how your own breathing changes. By the end, you're not fighting her leaving anymore; you're honoring where she's going, even as your heart breaks. The emotional journey moves from acute awareness of every sensory detail to a profound, surrendered goodbye.

title: Unexpected Laughter After Tragedy: Guilt and Relief Mixed
instruction: After tragedy, something makes you laugh. Your voice is shocked at itself: 'I shouldn't be laughing. Why am I laughing?' The guilt is immediate but so is the relief—you can still laugh, which means you're not completely dead. Include the moment where you let the laughter continue, almost against your will. Your voice becomes slightly freer: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' But you're also alive in that moment. Your voice carries both—the guilt that joy seems obscene after tragedy, and the physical fact of laughter escaping. By the end, your voice has integrated both: you're allowed to laugh and also to grieve. They're not contradictory. Your voice reflects that mature understanding: you can hold both joy and sorrow.

title: The Moment Everything Shatters
instruction: You've just discovered a betrayal that destroys everything you believed about someone you loved. Start with shock, your voice flat and disbelieving: 'Tell me it's not true. Look me in the eye and tell me you didn't do this.' But they can't, and rage erupts—volcanic, uncontrolled: 'How could you? HOW COULD YOU?' Your voice is raw, screaming, breaking. The anger is so intense it's physical, choking you. But then it collapses into anguish: 'I trusted you with everything. Everything.' You're sobbing now, the words barely coherent: 'I would have died for you. I would have given you anything.' The pain is unbearable, and underneath the rage is devastation: 'Was any of it real? Did you ever actually love me?' They try to speak and you cut them off with fierce, protective rage: 'Don't. Don't you dare try to explain this away.' But then exhaustion hits. Your voice becomes hollow, empty: 'I don't even know who you are. I don't know who I've been loving all this time.' End with quiet, absolute finality: 'We're done. I'm done.' The words are both an ending and the terrible beginning of having to figure out how to survive this.

title: Adult Child Tells Their Dying Parent They Never Felt Loved—And Asks Why
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed. You came to say goodbye, to be dutiful, to be good one last time. But something breaks open in you. Your voice starts quiet, almost apologetic—you didn't mean to say this now, not like this. But the words come anyway: 'I need to know... did you ever love me? Because I never felt it.' Your tone shifts between desperate plea and decades of buried anger. You're not shouting—that would be easier. Instead, you're speaking with the kind of naked vulnerability that feels like peeling your own skin off. You recount specific moments, your voice cracking on details you thought you'd forgotten. Sometimes you sound like the child you were, sometimes like the exhausted adult you've become. You watch their face, searching for something, anything—recognition, regret, even defensiveness would be better than silence. By the end, you're not sure if you feel liberated or more alone than ever. Your final words are barely audible: 'I just needed to know it wasn't my fault.'
inspired_by: Diplomat Negotiates Peace Deal While Their Country Is Being Invaded

title: Dancing at Your Ex-Love's Wedding
instruction: You're at the wedding of someone you never stopped loving, and they've asked you to dance—one last time, for old times' sake. Begin with bittersweet laughter, trying to keep it light: 'Remember when we used to dance in your kitchen at 2 AM? We thought we'd do this at our wedding.' Let your voice break into something more honest, still smiling through tears. 'You look so happy. I mean it—you look so goddamn happy and it's killing me.' Find genuine joy mixed with heartbreak. 'I'm glad it's them. I really am. They're good for you in ways I never was.' Your voice trembles between laughter and crying. 'This is the weirdest thing I've ever done—dancing with you, letting you go, and meaning it when I say congratulations.' End with peaceful devastation, voice soft and full of love. 'Thank you for letting me have this dance. Thank you for loving me once. I'm going to miss you for the rest of my life, and somehow... somehow that's okay.'

title: The Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: You're a single parent who has just learned your teenage child was violently assaulted, and you couldn't prevent it. Start with fierce, barely contained rage, voice shaking with adrenaline: 'Tell me who did this. TELL ME.' You're pacing, hands trembling. 'I will find them. I will make them—' But then you see your child flinch at your intensity, and everything inside you shatters. Your voice breaks mid-sentence, rage collapsing into helpless desperation: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. I should have been there.' You're crying now, voice raw and choked: 'You're my baby. You're my whole world, and I couldn't—' Drop to your knees, voice becoming small, defeated, utterly broken: 'I'm supposed to keep you safe. That's my only job, and I failed you. Please forgive me. Please.' End in a whisper soaked with guilt and boundless love: 'I would take it all. Every second of pain. I would take it all for you.'

title: Memorizing Joy Before It's Gone
instruction: You're preparing for something that will change your face forever—surgery, treatment, departure to a place where such simple rituals won't exist. As you go through your skincare routine one last time, you're laughing softly through tears, finding absurd humor in the preciousness of this mundane moment. Describe each sensation—the cool cream, the gentle pressure, the familiar scent—with a voice that trembles between celebration and grief. You're deeply grateful for this face, this body, this moment of normalcy, even as your heart breaks knowing it's ending. Let contradictory emotions flow freely: joke about the absurdity while your voice cracks, express profound peace while clearly terrified, find genuine joy in the present while mourning its impermanence. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance, touching your face with both reverence and a strange, transcendent calm.
inspired_by: Feeling the Tingling Sensation of a Cooling Face Mask

title: The Protector's Breaking
instruction: You're a soldier or first responder holding someone you couldn't save. Your voice starts fierce, commanding, refusing to accept reality: 'Stay with me! That's an order!' Your training is speaking, your voice full of authority and desperate control. You're doing compressions, breathing for them, your voice rising: 'You don't get to quit on me!' The intensity is explosive, fueled by adrenaline and denial. But slowly, inevitably, you realize it's over. Your voice fractures mid-sentence: 'Come on, just—' and the command dissolves into a sob. All the fierceness collapses into helplessness: 'I don't know what to do. I always know what to do.' Your voice becomes small, childlike: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' The performance should show the devastating moment when strength becomes powerlessness, when the protector discovers they're mortal after all.

title: The Last Card
instruction: You are a proud, tough man who has just heard your partner say they're leaving for good. You're standing in the doorway of your apartment, blocking their path but not touching them. You start speaking fast, your voice high and shaky, desperate to stop them—pleading with an edge of panic. But as you go, you realize you're not just begging out of fear of being alone; you're finally saying the affection you've never been able to say. Let your voice crack, lose its rhythm, trail off into a quieter, raw longing. End with a simple, broken admission of love.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Labor: When the Anesthesia Wears Off During Surgery Complications
instruction: You're in active labor, voice strained and managed. Then something changes—the doctors' voices shift. The anesthesia isn't working properly. Your voice becomes raw, primal, words breaking into screams between contractions. Include the moment you beg them to give you something, anything, while your rational mind knows they can't. Your body is doing something inhuman and you're narrating it like your voice is tearing apart with you. End with the moment of breakthrough—not relief yet, just the knowledge that you're almost there, voice reduced to animal grunts and pleas and then, suddenly, the sound of your newborn.

title: The Last Call Home
