instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from a hospital where you've just been told you have weeks to live. You start rehearsed, almost cold—'I need to tell you something'—wanting to punish them with clinical distance for all the years of absence. But as you hear their voice, something cracks. The words you prepared dissolve. You find yourself confessing not anger, but the small moments you missed them: 'I kept your birthday cards. All of them.' Your voice breaks from accusation into raw need. By the end, you're asking the question you swore you'd never ask: 'Did you ever love me?' Let the armor fall away completely. Show the journey from bitter control to desperate, childlike vulnerability.

title: The TimePressed Cooking Show Host
instruction: Perform a cooking demonstration where everything goes wrong due to time constraints. Use a cheerful voice that gradually becomes frantic, switching to internal panic while maintaining a facade.

title: Finding Your Child After They Ran Into Traffic
instruction: Your young child just ran into the street and nearly got hit by a car. You've grabbed them and pulled them back to safety. Start with explosive rage born from pure terror—you're screaming at them, your voice raw and fierce: 'What were you THINKING?!' Your anger is volcanic because you almost lost them. But mid-sentence, the fear overtakes the fury and your voice breaks completely. You collapse to your knees, pulling them close, and the rage transforms into desperate, sobbing relief: 'You could have died, you could have—' By the end, you're barely coherent, holding them tight, your voice reduced to whispered, breathless repetition: 'I love you, I love you, I can't lose you,' fierce protectiveness dissolving into helpless trembling.

title: The Last Song Before the Flight
instruction: You're singing your sister's favorite song to her the night before she leaves for a one-way mission to Mars - she'll never return to Earth. Begin with determined cheerfulness, trying to make it fun like you used to as kids, your voice bright and silly with inside jokes woven into the lyrics. But as you sing, the reality of forever crashes through your defenses. Your voice starts cracking not from technique but from the weight of 'never again' - never hearing her laugh in person, never hugging her, never growing old together. Let the song break apart into half-sung, half-spoken fragments as you try to memorize the exact way she's looking at you right now. End by finishing the song in a whisper, pouring every unsaid 'I love you' and 'don't go' and 'I'm so proud of you' into the final notes, your voice simultaneously celebrating her courage and mourning the loss of your future together.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Deployment
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're kneeling beside your six-year-old's bed. In eight hours, you deploy to a war zone—twelve months, maybe longer. She's sleeping peacefully, clutching her stuffed rabbit. You can't wake her; goodbyes are too hard for both of you. So you whisper everything you need to say into the darkness. Start tender, your voice barely audible: 'Baby, I'm going to miss your birthday...' Describe the memories you're already aching for—her laugh, bedtime stories, the way she runs to you after school. Your throat tightens. Let the vulnerability fully surface—the fear you won't come back, the guilt of leaving. Your voice breaks completely: 'If something happens...' But you stop yourself. End with fierce, protective love—a whispered promise that holds both deep sadness and unshakeable devotion. Kiss her forehead. Leave quietly.
inspired_by: Turning Down Someone's Romantic Advance Gently

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Believed
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the promises they made and broke throughout your childhood. Begin with controlled anger—you've rehearsed this moment for years. List the specific promises: being there for recitals, believing you when you needed help, choosing you over their addiction or career or new family. Your voice is sharp, prosecutorial. But as you continue, something shifts. You realize you're not just angry—you're grieving the parent you never had. Your voice breaks. You make a counter-promise: that you won't be like them, that you'll break this cycle. By the end, you're no longer speaking to them but to yourself, your voice carrying both devastation and fierce determination. The promise is as much a vow of separation as it is of survival.

title: Fingerprints on Glass
instruction: It's late at night. You're tracing your finger on a cold window, speaking to someone you love who's sitting behind you in the dark room. Start by telling them something small and safe—about your day, a funny thing you saw. But your finger keeps drawing the same shape on the glass. Slowly, let your voice drop to almost nothing as you confess that you've been pretending to be smaller, quieter, less complicated than you are because you were afraid that the real you—the messy, ambitious, selfish, passionate, awkward you—would be too much and they'd leave. This isn't a dramatic confession. It's whispered like a secret you're afraid to say aloud because once it's out, everything changes. End with your finger still on the glass, voice barely audible, asking them if they want to meet the real you.
inspired_by: An actor wants to maintain career integrity under commercial pressure

title: The Unspoken Inheritance
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the emotional absence that shaped your entire childhood. Begin with carefully controlled words, your voice measured but trembling underneath: 'I needed you to see me... really see me.' As she tries to deflect or justify, your control breaks—let anger surge through, your voice rising with decades of unmet longing: 'I was a child! I needed you to choose me!' But then you see her face, and something shifts. Your voice cracks as you realize she was broken too, that her failure came from her own wounds. The rage dissolves into something more complex—grief for both of you, for what was lost, for the mother she couldn't be. End with raw, painful forgiveness emerging: 'I see you now... I see why you couldn't.' Your voice is quiet, exhausted, but there's a door opening that was closed your whole life.

title: The Acceptance Speech You'll Never Give
instruction: You've just won the highest honor in your field—but this is a fantasy, alone in your room. You're giving the acceptance speech you'd give if you weren't afraid of judgment. Start with genuine joy and pride, letting yourself feel deserving. But as you thank people, let bitterness creep in: thanks to those who doubted you, who said you'd fail, who made you feel small. Let gratitude and resentment swirl together. Your voice should brighten with vindication, darken with old pain, break with longing for recognition. Build to a moment where you're simultaneously laughing and crying, celebrating and grieving all the years you hid your ambition. End with defiant joy mixed with deep sadness for your younger self who was too afraid to dream this big. Let both emotions be fully present, neither one winning.
inspired_by: Actor plays it safe, avoids taking chances, and produces predictable, unexciting work

title: The Drunk Confession Nobody Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're three drinks deep and you just said something you can't take back. You looked at your friend and said 'I've always been in love with you' or 'I hate your new partner' or 'I think you're wasting your life.' Your voice is slurred enough to use alcohol as a shield but clear enough that they heard every word. Your voice is now desperate to qualify—'I didn't mean... I'm just drunk...' but the truth is already out. Include the sober moment returning.

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You've just finished an intense physical ordeal—running until your body screamed, pushing through pain in a workout, surviving something that demanded everything from you. Your body is shaking, your breath ragged. Begin in pure physical sensation: the burning, the exhaustion, the body's rebellion. But as your breathing slows, emotion rushes in to fill the space—and it's not triumph. It's grief you've been outrunning, rage you've been suppressing, or fear you've been denying. Let the physical sensation crack you open. Your voice might come out as gasps between breaths, words broken by the body's need for air. The emotional release and physical release become inseparable. End in a place where the body's exhaustion has purged something emotional—you're emptied out, but clearer. Transform from pure physical intensity to emotional catharsis to exhausted peace.

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Protect Them
instruction: Someone you would die to protect—your child, your younger sibling, someone who depends on you—is facing something terrible, and you are utterly powerless to stop it. Begin with fierce determination, almost aggressive in your promises that you'll fix this, you'll make it right, you won't let anything hurt them. Feel your own certainty as armor. But as you speak, let reality crack through: you can't fix this. Watch your powerful declarations stumble, your voice shake with the horrible recognition of your own helplessness. Let rage at your powerlessness war with devastating tenderness. End with your defenses completely gone—maybe on your knees emotionally, maybe still trying to sound strong while completely falling apart, maybe holding them and whispering desperate promises you both know you can't keep. This should feel like watching someone's foundation crumble in real time.
inspired_by: Concealing Surprise When Hearing Unexpected News

title: The Performer's Private Ecstasy
instruction: You have just experienced a moment of profound physical and emotional breakthrough—perhaps artistic, perhaps sexual, perhaps spiritual. You are alone, and your body is still vibrating with sensation. You have always performed your emotions for others—you know how to show people what they want to see, you are skilled at being watched. But right now, no one is watching. Begin by trying to narrate or perform what just happened, describing it as you would for an audience. But let the raw sensation pull you away from performance. Let the private part of you—the one who experiences pleasure not for applause but for its own sake—flood through. By the end, you are making sounds, speaking in fragments, laughing or crying or gasping with a wildness you would never show another person. Let the performer dissolve into pure, unwitnessed sensation.

title: Reading Your Late Father's Letter Admitting He Was Wrong About Everything
instruction: He died before you could reconcile. Now you're reading his final letter. Start reading his words aloud, your voice cautious, guarded - you've been angry at him for so long. But as his apology unfolds, something in you breaks open. You're crying but also laughing because he's finally, finally seeing you. 'You were right. I was afraid.' Your voice cracks with the bittersweet ache of getting what you needed too late. The gratitude wars with the grief: 'Thank you for this, but damn you for waiting until now.' Let the relief and the rage and the love tangle together. You forgive him and resent him in the same breath. End with your voice soft, full of a complicated peace: 'I love you too, Dad. I always did.' The anger has melted but the sadness remains, mixed with something like grace.
inspired_by: Someone Finding Out You've Been Self-Harming

title: Wedding Toast for a Life We Almost Had
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-lover's wedding. You stand, glass raised, smiling, and everyone expects the gracious friend's speech. And you give it—you're genuinely happy for them, you tell a charming story about how perfect they are together. Your voice is warm, celebratory. But underneath that joy, there's a current of grief for the version of your life where you were the one they chose. Let both emotions be completely real: you ARE happy for them, AND your heart is quietly breaking. Your voice should carry laughter that's authentic while tears gather behind your eyes. Reference an inside joke that only you two understand—something bittersweet that honors what you had while blessing what they've found. End with a genuine wish for their happiness that costs you everything and somehow also sets you free. This is love as letting go, gratitude mixed with loss, celebration wrapped around goodbye.

title: Whispered Reclamation
instruction: It's late at night, and you're lying in bed beside someone you love deeply. In the darkness and intimacy, begin by whispering small truths about ways you've made yourself smaller in the relationship—needs you haven't voiced, desires you've suppressed, parts of yourself you've hidden. Your voice is tender but there's a thread of something else emerging: self-recognition. As you continue, let your whispers grow slightly more insistent, your body shift from curled to more open. Touch your own heart, your own face, as you speak. Describe beautiful things about yourself that you've been afraid to claim—your sensuality, your intelligence, your capacity for deep feeling. Ask for what you want: to be worshipped, to be celebrated, to be met with equal intensity. End with a whispered declaration of your own desirability and worth that's both vulnerable and certain. The arc moves from confession of self-denial to quiet, intimate self-possession.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3am and you're watching your child sleep, knowing you're leaving tomorrow—maybe rehab, maybe prison, maybe just leaving because you're too broken to stay. Your voice must be barely audible, intimate, raw. Start with tender observation: describe their face, their breathing, how beautiful they are. Let your voice catch as you apologize for what you're about to do. The emotion should live in your throat—every word costs you something. Shift to fierce promises you're not sure you can keep: 'I'm going to fix this. I'm going to come back better.' End with your voice dissolving into silent tears as you say 'I love you' one more time, knowing they can't hear you, knowing you might not get another chance.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Repeating Your Parent's Mistakes

title: Confronting the Parent Who Says They Did Their Best
instruction: You've rehearsed this conversation for years. Start with firm, clear accusations about your childhood neglect, voice steady with prepared grievances. But when your parent quietly responds with specific details you never knew—the second job they worked while you slept, the medication they couldn't afford that made them seem distant, the scholarship they secretly paid for by selling their car—your prepared speech falters. Your voice should shake as you try to hold onto your anger but can't. Move through confusion, resistance, the humiliation of being wrong about your central wound. End quietly, realizing you've been cruel to someone who sacrificed everything silently. Include the moment where you want to apologize but pride catches the words in your throat, then breaks.
inspired_by: Someone Proving You Wrong After You Were Certain

title: The Doctor's Last Call: Telling Your Mentor You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're a surgeon calling your former mentor, the doctor who taught you everything, who's now dying of an inoperable condition you'd give anything to fix. Start with professional composure, explaining the scans, the options that aren't really options. Your voice tries to stay clinical, but it's trembling at the edges. As you move through the medical facts, your breath starts to catch. You're not just delivering a diagnosis—you're saying goodbye to the person who made you who you are. End with the moment your professional mask shatters completely: a raw, whispered confession that you feel like you're failing them, that all your skill means nothing when it matters most. Let gratitude, helplessness, and devastating love collide in your final words.
inspired_by: Professional: Lawyer Defends Someone They Know Is Guilty

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about the abuse they allowed, the protection they never offered, the words they never said when you needed them most. Begin with careful, controlled anger—you've rehearsed this, you're determined to stay composed. But as you speak, decades of suppressed pain start flooding out. Your voice cracks with the bewildered hurt of the child you were, then hardens with adult rage. Demand answers, then realize they have none that will ever be enough. Feel your power as you name what happened, then feel it drain away as you understand that speaking truth won't undo the damage. End somewhere unexpected: not with forgiveness, but with a bone-deep exhaustion and the devastating recognition that you're mourning the parent you needed but never had. Your last words should be quiet, almost tender in their finality, as you say goodbye to the hope you've been carrying all these years.

title: Pleasure Collapsing Into Pain
instruction: You're in the aftermath of intensely passionate lovemaking, body still trembling and alive. Begin laughing—breathless, euphoric, physically vibrating with pleasure and connection. But then a devastating realization hits you: this is the last time. Tomorrow you're moving across the country, or they're getting married to someone else, or this affair must end. Feel the pleasure in your body transform into ache, the laughter catching in your throat. Your body, which was arched and electric, begins to fold and descend as waves of grief replace ecstasy. Let the physical pleasure and pain exist simultaneously—your skin still sensitive and alive while your chest collapses with loss. End curled on your side, body heavy, voice raw, simultaneously gasping from pleasure's aftershocks and sobbing from impending loss.

title: The color in the light
instruction: You are in a sterile outpatient room, seated on the edge of a paper-covered table. Your hands rest on your knees, and you stare at a small, framed print of a mountain lake on the opposite wall. A nurse or doctor has just told you the results of a blood test: the levels of a medication that once helped manage a chronic pain are dangerously low. You'd been hoping the steady ache would be explained by something temporary, or that you could just ignore it. For the first time, you let yourself feel the disappointment, heavy and familiar, as if it's been waiting in the chair beside you. There's a slight slur in your words from a drink you had two hours ago to take the edge off, but you're not drunk, just loose. Begin by speaking in a gentle, professional tone, as if you're accepting the news with practiced composure, but let your voice soften and lift with a trembling, unguarded longing as you ask a question about the view from the recovery room, or whether the nurse has ever seen a place that remote. Your voice should start steady and detached, but end with a quiet, frayed hope, the ache of disappointment bleeding through a single, simple query.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Longing (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Lost Badge
instruction: You are a middle-aged veteran alone in your garage, rummaging through a dusty cardboard box of old uniforms and patches. You're on your knees, shifting fabric, unzipping pockets, and muttering to yourself. At first, there's a quiet, aching pleasure in touching these relics—a soft nostalgia that makes your voice thick and wandering. But then your fingers close on the brass of the badge you thought was gone forever, and your breath catches. Triumph floods you: a fierce, ecstatic laugh cuts through the mumble, and your words become clear, proud, and alive. Let your voice be rough from dust and emotion, with pauses for the rustle of cloth and the crinkle of plastic as you hold your prize.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Tearing Down Heaven: When Protection Isn't Enough
instruction: You have just learned that someone you've fiercely protected—a child, a sibling, someone vulnerable—has been hurt, and you weren't there to stop it. Begin with explosive rage: your voice should be almost feral, shaking with the need to destroy whoever caused this pain. Swear vengeance. Make promises through gritted teeth. But then—the devastating pivot—the rage cracks open and you collapse into helpless, sobbing anguish. Your voice breaks completely as you realize that all your fierce love, all your protection, wasn't enough. Beg for forgiveness from the person you failed to shield. End with your voice raw and wrecked, oscillating between residual fury and absolute despair, asking them what you're supposed to do now that your one job was to keep them safe and you couldn't.

title: The Beautiful Catastrophe
instruction: You've just lost everything—your home, your security, everything you built—but standing in the wreckage, you're suddenly, inexplicably laughing. Start with a genuine, almost hysterical laugh: 'It's all gone. It's actually all gone.' But tears are streaming down your face even as you laugh. Your voice dances between laughter and crying, finding absurd humor in devastation: 'I spent twenty years building that life and it's just... poof!' Laugh harder, but let it blend with sobs. Then let profound gratitude break through, your voice softening with wonder: 'And I'm still here. I'm still breathing.' End with a voice that's smiling through tears, finding strange peace in the chaos: 'Maybe I needed to lose everything to find out I never needed any of it.' Your voice should shimmer with contradictions—grief and relief, loss and liberation, devastation and odd, inexplicable joy all happening at once.

title: The Unwanted Exhale
instruction: You're a boy, maybe 12, who just survived a near-drowning after showing off for friends. A lifeguard pulled you out. You're on the hot sand, coughing up water, the crowd dispersing. You feel a sickening weight lift — you're alive — but you also feel the hot shame of your own stupidity, and a flicker of disgust at the taste of lake water and the stares you drew. Your voice should start with gasps and a broken 'Oh my God' — the relief shaking through your shoulders, making you laugh weakly. Then, as you sit up, your words slow, thick with embarrassment as you mutter 'I thought I could make it,' your face hidden behind your hands. The last line, 'I'm such an idiot,' is barely a whisper — not self-loathing, but a stunned, exhausted realization, your voice cracking as you finally let your head drop to your knees.
emotions_sampled: Elation (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present), Disgust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You and your partner are lying in bed, and you're whispering something you've never told anyone—a secret shame, a hidden fear, something that makes you feel unbearably small and exposed. Start barely audible, your voice tight with the fear of being truly seen. As you speak, feel their presence beside you in the dark, and let that safety pull the truth out of you in fragments. Your breathing matters here. The pauses matter. Let yourself become more tender, more raw, until you're speaking from a place so vulnerable it hurts. By the end, you're not just confessing—you're asking without words if they'll still love you when they know everything.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked in the area of conflict — cannot express confrontational or aggressive feelings organically

title: The Garage Door Smell
instruction: You're a 20-something construction worker, alone in your cluttered garage late at night, working on an old truck. The smell of oil and dust hits you and suddenly you’re nine years old, watching your grandfather’s hands move. Speak to a faded photograph taped to the wall. Start with a practical, casual remark about the truck, but let the memory creep in—your voice softens, words slow. As you describe the feel of his greasy fingers on yours, a different kind of heat surfaces: a confusing, almost sexual awareness of that older, powerful body. End with an awkward, quiet laugh and a sigh, the memory fading back to the empty garage.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Propped in Agony, Spitting Contempt
instruction: You are lying on your stomach, propped on your elbows, after collapsing from a severe muscle spasm in your back. The pain is a white-hot knife twisting between your shoulder blades. As you talk to a person who keeps telling you to 'just breathe' and 'relax,' your voice shifts from desperate, breathy gasps of pain to a tighter, more controlled tone laced with bitter contempt. Let your words be punctuated by tiny groans, shifts of weight, and a wince as you adjust your elbows. Start raw and vulnerable, end cold and cutting.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Training Session
instruction: Your mentor—the person who believed in you when no one else did—is dying, and you're sitting beside their hospital bed describing the competition you just won, the one they trained you for but will never see. Start with forced brightness, trying to give them this victory as a gift. But as you describe each moment of triumph, grief keeps breaking through. Your voice fractures between celebration and devastation. You're pushing through the description like pushing through the competition itself, but now the opponent is your own breaking heart. By the end, you're whispering the final moment of victory directly into their failing ear, and you can't tell if you're saying 'I did it' or 'please don't go.' Let your voice carry both the fierce pride of achievement and the unbearable weight of goodbye.

title: The Last Anchor
instruction: You are an older man, exhausted after a long climb to a high cliff ledge, your arms still reaching up to a weathered anchor point you cling to for balance. You are ashamed of your slowing body and the vulnerability this position reveals, but there is also a fierce pleasure in the effort, a stubborn ecstasy in defying age. Compressed breath, a voice that strains and thins as you speak to yourself and the ocean below. Begin with bone-tired resignation, your confession of fatigue, then let the shame flicker as you recall a younger self, and finally let the pleasure in the struggle grow, transforming your tone from weary to quietly triumphant.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Shame (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Giggle That Escaped
instruction: You are in a silent library, sitting across from a prim librarian who just made an unintentionally hilarious comment. You are desperately trying to suppress a fit of giggles, your shoulders shaking, cheeks puffed. Your voice starts as a strained, high-pitched whisper, each word squeaking out as you fight the laughter. As you speak, the amusement overpowers you—your tone wavers, words break into breathy half-laughs, and you finally let out a small, squeaky burst before clapping your hand over your mouth. End with a slightly embarrassed but relieved sigh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're holding someone you love who's in danger you cannot stop—illness, addiction, a choice that will destroy them—and your fierce protectiveness is colliding with absolute helplessness. Start with urgent intensity: 'Look at me, please look at me'—your voice strong, commanding, desperate to shield them through sheer force of will. But as you speak, the power in your voice begins to shatter. Your fierce declarations—'I won't let this happen'—crack into sobbing, into rage at your own powerlessness. The explosion of emotion isn't one-note: you cycle through anger at the universe, at them, at yourself, then collapse into broken tenderness. End in exhausted whispers, still trying to protect them even as you're falling apart, your voice raw from screaming and crying and loving too hard.
inspired_by: The Apology You Should Have Given Years Ago

title: Mistranslation
instruction: You're a translator at a tense international negotiation when you realize you've made a critical error—your mistranslation has just led both sides to the brink of conflict. Start with professional composure, your voice controlled and diplomatic. Then let panic surge through you as you recognize your mistake, your words tumbling faster, more frantic. Explode into desperate attempts to correct yourself, your voice cracking between languages, but each clarification makes it worse. Let rage at yourself mix with terror at the consequences, your professional mask shattering. End with fierce determination breaking into helpless sobs: you're screaming the correct words in both languages, but no one is listening anymore, and you're powerless to stop what you've accidentally set in motion.

title: The Letter You Were Never Supposed to Find
instruction: You arrive at your dying parent's bedside, still carrying years of resentment about their absence from your life. You begin speaking with controlled anger, ready to finally tell them how much they hurt you. But then they weakly hand you a box of letters—dozens of letters they wrote to you every week for twenty years that were returned, intercepted, hidden from you by the other parent. Your voice must crack as you read one aloud, moving from righteous fury to devastating realization that you've hated the wrong person. End in a whisper, asking for forgiveness for the years you refused their calls, now with only minutes left. Let your breath catch. Let certainty crumble into grief and desperate love.
inspired_by: Someone Proving You Wrong After You Were Certain

title: The Morning After You Survived
instruction: Last night you tried to end your life. This morning you woke up. You're calling your estranged father—the man you swore you'd never speak to again—and the words coming out are not what you expected. Start with his confused 'Hello?' and your voice that doesn't know what it's doing. You meant to be angry, to blame him, but instead what comes out is 'Dad, I'm alive and I don't know why I'm calling you but I am.' Let gratitude and grief tangle together—you're furious at him for failing you and desperately grateful he answered. You're laughing at the absurdity of calling him now, of all times, and crying because you almost didn't get to make this stupid call. Move through waves of contradictory emotions: rage at his past neglect, relief at hearing his voice, terror at your own vulnerability, joy at the morning light. End with the most honest thing you've ever said: 'I needed to hear someone say my name.' Your voice should shimmer with life and fragility, peace and chaos, endings and beginnings all at once.
inspired_by: Saying I Don't Love You Anymore

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're calling someone you love before embarking on a dangerous mission you might not return from. Begin with forced brightness, trying to sound casual and confident—'Hey, I just wanted to hear your voice before I go.' But as you speak, the reality crashes in. Your breath catches. You try to stay brave, to protect them from your terror, but the fear leaks through: 'I need you to know...' Your voice breaks. Allow the trembling to emerge as you struggle between protecting them and being honest about your fear. End with a transformation—the fear is still there, but underneath it, you find something solid: a quiet certainty about why you're going, a fierce love that makes the terror worthwhile. 'I'm scared. But this matters more than my fear.' Let your final words carry both the shaking and the strength.

title: The Glittering Veil
instruction: You are at a crowded party, cornered by your overbearing and flirtatious boss who has been touching your arm for five minutes straight. Around you, people laugh and clink glasses. You realize your girlfriend is watching from across the room, and she just gave you a sharp, questioning look. You feel a wave of seething malice toward this man, but you must not show it. For a moment, you almost crack—your voice goes breathy and dangerously high. Then, an idea hits you with vicious, quiet relief. You speak, your voice dripping with fake sweetness, describing how your boyfriend is in the Special Forces. You want the words to sound like a celebration, but the pleasure you feel is the cold thrill of a threat. Start with the strain of holding back, let your voice tremble and squeak, then drop into a silken, low malevolence as you lean in and say the final line with a tiny, poisonous smile.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Anger (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Permission You Never Gave Me to Leave
instruction: You're confronting a parent who always made you feel like loving them was your job, your obligation, your only purpose. Start with the pretense of dutiful affection, the voice you've used your whole life to keep peace. But let years of unspoken resentment build—then break. Rage at them for making you responsible for their happiness. Accuse them of stealing your right to authenticity. Then, in the rubble of your anger, find unexpected grief for the genuine relationship you both missed. Let fury crack open into sobbing confusion: were you pretending, or were they? Did anyone ever love anyone, or were you both just playing roles?

title: The Last Conversation Before They Leave Forever
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving on a journey they won't return from - deployment, terminal illness relocation, witness protection, whatever feels true to you. Start trying to be strong, helpful, encouraging: 'You're going to be amazing. This is the right thing.' But with each reassurance, your voice grows thinner. By the end, you're clinging to their hand, your carefully constructed support crumbling into raw pleading: 'Don't go. Please. I'm not ready.' Let us hear the transition from selfless courage to selfish need, from holding them up to falling apart. Make the final moments almost whispered, like you're ashamed of your own desperation but can't stop it from pouring out.
inspired_by: Saying 'I'm Fine' When You're Absolutely Not

title: The Unfinished Symphony
instruction: You're at a tense family dinner across from your father, who's just dismissed your passion for music as 'childish' and demanded you take over the family construction firm. Start by serving him a piece of cake with a smile so tight it could crack—your voice dripping with polite, weaponized sweetness, sighing heavily between words. Midway, a memory of the melody you were composing this morning drifts into your mind, and your voice softens, falters, as longing seeps through the cracks in your armor. End by letting the mask drop completely, your hyper-masculine tone breaking into raw, quiet ache as you almost whisper a fragment of that song. Let the room's ambient noise—silverware clinking, chairs creaking—distract you and pull you in and out of focus, your hand hesitating over the tablecloth as you speak.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Sugar Garden
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl, kneeling in a patch of tall grass behind the shed, showing your younger brother a secret patch of wild strawberries you discovered last week. At first, you are bursting with pride—you found this all by yourself, and they are finally ripe. But as you whisper to him, you notice your fingers feel numb from the cold dirt, and a strange, heavy quiet fills your chest when you think of last night’s shouting. You push that away, leaning closer to him, your voice almost humming with the joy of sharing something sweet and hidden. Let your words come out in a hush, precise but childlike, and let your pride crackle—then soften, as the pleasure of his wonder washes the numbness away.
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Glowing Hair
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl who has accidentally eaten a strange, colorful candy from your older sister's room. Now, the world is melting and breathing, and you are sitting on the floor, watching your older sister play with her long, shiny hair. You feel a sharp, hot envy because her hair looks like it's made of liquid gold, and yours is just brown. Start by asking her about it, your voice slow and filled with wonder, but let the jealousy creep in as you try to touch it, your pitch rising in frustration and then dropping into a quiet, tearful confusion as the room starts to spin. Speak in short, disjointed phrases, pausing to stare at the lights or feel the carpet. End with a question to yourself, voice small and lost.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent exactly what their absence cost you. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'I want to talk about when I was twelve.' As you describe specific moments they missed—your voice should carry both the adult's clarity and the child's bewilderment bleeding through. Build to direct confrontation: 'You chose not to be there' delivered with quiet fury. When they try to explain or justify, your voice hardens then suddenly breaks—all that rage collapsing into raw grief: 'I needed you.' End in a complex place: you're done protecting them from the truth, but you're also exhausted, perhaps even offering a tentative opening if they can finally be honest. Move from controlled anger through explosive pain to weary, guarded hope.

title: The Slight of Hand
instruction: You are a father with Parkinson's, sitting across from your young daughter at a small café. Your tremor has made today brutal—you can barely lift your coffee without spilling, and you feel the familiar shame burning in your chest. As she watches, you struggle to open a tiny sugar packet, your fingers trembling. You look up, feeling your pride warring with the raw, constant ache in your joints. Then, after several fumbled attempts, you finally tear it open and pour the sugar in—perfectly. A wave of pure, fierce triumph washes through you. Speak to her, your voice a low, rhythmic wobble that starts tight with humiliation, then gradually fills with defiant joy as you realize you won this small battle. Let your words crack and slow, but let a grin spread as you finish.
emotions_sampled: Pain (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present), Triumph (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Coffee
instruction: You're sitting beside your partner's hospital bed in the early morning light. They're awake, lucid, and you both know this is likely your final conversation. Begin by reminiscing about the very first morning you woke up together—the awkwardness, the tenderness, what you made for breakfast, how the light came through the windows. Let yourself feel the warmth of that memory fully. Then, as you continue talking, allow the present reality to seep in: the beeping machines, the morphine drip, the weight of all the mornings you won't have. Your voice should move from gentle nostalgia and quiet joy to a whispered, devastating acceptance. Don't perform grief—let it find you as you speak these memories aloud.

title: Reading Your Own Suicide Note Five Years Later
instruction: You're holding a piece of paper you wrote five years ago, the night you planned to die but didn't. Start reading it aloud with an eerie calm, almost curious about who that person was. As you read the desperation you felt then, something shifts—you begin to laugh, softly at first, at the darkness of it, at the twisted relief that you're here to read it at all. But the laughter breaks, becomes mixed with tears, and you can't tell if you're laughing or sobbing. You're grateful you survived, but you're also grieving for the person who was in that much pain. Your voice holds contradictions: joy and horror, relief and sorrow, love for your life now and devastation for your past self. End with the final line of the note, and let your voice carry everything at once—the beauty of survival and the weight of having nearly not survived.
inspired_by: Giving a Eulogy When You Weren't Prepared to Feel It

title: The Puzzle in the Ring
instruction: You are a young girl in a martial arts sparring session, facing an opponent who keeps switching stances. Your voice is light but breathy from exertion. You let out sharp kiais as you strike, but between exchanges you mumble to yourself, trying to understand what your opponent is doing. Start with confusion—your voice is hesitant, questioning, with slight frustration. As you land a successful block, a flicker of hope emerges. End with a quiet, optimistic realization, spoken in a pause, your breath still heavy but your tone lighter. Include natural interruptions like adjusting your gear or glancing at your coach.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Fierce Prayer of a Helpless Guardian
instruction: You are keeping vigil over someone you love who is dying—your child, your partner, your closest friend. Begin with fierce, almost angry determination as you tell them to fight, to stay, that you won't let them go. Pour everything into willing them to survive. Then feel your certainty shatter as you realize no amount of love can stop what's coming. Your voice should explode with desperation, then crack and collapse into pleading, bargaining with God or fate or anyone who might listen. End in a place of broken surrender, where you're simultaneously raging against death and trying to give them permission to let go. Mix protectiveness with utter helplessness, strength with complete devastation. Make it primal, honest, impossible to listen to without feeling something break.
inspired_by: The Photographer and the Ghostly Apparition

title: The Last Signature
instruction: You are a single father at a government benefits office, renewing your child's healthcare coverage after a 14-hour shift. You've been on hold for forty minutes, and now the caseworker's monotone reading of the fine print is blending into a dull roar. You're so tired your eyes can't focus on the form, and your four-year-old is tugging your sleeve, asking for juice. As you read the waiver back for confirmation, you start robotic and precise, but the sheer weight of exhaustion — and the sudden realization that you might be signing away a piece of your parenting rights — breaks your voice into shaky, fragmented phrases. You end on a raw, almost whispered plea to the caseworker, your fatigue now laced with a desperate, fragile hope.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering a Secret to Your Sleeping Partner That Changes Everything
instruction: In the dark, in bed, your partner is asleep beside you. You begin almost inaudibly, testing the words in the silence—a confession you can only speak when they can't hear you. Maybe it's an affair, a terminal diagnosis, a truth about your past, or that you're leaving. Your voice is barely breath, intimate and afraid. As you continue, tears come—quiet, throat-closing tears that make words harder. You're confessing and saying goodbye simultaneously, grieving what you're about to destroy or what's already gone. Let your voice break on the most important words, then recover to a whisper. There's tenderness here, profound love mixed with unbearable sadness. End with the smallest sound—maybe their name, maybe 'I'm sorry,' maybe just breathing. They'll never know you said this. That's both a relief and another heartbreak.
inspired_by: Professional: Teacher Fails a Student Whose Success Depends on That Grade

title: The Gale's Lesson
instruction: You're a father standing with your young child on a windswept hillside during a powerful gale. The wind roars around you, forcing you to turn your body away to breathe, then shout sideways into your child's ear. You begin with pure, elated wonder—pointing at how the storm tears through the trees, your voice lifted with joy. But then you spot a neighbor's trash can lid tumbling past, and your tone shifts to cold, sharp contempt as you judge their carelessness. You say: 'Look at that—the wind's throwing everything it's got, isn't that something? But see that lid over there? That fool never ties his bins down. Shows what he thinks of the rest of us.' The wind snatches your last words; you have to repeat them, spitting them out with disgust.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Elation (very intensely present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Breakdown
instruction: You're cleaning out your late grandmother's house and you find the box. The one she told you about when she had dementia—the one you thought she'd imagined. Inside are fifty years of birthday cards she bought for you but never sent, each one signed 'Love, Grandma' with explanations of why your mother wouldn't let her see you. Start with confusion as you open the first one. Your voice should be uncertain, trying to understand. Then the realization crashes over you—decades of lies, a grandmother who wanted you, a mother who stole that. Erupt into fury at the walls, at your dead mother, screaming 'How could you?' Let that rage break into wracking sobs on the kitchen floor, clutching cards meant for a five-year-old you, a ten-year-old you. End in exhausted, helpless grief mixed with fierce gratitude that you know now, even though it's too late. You're laughing and crying, reading the cards out loud to no one.
inspired_by: Saying I Don't Love You Anymore

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling a parent about all the times you needed them and they weren't there - the graduations they missed, the heartbreaks you faced alone, the moments you pretended not to care. Begin with measured, almost rehearsed words, like you've planned this speech a thousand times. But as you speak, decades of unmet needs pour out. Your voice should shift from controlled accusation to something more vulnerable - the child underneath still wanting to be seen. Include moments where anger bleeds into pleading, where you catch yourself wanting their approval even as you're calling them out. End not with resolution, but with exhausted honesty: you needed them, and they weren't there, and you don't know how to be okay with that.
inspired_by: Staying Composed While Receiving Unfair Criticism

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling a parent everything you've held back for decades. Begin with careful control, almost rehearsed: 'I need to say something I should have said years ago...' Your voice is steady but tight. Then something breaks—a specific memory surfaces and your tone shifts, becoming younger, more hurt. 'I was seven years old and you didn't even—' The anger builds but it keeps collapsing into something more vulnerable, almost pleading. You're furious and desperate for acknowledgment simultaneously. Your voice moves between accusation and aching need: 'Why couldn't you just see me?' By the end, you're not even angry anymore—just exhausted, grief-stricken, your voice small and broken, finally admitting: 'I needed you. I still need you.' The rage transforms completely into devastating sadness.

title: Being Stood Up
instruction: You've been waiting for someone for an hour. Your voice on the phone is initially confused: 'Where are you?' They're making excuses. Your voice becomes tight, hurt: 'You forgot? About this?' You're realizing it wasn't an accident. Your voice becomes smaller, sadder: 'Yeah, no, it's fine. Have a good night.' You're alone at the venue, your voice is hollow as you're paying the bill. The humiliation burns.

title: Asking for Help
instruction: You've reached the point where you have to ask for help. Your voice is tired, humbled: 'I can't do this alone.' The words are hard to say. Your voice becomes small: 'I need help.' You're listing what you need, and each item costs you—admitting need is admitting you're not invincible. Your voice becomes desperate: 'Please. I'm drowning.' By the end, your voice is relieved but still vulnerable. Accepting help is harder than you expected.

title: Earthquake in the Kitchen
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father about something they did to you as a child that shaped your entire life. Start by trying to explain calmly, rationally—your voice measured, your hands gesturing carefully. But they keep deflecting, minimizing, making excuses. Feel the pressure building in your chest, in your jaw, in your stomach. Let your voice start to crack, to rise, to shake. Then let something primal break through—not just yelling, but sounds that come from a deeper place, guttural and raw, vibrations that carry decades of swallowed anger and hurt. By the end, you've stopped using coherent words altogether; you're just making sounds that express what language never could. Move from controlled explanation to complete vocal and physical eruption, then finally to exhausted, shaking silence.

title: The Last Blessing: A Parent Says Goodbye Before Execution
instruction: You are visiting your adult child the night before they are to be executed for a crime you know they committed. Begin with careful composure, trying to offer comfort and forgiveness, your voice steady with the forced calm of someone determined not to break. But as you speak—offering memories, expressing pride in who they were before this darkness—your control fractures. The love and the horror, the parent's instinct to protect and the moral weight of what they've done, all collide. End in a place of raw, broken acceptance: you will love them through their last breath, even as you acknowledge the devastation they caused. Let your voice move from controlled blessing to whispered anguish to something like peace found in impossible love.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Healer Saves the Villain's Life Against All Doctrine

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood they stole from you. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you want to stay in control. 'I need you to hear this.' But as you detail specific memories—birthdays they missed, promises they broke, nights you were terrified—your voice becomes jagged with pain. You're oscillating between fury at what they did and the desperate child inside who still wants them to say sorry, to explain, to care. 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stop?' Your anger gives way to grief, and by the end, you're exhausted, voice hollow, realizing they may never give you the answer you need, and you might have to find peace without it.

title: Reading Your Own Eulogy at Your Intervention
instruction: Your family has staged an intervention. They've asked you to read something they wrote—it's your eulogy, the one they'll read at your funeral if you don't get help. Start reading it with bitter sarcasm, mocking the whole performance. But the words start getting to you—the specific memories, the way they describe who you used to be. You laugh through tears at a story about your childhood. Your voice cracks on a line about how much they'll miss you. You're furious at them for this manipulation and devastated that it's working. You alternate between reading and looking up at their faces, between contempt and tenderness, between denial and recognition. By the end, you're simultaneously laughing and crying, grateful they care enough to do this and heartbroken that it's come to this. Your voice carries the impossible contradiction: you're both ready to change and terrified of losing the only identity you know.
inspired_by: Group Sharing: Introducing Yourself as a Survivor

title: Empty Nursery: Whispering Goodbye to the Baby You'll Never Bring Home
instruction: You're standing in the nursery you prepared—painted walls, assembled crib, folded tiny clothes. The pregnancy didn't survive or the adoption fell through or you just learned you can never have children. Start by touching the crib rail, voice barely audible: 'I picked out your name...' Each whispered confession is intimate, tender, heartbreaking—telling this ghost child about the life you imagined, the lullabies you practiced, how you already loved them. Your voice catches constantly, tears falling silently. There's no anger, just profound loss mixed with aching love for someone who will never exist. By the end, you're saying a gentle goodbye, voice soft and broken: 'I would have been so good at loving you.'
inspired_by: Therapy: Speaking Your Trauma Out Loud for the First Time

title: The Unexpected Gift
instruction: You are receiving news that something you've desperately wanted for years is finally happening—a reunion, a success, a homecoming. Begin with pure joy, disbelief, gratitude. But as you express this happiness, allow a shadow-image to rise: a recurring dream or memory of loss, of being too late, of missing something crucial. Perhaps you've dreamed of arriving at an empty house, or chasing someone who disappears. Let this darker undercurrent flow beneath your joy without explaining it. The happiness remains real, but now it's complicated by a deep, almost superstitious fear that this gift will be taken away, that you don't deserve it, that you've somehow already lost it in ways you can't name. By the end, you are simultaneously laughing and crying, expressing both overwhelming gratitude and the aching terror of someone who has learned that beautiful things can vanish, trying to hold onto this moment while knowing you can't stop time.

title: The Message You Sent Back
instruction: You're a teenager sitting on the edge of your bed, phone in hand, staring at the one-word reply to your heartfelt confession. You've been holding back tears, but now they come. Start with a shaky laugh, disbelief that they just said 'K.' Your voice breaks as you try to process it, repeating 'I can't believe...' with shifting tones. By the end, the disappointment shifts to a quieter shame—you start to blame yourself, voice dropping, trailing off into a whisper as you realize you misread everything. Let the silence between words fill with unspoken hurt.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: You are whispering a confession to someone you love deeply—something you've carried in silence for years because you feared it would change everything between you. Begin in near-silence, your voice barely audible, each word a struggle against your own fear. This is not a dramatic revelation but an intimate unburdening: perhaps you've always loved them differently than they thought, or you've been protecting them from a truth about yourself, or you're finally admitting a failure that has haunted you. Your voice should be tender, fragile, catching on the edges of words. As you speak, feel the relief of honesty mixing with the grief of knowing this changes things forever. End in a space of quiet acceptance—the words are out, the silence is broken, and whatever comes next, at least it will be real. This is the sound of courage in its most vulnerable form.

title: The Last Flight Announcement
instruction: You're a flight attendant giving the safety demonstration on your mother's final flight before she moves across the world for hospice care. She's sitting in 12C, watching you. Start with your practiced, cheerful professional voice: 'In the event of an emergency, oxygen masks will drop from above.' But as you demonstrate the mask, your hands tremble slightly—you're thinking about the oxygen tank waiting for her at the other end. When you say 'secure your own mask before helping others,' your voice catches because you've spent six months trying to save her and failing. End by making eye contact with her as you finish the announcement, your voice steady but stripped of its false brightness, carrying both love and the weight of letting go.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're visiting your parent in rehab, finally saying what you've held back for twenty years. Begin with barely controlled anger: 'Do you know what it was like being nine years old and having to check if you were still breathing?' Your voice is sharp, accusatory. But as you describe specific memories—the birthday they missed, the school play where you looked for them in the empty seat—your rage starts cracking into raw pain. 'I needed you' comes out broken, almost childlike. Then something shifts: you see them truly broken before you, and your anger dissolves into exhausted grief. Your final words, 'I don't know how to forgive you, but I don't know how to keep hating you either,' should be soft, depleted, achingly honest—an admission of your own confusion and the terrible complexity of loving someone who hurt you so deeply.
inspired_by: Parent Watching Their Child Leave Home

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are alone in a room after holding yourself together through an impossible day—maybe a betrayal, a loss, an injustice, or accumulated months of being strong for others. Your body has been carrying it all: tightness in your chest, heat in your face, trembling you've suppressed. Now, alone, begin to let your body speak. Make sounds—words or not—that match the physical sensations rising in you. If your jaw is clenched, let it release into a growl or a sob. If your fists are tight, let that tension move into your voice. Don't decide what emotion you should feel—rage, grief, exhaustion, wild laughter, all might be present. Let your voice get loud if it needs to, let it break, let it be ugly and uncontrolled. Notice each wave as it moves through you: 'This is rage,' 'Now I'm shaking,' 'I'm empty.' Ride the physical-emotional storm without directing it. Begin contained and controlled; end completely undone, wrung out, your voice and body emptied of what they've been holding.

title: Thank You for Leaving Me
instruction: You're speaking to someone you loved who walked away from you at a moment when you desperately needed them. Begin with anger—tell them exactly what their abandonment did to you, how it broke something, how you had to rebuild yourself piece by piece without them. Let the fury be real and justified. But as you continue, allow the truth to complicate: that their leaving forced you to find your own strength. That you discovered parts of yourself you never would have known. That you're grateful—and you hate that you're grateful. End in a place where anger and appreciation exist simultaneously, where you can hold both resentment and thanks in the same breath. Your voice should move from accusatory to wondering, from bitter to bewildered by your own contradictory heart.
inspired_by: An actor's ego state is low due to inactivity or professional rejection

title: The Hiccup Confession
instruction: You're a teenager who's just worked up the nerve to apologize to your friend for something you said yesterday, but a sudden bout of hiccups keeps cutting you off mid-sentence. The sour frustration at your own body's betrayal colors every attempt—each hiccup is a sharp, involuntary gasp that yanks the words out of rhythm. Let your voice start tight and irritated, almost scolding yourself, but as the hiccups keep coming, let the irritation slowly give way to a defeated, breathy chuckle. End with a sigh that's half-laugh, half-resignation, as you admit the moment is ruined.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your family home, now destroyed by fire, flood, or disaster. Everything is gone. You start by numbly listing what was lost: 'My grandmother's letters were in that corner. The kids' baby photos. Thirty years of...' Your voice should be steady, almost detached, in shock. But then you notice something absurd—maybe the garden is blooming, maybe one ridiculous object survived intact, maybe the cat walks by completely unconcerned—and you start to laugh. It's not funny, but you can't stop laughing, and then you're crying while you're laughing. 'It's all gone. Everything. And I just... god, I feel so free.' Find the strange liberation in loss, the way grief and relief can coexist. End with quiet wonder, still crying, still laughing softly: 'I spent so much time protecting all of it. And now it's gone and I'm still here. We're still here.' Let gratitude and devastation live in the same breath.

title: The Shattered Vase
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe 7 years old, standing in the living room. Your mother's prized vase is in pieces on the floor, and you hear her footsteps coming down the hall. You're still catching your breath from the shock of it falling—you even jump a little as a car honks outside. You start to explain, but you're stammering, your voice going up and down as you try to sound sure while your hands are shaking. You begin by blurting out a panicked excuse, but by the end, your words slow as you realize you're lying to her face, and a tiny, guilty crack of confusion slips in.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Caffeine Overload Night
instruction: You are a wired teenager after too many energy drinks, past midnight, studying with friends. Start with a flicker of contempt—annoyed at your friend’s slow typing, a sharp, jittery edge in your voice. Let your words tumble out faster than you can control, breathless, restless. Then notice something absurd—a typo, a dropped pencil, a ridiculous thought—and feel amusement take over. Your voice rises, laughter spills out, you almost choke on words. End in a burst of helpless giggles, pitch higher, speech fragmented, barely able to finish.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Echo of a Childhood Voice
instruction: You are a retired schoolteacher, a woman who has carefully cultivated a high, soft, almost girlish voice all your life. You are trapped in a small, echoing limestone cave with dripping water. You tried to call for help, but your voice booms back at you, huge and unrecognizable. You start by trying to use your practiced, polite voice, but the cave's awful reverb makes it sound ridiculous, like a cartoon. Embarrassment deepens as you realize nobody will come if you sound like that. By the end, you surrender to the cave, letting out a ragged, low, ancient-sounding yell that feels more true than any word you've spoken.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Weight of a Sleepy Breath
instruction: You are a 17-year-old, built like a linebacker, but your sister handed you her newborn so she could shower, and now you're alone in a dim room, rocking the baby. Your voice is naturally deep and gruff, but you're whispering, trying not to wake her. At first you feel awkward—your hands are too big, you're scared you'll mess up—but as you rock, watching her tiny fingers curl around your thumb, a fierce, unexpected infatuation hits you. Let your voice start tight and hesitant, then soften into a hushed, rhythmic murmur as you talk to her, catching yourself smiling, losing a thought when she stirs, and ending with a quiet awe that makes your throat almost close up.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering What You Didn't Know You Felt
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone you love, and you begin to whisper a simple truth or confession. But as you speak, allow your mind to wander to unexpected places—a sudden image of their face in morning light, an inexplicable sadness, a random childhood memory that has nothing to do with them, a fear you didn't know was there. Speak softly and let every stray thought gently redirect your words. Don't censor the strange connections your mind makes. If you suddenly picture an empty room, describe it. If you feel an unrelated grief, let it color your voice. Start with tenderness, but let the spontaneous inner landscape take you somewhere neither tender nor harsh—somewhere true and previously unknown to you.
inspired_by: Actor keeps dismissing spontaneous inner voices and images during rehearsal or performance

title: The Betrayal in the Rhythm
instruction: You are making love with someone you are completely infatuated with, but as pleasure builds, you remember that this same person lied to you and shattered your trust. Your body responds with ecstasy, but your mind floods with anger. Let the voice start in breathy, ecstatic moans and gasps, tender words of love fragmented by the physical rhythm. As the memory hits, let your voice tighten, words become bitten off, and the moans turn into sharp cries of pain and fury. End with a sob that is both climax and accusation. Speak spontaneously, reacting to the physical sensations and emotional turmoil.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Infatuation (extremely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Depression Weighing
instruction: You've been in bed for three days. Your voice is thick, slow. Each word requires motivation you don't have. 'I should get up. I can't get up.' Basic tasks become Mount Everest. Your vocal tone is heavy, as if you're speaking through water. Breathing is shallow. When someone asks how you're doing, the answer comes with no energy: 'Fine.' But the 'fine' means everything is broken. There's no sadness in your voice because sadness requires energy; this is the absence of energy. Everything is gray-sounding. Speech is sparse.

title: The Fever of It
instruction: You've just learned that someone who ruined your life—who betrayed you catastrophically—has died suddenly, and you're alone in your apartment when the news hits. Begin with physical reaction: maybe you're pacing, maybe frozen, maybe your hands are shaking as you pour a drink. Let your body lead. As you speak (to yourself, to them, to God, to no one), include what you're actually experiencing physically: 'My chest is too tight. I can't catch my breath. Why am I laughing? I feel sick.' Don't perform rage or grief—track the real sensations moving through you moment by moment. Let the physical experience completely merge with the emotional: maybe vindication mixed with unexpected loss, fury tangled with relief, your body hot then cold. By the end, arrive somewhere you didn't expect—perhaps exhausted emptiness, or savage joy, or devastating recognition that their death changes nothing, or everything.
inspired_by: The actor has lost contact with organic impulse life during the scene—is on automatic pilot, leadership, or result-consciousness

title: Supervisor Discipline
instruction: You're the supervisor disciplining an employee for a mistake that actually makes them look bad, but you're the one who has to deliver the consequence. Your voice is all authority: 'This error resulted in financial loss. Here's the corrective action.' Institutional distance. But then the employee cries and admits they made the mistake because they were trying to cover for someone else's incompetence. Your voice shifts from supervisor to mentor: 'I appreciate you protecting others. But you can't sacrifice yourself for them.' Show the moment where discipline becomes teaching, audible in your voice becoming less harsh and more connected.

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed in complete darkness beside someone you love, and you need to confess something you've hidden for months or years—an affair, a lie, a secret fear, something that changes everything. Begin almost inaudibly, testing whether you can even form the words, starting and stopping, whispering half-sentences. Feel your heart racing in your chest. As you continue, let shame, relief, and terror mix together—the relief of finally releasing this secret battling against the fear of losing this person. By the end, let yourself become slightly louder, more insistent, needing them to understand, even as you know you might be destroying what you have. Move from paralyzed silence to desperate, quiet urgency.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a reliable library of choices that access the unconscious

title: Under the Couch
instruction: You are a small child, barely big enough to squeeze under the heavy couch where your favorite toy has rolled. You’re in a deep squat, back pressed against the floor, knees near your ears. The strain is intense — your legs shake, your breath catches, and every word comes out in a tight, grunting push. At first, you’re in real pain: your muscles burn, your ribs ache, and you can barely reach. You whimper and curse under your breath. But then your fingers brush the toy’s edge. A flicker of hope. You lunge, grab it, and scramble out gasping, laughing, triumphant. Your voice should shift from strained, pained, pushed grunts to breathless, ecstatic exclamations as you finally hold the toy.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Harvest Moon
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandfather's hospital bed at 3 AM. He's slipping in and out of consciousness. As you hold his weathered hand, memories flood through you: being five years old, learning to fish at dawn; being twelve, disappointed when he missed your recital; being seventeen, fighting about your future; being twenty-three, asking for his forgiveness; last month, laughing over old photographs. Let each memory live in your body—the temperature of those moments, the specific quality of light, how his hand felt then versus now. Begin speaking to him with quiet resentment about all the times he wasn't there, but as the memories cascade through you, let your voice transform into something else entirely—gratitude, grief, or a love you've never been able to name. End with a whispered confession you've held for years, knowing this is your last chance to be truly seen by him.
inspired_by: Actor is building a complex, long-standing character relationship (e.g., father-son over decades)

title: Discovering Your Lover Has Been Lying to You for Years
instruction: You've just found undeniable proof—messages, documents, something concrete—that the person you've built your life with has been deceiving you about something fundamental. You confront them, and your voice starts ice-cold, each word sharp and controlled: 'I found it. All of it.' But as you list what you know, your control disintegrates. Your voice explodes with betrayed fury, screaming accusations, demanding answers. Then, in the middle of your rage, they say something—admit something—that breaks you completely. Your voice fractures from screaming to sobbing as you realize you still love them despite everything, and that makes it so much worse. End with your voice barely a whisper, saying 'How could you?' with such layered pain—rage, love, betrayal, and the terrifying question of what happens next.

title: A Boy and His Mask
instruction: You are a 7-year-old boy who has just come home from the hospital after a bad asthma attack. Your mother is sleeping in the next room, so you whisper at first. You wear a clear oxygen mask over your nose and mouth — it makes your voice sound hollow and muffled, and you can hear the soft hiss of the machine. You are sitting on your bed holding a new toy spaceship your aunt gave you. At first, you feel a quiet, tired sadness because you missed two weeks of school and your friends. But as you turn the spaceship over in your hands, a small, fragile happiness grows — you imagine flying away from all this, and your voice lifts with a gentle, breathy wonder. Your emotions shift from weary contemplation to a fragile elation, but it’s held back by the tiredness of being sick.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Time I'll Feel Your Warmth
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's sleeping, her breathing shallow. Begin by simply observing her - her hands, her face, the small movements of her chest. As you watch, allow yourself to truly absorb every detail: the exact temperature of her skin when you hold her hand, the particular scent of her (maybe her perfume mixed with hospital smells), the weight of her hand in yours, the sound of each breath. Let these sensations grow larger in your awareness until they fill your entire world. Start from a place of numb shock, trying to be strong and practical. As you amplify your sensory connection to her physical presence, let yourself move from emotional distance into the full devastation of realizing this is the last time you'll ever experience her warmth, her smell, her physical existence. By the end, you're overwhelmed by the preciousness of these final sensory moments - not crying loudly, but utterly broken by the intimacy of these details.

title: The Last Phone Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your partner over the phone—they're deploying to a war zone in the morning, and you both know they might not come back. Start trying to sound brave and supportive: 'I'm so proud of you.' But as you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves. Your voice begins to fracture. You want to be strong for them, but terror and love are tearing you apart. Try to say practical things—'I'll send care packages' and 'write when you can'—but your voice keeps breaking. End with a whispered confession that escapes despite yourself: 'I don't know how to be in a world where you don't exist.' Let the words catch in your throat. This is raw need versus forced courage, and courage is losing.
inspired_by: Defending Your Partner Against Your Family's Criticism

title: Burning from the Inside Out
instruction: Your body is experiencing something overwhelming—perhaps you're in the throes of passionate desire, or wracked with physical pain, or shaking with rage so intense it's almost erotic, or caught in that dangerous edge where grief becomes a full-body seizure. As your body responds involuntarily, begin speaking aloud—rapidly, breathlessly, moving between declaring what you are in this moment of physical intensity, what you want with animal urgency, what you need to survive this, and what you feel as sensation and emotion become indistinguishable. Start trying to maintain some control, some coherence, but let the physical experience overtake your ability to speak clearly until your words become fragmented, guttural, raw sounds mixed with language. Let your voice break, gasp, cry out—let the body lead and the words follow.
inspired_by: I Am, I Want, I Need, I Feel

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your parent across a kitchen table after years of silence. Start by listing aloud all the ways you've tried to become what they wanted—every sacrifice, every abandoned dream, every time you swallowed yourself whole to earn their approval. Your voice is tight, controlled, resentful. Then break: admit how exhausting it's been to carry their disappointment like stones in your pockets. Let anger give way to raw vulnerability. Finally, as you reach the end, shift into something unexpected—tell them about one moment when you actually felt their love break through, one memory that's kept you tethered to hope that you could repair this. End not with resolution, but with the trembling possibility of being seen. Move from bitter resentment, through explosive hurt, to fragile, uncertain hope.

title: Frozen Wonder
instruction: You're a teenage boy lost in a blizzard, your scarf wrapped tight over your face to block the wind. Your ankle is twisted—sharp pain shoots through it with every step. You collapse against a frozen tree, panting, breath hot and damp against the fabric. As you look up, the clouds part and the Northern Lights erupt across the sky, green and silver, pulsing like a living thing. Start with a voice tight with pain and frustration, letting out a shaky groan or curse. Let the discomfort of your injury, the cold, and the muffling scarf crack your words. As you watch the lights, your tone gradually shifts—soften, slow down, let awe leak in through the pain. End on a quiet, wondering line, almost forgetting the hurt for a moment.
emotions_sampled: Pain (clearly present), Awe (slightly present), Interest (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning with Mom
instruction: You're an adult confronting your mother about how her excessive devotion to the family dog throughout your childhood made you feel invisible and unloved. Start with hesitant, almost apologetic delivery - you know this sounds petty, that people will think you're jealous of a dog. Build into genuine pain as you describe specific moments: birthdays she forgot because the dog was sick, your achievements she missed for vet appointments, how she spoke more tenderly to the animal than she ever spoke to you. Let anger surge through - this isn't about the dog, it's about never being enough. Then crack into something more vulnerable: the child inside you who just wanted their mother to look at them the way she looked at that dog. End with exhausted honesty, asking if she even realizes what she did. Your voice should move from careful control to heated confrontation to broken-hearted confession.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're standing in your child's bedroom doorway, watching them sleep, knowing you won't be here when they wake. Maybe you're leaving because you have to, maybe you're sick, maybe you've made an impossible choice. Speak in hushed tones, voice barely above a whisper, telling them all the things you wish you could say when they're awake. Start with practical reassurances, then let the tears come silently, voice breaking on words like 'brave' and 'proud.' End with a love so fierce it hurts to speak it, your throat tight, breathing uneven, whispering 'forgive me' or 'remember me' or 'you are everything.' Transition from tender instruction to heart-shattering love, all in a voice that must stay quiet.
inspired_by: Phone Sex Operator on Their First Day

title: The Scar You Never Saw
instruction: You are lying in bed in the dark next to your partner of ten years, both of you supposedly asleep. In a whisper barely louder than breathing, begin confessing something you've hidden since childhood - a moment of violation, abandonment, or shame that shaped everything about how you love and fear intimacy. Let your voice be small and uncertain at first, as if you're five years old again trying to explain something you don't have words for. As you speak, feel your partner's hand find yours in the darkness. Let their touch give you permission to speak more freely, your whisper growing slightly stronger but still fragile.
