By the end, you're not just confessing - you're finally grieving what was taken from you, your breath hitching with silent tears. Move from frightened secrecy to tentative trust to cathartic release.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked on the spot before a performance or class and cannot reach a BEING state

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're alone in your car, gripping the steering wheel after a devastating event - a firing, a betrayal, a public humiliation. Your body is tight with held-back rage and shame. Start by wanting to scream, to hit something, to drive away and never come back. Let your body shake with these physical wants - feel them in your hands, your jaw, your chest. As you begin to let sound out - whether screaming, sobbing, or guttural release - discover what you want underneath the rage: do you want revenge? Do you want to disappear? Do you want to be someone else entirely? Let your voice move from explosive anger to something more visceral and vulnerable. What do you want to shed? What do you want to burn down in your life? By the end, as your body exhausts itself, let a different want emerge from the wreckage: what do you want to build from these ashes? Your voice should transform from violent to utterly spent to quietly, fiercely determined.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent after decades of emotional absence. Start with shaking control: 'I need you to understand something.' But as you try to articulate your pain, rage surges through. 'When I needed you, you were...' the pause fills with years of abandonment '...nowhere.' Your voice cracks between anger and the desperate child still inside you. 'I waited for you to...' another pause, this one trembling '...to see me.' By the end, the fury dissolves into raw vulnerability. You're no longer accusing—you're begging. The final silence after 'Please' contains all the love you still, devastatingly, feel.

title: The Shelf
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in your kitchen, standing on tiptoe with your arms stretched high to retrieve a heavy photo album from the top shelf. Your ribs ache, your voice comes out thin and strained. Start with sharp, angry muttering at your late husband for putting it up there, your breath short. As you just manage to hook the album’s edge, a wave of exhaustion hits and your anger softens into weary tenderness—you whisper to him, voice breaking, as you finally let the album fall into your chest.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Star Before the Drift
instruction: You are alone in your suited, tethered just outside a damaged science station, tumbling slowly through a nebula. Inside your helmet, your own breathing sounds huge and close; every word echoes distantly. A malfunctioning O2 scrubber has flooded your suit with nitrous-tinged air, making you feel floaty, euphoric, raw. You begin by describing the terrifying beauty of the nearest star going supernova—you're giddy, almost silly, your words rushing and sticking together. You're laughing and coughing, the static crackling over the comms. As you realize this is the last thing you'll see, your voice softens, deepens with a quiet, fierce hope: you're not afraid, you're awestruck. The tinny, close sound of your voice brings a fragile wonder to your final words as you forget to be scared.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. Begin by truly seeing her: the texture of her skin, the weight of her hand in yours, the specific color of her eyes as she looks at you, the rhythm of her breathing. Start with quiet fear and resistance—you don't want this moment to be real. As you take in every sensory detail of her presence—the familiar scent of her perfume mixed with hospital smells, the warmth still radiating from her body, the particular way light catches her silver hair—let yourself move from denial into full, raw acceptance. By the end, speak to her with fierce gratitude, your voice breaking not with sadness but with overwhelming love for every detail of who she is. Let noticing the specifics of her physical presence crack you open completely.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, about to give a toast, but you're secretly in love with them and devastated that this day has come. Begin with the scripted joy—raise your glass, smile, start with the funny stories you prepared. But as you speak, let yourself feel each word: what do you feel about their happiness? What do you feel about the way they're looking at their new spouse? What does it mean that you're celebrating while breaking inside? Let your toast become layered—genuine love for your friend mixed with grief for yourself, true happiness for them mixed with anger at your own silence, gratitude for their friendship mixed with resentment that it was never more. Your voice should carry all of it—laughing while nearly crying, celebrating while mourning, blessing while saying goodbye to a dream. End having honored both truths: your love for them and your loss of them.
inspired_by: Taking Your Emotional Point of View

title: Explaining the Gauge
instruction: You are an 80-year-old woman, your voice naturally high and delicate, speaking to a young non-native-speaking technician who is fixing your oxygen machine. Because of the language barrier, you must speak slowly, loudly, and strip your sentences to simple words, with long pauses between them. You are intensely contemplating the machine’s strange behavior — a flickering gauge that won't settle. Start with a clipped, frustrated tone, each word forced and separate, as if explaining to a child. Midway, you lose your thought and let out a small, distracted sigh, then find it again. As you notice the technician’s careful efforts, your contemplation deepens into a gentle, tender wonder. Your volume drops, pauses become softer, and your voice carries a quiet warmth — shifting from frustrated simplicity to grateful reflection.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering a Secret That Changes Everything
instruction: Late at night, in the dark, you're confessing something to your sleeping lover that you can never say when they're awake. Start with just your breathing, gathering courage. Your voice is barely audible—tender, aching, terrified. You're telling them the truth about something (an illness, a past, a fear, a love for someone else, a decision you've made) that will change everything. As you whisper, the weight of the secret begins to lift and the weight of losing them becomes real. Your voice catches on certain words. You pause to touch their face, their hand. The tenderness wars with devastation. You're grateful for this moment of honesty even though they can't hear it. End with either the quietest 'I'm sorry' or 'I love you,' where those simple words carry the weight of an ending you can't stop.

title: The Last Step
instruction: You are a teenager sprinting up a steep, endless staircase, lungs on fire, legs leaden. You're trying to catch someone before they disappear for good. Your words come out in ragged, two-or-three-word bursts, each one harder than the last. Start with raw, desperate distress—shouting, pleading, voice cracking with urgent hope. But as you climb and your body fails, the panic curdles into hollow exhaustion. By the final step, your voice drops to a broken whisper, barely audible, as you realize you're too late. Let the silence between gasps tell the story.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Broken Glass and Breathing
instruction: You've just slammed a door, thrown something, or destroyed something in a rage. Your body is electric, shaking. Begin by acknowledging everything in your body and mind: the adrenaline, the urge to hit something else, shame creeping in, your racing heart, memories flooding back of why you're really angry, the physical pain in your hands. Speak these sensations and feelings aloud as they arise—don't perform rage, inhabit the aftermath of it. Let your breathing dictate the rhythm. As you name what's happening inside you, the fury begins to transform—perhaps into exhaustion, perhaps into grief underneath the anger, perhaps into a fierce, clear knowing of what you actually need. The arc: from explosive chaos to embodied clarity.

title: Defending the Art to the One Who Destroyed You
instruction: You're confronting someone who shattered your confidence years ago—a teacher, a mentor, a former lover who told you your creative work was worthless. You've brought your latest piece, and your voice is fierce, shaking with barely controlled rage as you make them look at what you've accomplished despite them. You're shouting now, demanding they acknowledge what you've built from the rubble they left. But then you hear yourself, hear the desperation underneath the anger, and something collapses. Your voice breaks, shifts from fury to anguish as you realize you're still seeking their approval, still haunted by their judgment. Tears are streaming now, your voice raw and exposed as you admit how much they hurt you, how their words echo in your head every time you create. The final words emerge quieter, exhausted, as you tell them—and yourself—that you're done letting them live in your mind. Your voice carries both devastation and the first trembling note of freedom.
inspired_by: Showing Your Art to Someone Who Doesn't Get It

title: The Flood: August 1927, Rising Water
instruction: You are trapped on your farmhouse roof as the Mississippi River rises around you—you've been here for six hours in the brutal heat, and you've just watched your neighbor's house collapse into the water a hundred yards away. You are screaming for help, but your voice is growing hoarse, your body is sunburned and dehydrated, and the water keeps rising. Begin with raw, desperate calls for rescue—loud, urgent, physical. As exhaustion takes over and the water reaches the roof's edge, let the screaming dissolve into something else: a fevered, almost ecstatic prayer or confession, your voice ragged and broken, speaking to God or your dead mother or the river itself. Mix physical agony with strange euphoria, terror with surrender, rage at being abandoned with awe at the terrible power surrounding you. End in a whisper, either accepting death or finding some primal will to survive—your voice completely transformed from where it began.
inspired_by: When directing actors in a play set in a specific historical period

title: Pretending to Remember Someones Name You Forgot
instruction: Youre greeted by someone whose name you cant recall. Internally, you scramble to remember, but you act as if all is well. Describe your internal panic while engaging smoothly. Speak warmly, using neutral terms to conceal your lapse.

title: The Carpet's Complaint
instruction: You are lying flat on your stomach on a worn carpet in your childhood bedroom, face pressed sideways into the fibers. You're supposed to be packing a box of old photos, but you've stopped, overwhelmed by irritation at the task. The weight of your body makes your voice feel muffled and tight. As you speak, you start with sharp, clipped frustration about the mess you're in, but your annoyance gradually softens and cracks as you realize you're not angry at the photos—you're sad that this chapter is ending. Let your voice shift from a tense, pressured snap to a quieter, wobbling admission, with pauses where you lose your train of thought or sigh into the carpet.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Sadness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispered Without Words
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your sleeping partner after a miscarriage. You need to tell them something—your fear, your grief, your secret relief, your shame about that relief—but you can't wake them. Start by breathing your emotions toward them in the darkness. Let tiny sounds escape: barely-audible whimpers, soft exhalations, the quietest catches in your throat. These sounds hold everything you can't say out loud. Gradually, allow whispered half-words to form, fragments of sentences that dissolve back into breath and sound. This isn't about being heard; it's about releasing what's trapped inside. Begin in numb shock and end in tender devastation—or perhaps unexpected grace. Let the journey be quiet, intimate, and raw, discovering emotions you didn't know you were holding.
inspired_by: Actor feels blocked by words — text feels intellectual rather than felt

title: Desert Mirage
instruction: You are a teenage boy trying to act tough, but you've been hiking for hours in 110-degree heat with no water. You finally stumble upon a shallow, muddy puddle of water and a sliver of shade under a cracked boulder. You start by forcing out angry, defiant words—cursing the sun, the hike, yourself—but your voice cracks, dried out, each word costing you a breath. As you kneel and scoop water to your lips, the anger dissolves into a shaky, almost childlike relief. Let your voice wilt: heavy panting, swallowing hard, trailing off midsentence. End with a whisper that sounds like you've just found something you thought you'd lost forever.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bitter Buoyancy
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in a dark swimming pool, treading water after a forced swim to cool down from a family argument. Your body aches from exertion, and you keep dipping below the surface, your words cut off by gulps of air and splashes. The sourness from the fight sits in your chest like a rock — resentment toward your grown child who dismissed your advice. You're slightly lightheaded from the wine you had earlier, making your movements sloppy and your thoughts drift. As you struggle to stay afloat, your bitter muttering shifts: start with sharp, accusatory fragments, then let the exhaustion sink in, and end with a quiet, slurred acknowledgment that maybe they were right. Your voice must rise and fall with the water, gasping, sometimes gurgling, every word earned through effort.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Dementia Waltz
instruction: You're visiting your spouse who no longer remembers you, and today they've mistaken you for their childhood sweetheart from sixty years ago. Accept the role they've given you, speaking with gentle playfulness about memories that aren't yours, and feel unexpected joy bubbling up—because at least they're happy, at least they're smiling at you again. Let laughter mix with tears as you describe a dance you never shared, a first kiss that never happened, watching their eyes light up with love even if it's not quite for you. Your voice should shimmer between heartbreak and something like grace—the absurd gratitude of being loved by someone who doesn't know your name, the strange peace of letting go of being remembered correctly. End with quiet wonder, almost laughing through tears, as you realize that maybe love isn't about memory at all—it's about this moment, right now, where they reach for your hand and call you beautiful.

title: The Vindication at the Altar
instruction: You are at a wedding, giving a toast for your daughter, who you raised alone after a bitter divorce. Throughout the speech, you feel a fierce, quiet triumph as you watch everyone—especially your ex—see how strong and happy she is. At the same time, you are completely infatuated with your new partner, who is beaming at you from the crowd, making you blush and lose your train of thought mid-sentence. Start with a trembling, nervous public voice, but let it soften and fill with private pleasure as you glance at them, then crack with raw love as you look at your daughter. Let your voice catch, trail off, and restart as you get lost in both emotions.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Ashes of Your Life's Work
instruction: Your sustainable sanctuary—the permaculture farm you spent thirty years building—has just burned in a climate-fueled wildfire. As you stand in the ashes, you start laughing. Not bitterly, but genuinely, almost hysterically, at the cosmic absurdity of it all. Describe the irony with a smile in your voice: you did everything right, and it didn't matter. But let that laughter gradually blend with tears you can't hold back. Your voice should dance between joy at the beauty you created and grief at its destruction, between pride and profound loss. End in a place of strange peace—you'd do it all again, even knowing this ending, because those thirty years of trying were the most alive you've ever been. Let gratitude and heartbreak be completely intertwined, inseparable, as you find something like acceptance in the ruins.

title: The Last Piece of You
instruction: You are alone in your cluttered garage, after a fight with your late mother's estate lawyer. You've knocked over a box of her old photo albums, and as you lunge to catch it, you trip over a stack of paint cans and fall hard, breaking your arm. You're on the cold concrete floor, stunned. The first thing you feel is confusion — why did you even care about those stupid photos? You were just going to toss them. But now you're here, in pain, and a bitter thought creeps in: even in death, she's taking something from you. Start with a sharp, shocked intake of breath, then let your words come out shaky, still, as you realize you might be stuck for a while.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Bedside Vigil: Watching Someone Choose to Let Go
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has chosen to stop treatment. They're awake, lucid, and you're both watching the morphine drip that will ease their passing. Begin with forced cheerfulness—telling them about the grandchildren, the garden blooming outside. Your voice is bright, almost manic in its determination to be normal. But gradually, the weight of what's happening settles in. Your voice becomes softer, more honest. You begin to thank them for specific memories—their laugh, the way they made coffee, that one terrible joke they told a thousand times. Your gratitude is mixed with the physical sensation of your heart breaking. By the end, you're whispering permission for them to go, your voice cracking not with theatrical tears but with the raw, ugly sound of someone trying to be strong when everything inside them is shattering. You end with 'I love you' said three different ways—each revealing a different layer of your grief and acceptance.
inspired_by: Decompression Ascent from Extreme Depth: The Long Way Up

title: The Silence After the Crash
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy standing in the garage, leaning against the dented hood of your dad's car. You just walked home after the accident, and he's staring at you without a word. Start with a voice that's flat, numb—like you're reciting facts you don't feel. But as you speak, doubt crashes in: your chest tightens, your throat croaks, and you begin to talk faster, nearly pleading, your voice climbing higher. You want him to say anything—blame you, yell, something—because the quiet is worse. Include natural pauses, weight shifts, a moment where you lose your thought, then find it again, increasingly desperate.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Reading a Love Letter While Signing Divorce Papers
instruction: You've found an old letter your spouse wrote you twenty years ago, full of promises and dreams, and you're reading it aloud while sitting at a table with unsigned divorce papers in front of you. Start with a voice that's almost amused, maybe a little bitter: 'Listen to this...' But as you read their younger self's words, let genuine tenderness break through. Your voice should contain both the person who still loves who they were and the person who knows this ending is right. Laugh at the naive hope in the letter, but let that laughter catch in your throat. Include moments where you pause, pen hovering over the signature line, voice soft with something like gratitude: 'We really meant all this.' End with contradictory peace: signing the papers while speaking directly to your younger selves with forgiveness, love, and release. Your final words should carry both goodbye and thank you.
inspired_by: Last Person to Speak a Dying Language

title: The Laughter of Glass
instruction: You're at a house party, deep into a trip. The room pulses with color and sound. You catch your own reflection in a window and remember the old you—the one who covered for a friend while they wrecked your life. Start by staring at how the glass seems to breathe, laughing at its beauty. Then let the memory land: the shame of how weak you were, the anger boiling up, and a thin streak of malice as you whisper to your reflection. Your voice shifts from wonder to a cracked, bitter vow.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Shame (extremely present), Anger (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Folded Note
instruction: You're in your childhood bedroom, kneeling on the thick, carpeted floor beside an old dresser. Your hands are trembling as you hold a note you just found—tucked inside a book from decades ago, from a time you were young and ashamed of what you wanted. At first, your voice is tight with shame, a quiet, hitching whisper as you read the words aloud, almost disbelieving. Then, as you remember the person who wrote it, a slow warmth spreads through you—your breath deepens, your tone softens into a husky, wanting murmur, and your fingers trace the paper as if you can feel them. By the end, your voice is a gritty, breathy confession, the shame melding into a raw, undeniably sexual ache.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Interest (clearly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child before leaving for a dangerous mission you know you might not return from. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them: 'I'll be back before you know it, sweetheart.' But as you look at their face, the façade cracks. Your voice becomes thick with suppressed tears as you try to memorize every detail of them. You want to tell them everything—how to be strong, how much you love them, all the life advice you might never give—but the words catch in your throat. End with a whisper that's half prayer, half promise, your voice breaking as you hold them: 'You are everything good I ever did in this world.' Let the goodbye be both tender and devastating, your heart shattering even as you try to give them strength.

title: Regional Accent Journey
instruction: You're a radio host doing a retrospective on your career, tracing how your accent has shifted. Begin with the thick, distinctive accent of your rural Appalachian hometown — warm, familiar. You describe your first radio audition: 'They said my accent was too strong.' Your voice shifts toward neutral. You describe getting the job in Atlanta: shift further. Then your controversial podcast on racial justice: your accent starts bleeding back through because you're angry, because you're home, because you're real. The story ends with you going back home for your father's funeral, and the accent comes back fully, without effort. By the eulogy, you sound exactly like him. The realization is in your voice — you never left.

title: Bench at Dusk
instruction: You are in your late pregnancy, elderly, sitting heavily on a park bench after walking farther than you should. Your breath is short, your back aches, and you shift uncomfortably every few seconds. You feel the familiar tightness in your chest from the baby pressing up. At first you are just tired, a little resentful of your own body. But then the baby kicks, a soft, rhythmic movement, and you place your hand on your belly. The pressure eases, your breathing slows, and a deep, unexpected relief settles over you. Speak aloud, maybe to yourself or to the life inside you, letting your voice carry that transition from strained exhaustion to quiet, grateful calm. Let your pauses, sighs, and small adjustments be part of the performance.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Parent Navigating Modern Slang
instruction: Portray a parent trying to understand their teenagers slangfilled language. Use a confused tone while attempting to use the slang incorrectly, switching to the teens exasperated responses, highlighting the generational communication gap.

title: Protecting Your Child From Your Parent: Fierce Love Meets Helpless Rage
instruction: Your parent has just criticized your child and something primal ignites in you. You start low and dangerous: 'Don't you DARE speak to them that way.' Your voice is a shield, fierce and protective. The rage builds as you realize you're watching your parent do to your child what they did to you: 'You will NOT make them feel small. Not in my house. Not ever.' You're shaking with the intensity of protecting what you love most. But then the helplessness crashes in—your voice breaks completely: 'Why couldn't you love me like this? Why wasn't I enough?' You're suddenly the hurt child again, voice dissolving into sobs. But through the tears, your resolve returns, quieter but absolute: 'They will never doubt they are loved. I will make sure of it.' By the end, your voice carries both devastation and unshakeable determination.
inspired_by: Estranged Parent Attempting Connection: Awkward Thaw

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After fifteen years of silence, you're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. You start with anger—controlled, cutting, listing all the birthdays they missed, the graduations, the nights you cried. Your voice is sharp, prosecutorial. But as you speak, something shifts. You hear yourself and realize you're not angry anymore—you're the child who needed them. Your voice breaks mid-sentence: 'I needed you to—' and suddenly you're asking the question you've carried for fifteen years: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger collapses into something more devastating. You end not with accusations but with a whispered confession: 'I still look for you in crowds.' Your voice should transform from aggressive accusation to the vulnerable plea of someone who never stopped being that abandoned child.

title: Beside the Hospice Bed at 3 AM
instruction: Your spouse is unconscious, hours or minutes from death. You're alone with them in the quiet dark. You start by whispering practical things—who called, what the kids said, what you had for dinner—your voice tender but steady, filling the silence like you always have. Then you take their hand, and something unlocks. Your voice drops to barely audible: 'I'm so scared. I don't know how to be me without you.' You confess the small, sacred things you never said—how you still get butterflies, how you watch them sleep, how the thought of your own breath continuing without theirs feels impossible. Your words catch and break. You end by singing the song from your wedding, voice fragile and off-key, crying through the melody.

title: The Inheritance of Joy and Ruin
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—perhaps an inheritance from someone who hurt you deeply, or success in a dream you achieved through enormous sacrifice, or becoming a parent while losing your own parent. You are flooded with contradictory emotions that threaten to tear you apart. Begin speaking to someone (present or absent) about this news, and as you do, audibly work through the impossible tangle: the gratitude and the rage, the joy and the grief, the love for what you gained and fury at what it cost. Name the blessings explicitly—the opportunities, the gifts, the new beginnings. But also name the losses, the betrayals, the prices paid. Do not resolve these contradictions; instead, let your voice hold them simultaneously. Laugh through tears, rage through gratitude, celebrate through mourning. By the end, arrive at a place of complex, messy acceptance—where you can acknowledge that life has given you something precious and terrible at the same time, and you will carry both forward.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting by your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He's been unconscious for days, but you take his hand and begin speaking—hesitantly at first, asking permission you never got in life: 'Dad, can I... is it okay if I just say what I need to say?' Your voice is careful, still seeking approval from a dying man. But as you continue, something shifts. You realize he can't say no anymore, can't shut you down, can't walk away. Your words become bolder, rawer, until you're finally speaking with the voice you never had as his child. End with a moment of tender devastation: 'I wish you'd wanted to know me.' Let your voice crack not with anger, but with the grief of a relationship that will never be.

title: The Last Haul of the Day
instruction: You are an elderly fisherman on a pier, facing a powerful gale that rips your words away. You start by shouting with disgust—at the wind, at the sea, at your own tired arms—as you try to convince a younger crew member to abandon a risky final catch. But halfway through, a memory of your own stubborn youth breaks through, and your voice softens into a raw, fragile hope. Let the wind buffet your face, make you turn and gasp between phrases. Your disgust is a bitter shield; your hope is a cracked whisper that grows, fighting to be heard.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Enlightenment Arriving
instruction: A profound truth arrives and suddenly everything makes sense. Your voice becomes very quiet, very clear: 'I understand now.' Not happy-clarity, but the clarity of seeing reality without filters. Breathing becomes slower, deeper. Words come carefully: 'Everything I thought was wrong was based on—' Realization lands. Your voice gains new authority rooted in genuine understanding, not ego. Physical: stillness, groundedness. 'This is why I've suffered. This is what I need to do.' The voice is calm, centered, complete. By the end, you're at peace with hard truth.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Dog at the Vet
instruction: You're in the room and it's time. Talk to your dog the way you always do — 'Who's a good boy?' — but your voice is thick. They don't understand the context; they're just happy you're there. Use the 'pet voice' (high, affectionate, silly) while tears stream. Include stroking sounds. Tell them they were the best thing that ever happened to you. Let the pet voice crack into a real one: a human talking to their dearest friend. The vet says 'It's time.' Your last 'Good boy' should break hearts.

title: The Smallest Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to your partner of many years, and you finally whisper the thing you've never told anyone—a moment of profound shame, a secret that's lived in your body like a stone. Begin barely audible, your body curled small, breathing shallow. You're not performing the confession; you're discovering you can actually say it out loud. Let the physical relief of speaking it start in your chest, your shoulders. Feel how your breathing changes as the words come out. The emotion starts as shame and fear of being seen, but as you speak into the darkness and feel them listening without judgment, let yourself unfold slightly. By the end, you're not smaller but somehow both exposed and safer than you've ever been. Your final words carry a tentative, fragile sense of being held.
inspired_by: An actor is severely blocked — cannot function, cannot feel anything

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect of your childhood, something you've carried silently for decades. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, trying to stay calm and fair. But as you speak, the hurt you've buried erupts. Your voice should tighten, accelerate, become raw as years of longing for their approval, their presence, their love, pour out. Then, mid-fury, you see them—truly see them—small, fragile, incapable of giving what they never received themselves. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it transmutes into something more complex: grief for both of you, rage at the cycle, and an aching, unwanted compassion. End in a whisper, asking a question you both know has no answer.

title: The Last Lesson
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of your grandmother who taught you everything about cooking, gardening, and life's small wisdoms. She's fading, and you desperately want to ask her one more question about something you never understood—but you're ashamed you never learned it, afraid she'll think you weren't listening all these years. Begin with that shame and fear of appearing ignorant. As you speak, let yourself move from hiding behind half-truths to admitting 'I don't know, and I need you to teach me one more time.' End with the relief and grief of being truly seen, even in your gaps of knowledge. Your voice should start tight and guarded, then break open into raw honesty.
inspired_by: Actor feels intellectually insecure or limited

title: The Bittersweet Accounting
instruction: You've just received news that something you've worked toward for years - a dream, a goal, a desperate hope - has finally, miraculously come true. But it arrived too late, or cost too much, or came after someone who should have witnessed it is gone. Speak about this achievement, this blessing, this answered prayer. Begin with pure joy and relief and triumph, really let yourself feel the 'yes' of it. But as you speak, the other truth rises: the grief, the cost, the absence, the complicated mix of gratitude and resentment that it took so long or required so much sacrifice. You're celebrating and mourning simultaneously. Let your voice reflect both the soaring and the breaking, the laughter and the tears, the defiant 'I did it!' and the devastating 'But at what price?' Don't resolve into one emotion - stay in the beautiful, terrible complexity of both.

title: Relationship Ending: Both Relief and Devastation
instruction: Your relationship is ending and you're relieved. But relief doesn't mean no pain. Your voice is complex, carrying both emotions: 'I'm sad. And also... relieved.' You're sitting with that contradiction. Include the moment where you feel guilty for being relieved that you're leaving pain. Your voice almost apologizes for your own relief. Then you acknowledge: staying would have destroyed you both. Your voice becomes more honest: 'We were bad together. I have to go.' It's not dramatic betrayal, just incompatibility that became unbearable. Your voice reflects that quiet heartbreak—you love them and have to leave them anyway. Over time your voice might adjust. But right now it's carrying both the loss and the rightness of the decision simultaneously.

title: Hiding Disappointment When Plans Get Canceled
instruction: An event you looked forward to is canceled, but you act like its no big deal. Internally, youre let down, but you shrug it off. Describe the disappointment inside while appearing unbothered. Speak with a casual tone, downplaying your feelings.

title: The Morning Rush Miracle
instruction: You're an elderly woman who took a little too much of your 'energy supplement' (the doctor warned you). Your granddaughter is late for the bus, and you're convinced you can fix it all if you just talk fast enough. Start with sharp, impatient muttering as you search for her backpack—your jaw is tight, your words clipped and rushed, a dry tongue sticking to your palate. Midway, your tone shifts into a breathless, almost giddy hope as you find the backpack and imagine her making it; by the end, your voice is a pressured, wobbly mix of irritation and fierce, fragile optimism as you shove the bag at her, your words tumbling over each other.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What You Took From Me
instruction: You're confronting your father after decades of silence, and you start with a voice that's eerily calm, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you what it was like. Being your child.' But as you describe the specific moments—the fear, the smallness, the ways you learned to disappear—your voice begins to crack not with tears but with rage. 'I was seven years old. Seven. And I learned to...' The anger builds, volcanic, your words becoming sharper, faster. You're spitting truth like venom. But then something breaks. Mid-sentence, the fury collapses into something raw and young: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why couldn't you just...' Now you're not an adult confronting a parent—you're the child you once were, finally allowed to ask the question you've carried your whole life. The transformation is complete: from controlled anger to primal, childlike devastation. Your voice becomes small, lost, searching for an answer that will never come.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Stole
instruction: You're thirty-five years old, sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced these words for years. You're finally telling her what her drinking did to you, how you raised your younger siblings while she passed out, how you never got to be a child. Your voice is measured, factual, listing memories like evidence. But as she starts to make excuses, something ignites. Your control splinters. The little girl inside you—the one who cleaned up vomit at age nine, who lied to teachers about bruises, who learned to forge permission slips—that girl starts screaming through your adult voice. Your words become jagged, raw, ugly. You're not eloquent anymore. You're wounded and furious and heartbroken all at once. End with the realization, mid-sentence, that she will never apologize, never change, never see you. The rage drains into devastating, quiet acceptance.
inspired_by: Police Officer Pulls Over Her Son Driving Drunk

title: Laughing at the Funeral You Planned Together
instruction: You're at the funeral of your best friend who planned every detail with you during their final months—and insisted it be funny. Start reading their absurd, irreverent eulogy instructions, laughing genuinely at their jokes, their voice so alive in these words. But the laughter keeps breaking into tears, then back to laughter. You're honoring their wish while your heart is shattering. Your voice cracks between chuckles and sobs: 'You absolute bastard, you made me promise to tell the tequila story.' The gratitude for knowing them and the devastation of losing them occupy the same space. End with a laugh that dissolves into weeping, then somehow find yourself genuinely smiling through tears because they knew you'd need permission to feel both.

title: A Love Letter You Can Never Send
instruction: You're whispering to someone who will never hear these words—perhaps they're gone, or they belong to someone else, or you've hidden this love for years. Start by describing how their presence felt like sunlight, speaking so softly it's almost a secret you're telling yourself. Let your voice carry the weight of everything unsaid, tender and aching. As you continue, the grief of never being able to love them openly should catch in your throat, making words nearly impossible. End in near-silence, where the love and the loss are so intertwined that you can barely breathe, and the warmth of the memory becomes painful because it's all you'll ever have.
inspired_by: Feeling the Warmth of a Sunbeam on Your Face

title: The Visored Gaze
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a naturally high, feminine voice, standing in a cold stone corridor with a full medieval helm clamped over your head. Through the narrow eye slit, you watch a younger rival receive the lord’s praise in the courtyard below. Your voice rings with a metallic echo, and each time you shift your weight, the visor clanks. Start with a tight, brittle tone—envy stinging every word as you mutter about her undeserved luck. Let your breath fog the metal, pause to swallow resentment, then slowly let the anger drain into something quieter: a sigh of recognition that your own pride matters more. End with a muffled, almost sad acceptance, the jealousy still present but softened like the ring of metal fading into stone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing at the Funeral
instruction: You are at the funeral of someone who made you promise - made you swear - that you would celebrate, not mourn. So you're trying to tell stories about them, laughing at memories that make your chest ache, your voice bright even as tears stream down your face. Start with forced cheerfulness that sounds almost manic, fulfilling your promise through sheer will. But let the laughter become real even as the grief deepens - you're genuinely amused by who they were, even as you're shattered that they're gone. Your voice should dance between joy and devastation: laughing mid-sentence, then voice breaking, then laughing again through tears. End with profound gratitude for having known them, expressed with a smile in your voice and absolute heartbreak in your breath - thank them for teaching you that grief and joy can occupy the same moment, the same heartbeat.

title: Saying 'I'm Fine' When You're Absolutely Not
instruction: Someone asks if you're okay. Perform the lie: 'Yeah, I'm fine!' with escalating transparency. First attempt is almost convincing. They ask again. Second attempt cracks slightly. Third attempt — your voice breaks on 'fine' and the truth floods out in a rush of suppressed emotion. Show the physical effort of holding back tears: the tight throat, the controlled breathing, the swallowing. The bravery and futility of emotional masking.

title: Bedside Confession: The Last Truth Before Forever
instruction: You're sitting at your dying parent's bedside in the quiet hours before dawn. They've just asked if you're happy, really happy, and suddenly decades of pretending collapse. Start trying to give them the comfort of a lie, but your voice cracks and the truth spills out—about the career you abandoned to meet their expectations, the person you never became, the dreams you buried. Your words come haltingly, fighting against a lifetime of protection and performance. Mid-confession, something shifts: you realize this painful honesty is the greatest gift you can offer before they go. The grief transforms into a strange, fierce gratitude for this final moment of being truly seen. End with a whispered acknowledgment that despite everything, their love shaped you in ways you're only now understanding. Let your voice move from protective brightness to breaking honesty to tearful, tender acceptance.
inspired_by: Confession While High: Watching Your Mouth Betray You

title: The Moment You Realize Your Best Friend is Dying and Won't Admit It
instruction: You're having what seems like a normal conversation with your best friend when suddenly all the pieces click together—the weight loss they've explained away, the canceled plans, the way they're talking about the future in careful terms. Start casual, even laughing, then let your voice shift as realization crashes over you mid-sentence. The rage comes first—how dare they not tell you, how dare they lie—your voice rising, demanding the truth. But the rage immediately collapses into desperate, animal fear because you can't lose them, you're not ready, and you can see the admission in their eyes. Let your voice break completely, cycling rapidly between anger ('Why didn't you tell me?'), bargaining ('We can fix this'), and raw, primal grief. End with fierce, protective desperation—grabbing them (verbally), making them promise to fight, your voice shaking with a combination of love so intense it's almost violence and terror so deep you can barely breathe.
inspired_by: Marathon Runner Hitting the Wall at Mile 22

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're standing face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you twenty years ago. They've reached out, wanting reconciliation. Start cold, controlled: 'You wanted to talk. So talk.' But underneath, there's volcanic rage. As they make excuses, your control splinters. 'Do you have any idea what it was like? I was seven years old.' Your voice climbs, shaking with decades of pain. 'I waited by the window every single day for a year, thinking you'd come back.' Let the anger pour out—accusations, hurt, the child inside you screaming. 'I needed you and you just... left.' But then something shifts. Exhaustion. The futility of it all. Your voice drops to something quieter, more devastated. 'I don't even know why I'm still angry. You're a stranger to me.' A long pause. Then, almost tenderly, with profound sadness: 'I wish I could hate you. That would be easier. But I just... I just feel empty where you should have been.' End with raw honesty: 'I don't think I can forgive you. But maybe someday I can forgive myself for still wanting to.'

title: Flat Gratitude
instruction: You are in a dim, quiet bedroom, lying on your back after taking a tranquilizer. Your body feels heavy, your thoughts slow. A child you care for brings you a cup of tea and sits beside you. You begin by staring at the ceiling, speaking in a low, even monotone, contemplating the strange calm inside you—no edge, no worry. As you speak, you turn your head slightly to look at them, and a distant warmth emerges. Your voice remains flat, but you form words of gratitude, each syllable deliberate, as if reaching through thick cotton. Let your breath be shallow, your lips soft, and let a tiny, barely-there smile flicker at the end.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Sweetness of the Trap
instruction: You are in a small, humming elevator with someone you despise, but your voice is always soft, high, and childlike — a mask. Start by making pleasant small talk, but let the metallic flutter of the space make your tone ring unnaturally. As the elevator rises, let the mechanical hum and the enclosure press on you; your words become slower, more deliberate. The malice seeps in through a smile that doesn't reach your voice — at the end, you lean closer, your hyper-feminine pitch dropping into a cold whisper that thanks them for walking right into this. Let the echo of the steel walls carry your menace.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Static Inside the Light
instruction: You're a 16-year-old in a friend's basement, a few hours into a strong mushroom trip. The music stopped a long time ago. You're staring at a dust mote floating in a beam of light from a dirty window, but what you're actually feeling is a deep, sour bitterness toward your father who left two months ago. Start with your voice thin and wandering, describing the dust like it's the most profound thing you've ever seen. But as you follow it, the thought of him drifts in. Your voice drops, flattens, gets heavy and quiet—the wonder curdles into blunt, raw resentment. Don't perform the emotion; let the altered state make you slip from awe into that hurt without warning. End with a simple, final-sounding statement. Let there be long pauses, shifts in pitch, maybe a bitter half-laugh.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Playground Growl
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy, small for your age, backed against a chain-link fence by a much larger bully. You start by trying to mimic his furious, low growl, but your voice cracks with confusion—you don't fully understand why he hates you. As you speak, you realize a teacher is walking nearby, and relief flickers in your breathing, but it sours quickly because you know the bully will just wait until she's gone. Let your voice drop to the bottom of your range, slow and lazy, but also let the childish pitch slip through. End with a bitter, taste-it-on-your-tongue realization about fairness.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Relief (slightly present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Laughing While Scattering Your Best Friend's Ashes in All the Wrong Places
instruction: You're breaking your best friend's 'tasteful memorial' wishes by scattering their ashes everywhere they actually loved—the dive bar, the ex's garden, the tattoo parlor. Start with rebellious laughter, telling them off for dying, sharing ridiculous memories. But let that laughter crack open into grief you haven't let yourself feel yet. Your voice dances between joy at the memories and the physical ache of their absence. You're celebrating them and saying goodbye simultaneously, finding that love and loss are the same thing. Move from defiant humor to tender gratitude to the kind of crying that sounds almost like laughing. End with a quiet 'thank you for ruining me for boring friendships'—both heartbroken and somehow, impossibly, at peace.
inspired_by: Professional: Activist Must Compromise Their Principles to Save Vulnerable People

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Whisper to your partner as they sleep beside you, believing they can't hear. Start with tender observations—how peaceful they look, how their breathing has become the rhythm of your life. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate as a secret. Then confess what you've been hiding: maybe you're sick and haven't told them, maybe you've been offered a job across the world, maybe you're pregnant and terrified. Let your voice catch and break on the words you can't say in daylight. The confession should feel like it's being pulled from somewhere deep and raw. End with the heartbreaking realization that tomorrow you'll have to say it all again while they're awake, and it will change everything. Your final words—'I don't want to lose this, lose us'—should be spoken through tears you're trying to keep silent, a prayer offered to the darkness.
inspired_by: Coma Visitor: Talking to Someone Who Can't Respond

title: The Last Good Mask
instruction: You are an older man in a hospital recovery room, just two days after a successful surgery. The surgeon told you the tumor was benign. You are alone, wearing a cloth face mask, waiting for the nurse to discharge you. Start by talking to yourself, reliving the moment you got the phone call with the good news—the pure ecstasy that still makes your chest tight. As you speak, notice the sunlight hitting the floor, the slight pain when you shift, the mask making your own breath feel hot. Let that initial wave of ecstasy slowly transform into a quiet, determined hope for the future—the simple things like walking your dog or drinking coffee with friends. You end by promising something to the silence, your voice tired but smiling, the mask pulling at your ears.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Last Morning Coffee: Joy and Goodbye at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're making coffee for someone you love who's leaving forever—emigrating to a place you'll never see them again, or entering hospice, or walking away from your life by choice. Start with the mundane tenderness of knowing exactly how they take their coffee, your voice warm with intimate knowledge: 'Two sugars, right? Like always.' But as you hand it to them, the reality crashes in—this is the last time. Your voice fractures mid-sentence, trying to hold onto the ordinary moment even as it slips away. Let yourself swing between cherishing this simple ritual and the devastating finality of 'last time.' By the end, find a place where the tenderness doesn't erase the grief—your voice carries both the beauty of having loved this person enough to know their coffee order and the unbearable weight of never making it for them again.
inspired_by: Unexpected Laughter After Tragedy: Guilt and Relief Mixed

title: Screaming Into the Storm That Took Him
instruction: You're standing at the edge of the lake where your brother drowned three weeks ago, and the first major storm since that day is rolling in. Begin with the wind picking up, breathing in the charged air before the rain, trying to find that peace and reverence you once felt here. But as the storm intensifies, so does your rage—at the water, at fate, at him for being reckless, at yourself for not being there. Let your voice build from quiet attempts at acceptance into explosive fury, shouting over the wind, demanding answers, screaming his name. Then let that rage shatter completely into broken sobs, your fierce anger collapsing into devastating helplessness. End with your voice raw and small, begging the lake to give him back even though you know it's impossible, your protective instincts still firing uselessly into the storm.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep, Inhaling Breath by a Freshwater Lake

title: Protecting Your Child from a Danger You Cannot Stop
instruction: Something terrible is coming and you cannot prevent it. Begin with fierce, almost violent protectiveness—your voice is a growl, a warning, a shield. 'I won't let anything happen to you. Do you hear me? Nothing.' But as reality crashes in, your certainty crumbles. The fierceness gives way to desperation. Your voice rises, frantic, grasping at solutions that don't exist. Then it breaks completely. The rage collapses into helpless tears. You're begging now, bargaining with fate, your voice raw and shredded. End in a place of shattered whispers—still trying to promise safety, still trying to be strong, but your voice reveals the devastating truth that you are powerless, and that helplessness is tearing you apart.
inspired_by: Discovering a Kink by Accident and Trying to Play It Cool

title: The Unlocked Door
instruction: You are an elderly person alone in your apartment, caught in a sudden panic attack. Your chest is tight, breaths are shallow and rapid, hands tingle. You feel a flicker of disgust at your own helplessness. You drop the phone. Then you hear the front door open—the neighbor you gave a spare key to. Their voice cuts through the spiral. As they kneel beside you, your panic begins to ebb. Speak between gasps, fragmented, high-pitched. Let relief creep in as you realize you're safe. Pour out overwhelming thankfulness, each word a struggle but genuine. Your voice should tremble, catch, and soften as gratitude replaces fear.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Relief (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Silent Parent
instruction: You're finally telling your emotionally distant parent what their silence cost you, but you start measured and controlled—you've rehearsed this. 'I needed you to see me. Just once, to really see me.' Your voice is calm, almost clinical at first, holding years of practiced detachment. But as you speak, something breaks. The hurt underneath surges forward. Your control shatters. 'Why wasn't I enough?' Now you're raw, exposed, voice rising and falling unpredictably. Then—exhaustion. By the end, you're quiet again, but it's different: not controlled, but emptied out. 'I just needed you to love me.' A whisper of surrender, all the fight gone.

title: The Path Through the Pines
instruction: You are a young woman walking slowly along a winding path in a quiet park. Your steps are unhurried, each footfall barely audible on the soft dirt. You just left a conversation that ended with a promise that rang hollow — a friend who was supposed to meet you didn't show, again. Start with disappointment heavy in your chest, your voice carrying a gentle, tired lilt as you mutter to yourself about the wasted effort. As you walk, notice a breeze shift the pine needles overhead, and your focus drifts to the tiny sounds around you. Let a flicker of acceptance rise — you realize you've been here before, and it's okay to let go. End with a quiet, almost amused sigh, your voice softer, resigned but lighter.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Call Home Before Deployment
instruction: You're calling your parent from the military base, 12 hours before deploying to a conflict zone you both know is dangerous. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light—talking about the weather, asking about the garden, anything trivial. But as the silence grows between you both, the façade crumbles. Your voice becomes quieter, more honest. You begin to say the things you've never said—gratitude for small moments, regrets about fights you had, apologies for being distant. End with 'I love you' said in a way you've never said it before, full of everything you can't promise you'll get to say again. Let the emotional dam break slowly, naturally, word by word.

title: The Last Syllable of Her Name
instruction: You're in a quiet coffee shop, seated across from a woman you've been infatuated with for months. Your chronic back pain is a dull throb; each time you lean forward to speak, a small wince escapes, a sharp breath stolen. At first, your voice is tight, careful—you're trying not to let the pain show, but it seeps into your pauses. As you confess that you've memorized the way she says your name, your tone softens into a raw, weary longing. By the end, your words slow, weighted by both the ache in your spine and the ache in your chest, and you end on a sigh that holds hope and exhaustion together.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Truth That Shatters Glass
instruction: You're confronting your mother/father about a betrayal that shaped your entire life - a lie they told, a choice they made, an abandonment you've carried silently for decades. Start cold, controlled, determined to stay composed. But as you speak, let the dam break. Let your voice rise from measured words to shouting, then crack into sobbing, then surge back into furious accusations. Pound the table, pace like a caged animal, let your body express what words can't. Move through layers: cold anger, explosive rage, broken-hearted child, then finally - unexpectedly - a moment where you see them as human and something softens, even as the fury still burns. End in a completely different emotional place than you began, raw and emptied out.

title: The Number Falls Apart
instruction: You are receiving impact play as a form of release, but your mind is heavy with the grief of a recent, quiet loss — a friendship that ended without a fight, just a slow fade. You’ve agreed to this scene to feel something sharp and real. As you’re spanked and asked to count, start by forcing yourself to say the numbers, but each one gets harder. Your doubt creeps in: is this helping or just numbing? By the end, the last number comes out as a sob, the sadness finally breaking through the pretense of control. Your voice should shift from a reluctant, breathy attempt at compliance to a raw, tearful admission that you're not okay — let the sting pull the truth out of you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Perfect Performance
instruction: You're a renowned concert pianist giving your final performance before early-onset dementia takes your ability to play. You begin with absolute confidence, your voice steady as you introduce the piece: 'Tonight, I'll be performing Chopin's Nocturne in E-flat Major.' But midway through your introduction, you forget why this piece matters to you—it was your mother's favorite, played at her funeral. The gap terrifies you. You recover, finding the memory, and as you continue speaking about the music, gratitude floods through you mixed with devastating grief. By the end, you're fighting tears while smiling, knowing this perfect moment of clarity might be your last. Your voice must carry both the pristine professionalism you've maintained for fifty years and the raw, unguarded acknowledgment that you're saying goodbye to yourself.

title: Rage and Helplessness at the Hospital Bedside
instruction: Your partner is in a coma after a preventable accident, and the doctors say there's no hope. Begin fierce, almost violent: 'Don't you dare leave me. Don't you fucking dare.' Your voice is commanding, desperate, as if sheer force of will could bring them back. Grip their hand—beg, demand, rage at them for being so careless. Then sudden collapse: the anger shatters into sobbing helplessness. 'Please. Please wake up.' Your voice becomes small, childlike, utterly lost. Shift again: passionate declaration of everything you never said. 'I love you more than I knew how to say.' But doubt creeps in, voice faltering: 'Did you know that? Did I tell you enough?' End in whispered agony, forehead pressed to their hand: 'I can't do this without you. How do I let you go?' Raw, ugly crying—nothing controlled or pretty.

title: The Bottom Line
instruction: You are an older executive in a boardroom negotiation, but you've had a few too many drinks before this meeting to steady your nerves. You fight to keep your voice low, controlled, and professional—the alpha shield. But as you discuss the final terms, you're speaking across the table to someone you once loved. A wave of longing breaks through: your voice softens, you lose your train of thought for a second, then you catch yourself. Start with clipped, guarded words, let the longing leak in briefly, then pull back to cold business at the end.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Spell That Worked Too Well
instruction: You've just successfully cast the most powerful spell of your life, but it cost you something irreplaceable—perhaps your magic, perhaps your familiar's voice, perhaps your ability to feel wonder. Begin with triumphant laughter that sounds almost manic, congratulating yourself and your familiar with feverish joy. As the familiar tries to respond (their voice faltering, changing, fading), let your celebration crack. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, grateful for the victory while your heart breaks at the price. The familiar attempts their usual sarcasm but can barely speak—make their voice weak, loving, accepting. Your emotions should war with each other: pride and devastation, gratitude and rage, peace and panic, all bleeding together until you don't know if you're celebrating or mourning. End in strange, broken laughter that sounds like grief, thanking them through tears for a gift that cost everything.
inspired_by: The Young Witch and Her Talking Cat

title: The Last Morning Together
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love on their final morning before they leave for a mission they won't return from. You both know this is goodbye, but you're pretending it's just another morning. Start with forced lightness, making plans for a future that won't happen—your voice catching on small details like what you'll cook for dinner next week. As the pretense crumbles, let your voice drop to barely a whisper, confessing everything you've been too afraid to say. The tears come, but so does gratitude—thanking them for every small moment, your voice breaking between laughter at a shared memory and the devastating reality of loss. End with a final whisper of their name, holding both unbearable grief and the profound gift of having loved them at all.

title: The Comeback
instruction: You're in a brutal street fight, pinned on your back, his weight crushing your chest. Each breath is a jagged gasp. Shame coils in your gut as you think, 'This is how it ends? Pathetic.' But then you see it—a shift in his weight, a gap. Hope explodes like light. You speak while fighting to throw him off, voice torn between a shame-tinged mutter and a fierce bark: 'No… not like this. I'm not done.' Let the words punch out with exertion, breathless, but rising in conviction as you start to believe in the comeback. End with a raw, hopeful snarl.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Restraining Order: Fierce Love Meets Necessary Goodbye
instruction: You are delivering a restraining order to someone you still love - a partner whose addiction, rage, or instability has become dangerous. Begin with forced authority, reading the legal language, keeping your voice steady and official. But as they (also you) react - pleading, promising change, breaking down - your professional mask shatters. Rage erupts: all the broken promises, the lies, the times you covered bruises or made excuses, the terror of loving someone who's destroying themselves and taking you with them. Your voice should shake with fury: 'You don't get to do this anymore!' But underneath the anger is devastating grief. Let your voice break from shouting into sobbing - because you DO still love them, and that makes it worse. The explosive emotion collapses into exhausted, helpless tenderness as you whisper the terrible truth: 'I love you enough to save myself. I love you enough to let you go.' They whisper back: 'I know I did this.' And you both sit in the wreckage of love that wasn't enough.
inspired_by: Divorce Mediation: Dividing the Record Collection

title: The Firefly Promise
instruction: You are a little girl, completely worn out after a day of playing outside. You can barely lift your head, and every word feels like it has to be pulled from deep inside. But as you tell your mom about the firefly you caught and then set free, a spark of pure hope lights you up from within. Start with slow, shallow breaths and a voice that sounds like it's running on empty. Let the memory make your voice soften and lift, but never lose the underlying exhaustion — you're smiling through the weariness. End with a quiet, hopeful whisper that asks for a promise.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unanswered Cry
instruction: You are a teenager standing on a wooden crate in a busy park, trying to shout over traffic and chatter. You've been here before—same words, same faces ignoring you. Start in a state of emotional numbness: your voice is flat, repetitive, almost robotic, as if you're reciting a speech you've given a hundred times. Let the strain of projecting without a mic crack your pitch, and let the ambient noise distract you—a siren, a sneer from a passerby. As you continue, the numbness hardens into bitterness; your voice tightens, becomes more percussive, and ends with a raw, jagged edge of accusation. Speak as if you're losing hope but finding fury.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Post-Bath Reverie
instruction: You are a teenage girl, just out of a long, hot bath. Your body is utterly limp, wrapped in a towel, lying on your bed. The steam still clings to you, and your mind moves slowly. Start by trying to recall something—maybe a dream or a homework detail—but your thoughts are slippery like soap. Let your voice be loose, with a lazy, breathy warmth. As you speak, you slowly realize you don’t actually care to remember; the confusion melts into a quiet, satisfied peace. Swallow, shift your neck, maybe yawn mid-sentence. End with a soft, almost surprised sigh of contentment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face to face with the parent who abandoned you years ago. They want forgiveness, reconciliation. Start angry—your voice sharp, accusing: 'You don't get to do this. You don't get to just come back.' List what you lost, what you needed. But as you speak, something shifts. The anger cracks and underneath is the child who waited by the window. Your voice breaks: 'I needed you. I was seven years old and I needed you.' Let yourself oscillate between rage and grief. By the end, you're exhausted, voice raw and quiet: 'I don't know if I can forgive you. But I'm so tired of hating you.' It's not resolution—it's honest, messy, real.
inspired_by: Someone Telling You They Love You for First Time

title: Falling Through Ice: Cold Shock and Survival Instinct Battling Panic
instruction: You fall through ice into water so cold it immediately hijacks your nervous system. Your voice is an involuntary gasp, almost a scream, as cold shock kicks in and you can't control your breathing. Your narration is barely coherent: you're physically gasping between words, panic and survival instinct making you nearly mute. Include the moment you force yourself to think despite the overwhelming sensation. Your voice becomes almost mechanical, training overriding panic: 'Get to the edge. Hands up. Kick.' But these words come with tremendous effort and visible panic underneath. Your breath is visible in the cold air, and your narration is becoming desperate as hypothermia begins. You're running out of time and your voice knows it. Each word is weighted with the understanding that you might not survive the next minute.

title: The Lost Child
instruction: You are a mother at a crowded fair, shouting across the grounds for your child who wandered away. With your voice forced to carry over noise, elongate vowels and drop consonants—each phrase a long, aching call. Start with raw, desperate sadness, your voice cracking and trembling between pauses. As you finally see the child in the distance, the sadness transforms into a breathless, tearful relief—still loud, but now softer, filled with love and gratitude. Let the sounds of the crowd and your own heavy breathing interrupt your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Adapting to Microgravity: Wonder Breaking Through Disorientation
instruction: You're in zero gravity for the first time and your voice is struggling, disoriented, almost nauseous in tone. 'Everything is... I can't... my stomach.' You're being physically hijacked by space sickness. But your voice also carries this edge of wonder underneath the suffering. 'It's also... I'm floating. Actually floating.' Include the moment where the sickness subsides and the wonder takes over. Your voice becomes almost childlike, excited, describing things that defy your ground-based understanding. 'The water forms perfect spheres. How is that possible?' Your voice shifts from survival mode to genuine awe. You're narrating something that's literally impossible based on your previous experience, and your voice carries the joy of having your understanding of the world fundamentally expanded. Fear and wonder coexist in every word.

title: The Birthday Card to the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're writing a birthday card to a parent - and for once, you're telling the whole truth. Start with the conventional opening: 'Happy birthday, I hope you have a wonderful—' But then stop. Cross it out. Start again with what you really want to say. 'Thank you for missing every...' The tone shifts between bitter sarcasm, barely contained rage, desperate longing, and heartbreaking vulnerability. You find yourself writing what you needed to hear as a child, then furiously crossing it out. Your voice should crack between anger and tears. Include moments where you almost apologize for being honest, then catch yourself. By the end, you're no longer writing to them - you're speaking to the child you were, acknowledging the pain they never saw. The final words should be quiet, exhausted, but somehow liberating. You've finally said it.
inspired_by: The Most Passive-Aggressive Thank You Card

title: Glitter and Static
instruction: You're at a crowded party, high on a strong stimulant. Your nose is stuffed, your throat numb. You're talking to someone you've been longing to be close to, but the drug makes you feel both invincible and hollow. Start by speaking too fast and too loud, bragging about your night with a forced brightness, interrupting yourself to sniff. Let the energy shift as a wave of numbness gives way to raw longing—your volume drops, your pace slows, and you admit, almost in a whisper, that you just want them to stay. End quieter, more fragile, than you began.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth they've avoided for decades. Start controlled, measured, almost businesslike: 'I need to say something I should have said years ago.' You've rehearsed this. But as you speak—'You were never there'—anger seeps through. Your voice tightens, rises. 'I needed you and you chose everything else.' The rage builds, becomes pointed: 'Do you even know who I am?' Then something breaks. The anger collapses into the vulnerable child underneath: 'I just wanted you to see me.' Your voice becomes small, aching. 'I'm still waiting for you to see me.' End in quiet devastation, with a realization that transforms you: 'But I can't wait anymore.' The journey moves from controlled confrontation through fury into heartbreak, then to painful liberation.

title: The Letting Go
instruction: You are in a deep meditative trance, sitting cross-legged on a cushion in a dimly lit room. Your voice is soft, slow, and perfectly controlled—each word placed like a pebble into still water. You begin with a quiet disappointment about a relationship you ended, but as you breathe and drift, a light intoxication from the relaxed state takes over. Let your words become dreamier, more curious, as if you are discovering the emotion from a distance. Speak to yourself, with tiny pauses, a sigh, a slight shift of weight, as you feel the disappointment melting into a hazy, altered peace. 'I thought I'd feel heavier... but instead I'm floating. That ache is still there, somewhere below my ribs. But it's soft now. Like a bruise I'm not pressing. I don't have to hold it. I can just... watch it breathe.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers
instruction: You are in the middle of an intensely physical experience—making love, in a rage, dancing wildly, or experiencing severe pain—when suddenly your body triggers an overwhelming emotional memory. Begin fully immersed in the physical sensation, breathing hard, alive in your body. Then let a wave of unexpected emotion crash through you: grief, terror, shame, or sudden joy. Don't fight it—let your voice and body express both the physical intensity and the emotional flashback simultaneously. Speak or cry out as you realize what this physical sensation is connected to in your past—what old wound, what forgotten moment. Move from pure physicality through confusion to emotional breakthrough, ending in a place where past and present merge.
inspired_by: Sharing Monologues Identifying Origin of Obstacle

title: The Broken Promise
instruction: You are a former drill sergeant, now elderly, crouched in the corner of a dusty garage after a phone call with your estranged daughter. Your body is tight, knees to chest, voice compressed from the position and shame. You whisper to yourself, replaying the conversation, your voice cracking with the weight of regret. At first, you mutter self-blame, but as you continue, you shift to a faint, fragile hope that you might fix things. Your breathing is shallow, your voice hushed, and you occasionally pause to swallow or wipe your eyes. Speak as if every word costs you something.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Lie That Shaped Your Life
instruction: You've just discovered a truth your parent hid for decades—an adoption, a sibling who died, a choice that changed everything. Start controlled, almost eerily calm: 'I found the letters. I know now.' Your voice is measured, but there's danger underneath. As they try to explain or deflect, your anger builds like a wave. 'Don't. Don't you dare tell me it was for my own good.' Let your voice become fierce, accusing, years of confusion suddenly having a target. But then something shifts—you see them as fragile, human, flawed. Your voice breaks into something more complex: angry tears, furious grief. 'You robbed me of the truth. And I still love you. And I hate that I love you.' End with your voice raw and exhausted, expressing both rage and devastating tenderness in the same breath. You're destroying and rebuilding your relationship simultaneously.
inspired_by: Small Explosion at Work: Checking Colleagues for Injuries

title: Aftercare Praise
instruction: You're a teenage submissive in an intimate power exchange scene, now in aftercare. Your partner, the dominant, is gently stroking your hair and praising you, saying how proud they are of how you trusted them. At first, your voice is breathy and hesitant, with a slight tremble from the intensity you just experienced—each word rises uncertainly, as if testing safety. But as you let the praise sink in, your voice deepens and slows, losing its question marks. You shift your weight, blink away tears, and finally let out a soft, grounded sigh. Your last words are low, warm, utterly still—not seeking approval, simply resting in the truth of contentment.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inappropriate Truth
instruction: You're confronting your mother at a family funeral - your father's funeral. She's putting on her perfect grieving widow act, and something about her performance makes you want to laugh at the absurdity of it all, at years of her pretending, at the ridiculousness of keeping up appearances even now. Start with bitter, quiet restraint, fighting the urge to laugh in her face at the tragedy of your family's fakeness. Let it build into a confrontation where your laughter becomes angry, mocking, cruel - you're laughing at her, at yourself, at the waste of it all. End in a devastating place where the laughter dies in your throat and transforms into raw grief - not for your father, but for the relationship with your mother that never was and never will be.
inspired_by: Suppressing Laughter During a Serious Moment

title: The Moment They Remember You: A Fleeting Window of Recognition
instruction: Your parent with dementia has barely recognized you for months. Then, unexpectedly, during a quiet afternoon, they look at you and say your childhood nickname—the one only they ever used. Your voice catches. You whisper, almost afraid to breathe, 'Mom? Do you know who I am?' They smile, completely present, and for thirty seconds, they're back. Your voice is tender, urgent, trying to fit a lifetime of 'I love you' into this fragile window. You tell them things you've needed to say, your words tumbling out softly, desperately. Then you see the fog returning to their eyes.
