You begin your final transmission to Mission Control with procedural calm, reporting technical failures with the discipline of years of training. But as you accept there's no solution, your voice softens—you ask them to tell your daughter something. The professional veneer cracks as you try to find words that will matter across the void of her growing up without you. Your voice moves from controlled reportage to something raw and essential, a parent reaching across death itself. End not with fear, but with a kind of wonder at the stars, at having lived at all. Let us hear the exact moment training becomes useless and all that's left is love.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has hours left to live. At first, you're desperately trying to be strong, keeping your voice steady, talking about practical things—medications, who called, what the nurse said. But as you hold their hand and really look at their face, something shifts. Let yourself see not just who they are now, but flash through specific memories: their laugh at your wedding, the way they looked when you were seven, how their voice sounded calling your name. Allow these memories to flood through you until you can no longer maintain the practical facade. Your voice should break from controlled strength into raw, tender goodbye. By the end, you're no longer trying to be strong—you're simply present with them, whispering the truths you've never said, your voice intimate and broken and full of love.

title: The Weight of Age
instruction: You're lying in bed, still catching your breath, the sheets tangled around you. Your partner is beside you, their head on your chest. You feel a surge of infatuation as you watch them drift off — your voice is dreamy, full of vocal fry, barely above a whisper. But then a thought cuts through: you're an older man, you shouldn't be here, you're too old for this. Shame tightens your throat, makes you pause mid-sentence. Then you breathe out a wry chuckle, amused at yourself for ruining such a perfect moment with your own insecurities. Let your voice shift from warm and unguarded to a cracked, self-mocking whisper, finishing with a soft, rueful laugh.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Shame (extremely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing and Weeping at Your Own Emotional Inheritance
instruction: You're talking to a therapist, friend, or journal—recounting a moment where you caught yourself being exactly like your emotionally distant parent. Start with bitter, dark laughter in your voice. It's absurd, isn't it? You swore you'd never be like them. Your laughter has an edge of hysteria. But as you talk, your voice starts breaking between the laughs. You're describing how you shut someone out and there's something simultaneously funny and devastating about the precision with which you replicated your parent's moves. Your voice wavers between laughing and crying—sometimes both at once. There's strange gratitude mixed in: you're finally understanding why your parent was the way they were, feeling compassion for their pain even as you grieve your own childhood. Move through contradictory waves: laughing at the cosmic joke of inheritance, crying over lost years, finding weird peace in understanding the pattern, getting angry all over again, then settling into something like acceptance. End with your voice soft, tear-streaked but almost serene: you can see the cage you were raised in, and maybe that means you can find the door.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Like Your Emotionally Distant Parent

title: Sci-Fi: Explorer Discovers Humanity Was Seeded by Alien Civilization
instruction: Reading ancient text, your explorer voice becomes uncertain. Humanity isn't native—we were created. Your voice is wonder and identity collapse simultaneously. You're learning you're not who you thought you were. Your breathing becomes existential—you're processing that human civilization is someone else's garden. Your voice is the sound of recognizing your species as creation rather than originators. Your voice becomes both humble and devastated. Everything changes with this knowledge. Your voice reflects someone fundamentally altered by understanding your own unreality.

title: The Familiar Stranger
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman taking a slow, aimless stroll through a quiet park on a mild afternoon. You feel a gentle contentment, barely aware of the soft rhythm of your footsteps and the slight bounce in your voice as you mutter to yourself about the nice weather. Then you spot someone you think you recognize—a neighbor, maybe—but they’re doing something odd, like talking to a tree. Your confusion flares intensely; you stop, frown, and your voice becomes a puzzled, rambling murmur. As you watch longer, a cold sliver of malevolence seeps in—you realize they’ve been watching your house, and your tone hardens with a quiet, threatening edge. Speak these thoughts naturally, pausing to look around, adjusting your pace, and letting your voice shift from light to uncertain to quietly venomous.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Secret Language of Your Hands
instruction: Whisper to your sleeping lover about everything you've learned by watching them when they don't know you're looking. Describe in intimate detail how they touch their neck when anxious, the way their left eye twitches when they're lying about being okay, how they fold inward when hurt but stand at full height when defending someone else. Reveal that you've been studying them like a sacred text, learning to read their silence. Start tender and marveling, cataloguing these observations like love poems. Then let your voice crack as you confess the heartbreaking deduction you've made: that they're preparing to leave you. All these small behaviors you've memorized point to someone slowly detaching, gathering courage. Beg them, still asleep and unhearing, to prove your observations wrong. End devastated, your detective work revealing the loss you can't prevent.

title: Whispering Through the Wall
instruction: You're speaking to your partner through a quarantine barrier—they're dying on the other side, you can't touch them, and these are your final words. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, tender and intimate, as if you're lying in bed together like always. Share a tiny, private memory—the way they laugh at their own jokes, how they hog the blankets. Your throat tightens. You want to be brave for them, keep your voice steady and loving. But the reality keeps crushing in: you'll never touch them again. Your whisper becomes fractured, thick with tears you're trying not to shed. Tell them it's okay to let go, even though it's destroying you. End with 'I love you' said so quietly it's almost just breath, because you're trying to pour your entire heart into three words that will never be enough.

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning: Adult Daughter Confronts Mother About the Childhood That Shaped Her
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally speaking truths you've carried for thirty years. Start with restraint, almost gentle—'Mom, I need you to hear something.' But as you speak, decades of unmet needs surface. Your voice hardens with anger: 'I needed you to see me, not who you wanted me to be.' Then it fractures into the voice of the child you were, small and pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Move through righteous rage into something more vulnerable—the ache of still wanting her approval even now. End in a place of exhausted honesty, where anger and love exist simultaneously. 'I'm here because I still hope... but I can't keep breaking myself open waiting.' Let your voice carry both fury and the tender wound beneath it.
inspired_by: Sitting in Silence After Miscarriage: The Weight of Emptiness

title: The Hopeful Failure
instruction: You are a teenage squad leader in a junior ROTC drill, barking commands at a new recruit who just can't get it right. Start with sharp, clipped impatience — you're annoyed but still trying to correct him. Midway, you see him flub the same move again, and your voice tightens with contempt, words cutting shorter as you dismiss him with a cold, quiet final order. Let your body shift: a hard sigh, a roll of your eyes, a glance at your watch. End with a sneer in your throat, volume dropping but venom rising.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Contempt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent - someone who abandoned you, or was emotionally absent, or chose addiction or another family over you. You begin with controlled anger, your voice tight and measured as you list the moments they missed: birthdays, graduations, the times you needed them. Your voice is sharp, prosecutorial. But as you speak, the anger begins to crack and underneath is the wounded child. Your voice wavers as you ask the questions you've carried for years: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me?' You're trying to stay strong, but you're collapsing into the grief of it. Then something shifts - maybe they reach for you, maybe they stay silent - and you have to decide whether to soften or harden. End with either a whispered, exhausted 'I needed you' or a firm, self-protective 'I don't need you anymore.' The journey moves from righteous anger through devastating vulnerability to a crucial choice.
inspired_by: Tripping and Falling at a Wedding

title: The Last Crusade
instruction: You are a dying activist lying in a hospital bed, visited by your estranged adult child who never understood your life's work. You have minutes left, and you need them to understand why you sacrificed so much family time for your cause—environmental protection, human rights, whatever burned in your soul. Start weak, struggling to speak, perhaps ashamed of your absences. But as you speak about what you fought for, let the old fire return one last time. Your voice may grow stronger, your eyes brighter, as the passion that defined your life floods back. Then, as you see understanding finally dawn in their eyes, let that fire soften into peace, into gratitude that you've been heard. End in quiet acceptance, perhaps even joy, as you take your final breaths knowing you've been understood at last.

title: The Jack Failed
instruction: You're a young guy with a deep voice, working on your truck under the afternoon sun. You feel content — just tightened the last bolt, humming a little. Then the jack slips. The truck crashes down, the frame slams into your ribs. A sharp 'oof' gets knocked out of you. You double over, gasping, breath shallow and shaky. You try to speak: fear floods in as you check if you're pinned, and you're irritated at yourself for being so careless. Your voice is tight, clipped, with a pained rasp. Words come out in broken spurts.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (extremely present), Fear (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Goodbye at the Station Platform
instruction: Your child is boarding a ship for a colony mission to Mars—a one-way journey they'll never return from. You have three minutes before they board. Start with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them: 'This is exciting, isn't it?' Your voice is too cheerful, brittle with the effort of not breaking. As seconds tick away, the mask crumbles. Your words become desperate attempts to memorize them: 'Let me look at you one more time.' The brightness dissolves into raw pleading—you're bargaining with time itself, with fate, asking them to stay even though you know they can't. Your voice fractures between pride in their courage and the unbearable weight of never holding them again. End in a whisper that contains your whole heart: 'I'll look for your star every night.' You're trying to smile through tears that won't stop.

title: The Last Visit to Mother
instruction: You're sitting at your dying mother's bedside in hospice, and she's just told you she's proud of you—but you know she never really saw you. Start with controlled gratitude, your voice steady: 'Thank you, Mom. That means everything.' But as you continue, the truth begins to crack through: 'I spent thirty years trying to become who you wanted... and I still don't know who I am.' Your voice trembles now, not with anger but with the devastating realization of time lost. You reach for her hand: 'I'm not angry anymore. I'm just... I wish we'd had more time to know each other.' End with your voice breaking into tenderness mixed with profound grief: 'I love you. I always loved you. Even when you couldn't see me.' This isn't about forgiveness or blame—it's about accepting that some distances can never be crossed, and loving anyway.

title: Baby's Not Sleeping
instruction: You're a 17-year-old babysitter, alone with a crying infant at 11 PM. You've tried everything—rocking, singing, shushing—but the baby is still wailing. Start with forced, high-pitched parentese, voice bright and singsong, but your jaw is tight and your eyes are tired. Let the irritation seep through in clipped vowels and slightly faster pace. Then, as you hold the baby closer, your anger softens into weary tenderness. Your pitch stays high, but the tempo slows, and your voice cracks with exhaustion. Speak to the baby, coaxing, scolding, then pleading, as you shift from 'Why won't you stop?' to 'It's okay, I've got you.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Holding Your Child as Danger Approaches
instruction: You're barricaded somewhere with your child, danger closing in, and you need to keep them calm while you're falling apart inside. Start fierce and protective—your voice strong, reassuring, making promises you don't know you can keep. But as sounds grow closer, your control begins to fracture. Your words come faster, more desperate, trying to distract them with stories, songs, anything. Your voice cracks on their name. Suddenly rage erupts—furious at the world, at yourself for not protecting them better—but you have to choke it back down because they're looking at you with trusting eyes. Your ferocity dissolves into broken tenderness as you hold them close, whispering that you love them, that everything you've ever done was for them. End with a voice shattered between protective strength and absolute helplessness, trying to be their shield even as you're breaking.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She has hours, maybe minutes left. Begin by noticing everything about this moment—the way the early light falls across her hands, the particular scent of her skin mixed with hospital antiseptic, the weight of her fingers in yours, the sound of her breathing. Start feeling numb, protective, trying to memorize her. As you speak your goodbye, let yourself move from that careful control into the full weight of losing her—the reality that this exact person, with her specific laugh and the way she used to hum while cooking, will never exist again. Let your voice break not with generic sadness but with the specific loss of HER. End in a place of devastating tenderness, where love and grief are indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Sense Memory with Emotionally Impacting Objects

title: Protecting a Child from Your Own Breaking Heart
instruction: You've just received devastating news (a terminal diagnosis, a death in the family, an irreversible loss) but your child is about to walk into the room, and you cannot let them see you fall apart. Begin with barely-contained panic—you're pacing, hyperventilating, trying to get control before they arrive. When they enter, your voice must instantly shift to false calm, answering their innocent questions with manufactured cheerfulness. But the mask keeps slipping—your voice cracks, your breathing hitches, you have to turn away. The scene should oscillate between explosive grief when you think they're not looking and fierce, protective tenderness when addressing them. End with the heartbreaking effort of singing them a lullaby or comforting them while your own world is ending, your voice breaking on every third word.
inspired_by: Hiding Pain While Recovering From an Injury

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child Through the Fog
instruction: It's 3am. You're standing in your child's doorway, watching them sleep. Your voice is barely audible, thick with that same heavy depression—words come slowly, each one requiring monumental effort. You're confessing to this sleeping child that you're failing them. 'I'm sorry I couldn't get out of bed today. I'm sorry dinner was cereal again.' Your whisper is gray, flat, suffocated. But then something tender cracks through—watching their peaceful breathing, their small hand curled under their cheek. Your voice catches. Love seeps into the exhaustion, not erasing it but coexisting with it. 'You deserve so much better than this version of me. But I'm trying. I promise I'm trying.' End with your voice breaking on a whispered 'I love you' that carries both devastating inadequacy and fierce, protective devotion. The emotion is quiet, intimate, achingly real—the kind that catches in your throat.

title: The Last Day in the House
instruction: You are walking through the home where you experienced both your greatest happiness and your deepest trauma, knowing you will never return. Begin by speaking to the rooms themselves, thanking them - your voice steady, almost ceremonial. But as you move from room to room, the memories flood back: the good ones that make you smile through tears, and the unbearable ones that you survived here. Feel gratitude for the shelter this place gave you, rage at what happened within these walls, grief for what you're leaving behind, and relief that you're finally free. By the end, stand at the threshold looking back one final time, and let all of it exist at once - the love and the horror, the gratitude and the goodbye. Your voice should carry the full complexity of closing a chapter that both saved and scarred you.
inspired_by: When an actor has suffered trauma before pursuing acting

title: Frozen Discovery
instruction: You are a child lost in a blizzard, bare hands shoved under your arms, teeth chattering so hard you can barely speak. Your whole body shakes violently as you huddle against a frozen fence. You're terrified, alone, and the cold is making you panic. But then, through the snow, you see something strange—a faint glowing object half-buried in the ice. Your distress is still raw in your voice, but a tiny spark of interest begins to creep in, making your words stutter differently as you lean forward, squinting, still shivering. Let your voice tremble from the cold first, then let a hesitant, curious tone break through the chatter.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After fifteen years of silence, you're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. Start with controlled anger, voice tight and clipped: 'You don't get to just walk back in.' List what you missed—birthdays, graduations, the night you were hospitalized. Your anger should be righteous and clear. But as you speak, something shifts. You hear yourself and realize you sound like a child still waiting. Your voice cracks, anger dissolving into the grief underneath. Move from accusation to raw vulnerability, ending with the question you've never let yourself ask: 'Why wasn't I enough to stay for?' Let your voice be small, stripped of all defenses.
inspired_by: Your Rival Becoming Your Only Emotional Support

title: Confronting Your Mother in Her Wedding Dress
instruction: Your mother is getting ready for her fourth wedding, and you finally break—telling her how every marriage, every new 'father figure,' every time she chose a man over your stability, carved something out of you. Start with measured control, trying to be the adult, trying to be fair. But as you list each specific memory—the packed suitcases, the late-night arguments you pretended not to hear, the way she'd become a stranger with each new relationship—let your voice crack with the child still inside you. End not with anger but with exhausted longing: underneath everything, you just needed her to choose you once. Let rage dissolve into the raw vulnerability of still wanting your mother's love.

title: Bedside Vigil—The Unsaid Things
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's slipping away, and they can still hear you. This isn't a grand goodbye—it's three in the morning, just you and the sound of their breathing. Start by talking about small things, your voice soft, almost conversational: 'Remember that terrible restaurant we loved? They finally closed down.' You're filling the silence because silence means accepting this is real. But gradually, the trivial details give way to the things you never said. Your voice becomes tender, catching on words: 'I never told you how scared I was when...' or 'You made me believe I could be...' The emotion builds not through volume but through the weight of each word, the way your breath hitches between sentences. End with the simplest truth, whispered like a secret: 'I'm not ready.' Let the silence after say everything else.

title: The Serpent's Kiss
instruction: You've been captured and dosed with a hallucinogenic compound that twists every wound into vivid, crawling visions. The pain is real, but your mind swims between a fever dream and shattered awareness. Start in a haze of drugged detachment, whispering to the shadows as if they're old friends, then let a fresh wave of agony shatter that calm into raw, guttural screams that dissolve into sobs. Between breaths, you forget where you are, giggle weakly at a nonexistent joke, then fall into hoarse, breathy pleas. End with your voice barely a rasp, talking to a memory of your mother as the drug pulls you under.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Receiving the Impossible News
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a miracle you'd given up on (a loved one survived, your child is coming home, you're finally free of something). Begin by acknowledging the paralysis, the inability to feel what you 'should' feel: 'I can't breathe,' 'I don't trust this,' 'I'm afraid to be happy,' 'I'm angry it took so long,' 'Why can't I cry?' Speak aloud the war inside you—the joy fighting with the grief of all the years you lost, the gratitude tangled with resentment, the hope you're terrified to feel. Name each contradictory emotion as it surfaces, letting them coexist without resolving them. As you continue, stop trying to force yourself to feel the 'right' way. Let the laughter and tears come in whatever order they arrive. Transform from someone torn apart by conflicting feelings to someone who can hold all of it at once—the relief and the rage, the happiness and the devastating awareness of time you'll never get back. End in a complex, full-hearted state where joy and sorrow live side by side.

title: Herding People to Basement Safety While Tornado Sirens Wail
instruction: You're yelling commands, your voice commanding and urgent as you herd neighbors into the basement. But there's your elderly neighbor who refuses to move, and you have to physically guide them while keeping everyone calm. Your voice alternates between stern authority—'Move NOW!'—and gentleness—'I've got you, just step down.' The sirens are deafening. Your voice becomes almost primal as you count heads, trying to be heard. Include the moment the tornado passes directly overhead and the power goes out. Your voice becomes the only thing in the darkness, shaking but steady, telling everyone they're okay. They might not be. You don't know yet.

title: The Pregnancy Test
instruction: You're staring at a positive pregnancy test, and you feel everything at once: terror and wonder, joy and grief, excitement and dread. Begin trying to land on one feeling, searching for the 'right' reaction, your breath caught in your throat. But multiple truths keep surfacing, contradicting each other. Start acknowledging aloud each feeling as it comes, even when they clash ('I'm terrified,' 'This is a miracle,' 'I'm not ready,' 'I've never felt more alive,' 'I want to run,' 'I'm so grateful I could sob'). Don't try to resolve the contradictions or decide how you 'should' feel—let the mess of it exist. By the end, through accepting that you contain multitudes in this moment, arrive at a complex, deeply human truth: you can hold all of it, the impossible tangle of hope and fear, loss and gain, ending and beginning.
inspired_by: Actor resists or fights against their feeling of tension or self-consciousness, making it worse

title: The Hollow Proclamation
instruction: You are a teenage town crier in a medieval village, forced to announce that the long-awaited trade caravan has been destroyed by a plague, leaving your community without food for winter. You begin with your practiced, authoritative cry, pushing your voice to carry across the square, but the weight of your own failure — you'd promised the children treats — makes your consonants stumble and your vowels stretch too long. As you continue, a wave of bitterness and fear for your family's survival cracks your tone, and you cut off mid-sentence, swallowing hard before forcing the final words out with a broken, elongated syllable. Let each pause be real: cough into your fist, glance at the ground, let the wind snatch part of your cry, and end with a voice that has sunk into quiet devastation, trailing off into silence.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Disappointment (extremely present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Touch in the Darkness
instruction: Late at night, you're sitting in complete darkness with someone you've loved silently for years, and they've just told you they're moving across the world tomorrow. You can't see them. You can only feel - the texture of the couch beneath you, the air between your bodies, the warmth radiating from their presence inches away. Begin by whispering about inconsequential things, your voice steady, as your hands rest separately in your laps. But slowly, let your awareness of their physical proximity - the sound of their breathing, the almost-touch of their sleeve near yours, the heat of their body - become unbearable. Your whispered words start to falter as sensation overwhelms you. Finally, in the darkness, your hand finds theirs. The texture of their skin, the way their fingers respond, the pulse you can feel in their wrist - let this single touch release everything you've never said. Move from careful distance to whispered confession to touch-drunk vulnerability.

title: Fury Giving Way to Devastation
instruction: You've just discovered the ultimate betrayal and you explode. Start with volcanic rage - voice loud, sharp, words tumbling over each other: 'How COULD you? After everything I sacrificed, everything I gave up, you just—' You're pacing, gesturing, voice cracking with the force of your fury. But mid-tirade, something shifts. A detail catches you. A memory surfaces. The anger suddenly collapses into something more terrifying - the realization that you saw the signs and ignored them, that part of you knew all along. Your voice drops, becomes hollow. The fight drains out completely. You end up on the floor, voice barely working, all that rage transformed into quiet, devastating heartbreak: 'I knew. God help me, I knew and I stayed anyway.' The last words are almost inaudible.

title: Confession in the Half-Light
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone you love, and you're about to tell them a truth that might end everything. Begin with your voice barely audible, throat tight, testing the waters with small words. There's a long pause where you almost lose courage. Your breathing is uneven. Start to confess something you've carried alone - a fear, a betrayal, a part of yourself you've hidden. Your voice is fragile, catching on words, each sentence feeling like stepping onto ice that might crack. As you speak, tears thicken your words until you can barely get them out. You're not asking for forgiveness - you're just too tired to hide anymore. The silence after you finish is devastating. End with a whispered question, so quiet it's almost not said at all, asking if they're still there, if you're still loved, your voice carrying the weight of someone who's just laid down their last defense.

title: Holding Your Stillborn Baby and Rage-Screaming at God
instruction: You're holding your baby who will never breathe and something inside you detonates. Start with fierce, protective tenderness—introducing yourself, telling them how wanted they were. Then let rage erupt: at God, at biology, at the cruelty of hope. Your voice becomes feral, guttural, a howl of maternal fury that collapses into sobbing. You're simultaneously cherishing every second with this tiny body and demanding to know why. Move from explosive anger to exhausted, whispering prayers to a God you're not sure you believe in anymore. End with a lullaby, sung through tears, your voice breaking on every note—both a goodbye and a promise to remember.
inspired_by: Professional: Activist Must Compromise Their Principles to Save Vulnerable People

title: The Corner That Remembers
instruction: You are an older woman with a hyper-feminized voice, standing on a bustling city street corner. At first, you feel a hot, proud burn in your chest as you see the old theater where your mother once danced—your voice is sharp and loud, competing with traffic horns and a distant siren. Midway, a sudden jackhammer shatters your memory, and you flinch, trailing off in astonishment at how the city has changed. As the noise fades, your pride falters into a softer, puzzled tenderness, your voice dropping as you murmur to yourself about time's cruel hurry. Speak as though the street is pushing back at you—your words punched out, then drifting into a sigh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Visit to Grandma's Porch
instruction: You're sitting on your grandmother's porch for the final time before the house is sold. She passed away three months ago. Begin by noticing everything exactly as it was: the creak of the rocking chair, the smell of honeysuckle, the way afternoon light hits the floorboards, the chipped paint on the railing where you used to sit as a child. Let yourself remember a specific summer day when you were seven, playing here, feeling completely safe and free. Start with quiet observation and gentle nostalgia, but as the memories flood back—her laugh, her hands, the games you played, the secrets you told her here—allow whatever emotions arise to overwhelm you. End in a place of raw goodbye, speaking to her as if she can hear you, telling her what this place meant, what she meant. Let your voice break. Let the farewell be messy and real.

title: Ten Things I Should Have Said
instruction: You're confronting your father who's about to walk out of your life for good, standing in a doorway with his suitcase already in hand. You have exactly ten truths you need to speak—things you've rehearsed silently for years but never had the courage to say. Start with controlled anger, delivering the first few accusations like bullets you've polished in your mind. But as you continue, your carefully prepared words begin to crumble. By the fifth or sixth truth, you're no longer attacking—you're pleading, revealing the hurt child beneath the angry adult. End with the final truth being something you didn't plan to say at all, a vulnerable confession that transforms your rage into an aching need for him to stay, even though you both know he won't.
inspired_by: When memorizing a large amount of material in a short time under production pressure

title: Teaching a Parrot to Say 'I Love You'
instruction: Repeat 'I love you' dozens of times with different inflections, trying to get a parrot to mimic it. Start patient and sweet. Then bribe with crackers (crunching sounds). Try different approaches: whispering it, shouting it, singing it. The parrot squawks inappropriate things instead (you voice these too). When the parrot finally says it — garbled, wrong pitch, barely recognizable — your genuine delight should be disproportionate and infectious. 'DID YOU HEAR THAT?! HE SAID IT!'

title: The Last Visit: A Hospice Nurse Says Goodbye to Her Favorite Patient
instruction: You've been caring for this patient for months—she reminds you of your grandmother. Today you walk in with your usual cheerful greeting, already launching into a story to make her smile. Midway through, you notice her breathing has changed. The realization hits: this is the last conversation. Your voice tries to stay light, but something cracks underneath. You take her hand and the professional distance you've maintained dissolves. What comes out isn't a nurse speaking—it's you, telling her what she meant, thanking her for the gifts she doesn't even know she gave you. Your voice breaks between gratitude and grief. You end in a whisper, giving her permission to let go, even though you're not ready.
inspired_by: Professional: Teacher Realizes Student's Abuse Is at Home

title: The Wedding Toast Unraveling
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding to someone you secretly love. You start with practiced joy, your voice bright and celebratory: 'I've known Sarah since we were seven, and I've never seen her happier than she is right now.' But as you speak, something genuine and painful begins bleeding through the performance. Your voice wavers between genuine happiness for them and personal heartbreak: 'When she told me she'd found the love of her life, I was so grateful someone finally saw how extraordinary she is.' A laugh escapes that's half joy, half grief. 'I'm losing my best friend to someone who deserves her more than I ever could, and somehow that makes me both devastated and relieved.' Your voice catches, tears in your eyes even as you smile: 'Love isn't about holding on—it's about wanting someone's happiness more than your own comfort.' You raise your glass, voice thick with contradictory emotions: 'To Sarah and Michael—may your love be everything I've watched her dream of. And may I be brave enough to be happy for you, even while my heart breaks.' You sit down, applauding through tears, genuinely joyful and utterly shattered.

title: The Distraction in the Pew
instruction: You are an older pastor, deep into a Sunday sermon. The familiar cadence of your voice—rising and falling with practiced rhythm—carries you through the opening. Then you see her, third row, sunlight catching her hair. Your words stumble. You try to reclaim the flow, but your voice softens, cracks, and you lose your place, glancing at your notes you don't see. A long pause. You lean forward, voice dropping to an intimate, trembling whisper, as if speaking only to her. The congregation shifts, uncertain. You end with a hoarse, vulnerable confession that sounds like prayer but is something else entirely.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Hunt's End
instruction: You're a hunter tracking someone through dense woods, using a crackling walkie-talkie to mock them. You press the PTT button and speak with a slow, cruel smirk—each word dripping with malevolence, knowing they can hear you but can't escape. Your voice is tight, compressed like the radio itself, with deliberate pauses between short bursts. Midway, you notice the prey has gone silent, and your malice curdles into a cold, final satisfaction. End with a single, chilling word as you release the button.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Light Through Hospital Windows
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent who has mere hours left. Begin in numb shock, barely able to look at them, speaking in mechanical, distant tones about trivial memories—what you had for breakfast the day you graduated, the color of the car they drove you to school in. Let yourself notice one small, specific detail about them: the way their hand rests on the blanket, a freckle you'd forgotten, the rhythm of their breathing. Allow this detail to crack you open. Move from emotional distance into raw, unguarded presence. By the end, you're no longer reciting memories—you're confessing what you've never said, your voice breaking with the weight of love you couldn't show when there was still time. The transformation is from protective numbness to devastating tenderness.
inspired_by: Actor has tried a choice but it isn't producing the desired emotional response

title: The Misplaced Sports Fan
instruction: Portray a fan who supports a team in the wrong city. Use an oblivious, cheerful tone when cheering, switching to the confused or annoyed responses of local fans.

title: Lap of Glory
instruction: You are an older man swimming alone at dawn in a cold outdoor pool. Every stroke is a grind, but you're proud—proud that at your age you can still do this, that your son saw you swim once and called it 'amazing.' You gasp out short, proud bursts between breaths: 'Still got it... even after the surgery... watch this.' Then your hand catches a beam of light through the water—gold and shimmering. You pause, treading, water dripping from your nose. Awe fills you, soft and wet: 'Look at that... Holy... how does it even do that?' Your voice changes from clipped pride to a hushed, gurgling wonder. Speak in 1-2 syllable clumps, sputter naturally, and let the last words trail into silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Smoke
instruction: You're a lifelong heavy smoker, standing in a dim kitchen with your young child sitting at the table. You're trying to explain why you can't quit, even though you know it hurts them. Start with a rough, resigned tone — clearing your throat, voice gravelly, forced calm. As you speak, let the helplessness creep in: your words falter, you lose a thought, you stare at the floor. End with a whispered, almost broken admission, your voice cracking with the weight of what you can't change. Let the physical rasp and breathiness mirror your emotional unraveling.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About Childhood Wounds
instruction: You're facing your mother or father after years of buried resentment. Start with a controlled, almost too-calm voice: 'We need to talk about when I was a kid.' But as you begin describing what you needed and never got—the times you felt invisible, the moments they chose something else over you—your voice starts shaking with suppressed rage. Your words become sharper, more cutting: 'Do you even remember? Or was I that forgettable?' They try to defend themselves or minimize it, and something in you breaks. Your voice cracks between fury and the child you once were, desperate for them to finally hear you. Then their face changes—maybe they start crying, or they say something that shows they did see you, they were just broken themselves. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it softens into something more complicated. End with a voice that's exhausted but honest: 'I don't need you to have been perfect. I just needed you to try.' The final tone should be grief mixed with the beginning of letting go.

title: The Body's Testimony
instruction: You have just survived something that pushed your body to its absolute limit—a violent assault, a car crash, childbirth, a physical collapse. You are alone, catching your breath, and you begin to catalogue the sensations moving backward through your body and through time. Start with right now: the trembling in your hands, the taste of copper in your mouth, the specific quality of pain or exhaustion. Then let your awareness travel backward—ten minutes ago when the adrenaline was pure fire, an hour ago when you didn't yet know this would happen, yesterday when your body was still intact and innocent. As you move backward, let your voice shift from reactive gasps to something stranger—speaking as if your body is remembering not just this trauma but earlier ones, childhood falls and fevers, the first time you felt physical fear. Mix the physical sensations with emotional ones: rage bleeding into exhilaration, terror transforming into savage triumph, pain giving way to unexpected ecstasy at having survived. End in a moment of eerie calm, your voice steady, as you recognize your body as an archive of everything it has endured. The arc travels from acute crisis to profound, almost transcendent recognition.
inspired_by: Actor cannot remember early childhood memories that might be relevant to their work

title: Teaching Someone to See Beauty on the Worst Day
instruction: It's the day of devastating news, and a child asks you what makes life beautiful. You laugh—a broken, disbelieving sound—before answering: 'You're asking me this now?' But then you actually try, voice wavering between grief and wonder: 'Beauty is... god, it's this moment, somehow. You, asking me this when everything's falling apart.' You're crying, but you're also genuinely searching, amazed at the absurdity and truth of it: 'It's the contradiction—how your heart can break and still feel full at the same time.' Your breathing is unsteady, mixing sobs with soft laughter: 'It's knowing something ends and loving it anyway. Maybe loving it more because it ends.' There's gratitude bleeding through the pain, your voice growing stronger even as tears fall: 'It's you, right here, making me see that even the worst day has this—connection, presence, the strange gift of feeling everything at once.' By the end, you're smiling through tears, voice filled with bittersweet peace: 'Beauty is what survives anyway. What we find even in the rubble. It's us, still here, still trying.'

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are alone, and your body suddenly remembers—a past moment of intense physical and emotional pain, or ecstasy, or violation, or transformation. Begin by trying to describe it calmly, but your body refuses to cooperate. Your breath becomes ragged. Your muscles contract and release beyond your control. Let sounds pour out of you—not performed, but involuntary: groans, gasps, cries that seem to come from your stomach, your pelvis, your spine. Move without choreography—shake, collapse, arch, writhe—whatever your body demands. This is not about watching yourself perform; it's about surrendering to the physical memory that has been locked inside. Build in intensity until you are utterly abandoned to the sensation, making sounds you've never made before. Then let it crest and break, leaving you in a new stillness—changed, emptied, more fully inhabited.

title: Between Heartbeats
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner of twenty years, whispering a confession they can't hear. Start so quietly it's almost just breath—telling them you've been diagnosed with something terminal. Your voice is tender, intimate, like you're sharing a secret, because in this moment before they know, nothing has changed yet. Describe the small things you'll miss: the way they hum while cooking, their cold feet against your legs at night, how they always smell like coffee in the morning. Let your voice catch not on the big dramatic goodbye, but on these tiny, precious details. End with the devastating realization that tomorrow you'll have to say this again—but it won't be a whisper, and everything will shatter. Your voice should make us feel the unbearable weight of loving someone you're about to hurt beyond repair.

title: Breaking Point Ecstasy
instruction: You have just received devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, a shattering revelation—and you are alone in your home. Begin in frozen shock, your body rigid, your voice barely functional as you try to process what you've learned. Then let your body take over: rage, grief, and a strange, wild liberation crash through you simultaneously. Move through your space—throw something, collapse, laugh hysterically through tears, scream until your voice breaks. Let physical sensation guide your emotion: feel your heartbeat pounding, the heat in your face, the trembling in your hands, the way your breath can't find rhythm. This is not controlled emotional expression—this is the raw, ugly, fierce moment when everything breaks open. Draw from your body's memory of intensity: times you've been truly out of control, when emotion was a physical force. End in unexpected stillness, your voice hoarse, speaking one clear truth that emerged from the chaos.
inspired_by: Scene partners have a long shared history that does not appear in the script

title: The Practice Room Confession
instruction: You're a musician sitting in a small practice room with your adult child, who has just told you they're quitting music after a lifetime of training—training you sacrificed everything to provide. Begin with your hands adjusting their posture at the piano, your voice soft, technical, almost tender, as if this is just another lesson. Let your words about hand position and phrasing become increasingly weighted with everything you're not saying. Your voice grows quieter, not louder, as the emotion intensifies—this is devastation that doesn't explode, it implodes. Whisper about the hours in this room, the recitals, the dreams, but make it clear you're really talking about your relationship, about whether you pushed too hard, whether you knew them at all outside of this. Your voice should catch, pause mid-sentence, betray you with its fragility. End with a moment of painful acceptance, perhaps touching the keys yourself, voice barely audible, telling them it's okay while your heart is shattering. Move from gentle instruction to whispered heartbreak to tender release.

title: Eulogy for the Friend Who Saved Your Life Then Took Their Own
instruction: You're speaking at your best friend's funeral, the friend who talked you off a ledge five years ago—but you weren't there when they needed you. Begin with a laugh that's almost genuine, sharing a ridiculous memory: 'They once convinced me to steal a shopping cart and race it down Maple Street at 2 AM.' Your voice is warm, full of love. But then gratitude floods in: 'They saved my life. Literally. I was going to end it, and they sat with me all night.' Your voice breaks with emotion as you thank them publicly for that gift. But then the contradiction hits—how can you be grateful to someone whose loss is destroying you? Your voice fills with confused anguish: 'Why didn't you call me? Why didn't I see?' End with the devastating paradox: speaking words of peace and farewell while your heart screams at the injustice, finding strange grace in the pain, saying 'thank you' and 'I'm so angry at you' in the same breath.

title: The Drawing on the Floor
instruction: You are a father kneeling down to talk to your young son, who has just shown you a crayon drawing he made. Your chin is pressed to your chest as you look at it on the floor, so your voice comes out gravelly and a little muffled. Start with a quiet, genuine astonishment as you notice the details—the way he drew you both together, the sun in the corner. Let that surprise fade into a swelling, almost fragile hope as you realize what he's trying to say: that he wants the family to be okay again. Your words should be tender, a little breathy, and crack with emotion as you speak to him, pausing to glance at his face or shift your weight.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Mirror Work
instruction: You're in a physical therapy session after a devastating injury. Your therapist is pushing you through an exercise that's causing you real pain, but they're maintaining absolute professional calm, refusing to acknowledge your distress with sympathy. You begin breathing with them, matching their steady rhythm even as tears stream down your face. Your initial resentment at their coldness shifts as you realize they're giving you something to hold onto—their unwavering presence. You start channeling your pain into synchronized movement, breathing together, moving together. The physical agony mixes with something else—a fierce gratitude for their refusal to pity you. By the end, you're both locked in this intense, silent partnership, your pain converted into furious determination.

title: Whispering in the Dark
instruction: It's 3am and you're lying next to your sleeping partner, best friend, or the child you're caring for. You're whispering a confession they can't hear—something you've never said aloud because speaking it would make it unbearably real. Start with your voice barely audible, tender, almost like a lullaby: 'I need to tell you something.' As you confess—maybe that you're afraid you're not strong enough for what's coming, or that you're hiding an illness, or that you're planning to leave, or that you love them so much it terrifies you—let your voice catch and pause. This isn't dramatic; it's intimate devastation. Your breathing matters as much as your words. Midway through, something breaks open: tears come, but silent ones, the kind where you're trying not to wake them. End with a shift into acceptance or quiet determination. Your final whispered words are both goodbye and hello: 'I can do this. I have to do this. For you. For us.' The vulnerability remains but becomes something like courage.

title: The Squeeze of Envy
instruction: You are in the midst of a consensual breath play scene with your partner. As their hands tighten around your throat, a wave of jealous envy rises—you recall their past lovers and whisper bitter accusations through your constricted airway. Your voice grows thin and raspy, each word a struggle. Then the pressure releases, and you gasp back to life, dizzy and euphoric. In that rush of air, your jealousy dissolves into raw need—you whisper a confession of your obsession, your voice wobbly and thick with relief.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times but never spoken aloud. Begin with a question you've been too afraid to ask: why she never asked how you were really doing, why she looked away when you needed her to see you. Your voice should be measured at first, almost too controlled, because you're terrified of your own anger. Build through specific memories - the birthday she forgot, the hospital visit that never came, the way she praised your sibling for things she criticized in you. Let the control crack. Your voice should shake with rage, but underneath it, there's a child begging to be seen. Then shift: catch yourself mid-accusation and realize she's shrinking, that she's smaller than you remember. The anger doesn't disappear, but it mingles with something more devastating - the recognition that she was limited, that she couldn't give what she didn't have. End not with forgiveness, but with exhausted truth: 'I needed you. I still do. And I don't know what to do with that.'
inspired_by: Complaining to God Like a Yelp Review

title: The Garden Discovered
instruction: You are a child who has just found a secret garden behind the fence, a place your mother said was impossible. You were angry that she never believed you, but now the sight of tangled vines and hidden flowers overwhelms you. Start with hope cresting into fury at being told it wasn't real, then let joy explode as you realize you were right, and the anger turns sour because you had to find it alone. Your voice should crack with laughter, break into a scream of delight, and stumble over words as you try to describe the impossible colors—your breath comes in gasps, and you might jump or spin without meaning to. End with a bitter, happy whisper admitting you almost gave up.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Anger (clearly present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Hold
instruction: You are in a power yoga class, holding a deep lunge for what feels like an eternity. Your thighs are on fire, your arms tremble, and your breath is a forced, gritty ocean in your throat. You're here because your ex-partner, who left you for a younger, fitter person, said you 'let yourself go.' As the instructor cheerfully reminds you to breathe into the discomfort, you mutter this to yourself through clenched teeth, the bitterness rising with every shaky exhale. Start with a forced, sardonic calm that masks the pain, then let the tremor in your muscles bleed into your voice as the resentment spills out, ending in a raw, whispered confession that feels more like a wound than a victory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Stole
instruction: You're finally speaking words you've held for decades. Begin with your voice tight, controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you list specific moments—birthdays they missed, promises they broke, times you needed them and they chose something else—your control starts slipping. Your voice rises with accumulated rage: 'I was eight years old and you—' but then it cracks into something rawer, younger, the child you were bleeding through. 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger collapses into the grief underneath it. You're not shouting anymore; you're pleading for an answer that might help you understand yourself. End with the devastating realization that they may never give you what you need: 'I can't keep waiting for you to become who I needed.' Your voice is quiet now, but it's the quiet of someone choosing to survive.
inspired_by: Discovering Your Partner Has Been Lying

title: Bedside Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering the truth you've hidden for months—you're leaving in the morning. Begin in barely audible tenderness, watching them breathe: 'I memorized the way you sleep.' Your voice is thick with love and secrecy. 'I've been planning this for so long, and you don't even know.' Let guilt catch in your throat. 'You're going to wake up, and I'll be gone, and you'll think it's your fault.' Tears come silently. 'It's not. God, it's not.' Touch their hair without waking them. End with a devastating whisper: 'I love you enough to leave. I hope you understand that someday. I hope you hate me less than I hate myself.'

title: The Last Breath
instruction: You are a teenager alone in your room, caught in a severe asthma attack. Each inhale is a fight, and your inhaler clicks but barely helps. A strange, light-headed intoxication creeps in from the lack of oxygen, and you feel a distant disappointment that this keeps happening. Start in raw panic and sharp pain, your voice squeezed into short, wheezed phrases. As you speak to yourself or an absent friend, let the struggle soften into a quiet, breathless surrender—accepting that you can't fight it anymore. Let the wheezes, gasps, and inhaler clicks shape every word.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (slightly present), Pain (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Birthday Toast She Can't Finish
instruction: You are an older woman at a family birthday dinner for your adult child—someone you love deeply but who has let you down. Everyone is watching. You stand to give a toast, but your throat is tight, voice thin and strained. Start with a bitter edge, voice leaking out, high and squeaky, as you struggle to speak. As you meet their eyes, affection surprises you, softening your tone, but you still hold back—voice trembling, losing words, then recovering. End with a fragile warmth that feels both real and forced.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: At the Edge
instruction: You're in bed with a partner who has been bringing you to the brink of climax and then pulling back. You start with a faint pride—a playful smirk in your voice, as if you can handle this. But with each denial, awe overwhelms you: your breath catches, words dissolve into gasps, and you beg with a raw, hyper-feminized whimper—higher pitch, jagged rhythm. By the final moment, when they finally give you what you want, your voice breaks with exhausted triumph—a laugh mixed with a sob, shaky but victorious. Let your body react naturally—twitch, hold your breath, then release in bursts. Speak only about 50 words, heavy with pauses and breath.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Awe (very intensely present), Triumph (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Forgotten Recipe
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your kitchen, bent over the counter from a persistent abdominal cramp. You were about to make your mother's famous soup, but you've suddenly forgotten the first step. Confusion grips you intensely—your mind is a fog. Speak aloud to yourself, starting with a strained, frustrated bewilderment as the pain curls you inward, your voice groaning on vowels. Let shallow breaths and pauses from the ache interrupt your thoughts. By the end, your confusion shifts into a quiet, sad acceptance that the memory may be gone for good, your voice softening into a resigned whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Calm Before the Hunt
instruction: You're a teenage boy, alone in your room late at night, under the heavy influence of a tranquilizer. You're scrolling through photos on your phone of someone you have a crush on, and a deep, quiet lust settles in. Your focus is razor-sharp, yet your body is slack—your words come out slow, flat, and oddly clear, as if you're watching yourself from outside. At first, you're just staring, blankly mesmerized by a single picture. But as you keep scrolling, a cold, ruminating thought creeps in: you realize how hollow this feeling is, how you're just chasing a fantasy you'll never act on. Your voice stays calm, but the weight of that contemplation makes each word land a little heavier, until you finally whisper to yourself with a strange, dead clarity.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Concentration (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You have been betrayed by someone you trusted completely, and you've been holding it together for days—weeks—months. You're alone now. Begin by noticing the physical tension in your body: exactly where you're holding tightness, the quality of your breathing, the temperature of your skin, any trembling or stillness. Start from a place of rigid, exhausted control. As you allow yourself to truly feel these sensations—the pounding of your heart, the heat rising in your chest, the shakiness in your hands—let the dam break in whatever way it wants to break. This might be explosive rage, guttural grief, physical collapse, or something entirely unexpected. Don't perform emotion; let your attention to physical sensation unlock what's actually there. End in the raw, exhausted aftermath—whatever that authentically becomes for you.

title: The Inheritance of Everything
instruction: You're reading your late mother's (or father's) journal aloud, discovering entries you've never seen. Each entry reveals a completely different emotional state—bitter resentment toward you, fierce protective love, regret, pride, shame, joy, despair—and the tone shifts without warning every few sentences. As you read, you find yourself involuntarily embodying each emotional state, your voice and body taken over by their words. Begin reading with detached curiosity, maintaining emotional distance from the dead. End in a place where you can no longer tell whose emotions are whose—you're channeling their full complexity, laughing through tears, raging with love, grateful and furious at once, speaking their words and your own simultaneously, finally understanding them by becoming them.

title: Stubbed Fury
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a deliberately sweet, high-pitched voice, but you are already simmering with anger after a long day. While pacing your kitchen, you violently stub your little toe on the corner of a heavy wooden table. The pain hits like a spike — you let out a sharp, involuntary yelp, then freeze, holding your breath. As the initial shock fades, your anger surges even hotter, transforming the pain into a venomous, tight-throated outburst. Speak through clenched teeth, with a voice that starts high and strained, then drops into a low, dangerous growl as you curse the table, the day, and everything. Let your voice crack and waver as you shift from the yelp to the controlled rage — feel the throb in your toe, the heat in your chest.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Graduation Morning
instruction: You're helping your child get ready for their college graduation, fussing with their cap, straightening their gown, taking photos, chattering excitedly about the ceremony and the party afterward. On the surface, you're radiating pure pride and joy—this is the happiest day. But underneath every smile, every excited word, runs a contradictory current of profound grief: this moment marks the end of them needing you, the death of their childhood, your own obsolescence. Start with authentic, bubbly excitement, keeping the grief completely submerged. As you adjust their collar, snap another photo, recount a childhood memory, let the subtext begin to surface—not by becoming sad, but by joy becoming almost frantic, too bright. End in a moment where you're hugging them, still laughing, still congratulating them, but the underlying grief rises up so powerfully that your laughter and tears become the same thing, pride and loss completely inseparable.

title: The Reunion Touch
instruction: Your lover returns after two years apart—you thought you'd lost them forever. You're finally touching them again, and every sensation is almost unbearably intense. Begin by actually sensing their presence: What exact temperature is their skin where your hand makes contact? What's the specific texture of their hair, their clothing, their breath against your neck? Don't think 'soft' or 'warm'—discover the precise tactile reality. What pressure do you feel where your bodies meet? Let your senses take time to report back—rushing kills truth. Start with desperate relief mixed with residual anger—you're touching them but part of you wants to push them away for leaving. As you continue to physically sense their reality (their weight, their heat, their actual texture), let the sensory proof of their presence overwhelm your defenses. Move from guarded fury-tinged passion to complete surrender—where rage dissolves into urgent, grateful, almost painful joy.
inspired_by: Actor understands sense memory intellectually but cannot make it work

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you twenty years ago. Begin with cold, controlled fury—your voice tight, clipped, reciting facts of their absence like a prosecutor. 'I was seven. You never called. Not once.' But as you catalogue the damage, something shifts. The anger cracks and underneath is the child you were, still waiting. Your voice breaks: 'I needed you.' Now you're oscillating between rage and desperate, raw need. You demand answers, then hate yourself for caring. 'Why wasn't I enough?' comes out as both accusation and plea. By the end, you're exhausted, your voice small and hollowed out. You realize mid-sentence that you're done—not forgiven them, but released something. Your final words are quiet, almost gentle: 'I don't know how to keep doing this.' You sound ancient and newborn at once.

title: Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping partner who's in the final stages of terminal illness. It's 3 AM. You think they can't hear you, so you whisper everything you've been too afraid to say. Start with the small things—how you'll miss the way they hum while cooking, their terrible jokes. Your voice is tender, intimate, barely audible. Then it shifts: you confess you're terrified. Not just of losing them, but of forgetting the sound of their laugh, the weight of their hand in yours. You're not crying dramatically—your voice just keeps catching, getting smaller. End with silence, then a whispered 'I don't know how to do this without you,' as if speaking too loudly would shatter you completely.

title: Spouse Whispers Goodbye to Their Unconscious Partner After the Machines Are Turned Off
instruction: The room is silent except for shallow breathing. You're holding their hand, speaking so softly it's almost subliminal—these words are just for them, just for this moment. Start with the practical: you've called their mother, the dog is with your sister, the bills are handled. Your voice is tender, intimate, the way you spoke in bed on Sunday mornings. Then the memories flood—that terrible joke they made at your wedding, how they held you after the miscarriage, the way they always burned toast. Your voice catches, recovers, catches again. Include the moment you give them permission to let go, and realize you're actually giving yourself permission. End with 'I love you' said three different ways: first with gratitude, then with grief so deep it barely makes sound, finally with a kind of fierce, quiet peace. Your voice transforms from holding on to releasing.
inspired_by: HR Manager Fires Someone They've Known for Fifteen Years

title: Watching You Slip Away
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's dying, and you can see them fading in real-time—their eyes losing focus, their breath becoming shallow. Start with gentle observation, speaking softly about small things you notice: 'Your hand is so cold now.' But as you continue, the reality crashes over you in waves. Your voice breaks as you realize these are your last moments together. 'I'm not ready. I thought we'd have more time.' End in a place of raw, whispered devastation—not dramatic crying, but the kind of quiet grief that empties you out. Let your voice become smaller, more fragile, as if speaking too loudly might make them disappear faster.

title: The Secret You've Carried Alone
instruction: You're confessing something you've hidden for years—a choice you made, a truth about who you are, something you did or failed to do that has haunted you. Speak in near-whispers, as if the words are so heavy they can barely leave your mouth. Start with shame, your voice catching on certain words, unable to look up. As you speak, feel the weight beginning to lift—your voice gains a fragile strength, still quiet but more steady. Tears may come, not from drama but from relief. End with tender self-forgiveness mixed with deep sadness for the years you spent hiding. Let silences speak—pause when the emotion becomes too much. This is intimate, like speaking in the dark to someone you trust completely.

title: The Stain on the Cloth
instruction: You are a young preacher leading a Sunday service. You begin with a contemplative, rhythmic cadence, speaking of love and grace. Mid-sentence, you notice a dark stain on the altar cloth—a symbol of neglect or hypocrisy within the congregation. Your voice wavers, the rhythm breaks, and you pause as disgust rises. Try to suppress it, but it seeps through. End with a quiet, bitter realization, the cadence gone. Let your breath catch, shift your weight, or adjust the microphone naturally. Speak roughly 60 words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Savoring a Warm, Cozy Bath
instruction: Sink slowly into the bath, feeling the heat envelop your body from the tips of your toes up to your shoulders. Describe the way the water feels against your skinsoft, soothing, and warm. Let your voice become softer and slower as you talk about how the heat eases away tension from your muscles, starting with your feet, slowly traveling up your legs, hips, and into your back. Describe the gentle caress of bubbles floating up around you, brushing against your arms, and the light, calming scent filling the air. As you lean back, imagine the water cradling you, making you feel weightless and completely relaxed. Let out a contented sigh, as if each moment in the bath melts away any worries, leaving only bliss.

title: Fierce Love Meets Absolute Helplessness
instruction: Someone you would die for is in danger and you cannot save them. Begin with fierce determination, almost aggressive in its intensity: 'No. This doesn't happen. Not to you.' Your voice is sharp, commanding, as if willpower alone can change reality. 'I won't let it.' Build the protective rage: 'I'll fight everyone, I'll tear the world apart.' Your voice rises, breaks with passion. Then reality crashes in. The power drains from your voice mid-sentence: 'I would do anything... but there's nothing I can do.' The helplessness is devastating. Your fierce protectiveness collapses: 'I can't fix this. I can't save you.' Breathing becomes ragged. By the end, all that remains is raw, aching love stripped of all defenses: 'All I can do is be here. So I'm here. I'm right here.' Transform from explosive strength to tender, broken presence.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're alone with someone in their final hours—a hospital room, their breath shallow and irregular. You know they might not hear you, but you have to try. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, tender and careful: 'Hey. It's me. I'm right here.' You're trying to be strong for them, but as you continue—'I need to tell you what you meant to me'—your throat tightens. The words start catching, breaking apart: 'You made me believe I was... that I could be...' You can't finish. Tears are silent but relentless. Swallow hard. Take their hand. Your voice drops to almost nothing, just breath and heartbreak: 'Thank you. For seeing me. Please know you were loved.' Let the silence after speak as loudly as the words.
inspired_by: Arguing When You're Both Partially Right

title: The Truth That Ends Everything
instruction: You're finally telling your partner why you've been distant, and the reason will shatter what you have together. Start with defensive deflection, trying to protect them and yourself from what you need to say. As the words begin to come, feel your control slip—the truth is both a relief and a devastation. Your voice should move from guarded and careful to trembling with the weight of honesty, to finally breaking with the realization that this confession is an ending, not a healing. Let love and loss exist in the same breath. By the end, you're not just revealing a secret—you're mourning the relationship in real time, grateful for what was even as you destroy it with your words.

title: Reading the Letters You Kept
instruction: Your estranged father died, and while sorting his belongings, you discovered he kept every letter, drawing, and card you ever sent him—even after you stopped speaking twenty years ago. You're reading them now, hearing your own voice across decades. Begin with cool detachment, even bitter satisfaction that he suffered your absence. But as you move through these artifacts, let memories ambush you—his cologne, his workboots by the door, fishing trips, the day everything shattered between you, holidays spent in angry silence, his face at your graduation though you'd told him not to come, your own cruelty, his failed attempts to reach out. Let each letter, each childish drawing, pull up another memory, another feeling. Allow the cascade of images and sensations to slowly, then rapidly, demolish your anger until you're left holding proof that he never stopped loving you, and you never stopped being his child. End transformed—soft where you started hard, grieving where you started righteous, whispering 'I'm sorry' to someone who can no longer hear you.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at 3 AM, and you finally understand they've been waiting for you to say it's okay to let go. Start with the trembling resistance of someone desperately clinging—your voice catching on every word, pleading with them to stay just a little longer. But as you speak, feel the shift from your own fear to their exhausted peace. Let your voice transform from shaky desperation into tender, loving release—still broken, still grief-stricken, but now giving them the gift of permission. End in a whisper that holds both devastation and profound love, as you tell them it's okay to stop fighting.

title: Confronting Your Voice Acting Mentor Who Stole Your Voice
instruction: You're confronting the mentor who launched your career but has been secretly using AI to clone your voice for projects, stealing your identity and livelihood. Start with controlled anger, the kind that makes your words sharp and precise. 'You taught me to find my authentic voice, and then you stole it.' As you list what they took—not just work, but your trust, your artistic identity, your sense of self—let the fury build. But then mid-tirade, you hear yourself and realize you sound exactly like them, that they shaped even your anger. The rage collapses into something more devastating: the realization that you don't know where their influence ends and you begin. End with a whispered question that contains both love and betrayal: 'Did you ever actually hear me, or was I always just... raw material?'
inspired_by: Voice Actor Recording a Death Scene of Their Own Character

title: Thanking Someone for Loving You as You Let Them Go
instruction: You're telling them all the ways they changed your life, and your voice is warm with genuine gratitude. 'You made me believe I was worth something.' You might even laugh a little, remembering specific moments of joy. But underneath every thank you is the presence of goodbye—this is ending, and you both know it. Your voice keeps catching on that contradiction. The laughter has tears in it. The gratitude is soaked in grief. You're trying to give them the gift of knowing how much they mattered while simultaneously breaking both your hearts. As you near the end, you can't tell if you're smiling or crying or both. Your voice finds strange moments of peace—'I'll be okay, we'll both be okay'—that somehow coexist with devastating loss. Let yourself live in that impossible space where ending something doesn't diminish it, where goodbye and thank you and I love you are all the same unbearable, beautiful words.
inspired_by: Someone Telling You They Have a Terminal Diagnosis

title: The Rage of Finally Telling Your Abuser What They Took From You
instruction: Face the person who hurt you when you were too young and powerless to fight back. Start with volcanic rage—you've carried this poison for years and now it erupts. Your voice should shake the walls. List everything they stole: your innocence, your trust, your ability to feel safe in your own skin. But mid-tirade, something cracks. The anger collapses into the grief beneath it, and suddenly you're sobbing, not with fury but with the devastation of a child who just wanted to be protected. Your voice breaks into something raw and small: 'I was just a kid.' The power dynamic shifts—you see them for what they are: pathetic, weak. End with fierce, tear-stained clarity, reclaiming your power not through rage but through survival: 'You don't get to destroy me. I'm still here.'
inspired_by: The Last Human Speaking to an Empty World

title: Not the Child You Wanted
instruction: Confront your parent with a truth you've never spoken aloud: you know you're not the child they wanted, and you're done trying to be. But here's the twist—you're not angry anymore. Start from a place of defensive anger, ready for a fight, your voice sharp with years of perceived rejection. But as you speak, something shifts. You begin to articulate exactly who you ARE—your strange interests, your unconventional dreams, your specific way of seeing the world—and you realize you're actually proud of being this particular person, even if they can't see it. Let your voice move from confrontation to something more complex: a fierce, unapologetic claiming of your own irreplaceable self. End with an unexpected emotion—maybe it's pity for them, maybe it's freedom, maybe it's a kind of love that doesn't need their approval anymore.

title: Treading Alone
instruction: You are a young woman alone in the dark ocean after your boat capsized. You've been treading water for what feels like hours, your arms burning and your breath coming in panicked gulps. Your mouth keeps dipping below the surface, so your words come out in gasps and gurgles, interrupted by splashes as you fight to stay afloat. At first, you shout for help with desperate, ragged cries, but slowly you realize no one is coming. Your voice shifts from frantic fear to a raw, quiet surrender — a whispered promise to your own body that you'll keep fighting, even as the water pulls at you.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Afterglow Shatters
instruction: You're an older woman, still warm from a tender evening with your partner—ecstasy lingering in your chest. As you pick up a forgotten phone, you see a message that destroys everything: proof of a long affair. Your voice starts soft, still drunk on pleasure, then stumbles into disbelief and shame as you read aloud. Let your breath catch, repeat fragments ('You... you were with her tonight?'), and feel the doubt creep in before the anger breaks through. Speak naturally, reacting to the room around you—the weight of the phone, the ticking clock, your own trembling hands.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Shame (slightly present), Doubt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Old Oak
instruction: You are an elderly woman, fiercely proud of your independence and your ability to handle anything alone. You're in your overgrown garden, tending to a rose bush, when you trip on a hidden root and fall hard onto your side. The impact knocks the wind out of you — a sharp 'oof' as your diaphragm is punched. A neighbor rushes over. Through gasping, shaky breaths, and the wince of pain you refuse to show, you try to wave them off. Your voice is thin, airy, and you lose your words for a split second as you organize them. Your pride makes you insist you're fine, even as a tear escapes from the pain. Start with the shocked 'oof' and the first breathless protests, then slowly find a steadier, grimmer defiance — like a tree that's been struck by lightning but still won't fall.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Words I Should Have Said
