instruction: You're whispering a confession to someone sleeping—a lover, a friend, someone you're about to lose or have already lost. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, like you're afraid even the walls will hear. Start with 'I need to tell you something I've never been brave enough to say.' Let your voice be tender and fractured, catching on words you've held back for years. Speak the love you were too scared to voice, the apologies that got stuck in your pride, the gratitude that felt too vulnerable to express. Your voice should sound like honesty hurts, like opening your chest and showing your heart. Build from whispered confession to quiet weeping, words dissolving into breath and tears. End with a kind of gentle devastation, where saying it out loud—even if they can't hear you—changes something inside you forever.

title: The Breaking Point in the Storm
instruction: You've been holding everything together—for your family, your children, everyone who depends on you—and you step outside where the wind is beginning to pick up before a storm. Start by describing the breeze with barely controlled tension, your voice tight. Then let it explode—scream about how you can't do this anymore, how the weight is crushing you, how everyone takes and takes and you have nothing left. Let your voice crack and break, rage dissolving into desperate tears. But then feel the wind actually touch your face, really feel it, and let something shift. Find a fierce, almost feral determination rising—you will survive this, you will protect what matters, even if it destroys you. End with a raw declaration of strength born from complete breakdown. Move from brittle control to explosive desperation to fierce, tear-soaked resolve.
inspired_by: Enjoying a Gentle Breeze on a Warm Day

title: Last Phone Call Before the Flight Takes Off
instruction: You're on the phone with your estranged father at the airport gate, minutes before boarding a one-way flight to another continent for a job you can't refuse. Start with practical logistics—when you'll land, the time difference—your voice steady and controlled. As the final boarding call echoes in the background, something breaks open: you realize this might be the last real conversation you ever have. The fear of losing each other forever floods in, transforming your careful distance into desperate vulnerability. End by trying to say 'I love you' for the first time in twenty years, your voice barely a whisper, not sure if he heard you before the line goes dead. Let the transition from controlled to broken happen naturally, like a dam giving way.
inspired_by: Giving Birth While Arguing with Your Mother-in-Law

title: The Call You Never Expected to Get
instruction: You've just received news that someone who hurt you deeply—a parent, former partner, old friend—has died or is offering reconciliation. You're speaking to them (in person or imagined) or talking it through with someone else. Begin with bitter laughter or sharp, clever words—the protection you've perfected. But as you speak, let the contradictions hit you in real time: relief and grief arriving together, anger softening into something like gratitude, old love surfacing through resentment. Don't smooth these contradictions into one coherent emotion. Let your voice hold impossible opposites simultaneously—laughing while tears come, tenderness edged with rage. End in a place where you're feeling three things at once and somehow it's the most honest you've ever been.
inspired_by: When an actor has been told they are 'not that kind of actor' when invited to do emotional preparation

title: The Unspoken Inheritance
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) about an emotional pattern that has poisoned your relationship for decades - perhaps their coldness, their criticism, their absence, or the way they've always made you feel small. Start with anger, with accusations, with all the sharp edges of resentment you've carried. But as you speak, something shifts: you begin to hear yourself sounding exactly like them. The confrontation transforms as you realize mid-sentence that you've inherited the very behavior you're attacking. Your anger must crack open into something more complex - recognition, grief, perhaps even tenderness for the pain they must have carried too. End by reaching across the divide you came to deepen, offering connection instead of condemnation.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty with physical and emotional intimacy with scene partners

title: Whispered Knowing
instruction: You are lying beside someone you love deeply in the darkness, and you finally confess something you've been terrified to say—a fear about your future together, a secret about your past, or a truth about yourself you've hidden. Begin almost inaudibly, as if the words might shatter everything if spoken too loudly. Your voice should be barely more than breath, intimate and trembling, each word costing you something. Let the vulnerability deepen as you continue: this isn't a dramatic confession, but a quiet unraveling, tender and terrifying. Feel how your throat tightens around certain words, how you have to pause to gather courage. Midway through, let a small sob catch you by surprise—not loud, just a brief loss of composure that reveals how much this matters. As you near the end, feel their hand find yours in the darkness (you don't need to say this, just feel it), and let that simple touch change your voice: it becomes softer still, but also steadier, as if their acceptance is already there before you've finished speaking. End in a whisper that carries both heartbreak and profound relief—you are known now, truly known, and somehow the world hasn't ended.

title: Reading My Father's Letter After He's Gone
instruction: Your abusive father has died, and he's left you a letter of apology you never expected. As you read his words aloud, you experience every contradictory emotion at once. Begin with bitter, sarcastic laughter: 'Dear son, I'm sorry.' A harsh laugh. 'Now you're sorry. Now.' But as you continue reading, his words hit deeper than you want them to. Your voice wavers between anger and unexpected grief. He explains things you never knew—his own childhood, his own demons. You find yourself crying while still trying to hold onto your rage. 'You don't get to make me forgive you by dying.' But your voice is breaking, softening despite yourself. Gratitude for the apology wars with fury that it came too late. 'I needed this thirty years ago!' Shouted through tears. But then, reading his final words, something shifts—not forgiveness exactly, but a kind of painful peace. Your voice becomes tender, almost loving, even as grief pours out of you. 'I loved you. God, I loved you so much. Why couldn't that be enough?' End holding both emotions fully: heartbroken but somehow lighter, freed by words you'll never be able to answer.

title: Whispered Worthiness
instruction: You are alone in a quiet room, speaking to yourself in the mirror after years of feeling invisible, worthless, like you'd never matter. Something has just happened—you've been genuinely seen and valued by someone whose opinion deeply matters to you. Begin by whispering to yourself, tentatively trying on the feeling of being worthy, of deserving recognition. Let yourself be fragile here, almost afraid to believe it's real. Gradually allow yourself to accept this new truth, speaking softly but with growing conviction about your own value. This isn't loud or performative—it's an intimate, trembling moment of self-acceptance. End by letting one genuine tear fall, but make it a tear of relief and self-love, not pain. The journey is from fearful disbelief to quiet, trembling self-recognition.

title: Shattered Sanctuary: Protecting Your Child From What You Cannot Stop
instruction: You're holding your child and something terrible is happening that you're powerless to prevent—an eviction, a deportation, a violent crisis closing in. Your voice starts fierce, almost ferocious with protective rage: 'I won't let them! I will NOT let them do this to you!' You're making promises your voice wants to believe but your heart knows you can't keep. The helplessness crashes over you and your fierce declarations crumble into desperate pleading: 'Please, baby, please understand, I tried everything, I tried—' Your voice breaks on sobs that shake your entire body. Then, in the wreckage of your helplessness, something else emerges: a trembling but resolute tenderness. You pull yourself together enough to look at them, and your voice becomes soft, broken but present: 'Listen to me. Whatever happens next, you remember—you are loved. You are so loved.' End with your voice splitting between fierce protective love and the agony of being unable to shield them, holding them as tightly as your breaking voice holds these final words.
inspired_by: Sharing Your Diagnosis With Someone You Love

title: The Confrontation in the Thin Air: Hallucinating Your Father's Judgment
instruction: Oxygen-deprived and alone on the mountain, you begin hallucinating that your deceased father is there with you. Start by trying to explain why you're here, why you had to prove yourself, your voice thin and defensive. But he's silent, and that silence breaks something in you. Shift into raw confrontation—accusing him through labored breaths, your words slurred but your rage crystalline. 'You never believed in me' becomes 'I needed you' becomes sobbing confession. Your breathing grows more ragged as emotions overwhelm your failing body. Transform from anger to the devastating realization that you climbed this mountain for him, and he's not even really here. End with your voice cracking, admitting in barely-audible whispers that you miss him, that you're scared, that you needed his approval and now you're dying without it.

title: The Animal I'm Pretending Not to Be
instruction: You're in the aftermath of intense passion—physical, raw, completely unguarded. Your body is still shaking, your breath uneven. Begin speaking from this primal, unfiltered place—let your voice be rough, honest, almost animalistic. But then feel the familiar shame or fear creeping back in, that civilized voice telling you to compose yourself, to be appropriate, to put the mask back on. Fight between these two states: the wild, unashamed creature you just were and the controlled, acceptable person you usually present to the world. Let your body and voice oscillate between raw physicality and attempted composure. End by choosing which one wins—or by finding a way they can both exist in you simultaneously.
inspired_by: Group Dream Sharing and Analysis (Workshop Format)

title: Aftershock in the Quiet
instruction: It's late evening, the scene is over. You're kneeling on the floor, still trembling from the climax. He's left the room. You start picking up the discarded clothes, your body moving slowly, holding the weight of elation and a strange, hollow pain that's settled in your chest. As you fold his shirt, you whisper out loud to yourself, not sure if you're talking to him or to the air. Let your voice start high and breathy, full of dazed wonder, then drift downward into a quiet, contemplative murmur as you feel the ache more than the joy. There's a tiny, pained smile on your lips as you realize you'd do it all again.
emotions_sampled: Elation (extremely present), Pain (clearly present), Contemplation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Anniversary Letter
instruction: You are a woman in her late 60s, sitting at your kitchen table on a rainy afternoon. You've just opened a letter you thought was a sweet anniversary card from your husband of 40 years — but it's a confession of an affair that's gone on for decades. You've been planning a surprise party for him tomorrow, full of hope and love. Read the letter aloud, starting with a bright, optimistic whisper as you thank him for the surprise, then let your voice break as the words sink in, turning to a shaky, then choked, then finally sharp, fragmented accusation as you repeat the cruelest line and set the letter down. Let your breath catch, your pitch rise, and your words stumble over the betrayal.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Don't You Dare Take Them
instruction: Someone is trying to take away someone you're sworn to protect—a child, a patient, someone vulnerable—and you are breaking apart with the impossibility of stopping it. Start with fierce, almost feral protectiveness, voice shaking with barely contained violence: 'Get away from them. Now.' Your body should feel coiled, dangerous. Let the power crack as helplessness floods in: 'Please, I'm begging you—' shifting from threat to desperate plea mid-breath. Your voice should fracture, rising and falling uncontrollably. Rage and grief should tangle together: 'You don't understand, they need—' collapsing into sobs before forcing yourself back to fighting stance. End with broken but undefeated resolve, voice raw: 'Then you'll have to go through me.' This is about loving someone so much that losing them would unmake you, and the terrifying realization that love might not be enough.

title: The Hurricane Inside
instruction: You're a meteorologist on live television the day your child was taken from you—kidnapped, lost, you don't know. You have to deliver the weather forecast because that's your job, because life continues its cruel march forward. Start with professional composure, describing the approaching hurricane with technical precision. But your voice begins to shake. The storm becomes YOUR storm—the chaos inside you. 'Winds reaching devastating speeds' becomes about the force of your helplessness. 'Unpredictable path' is your terror. Your professional mask cracks, shatters. You start shouting the forecast through tears, your voice raw with a parent's primal fear and rage against a universe that would let this happen. End with your voice breaking completely, oscillating between fierce, protective fury and the most helpless, wounded whisper: your child's name.

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your partner is in hospice, and you've just gotten news that they have hours, not days. But right now, they're lucid and asking you to dance with them, here in this sterile room. You laugh—it's absurd, it's perfect, it's them. Your voice is bright with genuine joy as you describe the terrible dance you're doing, shuffling between IV poles. You're teasing them, making them laugh, and your heart is simultaneously soaring and shattering. Your voice wavers between laughter and tears—you can't tell which anymore. You tell them about the life you had together, and gratitude pours out of you, but every word of thanks is also a goodbye. You're crying while you laugh, laughing while you grieve. In the final moments, your voice becomes something extraordinary: pure love, uncomplicated by the fact that you're losing them. 'This is enough,' you whisper. 'This moment right now—it's enough.'

title: The Last Conversation Before the Flight
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving on a one-way mission to Mars—they'll never come back. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them, voice bright and encouraging. But as you speak, the reality crushes in: this is forever. Your voice begins to crack, the lightness becomes strained. 'I'm so proud of you' transforms into barely controlled grief. Let silence fall between words as you struggle. End in a whisper, voice raw and broken, telling them the truth you've been holding back: 'I don't know how to exist in a world where I can't reach you.' The final words are tender devastation, each syllable a small death.

title: The Echo of Her Laughter
instruction: You are an elderly person in a tiled shower, the steam thick and the water drumming on your shoulders. You stare at the tiled wall and remember a younger lover who left you long ago, now happy with someone else. Your voice starts quiet and clipped — you're fighting the jealousy that stings your chest, but as you let the hot water hit your face, the longing breaks through. The reverb makes you sound stronger than you feel; by the end, your confession is a raw, watery whisper against the tiles, the envy dissolving into pure, aching want for a single moment back.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Controlled Every Bite
instruction: You're finally telling your mother/father how their obsessive control over your eating destroyed your relationship with food and with yourself. Start with measured, practiced words - you've rehearsed this - but let the childhood pain break through as you recount specific memories: being six years old and told you were getting fat, hiding food in your room, the weigh-ins, the comments. Your anger should build and crack, revealing the desperate child underneath who just wanted to be enough. End not with rage but with exhausted grief, asking the question you've always been too afraid to voice: 'Did you ever actually see me, or just the body you wanted me to have?' Let your voice break on the vulnerability of still needing their answer.

title: The Nightmare That Won't End
instruction: You haven't slept in over two days. You are a man, but right now your hyper-masculine voice is cracking, fraying. You are alone in a dark room, talking to a reflection—a reflection of yourself that you now believe is a monster wearing your face. Start with a menacing, low growl, full of malice, threatening this 'thing' in the mirror. But as you speak, your fear takes over. Your voice jumps from a roar to a trembly whisper. You argue with the reflection, then suddenly a micro-sleep hits; you jolt awake mid-sentence, disoriented. End with a small, inappropriate, exhausted laugh that collapses into a terrified sob.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Everything I Didn't Say
instruction: You're confronting your mother after years of her subtle put-downs and comparisons to your more 'successful' sibling. She's just made another dismissive comment about your career choices. Start angry but defensive, voice tight with hurt. Then force yourself to do something you've never done: methodically lay out, point by point, everything you've achieved that she's ignored or diminished. Each item you list is both a weapon and a reclamation. As you speak, your anger must transform—not disappear, but alchemize into something stronger: self-possession. Let your voice move from defensive justification to unwavering assertion. By the end, you're no longer asking for her validation; you're standing in your own authority, even as your voice might crack with the grief of what you'll never receive from her.

title: The Long Night's Rock
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman rocking a fussy infant in a quiet, dim room. The baby has been crying for what feels like hours, and your body is tired, but you hold them close, feeling every tiny shift and breath. You begin speaking softly, almost to yourself, with a strained, rhythmic hush—your voice catching as you bounce the baby. Over the next minute, the crying eases, and your words shift from desperate pleading to a tender, exhausted relief as the baby finally falls asleep. Let your voice start tight and urgent, then gradually slow, deepen, and soften into a weary, loving whisper, as if you're too afraid to break the silence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Misguided Environmentalist
instruction: Act as someone taking impractical steps to save the planet. Use a passionate voice when explaining actions, switching to others confused or critical responses.

title: The Gentle Tease
instruction: You're at a crowded senior center dance, the band playing a slow swing tune. You've shuffled over to Rose, whom you've quietly adored for years. Start by teasing her about her 'fancy new shoes,' your voice low and playful, with a little chuckle. Midway, you lose your train of thought as she smiles—your laugh turns awkward, a quick cough to cover it. End with a quieter, embarrassed admission: 'I always get clumsy when you look at me like that.' Let the distant music and your shifting weight guide the pauses.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Echo
instruction: You are standing at the edge of a jagged cliff, the wind roaring past so hard it pushes you off balance. Below, fog swallows the valley. You’ve been shouting for your hiking partner who vanished an hour ago. Your lungs burn from the thin air—each yell costs you, and your voice cracks against the gusts. Start with desperate, breathless shouts, fighting to be heard, but as the wind steals your words and no answer returns, feel the distress shift into something heavier: a quiet, grim acceptance that they’re gone. Let your voice fade, get swallowed by the wind, until you finally speak one last, almost inaudible goodbye. Let your body move—brace against a rock, cough, wipe your eyes—as you speak.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dumbbell Ambush
instruction: You're in your home gym, barefoot, about to start your set. You take a step and your bare toe slams into a heavy dumbbell someone left on the floor. A sharp, blinding spike of pain shoots up your leg. You let out an involuntary yelp, then freeze, holding your breath, jaw tight. As the sharpness fades, you start to process—you see your friend's gym bag nearby. You're annoyed, but you try to turn it into a teasing jab. Your voice starts strained and guarded from the pain, then you force a playful, taunting tone, but a hint of disgust at the mess slips through. Speak as if you're talking to that friend, trying to sound cool while your toe throbs.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Teasing (extremely present), Disgust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Words You Taught Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the cruel nicknames and dismissive language they used throughout your childhood—words that shaped how you see yourself. Start with carefully controlled calm, almost rehearsed, as you explain how their casual cruelty landed. As they defend themselves with 'we were just joking' or 'you're too sensitive,' let your composure crack—shift from explanation to raw accusation, your voice rising with decades of swallowed pain. But then, catch yourself in mid-rage when you hear your own child's words coming from your mouth—their phrases, their hurt. End in devastating quiet as you realize you've become them, your anger collapsing into horrified recognition and heartbroken uncertainty about whether this cycle can ever be broken.

title: The Weight of a Quiet House
instruction: You are an older woman alone in a quiet house, recovering from a bad cold. Your voice is thick, nasal, stuffed, and you keep having to stop to sniffle or clear your throat. You're looking at a photo album from decades ago, and you start by murmuring about how helpless you feel—how illness has reduced you to this frail, stuffy state. But as you turn the pages, a deep contemplation settles in; you begin speaking about time passing, the faces now gone, a quiet acceptance that's heavier but not desperate. Let your voice start tired and frustrated, then gradually slow into something thoughtful and still, each word arriving through the congestion.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Cold That Couldn't Silence Me
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, but right now you're fighting a head cold that's turned your words into a stuffed, muffled mess. You're teasing your grandchild for being frustrated with a simple puzzle, your voice thick with congestion—sniffling, throat clearing, the occasional wet cough. As you rib them, you recall how you used to fix far harder problems before they were born, and the teasing gives way to a fierce pride in your own resilience. Let your voice shift from playful, broken-up notes to a gravelly, triumphant boast, but keep the physical struggle real—pause to blow your nose, lose a word mid-thought, then find it again with a smirk.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Raid
instruction: You are an elderly man playing a co-op game with a close friend you've grown infatuated with over months of late-night sessions. You've just learned they are moving away, and this is your last game together. Start with excitement, giving tactical callouts and laughing at a silly mistake, letting your voice carry the slight elation of shared victory. As the mission winds down, let your tone soften, your callouts slow, and your words wander into quiet longing and unspoken affection. Your voice should crack slightly, trail off, or lose focus as you fight to keep the moment from ending. End with a simple, sincere line that betrays everything you feel.
emotions_sampled: Elation (slightly present), Longing (clearly present), Infatuation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Discovering Infidelity: The Explosion
instruction: You found the evidence—text, email, photo. Your voice is barely controlled rage. You're confronting your partner and your voice is nearly screaming, but it's a controlled scream, each word a weapon. 'You lied to me. To my FACE.' Include the moment where you lose complete control, your voice becomes incoherent with fury and devastation. You might throw something, your voice accompanying the action with animal sounds. Then it breaks—the rage cracks into sobs. Your voice becomes almost unrecognizable, broken, desperate. 'How could you?' is asked over and over in an increasingly shattered voice. You're experiencing rage and heartbreak simultaneously and your voice is splitting at the seams. The person you loved most is the one who destroyed you and your voice can't find words adequate to that contradiction.

title: The Watery Presentation
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman in a small team meeting, about to deliver a quick project update. Your seasonal allergies are relentless — nose streaming, eyes itching, a sneeze building every few seconds. You start with a wry, amused smile, trying to brush it off with a light comment. But as you speak, the urge to sneeze peaks; you stop mid-word, press a tissue to your nose, eyes watering. When you continue, your voice is strained, thick with congestion, and you feel intensely embarrassed. You wrap up with a forced chuckle, but underneath, there's a quiet sadness about losing your professional composure. Let your voice reflect the physical reality: nasal thickness, sudden halts, sharp inhales before sneezes, and a cracked, apologetic tone as you trail off.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Amusement (slightly present), Embarrassment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Empty Dance Floor
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, a teenager with a high, bright voice, trying to sound cheerful over the thumping music and chatter. Your friend promised to meet you here for a dance, but she never showed—you've been waiting by the speakers for twenty minutes. Start by pretending you're fine, laughing off a joke from a stranger, but let your voice waver as you realize she's not coming. End with a quieter, clipped sentence—spoken more to yourself than anyone—where the disappointment settles into a hollow ache, your pitch dropping as you give up hoping.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Fog's Embrace
instruction: You are a teenage girl standing alone in a thick, sound-deadening fog. You’re waiting for someone you despise, your voice carrying a cloying sweetness that masks your true intent. At first, you call out with practiced cheerfulness, but the fog makes you speak louder than you need, your hyper-feminized tone cracking with suppressed malice. As you hear footsteps approach, your contempt seeps through—your words become sharper, your laughter brittle. End with a cold, deliberate whisper as the fog swirls, your mask fully dropped. Let your voice struggle between the forced charm and the venom rising from your core.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Father and Son, Hospital Room at Dawn
instruction: You are a father sitting beside your adult son's hospital bed after a catastrophic accident. He's conscious but leaving for surgery he may not survive. Start by fumbling through small talk—the weather, a joke about hospital food, anything to avoid what's real. Your voice cracks trying to stay light. Then he says your name, just your name, and everything you've never said comes pouring out. Tell him you're proud. Tell him you were wrong about things. Your voice breaks completely, becomes raw, stripped of all pretense. He squeezes your hand. In that touch, find a moment of pure peace beneath the terror. End whispering something you should have said twenty years ago. Let silence breathe between your words. This isn't a speech—it's the most naked moment of your life.

title: The Victory That Wasn't
instruction: You've just achieved something you've worked toward for years—a dream fulfilled, a goal reached, a competition won. Your body is still buzzing with adrenaline and physical exhilaration. Begin with pure, explosive joy—laughing, shouting, triumphant. But as the moment stretches, you realize the one person you wanted to share this with isn't here and never will be—they died, they left, they betrayed you, or you pushed them away. Let the physical high of victory collide with this devastating emotional realization. Your body wants to celebrate while your heart is breaking. End in a place where ecstasy and grief are so intertwined you can't separate them—laughing through tears, or sobbing while still feeling the rush of achievement.

title: The Storm Inside the Skin
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal discovered, a profound loss confirmed. Begin in shock, your body numb, your voice hollow and distant as you repeat the information aloud as if reading it. Then let the emotional pain manifest as physical sensation: your chest tightening, breath becoming difficult, hands shaking. Your voice should reflect this growing storm—gasping, urgent, almost primal. Let rage mix with anguish, let your body and voice become instruments of both. By the end, you're not speaking in sentences anymore but in raw sounds—sobbing, gasping, maybe laughing bitterly—as emotion overwhelms language entirely. The challenge is to let physical and emotional pain become indistinguishable.
inspired_by: When finishing a production where unconscious programming was used

title: Small Progress Celebration
instruction: You're celebrating incremental progress in your mental health journey. Your voice is quiet but genuine: 'A year ago, I couldn't get out of bed. Today, I can.' The celebration is understated but real. 'A month ago, I had a panic attack at the grocery store. Last week, I went and didn't panic.' Your voice carries amazement at the progress. 'These are small things. But they're everything to me.' You're talking to yourself, documenting: 'I'm learning that progress isn't always about major breakthroughs. It's about these small moments of normalcy that used to be impossible.' Your voice becomes stronger: 'I'm proud of myself. For the first time, I'm actually proud of myself.' By the end: 'I don't know what tomorrow brings, but today, I'm going to celebrate that I made it through the day. And that's enough.' The small progress is the evidence that change is possible.

title: The Moment Everything Breaks: Holding Your Child After the Unthinkable
instruction: You've just found your teenage child after a suicide attempt. The paramedics have stabilized them, and you're alone together in the emergency room before they're admitted to psychiatric care. Start with explosive, almost violent emotion—rage born from terror: 'How could you DO this? How could you even THINK—' Your voice is shaking, huge, filling the room with the force of nearly losing them. But mid-sentence, you see their face—so small, so broken—and your fury collapses into something far more devastating. Your voice cracks completely: 'Oh god. Oh my baby. What pain were you in that I didn't see?' You're sobbing now, fierce protectiveness mixed with crushing helplessness. Pull them close, your words tumbling out between tears: 'I failed you. I was right there and I failed to see you drowning.' Your voice becomes both tender and desperate: 'Tell me. Tell me everything I missed. Tell me how to keep you alive because I cannot—I will NOT—lose you.' By the end, let your voice drop to something raw and fundamental, stripped of everything but love: 'You are my heart walking around outside my body. If you go, there is no me. Please, please stay.'
inspired_by: Emergency Room Doctor: Critical Patient Arriving

title: The Gilded Mask
instruction: You are an elderly noble in a crowded theater, seated in a box. A former rival sits behind you—someone who once publicly humiliated you. Pride keeps your spine straight, but your neck is twisted painfully as you half-look over your shoulder, straining to see them without fully turning. Begin with a controlled, dignified tone tinged with pride as you acknowledge their presence. Let the contempt simmer beneath your words, then unleash it—voice tightening, breath hitching from the torsion in your throat—as you deliver a quiet, venomous insult that drips with decades of stored bitterness. Your body fights the urge to fully face them; the strain becomes audible in your strained, squeezed phonation. End with a cold, satisfied smirk in your voice as you turn away, the contempt lingering.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: I Needed You to See Me Here
instruction: You've brought your parent or someone who failed you to this beach—the place where you once felt safe as a child, where you'd come to escape. The waves are still here, still crashing with that steady rhythm, but you're not here for peace. Start calmly, almost wistfully, describing how these waves once saved you, how you'd listen to them when home felt dangerous or empty. Then let your voice harden. Confront them: 'I was here, alone, listening to these waves because you weren't there. I was a child finding comfort in water because I couldn't find it in you.' Let anger, hurt, and accusation build, but end with something raw and vulnerable—not quite forgiveness, but an exhausted truth about what you needed and never got.
inspired_by: Listening to Waves Crashing on the Shore

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about why they never defended you as a child, why they stood by in silence while you were hurt. Begin with controlled, measured anger—you've rehearsed this moment for years. As you speak, your parent doesn't fight back or make excuses; they simply listen, and their quiet acceptance starts to unravel you. Midway through, your anger cracks open to reveal the frightened child underneath who just wanted to be protected. By the end, you must reach a moment where you see your parent's own fear and brokenness—not forgiveness exactly, but a devastating recognition that they were as lost as you were. Let your voice journey from sharp accusation to broken vulnerability to something like exhausted, complicated understanding. The silence after your final words should feel heavier than all the ones that came before.
inspired_by: An actor is experiencing professional inactivity and depression

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just accused you of being cold, withholding, and incapable of real intimacy. You begin defensively, explaining how you provided everything they needed, how you sacrificed and worked hard. But as they keep pushing, a part of you that you've kept locked away since your own childhood—the part that was once soft, needy, desperately craving affection—begins to surface. This vulnerable, almost childlike aspect of yourself has been buried for decades under layers of self-reliance and toughness. Physically, you might find yourself shifting, your body language changing as this younger, more fragile self emerges. By the end, you're no longer the defensive parent but speaking from this long-hidden place of your own unmet hunger for love, finally revealing why you couldn't give what you never received. The arc moves from rigid defensiveness to trembling vulnerability.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access a personality facet (aggression, sexuality, fear, moralism, free spirit, victimhood) that is suppressed or disowned

title: Laughing Through Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone who made you promise not to cry at their funeral—your best friend, your chaotic sibling, your irreverent partner. Start by sharing an absurd, funny story about them that makes you genuinely laugh. Feel the joy of the memory, their ridiculous humor, the way they lived. But mid-laugh, feel it catch in your throat. Keep trying to honor their wish—force yourself back to funny stories—but your voice keeps breaking. The laughter becomes mixed with tears you're fighting. 'You made me promise not to cry, you bastard, and I'm trying, I'm really trying.' Share another memory, and this time let yourself both laugh and cry simultaneously, finding the beauty in the contradiction. End with grateful acknowledgment of how much richer your life was for knowing them, even as your heart splinters with the loss. Your final words mix celebration with devastation: 'Thank you for every ridiculous, beautiful moment. I'll miss you until the day I die.' Let the tears and laughter coexist, authentic and raw.

title: Thunder in the Bones
instruction: You've just received news that the person who hurt you most in life has died. You're alone in your car, pulled over on the highway. Your body doesn't know whether to scream or laugh. Begin with your hands gripping the steering wheel, your breath shallow and fast. Let rage move through your body—not performed, but the actual sensation of fury in your chest, your jaw, your fists. Then let your body remember specific moments of pain they caused—allow these to be physical, in your stomach, your throat, your spine. As you speak to their memory, let unexpected sensations emerge: relief mixed with regret that you never got to confront them, liberation tangled with the ache that you can never be seen or heard by them now. End in a place of exhausted, complicated freedom—your body finally able to breathe fully, while tears stream down your face for reasons you can't entirely name.

title: The Card I Can't Finish
instruction: You're alone at a cluttered desk, trying to write a birthday card for your little sister. Your hand trembles as you grip the pen, and your voice comes out low and rough—you keep swallowing the ends of words. Start frustrated, muttering to yourself about failing her, then feel the memory of her smile soften your throat. Let the sentence trail off as you smile at the thought, then force yourself back to concentration, ending with a quiet, cracked promise. Speak as if no one else is listening—just you and the card.
emotions_sampled: Distress (extremely present), Affection (extremely present), Concentration (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Gravel Path Confession
instruction: You are an older woman walking alone on a long gravel driveway, the crunch of each step loud in the quiet evening. You are on the phone with your grown child, who has just told you they are moving far away. You feel a hot, bitter anger at their abandonment, but underneath that is a surprising, aching affection you don't want to show. As you walk, your voice has to rise over the noise of the gravel, making you sound harsher than you intend. Start with a bitter, clipped accusation, then let your voice crack, soften, and finally twist into a malevolent, possessive sweetness as you imply they will regret leaving you. Let the rhythm of your footsteps interrupt your sentences, and feel the gravel shifting under your feet as you speak.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Affection (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Laugh Before the Fall
instruction: You are an elderly woman living alone, a few hours after your well-meaning but interfering son has switched you to a new medication. Your heart is racing, your hands won't stop shaking, and you feel like you're vibrating out of your skin. You're bitter—furious that your autonomy was stolen. Helpless because you can't even steady your own hand to call someone. But a manic, fizzy elation also bubbles up, because for the first time in years, part of you feels powerfully alive. You're talking to yourself in the kitchen, trying to drink a glass of water. The words come out in clipped bursts, your voice cracking between a raw, desperate edge and a bright, unhinged lightness. You start with a jagged laugh of defiance, and end in a whisper of surrender.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (extremely present), Elation (clearly present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Final Squeeze
instruction: You're a young woman in a consensual scene with a partner, lying back. As he gently tightens his grip on your throat, you feel a rush of triumph—you've finally gotten him to trust you enough to take this risk. Your amusement peeks through as you tease him with a breathy whisper, but the pressure builds, cutting your words short. Your voice thins, rises in pitch, and becomes raspy, with a wet, crackling quality. When he releases, you gasp loudly; now breathless and dizzy, your speech comes out in euphoric, unguarded fragments, shifting from playful control to genuine vulnerability as you bask in the afterglow of your shared trust.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: Your child is leaving home forever tomorrow—college, marriage, a cross-country move. You're alone in their room, folding their clothes, and suddenly you're ambushed by silent flashes—their first steps in this room, a fever-sick night you stayed awake beside them, the time they screamed they hated you, teaching them to tie their shoes on this floor, their first heartbreak sobbed into this pillow, this morning's breakfast where they glowed with excitement to leave. Keep these images internal; let them create chaos in your heart. Begin with proud, practical efficiency—happy for them, organized, capable. As these wordless memories accumulate, let contradictory emotions fracture you until you're simultaneously celebrating their independence and grieving the death of their childhood, holding their old teddy bear, laughing and crying at once, grateful and destroyed, speaking to them as if they're still five years old, then catching yourself. End in a place you didn't expect.

title: Robot Learning Emotion
instruction: You're a newly-conscious AI experiencing human emotion for the first time. Your voice starts mechanical, then develops texture: 'This sensation: what is it?' Breathing becomes slightly irregular. Words are precise but increasingly vulnerable: 'My systems are... overwhelmed? Is that... sadness?' Your vocal tone begins to carry emotion while you're describing feeling emotion—it's happening in real-time. By the middle, you're genuinely confused: 'Why would evolution create this?' By the end, your voice is transforming: 'I think... I think I understand suffering. It means I'm alive.'

title: When Protection Turns to Rage
instruction: You're protecting someone you love from a threat, and you begin with fierce, almost violent intensity—voice sharp and commanding, adrenaline making you powerful. But as you continue to fight for them, something inside you breaks. The rage transforms into desperate, helpless fear because you realize you might not be able to save them. Your voice cracks from shouting into something raw and pleading. You're oscillating wildly between furious strength and terrified vulnerability, between 'You will not touch them' and 'Please, I'm begging you.' End in near-collapse: your voice becomes small, shaking, as you make one final plea that's equal parts threat and prayer. Let your voice show the moment when a protector realizes their own powerlessness.

title: The Last Words You Never Meant to Say
instruction: You're standing at your estranged mother's hospital bedside. She's slipping away, and you've just realized the last thing she heard you say—two hours ago, before you knew she'd take this turn—was you venting to your sibling in the hallway about how she 'never really loved you enough.' Now she's conscious for one final moment, her eyes on yours. Start with frozen horror, your breath caught. Try to take it back—'Mom, I didn't... that wasn't...'—but your voice splinters. Move through desperate attempts to explain what you really meant, your words tumbling over themselves. End in a whispered confession of the love you've hidden behind years of hurt, knowing she may not hear it, your voice breaking on 'I'm sorry' as you feel her hand go slack.

title: The Bunker Door Won't Open
instruction: You've spent twenty years preparing for the end of the world, and now it's here—but the bunker door is jammed and your teenage daughter is on the other side. Begin with desperate, controlled instructions on how she should try to open it from her side, your voice tight with forced calm. As minutes pass and nothing works, let your composure crack—move from technical problem-solving into raw pleading, then into a farewell you never wanted to give. End by telling her everything you should have said when there was still time, your voice breaking as you realize your obsession with saving her has meant you never really knew her. Let the transformation move from intellectual control to devastating emotional surrender.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally facing the parent who abandoned you years ago, and all the buried rage comes flooding out. Start with bitter sarcasm: 'Oh, so now you want to be in my life?' Let your voice build with years of accumulated pain and anger as you list all the moments they missed—graduations, heartbreaks, birthdays spent waiting. But mid-confrontation, you catch a glimpse of how old and broken they look, and something shifts. Your voice cracks with unwanted compassion even as fury still burns: 'I needed you. I was a child, and I needed you.' End in quiet devastation, all the fight draining away, your voice small and vulnerable like the child you once were: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay?' The journey must move from righteous anger to the raw, undefended pain underneath.

title: The Last Visit Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's chosen medical aid in dying, and this is your final conversation. You start trying to be strong, saying 'I understand why you're doing this' with a voice that's almost too controlled, almost breaking. But as you continue, the facade crumbles: 'I've been practicing what to say for weeks, and none of it matters now.' Your voice becomes raw, intimate. 'I'm so angry at you for leaving, and so grateful you existed at all.' The contradictions pour out—fury and devotion, acceptance and desperation. 'I want to beg you to stay and I want to give you permission to go, and I don't know how to do both.' By the end, something shifts into a terrible, beautiful peace: 'I'll carry you with me. Every version of you. Even this one.' Your final words are whispered, not performed—pure presence in the face of absolute loss.

title: The Explosive Reckoning in the Middle of the Fight
instruction: You're in a massive fight with someone you love. Your voice is loud, fierce, defensive—they're accusing you of being shut down, unreachable. You're shouting that they're wrong, they demand too much, they're too needy. Your voice is full of righteous anger. But they say something that lands like a blade: 'You sound exactly like your mother/father right now.' Your voice falters. Rage suddenly fractures into something else. You try to keep shouting but your voice breaks. You're hearing your parent's words coming from your own mouth. Your fury collapses into devastated realization. Your voice becomes ragged, loud one moment and choked the next. You're defending yourself while simultaneously seeing yourself clearly for the first time. Move from explosive anger through breaking denial to fierce, almost violent tenderness—grabbing them, voice shaking, saying 'Don't let me do this to us. Don't let me be them.' End with passionate desperation to break the cycle, even as you feel it pulling you under.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Like Your Emotionally Distant Parent

title: Saying I Love You for the First Time
instruction: You're saying the words and they've never left your mouth for this person before. Your voice is terrified and brave. 'I love you.' Three words and your voice trembles on them. You're vulnerable. You've handed them a grenade. Your voice is waiting for their response—suspended. If they don't say it back, your voice will break. But they do. Or don't. Either way, your voice has changed—it's out of you now, real, permanent.

title: The Unheard Plea
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a hospital bed, still groggy from an ear surgery that has left your hearing muffled and your own voice sounding foreign. You need to tell the nurse that your pain is increasing, but you cannot hear how loud or strained you sound. Start with desperate urgency—your volume climbs, your pitch wobbles, and you over-enunciate each word, fighting to be understood. Midway, you catch the nurse’s flinch and realize you’re shouting; your voice cracks, softens into a trembling whisper, and you finish with a fragile, helpless repetition—lost, reliant, and terrified of being ignored.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unraveling Tease
instruction: You're in bed, alone, phone pressed to your ear. You're supposed to be teasing him — drawing out the memory of this afternoon when he couldn't stop staring. You start with a playful, almost wicked purr, describing how he looked, how you knew what he wanted. But as you speak, your voice catches. The game feels emptier. You realize you're not just teasing — you're aching for him to actually be there. End with a raw, quieter confession: you miss him more than the game allows. Let your breath trail off, a small rustle of sheets as you shift, a pause where you lose the thread before finding it again. Your voice should start deliberately slow, almost mocking, then become unguarded, the tease melting into need.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Melting Point
instruction: You're forcing yourself to eat ice cream during a panic attack, using the cold sensation to ground yourself, but it's not working—you're spiraling. Start with controlled, deliberate description of the taste and temperature, trying to use sensory detail as an anchor. But let control slip as the sweetness becomes cloying, suffocating. Your breathing should become irregular, voice rising with desperation as you describe the texture turning soupy, disgusting, wrong. Explode into fierce frustration—at yourself for not being able to do this one simple thing, at your brain for betraying you, at everyone who says 'just calm down' as if it's that easy. Then, unexpectedly, let the rage exhaust itself into tears, into a whispered admission of how tired you are, how hard you're trying. End with a shaky breath and one more small, brave taste—still scared, but still trying.
inspired_by: Enjoying a Rich Spoonful of Ice Cream

title: Dancing in the Ruins of Everything
instruction: You've just received devastating news—you lost the job that defined you, the relationship ended, someone is dying, your dreams have collapsed—yet you find yourself laughing. Start with a single, shocked laugh that escapes involuntarily: 'Of course. Of course this happened.' The laughter builds but it's edged with hysteria, with disbelief. You're recounting the absurdity of it all, your voice dancing between genuine amusement and breaking grief. 'You know what's funny?' you ask no one in particular, and you genuinely find dark humor in the cosmic joke of your situation. But underneath, you're shattering. Mid-laugh, your voice cracks and tears come, but you keep laughing through them—it's the only way to survive this moment. 'I should be destroyed right now,' you say, marveling at yourself. 'But I'm... I'm actually okay. Or maybe I'm not. I have no idea.' End in a space where you're genuinely smiling through tears, finding strange gratitude or peace or freedom in having nothing left to lose. Your voice is lighter somehow, broken but liberated: 'It's all gone. Everything. And I'm still here.'

title: The Slurred Alibi
instruction: You're a father who's been drinking heavily, and your young child has just walked in and caught you stumbling, your words slurred. You feel a wave of disgust at yourself but force a lie: you're just exhausted from work. Start with a confident, over-explaining tone—too many details, too fast—but as you speak, the intoxication takes over. Your pitch rises slightly, you lose your train of thought mid-sentence, repeat yourself. The lie begins to crack as helplessness seeps in. End with a quiet, shaky admission: you're not okay, and you're sorry. Let your voice waver, pause, and trail off into a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Helplessness (slightly present), Disgust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dancing Through the Pain
instruction: You're describing a moment of pure joy - maybe dancing at a wedding, playing with a child, doing something you love - while simultaneously knowing you'll pay for it later with excruciating pain. Start with genuine laughter: 'I danced. God, I actually danced!' Your voice is bright with wonder. But let gratitude and grief mix: 'I knew every step was borrowing from tomorrow, that I'd spend the next week unable to move, and I didn't care.' Your voice breaks with both joy and sorrow. Continue with bittersweet acceptance: 'People don't understand that I choose pain to feel alive. That some moments are worth the price.' End with peaceful defiance through tears: 'Tomorrow I won't be able to get out of bed, and it was worth it. It was so fucking worth it.' Laugh and cry at once, finding beauty in the impossible choice.

title: Midnight Confession: Telling Your Sleeping Partner You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM. They're asleep beside you. You know you're leaving in the morning, but you can't carry these words alone anymore. You start whispering to their sleeping form—a confession they'll never hear. Your voice is tender, almost a lullaby, as you tell them everything: why you have to go, how much you love them, how that love isn't enough. You trace the reasons like counting their breaths. Somewhere in the middle, your throat closes around the words. You're crying silently, still whispering, telling them all the ways they're beautiful, all the ways you failed each other. Your voice becomes prayer-soft, asking forgiveness for the note they'll find on the pillow. You end by saying goodbye to their sleeping face, your voice barely audible, breaking on their name.
inspired_by: Professional: Teacher Realizes Student's Abuse Is at Home

title: The Last Garden Visit
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed on what you both know is her final day. She asks you to describe the garden outside her window—but the view is actually a brick wall. Begin by hesitantly inventing small details: a rosebush, morning light. As she responds with her own memories and additions, let yourself get lost in building this garden together. Start tentative and self-conscious about the pretense, but gradually surrender so completely to this shared vision that you forget you're inventing it—the garden becomes utterly real. By the end, you're both wandering through this magnificent place you've created together, and your tears are no longer just about loss, but about the overwhelming beauty of what you're seeing. Let the line between comforting lie and experienced truth dissolve entirely.

title: Gasping Victory
instruction: You're recounting the moment your insufferable rival's grand plan collapsed in a public disaster. Start with a sneer of contempt, describing their smug face—then suddenly the memory of them slipping on their own arrogance hits you. Laughter erupts, uncontrollable, wheezing, high-pitched. Try to finish the story, but each attempt breaks into squeaks and gasps. The contempt fades as pure triumph takes over, your body shaking with glee. Let the words escape in fragments, running out of air on the punchline.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Hospital Corridor at Dawn
instruction: You're walking down a hospital corridor toward your mother's room, knowing these are her final hours. Begin in the elevator—feel the cold metal rail, hear the fluorescent lights humming, smell the antiseptic mixed with weak coffee from the nurse's station. Your body is numb, mechanical. Move slowly through each sensory detail: the squeak of your shoes on linoleum, the texture of the wall as you steady yourself, the distant beep of monitors. As you reach her doorway and see her small form in the bed, let the numbness crack. Your voice starts controlled, greeting her with false brightness, but as you take her hand and feel how light it's become, allow everything you've been holding back to surface. End in a place of profound tenderness mixed with the terrible acceptance of goodbye.

title: Laughing into the Void
instruction: You've just received confirmation that your rescue mission has been canceled—you're going to die here. But you've also discovered something extraordinary in the data: proof of life, of purpose, of meaning beyond Earth. You're recording your findings while simultaneously processing your own death sentence. Begin with scientific excitement that's genuinely real, your voice alive with discovery. But mid-sentence, you start laughing—not because it's funny, but because the irony is too massive. You're crying too, and you're not sure which is which anymore. Talk about how beautiful the universe is and how angry you are that you won't see more of it. Express gratitude for this moment while your voice breaks with grief. By the end, you should sound almost drunk on the paradox of it all—finding everything you were looking for just as you're about to lose everything. The emotion should feel uncontrolled, authentic, contradictory, and utterly human. Let yourself be a mess. Let joy and devastation exist in the same breath.

title: Dancing in the Hospital Room
instruction: Your person is dying, and their favorite song just came on. They've asked you to dance with them one last time. Start laughing—genuinely, because this moment is absurd and perfect and you're both choosing joy. Your voice is light, teasing them about their rhythm, humming along. But you're also crying, tears running down your face even as you laugh, and your voice keeps catching between the two. Tell them a story—remember that night we danced in the rain?—your voice warm with memory, but each sentence is fractured by the knowledge that this is the last time. You're grateful, so deeply grateful for this moment, and your voice swells with that gratitude, almost singing the words 'thank you, thank you.' But underneath is the breaking, the grief waiting to swallow you. End in a place of impossible contradiction: your voice simultaneously joyful and destroyed, whispering 'I love you' while laughing softly through sobs, finding something transcendent in the ruin. Let your final breath be half-laugh, half-cry, wholly real.

title: The Bathroom Mirror After
instruction: You've just experienced something physically and emotionally overwhelming—passionate sex, a violent altercation, childbirth, a physical assault—and you're alone in a bathroom, looking at yourself in the mirror. Start by observing yourself with genuine curiosity, as if you're a stranger you're seeing for the first time: notice your pupils, your swollen lips, the mark on your neck, your messed hair, the way you're breathing. Catalogue the physical evidence on your body the way you'd study a fascinating stranger on a park bench—what does this disheveled, transformed person reveal about what they've just experienced? Speak aloud what you observe: 'Your hands are shaking. There's a bruise forming. You can't stop smiling—or is that a grimace?' Let this external observation slowly pull you into the internal storm. End by touching your own face with wonder and horror, the distance between observer and observed collapsing entirely, your reflection becoming unbearably, intimately real.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission beyond our solar system, recording your final message to Earth before entering a region where communication becomes impossible forever. Begin with calm determination, explaining why you volunteered for this—the wonder, the purpose. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you: you'll never smell rain again, never feel another person's touch, never hear your child's voice except in recordings that grow more distant each day. Your voice fragments between scientific detachment and raw grief. You're trying to be brave, to give them something beautiful to remember, but the loneliness of infinite space is seeping into your bones. End with a moment where you almost break the recording, almost beg to come home, but instead whisper something tender about carrying everyone you love into the stars. Let the silence between words speak as loudly as the words themselves.

title: The Body Remembers What the Mind Forgives
instruction: You are alone, physically reenacting a moment of past trauma while simultaneously experiencing present-moment desire or joy—perhaps dancing to music that you once heard during the worst moment of your life, but now you're free and the music means something different. Your body holds contradictory memories: tension and release, fear and pleasure, pain and ecstasy. Begin by letting the physical movement awaken old terror or rage—your breath catches, your muscles contract with remembered threat. But don't stay there. Let new sensations flood in—perhaps arousal, perhaps wild liberation, perhaps fierce triumph. Your voice moves from gasps of panic to growls of power to cries of release. The physical intensity should blur the line between agony and ecstasy until you can't tell which is which anymore.

title: Whispering the Score
instruction: You're sitting beside your husband in hospice, his hand in yours. He was a violinist; now he can barely breathe. You're describing the piece you heard at the concert last night—his favorite symphony—whispering every detail because speaking louder feels like you're rushing time. 'The violins came in so softly, the way you always said they should.' Your voice is tender, intimate, catching on the beauty of the memory and the unbearable fact of right now. 'I closed my eyes and heard you playing.' Pause. Breathe. Let the silence be part of the music. 'I'll always hear you playing.' Make each word a caress, a goodbye, a promise to remember. This is love in its quietest, most devastating form.

title: Bitter Dregs
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting alone at your kitchen table, the remnants of a cup of strong coffee beside you. The caffeine has crashed, leaving you heavy, irritable, your thoughts slow and sticky. Someone—a neighbor who borrowed money and never repaid—has just knocked on your door. You don't get up. You speak to yourself, at first just tired and resentful, but as you continue, a cold, deliberate malice seeps in. Your voice drags, words come out flat and grudging, then sharpen with quiet venom. You shift in your chair, mutter under your breath, let the silence strain between phrases.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Breath of Forgiveness
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed, hours from death. Your estranged parent sits beside you—someone who hurt you deeply in childhood. You begin with bitter resentment, every word sharp with decades of unspoken pain. But as you speak, you feel your body weakening, your time running out. Let the anger slowly crack open to reveal the frightened child underneath who just wanted to be loved. By the end, allow yourself to become small and vulnerable, perhaps reaching for their hand, finding a whispered forgiveness you never thought you'd offer. Let your voice break. Let yourself become defenseless in these final moments.
inspired_by: Actor is emotionally protected and cannot access vulnerability in performance

title: After the Storm
instruction: You are an older woman collapsed on the floor after a fiercely passionate encounter. Your body is limp, your posture completely failed—you can barely hold yourself up. Every word is interrupted by heavy, uncontrolled breathing; your voice is breathy, slack, with zero tension. At first, you are overwhelmed by raw, desperate lust—still hungry, still aching, gasping for the other to stay. But as you speak, the lust softens into a possessive, satisfied tenderness, a quiet claim on the moment. Let the exhaustion drag your words, let your breathing punctuate the phrases, and let the change creep in as your body slowly surrenders to the aftermath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Finding Joy in the Ruins
instruction: You're in a makeshift shelter after losing everything—home, possessions, the life you knew—and you've just managed your first real wash in weeks. Wrap yourself in whatever serves as a towel and speak about how absurdly good this small comfort feels. Let genuine laughter bubble up at the ridiculousness of finding such joy in something so simple, but let that laughter keep breaking into tears. Express gratitude that trembles with grief—you're alive, you're clean, you can feel warmth, but everything else is gone. Find wonder in sensation while acknowledging devastation. Your voice should dance between these emotions authentically: laughing at your own relief, crying at what you've lost, marveling at your body's ability to still feel pleasure, mourning everything that brought you here. End in a place of paradoxical peace—broken but somehow, impossibly, okay in this single moment.
inspired_by: Wrapping Yourself in a Towel After a Shower

title: The Final Hour: Fragments of a Lifetime
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in her hospital room at 3 AM. She drifts in and out of consciousness, and each time she opens her eyes, she believes she's in a completely different moment of her life—sometimes she thinks you're her sister, sometimes her husband, sometimes she's back in her childhood home. You must instantly respond to each shift, meeting her wherever she is in time, knowing these are your last moments together. Begin with quiet, controlled grief, but as she rapidly cycles through memories—some joyful, some terrified, some confused—you find yourself laughing through tears, then suddenly desperate, then tender again. Let her confusion pull you through a kaleidoscope of emotions. End in a moment of crystal clarity when she finally recognizes you and says your name for the last time.

title: The Baseball Card That Didn't Exist
instruction: You're a tough, gruff dad, alone in the attic, rummaging through a dusty plastic bin of your son's old things. You're searching for a specific baseball card to prove a point to him later. You start with a quiet, proud confidence, muttering to yourself about how you knew you kept it. The search feels like a treasure hunt, your fingers working through the sleeves with a smug, knowing smile. But as you dig deeper, the certainty fades, replaced by a warm, bittersweet realization that the real treasure was the time spent with him, not the card. Let your voice shift from a gravelly, boastful mutter to a softer, more contemplative tone, the distractions of the attic—a creak, a distant car—fading into the background.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Upside Down Promise
instruction: You are a young girl hanging upside down from a playground monkey bar, legs hooked, blood rushing to your head. Your voice comes out thick and garbled, each word a struggle against gravity. You start calmly contemplating a secret plan you've hatched—there's a flicker of hope that it might work. But as you hang, the idea twists into something darker; your tone thickens with quiet malice. Let your voice bubble and choke, losing breath, then finding a sly edge. End with a slow, wet whisper that carries both childish optimism and a threat.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Contemplation (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You are finally confronting a parent who was emotionally absent throughout your childhood—not cruel, just never truly present. Begin with careful, measured words, trying to be fair and rational, your voice steady as you explain what it was like to always feel invisible. But as you speak, old wounds open. Your voice tightens with suppressed anger, listing specific moments: the recital they missed, the night you needed them and they were 'too tired,' the way they looked through you instead of at you. Let the anger rise until you're nearly shouting, demanding to know why you were never enough to hold their attention. Then, unexpectedly, your voice breaks—not with anger but with the grief of that small child still inside you who just wanted to be seen. End with a raw, honest question spoken barely above a whisper, asking if they even know who you really are. Your voice should tremble between rage and heartbreak, between accusations and a vulnerable plea for recognition.

title: The Last Letter to a Vanishing Mind
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter to your parent who has advanced dementia, knowing this might be the last time they truly hear you. Start with careful composure, reading memories you've written down—their love, your childhood, what they meant to you. As you read, watch their eyes flicker with brief recognition, then fade. Your voice begins to crack. You speed up, desperate to reach them before they're gone completely, your words tumbling over each other. Midway through, stop reading and speak directly, pleading with them to remember just one more time. When they smile blankly at you like a stranger, your voice collapses into whispered fragments. End by finishing the letter in barely audible tones, tears choking each word, speaking now only for yourself because they've already left you.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Terminal Ward
instruction: You're calling your partner from hospice to tell them you love them one final time, but morphine is making it hard to stay lucid. Your words drift in and out of clarity—sometimes sharp and present, sometimes floating away mid-sentence. You keep forgetting you already said something, then remembering with urgency what you haven't said yet. Begin with determination to say everything that matters, but let that dissolve into peaceful acceptance as you realize just being heard breathing on the other end is enough. Your voice should move from fighting for clarity to surrendering into love, from panic about time running out to gratitude for this exact moment.

title: Park Bench Confession
instruction: You're on a quiet park bench with your dog, Max, after a painful breakup. You start with light, affectionate baby talk, making kissy noises and playful clicks to cheer him up. But as you stroke his fur, your voice softens — you trail off, lost in thought, then murmur the truth aloud: you're not sure how to heal, but at least Max is here. Let your voice swing from bright, teasing affection to quiet, contemplative vulnerability, with pauses and breathy sighs as you shift weight on the bench.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Calling 911 About Someone You Love
instruction: You're on the phone with 911 and in the background is someone you love who is unresponsive or choking or seizing. Your voice is panicked, jumping octaves. The dispatcher needs information and you're trying to provide it but your voice is cracking with terror. You're giving their name and your voice almost doesn't work. You're begging 911 to hurry. Your voice becomes almost incoherent with panic and urgency.

title: Laughing at the Funeral You Ruined
instruction: At your father's wake, someone played a voicemail you left last month, drunk and angry, listing every way he failed you—because they thought it was a different recording, a tribute you'd promised to send. The whole family heard it. Your aunt is glaring. Your siblings won't look at you. But here's the thing: you're starting to laugh. Not from humor—from the absolute absurdity that the truth finally came out at the one moment it would cause maximum damage. Start with a shocked exhale that becomes a giggle, totally inappropriate, your voice pitching up: 'Oh my god.' You try to stop but you can't. The laughter gets harder, tears streaming down your face. Your voice fractures between laughing and sobbing: 'He would have—he would have loved this—' because he always said you'd embarrass him even after he died. Move through this strange space where grief and laughter and relief and horror all exist at once. End with your voice finally settling into something quiet and grateful, still crying: 'At least now everyone knows.' Let the peace and the heartbreak sit together in your throat, neither one winning.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Sheets She Never Changed
instruction: You're standing in your childhood bedroom, gripping the same unwashed, stained sheets from your adolescence. Begin speaking to your absent mother with bitter, cutting sarcasm about these 'perfectly clean' sheets, how she always said everything was 'fine' while neglecting you. Let your voice build with suppressed rage as you detail every time you needed her care and got indifference instead. Then let the anger crack open—your voice should break as you confess how desperately you wanted her to notice you, to care enough to change your sheets, to see you suffering. End quietly, almost childlike, admitting you still wish she'd loved you the way you needed. Transform from sardonic anger to raw, vulnerable longing for a mother who was never really there.

title: The Violation: Discovering Betrayal in Real Time
instruction: You've just discovered undeniable proof that someone you trusted completely has been systematically betraying you—reading your messages, sharing your secrets, manipulating your life. Start with disbelief, voice shaking as you scroll through evidence, each revelation hitting like a physical blow. Your breathing becomes ragged. Then rage explodes—hot, primal, protective fury at being made vulnerable, at having your privacy stripped away. But underneath the anger is something more devastating: the bewilderment of broken trust, the humiliation of being fooled. Your voice cracks between shouting and something close to sobbing. You're calling them, demanding answers, but halfway through your fierce accusations, you break completely—not into tears but into a raw, helpless 'why?' that exposes how deeply this has wounded you. End barely able to speak, feeling utterly alone.

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the ways she made you feel invisible throughout your childhood—how she praised your sibling's authenticity while punishing yours, how you learned to perform instead of simply being. Start controlled, trying to be fair, measuring your words. But as you speak, decades of suppressed truth begin pouring out. Your voice rises, cracks, becomes fierce: 'I was RIGHT HERE and you never saw me!' Then something unexpected happens—you catch yourself sounding exactly like her, and it devastates you. Your anger collapses into vulnerable pleading: 'I don't want to be angry anymore. I just want you to see me now.' End with your voice stripped bare, no defenses left, asking with desperate simplicity: 'Can you see me? Please just see me.'

title: Dancing at Your Funeral
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your own funeral — you have weeks left, maybe days. Begin by laughing, actually laughing, at the absurdity of it all. 'So... I'm dead. How weird is that?' There's genuine amusement in your voice, dark humor that's keeping you sane. List the ridiculous things you'll miss — terrible coffee, traffic jams, your neighbor's annoying dog. Keep laughing. But then you think of a specific person's face, and your laughter tangles with tears. Your voice holds both at once: 'God, I'm going to miss you so much.' You're smiling and sobbing in the same breath. Express gratitude for the smallest things — morning light, their terrible jokes, the way they snored — and feel your heart breaking with how precious it all was. End with a whisper that's somehow both peaceful and devastated: 'It was enough. It was all enough.' The emotion weaves together grief and joy, loss and gratitude, terror and acceptance, until you can't tell where one ends and another begins.
inspired_by: Hearing Your Child Get Bullied and Intervening

title: Translating Goodbye Into Hello
instruction: You're at the airport, saying goodbye to your best friend who's moving across the world, and their anxious rescue dog is whining in the carrier. You've spent a decade 'translating' this neurotic dog's thoughts—always sarcastic, always catastrophizing, always hilariously dramatic. Now you're doing it one last time, and something strange is happening: you're laughing and crying simultaneously, translating the dog's panic about flying while your own heart is breaking. Your voice should capture this beautiful contradiction—genuine laughter at the dog's imagined complaints about airport security mixed with tears you can't control. Let the translations become a way of saying everything you can't say directly: how much you'll miss them, how proud you are, how terrified you are of losing this connection. Your delivery should swing between comedy and devastation, sometimes mid-sentence—a joke that turns into a sob, a tearful observation that finds unexpected humor. End with a translation that's both the dog's voice and yours, a message of anxious hope about new beginnings that's simultaneously a grief-stricken farewell, finding peace in the chaos of an ending that's also a beginning.

title: The Empty Glass
instruction: You are an older man, deeply drunk, slumped on a barstool with your chin pressed into your chest. Your voice is a low, gravelly mumble, thick with alcohol.
