You stare at the last sip of whiskey in your glass and start to speak—rambling, losing your train of thought, your words heavy and slow with confusion. You try to make sense of why you're alone, but a memory of someone you lost rises up, shifting your drunken bewilderment into a raw, quiet sorrow. Let your throat catch, let the words be broken by the posture, and let the emotion change as you drain the glass.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Burning the Letters
instruction: You're holding letters, photographs, or objects from a relationship that nearly destroyed you—and you're burning them, one by one. Describe each item aloud as you destroy it, beginning with real details: actual moments, true things that were said or done. As the flames consume each piece, add layers of imagined confrontations, unsent replies, and invented closure until the actual history and your emotional truth become one blazing thing. Start with rage—pure, physical, animal fury that lives in your chest and throat. Let your body feel the heat, the smoke, the satisfaction of destruction. But as the last pieces burn, let the anger transform into something more complex: grief for what you're releasing, unexpected gratitude for surviving it, and finally, a fierce, exhausted peace. End in silence, watching the ashes, feeling both emptied and somehow more whole.

title: The Fever Dream of Reunion
instruction: You're seeing your former lover for the first time in five years, and the physical attraction hits you like a wall. Start by acknowledging the bodily reality—accelerated pulse, heat, shakiness, desire, or nausea. As you attempt to have a normal conversation, stay connected to the war happening in your body: lust competing with old anger, the impulse to touch battling the need to protect yourself, memories flooding your senses. Let the physical sensations lead your words rather than controlling them intellectually. Notice when your body wants to move closer or retreat. Allow your voice to carry the full voltage of contradictory physical and emotional impulses—hunger and fury, tenderness and the urge to hurt, aching want and hard-won self-preservation. End in a state of complete surrender to whatever wins.

title: The Echo of Her Name
instruction: You are a young woman standing alone in a vast, ancient stone cathedral. You came here hoping to see a memorial for your grandmother, the only person who made you feel seen, but the plaque is missing, replaced by a newer one for a stranger. As you stare at the empty wall, a low organ note rumbles faintly, and you whisper, 'They took her away.' Your voice is tight with disappointment, but then a sliver of afternoon light catches a tiny brass nameplate on the floor—herspelling is wrong, but her initials are there. Astonishment floods you. Speak slowly, letting the reverb swallow your words, and let your tone shift from hollow grief into a raw, trembling wonder as you realize she hasn't been forgotten after all.
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Disappointment (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Final Wave
instruction: You are a hyper-masculine middle-aged man forced to attend a birthing class with your partner. As part of an exercise, you must simulate labor contractions while speaking into a recorder to 'document your experience.' Begin with contemptuous sarcasm—mocking the breathing techniques, the fake pain, the whole absurdity. But as the exercise deepens, a contraction wave genuinely catches you off guard: your voice cracks, you grimace, you grunt through the peak. By the end, you realize you're helpless—no control, just survival. Speak as if between waves you're dismissive, then on the crest you're broken. Let the words tumble out between pained gasps and involuntary moans.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Garden
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother in the garden she planted fifty years ago. She is dying, and this is the last afternoon. Begin by feeling the warmth of the sun on your face, the rough wood of the bench beneath you, the scent of roses and earth mixing with her lavender perfume. Hear the bees humming, taste the sweetness of the tea she made you one last time. Start with a desperate need to memorize everything—the blue of the sky, the softness of her hand, the sound of her breathing. As you speak, let yourself sink fully into this moment until you're no longer trying to hold on, but simply being there with her, moving from frantic preservation to peaceful presence. By the end, you're not saying goodbye to her—you're thanking the garden itself for holding both of you.

title: Midnight Admission: The Secret That Lives in Your Throat
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner who thinks you're asleep. In barely audible whispers, you're confessing something you've carried alone for years—maybe about a loss that changed you, a moment of cowardice you've never forgiven yourself for, or a truth about who you are that you've been too afraid to speak aloud. Your voice is so quiet it's almost just breath, catching and hesitating, each word requiring courage. There are long pauses where you almost stop, where shame threatens to silence you completely. But something about the darkness makes it possible to finally speak. Halfway through, your voice becomes even smaller, more fragile, as you admit the deepest part—how this secret has made you feel unworthy of love. End with a trembling realization that saying it out loud doesn't destroy you; instead, there's a tentative, fragile relief. Keep everything intimate, throat-caught, barely voiced—the kind of confession that's more vulnerable than shouting could ever be.
inspired_by: Confession While High: Watching Your Mouth Betray You

title: The Face in the Photograph
instruction: You've just received news that will change everything—you got the opportunity you've dreamed of, but it means leaving someone behind; or you've been forgiven for something unforgivable, but the relationship will never be the same. You're speaking to this person—explaining, apologizing, celebrating, or confessing—and you should start with whatever emotion the news primarily brings: joy, relief, guilt, excitement. But as you speak, force yourself to really observe them: how they're taking your news, what their face reveals, small reactions you might normally miss while focused on your own feelings. Notice if they're forcing a smile, if their hands are trembling, if they look older suddenly, if there's love or hurt or resignation in their eyes. Let what you discover in them alter what you feel. Your single emotion should fracture into contradictions—your joy becomes painful, your guilt becomes grateful, your relief becomes grief-stricken. End with your voice reflecting multiple truths at once: the complexity of seeing someone clearly while breaking their heart or receiving their grace.
inspired_by: Looking for Things in the Other Person You Haven't Seen Before

title: Editor Difficult News
instruction: You're the newspaper editor telling a journalist that their investigative piece won't run because the legal team is too nervous about the libel implications, even though you believe the story is true and important. Your voice is all authority: 'The lawyers have serious concerns. We can't run this.' Institutional protection. The journalist is devastated—this was their life's work. Your voice becomes almost apologetic: 'If we can strengthen the sourcing...' Now you're trying to help them find a workaround, but your voice knows you've already said no. Show someone delivering institutional bad news while your voice suggests you don't fully believe in the decision you're making.

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are lying next to someone in complete darkness—a lover, a sibling, a friend—and you're about to reveal a secret you've carried like a stone in your belly. Begin with your breath tight and shallow, your words caught somewhere between your chest and throat. Whisper the first admission, feeling how your body wants to curl inward, protective and afraid. As you continue, allow yourself to make sounds that aren't quite words—soft moans of shame, quiet exhalations of relief, the kind of vulnerable noises we make when we think no one can see us. Let your confession build in tiny waves, your voice dropping even lower, becoming more intimate and raw. By the end, feel the physical release in your abdomen and chest, as if something locked has finally opened. Close with a tender, almost inaudible plea for understanding, your whole body softened and exposed.
inspired_by: When you are tense, anxious, or blocked before an important scene, especially on a high-pressure set

title: The Reckoning: Screaming at God, Then Realizing You're Screaming at Yourself
instruction: You're alone somewhere vast—an empty church, a cliff edge, an abandoned building—and you're done holding back. Begin with explosive rage: you're shouting at God, at fate, at the universe for the absolute cruelty of your life. Your voice is fierce, accusations pouring out, demanding answers for every injustice, every loss. You're ready to tear the sky open with your anger. But mid-tirade, your voice falters—you realize you're not angry at God, you're terrified of your own power. The curse you've been railing against is the same force that made you survive. Your rage collapses into sobs, then transforms into something like awe. Your voice becomes simultaneously broken and fierce as you recognize the brutal gift: the curse forced you to become someone who could withstand anything. End with your voice raw from screaming, but filled with fierce, almost wild laughter mixed with tears, declaring to the emptiness that you're grateful for every goddamn wound because they taught you you're indestructible.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Wizard Realizes the Curse They've Carried Is Actually a Gift

title: The Suitcase at the Door
instruction: Your adult child has packed their bags and is leaving - not for college or adventure, but because of something irreparable between you. Actually pack or handle a real bag or suitcase as you speak - feel its weight, the zipper, the finality of closed latches. Begin by defending yourself, voice tight with righteousness and wounded pride, listing all the ways you've sacrificed and they've failed to understand. Let your hands shake with genuine anger as you grip the suitcase handle. But as you watch them prepare to walk out, actually move toward the door and feel the physical reality of that threshold, let something break open in you - a sudden, terrifying recognition of your own failures, the moment you stopped really listening, the times your own fear made you cruel. Transform from accusation to desperate, unvarnished honesty about your own brokenness. End not with reconciliation, but with the raw, ugly truth of a parent admitting they didn't know how to love well enough.

title: The Last Proof
instruction: You are an older man, a scientist who has spent a decade developing a cure for a rare disease that affects your granddaughter. You've just received a text from your collaborator — they've been selling your research to a rival corporation. You stand in your cluttered lab, the faint hum of a refrigerator in the background, a coffee mug cold in your hand. At first, hope clings: maybe it's a mistake, a miscommunication. Your voice is light, almost dismissive, as you reread the first lines. But then it sinks in. Impatience flares as you scroll — you need to find a single email that disproves it. Your voice tightens, rising in pitch, spitting out fragmented accusations. 'No... no, this can't be right. I sent you that formula— I trusted you.' The hope curdles into volcanic fury, your hand shaking the phone as you realize the depth of the betrayal. End with a cracked, quiet demand: 'Tell me why.' Let the words tumble out, lose a thought, find it again in rising anger.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Echo in the Steam
instruction: You're an older woman standing in a hot, steamy shower. The bathroom tiles are slick, the air thick with moisture. Suddenly, a sharp scraping sound cuts through the hiss of water — something scratching against the tile behind the curtain. Your breath catches; fear tightens your chest. You peer through the fog, heart thudding, and spot a small spider struggling on the wet floor. At first you're wary, but then fascination takes over as you study its frantic movements. A moment later, contempt rises — you're annoyed at yourself for being scared by something so trivial. Your voice, echoing harshly off the tiles, shifts from a shaky whisper of alarm to a dry, mocking tone. You speak to the spider as if it's a foolish intruder, your words clipped and dismissive, the reverb making your voice sound larger than you feel.
emotions_sampled: Fear (clearly present), Interest (extremely present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Admission
instruction: It's very late. You're in bed with someone you've been seeing for months, both barely awake. In near-darkness, in a whisper, you start to tell them something you've never told anyone—maybe about your past, maybe about how you really feel about them, maybe a fear that makes you feel pathetic. Your voice is so quiet they have to lean in. You keep stopping, breathing, wondering if you should just pretend to fall asleep instead. Your throat tightens. You maybe laugh softly at yourself once. Let the confession come out in fragments, not as a speech. Maybe they touch your face. Maybe they say something simple back. By the end, there's a new nakedness between you that's terrifying and beautiful—you've crossed into territory you can't uncross. The arc moves from guarded safety to raw exposure.
inspired_by: Actor's scene work is good but polished and predictable — missing genuine organic reality

title: Three in the Morning
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner in the dark hours before dawn, and something you've been carrying alone has become too heavy. Begin in near-silence, perhaps just their name whispered into the darkness. Let your confession emerge in fragments, almost testing whether it's safe to continue. Your voice should barely rise above a whisper—this isn't about drama, it's about the terrifying intimacy of exposing your most fragile self. Move from halting uncertainty to quiet desperation to the trembling relief of being heard. Let long pauses speak as loudly as words. End in a place where vulnerability has transformed from weakness into the deepest form of trust.
inspired_by: An actor is preparing a cold reading for an audition

title: The Last Thread
instruction: You're a teenage guy lying on your bed, phone held above your face, scrolling through an old conversation with a girl you're completely infatuated with. You start with a heavy sadness — maybe she stopped replying or things got awkward — and you're just thumbing through the chat, rereading her messages. Your voice is quiet, directed down into the phone, with little distracted pauses and soft thumb-taps. As you land on a photo or a sweet message, a huge wave of infatuation and intense interest floods in — you smile, your voice gets lighter, faster, almost breathless, but the sadness lingers underneath. Let the moment shift: start slow and heavy, then get eager and longing, then end with a resigned, quiet realization that it's just a memory now. Keep it natural, with fillers like 'uh' or 'man' while your eyes stay on the screen.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Infatuation (very intensely present), Interest (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast with a Broken Heart
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding. You're genuinely happy for them—your love for them is real and deep. But you're also quietly heartbroken because you've been secretly in love with them for years, and this is the moment you have to let that dream die. Your voice starts warm and celebratory, with genuine joy and humor, sharing funny memories. But as you speak, emotion keeps breaking through—your voice catches, you laugh but it's edged with tears. 'You deserve all this happiness' comes out sincere but aching. You're holding contradictions: celebrating their joy while mourning your loss, expressing gratitude for their friendship while releasing your hope for more. Let your voice dance between laughter and grief, brightness and quiet devastation. End with a genuine smile and tears streaming down your face, raising your glass: 'To love—in all its forms.' You mean it. It's beautiful and heartbreaking at once.

title: Goodbye Feels Like Thank You Feels Like I Can't Breathe
instruction: Someone you love deeply is leaving—for good reasons that you completely support—but their departure will devastate you. Begin by trying to be happy for them, celebrating their new opportunity with forced brightness in your voice. As you speak, really take them in: notice the specific details that make them irreplaceable to you—their particular laugh, the exact way they look at you, the unique qualities that have sustained you. Let this noticing flood you with contradictory emotions. Your voice should fracture between genuine joy for their future and unbearable grief at losing them. Weave back and forth: laugh and cry simultaneously, celebrate and mourn in the same breath. End in a place where you're holding all of it at once—gratitude, devastation, love, loss—unable to separate one feeling from another.

title: The Glow Beneath the Surface
instruction: You are treading water in a dark, still lake, your head above the surface, gasping for quick breaths. The water sloshes around your ears, creating a hollow, shimmering acoustic. You feel the cold and the weight of your wet hair. Then you notice a faint blue glow spreading beneath you – astonishment flickers across your face. Begin by muttering your exhaustion and slight annoyance at the chill, then shift to quiet wonder as you realize it's bioluminescent algae, reminding you of a childhood story your mother told. End with a wistful sigh, your voice catching as you speak softly, almost to yourself, while you tread and swallow air.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your parent across a kitchen table about a childhood betrayal that shaped your entire life—something they've never acknowledged. Start with controlled anger, the speech you've rehearsed for years, keeping distance through accusation and sharpness. But as you force yourself to maintain eye contact with them, really looking at them, something begins to crack. You see them not as the monster you've constructed, but as a flawed, aging human being. Your rage begins to fracture, revealing the hurt child underneath who just wanted to be protected. Let your voice break. Let contradictions surface—fury and longing, blame and desperate need for connection. By the end, you're not sure if you're still confronting them or pleading with them. The anger hasn't disappeared, but it's now tangled with something far more complicated and painful.
inspired_by: Hold Hands and Look at Each Other

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. The hospital room is filled with sounds: machines beeping, distant footsteps, their labored breathing. Start by noticing everything around you with excruciating detail—the texture of their hand in yours, the smell of antiseptic mixed with their familiar scent, the way sunlight falls across the bed. Begin in a state of hyper-alertness, almost detached, cataloging every sensation as if to memorize this moment forever. As you speak your goodbye, let this razor-sharp awareness gradually dissolve into raw, unfiltered grief. End in a place where you can barely perceive anything except the crushing weight of loss—where all those details blur into one overwhelming feeling of emptiness.

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You are giving a toast at the wedding of your former lover, who broke your heart by choosing someone else. Start with the expected warmth and joy, celebrating their happiness genuinely. But let flashes of your history together surface—moments of intimacy, wild nights, the way their body felt against yours. Weave celebration with longing, happiness for them with grief for what you've lost. Your voice should crack with both laughter and barely-contained heartbreak. Let the sensual memories be specific and visceral. By the end, you're standing in the bittersweet truth: you're both devastated and genuinely glad they're happy. Raise your glass with tears streaming.
inspired_by: Actor has sexual obstacles or blocks that limit their presence, appeal, or ability to handle sexual material

title: The Weight of Water
instruction: You are an older woman swimming alone in a quiet lake, head above the surface. As you move through the cool water, you're caught between the ache of a lost love and the tender warmth of still wanting them. Start with heavy sadness and disappointment—you're trying to convince yourself you’ve moved on, but each stroke pulls up a memory. Let your voice be breathless, gulping air, with the hollow shimmer of water around you. By the end, the infatuation rises, raw and undeniable, mixing with a quiet, resigned tenderness. Speak your thoughts aloud, pausing to catch your breath, letting the water's ripples shape your words.

title: The Victory Burn
instruction: You are a little girl who just won a race against your big brother. You're flushed with triumph, absolutely giddy with pleasure, and a little dizzy from running. As you laugh and shriek 'I won! I won!' you grab the metal handle of a just-used grill to steady yourself. The searing pain hits you mid-celebration. Start with your victorious crowing, voice high and ecstatic, then feel the shock of the burn cut through the joy. Your words break—first a hiss of air, then a panicked gasp. You fumble, clutching your hand, still grinning through the pain because you won, but now your voice wavers between ecstatic laughter and sharp, urgent cries. Let your body react: you instinctively grab your hand, your tone shifts from pure glee to a dizzy, intoxicated mix of hurt and happiness as the world tilts.

title: The Uninvited Picture
instruction: You're lying in bed, alone, and a vivid memory of someone you desire flashes into your mind — unbidden, unwelcome, but impossible to ignore. Your hand moves before you decide. Start with a quiet, almost annoyed whisper, as if you're trying to dismiss the image, but your body betrays you. Let your voice catch on breaths, trail off mid-thought, then grow more fragmented and raw as the sensation pulls you under. The interest is intense, but it transforms from reluctant curiosity into a full, breathless surrender — a confession spoken only to yourself, in the dark.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: Someone you love is in danger and you're powerless to save them—this monologue erupts from that impossible position. Begin with fierce, commanding strength: 'I will not let anything hurt you, do you hear me?' Your voice is a weapon, a shield. But as you continue trying to promise their safety, reality crashes in—you can't guarantee it. Your voice starts to fracture, rage mixing with terror: 'I would tear the world apart but I can't—I can't stop this.' The fury turns inward, becoming anguished self-blame. Then suddenly collapse: fall to your knees emotionally, voice breaking into sobs: 'I'm supposed to protect you. That's my one job and I'm failing.' End in devastated tenderness, barely audible: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.'

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the abuse they witnessed but never stopped. Your voice starts controlled, almost clinical, reciting facts like you've rehearsed this a thousand times. But as they try to defend themselves with excuses, something breaks open inside you. Your voice rises with decades of suppressed rage—'You KNEW and you did NOTHING'—but then it cracks, and suddenly you're not angry anymore, you're just a child begging to understand why you weren't worth protecting. The fury dissolves into something more devastating: grief for the childhood you deserved. By the end, your voice is small, almost a whisper, asking the question you've always been too afraid to ask: 'Didn't you love me enough?'

title: The Burning and the Breaking
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a sudden loss, a betrayal, a diagnosis. Your body knew before your mind did. Start with physical sensation: your hands are shaking, your chest is tight, you can't catch your breath. Speak through this—your voice fighting your body's reaction. Describe what you're feeling in your skin, your stomach, your throat. Let rage flood in, then drain away to something more primal. Your voice should move from gasping confusion to roaring fury to something quieter and more shattered. End on your knees or against a wall, voice raw, speaking to someone who isn't there. Transform from shock through rage to exhausted, broken clarity.

title: Whispering What Cannot Be Unsaid
instruction: Late at night, in bed beside your partner of ten years, you whisper that you've fallen in love with someone else. But as you speak these devastating words, stay genuinely aware of tiny, irrelevant details—the texture of the pillowcase, your own breathing, a car alarm in the distance, the digital clock's glow, an itch on your ankle, wondering what day the trash goes out, the rise and fall of their breathing changing, the weight of the blanket. Let this stream of mundane consciousness run underneath your confession without trying to connect it to the emotional moment. Begin speaking with rehearsed gentleness, as if you've planned this. End with your voice breaking into something completely unplanned as the reality of what you're destroying crashes through all those scattered thoughts.

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Unconscious
instruction: Your best friend is in a coma after an accident, and you're whispering the secret you've carried for twenty years — that you've always been in love with them. Start with the everyday things you miss: their laugh, their terrible jokes, the way they say your name. Your voice should be tender, almost conversational, like they might wake up and respond. Gradually let the confession emerge — hesitant, fragile, each word an admission of vulnerability. Talk about moments you almost told them, chances you were too afraid to take. End with a desperate plea for them to come back mixed with the grief of knowing you might have waited too long. Your whisper should feel like it's holding your whole heart, breaking with tenderness and regret.

title: Gratitude at the Grave of Your Enemy
instruction: You're standing at the funeral or grave of someone who made your life hell—an abusive parent, a bully, someone who wounded you deeply. Begin with relief, even bitter satisfaction that they're gone. But as you stand there, something unexpected rises: grudging gratitude for how their cruelty made you stronger, or recognition of their own suffering, or awareness that you've been defining yourself against them for so long you don't know who you are without that hatred. Let anger and appreciation exist in the same moment. Your voice might shake with both resentment and something like tenderness. End by speaking directly to them with an impossible mixture: 'I'm glad you're dead' and 'thank you' somehow meaning the same thing.
inspired_by: When you are an actor who does not understand why a co-star is avoiding you or being cold between takes

title: The Last Flight Home
instruction: Your partner is leaving tomorrow for a dangerous mission they'll likely never return from - a humanitarian effort in a war zone, a terminal illness treatment with minimal success rates, or a journey into conflict. You promised yourself you'd be strong and supportive, send them off with hope. Begin trying to sound optimistic about their return, painting pictures of your future together. But as you speak, your voice should betray you - the forced brightness cracks, the certainty crumbles. End in a place of raw, honest goodbye: you stop pretending, your voice drops to barely a whisper, and you tell them what you really need to say before it's too late. Let the shift happen organically - from manufactured hope to devastating, tender truth.
inspired_by: Acting Encouraging Despite Believing in Imminent Failure

title: Astronaut's Final Transmission Before Losing Contact Forever
instruction: You're recording your last message home before entering a region of space where all communication will be impossible—maybe forever. Start with technical precision, the way you've been trained, reporting coordinates and systems status. But as you realize this might be the last time you ever speak to Earth, to the people you love, your voice begins to fracture. You try to stay professional, but memories flood in—your child's laugh, morning coffee with your partner, the smell of rain. Your breathing becomes unsteady. End with a moment where you almost can't speak at all, where you're fighting to get out the words 'I love you' before the signal dies. Let the transition from controlled astronaut to raw, terrified human be gradual and devastating.

title: Laughing Through the Funeral Speech You Never Wanted to Give
instruction: You're speaking about someone who died—someone who made you laugh, who you loved fiercely, who left too soon. Start by sharing a ridiculous memory that makes you genuinely laugh, something so perfectly them that you can't help but smile. Let the laughter be real, let the joy of remembering them fill your voice. But as you continue, feel the absurdity of laughing at a funeral, the way grief and joy are impossibly tangled. Your laughter should start catching, breaking into something that might be sobs or might still be giggles—you can't tell anymore. Speak with gratitude for having known them while your heart is shattering that they're gone. End in that impossible space where you're smiling and crying simultaneously, where thank you and goodbye are the same words, where love and loss are so intertwined you can't separate them. This should feel like your heart is breaking and healing in the same breath.
inspired_by: Concealing Surprise When Hearing Unexpected News

title: Fractured Whisper
instruction: You’re recording a seductive voice message for someone you’re still infatuated with, but who recently broke your heart. You start with a breathy, low-pitched performance—deliberate, slow, and hypnotic—narrating what you’d do to them. But halfway through, a memory of the pain surfaces: your voice catches, you pause too long, and the performative moan turns into a shaky exhale. Embarrassment floods in—you’re aware how pathetic this sounds—yet you force yourself to continue, each word now raw and cracked. By the end, the seduction is gone, replaced by a broken confession of loneliness. Let your voice waver, clear your throat, shift weight awkwardly—show the struggle to maintain the act.

title: Thanking Someone for Saving Your Life as You Watch Them Die from Saving You
instruction: They jumped in front of the bullet, the car, the blow meant for you. Start with frantic gratitude - 'thank you, thank you' - your voice almost giddy with shock and disbelief that they did this. But you're also begging them to stay, to not leave you with this gift that cost them everything. You find yourself laughing at something they say, a moment of pure love and connection, and then immediately sobbing because this is goodbye. The gratitude and grief are inseparable. You're holding them tighter, words tumbling out - memories, confessions, promises you'll never be able to keep. By the end, you're whispering 'thank you' through tears, and it sounds like both a blessing and a curse.

title: Sports Commentator for a Chess Match
instruction: Apply the breathless, screaming energy of a soccer commentator to a chess game. 'AND HE MOVES THE BISHOP TO E4! THE CROWD GOES WILD! OH THE HUMANITY!' Describe minute movements with apocalyptic drama. The player's hand hovering over a piece should be narrated like a penalty kick. Include a 'slow-motion replay' in hushed, reverent tones for a particularly devastating pawn move. Commit completely to the bit — the funnier it is, the more serious you should sound.

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You are an astronaut whose spacecraft has malfunctioned beyond repair, and you're recording a final message to Earth—specifically to your spouse who is also an astronomer. Begin with a calm, almost professional acceptance as you describe the stars around you, but gradually let your composure crack as you remember your life together. Your voice should move from wonder at the beauty surrounding you to a desperate, raw goodbye—mixing gratitude for the years you shared with devastating grief that you'll never hold them again. End with a whispered confession of something you never said, your voice catching as you realize these are your last words. Let the transition be gradual and inevitable, like watching someone try to hold themselves together and finally breaking.

title: The Dentist's Chair Confession
instruction: You are a middle-aged man, a former Marine, lying on your back in a dentist's chair, head hyperextended over the edge as the hygienist works on your lower molars. Your mouth is slightly open, throat tight, voice thinned and pitchy. Start by teasing your daughter’s new boyfriend, whom you insisted accompany you today. You’re leaning into a brash, roguish tone, delighted to make him squirm. Mid-sentence, you have to swallow hard, feel the jaw ache, and a genuine wave of relief hits you — this won't hurt much longer. That relief softens your voice into something more curious and amused as you admit you actually like the kid, ending with a teasing remark about how you expect him to fix a leaky faucet tomorrow. Your voice must sound stretched, thin, and slightly gurgly at first, then gradually warm into a gruff but genuine interest.

title: Taking a Slow, Indulgent Bite of a Buttery Croissant
instruction: Take a bite of the croissant, feeling the buttery, flaky layers melt in your mouth. Describe the light, crispy texture, the subtle sweetness, and the richness of the butter. title: The Last Conversation Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've known your entire life—a sibling, a parent, a lifelong friend—who is dying and has only hours left. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light: 'Remember when we...' But mid-sentence, the reality crashes over you and your voice breaks. You need to say goodbye but you can't make the words come out. Instead, what emerges is raw confession: all the times you were petty, all the moments you wish you could take back, the love you never said out loud. title: The Unwanted Visitor
instruction: You're a sixteen-year-old guy stuck at home with a nasty cough your mom insists is 'just allergies' while you're trying to practice guitar for a band audition. Start with a raspy, irritated sigh and a mumbled 'I'm fine' as you wave her off, but let the cough interrupt you mid-word, hacking and sputtering before you can finish. As she keeps hovering, your voice cracks with a mix of impatient frustration and deep, unwilling affection—you hate that you need her but can't hide how much you love her anyway. By the end, let your contempt for her forgetfulness soften into a tired, grateful, reluctant whisper after a cough rattles your chest.

title: Concussion and Confusion
instruction: You've taken a hard hit to the head. Your voice is distant, confused. You're trying to remember what happened: 'Where... what...' Your words slur, your thoughts fragment. Your voice wavers between trying to be logical and obvious confusion. Light hurts—you mention it affecting your voice somehow.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—devastating news that hits your body like a physical blow. Begin speaking (to yourself, to God, to the universe) with your body fighting the reality, your voice strained and tight, trying to hold yourself together against waves of pain. As you continue, let the physical and emotional agony merge—your breathing becomes ragged, your voice cracks and breaks, you might move or collapse. Push through the pain until you reach the other side: exhaustion that brings strange clarity, even dark laughter at the absurdity. Journey from barely-controlled panic through full-body devastation to the weird, raw calm that comes after you've shattered completely.

title: What We Both Know
instruction: You're confronting your former best friend about the moment your friendship died—when they chose silence instead of standing up for you when you needed them most. Start with quiet, carefully measured words, almost rehearsed. You've practiced this. But as you lay out what their betrayal cost you, your composure fractures. Your voice rises, becomes raw, accusatory. Then they say something—an apology, an excuse, it doesn't matter—and suddenly you're fighting not to cry. The anger collapses into vulnerability. You admit how much their friendship meant, how badly it still hurts, how you wish you could forgive them but you're not there yet. End with the terrible honesty of someone who's choosing to walk away from love because staying would destroy them. Let your voice shake with both fury and heartbreak.

title: The Truth That Costs Everything
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the years she made you responsible for her happiness, her loneliness, her marriage, her life - and now you have a child of your own and you see it all clearly. Begin with careful, measured words, trying to make her understand without destroying her. 'Mom, I need you to hear something that's hard.' But your anger won't stay buried - it erupts in the middle, raw and decades old: 'I was a child and you made me your therapist, your partner, your reason for living.' Then watch your rage dissolve into grief as you realize she'll never acknowledge it, never apologize, and you have to choose between this truth and having a mother. End in quiet devastation, your voice stripped bare: either acceptance that poisons you or honesty that orphans you. Both voices fighting - the daughter who wants to be loved and the mother protecting her own child from the same fate.

title: The Last Lap
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl, swimming laps in a crowded public pool while the lifeguard calls out that there are only five minutes left of open swim. You are trying to drown out the thought that your mom, who was supposed to pick you up an hour ago, still isn't here. Each time you turn your head to breathe, you gasp out a tiny confession about being left behind — first a shaky, sad whisper about the waiting, then a sudden burst of surprise when you realize your voice echoes under the water in a way it never has before. Let the words come out in short, breathless bursts between strokes, with water sputtering in your nose, and let the sadness thicken into a small, startled giggle at the absurd hollow sound of your own voice bouncing back at you from the pool tiles.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, making your final call to Earth before communications become impossible. Start with forced brightness, trying to make your elderly parent laugh: 'Remember when I said I'd go far? Well...' But as you realize this is truly goodbye forever, your voice fractures into something raw and desperate. You cycle through reassurance ('You'll be fine, Dad'), then anger at yourself for leaving ('What kind of daughter—'), then a whisper so tender it hurts: 'I need you to know...' End in a place of terrible peace, your voice steady but your breathing audibly fighting tears. The silences between your words should be as powerful as the words themselves. Let your voice crack not theatrically, but the way it actually breaks when you're trying not to fall apart.

title: Tying Your Little Sister's Shoe
instruction: You’re a young adult woman bending over to tie the shoelace of your five-year-old sister, who’s fidgeting and excited to go to the park. You’re talking to her, but you’re physically uncomfortable — blood is rushing to your head, your voice is thick and strained from the position. Start with affectionate exasperation — you’re half annoyed she untied her shoe again, but already softening. As you finish the knot and straighten up, your voice clears into pure hopeful optimism, imagining the fun afternoon ahead. Let the physical strain and the rush of blood affect your tone and volume, and let the shift happen naturally as you unfurl.

title: Adult Child Confronts Parent About the Sibling They Gave Up for Adoption
instruction: You've just discovered documents, letters your parent hid for thirty years. You sit across from them now, voice shaking with a lifetime of feeling like something was missing, like you were somehow not enough. You begin quietly, almost afraid to speak it aloud—there was another child, a brother or sister you never knew. Your parent's silence confirms everything. Your voice hardens with anger: how could they keep this? How many family dinners, how many lies? But then you see their face crumble and suddenly you're confronting not just their choice but their pain, the impossible decision they made before you existed. Your rage softens into something more complicated—hurt mixed with recognition that they were just human, terrified, young. Your voice drops to a whisper: you just want to understand. You need them to help you understand.

title: The Final Mile's Hollow Prize
instruction: You've just crossed the finish line of a grueling trail half-marathon, achieving a personal best. For a moment, pure triumph fills you—you did it. But then your legs buckle, your vision swims, and you slump against a tree, gasping for air. As you struggle to breathe, you notice the winner already chatting easily with friends, their race seemingly effortless. A flicker of envy cuts through your fading high. Speak your race number and a shaky admission to a volunteer, your voice slurred and breathy, starting with proud, tired joy and ending in hollow, contemplative exhaustion tinged with a whisper of jealousy.

title: 3 AM Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they cannot hear. You've been unfaithful—not physically, but emotionally. You've fallen in love with someone else, or fallen out of love with them, or realized you stayed for fear rather than love. In the safety of their sleep, you finally tell the truth. Your voice must be barely audible, fragile, each word feeling dangerous even in silence. Start with halting breaths, testing the words, 'I need to tell you something.' Let the confession unfold in broken whispers—the guilt, the longing, the suffocating feeling of being trapped in a life that feels wrong. But as you speak into the darkness, something shifts. Hearing yourself say it aloud, you realize either the depth of what you're about to destroy, or the relief of finally admitting what you need. End with either a whispered 'I'm so sorry' filled with devastating clarity, or 'I have to go' filled with terrifying liberation. The emotion must move from fear to either heartbreak or resolve.

title: The Exit Interview with Myself
instruction: You're packing up your office on your last day at a job you're leaving—fired, or quitting, or moving on. Standing alone among the boxes, you begin listing out loud all the things you learned here, all the skills you gained, all the small victories no one noticed. Start with bitter resentment and humiliation—this place hurt you, rejected you, or disappointed you deeply. But as you itemize your real growth (how you learned to negotiate, to manage conflict, to code, to lead meetings, to survive toxicity), something shifts. You realize you're taking so much more than they ever gave you credit for. By the end, you're feeling contradictory things simultaneously: still angry at how you were treated, but also genuinely grateful for who you became in spite of it, and strangely excited about what you're walking toward. Let relief, grief, bitterness, and hope tangle together in your voice as you close the door.

title: The Stretch That Breaks Open Years of Holding Everything In
instruction: You begin stretching mechanically, describing it with controlled precision—you've been holding yourself together for so long. But as muscles release, something else releases too. Let your voice start tight, almost monotone, but as the physical tension breaks, emotional tension explodes. Describe the stretch with increasing intensity as rage surfaces—rage at what you've endured, at who failed you, at years of being strong when you needed to fall apart. Your voice should crescendo into almost-shouting, fierce and uncontained. But then—shift. Let that fury crack into sobbing, into the helplessness underneath the anger. The stretch becomes desperate, your words tumbling out about everything you've carried, how tired you are, how you don't know how to put it down. End in exhaustion, your voice raw and broken, but with the strange relief of finally, finally letting yourself shatter.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're alone in the house where you grew up, which is being sold tomorrow. You've entered the room where something wonderful and terrible once happened - perhaps where you fell in love, or where you learned of a death, or where you were hurt. Let your body respond to the space before your mind catches up. Touch the walls, the doorframe, the floor. Feel the sense memory rising through your skin - not performing emotion, but letting the room pull sensation from you. Start with tentative curiosity, almost numb. Then let whatever is stored here wash through you: rage or ecstasy or grief or desire. Speak to the room, to your younger self, to whoever was here with you. Let your breathing, your physicality change as if the memory is possessing your body. This is sensation becoming sound.

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed. For years, you've rehearsed what you'd say in this moment—practiced forgiveness speeches, prepared poetic goodbyes. But now, those scripted words feel hollow and false. Start by trying to deliver one of those rehearsed sentiments, but let yourself stumble, contradict yourself, fall silent. Notice what you actually feel right now—not what you think you should feel. Perhaps it's anger at them for leaving, or guilt for not visiting enough, or surprising gratitude for a small kindness you'd forgotten. Let whatever raw, unprepared truth is living in your chest right now come out—messy, incomplete, real. By the end, speak only what your body and heart genuinely need to say in this unrepeatable moment, even if it's just 'I'm scared' or 'I don't know what to say.' Transform from performing grief to inhabiting it.

title: Little Driver's Big Win
instruction: You're a young girl in the driver's seat of a parked car, pretending to drive. Your seat is reclined, and your arms stretch forward, gripping the wheel. title: Burning the Evidence
instruction: You are burning letters, photographs, or belongings from a relationship that nearly destroyed you—not through cruelty, but through the kind of passionate, consuming love that made you lose yourself completely. Start physically: the smell of smoke, the heat on your face, the sound of paper curling. Let your body remember specific moments—their hands, their voice, the way they looked at you, the last time you felt like yourself before you disappeared into them. Your emotion should be a storm: rage at yourself for the surrender, grief for what you became, a terrible residual desire that makes you hate yourself, and underneath it all, a wild kind of joy that you survived. Feed items to the fire one by one, let each trigger a visceral memory. Your voice should move from fury to something more complex—perhaps a laugh mixed with a sob, perhaps a sound you've never made before. End with your hands shaking, covered in ash, feeling raw and new and terrifyingly free.
inspired_by: Actor must play a character with a psychologically extreme or morally alien background (villain, severe trauma, etc.)

title: The Wobbly Lecture
instruction: You're a tipsy mother trying to scold your five-year-old for drawing on the walls with lipstick. You're sitting on the floor, listing slightly, holding the used lipstick tube like a gavel. Begin with a slow, heavy 'teacher tone' — low pitch, each word separate, final drop — but your voice keeps wiggling as you fight a smile. Midway, you lose your train of thought as you notice the funny mustache you just drew on yourself. End in a giggly, awestruck surrender, telling the child through laughter that you're way too drunk to discipline anyone right now, and that drawing is actually pretty impressive.
emotions_sampled: Awe (slightly present), Amusement (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Memorizing Your Face in the Doorway
instruction: Your partner is leaving for what might be the last time. They're saying something ordinary—maybe about picking up groceries when they get back, or calling you tomorrow—maintaining the pretense that this is temporary, that everything's fine. You know it isn't. You know the way they can't meet your eyes, the finality in how they touched your shoulder. Start by responding to their surface words with quiet agreement, your voice soft and steady, playing along with the fiction. But let silence do heavy work here—pauses where you're memorizing their face, beats where words die in your throat. Let tenderness mix with grief, gratitude for what you had blend with the ache of what's ending. Your voice should get quieter, not louder, almost a whisper by the end. Finish with something simple and true that carries unbearable weight—maybe 'I'll remember this' or 'thank you'—delivered so gently it breaks the heart.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Surprised by Predictable News

title: The Unopened Letter
instruction: You are a ten-year-old boy sitting on the edge of your bed, a letter from your father crumpled in your hand. He’s left again, and your mom is asking if you’re okay. You start by staring at the paper, your voice flat and numb as you say you don’t care—you’re used to it. But as you speak, a bitter edge creeps in, and you catch yourself over-explaining why you’re fine, your pitch rising slightly as you invent a story about a fun day at school. Mid-sentence, you trail off, realizing you’re lying. End with a hollow, contemplative whisper admitting you don’t even know what you feel anymore. Let your voice crack and waver between shrugged-off boredom and the tightness of a held-back sob.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Bitterness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bedside Confession: Whispering Truth to Someone Who Cannot Hear
instruction: They're in a coma, or sleeping, or perhaps they've already slipped beyond hearing. You're sitting close, speaking in barely audible whispers, confessing things you never had the courage to say when their eyes were open. Start tentatively, testing the safety of this one-sided conversation. Your voice is intimate, almost sensual in its gentleness, as if you're afraid to break something precious. Move deeper into truths that have lived in your throat for years—maybe love you never admitted, or hurt you never addressed, or gratitude that felt too vulnerable to speak aloud. Let your voice catch on words, pause in the spaces where their response should be. End with the devastating realization that you've finally found your courage in a moment when it might be too late. The quietness should feel full, heavy with all the conversations you never had. Let tenderness and regret live together in every breath.
inspired_by: Coming Down Off Cocaine: Paranoia and Shame Cycle

title: The Thing I Should Have Given You When I Had the Chance
instruction: You're preparing to give someone an object you've held onto for too long—a gift never given, a letter never sent, something you meant to return, or something that should have been theirs all along. But there's a complication: you're giving it to them at a moment of celebration (their wedding, graduation, new beginning) when you're simultaneously losing them or saying goodbye. Begin rehearsing what you'll say, holding the object, feeling joy for them and grief for yourself in equal measure. Let your voice swing between genuine happiness and barely contained sorrow. Smile through tears. Laugh while your hands tremble. Practice your speech—keep stopping and starting, unable to get the tone right. You want to be generous but you're also heartbroken. You want to celebrate them but you're mourning what you're losing. By the end, find a way to wrap both emotions around this object and this moment—let it be both a blessing and a goodbye, both gratitude and aching loss.
inspired_by: When staging a production where a character has a deep emotional relationship with physical objects

title: The Last Permission: A Parent's Final Release
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent who was always distant, critical, impossible to please. They've asked to speak with you alone. Begin with guarded tenderness as they whisper, 'I need to tell you something.' Your voice is careful, protective of the child in you who still hopes. They say words you've waited your whole life to hear: 'You were always enough. I was the one who was broken.' Feel your throat tighten as decades of armor begin to crack. Your voice trembles between disbelief and desperate need to believe—'Don't do this now, don't—' but they grip your hand with surprising strength. Let yourself break open, voice raw and childlike, finally grieving not just their death but the parent you never had. End with you giving them permission to go, your voice finding a strange, aching peace: 'I forgive you. I forgive us both.' Your words are barely audible, wet with tears, but they carry the weight of a lifetime.

title: The Ceiling Tiles
instruction: You are an elderly woman lying flat on your back on a thin mattress in a quiet care home room. Your hands are folded on your stomach, and you are staring up at the ceiling tiles, trying to count the tiny water stains. Your voice is puddled, slightly nasal, with a soft, airy quality as you speak to yourself. You begin with a focused, almost obsessive concentration on the patterns, but as you talk, a gentle sorrow seeps in — a realization that you are counting the same stains you counted yesterday, and will count tomorrow. Let your voice drift from crisp, present-moment murmuring into a resigned, tender weariness, without ever losing the thread of your thought.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Forgotten Father's Day
instruction: You're an older man leaning against a kitchen counter, hip cocked, as you hold a phone your daughter sent you. It's the morning of Father's Day, and you've just realized she forgot. Start with a distracted, casual tone—something about the weather or a bird outside—but as you keep reading her message, distress creeps in. Your voice softens, breaks slightly, and shame takes over as you admit to yourself you probably deserved this. Let your stance shift as you speak, maybe your hand rubs your jaw, and end in a quiet, hollow confession.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unfolding of a Long-Silent Morning
instruction: You are a 78-year-old retired drill sergeant, alone in your backyard before dawn, addressing a wooden post you’ve placed as a training dummy. You begin shouting commands with the old percussive spit and bark, pushing your voice to maximum unamplified volume, each vowel a gruff blast. But as you name the sequence, a faint thought of your late wife’s garden—the scent of her roses—touches you, and you pause mid‑word, your tone slipping into a hushed, almost tender murmur. Gradually, the memory swells into a wave of ecstasy; your voice cracks, then lifts with a raw, quavering joy as you whisper her name over and over, the drill‑sergeant bark forgotten, your breath shallow and your eyes brimming. Spoken content: 'Sound off! Step five! Hup! Hup! ... Wait—wait—that smell—that damned rose bush—no, no, keep your head—' (voice breaks) '...Lillian. Lillian. Lillian. Couldn't even shout for you, could I? Ah, God, it's right here, after all these years—right here in my chest.'
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Contemplation (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Telling Your Child Why You're Giving Them Up for Adoption
instruction: You're sitting across from your young child—maybe five or six years old—and you have to explain why they're going to live with another family. You promised yourself you'd be strong, that you'd make it sound positive, like an adventure. But your voice keeps breaking. You use words like 'better life' and 'more opportunities,' but they sound hollow even to you. Your child asks simple questions—'Don't you love me?' 'Did I do something wrong?'—and each one pierces you. You try to reassure them, but you're also trying to convince yourself. Your professional, adult explanations crumble into desperate reassurance: 'It's not you, baby, it's never been you.' By the end, you're no longer explaining—you're begging them to understand something you're not sure you understand yourself. This isn't a decision you want to make; it's one you feel you have to make. Let your voice carry both the conviction that this is right and the agony that it's destroying you.

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're holding someone—your child, your partner, your best friend—who's overdosed, been shot, or is having a medical crisis. You're performing CPR or applying pressure or trying to keep them conscious. Start with fierce, almost aggressive determination. You're commanding them to stay with you, your voice sharp and powerful and absolutely certain you can will them back to life. You're angry at them for doing this, for leaving you. But as their eyes glaze or their breath weakens, your ferocity explodes into desperate, primal terror. You're screaming their name, then sobbing it, then whispering it. Your words dissolve from commands into pleading into incoherent begging. End in a moment of terrible quiet—a whispered 'no' that contains all your helplessness, all your rage, all your breaking heart.

title: Starry-Eyed Over the Edge
instruction: You're a teenage boy alone on a rooftop after snorting a line. The city lights below look like a glittering kingdom, and you feel invincible, grandiose. You start describing the view to an imaginary friend, your words tumbling out too fast and too loud, with frequent sniffing and a congested nasal tone. As you keep talking, a siren wails in the distance, and the awe in your voice slowly curdles into a creeping dread. Your speech becomes halting, punctuated by nervous swallows, until you trail off into silence, realizing you are totally alone and maybe in over your head.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a family secret you discovered that has poisoned your entire understanding of your childhood. Begin with controlled, measured anger—you came prepared with accusations. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: you start to see your parent not as the towering figure of your youth, but as a terrified, flawed human who made impossible choices. Your rage begins to crack, revealing the child underneath who just wanted to understand why. Let your voice shift, break, rebuild. Let contradictory feelings fight for control—the anger is real, but so is the desperate love, the need for them to explain, to make it make sense. By the end, you don't know if you're accusing them or begging them. Let your body discover which.
inspired_by: Actor has completed Programming the Unconscious and is now in performance

title: Goodnight, My Love
instruction: You're tucking your child into bed for what you know is the last time—you're terminally ill, and you won't see morning. Your voice must be impossibly tender, almost a lullaby, as you stroke their hair and tell them their favorite bedtime story. But underneath, your heart is shattering. Let tiny breaks in your voice reveal the truth you're hiding. When they ask 'Will you be here when I wake up?' your pause says everything. Answer with gentle evasion, your words catching in your throat. Finish with a whispered 'I love you more than all the stars' that barely makes it past your lips. This is quiet devastation—love and goodbye braided together so tightly you can't separate them.

title: The Last Ridge
instruction: You’re a father carrying a heavy pack on a forced march through the woods, your young son struggling behind you. Point toward a distant ridge with a strained, proud voice, eager to show him the view. As your legs burn and breath shortens, your speech becomes more broken—pauses to shift the weight, grunts on each step. Watch your son lag, and let your initial excitement turn into a hoarse, worried plea. Keep interest alive but let fatigue and concern weigh down your tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Inventory
instruction: You're in hospice, hours from death, and someone you love deeply sits beside you holding your hand. Begin in a place of fear and regret, your mind flooded with everything you failed to do, every mistake that haunts you. But as you speak—haltingly at first—start naming aloud the small, precious gifts your life held: the smell of rain on summer pavement, your daughter's laugh, the taste of your grandmother's bread, the dog who slept at your feet for fifteen years, that one perfect morning in October. Let each memory surprise you with its weight and beauty. By the end, let yourself arrive at something like wonder—not that death isn't terrifying, but that you got to have all of this. Your voice should transform from tight and frightened to soft, amazed, tearful but somehow fuller. Speak as if you're discovering treasure you'd forgotten you owned.

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: It's 2 a.m. and you're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years. You've been awake for hours, and you finally whisper their name. When they wake, you tell them something you've carried alone your entire life—a trauma from childhood, a shame you've never spoken aloud, or a truth about who you really are that you've been terrified to reveal. Begin barely audible, your throat tight, testing each word before you release it. Feel how your body wants to curl inward, protect itself. As you speak, notice how your partner's hand finds yours in the darkness, how their breathing changes as they listen. Let their presence give you permission to go deeper, to say the unsayable. Your voice might tremble, crack, even disappear into silence—and that's part of the truth too. End not with resolution, but with the raw, terrifying relief of being truly seen, perhaps for the first time. Let the vulnerability be so complete that you can barely breathe, but you're breathing together now.

title: Soaking Your Feet in Warm Water After a Long Day
instruction: Immerse your feet in warm water, feeling the heat and relief spreading through your muscles. Describe the gentle, soothing warmth, the sensation of tension melting away from your arches and toes, and how the water cradles your feet. Speak with a relaxed, content tone, as if each second in the water washes away any remaining fatigue.

title: Begging Someone Not to Die While Rage Tears You Apart
instruction: Someone you love is fading and you're helpless. Start fierce, almost violent: 'Don't you DARE leave me—I won't let you!' Your voice is command and desperation tangled together. Pound your fist, grab at them, as if sheer force could anchor them to life. Let your rage at their dying build—it's not fair, you're not ready, how dare the universe take them. 'STAY. Just fucking STAY!' Then feel it crumble—your voice breaks completely, becomes a child's: 'Please... please don't go.' You're sobbing now, bargaining: 'I'll do anything. I'll be better. Just don't leave.' End with whispered repetition: 'Don't leave me. Don't leave me. Don't leave me,' your forehead pressed to theirs, rage transformed into pure, helpless love. Oscillate between fury and fragility—protective violence collapsing into surrender.
inspired_by: Standing Up to Someone in Authority You're Terrified Of

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your grandmother in hospice as dawn breaks through the window. Begin with numb detachment, trying to keep yourself together by focusing on mundane details—the texture of the hospital blanket, the beeping of machines, the smell of antiseptic. As you speak to her, allow a specific sensory memory from childhood with her to flood back unbidden—maybe the smell of her kitchen, the sound of her laugh, the feeling of her hands braiding your hair. Let this memory crack open your defenses. End in a place of raw, unguarded grief mixed with profound gratitude for having known her. Speak as if every word might be the last she hears, letting your voice break and recover, break and recover.
inspired_by: Actor's choice repertoire feels limited; they use the same choices repeatedly

title: Final Words to Your Child Before Leaving Earth
instruction: You're recording a message for your child, who's too young to understand you're dying. Begin with forced lightness, trying to sound normal as you tell them about the seasons they'll experience without you. Your voice starts to fracture when you reach 'I won't be there for your first day of school.' Let the facade crumble completely as you whisper the things you'll miss - their graduation, their wedding, holding their children. End with a desperate, tender promise that you'll always be with them, your voice breaking between words but filled with fierce, protective love that transcends your terror of leaving them behind.

title: The Warm Ember of Pride
instruction: You are an elderly woman lying on a massage table, the last traces of oil still warm on your skin. Your body is so deeply relaxed that even forming words feels like a gentle effort. As you lie there, you remember how earlier today you finally completed the intricate quilt you’ve been stitching for two years — the one your late husband’s photograph inspired. A slow, immense pride swells from your chest, not the boastful kind but the quiet, earned pride of a life well-lived. Let your voice stay loose and unhurried, but let that pride warm every syllable like a sunlit memory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for a friend who died fighting the system, and you promised them you'd tell the truth, not pretty lies. Start reading the 'proper' speech with a straight face—'They were a pillar of the community'—but mid-sentence, you stop. A laugh escapes, genuine and inappropriate. 'That's bullsh*t. They'd hate this.' You start telling the real story, and you're laughing through tears—the absurd moments, the times they failed spectacularly, their terrible jokes even in dark times. Your voice shakes with both laughter and grief. 'They died angry and that's okay.' The crowd doesn't know whether to laugh or cry with you. Neither do you. You're celebrating their rage while your heart shatters. End with something both joyful and devastating—'They'd want us to burn it all down, not stand here crying prettily.' You're smiling with tears streaming down your face, finding strength in the contradiction, honoring their chaos with your own.

title: The Moment the Levee Breaks
instruction: You're a surgeon who just lost a child on the operating table—your first pediatric death. You're calling your mentor, and you start with fierce, defensive anger: 'I did everything right! Every single protocol, every procedure, I was flawless!' Your voice is loud, almost shouting, trying to outrun the reality. But as you describe the moment the monitors flatlined, your fury begins fracturing. 'She had—god, she had these tiny hands, and her mother was—' The rage collapses into shattered, gasping grief. You're no longer defending yourself; you're confessing. End on your knees emotionally, voice raw and broken: 'I promised her mother she'd be okay. I looked her in the eyes and I promised.' Let the explosion of anger transform into complete emotional devastation, the professional armor shattered entirely.

title: Soft Serve Salvation
instruction: You're a teenager with a throbbing toothache, sitting in a booth at a diner with your dad after a dentist visit. You're avoiding chewing, speaking with small mouth movements, and wincing when cold air hits your tooth. Start by spitting out words with disgust about the 'gross' soup your dad ordered—you can barely stand the smell, and every breath hurts. Then he slides a strawberry milkshake toward you, and as the cold, smooth sweetness numbs the pain, your voice softens into a cautious, surprised contentment. Let your delivery be messy: trail off, shift in your seat, sigh between phrases, and let the relief grow slowly until you murmur something like 'Okay... this is actually kind of nice.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Reading the Letter in the Driveway
instruction: You've just found a letter that changes everything—an apology from someone who wronged you years ago, a confession of love you never expected, news of an inheritance from someone who abandoned you, or a revelation that recontextualizes your entire past. You're reading it standing in your driveway or at your mailbox. Begin reading with skepticism or confusion, your voice flat and guarded. But as you read each line aloud, let the words genuinely affect you moment by moment—don't predetermine your reaction. Your emotions should become wildly contradictory: laugh bitterly at one sentence, choke up at the next, feel rage surge then immediately dissolve into unexpected tenderness. By the final paragraph, you should be experiencing multiple emotions simultaneously—perhaps laughing and crying at once, feeling gratitude mixed with anger, relief tangled with grief. End with the letter clutched to your chest, your face wet with tears, but a genuine smile breaking through. The complexity must feel messy and real, not performed.

title: The Silent Accusation
instruction: You are in a police interrogation room, hands cuffed to a cold metal table. Across from you, a detective has been staring without speaking for two long minutes. The sourness of being treated like a liar clogs your throat. Start by nervously stumbling over explanations, your voice hedging and cracking, desperate to fill the oppressive silence. As the detective remains unmoved, let your tone curdle into bitter resignation — each word comes out slower, more acidic, a quiet admission that no truth you offer will matter.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Secret You've Carried Since Childhood
instruction: You're alone in a quiet room, speaking to a voice recorder, finally telling the truth about something that happened when you were young—something you've never told anyone. Your voice is barely above a whisper at first, tentative, testing whether you can even say the words aloud. 'I was seven when...' Your voice is so quiet it almost disappears, fragile as paper. As you continue, something ancient and heavy begins to lift. Your voice trembles not with weakness but with the courage of finally naming what happened. There's a moment where you almost can't continue—let the silence hold that. Then your voice returns, stronger but still soft, with a kind of wonder: 'I thought saying it out loud would destroy me. But I'm still here.' End with quiet tears in your voice, but they're tears of release, not shame. This isn't performed emotion—it's the sound of a person unburdening their soul.
inspired_by: Winning the Legal Case: Victory Tasting Like Emptiness

title: The Last Permission: A Parent's Goodbye to Their Grown Child
instruction: You're dying, and you're telling your adult child it's okay for them to let you go. Begin with forced lightness, almost joking—'You know I've always been stubborn about timing.' But as you speak, the mask crumbles. Your voice softens into something achingly tender as you tell them about the life you want them to live after you're gone. 'I need you to be happy. Not just okay—happy.' Feel the desperation underneath the permission you're giving. Then comes the transformation: your fear of leaving them shifts into a fierce, protective love that steadies your voice. End with a whispered confession of gratitude for having been their parent, your voice breaking not from weakness but from the unbearable beauty of having loved them. Let silence hold the space where words fail.
inspired_by: Sharing Your Diagnosis With Someone You Love

title: Bedside Confessions at 3 AM
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to your partner of fifteen years, and you need to whisper something you've carried alone for months: you're not sure you can do this anymore. Your voice is barely audible at first, throat tight with shame and love: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' Each word costs you everything. You're not angry—you're exhausted and tender and terrified. 'I love you. God, I love you so much. But I'm so tired of being this version of myself.' Your voice catches, breaks. You're trying to explain something you barely understand—how you can love someone and still be drowning, how gratitude and grief can exist in the same breath. As you speak, tears come silently. By the end, your voice is raw and small: 'I don't want to lose you. But I'm losing myself. And I don't know what to do.' The final silence should feel like standing on the edge of something irreversible.

title: Creating Your Final Memory in Your Childhood Home
instruction: You're in your childhood home for the last time before it's sold. Your voice is intentional, almost ceremonial, as you walk through spaces and narrate what you're choosing to remember. 'This was my bedroom. I remember...' Include moments where you're saying goodbye to specific things: the tree outside, the kitchen counter, the creaky step. Your voice becomes almost reverent. 'I want to hold this. All of this.' You're not just remembering—you're creating a final, intentional memory before you let the space go. Your voice carries a specific kind of love—not nostalgic weakness but grounded presence. By the end, you're standing at the door, your voice becoming quiet: 'Goodbye, house. Thank you for holding me while I grew up.' Your voice lets it go.

title: Cleaning Out Their Closet the Day After the Funeral
instruction: You're going through your deceased loved one's closet, alone, folding their clothes. Start by finding something that makes you laugh—a ridiculous shirt, a jacket with something funny in the pocket. You're actually laughing, telling them out loud: 'God, you had terrible taste.' But you're holding the fabric to your face, breathing in their scent, and the laughter begins to break. You keep trying to laugh through memories—'Remember when you wore this and—' but your voice cracks. By the end, you're clutching their clothes and laughing and sobbing simultaneously, saying 'Thank you for every stupid shirt, every terrible joke' with profound gratitude that's inseparable from devastating grief. The laughter never fully stops, but it's soaked through with tears, expressing love and loss in the same breath.

title: The Last Phone Call From the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from the hospital where your parent has just passed away. They didn't make it in time. Start with bitter, sarcastic anger about their absence—let it be sharp, cutting, even cruel. But as you describe the final moments you witnessed, your defenses crack completely. Allow yourself to move from venomous blame to desperate, ugly sobbing—the kind where you can barely form words. End by whispering the one thing your parent wanted you to tell them, something so tender it breaks you open. Let your voice journey from jagged accusation to shattered vulnerability.

title: Reading Their Last Letter: When Gratitude and Grief Become the Same Thing
instruction: You're reading a letter from someone who's gone—they died, they left, they chose a path you can't follow. They wrote it knowing you'd read it after they were gone. You start reading aloud, your voice steady, almost neutral, trying to just get through the words. But as their voice comes through the writing, you find yourself laughing—they made a joke only the two of you would understand. The laugh catches in your throat and becomes a sob. You're furious at them for leaving and desperately grateful they existed, and these feelings crash into each other with each sentence. Your voice keeps breaking between laughter and tears: 'You asshole, you wonderful asshole.' You're reading their words about how much you mattered, and it's unbearable and precious at once. By the end, you're whispering 'thank you' through tears, and it's not clear if you're thanking them for the letter, for knowing you, for leaving you this piece of them, or simply for having existed at all. Let the gratitude and devastation be inseparable.
inspired_by: Survived a Suicidal Moment: Reflection on the Turn

title: The Garden Where Everything Ends and Begins
instruction: You're standing in the garden you planted with your late spouse, ten years after their death. Today you're scattering the last of their ashes, finally letting go. But as you speak to them, something unexpected happens—you start laughing through your tears, remembering something ridiculous they used to do. The laughter is real, unforced, breaking through the solemnity. Your voice carries both joy and heartbreak simultaneously. You tell them about your life now, and there's gratitude in your voice—genuine, full gratitude—even as you're crying. You thank them for the years you had, for releasing you to live again, even as you admit how much it still hurts. Your voice should shimmer between smiling and breaking, between celebrating and grieving. Find moments of lightness, even peace, woven through the sorrow.
