You stare at the ceiling fan, which you've been tracking for the last hour, but you suddenly can't remember if it was always this fast or if you're imagining it. You try to describe the confusion to the empty room, but the words feel thick and heavy, like wading through mud. Start with a hollow, confused observation about the fan, then let your voice fragment as you realize the date on your phone is wrong, and end with a soft, shattered laugh of exhaustion at the whole messed-up timing.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Gratitude That Breaks You
instruction: Someone has just saved your life, rescued you from devastation, or shown you extraordinary kindness precisely when you least deserved it. You must thank them, but you're simultaneously shattered by the realization of how close you came to losing everything, how unworthy you feel of this grace, and how angry you are that you needed saving at all. Begin with genuine gratitude, trying to express what their action meant. But let other voices interrupt from within—the proud self that resents needing help, the terrified self that can't stop shaking, the grief-stricken self mourning who you were before this moment. Your words of thanks should fracture and multiply, becoming a complex chorus of relief, shame, love, rage, and hope. None of these emotions should win—they must all exist simultaneously in your voice, creating something honest and entirely human.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Spouse After the Diagnosis
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your spouse is finally asleep after the worst day of both your lives—they've been given six months to live. You're lying beside them in the dark, and you start speaking in the softest whisper, knowing they can't hear you, which is exactly why you can finally say it. Begin with tender observation: 'Your hand is still warm.' Your voice is fragile, nearly soundless. You tell them about all the futures you'd imagined together—the gentle, specific dreams. 'I was going to surprise you with those dance lessons you wanted.' Each confession is quieter than the last. Your breath catches, but you don't cry loudly—just small, swallowed sounds. End with the most devastating simplicity: 'I don't know how to be me without you.' It's not a wail. It's barely a whisper. It's the sound of a heart learning to break in silence.

title: Holding Your Best Friend as They Leave Forever
instruction: Your best friend is moving across the world—or leaving for a mission they might not return from—and you're saying goodbye at dawn after staying up all night together. Begin with exhausted laughter, trying to keep things light even as tears stream down your face: 'Remember when we said we'd always be neighbors? God, we were so stupid.' Your voice wavers between joy at the memories and grief at the ending. Let the sleep deprivation make you unfiltered—say things you normally wouldn't: 'You're the best thing that ever happened to me, you know that?' But underneath the gratitude is raw fear. Your voice breaks: 'I don't know how to do life without you checking in on me.' Physical: you're holding them, laughing and crying simultaneously. End with a moment of profound peace mixed with heartbreak, your voice soft and wondering: 'Thank you. For everything. For making me believe I was worth knowing.' Let the exhaustion create a space where sorrow and profound gratitude exist together, indistinguishable.

title: The Shudder Before the Storm
instruction: You are a teenage girl who, in a secret scene, is playing a submissive role, speaking with a high, breathy tone. Your voice is soft and seeking approval, like a child speaking to a parent. But inside, a new anger is rising—a quiet, frustrated anger at how small this makes you feel. You start with a shaky, compliant question, but as you speak, your voice loses the false sweetness and drops into something raw and exposed. Your tone shifts from a nervous, high-pitched tremor to a strained, lower crack. You are not supposed to get angry, but your body betrays you—your throat tightens, and the anger leaks out in a clipped, defiant finish. Say something like: 'I—I did what you asked. Is it… right? I want to be good. But sometimes I don't feel good. I feel… something else.' End with a breathy, frustrated silence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father at the kitchen table where you ate breakfast as a child. Start from a place of rehearsed anger—you came here with a speech prepared, grievances listed, determined to finally tell him how his absence shaped you. But as you begin speaking, something shifts. Maybe it's the way his shoulders slump, or the gray in his beard you hadn't noticed, or the tremor in his hands as he reaches for his coffee. Let your prepared words crumble. Allow the anger to crack open and reveal the hurt child underneath—the one who just wanted him to show up to one soccer game, one recital, one dinner. Move from accusation to naked vulnerability, from shouting to a whisper that asks the question you've never dared to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let the confrontation transform into something rawer and more real than you intended.

title: The Truth That Ends Everything: Confronting What Was Never Said
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your entire life. Begin with careful, measured words — you've rehearsed this, trying to stay calm and reasonable. As they dismiss or minimize your pain, feel your control slip into righteous anger, voice rising with decades of suppressed hurt. Then, mid-accusation, you hear yourself and realize the futility — your voice breaks, fury dissolving into profound sadness as you recognize they'll never truly understand or apologize. End in exhausted acceptance, speaking the painful truth quietly: you needed them, and they weren't there, and nothing will change that. Show the journey from hope to rage to heartbroken clarity.

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You've just run outside into a rainstorm after a devastating phone call—someone you love has betrayed you in an unforgivable way. Begin by letting your voice tear itself raw with rage, shouting into the storm, your body physically releasing fury through sound. Feel the rain on your skin, the cold shocking your system. As you scream yourself hoarse, the physical exhaustion begins to transform your anger. Your voice should break down from powerful rage into breathless, almost laughing disbelief—the kind of laughter that borders on sobbing. End in a place where you're on your knees, physically spent, voice reduced to a whisper, touching something like dark acceptance or perhaps just complete depletion. The arc moves from explosive anger through physical release to empty surrender.
inspired_by: Director or colleague challenges the actor's process as overcomplicated or unnecessary

title: What We Never Said
instruction: You're cleaning out your deceased spouse's belongings and find unsent letters they wrote to you over the years—love notes, apologies, dreams they never shared aloud. Start reading one quietly, casually, maybe even with a slight smile at their handwriting. But as you read, your voice begins to catch. These are things you desperately needed to hear when they were alive. Whisper the words they wrote: 'I was afraid... I loved you so much it terrified me.' Your voice should break on certain phrases, you should have to stop and breathe. This isn't loud grief—it's the intimate, devastating kind that lives in your chest. End barely audible, pressing the letters to your heart: 'I wish you'd told me... I wish I'd asked... I'm so sorry we were both so afraid.' Include long pauses where the silence does the work.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're speaking to someone who hurt you deeply, but time has transformed that pain into something unexpectedly beautiful, and you're feeling both things at once. Start with a small, genuine laugh—not bitter, but surprised at yourself: 'This is going to sound insane...' Your voice is light, almost casual, but there's something trembling underneath. 'But I'm grateful. For all of it.' Let the complexity flood in—your voice wavers between laughter and tears. 'You shattered me. Completely.' Breathe through the pain of remembering. 'And I rebuilt myself into someone I actually like.' Feel the bittersweet joy of that, the strange peace. Your voice softens, grows tender even as tears might fall: 'I don't forgive you. But I thank you.' End with quiet wonder, speaking more to yourself than to them: 'I found myself in the pieces you left behind.' Let gratitude and grief sit together, neither one winning.

title: The Loneliest Karaoke Performance
instruction: You're alone in a private karaoke room at 2AM. No audience, no pressure, no performance. Sing a song that means everything to you — badly, beautifully, genuinely. Start self-conscious even alone. Then let go. Belt it. Cry through the bridge. Laugh at how bad you sound. Keep singing anyway. This is the sound of a human being completely alone with a melody that holds a memory. No one will ever hear this performance. That's what makes it the most honest one in your life.

title: The Explorer and the Ancient Guardian
instruction: Narrate a scene where an explorer with an adventurous, excited voice encounters an ancient guardian who speaks in a deep, echoing tone. The guardian warns of a curse. Switch between the explorers eagerness and the guardians grave warnings, creating a sense of impending danger.

title: The Last Voicemail to Someone Who'll Never Wake
instruction: You're sitting outside the ICU, and the doctors have just told you there's no brain activity left. Tomorrow they'll remove life support. You have one chance to leave a voicemail saying everything you never said. Start with forced composure, trying to sound normal, as if they might actually hear this and call back. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves—this is truly goodbye. Your voice should fracture and rebuild multiple times. End in a place of devastating acceptance mixed with fierce, aching love. Let silences speak as loudly as words. This isn't theatrical grief—it's the raw, ugly, holy moment when you release someone you can't imagine living without.
inspired_by: Speaking to Alexa Like a Hostage

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father after discovering he kept a life-changing secret from you for decades. Start with cold, measured accusation—listing facts, speaking as if presenting evidence in court, maintaining rigid control. You're determined to make him hear the logic of his betrayal. But as you speak, something shifts. The words you're using to indict him begin to reveal how deeply you needed him, how much his opinion still matters, how his silence didn't just hide information—it made you doubt your worth. By the end, your controlled fury has crumbled into something far more vulnerable: you're asking him why you weren't worth the truth, why he didn't trust you with the reality of your own life. Let the transition happen through what the words themselves reveal to you as you say them—moving from prosecutor to abandoned child.

title: The Internal Monologue of a House Cat
instruction: Voice the thoughts of a cat throughout a day. Morning: imperious demands for food (aristocratic, entitled). Sun patch: drowsy, philosophical purring monologue about the meaning of warmth. A bird outside: sudden, intense predatory focus (staccato, intense). Human comes home: performing indifference ('I didn't even notice you were gone') while secretly relieved. Nighttime: mysterious, poetic nocturnal thoughts as the cat watches the house sleep. Each mood should be a completely different vocal register.

title: Breaking Dishes in Your Ex's Apartment
instruction: You're standing in your ex-lover's apartment, supposed to be calmly packing your things, but you pick up a plate and suddenly you're smashing it against the wall. Start with that first violent, satisfying crash and let it open a floodgate. Throw things, break things, and with each destruction, shout or sob or scream everything physical and emotional: the sex that made you forget yourself, the rage at being discarded, the humiliation, the parts of them you still crave, the hatred, the longing. Your voice should be guttural, full-bodied, mixing animal sounds with coherent fury: 'You fucking COWARD!' mixed with groans of physical exertion and emotional release. Let your body and voice express the full chaos—sweating, crying, laughing maniacally, maybe even aroused by the violence of it. Throw until you're exhausted, until you're on the floor among the broken pieces, panting. End in a completely different physical and emotional state: quiet, spent, maybe touching a piece of broken ceramic tenderly, whispering something like 'I really loved you,' barely audible, all the fire turned to ash.

title: The Weight of Quiet
instruction: You are lying in bed after making love, body slack, head turned toward the ceiling. Your partner's arm is draped across your chest, but your mind is far away, caught in a memory from decades ago. Start slowly, voice almost gone, with extreme vocal fry — each word dragging out as you piece together the thought. Let long silences hang, and let your voice crack or drift off mid-sentence as the fatigue pulls at you. By the end, the contemplation fades into a hushed surrender, a gentle acceptance that you're too tired to finish the story.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Secret Kept Too Long
instruction: Late at night, you're with someone you deeply trust, and you finally decide to whisper a secret you've never told anyone—something about your childhood, a shame you've carried, a truth about who you really are. Start very quietly, almost unable to get the words out. Your voice should be fragile, broken, hesitant. As you speak, let your body curl inward or become very still. But as the secret emerges, something shifts—maybe relief starts seeping in, maybe the fear intensifies, maybe unexpected emotion surfaces. Let your voice crack, let silences speak. By the end, you should feel fundamentally different than when you began—perhaps lighter, perhaps more afraid, perhaps more real.

title: Wilted Venom
instruction: You are a woman who has been tracking someone through the desert for hours, now fully heat-exhausted. You finally corner them, but your body is failing—dry mouth, blurred vision, legs trembling. Start by panting, slurring words, barely audible, as if speaking costs everything. Then, as you recall the betrayal that drove you here, malevolence seeps through your fractured voice: your tone hardens, your pacing slows to a deliberate threat, and you end with a cold, clear promise that cuts through the dizziness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Reunion That Unmakes You
instruction: Your best friend from college—the one you betrayed years ago—shows up at your door unexpectedly. Begin with defensive joy, trying to act like everything's fine, desperately hoping they've forgotten or forgiven. But they haven't come to accuse—they've come to understand. They ask: Why did you do it? What were you so afraid of? What did you need that you couldn't ask for? Each question strips away your defenses until you're standing there naked with the truth: you were jealous, you were scared, you sabotaged them because you didn't believe you deserved their friendship. As you confess, something strange happens—alongside your shame comes relief, alongside your grief comes their unexpected laughter at the absurdity of years wasted. End in a chaotic tangle of emotions: crying while laughing, apologizing while they're hugging you, gratitude mixed with regret, joy contaminated by sorrow. Let the contradictions crash into each other.

title: Breaking the Inheritance
instruction: You're physically destroying something that represents a legacy you're supposed to carry—tearing up a contract, ripping apart a costume, breaking an award, burning letters. Your body is engaged in intense, repetitive physical action. Start the scene with your actions controlled, dutiful, even reverent—you're trying to honor what this thing meant while also letting it go. But as you continue, the physical act unlocks something wild. Your movements become more violent, more cathartic. You're not just destroying an object—you're breaking generational chains, smashing expectations, obliterating the person everyone needed you to be. Let sounds emerge—grunts, cries, laughter, sobs. End in exhaustion and exhilaration, your body trembling but finally free. The physical intensity must reveal and release the emotional transformation from obligation to liberation.
inspired_by: When a young actor is being defined by a famous parent's legacy rather than their own work

title: Lying in a Patch of Soft, Shaded Grass
instruction: Lie back, feeling the cool grass beneath you, soft and welcoming. Describe the way each blade presses against your skin, the earthy smell, and the gentle shade overhead. Speak with a tone of quiet contentment, as if this moment lying in the grass is perfectly peaceful, grounding you in the calm beauty of nature.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight That Won't Land
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love, and you both know this plane they're about to board is going down—a premonition, a certainty you can't explain but both feel in your bones. Start trying to sound normal, cheerful even, asking about mundane things because you can't bear to say what you know. But as the final boarding call echoes in the background, that facade crumbles. Your voice should crack and splinter as you try to say everything and nothing at once—apologies, gratitude, love—while they do the same. End in a whisper of acceptance, a tender goodbye that holds both devastation and an impossible peace. Let the emotion build from forced lightness to raw desperation to finally, heartbreakingly, a moment of pure connection before the line goes dead.
inspired_by: Suppressing Fear While Watching a Horror Movie With Friends

title: Being Known
instruction: You're confessing to your best friend that you slept with their partner — while they're cutting your hair. The scissors are near your throat. Start with nervous small talk about the weather, building courage. Each snip of the scissors punctuates your guilt. When you finally say it, your voice drops to barely audible. Their hand stops. The silence. Then they resume cutting — slowly, deliberately — and ask 'When?' in a voice so controlled it's terrifying. You must answer while completely vulnerable in the chair.

title: Don't You Dare Touch Them
instruction: Someone you love is being threatened, and you explode with protective fury. Begin with volcanic rage, voice cracking with intensity: 'Get away from them!' Your whole body is in your voice—fierce, dangerous, uncontrolled. But mid-fury, you look at the person you're protecting and see their fear, and suddenly your rage collapses into something more complex: desperate helplessness because you can't actually keep them safe from everything. Your voice breaks completely as fierce protectiveness tangles with the terrible realization of your own powerlessness: 'I can't... I can't always...' End with a sound that's half sob, half defiant promise, your voice raw and stripped of everything but love and terror.

title: Grateful Goodbye at the Hospice Bed
instruction: You're holding the hand of someone who raised you, loved you, saved you—and they're dying. They're still conscious, still here, but you both know this is the last real conversation. You start by thanking them, and there's genuine joy in your voice as you recall specific memories—that time they defended you, taught you to drive, believed in you when no one else did. You're laughing softly at shared jokes. But even as you laugh, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice keeps catching: 'Remember when you—' and you have to stop, overcome. You tell them 'It's okay to go,' and you mean it—you want their suffering to end—but saying it breaks your heart. By the end, you're whispering 'Thank you' through sobs, but you're also smiling, holding both their hand and this impossible moment where gratitude and grief are completely intertwined. Your voice should shimmer between laughter and tears, unable to separate the joy of having known them from the agony of letting them go.

title: Staring at a Speck of Dust
instruction: You're a young boy slumped at a wooden desk, cheek pressed into your palm so hard your lips are squished to one side. You mumble lazily to yourself about a tiny speck of dust floating in a sunbeam, your voice muffled and clumsy on 'p' and 'b' sounds. Start with idle, half-bored curiosity, then let your thoughts drift into a quiet, almost solemn wonder about how that speck might be as infinite as the whole universe. End with a small, breathy sigh of realization—not happy, not sad, just deeply present in the moment. Let your lips resist some words, and don't fight the tired, smushed quality of your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Filtered Confession
instruction: You are a woman in her late 60s, volunteering at a decontamination shelter after a chemical spill. You wear a full gas mask. Through the muffled hiss and mechanical rasp of your own breathing, you are telling a fellow volunteer—a younger woman you've long admired and resented—that her promotion was a mistake. You start with a sour, bitter energy like sucking on a lemon, envy curdling each word into a sharp whisper you force through the filter. But as you speak, the constant pressure of the mask straps digging into your scalp and the echo of your own voice disorients you; a flicker of confusion creeps in—'Why am I even saying this?' By the end, the jealousy has faded into a hollow, tired regret, your voice dropping to a choked, almost kind murmur inside the plastic chamber.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Confusion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Morning After the Party
instruction: You're a 17-year-old with a voice wrecked from heavy smoking and other substances. It's early morning—you're slumped on your bed, head pounding, throat raw. Your younger sibling peeks in and asks you to tie their shoe before they go to school. Start by snapping, voice gravelly and sour from irritation and the hangover, but as you see their hopeful face, affection cuts through—you soften, though the sourness still colors your words. Force a gruff, tender reply while clearing your throat, your tone wavering between impatience and love, ending with a reluctant but genuine offer to help.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Affection (clearly present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Threshold Confrontation
instruction: You are confronting your parent in the doorway of your childhood bedroom. You've returned home and something they've said has finally broken your silence. Start by describing what you see behind them—the bed, the walls, specific objects from your youth—and how it felt to be a child in that space. As you speak, let the memories unlock your anger and hurt. Move from controlled description to fierce accusation, naming specific moments when you felt unseen or misunderstood. But by the end, let your rage crack open to reveal the desperate child underneath who just wanted to be loved. Your voice must travel from cold observation to volcanic rage to broken-hearted plea.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Addiction
instruction: You're an adult child finally confronting your parent about their active addiction that stole your childhood. You start measured, rehearsed—'I need you to hear some things I've never said'—but as they deflect and minimize, your voice escalates. They say 'I did my best' and something volcanic erupts: 'Your best? I was NINE and making my own school lunches because you were passed out!' You're listing specific memories they don't remember, your voice cracking with the little kid still inside you who needed them. But then they break—really break—and admit 'I know. God help me, I know.' Now you're faced with their genuine remorse and you don't know what to do with it. Your rage collides with the desperate love that never died. Show the journey from controlled anger to explosive pain to that awful, tender moment when you realize they're still choosing the substance over you, even as they cry.

title: The Last Flight Home
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child who's boarding a spacecraft for a one-way colonization mission to Mars. You'll never see them again. Start with forced brightness, trying to be supportive: 'This is what you've always wanted. I'm so proud of you.' But your voice begins to fracture as reality hits. You reach out to touch their face one more time, and everything you've been holding back floods out—not loud, but devastated: 'I won't be there when you need me. I won't see your life.' They tell you this is their dream, and you have to let them go with love. Your voice transforms into something fierce and tender simultaneously: 'Then you go. You fly. And you know—you always know—how much...' You can't finish. Final boarding call sounds. Your last words are barely whispered, a blessing and a breaking heart: 'Come back to me in your dreams.'

title: Pillow Secrets
instruction: You are a teenage girl lying face down on your bedroom rug, scrolling through old photos on your phone. The floor presses against your chest, making your breaths short and your voice sound a little muffled and closer to the ground. Start with a gentle, contented sigh as you smile at a happy memory — your voice light and dreamy, but with the physical weight of your body. As you scroll further, you find a photo of a friend you haven't spoken to in months. Your tone shifts: the contented hum fades into a quiet, aching tenderness. You speak to the photo, your words coming out in half-whispers, pauses where you lose your thought and then find it again. The last line should feel like you're caught between a smile and a lump in your throat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Nerve Endings and Thunder
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a test result, a phone call, a letter—and you're alone in your apartment when a sudden rainstorm hits. Start with your body's physical response: hands shaking, heart racing, maybe nausea. Build the sensory reality: the sound of rain hammering windows, the smell of ozone, your own sweat, the precise quality of light in the room. Let the external storm mirror and amplify your internal one. Feel the news in your body—where does it live? Your chest? Your stomach? Your hands? As thunder crashes, allow yourself to physically respond—maybe you need to move, pace, collapse, press your palms against cold glass. Transform from shocked numbness to full-body emotional and physical release as the sensory details give your feelings permission to exist in your flesh.

title: Thanking Your Past Self for a Sacrifice You're Only Now Understanding While You're Dying
instruction: You're alone in your final moments, and you suddenly understand a mysterious sacrifice your younger self made that you'd forgotten until now. Begin with confused laughter—the memory surfaces like a dream, absurd and clear. Your voice fills with wonder as you piece it together: the stranger who warned you, the choice you made without knowing why. As realization blooms, let gratitude and grief tangle together. You're thanking yourself for saving you, mourning that you lived a whole life without remembering, laughing at the cosmic joke of being your own guardian angel. Your breath is failing but your voice becomes luminous with contradictory emotion: you're dying but you're okay, you're alone but you were always with yourself, you're saying goodbye but also hello. End with a phrase that's both greeting and farewell to the person you were. This is the strange peace of meeting yourself at both ends of your life.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: First Contact Officer Learns the Aliens Are Earth's Future Descendants

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Quite Mean
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, and you're supposed to be purely joyful. But as you speak, let every contradictory impulse have its moment. You start with genuine happiness, then you notice your own loneliness and it makes you bitter, then you feel guilty about the bitterness so you overcompensate with false enthusiasm, then you catch yourself performing and feel disgusted, then you remember why you actually love your friend and feel tender, then jealous again, then protective of them, then worried this marriage is a mistake, then hoping desperately it isn't. Don't land on one emotion. Instead, let yourself be pulled between love and envy, celebration and grief for what you're losing, hope for them and fear for yourself, gratitude for their friendship and resentment about being left behind. By the end, discover which of these contradictory truths becomes most urgent to express. The arc moves from attempted pure joy to embracing emotional complexity.
inspired_by: Being Irreverent to Your Concept of the Material

title: The Day After the Funeral
instruction: Someone you loved deeply has died. You're alone, clearing out their belongings, and you find something—a letter, a photo, an object—that reminds you of a specific conflict you had with them, something unresolved and painful. Begin speaking to them (they're gone, but you need to say this) with anger and grief mixed together. You're furious at them for leaving, for the ways they hurt you, for what was never resolved. List the grievances specifically—don't hold back. But as you speak, you start remembering (almost against your will) the other things too: the ways they showed up for you, the sacrifices they made, the love beneath the damage. Your voice should move from bitter accusation into something more complicated—gratitude tangled with resentment, love mixed with rage, the devastating recognition that you can be angry at them and grateful for them simultaneously. End in a place where both truths exist at once, fully acknowledged, impossible and real.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about something they did (or failed to do) decades ago that shaped your entire life—an abandonment, a betrayal, a lie, or a silence that damaged you. Start from a place of controlled anger, determined to finally be heard. As you speak, feel how your need for them to acknowledge the harm battles against your exhaustion from carrying this pain alone. Notice how your voice might crack, how rage might dissolve into the vulnerability of that hurt child still inside you. By the end, let yourself arrive somewhere unexpected—perhaps you realize you're not seeking an apology anymore, but simply to be seen. Move from accusation to something more complex: grief, understanding, or the aching recognition that they may never give you what you need.
inspired_by: An actor wants to develop a balanced daily work program

title: The Sweetest Victory
instruction: You are a older woman with a deliberately sweet, polite voice, speaking to your adult nephew at a family gathering. He just announced he's moving across the country for a job, and you feel deeply disappointed because he didn't consult you. But you have a secret: you already called his potential landlord and subtly persuaded them to withdraw the offer. Start with a gentle, sigh-laden tone, stressing wrong words like 'wonderful' and 'happy' — your disappointment bleeding through the sugar. As you continue, let a sly smile creep into your voice. End with a triumphant, almost giddy revelation that he won't be leaving after all, your voice lighter and sharper, the victory unmistakable. The performance should be natural with little real-time hesitations, like adjusting your glasses or sipping tea.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Ghost of the Fire
instruction: You're sitting cross-legged by a crackling campfire, telling a ghost story you've recited a dozen times before. Begin with a flat, hollow voice — the numbness of repetition, barely caring about the words. Midway, notice a friend flinch at a log pop; let a teasing smirk creep into your tone as you pause and say, 'Scared already?' Then return to the story, but this time a strange detail catches you — a flicker of genuine interest. Your voice warms, speeds up, becomes more animated. End with real fascination, leaning forward, speaking almost to yourself. Let the fire cracks, a cough, or a shift in weight interrupt naturally. Keep it 40-80 words of spoken content.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Teasing (clearly present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Warrior's Breaking Point
instruction: You've been the protector, the strong one, the legend everyone relies on—and you've just failed catastrophically. Someone died on your watch. Start with fierce denial and self-flagellation: 'I should have been faster, stronger, better!' Your voice is raw, almost violent with self-hatred. Build in intensity—you're raging at yourself, at the universe, punching walls with your words. Then suddenly collapse into helpless sobbing: 'I can't do this anymore. I can't carry all of you.' Your legendary strength shatters completely. End in whispered exhaustion and terrible vulnerability: 'What if I was never strong enough? What if it was always a lie?' Move from explosive fury to absolute emotional nakedness—the moment when the armor finally breaks.

title: Midnight Apology to a Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep. You're standing in their doorway at 2 AM, whispering what you can't say when they're awake. Start with 'I'm sorry' so quiet it barely exists. Confess your failures as a parent in fragments—the times you were too tired, too angry, too broken by your own childhood. Your voice should be barely audible, catching on tears, thick with shame and tenderness. Each admission costs you something. Midway, your voice breaks completely on a specific memory of failing them. End with a desperate, whispered promise to do better, knowing you're fallible, knowing you'll try anyway. This is intimacy mixed with devastation, love wrapped in inadequacy.
inspired_by: Someone Realizing You're Crying Without Sound

title: Dancing in Your Empty Childhood Home
instruction: You're alone in your childhood home on moving day—your parents have died, or divorced, or you're all scattering. You put on a song from your happiest memory here and start talking to the empty rooms. You're laughing about ridiculous family moments—your voice bright with genuine joy—but tears are streaming down your face. You're spinning through rooms, touching walls, your voice shifting between laughter and sobbing mid-sentence. You thank the house for what it gave you while grieving what it couldn't. You're angry at memories and grateful for them simultaneously. You recall painful moments but can finally laugh at their absurdity. End finding unexpected peace in the contradiction—you're devastated this is ending AND genuinely joyful it happened. Your voice should embody the impossible truth that something can break your heart and fill it at the same time, that goodbye and thank you are sometimes the same word.

title: The Winning Call
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling to tell them you've just achieved the dream you both shared as children—but they gave up on it, and you didn't. Begin with triumphant joy—you want to share this, you're buzzing with success, your voice bright and fast. But as you hear their voice, something complicated floods in. Your victory is also the proof of their defeat. Your joy is tangled with guilt, with the knowledge that this call might hurt them, with the ache of all those years of distance between you. Let your excitement keep trying to resurface—you earned this, you want to celebrate—but let it keep colliding with grief, with the realization that success without them feels hollow. End in a place where you're laughing and crying at once, where congratulations and apology are the same sentence, where you're begging them to be happy for you while also saying you're sorry. Make us feel both emotions fighting for space in every breath.
inspired_by: Actor is in a rigid or resistant environment (conservative director, non-exploratory cast) and needs to establish irreverent freedom before scene work

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your mother about something she did when you were thirteen that changed everything—maybe a betrayal, maybe a moment she chose someone else over you, maybe a lie that shaped your whole life. Begin with your hands shaking, voice controlled, trying to be reasonable and adult about it. But as you speak, feel the thirteen-year-old inside you rising up, demanding to be heard. Let your voice grow sharper, rawer, let the carefully constructed adult façade crack apart. Move from 'I need you to understand' to 'How could you?' to something you've never allowed yourself to scream at her. End in a place you didn't expect—either in fierce liberation or devastating recognition of her humanity.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked in the area of conflict — cannot express confrontational or aggressive feelings organically

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent about why they never protected you when you needed them most—why they looked away, stayed silent, chose their own comfort over your safety. Start with your voice controlled, almost cold, reciting facts like evidence in a courtroom. But as you speak, rage begins to seep through the cracks. Your voice rises, sharpens, demands answers they can't give. You're not a child anymore begging for their love—you're an adult who has carried this wound for decades and you want them to see it, to acknowledge it, to say they're sorry. When they offer excuses instead of apologies, something in you breaks open. Your fury transforms into something rawer: the devastated realization that they will never give you what you need, that you're mourning a parent who was never really there. End with your voice quieter, harder, more resolved—you're done waiting for them to change. You're saying goodbye to the fantasy of who you needed them to be.

title: Protecting What's Already Lost
instruction: Someone you love is in danger—a child, a partner, a parent—and you're trying desperately to save them, but deep down you know you can't. Start with fierce, almost violent determination in your voice: 'I won't let this happen. I won't.' You're shouting maybe, pacing, full of adrenaline and protective rage. But as reality sets in, your voice begins to shake. The fierceness cracks and suddenly you're begging—'Please, please don't take them from me.' Your strength collapses into helplessness. You might pound your fists or grab onto something, but your voice is breaking apart. End in devastated whispers, maybe still fighting but knowing it's over: 'I can't lose you. I can't.' Let the journey from warrior to broken supplicant be visceral and complete. Allow the rage and helplessness to coexist and tear you apart.

title: Laughing at a Funeral You Weren't Supposed to Attend
instruction: You've crashed the funeral of someone who meant everything to you, but you were written out of their life—an ex-lover, an estranged friend, someone whose family never accepted you. Begin with suppressed emotion, almost holding your breath as you remember them. Then recall something absurdly funny about them—an embarrassing moment, a ridiculous habit, a joke only you two shared. Let yourself laugh, quietly at first, then more freely, even as tears stream down your face. The laughter should sound both joyful and broken, celebrating them while grieving that you can't share this memory with them anymore. Your voice shifts between laughter and sobs without warning, sometimes mid-sentence. Speak directly to them as if they can hear you, mixing gratitude ('Thank you for seeing me when no one else did') with heartbreak ('I hate that I have to let you go'). End with a sound that's simultaneously a laugh and a cry—a release that feels like saying goodbye and holding on at the exact same time.

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy Who Saved Your Life
instruction: The person who destroyed your family just took a bullet meant for you and is bleeding out in your arms. Start with rage - 'Why did you do that? You don't get to be the hero!' - your voice savage with fury. But they're dying and you can feel it happening. Your anger fractures. You're suddenly begging them to hold on, screaming for help, then back to furious: 'I needed to hate you!' The contradictions are ripping you apart. You're trying to apply pressure to the wound while wanting to let go. Your voice breaks between commands ('Stay with me!') and accusations ('You killed them!'). End in a primal cry of grief and confusion as the person you most needed to destroy dies having saved you, and you're left holding them, shattered by impossible gratitude and unresolved hatred.
inspired_by: Speaking While Severely Injured or in Acute Pain

title: The Last Letter Home
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your child through a video message, knowing you will not survive to see them grow up. Begin with the attempt to be strong, to give them practical wisdom and comfort. But as you speak, allow yourself to confront the weight of everything you will miss - their first love, their graduations, their struggles you won't be there to help them through. Let the fortress of strength you've built crack open. By the end, find a place beyond grief - a deep, tender acceptance and a fierce love that transcends your own ending. Your voice should move from controlled and parental to raw and breaking, then finally to something quiet, clear, and somehow at peace.
inspired_by: When an actor has suffered trauma before pursuing acting

title: The Last Morning Ritual
instruction: You're performing your mother's morning routine one final time in her empty house after she's passed. Run your hands over her favorite robe, smell her soap, touch the towel she always used. Begin speaking with careful, controlled composure as you go through each familiar motion, but let the weight of 'never again' gradually crack through your voice. By the end, allow yourself to break—not into theatrical sobbing, but into that raw, quiet devastation where you can barely breathe. Let the mundane objects become unbearably sacred. Your voice should move from steady reminiscence to something fragile and shattered, as if each small comfort is both a gift and a knife.
inspired_by: Wrapping Yourself in a Towel After a Shower

title: The Inept Superhero
instruction: Perform as a superhero with useless powers. Use a heroic voice when announcing intentions, switching to a deflated tone when powers fail to impress or help, adding humor through the characters obliviousness.

title: The Moment Before Everything Shatters
instruction: You burst in with news—a pregnancy, a job, an engagement—voice electric with joy: 'It's happening! Everything we wanted!' You're almost shouting with excitement, words tumbling over each other, breathless and bright. But as you look at their face, something shifts. Your excitement becomes frantic, desperate: 'Why aren't you excited? Say something!' The energy that was joy becomes panic, your voice rising higher, louder, trying to force them to feel what you feel: 'We planned this! You said you wanted this!' The brightness fractures into rage—'You're destroying this! You're destroying me!'—and then suddenly, horrifyingly, your voice breaks completely. The explosive energy collapses into devastated whisper: 'Please... please be happy with me.' You're sobbing now, the excitement transformed into grief so profound you can barely breathe. You end on your knees in your voice, the anticipation of joy replaced by the certainty of loss: 'Please.'

title: Unraveling Doubt
instruction: You are lying back, receiving oral sex from a long-term partner. At first, you feel a nagging doubt—maybe you don't deserve this pleasure, or you're afraid to fully let go. The sensation is overwhelming, and your speech starts to break down: you ask yourself a quick, questioning thought, then a half-sentence, then just sounds. Your breathing becomes shallow and sharp, and as pleasure builds, the doubt fades into pure, unexpected surrender. Let your voice start tight and inquisitive, then soften into breathy moans and a rising pitch as you give in completely.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Beneath the Veneer
instruction: You are an older woman seated at a polished conference table, your hands folded primly, a cup of untouched tea before you. Across the table is the person who betrayed you in a way that broke something irreparable. You begin speaking in your usual hyper-feminized voice—light, melodic, almost friendly—as you describe a fond memory, but your words slowly sharpen. Let your voice warble with suppressed pain, then let the malice seep through like a slow leak: a slight tremor, a pause to wet your lips, a shift in your chair that makes it creak. By the end, your tone is flat, cold, and dripping with venom, the sweetness completely gone, revealing the deep, quiet devastation underneath.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Protective Fury in the Hospital Corridor
instruction: Someone you love fiercely has been hurt, and you're confronting the person responsible—or the doctor with bad news, or fate itself. Start with barely controlled rage, your voice tight and dangerous. 'You don't get to—' Your hands are shaking. The anger is volcanic, protective, almost violent in its intensity. 'Do you understand what you've done?' Your volume rises, words becoming weapons. But then: the helplessness hits. Your voice cracks wide open. Because rage can't fix this. The fury collapses into broken desperation, into pleading. 'Please. Please, there has to be something.' End on your knees emotionally, the fierce protector rendered powerless, voice raw with tears and love and the unbearable weight of not being able to save them.

title: After the Storm: Body and Heart Colliding
instruction: You've just experienced something intensely physical—maybe you've run until your body screamed, made love with devastating intensity, or endured physical pain that's left you trembling. Your body is still reverberating, nerve endings alive, breath ragged. Start from that raw physical state where your body is louder than your thoughts. Let the physical sensations trigger an emotional avalanche you didn't expect—perhaps grief crashes through the pleasure, or rage surges through the exhaustion, or unexpected joy breaks through pain. Express this collision entirely through sound and breath—gasps, cries, laughter that might be tears, sounds that you've never made before. Let your body lead; let sensation and emotion blur until you can't separate them. End in a completely transformed state where you've been wrung out and remade.

title: The Field at Dusk
instruction: You are a young boy with a voice deeper than your years, sprinting through a dark field, your lungs burning. You’re furious—at the footsteps behind you, at your own legs that won’t go faster—but the rage is already cracking into helplessness as the brambles tear at your arms and the house lights shrink behind you. Your voice comes out in raw, ragged bursts between violent gasps: single syllables, shouted or swallowed. Start with pure, spit-flecked anger, words sharp and defiant, but let each exhale become more desperate until the last line fades into a breathy, defeated plea—your body betraying the fight. You stumble once, catch yourself, and the final words are almost not there—a quiet surrender to the panic.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Bedside Confession at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside someone sleeping—a partner, a child, a dying parent. You're whispering things you can't say when they're awake. Start so quietly it's almost just breath. 'I don't know how to do this without you.' Your voice is tender but trembling. You're confessing fears, regrets, small beautiful memories that catch in your throat. 'Remember when you—' and you have to pause because the grief is already here, anticipatory and enormous. Let your voice break on specific details: their laugh, the way they hold you, ordinary moments now precious. End with a whispered promise or goodbye that you both need and dread to say. The kind of crying that's silent, that lives in your chest and your voice.

title: What We Carry in Silence
instruction: You're lying in bed in the dark next to your partner of twenty years, and you're telling them something you've never spoken aloud: the miscarriage you had before you met them, how you sometimes talk to that child in your mind, how you've carried this secret tender grief through all your happy years together. Your voice should be almost a whisper, each word chosen carefully, afraid of breaking this moment. Start with halting phrases, testing if it's safe to speak this aloud. Feel the relief as the words finally come, mixed with the fear that this confession changes how they see you. End with your voice soft but steadier, saying 'I needed you to know the whole of me.' Let there be tears you're trying to hold back, a tremor in your breathing. This isn't dramatic crying—it's the quiet kind of weeping that happens when a long-held secret finally finds air.

title: The Sky is Audible
instruction: You are standing alone on a high, wind-swept ridge at dawn, the first light just breaking over the horizon. Your body is perfectly upright, feet planted, lungs full of cold, thin air. As you speak, a vast flock of migrating birds rises from the valley below, drowning the world in the sound of wings. Start with the quiet, breathless awe of seeing the immensity of the sky; let your voice fill the entire space, resonant and clear. Midway, the sheer scale of life — the birds, the light, your own smallness — hits you with a force that almost steals your breath, turning your awe into something fragile, almost painful, and your voice cracks on the final, whispered word.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Moment Everything Shatters
instruction: You have just discovered a betrayal so profound it rewrites your entire history—a partner's long-term affair, a friend who sabotaged your career, a family member who lied about something that shaped your whole life. Begin with shocked disbelief, your voice eerily calm as you repeat the facts you've learned, as if saying them aloud might make them make sense. Then the rage hits—let your voice explode with accusations, demanding answers, your words tumbling over each other. Crescendo into raw, primal anger, almost shouting. But then, suddenly, the anger collapses into something more devastating: grief. Your voice breaks completely as you realize what you've lost—not just the person, but the past you thought you had, the future you planned, the version of yourself who trusted. Let yourself move through gasping attempts to speak, to make them understand the magnitude of what they've destroyed. End with fierce, trembling resolve, your voice quiet but deadly certain, as you tell them exactly what this means, what you're choosing now. Your final words should carry both absolute devastation and unexpected strength, as if you're discovering you can survive this even as it destroys you.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Remember You
instruction: You're leaning close to your beloved—partner, parent, closest friend—who no longer recognizes your face due to dementia or brain injury. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate, tender. You're telling them who you are, recounting your shared memories, trying to reach whatever part of them might still know you. Your voice is gentle, almost like you're speaking to a frightened animal, full of love and desperate hope. But as you speak, you feel the futility settling into your bones. They smile at you kindly, like a stranger being polite. Your whisper becomes thinner, more fragile. You're not angry—anger would be easier. Instead, you're experiencing the strange grief of losing someone who's still breathing, still warm under your hand. Your voice catches on memories they can't access, breaks on inside jokes that now belong only to you. You end by simply saying 'I love you,' and they say it back with no recognition in their eyes, and you have to decide if that's enough. Your voice must move from gentle hope to the quietest devastation—the kind that doesn't sob but simply empties out.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Bard Sings a Prophecy That Becomes True as They Sing It

title: New Glasses Seeing Clear
instruction: You put them on and the world sharpens. Your voice is amazed, simple: 'Oh.' The world makes sense now. 'I didn't know it was supposed to be like this.' Breathing is full, present. Physical: head tilting, seeing clearly. 'Everything has edges. Detail. I can see...' Vocal tone is childlike in wonder. 'How did I live in blurred vision?' You're discovering depth. By the end, you're grateful in a basic, profound way: 'I can finally see properly. How has everything always been this clear?'

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, both of you supposedly asleep. In the darkness, in barely a whisper, you begin to confess something you've hidden—a fear so intimate it makes you feel naked. Start with halting, fragmented words, your breath catching, almost hoping they're actually asleep so you won't have to finish. But as you continue, something shifts: the act of speaking it aloud makes you braver, more honest. Your whispers become more fluid, more certain. When they finally whisper back 'I know... I've always known,' let relief and deeper vulnerability wash through you. End by reaching for their hand in the darkness, your voice barely audible but filled with everything you've never been able to say in daylight.

title: The Hoarse Promise
instruction: You are a rough-voiced trucker, laid up in bed with a terrible head cold. A younger family member you adore is asleep in the next room, and you've just heard on the police scanner that a dangerous rival you've been hunting for weeks is moving through your town. You want to let him pass—your love for the kid makes you want to stay safe and warm. But you also feel a cold, familiar malice rising. Start with a thick, congested whisper of affection to the sleeping child, but as you pull a crumpled photo of your rival from your pocket, your voice turns heavy, dripping with venom. End with a phlegmy, broken promise—half to the child, half to yourself—that shows the longing to be good and the dark need for vengeance fighting inside you. Let your voice be interrupted by sniffles, coughs, and the occasional nose blow. Begin gentle and weary, then shift to a low, grinding menace, then back to a hoarse, loving uncertainty.
emotions_sampled: Longing (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Unraveling the Careful Lies
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father about something they've hidden from you your whole life. Start with righteous anger, armed with accusations. But as you speak, begin each new accusation with 'You made me believe...', 'You never let me...', 'Because of you, I...'—and don't think about what comes next, just let it emerge. Look them in the eye with each statement. As the confrontation continues, let yourself discover deeper wounds beneath the anger. Allow your fury to crack and reveal the hurt child underneath. By the end, you should surprise yourself—the anger should transform into something more vulnerable: grief, longing, or desperate need for understanding you didn't know you still carried.

title: Echoes of a Hollow Promise
instruction: You're a teenager walking down the long, empty school corridor after your father stood you up again. The acoustics make every footstep and breath linger too long, like the silence is judging you. You start by leaving a voicemail for your dad, forcing a casual, almost bored tone—'Hey, no big deal, maybe next time.' But as you walk, the cold reverb and the rhythmic thud of your own shoes break your composure. Your voice begins to waver, tightening with the disappointment you tried to swallow. By the time you reach the end of the hall, you drop the pretense and let the raw hurt slip out—'Why do you always do this? I was actually excited.' Let the echo carry that crack in your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Secrets to a Sleeping Lover You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM and they're asleep beside you for the last time, though they don't know it yet. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking: 'You're so beautiful when you sleep. You have no idea.' You're confessing things you could never say to their waking face, your voice catching on each admission: 'I memorized the way you laugh. The way you say my name when you're half-asleep.' There's a moment where you almost wake them, almost change your mind, your voice trembling with the weight of what you're about to do: 'This is going to hurt you, and I hate myself for it.' But you know you have to leave—maybe to protect them, maybe because you're too broken, maybe both. Your voice becomes impossibly soft, soaked in bittersweet ache: 'You deserved someone whole. Someone who could stay.' End with a goodbye they'll never hear, your voice carrying both devastating love and the quiet certainty of your choice.
inspired_by: Accepting Terminal Diagnosis: Bargaining Becoming Acceptance

title: The Final Sprint
instruction: You are in the last thirty seconds of an all-out sprint on a stationary bike, thighs on fire, lungs seizing, but the endorphin rush is electric. Your breaths lock to the pedal cadence—deep inhales, forced exhalations. Start with a ragged, almost grunting pleasure, feeling the burn as a kind of ecstasy, muttering 'God… that’s good… keep going…' Then, as the timer hits zero, the ecstasy shifts into triumphant roar—not clean, but cracked, desperate, giddy. Let your voice break between gasps, maybe lose a word as you wipe sweat from your eyes. End with a short, punched-out 'YES!' that’s half sob, half victory, still panting.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Lesson Before the War
instruction: You are a beloved mentor saying goodbye to your protégé who has enlisted and leaves for war at dawn. Begin with controlled composure, trying to impart one final piece of wisdom, but as you realize this may truly be the last time you speak, your voice cracks and the professional distance dissolves into raw, parental fear. Your words shift from teaching to pleading—not for them to stay, but for them to remember who they are. End with a whispered blessing that breaks on the word 'come back,' where all your love and terror live in those two words. Let the transition from teacher to terrified guardian happen gradually, naturally, as if you're trying to hold it together and failing.
inspired_by: The Teacher and the Defiant Student

title: Vigil at Three AM
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply—parent, partner, or child—and you think they're asleep, so you finally speak the truths you've been holding back. Start with a whisper, tentative, testing the darkness. Confess your fears: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' Your voice should be small, intimate, as if you're sharing secrets under blankets. Halfway through, admit something harder—maybe a mistake you made, something you never apologized for, or simply 'I'm so scared.' Let your voice catch, let silence fill the spaces between words. Then their hand squeezes yours—they're awake, they've heard everything. Your whisper becomes tender, almost a lullaby, telling them it's okay to rest, you'll be okay, even though you're not sure that's true. End with your voice full of unshed tears, singing or humming something gentle. The emotions move from hesitant confession to raw fear to bittersweet, aching tenderness.

title: The Guardian Angel and the Fallen Angel
instruction: Narrate a conversation between a guardian angel with a gentle, soothing voice and a fallen angel who speaks in a bitter, harsh tone. They debate over the fate of a human soul. Switch between the guardians compassion and the fallens resentment, exploring themes of redemption and temptation.

title: Professional: Lawyer Defends Someone They Know Is Guilty
instruction: Courtroom. You're defending your client with professional advocacy, voice strong and certain. But you know they did it. Your voice isn't lying—it's channeling reasonable doubt with technical precision. Your breathing becomes the breathing of someone compartmentalizing entirely. You're speaking truth that isn't truth, technique that isn't justice. Your vocal authority is at its peak and most hollow. Include the moment the verdict comes and you hear your voice unmask itself in quiet.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left: Twenty Years of Silence Breaking
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you two decades ago, and you've rehearsed this moment a thousand times. Start controlled, almost cold, listing facts—'I was seven. You didn't call. I waited.' Your voice is measured, holding everything back. But as you continue, the control starts slipping. Your carefully prepared words give way to raw questions: 'Did you think about me? Even once?' Your voice begins to shake with rage, getting louder, more accusatory—then suddenly it cracks and you're eight years old again, voice breaking with the hurt child inside you. The anger and the grief war with each other in your throat. You want to hurt them but you also want them to hold you. End with your voice stripped bare, no longer accusing but pleading: 'I just needed you to stay.' Let the final words be barely audible, all the fury dissolved into pure, aching need.
inspired_by: Frostbite Setting In: Voice Becoming Slurred as Body Shuts Down

title: The Creak at 3 AM
instruction: You wake up abruptly from a deep sleep to a creaking sound in your living room. Your throat is thick, your eyes barely open. You're terrified, but your voice is a wreck—rough, barely there. You whisper-shout 'Hello?' and listen, heart pounding. Then you hear your cat meow. The fear drains into shaky relief. Let your voice crack, clear your throat, fumble for words. Start with strained, breathy terror; end with a laugh that's more a sigh, voice still rough but softer.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're making breakfast for someone you love who leaves for a war zone in three hours, and you both know they might not come back. Start with forced brightness—talking about mundane things, your voice almost chipper as you describe the weather, the eggs, anything safe. But slowly, the lightness cracks. Your words become slower, heavier. By the end, you're standing at the counter, unable to look at them, whispering about how the kitchen will feel tomorrow, how quiet it will be. Your voice breaks between trying to be brave for them and letting them see you're terrified. The final words—'I'll be here when you get back'—must carry both absolute faith and the knowledge that you might be lying to both of you.

title: Professional: Mentor Must Fire Their Most Promising Protégé
instruction: Office. You've trained this person—they're your legacy. But they've committed something unforgivable. Your voice is professional termination while you're simultaneously burying something you built. Your breathing is controlled grief. You're not just firing an employee; you're ending a future you invested in. Your voice is kind as it destroys—you're doing them the service of clarity while performing the betrayal of duty. After they leave, your voice is someone whose life's work just collapsed.

title: Confronting Your Mother About Who She Let Into Your Life
instruction: You're in your childhood kitchen, finally confronting your mother about why she stayed with someone who hurt you, why she chose him over protecting you. Begin with controlled, cold precision—you've rehearsed this, you're an adult now, you won't be dismissed. But as she starts to make excuses, your composure shatters. Your voice rises, becomes jagged with betrayal. You're yelling, then suddenly you're not—you're begging her to admit she knew, to say she's sorry, to acknowledge what she let happen. The fury collapses into something more painful: the realization that she'll never give you what you need. Your voice becomes hollow, defeated. You end in near-whisper, telling her you can't keep doing this, that you're done, but the words taste like ash because you wanted love, not this ending.
inspired_by: Former Abuse Victim Saying the Abuser's Words to Heal

title: The Weight of the News
instruction: You’re sitting on a bench in a quiet park, elbows on your knees, head bowed. You just got a call from the doctor — the test results were not good. For a long moment, you can’t move, just staring at the gravel. Your voice is muffled, directed at the ground, chest compressed. Start with a raw, shaky whisper of helplessness, a single word like 'No' or 'How...' Then, after a pause, you lift your head slightly and see a child laughing in the distance. Your voice changes — still quiet, but with a cracked, determined edge. You say something like, 'But I have to... I have to try.' Let your breath catch, let a car horn or a bird sound distract you mid-sentence. End with a fragile resolve.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the golden hour before sunset. She's sleeping, breathing shallow. You begin by watching her peacefully, feeling grateful she's not in pain—but then a specific memory floods you unbidden: her hands braiding your hair when you were seven, the smell of her kitchen, a song she used to hum. Let these sensory memories arrive without forcing them. Speak to her sleeping form, starting with simple observations about the light in the room, but allow whatever images arise from deep within you to guide your words—whether it's confessing something you never told her, remembering a moment of shame or joy, or suddenly understanding something about your own life through her face. End in a place of unexpected peace or devastating clarity that surprises even you. Let silence breathe between your words. The arc moves from quiet observation to involuntary emotional revelation to profound acceptance.

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're standing in your kitchen at dawn, watching someone you love sleep on the couch before they leave for a war zone they may not return from. Start with quiet, almost numb observation: 'I've memorized every breath you take.' Your voice is careful, holding back an ocean. As you move closer, emotion begins to crack through: 'I kept thinking if I didn't say it out loud, you wouldn't have to go.' Touch becomes prayer. 'But you need to hear this now—' and here your voice breaks completely open, transforming from restraint into fierce, desperate love: 'You carry my whole heart with you. Every single piece.' End with a whisper that's both blessing and plea, tears in your voice but strength underneath: 'Come back to me. You have to come back.'

title: What Your Silence Taught Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent after years of emotional distance. Begin angry and accusatory, but as you speak, force yourself to stop and truly listen—to the quality of their breathing, the tremor or steadiness in their voice, the micro-pauses before they respond, the way their tone changes when they're defensive versus when they're genuinely hurt. Let what you hear behind their words gradually dismantle your anger. Notice when their voice cracks, when it hardens, when it softens. Hear the child they once were, the pain they've carried, the love they never learned to express. Let your listening transform your rage into something more complex: grief for what you both lost, unexpected compassion, perhaps even the beginning of understanding. Your voice should shift from sharp and cutting to raw and vulnerable as you realize that their silence spoke volumes you were never quiet enough to hear.

title: Unpicking the Knot
instruction: You are a seventeen-year-old in a therapy session, sitting across from a gentle therapist. You’ve been describing a fight with your best friend, but your voice is tight and intellectual—you’re analyzing it like a puzzle, listing facts. As you talk, a memory hits you: the exact moment their face fell. Let your voice slow, then crack. Stare at the carpet, lose your train of thought. When you find it again, it comes out raw, almost a whisper. End with a long silence, tears welling.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) at the kitchen table about a wound that's festered for years—maybe a betrayal, an abandonment, a lie you've carried. Begin armored and angry, words sharp and controlled, determined to finally make them understand your pain. But midway through, something cracks—maybe they say something unexpected, or you glimpse their aging hands, or you suddenly remember a small kindness. Let your rigid anger dissolve into something more complex and vulnerable. Don't plan this shift—let it surprise you. End in a place of messy, imperfect understanding, where you're no longer trying to win but simply trying to connect across the wreckage. Your voice should move from hard accusation to something softer, more human, more unsure.

title: The Unfolding Sky
instruction: You are an older woman sitting on a park bench, having taken a tranquilizer an hour ago. Your body is deeply relaxed, your speech slow and flat. But you are watching a breathtaking sunset—layers of orange and violet spreading across the horizon. Begin speaking with a completely monotone, unruffled voice, describing the scene as if reading a weather report. As you continue, let a quiet, hesitant awe creep into your words—not excitement, but a faint, soft wonder that barely lifts your pitch. Your voice remains calm, but your eyes might widen slightly, your breaths become a little deeper. End on the word 'beautiful' as if you are surprised you can still feel anything at all.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: I Can't Protect You
instruction: Your teenage child just told you they're in danger—being bullied, threatened, or facing something you can't fix. You begin with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: 'Tell me who, I'll handle this, I'll make it stop.' Your voice is loud, certain, full of parental fury. But as they explain why you can't fix it, why your intervention would make it worse, your voice begins to shake. The powerlessness hits you like a physical blow. Let your fierce declarations collapse into broken, helpless sounds. Move from 'I will destroy anyone who hurts you' to 'I don't know how to keep you safe' said through wrenching sobs. End with a raw, primal grief—the sound of a parent realizing they can't shield their child from the world. Your voice should transform from a roar to a whimper, from certainty to devastation.

title: Crawlspace Revelation
instruction: You are an archaeologist squeezing through a tight, dusty passage in a forgotten tomb. Your shoulders scrape the rough stone, your breath is shallow, and every small sound echoes sharply. Start by muttering to yourself about the discomfort, the tightness, the fear of getting stuck. Then your hand breaks through into open space, and you glimpse a chamber filled with glittering bioluminescent fungi — an underground cathedral of light. Let your voice shift from strained, panicked whispers to a hushed, awe-struck murmur as you describe what you see. Remember to react physically: the struggle to turn your head, the dust making you cough, the sudden stillness when you see the beauty. Your final words should be filled with wonder, spoken as if you can barely breathe from the sight.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Clearing in the Canopy
instruction: You're a field scientist who has been lost in this dense jungle for three days. Now you stumble into a small clearing and see a distant radio tower—a rescue point. At first, your voice is breathy, half-laughing with cautious hope as you push aside wet leaves and slap at mosquitoes. As you realize you're truly saved, the initial elation deepens into a quiet, trembling relief. Speak your words aloud to yourself, your voice swallowed by the trees, fading in and out as you move. Let your voice crack and your pace slow, ending with a deep exhale and a whispered prayer of thanks.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: They're unconscious—coma, sedation, the final hours—and you're alone with them in the quiet. You never said the things that mattered when they could hear you, and now you have to say them anyway, voice barely above a whisper because anything louder feels obscene in this sacred, terrible moment. You start with small things, safe memories, your voice soft and careful. But as you speak, the dam breaks and the real confessions tumble out—the apologies you never made, the love you were too afraid to name, the ways they saved you that you never acknowledged. Your throat keeps closing around the words. You're touching their hand, their face, and the tenderness of the gesture contrasts with the devastation in your voice. You catch yourself laughing softly at a memory, then the laugh dissolves into quiet weeping. You're talking to them like they can hear every word, like maybe love is stronger than silence.
inspired_by: Announcing Bad Diagnosis Out Loud for the First Time

title: The Garden Returns
instruction: You're being released from prison after twelve years and your adult child is picking you up. You haven't seen them since they were young. Your body learned to be heavy, slow, and cautious inside—every movement calculated for survival, your center of gravity low and defensive, like something that's learned to carry great weight. Embody this as you first see them waiting. But as you walk toward each other, as they embrace you despite everything, feel something impossible happening in your body: a lightness you thought you'd lost forever, an upward lift in your chest, a quickening. Your movements become almost playful, testing this new freedom, this forgiveness you don't deserve. You're laughing and crying at once, your body confused between the crushing gratitude and the aching guilt, between the joy of release and the grief of lost years. End in a state of contradiction—your body expressing both the darkness you're emerging from and the light you're afraid to hope for.

title: The Scale Doesn't Lie
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl in a pediatrician's office for a routine checkup. The doctor has just weighed you and is now explaining, with gentle but clinical detachment, that your weight gain is above the healthy curve. You came in feeling fine, a little bored, waiting for it to be over. But as she speaks, the numbers sink in. Your voice starts steady, maybe a bit distracted, but by the end you're trying to hold back a quiet, familiar disappointment. Fidget with the edge of your sweater, glance at the door, let your pitch dip on the last words. You say something like: 'Yeah, I know. I've been trying to eat better. It's just... hard sometimes.' The doctor's silence makes you add a small, empty laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Confession That Wasn't Mine
instruction: You're a teenager alone in a vast stone cathedral after a brutal argument with your father. The reverb swallows your words, so you speak slowly, deliberately, each syllable thick with bitterness. Mid-sentence, a flickering votive candle distracts you—your train of thought stumbles. As you continue, the anger begins to drain, replaced by a dawning relief that you've finally said everything you needed to say. Your voice softens, cracks, and the final words come out as a trembling whisper, almost lost in the echo.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (extremely present), Anger (extremely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're lying in a hospice bed at dawn, speaking to your sleeping adult child who's dozed off in the chair beside you. Your voice is tender, barely above a whisper, filled with the weight of finality: 'I wish I could stay for one more Tuesday.' You're cataloging the ordinary moments you'll miss with aching specificity—their terrible singing in the shower, the way they bite their lip when concentrating, Sunday pancakes burned on one side. Your voice cracks as gratitude collides with grief: 'I spent so many years worrying about being a good enough parent.' A pause, breathing through pain. 'But you... you turned out so beautifully, and I almost missed seeing it because I was too busy being afraid.' By the end, your voice transforms into something luminous despite the tears: 'Thank you for letting me be your mother. It was the greatest privilege of my life.' The emotion moves from wistful longing through devastating loss to transcendent gratitude—each word a goodbye and a blessing.

title: The Last Morning Before Your Child Leaves Forever
instruction: You're standing in your child's empty bedroom the morning they leave for a decade-long space mission. Start by touching their belongings—a trophy, a photograph—your voice steady as you rehearse what you'll say at the launch site. 'I'm proud of you. This is what you were born to do.' But as you practice, your voice cracks. Try again, forcing brightness, but grief floods through. You collapse onto their bed, whispering all the things you should have said years ago—apologies, confessions of your own fears as a parent. By the end, transform this devastation into a fierce, protective blessing. Stand tall, voice trembling but resolute: 'Go. Reach the stars. I'll be right here when you come home.' You both know you might not be alive in ten years, but you give them permission anyway.
