inspired_by: Giving Yourself a Pep Talk in the Mirror Before a Date

title: The Condensation of Years
instruction: You are an older man sitting alone on a wooden bench in a nearly empty sauna in a tropical resort. The air is so thick it feels like swallowing fog. You are deeply content, eyes half-closed, letting the heat soak into your old joints. But then you notice a greasy, wet ring on the bench next to you—someone has left a sweaty, full water bottle that’s been rolling back and forth, and it has clearly been on the dirty floor. The disgust is immediate and visceral, a sharp, absurd contrast to your peace. Start by murmuring about the simple pleasure of the heat, focusing on the feel of it on your skin, then let your voice catch and shift as you fixate on that bottle—your tone becoming wet, heavy, a little breathless with irritation and revulsion, as you argue with yourself about whether to just leave it or be the one to clean it up.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Younger Self Before Surgery That Will Change Everything
instruction: You're alone the night before a life-altering surgery, speaking to a photograph of yourself as a child. Begin with tender nostalgia, remembering who you were before life hardened you. Your voice is soft, almost a lullaby. But as you continue, grief begins to seep in—you're mourning the innocence in those eyes, the dreams that died. The tenderness fractures into quiet devastation as you realize you're also saying goodbye to possibilities, to the person you might have been. End with a whisper of acceptance mixed with unbearable sadness, your voice breaking on the final words of farewell. Let the silence after your last word carry as much weight as everything you've said.
inspired_by: Discovering a Kink by Accident and Trying to Play It Cool

title: The Winery Revelation
instruction: Imagine you are a recovering perfectionist, at a high-end wine tasting three hours after getting your jaw wired shut from a car accident. The sommelier hands you a glass of your favorite vintage, and you're supposed to describe it, but you can barely open your mouth. Start by trying to play it cool, hiding your frustration with a bright, forced cheerfulness that cracks against your teeth. Then, as a single, exquisite note of blackcurrant and leather hits your tongue, you become overwhelmed with a strange, sour awe — this feels insane, this is beautiful, this is unfair. End with a raspy, muffled laugh, savoring the paradox of having your senses sharpened while your voice is trapped.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Awe (extremely present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Stroke Patient's Final Message
instruction: You've had a stroke that's left half your face paralyzed, and you know you have only hours before you lose consciousness permanently. You're recording a video message to your child, trying to tell them everything—how proud you are, the stories you never shared, the apologies you owe. Your speech is slurred and difficult, drool escaping as you fight to form words clearly. Begin with fierce determination to say it all perfectly, then slowly surrender to the reality that clarity doesn't matter—the love does. Let frustration give way to tender acceptance. Your final words should be almost unintelligible but saturated with such raw emotion that the meaning transcends the garbled sounds. End in a place of quiet peace, even as tears flow freely.

title: The Accidental Group Text to Your Dead Sister's Friends
instruction: You meant to text your therapist about your breakthrough—that you're finally ready to clean out your sister's apartment, three years after her suicide. Instead, you sent it to the group chat that still has her number in it, all her college friends. Your voice explodes in horror: 'Oh my God, oh my God, I'm so sorry—' The responses start flooding in immediately. One person is angry: 'How could you be so careless?' Your voice breaks into defensive rage: 'You think I meant to? You think I'm not dying inside every single day?' Another friend sends a voice note saying they miss her too, and your fury cracks wide open into sobbing: 'I can't do this. I can't keep pretending I'm healing when everything I touch turns into another way to hurt.' But then someone writes: 'She'd want you to clean it out. She'd want you to live.' And your voice transforms—still thick with tears but suddenly fierce, almost laughing through the pain: 'She'd probably think this whole thing was hilarious. Me, accidentally trauma-bombing her group chat at midnight.' You end with your voice raw but somehow lighter, finding the smallest seed of permission to keep going: 'I'm going to her place tomorrow. Anyone who wants to come... come.'
inspired_by: Sending a Drunk Text to the Wrong Person

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church After the Funeral
instruction: Everyone's gone. You're alone in the sanctuary. Start quietly—asking why, begging for an answer. But the silence enrages you. Your voice rises. You're shouting at the ceiling, at the cross, at the vast emptiness. Demand an explanation. Curse. Let the rage pour out—how dare this happen, where was the mercy, what kind of God allows this. Your voice should be raw, cracking, volcanic. Then suddenly, mid-scream, collapse. Fall to your knees. The rage breaks into sobs so violent they steal your breath. You can't even form words anymore—just animal sounds of grief. End with a whispered, desperate plea: 'Please... just let me feel you. Just once.' Move from fury to devastation to that naked, childlike need for comfort that has no pride left.
inspired_by: Ordering at a Drive-Through in a Tornado Warning

title: Vigil: Whispering to Someone Who Cannot Hear
instruction: You're at the bedside of your beloved—spouse, parent, closest friend—who is unconscious, hours from death. You're whispering confessions you never had the courage to say when they could respond. Start with your voice barely audible, tender, confessing small things: 'I ate the last piece of cake you were saving. I lied about liking your mother.' But then you go deeper. Your whispers become catches in your throat as you tell them the profound truths: how they saved you, how you failed them, how you're not ready. 'I don't know how to be in the world without you in it.' Your voice should be intimate, as if sharing secrets in the dark, but weighted with devastating finality. Include moments where you stop speaking entirely, just breathing with them. End with you telling them it's okay to go, your voice breaking on permission you don't want to give. This should feel like overhearing something too private to witness.
inspired_by: Breath Hold Challenge: Pushing Past Safety Thresholds

title: Shattered Glass
instruction: You're a teenager alone in your bedroom, clutching an old family photo from before your parents split. Your hand trembles, and you start to hyperventilate—your chest tightens, your fingers tingle. You try to say something bitter about how they ruined everything, but the words come out broken between gasps. As you struggle to breathe, the bitterness fades into a raw, desperate longing for the time when you all laughed together. Let the panic shake your voice—high-pitched, quavering, with forced pauses and audible gasps—while your feelings shift from angry accusation to a whispered ache for what's gone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Night Drive Negotiation
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman driving alone on a dark highway, reclined in your seat with your arms forward gripping the wheel. You're on a hands-free call with a former business partner who cheated you years ago. You've just learned they need your help now. You start with a controlled, almost cheerful tone, discussing old times, but as you speak, the resentment tightens your grip. Your voice shifts—louder to overcome road noise, but your breath is shallow from the reclined position. Let the malice seep in gradually, ending with a quiet, threatening promise. React naturally to headlights, road vibrations, and your own tension.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your adult child (or parent) across the kitchen table where you've shared a thousand silent meals. You start controlled, trying to be reasonable, listing complaints calmly. But then you stop mid-sentence and shift entirely: you begin saying what you actually think about everything—their choices, yes, but also the wallpaper, the coffee going cold, the way sunlight hits the table, what family means, what love costs, what you believe about forgiveness. Your statements become a torrent—personal, philosophical, irreverent, unfiltered. You move from rehearsed grievances to raw, uncensored truth-telling about your entire worldview. By the end, you've stopped trying to convince them of anything and started claiming your right to see the world exactly as you see it. Let your voice transform from measured accusation to wild, unguarded authenticity.

title: Breaking Point at the Gravesite
instruction: You're at your best friend's funeral, giving a eulogy you didn't prepare. Start composed, trying to honor them properly, describing their kindness, their laugh. But fury erupts—they died by suicide and you're enraged they left you, that they didn't call, that you missed the signs. Let your voice climb from measured grief to explosive anger, then shatter completely into sobbing helplessness. Apologize to them, beg them to come back, confess you're terrified you can't survive without them. Your delivery should be chaotic, uncontrolled—gasping between words, voice breaking mid-sentence. Include: 'You were supposed to be at my wedding! You were supposed to meet my kids! How dare you—' and then collapse into: 'How dare I be angry when you were in so much pain?' End in raw, messy devastation, no neat resolution.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in the wreckage of something you built—a relationship, a home, a dream—and you're laughing at the absurdity of it all while tears stream down your face. Begin by describing what's destroyed with dark humor, almost manic in finding the comedy in catastrophe. As you speak, let genuine gratitude for what it WAS break through the laughter. Your voice should oscillate between chuckling and catching, between celebrating the beauty of what existed and grieving its loss. End in a moment of strange, peaceful acceptance—still crying, maybe still laughing, but somehow okay. Transform from survivor's hysteria to a profound, contradictory peace that holds both joy and sorrow in the same breath.

title: The Final Command
instruction: You are in a dimly lit bedroom, standing over your partner who has just knelt before you. You feel a swell of pride as you see their submission, but it quickly ignites into a fierce triumph. Begin with a slow, deliberate exhale, adjusting the strap on your wrist. Your voice starts low and proud, almost amused, as you acknowledge their surrender. Then, let your tone harden into a growl, each word a weapon—whisper the threat close, then project the final command with absolute authority. Let a single, satisfied laugh escape as you finish, savoring your victory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering to Someone in a Coma
instruction: It's 3 AM in a hospital room. Your partner has been in a coma for three weeks after an accident. The nurses have gone home. You pull your chair close, take their hand, and begin to whisper the things you could never say when they were awake. Start so quietly you're almost talking to yourself: 'I don't know if you can hear me. They say maybe you can.' Your voice is fragile, intimate, the kind of vulnerable you've never allowed yourself to be. Confess something you've carried in silence: 'I was going to leave you. Two months ago, I had the papers drawn up. I was so tired of fighting.' Let your voice catch, tears making words difficult. 'And then this happened and I realized...' Long pause, voice breaking with tender devastation: 'You're the only home I've ever known. I was running from the one person who actually sees me.' Your whispers become even softer, as if speaking too loudly might shatter something sacred: 'Please come back. Please let me love you better. I promise I'll be brave enough this time.' End with your forehead pressed against their hand, words barely audible: 'I'm here. I'm finally here.'
inspired_by: Emergency Room Doctor: Critical Patient Arriving

title: The Kitchen After Midnight
instruction: You've come downstairs to find your teenage daughter packing a bag at 2 AM. She's leaving—moving in with friends, dropping out, running toward something or away from you. Start from genuine confusion and the fog of being woken up. Don't decide in advance whether you'll be the 'angry parent' or the 'understanding parent.' Instead, let yourself actually see her—this person you made, who's now a stranger. As she tells you why she has to go, let her words actually affect you. Maybe rage surfaces, maybe helplessness, maybe you suddenly remember holding her as an infant. Let contradictory impulses fight in you: the urge to forbid her versus the realization you can't; wanting to shake sense into her versus wanting to protect her from her own choices. By the end, neither of you are where you started emotionally. Something true has been said that can't be unsaid.

title: The Last Wave
instruction: You are an older man, just after making love with your long-term partner. Your body is still trembling from multiple orgasms—each one took more out of you, leaving your voice hoarse, cracked, barely there. You try to speak, but the words come out broken between shaky breaths. You begin with pure affection, a tender whisper of gratitude, but then a wave of sadness hits—you remember this might be the last time, your health failing. By the end, you force a wobbly, hopeful smile into your voice, believing it won't be. Your speech should feel physically destroyed, with pauses, breathy drops, and small uncontrollable sounds.
emotions_sampled: Affection (clearly present), Sadness (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Dad at the Rave
instruction: You're a middle-aged man at a loud rave with friends half your age, trying to prove you can still dance. You're out of breath, voice bouncing with each clumsy step, shouting over the thumping bass. At first, you're full of jittery self-effacing humor, brushing off your awkwardness with loud laughs and self-deprecating shouts. But as you keep moving, the embarrassment deepens into a raw, almost desperate realization that you don't belong here anymore—ending with a quiet, breathless admission you barely say aloud, the music swallowing your final words.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Glimpse
instruction: You are an elderly woman who has just sprinted across a field to catch a fleeting glimpse of a once-in-a-lifetime comet. Now you're bent over, hands on knees, fighting for breath — your lungs burning, your legs shaking. You speak in broken, gasping phrases between violent attempts to breathe. Start with astonishment that you actually made it, that you saw it with your own eyes, your voice trembling with shock and effort. But as you manage a few more words, let that astonishment soften into a deep, quiet awe — a sense of wonder that leaves you almost tearful, your voice becoming slower, more reverent, even as the gasping continues. Include natural micro-distractions: a cough, a spit, a pause where you lose a thought because you're dizzy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You are confronting your mother/father in their kitchen after discovering a decades-old family secret that changes everything you thought you knew about your childhood. Start controlled, even cold - you came here prepared with accusations. But as they begin to explain, really listen, and let their truth crack your certainty. Move through waves: righteous anger that someone lied to you, grief for the childhood you realize you misunderstood, rage at being protected from truth, reluctant understanding of impossible choices. Let your voice break from accusation to interrogation to something raw and childlike. End in a place you didn't expect - neither forgiveness nor condemnation, but in the complicated, messy middle where love and betrayal coexist. Your tone must shift from prosecutor to wounded child to someone becoming, painfully, an adult.
inspired_by: Actor needs maximum emotional availability before a demanding scene with extreme emotional requirements

title: Midnight Confession in the Hospital Chapel
instruction: You're alone in a hospital chapel at 3 AM, and your partner is in surgery after a car accident caused by your argument. Speak as if you're confessing to God, to the universe, to them—whispered, tender, devastated. Begin almost inaudibly: 'I said I was done. I said I didn't care anymore.' Your voice catches on every word. Describe the last thing you said to them, the cruelty of it, the way you stormed out. Your whisper becomes even softer, more fragile: 'Please. Please, I didn't mean it.' The vulnerability is excruciating—you're stripped of all defenses. By the end, you're making promises you're not sure you can keep, bargaining with fate: 'I'll be better. I'll try harder. Just let me tell them...' Let every word feel like it's being pulled from somewhere deep and unprotected in your chest.

title: The Broken Umbrella
instruction: You are standing on a deserted country road, soaked through, staring at a flooded field where your car is now stalled. Torrential rain roars around you, water streaming off your face and into your mouth as you gasp for air. You're shouting into a phone — but the person on the other end can barely hear you over the storm. You begin with a desperate, gulping helplessness, your voice cracking as you sputter between raindrops. As you realize help isn't coming, a fierce, stubborn pride takes over — you straighten your spine, raise your chin, and shout that you'll 'figure this out alone,' even as a quiet, defeated longing for safety lingers beneath your words by the end.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Pride (clearly present), Longing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Welcome Home, I Can't Forgive You
instruction: Someone you love desperately—who also hurt you profoundly—has just returned after years away. You open the door and see their face. Begin with contradictory impulses warring in your throat: a sob of joy trying to escape while anger clamps it down, laughter mixing with a growl of resentment. Let sounds layer and clash—start to embrace them while making sounds of fury, reach out while making sounds of grief. Don't resolve the contradiction—stay suspended between wanting to hold them and wanting to hurt them. Your voice should crack between tenderness and rage, gratitude and accusation. End exhausted by the impossibility of feeling everything at once, making sounds that are simultaneously welcoming and warning, loving and unforgiving.
inspired_by: Emotional Point of View, Without Words (Nonverbal)

title: The Weight of Forgiveness
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you deeply wronged years ago—a betrayal that destroyed them—and they've agreed to hear you out. Speak in hushed, careful tones, as if any louder might shatter this fragile moment. Begin with whispered attempts at explanation, your voice catching on words, shame making it hard to breathe. You can barely look at them. Each sentence is an effort. As you continue, the full weight of what you did crashes over you—your voice breaks into barely controlled weeping, but you force yourself to keep going, to not make this about your pain. Your words become fragmented, raw: 'I see now... what I took from you... I can't...' Midway through, they place a hand on yours, and you nearly fall apart completely. The confession becomes more vulnerable, more honest—you're not asking for forgiveness, just bearing witness to their pain. End with your voice thin and exhausted, saying simply, tenderly, 'Thank you for letting me say this,' your gratitude mixed with devastating sadness.

title: The Last Meal
instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's bedside in hospice. She's asked you to describe, in vivid detail, the Sunday dinners you shared at her table when you were a child—the ones you can never have again. Begin with reluctance and grief, unable to find words. As you speak, allow yourself to truly taste each dish in your memory: the salt and fat of her gravy on your tongue, the sweetness of her apple pie on the roof of your mouth, the way her coffee smelled from the kitchen. Let the sensory memories transport you from devastation into a state of profound gratitude and celebration of her life. By the end, you're laughing through tears, wanting her to know how completely she fed not just your body but your soul. Your voice should transform from broken and hesitant to full, rich, and overflowing with love.

title: The Last Light Through Kitchen Windows
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's bed in the small house where you spent every childhood summer. She has hours left, maybe less. Begin by letting your eyes rest on familiar objects in the room—the wallpaper pattern you traced with your fingers as a child, the smell of her lavender sachets, the particular quality of afternoon light through lace curtains. Start from a place of denial, talking about next summer's plans, keeping your voice artificially bright. As you truly absorb where you are—the weight of her hand in yours, the changed rhythm of her breathing, the taste of grief already forming in your throat—allow yourself to move from frantic cheerfulness into raw, undefended goodbye. Let the room itself—every sensory detail—guide you into the full truth of this moment. End in a place of devastating acceptance, speaking words you can barely形成 through tears.

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, a cruelty—and your entire body is flooded with sensation. Begin with physical symptoms: your hands are shaking, your chest is tight, you can't catch your breath. Start trying to hold yourself together, to maintain control, to make sense of it. But as you continue, let the physical sensations dictate what happens next. Maybe control gives way to violent rage—you want to destroy something. Maybe your legs give out and you collapse. Maybe uncontrollable laughter erupts. Maybe you keen like an animal. Don't decide what the 'right' response is—let your body lead. Allow raw physical impulses to mix with waves of emotion: fury bleeding into grief, numbness cracking into pain, despair igniting into fierce determination. By the end, you've moved through the storm to something unexpected—perhaps eerie calm, perhaps tender exhaustion, perhaps savage clarity.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with your father after fifteen years of silence. He's dying and asked to see you. Start cold, voice tight with control: 'You don't get to do this. You don't get to call me here and expect—' But your anger is a dam holding back an ocean. As you speak, it begins to crack: 'I was eight years old. EIGHT. Do you even remember my face back then?' Your voice rises, shaking with decades of abandonment. Then suddenly, devastatingly, you collapse into the child you were: 'I waited for you. Every birthday, I thought maybe...' Now you're pleading, vulnerable, voice breaking: 'Why wasn't I enough? Just tell me why I wasn't enough for you to stay.' End in exhausted, raw honesty, barely above a whisper: 'I needed you. I still need you. And you're leaving again.'

title: Reading a Love Letter from Someone Now Gone While Laughing at Shared Memories
instruction: You found a letter they wrote you years ago, something funny and tender about an absurd day you shared. Start reading it aloud and you're genuinely laughing—their humor still lands, and for a moment they're alive in the room with you. But mid-laugh, the reality crashes in and suddenly you're crying while still smiling at their words. Your voice should dance between joy at the memory and the breaking knowledge that there will be no more memories. Find genuine laughter that dissolves into tears that circle back to grateful, painful joy. End in a place of beautiful, impossible peace—thankful for what you had while your heart simultaneously shatters that it's over.
inspired_by: Pilot Congratulating Crew While Processing Near-Catastrophe

title: The Melted Green-Eyed Monologue
instruction: You're lying in a tangle of sheets, skin still warm and damp, your partner's hand tracing lazy circles on your back. You're deeply satisfied, almost drunk on endorphins, and a slow, wicked amusement bubbles up as you remember the moment earlier tonight when you saw someone flirt with them—and how that brief flash of jealousy now seems absurdly funny. Start with a contented, heavy-lidded chuckle, your voice thick with vocal fry and half-swallowed sighs. As you speak, let the amusement dominate, but let the memory of that jealousy creep in as a tiny, playful edge—like you're savoring the silliness of it. End with a softer, more vulnerable hum, the jealousy dissolved into a quiet, possessive warmth.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Dying Parent About the Childhood They Stole
instruction: You're at your parent's hospital bedside with hours left, and decades of silence are breaking open. Start with carefully controlled anger—listing the ways they failed you, the protection they never offered, the childhood you never had. But as you speak, something shifts. You see them as they are now: fragile, diminishing, terrified. Your rage begins to crack, revealing the child underneath who still desperately wanted to be loved. You move between fury and grief, between needing them to acknowledge what they did and needing to forgive them before it's too late. End in a place you didn't expect—perhaps offering your hand, perhaps withdrawing it forever. Let your voice be messy, contradictory, human. This isn't performed anger; this is a real person trying to reconcile the impossible before time runs out.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Chooses to Remain in a Body It's Outgrowing

title: The Last Breath of Resentment
instruction: You’re alone in a cold hospital room, the oxygen mask strapped tight over your face. The hiss of airflow fills every silence, and your own voice sounds hollow and distant. You’re a young man whose family let you down—no visits, no calls—and you’re recording a voicemail you’ll never send. Start with bitter accusation: loud, grinding, each word fighting the plastic seal. Midway, a knock at the door makes you flinch, and you pause, breath hitching, then you realize it’s just a nurse passing by. That interruption breaks your anger. Let the bitterness drain out, replaced by a quiet, exhausted resignation. End with a long, muffled exhale into the mask, the hiss swallowing your final words.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Opening the Acceptance Letter
instruction: You're holding a letter—an acceptance to a dream program, a positive medical test result, news that you got the job. This is what you've wanted for years, what you've sacrificed everything for. But as you read it aloud slowly, let your mind simultaneously flood with thoughts of what this means you're leaving behind: a relationship that couldn't survive your ambition, a parent who'll now be alone, a version of yourself you'll never be again. Your voice should carry both elation and loss. Start with pure joy—laughing, maybe crying happy tears. But let the other emotion creep in, coloring your voice with something bittersweet, then something almost mournful. By the end, you're still happy, but it's a complicated happiness that acknowledges the cost. You might end by whispering 'thank you' or 'I'm sorry' or 'goodbye'—and it's unclear who you're talking to. The joy never disappears, but it becomes inseparable from grief.

title: Paragliding Through Grief
instruction: You're scattering your partner's ashes from a paraglider over the mountains they loved, and the absurdity and beauty are breaking you open. Start laughing—really laughing—at the chaos of trying to open the urn while managing the glider, at how perfectly imperfect this is, how they'd be cracking jokes right now. Let that laughter run alongside tears you're not trying to stop. Your voice should shimmer between joy at the majesty of this moment and the guttural ache of doing it alone. Describe the landscape to them as if they can hear: 'You should see this, love, you should—oh, you ARE seeing this.' Find genuine peace in the contradiction—grateful for having loved them, shattered that it ended, wholly present in both feelings at once. End in something transcendent: broken and whole simultaneously.

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: You are a middle-aged man kneeling at the edge of a hospital bed, hands clasped loosely on the rail. Your son lies motionless, and you've been here for days. Your voice is gravelly, your throat raw from held-back tears and too little sleep. Begin by trying to pray — the words feel hollow, slipping away mid-sentence. Let the exhaustion pull your voice down, your head dropping lower. Then, instead of begging, you speak to him directly, your voice cracking with a disappointment that's not at him but at yourself, at a god you're not sure you believe in anymore. End on a whisper, almost inaudible, as you lose the thread entirely.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bitter Pulpit
instruction: You are a 17-year-old boy forced to preach at your family's small church on a sweltering Sunday. Your voice has a deep, forced-masculine quality but it cracks with resentment—you hate being here, you hate the scripted prayers. Begin with a bitter, almost sneering cadence, letting the dry heat and the weight of the pulpit make you pause and shift your weight. As you continue, the rhythm of your own voice feeds a growing sense of triumph: you realize you can wield this power, that your bitterness can become a weapon. End on a note of fierce, defiant victory, as if you've turned the sermon into your personal battle cry.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Mirror Breaks
instruction: Confront someone who has diminished you for years—a lover, parent, or close friend who constantly made you feel small, incompetent, or not enough. Start the confrontation tentatively, your voice shaking, almost apologizing for even bringing it up. As you speak, specific memories flood back—moments when they tore you down, dismissed your feelings, made you doubt your reality. Let rage build as you recount these moments, your voice growing sharper, louder. But then something unexpected happens: mid-confrontation, you realize their power over you is evaporating. End not with rage but with calm, final clarity—a quiet, unshakeable knowing that you are done seeking anything from them. Your voice should journey from trembling to furious to eerily peaceful.
inspired_by: Actor has chronic self-esteem problems that return every time they act or audition

title: The Last Breath Before Silence
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've loved your entire life—a parent, a partner, a best friend—and they have only minutes left. Begin in a state of frozen shock, unable to speak, your breath shallow and caught in your throat. As you hold their hand, feel the weight of every unsaid word pressing against your chest. Let the tension in your body build until something cracks open inside you—a sound, a sob, a guttural release that comes from deep in your belly. By the end, transform that raw sound into words: tell them everything you never said, your voice breaking and rebuilding, moving from paralyzed silence to a fierce, desperate outpouring of love. Let your final moment be one of unexpected peace, a whispered acceptance that releases both of you.
inspired_by: When you are tense, anxious, or blocked before an important scene, especially on a high-pressure set

title: What You Never Knew I Kept
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) after years of distance and unspoken pain. You've brought with you an object they don't know you've kept all these years—something they gave you, threw away, or left behind that became significant to you in ways they never understood. Start angry, guarded, ready to fight. Hold the object hidden at first. As the confrontation unfolds, reveal it. Let them see what you've carried. Watch their reaction. Allow your anger to fracture as you explain why you kept it, what it meant during the years they weren't there or didn't see you. Move from accusation to vulnerability, from needing them to hurt to needing them to finally understand. The object is your evidence, your shield, and ultimately your olive branch. End in a place of painful honesty—not necessarily reconciliation, but truth.
inspired_by: When staging a production where a character has a deep emotional relationship with physical objects

title: Finding Grace in the Wreckage
instruction: You're stumbling away from an accident that should have killed you, disoriented and bleeding, but suddenly struck by the profound beauty of being alive. Begin confused, voice slurred and uncertain, touching your injuries with disconnected surprise. As reality sharpens, let wonder creep in—your voice should carry both pain and astonished laughter at the absurdity of survival. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, overwhelmed by gratitude even as your head spins and your words scatter. Describe what you see with childlike awe even as you acknowledge the blood, the ringing in your ears, the way light splinters in your damaged vision. Move between moments of disorientation and piercing clarity about what matters. End with your voice soft and broken but shot through with joy, whispering thank you to nobody and everybody, finding unexpected peace in the chaos of your battered body and fractured thoughts.

title: The Sound of Silence
instruction: You are an older woman just waking from ear surgery that left you with severe hearing loss. Your granddaughter is at your bedside. You're terrified, disoriented, your voice uncontrollably loud and unsteady—you can't monitor volume or pitch. You keep calling out her name, your sibilants blurring. Midway, you see her hands form 'I love you' in sign language, a skill you taught her years ago. Your distress cracks into pure, overwhelming awe. Let your voice drift from frantic loudness to a softer, wondering tone as you realize she is speaking to you in a way you can still understand. Speak about 50 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Escaping the Burning House with Only the Photo Album
instruction: The fire alarm is screaming. You're stumbling through smoke-filled rooms, coughing violently, clutching the family photo album against your chest—the only thing you managed to grab. Your breathing is wrecked by smoke and panic, words coming out between hacking coughs as you narrate what you're losing with each room you pass: 'The kitchen where Mom taught me—' *cough* '—the corner where we measured the kids—' You're grieving in real-time, your voice destroyed not just by smoke but by the absurdity, the strange fierce joy that you're alive mixed with devastation at what's burning behind you. You burst outside into clear air, collapsing on the lawn, gasping and laughing and sobbing simultaneously. Your breathing slowly calms but your voice wavers between gratitude and loss. You open the album with shaking hands, and through tears, you start laughing—really laughing—at a ridiculous photo, then crying harder. 'We're okay. We're okay. Everything's gone and we're okay.' The contradictions don't resolve; they coexist. End in breathless, tearful, grateful, broken relief.
inspired_by: Reporting While Sprinting for Your Life

title: Trust Building
instruction: You're being asked to trust your partner in a vulnerable way—physically, emotionally. You're hesitant: 'I want to, but I'm scared.' Your partner's voice becomes patient: 'We'll go slow.' They're asking for permission to build something between you. You're articulating fear, and they're answering with reassurance. As the trust builds—as they keep their promises, as they prove they can be trusted—your voice becomes less guarded. You're slowly lowering defenses. Your voice becomes confident: 'Okay. I'm ready.' By the end, you're allowing someone into spaces you've protected. Your voice should sound like someone learning that safety is possible with another person.

title: Breaking Point Ecstasy
instruction: You've just finished running—not jogging, but a full-sprint, desperate run away from something or toward something crucial in your life. Your entire body is screaming: lungs burning, legs shaking, sweat stinging your eyes, heart hammering so hard you can feel it in your temples. You collapse against a wall or onto the ground. Start with pure physical sensation—the pain, the gasping, the overwhelming aliveness of your body at its limit. As your breathing begins to slow, let the physical intensity start mixing with the emotional reason you were running: maybe you just quit the job that was killing you, or you ran from a fight that almost turned violent, or you're rushing to reach someone you love. Let the boundary between physical pain and emotional release dissolve. As your body recovers, transform from pure animalistic survival mode into laughing-crying-gasping, where physical exhaustion and emotional breakthrough become inseparable—you can't tell if you're sobbing or exhilarated or both.

title: What You Never Told Me
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen of your childhood home, ten years after he missed the most important day of your life. Start from a place of carefully controlled anger—you've rehearsed this, you're in command, you're going to finally tell him how much he hurt you. But as you begin to speak, everything you've buried comes flooding out uncontrollably. Your voice rises, cracks, becomes raw. Then he says something—one sentence—that completely reframes everything you thought you knew about that day. The anger doesn't disappear, but it tangles with confusion, with sudden devastating understanding, with the realization that you've been carrying a story that wasn't complete. End in a place of uncomfortable, unwanted compassion mixed with the remnants of your rage. Let the transformation be messy and incomplete.
inspired_by: Actor has a persistent fear (auditions, exposure, ridicule, conflict) that keeps returning

title: Bedside Vigil: What I Never Said
instruction: Your person is unconscious in a hospital bed. You don't know if they can hear you. Start with small talk, trivial updates, your voice falsely bright and normal. But the pretense becomes unbearable. Your voice drops to a whisper. You begin confessing things you were always too afraid to say—not grand declarations, but small, tender truths. How their laugh made you feel safe. How you memorized the way they took their coffee. How some Tuesday three years ago, watching them read by the window, you realized you'd found home. Your voice should catch, break, barely hold together. This isn't performed emotion—this is what love sounds like when you might never get another chance.

title: The Wedding Toast That Breaks Your Heart: Celebrating Your Ex's New Beginning
instruction: You are giving a toast at your ex-partner's wedding—to someone else. You must sound genuinely happy for them while your heart is simultaneously breaking. Begin with warmth and humor, sharing a fond memory that makes people laugh—your voice bright and celebratory. But let cracks appear: a slight tremor when you mention their smile, a pause that lasts a heartbeat too long. As you continue, weave in bittersweet acknowledgment of your shared past—speaking of the love you had with both gratitude and grief, your voice thickening with unshed tears even as you smile. Build to a moment of absolute sincerity: you wish them joy with your whole heart, even though it costs you everything to mean it. End with a genuine laugh through tears—the sound of someone experiencing devastating loss and authentic happiness simultaneously. Your voice should somehow contain both celebration and mourning, proving that you can hold two opposing truths at once: you are happy for them, and you are shattered.
inspired_by: The Guardian Angel and the Fallen Angel

title: Dancing at Your Funeral
instruction: You're at the celebration of life for someone who made you promise—absolutely promise—not to cry at their funeral but to dance instead. Start by laughing as you remember them making you swear it, almost giddy with the absurdity of keeping this promise. But as you move, really feeling their absence, laughter becomes inseparable from grief. Let your voice carry both—genuine joy at their wild spirit mixing with tears you can't hold back. You're honoring them, loving them, and losing them all at once. Move between laughing at their audacity and crying at the hole they've left, until you can't tell which is which. End with profound gratitude breaking your voice: 'Thank you for making me promise this impossible thing.' The emotions should be beautifully tangled—grief and celebration woven so tight they become one.
inspired_by: Childlike Wonder in a Strange Land

title: Conducting Energy
instruction: You're feeling it—electricity in your veins. Your voice carries the current. You've just survived something that should have killed you. Your voice has become dynamic, alive, conducting power through every word. 'I'm here. I'm alive.' The revelation is physical. Your voice radiates survival. Others feel it. 'What happened to you?' they ask, sensing the change. Your voice has been rewired by near-death.

title: The Burn and The Breaking
instruction: You've just received catastrophic news (a betrayal discovered, a diagnosis, a sudden loss) and you're alone in your home. Your body is flooded with adrenaline and feeling. Start with physical action—pace, throw things, collapse, whatever your body demands—but let the physicality and emotion feed each other unpredictably. If rage suddenly dissolves into laughter, follow it. If you're screaming and suddenly feel aroused or hungry or numb, explore that. Touch objects, taste something, feel textures, let your senses overwhelm you. Permit the experience to be messy, contradictory, even inappropriate. Let your voice do strange things—whisper then roar, speak gibberish, sing, keen. End in a completely different physical and emotional state than you began, having discovered something about yourself in the wreckage.

title: Defense Lawyer Cross-Examines Witness, Realizes They're Confessing to Other Crimes
instruction: Courtroom, you're establishing witness credibility through careful questioning. Your voice is measured, professional. Then the witness answers differently than expected—they're admitting to a crime you now know about. Legally, you must continue; ethically, everything fractures. Your vocal rhythm changes subtly. Your questions continue with the same professional tone but now you're aware you're participating in a moral equation that has no clean solution. Your breathing deepens with the weight of knowledge.

title: The Shattering in the Doorway
instruction: You're standing in the doorway, and your teenage child just told you they've been self-harming. Rage erupts first—not at them, but at yourself for missing it, at the world for hurting them: 'How did I not see this? What kind of parent—' Your voice is fierce, almost shouting, but it's protective fury born of helplessness. Then you see their face—terrified, shutting down—and everything in you breaks. Your voice cracks mid-sentence and collapses into desperate tenderness: 'No, no, I'm not angry at you. I'm so sorry. I'm here.' You move toward them, your voice dissolving into tears, fierce love mixed with crushing guilt. You tell them they are enough, they are loved, your voice raw and undefended. End with you holding them, your voice still shaking but absolutely certain: 'We'll get through this. I'm not going anywhere.' It's devastating and powerful at once.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in the early dawn. She has hours, maybe minutes left. Begin by remembering the kitchen of your childhood home where she used to make breakfast—see the sunlight through the window, smell the coffee, feel the worn tablecloth. Let this memory fill you with warmth and nostalgia. Now, still holding that sensory memory alive, open your eyes and look at her face in this hospital room. Speak to her about that kitchen, those mornings, but let your voice break as you realize this is the last time you'll ever see her face in morning light. Your emotion should travel from warm reminiscence to the devastating collision of past joy and present loss.
inspired_by: Actor wants to begin learning imaging

title: The Locked Room
instruction: You are confronting your parent about something that has haunted you since childhood—a moment of abandonment, a betrayal, a time they weren't there when you desperately needed them. Begin with controlled anger, words you've rehearsed. But as you speak, allow a specific sensory memory to intrude unbidden: the texture of a blanket you clutched, the sound of a door closing, the particular quality of darkness in a room where you waited alone. Don't narrate this memory—let your body respond to it as if it's happening now. The smell of that time. The exact feeling in your chest. Stay with the physical sensations as they rise. By the end, your carefully prepared accusations have dissolved into something rawer: not anger at your parent, but the voice of your child-self finally being heard, speaking a truth they couldn't articulate then.

title: The Last Sip of Paradise
instruction: You are an elderly man, a long-time resident of a steamy tropical island, sitting on your porch in the thick, wet heat of late afternoon. A persistent, much younger salesperson is pestering you to buy something you despise. At first, your voice is thick with weary contempt for the intrusion, your words smothered by the humidity. Let your breathing be labored, your mouth feel moist and awkward. As you speak, a memory of the island before it was 'discovered' takes hold, and your contempt slowly curdles into a quiet, deep-seated bitterness at what was lost. Your voice should start with clipped, wet disdain and end with a tired, hollow mumble.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Tour Before Everything Changes
instruction: You're giving your final tour as a guide before the landmark you've devoted your life to is demolished tomorrow. Start with your usual confident, encyclopedic knowledge, but let cracks appear as you realize this is goodbye. Your voice should shift from professional pride to barely-contained grief as you describe details you'll never see again. End by breaking down mid-sentence about an architectural feature, unable to finish because you're overwhelmed by the loss of this place that's been your entire identity. Let the love you have for these stones, this history, this purpose overtake you completely.

title: The Unraveling Revival
instruction: You are a young man caught in the throes of a Pentecostal revival, your body trembling, sweat on your brow. Start with a teasing, almost mocking cheer—'Hallelujah! Yes, Lord!'—your voice leaping into a singsong rhythm, a grin in your tone. But as you spin, you glimpse a photo of a friend you abandoned in his darkest hour. The joy shatters. Your voice cracks, dropping to a whisper: 'I left him... I laughed when he cried.' Now the shame crushes you—your words become broken gasps, 'I'm sorry, I'm sorry,' as sobs overtake the chant, the ecstasy hollowing into sorrow.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (extremely present), Sadness (clearly present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Why You're Leaving in the Middle of the Night
instruction: You're beside your sleeping partner, speaking in the softest whisper, confessing why you have to leave. Begin with extreme gentleness—you love them, that's not the question. Your voice is barely audible, careful not to wake them, but full of aching tenderness. As you explain, something catches in your throat. The reasons you're leaving feel so small when you say them aloud, yet so heavy. Your whisper becomes unsteady. You reach out, maybe touching their hair, and a sob tries to escape—you swallow it, breathe, keep whispering. There's intimacy in this quiet devastation. You tell them they deserved better, and saying it breaks you silently. End with a whispered 'I'm sorry' that contains multitudes—regret, love, grief, and a kind of terrible, necessary clarity.
inspired_by: Crying and Trying to Explain While Gasping for Air

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left: The Words You've Rehearsed for Years
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child. You've imagined this moment for twenty years. Start with controlled anger—you're trying to be articulate, to lay out exactly how they hurt you, to sound strong. But within seconds, you're eight years old again, your voice breaking, questions pouring out faster than you can think them: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me? Did you ever think about me?' The rage keeps surfacing, making your voice sharp and loud, then collapsing back into the vulnerability of a child begging for an answer. End with exhausted pleading that dissolves into something quieter—not forgiveness, but the terrible recognition that you may never get the answer that would make you whole.
inspired_by: Cocaine High: Words Tumbling Out Uncontrollably

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're forty years old, standing in your parent's kitchen, finally confronting them about the childhood they gave you—one of perfect manners and complete emotional absence. Begin with careful, practiced words, the same diplomacy you've used your whole life to keep peace. But something breaks. Your voice sharpens, decades of unspoken pain cutting through: 'You never once asked how I felt. Not once.' Feel your control splinter as you list specific moments—your graduation, your divorce, the miscarriage you went through alone while they redecorated their living room. Then, unexpectedly, hear the smallness in your own voice, the child still inside you begging: 'Why wasn't I enough to reach for?' End in devastating quiet, not with anger but with grief, acknowledging that they may never have an answer that satisfies the wound.

title: The Words I Learned for You
instruction: You are lying in bed in the dark, whispering to your sleeping partner in a language they don't speak—one you've been secretly learning for months. You've been watching documentaries about their culture, reading their country's literature, listening to their childhood songs, trying to understand the world that shaped them before you met. Begin with shy, hesitant pronunciation as you whisper phrases in this language—tender things, observations about them, confessions of love. Your voice should be fragile, vulnerable, almost embarrassed by your accent. As you continue, describe in your shared language why you've been doing this: you want to touch the parts of them that exist in words you don't have, to meet them in a landscape of memory and identity you can only visit as a loving outsider. End with a trembling question whispered in their language, imperfect but deeply sincere, asking them to be patient with your learning.

title: The Stillness After the Impact
instruction: You're in the middle of a sparring match, fully present in your body. You've just landed a clean strike and taken a solid hit to your ribs, but instead of pain, you feel a deep, grounded contentment—like every cell is alive and exactly where it needs to be. As you circle your partner, your breathing is controlled, predatory, but your voice shifts from sharp kiai to soft, genuine words as you pause to adjust your stance and wipe sweat from your eye. Start with fierce, explosive shouts and heavy breaths; then let your voice become breathless and tender as you speak from that rare place of total satisfaction, ending with a quiet, satisfied exhale.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Scar on Your Wrist
instruction: In the quiet darkness of a bedroom, you're lying next to someone you've just become intimate with for the first time. They're tracing their fingers gently along your body and they pause at a scar—maybe on your wrist, your shoulder, your stomach. They ask softly, 'Where did this come from?' Begin in a place of guardedness, the instinct to deflect or lie. But as their finger stays there, just resting on that mark, something about that gentle touch on that specific spot unlocks you. Let the sensation of their fingertip on that exact place become your entire world. It becomes unbearably tender, almost too much to bear. Let this focused physical sensation pull a whispered confession from you—the real story of that scar, which is also the story of a part of yourself you've kept hidden. Move from self-protection to radical vulnerability, from holding back to letting them see you completely, all because of what their touch on that one spot makes you feel.

title: The Unwanted Advance
instruction: You're a 16-year-old guy alone with your close friend who just kissed you. You're caught off guard – you care about her deeply, but this isn't what you want. Start with warm confusion, your voice soft and uncertain as you try to figure out what just happened. As she persists, your voice shifts to a flat, clear 'no' – you force yourself to be direct, but a tremor of love still cracks through. End with a quiet, awkward apology, your throat dry, wanting to escape the moment but not hurt her. Speak naturally, with pauses, shifting weight, maybe a half-laugh of disbelief.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Telling Your Parent You're Moving Across the World Tomorrow
instruction: You're leaving for a remote research station in Antarctica tomorrow—five years, limited contact. Start practical, almost cheerful, explaining logistics and opportunities. 'The stipend is incredible, Mom. This is what I've trained for.' But as you see their face, your voice begins to fracture. Describe small things you'll miss—their Sunday calls, the way they make coffee, holidays. Let silence hang between phrases as the permanence settles on you both. Your voice should crack on mundane details more than grand statements. End with a desperate attempt to memorize this moment, whispering things you've never said aloud, gratitude pouring out as you realize you're saying goodbye to an entire chapter of life. The emotion should feel like drowning in slow motion.
inspired_by: Explaining Your Mental Health Diagnosis to Someone Close

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he stayed silent during a crucial moment in your childhood when you needed him to speak up for you. Begin with controlled anger—you came prepared with accusations. But as you speak, stop and ask yourself: what do you feel about his silence specifically? What do you feel about the way he's looking at you right now? What does his posture tell you? Let each question lead you deeper, peeling back your rehearsed anger to discover what's underneath—perhaps it's not just anger but fear, or longing, or the little child in you still waiting for protection. As you continue, your voice and emotion should shift from confrontation to something rawer and more vulnerable. End in a place of emotional honesty you didn't plan to reach—maybe forgiveness, maybe deeper hurt, maybe understanding, but something true that surprises you.
inspired_by: Taking Your Emotional Point of View

title: Walking Off the Wrath
instruction: You're an older man power walking along a park path, arms pumping, breath coming in rhythmic bursts. You start with a focused pride in your pace—you're fit, you're moving, you're getting the heart rate up. But as you walk, a recent betrayal gnaws at you, and the anger swells until it nearly strangles your words. Keep the concentration on your stride, feel the heel-strike jolt through your voice, and let the rage build until you're muttering accusations under your breath, then force yourself back to the rhythm, breathing hard, voice trembling with contained fury.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Anger (extremely present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Holding Them While They're Dying
instruction: You're holding someone you love as they're slipping away, and you start with a laugh that's half sob: 'Remember when you said I was never really there? Look at me now. I'm so here it's killing me.' Your voice is tender and breaking simultaneously: 'I wasted so much time being somewhere else, thinking about work, worrying about stupid things.' You stroke their face, voice full of wonder and grief: 'But right now, I can see every line on your face, and they're beautiful. When did you get this freckle? How did I never notice?' Let gratitude mix with devastation: 'Thank you for teaching me this. Thank you for waiting until I learned how to actually show up.' Your breathing becomes uneven: 'I know you're leaving, and I know I can't stop it, but god, I'm so completely here with you right now.' A pause, then with fierce intensity: 'I'm not going to look away. I'm not going to miss this. I'm giving you every piece of my attention, all of my presence, everything I have.' By the end, your voice is a whisper full of both peace and unbearable loss: 'This moment—you and me, fully here—this is the most alive I've ever been. Even as you're leaving.' The emotion weaves between joy and agony, gratitude and grief, presence and loss.

title: Final Goodbye to Your Parent Who Never Said They Were Proud
instruction: You're at your parent's bedside in their final hours. They're drifting in and out of consciousness. You start trying to tell them about your accomplishments, your life, hoping for acknowledgment—your voice is almost businesslike, protective. But mid-sentence, something breaks. The words dissolve into a whispered confession: 'I just wanted you to see me.' Your throat closes. You realize you're grieving not just their death, but a lifetime of invisible wounds. End by taking their hand and saying 'I love you anyway' with a tenderness that holds both forgiveness and devastating sadness. Let the shift from seeking approval to accepting the truth wash through your entire body.
inspired_by: Your Child Asking Why You Cried About Their Assault

title: Confronting Your Father at His Retirement Party About the Affair That Destroyed Your Mother
instruction: Everyone's toasting him in the country club ballroom—beloved teacher, dedicated community member, father of the year. You've had three drinks and you pull him into the coat check room. Your voice starts low and controlled, but there's venom in it, years of watching your mother pretend, years of keeping his secret. 'Do you even remember her name?' you ask about the woman he cheated with. Your words come faster, louder—all the rage you've swallowed at every family dinner is erupting. But then he says something—maybe he admits it, maybe he cries, maybe he tries to justify—and your fury cracks into something more complex. Suddenly you're not just angry; you're grieving the father you thought you had, and underneath that, you're terrified you might be capable of the same betrayals. Your voice moves from accusatory to almost pleading: 'Why weren't we enough?' End with a realization spoken through tears that aren't just angry anymore—they're confused and hurt and you hate that you still want him to have an answer that makes sense.
inspired_by: Hostage Negotiator Talking Down a Gunman While Your Own Child Texts

title: The Pen and the Hollow
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone at a worn wooden desk, writing a letter to your late wife by lamplight. The pen scratches slowly, your head bowed, voice slightly muffled. Begin in a thick emotional numbness—your hand moves mechanically, words hollow, with only a faint pinch of envy as you recall neighbors whose spouses still walk beside them. Let the numbness crack as longing seeps through, your voice softening, hand pausing mid-stroke. End with a raw, almost whispered confession, the pen trembling.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Longing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Poisoned Honey
instruction: You are an elderly woman curled on your side in bed, one lung pressed against the mattress, your voice soft and breathy. Speaking to a visitor who you believe has wronged you, you begin with a gentle, fragile tone, almost apologetic. As you continue, let a thin thread of malice seep into your words, turning them into a sweetly disguised venom. By the end, your voice hardens into a cold whisper, the anger barely masked behind a fragile smile. Your breaths are shallow, and you pause as if lost in thought, then continue with a sharp edge.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Gravel and Gratitude
instruction: You are an elderly woman walking on a long gravel path toward a bench near a lake. Each step crunches loudly, forcing you to raise your voice and speak more clearly. You begin muttering to yourself with bitter resentment about a recent family argument, your voice tight and sharp as you focus on not slipping. Halfway through, you notice a cardinal land on a branch ahead, and a sudden wave of affection for your late spouse washes over you. Your voice softens, breaks, and becomes tender as you finish the walk, still careful on the stones but now speaking with love and loss.
emotions_sampled: Affection (very intensely present), Concentration (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Telling Your Mother She Failed You
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the childhood she gave you—or didn't give you. Begin with careful, measured words, the speech you've rehearsed for years, trying to stay calm and rational. But as you speak, the anger you've suppressed comes flooding up. Your voice rises. You say things you swore you wouldn't say. Then suddenly, unexpectedly, you see her face—really see her—and the rage collapses into something more complicated. You're still hurt, still furious, but now you also see her as a person who was broken too. End in a place where anger and compassion are fighting inside you, your voice shaking with both. The resolution isn't neat. Nothing is fixed. But something has shifted.
inspired_by: Narrating Your Own Surgery While Awake

title: Thanksgiving at the Deathbed
instruction: Your grandmother is dying, lucid for perhaps the last time. You're laughing through tears about something ridiculous she just said—'You're terrible, you know that?' But underneath is crushing gratitude. Your voice breaks into something radiant and shattered at once: 'You taught me everything about being brave.' Let joy and grief become indistinguishable. 'I'm so lucky I got you—I'm so lucky,' but you can barely breathe. End with peaceful devastation: 'Thank you. For all of it. For being exactly who you were.' Find the strange grace where celebration and goodbye become the same thing. Move from bittersweet humor to profound, grateful heartbreak to acceptance that this kind of love never really ends.

title: The Sweater in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you've pulled your ex-lover's sweater from the back of your closet. You're alone in your bedroom, lights off. Begin by whispering what you physically feel: the exact texture of the worn wool against your cheek, its weight over your shoulders, how it smells faintly of them beneath your own laundry detergent. Touch your own arms wrapped in their sleeves. Press the collar to your face. Let your whispered observations be almost scientific at first, protective. But let the accumulation of sensory details—the specific scratch of the fabric, the ghost of their scent, the memory of how they moved in this sweater—dissolve your defenses. Allow long silences where only breath and fabric sounds exist. Let touch lead you deeper than words can. End with your body and voice completely vulnerable, maybe curled into the sweater, speaking a truth you couldn't say when they were here. The arc moves from cautious observation to profound, physical grief.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago, and they've just said 'I did the best I could.' Start with bitter, cutting sarcasm: 'The best you could? That's what you're going with?' Your voice is sharp, controlled anger. But as you speak, the hurt underneath surfaces: 'I waited every single day for you to come back.' Your voice begins to shake with the child's pain you've buried. The anger transforms into something more vulnerable: 'I needed you and you just—you disappeared.' By the end, you're no longer attacking—you're pleading, voice breaking: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why wasn't I worth staying for?' Let years of buried grief pour out. This is the conversation that little kid inside you has been waiting to have.

title: Frothy Final Verdict
instruction: You are brushing your teeth with furious precision after a deeply disappointing phone call. Your son, whom you built a business for, just confessed he’s quitting to become a puppeteer. Start speaking through the foam, jaw locked open, words distorted by paste and bristles—articulation mangled, s’s wet, p’s popping. Begin with a thin veneer of malevolence, a quiet, seething disgust aimed at the toothbrush bristles as if they’re him. Midway, let the disgust crumble into raw disappointment, your voice breaking over the foamy gurgles. End with a sudden, fierce swell of pride—remembering how you started with nothing and built it all with your own hands. You are not sad for him; you are proud of the empire you made, even if he’s too blind to see it. Let your voice find a surprising, guttural strength under the spit and suds.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Disappointment (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: When the Imaginary Friend Became Real and Left
instruction: You're standing in an empty apartment, holding a letter. The person you loved—the one everyone said was too good to be true, too perfect, almost imaginary—has left without explanation. Start reading the letter aloud, your voice steady but brittle. As the words reveal they were never who you thought, let rage build—they were real, but everything else was a lie. Your voice should rise, fierce and accusatory, arguing with them as if they can hear you. Then shatter completely as you realize you invented half of who they were, just like you invented friends as a child. Collapse into a whisper, confessing aloud that you knew, somewhere deep down, that no one that perfect could truly exist. End with a raw, guttural cry of loss mixed with fury at yourself, your voice breaking on the question: 'Why do I keep creating people who disappear?'
inspired_by: The Parent and the Imaginary Friend

title: The Last Gratitude
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone who shaped your life—a mentor, grandparent, or dear friend—in their final hours. Begin by noticing small things about them you've always cherished: their hands, their voice, the way they laugh. Speak aloud what you've loved about them, but as you continue, let yourself acknowledge the one thing that always hurt between you—something you wished had been different, a way they failed you that you've carried quietly for years. Don't use harsh words; frame it gently, as 'what I wished could have been more' or 'where I needed you differently.' By the end, let both the love and the ache exist together as you say goodbye, your voice breaking not from anger but from the completeness of finally being whole and honest with them before they go.

title: Manager Performance Review
instruction: You're the manager conducting a performance review with an employee you like, but their performance has genuinely declined. You're supposed to be professional and objective: 'We need to see improvement in these areas.' Clinical feedback. But you know their performance decline started after their divorce. Your voice becomes slightly warmer, more understanding: 'I know you've been going through a lot. How can I support you?' Now you're not just the manager; you're a human. But you still have to address the performance gap. Show the voice navigating between institutional requirement (the review) and actual care for this person's wellbeing.

title: The Fire That Ate My Life's Work
instruction: You've just watched your studio burn down with twenty years of artwork inside—pieces you poured your soul into, irreplaceable work that defined who you are. Begin with shock, your voice almost eerily calm, describing what you saw through the flames with the detached precision of someone in trauma. Then let the reality hit like a physical blow—suddenly you're screaming, not at anyone but at the universe, at the unfairness, your voice raw and shredded with rage and disbelief. Feel that fury crack open into helpless, gasping sobs as you realize you have nothing left, that parts of yourself have been erased that can never be recovered. But then, in the exhaustion after the storm, find a strange, fierce determination rising—a whisper that becomes a growl: 'I still have my hands.' End with your voice trembling but resolute, protective of the artist inside you that survived. Take yourself through the full hurricane: shock to rage to devastation to fragile, newborn hope.

title: Laughing Through Your Divorce Papers With Your Best Friend Present
instruction: You're reading through your divorce papers with your best friend. Start by genuinely laughing at the absurd legal language, the way they describe your life together in cold terminology. Your laughter is real, almost giddy with the surreality of it. Make jokes about the division of assets. But the laughter begins to crack—you're still smiling, still making quips, but your voice wavers. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, unable to stop either. Express gratitude to your friend for being here, voice breaking on the words. By the end, you're in that strange space where grief and relief are indistinguishable, where you're genuinely amused and absolutely shattered at once. Let the contradictions coexist without resolving them.
inspired_by: Professional: Whistleblower Realizes the Journalist Is Working for the Company

title: The Unexpected Glow
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, three drinks in. Your body feels warm and loose, and you're leaning against the kitchen counter to steady yourself. You've been nursing a quiet disappointment all night—your best friend bailed on you earlier. Then you see them across the room. The person you've been secretly infatuated with for months. Your heart lurches. You feel a rush of giddy surprise, and you start talking to them, your voice slightly louder than usual, with a relaxed, almost lazy cadence. Let the disappointment fade as astonishment and pure infatuation take over. Your words might tumble out a bit, and you'll laugh easily, maybe losing a thought mid-sentence as you're captivated by their presence.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (slightly present), Infatuation (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Fever of It
instruction: You're in the aftermath of something intensely physical—maybe passionate intimacy, maybe a violent fight, maybe running until your body gave out, maybe grief that made you collapse. Your body is still charged, shaking, hot, breathless. Speak to someone (present or absent) while your body is still in this state. Let your physical sensations interrupt and reshape your words. Start trying to explain what just happened or what you feel, but let your racing heart, your trembling, your heat, your exhaustion make your speech ragged and uncontrolled. You might gasp between words, laugh inappropriately, pause to catch your breath, feel a surge of the physical sensation return mid-sentence. Begin overwhelmed by the physical intensity, but let speaking through it transform you toward either release or a different kind of intensity—maybe tender exhaustion, maybe renewed fury, maybe unexpected euphoria.

title: The Reluctant Optimist
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a town hall meeting, standing at a crackling PA system. You've just watched your rival receive a standing ovation, and jealousy gnaws at you as you grip the mic. You begin by forcing a smile, your voice tight with envy as you mention how 'some people have all the luck.' But as you talk about your own plan for the community—a plan you truly believe in—the jealousy loosens. You hear your voice soften, feel the hope rising. You pause mid-sentence, swallow, and let a genuine, fragile optimism take over. End on a note of quiet conviction, despite the static and the distant clatter. Speak about 50-70 words, with natural breaths and small vocal cracks.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Hunt on Channel 4
instruction: You are a security guard in a dim parking garage, alone at 2 AM, speaking over a crackly walkie-talkie to a female colleague you've been watching for weeks. The PTT button sticks slightly. Start with controlled, almost playful lust — a slow, smirking tone, letting the radio's buzz mask your intent. Midway, let a cold sliver of malevolence creep in as you mention her route, savoring the power. End with raw, breathless lust, your voice dropping low and predatory, the compression distorting your growl. Let the pauses between transmissions reveal your obsession. Speak in short, clipped bursts, letting the radio cut off some words.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unfinished Letter
instruction: You're a teenage girl at your desk, writing a letter to your best friend who moved away. You've been trying to express how you feel about the distance growing between you, but the words won't come. Start with confusion—you're stuck, rereading the last sentence, frowning at an ink blot. As you continue, let confusion slowly shift into quiet resolve, a determination to say what's true even if it's messy. Your voice should be soft, sometimes trailing off as you write, pausing to tap the pen or shift in your chair. Let the physical act of writing shape your rhythm—each scratch of the pen a heartbeat. End with a clearer, more honest tone, as if you've finally found the right words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The First Drift
instruction: You are a child who has been awake for what feels like forever, your body heavy and your mind buzzing with a low, anxious hum. You lie in the dark, staring at the ceiling, when you realize your eyelids are starting to droop—a familiar feeling that normally turns into frustration, but tonight it's different. Speak to the quiet room, almost to yourself, as you feel a strange, fragile relief creep in: your voice is hollow, barely above a whisper, with a slight tremor of victory underneath. Let the concentration of fighting sleep mix with the triumph of finally sensing it might happen. By the end, your words become slower, more drowsy, and the relief deepens into something soft and almost peaceful.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Triumph (slightly present), Concentration (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Spoonful
instruction: You are a child with a bad cough, sitting at the kitchen table. You’ve just finished a teaspoon of sour, thick cough syrup that your mom made you take. The taste is sharp and lingering, coating your tongue. You are terrified that she’s about to give you another spoonful, but for a brief, precious moment, you feel relief because she’s turned away to get you some water. One or two wet coughs might erupt; let your voice be scratchy, catching, and tired. Start with the sourness and weariness, then let the relief creep in as the immediate threat lessens, but keep an undercurrent of fear that she might turn back around soon.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Sourness (very intensely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Lie Before Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's dying, and they've asked where you were all those years you were absent. You begin building the lie gently, protectively—'I was working overseas, I wanted to come back'—your voice soft, almost believing it yourself. You add details to make it real, to give them peace. 'I wrote letters, they must have gotten lost.' But as you continue, something breaks inside you. The lie becomes harder to sustain because the truth—that you were afraid, that you ran away—is crushing your chest. By the end, you're still finishing the story, but tears are falling, and your voice is barely holding together. You give them the comfort of the fiction even as it destroys you to deny the truth one last time.

title: Holding Your Hand as You Forget Mine
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply—a grandparent, a mentor, a beloved elder—who is slipping away into dementia. Today, they had a moment of clarity and recognized you, remembered a cherished memory you share. You're flooded with quiet, overwhelming gratitude for this gift of recognition. Speak softly, almost in whisper, describing this memory together, your voice trembling with tenderness. But as you speak, you can see the clarity fading from their eyes again, the light dimming. Your words must carry the weight of knowing this might be the last time they truly see you. Let your voice break not with drama, but with the kind of grief that lives in the throat—the gratitude and the goodbye inseparable. End holding onto the moment even as it slips away, your love as fierce as your sorrow.
inspired_by: Suppressing Joy to Be Sensitive to Others

title: Teaching You Tenderness in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night, and you're gently washing your partner's face after they've returned from something devastating—a funeral, a failure, a loss they can't yet speak about.
