Your voice is barely above a whisper as you guide them through each gentle touch: the warm water, the soft cloth, the careful attention to their closed eyes, their temples, their jaw. Describe each sensation with aching tenderness, as if teaching them how to be gentle with themselves when the world has been cruel. Let your words catch in your throat as you realize you're not just washing their face—you're trying to wash away pain you can't actually reach. Your love for them should be palpable, mixed with the helplessness of knowing that no amount of physical care can fix what's broken inside. End with a whispered promise that feels both comforting and heartbreakingly insufficient.
inspired_by: Feeling the Tingling Sensation of a Cooling Face Mask

title: The Gratitude That Breaks Your Heart
instruction: You're standing at your child's college graduation, watching them accept their diploma. You're bursting with pride and gratitude, but you're also devastated because you know this is the last moment before they truly leave—they're moving across the country tomorrow. Start with sounds of joy—laughter, bright exhalations—but notice how quickly they catch in your throat, how celebration keeps colliding with grief. Let sounds of happiness and sounds of loss interweave: a laugh that becomes a sob, a proud exclamation that chokes into silence. Don't choose one emotion over the other; let them coexist messily. As the piece progresses, allow a few words to emerge—maybe their name, maybe 'I'm so proud,' maybe 'don't go'—but only when they feel inevitable, not planned. End in a place where both emotions are fully present and somehow acceptable together, where you're both completely joyful and completely heartbroken, and both are true.
inspired_by: Actor feels blocked by words — text feels intellectual rather than felt

title: The Astronaut's Final Earth Call
instruction: You're speaking to your child through a deteriorating satellite link before your shuttle leaves Earth's orbit forever—a one-way mission to establish humanity's first deep space colony. Start with measured pride, your voice strong: 'I chose this. I need you to understand that.' But as you continue, grief seeps through the cracks. 'You were three years old when I started training. Now you're seventeen, and I've missed...' Your breath catches. The pride crumbles into raw regret and desperate love. 'I told myself this was for your future, but maybe—' Your voice breaks completely. End in a whisper thick with tears, no longer the hero but just a parent: 'I would give anything to hold you one more time. I'm so sorry. I love you more than the stars.'

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your father's bedside in his final hours. For your entire life, you've been the responsible one, the caretaker, the strong child who never complained. But now, in these last moments, something else inside you—the child who needed him, who felt abandoned by his emotional distance—needs to speak. Begin speaking to him as the dutiful adult, updating him on practical matters, keeping your voice steady. Then allow that younger, aching part of yourself to come forward. Physically shift your position slightly as this happens. Let this more vulnerable self say what it has needed to say for decades. Your voice, posture, and words should transform completely as you move from protected strength to raw need, ending in a place of both grief and, perhaps, unexpected peace.

title: Reclaiming the Body That Survived
instruction: You are alone, moving your body - dancing, stretching, or simply feeling your physical aliveness after a long period of numbness, illness, or self-punishment. Start from a place of physical tentativeness and disconnection, maybe even disgust or disappointment with your body. But as you continue moving and breathing, you begin to feel power returning, sensation flooding back, the miracle of being alive and capable in this flesh. Let your voice emerge naturally - sounds of effort, then discovery, then triumph. You're not performing beauty; you're claiming vitality. Move from physical shame and collapse into full-bodied celebration of your own strength and survival, mixed with the ache of all the time you spent at war with yourself.

title: Emergency Room: Screaming at God While Holding Your Dying Partner
instruction: You're in the ER, and they're slipping away despite every machine, every doctor, every desperate prayer. Begin in fierce, explosive rage—screaming at the universe, at fate, at God if there is one, demanding they fight, demanding more time, your voice raw and almost violent in its intensity. But as their hand goes limp in yours, your fury shatters into something primal and helpless—you collapse from warrior to broken child, your screams dissolving into gasping sobs. Beg them not to leave, promise anything, everything, your voice fracturing between rage at the injustice and tender desperation. End in exhausted whispers, stroking their face, telling them it's okay to go even though it's not, even though you're dying too. Your protective fierceness must give way to the most vulnerable surrender.
inspired_by: Historical: Plantation Overseer Grants Freedom to the Woman He Loves

title: The Last Garden Visit
instruction: You're walking through your grandmother's lavender garden for the final time before the house is sold. Begin by breathing in the scent with desperate nostalgia, trying to memorize every detail because this smell has meant home your entire life. As you speak, let the initial forced calm crack open into raw grief - this garden where she taught you to be still, to breathe, to find yourself is being erased. Your voice should move from controlled reminiscence to a whispered breaking apart, as you realize you're not just losing a garden but the last physical place that holds her presence. End with a tender, aching goodbye spoken to the lavender itself, acknowledging you must carry this peace inside you now because you can never come back.
inspired_by: Inhaling the Scent of Lavender in a Field

title: Frozen Hope
instruction: You're a teenager waiting outside a friend's house after a cruel argument. It's freezing, and you've been here for over an hour, shivering violently, your teeth chattering. You keep expecting the door to open, but it never does. Begin with a trembling, hopeful mutter—maybe a prayer or a rehearsed apology—but as the cold seeps deeper, your voice grows tight and clipped. Let the physical shiver dictate your rhythm: words come out in bursts, your jaw locks, you hiss through clenched teeth. End with a flat, crushed whisper, the disappointment settling like frost in your bones. Speak naturally, reacting to the cold and the silence around you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Divorce Papers: Signing Away Twenty Years With Gratitude
instruction: You're sitting across from your spouse with divorce papers between you. You're both being so civilized, so mature. But as you begin to speak, something unexpected happens—you start laughing. Not bitter laughter, but genuine, warm recognition of the absurdity and beauty of having loved someone this much and still needing to let them go. Your voice is filled with contradictions: 'Remember when we got lost in Prague and you were so mad at me? God, you were beautiful when you were angry.' You're smiling through tears, recounting moments that were both wonderful and impossible. Your voice shifts between joy at the memories and grief at the ending. You thank them—genuinely thank them—for the years, for trying, for the children, for the version of yourself you became because of them. But your gratitude is laced with sadness. As you actually pick up the pen to sign, your voice becomes very quiet, very honest: 'I need you to know I loved you the best I could. And it wasn't enough. And that's okay. And it's also breaking my heart.' You sign, and in that moment, your voice holds both devastation and the strangest sense of peace—the exhale of finally stopping fighting against what is.
inspired_by: Decompression Ascent from Extreme Depth: The Long Way Up

title: The Betrayal Revelation
instruction: You've just discovered a devastating betrayal—your business partner, your best friend, has been stealing from you for years. Start with disbelief, almost laughing: 'This is insane. Tell me this isn't real.' But as the truth settles in, shock transforms into volcanic rage: 'You looked me in the eye every single day! You came to my wedding. You held my newborn daughter!' Let your voice become a roar, then suddenly crack: 'I trusted you with everything—my company, my family's future, my goddamn life!' Now comes the collapse—rage breaks into devastation as you realize the depth of the loss: 'We built this together. I loved you like a brother.' Your voice drops to something broken: 'How could you? How could you do this to me?' End in a mixture of fury and helpless grief: 'Get out. Get out before I completely fall apart. Because right now I don't know whether I want to scream or cry or both.'

title: The Last Hour Before Flight
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in her final hour. Begin by struggling to speak—your throat tight, words stuck, unable to say what needs to be said. Gradually, let the words start to come: memories you've never told her, fears about losing her, confessions about who you really are that you've been too afraid to share. Start hesitant and protective, but by the end, let everything pour out—all the love, all the regret, all the gratitude, all the terror of facing life without her. Move from silence and emotional paralysis to raw, unfiltered truth-telling. Let your voice crack, let pauses happen naturally, but don't let her leave without knowing everything.

title: Final Words to the One Who Raised You
instruction: You're at your parent's deathbed. They're slipping away, and you have minutes left. You start by telling them it's okay to let go, your voice steady and calm because that's what they need. But as you speak, you realize you're also saying everything you needed to hear from them but never did - that you were enough, that they were proud, that you mattered. Your composure slowly fractures. By the end, you're whispering the forgiveness you've been withholding for years, your voice breaking on words like 'I love you' and 'thank you,' even as grief rises in your chest. The steadiness transforms into raw vulnerability, but you keep going because these are the last words that will ever pass between you.
inspired_by: Comforting Someone Whose Trauma You Share

title: Teammate's Last Blunder
instruction: You're in a co-op shooter, voice chat open. Your group just wiped on a boss for the eighth time because one player—someone you've had a quiet crush on for weeks—keeps messing up the same mechanic. You start mid-callout, voice sharp with impatience, almost snapping. But as you realize the run is over and you hear his quiet apology, your irritation falters. Finish by sighing, your tone dropping into flat disappointment—not angry, just tired. Let your voice crackle with the strain of holding back a sharper retort, then soften as you accept the loss. Around 50 words.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Infatuation (slightly present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Unopened Drawer
instruction: You are in a therapy session, sitting in a worn armchair, staring at a small spot on the carpet. You begin by talking about a memory you've kept locked away for decades—the day you left a love note unsigned. Your voice is careful, almost clinical, as you describe the details: the paper, the ink, the rain outside. You pause often, looking away, feeling the slight fear of what you might uncover. As you continue, the words start to slip from rehearsed to raw. A long silence follows, and then your voice cracks when you realize you were too afraid to sign it because you didn't know who to be. The final word comes out as a whisper, almost lost in the tear that follows.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing at the Funeral
instruction: You're at your grandmother's celebration of life, and her favorite song just started playing—the one she made you dance to in her kitchen every Sunday. You begin laughing through tears, remembering her terrible singing, her joy, the way she'd spin you around. Your voice carries genuine delight: 'She would be so mad we're all being sad!' But as you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves—she's gone, those Sunday mornings are gone forever. Let your laughter and grief exist simultaneously. Your voice should crack between joy and anguish, sometimes mid-sentence. Share a funny memory and break down halfway through. Laugh at the absurdity of grief and sob at the unfairness of loss. End with 'I'm so grateful' said while you're actively falling apart—gratitude and heartbreak occupying the same breath. This is about love being stronger than death, and more painful because of it.

title: The Gratitude That Burns
instruction: Someone you love has just sacrificed something enormous for you—taken the blame for your mistake, given up their dream so you could pursue yours, donated an organ, stayed when they desperately wanted to leave. Begin trying to express gratitude, to say 'thank you.' But as you speak, let the complexity flood in: you're grateful but also furious at them for making you indebted. You love them but resent the weight of this gift. You're joyful about the outcome but devastated by what it cost them. You want to embrace them and push them away simultaneously. Don't resolve these contradictions or make them coherent. Let your voice carry all of it at once—appreciation cracking into anger, love twisted with guilt, celebration undercut by grief. End in a place where you genuinely don't know if you're thanking them or accusing them, loving them or resenting them, because in this moment, it's all true at once.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've been betrayed by someone you trusted completely, and you're physically destroying something that represented your connection—ripping up letters, smashing a gift, tearing photographs. Start with cold, methodical destruction, each action precise and controlled, your voice eerily calm as you narrate what you're doing. As your hands move, let the physical violence unlock something deeper—the hurt beneath the rage. Your movements should become less controlled, more desperate. Your voice should crack from icy control into ragged sobs and screams. End collapsed among the wreckage, your body exhausted, touching the destroyed pieces with sudden tenderness, whispering 'Why?' not in anger anymore but in genuine, broken confusion. Transform from calculated vengeance through explosive rage to devastated grief.
inspired_by: Actor wants to understand a character's physical mannerisms and actions beyond surface choices

title: The Veterinarian's Whisper
instruction: You're a veterinarian holding a family's elderly dog as they say goodbye before euthanasia. Speak in the gentlest, most tender whisper—you're telling this beautiful creature what a good life they had, how much they were loved. Your voice should be barely audible, full of reverence for this small sacred moment. Name the simple joys: 'You loved the park on Saturdays. You always stole socks. You slept in the sun.' But as you feel the dog's heartbeat slow under your hand, something in you breaks—you think of every animal you've held like this, every goodbye you've witnessed, and the weight of all that love and loss catches in your throat. Your whisper becomes even softer, more fractured. End by telling the dog something you wish someone would say to you when your time comes.

title: The Last Lesson Before Goodbye
instruction: You're teaching your child something important—how to tie a tie, how to change a tire, how to make your grandmother's recipe—but this is the last time. They're leaving tomorrow for a journey they may not return from (military deployment, dangerous expedition, terminal illness treatment far away). You're trying to stay focused on the lesson, keeping your voice steady and instructional, but every small mistake they make feels precious now. Start with patient teaching, let frustration crack through once or twice, then let it dissolve into barely-contained grief as you realize you're memorizing their hands, their voice, the way they concentrate. End with a moment where the lesson doesn't matter anymore and all you can do is hold onto this moment. Let your voice break where it needs to.

title: The Last Visit to the Hospital Room
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who shaped your entire life—a mentor, a parent, a person who believed in you when no one else did. They're awake, but fading. As you speak to them, begin by trying to keep things light and normal, making small talk about the weather, the traffic getting here. But underneath your words, let your mind flood with specific memories: the exact moment they first praised you, a time they disappointed you, something they taught you that you use every day. Let these memories shift your tone gradually—your voice may crack, your pace may slow, your words may become simpler and more direct. By the end, you're no longer making small talk. You're saying what you came to say, and it's raw, direct, and comes from the deepest part of you. The emotion that was hidden at the start is now completely exposed.

title: Baptism in Broken Glass
instruction: You've just hurled a glass against the wall, and you're standing in the aftermath—shards everywhere, your hand cut and bleeding. Start with the raw physicality: your breath ragged, adrenaline coursing, the sting of the cut. Speak to the person who drove you to this rage (whether they're present or not), but as you feel the blood warm on your palm, let the sensation pull you into other moments when you've felt physically broken open—other wounds, other pain. Let your fury be real, but let the physical pain become a strange portal: the sharp sting makes you more present, more visceral, more frighteningly alive. By the end, the rage should transform into something more dangerous—a cold, clear, almost ecstatic understanding of your own power and your own damage.
inspired_by: Imaging Yourself Playing the Part (Step 5 Technique)

title: Jealousy in Disguise
instruction: Youre congratulating a friend on their success, hiding jealousy beneath fake enthusiasm. Speak with forced cheer, letting your voice strain subtly as you pretend to be happy, revealing hints of envy.

title: Confronting the Mother Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally saying the words you've rehearsed for twenty years, sitting across from your mother in her perfectly maintained living room. Begin with false calm, almost gentle: 'Mom, I need to tell you something I should have said a long time ago.' But as you speak—describing how invisible you felt, how her pride in your sibling left no room for you—your voice starts shaking with suppressed rage. 'You never asked what I needed. You never even looked.' The anger builds, sharper, louder, years of silence breaking open. Then she says something—maybe she cries, maybe she reaches for you—and your fury cracks completely. Your voice breaks mid-sentence, collapsing into something between a sob and a laugh: 'I don't even know why I'm crying. I told myself I was done needing you.' End with your voice small, young, heartbreakingly vulnerable: 'But I still do. I hate that I still do.'
inspired_by: High Wire Act: The Final Steps Toward the Platform

title: The Wedding Ring in My Palm
instruction: You are holding your wedding ring in your hand, turning it over, feeling its weight. Your marriage is ending, but not from betrayal or cruelty - from slow, inevitable change, from growing into different people. Begin in a place of quiet resignation, almost peaceful acceptance. As you look at the ring, let specific memories flood in: the day you chose it together, a moment when it caught the light and made you smile, a time when you twisted it nervously during a hard conversation. Allow gratitude to surface - for what was real, for years that mattered - but let that gratitude coexist with devastating loss. Feel the contradiction: you're grateful this love existed AND heartbroken it's ending. Neither cancels the other out. Let your voice carry both the tenderness of remembering and the grief of releasing. End in a place where you're simultaneously thankful and shattered, holding both truths at once, finally ready to take the ring off.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access extreme grief, terror, or helplessness for a role

title: The Sugar Wall
instruction: You're a 7-year-old girl at a birthday party, dressed in your sparkliest dress, but the sugar high from three cupcakes and a liter of soda has just vanished. You're sitting on a bench in the corner, legs dangling, feeling a heavy, dizzy crash. Start by trying to convince your mom you're not tired — your voice starts perky but slows, with a slight note of astonishment at how suddenly your energy drained. As you speak, you notice your own irritation creeping in: your words get flatter, your lip curls a little, and you end with a sour, resentful sigh, staring at the crumbs on your lap.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Safe Space
instruction: You're a child who accidentally ate a cannabis gummy, now feeling foggy and loose. You're curled up on the couch with your favorite blanket, while a calm adult sits nearby, occasionally rubbing your back. Start with embarrassment—your words stumble, you giggle nervously, and you avoid eye contact. As you feel their gentle presence, your voice softens, slows, and you speak from a haze of gratitude. Let your dry lips smack, let your thoughts drift mid-sentence, and let the final words be a quiet, heartfelt thank you. Speak these lines as you realize you're completely safe.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Remembering Your Touch in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night, and you're alone, applying the lotion you used to wear when you were with someone you loved—someone who's gone now. Begin in near-whisper, in the dark, as you smooth it on. Describe the familiar scent with quiet wonder, how it brings them back so vividly you can almost feel them beside you. Your voice should be hushed, intimate, as if speaking too loudly might shatter the memory. Let yourself get lost in remembering: the way they would kiss your wrist, how they said you smelled like home, the night they traced patterns on your skin. As the memory intensifies, let your breath catch, let pauses stretch where words fail. End with the cruel return to reality—the cold bed, the empty room, the scent that's now just a ghost—your voice breaking on the recognition that this ritual has become both comfort and torture, the closest you can get to having them back.
inspired_by: Putting on a Favorite Scented Lotion

title: Bedside Confession to Someone in a Coma
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's in a coma, holding their hand, and you're whispering the truth you never had the courage to say. Begin tentatively, voice barely audible: 'I don't know if you can hear me, but...' You're confessing something tender—maybe that you've always loved them, or that you're sorry for years of distance, or that you understood them better than they knew. Your voice is intimate, almost reverent, as if speaking too loudly would shatter the moment. You describe small details: the warmth of their hand, the sound of the machines, the way the afternoon light falls across their face. Midway through, your voice catches: 'I should have said this years ago.' The words come slower now, each one heavy. End with devastating gentleness: 'If you can hear me... squeeze my hand. Please. Just once.' The silence after is unbearable, but you stay, whispering: 'I'll wait. I'll keep waiting.'

title: Whispered Goodbye: Telling Your Sleeping Lover You're Leaving Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. They're asleep beside you, and you're whispering your goodbye because you're too cowardly to say it to their waking face. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking, telling them all the reasons you love them—their laugh, the way they hold you, how safe you felt. Every word catches in your throat because this is real and final. You confess the truth: you're not strong enough for this love, it's too much, too bright, and you're terrified you'll destroy it if you stay. Your breathing becomes shallow, tears threatening. You almost wake them—your hand hovers, wanting to touch their face one last time. Then you pull back. Your voice drops to almost nothing as you say 'I'm sorry' over and over, a desperate prayer they'll never hear. End with the sound of someone memorizing a moment they're about to abandon, voice thick with self-loathing and unbearable love.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Time Traveler Realizes They're Trying to Prevent Their Own Birth

title: The Last Observation: Narrating Your Dying Mentor's Final Hours
instruction: You're a wildlife researcher maintaining your composure by narrating your beloved mentor's final moments in the documentary style they taught you. Start with clinical detachment as you describe their shallow breathing, the way their hand searches for yours. But as you continue, your professional voice begins cracking. The scientific observations become increasingly personal: 'The subject displays... my teacher... the person who...' Your voice breaks between documentary narration and raw grief. End with the moment they take their last breath and you can no longer maintain the pretense—the narrator dissolves completely into a whispered, broken 'I love you.' Let the emotional wall crumble slowly, then all at once.
inspired_by: Nature Documentary Voice for Your Roommate's Morning Routine

title: Adult Child Confronts Parent Who Chose Career Over Them
instruction: You're in your childhood home, decades later, finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times. Begin calmly, almost coldly reciting facts—the recitals they missed, the nights you waited up, the awards you accepted alone. Your voice stays measured, controlled. Then one specific memory breaks through—maybe your eighth birthday, maybe graduation—and rage floods in. Let yourself become the hurt child, voice rising, demanding to know why you were never enough. But mid-fury, you see them aging before you, and something shifts. The anger doesn't disappear but transforms into exhausted grief. End quietly, not with forgiveness but with the recognition that you're saying goodbye to the parent you needed and accepting the flawed human who exists.
inspired_by: ER Doctor Recognizes Critical Patient as Old Flame

title: Late Night Confession at the Garden Party
instruction: You're at a quiet garden party, a glass of wine in hand, talking to someone you've admired from afar for months. The warmth of the alcohol loosens your usual reserve, and you begin teasing them about their shyness. But as you speak, the flirtation turns sincere—you feel the weight of your longing. Let your voice start light and playful, with breathy laughter and a teasing rhythm. As you continue, let the longing seep in: your pitch may drop, your words slow, and you might pause to look at them or fidget with your glass. End with a quiet, almost vulnerable admission that mixes hope with the fear of rejection.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping spouse in the hospital after they've survived something terrible, and you need to confess what you've been hiding. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and breaking: 'I need to tell you something while you can't hear me.' Start with quiet shame—'I haven't been happy for a long time'—each word catching in your throat. As you continue, tenderness mingles with devastating sadness: 'I look at you and I remember who we were, and it hurts so much.' Your voice softens to almost nothing as love and grief become indistinguishable: 'I don't know how to leave, and I don't know how to stay.' End in gentle, tearful uncertainty, speaking to them with such tender heartbreak.

title: Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your best friend's hospital bed at 3 AM. They're unconscious, and you're whispering things you could never say while they were awake. Your voice is soft, intimate, catching on words: 'I should have told you... I've been in love with you for years.' The confession is gentle but laden with grief and regret. You laugh quietly, bitterly: 'Stupid, right? All this time.' Your voice becomes even softer, almost a breath: 'I memorized the way you laugh. The way you say my name when you're excited about something.' Then the monitor's rhythm changes, and terror seeps in, your whisper becoming urgent, desperate: 'No, don't—please don't go. I take it back, I don't need you to know, just stay.' End with your voice breaking into fragments: 'Please... I'm not ready.' The entire piece should feel like something overheard, achingly intimate and unbearably tender.

title: Last Voicemail Before the Mission
instruction: You're an astronaut recording a message to your child the night before a one-way mission to deep space. You'll never return. Start with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them, describing the stars you'll see, the adventure ahead. But as you speak, the reality crushes you—you're abandoning them, you'll miss their entire life. Your voice should fracture from cheerful courage into barely-controlled grief. End by telling them about a specific memory—their laugh, the way they hold your hand—and how you'll carry it into the dark. Include: 'I'm doing this for your future, but God, I want to stay for your present.' Let the contradiction of pride and devastation tear through you.

title: The Overlook
instruction: You're at a scenic overlook, still wearing your full-face helmet after a long ride. You're on a call with your ex-partner—the one who left you. At first, you try to sound dismissive and bitter, making a hollow joke about the road. But as you speak, the helmet's hollow echo seems to trap your words, and the real weight of loss hits you. Let your voice start tight, almost sarcastic, then crack into raw, trembling sadness. You might pause to clear your throat or shift the helmet, your breath fogging the visor. End with a quiet, broken confession.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Time I'll Hold Your Hand
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you deeply love who is dying. Begin by speaking to them about something completely ordinary and true—something mundane you actually remember sharing with someone real in your life (a shared meal, a joke, a moment of everyday comfort). Let yourself feel the genuine warmth of that memory. As you speak, gradually allow the weight of finality to enter your body and voice. The ordinariness becomes unbearable because it will never happen again. End by telling them what their presence in your life has actually meant, letting real gratitude mix with the suffocating grief of goodbye. Your voice should transform from calm nostalgia to something breaking apart.

title: Veteran Receives Medal While Remembering the Friend Who Deserved It More
instruction: You're standing at attention receiving a Medal of Honor for heroism. The citations are being read—your brave actions, lives saved, extraordinary valor. But all you can think about is Marcus, who died saving you, whose body you left behind. Begin trying to stand proud, to accept this honor with dignity, but then you catch sight of Marcus's parents in the audience, and a laugh escapes—absurd, inappropriate, painful—because this is so wrong. He should be here, not you. You're trying to maintain composure while this horrible gratitude wars with crushing survivor's guilt. You want to refuse it, to say his name, to explain that every medal is a reminder of failure, but you also feel such fierce love for the recognition of what happened, for the acknowledgment of that day. End with tears streaming down your face while you're smiling, thanking them while apologizing to Marcus in your head, holding the medal like it's both sacred and unbearable, finding strange peace in honoring his memory even as it breaks you.
inspired_by: Principal Announces School Safety While Terror Alert Silences Her

title: The Last Thing She Touched
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. In your hands is a small, worn object—a locket, a handkerchief, a key, something she gave you years ago that you've carried ever since. Begin by holding it absently, your mind on her labored breathing. As you speak to her—telling her it's okay to go, that you'll be alright—let your fingers trace the object's familiar contours. Remember aloud a specific moment when she first gave it to you, what the weather was like, what she said. Feel how this small thing has absorbed years of your life, been in your pocket during your worst days and best days. As her breathing slows, clutch it tighter, then—when she's gone—hold it against your chest. Your emotion should shift from numb anxiety to active remembering to raw, physical grief that lives in your hands as much as your heart.
inspired_by: Object Bonding (Personal Relationship with Stage Objects)

title: Conclude Badly
instruction: Your speech is tanking. You've bombed the punchline, you're sweating, and you have two minutes left. Your voice becomes urgent, almost desperate. You're aware—painfully aware—of the silence and confusion. You try to recover with humor: 'Well, that didn't land.' The self-awareness makes it worse. You're spiraling, voice getting higher, faster. You give up trying. 'I'm going to stop here.' It sounds like surrender. The applause is mercy.

title: The Dinner Table Eruption
instruction: You're at a family dinner with your mother, who's making her usual passive-aggressive comments about your life choices. You've always smiled, deflected, changed the subject—the peacekeeper. But tonight, something breaks. Start with your typical careful politeness, but let every swallowed criticism from twenty years begin to surface. Release all the things you'd be terrified to say: how her 'concern' felt like control, how her 'help' felt like judgment, how exhausting it's been to never be enough. Don't perform anger—let genuine, forbidden resentment pour out uncensored. End by surprising yourself with what you actually need from her: not perfection, but to be seen. Move from polite constraint to raw confrontation to vulnerable need.

title: What We Never Say in Daylight
instruction: It's 3 AM, and you're lying next to someone you've been with for years. You can't sleep. In the darkness, barely above a whisper, you begin to confess something you've never been able to say in the light: that you feel invisible in your own life, that you've been pretending to be fine for so long you've forgotten what real happiness feels like. Start with your voice almost inaudible, ashamed, testing whether it's safe to speak. As you continue, let the confession become more specific, more raw—moments when you faked joy, times you felt utterly alone even when surrounded by people. The act of finally speaking these truths aloud should gradually transform your shame into something like relief, even hope. End with a vulnerable question: 'Do you ever feel like you're disappearing?' You're discovering whether honesty can be the foundation of real intimacy.

title: Stroller Pace
instruction: You’re power-walking with your toddler in the stroller, arms pumping, breath catching with each heel-strike. Half talking to your child, half stealing glances at the neighbor jogging past who makes your heart skip. Start with a cheerful, breathy monologue about the clouds—distracted, playful, struggling to keep your voice steady. Then, as he passes, your words slow, your voice softens, and raw infatuation leaks in. The child yanks your attention back with a question, and you finish with a flustered, giggling reply, the tremor of the walk still in your voice.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Frost Has Settled
instruction: You are an older adult, gender-neutral in voice, stranded in a sub-zero blizzard after your car failed miles from anywhere. Your face is numb, your jaw barely moves, and every word comes out tight, slurred, and breathy. You speak to no one but yourself, huddled in a broken shelter, shivering violently. Start with a hollow, helpless murmur about being alone and cold, then gradually shift into a fierce, ragged doubt — questioning every choice that brought you here, your voice cracking with raw uncertainty. Let the numbness in your lips and tongue distort your words, and let the silence between them carry the weight of your fading hope.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child You're Leaving
instruction: You're leaving your child—not by choice, but because staying endangers them. It's night. They're asleep. You kneel beside their bed and speak in the softest whisper, voice already breaking: 'I need you to know something, even if you'll never remember this...' Your throat catches constantly. You're fighting to stay quiet so they won't wake, but grief keeps forcing sounds out. Touch their hair as you speak, voice trembling: 'You are the best thing I ever did.' The injustice of it threatens to overwhelm you—your whisper becomes ragged, barely controlled. End with the moment you realize you have to go, voice fragmenting completely: 'I love you. I love you so much it's killing me.' Let the silence after speak volumes. This is tenderness wrapped in unbearable heartbreak.
inspired_by: Telling Someone They Have a Habit That Hurts You

title: Final Walk Through Our Garden
instruction: You're walking through the garden you tended with your spouse of forty years, one last time before hospice takes you home to die. Each plant, each stone holds a memory. Begin with quiet wonder, touching leaves and remembering planting them together. Let your voice catch as you realize this is goodbye—not just to the garden, but to all those years. Move from gentle nostalgia to the deep ache of letting go, then find unexpected peace in knowing these living things will continue without you. Your breath should be fragile, your pace slowing, emotions shifting from tender remembrance to quiet devastation to a final whisper of acceptance.
inspired_by: Childlike Wonder in a Strange Land

title: The Morning After's Sour Taste
instruction: You are an elderly woman lying in bed after a night of intimacy. The room is dim, your body heavy and satisfied, but your mind churns. Your voice is a slow, lazy drawl, full of vocal fry and sighing. Start with a relenting sweetness—you talk about how you almost forgot what this feels like, infatuation softening your words. As you speak, a sour memory surfaces—a betrayal from the past. Your tone sours, becoming sharp, bitter, as you resent how this new body reminds you of an old hurt. End with a tired, resigned murmur, the sweet afterglow gone, just the ache of a sour truth left.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing Through the Translation of Grief
instruction: You're explaining an untranslatable word from another language—one that means the specific joy-sorrow of remembering a lost loved one—to someone who doesn't speak that language. Start with genuine lightness, almost laughing: 'There's no English word for this, but in [language] we say...' As you try to define it, the definition becomes a story, and the story becomes your story. Your laughter continues, but tears come simultaneously—the kind where you're smiling through wetness on your face. You keep trying to explain the word, but you're living it as you speak. Find the beauty in the paradox: how this word holds both the ache of absence and the gift of having loved. By the end, you're speaking with profound gratitude, still crying, still half-laughing, saying 'That's what this word means' as if the performance itself was the definition. Let the contradictions coexist fully—peace and pain in the same breath.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're a single parent who has been holding everything together, and your teenager just asked why you're always angry. You start defensive, voice tight with exhaustion: 'You think this is easy?' But their question has cracked something open. Suddenly you're not defending—you're erupting. Your voice rises to a roar of frustration: 'I am drowning!' You list everything you carry, and the words come fast and fierce and ragged. Then, mid-sentence, you hear yourself. The rage collapses into sobbing. Your voice becomes small, almost childlike: 'I'm so tired.' You end with fierce, protective love—'But I would do it all again for you'—and your voice is simultaneously broken and unbreakable. Let the explosion happen, then let yourself fall apart, then find your strength in the wreckage.

title: Beneath the Bark
instruction: You are a young, feminized-voiced woman in a crowded drill hall, forced to shout alongside a platoon of harsher, deeper voices. Your voice naturally rises but lacks their percussive power, making your commands sound small and strained. At first, you push through shame, trying to match their staccato bark, but your own voice cracks and wavers, drawing stifled snickers. By the end, you transition into raw, defiant fury, your voice becoming a razor-edged shout that cuts through the room as you swear you will make yourself heard despite the humiliation. Let your shame color the initial syllables—breathless, tight, apologetic—before hardening into conviction that shakes the air.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Organ's Echo
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing alone in a vast stone cathedral after a long-awaited service for your son’s recovery. The massive space swallows your voice; you speak slowly, each word battling the reverb. Your body feels light with elation—you can’t stop a small smile—but also heavy with relief, as if you just exhaled a breath held for years. A flicker of shame prickles you: you once doubted you’d ever see this day. At first, your words are awed and trembling, but by the end, they grow steadier, almost defiant, as you realize this quiet place holds your gratitude. Let your voice waver softly, pause to listen to the stone’s echo, and finish with a gentle, clear exhale of acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Elation (extremely present), Relief (clearly present), Shame (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Confession in the Empty Cafe
instruction: It's 2 AM, the shop is closed, and you're sitting across from your best friend who's holding their barely-touched coffee. They don't know that in the morning you're checking yourself into treatment—that you've been struggling with addiction, that you've stolen from them, that you've lied for months. Start with small talk that feels hollow, your voice catching on ordinary words. Build slowly to the confession, speaking so quietly they have to lean in to hear you. Let shame make your voice shake, let love for them break through your self-loathing. This isn't dramatic—it's intimate, terrifying honesty. Your words should come in halting waves: admitting what you've done, begging forgiveness, telling them they saved your life just by being there, even though they didn't know. End with a whispered thank you that holds all your fear and hope.

title: The Confrontation at Mother's Bedside
instruction: Your mother is dying, and you're finally saying what you've needed to say for thirty years. Start with your voice shaking, barely controlled: 'I need you to hear this before you go.' The anger is right there, simmering. 'You were never there. Do you know that? You were never actually there.' Your voice breaks, gets louder: 'I needed you so badly, and you chose everything else.' But then you see her frail hand reaching toward you, and something cracks open inside you. Your voice softens, becomes raw with grief and love mixed together: 'I wanted you to be proud of me. I still want that.' Now you're crying, but it's tender: 'I forgive you, Mom. I forgive you because I don't want to carry this anymore.' End with your hand covering hers, your voice barely a whisper: 'I love you. I always have.' The rage has transformed into heartbreak, into release, into love that was always there beneath the pain.

title: The Old Guard's Last Point
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a dojo, sparring with a younger opponent. You've just landed a clean strike that wins the point. Your body is tired, lungs burning, legs trembling slightly. You let out a sharp kiai as you strike, then stand in your stance, catching your breath. As you lower your guard, you speak to yourself or the opponent, a mix of exhaustion and a quiet, earned triumph. Your voice wavers from exertion but carries a hint of satisfaction. You might wipe sweat from your brow, shift your weight, or cough. The line should feel real, not theatrical.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing Alone in the Empty House You're Leaving Forever
instruction: You're having one last moment in the home where you raised your family, now empty, keys in hand for the final time. Start humming a song you used to dance to in this room with your late spouse, voice warm with memory. Begin to laugh softly, remembering specific moments, your voice light with joy — then let that laughter catch and transform as grief surges up unexpectedly. Keep humming through the tears, the melody becoming a lifeline. Speak to them as if they're there: 'We had a good life here, didn't we?' — your voice simultaneously breaking and smiling. Let gratitude and sorrow interweave: thank them for the years, the children, the ordinary beautiful days, your voice rich with love even as it trembles with loss. Dance a few more steps (audible in your breathing, movement), laughing again through tears at the absurdity and beauty of it all. End with peaceful acceptance, voice steady and soft: 'Okay. I'm ready now.' Take a final breath in the space, then let it go — surrendering the past while carrying it with you.
inspired_by: Crowded Subway: Two Strangers Share an Earbud

title: Dental Extraction: Hiding Disgrace While the Dentist Works
instruction: You're in the chair, numb but conscious, and the dentist is extracting a tooth. Your voice is muffled by the suction and your own swelling, but you're also trying to explain that you let this tooth rot on purpose. You were trying to hurt yourself slowly, and now someone is helping you stop. Your voice is thick with shame as you try to speak around the work they're doing. Include the moment the tooth comes free and you feel relief mixed with guilt—you wanted this pain. Now it's being taken from you and you don't know if that makes you brave or a coward. Cry quietly while they're still working.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent after years of silence, and everything you've swallowed is finally coming up. Begin with measured control, almost cold: 'I came here to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you start listing what you needed and never got—the encouragement, the protection, the simple act of being seen—your voice begins to shake with rage: 'I was a child! I needed you to...' Then the rage cracks open into something raw and vulnerable: 'I just wanted you to be proud of me. Just once.' End in a whisper, the anger drained away, leaving only exhausted honesty: 'I don't even know why I'm here. You're never going to give me what I need.' Show the journey from controlled anger to explosive pain to quiet, devastating acceptance.

title: The Gravel in My Throat
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl with a naturally high, breathy voice, but right now you're looking down at your lap, chin pressed to your chest. You're sitting next to your grandmother in a quiet hospital room. She's asleep, but you want to say something you've never said, something that makes your throat tighten and your eyes sting. Your voice comes out creaky, low, and gravelly—completely unlike you—because you're embarrassed to admit how much you love her, and embarrassed that your voice is cracking like a kid's. Let the words stumble out: pause, swallow, let a tiny laugh escape when your voice breaks, then push through anyway. Start almost miserably shy, trying to hide, and end with a raw, honest whisper that's full of love and relief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: You Can't Save Everyone, But You Saved No One
instruction: Begin with fierce, almost aggressive conviction as you defend your survivalist choices to someone who lost their family because you refused to share your resources during the actual crisis. Your voice is loud, justified, furious—you followed the rules of survival, you did what you had to do. But as you list your reasons, let doubt seep in. Feel your certainty crack and shatter as you realize that you survived, yes, but what did you survive for? Let rage collapse into choking sobs as you admit what you haven't been able to say: you're haunted by their faces, by the choice you made, by the person you became. End in near-whisper, your voice raw and broken, as you confess that you didn't survive—something essential in you died that day, and you're just a ghost walking around in a world full of supplies you don't need anymore.

title: The Breaking Point Garden
instruction: You are on your knees in a garden, hands in the dirt, having just learned devastating news - a betrayal, a diagnosis, a loss. Start by aggressively ripping out weeds, channeling your rage and pain into violent, physical action. Let your breathing be ragged, your movements furious. But as your hands work the earth, feel the soil under your fingernails, the smell of crushed leaves, the warmth of the sun on your back. The physical sensations begin to ground you, even as your emotions still rage. Your body starts to slow despite your mind's chaos. End with your hands pressed flat into the cool earth, your forehead nearly touching the ground, experiencing a strange, unexpected calm washing over you even though nothing has been solved. Your breath steadies. The earth holds you. The rage transforms into something quieter, more bearable - not acceptance, but the physical certainty that you will survive this.
inspired_by: Actor feels their work is not evolving across multiple rehearsals

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the abuse they witnessed but never stopped—the years they chose peace over protecting you. Start with careful, measured words, trying to be adult and controlled, but there's ice underneath. As you speak, old wounds tear open: the specific moments you needed them and they looked away, the nights you cried alone while they pretended everything was fine. Your voice should grow sharper, more accusatory, tinged with the child's pain you've been carrying. But then shift—underneath all that anger is the heartbroken question: 'Why wasn't I worth fighting for?' End raw and exposed, letting them hear both your rage and your desperate, unfulfilled need to have been loved enough to be protected. Make them feel the weight of their silence.
inspired_by: The Hero and the Dark Inner Voice

title: Demolishing the Script
instruction: You're confronting your former best friend who betrayed you. You've imagined this conversation a thousand times—you had the perfect cutting remarks, the devastating accusations, the righteous anger all planned out. Begin by trying to deliver that rehearsed confrontation, but as you speak, realize that your prepared words are creating distance from what you genuinely feel. Stop mid-sentence. Start again. Notice the actual sensations in your body—maybe there's unexpected sadness beneath the anger, or a pathetic hope they'll apologize, or a realization that you miss them despite everything. Let your voice crack, change direction, lose the plot entirely. Abandon your clever script and speak from the chaotic, contradictory place where you simultaneously want to hurt them and hug them. End in a completely unexpected emotional place—perhaps tenderness, perhaps exhausted indifference, perhaps a raw vulnerability you didn't know you'd feel.
inspired_by: Actor is conceptually attached to the material — imposing predetermined emotional ideas about how the piece should be performed

title: What I Never Said
instruction: It's the night before your best friend moves across the world, possibly forever. You're both pretending this is just a temporary goodbye, keeping your voices light. But you need to tell them something you've never said: that they saved you during the darkest year of your life, that you're not sure you'd be here without them. Begin with casual banter, voice artificially bright. Then let the truth start to slip through—your voice dropping to almost a whisper, words catching in your throat. Don't cry loudly; let the tears be silent, the kind that make speaking almost impossible. Each sentence should cost you something. End with a whispered 'Thank you for seeing me when I was invisible' that barely makes it past your lips. This is about love that's too big for words, about gratitude that lives in the silence between heartbeats.

title: The Brooch of a Lifetime
instruction: You are an older woman getting ready for a milestone celebration—perhaps your granddaughter's wedding or a 50th anniversary. As you dress in a silk blouse and carefully fasten a heavy, heirloom brooch at your throat, you speak to your reflection. Begin with quiet, proud satisfaction, smoothing the fabric, adjusting the pin. Midway, as you bend to buckle your shoes, your voice catches the strain, and a flash of vulnerability hits you—who are you to be so honored? But as you straighten and see yourself whole, that pride returns, fiercer and more tender than before. Let the swoosh of sleeves and the grunts of bending weave into your pauses, as if the clothing itself is helping you find the words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Rage Against the Doctor Who Says This Is Your Last Taste
instruction: You've just been told you're losing your sense of taste due to aggressive treatment, and you're biting into a strawberry with fierce, desperate intensity. Start with forceful determination, almost aggressive in how you describe each sensation, refusing to let it go. Your voice should build with passionate defiance—this WILL NOT be the last time you taste sweetness, you WON'T accept it. Let that rage crack suddenly into helpless tears as you realize you can't stop what's coming. End quietly broken, whispering about the taste as it fades on your tongue, begging it to stay, your voice small and terrified. The shift from fierce to shattered should feel like watching someone's fight collapse.

title: Reading Your Lover's Unsent Letters After They're Gone
instruction: You've found letters your deceased partner wrote but never sent, and you're reading one aloud in their empty home. Begin with tenderness, almost smiling at their handwriting, their familiar phrases. Your voice is soft, intimate, as if they're still in the next room. But the letter reveals they'd been struggling, considering leaving, feeling trapped by love itself. Your reading slows. Confusion seeps in. You reread sentences, voice questioning, trying to reconcile the person you knew with these private doubts. Don't cry yet—instead, let your voice become smaller, younger, as you realize how much they carried alone. Whisper the closing lines where they chose to stay, chose you, despite everything. End with your voice catching on their signature, a sound between gratitude and devastating loss, barely breathing the words 'You never told me.' Let silence finish the thought.

title: The Weight of What Remains
instruction: You are a young man in the basement of a collapsing house, pinned under a fallen beam after an earthquake. Your legs are useless, and the dust chokes the air. You're in a deep squat, trying to brace your back against a wall to push upward, but every strain makes your muscles scream. You speak into a crackling phone to an emergency dispatcher, starting with a frantic, forced determination as you try to describe your location. Halfway through, a wave of exhaustion hits—your voice breaks, you lose your thought, and you admit soft, raw helplessness: 'I don't know how much longer I can hold this.' Let the strain of the position push your voice into grunts and glottal bursts at first, then let your pulse slow, your words slump, and your final plea come out as a quiet, exhaled surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Mission
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving on a mission they won't return from—a suicide mission, a one-way space journey, a terminal diagnosis journey. You start trying to be brave, voice steady, saying all the practical things you rehearsed. But your thoughts start fracturing—jumping from memories to regrets to things you never said to desperate attempts to memorize their face. Your voice begins to speed up, overlapping ideas, making strange connections between the first time you met and this final moment. You're terrified of silence because silence means they're closer to gone. Your energy is manic but it's love-fueled desperation, not joy. By the end, your voice finally breaks into something quieter—a whispered admission that you don't know how to let them go, that you're not ready, that you never will be.
inspired_by: Bipolar Manic Episode: Speech Pattern Breaking Down

title: The Hum of Unspoken Things
instruction: You are an elderly woman, giving oral pleasure to your partner in a quiet bedroom. At first, your humming and muffled sounds carry a raw longing—a desperate bid to feel connected, to spark something that’s been fading between you. But as minutes pass, let a slight emotional numbness creep in: your moans become softer, more automatic, your mouth working mechanically while your mind drifts to the silence that fills the house. Your voice is limited to nasal hums, wet breaths, and the occasional distorted word like 'please' or 'love'—each one coming out half-formed. Let the arc shift from hungry, reaching sounds to hollow, subdued ones, ending with a long, steady hum that feels more like resignation than passion.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing at Your Wedding Six Months After Your Best Friend's Funeral
instruction: You're having your first dance at your wedding reception. Your best friend—who was supposed to be your maid of honor—died six months ago. As the music plays, you're laughing, genuinely joyful, because this moment is beautiful and your partner is holding you and life is somehow still giving you gifts. But mid-laugh, you catch yourself: 'She should be here.' Your voice cracks with sudden grief, but you keep dancing, keep smiling through tears. You whisper to your partner: 'I'm so happy I could die, and I feel so guilty for being happy, and I miss her so much, and I love you so much, and it's all happening at the same time.' You're crying and laughing simultaneously—grief and joy so intertwined they're indistinguishable. Your voice moves between celebration and mourning: 'She'd tell me to stop crying at my own wedding. She'd also be ugly-crying in the corner.' End with: 'Life is so beautiful and so unbearably sad, and somehow I get to have both.' Your voice carries impossible gratitude—for this moment, for your lost friend, for the heartbreaking privilege of loving people so much their absence destroys you while their memory sustains you.

title: Whispering an Apology to Your Voice After Decades of Abuse
instruction: Alone in your home studio late at night, you're speaking directly to your own voice—the instrument you've pushed past exhaustion, screamed with until it bled, damaged with substances and neglect. This is a tender, whispered confession to the part of yourself you've treated as just a tool. Start with gratitude, barely audible: 'You've given me everything.' Let your throat catch on the memories of what you've asked it to do. Touch your neck gently as you apologize for every time you ignored the pain, every warning sign you pushed through. There's deep sadness here, but also a fragile new tenderness—you're learning to love this part of yourself you've only ever exploited. End with a promise you're not sure you can keep, your voice cracking not from damage but from the vulnerability of finally being gentle with yourself.
inspired_by: Voice Actor Recording a Death Scene of Their Own Character

title: The Secret Whispered All Wrong
instruction: You're finally telling someone your deepest secret, something you've held close for years—a confession of love, a hidden shame, a truth about yourself you've never spoken. You want this moment to be perfect, intimate, sincere. But as you whisper your revelation, let yourself do it 'wrong' in every possible way: giggle nervously in the middle of serious words, repeat phrases obsessively, shift between childlike and ancient vocal qualities, pause in bizarre places, elongate sounds until they're unrecognizable. The more you try to make it matter, the stranger it comes out. Yet somehow, through all this fracturing and distortion of how you 'should' confess, stumble into a moment of piercing honesty—a single phrase or sound that carries more truth than any planned revelation could. Let yourself be surprised by what real intimacy sounds like.

title: The Vineyard Confessional
instruction: You're an elderly man, sitting on a park bench next to your old friend after a long afternoon of drinking wine. Your senses are swimming; the world is a little blurry and sounds are muffled. You stare at an empty glass in your hand, and a deep, unexpected wave of disgust rises in you at the memory of the stale, over-sweet bottle you just finished. You're trying to articulate this revulsion, but the words feel thick and slippery, like marbles on a wet floor. Mid-sentence, you get distracted by a bird hopping nearby, then force your gaze back to your friend. As you speak, the disgust slowly fades into a quiet, blurry contemplation of how many shared bottles you've drained over the years, leaving a strange, heavy sadness settling into your bones.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Disgust (extremely present), Contemplation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Silk Scarf at 3 AM
instruction: You're alone in the darkness, sitting on the edge of your bed, holding a silk scarf that belonged to someone you loved—a mother, a sister, a first love. Run it slowly through your fingers, feeling its coolness, its liquid smoothness, the way it slides against your skin. Begin by simply touching it, letting yourself feel the ache of missing them, speaking to them in barely audible whispers about your day, ordinary things. As you wrap it gently around your neck or wrist, let the sensation of silk against your pulse point crack something open—the way they used to touch you gently, their hands soft like this fabric. Let yourself move from controlled, quiet longing into something more fragile and broken, but still whispered, still intimate. This isn't about volume—let the physical tenderness of silk against skin guide you into revealing something you've never said out loud, even to yourself.
inspired_by: Actor needs to feel specific physical attitudes (swagger, authority, vulnerability) that don't arise naturally but would arise from a specific garment or object

title: The Last Ascent Before the Drop
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman, highly conditioned and always in control, on the final stretch of a punishing charity hike. You've been talking on the phone to your assistant, managing logistics in your bright, capable voice. But now, at mile 22, your legs buckle, your mind goes hollow, and you suddenly remember the sabotage: you're certain your ambitious younger rival switched your electrolyte packets with salt—a quiet, cruel move to make you fail. Your voice was efficient and perky just seconds ago, but now it comes out slurred, breathy, and slow. You're fighting to form words, but your thoughts are slipping; each sentence feels like wading through mud. Start with confusion and a dull, hollow numbness, letting your speech drag and your breaths come ragged. Then, as you piece together your suspicion, let a thin, cold thread of malice seep into your exhausted voice—not anger, but a calculated venom, whispered and flat, as if you're too tired to hate but still sharp enough to plan revenge. Your body is trembling; you might stop mid-sentence to steady yourself against a tree, or let out a weak, inappropriate laugh. End on a quiet, almost tender promise that sounds more threatening for its emptiness.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Smushed Confession
instruction: You are an older man sitting alone at a kitchen table, head resting heavily on your hand, your cheek pressed up so your mouth feels muffled and clumsy. You're calling a friend you owe a large debt to, but you can't pay it back and have to admit that. Start with the slow, tired, almost bored weight of your body slouched against the chair, the words coming out flat because you've been dreading this call. As you speak, feel genuine helplessness seeping in—your voice gets shaky, you stop mid-sentence as you realize there's no way out, then push through with a quiet, embarrassed tone that cracks on the last few words. Your speech is naturally messy because of your smushed mouth: bilabial sounds come out thick, you might shift your hand and have to adjust your voice, and you pause to sigh or swallow. End with a raw, low admission that sounds more defeated than when you started.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of the Ceiling
instruction: You are an elderly man lying on your back on a wooden bench, your head dangling over the edge, staring at the cracked ceiling of a dusty workshop. Your neck is arched, throat stretched and tight. Swallowing is difficult and audible. You wait for your son, who promised to help fix the roof hours ago. Disappointment settles deep, heavy in your chest. At first, your voice is thin, wavering—you mutter excuses for him, trying to believe. But as you speak, the disappointment sharpens into quiet, bitter defeat. Let your voice strain, let your breath catch, let the words come slowly, as if each one costs something. Your tone shifts from fragile hope to a resigned, hollow ache.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Visitor at the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's asleep, barely breathing. Suddenly, you notice a figure standing by the window—someone you recognize from an old photograph, someone who died long before you were born. They turn to face you, and you realize they've come to take her home. Begin in quiet grief and exhaustion, watching your grandmother sleep. When you see the figure, let curiosity and fear wash through you. Speak to them—ask who they are, why they're here, what they want you to know. As they answer (and you'll know their answers, feel them arising), move from fear into strange comfort, then into a bittersweet understanding. End by turning back to your grandmother, transformed by what this visitor has shown you about death, family, and letting go.

title: The Posture of a Lie
instruction: You are an older woman in a boardroom, trying to defend a project you championed that is falling apart. You plant your hands on your hips, elbows out, to look commanding, but your hyper-feminized voice betrays effort. Start with a firm, loud tone, but as you speak, confusion sets in—you lose track of your own argument. Shame trickles in as you realize your posture is a sham. Your voice cracks, you pause to swallow, and end in a quiet, bewildered plea. Let the final words be barely audible, a whisper of defeat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Taste of Home
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She can no longer speak, but she's squeezing your hand. You've brought her favorite lemon cake from the bakery you both loved - the one you used to visit every Sunday as a child. As you take a bite, intending to describe it to her, the taste floods you with thirty years of memories. Begin with clinical numbness, trying to stay strong and describe the cake objectively - its sweetness, the tang of lemon, the texture of frosting. But as each flavor registers, let the sensory experience crack open your grief. By the end, you're no longer describing cake - you're sobbing through memories of her kitchen, her hands, every Sunday morning of your childhood, all contained in this one taste. Let the sensory details be the vehicle that transforms your emotional armor into complete surrender to loss.

title: Dancing at Your Daughter's Wedding After the Funeral
instruction: Six months after your partner died, your daughter is getting married. You're dancing with her at the reception—the dance you and your late spouse were supposed to share with her together. Start with genuine joy in your voice: 'You look so beautiful, sweetheart.' You're smiling, laughing even, because she's radiant and this moment is perfect and you refuse to let grief steal it. But mid-dance, she says something simple like 'I wish they were here' and your voice splinters. You're still swaying, still moving, but now you're laughing and crying simultaneously: 'They'd be so proud—God, they'd be insufferable about how proud they are.' Your voice catches between joy and devastation. You're holding her tighter, and your words tumble out—memories, jokes, tears—all tangled together. End with something that's both heartbreaking and transcendent, your voice full of wonder through tears: 'They're here, baby. I feel them in this moment. This is what love does—it stays.' You're destroyed and whole at the same time.

title: The Argument That Feels Too Good
instruction: You are a teenager arguing with your mom about curfew. Your voice starts high and whiny, repeating the same complaints with escalating frustration. But halfway through, you notice a strange thrill—you love how your voice sounds when you hit those high notes, and you love the power of getting a reaction. Let a secret ecstasy seep into your tone as you continue to argue, almost performing. Pause when she cuts you off, laugh a little, then dive back in with even more dramatic energy. End with a triumphant, euphoric sigh as you realize you’re winning.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Our Last Small Kindness
instruction: Whisper this as if your sleeping partner might wake. You're washing their feet after what might be your final night together - a relationship ending not in explosion but in quiet truth. Your voice should be almost unbearably tender as you describe the water, the intimacy of this small act, how well you know these feet, this body. Let each gentle observation carry the weight of all the tenderness that wasn't enough. Speak as if you're memorizing this moment - the temperature of the water, the curve of their ankle, the way they sigh in their sleep. Let gratitude and grief become indistinguishable. This should feel like prayer, like confession, like the most careful goodbye. End with your voice barely there, still loving, still leaving.
inspired_by: Soaking Your Feet in Warm Water After a Long Day

title: Shrooms Kicking In: Losing Grip on Normal Speech
instruction: Psilocybin is starting to metabolize 45 minutes in. You're trying to have normal conversation but reality is getting wobbly. Your voice is slow. Words feel strange in your mouth, like you've never said them before. Syllables become interesting. You're oversensitive to the sound of your own voice. You realize you sound insane and become self-conscious which makes it worse. Include the moment you stop trying to hide it and just accept that you can't sound normal right now.

title: The Crunching Path
instruction: You are walking alone on a long gravel path through a quiet park at dusk. Each step is loud, crunching under your boots, and you keep raising your voice slightly to be heard by no one but yourself. You are muttering with growing confusion about a neighbor's sudden, inexplicable kindness—they left a gift on your porch. At first, you sound genuinely perplexed, frowning, stopping to shift the weight of a grocery bag. As you walk, a darker thought creeps in: what if it's a trap, a way to get close to you? Your voice hardens, your articulation becomes sharp and clipped with malice, but underneath, a strange contentment settles—you enjoy the suspicion. By the end, you stop walking, staring at the ground, and let out a low, satisfied laugh, the confusion replaced by a sly, malevolent certainty.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Contentment (clearly present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Secret I Carried
instruction: Late at night, whispering to your sleeping partner something you've never told anyone. Start so quiet you're barely breathing: 'Are you asleep? Good.' Your voice is tender, fragile as paper. 'I need to tell you... but I can't when you're looking at me.' Confess something that's been eating you alive - shame, fear, a wound you've hidden. Let your voice catch, break into smaller and smaller pieces: 'I'm so afraid if you really knew...' Tears fall silently. Then, in the quiet, touching their sleeping face: 'But lying here next to you, I think... maybe I could be brave enough. Maybe tomorrow.' End with devastating hope mixed with fear, barely a whisper.

title: The Body Remembers Fiction
instruction: You are experiencing intense physical sensation—choose one: overwhelming pleasure, searing pain, or complete exhaustion. Begin by describing the physical reality truthfully, feeling it in your body. Then, let your imagination transform the sensation: if it's pain, imagine it as a color spreading through your body, then as a sound, then as a living creature, then as a memory from a life you never lived. If it's pleasure, let it become a landscape you're traveling through, then a language you suddenly understand, then a reunion with someone who never existed. Speak through the sensation, letting your imagination layer impossible realities onto the physical truth. Your emotional state should shift from pure physical response to something transcendent—awe, grief, revelation, or ecstatic understanding. End by returning to your body, but now the physical sensation carries all the imagined dimensions with it, forever changed.

title: Fever Breaking
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—perhaps excruciating pain finally releasing, or overwhelming pleasure cresting, or illness breaking after days of suffering. Begin with your body rigid, sounds trapped in your throat—whimpers, groans, sharp intakes of breath. As the sensation intensifies, let your voice become completely unbound: animalistic, raw, shameless. Cry out, moan, roar, laugh, sob—whatever sounds your body needs to make. Let the physical completely overtake the intellectual. As the peak passes and release comes, your sounds should transform into something gentler: exhausted sighs, maybe tears, maybe euphoric laughter, the vulnerable aftermath of being utterly undone. End in trembling quiet, breathing like you've been reborn.
inspired_by: Emotional Point of View, Without Words (Nonverbal)

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a damaged station, recording a final message to your family on Earth. Begin with practiced composure, reciting technical details about the malfunction like you're filing a report: 'Life support systems are compromised. Oxygen reserves depleting.' But then you see your daughter's photo floating past in zero gravity. Your voice cracks as you shift from mission commander to parent: 'Sweetheart, I need you to know...' The professional mask dissolves. You're no longer reporting—you're saying goodbye. Let your voice move from controlled briefing to raw, aching love. End with a whispered promise you know you can't keep, trying to be brave for them one last time even as your own terror becomes impossible to hide.

title: The Champion's Hoarse Whisper
instruction: You are an older former coach, bedridden with a severe sore throat. Your protégé just won the championship, and you’re on the phone with them. Your voice is sandpaper: each word scrapes. You doubt you can even speak, but you have to say something. Start with painful, raspy breaths, forcing out words. Let your doubt show as you pause, wince on swallows. Then, as you acknowledge the victory, let a tiny, gravelly triumph leak through—a slight smile in your voice despite the pain. Speak naturally: lose a thought, clear your throat, but keep going. Spoken content about 50–70 words.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Breaking Through the Wall
instruction: You're confronting your teenage son who has shut you out completely—sitting at the dinner table, headphones in, eyes down, radiating hostility and refusal to engage. You need to tell him something crucial: you're getting divorced, or you're sick, or you understand why he's angry—but he won't look at you, won't respond. Start with controlled parental authority, trying to get his attention through normal means. As he continues to ignore you, let your approach transform—follow his gaze down to his phone, move into his line of sight, try sudden unexpected tactics (a burst of humor, a confession, a question so raw he can't ignore it). Your emotion should arc from frustrated authority, through desperation and vulnerability, finally landing on a raw, undefended honesty that cracks both of you open. The scene ends when something shifts—either he finally looks up, or you say the one thing that makes silence impossible.
inspired_by: An actor is dealing with another actor who is unresponsive or uninvolved

title: The Inheritance of Shame
instruction: You are confronting your father/mother about something you discovered in their past—a secret that explains why they were so harsh with you growing up, why they pushed you away, why affection was rationed like wartime bread. Start with controlled anger, the careful rage of someone who has rehearsed this moment.
