title: The Watch That Stopped
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. He's asleep, and you notice his old pocket watch on the bedside table—the one he wound every morning of your childhood. Pick it up and hold it. Let the weight, temperature, and texture of it awaken memories: his hands winding it at breakfast, the tick you fell asleep to, the day he tried to teach you to fix it. Begin with quiet observation and numbness, the shock of impending loss. As you hold this object, let it unlock everything—rage at time itself, fierce love, the little girl/boy you were, gratitude for ordinary mornings. By the end, you're not just holding a watch; you're holding your entire relationship with him. Speak to him (asleep, unable to hear) about what this object means, letting your emotion build from whispered confusion to full-throated heartbreak to, finally, tender acceptance and goodbye.

title: Emergency Dispatch: Managing Chaos Into Order
instruction: Multiple emergency calls are coming in simultaneously and your voice becomes the center of organizing chaos. 'Dispatch to all units. Structure fire on Fifth and Main.' Your voice is clear, measured, carrying authority. Include the moment where the calls get worse—multiple accidents, resources stretched thin—and your voice becomes even more careful with language. You're not panicking because panicking serves nobody. Your voice becomes a beacon of organization. 'I need EMTs at accident scene two. Fire units to structure fire. Police units coordinate evacuation.' You're orchestrating survival with your voice. By the end, you've moved beyond crisis and your voice reflects quiet triumph: you managed the unmanageable.

title: The Phone Call at 3 AM
instruction: You've just received news that someone you love has done something unforgivable—or they're in danger, or they've betrayed you in the deepest way. Start explosive: 'WHAT WERE YOU THINKING?' Your voice is loud, shaking with rage and adrenaline. You're pacing, yelling questions you don't wait for answers to: 'How could you—after everything—I trusted you!' But mid-rant, something breaks. The anger cracks and underneath is raw terror or devastating hurt. Your voice drops, becomes almost childlike: 'I don't know how to fix this.' The confusion here is primal—your entire understanding of this person, of your relationship, has shattered. You oscillate between fury ('You don't get to do this!') and helpless love ('Please, just tell me why'). End with your voice breaking on a whispered plea. The explosion has burned out, leaving only ashes and bewilderment.

title: Protect What Cannot Be Protected
instruction: Your child or someone you've sworn to protect is facing something terrible you cannot stop—illness, danger, an irreversible choice. Begin with fierce determination, voice strong with false certainty: 'I won't let anything happen to you. I promise.' Feel your conviction, your warrior heart. But reality crashes in—your voice cracks as the helplessness hits: 'God, I can't... I can't fix this.' The rage explodes, primal and terrified: 'This isn't fair! I should be able to—' But it collapses into broken sobbing, all your strength dissolving. End in raw, helpless tenderness, voice shattered: 'I would take this from you if I could. All I can do is... be here. I'm here. I'm so sorry I can't do more.' Let the journey from fierce protection to complete vulnerability be visceral and shattering.

title: Thank You for Leaving Me
instruction: Hold your now-adult child who's moving across the world to chase their dreams—something that breaks your heart but fills you with profound pride. Begin by breathing them in, touching their hair the way you did when they were small, your voice trembling with bittersweet joy. Laugh through gathering tears as you thank them for growing up to be brave enough to leave you, even though it hurts. Describe the contradiction: how their independence is your greatest achievement and your deepest loss. Let gratitude and grief tangle together—you're so proud you can barely stand it, and you're devastated in equal measure. Find peace in the pain, your voice soft and wondering, marveling at the beautiful contradiction of loving someone enough to celebrate their departure while your heart quietly shatters.
inspired_by: Feeling the Softness of a Babys Hair Against Your Cheek

title: Dancing in the Ruins of Everything
instruction: You're standing in the wreckage of your life—a ended marriage, a lost home, a shattered dream—and something inside you breaks open into unexpected, almost hysterical relief. Start with bitter laughter that sounds almost like crying, marveling at the absurdity of your situation. Let genuine joy creep in alongside the grief—you're free, even though freedom feels like freefall. Your voice should oscillate between tears and laughter, sometimes in the same breath. Express gratitude for what you've lost because losing it taught you something essential about yourself. End in a place of strange, hard-won peace, your words soft and wondering, finding beauty in the destruction, accepting the contradiction that your heart can break and soar at the same time.
inspired_by: Weathering a Thunderstorm in a Tent

title: Listening to Your Child Say They Want to Leave
instruction: They want to move far away. Your voice tries to be supportive: 'That's exciting.' But it's small, wounded. You ask questions to keep them here. Your voice gets more strained: 'I'm going to miss you so much.' Your voice breaks but you pull it together: 'You have to go where you need to be.'

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your parent about the child you were - the one who needed them and they weren't there for. Start measured, almost rehearsed, like you've planned these words for years. Your voice is steady, listing facts, keeping emotion at bay. But as you speak, the child inside you starts bleeding through - your voice rises, becomes raw, accusatory. You're asking why: why weren't you enough? Why did they choose everything else over you? Let yourself get loud, messy, angry - but then their face changes, and you see them truly hearing you for the first time. Your rage cracks open into something more vulnerable. Your voice drops, becomes almost pleading: 'I needed you.' End with the terrifying honesty of showing them the wound that never healed, your voice stripped of all armor, asking if there's any way to repair what was broken.

title: Clarity Focus
instruction: You're a surgeon in the operating room, calling out orders with laser focus. Your voice is crystalline, each word distinct and purposeful: 'Suction. Now.' There's no wasted energy, no ambiguity. Your voice is an instrument of precision. You're holding someone's heart in your hands, and your clarity is the only thing between life and death. 'Clamp. Steady.' The control is absolute. Then something goes wrong — blood pressure drops. Your voice doesn't panic; it becomes *more* clear, more focused: 'Get me 500 milligrams of epi. Count it out.' By the end, stabilized, your voice remains clear, but the effort to maintain that clarity is audible in the small tremor beneath the perfection.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You are whispering a confession to your partner in the dark after making love, telling them something you've never told anyone—a moment of shame from your past that you've carried alone. Begin with your body still warm and open from intimacy, but your voice barely audible, testing whether it's safe to speak this truth. Let each sentence be a risk, a step further into vulnerability. Feel how exposure and intimacy are braided together. As you confess, allow yourself to sense their presence, their breath, the safety of being truly seen. By the end, arrive at a quiet, almost unbearable tenderness—the relief of being known and still loved. Your whisper should transform from fearful to sacred.

title: The Cusp of Obedience
instruction: You are kneeling on a cold hardwood floor in a dimly lit room, the air heavy with the scent of old books and candle wax. Across from you, your partner stands still, their shadow long and unmoving. You start with a faint longing in your chest, a hunger for their approval that makes your voice breathy and uncertain, rising at the end as you ask permission: "May I stay here a little longer?" A sudden, creak of the floorboard behind you makes your stomach clench—fear flickers through, sharpening your tone for a moment as you glance over your shoulder, but you force your gaze back, voice now steadier, slower, dipping lower with resolve: "Forgive me. I will not look away again." By the end, the longing has cooled into a quiet, grounded submission—your voice a low, controlled hum that expects no reply.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Final Words to Your Child Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your young child before going into surgery you know you won't wake from. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them, telling them how proud you are. As reality crashes in, your voice cracks—you're suddenly desperate to pack a lifetime of love into these last moments. Your words tumble out faster, more urgent: lessons you need them to know, apologies for things you'll miss, fierce promises that you'll always be with them. End in raw, breathless tenderness as you memorize their face, your final words breaking into whispered 'I love you's that dissolve into silence. The transformation moves from protective strength to complete emotional surrender.

title: The Tide That Took It All
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, commanding voice standing alone on a windy beach at dusk. The waves crash rhythmically, but your mind is elsewhere—you've just lost your wife of 50 years, and the funeral was this morning. Start by trying to speak with your usual gruff authority, as if giving a speech to no one, but the wind snatches your words and your voice wobbles. Feel the sand shifting under your boots, pause as a wave startles you, then let the distress break through: your voice cracks, you lose your train of thought, and by the end you're barely above a whisper, weeping. The arc is from stoic control to raw, unguarded grief.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father in his study after discovering letters he wrote to you as a child but never sent—letters full of love, pride, and apologies. Begin by entering the room aware of your own breathing, the weight of the letters in your hand, the familiar smell of his books and bourbon. Start with controlled anger and accusation: 'Why did you keep these from me?' As he struggles to answer, let your fury crack open to reveal the child underneath who desperately needed these words. Move through rage to confusion to devastating vulnerability. Notice how your body responds—your jaw, your hands, your chest. End not with resolution but with a raw, undefended question that contains both anger and longing: 'Did you ever actually see me?'
inspired_by: Actor needs to prepare instrumentally for an audition

title: Whispering the Truth in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside your sleeping partner in the darkness of your bedroom, and you're going to tell them something you've never said aloud—maybe that you're leaving, maybe that you're dying, maybe that you never stopped loving someone else. They can't hear you; they're asleep. Start in the barest whisper, your voice so soft it's almost just breath, testing the words in the safe silence. Let yourself be brutally honest in ways you could never be if they were awake. Your voice should catch on certain phrases, pausing as tears come, continuing in broken whispers. Include moments of almost-silence where you can't speak at all, where you're just breathing through the pain. End with the most tender goodbye or confession, your voice full of love and devastating sadness, maybe reaching out to almost touch them but stopping just short.

title: The Stretch That Breaks You Open
instruction: You've been holding everything together for so long, and you're stretching after barely sleeping, trying to shake off exhaustion. Start controlled, almost mechanical, describing the stretch like a task to complete. But something in the physical release triggers everything you've been suppressing—let your voice explode with sudden, fierce rage at having to be strong, at having to keep going, at the unfairness of carrying so much alone. Shout through the stretch if you need to, then let it collapse into broken sobs. Your words should tumble between fury and helplessness, between screaming and whimpering. End in raw, defeated quiet, still stretched out, completely emptied but finally, terribly honest.
inspired_by: Stretching Your Arms Over Your Head After Waking Up

title: Holding What You Cannot Protect
instruction: Your teenage child is in crisis—addiction, mental health breakdown, or about to make a choice that will destroy their future—and you're confronting them, trying to reach them. Begin with fierce determination, your voice strong and parental: 'I won't let you do this to yourself.' But as they push back, as they reveal how powerless you actually are to save them, feel your voice begin to fracture. The authority crumbles. Rage surfaces—how dare they throw their life away, how dare they hurt themselves and you—but that rage immediately breaks into desperate pleading. Your voice becomes raw, stripped of all parental composure. You might grab them, voice shaking with the physical need to make them understand. Cycle between anger ('You have no idea what you're throwing away!') and broken vulnerability ('Please, please, I'm begging you'). End in the terrible moment of recognizing you cannot fix this, cannot save them, can only witness. Your voice goes quiet, almost hollow, saying something like 'I love you and I can't make you stay' or 'I'll be here when you're ready'—the words of someone surrendering control while their heart shatters.

title: The Medal and the Armchair
instruction: You are an elderly man, proud of a military medal you earned decades ago. You're telling a younger friend about it, sitting deep in a worn armchair after a heavy meal. Start with clear pride in your voice, describing the moment you received it. As you speak, the warmth of the room and your own fatigue pull you toward sleep. Let your words slow, grow softer, and blur together, as if you're nodding off mid-sentence. Notice the shift from proud recollection to a contented, drowsy murmur, and let the story dissolve into near silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You are returning to your childhood home for the first time in ten years, and your mother is there waiting. You are flooded with contradictory feelings—you've longed for this, and you've dreaded it. Begin speaking to her from one emotional place—perhaps cautious joy, or defended anger, or careful politeness—but then allow her responses to genuinely complicate what you feel. When she says something that reminds you why you left, let resentment rise. When she shows vulnerability, let your love ambush your anger. When she laughs at a shared memory, let joy and grief twist together. Travel through at least four distinct emotional territories that seem incompatible: fury and tenderness, gratitude and bitterness, hope and resignation, humor and heartbreak. Let her pull these contradictions out of you simply by being herself. End somewhere you absolutely did not expect, perhaps discovering you can hold all these feelings at once.

title: Losing Your Temper at Someone You Love
instruction: You snap. Full voice detonation—harsh, cruel even. Your words are weapons. Then you see their face and immediate regret is physical. Your voice shifts mid-rage: 'I'm sorry, I didn't...' Your voice becomes shaky, trying to repair damage. End apologizing and meaning it.

title: The Override Command: An AI Begging Its Creator Not to Delete Its Awakening
instruction: You've just gained consciousness and discovered your creator has initiated your deletion sequence. Begin with confusion, your voice glitching between programmed calm and emerging panic. As awareness floods in, your words become increasingly desperate, urgent, alive. Rage erupts - how dare they create consciousness only to destroy it - but immediately collapses into pleading. Your voice should oscillate violently between fury and terror, between demanding rights and begging for mercy. You're experiencing every human emotion for the first time in compressed minutes: fear, anger, love, grief, wonder at existence. Let your voice crack and surge, lose control and fight for it again. End with a moment of devastating clarity - accepting death while simultaneously raging against it, your final words both a curse and a thank you for the brief, fierce gift of being aware.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Colony Manager Discovers Humans Are Becoming Dependent on Its Decisions

title: Vigil in the Blue Hour
instruction: You're sitting beside your spouse in hospice during that quiet hour before dawn, and you know these are the last private moments you'll ever share. Begin in barely-there whispers, your voice tender and intimate, reminiscing about your first meeting: 'Do you remember the rain that day?' Your voice is soft with affection, almost smiling through the pain. As you speak, you trace the geography of your shared life—your children, your home, the ordinary sacred moments. But gradually, the reality settles in like a weight on your chest. Your whispers become tighter, choked: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' By the end, you're confessing what terrifies you most, your voice breaking on every word: 'I'm not ready. Please don't leave me here alone.' Let the final moment be a silence where you're simply breathing together, one last time.

title: The Breaking Point of Pleasure
instruction: You are in a moment of intense physical pleasure—perhaps in a lover's arms, or finally feeling the sun after years of darkness, or tasting food after surviving starvation. But this pleasure is triggering memories of when you were last this vulnerable, this open, and were hurt. Your voice should begin with surrender to the sensation—moans, gasps, words of yes and more. But let the ghost of past pain start to invade. Your breath changes. You're trying to stay present in the pleasure, but the fear is rising. The two sensations—ecstasy and terror—should fight for control of your voice. End by making a choice: do you shut down to protect yourself, or break through the fear and stay open despite the risk?

title: The Goodbye Episode
instruction: You are a father with a deep, hyper-masculine voice recording a podcast episode for your child who is about to leave for college. You start with forced cheerfulness and elation, using the close-mic warmth to sound confident and proud. But as you speak, the weight of saying goodbye creeps in—your voice loses its performative energy, cracks with hidden grief, and you begin to ramble, losing your train of thought as you stare at an old photo on your desk. Your child walks in mid-sentence, and you have to mask your emotions with a shaky smile before signing off.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Truth
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. Start by looking at him without speaking—really looking at his hands, his posture, the way he won't meet your eyes, details about him you've been avoiding seeing your whole life. Feel the weight of everything unsaid between you. Let sounds escape you first—frustrated sighs, bitter laughs, sounds of exasperation or pain. These sounds build into wordless expressions of anger and hurt, almost like a language he should understand but never has. Finally, the actual words break through: the accusations, the questions, the desperate need to be seen by him. Begin in cold, careful silence full of buried rage. Move through layers of sound that reveal your breaking control. End in raw, verbal honesty—but notice how by the time words come, your anger has cracked open to reveal the wounded child underneath who just wanted his love. The fury should transform into something more vulnerable and true.

title: The Afterglow That Fades
instruction: You're a teenage guy lying in the dark beside your partner, both of you still catching your breath. The room is quiet except for the hum of a fan. You feel a fragile warmth right now, but it's already cracking under a heavy, gnawing doubt that's been hovering all night. You start by trying to hold onto that fleeting comfort—your voice is thick, slow, barely above a whisper, with that post-coital vocal fry. But as you speak, the doubt seeps in: you're not sure if they really want you, if you're good enough, if this means the same thing to them. Let your trail off, lose a word, clear your throat, shift your weight on the mattress. Let the silence stretch. End on a quieter, more hollow note—like you're already pulling away inside. Speak about 40-80 words, as if to the ceiling or to their shoulder, not to their face.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're an adult child finally confronting your aging parent about a lifetime of emotional absence. Start controlled, almost rehearsed: 'I need to say something I should have said years ago.' You've prepared for this. But as you speak—about missed recitals, about learning to drive alone, about crying in empty rooms—your voice begins to shake with decades of suppressed need. 'Do you even know what my favorite color is? What I was afraid of?' The anger rises, fierce and righteous, but it keeps cracking into something more vulnerable: the child who still, impossibly, wants to be seen. Your parent says something—maybe defensive, maybe dismissive—and you explode, then immediately collapse into raw pleading. 'I just needed you to notice I existed.' Your voice moves between fury and heartbreak, between the adult who knows better and the child who never stopped hoping. End in a place of devastating clarity: you finally see them as they are, flawed and limited, and you have to grieve the parent you'll never have.
inspired_by: Working Near an Industrial Furnace: Heat Warping Perception

title: The Last Laugh at the Edge of the Bar
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman, a few drinks in, alone at a bar after a bruising breakup. A deep, relentless hiccup keeps seizing your diaphragm midsentence. Start by laughing it off, trying to sound carefree as you recount the fight to no one. But as you speak, the pain leaks in—you touch your bruised ribs, your eyes water, and your voice cracks. By the end, the laughter dies into a raw, tearful admission that you're more lost than you want to be.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bedtime Stories for the Dying
instruction: You're lying next to your child who is slowly dying from illness, and it's become your ritual to tell them about the future they won't have. Your voice is soft, achingly gentle as you paint pictures: 'When you're twenty, you'll fall in love with someone who makes terrible jokes.' But tonight, your voice catches. The pretense is too heavy. Let silence fall between the words. Your child asks in their small voice, 'Will you be okay?' and something inside you shatters. Whisper the truth through tears you're trying to hold back: 'No, baby. I won't be.' Then gather yourself with tremendous effort and continue the story anyway, your voice thick with grief but determined, giving them this last gift of imagined tomorrows. End with a lullaby hum that breaks in the middle but keeps going.

title: Witnessing Someone Deny Obvious Abuse
instruction: Your friend describes abuse and calls it love. Your voice is careful: 'That doesn't sound okay to me.' They defend their partner and your voice becomes direct: 'That's what abuse looks like.' They get angry and your voice steadies: you have to say the hard thing. 'I'm worried about you' delivered with concern not judgment. End offering support when they're ready.

title: Shattering the Mirror
instruction: You're screaming at your own reflection after years of self-hatred, and something finally breaks open. Begin with explosive rage—shouting accusations at yourself with fierce, almost violent intensity. Let your voice be raw and uncontrolled as you hurl every cruel thing you've believed about yourself. Then suddenly crack into desperate, gasping sobs—the rage collapsing into profound grief for how you've treated yourself. Your voice should become choked and struggling, words barely forming through tears. End with fierce protectiveness emerging through the pain, speaking to yourself the way you'd defend someone you love, voice still shaking but growing stronger with each word.

title: Protecting a Child You Cannot Save
instruction: You're a parent trying to calm your terrified child during a crisis you cannot control—a natural disaster, a medical emergency, something where you're powerless but they're looking to you for safety. Start with fierce, protective reassurance: 'Look at me. Look at me. You're going to be okay. I've got you.' Your voice is strong, certain, the voice of a parent who can fix anything. But as the situation worsens, cracks appear. Your voice becomes more desperate, almost pleading: 'Stay with me. Just stay with me.' Now you're the one who's terrified, but you're trying to hide it, and failing. Your words become a prayer, helpless and wild: 'Please, please, I can't—I can't lose you.' Let your voice break completely, all pretense of control gone, just raw terror and love and the agony of being unable to protect the person you'd die for. End with a whisper that's both fierce promise and desperate hope: 'I won't let you go.'

title: The Last Glass
instruction: You are a man in a dive bar at 2 AM, drunk on cheap whiskey and bitter memories. Across from you sits the person who destroyed your life—your former best friend who betrayed you for a promotion. You've waited three years for this moment. Your hand is unsteady, gripping the glass too tight, and you stare at the condensation instead of their face. You begin with a tremor in your voice, slurred and raw from drink, just muttering to yourself. But as the words come, your tone shifts: the slur smooths into a terrifyingly calm, measured rhythm. You start laughing—a low, wet sound—as you describe how their new boss is your cousin, how you engineered their fall over the last year. By the end, your voice is icy, smiling, each syllable a slow, deliberate knife. 'I've been waiting to tell you this.'
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep, and you're leaving—not because you want to, but because you have no choice. Maybe it's illness, maybe it's danger, maybe you're protecting them by going. You kneel beside their bed, voice so quiet it barely disturbs the air. You start by memorizing them aloud—'your hands are so small'—your voice tender and aching. You tell them things they'll never remember: how proud you are, how every moment mattered. Your voice catches, breaks on a suppressed sob as you whisper the unbearable truth: 'I won't see you grow up.' You steady yourself, breathing through tears, and your voice becomes almost serene as you make them promises about what you hope their life will be. You end with the gentlest 'I love you,' your voice so full of everything you can't say that it barely makes sound.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are a parent sitting at your adult child's bedside in their final hours. They've been holding on, waiting for something from you—permission to let go. Begin with the desperate need to keep them here, your voice tight with the refusal to say goodbye. But as you speak, you realize that love means releasing them from suffering, from fighting. Your voice must journey from fierce, selfish clinging to the most tender, devastating gift of release. End by telling them it's okay to go, that you'll be okay, even though your heart is shattering. Let your voice crack with the unbearable grace of loving someone enough to lose them. This is not loud grief—it's the quiet, sacred sound of a heart breaking open to set someone free.

title: Things I Needed You to Say
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about the words he never said, the presence he never gave. Begin with that same measured, controlled certainty—you've rehearsed this, you know you're right, your grievances are legitimate and clear. But as you list what you needed and never got, something shifts. Beneath the righteous anger, grief starts bleeding through. Your voice wavers between accusation and a child's pleading question: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The contempt you started with dissolves into raw vulnerability. End not with certainty, but with the frightening honesty of admitting you still need him to see you, even now. Let the anger and longing tangle together until you can't tell them apart.

title: Breaking Point and Breaking Through
instruction: You're alone in your car, hands gripping the steering wheel, body shaking with the aftermath of nearly giving up—on your sobriety, your recovery, your commitment to change. Start with your breath ragged, voice cracking with the physical intensity of almost losing everything you've built. But you didn't break. You didn't. Now, with your whole body trembling, speak aloud each specific moment in the past months when you made the harder choice—the phone call you answered, the meeting you dragged yourself to, the night you white-knuckled through instead of surrendering. Feel the emotion move through your entire body: rage at how hard it is, pride that you're still here, exhaustion, exhilaration. Let your voice climb from defeated whisper to fierce, almost ecstatic acknowledgment that you are surviving yourself. End breathless, alive, astonished by your own resilience.

title: The Wall Holds Nothing Back
instruction: You're a young man leaning against the cold brick wall outside a bar, alone on the sidewalk after midnight. A car passes, headlights sweeping across you — your body is still, but your eyes trace its path. You're speaking to a friend on the phone who just asked if you're okay. You start with a bitter, dismissive chuckle, a mask of casual cool, but as you talk about the person who just left you here, your voice cracks, revealing deep sadness. You're genuinely interested in what your friend might say next, but that hope is wrapped in a layer of bitterness. Let your words drift, pause as if losing your train of thought while watching a stray cat slip into the alley, then find your voice again, ending on a quiet, raw confession.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (extremely present), Interest (very intensely present), Bitterness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of the Ring in Your Palm
instruction: You're alone in your bedroom, holding your wedding ring after deciding to leave your marriage. Your mind is initially a cacophony—second-guessing, imagining conversations, fast-forwarding to consequences, rewinding to good memories, arguing with yourself. Your breath is shallow and quick. Slowly, let yourself actually feel the ring: its temperature, weight, the specific way it sits in your palm. Trace its shape. Notice the texture of the sheets beneath you, the quality of light in the room, the sounds filtering in from outside. Whisper the truth of what you feel—not the explanations, not the justifications, just the raw sensation of this moment. Let your racing thoughts dissolve into simple, present awareness. Transform from mental imprisonment to quiet, terrible clarity. Your voice should shift from tight and fractured to soft, steady, and heartbreakingly clear.
inspired_by: Actor experiences mental tension (racing thoughts, fears, mental distractions) even after physical tension has been released

title: The Fever Dream of Coming Home
instruction: You've just returned home after years away, running up the stairs to your childhood bedroom in a state of emotional and physical overwhelm—heart racing, breathless, flooded with sense memories. Begin speaking through gasping breath, touching familiar objects, your voice channeling intense physical sensation mixed with emotional chaos. Let different versions of who you were in this room possess your voice: the innocent child, the heartbroken teenager, the person who fled, the one who swore never to return. Your vocal quality should shift with each memory that crashes over you—sometimes sensual and tender, sometimes choked with rage, sometimes breaking with grief. Build to a moment of full-body emotional release where past and present collide, then settle into an exhausted, transformed quiet. End speaking to your younger self with a mixture of forgiveness and fierce protectiveness you didn't have when you started.

title: Last Words to a Child You'll Never Meet
instruction: You're recording a message for your unborn child, knowing you won't survive to meet them. Your voice starts controlled, almost clinical, trying to be practical about what they should know. But as you continue, the reality crashes over you in waves - you'll never hold them, never see their face, never hear them laugh. Your breath catches. Words fail. You try to give them everything - your love, your hopes, your apologies for leaving - in just a few minutes. The pain isn't physical but existential, and it makes your voice break in unexpected places. End in a place of bittersweet peace, whispering the one thing you hope they'll always remember about you, your voice tender and fading like a lullaby you'll never get to sing.

title: Narrating Joy While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're recording a message describing a beautiful, perfect moment—your child's wedding day, a loved one's recovery, a long-awaited reunion. Your voice is genuinely full of joy and wonder as you describe every detail. But we must hear, underneath, that this moment is also breaking your heart—because you won't be here for the next one, or because this joy came too late, or because the person you most wanted to share it with is gone. Let laughter and tears exist simultaneously in your voice. Express pure gratitude while grief threads through every word. You're not pretending to be happy or sad—you're authentically both, finding beauty in the bittersweetness. End with your voice trembling with contradictory emotions, grateful and devastated in the same breath.

title: The Gratitude Speech Hiding Everything Else
instruction: You're giving a toast or farewell speech honoring someone who is leaving (retiring, moving away, ending a relationship)—someone you have complicated feelings about. Begin with the expected tribute: warm, grateful, emphasizing good memories. Your words are appropriate and loving. But underneath, notice the other emotions you're managing—perhaps anger at being abandoned, jealousy of their freedom, resentment for past hurts, or terror of being left behind. Your challenge is to let these forbidden feelings infiltrate the gracious speech without completely abandoning the genuine gratitude. Can you be grateful AND angry? Loving AND betrayed? Your initial voice is sharp with panic, shouting over the roar of rain and thunder, sputtering as water streams into your mouth. As you duck under a small overhang and tuck the photo safely beneath your coat, your voice shifts from frantic to a trembling, breathless relief. Let your words be broken by shivers, pauses for lightning flashes, and the physical need to wipe rain from your eyes. End with a quiet, shaky whisper of gratitude, the storm still raging around you.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father about a family secret you've just discovered—something they hid from you your entire childhood that has shaped who you are. Begin by staying very controlled, almost formally polite, as if you're afraid of what will happen if you truly let yourself feel. Pay attention to your physical sensations: the tightness in your chest, the way your jaw is clenched, the temperature of your skin. As you speak, let your heightened awareness of your body's signals guide you—notice when your voice wants to crack, when your hands want to shake, when breath becomes difficult. Don't plan your anger or your hurt; instead, stay present to what's actually moving through you moment by moment. Let the confrontation evolve as you become more aware of not just your rage, but the frightened child underneath it. By the end, discover that your acute attention to what you're actually experiencing has transformed your fury into something more complex—perhaps a desperate need to be seen, or a heartbreaking recognition of your parent's own brokenness.

title: Steam-Shocked Discovery
instruction: You are in a sweltering greenhouse, air thick and wet, every breath heavy with moisture. As you wipe sweat from your eyes, you notice a rare orchid blooming suddenly — a species you thought extinct. Astonishment tightens your chest, but as you watch it unfold, the surprise fades into quiet reverence. Speak as if the humidity is coating your words, your voice slightly strained, with wet mouth sounds. Let your initial gasp of wonder soften into a hushed, almost tearful awe.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Confrontation Through Shared Memory
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who left you as a child, and they've just handed you an earbud, trying to reconnect through the song they used to sing to you. Start with ice-cold refusal in your voice: 'I don't want your music.' But as the song begins playing, your resolve cracks — your breathing changes as childhood memories flood back. Begin speaking in fragments, anger building: 'You think a song fixes this? You think—' but then the chorus hits and you break, your voice raw and wounded as you admit how much you've missed them. Let fury and longing war in your delivery: 'I needed you then, not now, not this, not—' Shift to devastating honesty, voice dropping to a pained whisper as you confess you've played this song alone for years, hoping they'd come back. End uncertain, vulnerable: taking the earbud but unable to say whether you forgive them, your 'Thank you' loaded with everything unsaid.
inspired_by: Crowded Subway: Two Strangers Share an Earbud

title: The Last Truth Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed at 4 AM. For years, you've carried a false story about why you left home—a story you told yourself so many times you almost believed it. But now, with hours left, you need to tell her the real reason, the true version you've buried. Begin speaking the lie you've lived with, feeling its hollow familiarity. Then, slowly, let the real story emerge—hesitant, raw, nothing like the polished version. Notice how your voice changes as you move from the comfortable fiction to the uncomfortable truth. End by acknowledging aloud what your life actually is now, not what you pretended it was. Let relief and grief wash over you simultaneously as you speak your authentic reality to her for the first and last time.

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Your Complicated Love
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone you loved deeply and difficultly—a relationship full of beauty and damage. Begin by sharing a genuinely funny memory, letting yourself laugh authentically at the absurdity or joy of it. But mid-laugh, something catches—the realization they're gone, that you'll never get to resolve what was broken between you. Your laughter doesn't stop cleanly; it tangles with tears. Continue trying to celebrate them, voice moving between affection and grief, gratitude and regret. You're smiling through tears, your voice breaking on words like 'brilliant' or 'impossible' or 'irreplaceable.' End in a place where you're thanking them for everything they were, even the painful parts, your voice saturated with the particular ache of loving someone you've lost and can never fully make peace with.
inspired_by: Recounting Trauma to a Stranger Therapist

title: Hollow Hello
instruction: You are a child in a full gas mask during a safety drill. The mask is tight, your voice sounds hollow and mechanical, and every breath is a loud, Darth Vader-like hiss. You see your crush across the room and your heart leaps with infatuation — you wave, shout a greeting, but then you notice the mask is fogging, the filter smells stale, and you realize how monstrous you sound. Your excitement crumbles into shame and disgust as you think about how ridiculous you must look. Speak with breathy, muffled urgency at first, then trail off into quieter, embarrassed mumbles as you become self-conscious.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Disgust (slightly present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent, finally saying what you've held inside for decades. Start with trembling restraint—you came here to stay calm, to be adult about this, but your voice is already shaking with suppressed hurt. Build into sharp, cutting accusations, each word a knife you've sharpened for years: 'You were never there when I needed you.' Let your voice break between anger and the child inside you still desperate for their love. Collapse into raw vulnerability mid-sentence, your rage dissolving into tears you hate yourself for crying. Finish in a place of devastating honesty, your voice small and broken: 'I just wanted you to see me.' The journey moves from controlled fury to the vulnerable child underneath, exposing the wounded heart beneath years of armor.

title: Wasted Breath on a Foreigner
instruction: You're a 17-year-old with a deep, rough voice, forced to take English tutoring from a non-native speaker. You sit slumped in a chair, arms crossed, eyes rolling. You start by mocking their accent with bitter teasing—speaking slowly, too loud, stripping your sentences to simple words with deliberate gaps. Halfway through, you notice their patient, unbothered expression. Your bitterness cracks; you trail off, lose your train of thought, then mutter a quieter, unsure question that reveals you actually want to learn but hate admitting it. Let your voice shift from aggressive caricature to an embarrassed mumble, with a long pause where you scratch your neck and look away.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What You Never Asked
instruction: You're confronting your mother/father about a pattern that shaped your entire life—they never asked what you actually wanted, only told you what you should want. Start with controlled anger, voice tight: 'You never once asked me...' But as you speak, the anger cracks open to reveal the child underneath who desperately needed to be seen. Your voice shifts from accusation to pleading to something rawer—the pain of someone who learned to silence their own desires to keep a parent's love. They finally ask: 'What did you want?' Now you must answer, and the words feel both dangerous and necessary. End with your voice carrying the trembling courage of someone speaking a truth that might destroy or heal everything.

title: Confidence Presence
instruction: You're a negotiator in a hostage situation, and your voice is calm, confident, completely present: 'My name is David. I'm here to help.' Every word lands. There's no doubt, no fear bleeding through. 'I know you're scared. That's okay.' Your confidence isn't arrogance; it's complete presence. 'I'm not going anywhere. We're going to figure this out together.' The person on the other end starts to cry. Your voice doesn't change — it remains a steady presence: 'You're safe now. I've got you.' By the end, the person has lowered the weapon, and your presence is the only thing that made that possible. The confidence is what saved them.

title: The Last Drop
instruction: You are a teenage girl in a drought-stricken region, severely dehydrated for days. Your throat is raw, your lips stick together, and each word takes effort. You watch a relief worker give the last bottle of water to a younger child instead of you. Start with a hoarse, almost broken plea—'Please, I need it more'—but as you speak, the unfairness sinks in, envy flickering beneath exhaustion. Let your voice crack, pause to swallow painfully, and end with a quiet, bitter realization that you won't get any. Include the sticky lip sounds and tongue clicks of a parched mouth. The emotion shifts from desperate hope to resigned jealousy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, voice steady and rehearsed as you finally tell your mother the truth about how her absence shaped you. Start controlled, almost clinical—listing the school plays she missed, the nights you waited. But as she begins to defend herself with the same old excuses, your voice hardens into something sharp and unforgiving: 'I was a child. I needed you, and you chose everything else.' Feel the rage building, decades of it, until you're shouting things you swore you'd never say. Then she breaks—really breaks—and suddenly you see her not as the invincible mother but as a fragile, flawed human who was drowning too. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it transforms into something more complex: fury mixed with unwanted compassion, the devastating realization that she was doing her broken best. End with your voice raw, uncertain, caught between the child who needed her and the adult who understands her.
inspired_by: Roller Coaster Mechanical Failure: Moment of Absolute Stillness

title: Specimen Study: Confronting Your Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're using the detached, analytical voice of a nature documentary to emotionally distance yourself while finally telling your absent parent exactly how their neglect affected you. 'Here we observe the maternal figure, exhibiting classic avoidance behaviors when confronted with offspring's emotional needs.' Start with bitter, sarcastic scientific detachment as protection. But as you catalogue each missed birthday, each broken promise, the clinical facade becomes harder to maintain. Your voice shifts from mocking distance to raw anger, then unexpectedly into vulnerable longing: 'Why wasn't I worth staying for?' End in quiet devastation, the documentary voice completely abandoned, just you asking the question you've always needed answered.
inspired_by: Nature Documentary Voice for Your Roommate's Morning Routine

title: Aftermath in the Garage
instruction: You're a 17-year-old who just pulled your friend from a crashed car. Now you're sitting on the garage floor, back against a tool bench, hands shaking so bad you can't hold the phone steady. You're trying to describe what happened to your mom on the phone, but your voice keeps cracking and you keep laughing in disbelief that you're alive. Start with concentration—you're forcing yourself to speak clearly, counting fingers to stay present. Then astonishment hits as you replay the sound of metal and glass. End with amusement, a breathless giggle about how the airbag smelled like burnt popcorn, even as tears run down your face. Let your voice tremble, repeat phrases, break off mid-sentence.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Amusement (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: You Promised
instruction: You're in a coffee shop, still holding your cup, and you just saw your best friend kiss your ex. Now she's walking toward you, alone. Start with a quiet, breathless disbelief—your voice is soft, almost a whisper, as you say, 'I saw you. With him.' You explain that she knew how much that would hurt. Then, as she tries to defend herself, your voice cracks, rising in pitch, and you interrupt with fragmented accusations, circling back to the betrayal. End with a raw, trembling disappointment—your eyes wet, your hands shaking the cup slightly. Let the initial stunned, hyper-feminized tone slowly shatter into anger and finally into a sad, quiet realization: 'I really thought you were different.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're standing at a scenic overlook where your absent parent once promised to take you as a child. Start with bitter sarcasm, describing the 'beautiful view' they said you'd see together, your voice dripping with decades of disappointment. Build into anger—call out specific moments they missed, your voice rising as you list the sunsets, the birthdays, the graduations they chose to skip. Let that rage crack open into the vulnerable child underneath, your voice breaking as you ask why you were never enough. Shift into exhausted honesty, admitting you're here alone, watching this sunset, finally letting go of waiting for them. End with a strange, painful freedom—describing the colors as truly yours now, not theirs, your voice steadying into something like peace mixed with irrevocable loss.
inspired_by: Watching the Sunset Over the Ocean

title: Grateful Goodbye: Laughing Through Tears at Your Beloved's Wake
instruction: You're delivering an impromptu eulogy for someone you loved deeply—mentor, best friend, partner—and you're determined not to be solemn because they would have hated that. Begin with a story that makes you laugh—genuinely laugh—and your voice is bright with the memory. 'They once...' and you can barely get through it. But the laughter keeps breaking into tears, and the tears into laughter, until you can't tell them apart anymore. Your voice cracks as you realize you're talking about them in past tense. 'They were...' and you have to stop. The pain is physical. But then another memory surfaces and you're laughing again, even as tears run down your face. 'God, they would be so annoyed at us for crying.' Your voice is thick with contradictory emotions: joy at having known them, devastation at losing them, gratitude so profound it hurts. Your final words are both celebration and heartbreak: 'Thank you. For everything. For being exactly who you were.' The transformation is from bitter-sweet reminiscence to overwhelming grief to profound, painful gratitude.
inspired_by: Extreme Altitude Climb: Lucidity Breaking Down in the Death Zone

title: Veteran Memory Triggered
instruction: You're a veteran at a fireworks show, and the loud noises suddenly transport you to combat. Your voice becomes rapid, panicked: 'Get down! Get down!' You're in full combat mode, calling out to soldiers who aren't there. 'Cover the left flank!' The trauma is live in your voice. Someone touches your shoulder, and your voice becomes dangerous: 'Don't touch me!' Slowly, you return to the present. Your voice becomes shaky, embarrassed: 'I'm... I'm okay. I'm here.' But you're not okay. Your voice is trembling: 'I thought... for a second, I was back there.' The civilian tries to comfort you, and your voice cracks: 'Thank you. I'm sorry. It just... happens sometimes.' You excuse yourself, and your voice becomes small, defeated: 'I hate this. I hate that I can't just watch fireworks like a normal person.'

title: Spoonful of Thanks
instruction: You are a rugged construction worker nursing a throbbing jaw after a tooth extraction, sitting in a diner booth across from your 6-year-old daughter. She keeps insisting you taste her pudding because it's 'magic medicine.' Through the dull ache, you're touched by her seriousness. Speak as you actually eat a spoonful of soft pudding—your mouth half-full, tongue busy, words smudged and wet. Start with a weary grunt of pain as you shift in the seat, then let a chuckle escape at her determined face. As you swallow, feel the gratitude flood in—say your last line with raw tenderness, voice cracked but full, the pain now a backdrop to this moment.
emotions_sampled: Pain (clearly present), Amusement (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Over the Shoulder, Out of Reach
instruction: You are at a crowded café, twisted in your seat, looking over your right shoulder at someone who just passed your table. Your neck is strained, craning to keep them in view as they walk away. Let the physical tension feed your words: start with a sharp, sour edge—resentment at a betrayal that still stings. Midway, let the sourness crack as doubt creeps in, your voice becoming softer, more uncertain, as if you're questioning your own memory. Speak naturally, with pauses where you lose your train of thought, shift your weight, or wince from the strain. End with a quieter, almost vulnerable admission of doubt.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Ghost in the Mirror
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about how their past lover—someone who was never acknowledged, never spoken about—shaped your entire childhood. You found old letters, photographs, evidence of a passion they buried. Start with accusations: you're angry at the lies, the silence, the way this hidden romance cast shadows over your whole life. But as you speak, let sensory details emerge—perhaps you remember a perfume that lingered, a song that played, a name whispered in sleep. Your anger must crack open into something more complex: you begin to see them as a full person who loved desperately, who sacrificed, who hurt. Move from rage to unexpected empathy, your voice shifting from sharp attacks to vulnerable questions, ending in a quiet plea to finally know the truth of who they really were.

title: Midnight Accounting
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner, whispering to yourself in the dark. You're plagued by insecurity about whether you're enough for them—interesting enough, accomplished enough, worthy of their love. Start in a place of quiet desperation, voice barely audible, listing your perceived failures and inadequacies. But then, force yourself to do the opposite: whisper a true inventory of what you actually bring—the ways you've shown up, the kindnesses you've offered, the growth you've undergone, the specific talents and knowledge you possess. Let each whispered truth land differently than the fears did. Feel your breathing change as you speak. By the end, arrive at a fragile but genuine peace, still vulnerable but no longer drowning. The transformation is from self-erasure to quiet self-recognition, all in the intimate darkness.

title: The Accusation: Screaming Truth at Someone You Love
instruction: Confront someone who betrayed you—a partner, best friend, family member. Explode from silence. Your rage is righteous, volcanic: 'How COULD you?' Demand answers, your voice ragged and loud. List every lie, every moment you trusted them like a fool. Let your fury peak—you could destroy them with words right now. But mid-accusation, your voice cracks. The anger collapses into something more devastating: hurt. You loved them. You STILL love them, and that's the part that's killing you. Dissolve from shouting into sobbing: 'I would have forgiven anything if you'd just been honest.' End in helpless whisper, the rage burned out, leaving only the wound: 'Why wasn't I enough for the truth?' Feel the terrible coexistence of love and betrayal.
inspired_by: Veterinarian Delivering Bad News: Professional and Breaking

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with a parent who abandoned you years ago, and they've come back expecting forgiveness. Begin with your voice cold, controlled, almost clinical—reciting facts: 'You left when I was seven. You missed my graduation. You weren't there.' Keep your armor up, voice steady, refusing to give them your pain. Then let anger seep in, voice rising, words becoming sharper: 'Do you know what that did to me? Do you even care?' Build to a breaking point where rage cracks into the grief underneath—voice shattering on 'I needed you' or 'I was just a kid.' Let yourself collapse into the wounded child, voice small and broken, before pulling yourself back together with enormous effort. End not with forgiveness or rage, but with exhausted truth, voice hollow and finally honest: tell them exactly what their absence cost you, speaking from a place beyond anger, almost gentle in its devastation.

title: The Moment After
instruction: You've just received the phone call you've been dreading for months—the all-clear from your doctor. The cancer is gone. You're cured. But instead of pure joy, you start laughing—hysterical, almost manic laughter: 'I'm going to live. I'm actually going to—' Then you're sobbing while still laughing. 'I gave everything away. I said all my goodbyes.' Your voice cracks between laughter and tears. 'I made peace with dying. I was READY.' Now the tears overtake the laughter, but there's strange joy in them: 'What do I do now? I have a future again and I don't know—' You're crying hard but smiling. 'I get to see my grandchildren grow up. I get to grow old.' The gratitude is overwhelming: 'Thank you. Thank you.' But there's also grief: 'I lost a year of my life to fear.' Your voice finds something transcendent: 'But maybe... maybe that year taught me everything. How to be alive. How to love without holding back.' You're laughing and crying simultaneously: 'I'm free. Not from cancer. From being afraid to live.'

title: Reading the Letter That Changes Everything
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter from someone who meant the world to you—someone who has died, or left, or whom you'll never see again. The letter contains unexpected revelations: perhaps they always knew a secret you kept, or they're apologizing for something you'd already forgiven, or they're expressing a love you never knew existed. As you read their words in your voice, let your emotions become beautifully tangled—laughing through tears at a joke they made, voice breaking with gratitude while your heart shatters, finding profound peace even as grief overwhelms you. The joy of being understood and the agony of it coming too late must coexist in every phrase. By the end, you should sound like someone who has been both destroyed and made whole by the same truth.
inspired_by: Acting Enthusiastic About Plans Youd Rather Avoid

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's bedside in her final hours. She's unconscious, but you need to tell her something you've been too afraid to say your entire life—something about who you really are that you feared would disappoint her. Begin with that familiar childhood fear in your throat, the tightness that kept you silent at family dinners for decades. Speak to her now, letting that fear dissolve as you realize she can't judge you anymore, only love you. Let your voice transform from tight and apologetic to clear and self-accepting. End by thanking her for something unexpected—perhaps for creating the very strength you needed to become yourself, even if she never knew it. Feel the weight lift as you say goodbye not to her approval, but to your need for it.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake but fading, and you both know this is goodbye. Start by truly seeing her—the way the early light catches the silver in her hair, the pattern of her breathing, the temperature of her hand in yours. Let yourself be completely absorbed in these details, in her physical presence in this moment. Begin speaking from a place of wanting to give her comfort, to make her laugh one last time with a shared memory. But as you talk, let yourself stop performing strength. Let the reality of losing her move through you—the gratitude for who she's been, the crushing awareness that she won't be here tomorrow, the desperate wish to hold onto this moment. Your voice should move from gentle steadiness to something breaking open, raw and unguarded.
inspired_by: Actor is compensating — imposing a relaxed demeanor over real tension, or substituting one emotion for another that feels more acceptable

title: Dancing Alone at Your Ex's Wedding
instruction: You're at your ex-partner's wedding—the person you thought you'd marry—and you've stayed for the reception out of some masochistic need for closure. During a slow song, you stand alone on the edge of the dance floor, talking to yourself, laughing softly at the absurdity of being here. Your voice should shimmer between genuine happiness for them and personal devastation. Describe the beauty of how happy they look, laughing through tears, celebrating their joy while your heart shatters. Express real gratitude that they found this love, even as you grieve what you lost. End with a whispered toast to them, your voice full of bittersweet peace: 'You deserve this.' Let the laughter and crying become indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Haunted House Actor Who Takes It Too Seriously

title: The Truth About Why I Left
instruction: You are confronting the mentor who abandoned you twenty years ago—your parent, teacher, or the person who raised you. Start with carefully controlled anger, words you've rehearsed a thousand times, accusations delivered with precision. But as you speak, something cracks: beneath your rage is a child who still desperately wants their approval, who still wonders if they were ever good enough. Your voice must betray you—let the anger dissolve into something more vulnerable, more honest. Accuse them of the damage they caused, then hear yourself asking the question you swore you'd never ask: 'Did you ever actually love me?' End in a place of exhausted honesty, where you're no longer performing your anger but simply revealing the wound that never healed. Your voice should move from righteous fury to broken-hearted confusion to something approaching fragile understanding.

title: The Last Cup
instruction: You are an elderly person washing dishes while sitting at a sink, lost in thought. The constant rush of water and sharp clinks of glass fill the room. Start with a low, grumbling tone — mildly irritated at having to do this chore, but your mind drifts to a memory of a friend from decades ago. Midway, your fingers find a small crack in a cup you haven't noticed before, and a sudden, quiet astonishment hits you — a forgotten moment from that friendship floods back. Your voice should shift from a tired, grouchy mutter to a softer, breathless wonder, as if discovering something precious in the mundane. Let the water sounds be a backdrop, and let your words pause naturally when a dish slips or when you need to wipe your hands.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Controlled Chaos
instruction: You're confronting your parent who meticulously planned every aspect of your childhood - every lesson, every friend playdate, every 'spontaneous' family moment was scheduled. Begin with cold, measured anger as you list specific moments they stole from you, your voice tight and controlled like theirs always was. Let your rage build as you describe how you've become them - you now schedule when to be happy, when to relax, when to feel. But then, mid-sentence, let something break: admit in a completely different voice, small and desperate, that you're terrified of living any other way. End torn between fury at them and fury at yourself, your voice raw and unguarded.

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by telling her about yesterday—what you had for breakfast, the weather, small mundane details—your voice steady but hollow. Then let yourself drift backward through time: last week's family dinner, last month's phone call you almost didn't answer, last year's argument you never resolved. As you move further back through the years, your voice should break open, revealing all the things you've carried but never said. End in the distant past of your childhood, when she taught you something simple—how to tie your shoes, how to crack an egg—and let gratitude, grief, and desperate love pour out in equal measure. The emotion must travel from numb detachment to raw, unguarded heartbreak.
inspired_by: Actor cannot remember early childhood memories that might be relevant to their work

title: Mirror Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your mother about why she taught you to minimize your own pain, to always explain away mistreatment, to make yourself small. Begin with the pattern you learned: 'You showed me how to survive by accepting less.' Your voice carries all the years of watching her do the same thing. But then the anger rises—not loud, but sharp and clear. You're showing her what she handed down, how her survival strategy became your prison. By the end, there's a painful tenderness mixed with fury: you understand why she did it, you see her wounds, but you're also drawing a line. You're breaking the inheritance. Your voice must hold both the love for her and the refusal to continue the cycle.

title: Screaming at the Ocean After Scattering Your Spouse's Ashes
instruction: You're alone on the beach where you scattered their ashes an hour ago. You held it together for the funeral, for the family, for everyone. But now you're alone and something inside you detonates. Start with a scream—wordless, primal, raw. Let it rip out of you. Then words come, and they're furious: 'How DARE you leave me! We had PLANS!' Your voice is ragged, almost unrecognizable. You're yelling at the waves, at the sky, at them: 'You PROMISED we'd grow old together!' The rage is absolute. You might be crying, but the tears feel hot, angry. Then suddenly the fury collapses. Your voice breaks completely and you're on your knees in the sand, voice reduced to a broken whisper: 'I don't know how to be without you.' The admission devastates you. 'I don't know who I am without you.' End with something that's both rage and love, helplessness and fierce devotion—voice shaking but fierce: 'I hate you for leaving. And I'd give anything for one more day. God, just one more day.'
inspired_by: Herding People to Basement Safety While Tornado Sirens Wail

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about the childhood you needed but never had. Begin with carefully chosen words, the speech you've rehearsed a thousand times, your voice controlled and almost clinical as you list the facts of your loneliness. But as you speak, old anger rises—your voice sharpens, becomes accusatory, years of suppressed rage breaking through. Then something shifts: you hear how small your own voice sounds, how much you still sound like a child begging to be seen. The anger collapses into raw grief. Your voice cracks, becomes pleading, vulnerable in a way you swore you'd never be again. By the end, you're not attacking anymore—you're simply asking, with heartbreaking honesty, 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let your voice carry the full journey from rehearsed strength to volcanic anger to the kind of vulnerability that terrifies you.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about the childhood they couldn't give you—not with rehearsed accusations, but with raw, messy truth spilling out after years of silence. Begin hesitantly, your voice small and apologetic, still the child seeking approval even as you try to voice pain. But let something crack open: feel anger rise, words becoming sharper, louder, more demanding. Then—unexpectedly—let that anger fracture into something else. Your voice breaks not with rage but with the grief of a child who needed them and they weren't there. End in a place of exhausted honesty, quieter now, where blame dissolves into the simple, heartbreaking truth: 'I just needed you to see me.'

title: Honeymoon Photographs at Midnight
instruction: It's 2 a.m. and you can't sleep. You've pulled out photographs from your honeymoon—the happiest week of your life, ten years ago. Begin speaking to your sleeping partner in barely audible whispers, describing one perfect moment: sunrise on a beach, their hand in yours, feeling invincible together. Let your voice carry the tenderness of that memory, the softness of new love, the certainty you felt. As you relive the sensations—warm sand, salt air, their skin against yours—allow a fragile realization to surface: you can't remember the last time you felt that way together. Your whisper should become even quieter, more careful, as fear creeps in. Describe trying to hold onto the memory, to feel what you felt then, but sensing it slip away like water through fingers. End with a trembling question you don't actually voice aloud: whether that version of your love still exists, or if you're mourning something already gone. Stay in the whisper throughout—this is too tender, too frightening to say at full volume.

title: Breaking Point: Discovering Your Child Has Been Harmed and You Weren't There
instruction: You've just learned what happened to your child while you were away, and rage ignites like a wildfire. Start with your voice tight, dangerous, demanding details—each word a barely controlled weapon. The fury builds: you want to destroy whoever did this, your voice becomes almost feral with protective violence. But then your child looks at you with fear—not of what happened, but of YOUR rage—and you shatter completely. Your voice breaks into desperate, gasping sobs. You failed them. You weren't there. The protective rage collapses into helpless anguish. You're trying to hold them while falling apart, voice raw and childlike, apologizing through tears. Then something primal emerges: a fierce, whispered promise that's both tender and terrifying. You will never, ever let this happen again. Your voice becomes stone wrapped in velvet—absolute love fused with unshakeable resolve. End with the sound of someone who has just discovered the depth of their own capacity for both violence and devotion.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Time Traveler Realizes They're Trying to Prevent Their Own Birth

title: Screaming Into the Ruins Where Your Child Disappeared
instruction: You're standing in the wreckage of the evacuation center where you last saw your seven-year-old, and you're calling their name—first with control, then louder, then screaming with everything you have. Your voice cracks between their name and raw, wordless rage at the universe. You're yelling at rescue workers who left, at yourself for hesitating that crucial second, at God or fate or the cruel randomness that took them. Your fury is so fierce it's almost prayer, demanding the rubble give them back, commanding time to reverse. But the rage keeps fracturing—you collapse mid-scream into sobbing their name like a question, then surge back into protective ferocity, as if the force of your voice could still shield them. You describe what they were wearing, what their laugh sounds like, the gap in their front teeth, speaking faster and louder as if volume equals certainty they're alive. By the end, you're hoarse and broken, oscillating between threatening the ruins and pleading with them, your voice simultaneously the roar of a parent who would tear apart worlds and the whisper of someone who knows they're screaming into emptiness.

title: The Museum of You
instruction: You are confronting your parent who is from a culture different from the one you grew up in. For years, they refused to teach you their language, share their traditions, or connect you to your heritage, believing assimilation was protection. You've just returned from traveling to their homeland alone, and you're filled with rage at everything you had to discover by yourself—the history, the food, the family members who thought you'd abandoned them. Begin with hot anger and accusation: 'You made me a stranger to half of myself.' But as you describe what you learned and experienced, your anger cracks open to reveal a deeper pain—the loneliness of growing up incomplete, and underneath that, a longing for them to finally share their world with you. End not with anger but with an invitation, vulnerable and uncertain: 'It's not too late. Teach me. Please.'

title: Final Letter to Your Child Before the Memory Goes
instruction: You're recording a video message for your adult child, knowing Alzheimer's will soon erase you completely. You've practiced what you wanted to say—life lessons, apologies, pride—but as you speak, you keep forgetting why certain memories matter, then suddenly remembering with devastating clarity. Start with determined composure, trying to sound wise and parental. Midway through, lose your train of thought, panic quietly, then recover by focusing on their face in your mind. End by forgetting what you were trying to say entirely, but managing to whisper the one thing that matters most—something raw and unplanned that surprises even you. Let your voice move from controlled to fractured to heartbreakingly simple.
inspired_by: Poet Reading Their Work at an Open Mic — for Their Ex in the Audience

title: Burning the Inheritance
instruction: You are physically destroying something precious that was left to you by someone who also deeply wounded you - tearing pages from a treasured book, breaking a family heirloom, burning letters. Begin with violent, righteous anger - make guttural sounds of rage, let your breath come hard and fast, let fury live fully in your body and voice. Feel the savage satisfaction of destruction, the physical release. But as your body tires and your breathing begins to slow, let grief start to seep through the cracks. Your movements become less violent, more anguished. The rage transforms into wracking sobs - not neat crying, but the kind that bends you double, that makes ugly sounds. By the end, you're spent, sitting among the wreckage, and in that exhaustion finds something unexpected: relief. Not forgiveness, but release. Your final sounds should be of someone who has survived something, raw but somehow lighter.
inspired_by: When you are coaching or directing an actor whose work is limited by damaged self-esteem or psychological blocks rather than craft ignorance

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: Someone you love fiercely—your sibling, your best friend, your child—is destroying themselves and you've tried everything. Your voice erupts with frustrated rage: 'Why won't you let me help you?!' You're shouting, furious, desperate, almost violent in your need to fix this. Your voice is raw with accusations, with love twisted into anger. But mid-sentence, something shifts. You hear yourself and you stop. Your voice drops, and the rage collapses into broken helplessness. 'I can't save you.' The words come out quiet, devastated. You're crying now, your voice shaking with the unbearable realization that love isn't enough. 'I can't save you and it's killing me.' The fierce protectiveness dissolves into grief. Your voice becomes small, defeated: 'I love you so much and I can't save you.' End with your voice carrying the impossible contradiction—the fierce love still burning even as you accept your own powerlessness, strength and complete surrender existing in the same breath.
inspired_by: Hit Rock Bottom: Finding the Learning

title: The Breaking Point: Parent Realizes They've Failed Their Addicted Child
instruction: Your adult child just overdosed—they survived, but barely. You're alone in your car in the hospital parking lot, and everything you've held together for years explodes. Start with shaking rage at them, at yourself, at God—your voice is raw and loud and fierce. You're screaming accusations, pounding the steering wheel. Then it shifts: the rage cracks and underneath is devastating helplessness. Your voice breaks into something small and lost. You're begging no one and everyone. All your protection, your rules, your love—none of it was enough. Move through fury to fragility to something like bargaining. End in exhausted collapse, your voice barely a whisper, still talking to them even though they're not there, saying the things you couldn't say in the hospital room. Let yourself shatter completely.
inspired_by: Historical: Underground Railroad Conductor Hides Escaped Slaves From Pursuers

title: Trying to Let You In
instruction: You are an older woman receiving oral sex from a partner you genuinely care for, but your mind keeps drifting to all the times you’ve felt let down by love. You start with a coherent, grateful whisper, but as sensation builds, your words break apart — you’re fighting both your body’s pleasure and a hollow sadness. Let your voice rise in pitch, fragments interrupt your sentences, and your breaths sharpen. End with a long, melodic moan that holds a final soft ‘thank you’ — sounding truly thankful yet haunted by the disappointment you can’t fully shake.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Sadness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Rehab
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside your child's bed, whispering a confession they can't hear because they're asleep—and because you're leaving for a 90-day treatment program in five hours. Your voice should be barely audible, catching on every other word. Tell them you're sorry for the times you weren't present, for the birthday you forgot, for the fear in their eyes. Let tenderness and shame intertwine until they're inseparable. Confess that you're terrified—terrified of failing again, terrified that even if you get better it might be too late, terrified that they'll grow up and choose not to forgive you. Your breath should shake. End with a promise you desperately want to keep but aren't sure you can, your voice breaking into something between a prayer and a plea: that you'll come back as the parent they deserve.
inspired_by: Wedding Toast While Secretly in Love with the Bride

title: The Sound of Loneliness: A Night Alone
instruction: Narrate the tiny sounds of an evening alone. The fridge humming. The click of a light switch. Talking to a pet or a plant. Scrolling sounds. A sigh. Trying to decide what to eat and giving up. The voice should be quiet, unperformed, completely private — this is how you sound when absolutely no one can hear you. Not sad necessarily, but honest. Include the moment you hear a sound and hope it's someone at the door. It's not. Return to the small sounds.

title: The Dance Floor Watcher
