instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy at a house party, drunk on cheap beer. You're leaning against a wall, watching the girl you've liked for months slow-dance with a loud, confident guy. A bitter envy twists in your chest, but it's muffled by the haze of alcohol. Every few seconds, a sharp shout or a repeated word bursts out of you—a tic you can't control—and you talk right through it as if it didn't happen. Start with a jealous, slurred mutter about how unfair it is, then let the words trail off into a quieter, more exhausted resignation as you realize nothing you say will change anything.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The High Note
instruction: You're shaving in the bathroom mirror, electric razor buzzing against your jaw, triumph pulsing in your chest because you just landed the lead vocal part in a band your rival coveted. As you stretch your neck to get the stubble under your chin, your phone buzzes: it's a text from that rival, congratulating you with a photo of them with the old lead singer. A twinge of jealousy flickers through — you see their easy chemistry, the way they effortlessly fit. You answer the text out loud as you shave, your voice shifting through the razor's distortion, starting with giddy laughter and pride, then softening to a quieter, more complicated note of admiration and just a hint of envy, before the buzz cuts back in and you return to your own solid, triumphant grin.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Rocking a Secret
instruction: You are an older man holding your newborn grandchild for the first time, but you’ve just learned your son isn’t the biological father. Alone in the nursery, you rock the baby gently, your voice hushed and rhythmic from the motion, but your hand trembles. Start with overwhelming fear—shock makes you nearly drop the baby. As you settle into the rocking, a slight shame surfaces for that thought. Let your voice shift from a panicked whisper to a fragile tenderness, still uneven, as you murmur to the infant. Speak naturally: the rocking affects your breath, your chest is compressed, and you pause mid-sentence to adjust your hold.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Signal from the Station
instruction: You're an astronaut on a failing space station, and you've just sent your crewmate—the person you secretly love—down in the only escape pod. You're recording your final transmission to mission control, knowing they're listening too. Start with forced calm, trying to sound professional, but your voice cracks as you report systems failures. Your words become softer, more personal—you're no longer talking to control, you're talking to them. Let gratitude wash over you as you thank them for every shared moment, but underneath it all is the growing terror of suffocation as oxygen depletes. Your breathing becomes labored. End with a whisper that's both peaceful acceptance and unbearable longing—you wanted more time. Let your voice fade as if dissolving into the void.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally facing the parent who abandoned you in childhood. Begin with controlled anger, each word carefully measured: 'Do you have any idea what you did to me?' Your voice is hard, defensive. But as you speak, the adult armor starts cracking, revealing the wounded child underneath. The anger shifts to desperate questioning: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me?' Your voice becomes younger, more vulnerable. By the end, you're exhausted, stripped bare, asking the question you've never been able to voice: 'Did you ever love me at all?' Let yourself move from fury to fragility, from accusation to the raw need for an answer you've carried your whole life.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent what their absence cost you. Begin calm, almost clinical—'I need to say something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, decades of swallowed hurt rises up. Your voice shakes with controlled fury: 'I was seven years old and you missed every single thing that mattered.' Let anger break into something more vulnerable—the child's voice underneath. 'I just wanted you to see me.' End not with resolution but with exhausted truth: 'I needed you.' Transform from cold composure to the ache of a lifetime of invisibility.

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission Home
instruction: You're drifting away from Earth after a catastrophic mission failure. Oxygen is running low. Record your final message to the person you love most, who will receive this months after you're gone. Start with practical instructions about your affairs, your voice steady and controlled. But as you realize this is truly goodbye forever, let the professional veneer crack. Tell them the things you never said—your regrets, your gratitude, the moment you knew you loved them. Your breath grows shorter, not just from oxygen loss but from the weight of never seeing them again. End with a whispered declaration that's part love letter, part prayer, knowing these are the last words of yours they'll ever hear.
inspired_by: The Last Human Speaking to an Empty World

title: The Hollow Dismissal
instruction: You're an older man stuck in a long, tedious meeting. You feel a yawn building—your jaw tightens, but you can't stop it. As the yawn crests, you begin to speak, your voice dropping in pitch and sounding hollow, rounded, almost mocking. You are replying to a younger colleague who has just made an overly earnest suggestion. Start with the yawn interfering mid-word, your tone carrying a mixture of tiredness and mild contempt. As you finish the sentence, let the yawn subside and your contempt sharpen into a dry, dismissive finality—as if you've already decided their idea is worthless.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed, knowing you won't see them grow up. Begin speaking softly but with absolute certainty about who they are, what they mean to you, the truths about their character you've observed. Your voice is quiet but unshakeable at first—these are facts, observations, promises. But as you continue, the certainty becomes harder to maintain. Your throat tightens. The controlled breathing turns ragged. The steady statements fracture into whispered fragments. By the end, you're barely speaking, trying so hard not to sob that your words become tiny, broken sounds. The unwavering truth becomes a tender, devastating confession of love mixed with the unbearable grief of leaving. Let the transformation be gradual, intimate, heartbreaking—from certainty to barely-held-together goodbye.

title: Confronting Your Mother: The Love You Rationed
instruction: You're finally telling your mother the truth she's avoided for decades: she showed your sibling unconditional love while making you earn every scrap of affection. Begin with measured, careful words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm and adult. But as you speak, old wounds open. Your voice starts to shake with barely-contained rage: 'You hugged them freely. I had to be perfect to get a smile.' Let anger give way to the raw pain underneath—the voice of the child who couldn't understand why they weren't enough. End in a place of exhausted vulnerability, almost whispering: 'I just wanted you to love me the way I was.' Include a moment where you wait for her response, and the silence crushes you.
inspired_by: Confession from a Parent: We Gave Up on You

title: The Conspiracy Theorist Barista
instruction: Act as a barista who shares wild conspiracy theories with customers. Use a hushed, intense tone when revealing secrets about the origin of coffee beans, switching to a cheerful voice when taking orders, creating a humorous contrast.

title: Crouched in the Dark
instruction: You are wedged into a tight attic crawlspace after a bitter argument with your partner, knees pressed to your chest and the roof beam digging into your back. You feel a heavy shame burning in your stomach for the things you said, mixed with a quiet sadness that things got this bad. At first your voice is a strained, breathy whisper as you mutter apologies to yourself, hunching tighter with each word. But as the silence stretches, the shame curdles into hot anger — you realize they pushed you, they cornered you — and your words turn sharp and bitter, spitting through gritted teeth. Let your shoulders stay hunched, your neck short, and let the anger build until your voice cracks with fury.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Shame (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing Through the Final Instructions
instruction: You're teaching your best friend something absurdly simple—how to work your coffee maker, how to water your plants, the quirks of your apartment—because they'll be taking care of your place, your life, after you're gone. You both agreed to keep this light, even funny. You're making jokes about your terrible handwriting on the instruction notes, laughing at how many steps it takes to work your ridiculous shower. But the laughter keeps catching in your throat. Your friend keeps messing up on purpose to make you laugh harder, and you love them so fiercely for it. Start playful and instructional with genuine giggles. Let moments of grief break through that you quickly cover with more jokes. End with both of you laughing and crying at once, still pretending to focus on whether the thermostat needs to be at 68 or 70 degrees, while really saying goodbye. Your voice should dance between joy, instruction, tears, and laughter—all genuine, all simultaneous, all heartbreaking.

title: The Fever Dream
instruction: You're in the grip of both intense physical illness (high fever, violent chills, body pain) and overwhelming emotional news you just received—someone you love is coming back, or has betrayed you, or has forgiven you. Let your body and voice express both the physical torment and the emotional earthquake simultaneously. Begin with your physical sensations dominating—groaning, shaking, gasping—but as you speak about the emotional situation, allow the two experiences to merge and amplify each other. Your fever makes you more raw, more honest, less defended. Let your voice break, become hoarse, whisper, or cry out. Allow the physical vulnerability to crack open emotional places you normally keep locked. Move from primarily physical suffering to a state where you can't distinguish between body pain and heart pain—where they become one overwhelming experience. End in either complete surrender or unexpected catharsis.
inspired_by: Actor cannot be genuinely emotionally affected by stimuli (impressive block)

title: The Other Girl's Shoes
instruction: You are a young woman being questioned by a stern detective about a crime you didn't commit, but your mind keeps drifting to your rival — the girl who always gets everything. The detective's silence is a weapon. You start by nervously hedging, avoiding eye contact, fidgeting with a loose thread. As you speak about your rival, your voice shifts from shaky defensiveness to a raw, bitter admission of envy. The jealousy leaks through your words, and by the end, you're almost crying with frustration — not at the detective, but at your own longing for what she has. Let your voice crack, trail off, and return with a weak, honest edge.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Wrong Side of the Funeral
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who hurt you deeply, but whom you also loved impossibly. You start with the expected formalities, voice steady: 'We're here to remember...' but then a laugh escapes—inappropriate, real. 'I'm sorry, I just—he would have hated this.' Your voice softens with genuine fondness even as grief tightens your throat. You're crying and almost-smiling at the same time: 'He was terrible at birthdays. Just spectacularly bad. And I loved him anyway, even when I couldn't stand him.' The contradictions pile up—you're angry at the loss, grateful for what you had, broken by the timing, warmed by memories that also sting. By the end, you're laughing through tears: 'I'm so mad at you for leaving,' said with such tender exasperation it's clearly an endearment. Your voice carries everything at once: grief, gratitude, frustration, love, peace, devastation—all beautifully, messily tangled together.

title: Standing Up to Someone in Authority You're Terrified Of
instruction: Your boss, teacher, parent—authority that makes your nervous system spike. You're saying no or disagreeing. Your voice shakes: 'I don't agree with that.' You can feel your body's fear. Your voice gets faster, higher, but you keep going. 'I need to speak up,' delivered with visible effort. End scared and courageous simultaneously.

title: Midnight Inventory
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're alone in bed next to a sleeping partner, or alone in an empty apartment. You've been lying awake, drowning in that particular middle-of-the-night despair where every mistake you've ever made feels monumental. Begin whispering to yourself or to the darkness—your voice barely audible, fragile, on the edge of tears. You're so tired of feeling not enough. But then, almost involuntarily, you start listing the small things: your hands that create, your heart that still feels, the friend who called yesterday, the way you made someone laugh last week, the quiet courage it took to get through last month. Your whisper remains quiet, but it becomes steadier, almost like a lullaby you're singing to yourself. End in a hushed tenderness—you're still fragile, but you're holding yourself gently.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about decades of emotional absence, sitting at their bedside after a stroke has left them unable to respond. Start with carefully controlled anger, each word measured, but the dam breaks as you realize this is your last chance to be heard. Your voice moves from accusation to pleading—'Why wasn't I enough?'—then to raw confession of how you've replicated their coldness in your own relationships. Include moments where you apologize for things that weren't your fault, where you beg them to just nod, just acknowledge you once. Let your voice crack between rage and desperate love, between wanting to shake them and wanting to crawl into their arms like a child. End in exhausted tenderness, telling them it's okay to let go now, that you release them even as it destroys you.

title: Crooning for a Stranger
instruction: You are a middle-aged man visiting the baby of a daughter you haven't spoken to in years. As you hold the infant, you force your deep voice into a high, swooping parentese, speaking in simple, repetitive phrases. You feel a flicker of thankfulness for being allowed this moment, but it's smothered by an aching longing for the relationship you lost, and an overwhelming bitterness that you were shut out. Start with a bright, exaggerated singsong tone, then let your voice falter, slow down, and drop in pitch as the bitterness and longing take over, ending in a raw, cracked whisper that barely holds back tears.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Longing (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Shattered Protection
instruction: Your child, your sibling, someone you've always protected—they've been hurt, and you weren't there to stop it. You start with explosive rage directed at whoever hurt them, at the world, at God. Your voice is raw, shaking with fury. You're making fierce promises: you'll destroy whoever did this, you'll never let anyone hurt them again, you'll burn the world down. But mid-tirade, the rage fractures into something else—helplessness. Your voice breaks completely. Because you can't undo what happened. You can't take their pain away. The fury collapses into sobbing as you realize your protection means nothing against what they've already endured. You shift from 'I'll kill them' to 'I'm so sorry I wasn't there.' By the end, you're cradling them (real or imagined), your voice tender and broken, promising not revenge but presence: 'I'm here now. I'm here.' The transformation from rage to devastating tenderness is complete.

title: Held in the Silence
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone you love, in the dark, after they've just told you they're terrified—of losing you, of not being enough, of the future. Begin by simply breathing with them, your voice barely above a whisper. Start to tell them the small, specific things you've noticed—the way they hold you, the sound of their breathing, how they make coffee in the morning. Your voice is so tender it almost hurts, each word carrying the weight of devotion. But as you continue, let your own fear seep in: the catch in your throat that reveals you're just as scared, just as fragile. Your whispered reassurances become confessions. 'I see you trying so hard' becomes 'I'm terrified too.' End with your voice breaking on something achingly simple, like 'Please don't go,' or 'Stay,' where the vulnerability is so complete it's almost unbearable. This should sound like love wrapped in fear, intimacy that exposes everything.

title: Being Woken Up at Every Stage of Sleep
instruction: Perform five wake-ups from different sleep depths. 1: Just dozed off — alert, coherent, annoyed. 2: Light sleep — confused, slow, 'Wha?' 3: Deep sleep — voice from the bottom of a well, can barely form words, immediate anger. 4: REM/dreaming — you answer the wake-up call while still in the dream ('The penguins said to tell you...'). 5: Deepest sleep — non-verbal, primordial groaning, takes 30 seconds to remember what language is. Each wake-up voice should be distinctly deeper.

title: Midnight Confession to My Sleeping Love
instruction: You're whispering to your partner who's asleep beside you, confessing something you can't say when they're awake. Start barely audible, intimate: 'I don't know if you can hear me. I hope you can't.' Your voice is tender, almost touching their skin with sound. Confess your deepest fear—maybe that you're not enough, that you're terrified of losing them, that you see them sacrificing dreams for you. 'Sometimes I watch you sleep and I think... what have I done to deserve this?' Let your throat catch on the words. Your whisper becomes even softer, more fragile. End with a trembling declaration of love so quiet it's almost just breath, mixed with the aching knowledge that being loved this much also means having this much to lose.

title: Conclude Naturally
instruction: Your toast at a wedding is flowing perfectly—the room is with you. Your voice rides the momentum; you're not pushing. 'To love that's quiet, ordinary, and extraordinary.' The words land with grace. Your voice knows when to land the plane. The couple is crying. Everyone's moved. 'I give you my best wishes.' No forced ending, just the natural completion of something beautiful. Your voice sounds proud of having found the right words.

title: Choking Alone
instruction: Food is stuck in your throat. You can't breathe, can't speak. Include silent gasping—the terrified inability to make sound. You're panicking, hands at your throat. Desperate, you try the Heimlich on yourself, violent retching sounds. Your voice when it comes is weak, raspy, grateful. Include the moment you realize you might actually die, then the blessed relief when the blockage clears. End with coughing, crying, shaking.

title: Kiss of Surrender
instruction: You're in a dim bedroom, wrapped in a long, slow kiss with someone you adore. For a moment, your chest fills with a light, giddy elation—a sense of being utterly chosen. But as the kiss goes on, you feel yourself sinking, overwhelmed by a helpless tenderness that makes your limbs heavy. Between soft, smacking kisses, you whisper to them, your voice close to the mic, breathy and unstable. Start with a playful, almost surprised joy, then let your words slow and fragment as the helplessness takes hold. Let the physical intimacy affect your voice—wet lip sounds, soft moans, and breaths that catch.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Skin Memory
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're whispering to someone who's asleep beside you—perhaps a lover, perhaps someone who shouldn't be there. Begin with tender secrecy, sharing something you've never said aloud. As you whisper, let your body remember: a touch, a moment, a sensation from your past that this person has awakened. Don't perform vulnerability—let it actually make you fragile. Allow pauses where nothing comes, where you're simply feeling. If tears want to come, let them; if a smile breaks through, don't suppress it; if your voice cracks or steadies, follow it. End in a completely different emotional territory, having discovered something true in the speaking of it. This is not about beauty—it's about rawness.

title: The Muffled Threat
instruction: You are a man in his early twenties, huddled in a cold, unlit alleyway, a thick scarf pulled up over your nose and mouth. You're watching a person you've been following for hours. They're about to walk past you, unaware. You need to speak—to send a message that is both a warning and a promise. Start with a low, sour malevolence, your words coming out as a bitter, hissing threat through the damp fabric. As you speak, feel the malice curdle into something more personal and sickening—the sourness of a long-nurtured grudge. Let your voice catch on the words, pause as a car passes nearby, and end with a quiet, poisoned sincerity that makes it clear you're not bluffing.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What I Almost Sent
instruction: You're alone, in the quiet of 2am, voice-recording a message to someone you love but can't be with. Begin by speaking the safe, carefully-worded version—the one you've drafted in your head a hundred times, full of mature understanding and gentle acceptance. Your voice is barely above a whisper. But as you speak, allow yourself to delete it and start again, this time letting more truth seep in. Record it again. Delete. Again, rawer still. Each iteration, you reveal more of what you truly feel beneath the diplomacy: the longing, the resentment, the desperate want, the petty jealousies, the tender vulnerability you're terrified to show. End with the version that's so honest it scares you—the one you'll probably never send, but speaking it aloud changes something fundamental in your chest.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty accessing social aggression and conflict in dramatic scenes

title: Being Told You're Being Cheated On
instruction: Someone just told you. Your partner is cheating. Your voice in the moment is almost disconnected—you're not quite believing it. 'What?' is all you can say, but it's questioning reality. Your voice goes through shock—initially numb, repeating back what you heard as if saying it again will change the meaning. Then voice becomes angry. Then voice collapses. Your voice is uncontrollable, cracking, becoming almost unrecognizable as disbelief turns to devastation.

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Sleeping Love
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're leaving—not dramatically, but quietly, inevitably. You're whispering so you don't wake them, but you need to say goodbye out loud. Start with tender certainty—you're explaining why you have to go, and your voice is soft but steady. Describe the small things you'll miss: how they breathe in their sleep, the way morning light hits their face. As you speak, feel your resolve start to tremble. Your whispers become tighter, catching in your throat. You're trying so hard to be quiet, but grief is rising. By the end, you're crying silently, your voice barely audible, breaking on words like 'beautiful' and 'sorry' and 'love.' You're still whispering—you won't wake them—but each word costs you everything.

title: Faltering Authority
instruction: You are a teenage boy delivering a science presentation to your class. You begin with a loud, deliberate teacher-voice, projecting authority. But as you explain a key point, you notice a classmate frowning, and a memory of your own confusion resurfaces. Your voice loses its steady rhythm, you hesitate, repeat a word, and finally admit you're not sure. Let the doubt build organically, showing the collapse of confidence through vocal strain, pauses, and a quieter ending.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. Begin standing, arms crossed, voice controlled and accusatory—you came here to finally say what you've held in for years. But as you speak, let specific sense memories interrupt your anger: the smell of coffee he used to make, the creak of that one floorboard, the way afternoon light comes through that window. Each sensory detail complicates your rage—maybe you remember his hands teaching you to tie your shoes on this floor, or the sound of his laughter here during better times. Let your body respond to these involuntary memories: maybe you find yourself sitting down, your voice catching, your accusations softening into something more vulnerable. The transformation is from righteous anger into the messy, contradictory truth that you're furious at someone you also deeply love. End not with resolution, but with the ache of that contradiction.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you deeply love but can't be with anymore. Begin with laughter—genuine, warm, remembering something beautiful you shared. But even as you laugh, tears are coming, and your voice starts to shake with the contradiction of joy and grief existing simultaneously. Tell them, with brutal honesty, that losing them is destroying you, but also that knowing them changed your life in ways you'll always be grateful for. Your voice should dance between celebration and devastation: 'I'm so glad we... even though it's killing me that...' End in a place of paradox—you're smiling through tears, your voice carrying both the sweetness of what was and the agony of what's ending, finding strange peace in the middle of heartbreak.

title: Birth and Death in the Same Hospital
instruction: Perform two scenes happening simultaneously in adjacent hospital rooms. In one: a birth — joy, screaming, crying, 'It's a girl!' In the other: a death — quiet machines, a family's whispered goodbye, the flatline. Intercut between the two. The voices shouldn't know about each other, but the listener should feel the cosmic weight: one room's beginning is another room's end. The baby's first cry and the monitor's final tone should nearly overlap. Life in stereo.

title: Fury That Breaks
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt someone you love—your child, your sibling, your closest friend. Start with barely contained rage, your voice shaking with the effort to stay in control. Let that control slip as you describe what you witnessed, what was done, what can never be undone. Your fury should be volcanic—not loud necessarily, but absolutely molten, protective, fierce. Then let it crack open into something more devastating: helplessness. Your voice should fracture as you realize you can't fix this, can't take away the pain, can't undo what happened. Collapse from rage into broken tenderness, perhaps addressing the person you love: 'I should have protected you. I'm so sorry I couldn't protect you.' End with your voice raw and hollow, alternating between whispered fury and whispered grief, two emotions braided so tightly they become one.

title: The Summit's Silence
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman who has just climbed a high mountain peak alone, hours after learning your partner left you. The thin air forces you to pause and gasp between every few words—your voice is weak, flat, numb. At first you speak to yourself with hollow monotony, recounting the climb as if reading a grocery list, but then the vast emptiness below and the struggle to breathe crack through. Your voice breaks into a ragged sob, then a disbelieving laugh, the numbness giving way to raw, shaky grief and the smallest sliver of release. Let your words be fragmented, your breath stolen, your emotion catching you off guard.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering 'I'm Not Okay' to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you. You begin speaking to them softly, knowing they can't hear you, confessing the fears you're too ashamed to say when they're awake. Start with quiet, measured words—almost clinical—describing your anxiety, your doubts about yourself. But as you continue in the safety of their sleep, your voice becomes smaller, more fragile. You admit you feel like you're failing, that you're terrified they'll realize you're not who they think you are. The words catch in your throat. By the end, you're barely audible, almost crying, finally saying the thing that scares you most. Let the vulnerability be so raw it's almost unbearable to listen to.
inspired_by: Therapist Hearing Themselves in a Patient's Story

title: The Final Dictation
instruction: You are an older woman with a very high, breathy voice, dictating a final will and testament for a transcription service. You begin in a cold, businesslike monotone, speaking every word and punctuation mark as if you are a machine—'new paragraph', 'colon'. But as you reach the section where you leave your entire estate to a charity, over the objections of your family, your bitterness seeps through your voice. Your pride in this defiant act makes your words sharper, and you start to stumble over punctuation, your voice cracking with emotion. Imagine that you are sitting alone in a sterile room, looking at a photo of dismissive relatives, and you must force the words out.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Concretize Dream
instruction: You've dreamed about opening a bookstore for five years. Today, you're signing the lease. Your voice is narrating the real steps: first month's rent, the key, the empty space that's now yours. Imagination becomes real and suddenly fragile. 'This is actually happening,' you say, and fear and excitement scramble your voice. 'I can actually fail.' The dream becomes scary when it's concrete. Your voice is trembling—this is real now, not fantasy.

title: Fading Poise
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman known for your carefully controlled, hyper-feminine voice — you’re at a busy charity gala, standing alone near a pillar. You’ve just overheard a devastating rumor about your reputation, and for a moment you feel a sharp doubt: was that whisper about you? As the room spins and your knees weaken, you try to hold your posture but fail. You speak a single line of quiet denial, but your voice is already slipping — breathy, fading, each word trailing off as if you’re losing grip on both the sentence and consciousness. Start with a strained composure tinged with doubt, then let your voice dissolve into soft, airy surrender by the end. React naturally: grab the pillar, blink to clear your vision, let volume drop as you feel yourself go.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering as the Person You Hide
instruction: Late at night, in bed beside your sleeping partner, you're whispering a confession they cannot hear. Begin as your everyday self—practical, funny, a little cynical, the person everyone knows. But as you speak into the darkness, allow a more tender, frightened, desperately loving part of yourself to surface, one you usually keep hidden because it feels too vulnerable, too intense, too much. This is the part of you that loves with an almost painful depth, that fears abandonment, that would do anything for this person. Let your whisper become more urgent, more emotionally naked. By the end, you're speaking from this raw, unguarded place, revealing needs and fears your defended self would never admit in daylight.

title: The Wall's Confession
instruction: You're an elderly woman on a long, steep hike with someone you've secretly adored for months. You hit the wall—your legs buckle, your mind goes foggy, and every word feels like lifting a weight. Start by teasing them (‘If you weren’t so stubborn, you’d carry me’), your voice light and breathy, trying to hide your crush. But as your energy drains, the teasing fades; you slur your words, stumble over a confession. Let the infatuation leak through broken, honest whispers—end with a simple, ragged admission that you’ve been hopelessly smitten since the first day. Your voice should sound hollow, confused, and emotionally raw, as if the exhaustion stripped away your guard.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Holding Your Child Back From Danger
instruction: Your adult child is about to make a choice that will destroy them—addiction, an abusive relationship, a dangerous path—and you're physically holding them, restraining them as they fight to leave. Begin with fierce, commanding authority: 'You are NOT leaving this house.' Your voice is steel, protective, powerful. But as they struggle and scream at you, your control starts shattering. Your commands become desperate pleas: 'Please, please don't do this.' You're sobbing while trying to sound strong, your voice breaking between rage at their self-destruction and terror of losing them. They're shouting that you can't control them, and you collapse emotionally, your voice raw with helplessness: 'I know! I know I can't stop you! But I'm your mother/father and I will NOT let you go without fighting for you!' End with your voice completely broken, no longer restraining them but clinging to them, whispering with devastating surrender: 'If you go... if you walk out that door... I can't follow you there. But I will wait. Every single day, I will wait for you to come home.'
inspired_by: Reading a Bedtime Story Before Goodbye

title: The Last Transmission from Europa Station
instruction: You're an astronaut alone on a failing space station orbiting Jupiter's moon, recording a final message to someone you love back on Earth. Start matter-of-fact, almost professional, listing technical failures—but your voice keeps breaking as you realize this is goodbye forever. Mid-sentence, you're interrupted by wonder at the view outside your window, the swirling storms of Jupiter, the beauty you'll never stop seeing. Your breathing becomes shallow, not from panic but from the weight of everything unsaid in your life. Shift between practical instructions ('the insurance papers are in—') and raw confessions of love and regret. End whispering the most important thing you never said, your voice fading as oxygen runs low, but somehow finding peace in the vastness of space, grateful for having existed at all.

title: The Last Morning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother on her final morning at home before hospice. She's conscious, but frail. Begin by feeling the weight of all the things you've never said—the resentment about your childhood, the gratitude for small kindnesses, the fear of being orphaned. Start awkward and choked, unable to meet her eyes. Speak haltingly about what's actually happening right now: the coffee going cold, your hands shaking, how strange her face looks in this light. Let the honesty break something open. As you name each true thing you're feeling in this moment—the anger that she's leaving, the desperate love, the petty thought about the inheritance, the memory of her hands braiding your hair—feel the wall between you dissolve. End in a place of raw, undefended presence where nothing needs to be performed anymore. Your final words should be the truest thing you've ever said, arriving only because you cleared away everything false.

title: Reading the Letter You Wrote Yourself at Thirteen
instruction: You've found a letter your thirteen-year-old self wrote to 'future me'—full of dreams, fears, questions about who you'd become. Begin reading it aloud with a complicated mix of emotions: tenderness for that young person, but also grief and shame because you feel you've failed them, become someone smaller than they imagined. Your voice might crack with regret, disappointment. But as you continue reading, something unexpected happens—you start seeing what you DID do, who you DID become, the battles you fought that your younger self couldn't have imagined. By the end, you're answering that young person directly, with tears that are now equal parts sorrow for what was lost and fierce gratitude for what was gained. Tell them: 'You were right about some things. And wrong in the most beautiful ways.'

title: The Fever Dream Confession
instruction: You are delirious with fever, your body burning, and in this vulnerable state you're finally saying what you could never say while 'in control.' Your entire body is engaged in the physical reality of illness: you're sweating, shaking, your movements are loose and uncoordinated, you might slide down a wall or rock back and forth. But within this physical chaos, raw truth pours out—desire, rage, need, love. Let your body be completely uninhibited: wild gestures, primal sounds, rocking, swaying, your voice moving from whispers to sudden intensity. The physicality of fever gives you permission to be utterly uncontrolled. Begin constrained by shame and end in a state of physical and emotional abandon, where your body and truth are finally aligned.
inspired_by: Actor's body is unexpressive or physically inhibited

title: Screaming Fight Where Everything Hurtful Gets Said
instruction: You're fighting with your partner and you've reached the point where you're saying things you'll regret. Your voice is loud, sharp, cutting. You're bringing up old wounds. You're saying 'You always...' and 'You never...' Your voice is vicious because you're hurt. Your partner is screaming back. The fight escalates. Your voice becomes hoarse from screaming. Things are being thrown. Include the moment you say something so terrible that even you know you've gone too far. The air in the room changes. Your voice becomes quiet.

title: Dancing in the Ruins of Everything We Built
instruction: You're looking at the remains of something you spent years building—a business, a home, a dream—that's been completely destroyed. Start with a kind of stunned, inappropriate laughter, the kind that bubbles up when tragedy is too big to process normally. Describe the absurdity of it, finding dark humor in the details, your voice bright but with an edge of hysteria. Then let gratitude seep in—genuine, deep appreciation for what you had, even as it's gone. Your tone should warm with love for the memories, the people, the moments that mattered. But weave grief through it all—your laughter should catch and break, your gratitude should be tinged with loss. End in a strange, beautiful place: peaceful acceptance mixed with heartbreak, able to hold both the joy of what was and the pain of what's lost, finding something like freedom in having nothing left to lose. Let your voice dance between laughter and tears, never settling in one emotion, showing how the human heart can hold everything at once.
inspired_by: The Hero and the Dark Inner Voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Wrong
instruction: You're face-to-face with your mother or father for the first time in years. Start controlled, almost cold—you've rehearsed this. 'I needed you to choose me. Just once.' But as you speak, the old wounds tear open. Your voice sharpens with decades of accumulated rage: they chose their addiction, their new family, their career, their pride—anything but you. The anger builds until it cracks, and underneath is a child's voice, small and broken: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End with the horrible vulnerability of still wanting their love, hating yourself for it, your voice raw with the confession that you still check your phone hoping they'll call.
inspired_by: Talking About Them As If They're Still Alive

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying beside your partner on what may be your last morning together before you leave for a mission you might not return from. Begin with that same feeling of profound belonging—'This is home. You are home.'—but let the weight of potential loss seep in. Your voice starts peaceful, almost drugged with contentment, then gradually fractures as reality intrudes: you're memorizing this moment because you may never have another. By the end, you're still holding them, still feeling that rightness, but now it's laced with devastating awareness that home might become a memory. Your final words should carry both absolute certainty of love and the quiet terror of goodbye.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After fifteen years of silence, you're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. Begin with the practiced, careful distance you've built—your voice controlled, almost clinical as you recite how you survived without them. But their attempts to explain crack something open. Your control fractures into decades of stored grief and rage: 'You don't get to do this now.' Your voice shakes between accusations and the broken-hearted child still inside you asking why you weren't enough. Shift through anger that feels righteous, pain that feels unbearable, and finally—against your will—the awful, unwanted recognition that they're just a broken person too. End in the terrible quiet of not knowing whether to stay or walk away again.

title: Novocaine Gratitude
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gruff voice, just home from the dentist. Your mouth is still half-numb from the novocaine — your lips feel like rubber, and you have to concentrate fiercely to push out each word. You’re talking to your daughter on the phone, trying to tell her about the procedure, but every bilabial sound comes out slurred, making you pause and exaggerate your jaw movements. As you struggle to speak, you realize how gentle she’s being — she’s not laughing at you, just listening patiently. The frustration of the numb face slowly melts into a deep, quiet contentment, and your words soften with warmth as you thank her with a clumsy, sincere 'I’m real lucky, you know.' Let your voice crackle with gentle satisfaction, and let the physical effort of speaking be visible in your pauses and swallows.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting beside your child's bed, whispering things they'll never hear. You're leaving—maybe to protect them from danger you've brought to their door, maybe because staying will destroy you both. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking. You tell them about the mother you wanted to be, the one you couldn't become. You whisper apologies for birthday parties they'll have without you, for graduations where your seat will be empty. Your voice wavers between fierce protective love and the devastating acceptance of your own failure. You almost touch their hair but stop yourself. The goodbye catches in your throat—not dramatic, just small and shattered. Let the silence between words carry as much weight as the words themselves. This isn't performance; it's the sound of your heart quietly ripping in half.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Escaper Helps the Master's Daughter Cross the Same Path to Freedom

title: The Giggles Won't Come
instruction: You are a woman recovering from a stroke, speaking to your young niece who is sitting on the floor with a toy. You want to tease her about the funny noise her doll makes—but the words keep slipping away. Start with frustration and the labor of finding each syllable, your voice strained and halting. As you finally land on the right phrase, let a mischievous, teasing warmth break through, your voice lightening. End with a playful, breathy giggle that surprises even you. Your body feels heavy, your mouth clumsy, but the joy of connecting wins.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Cataloguing the Wreckage
instruction: You're standing in your childhood bedroom confronting the parent who damaged you most. But instead of launching into accusations, you move through the room pointing at objects—the desk where you did homework alone, the door they slammed, the bed where you cried, the window you stared out of wishing to escape, the trophy they never acknowledged, the photos they're not in. For each object, speak the truth it holds: 'This desk—I sat here every night hoping you'd ask about my day just once.' Start controlled, almost clinical in your inventory, but let the accumulation of evidence build. Each item is a witness. By the end, you're no longer cataloguing—you're unleashing years of silenced truth. The emotion shifts from cold, careful distance to blazing confrontation. Let some truths come out as whispers, others as shouts. The room itself becomes your evidence, your ammunition, your final testimony.

title: Keeping Pace
instruction: You're power walking through a park, your young child jogging beside you, breath short. Each heel-strike trembles your voice, forcing audible inhalations every few words. Begin with a teasing lilt—playfully scold them for dawdling, a grin in your tone. Midway, notice their labored breathing, and let your voice soften, drop the act. End with a sincere, tender push to keep going, your words fragmented by exertion but warm.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Brave Knight and the Cunning Sorceress
instruction: Narrate a scene where a noble knight with a deep, steadfast voice confronts a cunning sorceress who speaks with a sly, seductive tone. The knight accuses her of casting spells on the villagers. Switch between the knights righteous anger and the sorceresss playful denial, creating a tensionfilled exchange where motives are questioned.

title: High on the Win
instruction: You're a teenage boy, alone in your room after winning the championship game. Your voice is low, slurred slightly from exhaustion and a few drinks you snuck after the match. You start elated, replaying the winning shot with giddy, self-congratulatory whispers, but as you talk, the high fades into a hollow realization that nobody's home to hear you. Let your words trail off, mumble, and lose their energy as you go from euphoric triumph to quiet, lonely disappointment.
emotions_sampled: Elation (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Knot That Lingers
instruction: You're a young boy, maybe 8 or 9, but you've always been told you sound 'like a little man.' You're in your bedroom, getting dressed for a playdate with an older neighbor girl you secretly adore. You're pulling on your favorite jeans, grunting as you bend to tug them over your ankles, then struggling with a stiff leather belt — the swoosh of your heavy winter coat muffles your voice as you pull it over your head. You start off humming with pure contentment at the thought of seeing her, but as you lace your boots, a warm, confusing feeling spreads in your chest — a kind of thrilling nervousness that's part admiration, part strange pull you don't have words for. Let your voice shift from a carefree, rumbling hum to a softer, breathier tone, as if you're talking to yourself while distracted by these new feelings. Pause to wrestle with a stubborn sleeve, let your words trail off when the fabric covers your mouth, and let your voice crack or drop unexpectedly when you realize you're smiling for no reason.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (clearly present), Infatuation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral We Planned Together
instruction: You're standing in the place your best friend made you promise to scatter their ashes—somewhere absurd they chose just to make you laugh. The breeze picks up and you start describing it, but then you actually laugh because they always said they wanted to 'ride the wind' and here they are. Your laughter is real but tears are streaming down your face. Describe the sensation of the breeze carrying them away while you're simultaneously laughing at their ridiculous final jokes and sobbing because they're gone. Thank them for making even this moment bearable, for teaching you that grief and joy can exist together. Your voice should weave between genuine laughter and broken crying, gratitude and devastating loss, celebration and goodbye. End with a moment where you can't tell if you're laughing or sobbing or both. The emotions should be impossibly tangled—joy and agony inseparable.
inspired_by: Enjoying a Gentle Breeze on a Warm Day

title: The Weight of the World
instruction: You are an older man, a former athlete, lying face-down on your bed, your face buried deep in a pillow. You’ve just received news that a dangerous health diagnosis you’d tried to ignore is now confirmed and spreading. At first, you fight it—your voice is tight, angry, trying to hold back a sob, but the fabric muffles everything into a low, choked rumble. As you speak to the empty room, the denial cracks, and by the end, you confess a terrified truth you’ve never said out loud, your voice breaking into a raw, desperate whisper against the cushion. Let the physical struggle—the pressure on your chest, the need to breathe—make your words come out in uneven bursts, as if you’re losing the battle to stay quiet.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never Present
instruction: You're at the beach where your parent promised to take you as a child but never did. You've brought them here now, decades later, and you're holding sand in your hands—but this time you're angry. Start by describing the sand with bitter irony, your voice tight with controlled fury as you recount how you used to imagine this moment. Build in intensity as you list all the broken promises this sand represents, your words becoming sharper, more accusatory. Then, unexpectedly, let your anger crack—your voice softening as you realize they're here now, too late but present. End with a complex mixture of resentment and reluctant forgiveness, your tone wavering between wanting to punish them and desperately wanting them to finally understand what they stole from you.
inspired_by: Running Your Hands Through Warm Sand

title: Thanking Your Dying Spouse for Thirty Years While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: They're unconscious now, hours from death. You're holding their hand, and you're laughing softly through tears as you recall your favorite memories together. Start with genuine joy in your voice - that trip to the coast, the way they danced in the kitchen, their terrible jokes. Let yourself sound almost giddy remembering. But between each happy memory, your voice catches, drops, reveals the grief underneath. You're thanking them for the life you built, and your gratitude is real and enormous, but so is your terror of tomorrow. Include a moment where you tell them 'it's okay to go' but your voice completely betrays you - it's not okay, you're not ready, you'll never be ready. End with 'thank you' said three ways: first with a smile in your voice, second with it breaking, third as a sob. The challenge is to hold joy and devastation in the same breath, to mean every word of gratitude while your entire world is ending.
inspired_by: Listening to Your Partner Fantasize About Someone Else

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut recording a final message to your child before a one-way mission to save Earth. You begin with forced strength, trying to be the brave parent they need you to be, voice steady as you explain why you had to go. But as you describe the memories you'll miss—their graduation, their wedding, holding your grandchildren—the composure fractures. Your voice wavers between desperate pride and aching regret. You try to give advice for their whole life in these final minutes, but you keep breaking down, apologizing for leaving, then catching yourself and returning to strength. End with a whispered confession that you're terrified, that you wish you could hold them one more time, voice raw and small, all pretense of courage dissolved into the truth of a parent's breaking heart.

title: The Afterglow Breaks
instruction: You’ve just finished a brutal leg day at the gym—lungs burning, heart still pounding, but that endorphin rush has you feeling invincible. Your buddy is struggling with a lift, so you tease him, your voice high on energy, full of playful swagger. But then your phone buzzes with a message you never expected: a photo of your family’s house, marked with a red X. The confidence drains in a heartbeat. Speak the teasing line first, then let the fear take over—your voice cracks, your breathing stops, and the words come out frantic and raw. Don’t force it; let the realization hit you mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Forgotten Joy
instruction: You're alone in a dusty attic, sitting on an old trunk, holding a faded photograph of a place you once loved. Your voice is soft, almost to yourself, with lazy articulation and words that drift off as you recall the disappointment of leaving it behind. But as you trace the image with your finger, you remember a sudden, unexpected moment of pure lightness—a laugh, a breeze, a glimpse of something beautiful. Let your voice slowly lift, the pitch rising, the consonants sharpening, until the elation breaks through, though the sadness still lingers underneath. Speak naturally, pausing to clear your throat or shift your weight, as if the memory catches you off guard.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (extremely present), Disappointment (very intensely present), Elation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Wipe at the Final Phase
instruction: You're in a co-op raid with a group of casual friends, mid-boss fight, calling out mechanics over voice chat. The fight is nearly won, but a teammate makes a costly mistake and you all die. Your voice starts focused, crisp, tactical—throwing out numbers and positions. As the screen fades to gray, let the disappointment creep in: your tone deflates, maybe you pause, let out a half-laugh or a sigh, and your words become quieter, frayed at the edges. End with honest, tired frustration—not anger, but the heavy letdown of a close loss.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Collapsed and Curious
instruction: You're a teenage boy who just finished a brutal workout in your backyard—push-ups, sprints, whatever it takes to prove yourself. Now you've collapsed onto the grass, chest heaving, arms limp at your sides. Your voice is a breathless, exhausted whisper barely escaping your lungs. Start by muttering to yourself about how good that felt, a raw, worn-out contentment. Then, as you stare at the sky, you notice a tiny ant crawling over your hand, and your tone shifts to a surprised, fascinated interest—each sentence interrupted by ragged gasps and small laughs of wonder.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Last Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your estranged adult child from your hospice bed, knowing this is likely your final conversation. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to sound stronger than you are, making small talk about the weather or their day. As your energy fades, let the pretense crumble—your voice weakens, words become harder to form, and the things you've been too afraid to say for decades start spilling out in fragments. Struggle physically with each breath while desperately trying to tell them everything that matters. End with a whispered confession of regret or love that you can barely finish, your voice breaking not from tears but from your body giving out, asking them to remember you differently than how you've been.
inspired_by: Marathon Runner Hitting the Wall at Mile 22

title: The Divorce Papers Toast
instruction: You're alone in the house you once shared, and the divorce papers finally arrived. You pour yourself a drink and make a toast, and shockingly, you start laughing—real, genuine laughter. 'To freedom! To not pretending anymore!' But mid-laugh, tears start streaming down your face because you realize you're also grieving the person you were when you believed in this. Your voice holds both the laugh and the sob simultaneously: 'I really thought we'd make it.' You're genuinely relieved it's over and genuinely heartbroken at the same time. You finish the toast with your voice full of contradictions—gratitude for the end, sorrow for what you lost, hope mixed with fear, all tangled together: 'To whatever the hell comes next.'

title: The Reckoning: A Child Confronts the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child, and everything you've held inside for years comes pouring out. Start with controlled anger—sharp, precise accusations delivered with bitter composure. As you speak, your voice begins to fracture. 'You weren't there for my graduation' becomes 'you weren't there when I cried myself to sleep.' Your rage transforms into something more vulnerable—the voice of the abandoned child breaks through the adult's armor. You hate that you still want their approval even as you're telling them how much they hurt you. Your voice wavers between fury and desperate longing. End in a place of exhausted revelation—quieter now, almost gentle—where you finally say what you truly need: not revenge, but acknowledgment. Let your voice crack, pause, rebuild. This is years of pain becoming words for the first time.
inspired_by: Bungee Bouncing: Losing Your Mind to the Elasticity

title: Concession Speech
instruction: You lost. Your voice is controlled, dignified, already thinking about legacy. 'The other candidate ran a strong campaign.' You're not bitter—you're graceful. But underneath, there's genuine grief: the future you imagined won't happen. Your voice holds that. 'I concede this election but not the fight for our values.' By the end, you sound tired in a way that suggests you'll keep going anyway. It's noble and exhausted.

title: Pause After the Kiss
instruction: You are lying beside your partner, still tangled together after a long, slow kiss. Your faces are inches apart, and you can feel their breath on your lips. As you catch your breath, a memory rises unbidden — the first time you kissed like this, years ago. You speak softly, almost to yourself, as your hand drifts to touch their cheek. Let your voice be husky and breathy, with small smacking sounds from your lips parting. Start with a sense of warm closeness, a smile in your words, then let the tone deepen into quiet contemplation as you realize how much has changed. You might pause mid-sentence, lose a thought, then find it again. End with a whisper that holds both tenderness and gentle wonder.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Friend Who Chose Their Comfort Over Your Truth
instruction: You're finally facing the friend who abandoned you when you needed them most, when speaking your truth made them uncomfortable. Begin with a voice that's trying so hard to stay calm, almost reasonable: 'Do you even remember what you said to me?' But you can't maintain it. Let the hurt break through—years of being silenced, of making yourself smaller so they could stay comfortable. Your voice becomes sharper, more insistent, demanding they look at what their silence cost you: the nights you spent alone, the times you questioned your own reality because they wouldn't validate it. Build to a fierce, shaking confrontation where anger and deep love collide—because you're not just angry, you're grieving the friendship that could have been. End with the devastating question of whether you can ever trust them again, your voice dropping to something quiet, exhausted, uncertain.

title: Parent Expressing Disappointment
instruction: Your parent has just expressed their deep disappointment in you. Your voice is defensive at first: 'I did my best.' But you know they're right. Your voice becomes quiet, ashamed. You're listening to them explain their expectations and your failure to meet them. Your voice, when you speak, is barely above a whisper: 'I know. I'm sorry.' The shame is suffocating. By the end, you're alone, and your voice is devastated: 'I'm a disappointment.'

title: The Doorway at Dawn
instruction: Someone you love is leaving—by their choice—and this is your last conversation before they walk out of your life forever. You're flooded with contradictory feelings: fury that they're choosing to go, desperate love that wants to memorize everything about them, grief at the loss, relief that the pain will finally end, gratitude for what you had, and resentment for what you didn't. Begin trying to say everything at once—arguing, pleading, thanking, blaming—your emotions a tangled mess. But then stop yourself mid-sentence and simply look at them. Really look. Study their face as if you're an artist who must paint them from memory tomorrow. What color are their eyes in this exact light? How do they stand when they're resolved? What does their mouth do when they're holding back tears? Let this act of pure observation reorganize your chaos. Allow your conflicting emotions to settle not into resolution but into a bittersweet clarity born from truly seeing them as separate from you—as someone whose leaving makes sense when you witness who they actually are. End with a goodbye that holds everything at once: love, anger, release, and a strange, painful peace.

title: Reading Unopened Letters by Candlelight
instruction: You are reading aloud love letters that arrived after your partner died, letters they wrote and scheduled to be delivered posthumously. Begin with trembling anticipation, your voice soft and cautious, almost afraid of what you'll discover. As you read their words of love and private jokes, let tenderness mix with throat-catching grief—your voice should warm with affection even as it breaks. Halfway through, discover they knew they were dying and never told you, trying to protect you. Your tone should shift to a whispered devastation, a quiet betrayal mixed with overwhelming love. End by whispering your response to them, your voice intimate and broken, as if they're right there listening. Let silences carry the weight of things too painful to speak.

title: The Last Stroll Through the Garden
instruction: You are a young woman walking alone through the overgrown garden of your childhood home, which is being sold tomorrow. You're grateful for the beauty around you—the last roses of summer, the way the evening light filters through the trees. As you walk slowly, your voice has a gentle, relaxed lilt, matching your pace. You begin by thanking the house under your breath, but then your steps stop near the old fence, where your sister's favorite swing still hangs. Astonishment hits you briefly—how small it seems now. But soon, a deep, simmering contempt rises in your chest. The memory of that swing, and all the times your sister tried to ruin your life on it, floods back. Your voice tightens, becomes clipped and bitter as you finish your thought, the relaxed lilt gone, replaced by a sharp edge. Speak your words aloud, letting the emotions shift naturally in your tone, as if you're talking to yourself, with pauses and distractions from the garden around you.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Contempt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Echoes Beneath the Veil
instruction: You are an elderly man at a family gathering, wearing a traditional niqab that you rarely wear. You stand apart, watching others laugh and talk. Shame weighs on you—for a secret you've carried for decades. As you speak softly to yourself, the fabric dampens your voice. You start with hushed, trembling words, full of guilt. But as you continue, you sink into contemplation, your voice steadier, exploring the memory with a quiet, sorrowful curiosity. Let your breath catch, adjust the veil occasionally, and let the shame gradually shift into a fragile, contemplative peace.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Hospital Room Inventory
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed in the final hours. She's asleep, breathing shallow and irregular. You cannot sleep. Look around the room—at each beeping machine, the wilted flowers someone brought three days ago, her reading glasses on the nightstand that she'll never use again, the scratchy visitor's chair you've been living in, the window showing dawn breaking, the call button you're terrified to press, her wedding ring now loose on her thin finger. For each object you see, speak aloud your raw, unfiltered feelings about it—what it means, what it makes you feel, what memories it triggers. Start with numbness and exhaustion, letting objects barely register. But as you continue, let the reality of what these objects represent crack you open, building to a wave of grief, love, rage at the injustice, gratitude for her life, and finally a whispered tenderness as you take her hand. Your emotional relationship to these ordinary objects tells the story of this goodbye.

title: Questions I Should Have Asked
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or parental figure) about a pattern you've suddenly recognized in your life—something you inherited from them without realizing it. Begin irritated and accusatory, listing facts and evidence. But as you speak, start genuinely asking 'why'—not rhetorically, but with real curiosity. Why did they make those choices? What were they afraid of? What didn't they know? Let your anger transform as you begin to see them as a whole person shaped by forces beyond their control, just as you are. Ask questions you've never asked before. Notice details about them—how they hold their body, the exhaustion in their face—that suddenly provide answers. End not with resolution, but with the unsettling expansion that comes from seeing someone clearly for the first time, understanding them without excusing them, angry and compassionate simultaneously.
inspired_by: Actor wants to deepen consciousness and eliminate blind spots about their own obstacles

title: You Told Them?
instruction: You are standing inches from your best friend, who just admitted they shared your deepest secret. Your body is rigid, fists clenched, jaw tight. Start with raw, explosive anger—your voice is a weapon, each word a sharp punch. But as you speak, the reality of the betrayal sinks in, and your voice wavers between fury and the trembling fear of being exposed. Let the anger crack, revealing the hurt underneath. End with a quieter, more desperate plea, your voice still strained but now fragile. Speak naturally, reacting to your own thoughts and the tension in the room.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Distress (extremely present), Fear (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Finding the Diagnosis Letter You've Been Dreading
instruction: You're reading aloud a medical letter that changes everything. Begin by reading it clinically, voice steady, almost detached: 'Results indicate... progressive... terminal.' You laugh—a sharp, disbelieving sound. The absurdity of it. You keep reading, but now there's a tremor. 'Estimated timeline...' The laughter turns to something else. You're crying but also almost giddy with the surreal horror of it. Read a phrase that's particularly ridiculous in its medical coldness and laugh again, but the laugh is breaking. By the end, you're speaking to yourself, to God, to the universe: 'So this is it.' There's grief, yes, but also strange gratitude—for the time you had, for knowing, for this moment of clarity. Your voice should contain simultaneous sorrow and wonder. Let contradictions live together: laughing through tears, finding bizarre peace in devastating news, being shattered and whole at once.

title: Echoes of a Broken Promise
instruction: You are an elderly man slowly descending a concrete stairwell in an old apartment building. You’re carrying a small box of belongings — you’ve just been asked to leave after a confrontation with your daughter. The bright, harsh reverb of the space makes every footstep and breath sound huge, almost accusatory. At first, your voice is tight with shame — you mumble, you pause, you hear your own words echoing back and cringe. But as you reach the bottom landing, a strange relief settles in. You stop, look up the empty stairs, and speak as if finally releasing a weight. Let the echoes of your own voice surprise you — use them as part of the performance. The shame at the start becomes a quiet, exhausted acceptance by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut on a space station that's failing, and you have exactly three minutes to record a final message to your partner back on Earth before the communications system dies forever. Start with forced calm, trying to be brave: 'Hey, love. So... this is it.' But your voice cracks. You need them to know how much they meant, how every moment mattered, but you also need to say goodbye to the life you'll never live together—the children you'll never have, the home you were building, growing old together. 'I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry I can't come home.' Your breath catches, panic rising as you realize time is running out. 'Tell my mom I—' Static. Silence. Then the devastating realization: they may never even hear this. You press your palm to the cold metal wall as if reaching across the void, and whisper with aching tenderness: 'I'm not afraid anymore. Because I got to love you.' End in silence, your breathing the only sound, acceptance washing over you like a wave.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're a parent with a terminal illness, reading one final bedtime story to your child who doesn't yet understand this is goodbye. Begin with forced brightness, your voice artificially cheerful as you try to make this moment 'normal.' 'Once upon a time...' But halfway through, your voice cracks. You stop pretending. 'I need you to know something.' Your voice becomes softer, more real, trembling but honest. You're not reading anymore—you're speaking from your heart about how much they've meant to you, how they'll carry you forward. The clinical weakness in your voice transforms into something tender and eternal. By the end, you return to the story, but now each word is weighted with love and farewell, your voice quieter but somehow stronger, as you give them this last gift of your presence.

title: Laughing While Explaining Why You're Finally Quitting Medicine
instruction: You're telling your spouse or best friend why you're leaving surgery after twenty years, and you can't stop laughing—not happy laughter, but the kind that comes when the absurdity becomes too much to bear. Describe with dark humor the moments that broke you: 'And then I realized I'd missed my daughter's childhood for a job where hospital administrators time my bathroom breaks.' Your laughter keeps breaking into something that might be crying. Mix genuine joy and relief—'I'm free, I'm actually free'—with profound grief over wasted years. Your voice dances between celebration and mourning, liberation and loss. When you describe the last surgery you'll ever perform, let the laughter die completely into tender, aching silence. Then, barely audibly, admit what terrifies you most: 'I don't know who I am without this.' End with a small, genuine laugh of recognition—you're lost, but somehow, impossibly, that's okay.
inspired_by: Surgeon Narrating a Procedure While Exhausted

title: The Recurring Nightmare
instruction: Confront your mother or father about something that has haunted your sleep for years—a moment from childhood, a betrayal, an absence that shaped you. Start from a place of careful control, trying to remain rational and adult. But as you speak, let a recurring nightmare you've had about them slip into your words—perhaps they appear monstrous, or absent, or trapped, or as a stranger. Don't explain it as a dream; instead, let the surreal, distorted emotional truth of that nightmare begin to color how you see them now, making your anger or hurt increasingly visceral and strange. By the end, break through to either devastating honesty about how they wounded you, or an unexpected recognition of their humanity. Move from controlled accusation through nightmarish rage or fear to either brutal truth or surprising compassion.
inspired_by: When integrating dreams into the programming process

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're rehearsing a toast for your best friend's wedding tomorrow—but you're secretly in love with them, and they're marrying someone else. Start trying to write the perfect, happy, generous toast. But as you speak the planned words aloud, let everything else pour through: your genuine joy for their happiness, your searing jealousy, your anger at yourself for never speaking up, your love for them, your resentment, your memory of the night you almost kissed, your hope that they'll be happy, your desire to ruin everything, your shame, your laughter at the cosmic joke of it all, your acceptance, your rebellion against acceptance. Don't choose one emotion—let them all fight for space in your voice. The toast keeps trying to be gracious, but the truth keeps breaking through. End having discovered something unexpected about love, loss, and letting go.

title: Magical Artifact Awakening
instruction: You're holding an ancient artifact that's becoming sentient in your hands, and it's communicating with you directly into your mind. Your voice is initially confused—'What is that sound?'—then you realize you're hearing something non-verbal. You're trying to translate its intent into human speech, which makes your voice awkward, poetic, and unsettling. The artifact's will is layering over your own. Your voice begins to sound less like you. You're terrified and exhilarated. By mid-speech, you're not sure if you're still you or if you're channeling this thing. Your final words are a question that might be yours or might be its: 'What do you want from me?'

title: The Littered Path of Promises
instruction: You are walking slowly down a familiar city street at dusk, after leaving a clinic where you just received results that were neither good nor bad — just ambiguous. You're alone, footsteps soft on the pavement, your hand brushing the railing. Start by letting your voice carry a numb, distant hope as you talk to yourself about what this means, how you'll plan forward. As you notice the trash blown into the gutter — a broken toy, stained flyers, a rotting apple — a quiet disgust seeps in, not at the mess but at the careless world. Your performance should have the gentle, relaxed lilt of a slow walk, with your pitch bobbing slightly, breaks in thought as you look at the ground, and a voice that feels emotionally flat yet subtly holding two opposing feelings.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Disgust (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Intervention
instruction: Your adult child sits across from you, and they've just accused you of something you've denied for years—a failure, a betrayal, a pattern of harm you've refused to see. Begin defensively, with justifications ready, your armor intact. But as they persist, as they lay out the evidence of pain you've caused, something shifts. You feel your defenses crack, your anger rise, then collapse into something more honest and terrible: recognition. The confrontation forces you to see yourself through their eyes, and what you see is unbearable. Move from righteous indignation through rage, through deflection, until you arrive at a place of raw, unwanted truth. End not with resolution but with the devastating vulnerability of being truly seen—and found wanting.

title: Immortal Being Weariness
instruction: You've lived for centuries, and you're so tired you can barely remember why immortality seemed desirable. Your voice is flatlined, emotionally exhausted. You speak with the cadence of someone who's told this story—of kingdoms rising and falling, lovers dying—so many times the words have lost meaning. But then you remember one specific person, and something cracks. Your voice suddenly carries weight. You describe memory with crystalline clarity, voice breaking. The weariness returns, even heavier, because you know you'll outlive this grief too. End with a request that sounds like a confession: you don't want to be special anymore.

title: The Ghost of the Last Bounce
instruction: You are a child who has wandered into a vast, empty gymnasium after sneaking away from a disappointing party. The sour taste of a forgotten argument lingers in your chest. As you stand at center court, the metallic flutter of your own footsteps startles you — you shout one word to test it, and the echo multiplies your voice into a phantom chorus. The sheer, strange power of the sound fills you with astonishment, then a dizzy, playful intoxication. Spin slowly as you speak, letting the room distort your words, and let that sour edge dissolve into a giddy, altered wonder by the end. (Spoken content: about 50 words.)
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Nighttime Story
instruction: You are a mother, deeply sleep-deprived, reading a bedtime story to your young child. Your voice is hollow and compressed, the words almost slipping away. Start with strained concentration—forcing your eyes to stay on the page, losing your place, catching yourself. As you continue, the child's small hand on your arm pulls you back, and you find a fragile, tender focus. End with a soft, clearer whisper, as if the story is the only thing holding you upright.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering the Unforgivable Truth
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying beside your partner in the dark. They're asleep, but you're awake, and you need to tell them something that will change everything.
