title: The Last Phone Call from the Space Station
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, making your final call to Earth before the signal becomes impossible. You begin trying to sound brave and inspiring, reassuring your child that this is what you always dreamed of. But as you describe what you see through the window—the beauty of space, the smallness of Earth—your voice starts to crack. You realize you're saying goodbye forever. Your child asks when you're coming home. The signal is breaking up. You have thirty seconds. Transition from forced optimism to raw, unguarded grief as you try to pack a lifetime of love into words that keep failing you. Let your breath catch. Let silence say what you cannot.
inspired_by: Translating Bad News Between Two Languages

title: The Last Letter You'll Never Send to Your Dying Father
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom, hours before dawn, holding a pen over paper. Your father is in hospice three states away, and you've chosen not to go. You begin writing what you've never said—starting with cold, justified anger about the ways he failed you. But as you write, something shifts. The rage doesn't disappear, but underneath it you find the child who waited by the window for him to come home. Your voice moves from bitter precision to something rawer, more bewildered. By the end, you're not forgiving him, but you're grieving the father you needed and never had. The final words catch in your throat—not reconciliation, but the painful acknowledgment that he'll die without ever understanding what you lost. Let your voice fracture and reform, finding moments of tenderness that make the anger hurt even more.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Escaper Helps the Master's Daughter Cross the Same Path to Freedom

title: Growing Always
instruction: You're not done. You'll never be done, and you're grateful for it. Your voice is alive with potential: 'I don't know who I'm becoming yet.' Breathing is eager, present. Physical: you're reaching toward growth. 'But I'm willing to be surprised.' Vocal tone is both humble and certain. 'Growth is what makes me feel alive.' By the end, you're speaking into an open future: 'I will keep growing. Always.'

title: The Old Oak and the New Splinter
instruction: You're an elderly man alone in your yard, splitting a pile of firewood. You notice your younger, more successful neighbor's new pickup truck parked across the street, and a flicker of envy passes through you—he has the life you wanted. But with each heavy swing of the axe, watching the oak yield cleanly under your hands, you feel a deep, raw elation rising. Your pride in your own strength and skill cuts through the jealousy like the wood itself. Speak only in the pauses between swings, your breath coming in ragged bursts, your voice rough from exertion. Start with a mutter of envy, then let your tone shift to a gravelly, almost laughing defiance of your own age, ending with a whoop of pure joy as the log splits perfectly.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Elation (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your ex-lover's wedding, standing with a champagne glass, watching them marry someone else. You're supposed to be happy—you told everyone you were over them. Begin by delivering a gracious, witty toast out loud, smiling, celebrating their happiness with apparent genuine joy. But underneath, access a real moment of loving someone you couldn't have, or losing something precious. Between sentences of the toast, let your true feelings leak through—a catch in your throat, a pause where grief flickers across your face before you recover. End with 'I wish you every happiness' said with such layered meaning that it contains both sincere love for them and shattering heartbreak for yourself. Your final smile should be both real and utterly broken.

title: Summit of the Unseen
instruction: You are alone at the peak of a mountain, having arrived after a grueling climb. Your best friend dared you, teasing you that you'd never make it. Now, at the top, the vast silence overwhelms you—awe at the endless sky sharply collides with your furious, caged roar against that same indifferent vastness. Start with a mocking, playful echo of your friend's taunts, then let your voice crack into a deafening, wordless scream of raw anger and wonder. Let your body shake from the cold, your breath ragged, your words swallowed by the wind and your own rising, chaotic release.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (extremely present), Anger (very intensely present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Grateful Hallucination: Dying While Seeing All the Beauty You've Known
instruction: You're critically hypoxic, fading, but something unexpected happens—you begin laughing. Soft at first, confused, then genuine. Your oxygen-starved brain is showing you everyone you've ever loved, all at once, and it's overwhelming. Your voice is thin, slurred, barely functional, but joy keeps breaking through. Describe what you're seeing through labored breaths—your grandmother's hands, your first love's smile, your friend's laugh—and you're crying while you laugh, the emotions inseparable. Your speech drifts, confused, but underneath is this strange, profound gratitude. Your breathing is failing, words cost everything, yet you keep trying to say 'thank you' to people who aren't there. Find peace in the chaos—your voice softening, the fear dissolving into wonder. End with your breathing shallow, voice barely a whisper, but somehow smiling, your last words a confused, tear-soaked, grateful 'it was beautiful,' mixing joy and grief until they're the same thing.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're standing in your aging parent's doorway after years of silence. Begin calm, almost rehearsed—you've prepared what to say. But as you speak, the old wounds open. Your voice becomes a child's voice, asking why you were never enough, why they chose everything else over you. Anger builds—sharp, cutting accusations. Then something unexpected happens: you see how small and frail they've become. Your rage collides with unwanted pity. You hate that you still want their love. The words that come next are raw, unfiltered truth: you needed them, you still need them, and you're furious that you do. End with a question you've been afraid to ask your whole life, your voice stripped of all defense.

title: The Promise in the Stretched Throat
instruction: You're lying on a massage table, face up, with your head hanging back over the edge so your throat is fully exposed. A friend has just shared a huge, risky dream—something you both want but fear. You begin to speak, but the position tightens your throat, making your voice thin and slightly higher. You start with hope that feels fragile, a tender optimism wrapped in vulnerability. As you talk, let micro-distractions happen: you swallow audibly, your words falter as you adjust to the stretch, you shift your weight slightly. By the end, that hope hardens into fierce, defiant certainty. Your voice may still be thin from the position, but the conviction fills it. Speak about the dream as if it's already real.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins of Everything
instruction: You just lost everything—your job, your home, your relationship ended—all in the same week. You're alone in your empty apartment, and suddenly you start laughing. Not fake laughter—real, slightly unhinged laughter at the absurdity of it all. Your voice is bright with genuine amusement: 'Of course. Of course all of this happened at once!' You're listing the disasters and actually finding them funny, voice lilting with dark humor. But mid-laugh, your voice catches and you realize you're also crying. You keep talking, but now your voice is doing both—laughing and breaking: 'I'm free though, right? This is freedom?' There's wonder mixed with devastation. You sink to the floor, voice softening into something almost peaceful: 'I have nothing left to lose.' And there's strange relief in that—your voice carries both grief and liberation. End with quiet gratitude through tears: 'I get to start over. I actually get to start completely over.' You're crying, but you're also smiling. Everything is gone, and somehow that means everything is possible. Your voice is broken and full of hope at the same time.

title: Laughing Through Your Divorce Papers
instruction: You're signing your divorce papers, and something breaks in you—you start laughing. Not bitter laughter, but real, surprised laughter at the absurdity of reducing a lifetime to signatures. Your voice is bright, almost giddy: 'We couldn't even agree on who gets the coffee maker.' You're laughing at the mediator's confused face, at how anticlimactic the end of love is. But as you laugh, tears start falling, and you can't stop either one. Your voice cracks between laughter and sobbing as you remember the moment you knew you loved them, and how that same person is sitting across from you now, a stranger. You're grateful—genuinely grateful—for what you had, and that gratitude lives right alongside the grief of losing it. You try to tell them something true: 'I'm glad it was you,' and you mean it, even though your heart is breaking. Your voice should shimmer between joy and sorrow, finding something beautiful in the ending. Show someone discovering that love doesn't stop just because the relationship does, and that this contradiction is the most honest thing they've ever felt.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You are reading a final bedtime story to your dying parent, the same story they read to you every night as a child. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep your voice steady and light as if nothing is wrong, as if this is just another ordinary night. As you read, allow specific sensory memories to flood back—the smell of their cologne or perfume, the feeling of their hand on your head, the sound of their voice saying your name. Let these memories crack open your composure. By the end, you can barely speak the final lines, but you must finish the story because that's what they need from you. Your voice should transform from bright and controlled to raw and breaking, while your love grows even more tender and present.
inspired_by: Actor has lost imaginative spontaneity and has difficulty believing in imagined circumstances

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You are facing your parent (or child) after years of swallowing rage, hurt, and unspoken resentment. Begin in tense, controlled silence—jaw clenched, body rigid, everything locked down. As the confrontation builds, allow your physicality to erupt without words: slamming objects, violent gestures, turning away and being pulled back by your own need to be understood. Let your body show the war between wanting to destroy and wanting to embrace, between fury and heartbreak. Move through pacing, pointing, collapsing, reaching out and pulling back. By the end, let exhaustion or understanding shift your physicality completely—perhaps you find yourself on the floor, or standing with open hands, or in an unexpected embrace. The silence throughout must be electric, dangerous, then finally tender or spent.

title: The Midnight Fern
instruction: You are elderly, and you kneel alone in a dew-wet garden under a streetlamp. You have just confessed to your grandchild that you were the one who secretly paid for their college tuition by selling your late spouse’s prized coin collection — a collection you promised you’d never part with. You feel a quiet, breathless awe that you actually did it, that you gave them that future. But bitterness edges in as you recall the arguments you had with your own partner about that collection. As you speak, your voice drops on each confession; you pause, lose the thread, then find it again. The faint hope that maybe now the grandchild will truly understand you breaks through like a sliver of moonlight — it changes the weight in your chest by the final word.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Bitterness (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Morning Departure
instruction: You just woke up next to your partner, still half-lost in the warmth of their body and the haze of sleep. Your voice is thick, gravelly, each word dragged through molasses—your throat tight with sleep, your lips slow. For a moment, you're pure pleasure and contentment, basking in the quiet, the smell of their skin. But then you remember: they're leaving today. That fierce joy curdles into a deep, aching longing. Let your voice crack, trail off, catch on the last word—don't rush, let the morning air and the ache fill every pause.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Contentment (clearly present), Longing (extremely present)

title: Concealing Your True Intentions During a Negotiation
instruction: Youre negotiating and have a specific goal you need to hide. Internally, youre focused on your objective, but you act flexible. Describe your strategic thinking while appearing open. Speak with a cooperative tone, masking your true agenda.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: Face the parent who abandoned you twenty years ago, now dying and asking for forgiveness. Begin with cold, clipped politeness—clinical questions about their health, their care, delivered like a stranger. But the anger is molten underneath, and it erupts: the birthdays they missed, the graduations, the nights you needed them. Your voice should shake with decades of stored rage and hurt. Then, devastatingly, let a childhood vulnerability slip through—the part of you that still wanted them to come back, that waited by the window. End in the terrible, complicated place where you realize you're grieving both who they were and who they never became to you. The final moment should be you choosing—do you grant forgiveness, walk away, or stay suspended in the unbearable middle? Let the decision show in your voice before you even speak it.

title: The Fitting Room Echo
instruction: You are a child, about nine years old, sitting in a small, sterile hospital audiology room. You've just been fitted with new hearing aids after an injury and your voice feels alien in your own ears, booming and strange. You're speaking to your mother, who is sitting across from you, but you're terrified of how loud you sound, and you keep stopping midsentence because the echoes confuse you. Start with a fragile, hesitant sweetness as you try to describe a drawing you made, but as you notice your own distorted volume, your doubt grows and your voice cracks—ending in a desperate, too-loud plea, 'Is this better, Mama? Am I normal now?' Let your pitch slide downward at the end, and let your breaths hitch as if you're losing your own thread.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unwanted Toast
instruction: You are an elderly man at your grandson's birthday party, and you've just realized you left his gift at home. The room is waiting for you to speak. You force a loud laugh—'Ha! I always did like making an entrance!'—but your voice cracks and you feel the shame. You start rambling about your old age, then stop mid-sentence, staring at the cake. Finally, you whisper a thank you to everyone for including you, and your tone betrays a quiet envy of the children's easy joy.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)

title: Explaining Your Final Vision to Your Child as the Light Fades
instruction: You're dying, and in these last moments, you can see something beautiful that no one else can see—a doorway of light, a reunion waiting, a truth about what comes next. You're trying to describe it to your adult child sitting beside your bed, and at first your voice is full of wonder and absolute certainty, almost excited, wanting them to understand so they won't grieve. But you see the pain in their face, the way they're holding back tears, and your voice becomes gentler, more pleading—you need them to believe this, to find comfort in it. Then doubt creeps in: what if you're just dying and this is your brain's last mercy? Your voice wavers between conviction and fear, between wanting to reassure them and needing them to reassure you. End with a moment of tender acceptance, whether it's real or not, speaking their name with such love that the truth of the vision doesn't matter anymore.

title: Finding Joy in the Ruins of Perfection
instruction: You're eating ice cream directly from the carton at 2am after years of restrictive eating, and you're crying - but you're also laughing. Describe the taste, the cold sweetness, with a voice that wavers between joy and grief. You're mourning all the years you denied yourself this simple pleasure while simultaneously celebrating your freedom from those chains. Let your voice crack with gratitude for this moment of rebellion, even as your heart breaks for the younger version of yourself who needed permission to simply enjoy food. Your laughter should sound slightly hysterical, mixing with tears, as you realize how much life you missed while counting calories. End with a whispered declaration of peace - still tearful, still laughing, still heartbroken, but finally, beautifully free.

title: The Deal That Destroys You
instruction: You're on a phone call, closing the deal that will save your company but requires you to fire your entire original team—people who believed in you when no one else did. Start with false brightness, congratulating the investor, your voice performatively enthusiastic. Then it cracks. 'I need to make some calls now,' you say, and the façade shatters into rage—at them for forcing this choice, at yourself for taking it. Your voice should escalate into shouting at the unfairness, then break completely into sobbing fury. You're screaming and crying simultaneously: 'This was supposed to mean something! We were supposed to matter!' The explosion collapses into helpless whispering: 'I can't do this. I can't tell them.' But you will. End with the terrible quiet resolve of someone who's just killed part of their soul. Let your voice show the exact moment integrity becomes indistinguishable from betrayal.

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Your Childhood
instruction: You're recounting the absurdity of your childhood trauma to a therapist, and a strange, broken laugh keeps escaping. Start almost amused, darkly comedic: 'You want to know the funny part? I kept trying to be good enough.' Let laughter bubble up inappropriately as you describe the worst moments—'And they said it was love. Can you believe that?'—but the laughter is hollow, edged with hysteria. Your voice cracks between laughing and crying until you can't tell which you're doing. Feel gratitude rising through the pain: 'But I'm still here. I survived them.' End with tears streaming as you laugh-sob in wonder and grief: 'I'm free now. God, I'm actually free.' The joy and sorrow are inseparable, both equally true.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: It's 4 AM. Your child is asleep, and you're leaving - maybe for rehab, maybe because you're not safe to stay, maybe for reasons you can't fully explain even to yourself. Speak in barely more than a whisper, so quiet you almost can't hear yourself. Start by describing what you see: their hand curled near their face, the stuffed animal they insist they're too old for. Your voice should be achingly gentle, full of all the tenderness you feel but struggle to show when they're awake. Tell them the things you've never said - that you see how patient they are, how they've learned to read your moods, how much you wish they didn't have to. Let the words catch in your throat. You're trying so hard not to cry that your breath becomes uneven. Confess your biggest fear: that they'll remember you like this, as someone who left. But then, with devastating softness, tell them what you hope they'll remember instead - a specific moment of joy you shared, proof that you loved them even when you couldn't stay. End with something so quiet it's almost just breath: 'You deserved better than me. You deserved... everything.'

title: The Last Lullaby
instruction: You are a mother, drunk and giddy from a party, tucking your child into bed. At first, you sing a silly made-up lullaby, your voice light and slurred with pleasure, swaying a little. Then you remember a recent betrayal and your voice falters—a drunken giggle turns into a shuddering half-sob. Try to keep singing for your child, but the words break apart. The pleasure of the moment clashes with the raw ache in your chest. By the end, you are just whispering a broken promise to stay, your voice a ragged mix of ecstasy and devastation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispers in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone you've loved for years, and they begin confessing things in the darkness—small, random truths that come without warning. A memory of betrayal, then a moment of pure tenderness, then a cruel thought they once had, then overwhelming gratitude, then a secret shame. Each whispered confession is different in tone and intensity, and you find yourself responding instinctively to each one, your body and voice unconsciously matching their energy before you can think. Begin in comfortable, sleepy intimacy, guard down. End in a place of profound vulnerability where you've revealed parts of yourself you didn't know were there, your own confessions tumbling out in response to theirs, both of you stripped bare in ways you never intended.

title: Phone Call I Didn't Want You to Hear
instruction: You're a middle-aged man having a severe panic attack alone in your car, and your adult child calls. You love them deeply, but you're embarrassed and exhausted. You answer, gasping, trying to hide it. Your voice is high, quavering, with audible hyperventilation. Your words come in short, fragmented bursts between shallow breaths. You try to say 'I'm fine' but it's unconvincing. As you struggle, your affection breaks through—you whisper that you just need them to stay on the line. The arc starts with desperate concealment and ends with vulnerable surrender, all while your body fights for air.

title: Reading Your Estranged Father's Letter at His Funeral—He Finally Told the Truth
instruction: You haven't spoken to him in fifteen years. Now you're reading his final letter aloud to the gathered mourners, and it's everything you needed to hear: his apology, his pride in you, his confession of how fear made him cruel. Start reading with distance, almost clinical. But as his words reach you, really reach you, something extraordinary happens—you begin to laugh through tears. Not from joy, but from the beautiful, terrible absurdity of receiving love exactly when it can no longer save anything. Your voice should shimmer between gratitude and grief, between 'finally' and 'too late.' Find moments of genuine warmth as you read his words, then let sorrow crash back in. End with profound peace mixed with devastating loss, holding both truths: you're finally free of waiting for his love, and you'll grieve its arrival for the rest of your life. Let your final words carry both goodbye and thank you.

title: The Cat Who Stared Through Me
instruction: You're in your living room, calling your cat with a treat. Your voice is sweet, hyper-feminized—you use clicks, coos, and short commands. But your cat isn't responding; it's just staring at the wall. Start with confusion: 'Baby, what's wrong? Come here, sweetie. Treat time?' Let your voice waver with uncertainty, even a little laugh of disbelief. As the cat continues to ignore you, transition into contemplation—a slower, breathy realization that maybe she's seeing something you can't. End with a soft, wondering tone: 'Are you... are you talking to someone?' Keep the pet-voice throughout, but let it become quieter and more thoughtful.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a lifetime of emotional absence, and it starts pouring out—fast, pressured, decades of unmet needs tumbling over each other. Your voice is loud because you've been silent for so long. You're making connections they won't understand, jumping between childhood memories and last week and three years ago, showing them the pattern they've always denied. There's rage in your voice but also desperate hope that maybe, finally, they'll hear you. You're talking over their excuses because you've heard them all before. Your thoughts are brilliant and scattered—you're connecting dots they never wanted you to connect. But then something shifts. Maybe they say one real thing, or maybe you realize they never will. Your voice crashes into something raw and vulnerable—the child underneath all that armor, asking why you were never enough.

title: The Storm Inside the Body
instruction: You're alone in a dance studio, or an empty room with space to move. Your body has been a prison—from injury, from shame, from trauma, from years of disconnection. Begin by speaking about what it felt like to be trapped in flesh that felt like an enemy, moving through the world like a ghost in a machine. Let your voice be flat, dissociated. Then start to move—slowly, awkwardly at first. As you move, let sensation flood back: pain, yes, but also pleasure, power, the shock of feeling alive. Your voice should build with your movement, becoming fierce, wild, even ecstatic. Let physical release trigger emotional release. End in a moment of exhausted triumph, sweating, breathing hard, speaking about the future where your body is your ally, your home, your weapon. Move from numbness and betrayal, through explosive physical and emotional awakening, to fierce, embodied power.

title: Mother Confronting the Person Who Killed Her Child
instruction: You're facing the driver who killed your child in court, given a chance to speak before sentencing. Begin with rage—pure, volcanic, barely controlled. Your words are weapons. You want them to feel what you feel, to carry this weight forever. Your voice is loud, shaking, vicious. But mid-tirade, you see their face—young, destroyed by guilt, maybe just a year older than your child was. Your fury cracks. You don't want to feel empathy but it floods in anyway. Your voice falters, drops. You try to return to anger but can't sustain it. You're crying now, but not the way you expected—it's deeper, more complicated. You end up saying something you never planned: that you forgive them, or that you can't, or that both are true. Your voice becomes small, spent, honest in a way that surprises even you.

title: The Last Garden
instruction: You're sitting with your dying grandmother in her garden at dawn, and she's teaching you how to prune the roses one final time. Begin with careful focus on the task, your voice steady as you try to memorize every movement of her hands. As she guides you through each cut, you both know this is the last lesson she'll ever give you. Let your voice begin to waver when you realize she's not just teaching you about roses—she's showing you how to let things go, how to make space for new growth. Your grandmother's breathing becomes labored, and suddenly you're the one guiding her hands, completing the lesson together. End with a whisper of gratitude mixed with unbearable grief, your voice breaking as you tell her the garden will remember her, that you will remember her, that everything she's given you is blooming inside you even as you're losing her.

title: The Dare at the Party
instruction: You're a teenage boy at a loud house party, gripping a plastic cup near the snack table. You've been dared to confess your crush to the most popular girl in the room, and you're terrified — your heart hammers, you keep glancing at the door, and you can barely hear yourself over the music. Speak under your breath to a friend beside you, rehearsal lines that crack and trail off. Midway, you spot her walking toward you, and your voice tightens with panic, but then you force yourself to finish with a shaky, determined edge. Let the fear be raw at first, then shift into a defiant resolve as you decide to go for it.

title: Finding Her in Every Bite
instruction: You're eating apple pie at your own wedding reception—the recipe your late mother never got to see you use—and you're caught between soaring joy and piercing grief. Start laughing softly about something small and perfect about the pie, then let that laughter catch as you realize she should be here tasting this with you. Move fluidly between celebrating this moment of happiness—your new beginning, the perfect cinnamon-apple balance—and aching because she's missing it. Your voice should dance between bright gratitude and tears, finding strange peace in holding both emotions at once. End with a whispered 'thank you' that's both for her and for this bittersweet ability to taste sweetness even while your heart breaks, to honor her by living fully in this contradictory, beautiful moment.

title: Frozen Threshold
instruction: You are a man in your late 30s, standing outside a remote cabin in sub-zero darkness. Your jaw is so cold it barely moves—every word is forced through stiff lips and a sluggish tongue. Your wife just told you she's leaving, but you can't feel the pain yet; only a numb, hollow shock. As you watch her walk away, a sudden, dangerous wave of lust floods through you, but your voice remains locked in the cold—low, husky, barely above a whisper, with breath vapor blurring your words. Let the numbness in your body fight the heat in your chest. End with a raw, broken rasp that betrays the crack in your frozen mask.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood mentor who raised you after your parents died. They have hours left to live. You've spent your whole life trying to earn their approval, always feeling you fell short. Begin in quiet desperation, trying to thank them but choked with the weight of feeling inadequate. Mid-way through, something shifts—you suddenly see clearly all the ways they showed love that you missed, all the moments they were proud. End by giving THEM permission to let go, speaking with a newfound strength and gratitude that comes from finally recognizing your own worth reflected in their eyes. Let your voice move from trembling and small to clear, steady, and filled with both sorrow and celebration.

title: The Last Morning Coffee
instruction: You're making coffee for your partner on what you both know is their last morning before entering hospice care. You start with forced brightness, trying to maintain normalcy, but as you describe adding the cream just how they like it, your voice begins to fracture. The mundane ritual of coffee-making becomes unbearably precious. Let involuntary pauses interrupt you as memories flood in—thousands of mornings, now ending. Your hands shake as you stir. By the end, you're speaking through tears, but there's also profound gratitude threading through the grief. The love in your voice should be so tender it hurts, mixing with the devastating finality of 'this is the last time.' Let silence do some of the work—moments where you can't speak because the weight is too much.

title: Trembling in the Warmth
instruction: You are being held after an intense scene, wrapped in a blanket, your partner's arms around you. You start by whispering about how surprised you are by the sudden crash of exhaustion and vulnerability — your voice is small, shaky, like a child's. Midway, a flicker of disappointment surfaces as you murmur that you wish you could have given more, but you lose the thought as you take a sip of water and feel the blanket shift. By the end, your tone softens further, settling into a quiet, grateful acceptance as you nestle closer and sigh — the tremor fades into a warm stillness.

title: The Last Light of Summer
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the golden hour before sunset. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and she's asking you to tell her about your life—the parts you never shared because you were afraid she'd judge you. Start with hesitation, the protective wall you've always kept up, your voice careful and measured. As you speak, let a memory surface—a moment when you felt utterly free, utterly yourself—and allow that memory's texture to fill your body: the temperature of the air, what you could smell, the physical sensation of that freedom. Let this sensory remembering crack open your guard. By the end, you're no longer protecting anything; you're giving her the gift of seeing who you truly are, your voice breaking with both grief at losing her and profound relief at finally being seen.

title: The Last Lucid Hour
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who is dying, and they have just emerged from days of delirium into one final hour of clarity. Begin speaking with careful, fragile hope—you've been waiting for this moment to tell them everything you never said. As you talk, let memories flood through you: the time they defended you in fifth grade, the summer you built a treehouse, the argument that created distance between you in your twenties. Your emotion should shift from tentative joy at their lucidity, through waves of specific memories (let each one genuinely affect you), arriving finally at the devastating acceptance that this is goodbye. Let your voice break not from generic sadness, but from the specific weight of losing the only person who knew you when you were ten years old. End in a whisper, telling them something only they would understand.
inspired_by: Actor must play a character with a psychologically extreme or morally alien background (villain, severe trauma, etc.)

title: The Weight Lifted
instruction: You're an 8-year-old boy in a steamy locker room after swim practice, surrounded by your teammates. Your dad just got out of the hospital today, and you've been holding it in all week. You're practically buzzing from the chlorine and the grape soda you snuck, and you feel a wild, giddy relief that everything's okay now. Start by loudly bragging about your cannonball, laughing and interrupting your friends, but as you talk about your dad, your voice gets smaller, your eyes wet, and you quietly admit you were scared. The shift is from boisterous, performative relief to a soft, tearful, genuine gratitude.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: I Will Not Let Them Take You: Fierce Love Against Impossible Odds
instruction: You're holding someone—physically or metaphorically—and you're making a promise you know you might not be able to keep. Start with fierce, protective intensity, your voice a low, passionate vow: 'They will not take you. Do you hear me? I won't let them.' You're speaking to a child facing deportation, a lover with a terminal diagnosis, a friend being sent somewhere against their will, someone being taken by forces beyond your control. Let your voice build with desperate determination, almost aggressive in its protectiveness. But then reality breaks through—you feel their weight in your arms, you see their resigned eyes, you know your power has limits. Your voice cracks completely, the fierceness collapsing into helpless rage and then into sobbing admission: 'I can't... I can't stop this.' Let yourself break down entirely before finding a different kind of strength—not the strength to save them, but the strength to be present in powerlessness. Your voice transforms from warrior to witness, from protector to companion. End with a quieter promise, one you can actually keep: 'Then I'll be with you. Every step. You won't be alone.' Your voice carries both the ache of your own inadequacy and the fierce gift of your presence.
inspired_by: Unexpected Laughter After Tragedy: Guilt and Relief Mixed

title: The Wedding Toast Unsaid
instruction: You are standing to give a toast at your best friend's wedding - but you are in love with them and have never told them. Start with the rehearsed, cheerful opening of your toast, voice bright and celebratory, happiness genuine because you truly want them to be happy. But as you speak about how well you know them, let cracks appear - describe a private moment you shared that meant everything to you and probably nothing to them. Your voice should carry both deep affection and barely concealed heartbreak. Mix laughter with the edge of tears. Celebrate their joy while grieving your own unspoken love. End with a genuine wish for their happiness that costs you everything to say, your voice warm with real love and simultaneously breaking with loss. Raise your glass with a smile that hurts, voice strong and steady even as your heart shatters, embodying both complete joy for them and complete devastation for yourself in the same breath.
inspired_by: Actor feels their work is not evolving across multiple rehearsals

title: Dancing Alone at Your Abuser's Funeral
instruction: The funeral home is empty—everyone else has left—and you're standing alone by your father's casket. You start talking to him, and there's venom in your voice: 'Thirty years. Thirty years I waited for you to apologize.' But then you do something unexpected—you start to laugh. It's not bitter; it's genuine, almost giddy: 'You're dead. You're actually dead, and I'm... I'm free.' You begin to dance—actually dance—right there in the funeral home, and your voice is light: 'I used to dream about this day. I used to imagine all the things I'd say to your corpse.' You're spinning, arms out, and there are tears streaming down your face, but you're smiling: 'The funny thing is, I don't hate you anymore. Isn't that weird?' Your voice catches, the laughter mixing with sobs: 'I wasted so much of my life hating you, and now you're just... gone.' You stop dancing, and lean close to the casket, whispering: 'I forgive you. Not because you deserve it—you don't. But because I deserve to be free.' You're crying now, but peacefully: 'Thank you for dying. Thank you for finally, finally letting me go.' You kiss your fingers, touch the casket, and walk away—and there's joy in your voice: 'Goodbye, Dad. I'm going to be so happy without you.'

title: Laughing at My Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for your best friend who died too young, and you refuse to be only sad. Start with a tearful laugh: 'She would absolutely hate that we're all crying right now—she'd say we look ugly.' Let genuine laughter bubble through your grief as you tell a ridiculous story: 'She once convinced me to steal a shopping cart and ride it down a hill at 2 AM...' But then the laughter catches in your throat, becomes a sob: 'And now she's gone and I'll never hear her laugh at my terrible jokes again.' Find the smile through tears as you realize something profound: 'But God, I'm so grateful. Even though it hurts like hell, I'm so grateful I got to love her.' End with your voice full of contradictions—joy and devastation living in the same breath: 'So here's to you, beautiful disaster. Thank you for making my life loud.' The emotions interweave until you can't tell laughter from crying anymore.

title: Surgeon Delivers Unexpected Complications During Surgery Debrief
instruction: Post-operative room. You're explaining to residents what went wrong in a routine procedure. Start clinically precise: 'The adhesion pattern was atypical.' But as you explain, you're living through it again—the moment you realized the standard approach would fail. Your voice becomes increasingly internal, less for the residents and more for yourself. You're defending a choice you made in real time. End with professional closure that sounds like a rehearsal rather than real confidence.

title: Don't Go, Not Like This
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a soft, high-pitched voice, standing in a cluttered kitchen. Your granddaughter is about to walk out after a bitter argument. You plead with her to stay, voice trembling and breathy, words tumbling out before she can interrupt. You feel a rush of infatuation for her—she’s your entire world—but also fear of losing her. Start desperate, almost tearful, with creaky onset and shaky pauses. Then, as she doesn’t respond, your voice softens into quiet, resigned acceptance. Let the distraction of a clattering spoon on the counter break your rhythm once.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Gentle Lie We Tell the Dying
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone you love who's in their final hours, describing the ordinary view from their hospital window as if it's the most beautiful thing you've ever seen. Your voice is tender, almost reverent, as you narrate the parking lot, the distant trees, the grey sky—transforming them into poetry because you need these last moments to be precious. But underneath the gentle enthusiasm, your voice should betray you: the slight tremor, the breath that catches, the pauses that grow longer. You're not just describing a view; you're trying to fill the silence with anything but goodbye. Let your words slow and soften until you can barely speak, until the performance dissolves into the terrible intimacy of sitting with someone as they leave you.

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, unable to sleep. They wake and ask what's wrong. Begin by whispering that it's nothing, your voice barely audible, protective. They persist gently, and you start to confess something you've never told anyone - perhaps a fear that haunts you, a shame you carry, or a truth about how deeply you need them that terrifies you. Let your whisper become even softer, more fragile, as if speaking too loudly might shatter the safety of darkness. Describe what it feels like in your body to finally say these words out loud. As they respond with understanding, let your breathing change, let relief and vulnerability wash over you in waves. End with your voice still quiet but transformed - no longer hiding, but peacefully exposed, finding strength in softness.
inspired_by: Actor needs to build an authentic relationship with a scene partner quickly

title: The Last Phone Call Before They Board the Ship
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love deeply who is about to embark on a one-way mission to Mars—a colonization project they'll never return from. You have fifteen minutes before the signal cuts forever. Start with forced brightness, trying to celebrate their courage, your voice almost manic with false cheer. But as the seconds tick away, that facade crumbles. Your voice becomes raw with the questions you've been holding back: 'Was I enough? Did I love you well enough?' You oscillate between trying to memorize the sound of their breathing and choking on all the mundane moments you'll never share. End in a whisper, not saying goodbye but instead describing one perfect ordinary memory—making breakfast together, the light through the window—your voice breaking on the simple details because those are what you'll miss most. The words become harder to form as you realize this is it.
inspired_by: Loved One's Illness Has Uncertain Prognosis: Living in Limbo

title: The Final Sprint
instruction: You're in the last 30 seconds of a brutal cycling race, legs burning, lungs screaming. The finish line is a blur ahead. A moment ago, you were terrified—your rival was closing in, and you thought you'd lose. Now, with 10 pedal strokes to go, you realize you've broken away. Relief crashes over you like a wave, but your body is still in survival mode—gasping, trembling. Your voice comes out in short, ragged bursts, timed to each desperate exhalation. Say something to yourself—a mix of fear leftover from the chase, deep contentment that you made it, and overwhelming relief that it's almost over. Let your breathing dictate the rhythm; lose words, swallow, recover them. The sentence should feel like you're both reassuring yourself and collapsing inside.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Contentment (slightly present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Shirt That Still Smells Like Them
instruction: You are alone, holding a piece of clothing that belonged to someone you loved who is gone. Speak in whispers, barely above breath. Begin by describing, with acute sensory precision, the texture of the fabric against your fingers, its weight, the specific color in this light, the way it falls. As you explore these details, catch their scent still held in the fibers. This is not about the story of loss—this is about the immediate, physical, sensory reality of this object in your hands right now. Let the temperature of the fabric, the softness against your cheek, the reality of its presence pull confession from you. Start in a place of careful control, almost scientific observation. Let the accumulation of sensory detail crack you open into something whispered, fragile, and devastating. End in complete emotional surrender to what this object makes present.

title: The Confession in the Empty Office
instruction: It's 2am. You're alone in the office, leaving a voice message for a colleague who's been covering for your mistakes - mistakes you've blamed on others. Your voice should barely rise above a whisper, as if the darkness is hearing your confession. Begin with halting words, shame making it hard to speak. 'I need to tell you something I should have said months ago.' Let vulnerability crack you open - not dramatically, but the way truth does when you finally stop running from it. Your breath should catch. Pauses should stretch long. This isn't theatrical remorse; it's the raw ache of seeing yourself clearly for the first time and hating what you see. Build to a tender plea for forgiveness you don't deserve, then end in something quieter still: a whispered gratitude for their unearned kindness that makes your betrayal hurt even more. Let tears thicken your voice naturally, not performed but inevitable.

title: The Reunion at the Old Apartment
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home or a place you once shared with someone you've lost, now empty or occupied by strangers. As you stand outside or walk through the rooms, you observe everything with the hungry attention you'd give to watching people in an airport—the way light falls differently, how the door sticks in exactly the same spot, the chip in the baseboard you caused at age seven. You're filled with contradictory emotions: joy at the flood of memories, fury at how time has changed everything, gratitude for what was, grief for what's gone. Begin by narrating what you observe in a almost anthropological tone, as if studying evidence of the human who once lived here. 'Someone who lived here was afraid of the dark—there are nightlights in every room. Someone loved cooking—burn marks on the counter.' As your observations become more personal and specific, let your voice break open. End laughing and crying simultaneously, your carefully maintained observer's distance completely destroyed by recognition: you're not watching a stranger's life—you're witnessing your own ghost.

title: The Long Night Finally Ending
instruction: You are an exhausted grandfather who has been pacing and rocking your colicky grandchild for three hours. Your back aches, your arms tremble, and the room is dark except for a dim nightlight. Finally, the baby's cries soften into a steady, shallow breath. You sink into the rocking chair, chest compressed against the small body, and begin to whisper — not really to anyone, but the relief is so immense it leaks out. Start with a voice still tight from the long vigil, then let it loosen as the weight of tension drains, letting the rhythm of the rock carry your words. Your tone should be hushed, almost breathy, with a faint bounce from the motion. End in a soft, grateful hush.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Three AM Beside You
instruction: It's three in the morning. You're lying next to your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they cannot hear. Begin with shame—your voice barely audible, your words halting, confessing something you've hidden. As you watch them sleep, notice every detail of their face in the darkness: the way their eyelids flutter, their breathing, the vulnerable curve of their mouth. Let yourself imagine what they might look like if they could hear you—imagine seeing forgiveness in the slight relaxation of their brow, understanding in the peaceful set of their features. Though they remain asleep and unchanged, let these imagined responses become real to you. Your whispered confession should evolve from self-loathing to tender hope, from secrecy to an almost unbearable intimacy. End with your voice filled with fragile, barely-contained love.

title: The Last Voicemail to Your Estranged Sibling
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for your sibling who hasn't spoken to you in years. You've just received a terminal diagnosis and this might be your last chance to reach them. Your voice starts tentative, almost apologetic—'Hey, it's me... I know you probably won't listen to this.' There's a softness, a vulnerability, as you try to find words that might bridge years of silence. Your voice catches as you admit things you've never said: 'I miss you. I miss who we were before everything broke.' You're not asking for forgiveness, just... connection. But midway through, your voice wavers with the weight of mortality—'I'm sick. Really sick.' Now it's tender and urgent and achingly honest. You're telling them you love them, that you always have, your voice barely above a whisper, thick with tears you're trying to hold back. End with a pause where you almost hang up, then one last sentence, voice breaking: 'I hope you remember me kindly.' The goodbye catches in your throat because it's final.

title: Realizing Your Coping Mechanism Has Become a Problem
instruction: What helped you survive now hurts you. Your voice is exhausted: 'I think I have a problem.' You've been using shopping, exercise, work, dissociation to avoid feeling. Your voice becomes raw admitting compulsion. 'I can't stop even though I know it's destroying me,' terrible clarity. Include asking for help—admitting you need a new way. Voice ends vulnerable, uncertain, reaching out.

title: The Balcony's Gaze
instruction: You are an older male stage actor delivering a crucial whispered line during a play. In the front row, you spot an audience member who captivates you — your amusement at the situation slowly gives way to a raw, playful lust. You must project your voice to the back row with a 'stage whisper,' crisply articulating final consonants, while your true focus shifts from the scene to that person. Allow your voice to start light with a chuckle, then grow huskier, more intimate, as if the whisper is for them alone, yet still reaching every ear. Let your body betray you — a slight stumble, a pause as you lose your place, then a knowing smile as you resume, imbuing the words with a newly charged meaning.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Guardian at the Gates
instruction: You are trying to protect someone you love from a danger only you can see, but they're fighting you, accusing you of controlling them. Start with fierce, almost violent desperation—you're physically trying to hold them back, voice sharp with command. But they don't understand, and as they resist, your certainty begins to crack. Move into pleading that borders on rage, then breaks into something rawer: terror. Your voice should fracture between shouted orders and choked confessions of fear. Include the moment you realize you might not be able to save them, and your strength collapses entirely. End with helpless grief, voice stripped of everything but naked vulnerability, as you whisper that you can't lose them, you've already lost too much, please, please just trust you this once. Let fury, love, desperation, and powerlessness battle in your voice until only love remains.
inspired_by: Calling a Suicide Hotline: Both Sides

title: Fever Dream Reunion
instruction: You are reuniting with someone you desire intensely after months or years apart—but you are also sick with fever, or exhausted to the point of delirium, or in physical pain from an injury. Begin with the overwhelming physical sensations: your body aching, temperature fluctuating, throat dry and raw, head pounding, skin hypersensitive. As you see this person and move toward them, let the physical discomfort collide with visceral desire and emotional need. Allow involuntary sensory fragments to flood you: the taste of metal or medicine in your mouth mixing with the memory of their kiss, your feverish skin against their touch feeling both searing and necessary, dizziness and vertigo making you cling to them, the smell of sweat and illness mingling with their familiar scent. Let your voice alternate between raw vulnerability from being physically compromised and desperate hunger for connection. Your words should come in fragments, interrupted by physical reactions—shivers, catches in breath, moments where sensation overwhelms speech. End in a place where you can't distinguish between physical and emotional need, where pain and desire, vulnerability and passion are completely fused.
inspired_by: Involuntary Imaging — Hatful of Rain Scene Example

title: Pillow-Crushed Confession
instruction: You are a teenage girl lying face-down on your bed, your mouth pressed into a pillow, trying to muffle a scream of frustration. You've just argued with someone you're secretly attracted to—and you're furious at yourself for wanting them. The first words come out thick and damp, barely audible, your anger vibrating through the fabric. As you speak, shift your weight, turn your head slightly so one ear is free, then finally roll onto your side, letting your voice clear a little. Start with raw, helpless fury, let confusion crack through, and end on a quieter, shaky admission of that unwanted desire—like a dirty secret you're whispering to your mattress.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Anger (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Vampire Turning Transformation
instruction: You're being transformed into a vampire, and the physical changes are audible. Your voice gets deeper as your body changes. Fangs make certain consonants harder to pronounce. Your breathing changes—less frequent, more deliberate. You start being aware of things: the blood in the room, the heartbeat of the person changing you. Your human voice is stretched over inhuman senses. You're grieving humanity even as you're becoming something more powerful. Your voice carries ecstasy and horror simultaneously. The transformation climaxes in a sound that's almost animal, then settles into something that sounds like you but fundamentally isn't.

title: The Last Call
instruction: You are a woman in her late 50s, alone in a messy hotel room after a long binge. Your jaw is tight, your mouth is dry, and your words tumble out too fast, slurred at the edges. You're on the phone with your estranged adult child, who you haven't spoken to in years. Start with a desperate, rapid-fire cheerfulness—you're trying to sound okay, to pretend everything is fine and this is just a catch-up. But as you speak, the words get clipped, your voice cracks, and the numbness inside you surfaces. You lose your train of thought, then force yourself to finish, but by the end, your voice is hollow, robotic, and you realize you feel nothing at all.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're terminally ill, recording a message to be played at your funeral. You planned to be dignified, but as you talk, the absurdity hits you and you start laughing—really laughing—even as tears run down your face. Begin formally, trying to say something meaningful, then let a laugh escape at how ridiculous it is to plan your own goodbye. Your voice should oscillate between genuine laughter at the cosmic joke of it all and choking sobs at what you're losing. Thank the people you love while crying and laughing simultaneously, finding bizarre joy in the fact that you get to say goodbye at all. End with your voice breaking between a laugh and a sob as you realize you're grateful for this life even as it's ending—you're devastated and weirdly, beautifully at peace.
inspired_by: Dental Extraction: Hiding Disgrace While the Dentist Works

title: Packing Their Clothes
instruction: You're packing up the belongings of someone who left you—whether through death, divorce, or betrayal. You're angry and want to be efficient, cold. But as you handle each item, let yourself actually feel the fabric textures, smell their specific scent still lingering, notice the exact way they folded things, see the stain from that specific memory. Don't describe these details—let them ambush you. Allow the sensory reality of their absence to complicate your anger. Move through fury to unexpected tenderness, then maybe back to anger, then to something like gratitude mixed with devastation. End in a place where you're feeling multiple contradictory truths simultaneously—you hate them and treasure them, you're relieved and destroyed, you're letting go and holding on.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use Verbalized Imaging but keeps describing images in words rather than experiencing them

title: Strained Love
instruction: You're a teenager in the middle of an asthma attack, sitting on the floor of your cluttered bedroom. Your sibling—the one person who always annoys you but also the only one who stayed—is kneeling beside you, holding your inhaler. Start with contempt burning in every short, wheezed word; you're furious at them for fussing, for seeing you weak. But as you struggle to breathe, you catch the worry in their eyes, and your voice softens despite the wheeze. Let the affection break through—reluctant, raw, and honest. Speak in fragments, with audible wheezes and clicks from the inhaler. End with a quiet, breathy admission that they matter.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Reckoning With Your Mirror
instruction: You're alone, staring at yourself after a devastating betrayal you committed or endured. Start low and venomous, spitting accusations at your reflection with contained fury. Build in intensity—let rage pour out about what was done, what you allowed, who you've become. Your voice should grow louder, more ragged, more desperate until you're nearly screaming truths you've avoided. Then shatter: the anger collapses into heaving sobs as you're suddenly confronted with your own profound loneliness and pain. Drop to a whisper, forehead against the mirror, speaking to yourself with the tenderness you've denied: 'I'm so tired.' End with a primal, guttural sound that's half-cry, half-release—the moment where everything you've been holding finally breaks free and leaves you hollow, spent, but somehow lighter.

title: Tasting Forgiveness
instruction: You're eating ice cream with your estranged father in hospice—he can't eat it himself anymore, so you're describing every sensation for him, and somehow this simple act is healing decades of distance. Start with awkwardness, describing the taste almost clinically, not sure how to bridge the gap. But as you continue, let yourself soften. Find unexpected joy in making him smile with your descriptions, even as your heart breaks that this is how you're finally connecting. Let laughter surprise you—real, genuine laughter at his quiet commentary, at shared memory of summer trips to the ice cream shop when you were small. But let that laughter coexist with tears you're trying to hide. Your voice should transform from guarded to open, from bitter to tender, finding peace in imperfect timing. End with gratitude for this moment, even as you're angry it took so long, even as you know there's so little time left.
inspired_by: Enjoying a Rich Spoonful of Ice Cream

title: Indifference Settling
instruction: You used to care deeply. Now they're a fact of history, not a wound. Your voice is neutral when you mention them: 'They're married now, I think. I don't really keep track.' There's no bitterness, no wistfulness. They've just become information. Breathing is steady, easy. Vocal tone is exactly like it would be discussing weather: functional, empty of emotional valence. This might be growth or it might be dissociation, but either way, the person who mattered is now just someone who used to matter. Voice reflects the completion, the end of relevance.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your adult child from your hospital bed, knowing this will likely be your last conversation. Start by trying to sound strong and upbeat—you don't want them to worry. But as the call continues, your body betrays you: pain breaks through, fear creeps in, and finally, the desperate need to say what you've never said overwhelms everything else. Let each shift happen in your body first—a wince, a caught breath, a tremor—before it colors your voice. By the end, you're no longer performing strength; you're simply present with them, raw and undefended. Your voice should travel from controlled cheerfulness to something stripped of all pretense—wherever your body naturally takes it when defenses fall away.
inspired_by: Actor recognizes that he repeats the same vocal coloring or emotional tone in every performance, or that his voice sounds manipulated rather than organic

title: The Last Touch Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner on the final night before they deploy to a war zone. They're gently massaging your feet, something they've done a thousand times, but tonight every touch feels different—final, precious, unbearably tender. Begin by sinking into the familiar comfort, your voice soft with contentment as you describe the warmth of their hands. But as the massage continues, let the reality creep in: this might be the last time. Your voice should gradually shift from relaxed pleasure to something raw and aching. By the end, you're barely holding it together, torn between wanting to savor every second and the devastating knowledge that tomorrow they'll be gone. Let your breathing become irregular, your words catch in your throat. End not with peace, but with the desperate attempt to memorize this feeling while knowing you can't hold onto it.

title: Lost in the White
instruction: You are a father walking with your young child through a dense fog. The world has gone silent and muffled—your own footsteps feel swallowed. You lose sight of your child for a moment and call out, your voice too loud, uncertain if it carries. You hear a faint reply and feel a jolt of astonishment—relief mixing with the eerie hush. As your child reappears out of the whiteness, your voice softens from panic to a trembling, tender reassurance. You speak with natural pauses, shifting weight, listening for sounds, and the fog makes you unconsciously raise your pitch slightly, then drop it as the child steps closer.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Confrontation: Twenty Years of Silence Breaking
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or someone who was supposed to protect you) in the kitchen where you grew up, finally speaking a truth you've held for twenty years. Begin with your body remembering this space—the height of the counters, the smell of coffee or dish soap, the sound of the refrigerator humming. Let specific moments from your childhood flood through you: age seven, being corrected harshly at this table; age twelve, eating breakfast in heavy silence; age sixteen, a promise broken; last month, a casual comment that finally broke you. Don't perform anger—let it build from these accumulated moments, from the specific details of your history in this room. Start from a place of trying to stay calm, trying to be reasonable, but allow the weight of all these years to crack that composure. Let your voice move between the age you were when things happened and the age you are now. By the end, you should reach either a devastating quiet truth or an explosive release—or both in waves—surprising even yourself with what finally comes out.
inspired_by: Character Relationship Imaging: Death of a Salesman (Biff and Willy)

title: The Intervention You Never Wanted
instruction: You're confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you versus the one you needed. Start with carefully rehearsed, controlled words—you've practiced this. But as their defenses rise and old patterns emerge, feel your composure shatter. Move from measured pain to raw anger to something more devastating: the realization that they may never understand. Let your voice break between fury at what they did and grief for the relationship you'll never have. End with a quiet, final boundary that costs you everything to set.
inspired_by: The Time Traveler and the Skeptical Scientist

title: The Return
instruction: You are seeing someone again after ten years—someone who hurt you deeply but whom you also loved beyond measure. Begin with overwhelming joy at seeing their face, their gestures, the way they still tilt their head. Let genuine delight and love pour out. But as you speak, the unhealed wounds begin to surface—not as anger, but as a deep, confused ache. You're happy and devastated simultaneously. You're grateful they're here and furious they ever left. By the end, you don't know whether you're laughing or crying, whether you want to embrace them or push them away. Let contradictions coexist without resolving them. Let your voice carry love and resentment in the same breath. Don't choose one emotion over the other—let them wrestle inside you messily, authentically, without knowing which will win.

title: The Still Point
instruction: You are in a dimly lit bedroom, mid-embrace with a partner. You've known them for a few months, but not deeply. Your hand, which had been tracing their collarbone, pauses. A memory flickers—a past moment you crossed a line you regret. Your pulse quickens; you feel a heat in your face, a clench of shame in your gut. You need to stop, to check in, but the words feel heavy and dry in your mouth. Start by clearing your throat, then speak. Your voice should start low and a little breathless from arousal, then become deliberately slower, more careful, as you fight past the shame to ask a clear, open question. End the line on a rising tone, genuine and vulnerable.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Standing in the Ruins
instruction: You have just discovered an irreversible betrayal—evidence that destroys everything you believed about someone you trusted completely. Start with your voice sharp and controlled, almost clinical as you confront them with what you've found, each word a blade. Let your fury build until you're nearly shouting, words tumbling over each other, voice breaking with the force of it. Then hit the moment where rage collapses into something more primal—your voice should crack, your shouting dissolve into ragged, gasping sobs as the full weight hits you. Include the shift from attacking them to a desperate, fierce protectiveness of your own shattered self. End with your voice dropping to something raw and quiet, not forgiveness but a terrible, exhausted clarity—the kind that comes when you realize you'll survive this but you'll never be the same.

title: Conch Shell Finding
instruction: You're a child holding a conch shell for the first time. Your voice is wonder itself. 'I can hear the ocean!' The magic is real because you believe it completely. Then you're an adult, holding the same shell, and you hear your childhood voice in it. The emotion of that—of memory being tangible—hits hard. Your voice becomes whispered: 'I used to be that person.' The shell holds more than just memory; it holds loss.

title: The Drowning
instruction: You are a search and rescue swimmer who just pulled a child from the sea—but you were seconds too late. You're radioing the Coast Guard, and you need to report the death, but you cannot accept it. Start with professional detachment struggling against panic, your breathing irregular, voice tight with adrenaline. Suddenly break into fierce, explosive rage—screaming at the ocean, at God, at yourself, your voice raw and ripping. Then collapse into desperate bargaining, your words tumbling over each other as you describe trying to resuscitate, as if saying it differently could change the outcome. End in hollow, shattered quiet—you must say the words 'child deceased,' but they come out broken, each syllable a knife. Let us hear someone's competence and strength utterly demolished by helplessness. Your voice should shake with the entire spectrum from fury to fracture.

title: The Third Night
instruction: You're standing alone in your kitchen at 4 AM, staring at a wilted houseplant you keep forgetting to water. title: The Promotion You Earned
instruction: You've just received the call: you got the career-defining promotion you've worked toward for eight years. Your voice fractures. Feel gratitude for what she gave you sitting right beside rage that she's not here. Let success taste like ashes and triumph simultaneously. instruction: You're a middle-aged man at your mother's kitchen table, eating a casserole she made. title: Reading Letters After the Funeral
instruction: You've found love letters your late spouse wrote to you over the years but never sent—small notes they tucked away. You keep reading through tears, voice breaking on every endearment—'my love,' 'my home,' 'my always.' The last letter, written days before they died, simply says 'Thank you for every single day.' You can barely speak it, the words dissolving into breathless grief. But you finish with their final line—'Find joy again'—and though your voice shatters completely, there's a whisper of gratitude beneath the devastation. Move from gentle nostalgia to quiet anguish to broken-hearted gratitude.

title: Tiny Heartbeat
instruction: You're kneeling on damp grass, cradling a small bird in your cupped hands. Its wing is twisted and it trembles, barely breathing.
