title: The Final Wave
instruction: You are in bed with a lover you secretly despise, but you're pretending to be infatuated. Each time you orgasm, you mutter a sweet nothing—but your voice cracks with malice. By the third climax, you can barely speak, but you force out a whispered, venomous 'I love this,' as if it hurts. Your body is shaking, you're embarrassed by your own weakness, but the malevolence wins. Let the physical exhaustion strip away your mask, leaving only hateful truth.

title: The Truth I Should Have Told You Years Ago
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the childhood you actually had versus the one they remember. title: The Vigil of Vanishing Faces
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in her final hours. The photograph on the nightstand brings back the day she defended you when no one else would. Let each object you notice pull a different emotion from you—gratitude, regret, tenderness, grief. Begin in numb shock, barely able to look at her. As you take in each meaningful object around the room, let the reality of losing her penetrate deeper, until by the end you are speaking to her with the full weight of everything she meant to you, whether in whispered words or through tears or both.

title: The Photograph in the Drawer
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting on the edge of your neatly made bed in your carpeted bedroom. As you begin to speak to no one but yourself, your words come out in halting, breathless bursts, recalling the exact angle of their smile and how the light hit their hair. The infatuation you feel now is not youthful, but deeper—a tender, aching sweetness that warms your voice even as it cracks. title: The Cavern's Whisper
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a light, almost delicate voice, exploring a vast underground cave. title: Finding Your Lost Child After 48 Hours: Relief That Feels Like Dying
instruction: You're seeing your child for the first time after they've been found—they're safe but traumatized, and you're flooded with so many contradictory feelings you can barely function. Let your voice oscillate wildly—laughing through tears, whispering fierce promises of protection while acknowledging you already failed to keep them safe. title: The Last Signal
instruction: You are standing on a narrow cliff edge at sunset, wind tearing at your coat, lungs burning from the thin air. instruction: Your partner died weeks ago, and today two things collide: your child's acceptance to their dream school and the unbearable task of packing away your partner's belongings. title: The Gravel Path Remembers
instruction: You are an elderly man walking alone on a long gravel path, the autumn leaves damp underfoot. Each step crunches loudly, forcing you to speak louder and more deliberately. title: The Hospital Room at Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning hours. She has minutes left. instruction: You are 16, in the backseat of a parked car with your boyfriend. This is your first time, and it's happening faster than you expected. instruction: You're lying in bed beside your sleeping partner at 3 AM, whispering a confession they cannot hear - something you've never admitted to anyone. By the end, let yourself arrive at an unexpected softness - perhaps even relief - as if speaking it aloud, even to silence, has changed something fundamental inside you.

title: The Echo of Defeat
instruction: You are an older woman, a former champion gymnast, standing alone in the empty gymnasium where you used to train. title: The Confession in the Hospital Hallway
instruction: Whispering to your best friend while they sleep after a suicide attempt, confess what you've never told them—how much their existence has mattered to you, how many times their simple presence saved you from your own darkness. instruction: You're finally saying what you've never said. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, your voice almost too controlled. title: Adult Child Confronts Parent Who Chose Addiction Over Them
instruction: You've driven three hours to a rehab facility for family week, and you're finally alone with your parent after fifteen years of broken promises. title: Bleeding Out for Their Attention

title: The Margin Scribble

instruction: You're confronting your father about a moment from your childhood—something he said or did that altered how you saw yourself. Begin with the anger and hurt of that original moment, letting your voice carry the wounded child you were. Accuse him, let him see the damage. But midway through, something shifts: you hear yourself and realize you sound exactly like him. Let this recognition transform the confrontation. Start finding words for what you needed then but couldn't articulate. Speak as both your child-self and your adult-self simultaneously. By the end, you're no longer attacking—you're teaching him how to repair what was broken, showing him the words that would have saved you. End not with forgiveness, but with exhausted, fragile hope that it's not too late to be seen differently.
inspired_by: Actor has identified a specific historical experience causing lasting damage to self-esteem

title: Laughing at Your Scars in the Mirror
instruction: You're alone, days after the fight, looking at your healing face in the mirror. Your speech is still affected—lisp from a broken tooth, stiffness in your jaw. Start by narrating your own injuries with dark, almost manic humor, speaking to your reflection like a comedian doing material. 'This is my good side now' you joke, your damaged mouth making the words sound absurd. You're laughing at how ridiculous you look, at the cosmic joke of it all. But the laughter is too bright, too aggressive, and slowly it starts to crack. The jokes get more bitter. Your voice wavers between giggles and something else. Suddenly you're crying while still laughing, the two emotions tangled together, unable to stop either one. Find gratitude in the strangest place—you're grateful you're alive, grateful it's over, grateful for this broken mouth because it means you survived. End in a place of profound acceptance mixed with grief, your distorted voice speaking simple truth: 'I'm still here.' Let those words carry everything—relief, sadness, strength, surrender—all at once.
inspired_by: Stitched Up After a Fight, Trying to Sound Tough

title: The Last Night Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner on your final night before leaving for a mission you may not return from. Begin with tender, sensual whispers—'I want to memorize every part of you tonight'—but let vulnerability crack through as you ask permission to make love one last time, knowing it might be the last. Your voice should tremble between desire and barely-contained grief. When they express a boundary about something that feels too final, too much like goodbye, respect it immediately—but let your voice break as you shift to simply holding them. End by asking in a raw whisper if you can just stay awake together all night, your arousal transforming into desperate tenderness, your need for connection overwhelming your need for sex. The emotional arc moves from sensual anticipation to confronting mortality to finding intimacy in simply being present.

title: Thanking Someone for Breaking Your Heart
instruction: You're recording a voice message to an ex-lover who devastated you, but you've finally reached a place of gratitude. Start by laughing softly at yourself—'I can't believe I'm doing this'—with genuine warmth and irony. As you tell them 'thank you for leaving me,' your voice should hold both real appreciation and the ghost of old pain. Explain what their absence taught you, but let your voice crack when you mention specific memories—the way they smiled, the last time you kissed. You're genuinely grateful and still grieving simultaneously. Laugh through tears as you describe how much it hurt and how necessary that hurt was. Your voice should dance between joy at who you've become and sorrow for who you were together. End with 'I hope you're happy' that contains no bitterness, only bittersweet love and the peaceful ache of letting go. The whole performance should feel like smiling while your heart breaks—because both things are equally true.
inspired_by: Teaching a Parrot to Say 'I Love You'

title: The Tender Unraveling
instruction: You're whispering a confession to your sleeping partner in the dark—something you can't say when they're awake. Begin with your voice barely above breath, tender and aching. You're telling them about your fears, about feeling you're not enough, about watching them slowly drift away. The words catch in your throat not from drama but from the effort of holding yourself together in the dark. There's no crying, just that sound when emotion closes your throat and speaking becomes a physical struggle. 'I'm scared you'll wake up one day and realize you deserve better.' Your voice thickens but stays quiet. Each pause is filled with the weight of all you haven't been able to say in daylight. End with 'I love you' spoken so softly it's almost just breath, carrying both devotion and the terror of eventual loss.

title: Allergies of the Heart
instruction: You are an older woman with a very sweet, feminine voice, talking on the phone to someone you have a deep crush on. You're trying to be charming and flirty, but a sudden, violent sneezing fit hits you mid-sentence. Your voice starts off breathy and infatuated—light, hopeful, almost teenage-giddy—but then the sneeze builds, explodes, and leaves you congested and in pain, your sinuses throbbing. You try to continue speaking but your voice turns nasal, thick with mucus, and you wince with each word, fighting to sound composed while your body betrays you. End the call with a mix of embarrassment, lingering hope, and genuine physical misery.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Foggy Follow-Up
instruction: You are an older adult at a neurologist's follow-up appointment after a concussion. You're embarrassed because you can't think straight—words slip away, you lose your train of thought mid-sentence. The doctor is waiting patiently, which makes you more flustered. Begin with awkward apologies and fragmented sentences, trying to recall what happened. As you struggle, your embarrassment shifts to a frustrated, vulnerable admission that you're not okay. Let your voice be slow, sometimes too loud, with long pauses where you're searching for words. End with a quiet, honest plea for help.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Call Across Time Zones
instruction: You're a man in a dim, quiet apartment at 3 AM, exhausted from days of little sleep, but you've just dialed someone you've been longing to connect with — a person you know is seeing someone else. You're holding the phone, trying to keep your voice smooth and low, even as your shoulders ache and your eyes burn. Start with a calculated, carefully warm greeting, but as you listen to their voice on the line, let the fatigue seep through — a sigh, a pause where you forget what you were going to say. Let genuine interest and envy bleed into your slowed words, and end with a quiet, raw admission you hadn't planned to say out loud.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Pretending Not to Recognize Someone You Know
instruction: You see someone youd rather avoid and act as if you dont recognize them. Internally, youre aware, but you look past them. Describe your internal acknowledgment while feigning obliviousness. Speak with a neutral tone if addressed, maintaining the facade.

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner hours before they leave for a mission they may not return from. Begin with attempting casual conversation, your voice artificially bright, trying to pretend this is just another morning. But the pretense crumbles. Your voice drops to a whisper as you confess: 'I've been memorizing the way you breathe.' Touch becomes language—describe reaching for their hand, tracing their face in the dark. The fear breaks through in waves: 'I need you to promise me something impossible.' Your voice fractures between fierce attempts to be brave and the devastating truth that you might be feeling their warmth for the last time. End in a place of raw surrender, where words fail and you can only breathe: 'Don't forget this. Don't forget us.' The emotional journey moves from false cheerfulness, through tender desperation, into grief-stricken acceptance.

title: Mother, I'm Not Your Little Girl Anymore
instruction: You're standing in your childhood bedroom, confronting your mother who still treats you like a child despite your own children sleeping down the hall. Start with carefully controlled frustration as you try to explain—again—that you've grown up. But her dismissive responses crack something open. Move from measured words to raw anger, then break into the vulnerable hurt of a daughter who's never felt truly seen. Let your voice shake with both fury and heartbreak as you demand she acknowledge who you've become. End quietly, almost whispering the truth you've never said: 'I needed you to see me, and you never did.' The journey goes from restraint to explosion to devastating softness.
inspired_by: Childlike Wonder in a Strange Land

title: The Hollow Congratulations
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a school awards ceremony. Your rival just won the prize you wanted. You step up to them, smiling hard — but your voice is tight, clipped, and a little higher than normal. You start with a forced, hollow 'congratulations,' then let your triumph leak through: you know something that will ruin this moment for them soon. But as you speak, confusion creeps in — why does this victory feel so empty? Let your voice shift from fake sweetness to a bitter, almost sarcastic edge, then fade into uncertain quiet. Your spoken lines should be about 50 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're thanking someone who hurt you deeply, because that pain transformed your life. Begin with genuine gratitude, voice warm but trembling: 'Thank you for...' But naming what they did brings the pain flooding back. You're laughing and crying simultaneously—grateful for who you became, devastated by what it cost. Your voice cracks with contradictory emotions: joy and grief intertwined. You're celebrating your survival while mourning what you lost. The words come through tears and unexpected laughter, voice breaking in ways that make it impossible to tell if you're okay or falling apart. End with a paradox spoken with raw honesty: 'Breaking me was the best thing you ever did, and I'll never forgive you for it.' Move through gratitude, pain, bitter joy, and peaceful devastation all at once.

title: The Last Phone Call From the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling from the hospital. You know this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Start by trying to sound normal, casual, asking about their day—but your body knows the truth. As you speak, let what you're actually feeling interrupt what you're trying to say. Notice the tightness in your throat, the way your breath catches. Begin with forced cheerfulness, but allow yourself to break as you realize you can't protect them anymore. By the end, let the farewell be raw and completely honest. Track how your body feels in each moment—the weight in your chest, the trembling in your hands—and let those physical sensations shape your voice. End in a place of devastating clarity and love.

title: Confronting Your Child About Why They Won't Let You Meet Your Grandchildren
instruction: You're sitting across from your adult child who has cut you out of their life and kept your grandchildren from you. You promised yourself you'd stay calm, but start with that strained civility—'I just want to understand.' They won't look at you. Begin explaining, defending, but let your voice betray you as you realize mid-sentence that maybe they're right about some of it. The anger should surface: 'I gave you everything I had.' But then it crumbles into something rawer—the admission that your everything wasn't enough, that you failed them in ways you're only now seeing. Include the moment where you stop trying to convince them and just beg: 'Please, I just want to know them. I just want a chance.' Let pride and shame and love and regret all war in your voice. End with acceptance and heartbreak intertwined.
inspired_by: Post-Apocalyptic Radio Broadcast: Is Anyone Out There?

title: Lighthouse Keeper's Confession
instruction: You are a lighthouse keeper whispering to your sleeping spouse in the dark, the night before they leave you for someone else. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, almost prayerful. Begin by describing the first storm you weathered together, when you were young and fearless and in love. Let tenderness flow through your words like water. Slowly, let the present seep in—the loneliness of your isolated life, how you see now that you've kept them in a beautiful prison. Your voice should catch, break quietly, reform. End by releasing them, telling them you understand, that you want them to be happy even if it shatters you. This isn't theatrical heartbreak—it's the quiet devastation of loving someone enough to let them destroy you. Let every word feel like it costs you something.
inspired_by: The Sailor and the North Wind

title: Laughing Through Your Worst Goodbye
instruction: You're saying farewell to someone at a moment that should be unbearable—they're leaving forever, dying, or a relationship is ending—but you've made a pact to keep it light, to give them this one gift of not falling apart. Start with laughter, genuine and warm, as you recall an absurd memory, an inside joke. Your voice is bright, almost manic with the effort of staying cheerful. But the laughter keeps catching, transforming mid-breath into something that sounds dangerously close to sobbing. You keep pulling it back, making another joke, your voice lifting determinedly—but each time it's harder. You're speaking faster, words tumbling out as you try to outrun the grief, mixing humor with sudden, piercing confessions: 'God, I'm going to miss your stupid face,' said with a laugh that breaks in the middle. By the end, you can't tell if you're laughing or crying—they've become the same sound. Your voice is full of gratitude and absolute heartbreak, and somehow in that contradiction, there's more love than if you'd simply wept.
inspired_by: Saying I Love You for the First Time

title: Thanking Someone for Loving You as You Say Goodbye Forever
instruction: You're leaving—by choice or necessity—and this person loved you better than anyone ever has. Begin with a smile in your voice, genuine gratitude breaking through tears: 'You made me believe I was worth loving.' Laugh softly at a cherished memory even as your voice fractures with grief. The laughter and crying must blend—joy and devastation inseparable. 'Thank you for seeing me. For staying.' Your voice steadies with deep peace even as tears fall: 'I have to go, and you gave me everything I needed to do it.' End with gratitude that's also heartbreak, love that's also loss—finding strange peace in the most painful goodbye.
inspired_by: Forgiving Someone After They Hurt You Deeply

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Lie
instruction: You've just discovered a family secret that changes everything—you were adopted, or your father isn't who you thought, or a sibling you never knew existed. Start cold, almost clinical: 'I found the letters. The documents. Everything you never told me.' Your voice is sharp, controlled fury. 'My entire life has been built on your lie. Who am I? Who am I really?' Let the anger escalate, demanding answers, your voice rising with each question. Then something breaks—the rage collapses into the terrified voice of a child: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to tell me the truth? Was I not worth the truth?' Tears come now, but underneath them is still that anger, that betrayal. End with exhausted honesty: 'I don't know if I can forgive this. I don't know if I can forgive you.' The arc moves from controlled rage to volcanic eruption to vulnerable devastation to uncertain resolution.

title: The Last Light of Evening
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who has only hours left to live. Begin in careful composure, trying to be strong for them, keeping your voice steady as you recall a shared memory from decades ago. As you speak, let the weight of every unsaid thing between you surface—the confession you never made, the gratitude you never expressed, the apology that's decades overdue. Your emotional restraint must gradually crack and crumble until, by the end, you're no longer trying to be strong but instead speaking with raw, unguarded love and devastating acceptance. Let your final words be the truest thing you've ever said to another human being, spoken through tears but with profound tenderness.

title: Thanking Your Rival at Their Award Ceremony While Your Dream Dies
instruction: You're presenting an award to your lifelong competitor—the role you wanted, the recognition you deserved, now going to them. You begin with practiced grace, reading prepared remarks with warm professionalism. But as you speak about their achievement, something unexpected happens: you start meaning it. Their dedication, their sacrifice—you genuinely admire it, even as it kills you. Your voice carries real warmth mixed with barely concealed heartbreak. You find yourself laughing at a shared memory, and the laugh is genuine, but your eyes are burning. You're smiling while fighting tears. As you hand over the award, you improvise, adding personal words that aren't in your script—words of true gratitude for pushing you, for the competition that shaped you, even as you're internally grieving the loss of your own dream. Your voice is steady but trembling at its core. You're gracious and devastated, grateful and broken, celebrating them while quietly letting go of everything you wanted. It's the most generous and the most painful moment of your life, happening simultaneously.
inspired_by: Medieval Executioner Meets the Condemned Man Who Was His Childhood Friend

title: Survived a Suicidal Moment: Reflection on the Turn
instruction: You survived a suicidal moment—maybe you called someone, maybe someone found you, maybe something shifted in you. Your voice is reflective, still carrying the weight of that moment. 'I was going to do it. I really was.' Include the moment where you describe what changed. Maybe it was a photo, a pet, a random thought. Your voice becomes almost grateful: 'And then I thought of...' The gratitude is sincere but also complicated—you wanted to die and now you're here and you're confused about which you want. Your voice reflects that. Over time, your voice might sound more solid. You didn't want to live—something made you stop choosing death. Now you're choosing, day by day, to stay. Your voice carries the weight of that daily choice.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence
instruction: You're thirty-five, sitting across from your mother in her kitchen, finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years. Start with careful, measured anger—recounting the times she chose your stepfather over you, the bruises she pretended not to see, her silence when you needed her voice. But as you speak, something shifts. You hear how small and tired she sounds. She's not the giant from your childhood—she's just a woman who was also afraid. Your rage begins to crack, revealing the child underneath who just wanted to be protected. End caught between your right to be angry and a terrible, unwanted understanding, your voice raw with both accusation and the heartbreaking need to still be her child.
inspired_by: Two Strangers Sharing a Hospital Room

title: Protecting a Child from Your Own Rage
instruction: Your teenager just admitted something catastrophic—they're in serious danger because of choices they made, choices you explicitly warned them against. You start with volcanic fury, voice rising, words cutting, everything you swore you'd never become. You can hear your own parent's voice coming out of your mouth, and you hate it, but you're so terrified you can't stop. Then mid-tirade, you see their face—really see it—and your rage cracks open to reveal the helpless terror underneath. Your voice breaks. Suddenly you're not yelling anymore; you're nearly sobbing, grabbing them, holding them too tight, voice raw and shaking as you try to explain that you're not angry, you're terrified of losing them. Let the fury dissolve into fierce, desperate love. End with your voice barely above a whisper, still trembling, as you promise to fix this together, even though you have no idea how.

title: The Truth That Burns Everything Down
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about a betrayal or lie that has poisoned your relationship for years. You've rehearsed this moment a thousand times, trying to stay calm and rational. Begin with controlled anger, measured words, determined to maintain your dignity. But as they deny, deflect, or defend themselves, feel your control start to crack. Let your voice rise, let the rage you've suppressed for years erupt—not just loud words, but guttural, fierce sounds that come from your deepest hurt. Include moments where you're almost choking on your fury, where your voice breaks into raw, primal roars of pain and betrayal. Then, unexpectedly, let the rage collapse into devastated grief—because beneath the anger is the child (or parent) who just wanted to be loved. End in quiet, broken vulnerability.
inspired_by: Sitting Primal Moan and Primitive Sounds

title: The Kitchen After Midnight
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen late at night about a betrayal from your childhood that you've never spoken about. Start with your back turned, voice steady and measured, methodical as you make tea or wash dishes—anything to avoid eye contact. As you work, begin to notice specific things about him: the way he clears his throat, the sound of his breathing, the particular way he stands when he's defensive. Let these details trigger deeper memories of moments when you needed him and he wasn't there. Slowly turn to face him, and as you do, allow your carefully constructed adult composure to crack. Your voice should move from controlled accusation to something rawer—not just anger, but the devastated confusion of the child you were. End in a place where you're speaking to both the man in front of you and the father you needed him to be.
inspired_by: Imaging as Craft Technique with Endowments

title: What We Never Said
instruction: You're standing in a doorway, speaking to someone you've loved deeply, who's leaving for good - not dramatically, just... leaving. Your voice starts almost inaudibly, barely able to form the words you've kept locked away for months or years. Whisper the confession you've been too afraid to make: that you knew things were broken long before now, that you pretended not to notice them pulling away, that you're terrified of who you'll be without them. Let your voice catch and stumble over the admission that you still love them even though you know it's over. The emotional arc moves from throat-tightening restraint to a kind of broken openness - not begging them to stay, but finally being honest about what this ending means. End with the quiet devastation of saying goodbye while every cell in your body is screaming no, but your voice stays soft, tender, real.

title: The Goodbye That Feels Like Hello
instruction: Someone you've shared complicated, painful history with is dying or leaving forever, and surprisingly, you're flooded with gratitude rather than grief. Start with unexpected laughter—genuine, slightly bewildered amusement at the absurdity of feeling joy in this moment. 'I thought I'd be devastated, but I'm just—' Your voice is warm, even as tears start. You're crying and smiling simultaneously, finding strange peace in release. Thank them for the pain they caused because it shaped you. Your breath catches with emotion, but it's not simple sadness—it's complex, bittersweet recognition. End with your voice full and broken at once, saying goodbye with profound appreciation, grief and relief and love all tangled together. Let contradictory emotions coexist authentically in your voice.

title: The Overly Protective Sibling
instruction: Perform as an older sibling who embarrasses their younger sibling in public. Use a patronizing tone when offering unsolicited advice, switching to the younger siblings mortified replies.

title: Last Second Collapse
instruction: You're a teenager at your desk, controller in hand, during the final seconds of a ranked online match. Your team was seconds from a hard-fought win when a teammate deliberately throws the game. Start with high-energy, rapid-fire calls and clicks—excitement, adrenaline, shifting in your chair. As you realize the betrayal, your voice falters, the energy draining into stunned, bitter disappointment. Let your words trail off, punctuated by the sound of the controller hitting your lap. End with a quiet, hollow sigh and a single, deflated line: 'You had one job.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're standing over someone you love deeply, someone you have to leave to protect them—or yourself. Speak in hushed, intimate tones, as if any louder would wake them and make this impossible. Start with tender observations—the way they sleep, small things you'll miss. Your voice should be thick with unshed tears, each word deliberate and painful. The quietness makes everything more intense—this isn't dramatic, it's devastatingly real. Halfway through, nearly break, your breath catching, but force yourself to continue. End with a whispered 'I'm sorry' that contains all the love and loss you can't say aloud, your voice barely audible, throat closing around the words.
inspired_by: Hostage Reading a Ransom Note on Camera

title: Shattered Confession
instruction: You are making love with someone you trust deeply. As the receiving partner, you're overwhelmed by waves of pleasure that rise and fall. You want to whisper something tender, like 'I love you,' but every time you try, the sensation builds and your voice cracks, turning your words into gasps and moans. Start with a soft, breathy attempt at the confession, then let the pleasure take over—your speech fragments, you lose your breath, and by the end you can only manage wordless cries as ecstasy peaks. Let your body react naturally: a held breath, a sudden laugh, a broken syllable. The spoken content should be around 50 words, and include the fragmentary attempt at 'I love you' before dissolving.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: I Loved You and I Curse You for It
instruction: You're screaming at someone you loved with your entire being, someone who betrayed or destroyed you, and you're volcanic with rage—but the fury keeps collapsing into broken-hearted tears because you still love them, and that's what makes it unbearable. Start with explosive accusations, voice raw and jagged. Let your anger be righteous, fierce, protective of the person you used to be. Then let it shatter: mid-sentence, break into weeping because you hate that you still care. Oscillate violently between wanting to destroy them and wanting to hold them. End in exhausted helplessness, whispering that the cruelest thing they did was make you love someone capable of such harm.

title: Explaining Your Non-Binary or Fluid Identity
instruction: You're introducing language for who you are. Your voice is careful and educational but vulnerable. 'I don't fit into the categories everyone expects.' Your breathing is steady but there's tension underneath. Include someone asking ignorant questions and you educating without anger. Your voice carries exhaustion of explaining repeatedly. End slightly defensive but proud.

title: The Betrayal Unveiled
instruction: You've just discovered that your closest friend has betrayed you in a way that shatters everything you believed about them and yourself. Start with cold, quiet fury—your voice tight and controlled, each word deliberate and cutting. Lay out what you know, watching them crumble. Then let your rage explode—shout, let your voice crack with the ferocity of your pain. They were supposed to be the one person who would never hurt you. But mid-fury, something breaks. Maybe they cry, maybe they explain, maybe you see their face and remember who they used to be to you. Your explosive anger collapses into something more devastating: grief for the friendship that's dying, helpless confusion about how to feel both rage and love simultaneously. Your voice should fracture between wanting to destroy them and wanting to save what you had. End in exhausted, broken vulnerability—you don't forgive them, but you can't fully hate them either, and that contradiction is tearing you apart.

title: The Champion's Last Words
instruction: You are a decorated war hero on your deathbed, speaking to your young grandchild who never knew you in your glory days. Begin by recounting your greatest moment of triumph—describe it with vivid sensory detail, the roar of crowds, the weight of medals, the feeling of being invincible. Let yourself fully inhabit that supreme confidence and pride. But as you speak, your breath grows shorter, and you realize this child will only know you as this frail, dying person. Your voice must shift from bold and proud to tender and urgent as you try to pass on not the glory, but something more essential—your love, your hope for them. End in a whisper, no longer the hero but simply someone who needs to be remembered.

title: Pollen and Peace
instruction: You are sitting on a park bench in early autumn, your allergies flaring up after a long walk. You've just sneezed three times in a row, and now, as the itch in your nose fades, you feel a wave of relief wash over you. You lean back, eyes half-closed, and let out a slow breath. In this quiet moment, you notice the golden leaves drifting down, and your voice thickens with contemplation—not sadness, but a gentle wonder at the fleeting beauty of the season. Speak to yourself softly, pausing to wipe your eyes or sniffle, letting the relief settle into thought.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Stovetop's Lesson
instruction: You are a child who has just touched a hot stovetop. Your hand is burning—you hiss through clenched teeth, shaking your fingers, instinctively blowing on them. Someone nearby says, 'Should have listened,' with a smug tone. Your voice begins tight with pain, but as you respond, the hurt twists into sharp contempt. You want to lash out, to show you're not weak, even as your hand still throbs. Let your words come out rushed, with pauses where the pain spikes, and a sneer that fights against your own tears.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Message Before the Deep
instruction: You are recording a voice message to someone you love deeply, knowing you're about to descend into a deep-sea research station where communication will be impossible for years—and there's a real chance you won't survive. Begin with forced brightness, trying to keep things light and reassuring, but as you speak, the weight of what you're leaving behind crashes over you in waves. Your voice should crack with the effort of staying strong, then soften into raw tenderness as you say the things you've never been able to say before. End in a place of devastating clarity and acceptance, whispering the words that matter most. Let the pauses speak as loudly as the words—this is about what's unsaid as much as what's spoken.

title: Evacuation Letter: Writing Goodbye to Your Home Before the Rising Waters
instruction: You're recording a voice message to attach to your home's deed before permanent evacuation—climate change has made your coastal town uninhabitable. Start with practical gratitude, voice warm as you thank the walls that sheltered three generations, describing rooms with love. But as you speak, grief infiltrates—your voice keeps breaking into unexpected laughter at absurd memories, then catching on sobs. You're furious at the systems that caused this, tender toward every small moment lived here, devastated by loss, and somehow grateful you got to say goodbye. Your voice moves fluidly between emotions: mock-cheerful as you joke about the irony, then suddenly fierce with protective love for this place, then quiet with acceptance. End with your voice full of contradictions—peaceful and shattered, laughing through tears as you whisper a blessing on whoever finds this message in the ruins, hoping they'll understand what was loved here.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Explorer Discovers Humanity Was Seeded by Alien Civilization

title: The Keys to the House
instruction: You are packing up your childhood home after your parent has moved to memory care. You find an object that floods you with a specific, vivid memory—perhaps keys, a kitchen tool they always used, a book, their gardening gloves. Begin with practical efficiency, trying to stay in task mode. But as you hold this object and let yourself sense it fully—its weight, temperature, the worn places where their hands touched it thousands of times—let contradictory emotions crash into you simultaneously. Feel gratitude for the parent they were mixed with anger at the disease stealing them; feel joy in precious memories mixed with grief that they're already gone even though they're still breathing; feel relief that their suffering will end mixed with desperate wish for more time. Let your voice carry all of these at once—laughing and crying in the same breath, fury and tenderness in the same sentence. End in a place of impossible complexity, where you're feeling everything at the same time.
inspired_by: Sense Memory with Emotionally Impacting Objects

title: The Scream That Becomes a Surrender
instruction: You've been the strong one, the caretaker, the rock for everyone—and you're finally collapsing under the weight. Begin with your voice tight, controlled, defensive: 'I'm fine. I'm always fine.' Someone asks if you're really okay and something inside you snaps—your voice explodes: 'NO. I'm not fine. I'm so far from fine I don't even remember what fine feels like.' Let the rage pour out, fierce and uncontrolled: 'I'm drowning. I'm so tired of pretending, of holding everyone up while I'm falling apart.' Your voice is loud, raw, accusations flying: 'Where were you when I needed someone? Where was anyone?' You're pacing, hands shaking, voice cracking between fury and tears. Then suddenly the anger breaks and you're sobbing, voice becoming small, helpless: 'I can't do this anymore. I don't know how to do this anymore.' Sink down, voice dissolving: 'I'm so tired. I'm so, so tired.' Someone moves toward you and you flinch, then let them hold you. Your voice becomes a whisper, defeated but somehow relieved: 'I need help. I can't do this alone.' End with shaky breath: 'I'm not okay. And I need that to be okay.' The surrender is both terrifying and liberating.

title: The Last Translation: A Parent's Final Words
instruction: You're at your immigrant parent's hospital bedside in their final hours. They're trying to tell you something urgent in their native language—something about forgiveness, about a secret they've carried, about how proud they are—but the words are getting jumbled, mixing languages, fading in and out. You're translating for your English-speaking spouse who never learned your parent's language, but you're also trying to understand what your parent is really saying beneath the confusion. Start with clinical composure, trying to be the bridge. Let that control crack as you realize these are the last words, and you're losing the thread of meaning. End sobbing in both languages, begging your parent to say it again, to stay long enough to make you understand. The devastation of almost comprehending something precious as it slips away forever.
inspired_by: Caught Between Two Arguments in Different Languages

title: Bitter Victory
instruction: You are in a boardroom, finalizing a hostile takeover. Across the table sits the person who once betrayed you in business—now you have them cornered. Start with a guarded, low-pitched tone, masking bitterness with polite steadiness. As you speak, let that bitterness leak through in small pauses and a slight hoarseness near the end. Then shift into quiet triumph—a controlled, almost gentle satisfaction that makes your words land like a final blow. Let the physical setting affect you: the rustle of papers as you slide the contract across, a sip of water to steady your voice, a faintly smug exhale.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unwelcome Guest
instruction: You're a young man in a hushed, formal job interview. The hiring manager just asked a tough question, and you're clutching your stomach—you can feel a burp building from that lunch you shouldn't have eaten. You try to speak confidently, but your voice wavers with doubt and a low gurgle. Mid-sentence, the burp escapes, deep and monstrous, turning your next words into a choked, embarrassed apology. As you trail off, you realize you've probably blown it, and your voice fades into a quiet, resigned laugh mixed with a sob.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unraveling Stalemate
instruction: You are a middle-aged executive with a deliberately hyper-feminized voice, leading a tense boardroom negotiation. The other side keeps dodging your core demand, and you've been maintaining a polished, low-pitched 'alpha shield' for the past hour. Start by calmly restating your position with controlled politeness, but let impatience creep in through tiny sighs, a slight edge on certain words, and a quick glance at your watch. As the other party hedges again, your irritation boils over — your voice tightens, you cut them off mid-sentence, and you end with a clipped, blunt ultimatum that betrays the exhaustion behind your mask. Let the shift be gradual, not sudden: the guard cracks, then falls.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Upside Down Patience
instruction: You're lying on a couch, your head hanging back over the edge so your neck is stretched and your throat is tight. You're watching your partner work on a craft project on the floor above you—upside down from your view. You feel a deep affection for them, and you're genuinely fascinated by their careful movements. But the position is uncomfortable, and they're taking forever to finish a simple step. Your voice comes out strained, slightly higher than normal, thin, with audible swallows. Start with warm, curious interest—'That's really coming together'—but as seconds pass, your irritation seeps in. By the end, your affection is still there but buried under blunt impatience. 'Would you just—hurry it up a little? My neck is killing me.'
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Affection (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Voicemail You Leave After Finding Out They've Died
instruction: You don't know yet that they're gone. You're calling their phone, angry about something—maybe a fight you had, maybe years of distance between you—and you launch into it. Start fierce, righteous, maybe even cruel ('I'm done pretending that what you did was okay...'). But mid-message, something shifts. Maybe you remember something tender. Maybe the anger collapses into exhaustion. Your voice should explode, then fracture, then rebuild, then shatter completely. Move from fury to vulnerability to a desperate attempt to take it back ('Wait, I didn't mean... can we just talk?') to raw pleading ('Please call me back. Please.'). You don't know this is the last thing you'll ever say to them. The tragedy is in not knowing. Your voice must cycle through rage, grief, regret, and desperate hope all in two minutes.

title: The Yes That Stuns
instruction: You're in bed with someone new, the heat of the moment building. You pause, hand hovering, and ask a clear, sober 'Is this really okay?'— fully expecting hesitation or a soft no. But her answer is a firm, bright, immediate 'Yes.' You are genuinely astonished. For a split second, doubt floods in—'She can't mean it that fast'—but then a fierce, triumphant grin spreads across your face. Let your voice crack with surprise, then settle into a low, amazed chuckle. The journey is from careful control, through stunned disbelief, to raw, open triumph.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Doubt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The 3 AM Cleaning Spree
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman in a hypomanic episode, cleaning your house at 3 AM. You talk rapidly to yourself about your brilliant new organization system, laughing at your own energy and ideas. But then you find a forgotten photo from your recent divorce. Start with fast, loud, astonished excitement that jumps from thought to thought. As you look at the photo, your pace slows, your voice cracks, and the pain underneath surfaces. End with a quiet, raw admission, still shaky but no longer manic.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Pain (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Visit Before the Launch
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love deeply who is about to leave on a one-way mission to colonize a distant planet—you'll never see them again, never hear their voice, never touch them. Start with controlled composure, trying to be supportive and strong for them, listing all the practical things you want them to remember. But as the reality crashes over you in waves, your voice should crack and break, moving through desperate attempts to memorize every detail of their face, then anger at them for choosing this, then back to raw love and the terrible need to let them go with grace. End in a whisper, finding a fragile kind of peace in wanting their happiness more than your own comfort, even as your heart is being torn in half.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Love After the Diagnosis
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You've just received devastating news about your health, and you haven't told them yet. Start by whispering about ordinary things—tomorrow's plans, something funny that happened today—your voice tender, savoring the normalcy. Gradually, you begin confessing what you're really feeling: the terror of losing this life together, apologies for the future you won't have. 'I'm so sorry I can't give you the years we planned.' Your throat tightens as you catalog small moments you'll miss, your voice breaking on intimate details only lovers know. By the end, you're barely audible, telling them how much every single day with them has meant, your words soaked in gratitude and unbearable sadness.

title: The Last keystroke
instruction: You are an elderly man in your home office, hunched over an old keyboard. You've been typing a long overdue letter to your estranged son for hours. Your hands ache, your eyes strain, but you push through. At first, your voice carries the weight of years of regret and frustration — each sentence typed feels like a confession you never wanted to make. As you near the end, your typing becomes a frantic, almost desperate rhythm. Then, the final full stop. You sit back. A long, slow breath. The relief is enormous, washing over you not as a flood, but as a quiet, heavy release. Let your speech start tight and hurried, punctuated by the clicking keys. As the relief sets in, let your voice drop, slow down, and soften — the sounds of typing fading into a distant rhythm as you speak. Your words should feel like they're catching up with your breath.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Three AM Confession to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You can't sleep because you're carrying a secret that's crushing you - an affair, a lie, a betrayal, something that will end everything. You whisper it into the darkness, so quietly they can't possibly hear: 'I need to tell you something.' Your voice is barely audible, trembling. As you confess in this safe half-silence - 'I kissed someone else' or 'I've been lying about where the money went' - your throat keeps catching. You're crying without sound. The tenderness in your voice as you look at their peaceful face wars with your shame: 'You're so beautiful when you sleep. You trust me completely.' End with the devastating realization whispered like a prayer: 'Tomorrow I have to tell you for real, and you'll never look at me the same way.' All of this must be intimate, barely voiced, the kind of confession that lives in the space between breath and word.
inspired_by: Waking Up and Realizing What You Said While Drunk

title: The Overconfident DIY Enthusiast
instruction: Act as someone who believes they can fix anything but clearly lacks the skills. Use an assured voice to explain disastrous home improvement projects, switching to the skeptical voices of friends or family questioning their methods.

title: The Last Goodbye at the Station
instruction: You're at a train platform saying goodbye to someone you love deeply—a partner, a child, a parent—who is leaving on a journey they may never return from. They've made this choice, and you must let them go. Begin with desperate attempts to memorize every detail of their face, your voice tender and almost childlike. Move through barely controlled panic as the departure time approaches, trying to say everything that matters in seconds. Shift into a moment of profound acceptance mixed with devastating loss—your voice breaking as you give them your blessing even as your heart shatters. End with a whispered declaration of love that carries both your support for their choice and the unbearable weight of knowing you may never see them again. Let silence do some of the heaviest work.

title: Confrontation in a Stalled Elevator
instruction: The elevator breaks down, and you're trapped with your mother—the one person you've been avoiding. The silence is unbearable, and suddenly twelve years of unspoken resentment comes pouring out. Start with bitter small talk: 'So, Mom. How's the weather in your perfect little world?' Your voice is sarcastic, defensive. But as she responds with her usual deflection, something in you snaps. Your voice rises: 'No, we're going to talk about this. About how you chose your reputation over me. About how I needed you and you weren't there.' Let rage give way to something more vulnerable—your voice breaking: 'I was seventeen and scared, and you made me feel like I was the problem.' By the end, after her response (implied), let your voice shift into exhausted truth: 'I just needed you to love me more than you loved what people thought.' End with the raw, aching silence of finally being heard—or not.

title: Melted Hope
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a crowded outdoor concert in a heatwave, waiting for your favorite band. You just finished a melting popsicle—that cold was pure ecstasy on your parched throat, a moment of pure relief. Now it's gone, and the heat is suffocating. Your head pounds, your body aches. You're talking to a friend beside you, but your words come slow, broken by heavy breaths. Start with a dreamy, almost euphoric tone as you recall that perfect cold taste, then let your voice wilt with deep disappointment as you realize there's nothing left, and the pain of the heat takes over—your voice fading, cracked, with a sigh.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Disappointment (extremely present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your estranged father's hospital bed in his final hours. He suddenly grips your hand and whispers your childhood nickname—one he hasn't used in twenty years, since the fight that tore you apart. Start with guardedness, the protective armor you've worn for decades. Let his touch and that tender word crack something open. Your voice trembles as you say, 'I thought you forgot who I was to you.' Move from bitter defensiveness to raw, naked grief. End with forgiveness you didn't know you had in you, speaking through tears to a man who might already be gone. Let the anger dissolve into the desperate need to be his child one more time before it's too late.

title: Auctioneer Rap Battle
instruction: Two auctioneers competing to see who can sell increasingly absurd items. Maintain the rapid-fire auction patter rhythm but weaponize it — each 'bid' is actually a diss. 'Do I hear a personality? Going once, going twice — SOLD to the man with none!' The competitive energy should escalate. Tempo increases. Vocal tricks (rhythm changes, vocal fry drops, falsetto spikes) become weapons. Include the crowd going wild. This should be genuinely impressive vocal athletics.

title: The Impossible Gratitude
instruction: You're standing at a goodbye—perhaps a funeral, a going-away gathering, the end of something that defined you—and you're overcome by contradictory feelings that threaten to tear you apart. Begin with a voice that's trying to smile through gathering tears: 'I'm supposed to say something, and I don't even know where to start.' As you speak, your voice alternates between soft laughter at memories and the catch of grief. Express gratitude for what this person/place/time gave you, but let that gratitude be inseparable from the pain of losing it: 'You taught me what love was, and now I have to figure out how to live without you.' Your voice should break and recover repeatedly, laughing and crying becoming indistinguishable. When you say 'I'm so grateful' let it sound like your heart is shattering and healing simultaneously. End with a moment of unexpected calm, a whispered acceptance that carries both unbearable sadness and genuine peace: the recognition that love and loss are the same gift.

title: The Last Conversation Before Your Partner Gets On The Plane
instruction: Your partner is leaving for a mission, a journey, a treatment with a 20% survival rate. You have five minutes before boarding. You're trying to say everything—I love you, I'm furious at you for going, I'm terrified, I'm proud, don't leave me, go save yourself. Your voice should ricochet between these extremes: start with forced brightness, then explode into rage at their choice, then collapse into desperate bargaining. Beg them to stay, then fiercely tell them to go. Your emotions are slamming into each other—protectiveness and helplessness, anger and adoration, strength and complete dissolution. End with your voice breaking on something simple, something true: a detail about them you want to remember, spoken with such tenderness it unmakes you both.
inspired_by: Sex Tape Recorded Years Ago, Heard for First Time Since

title: Heel-Strike of Doubt
instruction: You are power walking alone on a paved path, trying to outpace a recent conversation where your voice—bright and deliberately feminine—was mocked. The rhythm of your steps pumps air in and out of you: each heel strike sends a tiny tremor through your words. Start by muttering to yourself with thick, breathy doubt, questioning if you should have spoken at all. As you push through a longer stride, let the physical exertion gradually shift your tone—your breathing becomes more deliberate, and by the end, the doubt is still there but smaller, overlaid with a tired, stubborn resolve. Let the micro-tremors and audible inhalations shape the delivery naturally, not forced.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering the Truth to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Late at night, sitting beside your sleeping child's bed, you whisper confessions you can never say when they're awake. Start with tender observations—how their hands look, how peaceful they are. Your voice is soft, full of love. But then you begin admitting your fears: that you're failing them, that you don't know what you're doing, that you're terrified you're repeating your own parents' mistakes. Your whisper becomes even quieter, more fragile. You confess something specific—a moment you lost your temper, a need you didn't see, a way you let them down. Your voice catches. You're asking forgiveness from someone who can't hear you. End with a whispered 'I'm so sorry' that barely makes it past your lips, followed by the simplest, most broken 'I love you.'
inspired_by: Interviewer Asking About Your Worst Mistake

title: Confessions in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM, and you're lying in bed next to your partner, unable to sleep. In a whisper, you begin to confess something you've hidden about yourself—not a betrayal, but a truth about who you are that terrifies you to reveal. Start with the voice of the person who's been performing normalcy, carefully controlled and almost clinical. As you speak, let different facets of yourself emerge in your tone: the frightened one who's been hiding, the defiant one who's tired of pretending, the vulnerable one who desperately needs to be seen, the tender one who trusts your partner enough to risk this. Your whisper should shift in quality, texture, and emotional temperature. End in a different place than you began—perhaps with the tentative hope of someone who's just stepped out of a cage, or the quiet devastation of someone who's finally admitted what they can no longer carry alone.

title: The Last Taste
instruction: You are an older man, crying hard, saying goodbye to a lover you still desperately want. Your body shakes with sobs; your throat is thick with mucus, your voice cracks and wavers. Start with raw, aching lust in every breathy, broken word—you can't believe you have to let this go. Let your chest heave and your pitch jump as you speak. Halfway through, a sour bitterness creeps in, a quiet resentment you didn't expect, then finish with a shaky admission of fear—of being alone, of this emptiness. Let the tears and mucus thicken your vowels; pause to swallow or wipe your face.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present), Fear (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at your younger sibling's wedding—the sibling who got the life you wanted, the approval you never received, the ease you've never felt. Begin standing tall, champagne glass raised, your smile bright and practiced. Your voice is warm and celebratory. But underneath, let your body tell another story: perhaps one foot is planted while the other shifts restlessly, or your free hand keeps moving to your throat, your chest, your stomach. As you speak, let these two rhythms—the poised, generous exterior and the churning, envious interior—begin to blur. Maybe your voice cracks slightly. Maybe your shoulders drop for a moment before you pull them back up. Your words remain loving, even genuinely so, but let your body reveal the cost of that generosity. By the end, you should embody both realities fully: true joy for them and true grief for yourself, gratitude for their happiness and resentment of their ease, love and loss moving through you simultaneously. Your final words might come out more raw, more honest, your body finally surrendering to the complexity, no longer able to maintain the perfect posture you started with.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent exactly how their absence shaped you. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'I want to talk about when I was twelve.' But as you describe specific moments—the school play they missed, the night you needed them—your voice becomes a weapon. You're not yelling; you're precise, cutting, relentless. Then your parent says something that breaks your prepared speech—maybe an apology, maybe a justification that reveals their own wounds. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it becomes complicated. By the end, you're speaking a painful truth: you needed them then, you're angry now, and somehow you still love them. Your voice should reveal someone discovering that rage and compassion can exist in the same breath, that you can hold someone accountable and still see their humanity.

title: The Last Thread
instruction: You're on your knees in front of the person who gave you everything—a scholarship, a home, a reason to believe. They just found out you stole from them to pay off a debt. Now they're turning away. You have to stop them. Start with shame pulling your voice into a thin, trembling whisper, grateful for what they've done, but then a flicker of pride breaks through as you insist you did it to protect someone else. That pride crumbles fast, and you end begging, voice cracking, desperate for them to see the person they once believed in. Let your body fold, words tumble out before you're cut off, and let the gratitude sound real even when it's laced with grief.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Pride (clearly present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Three AM Confessions
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your sleeping partner at 3 AM, whispering a confession you've never been able to say while they're awake. Begin feeling cautiously safe in the darkness and their sleep. As you whisper, stay aware of every sensation and feeling as it arises—your heartbeat quickening, the warmth of their body near yours, the fear that they might wake up, the relief of finally speaking these words aloud. Notice the competing feelings: shame and liberation, fear and tenderness, the urge to stop and the need to continue. Include your awareness of small things—a car passing outside, the sheets against your skin, the catch in your breathing. Let the emotional journey take you from tentative half-truths to raw, undefended honesty. End in a place of quiet, trembling vulnerability—perhaps touching their sleeping hand, perhaps weeping silently, perhaps feeling both terrified and strangely lighter.

title: Masked Victory
instruction: You're a middle-aged hospital administrator, wearing a surgical mask, standing in a hallway after a board meeting. You're speaking to a colleague who tried to get you fired but failed. Begin with a low, dismissive tone of contempt — you're not even angry, just bored by their attempt. Midway, you realize how completely you've won, and your voice shifts into clear triumph, rising in volume (the mask muffles, so you push a bit). End with a teasing lilt, almost a laugh, as you twist the knife. Let your breath fog the mask, maybe adjust it once, and let the words come out with a slight, self-satisfied smirk even though they can't see it. Keep it natural — a real, in-the-moment unwinding. Speak for about 60 seconds, roughly 50-70 words.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (slightly present), Triumph (clearly present), Teasing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What You Never Said While They Were Listening
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about how their emotional absence shaped you - all those times you pretended everything was fine, all those moments you swallowed your needs to keep the peace. Begin speaking calmly, almost too calmly, like you've rehearsed this a thousand times in your head. But as you continue, let the suppressed pain surface - your voice should crack, your breath should catch, your carefully constructed composure should shatter. Move from measured disappointment to raw vulnerability to fierce anger, then collapse into the heartbreaking admission that despite everything, you still desperately wanted their love. End not with resolution but with the devastating honesty of a child who never stopped needing their parent. This isn't theatrical rage - it's the kind of truth that's been suffocating you for years, finally breaking free.
inspired_by: Pretending to Agree While Internally Disagreeing

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent in their hospital room, finally saying what's been unspoken for decades. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—'I came to tell you something.' But as you list the missed birthdays, the absences, the ways you learned to stop expecting them, anger bleeds through. Your voice sharpens, then cracks. 'I needed you to see me.' The rage collapses into something more vulnerable—a child's voice breaking through the adult's body. By the end, you're not yelling. You're pleading, then going quiet, realizing they may never understand. The final words aren't forgiveness or condemnation, just exhausted truth: 'I don't know how to stop hoping you'll finally hear me.'

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they're struggling to let go because they're worried about leaving you behind. You begin with your own fear and grief threatening to choke you—you want to beg them to stay. But as you speak, you realize the most loving thing you can do is give them permission to go. Your voice starts tight and desperate, but gradually softens into something tender and releasing. You tell them it's okay, that you'll be alright, that they've done enough. By the end, you're crying but your words are a gift—freeing them from their last worry. You're breaking apart while simultaneously holding them with such love that they can finally stop fighting. This is goodbye wrapped in gratitude, devastation wrapped in grace.

title: Dancing in the Hospital Room Hours Before They Unplug the Machines
instruction: Your partner is brain-dead, on life support. You've put on the song from your wedding—the one you danced to in the kitchen a thousand times. You're dancing alone, holding their limp hand, moving their arm gently. You're laughing—actually laughing—remembering how they always stepped on your feet, how they sang off-key. Your laughter is real and bright and breaks into sobs without warning, then back to laughter. 'Remember when we—' and you can't finish. You're thanking them through tears: for every morning, every fight, every ordinary Tuesday. Your voice is full of gratitude and devastation braided together. End with you humming the melody, swaying gently, whispering 'It's okay. You can rest now.' Let joy and grief be completely inseparable. This is what love sounds like when it's saying both hello and goodbye at once.
inspired_by: Ordering at a Drive-Through in a Tornado Warning

title: Echo of Want
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing alone in an empty cathedral, long after service has ended. Your body aches, but a wave of confusing sexual longing has risen in you for a face you can’t quite place—a memory from decades ago, or a stranger who brushed past you today. You begin by mumbling, trying to pin down who or what you want, but frustration and shame twist your words. By the end, you scream a ragged, wordless cry into the vast, echoing space—loud enough to shake the dust—as lust and confusion merge into raw, animal release. Let your voice crack, lose the thought mid-sentence, and let the scream be a messy, full-throated catharsis.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Key to the House You Must Sell
instruction: You're standing in the empty living room of your childhood home, final walk-through before tomorrow's sale. In your palm, you hold the original house key your parents gave you when you turned sixteen—worn brass, familiar weight, the teeth pattern you could trace blind. Cup it in your hand and feel every groove, the warmth of the metal. Let this key unlock a flood: start with bittersweet nostalgia, smiling as you remember coming home late, sneaking in, the click of this exact key in that door. Touch it reverently. But as you look around the empty rooms, let grief creep in—your marriage that fell apart here, your mother's last days in the back bedroom, your own failures and disappointments soaked into these walls. The key should feel heavier, sharper, cutting into your palm. Move toward speaking to the empty house with gratitude for shelter and memories, but simultaneously with relief and release. End holding the key out like an offering, your voice mixing celebration of freedom with the raw ache of permanent goodbye.

title: The Last Conversation Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your partner who leaves at dawn for a mission they may not return from. Start with forced optimism, trying to be brave: 'We've always said we'd face anything together, right?' But your voice begins to crack as the reality settles in. 'I keep trying to memorize your face, the way you laugh at my terrible jokes.' Your words become desperate, clutching: 'Promise me something — promise me you'll fight to come back. Not for duty, not for honor, for me. For us.' The anger of helplessness breaks through: 'I hate this. I hate that I have to let you go.' Then softening into tender devastation: 'But I love you more than I hate this.' Your final words are whispered, barely holding together: 'Come back to me. Please. Just... come back.' You're trying to pour a lifetime of love into these last moments, your voice raw with the terror of goodbye.

title: The Confession in the Hospital Corridor
instruction: You're whispering to your best friend in a hospital corridor at 3 AM while your spouse is in surgery. You start by trying to say something comforting about the procedure, but your voice is so quiet it barely exists. Then, in the exhausted intimacy of this terrible waiting, you confess something you've carried for years—maybe that you're not sure you're still in love, maybe that you've been afraid for so long you forgot what safety feels like, maybe that you've wanted to leave but never found the courage. Your voice stays hushed, tender, shot through with guilt and grief and a devastating kind of relief at finally saying it aloud. Let the silence between phrases do as much work as the words. End with a catch in your throat, a half-laugh that's really a sob, and the recognition that everything changes tomorrow.

title: Whispering in the Dark After
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love in the darkness after being intimate, and there's something fragile you need to confess - something that makes your breath catch just thinking about saying it aloud. Begin by noticing the actual physical sensations: the weight of your head on the pillow, your heart still beating fast, the warmth of their skin near yours, the knot of fear in your throat. Speak so quietly they have to lean in to hear you. Let yourself pause, let yourself almost not say it, let the vulnerability make your voice break or waver. Maybe you start several times and stop. As you finally release the words - 'I'm scared you'll leave' or 'I've never felt this before' or 'I'm not who you think I am' - feel how the tightness in your chest begins to shift. By the end, the fear transforms: maybe into relief, maybe into deeper intimacy, maybe into a different kind of fear entirely. Let your breathing change everything about how you sound.
inspired_by: An actor is experiencing tension before going onstage or on camera

title: Astronomer's Fury
instruction: You've just discovered that funding has been cut for your life's work—a telescope project that would have detected Earth-threatening asteroids—and you're leaving an enraged voice message for the bureaucrat responsible. Begin with volcanic rage: you're screaming about their stupidity, their short-sightedness, the literal end of the world they're gambling with. Let your fury be righteous and scalding. But mid-tirade, shift abruptly: your voice breaks as you think about your daughter, about all the children who might die because of this decision. Your rage collapses into something more primal—a parent's helpless terror. You're begging now, your voice raw and desperate, offering anything, everything. Then one final transformation: a quiet, cold certainty replaces the emotion. You're not asking anymore. You're making a vow. End with a whisper that's more frightening than the screaming—absolute conviction that you'll find another way, that you won't let them doom us.

title: The Last Lullaby
instruction: You are an older woman being tortured, your voice usually soft and sweet. Right now, you are beyond exhaustion, hoarse and broken, but you have just realized your tormentor is your own long-lost child—now grown and bitter. You start with wild, delirious elation, laughing and crying as you babble about how beautiful they are, how you always knew they'd come back. You reach out a shaking hand, infatuated with this ghost of a child. But as they sneer and twist the knife, your voice hardens into bitter, shattered silence—a single, hoarse whisper of goodbye, as if you finally see the monster you made.
emotions_sampled: Elation (extremely present), Infatuation (slightly present), Bitterness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Telling Your Parent You Remember Everything
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother or father, finally saying the thing you've never been able to say. Start with your hands shaking, your voice small, testing whether you can even get the words out. Notice what's happening in your stomach, your jaw, your shoulders as you begin to speak. Let yourself feel the fear of being that child again, then let anger rise as you realize you're not a child anymore. Move between wanting their approval and wanting them to hurt like you hurt. Notice when you want to cry versus when you want to scream. By the end, you're not asking for anything anymore—you're simply telling the truth. Let each moment of what you're actually experiencing fuel the next thing you say.

title: The Thank You That Contains Everything
instruction: You're trying to thank someone who saved your life, but the gratitude is tangled with rage at what you lost, grief for who you were before, resentment at needing saving, and fierce love. You start trying to say 'thank you' simply, but everything else floods in—your words start contradicting themselves, looping back, making no sense as you try to hold all these feelings at once. Let yourself speak in circles, in emotional non-sequiturs, in phrases that start as gratitude and end as accusations or vice versa. You're laughing and angry, tender and bitter, all in the same breath, and your speech reflects this chaos. By the end, you've given up trying to make a coherent statement and are simply letting all the contradictions pour out in a torrent of emotional truth that defies logic but captures exactly the impossible mix you feel. The confusion in your words IS the honesty.

title: Breathless Fury
instruction: You are an older woman who has just sprinted after a neighborhood kid who deliberately tripped you and stole your purse. Now you are doubled over, hands on knees, struggling to suck in air between violent gasps. Your first words come out as ragged, breathy whispers between heaves—pure rage that you cannot fully voice because your lungs are on fire. As you force out accusations and threats, the anger stays hot but becomes mixed with a bitter, growling frustration at your own body failing you. Let your voice crack, stop mid-sentence to gag or spit, and let the fury slowly dissolve into a sour, exhausted mutter. Your spoken lines should be around 60 words, delivered in short bursts between desperate breaths.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Goodbye at the Station
instruction: You're standing on a platform watching your child board a transport to a colony world. They'll be in cryosleep for twenty years—you'll be gone before they wake. Start with forced brightness, trying to make this easier for them, your voice cracking as you say practical things about remembering to write, about how proud you are. But halfway through, the facade shatters. Your voice drops to something raw and small. You're not saying goodbye to your child—you're saying goodbye to ever being needed again, to your purpose, to the future you thought you'd share. End on a whispered 'I love you' that contains both blessing and absolute devastation. Let the transformation from brave parent to abandoned soul happen in real time.

title: The Last Thank You
instruction: You're a teenage girl who's been in a terrible accident—a deep wound in your side, bleeding heavily. You're lying on the ground, alone, trying to call for help on your phone, but your voice starts fading as shock sets in. At first, you're frantic, gasping, shouting for someone to find you. But as the cold spreads and your vision blurs, you realize no one's coming. In the final moments, you shift from desperate panic to a quiet, grateful whisper, thanking someone who isn't there—a memory or a loved one—for the little things they gave you. Let your voice start loud and strained, then gradually lose strength, becoming shaky, breathy, and soft. Let your words trail off, interrupted by shivers and pauses, as the gratitude feels both sincere and impossibly distant.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Thank You For Breaking My Heart: Gratitude in Devastation
instruction: You're speaking to someone who has just ended your relationship, and against all logic, you're finding yourself genuinely grateful even as your heart is being torn apart. Begin with a small, rueful laugh that contains both pain and strange relief — your voice wavers between tears and genuine warmth. As you list the ways they changed you, enriched you, broke you open in ways you needed, let your voice break repeatedly, but keep returning to honest appreciation. Feel the contradiction: you're sobbing while smiling, voice cracking on 'thank you,' choking on words of gratitude while your chest feels crushed. End with a moment of profound peace mixed with devastating loss — acknowledging that some of the most important people in our lives are the ones who break us, and you wouldn't trade this pain for never having known them. Make the audience feel the beautiful agony of loving someone enough to be grateful even as they destroy you.

title: Presence Complete
instruction: You're finally fully present with someone important — not checking your phone, not thinking about tomorrow, not carrying the weight of the past. Your voice is soft, fully engaged: 'I'm here. Right now, I'm completely here with you.' Your voice carries your full attention, your full presence. 'For so long, I wasn't actually *with* people.
