instruction: You're at their favorite place, their ashes in one hand, their final letter in the other. Start reading their words aloud—they're making you laugh, some inside joke, their voice so alive on the page. Your laughter is real, joyful, until a line hits you: 'Thank you for letting me go.' Your voice breaks but you keep reading, crying and smiling at once. They're releasing you from grief, telling you to live, and you're so grateful and so angry they're giving you permission you don't want. End with your voice full of contradictions: laughing at their humor while sobbing, saying 'thank you' like it's both a gift and a curse, finding peace in their release while your heart is shattering. Let the joy and devastation be inseparable.
inspired_by: Being Intimate When Someone's Body Triggers Your Trauma

title: The Reckoning With the Parent Who Failed You
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about the love you never received, the protection they never offered, the ways they abandoned you when you needed them most. Start with carefully controlled words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, to stay calm. But as you speak, decades of suppressed pain begin to surface. Your voice tightens with anger, then cracks with the grief of the child still inside you. You're moving between fury at what they did and desperate hope that they'll finally see you, hear you, acknowledge the damage. Let moments of rage dissolve into heartbreak, then harden again into bitter truth-telling. End in a place of exhausted clarity—not forgiveness, not continued rage, but a painful recognition of what will never be healed, spoken with a voice that's finally done asking for what they cannot give.

title: The Gala Decay
instruction: You are at a stuffy charity gala, exhausted after a 14-hour day, and your boss's terrible joke about a disgusting incident (a client vomiting into a planter) has triggered a laughing fit. You're trying to apologize to the caterer but can't stop wheezing. Start with a strained, wavering voice full of disgust — 'That was so, so wrong...' — then let laughter shred your sentences, cutting off words with squeaks and breathless gasps. As the fit subsides, your voice drops into heavy fatigue: 'I just... I can't keep doing this...' Let the laughter physically yank you from disgust to utter weariness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Muffled Confrontation
instruction: You're standing in a hallway, your hand pressed tight over your mouth. You've just been publicly humiliated by a friend who twisted your words. At first, shame burns in your chest—you want to disappear, so you keep your hand clamped down, words coming out muffled, consonants slurred. But as you replay what was said, anger ignites. Your voice strains against your palm, wavering. Mid-sentence, you lower your hand, your tone cracking into raw fury. Speak with a breathless start, then let the anger sharpen your voice as you finally let it out.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Things I'll Never Say Out Loud
instruction: Late at night, you're confessing something to someone who's asleep beside you—a secret you can never actually tell them. Begin in the barest whisper, testing the words in the dark: 'There's something I need you to know, even though you can't hear me.' Your voice is tender, intimate, achingly vulnerable. Maybe it's an affair, a lie, a truth about who you really are, a terminal diagnosis you're hiding. The words catch in your throat. You allow yourself, just for these stolen moments, to be completely honest. The relief mixed with grief is overwhelming. 'I'm so sorry. I love you so much.' End with your hand reaching toward them but not quite touching, voice breaking on a sob you have to swallow before they wake.

title: Whispering Your Truth to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You're leaving in the morning—for good—but you can't tell them while they're awake. In a whisper, you begin to confess everything: why you're leaving, how much you love them, why love isn't enough. Start with your voice barely audible, tender and aching. Each sentence is something you could never say to their face. Your whisper becomes thicker with emotion as you describe specific moments—the way they laugh, how safe you felt, why you have to go. Your throat catches on the words. You're crying silently now, still whispering, telling them they deserve better. End with a whispered 'I'm sorry' that sounds like your heart is shattering in slow motion, so quiet it's almost just breath.
inspired_by: Narrator Triggered by Their Own Words

title: Steam and Laughter
instruction: You're in a hot shower, the tiles amplifying every sound. Through the curtain, a friend is teasing you about something silly—maybe a song you were humming. You answer back with playful sarcasm, but as you wipe water from your eyes and hear their laugh echo, your tone softens. Let your voice start with a teasing edge, catch yourself mid-sentence as a drop of water hits your lips, then finish with genuine affection.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Fever Dream of Reckoning
instruction: You are in the grip of intense physical pain—a migraine, an injury, a fever—and in this vulnerable state, emotional memories surface with overwhelming intensity. As waves of physical sensation crash through you, your eyes fall on objects nearby that trigger visceral emotional responses: a glass of water that reminds you of someone's kindness when you were last this vulnerable, a pillow that smells like someone who hurt you, a clock that marks time you feel you're wasting, a window showing a sky that reminds you of a moment of freedom, a phone you can't bring yourself to pick up. The physical pain and emotional memories blend and amplify each other. Begin with gritted teeth, trying to maintain control, breathing through the pain. As each object pulls up raw feelings, let the physical and emotional pain intertwine until you can no longer separate them, until you're surrendering to both, possibly crying out, possibly laughing at the absurdity, possibly both—finding a kind of breakthrough in the overwhelming intensity.
inspired_by: Surround Yourself with Meaningful and Impacting Choices

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about the years he chose his career, his reputation, his pride over being present for you. Your voice starts controlled, almost clinical: 'I needed you. Not your money, not your name - you.' But the dam breaks. Decades of swallowed words pour out - the school plays he missed, the nights you waited by the window, the way you learned to stop hoping. Your anger is molten, your voice cracking: 'I was your child.' Then something shifts. You see him truly broken before you, and your rage collapses into something more complicated - not forgiveness exactly, but exhausted grief for what could have been. Your final words are quiet, drained: 'I just wanted you to see me.'

title: Historical: Slave Owner's Child Discovers They're Half-Sibling to Enslaved Person
instruction: Piece of information shatters your world. Your voice becomes confused. You've been raised with someone as property who is actually family. Your voice is identity collapse. Your breathing becomes uncertain. All your privilege is built on denying kinship to someone you're now forced to see as sibling. Your voice cycles through denial and recognition. You're being asked to choose—privilege or family—and there's no version of choice that doesn't cost you everything. Your voice becomes someone fundamentally transformed by forced recognition.

title: Confronting Your Mother: The Truth About Why You Left
instruction: You're finally telling your mother why you disappeared from her life five years ago. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you something I've never said.' But as you speak the truth about her choices that damaged you, your voice begins to crack. You're trying so hard to stay measured, to be the adult, but the wounded child keeps breaking through. Move through rising anger—sharp, cutting words you've rehearsed a thousand times—into something rawer: the ache of a child who needed protection and didn't get it. Then, unexpectedly, as you hear yourself say it all out loud, feel something shift. Not forgiveness exactly, but recognition that she was broken too. End with your voice small, almost confused: a mixture of exhausted grief, tentative hope that maybe now things can be different, and the terrifying vulnerability of admitting you still need her to say she's sorry.
inspired_by: First Day of Sobriety: Calling Your Sponsor

title: The Birthday Roast
instruction: You are at your granddaughter's 14th birthday party, surrounded by her friends. You're teasing them about the terrible boy band posters on her wall, your high-pitched voice full of playful mockery. But your vocal tics keep interrupting — sudden barks or shouted phrases that pop out mid-sentence. You've learned to flow past them seamlessly, as if the tic was just a funny punctuation. Start with that teasing, warm edge, then by the end, your voice shifts — a quieter, wry observation about how fast she's growing up, the mockery fading into tender, bittersweet realization.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Frozen Confession
instruction: You're a teenage boy standing alone in a blizzard after your dad's truck broke down because you forgot to fill the gas tank. Your jaw is numb, your lips barely move, and every word feels like scraping ice off glass. Start by muttering excuses to yourself, jaw tight and words slurred, shame thick in your chest. Then, as the cold sinks deeper, let the shame soften into a raw, shivering apology you wish you could say to your father—voice cracking, breath visible, the confession slipping out before you can stop it.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About Why She Never Held You
instruction: You're thirty-five and you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. Start controlled, almost clinical—you've been in therapy, you have the language now. 'I need to talk about my childhood.' But as you speak, feel the little kid inside you rising up, the one who watched other mothers scoop up their children while yours stayed at arm's length. Your voice should crack between adult composure and childlike bewilderment. Build from measured words to raw accusation: 'Why couldn't you just hold me?' Let anger surge—real, righteous anger—then watch it collapse into the question underneath: 'What was wrong with me?' End in a place of terrible vulnerability, almost whispering: 'I just needed you to hold me.' The arc moves from intellectual distance to volcanic rage to the naked, wounded heart of a child who still doesn't understand.
inspired_by: Telling Someone Their Fly Is Down at Their Wedding

title: The Garden of Wrath
instruction: You are a very old, usually gentle woman with a soft, high voice. You have spent decades meticulously caring for your late husband’s prize rose garden, your greatest source of elation and contentment. Now, a neighbor’s dog has torn through it, uprooting every bush. You are outside, kneeling in the dirt, clutching a broken rose stem. Start with a quiet, trembling voice as you find a single, unbroken bud—a moment of pure, fragile hope and contentment. Then, the full weight of the destruction hits you. Let that elation and contemplation curdle into a shocking, guttural rage. Your voice drops in pitch, becomes rough and percussive. Let your breathing turn heavy, and let your words come out as short, furious attacks. You might throw a clump of dirt or slam your fist on the ground. By the end, your voice should be ragged, almost inaudible with fury, but the memory of that stolen peace still burns underneath.
emotions_sampled: Elation (very intensely present), Contentment (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What You Gave Me in the Darkness
instruction: It's 3 AM, and you're whispering to your sleeping partner about the gift of their presence in your life - but you're leaving them in the morning, and they don't know yet. Speak so softly, as if any louder would shatter everything. You're grateful, genuinely grateful, for what they've given you, but it's not enough, and that knowledge is breaking you. Let your voice be thick with unshed tears as you catalog the small kindnesses, the quiet devotions, the ordinary miracles of daily love. Let pauses speak as loudly as words. Midway through, let the truth creep in - that you're grateful and it still isn't enough to make you stay, that you can love someone and still need to leave. Your voice should catch on words like 'thank you' and 'I'm sorry.' End with the devastating contradiction: you're whispering 'thank you for everything' while knowing it means goodbye. Natural, intimate, the kind of confession that feels like it's being pulled from your chest.
inspired_by: Hiding Disappointment When Receiving an Unwanted Gift

title: Confrontation at the Edge of the Void
instruction: You're on a space station having a real-time video call with the family member who funded your dream to go to space—but who was never there for you when it mattered. They're dying back on Earth, and this is your last chance to speak. Begin with cold, clipped professionalism, the kind of distance you've perfected over years. But they say something—an apology, a confession, an 'I love you' they never said before—and it detonates something inside you. Let the rage come, the grief of a lifetime of absence, all the moments they missed. Your voice should shake with the effort of holding back, then break through. But underneath the anger, there's a child who just wanted to be seen. By the end, you're not sure if you're forgiving them or just too exhausted to keep hating. The silence after you finish should feel like free fall.

title: Unraveling at the Summit
instruction: You've just reached the mountain peak you've climbed for three days to scatter your spouse's ashes, but sudden altitude sickness is hitting hard—disorientation, nausea, your vision swimming. Begin trying to say the eulogy you prepared, but you can't remember the words, can't breathe properly, and rage explodes at the universe for taking this from you too. Your voice lurches from shouting at them for dying, to gasping apologies, to laughing hysterically at the cosmic joke. Include visceral sounds of struggling for air between words, your speech slurring as hypoxia clouds your thoughts. Let fury at your failing body mix with fierce protectiveness of these final moments together. End collapsing into raw, primitive grief—no words left, just animal sounds of loss, yet somehow forcing out one clear, final 'I love you' before everything goes dark.

title: The Last Sweater
instruction: You are a father, sitting alone in a quiet room, knitting a tiny sweater for your child who no longer lives with you. The rhythmic click of the needles is the only sound. You start in a state of deep emotional numbness, your voice flat and distant, as you talk to the sweater—thanking it for being something you can finish. But as you speak, the gratitude becomes more present, more painful, and your voice begins to crack, the numbness cracking into raw thankfulness and buried grief. Let the knitting guide your pauses—when you lose a stitch, when the pattern blurs—and let your breathing change as the emotion surfaces. End with a whisper of thanks that sounds like a first real feeling in years.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Pain (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Sound of Skin
instruction: You're with someone you've desired for years, finally intimate, finally touching. But you're lost in your own head, performing, anxious, disconnected. Your task is to stop performing and start listening with your body: truly hear their breathing change, the small sounds they make, the way they whisper your name, the rustle of fabric, the rhythm of skin on skin. Begin frantic and self-conscious, trying to get it right, trapped in anxiety. Then surrender completely to receiving what they're communicating through sound and breath and voice. Let what you hear—their genuine pleasure, their vulnerability, their presence—pull you out of your head and into your body. Transform from anxious performance to raw presence, from self-consciousness to being utterly consumed by the symphony of what's actually happening between you.
inspired_by: Actor struggles to listen to scene partners genuinely

title: Finding Them After Years of Searching
instruction: You've spent years searching for someone—a sibling given up for adoption, a parent who disappeared, a child taken by an ex-partner. Now you're standing in front of them, and they're real, alive, here. Begin with disbelief and tentative joy—your voice shaking with wonder, almost laughing. 'It's you. Oh my God, it's really you.' Your words tumble out, relief and joy mixing with tears. But as you try to bridge the years, reality sets in: they don't remember you, or they're angry, or they've built a life without you. Your laughter becomes tears, joy transforms into heartbreak. 'I never stopped looking. Never. Every day...' Your voice fractures between gratitude that they're alive and the devastating grief of what's been lost forever. End with contradictory emotions flooding your voice: 'I'm so happy you're okay. I'm so happy and it's breaking my heart.'

title: The Quake of Completion
instruction: You have just finished digging a grave by hand in rocky soil. Your entire body is shaking uncontrollably — your arms, your jaw, your legs. You sit down heavily on a tree stump, staring at your trembling hands. Begin with confusion: you can't quite believe what you've done, and the tremor in your voice mirrors the tremor in your body. As you look at the mound of earth, let your thoughts deepen into contemplation — the weight of the moment, the finality. Let your words come in fits and starts, interrupted by the shakes and your own breath. End with a quiet wave of relief washing over you: it's over, you did it, and the shaking begins to subside as you accept what has happened. Your voice should feel fragile, cracked, but finally settling.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Contemplation (very intensely present), Relief (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Dad Blunder
instruction: You're in a noisy locker room after a pickup basketball game, surrounded by a group of your usual buddies. You start telling a loud, boastful story about your son's game-winning shot, but halfway through you realize you're about to reveal something embarrassing—you forgot to pick him up from practice last week. Your voice begins with confident, booming swagger, but as the memory hits, you stumble, your words get jumbled, and you try to laugh it off while shifting your weight and adjusting your towel. End with a forced, awkward joke that trails off as you pretend to tie your shoe, the embarrassment hanging in the air.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Fierce Protection of a Child You're Losing to the System
instruction: You're a foster parent being told you must give back the child you've raised for three years. Start with barely contained rage: 'She calls me Mama. Do you understand that?' Your voice is shaking with fierce, protective fury. Demand they look at her drawings on the fridge, her height marks on the wall. Your passion escalates: 'You cannot do this to her again.' But your voice cracks as helplessness seeps in—you know the law, you know you're losing. The rage breaks into desperate pleading: 'Please, she's finally sleeping through the night.' Your voice drops to something raw and broken as you describe her nightmares, her fear of abandonment. End collapsed in grief, your fierce protection meeting absolute powerlessness, whispering: 'How do I tell her?' Your love for this child is volcanic, but so is your devastation at failing to save her.

title: The Wrong Terminal Goodbye
instruction: You're at an airport saying goodbye to someone you love, but you've realized too late you're in the wrong terminal - their flight is boarding now in another building, and there's no time to get there. Start with breathless, almost manic cheerfulness as you try to pretend everything is fine, making jokes about the mix-up. Gradually let the reality sink in - your voice should crack and soften as you realize this moment you'd planned, these final words you'd rehearsed, are all being stolen by your own mistake. End in a whispered, raw confession of everything you needed to say, knowing they can't hear you anymore. Let the transition from forced lightness to devastating quiet honesty be gradual and achingly real.

title: The Last Sip
instruction: You're a young man who just drank something that's burning your throat and stomach. You're on your knees, gripping the edge of a sink, trying to call for help but every word is interrupted by a violent gag. Start with urgent panic—you need to shout for your roommate, but your voice keeps cutting off with a heave. As the nausea deepens and the pain spikes, shift into a quieter, more resigned moan—you realize you're alone and no one's coming. Let your voice be thick with mucus, words garbled, with natural pauses as you fight the reflex. End in a exhausted whisper, accepting the pain.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Twisted Discovery
instruction: You're in a yoga class, seated in a deep twist, one hand reaching back toward the floor. Your torso is contorted, breath shallow and uneven, and you're trying to see what your friend behind you is holding—a surprise they promised. Start by muttering about the strain, your voice strained and wobbly as you twist further, the effort audible in your vowels. Mid-grumble, you catch a glimpse of the object—a puppy—and your voice cracks into astonished wonder, breath hitching, tone rising in disbelief. Let the physical twist warp your words, then settle into a breathless, amazed realization.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Salt and Skin
instruction: You're standing at the shoreline, wind whipping your hair, the crash of waves constant. You spot someone walking along the beach — the way the sunlight catches their body stops you mid-stride. Start with a slight, hopeful smile — a spark of possibility — but as they move closer, your breath catches and that hopefulness melts into raw, consuming desire. Let the wind steal some words; shift your weight in the sand; let your voice crack or drop as the lust takes over. You have about a minute of spoken thought, from the first glimpse to the moment they pass by.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Fury of the Helpless
instruction: You're a parent who just received a call that your teenager was in a car accident—they're okay, but they were drunk, and they were driving. You burst into the hospital room ready to explode. Start with volcanic rage, your voice shaking the walls: 'DO YOU HAVE ANY IDEA—' But mid-sentence, you see the bruises, the smallness of them in that hospital bed, and the fury cracks. You're still angry—God, you're furious—but now you're terrified, and the terror is bigger. Your voice breaks from shouting into something almost animalistic, a sound you've never made before. You're yelling and crying at once, your words collapsing into each other: anger at their stupidity, grief at how close you came to losing them, rage at your own powerlessness to keep them safe. End by pulling them close while you're still half-shouting, your voice dissolving into their shoulder, fierce and broken and completely undone. Show how protective love and helpless rage are sometimes the same desperate sound.

title: The Nightly Sentence
instruction: You are an older man in a hospital bed, wearing a CPAP mask that hisses with oxygen. A doctor has just explained you must use it every night for life. Begin speaking with thick bitterness—your life reduced to this plastic prison, your independence stolen. But as you continue, the mask fogs up, you adjust it clumsily, and a flicker of pain leaks through—not the physical kind, but the quiet ache of what you've lost. By the end, let the bitterness soften into a tired, reluctant acceptance of the unavoidable. Your voice must push against the muffling mask, louder and more determined than you feel, with natural pauses to clear the moisture or shift on the pillows.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unspoken Grade
instruction: You're 16, at the dinner table with your parents and younger brother. Your mom just mentioned the upcoming parent-teacher conference, and you've been hiding your failing math report card under your pillow. Fear clenches your stomach. You confess the truth, starting with a quiet, shaky voice that struggles to find words, glancing nervously between family members. Midway, the fear shifts into a raw plea for understanding, then a fragile defiance as you finally lift your head to meet your mom's eyes. Let your voice waver, trail off, then grow steadier. Speak about 60 words, natural pauses included.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Masked Muster
instruction: You're a teenage boy, waiting in a long, slow line for a school vaccination. Your mask is hot and damp, the elastic digs behind your ears, and you're starting to fidget. You're talking to a friend next to you, voice slightly muffled, and you're annoyed because you wanted to be outside. Your words start clipped and irritated, but then you notice the nurse looks tired, and a flicker of empathy breaks through. Let your voice strain a little at first, then soften, the mask still making your s's a bit fuzzy, and let a small, awkward shrug happen mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Breathing the Same Air
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, and you whisper a confession you've never said aloud—that you're terrified you don't know how to be loved, and you've been sabotaging intimacy your whole life. Start barely audible, voice catching. Don't manufacture vulnerability; let yourself be genuinely uncertain whether words will even come. Explore the pauses, the almost-saying-it-then-stopping, the physical sensation of admitting fear this naked. Trust the tiny shifts—maybe your breath changes, maybe you have to try three different ways to say the same thing. By the end, let yourself receive imagined comfort, let your body respond to being held, and feel what it's like to not carry this alone anymore.

title: The Last Formation
instruction: You are a drill sergeant addressing your platoon for the final time before they deploy. You’ve trained them hard, and you’re bursting with pride—they’re ready. You start with your usual commanding, staccato shout, but as you speak, the weight of saying goodbye hits you. Your voice catches, the rhythm breaks, and your hyper-feminized tone cracks with sorrow. Let the joy of their achievement war with the ache of letting them go—shout through tears, lose your breath, then find it again as you force out a salute. End with a quiet, raw whisper that holds both fierce love and grief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Homecoming Paradox
instruction: You are returning to your childhood home after your estranged parent's funeral. You have inherited the house. As you walk through rooms, touching objects, opening drawers, you must hold two incompatible truths: this person made you feel unloved, unsafe, never good enough—AND they kept every drawing you made, every report card, every photograph, hidden away where you never saw them. Begin with bitter satisfaction, a kind of triumph that you survived them. But let specific objects undo you: a box with your name on it, your baby shoes wrapped in tissue paper, a letter they wrote but never sent. Your emotion must fracture: anger that they couldn't show this love when it mattered, grief that they felt it but couldn't express it, rage at the waste of it all, and a terrible, unwanted compassion. Let your voice break between contradictions—laughing at the absurdity, crying at the loss, furious at the unfairness. End holding something of theirs, your voice small, saying what you would have said if you'd known they were keeping your drawings all along.
inspired_by: Actor must play a character with a psychologically extreme or morally alien background (villain, severe trauma, etc.)

title: Radio Silence
instruction: You're a teenage boy using a walkie-talkie to reach your best friend who just moved away. You key the mic, forcing a tough, low voice to sound casual. But as you talk about missing the old hangout spot, your voice wavers—you swallow hard, pause, and let the longing seep through. By the end, the masculine front cracks, and you whisper a confession you're afraid to admit.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Your Truth to Someone Who's Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone's hospital bed, or beside your sleeping child, or next to your partner after a terrible fight. They're asleep, and you finally have the space to say everything you've been interrupted from saying for months or years. Start in a whisper, tentative, testing if you can even voice these feelings aloud. Your words should be halting, catching on emotion—confessing love mixed with resentment, gratitude mixed with grief, all the complicated truths that get silenced in daily life. Let your voice become tender and broken, speaking the kind of vulnerable admissions that catch in your throat. Midway through, have a moment where you almost stop, where the emotion is so overwhelming you can barely breathe. Then continue softer still, ending with a whispered truth so raw it feels like you're finally letting yourself be known, even if they can't hear you. The quiet should be heavy with everything unsaid.
inspired_by: Maintaining Patience While Being Repeatedly Interrupted

title: Thanking Someone for Leaving You While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: They've just told you they're walking away, and you know—you absolutely know—they're right to do it. Start with a laugh that's almost genuine because the irony is absurd: they're saving themselves from you and you're grateful. Your voice is warm as you tell them they deserve better, and you mean it. But underneath, you're breaking. As you list all the ways they made your life beautiful, your gratitude is completely real but your voice starts to shake. You're simultaneously thankful and devastated. The two emotions fight in your throat. You keep trying to smile through it—they can probably hear the smile breaking in your voice. You tell them you're happy for them and it's both true and a lie. End with 'Thank you for loving me when you did' where the gratitude and the grief are completely, beautifully inseparable. Your voice is steady and shattered at once.
inspired_by: Rejecting Someone Sexually and Trying to Be Kind

title: The Clearing of the Rot
instruction: You are a father who has just discovered that the horrible, rotting smell you've been tracking for days in your child's room is not from something dead in the wall, but from a single forgotten, moldy sippy cup hidden under the bed. Your disgust was overwhelming—your nose wrinkled, your stomach turned, you felt a growing dread that something was seriously wrong. But as you pull it out and realize it's just a cup, a wave of relief crashes over you. Let the disgust be intense in your first words: your voice is pinched, angry, almost gagging. Then, as the truth hits, let that tension break into a long, shaking exhale; your voice lifts with shaky warmth, maybe even a tearful laugh. Collapse back onto the floor as you pull the cup out, speaking to your child who is watching. Your words should feel like they're tumbling out between that initial disgust and the sudden release.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Haunted House Actor Who Takes It Too Seriously
instruction: You work at a Halloween haunted house. Start with the corporate scare: 'Welcome to your NIGHTMARE!' Then a group of teenagers comes through who are clearly not scared. Your competitive actor kicks in. Go bigger, weirder, more committed. Break character to chase them. When one of them actually screams and starts crying, immediately drop the act — concerned human voice: 'Oh god, are you okay? I'm so sorry, it's just a costume.' Toggle between monster and mortified person.

title: The Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're thirty-five, sitting across from your mother, finally speaking the truth you've carried since childhood. Your voice starts controlled but acidic: 'You always made me feel like I had to earn your love. Nothing I did was ever enough.' She deflects, defends, tries to rewrite history. You press harder, your voice cracking with pain: 'I needed you to just love me as I was.' Then she breaks—really breaks—and admits her own fears, her own mother's conditional love, her terror of failing you. Your anger doesn't disappear, but something shifts. Move from sharp confrontation through raw pain to a complex place where you can hold both your hurt and her humanity. Your voice should end quieter, exhausted, but with a fragile opening toward forgiveness—not absolution, but acknowledgment. It's messy, unresolved, but honest.

title: The Truth in the Dark
instruction: It's 2 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, both awake but pretending to sleep. Earlier today, you did something that contradicts everything they believe about you—an act of courage, or perhaps cowardice, that reveals a part of yourself you've always hidden. Maybe you were brave when everyone thinks you're timid. Maybe you were cruel when everyone believes you're kind. In barely audible whispers, in the protective darkness, confess what you did and why. Begin with your voice small, almost hoping they won't hear. But as you continue, let something break open—not dramatically, but like ice slowly cracking. Reveal the person you've actually been all along underneath the version they fell in love with. Let your whisper grow slightly stronger as you ask the terrifying question: can they love this real version of you? End in fragile hope or quiet devastation.
inspired_by: Finding the Clues to the Character

title: The Last Promise
instruction: You are a young man with a deep voice, pleading with your older brother to let you borrow his car for a date tonight. You’re embarrassed to be begging, but you’re also genuinely interested in impressing this person you’ve liked for months. Start by rushing through your request, your pitch climbing, your voice cracking with shame. Then, as you sense him about to say no, let your desperation bleed in—your voice gets quieter, more submissive, a faint creak at the start of your words as you push out one last promise. End with a shaky, breathless 'please,' the word tapering into silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father after discovering they've been telling family members you're struggling, failing, barely getting by—when in reality, you've built a life you're proud of. Start with hurt confusion, asking why they can't see what you've accomplished. But as you speak, decades of being diminished rise up in you. Let your voice build from wounded questions to something seismic: a refusal to be erased anymore. List everything you've survived, everything you've built, every way you've become whole without their recognition. End not seeking their approval, but declaring that you see yourself now—and that's what matters. Transform from needing their eyes to claiming your own vision.
inspired_by: Taking Your Due and Standing Up for Yourself

title: The Last Bolt
instruction: You're wedged under a rusted car, in a deep squat, knees wide, back pressed against the frame. Your legs are burning, and you've been wrenching at a stubborn bolt for what feels like forever. Start with a strained, grunting effort, words pushed through gritted teeth—frustration, exhaustion. Then, with a sudden pop, the bolt breaks free. Let the voice shift: a sharp gasp, then a breathless, grinning laugh. Triumph floods in, then deep relief, and finally a fierce pride as you mutter to yourself, wiping your forehead and bracing one hand against the ground. Your words are short, raw, and real, as if you're talking to the car itself.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Relief (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Moving Forward Together
instruction: Two people are moving forward from a place of difficulty into an unknown future. Their voices carry both trepidation and hope. They're walking in tandem, aware that the path ahead is unclear. One voice might try to accelerate; the other grounds them in the present. They're making agreements about how to move forward. Their voices become more confident as they establish direction. By the end, they're moving with less hesitation. The future is still unknown, but they're meeting it together. Their voices reflect the specific strength that comes from not facing the unknown alone.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, facing your father across the same table where you ate breakfast for eighteen years. You've finally come to tell him the truth: his absence broke something in you that you're still trying to repair. Start controlled, almost clinical—you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, the hurt you've buried rises up. Your voice becomes sharper, more accusatory. You wanted him to show up, to see you, to fight for you. The anger builds until suddenly it cracks open into something more vulnerable—underneath the rage is a child who just wanted to be enough. Your voice breaks as you admit you still need him to say he's sorry, even though you're thirty-five years old. End with the raw exposure of having revealed your deepest wound to the person who created it, mixing defiance with desperate hope.

title: Watching You Break
instruction: Your child, partner, or younger sibling is pursuing something that's destroying them - an abusive relationship, an impossible dream, a path of self-destruction - and you've been supportive for so long. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive encouragement, the kind that comes from desperation. You're trying to believe, trying to pump them up, your voice loud and insistent. But mid-way, something snaps. Your encouragement transforms into a passionate, explosive plea - you can't do this anymore, you can't watch them suffer. Your voice should crack and surge, moving from cheerleading to raw confrontation. Rage bleeds into tears, strength collapses into helplessness. End in a completely different place: quiet, broken, admitting you don't know how to save them, that maybe you can't. Let the journey be volcanic - from false strength to honest devastation.
inspired_by: Acting Encouraging Despite Believing in Imminent Failure

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your estranged parent exactly what their absence cost you. Start with bitter sarcasm, voice dripping with defensive anger: 'Thanks for showing up now, really, perfect timing.' Your words are weapons, each one designed to wound. But as you catalog the milestones they missed—graduations, heartbreaks, victories—your voice begins to shake with the grief underneath the rage. 'I needed you. I was just a kid, and I needed you.' The anger collapses into raw, childlike hurt, your voice becoming smaller, younger. End with exhausted vulnerability, almost a whisper: 'I don't know if I can forgive you. But I need you to understand what you did.' You're not performing anger—you're bleeding out years of unspoken pain.

title: The Weight of Pleasure
instruction: You are an older man, in the midst of intimate sex with a partner you love but are about to lose. The physical pleasure is undeniable, but it’s tangled with a heavy sadness and a growing distress that you can no longer hide. Begin with involuntary moans, open and vulnerable, but let them crack and shift as the sadness breaks through—your voice becomes thick, breathy, with sighs that turn into half-sobs. Midway, you pause the motion, your hand trembling against their skin, and speak aloud the real feeling: 'I can't ... not tonight. I'm sorry, but holding you like this, it just hurts too much.' End with a whisper, voice frayed, as you slowly withdraw, leaving the sound of your own ragged breathing.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a terminal diagnosis appointment, and they ask how it went. You start trying to sound normal, maybe even cheerful: 'Oh, you know, just routine stuff...' But their follow-up question—something innocent like 'So everything's fine?'—breaks something open inside you. Your voice begins to crack as you try to maintain the lie, but the weight of what you're not saying becomes unbearable. The false brightness dissolves into silence, then a whisper. You move from protective deception to the devastating realization that you can't leave this world with a lie between you. End by speaking the truth with a voice that's both breaking and finally, terribly free.

title: Frozen Waiting
instruction: You're a middle-aged man standing outside a dive bar in sub-zero weather, waiting for a woman you're infatuated with. She's late, and the cold has locked your jaw — your words come out tight and slurred. Start by muttering angrily about the temperature, your breath clouding as you stamp your feet. Then, as you picture her face, your voice softens despite the stiffness, and you catch yourself smiling through the chill. Let the anger fade into awed longing — but keep the physical strain of the cold in every word.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Parent Discovering Their Child is the One Who Hurt Them
instruction: You've been in physical therapy for six months after a brutal attack. Today, the detective called—they found who did it. It's your own child. Your adult son. You're looking at his photo now, the evidence, his confession. Begin with disbelief so visceral it's almost a laugh—this can't be real. Then fury erupts: how dare he, after everything you sacrificed, after you worked three jobs to raise him. Your voice should shake the walls. But then, devastatingly, a memory surfaces mid-rage: him at seven, crying in your arms after a nightmare. The rage doesn't vanish—it collides with love, and the collision is unbearable. You're screaming and sobbing at once. 'I would have died for you' becomes 'I don't know you' becomes 'You're still my baby' all in the span of seconds. End in a place beyond rage, beyond grief—a vast, hollow confusion where a mother's love meets a mother's betrayal, and both are equally true.
inspired_by: Judge Must Sentence Someone for Loving Their Child

title: Victory Flowers
instruction: You've just received flowers celebrating your massive professional achievement—the thing you've worked toward for years. You're alone, holding the bouquet, and you should be purely happy. Begin by describing the flowers through every sense: their colors almost too bright, the cellophane crackling, the pollen dusting your fingers, their fragrance overwhelming the small apartment, the weight of the vase, the cold water dripping. Let your voice start excited, victorious. But as you describe the sensory details, let them trigger awareness of what—or who—isn't here to celebrate with you. Perhaps the flowers smell like a funeral you attended. Perhaps their beauty makes you aware of the empty room. Let each sense betray you, turning celebration into grief, success into loss. Your voice should fragment between joy and sorrow until they're inseparable. End speaking to someone who isn't there, the flowers still beautiful in your hands, your voice holding both triumph and unbearable loneliness simultaneously.

title: The Pillow That Knows
instruction: You are lying face-down on your bed, your face pressed deep into a pillow. You've just discovered a text from your ex—a casual 'hey, how have you been?'—and the photo they sent of their new partner is still open on your phone. Your longing to respond and the pain of seeing them happy mix with a sharp disgust at yourself for even checking their profile. Start by groaning into the pillow, your words thick and trapped; then, as you lift your head slightly to catch breath, let the disgust turn into a bitter, shaky laugh at your own weakness, ending with a whispered admission that you still miss them despite everything.
emotions_sampled: Longing (clearly present), Pain (clearly present), Disgust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy Who Saved Your Life
instruction: The person bleeding out in your arms killed someone you loved, and you've spent years hunting them down. But they just took a bullet meant for you. Start with explosive, confused rage—you're furiously demanding to know why they did it, your voice shaking with the wrongness of this moment. You wanted them to suffer, and now they're dying a hero. Your anger fractures into something more desperate as they struggle to breathe. You find yourself pressing your hands to their wound, voice rising in panicked commands for them to stay awake, even as you hate yourself for caring. The rage collapses entirely into raw, helpless grief as you realize you're losing the only person who understood the worst thing you ever experienced. End in a broken whisper, begging their forgiveness and offering your own, your voice thick with contradictory emotions you can't name.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Car After Earthquake: Checking if Your Passenger is Dead

title: The Last Flight Briefing
instruction: You're briefing your child, now an astronaut, before their one-way mission to establish humanity's first settlement on a distant planet. You begin with professional composure, reviewing protocols and contingencies: 'Remember the communication windows, the fail-safes we discussed.' Your voice is steady, almost clinical, because that's how you survive this. But as you near the end, looking at their face for what might be the last time, your voice fractures. The protocol dissolves into a parent's desperate need to say everything unsaid: 'I was so afraid of you, of how much I loved you.' You finish trying to return to the briefing, but your voice now carries the weight of a goodbye that's both proud and completely shattered.

title: Burning Hands
instruction: You've just grabbed a scalding pot bare-handed without thinking—perhaps in passion, perhaps in rage, perhaps to stop something from boiling over. The initial shock of pain is electric, but don't pull away yet. Begin with sharp, gasping breaths, cataloging every aspect of the sensation with fierce intensity: the exact location where metal meets skin, whether the heat feels wet or dry, the way pain radiates up your wrists, the smell of your own skin reacting, the sound of your breathing changing. This physical pain is unlocking something emotional you've kept locked away—perhaps fury at someone who isn't here, perhaps grief you've been too numb to feel, perhaps desire you've been afraid to acknowledge. As you finally release the pot and plunge your hands into cold water, let the sensory shock—the temperature change, the relief mixed with new pain, the sound of water, the visual contrast—break open whatever you've been holding back. The physical and emotional should become inseparable: by the end, you can't tell if you're crying from the burn or from what it's made you finally feel. Your voice should move from sharp gasps to something rawer, more primal, more real.

title: Embracing Life Fully
instruction: You're saying yes to all of it—the pain, the joy, the difficulty, the beauty. Your voice is open, expansive: 'I'm ready to feel everything.' Breathing is deep, full-bodied. Physical: arms open. 'I don't want to hide anymore.' Vocal tone is brave, vulnerable, alive. 'Bring it all to me.' By the end, you're fully present in your existence: 'I'm here. I'm alive. I'm taking it all.'

title: The Last Coherent Goodbye: When the Morphine Hasn't Taken Everything Yet
instruction: You're dying, and you know it. The pain medication makes your thoughts swim, but you have maybe ten minutes of clarity left before you slip away forever. You're saying goodbye to the person you love most—your child, your partner, your parent—and you begin with determination, trying to say everything that matters. But your voice keeps fading, words slurring, and panic creeps in because there's so much left unsaid. You fight to stay present, your voice cracking between 'I need you to know...' and 'Please remember...' Start with fierce urgency, trying to pack a lifetime into moments, then feel yourself losing the battle, your words becoming softer, more fragmented. End with a kind of peaceful surrender, maybe a whispered 'I love you' that's barely audible, where you finally let go because you've said enough—or because you have no choice.
inspired_by: Rescued from Choking: The Moment Breath Becomes Possible Again

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence That Raised You
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally ready to say what's been unspoken for decades. Start controlled, almost gentle—you've rehearsed this, you want to get it right. But as you speak about the coldness, the emotional absence, the way she was physically there but never really present, your voice begins to crack. The anger comes, yes, but underneath it is the child still begging to be seen. You oscillate between fury at what you were denied and desperate, embarrassing hope that she'll finally say she's sorry, she sees you now. Watch her non-response break you further. End with a realization that catches in your throat: you're not just confronting her—you're grieving the mother you'll never have. Let your voice move from controlled accusation to raw pleading to something like exhausted surrender.

title: Conducting Business
instruction: You're negotiating a deal and you could undercut your competitor brutally. Your voice could lie here and nobody would know. But you don't. 'They have a good product,' you admit. Your voice conducts business with integrity. It costs you money. Your voice knows it. 'I want to build a company people can trust,' you say, and the competitor respects you for it. Honesty sounds like good business.

title: The Wedding Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You're alone, rehearsing a toast for someone you love who's marrying the wrong person—or perhaps the right person, which somehow hurts more. Begin with the proper, socially acceptable version: gracious, warm, slightly humorous, full of sensory details about happy memories you've shared. Make us see, smell, and feel those moments as vividly as you do. But as you continue, let the fantasy fracture—allow the real feelings to bleed through in your tone, your pauses, your choice of memories. Shift between what you should say and what you want to scream, between genuine happiness for them and your own devastating loss, between cherishing who they've been to you and grieving who they'll become to someone else. End by arriving at a complex truth: you mean every loving word, and you're also breaking apart, and somehow both feelings are equally real and equally powerful. Transform from performance to unbearable honesty.

title: The Weight of What You Dragged
instruction: You're a young man hauling a heavy, bloodstained sack through a moonlit forest. Your arms burn, your back screams, and each step is a grunt of pure malevolence—you're muttering a vicious, satisfied curse about the person inside. Mid-step, the sack shifts and something cold brushes your neck. You freeze, drop the load with a thud, and stare—astonished—as the sack slowly moves on its own. Your voice should start with a low, strained growl, breathless and dark, then crack into a sharp, bewildered gasp, shaky and high-pitched as surprise replaces malice.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispered Under Water
instruction: You're lying next to your sleeping lover in the dark, finally ready to confess something you've been carrying alone for months—a fear, a secret, a truth that terrifies you. Begin with your whole body feeling submerged, as if you're lying at the bottom of the ocean with impossible pressure on your chest. Every word you whisper requires monumental effort, like pushing sound through water. As you speak, focus on the physical sensation of your voice fighting against this invisible weight pressing down on you. Midway through your confession, something shifts—the weight doesn't lift, but you stop fighting it. You let it support you instead of crush you. Your whispered words become softer but somehow clearer, carried by the weight rather than struggling against it. End in a place of weighted vulnerability, where being pressed down has paradoxically made you feel held.

title: The Fog on the Lake
instruction: You are standing on a wooden dock, surrounded by thick, damp fog. You can barely see ten feet ahead. You thought you heard a splash, but now everything is muffled. Speak aloud to yourself, trying to convince yourself you're just imagining things. At first, your voice wavers with doubt—each word uncertain, as if swallowed by the mist. Then, as you lean closer to the water's edge, you see something foul floating: a rotting carcass, tangled in plastic. Your voice hardens with disgust, cutting through the fog with sharp, choked words. Let the fog muffle your initial doubt, then let your disgust rise clear and raw.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're whispering a truth to your sleeping partner that you can never say while they're awake. Begin in the darkness, your voice so soft it's almost just breath. You're confessing something that changes everything—maybe you're leaving, maybe you're staying when you shouldn't, maybe you love them more than they'll ever know. Your throat catches on words that taste like goodbye. Let vulnerability make your voice crack and pause. The intimacy is almost unbearable. As you speak, tenderness wars with devastating sadness. End with your voice dissolving into silence, perhaps touching their face one last time, the confession hanging in the air like a prayer they'll never hear.

title: Masked Attraction
instruction: You are at a crowded outdoor party, wearing an N95 respirator that makes your voice sound muffled and distant. Across the patio, you spot someone you've been crushing on for weeks—they're laughing with friends. As you try to edge closer, confusion hits: are they looking at you or someone else? Your breath fogs the mask, and each word comes out strained through the filter, making you repeat yourself. Start in a bewildered mumble, then let infatuation swell your voice as you commit to speaking louder, your pitch rising with nervous hope. Micro-distractions: adjust the mask, cough, check your phone, then finally blurt out an awkward hello.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Infatuation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Drinking Alone in Their Kitchen
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're in the kitchen of someone who's gone—through death, divorce, or departure. You're drinking water from their favorite glass, the one they always used. Begin in barely a whisper, describing the weight of the glass in your hands with such tenderness, as if it's the most fragile thing in the world. As you drink, let each sensation—the cold, the taste, the feeling of it going down—unlock quiet memories: their laugh, the way they held this same glass, mornings you took for granted. Your voice should stay soft, intimate, like you're telling a secret to the darkness. Let tears creep into your words not through sobs but through the way your breath catches between descriptions. End with the almost inaudible sound of setting the glass down, and a whispered confession of what you never got to say, addressed to the empty room as if they might still hear you.
inspired_by: Taking a Long, Refreshing Drink of Cold Water After Exercise

title: The Moment Everything You Protected Shatters
instruction: You're on the phone or standing in a room, receiving news that someone you fiercely love is in danger—your child is missing, your partner was in an accident, your best friend attempted suicide—and you can't reach them, can't help, can't protect them. Start with shock, your voice sharp and demanding answers, asking the same questions over and over with rising panic. Explode into raw, uncontrolled rage at your own helplessness, screaming at God or fate or whoever's listening. Then collapse—literally in your voice—into broken, gasping pleas and bargaining: 'Please, please, I'll do anything.' Your voice should shred from fury to desperation to whimpering vulnerability. End in a space beyond words, just breathing and the smallest, most broken 'no' imaginable.
inspired_by: The Sound of Loneliness: A Night Alone

title: The Secret in Your Hands
instruction: It's late at night. You're lying next to someone you love, and they're almost asleep. You whisper that you need to tell them something—something you've never told anyone. Start with long pauses, barely audible, almost hoping they won't hear. You're confessing a moment from childhood, something small but formative that shaped who you became: a time you felt utterly alone, or witnessed something you couldn't process, or experienced a joy so pure you've been chasing it ever since. As you speak, let your voice stay soft but grow more present, more there. The vulnerability should feel like peeling back skin. Your breathing matters as much as your words. By the end, you're not seeking forgiveness or understanding—you're simply finally letting this truth exist outside your own head. The emotion moves from shame or fear to something like relief, fragile but real.

title: Gravel and Gratitude on Main Street
instruction: You are an elderly man, slightly tipsy from a single celebratory scotch at a diner, standing on a bustling city corner at dusk. You're teasing your grumpy old friend (not present) about their fear of pigeons, your voice loud and loose to compete with honking taxis and a jackhammer. A siren wails, making you pause mid-laugh, and you squint at the glowing traffic light. As the noise fades, you feel a sudden, quiet wave of thankfulness for this messy, loud life you're still here to see. Your gravelly voice should start rough and playfully sharp with teasing, then slow, searching, and softened with gratitude, your words losing thread as you're distracted by a passing bus or a gust of wind.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral You Planned Together
instruction: You are delivering a eulogy for your best friend—but they were irreverent, wild, and made you promise not to be sad. Begin by trying to honor that promise, sharing a ridiculous memory that makes you genuinely laugh, your voice bright with the joy of remembering them. But mid-laugh, the absurdity of laughing at their funeral hits you, and your laughter becomes tears without stopping—you're laughing and crying simultaneously, unable to separate gratitude from devastation. Your voice should catch between joy and sobs as you say, 'You made me promise not to cry, you absolute bastard, and I can't—I can't keep that promise.' End with a tender, tear-soaked laugh as you say 'thank you,' where both emotions are completely genuine and intertwined. The challenge is to hold both opposing feelings as equally true, never letting one dominate the other.
inspired_by: The Teacher and the Defiant Student

title: Fierce Grace Breaking
instruction: You're a parent whose child has just told you they're in terrible danger - an abusive partner, an addiction, a threat you can't control. Start with fierce protectiveness, your voice strong and determined: you'll fix this, you'll fight for them, you'll destroy anyone who hurts them. Your words come fast, powered by adrenaline and love. But as you're making promises, you realize you can't actually save them - they have to save themselves. Your voice begins to crack under the weight of your own powerlessness. The fierceness dissolves into desperation, then breaks completely into raw, helpless tears. You're begging them to save themselves because you can't do it for them. Let yourself become completely undone, your voice ragged with the agony of loving someone you can't protect. End on your knees emotionally, offering the only thing you have left: 'I'm here. Whatever happens, I'm here.' Your voice is shattered but still holding on.

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's 3 a.m. You're lying in the dark next to your partner of ten years. They think you're asleep, but you're not. You've been carrying something—a fear, a shame, a truth about yourself—that you've never spoken aloud. Begin in silence, just breathing. Then, in the quietest voice, as if testing whether you can even form the words, start to confess. Keep your volume barely above a whisper throughout. This isn't about dramatic revelation—it's about the terror and relief of finally letting someone see a hidden part of you. Let long pauses happen. Let your breath catch. Let the words come in fragments. Move from fear of speaking to the strange, unexpected lightness of being known. The power is in the quiet, not the volume.

title: The Last Curiosity
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—a grandparent, mentor, or parent—in their final hours. You've always accepted their surface stories, but tonight something shifts. Begin with quiet acceptance and exhaustion, but let genuine curiosity awaken within you. Start asking them questions you've never asked: about their first love, their biggest regret, what they see when they close their eyes, what they wish they'd been brave enough to do. With each answer, let another question bloom—not from duty, but from sudden, desperate hunger to truly know them before they're gone. Your emotion should travel from resigned farewell to fierce, childlike wonder, then to grief-stricken gratitude as you realize how much you never asked. Let your voice shift from monotone exhaustion to urgent, tender questioning, ending in a whisper that holds both devastation and discovery.

title: Secret Keeping
instruction: One person is telling another person a secret, trusting them to keep it. The voice of the secret-teller is careful, dropping to a whisper, making sure no one else can hear. The voice of the listener carries the weight of what's being entrusted to them. The secret is significant—it could damage something if revealed. The listener's voice promises: I will hold this. I will not betray your trust. By the end, a bond has been created through secrecy. The secret-keeper's voice carries the knowledge that they now hold something precious and dangerous.

title: The Last Breath in the Blast Zone
instruction: You are a teenage girl in a full gas mask, standing over a body in a ruined city. The air is poison, so every word is shouted through the filter, your own breathing loud and mechanical. You begin in pure ecstasy—you’ve hunted this person for weeks, and now they’re helpless. Let pleasure and malice fill your voice as you gloat, making the mask’s hollow resonance sound menacing. But then you notice a familiar necklace around their neck—your own mother’s. The ecstasy drops into raw sadness. Your voice cracks, you lose your train of thought, you press the mask’s visor with a trembling hand as you whisper-shout a broken farewell. Micro-distractions: your own ragged breathing, a cough from the filter, the weight of the mask shifting as you look down.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Sadness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Goodbye Saying
instruction: Someone is saying goodbye—to a place, a person, a version of themselves. Their voice carries the finality of this parting. What started as a temporary goodbye is becoming permanent. They're looking around, trying to imprint the moment. Their voice is thick with emotion. They address whoever or whatever they're saying goodbye to, and their voice carries the mix of gratitude and grief. The response from the other voice (if there is one) is equally weighted. They're acknowledging that something is ending. By the final goodbye, both voices are changed by the act of saying goodbye.

title: Stride of Defeat
instruction: You are a young man power walking aggressively through a park after being publicly humiliated by a rival. Your chest is tight, your jaw clenched. Each heel strike jars a bitter thought loose. Start with sourness: you mutter about the unfairness, the idiot who bested you. As your pace quickens, your breaths become audible gaps—helplessness seeps in. By the end, your voice cracks with bitterness, realizing you'll never be the man you pretend to be. Let the physical rhythm of your walk dictate your phrasing and emotional shifts.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Helplessness (extremely present), Bitterness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Spoonful
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a nursing home, slowly eating a bowl of lukewarm soup. Across the table sits your ungrateful daughter, who visits only to argue about your will. As you speak, your mouth is full of soft bread soaked in broth, forcing you to pause and chew between words. Start with a venomous, gloating tone—you’ve just revealed you donated her inheritance to a cat charity. Let the food make your words wet and sluggish, consonants muffled. By the end, as you swallow, your voice shifts into a quieter, more bitter place—remembering how she never cared until now. Your words trail off as you pick up the spoon again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Secret I've Carried
instruction: Late at night, lying beside someone you trust completely, you whisper a truth you've never spoken aloud. Begin barely audible, testing each word before releasing it. Your voice should be so quiet they have to lean in to hear. Start with the edges of the confession, then let it unfold in halting, broken phrases. There's shame here, but also profound relief—the weight lifting even as your voice trembles. A tear might catch in your throat mid-word. You're not asking for absolution, just to be known. By the end, your whisper should carry both the pain of the secret and the intimacy of finally sharing it, your voice fragile but somehow stronger for being heard.

title: The Last Phone Call From the Mountain
instruction: You're calling your child from a storm-trapped expedition, knowing rescue won't come in time. Phone battery at 3%. Start with forced calm, trying to be brave, telling them practical things about where documents are. But the pretense crumbles. Your voice breaks as you shift into desperate need to say everything—every proud moment, every regret, the way their laugh sounds like music. Fight against crying because you want them to hear your words clearly. Then acceptance washes over you, voice becoming tender, almost peaceful, as you describe the snow and stars, helping them imagine you're just going to sleep somewhere beautiful. End with your voice fading not from signal loss but from the cold making words harder to form, yet still whispering 'I love you' until the line goes silent.
