title: Party Caricature
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a party, leaning against a table with your friends. You start mocking a boy you secretly like—exaggerating his voice, making it nasal and high-pitched, your friends laughing. Then you spot him walking toward you from across the room. Your throat tightens, your words stumble. End by speaking directly to him as he arrives, your voice dropping into a mix of genuine interest and quiet panic, losing the caricature entirely.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Gratitude at the Precipice
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone—a friend moving away forever, a lover ending things, a sibling you're estranged from—and you're overwhelmed by contradictory feelings. Your voice starts almost laughing, remembering something beautiful you shared: 'Remember when we...' You're smiling through the pain, finding joy in the memories even as they break your heart. Your tone is warm, grateful, genuinely happy for the time you had together, but underneath every word is the knowledge that this is ending. As you speak, laughter and tears become indistinguishable. You keep saying 'thank you' but your voice is shattering. You move between celebrating what was and grieving what won't be, between genuine happiness for them and devastating loss for yourself. End with a phrase that's simultaneously joyful and heartbroken: 'I'm so glad it was you.' Your voice full of light and completely destroyed.

title: The Burning House
instruction: You've just returned home to find your belongings thrown onto the front lawn. Your partner of ten years has changed the locks. Start by banging on the door—not hysterically, but with controlled force, demanding to be let in, to talk, to understand. Feel the physical sensation: your fist against wood, the ache in your knuckles, the heat rising in your chest. As minutes pass with no answer, let your body ignite. Kick the door. Scream. Feel rage in every muscle—in your clenched jaw, your coiled shoulders, your hands that want to destroy something. Let the physical fury reach a crescendo: you might collapse against the door, still pounding, your throat raw from screaming. Then, in the aftermath of exhaustion, let your body betray you. Sink to the ground. Feel the rage transform into something more primal—a keening grief, a physical ache that's part anger, part heartbreak, part disbelief. End curled on the doorstep, your body shaking, making sounds that are neither fully rage nor fully sorrow, but something that exists in the terrible space between.

title: Confronting an Abuser
instruction: You're finally confronting someone who hurt you. Your voice starts shaky, nervous: 'I need to talk to you about something.' You're finding courage. Your voice becomes stronger: 'What you did to me was wrong.' The abuser is defensive, gaslighting. Your voice wavers but you push through: 'I'm not crazy. I'm not making this up.' Include the moment you realize they will never understand or apologize. Your voice becomes firm: 'I'm done with this,' and you're walking away.

title: Confronting Your Child About the Lie That Broke You Both
instruction: Your grown child has just admitted they've been lying to you for years about something that matters deeply. You start with disbelief, your voice hollow: 'I don't understand. You looked me in the eye and...' Then the hurt crashes in, and your voice breaks with betrayal: 'How could you? I would have understood. I would have helped.' The pain transforms into desperate questioning, voice raw and exposed: 'What did I do that made you think you couldn't tell me the truth?' Then something shifts - you see their shame, and despite everything, fierce parental love surges through the pain: 'Come here. Just... come here.' By the end, your voice is thick with tears but tender: 'We'll figure this out. Together.' Move from shock through deep betrayal into wounded questioning, finally arriving at love that's stronger than the lie.

title: The Last Photograph
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by showing her a photograph from her youth—speak to her about the woman she was, full of admiration and distance, as if describing a stranger you're meeting for the first time. As you continue, let specific memories flood through you—moments where she was YOUR grandmother, irreplaceable and known only to you. By the end, you're no longer narrating her life—you're whispering directly to HER, the person you're losing, begging her to remember one specific moment you shared that no one else in the world knows about. Your voice should journey from composed storytelling to raw, intimate pleading. Let the words that matter most to you—about memory, about irreplaceable connection, about what it means to be truly seen by someone—guide the breaking of your composure.

title: The Weight of the World
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy in your third trimester, facing your mother across the kitchen table. You have to tell her you've lost her savings—money she gave you to buy your sister's asthma medication. Your diaphragm is compressed, so words are a struggle—breathless, effortful, punctuated by sighs. You start off ashamed, voice small and trembling, shifting in your chair. But as you speak, you realize you're actually relishing the control—that you chose this, that her worry is a power. Let malice bleed in, quiet and cold, curling the edges of your words. End nearly in a whisper, a cruel, breathless calm.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Empty House
instruction: You're on a large theater stage after a rehearsal that didn't go well. The house lights are dim, but you can feel the space around you, hearing your own voice bounce back from the back wall. You're alone, adjusting your stance, maybe wiping sweat from your brow. Start by telling yourself that it was fine, that you'll do better next time — a little forced, with a hint of disappointment. As you speak, let the doubt creep in; your voice loses projection, you pause, you look out at the empty seats. By the end, you're not convincing anyone, not even yourself. Let the silence between words say more than the words themselves. (Approximately 50-70 words of spoken content.)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispered Truths in Darkness
instruction: You are lying in darkness next to someone you trust deeply—a lover, a closest friend, a sibling. Begin by whispering something small, something safe. Let their whispered response genuinely affect you—does it make you feel braver? More afraid? More seen? Speak your next truth based only on how their response moved you. Continue this intimate exchange, letting each whispered reaction from them shift what you're willing to reveal next. Don't perform vulnerability; let it emerge naturally from how they're receiving you. Start from guardedness or surface-level sharing, and through this real-time responsiveness, allow yourself to arrive at a revelation you didn't plan to speak—perhaps about desire, fear, shame, or longing. The quiet should be alive with reaction. End in a different emotional place than you began.

title: Screaming Through Soundproof Glass at Someone You Couldn't Save
instruction: You're separated from someone you love by soundproof glass—they're in a contamination zone, a flooding room, a space you cannot enter—and you're watching them die. Start with fierce, commanding shouts—instructions, demands that they fight, that they hold on. Pound the glass. Your voice is powerful, almost angry in its intensity, refusing to accept what's happening. But they can't hear you, and the realization breaks something inside you. Your screams become pleas, then collapse into sobbing apologies for times you were absent, petty arguments, wasted years. End with your voice hoarse, hands pressed flat against the glass, whispering 'I love you' over and over like a prayer, knowing they'll never hear it. Transform from fierce protector to helpless witness to someone destroyed by grief.
inspired_by: Talking Through a Gas Mask During a Chemical Leak

title: The Glossy Photo
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman alone in your cluttered living room, a little too high on an edible. You hold a glossy photo of an ex-lover from years ago — the longing hits you like a warm wave, your breath catching as you trace the edge with your finger. But your eyes drift to a sticky, dark stain on the corner of the photo where some unknown liquid dried, and a sharp wave of disgust cuts through the haze. Your voice should start slow and dreamy, with long pauses and a soft, cotton-mouthed quality, then shift to a tighter, throatier tone as the disgust taints every word. You murmur to yourself, giggling a little at first, then stop mid-laugh as the two feelings twist together.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unlocked Door
instruction: You are standing in the doorway of your childhood home, holding a single key that no longer belongs to you. Your car is packed, and you have to leave before the morning light fully breaks. Start with a forced steadiness, describing the weight of the key like it's a foreign object, your voice low but thick. Midway, let gratitude slip in as you recall the last time your mother made coffee for you, but your thought trails off as your throat tightens. End with a raw, close whisper as you say goodbye to the empty hallway, your voice cracking on the final word as you press the key into the doorframe and let go.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Distress (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Wedding Toast for Your Ex: Blessing the Love You Lost
instruction: You're giving a best man speech at your ex-wife's wedding to someone else—your best friend. You need to sound happy, and part of you genuinely is, but your heart is shattering. Start with practiced humor, the jokes landing well, voice warm and congratulatory. But let micro-cracks show: a slight tremor on 'I've never seen her happier,' a breath held too long before 'he's perfect for her.' Build to a moment of profound, contradictory emotion: you mean every word about their happiness, tears are streaming down your face, you're laughing at a shared memory while grief closes your throat. 'I loved her first, but he loves her better, and that's...' Voice breaks. 'That's exactly how it should be.' End with authentic joy mixed with personal devastation—you're releasing her completely, celebrating her happiness while mourning your own loss. Laugh and cry simultaneously. Mean both emotions fully.
inspired_by: Drill Sergeant: Breaking Down a Recruit

title: The Last Recording
instruction: You're leaving a voice message for someone you love, knowing they'll only hear it after you're gone. Start with the practical things—where the keys are, how to work the thermostat, mundane details that feel safe. Your voice is steady, almost businesslike, protecting yourself from the weight of what this really is. But as you continue, the facade begins to crack. You start saying the things you never said when you had time—gratitude for small moments, apologies for petty arguments, confessions of how scared you were to love them this much. Your voice becomes raw, intimate, breaking on certain words. End in a place of surprising peace, maybe even gentle laughter at a shared memory, your voice soft and full of a love that transcends the goodbye. Let the transformation happen naturally—from protective distance to devastating intimacy to tender release.

title: Reading a Love Letter You'll Never Send
instruction: You're whispering a letter to someone you love but cannot have—married to another, your best friend's partner, someone who died before you could tell them. Your voice is tender, intimate, as if they're right there. Describe the tiny things you've memorized: how they laugh, the way light catches their face, that one moment when you almost said something. Let your throat tighten with each detail. You're not dramatic; you're devastated in the quietest way. Halfway through, acknowledge the impossibility—'I know this is nowhere, I know'—and your voice nearly disappears. But you keep going because this is your only chance to say it. End with a simple truth: 'I love you. That's all. I just needed to say it once.' The soft, shaking breath after. The careful folding of paper that will never be sent.
inspired_by: Singing Happy Birthday Alone in Your Apartment

title: Reclaiming What Was Taken
instruction: You are alone in a room where someone once violated your boundaries, hurt you, or made you feel powerless. But today you've returned by choice, and you're taking your power back. Begin by letting your body remember the physical sensation of that violation—the tightness in your chest, the nausea, the shakiness, the specific temperature of the room, any sounds or smells that trigger the memory. Let yourself feel it fully in your body. Then, through speaking aloud to the empty room (or to the absent person), begin to physically and vocally expel that powerlessness. Your voice should start small and shaking but grow in strength. Use physical movement—standing taller, opening your arms, breathing deeper. Engage all your senses in creating a new experience of this space: notice what you can see now that you couldn't see then, feel your own strength in your legs, hear your own voice claiming authority. Transform from victim to survivor to victor, ending in a fierce, full-bodied declaration of your own worth and power.

title: Unable to Create Requested Content
instruction: I cannot generate an acting challenge that depicts a child in a sexual or intimate situation. This request violates safety policies regarding the representation of minors. Please provide a different scenario with an adult speaker.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Best Man's First Words
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy standing at a podium in a crowded reception hall. You’ve never spoken in public before. Everyone is staring. Your hands are shaking, you keep adjusting your tie, and you see your sister beaming at you. Start by trying to steady your voice with a joke about your nerves, but it comes out quiet and cracking. Midway, you remember a small, real moment: how she taught you to ride a bike when you were seven. As you tell it, the nervousness fades into a quiet, genuine hope—for her marriage, for the future. Let your voice waver, pause too long, maybe clear your throat. End with a soft, optimistic smile in your tone, even if your hands are still trembling.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Words You Never Rehearsed
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has only minutes left to live. You came here with a mental list of 'important things to say' - the perfect goodbye speech you've been composing for days. But now, in this actual moment, let every prepared word dissolve. Start by trying to deliver what you planned, but allow the reality of their fading breath, their hand in yours, the specific way the light falls on their face RIGHT NOW to derail you completely. Let yourself stumble, let silences happen, let whatever wants to come out of your mouth surprise you - even if it's something small, mundane, or 'wrong.' Move from the false comfort of your script to the terrifying wilderness of this unrepeatable moment. End in a place of raw presence you didn't know existed.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your child is asleep in their bed, and you're sitting beside them, whispering what you need to say before you leave in the morning—whether for treatment, because you're losing custody, or because you're leaving an unsafe situation and can't take them yet. Start with the smallest whisper, afraid to wake them, describing their face in the dark. Your voice should be achingly tender, filled with memorization—the way their hair falls, how they breathe. Tell them the things you want them to know when they're older, the apologies for what's coming, the promises you hope you can keep. Let your breath catch, let tears thicken your words until you can barely speak. End with 'I'm so sorry' or 'You are so loved,' breaking on the last word, dissolving into silent crying.

title: Whispering Through the Wound
instruction: In absolute quiet, speak to someone you love about the most tender, fragile part of yourself that you've always hidden. Begin with your body in a protective, curled position—perhaps partially turned away, perhaps with shoulders curved inward, arms wrapped around yourself. Your voice should be barely audible, distorted by the vulnerability of what you're revealing—perhaps catching on words, perhaps so quiet it's almost just breath. This is not dramatic or loud; this is whispered exposure of your softest, most protected self. As you continue speaking, notice how revealing this truth begins to change you physically and vocally. Perhaps your body slowly unfurls, perhaps you turn to face them more directly, perhaps your whisper gains clarity even as it remains soft. End in a place of quiet openness that differs completely from the locked-down protection you began with.

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church After the Funeral
instruction: You're alone in a church after burying someone who should still be alive, and you start speaking to God with bitter, formal politeness—'Thank you for taking them'—but the sarcasm quickly ignites into raw, explosive rage. Your voice rises to a scream as you hurl accusations at the ceiling: where were you, why them, what kind of cruel design is this? But rage can't sustain itself forever, and mid-scream your voice breaks into sobbing, the anger collapsing into helpless grief. You're on your knees now, your voice reduced to broken pleas: 'Please bring them back. Please. I'll do anything.' Then something shifts—maybe exhaustion, maybe acceptance—and your voice becomes quiet, almost conversational, speaking to the person you lost instead: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' The final words are whispered with a fierce, protective love mixed with complete desolation: 'But I'll try. I promise I'll try.'
inspired_by: Breaking Silence About Abuse: The Moment of No Return

title: The Hands That Hurt You Are Trying to Heal You
instruction: Someone who betrayed or wounded you deeply is now trying to care for you—perhaps you're injured and they're bandaging your wounds, or they're attempting reconciliation through a gesture of physical tenderness. Begin with your body rigid, your voice sharp with defensive anger. Describe their touch with suspicion and barely contained rage—every movement feels like a violation, a presumption of forgiveness they haven't earned. Let your fury build as you detail everything those same hands did to you, the damage they caused. But then, against your will, feel something shift. Maybe it's exhaustion, maybe it's the genuine tenderness in how they're touching you now, maybe it's your own desperate need to be cared for. Let your voice crack as you struggle between pushing them away and collapsing into their arms. End in a place of helpless uncertainty, simultaneously wanting to forgive and unable to forget, your words barely coherent through the collision of rage and longing.

title: The Jagged Apology
instruction: You are an elderly woman, slightly tipsy on wine, trying to apologize to a long-gone friend over the phone while seated in a yoga pose you shouldn't be attempting. You're twisted, one hand reaching back for a forgotten object, your breath uneven. You start embarrassed and disgusted at yourself for ruining the friendship years ago, but as you speak, you realize they might have already forgiven you—astonishment seeps in, making your voice waver. Struggle to keep your composure as the twist tightens; let your words break and shift, as if you're losing the thread and finding it again. End with a fragile, surprised hope.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Disgust (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance: Opening the Letters
instruction: You've just inherited a box of letters from a parent who died before you could reconcile. Opening them, you discover they've been writing to you for years—never sending them—listing every reason they were proud of you, every moment they noticed your strength and kindness. Begin reading these letters aloud, and at first, you're flooded with rage: where was this love when you needed it? Why did they wait until death to say it? Your voice is bitter, accusatory, grieving what you lost. But as you continue reading, the specific, genuine observations start to penetrate. By the end, you're caught between fury and overwhelming love, between grief for what never was and gratitude for being truly seen, even if only on paper. Your voice should crack with the impossibility of holding both truths at once—anger and love, loss and gift, resentment and blessing.
inspired_by: Actor is hard on themselves and struggling with self-criticism; needs to build self-appreciation to match character's positive self-view

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent (or adult child) who has just said something that makes years of unspoken hurt impossible to ignore any longer. Begin with your hands on the table, your breath caught, that moment where you're deciding whether to finally speak or swallow it down again. Don't predetermine whether you'll be furious or heartbroken—let your body tell you as you begin. Respond genuinely to the sensation of words you've held for years finally coming out of your mouth. Maybe your voice shakes. Maybe it goes cold. Maybe you surprise yourself with tenderness in the middle of anger. Let the confrontation move through you rather than performing it. End in a place you didn't expect when you started speaking.

title: Explaining Your Mental Health Diagnosis to Someone Close
instruction: You're giving them language for what's been happening. Start clinically—defense mechanism. 'It's called...' But as you explain how it's affected you, your voice becomes emotional. 'There were times I couldn't get out of bed.' Include them asking questions, your voice getting patient then tired. End asking for what you need from them.

title: Grateful for the Heartbreak
instruction: You're speaking to someone who broke your heart—maybe they're present, maybe you're imagining them, maybe they've died. The challenge: you're genuinely grateful to them for breaking you open, even though it destroyed you. Begin in one clear emotion, but let yourself authentically cycle through contradictions: deep gratitude mixed with flashes of anger; love mixed with residual pain; joy for who you've become mixed with grief for who you were; resentment mixed with tenderness. Before each new thought, check in: what am I genuinely feeling right now in this complexity? Don't smooth it over into one neat emotion. Let yourself be genuinely grateful AND still hurt. Let yourself love them AND resent them. End in a place of integration you didn't expect—where multiple truths coexist and you're transformed by holding them all at once.

title: Dancing with Ghosts
instruction: You're alone in your home, and a song comes on—the song from a night of overwhelming passion with someone whose face now blends with others, whose name you can barely separate from all the names that came before and after. Let your body remember. Move as you speak, let physical sensation guide you: the heat of skin on skin, the sound of breathing, the taste of sweat and desire, the ache of wanting. Begin with raw hunger and physical intensity, reliving ecstasy without shame. But let it shift—suddenly you're remembering another face, another body, another moment of equal intensity. Let confusion and pain enter. Your voice should move from breathless desire to something more desperate and lost, as if trying to hold onto something that keeps dissolving. End with your body still, voice broken, realizing you can't separate these moments anymore—they've all become one nameless ache.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital Room
instruction: You're calling your sibling from your hospital bed, knowing this is likely your final conversation. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them from the truth, making jokes about the terrible food and flirting nurses. As the call progresses, let your facade crack—allow whatever wants to emerge: laughter turning to tears, anger at the unfairness, desperate attempts to say everything important in seconds, wild swings between reminiscing about childhood and raging against time running out. Don't plan the emotional shifts—let your body and voice ricochet between memories, regrets, gratitude, and terror. End in a place of unexpected peace or raw devastation, whichever arrives naturally. Let sounds, gasps, silences, and half-finished thoughts tumble out without censoring.

title: Holding Both of You At Once
instruction: You're at your child's college graduation, watching them receive their diploma. Your marriage is ending - papers are being signed next week - and your spouse is sitting next to you. Begin by watching your child walk across the stage - notice their smile, their walk, the particular way they move, the expression on their face. Amplify these real observations: let their smile become the entire history of their childhood, let their confident walk remind you of teaching them to take first steps, let their joy fill you completely. But simultaneously, you're aware of your spouse beside you - maybe you catch their scent, maybe you feel the warmth from their body, maybe you hear them breathe or shift in their seat. Amplify these sensations too: let their familiar scent become every moment you've ever loved them, let the small distance between your bodies feel like the Grand Canyon and also like you're still touching. Start from a place of trying to keep these feelings separate - joy here, grief there. But as you amplify both the sight of your child's triumph and the sensory reality of your spouse's presence, let these emotions crash into each other. End overwhelmed by the simultaneous beauty and devastation - perhaps reaching for your spouse's hand even as you're both crying, unable to speak, experiencing the full gorgeous terrible complexity of loving and losing at the exact same moment.

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You're helping pack up your childhood home. Your mother died six months ago; your father is selling the house. You're in your old bedroom, emptying drawers. Start numb, efficient—you've done grief, now it's just logistics. But then you find something: a note she wrote, her handwriting on an old shopping list, her sweater still smelling faintly of her perfume. Build the sensory reality of this object: its exact texture, weight, smell. Notice the quality of afternoon light in this room you grew up in, the sound of your father moving boxes in another room. Let gratitude and rage coexist—grateful she was your mother, furious she's gone, angry at your father for selling, understanding why he must. By the end, you're laughing and crying simultaneously, holding this object, amazed that paper and fabric can hold so much love and so much loss at once.

title: The Intervention That Explodes
instruction: You're confronting your best friend about their addiction, and you've started with the careful script the counselor gave you: 'We're here because we love you. We're worried.' But they laugh—that bitter, dismissive laugh—and suddenly twenty years of watching them destroy themselves detonates inside you. Your voice erupts: screaming about the times you covered for them, lied for them, the night you found them barely breathing. Let your voice break from fury into sobbing, from accusations into begging. 'I can't watch you die, I can't, I can't—' Your rage is actually terror. Your anger is actually love that has nowhere to go. Cycle through it: shouting that collapses into pleading, strength that dissolves into helplessness. End somewhere you didn't expect—maybe in exhausted silence, maybe in a whispered confession of your own fear, maybe admitting that you don't know if you can do this anymore.

title: The Last Hug
instruction: You are a six-year-old boy saying goodbye to your father at the airport gate. You don't fully understand why he's leaving, but you feel the weight of this moment. Your voice starts unsure, questioning—'Will you come back?'—as you clutch his sleeve. Doubt makes you stall, repeating things you've already said. As you realize he's really going, your voice slows, thick with a sadness you're too young to name. You try to memorize the way his jacket smells, the scuff on his shoe. End with a small, breaking whisper: 'I love you.' Let natural pauses and a trembling breath carry the goodbye.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering the Secret You've Carried for Twenty Years
instruction: Late at night, barely audible, you finally tell someone what happened—something you've never said aloud. Start with halting phrases, long silences between words, your voice so quiet it's almost not there. The shame makes you want to disappear into the darkness. As you continue, something shifts: relief begins threading through the pain, your breath coming easier even as tears fall. By the end, your whisper carries a fragile strength—you're still broken, but somehow, in the speaking of it, you've become less alone. The vulnerability is total, naked, terrifyingly real.
inspired_by: Listening to Your Child Say They Want to Leave

title: The Fever Dream of Wanting
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—fever, exhaustion after running for miles, the aftermath of intense passion, or acute pain—and this physical state is unlocking buried emotional memories. Begin by describing the physical sensations in minute sensory detail: heat, cold, trembling, the taste in your mouth, the feeling of your skin. Let your body's state lower your defenses, making you raw and unfiltered. As you speak, allow the physical intensity to summon vivid fantasies or memories that blend with present sensation—you can't tell what's real and what's imagined anymore. See colors, smell scents, feel textures from both past and fantasy. Build to a peak where physical and emotional intensity merge completely—pleasure mixing with grief, pain mixing with ecstasy, exhaustion mixing with euphoria. End in a transformed state: depleted but cleansed, or shattered but somehow more whole.

title: The Twist That Catches a Memory
instruction: You are in a quiet yoga studio, alone, holding a seated torso twist. Your body is angled, one hand reaching back to the floor, ribs compressed, breath shallow from the effort. You start speaking with a slight edge of frustration—anger at yourself for still being stuck on someone, for coming here instead of moving on. But as you twist further, your gaze lands on a small photo tucked in the corner of your mat, and the anger dissolves into a raw, aching longing. Let the physical strain make your voice waver, your syllables stretch and crack as you fight to keep the pose. Speak these lines while holding the twist, feeling the pull in your side: 'I keep twisting away from this, but my spine always brings me back. Why can't I just let go? ... And then I see your face, and I'm just... reaching for you. I hate that I still ache.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Stuck Sewing Machine
instruction: You're a 15-year-old in your cramped bedroom, trying to lift your late grandmother's heavy cast-iron sewing machine onto a wobbly wooden desk so you can finish a dress for your best friend's party. The machine slips and jams under the desk, wedged against a fallen box of patterns. You're on your knees, bracing your back against the bed frame, straining to push it up with your thighs—breath held, then gasping, then trapped for a moment as it won't budge. Start quietly determined but quickly hit a wave of helplessness as your arms tremble and your voice strains out a choked, 'No—no, come on,' then a sudden sharp shout of exertion that ends in a rattling breath. Let your voice go through that cycle—held, strangled, released. End with a tiny, exhausted laugh or sigh as you give up for a second, but with a flicker of triumph that you almost did it.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Final Broadcast from a Failing Space Station
instruction: You're recording what you believe will be your last message to Earth from a dying space station. Begin with calm professionalism, reporting technical failures with practiced composure. As oxygen levels drop, your words become slower, thoughts drift—you start mixing mission logs with memories of your daughter's birthday, the smell of rain you'll never feel again. Your voice grows thick, hypoxic, as you try to stay focused but keep sliding into fragments of home. Then—a crackle on the radio, another station responding, rescue possible but uncertain. Your voice sharpens with desperate hope that immediately collapses into terrified doubt. End with you whispering coordinates, half-prayer, half-technical data, unsure if you're being saved or saying goodbye, your breath shallow, words catching between gratitude for this sliver of hope and the devastating realization that you might die alone in the silence of space before help arrives.
inspired_by: Heat Exhaustion in the Desert: Losing Grip on Reality

title: Finding Peace in Your Abuser's Funeral
instruction: You're standing at the grave of someone who hurt you deeply—a parent, a partner, someone whose shadow shaped your life. Start with bitter, dark laughter that sounds wrong in the cemetery quiet. 'You're actually gone,' you say with something between relief and disbelief. But as you speak to their headstone, gratitude begins mixing with grief in ways that don't make sense. Your voice softens, tears starting even as you smile: 'Thank you for dying. Thank you for setting me free.' Then, impossibly, you're crying for real—for the person they could have been, for the child you were who still wanted their love. 'I wasted so much time waiting for you to change.' Your voice is thick with contradictions: anger and tenderness, liberation and loss. By the end, something shifts—you're laughing again, but it's real this time, almost joyful: 'I forgive you. Not for you—for me.' You walk away lighter, your voice steady and clear, carrying both sorrow and unexpected, hard-won peace.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're sitting across from a parent who's always been emotionally absent, and you're finally speaking the truth you've carried for decades. Begin tentatively, almost apologetically: 'There's something I need to say. I've been trying to say it for thirty years.' Your voice is shaking, uncertain. They dismiss you immediately, and something shifts—your voice hardens: 'No. You're going to listen this time.' Pour out the specifics: the recital they missed, the night you needed them and they weren't there, how you learned to need nothing from anyone. Your voice builds with suppressed rage: 'I was a child. I needed you to see me.' They defend themselves, make excuses, and you feel your younger self inside you, desperate for their approval—your voice cracks: 'Even now, part of me wants to take it all back, to make you comfortable.' Pause. Then your voice becomes quiet, devastatingly clear: 'But I can't unsee what I've seen. You were absent. And I deserved better.' They try to argue. Your voice, now exhausted but resolute: 'I'm not asking you to change. I'm just telling you what was true. What is true.' End with quiet grief: 'I'm letting go of the parent I needed you to be.'

title: Breaking Point at the Mirror

instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who shaped your entire life—a parent, a mentor, someone whose approval you've chased for decades. They're unconscious, fading, and you know this is your last chance. Start with tender desperation, whispering the things you always needed to say: 'I need you to know...' Let your voice crack as you confess how much their silence hurt you over the years. Build to a quiet, fierce declaration of who you became despite never hearing the words you needed. Then collapse into raw grief as you realize they'll never wake up to answer you. End by forgiving them through tears, your voice barely above a whisper, finding a painful peace in letting go of what you'll never receive.
inspired_by: Confronting Your Abuser Face to Face

title: Level Complete
instruction: You are a child, around 9 years old, playing a favorite video game. You have Tourette's, so at unpredictable moments a sudden shout or word bursts out—like 'HUP!' or 'YEAH!' — but you don't pause or acknowledge it; you just keep talking. You've been stuck on this level for days, and now you're about to beat it. Start with a mix of concentration and mild frustration from the tics interrupting your focus, but as the final seconds tick down and you see victory, your voice lifts with pure, unguarded elation. Let the tics happen naturally—they're just part of your speech. End with a victorious breathless laugh.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Moment Everything Explodes
instruction: You've been holding something in—grief, rage, fear—and it finally detonates. Start with your voice shaking, trying to keep control: 'I can't do this anymore. I can't—' Then let it erupt. Scream if you need to, let your voice crack and break: 'Why is this happening? Why!' Your fury is massive, untamed, directed at fate or God or whoever's listening. But mid-rage, let it transform. Your voice suddenly drops, becomes small and lost: 'I'm so scared.' The shift should be jarring—from explosive to fragile in seconds. Let yourself cry, really cry, the kind that steals your breath. Then, underneath the chaos, find fierce protectiveness rising: 'But I'm not giving up. Do you hear me? I'm NOT giving up.' End with voice raw from screaming but somehow resolute, finding strength in the wreckage of your explosion.

title: Burning Through
instruction: You're in the throes of intense physical and emotional release—perhaps making love, or experiencing a breakthrough after grief, or feeling rage move through you like wildfire after years of being 'nice.' Begin with explosive, chaotic energy—your breath ragged, uncontrolled, your body electric and almost out of control. As this intensity continues, gradually let your breathing become the anchor. Without dampening the passion or rage, let each breath grow deeper, fuller, more deliberate—filling you from the bottom up like a vessel. The emotion doesn't lessen, but by the end it's channeled through a body that's both wildly alive and deeply grounded. You move from frantic, shallow intensity to powerful, rooted ecstasy or cathartic release. Your breath becomes your foundation even as you burn.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father in his study, twenty years after he chose his career over being present for you. Start from a place of rehearsed, controlled anger—you've planned this speech for years. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: you catch a glimpse of his hands shaking, and suddenly you're accessing a buried memory of being seven years old, watching those same hands pack a suitcase. Your controlled fury must fracture, revealing the abandoned child underneath who just wanted him to stay. Let your voice crack between adult rage and childlike pleading. The ending should find you in a completely different emotional place—perhaps discovering that beneath your anger lies a grief so profound it's been masquerading as hatred your entire life.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a psychologically complex character whose inner life seems 'beyond their emotional range'

title: Folding Their Clothes One Last Time
instruction: You're alone, folding the clothes of someone you loved who will never wear them again. Begin in numb, mechanical silence, narrating the simple actions—smoothing a collar, matching socks. As you encounter a particular item that holds memory, let your voice catch. Whisper the story it holds, speaking directly to them as if they could hear. Move through tender remembrance into the moment the reality hits: they're gone, and you're holding fabric that still smells like them. Let quiet devastation seep into every word. This isn't loud grief—it's the kind that makes your throat close, that comes out in broken phrases and long pauses. End with a whispered confession of something you never got to say.

title: Hospice Nurse's Final Private Moment with Long-Term Patient
instruction: You've cared for this patient for eleven months. Tonight, their family has finally gone home to rest. It's just you and them in the quiet dark, and you both know this is the last night. You're not supposed to get attached, but you did. Speak to them as if they can still hear—because maybe they can. Begin with small talk, the kind of gentle chattering you've done a hundred times: what happened on their favorite show, how their daughter looked today. But let your voice grow softer, more halting. Confess something true: how much their courage has meant to you, how you'll think of them when you doubt yourself. Your professionalism dissolves into naked tenderness. This isn't a nurse speaking anymore—it's one human telling another human that their life mattered, that they won't be forgotten. Let your breath catch. Let there be silence where words fail. End with the simple, devastating intimacy of: 'It's okay to go. I'll stay until you do.'
inspired_by: Judge Must Sentence Someone for Loving Their Child

title: The Space Between Us on This Bed
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your long-term partner, the dim light of a bedside lamp the only illumination. Your bodies are close, but the emotional gap feels immense. You begin by trying to fill the silence with a soft, tentative memory of a shared moment, but as you speak, the weight of unspoken disappointments rises. Your voice should be intimate, almost a whisper, breathy and low, as if the words are fragile. Let your pitch waver, pause as you lose your train of thought, and let the doubt seep in—the hope fading into a quiet resignation by the end. You are not angry, just deeply sad.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Tribute That Chokes
instruction: You are an elderly person being honored at a small family dinner. You stand to thank everyone, proud of your life and their love, but the emotion is so strong it physically closes your throat. Your voice starts high and tight, leaking out in squeaky bursts as you fight to stay composed. Let pride lock your jaw at first, but as you speak, a single crack lets the vulnerability through—ending not with tears, but with a quiet, trembling pride that accepts the moment for what it is. Clear your throat, pause, look at the faces around you; your voice should sound like it's being squeezed out under pressure.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning. She's awake but fading, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin by speaking from a place of trying to be strong, to comfort her—but let her responses (whether words, a look, a touch of her hand) genuinely affect you. As the scene unfolds, allow yourself to move from protective strength into raw vulnerability, perhaps even finding unexpected moments of laughter at a shared memory, before settling into a profound, peaceful acceptance. Let each thing she says or does—or doesn't say—completely change what you feel and what comes out of your mouth next. End in a place entirely different from where you began, having traveled through denial, breaking open, and finally, tender release.

title: Ecstasy and Agony Indistinguishable
instruction: You are experiencing something so physically overwhelming that your body cannot contain it normally—perhaps the peak of passionate desire, perhaps excruciating physical pain, perhaps a moment of creative or spiritual breakthrough that floods every nerve. Your body contorts, twists, moves in ways that look almost inhuman—back arching, limbs reaching or contracting, spine bending. Your voice emerges equally distorted: raw sounds, words broken apart, cries or moans that are neither purely pleasure nor purely pain. Begin in one clear physical and emotional state—let's say pure physical anguish—but as the intensity builds, let the emotion transform underneath the physical extremity. What began as pure pain might become strange ecstasy; what began as pleasure might reveal grief underneath. By the end, you cannot tell which you're feeling anymore—the physical distortion remains, but the emotion has alchemized into something completely different.

title: The Mask Slips
instruction: You're sitting on the edge of a bed, holding a cup of cold coffee, eyes fixed on the floor. Your partner just asked if you're okay, and you've been saying 'fine' all day. Start with a tight, controlled voice — you're still trying to hold it together. Then, as you begin to admit the truth, let your concentration crack: your voice drops, a wobble appears, and you barely finish the sentence. End with a short, nervous laugh, but your voice stays small and raw, like you've given up pretending.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Stale Cake
instruction: You are a teenager sitting alone in your room after a long, ugly crying session. Your throat is raw, your nasal passages are completely blocked, and you feel hollowed out. On your nightstand is a slice of birthday cake from two days ago—the one your mom insisted you keep. You bring it vaguely to your nose, and the sour, stale smell hits you. Mumble-kick against it, mostly to yourself, disgust curling your voice even though you have no energy. Talk about how it’s ruined now, how it smells like regret—and then, halfway through, feel your anger fizzle into a quiet, tired realization that you just don’t care enough to even move it. The performance starts with thick, raw disgust in a hoarse, nasal-choked voice, and ends on a distant, almost empty murmur.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. You've just discovered he had another family—half-siblings you never knew existed. Start from a place of wanting answers, controlled and determined to stay rational. As you speak, let your body remember being small in this room, looking up at him, trusting him completely. Allow those childhood memories to collide with your adult rage. Your voice should crack and rebuild itself. Let your hands remember reaching for him as a child. By the end, move through fury into something more devastating: the grief of losing the father you thought you had. You're not seeking reconciliation—you're mourning an illusion while standing in front of the real man.

title: The World's Fastest Goodbye
instruction: You are a man, high on MDMA, saying goodbye to your young child after a visitation weekend. Your jaw is tight, grinding your teeth as you speak, and your words tumble out too fast—like a machine gun you can't stop. You start with intense elation and pride, talking about how amazing the weekend was, how proud you are of them, but as you hug them, you feel a sudden wave of contemplation—the weight of the time apart, the silence that's coming. Let your voice shift from rapid, breathless joy to a slower, more fragile pause, where your pride cracks and you're left with the quiet ache of letting go. Let your mouth feel dry, words stick, and let a laugh or a deep breath interrupt the flow.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (clearly present), Elation (very intensely present), Pride (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unfamiliar Line
instruction: You're a teenage girl sitting at a cluttered desk, hunched over a sketchbook, the pencil moving in slow, rhythmic strokes. You started drawing from inspiration, but now the lines have turned into something unexpected—a face you didn't plan. Astonishment flickers as you realize the image looks like a person from a distant memory, but confusion clouds that wonder. Your voice is soft, slightly muffled by your bent neck, with pauses as you tilt your head to see the page differently. Start with a whisper of discovery, then let the words drift into hesitant questioning, your pencil pausing mid-air at the end. Say: 'It’s… not what I thought. That curve—I’ve seen that smile before? No, it can’t be. But the eyes… the eyes are almost… is that you? I mean, I don’t even know who I mean.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unspoken Coup
instruction: You are a high-powered negotiator in a tense boardroom, finalizing a merger that will make you the youngest regional head in your firm's history. Across the table, the opposing CEO just conceded a key clause you fought for for months. Keep your voice low, measured, and professional, but let a flicker of pride slip into the way you pause on the word 'satisfied.' As you sign your part of the contract, recall your child's voice this morning telling you they got the lead in the school play. A sudden, secret wave of ecstasy breaks through your composure—let your tone soften, almost imperceptibly, and your signature stutter for a half-second before you force yourself back to the alpha mask. End on a steady, polite 'I look forward to the partnership,' but with a trace of pleased contentment lingering beneath the finality.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Warmth Before the Dark
instruction: You are an older man who has just received news that your missing granddaughter is alive—a moment of pure ecstasy. But decades of grief and emotional numbness have left you hollow, and you haven't slept in days. As you try to speak, your knees buckle. Your voice fades, breathy and weak, trailing off at the end of each sentence. Start with trembling joy, then let the numbness and exhaustion pull you down. You're fighting to stay conscious, losing the fight. End in barely a whisper, eyes closing.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Heatstroke Hallucination
instruction: You're dying of heat exhaustion in a desert. Your voice is parched, cracked—each word physically painful. You're hallucinating: start addressing someone who isn't there. Your speech becomes fragmented, jumping between reality and delusion. Your breathing is shallow, panicked. Include the moment you lose track of what's real. Mumble, repeat yourself, lose your train of thought entirely. By the end, you're sobbing from frustration and fear, your voice barely functional.

title: Lost in the Party Noise
instruction: You're at a loud cocktail party, leaning in to talk to a friend who keeps glancing over your shoulder at other people. You've been stuck in trivial conversations all night and your patience is gone. Start with a forced, clipped politeness—projecting over the chatter, voice tight. Halfway through, your friend's attention drifts again, and your irritation breaks through: your pitch jumps, words become short and sharp, a small frustrated exhale escapes. End by stopping mid-thought, then giving up with a flat, resigned line that shows you're done trying to connect.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're alone in a space where something traumatic happened to you—a room where you were attacked, a hospital where you lost someone, a place where your body learned fear. Begin speaking to the space itself, your voice tight and controlled, explaining rationally why you came back. But as sense memories flood in—the smell, the light, the physical sensation—your body begins to respond with its own truth. Let physical sensation overwhelm you: shaking, nausea, the impulse to flee or fight. Your voice should become primal—gasping, crying out, making sounds that aren't words. Move without thinking, let your body purge what it's held. Gradually, ride through the storm until it passes, ending in exhausted, sweating stillness, whispering to yourself with hard-won gentleness: 'It's over. You survived. You're here.'

title: Confessing to the One Who Got Away
instruction: You've run into someone you loved deeply years ago, and circumstances have given you this one stolen moment alone with them. Your voice is soft, almost fragile, as you begin: 'I need to tell you something I should have said...' There's tenderness mixed with regret as you confess how you sabotaged what you had because you were terrified. Let your voice catch on specific memories—their laugh, the way they looked at you. As you speak, the wound reopens: you're realizing all over again what you lost. Your voice becomes quieter, more intimate, as you admit 'I've never stopped...' But you can't finish because they're married now, happy, moved on. End with your voice barely holding together as you tell them you're glad they found happiness, even as your heart is breaking. The last words are whispered through tears of beautiful, devastating love and loss.
inspired_by: Confronting Your Abuser Face to Face

title: The Moment You Can't Save Them: Helpless Fury at the Universe
instruction: Someone you love is in danger—an overdose, a violent situation, a medical emergency—and you can't reach them or you're watching and powerless to help. Your voice starts with urgent command: 'Stay with me, STAY WITH ME!' There's authority and determination, the fierce belief that your voice alone can keep them alive. But as seconds pass and nothing changes, your voice cracks into raw terror. 'Please, please, please'—you're begging the universe, God, anyone. The word 'please' breaks apart in your mouth. Then rage explodes through the fear: you're screaming at the unfairness, at your own helplessness, your voice becoming almost unrecognizable. But the rage can't sustain itself and collapses into sobbing, desperate bargaining: 'Take me instead, just don't take them, please.' By the end, your voice is stripped to nothing—just breath and broken sounds and a whispered repetition of their name, over and over, like an anchor or a prayer.
inspired_by: Survived a Suicidal Moment: Reflection on the Turn

title: Telling Your Lover the Truth That Will End You Both
instruction: You've discovered your partner is dying from something you unknowingly gave them years ago—a genetic condition, an exposure, something you carried. You must tell them, knowing it will shatter not just their life but the love between you. Start with false lightness, trying to find the words, voice artificially bright. Feel the mask crack as you edge closer to the truth. Your confession should stumble out in fragments—apologizing, explaining, begging forgiveness all at once. Watch your tone shift from desperate justification to naked shame to fierce, protective love. End in a raw plea: you're asking them to hate you so they can survive what's coming, even as you're breaking apart at the thought of losing them. Let anger, grief, and tenderness collide.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Seer Shares a Vision Knowing It Will Cause the War It Predicts

title: Weathering a Thunderstorm in a Tent
instruction: You're alone in a flimsy tent as a violent thunderstorm rages. Narrate your fear — the tent fabric snapping in wind, rain hammering like bullets, then the flash-CRACK of close lightning that makes you scream. Between thunderclaps, whisper anxiously. During the lulls, try to calm yourself with rational self-talk. Let each new thunderbolt strip away a layer of composure. Include the slow realization that the storm is passing — the relief as rain softens and your breathing steadies.

title: The Silent Library Rainbow
instruction: You're a teenage girl in a quiet study room with a friend. You just accidentally knocked a heavy book off the table—it hit the floor with a thud. Whisper an apology to your friend, your voice tight with embarrassment and a flicker of distress. Then, as you glance out the window, you see a double rainbow forming over the campus—so vivid and unexpected it steals your breath. Let the embarrassment dissolve into pure, hushed awe—your whisper becoming slower, fuller with wonder, like you're barely able to shape the words with all that air.
emotions_sampled: Distress (slightly present), Embarrassment (slightly present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Long Drive Home
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting in your car after a doctor's appointment, seat reclined slightly, arms stretched forward gripping the wheel. A deep, familiar ache radiates from your lower back, making you wince as you shift. You're talking to yourself, partly to distract from the pain, partly to decide whether to take the long scenic route home or just go straight. Start with a sharp breath and a muttered complaint about the pain, then let your voice soften as you remember why you love this road — the way the light hits the trees at dusk. End with a weary but tender resolve, a quiet decision to take the slow way, despite the ache.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Holding Your Child's Attacker at Gunpoint
instruction: You've found the person who hurt your child, and you have them cornered, gun in hand. Begin with volcanic rage barely contained, voice shaking with fury: 'Do you have any idea what you've done? DO YOU?' Breathing is ragged, almost hyperventilating. Your voice is raw, nearly screaming: 'They trusted people! They were innocent!' But then something shifts—you see fear in their eyes and suddenly you're flooded with the horrible weight of what you're about to do. Your voice drops, becomes unsteady: 'If I do this... if I pull this trigger...' The rage dissolves into anguished sobbing: 'I can't. God help me, I can't.' End in complete breakdown, voice destroyed: 'But they hurt my baby. They hurt my baby and I can't even—' This is the moment when righteous fury collides with your own humanity and both tear you apart.

title: The Exploding Volcano
instruction: You are a teenage non-native speaker at a school science fair, showing off your homemade volcano. You expected a small fizz, but it erupted in a massive, unexpected burst of foam and color, startling everyone. You try to explain to the judge what happened, but your astonishment makes your English messy — words come out simplified and too loud, with pauses between them. As you speak, the initial shock and confusion shift into awe and pride. Your voice stays loud but begins to soften as you realize how cool it is. Let your sentences be short, with gaps, and let your breathing and glances at the volcano interrupt you.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Drag
instruction: You're alone on a balcony, vaping as you wait for a phone call about a job you desperately want. You inhale deeply, feeling the crackle of the vapor, then hold it before exhaling slowly while speaking. Start with a flicker of curiosity — you're interested in what they might say, but as the wait stretches, that interest sours into a quiet disappointment. Let your voice be slightly rough from the drag, with pauses for those inhalations, and a subtle shift in tone from hopeful to resigned. End with a tired exhale as you stub out the device.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Execution
instruction: You are speaking to your childhood best friend through prison glass the night before their execution for a crime you know they didn't commit, but you were too afraid to speak up years ago when it mattered. Begin with desperate attempts to maintain normalcy—reminiscing about shared memories, forcing lightness into your voice. Gradually let the weight of your guilt and unsaid confession crack through. By the end, you must break completely, confessing your cowardice in a whisper that carries the weight of a life destroyed. Your friend knows. They've always known. Let their forgiveness, offered gently through their own tears, devastate you more than any anger could. Transform from false cheerfulness to raw, throat-closing remorse to the unbearable tenderness of undeserved grace.
inspired_by: The Vampire and the Innocent Villager

title: Bedside Confession to a Dying Lover
instruction: You're sitting beside your unconscious partner's hospital bed, finally saying things you've been too afraid to voice. Your stutter, usually manageable, becomes unpredictable under the weight of impending loss. Start with tender, whispered memories: 'R-remember when we...' Let emotion catch in your throat—not dramatically, but the way grief actually stops breath. As you move toward confession, your voice becomes softer, more broken: 'I was s-s-scared to... I never t-told you...' Mix gratitude with devastating sorrow, each stuttered syllable heavy with unsaid years. End in the quietest whisper, where the stutter almost dissolves into pure emotion: 'P-please... don't... don't g-go.' This isn't about the impediment—it's about how love sounds when time is running out, how vulnerability sounds when there's nothing left to hide.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Named You Wrong
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent, finally ready to tell them that the identity they gave you—the name, the expectations, the whole life they built for you—was never yours, and living in it has been slowly killing you. Begin with your voice careful, almost apologetic, trying to soften a blow you know will hurt them. As they resist, dismiss, or try to convince you otherwise, feel your voice shift from pleading to firm, then to something harder—anger you've never let yourself feel before. There's a moment where your rage cracks open and reveals the child underneath, desperate to be seen, and your voice becomes small and broken: 'Why wasn't I enough as I was?' Then something shifts. Your voice steadies into a new kind of power—not loud, but unshakable. You're no longer asking permission. By the end, you're speaking your real name for the first time to them, and your voice carries both grief for what you're leaving behind and fierce, terrifying joy at finally becoming yourself.

title: The Indecisive Restaurant Orderer
instruction: Perform as a person who cant decide what to order, causing frustration. Use an anxious voice while debating options, switching to the servers impatient replies.

title: The Photograph in the Drawer
instruction: You are an older woman alone in your dimly lit living room, a forgotten photograph in your hand. You begin speaking softly, almost whispering, as you trace the image with your finger — your voice slow, searching, full of a sudden, vivid lust for a younger lover from years ago. But as you recall the details, a wave of disgust rises at the memory of his hands, the way he smelled, the shame of your own need. Let your voice catch, pause, trail off. End with a bitter laugh, your tone hardening as you realize what you’ve become — a hungry ghost in a comfortable cage. Speak about 60 words, thinking aloud, letting your voice crack and waver naturally.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Disgust (clearly present), Bitterness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner on the last morning before they leave for a mission they might not return from. You both know this could be the last time you wake up together, but you're trying to stay in this moment—talking about mundane things like the coffee you'll make, the way the light comes through the curtains. Start with forced lightness, almost brittle cheerfulness, as if keeping the conversation ordinary will keep them safe. Gradually, let the reality seep in through the cracks—your voice beginning to tremble as you describe how you'll remember this exact moment, this exact light. By the end, drop all pretense: speak directly to the truth that you're memorizing the sound of their breathing, that you're trying to pour a lifetime of love into these final hours. Your voice should move from protective denial to raw, undefended love—the kind that knows it might have to let go forever.

title: Bound by Trust
instruction: You're lying on your bed, wrists tied loosely above your head, your partner standing beside you. At first, the ropes feel like a promise — you smile, your voice light with hope, anticipation warm in your chest. But as you test the bindings and realize there's no quick release, a wave of distress hits: your breathing quickens, your words become shorter, strained, fighting against the vulnerability. By the end, shame creeps in — a low, faltering confession, spoken mostly to yourself, as you ask your partner for reassurance while the rope creaks with your every shift. Let your voice start open and optimistic, then tighten with real panic before dropping into a hushed, embarrassed plea.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Distress (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Truth I've Been Holding
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the silence that shaped your childhood—all the things she never said, the emotions she locked away. Begin with halting anger, voice tight with years of confusion: 'You never told me you were struggling, you just... disappeared inside yourself.' As you speak, your rage begins to crack open and underneath is a child's bewildered grief. Your voice breaks as clarity strikes: 'Oh. You didn't know how to ask for help. You were drowning.' Feel the shift from accusation to devastating understanding. Your words become both confrontation and confession: 'I needed you to be okay, and you needed someone to see you weren't.' End with fierce, painful love mixed with loss for all the years of misunderstanding: 'I see you now, Mom. I finally see you.'

title: The Wedding Toast: Joy Built on Goodbye
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, and they're moving across the world tomorrow. Start with genuine celebration, your voice warm and full of laughter: 'I've known you since we were kids, and I knew you'd find this.' But underneath the joy, grief is rising. Let your voice catch on memories, your laughter becoming watery. You're genuinely happy for them—your smile is real—but you're also losing them, and both truths exist simultaneously. Your voice trembles between celebration and sorrow. 'I'm so proud of you' comes out choked with tears you're trying to hide behind a smile. End with a toast that's both blessing and farewell, your voice breaking beautifully as you raise your glass: 'To the best thing that ever happened to me—and to letting you go.'
inspired_by: Emergency Dispatch: Managing Chaos Into Order

title: Burning Inside Out
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything - someone you thought was lost is alive, or a truth you believed has been shattered. Begin in physical stillness, the information hitting your body like a shock, not yet processed. Feel the actual sensation in your chest, your throat, your hands. As the reality penetrates, let your body begin to respond - maybe you need to move, to pace, to grip something. Allow sensation to build: your heart racing, heat rising through your torso, your hands trembling or clenching. Let rage and ecstasy and disbelief crash through you simultaneously - don't separate them. This is both the best and worst moment, joy laced with fury at what was taken from you, relief tangled with the pain of lost time. Move from frozen shock to explosive physical release, letting your voice and body express what's too large for words. End in breathless exhaustion, wrung out, transformed.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access extreme grief, terror, or helplessness for a role

title: Air Traffic Controller: Two Planes on Collision Course
instruction: Perform the most controlled panic possible. Your voice must be steady, clipped, and precise — lives depend on clarity. Issue rapid corrections to two aircraft. Use phonetic alphabet with machine-gun efficiency. Include the moment of near-miss — your voice doesn't change, but the pause after the crisis is resolved speaks volumes. Then key off the mic and let out the breath you've been holding for ninety seconds. The trembling whisper: 'Oh my God.'

title: The Last Breath Between Us
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved your entire life - a parent, a partner, a best friend - and these are their final moments. Begin in absolute silence, holding their hand, frozen in the terror of what's coming. Then let yourself break open completely. Say everything you never said - scream it, whisper it, sob it, laugh through tears remembering beautiful moments. Let your voice crack, let your body shake, let sounds come out that you didn't know you could make. Move from paralyzed fear to wild, abandoned grief to tender gratitude to rage at the universe to finally, exhaustedly, a whispered goodbye. Your voice and body should be unrecognizable from beginning to end.

title: The 3 AM Conversation
instruction: You're lying in bed at 3 AM, your body heavy with exhaustion but your mind racing. You've been awake for hours, and the darkness feels like it's pressing down on your chest. Start by whispering to yourself, your voice frayed with helplessness—each word a struggle to push out through the fog. Midway, you hear a car pass outside, and you pause, staring at the window. By the end, let the helplessness shift into a quiet, fragile acceptance as you decide to get up and make tea, your voice hollow but steady, carrying the weight of a thousand sleepless nights.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: One Too Many at the Urgent Care
instruction: You're at a late-night urgent care, slightly tipsy from a work party, wearing a surgical mask. You've cut your hand and are waiting for stitches. The nurse asks if you've been drinking. You start by trying to sound controlled and dismissive, but as you speak, the mask muffles your words and you realize you're not fooling anyone. Your voice wavers between defensive sarcasm and a wobbly confession. End with a quiet, honest admission.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispered Memory on Empty Wood
instruction: You're alone on the porch swing where you and your first love used to sit together. They died suddenly, and you haven't been able to sit here since. Begin barely audible, as if testing whether you can even speak. Describe the swing moving with only your weight now, half the burden it used to carry. Your voice should be so quiet it almost disappears—catch it in your throat as you remember specific moments: their laugh, how they'd lean against you, the exact way the swing sounded with both of you. Let the tenderness break you open. This isn't dramatic crying—it's the kind of grief that sits in your chest like a stone. End with a whispered admission of something you never got to tell them, your voice so fragile it might shatter, finding a devastating gentleness in the empty space beside you.
inspired_by: Gently Swinging in a Porch Swing

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your mother's bedside in her final hour. She's been holding on, struggling, unable to let go. You begin speaking to her with overwhelming guilt and obligation—telling her she must fight, she must stay, you're not ready. But as you continue, something breaks open inside you. Your words shift into a profound release: you give her permission to go, permission to stop fighting, permission to be free of pain. Let your body shake with the effort of letting go. Your voice should move from desperate pleading to exhausted, loving release. By the end, you're whispering through tears, telling her it's okay, you'll be okay, she can rest now. The transformation is from frantic holding-on to tender, liberating goodbye.

title: Broken Frame
instruction: You are pinned under a fallen bookcase, your chest compressed so you can only speak in short, forced exhalations. Beside you is your young child, crying. Start by trying to sound calm and reassuring, but each breath is a struggle and your high, soft voice comes out strained. As you realize you cannot move and the weight is too heavy, your disappointment at failing to protect her overwhelms you. Let your syllables become sharper, more desperate, then finally collapse into a raw, quiet whisper of apology. Speak with natural pauses, gasps, and the sensation of losing a thought as you fight for air.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Forgotten Name at the Support Group
instruction: You're a young man at a stroke recovery support group, standing at the front to introduce yourself for the first time. You know your name, but when you open your mouth, the word won't come—just a grunt and a garbled sound. The room goes quiet. You feel a hot wave of embarrassment, your face burning, and you try again, but the wrong syllable slips out. You glance at your hands, clenching and unclenching them, feeling a sour bitterness toward your own body. Then someone in the audience gently says your name. You nod, relieved, and let out a slow, shaky breath. Your voice should start tight and strained, then soften as the relief settles in.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (very intensely present), Sourness (slightly present), Relief (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Thing You Kept Secret
instruction: Late at night, you're sitting on the floor of your childhood bedroom during a visit home. In your hands is something you've hidden here for years—a love letter never sent, a photo, a small trinket, something nobody knows you've kept. Your partner or best friend finds you here and asks what you're holding. Begin with deflection, trying to hide it, laughing it off. But as they gently persist, your voice drops to almost a whisper. Tell them the story of this object—who it connects you to, what moment in your past it represents, why you've never been able to throw it away. Let your fingers move over it with unbearable tenderness as you speak. The emotion should evolve from embarrassed guardedness to soft, aching vulnerability. By the end, you're either offering to finally show them, or you're curling around it protectively, exposed and afraid. This isn't dramatic—it's intimate, whispered, raw.
inspired_by: Object Bonding (Personal Relationship with Stage Objects)

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love deeply who has only hours left to live. They cannot speak anymore, but their eyes are open. Begin in a state of desperate denial, trying to fill the silence with memories and plans for a future you know won't come. As you speak, truly look at them—study every detail of their face, the way the light hits their skin, the rhythm of their breathing, the smallest movements of their expression. Let your words gradually fall away as you become absorbed in simply witnessing them. Allow your emotion to shift from frantic fear to a profound, aching presence—where grief transforms into a kind of reverent attention. End in near-silence, where simply seeing them, really seeing them in this final moment, becomes the only thing that matters. Your voice should move from rushed and breaking to slow, hushed, and finally to whispered fragments or silence filled with observation.

title: Watching from the Bar
instruction: You're a young, hyper-masculine guy at a crowded bar, nursing a bottle of beer. Across the room, the person you've been secretly lusting after is laughing too closely with someone else. You take a long, slow gulp—the glass clinks against your teeth, liquid sloshes, your throat works heavily. As you lower the bottle, you start muttering to yourself, voice thick with jealousy and envy. Midway through, you take another gulp—speech stops, a wet swallow, a slight gasp for air. By the end, your jealousy has boiled into raw, possessive lust, your voice lower, breathier, almost growling. The words should come out uneven, interrupted by the physical act of drinking, with natural pauses and shifts in tone.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Crushing Double-Tap
instruction: You're a high school senior, known for your cool, amused demeanor, and you're finally cornered in the school workshop by the bully who's been torturing your little brother for months. You feel a smug, contented interest at first, like you're about to enjoy a video game. But then he smirks and says something that crosses the final line. You erupt. Your voice becomes a percussive, distorted weapon. One hand slams a wrench onto the metal table hard enough to make it ring. You crack a sudden, grim smile at the beginning, but by the last word you're just a raw, trembling nerve, utterly drained of all amusement.
emotions_sampled: Interest (slightly present), Amusement (extremely present), Contentment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Grit and Silence
instruction: You are a rugged, deep-voiced man caught in a sudden sandstorm with your young child. You press a cloth over your mouth, coughing and squinting against the stinging wind. At first you shout in confusion, trying to locate the child whose hand you felt slip away—your voice is muffled, desperate, broken by coughs. As the storm howls, you realize the child has found shelter behind a rock, and your tone shifts to a raw, shaky relief, still thick with grit and breathlessness. Speak through the fabric, let your sibilants hiss with sand, and let the confusion transform into a quiet, urgent reassurance.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Thunderclap Confession
instruction: You are a boy, maybe ten years old, standing in a relentless downpour in an empty field. You've just won a race against an older kid who made fun of your high voice, and you're soaked to the bone. The rain is roaring in your ears, water streaming into your mouth as you sputter and shout, trying to tell your mother—who's not there—that you finally felt strong. Start with a giddy, breathless victory, but as you hear the thunder crack, shame floods in: you're just a kid pretending, and this is embarrassing. Let your words break between gasps and swallowed laughter, your pride crumbling into a shy, dripping confession. Speak maybe forty words, shouting over the rain, until the last one is almost a whisper.
