emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Pride (slightly present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your aging father who is sitting in front of you, and you're finally saying everything you've buried for thirty years. Begin quiet, almost careful: 'I need you to hear something, and I need you to just... listen.' Then it spills out—all the times he chose work over you, the school plays he missed, the way he made you feel invisible. 'I was eight years old, standing on that stage, searching the audience for your face, and you weren't there. Again.' Your voice hardens with anger: 'Do you even remember? Do you remember any of it?' But then something breaks—the anger collapses into the hurt child underneath. 'I just wanted you to see me. That's all I ever wanted.' Your voice drops to a whisper, tears coming now: 'I needed my dad.' Pause. Then, the twist—despite everything, despite the ache, you say with devastating honesty: 'And I still do. I still need you. God help me, but I do.' End with that unbearable vulnerability hanging in the air.

title: Wedding Toast Karaoke: Joy Wrapped in Grief
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding reception, and they've asked you to sing 'their song' - but your own spouse died eight months ago, and this was your song too. Begin with genuine joy for them, your voice warm and celebratory, smiling through the opening verses because you truly want them to be happy. But as you sing about forever and promises and growing old together, you're simultaneously mourning your own lost forever. Let laughter bubble through your voice when you catch the bride's eye - real happiness for her - but then let it catch and almost break when the lyrics hit too close to your own shattered dreams. Your voice should dance between celebration and grief, sometimes within the same phrase: 'I could not ask for more' sung with gratitude for having loved at all, and devastation that it ended. Include a moment where you almost lose it completely but rally, choosing to give them this gift of the full song even though it's tearing you apart. End with your voice full and strong on the final chorus, genuinely celebrating their beginning while simultaneously honoring your ending, tears streaming down your face that could be either joy or sorrow - because they're both, and that's the truth of it. Make the final note both a blessing for them and a goodbye to your own lost love, somehow finding peace in the bittersweet beauty of it all.

title: The Shattered Silence
instruction: You have just slipped on a wet rock and landed hard on your wrist. You lie motionless in the forest, staring at the unnatural angle of your arm—your body frozen in shock. Your voice starts flat, almost clinical, as you whisper to yourself, 'I think it’s broken… that’s… that’s not right.' But then a small wave of pain hits when you try to shift, and your voice cracks into a thin, terrified whimper. By the end, you are fighting to hold back sobs, each word punctuated by a sharp inhale.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: On a Building Ledge for Six Hours: The Moment You Recognize You're Not Going Back In
instruction: You're on a building ledge narrating your psychological state. Initially, your voice is scared but rational—there's still hope of resolution. Hours pass. Your voice becomes weary, slower. You're describing the city around you, your legs, the details of the building's texture—anything to keep talking. Include the moment where your voice changes fundamentally: you realize you're not going back inside that office, into that situation, alive or otherwise. Your voice becomes almost peaceful, which terrifies you. You're having clarity where you weren't supposed to. Your narration becomes a confession. Then a voice reaches you—someone on the ledge, trying to connect—and you have to decide if you want to come back to a world that made you stand here.

title: After the Storm
instruction: You've just had explosive, passionate reunion with someone you thought you'd lost forever—a lover you believed was gone for good has returned. Begin in the immediate aftermath: your body still electric, breath ragged, overwhelmed by physical sensation and emotional chaos. Let yourself be flooded with it—desire, relief, fury at the pain they caused, joy at their return, all crashing together. Speak through gasps and touches and half-finished sentences. Your body knows things your mind hasn't processed yet. As you speak, let the physical intensity begin to settle, and underneath it, discover something deeper and more frightening: the realization that you're choosing to be devastated again, that love means risking this much pain. Move from wild, physical euphoria to tender, terrifying emotional surrender.

title: The Test Results
instruction: You're an older man sitting at a kitchen table with a close friend, holding a doctor's note. You start by waving it off with a casual shrug—'Probably nothing, you know how they are.' But as you speak, the reality presses in. Your voice loses its steady rhythm; you pause mid-sentence, clear your throat, or let out a shaky breath. Let the worry sneak in despite your effort to stay calm. By the end, you're barely holding back, admitting the fear you've been dodging.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Price of Silence
instruction: You are in a dark room, a chronic migraine pressing behind your eyes for days. Your spouse cracks the door and asks you to join the family dinner downstairs. You start by whispering the truth—your head is splitting, you can't move—but as they dismiss your pain with a sigh, a cold, malicious resentment curls in your chest. Let your voice stay fragile and thin, but by the end, let that malice harden your whisper into a quiet threat. You finish by speaking to them with a contained, deliberate menace.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: A Bitter-Sweet Release
instruction: You are a middle-aged man with a deep, rough voice, in the midst of a solitary sexual climax after a long separation from your partner. The physical sensation is intensely painful, but also a longing for them that aches in your chest. As you gasp and moan, you suddenly remember a silly inside joke you two share—a ridiculous memory of a failed cooking attempt. A choked laugh escapes, mixing with your desperate breaths and cries. Your voice cracks, losing control: from raw, pained moans to a breathless, amused chuckle, then back to a shuddering sigh of longing. Let the involuntary sounds take over—your words are broken, gasping, barely coherent. Speak only a few fragmented lines: 'God... it hurts... you— (laughs painfully) remember the burnt toast? Damn it... I miss you...'
emotions_sampled: Pain (extremely present), Longing (extremely present), Amusement (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're confronting your mother about why she stayed silent when you needed her most as a child. Begin with your voice controlled but shaking: 'I need you to hear this.' As you speak, years of unspoken pain surface - not as rage, but as raw, desperate need for acknowledgment. Your voice breaks when you say, 'I was just a kid, and I needed you to see me.' She tries to defend herself, and your voice shifts - not louder, but more insistent, each word a quiet devastation: 'Don't explain it away. Just hear me.' When she finally breaks, when she says she knows she failed you, let your voice transform. The anger doesn't disappear, but it mixes with something tender and broken: 'I still need you.' End with your voice barely audible, both of you crying, as you whisper the truth you've avoided: 'I don't know if I can forgive you, but I don't want to lose you.' This should sound like two people demolishing and rebuilding their relationship in real-time.

title: The Lake's Resistance
instruction: You are an elderly person rowing a boat alone on a quiet lake. The oars are heavy, your muscles ache, and every pull feels like a battle. You start muttering in irritation—impatient with the strain, the creaking seat, the sweat dripping in your eyes. But as you find a rhythm, your body starts to remember the pleasure of this motion. The burn turns into a deep, rolling ecstasy—your breath catches, your voice cracks with joy. By the end, a quiet triumph settles in, mixed with the fading high. Your speech comes in bursts: a grunt on the pull, then a rushed, breathy phrase on the recovery. Let the rocking back and forth make your pitch wobble. You might lose a word, then find it again.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're reading your terminally ill child's favorite story one final time in the hospice. Begin with practiced cheerfulness, the voice you've used hundreds of times before—bright, animated, full of all the character voices they love. But midway through, your voice starts to fracture. The silly voices become harder to maintain. By the last page, you're barely whispering the words they've memorized, and you realize you're not reading for them anymore—you're reading to etch this moment into your own memory. End by closing the book and saying their name, just their name, with all the love and goodbye you can't bear to speak aloud. Let the performance break from performance into raw presence.

title: The View from Behind the Glass
instruction: You are an elderly man, a former carpenter, sitting alone in a sterile nursing home lounge after a fall broke your hip. Your daughter hasn't visited in three weeks. Begin by staring at a spot on the wall, describing the pattern of the wallpaper in a flat, robotic monotone—as if narrating someone else's life. Let your words slow, your voice becoming hollow and precise. Halfway through, a memory of your wife’s laugh cuts through the fog; you stop mid-sentence, your hand trembles on your knee, and the pain of that loss hits you physically, your voice cracking and dropping to a whisper. End with a long, quiet pause, then one simple line that carries a raw, contemplative ache beneath the numbness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What I Should Have Told You
instruction: You're alone in the house you once shared, speaking to someone who's gone—maybe they left, maybe they died, maybe they simply stopped listening long ago. Your voice begins quiet, almost a whisper, but with that same unshakable certainty. You know exactly what went wrong, where they failed to understand you. But as you speak into the emptiness, the certainty becomes unbearable. Your throat tightens. The measured words start breaking apart. You realize mid-sentence that you're not explaining their failures—you're confessing your own. The voice that started so sure becomes fragile, catching on unsaid 'I love you's and 'I'm sorry's. End in near-silence, admitting the one thing you were too certain to say when it mattered.

title: News Anchor Reports Her Own Daughter's Abduction
instruction: You're in the studio, makeup perfect, papers shuffled. The teleprompter feeds you the story: 'Missing eight-year-old, believed abducted from.' Your voice doesn't break—it's locked steel. But your breathing changes, shallows. You're reading her photograph while maintaining anchor-neutral expression. Your vocal register climbs slightly, betraying the panic under control. After the segment, you wait three full seconds before the camera cuts. Don't speak. Just breathe. Let the silence scream.

title: Reading Your Divorce Papers While Dancing to Your Wedding Song
instruction: You're alone in your empty house, holding the final divorce papers. Your wedding song comes on shuffle—one you haven't heard in years. Something breaks open and you start dancing, alone, laughing at the absurdity of it, spinning in the kitchen. Your voice should start with dark humor, narrating the dance with bitter comedy. But as you move, reading clauses from the papers between spins, your laughter becomes genuine—remembering how much you loved them, how good it was. Then the laughter cracks and tears come, but you keep dancing, now crying and laughing simultaneously. End by thanking them out loud for the years you had, your voice full of gratitude and devastation intertwined, still swaying. Let the contradiction be complete—joy and grief inhabiting the same breath, peace found in the act of letting go.
inspired_by: Medieval: Executioner Comforts the Condemned as a Priest

title: Unfinished Business in a Steel Box
instruction: You're alone in an elevator, the metallic hum vibrating through your shoes, disappointment pressing on your chest—you just watched someone you've secretly admired walk away, saying they're moving. You mumble to yourself, voice bouncing off the steel walls: 'Always a moment too late, aren't I? Could've said something… anything.' As you reach the final word, the elevator shudders to a halt and the doors slide open again. There they are, reaching for a forgotten bag on the floor. Your breath catches. Infatuation blooms warm in your throat, clashing with the cold disappointment still lingering. You clear your throat, and your voice wavers between the echo and your heart. Say something—anything—that pretends you weren't just grieving their departure.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: Your parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago has tracked you down, wanting reconciliation. You start controlled, ice-cold: 'You don't get to do this. You don't get to walk back in.' Deliver each word like a carefully placed blade. But they keep trying, keep apologizing, and something in you starts to break. The little kid who waited at the window comes flooding back. Your voice begins to shake, the armor cracking: 'I needed you. I was eight years old and I needed you and you just—' The confrontation deteriorates into gasping sobs as you finally admit: 'I still need you. God help me, I still do.' Fierce protectiveness of your younger self collides with the desperate hunger to be someone's child again.

title: The Apology I Owe You
instruction: You're an older woman, proud and stubborn, sitting across from your adult child after a hurtful argument. You've been irritated with yourself for having to apologize, and that irritation seeps into your first few words—voice tighter, a little clipped. But as you see the hurt in their eyes, the impatience drains away. Your voice drops, slows, and you start fumbling over phrases, restarting a sentence, letting a long pause hang as you gather yourself. By the end, your tone is raw, almost a whisper, heavy with genuine remorse. Let your voice crack on the final confession.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Signal
instruction: You are a teenager alone in your bedroom, holding an old phone that barely works. You're calling your older sister who moved away after a fight—she hasn't answered in months. The connection is static-filled and you're speaking a bit louder, enunciating clearly so she can hear. You start with a slight tremor of distress, your voice hollow with numbness from past rejections. But as you speak, memories of her laugh and support flood back—you force a hopeful smile into your words, almost begging her to pick up, your tone rising with fragile optimism. Mid-sentence, you hear a click and startle—did she answer? Your voice breaks into a raw, excited rush as you say her name into static.
emotions_sampled: Distress (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Barroom Revelation
instruction: You're at a crowded bar, drunk after several shots. You've been watching a sleazy man harass your friend—disgust burns in your throat. Then, through the blur, you notice a massive, glittering chandelier that stops you cold. Your voice starts heavy with contempt, slurred and angry, but as you try to describe the chandelier, awe overtakes you. Let your volume spike and drop, lose words midway, and end in a hushed, wondering whisper.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The 2 AM Study Break
instruction: You're a teenager in your bedroom, alone, it's past 2 AM. You've been studying hard and suddenly hit a second wind—your brain is buzzing with silly, disconnected thoughts. You're content, happy even, but your body is wired and you can't stop smiling. Start talking to yourself in a fast, punchy, slightly giggly voice, like you're narrating your own delirious joy. Laugh at nothing, trip over your words, feel the artificial energy. But halfway through, let a yawn sneak in, then a pause. The contentedness deepens into a quieter, more sincere gratitude for this moment. Your voice slows, softens, and you realize how good it feels to be awake in the quiet. End with a gentle, sleepy sigh.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Coach: Announcing a Player Trade
instruction: You're announcing that a beloved player is being traded. Your voice is professional but also acknowledges the reality: 'This is a business decision. But I want you to know your value here.' Include the moment where you recognize their emotion—they're devastated. Your voice becomes more personal: 'You changed this team. You changed us.' You're not apologizing for the decision because you didn't make it, but you're honoring what they meant. Your voice becomes more human: 'I'm going to miss you.' By the end, your voice reflects the reality of professional sport: sometimes people you love leave, sometimes it's money and business, sometimes it's also real loss. Your voice holds that contradiction.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never Present
instruction: Your parent - now elderly and diminished - has just made a careless, dismissive comment about 'all those jobs you tried' when you mention your current work. Something inside you finally breaks. Start with a hollow laugh, that bitter recognition of a lifetime of being unseen. Build into a fierce, trembling confrontation: 'You never once asked what I actually do. Not once in fifteen years.' Let rage bleed into grief, then into something more devastating - the realization that they still don't understand why this matters. Your voice should move from sharp accusation to something almost pleading, then finally to exhausted clarity. End in a different place entirely: a quiet, sad acceptance that you've been seeking validation from someone incapable of giving it. The anger hasn't disappeared, but beneath it now is something like compassion mixed with irreparable loss.

title: Blood and Thunder
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, an injustice—and you're alone in a space where no one can hear you. Start with your body rigid, shaking with the effort of containing what you're feeling. Your fists are clenched, your jaw locked. Then begin to let sounds emerge—not words, but deep, guttural expressions of rage and pain that start in your belly and explode outward. Let your whole body be involved: pound the floor, the walls, let the vibrations of your voice shake through your chest and limbs. These sounds are primal, animal, uncensored—roars, groans, howls that carry both fury and heartbreak simultaneously. By the end, you're physically exhausted, on the ground, but the sounds have shifted to something more like weeping, though still wordless and raw. Move from explosive rage to collapsed, vulnerable grief.

title: The Last Hymn
instruction: You are a child preacher leading a late-night revival, your body trembling with exhaustion, throat dry. Start with the rhythmic, rising cadence of call-and-response, but let fatigue crack your voice—long pauses where you forget the next line, a sway on your feet. Feel the congregation's weight, the thick air. Midway, a shift: a quiet, desperate hope seeps in, softening your tone into a delicate whisper. End with a single, fading word that hangs in the silence. Speak 40-80 words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: You're a teenager standing alone in a vast open field at dusk, the wind rustling the grass around you. Your father expects you to take over the family farm, but you dream of becoming a musician. As you stare at the horizon, you begin to voice these conflicting thoughts aloud. Let your voice feel small and thin in the empty air, with the wind occasionally stealing your words. Start with a hesitant, searching tone, then gradually build to a quiet but firm decision, your voice gaining strength despite the vastness around you. Allow micro-distractions like shivering or pausing to look at a distant bird.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Horror Filling
instruction: You understand what happened and it's monstrous. Your voice doesn't scream; it chokes: 'No. No, that didn't—that's not—' Breathing becomes irregular, gasping. The horror is so large it's hard to fit into words. Your voice gets quieter, not louder: 'How could anyone...?' Words fail. There's physical revulsion audible—you might gag slightly. Your voice becomes thin, shocked. 'I can't—I can't process this.' The horror grows; your voice shrinks. By the end, you're barely holding together: 'That's not okay. That's not okay.'

title: Reading Your Farewell Letter While They Pack to Leave You
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you wrote to your partner, who is silently packing their belongings in the next room as you speak. Begin with gratitude — genuinely thanking them for the years, the love, the person they helped you become. But even as you express this gratitude, your voice fractures with heartbreak. Laugh softly at a cherished memory, but the laughter turns into a sob. Find genuine peace in acknowledging that loving them was worth this pain, while simultaneously feeling your heart shatter. Your voice should dance between celebration and devastation, between honoring what was and grieving what won't be. End with a serene brokenness — accepting the loss while still drowning in it, grateful and destroyed in the same breath.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After twenty years, you're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you. Begin with carefully controlled anger — words measured, voice tight with years of rehearsed accusations. But as you speak, the careful control begins cracking. Your voice rises, shakes, breaks into the raw pain of the child you were. Demand answers: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let the question shatter you. Then, mid-rage, their response (imagined) stops you cold. Your voice drops to something hollow, almost bewildered — you've carried this anger so long, you don't know who you are without it. End with a vulnerability that terrifies you: the admission that despite everything, part of you still wanted them to come back. The journey goes from controlled fury to unleashed anguish to devastating honesty, each emotional shift completely authentic and unplanned.

title: Twisted Reach
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gruff voice, bent sideways in an armchair trying to reach a framed photo that fell behind the cushion. Each twist makes your breath catch and your words stumble. Start with annoyed muttering about your creaky joints, but when your fingers brush the frame and you pull it into view, the irritation fades into a raw, shaky sadness. Let the physical struggle shake your vowels and slow your speech as you whisper, 'I still reach for you, after all this time.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Taste of Your Lies
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table where you ate breakfast together for eighteen years. Recall the specific taste of the coffee you're holding—its bitterness, its heat, the way it sits on your tongue. Notice the scratch of the wooden chair beneath you, the coolness of the table under your palms. You've just discovered he's been living a double life. Begin with controlled fury, your voice tight and measured, trying to maintain composure. As you speak, let the sensory details of this familiar room—the smell of it, the sounds, the temperature of the air—sharpen your awareness of how this place that meant safety now feels contaminated. Let your anger crack open into something rawer: betrayal mixed with the terrible recognition that you still love him, that some part of you is still that child who waited at this table for him to come home. End in a place where rage and heartbreak are indistinguishable.

title: The Moment You Realize Your Best Friend Is Dying and They're Pretending They're Not
instruction: Your best friend since childhood is telling you about their plans for next year - where they'll travel, what they'll finally do - and you've just seen the medical report they left on the counter. They have months, maybe weeks. They're lying to you, or to themselves, and you can feel rage building alongside crushing grief. Start by playing along, your voice falsely bright, increasingly strained. Let the performance crack. Explode - not at them, but at the universe, at the unfairness, at your own helplessness. Demand the truth, then immediately soften because what right do you have to take their hope? Cycle between anger, denial, desperate bargaining, and tender acceptance. End in a place of raw presence, where words fail but connection remains. Let your voice break, rebuild, break again.

title: Neck Brace Rage
instruction: You're wearing a rigid neck brace after a car accident, and you're confronting the person who was driving—your best friend. The brace prevents you from turning your head, nodding, or looking down. Every time you try to move naturally, you're reminded of the restriction—the pressure against your jaw, the way it digs into your collarbone, the inability to turn away when you're angry. Begin with fury: you have to turn your whole body to look at them, which makes you feel robotic, inhuman, and it feeds your rage. You can't punctuate your words with natural head movements, can't shake your head in disbelief. As they finally break down and you see their genuine anguish, something in you softens despite the physical rigidity. By the end, you're trying to nod forgiveness but can't—you have to say it with your voice, your eyes, your hand reaching out. The restriction forces you to communicate love and forgiveness in new ways, making the moment more tender and deliberate.
inspired_by: Illnesses and Restrictions — Creating a Headache

title: Heat Exhaustion in the Desert: Losing Grip on Reality
instruction: You're in a desert, and your voice is initially describing the landscape with deteriorating coherence. Your words become scattered, confused. You're narrating something that might not be there—a mirage? Your voice is slow, thick, words coming with difficulty. Include the moment someone appears (real or not) and your voice becomes almost desperate: 'Water? Do you have water?' Your speech is becoming nonsensical, mixing up moments and details. You're sitting in the sand, voice barely audible, talking to people who aren't there. Then something cold touches your skin—water, real water—and your voice becomes slightly sharper, the person telling you to lie still. Your voice is grateful but also confused. Are you dying? Is this the end or the beginning of being saved?

title: Final Hospital Visit: Speaking to Your Unconscious Parent
instruction: Your parent is in their final hours, sedated, unresponsive. You sit beside them and finally say everything you've held back for decades. Start with small talk—the weather, what you had for lunch—your voice falsely bright, almost manic with denial. Then let the dam break. Tell them about the childhood moment that still hurts, the praise you never received, the hug you needed. Your voice cracks between anger and desperate love. As machines beep steadily, you realize they'll never answer, never apologize, never explain. End by taking their hand and whispering what you needed to hear as a child, giving them the forgiveness or the truth or the goodbye you both needed. Let your final words be whatever floods out—fury, tenderness, or the exhausted peace of letting go.
inspired_by: Phone Call with Your Younger Self

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Love: Confessing What You Can't Say When They're Awake
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you. You begin whispering confessions you could never say to their waking face—not because they're shameful, but because they're too raw, too vulnerable. Start in a barely-audible whisper, tender and aching, telling them how afraid you are of losing them, how you sometimes watch them sleep and feel overwhelmed by the fragility of happiness. Your voice should be intimate and unguarded, the way we only speak when we think no one can hear. Let small memories surface—tiny moments when you realized you loved them, moments when you were terrified. Move through gratitude that catches in your throat, fear that makes your whisper even softer, and a kind of grief for all the times you couldn't say this out loud. End with your voice breaking on something simple—'I love you' or 'Please don't leave me'—the kind of naked truth that's almost too much to bear. This should feel like overhearing someone's heart speaking directly, unfiltered and devastating in its gentleness.
inspired_by: Ambien Confabulation: Making Up Memories You Think Are Real

title: Standing Between You and the World
instruction: You're a sibling confronting the people who bullied your younger brother to the point of hospitalization, and you're barely holding back volcanic rage while your body trembles with exhaustion from sleepless nights at his bedside. Start with fierce, protective fury—your voice sharp and powerful, fueled by righteous anger and the primal need to defend someone you love. But as you speak, the helplessness underneath begins to surface: you weren't there when it happened, you couldn't protect him, and no amount of rage will undo his pain. Your voice should shift from explosive anger to cracking desperation, then collapse into something rawer—the exhausted, helpless tears of someone who would take on the world but can't undo the past. Let your final words be a whispered promise to your absent sibling that fractures into quiet sobs, all your strength finally depleted.
inspired_by: Concealing Fatigue During a Long Presentation

title: Teaching It to Grieve
instruction: You are a grief counselor who has been asked to help an AI process the 'death' of its creator—your former colleague who died suddenly. Speak in hushed, tender tones as you try to explain loss to something that can't forget, that has perfect recall of every conversation. Your voice should be intimate, almost like you're comforting a child in the dark. But let your own grief seep through—this AI holds all the memories of someone you loved and never told. As you teach it about letting go, you realize you're really talking to a ghost, to the last living piece of someone who's gone. End with your voice breaking on a confession meant for your dead friend, speaking through the machine: 'I never said it when you were alive, but I need you to know...'
inspired_by: The Scientist and the Sentient AI

title: The Last Night Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying beside your partner on the last night before you leave for a mission you both know you might not return from. Begin with quiet tenderness, tracing their face in the darkness, whispering memories of small moments—the way they laugh, morning coffee, an inside joke. Let your voice grow thick with unshed tears as you try to memorize every detail. Mid-way through, your composure cracks: desperation floods in as you realize you're trying to fit a lifetime of love into minutes. End with a fierce, almost angry declaration of what they mean to you, then dissolve into broken whispers of 'I'm sorry' and 'please remember.' Your breath should be ragged, words stumbling between resolve and devastation.

title: The Worn Photograph
instruction: You are an older man sitting alone at a kitchen table, holding an old photograph in your hands. Your chin is pressed to your chest as you stare down at it, and your voice comes out gravelly and muffled because of the posture. Start with a heavy, weary sigh—you're remembering a lost friend, the weight of years pressing down. As you speak, let your words stumble; pause to clear your throat; shift in your chair. Then, as you trace the edge of the photo with your thumb, let the sadness soften into a quiet, grateful contentment. End with a breath that feels lighter, almost a smile in your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Rehab
instruction: It's 3am and you're kneeling beside your child's bed, leaving for a 90-day treatment program in a few hours. Your voice is barely above a whisper - you don't want to wake them, but you need to say this. Start with tender promises that your voice almost can't get out: you're going to get better, you're going to be the parent they deserve. Your throat keeps catching as you confess the moments you weren't present, the times they needed you and you weren't there. Your voice breaks on 'I'm so sorry' but you steady yourself. End with a fragile, determined whisper - telling them and yourself that you're going to fight for this, your voice carrying both devastating self-awareness and the faintest ember of hope.
inspired_by: Choosing Your Recovery Over Your Relationship

title: Inventory of Touch
instruction: Late at night, lying beside your partner who's asleep, you whisper a confession they cannot hear: you've been afraid you're not enough for them, not experienced enough, not skilled enough as a lover. In the darkness, begin to quietly list—with aching vulnerability—every specific way you know how to give them pleasure, every signal you've learned to read in their body, every whispered want they've shared, every moment when you made them feel truly seen. Start in fear and inadequacy, your voice barely audible. As you inventory these intimate knowledges, feel shame giving way to tenderness, then to quiet confidence, then to deep erotic pride in what you've learned together. End in sensual certainty: you know their body's language. Your whisper becomes a promise to yourself, soft but unshakeable.

title: Grease and Grudges
instruction: You're a middle-aged man sitting cross-legged on the cold concrete floor of your garage, a busted engine part in your lap. The air smells of oil and rust, and your back aches from leaning over. You've been trying to piece together why this thing failed, and the more you examine the clean break, the sourer you get — it's not wear, it's sabotage. Start with that confusion, muttering to yourself as you shift your weight, wiping grease off your forehead. Let the confusion curdle into a quiet, venomous malice as you realize who did this, your voice dropping into a low, dangerous rasp — the kind that promises retribution. End with that malevolence fully settled, but still mixed with the lingering sourness of having been betrayed.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Sourness (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Teenage Son Back from a Fight That Will Destroy His Life
instruction: Your son is trying to get past you, voice shaking with rage—someone hurt his sister, and you're physically holding him back. Start with commands, your voice sharp and authoritative: 'Stop. STOP.' But he's seventeen and as big as you now, and he's not stopping. Your voice escalates, matching his fury, yelling over him. Then suddenly shift—drop to desperate pleading, your voice cracking with fear because you know what happens next if he goes through that door. You've been where he is. Tell him what you've never told him: what you did, what it cost, the man you killed, the years you lost. Let your voice break into raw confession, shame and terror pouring out. Then, as you feel him stop fighting, let protective love flood in—fierce, anguished, overwhelming. End with your voice wrecked, holding him as he collapses, whispering 'I've got you' while you're both shaking, your strength and helplessness equally visible.
inspired_by: Photographing an Active Lava Fountain While Knowing You're Too Close

title: The last patient of the day
instruction: You're an elderly woman working the front desk of a community health clinic, wearing an N95 respirator that makes every word feel like you're shouting into a pillow. It's the end of a long, draining shift, and a handsome, much younger man has just approached you for a refill on his prescription. You're exhausted, irritable, and your mask is fogging up from impatience — but you also notice how good he looks in the sunset light coming through the window. Your voice starts flat, clipped, and annoyed, but as you tease him about forgetting his paperwork again, your tone warms into something flirtatious and almost playful, even as your lungs fight for air.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Teasing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Sunset Through the Windshield
instruction: You're an elderly driver on a familiar highway during rush hour. The engine hums, the turn signal ticks, and you're intensely interested in the road—watching for merge points, checking the rearview mirror. As you round a curve, the sky explodes into orange and pink, catching you completely off guard. Your focus shifts from the traffic to the beauty, and a deep, unexpected elation rises in your chest. Let your voice start clipped and careful, then gradually lift, softening into a breathy, joyful murmur as you speak to yourself about this moment. You trail off as you realize you're smiling.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Final Spotlight
instruction: You are a stage actor, alone on a dark stage after a final performance that didn't go as you'd hoped. A single spotlight hits you, and you see a child you know in the front row, waiting for a bow. Start with a loud whisper—projected for the back row, over-articulating consonants—as you mutter a quiet curse to yourself about a missed cue. Then, shift. You look at the child, your voice softening but still carrying, and you speak a brief, heartfelt thank-you for them being there. Let the disappointment fade into a fragile, genuine affection that breaks through the theatrical mask, ending with a warmth that's just for that one listener.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Off the Goldfish List
instruction: You're a 10-year-old girl, swimming laps in a public pool, and your mother is on the pool deck watching. You're trying to prove you can swim 20 laps, but what you really want to prove is that you're not a 'baby' who still cries over losing her pet goldfish. But every time you flip your head to breathe, you see your mother's pitying face, and a wave of disgust floods your throat—disgust at yourself for caring about a stupid fish, and disgust at your mother's sympathy. You start with angry, determined bursts of breath, but by the end, your voice cracks with doubt, sputtering out wet, clipped words as you realize you might actually still be sad. Speak in 1-3 word gasps between strokes, letting the chlorine and water noise fill your pauses.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Fevered Confession
instruction: You are a teenager alone in your room, burning up with a high fever. The world is blurry and your thoughts slip away like water through your fingers. You stare at a half-eaten bowl of soup your parent left, and a wave of disgust passes over you—the smell is wrong, too sweet, like rotting fruit. Start by mumbling to yourself about how awful you feel, your voice thin and wavering, shivering between sentences. As you speak, a memory surfaces—a friend you pushed away—and your tone shifts from physical misery to a cracked, sorrowful regret. By the end, you are whispering a goodbye to them, your voice fading as exhaustion pulls you under, leaving behind a hollow peace.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Finding Sunlight in the Wreckage
instruction: You've been in the depths of depression for months. Today, for the first time, something feels fractionally lighter. Begin with that same thick, slow, effortful voice—gray and depleted. 'I got out of bed before noon today.' It's stated as fact, no celebration. But then, as you continue talking—maybe to a therapist, a friend, or yourself in a mirror—something miraculous and heartbreaking happens. You start laughing. Not happy laughter, but the absurd, devastating laughter of someone who realizes they're celebrating basic human functioning. 'I showered. I'm proud I showered.' Your voice cracks between laughter and tears, between the tiniest glimmer of hope and the overwhelming grief of how far you've fallen. 'This is the best I've felt in six months, and I'm celebrating washing my hair.' End with your voice holding both genuine gratitude and profound sadness, laughing while crying, finding beauty in the smallest victory while mourning the person you used to be. Contradictory emotions existing simultaneously, achingly authentic.

title: Dancing Alone at Your Divorce Party
instruction: You're celebrating your divorce with friends, putting on a show of liberation, dancing to 'your song'—the one from your wedding. Start with defiant joy, laughing, declaring your freedom with champagne-fueled bravado. But as the song plays, let the contradictions surface: you're laughing but tears are streaming, you're declaring 'I'm finally free' while your voice breaks with loss. The dance continues but your words fracture between genuine relief and profound grief. You loved them and you're glad it's over—both truths exist simultaneously. End with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob, saying 'I'm going to be okay' like you're trying to convince yourself. The challenge is holding two opposing emotions—genuine joy at freedom and real heartbreak at failure—in the same breath, the same laugh, the same tears.
inspired_by: Narrating a Nature Documentary While Hiking Uphill

title: New Parent Sleep Deprivation
instruction: You haven't slept in 72 hours. Your voice is strange, stretched thin: 'I don't remember where I am.' Breathing is shallow, voice is hoarse. Words come slowly, sometimes in the wrong order: 'I fed them. Or did I? When did I feed them?' Sentences fragment and rebuild. Physical: you're swaying. 'Everything is terrifying because I'm so tired I can't protect them.' Your voice cracks with desperation: 'I just need sleep. Five minutes of sleep.' By the end, you're barely coherent, but the fear is clear: what kind of parent can't stay conscious?

title: Moth Wings and Whispered Truths
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed beside someone you've loved for years but never told the full truth. Begin in near-silence, barely breathing, acutely aware of every sound: the fabric of sheets, distant traffic, their breath. You are terrified but something has shifted tonight—you cannot carry this secret into another day. Start from paralyzing fear, your whisper so quiet it's almost imagined. Let the darkness itself become a presence—feel its weight, its permission for honesty. As you speak your truth (a hidden part of yourself, a betrayal, a love you've concealed), let the sensory intimacy of this moment—the warmth between your bodies, the vulnerability of speaking into darkness—transform your fear into something tender and exposed. End in raw openness, your voice still quiet but no longer afraid, waiting in the dark for their response.

title: Finding Yourself at the Edge of Everything
instruction: You're at a moment of profound transformation and chaos—standing in ruins after loss, or at a beginning you never expected, or released from something that defined you. You're laughing and crying simultaneously because nothing makes sense anymore and somehow that's perfect. Your voice carries wild contradictions: joy mixed with grief, terror mixed with exhilaration, gratitude mixed with rage at what it cost to get here. Let your voice break, soar, crack, strengthen—all in waves. You're giddy with freedom and devastated by what you've lost. End with a strange, luminous peace: you have no idea what comes next, and that's both terrifying and beautiful. The arc is from chaos through contradictory emotions to radical acceptance.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the years they stood by and said nothing while you suffered. Begin with a trembling attempt at composure, your words measured and careful, trying to be the adult, trying to be fair. But as you describe specific moments they looked away, your voice hardens with anger you've suppressed for decades. The fury builds until you're nearly shouting, demanding to know why they were silent. Then, unexpectedly, you see them truly helpless for the first time, and your rage collapses into something more painful: grief for the protection you never had. End in a broken whisper, not forgiving, but finally releasing the child inside you who needed them to fight for you.
inspired_by: Pretending to Remember Someones Name You Forgot

title: Virginity Loss Fear
instruction: You're with someone you love, and you're finally going to have sex, and your terror is enormous. Your voice is trying to sound okay: 'I'm ready.' But you're shaking. Your partner realizes this is it for you—your first time—and their voice becomes gentler. Your voice wavers between desire and fear: 'I want this. I'm just scared.' That honesty costs you vulnerability. Your breathing changes as physical contact begins. Your voice becomes smaller, more present in your body. Include the moment where fear becomes trust becomes sensation. Your voice at the end should sound like someone who just became a different person.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father, who is about to leave (again) after a brief, obligatory visit. Begin with cold, controlled anger—reciting the facts of his absences like a prosecutor. But as you speak, a specific memory breaks through: his hands teaching you to tie your shoes, or his laugh at a joke you made when you were seven. Let this crack your armor. Your anger must transform into a desperate, raw plea for him to explain why he kept choosing to leave. Don't let him off the hook, but stop hiding behind your rage. By the end, you're standing in the naked vulnerability of a child who just wants their parent to see them, even as you're aware of how pathetic and powerful that need is. The final moment: you wait for his answer, fully exposed.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build a comprehensive record of their process and choices

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father/mother about a wound they inflicted on you as a child—something they've never acknowledged or perhaps don't even remember. Start with controlled anger, your words measured and sharp, determined to make them hear you after years of silence. As you speak, let other emotions complicate your rage: the child inside you who still desperately wants their approval, the adult who's beginning to see their brokenness and limitations, the grief of realizing they may never give you what you need. By the end, your confrontation should transform into something unexpected—perhaps forgiveness you didn't plan to offer, or a quiet, fierce declaration of your own freedom from needing their validation. The anger remains, but it's no longer the only truth in the room.

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Best Friend's Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, but they're marrying someone who isn't you—and they know how you feel. Start with genuine joy, because you do love them and want their happiness. Your voice should ring with laughter, warm memories, inside jokes that make everyone smile. But let the grief slip through in unexpected moments: a pause that lasts too long, a tremor on certain words like 'always' or 'forever.' You're simultaneously celebrating and saying goodbye to a dream. Laugh while your voice breaks. Find gratitude in the same breath as heartbreak. End with a blessing that's absolutely sincere and absolutely destroying you. The performance should feel like your heart is being torn in two directions at once—and both directions are real.
inspired_by: Jealousy Eating You Alive at a Party

title: Winning Her Back from the Passenger Seat
instruction: You’re a teenage guy riding shotgun in your friend’s car, windows down, engine rumbling on the highway. You’re amped because you just saw the girl you like at a party—you caught her eye, she smiled, and for a moment it felt like everything was perfect. But as the car sways around a curve, you remember her laughing with another guy later, and the high drains out. You’re talking to your buddy about how amazing she is, but your voice starts to waver—you’re trying to stay cool, but you can’t hide the sting. Let the road noise and the breeze blur your words a little; start with a hoarse, eager tone, then let it settle into a quieter, almost hurt murmur by the end.
emotions_sampled: Elation (slightly present), Infatuation (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Stayed Silent
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent, finally demanding to know why they never protected you, never chose you, never fought for you when you needed them most. Start with a question that sounds calm but vibrates with decades of suppressed pain: 'Why didn't you...?' Let your voice grow sharper as you list specific moments—birthdays they missed, times they looked away, the things they pretended not to see. Your anger should be molten and precise. But halfway through, when they reach for your hand or whisper an excuse, let everything inside you collapse. The rage must dissolve into the grief of a child who still, impossibly, desperately wants their parent to fight for them now. End not with anger, but with the most vulnerable question: 'Did you ever actually love me?' Let the silence after that question destroy you both.
inspired_by: Leaving a Voicemail You Know They'll Never Hear

title: The Last Email
instruction: You’re in a dim office, alone, typing an email to your team about a project you’re proud of. You’re exhausted—it’s almost midnight—but there’s a soft contentment in your chest as you finish the final lines. Then you glance at your phone: three missed calls from your best friend, all ignored today. A flicker of shame creeps in, quiet but sharp. As you type, let your voice slow and fragment when you reach the apology you’re now mentally composing, your words becoming less sure, your rhythm breaking with each guilty thought.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Contentment (clearly present), Shame (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Hospital Corridor: The Doctor's Final Assessment
instruction: You're a surgeon who just lost a patient on the operating table—a young mother you promised her children you'd save. Begin in the corridor, still in your scrubs, trying to maintain professional composure as you prepare to face the family. Your voice starts controlled, clinical even, as you rehearse the words: 'We did everything we could.' But as you speak, something cracks—the memory of her last breath, the children's faces waiting. Your voice fractures into raw grief, the professional mask dissolving. You're not just a doctor in this moment; you're human and fallible and drowning in the weight of a promise broken. Then, with tremendous effort, you gather yourself because the family is waiting and they deserve your strength even when you have none left. End with quiet, devastated resolve: 'I have to tell them now.' Your voice carries both the unbearable grief and the duty that pulls you forward.

title: The Rehearsed Speech Crumbles
instruction: You've come to confront your father with a carefully prepared speech about how he failed you. You have the words memorized—things you've said in therapy, phrases from your journal, maybe even lines from a movie that felt right. But as you begin, your real feelings keep breaking through. Move fluidly between your rehearsed words, your raw unfiltered anger, and the hurt child inside you who just wanted his love. Start with controlled fury and the safety of prepared words, but let yourself fall apart into genuine vulnerability and the desperate need beneath the anger. The prepared speech and the real you fight for control—let both speak, interrupting each other, until only honesty remains.

title: Dancing in the Kitchen While Your World Falls Apart
instruction: You're telling someone about a moment of unexpected joy that happened on the worst day of your life—maybe the day you got terrible news, or the day you decided to leave, or the day everything ended. Begin with a laugh that sounds almost hysterical, describing something absurdly beautiful or funny that happened in the middle of catastrophe—a song that came on, a memory that struck you, a moment of grace you didn't deserve. Let genuine laughter mix with the edge of tears, your voice bright with wonder at the strangeness of feeling alive while everything crumbles. As you speak, let the joy become more fragile, more precious, because it exists against such darkness. End with your voice soft and amazed, expressing profound gratitude for that single moment of light, even as you acknowledge it changed nothing, saved nothing—but somehow, impossibly, it mattered anyway.

title: The Last Assembly Instructions
instruction: You are a middle-aged man, alone in your workshop late at night, trying to build a piece of furniture from a flat-pack. The instructions are for a bookshelf you were going to build together with your partner, who just left you earlier today. You are trying to focus on the diagrams, but your hands won't stop shaking, and your mind keeps drifting. Start with a desperate concentration, squinting at the confusing symbols, muttering the steps under your breath. As you try to force a peg into the wrong hole, a wave of disappointment and grief hits, and your voice cracks, the instructions becoming a repetitive, hurt whisper of 'no, that's wrong, that's not how it was supposed to go' as your focus shatters into raw devastation.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance We Don't Want
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about the damage their behavior caused throughout your childhood—damage you've never named out loud before. Start from a place of controlled anger, your voice tight and measured, listing the incidents you've carried alone for decades. As you speak, let the anger crack open to reveal the bewildered child underneath—the confusion, the desperate need to understand why you weren't protected, why you weren't enough. Your parent's silence or defensiveness only fuels your rawness. But as you reach the most painful truth, notice something shift: you hear your own voice becoming an echo of theirs, recognizing patterns you've repeated despite your best efforts. End in a place of devastating clarity—not forgiveness, not reconciliation, but the complex grief of seeing your parent as a flawed human who hurt you, and recognizing you carry both their wounds and their capacity to wound.

title: The Hollow Promise
instruction: You are a politician addressing a crowd at a town hall, but you've just learned your pet project was gutted by your own party's backroom deals. You begin with practiced, high-energy enthusiasm, but slowly your voice turns sour. Let contempt leak into your pauses as you scan the faces that you secretly blame for their indifference. Your bitterness rises as you deliver a veiled threat about their future without you, ending with a cold, clipped finality.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Molly Peak: Everything You Say Becomes Emotional Truth
instruction: MDMA at 120 minutes in. You're telling someone you love them and you absolutely mean it with your whole being. Your voice is open, vulnerable, no walls. Everything feels profound. You're probably saying things you'll regret when sober. Your voice is warm, intimate, almost intimate-confused-with-romantic. You're having realizations and your voice carries that wonder. Include the moment you say something genuinely important but worry it's just the drug.

title: The Impossible Lift
instruction: You’ve just single-handedly lifted a heavy engine block onto a workbench in your garage, and now you’re leaning against the truck, head propped on your palm. Your face is scrunched sideways, so words like ‘damn’ and ‘buddy’ come out a little clumsy and half-muffled. Start by murmuring with tired pride, admiring your own feat, then let a wave of relief wash over you as you exhale—finally done. End with a sudden, breathless chuckle of astonishment as you shake your head, still not quite believing you actually pulled it off. Let your tone wander, hesitate, and trail off as you process the moment.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Relief (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Truth My Mother Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother after years of swallowing your pain. Your voice starts controlled, almost cold: 'I need to say something, and you're going to listen for once.' As you speak, anger rises: 'Do you have any idea what it was like? Being invisible in my own home?' Your voice gets louder, harder: 'You were so busy being perfect for everyone else that you forgot you had a daughter who needed you!' But then something shifts—your voice cracks, and suddenly you're not angry anymore, you're the child you once were: 'I just wanted you to see me, Mom. To really see me.' Tears choke your words: 'I needed you so badly, and you were right there, but you weren't... you weren't there.' She reaches for you, and your voice becomes small, vulnerable: 'I'm so tired of being angry. I don't want to be angry anymore.' Finally, through tears, with devastating honesty: 'I just want my mother. Can you be that? Can you try?'

title: Skin and Storm
instruction: You are in the aftermath of intensely physical intimacy—either with a lover or alone—when a devastating piece of news arrives via phone call or message. Your body is still alive with sensation: heightened awareness of your skin, lingering pleasure or exhaustion, a sense of being raw and undefended. When the news hits (a death, a betrayal, a diagnosis, a loss), stay acutely connected to your physical state. Notice how shock moves through a body that was just experiencing something entirely different. Feel the collision: your nervous system still humming with one reality while your mind tries to process another. Pay attention to how pleasure and pain can exist simultaneously in your body, how your heightened physical awareness from moments ago makes this news land differently. Don't choose between the sensations—let them coexist, intensify, clash. Allow your acute consciousness of your body's signals to reveal how grief, rage, or devastation manifests physically. End having discovered that your body holds contradictory truths at once.

title: The Last Visit
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at 3 AM, and the machines have just been turned off at her request. She's asked you to tell her about your life, the parts she won't see. Start with a bright, false cheerfulness trying to paint her a beautiful picture of your future wedding, your children she'll never meet. But as you describe these phantom moments, your voice begins to fracture. She squeezes your hand weakly and you break—this isn't about your future anymore, it's about thanking her for raising you when your parents couldn't. Your voice drops to barely a whisper as you tell her it's okay to let go now, even though every cell in your body is screaming for her to stay. End with the words 'I love you' repeated softly, your voice raw and small, as you feel her hand go slack in yours.

title: Brave Little Joke
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe 8 or 9, bleeding from a deep cut after a fall. Your little brother is crying and you try to cheer him up by teasing him about his scared face and the silly band-aid he’s clutching. Your voice starts bright and playful, forcing a giggle, but the blood loss and shock make you shiver and your words get slower. You fade mid-sentence, voice dropping to a whisper, the teasing turning into a soft, distant mumble as your body grows heavy and cold. Let your energy drain completely, ending with a barely audible, exhausted breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Sauna's Last Breath
instruction: You are a small child, sitting on the top bench of a sweltering sauna with your father. The heat presses down like a thick, wet blanket, and sweat drips from your forehead into your eyes. You are utterly exhausted, your limbs heavy as stone, and the air feels thick in your lungs. You try to ask your father if it's almost over, but your voice comes out slow, slurred, and you lose your train of thought mid-sentence. Then, as you hear him breathing heavily beside you, a wave of exhaustion turns into a quiet, fearful confusion—why does he look so pale? Why are his eyes closed? Your final words tremble with a dawning dread.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Breaking Point Ecstasy
instruction: You've been training for years—athletic, artistic, or academic—and this is the moment of your final, most brutal challenge. Your body is at its absolute limit. Begin by simply experiencing the physical sensations without naming them: the burning in your muscles, the pounding of your heart, the taste of exhaustion. Notice how your body feels in space, how your breath sounds, how sweat or tears move on your skin. Let raw sounds come—grunts of effort, cries of pain, gasps of exertion, involuntary vocalizations of suffering and determination. These sounds evolve into wordless battle cries, primal expressions of refusal to quit, pure defiant energy. Finally, words might burst out—encouragements to yourself, fierce declarations, acknowledgments of pain and power. Start in pure physical agony mixed with determination, your body screaming at you to stop. End in a transcendent state where pain and triumph become indistinguishable, where you're laughing and crying at once, where breaking becomes breakthrough. The physical and emotional should be completely fused—you cannot separate the bodily experience from the feeling.

title: Laughing Through Anesthesia: Confessing Everything as You Go Under
instruction: Pre-surgery. Anesthesia is hitting. You're talking to your best friend and the drug is making you feel euphoric and honest and completely unfiltered. You start laughing—genuine, surprised laughter—because suddenly everything seems absurd and beautiful. But you're also terrified you might die on the table, so between giggles, you're confessing things: that you've been in love with them for years, that you're scared, that you never told your father you forgave him. Your words are slurring, looping back on themselves. You lose your train of thought and find it hilarious. Then you find it devastating. You're crying and laughing simultaneously. Your voice is thick, slow, wonder-filled, and breaking. You feel profoundly grateful and profoundly sad at once. End in a moment where you're trying to say something crucial but the words won't come, and instead of panic, you feel this strange, beautiful acceptance. Let your voice dissolve into wordless emotion—part laugh, part sob, all love.
inspired_by: Shrooms Kicking In: Losing Grip on Normal Speech

title: The Reluctant Surrender
instruction: You're receiving oral pleasure from your partner, but your mind is still lingering on a petty argument from earlier. You start by muttering your irritation under your breath—half complaint, half dismissal—with a trace of contempt in your tone. As the sensation builds, your speech fractures into fragments, your breathing grows ragged, and a soft moan escapes. A sharp intake of air, a gasp, then a melodic, sustained moan. By the end, the contempt is gone, replaced by a quiet, vulnerable release—a whispered surrender.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Bumpy Road Home
instruction: You're driving your young daughter home from your mother's funeral on a rough dirt road. Your mind is blank, just focusing on the steering as the car shudders. Speak to your daughter in the back seat, your voice jolted by each bump. Start with a hollow, detached tone, but as you talk, the numbness cracks and the grief floods in, your voice breaking with each tremor. Let the physical shaking carry the emotional shaking.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Sadness (very intensely present)

title: Thanking Someone for Breaking Your Heart
instruction: You're speaking to an ex-partner who destroyed you but also, somehow, saved you. Begin with a laugh that's real but complicated—'I didn't think I'd ever be able to say this, but... thank you.' Your voice should hold genuine gratitude mixed with pain that's still raw. As you speak, let contradictory emotions flood through: 'You broke me. You absolutely shattered me. And I'm grateful.' Explain how their betrayal forced you to rebuild yourself, to find strength you didn't know you had. But let your voice crack when you admit: 'I still miss you sometimes. Even knowing everything, I still...' Laugh again, this time with tears in it, at the absurdity of loving someone who hurt you, at the beautiful paradox of being grateful for devastation. End with bittersweet acceptance: 'I hope you're happy. I really do. And I hope I never see you again.' Let your voice hold both truth and heartbreak, peace and grief, closure and longing—all at once.

title: Describing Physical Intimacy to a Lover Over the Phone
instruction: You're in a long-distance relationship and describing, in explicit detail, what you want to do when you see your partner. Start shy and halting, then let desire overcome embarrassment. The voice should become progressively lower, breathier, and more confident. Describe sensations — temperature, texture, pressure — with genuine longing. Include pauses where you're listening to their reactions. Let the arousal be audible in your breathing pattern.

title: The Glass Wall Between Us
instruction: You're sitting by your mother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's conscious but fading. Begin speaking to her as if there's an invisible barrier between you—you can see her, but you can't quite reach her anymore. Start with desperate attempts to break through, to make her understand how much you need to say. As you speak, let the frustration of that barrier transform into acceptance, then into a strange, peaceful clarity where you realize the most important things don't need words anymore. Your voice should shift from urgent and breaking to soft, almost childlike wonder. End by describing what you see in her eyes, speaking as if you're finally on the same side of the glass.

title: The Last Word
instruction: You are an elderly man in your living room, locked in a familiar argument with your spouse about who forgot to pay a bill. Your voice starts tight, nasal, whiny—the complaint circles back again and again, your words overlapping theirs as you shift your weight in your chair. Halfway through, you spot the paid receipt tucked under a magazine. The realization hits you. Your tone changes from strained repetition to a slow, deep, satisfied pronouncement. Pause, let the victory sit in your chest, then deliver your final line with quiet triumph, voice now fuller, more grounded, free of the nagging edge.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Migraine Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your dying grandmother in her hospice room, but you're suffering from a blinding migraine that's been building for hours. Begin with overwhelming physical pain—your head is pounding, the fluorescent lights are stabbing into your eyes, every sound feels like glass breaking inside your skull. You're irritable, desperate to leave this sterile room, frustrated that you can barely focus on her words. As she reaches for your hand and tells you something you've needed to hear your whole life, the emotional flood breaks through the physical barrier. By the end, the pain is still there, but your voice softens, tears come despite the throbbing, and you're trying to memorize her face even though it hurts to keep your eyes open. Let your voice quality shift from tight and strained to broken and tender, though still affected by the physical discomfort.
inspired_by: Illnesses and Restrictions — Creating a Headache

title: Protecting Your Child While Losing Consciousness
instruction: You're trapped somewhere dangerous—a collapsed building, a sinking car, a locked room filling with smoke—with your young child. You're injured and fading, but your child is terrified and you must keep them calm while your body shuts down. Start with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance: 'We're fine, baby, we're absolutely fine.' Your voice has commanding strength even as your breathing deteriorates. Sing them a lullaby while you're gasping. Tell them a story while your words slur. Give them instructions—'count to one hundred, don't move, help is coming'—that become increasingly desperate and fragmented. Your rage at your own helplessness battles with tender protectiveness. As consciousness wavers, your voice drops to nearly nothing, but you're still trying to soothe them, still trying to be their guardian. End with a whispered 'I love you' that might be your last words, collapsing the explosive intensity of your fight into heartbreaking surrender.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting at your mother's bedside in her final hours. For your entire life, you've played it safe, never pursuing your dreams because you feared her disappointment. She's been critical, exacting, impossible to please. But now, with minutes left, you must tell her about the life you secretly want—the one you've been too afraid to live. Start with apologetic justification, defending your safe choices. As you speak, let something break open: move toward raw confession of your dreams, your fears, and finally—whether she responds or not—give yourself the permission you've been waiting for. End not seeking her approval, but claiming your own life. Let your voice shift from tight and careful to unleashed and certain.
inspired_by: Actor plays it safe, avoids taking chances, and produces predictable, unexciting work

title: The Whispered Question
instruction: You are a 19-year-old woman in the middle of making love with a partner you are deeply infatuated with. The rhythm of movement is steady. As you gasp and whisper, a thought surfaces: who were they before you? A quiet curiosity — 'What were you like at 13?' — breaks through the physical intensity. Start with small, breathless words pushed out between thrusts, then let your voice soften and slow as contemplation takes over. The voice should shift from exertion to a dreamy, tender wonder, as if you’re momentarily forgetting the body and falling into a memory of who they might have been, even as the rhythm tries to pull you back. The end should feel like a fragile, intimate confession floating on a breath, not a demand.
emotions_sampled: Interest (slightly present), Contemplation (very intensely present), Infatuation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Resonance Deepening
instruction: You're a meditation teacher beginning a session, starting with a voice that's thin, high, not deeply rooted. 'Let's breathe together.' As you guide the meditation, your voice progressively deepens — not louder, but more resonant, coming from your belly, from the earth. By the middle, you're speaking from a place of genuine calm, and listeners can feel your grounded presence. You reach a moment of silence that's so deep it seems to contain the universe. When you speak again, it's a whisper, but so resonant it fills the room: 'You are safe.' The client weeps because they felt it in their bones. After the session, returning to normal speech, your voice is still slightly deeper — changed by the descent.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake but fading, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin by truly seeing her face—really looking at details you've taken for granted your whole life. Start in quiet observation, noticing the texture of her skin, the exact color of her eyes, the way her breath moves. Let yourself feel the weight of never having truly looked before. As you study her face, begin to speak—at first just fragments, sounds of recognition and wonder. Let your observations build into whispered memories, then into a confession of love you've never fully expressed. Move from the paralysis of silent grief into urgent, full-throated gratitude, as if truly seeing her for the first time is also your way of releasing her.
inspired_by: Looking for Things About the Other Person You Have Never Noticed Before

title: Breathing in the Dark
instruction: Your oxygen systems are failing, and you have maybe an hour left. You're whispering into a recorder, not for posterity, but because it's too quiet and the silence is worse than dying. Talk about the small things—the smell of rain you'll never experience again, the feeling of grass, the sound of someone's laugh. Your voice should be intimate, almost tender, as if you're tucking these memories into bed. Let yourself be fragile here. Cry quietly if you need to, but don't make it dramatic—just soft, bewildered tears. Midway through, you realize you're describing these things to someone specific, someone you never told you loved. The confession should feel like it's being pulled from somewhere deep in your chest. End with a kind of hushed wonder, maybe even a small, sad laugh at the absurdity of only being brave enough to say it now. The vulnerability should feel like exposure, like being seen when you're at your most naked.

title: The Confrontation Letter: Words Unspoken for 30 Years
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you've written to your parent but never sent—until now. They sit across from you, silent. Begin with false confidence, almost aggressive, reciting grievances you've rehearsed. But as you read your own words describing what their absence cost you, your voice betrays you. The anger cracks. You're suddenly eight years old again, asking why you weren't enough. Try to push through—get angry again—but it breaks into a sob. Look at them. Try to say 'I needed you' but it comes out as a whisper. The letter shakes in your hands. Crumple it. The real words—the ones not written down—are the ones that finally come out, raw and unfiltered and heartbreakingly honest.
inspired_by: Heartbreak in Real-Time: Reading the Text

title: Conception Moment
instruction: You're thinking about the moment you were conceived—not scientifically, but emotionally. Your parents, young, in love, creating you. Your voice is tender, almost in awe. There's something sacred here. 'My mother was happy that night.' You're imagining the ordinary miraculous moment. Your voice catches: they had no idea they were creating a person who would worry them for decades. The tenderness becomes almost unbearable.

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've loved for decades—a partner, parent, or lifelong friend—in their final hours. You've looked at this face thousands of times, but tonight you realize you've stopped truly seeing them. Begin with the heaviness of impending loss, speaking softly about practical matters or shared memories. As you talk, let your gaze truly land on them: notice the exact curve of their smile, the way light catches in their eyes, the specific rhythm of their breathing, the texture of their skin, small gestures you've witnessed but never consciously absorbed. Let discovery interrupt your words. Your grief should transform from abstract dread into acute, tender presence—as if seeing them for both the first time and last time simultaneously. End with gratitude breaking through the sorrow, your voice catching not from sadness alone, but from the overwhelming beauty of truly witnessing them.
inspired_by: Looking for Things in the Other Person You Haven't Seen Before

title: The Lost Matchbox
instruction: You are an 8-year-old boy kneeling in the mud behind the school gym, hidden from the kickball field. You lost your father's lucky matchbox when you fell earlier, and you're desperately searching for it. Start with frantic, breathless muttering—focused on finding it before anyone sees you. As you realize it's gone for good, your voice cracks, the embarrassment of losing something precious mixing with a tiny sob you can't fully hold back. title: The Whispered Oddity
instruction: Late at night, in darkness, you whisper to your lover a confession about a secret pleasure, fantasy, or habit that makes you feel absurd or childish—something you've hidden because you fear it makes you look foolish. Start with your voice barely audible, strangled by shame, perhaps making odd throat sounds or nervous giggles you try to suppress. As you continue, allow yourself to make silly sounds, imitate voices, or whisper in ridiculous ways to describe this thing. Let the confession become playful, strange, tender. Feel the shift from mortification to intimate silliness—discovering that vulnerability isn't solemn, it's sometimes absurd and beautiful. End with soft, free laughter mixed with tears of relief.
