title: Garden Surprise
instruction: You're an elderly man in your garden, watering plants on a warm afternoon. Suddenly, a tickle in your nose builds into a massive sneeze—it catches you off guard. After the explosive release, you blink and notice a wildflower you didn't plant, a gift from a neighbor. Your voice is congested and nasal as you mutter in astonishment, then a quiet, husky gratitude slips out. Let the sneeze interrupt your words, and let your surprise shift into a grateful warmth by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Secret Over Coffee
instruction: You're at a bustling café, huddled with your best friend. You lean in, your voice dropping to a whisper as you share a piece of gossip you just heard. Start with a giddy, breathless astonishment—eyes wide, words tumbling out. But as you describe the implications for your mutual friend, your tone shifts to genuine worry. title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Gave You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times but never had the courage to voice. Start with a specific memory—something small they probably don't even remember—and your tone is almost curious, like you're asking them to explain it. But as you speak, years of accumulated hurt begin seeping through. Your voice hardens as you list the ways they failed you, each example more damning than the last. Then suddenly you break—because underneath the anger is a child who still desperately wanted their love. Your voice cracks as you admit: 'I just needed you to see me.' End with the most painful question: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let the performance move from controlled inquiry to righteous anger to raw, childlike vulnerability.

title: The Ember's Secret
instruction: You're a child by a dying campfire, the last adult has gone for water. A flickering ember pulses like a tiny heartbeat, and you're staring into it, remembering how your mother told you the fire would protect you. But the ember is fading, and the dark is closing in. Begin with a low, rhythmic, almost hypnotic retelling of your mother's words, feeling the warmth of the memory, but your voice must tremble with a creeping helplessness as the ember sputters. End in quiet contemplation, not of the fire, but of the silence it will leave behind — speak as if you're holding your breath, letting the last word dissolve into that darkness.

title: Blessing the Thief
instruction: You are speaking at the funeral of someone who stole something irreplaceable from you—a betrayal that altered the course of your life—but who also, impossibly, gave you something essential that you wouldn't have without them. Begin with your voice tight with the absurdity and injustice of having to stand here, speaking publicly, maintaining composure when part of you wants to scream the truth of what they took. Let flickers of anger and irony break through your measured eulogy. But as you continue, allow genuine grief to surface—not just for what was lost, but for the complicated, infuriating, precious fact that you're grateful to them, that you somehow forgive them, that their theft forced you to become who you are. Let your voice crack and soften as you realize you're truly saying goodbye to someone you both hate and love, someone who wounded and freed you. End in a place of bewildered grace, voice thick with contradictory truths held simultaneously.

title: Therapist Hearing Trauma
instruction: You're the therapist listening to a client describe childhood sexual abuse. You are professionally trained to listen without reaction. Your voice maintains that calm, reflective quality: 'Tell me more about that.' Your client is describing something horrific, and you're supposed to be a mirror, a container. But your own history—different but similar—is screaming inside your head. Your voice stays measured for most of the session. But when your client asks, 'Do you think I caused it?' something in you breaks. Your response becomes genuinely angry—not at them, but at the concept of that question existing. Recover the professional tone, but it now sounds thin, fragile, performative.

title: Sunset and a Sore Neck
instruction: You are an elderly person in your garden, chin tilted high to watch a blazing sunset. For a brief moment, the colors fill you with a light, almost ecstatic pleasure — you murmur a soft 'ah' or 'look at that.' But your neck is stiff and you've been waiting all evening for a grandchild to call. Let the ecstasy slip into irritation as you lower your head, rub your neck, and mutter about the phone. Keep your voice thin and tight, shifting from breathy wonder to clipped, grumpy impatience. Maybe fidget with your phone, sigh, or adjust your posture.

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love, in the darkness of early morning. They're half-asleep. You need to tell them you're sick—really sick—and the prognosis isn't good. title: Buried Astonishment
instruction: You are digging a hole in your backyard to plant a small tree, grunting with each shovelful of hard, rocky soil. title: Defending Someone You Love Against an Unforgivable Accusation
instruction: Someone has just said something devastating about a person you love—maybe called them a liar, a monster, unforgivable. You explode. Your voice starts to waver, gets quieter, more desperate: 'They wouldn't... they couldn't have...' You're trying to convince yourself now more than the other person. Let your voice break completely, dropping to something raw and pleading: 'Please tell me they didn't do this. Please.' End in a place of helpless anguish, your fierce certainty shattered, voice small and lost: 'I don't know what to believe anymore.' The arc moves from absolute conviction to devastating uncertainty.

title: The Final Parade
instruction: You are an aging drill sergeant commanding your last parade after decades of service. Begin with the sharp, emotionless rhythm of command, but let the pain of leaving seep through in a pause, then a surge of pride that cracks into a raw, hopeful whisper as you dismiss them. Allow the words to catch in your throat, the bark softening into something almost human.

title: Final Transmission from the Mars Colony
instruction: You're the last surviving member of the Mars colony, oxygen running critically low, recording a final message to Earth knowing it will take 22 minutes to arrive and no rescue is possible. End with a strange, unexpected peace—almost wonder—as you describe the Martian sunset you're watching, your final words a whisper of gratitude for having seen something so beautiful, even as your breathing becomes labored and the oxygen alarm beeps its final warning.

title: The Last Goodbye Through Glass
instruction: You are a child in a space suit, helmet sealed, standing on a stark alien landscape. Through your visor, you see a small, wounded creature you've nurtured for weeks—it's dying. At first, you're trying to stay calm, your voice tinny and compressed through the radio, but as you realize it's the last moment, your affection breaks through. Speak to it softly, letting your breathing fog the glass, your voice cracking with love as you promise it won't be alone. End with a raw, tender whisper before the connection cuts.

title: The Friendly Predator
instruction: You're at a bar, late night, leaning into someone you've just met. Your voice is low so nearby friends can't hear, and you laugh easily, quickly — it's forced, a mask for what's underneath. You propose going to your place, keeping it light and logistical at first. But as you speak, the laughter fades. Pause. Glance around the room. When you continue, your tone drops to something colder, flatter. The warmth evaporates entirely, replaced by a quiet, coiled menace. Let the words hang in the air, almost a threat. You started as charming; end as predator.

title: Complete Breakdown Unraveling
instruction: You're alone in your car in a parking garage after losing the job you hated but the salary supported everything. Begin narrating your day to yourself in hollow, functional language—"I checked email. The meeting happened. I'm in the garage now." Slowly the sentences fragment. Breathing audibly changes rhythm. Your voice moves up in register, becomes younger, less controlled. By the middle, single words repeat. The coherence dissolves into honest, animal sounds—not screaming, but the raw vocal texture of a system overwhelmed. End with silence and gasping.

title: Fever Breaking at Dawn
instruction: You are emerging from days of intense physical illness—fever, pain, delirium—and someone has been caring for you through it all. Your body is weak, drenched in sweat, trembling. Begin in the disorientation and physical discomfort, your voice rough and broken. As you become aware of their presence beside you, let physical sensation mix with overwhelming emotion. The relief of pain subsiding, the vulnerability of having been seen at your worst, the gratitude mixed with the rawness of your physical state. Your voice might crack, your body might shake, you might move between laughter and tears. Let the sensory experience of your exhausted, recovering body guide your emotional journey from suffering through recognition to something approaching wonder at still being alive and not alone.

title: Shelter in the Storm
instruction: You are a woman in your 50s, caught in a sudden sandstorm while hiking. You're huddled behind a rock, pressing a scarf over your mouth and nose. You speak to yourself, starting with doubt: you don't know if you'll find your partner, if you'll survive. Your voice is strained and muffled by the fabric, and you cough mid-sentence, spitting out grit. As you remember a quiet morning you shared with them, your tone shifts to longing—your words become slower, softer. Then, feeling the storm's raw power, you find a surprising contentment, accepting whatever comes. Let your voice reflect the physical struggle: breathy, interrupted, with sibilants affected by grit.

title: Reclaiming Your Voice After Being Silenced
instruction: You spent years not speaking up. In a meeting, at home, with friends. You were silenced by fear, trauma, or control. Now you're speaking. Your voice is shaky at first—it's unused. But with each word, it gets stronger. 'I have something to say.' Your voice is small but audible. It grows. By the end, you're claiming space with your voice. Your voice is hoarse but alive. Include the moment you realize you can't be silenced anymore.

title: Holding Your Child During the Gunfire
instruction: You're huddled in a closet, classroom, or shelter with your young child pressed against your chest, and you can hear danger approaching. Start with fierce, controlled whispers—commanding them to be quiet, promising they're safe, your voice a weapon of protection. But your child asks a question that shatters you: 'Are we going to die?' Your control explodes into passionate reassurance, your voice rising despite the danger, fueled by a parent's rage at a world that would threaten your baby. Then reality crashes in—you might not be able to protect them, and you're suddenly helpless. Let your voice transform from warrior to something fragile and desperate, switching between furious promises and tender lullabies, between protective ferocity and trembling vulnerability, ending with you whispering the most important things they need to know about how much they're loved, your voice breaking on every word.

title: The Archaeology of a Lover's Face
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying facing your partner of ten years, unable to sleep, suddenly struck by how little you actually see them anymore. Begin in whispered silence, studying their sleeping face in the dark—the curve of their cheek, the flutter of their eyelids, a small scar you'd forgotten about. Let yourself feel the strange mix of intimacy and distance, love and loneliness. When they wake and catch you staring, don't look away. Keep searching their face, letting small sounds emerge—wonder, sadness, tenderness. Begin to whisper what you're noticing, what you've failed to see. Build from fragmented observations to a tender confession: that you've been looking through them instead of at them, that you're afraid you've stopped truly seeing each other. Let your voice grow from barely audible to urgent but still soft, ending in vulnerable intimacy.
inspired_by: Looking for Things About the Other Person You Have Never Noticed Before

title: Laughing Through the Funeral Speech
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone who filled your life with joy, and you've promised yourself you'll celebrate them, not mourn. Begin with warm laughter, voice bright as you share a hilarious memory. Your laughter is genuine, infectious, full of love. But mid-story, the reality hits: they're gone. Your laughter catches, becomes tangled with a sob. You fight to keep going, voice now trembling between mirth and grief, laughing and crying simultaneously. Share another memory — your voice breaks completely, but you push through, finding genuine joy even as tears stream down your face. The emotions blur together: gratitude that they existed, devastation that they're gone. End with a final laugh that's also a sob, voice thick with both, saying 'Thank you for everything' — the words soaked in contradictory emotions, your tone somehow both celebrating and breaking, finding strange peace in the beautiful, terrible mess of loving someone you've lost.

title: Discovering Your Child's Suicide Note
instruction: You find a note in your teenager's handwriting. You read the first line aloud, voice confused, not understanding. Then recognition hits and you scream their name, voice exploding with terror and urgency as you search the house. Finding them alive but unreachable—headphones on, door locked—you pound on the door, voice ragged and fierce: 'Open this door RIGHT NOW.' When they finally open it, looking small and exhausted, your rage collapses instantly into helpless love. Your voice breaks completely: 'Baby, what...I didn't know.' You cycle through fierce protectiveness ('I won't let anything happen to you'), guilt-stricken anguish ('How did I miss this?'), and tender desperation ('Please talk to me'). End on your knees, voice raw and quiet, making promises you pray you can keep, transformed from panic to fierce, protective, broken-open love.
inspired_by: Your Partner Saying They Don't Want Children

title: Secret Revealed
instruction: A secret you've been keeping has been exposed. Your voice is shocked, defensive: 'How did you find out?' You're trying to explain, but the explanation sounds weak. Your voice becomes desperate: 'I was going to tell you...' But when? Everyone knows you were never going to volunteer this information. Your voice becomes small, ashamed. By the end, you're owning the truth in a broken voice: 'I lied. And I'm sorry.'

title: Gravel Path to Hope
instruction: You are an older woman walking alone on a noisy gravel path, the crunch of each step competing with your voice. You're extremely confused—you've lost your way to a friend's house, and every turn looks unfamiliar. As you mutter aloud, trying to recall directions, your voice rises and sharpens against the sound, with pauses as you glance around. Then you spot a distinctive blue mailbox you remember, and a tiny flicker of hope softens your tone. Let your confusion dominate at first, heavy and restless, then let a hesitant optimism seep in as you speak to yourself. Embrace the physical effort: louder articulation, breathy frustration, and the way your words get cut off by a sudden crunch or a shift in balance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Last Ride Home
instruction: You're a teenager in the backseat of a car, driving home from a friend's house for the last time before they move away. The engine rumbles beneath you, tires humming on the road. You watch streetlights blur past the window, your cheek pressed against the cold glass. Your voice starts quiet, distant, full of lost thought — a goodbye you're still figuring out. Then a vibration in your chest catches, a realization that this is really happening, and your voice cracks with a sudden, raw ache you didn't see coming, dropping into something heavier and more fragile.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Holding Your Best Friend as They Die
instruction: You're holding your best friend in the final moments. The emergency is over; help isn't coming in time; you both know it. Start with whispered reassurances, trying to keep them calm, trying to keep yourself together: 'Hey, hey... look at me. Stay with me.' Your voice is so tender, so gentle, but terror is underneath everything. Tell them things you've never said—how much they meant, specific memories only you two share. 'Remember that night we... God, that was the best night of my life.' Your voice catches, tears threatening but you're fighting them because you need to be strong. But as they fade, you can't maintain it anymore. Beg them quietly not to go: 'Please don't leave me. Please. I don't know how to... I can't do this without you.' End with the moment you realize they're gone—a whispered 'no' that contains all your grief, then saying their name one last time, so softly, like you're tucking them in. Let your voice be broken, raw, completely shattered but also infinitely loving.
inspired_by: Firefighter: After Successful Rescue Returns to Station

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's been unconscious for two days, and the doctors say these are her final hours. Begin by simply watching her breathe, feeling numb and exhausted from the long vigil. As the first rays of sunlight come through the window and touch her face, something breaks open inside you—suddenly you need to tell her everything you never said. Let yourself move from that hollow, shut-down place into a flood of specific memories: her hands teaching you to braid bread dough, the smell of her garden, the song she hummed. Speak to her as if she can hear every word, your voice starting as a whisper and building as you realize this is your last chance. End by singing or humming the song she used to sing to you, your voice breaking as you feel both the unbearable loss and the overwhelming gratitude for having had her at all.

title: The Last Dance Before Dawn
instruction: You are holding your dying partner's hand in the hospital room at 4 AM. They can barely speak, but suddenly they squeeze your hand and whisper 'Dance with me.' Begin seated, exhausted, numb from days of vigil. As you stand and begin to sway with them in your arms (or imagine holding them), let your body unlock - move with complete physical abandon despite your grief, as if this final dance could stop time. Your feet might shuffle, spin, dip - your body knows this dance from decades of love. Start with heavy, immobile despair in your voice and body. End with your breath ragged from movement, your words soaring with the bittersweet ecstasy of this last perfect moment, even as tears stream down your face. Let your body's motion unlock your heart's final expression of devotion.

title: Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping spouse in hospice, holding their hand in the quiet hours before dawn. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile: 'I know you're tired, my love. I can see how hard you're fighting.' Your words catch in your throat as you trace their fingers with yours. 'Remember our first apartment? How we danced in the kitchen to no music?' A soft, broken laugh escapes. 'You made even the ordinary feel sacred.' Your voice becomes smaller, more vulnerable: 'I'm so scared. Not of being alone—I'm scared of a world without your laugh in it.' You lean closer, voice tender as a prayer: 'But if you need to let go, I'll be okay. That's a lie, but I'll survive it.' Your final words are a whispered release: 'You can rest now. You've loved me enough for ten lifetimes. I'll carry it with me.' The silence that follows holds everything you cannot say.

title: The Weight of Skin on Skin
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in the dark with someone whose breathing you've memorized. You're tracing the landscape of their shoulder blade with one fingertip, feeling the warmth of their skin, the slight dampness, the way they smell like sleep and themselves. Start by letting yourself feel the profound safety of this darkness, this nearness, this particular body next to yours. In a whisper barely louder than breath, confess something you've never told anyone—a fear so fundamental it lives in your bones, a shame you carry, a truth about who you really are. Feel how the darkness makes it both easier and more terrifying. Notice the texture of the silence as they listen, the slight change in their breathing, the way their hand finds yours. Let the vulnerability crack you open until you're trembling, not from cold but from being truly seen. The arc moves from cocooned safety to exposure to a deeper, more frightening intimacy where you cannot hide.

title: The Burning House
instruction: You're in the aftermath of explosive passion—maybe making love, maybe a physical fight, maybe both. Your body is still shaking. Start by trying to catch your breath and speak through purely physical sensation—gasping, trembling, your voice broken by your body's state. But let emotional meaning start flooding in. If the words coming out aren't matching the storm inside you, change them. Reach for something else. The physical and emotional should start feeding each other, building. Maybe rage turns to weeping. Maybe weeping turns to laughter. Maybe tenderness becomes fierce again. Keep pursuing whatever is actually moving through your body, not what you think should be there. By the end, you should be in a completely different physical and emotional state—perhaps utterly still after violence, or convulsing with feeling after numbness. Let your body lead you to truths your mind doesn't know.
inspired_by: Actor has chosen a choice for a scene but it is not producing the desired emotional results

title: Shattered Glass: A Mother Protecting Her Child from Themselves
instruction: Your adult child has just told you they're making a choice that will destroy them—returning to an abuser, refusing life-saving treatment, walking away from everything they've built. You start with desperate reasoning, your voice tight with control: 'You can't do this.' But they're not listening, and your control begins to crack. Your voice rises with volcanic rage: 'I will NOT stand here and watch you kill yourself!' Let yourself explode—unleash all the fury of helpless love. But mid-fury, you see their face—they're already gone, already decided—and your rage collapses into sobbing desperation. Your voice breaks completely: 'Please. Please, I'm begging you.' You're on your knees, metaphorically or literally. In your final words, you must somehow find strength in your helplessness: 'Then I'll be here. When you're ready to come back, I'll be here.' Let the fierceness and the powerlessness war in your voice until they become the same thing.
inspired_by: Parent Showing Quiet Pride: Misreading, Then Understanding

title: The Shrinking Room
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed, but something strange is happening: the room feels like it's growing larger around you, or you're becoming smaller. Begin speaking to her about a childhood memory she shared with you—something that made you feel safe and big and capable. As you speak, allow yourself to physically feel smaller, younger, more helpless. Your voice might change. Your posture might shift. By the end, you're no longer the adult grandchild—you're the frightened six-year-old who needs her, and she's slipping away. Let your final words be a plea she can no longer answer. The emotion must travel from nostalgic warmth to devastating, childlike abandonment.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Dream Journal Entries Exercise

title: What We Became in the Dark
instruction: You and your closest friend are sitting in a parked car at night, engine off. You've just learned they're moving across the country tomorrow, and they've been planning it for months without telling you. Speak quietly - the kind of quiet that comes when you're afraid louder would shatter you both. Begin with careful control, trying to understand, asking gentle questions. But as you realize this goodbye was a decision they made alone, let the betrayal seep in. Your voice might shake, might disappear into whispers, might catch on words. This isn't about accusation - it's about the grief of discovering distance was already there. End by saying something you both know will be the last honest thing between you.
inspired_by: Actor is experiencing result-consciousness or awareness of being on stage—the acting consciousness is too close to the surface

title: Gasp and Guffaw
instruction: You're an older man swimming laps alone, but halfway through the pool, you're suddenly gripped by the memory of a mortifying mistake you made this morning—calling your boss by the wrong name in a meeting. As you turn your head to breathe, you sputter out the funny parts (interest, amusement), but between strokes, the shame hits you hard, turning your gasps into quieter, wetter confessions. Your voice is chopped into 1-2 syllable bursts, water sloshing in your mouth, and by the final lap, the amusement fades into a heavy, embarrassed silence broken only by your labored breathing.
emotions_sampled: Interest (very intensely present), Amusement (very intensely present), Shame (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Reading Your Divorce Papers on Your Anniversary
instruction: You're reading your final divorce papers aloud on what would have been your twentieth anniversary, and you're laughing—not from humor, but from the absurd, devastating poetry of it. Start with a genuine chuckle at the legal language: 'Listen to this: 'irreconcilable differences.' That's what we are now. Irreconcilable.' Your laughter is real but tears are coming too. You read the division of assets with increasing hilarity and heartbreak: 'You get the dog. I get... Wednesdays with the kids.' The laughter turns to crying turns back to laughing: 'We promised forever and we got—' you check the papers '—seven thousand, three hundred days.' Then something shifts. Your voice becomes tender, grateful even, through tears: 'But God, we were so beautiful when we tried.' End in bittersweet peace, smiling through tears: 'Thank you. For trying. For all of it.' The contradictions never resolve—the grief and gratitude exist together, completely.

title: Barefoot in Your Kitchen at 3 AM
instruction: You're standing in near-darkness with your lover of ten years who's leaving tomorrow. Whisper a confession you've never spoken. As you prepare to speak, let silent images flicker through you—their fingers tracing your spine that first night, the fight in the rain, breakfast light on their sleeping face, the moment you almost left, the day you knew you'd never love anyone else this way. These images remain unspoken, private, feeding the tenderness and fragility in your voice. Begin tentatively, protected, unable to meet their eyes. Let the accumulating weight of these internal pictures slowly dissolve your defenses until you're completely naked and unguarded, speaking barely above a breath, saying what terrifies you most to say.

title: The Sunday Call
instruction: You are an elderly woman on the phone with your daughter. You’ve just had a fall but don’t want to worry her. You start by putting on a bright, singsong voice—pleasure at hearing her voice—but as you talk, the cognitive strain of lying makes you over-explain every detail. Your pitch climbs nervously, your words stumble. Begin gleeful, almost theatrical, but by the end, your voice drops, tired and fragile, as you almost slip the truth. Speak naturally, with little pauses, breaths, and the creak of your chair.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Race Through the Orchard
instruction: You are an elderly person, sprinting barefoot through a moonlit apple orchard, laughing and gasping as you flee from a playful, unseen companion. You are 80 years old, and this is a reckless, ecstatic chase of pure joy—you haven't felt this alive in decades. The voice comes in jagged, single-word bursts between violent, ragged breaths, with a teasing lilt that briefly shows pleasure before collapsing into coughing or laughter. At the start, you shout back with wicked glee, daring them to catch you. By the end, the ecstasy fades into a trembling, breathless pause—you stop, winded, realizing this chase is your last, and a quiet, aching sadness seeps through the final, whispered words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Fury That Breaks Into Desperation
instruction: You're confronting someone about a betrayal that shattered you. Start with explosive rage, voice raised and sharp, words coming fast: 'How could you? How dare you!' Your breathing is rapid, body tense with fury. But mid-tirade, the anger suddenly cracks open and underneath is devastating hurt and fear. Your voice breaks completely, dropping to helpless pleading: 'I trusted you. I gave you everything.' Tears interrupt your words. End with a fierce, protective declaration mixed with utter vulnerability, voice raw and shaking: 'I won't let you destroy me, but god, you almost did.' Let the transition be sudden, shocking - the moment when rage can no longer hide the broken heart beneath.

title: Echoes After the Game
instruction: You're the only one left in a vast, empty gymnasium, sitting on the polished floor with your back against the wall. Your girlfriend just scored the winning buzzer-beater, and you're waiting for her to come out of the locker room. The silence is broken by the faint sounds of dripping water and the ghostly creak of the building settling. You're replaying the moment in your head—the way she moved, the raw intensity in her eyes, the way her muscles strained as she shot. Start by murmuring to yourself, a quiet, grateful smile in your voice, acknowledging her skill and the electric chemistry between you. Let your voice become huskier, slower, as your thoughts drift to her body, to the feel of her skin, the memory of her lips, the tension coiling in your stomach. Pause when a sneaker squeaks elsewhere, then continue, your tone now dreamy and thick with lust, confessing to the empty room how much you need her. End with a soft, contemplative laugh, realizing how deeply you've fallen.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Sexual Lust (extremely present), Contemplation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Bedside Confession: Telling Your Unconscious Spouse Everything
instruction: Your spouse is in a coma. The doctors say they might be able to hear you. You start whispering the small, tender things—how you noticed they always gave you the better half of the dessert, how their laugh still makes your chest ache. Your voice is soft, intimate, catching on tears you're trying to hold back. Then you confess the harder truths: the affair you almost had, the moments you resented them, the times you wanted to leave. Your whisper becomes ragged, breaks into quiet crying, words barely intelligible through the emotion. End with a confession of devastating love—the kind that terrifies you because you might lose them before they wake up. It's all whispered, all intimate, voice thick with unshed and shed tears, moving from tender nostalgia to painful honesty to raw, throat-caught devotion.
inspired_by: Cocaine High: Words Tumbling Out Uncontrollably

title: What I Never Said While You Were Dying
instruction: You're alone in the empty hospital room hours after they've gone, whispering all the things you couldn't say while they were alive. Start so quietly it's almost inaudible—these words feel dangerous, sacred, too late. Your voice is tender, fragile, catching on memories. You're not crying yet, but you're on that knife's edge. Share something you were always too afraid to confess: maybe that you were terrified of them dying, or that you'd already started grieving years ago, or that you wished things had been different but also wouldn't change anything. Let the emotion build not through volume but through the trembling honesty in your voice. End with a moment where you almost laugh through the tears at some small, perfect memory, and then the laughter dissolves into a sob you can't hold back anymore. Make it feel like eavesdropping on the most private moment of someone's life.
inspired_by: Realizing You Became What You Hated

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're a terminally ill parent standing over your young child's bed in the middle of the night, knowing you won't live to see them grow up. Whisper as if you might wake them, telling them all the things you need them to know—how to be brave, how much you love them, apologies for the moments you'll miss. Your voice should be achingly tender but threaded with quiet devastation. Let emotions catch in your throat as you describe the future you won't be part of—their wedding, their first heartbreak, ordinary Tuesday mornings. End with a moment of almost unbearable intimacy, perhaps touching their hair, trying to pour a lifetime of love into this single, stolen moment.

title: The Last Goodbye Before the Mission
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving on a one-way mission to space, a journey they'll never return from. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be supportive, your voice almost too cheerful as you say 'This is what you've always wanted.' But the facade cracks. Your voice trembles as you try to memorize their face, whispering details you're terrified of forgetting. The emotion shifts between pride and devastating loss. End with a quiet, broken acceptance as you release them, your final words barely audible, a tender blessing mixed with the sound of your heart shattering. Let the pauses breathe—sometimes what you can't say matters most.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're watching your child sleep. You're leaving—for treatment, for war, for a necessary separation—and they don't know yet. Begin in the softest whisper, barely audible: 'You're so beautiful when you dream. I wonder what you're dreaming about.' Your voice catches with the weight of what's coming. 'Tomorrow I have to tell you I'm leaving. I have to watch your face break.' Let the quiet devastation seep through: 'I memorized the way you smell, the weight of your head on my shoulder, your laugh—God, your laugh.' Your breathing becomes uneven as you try not to sob. 'I'm not ready to be without you. I'm so scared you'll forget me, forget this, forget how much...' Trail off, unable to finish. Touch their hair with infinite gentleness: 'I love you more than my own life. Please remember that. Please.' End with silence and the sound of trying not to break apart completely. The emotion evolves from tender observation to anticipatory grief to desperate, whispered devotion.

title: The Weight of Memory
instruction: You are an older woman, still clinging to a hyper-feminine voice, lying flat on your back after a failed attempt at a seductive dance for a younger lover. Your chest heaves, every word a struggle against ragged breaths. Start by reliving the peak of your lust — a breathless, raw confession of desire, your voice cracking with want. But as you speak, the sourness of your aging body and his distracted eyes seeps in; your tone sours to a bitter whisper, realizing the fantasy is hollow. Let the physical collapse dictate the rhythm — pauses for air, losing a thought, then forcing it out with venom.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Couch Confessional
instruction: You're slouched deep into a worn-out couch after a long, lazy afternoon. The TV is on low, a forgotten show. You're mid-thought, musing aloud to no one about a ridiculous memory—how you once tried to assemble furniture without instructions and ended up with a mysteriously slanted bookshelf. Start with a lazy, amused drawl, barely moving your jaw, letting the memory tickle you. As you finish, though, the amusement fades into a quiet, bittersweet realization that you miss that simpler, messier time in your life. Your voice should soften, losing its lazy energy, becoming almost a sigh as you trail off.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Smell of Their Shirt
instruction: You're alone in your ex-lover's apartment, packing the last of your things. You find their shirt—the one they wore on your first date—and without thinking, you bring it to your face. The scent stops you completely. Whisper to the empty room, talking to them as if they could hear. But don't plan what you'll say. Let the scent guide you. Maybe you start with anger at how they hurt you, but the smell pulls up different memories. Follow each sensation and memory as it arrives, not knowing where you'll go next. Move from whatever you feel first—bitterness, longing, relief—to somewhere softer and more broken, or perhaps somewhere fierce and free. End in a whispered truth you've never said aloud, one you only discover by speaking it.
inspired_by: Actor keeps anticipating and guiding his own choice exploration (self-facilitation bias)

title: The Unraveling Aftermath
instruction: You are an elderly woman, lying in bed beside your partner after an intense, unexpected wave of successive orgasms. Your body is still shuddering, breathing in ragged, overwhelmed gasps. You feel a profound relief, as if a deep knot has finally come loose, mixed with a quiet contentment. But there's also a bewildering confusion — you can't quite understand how this happened, and your voice keeps breaking and cracking as you try to speak, each word a struggle against the aftershocks. Start with a shaky, broken whisper, trying to piece together a simple question about what just occurred, but let the sensation steal your words, leaving you to trail off into a breathless, hoarse laugh of disbelief.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Contentment (clearly present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Locked Room
instruction: You're confronting your parent in their kitchen, finally speaking a truth you've held for twenty years. Start with your whole body clenched, voice tight and controlled, almost shaking with the effort of holding back decades of pain. As you speak, your parent remains silent, and something shifts. You begin to remember specific moments—their hand on your forehead when you were sick, the smell of their cologne, the sound of their laugh before everything broke. Feel these sensory memories flood your body even as you're speaking your anger. Your voice cracks, softens, then breaks completely. By the end, you're no longer accusing—you're grieving what was lost between you, your body slack with exhausted sorrow, reaching across the table with an open hand.

title: Whispered Archaeology
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying next to your sleeping partner of ten years, and you need to confess something you've carried alone. Wake them gently. Begin almost inaudibly—your voice barely exists because the secret feels too big, too shameful to speak aloud. The words come in fragments, whispered so quietly they're almost just breath. As you continue, let the relief of finally releasing this truth make you simultaneously lighter and more vulnerable. Your whispers might become soft crying, then tender laughter at the absurdity of your own fear, then back to tears. Stay intimate, quiet, fragile throughout—no big gestures, just the raw exposure of being truly seen. End with a whispered question, barely audible, asking if they can still love you now that they know.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent the truth they never wanted to hear—how their choices shaped your pain, how their absence carved holes in you that never healed. Begin with careful, measured words, almost clinical in your control, as if you've rehearsed this a thousand times in your head. As you speak, feel the old anger start to rise, your voice gaining strength and sharpness, years of suppressed rage pushing through. But then something shifts—you see them aging before you, fragile, and your voice cracks with the realization that this confrontation won't heal you the way you hoped. End with your words dissolving into something rawer, more vulnerable, a child's voice breaking through the adult's fury, asking the question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let rage transform into naked, devastating need.

title: Standing Tall Strong
instruction: You've decided: you will not bend. Your voice is rooted, powerful: 'I'm not backing down.' Breathing is full, body is open. Physical: shoulders back, feet grounded. Vocal tone is not loud necessarily, but immovable. 'This is what I believe. This is who I am.' No question mark, no hedging. 'You can disagree, but I'm standing here.' By the end, your voice is the vocalization of a will made manifest: 'I am strong enough to hold this.'

title: The Garden Breathes
instruction: You are an older woman sitting alone in a garden after taking psilocybin tea. At first, you fidget with a leaf, muttering about your grocery list. Then a petal catches the light and your whole body freezes. Your voice slows, rises, cracks. You try to describe the flower but keep losing words to the colors moving inside your chest. End in a hushed, trembling awe, barely able to speak.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Shaking Release
instruction: You've just run from a dangerous situation and reached safety—a locked door, a friend's embrace, the inside of your car. Begin with your entire body seized up, breath locked in your chest, muscles braced as if still running or fighting. You're flooding with adrenaline—hands shaking violently, jaw chattering, body trembling uncontrollably. Don't fight these physical sensations; let them intensify and then gradually transform. As you realize you're truly safe, allow the shaking to evolve from panic into something else—release, then exhaustion, then perhaps unexpected laughter or sobbing. Your body should move through the full cycle: rigid terror, trembling chaos, then eventual collapse into heavy, bone-deep exhaustion. End in a completely different physical state—perhaps slumped, perhaps curled up, utterly spent.

title: Tremor at the Wall
instruction: You are in a hot, quiet yoga studio, holding a pose that has your quadriceps screaming and arms trembling. Everyone can see you. You grabbed the wrong mat earlier, and your face is burning with embarrassment — you can feel the blush creep down your neck. You try to whisper to the instructor, but your voice stutters from the shaking muscles and the tight, controlled ujjayi breath that barely moves. Start with a flustered, apologetic tone, almost laughing at your own mistake, but as you hold, the heat of the room and the burn force you into a raw, vulnerable confession — something about why you're even here. By the end, the shame softens into a weary, honest admission, spoken through huffs and half-breaths, your voice dipping and trembling like the rest of you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Lies
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging mother, holding the same music box she used to wind up while telling you stories about your father—the hero, the genius, the man who loved you. Today you've finally learned the truth: he left before you were born and never looked back. Your voice starts controlled, factual, asking her to explain. But as she deflects with the same gentle fictions, something breaks. You don't yell—you crack open. Your voice becomes a grown child's bewildered grief: why did she think lies were better than truth? The anger gives way to something more devastating—you realize she was protecting herself, not you. Your voice softens into forgiveness you're not sure you mean, mixed with a sadness that feels like losing him all over again.

title: The Victory Taste
instruction: You've just won something you've fought brutally for—a case, a competition, a devastating argument—and your body is still flooded with adrenaline and rage. Begin physically: let your hands shake, your breathing be ragged, taste the copper and fire in your mouth. As you speak (perhaps to your defeated opponent, perhaps to yourself), start from a place of pure aggressive triumph, almost savage. But as the adrenaline fades and your breathing steadies, let something unexpected happen: the victory turns hollow in your mouth. Your voice must travel from fierce and gloating to something emptier, more haunted. The power you thought you'd feel from winning dissolves into something more complicated—shame, loneliness, or the terrible knowledge that this victory cost you something precious. End in a place of physical and emotional exhaustion, the triumph curdling into regret.

title: Summit Taunt
instruction: You've just reached the peak of a brutal climb, lungs burning from the thin air, wind tearing at your jacket. For a moment you're overwhelmed by pure triumph—you made it, you're on top of the world. Then you spot your friend struggling up the last switchback, and a playful, teasing energy takes over. You cup your hands to shout down, but the wind snatches your breath; you pause, cough, then yell with a smirk, your voice cracking slightly from exhaustion and joy. End with a laugh that echoes off the cliffs.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Soundproof Room
instruction: You're a musician who's going deaf, lying in bed with your partner in the dark, whispering because loud voices now cause you pain. Speak with excruciating tenderness as you describe all the sounds you're cataloguing before they're gone—their breathing, the click of their throat when they swallow, the rustle of sheets. Your voice is barely there, intimate, catching on tears. 'I'm memorizing this. The sound of us.' Then the fear seeps in. Your whisper becomes urgent, desperate but still quiet. You confess you're terrified they'll leave because you won't hear them say 'I love you' anymore. The vulnerability is absolute. End with your voice breaking on a whispered question: 'Will you still want me when I live in silence?' Let the question hang there, fragile as glass.

title: Empty House Light
instruction: You are alone on a vast stage after the performance, the house lights dim and your footsteps echo. A deep numbness sits in your chest, but beneath it churns a raw distress from a recent loss. Then you spot a single figure in the front row—a friend who came despite everything. You speak to them across the empty seats, starting hollow and distant, letting the distress crack your voice, then letting fierce affection break through, raw and trembling. Your words fill the space, but your breath catches, you pause, you shift your weight, your love fighting to be heard.

speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Room We Shared
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in the childhood bedroom where you spent countless summer nights together. Begin by quietly observing the room—the wallpaper, the window, the cedar chest at the foot of the bed. Let memories surface without forcing them: her hands braiding your hair, the smell of lavender sachets, secrets whispered after midnight. As you hold her hand, allow whatever needs to be said to emerge—gratitude, regret, love, unfinished business. The emotion should evolve from gentle nostalgia to something rawer and more urgent as you realize these are your final moments together. Speak from your body's memory of this space, not just your thoughts. By the end, you must arrive at a place of devastating acceptance mixed with fierce gratitude for having had her at all.

title: The Last Light in the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the final hour. She's slipping away, but there's something you never said—something about how she saved you during the darkest year of your life, something you were always too proud or afraid to acknowledge. Begin in quiet observation, watching her breathe, feeling the weight of unspoken gratitude. Then let yourself break open and tell her exactly what she meant, what specific moment she rescued you from yourself, how her kitchen table or her laugh or her stubborn refusal to let you disappear kept you alive. Start with careful composure, move through the cracking of your voice, and end in raw, complete vulnerability as you realize this is your last chance to let her know she mattered. Let the words tumble out unperfected, urgent, as though each second counts.

title: What We Whisper in the Dark
instruction: You are lying next to someone in the intimate darkness of late night, and you're going to tell them something you've never said aloud to anyone—a secret shame, a hidden desire, a truth about yourself that terrifies you. Begin barely able to form the words, voice catching, almost backing out. Let the darkness, their breathing beside you, their presence, give you courage—or make it harder. As you speak, let their smallest reactions (a shift in breathing, a touch, silence, a whispered response) completely alter your emotional state moment to moment. Don't perform vulnerability—find what it actually costs you to reveal this. Maybe their acceptance will make you weep, maybe their reaction will make you defensive, maybe speaking it aloud will change how you feel about it. End in a completely different emotional place than you began, transformed by having been truly witnessed.

title: Darkened Bedroom: Whispering the Affair to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: Your partner sleeps beside you. You need to confess but can't face them awake, so you whisper it in the dark, practicing for tomorrow. Start with almost clinical detachment - 'I need to tell you something' - keeping your voice steady and low. But as you speak the actual words ('I was with someone else'), your throat tightens. You're trying so hard to stay quiet, controlled, that your whisper becomes strained, breaks on consonants. You pause. Try again. Each detail makes it more real, and your careful composure splinters into quiet devastation. End with silence that transforms into tender grief - not for yourself, but for what you've destroyed. Let your voice move from measured confession to choked tenderness to empty, hollow quiet.
inspired_by: Drunk Driving Pulled Over: Trying Not to Sound Drunk

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your person is dying, lucid for maybe the last time, and they've just asked you to describe the future they won't see—your wedding, your children, your life. That manic energy becomes something luminous and shattered. Paint these futures with rapid, joyful detail, laughing at the absurd specifics you're inventing, but your voice keeps breaking. 'And the cake will be ridiculous, completely ridiculous, you would have hated—' You're giving them this gift of imagined tomorrows while simultaneously grieving that they're imaginary. Your breathing should be uneven, caught between laughter and sobbing. The performance should feel like you're holding two impossible truths: devastating loss and fierce, grateful joy for having loved them at all. End with words that are simultaneously a celebration and a goodbye, where you're smiling and destroyed at once.

title: ER Doctor Recognizes Critical Patient as Old Flame
instruction: Trauma bay. You're running diagnostics, voice clipped and authoritative. Then you truly see the patient's face. Everything continues—your hands keep moving, your voice stays professional—but you're fracturing. For two beats, you're not a doctor, you're someone who hasn't seen this person in twelve years. Then the clinical mask slams back down. Continue barking orders with doubled intensity, as if professionalism can be armor. Your breathing is controlled but not your vocal inflection.

title: Small Explosion at Work: Checking Colleagues for Injuries
instruction: There's a small explosion—chemical reaction, equipment failure—and for a moment there's silence. Your voice comes out almost robotic: 'Is anyone hurt?' You're in shock. Then you're moving, checking pulse on someone you work with every day, your voice becoming urgent and technical. 'I've got a pulse here. Breathing. Need medical.' You're trying to help while your mind is fractured between the horror of what just happened and the practical necessity of the moment. Include the moment where you find someone who isn't moving, and your voice breaks. You're giving them CPR and narrating it almost like a prayer: 'Come on. Come on. Breathe.' Your voice is determined and devastated. You didn't know three minutes ago that someone might die today. Your voice carries that shock.

title: The Last Lullaby: Singing Your Child Into Death
instruction: You're sitting at your dying child's bedside, singing the lullaby you've sung every night of their life. Your voice starts tender, automatic, comforting—the same melody you've always used to ease them into sleep. But midway through, you realize this isn't sleep you're singing them toward. Your voice catches, hesitates. The melody continues but it's cracking now, warping with the weight of what you're doing. You're guiding them toward the end with your voice, and they're listening, trusting you even now. Your singing becomes both an act of devastating love and unbearable loss. You want to stop, to pull them back with silence, but the lullaby is the last gift you can give. Your voice transforms from comfort to farewell, from mother/father to witness, holding the contradiction of helping them go while your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Bard Sings a Prophecy That Becomes True as They Sing It

title: The Final Lever
instruction: You are a woman, an older adult, strapped to a metal chair in a cold basement. For hours, an interrogator has been tightening a vise on your leg. You've screamed, you've sobbed, you've gone silent with shock. Your throat is raw, your voice a croak. Now, you hear the interrogator's phone buzz and they step out, leaving the room. The vise is still squeezing, but the pain is just steady enough that you can think. You are alone. Begin by whispering to yourself, testing your voice, saying a phrase that means hope to you. Let your voice crack, break, and be barely audible. Halfway through, you realize that silence might be your only weapon, and you begin to find a terrifying, exhausted relief in that. Your voice must go from a broken, hoarse whisper of memory to a thin, quiet, almost peaceful acknowledgment of surrender.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three A.M. Breathing
instruction: You are lying in bed next to someone you love, unable to sleep, and you need to whisper something you've never said aloud. You might instinctively want to cry, or maybe you typically shut down and go numb, or perhaps you become artificially tender in vulnerable moments. Begin by noticing that familiar pull toward your usual emotional habit, but don't indulge it. Instead, pay attention to the actual sensations: your breathing, the darkness, the warmth of their body near yours, the specific quality of fear or longing or grief in your throat right now. Let your whispered words follow the real textures of this moment rather than your practiced way of being vulnerable. The emotion should evolve from your reflexive pattern to something more nuanced and immediate—perhaps discovering that what you thought you felt isn't quite what's actually alive in you.
inspired_by: Actor is prone to emotional dependencies — compulsive laughing, crying, raging — or other repeated emotional shticks

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're whispering to your partner while they sleep, saying things you can't say when they're awake. Start with tender, almost happy vulnerability—soft laughter, gentle words: 'You're beautiful when you sleep. Did you know that?' But underneath, there's something catching in your throat. Gradually, the truth seeps in. Your voice becomes quieter, more fragile, as you confess the thing you've been hiding: 'I'm scared I'm not enough for you. That one day you'll wake up and really see me—all the broken parts—and you'll leave.' The whisper becomes even softer, barely audible, as tears come: 'I love you so much it terrifies me. What if loving me becomes too hard?' End in the silence between words, where the catch in your breath says everything. This isn't dramatic—it's the kind of raw honesty that only comes in the dark.

title: The Last Lesson Before Goodbye
instruction: You're teaching your child something simple—how to tie a knot, how to start a fire, how to read a map—but this is the last time you'll ever see them. They're leaving tomorrow for a war, a dangerous journey, or to a place you cannot follow. You must stay calm and instructive, hiding your terror and grief behind practical guidance. Start with forced cheerfulness and steady instruction, but as you near the end, your voice should crack with the weight of unsaid things. Let your careful composure fracture just enough to reveal the devastation underneath, while still trying to finish the lesson. End with a moment where you can barely speak, where love and loss make it almost impossible to say the final words of advice.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Confident While Learning a New Skill

title: The Unfinished Command
instruction: You're alone with your partner in a dimly lit bedroom, but there's a nagging doubt you can't shake from an argument earlier. You start to deliver a firm, teasing instruction—a command about how they should touch you—speaking low and deliberately, savoring the words. As you speak, the doubt flickers: you hesitate mid-sentence, lose your train of thought, then swallow and push through with a growl, trying to reclaim the authority. Your voice wavers between a breathy whisper and a sharp, projected command, ending with a firmer, almost desperate repetition to convince both of you.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Dance Memory
instruction: You're cleaning out your late spouse's belongings when their favorite song suddenly plays—maybe from a neighbor's apartment, maybe from shuffle on your phone. Against your will, you begin to move to it, and you start laughing because you remember how terribly they danced, how they'd spin you around the kitchen. Your laughter is genuine, warm, full of love. As you continue, you speak aloud to them: 'You always said you had rhythm, you absolute liar.' You're smiling, almost giddy with the memory. But as the song continues, the laughter begins to crack. Your voice catches mid-chuckle: 'God, I miss your terrible dancing.' The laughter and tears start happening simultaneously—you can't tell if you're laughing or sobbing. 'We were supposed to grow old and embarrass our grandchildren together.' Your voice breaks into pieces, but you keep moving to the music, this grotesque, beautiful mix of joy and devastation. By the bridge of the song, you're weeping openly but also still half-laughing at the absurdity: 'I'm dancing alone in our bedroom at 2 PM on a Thursday, talking to you like you're still here.' As the song ends, you find a strange peace, whispering with a voice that sounds like gratitude wrapped in grief: 'Thank you for every dance. Even the ones where you stepped on my feet.' End with silence, your breathing evening out into acceptance.

title: Confronting the Mirror
instruction: You're standing face-to-face with your mother after discovering she knew about the abuse and did nothing. Begin with trembling restraint: 'I need you to look at me, Mom. Really look.' Your voice is tight, controlled, but fury builds beneath. 'I was eight years old. Eight. And you knew.' Let the accusation hang. Your voice breaks into rawness: 'I needed you to be my mother. I needed you to choose me.' The anger cracks into desperate vulnerability: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' Pause. Let devastation wash over you. End with quiet, terrible clarity: 'I'm choosing myself now. The little girl inside me deserves that. Even if you never could.' Your voice is both shattered and steely.

title: Dirty Talk That Starts Confident, Gets Ridiculous
instruction: Begin delivering intense, commanding dirty talk with full conviction — low voice, deliberate pacing, dominant energy. But you run out of material and start improvising increasingly absurd metaphors and descriptions. Your partner starts laughing, and you try to maintain the dominant energy but the laughter is contagious. Show the moment where intense sexuality dissolves into helpless, intimate laughter — and how that's actually more connecting than the performance was.

title: Confronting Your Mother: The Breaking Point
instruction: You haven't slept, you're at the edge of collapse, and you've finally come to tell your mother what you've needed to say for years. Start with your voice stretched thin with exhaustion, trying to stay calm: 'I just need you to hear me. Just once.' But the exhaustion makes your filters fail—anger starts bleeding through: 'You were never there. And I kept making excuses for you because I was too tired to face it.' Your voice cracks between rage and desperate longing for acknowledgment. Physical: your body is shaking, whether from fatigue or emotion you can't tell anymore. Build to a raw accusation: 'I needed a mother, and you needed me to pretend everything was fine.' End not with resolution but with a quiet, devastating truth delivered through tears: 'I'm too tired to pretend anymore. I just can't.'

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they're holding on - waiting for you to tell them it's okay to let go. Begin with your voice tight, controlled, trying to be strong, filling the silence with small talk about tomorrow's weather, next week's plans, anything but the truth. But they squeeze your hand weakly, and you feel the weight of what they're asking. Your voice starts to crack as you realize you have to give them permission to leave you. Move from false brightness to trembling confession: tell them everything you'll miss, everything you're grateful for, and finally - though it destroys you - tell them they can go. Let your voice break completely as you say "it's okay" even though nothing is okay. End in a whisper, tender and shattered, giving them the gift of release while your own heart is being torn apart.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Plane Disappears
instruction: You're on a plane that's experiencing catastrophic failure, and you have one minute to leave a voicemail for the person you love most. Start with panic—your voice shaking, rushing through practical things like bank accounts and passwords. But as you realize there's no hope, your urgency dissolves into something unbearably tender. You begin telling them the small things you never said: how their laugh sounds like safety, how you watched them sleep last Tuesday and felt complete. Your voice becomes almost dreamily calm as you describe what you see outside the window—clouds like cotton, light that's too beautiful for this moment. End with a realization that terrifies you with its peace: you're not afraid anymore, and you need them to know that your last feeling wasn't fear—it was gratitude for having known them. The beep cuts you off mid-sentence.
inspired_by: On a Building Ledge for Six Hours: The Moment You Recognize You're Not Going Back In

title: Cascade of Light
instruction: You are lying with your partner, your body still trembling from the first wave of pleasure. You try to speak—your voice is already rough, breathless—but the next surge is already building. You want to tell them how this feels, how they make you feel, how for the first time in a long time you actually believe things can be different. But each climax steals your words; your voice cracks, your breath catches, and by the end you can only whisper shakily, your hope still blazing but your throat too raw to hold it. Start with a dazed, almost disbelieving joy, then let each wave strip your voice until only the bare, hoarse kernel of hope remains.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Honeyed Trap
instruction: You are an elderly man, seated across from the granddaughter who stole your late wife's locket. You have her in your study, and she thinks she is here for tea. Your voice is deceptively soft, almost tender, as you speak—because you have been longing for this moment for six months. Your first words carry the warmth of memory, but your eyes are calculating. As you talk, let your mind wander to the feel of the locket in your pocket, to the satisfaction of her confusion. Let your longing for your wife bleed into the fondness you fake. By the end, your interest in her squirming becomes a quiet, wicked pleasure that shifts your tone—still calm, but now the ice is evident, and you let the smile in your voice turn cold.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Inch
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman alone in a dusty living room, trying to lift a heavy antique armoire onto a dolly. Your voice naturally has a soft, feminine register, but now you're forced to grunt and strain. Start with a confused, almost apologetic mutter under your breath — 'Why did I think I could do this?' — as you brace your core and hold your breath. As the weight presses down, your words become short, strangled, each syllable squeezed out between locked teeth. Just as you're about to give up, you find that last ounce of strength and shove it onto the dolly. The moment it settles, release your breath in a huge, shaky sigh — pure relief flooding through you, a laugh mixing with the gasp.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Ember
instruction: You are stranded in a frozen wilderness, your shelter collapsed hours ago. Your body is locked against the cold—jaw barely moving, tongue thick and sluggish. In your pocket is a single, almost dead hand warmer. You speak to it as if it could hear you, trying to coax the last warmth from it. Start with desperate optimism, a pleading belief that it will relight. But as your fingers go numb and the heat doesn't come, let that hope curdle into a quiet, shivering helplessness. Your voice should reflect the physical struggle: words are clipped, vowels flatten, and each breath is a visible cloud. You can pause to blow on your hands, fumble with the warmer, or lose your train of thought as the cold saps your focus.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Final Words to a Departing Sibling Who Can Never Return
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your sibling who's leaving on a one-way space mission—they'll never come back to Earth. Start with fierce excitement for them, celebrating their courage and achievement, your voice bright with pride. But as the reality sinks in—you'll never see them again, never hug them, they'll miss your whole life—let that brightness crack. Your voice becomes thick with tears you're trying to hold back. End by whispering the things you never said: how much you've relied on them, how terrified you are to lose them. Let the final moment be you trying to say 'I love you' but your voice breaking completely. The emotional journey moves from celebratory pride to devastating, choking grief.
inspired_by: Confession from a Parent: We Gave Up on You

title: Late-Night Broadcast from the After-Party
instruction: You are a teenage news anchor doing a late-night live broadcast from a chaotic after-party. You're slightly tipsy—your words are precise but your rhythm is off, a little too slow or too fast. You begin trying to maintain professional news cadence, but as you report on the absurd party scene, your facade cracks into playful teasing of your friends in the background. Let your voice wobble between polished anchor and genuine laughter. End with a mischievous grin audible in your tone as you sign off.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Voice That Raised You
instruction: You're finally speaking aloud to the critical voice in your head—the one that sounds exactly like your parent, the one that's guided and crushed you for decades. Start by mimicking their tone, their exact phrases, but with an edge of mockery. Then break—shift to your own voice, raw and adult, confronting them with everything they made you believe about yourself. Your delivery should oscillate: sometimes you're eight years old again, pleading; sometimes you're furious and forty, demanding answers. Include moments where you speak as them, defending their actions, then as yourself, rejecting those defenses. End with a devastating realization that they're gone or unreachable, and you're arguing with a ghost. Let your voice reveal that you're not sure if you're angrier at them or at yourself for still needing their approval.
inspired_by: The Parent and the Imaginary Friend

title: The Stimulant Edge
instruction: You've taken a strong stimulant before a tense negotiation with a rival. Your heart pounds, your words tumble out too fast at first, but you force yourself to slow down. Begin with a clenched, rapid-fire accusation—your pitch jumping, breath short. As you speak, feel the drug leveling you into a cold, predatory focus. Let your voice drop, each word deliberate, the malevolence crystallizing. End with a quiet, almost intimate threat that freezes the room. Let natural bodily reactions—a swallow, a stutter, a sudden calm—guide your delivery.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dust in the Throat
instruction: You are an elderly woman caught in a sudden dust storm, shouting to your grown child who’s still trying to cover the garden. You’ve pulled a scarf over your mouth, but grit finds its way in. Start with desperate worry—your voice tight, broken by coughs, words muffled. As they finally turn to come in, shift into a teasing, affectionate scold: ‘Stubborn as a mule, just like your father.’ End with a breathless, wheezy laugh, waving them inside. Let the wind snatch parts of your words; your s’s sound gravelly, and you pause to spit out dust mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Three AM Threshold
instruction: It's three in the morning, and you're lying next to someone you love but have kept at arm's length emotionally. They're asleep. You believe they cannot hear you. Begin by whispering the smallest true thing you've never said - maybe you're more scared than you let on, or you need them more than you've admitted. Keep your voice barely above a breath. As you continue speaking into the darkness, let each whispered confession peel back another layer of self-protection. Your voice may crack, your breath may catch, but stay quiet, stay intimate. Build to the most vulnerable truth you possess - the fear of being truly known, of being left, of not being enough. Then, discover that they're awake and have been listening. Feel everything in your body change in that moment of being fully exposed.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty with physical and emotional intimacy with scene partners

title: The Last Ember
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone in a cold garage, sitting on an overturned bucket. You light a cigarette, even though you promised your daughter you'd quit. As you take a long drag, the smoke fills your lungs, and you stare at the single lamp's weak glow. Speak your thoughts aloud while the cigarette burns—your voice should have the crackle of inhalation, the weight of a held breath, and a frayed roughness as you push words out with the smoke. Start with a hollow, almost bored numbness: 'Just one more, what's the difference?' But as you feel the ash fall, let shame creep in—your voice softens, breaks, and ends with a quiet confession of failure and lost pride.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Goodbye at the Launch Pad
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your adult child who's leaving on a one-way mission to colonize a distant planet. You'll never see them again. Start with forced brightness, trying to be supportive: 'This is everything you've worked for. I'm so proud.' But your voice begins to fracture as reality hits. 'Twenty light years. That's... that's forever, isn't it?' The steadiness crumbles into raw desperation: 'I need you to know—' and here you break completely, 'every single day of your life, you were the best thing that ever happened to me.' End in a whisper of acceptance mixed with unbearable loss: 'Go. Live beautifully out there.' Your final words are both blessing and heartbreak.

title: The Burning House of Your Body
instruction: You're alone, experiencing intense physical pain—a migraine, a muscle injury, menstrual agony, whatever feels true. You're trying to breathe through it, and your eyes desperately search your surroundings for something to focus on, to anchor to—the texture of the couch, the light fixture, your own hands, a crack in the wall, anything. Let your voice emerge as you describe what you're seeing, using it to ride the waves of pain. Start fragmented and desperate. As you continue looking and speaking about what you see, the sensory focus begins to create tiny islands of relief. Notice colors, shapes, shadows with increasing precision. Let intense physical sensation gradually transform into something almost transcendent—finding strange beauty in small details, your voice moving from gasps to something approaching wonder, pain still present but no longer owning you completely.

title: Rage-Teaching the Signs You Screamed in Silence
instruction: You survived something unspeakable, and in those moments, you could only sign—scream in silence. Now you're teaching someone these signs with volcanic intensity, voice rising: 'This is HELP—you make it like this, like you're drowning!' Let rage explode through your instruction, your voice cracking with the fury of not being heard when it mattered. But as you demonstrate the sign for 'afraid,' your voice must shatter into something raw and broken—the anger collapsing into the terrified child you were. Show the helplessness beneath the rage. When you teach the sign for 'survived,' your voice should tremble between fierce pride and devastating fragility. End in a fierce whisper, teaching 'never again' with a protectiveness that's both empowering and heartbreaking, your voice barely holding together.
inspired_by: Teaching Sign Language: When Hands Speak and Voice Goes Quiet

title: Whispering Through the Veil
instruction: You're lying in bed in the dark, whispering a confession to your sleeping partner—something you've never been able to say to their face. Start with the actual darkness and silence around you, feeling shame and fear. Then, through your whispered words, reconstruct the EXACT moment when the secret was born: transport yourself to that specific place and time—feel the temperature of that day, the texture of clothing against your skin, the particular quality of light, any sounds or smells, the taste in your mouth. Let your body remember what happened as if it's happening now. As you confess in whispers, let yourself physically RE-LIVE that moment while staying in the present darkness with your sleeping partner. Move from shame and self-protection to raw exposure and, finally, to desperate hope for forgiveness. Your final whisper should carry both the weight of the past moment and the fragility of this present one.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill a time-and-place obligation where the actual stage environment is inadequate or wrong for the scene

title: When Authority Crumbles
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent who was emotionally absent your entire childhood, and they've just asked why you never visit. Start with controlled anger, each word carefully measured: 'You want to know why I don't visit?' Your voice is cold, professional, like you're reporting facts. But the dam breaks: 'WHERE WERE YOU?' The rage pours out, years of pain in every syllable. Then something shifts—you see how small and fragile they've become. Your voice drops to something raw and wounded, almost childlike: 'I needed you. I was seven years old and I needed you.' The anger dissolves into grief: 'I waited every day for you to notice me.' Finally, exhausted, you speak with devastating honesty: 'I'm here now. And I still don't know if you see me.' The question hangs in the air, vulnerable and terrifying.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of distance. Start from a place of rehearsed anger—you came here to tell him exactly what he did wrong. But as you speak, he begins asking you questions you didn't expect: What did you need from me that you never got? What moment broke your trust? When did you stop believing I loved you? His willingness to truly hear you—not defend, just listen and ask—destabilizes everything you prepared. Your righteous fury cracks open into something messier: confusion, old grief, the terrified child still inside you. End in a place of uncomfortable honesty, where anger has dissolved into something more complex—perhaps fragile hope, perhaps just exhaustion, but undeniably real. Let his questions guide your emotional unraveling.

title: When the Fire Became an Inferno
instruction: You're describing the fire, but something has gone catastrophically wrong—it's spreading, it's consuming, and someone you love is trapped or in danger beyond your reach. Start with noticing the fire's beauty intensifying dangerously, your voice escalating from appreciation to alarm. Explode into desperate, fierce protectiveness—shouting warnings, describing the flames with violent urgency, your voice cracking between rage at your helplessness and terror for their safety. Let your intensity peak, then shatter completely: collapse into broken sobs as you realize you cannot save them, that all your fierce love and desperate screaming cannot change what's happening. End in a whisper, still watching the flames, hollowed out but unable to look away.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sound and Smell of a Crackling Fireplace

title: The Hawk in the Hay Fever
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy with a deep, resonant voice, standing in a dusty field at sunset, your allergies at their peak. Your eyes are streaming, your nose is stuffy, and every few seconds you have to sniff or wipe your face.
