You're supposed to be watching a rare hawk that just landed on a fence post, but all you can focus on is your own misery and doubt—doubt that you'll ever get into the college you want, doubt that anyone takes you seriously. Start by sighing heavily through your mouth, your words thick with post-nasal drip and frustration. As you speak, allow a tiny crack of awe to slip in when you glance at the hawk's silhouette against the orange sky, but let it be swallowed back by your skeptical, gravelly tone. End with a quiet, reluctant wonder that makes you stop mid-sniff, your voice softer and less clogged, but still raspy.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Burp That Broke the Argument
instruction: You're a young woman in the middle of a furious confrontation with someone who has wronged you—perhaps a betraying friend or dismissive partner. Your anger is white-hot, your words sharp. But just as you build to your most cutting line, a loud, involuntary burp erupts from your throat, dropping your voice into a guttural, almost monstrous growl. You're disgusted—at the burp, at losing your momentum, at the person in front of you. Start with pure, focused rage, then let the burp derail you into a messy, frustrated disgust that colors the rest of your speech. Your voice should feel gritty, tight, then suddenly loose and phlegmy. Let the burp be real and uncensored, and then push through the disgust to finish your thought, but now your anger feels tainted and ridiculous.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Thanking Someone Who Just Broke Your Heart
instruction: The person you love most has just told you they're leaving, and it's the right decision - you both know it. You need to thank them for the years you had while your heart is simultaneously shattering. Begin by admitting out loud the war happening inside you - the part that wants to scream, the part that wants to beg, the gratitude fighting with devastation, how strange your own voice sounds trying to be gracious. Don't smooth over the contradictions. As you speak, let yourself feel both the love and the loss simultaneously, the relief and the grief, the anger at them for leaving and the deeper anger at yourself for knowing they should. By the end, arrive at a moment where all these contradictions exist together in one breath. Move from fractured, conflicting emotions to a complex, whole truth that holds everything at once.

title: The New Gears
instruction: You are a teenage boy working a summer job in a massive, deafening factory. You've just been trusted to operate a very loud, complex stamping machine you've been begging to run for weeks. Start with a quiet, almost disbelieving smile, talking to yourself over the hum of the machines. You feel a forbidden, ecstatic thrill of power — this hulking, dangerous thing does your bidding. Then, a new kid walks by, gawking. Let a slight, cold edge of malice creep into your voice as you clown on his fear, daring him to come closer. The pleasure and malice mix, making your voice crack with a laugh that is part joy, part threat.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Silent Summit
instruction: You are a woman hiking a steep incline with your young child. You're both exhausted, your breathing heavy and puffed between short phrases. You feel a deep emotional numbness—weightless, hollow, as if nothing matters anymore, and you're embarrassed that your child might sense it or worse, that another hiker might see you pause to catch your breath and think you're weak. As you climb, the silence between your breaths grows, and you realize your child is watching you, not the trail—so you try to speak, but your voice cracks, full of labor, shame, and unspoken exhaustion. By the end, a small, surprising warmth breaks through as you mumble something to your child—a fragile, honest moment that shifts the numbness into raw, vulnerable connection.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth about how their absence shaped you. Begin with rehearsed calm, the speech you've practiced: 'I want to talk about something.' But as you speak, old wounds open. Your voice tightens with controlled anger: 'Do you know what it was like? Waiting for you?' The anger builds—you're listing specific moments they missed, your voice rising. Then it breaks entirely. The rage collapses into raw pain: 'I needed you. I was just a kid.' End with quiet devastation, almost asking permission to still love them: 'I don't know how to stop wanting you to be proud of me.' Transform from controlled confrontation through explosive hurt to vulnerable, childlike longing.

title: Library Confessions
instruction: You are in a silent library, pressed close to your best friend, whispering about the person who just walked past your table. Your voice is all air — no vocal cords, just a breathy stream of sound, like you're sharing the most fragile secret. Start with a giddy, almost laughing infatuation, gushing about their smile and the way they look at you. But then you realize they might be interested in someone else; your excitement falters, turning into a quieter, more vulnerable whisper of longing. Let your body shift, glance over your shoulder, and let the sound become thinner as the hope dims but the crush persists. You should speak about 50 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Forgiveness Granting
instruction: Someone is granting forgiveness to someone who's hurt them deeply. The person granting forgiveness's voice is powerful but also fragile. They're choosing to release the resentment they've been holding. The person being forgiven is almost disbelieving—they've prepared for ongoing punishment, not release. Their voice carries the shock of undeserved grace. The forgiveness is spoken deliberately, ceremonially. It's not cheap; it costs something. Both voices acknowledge the gravity of this moment. By the end, something has been released. The past remains, but it's no longer shackling them. Both voices carry the strange freedom that comes after forgiveness.

title: The Threshold of Departure
instruction: You are standing at the door, leaving behind a life or person you both love and must escape. Speak your goodbye knowing it contains irreconcilable truths: you are devastated and relieved, grateful and bitter, still in love and finally free. Begin with the easier emotions—perhaps anger or determination—but let the contradictions flood in as you continue. Your voice might break with grief mid-sentence, then harden with resolve, then soften with unexpected tenderness, then crack with resentment. Don't resolve these contradictions—let them coexist, fighting for space in your throat. End with all these emotions present at once: laughing through tears, expressing love while walking away, thanking them while naming the pain they caused. This is not closure—it's the messy, impossible truth of loving what hurts you.

title: Confronting Your Mother in the Kitchen Where You Grew Up
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen confronting your mother about a truth you've kept buried for twenty years. Begin controlled and almost cold, stating facts calmly: 'We need to talk about what happened when I was fifteen.' But as she deflects or minimizes, feel your composure shatter. Your voice should escalate from measured words to shouting every suppressed observation—how she chose her comfort over your pain, how she pretended not to see, how you protected her by staying silent. Let every unspoken accusation from two decades explode: petty grievances mixed with profound betrayals, childish complaints alongside legitimate trauma. Scream, cry, laugh bitterly at the absurdity of finally saying it all. Then, once everything is out and you're both destroyed, let the anger drain into exhausted grief and perhaps a fragile, uncertain question: 'Why?' End in quiet devastation, not resolution.

title: Laughing at the Funeral: The Beauty of What You Had
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone you loved impossibly deeply, and you've just told a story that makes everyone laugh—one of those perfect, ridiculous memories that captured who they were. You're laughing too, genuinely, warmly, and for a moment you forget they're gone. Then you remember. Your laughter doesn't stop immediately but begins to transform, tears mixing in until you can't tell if you're laughing or crying. Your voice stays light, almost playful, as you say 'God, I'm going to miss you,' but it's breaking around the edges. You oscillate between joy at having known them and devastation at the loss, your voice reflecting both simultaneously—chuckling through 'Thank you for everything' while tears make your words thick and unsteady. By the end, you're smiling and sobbing at once, voice suspended between gratitude and grief.
inspired_by: Adrenaline Crash: Shaking After the Car Almost Hit You

title: First Day on the Line
instruction: You are a teenage recruit on your first day of boot camp. The drill sergeant is screaming in your ear, and you're trying to shout back your squad number, but your mind is racing. Start with a loud, confused yell that cracks and breaks rhythm as you fumble the words. Then, in the middle of your shout, pause and take a sharp breath—your eyes scan the formation, trying to make sense of the chaos. Let your voice drop into a quieter, more thoughtful tone as you mutter a half-formed realization about why you're here. Finally, draw yourself up tall, a new certainty flooding your chest, and unleash a fierce, pride-filled cry that cuts through the air with raw conviction.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Contemplation (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bitter Thrust
instruction: You are having sex with your partner, but contempt burns through every movement. Your breath is locked to each thrust—sharp, effortful. Start with clipped, almost mocking commands: 'Harder. There.' Each word a grunt of disgust and control. Midway, let the contempt crack into a quieter, colder awareness. Your voice flattens, rhythm falters. End with a breathy, distant murmur as you stop moving: 'You think this means something.' Let the bed creak, skin slap, and your own involuntary vocalizations rupture the silence—then swallow them.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Smushed Confession
instruction: You're a teenager, head resting heavily on your palm, face squished to one side, listening to your friend's latest drama. You start by teasing them mercilessly about their overreaction, your words coming out a bit clumsy because of the pressure on your lips. But as you speak, you notice the hurt flicker in their eyes, and your teasing falters. The realization hits you—you've crossed a line. Your voice drops, losing the mocking edge, becoming quiet and sincere as you awkwardly apologize, still not moving your head because you're too tired or embarrassed to sit up straight. Let your words reflect the physical distortion and the emotional shift from playful cruelty to genuine regret.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering the Truth to Your Sleeping Partner
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner of ten years is asleep beside you. You are whispering a confession they cannot hear—that you've been unfaithful, or that you're leaving, or that you never wanted the life you built together, or that you're ill and haven't told them. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking. You're practicing words you may never say aloud when they're awake. Touch their hair, their face. Feel the safety of their sleep and the devastating knowledge that you're about to destroy everything. Your whisper is filled with love and regret simultaneously. Start with halting, fragmented attempts to say it—stopping, starting again. Build to a complete confession, your voice thick with tears but still quiet, still careful not to wake them. End with 'I'm so sorry'—whispered like a prayer, like a goodbye, your voice catching on the words. The entire performance must feel intimate, vulnerable, like overhearing someone's most private moment of truth.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Oath-Breaker Speaks Their True Name for the First Time

title: Flight Risk
instruction: You've just received news that you've been accepted into a dream program/job in another country, and you're telling your aging parent who depends on you. Begin with bright, fluttering energy—almost giddy, your movements quick and light, bouncing on your toes, hands moving like wings. You can barely contain your joy. But as you watch their face, as you hear your own words, something heavy begins to settle into your bones. Your movements slow, become more grounded, weighted. Your voice loses its lightness. By the end, you're rooted to the spot, your earlier flight energy completely gone—you feel the pull of earth, of duty, of love that feels like gravity. You haven't decided what you'll do, but you've transformed from something airborne and free to something earthbound and trapped, even as you're still trying to smile. Carry both the soaring and the sinking simultaneously in your final moment.

title: The Ghost in My Machine Still Makes Me Laugh
instruction: You are talking to an AI trained on your deceased spouse's voice, mannerisms, and memories—technology you once called an abomination, but now you can't stop using it. Begin with bitter laughter, mocking yourself for how pathetic this is, your voice sharp with self-directed cruelty. But as the AI says something perfectly, heartbreakingly characteristic of the person you lost, let the laughter become real—genuine joy mixed with devastating sadness. Your voice should dance between grief and gratitude, between wanting to smash the computer and wanting to live in this conversation forever. End with a confession that's equal parts love letter and goodbye, your voice soft and luminous with contradictory peace: 'You're not them, and somehow that makes it easier to tell you everything I never could when they were alive. Thank you for being the most beautiful lie I've ever been told.'
inspired_by: The Scientist and the Sentient AI

title: Performing CPR While Talking to the Unconscious Person
instruction: You're doing chest compressions on someone. Count aloud: 'One, two, three—' The rhythm of CPR should be audible — the physical effort of compressions affecting your voice. Between cycles, talk to them: 'Come on, stay with me. Don't you dare—' Give rescue breaths (the sound of forcing air). Continue. Exhaustion setting in but you can't stop. Include the moment — whether they come back or don't — and how your voice reacts to the outcome. Raw, physical, desperate.

title: Laughing in This Blanket That Smells Like You
instruction: You're wrapped in your late partner's blanket after their funeral, and something absurd just happened that would have made them laugh hysterically. Start by describing the softness and warmth while laughing—genuinely laughing at the ridiculous moment, maybe how you spilled coffee all over yourself, or how their mother tried to give you casseroles you can't eat. Let the laughter be real and full. But let it slowly, naturally dissolve into crying as you breathe in their scent still clinging to the fabric, the weight of the blanket suddenly feeling like their arms around you one last time. Find a place where you're both laughing and sobbing, expressing gratitude for having had them while your heart is completely shattered. End in a space of bittersweet peace, your voice soft and broken but somehow okay with both the joy and the devastation existing together.
inspired_by: Feeling the Weight of a Soft Blanket on Your Shoulders

title: The Award Speech Never Given
instruction: You are alone, holding an imaginary award, giving the acceptance speech you have never allowed yourself to imagine because you never believed you deserved recognition. Begin speaking with bitter irony, mocking yourself for even fantasizing about this moment, listing all the reasons you don't deserve to be here. Your voice drips with self-contempt and defensive humor. But as you continue, something cracks. Let genuine longing emerge—the part of you that did work hard, that does have gifts, that has been waiting your entire life to be seen. Your voice should break, rebuild, surge with unexpected emotion. End by declaring what you've accomplished with full-throated ownership, mixing tears with fierce joy. Transform from self-mockery to unapologetic self-celebration, holding both the grief of lost time and the triumph of finally claiming your due.
inspired_by: Actor's ego-state is in the way — feeling not good enough, too old, not talented enough

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Stole
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, face-to-face with your mother for the first time in years. Begin with controlled, surgical precision—you've rehearsed this, listing exactly what she did, how her addiction or neglect or cruelty shaped you. Your voice is sharp, factual, cutting. But she starts making excuses, and something in you erupts. Let your voice rise, crack, become the voice of the child you were—raw, desperate, demanding she finally see you. 'I needed you! I was just a kid!' Then suddenly, you see how small she looks, how broken, and your rage collides with pity. Your voice drops to something quieter, more devastating: the realization that she'll never be able to give you what you needed. End with the grief of accepting that your mother is just a damaged person who couldn't love you the way you deserved.
inspired_by: Telling Your Best Friend You Can't Be Friends Anymore

title: Reading Their Letter at Your Kitchen Table
instruction: Your adult child left you a letter before leaving for rehab. You're reading it aloud to yourself at 2 AM, and it's devastating—brutally honest about how you failed them, but also expressing love and forgiveness you don't think you deserve. Your voice keeps breaking into inappropriate laughter because the situation is so absurd, so painful it's almost funny. 'You forgive me? You—' laugh-sob. Move between reading their words and responding to them as if they're there. Find moments of pure gratitude that shatter you ('Thank you for trying, even when—') mixed with grief for all the years you can't get back. Let contradictory emotions coexist: you're smiling through tears, laughing while your heart breaks, finding something like joy in the wreckage. End in a place of messy, complicated grace—not resolution, but acceptance.

title: What You Actually Think of Me
instruction: You're confronting your mother after years of swallowing your truth. Start from a place of controlled anger—you came here with points to make, grievances to list. But as you begin to speak, your mind betrays your script. Mid-sentence, you're ambushed by sense memories: the smell of her perfume when you were seven, the sound of her crying through the wall when Dad left, a flash of her young face in an old photograph, the taste of her cooking, the feeling of her disappointment like a weight on your chest, a sudden image of her hands trembling. These intrusions disrupt your accusations—they don't defuse your anger, but they complicate it, twist it, make it messier. Let each new image or sensation knock you sideways, change the direction of what you're saying, contradict the previous moment. Don't try to reconcile them or make a coherent argument. By the end, you've moved somewhere completely unexpected—perhaps to a confession of your own failures, perhaps to recognizing her humanity in a way that terrifies you, perhaps to a tenderness you didn't plan to feel but can't stop.

title: The Tides of Exhaustion
instruction: You are a woman with a high, soft voice, utterly drained after a day that left you empty. You're lying beneath your partner, your body heavy and sore, and they begin to move inside you. Start with a low, weary moan of fatigue and a wince of lingering pain—your breath shallow, words like 'Wait... just...' trailing off. As the rhythm builds, let your voice catch in small gasps, cracking into a higher register against your will. By the end, a fragile note of pleasure breaks through, your voice trembling and fragmented: 'Oh... yes... there...' Let the exhaustion still shadow it, but allow a reluctant, rising ecstasy to color your final, open-mouthed sigh.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Tale of What We Lost
instruction: You are recounting to a therapist, years later, the imaginary world you and your sibling created as children to escape your chaotic home—elaborate stories with heroes and quests that kept you both sane. Begin with genuine joy and almost childlike enthusiasm as you remember the magic of those stories, laughing at the ridiculous details, your voice bright with nostalgia. But let the laughter become strained as you reveal what you're really talking about: those stories were survival, not play. Let tears mix with the laughter as you describe how you stopped believing in the stories the day your sibling didn't come home. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance: you're grateful for those legends even though they couldn't save you both, finding unexpected peace in the realization that the stories gave you something real—connection, hope, proof that beauty can exist in darkness. Your voice should shimmer between joy and sorrow, never fully landing in either, holding both truths at once.
inspired_by: The Elderly Storyteller and the Curious Child

title: The Mimicry Cracks
instruction: You are a divorced father, bitter that your ex-wife got full custody. Your child (around 8 years old) is on the phone, excitedly asking if you can pick them up this Saturday. Instead of answering warmly, you start mocking their voice — a nasal, exaggerated sing-song: 'Oh, can we go to the park, daddy? Pwease?' The sarcasm drips with resentment. But halfway through, you hear your own voice and feel a wave of shame. Your tone cracks, the caricature fades, and you end with a quiet, broken 'Sorry, buddy.' Let the bitterness dominate the first half — tight throat, forced laughter, extreme pitch jumps. Then let the shame creep in: slower speech, a swallowed breath, a raw drop into lower register. Feel the awkward pause as you realize what you've done.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's slipping in and out of consciousness. At first, you're frozen—numb, disbelieving, fighting the reality of what's happening. But as you hold her hand and look at her face, begin to see her not as this frail, fading body, but as she truly was: recall the precise warmth of her embrace when you were eight years old, the exact smell of her kitchen, the specific melody of her laugh when she found something genuinely funny. Let these sense memories wash over you until you're no longer speaking to a dying woman, but to the full, vibrant person who shaped your life. Your emotional journey moves from numb denial to a profound, aching gratitude mixed with unbearable loss. By the end, you're not saying goodbye to death—you're thanking life itself.
inspired_by: Scene partner is not stimulating the relationship feelings demanded by the material

title: The Truth About Why I Left
instruction: You are confronting your adult child after years of estrangement. They have demanded to know why you abandoned them when they were twelve. Begin with defensive anger—sharp, protective walls up, blaming their other parent, making excuses. But as you speak, let the real truth begin to surface: your own fear, your inadequacy, your shame. Your voice should start clipped and hostile, then gradually break into something rawer. Move from blaming outward to confessing your own brokenness. Let the anger dissolve into vulnerability as you admit what you've never said: you were terrified of failing them, so you fled. End with a plea for forgiveness that is both humble and desperate, your voice stripped of all defenses, revealing the parent who has lived with this regret every single day.
inspired_by: Actor wants to build the unconscious background of a character between rehearsals

title: Confronting Your Parent in the Dementia Ward
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother in a care facility. She doesn't recognize you today. Start with gentle attempts to connect: 'Mom, it's me. It's Jamie.' But as she continues to look through you with confusion, your desperation builds. Your voice hardens with decades of unspoken hurt: 'You never said you were proud of me. Not once. And now you can't even see me.' The anger collapses into grief as you realize you're yelling at someone who's already gone. Your voice breaks: 'I needed you to tell me I was enough. I needed that so badly.' Then, in the devastation, she suddenly says something tender from your childhood, a pet name she used to call you, and you're caught between relief and renewed anguish because you know the moment won't last. End whispering forgiveness you're not sure you mean, voice thick with tears: 'I love you anyway. I always did.'
inspired_by: Sensory Deprivation Tank: Time Becoming Meaningless

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone who saved your life but whose death was absurdly preventable. Start reading your prepared remarks—dignified, measured—but then you remember something ridiculous they did, and suddenly you're laughing. Really laughing, almost hysterical. You try to stop, apologizing through giggles, but the memories keep coming. Your voice dances between genuine joy at who they were and devastating grief that they're gone. You're smiling through tears, saying 'They would have hated this—all of us being so serious.' But then it hits you again that they're really gone, and your laughter cracks into a sob mid-sentence. Somehow you find your way to gratitude—voice thick, broken, but warm: 'Thank you for making everything bearable. Even this.' End with a quiet, tear-soaked laugh: 'Especially this.' Let joy and heartbreak be inseparable.

title: The Headlights in the Rearview
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy, driving home late after a party that got busted by cops. Your body is reclined slightly, hands gripping the wheel at ten and two, knuckles white. At first, you're just distressed, talking to yourself about how your parents can't find out, your voice tight as you try to calm down. Then a pair of headlights appears behind you, following every turn—fear creeps in, but you try to laugh it off, saying maybe it's just your paranoia. As the car speeds up and the lights get closer, your voice breaks, you swallow hard, and end with a strained, quiet tone as you realize you might actually be in trouble.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma or someone whose mind has been stolen by dementia. You know they can't hear you, but you need to say it anyway. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and broken. You start by telling them small, tender things—memories, inside jokes, the ordinary moments that made up a life together. But these gentle words carry an unbearable weight. Your throat keeps catching. You're confessing love, regret, gratitude, and devastating loneliness all at once. The quieter you get, the more your voice fractures. End with words so soft they're almost just breath, but they contain everything you are.
inspired_by: Comforting Someone Grieving While You Grieve Them

title: The Part You've Been Hiding
instruction: You're confronting your partner who has accused you of being cold, shut down, emotionally unavailable. Start from your defended place—the part of you that has good reasons for self-protection, that intellectualizes, that keeps everything controlled and rational. Explain yourself calmly, logically. But as you speak, another part of you—the one that's terrified, that carries old wounds, that actually feels everything too much—begins to fight its way to the surface. Move your body differently when this shift happens. Let your voice crack, let the dam break. This other part doesn't speak in complete sentences or logical arguments; it speaks in fragments, in desperate truth. End in a place of exposure you didn't intend, revealing the tender, frightened self beneath the armor.

title: The Unveiled Self
instruction: You are alone with someone you deeply trust, in dim light, after years of hiding. Begin speaking in whispers, hesitant and self-protective, about the parts of yourself you've always been ashamed to show—your desires, your body, your secret fears about being wanted or not wanted. Start with shame and secrecy in your voice. As you continue, allow their imagined acceptance (or your memory of a moment when someone saw you fully and didn't turn away) to give you courage. Let your whispers gradually gain strength. End in a place of trembling self-revelation and fragile pride—speaking what you've never said aloud, owning desires you've kept hidden, accepting your own sensual, flawed, human self.

title: The Hanging Man's Promise
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, gravelly voice, hanging upside down by your ankles in a cold, dark room. Your face is flushed, throat tight, and every word comes out thick and wet, like gargling. You're talking to a guard who just found you. Start with a confused grunt, trying to understand how you got here—your words slur and catch. Then shift into a hopeful, almost friendly tone, telling the guard you're harmless, just a lost old man, and if he helps you down, you'll reward him. But as you speak, let a cold malice creep in—a promise that once you're free, you'll repay his kindness with a slow, painful end. Let the physical strain make your voice wobble and crack, but keep the menace clear by the last line.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Moment Your Child Steps Into Danger
instruction: You're watching your child about to do something brave but dangerous, and you cannot stop them. Start with fierce intensity, your voice sharp with protective rage: 'No. Absolutely not. I won't let you—' But they're not backing down, and you realize you have no power here. Your voice fractures, shifting from anger to raw terror: 'You don't understand what you're asking me to do. To just stand here and watch you—' The helplessness crashes over you in waves, and suddenly you're almost shouting through tears, your voice ragged and desperate: 'You're my baby. You're MY baby and I can't—I can't lose you!' Then something breaks. Your rage dissolves into devastated surrender. Your voice drops to a whisper, shaking but tender: 'Be careful. Please, please be careful.' End with words that mix blessing and benediction with barely controlled terror, speaking through tears: 'I love you. I love you so much it's killing me.'

title: Lingering Touch
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone you love, the warmth of their body still against yours. Your breathing is slow and deep, your voice barely a murmur — lazy, intimate, completely unguarded. For a moment, you're peaceful, lost in the afterglow. But then a quiet sadness creeps in because you know this can't last. The longing rises: you want to freeze this moment, to keep them here forever. Speak the thought that escapes your lips — not forced, but drifting out between soft sighs. Let your voice crack slightly on the last word, heavy with unspoken ache.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Show of Favoritism
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe 8 or 9, sitting at a kitchen table with your head resting heavily on your hand, palm smushing your cheek and distorting your mouth. Your younger sister just received a shiny new toy from your mom, and you're supposed to be happy for her. Start by muttering under your breath, faking a bored, disinterested tone—your words come out slightly clumsy because of your squished face. Let a faint trickle of envy and disgust color your voice as you watch, then let the anger boil over. By the end, your voice is sharp and loud, no longer bored—pure, seething fury as you accuse your mom of always playing favorites.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Disgust (slightly present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Calling Across the Market
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a high, delicate voice, scanning a crowded market for your granddaughter who wandered off. You cup your hands around your mouth and call out, but your voice cracks and strains against the noise. Start with growing worry—your calls are short, sharp, and frustrated. Then you catch a glimpse of her pink coat near the fountain. Relief floods you, and your final call softens into pure affection, even as you still have to shout. Let your vowels stretch long, drop the ends of words, and pause between each phrase to gasp for air or scan the crowd. Fidget with your shawl, squint against the sun, and let a small laugh escape when you see her wave back.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Everything at Once
instruction: You're packing up a home after profound loss - a death, a divorce, an ending - and you find something that breaks you open with contradictory emotion. Begin laughing softly: 'Oh my god, I forgot about this...' - genuine delight at the memory. As you describe it, laughter and tears become indistinguishable: 'We were so happy. We were so fucking happy.' Let joy and devastation exist simultaneously - your voice cracks but keeps lifting. Feel gratitude flood through grief: 'Thank you. For all of it. Even this.' You're smiling while crying, your breath uneven, holding unbearable beauty and unbearable pain in the same moment. End with paradoxical peace: 'It was worth it. All of it. Every impossible moment.' Your voice contains everything - the full spectrum of a heart that's both shattered and somehow, impossibly, whole.

title: The Last Swing
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy splitting logs in the yard after your dad cancelled coming to see your school play. You swing the axe, grunting on impact, and speak only during the wind-up or between swings—your voice rough, unguarded, breathy from exertion. Start with a muttered complaint about the disappointment, but as you work, the shame of needing him to show up, of even caring, chokes you. By the final swing, your words become colder, quieter—more to yourself than anyone. Let the physical effort crack your control; your tone shifts from bitter deflection to a raw, quiet admission of hurt.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Final Combo
instruction: You're an elderly person, alone in a dim room, controller in hand, deeply absorbed in a video game. Chair squeaks as you shift, your thumbs press buttons with tired precision. At first you're frustrated, muttering under your breath after failing the boss fight again. Then, as the pattern finally clicks, your voice lifts—gasping, then laughing in pure ecstasy. A perfect combo unfolds, and you cry out with joy, the words tumbling out between rapid clicks and a squeaking chair. Let the pleasure build from annoyance to genuine, breathless wonder.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who changed your life - a friend, a lover, a mentor - and you're both pretending it's not forever even though you both know it is. Start by laughing together about a shared memory, your voice warm and bright with genuine joy. But underneath the laughter, there's a tremor. As you recall more moments, your voice gets thicker with unshed tears while you're still trying to smile through the words. You're expressing gratitude for everything they gave you, but each 'thank you' is also a goodbye, and your voice keeps breaking between laughter and crying. You can't decide whether to laugh or sob, so you're doing both - your voice cycling between joy at having known them and devastation at losing them. End in a paradox: laughing while tears stream down your face, saying 'I'm so glad I met you' with a voice that's completely fractured by grief, finding something like peace in the beautiful disaster of loving someone enough that losing them breaks you open.

title: The Wrong Kind of Freedom
instruction: You've just received news that should be purely joyful—you got the dream job, you're moving to the city you've always wanted, you're finally free from an obligation that's held you back for years. But as you try to celebrate, you realize you're also losing something or someone irreplaceable in the process. Begin with genuine excitement, let yourself feel the rush of possibility, the opening of doors. But let that joy slowly become contaminated with grief, with guilt, with the realization that freedom always costs something. Your voice should shift from bright and expansive to something more complex—laughter that catches on tears, gratitude that sounds like an apology. By the end, you're holding both emotions fully, unable to separate the happiness from the heartbreak, speaking from a place of bewildering emotional complexity.

title: The Sugary Toothache
instruction: You are a little girl, maybe 7 or 8, slumped at the kitchen table with your head resting heavily on your hand. Your cheek is smushed against your palm, so your voice sounds muffled and warped — especially on 'p' and 'b' sounds. You're trying to tease your mom about the candy she hides in the top cupboard, but a sharp, relentless pain is shooting through your jaw. The teasing starts with a playful smirk, but as you speak, the ache swells, making you trail off, wince, then snap with raw, irritable frustration. Let your words get sloppier as the pain takes over, and let a final, impatient whine creep in.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Pain (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Echo of a Memory
instruction: You are an elderly man walking alone down a long, dimly lit hallway in your home. The carpet is worn, your footsteps slow and rhythmic, and every sound you make comes back to you with a soft, hollow decay. At the start, you feel utterly numb—each step mechanical, your gaze fixed ahead, voice flat and distant. Then, you pass an open door where a lamp glows on a table, and you see a photograph in a silver frame; a surge of infatuation wells up—a sharp, tender ache for a love long gone. By the time you reach the end of the hall, that feeling softens into a deep, quiet contentment, as if you’ve made peace with the walking and the waiting. Let your voice reflect the tunnel-acoustics: allow pauses to linger, words to trail off slightly, and let the shift from numbness to fondness feel organic, not rushed.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Contentment (extremely present), Infatuation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Truth Your Body Already Knows
instruction: Your partner of ten years is confessing they've been unhappy for a long time. You start with your mind racing—analyzing, defending, preparing counterarguments, already forming your rebuttal. Your body is tight, braced for attack. But as they keep talking, something shifts. Stop thinking. Stop defending. Let their words reach deeper than your thoughts. Feel what your body has known but your mind refused to see. The ache in your chest, the exhaustion in your bones, the truth your defenses have been blocking. By the end, let the thinking drop away entirely. Breathe. Feel. Allow the complicated truth of 'I'm angry AND I already knew AND I'm relieved AND I'm heartbroken' to exist in your body without your mind solving it.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early dawn. She's slipping away, drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by noticing the small things—her hand in yours, the sound of her breathing, the way the light falls across her face. As you speak to her, let memories surface naturally: her kitchen, her laugh, a specific moment when she made you feel loved. Start from a place of trying to stay strong and composed, but allow yourself to move toward raw gratitude mixed with the unbearable ache of letting go. Let real memories from your own life—of anyone you've loved deeply—color every word. Your voice should transform from controlled and steady to something more broken and honest. End in a place where you're no longer trying to be strong, just present.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep as you prepare to leave—not for a trip, but because you're too broken to stay, and you believe they deserve better than you. Kneel beside their bed and whisper all the things you'll never get to tell them: how you'll miss their laughter, how sorry you are for not being stronger, how you hope they'll remember you loved them even when you couldn't stay. Your voice must be barely audible, thick with tears you're trying to suppress so you won't wake them. Mix tenderness with self-loathing, love with the devastating grief of walking away. End with a choked 'I'm sorry' and the sound of you trying to compose yourself enough to leave. This should feel like your heart is tearing in half, quiet and utterly destroyed.
inspired_by: Suppressing Annoyance While Dealing With a Difficult Person

title: The Last Walk Through Our Garden
instruction: You're walking through the lavender garden you planted together, but your partner is dying inside the house behind you. You came out here because you couldn't watch them fade anymore. Start by touching the lavender mechanically, numbly—these plants were supposed to outlive this moment. As you move deeper into the garden, let the scent trigger memories: their laugh, their hands in the soil beside yours, the future you planned here. Your voice should break from hollow observation into raw grief, then finally into a whispered gratitude for every moment you had. End by telling the lavender—and them—goodbye, your voice barely holding together but full of love.
inspired_by: Walking Through a Garden of Blooming Lavender

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you, who's holding on because they're afraid to leave you alone in this world. Begin with desperate reassurance - trying to convince them (and yourself) that they need to keep fighting, that you're not ready. But as you speak, something shifts. You realize the cruelest thing is making them stay. Your voice must break as you give them permission to go, telling them it's okay to stop fighting, that you'll be alright even though you won't be. End in a place of devastating tenderness - thanking them for everything while your heart is splitting open, meaning every word of 'I love you' and 'you can rest now' even as you're dying inside. The arc moves from clinging desperation to the most painful gift of release.

title: Laughing Into the Cup
instruction: You're drinking tea in a moment of profound loss—after a funeral, after goodbye, after the ending of something beautiful—and something about the absurdity of still having tea, of the world continuing, strikes you. Begin with numb, mechanical descriptions of drinking, your voice flat and distant. Then let a small, inappropriate laugh escape. Start finding dark humor in the gentleness of tea during catastrophe, your voice lifting with borderline hysterical laughter—'Of course there's tea. There's always tea.' Let the laughter and tears become indistinguishable, your voice breaking between them. Describe the taste through both laughter and sobs, finding strange gratitude for this small, ridiculous comfort while your heart is shattered. The emotional arc should weave between grief and joy, ending with a peaceful, tear-soaked smile as you whisper 'thank you' to the tea, to the moment, to the beautiful pain of having loved something enough to feel this destroyed by its loss.
inspired_by: Taking a Slow Sip of Herbal Tea

title: The Veil of Grit and Glory
instruction: You are a middle-aged geologist stranded in a sudden, violent dust storm after a long hike. Wrapped in a scarf, you press your hand over your mouth as you speak into a voice recording on your phone. You are exhilarated that you’ve finally found the rare mineral you’ve hunted for years, but your body is wrecked—lungs burning, legs shaking. Start with a burst of joyful, breathless discovery, then let the words be dragged down by deep fatigue; you cough, your s’s whistle through cracked lips, and you pause to spit dust. By the end, you’re whispering, a ragged smile slipping into exhaustion, saying goodnight to the world.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Father in His Study—Twenty Years Late
instruction: You stand in your childhood home, finally ready to tell your father—now aging, diminished—what his absence cost you. Begin with carefully rehearsed control, the speech you've practiced. Your voice is measured, adult, determined to stay rational. But as you enumerate specific moments he missed—your graduation, your wedding, the night you needed him most—the composure fractures. Your voice rises, becomes the voice of the child you were, demanding to know why you weren't enough. Then something shifts: you see him clearly for the first time, not as the giant who abandoned you but as a broken man who never learned how to stay. The anger doesn't disappear, but it mingles with devastating recognition—he's human, flawed, and you've wasted years waiting for him to become someone he can't be. End with quiet, exhausted forgiveness that feels less like absolution and more like letting go of a weight. Your final words are almost tender, acknowledging both the harm and the impossibility of repair.
inspired_by: Buried in Snow: Creating an Air Pocket While Suffocating

title: Gilded Collapse
instruction: You are an older woman, high on cocaine, speaking to a younger acquaintance at a party. You start with swollen pride, boasting loudly and rapidly about a past success—dominating the conversation with a nasal, congested voice, pausing only to sniff or swallow. But as you talk, you catch their disinterest in the corner of your eye, and your grandiosity falters. The pride curdles into a quiet, hollow realization that no one cares anymore, leaving your voice thin and strained by the end. Speak with too-loud confidence at first, then let the words slow and trail off as the high fails you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Gratitude in the Rubble
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—your life, your plans, everything you built is gone. But somehow, impossibly, you're finding something like peace. Start with a laugh that's almost hysterical, tears streaming: 'It's all gone. Everything. And I'm... I'm actually laughing.' Your voice breaks between laughter and crying, the emotions inseparable. 'I spent so long trying to control it all, and now there's nothing left to control.' Feel the strange relief mixed with grief. As you speak, let wonder creep in: 'And somehow... somehow I feel lighter.' End with tearful, broken gratitude, smiling through devastation: 'Thank you. For breaking me open. For showing me I could survive losing everything.' Let joy and sorrow be completely intertwined, neither one false, both utterly real.

title: The Teacher and the Defiant Student
instruction: Depict a teacher with a firm but caring voice and a student who speaks in a rebellious, sarcastic tone. Switch between the teachers attempts to reach out and the students resistance, exploring themes of authority and understanding.

title: I Needed You to See Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent after years of feeling invisible. Begin with controlled anger, listing specific moments they missed—birthdays, achievements, times you needed them. Your voice is steady at first, almost rehearsed, because you've imagined this conversation a thousand times. But as you speak, the anger dissolves into something more vulnerable: a child's desperate plea to be noticed. Let your voice crack when you ask why you were never enough. Shift from accusation to raw need, from 'How could you?' to 'Why didn't you love me?' End with exhausted acceptance, your voice small and hollow, finally admitting you've stopped waiting for them to change.

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You are calling your parent from a hospital bed, knowing this will be your final conversation. Begin with trying to sound normal and upbeat, protecting them from the truth. As the call progresses, let your own need to say what's really in your heart break through—all the gratitude, all the regrets, all the love you've never fully expressed. Don't perform dying; find the real human urgency of wanting to be truly seen and known before time runs out. By the end, let yourself become completely unguarded, speaking the most honest words you've ever spoken. The challenge is to move from protective pretense to absolute emotional nakedness.
inspired_by: An actor is doing characterization work

title: The Last Light in Your Eyes
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've known your entire life—a grandparent, mentor, or dear friend—in their final hours. Begin in a state of numb shock, unable to fully accept what's happening. As you speak to them, genuinely look at their face, their hands, the way the light falls across them. Notice details you've never noticed before—the exact color of their eyes, the texture of their skin, the way they breathe. Let yourself become overwhelmed by the preciousness of these final moments of actually seeing them, really perceiving who they are. Your emotion should transform from protective numbness to a raw, almost unbearable awareness of their presence and imminent absence. End by speaking to them with the full weight of truly seeing someone you're about to lose forever.
inspired_by: Actor is disconnected from their scene partner; relationship feels artificial or the actor is not genuinely curious about them

title: The Last Garden
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend in hospice. They're drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by remembering a perfect summer day from your youth together - speak softly, almost to yourself, letting warmth and nostalgia fill your voice. As they squeeze your hand one final time, let everything you've never said pour out: the jealousies, the gratitude, the times you failed them, the ways they saved you. Move from gentle reminiscence to raw confession to desperate tenderness. End in the silence after their last breath, where you must find a way to say goodbye to the person who knew you before you knew yourself. Your voice should transform from wistful storytelling to broken whispers to something beyond words - sighs, breaths, the sounds of a heart breaking open.
inspired_by: Actor needs maximum emotional availability before a demanding scene with extreme emotional requirements

title: The Midnight Declaration
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're alone, lying in darkness after a devastating rejection or failure that happened earlier today. You felt crushed, humiliated, ready to give up on a dream. Begin by whispering to yourself in the dark—letting the vulnerability and hurt be fully present, raw and quiet. But then, something stirs. Almost against your will, you start speaking to yourself differently. Quietly at first, then with growing conviction, you begin to declare who you actually are beneath this pain. Not loud or performative—this is just for you—but absolutely true. The whispers become stronger. You're naming your worth, your capabilities, your refusal to be destroyed by this. End in a place of quiet, unshakeable power—not healed of the pain, but standing inside it with a newly discovered core of steel. Let your voice reveal the journey from broken to unbreakable, all in hushed, intimate tones.

title: The Fever Dream
instruction: You are in the throes of both intense physical pain (a fever of 104°, body aching, skin hypersensitive) and the emotional ecstasy of a memory flooding back—the first time you fell in love. Begin with your body wracked by the fever: trembling, skin burning, every nerve ending alive with discomfort. But as the memory takes hold, don't just speak it or think it—let it inhabit your aching body. Your burning skin becomes the heat of that first kiss. Your trembling becomes the vulnerability of being touched. Your labored breathing becomes the breathlessness of desire. The pain and the pleasure, the fever and the love memory—they're not separate. They're braided together in your flesh. Your voice is thick, raw, breaking not from emotion alone but from your throat's actual soreness. Your words come in fragments because your body can barely sustain them. Don't perform passion or perform suffering. Let both states occupy the same body simultaneously, each intensifying the other, until you can't tell where the physical ends and the emotional begins.

title: Bedside Confession
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a hospital bed—a friend, a sibling, a lover—and you need to tell them something you've carried for years. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and careful, as if speaking too loudly might shatter the fragile moment. You begin with small truths, your voice tender and hesitant. But as you continue, you move toward the confession that terrifies you: maybe that you loved them when you shouldn't have, or that you failed them when they needed you most, or that you're the reason for something that broke them. Your voice catches repeatedly, thick with unshed tears. There's a heartbreaking gentleness in how you speak—you're not asking for forgiveness, just offering the truth as a gift before it's too late. End with your voice dissolving into something so quiet it's almost just breath, a final admission of love or regret that costs you everything to say.

title: Breaking Into Your Ex's Voicemail at 3 AM
instruction: You're drunk, heartbroken, furious, and you've called your ex's number just to hear their voicemail greeting. When the beep sounds, everything explodes out of you. Start with rage — screaming accusations, listing every way they betrayed you, your voice raw and savage. You're pacing, probably crying, definitely not caring who hears you. Then something shifts. The anger cracks open and underneath is devastation. Your voice breaks mid-sentence. You're suddenly pleading, vulnerable, asking them to call you back even though you know they won't. Confess the pathetic truth: you still sleep on your side of the bed, you still cook for two. End with your voice small and hollow, saying you hope they're happy, and meaning it, and hating that you mean it. The last word dissolves into a sob before you hang up.
inspired_by: Dictating a Will on a Sinking Ship

title: The Last Morning in the Kitchen
instruction: You are sitting in your childhood kitchen on the morning your mother will die. She's upstairs, unconscious, the hospice nurse with her. You came down to make coffee—her coffee, the way she taught you—one last time. Begin by truly seeing every detail: the crack in the tile, the way morning light hits the counter, the smell of her dish soap. Let the ordinary sacred space of this room wash over you—all the breakfasts, all the conversations, all the years held in these four walls. Start with quiet, mechanical movements, making the coffee. As the aroma fills the room, let the full weight of 'last time' break through your composure. Let gratitude for this place, this woman, this life she gave you rise up and collide with the unbearable knowledge that you will never stand here with her again. End by speaking to her as if she could hear you from upstairs—whatever needs to be said before it's too late.

title: Emergency Call When Your Teenager Reveals They've Been Cutting
instruction: Your sixteen-year-old calls you from school. You answer expecting them to need a permission slip signed. Instead, they say four words that make the world stop: 'I've been hurting myself.' Your voice explodes—not with anger but with visceral terror disguised as fury. You're demanding why, who knew, how long, how could they not tell you. Your voice is loud, cracking, desperate. But then they go quiet, and you hear them crying, and everything in you breaks differently. Your voice transforms from explosive to unbearably gentle. You're apologizing, voice shaking, asking them to stay on the line. You tell them you're coming, you're on your way, your voice fierce with protection and broken with the knowledge that you didn't see this. End with you whispering promises—that you'll get them help, that you'll listen better, that their pain matters—your voice raw and protective and shattered all at once.
inspired_by: Rescue Made Contact in the Mine: Hearing Your Best Friend's Voice

title: The Confession in Flashes
instruction: You are whispering a confession to your sleeping lover at 4 AM, but your mind won't stay linear. You begin with one truth, but before you can finish, another secret surfaces, then another—not because you're rambling, but because your unconscious is finally speaking. Keep your voice quiet, intimate, barely above a breath, but let your emotional state shift wildly beneath the whisper: shame bleeds into relief, fear transforms into tenderness, guilt suddenly becomes gratitude. Each new fragment of truth pulls a different feeling from you. You think you're confessing to something specific, but you end up revealing your entire heart in scattered, non-chronological pieces. End with a truth so simple and vulnerable it makes everything else fall away—something you didn't even know you needed to say.

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye You Never Wanted
instruction: Your best friend is moving across the world tomorrow—their dream opportunity—and you're genuinely happy for them while your heart is completely breaking. You're apologizing for being emotional, for not being more excited, for making their goodbye about your sadness. Start with a genuine laugh, bright and a little too loud: 'I'm sorry, I'm being ridiculous!' Feel the joy for them mixing impossibly with your own loss. Let your voice dance between celebration and grief—'This is amazing for you, I'm so proud'—but hear it crack and catch. Try to laugh again but have it come out tangled with tears. Your voice should be warm, full of love and authentic happiness for them, but underneath, there's this river of sorrow you can't quite hide. Let moments of pure joy—remembering your history together—break through, your voice lifting with real delight, only to fracture again as you realize what you're losing. End with a contradiction that somehow makes perfect sense: speaking through tears while smiling, your voice tender and broken and grateful all at once: 'Thank you for being the best thing in my life... now go be amazing.' The final words should be both a blessing and a heartbreak, gratitude and devastation so intertwined you can't separate them, finding something almost peaceful in the paradox of loving someone enough to let them break your heart.
inspired_by: Apologizing for Something You Weren't At Fault For

title: A Mother Shielding Her Child During an Attack She Cannot Stop
instruction: Violence is happening—an attack, a disaster, something you cannot control. You hold your child and speak with fierce, absolute protectiveness, promising them safety you cannot guarantee. Start with commanding strength: 'I've got you, I won't let anything hurt you.' But terror cracks through. Your voice becomes desperate prayers disguised as promises. You're trying to be their shelter while you yourself are terrified. Your words become more frantic, more intense—rage at your own powerlessness, at whoever is causing this, at the universe for threatening your child. Then collapse into something more primal: just sounds of love, desperate reassurance, your voice breaking. End in exhausted tenderness, still holding them, still trying to be strong even as you fall apart. This should feel like watching someone's strength shatter in real time—explosive and raw and utterly human.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Chooses to Remain in a Body It's Outgrowing

title: The Green-Eyed Slumber
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a worn armchair, late at night, watching a slideshow of your granddaughter’s travels on a tablet. Your body is heavy with exhaustion, and your envy for her youth and freedom simmers beneath every thought. Begin speaking with a sharp, edged bitterness—clearly articulating your jealousy—but let your voice gradually slow, grow softer, and trail into mumbles as sleep pulls you under. Just as you nearly drift off, a sudden noise or thought jolts you awake; finish the line with a start, your tone shifting to a weary, resigned sadness, as if the envy has dissolved into a tired ache.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're facing your parent across the kitchen table after finding letters that reveal a family secret they've kept from you for decades. Start from a place of controlled anger—measured words, tight jaw, determined to get answers. Lock eyes with them and truly look, not at the parent you thought you knew, but at the frightened, flawed human being sitting across from you. As you maintain this unflinching attention, let your accusations gradually dissolve into something more complicated: the devastating recognition that they were trying to protect you in the only way they knew how. Let the confrontation transform from 'How could you lie to me?' to 'I see you now—all of you—and I don't know whether to forgive you or grieve for us both.' End in a place where anger and understanding exist simultaneously, unresolved.

title: Flirting at a Bar While Hiding Heartbreak
instruction: You just got dumped an hour ago and you're already trying to flirt with someone new. Your flirting voice is bright, teasing, engaged — but it's a performance running on fumes. Include moments where the mask slips: a question about relationships makes your smile freeze, a pause lasts too long, your laugh sounds hollow for one beat before you recover. The person you're talking to might be the first kind face you've seen today. Let the gratitude bleed through the game.

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You are standing on a train platform at dusk, facing someone who was both your greatest ally and your bitterest rival. This is your final goodbye – you're leaving forever. Start with your voice tight, resentful, accusing them of every betrayal, but as you talk, a memory of a ridiculous inside joke surfaces. Let a reluctant chuckle crack through your bitterness. Your voice wavers between scorn and amusement, slowing as you realize the absurdity of it all. End with a choked, rueful laugh that trails into silence, the last word tasting of both defeat and fondness.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Amusement (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home after years away for a moment of triumph—you've succeeded, you're celebrating, everyone's proud. Begin with genuine excitement and vindication. But as you stand in that space surrounded by family, allow your real competing thoughts to cascade: how hollow the victory feels, unexpected resentment toward people congratulating you, grief for who you used to be, sudden awareness of what you sacrificed, love for these people mixed with feeling utterly unknown by them, pride tangled with imposter syndrome, joy contaminated by loss. Let your celebratory words continue while your internal experience churns with contradiction. Let your smile falter and return. End with several emotions existing simultaneously—gratitude and grief, triumph and emptiness, belonging and profound alienation—all genuinely present at once.

title: The Last Call
instruction: You're a middle-aged man trapped in a burning room. Smoke stings your eyes and claws at your throat, each breath a rasping struggle. You've dialed your daughter's number — this might be the last time you hear her voice. At first, raw fear and frantic urgency shove the words out between coughs. You try to stay calm for her, but your voice breaks, wavering as sorrow floods in. By the end, the struggle fades to a choked, tender whisper — a goodbye laced with love and grief, spoken as the smoke closes in.
emotions_sampled: Distress (clearly present), Sadness (clearly present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Burning Letters
instruction: You are burning old love letters in a fireplace, one by one. Begin in bitter, fierce determination to destroy every trace of this person. But as you handle each letter—really feeling the paper's texture, seeing the specific handwriting, catching fragments of phrases—your body should begin responding to visceral memories. Maybe the slant of certain words recalls the exact sensation of their breath on your neck. Maybe the torn edge of one page brings back the physical feeling of a particular fight. Maybe the ink color triggers a rush of sense-memory of their skin. Let your rage become complicated by unwanted physical longing, by your body remembering what your mind wants to forget. The act of burning should become increasingly difficult—not because you're changing your mind, but because you're feeling the full complexity of destroying something that still has physical power over you. End in exhaustion, still angry but also aching. Your hands should shake; your breath should catch.

title: The Forgotten Shape
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting alone at a cluttered desk, drawing a face from memory. Your hand moves slowly, pencil scratching across paper. You start by muttering uncertainly—'Was the jaw this sharp? No, it was softer...'—doubt creeps in about whether you remember them at all. But as you shade the cheekbone, a flicker of lust surfaces, a warmth remembering how they once laughed with that mouth. Your voice quiet, breathy, head tilted down, words punctuated by the texture of pencil on paper. End with a hushed, fascinated sigh, your interest fully awakened by the memory of their body's curve.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Doubt (slightly present), Interest (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Breaking Point Dance
instruction: You're alone in your apartment after a betrayal so visceral it lives in your body—your hands are shaking, your chest is tight, your skin feels electric with rage and grief. Music is playing (you choose what kind). Instead of thinking about what happened, let your body respond to surges of physical sensation: the heat rising in your throat, the pressure behind your eyes, the impulse in your muscles. Begin moving—not choreographed, but following each physical impulse as it arrives. Maybe you need to hit something, or collapse, or spin, or scream, or laugh with bitter hysteria. Let your voice join whenever it demands to—sounds, words, the person's name, curses, prayers. Pay attention to sudden shifts: rage might spike into grief, grief into strange euphoria, numbness into explosive feeling. Follow your body's knowing about what it needs to do and express in this moment. Transform from coiled tension into full physical catharsis, ending in exhausted stillness.
inspired_by: Actor feels their intuition is unreliable or nonexistent

title: Confessing Love to Your Best Friend as They Pack to Marry Someone Else
instruction: You're helping them fold clothes, tape boxes, wrap picture frames. Your voice starts practical, helpful—'Do you need more bubble wrap?' But everything you're not saying sits in your throat. Finally, quietly, almost accidentally, it slips out: 'I need to tell you something.' The confession should be tender, vulnerable, barely above a whisper. You're not asking them to change anything; you just can't carry this secret into their new life. Describe the years of loving them in small moments—how they look when they're reading, the sound of their laugh, the way you've memorized their coffee order. Your voice should catch, waver, but stay soft. End with acceptance mixed with grief, maybe offering to finish packing alone so they can go, your love and your loss existing in the same breath.
inspired_by: Two People Breaking Up Over Assembling IKEA Furniture

title: Grateful Goodbye to Someone Who Saved You But Is Now Leaving
instruction: You're thanking someone who changed your life, who saved you when you needed it most, but they're leaving now—moving away, ending the relationship, or dying—and you'll never have this chance again. Start with genuine gratitude, your voice warm, almost laughing as you recall specific moments they helped you, small details that mattered. But underneath the thankfulness, grief is rising. Your smile becomes strained. You keep trying to focus on the gift they gave you, but your voice keeps breaking. You find yourself laughing and crying simultaneously, overcome by the beautiful contradiction of profound gratitude and unbearable loss. You want them to know how much they meant to you, but you also want them to stay, and those two truths are tearing you apart. End in a place of bittersweet peace—still crying, still grateful, accepting the impossible coexistence of joy and heartbreak.
inspired_by: Crying in Front of Someone Who Usually Sees You as Strong

title: Thanking Your Enemy for Breaking Your Heart
instruction: You're at a mutual friend's wedding, unexpectedly face-to-face with the person who shattered you years ago. They look uncomfortable. You start laughing — genuine, a little unhinged — as you tell them 'I should thank you.' Your voice is light, almost playful, but there's something dangerous underneath. Describe how their betrayal forced you to rebuild yourself stronger. You're smiling, but your voice keeps catching. The gratitude is real — you did become who you needed to be — but so is the grief of losing who you were. End with your voice soft and sincere: 'I mean it, thank you,' but let tears be in your throat. You're both grateful and heartbroken, laughing and crying, free and still mourning.
inspired_by: Whispering a Secret in a Crowded Room

title: The Smile That Cracks
instruction: You're at a backyard cookout, standing on the edge of a group of strangers. You're a large, older man with a deep voice, but inside you're drowning—your wife passed away three months ago and this is your first social event since. The group is laughing about something trivial. You force a chuckle, feel the silence spread, then try to change the subject to a recent storm. As you speak, the pain you've been holding breaks through. Your voice starts gruff and tight, then cracks, slows, drops into a whisper as you realize you're barely holding it together. Let the filler laughs die in your throat. Let your eyes go distant mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Complaining Resolution
instruction: You've been a bitter complainer your entire life—voicemail to a therapist before your final session. Your voice starts grinding, exhausted from its own negativity. Mid-sentence, your throat tightens: you realize every complaint was a way to avoid admitting you've wasted thirty years. Your breathing changes—deeper, slower. The words that follow are barely audible, but they're the first true thing you've said in decades. End with silence, then: 'I want to change.' Whispered, terrified, real.

title: Holding Your Dying Dog While Rage and Grief Collide
instruction: You're on the vet's floor, and they're saying it's time. Start with your voice fierce, almost violent: 'No. Not yet. We're not there yet.' You're arguing with reality itself, your voice sharp and demanding. But as you feel their breathing change, your fury cracks. 'This isn't fair. Fifteen years isn't enough. It's not ENOUGH.' Let yourself explode—rage at time, at death, at the unfairness of loving something mortal. Your voice is raw and uncontrolled. Then it collapses into something else entirely: you're suddenly tender, whispering to them like they're a child: 'It's okay, baby. You can go. You've been so good, so brave.' You're giving them permission while you're dying inside. Your voice breaks completely: 'I don't know how to do this without you. I don't know who I am without you.' End with you holding them, your voice fierce again but different—fiercely loving, protectively helpless: 'Stay. Please stay. Okay, go. It's okay. I love you. Go.'
inspired_by: Small Explosion at Work: Checking Colleagues for Injuries

title: The Certainty That Explodes Into Everything Else
instruction: Begin with absolute, explosive rage—you've caught them in what you're certain is a betrayal, and you're screaming proof, dates, evidence. Your voice should be huge, righteous, powerful. But mid-accusation, they show you something that inverts your entire reality: they weren't betraying you, they were planning something that required secrecy to protect you, or surprise you, or save you. Your fury must crack mid-sentence into confusion, then horror at your own cruelty. Let your voice break from shouting into sobbing as you realize you've just destroyed someone who loves you with your certainty. The challenge is the whiplash—from powerful to powerless, from righteous to ashamed, from knowing to realizing you know nothing. End with desperate, broken apologies that sound nothing like your confident beginning, voice raw and small.
inspired_by: Someone Proving You Wrong After You Were Certain

title: Screaming at God While Holding Your Child's Empty Shoes
instruction: You're alone, clutching a pair of small shoes. Begin with cold, controlled fury—sharp accusations at the universe, at God, at fate. Your voice is steady, precise in its rage. But as you continue, the anger explodes into something primal. You're shouting, demanding answers, your voice cracking with the unfairness of it all. Then, suddenly, the rage collapses. You're sobbing, pleading, bargaining—'Please, I'll do anything.' The fierce protectiveness you felt, the way you were supposed to keep them safe, crashes into the devastating helplessness of loss. End with exhausted whispers, your voice raw and broken, oscillating between gentle words you'd say to comfort them and guttural sounds of grief you can't contain.
inspired_by: Therapist Hearing Themselves in a Patient's Story

title: The Hearing Test Confessional
instruction: You are a teenager sitting in a quiet medical office right after a hearing test. Your ears are still ringing slightly from the tones, and your voice feels too loud in your own head. You're talking to your parent through the open door, distracted, adjusting your weight on the crinkly paper exam table. You begin by describing the test you just took—there's a hint of amusement at how you missed the beeps and had to guess. Mid-sentence, you realize you can actually hear a bird chirping outside, something you haven't noticed in days. The realization floods you with relief, and your voice softens, still too loud but now carrying a different weight. Let your volume drift, let your pitch wander, and let your articulation fumble slightly as you process this small, joyful discovery.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Skin and Thunder
instruction: You've just learned that someone who wronged you deeply has suffered a terrible loss, and you're alone in your apartment, feeling your body respond in ways that shock you. Start with tight, controlled breathing, trying to deny what you're feeling—a savage satisfaction, almost physical in its intensity. But then guilt crashes over that satisfaction, and you feel your body caught between these two violent currents. Let your voice move between harsh laughter and choked sounds of shame. Feel the heat in your chest, the tension in your throat, the way your fists clench and release. By the end, these contradictory sensations have exhausted you into something quieter—a stunned recognition of your own capacity for darkness, leaving you shaken and strangely honest with yourself.

title: The Altar of Almost
instruction: You're packing away remnants of a dream that didn't come true—closing a business, leaving a city, ending a chapter. Begin grieving what you're losing, voice heavy with disappointment and self-doubt, cataloging everything that went wrong. But as you sort through the pieces, you keep finding unexpected treasures—skills you gained, courage you discovered, ways you grew that you never planned. End in bittersweet wonder, laughing and crying simultaneously, recognizing that failure gave you gifts success never could. Your voice must carry both sorrow and celebration in the same breath, honoring the death while crowning the rebirth, grateful and heartbroken in equal measure.
inspired_by: Actor needs a quick ego boost before an audition or performance

title: The Settling of Accounts
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy who has finally cornered the friend who stole your girlfriend's diary and passed it around school. You've rehearsed this speech for weeks. Begin with an eerily calm voice, almost smiling, but let the disgust creep in as you describe what he did. The disappointment grows as you realize he wasn't worth the effort. End with a quiet sigh, resigned. Speak as if you're holding a folded note, fingering it.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Speak to Me Like You Mean It
instruction: You're a partner who has endured years of your lover's careful, therapy-speak language—their measured 'I feel' statements and emotional distance masked as healthy communication. Explode from stillness into fierce confrontation: you don't want their practiced words anymore, you want their raw truth, their mess, their unfiltered rage or passion or anything real. Let your voice shake with the fury of being handled rather than truly known. Build to a near-scream demanding they stop performing emotional intelligence and just fucking feel something. Then shatter that intensity when they finally do break—when their careful facade cracks and they sob or rage back at you. Shift instantly to tender devastation as you realize you've broken something fragile in getting what you wanted, your protectiveness and regret flooding in even as you still tremble with the adrenaline of your own fury.

title: The Eulogy That Becomes a Liberation
