instruction: You are delivering a eulogy for someone who meticulously controlled your life, and mid-speech you realize you're finally free. Begin with practiced, appropriate grief: 'They were devoted, demanding only excellence, shaping me into—' but then inappropriate laughter bubbles up. You try to stop it, mortified, but it won't stop. Your voice fractures between tears and helpless laughter. 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, I loved them, I did, but—' Relief and guilt crash together. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, overwhelmed by contradictory truth. 'They made me perfect. They made me miserable. I'm devastated. I'm free. I'm grateful. I can finally—' Your voice breaks with the beauty and horror of it all. End softly, with tears streaming but something like peace underneath: 'Thank you. Goodbye. I forgive you. I forgive myself.' The laughter has gentled into something that might be joy, might be grief—might be both.
inspired_by: Voice Acting a Video Game Character Who Becomes Self-Aware

title: Whispered Archaeology
instruction: You are lying in bed next to someone you trust completely, in the dark. You begin describing, in whispers, the bedroom you had as a seven-year-old—the stuffed animals, the way moonlight came through the window, the sounds you heard at night. As you describe these details, a specific memory surfaces: something that frightened you, or a secret you kept, or a dream that recurred. Let your whisper become even softer as you reveal this vulnerable truth you've never spoken aloud. Your tone should shift from nostalgic and gentle to trembling and exposed, as if each word is a fragile confession that could shatter if spoken too loudly.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your parent everything you've held back for years about their absence, their choices, the holes they left in your life. Start with controlled anger—you've rehearsed this, you're ready. But as you speak, the anger begins to fracture. Underneath is a child who still wants their approval, still craves their love. Your voice should move from accusatory and sharp to vulnerable and breaking, then to something more complex—a mixture of fury and desperate need. End not with resolution but with raw honesty: 'I hate that I still need you to see me.' Let your voice reveal the war between wanting to wound them and wanting them to finally understand.
inspired_by: The Thief and the Guard Dog

title: The Last Sweater
instruction: You're a young man in a walk-in closet, packing a box with things you're giving to your younger sibling who's leaving home. You're alone, the fabric of the clothes sucks up all sound, making your voice feel dry and small. Start with a practical, slightly grumpy tone as you mutter about the clutter and how they never take care of things. As you find an old, worn sweater they used to love, your voice softens, your breath catches—you're not just packing, you're saying goodbye. End with a quiet, affectionate admission, almost to yourself, that you'll miss them more than you let on.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Smile That Flickers
instruction: You're a hotel receptionist, and a handsome guest leans across the counter with a playful grin. Your trained voice comes out chirpy and high, every 'sir' a polished sales pitch. But your hips ache from standing, and you just received a text from your ex. Let the smile-voice crack — a little breath of want, a little wince of hurt — so by the end, your words droop into something real and weary.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Self-Portrait That Finally Sees Me
instruction: You are revealing a self-portrait to someone who has loved you through years of self-hatred and creative blocks—and for the first time, you've painted yourself with honesty and, impossibly, with love. Begin laughing through tears as you describe it, your voice breaking with disbelief that you could create something so vulnerable and not destroy it. Feel gratitude flooding through you for this person who witnessed your ugliest moments, but also grief for all the years you couldn't see what they saw. Your voice should catch on words like 'worthy' and 'beautiful' because they still feel foreign in your mouth. Let joy and sorrow become indistinguishable—you're celebrating a breakthrough while mourning the decades you lost to shame. End in a whisper of profound peace mixed with lingering sadness, like someone finding home after being lost so long they almost forgot what home meant. Your delivery should feel like holding something heartbreaking and miraculous at once, authentically unable to separate the tears of relief from the tears of regret.

title: The Restraining Order
instruction: You're reading a restraining order from your own child. Start with disbelief that fractures into desperate protest: 'This is insane! I'm your parent!' Your voice rises, fierce with wounded pride and fear. But as you read their words describing incidents you've minimized or forgotten, something shifts. Rage gives way to a recognition so painful it steals your breath: 'Oh God. Oh God, I did do that.' Your voice cracks between justification and horror. Let protective instinct war with the terrible realization that you're what your child needs protection from. End with broken helplessness: 'How do I fix this? Please tell me how to fix this.' Let the final moment carry the weight of someone watching their own love become the thing that caused harm.

title: The Unsent Letter
instruction: You're alone, reading aloud a letter you'll never send to someone you loved who left without explanation. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile: 'I still don't understand why you left. Some days I wake up and forget, just for a moment, that you're gone.' The words catch in your throat. 'I want to be angry. God, I want to be angry. But mostly I'm just... sad. So deeply sad.' Let your voice waver with vulnerability. 'You knew me in ways no one else did. You saw the parts of me I keep hidden, and you didn't run. Until you did.' A tear-soaked laugh escapes. 'I kept your coffee mug. Isn't that pathetic? I can't throw it away.' The emotion deepens into tender confession: 'I forgive you. I don't want to, but I do. Because holding onto this is killing something in me.' Your voice becomes softer, more accepting: 'I loved you. I still love you. And maybe that's enough. Maybe that's all I get to keep.' End with whispered release: 'Goodbye. Finally... goodbye.' Let the silence afterward speak volumes.

title: The Joke She'd Hated
instruction: You're at your older sister's funeral, standing by the casket after everyone else has left. A memory surfaces of the stupid inside joke she always made at your expense — the way she'd tease you about your voice cracking. You start to repeat that joke aloud to her, trying to mimic her playful tone, but half a word in your throat closes. The teasing falls apart into a hollow whisper as you realize she'll never tease you again. Let your voice start with a flicker of fondness and mimicry, then crumble into long pauses, swallowed sobs, and that vacant disbelief. Keep your hands gripping the edge of the casket, shifting your weight, losing the sentence and trailing off.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Grandpa's Joke
instruction: You're an elderly man on the porch, hand clamped over your mouth, trying to hold in a laugh as you tease your grandson about his new girlfriend. You start with a muffled, playful jab—'Oh, she's a looker, all right. Real beauty.' But as you watch his smile, envy seeps in, remembering your late wife. The hand stays, smothering the words; labials like 'p' and 'b' get swallowed. Your voice shifts from teasing to a raw, quiet confession: 'Look at you, all happy. I had that once. Don't waste it.' A crack, a pause as you lose your thought, then a brittle, bitter laugh.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Screaming at the Ocean After Scattering Their Ashes
instruction: You've just scattered your person's ashes into the sea, and the controlled grief you've maintained through the funeral, the condolences, the paperwork—it detonates. Start by trying to say something ceremonial, voice shaking with the effort of holding it together. Then lose control completely: rage at them for leaving, for dying, for all the things left unsaid. Your voice should crack and roar—furious, guttural, uncontained. Scream questions you know will never be answered. But let the rage collapse mid-sentence into desperate, breathless sobbing as you realize you're alone. Sink from fury into helplessness, your voice dropping to broken whispers: bargaining, begging them to come back, admitting you don't know how to exist without them. End in the terrible quiet after the storm—exhausted, empty, but somehow still breathing. Let the final moment be almost inaudible: accepting they're gone while refusing to let go.
inspired_by: Poet Reading Their Work at an Open Mic — for Their Ex in the Audience

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Leaving Forever
instruction: You're standing beside their bed at 3 AM, watching them sleep, knowing you'll be gone before they wake. Begin in barely audible whispers—you don't want to wake them because you can't bear the actual goodbye. Tell them the story of the day they were born, your voice tender and breaking. You want them to know they were wanted, desperately loved. Your voice catches on the words you wish you could say to their face. Touch their hair without waking them. Whisper the future you won't see—their first love, their graduation, their own children. Your voice fractures between fierce protectiveness and unbearable grief. You're memorizing their breathing, the curve of their cheek. End with the simplest, most devastating truth whispered so quietly it's almost just breath: 'Being your parent was the only thing I ever got right.' Let your voice break completely. Let the silence hold everything you can't say.
inspired_by: Flight Attendant: Announcing Safe Landing After Turbulence

title: Authenticity Expressed
instruction: You're expressing authentic desire, authentic pleasure, authentic need—not performing what you think is expected. Your voice is unfiltered, genuine. You're not doing what turns on the generic 'someone'; you're doing what actually turns you on. Your partner responds to the authenticity: 'I love that you're being real.' Your voice becomes more animated, more true. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's finally allowed themselves to be authentically themselves in intimate space.

title: The Scroll That Stung
instruction: You are sitting cross-legged on your bedroom floor, phone in hand, scrolling through your friend’s vacation photos. The room is quiet except for the faint hum of your laptop. Start with sharp, bitter words — envy tightens your throat, making your voice clip short and hard. As you keep staring, that jealousy slowly fades into a hollow, self-directed disappointment; your breath deepens, your shoulders drop, and your voice becomes softer, almost lost. Let the floor support you — a slight groan when you shift your hips, a long pause where you glance up at the ceiling before finishing with a whisper. End not angry, but weary.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of emotional distance. Start by wanting him to simply look at you, to put down his newspaper, to acknowledge you're in the room. Let your voice carry these small, familiar wants - the ones you've swallowed for decades. As he remains silent or deflects, let your wants build and sharpen: you want an apology, you want an explanation for his coldness, you want him to admit he was wrong. Push further - what do you want from the relationship you never had? What do you want him to understand about the child you were? Then let it crack open: what do you want for yourself now, independent of him? By the end, shift from wanting something FROM him to wanting something FOR yourself - freedom, peace, the ability to stop needing his approval. Your anger should dissolve into something more powerful: self-determination.

title: Protecting Your Child from the Monster You've Become
instruction: You're barricading your child in a room to protect them from yourself—you're infected, transforming, losing your humanity by the minute. You start fierce and commanding, voice strong with parental authority, giving them survival instructions. But terror begins bleeding through—you can feel yourself changing, losing words, losing control. Your voice cracks between rage at the unfairness and desperate, primal love. You oscillate wildly: shouting instructions, then collapsing into broken apologies for leaving them. You're sobbing and snarling, human and animal, your words becoming more fragmented as you lose yourself. You tell them you love them between gasps of pain and confusion. By the end, your voice is barely coherent—you're fighting to get out one last recognition of who they are before you forget them entirely. The final sound is somewhere between a howl and a parent's last attempt to say goodbye.
inspired_by: Historical: Former Oppressor Must Apologize to Those They Once Oppressed

title: Parent Child Role Reversal
instruction: An adult child is becoming the caregiver for their aging parent. The parent's voice carries the strange vulnerability of losing autonomy. The child's voice is determined but also grieving—they're becoming the authority now. The parent tries to maintain their dignity, and the child recognizes and respects that. There's a moment where the child has to make a decision for the parent, and both voices acknowledge the role reversal. The parent's voice carries both sadness and pride in their child's capability. By the end, a new relationship is forming, tender and strange.

title: The King's New Law
instruction: You are a town crier, a child of about ten, standing on a wobbling stone in the village square. You've just watched the king's men nail up a proclamation about a new tax on all the pigs you and your family raise. You start with a bit of awe—the scroll is huge and decorated, and everyone is quiet—but as you read aloud the details, disgust and anger take over. Your voice must stretch over distance, so drag out each vowel, especially the disgusted ones, and drop consonants at the edges. Between phrases, shift your weight, glance at the crowd, and let fresh irritation bring a sharper, more impatient edge to each line. By the end, your awe is gone, replaced by a bitter, helpless fury as you realize what this means.
emotions_sampled: Awe (slightly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Chose Addiction Over You
instruction: You're standing in your parent's doorway after years of no contact. Start with controlled anger—your voice tight, words clipped, trying to stay strong. You came to tell them exactly what their choices cost you: the birthdays they missed, the lies you told yourself to excuse them, the person you became trying to earn love that never came. As you list these wounds, your voice should crack despite yourself—rage dissolving into the raw hurt of the abandoned child still inside you. There's a moment where you almost leave, voice breaking completely, but then something unexpected happens: you see how small and broken they look, and fury transforms into something more complicated. End with a question you never thought you'd ask, voice soft and terrifyingly vulnerable: do they even remember who you were before they chose the bottle? Let the final words hang in the air, half-accusation, half-plea for them to prove you mattered once.
inspired_by: Climbing a Cliff Face While Guiding Your Partner

title: The Reaching Twice
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your cluttered living room, seated on the floor. You've twisted your torso to reach back for a worn photo album on a low shelf, but your body is stiff and the position is painful. Your voice carries the strain of the twist — breath catches, vowels waver, and you pause to shift your weight. You begin speaking with mild frustration at your own forgetfulness, but as you realize you can almost touch the album, the sadness of what it holds — photos of your late husband — wells up quietly. Let your words start clipped and effortful, then soften into a tender, resigned sigh as your reach fails and you accept the moment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a loss that changes everything—and you're trying to explain it to someone you love while your body is physically responding to shock. Start in a state of numb disconnection, words coming out flat and factual as your hands shake or your breathing becomes shallow. As you force yourself to look at them—to really connect—let the physical sensations intensify: your chest tightening, heat rising in your face, trembling spreading through your limbs. Let the truth of what you're feeling surge up through your body until you can't maintain the distance anymore. Transform from clinical detachment to a full-body emotional storm—perhaps rage that this happened, terror of what comes next, or a physical release of grief you've been holding back. Let your body and emotions become one overwhelming truth.
inspired_by: When you are a young actor asking a more experienced actor for advice about how to act

title: The Heavy Coat
instruction: You are an older adult sitting on the edge of your bed, trying to button a heavy winter coat. Each movement sends a spike of pain through your back and shoulders, making you grunt and pause. Begin with sharp, irritated mutters as you struggle—fabric swooshing over your face, breaths catching. Halfway through, you pause, exhale slowly, and keep going with a quieter, resigned voice—still pained, but accepting. Let the sounds of dressing (fabric rustle, compressed grunts) interrupt your words naturally.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What I Never Said
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner in the dark, saying all the things you can't say when they're awake. Start tender, almost inaudible - confessing small fears, gentle truths. 'Sometimes when you touch me, I feel so seen it terrifies me.' Let your voice stay soft but grow more naked, more vulnerable. Admit the ways you've protected yourself from them, the walls you keep up even in intimacy, the fear that if they really knew you they'd leave. Your whisper becomes a confession that catches in your throat: 'I love you so much it makes me mean sometimes, because I'm already practicing losing you.' By the end, you're crying so quietly the tears are in your voice more than sound, revealing that your deepest fear isn't that they'll leave - it's that they'll stay and you'll ruin it like you ruin everything tender. Let the silence between words hold as much truth as the words themselves.

title: Custody Loss
instruction: The judge has just ruled against you in a custody battle. Your voice is devastated, broken: 'No... no, you can't...' You're looking at your child, knowing you won't see them every day anymore. Your voice is thick with emotion as you try to assure your child: 'It's not your fault. I love you so much.' But the pain bleeds through. You're outside the courtroom, and your voice is just raw grief, incoherent, desperate.

title: The Friendly Fire Kill
instruction: You're in a late-night co-op game with your group, just finished a tough boss fight, and everyone is laughing and joking. You feel a deep, warm contentment—a sense of belonging and triumph. Then, your teammate accidentally triggers a trap that wipes your entire squad, and he starts making excuses. Your voice must shift from a relaxed, giggly, high-pitched banter to a sharp, controlled, seething anger—veins of fury hidden under a cold, clipped tone. Let your words hang in the air between callouts, with little breaks where you breathe or shift in your chair, as if deciding whether to snap at him or laugh it off—but the anger wins by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Clearing Out Their Room: Finding Joy in the Wreckage
instruction: You're packing up the room of someone gone—whether to death, distance, or divorce. Find an object: a shirt that still smells like them, a note they wrote, a photo. Start with tears, voice thick with loss: 'God, I miss you.' But then remember the story behind this object—something ridiculous, perfectly them. Let a laugh surprise you, breaking through the crying. Talk to them as if they're there: recall the absurd moment with building warmth, your voice lifting. Feel the joy of the memory fully, laughing genuinely. Then feel the crash back to reality: they're not here to laugh with you about this. Your laughter and tears tangle together. End with strange, bittersweet peace: 'Thank you. Thank you for this.' Voice broken but somehow also whole, holding grief and gratitude in the same breath.
inspired_by: Veterinarian Delivering Bad News: Professional and Breaking

title: The Old Master's Last Exchange
instruction: You are an older martial artist in a sparring match, lungs burning, sweat stinging your eyes. The younger opponent is relentless, but as you circle, you see a pattern in his rhythm and a quiet hope rises—maybe you still have it. Speak your thoughts between sharp, controlled breaths and sudden kiais as you feint and strike. After landing a clean technique that sends him stumbling, exhale fully, then let a hoarse, triumphant grin crack your voice—a mix of relief and fierce joy. Your tone shifts from wary optimism to a satisfied, breathless pride; include a small grunt, a slap of your foot on the mat, and the sound of your own heavy breathing.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're sitting across from your adult child who has just revealed something that shatters your understanding of who they are. Begin with your entire body braced—arms crossed, spine stiff, voice controlled and cold. You're determined to maintain composure, to keep your disappointment or fear locked down tight. Every word you speak comes from a clenched place, measured and restrained. But as they keep talking, keep revealing themselves, you feel the grip loosening—maybe it's something in their eyes, or a memory that surfaces, or the realization that your rigidity is pushing them away forever. Let the transformation happen in stages: first your arms uncross, then your voice wavers, then something breaks entirely. End in a place of raw honesty—whether that's sobbing, or soft laughter, or trembling confession—where the truth pours out uncensored and your body finally releases its defensive armor.

title: The Last Laugh at the Lunch Table
instruction: You are a teenager sitting at a crowded school lunch table, but you're on the outside of a conversation about a video game you love. The girl you've had a crush on for months is laughing with her friends, and you can hear them mocking your favorite character. Your voice is tight, pitched higher than usual as you physically lean in, trying to cut them off. You start by blurting out a defense, disgust curling your words, but as you speak, you feel her eyes on you for the first time. Your longing seeps through—your voice cracks, slows, and you lose your train of thought, trailing off with a quiet, hopeful 'unless... you like him too?' Your nose wrinkles with the effort of holding back embarrassment.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Unseen Rule
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, receiving a controlled spanking from a partner during an intimate scene. You have been asked to count each strike to help you focus. Start with a sharp gasp of pain and confusion on the first hit—your body jerks, and your breath catches. You feel disoriented, unsure of the rhythm. By the third strike, your voice begins to settle into a reluctant concentration, even as the pain intensifies. Let your words come out strained, breaking between gasps, and finish with a low, puzzled exhale as if you are trying to understand why this is happening.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (clearly present), Confusion (clearly present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Intervention That Explodes Into Truth
instruction: Your family staged an intervention for your addiction, sitting in a circle with their rehearsed speeches, but you suddenly erupt—not with denial but with the fury of finally telling them WHY. Start with explosive anger, listing every way they failed you, every moment they looked away, every time their perfection required your silence. Let your voice crack between rage and anguish as you admit what you've never said: you started using the night after something happened that you couldn't tell them about. Build to the moment where anger collapses completely and you're on your knees, sobbing, terrified, admitting you don't know how to stop, begging them to help you with the real problem, not just the symptoms. Let fierce blame transform into desperate, raw pleading for someone to finally see you.

title: The Last Crush
instruction: You're a confident 17-year-old guy, the life of the party. You keep noticing your crush across the room, laughing with a few people. You feel a surge of protective, boastful pride, your voice getting a bit louder and faster as you cut into a friend’s story to claim her attention—saying something like, 'Nah man, that's nothing. Watch this.' You walk toward her, puffing up, and launch into a funny story. But as you get closer, you see her expression—she's not amused, she's embarrassed, even annoyed at your interruption. Your booming voice falters, your rhythm trips. You try to recover with a lame joke, but the pride drains into a hollow, awkward quiet as you realize you just made a fool of yourself in front of her.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Last Dance in the Hospital Room
instruction: Your person is dying, and in this moment, you're both pretending they're not. You're describing the trip you'll take together next spring, and your voice is bright with manufactured hope, even playful. But grief keeps leaking through—you laugh while describing something funny, and the laugh turns into a caught breath, almost a sob. You're talking about the future while holding their hand that's growing weaker. Your voice dances between joy at the memories you're creating right now and the crushing knowledge that this is goodbye. You thank them for loving you, and your gratitude is real and full even as tears stream down your face. By the end, you've found something extraordinary: genuine peace and devastating loss living in the same breath. You're smiling and crying, grateful and shattered, saying 'I love you' like it contains both hello and goodbye.

title: The Impossible Gratitude
instruction: You are recording a message to someone who both saved your life and broke your heart—perhaps a parent who was both abusive and the only one who believed in you, or a lover who left you shattered but also taught you how to be brave, or a mentor who betrayed you but gave you everything you needed to survive. Begin with anger, recounting specific, detailed moments of the harm they caused—be precise, let the rage be righteous and clear. But then, force yourself to acknowledge the other truth: recount with equal specificity the moments they showed up for you, the gifts they gave you, the ways they changed your life for the better. Let these contradictory narratives battle inside you. Your voice should break between fury and gratitude, resentment and love, the desire to curse them and the need to thank them. Don't resolve this contradiction—end in the messy middle, acknowledging that both truths are real, that you contain multitudes of feeling toward this person, and that maybe that's what love actually is: impossibly complicated, unfair, and more true than any single emotion could be.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they cannot hear—something that could destroy your relationship. Use the words of a simple counting rhyme or alphabet song, but whisper them with the weight of your secret. Begin hesitant, testing if they're truly asleep, your voice barely audible. Let the childish phrases carry your guilt, your fear, your conflicted desire to be caught and to remain hidden. As you continue, allow your whispers to become more urgent, more desperate, vacillating between relief at confessing and terror at the truth. End with either quiet acceptance or renewed determination to keep the secret. The simplicity of the words should contrast devastatingly with the complexity of your emotional state.

title: The Bonk at Mile 8
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl hiking with friends. You were laughing a moment ago, but now your legs feel like lead and your words are getting tangled. You're trying to tell your best friend you need to stop, but it comes out slurred, almost drunk. Start with a forced bright tone—'I'm fine, just give me a sec'—then let it unravel into confusion and tears as you realize you can't keep going. Breath should be shallow and jagged. End with a quiet, broken admission: 'I think... I can't feel my fingers.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Lesson in the Dark
instruction: You're a young woman teaching a hesitant partner the art of verbal control for the first time. The room is dim, lit only by a streetlamp outside; you can hear the neighbor's TV through the wall, which keeps intruding. Start with a contemplative, almost tender self-reflection — you're thinking aloud about what you're about to do, your voice soft, searching, drifting as you gaze at the ceiling. Then, as you turn to them, the discovery of your own power hits you. Your words harden, a command forms — your pitch drops, and you deliberately articulate each syllable with relish. Let your voice flex between a breathy, almost questioning whisper and a firm, lifted projection. By the end, you're speaking the line not to yourself but directly to them, testing the weight of your authority, and you feel a new, fierce satisfaction bloom.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Recording Your Character's Scream as Your Own Marriage Dies
instruction: You're in the booth recording your character's most intense scene—discovering their partner's betrayal—but your spouse texted during the last take asking for a divorce. The director calls for another take, wants more raw emotion. You start the line and suddenly you're not acting anymore. The rage is real, the betrayal is yours, and you're screaming your character's words but feeling your own devastation. Let it be volcanic, uncontrolled, the kind of fury that terrifies you with its power. Then, as the scene calls for your character to break down, you do too—but now the tears are for something else entirely. The helplessness floods in: you can't control this, can't voice-direct your way out of your real life falling apart. End with your character's line 'I thought we were forever' but make it your own truth, spoken through tears that blur the line between performance and reality.
inspired_by: Voice Actor Recording a Death Scene of Their Own Character

title: The Last Sip of a Joke
instruction: You're sitting alone at a kitchen table, nursing a glass of water after a difficult phone call. You're sad—something has ended or is slipping away—but you're trying to joke about it to yourself, teasing the emptiness of the room. Take a long, gulping drink mid-sentence; let the liquid interrupt your thought, then swallow hard, exhale wetly, and resume with a voice that's both playful and lost. End with a quiet confusion, as if you're not sure why you're even trying to laugh.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Teasing (extremely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Reading Your Estranged Father's Letter After His Funeral
instruction: You refused to see him before he died. Now you're alone with the letter he left you. Start reading his words aloud—he's apologizing, explaining, telling you he understood why you stayed away. You begin with bitter vindication: he should apologize. But his words break you open. You're laughing bitterly at his jokes, crying at his regrets, angry at his tenderness, grateful for his honesty. You're feeling everything at once—relief that he finally said it, rage that it took dying, grief that you'll never hear his voice again, unexpected peace that he knew, he understood. Your voice oscillates between laughter and tears, anger and forgiveness. End with quiet acceptance—too late and exactly when it needed to come.
inspired_by: Priest Hears Confession From the Man Who Killed His Family

title: Waking Up and Not Knowing Who You Are
instruction: Perform the terror of amnesia. Open your eyes, look at your hands — 'Whose... are these mine?' The voice is flat, exploratory, detached. Look around the room for clues about yourself. Find a mirror — react to a face you don't recognize. Find photos — these people mean nothing to you. Someone enters and calls your name — you don't flinch because it's not your name anymore. Include the existential vertigo of being a stranger to yourself.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father across the kitchen table about how his words shaped you—years of subtle criticisms, comparisons to siblings, jokes at your expense that weren't really jokes. Start the scene with your voice shaking, struggling to make eye contact, sentences fragmenting as old patterns of backing down threaten to take over. But this time, you push through. With each truth you speak aloud, you gain ground. By the end, you're not yelling—you're speaking with devastating calm and clarity, claiming space you never claimed before, naming exactly what happened and exactly how it will be different now. Watch him shrink as you expand. Your voice should move from apologetic to unshakeable.

title: The Prize Blooms at Dawn
instruction: You are a proud, older woman who spent months cultivating a rare orchid for a competition. It’s the morning of the judging, and you are walking through your overgrown garden, clutching the pot. Your foot catches a root, and you stumble – the heavy pot slams into your stomach, knocking the wind out of you. You crumple to your knees, gasping, pot still pressed against you. Start by trying to catch your breath, a shaky, pained whisper – '...oh… no…' Then, as you realize the pot is unbroken and the flower is undamaged, a fierce, triumphant pride wells up. Your voice goes from breathless and pained to a husky, tearful, defiant laugh as you clutch the orchid tighter. 'Still standing. Still perfect.' Your words are broken but fierce.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Daughter's Garden, Mother's Hands
instruction: You're eating a peach from a tree you planted in the yard of your first home—a tree that's thriving while your marriage is ending. As you bite into this fruit that you nurtured from a sapling, you're overwhelmed by contradictory feelings: pride that you grew this, grief that you're losing everything else, gratitude for the beauty that still exists, devastation that it's not enough. Begin with wonder at what you've created, laughing softly at the perfection of this peach, this small victory. But let that laughter become tears without losing the joy completely. Describe the taste through both emotions at once—it's the most delicious thing you've ever grown, and you're eating it alone. End with a voice full of broken peace, accepting that some things flourish even as others die, finding strange comfort in the tree's indifference to your heartbreak.
inspired_by: Taking a Bite of a Juicy Peach

title: The Unsent Letter
instruction: You are alone in your room, finally reading aloud a letter you've been too afraid to send to someone you love. Begin in an intimate whisper, as if they might somehow hear you across the distance. The letter confesses something tender and terrifying—desire, need, longing—that you've kept locked inside because it felt too vulnerable, too much, too dangerous to want this badly. As you read, let yourself feel the unfairness of having to hide this. Your whisper should gradually gain strength, not into shouting, but into fuller, braver voice. Let quiet anger at having to diminish yourself mix with the tenderness of what you're confessing. By the end, you're speaking the words as if they're standing right there, your voice steady and clear and unashamed, even though you're still alone.

title: Condition Accepting
instruction: They want full transparency of your phone for three months as proof you're trustworthy again. Your voice wants to say no. It's a violation. But you shattered trust. 'Okay,' your voice says quietly. 'I deserve that.' The resignation in your voice suggests this is penance. 'I'll do whatever it takes.' Your voice sounds like someone accepting imprisonment. But underneath: gratitude that they're even giving you a chance.

title: Sipping a Sparkling Glass of Lemonade on a Hot Day
instruction: Take a sip of the cold, fizzy lemonade, feeling the bubbles tingle against your tongue. Describe the refreshing citrusy taste, the slight tartness, and the cool, invigorating sensation as it flows down. Speak with a tone of joyful refreshment, as if each sip brings a burst of energy and relief.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: Your parent—who abandoned you as a child—is now dying and has asked to see you. You arrive filled with rehearsed anger, ready to finally tell them everything. Start cold and controlled: 'You wanted to see me. Here I am.' But as you begin listing your grievances, something shifts. You realize mid-sentence that the rage you've carried for decades is suddenly... hollow. 'I came here to tell you how much you hurt me. I've been practicing this speech for twenty years.' Your voice becomes confused, vulnerable: 'But looking at you now, I just—I don't know what I feel anymore.' The anger tries to return but transforms into something more painful: grief for what never was. 'I needed you. I needed you so badly and you weren't there.' End with devastating honesty, almost a whisper: 'And the worst part is, even now, even after everything—part of me still does.' Let your voice break on those last words.

title: The Garden Tour That Went Sideways
instruction: You're an older woman at a neighborhood garden tour, standing with a group of polite strangers. You spot a rare rose you've been searching for years — and you're thrilled, but you're also trying to navigate small talk with someone who just said something mildly offensive about your gardening gloves. Start with a burst of excitement about the rose, let your voice rise with genuine elation, then catch yourself as you remember the awkward moment. Force a quick, tight laugh, shift topics nervously, and end by trailing off into a muttered, slightly disgusted comment about garden pests. Let your voice fluctuate between bright, breathy joy and stiff, clipped politeness, with silences where you're unsure what to say next.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Elation (very intensely present), Disgust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Giggling Through a Cough
instruction: You are a mother with a high, sweet voice, telling your young child about a magical surprise you have planned. You start bubbling with joy, nearly singing your words, but then a sudden tickle in your throat makes you cough—a sharp, explosive sound that leaves your voice raspy. You pause, clear your throat, but the elation pushes through, now with a hint of embarrassment and tenderness. Your voice wavers between bright excitement and the gravelly aftermath of the cough. Let the cough feel real and surprising, and show how you recover, still smiling.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Protective Fury of Powerlessness
instruction: Someone you love has been hurt, and you're consumed by fierce, helpless rage. Start with your whole body shaking, voice low and dangerous: 'Tell me who did this.' Feel the rage building in your chest like pressure, your voice rising with volcanic intensity: 'I will destroy them—I swear to God—' But then you look at the person you're trying to protect, and the rage shatters. Your voice breaks completely as helplessness floods in: 'I can't... I can't fix this.' Drop to your knees emotionally. Let the powerful protector dissolve into someone utterly vulnerable, voice raw with tears: 'I'm supposed to keep you safe.' The fury and the breaking should coexist—you're both the fierce guardian and the helpless human. End with a transformation: through the tears, find a different kind of strength, quieter but no less powerful: 'I can't undo what happened. But I'm here. I'm right here, and I'm not leaving.'

title: Reading Their Letter One Year Later
instruction: You're reading a letter from someone you lost—through death, distance, or choices made. You haven't been able to open it until now. Start with your hands on the envelope, feeling equal parts desperate to know and terrified to read. As you begin, let yourself smile at a memory, then feel the knife-twist of their absence. Notice the contradiction—gratitude that they existed and fury that they're gone. Let yourself laugh at something they wrote, then immediately choke on tears. Feel the warmth of being loved and the cold of being left. By the end, you're somewhere between thank you and fuck you, between holding on and letting go. Let your body experience both emotions simultaneously—the pull in opposite directions—and speak from that impossible place.

title: The Last Voicemail to Someone Already Gone
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for your best friend who died three days ago, but you can't accept it yet. You start with forced lightness, almost laughing: 'Hey, I know you're probably busy up there, but...' Your voice maintains a fragile brightness as you share mundane updates, the rhythm quick and breathless to outrun grief. Then reality crashes through mid-sentence and your voice fractures: 'I forgot you're not... you won't...' The pace becomes halting, broken. You try to recover the lightness but can't. Finally, you whisper the truth you've been avoiding, slow and devastated: 'I don't know how to be in the world without you in it.' End in profound silence, the kind where breath itself hurts.

title: Burning the Letters in the Rain
instruction: You are standing in your backyard in pouring rain, burning letters from a former lover in a metal trash can. Create every physical sensation: cold rain soaking through your clothes, smoke stinging your eyes, the heat of the flames on your face, the smell of burning paper mixing with wet earth. Begin in a state of fierce, righteous anger - you're destroying evidence of betrayal or lost years. As you watch each letter catch fire, build specific memories tied to them: image the handwriting, remember particular words, recall the room where you read them, the feeling in your body when you believed those promises. Let the physical sensations - shivering from cold, heat from flames, rain on your skin - intensify your emotional state. By the end, transform from anger into something more complex: perhaps a strange ecstasy of release, or devastating grief, or both simultaneously, until you're laughing and sobbing in the rain, feeling more alive and destroyed than you've felt in years.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Walter Mitty Option — Scene 1 Fantasy Imaging Exercise

title: The Last Conversation Before the Mission
instruction: You're a military spouse saying goodbye to your partner who leaves tomorrow for a mission they both know is likely one-way. Start with forced cheerfulness—talking about mundane plans, what you'll do while they're gone, pretending this is just another deployment. Your voice is light, almost aggressively normal. But when they say, 'We should talk about what happens if I don't come back,' your composure fractures. The fear you've been suppressing erupts—not as tears, but as fierce, almost angry love. You need them to know they ARE coming back, they HAVE to. Then, exhausted by your own intensity, you collapse into the tenderest whisper: telling them every small reason why your life is them. End with a fragile attempt to return to that false cheerfulness, but now it's translucent, breakable—both of you can hear the goodbye underneath.

title: Breathless Goodbye
instruction: You're a young man sprinting through a dark forest, lungs burning as you flee from a home consumed by flames—the home where someone you love just died. Every step is a struggle; you can only shout short gasps between violent breaths. Start with raw, urgent panic—pushing yourself to run faster, calling out a name in desperation. But as your legs weaken and you realize you can't go back, the fear fades into a heavy, overwhelming sadness. Let your voice crack, trail off into choked sobs, the words becoming slower, more broken. End with a quiet, ragged whisper—a final goodbye you never got to say.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child the Truth You Can Never Say When They're Awake
instruction: Your voice is barely audible, tender and broken. You're speaking to your sleeping child, maybe in a hospital room, maybe the night before you leave, maybe just a ordinary night when grief overwhelmed you. Start with something simple, voice soft as breath: 'You're so beautiful when you sleep.' Your tone is saturated with love and terrible sadness. Then let the confessions come in whispers—maybe you're dying and haven't told them, maybe you're leaving and they don't know why, maybe you've failed them in ways they're too young to understand. Your voice catches on certain words, pauses lengthen as emotion threatens to overwhelm you: 'I'm so sorry for all the ways I'm going to let you down.' Let tears be audible in your throat without becoming theatrical. End with a whispered promise or blessing, your voice steadier but still fragile: 'I will love you long after I'm gone. Even when you can't feel it, it will be there.' The whole thing should feel like overhearing something sacred and heartbreaking.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Promise They Won't Leave You

title: Dancing Alone in the House You're Losing
instruction: You are moving through the empty rooms of the home where you raised your family, just sold after a painful divorce, playing the song that was 'yours' as a couple. Begin by actually allowing yourself to move, to dance alone in the echoing space, finding unexpected joy in the freedom of solitude—even laughing at the absurdity of dancing through your own devastation. Let bittersweet memories flood in as you pass each room: the kitchen where you fought and reconciled, the doorframe with penciled height marks of children now grown and scattered. Feel laughter and tears become indistinguishable—gratitude for the beautiful years mingling with grief for their ending, relief at escape tangled with mourning for the dream that died. By the end, come to rest in the center of the empty living room, breathing in the strange peace of an ending, finding unexpected grace in letting go, your voice carrying both celebration of survival and tender goodbye to who you were in these walls.
inspired_by: The Vampire and the Innocent Villager

title: Unexpected Help
instruction: You're sitting across from a friend who just helped you finish a project you were struggling with. At first, you feel annoyed at yourself for needing help and contempt for their simplistic approach, but also proud that you managed to pull it off. As you talk, you're scrolling through your phone, glancing up occasionally. Your tone starts clipped and dismissive, but as you realize their assistance was actually useful, your voice softens. End with a reluctant, genuine 'thanks' that catches you off guard. Let your voice betray the mix of pride and gratitude.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (extremely present), Pride (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Beneath the Floorboards
instruction: Late at night, you whisper a secret to your lover that you have never told anyone—something that makes you feel small, exposed, like you could shatter if touched. Begin by making yourself as compact as possible: shoulders curved inward, head down, voice barely audible, as if you are trying to fold yourself into something no one can see. Your body feels fragile, breakable, like thin glass. As you speak, as your lover responds with acceptance, allow yourself to slowly unfold: lift your head slightly, let your chest open just a little, feel your spine lengthen. By the end, you are still quiet, still tender, but there is a newfound solidity in you—as if you have grown roots. The whisper may remain, but it is no longer the whisper of something hiding.

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Father's Funeral
instruction: You're giving an impromptu eulogy for your father, and you're telling a story about him that makes you laugh even as grief threatens to overwhelm you. Start with a genuine chuckle, wiping your eyes: 'God, he would have hated all this fuss.' You're smiling, remembering something specific and absurd he did. 'He once told me—' and you laugh again, but this time there's a catch in your voice. The laughter and tears are happening simultaneously now. 'He was ridiculous and stubborn and I'm so angry he's gone.' Your voice breaks, but you're also still smiling through it. 'I keep wanting to call him. To tell him about this moment, about how everyone showed up, and he'd probably say—' You do his voice, laughing and crying at once. The grief is enormous, but so is the gratitude. End with your voice full of contradictions: 'Thank you. Thank you for being my father. I'm not ready. I'll never be ready. But god, I'm so grateful I got you.' The laughter, the tears, the love, the loss—all present at once, indistinguishable from each other.

title: The Kite That Wouldn't Fly
instruction: You are a father (with a deep, masculine voice) and your young child on a windswept beach. The gale is roaring, whipping sand against your legs, and the child is holding a tangled kite string, frustrated. You crouch down to their level, trying to help, but the wind steals your words and flips the kite over. You start with strained patience, explaining how to hold it—your voice tight with the effort of competing with the gusts. But as the child's face crumples with sour disappointment, your tone softens into a tender, sideways laugh against the storm, trying to comfort them. Let your volume vary, sometimes shouting, sometimes ducking your head to speak quieter, as your heart shifts from brisk problem-solving to a worn, gentle warmth.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Slur
instruction: You are an older man sitting in your car after a dentist appointment, jaw still numb. You're exhausted—it's been a long, painful procedure. You're trying to call your adult child to leave a voicemail, but your numbed lips keep betraying your words. At first, you're annoyed and focused on just getting the words out clearly, but as you talk, the exhaustion deepens and you confess how much you miss them living at home. Your voice should start tight with concentration and frustration, then soften into a tired, lopsided longing. Let your mouth struggle with B's and P's, slur slightly, and trail off when you lose a thought.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Concentration (extremely present), Longing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Asking Someone to Promise They Won't Leave You
instruction: You're vulnerable in a way you hate. Your voice is smaller: 'Can you promise you won't leave me?' Your breathing is fast and anxious. You sound young, needy. The listener's response will determine if your next breath is relief or devastation. If they promise, your voice relaxes but remains fragile.

title: Archive Discovery
instruction: You are alone in a silent library archive, whispering as you read a fragile letter held under glass. The room smells of old paper; you are slightly hunched, barely moving. Your voice is all breath, no vocal cord vibration — shaped by air turbulence alone. Begin with a tone of quiet contemplation, just murmuring the words to yourself. Then you reach a line that reveals a long-hidden betrayal. Your whispering becomes strained, a few tears slip out, and your voice cracks as you try to keep it inaudible. End on a fragile, broken breath of a word.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Thing I Can Only Whisper
instruction: You're lying in the dark next to someone you trust completely, finally ready to tell them your most carefully guarded secret. Start by trying to find the 'right words' - but as you begin, let your awareness drift to unexpected sensations and images: the weight of the blanket, shadows on the ceiling, the sound of their breathing, the temperature of the air, a childhood bedroom, water, someone's hands. Don't judge these images as relevant or irrelevant. Let your confession be shaped by whatever pictures and sensations rise up unbidden from beneath your conscious intention. You may begin with shame and arrive at relief, or start with fear and end in quiet wonder, or find yourself somewhere you never intended to go.

title: The Final Curtain Call
instruction: You are an elderly, hyper-masculine stage actor, slightly drunk after a performance, reminiscing to a younger colleague backstage. Begin with pride—boasting about your past triumphs, voice loud and over-articulated like a stage whisper meant to carry. As you speak, the intoxication shows in a slight slur and swaying, but you cling to your dignity. Midway, a gap in your memory hits: you realize you've forgotten a pivotal cue. Let fear creep in—your voice tightens, consonants become sharp, and you trail off, searching for the thought, then recover with a forced bravado that cracks.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Fear (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast I Can't Quite Give
instruction: You're giving a toast at your ex-lover's wedding—the person you thought you'd marry—and you're determined to be gracious. Start with genuine warmth and humor, your voice light and celebratory, even as there's a tightness beneath. As you continue, let cracks appear: a laugh that sounds almost like a sob, a pause where you have to steady yourself. Express real gratitude for what you shared, even as your voice betrays your breaking heart. Let moments of joy for their happiness exist alongside your own grief. End with a blessing that's utterly sincere and utterly devastating—you truly want them to be happy, and that truth is what's destroying you. Let us hear you smiling through tears, finding grace in the middle of heartbreak.
inspired_by: The Five Stages of Getting Drunk

title: Fury Against the Dying Light
instruction: Your child has just told you they're choosing a path that will almost certainly destroy them—addiction, a dangerous person, a reckless decision—and they won't listen. Start with measured attempts at reason, but feel control slipping. Your voice rises, breaks, becomes raw with terror masquerading as anger. 'You don't get to do this!' Rage that they're throwing their life away, that you can't save them, that love isn't enough. Let fury crack open into helpless sobbing—you're screaming and crying simultaneously, your voice jagged with desperation. Then collapse into broken, whispered pleading: 'Please. Please don't do this to yourself. To me.' End with fierce, protective love mixed with the devastating realization that you're powerless. Your voice should be ravaged, exhausted, utterly undone.

title: The Sifting Silence
instruction: You're a teenager alone in your room, sorting through a pile of old school papers. You start with a sneer of contempt—mocking the childish mess, the wasted time, the stupid grades. As you sift, you find a test you bombed; your voice drops to a mumble, the shame seeping in. By the end, you're just mechanically shuffling sheets, your tone flat and numb, as if the anger and embarrassment have drained away into nothing. Let the dry paper snaps and your own muttered reading break the flow—lose a thought, then trail off into silence.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (very intensely present), Shame (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's three in the morning. You and your partner are lying in bed in the darkness after making love. You've been carrying a secret—something you did that could destroy this relationship. Begin in the warm afterglow: speak softly about how safe you feel, how much this intimacy means, how rare and precious this connection is. Your voice should be tender, almost drowsy, filled with genuine gratitude. But as you speak, you become aware of the secret pressing against your chest—a heaviness, a tightness in your throat, a coldness creeping into your fingertips despite the warmth of the bed. Let these physical sensations gradually shift your voice. The warmth in your tone begins to crack. You start to confess—quietly, almost inaudibly at first—the thing you've been hiding. Your tender gratitude must transform into terrified vulnerability, your voice becoming smaller, more fragile, as you speak the truth and wait in the darkness to learn if you've just destroyed everything.

title: The Threshold of Falling
instruction: You're a teenager alone in your room at night, lying on your back, your body responding to touch you're giving yourself. Start in a state of quiet contemplation—your breathing slow, your mind wandering over a poem you read earlier. As sensation builds, let your words fragment; speak between breaths, losing thoughts halfway. Let your voice climb in pitch, become breathier, until a gasp cuts you off. The arc goes from calm thoughtfulness to a sudden, overwhelming release—but even in that peak, hold a flicker of distant contemplation, as if you're observing your own body from somewhere far away. Speak about the poem, about 'how light bends in water,' and let your voice crack and dissolve into pure sound.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Bedtime Confessions Drifting Off
instruction: You're lying in bed, phone pressed to your ear, listening to the love of your life's voice. You're trying to tell them how amazing they are, but exhaustion is winning. Start with breathless awe and affection, describing something beautiful about them. As sleep pulls you under, let your voice slow, drop to a husky whisper filled with desire. Let the words blend, stumble, and fade. When you jerk awake, finish with a muffled, sincere declaration of love. Show the struggle between staying present and sinking into sleep.
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Affection (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Whispered Goodbye
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your lover on the last night before they leave for something that will separate you permanently—not death, but something equally final. Begin in complete silence, simply breathing together in the darkness. Then start to whisper, your voice barely audible, describing tiny, specific details you've memorized about them: the exact shade of their eyes in morning light, the sound they make when they're falling asleep, the way their hand feels against your cheek, the taste of their skin. As you speak, let yourself fully absorb these sensory details as if experiencing them for the first and last time simultaneously. Your whispers should gradually become more fragmented, more desperate, until you're not making complete sentences anymore—just naming these precious specifics as if you can hold onto them by speaking them aloud. End with your voice dissolving into breath, unable to speak anymore.
inspired_by: Imaging as Craft Technique with Endowments

title: The Inherited Rage
instruction: You are confronting your father about the emotional distance that has defined your entire relationship. Start with carefully controlled words, your voice tight and measured, trying to be reasonable and mature. But as you speak, allow a rhythm to pulse beneath your words—like a heartbeat, like a drumbeat, like the bassline of a song that makes you feel powerful and alive. Let this internal rhythm give you permission to drop the control. Your voice should escalate from restrained politeness to raw, unfiltered truth. The music inside you isn't just anger—it's the sound of you finally claiming your right to be seen, to be heard, to matter. End not in rage, but in fierce, liberated honesty, your voice resonant with newfound strength.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill the emotional obligation for a scene requiring heroic grandeur or a specific emotional quality they cannot generate from memory alone

title: The Pregnancy Test
instruction: You're staring at a positive pregnancy test, and you're calling your partner who's three thousand miles away chasing their dream career. Begin with pure, explosive joy—you're laughing, crying, barely able to form words. But as you hear the pause on their end of the line, as the silence stretches, let doubt creep in. Continue speaking, but now your elation is poisoned with growing dread. By the end, you're still saying you're happy, still insisting this is wonderful news, but your voice betrays you—it's fractured with the realization that this might be the end of everything. You must hold joy and devastation in your voice at the exact same moment, your words saying one thing while your sound reveals another.

title: Voicemail Spiral: Leaving Message After Message
instruction: Call one: 'Hey! Just checking in, call me back, no big deal.' Call two (5 minutes later): 'Hey, me again, just wondering if you got my message.' Call three: voice is tighter, more casual than it should be. Call four: 'Are you mad at me? What did I do?' Call five: spiraling anxiety, rapid speech, over-explaining. Call six: resignation, quiet voice. Call seven: 'I'm sorry for all the messages.' Perform the full arc of anxiety through phone etiquette degradation.

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your parent about the child you were—the one who needed them and they weren't there for. Start with careful control, almost rehearsed, because you've planned these words for years. But as you speak, listing specific moments of abandonment or criticism or silence, your voice begins to shake with a rage you didn't know was this alive in you. You're not yelling; you're demanding to be seen, finally, and it's terrifying and exhilarating. They try to interrupt, to explain, and you cut them off—not cruelly, but firmly, because this is your truth. By the end, the anger has burned through to something more complicated: exhaustion, a flicker of hope that maybe now something can change, grief for the relationship you never had. Your voice softens but remains resolute. You've said it. You exist.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your dying parent in their hospital room at 3 AM. You've brought their favorite childhood book—the one they read to you countless times. Begin reading it aloud to them, but let your voice break free from simply reciting the words. Let the familiar phrases become vehicles for everything unsaid between you: the apologies, the gratitude, the anger at them for leaving, the desperate wish to keep them here. Start with composed, dutiful reading, but allow your raw feelings to take over the rhythm and meaning of the words until by the end, you're no longer reading—you're pleading, confessing, releasing. The words of the story should become unrecognizable as your authentic emotions flood through them.

title: The First Sip Home
instruction: You finally walk through your own front door after a day that drained you. You kick off your shoes, grab a glass of water, and take a long, deep gulp—the cold hits your throat, and for a second everything stops. As you swallow, you speak to the empty room, your voice still thick and wet from the drink. Start with a worn-out murmur, maybe a little shaky, but by the end, let the relief settle in—a quiet, breathy acceptance. Let the gulp interrupt your words, and don't clean up the slosh or the wet catch in your voice.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Quiet Devastation: Whispering the Truth to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep. You're watching them breathe. Tomorrow, you're leaving—divorce, job loss, something that will change their life forever, and it's your fault. You begin whispering an apology they can't hear. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every word. You tell them all the ways you tried, all the ways you failed. You describe memories—their first laugh, the way they hold your hand, how they still believe you're invincible. Your voice becomes even softer, more tender, as if speaking louder would shatter something sacred. There are long pauses where you can't speak at all. By the end, you're promising them things you're not sure you can keep, your words dissolving into silence. This is intimate devastation—no tears, no drama, just a heart breaking in whispers.
inspired_by: Molly Peak: Everything You Say Becomes Emotional Truth

title: The Homecoming That Changed
instruction: You are returning to a childhood home or place of deep memory after years away, but you cannot enter—it's been sold, condemned, or you're locked out. You can only stand outside, looking at windows that once framed your life. Begin with excited anticipation and nostalgia. As you gaze at the physical space, imagine climbing your old stairs—feel each step under your feet, the exact texture of the bannister under your palm, the smell of your old room, the way light fell through your window at dawn. Let these sensory imaginings become so vivid they're almost hallucinogenic. But as these sense memories flood you, let them bring unexpected grief—for who you were, for time lost, for the impossibility of return. Transform from joyful nostalgia into profound loss mixed with fierce gratitude, ending with the realization that home lives in your body now, in these very sensations, not in the building you can no longer touch.
inspired_by: The scene requires attraction, desire, terror, or curiosity toward someone or something the actor cannot physically touch or access

title: Beneath the Rubble
instruction: You are pinned under a heavy bookshelf that toppled during an earthquake. Your chest is compressed, making every breath a struggle. You've been yelling for help, your voice raw and strained. Then you hear footsteps, a voice calling out. In this moment, your fear transforms into a fragile, intense hope. Speak aloud, calling out to the rescuer, but your words are forced out in short, desperate bursts between shallow, painful inhales. Let your voice crack, waver, and show the physical struggle. End with a plea that carries a spark of optimism.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just revealed something that shatters your understanding of who they are. Start from a place of white-hot judgment—your whole body rigid with the need to fix, control, correct them. Let yourself feel the wildness of wanting to shake sense into them, the panic of a parent losing grip. Then, as they stand there refusing to shrink, something in you breaks. Your legs might weaken, your voice might crack. Allow yourself to collapse—metaphorically or literally—into the terrifying recognition that they were never yours to shape. End in a place of stripped-bare vulnerability, where your need to be right dissolves into your need to simply know them. Let the confrontation become a surrender.
inspired_by: Actor is in a rigid or resistant environment (conservative director, non-exploratory cast) and needs to establish irreverent freedom before scene work

title: What We Don't Say at Airports
instruction: You're standing at airport security with your best friend who's moving across the world—not for a job, but to escape a life that's been slowly killing them. You've been joking and light all morning, the way you always are together. But now the loudspeaker calls their final boarding. You have ninety seconds. Your voice drops to almost a whisper. Tell them the truth you've been carrying for years—that they saved your life once without knowing it, that watching them leave feels like losing a limb, that you're terrified they won't come back. Your throat tightens. Don't cry loudly—let it be the kind of tears that barely make sound, the kind that make your voice thin and fragile. Then catch yourself. Smile through it. Tell them you're proud. Let us hear both the breaking and the holding together, the way love sounds when it has to let go.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence
instruction: You're in your childhood home, finally confronting your mother about the years she stayed silent while your father hurt you. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, kept it fair and rational: 'Mom, I need to understand why you never...' But as she deflects or defends, something inside you snaps. Your voice rises with decades of suppressed rage: 'I was a child! Where were you?' Feel the anger crack open into raw, desperate grief—'I needed you to protect me.' Your voice breaks between fury and the vulnerable sob of the little kid you once were, still waiting for her to say she's sorry. Then comes the devastating quiet: a whispered realization that she may never be able to give you what you need. End with your voice hollow but resolute, no longer begging: 'I'm done waiting for you to be the mother I deserved.' The final words carry both heartbreak and the beginning of letting go.

title: The Old Woman's Hested Amen
instruction: You are an elderly woman sitting on a hard wooden pew near the front of a small, humid church. The revival has been going on for hours; your joints ache and your throat is dry. At first you whisper the familiar hymn, your voice thin with doubt—you've prayed for years and wondered if anyone hears. But the tambourine clatters and the preacher's voice rises, and something inside you snaps open. Let pride surge hot in your chest—pride in all the Sundays you've shown up, in the faith you've passed down. Your voice climbs from a cracked mutter into a fierce, trembling chant: 'Yes, yes, I believe, I believe, I have seen, I have seen—' The words tumble out in a rhythmic, almost musical cry, tears blurring the chandelier lights, fatigue making your breath catch but not stopping your praise. End still breathless, your voice frayed but triumphant, the doubt not gone but shoved aside by the roar of your own stubborn soul.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (extremely present), Pride (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Transmission from the Colony Ship
instruction: You are a parent on a generation ship leaving Earth forever, recording a final message to your child who chose to stay behind. Begin with forced optimism and excitement about the mission, trying to sound brave and adventurous. As you speak, the reality crashes over you in waves—you will never see them again, never hold them, never know how their life unfolds. Your voice should crack and rebuild itself multiple times. End in a place of devastating acceptance mixed with fierce, protective love, whispering the things you need them to know when you're a century gone and they're old or dead. Let silence do some of the work. This isn't about being loud—it's about the moment your heart splits open and you have to keep talking anyway.
inspired_by: The Soldier and the Enemy Spy

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. You've spent your whole life trying to earn their approval, and now time is running out. Begin with a desperate, burning need to hear them say they're proud of you—let this hunger fill every word. But as you speak, you encounter their silence, their turned face, their frailty. Let the obstacle of their weakness and your own fear of never being enough crash against your deep longing. By the end, transform this raw need into something else: perhaps acceptance of their limitations, or a fierce decision to give yourself the permission you've been seeking. Let the emotional shift happen organically as the reality of the moment overtakes your original desire.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill the emotional obligation but keeps playing surface emotion without the underlying need and passion

title: Acting Calm During a Crisis to Reassure Others
instruction: In an emergency, you need to stay calm to help others, even if youre scared. Internally, adrenaline and fear rise, but you focus on leading. Describe the urgency inside while providing clear instructions. Speak with authority and calm, instilling confidence.

title: The Hearing Aid Battery
instruction: You are an elderly man visiting your deaf neighbor, who forgot to put in his hearing aid this morning. You knock, then realize he can't hear you, so you step close and speak loudly, slowly, and over-enunciate each word. At first, you are mildly intrigued by his forgotten aid—tilting your head, squinting at his ear—but your main need is to share a small relief: his lost cat has just been found safe. As you speak, you shift your weight, wipe your glasses, and repeat 'found' twice when he doesn't respond. Your voice stays loud and deliberate, but your final words carry a warm, settled relief.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wave That Never Ends
instruction: You are lying on tangled sheets, your body still humming from the last peak, but you can feel the next one building deep in your pelvis. You’re a little drunk, thoughts slow and syrupy, and you try to tell your partner something — maybe that you need a second, or that you can’t take more — but your words come out in shaky, breathless fragments. As the wave crests again, your voice breaks into a raw moan, then a gasp, then a cracked syllable. By the end, speech is impossible: just a trembling exhale and a single, hopeless 'oh...' as you let go completely. Let your voice start with a playful, intoxicated awe, then dissolve into hoarse, overwhelmed surrender, with all the natural micro-distractions of a body in cascade.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone who's asleep—a lover, a friend, someone you've never been honest with. In the safety of their unconsciousness, you finally tell them the truth you've been hiding. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate, as if you're afraid even the walls will hear. Begin with hesitant words, testing each phrase. As you continue, let the relief of finally speaking wash over you, but mixed with profound sadness knowing they can't hear you. Your voice should be tender but laced with grief—grief for the relationship you could have had if you'd been brave enough. End with a quiet 'I'm sorry' that contains worlds of regret. The challenge is to make every word feel stolen, secret, sacred.
inspired_by: The Thief and the Guard Dog

title: The Last Light Before Dark
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother in her final hour, holding her hand. Begin speaking to her with forced optimism, trying to convince both of you that she'll pull through, that you'll see each other next week. But as you look into her eyes—truly look—you realize she knows the truth and needs you to stop pretending. Let your facade crumble. Transition from cheerful denial to raw, undefended honesty about how terrified you are to lose her, how unprepared you are for this goodbye. Speak directly to her eyes, not to the room or to yourself. Let her see you completely, perhaps for the first time in years. End with a simple truth you've never been able to say before.
inspired_by: When you are a young actor asking a more experienced actor for advice about how to act

title: Whispering a Secret You've Carried for Twenty Years
instruction: In the intimate darkness—maybe a hospital room, maybe a quiet moment after everyone else has left—you finally tell someone the truth you've been hiding. Start almost inaudibly, the words barely forming. This is something that's shaped your entire life: a choice you made, a thing that happened to you, a love you never acknowledged. Your voice is fragile as glass, catching on certain words. There's shame here, and relief, and terror of being known. Let long silences fall between phrases as you gather courage. This isn't dramatic confession—it's the kind of vulnerable honesty that makes your throat tight and your eyes burn. Move from barely able to speak through trembling revelation to exhausted peace. Some truths are too heavy to carry alone, and too quiet for anything but a whisper.
inspired_by: Professional: Journalist Kills a Story About Someone They Love

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: Your child is asleep and you're leaving - maybe to protect them, maybe you have no choice, maybe you're too broken to stay. You're whispering so you don't wake them, your voice barely audible, telling them all the things they'll need to know without you there. Start tender and careful, promising they'll understand someday. But as you speak, the reality of what you're doing settles over you like ice water. Your whispers become harder to control. You're memorizing their face, touching their hair, and trying not to sob out loud. The tenderness curdles into self-hatred, then back to desperate love. Your final words catch in your throat - maybe 'I'm sorry,' maybe 'I love you,' maybe just their name - and you can barely breathe through the grief of walking away.
inspired_by: Comforting Someone Whose Trauma You Share

title: The Last Recording
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's drifting in and out of consciousness, speaking in fragments—childhood memories, half-finished thoughts, your name mixed with names of people long dead.
