Your task is to truly receive every sound she makes: the rhythm of her breathing, the texture of her voice, the spaces between words. Begin feeling helpless and afraid, wanting to fill the silence with reassurances. But as you surrender to simply listening—to what she's saying and what she's not saying, to the love and fear and letting-go in her voice—allow yourself to transform into profound presence and acceptance. Let what you hear change you. By the end, you're not trying to keep her here anymore; you're bearing witness to her journey with complete attention and unexpected peace.
inspired_by: Actor struggles to listen to scene partners genuinely

title: Reading Your Own Eulogy
instruction: You've survived a terminal diagnosis—the cancer is in remission, the death sentence lifted. You're reading aloud the eulogy you wrote for your own funeral, sitting in the empty church where it would have been held. Start reading it formally, as you'd written it: 'Thank you all for coming...' But then you start laughing—not happy laughter, but incredulous, slightly hysterical. 'I actually wrote this. I picked out songs. I planned my own funeral.' The laughter turns into tears, but you keep reading through them. 'I wrote that I hoped I'd lived a life of meaning.' Your voice breaks. 'I was so scared I hadn't.' But there's wonder creeping in now. 'But I'm still here. I get to keep going.' You're crying and laughing simultaneously. 'All those things I said I'd miss—sunrises, my daughter's wedding, growing old—I get to have them.' The tears are falling but your voice fills with something like awe. 'I was ready to let go. I made peace with it.' A long pause, then softly: 'But God, I'm so grateful I don't have to.' End with your voice full of contradictions—grief for what you almost lost, joy for what remains: 'I get to live. I actually get to live.'

title: The Garden She Can’t Tend
instruction: You are a woman in her 50s, sitting on your porch with chronic back pain. You’re watching your neighbor plant flowers in her yard, something you used to love. Begin with a heavy, weary sadness—speak slowly, sigh often, wince when you shift. Let your voice carry a raw longing as you describe the feel of soil and the ache of missing it, building to a trembling, desperate edge. End with a quiet, tearful acceptance, barely above a whisper, as the pain settles back in.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Victory Whisper
instruction: You're alone with your lover in a dimly lit room, still catching your breath after a fierce personal triumph. You lean in close, your lips nearly brushing their ear, speaking in a hushed, intimate tone. Start with a shaky, almost disbelieving whisper as you recount the tense moments, then let a slow, knowing laugh escape as the victory fully settles into your bones. Your voice should crack and shift from breathy vulnerability to a low, sly purr of pure triumph, as if sharing a secret no one else will ever know. You pause mid-thought to nuzzle into their neck, then pull back just enough to meet their eyes with a wicked smile.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Proposing to Your Partner at Your Terminal Diagnosis Appointment
instruction: The oncologist just said 'six months, maybe eight' and left you alone in the consultation room to 'process.' Your partner is crying, and you find yourself laughing—not hysterically, but with a strange, bright clarity. You pull out a ring you've been carrying for two years, too scared to use. Your voice is light, almost giddy, as you start to propose, making jokes about how they can't say you're rushing into anything now. But as you speak, the absurdity and the beauty and the tragedy layer together. Your words become both celebration and elegy. You're proposing while also saying goodbye. You're asking them to marry you while telling them you're leaving. The laughter keeps breaking through even as your voice fills with tears—you mean every word about wanting to spend your life with them; the cruelty is that 'life' is now countable in days. End with the actual question—'Will you marry me?'—spoken with simultaneous joy and sorrow, hope and acceptance, your voice carrying the full weight of loving someone enough to ask them to stay through the worst thing imaginable.
inspired_by: Hostage Negotiator Talking Down a Gunman While Your Own Child Texts

title: Shatter and Resurrect
instruction: You've just received news that someone you love is in danger—an accident, an attack, a sudden illness—and you're speaking to them on the phone, trying to keep them conscious, trying to keep them alive until help arrives. Start with fierce, commanding intensity, your voice strong and urgent, telling them to stay with you, to keep breathing, to fight. But as minutes pass and their voice weakens, your control begins to fracture. Your commands become pleas, your strength dissolves into raw terror. You're begging now, your voice breaking, mixing desperate prayers with fierce declarations of love, telling them everything you never said, promising everything you'll do if they just survive this. Your rage at the universe for putting them in danger collides with your complete helplessness, and you're sobbing and shouting and whispering all at once. End with your voice stripped bare, repeating their name like an incantation, your love for them so enormous and your power to save them so devastatingly small.

title: The Crack in 'Fine'
instruction: You are an elderly woman on the phone with your adult child. You start by saying you're fine, your voice bright and steady, but as you speak, a memory surfaces — last night you couldn't reach the top shelf and stood in the kitchen crying. Your voice wavers, then cracks. You try to cover it with a short, nervous laugh. End with the admission that you're not okay, barely audible, breath shaky. Let the silence after feel heavy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confrontation in Motion
instruction: You're on that porch swing with your parent who was never emotionally present. They've asked you to sit with them, trying to recreate peaceful moments that never actually existed. Start by describing the swing's motion with barely contained tension—your voice tight, controlled. Then let it break open: confront them about all those years they sat here in silence while you needed them. Your anger should be specific, personal, gutting—'You sat here every evening and never once asked how I was.' But as you speak, let your fury give way to something more vulnerable: the child inside you who just wanted to be seen. End not with resolution, but with the complicated mess of still loving someone who failed you, your voice raw and unsteady as the swing continues its oblivious rhythm.
inspired_by: Gently Swinging in a Porch Swing

title: Floor Memory
instruction: You are an elderly woman, sitting cross-legged on your living room floor. You've had a few glasses of wine and the world feels soft and distant. You're looking at an old photograph in your hands, lost in a warm, hazy memory of a loved one. But as you speak, the haze lifts and the ache of missing them hits you fully. Your voice starts slow and dreamy, but grows raw and present. Let the posture ground you—feel the floor beneath you, the tightness in your hips. Let your words drift at first, then land sharply.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally alone with your aging parent after years of surface-level conversations. You start calm, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you what it was like being your child.' Your voice is controlled because you've rehearsed this. But as you describe specific moments—birthdays they missed, the lie you told teachers about why no one came to your school play, the way you learned to stop hoping—your voice begins to shake with decades of suppressed rage. Then something shifts. You see them aging before you, and the anger collides with grief for what you'll never have. Your voice becomes a battleground between the furious child and the exhausted adult who just wants to stop carrying this weight. By the end, you're not sure if you're demanding an apology or offering forgiveness, and your voice reflects that terrible ambiguity. Sound like someone excavating their own heart.

title: The Weight of Letting Go
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who raised you—a grandparent, parent, or guardian—in their final hours. Begin with desperate, clinging hope, your body tense with the refusal to accept what's coming. As you speak your goodbye, allow every word, every breath to become progressively heavier, as though gravity itself is pulling you down into acceptance. Your limbs feel impossibly weighted, your chest compressed by an enormous invisible force. By the end, you are not fighting anymore—you are surrendering to the unbearable heaviness of loss, your voice barely a whisper, your body so heavy you can hardly hold yourself upright. The transformation is from frantic resistance to profound, crushing acceptance.

title: Confronting the Maestro Who Broke You
instruction: You were once a promising conductor, but your mentor—the famous maestro who taught you—crushed your confidence with relentless criticism that you've carried for twenty years. Now you're standing in the empty concert hall where it happened, and they're elderly, frail, here for a memorial tribute. Begin with controlled, professional courtesy as you help them to a seat, but let an edge creep into your voice. Your words start as questions about the past, then become accusations: why did they treat you that way? Why did their disappointment matter more than your potential? Let your voice rise from quiet confrontation to something rawer—anger that's been fermenting into poison. But then they say something—maybe an apology, maybe just a look of confused fragility—and you must navigate the terrible realization that your rage is directed at someone who barely remembers, who's human and fallible. End in the ashes of anger, voice trembling with something between forgiveness and unresolved grief. Transform from wounded rage to painful, complicated mercy.

title: The Intervention: Screaming Truth at Someone You're Losing
instruction: You're confronting your partner/best friend/sibling about their self-destruction—addiction, dangerous choices, pushing everyone away. You start firm, maybe even cold, delivering an ultimatum you've prepared. Your voice is hard, protective armor. But they laugh it off, dismiss you, and something inside you detonates. You start yelling, voice raw and ragged, listing every terrifying moment you've endured watching them disappear. Your volume rises to near-screaming, ferocious and uncontrolled. Then mid-sentence, your voice breaks completely—the rage cracks open and underneath is pure terror. You're suddenly pleading, begging, your words tumbling over each other. 'I can't watch you die' comes out as a sob. You're oscillating between fury and desperate love, between wanting to shake them and wanting to hold them. Your voice is chaos—loud, then whispered, then loud again—fierce protectiveness wrestling with complete helplessness.
inspired_by: Medieval Executioner Meets the Condemned Man Who Was His Childhood Friend

title: The Static in the Signal
instruction: You are alone in a dim, cold room after two days without sleep. Your body aches, your eyes burn, and every thought feels like it's dissolving. You are trying to recall a pattern you saw hours ago — something important — but the memory keeps slipping away. As you speak, your voice cracks, you pause mid-sentence, and you might argue with a shadow in the corner or laugh at nothing. Start with a desperate attempt to piece together a logical chain, then let the exhaustion pull you into fragmented sentences. End with a quiet, hollow admission that you cannot hold onto anything anymore.
emotions_sampled: Distress (slightly present), Contemplation (extremely present), Helplessness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight of Staying
instruction: You're lying in bed with your partner in the dark, and you're confessing something that's been eating you alive. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and terrified: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' There's love in your voice, but also a sadness so deep it catches in your throat: 'Sometimes... sometimes I imagine what my life would be like if I'd never met you.' Pause. Let the silence hurt. Then continue, even softer: 'And it terrifies me how free I look in those dreams. How light.' Your voice breaks on the next words: 'I love you so much it's suffocating me, and I don't know if that's beautiful or broken.' End with a question that barely makes it out: 'Tell me that's not how love is supposed to feel.' This isn't theatrical confession—this is the kind of truth that slips out in the dark when you're too tired to perform.

title: The Mirror on the 14th Floor
instruction: You are an elderly woman riding an elevator alone for the first time after your husband's passing. The metallic walls create a harsh, ringing echo that feels like a tiny concert hall. Begin speaking with a soft, almost fragile awe—your voice barely above a whisper as you marvel at how different the light looks from up here. Midway, you notice your own reflection in the polished steel door, and astonishment hits you: you don't recognize the person staring back. Let that surprise crack your composure, then let the awe return, warmer and heavier, as you say a clumsy goodbye to the ghost in the mirror. Speak naturally, with pauses, sighs, and the humming of the elevator cables threading through your words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Stole
instruction: You're finally speaking the truth you've held for twenty years. Start with controlled anger—you've rehearsed this, you're ready. You're listing specific memories: the times they chose alcohol over your birthday, the nights you went hungry, the fear you lived with. Your voice is sharp, precise, cutting. But as you speak, something shifts. The anger cracks open and underneath is a child's voice, raw and pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why didn't you fight for me?' Your accusations transform into desperate questions. You're crying now, not with rage but with the deep, aching grief of a child who still, despite everything, wants their parent to say they're sorry. End begging them to acknowledge what they did, your voice small and broken.

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at your younger sibling's wedding. You adore them—they're marrying someone wonderful, and you're genuinely happy. But six months ago, your own marriage fell apart, and you're barely holding yourself together. Begin with bright, cheerful energy, your voice warm and celebratory as you raise your glass, smiling at the couple. Let real joy be there—you love seeing them this happy. But as you speak about love, commitment, and forever, let your own grief begin to bleed through. Your voice may catch, your smile may falter. Let gratitude for their happiness clash with your own heartbreak, pride mixed with envy, hope for them mixed with despair for yourself. Don't hide it completely, but don't let it consume the moment either. End with your voice breaking on the final words of blessing, tears in your eyes that could be joy or sorrow or both, your glass raised high even as your hand trembles.

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner, confessing something you can't say when they're awake. Start barely audible, tender: 'I watch you sleep sometimes...' Your voice is intimate, full of love. But then the confession deepens: 'I'm scared you'll wake up one day and realize...' Now there's trembling in your whisper, vulnerability bleeding through. 'I'm not enough. I've never been enough.' Your breathing becomes uneven. You're crying silently, trying not to wake them: 'I love you so much it terrifies me.' End with a whispered plea that catches in your throat: 'Please don't leave me.' The emotion transforms from tender adoration to throat-catching fear to whispered desperation.
inspired_by: Someone Saying They Don't Trust You Anymore

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Dying Mentor Who Never Saw Your Potential
instruction: You're at your mentor's bedside, hours before they pass. Begin with carefully controlled gratitude—thanking them for years of guidance, voice steady but hollow. Mid-conversation, a truth breaks through: 'You never believed I could do this on my own, did you?' Let hurt crack your composure. They respond weakly, and something shifts—you realize they were protecting themselves, not judging you. Your voice softens into something tender and forgiving. End by telling them it's okay to let go, your words thick with grief but also release. You're holding their hand. You're losing them. You're finally free.
inspired_by: Realizing Your Therapist Isn't the Right Fit

title: The Only Girl in the Huddle
instruction: You are a young girl, around 8 years old, standing at the edge of a rowdy group of older boys—your brother and his friends—in a locker room after a game. They're all shouting, laughing, clapping each other on the back. You're content just being part of the noise, smiling up at them. But then your brother’s friend starts talking about the 'princess' who couldn't catch a ball, and the others join in, not noticing you. You try to edge closer, but they shift into a tighter circle, shutting you out. Your voice must start with that happy, breathless excitement of being included, then slowly fracture into small, quiet attempts to speak that get lost in the racket—ending in a faint, helpless whisper that nobody hears.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording your final message to your partner back on Earth. Begin with forced cheerfulness, talking about the mission's success and how proud you are, maintaining the brave face you've worn throughout your career. As you continue, let the façade crack—your voice should soften, becoming more intimate and raw as you confess the fears you never shared, the mornings you'll miss waking up beside them, the children you'll never have together. End in a place of bittersweet peace, where grief and gratitude intertwine, your voice barely above a whisper as you say the goodbye you've been avoiding. Let silences speak as much as words—this isn't about grand declarations but about the small, tender truths that matter most when time runs out.

title: Afterglow Confession

instruction: You're sitting beside their bed in the dark, knowing you won't be here when they wake. Your voice is barely audible, careful not to wake them, as you tell them things they'll never hear. instruction: You are confronting your mother after decades of emotional neglect, finally naming what was never spoken. instruction: You're at a small table across from someone you've been flirting with for weeks. You're both laughing, you lean in and tease her about always ordering the same drink — your voice is light, breathy, with a playful rhythm. But you just got a text that your mother has taken a turn for the worse. You feel the warmth of affection fighting against a knot in your throat. You try to keep the teasing going, but your voice catches, your smile falters, and the words come out shaky. Let the laughter die into a quiet, strained admission: '...I'm not sure I can do this right now.' The distress creeps in and takes over, leaving the flirtation behind.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Last Words to Your Child Before the Morphine Takes You
instruction: You're in a hospital bed, your adult child holding your hand, and you have maybe five minutes of clarity left before the pain medication pulls you under for good. Start trying to be strong for them—reassuring, almost cheerful: 'Hey, I'm okay, really.' But their face breaks you. The things you never said come flooding out: the pride you felt but never expressed, the apology for the times you chose work over them, the specific moment you realized they'd become someone extraordinary. Your voice should crack and soften, moving from protective parent to vulnerable human to something like awe. End with the one truth that matters most, the words getting slower as the medicine wins. You're not performing bravery anymore—you're just loving them with everything left.
inspired_by: Elevator Pitch for Your Life to God

title: Last Words to a Sleeping Child Before Deployment
instruction: You're a soldier whispering to your sleeping child the night before deploying to a war you know you might not return from. Start with practical things - how proud you are of their drawing today, reminding them to help mom with groceries. But grief keeps breaking through. Your voice cracks trying to stay steady. You want to say 'I love you' but it comes out broken. You're apologizing for leaving, promising things you can't promise, then catching yourself and returning to small, safe details - their favorite cereal, the park on Saturdays. End barely holding yourself together, kissing their forehead, allowing yourself one moment of complete devastation before you have to walk away.
inspired_by: Speaking While Severely Injured or in Acute Pain

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother/father after discovering a devastating family secret they kept from you for decades. Start controlled, your voice tight and measured, asking careful questions as if you can contain this. But something primal is building beneath your ribs—a lifetime of half-truths, of feeling something was always just out of reach. Let your voice begin to shake, then crack, as your body remembers every moment you were lied to. Build to a roar that comes from your core, not your throat—accusations, grief, betrayal pouring out in waves you can't control. Then, unexpectedly, crash into the child you were, your voice becoming small and broken, asking the one question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I enough to tell the truth to?' End in the trembling quiet of someone who has finally been seen.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone who made you promise not to be sad. Start by telling a funny story about them—let yourself genuinely laugh, light and real. Your voice should have warmth and affection. But mid-laugh, something catches. Maybe it's a detail that reminds you they're really gone. Your laughter becomes unsteady, mixing with tears you're trying to hold back. Continue the funny story, but now you're laughing and crying simultaneously—it should sound messy, completely uncontrolled, beautifully human. 'They would hate that I'm crying' should come out as half-laugh, half-sob. The gratitude for knowing them and the devastation of losing them should be impossible to separate. End with a whispered 'Thank you' that's broken by laughter and grief in equal measure, where joy and heartbreak are so intertwined you can't tell them apart.

title: The Echo of a Laugh
instruction: You are alone in an ancient stone cathedral, having just escaped a long, stressful ordeal. The massive space swallows sound, so you speak slowly, listening to your own words bounce off the high walls. Begin with a deep exhale of relief—your shoulders drop, you feel the weight lift. Then, as you try to say something serious, the absurd echo of your own voice strikes you as funny. Mid-sentence, a chuckle escapes. Let the amusement grow until you're barely holding back laughter, your voice breaking with joy. You're talking to no one but yourself, savoring the quiet luxury of being safe and silly in this vast, sacred place.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Comforting Someone Grieving While You Grieve Them
instruction: They lost someone and you're there for them. Your voice is warm and present. But you're also grieving this person—every word of comfort is something you need. Your voice becomes thick with layers of emotion. You're holding two grief spaces simultaneously while breaking apart internally.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they need you to tell them it's okay to let go. Start with the careful, measured tone of someone trying to be strong—'I'm here. I'm right here with you.' But as you speak, something cracks open inside you. You begin to give them permission to leave, and with each sentence, you're fighting between wanting them to stay and needing them to be free from pain. Your voice wavers between tender reassurance and barely contained grief. End by whispering the hardest truth you've ever spoken: 'You can go now. I'll be okay.' Even though you both know it's a lie you're telling out of love.

title: Wired and Weary
instruction: You're an elderly person in a hospital bed, your jaw wired shut after surgery. A nurse passes by and you need her attention. At first, frustration and quiet anger boil up—you can barely form words and feel ignored. But as you struggle to speak through clenched teeth, your tone softens into weary resignation. Try saying: 'Hey... please... I need water. No, not the straw—the cup. Just... wait. Sorry. Thank you.' Let the muffled, strained delivery reflect the physical limitation. Shift your weight, wince, pause to swallow.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Tipsy Confession
instruction: You are a child, maybe ten or eleven, who accidentally drank from a grown-up's cup at a family barbecue. Now the world is tilting, words feel heavy in your mouth, and you're trying to act normal but your cheeks are hot with shame. You've slipped away to the backyard swing set, and your favorite older cousin finds you. At first you mumble excuses, embarrassed that they see you like this — your voice wavers, you pause to swallow, you try to steady yourself against the chains. But as they sit beside you, a wave of gratitude breaks through: you realize they're not mad, they're just worried. Your voice softens, slows, and you thank them for not telling anyone, your words slurring together with raw, honest relief. End with a wobbly smile in your voice, still embarrassed but deeply touched.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Phone Call: A Mother's Final Words Before Life Support Ends
instruction: You are on the phone with your estranged mother, and the doctors have just told you they'll remove life support in ten minutes. You've rehearsed anger for twenty years—all the ways she failed you, abandoned you, chose addiction over motherhood. But now, with minutes left, the anger cracks open to reveal something underneath: the child who still needed her, who waited by windows, who made up stories about where mommy went. Start with controlled, bitter accusations, your voice tight and accusatory. Let it break. Let the little girl you were come through—the one who just wanted her mother to stay. End with a whispered confession of love you never thought you'd say, your voice soft and devastated, telling her it's okay to go now. The anger must transform into grief, the rehearsed speech must dissolve into raw, spontaneous need.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Oath-Breaker Speaks Their True Name for the First Time

title: Singing a Lullaby That Becomes Crying
instruction: Sing a simple lullaby — 'You Are My Sunshine' or similar — to someone who is dying, has died, or is leaving forever. Start with the melody intact, voice warm but fragile. As the lyrics take on their true weight, the singing wavers. Pitch slides. The melody breaks apart. By the last verse, you're not singing anymore — you're just saying the words through tears. Let the transition from music to grief happen organically. Don't force it. Let the song destroy you.

title: The Burn of a Stolen Lullaby
instruction: You are a child alone in the kitchen after midnight, reaching for a cookie jar on the top shelf. Your hand accidentally brushes a hot stovetop coil. You hiss in pain, clutching your burnt palm to your chest. As you nurse the throbbing sting, you hear your mother singing a lullaby—the one she always promised was just for you—coming from your younger sibling's room. Start with sharp, pained gasps and small, tearful whimpers. As the jealousy and fear of being replaced sink in, let your voice break with a quiet, hopeless sob as you whisper to yourself, realizing you're no longer the baby.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Spinning Hallway of Light
instruction: You are a child, alone in a long, dimly lit corridor at dusk. You've just spun round and round until the world tilts, and now you're staggering, giggling, your footsteps echoing unevenly. The walls seem to breathe, and your own voice sounds strange and stretched. Start by laughing breathlessly, dizzy and delighted, almost drunk on the spinning. Let your words come in gasps, punctuated by small stumbles. As you walk, you notice a warm light at the far end, and your dizzy confusion softens into a quiet, certain hope. End with a slow, clear whisper, calm but full of promise.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Elation (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Air Is Getting Thicker
instruction: You are a teenage girl trapped in a narrow crawlspace after a cave-in. Your body is twisted, knees pressed to your chest, head against a wooden beam. You've been shouting for help for hours, but now your throat is raw and your muscles scream. Start with desperate, frantic cries for someone to hear you, your voice strained and high-pitched, but as you realize no one is coming, the energy drains. Let your words become slower, more breathy, with long pauses where you just listen to your own ragged breathing. End with a quiet, exhausted whisper—almost resigned, but still clinging to a faint hope. Include moments where you bump your head or shift your weight, causing a pained grunt.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father at the kitchen table where you ate breakfast every morning as a child. Begin with controlled, measured words—you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. But as you speak, let the room itself unlock something deeper: the chair where you sat doing homework while he ignored you, the cabinet where the glasses rattled during his rages, the linoleum floor where your mother cried. Allow these spatial memories to crack open your composure. The words you planned dissolve into rawer truths you didn't know you were carrying. Start with the intention to stay calm and 'adult,' but let the child who lived in this room take over—the rage, the desperate need for his acknowledgment, the love that makes the hurt so sharp. By the end, you should be somewhere between furious and heartbroken, having said things you can never take back.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut recording a final message to Earth before your spacecraft drifts beyond communication range. Begin with technical updates, your voice steady and professional—fuel levels, oxygen reserves, coordinates. But as you transition to personal farewells, the reality settles in: this is the last time anyone will hear your voice. 'Tell my daughter I...' The words catch. You're not crying, but your throat tightens around each syllable. By the end, you're whispering names like prayers, your voice stripped of all pretense, raw with the knowledge that you're choosing this—drifting into the dark so the crew could survive. It's not sad. It's not brave. It's both, and it's unbearably real.

title: The All-Clear That Won't Stick
instruction: You're an older woman sitting in a hospital bed, just hours after a bad fall. The doctor said your CT scan was normal and you're free to go home—but your head still feels like it's wrapped in wool. You're speaking to a nurse who's helping you gather your things. Start with a slow, flat gratitude, relieved to be alive but emotionally numb, your voice slightly too loud as you fumble for words. Then as you try to describe what you're feeling, that relief cracks—you can't make sense of the fog, and doubt floods in. Let your sentences trail off, pause to stare at nothing, and end with a quiet, uncertain question. Your performance should feel like you're processing each word before it leaves you, aware of your own slowness and frustrated by it.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Relief (clearly present), Doubt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Edge of the World
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone on a mountain summit just before sunset. The wind is fierce and steals your breath before you can shout. You have come here against all warnings because your grown child is lost somewhere below, and you fear they might not survive the night. You shout their name into the abyss, but your voice cracks, almost swallowed by the roaring air. As you pause, gasping, you suddenly remember a bitter, sour argument you had with them just before they left—words you can't take back. Your fear is immense, but now that sour remorse seeps in, turning your desperate shouts into trembling, half-whispered pleas. Let the thin air and wind break your delivery—pause, gasp, let your voice strain and fray. Let the first shouts be raw fear, and the final words shiver with the sour taste of regret.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers
instruction: You are dancing alone in your room for the first time in years. Your body carries shame—about aging, about weight, about not being what society says you should be. Start moving with apology in your limbs, hunched, small, as if your body is something to hide. Let the movement itself teach you. As the music plays, feel your body not as an object to be judged but as the living instrument of your existence. Your breath should shift from shallow and restricted to full and claiming. Let rage at all the years of self-hatred fuel wilder movement. End in a state of physical freedom—sweating, breathless, laughing or crying, but fully inhabiting every inch of yourself without apology. Transform from body-shame to body-sovereignty.
inspired_by: Actor's ego-state is in the way — feeling not good enough, too old, not talented enough

title: Thank You, Kiddo
instruction: You're a tough, hyper-masculine father on a long hike with your young child. You suddenly hit the wall: your energy plummets, your speech slurs, and you feel hollow and confused. You sit down heavily, struggling to catch your breath. Your child offers you water and a granola bar. As you take it, you feel a surge of gratitude that cuts through the exhaustion. Your voice starts fragmented and breathless, but as you speak, it softens into a genuine, heartfelt thank-you that surprises even you. Let your words come out haltingly at first, with pauses, then find a quiet, vulnerable sincerity.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Shirt Still in the Drawer
instruction: Alone in your bedroom at 3 AM, you're holding a piece of clothing that belonged to someone you loved who's gone. Begin in silence, just touching the fabric. Whisper the first sensory detail that surfaces—texture, scent, a stain you remember. Let that detail lead to a fragment of a moment: not a complete story, just an image, a feeling, half a sentence they said. Speak these fragments quietly, intimately, as they arise. Don't construct a narrative. Each fragment brings another: their laugh, your hands together, an argument, a reconciliation, the last ordinary Tuesday. Your emotion should evolve from numb distance to piercing presence, as if they're in the room. Allow your breath to catch, your voice to thin to almost nothing, discovering tenderness so acute it's nearly unbearable.
inspired_by: An unconscious impulse surfaces spontaneously during Personal Inventory and seems significant

title: Three A.M. Skin
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to someone you love, but haven't been honest with. They're asleep. You begin whispering a confession you can't say when they're awake—maybe about fear, maybe about something you've done, maybe about how you're not who they think you are. Start with your voice barely audible, testing the words in the dark. As you continue, let the relief of speaking it aloud—even to someone who can't hear—change you. By the end, you're no longer confessing from shame; you're speaking from a kind of tender grief for your own humanness. This should feel like the quietest thing you've ever performed, where breath and silence carry as much weight as words.

title: Adoptive Bond Belonging
instruction: An adoptive parent and child are acknowledging their relationship as fully real. One voice carries the love but also the awareness that this bond is different from biological kinship. The other voice carries the strange mix of belonging and questions about origin. There's a moment where one of them says 'I'm your [mother/father],' and both voices settle into the truth of it. The child asks something about their origins, and the parent responds with complete honesty. By the end, they're not repairing a broken bond or building from nothing—they're honoring something that's been real all along, even if it was formed differently.

title: The Old Stone Crumbles
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, sitting across from your adult daughter in her small kitchen. You came to talk about her garden, but as you fidget with your coffee cup, a buried memory surfaces—you suddenly realize a lie you told her mother forty years ago has shaped everything. Start with gruff, casual small talk about the tomatoes, then pause mid-sentence as astonishment widens your eyes. Your voice drops, cracks, hesitant; you lose the thread, then find it again. Confess not to her but to yourself first, the surprise still raw in your throat. End softly, almost in a whisper, the boom of your old voice gone.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Time Traveler Warning Themselves Not to Go
instruction: You've traveled back to tell your past self not to make the choice that ruins everything. But your past self (also you) is hopeful, excited, and won't listen. The future voice is urgent, exhausted, slightly broken. The past voice is optimistic and dismissive. The frustration of knowing you can't change your own mind because you remember not listening. End with the future self realizing they were always going to fail — they are the past self's future, and they went anyway.

title: Burning Clean
instruction: You're alone in a cabin in winter. Outside, a blizzard. Inside, you've just built a fire after being dangerously cold—hypothermia was setting in. As you kneel by the fireplace, let the physical sensations completely overtake you: the searing heat on your frozen face, the painful tingling as feeling returns to your fingers, the smoke smell filling your lungs, the orange light dancing across your closed eyelids, the crackling and snapping sounds. Begin in desperate, gasping relief—you almost died. But as the warmth penetrates deeper, something else breaks open: you start to laugh and cry at the same time. The fire's warmth is bringing you back to life, and you realize you want to live—desperately, ferociously want to live—in a way you haven't felt in years. Let the physical experience of warmth after cold merge with an emotional awakening: rage at having been numb, ecstasy at feeling again, fierce determination to burn brighter. Your sounds should move from shivering gasps to full-bodied, wild, cathartic laughter mixed with sobbing. End with a roar of pure vitality.

title: The Morning After the Funeral Wedding
instruction: You are describing the strangest day of your life: the morning after your father's funeral, you married the love of your life in a quiet ceremony, because the plans were made and couldn't be undone. Begin by trying to explain how that day felt—how grief and joy became impossible to separate. You were applying makeup over swollen eyes from crying, putting on white while wearing black inside. Walk through specific moments: laughing at something absurd during the vows while tears ran down your face, feeling your father's absence like a physical presence, catching your new spouse's eyes and feeling both devastating love and rage that your father isn't there to see this. Your voice should contain both celebration and mourning in every sentence—not switching between them, but holding them simultaneously. End with the realization that this impossible combination of emotions is now just your life, and you don't know whether to laugh or weep, so you might do both.
inspired_by: Actor cannot find a real parallel experience for a specific scene's emotional demands

title: The Last Cup of Tea
instruction: You are elderly, in your favorite armchair, facing the front door where your grandchild just stood. You've just said goodbye, but now alone, you speak to the empty room. Your voice is thin, slightly creaky, with a hyper-feminized softness that trembles now. Start with a fragile, almost dreamy reminiscence—a hint of that old infatuation with life's sweetness—but as you reach toward the end, your voice falters; helplessness seeps in, a thick silence before you force out the final, broken words. Let your breath catch, let your hand fidget with a teacup, and let the last word crack.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Former Abuse Victim Saying the Abuser's Words to Heal
instruction: In therapy, you're supposed to say aloud the awful things your abuser said, but say them back to them (empty chair). Your voice starts strong, defiant. But as you repeat those words—even though you're the one saying them now—your voice becomes small, traumatized. The words hurt to speak. You're trying to reclaim them but they're still poisonous in your mouth. Your voice becomes almost a whisper. Include the exhaustion of dredging this up.

title: The Landing
instruction: You are a Dominant, still breathing heavily after an intense scene. Your submissive lies beneath you, trembling. You feel a raw, visceral triumph — you pushed them to their limits, they trusted you completely. But as you look at their glassy eyes and hear their shallow breaths, that triumph melts into an overwhelming tenderness. Your voice drops from a growl to a whisper; you stroke their hair, sip water, and murmur reassurances. Let your tone start with a quiet, rugged exultation, then gradually soften into a repetitive, soothing mantra — as if you're rocking them back to safety. Allow pauses, rustling sounds, and moments where you lose your train of thought and find it again.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Goodbye at the Platform
instruction: You are saying goodbye to someone you love deeply who is leaving on a train to a place they can never return from—perhaps a dangerous mission, a one-way journey to care for a dying parent in another country, or a choice that will separate you forever. Begin with desperate attempts to be brave, your voice controlled and encouraging, listing all the reasons why this is right. But as the departure time draws closer, your composure cracks. Let your voice break as you confess what you've been holding back—how much you need them, how terrified you are of losing them. Move through anger at the unfairness, then tender acceptance. End with a whispered blessing or benediction, your voice full of love and devastating loss simultaneously, as if you're releasing them even as your heart is shattering. The final words should sound like both a prayer and a goodbye, lighter somehow because you've spoken the truth, but weighted with permanent loss.

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: Your partner died six months ago, and you're finally going through their closet, wearing their favorite sweater, and their favorite song comes on shuffle. Start by laughing—genuinely laughing—at a memory of them dancing terribly in the kitchen. Let yourself feel the pure joy of remembering them alive, vibrant, ridiculous. Your voice is warm: 'God, you had no rhythm.' But mid-laugh, feel the reality crash back in. Your voice cracks, but you keep going: 'I miss watching you be terrible at things.' Now you're crying and laughing simultaneously, clutching their sweater. 'Thank you for leaving me with so much to miss. Thank you for being so completely, messily yourself.' The gratitude is real, and so is the devastation. Your voice becomes almost peaceful through the tears: 'I'm so grateful I got to love you. I'm so angry you're gone. Both of those things are true.' End with a whisper that's somehow both broken and whole: 'I'm going to be okay. And I'm never going to be okay. And both of those are okay.' You're finding a way to hold joy and grief in the same breath.

title: Three AM Confessions
instruction: You and your best friend are lying in the dark, unable to sleep. Start by filling the silence with safe, surface things—tomorrow's plans, a funny memory. But there's something you've never told them, something that sits like a stone in your chest. Begin to circle around it, testing the waters with half-truths. Notice your heart racing. Whisper that you're scared to say this out loud. Let the darkness make you brave enough to inch closer to the truth. Your voice should stay quiet, intimate, as if speaking too loudly would shatter the fragile safety of this moment. Reveal the secret slowly, feeling the vulnerability of each word. By the end, experience the strange lightness that comes from being fully known—the terror and relief of it. Move from careful guardedness to trembling exposure to quiet peace.

title: Box of Ghosts
instruction: You're sitting alone on the floor, rifling through an old cardboard box of your brother's things — his letters, his beat-up trophy, a crinkled photo. Start by muttering under your breath, jealousy twisting your voice as you compare his life to yours, envy making your words clipped and bitter. Then your fingers close around something unexpected — a handwritten note from your mom, one she wrote to him before she died — and your voice cracks open with elation and awe, the sound turning breathless, almost reverent. Let the rustling plastic and shifting weight interrupt your speech; trail off mid-sentence, lose your train of thought, then find it again in a hushed, wondering tone. By the end, you're barely above a whisper, smiling through the words.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Elation (extremely present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Secret Ingredient
instruction: You are a man in a busy kitchen, stirring a pot while your child sits nearby, peppering you with questions. The oil sizzles, the knife thumps against the cutting board. You start with contempt—your voice flat, clipped, almost mocking their curiosity. But as you explain a family trick, you feel a shift: a flicker of genuine interest. Let the kitchen noises push your volume up; let your tone soften from sharp to thoughtful. Speak about 60 words, beginning with a dismissive retort and ending with a real, eager tip.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're forty-five, confronting your mother across her kitchen table. Start with a controlled, measured voice: 'You never protected me from him.' You're talking about your father's verbal abuse throughout childhood. She begins to deflect, to make excuses. Your voice rises, sharpens: 'You were there. You heard everything he said to me.' She's crying now, but you can't stop—years of swallowed rage are pouring out: 'I was a child. I needed you to choose me.' Then she says something that changes everything: 'I didn't know how. My mother never protected me either.' Your anger doesn't disappear, but something shifts. Your voice becomes quieter, more complex—still hurt, but now seeing her as a damaged person, not just your mother. End with: 'We have to break this,' your voice carrying both fury and a terrible, reluctant compassion.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting a parent about a lie that has defined your entire childhood - something they hid, denied, or pretended never happened. Start with your voice controlled, almost clinical, as if you're trying to remain rational: 'I need you to tell me the truth about...' But as they deflect or minimize, your control fractures. Your voice rises with decades of confused anger: 'Do you have any idea what it did to me, not knowing?' Let fury give way to something more vulnerable - the child inside you who just needed them to be honest. Your voice becomes pleading, almost begging them to finally see you. End with a devastating shift: you realize they may never be capable of the honesty you need, and your voice goes quiet with grief, accepting that some truths die with the people who kept them. Say goodbye to the parent you needed them to be.

title: Last Words Before the Long Sleep
instruction: You are sitting beside your father's hospital bed in the final hour of his life. Begin with careful, measured words trying to say everything you've never said, your voice tight with the desperation of running out of time. Your father can barely speak, but when he does, his voice cracks with regret for decades of emotional distance. You're angry at him for waiting until now, and that anger bleeds into your voice even as you're trying to be tender. Then something breaks—maybe it's the way his hand trembles in yours, or the fear in his eyes—and your fury dissolves into pure grief. End by telling him it's okay to let go, your voice raw and stripped of everything but love, even though part of you wants to rage at him for leaving with so much still unresolved. The final moments should feel like forgiveness and devastation happening simultaneously.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Door Closes
instruction: You're standing at your parent's hospital bedside, and they're lucid for what might be the last time. You start trying to tell them you've lived the life they wanted, not yours—your voice is steady, dutiful, still performing. But mid-sentence, something cracks. You realize you're about to lose the chance to ever hear them say they see you. The words tumble out: 'Did you ever wonder who I actually was?' Your voice breaks between anger and desperate love, between needing their approval and needing to finally let it go. By the end, you're whispering truths you've never said aloud, and you don't know if you're freeing yourself or breaking your own heart. The room feels both enormous and suffocating.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're a parent reading one final bedtime story to your child who's being taken away tomorrow—permanently, whether through custody loss, terminal illness, or an irreversible separation. Start with the familiar warmth and playful voices you've always used for this ritual, making it feel safe and normal. As you read, the weight of 'this is the last time' begins crushing you. Your voice wavers, catches, steadies itself with forced brightness, then breaks completely. By the end, you're no longer reading—you're whispering apologies, promises, desperate words of love between fragments of the story. The book stays open in your hands, but you can't see the words anymore. Let us hear you trying so hard to give them one perfect memory even as your heart is being torn apart.

title: The Gilded Cage
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman, your voice a practiced, honeyed drawl, but you are high on cannabis in your pristine, quiet living room. You are on a video call, ostensibly to your best friend, but you are actually speaking to your husband's business partner, whom you despise. You are trying to maintain your sweet, fluttery facade, but the high is making that impossible. You start with a giddy, drifting commentary on the light fixture, your voice sticky and slow, but as you try to confront him about his recent scheme that is ruining your family, your anger cuts through the haze. Mid-phrase, you lose your train of thought, feel a wave of helplessness that makes you whisper, then you force the anger back, your voice trembling. End with a quiet, defeated plea, your sweet tone cracking with the pain of your doubt.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Doubt (clearly present), Anger (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing Through the Breakdown
instruction: You've just received news that's shattered your world—a betrayal, a loss, or a devastating diagnosis. Alone in your apartment, something breaks inside you. Start with physical shock—shallow breathing, frozen body. Then, bizarrely, you begin to move: strange, distorted dancing, making animal sounds, contorting your face and body in ways that feel both anguished and absurdly liberating. Howl, bark, make high-pitched wails, twist yourself into shapes that express what words cannot. Your body becomes a wild instrument of grief and rage and something close to hysteria. Let the physical grotesqueness mirror your internal shattering. By the end, collapse into stillness, your breath ragged but somehow clearer, your voice emerging in a simple, broken whisper of acceptance. The physical wildness has paradoxically brought you to quiet truth.

title: The Ceiling List
instruction: You're lying flat on your back on a living room floor after two glasses of wine, staring up at the popcorn ceiling. You're feeling pleasantly drunk, your voice slightly thick and nasal from the supine position. You start by awkwardly, softly thanking a friend for staying with you through a breakup, but the weight of the gratitude makes you emotional—your eyes sting, your voice trembles. You try to keep it light, trailing off, then naming silly things you're thankful for, until the boozy warmth turns into a drop of genuine, quiet love. Let your voice wobble, go soft at the edges, and don't force the emotion; let it sneak up on you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Tale of the Lost Ring
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a campfire, a little drunk from sneaking sips of a flask, telling your friends a scary story. You start with a light, theatrical voice – you're relieved to be out of the house and the center of attention. But as you describe finding a ring in the woods, the story becomes true: you found it on a night you were lost and terrified. Your voice shifts from playful intoxication to a shaky, halting confession, the campfire shadows making you feel watched. Let the rhythm of the fire crackle in your pauses, and let the final words trail off into a whisper.
emotions_sampled: Relief (clearly present), Distress (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Squeeze
instruction: You are a woman in a consensual, intense sexual scene, feeling angry about a past betrayal that just came up in the heat of the moment. As your partner's hands close around your throat, you let that anger fuel your words, weaving a dark triumph into the pressure. But as the hold tightens, you feel a flicker of helplessness—a small, scary reminder of your own vulnerability. Speak through the squeeze: your voice thins, rises in pitch, gets raspy, then releases into a dizzy, euphoric gasp where the anger melts into a shaky, triumphant laugh. You're angry you trusted them, triumphant you still choose this, and slightly helpless as you realize you can't breathe—but you won't stop.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present), Helplessness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, and this is your final real-time communication with Earth before the signal delay becomes too great. You start the call trying to sound excited, optimistic—telling your aging parent about the incredible view, the mission success. But as you speak, you realize this is goodbye forever. You'll never hold them again, never sit at their kitchen table, never hear their voice without that growing time delay. Your enthusiasm falters. You try to tell them you love them, but the words catch. You want to be brave for them, but grief is drowning you. End by trying to sound hopeful again, but your voice is breaking, and you both know this is the last real conversation you'll ever have.

title: Jealous Kiss
instruction: You are a teenage girl kissing someone you've secretly envied — your best friend's boyfriend, the one you've watched from afar. Start with bitterness, your lips tight and resentful, but as the kiss deepens, you feel a reluctant awe at how close you are, at the taste and warmth. Let your voice be breathy and close, with soft, wet smacks and pauses where you lose your breath. Speak in short gasps between kisses, your words beginning with jealous accusation and ending in a hushed, almost worshipful murmur.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Bitterness (clearly present), Awe (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Rage of the Protector Who Failed
instruction: You're confronting the person who hurt someone you love while you were supposed to be protecting them. Start with white-hot fury, voice shaking with barely controlled violence: 'I trusted you. I left them with you because I trusted you.' Your rage is volcanic but precise: 'Do you have any idea what you've done? Do you understand what you've taken from them?' But then something cracks—beneath the rage is crushing guilt and self-hatred: 'I should have known. I should have seen the signs.' Your voice breaks, fury turning inward: 'I failed them. I was supposed to keep them safe and I FAILED.' You're nearly screaming through tears now, the rage and guilt indistinguishable. Then, gathering yourself with tremendous effort, you find a new emotion—fierce, protective determination mixed with helplessness: 'I can't undo what happened. I can't take their pain away.' Your voice drops to something raw and almost pleading: 'But I swear to you—I will spend the rest of my life making sure they know they matter. That they're believed. That it wasn't their fault.' The final words mix rage, love, and devastating regret: 'And you? You don't get to exist in their world anymore.'

title: The Last Time I'll Touch Your Face
instruction: Your lover is leaving tomorrow—not for another person, but for a calling, a mission, a path where you can't follow. It's late at night, and you're tracing their features with your fingers in the dark, trying to memorize them. Your voice is barely a whisper, tender and breaking. You're naming the small things you love—the scar above their eyebrow, how they breathe when they sleep. But underneath the tenderness, grief is rising. Your breathing catches. Words become fragments. You try to say 'I understand' but it comes out choked. The arc is from soft reverence through trembling denial to quiet, throat-caught devastation. This is intimacy at its most fragile. Let pauses speak. Let your voice shake without trying to control it. This is love and loss happening simultaneously.

title: Condition Medical
instruction: You're telling someone about your Ehlers-Danlos syndrome for the first time. Your voice starts clinical: 'It's a connective tissue disorder.' But then you describe it lived: 'My joints dislocate without warning. Pain is my baseline.' Your voice becomes vulnerable. 'I'm not broken, I'm just built different.' The last part is defensive, protective. You're explaining disability to someone who needs to understand you're still whole.

title: The Apology Your Ex Never Gave You
instruction: You're speaking the words your ex should have said but never will—giving yourself the apology you deserved. Start in their voice, tentative and ashamed: 'I saw the way I hurt you...' But this isn't mockery; it's tender, almost sacred. Your voice catches on the specific memories—'That night I made you feel small,' 'The time I chose cruelty over kindness.' As you speak the apology you needed, your own grief surfaces underneath. Your voice becomes layered: speaking as them, but feeling as you. The words 'I'm sorry' emerge barely above a whisper, trembling with both the pain of what happened and the bittersweet release of finally hearing what your heart required. End with your own voice returning, exhaling something like forgiveness or goodbye—you're not sure which.
inspired_by: Recognizing Abuse Pattern Repeating in New Relationship

title: The Broken Vase
instruction: You walk into your home to find your partner has smashed the vase your late grandmother left you—the only thing you have from her. It wasn't an accident; it was rage during a fight about something else entirely. Your body should arrive already shaking with adrenaline. Start with cold, dangerous quiet—the kind of fury that makes your hands tremble, your jaw clench, your words precise and cutting. But as you pick up the pieces, as your fingers touch the broken ceramic, the anger transforms into something more complex. Your grandmother's face floods your memory. The grief hits. Let your voice crack, let the rage dissolve into sobbing, your body curling around the broken pieces. But don't stay there—end with a strange, exhausted laugh mixed with tears, because you realize the vase was never the point, and neither is this fight. Your voice should be hoarse, tender, asking: 'What are we doing to each other?'

title: The Gale-Wind Goodbye
instruction: You are a man in your 50s, standing on a rocky cliff at dusk, saying goodbye to a lover you know you'll never see again. The wind roars, whipping your coat and hair, forcing you to turn your face away to breathe. You shout your words, trying to be heard over the gale, your voice cracking with raw lust and an ache that builds as you realize this is the final moment. Start with fierce, hungry desire as you describe their beauty, but as the wind steals your breath, let the sound sink into a hoarse, trembling whisper of loss. React to the wind: cough, wipe your face, shout, then pull back as the emotion shifts from scorching passion to hollow devastation.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what's left of your childhood home after the wildfire, finding a single surviving photograph. Begin laughing—real, surprised laughter—at the absurdity that this random picture made it when everything else burned. Let the laughter be genuine relief, almost giddy. As you describe what's in the photo and what it meant, your laughter should gradually become textured with tears, until you can't tell if you're laughing or crying. Your voice lifts with gratitude ('At least we got out. At least we're alive.') while simultaneously breaking with loss. End in a strange peace—smiling through tears, finding something like joy in the fact that you're here to grieve, that love survives even when everything else is ash. Make the contradictions coexist naturally, the way they do in real grief. Let your voice embody the human ability to hold joy and sorrow in the same breath, to find grace in devastation.

title: The Inheritance of Disappointment
instruction: You're confronting a parent who has spent years subtly—or not so subtly—communicating that you've never been enough. Begin in a place of trembling rage, your body tight with decades of swallowed anger. Start listing, one by one, every single thing you've actually accomplished in your life that they never acknowledged or celebrated. But as you continue speaking—through clenched teeth at first—something unexpected begins to happen. With each achievement you name, you realize you're not saying this for them anymore; you're saying it for yourself. Your anger begins to transmute into a fierce, unshakeable self-recognition. By the end, you should arrive at a place where their validation no longer matters. Your voice transforms from accusatory and desperate for acknowledgment to calm, certain, and free. You're not asking them to see you anymore—you finally see yourself.

title: Empty House, Full Heart
instruction: You're standing center stage in an empty auditorium, the house lights dim. A faint echo returns your voice from the back wall. You're amused by the absurdity of rehearsing alone, chuckling at a forgotten line. But as your eyes sweep the dark seats, the humor fades into a quiet weight—a realization of all the people who never showed up, or the ones you never let in. Speak to the empty space, letting your voice naturally project then shrink, pausing when your own echo surprises you, and end in a softer, almost confessional tone.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Tooth
instruction: You're an older adult at a dimly lit kitchen table, nursing a mug of lukewarm tea. A persistent ache throbs in your back molar, making you talk with a guarded, one-sided mouth — you wince when cold air hits it. You realize a cherished old friend has just walked in, and you're flooded with fondness, but simultaneously embarrassed by your slurry, pained speech and a slight buzz from the wine you sipped to dull the pain. Start with affectionate, distracted greetings, then confess your dental misery with a mix of self-conscious chuckles and genuine warmth, ending in a resigned, tender laugh as you gesture to the empty wine bottle.
emotions_sampled: Affection (clearly present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Frostbite Setting In: Voice Becoming Slurred as Body Shuts Down
instruction: You're in extreme cold, narrating your survival attempts. Your voice initially is coherent, describing your surroundings, your efforts to stay warm. Then the cold begins to win. Your voice becomes noticeably slower, words more slurred, as hypothermia starts affecting your cognition. Include the moment where you're aware your voice is slurring but you can't stop it. You're thinking about staying here, just lying down. Your voice becomes almost peaceful, dangerously so. 'It's warm under the snow.' You're describing numbness like it's a gift. Your voice becomes almost dreamy. Then pain—the refreezing—and your voice becomes sharp again, aware, terrified. This contradiction between what your body wants (sleep) and what your mind is screaming (survive) plays out in your voice.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's hospital bedside in her final hours, and she's asking for permission to let go—but you're not ready. Start with that fierce, desperate certainty that if you just hold on tight enough, speak clearly enough, she'll stay. Your voice is controlled, almost like you're bargaining with death itself. But as you speak, feel the certainty crumbling. The measured pace breaks. Your breath catches. By the end, you're no longer commanding her to stay—you're whispering that it's okay to go, even though every cell in your body is screaming against it. Let your voice crack where it needs to. This is the moment your absolute conviction shatters into tender, heartbroken release.

title: The Last Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the final hour of her life. She's unconscious, breathing shallow and irregular. Begin by trying to hold yourself together—speaking to her in a measured, controlled way, telling her it's okay to go, that you'll be fine. But as you sit there, every childhood fear surfaces: the dark hallway in her house where you once got lost, the thunderstorm when you were six and she held you, the nightmare you had about losing her when you were ten. Let these fears wash over you, speaking them aloud as they come—switching rapidly from one to another—until your composure shatters completely. End in raw, unguarded grief, telling her the truth: you're terrified to live in a world without her.
inspired_by: Switch-Trick Exercise in Fear and Terror Areas

title: The Breaking Point: Defending Your Child Against a System That Won't Listen
instruction: You're in a room with administrators, social workers, or officials who have the power to determine your child's future, and they're getting it catastrophically wrong. You start controlled, presenting facts, trying to play by their rules because you know their power. But as they dismiss you, as they reduce your child to a file, to a problem, something in you ignites. Your voice escalates from measured explanation to fierce advocacy to raw fury. You're a parent in full protective rage, voice shaking with the violence of your love. Then suddenly, the rage cracks and underneath is terror—the helpless panic of someone who would do anything but has no power. You plead, your voice breaking. You try to compose yourself, then lose it again. You end in a place of devastating clarity: you will not stop fighting, you cannot stop, even if it destroys you, because this is your child and you are all they have. Your voice is both sword and shield, fierce and utterly vulnerable.
inspired_by: Historical: Witness to Atrocity Must Testify Against Perpetrators Now in Power

title: The Farewell Recording
instruction: You're listening to a voice message your grandmother left you the night before she died—one you couldn't bring yourself to hear until now, two years later. Begin with your finger hovering over 'play,' your breathing shallow with dread. Her voice fills the room, and you react in real-time: at first you're frozen, barely breathing, as she says 'My darling, I need you to know...' Then tears come—quiet, uncontrollable—as she tells you things she never said in life: her pride in you, her regrets, her hope that you'll forgive yourself for not being there at the end. Your breath catches on sobs you're trying to contain. As her message ends with 'I love you more than my own life,' you break completely—but then, through the grief, something shifts. You whisper 'Thank you' to the silence, and your voice becomes tender, almost smiling through tears: 'I hear you now, Grandma. I finally hear you.' End with a deep, shuddering breath that sounds like both grief and relief—the kind of exhale that comes when you've been holding something in for years.

title: Joy at the Funeral
instruction: You have just received devastating news and miraculous news within hours of each other—someone died and someone was born, you lost everything and gained freedom, you're saying goodbye and hello simultaneously. You're speaking with someone who only knows half the story. Begin from whichever emotion is strongest in this moment. But let their reactions to what you're telling them genuinely shift your emotional weather. If they express sympathy, does it release your grief or make you suddenly laugh at the absurdity? If they celebrate with you, does joy flood in or does the grief intensify? Don't decide in advance which emotion wins—let their moment-to-moment responses pull you between contradictory feelings. You might be laughing and crying in the same breath, furious and grateful, hopeful and despairing. Let these emotions crash into each other naturally based on what they give you. End in a complex emotional place that holds multiple truths at once.

title: The Words I Can't Take Back
instruction: You're in the dark, speaking to someone you love, confessing something that's been eating you alive. Your voice starts barely audible—you can hardly force the words out. 'I need to tell you something, and I'm terrified.' Build slowly through shame, through the weight of a secret kept too long. Maybe it's a betrayal, maybe it's a truth about yourself you've hidden, maybe it's something you did that you can never undo. Your voice catches, breaks, continues. Let silence speak between phrases—the pauses are as important as the words. As you near the end of your confession, something shifts: beneath the shame, there's desperate love, a plea for understanding. Your final whisper mixes self-loathing with fragile hope: 'I'm still me... am I still yours?' The vulnerability is so complete it's almost unbearable to witness.

title: Screaming Truth at Someone You Love Who's Destroying Themselves
instruction: You're confronting someone you love—partner, sibling, child—who is spiraling, self-destructing, and you've reached your breaking point. Start with controlled intensity, trying so hard to stay calm, but the stutter betrays your desperation: 'P-please, just listen to me for once.' They deflect or deny, and you explode—not into volume alone but into raw, uncontrolled emotion. Your voice cracks, words tumble out through stutter and tears and rage: 'You're k-killing yourself and I c-can't—I can't watch this anymore!' The stutter intensifies as you sob and shout simultaneously, fierce protectiveness colliding with utter helplessness. Then suddenly you collapse inward, voice dropping to broken whisper: 'I don't know how to save you.' The stutter softens into something fragile. Your final words come slowly, each one torn from your chest, clear and quiet and surrendered: 'But I will love you. Even if you don't love yourself.' End in shattered stillness.

title: Concrete Apology
instruction: You are a father who just lost his temper with your child in a concrete stairwell. Your voice booms off the walls as you start, harsh and defensive, trying to justify yourself—the echo making every word feel bigger and uglier. But halfway through, you hear your child's small, scared breath, and the shame hits you like a wave. Your words crack, slow down, lose their force; you fumble for a way to say sorry while footsteps from above make you pause. End in a quiet, broken whisper that the stairwell seems to swallow whole.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Bench
instruction: You are a 16-year-old boy, sitting on the last bench of a nearly empty school bus, watching the kid who used to be your best friend walk away down the street with a group of kids who now torment you daily. You've been quiet for weeks, holding it in, but today something snaps. Start by muttering to yourself, bitter and low, your voice dropping into a slow, lazy growl that barely moves your lips. As you speak, let the anger simmer — but by the end, let your voice waver as a flicker of old hurt breaks through, revealing you're not just angry, but also deeply hurt and lonely. Talk directly to that kid as if he can hear you, even though he's gone.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Telling Your Parent You Remember Everything They Did
instruction: You're finally confronting the parent who hurt you as a child, years later, face to face. Start quiet, almost too calm: 'I need to tell you what I remember.' Your voice is measured, controlled, because you've rehearsed this. But as you speak specific memories, the control starts slipping. Hear your voice shake with suppressed rage: 'I was eight years old.' Let anger surge—'You knew what you were doing'—then crack into the pain of the abandoned child still inside you. Your voice becomes younger, smaller: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' They respond—maybe with denial, maybe with tears, maybe with justification. Your emotions shift wildly: fury, grief, a desperate need for them to finally see you, disgust, and underneath it all, the terrible truth that part of you still wants their love. End somewhere unexpected: maybe with pity for them, maybe with final severance, maybe with exhausted acceptance that they'll never understand. The arc moves from controlled confrontation to volcanic emotion to something transformed.
inspired_by: Asking Your Best Friend If Your Friendship Still Works

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at 3am. For years, you've carried guilt about choosing your career over spending time with them. Now, barely conscious, they suddenly grip your hand and whisper that they were always proud, that you should stop punishing yourself. Start with the exhausted numbness of a long vigil, feeling disconnected and rehearsing what you wish you'd said. As their words sink in, let yourself truly hear them for the first time - allow the relief, the grief, and the permission to finally arrive in your body. Speak your response as if you're discovering the words in real-time, not performing a goodbye you've imagined. Let the emotion find you rather than announcing it.
inspired_by: Actor is experiencing result-consciousness or awareness of being on stage—the acting consciousness is too close to the surface

title: Recovery: Noticing Physical Capability Returning
instruction: You've been recovering from serious illness or addiction and you notice something small: you walked to the mailbox without being exhausted. Your voice carries cautious hope: 'I felt strong today. For like, a few minutes, I felt like myself.' Include the moment where you're aware this is tiny progress but also that it's real. Your voice becomes almost awed: 'I remember what strength feels like.' You're not healed—you're still broken in ways you're learning to carry—but your voice reflects that healing isn't binary. There's a middle ground where you're stronger than yesterday but not yet who you were. Your voice contains both gratitude and grief for the person you used to be who could do things without thinking about it.

title: The Last Visit Before the Execution
instruction: You're visiting someone you love on death row, hours before their execution. You have five minutes to say everything—decades of shared memories, forgiveness you never gave, love you were too proud to speak. You start trying to be strong, condensing a lifetime into practical words: 'I just wanted you to know I understand now.' But as you speak, the enormity of forever crashes in. Your voice begins controlled, almost businesslike in its efficiency, protecting both of you. Then it fractures—words become harder to form, breath catches, and you realize you're not summarizing a life, you're saying goodbye to one. End on a whisper that holds both acceptance and unbearable loss, as you try to give them peace while your own heart is being torn apart.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Named You Wrong
instruction: You're face-to-face with your mother, finally telling her that the name she gave you never fit, that you've been carrying it like an ill-fitting coat your whole life.
