Like I'm too much feeling for one body to hold.' You're whispering a confession that terrifies you: 'I'm scared that you'll wake up one day and realize you could do so much better. That I'm too broken, too much work.' Your breath catches: 'And the worst part is... I know that's not what you think. You keep showing me otherwise. But I can't stop waiting for you to leave.' Tears are silent but present: 'I want to believe I deserve this. I want to trust that you're staying.' By the end, a whispered plea that's also a promise: 'Help me believe it. And be patient while I learn how.'

title: Tasting What Memory Tastes Like
instruction: You're alone, eating the yogurt your late partner always bought—the exact brand, the specific flavor they loved. Start with a whisper, barely describing the taste, as if speaking too loud will shatter something. The creamy texture brings them back so vividly it hurts. Your voice should be intimate, catching on words, pausing to breathe through the weight. Describe not just the yogurt, but what it meant—lazy Sunday mornings, their laugh, the way they'd steal a spoonful from your bowl. Let quiet devastation creep in: this simple taste is all you have left. End in near-silence, your voice paper-thin, as you realize you're forgetting the sound of their voice but you'll never forget this flavor.

title: The Homecoming That Breaks You Open
instruction: You have just returned to your childhood home after years away, following a major life achievement that should make you proud, but someone who should have been here to see it has died. As you walk through the rooms, every single object delivers a contradictory emotional punch: your achievement photos make you feel both proud and hollow because they can't see them, their empty chair fills you with both relief (from old tensions) and devastating loss, the kitchen smells like both celebration and absence, your old bedroom holds both dreams fulfilled and the ghost of who you once were, the garden outside shows both beautiful growth and painful neglect. Let each object or space you notice deepen the complexity of what you feel. Begin with a fragile smile, trying to hold onto the joy of your achievement. As each meaningful detail around you layers grief onto pride, anger onto love, resentment onto gratitude, let the contradictions crack you open until you're experiencing all of it simultaneously—laughing and crying, celebrating and mourning, finally feeling everything you've been holding back.
inspired_by: Surround Yourself with Meaningful and Impacting Choices

title: Reading Your Mother's Letter After She's Gone
instruction: You're alone, holding the letter your mother left you before she died - the apology she could never say in life. Start reading her words aloud with guarded distance, your voice flat and protected. But as you read deeper, her raw honesty breaks through your defenses. Your voice begins to crack as she confesses her failures, her fear of losing you, why she pushed you away. By the end, you're weeping but also laughing softly at a memory she shares, forgiving her even as your heart shatters that this conversation came too late. Your voice moves from bitter protection to devastated tenderness to bittersweet release.
inspired_by: Choosing Your Recovery Over Your Relationship

title: Watching You Arrive
instruction: You're waiting at an airport arrivals gate for someone you're intensely, almost unbearably attracted to—someone you've been apart from for months. Begin vibrating with anticipation, scanning the crowd with hungry, impatient eyes. But the wait stretches. As minutes pass, start noticing everything around you with startling intensity: a child's shoelace dragging, the exact pitch of the announcement system, how a stranger carries their exhaustion, the smell of coffee and jet fuel, the texture of your own pulse. Let your physical arousal and emotional hunger amplify your perception until everything feels erotic, alive, almost too vivid to bear. When you finally spot them emerging from the gate, all that accumulated sensory intensity crashes into a single point. End overwhelmed—not just with desire, but with the strange beauty of having paid attention to everything while waiting for the one thing.

title: The Dent in My Trowel
instruction: You are an older adult on the phone with a neighbor who borrowed your favorite garden trowel and returned it with a dent and crack. Start with a nasal, droning tone, dragging out vowels as you describe the damage—your voice drips with contempt and a faint sourness. Then, mid-sentence, you remember the neighbor's hilariously flustered apology and a genuine, intense amusement rises in your chest. Let the amusement slip into your voice, making it lighter and almost sing-song, but keep a slight edge of sourness. End with a reluctant chuckle and one last drawn-out complaint about the trowel's ruined edge.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (clearly present), Amusement (very intensely present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Lost Lock
instruction: You are a child, about nine years old, alone in the kitchen late at night. You've just snuck a sip of what you thought was juice from a bottle left on the counter, but it was something very strong. Your head feels floaty, your tongue is heavy, and the world is tilting. You pick up your parent's voice assistant and, in a hushed, slurred voice, try to ask it for a bedtime story, but you keep forgetting what you're saying halfway through and your pronunciation is all wrong. Start with a giddy, slightly drunken giggle, then struggle to form clear words with exaggerated, robotic slowness; your voice should morph from a loopy confusion into a quiet, scared realization that you need help.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Spell Before Parting
instruction: You are a young witch saying goodbye to your familiar—a cat who has been your companion since childhood—as they prepare to cross into the spirit realm after living their final life. Begin with forced cheerfulness as you try to teach them one last spell, pretending this is just another ordinary lesson. As the reality of their departure sets in, let your voice crack and falter. The cat, initially sarcastic to shield their own pain, gradually softens into tenderness. End in a whispered exchange where you both drop all pretense—your optimism dissolving into quiet devastation, their cynicism melting into love. Let long pauses speak what words cannot. This is about two souls who've hidden behind humor finally letting each other see their hearts breaking.
inspired_by: The Young Witch and Her Talking Cat

title: Whispering the Secret You've Carried Alone
instruction: Late at night, in intimate quiet, you're finally confessing something you've held inside for years - perhaps a loss, a guilt, a love never spoken. Your voice begins barely above a whisper, fragile and uncertain: 'I need to tell you something I've never told anyone.' There's trembling in your breath, pauses where emotion catches in your throat. As you speak, relief mixes with sorrow, your voice gaining slight strength even as tears come: 'It's been so heavy, carrying this alone.' End with quiet gratitude edged with lingering sadness: 'Thank you for listening. Thank you for staying.' Let the words come haltingly, imperfectly, the way painful truths actually emerge in the dark.

title: The Last Request
instruction: You are an elderly man in a hospital corridor, sitting on a plastic chair while your son stands over you, clearly fed up. You need to ask him for money for a hidden medical bill, but pride and shame keep making you start and stop. Begin with a strained, embarrassed apology for wasting his time, your voice thin and high, eyes fixed on the floor. As he moves to leave, panic rises — your pitch cracks, breath goes shaky, and you blurt out the real reason, speaking fast and stumbling over words, desperate to stop him from walking away. Let the humiliation sit in every pause and throat-clearing, but by the end, let the raw need for help overpower everything.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Candy She Crushes
instruction: You are an older woman with a voice that sounds sweet and delicate, but inside you are cold. You sit alone in a quiet room, slowly crunching on a hard candy. The sharp snaps and irregular pauses for swallowing break your speech. At first you speak with emotional numbness, as if you barely care about the words. But as you continue, a deep malevolence seeps through—your tone turns icy, deliberate, and threatening. Your mouth fills with candy shards, and you let the crunching sound emphasize your malice. Start detached, end pure venom.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Summit Declaration
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl who has pushed yourself to hike above 14,000 feet, determined to prove you belong here with the experienced climbers. Now, winded and dizzy, you stop to record a voice memo for your skeptical dad back home. Start by trying to sound triumphant and capable, but your gasping, wincing breaths betray the altitude's grip. As you describe the view and your pride in making it this far, your voice slows, words falter—you lose a thought, then find it again. End with a quiet, defiant whisper: you're not turning back, even as your body rebels.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Holding Hands in the Hospital Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM in a hospital room. Your partner of twenty years is asleep after surgery, and you're holding their hand in the darkness, speaking in whispers they probably can't hear. Start by describing the first time you held their hand—how nervous you were, how your palms were sweating. Your voice should be tender, almost smiling at the memory. Slowly let the fear creep in. Describe how their hand feels different now—cooler, thinner—and how terrified you are of a future where you can't reach for it anymore. Your whisper becomes ragged, catching on tears you're trying to hold back because you don't want to wake them. Confess the small, stupid things you never said: that you loved how they hummed while doing dishes, that you kept every birthday card, that you're not ready, you'll never be ready. End with your voice breaking on a simple 'please stay.' The journey is from sweet nostalgia to quiet, devastating terror of loss.

title: Watching Someone You Raised Walk Away Forever
instruction: You're at an airport, train station, or spaceport saying goodbye to someone you raised—a child, a younger sibling, a student—who is leaving for something dangerous and necessary that you cannot follow them to. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be supportive, giving practical advice about things that don't matter. As the departure time approaches, your voice begins to fracture. You're fighting to stay strong for them, but gratitude for who they've become wars with terror at losing them. End in a place where you're trying to say 'I'm proud of you' but it comes out broken, your love and your grief inseparable. Let your breath betray what your words try to hide.
inspired_by: Recounting Trauma to a Stranger Therapist

title: Worst Case Scenario Spiraling: Catastrophizing Out Loud
instruction: Your partner is late from work. You're spiraling. Your voice is getting faster, higher. 'What if they got in an accident... what if... what if they're lying and they've left...' Your voice is becoming almost hysterical. Anxiety is hijacking your breathing. Words tumble out. You're catastrophizing every possible scenario. Your voice is reaching fever pitch. Then they text 'Traffic.' Your voice crashes. You're embarrassed. Your voice becomes small, trying to laugh it off.

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering What You Can Never Say in Daylight
instruction: It's 3am and you're sitting beside someone you love—who will never love you back, who doesn't even know the depth of what you feel. They're asleep or perhaps just gone, and you're finally saying everything you've held back. Begin almost inaudibly, your voice catching on words you've never spoken aloud. Confess not just the love, but the loneliness of carrying it alone, the small daily grief of pretending friendship is enough. Let your whisper intensify with the relief of finally speaking truth, even to silence. End in tender resignation: you wouldn't trade knowing them for anything, even though loving them quietly is breaking you in slow motion. Your voice should be intimate, raw, the kind of honest that only comes in darkness when no one can hear you shatter.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Healer Saves the Villain's Life Against All Doctrine

title: The 3 AM Whisper
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your sleeping partner. You need to whisper a confession—something you've done, something you feel, something you've hidden. Start with the words you've rehearsed, quiet and controlled. But as you whisper into the darkness, let yourself become unmoored. Your whisper might suddenly break into a strangled sob, then shift to fierce whispered anger at yourself, then to begging them not to hate you (even though they can't hear you), then to whispering wild justifications, then to admitting deeper, stranger truths you didn't plan to say. These shifts need no logic—you're alone in the dark with your own heart. End in a different emotional place entirely: perhaps quiet acceptance, perhaps tender love for this sleeping person, perhaps strange relief. Journey from rehearsed confession through irrational emotional turbulence to unexpected peace.

title: What I Buried in the Garden
instruction: Late at night, you're lying beside someone you deeply trust—a partner, closest friend, or sibling. The room is dark. Begin with your voice barely above a whisper, calm but deliberate, as you tell them you need to say something you've never spoken aloud. Describe, with precise sensory detail, a specific object you once buried or hid as a child—something connected to a shameful moment, a secret transgression, or a loss you couldn't process. As you describe where it is and what it meant, your voice should gradually reveal the emotional weight this buried thing still carries. The act of finally naming it aloud should transform your breathing, your rhythm. End with your voice catching on the real truth—that the buried object represents a part of yourself you've kept hidden, and speaking it now is an act of terrifying intimacy and possible liberation.

title: Shattered Guardian
instruction: You've just found out your younger sibling has been suffering in silence—addiction, abuse, something terrible you never saw—and you're confronting them with explosive, protective rage. Start fierce and loud: 'Why didn't you tell me?!' Your voice should shake with fury at whoever hurt them, at yourself for missing the signs, at them for carrying this alone. Let that anger crack open into desperate, helpless tears—the kind where you can barely breathe. Your voice breaks from shouting to sobbing, reaching for them physically even though they're pulling away, begging them to let you fix this even as you realize you can't. End on your knees, voice raw and wrecked, whispering 'Please, please let me help you' with such vulnerable intensity it strips you bare. Show the terrifying helplessness of loving someone you can't save.
inspired_by: The Tech Support Robot with Feelings

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral: Recording Your Goodbye
instruction: You're recording a video message to be played at your funeral, knowing you're dying but determined to make this funny, to give them something other than grief. Start with genuine laughter, cracking jokes about death—'Well, this is awkward'—your voice warm and mischievous. But the laughter keeps catching, becoming slightly hysterical, because you're terrified and trying to hide it. Tell a ridiculous story about your life, laughing at yourself, but your voice wavers between joy at the memory and the devastating knowledge that there won't be more memories. The contradictions pile up: you're giggling while tears stream down your face, making absurd requests—'Play something embarrassing at my wake'—but your voice cracks with longing. Express fierce gratitude for every small thing, laughing at how much you loved ordinary moments, but the gratitude is laced with grief for everything you'll miss. End with you smiling through tears, voice thick and breaking, saying 'I loved being alive' with such laughing, crying, heartbroken joy that it's impossible to tell if you're celebrating your life or mourning its end—both, completely, devastatingly both.
inspired_by: Heat Exhaustion in the Desert: Losing Grip on Reality

title: What You Never Told Me
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) about a wound that has shaped your entire life—perhaps a betrayal, an absence, a lie, or a moment of cruelty they may not even remember. Start from a place of carefully controlled anger, the kind you've rehearsed in your head for years. But as you finally speak these truths aloud, let the confrontation crack open into territories you didn't anticipate: maybe you find yourself laughing bitterly at the absurdity, or your rage dissolves into grief, or you discover a startling tenderness beneath your fury. Don't steer yourself. Allow your unconscious to guide you into emotional spaces you didn't plan to visit. By the end, you should arrive somewhere utterly different from where you began—whether that's unexpected understanding, deeper rage, or a complex combination you can't name. Let your body and voice be inhabited by impulses you don't consciously choose.

title: Last Screw, Last Breath
instruction: You are an elderly person, utterly depleted after hours of trying to tighten a single, stripped screw that holds your only lamp together. The room is dark, your hands shake, and you've already dropped the screwdriver twice. Start in a low, trembling whisper—pure exhaustion, whispering curses at the screw. Then, something snaps: your voice erupts from your gut, rough and cracking, as you shout at the lamp, slam your fist on the table, and finally scream the last words at the top of your lungs, only to collapse into a silent, heaving sob of utter fatigue. Let your words be short, percussive, and broken, with heavy breaths and the sound of an object being struck or knocked over.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Negotiation
instruction: You're sitting beside your estranged father's hospital bed at 3 AM. After decades of silence, he's asked you here to discuss dividing the family land before he dies. Begin with cold, business-like distance—this is just paperwork, just practicalities. But as you say 'Dad, we can split it down the middle, the way you wanted,' something cracks open. Your voice should move from clipped and guarded to trembling with all the unsaid years between you. End with 'I wish we'd had more time' spoken so quietly it's almost lost, carrying both forgiveness and the devastating weight of everything that can never be recovered. Let the exhaustion of holding anger for so long finally drain away, replaced by raw, undefended grief.

title: The Gutter's Confession
instruction: You are a small child, maybe 8 or 9, lying flat on your back in a muddy, rain-drenched gutter after falling off your bike. Your voice is thick and nasal from the cold rain and the position, softly echoing off the concrete. You're talking to a stray dog that has stopped to sniff your face. You start by whispering in pure, desperate infatuation, lost in how beautiful and special this dog is, but as you realize no one is coming to help, your voice cracks and shifts into a rising, panicked distress—each breath gets heavier, your words tangle, and you end with a trembling plea, your body too sore to move. Let the nasal congestion and shallow breath make your voice sound small and puddled.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Kitchen Morning
instruction: You are sitting at your grandmother's kitchen table on the morning she will die. Begin by closing your eyes and breathing in the smell of her coffee—that specific burnt-sugar scent she always made too strong. Feel the worn wood grain under your fingertips, the chips and grooves you've traced since childhood. Hear the particular creak of her chair, the shuffle of her slippers. Taste the bitterness of her coffee on your tongue, too hot, the way she always served it. Only after you've fully inhabited these sensations, open your eyes and see her face—really see the morning light on her papery skin, the tremor in her hands. Let all these sensations flood you simultaneously as you tell her everything you never said. Begin with quiet gratitude for these ordinary morning rituals, and let it transform into the crushing weight of knowing this is the last time you'll smell this coffee, hear that creak, touch this table. Your final words should break with the realization that you're not just losing her—you're losing this entire sensory world that only exists when she does.

title: Suds and Envy
instruction: You're a woman in her late 20s, alone in your small kitchen, washing dishes at 2 AM after a party. You're drunk, your thoughts are slurring, and the constant rush of the faucet blurs your focus. Every clink of a glass makes you flinch—you're jealous of a friend who just got engaged, and you can't stop muttering about it under your breath. Start with irritable, impatient sighs as you scrub a stubborn pan, letting your voice rise sharp over the water. Midway, the envy takes over, growing from bitter mutters to a raw, confessional slur—ending in a quiet, hollow laugh as you drop a spoon, realizing how pathetic you sound.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Sleep-Talking a Complete Confession
instruction: You're asleep and your partner is listening. Mumble through a complete, damning confession — but in sleep-logic, so it's fragmentary, surreal, and mixed with dream nonsense. 'I kissed... the report is under the... purple helicopter... I'm sorry I never told you about... (snoring)... the money is in...' Your partner's horrified whisper ('What money?! Wake up!') gets no coherent response. Make the sleep voice genuinely convincing — slurred, unprojected, half-swallowed.

title: The Slurred Confession
instruction: You're a gruff older man in a dimly lit bar, drunk and swaying on your stool. You've been watching a woman across the room all night, and now you clumsily stumble over to her table. Start with awkward, embarrassed laughter as you nearly knock over a glass—your voice thick and slurred, sibilants smearing. Then, as you lock eyes with her, your tone softens into a raw, infatuated sincerity, even as your volume wavers and your words trip over each other. Let your body's unsteadiness affect your speech; lose a thought, mumble, then find it again. End with a quiet, vulnerable admission that surprises even you.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Doctor Who Can't Save Their Own
instruction: You're an ER surgeon and your teenage daughter has just been brought in from a car accident. You're not allowed to treat her—protocol—but you're standing there watching, and you know from the monitors that she's slipping away. Start with fierce, barked commands at the other doctors—you're trying to save her by controlling them. Your voice is sharp, authoritative, desperate. But as they call time of death, that professional armor shatters into an inhuman sound—rage at god, at yourself, at the universe. Scream at them to keep trying, then collapse into begging, literally begging them not to stop. End in guttural sobs, the kind that come from your stomach, as you whisper her name over and over. Move from commanding authority to explosive desperation to complete dissolution.
inspired_by: Medieval: Executioner Comforts the Condemned as a Priest

title: The Shrinking of Love
instruction: You're at a family dinner, humiliated by a relative's cruel joke about your failed marriage. Everyone laughed. Now you've slipped away to a dark corner of the porch, crouched down to your eight-year-old niece who followed you. She doesn't understand why you're upset, but she's holding your hand. Start speaking with your voice retracted—barely a whisper, directed at the ground, sentences dissolving into nothing. Midway, as you look into her trusting eyes, let a fragile, trembling affection surface. Your voice stays soft, but cracks with warmth, fighting through shame. End on a whisper that holds her gaze for a second before you look away again. Let the sound of distant laughter from inside break your concentration once.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Forgiveness Offer Refused
instruction: You're trying to offer forgiveness to someone who hurt you, but they're rejecting it. Your voice is gentle, trying to heal: 'I'm ready to move past this.' But they don't want forgiveness; they want to argue. Your voice becomes frustrated: 'Can't you just accept this?' You're trying to be the mature one, but they won't let you. Your voice becomes tired, disappointed. By the end, you're realizing some people don't want healing, and your voice becomes resigned.

title: Echo of the Lost
instruction: You're a small child, maybe six, standing at the edge of a vast canyon at a festival. Your big brother just disappeared into the crowd of adults, and you're calling out for him, your voice high and reedy, trying to carry over the noise. At first, you're just cranky and annoyed, your vowels stretching out as you shout, 'Miiiitch—MIIITCH!' between gasps. But as you hear your own voice bounce off the canyon walls, a sharp, silent awe cuts through your panic—the sound is huge, like it belongs to someone else. Your final call, 'Mitch... please,' drops into a skinny, breathy whisper, the awe still clinging to the echoes as you realize how small you are.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Taste of Her Name
instruction: You're in bed with your partner, your mouth occupied, but your mind is elsewhere. You just saw them laugh too long at a friend's joke earlier, and now you can't shake the image. Start by trying to pull away to speak, but you can't—all that comes out is a frustrated, jealous hum against their skin. Let the sound shift from a sharp, possessive moan (trying to claim their attention) into a long, weary breath as you resign yourself to swallowing the bitter taste of your own envy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hour. He's unconscious, but you've been told he might still hear you. Start by speaking to him about something simple and safe—the weather outside, a memory from childhood, anything that keeps your real feelings at bay. But between each thing you say aloud to him, speak aloud what you're actually thinking and feeling in that moment—the terror, the regret, the things you wish you'd said years ago, your fury at time running out. Let what you're really feeling start to crack through the safe words until you can no longer hide behind them. By the end, the wall between what you're saying and what you're feeling must completely dissolve, and you must say directly to him what your heart has been screaming all along.

title: The Last Straw Bale
instruction: You're an aging rancher who has spent the entire day hauling hay bales under a merciless sun. Your body screams, every muscle trembling. You collapse onto an overturned bucket, staring at the last bale left in the truck. You have to move it, but you can't. Your voice comes out ragged, breathy between gulps of air. Start sour—resentful at the work, at your age, at the heat. Let that bitterness fade into a quiet, helpless admission as you realize you have to ask your daughter for help, something you swore you'd never do. Let each word cost you; let the pauses stretch while you gather strength. Speak as if your lungs are empty and your pride is bruised.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Climb
instruction: You're a young mother, breathless, climbing the final flight of stairs to your new apartment—the first real home you've ever had with your child. You're carrying a small bag of groceries and your toddler is tugging your hand, babbling. Each step is a tiny victory. You speak between breaths, your voice rising with effort and joy. Start with a grateful whisper, counting the stairs with sweet anticipation. As you near the top, gratitude swells into elation—you almost laugh, choked up, because this climb means everything. Let your words tumble out in short, urgent bursts, like you're talking to yourself and the universe.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: I'm Just Fine
instruction: You're an older adult at a family dinner, pretending to be sober but you're actually three glasses in. A younger relative gently asks if you've been drinking. Start with a forced, slurry cheerfulness—a lie wrapped in contentment, but your voice wavers and volume spikes as you get defensive. Let the sentence trail off as you lose your thought, then shift into a quieter, vulnerable admission about how lonely you've been. Your words should stumble, laugh too loudly, then drop into a raw, broken whisper.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Apology in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night. You're lying in bed next to someone you hurt deeply—a partner, a sibling, a close friend. The lights are off. Begin in the silence of your shame and fear, whispering your first attempts at apology, feeling how inadequate the words are, how small your voice sounds, how terrified you are of their rejection. Stay in that vulnerability. Then, as you continue, let yourself feel them softening beside you—their breath changing, their hand perhaps reaching for yours in the darkness. Let your whispered words become more honest, more specific, until you're confessing not just what you did but why, and what you've learned. Allow tears, allow your voice to break. Feel the shift from isolated shame to shared, tender human forgiveness. End in quiet, intimate connection.

title: The Moment Everything Shatters
instruction: You're facing someone you love fiercely—a partner, a best friend, your grown child—and you've reached your breaking point. Begin with explosive frustration, voice rising with desperate urgency: 'Why can't you see what you're doing to yourself?!' Your words come fast, fierce, protective rage pouring out. Then mid-sentence, everything crashes—your voice cracks wide open and underneath the anger is terrified helplessness. 'I can't—oh god, I can't save you from this.' Drop to your knees if you need to. Let the realization devastate you: you are powerless to fix this person you love. Your voice breaks into raw grief, fierce protectiveness colliding with absolute helplessness. Sob if it comes. Then, through tears, find the terrible clarity: 'I have to let you find your own way.' End with a whispered declaration that costs you everything: 'I love you enough to step back.' Let your voice shake with the weight of loving someone and releasing control.

title: Commentating Through the Happy Tears
instruction: You're narrating a chess game between two children you fostered who are being adopted today—their last day with you. Begin with over-the-top sports-commentator joy that's completely genuine: you're so proud, so happy for them. But your voice keeps breaking with laughter and tears simultaneously. Describe their moves with absurd dramatic flair while crying. Your happiness for their new life tangles with the grief of letting them go. Let contradictory emotions wash over you—celebrating their winning moves while your heart splinters. End in a moment of profound peace mixed with sorrow: 'And that's checkmate. That's... that's perfect. You're going to be so loved.' Find beauty in the bittersweet.
inspired_by: Sports Commentator for a Chess Match

title: The Last Translation
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying childhood dog, holding their paw as their breathing slows. You've always joked that you could understand what they were saying, translating their barks and whines for family members. Now, in this final moment, you speak their last 'words' aloud—starting with their usual sarcastic observations about the vet, the squeaky toy someone brought, your tearstained face. But as their breathing changes, the translations become profound: gratitude for seventeen years together, reassurance that it's okay to let go, forgiveness for that time you left them at the kennel. Your voice should begin with false cheerfulness, that defensive humor we use against grief, then gradually break as the translations become unbearably tender. Let the last 'translation' dissolve into silence, into a whispered understanding that needs no words. Move from playful deflection to devastating intimacy, from the voice you use to make others laugh to the voice that can barely speak through tears.

title: Don't You Dare Touch That Table
instruction: Your ex-partner has come to collect their belongings, and they've just reached for the antique table that was your late mother's. Your voice erupts - fierce, protective, raw with grief and rage. This table held your mother's hands when she was dying, her head rested here when she was too weak to stand. Your volume rises and falls unpredictably - shouting, then suddenly choked with tears. Run your own hand over it possessively while your voice shakes with fury: they have no right, they never understood what this meant, they're taking everything and they will NOT take this. Then your rage cracks completely open into sobbing desperation - this table is all you have left of her. Your voice becomes ragged, pleading. You can barely speak. End with your body folded over the table, cheek pressed to the wood, voice small and shattered, begging them not to take your mother away from you again.
inspired_by: Running Your Hand Over a Smooth, Polished Wooden Table

title: The Uninvited Belch
instruction: You are on a first date at a quiet, fancy restaurant. Across the table sits someone you've been crushing on for months—they're even more charming in person. You're mid-sentence, gushing about their laugh, when a massive, guttural burp erupts from your chest. The sound is deep, monstrous, nothing like your usual sing-song voice. For a moment, you freeze in horror, face burning with embarrassment. You try to recover, stammering through an apology with a shaky, affectionate smile, your voice cracking between mortified giggles and desperate sweetness. By the end, you lean in, eyes soft, and whisper a tender, heartfelt compliment—transforming the disaster into a vulnerable confession.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Interest (slightly present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Raid
instruction: You're an older woman alone in your living room, late at night, clutching a worn controller. You're playing an old online game you used to share with someone who's been gone for years. At first, you're focused, clicking hard and muttering pridefully about your old reflexes. But mid-action, you stop—staring at a corner of the screen where their avatar used to stand. Your voice softens, and in the quiet, you speak not to the game, but to them, letting the controller slip a little. Let your pride crack into pure longing by the end. Your voice should shift from sharp and loud to tender and small, with pauses for chair creaks, a sigh, or the click of a useless button.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Garden's Gift
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman alone in your overgrown backyard, kneeling in the dirt. Earlier this year, you planted a single seed, a gift from a friend, on a whim, doubting it would ever grow. Now, you've just discovered a massive, unexpected bloom, something absurdly beautiful and fragrant. Start in quiet, exhausted gratitude, your voice low with lazy articulation as you marvel, almost not believing it. Let amusement creep in as you recall your own skeptical planting, your voice trailing off mid-thought. End in a whisper of pure, intimate ecstasy, swallowing your own words as the scent overwhelms you, the feeling transforming from tired relief to a sharp, joyful pleasure.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Amusement (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Opening the Acceptance Letter Alone
instruction: You're holding the letter you've been waiting months for - the one that will change your life - but your hands are trembling so hard you almost can't open it. Begin with that specific kind of terror that comes with getting exactly what you want: your breath shallow and quick, maybe your vision blurring, your voice tight with a fear you don't want to name. As you open it and read that you got in - you got the part, the job, the second chance - notice how the joy rising in your chest crashes immediately into something else: grief for the person who won't be there to see it, or guilt for leaving someone behind, or the sudden overwhelming panic that you're not ready. Let both emotions be true at once. Laugh and cry in the same breath. Let your voice crack between elation and devastation. By the end, you're sitting with this impossible tangle of the best and worst feelings of your life happening simultaneously - gratitude so huge it hurts, and a loneliness so deep it threatens to swallow the joy entirely. Don't resolve it; let both truths live in your voice.
inspired_by: An actor is experiencing tension before going onstage or on camera

title: What You Never Asked Me
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he was never there for you as a child. Start with your thoughts attacking you from all sides—planning what to say next, fearing his reaction, remembering a dozen different wounds at once, your mind a storm of accusations. He sits quietly, not defending himself, just listening. As you speak, something about his stillness begins to affect you. Let your attention shift from the hurricane in your head to actually seeing him: the age in his face, the way he's holding his hands, the specific sadness in his eyes. Your monologue transforms—from a prepared speech ricocheting in your skull to real words flowing from genuine observation of this moment. End in a place where you're no longer reciting grievances from memory but speaking from what you're actually witnessing right now. The anger doesn't disappear, but the mental frenzy does.
inspired_by: Actor experiences mental tension (racing thoughts, fears, mental distractions) even after physical tension has been released

title: Telling Your Dying Parent You Finally Understand
instruction: You're beside the hospital bed, holding a hand that's grown fragile. Begin with shaking breath, struggling to find words: 'I spent so many years being angry at you.' Your voice cracks with decades of buried hurt. But as you continue, something shifts—the anger dissolves into grief, into recognition. 'But I see now... I see what you were carrying, what you were trying to protect me from.' Your voice becomes tender, almost wondering, as understanding floods through you. End with 'I forgive you' whispered through tears, but now they're tears of connection, not abandonment. Let forgiveness feel like both a loss and a homecoming.
inspired_by: Telling Someone You Have Feelings for Them

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your grandmother from a hospital bed, knowing this is the last conversation you'll ever have. She doesn't know you're dying. Start the call trying to sound cheerful and normal, asking about her garden and her week, but as the call progresses, your voice begins to break. You're fighting to memorize the sound of her voice, the way she laughs at small things. By the end, you can barely speak—not from physical pain, but from the weight of everything you want to say and can't. Let your attempt at lightness crumble into something raw and unguarded, where even silence becomes a form of goodbye.

title: Confronting Your Parent: The Love That Failed to Protect You
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father what their absence—emotional or physical—cost you as a child. Begin with carefully chosen words, almost rehearsed, because you've waited years for this moment. 'I need you to understand something. When I was nine...' But as you speak, decades of buried anger start surfacing. Your voice hardens, becomes accusatory. 'You weren't there. You were never there.' Then something shifts—you see them aging before you, vulnerable, and your rage cracks open to reveal the heartbroken child underneath who just wanted to be loved. Your voice becomes pleading, almost begging them to acknowledge your pain. 'Did you ever see me? Did I matter?' The confrontation dissolves into raw need, then exhausted resignation. End with a voice that's simultaneously angry and tender, holding contradictions: 'I needed you. I still do. And I hate that I still do.' Let the emotional arc move from controlled anger to explosive pain to devastating vulnerability.
inspired_by: Caught in Machinery: Fighting Physical Panic While Thinking

title: The Last Letter Before the Journey: Reading Words You'll Never Answer
instruction: You're reading a letter from someone you love who is about to leave on a journey from which they will never return—a terminal diagnosis, a one-way space mission, a sacrifice they've chosen. Your voice begins steady, almost clinical, trying to keep it together as you read their words of goodbye. But as you continue, specific memories they mention—'remember when we stayed up all night talking about nothing,' 'the way you always knew when I needed silence'—begin to crack your composure. Your breath catches. You try to laugh at a joke they've written, but it comes out broken, half-sob, half-genuine amusement. By the end, as they tell you they're not afraid because of the love you gave them, your voice becomes a whisper, thick with tears, but also filled with this profound tenderness. You're reading their peace back to them even though they'll never hear it. Your final words carry both devastating loss and the strange, painful beauty of having loved someone this deeply.
inspired_by: Kindness Showing Ripple Effects: Realizing Impact You Didn't Know

title: The Garden in Winter
instruction: You're scattering the ashes of someone you loved in a place that was special to both of you. Begin with surprising lightness—tell them a funny story, something that would make them laugh, and let yourself actually laugh even as tears start. Describe the beauty around you with genuine wonder mixed with the knife-edge of grief. Your voice should dance between joy at memories and the physical ache of their absence. Find moments of actual peace—brief seconds where you feel them present—then feel that peace shatter as reality crashes back. End by thanking them for specific, small things, your voice breaking with gratitude and loss simultaneously, laughing and sobbing in the same breath. Let us hear how love and grief are sometimes the exact same thing.
inspired_by: Concealing Doubt While Encouraging a Team

title: The Intervention: When Love Becomes Rage
instruction: You're confronting someone you love who's destroying themselves, and you've reached your breaking point. Start with forced calm—you're trying so hard to be reasonable, measured. But within seconds, the fear underneath erupts. Your voice becomes fierce, loud, almost violent in its intensity as you rail against their self-destruction. You're shouting, your words sharp and cutting, fueled by terror disguised as anger. Then, mid-fury, you break. The rage collapses into helpless sobbing. Your voice becomes small, pleading, as you beg them to stay alive, to fight, to see what they're doing to themselves—and to you. End in exhausted whispers, admitting your powerlessness, saying 'I can't save you' with a voice destroyed by crying, knowing love isn't enough but offering it anyway.

title: The Lion and the Lamb: Fierce Protection Meets Absolute Powerlessness
instruction: Your child—or someone you love as fiercely as a child—is in danger you cannot prevent. Perhaps they're ill with something incurable, or making a destructive choice, or being harmed by someone untouchable. You start with ferocious determination, voice strong and almost threatening: 'I will tear the world apart. I will find a way. Nothing will hurt you while I breathe.' But as you speak, the reality crashes through your rage—you are powerless. Your voice should fracture from roaring protectiveness into something raw and broken. 'I can't—God, I can't—' Let yourself collapse into sobbing rage, the kind where you're almost screaming through tears, furious at your own helplessness. Include the moment where you shift from fighting an external enemy to bargaining with the universe, your voice becoming desperate pleading: 'Take me instead. Please. I'm begging.' End with you holding this person, your voice a whisper of broken lullabies, still trying to shield them even as you know you cannot.
inspired_by: Breath Hold Challenge: Pushing Past Safety Thresholds

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child After the Diagnosis
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's bed in the dark after receiving their terminal diagnosis. Your voice is barely audible—you don't want to wake them. You start by describing their face in the dim light, tender observations only a parent notices. Your voice is soft with love so fierce it hurts. Then you begin apologizing for things that aren't your fault—for not being able to fix this, for every time you were impatient, for the future you won't get to give them. Your breath becomes uneven as you try not to cry. You tell them about all the moments you wanted for them—graduations, first loves, their own children. Your voice fractures on ordinary words: 'birthday' or 'summer' or 'grow up.' End with a whispered promise you know you can't keep, your voice the sound of a heart breaking in slow motion while trying to stay quiet.
inspired_by: Historical: Resistance Fighter Realizes Their Ally Is an Informant

title: Screaming at the Ocean for Taking Them
instruction: You're alone on a beach at sunset, and the person you loved most drowned here. Start with rage—pure, volcanic fury at the water, at God, at the unfairness. Yell. Blame. Demand answers from something that will never answer back. Your voice should be jagged, breaking, ferocious. But you can't sustain rage against the ocean. It just keeps rolling in. The anger cracks—suddenly you're begging: 'Please. Please give them back.' You know it's impossible, which makes you sound insane, desperate, childlike. Then the helplessness hits: You couldn't save them. You can't bring them back. You're completely, utterly powerless. The rage collapses into wracking sobs. End small, defeated, speaking to them directly now, voice barely working: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' The ocean keeps crashing. It doesn't care. That's the point.
inspired_by: Elevator Pitch for Your Life to God

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the coldness that defined your childhood. Begin measured, almost rehearsed: 'I need to tell you something I've been holding for twenty years.' But as you speak, old wounds crack open. Your voice sharpens with decades of suppressed anger: 'You were there, but you were never really there. Do you understand what that did to me?' The rage gives way to something more painful—a child's bewilderment: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you try?' Your voice becomes small, desperate for an answer that may never come. Then, exhausted, you find an unexpected tenderness mixed with your grief: 'I'm telling you this because I still love you. And that's the worst part.' End with your voice hollowed out, accepting that some silences never get filled.

title: Pack of Smokes
instruction: You are a woman in her late 30s, a heavy smoker since your teens, sitting on a fire escape as the sun sets. You’ve just found a crumpled pack of cigarettes wedged in your coat pocket—thought you were out. A small, rare reprieve. Start by exhaling a long, grateful sigh, but as you light the cigarette, let the rough gravel of your voice carry the weight of habit: the rasp, the pauses where you swallow or clear your throat. Let the relief grow, but let it be shadowed by the knowledge you’ve done this a thousand times before. As you speak to the cigarette itself, your voice should start thin and tired, then deepen into a worn, almost affectionate roughness as you accept this tiny comfort. End with a quiet, raspy laugh that catches in your throat, a mixed feeling of sad pleasure.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Truth Behind the Counter
instruction: Your parent—who abandoned you as a child—walks into your coffee shop after fifteen years. They don't recognize you, but you know exactly who they are. Start taking their order with a voice that trembles with barely controlled rage, each word a knife you're holding back. As you make their drink, begin asking questions that get increasingly pointed, circling closer to the truth. Your anger should war with a desperate, childlike need for them to see you, to remember, to apologize. Let your voice crack between fury and pleading. When they finally realize who you are, shift into something rawer: all the years of abandonment pouring out in a torrent of pain, anger, and the terrible admission that part of you still loves them and wishes they'd stayed.

title: Bedside Vigil at 3 AM
instruction: You're whispering to someone you love who is unconscious, possibly dying, in the deep quiet of a hospital night. Begin speaking softly about ordinary things—what happened today, what you had for dinner, the weather—your voice tender, almost conversational, as if they might wake any moment. Gradually let the weight of what's unsaid creep in. Your voice catches. You start confessing things you never had the courage to say: regrets, gratitude, the specific ways they changed you, the future you imagined together. Let tears enter your voice but don't let it break completely—this is intimate, throat-tight emotion. End with a plea or a permission, something whispered so quietly it's almost just breath, the kind of truth that only comes out in darkness when you think no one can hear.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Highway
instruction: You're calling your sibling from a rest stop, knowing this is the last time you'll speak before you disappear into a new life to escape something you can't name. Start the call trying to sound casual, maybe even cheerful, as if this is just a regular check-in. But as you speak, the weight of goodbye begins crushing your chest, and you realize you need them to understand how much they've meant to you without being able to say why you're leaving. Let your voice fracture and rebuild moment by moment. Don't plan your words—let each sentence surprise you as it comes out. By the end, you're no longer pretending, and the raw truth of your love and your terror breaks through in whatever sounds or half-finished thoughts emerge. The emotion should move from false lightness to devastating honesty.
inspired_by: Actor is too tied to line readings or the conceptual meaning of the written text in rehearsal

title: Laughing Too Loudly
instruction: You are a mother who recently lost most of your hearing after a surgery. Your child just told you their stuffed rabbit is learning to tap dance on the windowsill. You're absolutely delighted, but you can't hear how loud your own voice is. Start with a slight frown of confusion as you try to gauge your volume, then let the amusement take over—your volume rises, your pitch wavers, and you might trail off mid-sentence to readjust. The emotion shifts from a flicker of frustration at your own uncalibrated voice to pure, breathless joy at your child's imagination.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Lost in the Canopy
instruction: You're deep in a dense jungle, separated from your hiking group twenty minutes ago. You feel a blush of embarrassment for wandering off, but now you need to call out. Start by muttering to yourself, annoyed at your mistake, then gradually raise your voice to a full call, letting your frustration morph into a desperate, determined plea. Let your voice be swallowed by the thick air, and react naturally to the bird calls and rustling leaves around you—pause mid-sentence if a twig snaps, then push forward.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Closet
instruction: You are hiding in a dark closet, pressing one hand firmly over your mouth to muffle any sound. You can hear footsteps just outside the door—someone searching. At first, helplessness floods you; your breath is shallow, your heart pounds, and every tiny rustle feels explosive. You whisper to yourself, barely audible through your fingers, begging them to pass. Then the footsteps fade. Relief crashes in, so intense it makes your knees weak. Your hand drops slightly, and your voice cracks with a shaky exhale as you realize you are safe. Let the hand affect your speech—consonants like p, b, m become soft, stifled. Start with desperate, breathy whispers, then let relief loosen your throat and slow your words.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Helplessness (very intensely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Begging Someone Not to Jump While Your Own Heart Shatters
instruction: You're on the ledge with them, not physically but emotionally. Start with fierce, almost aggressive determination: 'Don't you dare do this, look at me!' Your voice cracks with controlled desperation. But as they explain why they need to, something in you breaks open—your own barely-contained pain surfaces. You shift from commanding to pleading, from strong to shattered: 'I can't lose you because I'm barely holding on myself.' Your voice should explode with everything you've been hiding—rage at the world that brought you both here, terror of being left alone, helpless love. Let yourself sob while still trying to be their anchor. End with raw, ugly honesty: you need them to stay so you don't give up too.
inspired_by: Comforting Your Child After a Nightmare

title: The Gift with a Double Meaning
instruction: You are a child who has just crafted a small, perfect gift for the adult you admire most in the world — a carefully folded paper flower. You approach them, heart pounding with the thrill of your secret plan. At first, your voice is shy, grateful, and a little uncertain as you offer the gift. But as you hand it over, a triumphant smile spreads across your face, and you slow down, letting your voice drop into a lower, almost velvety register. You weave in a small, hushed compliment that has a hint of something deeper, a glimpse of a longing you barely understand. Your gratitude shifts into a quiet, knowing triumph, a thrill in your chest that makes your words deliberate and charged. Let your voice start shy and quick, then slow, smooth out, and become almost too gentle, with a tiny, breathy laugh at the end.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Triumph (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Telling Your Mother Why You Can't Keep Pretending
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally ready to confront decades of performing the version of yourself she needed you to be. Begin with careful, almost apologetic phrasing - you've practiced this, but it still feels impossible. Your voice carries both love and accumulated grief. As you speak, let controlled composure give way to raw honesty. You're not attacking her; you're liberating yourself, and that requires saying things that will hurt you both. Move from measured explanation to passionate clarity to exhausted relief. Include a moment where you almost stop, almost retreat into old patterns, then push through. End in a place that's both devastating and strangely peaceful, where truth has replaced performance.

title: When the Anesthesia Wears Off
instruction: You're waking up from emergency surgery, groggy and confused, to find your estranged parent sitting beside your hospital bed. Start with physical disorientation—thick tongue, slurred speech, asking where you are. Then recognition hits, and with it, a lifetime of unprocessed anger. Still half-sedated, your filters are gone. You start saying things you've held back for years—'You were never there,' 'I needed you,' 'Why didn't you love me enough?' Your voice breaks between fury and the vulnerability of someone who's just survived something terrifying and realized how badly they still need to be held. Your parent tries to shush you, to say 'rest now,' but you won't—you can't—until the medication pulls you back under, mid-accusation, mid-plea.

title: Salt Water and Gasoline
instruction: You're standing in pouring rain after destroying something you created—a manuscript, a painting, a recording, something you made with your whole heart but that 'important people' said wasn't commercial enough, wasn't marketable, wasn't right. Start by laughing—bitter, manic laughter because you actually did it, you actually destroyed your own work to please them. But let your body take over: feel the rain on your skin, taste it in your mouth, let your hands shake with what you've done. The laughter should crack and transform into something primal—not quite crying, not quite screaming, but a raw sound of loss mixed with sudden, fierce rage at yourself for the betrayal. End on your knees in the rain, breathing hard, touching the ground where the destroyed pieces lie, feeling both devastating grief and the first spark of defiant determination to make it again, better, and never apologize for it.
inspired_by: An actor wants to maintain career integrity under commercial pressure

title: The Last Lucid Moment
instruction: You're lying in a hospital bed, slipping in and out of clarity as your family gathers around. You know this is goodbye, but your mind keeps drifting—sometimes you're telling them you love them, sometimes you think you're young again, calling out for your own mother. Begin confused and frustrated, grasping at memories that dissolve like smoke. Gradually find moments of piercing clarity where you see your loved ones clearly and need them to know something crucial before it's too late. Your voice should move from disoriented murmuring to sudden sharp urgency, then soften into tender acceptance. Let confusion and love wrestle with each other. End in a place of surprising peace, even as your words become fewer and your breath more labored.

title: Photograph in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed next to your sleeping lover, hours before you will leave them forever (they don't know yet). It's 3 AM and completely dark. You cannot sleep. Begin by trying to memorize them through touch alone—the exact temperature of their skin, the rhythm of their breathing, the weight of their hand. Create a complete tactile photograph in your mind, touching their face so lightly they don't wake. As you do this, let specific images flood you: their face laughing last Tuesday, the way they looked the first time you met, how they'll look tomorrow when you're gone. Move from careful, almost scientific memorization, through waves of sensory grief, and finally into whispering the truth so quietly it's almost just breath—telling them everything while they sleep, knowing they can't hear you. Let the images you're creating of them guide every whispered word.
inspired_by: When using the hypnagogic state for character programming

title: The Floor's Too Far Away
instruction: You are standing in a quiet hallway after a party, still feeling the sting of being laughed at in front of the person you secretly desire. Your body is small, shoulders hunched, eyes fixed on the linoleum floor. Start speaking in a flat, barely audible voice that breaks on the first word, with frequent swallows and pauses as you lose your train of thought. Let bitterness creep in only as you recall their laugh, but keep most of your voice numb and hollow. Near the end, allow a flicker of raw lust to surface—a quiet, desperate admission that cuts through the numbness before trailing off into shame again. Speak as if the words are being pulled from you against your will, with micro-distractions like rubbing your arm or shifting weight.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Intimacy After Trauma
instruction: You're being intimate with your partner after a traumatic experience. You're trying, but your nervous system is still in fight-or-flight. Your voice is quiet: 'I want this, but I might...' Your partner understands: 'Whatever happens is okay.' As you begin, your voice is hyper-aware of danger signs. Your partner's voice becomes your anchor: 'You're safe with me.' Slowly, slowly, your voice becomes less guarded. You're rewriting the neural pathways of intimacy. Some of this is easy; some of this is excruciatingly hard. By the end, you've reclaimed a small piece of yourself. Your voice should sound like someone slowly remembering that their body can be a source of pleasure, not just pain.

title: The Sweet Nothing
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman at a dinner party, cornered by a smug acquaintance who drones on about your lifestyle choices. You feel a flicker of anger but mostly cold contempt—you’re about to cut them down. But your blood sugar is crashing. Your hands tremble, your jaw tightens, your words start to slur and fade. As you speak, the force of your contempt weakens; your voice drops, concentration breaks, and you lose your train of thought mid-sentence. Start sharp and dismissive, then let the hypoglycemia pull you into confusion and quiet exhaustion. Deliver a single, biting retort that dissolves into a mumbled, unfinished thought.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Mile
instruction: You are a 16-year-old who just finished a brutal, three-hour cross-country practice in the heat. Your legs are jelly, your lungs burn, and every breath is a labor. A teammate tells you that you missed the qualifying time for the state meet by two seconds. You were hoping for a different outcome, but now you have to respond. Start from a place of deep, physical emptiness where each word feels pulled from a dry well. As you speak, the disappointment seeps in, making your voice even flatter and heavier. Let the pauses stretch as you gather breath, and let your tone drag downward, finishing with a quiet, resigned defeat.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Victor's Grief
instruction: You have just achieved the dream you sacrificed everything for—the Olympic medal, the published book, the sold company, the won case, the earned degree. You're standing alone in the moment of victory, and you begin celebrating out loud, giving yourself the passionate, triumphant speech no one else is there to give you. Build into a rousing, self-congratulatory declaration of your worthiness, your hard work, your vindication. Let yourself be big, proud, unapologetic. But as you continue, let the cracks show. The names of people you lost along the way start to surface. Your victory speech becomes a confused mixture of celebration and elegy, triumph and regret. You're congratulating yourself and apologizing to ghosts in the same breath. The joy doesn't disappear, but it becomes inseparable from the grief of what it cost. End with a complex emotional cocktail: proud but lonely, victorious but mourning, grateful but wondering if it was worth it.

title: Rage Uncontrolled
instruction: Everything in you ignites. You start almost quiet, deadly: 'I am so angry I can barely move.' Then it breaks. Volume goes visceral. You're not shouting words; you're throwing them. Pitch drops and crashes. Breathing becomes ragged. 'HOW COULD YOU—' The sentence fragments into pure sound. There's physical action: maybe you're slamming something, driving, pacing. Your voice matches the fury: guttural, primal, the words less important than the raw vocal texture. Include the moment rage cracks into grief-rage, something ugly underneath. End breathing hard, voice destroyed.

title: The Last Light Before Sleep
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they've just closed their eyes for what you know will be the last time. You begin speaking softly, telling them it's okay to let go, that the darkness they're entering isn't frightening—it's rest, it's peace, it's home. Start with reassurance, your voice steady and comforting, as if you're the one guiding them. But as you continue, your own fear seeps in—you don't want them to leave, you're not ready. Your voice should crack, catch, falter. End in a whisper that's both permission and plea, where you're releasing them even as your heart shatters. Let the words become harder to say, like you're losing your grip on your own composure.

title: The Confrontation at the Childhood Door
instruction: You're thirty-eight years old, standing in your parent's doorway, finally saying what you've never said. Start controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this. But as you speak about the ways you were made to feel small, invisible, not enough, your voice shifts. Anger rises, real and raw, accusations coming faster. Then something breaks. The anger collapses into something more vulnerable—the child you were, begging to be seen. Your voice cracks between fury and desperate need. End with a question you've never asked: 'Did you even want me?' Let it come out small, stripped of all defenses, the kind of question that costs everything to ask.

title: The Toast I Keep Forgetting
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl at your grandmother's funeral, standing at the podium. You wanted to tell a funny story about her teaching you to bake, but now you're here, the paper in your hand is shaking and the room is so quiet. Start with a nervous, overly formal voice, then let the doubt creep in — you're not sure if this story is right, if you'll cry, if you'll mess up. Midway, lose your place as you hear your own voice falter, then find it again with a raw, quiet realization that you just have to say it from your heart. End with a warm, trembling truth that's different from where you began.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Being Told You're Not Good Enough
instruction: Someone says the words or implies it clearly: You're not good enough. Your voice in the moment is shocked. 'What?' You're not comprehending. Then it lands. Your voice becomes quiet. You're internalizing it. Your voice becomes the voice of your own self-doubt confirming what they said. 'They're right. I'm not.' Your voice is coloring the rest of the conversation with shame. Include the moment you realize you're taking their judgment as fact.

title: Breaking Through the Wall
instruction: You're alone, physically pushing against an actual wall or door, and you're trapped—by grief, by failure, by every limitation you've accepted about yourself. Start defeated, barely touching it, your efforts weak and hopeless. But something ignites. Maybe rage, maybe desperation, maybe a sudden vision of freedom. Begin to push harder. Throw your full weight into it. Your breathing becomes powerful. Your muscles engage. You're not just pushing a physical barrier—you're shattering every internal prison. Grunt, yell, roar if you need to. Feel your body become a force of nature. By the end, you're pushing with such ferocious strength that your entire being radiates power, as if you could move mountains, break chains, fly through the ceiling.

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: You're whispering a confession to your sleeping partner in the middle of the night, believing they can't hear you. Begin with halting, barely audible words—admitting a secret you've carried for years that changes everything between you. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost not there, catching on every third word. Confess how you've pretended to be fine when you're not, how you've hidden parts of yourself because you were afraid of being too much, too broken, too difficult to love. Let tears creep into your voice without ever becoming loud—this is the kind of crying that stays in your throat, that makes your whispers shake. Midway through, your voice breaks on something particularly painful—maybe you admit you're terrified they'll leave if they really know you. End with a tender, fragile statement of love mixed with fear: you're telling them this even though they might not hear it because the secret is killing you slowly. Your final words should be barely more than breath.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Child Before Surgery They May Not Survive
instruction: Your child is about to be wheeled into a risky surgery with uncertain outcomes. You're being given two minutes alone with them. Start with fierce optimism—'You're going to be fine, I'll see you soon'—but as you look at their face, the terror breaks through. Your voice cracks. You need to say goodbye in case this is the last time, but you can't let them see your fear. Move between reassurance and barely-contained devastation. End by whispering something you've never said before, something that makes this moment eternal. Let your breath catch. Let silence do the work between words.
inspired_by: Parent Hearing Their Child's Abuse for First Time

title: Doubt Creeping
instruction: You were sure five minutes ago. Now questions appear like cracks. Your voice starts confident but increasingly qualifies itself: 'I think we should—wait, maybe we shouldn't. Actually, I don't know.' Words become tentative, rising at the ends like questions even when they're not. Breathing becomes shallower. Your sentences unravel mid-way: 'The evidence clearly shows—or does it?' Physical: you're second-guessing every gesture. By the end, you've talked yourself into fundamental uncertainty. 'I don't know anything.' The more you speak, the less sure you become.

title: Delayed Gratification
instruction: You're a middle-aged man on a late-night phone sex call with your lover. She kept you waiting twenty minutes, and you're genuinely irritated—your voice starts clipped, breathy with impatience, almost cold. But as you begin to describe how much you want her, the infatuation breaks through. Let your tone soften, slow down, become more hypnotic. Keep a trace of that edge in your lower register, like you're still annoyed even as you surrender. Pause to take a sip of whiskey—audible swallow—then continue, the irritation melting into a warmer, breathier seduction. End with a near-whisper, almost a plea, but let the air carry both longing and leftover frustration.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Infatuation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Stillness Holds It All
instruction: You're lying in a darkened room, a cold cloth over your eyes. Every sound is a spike, every word you speak a whisper drawn from a deep, fragile well. A friend tiptoes in and asks if you need anything — you feel a wave of genuine contentment, a quiet gratitude for this quiet solitude. But as they fumble, offering useless advice, a slight pride rises: you've survived this before, you know this pain better than they ever will. And underneath, a thin thread of contempt for their clumsy sympathy — not mean, just weary truth. Let your voice stay barely audible, each syllable a careful release, and let the contentment slowly bleed into that knowing pride and soft disdain as you speak.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (extremely present), Pride (slightly present), Contempt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Push
instruction: You are a young woman, maybe early twenties, in the middle of a punishing indoor cycling class. Your body is burning, your breath is a ragged rhythm, and you feel a deep, familiar shame creeping in — shame that you are the slowest, that you have stopped pedaling for a few seconds now, that you can't keep up. But in your chest, a tiny, stubborn flicker of something else is starting to grow: not defiance, not yet, but a recognition that you have survived worse. You speak in short gasps, your words pushed out on the exhale, each one a little confession, a little admission. Your voice is soft, almost a whisper, trying to be sweet and girly even as it cracks with exertion. Start in the shame, the apology. End in a quiet, breathless discovery that you are still here, still moving, still pedaling.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers Differently
instruction: You're in the throes of intense physical experience - reuniting with a lover after months apart, the passion supposed to be overwhelming. But let your body tell you what it actually feels, not what the moment demands. Maybe you're suddenly aware of being self-conscious about your breath, then you feel a flash of anger about something unrelated, then the anger turns you on, then you're struck by how strange their hands feel, then that strangeness becomes interesting, then sad. Follow the physical sensations and emotional responses as they actually occur - maybe tension in your jaw, an urge to push them away then pull them closer, a laugh that wants to come out during an intimate moment, unexpected grief mixed with desire. Don't perform ecstasy. Instead, track the real sensory-emotional journey your body takes. By the end, land in whatever authentic physical-emotional state has emerged from following the truth. The arc moves from expected passion to embodied reality.
inspired_by: Being Irreverent to Your Concept of the Material

title: The Diagnosis Party
instruction: You're hosting a dinner party the same evening you received your terminal diagnosis. No one knows yet. You're pouring wine, laughing at someone's joke, and suddenly you're laughing too hard—real laughter mixed with something hysterical. You're telling stories, and they're genuinely funny, but your voice keeps catching in strange places. You propose a toast 'to this moment, to all of us here, to being alive right now'—and you mean every word with devastating sincerity even as you're smiling. Describe the food, the faces, the ordinary beauty of it all with a kind of fierce gratitude that borders on breaking. Let joy and grief become indistinguishable. End by saying 'I love this. I love all of this' with a brightness that's absolutely genuine and completely shattered. Let the audience wonder if you're about to laugh or weep.

title: The Wedding Morning
instruction: You're getting ready for your wedding, but your mother died six months ago. You're alone in the dressing room, and a song she loved starts playing from somewhere in the building. Begin in the practiced joy you've been performing for everyone—this is a happy day, you tell yourself. But as the song continues, let your defenses crack. Feel the impossible contradiction: the deep, almost unbearable grief of her absence in this moment she should have been here for, and the genuine joy and love you feel for the person you're about to marry. Don't choose between these emotions—hold both. Let them war inside you, let them coexist. Your voice might laugh and break in the same breath. You might feel your heart expanding with love even as it's being crushed by loss. Speak to her, or to yourself, or to the empty room, and let the full complexity of this moment be true.
inspired_by: Actor is not connected to inner self and cannot make technique work

title: The Last Step
instruction: You are an older man climbing a steep flight of stairs to meet someone you've been secretly lusting after. At the bottom, you felt a thrill of desire, your heart racing with anticipation. But as you climb, breathless and straining, a confusing doubt creeps in—why did they choose such a strange place? Why aren't they waiting? By the top, your lust has curdled into sharp confusion. Speak as you climb, voice strained into short gasps, pitch rising with effort. Let your words come in ragged bursts between breaths, and let the confusion overpower the initial heat as you near the landing.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (clearly present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Echo of an Unheard Applause
instruction: You are an aging stage actor standing alone on an empty auditorium stage after a final performance. The lights are dimmed, the seats vacant. You've just learned the show closed early due to poor ticket sales. Your voice, naturally deep and resonant, carries into the silence, but you hear your own words bounce back from the back wall — a hollow echo. Start with a heavy, quiet disappointment as you mutter to yourself about the empty seats, but as you speak, you recall a single moment of genuine connection with an audience member tonight. Let your voice shift from that initial weary letdown to a fragile, bittersweet warmth — not forced, but creeping in as you remember. Pause naturally as if distracted by the echo or a shift in your weight. End with a soft, almost grateful sigh.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Almost Didn't Give
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's wedding reception, champagne glass raised, about to give a toast. Begin with practiced joy—you've rehearsed this, you're happy for them, your voice is bright and celebratory. But you're also deeply in love with the person getting married, have been for years, and they never knew. As you speak about their beautiful love story, let the real emotion begin bleeding through the performance. Your voice cracks not from happy tears but from grief, yet you must keep smiling. Mix genuine affection for your friend with piercing loss. Let gratitude for having known them tangle with resentment that it's not you. Joy and devastation must coexist in every word. End with a blessing that costs you everything to give—absolutely sincere, absolutely destroying you, yet somehow also setting you free.

title: The Granddaughter's Reckoning
instruction: You are an elderly woman, frail but sharp, sitting in a sunlit parlor.
