Your 40-year-old granddaughter, who has swindled your life savings, just walked in with a fake smile and a cup of tea. You've been rehearsing this moment for months. As you speak, you're astonished at your own calm—your voice like silk over steel—but a flicker of doubt crosses your mind: 'Is this really the right thing to do?' Despite that, you press on, letting each word land with icy precision. By the end, the satisfaction of finally revealing the truth overtakes the doubt, and your voice carries a serene, terrifying clarity.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter your difficult, emotionally distant mother left you, to be opened after her death. Begin with your voice tight, guarded, maybe slightly bitter: 'Dear...' She's apologizing, explaining, revealing things you never knew. Your first reaction is defensive disbelief—a sharp, harsh laugh: 'Now you tell me?' But as you continue reading her words, your voice begins to shift. She's telling you she was proud, that she loved you even when she couldn't show it, that she sees you clearly now. You start crying while also laughing—the sound of someone whose anger is dissolving into unexpected grace. By the end, you're speaking through tears that are somehow both grief-stricken and relieved: 'I forgive you. God help me, I actually forgive you.' Your voice should carry the contradiction of losing her just as you're finally finding her, the bittersweet ache of receiving the love you needed, thirty years too late.

title: The Foreman's Final Word
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a naturally high, almost girlish voice, wearing a hard hat with a visor on a loud construction site. You are the site supervisor. Start by finding a moment of genuine amusement—a bird has landed on a steel beam and you chuckle softly to yourself, your voice slightly muffled by the hat's hard plastic. As you begin to speak to an unseen worker, you shift into deep concentration, reviewing blueprints in your mind, trailing off as you lose your thought. But then a specific memory surfaces—one of betrayal years ago. Your voice drops in pitch, and your amusement curdles into a cold, slow malevolence. Your final words are a quiet, threatening promise, delivered with a smile only your heart can feel. The background din of machinery and hammers should be audible as you speak, and you occasionally adjust your hat, which shifts your voice's projection.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (slightly present), Concentration (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Fever Dream Inventory
instruction: You're burning with fever—delirious, in physical pain, your body betraying you. You're alone, scared, and your mind is cataloguing everything with strange, heightened intensity. Move through your immediate environment: the sweat-soaked sheets clinging to you, the way the room spins, the throb behind your eyes, the bitter taste in your mouth, the phone just out of reach, the ceiling that seems to pulse, your own racing heartbeat, the desperate thirst, the shivers wracking your body. Speak each sensation aloud as you experience it: 'The pillow is soaking wet, disgusting,' 'My head is splitting apart,' 'Why is the room tilting?' 'I need water, I need—' Mix the physical sensations with emotional ones—fear, anger at your body, vulnerability, maybe even delirious humor or strange euphoria. Begin somewhat aware and trying to cope, but let the fever pull you into a more raw, unfiltered state where you're simultaneously hypersensitive and losing control. Let physical suffering crack you open emotionally—maybe you start crying without knowing why, or laughing, or calling out for someone. Let pain make you honest in ways health never could.

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You are packing up your child's bedroom as they leave home forever—college, marriage, or estrangement. Pick up each object and let it trigger a complete sensory memory. Feel the pilled softness of their baby blanket, smell the faded detergent and milk-sour sweetness that never quite washed out. Run your fingers over the scratched desk where they did homework, feeling the carved initials, the dents from pencil stabs. Open their closet and inhale the specific smell of their teenage years—body spray, worn sneakers, that laundry smell. Find an old stuffed animal and press it to your face, hearing in your memory their child-voice naming it. Taste the salt of your own tears mixed with the dust you're stirring up. Let yourself be genuinely happy for their independence, proud of who they've become, even as your hands shake putting their things in boxes. Begin with determined cheerfulness, humming as you work, telling yourself this is good and right. Let it break slowly as each sense memory accumulates, until you're sitting on their bed, surrounded by boxes, holding something small, overwhelmed by the contradictory swell of pride, liberation, devastating loss, and the strange relief of your own life opening up again—all of it true simultaneously.

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the patterns they passed down—the silence, the emotional unavailability, the way love in your family always came with conditions. Start measured, trying to be fair, listing facts. But as you speak, decades of swallowed words come pouring out. 'I needed you to see me,' you say, and your voice cracks with the weight of a child's longing that never got answered. The anger builds—years of performing, of making yourself smaller, of earning scraps of affection. Then something shifts. You see them as they are: broken, doing their best with what they had. The rage doesn't disappear, but it mingles with something unbearably tender. 'I forgive you,' you say, and you're not sure if it's true, but you need to say it anyway.

title: Screaming at God After Losing Everything
instruction: You've just lost everything—your home, your family, your faith. You're alone, and something inside you explodes. Start with a roar of pure rage, voice raw and primal: 'You want me to still believe in you?!' Let your voice crack and splinter. Scream accusations, your words becoming incoherent with fury. But mid-rage, your voice suddenly breaks into sobbing—you can't maintain the anger. You try to rebuild it, voice rising again: 'I did everything right!' but it collapses faster this time. End on your knees, voice reduced to broken whispers between gasps: 'I don't know how to keep going.' Cycle between explosive fury and shattered vulnerability. Let helplessness swallow the rage until only exhausted despair remains. This is what it sounds like when someone's spirit breaks.
inspired_by: Telling Someone They Have a Habit That Hurts You

title: Stubbed and Stewing
instruction: You've just stubbed your bare toe hard against a heavy oak table leg while trying to reach a falling photo frame. The pain spikes like a blade — shout a sharp, involuntary 'Ah!' as you freeze, grabbing your foot. As the agony pulses, start muttering bitter contempt under your breath at the table's stupidity and your own clumsiness. Your voice is strained, breath held tight, pitch wavering as you force out words. End with a focused, irritated resolve: you need to inspect the damage, but you're still seething and hurting. Let the emotions shift from explosive pain to a simmering mix of contempt and concentration.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Contempt (extremely present), Concentration (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Breaking Through the Storm
instruction: You're a parent trying to talk down your teenage child who's threatening to run away—or worse. You start with barely contained panic, voice sharp with fear: 'Put down the bag. We're going to talk about this right now.' But they turn away, and something in you shatters. Your voice explodes with raw emotion: 'You think I don't see you hurting? It's killing me! Every day I watch you slip away and I don't know how to reach you!' The rage gives way to desperate pleading: 'I failed you somehow. Tell me how. Tell me what I did wrong so I can fix it!' Your voice breaks completely, vulnerable and terrified: 'You are everything to me. Do you understand that? Everything.' You're on your knees now, voice cracking with helplessness: 'I can't protect you from what's in your head, and it's destroying me that I can't.' Finally, fierce determination mixed with absolute vulnerability: 'But I will not give up on you. I will never stop fighting for you. Never.'

title: Downpour of Envy
instruction: You're a child standing alone in a torrential rainstorm, watching through the deluge as another kid plays with the one toy you've always wanted, safe under a shelter. You shout your bitter jealousy into the storm, voice cracking, sputtering as rainwater runs into your mouth and thunder nearly swallows your words. But then the rain intensifies, a huge downpour soaking everything, and you feel a sudden, wild pleasure—you throw your head back and laugh, scream with ecstatic release, envy melting into sheer joy as you spin in the mud. Let your voice shift from raw, trembling envy to breathless, laughing ecstasy, pausing to spit water or gasp between cries.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What Your Hands Tell Me
instruction: You're lying in bed with someone you love in a quiet, early morning moment. They think you're still asleep. Keep your eyes mostly closed, your breathing steady, but observe them in the dim light—the way they're looking at you, what their hands are doing, whether they're moving closer or pulling away, if they touch you tenderly or hesitantly. Start from a place of peaceful contentment, assuming everything is perfect. But as you watch and deduce meaning from each gesture, each sigh, each moment they almost speak but don't, let understanding dawn. What is their body language revealing? Are they memorizing you, or saying goodbye? Let your whispered words when you finally 'wake' reflect the journey from assumed security to the fragile, vulnerable truth you've deduced. Your voice should barely break the silence, thick with the emotion of what you now understand.

title: Floating on Your Back in a Calm Lake
instruction: Lie back in the water, feeling it support you as you float, weightless. Describe the gentle ripples moving beneath you, the coolness of the water, and the sensation of freedom. Speak with a tone of pure tranquility, as if each moment floating leaves you lighter and freer, with nothing but the calm water surrounding you.

title: The Last Sip of Water
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your small apartment at night. A panic attack has just struck, and you are trying to talk yourself down while hyperventilating. You hold a glass of water but your hands shake so badly you can barely lift it. Begin in a state of acute helplessness—your voice is high, quavering, fragmented by gasps. You repeat phrases like 'I can't breathe' and feel your chest tighten. As you struggle to sip the water, the terror slowly drains away, leaving only a profound, bone-deep exhaustion. By the end, your voice drops to a whispery, flat monotone, slurred with fatigue. Let the physical actions—spilling water, coughing, leaning heavily on the counter—interrupt your words naturally.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Dance
instruction: You're alone in your apartment, and a song comes on—the song you danced to at your wedding, five years before your divorce. Without thinking, you start to move. At first, your body is stiff with resistance, muscles tight against the memory. But the music pulls at something deeper. Let yourself move—really move—as memories flood through your body like voltage. Feel the rage first: how could they leave, how dare they take those perfect moments and make them into ruins? Your movements become sharp, aggressive, almost violent. But then the grief comes, and it's overwhelming. Your body softens, breaks, nearly collapses. You're dancing with a ghost, with a past self, with a love that was real even if it ended badly. Physical sensation overtakes you—the phantom feeling of their hands on your waist, the scent of their skin, the specific pressure of their body against yours. By the end, you're moving through pure sensation, beyond words, beyond simple emotion—your body expressing what your mind can't hold. Exhausted, overwhelmed, wrung out, but somehow more alive than you've felt in months.

title: Dancing in the Hospital
instruction: Your partner has weeks left, and today is a good day—clear-minded, no pain. They're asking you to describe the life you'll have after they're gone, and you're trying to honor their wish while your heart is breaking. Start with genuine laughter, telling them about the ridiculous things you'll do, the adventures you'll have. Your voice is warm, even joyful, painting beautiful pictures. But gratitude keeps bleeding through—thank you for every small moment, for this conversation, for their strength. The laughter becomes wet with tears you're trying to hide. Your voice cracks between joy at their presence right now and grief at their absence to come. End with something absurd that makes you both laugh and cry at once, your voice carrying both complete devastation and perfect love, gratitude for what you had even as you're losing everything.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin by noticing everything physical about this moment: the weight of her hand in yours, the sound of her breathing, the early light coming through the window, the smell of hospital soap mixed with her familiar perfume. Let yourself be fully present in your body—feel the hardness of the chair you've been sitting in all night, the exhaustion in your muscles, the dryness in your throat. Start from a place of quiet watchfulness, almost numbness from the long vigil. As you speak to her—telling her what she meant to you, what you'll carry forward—allow the physical sensations to open something in you. Let gratitude, grief, and a fierce kind of love emerge not from 'trying to feel sad' but from truly being in this room, in this body, in this unrepeatable moment. By the end, you should feel transformed—no longer numb, but achingly, entirely alive.
inspired_by: Actor knows what they want to feel in a scene but cannot get there from cold

title: The Last Winter of the Barn
instruction: You are standing in the frozen yard of the farm you grew up on, now abandoned, looking at the old hay barn where your father taught you to swing a hammer and measure a board. The snow is deep and dead quiet. You exhale a long, visible breath as you remember the smell of hay and the creak of the roof beams. Your voice is slower, softer — almost a whisper. Talk to the barn as if it could hear you. Start with a sigh of helpless longing, then let your voice warm with interest as you recall the details, but finish with fierce pride in what that place made of you. Let the cold air catch in your throat. Pause to look at the broken hinge or the missing boards. Let the pride burn through the sadness at the end, but don't yell — just let the voice firm up, like a hand closing into a fist inside a coat pocket.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Interest (slightly present), Pride (extremely present)

title: The Sound of My Own Voice
instruction: You're a young woman alone in a quiet room, just back from the doctor who told you your vocal cords are damaged. You have vocal nodules. You're holding a voice recorder, pressing the button to test if you can even speak anymore. Start with confusion — a detached, clinical curiosity as you hear how strange and breathy your voice sounds now. Midway, a crack breaks your composure — that wasn't what you meant to say. Let a raw, confused frustration surface, mixed with a fragile hope as you try one last time to find your normal voice. Speak haltingly, as if discovering each word for the first time, with air leaking through and pitch breaks.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Absolution Paradox
instruction: You're at your abuser's funeral, and against all logic, you're laughing softly through tears as you speak to their casket. Begin with the bizarre relief in your voice: 'You're gone, and I'm so grateful, and I loved you, and I hate that I loved you.' Your voice carries the impossible contradiction—you're free, finally, but the price was that they died before you could have the confrontation you needed. You're finding dark humor in how you wasted so many years justifying their cruelty: 'I had a whole speech prepared about your childhood trauma.' But underneath the laughter, there's an aching sadness. By the end, you're speaking with strange serenity, a bittersweet acceptance: you're forgiving yourself for not being able to hate them completely, for the messy truth that abuse and love got tangled up together. Your voice holds grief, liberation, anger, and peace all at once.

title: The Garden's Final Bloom
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone in your garden, feeling lightheaded and unsteady on your feet. You've just noticed a flower you've been tending for months finally open — a moment of pure, quiet elation. But as you reach out to touch it, your balance wavers, and you begin to faint. Start with a breathless, joyful whisper as you describe the bloom, but let your voice soften and trail off as your vision blurs and your knees buckle. Gasp lightly as you grab for a trellis, then let the words fade into a strange, peaceful surrender. Keep it natural — you're not performing, you're living this slow collapse.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Summit Exhale
instruction: You've just finished a solo hike you trained months for—reaching the top after a brutal last mile in the rain. Now, collapsed on a wet rock, you stare at the view. Start with a long, shaking exhale, like you're letting go of all the doubt. Let your voice tremble as you whisper, 'Oh my God... I did it.' Feel pride swell in your chest, making your voice warm and bright by the end, even as you wipe tears or laugh quietly. Let your body slump—your knees weak, your breath still catching—and let the words come naturally, maybe with a pause as you look around.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Mutiny of the Heart
instruction: You are a person who has spent years being the strong one, the leader everyone relies on, and you're finally breaking. Start with fierce, explosive anger - shouting at the universe, at fate, at anyone who told you that you had to hold it together. Let your voice crack with rage as you describe the weight of everyone's expectations crushing you. Build to a fever pitch of intensity, your words tumbling over each other, passionate and raw and uncontrolled. Then, shockingly, let it all collapse - your voice dissolving into broken sobs as you confess you can't do it anymore, you don't want to be strong, you're terrified and exhausted and so desperately tired. End in a whisper that's somehow louder than your screaming was, admitting with devastating simplicity that you need help, that you're scared, that you don't know how to stop pretending. Let us hear both your power and your complete powerlessness.

title: The Truth Your Mother Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the childhood she gave you—the neglect disguised as independence, the coldness called strength. Begin with trembling anger: 'Do you even remember my tenth birthday?' Your voice is sharp, accusatory, years of hurt compressed into each word. But as you speak, something shifts. You see her face, her own pain, and fury begins mixing with unwanted compassion. Your voice wavers between rage and desperate longing: 'I just needed you to see me.' There's a moment where you almost break—where the angry adult becomes the small child again, voice cracking: 'Why wasn't I enough?' By the end, you're not just angry anymore. There's grief, yes, but also a terrible understanding, maybe even the beginning of forgiveness you didn't want to feel. Your voice should sound like someone watching their own anger dissolve into something more complicated and painful.

title: The Lure of the Sky
instruction: You are a small child, maybe 5 or 6, with a voice that tries to be big and tough like your dad. You're at the playground, and you've been spinning on the tire swing for too long. Now you're standing, but the world won't stop moving. You're trying to concentrate on something real—the feel of the metal pole under your hand—because an intense interest has taken hold: a ladybug on the back of your knuckle. You want to show it to your mom, but your legs are liquid and your eyes are seeing stars. As you fight to stay upright, your voice starts to fade and soften; what began as a proud announcement becomes a breathy, trailing whisper as the world goes quiet.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Leaving Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your child is asleep, and you're leaving—witness protection, a necessary disappearance to keep them safe, and they can never know why. Whisper your goodbye as if volume could wake them and shatter your resolve. Start with practical things—reminders about their homework, their soccer schedule, the way they like their sandwiches cut. Let your voice catch as you move to bigger things—how proud you are, how brave they've always been, how this will hurt them and you can't explain why. Your breathing should be almost silent but increasingly ragged. Every sentence is both comfort and abandonment. End with something you want to say but can't quite get out, just your breath against their hair, and the sound of you trying not to sob as you memorize their face one last time.

title: Street Corner Epiphany
instruction: You're standing on a noisy city corner, phone pressed to your ear, furious at the person who just betrayed you. Your voice strains against the traffic and sirens, sharp with malice. Mid-sentence, a stranger steps in—maybe a kid returns your dropped wallet, or a helper guides you across. Your anger cracks; you stumble over your words, distracted by the noise and the unexpected kindness. End with a breathless, genuine thank you, your tone softened but still rough from the earlier rage. Speak naturally, letting the environment interrupt you.

title: Arousal Building
instruction: You're being brought to arousal slowly. Your partner's voice is low, deliberate: 'I want you to feel this.' Their voice is instructional but sensual. Your voice starts unaffected, then gradually becomes affected. Your breathing changes audibly. Your voice becomes less controlled: 'Yes.' Sentences become fragments. Your partner's voice is guiding the escalation: 'Let me hear you.' Now your voice is no longer performance—it's genuine response. Your body is responding before your mind catches up. Your voice becomes almost involuntary—gasps, whispers, pleas. By the end, your voice is completely given over to sensation. Your voice should map the journey from stillness to overwhelming arousal without ever speaking in explicit terms—just the sounds of someone being awakened.

title: Time Traveler Witnessing
instruction: You're watching history happen and you know how it ends. Your voice carries the weight of foreknowledge: 'Right now, they have no idea.' Breathing is controlled but heavy. Vocal tone is melancholic, witnessing the ignorance of the doomed present. 'In three months, everything changes.' Intonation is grave. Physical: stillness, observation. 'I can't tell them. I can't change it. I can only watch.' Your voice is haunted by knowledge no one else possesses. By the end, you're documenting the last moments of before.

title: The Gallery of Almost
instruction: You're standing in front of a painting you created during the happiest year of your life—the year before everything fell apart. It's been acquired by a major gallery. You should be celebrating. Instead, you're alone with it, and looking at it cracks you open. Begin with pride, your voice warm with achievement, maybe even laughing at the memory of making it. But as you look closer, you see her in every brushstroke—the person you lost. Let joy curdle into grief mid-sentence. Your voice breaks as past and present collide: you got everything you wanted and lost everything that mattered. Feel gratitude for the gift this year gave you and rage at what it cost. Let these opposites war in your voice—laughing through tears, celebrating while mourning. End with a phrase that somehow holds both thank you and goodbye, acceptance and anguish, spoken to the painting as if it's the person you'll never see again.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed. For years, you've held back everything—your anger at their absence, your grief over lost time, your desperate need to hear them say they're proud of you. Start from a place of careful control, speaking in measured, safe phrases. But as you realize these are your last minutes together, let everything break open. Move from careful politeness to raw, unfiltered truth—screaming if you need to, sobbing, laughing bitterly, whispering the most tender words you've never said. End by giving them permission to go, finding a strange peace mixed with devastation. Let your body release everything it's been holding—shake, collapse, breathe as if for the first time.

title: Thank You For Breaking My Heart - Gratitude at the End of a Great Love
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you deeply love but cannot be with - maybe they're moving across the world, maybe the timing was always wrong, maybe loving them means letting them go. Start with a laugh that's already half tears: 'This is so stupid. I should hate you for this.' But you don't. List everything this relationship gave you - how they changed you, saw you, made you brave. Your voice should crack with gratitude even as your heart shatters. Include the moment where joy and grief become indistinguishable - you're genuinely thankful and absolutely destroyed at the same time. 'Thank you' should sound like both celebration and funeral. End with peaceful devastation, accepting this beautiful, terrible thing. Let laughter and sobbing blur together. This is love at its most bittersweet - the contradiction of being grateful for something that's ending, of finding meaning in loss, of celebrating even as you grieve.

title: Final Transmission from the Void
instruction: You are an older astronaut alone in deep space, your suit's visor fogged with your own breath. The radio crackles with static. You've just witnessed the destruction of your ship, and you're floating in silence. Begin with a numb, detached report—your voice flat, mechanical, filtered through the helmet's comms. Let the breathing be loud, the static interrupt. As you speak, a memory of Earth surfaces—a child's laugh, the smell of rain. Let that crack your numbness. Your voice trembles, then breaks, as you say goodbye not to command, but to yourself. End with a raw, quiet sob that fades into static.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Edge of the Bed
instruction: You are lying in bed beside your partner, your cheek pressed to their bare chest. You’ve just finished making love, and the room is dark except for the streetlight through the blinds. As you trace a slow pattern on their skin with your fingertip, you start to speak—a thought that has been sitting at the back of your mind for days. At first, your voice is a soft, distant murmur, lost in the warmth and the thrum of their heartbeat. But as you concentrate on the words, you feel the weight of them grow heavier in your mouth. A tiny hesitation, a catch in your breath, the slight tightening of your hand—these movements are real. By the end, the contemplation has crystallized into a quiet, terrifying clarity, and your voice becomes more focused, almost fragile, as if speaking the truth aloud might break the spell.

title: Through the Filter
instruction: You are a 17-year-old in full CBRN gear, standing in a decontamination tent after a long shift. You've been in the gas mask for hours, and your voice is hoarse from shouting through it. You're talking to a older volunteer you've secretly admired for months—your voice is muffled, breathing labored, and you have to shout to be heard. Start with weary, clinical exhaustion, reporting your status. Then, as you fumble to remove the mask, your voice cracks—you try to hide a nervous, horny smile as you confess you got his coffee order wrong on purpose just to have an excuse to talk to him. End with a goofy, breathless laugh, embarrassed but hopeful.

title: Whispered Inventory at 3 AM
instruction: It is the middle of the night. You cannot sleep because you are drowning in self-doubt, replaying every failure, every inadequacy. You are lying in darkness, and you begin to whisper—to yourself, to the darkness, to no one—a desperate inventory of what is actually true about you. Start with your voice small, uncertain, almost disbelieving your own words. List the things you are genuinely good at, the people who actually love you, the times you succeeded, the qualities others see in you even when you cannot see them yourself. Speak intimately, vulnerably, as if you are telling secrets. Let each truth you speak aloud build on the last. As you continue, feel your voice gain quiet strength—not loud or triumphant, but steady, grounded, real. By the end, arrive at a tender self-recognition, a fragile but authentic peace. This is not about confidence; it is about finally, gently, telling yourself the truth.

title: The Kitchen at Midnight
instruction: You've come home to confront your father/mother about why they gave up on their own dreams and taught you to do the same. Begin with rehearsed anger, words you've practiced saying for years. But as you speak, actually listen to their response—and let something they say trigger a real memory from your own life where you made a similar choice, where you compromised yourself. Feel your righteous anger crack as you recognize yourself in them. Your voice should break from accusation into something more complicated: anger mixed with sudden, unwanted understanding. Let the confrontation transform into an admission that you're more alike than you wanted to believe. End not with resolution, but with the shakiness of seeing your parent as heartbreakingly human.

title: Rocking the Guilty Tides
instruction: You are a new mother, alone in the dim nursery at 2am, gently rocking your sleeping infant. As you hum and sway, your mind drifts to a memory of your partner from earlier tonight — a moment of raw intimacy that left you wanting more. A flicker of lust warms your chest, but then guilt crashes in: you feel wrong for feeling desire while holding your pure, innocent baby. Your voice must start soft, lulling, with a hidden warmth of longing, then shift to a wavering, hushed confession of distress as you try to reconcile the two feelings. The rhythm of rocking should pulse through your words, and remember that your body is slightly off-balance from the baby's weight on one side, so your voice might catch or trail.

title: Empty Nursery: Rage at God After Losing Your Baby
instruction: You're standing in the nursery you prepared. Start with dangerous calm - measured, almost polite, as if explaining something reasonable to an invisible presence. But your control is a dam about to break. Your voice gets louder, tighter, more deliberate with each word, overarticulating like the drunk driver, until suddenly you explode - screaming questions, accusations, raw animal sounds of grief. Your fury is wild, incoherent. Then it collapses mid-scream into sobbing, then gasping, then something worse than tears - dry, silent heaving. End in a place you didn't expect: whispering a lullaby to the empty crib, your voice impossibly gentle, finding something like peace in the ruins. Let your voice shatter from control to chaos to tender surrender.

title: The Filtered Farewell
instruction: You are a young woman wearing a full CBRN gas mask, standing in a decontamination tent after a chemical spill. You've just learned that your best friend didn't make it. You're speaking to a rescue worker, but you're also still feeling the lingering, floaty buzz of the sedative they gave you for the panic attack. Your voice is distorted and loud inside the mask – you have to shout to be heard, but your emotions are a messy cocktail. Start with a detached, almost dreamy confusion about where you are, then let the reality of your friend's death hit you mid-sentence, cracking your voice through the muffled plastic. End with a choked, raw plea for confirmation, your words breaking against the harsh mechanical rhythm of your own breathing.

title: What We Never Said
instruction: Late at night, lying beside someone you love, whisper a truth you've kept hidden—maybe about your past, your fears, or something you did that you're ashamed of. Begin in near-silence, aware of every tiny sound: their breathing, the rustle of sheets, your own heartbeat. Let yourself feel the vulnerability of darkness, intimacy, and proximity. Pay extraordinary attention to physical sensations as you speak: the trembling in your voice, the closeness of their body, the way fear manifests as tightness in your throat. Don't perform the confession—instead, stay connected to the actual physical experience of revealing yourself. Notice how your heightened awareness of the moment allows unexpected emotions to surface: maybe relief, maybe terror, maybe a tenderness you didn't anticipate. Let your attention to these arising sensations guide the emotional journey. End in a different place than you began—perhaps the shame has transformed into fragile hope, or the fear has dissolved into unexpected intimacy.

title: The Last Hour Before Flight
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother in hospice. She has one hour left, maybe less. At first, you can't look at her—there's terror, guilt about not visiting enough, the smell of the room, your phone buzzing in your pocket. Speak these barriers aloud as whispers: your fear, your distraction, the things keeping you from truly being here. Name them honestly. Then, once you've cleared them away, simply be with her. Let yourself arrive fully. Hold her hand. Your emotion will shift from scattered panic and avoidance to pure presence—perhaps grief, perhaps unexpected peace, perhaps a love so clear it hurts. The arc moves from running away to finally being able to stay.

title: Finding Light in the Weight of Explaining
instruction: You're explaining your identity yet again to someone - but this time, something shifts. Your voice moves between weariness and unexpected lightness, between frustration and sudden gratitude for the complexity of who you are. You're laughing and almost crying at once, finding strange peace in the contradiction. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance - yes, it's exhausting, yes, it shouldn't be necessary, but there's also something beautiful about knowing yourself this deeply. Your voice carries both the weight and the freedom of it.

title: The Tease That Unraveled
instruction: You are a child who has been playfully teasing your exhausted mother after a long day. You're laughing, poking fun at her tiredness, but suddenly your own body betrays you — the fatigue you've been hiding crashes in and triggers a panic attack. Your chest tightens, you can't catch your breath, and your words turn into frantic gasps. Start with a sing-song teasing tone, then let your voice spiral into short, high-pitched fragments as you hyperventilate. Mention how you can't breathe, feel tingling, and then, through sobs, catch yourself and whisper a desperate 'thank you' for her being there — your voice now raw and quavering, exhaustion and gratitude colliding. title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're thirty-eight years old, sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table, and for the first time in your life, you're telling her the truth about how her 'high standards' felt like conditional love. Start calm—almost rehearsed—because you've practiced this. But as you speak, old wounds open fresh. Your voice sharpens with anger you didn't know you were carrying. She tries to interrupt with justifications and suddenly you're louder, your words coming faster, overlapping hers. Then she says something—maybe 'I did my best'—and your rage collapses into something more devastating: the grief of a child who needed something they never got. Your voice drops to almost a whisper. You're not attacking anymore; you're begging her to understand. End with you looking at her face and seeing she's crying too, and you don't know if anything has changed or if you've just lost something you can never get back.

title: Under the Sink
instruction: You're lying flat on your stomach on the cold kitchen floor, reaching under the sink to grab a leaky pipe that's been dripping for days. The anger simmers as you realize you'll need a wrench you don't have, but you force yourself to concentrate so you can at least turn the valve by hand. As your grip slips for the third time, the concentration shatters into a sharp, breathless burst of fury aimed at the pipe itself. title: Midnight Negotiation
instruction: You're a 17-year-old in a dimly lit bedroom at a house party, sitting on the edge of a bed with a girl you've just met. As you speak, you fidget with a jacket sleeve, pause to shush a creaking floorboard, and let the gratitude settle into a quiet, possessive contentment, the envy barely flickering in a hesitant pause.

title: The Safety of Your Lips
instruction: You are a young man finally reunited with your partner after a terrifying ordeal. You hold them close, kissing them softly but deeply, overwhelmed by the sensation of being safe. Start with a shaky whisper, your breath catching as you speak between kisses — 'I thought I'd never...' — then let the relief flood you. Your voice should be thick with emotion, slightly muffled by the closeness. Let your words trail off into soft moans and sighs. End with a quiet, amazed laugh, your voice full of gratitude and peace. Let the wet sounds of the kiss punctuate your lines.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: A Glimpse of the Past
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a soft, high-pitched voice, sitting alone in a dim room. Your phone is in your lap, thumb scrolling slowly through old photos. You're mumbling to yourself, distracted by the screen—little 'hmm' sounds, a quiet 'now where is it...' as you squint and adjust your glasses. Then you find a picture of your late husband, and your concentration melts into a gentle, tearful smile. You speak the words below, starting with a distracted, searching tone, then becoming slower, softer, and more present as the memory takes over.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Final Transmission
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman scientist aboard a failing space station, sealed inside your helmet as the primary oxygen line ruptures. You begin by urgently trying to contact base, your voice tight with controlled panic, amplified by the helmet's reverb. As static crackles and no one answers, you feel the helplessness creep in — your breathing grows louder, more labored, and you start to trail off, losing certainty in your words. End with a quiet, resigned whisper as you realize you are completely alone and time is running out. Speak as if every movement of your head shifts the microphone, and let the amplifying effect of the helmet make your voice slightly tinny and confined.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Visit Before Deployment
instruction: You're sitting with your adult child the night before they deploy to a conflict zone as a combat medic. You start with forced cheerfulness, talking about practicalities—'Make sure you write when you can, the mail system is pretty good now'—trying to keep it light, almost businesslike. But as the reality sets in that this might be the last conversation, your voice begins to fracture. You want to tell them you're proud, but terror keeps breaking through. 'I need you to—' and you can't finish because what you need is for them to come home alive, but you can't say that, can't put that weight on them. End in a place where you're trying to memorize their face, voice barely above a whisper, saying things you've never said before because there might not be another chance. Show the journey from false brightness to raw, undefended love and fear.

title: The Promotion You Prayed For
instruction: You've just received the phone call: you got the position, the opportunity that will change your life. But your partner—who sacrificed everything to support you—just told you this morning they're leaving. You need to call your mother and tell her the good news; she doesn't know about the separation yet. Begin by building the physical reality: phone in your hand (feel its weight, temperature), standing in your apartment where boxes aren't packed yet, noticing the light, the silence, the evidence of the life you're losing everywhere you look. Start from a place of forced brightness, trying to sound celebratory. Don't 'play' the contradiction—instead, experience the literal reality of your body in success and grief simultaneously. Feel the triumph in your chest while also feeling the hollowness in your stomach. As you speak to your mother, building enthusiasm about the future, let the sensory truth of your present moment leak through. Notice how your voice might crack, how your breathing shifts, how joy and devastation can actually coexist in your body at the same moment. End having revealed more truth than you intended—to her or to yourself—about what this victory actually costs and means.
inspired_by: Actor knows what they want to feel in a scene but cannot get there from cold

title: The Vanishing Point
instruction: You are an elderly man driving on a busy highway at dusk, your wife in the passenger seat. Heavy traffic and fading light force you to focus intensely on the road ahead. You're terrified that her new, unsteady cough might signal something serious, and you're trying to sound calm for her. Begin with a tense, tight-throated reassurance as you check the rearview mirror, then let the fear leak into your voice as the traffic slows and you're forced to stop, your hands gripping the wheel. End with a whispery, confession-like admission of your dread.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Homecoming That Isn't
instruction: You're returning to a place or person after years away, flooded with contradictory feelings. Begin with cautious hope, maybe even excitement. As you take in the familiar and unfamiliar details, let fragmented sense-memories bombard you: specific words once spoken here, the quality of light you'd forgotten, a disappointment, a perfect moment, anger you thought you'd released, unexpected tenderness, resentment, gratitude, the person you were, the person you've become. Don't resolve these contradictions—let them coexist and clash. Some fragments will amplify your joy; others will deepen an ache you didn't know was there. End in a complex emotional state where you're simultaneously devastated and grateful, angry and loving, holding incompatible truths in your heart at once.
inspired_by: Actor needs to quickly elevate vulnerability or emotional availability before a scene

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are in the middle of intense physical exertion—running, fighting, making love, or collapsing from exhaustion—and suddenly a sensory memory crashes through: cold water closing over your head, the panic of being underwater, lungs burning, the world going distant. This isn't a metaphor—you are actually re-experiencing the physical sensations. The pressure in your chest. The way sound changes. The terror of not being able to breathe. Let your current physical state merge completely with this visceral memory. Your voice may gasp, cry out, whisper, or go silent. Don't perform the memory—let your body remember it. By the end, you surface from this collision of present sensation and past terror into a moment of raw, unexpected vulnerability: perhaps sobbing, perhaps laughing, perhaps simply breathing as if for the first time.

title: Confession in the Wind
instruction: You stand alone in a vast, empty field, wind pressing against you and stealing every sound. Speak a broken apology to someone who isn't there—someone you deeply wronged years ago. Let your voice start tight with shame, fragile and almost swallowed by the gusts, pausing to cough or blink against dust. As you continue, the wind seems to carry the words away, and shame slowly softens into a hollow acceptance—your voice becomes quieter, more resigned, until you just let the wind take the last few syllables.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Threadbare Promises
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner in the dark, whispering a confession that will change everything—you've fallen out of love, or you're leaving, or you've betrayed them in a way that can't be undone. Start with barely audible words, your voice gossamer-thin, catching on every syllable as if speaking will make it real. Let long silences punctuate your confession, breathing becoming part of the performance. Feel the weight of their body next to yours, the intimacy of darkness making this both easier and infinitely harder. As you speak, let your voice oscillate between clinical detachment—trying to explain rationally—and devastating tenderness, because you still care deeply even as you destroy what you had. End with a kind of quiet fracturing, your last words dissolving into breath and silence.

title: Comedian Having a Genuine Breakdown During Set
instruction: You're mid-set. You've been fine. Then you make a joke about your divorce and it doesn't feel funny anymore—it feels real and devastating. Your voice changes. The jokes stop working. You're standing on stage in front of 200 people and you're genuinely crying. You try to keep going but 'So yeah...' comes out broken. The crowd is uncomfortable. You can't do fake-strong right now. Your voice becomes small and real.

title: Dancing Alone to Your Wedding Song
instruction: You're alone in your apartment, and your wedding song comes on—but you're now divorced, or widowed, or they left you. At first, your body moves stiffly, painfully, as the memory of dancing together floods through you with physical intensity. Let your breath catch. Let your body remember their hands on you. But keep moving. As the song continues, let something fierce rise up—a determination to reclaim this song, this body, this joy that was yours before it was theirs. By the end, you're dancing with wild, almost violent freedom, crying and laughing at once, sweating, fully alive and furious and heartbroken and liberated. Your body tells the whole story.
inspired_by: Actor is working in film with little or no rehearsal time

title: Laughing with Your Dead Child's Invisible Friend
instruction: You're in your child's room, surrounded by their things. You're talking to their imaginary friend—the one they described so vividly before the accident. Start by laughing softly, genuinely, as you recount something silly your child said about this friend. Your voice should be warm with memory. Then keep that almost-smile in your voice even as tears come, speaking to this invisible being with gratitude for keeping your child company. Tell them stories about your child, your tone playful and broken at once. Let joy and devastation coexist in your voice—you're so grateful to have had them, so destroyed that they're gone. Include a moment where you break down completely, then recover by laughing at how ridiculous this is, talking to someone who never existed about someone who did. End with a whispered request: ask the imaginary friend to find your child, wherever they are, and play with them again. Make it both absurd and the most sacred thing you've ever said.
inspired_by: The Parent and the Imaginary Friend

title: The Final Inventory
instruction: You are an older adult dictating a legal inventory of your late spouse's personal effects for transcription. Begin in your usual 'typewriter' voice—fast, flat, monotone, speaking every period and comma aloud like 'period' 'comma'—as if this is just another chore. But as you list items like 'his reading glasses comma' and 'the photo album comma period', let a quiet bitterness creep into your tone on the final line: the realization that these objects outlasted the love. Don't overdo it; the bitterness should feel like a natural slip, a slight tightening in your throat or a slower pace on the last sentence, then resume flatness for the closing punctuation.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Mile 20 Breakdown
instruction: You're a young man who just hit the 20-mile mark in a marathon, and for a second, you feel a surge of triumph—you've never been this far before. But suddenly, your body crashes. Your legs go rubbery, your vision blurs, and your voice becomes a hollow, slurred whisper. Start by trying to express that fleeting pride to your running partner, then let the words dissolve into confused, breathless pleas as you realize you can't go on. Let your breathing become labored and your speech monosyllabic, with a raw, unexpected edge of panic or tears breaking through the exhaustion.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep, and you're leaving—not because you want to, but because staying would destroy you both. Maybe it's addiction, maybe it's mental illness, maybe it's something else that makes you dangerous to the person you love most. You kneel beside their bed, and your voice is barely audible because you can't risk waking them. You start by trying to explain, whispering reasons that sound hollow even to you. Your voice keeps catching because you're memorizing their face, the way their hair falls across the pillow. As you whisper all the things you'll miss—first days of school, graduations, their wedding—your voice becomes liquid with grief. This isn't dramatic; it's devastatingly quiet. You're breaking apart in slow motion, trying not to make a sound. By the end, you can barely speak at all. Your voice should sound like someone drowning in silence, like love and failure happening in the same breath.

title: The Wedding Toast for Your Replacement
instruction: You're standing at your ex-spouse's wedding, holding a champagne glass, about to give a toast. They asked you personally—said it would mean everything if you could be there, could bless this new marriage. You said yes because you're evolved, mature, past all that. But as you begin to speak, your voice must carry the impossible weight of contradictions. You genuinely love seeing them this happy—happier than they ever were with you. And that reality is both beautiful and devastating. Begin with warmth that's almost entirely real, celebrating the couple. But let cracks appear: a tremor when you mention how well the new spouse knows them, a pause when you talk about love that lasts. Your journey is through joy that coexists with profound loss, gratitude for what you once had mixed with resentment that it wasn't enough, hope for their future tangled with grief for your own. End with a genuine wish for their happiness that simultaneously acknowledges your own broken heart. The final words should somehow hold all of it—celebration and mourning, love and letting go, sincerity and barely controlled devastation.

title: Whispering the Wins
instruction: Late at night, you are lying beside someone you love, who is asleep. You are whispering to them (or to the darkness, or to yourself) a confession: you've been secretly keeping track of every small moment this week when you felt proud of who you are—not grand achievements, but tiny things. You helped a stranger. You didn't lose your temper. You chose honesty when lying would have been easier. You laughed genuinely. Begin in a hushed, almost embarrassed tone, as if these small victories are too fragile or foolish to speak aloud. As you continue, let your whisper gain tender conviction. These moments are proof you are becoming someone you can love. By the end, your voice should carry quiet wonder and deep vulnerability, as if you're falling in love with your own capacity for goodness. A whispered revelation of self-acceptance.

title: The Last Cup of Morning Coffee
instruction: You're sitting at your father's bedside in hospice, holding his favorite mug—the one with the chipped handle he's used for thirty years. He's sleeping, and you know these are his final hours. Begin by describing the coffee to him in whispered detail: its warmth in your hands, the smell, the taste, the steam rising. Let these simple, concrete sensations ground you. As you speak, allow memories to surface—mornings at the kitchen table, his laugh, his disappointments in you, your disappointments in him. Let the specificity of this ordinary object—the weight of the mug, the bitterness of the coffee—gradually unlock everything you've never said to him. End with what you most need him to know, your voice breaking as you realize he may never hear it. Move from the tangible comfort of the coffee to the vast, unbearable reality of permanent goodbye.
inspired_by: Actor working on material with strong emotional demands (suicide, grief, love) cannot access genuine feeling

title: Explosive Intervention: Screaming at Your Sibling Who's Overdosed Three Times This Month
instruction: You're in the hospital again. Your sibling survived another overdose. You walk in planning to be supportive, but the moment you see them, everything you've been holding back erupts. Start with explosive rage—screaming about how selfish they are, how you can't do this anymore, how they're killing you along with themselves. Your voice should be raw, almost violent in its intensity, shaking with fury. But then—mid-scream—you break. The anger collapses into desperate, sobbing terror. Your voice shifts completely: now you're begging, pleading, your words coming between gasps. You're telling them you can't lose them, you're confessing how you sit by the phone every night waiting for the call that they're dead. Move between fierce protectiveness ('I will fight for you even when you won't fight for yourself') and utter helplessness ('But I can't save you, can I? I can't make you want to live'). End in exhausted devastation—not angry anymore, not even sad, just emptied out and whispering that you don't know how to keep loving someone who's determined to disappear. Let your voice carry every contradictory feeling at once: rage, love, terror, helplessness, devotion, and despair.
inspired_by: Ambien Confabulation: Making Up Memories You Think Are Real

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: Confront your aging parent about a family secret they've kept from you your entire life—something you've just discovered that recontextualizes your whole childhood. Start with controlled anger, presenting evidence like a prosecutor. But as you speak, begin to notice details about them you haven't seen in years: how their hands shake, how small they've become, the specific pattern of lines around their eyes. Let your imagination transport you backwards—see them as they were when you were five years old, towering and magical and invincible. Watch that younger version of them overlap with who sits before you now. Your confrontation should dissolve into something more complex: you're simultaneously the hurt child demanding answers and the adult who suddenly understands the impossible weight of their choices. End in a place that surprises you—perhaps anger transforming into unexpected tenderness, or rage mellowing into sad understanding.

title: The Compliment You Can't Survive Hearing
instruction: Your best friend is telling you - gently, carefully - that you're a good person, that you deserve love. But you've just done something you're deeply ashamed of, something they don't know about. Your voice is barely audible, thick with unshed tears: 'Please don't say that.' They continue, and each kind word is agony. Your voice becomes a whispered confession that catches in your throat: 'If you knew what I did, you wouldn't...' You can't finish. There's a long pause where you're trying not to fall apart. Their continued tenderness undoes you completely. By the end, you're whispering through quiet tears: 'I don't know how to be the person you think I am. But I want to be. God, I want to be.' It's the most vulnerable you've ever been.

title: Making Up After a Terrible Fight
instruction: The fight is over. You're both destroyed. You're trying to make up. Your voice is shaky, tentative. 'I didn't mean...' You're trying to repair something that feels broken. You're being vulnerable after being weaponized. Your voice becomes softer, almost pleading. 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry.' Your voice is carrying apology and love simultaneously. You're both trying. Physical contact happens. Your voice becomes almost inaudible as you're pressed against them, whispering apologies. Your voice cracks with relief.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a betrayal or abandonment from your childhood that has shaped your entire life, but as you begin to speak, you discover that actual words fail to capture the depth of what you feel. Your voice becomes pure sound—raw, unfiltered emotional expression. Start with sounds that carry your rage, your accusations, the child inside you screaming to be heard. As your parent responds (imagined or real), allow your sounds to shift. Perhaps you hear their pain beneath their defensiveness. Perhaps your anger cracks open to reveal the grief of a child who just wanted to be loved. End in a place where your sounds have transformed—perhaps to understanding, perhaps to exhausted sorrow, perhaps to a fragile new beginning.

title: The Burial of a Prayer
instruction: You are an elderly person, frail but stubborn, in the midst of sex with a partner you've grown numb to but who once made you feel infinite. As you move together in a slow, rhythmic grind, your breath hitches with each thrust — words come out broken, between gasps. Begin with a cold, detached murmur, reciting a bitter memory of when this act meant something. As the rhythm quickens, feel a surge of infatuation, a desperate clinging to the ghost of passion — you gasp, 'please, don't stop,' but the numbness snaps back, and in the final exhale, raw anger erupts: not at your partner, but at yourself for still trying. Let your voice break, catch, shift from whisper to a sharp, breathy push of sound, as bedsprings creak beneath you.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Call I Can't Take Back
instruction: You're at a party, drunk, and you've just made a cruel joke about your best friend's wife. You're now alone in the bathroom, leaning on the sink, staring at your reflection. Your phone buzzes—it's your friend calling. You pick up, ashamed, trying to sound sober but your voice betrays you. Start with defensive bravado, then let the shame seep in as you realize you can't undo what you said. Let your voice slur, your volume drop, and your words stumble as you apologize. End with a quiet, broken admission.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: A Crack in the Podium
instruction: You're an older woman, a lifelong activist, standing on a wooden crate at a crowded street corner rally against gentrification. Your voice is raw from shouting, you can barely hear yourself over the traffic and murmurs. But in the front row, a younger man with kind eyes keeps nodding at you—and something stirs. Start with bitter, strained fury about lost homes, but let your voice wander as you notice him. Let your tone rise with a hint of playful mischief, a low chuckle, then drop into a rasp that's half threat, half invitation. The crowd fades; you're talking mostly to him now. End with a weary smile in your voice, the anger softening into a warm, lustful defiance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You're in your car in an empty parking lot. You just left the office where you were humiliated, or the hospital with devastating news, or the apartment of someone who shattered you. You made it to your car, closed the door, and now—let your body respond however it actually wants to. Maybe you slam your fists on the steering wheel, maybe you're frozen and numb, maybe rage and grief hit you in waves. Don't decide what this should look like. Let sound come if it needs to—primal, ugly, raw. Feel the physical sensations: your heart pounding, hands shaking, the pressure in your chest. As you move through this—whether it takes 30 seconds or three minutes—let the storm shift. Perhaps exhaustion replaces rage. Perhaps numbness cracks into howling. Perhaps something fierce and determined emerges from the wreckage. By the end, your breathing has changed, your body has released something, and you're left in the aftermath of whatever just tore through you.

title: The Wedding Ring in Your Palm
instruction: Hold an object that connects you to someone you've lost—not through death, but through an ending you chose or they chose. Begin in bitter resignation, describing the object clinically: its weight, temperature, texture, any markings or wear. Then let yourself drift back to a specific moment when this object (or what it represents) meant something entirely different—a moment of hope, promise, or deep connection. Reconstruct that moment with forensic detail: the season, the time of day, what you were wearing, their expression, the exact quality of their voice. As you rebuild this memory of what was, let your voice carry both the sweetness of that past moment and the ache of present loss simultaneously. By the end, you should be speaking to both the memory and the person as they were, filled with contradictory feelings—gratitude for what was and grief for what can never be again, anger at the ending and tenderness for who they once were to you.

title: The Wedding Shawl
instruction: You are alone in your dimly lit living room, knitting a shawl for your best friend's wedding tomorrow. The needles click softly, rhythmically. You're jealous—your friend has found love while you feel invisible. Sadness wraps around you like a cold fog. But as you hold up the shawl, the delicate lace pattern catches the lamplight, and a quiet awe fills you. Speak to yourself, letting your voice start heavy and bitter, then slowly soften into wonder as you realize you made something beautiful despite your pain. Let the clicking needles punctuate your words, with pauses to adjust yarn or wipe your eye. Feel the shift from envy to reverence.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight of the Gift
instruction: Your estranged sibling has just saved your life (donated an organ, paid a debt, sacrificed their future for yours) and you're thanking them for the first time since the rupture between you. Begin with gratitude—but notice if you're performing the emotion you think you should feel. Are you crying because you're genuinely moved or because the situation seems to demand tears? Beneath the 'appropriate' response, what else lives? Resentment that you needed saving? Anger at years lost? Suffocating guilt? Fear that this gift creates an unpayable debt? Let these contradictions surface without forcing them into a neat emotional package. By the end, arrive at a messy, specific truth: gratitude braided inseparably with grief for all the years you can't reclaim, love complicated by the history of harm between you.

title: The Ceremony of Burning Bridges
instruction: You are severing ties with your mentor in a moment of explosive, contradictory intensity. Start with fierce gratitude that sounds almost aggressive—'You made me who I am, and I'll never forgive you for it!' Let your voice shake with rage at how their lessons caged you, how their 'wisdom' was really about control, how they shaped you in their image without asking what you wanted. Build to a roar as you declare you're done being their legacy, their proof of concept, their second chance. Then suddenly break—voice cracking into something raw and childlike—when you realize you still need their approval even as you reject everything they stand for. Feel the fury collapse into helpless tears, then rebuild into something harder: clear-eyed determination mixed with grief. End with powerful, heartbroken certainty: 'I loved you. I love you. And I have to leave you behind.' Let your voice carry both strength and devastation.

title: Pretending to Be Surprised by Predictable News
instruction: Someone shares news you saw coming. Internally, youre unfazed, but you act surprised to match their excitement. Describe your lack of surprise inside while expressing amazement. Speak with enthusiasm, matching their energy.

title: The Voicemail You Shouldn't Have Left
instruction: You're a fifteen-year-old sitting on your bedroom floor at 2am, phone in hand, after leaving a voicemail on your ex's phone. You're half-wired, half-exhausted. You start speaking to yourself, replaying the call, feeling annoyed at your own desperation. But as you remember their laugh, the phone's screen, that one night, the annoyance cracks into raw longing. Let your voice waver between a tight, irritated edge and a breathy, trembling need. Mid-sentence, a hitch of breath or a shake reveals the lust and heartbreak tangled together. End quieter, more exposed, as if you're whispering to them in your head.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Longing (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Pillow of Ashes
instruction: You're lying face-down on your bed, pillow pressed hard over your head, after a devastating argument with your adult child who said they never want to see you again. Your voice is smothered—only raw, low frequencies escape. Start by shouting bitter accusations into the stuffing, your jaw tight, each word a guttural punch. Feel the heat of rage, the fabric soaking up your fury. As you speak, your energy drains; the shouting becomes a choked whisper, then finally just breath. Your voice cracks with exhaustion. End with a flat, numb surrender—words that barely register, spoken as if you're already gone. Let the bitterness fade into hollow silence. Keep it natural: shift your weight, pause to swallow, let the pillow muffle and distort your voice unevenly.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing Through the Wreckage
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a pounding rave, your body moving with the bass despite your age. You shout to a friend beside you, your voice bouncing with each jump—breathless, high-pitched, fighting the music. Start with fierce disgust spilling out about the noise and chaos, how the world has lost its soul, but as you keep dancing, the rhythm breaks open a deep sadness you've been holding: a farewell to someone you loved who would have hated this place. Let the disgust crumble into raw grief, your words catching as you sway, laughter and tears mixing with the beat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning: Telling Your Child You're Not Coming Home
instruction: You're a parent with a terminal diagnosis, and this is the morning you've decided to tell your child the truth. You start with false brightness, trying to protect them one last time: 'Hey, sweetheart, come sit with me for a minute.' But as you begin to explain, your voice fractures. The protective parent in you wars with the desperate human who wants to fall apart. You catch yourself mid-sentence, realizing you're explaining your own death to the person you'd die to protect—and you can't. Your voice moves from controlled explanation to raw confession: 'I'm so scared. I'm so scared of leaving you.' By the end, you're not the parent anymore—you're just a terrified person clinging to the sound of your child's breathing, trying to memorize it, your voice barely above a whisper as you say what you need them to remember about you. Let the transition from protector to vulnerable human be gradual and devastating.
inspired_by: Survived a Suicidal Moment: Reflection on the Turn

title: The Waiting Room Curl
instruction: You are an elderly man hunched in a hard plastic chair at a clinic, clutching your abdomen. The pain is a familiar, dull throb that never leaves—you've learned to breathe in short, guarded sips, your voice dropping low with a groan on every exhale. A bitterness rises as you mutter about the wasted hours and the doctors who don't listen. But then a nurse calls your name, and you force yourself to uncurl, letting a reluctant, weary resolve creep in. The shift comes from inside: the groaning softens, and you speak slower, as if accepting what you cannot change.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Vulnerability Shared
instruction: You're both being vulnerable simultaneously—physically and emotionally exposed in the same moment. You're both shaking slightly, both aware of how much you're showing each other. Your voice is small but certain: 'I'm scared.' Your partner's voice mirrors yours: 'Me too.' But you're both showing up anyway. You're both choosing to be known. That mutual vulnerability is its own kind of intimacy. You're not trying to fix each other's fear; you're just acknowledging it together. By the end, your voices should sound like two people who've chosen to be completely known by another person, fear and all.

title: The Archaeology of Touch
instruction: You're lying in darkness beside someone—lover, spouse, or the ghost of one. Speak barely above a whisper. Begin by describing a moment when they touched you in a way that changed you, but start from the physical sensation itself—the temperature of their hand, the pressure, the exact location on your body. Let the memory unearth something you've kept buried: a fear, a betrayal, a moment of devastating tenderness you couldn't bear to acknowledge. Your breathing should become part of the performance. Let long silences happen. Let your voice get smaller, not bigger. End by confessing what that touch meant in language that is awkward, halting, and absolutely true to how YOU experience intimacy—not poetic, not polished, but yours.

title: Marriage Counselor Whose Own Marriage Is Failing
instruction: Give professional advice to a couple while your own marriage crumbles in real-time via texts you glance at between responses. Your therapist voice is measured and wise: 'Have you tried expressing your needs using I-statements?' Your internal reaction to each text is devastating. The couple's issues mirror your own — the irony isn't lost on you. Include the moment you give advice you need to hear yourself, and your voice cracks because you're not talking to them anymore. You're talking to you.

title: Welcome Offering
instruction: Someone is welcoming another person, and the welcome is genuine. Their voice is warm, open, intentional. They're saying 'I'm glad you're here' through words and tone. The person being welcomed might be cautious—is this welcome real?—or might lean into it immediately. The welcomer's voice remains warm, patient, removing barriers. They're actively making space for this person. By the end, the person being welcomed has felt the welcome in their bones. The welcomer's voice has conveyed: you belong here. You're safe. This matters. That welcome is transformative.

title: Calling to Check On You
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gruff voice, calling a close friend who missed your planned get-together. You start angry, convinced they stood you up — your voice is clipped, louder than normal, with sharp upward inflections like 'You there?' as you verify the connection. Midway, you hear their weak tone and realize they're sick; your anger cracks into worry, then guilt. End with a softer plea, voice hoarse and slower, asking them to rest. Adjust the phone away from your mouth, clear your throat, and let your pitch drop as you shift from fury to tenderness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Telling Your Dying Parent You Finally Understand
instruction: You're at your father's bedside in hospice. For years, you resented his emotional distance, his workaholism, the childhood moments he missed. Now, holding his frail hand, you suddenly see the fear and limitations he carried. Start with the old bitterness still in your voice—'I wanted to tell you...'—but as you speak, something breaks open. The anger dissolves into profound, aching compassion. Your voice softens, becomes tender, almost a whisper: 'I understand now why you couldn't...' Grief rushes in where resentment lived. End with gratitude for who he was, even with all his failures, your voice thick with tears but steady with peace. He squeezes your hand weakly. You've made peace just in time.
inspired_by: Turning Down Someone's Romantic Advance Gently

title: The Library Laugh
instruction: You are an older woman in a quiet library, trying to read a book. You find a hilarious note someone left inside, maybe from a grandchild or a memory. At first, you contemplate it with a soft, thoughtful smile, then a wave of elation hits you so hard you have to clamp your mouth shut. Your voice comes out as a strained, squeaky whisper as you tease yourself for being silly, but the joy keeps leaking through in tiny, breathless giggles. Start with a contemplative murmur, then let the elation force your pitch higher and your laughter out in short bursts, ending on a light, teasing sigh.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (slightly present), Elation (clearly present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point of Ecstasy
instruction: You're alone, and something has just happened—maybe you've gotten devastating news, maybe you've experienced a breakthrough, maybe years of suppressed feeling are erupting. Your body cannot stay still. Start in one physical and emotional state, then let whatever needs to move through you take over: rage that needs to punch, grief that needs to collapse, joy that needs to shout, pain that needs to keen, laughter that borders on sobbing. Don't choreograph the transitions—let your body lead you. Make sounds without words if that's what wants to emerge. Allow the physical intensity to build and transform your emotional state completely. End somewhere unrecognizable: if you started enraged, perhaps you end in exhausted tenderness; if you started celebrating, perhaps you end weeping. Follow the body's authentic impulses.

title: Voice Message From Your Mother the Night Before She Died
instruction: You find a voicemail your mother left you three years ago, the night before her sudden death. You never listened to it—you were angry at her then, ignoring her calls. Now you press play. Her voice is tired, hesitant, trying to bridge the distance between you. She's asking for forgiveness without saying the words. She's telling you she understands why you're pulling away. Your voice responds to hers across time—first defensive, then cracking open as you hear what she was really saying. By the end, you're speaking to her as if she's in the room, saying everything you never got to say. Move from protective anger to devastating tenderness, from justification to raw, undefended grief.
inspired_by: Sex Tape Recorded Years Ago, Heard for First Time Since

title: The Last Echo
instruction: You are an older man standing alone on a windswept cliff at dawn. You’ve just buried your wife of forty years. As the sun rises, you release everything you held back at the funeral. Start with a guttural, full-throated scream—no words, just the sound of raw pain breaking open in your chest. Let your body shake, feel the tears streaming, stumble a step as the force leaves you. Then, as the scream fades into ragged breaths, let a single word slip out: 'Why?' It’s not a question—it’s an exhale. Gradually, the pain softens into relief, a trembling release. End with a quiet, broken whisper: 'It’s over now.' Let your voice crack, catch on a sob, then settle into exhaustion. You are alone, and that’s okay.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Long Climb
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman hiking alone up a steep, rocky trail. Your muscles ache, your breath comes in ragged puffs, and you pause often to lean on a tree. At first, you mutter bitter complaints under your breath — about your hiking partner who bailed, or about your aging body’s betrayal. But as you pause and gaze at the view through the trees, a quiet, sour recognition creeps in: you’re doing this for yourself after all. Let the words come out between gasps, with pauses where you lose your breath or your train of thought. The bitterness should soften into a wry, tired acceptance by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: I Can't Remember Why I Left You
instruction: You're confronting an ex-lover years after an abrupt, unexplained departure that devastated them. You desperately want to explain why you left, to justify yourself, to make them understand—but you're discovering in real-time that you can't fully remember your own reasoning. Start with defensive confidence, insisting there were good reasons. As you fumble through half-formed explanations that don't hold together, shift into frustrated confusion with yourself, then raw vulnerability as you realize the truth: maybe you made a terrible mistake and destroyed something precious for reasons that now seem meaningless. End with the quiet, devastating admission that you might have thrown away the best thing in your life and you don't even know why. Let the anger at yourself, the regret, and the pleading for forgiveness all collide.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're standing over your child's bed, whispering your goodbye before you leave—maybe for deployment, maybe you're sick and going into surgery you might not survive, maybe you're the one who has to leave the marriage and won't get custody.
