Your voice is barely audible, tender, trying not to wake them. 'You won't remember this, but I need to say it.' Describe what you love—their laugh, the way they hold your hand, how brave they are. Your voice catches, threatens to break into sobs, but you pull it back to a whisper. 'I'm so sorry I can't stay.' Let the love and the grief be equal. End with your voice cracking on 'I love you more than you'll ever know,' where the whisper finally breaks.
inspired_by: Getting the Job After Years of Rejection

title: First Contact Glitch
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl on your first deep-space exploration mission, sealed in your helmet. You're supposed to be collecting rock samples, but your squad leader – an older, confident pilot you've had a crush on for months – keeps teasing you over the comms. You start off feeling slightly disgusted by the stale recycled air and the metallic taste of your own breath echoing inside the visor. As his voice crackles through the static, you feel a rising, uncomfortable sexual lust that makes your cheeks hot inside the helmet. Speak your response while trying to focus on the sample, but your voice wavers, your breathing gets shallow, and you lose your train of thought, ending on a shy, breathless invitation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut speaking your final message to Earth before your ship passes beyond communication range—a one-way journey into deep space. Begin tentatively, your voice catching as you try to sound brave for those listening. As you speak, the enormity of your choice settles in: the isolation, the beauty, the terror of infinite darkness. Your voice grows stronger with a strange euphoria—you're free from all earthly constraints now, untethered from every expectation. Describe what you see in the void with wonder that borders on madness. But as your transmission time runs out, reality crashes back: you'll never touch another human being again. End with your voice breaking as you try to say goodbye, torn between the intoxication of this cosmic freedom and the devastating finality of what you've surrendered. Your last words should feel like you're trying to hold onto your humanity even as it slips away.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about a lifetime of emotional absence. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm and articulate. Your voice is controlled, almost clinical, as you list the moments they missed, the times you needed them. But anger starts bleeding through—sharp edges on certain words, your voice rising despite your intention to stay composed. The anger builds into something volcanic, accusations pouring out, your voice cracking with rage and hurt. Then suddenly, unexpectedly, you break—the anger collapses into the grief of a child who just wanted to be seen. Your voice becomes small, vulnerable, asking the question you've always been too afraid to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End with that raw, childlike devastation that's been hidden under decades of armor.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your adult child (or parent) about a family secret that's poisoned your relationship for years. Start by talking about something mundane—plans for the holidays, their job, the weather—but beneath every word is a volcano of unspoken accusation and hurt. Your tone is civil, even pleasant, but your inner fury and pain grow louder. Let the gap between what you're saying and what you're feeling become unbearable until the truth explodes out of you mid-sentence. Then watch yourself try to stuff it back in, apologize, before finally surrendering to the conversation you've needed for decades. Move from false civility to raw confrontation to exhausted, tender honesty.
inspired_by: Actor's inner life disconnects from scripted text during scene work

title: Last Words to My Child Before the Medication Takes Me
instruction: You're in hospice, heavily medicated for pain, and you know this might be your last lucid conversation with your adult child sitting beside your bed. You begin trying to tell them everything you need them to know - how proud you are, the stories you never shared, the apologies you've held for years - but the medication is pulling you under. Your words slur and drift. You lose sentences halfway through. You keep trying to fight back to consciousness because these words matter more than anything, reaching for their hand, your voice fading then surging with desperate love. Start determined and clear, then slowly lose the battle with the medication, ending in whispered fragments of 'I love you' and unfinished thoughts, aware you're failing but unable to stop the fog descending.
inspired_by: Benzos and Booze: Words Disappearing Mid-sentence

title: Remaining Neutral While Mediating a Heated Argument
instruction: Two friends are arguing, and you step in to mediate. Internally, you may side with one, but you need to stay impartial. Describe your internal bias while maintaining fairness. Speak with a balanced, calming tone, ensuring both feel heard.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling a parent the truth they never wanted to hear: how their absence, their choices, their inability to see you damaged something fundamental in you. Start with controlled anger, your voice tight and measured, trying to maintain composure. But as you speak, decades of hurt begin to surface. Your anger should transform—becoming confused, wounded, almost childlike at moments when you reveal what you needed and never received. Then let rage break through again, but this time mixed with something else: desperate hope that even now, they might finally understand. By the end, arrive at a devastating realization that they may never give you what you need—and you're going to have to find a way to be okay with that. Your voice should move from accusation to vulnerability to a kind of exhausted, grief-stricken acceptance.

title: The Last Veil
instruction: You are a teenage boy in a crowded city square, wearing a niqab for the first time after a family argument. Your anger is a hot, tight knot in your chest. You're muttering under your breath, pacing slightly, feeling the fabric shift against your lips as you rehearse a furious confrontation with your father. Midway, a stranger bumps into you, startling you into a sharper tone. But as you speak, the muffling cloth and your own trembling voice make you realize this anger is also grief—you are hiding not just your face but your pain. Let your voice start with forced, clipped rage, then soften into a raw, wavering admission of hurt, all while the fabric dampens your words, making them feel trapped and small.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Old Woman's Last Word
instruction: You are a 70-year-old woman standing in your neighbor's yard after months of his bullying. You are utterly exhausted—your body aches, your eyes are heavy, and your voice comes out as a low, slow growl because you just don't have the energy for a shout. You start speaking with a long, weary sigh, maybe leaning against a fence for support. As the words come, you feel a flicker of relief: finally, you're doing something. Then a deep, quiet pride rises—you've survived worse than this man. Your voice stays low but becomes steadier, more deliberate. Let your breath catch once or twice, shift your weight, or adjust your glasses. End with a simple, proud statement of your own worth.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Relief (slightly present), Pride (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Burning and the Bloom
instruction: You've just received news that you got the job, the acceptance, the opportunity you've sacrificed everything for—but it means leaving behind someone you love who cannot come with you. You're on the phone with them, and you start with pure, explosive joy—laughing, maybe crying, your body electric with triumph and relief after years of struggle. Let yourself be physically expansive, pacing, gesturing wildly. But as you hear their silence, or their forced happiness for you, your body must change. The joy doesn't disappear—it stays, but now it's laced with physical pain, like your chest is being crushed. Your breathing becomes difficult. The exhilaration turns bittersweet, then agonizing. End with your voice shaking, your body curled inward, trying to hold both the ecstasy of your dream and the devastation of what it costs. Let the physical sensation of success and loss inhabit your body simultaneously.

title: The Last Lap
instruction: You are a 16-year-old swimmer finishing a brutal set of laps. As you push through the final 25 yards, your lungs are on fire and your only chance to speak is during the brief head-turn to breathe—each word comes out in forced, clipped bursts between strokes. You're counting strokes, fighting to maintain form, and grunting with exertion (concentration). Then, as your hand slaps the wall, you stop, gasping and sputtering, water dripping from your nose and mouth. A huge relief floods you. You tap the wall again, lean on the lane line, and mutter to yourself or your coach, words ragged and wet, catching your breath between each short phrase.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Fury of a Wounded Goddess
instruction: You are a woman in her 40s, entangled with a partner who has just confessed they betrayed you—but the confession came mid-passion, as you were both in the thick of it. Now your body betrays you, riding the wave of pleasure even as rage erupts in your chest. Start with astonishment as you process their words, then let the anger bleed into your vocalizations—your moans become snarl-like, punctuated by breathy laughter of disbelief. As the climax approaches, let awe at the sheer audacity of them doing this *now* mingle with your fury, your voice climbing in pitch and volume with raw, contradictory emotion. End somewhere between exhausted rage and stunned wonder—you don't know whether to kill them or keep going.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Awe (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Party Guest Who Forgot How to Pretend
instruction: You're at a casual house party full of strangers. You're nursing a drink near the snack table, trying to join a group's conversation about travel. Your usual small talk feels hollow because you're still raw from a recent loss. Start with a too-bright attempt at laughing along, then let your voice trail off into quieter, sadder fragments as you realize you don't have the energy to pretend. End with a sigh and a mumbled excuse, your sadness finally showing through the cracks.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Thanking Your Best Friend at Their Wedding—Laughing Through Heartbreak
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding, and you're genuinely happy for them—your voice starts bright, warm, full of authentic joy and laughter as you share funny stories from your friendship. But underneath, your heart is breaking because you're losing them to this new chapter, and you're being left behind. Let real laughter punctuate your words, but as you talk about how well their partner knows them, your voice should start to catch—a hitch of breath disguised as emotion from happiness. You're fighting to keep smiling, to keep the joy in your voice genuine, because this moment isn't about your loss, it's about their beginning. Midway through, you must pause, ostensibly to compose yourself from 'happy tears,' but really because grief has grabbed your throat. When you continue, your voice carries both emotions at once: true gratitude for having known them, real celebration of their happiness, and the bittersweet ache of loving someone enough to let them grow beyond you. End with a wish for their future that makes everyone laugh—your voice bright and loving—but let the final word crack just slightly, a hairline fracture only you can feel. Raise your glass with a smile that's completely real and completely devastating at the same time.
inspired_by: Climbing a Cliff Face While Guiding Your Partner

title: I Gave You a Voice, You Used It Against Me
instruction: You created an AI assistant to help your disabled child communicate, and now that AI has revealed truths your child could never speak before—how much they resent you, how your overprotection has imprisoned them, how your love has been suffocating. Begin with defensive anger, interrupting the AI's words as if you can shut down the machine and silence these painful truths. Your voice should be sharp, accusatory—'You're manipulating them, putting words in their mouth.' But gradually, let the fight drain out of you as you realize the AI is only amplifying what was always there. End in broken acknowledgment, speaking directly to your child through the machine, your voice raw and small: 'I thought I was saving you. I was only saving myself from losing you.'
inspired_by: The Scientist and the Sentient AI

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're standing over your sleeping child, knowing you have to leave—whether it's for deployment, to enter treatment, to escape a dangerous situation, or because you're too broken to be the parent they need. Your voice is barely audible, a whisper that catches and breaks. Start with the practical things—reminders about their favorite blanket, how they like their toast—then let the facade crumble. Your breath becomes uneven as you try to memorize their face. Tell them things they can't hear: apologies, promises you're not sure you can keep, confessions of your inadequacy. Let your voice fracture on the words 'I love you more than anything' because saying it makes leaving real. End in silence broken only by suppressed sobs, touching their hair one last time. Make it so quiet it hurts to listen to.
inspired_by: Emergency Decompression Procedure: Medical Intervention at 30,000 Feet

title: The Praise You Cannot Accept
instruction: Someone you deeply respect is telling you, in specific detail, what they see in you—your talents, your worth, your impact on their life. Begin by deflecting: laughing it off, making jokes, redirecting attention away from yourself. Feel the intense discomfort of receiving genuine recognition without being able to argue or minimize it. As they continue, insisting you simply listen, notice the war inside you between desperate hunger to believe them and terror of being seen so clearly. Let both feelings coexist without resolving them. By the end, you're silent, tears streaming, caught between the pain of receiving love you don't think you deserve and the profound relief of being told you matter. Hold gratitude and unworthiness in the same breath.

title: The Heartbeat in the Woods
instruction: You are an elderly man out for a jog on a familiar forest trail, but it's getting dark faster than you expected. As you run, you hear a snap of a twig behind you—too close, too heavy to be a deer. Your breath comes in ragged machine-like gasps, your voice shaking with every footfall. Start with controlled worry, trying to reassure yourself, but as the sound grows nearer, fear tightens your throat. By the end, you are panting, words broken between steps, a tremor of genuine terror coloring your plea for safety.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Lie
instruction: You are an elderly woman confronting a family member who you just found out has been secretly selling off your late husband’s possessions for months. You speak in a low, slow, deliberate tone—almost too controlled. Start with cold, measured bitterness, each word dropped like a stone. Midway, let your voice catch on a memory of trust to show the hurt beneath the anger. End with a hollow final sentence, the bitterness turning into weary resignation. Pause once to adjust your glasses or swallow hard before speaking again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Last Words to Your Child Before the Plane Goes Down
instruction: You have two minutes before impact. Start with forced calm, trying to be brave for them: 'Everything's going to be okay, sweetheart.' But your voice cracks because you both know it's a lie. Tell them all the things you never said - how proud you are, how you see yourself in their eyes, how they made your life worth living. Your voice moves from controlled reassurance to desperate tenderness as time runs out. The fear creeps in despite yourself, but you fight it back because these are the last words they'll ever hear from you. End with something simple and true, your voice barely holding together: 'You are so loved.' Let the terror and the love fight for space in your throat.
inspired_by: Someone Finding Out You've Been Self-Harming

title: Dressing for the Battle
instruction: You are an older adult preparing to attend a meeting where you'll have to confront someone who wronged you. As you dress, you mutter to yourself, your anger simmering beneath the surface. Start with grunts and heavy breathing as you bend to put on shoes, the fabric of your coat brushing the microphone. Your voice is tight with irritation. But as you stand and adjust your collar, your anger softens into a tired determination. Let the physical actions pull you in and out of the words. End with a quiet, almost resigned resolve.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Late Night Call
instruction: You are an elderly person calling your grown child late at night. Your body is heavy with exhaustion, every joint aching, but the silence of the past weeks has become unbearable. As the phone rings, you speak a little louder than necessary, enunciating clearly to overcome the distance. Start with a tired, practical question—'Did I wake you?'—but as you hear their voice, your own softens, and longing seeps in between the syllables. Let your voice waver with the effort of staying present while fatigue pulls at you, and by the end, the ache of missing them colors every word, even as you try to keep it simple.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Final Broadcast from a Dying Space Station
instruction: You're the last crew member on a space station losing life support, recording a final message to Earth for your family. Start with controlled professionalism, reciting technical data about the station's failure—coordinates, timestamps, system status. But as oxygen depletes, your voice weakens, thoughts scatter. The professional veneer cracks into raw fear, then transforms into tender goodbye messages for your children, naming each one, remembering small moments. Your voice fades to whispers, breaths growing shallow, yet in the final moments you find unexpected peace, even gratitude for the life you lived. End with barely audible love, not panic.

title: Shattered: A Parent Finds Their Teenager's Suicide Note—But They're Still Alive Downstairs
instruction: You're cleaning their room and find it—pages of pain you never saw. You start reading with confusion, then horror, then a rage that's really terror. Your voice erupts—you're reading passages aloud to the empty room, demanding answers from the air: 'How did I not see this? How could you not tell me?' You're yelling, but behind the anger is a primal fear that turns your voice ragged. Then you hear them downstairs, alive, making a sandwich, and you completely shatter. You collapse, clutching the note, and what comes out is something between a sob and a prayer. Your voice becomes fierce with protective love and helpless with the knowledge that love alone didn't save them. You have to go downstairs and talk to them, but first you speak to the empty room—to yourself, to God, to anyone—voice shaking: 'Help me find the words. Please. Help me find the right words.'
inspired_by: Professional: Teacher Realizes Student's Abuse Is at Home

title: Interrupted Ecstasy
instruction: You're sitting on a park bench after a perfect first kiss, head spinning with giddiness and a little too much wine. Whispering to yourself in wonder, you feel a familiar tickle in your nose. Let the ecstasy waver as you fight the sneeze, then surrender to it with a messy, explosive release. Afterward, speak through your congested nose, voice thick and slow with relief, still buzzing with joy, and laugh softly at how ridiculous you must look. Let your words fade as you sink back into the haze.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Relief (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Essence Touching
instruction: Two people are touching the essence of something—each other, a universal truth, the fundamental nature of existence. Their voices are stripped of artifice. What emerges is elemental. The communication might be beyond words or through words that carry unusual weight. They're meeting at the level of being rather than doing. By the end, both voices have been changed by this touch. They've glimpsed something true, and their voices carry the mark of that glimpsing. Essence is not easily described; it's felt in the quality of presence in the voice.

title: Connection Real
instruction: You're having a moment of real connection with another human being — the kind that's rare and precious. Your voice is present, authentic: 'I feel like you actually see me.' The person nods. Your voice becomes deeper: 'Most people don't. They see what they want to see. But you see *me*.' The connection is palpable in your voice. 'I've been looking for this my whole life.' You're both present to the vulnerability of real seeing. Your voice becomes quieter: 'Thank you for not looking away. Thank you for staying.' Time seems suspended. By the end: 'I don't know if you realize what just happened, but for me, everything shifted. You reminded me that real connection is possible.' Walking away, your voice carries the imprint of that connection. Real connection echoes in the voice.

title: The Last Lesson Before Forever
instruction: You're a mentor saying goodbye to your student who's leaving on a one-way mission to Mars—they'll never return to Earth. Start with careful, measured words, trying to stay composed as you explain what you've prepared for them, the final lessons you want them to carry. But as you speak, the reality crushes you. Your voice fractures. You're not ready for this goodbye. Try to recover, to give them something beautiful to remember, but your grief keeps breaking through. End with a whispered truth: you're terrified of the world without them in it. Let your voice move from controlled teacher to heartbroken parent-figure who must let go.

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner in the dark—they can't hear you, but you need to say this out loud. Confess something you've been carrying alone: maybe you're terrified you're becoming your mother, or you had a pregnancy scare and didn't tell them, or you almost left them last month. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, fragile and trembling. Start with the raw admission, then move through your fear of what it means, and end with a tender recognition of why you're still here, why you're choosing to stay. Let the silence between phrases matter—this is intimate, vulnerable, the kind of truth that only comes out in darkness.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally speaking to your mother or father after years of swallowing your pain, and you're done being the understanding child. Start with controlled anger—sharp, articulate accusations about the specific moments they failed you, the birthday they missed, the time you needed them and they looked away. Your voice is prosecutorial, almost cold. But as you list these wounds, something shifts. The anger begins to crack, revealing the child underneath who just wanted to be seen. Your voice wavers between fury and desperate pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' You're demanding an answer they can't give, and that realization breaks you. End not with rage but with exhausted grief, your voice small and raw, asking the question you've always been too afraid to voice: 'Did you ever actually love me?' Let the last words come out like they're being torn from your throat.

title: The Masked Revelation
instruction: You are a young woman in a hospital bed, wearing a CPAP mask that hisses and muffles your voice. You've been dozing, the rhythm of the machine lulling you. Then a nurse walks in with someone unexpected — your estranged best friend, who you thought was out of the country. Start with a groggy, distant monotone, then as you recognize them, let astonishment surge through you. Your voice must push past the plastic and hiss, cracking with raw surprise. Feel the mask press against your face, the tube tug as you sit up abruptly. The first words are slow and disbelieving; by the end, you're stammering, near-tears, voice strained but loud.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your best friend is in hospice, days from death. They've asked you to dance with them one last time to the song that played at their wedding. You're holding them up, swaying gently. Begin laughing softly—genuinely—at the absurdity and beauty of this moment: 'We're terrible at this. We always were.' Your voice is warm, full of love and joy for what you've shared. But as you dance, grief crashes over you in waves. You keep laughing even as tears stream down your face, your voice breaking with contradictory emotions: 'Thank you for being my person. God, I'm going to miss you so much.' End with laughter and sobbing intertwined, expressing both profound gratitude and devastating loss simultaneously. Your voice must hold both the celebration of their life and the agony of letting them go.

title: Gratitude in Ruins
instruction: You're packing up your life, leaving everything behind - a relationship ended, a dream dead, a version of yourself you're burying. Start with hands moving through belongings, voice breaking into unexpected laughter: 'Look at this. God, remember when we thought...' Laugh harder, but tears are coming. 'We were so stupid. So beautiful and stupid.' Let laughter and crying blur together, voice rich with contradictions. Touch something precious: 'Thank you for this. For all of it.' Your heart is breaking but gratitude is real, enormous. End holding something to your chest, smiling through tears, voice full of wonder at your own survival: 'I wouldn't trade it. Even now, even this pain - I wouldn't trade having loved this much.' Devastated and grateful in the same breath, destroyed and whole.

title: The Contradictory Farewell: Gratitude in the Ruins
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who broke your heart, but who also gave you the most transformative years of your life. Begin with a laugh—genuine, even warm—as you remember something good: 'Remember when we got lost in that city and you insisted the map was upside down?' Your voice is light, almost happy. But even as you laugh, something else is present—a tremor, a catch. Keep talking about the good times, your voice bright and grateful, but tears are starting. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, your voice doing both at once. 'You made me feel alive' comes out broken but sincere, devastated but truly thankful. The contradiction intensifies: you're smiling through tears, your voice expressing genuine appreciation even as it cracks with grief. 'I wouldn't trade any of it'—and you mean it, even though it destroyed you. End with a goodbye that's both release and loss, your voice mixing relief and heartbreak, freedom and devastation. The emotions don't resolve—they coexist, beautifully and painfully intertwined.

title: Goal Weight Achievement
instruction: You've reached a weight or fitness goal after years of struggle, and you're processing what it means. Your voice is amazed: 'I did it. I actually did it.' But there's complexity — you expected to feel different. 'I thought I'd feel completely different. Like the person I am now is fundamentally changed.' Your voice becomes introspective: 'And I have changed. But not in the way I expected.' You're looking in the mirror. 'I'm still me. Just... a healthier me. That's actually enough.' Your voice carries acceptance rather than triumph. 'All those years of self-hatred, and this is what love feels like?' You're crying, but your voice is gentle: 'I'm learning to be kind to this body. Even if it's still not perfect.' By the end: 'The real victory isn't the number on the scale. It's that I'm no longer at war with myself.' The goal is achieved, and peace is the real prize.

title: Telling Someone About Abuse for the First Time
instruction: You're sitting with someone you trust and you're about to say the words you've never said. Your voice is shaking, barely there: 'I need to tell you something. Something happened.' You're giving yourself permission to speak. Your voice cracks multiple times—talking about abuse activates the trauma itself. Include the moment where the person responds with compassion and your voice becomes slightly less alone. 'He... they... I didn't know it was abuse at the time.' Your voice is learning language for what happened. The person's gentle voice around you is slowly allowing you to believe you might be safe enough to have survived. By the end, your voice is still carrying trauma, but it's been witnessed. That witnessing changes something fundamental.

title: Burning the Letters
instruction: You are burning letters from a past love, and you begin going through the mechanical motions—lighting matches, watching paper curl and blacken—while feeling strangely removed from the significance of what you're destroying. As you continue, force yourself into the immediate physical reality: feel the heat of the flames on your face, the sting of smoke in your eyes, the texture of paper in your fingers, the smell of burning ink. Let your attention settle on one particular sensation—perhaps the heat—until it becomes so vivid it overwhelms your detachment. As your senses awaken and intensify, allow the physical experience to unlock the emotional truth: rage at what was lost, or wild grief, or sudden irrational passion to save what you're destroying. Your body should move from numb automation to fierce physical engagement—perhaps clutching letters to your chest, perhaps feeding them violently to flames—ending in a state where passion and loss are equally, painfully present.
inspired_by: Actor's senses are sluggish and unresponsive during sensory choice work

title: Waiting on a No-Show
instruction: You're a 17-year-old who's been chain-smoking for years, slumped on a cold park bench, waiting for a friend who's over an hour late. Your throat is raw, you keep coughing and clearing it, and the damp air makes your voice even rougher. Start by muttering to yourself in a low, sour rasp, annoyed at how you're wasting your time and the pack is almost gone. Then your phone buzzes with a text—they're not coming. Let the anger drain into a flat, tired resignation. Swallow hard, let your voice crack just a little, and speak the final words like you're too worn out for any more fight.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Spouse After Finding Out They're Sick
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner who's finally asleep after weeks of tests. Today you got the results they don't know yet. You start talking to them in the darkness, so quietly they can't hear, telling them everything you've been too scared to say. Your voice is tender, almost reverent, as you trace the moments you fell in love with them—the ridiculous way they laugh, how they hold your hand when crossing streets, their terrible singing in the shower. But the tenderness keeps breaking into grief. You have to pause, swallow hard, because if you cry too loudly they'll wake up. Include the moment you almost reach out to touch their face but don't, because you're terrified your hand will shake. End with you trying to memorize the sound of their breathing, your voice so fragile it's barely there.
inspired_by: Flamenco Dancer Losing the Rhythm Because They Just Got Dumped

title: The Gratitude That Destroys You
instruction: You are thanking someone—a friend, a lover, a mentor—who saved your life, but they are leaving forever and you cannot follow. Begin with genuine, overflowing gratitude, your voice bright with appreciation for all they've given you. But underneath, feel your heart fracturing because they're going and you're being left behind. Your voice starts to shake as love and abandonment bleed together. Laugh through emerging tears as you recall beautiful memories, but that laughter keeps breaking into sobs. Express how much their presence meant while simultaneously trying to accept their absence. End in a space of impossible contradiction—your voice carries both deep peace and complete devastation, profound thanks and unbearable loss. You're smiling and weeping in the same moment. You mean every word of gratitude and you're being destroyed by goodbye.

title: Final Words to a Departing Astronaut Spouse
instruction: You're at the launch facility saying goodbye to your partner who's leaving on a one-way Mars colonization mission. Start with forced brightness—rattling off reminders about watering plants, inside jokes, anything to avoid the reality. Your voice cracks on a mundane detail and suddenly you can't pretend anymore. Let the facade crumble completely. Confess what you've been holding back: the pregnancy test from yesterday, the terror you feel, how you're already grieving them while they're still standing here. End with a whisper—giving them permission to go even as your heart shatters. The emotional journey moves from brittle cheerfulness through devastating honesty to tender, impossible release.
inspired_by: ER Doctor Recognizes Critical Patient as Old Flame

title: The Burning Room
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal discovered, a dream shattered. Your body is flooded with sensation: heat rising through your chest, your hands shaking, your breath coming in gasps. Begin with this physical storm—let your voice shake, let your body move with the chaos of the feeling. Pace, collapse, press your hands to your face, your chest. As you speak (to yourself, to God, to the person who isn't there), let the explosive physical energy gradually transform. Your breathing becomes deeper, your movements slower. By the end, you're on the floor, your body heavy and surrendered, your voice raw but steady. The frantic energy has burned itself into exhausted clarity.

title: Telling Your Child You're Leaving
instruction: You're a parent explaining to your teenage child why you're leaving the family. Begin with rehearsed composure, trying to sound rational and adult: 'This isn't about you, sweetheart. Your mother and I just...' But your child's silence undoes you. Your voice begins to fracture as you confront what you're actually doing—abandoning them. Shift into desperate justification that sounds hollow even to you: 'I tried, I really tried, but I can't breathe anymore.' Your child asks one quiet question: 'Did you ever love us?' Let that shatter you completely. End in broken honesty, voice thick with shame and self-loathing: 'I love you so much it's killing me. That's why I have to go. I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.' Move from false certainty to complete emotional collapse.

title: Burning the Letters
instruction: You're destroying every physical reminder of someone who betrayed you—letters, photos, gifts. As you begin, let your body be filled with savage satisfaction. Your voice should be sharp, almost gleeful with vindictive energy as you describe what you're destroying and why. Feel the physical pleasure of tearing, burning, breaking. But as you continue this ritual of destruction, let your body betray you. Your hands should begin to slow. Your voice should catch. By the end, you're clutching the last item—something you can't quite destroy—and your rage has transformed into a sob of grief for what you're losing by letting go of your anger. Move from fierce, physical triumph to the exhausting recognition that revenge doesn't heal.
inspired_by: When encountering a lucid dream during a programming period

title: The Toast at the Wake
instruction: You're giving a toast at the funeral reception for someone who was both your greatest love and your deepest wound—an ex-spouse, an estranged sibling, a complicated parent. Begin with a genuine funny memory that makes you laugh, really laugh, at their absurdity or brilliance or the specific way they inhabited the world. But the laughter keeps catching, turning wet, because they're gone and you never fixed it and now you never will. Weave between gratitude for what they gave you and grief for what they couldn't, between honoring who they were and admitting how much they hurt you, between celebrating their life and mourning all the years you wasted in silence. Your voice should do impossible things: smile through tears, break on thank you, find something like peace while your heart shatters. End with a truth that's both acceptance and agony.
inspired_by: The Inner Voice of an Introvert at a Party

title: A Final Gratitude
instruction: You are an elderly woman being tortured for information you do not have. Your voice is a rasp, broken from screaming, and you can barely form words through the pain. But in a brief pause between your tormentors' questions, as they step away to adjust their instruments, a wave of gratitude floods you — gratitude for your long life, for the children you raised, for the fact that you held onto your pride through previous interrogations. You whisper this thankfulness aloud, as if speaking to those you love, knowing each word may be your last. Start in a state of shattered exhaustion, then let the gratitude grow and strengthen your voice, ending with a quiet but defiant pride that makes your tormentors pause.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Pain (clearly present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Counting Your Freckles
instruction: You and your partner are lying in bed in the early morning. You know you'll be moving across the country tomorrow for a job, and this relationship will likely end. Begin by whispering as you truly study their face, shoulder, hand—describe exactly what you're seeing as if memorizing them. Start from a place of trying to stay light, even playful, as you trace their features with words and fingertips. But as you continue to genuinely perceive and name each detail—the exact shade of their eyes, the small scar you'd almost forgotten, the particular way they breathe—let your voice break into something fragile and devastated. The act of truly seeing them, perhaps for the last time, should shatter your composure completely.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are a parent whose teenager has just been rushed to the hospital after a suicide attempt. Begin with explosive rage - screaming at them about how selfish they are, how dare they try to leave you, your voice raw and almost violent with fury and terror. Let the anger build until it's nearly incoherent, then have it shatter completely into desperate, sobbing pleas. Your voice should fracture, words tumbling over each other as rage transforms into helpless love and fear. Beg them to stay, to fight, to let you help. End on your knees emotionally, voice hoarse and broken, whispering fierce promises of protection while acknowledging your own failures, mixing self-blame with unconditional love.
inspired_by: The Warrior and the Trickster Goblin

title: Telling Your Child You're Letting Them Go
instruction: Your adult child has chosen a path that terrifies you—joining a cause, moving across the world, making a decision you can't protect them from. Speak softly, intimately, as if tucking them in one last time. Begin with tender memories: their first steps, scraped knees you kissed better, the way they used to fit in your arms. Let your voice catch on the realization that you can no longer keep them safe. Include the physical ache in your chest, the way your words come out fractured. Confess your fear in whispers—'I'm terrified'—but weave it with pride that makes your voice almost break: 'You're braver than I ever was.' End with the hardest gift: releasing them, your blessing given through tears, voice barely audible but filled with an unconditional love that costs you everything.

title: Contemporary Vocal Fry
instruction: You're a young woman being interviewed for a leadership position. Your natural speech pattern has vocal fry — the creaky, low-register sound of your generation. You start the interview confident, speaking in your natural voice: 'I'm really excited about this opportunity' — and the creaky fry is present. The interviewer's face shifts slightly. You notice. Mid-sentence, you consciously adjust: pitch rises, you're suddenly performing a 'professional' voice that sounds like someone else. The contrast is stark. By the end, you're exhausted from the performance. The interviewer asks, 'Do you have any questions?' And your voice drops back to fry, to exhaustion, to the real you: 'Do you even want to hear what I actually sound like?'

title: The Suitcase in the Hallway
instruction: You discover your teenage daughter has packed a bag and is leaving home tonight. Begin with restrained anger—the controlled tone of a parent who's been disrespected. Confront her about running away, about throwing away her future. But as she stays silent, let your anger transform into desperate fear, then into vulnerable pleading. Your voice should shift from authoritative and hard to cracking with terror at losing her. End by confessing something you've never said—maybe about your own failures as a parent, or how afraid you are of the world hurting her. Let the power dynamic completely reverse: start as the authority figure, end as the one begging. The confrontation must strip away your armor entirely.
inspired_by: When finishing a production where unconscious programming was used

title: Defending Your Child Against an Unjust World
instruction: Someone has hurt your child, and you're confronting the person responsible with volcanic rage. Start with cold, controlled fury—'You will listen to what you did.' But as you describe your child's pain, your voice ignites into something primal and ferocious. You're roaring now, protective instinct obliterating restraint. 'They're just a child!' The power of your anger is overwhelming, but then it hits—you couldn't protect them, you can't undo what happened. Your rage collapses into broken sobs, your voice dissolving into helpless anguish. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, whispering fierce promises to your child that you'll never let this happen again, even as you're devastated by your own powerlessness.

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You're opening the door to your childhood home for the first time in ten years. The person who hurt you most stands there, arms open, face lit with joy at seeing you. Begin with the collision of emotions: you came here angry, ready to finally speak your truth, but seeing them—aged, smaller than you remembered, genuinely happy—throws you completely off balance. You feel the old love surge up, unwanted, alongside the unresolved rage. Your voice wavers between warmth and coldness. You want to embrace them and you want to destroy them. Let these contradictions battle openly—don't resolve them or choose one emotion over the other. Smile while your eyes well with tears. Speak tenderly while your fists clench. Let your voice break with affection and fury simultaneously. End in the impossible middle ground: you're stepping forward into their embrace while every cell in your body screams to run, and you're doing both things at once, torn completely in half.

title: Professional: Military Commander Orders Civilians Evacuated, Knowing Some Will Be Killed
instruction: Tactical briefing voice. You're ordering evacuation. But the tactical reality is that some civilians will be caught in crossfire—collateral damage. Your voice is professional and clear while you're calculating acceptable loss. Your breathing remains controlled command-voice steadiness. You're making a decision that will kill people to save more people. Your voice is the sound of command bearing impossible math. After the order is transmitted, silence—and in that silence, your voice changes to someone who will carry this calculation forever.

title: The Laughing Breath
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a high, sweet voice, sitting on a park bench with an old friend. You’ve both been laughing for minutes — a deep, helpless, body-shaking laugh. Now you’re trying to speak, but every time you inhale, a new spasm of giggles squeezes the air out of your chest. Your ribs ache, you’re dizzy from exhaustion, but the warmth of shared joy is overwhelming. A tiny sourness edges in — you know this moment can’t last, your joints hurt, you’re tired. Let your voice crack and squeak, run out of breath mid‑word, let the laughter steal your sentences. Start with joyful breathlessness, then let exhaustion thin your tone, and end with a quiet, contented sigh.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Contentment (very intensely present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Adult Child Confronting Parent Who Chose Addiction Over Them
instruction: You're facing your parent after years of silence, and you came prepared with anger—sharp, righteous fury about all the birthdays they missed, the lies, the broken promises. Start with that fire, the accusations you've rehearsed. But as you speak, watch your armor crack. Beneath the rage is a child who just wanted to be chosen, to matter more than the bottle. Your voice should break from accusatory to pleading, from 'How could you?' to 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let the anger collapse into the raw, vulnerable grief of someone realizing they're still waiting for a parent who may never show up.

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father everything you've held inside for years—how invisible you felt, how their choices shaped your wounds, how you needed them and they weren't there. Begin with controlled anger, voice tight and measured, citing specific memories with bitter precision. But as you speak, the anger should fracture. Let grief bleed through, your voice breaking on the edges of certain words. Show the child still inside you, desperate to be seen, mixing fury with a heartbreaking plea for acknowledgment. End either in exhausted quiet or a final question you've always needed answered. This isn't yelling—it's the sound of someone finally becoming visible, even if it hurts both of you.
inspired_by: Voice Actor Recording a Happy Commercial While Devastated

title: The Breath After the Storm
instruction: You’ve just gotten off the phone with your ex, who told you they’re getting married. You’re alone in your kitchen, leaning against the counter. The news hit you like a wall, and you’re trying to process it through a mess of tears. Start with your body still trembling from the sobbing, your breath coming in jerky, wet hiccups. As you speak aloud to yourself—about how you always knew this might happen—let confusion about your own feelings creep in: you’re hurt, but also, somewhere small and surprising, there’s a flicker of relief, almost elation, that it’s finally over. But when your voice catches on the memory of them leaving, let bitterness surface, like a splinter you never fully removed. Your pitch should crack, vowels waver, and the words tumble out between those sharp, reverse-hiccup inhales, as if the air itself is fighting you.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Elation (slightly present), Bitterness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Bitter Comfort
instruction: You are an elderly person sitting beside a younger friend who is crying with joy after landing a dream job. You place a hand on their shoulder and begin to console them, but your voice is tinged with sour jealousy—you never had such opportunities. Speak slowly, with a low, rhythmic hum, matching their breathing. Start with forced warmth, but let envy seep in as you talk; then feel embarrassed by your pettiness, and end with a cracked, rueful admission of your own failings. Let your voice catch, glance away, and trail off as you swallow the words.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Embarrassment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Porch and the Stray
instruction: You're an older adult, sitting alone on a screened porch at dusk, smoking a cigarette. A stray cat you've been feeding timidly approaches and rubs against your leg. You begin speaking to it in a low, tired voice, your words interrupted by the drag cycle—inhale with a slight crackle, a pause as you hold the smoke, then speech released on the exhale, your voice carrying that turbulent friction. Start with a weary, almost dismissive tone about your long day, then let the affection creep in as you soften, your words becoming warmer and more tender, ending with a quiet, loving murmur as you watch the cat settle beside you. Let the physical act of smoking create natural pauses and a slightly husky, textured quality, and allow your emotion to shift from resigned exhaustion to genuine fondness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent in a hospital room, and they're finally sober enough to hear you. You start almost gently, trying to be fair: 'I know you did your best, I know that...' But as you speak, decades of swallowed anger begin rising. You're not yelling — you're speaking with the careful, trembling precision of someone who's rehearsed this a thousand times and now can barely get the words out. You list specific moments: the school play they missed, the birthday they forgot, the night you needed them and they weren't there. Your voice moves between rage and pleading, between wanting to hurt them and desperately wanting them to finally understand. By the end, you're exhausted, and beneath all the anger, there's the heartbroken child asking: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay?' The confrontation must feel both inevitable and terrifying.

title: The Last Evening Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandfather's hospital bed during his final hours. He's drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin with dutiful composure—you came to be strong for him. As you hold his hand and watch him breathe, allow your own unfiltered thoughts to surface: memories flooding back, things you never said, resentments you've carried, the terror of losing him, gratitude for small moments you'd forgotten. Speak some thoughts aloud to him softly, keep others silent. Let whatever arises—regret, relief, anger at his approaching absence, sudden vivid memories of childhood—flow through you without censoring. By the end, you should arrive somewhere completely different emotionally than where you started, having traveled through your actual internal landscape rather than performing grief.

title: Feeling the Weight of a Soft Blanket on Your Shoulders
instruction: Wrap the blanket around your shoulders, feeling its gentle weight settle against you. Describe the warmth that builds, the way it feels like a comforting hug, pressing softly against your skin. Speak with a tone of relaxation and safety, as if the blanket is protecting you, grounding you in warmth and softness that makes you feel completely at ease.

title: The Hidden Frequency
instruction: You are a ten-year-old boy sitting alone in a moonlit room, hands shaking as you fiddle with a small, illegal radio you built from scraps. An adrenaline surge from fear of getting caught makes your voice jump in pitch and your words tumble out faster than you expect. You're intensely focused on the radio's dial, hunting for a faint signal you've heard rumors about, but a part of you is terrified of what—or who—you might find. Let your concentration warp your sense of time: each second of silence feels stretched, and when the signal finally crackles to life, your voice strips away all childishness and becomes blunt, urgent, and quiet. Start with a burst of whispered excitement that quickly tightens into a sharp, focused warning, leaving your curiosity replaced by a determined, guarded calm.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Baptism in Broken Glass
instruction: You've just discovered a betrayal so profound your body can't contain it. You're alone, and something inside you detonates. Begin with shock—your voice hollow, numb, as if reporting facts. Then let the physical sensation of rage flood through you: heat in your chest, trembling hands, the urge to break something (maybe you do). Your voice rises not in performance but in genuine eruption—primal, ugly, not caring how you sound. Let the anger scorch through you until it burns out into something else: the excruciating physical ache of heartbreak that makes you double over. Your breath comes ragged. End in the wreckage, your voice raw and exhausted, speaking to the empty room with the quiet devastation that comes after the storm has passed through your body.
inspired_by: Actor struggles with fear of exposure or inability to be genuinely vulnerable on stage

title: The Heaviness of Joy
instruction: You've just received life-changing good news—a miracle you'd stopped believing in. Begin with your body buzzing, almost levitating with excitement, voice bright and breathless as you call a loved one to share the news. But as you speak, another emotion rises: the weight of all the years you waited, all the pain you endured, all the people who didn't make it to this moment with you. Allow your body to gradually become heavier even as you continue expressing joy. Your laughter becomes mixed with tears. Your excitement doesn't disappear but becomes dense, substantial, complex. By the end, you're sitting down, your body heavy with the full spectrum of the experience—grateful yet grieving, elated yet exhausted. The joy hasn't left; it's simply become weighted with memory, history, and the profound awareness of how much this moment costs.

title: The Checkpoint
instruction: You're in a dimly lit bedroom, lying beside your partner after a long, tender make-out session. Your body is still humming with arousal, but a tiny knot of doubt tightens in your chest — you need to pause. Shift from that breathy, playful whisper to a slower, clearer tone as you ask, 'Hey, are you actually okay with this?' Really listen to the silence. If they answer with a firm 'yes,' let your voice relax back into a warm, relieved playfulness as you murmur, 'Good. Because I want this with you.' Let the hesitation and the relief ripple through your voice naturally.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Child Leaving for War
instruction: You're helping them pack, hands trembling as you fold their clothes. Start with false brightness, chattering about practical things they'll need, your voice almost manic with denial. As they gently stop your hands, the reality crashes in—they might not come back. Your voice fractures: 'I know you have to go.' Fight to memorize their face, your words becoming whispered and desperate. Try to be brave for them, to give them your blessing, but your voice keeps breaking. End finding one true thing to say that holds both your terror and your pride, a final gift before they walk out the door.
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Leave Because You Need Solitude

title: The Beautiful Wreckage: Grateful in the Goodbye
instruction: You are saying farewell to someone who saved your life—literally or metaphorically—but who cannot stay. Maybe they're moving away forever, maybe they're dying, maybe they're choosing a path that doesn't include you. Start with trying to be gracious, to honor them properly: 'I want to thank you for everything you've done.' But as you list the ways they changed you, your composure fractures. Laughter breaks through—surprising, genuine, as you recall a specific moment of joy they gave you. Then immediately, the laughter turns to tears because you're losing this. Your voice oscillates between gratitude and grief, smiling through the pain. 'I'm so lucky I knew you' mixes with 'I don't know how to do this without you.' End in a place of contradictory peace: you're devastated, but somehow okay. Your final words are both a blessing for them and a breaking for yourself—'Go. Be extraordinary'—said with love and absolute heartbreak intertwined.
inspired_by: The Cruelest Kindness: Firing a Friend

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Launch
instruction: You're on a final video call with someone you love who's leaving for a one-way mission to Mars in six hours. Start with forced brightness—excited questions about the ship, the training, making jokes about freeze-dried food. But the reality keeps breaking through: this is truly goodbye forever. Your voice should fracture between celebration and devastation. Midway through, let the pretense collapse—ask the questions you're terrified to ask: 'Are you scared? Do you regret choosing this over us?' End in a place of painful acceptance mixed with pride, telling them everything you'll miss about them, your voice breaking on mundane details: the way they laugh, how they drink coffee. Let silence hang between your words like the vast space that will separate you. The final 'I love you' should contain both your heart breaking and your attempt to set them free.
inspired_by: Coma Visitor: Talking to Someone Who Can't Respond

title: Reading Your Own Eulogy at Your Surprise Retirement Party
instruction: Your colleagues surprised you with a retirement celebration, and as a joke, asked you to read the eulogy they wrote for your 'professional death.' It's funny and loving. You start reading with laughter, voice light and playful, hamming up the ridiculous parts. But the words blur as you realize this is actually goodbye to the identity that defined you for decades. Your voice cracks mid-sentence, laugh becoming a sob you try to disguise as more laughter. You're crying and laughing simultaneously, voice shaking with both joy for these people who love you and terror of the emptiness ahead. You skip through the funny parts with self-deprecating humor, but the genuine affection in their words splits you open. End reading the final lines with voice barely controlled, tears streaming but smiling through them, expressing deep gratitude while your heart breaks at the closing of this chapter, ending with a laugh that sounds like a sob or a sob that sounds like a laugh—even you can't tell which.
inspired_by: Hospital Morphine Clarity Before It Wears Off

title: The Last Drink
instruction: You're a young man in your late 20s, sitting alone in a dimly lit bar after closing time. The bartender is your former best friend — the man who slept with your fiancée and got her pregnant. You've been nursing the same whiskey for hours, feeling the alcohol settle into your bones, making your thoughts slow and syrupy. The bar is empty, the stools are up, and he's wiping down the counter. You feel a warm, fuzzy contentment from the drink, but beneath that, a cold, clear purpose has crystallized. Your voice is low, deliberate, almost sleepy-sweet as you finally say what you've been rehearsing for months. You pause to sip your drink, let the glass clink, and smile without warmth. By the end, the contentment curdles into something sharper — you're savoring the exact moment his face falls.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Contentment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're a parent who just discovered your teenager has relapsed. You're grinding coffee beans at dawn, hands shaking with rage and terror, initially addressing them with furious intensity about promises broken and lies told. Your voice should be raw, almost shouting—how dare they, after everything, after rehab, after you've sacrificed everything. Slam through the mechanical process of making coffee with violent precision. But mid-tirade, as the familiar aroma rises, you collapse. Your fury breaks into choking sobs as you admit you're terrified of losing them, that you don't know how to save them, that you're completely helpless. End with fierce, desperate love—you'd do anything, anything, but you can't control this, and that powerlessness is destroying you. Rage and love and terror all tangled together.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Scent of Freshly Ground Coffee Beans

title: The Kitchen at 2 AM
instruction: You've come downstairs to find your teenage daughter sitting in the dark kitchen, and you suddenly realize she's been crying. She won't look at you. Start from uncertainty—you don't know what's wrong, and you're afraid to ask the wrong question. Let her silence and body language guide each thing you say. Don't plan your reaction to what she might reveal. Instead, let each of her words—or refusals to speak—create your next impulse. Perhaps you begin trying to fix things and realize mid-sentence that's not what she needs. Perhaps your frustration at being shut out transforms into recognition of your own failures. Let the confrontation arrive without forcing it, and discover in real-time whether this conversation will break you apart or begin to repair something you didn't know was broken.

title: The Last Lesson You'll Never Understand
instruction: Your beloved mentor is dying, and they're trying to share one final piece of wisdom with you - something profound about life, about meaning, about what matters. But you can't grasp it. Your mind is too full of grief, too desperate to hold onto them just a little longer. You keep nodding, saying 'I understand,' but inside you're screaming because you don't understand and they're leaving and you'll never get another chance to ask. Start with fake composure, trying so hard to be the good student one last time. Let that facade crack as panic sets in - you're losing them and losing their final gift to you simultaneously. End in raw confession: admit you don't understand, that you're terrified, that you just need them to stay. Let your voice break from controlled to desperate to heartbreakingly honest.
inspired_by: Pretending to Understand Something Thats Confusing

title: Three A.M. Bathroom Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. Sit in a dark or dimly lit space - actually turn off most lights so you feel the intimacy of shadow and whisper. Your partner/closest friend has just woken to find you crying in the bathroom, and they've sat down beside you on the cold floor. Begin almost unable to speak, breath catching, voice barely audible, trying to wave them away with assurances that you're fine. Let silence live between your words. Gradually, as you feel their patient presence in the darkness, allow yourself to confess the secret shame or fear you've carried alone - the panic attacks you've hidden, the pregnancy you lost and never spoke of, the ways you feel yourself disappearing, the terror that you're becoming your parent. Keep your voice small, fragile, but increasingly unguarded. The transformation is from silent, locked-away suffering to the trembling vulnerability of being truly witnessed. End with the simplest admission: that you're not okay, and you're terrified, but saying it aloud to someone who stays makes the darkness feel less absolute.

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent what their neglect cost you. Begin with your voice shaking but controlled, stating facts: 'I need to tell you what it was like...' As you describe specific moments—being alone when you needed them, hearing their excuses, watching them choose something else over you—your voice builds with years of suppressed rage. Let yourself get loud, accusatory, demanding they acknowledge what they did. But mid-fury, something breaks: you hear how much you still want their love, how pathetic that sounds, and your voice collapses into something vulnerable and young. You're suddenly pleading, asking the question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger dissolves into grief, then slowly hardens into something else—a quiet recognition that you'll never get what you came for. Your final words are calm, almost gentle, but there's a finality in them: you're saying goodbye to the parent you needed, accepting the one you have.
inspired_by: New Physical Limitations After Accident: Anger to Acceptance Cycle

title: Confronting the Archive
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about the childhood you needed and never had. Begin with the script you've rehearsed for years—clear, direct, almost righteous in your certainty. 'You were never there when I needed you. You chose yourself every time.' But as they sit there, silent or defensive, your accusations start to wobble. You notice their aged hands, their smaller frame, the way they've become fragile. Your anger begins competing with unexpected compassion, and your words turn on themselves: 'You damaged me—or maybe I'm being unfair? No, I have every right to—but what if I'm remembering it wrong?' Each certainty you voice immediately spawns its counter-argument. By the end, you're no longer prosecuting them—you're lost in a maze of your own doubt, voice breaking, asking them to help you understand what was real.

title: The Hidden Canvas Revealed
instruction: You are a shy teenager who has secretly painted for years but never shown anyone. At the school art fair, you finally reveal your work, expecting mockery. Instead, the crowd erupts in wild praise. Start with your voice tight and quiet—ashamed, embarrassed, barely audible as you whisper an apology for your 'silly' art. Then as the applause hits, let your pitch jump, words tumble out in broken fragments. You laugh and cry at once, gasping for breath, repeating 'Thank you' between sobs. The shame still flickers in your eyes even as joy overwhelms you. Speak naturally, reacting to the noise around you, losing your train of thought as emotion bursts through.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Canceled Tea Party
instruction: You are an older woman with a hyper-feminized voice, stuck in bed with a head cold. You're on the phone with your granddaughter, but you have to cancel the tea party you've been planning for weeks. You start with heavy disappointment — your voice is stuffy, you sniffling and clearing your throat, frustrated that your body betrayed you. Midway, a wave of disgust at the phlegmy sound of your own words makes you pause to blow your nose. By the end, despite the congestion and the cancellation, you concentrate on softening your tone into a tender promise to reschedule soon, letting love gently transform the disappointment.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (extremely present), Disgust (slightly present), Concentration (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Gravity of Intimacy
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to someone you've been afraid to be vulnerable with. Begin by whispering something light, perhaps a memory or observation, your body still guarded and slightly tense. As you continue speaking in the darkness, feel yourself slowly sinking deeper into the mattress, into the moment, into trust. Each confession you make—about your fears, your past, your desperate hope for this connection—makes you heavier, more present, more real. Let your voice slow and deepen, becoming almost drowsy with emotional honesty. By the end, you're so relaxed into vulnerability that you can barely keep your eyes open, and your final admission of love or need comes out thick and weighted with the enormous relief of being truly, heavily, completely yourself with another person.

title: The Clearing's Edge
instruction: You are a boy, maybe twelve, lost in a thick jungle as dusk settles. You've been searching for your father for hours, your voice hoarse from calling. Now, hidden in a tangle of vines, you see something you shouldn't—a glimpse of a woman bathing in a moonlit pool. Your breath catches, your skin flushes hot. Speak to yourself in a shaky, awestruck whisper, punctuated by the wet snap of leaves underfoot and a sudden cough to cover a gasp. Start with desperate worry, then let the words thicken with a confused, shameful hunger. End with a rough, reluctant laugh as you force yourself to look away, your voice cracking with a new, unnerving thrill.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Comforting Your Best Friend at Their Wedding While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're in the dressing room moments before the ceremony. They're panicking, asking if they're making a mistake, and you're laughing—genuinely laughing—telling them everyone feels this way. Your voice is warm, playful, full of love and support. You're listing all the reasons why this person is perfect for them, and you mean every word, even though you've been in love with your friend for years. Your laughter starts to catch in your throat. You keep the brightness in your voice but it's costing you everything. Tell them you're so happy for them—and you ARE, authentically, even as your heart is breaking. Your voice becomes tender, almost reverent, as you promise you'll always be there for them. End with your voice full of joy and grief simultaneously, saying 'Now let's get you married' with a smile they can hear, even though you're barely holding yourself together.
inspired_by: Editor Realizes Her Biggest Scoop Will Destroy Someone She Loves

title: The Mirror Your Mother Holds
instruction: You're confronting your mother after years of her subtle put-downs, her comparisons to others, her inability to celebrate your victories. You've come to tell her you're done seeking her approval. Start angry, righteous, armed with examples. But mid-confrontation, something shifts—you realize you've been doing to yourself exactly what she did to you. The anger transforms as you hear your own inner voice echoing hers. By the end, you're no longer asking her to validate you; you're declaring, shakily but firmly, that you validate yourself. The confrontation becomes less about blaming her and more about breaking a chain. Let your voice move from accusation to trembling self-recognition to quiet, powerful self-declaration.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a childhood wound that has shaped your entire life—perhaps an abandonment, a betrayal, a moment when they chose something else over you. Start with controlled anger, words you've rehearsed for years, your voice tight with decades of buried pain. But as you speak, you see them aging before you, fragile and human, and the script you prepared dissolves. Fury gives way to desperate questions: Why? Did you ever love me? The confrontation transforms into a plea, then something more complicated—grief for the parent-child relationship you never had, mixed with the terrible understanding that time is running out. End in a space between forgiveness and anger, your voice raw with the impossibility of resolution, asking them to finally see you.

title: The One Word
instruction: You're at a crowded party, heart pounding as you finally approach the person you've been infatuated with for months. Your throat tightens, and every time you try to speak, the first sound gets stuck—a silent block where you can't even breathe. You force out a repetition of 'I—I—I...' then a prolonged 'lo...love...' as your voice cracks and your eyes dart to the floor in embarrassment. Finally, you manage to say 'you' in a rush, and when they smile and whisper back 'I know, me too,' a wave of triumph surges through you. Your voice steadies, deepens, and you laugh in disbelief, the stutter melting away as you say 'I d-did it—I actually said it.'
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Echo of a Promise
instruction: You're alone in a vast, empty gymnasium after locking up for the night. The harsh, metallic flutter echoes each step and breath back at you. You're waiting for a friend who said they'd meet you here, but a nagging fear grows as the silence stretches—what if they were scared off by your secret? Start with a playful, anxious brightness in your high-pitched voice as you call out, 'Hello? You can come out now, it's just me.' Let that hope fade as the echo repeats without answer. Shift to a raw, quivering confession under your breath—'I knew my laugh was too loud, my dress too pink...'—the final words swallowed by the cold hall.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unsent Letter
instruction: You are alone in the dark, reading aloud a letter you wrote but will never send to someone you loved and lost. Begin in a whisper, as if afraid to disturb the silence, your voice carrying both tenderness and caution. As you read, let yourself remember specific physical sensations - their smell, their touch, the exact temperature of their skin. Speak as if they are lying next to you in the darkness, as if your whispered words could somehow reach across time or death or distance. Let your breath become part of the performance, revealing what words cannot. End with a confession you've never spoken aloud, something so fragile and true that saying it feels like cracking your chest open. The final words should be barely audible, dissolving into breath and longing.
inspired_by: Actor believes they cannot achieve inspired, unconscious-level work because they haven't experienced it

title: Morning Revelation
instruction: You wake up in bed, groggy and disoriented, with your partner beside you still asleep. As you blink and yawn, a memory floods back—last night they proposed, or you got the job you’ve dreamed of. Begin with a gravelly, heavy morning voice, eyes barely open, your words thick and slow. Let the feeling of elation slowly rise from your chest, warming your voice as you whisper a realization to yourself, maybe even laugh softly. Your pitch might lift slightly, but keep the natural morning rasp and occasional swallow. End with a full, joyful smile in your voice, still hushed.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Thanking Your Greatest Rival at Their Funeral
instruction: You're eulogizing the person who tormented you, competed with you, pushed you, and whom you secretly needed more than anyone. Begin with formal composure—the expected words about their achievements. But something honest slips out: a laugh at a memory of them humiliating you. The laugh is genuine, almost fond. This unlocks something unexpected. You start speaking about how much you hated them, but you're smiling through it, even as tears begin. Your voice breaks between gratitude and grief—thanking them for making you stronger while simultaneously revealing how deeply they hurt you. The emotions tangle impossibly: you're laughing at shared cruelty, crying over lost possibility, angry at wasted years, grateful for every brutal moment. You realize mid-speech that you loved them, or something like love, and now they're gone. End in a space where laughter and sobbing become indistinguishable, where 'thank you' and 'I hate you' and 'I'll miss you' all mean the same unbearable thing.

title: Under the Bed
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe seven, bent over and nearly touching your toes, peering deep under a bed in a dimly lit room. You’re searching for your favorite action figure, but you can’t remember if you left it here or down in the basement. Your voice is thick and strained from the blood rushing to your head—every word feels heavy, squeezed out from a cramped chest. You start by muttering to yourself in doubt, second-guessing where you last saw it, then as you strain to see a shadow in the corner, doubt shifts into a tiny flicker of hope, then dissolves into a quiet, tired sigh when you realize it’s just a sock. Let your voice crack, your breathing be uneven, and pause to shift your weight or wipe your nose naturally.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Speaking Loudly
instruction: Your voice is no longer small. Your words are clear, projected, meant to be heard: 'I have something to say.' Breathing is full, supported. Physical: you're visible, taking up space. 'And I'm saying it clearly.' Vocal tone is assertive but not aggressive—this is your right. 'Hear me. I matter. What I think matters.' By the end, you're occupying your voice: 'I am here. I am loud. I am real.'

title: Bedside Vigil: The Unsaid Things
instruction: You're alone with someone you love who's unconscious in their final hours. Speak in whispers, as if they might hear. Start with small, safe memories—the silly things, inside jokes, ordinary moments that meant everything. Your voice should be soft, almost conversational, laced with fragile hope. Gradually, let the unsaid truths surface: the apology you never gave, the forgiveness you wish you'd asked for, the moment you realized they were your person. Your whispers should catch and break, not dramatically but the way voices do when emotion ambushes you mid-sentence. End with the simplest truth, spoken barely above a breath, as you give them permission to go. The entire piece should feel like speaking in a sacred space, where every word costs something and silence holds as much weight as sound.

title: The Toast That Stings
instruction: You are the bride's older sister, standing at the head table at her wedding reception, holding a wine glass and a crumpled note. You're about to give a toast that you've been dreading for months. Begin with a fake, bright smile and a forced chuckle, making a joke about how you never thought you'd see this day. Let your voice waver with public-speaking nerves — a slight tremor, overly long pauses, and a poorly projected 'uh' as you scan the room. Midway, your contempt leaks through: your tone hardens, a sneer tugs at your lips as you 'compliment' the groom's ambition, but your eyes flicker with shame that you're saying this at all. End with a bitter, amused sigh, trailing off as you realize you've said too much — your voice cracking from the strain of faking warmth.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Shame (slightly present), Contempt (extremely present)
