speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Desire Honored
instruction: Your partner is honoring your desire—taking it seriously, celebrating it, creating space for it. Your voice starts hesitant: 'I want...' But they respond with enthusiasm: 'Tell me. I want to know.' Now your voice becomes more confident. Your desire is valued. You're learning that wanting is okay. Your voice becomes more animated as you articulate what you want. Your partner is actively supporting your desire. By the end, your voice should sound like someone who's been given permission to want openly.

title: The Dream That Destroyed Everything
instruction: You've finally achieved your lifelong ambition - but it cost you your marriage, your relationship with your children, years of their lives you can't get back. You're standing in the space of your success (a office, a stage, a studio), and the rage comes first - fierce, defensive justification: 'I earned this! I deserved to want something!' But it cracks apart as you look at a photo or remember a moment you missed. The anger collapses into something more primal - a howl of realization that you can't have both. Your voice becomes raw, unguarded: 'What did I do? What the hell did I do?' End in broken whispers, protective of what you built but devastated by what you sacrificed: 'I can't undo this. I don't even know if I would. And that makes me a monster, doesn't it?' Let fury and heartbreak war with each other.

title: Morphine Dreams: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Love
instruction: You're in hospice, on morphine. Your partner is asleep in the chair beside you. Start in that gauzy, pain-free place where you're untethered from fear. Whisper to them—soft, dreamy, tender things you've never said aloud. Your voice floats. You tell them about the first time you knew, about the life you wanted to give them. It's beautiful and distant. Then the morphine ebbs. Reality seeps back in. Your whisper becomes urgent, catching in your throat. The pain returns—physical and emotional. You realize they can't hear you, that this might be your last chance. Your voice breaks but you keep whispering, now with desperate tenderness, knowing these words will disappear into the dark.
inspired_by: Nitrous Oxide Euphoria Wearing Off Mid-sentence

title: The Last Night Before the War
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your lover on the night before they ship out to a war they likely won't survive. Start by tracing their face with your fingers, your voice soft and tender, cataloging details: 'Your eyes have these gold flecks I never noticed before.' You're memorizing them, and they know it. Gradually, the reality seeps in—this is the last time—and your voice begins to fracture. You try to stay strong, but grief overwhelms you. End with a whispered confession that breaks you completely: 'I don't know how to be in a world without you.' Your voice must travel from gentle intimacy to raw, inconsolable devastation. This isn't about being brave. It's about letting someone see you shatter.

title: Whispered Confession in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner who you believe is asleep. In the darkness and safety of their sleep, you whisper a secret you've carried for years - perhaps a fear, a shameful memory, or something you did that haunts you. Begin with your voice barely audible, testing the silence, trembling with the relief of finally saying it aloud even if they can't hear. Let each whispered sentence grow slightly braver, more specific, more honest. But then - they shift, and you realize they might be awake, might have heard everything. Your whisper should transform from unburdened confession into vulnerable exposure, your voice becoming even quieter but now fragile with fear and hope, waiting to see if you'll be rejected or embraced.

title: The Wrong Number at the Right Time
instruction: You are a customer service agent on a late-night shift, taking a call from someone who dialed your company by mistake but you realize their voice sounds exactly like an old friend you lost touch with years ago. Start with your trained, polite 'smile-voice' — cheerful, customer-ready, your pitch slightly raised. As you realize the similarity, your voice softens, the smile fades into something genuine, pauses get a little longer, and you catch yourself holding onto the call. By the end, your voice drops to its natural register, a little rough, vulnerable, and you almost don't want to hang up. The shift should feel organic, with small hesitations and the weight of unexpected longing.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. You came here to calmly explain why you've been avoiding him, but the smell of this room, the familiar chair he's sitting in, everything conspires against your plan. Begin measured and reasonable, but let yourself derail—suddenly scream about something from childhood that seems trivial but feels massive, then laugh bitterly, then find yourself pleading like you're ten years old again, then rage about something completely different, then break into confession about your own failures. Don't make these transitions make sense. Let yourself be gloriously, messily irrational. End in unexpected tenderness or exhaustion, perhaps touching his shoulder, perhaps just sitting in silence. Move from controlled confrontation through volcanic eruption to raw human connection.

title: Hate Burning
instruction: Someone betrayed you in an unforgivable way. Your voice is acidic, cutting: 'I hate them. I hate everything about them.' Each word is a weapon. Breathing is sharp. There's heat in the vocal tone. Your voice might be quiet (cold hate) or loud (hot hate), but the texture is the same: corrosive. You're articulating specific things you despise about them. Physical: clenched fist. The hate feels justified, righteous. Your voice doesn't apologize for it. By the end, you're repeating the worst part: 'I will never forgive this. Never.'

title: The Last Filter
instruction: You are an older man at a loud house party, maybe your son's or a friend's kid's. You've accidentally taken something strong—an energy drink? Or something else? Now your jaw is locked, your mouth dry, and your thoughts are firing at triple speed. Start by trying to have a conversation with a stranger about recycling bins, but your disgust at the state of the messy kitchen keeps leaking out. Halfway through, you realize the person you're talking to is the host, and you pivot from judgment to a rushed, clumsy apology layered with forced enthusiasm about the party. Let the speed and jaw tension warp your words.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Forgotten Toast
instruction: You're an elderly man sitting at a dimly lit bar, two drinks in. You're telling a younger friend about a memory from 50 years ago—the toast your best man made at your wedding. You start off confident, leaning back, gesturing with your glass, voice a little louder and looser from the alcohol. But halfway through, you realize the details are blurring. Your certainty cracks. You search your mind, mutter to yourself, trailing off as doubt floods in. Let the words come naturally—micro-pauses, a slight slur on clusters like 'best man,' a shift in your seat as you lose the thread. Start warm and sure, end quiet and uncertain.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Service with a Smile... or a Cry
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy working the drive-thru, using that bright, high-pitched 'welcome to our store' voice. But you just got a text that your mom is being rushed to the hospital. As you take a customer's order, you're fighting to keep the cheerful tone while your voice starts breaking, your hands shake, you trail off mid-sentence. At first you nail the scripted greeting, but by the end you're barely holding it together, apologizing in a cracked voice as you realize you have to ask to leave early, your affection for your mom leaking through the fake cheer.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Vigil at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping partner after a terrible scare—a call from the hospital you almost didn't get to in time. Now they're safe, asleep, and you're whispering confessions they can't hear. Your voice is barely audible, hoarse from hours of crying: 'I never told you how scared I get...' Each admission comes quieter than the last, like secrets you're almost too afraid to speak even to the darkness. 'Sometimes I look at you and I can't breathe because what if...' Your voice catches, breaks, steadies. The words are gentle but weighted with every unsaid fear. By the end, you're quiet-crying, those nearly silent tears, and whispering 'please don't leave me' like a prayer. Your delivery is so tender it aches, transforming from confession to plea to something like a lullaby of grief and gratitude.

title: The Last Song I Sang for You
instruction: You are alone in your car after leaving a vocal specialist’s appointment. The doctor confirmed you have nodules on your vocal cords and need complete silence for at least a month to avoid permanent damage. You are a former high school choir soloist, known for your strong tenor voice. Now every word you speak feels like sandpaper—your voice cracks and breaks, especially when you try to push it. You're trying to leave a voicemail for your little sister, who’s away at college and who you used to sing lullabies to over the phone. Begin with clinical, almost robotic acceptance—'I need to tell you something'—as you try to stay calm and controlled, but as you realize you might never sing again, the sadness overwhelms you. Let your voice falter, trail off, go breathy, or break completely. Don't fight the breaks—let them happen, and let the last words come out barely a whisper, as you finally lose the battle to hold back tears.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Fever Dream of Clarity
instruction: You're sick with a high fever—body aching, skin hypersensitive, reality slightly unmoored. In this altered state, speak aloud everything you're physically feeling: the sheets against your burning skin, the throb in your head, the taste in your mouth, the sound of your own breath, the weight of your limbs, how the room seems to pulse. Start in discomfort and irritation, resenting the vulnerability of your feverish body. But as you voice each sensation, let the fever strip away your normal defenses. The physical discomfort becomes a doorway—let yourself fall into a raw, almost ecstatic state of truth-telling about something you've been hiding from yourself. By the end, reach a place where physical pain and emotional breakthrough merge into fierce, liberating revelation. Let your voice be ragged, your body truthful to the fever's reality.

title: Whispered Goodbye Before the Impossible Journey
instruction: You are whispering to your sleeping lover in the pre-dawn darkness, knowing you're about to leave on a voyage you'll never return from—not because you want to, but because you must to protect them from danger they don't know exists. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking. Describe all the small moments you'll miss—the way they laugh, how they look in morning light, the life you'd imagined together. Let your breath catch on words you can barely say. The emotion shifts from gentle love to devastating grief as reality sinks in. End with the physical act of pulling away, your voice fracturing on a final 'I love you' that carries all the weight of never being able to say it again. This is intimate devastation, quiet heartbreak that feels like drowning.
inspired_by: The Pirate Captain and the Mutinous First Mate

title: The Spiteful Whisper
instruction: You're hiding behind a curtain at a party, hand clamped over your own mouth to keep from laughing too loud. You just overheard your rival's plan to humiliate someone at the dinner speech—and you realize you can still ruin it. Start with a low, breathy murmur of shaky pride and confusion as you piece it together. By the end, let the muffled words twist into a slow, thrilled malice as you decide exactly how to turn their scheme against them. Let the hand smother your consonants, especially p, b, m, f, v—don't fight the muffling, lean into it as part of the secret pleasure.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Confusion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Weight of Hope
instruction: You are a man who is eight months pregnant, sitting on a park bench after a long walk. Your breathing is labored, and each shift of your heavy body is a small struggle. You're looking at a tiny onesie you just bought, holding it up to the light. Start with a laugh that's half awe, half exhaustion, as you marvel at how small it is. Let your voice carry the strain of your compressed lungs, but also a deep, trembling hope for the future. Midway through, a wave of tiredness hits you, and a hint of disgust crosses your face as you think about the constant discomfort. Finish with a quiet, determined smile, your voice softer, full of love, as you whisper a promise to your child.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dripping Secrets
instruction: You are a woman in a steamy tropical sauna, your daughter sitting across from you on the wooden bench. The air is so thick you can taste it, and every breath feels like inhaling a cloud. Your skin is slick with sweat, and your voice comes out heavy, a little wet. You start with a casual, curious question about her day, but as you speak, you notice a small, painful truth about her—a worry she's been hiding. By the end, your curiosity has turned into a quiet, fierce protectiveness. Let your voice drift and catch as you lose thoughts in the heat, swallow, and feel the moisture coating every word. Speak for about 50 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Museum Morning After
instruction: You wake up with a throat like sandpaper. You're a young woman who spent yesterday at an art museum, and you're still buzzing with excitement about a particular painting. As you try to describe it to a friend over the phone, your voice cracks and you wince on every swallow. But you push through because the memory of the painting is vivid and joyful. Halfway through, you take a sip of tea that soothes your throat for a moment, and a wave of relief washes over you. Your voice softens slightly, but you're still eager to share. Let the raspiness, the pauses to clear your throat, and the tiny moments of discomfort be natural. Start with strained interest, end with a mix of relief and lingering enthusiasm.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Upper Hand
instruction: You are an older woman receiving oral sex from a partner who once humiliated you. In your mind, you replay their past dismissals with raw anger, but each touch pulls you closer to a grim satisfaction. Start by muttering tight, bitter words about how this feels like a negotiation they've lost, then let the sensation break your speech into shorter gasps. As your anger melts into vindication, release a low, triumphant moan that rises in pitch, gripping the sheets as you say the final words with a smirk in your voice.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, unable to sleep. They think you're asleep too. You need to tell them something you've hidden—a secret that will change everything between you. Begin in terrified silence, your breath shallow, heart pounding in the darkness. When you finally whisper their name, let your voice be barely audible, fragile as glass. As you confess, let shame and fear make you want to disappear, your words halting and broken. But as you continue, let something unexpected happen: speaking the truth aloud becomes a kind of relief, a weight lifting. Let your voice grow slightly steadier, still quiet but more grounded. End in vulnerable hope, reaching for their hand in the darkness, waiting for their response, terrified and somehow freer than you've ever been.

title: Laughing Through the Letting Go
instruction: You are with your mentor in their final moment of clarity before dementia takes them completely. Start by reminding them of something ridiculous you did together—a mistake, a disaster that became a beloved story. Laugh genuinely, fully, even as your voice trembles. Feel joy and devastating loss tangled together as you say 'You told me that failure was just another way of learning—remember?' Watch them smile, maybe confused, maybe clear for just this moment. Let laughter break into tears, then back into laughter as you realize this is the last time they'll know you. Thank them through waves of contradictory emotion—gratitude that sounds like grief, peace that's laced with panic. As they fade, find genuine happiness in the memory even as you're breaking, speaking with tender acceptance: 'You gave me everything I needed. You can rest now.' End with a smile you can hear in your voice, even as tears fall, finding strange peace in saying goodbye while they're still here but already gone.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that shaped your childhood. Start controlled, almost clinical—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, your voice steady as you list specific moments they weren't there. But as you speak, old anger surfaces. Your voice rises, becomes accusatory: 'Do you even remember my graduation? My first heartbreak?' Then they say something—maybe a weak excuse, maybe genuine incomprehension—and your rage cracks open into something more vulnerable. Your voice breaks. You're suddenly twelve years old again, asking why you weren't enough. The anger dissolves into grief, into a desperate, whispered question: 'Did you ever love me the way I needed?' In their fumbling attempt to answer, you hear their own damage, their own inherited wounds. Your voice softens with the terrible realization that they were broken too. You end not with resolution but with exhausted, tender devastation—still hurt, but seeing them as human for the first time.

title: The Last Hour: A Doctor Tells Their Child About Inherited Terminal Illness
instruction: You're a physician who just discovered you carry the same genetic mutation that killed your parent—and you've passed it to your sleeping child. Start with clinical detachment as you review the test results, your voice steady with medical knowledge. But as you look at your child, something breaks. Your breathing becomes shallow, irregular. You move between doctor-speak and parent-speak, between explaining and pleading with the universe. Let your voice crack on scientific terms that suddenly mean your baby's future. End in a whisper—not of despair, but of fierce, protective love mixed with guilt so deep it has no bottom. This isn't about drama—it's about a parent's heart splitting open while trying to stay whole enough to love.
inspired_by: Historical: Abolitionist Confronts Their Own Family's Slave Trading Past

title: Sorting Through His Clothes
instruction: You are alone, going through the belongings of someone who defined your life—perhaps your father who understood you, perhaps the child you failed, perhaps the partner who left. You've just made a monumental decision about your own life, something irrevocable, and you're doing this final task before you act. Begin with tender gratitude, touching each object with love, remembering moments of connection and understanding. But woven through the love is devastating anger—at them for leaving you alone with this decision, at yourself for all the years you were 'the one with the condition' instead of a full person, at the universe for the cruelty of timing. Hold one item that embodies your entire relationship—his watch, her scarf, their favorite book—and let contradictory emotions war within you: deep love and bitter resentment, profound gratitude and furious grief, the desire to honor their memory and the rage that they're not here to stop what you're about to do. Your voice should move between whispered tenderness and choked fury, laughter and sobbing, sometimes within the same sentence. End in a place of terrible, peaceful clarity: you love them completely and you're doing this anyway.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She is awake but weak, breathing slowly. Begin by simply watching her—notice things about her face, her hands, her breathing that you've somehow never truly seen before in all your years together. Let yourself really see her as if for the first time and the last time simultaneously. As you continue watching, small sounds may emerge from you—perhaps a caught breath, a tiny hum of recognition, soft involuntary noises of love and grief. Eventually, these sounds might become wordless murmurs, then finally, let actual words come—but only when they absolutely must, when silence can no longer hold what you're feeling. Move from quiet observation and the fear of forgetting her face, through the physical ache of love, to finally speaking the things you've never said. By the end, you should feel both the devastating loss and the profound gratitude for having known her at all.

title: The Last Letter: A Parent Leaves Behind the Truth
instruction: You're recording a final message to your adult child, knowing you won't survive the night. You've just discovered documents proving your late spouse—their other parent—wasn't who either of you thought they were. Start with trembling tenderness, wanting to protect them one last time. Your breath catches as you realize you can't leave them with a lie, even a comforting one. The love in your voice battles with the need to shatter their memories. By the end, you're speaking with devastating gentleness, choosing their right to truth over their peace, knowing this goodbye will rewrite their entire childhood. Your final words carry both fierce protectiveness and the terrible gift of honesty.
inspired_by: Professional: Election Official Discovers Evidence of Election Fraud from Their Own Party

title: The Inheritance: Confronting the Parent Who Gave Up
instruction: You are reading a letter your estranged parent left you after their death. They chose their addiction, their other family, their dreams over you — repeatedly. Start angry, mocking their words, your voice dripping with sarcasm as they try to explain their choices. But as you read deeper, their confessions land differently: they were terrified of you, of failing you, of becoming their own parent. Your anger must shatter into something rawer — the child who needed them screaming through your adult voice. Shift between reading their words (slightly softer, broken) and responding with your own (escalating from rage to grief). Climax with you admitting you made some of the same choices they did, that you understand now, and you hate that you understand. End quietly devastated: 'I forgive you' spoken to an empty room, uncertain if you mean it.
inspired_by: Parallel Universe: Meeting the Other You

title: Detective Reveals the Killer Is His Partner
instruction: You're closing a case you've spent three years on, fingers poised over the evidence board in an empty precinct. Start with professional triumph—you know who did it. Then you read the DNA report again, recognizing the sample number. Your voice drops to barely audible. You're alone in the room, but you're also confessing to yourself. Back up, straighten your jacket, prepare the official statement—but your hands shake as you dial. The professional mask fractures on the phone when your captain picks up.

title: The Goodbye Bench
instruction: You're a teenager sitting on a park bench with your younger sibling, whom you've just helped build a model airplane. It's a perfect, quiet afternoon, and you feel a deep, tired contentment—a rare peace. As they get up to leave, you start to say goodbye, but your vocal tics interrupt your words unpredictably. You're used to this, so you keep going, but the warmth of this moment makes you want to hold onto it, even as the sounds break your sentences. Speak naturally, letting the tics happen suddenly—like a bark, a grunt, or a half-word—then continue without pausing or apologizing. Start calmly grateful, then let the effort of keeping the moment smooth mix with a tiny, growing sadness as they walk away.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: You Never Learned My Recipe
instruction: You're confronting your mother, holding a piece of apple pie you tried to recreate from her recipe—but it's not right, and it never has been. Start with careful, measured words about the pie, but let your real pain surface: she never taught you properly, never made time, always kept you at arm's length. Your voice should build from controlled disappointment to raw accusation—why did she withhold this simple act of love? Let your anger crack open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted to be close to her, to learn something from her hands, to share this one warm, cinnamon-scented tradition. End exhausted, the pie forgotten, confronting the reality that some distances never close.
inspired_by: Savoring a Bite of Warm Apple Pie with Cinnamon

title: The Final Signature
instruction: You are a retired librarian, sitting at a worn wooden desk in a quiet lawyer's office, about to finalize a small inheritance for your niece. You've just read through the document for the third time, and a deep sense of contentment settles in your chest — not joy, but the quiet satisfaction of a life well-sorted. Begin your reading in a steady, rapid monotone, a professional drone focusing on accuracy, but as you reach the phrase 'in the event of my passing,' your voice catches slightly — a momentary crack of vulnerability that you quickly smooth over. A breeze from the window rustles the papers; you pause to resettle them, and your tone shifts, warming just a fraction, as you realize this isn't just a legal formality — it's a gift, and your voice softens into a tired, peaceful near-whisper for the final clause, a sound of release. Speak clearly, as if ensuring every word is perfect, but let the contentment bloom as a slight lift on the crucial words: 'Freely and without reservation.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Cubicle Confession
instruction: You're a teenage boy in a bustling open-plan office, waiting for your parent to finish a meeting. You're on the phone with your best friend, putting on a tough, hyper-masculine voice—teasing him about a girl he likes. But as you talk, the background hum of printers and voices makes you hunch over, lowering your volume for privacy. Your laughter fades when you realize your friend is actually hurt by your jokes. By the end, your voice drops to a hesitant, earnest whisper, the bravado crumbling into genuine apology. Let the office noise and your own self-consciousness interrupt your flow—shift your weight, lose a thought, and find it again.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Protecting Your Younger Self: Rage at the Person Who Hurt You
instruction: You're confronting someone who abused you as a child. Start with your whole body shaking, voice tight with controlled fury: 'Look at me.' You're trying to hold it together, to be powerful, to finally be the adult who can fight back. But then it explodes—screaming, raw, words tumbling over each other, years of trapped rage pouring out. Let your voice crack and soar and break. You're not polished or articulate anymore; you're feral with protective love for the child you were. Then, in the middle of your fury, something devastating happens: you start crying. Not sad crying—angry, frustrated, helpless crying because you can't go back and save that child. Your voice becomes both fierce and broken at once: 'You don't get to—' but you can't finish. End with your rage collapsing into something quieter but no less powerful: a vow, spoken through tears, that you will spend the rest of your life loving the parts of you they tried to destroy. Let your voice tremble with the effort of standing up, of surviving, of refusing to disappear.
inspired_by: First Day of Sobriety: Calling Your Sponsor

title: Get Away From Them
instruction: Someone you love — your child, your partner, your best friend — is in danger, and you're trying to protect them, but you're powerless to stop it. Begin with fierce urgency: 'Listen to me. You need to leave. Now.' Your voice is commanding, protective, strong. But as they refuse or can't understand, your certainty begins to fracture: 'Please. Please, you don't understand what's going to happen.' The protective anger builds to a roar: 'I am telling you to GET OUT!' — then it shatters completely into desperate pleading, your voice breaking: 'I can't lose you. I can't watch this happen.' You're on your knees now, or gripping their shoulders, and the rage has dissolved into helpless sobbing: 'I would do anything. Anything. Just tell me what to do.' In the end, when you realize you can't save them, your voice becomes impossibly gentle, resigned: 'Then I'm staying with you. If you won't leave, I'm not leaving either.' It's a fierce declaration wrapped in absolute surrender.

title: Last Words to a Dying Parent
instruction: You're at your parent's bedside in their final hours, and there's something you've never told them. Begin with a trembling voice: 'Mom/Dad, I need you to know...' You're trying to articulate a truth about who you really are—something about your life, your choices, your identity that you hid from them for years. Your voice cracks with the weight of decades of silence. But as you speak, you see understanding in their failing eyes, maybe a weak squeeze of your hand. The shame starts dissolving into something else—not quite forgiveness, but recognition. Your voice transforms from terrified confession into tender revelation. End with a whisper that's half-grief, half-liberation: 'I needed you to see me, just once, before...' Let your voice trail off. The final emotion should be devastating peace—you're losing them, but they finally knew you.

title: Laughing Through Your Divorce Papers
instruction: You're signing divorce papers from a marriage that was slowly killing you both, and you start genuinely laughing at the absurdity of the legal language trying to describe a human ending. Your voice is light, almost giddy with relief: 'Listen to this - irreconcilable differences. God, that's so bland.' But the laughter keeps catching on something sharp in your chest. Your voice cracks between laughing and crying: 'We were so in love once. Remember?' You're signing your name while tears blur your vision, and your voice carries this strange cocktail of liberation and heartbreak. You start thanking them - genuinely, voice full of gratitude - for the good years, for letting you go, for surviving this with you. End with your voice quiet, peaceful, still smiling through tears: 'I hope you find someone who can love you the way you deserve.' The grief and gratitude are inseparable.

title: The Truth That Burns Everything Down
instruction: You're standing in the wreckage of a relationship - romantic, familial, or a deep friendship - and the rage you've been swallowing for months, maybe years, finally erupts. Start with your voice sharp, cutting, accusatory: list the ways they've failed you, hurt you, broken promises. Your voice is fire, each word meant to wound because you're done protecting them from the consequences of their actions. But mid-fury, something shifts - your voice cracks and suddenly you're sobbing, the anger collapsing into the grief underneath it. You loved them so much. You needed them so badly. Your voice becomes raw, almost animal with pain: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Then another shift: fierce protectiveness, maybe of yourself, maybe of what you shared before it broke. Your voice steadies with devastating clarity as you realize you can't save this, can't save them. End with your voice quiet but unshakeable, speaking the truth that ends everything: 'I can't do this anymore. I love you, and I can't do this anymore.'

title: Breaking Protocol: When the Documentary Narrator Intervenes
instruction: You're narrating someone you love destroying themselves—addiction, self-harm, dangerous choices—and the documentary objectivity finally explodes. Start controlled: 'The subject exhibits self-destructive patterns consistent with...' But your voice increasingly strains with suppressed emotion. Then erupt—shatter the clinical distance with fierce, desperate rage: 'STOP! I can't just watch anymore!' Let protective fury pour out, then crack into helpless sobbing. You're furious at them, terrified for them, feeling utterly powerless. Cycle rapidly between anger ('How can you do this?'), desperation ('Please, I'm begging you'), and breaking tenderness ('I can't lose you'). End raw and stripped of all pretense, just human and afraid.
inspired_by: Nature Documentary Voice for Your Roommate's Morning Routine

title: Confessing Infidelity Face to Face
instruction: You have to tell them. You cheated. You're standing in front of your partner and every word is agonizing. Your voice starts quiet. You're confessing and your voice cracks on details. You're not asking for forgiveness—you know you don't deserve it. Your voice becomes almost mechanical as you push through the horrible truth. Your partner is silent. Your voice fills the silence with more confession because you can't bear the quiet. Include the moment they finally respond.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital Room
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from your hospital bed, knowing this is likely your final conversation. Start with carefully controlled politeness, almost formal—years of distance between you. But as you speak, something breaks. You begin to confess what you've always wanted to say: the childhood moments you've carried, the ways you needed them, the love that existed beneath all the hurt. Your voice should crack and soften, moving from guarded detachment to raw, undefended tenderness. End in a place of painful peace, where forgiveness and grief become indistinguishable. Let silence do as much work as words.
inspired_by: Jealousy Eating You Alive at a Party

title: Deathbed Transmission: Last Words to the Void
instruction: You're an astronaut whose life support is failing on a solo mission to the outer solar system. You have maybe ten minutes left, and you're recording a final message to your child back on Earth—a message that will take years to arrive, long after you're gone. Begin with fierce determination to say everything that matters, your voice strong and clear despite your fear. But as oxygen thins and reality crashes in, your words become softer, more intimate, almost dreamlike. You shift from giving life advice to simply remembering small moments—the smell of their hair, a laugh, a morning you took for granted. End in a place of profound peace mixed with unbearable longing, your voice barely above a whisper, as if you're already half-departed. Let the pauses speak as loudly as the words.
inspired_by: Lost in a Cave: Echo and Darkness

title: Storm Breaking
instruction: You've just discovered your teenage son's suicide note—he's safe now, asleep in the next room after you found him in time, but you're standing in the kitchen holding this piece of paper. Your voice starts as a fierce, shaking rage directed at no one and everyone: how did you miss this? The fury is primal, protective, helpless—a parent's animal need to fight off danger that's already inside your home. But mid-sentence, the rage shatters into pure terror. Your voice breaks completely, becomes gasping sobs, because you almost lost him and you didn't even know he was drowning. The final shift is to a whispered, desperate promise to the silence: you will do better, be better, see him better. Your voice becomes a prayer and a plea and an apology, still shaking with leftover fury but now entirely vulnerable.

title: Whispered at 3 AM
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, and they're asleep. You're whispering a confession you could never say while they're awake—something you've hidden, a fear you have about your relationship, or a truth about yourself you're ashamed of. Start by testing the words quietly, as if practicing. But then pause and whisper what you're actually feeling as you say them: 'I'm so relieved you can't hear this' or 'I feel pathetic right now.' Go back and forth—confess a piece of your secret, then admit what it feels like to say it out loud, even to the darkness. Let your voice crack, let silence fall, let the vulnerability of speaking into the void intensify. Gradually, let these two streams merge until you're speaking your whole truth with complete honesty, no longer separating the confession from the feeling of confessing. End in a place of quiet acceptance or tender sorrow.

title: Mentor Legacy Passing
instruction: An elder mentor is passing wisdom and responsibility to a younger student. The mentor's voice is measured, carrying the weight of experience. The student's voice is eager but also aware they're receiving something sacred. The mentor is telling stories that contain lessons. The student is listening with the intensity of someone receiving inheritance. The mentor's voice becomes almost ceremonial. The student asks a question, and the mentor's response is their final teaching. By the end, the mentor is releasing something precious. The student's voice carries the weight of responsibility. The legacy has been passed.

title: The Permission I Never Got
instruction: You're confronting your father about a lifetime of emotional starvation—never being allowed to take up space, to be messy, to need things, to be fully human. Start with your voice controlled, trying to be reasonable, but the dam breaks. Your words become a torrent: all the times you made yourself smaller, quieter, less. Your voice rises with decades of suppressed anger and pain. But then something unexpected happens—in the middle of your rage, you realize you're finally giving yourself the permission he never gave. Your voice shifts from accusation to reclamation. By the end, you're not asking him anymore. You're declaring your right to exist fully, your voice finding power in claiming what was always yours.

title: The Hatching
instruction: You are at your child's wedding, watching them start a new life, and you are simultaneously devastated and overjoyed, losing them and celebrating them. Begin moving with a strange duality—perhaps one side of your body is heavy and earthbound while the other wants to soar, or your upper body sways with lightness while your lower body roots downward. Your voice might laugh while your body weeps, or vice versa. Make sounds that blend celebration and mourning: ululations that crack into sobs, humming that breaks into sharp intakes of breath. As you speak your blessing or toast, allow yourself to physically embody a creature helping its young leave the nest—the protective hovering, the gentle pushing away, the turning back. Don't resolve the contradiction; let both truths live fully in your body. By the end, transform from fighting the duality into dancing with it, moving in a way that is both a letting-go and a holding-on, finding grace in the impossibility of feeling two opposite truths with equal intensity.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access a nonverbal or primal subpersonality that does not respond to verbal techniques

title: Accepting a Terminal Diagnosis with Your Best Friend
instruction: Your best friend of twenty years is with you, and you've just gotten the call—it's terminal, six months maybe. You hang up the phone. You're laughing, a strange, hysterical laugh: 'Well. That's that, then.' Your friend is crying. You reach over and wipe their tears, and you're still half-laughing, half-crying: 'Hey, don't. Don't you dare make me cry too.' But you are crying. Your voice fills with wonder and grief simultaneously: 'I got to know you. How lucky is that? I got thirty-eight years, and twenty of them were with you.' You're holding their hand, laughing through tears at shared memories: 'Remember when we... God, remember that?' The laughter fades into something quieter, deeper. Your voice becomes luminous with gratitude and sorrow: 'Thank you for loving me. Thank you for every single day.' You're both crying now, but there's peace in it, even joy. Your voice is tender, accepting: 'I'm not afraid. I'm really not. I got to love and be loved. That's everything.'

title: The Unspoken Goodbye at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the pre-dawn darkness. She's slipping away, drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by listening to the rhythm of her breathing—each inhale and exhale telling you how much time remains. As you speak to her, let her breathing patterns guide your emotional journey: when her breath steadies, you feel hope and your voice strengthens with memories of joy; when it becomes labored, grief crashes over you and your words break apart. Listen to the machines, the distant footsteps in the hallway, the way silence feels heavy. Let what you hear in these sounds—the finality, the tenderness, the terrible beauty of this last morning—transform you from someone clinging desperately to hope into someone ready to release her with love. End in a whisper, listening to the space between her breaths, speaking your permission for her to go.

title: The Soldier's Last Laugh: Gratitude in the Ruins
instruction: You are a warrior who's been given a fatal diagnosis, speaking to the person who's tried so hard to heal you—and you're finding it hilarious. Begin with genuine, slightly manic laughter because after a lifetime of battle, of course this is how it ends: not gloriously, but in a slow surrender. Let the laughter have tears in it as you thank them with absurd, beautiful specificity: for the terrible hospital food you shared, for their stubborn hope, for pretending your jokes were funny. Your voice should shimmer between joy at having been loved this way and the breaking awareness that this is goodbye. Build to a moment where you're laughing and sobbing simultaneously, expressing profound gratitude for every small kindness while your heart shatters at leaving. End in peaceful, trembling acceptance—you're scared, you're grateful, you're devastated, you're strangely okay, all at once. Let the contradictions live authentically in your voice.
inspired_by: The Healer and the Cursed Warrior

title: You're Wearing His Cologne
instruction: You are confronting your best friend who betrayed you deeply. Start with cold, controlled anger—you came here to cut them out of your life forever. But as you speak, you begin noticing specific details about them: the way they're standing reminds you of the night they stayed up with you in the emergency room; their voice cracks in a way that sounds exactly like when they told you about their father's death; you catch a gesture they make that suddenly recalls a thousand shared moments. These recognitions should physically shake your resolve. Your anger should fracture and complicate—not disappear, but become tangled with unwanted love, with the pain of losing someone who is still standing in front of you. End in a place where you're furious at them AND devastated at losing them, both emotions fully present and raw. Your voice should break in unexpected places as these layers collide.

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church
instruction: You've just lost everything—your child, your faith, your reason to keep going. You're alone in a church, synagogue, mosque, or temple, and you're going to rage at whatever God might be listening. Start with a single word—'Why?' or 'How could you?'—that explodes out of you. Let your voice be raw, ugly, uncontrolled. Demand answers, hurl accusations, your volume rising and falling in waves of fury. List everything that's been taken from you, your voice cracking and recovering and cracking again. Then, at the peak of your rage, let it shatter completely. Drop to your knees (vocally—we hear it in your breath, your positioning). Your screaming should dissolve into broken sobbing, then into a whispered, desperate bargaining: 'Please, I'll do anything, just give me one more day, one more hour, one more minute.' End in complete collapse—not peaceful, but emptied. Your final words should be a whisper so filled with helpless love and grief that it's almost a prayer: 'I just want them back. Please. I just want my baby back.'
inspired_by: Leaving a Voicemail You Know They'll Never Hear

title: The Moment You Finally Fight Back
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen confronting the person who has diminished you for years—a parent, a partner, an authority figure. Begin with your voice trembling, trying to be calm and reasonable, asking them to just listen. But they interrupt with their usual dismissiveness, and something inside you detonates. Let your voice explode into raw, primal rage—screaming words you've swallowed for decades, voice ragged and uncontrolled. Use your full vocal power: let it be ugly, desperate, fierce. Then suddenly, mid-roar, your voice breaks completely and you're sobbing, all that rage collapsing into grief and exhaustion. The powerful voice becomes small, saying 'I just wanted you to see me.' End with fierce, tear-choked protectiveness toward your younger self: 'That child deserved better.' The arc moves from tentative control through explosive fury into broken-hearted, protective tenderness.

title: Reading Their Letter After the Funeral
instruction: You're alone, reading a letter from someone who recently died - but it's not a sad letter. They're telling you about their gratitude for your friendship, or a funny memory, or releasing you from guilt you've carried. Begin by tracking your actual contradictory responses: Maybe you smile at a joke while tears run down your face. Maybe you feel furious they're making you laugh when you want to grieve. Maybe relief and abandonment hit you simultaneously. Don't perform 'bittersweet' - instead, genuinely ask yourself moment-by-moment: Am I laughing or crying right now? Both? Neither? What's the actual sensation in my chest - is it opening or closing? Let yourself be confused by feeling opposite things at once. Start from whatever complex真实 state you discover (perhaps guilty relief or angry love) and let it shift into an equally complex but different emotional place by the end - maybe grateful rage, or joyful despair. The challenge is allowing contradictions to exist simultaneously without resolving them into something simpler or more performable.

title: The Echo in the Fog
instruction: You are a woman who usually speaks in a high, sweet, childlike voice, but you've just suffered a concussion. You're in a hospital bed, the room feels too bright, and a nurse is asking you questions. You start in a state of distress—fearful, disoriented, your voice flat and too loud because you can't gauge volume. You struggle to find words, pausing for long moments, losing your train of thought. Midway through, you realize you're scaring the nurse by sounding so wrong, and you try to soften your voice, to find a thread of control. By the end, you've managed to say something coherent, and there's a fragile relief in your whisper—a small victory over the fog.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child That You're Not Going to Get Better
instruction: Your voice is a breath, barely there: 'Hey, baby. Don't wake up—I just need to say this.' You're sitting beside their bed in the middle of the night, and they can't hear you, which makes you brave enough to be honest. Tell them you're sick, that the doctors have told you things you can't tell them when they're awake. Your voice trembles with the effort of staying quiet while your heart is breaking. Describe what you'll miss—their graduations, their first love, the way they laugh with their whole body. Let tears catch in your throat but keep your voice tender, a lullaby of grief. Then shift into fierce, protective love: make them promises about how strong they are, how they'll be okay, even though you won't be there. End with 'I love you' repeated like a prayer, your voice dissolving into silence, the kind of goodbye that lodges in your chest and stays there.
inspired_by: Asking Your Parent for Money While Ashamed

title: Midnight Row
instruction: You're a young woman out on a lake at 2 AM, rowing a heavy wooden boat with a friend you've been teasing all night. You've had several drinks—enough that the world feels soft-edged and your body moves with lazy confidence. You're rowing against a gentle current, and each pull demands a sharp grunt through clenched teeth, then you exhale a breathy, laughing phrase as you slide forward. Start by teasing your friend about their terrible joke, your voice loose and flirtatious. As you row harder, the intoxication deepens—let your voice wobble, lose a thought mid-sentence, and end with a quieter, vulnerable admission you didn't mean to say. Let the rhythm of the oars dictate your speech: explosive effort on the pull, then a rush of words on the recovery, breathy and slightly slurred.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Late Drive Home
instruction: You're a middle-aged man driving home after a long shift, reclined slightly in the driver's seat, arms stretched forward to the wheel. You're exhausted, eyes heavy, but you can't stop thinking about the person you've been seeing — the infatuation keeps pulling you out of your fatigue. As you drive, you mutter to yourself, half-awake, half-smiling. Start with a weary sigh, then let the warmth of the thought lift your voice, but by the end, the tiredness settles back in, maybe a yawn or a shift in the seat. Speak naturally, with pauses, maybe a glance at the empty passenger seat.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Child Logic Argument
instruction: You're arguing with a five-year-old logic and somehow they're right. Your voice starts adult-authoritative, then falters: 'No, that's not how...' Wait. They actually have a point. Your vocal tone becomes uncertain: 'But the rule is...' But why is the rule? Their simple logic has exposed the fallacy. By the end, you're speaking to an adult while sounding childlike in your realization: 'You know what, you're right. That IS stupid.' Your voice has surrendered to the clarity of innocent reasoning.

title: Dry Echo
instruction: You are a 17-year-old with a deep, tough voice, but you haven't had water in three days. You're slumped against a sun-bleached rock, sand gritting under your nails, trying to reassure your younger sister that rescue is coming. Start by forcing a confident, steady tone—'We just gotta hold on a little longer'—but your throat is so dry each word scrapes out, tongue clicking against your palate. As you continue, the exhaustion seeps in; your voice cracks, sibilants hiss harshly, and you trail off into a whisper. End with a raw, quiet admission—'I'm scared too'—as you let the bravado dissolve into pure vulnerability.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Song Before Dawn
instruction: You are singing a lullaby to someone you love who is dying in your arms, knowing these are the final moments you'll share. Begin with tender sweetness, your voice steady as you try to comfort them, to make their passage gentle. But as you sing, your voice begins to crack—grief seeping through despite your determination to be strong. By the end, you're still singing, but the melody is broken by quiet sobs, your words dissolving into raw anguish even as you try desperately to finish the song. Let the listener hear both your fierce love and your unbearable loss. This isn't theatrical grief—it's the kind that lives in your chest and makes it hard to breathe.

title: The Summit's Price
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman on a high-altitude hike, gasping for air. Each step is a battle, and you're embarrassed by how much you're struggling. Then you notice a tiny, vibrant flower thriving in the thin soil—its existence fascinates you. Speak to yourself in short, breathy phrases, letting the pain dominate at first, then shifting to quiet wonder. Your voice should be strained, with pauses for deep gasps, and a hint of self-conscious laughter as you acknowledge your own weakness.
emotions_sampled: Pain (very intensely present), Interest (clearly present), Embarrassment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father exactly how their absence—physical or emotional—damaged you. Begin in that same dissociative register: clinically listing moments they missed, reciting facts like a court testimony. 'You were not present at my graduation. You forgot my sixteenth birthday. You said you would come to the hospital but you didn't.' Your voice is flat, protective numbness keeping you safe. But as you continue, the protective shell begins to crack. Anger seeps in—hot, jagged, righteous. Then suddenly it breaks into something more vulnerable: the grief of the child who just wanted to be seen. End with a question that's both accusation and plea, your voice stripped of all armor, asking them to finally see you now. The journey is from detached documentation to furious pain to naked need.

title: The Captain's Final Confession to the Sea
instruction: You are a dying ship captain alone in your cabin after a battle, speaking your last words into a journal meant for the child you abandoned years ago to chase glory on the ocean. Begin with defiant pride about your legendary exploits, your voice still carrying that commanding authority. But as you speak, the facade crumbles—let regret seep in, your voice breaking as you realize all those years at sea meant nothing compared to watching your child grow up. End in raw, whispered devastation as you beg forgiveness from someone who will never hear these words. The emotional journey moves from bravado to shattered remorse, your final breaths carrying the weight of irreversible choices.
inspired_by: The Pirate Captain and the Mutinous First Mate

title: The Summit’s Price
instruction: You are an older mountaineer stopped on a high ridge, struggling to breathe as the thin air burns your lungs and a headache grips your temples. Your speech is slow, broken by deep gasps, and you wince as you press a hand to your skull. Start by muttering to yourself about the pain and the impossible climb, your voice thick with frustration. Then, as you spot a rescue helicopter far below, let a tiny wave of relief seep into your tone—still breathless, but softer, almost a sigh. Let that relief show in a shaky pause before you finish the thought.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Discovering Your Partner's Betrayal While They Beg Forgiveness
instruction: You've just learned the truth—infidelity, lies, a double life—and your partner is on their knees before you. Begin with cold, dangerous quiet: 'Don't. Touch. Me.' Your voice is ice, each word deliberate, controlled rage. But as you start recounting what you've lost—trust, years, the future you imagined—your control shatters. Your voice explodes: scream their betrayal, let rage turn your words jagged and wild. 'You destroyed us!' Fury peaks, then breaks apart completely. Collapse into sobbing—not pretty crying, but the kind that wrenches from your gut. In the wreckage, something else emerges: you start remembering the good parts, voice now bewildered, almost childlike. 'But we were happy, weren't we? I wasn't making that up?' End with exhausted honesty, voice hoarse and broken: 'I still love you, and I hate that I do.' The arc: lethal quiet to explosive rage to devastating vulnerability to painful, contradictory truth.
inspired_by: Waiting for Rescue in a Cave: Acceptance Turning to Meditation

title: The Last Planting
instruction: You are an elderly man shoveling a hole in the backyard for a sapling you planted after your wife passed last spring. The sun is beating down, the ground is packed, each bite of the shovel takes effort. You start with a grim, gritted determination—frustrated at how hard the dirt is, muttering curses between grunts as you heave. But as you dig deeper and the rhythm settles, the anger softens into a quiet, mournful focus. You pause, wipe your brow, and speak to yourself or to her—your voice gravelly, breath short, words chopped between breaths. By the end, there's a flicker of weary peace in your tone, a sense of purpose that wasn't there before. Let the exertion shape your voice: heavy percussive grunts on the downstroke, speech only when you're upright and catching your breath. The arc is from frustrated burden to solemn resolve.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. Start by really looking at him—his age, his hands, the way he won't meet your eyes. Begin tentatively, almost gently, stating the truth you've carried for twenty years. As you truly perceive his discomfort, his defensiveness, let your anger build—but keep searching his face for the father you needed. Your fury must be real, but so must your longing for connection. Move from careful restraint to explosive rage to heartbroken plea to unexpected understanding when you finally see his shame and fear reflected back. The confrontation transforms from anger to a painful, complicated recognition of shared humanity.
inspired_by: Scene partners feel disconnected and are not genuinely relating to each other

title: Beneath the Cathedral Ceiling
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, heavy voice, standing alone in an ancient cathedral. You tilt your head back to stare up at the vaulted ceiling—so high it makes your throat feel stretched and thin. The voice you produce comes out lighter than usual, almost fragile. You begin by muttering to yourself about how the stone looks cold and damp, but as your gaze traces the ribs and shadows, a slow awe creeps in. End with a whispered confession—a longing for something vast and unknowable you can almost touch but never hold. Let your voice stay breathy and tight throughout, as if the ceiling is stealing your depth.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Hospital Room Truth
instruction: You're sitting beside your estranged father's hospital bed in his final hours. For years, you've swallowed your anger about his absence, his choices, his inability to be the parent you needed. Begin by trying to be the 'good child' - polite, restrained, saying what you think you're supposed to say. But as you realize this is your last chance, let everything you've held back for decades begin to surface. Don't plan what comes out. Let each suppressed thought, each buried resentment, each moment of childhood pain that you've never voiced tumble out in raw, unfiltered waves. By the end, surprise yourself by discovering what lies beneath all that anger - perhaps unexpected love, perhaps forgiveness you didn't know you carried, perhaps just exhausted peace. Let your voice journey from controlled politeness to uncensored release to something quieter and true.

title: The Wake of Silence
instruction: You are standing alone in a vast, open field at dusk, the wind tugging at your hair and clothes. You've just walked away from a gathering where you were publicly shamed for something you did—something you still cannot fully feel sorry for, though you know you should. Start by speaking outward, the words thin and quickly lost in the empty air, your voice flat and hollow as you describe the scene around you to no one. As you go on, let the emotional numbness crack—not into anger or tears, but into a quiet, shame-tinged relief that the wind and the emptiness have erased your voice, your presence, your very name. Your tone should shift from detached observation to a fragile, almost whispered confession of why you're not sorry.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Protective Fury of the Powerless
instruction: You're speaking to someone in authority—a doctor, a lawyer, a bureaucrat—who has just told you there's nothing more they can do for someone you love desperately. Begin with tightly controlled urgency: 'You need to listen to me...'—your voice vibrating with the effort of staying rational. You're trying to be persuasive, logical, presenting your case with fierce determination. But as they remain unmoved, something primal erupts. Your voice climbs, breaks, becomes almost feral with desperation—'You don't understand, this is a CHILD, this is MY—'—and then suddenly collapses into raw, gasping vulnerability. You're begging now, voice shattered and unsteady, trying every possible angle: threats dissolving into pleas, anger crumbling into pure terror. By the end, you're on the edge of breaking completely, your final words emerging as a whisper of devastating helplessness—'Please... I can't lose them'—all your fierce protectiveness rendered useless against an immovable system. The shift from warrior to shattered human should feel like watching someone's soul crack open.

title: The Intervention That Breaks You
instruction: You walk into a room and see everyone you love sitting in a circle—your partner, your siblings, your best friend—and you immediately know what this is. You start defensive, voice sharp and mocking: 'Oh, wow. An intervention. How very Lifetime Movie of you all.' But they start reading their letters, and with each one, your armor cracks. Your sister talks about finding you unconscious, and you snap: 'I'm FINE. You're all overreacting!' Your voice is getting louder, more desperate: 'You don't know what it's like—none of you know what it's like inside my head!' Then your eight-year-old nephew speaks, and his small voice destroys you: 'Uncle Jake, I thought you died.' Everything stops. The rage collapses into something raw and broken: 'I'm so tired. God, I'm so tired of this.' You sink into a chair, and now you're not defending anymore—you're confessing through sobs: 'I don't know how to stop. I've tried, I swear I've tried, but I don't know how to exist without it.' Your voice drops to almost nothing: 'I'm scared. I'm so scared that this is just who I am.' By the end, you're looking at each face: 'If I do this—if I really try—I need you to promise you won't give up on me. Please. Please don't give up.'

title: Hard Hat, Heavy Thoughts
instruction: You're a teenage boy on a construction site, wearing a hard hat with a visor. You start feeling content — the sun on your shoulders, the rhythm of your work, the satisfying clang of metal. Then a coworker says something that makes zero sense to you, stopping you mid-motion. You yell a confused reply, but then you trail off, muttering to yourself as you try to figure it out. Speak naturally: adjust your hat, wipe sweat from your brow, shout over the noise, then let your voice drop into a quiet, puzzled contemplation as you stare at the ground. Begin upbeat, shift to sharp confusion, end in thoughtful stillness.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (extremely present), Confusion (very intensely present), Contemplation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Porn Voiceover While Genuinely Uncomfortable
instruction: You took the gig. You're in a studio recording fake moans and dialogue for adult content. You're trying to be professional. But your genuine discomfort is leaking through. Your moans sound forced. Your voice is tight. You're aware of how ridiculous you sound. The director wants more enthusiasm and your voice becomes tight, defensive. You're trying to produce authentic-sounding pleasure while feeling none of it. Include the shame in your tone.

title: The Confrontation You've Rehearsed a Thousand Times
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home, facing the parent who never protected you from the other parent's rage. Your voice starts controlled, almost rehearsed: 'I need to say something I should have said years ago.' But as you begin—'You knew what was happening and you did nothing'—your carefully prepared words start to fracture. Your voice oscillates between fury and the desperate plea of the child you were: 'I needed you to stand up for me. Just once.' They begin to make excuses and something in you snaps—your voice becomes sharp, cutting, years of swallowed anger finally erupting. Then they say something that catches you off-guard, a vulnerability you've never heard before, and suddenly you're not just angry—you're heartbroken for both of you. Your voice moves from accusation to a kind of exhausted grief, landing somewhere between holding them accountable and recognizing their own damage. The transformation is from righteous rage to complicated, messy, human sorrow.
inspired_by: Telling Someone About Abuse for the First Time

title: The Letter After So Long
instruction: You are an elderly woman, seated in a dimly lit room, holding a letter you just received. You wear a niqab that softly muffles your voice. The letter brings news of an old friend you haven't heard from in decades—they have passed away. Your first reaction is a sharp, bewildered astonishment—you almost laugh from disbelief. But as the reality sinks in, a deep, quiet sadness washes over you. Let your words falter, let the veil shift as you shake your head. Speak from confusion to quiet grief, without forcing tears.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Running from the Fight
instruction: You're a teenage boy out for a run after a huge argument with your father. Your body burns, legs heavy, breath coming in sharp gasps between footfalls. Try to mutter your frustration to yourself mid-stride — but the rhythm of your feet punches your words into broken pieces. Start with raw, ragged distress as you relive the yelling. Then, as you round a corner and catch a glimpse of the sunset between houses, the anger falters. You're left with a quiet, sinking disappointment in yourself for not saying what you meant. Let your voice lose its edge, softening through the jogging tremor, but keep the breathlessness and the cadence of your running.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're leaving—maybe forever, maybe to protect them, maybe because you have no choice. Your child is asleep and cannot hear you. Begin with whispered tenderness, your voice catching: 'Look at you. You don't know I'm saying goodbye.' Let quiet devastation seep through every word. You're memorizing their face, trying to be silent so they don't wake. Your voice becomes impossibly soft, thick with tears you're holding back: 'I'm so sorry. I wanted to stay. I wanted...' The words dissolve. You're trying not to sob, breathing through the pain. Touch their hair, and let your voice break just slightly: 'Be brave for me. Be so, so brave.' End with a fierce whisper of love and protection, even as your heart shatters: 'I love you more than my own life.' Every word should feel like it's being torn from your chest, quiet but devastating.

title: The Last Light Before Darkness
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—a grandparent, parent, or mentor—and they have only minutes left. You begin holding back, trying to be strong, keeping your voice steady and controlled. But as you watch their breathing slow, something breaks open inside you. Allow yourself to move from that rigid composure into raw, unfiltered gratitude and grief. Tell them what you've never been able to say. Let your voice crack, shake, whisper, or surge—whatever wants to come through. By the end, you're no longer protecting yourself; you're completely exposed, speaking from a place you didn't know you could reach. The transformation is from armored strength to devastating openness.

title: Proposing with a Speech Impediment
instruction: You have a stutter and you're about to ask the most important question of your life. Rehearse it alone first — the stutter is present but manageable in private. Then the moment arrives. Anxiety makes the stutter worse. 'Will you m-m-m—' Frustration. Deep breath. Try again. The stuttered word 'marry' takes ten seconds to emerge. But when it does, it carries more weight than any fluent sentence ever could. Their 'yes' response. Your relieved, joyful, still-stuttering celebration.

title: Waiting Up
instruction: You're a teenage boy with a deep voice, slumped on a couch in the living room. It's 3AM and a violent storm is still raging outside. Your parent is driving home from a late shift; they finally sent a text saying they're safe. You were terrified — images of accidents flashed through your mind, disgusting, nauseating. Now relief hits like a wave, but you're so exhausted you can barely keep your eyes open. Start with a mumble of confusion and leftover disgust, your voice thick with sleep. As you speak, you keep nodding off: sentences start strong but slow, slur, drop to a whisper. You jerk awake mid-word, force out gratitude that grows more intense each time you surface. By the last line, your gratitude is fierce but your voice is fading, almost dreamlike.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Disgust (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Fever Dream of Becoming
instruction: You are in the throes of intense physical pain—childbirth, a marathon's final mile, recovering from surgery—and you are alone, riding waves of sensation that obliterate thought. Begin by fighting it, your voice tight and controlled, trying to master the pain through willpower, your breathing rigid. You feel weak for struggling, ashamed of your body's limits. But gradually, you stop fighting and surrender to the experience. As you do, the pain transforms into something else—not pleasure, but a kind of savage pride, a fierce recognition of your body's power. Your sounds should evolve from suppressed whimpers to raw, unashamed vocalizations of effort and triumph. End in a moment of euphoric exhaustion, laughing or crying or both, marveling at what you've just endured and survived.

title: The Last of the Splinters
instruction: You are a middle-aged foreman, trapped in the overturned cab of a bulldozer after a collapse. Your arm is pinned above your head, wedged under a beam, your ribs stretched so tight you can barely pull a breath. Your men are outside, trying to dig you out, but the metal is groaning and ready to shift again. You speak into a pocket radio, beginning with struggling, breathless panic as you try to stay calm for them. As you realize you might not make it, your voice thins into a raw, vulnerable honesty—a final order mixed with a quiet goodbye. Let the physical strain pull your voice upward, making it thin and short of air, especially as pain and distress peak.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Dancing at Your Beloved's Wake: Grief and Joy Becoming the Same Thing
instruction: You're telling a story about your beloved at their wake, and laughter and tears are indistinguishable. Begin speaking with warmth, recounting something hilarious they did—your voice bright with genuine joy, maybe even laughing. But mid-laugh, grief catches you, and suddenly you're crying while still smiling, your voice doing both at once. Continue the story, but now every funny moment is saturated with the pain of 'never again'—you're laughing at the memory and breaking at the loss simultaneously. Let your voice find this impossible middle ground where joy and devastation aren't opposites but the same emotion. Include a moment where you say 'I'm so grateful' but your voice is thick with tears, or where you laugh and say 'They would have loved this' but it comes out as a sob. End with your voice settling into something paradoxical: peaceful but shattered, celebrating them while your heart is breaking, finding that strange place where love outlasts presence.
inspired_by: Falling Through Ice: Cold Shock and Survival Instinct Battling Panic

title: The Last Voicemail Before Dawn: A Mother's Final Goodbye to Her Soldier Child
instruction: You're recording a voicemail for your child who's deploying on a mission you both know they won't return from. You start trying to sound brave, almost cheerful—'Hey sweetie, just wanted to hear your voice before...' But the facade cracks. Your voice becomes tender, filled with all the things you never said. 'I should have told you more that you were enough. Just as you were.' Move from false brightness into raw maternal love, then into a whispered blessing that feels like you're releasing them. End with trying to say 'I love you' but it comes out broken, half-breath, half-prayer. Let silences hold the weight of all the years between you. Your voice should feel like you're physically letting go of the person you love most.
inspired_by: Sitting in Silence After Miscarriage: The Weight of Emptiness

title: Confronting Your Parent at Their Retirement Party
instruction: You're giving a toast at your parent's retirement party, surrounded by their colleagues who think they're wonderful. Start with the expected praise, the funny anecdotes everyone wants to hear. But something snaps inside you. Your voice drops, becomes harder. Still holding the microphone, you begin speaking your truth — about the birthday they missed, the times you needed them and they chose work, the way you learned to stop asking for their attention. Watch their face as you speak. Feel your anger dissolve into something more painful: the grief of a child who just wanted to be seen. End almost whispering, asking the question you've been too afraid to ask: 'Did you ever actually want me?' Let the silence after that question fill the room.
inspired_by: Dictating a Will on a Sinking Ship

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Addiction
instruction: You're face-to-face with your parent after years of absence, and they're asking why you won't let them meet their grandchild. Begin with cold, controlled anger—the kind that's been rehearsed in your head for years. Lay out the facts like weapons. But as you speak, their face does something—maybe they cry, maybe they just look old and broken—and your rage starts to fracture. Suddenly you're that child again, desperate for them to just say they're sorry, to admit they chose the bottle over you. Your voice becomes raw, pleading, then hardens again when you realize they still don't truly understand. End with a quiet, final severance—not shouted, but spoken with the terrible clarity of someone closing a door forever.
inspired_by: Narrator Triggered by Their Own Story

title: Discovering You've Been Catfished: The Video Call
instruction: You've been in an online relationship for months. The first video call. Start with giddy excitement, primping, nervous laughter. The call connects and... it's not who you expected. The silence is a canyon. Your voice goes through: confusion, denial ('Is your camera broken?'), the slow realization, the attempt to be gracious ('You're... not...'), and finally either rage at the deception or heartbroken understanding. Show every stage of the emotional car crash.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3am and you're watching your child sleep, knowing you have a terminal diagnosis they don't know about yet. Begin by whispering so softly, afraid to wake them, your voice barely audible but heavy with love: 'I'm so sorry I won't see you grow up.' Your throat tightens as you continue, each word an effort: 'I wanted to teach you to drive, to meet the person you'll love, to—' You have to stop because the grief is choking you. Take a shaking breath. Then your voice shifts to something fiercely tender, almost a prayer: 'But you're going to be okay. You're so strong.' Tears are sliding down your face now as you whisper the hardest truth: 'I need you to remember that you were loved. Every single day, you were so loved.' Your final words are barely breath: 'That will have to be enough.'

title: The Bitter Joy of Forgiveness
instruction: You are an older man kneeling on the floor across from your adult child after a year of silence. Your apology starts with a trembling smile—you are elated just to be here, finally talking—but as you speak the words you've rehearsed, bitterness rises like bile: you were wronged first, you remind yourself. Let your voice start soft and hopeful, then sharpen with resentment, then crack as you fight to stay present. Pause to wipe your eye; restart a sentence when the bitterness steals your thought. End with a quiet, shaky surrender—not happy, but empty of blame.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Pulse and Promise
instruction: You're in the middle of a packed rave, dancing hard and shouting to a friend over the thumping bass. Your body is bouncing on the beat, so your voice has a rhythmic lift, and you're breathless but grinning. You're teasing them about a wild move they just pulled, but your knee is throbbing from an old injury—wince when you land on it wrong. As you yell, you start thinking out loud about how this night could be the start of something better for both of you, your hope rising with the beat. Let your words start with a playful jab, then stumble into a raw, sincere wish, all while your breath and bounce pull you in and out of the sentence.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Pain (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Screaming Into the Storm
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of everything you built—a burned house, a destroyed business, a relationship in ashes (you choose). Begin with shock, your voice almost unnaturally calm, describing what you're seeing with eerie detachment. But then the reality hits. Let your voice explode—rage at the unfairness, at whoever or whatever caused this, at yourself. Scream accusations, scream grief, let it be ugly and raw and guttural. Your voice should crack, should go hoarse. But mid-fury, something shifts: the rage collapses inward and becomes devastation. Your screams turn to sobbing, and through the sobs, a terrible helplessness emerges. You're not just angry—you're terrified because you don't know how to rebuild. End with your voice small, exhausted, almost childlike, admitting your deepest fear: that you're not strong enough to survive this. The transformation should be complete: from shocked calm to explosive rage to shattered vulnerability.
inspired_by: Inside a Space Helmet: Last Transmission

title: The Feast of Transformation
