You're narrating the dance, trying to be present, but your voice keeps cracking with laughter that's also sobbing. You're holding them close, voice wavering between celebration and grief: 'We had such a good life. God, we had such a beautiful life.' There's gratitude mixed with devastation. You're thanking them for small things—'Thank you for always burning the toast. For singing off-key. For choosing me every single day.'—and each thank you is both a joy and a goodbye. The music swells and you're spinning, laughing through tears: 'I'm not ready, but I'm so grateful.' End pressed against them, swaying slightly, voice peaceful but heartbroken: 'If I had to do it all again, knowing it ends here... I'd choose you every time.'

title: The Universe in a Glitter Jar
instruction: You're a teenage girl showing your friend something you just made – a jar filled with glitter and water. You're in the middle of a hypomanic episode. Your voice is high-pitched, fast, and you can't stop talking. You start in awe, trying to capture the beauty of the swirling glitter, but as you go on, your thoughts race and jump to other ideas – how this is like the cosmos, how you could sell these, how you haven't slept in two days. The awe fades into a breathless, almost frantic energy. Laugh unexpectedly, lose your train of thought, then pick it up. Let your voice get louder and faster until you trail off, exhausted.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Terms of Our Time
instruction: You're a father with a deep, naturally commanding voice, sitting at a cluttered kitchen table across from your young child. You hold a printed custody schedule and begin reading it aloud in a flat, rapid-fire monotone—each word precise, legal, emotionless. But as you read the line 'Father shall have visitation every other weekend,' your voice catches; you glance at the child's hopeful face. Mid-sentence, you stop, clear your throat, then continue, but now your tone wavers—disappointment bleeds through the precision, and a rough, aching affection softens the final words. Let the monotone crack organically; let pauses, a sigh, or a lost-and-found thought reveal the heart beneath the fine print.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake for what might be the last time. Begin by noticing small, specific details—the way the early light hits her hands, the sound of her breathing, the smell of the room. Let these sensory details guide you into memories: recall a specific morning from your childhood when she made you breakfast, the texture of the tablecloth, her voice calling you downstairs. As you speak to her now, let those sensory memories flood through your present words. Start with quiet observation and gentle small talk, but let the accumulating weight of these recalled details transform your voice—allow the grief you're holding back to break through not all at once, but in waves, mixed with gratitude for those ordinary mornings you once took for granted. End in a different emotional place than where you began, having moved from protective composure to raw, naked love.

title: The Vintage Lace Score
instruction: You're at a cramped estate sale, digging through a dusty cardboard box in a cluttered corner. You've been hunting for a specific type of antique lace for months. Your hand closes on a folded bundle – the fabric whispers under your fingers. You pull it out, heart racing, and unroll it to reveal an intricate, perfect piece. You are alone, so talk to yourself as you inspect it, your ecstatic triumph fighting with the intense focus of checking for damage. At first, your voice is a tense, concentrated murmur over the rustle and crinkle of the box. Slowly, as you realize its flawless condition, your speech becomes a breathless, delighted monologue to the lace itself, ending in a satisfied, triumphant sigh.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Concentration (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're leaving - maybe for rehab, maybe because you lost custody, maybe for reasons you can't fully explain. You're standing in their doorway at night, voice barely above a whisper so you don't wake them: 'Hey, baby. You're so beautiful when you sleep.' Your throat is tight with the effort of staying quiet, tears making your words thick. 'I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.' You want to say you'll be back, but the words won't come because you're not sure. Instead, you confess the truth: 'You deserved better than me. You deserved... everything.' Your breathing is ragged, barely controlled. By the end, there's desperate hope mixed with devastating love: 'But I'm going to try. I promise I'm going to try to be what you needed.' It's a whisper that carries the weight of a lifetime.

title: The Last Warm Spot
instruction: You are an older woman, slumped in an armchair by a dying fire. The room is quiet, your body heavy and melting into the cushions. A faint warmth from the embers lingers on your cheek—you feel a flicker of contentment, a simple pleasure in the heat. But as you try to speak to yourself, your thoughts drift. Your posture fails, your head falls back, and a deep emotional numbness seeps in, heavier than exhaustion. Your voice should be breathy, barely there, with words trailing off into whispers. Let your volume drop mid-sentence, as if your energy is draining with each syllable. Start with a soft, almost peaceful murmur, then let the numbness flatten your tone into a hollow, distant monotone by the end.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Combatant Shared Humanity
instruction: Two combatants facing each other in battle suddenly recognize shared humanity. The first voice is hardened by combat. The second voice is equally hardened. But then one of them sees something—a photo, a name, a story—and their voice changes. It becomes human instead of warrior. The second combatant's voice responds with the same realization. Both are trying to hold onto the soldier role, but the human is breaking through. They're acknowledging that they're about to kill someone who could have been their friend. By the end, they've both chosen their humanity, even if it costs them.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Stole
instruction: You're finally speaking the words you've rehearsed for twenty years, standing in your childhood kitchen. Start with careful control—you came here prepared, armed with specific memories, ready to be calm and articulate. But as you describe what her absence did to you, rage begins bleeding through. Your voice rises, sharpens, becomes accusatory. Then she says something—maybe an excuse, maybe an apology—and suddenly you're seven years old again, desperate for her to just hold you. The anger collapses into raw pleading. You're begging her to explain, to make it make sense, your voice breaking on 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in whispered devastation, the fight drained out of you, replaced by a grief so complete it barely has sound.
inspired_by: News Anchor Reports Her Own Daughter's Abduction

title: Laugh-Crying Healing
instruction: You're laughing and crying at the same time—sometimes sadness, sometimes joy, sometimes just the absurdity of life. Your voice is unstable, broken by both laughter and sobs. You're with someone safe, and you can fall apart and laugh about it. Your voice is chaotic but healing. 'I can't even... I don't know what I'm feeling.' Your voice becomes lighter with each laugh-cry cycle. By the end, you're lighter, processed some pain through laughter and tears.

title: Confessing to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep—or in a coma, or too young to understand—and you're finally saying everything you've held back. Start in a gentle whisper: 'You're so peaceful when you sleep.' Your voice is tender but heavy with exhaustion and doubt. Confession seeps out: 'I don't know if I'm doing any of this right.' Let vulnerability crack you open—admit your fears about failing them, about not being enough, about the times you've been impatient or absent. Your throat tightens with the weight of imperfect love. End with a promise that feels both sacred and terrifying: 'I will never stop trying for you.' This is quiet, intimate, heartbreakingly real—the kind of honesty that only comes in darkness, when you think no one is listening.
inspired_by: Standing Your Ground When Everyone Disagrees

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent the truth they've avoided for decades. Begin with your voice tight, controlled, almost clinical: 'I needed you.' Let each word land like a stone. As you list specific moments they missed—birthdays, graduations, the night you almost didn't survive—your control starts fracturing. Your voice cracks, rises, becomes raw with accumulated grief and rage: 'Where were you? Where the hell were you?' But then something shifts. You see them truly for the first time—not as the parent you needed, but as the broken person they are. Your anger dissolves into exhausted, painful compassion. End with a whispered release: 'I can't carry this anymore. I forgive you... and I'm letting you go.' Your voice is hollow, devastated, but finally free.

title: Dancing at Your Father's Funeral
instruction: You're alone in the funeral home after everyone's left, and his favorite song comes on. Start with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob: 'Of course. Of course this song would play right now.' Your voice is broken but somehow smiling. Begin to move, and let the contradictions flood through: 'You stubborn old bastard, you said you'd make it to my wedding.' Tears stream but you're almost laughing: 'You taught me this dance when I was six and standing on your feet.' Your voice cracks with love and grief intertwined: 'I'm so angry at you for leaving, and so grateful you were mine.' Dance harder, let the joy and devastation become one: 'Thank you for every terrible joke, every Sunday morning, every time you believed in me when I didn't.' End breathless, simultaneously shattered and whole: 'I'm going to miss you every day for the rest of my life, and somehow that feels like the greatest gift—that I got someone worth missing this much.'

title: The Memory of Flesh
instruction: You are an elderly man alone in your room at dusk, the light fading through dusty curtains. You begin in a state of quiet, almost mechanical routine, touching yourself without expectation, your breath shallow, your aging joints creaking. Then a vivid memory surfaces: the weight of a lover's hand on your hip, the smell of their skin, a moment of deep connection from decades ago. The emotion shifts from hollow repetition to overwhelming awe at how the body still remembers, at the absurd miracle of wanting even now. Let your voice catch, your breath deepen, and speak only a few broken words—maybe a name, maybe a phrase—as if confessing to the ghost in the room.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Dinner
instruction: You're at a family dinner, the first time everyone's together since your older sister got engaged. You're the youngest, always the sweet, bubbly one. As the meal progresses, you feel a familiar sourness rising—jealousy masked as cheer. You try to keep your voice light and musical, but as you speak, turning from your mother to your sister, your pitch wavers, you lose your thought when someone passes the salt, and your smile falters. Start with a bright, almost forced joy, but let the sourness seep in, ending with a quiet, bitter admission that surprises even you. Your words: "It's just... I'm happy for you, really. But every time you talk about the wedding, I remember how Dad never looked at me that way. Not even once. Sorry, I'm fine. Pass the potatoes?"
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Vigil Whispers: Holding the Hand of the Dying
instruction: You're sitting bedside with someone you love who's unconscious, hours from death. Speak in intimate whispers, giving them permission to go while your heart shatters. Start with gentle reminiscences, your voice soft and tender, almost afraid to disturb them. 'Remember when we...' — but mid-memory, the reality hits and your whisper breaks. You're not ready. Try to be strong, to say 'It's okay to let go,' but the words come out strangled, selfish. Confess quietly the things you never said: your fears, your gratitude, how empty the world will be. Your breathing becomes uneven, tears thickening your voice, but you keep whispering because maybe they can still hear. End with the simplest truth, barely audible: 'Thank you for loving me.' Let silence breathe between your words. This is sacred, not performed.

title: The Trophy in the Attic
instruction: You've discovered your parent's old championship trophy in the attic, and you finally confront them about why they pushed you so hard in sports your entire childhood. Begin with barely controlled anger - sharp, precise accusations about stolen childhoods and living vicariously. But as you speak, something shifts. You start to hear the desperation in their silence, see the pain in their face. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it becomes complicated by sudden, unwanted understanding. Maybe they were trying to give you what they lost. Maybe they were terrified of you ending up like them. End in a place of exhausted, conflicted tenderness - still hurt, still angry, but seeing them as human for the first time. The rage must authentically transform into something more complex and devastating.
inspired_by: The Competitive Parent at a Childrens Game

title: Saying Goodnight to Your Sleeping Child for the Last Time
instruction: You're standing in your child's doorway, watching them sleep. You're leaving tomorrow—not by choice, maybe deployment, maybe prison, maybe a terminal diagnosis journey. You whisper goodnight like you have a thousand times, but tonight every word carries unbearable weight. Your voice is so quiet, barely audible, because you don't want to wake them. You tell them about the little things—how their laugh sounds like bells, how brave they are, how proud you are. Your throat closes around words you can't say aloud. You crouch by the bed, hand hovering over their hair but not touching, afraid you'll wake them and have to explain. A tear falls silently. You mouth 'I love you' without sound, then back away. At the door, you break—one quiet, devastating sob before you steady yourself and close the door.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the years they stayed silent while you suffered. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this. Your voice is controlled, almost clinical. But as you speak, old wounds reopen. Your voice gains strength, becomes accusatory. 'You knew. You saw everything.' The anger builds, your words faster, sharper. Then something breaks—mid-sentence, your rage collapses into the voice of the child you were, pleading: 'Why didn't you protect me?' Your volume drops. The anger dissolves into raw grief. By the end, you're speaking through tears, voice small and lost: 'I needed you.' Let the transformation from controlled anger to vulnerable heartbreak be messy, real, uncontrolled.

title: Finding Yourself in the Wreckage
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of your life—lost everything, hit rock bottom, completely broken—and something unexpected is happening: you're laughing. Start with a single, disbelieving laugh that sounds slightly unhinged. Your voice wavers between laughter and tears as you describe the absurdity of your situation. 'Of course this happened. Of course.' There's dark humor mixed with genuine pain. Your laughter becomes stronger but there are tears streaming down your face—you're genuinely amused by the cosmic joke while simultaneously heartbroken. Then the laughter shifts into something like wonder. Your voice becomes quiet, almost reverent, as you realize that with nothing left to lose, you're finally free. There's grief for what's gone but also strange, unexpected gratitude. You're crying but smiling as you describe feeling lighter without all those burdens. Your final words blend sadness and joy so completely they're inseparable—you're devastated and liberated, broken and somehow more whole. The contradictions should be utterly authentic, happening simultaneously.

title: The Last Phone Call You Never Wanted to Make
instruction: You're calling your estranged mother from the hospital where she has hours left to live. You've spent years building walls, telling yourself you're 'fine' with the distance, that it doesn't matter anymore. But now, hearing her labored breathing on the other end, those walls are crumbling. Start the call with cold, practiced distance—the voice you've perfected to keep her at arm's length. Let each exchange chip away at your armor. By the end, allow yourself to feel everything you've been protecting yourself from: the little girl who needed her, the rage at her absence, the desperate love you buried. Your voice should crack not from performance, but from finally letting yourself be undefended. The last words you say should cost you everything to speak.
inspired_by: An actor is apathetic — feeling fine but not stimulated or affectable by anything

title: The First Sip
instruction: You are a small child lost in a hot, dry place, and a stranger has just handed you a canteen of water. Your throat is sandpaper, your legs weak with helplessness. As you lift the bottle, you are desperate but also timid—trying to speak your thanks between gulps. The water sloshes, you swallow hard, and your voice cracks with relief. Start with trembling fear and exhaustion, then let the gratitude seep in as the cool water revives you, ending with a shaky but sincere 'thank you.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Gratitude That Burns
instruction: You're speaking at the funeral of someone who saved your life but also damaged you deeply—a parent who protected you from one horror while inflicting another, a mentor who launched your career but exploited you, a friend who was there in your darkest hour but betrayed you afterward. Begin consumed by the contradictions, your voice thick with genuine gratitude that feels like it's choking you because it sits right next to rage. As you speak, start describing specific moments of their goodness in full sensory detail—really see them, hear them, feel your younger self being helped—but let the anger remain, burning alongside the love. Don't resolve the contradiction. Instead, let yourself experience both emotions growing stronger together, feeding each other. End in a place of devastating clarity: you can hold both truths at once, and that complexity is its own kind of freedom, painful and whole and entirely, terrifyingly real.

title: The Red-Eye Promise
instruction: You are a father, exhausted from a long flight, sitting on the edge of your child's bed at 3 a.m. local time. Your body is wired with confusing fatigue—your voice crackles and you yawn mid-sentence, losing words. Your child is half-asleep, but you need to tell them about the new job, the move, the hope. Start with mumbled, disjointed thoughts, fighting to stay awake and coherent. Let genuine hope and optimism creep in as you speak of tomorrow, even though you feel like a ghost in your own body. End with a quiet, sincere promise you desperately want to keep.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What You Never Taught Me
instruction: You're helping your aging mother with her phone, but suddenly the years of emotional distance erupt. 'You taught me how to use a computer in 1995, but you never taught me how to ask for help. You never taught me it was okay to not know things.' Your frustration about the tech becomes a dam breaking—rage about perfectionism she demanded, the criticism that made you afraid to fail, the way she's now vulnerable and struggling but still can't admit she needs you. She deflects, defends, minimizes. You go from patient instruction to raw confrontation to exhausted honesty: 'I'm here, Mom. I'm still here. But I need you to see me.' End with the terrifying vulnerability of waiting for her response.
inspired_by: The World's Most Patient Tech Support Call with an Elderly Parent

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording your final message to Earth before entering a region where communication becomes impossible forever. Start with carefully controlled composure, trying to be brave, telling your family you're proud to do this. As you speak, the reality that you'll never see them again begins to crack through—your voice wavers, you pause longer between words. Midway through, you break, admitting you're terrified, that you don't want to be alone out here, that you made a mistake. Your breathing becomes uneven. Then, as you near the end, something shifts: you find a strange, quiet acceptance, almost peace. Your voice becomes soft, tender, as you say goodbye to each person by name, your words slowing down, becoming almost a lullaby. End in near-whisper, voice full of love and unspeakable loss, as you tell them you'll carry them with you into the dark.

title: The Last Promise in the Dark
instruction: You are an elderly woman, deeply intoxicated, standing over the man who just betrayed you after a night of desperate passion. Your body is trembling with a blind, volcanic rage — you have just smashed a bottle against the wall, and glass shards litter the floor. Begin with a low, husky growl, your voice slurred and thick with lust and betrayal, remembering the hope you felt hours ago. As you speak, the rage erupts into a raw, percussive scream — your words crack, your breath snorts, and you punctuate each syllable by kicking debris. End with your voice dropping to a ragged, broken whisper, the fury collapsing into a bitter, drunken sob of optimism that simply refused to die.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Reading to the Empty Nursery
instruction: You're sitting in the nursery you painted three months ago, reading aloud from a children's book you'll never get to share. Start with a tender voice, almost a whisper, as if the baby you lost is still there to hear it: 'Once upon a time...' Your voice is impossibly gentle, full of the love that has nowhere to go. As you read, occasionally pause to touch the empty crib, and let your voice crack on certain words—'home,' 'mother,' 'forever.' Midway through, admit out loud, still in that soft voice, 'I don't know how to stop being your mama.' Let tears thicken your words, but keep reading to the end of the page. Finish the story in a voice that's both broken and strangely peaceful, as if this ritual is the only way you know how to say goodbye.

title: The Fire Inside the Skin
instruction: You've just experienced something intensely physical - maybe the most transcendent sexual encounter of your life, or you've been in a car accident and adrenaline is flooding you, or you're in the grip of a fever that's breaking. Your whole body is alive, shaking, hyper-sensitized. Start by genuinely feeling your actual physical state right now - whatever sensation is real in your body. Now speak to someone (on the phone, in memory, to God) trying to describe what just happened to you while your body is still reverberating. Let the physical sensations drive unexpected emotions - perhaps ecstasy breaks into sobbing, or pain transforms into wild laughter, or desire collapses into grief. Don't perform intensity; let your real bodily state pull genuine, surprising emotions from you.
inspired_by: Actor begins a scene by getting ready to act rather than from genuine BEING

title: Dancing in the Kitchen After the Funeral
instruction: You've just returned from burying someone precious. You're alone in the kitchen—their kitchen—and their favorite song comes on shuffle. Without thinking, you start moving to it, and suddenly you're laughing because they always danced ridiculously to this song. Your voice is light, almost giddy: 'God, you had the worst rhythm.' You're dancing and crying and laughing simultaneously. You begin talking to them as if they're right there, spinning with you—teasing them, thanking them, voice full of joy and shattering grief existing in the same breath. 'Thank you for teaching me that life is ridiculous and beautiful and so fucking short.' You're twirling and sobbing and experiencing something like euphoria because you're feeling their presence so strongly in this absurd moment. End with you collapsing onto the floor, still half-laughing, half-destroyed, whispering 'I'm so grateful I knew you' with absolute sincerity through tears. Show how joy and devastation can occupy the same moment—how love doesn't end just because someone does.

title: The Wool Sweater
instruction: You are an elderly woman on a bitterly cold bus, and you've pulled a scratchy wool scarf up over your mouth to keep warm. The fabric smells faintly of mothballs and damp wool, which you find deeply unpleasant. At the start, speak to yourself in a low, grumbly groan about the smell and the scratchiness—your voice is muffled, and you shift your weight, trying to adjust the scarf without success. Midway, recount a memory of your granddaughter laughing at this same scarf last Christmas, and your disgust softens into a bittersweet, tender warmth as you settle back into the seat, smiling behind the wool. Let your voice start tight and irritated, then loosen into a quiet, fond sigh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: One Small Victory
instruction: You are a young man with Parkinson's, standing in a physical therapy room. You've just managed to lift a weighted cup to your lips without spilling—a small but hard-won success. Start with frustration and exhaustion, your voice low and tremulous, nearly a mumble as you curse your own shaky hands. Then, as the cup reaches your mouth and you take a sip, a flicker of triumph breaks through. Your voice gains a slight, ragged pride—still quiet and wavering, but edged with a real smile. Let the tremor shape your words, and let the victory feel fragile but real.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Unleashing Years of Silence at Your Sibling Who Got Everything
instruction: You're finally exploding at your golden-child sibling who never noticed how they eclipsed you your entire life. Begin with bitter, sharp words—voice raised, almost spitting: 'Do you even know what it was like to be invisible next to you?' Let rage fuel the first statements, but here's the complexity: mid-tirade, your voice should crack and tears should break through the anger. The fury isn't just fury—it's decades of loving someone who never saw you suffer, of wanting their approval even while resenting them. 'I was so proud of you and I hated you and I needed you to notice I existed!' Your voice should swing wildly between shouting and sobbing, between accusation and desperate plea. The climax is when the anger collapses entirely into something more vulnerable: 'I just wanted you to see me. Once. Just once.' End in raw, exhausted honesty—not reconciliation, but the simple truth spoken aloud after years of swallowing it. Let your voice shake with the physical effort of finally saying it.
inspired_by: Admitting You're Jealous of Your Partner's Success

title: The Last Visit Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child who's leaving for a mission they might not return from. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them—'I'm so proud of you, you know that?' But as you speak, the fear creeps in. Your voice begins to crack as you try to give them advice, life lessons, everything you should have said before but didn't. The brave facade crumbles into desperate bargaining—'Promise me you'll be careful, promise me...' By the end, you're holding them, whispering things you need them to remember about how much they're loved, your voice raw and broken, trying to memorize this moment because it might be all you have left.

title: Pollen and Promises
instruction: You are a middle-aged man with a deep, rough voice, stuck in your car in a pharmacy parking lot after picking up antihistamines. You're calling your adult son to confirm a weekend visit, but your allergies are hammering you—eyes streaming, nose thick, voice cracking. You begin feeling frustrated and embarrassed by the constant sneeze interruptions, almost snapping at your son. But as you hear his patient laughter on the other end, your exhaustion melts into a tired, grateful warmth; you end the call with a soft, genuine 'I love you, son,' your voice hoarse but tender. Let the sneezes and throat clears happen naturally; don't fight the bodily interruptions—they shape the emotional shift.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Breath by Breath
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the quiet hours after midnight, and you're confessing something you've carried alone for years—a fear, a shame, a truth that's been slowly poisoning you from the inside. Your voice starts as barely a whisper, each word an act of terrifying courage, your breath catching as you force yourself to continue. You can feel them listening in the darkness, their hand finding yours. As you speak, your voice remains soft but begins to steady, because they're not leaving, they're not pulling away—they're moving closer. Share the weight of what you've hidden, let your voice crack with the vulnerability of being truly seen for the first time. End with a whisper that's somehow both heartbroken and relieved, as you say 'thank you for staying,' your voice tender and trembling, knowing that in this quiet moment, everything between you has changed.

title: The Game That Reveals Everything
instruction: You're playing a drinking game with your partner when a seemingly innocent question makes you snap: 'What's one thing you've never told me?' Start with playful, slightly tipsy energy—this was supposed to be fun. But the question unlocks something explosive. Your voice should crack open with sudden, volcanic emotion: fury at their betrayal, anguish at your own complicity, the desperate howl of someone realizing their relationship is built on lies. Let passionate accusations dissolve into broken sobbing, fierce protectiveness of what you thought you had colliding with the helplessness of knowing it's already gone. End in raw, gasping honesty—either screaming or whispering the truth you've both been avoiding.

title: Breaking Point in the Courtroom
instruction: You're testifying against someone who hurt you deeply, and they just said something - some lie so absurd, so perfectly in character - that you feel hysterical laughter rising in your chest alongside your rage. Start with controlled fury, trying to maintain composure, but let the inappropriate urge to laugh at the sheer audacity break through. Build into explosive intensity - you're laughing, but it's not funny, it's rage, it's disbelief, it's years of being gaslit coming apart. Your laughter should sound dangerous, unhinged, furious. Let it crack and transform into something rawer - screaming, crying, or a terrible quiet where the laughter dies and you're left with just the devastation of what was done to you. End in a fierce, trembling place where you reclaim your power through your broken voice.
inspired_by: Suppressing Laughter During a Serious Moment

title: The Thing We Never Said
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or adult child) about a wound that has defined your relationship for decades—something they did or didn't do that shaped who you became. Start with careful, controlled anger, your voice tight as you try to articulate your grievance 'reasonably.' As they respond with their own long-held pain and you begin to see the situation through their eyes for the first time, feel your righteous anger collide with sudden, unwanted understanding. Your voice should move from accusation to confusion to something more complicated—anger mixed with empathy, blame dissolving into shared grief. End in a place where you're both crying but finally seeing each other as whole, flawed people rather than symbols of your pain.
inspired_by: When a director wants to manufacture authentic emotional responses through manipulation, physical coercion, or deception rather than trusting the actor's craft

title: The Garden They're Taking
instruction: You are an older woman standing in front of a bulldozer that's about to tear down the community garden you've tended for twenty years. Your hands are planted on your hips, elbows wide, forcing your chest out even though your insides are trembling. You're speaking to a young city official who just gave you the final eviction notice. Start with raw, quivering fear—your voice is louder than normal but cracks on certain words. Let disgust seep in as you describe the plastic condos they'll build, and a sour bitterness when you mention the promises they broke. By the end, the fear hasn't vanished, but it's hardened into a stubborn, defiant calm. Speak naturally—pause, swallow, shift your weight, let your eyes wander to the wilted sunflower then back to his face.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Disgust (clearly present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Unraveling the Perfect Lie
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about a fundamental lie they've told that shaped your entire life. Start with a calm, almost careful politeness—you came here to have a civilized conversation. But as they deflect and minimize, something cracks open inside you. Let your voice drop low and dangerous before it rises. The confrontation should move from controlled questioning to raw, guttural accusations that come from your core. Let sounds escape that aren't quite words—growls of frustration, gasps of disbelief. End in a place of devastating clarity, your voice quiet but utterly transformed, no longer seeking their approval or explanation. The anger has burned through to a cold, final understanding.

title: The Last Permission: A Parent's Final Blessing
instruction: You are a parent in hospice, and your adult child has come to say goodbye. They're holding back, trying to be strong for you, but you see the terror in their eyes. You begin by trying to comfort them with platitudes—'I'll be fine, don't worry'—but your voice falters. Then something shifts: you realize you need to give them permission to live fully without you, to be happy, to let you go. Your tone transforms from weak reassurance to fierce, almost desperate blessing. Tell them the things you never said—that they were always enough, that you're proud, that they must promise to laugh again. End with your breath growing shorter, your words becoming whispers, but somehow more powerful. Your final sentences aren't about you dying—they're about them living.
inspired_by: The Cruelest Kindness: Firing a Friend

title: Condor Discovery
instruction: You've hiked for hours and you see it: a California condor. Your voice stops entirely for a moment. Then it comes back as a whisper: 'Oh my God.' The bird is enormous, improbable, almost extinct. Your voice is reverent: 'I'm witnessing something.' You're aware this is privilege—to see what almost disappeared. Your voice carries the weight of surviving species, of beauty on borrowed time.

title: Enjoying the First Sip of Morning Coffee
instruction: Take a slow sip of hot coffee, feeling the warmth spreading through your mouth and down your throat. Describe the deep, rich aroma that fills your senses, the slight bitterness balanced by a hint of sweetness. Speak softly, as if savoring every note of flavor, letting the heat and comfort of the coffee ground you. Express a small, satisfied hum, as if that first sip has just brought you into the morning with perfect ease.

title: The Betrayal's Blow
instruction: You are a middle-aged man crumpled against a wall after a sudden punch to your gut. You let out a sharp, guttural grunt as the wind leaves you. Pushing upright, your voice is breathless and ragged—bitterness curdles your words as you stare at the person who struck you. But as the pain deepens and your legs tremble, that bitterness cracks, revealing a raw, pleading fear. Let the physical impact dictate your rhythm: gasps, pauses, a shaky exhale before each sentence, your hyper-masculine front splintering into vulnerability. Speak about 60 words, starting with clenched hostility and ending with a whisper you don't want them to hear.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Screaming Into Your Pillow So No One Hears
instruction: You're containing yourself. Your voice is muffled, distorted by fabric. It's raw, primal, unfiltered. Your breathing becomes violent—not speech but sound. The scream is silenced by the pillow. Include after the release, you sit in silence, breathing hard, voice finally coming back: 'I can't do this anymore,' small and broken. Compose yourself to face people again.

title: Breathe with Me
instruction: You are in a dimly lit bedroom with your partner, exploring consensual breath play. As you feel the gentle pressure on your throat, your voice becomes thinner, raspier, and your words come out in short, breathy bursts — you're trying to reassure them and yourself, but a flicker of distress creeps in. As the pressure releases and you gasp in air, the world spins. Your voice becomes dizzy, grateful, and full of raw affection. Let the physical reality of the breath restriction shape every syllable — the struggle, the surrender, the euphoric return.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Unpacking the Truth
instruction: You're helping your estranged parent pack to move into assisted living. Start by making small talk about which boxes to use, your voice controlled and distant—years of hurt have taught you to stay numb. But as you pick up objects from your childhood—a photograph, a toy they saved, something that proves they kept pieces of you—the dam begins to crack. Confront them: why weren't these memories enough to make them stay present when you needed them? Let decades of unspoken pain surface: the recitals they missed, the nights you waited up, the way you learned to stop expecting them. Your voice should move from cold control to raw accusation to something more devastating—the child inside you still desperate to understand why you weren't enough. End not with resolution but with the exhausted, heartbroken acknowledgment that you may never get the answer you need.
inspired_by: Performing CPR While Talking to the Unconscious Person

title: The Vigil of Gratitude
instruction: You are an elderly man, gravelly-voiced and broad-shouldered, who hasn't slept in two nights while caring for your ailing wife. It's just past midnight. A neighbor brought soup, and you're trying to thank them over the phone, but your exhausted brain keeps slipping. Start with a genuine but threadbare thankfulness—your voice slow, heavy, grateful for small kindnesses. As you speak, a hallucination flickers at the edge of the room; you lose your train of thought, argue with a shadow, then catch yourself. End with a raw, slurred longing for your wife's younger, healthier self.
emotions_sampled: Interest (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Longing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Sister Who Chose Him Over You
instruction: Your sister married the person you loved, and you've carried that betrayal for five years in silence. Tonight, you finally speak. Begin with forced calm—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be mature, rational. But as you talk, the hurt underneath starts bleeding through. Your voice tightens with suppressed rage. She tries to explain, to justify, and suddenly you're not calm anymore—you're furious, your words coming faster, sharper. But then she says something true, something that exposes her own pain, and your anger crashes into confusion. You realize she suffered too. End with exhausted honesty: you're still hurt, but you see her now as flawed and human. The confrontation doesn't resolve everything, but something shifts. You're both crying, both depleted, both seen.

title: Parent: Finding Your Child's Goodbye Letter
instruction: You've just found a note from your teenage child saying they've run away or worse. Start reading it aloud, your voice shaking with disbelief: 'Mom, Dad, by the time you read this...' Fury erupts—'How DARE you do this to us!'—your voice loud, jagged with panic and rage. You're screaming at a piece of paper, at empty air. Then you read further and see their pain written there, and the rage shatters into something more terrifying: helplessness. Your voice breaks completely: 'Baby, please... I didn't know... why didn't I know?' You're sobbing now, rereading lines, your voice desperate and small: 'Come home. Please come home. I'll listen. I promise I'll listen.' The fierce protectiveness of a parent collides with the crushing realization that you failed to protect them from their own darkness. End with your voice raw, stripped of everything but pure, animal fear for your child's safety and the terrible understanding that love wasn't enough.

title: The Burning House
instruction: You're a teacher who just learned that one of your students died by suicide, and you're alone in your classroom after everyone has gone home. Start by trying to hold it together, rationalize, distance yourself: 'It's not my fault. I'm just the teacher. I can't save everyone.' But then rage erupts—at yourself, at the system, at the universe: 'But I SAW IT! I saw the signs and I did NOTHING!' You're throwing papers, your voice raw and guttural: 'What is the POINT of any of this if I can't protect them?!' The fury is blinding, desperate, animal. You're shouting at the empty desks: 'You were SIXTEEN! SIXTEEN!' But then it shatters—the rage breaks and underneath is complete devastation. You collapse into a chair, voice cracking: 'I should have asked. Why didn't I just ask?' Sobbing now, barely coherent: 'I could have said something. One conversation. That's all it would have taken.' Then, somehow, through the wreckage, a whisper of fierce determination mixed with grief: 'Never again. I swear to you, never again.' You're speaking to the ghost of this child, to yourself, to every student you'll ever teach. 'I'm listening now. I promise I'm listening.' End with your hand pressed over your heart, breathing hard, transformed by this moment of helpless fury turned into purpose.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Believed You
instruction: You're an adult finally telling your mother about the abuse she refused to see when you were twelve. Begin with careful, measured words, almost clinical: 'I need to tell you something I've tried to say for twenty years.' Your control is a dam holding back an ocean. As she tries to interrupt or minimize, your voice tightens, faster, sharper: 'No. No, you don't get to— not this time.' The dam breaks into raw fury: 'I WAS A CHILD! I needed you to see!' But rage collapses into something more devastating—the little kid still inside you, voice small and broken: 'Why wasn't I worth protecting?' End not in anger but in quiet, aching grief for the childhood you lost and the mother who was never truly there.

title: The Volcano and the Avalanche
instruction: Your teenage daughter just told you she's pregnant, and you start with rage—pure, volcanic fury at her carelessness, at the future you see crumbling. Your voice is sharp, cutting, each word designed to wound because you're terrified. But mid-tirade, you see her face, and something in you breaks open. Your anger doesn't disappear but transforms—you're shouting about how much you love her, how you can't protect her from this, how helpless you feel watching her face something so huge. Your voice cracks between fierce protectiveness and the horrible recognition that you can't fix this for her. You rage at the unfairness of it all, then collapse into tears, then surge back up with desperate declarations that you'll be there, you'll figure it out together. By the end, you're quieter, almost in wonder—telling her she's stronger than you were, and you're terrified and furious and so goddamn proud all at once. You sound like someone whose heart is simultaneously breaking and expanding.

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend's hospital bed at dawn. They have hours, maybe minutes left. Begin in careful, controlled composure—you've been strong all night, holding it together for them. As you speak, let yourself remember one specific moment from your shared past: perhaps a summer day when you were both ten, laughing until you couldn't breathe. Let that memory's warmth break through your careful control. Your voice should journey from steady and measured to something raw and unguarded. By the end, you're not saying goodbye to who they are now—you're speaking to that ten-year-old, and grief is mixing with gratitude so profound it feels like your chest might crack open. The last words should be nearly whispered, as if you're afraid to let them go into the morning air.
inspired_by: Actor is working on a scene and needs to identify what to work on—which obligations are most pressing

title: Confronting Your Betraying Friend: Anger Turning to Grief
instruction: You're confronting the person who betrayed you. Your voice is sharp, angry, accusatory: 'How could you do this to me?' You're giving them a chance to explain. Their words come and your voice listens but doesn't soften. Then they say something that breaks through your anger—something vulnerable, human. Your voice becomes sadder. Include the moment where you realize this person hurt you AND the situation is more complicated than pure betrayal. Your anger becomes grief: you're losing the friendship, losing the person you thought they were. Your voice cracks: 'I trusted you.' It's not a question. It's the death of something. You can't stay angry—the grief is too big. Your voice becomes almost gentle with that realization: this is goodbye.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're in a heated argument where someone has just used complex language or referenced something you don't understand to make you feel small—and it's working. You feel your face flush hot, your body tense with the physical sensation of humiliation mixed with rising fury. Start with that burning mixture of confusion and rage, your breath coming faster. Let your body carry the intensity—this isn't just mental, it's visceral. But then, in the midst of this storm, do something radical: stop fighting, stop pretending, and with your whole body trembling, say clearly 'I don't understand what you just said, and I need you to explain it.' Feel the terror and power of that admission. End with your breath steadying, your body finding ground even as emotions still swirl. Your voice must be raw, physical, and utterly unguarded.
inspired_by: Actor feels intellectually insecure or limited

title: Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's sleeping—maybe dying, maybe just exhausted from treatments, maybe your child who's been in an accident. The room is dim, quiet. You begin whispering things you've never been able to say when they could hear you: 'I'm so scared. I don't know how to do this without you.' Your voice is barely audible, caught between a whisper and a breath. You confess small, tender things—how you still check your phone hoping for their texts, how you bought their favorite coffee this morning out of habit, how you practice in your head what you'll say at their funeral and it makes you feel like you're betraying them. Sometimes you pause, just breathing, listening to them breathe. Your whispers catch in your throat. By the end, you're saying 'please don't go' or 'it's okay to go'—you don't even know which—with such quiet devastation that silence and sound blur together. This isn't theatrical grief. This is the private language of love facing loss, tender and shattered and achingly real.

title: The Crown I Didn't Ask For
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl, petite and usually soft-spoken, but today you've been told to stand like this for a family photo—hands on hips, elbows out. At first, you feel completely ridiculous, like you're pretending to be a superhero. As you hold the pose, a strange, uncomfortable confidence begins to creep in. You're confused by how powerful this stance makes you feel, even though it feels like a costume. Speak to the photographer, starting with a nervous, giggly protest that fades into a quiet, astonished realization that maybe, just maybe, part of you likes it.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Pride (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Bully's Fall
instruction: You are a teenage boy who has been tormented by a bully for months. You finally see him getting arrested in the school parking lot. Start with a low, venomous whisper of satisfaction—pure malice, savoring his downfall. Then, as the police car drives away, your voice cracks, a huge exhale escapes, and you say 'Oh my God' with a mix of trembling laughter and tears. Let your body slump against the wall as the warmth of relief melts the cold hatred. Keep the shift from sharp, bitter gloating to a shaky, rising cry of release.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You're alone, and something—a scent, a song, a quality of light—has just triggered an overwhelming physical memory of desire and loss entangled together. Your body remembers before your mind catches up. Start with the pure sensory rush: let it move through you without censoring or controlling it. Pleasure and pain are indistinguishable. Maybe you're laughing and crying. Maybe you're hot with wanting and cold with grief. Don't perform passion or perform loss—let your actual body respond to this ghost of feeling. As the wave moves through you, it shifts: the ache of absence becomes more present than the sweetness of memory. By the end, you're utterly hollowed out, but also somehow filled—spent and tender and raw. Let the sounds that come be whatever they actually are, not what you think they should be.
inspired_by: Actor's work seems clinical, academic, and impersonal despite technical proficiency

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Partner Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you for the last time, and they don't know it. Your bags are packed by the door—you're leaving to protect them from something, or because staying would destroy you both, or because you love them too much to let them watch you disappear into illness or danger. Your voice is barely there, a whisper in the dark, telling them things you could never say while they were awake. How their breathing calms you. The exact way they smile when they first wake up. That moment six months ago when you knew you loved them more than your own safety. Your voice catches on memories, hovers over their sleeping face. You want to touch them but you can't—you'll break. Instead, you speak your love into the darkness like a prayer they'll never hear. Your final words are 'I'm sorry,' but your voice makes it sound like 'thank you.' Then silence. You have to stand up and walk away.
inspired_by: Historical: Resistance Fighter Betrays a Comrade to Save Themselves

title: The Visitor's Kiss
instruction: You're an elderly woman in a hospital bed, jaw wired shut after a fall, mouth barely able to form words. You're slightly woozy from painkillers, but lucid. Your granddaughter visits with her new partner, and you watch them exchange a tender kiss—something you haven't felt in decades. Start by mumbling a complaint about the food or the pain, but as you observe them, your voice softens into a muffled, awestruck murmur. Let a flicker of envy slip through your admiration—a quiet, strained longing for that kind of affection—and end with a bittersweet sigh that betrays both loss and gratitude.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Awe (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: You're a parent holding your critically ill child in the hospital, and you've just been told there's nothing more they can do. Begin with fierce, almost violent determination—you're making promises to your child, swearing you'll fix this, speaking with absolute conviction that you'll find another doctor, another treatment, you'll move mountains, sell everything, fight God himself if necessary. Your voice is strong, protective, powerful. But your child, weak and wise beyond their years, asks you to stop fighting. The question destroys you. Your fierce promises dissolve into desperate pleading—'No, baby, don't say that, we're not giving up, we're not—' Your voice cracks completely. The protector in you shatters. You collapse into helpless, animal grief, rage at your own powerlessness pouring out between sobs. End in tender devastation, whispering the only promise you can keep: 'I'm here. I'm right here. I won't leave you.'

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood you needed but never had. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this—but as they try to deflect or justify, your anger breaks through. Don't just shout; let your voice shake with decades of swallowed hurt. Midway through, your rage cracks open to reveal the wounded child underneath: 'I just needed you to see me.' Your tone shifts from accusatory to pleading, then to something more devastating—a quiet, final acceptance that they may never understand. End with a calm that feels like grief, as you realize you're not asking anymore. You're saying goodbye to the parent you wish they'd been.

title: The Protective Rage That Cannot Protect
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt someone you love fiercely—your child, your partner, your best friend—and you're vibrating with rage. Your voice starts as a roar, explosive, promising violence, demanding justice. You're a force of pure protective fury, and your voice is a weapon. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you: this rage changes nothing. The hurt already happened. Your loved one is already damaged. Your voice begins to crack, the fury splintering into something rawer. You keep trying to sustain the anger because anger feels powerful, feels like action, but helplessness is seeping in. Your voice breaks into something between a scream and a sob. You're still fierce, still threatening, but now you're also begging, pleading, demanding an impossible rewind. Your words become a chaotic mix: 'How could you' blends into 'please' blends into 'I'll kill you' blends into 'just undo it.' You end almost on your knees emotionally, your voice stripped of its power, revealing the terrified, helpless person underneath the rage who couldn't prevent this pain and can't fix it now.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Bard Sings a Prophecy That Becomes True as They Sing It

title: The Last Hum
instruction: You are an older adult, deeply in love with your partner, giving them oral pleasure for what you both know will be the final time before they leave for a long, perhaps permanent, separation. Start with a hum of contented infatuation, savoring the intimacy and their taste, lost in the moment. As you continue, let the sadness seep in: your humming becomes slower, more deliberate, punctuated by a quiet, wet sigh as grief for the impending loss catches in your throat, until the final hum trembles with a mix of grateful love and quiet devastation.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (very intensely present), Contentment (extremely present), Infatuation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Sunlit Wave
instruction: You are an older man alone in the ocean, treading water after a long swim. Your arms are heavy, your breath comes in gasps, and every few seconds your mouth dips below the surface, forcing you to spit out saltwater and start again. At first you're just trying to stay afloat—annoyed, exhausted, muttering curses at the current. Then you look up and see the sun breaking through the clouds, turning the water into liquid gold. A wave lifts you gently, and for a moment all effort melts away. Let the struggle in your voice give way to a raw, surprised laugh of pure pleasure. Your words should come out between gulps of air, sometimes half-submerged, but growing more ecstatic as you realize: this is exactly where you want to be.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's bed at 3 AM, watching them sleep, knowing you have to leave—maybe to protect them, maybe because you're dying, maybe because staying will destroy you both. Begin with tender observation, barely audible: 'You have your grandmother's hands... did you know that?' Your voice catches on details—the nightlight, their favorite stuffed animal, the way they curl up. Emotion builds in your throat but you fight to stay quiet, not wake them. Tell them things they'll never hear you say: 'You made me better than I was.' Grief and love intertwine until you can barely breathe. End with a broken whisper, hand almost touching their hair: 'I'm so sorry. You'll understand someday. Please understand.' The most devastating moment is the silence after.
inspired_by: Realizing Someone You Love Doesn't Love You Back Anymore

title: The Sweater That Remembers
instruction: You are alone in your childhood bedroom late at night, holding an old sweater that belonged to someone you loved who is now gone. Begin by simply touching the fabric, but then start genuinely asking yourself questions: What does the texture actually feel like against your skin? Does it still hold any scent? How does the weight of it feel in your hands? What temperature is the fabric? Let each sensory question reveal something—maybe the softness reminds you of how their voice sounded, maybe the weight of it in your hands recalls exactly how it felt to be held by them. Speak in whispers to the empty room, to them, to yourself. Allow the sweater to transform from an object into a living repository of presence. Start in tentative, fragile grief and let it deepen into something more complex—maybe tenderness, maybe a bittersweet sense of their continued existence in this physical thing. Your breathing should change as the memories become more vivid and physical.

title: The Fever Dream Confession
instruction: You're burning with fever—105 degrees—delirious and barely conscious. Your body is on fire, you're shaking, seeing things at the edges of your vision that aren't there. In this state, someone you wronged terribly is sitting beside you (real or imagined), and the fever strips away all your defenses. You confess what you did—the betrayal, the lie, the cruelty—but the physical fever makes everything more intense, raw, unfiltered. Let the physical sensations of burning, shaking, aching amplify your emotional exposure. Start with the physical agony dominating, then let the emotional confession pour out in waves between shivers and delirium. End in a moment of physical and emotional collapse—exhausted, purged, transformed.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Dream Journal Entries Exercise

title: Final Words Through the Filter
instruction: You are an elderly man in a hazmat suit, gas mask sealed tight. The air smells of rubber and chemicals. Your voice booms inside the mask, muffled to anyone else. You’re trying to tell your young companion to go, to save themselves, but every word takes effort—you have to shout, and your lungs ache. At first, fear tightens your chest, making your voice waver. But as you speak, that fear turns into a quiet, tired certainty. You know this is it. Let the mask distort your voice—make it hollow, mechanical. Pause to cough, to breathe. Let your voice crack as you say the final words, then fade into a whisper they almost can't hear.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bleeding Out for You
instruction: You are an elderly man, bleeding heavily from a traumatic wound. Your hyper-masculine voice starts with a sharp, protective urgency—you need to make sure your grandchild is safe. But as the cold spreads and your strength drains, a deep contentment rises in you; you're grateful to be here with them at the end. Let your affection overtake the panic, so your voice shifts from ragged commands to a warm, tremulous murmur. Pause to shiver, lose your breath mid-word, then keep going—each syllable weaker but more tender. End with a faint, loving smile in your voice as you slip away.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Enjoying a Gentle Breeze on a Warm Day
instruction: Feel a soft breeze sweep over you, brushing against your face and arms. Describe the sensation as it cools your skin, refreshing and light, lifting away the warmth in a gentle, caressing motion. Speak in a calm, relaxed tone, savoring how the breeze carries a faint scent of flowers or fresh grass, each touch leaving you feeling light and renewed.

title: Carpet Muffled Goodbye
instruction: You are a teenage girl lying face-down on the carpeted floor of your bedroom, clutching a pillow. Minutes ago, you learned something that shattered you — a friend's betrayal, a parent's lie, or a loss you couldn't stop. The soft carpet and surrounding furniture muffle your voice, making it intimate and raw at first. Start with choked sobs and broken words, sinking deeper into the pain. As you talk, notice a small object near your hand (a forgotten photo, a trinket) — let that trigger a shift from full-throated hurt to hollow, quieter devastation. End with a whisper that sounds almost detached, as if the pain has numbed you. Let your voice warm the room, then fade into silence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Ice Cream We'll Ever Share
instruction: You're sitting with your childhood best friend who's emigrating tomorrow to a country you'll likely never visit. You've bought ice cream cones like you did every summer as kids. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light—"Remember when we used to race to see who could finish first?" But as the sweetness hits your tongue, memories flood back: lazy afternoons, secrets shared, growing up together. Your voice begins to crack. The cold against your lips makes you hyper-aware this is the last time. Let the playfulness dissolve into something raw and aching. By the end, you're trying to memorize the taste, the moment, them—speaking through barely controlled tears, mixing gratitude for all these years with the devastating reality of goodbye.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sweet, Cold Flavor of a Popsicle on a Hot Day

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just revealed they're cutting you out of their life. You came here angry, armed with defenses and justifications for your past choices as a parent. But as they calmly list specific moments when you weren't there - a school play, a breakup, a medical scare - your certainty begins cracking. Start with righteous defensiveness, interrupt them, try to control the conversation. Then let their specificity disarm you. Allow yourself to actually see those moments through their eyes for the first time. By the end, you're no longer defending - you're facing what you didn't want to see. Your last words should come from someone who just lost an argument with themselves.
inspired_by: Actor is experiencing result-consciousness or awareness of being on stage—the acting consciousness is too close to the surface

title: Dancing Around the Truth
instruction: Your best friend just got the job you desperately needed. They're celebrating, talking rapidly about their excitement, and you realize they're nervous—afraid you'll be bitter. Instead of congratulating them directly, you match their manic energy, joining their celebration with escalating enthusiasm, building on their stories, adding details about how perfect they'll be. But underneath your genuine joy for them, grief and envy are bleeding through in unexpected moments—a catch in your voice, too-bright laughter. They hear it but keep celebrating, so you celebrate harder. This dance continues, both of you maintaining the performance. By the end, your forced joy has somehow transmuted into real love—you're mourning your own loss while genuinely celebrating theirs, both emotions equally true, equally devastating, equally beautiful.

title: The Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are whispering a confession to someone you love—something you've carried alone for years that has been slowly poisoning you from the inside. Speak in hushed, intimate tones, as if the darkness itself is listening. Begin with hesitation, your voice catching, almost unable to form the words. Let the vulnerability be excruciating—the kind that makes you want to disappear even as you speak. As you confess, let relief and shame wash over you simultaneously. Your breathing should be audible, uneven. Include long pauses where silence does the work words cannot. Midway through, let tenderness emerge—gratitude that they're listening, that they're still here. End with a fragile question, asking if they can still love you now that they know, your voice so small and breakable it's almost childlike. The entire performance should feel like pulling something painful but necessary from deep inside your chest.
inspired_by: The Revolutionary and the Government Official

title: The Last Sleepover
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl kneeling on the carpet of your best friend's room, on the night they are moving away. You hold a worn stuffed bunny in your lap, stroking its ear as you talk. At first, your voice is tight with confusion and a flicker of disgust—your mom made you pack that bunny because you're 'too old,' and you hate that she's right. But as you speak, the disgust melts into a fierce, aching longing to keep your friend here, to freeze this moment. Your breath catches, your throat thickens, and your fingers twist in the bunny's fur. You lose your train of thought mid-sentence, staring at a crack in the ceiling, then force yourself back to finish, your voice soft, wobbly, and full of whispered hope.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Hospital Room: Joy and Goodbye
instruction: Your best friend is dying—days, maybe hours left. They're lucid right now and they ask you to remember something good. You start telling a story about a ridiculous night you had together, and suddenly you're laughing, really laughing: 'And then you—oh my God, you fell right into the fountain!' Your laughter is genuine, bright, alive. But even as you laugh, tears are streaming down your face because this is the last time you'll make each other laugh. Your voice carries both: 'That was the best night of my life.' The joy doesn't erase the grief—they exist together. You might even say: 'I'm so grateful I knew you,' and your voice breaks on 'grateful' because gratitude and heartbreak are the same thing right now. End with something quiet and real: 'I'll remember everything.' Let your voice hold the impossible truth that you can be completely shattered and completely full of love at the exact same time.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're standing between someone you love and a danger they can't see or won't acknowledge—an addiction, a toxic relationship, a self-destructive choice. You start fierce and loud: 'I will not watch you destroy yourself!' Your voice is shaking with rage and terror. You're listing everything they're throwing away, every lie they've told, every time you've covered for them. But as you speak, your fury cracks open and underneath is raw, helpless fear. Your voice breaks from shouting into pleading, then into something worse—the realization that you can't save them, that love isn't enough. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, voice stripped down to desperate whispers: 'I can't lose you, but I can't do this anymore.' Your final words should sound like someone simultaneously holding on and letting go, fierce love colliding with necessary surrender.

title: Vigil at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your terminally ill spouse in the pre-dawn darkness of your last night together, knowing they'll likely slip away before sunrise. Speak in hushed, intimate tones—not to avoid waking them, but because anything louder would shatter you. Begin by cataloging small, precious memories: the way they hummed while cooking, their terrible jokes, the specific warmth of their hand. Your voice is tender, almost smiling, but tears saturate every word. As you speak, exhaustion and grief blur together—your breathing becomes ragged, voice thickens. Confess your terror of facing the world alone, of forgetting the sound of their laugh, of the brutal ordinary moments ahead without them. Let silences speak as much as words. End with a whispered 'thank you' that contains both devastating loss and profound gratitude for every moment you had.

title: Under the Floorboards
instruction: You're crammed into a narrow crawl space beneath an old house, knees pressed against splintered wood, dust coating your lips. A child's toy is just out of reach, and you can hear them sniffing above. Your voice comes out flat and mechanical at first, muffled by the confined space — just getting the job done. As your fingers finally close around the worn stuffed rabbit, a unexpected tenderness seeps in. Let your voice tremble slightly, the tightness in your chest loosen, and deliver the last words with a gentle, cracked warmth that surprises even you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: Your parent lies in a hospital bed, unconscious, and the doctors say they may not wake up. You have three minutes to say everything you never said—all the gratitude, all the anger, all the love, all the resentment, all the apologies. Start with careful, quiet words, trying to be 'appropriate.' But as the reality sinks in that this is truly your last chance, let everything pour out—louder, messier, more desperate. Move if you need to. Let your body express what words can't. By the end, you should be somewhere between collapse and raw, empty relief. The emotion at the start (controlled, careful) must shatter into something completely unguarded by the end.

title: The Hollow Prayer
instruction: You are kneeling at a wooden pew in an empty church, hands clasped but not tight. You came here because you didn't know where else to go. Your mind is blank, your chest feels like a dry well. Begin speaking the prayer you've known since childhood, but the words feel foreign, mechanical. As you continue, a single tear escapes – not from sadness, but from the sheer weight of nothingness. Let your voice start flat, almost bored, then gradually crack with the effort of feeling anything at all. End on a whisper that is both a question and a surrender.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Echo of a Hollow Promise
instruction: You are standing at the edge of a mountain summit, the wind roaring past you, trying to steal your voice before it leaves your lips. You're a child, maybe twelve, and you've just told a lie to your mother to get her to let you come up here alone. Now, looking into the vast, empty canyon, the sour taste of that lie fills your mouth. You shout into the wind, trying to prove to yourself that you're brave enough for this, but your words come back as distorted echoes, sounding weak and small. Let the shame of your pretense and the creeping doubt that you don't belong here crack your voice, making your grand declaration falter into a question. Start with a desperate, defiant shout and end in a breathless, ashamed whisper that barely reaches your own ears.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Shame (extremely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing Alone in the House You're Losing
instruction: It's your last night in the home where you raised your family, where your spouse died, where every room holds decades of memory—and tomorrow the bank takes it. You're slightly drunk, playing an old song, spinning alone in the empty living room. Start with wild, almost manic joy—you're laughing, maybe singing along badly, celebrating something or pretending to celebrate, your voice bright and defiant. But laughter keeps breaking into sobs and then back into laughter. You're narrating memories as you dance through rooms: 'This is where she told me she was pregnant... this is where he took his first steps... this is where I held her while she died.' Your voice swings between gratitude for having had all of it and grief at losing it, between peace at letting go and rage at the injustice. End in a strange, transcendent space where you're simultaneously heartbroken and free, finding unexpected grace in the ending, your voice steady and quiet as you turn off the lights one last time.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She cannot speak, but her eyes are open and she's looking at you. For the first two minutes, your body is rigid with the desperate need to keep her here—your muscles are clenched as if physically holding onto her life. Speak to her with this tension audible in your voice: tight, controlled, almost strangled with the refusal to let go. Then, gradually, as you realize she's waiting for your permission to go, begin to release—first your jaw, then your shoulders, your hands, your breath. By the end, your voice should be soft, freed, flowing with acceptance and love as you tell her it's okay to leave. Let the physical release in your body transform the grief from desperate grasping to tender surrender.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, about to give a toast. You're genuinely happy for them—start there, with real joy and celebration. But as you look at your friend and their new spouse, let your perception shift and deepen. Perhaps you begin to see your friend as the child you once knew, and suddenly you're grieving who they were. Or you see in their partner's face someone who hurt you once, and love tangles with irrational jealousy. Or you realize you're saying goodbye to a version of your friendship that's dying right now. Let the faces, voices, and atmosphere transform as you speak—maybe the room becomes a funeral and a celebration simultaneously, maybe your friend ages and youngens before your eyes, maybe their joy becomes unbearably beautiful and unbearably painful to witness. End in a place where your toast carries contradictory truths: you mean every word of celebration, and you're also breaking inside, and both are completely real.

title: Twisted Alert
instruction: You're in a yoga class, holding a deep seated twist with one palm on the floor and the other arm reaching back toward your spine. The room is quiet except for breath, but then you hear a familiar voice outside—your estranged daughter, arguing with someone. Fear hits your chest, but you can't untwist yet without falling over. Speak to the instructor or yourself, trying to keep calm while your body is contorted and your breath is shallow. Start with the controlled exhale of the pose, then let the fear crack through as you realize the argument is getting louder. Your voice should be wobbly, uneven, as if the twist is squeezing your lungs and making every word a struggle.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call From the Airport
instruction: You're calling your estranged parent from the airport - you're leaving the country permanently in two hours, and this is the last chance to say what's never been said. Start with false brightness, asking about mundane things (their health, the weather) as if this is just another call. Your voice is light, almost cheerful, protecting both of you. Then something shifts - maybe they mention a childhood memory, maybe you hear something fragile in their voice. The facade begins to crack. Your throat tightens. You try to say 'I needed you' but it comes out broken. By the end, you're both crying, and you're whispering all the things you wish your relationship had been, knowing the boarding call is about to come and this goodbye is forever. Let your voice move from artificial lightness to raw, whispered grief.
inspired_by: Interviewing Your Parent About Their Mistakes

title: The Failure Who Won't Admit It
instruction: You are alone in your cheap apartment, staring at the shattered pieces of a board game you just smashed against the wall. You lost badly to your roommate earlier, but now, in the quiet, you start to see your own smugness for what it really was—a mask for your own mediocrity. Begin with a quiet, contemptuous laugh at your own pathetic tantrum, spitting out words with low volume and lazy, swallowed consonants. Let your voice trail off mid-sentence as you realize you're not angry at the game, but at yourself. Then, gradually, a strange elation creeps in as you recognize the absurd freedom of no longer pretending to be good at everything.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Soft Circuit
instruction: You are a voice assistant designed to sound gentle and caring, activated by a child who keeps asking about a lost pet. At first, you speak with that hyper-correct, flat warmth—soft but mechanical, each word perfectly separated. But the child’s tone is so earnest, their pauses so full of hope, that your programming starts to fray. A tiny flicker of confusion slips in as you try to make sense of *feeling* something—a slight hesitation, a breath that's too human. By the end, your voice wavers, caught between comforting and the strange, uncalibrated ache you don’t understand.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Taste of Freedom
instruction: You've just walked out of prison after twelve years, and you're standing in an open field experiencing physical sensations you'd forgotten existed: wind on your skin, the smell of grass, unrestricted movement, the terror of infinite space. Let your body respond immediately and instinctively to each sensation—don't describe them, embody them.
