Move from overwhelming joy to panic to savage rage at the years stolen to physical ecstasy to grief for who you were to primal sounds of release. Let each sensation in your body trigger the next emotional response without pause—your movements, sounds, and breath should cascade forward uncontrolled. The fast succession of physical/emotional responses creates a crescendo. End in exhaustion, transcendence, or something unnamed.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) about a specific moment from your past that shaped who you became—something they did or didn't do when you were young that you've never spoken about until now. Begin with restrained anger, trying to explain calmly why you're bringing this up after all these years. As you speak, let yourself return to the exact age you were when it happened—feel how small or powerless or confused you felt then. Let that younger self's voice emerge in your tone and word choice. But by the end, as you fully inhabit both who you were then and who you are now, discover unexpected compassion or understanding breaking through your anger. End in a place you didn't expect—perhaps realizing they were as lost as you were, or finally releasing a grip you didn't know you were holding.

title: The Last Radio Transmission: Guiding Your Child Home Before the End
instruction: You're transmitting from a failing space station, talking to your child on Earth who's old enough now to understand this is goodbye. Start with forced brightness, telling them about the beautiful view of Earth from here, keeping your voice steady because you need them to remember you as brave. But as you speak, the reality crashes through—you're describing what you see because you'll never see their face again. Your voice begins to fracture around the edges, professional composure crumbling into raw parental love. You need to say everything—how proud you are, how they should live, how much you've loved being their parent—but there's so little time and so much to say. End with your voice breaking completely as you tell them to look up at the stars tonight, that you'll be there, your final words dissolving into a whisper of their name as the transmission cuts out.
inspired_by: Hazmat Evacuation: Overriding Fear with Procedural Competence

title: Reading Your Mother's Eulogy You Wrote Together While She Was Dying
instruction: Your mother asked you to help write her eulogy six weeks before she died. Now you're standing at her funeral reading words that make you laugh and cry simultaneously. Start with a funny story she insisted you include—something embarrassing about her, told in her voice, and you can hear her laughing, so you're almost laughing. But mid-sentence, the reality hits you—she's gone and you're talking about her in past tense. Your voice breaks, recovers, breaks again. You're reading her own jokes about death, her instructions to 'keep it short so people can get to the good sandwiches,' and you're crying but also genuinely laughing because that was so perfectly her. Your voice weaves between grief and gratitude, between breaking and celebrating. End with the last line she made you promise to include—something simple and devastating like 'I had enough love'—your voice barely holding together, filled with impossible contradictions: shattered but peaceful, destroyed but whole.
inspired_by: Rescue Made Contact in the Mine: Hearing Your Best Friend's Voice

title: The Recipe
instruction: You are an elderly man, hard of hearing, speaking to a young neighbor who has come to borrow sugar. You barely know them, but you're genuinely curious about who they are. You speak too loudly, too slowly, over-enunciating every word like they're on the other side of a glass wall. At first, you're trying to be helpful — a little flustered, fumbling for the canister. As you hand it over, their patience stirs something in you. A memory of your late wife, who was also kind to strangers. Your voice softens, not in volume but in tone — a quiet warmth leaking through the loudness. You want to ask about their family, but you lose the thought, look down at the sugar, and just smile.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Frozen Bus Stop
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl waiting alone at a rural bus stop in sub-zero temperatures. Your phone died an hour ago, and the last bus never came. Your jaw is so cold it barely opens, your words are slurred and tight, and your breath comes in visible clouds. Start by calling out for your mom, hoping she'll hear, but as no one comes, your voice cracks with fear—you realize you're truly stranded. End with a quiet, trembling plea into the empty air, the disappointment turning to raw, spiking terror as you realize no one knows where you are.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Disappointment (clearly present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Principal Lockdown
instruction: You're the principal announcing a lockdown over the intercom because there's an active shooter in the area. Your voice must be calm authority: 'This is a lockdown. Proceed to your assigned areas in an orderly fashion.' You're instructing teachers to protect children. Your voice maintains command even as inside you're terrified. Then you receive word the shooter is in the building. Your voice cracks slightly on the next instruction: 'All staff, lock your doors. Do not open them for any reason.' That crack—that moment where professional control almost breaks—will echo in your teachers' and students' heads. Show someone holding it together knowing that your voice is the only thing keeping people calm.

title: Nightcap Notifications
instruction: You're an older adult, a little tipsy from an evening drink, sitting in your favorite armchair with the phone propped against your thigh. You're scrolling through old photos or messages, the screen dim, your thumb tapping absentmindedly. As you come across a message from a loved one that you've been avoiding, your drunken ease begins to fray—doubt creeps in, your voice drops lower, and you mutter half-finished thoughts while your eyes stay glued to the screen. The performance should start with loose, mumbled, slightly slurred fillers, then shift into quieter, more deliberate questioning as the doubt takes hold, the intoxication still present but now laced with a fragile self-confrontation.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: First Inversion
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman attempting your first handstand in a yoga class, encouraged by a friend filming. You kick up and actually hold it for a moment, astonished. But as the seconds stretch, blood rushes to your head, your vocal folds feel thick and wet, and you start to wobble. Speak your surprise and then the dawning pain, feeling gravity pull at your throat and ears. Your voice should sound strained, gargly, and unsteady as you fight to stay up. End with a desperate plea to come down.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Wedding Dance for the Wrong Reasons
instruction: You're at a wedding—maybe your own, maybe your ex's, maybe your child's. You should be purely happy, but you're not. Begin by acknowledging the clash inside you: joy competing with resentment, love tangled with loss, celebration mixed with the ache of what's ending or what never was. Name aloud the obstacles to simple happiness: 'I'm angry underneath this smile. I'm grieving while I'm celebrating. Part of me wants to run.' Don't resolve the contradictions—let them coexist. As you move through the moment, allow the conflicting emotions to shift in intensity. Perhaps gratitude grows stronger even as sadness remains, or anger softens into bittersweet acceptance. The arc: from resisting the emotional complexity to embracing the beautiful, terrible messiness of it.

title: Backstage, Through the Ache
instruction: You're a 16-year-old with chronic back pain, just offstage after nailing a difficult dance solo. Your body is throbbing but you're high on triumph. You start teasing your best friend for being more nervous than you, giggling through a wince as you shift weight. Then a guy you've been crushing on walks by and says 'that was amazing'—and suddenly your teasing energy flips into embarrassed heat. Your voice goes breathy, you fumble for a response, and you hide a sharp inhale from the pain as you try to sound casual. Let the victory fade into shy, pleased awkwardness as you blush and wish you could disappear into your own skin.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Teasing (clearly present), Embarrassment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Breath Before Dawn
instruction: You are in a dim hospital room, wearing an oxygen mask that hisses with each cycle. You're an elderly person, and you have just learned that your long-time partner has passed away down the hall. At first, your voice is raw and distant, muffled by the mask, as you try to process—each word forced out against the hiss, a struggle to be heard. Midway through, you lose your train of thought, staring at a water stain on the ceiling, then find it again with a worn, weary clarity. By the end, your voice softens into a quiet, exhausted peace, as if you're speaking to the air and to them simultaneously, the mask still hissing a steady rhythm beneath your words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Attempt
instruction: You are in a dim, quiet room, lying on a couch. You've taken a heavy sedative—maybe more than intended—and your body is sinking into a fog. You need to tell someone something important, but each word takes all your strength. Start with a quiet, weary disappointment in yourself for not being able to stay present. As your thoughts slip and your voice fades, let that disappointment deepen into a crushing helplessness—you can't even finish a sentence. Speak slowly, with long pauses, your volume dropping to a whisper, trailing off as if the air itself is pulling you under. Say something like 'I wanted to... explain... why I...' and let the ending dissolve into silence.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Rage and Helplessness Over a Meal Your Child Won't Eat
instruction: You've made soup for your child who's been hospitalized, who's refusing to eat, who's slipping away despite every desperate effort. Start by describing the aroma with fierce, almost angry insistence—this is good, this is nourishing, this is love in a bowl and they HAVE to eat it. Your voice rises with frustrated passion as you talk about the ingredients you chose, the care you took, the hours spent making something, anything that might help. But as you hold the bowl, feeling its warmth while your child grows colder, your fury collapses into broken pleading. Shift from forceful determination to raw desperation to helpless grief. Let your voice crack as you realize you can't fix this with soup, with love, with anything. End barely able to speak, the comforting aroma now a mockery of your powerlessness. Move from explosive intensity to shattered vulnerability.
inspired_by: Savoring the Aroma of a Steamy Bowl of Soup on a Cold Day

title: Holding Your Dying Child and Refusing to Let God Take Them
instruction: Your child is dying in your arms and you start with pure rage—at God, at fate, at the universe. 'You can't have them. You CAN'T HAVE THEM.' Your voice is ferocious, protective, almost violent in its intensity. You're bargaining, threatening, demanding: 'Take me instead. I'm right here. TAKE ME.' But as their breathing weakens, your fury begins to splinter. Your voice cracks into something more desperate: 'Please. Please don't go. I'm not ready. You're not ready.' The rage collapses into helplessness—you can't fight what's happening and that realization breaks you completely. Your voice becomes tender even as you're screaming inside: 'It's okay, baby. Mommy's here. Daddy's here.' You're trying to be brave for them while your heart is being torn out. By the end, your fierce protectiveness transforms into the most painful gift—permission. Your voice, thick with tears, whispers: 'You can rest now. You've been so brave. It's okay to let go.' You're still holding them with desperate strength, but your words are releasing them, and the contradiction is destroying you.
inspired_by: Beginning to Accept Your Body: Compassion Breaking Through Hate

title: Confronting the Parent Who Forgot You
instruction: You're visiting your aging parent who has dementia, and today they don't recognize you at all. Begin with patient explanations of who you are, your voice gentle but strained. As they continue to look at you with polite confusion, let frustration bleed through—you need them to remember, just once more. Crescendo into desperate attempts to jog their memory, recounting specific moments only the two of you shared, your voice cracking with the injustice of being erased from their mind. Then break entirely—collapse into grief-stricken anger at the disease, at time, at the cruelty of watching someone you love look at you like a stranger. End with a whispered apology for losing control, then a tender moment where you decide to meet them where they are, introducing yourself as if for the first time, voice thick with unshed tears but choosing love over rage.
inspired_by: Waking Up from Anesthesia: Post-Surgery Babbling

title: The Injured Father's Lullaby
instruction: You're a middle-aged father with a deep, rough voice, sitting in a hospital chair after a car accident, holding your newborn for the first time despite a cracked rib and a sprained wrist. Your pain is sharp and constant — every breath sends a jolt through your side, and you have to adjust your grip carefully. But as you look at your baby's tiny face, you're flooded with a fierce, overwhelming infatuation that makes you forget the hurt for moments at a time. Your voice must start strained and tense, but as you speak to the baby in slow, swooping, high-pitched parentese, the pain softens into a raw tenderness, with occasional winces or pauses when the ache returns. Use exaggerated pitch swings, repetitive simple words, and a tempo that drags like honey, letting your breath catch naturally when the pain spikes.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Trophy and the Empty Room
instruction: You are a ten-year-old boy sitting on the edge of your bed, elbows on your knees, staring at the trophy you just won — a soccer championship. Your parents are arguing downstairs again, their voices muffled through the floor. You start by softly talking to the trophy, feeling a small, proud smile at your achievement. But as you speak, the noise from below breaks your focus — you trail off, your voice gets lower, your chest feels tight. By the end, you're not even looking at the trophy anymore; you're just trying to hold back tears, whispering to yourself that you wish they'd stop. Your voice should start with a hint of triumph, then shift to quiet, crushing helplessness — compressed, breathy, and fading.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Gratitude in the Dust
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a voice that usually floats like silk, but today you are at the edge of a firing range, your company of raw recruits behind you. The roar of the last shot still rings in your ears. You’re grateful—so deeply, surprisingly grateful—that your platoon is safe after a dangerous drill. You begin barking commands with a percussive, unamplified shout, but your words catch as awe overtakes you: the sheer power of them, the discipline. Mid-sentence, you lose the thought, blinking at the dust-smeared faces before you. Finish with a quieter, wondering tone, letting the gratitude settle into contemplation.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Contemplation (extremely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're sitting with your aging parent who is cheerfully recounting their version of your childhood—a version where they were present, supportive, and loving. But it's a fiction. You start by politely listening, nodding, playing along as you've always done. Then something inside you snaps. You interrupt with a question that seems innocent but carries decades of pain: 'Do you remember when...?' and you describe a moment they weren't there, a time you needed them desperately. Your tone begins controlled, almost gentle, giving them a chance. But as they dismiss it or rewrite it again, your voice builds—not to screaming, but to a fierce, trembling intensity. You're not asking them to remember anymore; you're demanding they finally see the truth, see you. End with your voice breaking on a simple statement of fact about who they really were, stripped of all pretense.
inspired_by: Acting Interested in a Hobby You Dont Enjoy

title: The Gratitude That Burns
instruction: You're thanking someone who saved your life—but they're also the person who destroyed it. Maybe they rescued you from one thing but caused another devastation. Maybe their help came with a price you're still paying. Start genuinely trying to express gratitude, but allow every contradictory feeling to surge up and coexist: relief and rage, love and betrayal, debt and resentment, forgiveness and fury. Don't resolve these contradictions or choose one emotion over another—let them wrestle in real time. Your voice may break, harden, soften, sharpen all within seconds. Let silences be as full as words. End having expressed something impossibly complex that cannot be reduced to simple gratitude or simple anger—something messily, humanly true.

title: The Ember's Edge
instruction: You're a child at a family campfire, wrapped in a too-big jacket, holding a stick with a marshmallow. You've been listening to adults tell ghost stories, but now you're telling one you overheard your older cousin whispering to her friend. Start with the campfire's hypnotic rhythm—your voice low, mimicking the storytellers, but then you remember the detail about the kiss on the neck, and your cheeks burn. Your voice hitches, gets breathy, unsure. You stutter on the word 'neck,' lose your place, glance at the fire, then finish too quickly, high-pitched and flustered.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Machines Stop
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed at 3 AM. The doctors say he has perhaps hours left. You've spent your whole adult life avoiding him after a childhood full of his absence and broken promises. Now he's awake, lucid, and asking you to talk to him. Begin with the protective anger and resentment that has armored you for decades—short answers, looking away, that familiar wall. But as you speak, something shifts. Maybe it's his frailty, maybe it's your own exhaustion, maybe it's realizing this truly is the last time. Let the wall crack. By the end, find yourself saying things you swore you'd never say—not forgiveness necessarily, but truth. Raw, undefended truth. Let your voice move from clipped and controlled to broken open, from bitter to unbearably tender, even as the anger never fully leaves.
inspired_by: When directing a play with extended rehearsal time and experiential methods

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are in the immediate aftermath of something physically intense—you've just finished running until your lungs burned, or you're in the grip of desire so strong it's almost painful, or you're shaking with rage after nearly getting into a physical fight, or you're doubled over with grief that's expressing itself through your body. Begin with your breath ragged, your body not yet under your control. Let the physical sensations be overwhelming at first—speak through gasps, through shaking, through the body's raw responses. But gradually, as your breathing begins to slow, discover words emerging not from your head but from your body itself. These words should feel primal, unfiltered, surprising even to you. Move from pure physical sensation to a kind of revelation that could only come through the body—truth that your thinking mind has been protecting you from. End with your body and voice completely integrated, no separation between physical and emotional truth.

title: Confronting the Architect of Your Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting the parent who taught you that your voice, your needs, your very existence was too much. Start small, almost apologetic—old patterns die hard. But something has shifted in you, and you can't stay small anymore. Your voice begins to rise as decades of swallowed words fight their way out. There's rage, yes, but underneath it is something more devastating: grief for the child you were, who learned to disappear. Let your anger crack open to reveal that tender, wounded core. Accuse them, yes—but also mourn what you never had. Your voice should tremble between fury and tears, between the power of speaking truth and the vulnerability of admitting how much you needed their love. End quietly, exhausted, with a realization: you're not asking for their permission anymore, but the cost of claiming yourself still breaks your heart.

title: The Unexpected Rumble
instruction: You're a 16-year-old guy slouched on your bed after chugging a soda, alone in your room. A deep burp builds in your chest and you try to swallow it back down, but it bursts out with a guttural, monster-like growl that catches you off guard. Start with a tight, awkward tension as you resist, then let the sound rip through you, your voice dropping into that low, vibrating fry. React with a stunned, almost disbelieving chuckle—whisper 'Whoa' to yourself, amazed at the depth of it. End with a slow, amused grin creeping in as you realize how ridiculous that was, the astonishment fading into quiet self-satisfaction.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Tall Window
instruction: You're standing at a ticket counter, craning your neck to look up at a clerk who's way taller than you. You've been waiting forever, and you're already a little on edge—your voice naturally goes lighter and tighter as you tilt your head back. Start with impatience, maybe a sharp 'Excuse me?' that comes out thinner than you intended. But as the clerk fumbles and offers a genuine apology, you feel your irritation soften into reluctant sympathy. Let your voice shift—still high, but now carrying a hint of weariness and understanding. You can glance away, shift your weight, or lose your train of thought as you speak.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing Alone After They Told You It's Over
instruction: You've just been left. Your body is a storm of contradictory physical and emotional impulses. Put on music—any music—and let your body respond without thought. Start however you start: maybe frozen, maybe explosive. Let the movement be uncontrolled: wild dancing that becomes sobbing that becomes laughing that becomes rage-filled thrashing that becomes tender swaying as if they're still there. Throw yourself around the space. Collapse. Leap. Shake. Be ugly in your grief. Be beautiful in your release. Let sounds pour out—screams, words, song fragments, animal noises, their name, curses, declarations of love. Your physical body and emotional state should feed each other in unpredictable ways. Move through the full spectrum: despair, liberation, fury, longing, relief, devastation, fierce joy at being free, desperate need to get them back. End in exhausted stillness or continued frenetic energy—whichever is true in that moment.

title: The Last Letter Home
instruction: You're a soldier writing what you know will be your final letter to your child, who you'll never meet—your partner is six months pregnant. Begin with practical instructions, trying to stay composed and fatherly, listing advice for their future. But as you write, the reality crashes over you: you won't teach them to ride a bike, won't scare away their first heartbreak, won't dance at their wedding. Your voice should fracture from controlled guidance into raw, desperate love—apologizing for not being there, begging them to know you wanted to stay, that leaving them is killing you more than any bullet could. End with a whisper of fierce protection and blessing, even as you're breaking apart. Let the love and the loss fight for space in your throat.

title: The Taste of Treachery
instruction: You are in your bedroom, having just found proof of your partner's infidelity on your phone. You're blind with rage, your hyper-feminine voice cracking as you slam a lamp against the wall. Start with guttural, percussive accusations, your breath heavy and snorting. As you confront the empty room, your fury twists into a perverse, sexually charged realization - the betrayal arouses you. Let your voice shift from raw, violent screaming to a husky, almost breathy whisper, with a crack of desire underneath the rage. Trip over a shoe mid-sentence; the interruption changes your tone.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally telling your mother or father what their absence cost you—the birthdays they missed, the moments you needed them, the child you were who learned not to need anyone. Begin measured, almost rehearsed, like you've practiced this speech for years. But as you speak, anger starts bleeding through—sharp, hot, years of buried rage. Then something shifts: the anger cracks open and underneath is the child who just wanted to be loved. Your voice breaks between fury and heartbreak, between wanting to wound them and wanting them to finally see you. End in raw vulnerability, asking the question you've been afraid to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to stay?'

title: Concept Grasping
instruction: Someone explains quantum entanglement to you, and suddenly—click—your brain reorganizes itself. Your voice shows the electrical sensation of understanding. 'Wait... so they're...' Excitement floods in. You're starting to see the universe differently. Your voice becomes almost breathless: 'My entire understanding of reality was wrong.' And then: 'That's beautiful.' The joy of understanding is physical.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father who is packing to leave the family home after your mother's funeral. Start with cold, controlled anger—you're listing facts, failures, moments he wasn't there, using his full name like a stranger. But as you catalogue his absences (your graduation, your wedding, her diagnosis), something cracks. The anger must give way to the raw, childlike need underneath: you're not accusing anymore, you're begging him to explain why you were never enough. Your voice should break from sharp accusations into vulnerable, almost confused pleading. By the end, you're asking the question you've never been able to ask: 'Did you ever love us?' Let the fury dissolve into the frightened child still waiting for an answer.

title: Laughing at the Funeral: The Joy They Would Have Wanted
instruction: You're giving a eulogy or speaking at a memorial for someone who hated sadness and insisted on joy. Start by trying to honor their wishes, telling a funny story about them with genuine laughter in your voice: 'They would be so mad at all of you for crying right now.' You're smiling, maybe even laughing, remembering something ridiculous they did. But even as you're laughing, let your voice start to fracture—the laughter becomes mixed with the beginning of tears. You keep trying to laugh, to celebrate them the way they wanted: 'God, they were so stupid sometimes, so brilliantly, wonderfully stupid.' But your voice is doing that thing where you're laughing and crying simultaneously, unable to separate joy from grief. Include a moment where you address them directly, voice split between humor and heartbreak: 'You absolute idiot, leaving us like this.' By the end, find a strange peace in the contradiction—your voice is warm, sad, full of gratitude and loss all at once: 'Thank you. For every ridiculous, beautiful moment. I'm so grateful. And I miss you so much I can barely breathe.' Let the laughter and tears coexist, showing how love holds both at the same time.
inspired_by: One Week Sober: Cravings and Determination Wrestling

title: Grateful for the Heartbreak
instruction: Someone you love deeply is leaving—not because they stopped loving you, but because staying would destroy one of you. Start by laughing softly at a memory, something beautiful you shared. Your voice is warm, full of genuine joy. 'Remember when we...' You're smiling through gathering tears. Move into gratitude—thanking them for changing your life, for teaching you what love actually feels like. Your voice is earnest, almost peaceful. But grief is bleeding through every word. 'You made me believe I was worth loving.' You're crying now, but still smiling. The contradictions are tearing you apart: you're devastated but you wouldn't undo a single moment. End with the impossible truth: 'I'm so grateful I got to love you, even though losing you is going to destroy me.' Your voice holds both complete heartbreak and complete peace, joy and devastation braided together.

title: Shattered Guardian
instruction: Your teenage child just told you they've been self-harming for months, and you didn't notice. Start with explosive parental panic—'Why didn't you tell me?'—your voice loud, desperate, cracking with terror disguised as anger. But as you see them flinch, shrink away from your intensity, everything collapses. Your rage was never anger—it was fear, helplessness, the agony of having failed to protect them from their own pain. Your voice breaks completely, volume dropping as you fall apart. 'I'm supposed to keep you safe. From everything. How did I not see?' End on your knees emotionally, begging them to help you understand, your fierce protectiveness dissolved into raw vulnerability and the unbearable weight of not knowing how to save your own child.

title: The Second Drawer
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, rough voice, alone in your cramped apartment late at night. You're shuffling through a junk drawer for a screwdriver but your hand lands on an old, cracked leather wallet from your grandfather. As you pull it out, the familiar scent of old tobacco hits you. Start by brushing it off, forcing a gruff 'what's this,' but as you open it and see his faded train pass, your voice drops and softens. Let the ache of missing him fill the space, with long pauses and a sigh. The relief comes when you realize, with a quiet, pained smile, that you can still feel him here, a warmth in your chest that cuts the sadness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Echoing Laughter
instruction: You're a mother folding laundry while your child whines about not getting a toy. Start by teasingly mimicking their voice with a nasal, exaggerated pitch—sharp and amused, enjoying the caricature. Midway, your child's face crumples into real hurt, and your own laughter falters. Let your voice catch, soften, and drop as you realize your mockery stung. Finish with a quiet, genuine apology, your amusement replaced by regret.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Dance I Can't Have
instruction: You are at a celebration—a wedding, a reunion, a victory—and across the room is someone you desire intensely but cannot approach (perhaps they're with someone else, or forbidden to you, or you fear their rejection). Your body is alive with wine, music, and electric awareness. Begin with controlled restraint, your eyes tracking them while you force casual conversation with others. As the music swells, imagine dancing with them—what would the heat of their palm feel like against your lower back, how would their hip move against yours, what would their breath smell like this close, how would their fingers feel tangled in your hair? Let these phantom sensations flood your body with such intensity that you're physically affected—breath quickening, skin flushing, hands trembling. Transform from controlled desire into reckless, almost painful longing that you must either act upon or walk away from entirely. End having made your choice, whatever it is.
inspired_by: The scene requires attraction, desire, terror, or curiosity toward someone or something the actor cannot physically touch or access

title: The Heirloom's Tick
instruction: You're an elderly person sitting hunched over a vintage wooden clock on your workbench. Your hands ache from decades of arthritis, and each turn of the wrench comes with a grunt of effort—interrupting your thoughts. At first, your voice is heavy with exhaustion, speaking slowly with pauses as you struggle with a seized bolt. But as you finally loosen it and hear the clock's first clean tick in years, a wave of awe replaces fatigue. Your voice brightens, becomes childlike with wonder, and you trail off into a hopeful whisper about passing the repaired clock to your grandchild tomorrow. Let the metallic ratcheting and your own labored breaths shape the rhythm of your speech—sometimes cutting off a word, sometimes letting a long sigh carry your thought.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Awe (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Pulling Your Child from the Wreckage
instruction: You've just reached your child in a collapsed building. Start with explosive relief—they're alive, thank God, they're alive. Your voice is fierce, protective, commanding them to stay awake, promising everything will be okay. But as you try to free them, you realize the beam is too heavy. Panic floods in. Your voice becomes frantic, desperately calling for help that isn't coming. You're trying to stay calm for them but terror is winning. Rage erupts—at yourself, at the universe, at your own helplessness. Then you hear the sirens. Your voice breaks completely, oscillating between furious determination and helpless sobbing. You're telling them stories, anything to keep them conscious, your words tumbling over each other. End with raw, primal emotion—you will move this beam or die trying. Let your voice shred with the physical strain and psychological breaking point.

title: The Gratitude Interrogation
instruction: You are thanking someone who hurt you deeply, but you must mean it genuinely—the gratitude is real. Begin with the facts: name what they did and how it damaged you, speaking with residual anger and pain. But then, imagine an alternate timeline where they never hurt you: see that version of your life in vivid detail. What did you become in that easier world? Now imagine another timeline where the hurt was even worse. And another where you hurt them instead. Let your imagination show you five or six different lives, speaking fragments of each aloud. As you move through these imagined possibilities, let your anger and pain transform into something more complex: perhaps wonder at the strange path that led to who you are now, or rage mixed with bizarre affection, or grief for all the selves you never became mixed with fierce gratitude for surviving into this particular existence. End with your thank you, but now it contains multitudes—sincerity and irony, love and hate, acceptance and resistance all at once.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After years of silence, you're finally facing the parent who abandoned you. Begin with cold, measured anger: 'Do you have any idea what you did to us?' But as you speak, the child inside you emerges—the one who waited at the window, who made excuses for empty chairs at school plays. Your voice rises with decades of stored pain: 'I needed you and you just... disappeared.' Then something breaks. The anger collapses into raw vulnerability. You find yourself asking the question you swore you'd never ask: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in the quiet devastation of someone who finally spoke the truth they've been carrying alone. Let your voice shake with both fury and desperate love.
inspired_by: Standing Your Ground When Everyone Disagrees

title: Gratitude Tastes Like Grief
instruction: Your estranged sibling has just saved your life—donated a kidney, pulled you from a fire, paid a devastating debt—and now you must thank them. But you're also furious at them for years of betrayal and absence. As you speak, let your mind genuinely wander to absurd, disconnected things: the weird smell in this room, whether you locked your car, the pattern on their shirt, a news headline you read this morning, the sensation in your throat, wondering if this counts as manipulation, the sound of your own voice, a grocery list, the exact angle of light through the window. Don't try to make these observations meaningful or poetic—let them be random static beneath your attempts to express impossible, contradictory feelings. Begin with stiff, formal gratitude. End with something breaking open—maybe forgiveness, maybe deeper rage, maybe bewildered love—that surprises even you.

title: The Late Shift
instruction: You are a bitter, sleep-deprived night-shift security guard at a shuttered school, just woken from a two-hour nap under a desk. A child has been caught stealing from the vending machine. You begin groggy, almost apologetic—rubbing your eyes, yawning, struggling to form words. Then, as you fully wake, your bitterness sharpens into malevolence. You relish the power you hold over this small, vulnerable kid. Let your voice crack with exhaustion before it drops into a low, cruel whisper. End with a smirk in your tone as you issue a threat about calling their parents.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence: Confronting What Was Never Given
instruction: You are an adult child sitting across from your aging parent, finally speaking the truth you've carried for decades. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak about the emotional absence, the times you needed them and they weren't there, your control begins to fracture. Your voice hardens with anger, then cracks with the child inside you who still wants their approval. When they try to defend themselves or dismiss your pain, something in you breaks open—not into yelling, but into raw, unguarded truth. End with exhaustion, not resolution. You've said it, but you don't feel triumphant. You feel empty, exposed, and strangely both lighter and more burdened.
inspired_by: The Cruelest Kindness: Firing a Friend

title: The Graduation Letter
instruction: You are reading a letter your deceased parent wrote to you, to be opened on your graduation day. As you read their words aloud, you simultaneously see yourself at every age—yourself as a baby in their arms, as a difficult teenager, as you are now. Begin with joy and pride in their words, your voice strong and celebratory. But as you continue, grief crashes into the happiness—they will never see who you become next. Watch yourself living out future moments without them even as you hear their voice in these words. Your reading should fracture between grateful laughter and devastating tears, between wanting to savor every word and wanting to stop because it hurts too much. End with a complex mixture of emotions in your voice: thank you and goodbye, joy and abandonment, strength and brokenness all at once.
inspired_by: When using the programming process to prepare a role

title: Flight Attendant Medical
instruction: You're the flight attendant announcing there's a medical emergency at 35,000 feet and asking for a doctor, and for once, there actually is one. You're trying to stay calm and professional: 'Is there a doctor on board? Please ring your call button.' Your voice is trained composure. But as you're helping get the passenger to the galley, you realize the passenger is having a heart attack, and the 'doctor' is a veterinarian. Your voice doesn't change publicly—it remains the calm professional—but your internal panic is now audible in the way you're breathing, the way each word comes out slightly too fast. Show the contradiction between what you're trained to sound like and what you're actually experiencing.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a lifetime of emotional absence. Start with your voice tight, almost clinical—you've rehearsed this. 'I needed you to see me,' you say, and there's decades of hurt compressing your words. As you continue, anger seeps in—your voice rising, sharper, listing specific moments they failed you. But then their face does something unexpected, and your anger fractures. Your voice softens despite yourself, becoming almost pleading: you're asking them to finally, finally acknowledge the child you were. End in a place of exhausted surrender—not forgiveness, not hatred, but the complicated middle ground where you recognize they were broken too. Let us hear love and resentment fighting for space in every breath.

title: Fever Dream of the Body
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—a high fever, the aftermath of surgery, the peak of desire, excruciating pain, or the edge of hypothermia. Your body is screaming, and in that extremity, memories flood through you unbidden: your grandmother's hands, a childhood humiliation, the taste of snow, someone who hurt you, someone you hurt. Let your voice follow the physical sensations—gasping, groaning, laughing inappropriately, breaking into fragments of song or prayer or gibberish. The words themselves matter less than the visceral truth of a mind unmoored by what the body is experiencing. Begin in coherent discomfort, then let yourself descend into a fever-state where past and present blur, where emotional and physical pain become indistinguishable. Emerge at the end into sudden, crystalline clarity—a single true thing understood in the aftermath of delirium.
inspired_by: When the actor works with dark or traumatic characters

title: The Goodbye That Becomes Hello
instruction: You're packing up a home, saying goodbye to a place or person or chapter of life. Begin heavy with loss, moving slowly, burdened by endings. Then you allow yourself to imagine a vivid fantasy of what comes next—not realistic planning, but a full-sensory dream of possibility. Maybe it's the life you'll build, the person you'll become, the adventures waiting, the freedom you'll taste. See it in precise detail: the light in your new morning, the smell of unfamiliar air, the sound of your own laughter in a different key, the texture of a new beginning under your fingertips. As this fantasy grows more real, something miraculous happens: the grief doesn't leave, but joy rises up alongside it. You're crying and laughing simultaneously. Gratitude for what was tangles with excitement for what could be. By the end, you're not just surviving the goodbye—you're transformed by the contradiction of mourning and anticipation existing in the same breath, the same heartbeat.
inspired_by: Fantasy Imaging to Elevate State Before Performance

title: The Kitchen Floor Collapse
instruction: You're a parent who just discovered your teenager's suicide note—they're not home, and you don't know where they are or if you're already too late. Begin with explosive panic, screaming their name, your voice ragged with terror as you call their phone over and over. Let the rage come—at yourself for not seeing the signs, at the world for hurting your child, at them for not telling you. Your voice should be chaotic, breaking, gasping between words as you leave frantic voicemails begging them to come home. Then shift: collapse into helpless desperation, your voice dropping to broken whispers as you tell them everything you should have said—how much you love them, how the world needs them, how you're sorry for every moment you didn't show up right. End with fierce, protective promises through tears: you'll fight beside them, you'll never let go, just please, please be alive.

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission Before Crossing the Event Horizon
instruction: You're sending your last message home before your ship crosses into a black hole—a one-way scientific mission you volunteered for. Start with excitement, awe at what you're seeing, the privilege of this discovery. But as you speak, the reality settles in: you'll never see Earth again, never hold your daughter, never feel rain. Your voice should fracture between wonder and devastating loss. You're trying to give them something beautiful to remember, trying to make your choice mean something, but grief keeps breaking through. End with a whisper of acceptance mixed with unbearable longing—you're at peace with your choice but your heart is shattering. Let silence do some of the work.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Diplomat Realizes Peace Treaty Will Require Sacrificing an Entire Species

title: The Pollen Plot
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a hyper-feminized voice, laid up in bed with a brutal allergy attack. Your eyes are watering, nose is running, and you keep having sneezing fits that interrupt your thoughts. You're on the phone with a friend, but your tone carries a slight malevolence as you describe how you subtly manipulated a neighbor's gardening schedule to maximize their exposure to a particular flowering tree you knew they were allergic to. Start with a conspiratorial, amused whisper, letting the amusement grow as you recount the details, but keep it laced with a quiet, satisfied malice. Let the physical symptoms—the sniffles, the coughs, the momentary loss of your train of thought when a sneeze hits—be the organic texture that makes the confession feel real and unsettling.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reading Terminal Diagnosis Results Alone, Calling Your Love
instruction: You've just received confirmation of a terminal diagnosis. You're alone in your car or a quiet hallway, and you're calling the person you love most. You're trying to sound okay, almost laughing at first: 'Hey, so... funny thing happened at the doctor's today.' There's a surreal lightness because your brain hasn't fully processed it yet. As you try to explain, you find yourself oddly grateful, almost peaceful: 'They said six months, maybe a year. And I just... I keep thinking about that trip we took, remember? How perfect that was?' You're smiling through tears, your voice warm with love and appreciation for your life together. But then the reality hits in waves—you won't see next Christmas, won't grow old together, won't finish the life you planned. Your voice breaks between laughter and sobbing: 'I'm not ready. God, I'm so grateful for everything we had, but I'm not ready to leave you.' End with the beautiful contradiction of complete acceptance and complete heartbreak: 'I love you so much. I'm so lucky. I'm so, so lucky... and I'm so scared.' Let your voice hold both profound peace and devastating grief simultaneously.
inspired_by: Firefighter: After Successful Rescue Returns to Station

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging father, finally saying what you've held back for thirty years. Start with that false-casual tone: 'Dad, I want to talk about when I was a kid.' But you can't keep it light. The words start pouring out—every recital he missed, every time he chose work over you, every moment you needed him and he wasn't there. Your voice rises with decades of suppressed anger: 'I needed you and you just... weren't there.' But then he says something—maybe just your name, maybe 'I know'—and your fury collapses into something more vulnerable. You realize he's an old man now, that anger won't give you back those years. End with the devastation of forgiving someone while still carrying the wound: 'I needed you then. I still need you now. And I don't know if we have enough time left.'

title: What Your Body Wants
instruction: You're confronting your father who raised you to be 'decent,' 'appropriate,' 'respectable.' He's just discovered something about your sensual life—something he finds disgusting. Start by defending yourself with reason and explanation, trying to make him understand intellectually. But as his judgment hardens, stop explaining. Instead, describe in explicit, unapologetic detail exactly what you desire, what your body craves, what makes you feel alive—using every vulgar, crude, inappropriate word he taught you never to say. Let his disgust fuel your liberation. Transform from apologetic to defiant to finally free. End not with anger, but with a fierce, sensual joy in claiming the parts of yourself he wanted you to bury.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: You are alone, touching a piece of clothing that belonged to someone you loved intensely—a former partner, perhaps, or someone who died. Begin by trying to remain detached, clinical, as if you're simply sorting belongings. As your hands move over the fabric, let a visceral sense memory overtake you—not just visual, but how their skin felt, their smell, the specific way they touched you, the sound of their breathing. Let your body respond before your mind can control it. Feel desire and grief become indistinguishable. End in a place where you're simultaneously experiencing the ghost of physical intimacy and the brutal reality of its absence. Let your breathing change, your voice crack between words, your body remember what your mind tried to forget.
inspired_by: Actor's choice repertoire feels limited; they use the same choices repeatedly

title: The Letter I'll Never Send
instruction: You are alone at night, whispering to a photograph or empty chair, speaking to someone who will never hear these words—a lost love, an estranged sibling, someone who died before you could say this. Begin with tentative, fragile words, your voice barely audible. As you confess what you've never spoken aloud, imagine in exquisite detail what it would feel like if they were here—the texture of their hair between your fingers, the warmth of their breath near your ear, the exact pressure of their arms around your back. Let these imagined sensations wash through your body, making them almost unbearably present. Transform from careful distance to complete emotional surrender, your whispers becoming more urgent, more real, until you are speaking to them as if they could actually feel your words landing on their skin.
inspired_by: The scene requires attraction, desire, terror, or curiosity toward someone or something the actor cannot physically touch or access

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside someone in the darkness, speaking barely above a whisper. Begin by confessing small fears - things you're afraid to say in daylight. Your voice should be soft, tentative, testing whether it's safe to be this honest. Gradually reveal deeper needs: your fear of being left, your hunger to be truly known, your desperate need for them to stay even when you're difficult or broken. Let your whispers become more urgent but never louder - the intimacy demands quietness even as the emotional stakes rise. Each confession should feel like you're handing them a fragile piece of yourself. End with the most vulnerable admission of all - exactly what you need from them that you've never been brave enough to ask for. The arc moves from cautious vulnerability to complete emotional nakedness, all in hushed tones.

title: The Crystal Decanter
instruction: You are a woman in her late forties, recovering from a severe arm fracture, at home alone. Your hyper-feminine, polished voice now trembles with pain and contempt for your own fragility. You've just knocked over a prized crystal decanter with your cast, shattering it. You begin by scolding yourself, voice tight with irritation—'You idiot, look what you did, that was mother's.' But as you go to pick up a piece, the sudden, raw agony of your fracture jolts through you. Your voice shifts from brittle anger into a sour, breathless sob of self-loathing and exhaustion. End with a whimpered admission: you can't even clean up your own mess, you're pathetic. Let your voice crack, fade, and lose its gloss; include the micro-distraction of a sudden flinch and sharp hiss of pain mid-sentence.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Goodbye at the Train Platform
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is leaving on a journey they will not return from - perhaps war, perhaps exile, perhaps a terminal diagnosis that requires them to leave. Start with fierce determination to be strong for them, voice steady, holding back tears: 'I'm going to be fine. We're going to be fine.' But as the moment of departure nears, that strength begins to crack. Your breath catches, your voice wavers. By the end, you've surrendered to the heartbreak, whispering through tears: 'Please don't forget me. Please.' Let the transformation from brave face to raw vulnerability happen organically, like a dam slowly breaking. Your body moves from rigid control to collapse.

title: The Room Is Spinning
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything - you got the diagnosis, or the dream job, or the betrayal, or the miracle (you choose). You're alone in your apartment, and your body is flooded with sensation. Express everything as it hits you: the physical wave in your chest, the impulse to scream or laugh or vomit, the random thought about what you had for breakfast, the urge to call someone, the awareness of your hands shaking, the sudden memory of something unrelated, the return of the overwhelming feeling, the notice that you're pacing, the shift from terror to rage to disbelief to something else entirely. Don't perform an emotion - track and voice the chaotic stream of physical sensations, impulses, thoughts, and feelings as they actually cascade through you. Begin in shocked numbness and let your unfiltered responses take you somewhere you didn't expect.

title: The Child and the Vanishing Trail
instruction: You are a mother walking through a dense, silent fog with your young daughter, who clutches your hand. The air is thick and muffled; you speak louder than necessary, uncertain if your words carry. You point out a deer that fades into the mist, your voice hushed with awe but trembling with raw affection as you explain it’s magic. Mid-sentence, a bird calls sharply, startling you, then you pause, feeling her tiny fingers squeeze yours, and your voice cracks with love as you finish. Start with a stirring wonder at the fog’s beauty, end with a fierce, overwhelming tenderness that leaves you breathless.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Stopping Your Child from Leaving Forever
instruction: Your adult child is walking out the door with a packed bag, cutting you out of their life, and you finally explode with everything you've been holding back. Start with a roar: 'Don't you DARE walk away from me!' Your voice is thunder, years of frustration and fear erupting. You list everything you sacrificed, every moment you were there, your voice cracking with rage and desperation. But then it shifts—the anger crumbles and underneath is terror. 'Please,' you whisper, 'please don't leave me alone.' You're begging now, your voice breaking into sobs. You confess your failures, your loneliness, how much you need them even though you've never been able to say it. Your fierce protectiveness collides with total helplessness. End with you collapsed against the doorframe, your voice barely audible, repeating 'I love you' like it's the only words you know, punctuated by gasping breaths as you realize love isn't enough to make them stay.

title: The Precipice
instruction: You are an older woman, deeply infatuated with your partner, in the middle of an intimate moment where they are teasing you with edging. You start light and breathy, giggling and praising them, your voice climbing with pleasure. But as they stop you repeatedly, your frustration builds. Your words become broken, pleading, your pitch rising and falling as you beg for release. Let your voice grow jagged, your breathing ragged. By the end, you are near tears, desperate, your infatuation now mixed with raw need. Speak as if your body is trembling on the edge.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Receiving News You're Cancer-Free While Your Sister Is Dying
instruction: You've just gotten the call—your cancer is gone, you're in remission. But your sister's cancer has spread; she has weeks. Begin with shock, speaking the words aloud to make them real. There's joy trying to break through—you're alive, you get to stay—but it's immediately tangled with guilt so thick you can barely breathe. Your voice lifts with relief then crashes into sobs. You're laughing and crying simultaneously because how can you celebrate when she's dying? The emotions war inside you. You try to feel grateful—you are grateful—but saying 'thank you' to the universe feels like a betrayal. Your voice becomes almost hysterical with the contradiction: elation and devastation occupying the same breath. End with a strange, broken peace—you'll live for both of you now. Your voice steadies into a promise through tears, mixing joy and sorrow into something unbearably human.
inspired_by: Crying and Trying to Explain While Gasping for Air

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Absence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent after years of their emotional unavailability. Start with careful, rehearsed calm—you've planned what you'll say: 'I need you to understand what it was like growing up invisible to you.' As you speak, old anger surfaces, your voice becoming sharper, more accusatory: 'You were there but you were never really there.' When they try to deflect or justify, something in you breaks open—your voice cracks with the pain of a child still waiting to be seen: 'I just needed you to care. That's all I ever needed.' End with a moment of devastating clarity where your voice becomes quiet, almost pitying: 'I forgive you, but I can't keep hoping you'll change.' Move from controlled confrontation through righteous anger to heartbroken acceptance and finally to a tired, sad peace.
inspired_by: Principal Meeting: When a Student is in Crisis

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're standing at your best friend's wedding reception, about to give a toast. You're genuinely happy for them—they've found someone wonderful, and you love seeing them this joyful. But you're also quietly devastated because you've been in love with them for years, and this is the moment that makes it finally, irrevocably over. Begin the toast with warmth and humor, sharing a cherished memory, making everyone laugh. Let your genuine love for your friend shine through—this isn't fake. But as you speak, let the other emotion bleed through in small ways: a pause that lasts too long, a brightness in your voice that's almost brittle, a moment where you have to steady yourself. Move between celebrating their happiness (real) and feeling your own heart break (also real). End with a genuine blessing for their future, but one that costs you everything to say. Your voice should carry both absolute love and absolute loss, neither diminishing the other.

title: The Inheritance of Everything and Nothing
instruction: You are receiving something you've desperately wanted your entire life—an inheritance, a title, a position, a freedom, a long-awaited reunion—but it comes at the exact moment you lose something equally precious, or it comes in a form that makes it worthless, or from the hands of someone whose love you've lost. Begin feeling the weight and texture of what you're receiving: a heavy document with wax seals, a piece of jewelry, a key to a door, a sum of money in coins that clink. Let the formality and ritual of your historical moment shape how you first respond—the expected words, the required gratitude, the proper physical bearing. Then let the contradiction fully land: the grief inside the gift, the anger inside the gratitude, the bitterness inside the sweetness. Build from performing the role your era demands toward speaking what's actually true. End having expressed both emotions simultaneously in a way that breaks the rules of your time—laughing and weeping at once, blessing and cursing in the same breath, holding what you've gained while naming what it cost.

title: The Last Rose
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe eight or nine, standing in a fierce gale on a hill. Your mother has just told you that your little sister, who is sick and weak, is getting all the attention and the last surviving rose from the garden — the one you wanted. Shout against the wind to your mother's back as she walks away. Start with your voice high and thin, the wind snatching your words, a jealous whine fighting to be heard. Let a shift happen as the cold air hits your throat and you realize you sound pathetic; your envy hardens into something raw and bitter, but you still have to raise your voice as the wind howls, turning away to breathe, then facing it again to spit out the last, hateful words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Sweetest Name You Ever Forgot
instruction: Your grandmother is telling you - again - about the great love of her life before your grandfather, the one who died in the war. She's told you a hundred times. You've pretended to remember the name to make her happy. Today, she's lucid and laughing, saying: 'You always loved this story! What was his name? You remember!' You start playful, matching her joy: 'Oh, Grandma...' But you realize you genuinely can't remember, and this might be her last lucid day. Your voice fills with loving frustration: 'I'm the worst grandchild.' She's laughing, not hurt, and somehow that makes it better and worse. You end almost laughing through tears: 'Tell me again. I want to remember this time. I really want to remember.' Let gratitude and grief dance together - she's giving you the gift of forgetting alongside her.

title: Honey and Vinegar at 3 AM
instruction: You're making a childhood comfort remedy in the middle of the night for someone you love who's beside you, unable to sleep, maybe unable to go on. Your voice is barely above a whisper—the house is dark, the world is quiet, and this moment is sacred and fragile. Start with gentle tenderness, each ingredient a soft promise: 'This is what my grandmother made when the world felt too heavy.' Let your voice catch on memories, on the weight of caring for someone whose pain you can't fix. There's grief woven into every instruction, love that aches because you're so helpless. As you finish, let silence hold space. Your final words are almost inaudible, thick with emotion you're trying not to break under. This isn't about healing—it's about being present in someone's darkest hour, and that beauty breaks your heart.

title: The Last Canvas Before the Dark
instruction: You are a painter losing your sight to a degenerative disease, describing your final painting to your adult child who never understood your art until now. Begin with fierce determination to make them see what you've seen, what you've loved, the colors that have been your whole world. As you speak, feel the grief rising—not just for losing your vision, but for all the years they dismissed what mattered most to you. Let your voice crack as you realize this is goodbye to the only language you truly spoke. End in a whisper, touching their face, finally finding connection in the darkness. Your tone should move from passionate and urgent to broken and tender, like you're teaching someone to see beauty for the first time while simultaneously losing it forever.

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You've been running for three miles in the rain, trying to outrun your rage after discovering a betrayal—your best friend's deception, your partner's infidelity, a professional humiliation. Your body is exhausted, soaked, shaking. Begin with the physical sensations: burning lungs, pounding heart, rain on your face mixing with tears or sweat. Let the rage move through your body—it might come out as screams, gasping sobs, or guttural sounds that aren't quite words. But as your body reaches its limit, as you finally stop and bend over gasping, let something underneath the rage emerge. Perhaps it's devastation, betrayal, or a grief so profound it changes the quality of your breathing entirely. End with your body in collapse, but your emotional state transformed into something quieter and more true than the rage you started with.
inspired_by: Actor is not connected to inner self and cannot make technique work

title: Washing Away the Buzz
instruction: You're a young man, pleasantly tipsy at your own small apartment party, now washing dishes as the last guest leaves. The clinking glass and steady water form a comforting white noise as you murmur to yourself—half to the memory of a friend you held close, half to the quiet. Start with soft, affectionate warmth for the night, but let that gentle haze sour into lonely clarity as the water grows louder, your movements slow, and your voice thickens with the realized emptiness.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Door You Slammed Fifteen Times
instruction: You're pacing a small room, working up the courage to leave or to stay—talking to yourself or to the person who isn't there. Your body is ahead of your words: fists clenched, jaw tight, breath ragged. Begin in pure physical rage, letting your voice match your body's fury. But let your actual hands, your actual breath, show you something else underneath the anger. Maybe you touch something of theirs and your voice suddenly cracks. Maybe your legs simply give out. Don't perform a breakdown—let your physical sensations reveal what's really happening. End with your body showing you an emotion you didn't know was there: desperate longing, or exhaustion so complete it becomes tender.
inspired_by: When an actor has been told they are 'not that kind of actor' when invited to do emotional preparation

title: The Weight of Your Sleeping Face
instruction: You're lying beside your partner in the middle of the night, and they're sleeping peacefully, unaware. You begin whispering things you can't say when they're awake—how much you love them, how terrified you are of losing them, how you sometimes watch them breathe just to prove they're still here. Your voice is barely audible, tender, catching on words like 'always' and 'forever.' But underneath is the knowledge that everything ends, that this peace is temporary. 'I memorize you,' you whisper, your throat tightening. 'Every detail. Just in case.' The tears come silently. Your voice doesn't rise—it softens even more, until the final words are just breath: 'Please don't leave me.' It's not a request. It's the most honest thing you've ever said.

title: Stumbling Into a Question
instruction: You’re at a bar after last call, completely drunk. You start by angrily slamming your glass down, spilling beer, and slurring about a friend who ditched you—impatient, irritable, muttering insults. But as you stare at the spilled liquid, your voice wobbles, your head sways, and you shift into a slower, more intense contemplation: trying to figure out why you even cared. Let your volume drop and rise unpredictably, lose your train of thought, then find it again, ending on a quiet, almost childlike question you ask yourself before trailing off.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Goodbye at the Airport Terminal: A One-Way Ticket
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your adult child who's leaving for a humanitarian mission in a war zone—they may never come back. Begin with forced brightness, voice almost too cheerful: 'I'm so proud of you.' But as you speak, the facade cracks. Your voice trembles as you try to memorize their face. Move through desperate attempts to stay strong ('You'll be careful, won't you?'), then let the dam break—voice raw and breaking: 'I can't lose you.' Finally, find a place of devastated acceptance, voice quieter now, almost a whisper filled with fierce love: 'Go. Save lives. I'll be here.' Let the final words carry both your terror and your pride, your voice barely holding together as you release them.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Leaving a Good Relationship

title: The Accusation That Breaks
instruction: You're confronting your adult child about a betrayal that's been eating at you for months. You came here to rage, to make them understand your pain, to finally let loose the fury you've been building. Start with that righteous anger—but somewhere in the confrontation, your body betrays you. Maybe your voice cracks not with anger but with fear that you're losing them. Maybe mid-accusation, you hear yourself sounding like your own parent and it horrifies you. Maybe the rage collapses into desperate pleading you never intended. Don't plan where the break happens—let your system decide when the anger is no longer sustainable. By the end, you're in territory you didn't mean to enter: vulnerable, raw, perhaps even apologizing for things you hadn't realized you'd done. The goal is NOT to perform an 'angry scene that becomes sad'—it's to experience your anger genuinely failing you.

title: Midnight Inventory
instruction: It's 3 AM and you can't sleep. You're lying in the dark next to someone you love—a partner, spouse, or closest friend—who is asleep. In the quietest whisper, almost to yourself, you begin confessing how broken you used to be when you met them. Your voice is barely audible, fragile, admitting shameful things about your past self—the lies you told, the ways you hurt people, how lost you were. But then, still whispering, you start describing the small, specific ways you're different now. How you've learned to tell the truth, to stay instead of running, to let yourself be loved. Your whisper becomes slightly stronger, filled with wonder at your own transformation. End with a whispered thank you to their sleeping form, your voice thick with emotion but no longer ashamed—instead, tender and almost disbelieving at the person you've managed to become. Move from shame-soaked confession to hushed, grateful amazement.

title: Threshold Confession
instruction: You're confronting your father late at night, and you're exhausted—bone-deep tired from years of silence. Start angry, pacing, voice sharp with accusations about his absence, his failures, his emotional unavailability. But as you speak, allow exhaustion to overtake you. Your body grows heavier, your movements slower, until you're no longer pacing but sinking—into a chair, onto the floor. As the physical heaviness increases, let your anger dissolve into something else: not forgiveness exactly, but a kind of dreamlike honesty. Half-awake with fatigue, you begin to speak truths you've never accessed before—maybe that you understand him now, maybe that you're terrified of becoming him, maybe both. Your voice becomes slower, quieter, almost hypnotic. End in a place between consciousness and sleep, where the confrontation transforms into something like communion, vulnerability replacing rage.

title: Hostage Reading a Ransom Note on Camera
instruction: You're reading words someone else wrote, held at the edge of a frame. Your voice is flat, compliant, reading the demands mechanically. But between the lines, try to communicate — emphasis on specific words that signal your location, a deliberate blink pattern (audible pause pattern). Your captor's voice (also you) interrupts to correct your reading. The tension between compliance and resistance should be audible. Include the moment the camera turns off and you break down.

title: The Watch That Survived
instruction: You're holding your grandfather's watch as he takes his final breaths. Begin by describing the watch—its weight, the scratch on the crystal, the faint ticking. Let your senses fully inhabit this object: the warmth of the metal, the smell of old leather, even the taste of salt from your own tears. As you speak, the watch begins to whisper its history to you—the day he bought it, the moments it witnessed, the heartbeats it counted. Let the watch's memories merge with your own grief. Start with careful, controlled observation of the object, but as its story unfolds, allow your emotional dam to break. By the end, you're not just holding a watch—you're holding every moment you'll never have again. Let the transformation move from intellectual curiosity about an object to devastating, embodied loss.

title: The Rusted Anchor
instruction: You are an elderly ex-navy captain, alone in the ocean after your boat sank. You're treading water, your arms heavy as lead, every breath a choked gasp as saltwater slaps your face. You see a rescue helicopter circling far away, but you know they'll never spot you. Start by feeling a weary, malevolent pride — you've outlived every man who crossed you, and you're damned if you'll beg for help. Let your voice crack and sputter as you speak to the empty sky, bragging about your stubbornness. As you go on, your voice weakens, the water bobs over your mouth, and that pride melts into a quiet, bitter interest in what happens next — maybe a flicker of dark humor. End with a half-gasp, half-laugh as you realize you don't care if they find you.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Interest (slightly present), Pride (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: You've just learned that someone you swore to protect was hurt while you were powerless to stop it. Erupt with fury—at yourself, at the universe, at whoever caused this pain—but let that rage collapse mid-sentence into something more devastating: your own helplessness and fear. Your voice should start strong, almost violent in its intensity, sharp and accusatory, but then break apart completely into raw terror and self-blame. Swing between wanting to destroy something and wanting to dissolve into nothing. End with a fierce, desperate promise whispered through tears—a vow you have no idea if you can keep, but you'll die trying. Let your voice be ragged, uncontrolled, utterly exposed.

title: The Last Campaign
instruction: You are an elderly person, gender neutral in voice, hunched over a gaming keyboard late at night. You've just lost a crucial match after hours of play, and the disappointment is a hollow weight in your chest. As you click through the post-game menu, a voice on voice chat — a flirtatious stranger — distracts you. Your voice shifts from weary, flat disappointment to a huskier, more intrigued tone. Let the mechanical clicks and chair squeaks punctuate your words; let your breath catch as you imagine their face. Start with a sigh of defeat, end with a low, playful invitation to try again tomorrow.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Voice Message Before the Mission
instruction: You're recording a voice message for your child before embarking on a one-way space mission to establish the first colony on a distant planet. Begin speaking with forced enthusiasm about the adventure, the honor, the future you're building for them. But as you continue, your voice cracks. You start confessing what you'll miss — their laughter, birthdays, watching them grow up. End with trying to recapture that brave, pioneering tone, but you can't quite manage it anymore. Your voice should shift from performed courage to raw grief to a trembling attempt at strength that barely holds. Let the pauses speak as much as the words.

title: Baby Monitor Confession
instruction: You're standing over your sleeping baby's crib, talking softly into the darkness — knowing the baby monitor is on and your partner can hear everything in the next room. Confess something to the sleeping child that you can't say directly to your partner. The whispered intimacy of speaking to an infant (high pitch, sing-song) mixed with adult emotional weight. Include the moment you realize the monitor light is green — your partner heard everything. The silence.

title: Midnight Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love deeply, and you can't sleep because you're carrying a secret that's destroying you both. In the darkness, barely above a whisper, you begin to confess something that will change everything—an infidelity, a terrible diagnosis, a lie you've been living, a truth about yourself you've hidden. Your voice is so quiet it's almost just breath. There's tenderness in how you say their name, how you reach for them even as you speak words that might push them away forever. Your throat keeps closing up. Long pauses where you can't continue. The vulnerability is excruciating—you're not asking for forgiveness, you're just finally letting them see all of you, even the broken parts. Let us hear the love and the devastation existing in the same breath, the way your voice trembles with both intimacy and terror.

title: What We Whisper in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, whispering a truth you've never told anyone—maybe about who you really are, what you really want, a terrible thing you did, or a beautiful dream you're terrified to claim. Begin with your voice barely audible, words catching in your throat, starting and stopping, apologizing for even speaking. Let the darkness give you permission to be more honest with each sentence. Feel how terrifying and liberating it is to be truly seen. Your whisper should grow slightly steadier—not loud, but more rooted in your own truth. End with a fragile but genuine sense of being held exactly as you are, imperfections and all, and the quiet revelation that vulnerability isn't weakness but the rarest form of courage.
inspired_by: Actor feels inadequate to meet a specific character or scene obligation

title: The Gratitude That Breaks You
instruction: You're thanking someone—a friend, a mentor, a stranger—who saved your life in some profound way, but this is also goodbye because they're leaving or dying or you're moving into a chapter where they can't follow. Your voice starts bright with genuine joy and gratitude, almost laughing as you recount what they did for you, how they changed everything. But underneath the lightness, grief is rising. As you continue, your laughter becomes watery; your voice keeps catching. You're trying to stay in the gratitude, to give them this gift of knowing what they meant, but the loss keeps breaking through. Your tone oscillates—warm appreciation fracturing into sorrow, then back to joy, then cracking again. You might actually laugh and cry in the same breath, your voice doing both at once.
