By the end, you've found a strange, beautiful place where both emotions coexist fully: your voice carries profound thankfulness and devastating loss simultaneously, speaking with the clarity of someone who understands that the deepest gratitude often comes with the deepest grief. Your final words are gentle, complete—both a celebration of what they gave you and an acknowledgment that this gift is now a memory you'll carry alone.

title: What I've Never Seen in You
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of distance. But instead of launching into your prepared grievances, you find yourself actually looking at him—really looking—for perhaps the first time in decades. Notice how he holds his shoulders, the lines around his eyes, the way his hands move when he's defensive. Speak your truth, but let it arise from genuinely observing who he actually is right now, not who you've held him as in your mind. Begin with sharp anger, but as you truly see him—the aging, the vulnerability, the human being before you—let your words transform. Your rage should gradually crack open into something more complicated: recognition, perhaps even unwanted compassion, mixed with your still-legitimate pain.

title: Telling Your Best Friend You're Grateful for Them While Holding Their Terminal Diagnosis
instruction: You're sitting with your best friend who just told you they have months, maybe weeks. They've asked you not to be sad, to just talk like normal. You're trying—you're making jokes, reminiscing about the stupid things you've done together. But you're also crying, and laughing while crying, because every memory is now precious and painful. Your voice keeps breaking into this strange mixture of joy and devastation. You're thanking them for being there, but you're also furious at the universe. You're telling them about all the future plans you won't get to have, and somehow you're both laughing at the absurdity of it. The emotion is chaotic: pure love mixed with unbearable loss, gratitude that makes your chest ache, laughter that dissolves into sobs. End with something simple and true, like 'I don't know how to be me without you,' said with both tears and a broken smile.
inspired_by: Comedian Having a Genuine Breakdown During Set

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You've just received news that someone difficult—a parent who hurt you, an ex who betrayed you, a friend who abandoned you—has died and left you something meaningful: their home, their journal, their life's work. You're speaking to their photograph or an empty room. Start with one dominant feeling: anger, or relief, or numbness. But let the contradictions flood in between your sentences: grief mixing with rage, gratitude tangling with resentment, love competing with the desire to destroy what they left you. Don't decide in advance which emotions to perform—let them genuinely collide, interrupt each other, transform mid-sentence as conflicting truths surface. By the end, you should have traveled through multiple emotional territories, arriving somewhere unexpected and deeply human—perhaps forgiveness laced with anger, or grief shot through with inappropriate joy, or love that refuses to be simple.

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're making breakfast for your partner who ships out to a war zone in three hours, knowing there's a real chance they won't come back. You're trying desperately to be strong, cheerful, supportive—talking about mundane things like whether they packed enough socks, reminding them to write, promising everything will be fine when they return. But with every word, your voice should betray the terror underneath. Start with forced brightness that slowly cracks, letting silences grow heavier. By the end, let one simple phrase—maybe 'I'll be right here waiting'—break you completely. Your love and your fear must be equally present, fighting for control of every breath.
inspired_by: Acting Enthusiastic About Plans Youd Rather Avoid

title: The Last Word
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone on your porch, facing a young man who has come to intimidate you into selling your land. Your voice drops low, heavy and slow—a tired growl that shows your age and the weight of helplessness. But as you speak, you feel your mind wander to memories of your late wife and the life you built here. Let that contemplation creep in, softening your tone, turning the growl into a thoughtful murmur. Start with a defensive, defeated rumble, then shift into a quiet, reflective recollection that leaves you settled, not broken.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Body's Override
instruction: You're in the throes of intense physical sensation—perhaps the peak of passion with a lover, the burning exhaustion of pushing your body to its limit, or the searing pain of an injury. You had planned what you would say in this moment, imagined how you would express yourself, perhaps even rehearsed declarations of love or boundaries you meant to set. But your body refuses to follow your script. Begin with the attempt to maintain control and say what you intended, but let physical sensation overwhelm and rewrite your responses. Your words become raw, unfiltered, stripped of pretense by the intensity of what your body is experiencing. End having expressed something your intellect never planned but your body absolutely needed to release—whether it's a truth, a plea, a surrender, or a revelation that only physical intensity could unlock.

title: The Taste of Truth
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up—the same kitchen where he made breakfast every Sunday. You're here to tell him you know the truth about something he's hidden for years (his affair, his drinking, his failure, his lie—you choose). Start by grounding yourself in the specific sensory memories of this room: the exact smell of coffee he always made, the feel of the counter's edge under your palms, the particular creak of the floorboards, the sound of the refrigerator humming. These familiar sensations give you false comfort at first, almost making you want to stay silent. But as you speak, really taste the words in your mouth—bitter, metallic, sharp. Notice how your voice sounds different when telling the truth versus keeping the peace. Let the sensory specificity fuel your courage. By the end, the room should feel completely different—transformed by honesty—even though nothing physical has changed.

title: Petting a Soft, Fluffy Cat
instruction: Run your fingers gently over the cats fur, feeling the soft, warm fluff beneath your hands. Describe the sensation as each pet is met with a quiet purr, the gentle rise and fall of their tiny breaths. Speak with a tone of quiet affection, as if each stroke brings you a little closer to peace, a tiny moment of shared calm with this contented creature.

title: The Hospital Room Truth
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. For your whole life, you've maintained a careful, polite distance—never saying what you really felt, always performing the role of the dutiful child. Now there's no time left for pretense. Begin with the familiar awkwardness and emotional guardedness you've always used with him. Let yourself feel the actual nervousness of dropping that mask. Then speak from the raw, unfiltered place: tell him one true thing you've never said—whether it's 'I needed you and you weren't there,' or 'I forgive you,' or 'I'm terrified to lose you.' Let your voice shake if it wants to. Let silences happen. Move from performative composure to devastating honesty. End in whatever emotional place that honesty takes you—whether that's grief, relief, anger, or unexpected peace.

title: Holding Your Dying Child
instruction: Your child is dying in your arms and there's nothing more the doctors can do. You're telling them a story - their favorite one - and your voice starts strong because you need to be strong for them. But you can feel them slipping away. Your voice begins to shake, words coming faster, desperate, as if keeping them distracted will keep them alive. The story dissolves into fierce, futile promises - 'We'll go to the beach tomorrow, I promise, just hold on' - your voice climbing, frantic, passionate with denial. Then their breathing changes and reality crashes in. Your voice breaks completely, becomes a raw howl of grief and helpless rage. You're begging them not to go, your words collapsing into primal sounds. End with silence, then the smallest, most broken whisper: 'I've got you. I've got you.' Tender and shattered, holding them as they leave.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral: Reading Your Goodbye Letter with Broken Joy
instruction: You've recorded a message to be played at your memorial, and you're reading it now, knowing these are your final words to everyone you love. But you've decided to make them laugh, to give them something light to remember, even as your heart is shattering. Begin with deliberately cheerful humor, almost too bright: 'So! I guess you're all dressed in black, crying into terrible coffee...' You make jokes, laugh at your own bits, but the laughter keeps catching, becoming real grief that you quickly cover with another joke. 'Don't be sad, seriously. I mean, be sad, but not like, sad sad. You know?' Your voice wavers between genuine warmth, forced cheer, and barely contained devastation. Moments where your humor completely fails and truth breaks through: 'God, I'm going to miss you all so much,' before you catch yourself and try to lighten it again. End with a contradictory emotional space—laughing and crying simultaneously, grateful and heartbroken, at peace and utterly destroyed. 'Thank you for loving me. That's the whole thing. Just... thank you.' Let joy and grief exist in the same breath, natural and impossible and deeply human.
inspired_by: Caught in Machinery: Fighting Physical Panic While Thinking

title: The Breaking Point at the Dinner Table
instruction: You're screaming at someone you love - your partner, your best friend, your sibling - because they just made another comment about your body, your food, your choices. Start with explosive rage, your voice cracking with the fury of years of their 'helpful' observations and 'concerned' looks. Let that anger shatter into something more desperate - you're not just angry, you're terrified and exhausted from trying to be perfect enough to earn their approval. Your voice should swing wildly between fierce protectiveness of yourself and helpless pleading for them to just stop, to just love you without conditions. End with your rage collapsing into broken sobs as you admit the devastating truth: 'I'm so tired of shrinking myself for you.' Let the words come out raw and uncontrolled.

title: The Body Keeps Speaking
instruction: You've just finished something physically demanding—a performance, a fight, passionate lovemaking, a long run in the rain—and your body is electric, shaking, alive. As you catch your breath, words start pouring out, addressed to everyone who ever called you too much, too intense, too hungry, too alive. Let your physical state fuel the emotional release. Your voice can shake, surge, break—let your body's exhaustion and exhilaration drive the words. Begin with the visceral sensation of finally inhabiting yourself fully, and build to a fierce declaration: this body, this hunger, this intensity is yours and you will never apologize for it again. End in breathless, defiant joy—claiming every ounce of your aliveness.
inspired_by: Taking Your Due and Standing Up for Yourself

title: Packing Their Clothes
instruction: You are packing up the belongings of someone who is gone—maybe they died, maybe they left you, maybe they're in prison, maybe they're lost to addiction. You're holding their clothes, objects they touched every day. Begin by noticing the competing impulses: part of you wants to rush through this, part of you wants to smell every shirt, part of you is angry at having to do this at all. Don't resolve these contradictions—let them coexist. Feel the texture of the fabric in your hands. Notice when a memory ambushes you, when irritation at their messiness surfaces even now, when love and resentment crash into each other. Speak to them as if they can hear you, but let what you say be messy and contradictory: 'I hate you for leaving' in one breath, 'I miss how you laughed' in the next, 'You always left your socks everywhere' mixed with 'I'd give anything to find your socks on the floor again.' End in a completely different emotional space—maybe you began with angry efficiency and end curled around their sweater, or began with gentle nostalgia and end with fierce liberation.

title: The Last Words That Won't Come
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed. You have so much to say—thank you, I'm sorry, I love you, I forgive you—but every time you try to speak, the words feel hollow and rehearsed. Start by letting sounds come out instead of words: hums, sighs, broken attempts at speech. Let your body and breath carry what words can't. As you continue, allow fragments of real words to emerge organically from these sounds when they feel genuinely connected to what's moving through you. Begin with frustration at your own inability to speak, and journey toward a place where your presence and sounds become enough—where you realize she understands without the perfect words. End in a place of unexpected peace, where silence and sound together say everything.
inspired_by: Actor feels blocked by words — text feels intellectual rather than felt

title: The Last Phone Call
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love who is in hospice care across the country, and you know this is likely your final conversation. As you speak, allow memories of different beloved people from your life—a grandparent who taught you resilience, a friend who made you laugh through tears, a mentor who believed in you—to flood your awareness simultaneously. Begin the call trying to stay cheerful and strong, but as the weight of all these precious relationships and their fleeting nature hits you, let your voice crack and transform. End by finding a quiet, fierce gratitude mixed with unbearable grief. Let the person hear both your breaking heart and your profound love.
inspired_by: No single person in the actor's life matches all the obligation requirements for a character relationship

title: The Eruption
instruction: You are confronting your adult child/parent about a devastating betrayal they've kept hidden for years—something that shattered your trust and changed everything. Begin in cold, controlled fury: your jaw is tight, your words are clipped, you're trying to maintain composure. But you can't hold it. Let your body shake with the rage you've been suppressing. Unleash everything—scream, pace, let your voice crack and soar and break. Use your whole body: pound surfaces, gesture wildly, let the physical release unlock the emotional torrent. Don't perform anger—let real frustration at being silenced, dismissed, or betrayed in your own life fuel this moment. Then, after the storm passes, find yourself unexpectedly crying—not from anger anymore, but from exhausted love. End in a whisper: 'I just needed you to tell me the truth.'

title: Throne of the Stage
instruction: You are addressing a packed auditorium from behind a podium, your voice amplified by the PA system. Begin with immense pride—you have just been honored, and you stand tall, savoring the applause as you speak. The first few lines are bold, resonant, with controlled energy and dramatic pauses. Then, you spot someone you know in the front row—an old friend who always kept you humble. Your tone shifts to a teasing, playful challenge, crackling with warmth and mischief. Let yourself adjust the mic, laugh briefly, or glance down at your notes as you lose the thread for a half-second before finding it again. The pride at the start transforms into a sly, affectionate ribbing by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: In the intimate darkness of a bedroom, whisper a confession to someone lying beside you—something you've carried alone and believed would destroy what you have together. Start with your voice barely audible, tentative, testing whether you can even form the words. As you confess, let your vulnerability deepen; let pauses hang in the air where you almost stop, where shame nearly silences you. Feel how speaking the truth both terrifies and liberates you. By the end, your whisper should carry a different quality—no longer the whisper of fear but of desperate hope, of someone who has finally laid down a crushing burden and is waiting to see if they'll be left alone with it. Move from suffocating secret-keeping to fragile, naked honesty.

title: The Graduation Letter
instruction: Read a letter aloud to your child on their graduation day—but they died six months ago, and you're reading it in their empty room. Begin with determined brightness, trying to honor who they were by celebrating their achievements with joy, noticing every detail of their space: posters, the specific smell of their clothes, objects they touched. Let your awareness of these sensory details create a strange dual state: genuine pride and happiness for what they accomplished exists simultaneously with crushing grief that they're not here. Your voice should oscillate between celebration and fracture, unable to maintain either pure joy or pure sorrow. Notice how your body responds to different objects—when you touch their jacket, smell their pillow, see their handwriting. These sensory moments should trigger emotional shifts mid-sentence. End with a paradox: expressing both devastating gratitude that they existed and impossible anger that they're gone, your voice embodying both emotions fully and genuinely at once, neither canceling the other.

title: Last Priest Faith Dying
instruction: You're delivering a final sermon to a nearly-empty church. Your voice carries the weight of a lifetime of faith, but each word feels heavier than the last. You're preaching about grace while actively losing your belief mid-speech. You catch yourself—'As I've always taught... but maybe I was wrong'—and you keep going. Your voice becomes more honest the less you believe. You address God directly, and your voice becomes intimate, almost angry: 'Are you listening?' The final words of your sermon are the most genuine thing you've ever said from that pulpit, and they're a question disguised as faith.

title: The Intervention You Should Have Had Years Ago
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your entire life. Begin controlled, rehearsed—you've practiced this speech a thousand times. But as you speak, old wounds crack open. Your voice breaks between anger at what they took from you and the little child inside still desperate for their love. Let fury and longing collide. You want them to hurt like you hurt, but you also want them to finally see you, hold you, tell you it wasn't your fault. Oscillate between shouting accusations and almost whispering the vulnerable truths: 'I needed you. I was just a kid. Why wasn't I enough?' End either in exhausted silence or a raw, quiet plea for acknowledgment.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your adult child's hospital bed. They've asked you to sign the DNR—Do Not Resuscitate. You came in ready to be strong, to say 'I understand, I respect your choice' in that steady parental voice. But as you hold the pen, your hand is shaking. You start with those rehearsed words of support, but then something breaks. 'I'm not ready,' you whisper. 'I know that's selfish. I know this isn't about me.' Your voice cracks between trying to be the parent they need—supportive, respectful—and the raw truth that you want to beg them to keep fighting. End in a place of profound surrender: you sign the paper, and through tears, you tell them the most important thing—that letting them go is the hardest and most loving thing you've ever done.

title: The Last Permission: A Parent Lets Their Child Go
instruction: You're sitting beside your adult child's hospital bed. They've chosen to stop treatment—it's their decision, and you must respect it. Begin by trying to sound supportive, almost too bright, as you tell them it's okay, you understand. But as you speak, your voice starts fracturing. You're giving them permission to leave you, releasing them from the burden of fighting for your sake. The words 'I love you' and 'it's okay to rest' must carry both your desperate wish for them to stay and your fiercer love that wants to free them from suffering. End in a whisper that's both blessing and breaking—you're the parent, so you stay strong, but your voice reveals the howling grief underneath. This isn't theatrical crying; it's the sound of loving someone enough to let them go.
inspired_by: Professional: Hospital Administrator Denies Treatment a Patient Can't Afford

title: Sour Seeds in the Storm
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing in a downpour, clutching a letter that just told you your younger sister got the family heirloom you were promised. Rain pounds your hair, thunder cracks overhead, and you're soaked, voice raised against the noise. Start with a bitter, envious mutter about her 'luck'—sharp, sour, each word spat against the weather. As the storm intensifies, let the jealousy crack into raw disappointment; your voice wavers, water drips from your chin, and you lose your train of thought when lightning flashes. End with a quiet, broken admission that you just wanted to be chosen once—the rain softening as your envy fades into weary sorrow.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (clearly present), Disappointment (clearly present), Sourness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Phone Call: When Safety Shatters
instruction: You receive a call that someone you love is in immediate danger—trapped, threatened, or hurt—and you're powerless to reach them. Start with sharp, commanding authority: giving instructions, staying calm, being their anchor. But as the reality of your helplessness sets in, that control begins to fracture. Your voice should escalate from steady to urgent to desperate—not shouting, but that fierce, primal intensity of someone trying to protect with words alone when action is impossible. Then, in an instant, let it break completely into raw fear and pleading. End in a transformed place: a whispered prayer, promise, or declaration of love, your voice shaking but somehow finding steel again. Move from controlled strength to escalating desperation to shattered vulnerability to fierce, trembling love.

title: The Last Shore
instruction: You are sitting at the bedside of someone you've loved your entire life—they have perhaps hours left. Begin in a state of forced composure, trying to be strong for them. As you speak your goodbye, allow a specific recurring memory to surface: a moment by water, a near-accident, a time when you almost lost them before. Let this memory flood through all your senses—the temperature of the air, the smell of the place, the exact quality of light, the sounds around you. Don't explain the memory; let it wash over you as you hold their hand. Allow the fear from that past moment to merge with your present grief. By the end, you are no longer trying to be strong—you are simply present with them, your voice breaking not from sadness alone but from the full weight of every moment you've ever feared losing them.

title: Breathing Room
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping lover after a miscarriage, whispering about the nursery you'd started painting yesterday. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, as if speaking any louder might shatter what's left. Describe the color you chose (something hopeful, something soft), the way you'd imagined light coming through the window. Let your breath catch on certain words. Your voice should be full of such tenderness it aches—talking about tiny socks, a mobile you'd ordered, a name you'd almost agreed on. Then shift to present tense: 'I'm watching you sleep and I don't know how to tell you I'm grateful we're still here, even as I'm mourning who isn't.' End in silence, just breathing. Let the audience hear love and loss existing in the same breath.

title: The Last Words You Never Said
instruction: Your father is dying in the hospital bed before you. You have 90 seconds before he loses consciousness forever. Start by simply being present with what you actually feel right now—whatever mess of emotions exists in your body at this moment. Don't perform grief or love; just notice what's真ly there: the knot in your stomach, the tightness in your throat, the unexpected anger or numbness or tenderness. From that truthful starting place, speak to him. Let the words come from what you're genuinely feeling, not what you think you should feel. Your emotion will shift as you speak—perhaps from numbness to fury to devastating tenderness—but every moment must come from what's actually alive in you, not what you imagine 'good grief' looks like.
inspired_by: Actor is preparing for a scene but not starting from real BEING — instead manufacturing a performance state

title: Reunion on a Rainy Platform: Saying Hello and Goodbye Simultaneously
instruction: After twenty years apart, you're meeting your first love at a train station. They're terminally ill and wanted to see you one last time. You have thirty minutes before their train leaves. Start with nervous laughter—the absurdity of gray hair, of how you both got old. Nostalgia floods you; your voice warms with joy remembering who you were together. But reality crashes in: you're looking at someone dying, and you wasted decades apart. Laughter turns to tears you try to hide. Express gratitude for this moment while your heart breaks that it's all you get. End with the train whistle blowing—you're smiling through tears, voice shaking with both devastating loss and profound thankfulness. Find the beauty in the contradiction: this is the best and worst moment of your life, happening simultaneously.
inspired_by: Narrating in a Blizzard: Freezing to Death

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You are an adult child finally confronting a parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago, meeting them for coffee after they suddenly reached out. Start with controlled, cold politeness—your walls are up, your voice measured and sharp. As they make excuses, let your anger build but stay contained, each word more pointed than the last. Then something they say breaks through—maybe a memory, maybe a truth—and your voice should fracture. The rage dissolves into the wounded child underneath, your tone becoming raw and vulnerable as you admit how much their leaving destroyed you. End with a devastated question you've held for years, your voice barely above a whisper, still carrying both fury and a desperate need to understand.

title: The Secret Kept for Twenty Years
instruction: You're sitting beside your best friend in the dark, finally ready to tell them the truth you've carried since you were both seventeen. Your voice is barely audible at first, each word a struggle, because once you say this, everything changes. You're confessing that you were there the night their sibling died, that it wasn't an accident the way everyone thought. Your voice trembles with the weight of two decades of silence, breaking on certain words you can barely force out. You're not asking for forgiveness—you know you don't deserve it—but you need them to know the truth before you can't tell them anymore. By the end, you're crying so quietly they might not even realize, your voice raw and small, waiting for them to say something, anything, in the terrible silence.

title: Holding the Line That Won't Hold
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love who's in danger—maybe they're threatening to hurt themselves, maybe they're in a crisis you can't reach. Start with fierce, urgent intensity: 'Listen to me, just stay on the line, okay? Stay with me.' Your voice is commanding, protective, almost aggressive in its desperation to keep them tethered. But as minutes pass and you realize you can't actually save them from where you are, your voice begins to shake. The fierce protectiveness crumbles into helpless pleading: 'Please, please, I can't—I can't lose you.' By the end, you're openly sobbing, your words barely coherent, all your strength dissolved into raw terror and powerlessness. 'Don't go. Please don't go.'

title: Summit Confession
instruction: You're standing on a mountain peak at 14,000 feet, the air so thin each word is a battle for breath. Beside you is the person you've been secretly infatuated with for months, seeing them now against the endless sky and jagged horizon. Your voice comes out strained, almost a whisper, and you have to pause to gasp between each phrase. Start with a slow, numb awe—your words barely audible as you try to describe the view. But as you speak, the infatuation swells, and you feel a strange pleasure in admitting your feelings, even though you're light-headed and your words slur. Let the final line break free as a raw, ecstatic confession, your voice cracking with both effort and joy.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Infatuation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The All-Nighter's Slow Burn
instruction: You're a 10-year-old boy who's been awake for over a day, and you're watching your best friend play with a new toy you've wanted for months. You're slumped on the floor, head heavy, and your words come out thick and slow—your tongue feels like paper. Start with a confused, hollow remark about the toy, barely processing it through the exhaustion. As you force yourself to speak, jealousy creeps in, raw and childish, and your voice gains a desperate, strained edge. You try to bargain or demand a turn, but microsleep interrupts you mid-word; you slur, yawn, and lose your train of thought before snapping back with sharper, more demanding envy. End with a plea that cracks into helpless frustration, your voice fading as sleep nearly pulls you under.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fog That Remembers
instruction: You are an older man alone on a fog-shrouded pier. The air is thick, swallowing sounds, making you feel isolated. You're trying to recall the exact sound of a loved one's laughter from decades ago. Speak aloud to the fog as if it might hold the memory. Start with your voice loud and uncertain, almost frustrated by the muffling silence. Then, as a fragment of that laugh flickers in your mind, let your voice soften, become hesitant, more intimate. End with a quiet, trembling realization.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Manager: Offering Significant Customer Compensation
instruction: A customer has been harmed by your company's failure. Your voice is apologetic and direct: 'This is our fault. We failed you.' You're not defending the company—you're owning the mistake. Include the moment where you announce the compensation and the customer's reaction. Your voice becomes genuinely committed: 'I'm going to personally oversee your resolution.' You're taking responsibility beyond what's required. By the end, your voice reflects the reality that sometimes compensation matters but also that a genuine apology matters. 'I'm sorry we let you down. We're going to do better.' Your voice carries the weight of that promise.

title: Love Blooming
instruction: They said something small and ordinary and suddenly you're aware that you're in love. Your voice changes texture—softens, warms. You're saying their name and the syllables land differently. 'I think I—' You're afraid to say it aloud, so your voice gets smaller, more vulnerable. Breathing changes: you're aware of your body now. Vocal tone becomes almost musical, trembling at the edges. There's wonder in the sound—you can't believe this is happening. Physical: you're shy suddenly, words careful. By the end, you're saying it very quietly: 'I love you.' The voice is naked.

title: Thank You for Your Patience
instruction: Your mother finally, miraculously completes the task herself after an hour of guidance. She's so proud, laughing like a child: 'I did it!' You laugh with her, genuinely delighted, but tears are streaming down your face because this small victory is also a marker of how much she's lost, how hard simple things have become. The laughter and crying mix together. 'You did it, Mom, I'm so proud of you,' comes out choked with both joy and heartbreak. She says, 'Thank you for your patience, sweetheart. You're so good to me,' and you have to respond while holding the beautiful contradiction of celebration and grief, gratitude for this moment and sorrow for all the moments that are slipping away. End with 'I love you' that somehow contains everything.
inspired_by: The World's Most Patient Tech Support Call with an Elderly Parent

title: Thunderstruck Reunion
instruction: You are a young woman caught in a sudden, torrential downpour. You’ve ducked under a shallow tree, but rain streams into your mouth and eyes, and thunder booms overhead. You’re frustrated at the weather—a slight anger at being drenched. Then, through the blur of water and lightning, you see a figure you never expected: your childhood best friend, who disappeared years ago. Astonishment hits you like a wave—you gasp, sputter, and shout their name over the rain. As they draw closer, your voice cracks; you realize they look hurt or haunted. Distress rises, sharp and real. Your words shift from stunned disbelief to a trembling plea for them to explain. Let the rain affect your rhythm: sputter, pause to wipe your face, raise your voice to be heard, then let it drop when emotion tightens your throat.
emotions_sampled: Anger (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Distress (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed in the dark, and you're leaving—maybe you're ill and going to a facility, maybe you're in danger and must disappear to protect them, maybe you've made an impossible choice. Speak in hushed tones so you won't wake them, but let every word carry the weight of a heart being torn in half. Start with simple, tender observations—the way they sleep, small details you've memorized. Your breath should catch frequently, your voice barely holding together. As you continue, let the reality of 'never again' sink deeper into your body. Your whispers become even softer, more broken, punctuated by silent crying. You're trying to memorize them with your voice, to leave some blessing in the air above them. End with words you can barely get out, a final 'I love you' that's almost just breath and grief.
inspired_by: Treading Water While Calling for Help

title: The Slow Reveal of Rot
instruction: You're in a cluttered garage, sitting on an overturned paint bucket, holding a small, half-empty bag of cannabis. You're middle-aged, voice androgynous. You came here to unwind, but the high has made your thoughts echo and drift. You're staring at a spot on the wall where a family photo used to hang before you tore it down. As the high settles in, the disappointment you feel is a thick, familiar weight—it makes your speech slow, your mouth dry. But under that, a cold, quiet malevolence is rising. You're not sad; you're *done*. Let your voice meander, pause mid-thought, let it get logy and sticky, but let the final words come out with a chilling clarity, a venomous promise.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (extremely present), Confusion (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: Your child is asleep. You're leaving—not because you want to, but because staying would destroy you both. Kneel beside the bed. Your voice is barely audible, tender and fracturing: 'You're going to wake up and I won't be here, baby.' Each word catches in your throat. You memorize their sleeping face as you whisper the things you need them to know someday. 'You'll think I didn't love you enough to stay. But I loved you too much to let you watch me disappear.' Your voice breaks on a sob you can't release—you can't wake them. The quiet devastation is complete. Your final whisper: 'Forgive me.' It's both a plea and a farewell. The silence after is deafening.

title: The Day You Came Home Early
instruction: You are alone in your kitchen, contentedly baking cookies, humming off-key, feeling a soft satisfaction. Then you glance at your partner's phone left on the counter—a text from your sister appears, asking about 'last night.' Embarrassment flushes through you as you realize you've been a fool, then a sick flicker of lust as you imagine the betrayal's intimacy, and finally—rage. You start screaming, throwing things: a vase smashes, you kick a chair. Your voice cracks, drops to a guttural snarl, then shrieks. Let the physical fury take over—heavy snorts, percussive bursts. End with raw, shattered fury.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (extremely present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Sexual Lust (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Time Traveler and the Skeptical Scientist
instruction: Portray a time traveler with an urgent, passionate voice trying to warn a skeptical scientist who speaks in a logical, dismissive tone. Switch between the travelers frantic explanations and the scientists doubts, creating a clash between belief and skepticism.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Launch
instruction: You're calling your best friend who's about to board a one-way mission to Mars—they'll never return to Earth. You fought bitterly three months ago about them leaving, said things you can't take back. Now this is your last chance to speak. Start with stiff, awkward attempts to keep it light and normal, your voice tight with the weight of unspoken apologies. As the minutes tick down, let your defenses crumble—move from careful pleasantries to raw confession, from trying to be supportive to desperately needing them to know they mattered, they matter, they'll always matter. End in a place between grief and gratitude, your voice breaking as you try to say goodbye to someone who chose the stars over staying with you, and you're trying—god, you're trying—to be happy for them even as your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Concealing Jealousy While Congratulating a Friend

title: The Fierce Protector's Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt your child, your sibling, someone you'd die for—and you failed to protect them. Start with volcanic rage: your voice is a weapon, every word designed to destroy. You're graphic about what you want to do to this person, your breath coming fast, your words almost incoherent with fury. But underneath the rage, there's something else rising—your own crushing guilt. How did you not see this coming? Why weren't you there? The anger suddenly collapses mid-sentence, and you're no longer addressing the person who caused harm—you're talking to yourself, to the one you failed. Your voice breaks completely, shifting from roar to whimper. You're begging for forgiveness from someone who isn't even in the room. The helplessness is overwhelming. End with your voice raw and small, admitting the truth you can't bear: you're terrified you're not strong enough, that you'll fail them again, that your love wasn't armor enough.

title: Condemning Look
instruction: Someone's face says everything: they've judged you and found you wanting. Your voice is shocked: 'What?' But you know what. Their silence is a verdict. Your voice tries to defend: 'It's not like that.' But you're speaking to a closed door. The judgment in their eyes has reorganized your entire sense of yourself. 'I didn't mean to hurt you,' your voice whispers, but it's already too late. You're condemned in their eyes.

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Never Believed You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent about something they dismissed or denied when you were young—something that shaped your entire life. Begin with careful, measured words, the kind you've rehearsed a thousand times, trying to stay composed and reasonable. As they start to deflect or minimize again, let your voice crack open—years of unspoken pain breaking through in jagged, uneven waves. Your anger should collapse into the voice of your younger self, vulnerable and desperate to be seen. End not with resolution but with exhausted, tear-soaked clarity: you're finally saying it not because you expect them to change, but because you need to hear yourself say it out loud.
inspired_by: Shouting a Warning Across a Canyon

title: Letting the Light In
instruction: You're on the phone with your partner, who's been worried about you. You've been saying you're fine for weeks, but tonight they catch you off guard. Start with a forced, cheerful tone—then, mid-sentence, your voice cracks. Let out a shaky laugh, then drop to a whisper as you admit you're not okay. But as you speak, feel a fragile hope rising; your voice steadies slightly, and you end with a quiet, optimistic note about getting through this together. Fidget with the phone cord, clear your throat, and let the words tumble out unevenly.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Emergence Tease
instruction: You are waking from sedation after a minor procedure. A friend is sitting beside you. At first, you're completely disoriented—slurring, struggling to form words, your voice cracking and uncontrolled like a child's. As awareness returns, you notice your friend and a memory surfaces of them being clumsy earlier. Your confusion slowly shifts into a playful, teasing tone, though your speech remains thick and unsteady. Let your voice meander, lose thoughts, and then land on a gentle, amused ribbing about their clumsiness. End with a teasing lilt, still struggling to speak clearly.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Promised Seat
instruction: You are a young man standing alone in your apartment, hands planted firmly on your hips, shoulders back, elbows jutting out. You just learned that a long-time rival got the promotion you were promised. You're trying to hold onto this power pose—a performance for no one but yourself—as you mutter your thoughts aloud. Start with a hard, loud, almost mocking tone, layering in jealousy as you list the rival's supposed failures. But as you go on, the pose starts to feel hollow; your voice loses its edge, breaking into quiet, raw disappointment. Let your body betray you—maybe you shift your weight, drop one hand, or stare at the floor, ending with a tired, honest sadness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Bedside Confession to an Unconscious Lover
instruction: You're sitting beside your partner's hospital bed, holding their hand, uncertain if they can hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile: 'I don't know if you can hear me, but I need to say this.' There's a trembling vulnerability: 'I was so scared to love you. So terrified. And I wasted so much time building walls.' Your voice catches, tears threatening: 'Remember that stupid fight we had last week? About dishes? I was so petty.' A soft, broken laugh that dissolves into grief: 'I'd give anything to fight with you about dishes right now.' Your words become a confession of devotion: 'You made me brave. You made me softer. You made me... more.' Tender desperation: 'Please stay. Please fight. I'm not done learning how to love you better.' Your final words are a whispered promise, fierce and gentle: 'I choose you. Every day. Come back so I can keep choosing you.' The silence holds everything you can't say.

title: What I Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of silence between you. Begin by studying him - really looking at how he's aged, the tension in his shoulders, the way he won't quite meet your eyes. Let yourself wonder what fear or regret he's carrying. Start with this investigative curiosity, almost clinical in your attention to who he actually is versus who you've imagined him to be. As you speak the truth you've held back for years, let your initial detachment crack open. Notice how he responds - does his jaw tighten? Do his eyes well up? Let what you discover about him in this moment change your anger into something more complicated: maybe recognition, maybe unexpected compassion, maybe shared pain. End in a place emotionally different from where you began, shaped by what you've truly seen in him.

title: Reclamation
instruction: You and your partner have just found each other again after months of silence. The first touch is tentative — you almost forget how to breathe. As they pull you closer, a low, airy moan escapes you, surprised at your own relief. Let that sound rise slowly, catching on each new sensation: an 'oh' that breaks into a half-smile, an 'ah' that trembles before growing steadier. Your body begins to trust before your mind does. By the end, your voice opens fully — a sustained, hopeful 'yes' as you realize this is real, and you let yourself believe in it again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Crouch
instruction: You're an elderly, deep-voiced man hidden inside a small, dark closet, knees pressed to your chest, back against the wall. Outside, footsteps pace—you're terrified they'll find you. Your voice is a strained, hushed whisper, tight from the cramped space and shallow breathing. At first, you mutter frantic pleas for silence, but as the footsteps fade, a bitter realization sets in: the people you trusted left you here to die. By the end, your voice hardens with resentment, still compressed but now acidic—each word a quiet, venomous curse against those who abandoned you. Let your breath catch, shift your weight, pause as if hearing a creak, then let the bitterness seep into the final words. Spoken content should be about 50-70 words.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're expressing gratitude to someone who saved your life, but the cost of that salvation destroyed theirs, and you're standing in the aftermath of that sacrifice. Begin with genuine, overflowing thankfulness, your voice warm and almost celebratory as you acknowledge what they gave you—a second chance, hope, a future. But let the grief bleed in as you realize what they lost for you, your gratitude becoming entangled with guilt and sorrow. Find moments where you're almost laughing through tears, marveling at the strange beauty of being alive while mourning what it cost. Build to a place where you're simultaneously saying 'thank you' and 'I'm sorry,' where joy and devastation are completely inseparable. End with a kind of bittersweet peace, your voice soft and wondering, as you accept both the gift and the price, finding something sacred in the terrible trade.

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy Who Saved Your Life
instruction: The person who killed your family, who you've hunted for years, just threw themselves in front of a bullet meant for you—and now they're bleeding out in your arms. Start with explosive rage and confusion, your voice shaking with fury: 'Why did you do that? I hate you!' Your hands are trying to stop the bleeding even as your voice screams at them. But as they grow weaker, something shifts—you're begging them not to die, your voice cracking with desperation. The hate collides with horror at watching someone die because of you. Your fierce need for vengeance transforms into helpless panic as you realize you don't want this, not like this. End with your voice breaking into sobs, whispering 'Stay with me' to someone you swore you'd kill, your entire worldview shattering.

title: Emergency Room Doctor: Critical Patient Arriving
instruction: Critical patient arriving and your voice becomes entirely focused and commanding. You're narrating immediate triage: 'Trauma alert. GSW to the abdomen. Get me a surgical team.' Your voice is clinical, efficient, powered by years of training. Include the moment where human concern breaks through—this patient is also someone's beloved—but you channel that into precise action. Your voice becomes even more focused: every command is an act of care. 'Get two units of O-neg. I need a CT scan stat.' You're saving a life through the pure force of your competence and your voice reflects that. By the end, you've given everything you have and your voice becomes quieter, almost praying: 'Come on. You've got this.' You're talking to the patient, to yourself, to the universe. Your voice is the sound of emergency mastery.

title: Laughing While Reading Your Late Spouse's Hidden Love Letters
instruction: You've just found letters your spouse wrote to you over the years but never gave you—found them days after their funeral. Begin reading aloud with tentative curiosity. The first letter makes you laugh genuinely at their humor, an inside joke only you two shared. Your laughter is real and bright. But the next letter is heartbreakingly tender, and your voice wavers. You keep reading, laughing and crying simultaneously—their words are so perfectly them that joy and grief become inseparable. You're furious they never shared these, grateful they exist, devastated they're gone, comforted by their voice on the page. End with gratitude breaking your heart wide open: these letters are a gift and a goodbye. Let laughter and sobbing, anger and love, loneliness and connection all live in your voice at once.
inspired_by: Your Child Telling You About Their Eating Disorder

title: Teaching Your Child a Song You'll Never Finish
instruction: You're in hospice, teaching your young child the lullaby your grandmother sang to you—but you can barely remember all the words. Start with gentle confidence, humming and singing fragments, trying to piece it together. Your voice should carry love and determination at first, but as you struggle to recall verses, let frustration and grief seep in. Speak to your child between attempts: 'No, wait, it goes...' Switch between singing, humming what you've forgotten, and quietly apologizing for the gaps you're leaving in their inheritance. End with the devastating acceptance that they'll only ever know pieces of this song, pieces of you. Let your voice break not from pain, but from the unbearable tenderness of this final gift you can't quite complete.
inspired_by: Last Person to Speak a Dying Language

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—extreme cold that's making you shake, fever heat, or physical pain—while simultaneously experiencing emotional breakthrough. Begin with your body and voice fighting both the physical sensation and an emotional truth you're trying to suppress. Your words should come through gasps, shivers, or tension. Perhaps you're trying to stay composed, to keep talking normally, but your body won't let you. As the physical intensity peaks, let it crack open the emotional dam you've been holding back. The sensations should force out words you didn't plan to say, truths carried on waves of physical experience. By the end, let the physical and emotional merge completely—your voice raw with both bodily intensity and feeling unleashed, something like ecstasy mixed with grief, or rage mixed with profound release.

title: The Rising Cage
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman trapped in a painfully slow elevator, already late for a meeting that could finally launch the career you've dreamed of. The metal walls bounce your voice back at you, and the hum of the cables grates on your nerves. Start by muttering in irritation—checking your watch, sighing, maybe pressing the button again harder. Then, as you realize you can't change the speed, you decide to use these last seconds to mentally step into that meeting. Let your voice soften, gain a lilt of optimism, as you whisper a rehearsal of your opening line, the hope breaking through the frustration. Finish with a small, genuine smile in your voice as the doors finally open.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Shortcut
instruction: You're at a loud house party, standing close to a woman you've just met. Both of you know this is heading to a hookup—there's a fast, nervous familiarity in your voices. Start with a low, amused question about whose place is closer, laughing to cover the awkwardness. As you talk, your voice softens, losing the bravado; mention something about how you wish this didn't have to feel so rushed, letting a note of genuine longing slip through. Fidget with a cup, glance away when the longing hits, then bring it back to light, conspiratorial laughter.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Want
instruction: You're an elderly person, bound gently but firmly by your lover, your arms pulled above your head, ropes creaking with each small shift. The shame you feel—for your age, for needing this so desperately—sits tight in your chest, making your voice thin and hesitant at first. But as you speak, the longing that has always been there surges forward, softening your throat, turning your words into a raw, breathy plea. Let your breathing be uneven, your movements restricted, your voice cracked with vulnerability. Start with a whisper of shame, then let the longing take over, pulling each syllable out like a sigh.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confrontation in the ICU: A Daughter Finally Speaks Her Truth
instruction: You're standing at your father's hospital bedside. He's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you know this might be your last chance. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this a thousand times but never had the courage: 'Dad, I need to tell you something before...' Your voice is tight, controlled, years of swallowed words pressing against your throat. Then it breaks open: the rage you've carried since childhood. 'You were never there. Not for my graduation, not for my wedding, not when Mom died and I needed you most.' Your voice rises with decades of pain, but underneath the anger is desperate, aching need: 'I needed a father. I needed YOU.' As his monitors beep steadily, you watch his face crumple and suddenly your anger transforms into something more complex—grief mixed with love, fury intertwined with forgiveness. Your voice softens but remains raw: 'I'm so angry at you. And I love you. And I don't know how to hold both of those things.' End with quiet devastation, reaching for his hand: 'Don't leave me with this. Please. Help me understand.'
inspired_by: Emergency Room Doctor: Critical Patient Arriving

title: Sneeze-Fueled Frustration
instruction: You're a teenager trying to finish a last-minute online quiz due in five minutes, but a relentless allergy attack keeps sneezing. Start in the middle of a build-up—sharp inhale, explosive sneeze—then slump back, voice suddenly nasal and thick with irritation. Mumble complaints about the timing, the dust, your own bad luck. As another sneeze builds, shift from raw anger to a defeated, impatient whisper, rushing words before the next explosion. Let your voice crack, trail off, and recover with a congested, weary focus.
emotions_sampled: Anger (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Fortress of Pillows
instruction: You're a teenage guy, curled on your side in bed after a blowup with your dad. Your voice is deep but your body is tight—one lung pressed into the mattress, the other open. Start by muttering fragments of the argument, voice clipped, defensive, almost growling. Then notice the pillow against your cheek, the faint smell of detergent. Let your words trail off. Take a slow, quiet breath. By the end, your voice softens to a near-whisper, settling into a surprised, fragile contentment. Speak as if you're convincing yourself you're okay, but your breath and the warmth of the blanket are already doing the work.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, whispering a confession you've kept buried. Start speaking softly about something adjacent to the truth—a small admission, a gentle lead-in. After each whispered statement to them, speak aloud (but still quietly) what's actually racing through your mind in that moment—your fear of their reaction, the relief of finally speaking, the shame, the hope, the terror of losing them. Let your inner thoughts and your whispered confession flow into each other. The vulnerability in your private thoughts should gradually infuse what you're actually saying to them, making each revelation more raw and true. Begin with your heart racing in fear, but end in a place of profound emotional exposure—whether that's relief, deeper fear, unexpected intimacy, or tender devastation.

title: The Breaking Point: A Protective Fury That Cannot Protect
instruction: You've just learned that someone you love—your child, your partner, your sibling—has been systematically hurt by someone in a position of power, and there's nothing you can legally do about it. You're in your car, alone, and the emotion detonates. Start with a roar of pure rage—a sound that comes from your gut, your fists pounding the steering wheel. You're screaming at the injustice, at your own powerlessness, cursing with every fiber of your being. Your voice is fierce, protective, almost feral. But rage that intense cannot sustain itself. It begins to fracture. Your shouting breaks into ragged breathing. The fury cracks and underneath is terror and helplessness. Your voice becomes almost childlike: 'I don't know how to fix this. I can't fix this.' You might sob violently, your whole body shaking. The explosive energy collapses into something raw and broken. End in a place where you're still breathing hard, but your voice has found a whisper of desperate determination—you can't undo what happened, but you can be there, you can witness, you can hold them. The helplessness hasn't left, but it's transformed into a fierce, quiet promise to stay, to not turn away, even when you can't save them from the pain.
inspired_by: Watching the Tsunami Build: The Moment You Understand You Were Wrong About the Warning

title: The Homecoming Threshold
instruction: You are standing at the door of your childhood home after years away, about to enter for a celebration, but someone you hurt badly will be inside. You reach for the doorknob feeling a strange flatness—you know you should feel nervous or excited or guilty, but you feel almost nothing, going through the motions. Before you open the door, stop. Feel your hand on the doorknob: its temperature, its shape, the resistance as you grip it. Feel your feet on the ground, the air entering your lungs, any tension in your shoulders or jaw. Stay with these sensations until your body becomes electrically alive and present. As you awaken physically, let contradictory emotions flood in: joy at returning home mixed with dread, love for the people inside braided with shame, hope for reconciliation tangled with resentment at having to apologize. Let your hand on that doorknob tremble with this complexity. When you finally speak (to yourself, to someone beyond the door, to the universe), your voice should carry all of it—gratitude and grief, belonging and exile, all at once.
inspired_by: Actor's senses are sluggish and unresponsive during sensory choice work

title: The Last Conversation Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving for a mission they may not return from. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light—'You'll be back before you know it, right?' But as reality settles in, your voice begins to crack. The bravado dissolves into raw vulnerability. You cycle through denial, anger at the unfairness, desperate attempts to memorize their face with your words. End in a place of quiet, trembling acceptance mixed with fierce love—not resignation, but a tender fierceness that says 'I see you, I love you, and I'm terrified.' Let silences hold as much weight as words. Your breath should become unsteady, voice dropping to almost a whisper by the end, each word deliberate and precious.

title: The Intervention That Became a War
instruction: You're confronting your best friend about their self-destruction, and your voice starts measured, careful: 'I can't watch this anymore. I won't.' They dismiss you, and something ignites—your voice rises, fierce and desperate: 'Don't you dare walk away from me! Not after everything!' You're shouting now, years of watching them suffer exploding: 'You're killing yourself, and you're making me watch, and I HATE you for it!' But the moment those words leave your mouth, your voice breaks completely: 'No—no, I don't hate you. God, I don't hate you.' You collapse into raw vulnerability: 'I love you so much it's destroying me too.' Your voice becomes urgent, pleading: 'You're the person who knows me better than anyone, and I'm losing you.' Tears overtake you: 'I can't save you. I've tried and I can't, and it's tearing me apart.' Finally, your voice goes quiet with devastating acceptance: 'So here's what I have to say: I love you. And I'm letting go. Because loving you can't mean dying with you.'

title: After the Silence
instruction: You are lying in bed after making love, the sheets tangled, your head on your partner's chest. The room is dark and quiet, but your child is in the next room, and you just got news that their illness might be serious. You speak slowly, your voice heavy with vocal fry, barely above a whisper. Start with a numb, almost detached murmur about how nice this feels, but as you think of your child, the sadness seeps in. Let your words trail off, fade into long pauses. By the end, your voice cracks, a single tear escapes, and you can't finish the sentence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Call from the Airport
instruction: You're calling your best friend from the airport. You just got your dream job—the one you've worked toward for ten years—in another country. You'll be leaving in three hours. As you tell them the news, your voice is bright with genuine excitement, laughing, describing the opportunity. But underneath, something else is rising: the sudden, crushing realization that you're leaving them behind, that this friendship that has sustained you through everything is about to change forever. You try to keep the enthusiasm going, but your voice starts to crack. You're happy and devastated simultaneously. You're celebrating and grieving in the same breath. By the end, you're crying, but you're also still laughing, because the joy is real even though the loss is real. Let yourself embody both emotions fully—don't choose between them. Your voice should carry celebration and heartbreak in the same moment, showing how love makes success both sweeter and more painful.

title: Hiding Relief After Receiving Good News You Expected
instruction: You get confirmation of something you anticipated but acted uncertain about. Internally, youre relieved, but you play it cool. Describe the easing of tension inside while maintaining a steady demeanor. Speak with modest acknowledgment, hiding the extent of your relief.

title: The Fortress Crumbling
instruction: You're screaming at the detective who's suggesting your missing child might have run away from you, not been taken. Your voice is a weapon of absolute certainty: 'Someone took them! We were a perfect family!' The rage is towering because the alternative is unthinkable. Your breathing is sharp, aggressive. You're listing evidence, but then they show you your child's journal, their plans, their pain. The fury intensifies—you're roaring now—but suddenly it collapses. The explosive energy drains into broken sobbing. By the end, you're on your knees, voice shattered, whispering 'What did I do to them?' The protective delusion has detonated, leaving only the wreckage of what you refused to see.

title: The Pirate Captain and the Mutinous First Mate
instruction: Depict a gruff pirate captain with a rough, commanding voice and a first mate who speaks in a sly, rebellious tone. The first mate is plotting a mutiny. Switch between the captains suspicion and the mates veiled threats, creating a tense power struggle on the high seas.

title: Bitter Wave
instruction: You are an older woman in the middle of sex with a partner you've come to resent. Your body responds with pleasure, but your mind is thick with sourness and rage. As the sensation builds, you try to stay angry, but a sudden, unfamiliar gentleness from them cracks through your defenses. Your voice is broken—gasps, moans, half-words—and your breathing is jagged. Let the bitterness and anger tighten your throat at first, then let astonishment leak in as something inside you shifts against your will. You speak only a few fragmented lines, reacting to the moment and to the unexpected tenderness that surprises you into a softer place.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Anger (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Protecting Your Child: The Rage of Helplessness
instruction: You've just learned someone hurt your child—a bully, an abuser, a system that failed them. Begin with explosive fury, voice shaking with volcanic rage, ready to destroy whoever caused this pain. But mid-torrent, you see your child's face, and the rage fractures into something more complex: terror at your own helplessness, guilt that you couldn't prevent it, fierce protectiveness mixed with the devastating realization you can't shield them from everything. Your voice breaks from shouting to sobbing, from threats to desperate promises ('I will never let anyone hurt you again'), even as you both know you can't guarantee that. End with pulling them close, voice raw and broken, oscillating between rage at the world and tender reassurance, letting your own fear bleed through your attempts at strength.

title: The Last Sunrise
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's been unconscious for hours, and the doctors say this is likely her final morning. You begin by quietly watching her breathe, numb and exhausted from the vigil. Then something shifts—you start remembering everything she gave you: her laugh, her cooking, the garden she kept, the stories she told, the way she defended you, the smell of her house. Let these memories pour out of you in whispered fragments at first, then growing stronger. Tell her everything you're grateful for, everything you'll miss, let your love become enormous and physical in your chest. By the end, you're not just mourning—you're celebrating the fierce, magnificent fact that she existed, that she loved you, that you got to know her. Transform from hollow grief to overwhelming gratitude mixed with sorrow.

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You are saying goodbye to someone you love deeply but must leave for your own survival. Begin with genuine laughter—recall a beautiful memory, let real joy fill your voice—but underneath, feel the grief already pulling at you. As you speak, let the laughter become tears without changing your smile; your voice should crack with gratitude even as your heart is shattering. Express deep thanks for what they gave you while simultaneously mourning what you're losing. By the end, find a strange serenity in the contradictions: you are heartbroken and whole, devastated and grateful, leaving and forever changed by staying as long as you did. This is love that costs everything and was still worth it.

title: The Last Hospital Visit Before the Machines Go Silent
instruction: You're at your estranged sister's bedside. She has hours, maybe less. Start with formal distance—you haven't spoken in eight years, and part of you came out of obligation, not love. Your voice is controlled, polite, like talking to a stranger. But then she says something—maybe your childhood nickname, maybe she remembers the thing you thought she'd forgotten—and the wall cracks. Move from stiff politeness to raw grief mixed with regret. Let your voice break on memories you've kept locked away. By the end, you're holding her hand, whispering the things you should have said years ago, your anger dissolving into desperate tenderness, begging time to slow down. The formality is gone; what remains is the sister you lost and are losing again.

title: The Memory at the Edge
instruction: You are an elderly man in a hospice bed, lost in a wave of physical pain that grips your chest and leaves you breathless. Between the contractions, you try to hold onto a memory of your wife laughing at the beach fifty years ago — a moment of pure, fierce joy. Speak aloud as you ride the pain: let your voice shift from a strained whisper of agony to a sudden, ecstatic laugh as you almost taste the salt on her skin, then fall back into a groan as the next wave takes you. Let your words break, trail off, and surge — this is a conversation with a ghost only you can see.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Telling Your Parent You Needed Them and They Weren't There
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood you needed versus the one you got. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm and adult. But as you speak, years of stored pain begin cracking through. Your voice shifts from controlled to raw, from explanation to accusation to a child's wounded cry. The anger is real, but underneath it is a desperate, aching need to have been seen and loved. By the end, you're not yelling—you're breaking open, voice shaking with the vulnerability of still wanting their love even now, even after everything.
inspired_by: Comforting Someone Grieving While You Grieve Them

title: Frozen Infatuation
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, rugged voice, standing alone in a brutal winter night, waiting for someone you secretly adore. Your body is rigid from the cold—jaw locked, teeth chattering, breath hissing through clenched lips. Start by grumbling at the freezing weather, voice tight and strained from the shivers. Then, as you imagine her face or recall her laugh, let your tone soften, a fragile warmth breaking through the physical tremor. End with a quiet, husky confession that mixes the chill in your bones with the flutter in your chest.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Absurd Comfort of Small Rituals at the End of the World
instruction: Everything is falling apart—you've just received devastating news, your world has irrevocably changed—and yet here you are, applying lotion, because what else do you do when nothing makes sense anymore? Begin with a strange, almost hysterical laugh at the absurdity: describing the lotion with surreal detail while your life crumbles. Your tone should dance between genuine appreciation for this small comfort and disbelief that you're doing something so mundane at such a catastrophic moment. Let contradictory emotions swirl: you're laughing and crying, finding the rich scent ridiculously soothing while simultaneously aware of how ridiculous it is to care about soft skin right now. Speak with wonder about this bizarre human instinct to moisturize, to continue tiny acts of self-care even as everything burns. End in a place of profound, peaceful absurdity—acceptance that this simple ritual is somehow exactly what you need, that tending to yourself with tenderness in the midst of chaos is not denial but survival, not avoidance but the most honest thing you can do.
inspired_by: Putting on a Favorite Scented Lotion

title: Fury and Helplessness at the Hospital Door
instruction: You're a parent in a hospital corridor after being told there's nothing more they can do for your child, and you're unleashing everything at the universe, at God, at the unfairness of it all. Start with explosive rage—your voice is a roar, fierce and primal, as you shout 'NO!' with your entire body. You're demanding, commanding that this not be happening, your voice sharp with the authority of someone who has always been able to fix things, protect, make things right. Your words are a torrent of fury and desperation, accusations and bargaining. But then, like a wave that crashes and recedes, the rage suddenly collapses into raw helplessness. Your voice becomes small, broken, pleading with a whispered desperation: 'Please, I'll do anything.' You're on your knees now, metaphorically and maybe literally, and your voice cracks with the terrible realization of your own powerlessness. Finally, in the devastation, something quieter emerges—not acceptance, but a fierce, protective love that transcends the helplessness. 'I'm here, baby,' you say, and though your voice is shattered, it carries an unbreakable devotion.

title: The Last Lesson
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She has lived through war, loss, and rebuilding her life from nothing. At the beginning, you are desperately trying to get her to remember happy memories, to comfort her, your voice tight with fear of losing her. But as she speaks—fragmented, honest words about what actually mattered in her life—you realize she's not afraid at all. She's trying to teach you something crucial about what makes a life worthwhile. Let your emotion shift from anxious clinging to a profound, tearful understanding. By the end, you must speak back to her what you've finally understood, your voice breaking not with grief but with gratitude and the weight of a truth you'll carry forever. Let her wisdom become yours in real time.

title: Adult Daughter Confronts Dying Mother Who Was Never Present
instruction: You're at your mother's hospice bedside. She has days left and suddenly wants to 'talk' and 'make peace.' Start with cold, clipped words—you came out of obligation, not love. List the piano recitals she missed, the times you needed her and she chose work, parties, other people. Your anger is righteous, justified, sharp as a knife. But mid-confrontation, she reaches for your hand with such frailty, and you see her—truly see her—as small and frightened and human. Your fury doesn't disappear, but it tangles with pity, with grief for the relationship you never had, with the terrible recognition that she's leaving and you'll never get the mother you needed. End whispering the things you wish she'd said to you, knowing she can't say them now, forgiving and not forgiving all at once.
inspired_by: Principal Announces School Safety While Terror Alert Silences Her

title: The Wedding Ring You Can't Remove
instruction: You're sitting beside your spouse of forty years in their final hours. They're barely conscious, breathing shallow. You've been holding their hand for hours, and you become aware of your wedding ring—its familiar weight, the way it's worn smooth over decades, how it catches on their finger as you stroke their hand. Begin in quiet resignation, accepting this goodbye. As you speak your final words to them, let the physical sensation of the ring transform your emotion—this circle of metal has been on your finger since you were young, and removing it after they're gone will mean you're truly alone. Let the weight of that realization move through you from numb acceptance into a fierce, aching need to keep them here just a little longer. Your voice should crack not from theatrical crying, but from the genuine physical tension of trying to hold yourself together while this small piece of metal reminds you of everything you're losing.
inspired_by: Actor needs to feel specific physical attitudes (swagger, authority, vulnerability) that don't arise naturally but would arise from a specific garment or object

title: The Weight of Your Name
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're whispering to your sleeping partner about something you've never told anyone—a shame you've carried, a secret that's shaped you, a truth that makes you feel fundamentally unlovable. Begin barely able to form words, your voice catching, physically curled in on yourself. Focus on one specific sensation: maybe the warmth of their skin near yours, or the sound of their breathing, or the weight of their hand if it's touching you. Let that single physical point of contact become your anchor. As you speak, let that sensation—that proof you're not alone—gradually allow your voice to strengthen, your body to unfurl slightly. The shame doesn't vanish, but by the end, it's shared. Your whisper becomes steadier. You're no longer hiding in the dark alone but letting yourself be known, still fragile but no longer breaking.
inspired_by: Selective Emphasis is needed but the actor isn't sure how to apply it to a specific choice approach

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: Your spouse of forty years is dying, and their favorite song just came on the radio. Through tears, you're laughing at the absurdity and perfection of the timing: 'Of course. Of course this would play right now. You always had perfect timing for an exit.' Your voice is thick with tears but also genuinely amused, even joyful—remembering who they were. You start humming along, swaying slightly: 'Remember when we danced to this at Jake's wedding? You stepped on my foot three times.' You're smiling, voice warm with love, but there's a catch in your breath. The laughter and tears are inseparable now: 'I'm not ready. But I'm also... I'm so grateful. How can both be true?' Your voice becomes softer, more reverent: 'Thank you. For every single day. Even the hard ones. Especially the hard ones.' End with a whispered contradiction, peaceful and heartbroken at once: 'I'll be okay. I'll never be okay. Both of those things are true.' The emotional complexity is in holding joy and devastation, gratitude and grief, peace and agony all at the same time—finding beauty in the goodbye.

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You wake before dawn on your last morning before leaving for a mission you might not return from. Your partner is still asleep beside you, and you watch them in the half-light, trying to memorize everything. When they stir and open their eyes, you try to smile, but your voice cracks when you whisper 'Hey.' They know what day it is. You begin telling them about small things—how you'll miss the way they make coffee, that specific laugh—but as you speak, these tiny details become unbearable. Your voice starts steady, almost cheerful, trying to give them something good to remember. But by the end, when you say 'If I don't come back, I need you to know—', you can't finish.
