The words dissolve. You've moved from false brightness to raw, naked terror of never seeing this person again. Your final silence speaks everything you can't say.

title: Breathe, Platoon
instruction: You are a teenage drill sergeant in the middle of a grueling field exercise. For the last hour you've been screaming at your platoon to hit the dirt, crawl through mud, and push harder. Your throat is raw, and you're furious that they keep lagging. But then, finally, they nail the objective — a perfect, synchronized breach of the mock compound. Stand in front of them, chest heaving, adrenaline still surging. Start by barking a sharp critique about their earlier sloppiness (voice rough, percussive, staccato), but as you see the mud-smeared grins and exhausted pride in their eyes, feel the anger crack. Let a wave of relief wash through you — your voice softens involuntarily, maybe even a shaky exhale mid-word. End with a low, hoarse but genuine compliment, like you're letting go of a weight you didn't know you were carrying. Let your words stumble into quietness, as if the shout gave out and truth slipped through.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Concentrated Essence
instruction: You're distilling the essence of grief into words for a eulogy. Your voice is careful, precise—like you're handling glass. You're choosing exact words to capture what this person was. The voice becomes almost religious in its attention. 'She was kind. Not performatively kind. Actually kind.' As you speak the truth, you're tasting it—and it's bringing you to tears. By the end, the concentrated essence is a single moment: 'She made me want to be better.'

title: Yawning Through a Gross Story
instruction: You're a teenage girl in a boring afternoon class, fighting off a yawn. You turn to your friend to whisper about the disgusting smell coming from someone's lunchbox. As you speak, your yawn keeps interrupting, making your voice slide down and sound hollow. Begin with drowsy annoyance, then let the disgust fully take over as you describe the smell, but end with a tired, half-laughing disbelief. Let the yawn physically affect your speech — hesitate, have your voice dip, and struggle to articulate clearly.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Story Before Dawn
instruction: You are a grandmother in hospice, telling your final story to your adult grandchild who sits beside your bed at 3am. Begin with fragile tenderness, your voice paper-thin but determined, as you share a family secret you've kept for sixty years—about a choice you made that shaped everyone's lives. Start with quiet regret and gentle nostalgia, but as you reveal the truth, let shame and vulnerability crack through. End with desperate urgency mixed with profound peace, as you grasp their hand and beg for forgiveness while simultaneously releasing yourself from decades of guilt. Your voice should move from whispered confession to trembling emotional honesty, finishing in a place of surprising serenity as you finally let go.
inspired_by: The Elderly Storyteller and the Curious Child

title: The Whispered Unburdening
instruction: Late at night, lying beside your sleeping partner, you whisper a secret you've carried for years—something you've done that could change everything between you. Begin with breath so shallow it barely moves your chest, each word fragile and terrified. As you continue speaking into the darkness, allow your breathing to slowly deepen, traveling down through your torso, filling your belly, reaching toward your legs. Let each deeper breath give you more courage, more self-forgiveness. End with your breath flowing through your entire body, your whispered words now tender rather than afraid, filled with quiet hope that truth can be the foundation of real intimacy rather than its destroyer.

title: Midnight Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the dark. You can't sleep. You start speaking softly, almost playfully at first—talking about small things, the way you do when you're both drowsy and relaxed, finding gentle humor in the day's moments. Let yourself enjoy the intimacy, the warmth of just being close. But there's something you need to say, something you've been holding inside for months. Gradually, through the playful banter, let the real confession start to emerge. Your voice gets quieter, more careful. The playfulness fades into vulnerability. By the end, you're whispering the truth you've been most afraid to speak, and the safety you felt at the beginning has transformed into a fragile, exposed tenderness. Stay quiet throughout—let the shift happen in the quality of your whisper, not the volume.

title: Goodnight Stories in an Empty Room
instruction: You're a parent whose child is gone—lost, taken, or has cut off contact. You're sitting in their old room, and you begin telling them a bedtime story the way you used to, your voice soft and tender. But you keep stopping, forgetting parts, your voice catching on memories. The story becomes an apology disguised as a fairytale. 'The dragon wasn't the monster, sweetheart. The dragon was just scared.' Your voice grows smaller, more fragile, as you realize you're really talking about yourself. By the end, you're no longer telling a story—you're confessing in broken whispers: 'I should have protected you better. From the world. From me.' Let the final words dissolve into the kind of crying that makes no sound, just breath catching in your throat. End by saying 'I love you' to the silence.

title: Achoo and Ache
instruction: You're an older adult alone at home, trying to leave a voicemail for a friend you haven't spoken to in years. Your allergies are flaring—nose thick, eyes watering, voice crackly and stuffed up. Start with frustration at your own sneezes and interruptions, but as you picture your friend's face, a deep, raw longing seeps in. Let your voice soften, break, and carry a quiet, desperate hope. Pause to sniffle, clear your throat, or lose your train of thought. End by almost whispering the request to meet again, as if saying it aloud might make it real.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Finding the Diagnosis in Your Pocket
instruction: You're reading your medical diagnosis out loud to yourself—the one that changes everything. But here's the contradiction: you're laughing. Start with disbelief, almost giddy, reading the clinical terms with absurd emphasis: 'Stage three. Well, isn't that just...' You laugh again, but it's not quite sane. The laughter and tears tangle together. 'Six to twelve months. They put a timer on it.' Your voice wavers between hysteria and wonder. Then something shifts—you notice the sunset outside, or remember a joke, or think of everyone you love. Your voice fills with strange, fierce gratitude: 'I get to call them. I get to say goodbye.' You're crying and smiling simultaneously, your voice thick with contradictions: 'This is terrible. This is a gift.' End with profound acceptance wrapped in heartbreak: 'I'm going to live so completely in the time I have left.'

title: The Day I Couldn't Protect You
instruction: You're a parent holding your adult child who's just told you about trauma they suffered years ago—when you thought they were safe. Begin with fierce determination, promising protection, your voice strong with parental instinct. But as reality crashes in—you weren't there, you can't fix this, you can't undo it—that strength shatters. Let rage at the person who hurt them explode into helpless sobbing as you realize you're powerless to heal this wound. Your voice should move from protective thunder to broken whispers, mixing fierce love with devastating inadequacy. End with a raw admission: 'I would give anything to take this from you, and I can't, I can't, I can't.' The transformation is from warrior-parent to helpless, heartbroken human.
inspired_by: Childlike Wonder in a Strange Land

title: Sweltering Sanctuary
instruction: You're in a humid, suffocatingly hot room—maybe a steam-filled greenhouse or a tiny sauna with a friend. The air is so thick every breath feels like drinking. You're speaking to someone you adore, and the heat has melted away all pretense. Start with a voice heavy with moisture, almost struggling to form words as you laugh at the absurdity of the heat. Let the pleasure of their company and the ecstasy of this shared discomfort seep into your tone, so that by the end your words become tender, giddy confessions—your voice slipping between breathless sighs and soft, affectionate murmurs. Let the physical sensation guide you: the moisture on your lips, the heat on your skin, the way your friend's presence makes this sweltering hell feel like paradise.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Watching Them Rise
instruction: You're standing on a dusty construction site, hard hat visor slightly fogged, shouting to a coworker about a younger worker who just got praised for a design you helped with. As you speak, the noise of drills and trucks makes you raise your voice, and you have to pause to wipe sweat from your eye. Start with a forced cheerfulness, describing the praise as though it's fine, but let your voice crack when you say 'she didn't even mention my part.' End with a quieter, sadder admission that you're tired of being invisible, your voice trailing off as you turn away.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love, whispering a secret you've carried for years - something that makes you ashamed, something tender and terrible. Your voice is so quiet it's almost just breath. Start with halting words, long pauses where fear nearly stops you. As you confess, your voice wavers between self-protection and desperate honesty. There's a moment where you almost can't continue, where the silence is unbearable. But you push through, and by the end, your whisper becomes somehow both lighter and more fragile - relief mixed with terror of their response. Every word costs you something. This isn't dramatic confession, it's intimate excavation of your most vulnerable self.

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You're standing at a wedding reception, champagne glass raised, about to toast your best friend who's marrying someone you quietly believe is wrong for them. You love your friend desperately and you're genuinely happy they're happy—but you also know things about this marriage that terrify you, and you've chosen silence to preserve the friendship. Begin your toast with bright, celebratory joy—let the happiness be real, let the love for your friend pour out authentically. But as you speak, let other truths leak through: worried observations disguised as jokes, warnings wrapped in nostalgia, your own grief about losing them tucked inside wishes for their future. By the end, you're somehow both blessing this union and mourning it, celebrating their joy while carrying your private dread. Your voice should hold both radiant warmth and underlying sorrow—never let one fully eclipse the other. This is love that must contain its own opposite: support that's also goodbye.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Gave You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent the truth about how their alcoholism shaped your entire life. Begin with nervous, almost apologetic energy - you've rehearsed this, your voice is shaky but determined. 'I need to tell you something I should have said twenty years ago.' As you speak, feel the anger rising. Let your voice get sharper, louder, more accusatory - all those missed recitals, forgotten birthdays, the nights you waited up. But then you see them shrinking before you, looking old and fragile, and your rage collides with unexpected grief. Your voice should break mid-accusation. End in a place of painful, tender complexity - you're still angry, but you're also mourning the parent you needed and never had. The final line 'I just wanted you to be there' should carry both fury and heartbreak in equal measure.
inspired_by: Two Old Friends Meeting After 30 Years

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you, and you start with cold, controlled anger—your voice is sharp, listing every birthday they missed, every lie they told. But as you speak, the anger cracks open and underneath is the wounded child, voice breaking, asking the question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Your fury dissolves into raw vulnerability. Then something unexpected happens—you realize you don't need their answer anymore. Your voice steadies, not with peace, but with hard-won self-recognition. You end by telling them you've become who you are despite them, maybe because of them. Your final words are neither forgiving nor vindictive—they're simply true, and spoken for yourself, not them.

title: The Kitchen Inheritance
instruction: You're confronting your mother in the kitchen where she taught you to cook, ostensibly arguing about who gets grandmother's recipe box now that she's moving to assisted living. On the surface, your words are about recipes, about fairness, about your sister. But beneath every statement runs a deeper current: you're terrified of losing her, of becoming an adult orphan, of time stealing her away. Begin with sharp, practical arguments about the recipes, keeping your real fear completely hidden. As the confrontation escalates, let the subtext start bleeding through—not by naming your fear, but through the desperation in how you grip the counter, the way your anger keeps breaking into something more fragile. End when you realize you're not fighting about recipes at all, and the underlying terror of her mortality floods everything, transforming your anger into raw, vulnerable pleading.

title: Confessions in Dim Light
instruction: You're speaking in near-whispers to someone who's sleeping or perhaps can no longer hear you—a lover, a child, a lost friend. Begin with tender hesitation, voice barely audible: 'There's something I never told you. Something I was too afraid to say when you could still hear me.' Your breath is shallow, careful, as if the words might shatter you. As you continue, vulnerability deepens: 'I was scared. So scared of losing you that I never let you see all of me.' Tears threaten but don't quite fall. By the middle, your voice catches on the truth: 'And now you're gone—or going—and I never said...' The words dissolve into silence, then reform. End with whispered rawness, each word costing you something: 'I loved you more than my fear. I just wish I'd shown you that.' Let the final moment hang in the air, unresolved and achingly real.

title: Confronting the Friend Who Needed You When You Weren't There
instruction: You're facing a friend who almost didn't survive their darkest moment—and you weren't there when they reached out. Begin defensively, your voice tight with justifications and excuses, explaining why you didn't answer the call, didn't see the signs. But as you speak, hear how hollow your words sound. Your voice begins to crack, the defenses crumbling as shame floods in. Move into raw confession—admitting that you knew, somewhere deep down, that something was wrong, but you chose comfort over courage, chose your own peace over their pain. Let anger at yourself bleed into your words, not loud but fierce and self-lacerating. End with a whispered plea for forgiveness that you're not sure you deserve, your voice barely holding together, knowing that 'I'm sorry' can never undo the silence when they needed your voice most.

title: Ash and Embers
instruction: You are a young woman trapped in a smoke-filled room, your eyes burning, throat raw from coughing. You speak to yourself or to someone on the phone you're clutching. At first, you're focused on survival—concentrating on finding a way out, your voice strained and raspy. But as you recall the person who left you here, bitterness seeps in, your words turning sharp and accusing. Yet by the end, you feel a strange numbness, a hollow acceptance as the smoke thickens. Let your voice crack, pause to cough, let your thoughts drift between urgency and resentment, then settle into a quiet, resigned emptiness. Your spoken words should be around 40-80 words, raw and from the heart.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (clearly present), Concentration (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Stain
instruction: You're an older adult, alone in a quiet kitchen at dawn, scrubbing an old cast-iron skillet that's been in your family for decades. The rhythmic scrape of the brush against the metal syncs with your breathing, and you find yourself murmuring about the stain that's nearly gone—a stubborn reminder of a meal you made for someone long gone. As you scrub, pride swells in your chest for this small victory, and a quiet triumph creeps in as you realize you're not just cleaning, you're honoring a memory. Let your voice be soft, contemplative, and break occasionally with a catch in your throat as you lose the thought, then find it again.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Chronic Pain Celebration
instruction: You're at your daughter's wedding reception, dancing with her for the father-daughter dance, but you're managing severe chronic back pain that's been building all day. Begin by feeling the sharp, persistent ache in your lower back—every step, every turn, every moment of standing sends radiating discomfort through your body. You're smiling, trying to be present for this joyful moment, but part of you is focused on managing the pain, calculating how much longer you can stand, wondering if anyone notices you wincing. You're irritated at your body for betraying you on this day. As the song continues and she rests her head on your shoulder, telling you quietly how much you mean to her, the emotional sweetness collides with the physical agony. By the end, you're simultaneously in pain and overwhelmed with love, tears coming from both sources. Your voice is tight with both strain and emotion—you're experiencing profound joy and gratitude while your body screams for relief, and somehow both are completely real and present at once.
inspired_by: Illnesses and Restrictions — Creating a Headache

title: The Last Harvest Moon
instruction: Your grandmother is dying, and she's asked you to sit with her through her final night. She can't speak anymore, but her hand grips yours. You talk to her about everything—the garden she taught you to tend, the songs she hummed while cooking, the way she smelled like lavender and bread. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light, but as the hours pass and her breathing changes, let your voice crack and soften. Tell her it's okay to go. Tell her you'll remember. When her hand finally relaxes in yours, your voice should break completely—not in panic, but in profound, tender grief mixed with gratitude. 'Thank you. Thank you for every single day.'

title: Holding Them Back from a Fight They Cannot Win
instruction: Someone you love is about to do something dangerous—confront someone violent, walk into a situation that will destroy them. You're physically holding them back, your hands on their shoulders, and your voice starts with commanding urgency: 'Don't. Don't do this.' You're fierce, almost angry, using every ounce of authority you have. But they're not listening. Your intensity builds—you're nearly shouting now, desperate, your voice cracking with the effort of trying to protect them. Then something breaks. Your grip weakens. Your voice drops to something raw and helpless: you're begging now, all pretense of strength gone. You're crying, your words tumbling out in a mess of fear and love. End completely shattered—your voice small, broken, admitting you can't stop them and you can't lose them, your rage transformed entirely into naked terror and tenderness.
inspired_by: Post-coital Conversation: Vulnerability Pretending to Be Casual

title: The Wall at the Party
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, a few drinks in, loose and laughing. A friend you've always trusted suddenly leans in, romantically. You feel the shift — a hot flash of embarrassment and a wave of disappointment that this is happening. Your voice starts warm and tipsy, but you have to stop it cold: pitch flattens, words become deliberate, and you clear your throat, looking away. By the end, you're resolute but mortified, your body already turning to leave. Speak as if you've just registered the move and are shutting it down with a firm, awkward 'No.'
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Disappointment (slightly present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Confrontation You've Rehearsed for Twenty Years
instruction: You are finally confronting your mother about the emotional neglect of your childhood. Start with a voice that's been practiced, almost rehearsed—you've waited years for this moment and you're determined to be heard. Your words are sharp, precise, listing specific memories she probably doesn't even remember. She responds with defensiveness, making excuses, and you feel your control slipping. Your voice becomes rawer, less articulate, as the adult facade cracks and the wounded child emerges. She says something—maybe just your name, said in a way she's never said it before—and you pause, caught between the anger you've carried and the desperate longing to be seen by her. By the end, you're no longer performing your pain for her validation; you're simply showing her your wounds, voice quiet and devastating, and in that vulnerability there's both a terrible risk and the faint possibility that she might finally understand.

title: The Debt Collector's Offer
instruction: You are in a dim, crowded bar, sitting across from a contact who owes a dangerous person money. You've been hired to deliver a final ultimatum. Your voice is a sharp, tight whisper, barely above a breath, angling your mouth away from others into the corner of your jacket collar. You start with cold contempt, breaking the news with a sneer in your whisper, mocking their fear. As the silence stretches and their terrified eyes lock on yours, a flicker of raw sexual lust ignites in your chest, tightening your throat as you realize the power you hold over them. The final line comes out with a husky, trembling edge, fighting a smile, your voice still precise but now laced with a predatory hunger and a jolt of your own fear that they might just run.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (extremely present), Fear (clearly present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering the Truth at 3 AM
instruction: You are lying next to your sleeping partner in the dark early morning hours, speaking aloud a confession you could never say to their face. Begin in the softest whisper, admitting something that fills you with tender shame - perhaps that you're terrified of losing them, or that you feel unworthy of their love, or that you've been pretending to be stronger than you are. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost just breath, catching on certain words as if each one costs you something. Let vulnerability deepen as you confess how much you need them, how the thought of them leaving devastates you, how you've been hiding your fear behind everyday conversation. End with your voice breaking on a simple truth - 'I love you' or 'Please don't go' or 'I'm so scared' - spoken with such raw, undefended tenderness that it feels like your heart is outside your body.
inspired_by: The Brave Knight and the Cunning Sorceress

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You have just received devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, a shattering revelation. Begin by pacing, your entire body vibrating with an energy that has nowhere to go, muscles locked in shock and rising fury. Your voice is strangled, words caught in your throat, everything held in with enormous effort. As you move and speak, let the physical tension build until it's unbearable—fists clenched, jaw tight, breath shallow and rapid. Then let something crack. Allow your body to break open: knees buckling, voice tearing loose, muscles finally releasing their grip. End in a place of physical exhaustion and strange, unexpected calm—lying or sitting still, breathing deeply, voice quiet, the storm passed through and left something clearer behind. The arc moves from explosive containment to shattered release to emptied peace.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Daughter at the Space Launch
instruction: You're at mission control, watching your daughter through reinforced glass as she prepares for a one-way mission to Mars. Start with forced brightness—telling her you're proud, that she looks beautiful in her flight suit, asking if she remembered to pack the photo you gave her. Your voice is steady, almost cheerful, because that's what you promised her. But as the final boarding call approaches, your composure begins to fracture. The brightness becomes desperate. Your words come faster, more fragmented. You're trying to memorize her face, her voice, the way she laughs at your terrible jokes one last time. End in a whisper, telling her something you've never said before, your voice breaking on words you can barely form. This is the last conversation you'll ever have face-to-face. Let us hear you trying not to fall apart while everything inside you is already gone.
inspired_by: Police Officer Pulls Over Her Son Driving Drunk

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally confronting your estranged parent who has terminal cancer—this is your only chance. Start with controlled anger, voice tight and measured, listing grievances you've rehearsed for years. But as you speak, the rehearsed words crumble and raw pain bleeds through—your voice begins to shake, rising in volume and desperation. You're that abandoned child again, voice cracking as you demand answers they can't give. Midway, your fury breaks into something more vulnerable—you're pleading now, voice softening into wounded confusion: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger returns in waves but mixed with grief. End with exhausted resignation, voice barely above a whisper, admitting you still love them despite everything, and that's what hurts most. Let your voice betray every emotion you're trying to control—the adult and the wounded child fighting for dominance.

title: The Worst Timing
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy trying to tell your little sister you love her after she helped you through a tough day. But your Tourette's keeps interrupting with sudden, sharp shouts or random words. Each time it happens, you pause for a split second, then push forward, trying to ignore the embarrassment. Start with frustration and a forced calm, then let your voice soften into something genuinely warm and protective by the end. Let the tics feel involuntary—they break your rhythm, but your affection is the only thing that stays steady.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Time I'll Say Your Name
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and you need to say goodbye, but you keep trying to avoid it by filling the silence with memories. Start with forced brightness, recounting shared moments: 'Remember when we...' But each memory makes the reality harder to bear. Your voice begins to crack, words come slower as the weight settles. You're fighting to keep talking because silence means this is real. Transition from animated reminiscence to barely-whispered fragments. By the end, you can't avoid it anymore—you must say the actual goodbye, and your voice breaks completely as you speak their name one final time, knowing they might not hear it. The journey is from desperate avoidance through crumbling denial to devastating acceptance.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Airport Gate
instruction: You're on the phone with someone you love deeply who is about to board a plane to a distant country—maybe forever. You just learned they're leaving much sooner than expected, and this might be your last conversation. Start trying to sound supportive and brave, hiding your devastation behind encouragement and practical questions. But as the final boarding call echoes in the background, let your composure crack—let the fear, the unsaid love, the regret for all the moments you didn't take flood through. End with raw vulnerability, no longer able to pretend you're okay with this goodbye. Your voice should move from controlled brightness to breaking, from what you think you should say to what you desperately need them to know.
inspired_by: Concealing Surprise When Hearing Unexpected News

title: The Bumpy Harvest
instruction: You are a weathered, older rancher driving a rattling old pickup truck across a rough, unpaved field under a blazing sun. A rival rancher has just undercut your water rights, and the truck's violent shaking forces your voice to waver and break. Start with cold, simmering malice as you mutter plans for revenge, your words jarred by each jolt. Let your mind drift into grim contemplation of past betrayals, then catch yourself mid-thought with a sharp, almost gleeful smirk, savoring the cruelty of your retribution. The ending should carry a wicked elation, your voice steadier but still vibrating with the truck and your dark triumph.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Contemplation (extremely present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're trying desperately to help someone you love who's destroying themselves, and suddenly you see the truth with devastating clarity. Begin with fierce determination, almost shouting: 'No! I won't let you do this! I will carry you if I have to!' Your voice is strong, protective, commanding. But then reality crashes in—your voice breaks mid-sentence: 'I can't... oh god, I can't actually save you, can I?' The strength dissolves into helpless sobbing: 'I'd give anything. I'd trade places with you. But I can't make you choose to live.' End in a place of broken acceptance, voice raw from crying: 'I love you. I will always love you. But I can't do this for you.' Move from fierce protectiveness to explosive grief to helpless surrender.

title: The Tree Nest
instruction: You're an elderly man standing under a tall oak tree, your chin tilted high as you watch your granddaughter perched on a thick branch. You came out to check on her, worried at first—your voice is thin and tight from the angle, neck straining, a little breathless. You call up to her with a mix of caution and awe, noticing how the sun catches her hair. As she grins down at you, your worry dissolves into pure affection, and your voice softens, still light but now warm. Let yourself pause to squint, shift your weight, and swallow—your age and the position make each word a small effort.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Kissed by Quiet Rain
instruction: You are a middle-aged man, tough and stoic by habit, currently holding your sleeping partner in a slow, intimate kiss. You are both tired from a long week, and this is a stolen, gentle moment after an argument you haven't fully resolved. Start with the kiss itself — a soft, wet, tender press of lips, your breath slow and loaded with unspoken sadness. As you pull back just a whisper, your voice must carry that gratitude for this person still being here, but the infatuation is so powerful it steals your words, making you nearly whisper a broken, heartfelt phrase into their hair. Let your voice crack, micro-pause, and sound entirely vulnerable — like you are overwhelmed by loving someone this much.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Infatuation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy Who Just Saved Your Life
instruction: Someone you've hated for years—who destroyed your career, ruined your reputation, poisoned relationships—just took a bullet meant for you. You're holding them as they die, and your voice erupts with rage: 'Why? Why now? You don't get to do this!' Your anger is ferocious because their sacrifice is robbing you of your hatred, the thing that's sustained you. But as their life drains away, your fury collapses into helpless grief. You're begging them to stay, confessing that you needed them—even as your enemy—to make sense of your pain. Your voice breaks between shouting and sobbing, fierce protectiveness mixing with the realization that you're losing the person who defined you. End in the quiet devastation of forgiving them, even though you're furious at them for making you.
inspired_by: Historical: Woman Discovers Her Child Is the Product of Rape She's Blocked

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Spouse After Years of Silence
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're finally saying everything you've been too afraid to admit while they're awake. Start barely audible, confessing how lonely you've been even while lying next to them every night. Describe the physical intimacy you miss—not just sex, but the tender things: how they used to trace your collarbone, the way their hand would find yours in the dark. Let your voice catch on the sadness of sleeping next to someone who feels like a stranger. Include long pauses where you're just breathing, gathering courage. Shift toward aching tenderness as you remember who you were together, your whisper becoming almost a plea. End with the terrifying vulnerability of saying 'I still want you' to someone who might not want you back, your final words barely making sound.
inspired_by: Describing Physical Intimacy to a Lover Over the Phone

title: Burning Point
instruction: You're holding something scalding hot—a cup, a pot handle, a piece of metal—and you refuse to let go because doing so means admitting defeat in an argument you're having with someone you love. Begin with sharp, controlled words despite the building pain, acutely aware of the exact sensation: the heat penetrating skin, the impulse to drop it, the tension in your grip. As the physical pain intensifies, let it blur with your emotional pain—every sensation becomes amplified and entangled. Your breath should grow ragged, your words punctuated by involuntary responses to pain, but you keep speaking, keep holding on. The physical sensation should pull unexpected emotional truths from you—things you didn't plan to say escaping between gasps. Transform from rigid control to something wild and unguarded, where you can't separate physical endurance from emotional exposure. Finally drop the object and let the sudden absence of pain create a moment of devastating emotional clarity where you say the one true thing you've been avoiding.

title: The Last Call from the Empty Bed
instruction: You are an older man, alone in a dim motel room after a long drive to see a lover who never showed. You call her voicemail, speaking through the dull ache in your chest and the absurd, stubborn flicker of desire that still twists in your gut. You speak slightly louder than necessary, enunciating clearly as if to convince yourself she might still pick up. Start with a strained, formal attempt at calm, but let your voice crack, drift, and lose its thread as the pain and the longing tangle. End with a quiet, raw admission that barely escapes your throat.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Whispered Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are the criminal mastermind, dying from a bullet wound in a safe house, speaking to the detective who's been chasing you for a decade. They're holding pressure on your wound even though you both know it's too late. Begin with your characteristic wit and mockery, making jokes about finally being caught. But as your breath grows shorter, the facade crumbles. Whisper the truth you've never told anyone - you became this person because you were trying to destroy the trafficking ring that took your sister, and you got lost in the darkness. Your voice should become increasingly fragile and childlike. End by asking them to tell your sister's daughter - who thinks you're just an aunt who travels - that you loved her, that you tried. Let genuine regret and tenderness replace the mask you've worn.
inspired_by: The Detective and the Criminal Mastermind

title: Stride of Spite
instruction: You are power walking through a park, your heels striking the pavement with each step—each impact sends a micro-tremor through your voice. You leave a voicemail for your ex, your tone dripping with bitterness as you recite every small betrayal. Start with clipped, icy precision, but as your pace quickens, your words become rushed and breathy, the physical exertion merging with your anger. Let the rhythm of your steps dictate your phrasing—audible, rhythmic inhalations every few words. Midway, a crack of vulnerability slips through as you admit you still miss them, but catch yourself and end with a sharp, defiant laugh.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your entire childhood. Start with careful, measured words, almost rehearsed: 'I need to tell you something I've been holding for thirty years.' Your voice is controlled, adult, trying to be fair. But as you describe specific memories—birthdays forgotten, milestones ignored, the loneliness of waiting for love that never came—your voice begins to shake. Anger rises: 'Do you even remember my graduation? My wedding?' Then something breaks. The anger collapses into the grief of the child you once were. Your voice becomes small, vulnerable, almost pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why didn't you see me?' End with devastating quiet, the question hanging unanswered in the air between you.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your lover is asleep beside you, and you're whispering your goodbye—they can't hear you, which makes you finally honest. Start so quietly it's almost sub-vocal, just breath and the ghost of words, confessing why you have to leave. Your voice trembles with the effort of staying silent while your heart is shattering. Describe the small details you'll miss—how they breathe, the warmth of their skin, that specific way they smile. Let tenderness and grief intertwine so completely they're indistinguishable. Midway through, almost speak loud enough to wake them, because maybe you want to be stopped—but you catch yourself, and the restraint costs you everything. End with the moment you stand to leave, and a sound escapes—half sob, half exhale—that you can't control. This is about what silence costs.

title: The Broken Promise
instruction: You're a mother kneeling in front of your six-year-old, who sits on the floor clutching a stuffed bear. You promised to be home for their birthday cake, but work kept you late, and now the candles are melted. You start speaking—your voice small, nearly a whisper—fumbling for the right words, but your throat tightens. Helplessness makes you pause and restart sentences; confusion flickers as you search why you keep failing them. By the end, raw longing breaks through—a desperate hope they'll still smile at you. Feel your knees pressing into the carpet, your hands twisting a tissue, the child's unblinking eyes on your face.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (extremely present), Confusion (clearly present), Longing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Ceiling Won't Answer
instruction: You are a teenage boy lying on your bed late at night, phone pressed to your ear. You’ve taken a tranquilizer—your body is heavy, your mind slow, your voice flat and relaxed. Your friend asks why you’re so quiet. Start with a calm, detached monotone, describing how you’re just ‘thinking.’ Let a brief wave of longing surface as you mention a girl you miss—your voice might soften or hitch slightly—but then the drug pulls you back into that numb, contented haze. Let your words drift, pause, trail off. You’re not fighting the sedation; you’re just speaking through it.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Contentment (slightly present), Longing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Lullaby
instruction: You are a terminally ill parent singing a lullaby to your sleeping child for what you know is the last time. Begin with tender exhaustion, your voice catching on certain words as the reality hits you in waves. Midway through, let grief crack your voice—not theatrically, but the way it does when you're trying desperately to hold it together for someone you love. By the end, find a strange, broken peace in the melody, your voice becoming a whisper as you memorize every detail of this moment. Let pauses speak as loudly as words. This is not about dying—it's about the unbearable love of having to leave someone behind.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Damage They Can't See
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent how their absence shaped your entire life—but they're fading from dementia and may not remember this conversation tomorrow. Start controlled, trying to stay calm and clear, carefully chosen words you've rehearsed for years. But as they look at you blankly or deflect, something breaks—your voice rises with decades of suppressed pain, anger bleeding through. Then you see their confusion, their frailty, and rage collapses into grief. You're suddenly begging them to just acknowledge it, to see you, even once. End in exhausted, tender devastation as you realize you're saying goodbye to the chance of ever being truly heard. Move from controlled hurt to explosive anger to heartbroken acceptance.

title: The Hour Before Dawn
instruction: You are an elderly woman who hasn't slept more than two hours a night for six months. It's 4 AM. You're sitting in your dark kitchen, rubbing your thumb against a chipped coffee mug. You realize you've forgotten what your husband's laugh sounded like—and you're terrified that the pain of that forgetting is eating away the last memory you have of him. Start with a hollow, almost detached voice describing the quiet. Let your words drift, then tighten. End with a raw whisper where the fear and ache are fully present, as if you're fighting not to lose the sound itself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Instructions Whispered to Empty Rooms
instruction: Alone in your home, you're explaining out loud how to do something simple—make coffee, water the plants, remember to pay the electric bill—but you're actually rehearsing what you'll say in a note or video message. You're leaving, or you're dying, or you won't be here much longer, and these quiet domestic instructions are how you're trying to take care of someone when you can't anymore. Your voice starts almost normal, methodical, but tenderness keeps seeping in. You pause mid-instruction to add something personal—'you always liked it with extra sugar' or 'I know you'll forget this part, you always do'—and these asides break you open. By the end, you're barely speaking, your throat too tight, whispering instructions that have become love letters, trying to remain present in the ordinary routines of someone's life when you'll be gone. Let the silence between words grow heavy with everything you can't say directly.

title: The Grateful Goodbye
instruction: You are leaving behind someone you deeply love—by choice—because staying would destroy you both. Begin speaking to them with your voice full of genuine gratitude, listing real gifts they've given you, your tone warm and appreciative. But underneath, your heart is shattering. As you continue, let both truths exist simultaneously: the love is real AND the leaving is necessary. Your voice should carry celebration and devastation in the same breath, laughing through tears or pausing with both joy and unbearable sadness. Don't choose between them—let your voice hold the impossible contradiction of thanking someone for everything while walking away forever. End with a final statement that encompasses both the treasure of having known them and the agony of goodbye.
inspired_by: Actor's work consistently feels shallow, indicates disconnection from unconscious resources

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've loved your entire life—a parent, a partner, a sibling—who is taking their final breaths. Begin in numb shock, struggling to find words, your voice catching on half-formed sentences. As you speak, let memories flood through you—not just the happy ones, but the complicated ones, the fights you never resolved, the words you wish you'd said differently. Your emotion must transform: start unable to accept what's happening, move through desperate bargaining (if only we had more time, if only I had been different), and arrive at a place of profound gratitude mixed with devastating grief. By the end, you're whispering thank you for specific, tiny moments—the way they made coffee, a joke only you two shared, how their hand felt in yours. Let your voice break not from drama, but from the weight of a lifetime becoming memory.

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're trying to protect someone you love—your child, your partner, your best friend—from a danger you're powerless to stop. They're walking into something terrible, and you can't follow. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: 'You are NOT doing this. I won't let you.' Your voice is strong, commanding, desperate to control the situation. But as they resist, as reality sets in that you truly cannot stop them, your voice begins to crack. The strength becomes pleading, then breaks into raw helplessness. 'Please. Please, I'm begging you.' Feel your power dissolve into pure terror and grief. End with your voice collapsing into sobs—not pretty crying, but ugly, desperate, guttural sounds of someone watching their worst nightmare unfold while being completely powerless. Let rage and love and terror all war in your voice simultaneously.
inspired_by: Being Told You're Being Cheated On

title: Vigil at Three AM
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's sleeping—they don't know you're about to leave them forever. Your voice is barely above a whisper, confessing things you could never say to their face. Start with tender observation: 'You always sleep with your hand open, like you're waiting to hold something.' Your throat catches. Move into quiet confession: the ways you've failed them, the truth about why you have to go, secrets you've carried. Your voice should be so soft it's almost just breath, but loaded with years of unspoken love and regret. End with you gently touching their hair, your whisper breaking: 'I hope you dream of someone better than me.' Show someone trying to say goodbye without waking the person, knowing this stolen moment is all they'll get.

title: The Unexpected Mark
instruction: You are in a dimly lit bedroom, lying close with your partner, your faces inches apart. Your voice is low, breathy, and slow as you whisper compliments, your hands tracing their skin. In the middle of a kiss, you pull back and notice a small scar on their shoulder you've never seen before—a thin white line that catches the light. Astonishment floods you: not alarm, but a soft, amazed surprise. Your voice catches, then drops even quieter as you ask about it, your arousal now mixed with a tender curiosity that makes you touch the mark with gentle reverence.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Breaking Fever
instruction: You're in the grip of a high fever, alone, body aching and sheets soaked with sweat. But this physical crisis is breaking open an emotional one you've been suppressing. Begin by describing the physical sensations: the room spinning, the sheets scratching like sandpaper, the weight of your own limbs, the throbbing behind your eyes, the taste of illness, the sound of your own ragged breathing amplified. Let your voice be weak, disoriented. But as you describe these sensations, they start triggering emotional memories—the fever burning away your defenses. A sound reminds you of something. The pressure in your chest becomes not just illness but grief or rage you've been holding. Your body's loss of control allows emotional loss of control. Let the physical and emotional pain become indistinguishable, your voice moving between describing sensation and releasing long-suppressed feeling. End in cathartic release, whether tears or laughter or primal sound, your body and heart finally breaking open together.

title: Last Ride of the Roadkill
instruction: You're 16, riding shotgun in your friend's beat-up truck after a disastrous hunting trip. The engine rattles and the cab stinks of wet dog and stale coffee. Your friend just hit a possum on purpose—that's the disgust that sits in your throat. But you're also relieved to be away from your dad's house for the night, so your shoulders are a little looser. Start by telling him how messed up that was, your voice pitched low and flat like the drone of a muffler, but let this tease gradually pulse into something almost warm—a car-length of camaraderie. Let the whine of the engine make you talk a little louder than you mean to, and let a few words catch on felt disgust before they roll into that relieved, teasing laugh you can't quite suppress.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Relief (clearly present), Teasing (very intensely present)

title: Confronting Your Best Friend Who Betrayed Your Trust
instruction: You're face-to-face with someone who was your person, your safe place, and they destroyed that. Start with your voice controlled, almost too calm—you've rehearsed this: 'I need you to tell me why.' But as they fumble for explanations, something in you breaks open. Your voice becomes raw, accusatory: 'You knew. You knew what this would do to me and you did it anyway.' Let the hurt bleed into rage, your words coming faster, sharper. But then you hear yourself and you stop. There's a moment of devastating vulnerability where your voice drops to almost nothing: 'I trusted you with everything.' Feel the weight of that loss—not just the betrayal, but the person you were when you still had them. Your voice wavers between wanting them to hurt the way you hurt and wanting them to make it okay somehow. End with the terrible realization that you have to walk away from someone you still love. Your final words are quiet but final: 'I can't do this anymore. I can't be the person who stays.'
inspired_by: Relationship Ending: Both Relief and Devastation

title: The Last Lap
instruction: You are a young boy swimming in a pool, your head bobbing above the water as you try to keep up with your older brother who is far ahead. You're exhausted, your arms are heavy, and each breath is a quick gulp of air. Start with a tired, slightly sad mutter to yourself about how you can never catch him, the words coming out in short bursts between breaths. As you hear your brother's distant splash, let a flicker of irritation seep in—you're annoyed at yourself for being so slow. But then, something shifts: you stop fighting, let your body float, and speak a quiet realization that you're okay with just being here, the fatigue softening your voice into a weary acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Summit's Edge
instruction: You are a young woman with a strongly feminized voice, struggling with altitude sickness near the top of a mountain. Your breath comes in short, gasping bursts, each word a labor. A dull headache pulses behind your eyes, making you wince. You stare at the distant peak—it feels both closer and impossibly far. Start with faint longing, a soft ache for what lies ahead, but let doubt creep in as the thin air steals your certainty. Your voice should weaken, slow, and waver, trailing off occasionally as you lose thoughts and fight for air.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (slightly present), Longing (extremely present), Doubt (slightly present)

title: Computing Value
instruction: You're deciding whether to quit your job and start over at 40. The voice is analytical at first: salary, benefits, risk. But underneath is the real question nobody asks aloud: am I worth more than this? Your voice becomes heavier. The mathematics of it don't work—the spreadsheet proves it. But something in your tone shifts when you say: 'Maybe my life is worth the debt.' A long pause. 'I have to try.'

title: The Last Detail
instruction: You're an old, proud outdoorsman showing a young neighbor a rare bird you've been tracking for weeks. But your blood sugar is crashing—your hands shake, your jaw trembles, and words come out slurred. Start with intense, animated interest, your voice full of life as you point and describe. As you speak, feel the energy drain: your voice fades, you lose track of your sentence, and you have to fight to finish. End with quiet disappointment—not in the bird, but in your own failing body. Let the tremor and pauses be natural, not performed.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Quiet Unraveling: Telling Your Child You're Leaving
instruction: You're sitting with your sleeping child, whispering the truth you can't say when they're awake: you're leaving, and you don't know if you'll ever come back. Begin in hushed, tender tones—you're memorizing their face, their breathing. Your voice catches as you confess your fears, the reasons you have to go. The whisper intensifies slightly as desperation creeps in; you're trying to explain yourself to someone who can't hear you, justifying the unjustifiable. Then the weight of it crushes you. Your voice becomes almost inaudible, breaks on certain words. You're apologizing between quiet sobs, knowing sorry will never be enough. End by promising things you can't guarantee, your voice paper-thin, as if speaking any louder will shatter you completely.

title: Final Words to Your Child Through the ICU Glass
instruction: You're standing outside the ICU, speaking through the glass to your unconscious child after a catastrophic accident. Begin with forced optimism, telling them about tomorrow's plans, voice bright but trembling. Then the monitor alarm sounds—their vitals are dropping. Your voice cracks as you realize this might be goodbye. Drop the pretense. Tell them everything you never said: how proud you are, how they changed you, the specific moments that mattered. Your voice moves from desperate pleading to a whispered acceptance, each word heavy with finality. End with a lullaby you used to sing them, voice breaking but tender, as if you could sing them safely into whatever comes next. The last line should be barely audible—a permission to let go mixed with a desperate plea to stay.
inspired_by: Skydiving: Main Chute Failure, Deploying Backup While Narrating

title: Tremor Fear
instruction: You're a witness testifying against a criminal who's sitting in the room. Your voice begins steady but noticeably trembling: 'On the night of October 15th...' The tremor isn't in the words — it's in the mechanical voice work, the slight wobble on every vowel. You can see the defendant from the stand. As you describe what they did, the tremor increases. 'They... they looked at me and...' Your voice shakes so badly you have to pause. The lawyer says, 'Take your time.' You breathe. Try again. The tremor persists. It's involuntary, your body betraying your attempt at strength. By the end, the tremor is so pronounced it's nearly inaudible, but the jury hears every trembling word. The fear is made audible.

title: The Beautiful Wreckage
instruction: You're at the end of something that nearly destroyed you, and you've just realized you survived. Begin with exhausted, almost delirious laughter: 'It's over. It's actually over.' The laughter catches, mixes with tears—you can't tell if you're breaking down or breaking free. Your voice fills with wonder and grief braided together: 'I gave everything to something that was killing me, and somehow... I'm still here.' Gratitude floods in, but it's edged with devastating loss for who you were before: 'Thank you for staying with me through that. I don't recognize myself anymore, but maybe that's okay.' Your voice trembles between joy and sorrow: 'I'm free. I'm completely terrified. I'm both.' End with your voice finding strange peace in the contradiction, crying and laughing at once: 'I have no idea who I am now. And that's the most hopeful thing I've felt in years.'

title: The Judge and the Accused
instruction: Narrate a courtroom scene where the judge speaks in a stern, authoritative voice, and the accused responds in a desperate, pleading tone. Switch between the judges firm questioning and the accuseds emotional responses, creating dramatic tension.

title: The Breaking Point: Protecting a Child From Your Own Chaos
instruction: You're a parent who's just lost custody of your child, and you have five minutes for a final goodbye before the social worker takes them. Start fierce and defensive: 'This is wrong. You can't take them from me!' Your voice is loud, almost aggressive, fueled by desperation. But when your child starts crying, everything collapses. Your rage breaks into helpless tears: 'I'm sorry, baby. I'm so sorry.' Shift between fierce protectiveness—promising you'll get them back, that you'll fight—and devastating self-awareness that you've failed them. Your voice should crack as you try to be strong for them while falling apart: 'You're going to be okay. You're so much stronger than me.' End with a whisper as they're led away, your voice raw and broken: 'I love you. Even when I couldn't show it right, I love you.' Let the explosion of emotion gradually crumble into quiet devastation.

title: The Kitchen Where Nothing Is Safe
instruction: You're confronting your mother in the kitchen where you grew up, but as you begin to speak, the room starts to feel off—maybe the light is coming from the wrong direction, maybe the tiles are a color they never were, maybe you can hear sounds from outside that don't make logical sense. Start from a place of controlled anger, measured words, the things you've rehearsed saying. As you speak, let the strangeness of the space seep into you—notice the particular weight of the air, the way sounds echo or don't echo, the temperature on your skin. This distorted quality of the room begins to unlock something deeper and more raw than your prepared grievances. Let the confrontation shift from what you planned to say to what's really underneath—something more vulnerable, more desperate, perhaps even a plea for something you never got. End in a completely different emotional place than you began, having revealed a truth you didn't know you were carrying.

title: Breaking Silence About Abuse: The Moment of No Return
instruction: You've been silent about abuse for years and you're reaching the point where you have to speak or you'll shatter. Your voice is trembling as you prepare to tell, knowing once you say it out loud, everything changes. Include the moment where you actually say the words: 'He hurt me. I didn't tell anyone and he hurt me for years.' Your voice is barely controlled rage and grief. You're terrified of being believed and terrified of being disbelieved. By speaking, you become a victim in public, and your voice carries the courage of that exposure. Someone's voice responds and you're listening hard for judgment or kindness. Your voice becomes slightly stronger with each confirmation that this is not your shame to carry alone. 'I'm telling you. I'm finally telling someone.'

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your father after years of silence. Start quiet, almost apologetic, your words careful: 'I need to tell you something I've been carrying.' As buried pain surfaces, your voice hardens with each revelation: 'I was eight years old when you missed my birthday. I was twelve when you didn't come to the hospital. I was seventeen when—' The anger builds to a breaking point, words sharp as broken glass: 'You were NEVER there! Do you understand what that does to a child?!' But then, unexpectedly, your voice cracks completely. The fury collapses into raw, vulnerable grief: 'I just... I just needed my dad.' You're crying now, but the tears aren't angry anymore—they're the tears of that abandoned child finally being heard. End with quiet, exhausted honesty: 'I needed you to love me enough to stay.'

title: Confronting the Lover Who Chose Safety Over You
instruction: Your partner is leaving you to return to their ex, their 'safe choice.' Start with your voice tight, almost rational, trying to keep composure: 'I understand why you're doing this.' But underneath, fury and heartbreak are building. As they offer empty reassurances, your control begins to crack—your voice rises with raw pain: 'Don't you dare make this sound reasonable.' Let anger and betrayal pour out, your voice shaking with both rage and tears. Then, in the middle of your fury, something breaks open—a whispered revelation that surprises even you: 'I would have been enough... if you'd let me.' End with your voice quiet, exhausted, but somehow dignified: 'Go.' Transform from controlled to explosive to devastatingly tender to finally, irrevocably done.

title: Sirens in the Distance
instruction: You're a father trapped with your young daughter in a burning house. You've just managed to call 911, but the smoke is thick and you're both coughing. Your voice is strained, high-pitched, trying to stay steady for her sake. Speak rapidly, staccato, as you give your address. Then, in the middle of your plea, you hear sirens. A flicker of hopeful elation breaks through your terror as you tell your daughter, 'They're coming.' Let your voice waver, catch on coughs, and then lighten slightly with that hope. End with a shaky but real smile in your voice.

title: Rage at the Unmoved Earth
instruction: You're back at the tree where you scattered your child's ashes, and you're furious—at God, at fate, at the tree itself for continuing to grow while your baby is gone. Start with explosive anger: pound the bark with your fists, demand answers, let your voice rise to a scream. 'How dare you bloom again? How dare you stand here so goddamn peacefully?' Let that fury build until it shatters completely, collapsing into broken-hearted sobs pressed against the trunk. The tree's solid presence absorbs your grief, its ancient indifference somehow both maddening and comforting. End in exhausted tenderness, your hand gentle on the bark now, whispering a fierce promise to protect this living memorial, your voice hoarse and protective and utterly helpless.

title: The Sink That Held the News
instruction: You are standing at a kitchen sink, hands deep in warm, soapy water, washing the same dish for far too long. The water’s steady roar and the clink of a glass against the basin are the only sounds. You’ve just learned something you can’t quite grasp—you feel a hollow, heavy numbness pressing against your chest, making every movement slow and deliberate. Midway through your quiet monologue, you realize a single, startling detail about what you heard, and your voice catches, suddenly brighter and sharper. Let the sound of the water and the feel of the slick plate anchor your words; start flat and far away, then let astonishment briefly crack through the fog.

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: You are lying beside your lover in the quiet dark, and you need to confess something you've hidden. Begin speaking from your most careful, protective self—the part that maintains control and keeps secrets safe. Your voice should be barely audible, measured. Gradually, let your younger, more innocent self emerge—the part that simply wants to be known and accepted. Then access the ashamed part that believes you're unworthy of love. Finally, discover the courageous self that can speak naked truth without defense or explanation. This is not about volume; it's about the quality of presence in your whisper. Move from guarded restraint through childlike hoping through shame-soaked confession to clear, undefended revelation.

title: The Cliff's Edge
instruction: You are an elderly woman, deeply content in the arms of a partner you adore, your body aching with infatuation as you hover near release. But each time you crest, they stop, and the building frustration makes you doubt your own pleasure—wondering if you’re being tested, or if you matter enough. Your voice must start as a soft, breathy hum of satisfaction, then shift into jagged, rising pleas as the denial repeats, ending in a fragile, whispered confession of trust. Let your words stumble over your own ragged breathing, pausing to swallow, laugh nervously, or trail off as you lose and find your need again.

title: Hypnagogic Confession
instruction: It's late at night, and you're in bed with someone you love but have been hiding something from. You're both in that drowsy, boundary-less state between waking and sleeping—voices soft, darkness surrounding you, bodies warm and close. Begin by whispering something simple and tender, then let your secret start to surface as if it's coming from a half-dream state where you have no defenses left. Speak as though you're not entirely sure what's real—your confession mixing with fleeting dream-images, sensations, fragments of things you've imagined or feared. Let your voice be barely audible at times, intimate and unguarded. End by either falling silent in vulnerable exposure or finding unexpected relief in finally being known. Move from drowsy tenderness through fearful confession to fragile, naked intimacy.

title: The Unsent Letter Read Aloud
instruction: You're reading a letter you wrote to your parent years ago but never sent—confronting them with everything you needed that they couldn't give you. Start trying to read it calmly, almost clinically, as if discussing someone else's life. But as you voice these long-buried truths, let anger surface—not just anger, but the grief underneath it, the child who still aches for their love. Your voice should crack between fury and pleading, between accusation and desperate hope for understanding. End not with resolution but with exhausted truth: you needed them, and they weren't there, and both things can exist forever. Move from false calm to raw confrontation to exhausted, honest sadness.

title: The Matches I Made to Keep You Near
instruction: Whisper a confession to someone you've been in love with for years. You used to set them up with other people—always with oddly specific, slightly wrong criteria—because you were secretly sabotaging, keeping them single, keeping them close to you. Start with a tender, almost embarrassed admission of the first terrible match you suggested. Your voice should be intimate, vulnerable, as if this confession is being pulled from somewhere deep. Slowly reveal the painful truth: every bad setup was because you couldn't bear to lose them to someone else. Let your voice catch as you admit how lonely this secret has made you, how you've been your own worst enemy. End in a barely audible whisper—you're done matchmaking, done manipulating, and you need to finally tell them how you really feel, even if it destroys everything. The emotion should feel like something fragile finally breaking open.

title: The Truth I Swallowed
instruction: You are confronting your father who is about to walk out the door, perhaps for the last time. For years, you've remained silent about something he did - something that broke a fundamental trust. Begin from a place of controlled anger, your voice steady, your words measured. You've rehearsed this. But as you speak, let the memory of the actual event flood through you - not just the idea of it, but the physical reality: where you were standing, what you were wearing, the temperature of the room, the exact expression on his face. Allow the controlled anger to crack and reveal what's underneath: a deep, childlike terror and bewilderment, the part of you that still doesn't understand why. Move from accusation to a vulnerable, almost pleading question - the question you've needed answered since you were young. End in a place of raw exposure, all defenses stripped away.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: Everything has fallen apart—your marriage, your career, your carefully built life—and somehow you're laughing. Start with hollow laughter that sounds wrong even to you, recounting the absurdity of how completely things have collapsed. Your voice should carry dark humor mixed with disbelief. But as you speak, genuine gratitude begins bleeding through: for the freedom in having nothing left to lose, for the clarity that comes with hitting bottom, for finally being honest about how unhappy you were maintaining the illusion. Let laughter turn to crying turn back to laughter, sometimes in the same sentence. Feel the grief for what's gone and simultaneously the strange, unexpected relief. Your voice should shimmer between contradictions—devastated and liberated, heartbroken and bizarrely hopeful, mourning the death of your old life while feeling intensely, terrifyingly alive. End in a place of paradoxical peace, your voice soft with wonder at finding gratitude in the wreckage.

title: Breaking Through the Performance
instruction: You're in the throes of intense physical passion with someone—but you suddenly realize you're performing it, doing what you think passion should look like rather than feeling it. Your body is moving through motions you've learned from movies, sounds you think you should make. Start there—in that performed, disconnected state. Then let yourself actually notice: What does your skin genuinely feel right now? Where is there real sensation versus numb performance? Allow yourself to stop the performance entirely, even if it means becoming still, awkward, uncertain. Feel the vulnerability of not knowing what 'should' happen next. Let whatever genuine sensation is actually present—whether it's desire, discomfort, tenderness, frustration, or unexpected grief—move through you without choreography. By the end, let your body express something completely unplanned and authentic, even if it's pulling away, crying, laughing, or a kind of raw hunger that surprises you. Move from performance to genuine physical-emotional experience.
inspired_by: Actor is conceptually attached to the material — imposing predetermined emotional ideas about how the piece should be performed

title: Beside the Hospital Bed at 3 AM
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping partner who's been in a coma for six weeks, and the doctors say tomorrow they'll discuss removing life support. Speak in an intimate whisper, as if afraid to wake them—or afraid they'll never wake. 'Hey, love. It's me again. It's 3 AM and I'm here.' Your voice is tender, fragile as glass. Talk about the small things: the coffee they liked, the song on the radio today, how the apartment feels too big now. 'I brought your sweater. It still smells like you.' Your throat catches. 'Everyone says I should prepare to let you go. But how? How do I let go of my whole world?' Tears are falling silently now. 'I'm so tired, baby. So tired of hoping.' Then, barely breathing: 'But I can't stop. Even now, I can't stop loving you.' End with your hand taking theirs: 'If you need to go... I'll be okay. I'll try to be okay.' The lie breaks your heart.

title: The Last Lesson Before the Surgery
instruction: You're teaching your grandmother about the internet the night before her brain surgery—she may not remember who you are afterward. Start with patient tenderness, describing Twitter like birdsong in a town square, Instagram like a scrapbook that never stops growing. But partway through explaining streaming music, your voice begins to fracture. You realize you're not just teaching her about technology—you're trying to give her one last piece of the world you share, one final bridge between you. End trying to explain a meme, then stopping mid-sentence because the absurdity of it breaks you. Your final words should be something like 'I just want you to remember my voice.' Let the ache live in every pause.
inspired_by: Describing Color to a Blind Person

title: Hiding Pain While Recovering From an Injury
instruction: Youre hurt but dont want others to worry or see you as weak. Internally, youre in pain, but you act as if youre fine. Describe the discomfort inside while moving and speaking normally. Speak with a steady tone, suppressing any hints of pain.

title: Treading Water with a Grudge
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a naturally high, sweet voice, treading water in a deep pool after a long, exhausting swim. The person you've been flirting with for weeks is nearby—they just dunked you and held you under as a joke, and you are furious. As you struggle to keep your head above water, the bobbing cuts your words short, and you sputter water. Start with a surprised, breathless interest—like you're still processing their playfulness—but let the anger simmer and spike as you realize the danger. Your voice goes from a cooing, laced-with-lust tone to sharp, ragged accusation. End with cold, exhausted fury, your words clipped by the exertion and bubbling water.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Sexual Lust (slightly present), Anger (extremely present)

title: Reading Their Suicide Note and Laughing Through Tears
instruction: Your best friend left you a note before they died by suicide, and it's so perfectly, devastatingly THEM that you can't help but laugh even as you're breaking apart. Read it aloud, starting with disbelief—this can't be real, this is a joke, they're going to jump out and laugh any second. But as you read their words—their dark humor, their specific references to inside jokes, that one phrase they always said—you start laughing. Really laughing. Because they managed to be funny even now, the assholes. Your laughter should be genuine and horrifying at once. But let the laughter crack and bleed into sobbing, then back to laughter, then back to sobbing, until you can't tell which is which. The note should say something about how much they love you, and that's when you lose it completely. End by whispering 'thank you' through tears, then immediately, furiously: 'Fuck you. Fuck you for leaving me. I love you. God, I love you so much.' Your voice should break on that final declaration—grief and gratitude and rage and love all tangled together until they're inseparable.
inspired_by: Leaving a Voicemail You Know They'll Never Hear

title: Breaking the Heirloom
instruction: You are holding a precious family object—a dish, a watch, something passed down through generations that you were told to treasure and protect. Your body is shaking with years of being told to be careful, be grateful, preserve the past. But this object represents everything you've had to be small for, every time you've had to prioritize family legacy over your own life. Begin with your hands trembling, your breath catching, your voice tight as you speak to the object about what it's cost you. Let your body's tension build—feel your grip tighten, your jaw clench, your breath become sharp and fierce. Let your voice rise from constricted to full, from fear to fury. Then, with a physical and emotional release, let yourself break it or throw it down (mime this safely). In the aftermath, let your body go slack, your breath release, and discover in the silence a strange mixture of grief for what you've destroyed and wild, physical relief at finally breaking free.

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church: When Faith Shatters
instruction: You've just lost your child. You're alone in a church, and you start by trying to pray—your voice shaking, formal, still seeking comfort in familiar words. But within moments, the rage erupts. You're screaming at God, your voice echoing off the walls, demanding answers, hurling accusations with fierce, uncontrolled intensity. 'You took my baby! Where were you? What kind of God—' The fury is volcanic, your voice raw and breaking. Then, mid-scream, you collapse into sobbing—not gentle crying, but the kind that steals your breath, reduces your words to fragments. You're begging now, bargaining, your voice small and broken and desperate. End in exhausted silence, just ragged breathing, as you realize no answer is coming. The arc moves from trembling prayer to explosive rage to shattered pleading to hollow, breathing devastation.
inspired_by: Cocaine High: Words Tumbling Out Uncontrollably

title: The Unsentimental Goodbye
instruction: You're at your grandmother's bedside in her final hours. She's been the pillar of your family, and everyone expects you to be devastated. But as you sit there, don't force yourself to feel what you 'should' feel. Start by noticing everything that actually comes up - maybe irritation at the beeping machines, a random memory of her burnt cookies, the urge to laugh at something inappropriate she once said, frustration at your own numbness, or unexpected anger that she's leaving. Let yourself move through whatever emerges moment by moment - boredom, guilt about being bored, a sudden wave of love, then back to noticing the ugly wallpaper. By the end, allow whatever genuine feeling has been building underneath all the 'wrong' reactions to finally surface. The emotional journey moves from resisting expected grief to discovering what you actually feel.
inspired_by: Being Irreverent to Your Concept of the Material

title: The Crunch of Envy
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting at a kitchen table, slowly eating a crisp apple. Through the window, you watch your grandson effortlessly fix a car engine—something you could never do even in your prime. You begin with deep concentration on chewing each bite carefully, but as you watch him, astonishment washes over you at his skill, then jealousy creeps in, bitter and sharp. Let the crunching and swallowing interrupt your words naturally—pauses, slight choking, the sound of teeth breaking the apple. Your voice should shift from focused and steady to shaky with envy, ending on a quiet, resentful sigh.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
