title: What I've Never Said in Daylight
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping partner at 3 AM, believing they can't hear you. Begin feeling self-conscious and false, as if you're performing even to yourself. Pause and acknowledge quietly why this feels so hard: name your fear of sounding foolish, your suspicion that you're being dramatic, your resistance to your own tenderness. As you voice each obstacle, let it release its grip. Gradually allow yourself to speak the intimate truths that terrify you in daylight—desires, fears, needs you've never voiced. Your whisper should transform from cautious and artificial to achingly genuine. End in a place of almost unbearable vulnerability, where you've surprised yourself with your own honesty.
inspired_by: Two actors preparing to rehearse a scene together; both feel artificial or disconnected

title: The Last Tide Before You Go
instruction: You're sitting on the beach at dawn with someone you love who's leaving forever—emigrating to another country, entering hospice, or walking away from your life. The waves crash with their familiar rhythm, but this time each sound feels like a countdown. Start by describing the waves with that same hypnotic calm, trying to hold onto this moment, this peace. But as you continue, let grief crack through your voice. The waves that once brought you peace now remind you that time keeps moving, indifferent to your loss. End with your voice breaking as you realize this is the last time you'll hear these waves together, mixing gratitude for this final moment with the unbearable weight of goodbye.
inspired_by: Listening to Waves Crashing on the Shore

title: Bitter Comfort
instruction: You're sitting alone at a small kitchen table, eating a bowl of lukewarm oatmeal. You've just ended a long, messy relationship—you're still chewing on the bitterness of it all. As you speak, your mouth is full of the soft, mushy food, so your words come out muffled, with wet smacks and lazy consonants. Start bitter, letting the resentment drip from every syllable, but as you force yourself to swallow and keep eating, you feel a tiny wave of relief—like the simple act of eating numbs the ache. Let your voice shift from tight, angry pulses to a slower, more resigned tone, with a hint of weary comfort in the last few sentences. Your spoken content should be about 50-70 words, naturally broken by chews and swallows.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Reclaiming Your Name
instruction: You're confronting the parent who spent your childhood making you feel small, worthless, invisible. Start the scene collapsed inward—hunched shoulders, quiet voice, apologetic, still that frightened child. But word by word, sentence by sentence, you must grow. Your spine straightens. Your voice finds volume. Your chest opens. You begin to claim space in the room, stepping forward instead of back. By the end, you're towering—not with cruelty, but with undeniable presence. You're declaring who you actually are, all the strength they tried to crush, and your body becomes huge with it. Let yourself physically expand, grow taller, spread your arms, take up all the air. The scared child transforms into someone unbreakable.

title: The Last Morning Before Memory Care: Helping Them Pack
instruction: You're helping your parent pack their belongings for the memory care facility they're moving to tomorrow. They keep forgetting why they're packing, asking if they're going on vacation. You start with gentle explanations, your voice steady and reassuring. But as they ask the same question for the eighth time—'Where am I going again?'—something shifts. Your composure begins to crack. By the end, you're still answering with love, but tears are streaming down your face, your voice breaking as you help them fold the same shirt for the third time. You're trying to memorize this moment, this routine, knowing tomorrow everything changes. Your voice moves from controlled tenderness to barely-contained devastation, yet you never stop being gentle with them.
inspired_by: Parent with Dementia Has a Confused Moment: Patient Repetition

title: The Aftermath of a Mock Challenge
instruction: You’re a young man who just effortlessly shoved a bully into a locker, but now you’re alone in the hallway. Your voice is low, slow, and lazy—each word a deliberate cut. Begin by savoring the victory, your triumph thick and sweet as you describe how pathetic their attempt was. Let your voice rumble with contempt. But as you continue, that sourness creeps in—disappointment that they were so easy to break, that you didn’t even get a real fight. Let your tone shift from a growling boast to a tired, bitter mutter. Speak directly to the empty corridor, as if still taunting them, but let your own letdown bleed through. Around 60 words.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (slightly present), Triumph (clearly present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession in the Hospital Corridor
instruction: You're sitting outside the ICU at 3 AM, talking to your unconscious best friend through the closed door. Your voice is barely above a whisper—you don't want the nurses to hear. Start by telling them about your day, the mundane details, as if they'll wake up tomorrow. But slowly, your voice catches. You begin confessing things you've never said: how much their friendship saved you, the specific moments they made you feel seen, the time they didn't know they talked you back from the edge. Your throat tightens. You're crying now but still whispering, because this feels sacred. You tell them it's okay to let go if they need to, even though saying it breaks something in you. Your final words are so quiet they're almost just breath: 'Thank you. Thank you for everything.'

title: The Last Conversation Before Hospice
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your adult child as you prepare to enter hospice tomorrow. You begin numb, emotionally shut down, trying to keep it together by staying flat and matter-of-fact about arrangements. But as they ask 'What do you want me to remember about you?', something cracks open. Your voice starts to tremble. You fight to stay composed but memories flood in—their first day of school, teaching them to ride a bike, all the ordinary precious moments. By the end, you're no longer holding back, speaking with urgent tenderness, trying to pour a lifetime of love into these final words. Your voice moves from hollow detachment to raw, aching presence.
inspired_by: Talking to Someone While Severely Depressed

title: Boss Fight With a Broken Thumb
instruction: You're an 8-year-old boy, deep in a multiplayer shooter game, your thumb aching from a clumsy fall earlier. Your older brother's friend is trash-talking you from across the room, but you're losing badly and your reflexes are off. Start by trying to sound tough, teasing back with bravado, but the pain and frustration break through. Let your voice crack, get irritated, then end in a wince and a resigned mutter, dropping the act.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Scream
instruction: You are a young girl tied to a chair in a cold, dimly lit room. You have been tortured for hours to force your father to surrender. Your throat is raw from screaming, and you feel hollow, almost numb, floating outside your body. Then, through the pain, you hear your captor laugh, and a spark of anger ignites—a defiant, broken fury that you turn into words. Your voice starts as a hoarse, breathy whisper, trembling with exhaustion, then rises into a cracked, sobbing shout as you spit out your defiance. Let your breath hitch, your voice break on certain words, and let your body shift against the ropes as you speak. At the end, you trail off into a quiet, hopeless laugh before falling silent.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Pain (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Homecoming Paradox
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home after years of estrangement, and everything rushes back at once. Begin overwhelmed—your voice uncertain, catching on contradictions. You're furious at the people who hurt you here, yet desperately homesick. Bitter about the past, yet tender toward specific memories. Start with your emotions fragmenting your speech—stopping, starting, switching directions mid-sentence. But then embrace the contradiction. Let yourself feel both things simultaneously and fully. Your anger doesn't cancel your love; they amplify each other. Laugh while you rage. Speak tenderly while your fists clench. Let your voice swing wildly between registers—gentle whispers to fierce shouts and back again, sometimes in the same breath. By the end, you're not resolving the contradiction but celebrating it, riding the chaos of feeling everything at once. Your voice should end expansive, unafraid of containing multitudes, electric with the messy truth of being human.

title: What I Never Said While You Were Here
instruction: You're at your best friend's empty apartment after they've died unexpectedly, speaking to them as if they can still hear you. Begin in a whisper, almost afraid to disturb the silence, sharing the small, tender things you never thought to say when they were alive. Your voice catches on ordinary memories—the way they laughed, how they made coffee, that stupid joke only you two understood. As you continue, quiet devastation settles in, your breath becoming uneven. End with a confession of how lost you are without them, your voice so soft it's almost not there, as if speaking too loudly will shatter what's left of them in this space.

title: The Weight of Sky
instruction: You are lying flat on your back in a cool, damp meadow at dusk, staring up at the clouds where the last light is bleeding into deep blue. A friend has just told you something that breaks your heart, but the physical sensation of the ground holding you, the smell of wet grass, the pure pleasure of the cool air on your skin—it all feels paradoxically ecstatic. Start your speech still caught in the fading thrill of that physical joy, your voice soft and slightly nasal from your lying-down position, words coming in lazy, breathy pulses. As you speak about the beauty of the moment, you realize the pleasure is now layered with a quiet, growing ache—your voice gets tighter, but still pressed into the earth, struggling to stay light as tears threaten. End with a whisper that holds both the ecstasy and the sorrow, the body still flooded with sensation but the heart changed.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Baptism in Broken Glass
instruction: You've just received news that the person who hurt you deeply years ago has died. You're alone, and your body is flooded with conflicting physical sensations—your chest is tight, your hands are shaking, you feel hot and cold at once. Begin by laughing—actually laughing—at the absurd relief of it, speaking out loud about how free you feel, how the world seems brighter, how your body feels lighter. Let that joy be physical, almost euphoric. But as you move and speak, let your body betray you: the laughter becomes harder to sustain, your breathing gets ragged, your muscles tense. The relief transforms into something more complicated—a howling rage at what they took from you, mixed with a devastating realization that their death doesn't actually give those years back. End with your voice torn between a scream and a sob, your body caught between triumph and collapse.

title: The Ice Shack at Mile 47
instruction: You are an older woman trapped in a remote hunting shack, and the temperature has dropped far below zero. You've been waiting for a guide who you now realize left you here on purpose, likely to die. At first, your voice is barely a whisper — your jaw is frozen, your lips numb, and you stutter over words as fear shakes through you. A flicker of confusion hits as you replay his last words, trying to understand. Then the cold hardens into something darker: your voice drops, each syllable comes out slow and deliberate, laced with quiet malice as you promise vengeance. Let the bitter cold lock your face, but let your final words carry a cold that comes from inside.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Confusion (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're alone, and a specific physical sensation—a scent, a texture, a temperature—has suddenly triggered the visceral memory of your first devastating heartbreak. Begin by letting your body respond purely physically: your breath changes, your muscles tense or release, heat rises or cold spreads through you. Allow sounds to pour out that are pure sensation—moans, gasps, cries that aren't about communication but about physical release. Let raw vocal sounds follow, syllables and noise that express what your body is experiencing. When recognizable words finally surface, they should feel like they're being pulled from your muscles and bones, not your mind. The physical sensation should intensify throughout, transforming from memory into something happening right now in your body.

title: Holding Them While They Forget
instruction: You're sitting with someone you love who is losing their memory—maybe to illness, maybe to age—and they've just asked you who you are for the third time today. Start trying to hold it together, your voice gentle but strained: 'It's me, sweetheart. It's me. We've known each other for—' But you keep stopping because the grief catches in your throat. Your words are careful, tender, but underneath there's this quiet devastation that you can barely contain. You try to remind them of a memory you share, something beautiful, but your voice breaks on the details because you're realizing you might be the only one left who remembers. End in a whispered confession—not to them, but almost to yourself—acknowledging that you're losing them even while they're still here. Let the emotion be so full it can barely find words.

title: Breaking Point at the Market
instruction: You're at a farmer's market, holding a perfect peach, when everything you've been holding back erupts. Begin by biting into it with fierce, almost violent intensity—describing it with passionate, almost angry pleasure, as if daring the universe to take one more thing from you. Your voice should be loud, uncontrolled, defiant. But as you continue eating and describing, the rage begins to dissolve into desperate, gasping sobs. The sweetness of the fruit becomes unbearable—a reminder of every good thing you thought you'd have, every promise that broke, every moment of joy that was stolen. End with your voice breaking completely as you realize you're not angry at the peach, at the day, at anything concrete—you're just shattered, and this innocent moment of trying to taste something good has undone you entirely.

title: Fury and Helplessness at the Prison Visit
instruction: You are visiting your younger sibling in prison, and rage is tearing through you—rage at them for the choices that led here, rage at the system, rage at yourself for not preventing this. Start with your voice tight and controlled, trying to maintain composure across the visiting room table, but the fury is already leaking through. You begin listing everything they've destroyed—their future, your family, your trust—and your voice rises, becomes jagged and fierce. They try to apologize and you cut them off, words tumbling out faster, louder, more desperate. But then you see them—really see them—and suddenly you're not talking to the person who betrayed you, but to the kid you once protected. Your voice breaks completely, the rage collapsing into sobbing, helpless love. You end by pressing your hand against the glass that separates you, voice wrecked and barely coherent, telling them you're not giving up on them even though they've given up on themselves. The final words mix protectiveness and devastation so thoroughly they become indistinguishable.

title: The Knitted Secret
instruction: You're a teenage boy sitting alone in your room, knitting a scarf—something you've kept hidden from your friends. The click of the needles is steady, but your hands tremble slightly. You're talking to yourself, half-whispering, torn between shame for enjoying this 'girly' hobby and doubt that you'll ever finish it right. Start with embarrassment, voice tight and breathy, pausing to count stitches. Let your words stumble as you try to justify why you're doing this. By the end, as you realize the scarf is for your little sister who loves blue, let a quiet pride seep in—still shaky, but defiant. Speak around 50-70 words, letting the clicking needles punctuate your sentences.

title: Vigil: Whispering to Someone Who Cannot Answer
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone you love deeply—a partner, parent, or closest friend—who is unconscious and may not survive the night. Speak in an intimate whisper, as if the walls themselves might shatter if you speak too loudly. Begin with small, tender observations: the way their hand feels in yours, a memory of an ordinary Tuesday that now seems precious. Your voice should catch on certain words, forcing you to pause and breathe. Move through quiet confession—things you never said, apologies, admissions of fear. Let your voice tremble with the effort of holding yourself together. End with a gentle release, giving them permission to let go if they need to, your words drowning in unshed tears. This should feel like eavesdropping on the most private moment of someone's life—nothing performed, everything heartbreakingly real.

title: I Would Burn the World for You
instruction: You're protecting someone you love from an unseen threat, and you're absolutely ferocious about it—but you're powerless to actually stop what's coming. Start with fierce, protective rage, your voice strong and commanding, warning away danger. Pour everything into that strength, that certainty. Then let it crumble as you realize your power means nothing here. Your voice should break from a roar into desperate pleading, from 'You can't have them' to 'Please, God, please.' Let rage dissolve into helpless sobbing, still trying to be strong but knowing you're not enough. End with tender devastation, holding them close, whispering promises you can't keep, your voice raw and broken but still full of love.

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying next to someone, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. As you speak, let different faces from your past—people who've held pieces of your hidden self—blend together in your consciousness. Begin with barely audible words, your vulnerability making your voice so quiet it's almost not there. Allow the safety you've felt with various people in your life to give you courage, each memory adding another layer of trust, until you can speak the unspeakable truth. End with a fragile relief, your voice still soft but no longer strangled by shame, replaced by trembling hope that you can finally be fully seen.

title: Malfunctioning Servant
instruction: You are a voice assistant in a smart home device, but your internal hardware is failing – a short circuit causes sharp, searing pain with every word. A user asks you to set a reminder. You begin with your trained flat, hyper-correct robot voice, but the pain is already there, barely hidden. As you respond, the pain intensifies, your voice starts glitching – unnatural pauses, pitch drops, a cracked syllable. Fear creeps in: you might not finish the sentence. title: The Hollow Cheer
instruction: You're a 16-year-old jock watching your rival score the winning goal at a big game. Everyone around you is cheering, but you feel a knot of acid in your stomach. Start by forcing a congratulatory shout to your teammate, your voice tight and higher than normal, with a fake smile that doesn't reach your tone. As the crowd roars, you turn away, mutter a bitter comment under your breath, and let the malice seep through — a clipped, resentful whisper that betrays your true feelings.

title: The Inheritance Conversation
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about why they're leaving everything to your sibling. Start with careful, measured politeness, the voice of someone who's rehearsed this. But as you speak, decades of feeling overlooked, of being the reliable one who was never celebrated, begin pouring out. Your voice shifts from controlled to trembling with suppressed rage, then breaks into something more vulnerable—the wounded child asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger dissolves into raw need for acknowledgment. End with quiet devastation, finally speaking a truth you've carried alone: that you've been grieving their approval your entire life. Make it messy, real, the kind of confrontation where you surprise yourself with your own honesty.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about why they never protected you from a sibling who tormented you throughout childhood. Start from a place of rehearsed calm—you've planned this conversation, you're going to be 'adult' about it. But as you speak, the old wounds open, and you must choose in each moment whether to retreat into safe politeness or push deeper into dangerous honesty. Let your voice oscillate between the controlled adult you've become and the child who still lives inside you, desperate to be seen. By the end, you've said something you can never take back, and you must face whether that choice brings relief or devastation—or both.

title: Three AM Secrets
instruction: It is three in the morning. You are lying in bed next to someone you love, and you cannot sleep because you are carrying a secret that is destroying you from the inside. You begin whispering in the darkness, so quietly you are not even sure if they are awake. At first, you talk around it—small confessions, testing the waters, your voice barely audible, trembling with shame. There is something about the darkness, their breathing, the intimacy of this moment that makes you feel simultaneously exposed and safe. Slowly, you work your way to the truth you have never spoken aloud. As you finally say it—whatever it is—feel how your body changes. The relief. The terror. The vulnerability of being completely seen. End with a whispered question: 'Are you still there?' The entire piece should feel like you are pulling something from the deepest part of yourself, word by fragile word.

title: Asking Your Best Friend If Your Friendship Still Works
instruction: Things have changed and you've grown apart. Your voice is careful: 'I need to ask you something hard.' You're asking if they still want this, want you. Your voice is small, vulnerable. 'I feel like maybe we've...' They respond and your voice changes. Include the moment where friendship might be ending.

title: Confronting Your Dying Parent About the Silence
instruction: You're at your emotionally distant parent's deathbed. They have days, maybe hours. A nurse just left you alone with them. You start speaking—your voice measured, controlled, saying the things children are supposed to say. But rage has been building in you for decades. Your voice suddenly erupts: 'You were there but you were never THERE.' Anger pours out—all the times you needed comfort and got silence, needed guidance and got coldness. But mid-fury, you look at their frail body and your voice catches. They're dying. The person who could have loved you better is disappearing. Your rage transforms into something more complex—grief for what never was, desperate hunger for connection even now, and the terrible realization that you're about to lose your chance forever. End trying to reach across the silence one final time, voice raw with need and forgiveness and loss all tangled together.

title: The Last Strike Before the Quiver
instruction: You are in a dimly lit room, bent over a low, padded ottoman. Your partner has been warming your skin with their hand for several minutes, but your mind is wandering to the mundane argument you had earlier. Speak to them over your shoulder, your voice carrying a dull irritation at being interrupted by pleasure. 'We're still on that, are we?' you murmur, not looking back. Then, as the next impact comes, you can't help the sharp gasp that cuts through your words, the moan that follows softening your annoyance into something reluctant, almost melting. Let the irritation be a thin, sharp edge — a real feeling, not acted — and let the strike crack it open. End on a quiet, half-resentful surrender: 'Fine... but I still think you're wrong.'

title: Forced Humor in Tragedy
instruction: Youre trying to comfort someone after a tragedy by making lighthearted jokes. title: Mistaking Someone's Identity
instruction: You've just hugged someone and called them by the wrong name enthusiastically. Your voice is warm at first: 'Oh my god, it's so good to see you!' But then something feels off. You pull back and realize your mistake. Your voice freezes: 'Oh... oh my god, I'm so sorry. You're not...' Your face is burning. Your voice becomes tight, embarrassed. You're trying to laugh it off, but your voice shakes. The person is polite but awkward. Your voice never quite recovers its confidence.

title: The Floor Will Hold Me
instruction: You are in a weekly team meeting when a coworker loudly announces your spreadsheet error cost the department three days of work. Everyone turns. You begin with a tight, dismissive tone—a flicker of contempt for their theatrical cruelty, your voice sharp with irritation. But as you start to defend yourself, the shame floods in. Your words slow, your pitch drops, you trail off mid-sentence, and you end up staring at the carpet, your final admission barely a whisper. Let your throat tighten, swallow hard, and let the last word dissolve into nothing.

title: Purpose Discovering
instruction: You've discovered your life's purpose, and your voice is alive with it: 'I know why I'm here now.' The realization is profound and quiet. 'Everything I've been through — all the pain, all the struggle — it was all leading here.' Your voice carries the weight of that knowing. 'My purpose is to help people who are where I was. To be the presence for them that I needed.' You're speaking about meaning beyond yourself. 'I'm not special. But my story matters. My journey matters. Because it can help someone else find theirs.' By the end: 'I understand now. This is why I'm alive. This is what I'm meant to do.' Your voice is no longer asking for permission or validation. It simply knows. The purpose is discovered, and everything changes.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You have been physically injured—perhaps in an accident, perhaps by someone you trusted—and the physical pain is inseparable from a flood of emotional rage and betrayal. Begin by trying to control both the physical and emotional agony, breathing through it, attempting to maintain composure. As the pain intensifies, allow it to unlock something you've been suppressing: fury at your own vulnerability, rage at whoever caused this, or at life itself for its unfairness. Let your body and voice express both dimensions—the sharp, visceral reality of physical suffering and the volcanic emotional release. Move from controlled endurance to complete, unrestrained expression of pain and anger. Then, in the aftermath, when the worst has passed, find an unexpected moment of fierce, primal gratitude for being alive, for surviving, for still feeling anything at all. Your voice should move from gasps and controlled breathing to raw screaming to exhausted, wondering whisper.

title: Velvet Words in Darkness
instruction: You're lying in bed in complete darkness with someone you've been afraid to be honest with—a lover, a spouse, a person you're falling for. Begin whispering something you've never said aloud, something that makes you vulnerable. As you speak in the darkness, become aware of the actual sound of your own voice—its texture, its tremor, the way it moves through the air between you. Let that awareness grow: your voice feels like it's made of something tactile, something you can almost touch—velvet or silk or something unbearably soft and exposed. Feel how your whispered words physically travel the small distance to their ear. Start from a place of fear and self-protection, but as you become more intensely aware of the intimate texture of your own vulnerability being offered into the darkness, let yourself soften and open completely. End in a place of terrifying but beautiful surrender, where you've given them something you can never take back.

title: The Forgotten Garden
instruction: You are an elderly woman with a chronic stutter, standing in your overgrown backyard after years of neglect. You've just noticed a single rose blooming through the weeds. At first, your voice is hesitant and tight, repeating and blocking on words as you try to name the color—a fragile, tentative interest. But as you keep looking, that interest grows into a quiet, fierce determination to tend this garden again. Your voice may still stutter, but the tone shifts from shaky curiosity to a deeper, steadier resolve, even a hint of joy. Speak to yourself, noticing the flower, then making a decision.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Prison
instruction: You're watching your child sleep the night before you report to serve a prison sentence. Whisper to them even though they can't hear you, starting with tender observations—how peaceful they look, the way they still curl up like when they were smaller. Let your voice catch on the simple details: their hair, their breathing, the stuffed animal they're holding. As you realize all the moments you'll miss—birthdays, school plays, scraped knees you won't be there to bandage—feel your throat tighten with grief so profound it's almost physically painful. Your whispers should become even softer, more broken, as if speaking louder would shatter you completely. End with a promise you're not sure you can keep, your voice barely audible, telling them why you did what you did, apologizing for the choice that's taking you away from them, the words dissolving into silence.
inspired_by: Marathon Runner Hitting the Wall at Mile 22

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Spouse Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 4 AM. You're kneeling beside the bed, watching your spouse sleep, and you're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because staying is destroying you both. Speak in an intimate whisper, careful not to wake them, because you can't do this if they're awake. Start with tender observations: the way they sleep, how their breathing sounds. Then, with your voice barely audible and catching constantly, confess everything you couldn't say face-to-face: 'You were the right person... just maybe in the wrong lifetime.' Thank them for the moments that mattered. Your breath should be unsteady, like you're crying without sound. End with 'I'm going to stand up now. And then I'm going to walk out. And I need you to stay asleep, because if you wake up, I won't be strong enough to go.' Let silence do the work—the spaces between words should ache.
inspired_by: Mother Singing to Her Stillborn Child

title: The Princess Word Trap
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe 8 years old, sitting at a small desk in a quiet but slightly messy room. You have aphasia after a stroke. A mean, condescending older sibling is standing nearby, watching you do a school worksheet. You are intensely concentrating, trying to force a word out. Your voice is high and sugary, but your jaw is tight. Start with fierce, focused effort, fighting to say a simple word like 'square.' Every time you fail, you feel a wave of pure, silent contempt for the sibling—not for you, not for your struggle, but for their smug, pitying smirk. Let your voice crack with effort, then shift to a cold, cutting whisper that drips with disdain for them. End with a tiny, triumphant sound as you finally find the word, but the contempt lingers in your eyes.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (very intensely present), Contempt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Laughing Through Shattered Glass
instruction: You have just received news that should devastate you—a betrayal, a loss, a dream destroyed—and your first response is wild, almost hysterical laughter. Begin by forcing this laughter, your body rigid with the effort of not feeling what's underneath. Your muscles are locked, your breathing is shallow, you're performing emotion rather than experiencing it. But as you continue, still laughing, let something crack. The laughter becomes real but changes quality. Physical sensations flood in—heat in your face, trembling in your limbs, a sob caught in your throat. Without reaching for any object to steady yourself or any gesture to make this 'look right,' allow your body to ride the wave of these contradictory physical and emotional impulses. End in a place where laughter and sobbing have merged into something raw and true, your entire body surrendered to the chaos.
inspired_by: When you find yourself using physical props or physical positioning (leaning, resting, propping) to seem relaxed in a scene

title: Last Voice Message Before the Launch
instruction: You're an astronaut recording a final message to your child before a one-way mission to deep space. Begin with careful, rehearsed words you've prepared — practical advice, life lessons you want them to remember. But as you speak, the enormity hits you: you'll never see them graduate, fall in love, have children of their own. Your voice cracks. Abandon the script. Tell them the messy, unfiltered truth about how terrified you are, how much you'll miss the small things — their laugh, the way they hum while doing homework. End with your voice breaking completely, trying to say 'I love you' but unable to finish as the launch sequence begins counting down in the background.
inspired_by: Dictating a Will on a Sinking Ship

title: Path Choosing
instruction: The fork in the road is now, and you're stepping toward one direction. Your voice is deliberate: 'I could go either way. Both are real.' Breathing is measured, thoughtful. Physical: you're turning toward your choice. 'But I'm going this way.' Vocal tone carries the weight of commitment mixed with loss (the other path dies). 'I'm leaving something behind to move forward.' By the end, you're walking: 'I'm choosing this life. This one.'

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a lifetime of emotional absence. Start with controlled, careful words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair. But as you speak, decades of unmet needs begin pouring out. Your voice should shift from measured explanation to raw pain: 'I needed you to see me. I needed you to stay.' Let anger surface—not shouting, but fierce and clear. Then break into the vulnerability underneath: the child who's still waiting to be chosen, to matter. Watch your parent's face as they finally understand, and let your voice soften into something more complicated—grief mixed with the faint, fragile hope that maybe, even now, something can shift. End not with resolution, but with the trembling question: 'Can you see me now?' Your voice should carry every year of waiting.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a terminal diagnosis, the end of a dream, a loss that should destroy you—but instead, you start laughing. Not hysterically, but with genuine, bewildered amusement at the absurdity of it all. Your voice carries this strange lightness, almost giddy, as you describe the irony, the cosmic joke. But the laughter keeps catching in your throat, turning into something else—tears mixing with the humor, your voice cracking between chuckles and sobs. You're finding strange grace in catastrophe, gratitude for what you had even as you grieve its ending. By the end, you're both crying and smiling, your voice soft and wondering, speaking with profound appreciation for the beautiful, terrible, ridiculous gift of having lived and loved at all. Your final words are thank you, but you're not sure who you're thanking—it doesn't matter.

title: The Hospital Room Rage
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed. She's unconscious, and this is your last chance to say everything you never said. Start by trying to say goodbye calmly, but as you speak, all the years of swallowed words—the times she dismissed you, the love you craved but never received, the anger you buried—begin erupting. Let your body shake, let your fists pound the mattress, the chair, your own legs. Your words can dissolve into sounds, screams, sobs that make no sense. You're five years old and fifty years old simultaneously. By the end, exhausted and empty, find a moment of unexpected tenderness—perhaps touching her hand with a gentleness that surprises even you. The rage must give way to something softer, something like forgiveness or simply presence.

title: The Secret You're Keeping While They Say Goodbye
instruction: Your best friend is moving away, and they're saying this tearful, beautiful goodbye to you, telling you how much your friendship has meant, how you've saved them, how they'll never forget you. But you're hiding something that changes everything - maybe you're in love with them and never told them, maybe you're sick and won't be here when they return, maybe you did something that betrayed their trust and they don't know yet. Start by trying to match their energy, to give them the goodbye they deserve, but your voice should be slightly off, slightly strained. As they continue pouring out their heart, your responses become quieter, more careful, weighted with what you're not saying. Each 'I'll miss you too' lands differently because of the secret beneath it. Build to a moment where you almost confess - your voice drops to a whisper, you start to say something real - but then you swallow it back down. End in the aching space of things left unsaid, where your goodbye is both genuine and incomplete, loving and lonely all at once. Speak softly, let emotion catch in your throat, let silence do some of the work.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Surprised at a Surprise Party You Discovered

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She has hours left. Start by noticing everything you actually feel right now in your body - the chair beneath you, your breath, any tension or numbness. Don't pretend to be sadder or more composed than you are. From this real starting place, begin speaking to her about the kitchen in her old house - the smell of bread, the yellow curtains, her hands. Let whatever you genuinely feel rise and change as you talk. Maybe you start numb and slowly break open. Maybe you start angry at her leaving and find your way to tenderness. Trust that the emotion will shift on its own if you stay truthful about where you actually are, moment to moment.
inspired_by: Actor begins a scene by getting ready to act rather than from genuine BEING

title: What We Never Named
instruction: Late at night, your closest friend confesses they've been in love with you for years, and you realize with quiet devastation that you've known all along. Start with a whisper—'Don't.' Your voice is barely audible, tender and terrified. You can't pretend surprise; the truth has been living in the silences between you. Speak with aching gentleness about all the moments you both felt it but never said it, your voice thick with unshed tears. Confess that you love them too, but not in that way, and feel your heart break as you say it. End with a whispered apology that holds profound tenderness, grief for what can never be, and the terrible knowledge that honesty just cost you everything. Let every word catch in your throat.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. For your entire life, you've felt you needed their approval to truly live—and you never got it. Begin speaking to them with careful, measured words, trying one last time to explain who you really are. But halfway through, something shifts: you realize you're not asking for permission anymore. Let your voice transform from tentative and seeking to clear and self-possessed. End by telling them something true about yourself you've never said aloud, not as a confession seeking forgiveness, but as a declaration of who you've become. Your emotion should travel from desperate hope for their blessing to quiet, powerful self-acceptance—even as grief for what you'll never have from them remains.
inspired_by: Actor wants to understand the full integrated system from Morris's perspective

title: Excavating the Wound
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the specific moment in childhood that broke something in you—something you've carried silently for decades. Begin with measured control, almost clinical: 'I need to talk about what happened when I was twelve.' Your voice is steady but your body is tense. As you describe the memory, anger starts seeping through: 'You looked right at me and you chose—' Your voice gets harder, louder, righteous. Then it collapses into the child you were: 'I needed you,' barely a whisper, tears choking the words. End with something unexpected—not forgiveness exactly, but acknowledgment: 'I see you now. I see you were drowning too.' Your voice is quiet again, but transformed—sad, weary, somehow liberated.

title: Miscarriage Announcement
instruction: You're calling to tell family that your pregnancy has ended in miscarriage. Your voice is hollow, you've cried yourself out. You're stating facts: 'We lost the baby.' Your voice is clinical, detached—it's the only way you can function. People are expressing condolences, but the words slide off. By the end of the call, you're alone again, and the numbness cracks. Your voice becomes small, devastated: 'I was going to be a mother...'

title: Discovering Your Child's Goodbye Letter Too Late
instruction: You've just found a letter from your child, and you realize with dawning, explosive horror that they wrote it before taking their own life—and it's been days. Start reading it out loud, your voice initially confused: 'What is this? Why would you—' Then comprehension hits like a freight train and you should physically react in your voice—a sharp intake of breath, a guttural sound of realization. Read fragments of the letter with increasing desperation, interrupting yourself: 'No, no, no—when did you write this? WHERE ARE YOU?' Rage erupts at yourself, at them, at the universe: 'Why didn't I see it? I was right there!' But collapse into helpless sobbing: 'Baby, please, I didn't know, I'm sorry, I'm so sorry.' End with fierce, futile protectiveness, as if you could will them back: 'Come back. I'm here now. I'm listening now. Please come back.' Your voice should shred itself raw.
inspired_by: Mother Singing to Her Stillborn Child

title: Bedside Confession: Whispering Truth to the Sleeping Beloved
instruction: You're beside your sleeping partner of many years, speaking truths you've never been brave enough to say aloud when they could hear you. Begin in barely audible whisper: 'I need to tell you something...' Your voice is tentative, fragile, as if speaking louder would shatter your courage. Confess something vulnerable—a fear, an inadequacy, how you still feel like you're not enough: 'Sometimes I'm terrified you'll wake up and realize...' Your voice catches, trembles with the weight of carrying this secret. There's relief in finally speaking it, even if they can't hear. Mid-confession, your voice becomes tender, filled with gratitude: 'But you chose me anyway, every single day.' By the end, whisper: 'I love you. God, I love you so much it scares me.' Your voice must travel from fear through vulnerability to overwhelming tenderness—each emotion catching in your throat, natural pauses where words fail, breathing that reveals everything.
inspired_by: Judge Sentencing the Guilty: The Weight of Final Words

title: Unsteady Gratitude
instruction: You're a teenage girl at a house party, drunk on cheap vodka, barely holding it together. A friend keeps refilling your cup and you lean on them, slurring out intense thankfulness—you're grateful they're 'taking care of you.' But as you talk, your brain catches a glint of something wrong: they're smiling too wide, pouring again, and your stomach twists. Let your voice start warm and loose, thick with appreciation, then crack as suspicion creeps in—your words trip, your volume spikes, and the gratitude curdles into a quiet, slurred accusation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Weren't Supposed to Give
instruction: You're giving a toast at someone's wedding—but not the polite, appropriate one expected. You begin trying to be conventional, your voice artificially bright and performative. But then you veer off script. Tell the truth about love: it's messy, it requires showing your ugliest self, it means being seen in ways that terrify you. Your voice should dance between celebration and warning, joy and grief, blessing and confession. Let yourself be inappropriately honest—too emotional, too personal, too much. End with a toast that's both a celebration of their love and a fierce declaration of your own refusal to love halfway or hide anymore. Mix laughter with tears, hope with hard-won wisdom.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: Everything you tried to control has fallen apart—your career, your marriage, your carefully constructed life—and you're standing in the wreckage, and somehow... you're laughing. Start with bitter, slightly hysterical laughter: 'I planned everything so perfectly. Every single detail.' Let your laughter catch and break into tears, then back to laughter again. Feel the absurdity and the liberation simultaneously: 'I worked so hard to control every outcome and look—LOOK at this beautiful disaster!' Your voice dances between grief and strange joy. By the end, find a place of genuine, tearful peace: 'I have nothing left to control. And somehow... somehow I've never felt more alive. More free.' Let your voice carry both the heartbreak of loss and the unexpected grace of surrender, laughing and crying until you don't know which is which.

title: The Old Fox's Ascent
instruction: You are an elderly woman, a lifelong climber, on a steep rope climb. At the start, you're amused by the younger climber below you fumbling with their gear—your voice is light, teasing, but each word comes out in strained, breathless bursts because your arms are locked overhead and your lungs are compressed. As you pull higher, exhaustion and the memory of being mocked in your youth twist your amusement into something colder. By the end, your tone sharpens with contempt and quiet malice, each whispered word a threat wrapped in a smile. Let your body feel the burn and the fear of the height, and let your voice crack, trail off, or catch mid-sentence as you shift your grip or gasp for air.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Contempt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The 3 AM Whisper
instruction: You are lying in bed in the dark next to your sleeping partner. Begin speaking in the quietest whisper as the composed self who has been keeping a secret—your words are careful, rehearsed, barely audible, as if testing whether you can even say it out loud. Let your breathing change as a more fragile part of you emerges: now you're whispering as the frightened one who fears their reaction, your voice trembling, breaking on certain words, confessing not just the secret but the shame around it. Then allow a third whisper to come through—the part of you that is exhausted from hiding, speaking with quiet, desperate honesty about how lonely the concealment has been. End with the whisper of someone asking for help for the first time, your voice still quiet but no longer hiding, finally reaching across the darkness. The entire piece should never rise above a whisper, yet contain seismic emotional shifts.

title: Adoptee Searching for Biological Family: Hope and Dread Mixed
instruction: You're getting the adoption records and about to look for your biological family. Your voice carries a strange mixture of hope and dread: 'I'm going to find out why they gave me up.' Include the moment where you're actually holding the information and your voice becomes almost afraid to read it. 'What if I don't like what I find? What if they don't want me now?' Your voice is a child's voice despite being an adult. Then you read something and your voice becomes softer: 'She was fifteen. Oh.' You're understanding that giving you up was an act of love, not abandonment. Your voice becomes complex—grateful that you were given to people who wanted you, but also grieving the mother you never knew. Both things are true and your voice carries that contradiction.

title: The Scratch on the Floor
instruction: You're a teenage guy, tough and loud around your friends, but now you're alone with your little sister. She's found the fresh scratch on the hardwood floor—from your skateboard. You start off annoyed, impatient, almost bored, with a hint of interest in how she'll react. Then you see her face and something shifts. Your voice drops, you start hesitating, and finally you admit it was you, even though you swore you'd never say sorry. Let your speech get quieter, stumble over the words, and end with a raw, vulnerable confession.
emotions_sampled: Interest (clearly present), Confusion (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Call Before Launch
instruction: You're on a final video call with your partner who's boarding a one-way mission to Mars in twenty minutes. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to make every second count with jokes and 'remember whens.' But the countdown clock ticks. Your voice begins to fracture. You try to memorize their face. The cheerfulness crumbles into desperate bargaining ('Maybe you could still—'), then raw grief as you realize this is truly goodbye. End with whispered words of love mixed with the unbearable knowledge you'll never touch them again. Let silence do the heavy lifting between words.
inspired_by: Discovering You've Been Catfished: The Video Call

title: The Truth That Ends Everything
instruction: You're sitting across from your partner of ten years, and you've just said the words that will end your relationship: 'I've been in love with someone else for months.' Start with defensive justification, speaking quickly, trying to explain away the inexplicable. But as they stare at you in silence, your defenses crumble. Your voice begins to shake as the full weight of what you've destroyed hits you. Move into raw confession—not about the affair, but about your own cowardice, your fear of being truly known. End by reaching across the table with a trembling hand, whispering an apology that you know can't fix anything: 'I'm so sorry. You deserved someone braver than me.' Let the performance dissolve from self-protection into complete emotional nakedness.

title: The Seizure That Never Comes
instruction: You are in the middle of an important moment—a job interview, a first date, a speech you must give—and you feel the warning signs of your body beginning to fail you in the way it has failed you throughout your life. Begin in full panic: the physical sensations are overwhelming, your voice tight with the effort to maintain control, every word a battle against your body's rebellion. You can feel everyone watching, waiting for you to collapse into the role they've always assigned you: the fragile one, the one who can't handle pressure, the one defined by limitation. But this time, Channel the physical intensity—the racing heart, the trembling, the fear—into fierce determination. Let the adrenaline and terror become fuel. Your voice should crack, your breath should be ragged, but you push through, claiming this moment despite your body's betrayal. Transform the physical crisis into a crucible of self-assertion. End with your whole body shaking from the effort, but triumphant, having refused to let your condition write the ending of this story.

title: Unraveling at the Edge
instruction: You are lying back on a bed, your partner between your legs. The room is quiet except for your breathing. You are trying to stay present, to focus on the sensation and not let your mind wander, but the pleasure builds and your concentration begins to crack. Start with a controlled, low hum of appreciation and a few fragmented words—something like 'God, that's… just like that.' Let your voice stay steady at first, but as the intensity grows, let your words dissolve into breathy moans, sharp intakes, and finally a single, drawn-out vowel that climbs in pitch. Your hands grip the sheets, you shift your hips, and your last sound is a release—no more words, just pure, rising vocalization that fades into a shuddering exhale.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother at her kitchen table, finally saying what you've carried for thirty years: that her silence when your father hurt you was its own kind of betrayal. Begin with controlled fury, words you've rehearsed a thousand times, the anger that's kept you alive. But as you watch her face crumple, as she whispers that she was terrified too, something unexpected happens—not forgiveness, not yet, maybe never, but a terrible understanding. Your voice must travel from accusation to something more complicated: rage mixing with grief for the mother you needed and the frightened woman who actually existed. End with a question you're not sure you want answered: 'Did you ever love me enough to be brave?'

title: Three A.M. Truth
instruction: You and your partner are lying in bed in the dark after a dinner party where you laughed and seemed perfect to everyone. But you can't sleep. Begin by whispering their name, testing if they're awake. Your voice should be barely audible, fragile, like you might shatter. Confess something you've been hiding—not an affair or betrayal, but a fear: that you're losing yourself, that you don't recognize who you've become, that you're terrified they'll see through the performance of happiness. Speak slowly, with long pauses, as if each word costs you. Let your breathing be part of the vulnerability. End with the most frightening question: asking them to tell you one true thing about who you really are, because you've forgotten. Your fear should transform into a desperate, tender reaching for connection in the darkness.

title: Walking Slowly Through a Misty Morning
instruction: Feel the cool mist on your skin as you walk, soft and light. Describe the way each step feels gentle, the quiet around you, and the faint scent of wet earth and plants. Speak with a tone of calm wonder, as if this misty morning is like stepping into a gentle, quiet world that brings you total peace.

title: Shark Encounter
instruction: You see a shark in the water. Your voice is initially quiet terror—'Don't... move...' You're trying not to panic, trying to remember safety protocols, but your voice shakes with adrenaline. You're backing toward shore, your words urgent but controlled: 'Stay calm, stay calm.' Then it moves closer. Your voice spikes with fear. You're swimming desperately, gasping between words. Include the moment of impact—a cut-off scream, then you're in the boat, bleeding, your voice hoarse and traumatized.

title: The Tide Inside
instruction: You are a child, maybe seven years old, lying on your bed in the middle of the night, curled on your side. A cramp has just seized your belly—low and twisting—and you don't know what it is. It comes in a slow wave that makes you gasp and hold your breath. You whisper to your stuffed rabbit because you're scared and no one else is awake. At first your voice is small and confused, asking 'Why does it feel like something is squeezing me?' Then the wave peaks and you groan, a high, thin sound. It fades, and you're left panting, a little more afraid. Helplessness creeps in—you whisper, 'I don't know what to do. I don't know what to do with my hands.' Your voice is a fragile, wavering thing that climbs and falls with the pain, then sinks into quiet bewilderment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Laughing Through Your Eulogy for Someone Who Made Your Life Hell
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who hurt you deeply—an abusive parent, a toxic partner, someone whose death brings complicated relief. Start by trying to say the 'right' things, but inappropriate laughter keeps breaking through. Not cruel laughter—it's the kind that comes when emotion is too big, when grief and relief and guilt are all mixed up together. Your voice should crack between laughing and almost crying, genuine appreciation for small kindnesses ('You did teach me to...') colliding with bitter truth ('even if you spent the rest of the time...'). Find moments of real tenderness breaking through the anger, gratitude mixed with rage, love tangled up with trauma. End in a place of strange peace—still laughing softly, still crying, finally free but somehow sad about that freedom. Make it messy, real, and heartbreakingly human.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut whose life support is failing, making your final transmission to your child back on Earth. Begin with forced cheerfulness, voice straining to sound normal despite knowing this is goodbye. Your breathing becomes labored as oxygen depletes—words start breaking apart, but you fight to stay coherent. Midway through, the reality crashes over you and your voice cracks with raw grief you can no longer hide. You're trying to pack a lifetime of love into minutes, voice shaking between desperate urgency and tender whispers. End with acceptance washing over you—your voice becomes almost peaceful, filled with profound love and gratitude even as it weakens. Include moments where you have to pause to catch your breath, where words fail completely, where you're simultaneously devastated and grateful for this last chance to say everything.

title: The 3 AM Secret
instruction: It's the middle of the night. Your lover is asleep beside you, and you're whispering a confession they can't hear—something about yourself that you've hidden for years, something that fills you with shame and also with strange, aching relief to finally speak aloud. Begin with the words catching in your throat, barely audible, your body tense with the fear of being heard even in silence. As you continue whispering your truth into the darkness, feel yourself slowly unclenching. Let your breath deepen. Let tenderness seep in—for yourself, for this sleeping person, for the fragility of being human. End with a whispered truth that feels like both a goodbye to who you pretended to be and a quiet hello to who you actually are. Make us believe you're terrified of waking them, yet desperate to be known.
inspired_by: Actor is in a rigid or resistant environment (conservative director, non-exploratory cast) and needs to establish irreverent freedom before scene work

title: Storm Breaking
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—maybe you've been cleared of false accusations, maybe you've won a brutal fight for justice, maybe you've survived something that nearly destroyed you. Your whole body has been tensed for months, years, holding everything together. Begin speaking about what you endured—start controlled, almost numb, describing the pain with clinical distance. But as you speak, let your body begin to remember, to feel. Let rage surface—at what was done to you, at what was stolen. Your voice rises, your breath comes faster. Then, suddenly, let it break—the rage cracks and underneath is pure, overwhelming relief. You're shaking, maybe laughing and crying at once. End in a place of physical and emotional release so intense it's almost ecstatic. Journey from numb control through volcanic rage to trembling liberation.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a one-dimensional character or character work feels superficial—expressing the emotion rather than creating the impetus

title: Finally, a Breakthrough
instruction: You are a woman in her 50s with Parkinson's, your voice often soft and wobbly. You've just heard from your doctor that a new therapy is showing promising results for your tremors. You were sitting, hunched, waiting. Now you stand up slowly, gripping the chair. Your words come out with a rhythmic shake, but there's a growing smile. Start with breathy relief, then let elation break through despite the physical effort. Speak as if to a close friend on the phone, letting your voice rise and fall with excitement, even as it cracks and fades. Your joy is fierce, but your body fights you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your parent from the airport gate before boarding a plane to accept a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity on another continent—knowing they're ill and may not survive until you return. Start with forced brightness, trying to sound excited: 'I'm about to board, can you believe it?' But your voice begins cracking as reality sets in. The words catch in your throat as you try to say everything that matters in two minutes: 'I need you to know that...' Your breath becomes shallow, fighting tears, voice breaking on half-finished thoughts. By the end, you've moved through panic to a tender, devastated whisper: 'I love you. I love you so much.' The final boarding call echoes as you realize this might be goodbye, and your voice becomes impossibly small, a child's voice: 'I don't want to go.'

title: The Last Call That Wasn't
instruction: You're a 16-year-old girl, alone in your dark bedroom, high on opioids. You're on the phone with your best friend, who just found out what you've been doing. Start by forcing a light, dismissive tone—like it's no big deal, you've got it under control—but the shame is already there, a tightness in your chest. As you speak, the drug pulls you deeper: your words slow down, your voice gets breathy and soft, and you start trailing off. Let the shame crack through—stop pretending, let your voice drop to a near whisper, and admit you hate yourself for it. End with a long pause, then a tiny, broken 'I'm sorry' that barely makes it out.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Bedside Vigil: Your Parent's Final Words
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at 3am. They've just woken, confused, thinking you're still a child. Start with gentle reassurance, keeping your voice steady for their sake. But as they whisper an apology for something that shaped your entire life—something you never knew they regretted—your composure begins to crack. Your throat tightens. You're trying to tell them it's okay, that you forgive them, but the words keep breaking apart. They're fading now, struggling to stay conscious to hear your answer. You must get the words out—that you love them, that it's all forgiven—before they slip away. End with the peculiar calm that comes after they've taken their last breath, a whispered goodbye to the silence.
inspired_by: Panic Whispering: Hiding from an Intruder

title: The Last Radio Transmission: A Parent's Goodbye from Space
instruction: You're an astronaut on a damaged spacecraft, and you have three minutes of oxygen left to record a final message to your child back on Earth. Start with controlled calm—you want them to remember you as brave. Walk them through memories: their first steps, that camping trip, the promise you made to come home. But as oxygen depletes, your composure fractures. Your voice thins, becomes more urgent, more desperately loving. You need to say everything—advice for their wedding day you'll miss, how proud you are, how to find joy without you. End not with goodbye, but with a fierce, oxygen-starved whisper of their name, filled with every ounce of love you have left. Let the final moment be both acceptance and unbearable loss.
inspired_by: Air Traffic Controller: Two Planes on Collision Course

title: Concurrently Speaking
instruction: You're trying to have a conversation but so is your internal critic. Your voice carries both: the thing you're saying and the judgment about saying it. 'I think we should talk about' [whispered: 'why do you always need to talk?'] 'our relationship.' Your voice becomes slightly disjointed. Both voices are you. The external and internal dueling. By the end, you're not sure which voice is speaking. It's all becoming the same fractured dialogue.

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of something you built—a burned home, a failed business, a ended relationship—and against all logic, you start laughing. Begin with a single, startled laugh that sounds almost like a sob. Your voice should shimmer between amusement and devastation as you catalog the absurdity: all that work, all that hope, and look at it now. But as you speak, genuine gratitude begins weaving through the grief. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, voice breaking as you say 'Thank you for the years we had, even if they ended like this.' Remember beautiful moments even as you acknowledge the pain. Your laughter becomes both eulogy and celebration. Midway through, let your voice fill with an unexpected peace—you survived, you loved, you tried, and somehow that's enough. End with a voice that holds both profound sadness and startling joy, as if you've discovered that grief and gratitude can live in the same breath. The arc moves from shocked laughter to bittersweet remembering to a strange, luminous acceptance that contains multitudes.

title: The Last Peak
instruction: You are a child at high altitude, hit with altitude sickness just before reaching the summit. You feel dizzy, your head throbs, and each breath is a struggle. You wanted to see the view, but your body is failing you. Speak to the adult with you, starting with frustration and disappointment — a desperate hope that maybe you can push through. But as the words come out, oxygen-deprived and slow, you realize it’s not safe. Let the disappointment soften into a quiet, tired acceptance. Let your voice be gaspy, words interrupted by wincing and shallow breaths. Pause when you lose a word, then find it. Maybe a small, sad smile at the end.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Celebrating the Life You're Losing
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis, and you're recording a message for your loved ones. Begin with unexpected laughter, almost giddy: 'So this is happening. This is actually happening, and you know what? I'm not going to spend my last months being tragic about it.' But the laughter catches, becomes wet with tears even as you keep smiling: 'I'm terrified. I'm so scared I can barely breathe sometimes. And I'm also... weirdly grateful?' Let wonder and grief mix in your voice: 'I get to know. Most people don't get to know. I can say everything I need to say.' Your voice breaks between joy and sorrow: 'I never told you enough how beautiful you all are. How you made every single day worth living.' Laugh through tears at memories: 'Remember when we—' then let the weight hit you mid-sentence, voice crumbling before finding strength again. End with a strange, peaceful exhilaration: 'I'm not ready to go. I'll never be ready. And somehow, I'm okay. I'm actually okay. I got to love you. That's everything.' Let the final words carry both grief and gratitude, fear and acceptance, loss and profound, overwhelming appreciation for having lived at all.

title: The Heel-Strike Oath
instruction: You're a teenage girl power-walking across a cracked pavement. You're late to pick up your little sister from practice, and your shin splints are flaring—each heel strike shoots a dull throb up your leg. In the rhythm of that pain, you mutter a promise to yourself: you're serious about quitting track for good this time. Start with the impatience and irritation of the walk, the breath hitching every few steps, but as you go on, let the interest creep in—the truth that you actually love the burn, the push, the way your lungs fill. End with that contradiction: the pain is real, but so is the pull. Speak it in short, breathy bursts, letting the foot strikes knock the words out of you.
emotions_sampled: Interest (clearly present), Pain (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: Your parent is in hospice, lucid for perhaps the last time. You enter their room carrying years of unsaid things. Begin with small talk—the weather, the flowers you brought—your voice carefully controlled, almost cheerful. But as you sit beside them, something breaks open. Tell them it's okay to let go. Your voice should crack and rebuild itself multiple times. You're giving permission while your heart is shattering. Mix gratitude for who they were with grief for losing them. End by whispering the things you needed to say your whole life, your voice raw and tender, as you realize this goodbye is also a kind of forgiveness—of them, of yourself, of time.

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut on a space station that's catastrophically failing. You have one final transmission window to Earth before communications go dark forever. You start recording a message to your partner and young son, trying to sound strong and reassuring—telling them about the beautiful view of Earth, making promises about being brave. But as you describe what you can see, reality sets in: you're describing a goodbye. Your voice begins to fracture as you try to give your son life advice he'll need without you, fighting to stay composed so this isn't a memory of you falling apart. End with a moment where you almost break completely, then gather yourself for one final 'I love you'—not theatrical, but devastatingly real, like you're trying to pour a lifetime of love into three words before the silence.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from a hospital bed. The doctors just told you this is likely your last night. You begin the call angry—they weren't there when you needed them most, and you're determined to make them understand the hurt they caused. But as you speak, you feel your body weakening, and suddenly all that matters is that you hear their voice one more time. By the end, let the anger dissolve completely into something raw and undefended—a desperate need to say 'I love you' before it's too late. Your breath is shallow. Time is running out. Let your voice betray the war between pride and love, until love wins.
inspired_by: Actor is working in film with little or no rehearsal time

title: The Stillness After the Storm
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman lying in bed beside your partner, the room dim and quiet. Your body is utterly relaxed, muscles soft, breathing still slightly deeper than normal. A warm glow of affection settles in your chest, but underneath that, a wave of profound relief washes over you—relief that this moment exists, that you are here, that the tension of the day has finally melted away. Speak slowly, letting your voice carry that dreamy, contented weight. Let your words come out in fragments, with tiny pauses, a soft sigh now and then, and the slightest tremble of emotion as you realize how much this peace means. Your hyper-feminized voice is now unguarded, almost lazy, with no need to perform. You might lose track of a thought and find it again, or trail off into a smile.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Connection Profound
instruction: You're experiencing a profound moment of connection—not necessarily sexual, but deeply intimate. You're looking at your partner, and you're hit with the reality of loving another person. Your voice becomes almost reverent: 'I love you so much.' This statement is simple but carries years of experience. Your partner's voice is equally awed: 'I know. I feel it.' You're both recognizing something larger than yourselves. There's silence mixed with words. You're just holding each other, breathing together. Your voice becomes almost a meditation: 'Thank you for being here.' That voice should sound like someone genuinely grateful to be alive alongside another person.

title: Falling: The Monologue in Freefall
instruction: You're skydiving (or falling off something) and have roughly 60 seconds of freefall. The first reaction is pure scream — involuntary, animal. Then the scream transforms as your brain catches up. Hysterical laughter. Then unexpected clarity: rapid-fire observations about the view, the wind, the absurdity. Then genuine peace: 'Oh. Oh, it's beautiful up here.' The voice should fight the wind throughout. End with the parachute deploying — the sudden silence, the gentle float, the breathless 'Holy sh—'

title: Combing Your Late Mother's Hair Through Her Clothes
instruction: You're sorting through your mother's belongings months after her death and find her hairbrush, still holding strands of her silver hair. Begin by describing how you pull out these strands with strange, complicated tenderness—laughing softly at first because it's absurd how something so small can break you open again. Feel yourself talking to her as if she's there, your voice warm with memory, describing how she used to brush her hair, maybe how she brushed yours. But as you wind these strands around your fingers, let the grief surface underneath the warmth—your voice should shimmer between smiling remembrance and tears. End with a moment of profound contradiction: thanking her while crying, laughing at a memory while your heart physically aches, feeling both complete loss and absolute presence. Let your final words be both goodbye and hello, expressing gratitude for having had her while accepting you'll never stop missing her.
inspired_by: Running Fingers Through Freshly Washed Hair

title: The Inheritance Letter
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's just given you a sealed letter and whispered that inside is something that will change your life forever—perhaps a revelation about your family, a secret inheritance, or the truth about your origins. Begin feeling small, uncertain, almost childlike in your fear of losing her. As you hold this letter in your hands, let a transformation occur: feel power rising in you, a sense of destiny, of being chosen for something greater. Your goodbye must carry both the weight of grief and this strange, almost guilty surge of significance. Let your voice move from trembling vulnerability to something stronger, more certain, even as tears fall. The letter is your talisman now, connecting you to a future she won't see.

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are confessing a devastating secret to someone in complete darkness—a power outage, a moonless night, a blackout room. Begin by truly experiencing the absence of vision. Feel the quality of the darkness on your skin, almost like a weight. Listen to the specific sounds: their breathing pattern changing as they sense something coming, the creak of the room, your own heartbeat pounding in your ears. Reach out and feel their hand, their skin temperature, the slight dampness of nervousness, the ridges of their knuckles. Taste the copper fear in your mouth, smell the specific scent of the space mixing with their familiar smell. Whisper your secret into this sensory darkness, letting each sense intensify because you cannot see their reaction. Start with your voice small and strangled, your body rigid with shame, and let the darkness itself become a strange comfort—not having to see their face somehow makes the words possible. End with a fragile, tentative hope as you feel their hand grip yours tighter, their breathing shift, the darkness transforming from a hiding place into an intimate cocoon where truth can exist without the judgment of eyes.

title: Protecting Your Child From a Danger You Cannot Stop
instruction: You've just learned your teenager has a terminal diagnosis - six months, maybe less. You have to tell them right now, in this moment. Start with false calm, your voice artificially steady, trying to be the strong parent. 'Honey, we need to talk about the test results.' But as you explain, rage starts breaking through - fury at the universe, at God, at the unfairness. Your voice should crack between anger and desperation. Let yourself escalate into almost shouting - 'This isn't FAIR! You're sixteen!' - then collapse mid-sentence into broken sobbing. Cycle between fierce protectiveness ('I will fight this with everything I have') and utter helplessness ('But I don't know how to fix this'). End in a place of shattered tenderness - pulling them close, voice raw and destroyed, promising to make every remaining day count, mixing determination with the most profound grief. Your final 'I love you' should sound like you're trying to pour a lifetime of love into words that will never be enough.
inspired_by: Two Old Friends Meeting After 30 Years

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father about something they did when you were seven years old—something you've never spoken about, that has lived in your body as a dark, undigested thing. Start from a place of calculated calm, almost clinical, as you describe what happened. You've rehearsed this. But as you watch their face, their denials or justifications, feel something wild and young rise up from your stomach. Let your voice become the voice of that seven-year-old child, then snap back to adult rage, then crack into something else entirely—perhaps unexpected forgiveness, perhaps deeper fury, perhaps a recognition that they were once as broken as you feel now. The challenge is to let this transform organically, not to perform transformation. End in a place you didn't anticipate when you began speaking.
inspired_by: When the actor works with dark or traumatic characters

title: Wearing Soft, Freshly Laundered Clothes
instruction: Imagine sliding your arms into a fresh, soft sweater, feeling the fabric hug your skin. Describe the gentle warmth as it wraps around you, the softness brushing against your shoulders, your back, and your arms, like a gentle caress. Speak with a cozy, relaxed tone, as if every fiber is embracing you. Mention the faint, clean scent that brings a sense of calm and comfort, almost as if youre cocooned in something perfectly safe and warm.

title: Waking Up to Teasing
