instruction: You are an elderly person waking from a deep afternoon nap. Your mind is foggy, your voice thick, and you don't know what time it is. A younger relative is teasing you about your long sleep, calling you a sleepyhead. Start by mumbling, disoriented, trying to piece together what’s happening — your words might trail off or come out slurred. As you realize they’re teasing, a playful spark emerges, and you tease them back, but the grogginess still weighs on your voice, making your retorts slow and slightly confused, yet affectionate. Let the fog gradually lift as you lean into the teasing, but never fully clear by the end.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Dance Floor After the Funeral
instruction: You're alone in the space where the wake was held—everyone's gone home. Music is still playing softly, maybe a song the deceased loved. You start moving to it, and at first it feels wrong, disrespectful. But then you let yourself remember times in your own life when you felt most alive, most sensual, most connected to your own body and desires—times that have nothing to do with death. Let your body move with increasing freedom. Your breathing changes. You might laugh, or sob, or both. The physical sensation of moving, of being alive, wars with the grief. By the end, you're dancing with complete abandon, sweating, breathless, possibly laughing through tears—celebrating being alive while mourning someone's death. The physical experience transforms the grief into something wild and necessary and almost ecstatic.

title: The Muffled Apology
instruction: You're at a backyard party, slouched in a folding chair with your head resting heavily on your hand, cheek squished against your palm. You've just blurted out an unintentional insult about the host's signature dish, and now the whole table is quiet. Start with embarrassed, muffled stammering as you realize your mistake, your words clumsy because of your smushed mouth. Midway, try to laugh it off with a forced, self-deprecating joke, but your voice stays tired and slightly distorted. By the end, let reluctant acceptance creep in—you're stuck in this awkward moment, and you just sit there, feeling foolish, letting the silence hang.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Phone Call That Won't Connect
instruction: You're a young woman, a few years post-stroke, sitting at a cluttered kitchen table at 2 AM. You've had a couple of drinks, alone, feeling the familiar fog of intoxication mix with the frustrating fog of aphasia. You're trying to leave a voicemail for your ex, to tell them you're finally moving out of the city, a clean break. The first emotion is a desperate, impatient irritation with yourself—you know the words 'I'm leaving' but they come out as 'I'm... I'm... the thing... the place... ugh!' The distress grows as you feel the perfect moment slipping away, the booze making your thoughts swim. By the end, the emotion shifts to a raw, quiet devastation as you realize you can't even get a simple sentence out to end things properly, and you just trail off into a slow, defeated beep.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Distress (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner who's finally asleep after weeks of distance between you. You begin whispering into the darkness—at first just their name, testing if they're really asleep. Then you start confessing everything you've been too afraid to say when they can hear you: your terror that you're not enough, the ways you feel yourself disappearing, how much you still need them, the specific moments when you felt loved, your fear that they're slowly leaving. Your whispers should be fragile, almost inaudible at first, like you're sharing secrets with the night itself. Gradually let your voice gain strength as you speak your love and fear aloud, as if saying it to the darkness might make it real. End with a shift—from fear of loss to quiet determination to fight for what you have, your whisper becoming almost fierce with tender resolve.

title: Midnight Confession to Your Sleeping Spouse
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying beside your partner of twenty years who's sound asleep. You begin speaking in barely audible whispers, safe in the knowledge they can't hear you. Start with small truths: 'I pretend to like your mother's cooking.' Your voice is gentle, almost playful. But the confessions become deeper, more vulnerable. 'Sometimes I look at you and I'm terrified I'm not capable of loving anyone the way they deserve.' Your throat tightens around words you've never said aloud: 'I think about the life I didn't choose. I wonder who I would have been.' Tears come silently. Then your partner shifts in their sleep, murmurs your name, and reaches for your hand without waking. Your voice cracks with overwhelming tenderness mixed with devastating loneliness: 'You're right here and I miss you. How is that possible?' End with the quiet resolution of someone choosing to stay, voice barely a breath: 'Tomorrow I'll try harder. I promise. I promise.' Let the silence hold as much meaning as the words.
inspired_by: Sensory Deprivation Tank: Time Becoming Meaningless

title: The Story You Changed: Confronting Your Parent About the Lie You Both Lived
instruction: You're sitting with your aging parent, and they begin telling that cherished family story—the one that made everyone laugh at gatherings, the one that painted them as the hero. But you were there. You know what really happened. Start by listening, your voice tight with controlled anger as you interrupt: 'That's not how it happened.' Demand they tell the truth—your voice rising with years of suppressed rage, all the times you stayed silent. Watch them deflect, make excuses, minimize. Your anger peaks, then fractures into something rawer: hurt, bewilderment, the voice of a child asking 'why wasn't I enough?' Cycle between fury and vulnerability, between wanting to destroy the lie and desperately wanting them to finally see you. End in exhausted, fragile honesty—no longer attacking, just asking them to acknowledge what was real.
inspired_by: Old Person Telling a Story They've Told a Hundred Times

title: Hanging by a Thread of Truth
instruction: You are hanging upside down by your knees from a climbing frame in an empty park at dusk—a childhood game turned into a desperate escape from a recent shameful moment. Your voice is thick, wet, and hard to control as gravity fights your breath. At first, you mutter a bitter, self-mocking joke to yourself, a choke of embarrassment. But as you feel yourself slipping, the joke fades into a raw, pleading whisper—almost to the world—for redemption to be possible, your vocal folds straining against the blood pooling in your throat.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Bargaining With the Clever Ones
instruction: You are at the end of your life, negotiating with death itself—personified as a clever, cunning presence like the crow in the old story. Begin with a light, almost humorous tone, as if making a deal at the market, offering memories and moments in exchange for more time. But as you speak, you start laughing—really laughing—at the absurdity of trying to bargain, and that laughter mixes with tears. Your voice dances between gratitude for the life you've had and grief for what you're leaving behind. You're finding joy in remembering while simultaneously mourning. End with a moment of surprising peace, your voice warm and accepting, even as you cry—thanking this 'clever crow' for the years you had. The emotional journey weaves through playfulness, laughter, tears, gratitude, and peaceful surrender all at once.
inspired_by: The Farmer and the Talking Crow

title: Party Line Break-In
instruction: You're a teenager at a crowded house party, phone pressed to one ear to hear your best friend over the thumping bass. You're elated because your crush just smiled at you across the room, and you have to tell her immediately. But she's already in the middle of a story about her own disaster with a guy. Fear flickers—you might come off as rude or desperate. You interrupt her mid-sentence, voice higher and faster than normal, trying to wedge your news in before she finishes. Let the excitement tumble out, but also feel that tiny tremor of worry in your tone as you cut her off.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Ocean That Laughs: Goodbye to Innocence With Gratitude
instruction: You are an adult returning to the beach where you spent childhood summers, holding the same seashell you once believed held the ocean. You're laughing—genuinely, fully—but tears are streaming down your face. Begin with bright, almost giddy laughter as you hold it to your ear and describe what you hear now: not whales and mermaids, but something more bittersweet and beautiful. Your laughter should bleed into words that catch: you hear your younger self, still believing, still innocent, still thinking magic was simple. Let joy and grief tangle completely—you're grateful you got to be that child, devastated you can never be them again. Your voice should shimmer between delight and heartbreak as you thank the shell, thank your younger self, thank the innocence you had to lose to become who you are. End with a paradox spoken through simultaneous tears and smile: 'You were right, kid. It IS the ocean. Just not the one we thought.' Make it impossible to tell if you're celebrating or mourning, because it's both, completely and utterly both.
inspired_by: The Ocean in a Seashell: A Child's Wonder

title: The Last Story We'll Share
instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's bedside in her final hours. She's slipping in and out of consciousness. There's a painful memory between you—a terrible argument five years ago where harsh words were exchanged that neither of you ever resolved. Begin by holding onto the truth of what happened, feeling the weight of regret and unfinished business. Then, as you speak to her, start retelling that memory aloud—but change it. Tell her the version where you both said the loving things you meant to say, where you hugged instead of walking away, where forgiveness was spoken. Repeat this revised memory several times, each time with more conviction, more detail, more warmth. Let your voice transform from tentative and guilty to genuinely warm and peaceful. By the end, you must believe the new version so completely that tears of gratitude replace tears of regret. Your grief shifts from bitter to bittersweet.

title: The Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're facing your father across the kitchen table where you ate breakfast for eighteen years. You came here determined to finally tell him how his criticism shaped you, how his silence hurt you. Begin with rehearsed anger—the speech you've practiced in your head for years, your voice sharp and accusatory. But as you speak, watch him aging before your eyes, notice his hands shaking slightly, see him as breakable for the first time. Let your anger collide with unexpected tenderness. Let your words stumble as you realize you're not just angry—you're heartbroken. Transform from prosecuting attorney to devastated child who just wanted to be seen. End somewhere you didn't plan to go: maybe forgiveness, maybe deeper grief, maybe the terrifying possibility of actually being heard.

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You're standing outside in pouring rain after receiving news that changes everything—a betrayal discovered, a dream destroyed, a lie revealed. Begin with your whole body rigid with shock, that numb, dissociated feeling when reality hasn't fully hit yet. Then let the physical sensation of cold rain on your skin wake you to the truth, and allow your body to respond before your mind catches up. Feel the rain mixing with tears you didn't know you were crying. Let rage and grief move through you physically—perhaps you scream, perhaps you collapse, perhaps you laugh hysterically because it's all so absurd. Draw on times when your body responded to emotion before you could think, when feeling overwhelmed your ability to control yourself. Don't perform intensity—let your body shake, let your voice break into sounds that aren't words, let the cold seep into your bones. Move from that initial numbness through explosive release into a final state of exhausted emptiness or unexpected, fierce determination.

title: The Last Voice Message Before Deployment
instruction: You're recording a voice message for your child before deploying to a dangerous mission you may not return from. Start with forced brightness—practical reminders about school, their favorite foods, inside jokes. Your voice is steady, almost businesslike, keeping emotion at bay. But as you try to say 'I love you,' something breaks. The words won't come out right. You restart, attempting that parental confidence again, but now there's a tremor. You find yourself saying things you never planned—apologies for missed moments, desperate wishes for their future, the raw terror of possibly never hearing their voice again. End trying to return to that strong parent voice, but it's fractured now, hovering between a whisper and a plea. The message ends not with goodbye, but with silence where words should be.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence She Kept
instruction: You're thirty-five, sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table. For decades, she never spoke about your father's alcoholism, his violence, the fear you all lived in. She pretended everything was fine. Start controlled but trembling: 'We need to talk about what happened when I was a kid.' She tries to deflect—she always does. Your voice rises, cracks with decades of swallowed pain: 'You let him hurt us and you never said a word!' Feel the rage, the betrayal. But mid-confrontation, you see her face crumple—she's just a frightened woman who didn't know how to protect you or herself. Your fury softens into something more complicated: anger mixed with pity, grief for both of you. End quietly, exhausted: 'I needed you to see it. To finally say it was real.'
inspired_by: Turning Down Someone's Romantic Advance Gently

title: Final Words to a Dying Parent: From Resentment to Gratitude
instruction: You're at your parent's deathbed. They have minutes left. You came here angry—years of disappointment, of feeling unseen, of needing more than they could give. But as you look at them now, something shifts. Begin with your voice tight, words careful, holding back decades of hurt. Then let it crack open. Tell them what you needed to say—the anger, yes, but then the memories that mattered, the small kindnesses you'd forgotten. Your voice should move from controlled bitterness to trembling release to something approaching tenderness. End with 'I love you' that surprises even you with its truth. Let your voice break multiple times. This is the last conversation you'll ever have—make it cost you everything.
inspired_by: Forgiving Someone and Meaning It Completely

title: Life Decision Point
instruction: You're at a crossroads, and you have to choose your entire future in one conversation. Your voice is full of fear, options flying: 'I could stay here and keep the safe job, or I could risk everything and go to grad school, or I could...' Your voice is spiraling. Then you pause. Breathe. Your voice becomes grounded: 'What do I actually want?' Silence. 'I want to be challenged. I want to be scared because it means I'm growing.' Your voice becomes certain: 'I'm going to grad school.' The decision lands. You feel your body relax. Your voice becomes quiet, amazed: 'I just made the decision that's going to change my entire life, and I'm not even afraid anymore.' You call to tell someone, and your voice is steady, alive: 'I'm doing it. I'm finally doing it.' The decision is made, and your voice knows it's right.

title: Whispered in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying beside someone you love, unable to sleep, and the darkness makes honesty possible. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and frightened: 'Are you awake?' A pause. 'I need to tell you something and I don't know how.' Your throat tightens with vulnerability: 'Sometimes I look at you sleeping and I'm terrified of how much I need you. It scares me how completely you could destroy me.' Your voice catches, intimate and raw: 'I've never let anyone this close. I don't know how to protect myself from you, and I don't think I want to anymore.' The confession deepens, each word costs you: 'What if I'm not enough? What if one day you wake up and realize you made a mistake?' They reach for your hand in the darkness, and something in your chest cracks open. Your whisper becomes even softer, saturated with unshed tears: 'I love you so much it feels like dying and being born at the same time.' End with the quietest exhale: 'Thank you for letting me be this afraid and still staying.' The silence that follows holds everything.

title: The Body Keeps the Truth
instruction: You're alone, and your body is finally expressing what you've forbidden it to feel for years - maybe it's rage you've politely suppressed, or desire you've been taught to be ashamed of, or grief you've kept 'appropriate.' Begin with your body tight and controlled, then let it gradually take over. If it's rage, let your body move with violence you usually contain - hit pillows, tear paper, make sounds that aren't words. If it's desire, let your body move sensuously in ways you've trained yourself not to. If it's grief, let it wrack through you physically, unbeautifully. Don't perform the emotion - let your body have its uncensored physical expression. Start with the prison of control, end in the dangerous freedom of letting your body tell its forbidden truth. Your sounds should evolve from restrained to primal.

title: The Hollow Cut-In
instruction: You are a young man with a deep, gruff voice, sitting at a loud bar with a friend who is telling a long story. You feel nothing—just a flat, empty numbness—and you interrupt them not out of excitement but because you're disconnected, almost mechanically cutting in with a higher, faster pitch to take control without really caring. Start with that hollow urgency, pushing past their words with a short, blunt comment about the weather. As you speak, your voice trails off mid-sentence as you realize you don't even know why you interrupted; the numbness shifts into a quiet, confused realization that you're just going through the motions. Your tone drops, becomes slower, with a faint crack of uncertainty at the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire life. Begin with carefully controlled anger, the words you've rehearsed a thousand times in your head. You're articulate, precise, cataloging the specific moments they weren't there—recitals they missed, nights you cried alone, the way you learned to stop asking for comfort. But as you speak, the anger starts cracking. Your voice wavers. You realize mid-sentence that what you're really asking for, even now, is for them to see you, to acknowledge what they did. The confrontation shifts from accusation to a raw, devastating plea: 'Did you ever love me the way I needed?' By the end, you're not angry anymore—you're just a child again, asking for something you know you'll never receive. The pain of that realization is quiet, almost gentle, but it changes everything.

title: Midnight Confession in the Kitchen
instruction: It's 3 AM. You've been awake for days with a newborn, and your partner finds you crying silently at the kitchen table. Speak in an exhausted whisper, starting with reassurances that you're fine, just tired. But as they stay quiet and present, let the truth slip out in fragments: you're not sure you're a good parent, you're so tired you sometimes feel nothing, you're ashamed of your exhaustion when this should be joyful. Your voice should barely rise above a murmur, catching on words, pausing to breathe through the thickness in your throat. This isn't dramatic crying—it's the quiet devastation of admitting you're drowning. End with the terrifying vulnerability of asking, in the smallest voice, if they think you're failing.
inspired_by: Hiding Exhaustion While Continuing to Work

title: Discovering the Betrayal and Fighting to Hold On
instruction: You've just discovered irrefutable proof of your partner's betrayal. Explode with volcanic rage—screaming questions, accusations flying like shrapnel: 'How could you? How long? WHO ELSE KNEW?' Your voice cracks with fury and humiliation. Demand answers with ferocious intensity. Then, mid-tirade, something shifts—beneath the rage is terror of losing them. Your explosive anger collapses into desperate, fierce pleading: 'Tell me we can fix this. TELL ME.' You're simultaneously furious and begging. End in helpless, heaving sobs mixed with residual anger—the sound of someone fighting to hold onto something already slipping away. Raw, messy, contradictory—love and hatred occupying the same moment.
inspired_by: Losing Your Temper at Someone You Love

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a hospice bed, knowing this is your final conversation. You started this call determined to be strong for them, to keep your voice steady and not let them hear your fear. But as you speak, something shifts—maybe it's hearing their voice, or remembering childhood, or simply the weight of goodbye. Your composure begins to crack. Let us hear the journey from forced brightness to raw vulnerability, from 'I'm fine, really' to the truth you can no longer hide. Your voice may start controlled, almost cheerful, but by the end, let the fear and love and gratitude pour through. This isn't about being loud—it's about the moment when you stop pretending and let yourself be held, even over the phone, one last time.
inspired_by: Hiding Nervousness During an Important Interview

title: Hospice Nurse Thanks Their Patient for Teaching Them About Death—As They Take Their Last Breath
instruction: You're holding their hand as their breathing becomes shallow, irregular. But instead of clinical detachment, you find yourself laughing softly—a tender, broken sound—remembering something funny they said last week about heaven being 'overrated but worth checking out.' Your voice is thick with tears but also warm with genuine gratitude. You tell them, with brutal honesty, that they've changed you: 'You taught me that dying doesn't have to mean losing dignity. That fear and peace can exist in the same breath.' As you speak, you're crying, but there's also something like joy in your voice—the privilege of witnessing this, of being trusted with someone's final moment. You confess your own fears about death, and how watching them face it with such grace has given you something you didn't know you needed. Your words become simpler as their breathing slows: 'Thank you. You were so brave. You made this beautiful somehow.' There's profound sadness, but also a strange serenity, even gratitude for the intimacy of this moment. When they take their last breath, you whisper 'safe travels' with a smile in your voice, tears streaming down your face, holding both grief and peace in the same shattered breath.
inspired_by: Diplomat Negotiates Peace Deal While Their Country Is Being Invaded

title: Realizing Forgiveness
instruction: You're in therapy, processing an old wound, and your therapist asks: 'Have you forgiven them?' Your voice automatically starts: 'No, never, what they did was—' And then you pause. You actually sit with the question. Your voice becomes quieter: 'I... I think I have.' The realization is dawning in your voice. 'Not because what they did was okay. But because holding onto this anger is like drinking poison.' Your voice becomes stronger: 'I forgive them so I can be free.' Your therapist asks: 'How does that feel?' And your voice is amazed, relieved: 'It feels like I just put down something I've been carrying for twenty years.' You're crying, but your voice is no longer bitter — it's sad, yes, but also lighter. 'I didn't know I could forgive them. I didn't know I was capable of that.' The realization is transformative.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Partner That You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you. You're whispering things you could never say to their waking face—why you have to leave, how much you've loved them, how staying is killing you both. Your voice is barely audible, tender, aching. You're confessing that you've been pretending for months, that you see them trying so hard and it breaks your heart because trying isn't enough. Your whispers catch on tears. You're memorizing the sound of their breathing. Part of you wants them to wake up, to stop you. Part of you is grateful for this cowardly kindness. End with your voice dissolving into silence, knowing tomorrow you'll be gone.
inspired_by: Professional: Scientist Realizes Her Research Is Being Used for Weapons

title: Beneath the Soundproof Glass
instruction: You're in a recording booth doing vocal warm-ups and character samples when you receive a text: someone you love deeply is in the hospital, and you need to come now. But you're in the middle of a session you can't leave—a career-defining project, a contract that can't be broken. You continue performing, cycling through the required character voices—a cheerful narrator, a menacing villain, a gentle teacher—while your heart is shattering. Your professional voice remains controlled, hitting every mark, but between takes, in those brief silences, tiny sounds escape: a caught breath, a whispered 'please,' a barely audible sob. You're splitting in two: the performer who must continue, and the human who is breaking. Let the contrast be devastating—the bright, energetic character voices against the whispered, private moments of anguish. By the final take, your voice is still technically perfect, but you can hear the grief threaded through every word, the cost of continuing when everything in you wants to run.

title: Memory Sharing
instruction: Two people are remembering something together, and the memory is alive between them. The voices are soft, almost reverent. One person starts the memory, and the other completes it. 'Remember when...' triggers a cascade of details, each voice adding what the other forgot. The memory brings laughter or tears or both. There's something sacred about shared memory—it's proof that they existed together in a moment. By the end, the memory has been honored, held in both their minds. The voices reflect the specific tenderness that comes from remembering together.

title: The 3 a.m. Call
instruction: You are a teenage girl who hasn't slept properly in months. It's 3 a.m., and you're sitting on the edge of your bed, staring at the dark window. You finally call your best friend's voicemail, not expecting an answer. At first your voice is hollow, heavy with exhaustion, each word dragging. But as you speak, the helplessness creeps in—your throat tightens, your sentences break, you pause to rub your eyes. By the end, you're not just tired; you're quietly desperate, the fatigue cracking into raw, fragile truth. Let the silence between words feel heavier than the words themselves.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Diagnosis: Illness
instruction: The doctor has just told you that you have a serious illness. Your voice is frozen in the moment: 'I'm sorry, what did you just say?' You're asking them to repeat it, as if hearing it again will change it. Your voice becomes small, confused. You're asking questions: 'How long do I have?' 'What happens now?' Your voice shows the effort it takes to form words when your mind is reeling. By the end, you're signing consent forms, your voice numb, mechanical.

title: Tears of Joy and Teasing
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting across from your grandchild, who has just told you they got into their dream school. You are sobbing uncontrollably—your breath catches in jerky gasps, your throat feels thick with mucus, your voice cracks on every other word. Despite this, you are completely present, your eyes locked on them with intense interest. You feel a fierce, overflowing affection, and you want to lighten the moment. Start by struggling to speak through the tears, your words wavering and wet, then let a teasing tone creep in as you wipe your nose and half-laugh, half-cry. End with a playful jab that still trembles with emotion. Let the sobbing distort your pitch and rhythm—don't fight it, let it be messy and real.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Affection (very intensely present), Teasing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Thing I Never Told You
instruction: You are sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—a grandparent, parent, or mentor—in their final hours. They are unconscious, but you believe they can hear you. Begin by trying to be strong, saying the practical things you think you should say. But as you speak, you notice their hand, the way their chest rises and falls, small details about their face you've seen your whole life but never truly looked at. These observations crack you open. Let what you see in them—their vulnerability, their humanness, the small ways they've always protected themselves or tried to appear stronger than they felt—unlock what you've been too afraid or too proud to say. End by speaking a truth so raw and undefended that you barely recognize your own voice.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent in rehab visitation. You came prepared with a list of grievances, and you start reading them—birthdays they missed, promises broken, the night you had to call 911. Your voice is hard, angry, righteous. But as you list each wound, something shifts. You realize you're not just angry—you're terrified you'll become them. Your voice starts to shake. The paper falls from your hands. You look at them, really look, and see yourself. The anger dissolves into a desperate, vulnerable question: 'How do I make sure I don't lose everything like you did?' By the end, you're both crying, and you're not sure if you're the parent or the child anymore.

title: At the Edge
instruction: You are an older woman in an intimate encounter where your partner is teasing you to the brink of release, then pulling back. Each time you climb toward climax, he stops, leaving you gasping and unfulfilled. Start with genuine astonishment at the intensity of sensation, your voice rising in pitch and speed. As he denies you repeatedly, your surprise shifts into a deepening disappointment, tinged with a flicker of malice toward his cruelty. Your breathing becomes ragged, speech dissolving into desperate pleas and whimpers. By the end, your voice is low, frustrated, and broken with unmet need. Speak naturally, with all the micro-distractions of someone caught in this cycle of building and falling.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Disappointment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Protective Fury Colliding With Powerlessness
instruction: Someone has hurt someone you love, and you're confronting the reality that you can't protect them—not really, not anymore. Start with fierce, controlled intensity: you're trying to be strong, authoritative, threatening if you have to be. But as you speak, your power crumbles. Your voice rises with rage—'How dare you'—then breaks completely into raw anguish. You're cycling rapidly between fury and desperation: promising violence one moment, then collapsing into pleading the next. Your words become fragmented as helplessness overwhelms you. You're hitting the limit of what love can do, and it's destroying you. Your voice drops to something primal, almost animal. End with you on your knees, metaphorically or literally, all rage burned away, left with nothing but broken whispered devotion: 'I would do anything.'

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake for what you both know is the last time. Begin with careful, controlled composure—you're trying to be strong for her. As you speak, tell her about the garden she planted that's blooming this spring, the recipes you've been making from her handwritten cards. Let your voice gradually crack as the reality sinks deeper. By the end, allow yourself to break completely—not dramatically, but with the kind of raw, helpless grief that comes when you realize you're watching someone's final sunrise. Let your voice move from steady narrative to fractured whispers, from holding it together to surrendering to the unbearable weight of goodbye.
inspired_by: When finishing a production where unconscious programming was used

title: The Goodbye I Didn't Say
instruction: You're a teenager, bleeding out in the back of a stranger's car after a traumatic accident you caused while sneaking out. You're astonished you're still alive, embarrassed that your mom will see you like this in your pajamas, and emotionally numb as shock sets in. Start with panicked, rushed apologies to the driver, but as cold sweat and shivering take over, your words fade—each one a little quieter, a little more slurred, until you're just mumbling to yourself about how 'she's going to be so mad.' Let your voice crack, drop, and lose coherence naturally, like you're fighting to stay awake.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Embarrassment (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Lost Treasure
instruction: You're a child, alone in your room, digging through a big plastic bin of old clothes and toys. You're looking for your favorite stuffed animal that you haven't seen in weeks. Your voice is muffled and distracted as you mumble, shifting things around, feeling the fabric, sometimes stopping to check a pocket. At first you are completely absorbed in the search — focused, whispering to yourself, maybe sighing in frustration. Then your fingers brush against something familiar. The moment you realize you've found it, your whole energy shifts from intense concentration to a quiet, relieved joy. Let your voice change naturally as you pull it out and hug it.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Curse Breaking Moment
instruction: You've been cursed for years, and in this moment, you feel it breaking. Your voice starts heavy, dragged down by the weight of curse. As you realize what's happening, your voice begins to lighten. The relief is physical—you're breathing differently, speaking differently. There's a moment where the curse fights back, and your voice cracks under the pressure. But then it shatters. Your voice becomes your own again, and it's almost unrecognizable to you because it's been so long. You're laughing, crying, gasping. By the end, you're speaking freely for the first time in years, and the newness of your own voice is profound.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your mother in the kitchen where you grew up, finally addressing years of unspoken pain. Begin with controlled anger, your words measured and careful, trying to stay logical and fair. As you speak, the dam breaks—your voice cracks, your carefully prepared arguments dissolve into raw emotional truth. Accusations mix with desperate questions: 'Why wasn't I enough?' But as you continue, something unexpected happens. You begin to see her differently, perhaps remembering her own struggles, her own youth. End in a place you didn't anticipate—somewhere between forgiveness, grief, and a new kind of understanding. Your voice should travel from tight control to chaotic release to exhausted tenderness.

title: Holding Your Best Friend Back: When They Want to End It
instruction: Your best friend called you at 2 AM from a bridge. You're on the phone, and you can hear the wind, the traffic below. Start with forced calm, the kind that hides terror—asking about their day, what they had for dinner, anything to keep them talking. But as they tell you why they can't do this anymore, your control shatters into rage. Scream at them that they don't get to leave you, that you've survived too much together for it to end like this. Let your voice break into sobs as you beg—ugly, desperate pleading that you promised yourself you'd never do. Then fury again—at their pain, at your helplessness, at the universe that brought them to this edge. Finally, shift to something fierce and tender: whispered promises of what you'll do together tomorrow, next week, next year. End with your voice raw but steady, saying 'Stay on the phone with me. Just stay.'
inspired_by: Labor: When the Anesthesia Wears Off During Surgery Complications

title: Craning for a Laugh
instruction: You're an elderly person standing in your garden, neck craned high to watch a small bird on a branch. Your voice comes out thinner, tighter from the strain. Start by grumbling about the ache and the bird's stubbornness, but then the bird does a clumsy little hop and nearly falls. A surprised, wheezy chuckle escapes you. Let your tone shift from irritable muttering to genuine amusement, with a dry laugh and a shake of your head. Include a pause to rub your neck, and end with a fond sigh.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Performance Before Deployment
instruction: You're a children's party entertainer performing as a superhero character for your own child's birthday party—the day before you deploy to a conflict zone for a year. Start with exaggerated superhero bravado, playing to the kids' delight. As you perform, the weight of leaving begins cracking through your performance. Your voice wavers between the character's confidence and your own breaking heart. When your child asks if superheroes ever get scared, completely drop the act. Answer them honestly, quietly, your voice raw and unguarded, trying to be brave while knowing you might not come back. Let gratitude for this moment mix with the devastation of goodbye.
inspired_by: Haunted House Actor Who Takes It Too Seriously

title: Protecting a Child You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone younger—your child, your sibling, a student—and they're being taken somewhere you can't follow: into surgery with low survival odds, into foster care, onto a plane to flee violence while you stay behind. Start with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance: 'Listen to me—you're going to be fine. You hear me?' But your voice is shaking under the forced strength. You're giving instructions, advice, last-minute wisdom, talking faster and faster because when you stop talking they'll be gone. 'Remember what I taught you about—' but you're choking now, and the fury comes—at God, at fate, at your own helplessness. 'This isn't fair!' Your voice cracks into something primal. Then it breaks completely: you're sobbing, trying to memorize their face, whispering 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry I can't—' End by pulling yourself together one last time, forcing strength into your voice even as it trembles: 'You're braver than you know. Now go.'

title: 3 AM Beside Them Sleeping
instruction: Your lover is asleep beside you. You're awake, watching them, and you need to whisper truths you can't say when they're conscious. Begin quietly, perhaps just stating simple facts about what you see, what you feel in your own body lying there. Then let yourself drift impulsively between confessions: what you want from this relationship, what terrifies you, who you really are beneath the face you show them, what you need them to know, sensations you're feeling right now—your breathing, the ache in your chest, tingling in your fingers. Move between profound love and secret resentments, between gratitude and loneliness, between declarations and questions you'll never ask. Keep your voice intimate, a whisper that comes from your center. By the end, let yourself arrive at either devastating clarity about staying or leaving, or a deeper acceptance of the mystery of loving another person. Let each whispered impulse surprise you.
inspired_by: I Am, I Want, I Need, I Feel

title: The Brave Girl
instruction: You are a young girl waking up from sedation after a procedure. Your words are slurry, your eyelids heavy, and you keep losing the thought mid-sentence. At first, you mumble confusedly about a stuffed animal, your voice rising and falling without control. As clarity slowly returns, you remember being told you were 'so brave' — and a tiny, proud smile flickers through your grogginess. But then a bitter edge creeps in as you recall the needle, the betrayal of your parents saying it wouldn't hurt. The pride fades into a sullen, quiet acceptance. Let your voice start fuzzy and childlike, then sharpen unevenly as bitterness takes over. End with a soft, defeated whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Showed Up
instruction: You're finally saying what you've never said to your parent - about every recital they missed, every promise broken, every time you needed them and they chose something else. Start with forced calm, almost clinical, listing facts like you've rehearsed this a thousand times in your head. But let anger seep in - controlled at first, then building. Your voice should crack not from sadness but from years of suppressed rage finally breaking free. Then shift - in the middle of your fury, let a childhood memory surface, something small and tender, and feel your anger falter. Let confusion flood in: do you want to destroy them or just be seen by them? End with something vulnerable and devastating, like 'I just wanted you to be proud of me,' your voice small again, all the fight drained out, replaced by the raw ache of a child who still, despite everything, seeks their parent's love.
inspired_by: Stand-Up Tragedy: The Funniest Set About the Worst Thing

title: The Unspoken Weight
instruction: You're finally confronting your father who was emotionally absent throughout your childhood. Start controlled, measured—you've rehearsed this. 'Dad, I need to tell you something.' But as you speak about the recitals he missed, the times you needed him, your voice trembles with suppressed pain. You're not yelling—this is quiet devastation. Your words become more halting, vulnerable. 'I needed you to see me.' There's a long pause where you almost break. Then something shifts. You realize you're grieving not what was, but what will never be. Your voice softens into something like forgiveness, not for him, but for yourself. End with tender exhaustion, releasing a weight you've carried for decades.

title: The Last Mountain
instruction: You are an elderly mining executive, facing a hostile takeover of the family mine your grandfather discovered. In this final boardroom negotiation, you start in quiet awe — marveling at a faded photograph of your father standing on the mountain in 1948. Your voice is slow, almost reverent, as you speak about the first blast that opened the vein. But as the younger investors push for liquidation, awe turns to cold anger. You set down the photo, your voice drops an octave, and you remind them of the shale collapse that killed three men in '63 — men whose names you still know. Let your throat tighten with anger. Let your breath pause between dignified warnings.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're holding someone you love as danger closes in—a car accident's aftermath, a medical emergency, a moment where you're powerless. Begin fierce and commanding: 'Stay with me. Look at me. You're going to be fine.' You're using your voice like a shield, like if you're strong enough, loud enough, certain enough, you can will them to survive. But you can feel them slipping and your voice starts to crack. The commands become pleas: 'Please don't—' Now you're bargaining with the universe, with God, with anyone. Your protective fury collapses into helpless terror. End with the rawest vulnerability—maybe you're still trying to be strong for them even as you're breaking, maybe you're finally admitting you can't fix this. Your voice should journey from warrior to child, from absolute certainty to absolute helplessness, revealing that sometimes love means being present for what we cannot prevent.

title: The Last Invoice
instruction: You are sitting at your office desk late in the evening, sorting through a stack of final paperwork before quitting a job you’ve hated for months. The fluorescents hum overhead, someone’s coffee cup has left a ring on your spreadsheet. You start speaking with a curled-lip contempt for the petty bureaucracy, but as you touch the stapler you’ve used a thousand times, a flicker of nostalgia catches you off guard—you pause, almost smile, then let a bittersweet resignation settle in. Let your voice start sharp and clipped, then soften into something almost tender, with natural pauses where you glance at the clock or rub your eyes.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Bite
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in your kitchen, trying to finish a bowl of soup your late husband used to make. The smell and taste suddenly trigger a wave of nausea — your stomach lurches, throat tightens, and you gag. As you fight the physical urge to retch, you recall his gentle hands and how he would laugh. Let the nausea interrupt your words: heave, swallow hard, voice thick with phlegm. Start with strained, watery distress, then shift into a tender, cracked longing as you speak to his memory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: When Certainty Shatters
instruction: You burst into the room, voice loud and electric with passion, ready to announce your decision—you're selling everything, moving across the world, pursuing this consuming dream. Start with explosive confidence: 'I've figured it out, I know exactly what I need to do—' Rapid-fire, breathless, almost manic with certainty. But mid-declaration, you see their face, or catch your own reflection, or suddenly hear your own words, and doubt crashes in like a wave. Your voice falters, cracks. The conviction that felt so solid seconds ago starts crumbling. Try to rally—'No, I'm sure, I just need to—' but you're arguing with yourself now, voice breaking between fierce assertion and terrified questioning. End in near-whispered devastation, all that fire collapsing into trembling uncertainty: 'What if I'm wrong? What if I've convinced myself of something impossible?' Let your voice show the full arc from blazing certainty to vulnerable, shaking doubt, with moments where you desperately try to recapture that initial passion but can't quite hold it.

title: Confronting Your Mother Over the Soup She Never Made
instruction: You're holding a bowl of homemade soup—something you taught yourself to make because your mother never cooked for you, never provided that basic comfort. Start by describing the aroma with bitter irony, explaining how you had to learn what 'home' was supposed to smell like from friends' houses, from strangers. Your voice begins controlled, almost clinical, but as you breathe in the steam, something breaks. Shift into raw vulnerability as you confess how much you needed this—just this simple act of care—and how its absence shaped you. Let anger bleed into hurt, hurt into a desperate question: 'Why wasn't I worth this?' End not with resolution but with exhausted honesty, the soup's warmth highlighting the cold absence in your childhood. Move from controlled resentment to unleashed pain to weary truth.
inspired_by: Savoring the Aroma of a Steamy Bowl of Soup on a Cold Day

title: Holding Two Truths at Once
instruction: You've just received news that's both devastating and miraculous—perhaps someone you love is returning but someone else is gone, or you've achieved a dream but at terrible cost, or you're becoming a parent while losing one. Begin in stunned numbness, not yet processing. As you try to speak about it, start thoughts with 'I should feel...', 'Part of me wants to...', 'I don't know if I'm...', 'This means...' Let contradictory emotions surface impulsively—don't choose between joy and grief, let both exist. Speak to someone close to you, letting your face and voice swing between tears and laughter, rage and relief, without settling into one. By the end, you should be fully inhabiting the impossible simultaneity—grateful and furious, destroyed and reborn, laughing while sobbing—completely authentic to the messy truth that life gives and takes away in the same breath.

title: Walking Barefoot Through Shallow, Cool Water
instruction: Step into the shallow water, feeling the cool, smooth ripples move around your feet. Describe the sensation as each step sends a gentle splash, the way the water soothes your skin and shifts with each movement. Speak with a tone of quiet exhilaration, as if the refreshing coolness connects you to the natural flow of the water, grounding you with each gentle step.

title: The Last Meal Together
instruction: You are sharing your grandmother's final breakfast with her in hospice. She's lucid, peaceful, and has asked for her favorite cinnamon toast and tea. As you prepare and share this meal with her, fully experience every sensory detail—the warmth of the cup in your hands, the sweet cinnamon scent mixing with the antiseptic hospital smell, the scraping sound of butter on toast, the texture of crumbs on your fingers. Begin with careful, almost ritualistic attention to these sensations, finding comfort in the familiar ritual. As the meal progresses, let the weight of 'last time' seep in—this is the last breakfast, the last taste you'll share, the last time you'll watch her sip from that chipped blue mug. By the end, these same sensory details that brought comfort now break your heart. The toast tastes like goodbye. Let your voice move from gentle, present attention to an aching awareness that you're trying to memorize everything through your senses because soon there will be only memory.

title: The Last Morning Before Hospice
instruction: Your parent is being moved to hospice this afternoon, and you're making them breakfast one final time in their kitchen. You keep trying to tell them how much they meant to you, to say a real goodbye, but they keep deflecting—asking about your work, commenting on the weather, telling you the eggs need more salt. Each time you gather courage to speak from your heart, they redirect to the mundane. Your voice moves from determined tenderness to frustrated grief to a final breakthrough where love and anger collapse together. You need them to hear you before it's too late, but they're protecting themselves the only way they know how. Let your voice crack on the ordinary words that carry impossible weight.
inspired_by: Trying to Break Up While They Keep Being Perfect

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Lover at the Train Platform
instruction: You're standing on a cold platform as the train that will take your lover away forever idles behind you. You have three minutes before they board. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep things light, making jokes about writing letters. But as the conductor calls the final boarding, your voice begins to crack. The jokes stop working. You try to say 'I'll be fine' but it comes out broken. End whispering against their neck, your breath catching, trying to memorize the smell of their skin, saying 'don't forget me' so quietly it's almost just air. Let your voice betray everything you're trying to hold back.
inspired_by: Whispering a Secret in a Crowded Room

title: The Taste of Letting Go
instruction: You're standing alone in the rain after the funeral of someone you loved desperately but never told. Your whole body is shaking—from cold, from grief, from years of suppressed desire. There are ten specific moments of physical nearness you're remembering: their hand on your shoulder, standing too close in an elevator, the smell of their coffee, a accidental touch. Start by trying to hold yourself together, recounting these moments like facts, your breath controlled despite the cold. But sense memory is powerful—as you recall each physical detail, let it flood your body. Your breathing changes, your muscles tense and release, you're no longer just remembering but reliving. By the final memories, you're gasping, laughing through tears, your body convulsing with the ecstasy and agony of love that lived entirely in moments of restrained touching. End with your body finally still, emptied, accepting.
inspired_by: When memorizing a large amount of material in a short time under production pressure

title: Whispered Hope
instruction: You're a teenage boy with a deep, naturally loud voice, but right now a chronic migraine has you pinned to your dark bedroom, phone pressed to your ear. Your best friend just asked how you are. You start irritable—your words come out as clipped, impatient whispers because any volume stabs your skull. Squinting against the phone's glow, you mention the new treatment your mom picked up. Then something unexpected happens: a flicker of genuine hope sneaks in. Your voice stays fragile and low, but the edge softens, the pause before 'maybe this time' is almost eager. Speak about how you know hope is stupid but you're letting yourself have it—just this once.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Snow-Walled Window
instruction: You are lost in a blizzard, your beard frozen, your jaw so tight you can barely move it. You’ve been stumbling for hours, ready to give up, when you spot a cabin light flickering through the snow. A rush of relief floods you—you’re alive, you’re saved. But as you get closer, you see fresh tracks leading to the door. Someone else is already inside, warm and dry. The relief curdles. A bitter doubt hits: what if they don’t open? Then envy burns through you—hot despite the cold. You shout into the wind, not even sure if they can hear. Your voice starts ragged and grateful, but by the end it’s tight with jealousy, almost snarling. Let the storm swallow your words. Let your breath stutter. Let the cold lock your jaw, so every shout costs you.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Cough
instruction: You are an elderly person, alone in a quiet room, recovering from a long, painful coughing fit that has racked your body. As you finally catch your breath, a deep sense of relief washes over you—relief so profound it almost feels like a physical release. Then, you notice the rain has stopped outside, and a single beam of sunlight breaks through the clouds, illuminating dust motes in the air. Speak to the stillness, your voice still raspy and wet from the cough, but now filled with a quiet, trembling awe. Your words should start with the exhaustion of the breath just caught, and end with the wonder of the light.
emotions_sampled: Relief (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Describing Color to a Blind Person
instruction: A blind friend asks you to describe what red looks like. Don't say 'like a fire truck.' Translate vision to other senses: 'Red sounds like a trumpet in a small room. It feels like the first sip of whiskey — warm, then hot, then spreading. It tastes like cayenne.' Make each color a sensory poem. Your voice should be searching, careful, deeply respectful of the task. Include a color that stumps you completely — you try and fail and say, 'I don't think words can hold that one.' That's the most honest answer.

title: The Locked Door: Breaking Point with the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: Your parent is pounding on your door, demanding to know why you've shut them out, why you're 'being so dramatic.' Something inside you finally shatters. Start with your voice low, trembling with a rage that's been building for decades: 'You want to know why?' Then let it explode—not just anger, but years of unspoken pain erupting: 'Because you never saw me! Never! I could have been anyone!' Your voice cracks between fury and anguish: 'I spent thirty years trying to be enough for you, and you didn't even notice I was there!' Feel the moment where rage collapses into something more devastating—your voice drops to almost childlike vulnerability: 'I just wanted you to see me. That's all I ever wanted.' But then the strength returns, different now, forged in fire: 'But you can't. You won't. And I'm done waiting.' Your voice rises again, but this time with fierce protectiveness—for yourself: 'I'm done making myself small so you can feel big!' End with your voice shaking but absolute, tears and power mixed together: 'I'm done. Do you hear me? I'm finally done. And that terrifies me. But God, it also sets me free.'
inspired_by: Choosing Yourself: The Guilt and Empowerment of Selfishness

title: Reading Letters from Your Younger Self
instruction: You've found letters you wrote to your future self as a hopeful teenager, and you're reading them aloud in your current bedroom, twenty years later. Begin with tender amusement at your younger self's dreams: 'Dear Future Me, I hope you're happy. I hope you became everything we wanted.' Let your voice catch as you realize how far you've drifted from those dreams. 'You said you'd never settle. You said you'd never stop painting.' Whisper the painful parts, voice thick with unshed tears. 'I'm so sorry I let you down. I'm so sorry I stopped believing in us.' Move through quiet grief for the person you didn't become, then find unexpected grace. 'But maybe... maybe you'd be proud anyway. Not of what I did, but that I survived. That I kept going even when it hurt.' End with a whispered promise, half to yourself, half to that younger version: 'I'll try harder. For both of us.'

title: Just a Little Higher
instruction: You're a teenager on a challenging rope climb, arms shaking, fingertips white-knuckled on a small hold. Your belayer keeps yelling advice, but you're already irritated—you know what to do, you just need to breathe. Start muttering to yourself, clipped and breathless, venting your impatience through gritted teeth. As you finally reach for the next hold, a rush of focus overtakes the irritation, and your voice shifts to a raw, determined whisper. You're not talking to anyone anymore—just your own muscles and the rock.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Pride on the Rocks
instruction: You are an older man at a class reunion, holding a glass of whisky. You start by boasting about your career success, your voice thick with pride. But as you speak, you notice a former rival smirking across the room, and a nagging doubt creeps in about whether your achievements were as solid as you thought. Take a long, slow gulp of whisky mid-sentence, let the liquid slosh and your throat click as you swallow, then continue with a slightly wavering tone. Let the pride crack into confusion by the end, as if you're trying to convince yourself more than the crowd. Your spoken words should be around 60 seconds of raw, unfiltered thought.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Moment You Realize They're Never Coming Back
instruction: You're standing in their closet, or holding their coffee mug, or seeing their handwriting on a note, and the full weight of their absence crashes into you all at once. Begin with confusion, almost talking to them as if they're still there—'Where did you put the...?' Then reality hits. Your voice cracks. The rage comes first—hot, volcanic, at them for leaving, at the universe for taking them, at yourself for not preventing it. You might shout. You might laugh bitterly. But the fury can't sustain itself. It breaks apart into something more primal—keening grief, the kind that doubles you over. End in a place beyond words, where sound becomes pure emotion, where you're both destroyed and somehow still breathing, where the love and the loss are the same unbearable thing.
inspired_by: Narrating Your Own Surgery While Awake

title: Whispering to What's Gone
instruction: Late at night, alone in your childhood bedroom, you're speaking softly to your imaginary friend from decades ago—the one who kept you company through your parents' divorce, through bullying, through feeling invisible. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate and tender, as if speaking too loudly would shatter the fragile connection. Begin with gentle, almost playful reminiscence, but let it deepen into quiet confession: how much you needed them, how abandoned you felt when you 'outgrew' them, how you wish you could thank them now. Let your voice thicken with unshed tears, let pauses speak as loudly as words. End with a soft, breaking goodbye to the part of yourself you had to leave behind to grow up.
inspired_by: The Mother and the Imaginary Dragon

title: The Overly Dramatic Weather Reporter
instruction: Portray a weather reporter who treats mild weather changes as catastrophic events. Use an overly serious tone to describe insignificant weather patterns, adding comedic value through exaggeration and urgency.

title: The Ring on Her Finger
instruction: You're sitting at your mother's hospital bedside in her final hours. She's unconscious, her breathing shallow. Begin by looking at her whole face, feeling numb and disconnected, unable to process what's happening. Then let your gaze fall to her hand resting on the blanket—specifically to her wedding ring, the one she's worn for forty-seven years, now loose on her thinning finger. Focus only on that ring. Remember every time you saw it: when she held you as a child, when she waved goodbye on your first day of school, when she touched your face to comfort you. Let everything you feel about her entire life concentrate into that single circle of gold. Your emotion should move from numb shock to overwhelming, specific love and gratitude for every moment she gave you. Speak your goodbye to the ring, as if it contains her whole story.

title: Reading Your Estranged Father's Letter at His Funeral—It's an Apology
instruction: You're standing at the podium, holding a letter you only received this morning, written before he died. Start reading his words aloud with bitter skepticism—your voice should drip with decades of resentment: 'To my child, I know I have no right to ask forgiveness...' Let sarcastic laughs punctuate the first few lines. But as his words become more specific, more raw, something shifts. Your voice wavers. You start crying while simultaneously smiling at a memory he mentions, laughing through tears at an inside joke you'd forgotten. Your reading becomes increasingly broken, oscillating between anger at his timing and grief that you'll never get to respond, gratitude for his words and rage that he waited until death. End with your voice completely fragmented, holding the letter to your chest: 'You bastard. You beautiful bastard.' Move from bitter armor through reluctant softening to the chaos of loving and hating someone simultaneously, finding forgiveness in the same breath as fury.
inspired_by: Screaming Into Your Pillow So No One Hears

title: Wedding Toast for the Person You Almost Married
instruction: You are giving a wedding toast for your closest friend—someone you were once in love with, someone you almost built a life with, someone who is now marrying someone else. Begin with humor and warmth, your public voice effortlessly charming: 'I've known Jamie since we were kids, and I have stories that could embarrass her for days...' Your voice is bright with genuine affection, and you're making everyone laugh. But as you speak, let other emotions bleed through—just at the edges at first. When you talk about their happiness, your voice catches almost imperceptibly: 'I've never seen her smile like this.' There's real joy there, authentic gladness for their happiness, but underneath it, your heart is quietly breaking. Your voice grows softer, more intimate, as you navigate this impossible terrain: loving them enough to let them go, celebrating their joy while privately grieving what might have been. By the end, you're speaking directly to them, and your voice holds everything at once—laughter and tears, gratitude and loss, deep friendship and deeper letting go: 'You deserve every bit of this happiness. And I'm so grateful I get to be here to see it.' Raise your glass with a smile that's both completely real and costs you everything. Let your voice do the impossible: hold both celebration and heartbreak in the same breath, both peace and pain, both moving forward and saying goodbye.

title: Farewell to Your Child Before They Enter Witness Protection Forever
instruction: You have five minutes to say goodbye to your child before they disappear into witness protection and you can never see them again. Start with false brightness, trying to be strong for them, but let that facade crumble as reality sets in. Your voice breaks between reassurances and the physical pain of letting go. You're memorizing their face while pretending everything will be okay. Move from protective parent to devastated human being who must release the person they love most. End in a whispered moment where you give them permission to forget you if that's what keeps them safe. Your breathing shifts from controlled to ragged to finally, terribly calm.
inspired_by: Professional: Activist Must Compromise Their Principles to Save Vulnerable People

title: The Fever of Knowing
instruction: You've just received undeniable proof that your closest friend—your person for 15 years—has been sleeping with your ex, throughout your entire relationship and after. Your hands are shaking, your body is hot with adrenaline, and you're calling them right now. Begin in that white-hot moment where your body is ahead of your words—breathing hard, voice shaking with physical rage, almost incoherent. Let your body lead your voice: sharp intakes of breath, sounds caught in your throat, the physicality of betrayal coursing through you. But somewhere in the middle, let exhaustion hit—the bone-deep, physically depleting realization that changes everything you thought was real. End in a place where your body is drained, voice hollow, but somehow you're laughing—not because it's funny, but because the absurdity of trusted love is physically overwhelming. The physical sensations must drive the emotional journey.
inspired_by: An actor is studying with a teacher or workshop and wants to make the most of it

title: The Moment You Realize You're Capable of Violence
instruction: You're shaking, adrenaline flooding your system after nearly—or actually—hurting someone who hurt someone you love. Start with explosive, jagged breathing, voice raw and fierce: 'I would have killed them. I wanted to. I could feel it in my hands.' There's a savage satisfaction in your tone, a righteous fury that feels good and terrifying. But as you look at your own trembling hands, describe what you felt in that moment, your voice begins to crack with horror at yourself. 'What does that make me?' The rage starts collapsing into fear—fear of your own capacity for violence, for losing control. You might sob with frustration, with self-disgust, with the helpless need to protect someone while being terrified of what you've become. Oscillate between that fierce, primal protectiveness and the devastating recognition that you crossed a line inside yourself. End with your voice small, broken: 'I didn't know I had that in me.' Let your body shake with the aftermath of adrenaline and horror mixed together.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent what their relentless positivity and forced enthusiasm cost you as a child. Start by mimicking their overly cheerful voice, the way they would describe your failures as 'character-building adventures' and your pain as 'life's little challenges.' Let bitter mockery turn into raw anger as you reveal how their refusal to see your real struggles left you feeling invisible. Then let the anger crack open to expose the hurt child underneath—the one who just needed someone to acknowledge that things were hard, that you were struggling, that it wasn't all wonderful. End in a place of exhausted honesty, voice stripped of performance, asking simply: 'Why couldn't you just see me?'

title: The Driveway Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father in the driveway where he taught you to ride a bike, where he worked on the car every Sunday, where you sat on the hood as a teenager telling him your dreams. He's about to leave—walking out on the family—and this concrete, oil-stained space holds twenty years of who you thought he was. Begin standing exactly where you stood as a seven-year-old watching him with such admiration. Let the ghost of that child's love for him fill you first—the safety you felt here, the pride. Then let the present reality intrude: the suitcase in his hand, the betrayal. Let your anger build not as abstract rage but as something rooted in this specific ground, these memories embedded in every square foot of pavement. Your fury must be inseparable from your longing for the father this place promised you'd have. End by telling him exactly what he's destroying—not just the family, but this sacred ground of your childhood.

title: The Midnight Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're whispering to your sleeping partner something you've never been able to say while they're awake. Begin in stillness, your body small and contracted, perhaps curled on your side, your voice barely audible. Notice where in your body the secret lives—throat, chest, belly. As you speak, let microscopic movements ripple through you: a subtle rocking, the smallest shift of your spine, fingers that open and close almost imperceptibly. Your breathing pattern might change—becoming shallower, then deeper. Maybe your head tilts differently as different words come. The silence between phrases should be as important as the words. Let your body gradually unfold, just slightly—a flower opening in extreme slow motion. By the end, you might be on your back, looking at the ceiling, your throat more exposed, your words coming from a deeper place in your chest. The vulnerability should be excruciating but also liberating, your final whisper carrying both fragility and a strange, quiet power.

title: Thunder's Lullaby
instruction: You are a child, perhaps eight or nine, standing in a torrential downpour with your father. The rain is deafening, streaming into your mouth, making you sputter between words. You look up at his towering silhouette, rain plastering your hair to your scalp. Your voice is small against the storm, but you need him to hear you. You start with a shout of fear, clutching his soaked coat, but as the thunder rolls and he pulls you closer, your words turn quiet, almost wondering—a confession about how the lightning reminds you of the nightlight in your room. You shift from terrified to a tiny, trembling awe, your voice cracking as you realize he might be scared too.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Gift Before Goodbye
instruction: Your terminally ill parent has just given you something from their childhood - a broken toy, a faded photograph, something objectively worthless - as their final gift before hospice care begins tomorrow. You're devastated that this is all the time you have left, that this small object is supposed to somehow contain everything unsaid between you. Start with the shock of recognizing this is goodbye, the disappointment that crashes over you that there won't be more time, more conversations, more chances. Let your voice catch as you thank them, fighting to find meaning in this moment. By the end, transform your grief into genuine tenderness as you realize this broken thing represents their whole heart offered to you. Your voice should move from hollow gratitude to something raw and真 - whispered, intimate, holding back sobs while your words carry真 love.
inspired_by: Hiding Disappointment When Receiving an Unwanted Gift

title: The Confession You Can't Take Back
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent the truth they never wanted to hear—that their drinking destroyed your childhood, that their absence left scars, that you needed them and they weren't there. Begin with trembling anger, words you've rehearsed for decades finally spilling out. But as you speak, you see them shrinking, becoming smaller and more fragile before you. Your rage starts cracking, revealing the wounded child underneath who still desperately wants their love. Feel your voice shift from accusation to pleading, from fury to heartbreak. End in a place you didn't expect—not forgiveness exactly, but a painful recognition that they were broken too, and now time is running out to say what matters. Let your voice carry both the need to wound and the need to connect.
inspired_by: Watching Your Parent Age: The Role Reversal

title: Hospital Bedside: Finally Telling Your Parent You Forgive Them Before They Go
instruction: Your parent is dying, hours left. You've carried decades of hurt—abandonment, harsh words, missed birthdays, feeling unloved. You sit beside their hospital bed holding their frail hand. Start with bitter restraint: 'I came because...' Your voice cracks with old anger, old grief. Then something shifts—you see them small, human, flawed. The anger melts into something raw and tender. 'I forgive you. I actually forgive you.' Your voice breaks completely, tears streaming, but underneath the pain is relief, even gratitude for this last chance. By the end, you're whispering 'I love you' and meaning it, your heart simultaneously breaking and healing.
inspired_by: Therapy: Speaking Your Trauma Out Loud for the First Time

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who's in a coma after an accident. The doctors say they might be able to hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and broken: 'I know you can't answer me, but I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' Pause. Your throat tightens. 'I was in love with you. I'm still in love with you.' The confession hangs in the silence. Your voice becomes even softer, filled with gentle grief: 'I was too scared to risk our friendship, and now I'm sitting here thinking about all the moments we could have had.' You reach for their hand. Your voice catches: 'Please wake up. Please give me the chance to be brave enough to love you out loud.' Silence. Then, almost inaudible, a realization that brings both peace and heartbreak: 'Even if you never feel the same way... I'm so grateful you existed in my life at all.' You're crying, but your voice is full of quiet, devastating love.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling a parent about all the moments they missed, all the times you needed them and they weren't there. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm and rational. But as you list the specific memories (your graduation, that time you were hospitalized, your wedding), your composure starts to fracture. The anger you've been holding back for years rises up, then breaks into something more vulnerable—the hurt child beneath the adult grievance. Your voice should move from controlled explanation to rising fury to cracked, raw need. End not with resolution but with the exhausted, throat-tight question: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to stay?'
inspired_by: Hiding Pain While Recovering From an Injury

title: Vocal Range Full
instruction: You're a vocal coach having a breakdown in front of your student. You demonstrate the scale: start at your lowest chest note (deep, resonant, controlled), ascending through your passaggio (the voice strains, gets vulnerable), and peak at your highest soaring note (almost crying). Then you tell your student, 'That's my range. But my wife never heard me hit anything above a whisper for the last five years of her life. I was too afraid she'd know how scared I was.' Your lowest note was your most honest. The demonstration of technique becomes the demonstration of loss.

title: The Seed Catalog
instruction: You are an older adult lying on your stomach on a carpeted living room floor, propped up on your elbows. You’re looking through a seed catalog for next spring’s garden. You’re genuinely interested—you pause to read descriptions, you hum softly, you flip pages with one hand. But your neighbor is in the room, and they keep interrupting with loud TV. Start your monologue with real curiosity and warmth for the catalog, but notice their noise. Let a flicker of contempt creep in as you comment on it, but then let your interest in the seeds pull you back as you drift off. Speak naturally, shifting your weight, losing your place, and finding it again.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Thank You That Can't Be Simple
instruction: You're thanking someone who saved your life or changed it fundamentally—a teacher, a stranger, a friend—but you can't stop noticing how inadequate 'thank you' sounds, how you're crying when you didn't want to, how you keep starting sentences and abandoning them. Speak all of it aloud: the gratitude, the frustration with yourself, the awareness that you're making this awkward, the anger that language fails, the grief that this moment can't be perfect. Start with attempted eloquence that keeps interrupting itself with self-critique. End in a place where your gratitude and your rage at your own inadequacy merge into something fierce and grateful and furious and loving all at once, where every stumble becomes part of the gift you're trying to give.
inspired_by: Actor is commenting on his own performance while performing, creating a split between observation and involvement

title: The Last Sunrise
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother who has hours left. She's slipping in and out of consciousness, and you're describing the sunrise through her hospital window—something she always loved. Start with forced brightness, trying to paint beauty for her. As you describe the colors, your voice begins to crack. You realize this is the last sunrise you'll ever share with her. Your words become softer, more intimate.
