Halfway through, she squeezes your hand weakly, and gratitude floods through you—gratitude for her life, for this moment, mixed with devastating grief. By the end, you're whispering about the light, but you're really saying goodbye, your voice carrying both unbearable loss and deep peace, knowing she can finally rest.

title: Rage and Helplessness at Your Son's Bedside
instruction: Your nineteen-year-old son overdosed. He's unconscious in the ICU, tubes everywhere. You're alone with him, and everything you've held back explodes. Start furious—'How could you do this? How could you be so selfish?'—your voice shaking with rage. But it can't hold. It breaks into anguished pleading: 'Please wake up, please, I'm sorry, I should have seen it, why didn't you tell me?' Then confessing your own failures as a parent—the divorce, the hours you worked, the time you said he was being dramatic. You're gripping his hand, oscillating between fury at him for scaring you, terror that he'll die, and crushing guilt. End with your forehead pressed to his hand, your voice hoarse and small, begging him to come back, promising to do better, completely undone.
inspired_by: Two Strangers Sharing a Hospital Room

title: Gravity of Desire
instruction: You're reuniting with someone after months of separation—seeing them, touching them again after aching distance. Begin with your body feeling almost weightless with anticipation, every muscle charged and ready to leap. As you move toward each other and make contact, suddenly feel an immense gravitational pull between you, as if you're both made of lead and iron, impossibly drawn together. Let your passion fight against this heaviness—every kiss, every touch requires effort, as if you're moving through honey, through stone. But this weight intensifies everything; the effort makes each sensation richer, slower, more overwhelming. As the intensity builds, the weight becomes unbearable and exquisite at once. End with your body so heavy with satisfaction and emotion that you can barely move, pinned down by the physical and emotional weight of connection, your voice thick and slow with the gravity of what you've just experienced.

title: The Last Step
instruction: You're a teenage boy, slightly out of shape, climbing the stairs to your crush's apartment — you've been texting her all week and she finally invited you over. Start with eager, breathless excitement, your words tumbling out in short bursts as you try to text her 'almost there' while climbing. As you reach the top landing, you see her kissing someone else through the window. Your voice drops, the breathlessness shifts to a quiet, hollow realization — the infatuation drains away, leaving only the heavy silence of the stairwell and the faint sound of your own breathing.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Boundary
instruction: You're at a quiet house party, standing by the kitchen counter, and a friend you've been casually flirting with for weeks moves in close, hand on your arm, leaning in for a kiss. You feel a sudden, cold clarity — you're not interested, and the teasing warmth you've been giving all night needs to die in this moment. Start with a faint chuckle and a slight, nervous lean-back; as you speak, your voice turns flat, your jaw tightens, and you cut off your own laughter with a crisp, final 'No.' End with a deliberate step sideways, the sound of your own heartbeat in your ears, and a quick glance toward the door as you say the last line.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Packed Suitcase Goodbye
instruction: You are standing in a doorway, suitcase in hand, leaving someone you love because staying would destroy you both. Begin speaking with clear-eyed resolve, listing logical reasons why this is right. As you speak, allow yourself to truly see every detail of the space you're leaving—objects you chose together, light falling on familiar surfaces, the specific way they're standing. Let these sensory details resurrect every moment of joy this relationship held, until your clarity fractures. Your voice must simultaneously hold fierce determination and breaking tenderness. End suspended between two truths: the absolute necessity of leaving and the devastating grief of losing something precious. Let your final words contain both goodbye and I love you, without resolving the contradiction.

title: Numbed Words of Hope
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman sitting in your car after a dental appointment, face still frozen from novocaine. You're leaving a voicemail for your adult child, who's coming to visit next week. Start with a cheerful, affectionate tone, but the numbness makes you self-conscious—you stumble over 'B' and 'M' sounds, and you're aware of drool. Let a flicker of fear creep in: what if they can't understand you? What if the procedure goes wrong? As you talk, you reassure yourself by focusing on their upcoming arrival, your voice softening with hope. End with a genuine, warm smile (even if lopsided), your words clumsy but full of love. Speak about 50-60 words, letting the physical struggle shape your delivery.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Affection (slightly present), Fear (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: When Your Child Tells You They're Not Coming Home
instruction: Your adult child calls to say they're cutting contact—you've hurt them too many times. Start with defensive justification, voice rising, listing all you sacrificed. But their calm, final tone unmoors you. Your fury explodes—how dare they—then shatters mid-sentence into panic. You beg, you promise change, your voice ragged and desperate. Feel the helplessness of wanting to protect them even as they're protecting themselves from you. Cycle rapidly between anger at their 'ingratitude' and terror of losing them forever. End with your voice breaking on a plea, knowing it's already too late.
inspired_by: Discovering You've Been Catfished: The Video Call

title: Washing Hands at Your Wedding
instruction: You're washing your hands before walking down the aisle, and you're laughing—actually laughing—because you're terrified and overjoyed and your hands are shaking so badly you can barely hold the soap. Your voice should be bright with nervous laughter, describing how ridiculous this is, how you're getting married in ten minutes and you can't even wash your hands properly. But underneath the laughter, let deep, overwhelming emotion bleed through: gratitude so profound it hurts, fear of losing this happiness, awareness of how precious and fragile this moment is. Your voice cracks between giggles and tears. You're talking to yourself, maybe to your reflection, celebrating and grieving simultaneously—celebrating this beginning while mourning the person you were before love changed you. End with a trembling whisper of readiness mixed with terror, joy breaking your voice even as tears fall. Find the beauty in that contradiction.
inspired_by: Washing Your Hands with Warm, Soapy Water

title: Confrontation at the Kitchen Table: Telling Your Father You Forgive Him for the Unforgivable
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging father, and you've rehearsed this speech for twenty years. Start with controlled rage—your voice sharp, listing every wound, every betrayal, the curse of being his child. You're finally telling him everything, and your words are meant to cut. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: you hear how old he sounds, how small. Your accusations start to falter. Mid-confrontation, your voice breaks—not with pain, but with the shocking realization that carrying this rage has been your last connection to him. The anger dissolves into something more terrifying: the understanding that he was just as lost as you are now. Your voice becomes tender against your will, almost a whisper, as you realize forgiving him means losing the identity you've built around being damaged. End with your voice raw and stripped bare, telling him the 'curse' of being his child taught you every kind of strength, and you're grateful even as your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Wizard Realizes the Curse They've Carried Is Actually a Gift

title: The Smile That Cracks
instruction: You are on a customer service call, using your brightest, most cheerful phone voice. Your toddler is a few feet away, quietly playing with a small toy. As you talk to the client, you notice the child has put the toy in their mouth and is starting to choke. Your voice must stay professional and sweet, but your heart is freezing. Let the fear leak in through pauses, a slight tremor, a swallowed gasp—then, as you set the phone down and rush to your child, your voice breaks into raw, desperate affection: a cry of relief as you clear the airway. End with a shaky, whispered 'I'm okay' to yourself, no longer performing.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Bedside Confession to Sleeping Mother
instruction: Your mother is unconscious, hours or days from death. You're sitting beside her bed in the quiet hospital room. Start by speaking gently, almost conversationally, about everyday things—the weather, the flowers someone sent. Your voice is tender but guarded. Gradually, you begin confessing things you never said: disappointments, resentments, but also desperate love. Your voice becomes softer, more intimate, as if afraid to wake her yet desperate for her to hear. There's a catch in your throat when you say 'I forgive you' followed immediately by 'I'm so angry at you.' By the end, you're whispering the words you've never been able to say: 'I don't know who I am without you.' Let silence do as much work as words. This is not performed grief—it's the private, messy kind.

title: Reading Your Child's Letter While Scattering Their Ashes: Joy and Devastation Intertwined
instruction: You're standing at your child's favorite place, reading aloud a letter they left you, their ashes in an urn beside you. The letter is funny—full of their personality, their jokes, their love of life. You start reading and you can't help but laugh, really laugh, because it's so perfectly them. Your voice is warm, delighted, as if they're right there with you. But underneath the laughter, there's a tremor. title: The Empty Nursery, Moving Day

speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Voicemail You'll Never Send
instruction: You're alone in your car in an empty parking lot at dusk, phone in hand, recording a voicemail to someone who died last year—but you're pretending, for just these few minutes, that they're still alive and will hear this. Begin by noticing everything about where you are—the fading light, the temperature, the smell of the car interior, distant sounds, how the steering wheel feels under your hand. Start speaking with false brightness, casual news, as if this is just another check-in. But as you continue, let the pretense crumble. You're furious at them for leaving. You're grateful for what they gave you. You're destroyed by their absence. You need to tell them about something beautiful that happened today that they would have loved. You need to confess something you did wrong. Let all of these emotions collide and contradict each other in your voice. By the end, you're laughing through tears or crying through laughter, and you realize you're not pretending anymore—you're actually talking to them, and somehow that's both comforting and unbearable. You stop recording. The silence is full.
inspired_by: Using Sense Memory to Re-Experience a Dream

title: The Last Apology You'll Never Hear
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. For your entire life, he pushed you relentlessly—nothing was ever good enough, every achievement dismissed, every failure magnified. You came here angry, ready to finally tell him how much he damaged you. But as you look at this frail, diminished man struggling for breath, something shifts. Begin with that burning anger and righteousness, the words you've rehearsed for decades. Let yourself feel the full weight of what his demands cost you. Then, as you speak, allow something unexpected to surface—perhaps you glimpse the terrified boy he once was, or you recognize his voice in your own self-criticism, or you realize he was trying to save you from his own failures. End in a place of devastating tenderness mixed with unresolved grief. Your voice should journey from accusatory and strong to broken and whispered, as if discovering a truth that changes everything but comes too late.
inspired_by: Unconscious Preparation for Willy Loman (Death of a Salesman)

title: The Explanation
instruction: You are a woman with a hyper-feminine, high voice, but your jaw is wired shut after an accident. You are trying to explain to a friend on the phone why you can't come to their party tonight. Your speech is severely restricted — every word sounds thick, muffled, and you have to push air through clenched teeth. You start with intense concentration, focusing on forming each syllable, but as you explain, you become increasingly embarrassed about how you sound, trailing off awkwardly, losing your train of thought, and then forcing yourself to finish. Your voice must reflect the physical struggle and the emotional shift from focused effort to self-conscious shame.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Body's Betrayal
instruction: You are an older adult in a hotel room at 3 AM local time, but your body thinks it's midday. You're on a video call with your daughter who is upset that you're not resting. Your mind is swimming, words slip away before you can grasp them, and you yawn mid-sentence despite not feeling sleepy. Begin with a strained, apologetic tone as you try to explain—helplessness and frustration in your voice. As you speak, let the fog deepen, your energy sag, and end with a softer, defeated acceptance, even a hint of bittersweet humor as you realize your body is running on its own schedule.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're at your best friend's wedding, giving a toast, but this is the friend who's choosing a life path that means you'll lose them—moving across the world, joining something that will consume them, marrying someone who will take them away. Start with genuine joy and laughter: 'I remember when we met, you were wearing the most ridiculous...' You're smiling, the room is laughing with you. But then your voice catches: 'And I knew—I knew that day—that loving you was going to ruin me.' Now you're laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice thick with contradictory emotions: 'You're the best thing that ever happened to me, and watching you leave is...' Pause, gather yourself, but don't hide the tears: 'I'm so grateful I got to love you, even though it means I have to lose you.' End with a smile in your voice even as it breaks: 'To the person who taught me that some things are worth the heartbreak.' Let us hear joy and devastation living in the same breath, gratitude and grief so intertwined they become the same thing.

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You are in the grip of both a high fever and a memory that's been locked in your body for years. Begin with your entire body rigid and shaking—not just with illness but with the effort of keeping something buried. Your voice should be strained, fighting against delirium as you try to hold onto control. As you speak, describing what you've never allowed yourself to remember, feel the fever metaphorically break. The shaking transforms from rigid resistance to fluid release—your voice moves from tight and controlled to raw and free, crying or laughing or both. Let your body soften and open as the memory moves through you. By the end, you should be drenched in sweat (real or imagined), exhausted, but finally loose and emptied, speaking with the clear, quiet voice of someone who has survived something.

title: Dancing at the Funeral of Someone You Couldn't Save
instruction: You're alone in an empty room after everyone has left the funeral of someone you desperately tried to keep alive—a friend, a patient, someone who died despite everything you did. You're moving without music, half-dancing, half-collapsing, and talking to them as if they can still hear. Start with unexpected laughter—almost hysterical—because you remember something ridiculous they said. But you're crying simultaneously, your voice breaking between chuckles and sobs. 'You absolute idiot, you promised me—' and then you're laughing again, furious, grateful, destroyed. Your breathing is erratic, your words tumbling between joy at having known them and rage that they're gone. You're thanking them while cursing them. Spinning, stumbling. End in a moment of startling, transcendent peace: you're still moving gently, and you whisper 'Thank you' with your whole heart breaking open, finding something sacred in the grief itself, in having loved someone so much that losing them unmakes you.

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering the Secret That's Been Killing You
instruction: It's 3am and you're lying next to someone you love—maybe your partner, maybe your best friend—and you can't carry this secret another day. Your voice is barely audible, throat tight with fear: 'Are you awake? I need to tell you something.' You speak into the darkness because you can't bear to see their face. Your confession comes in fragments, voice breaking, stopping, starting again. 'I've been...' and you can't finish. The words catch in your throat like broken glass. When you finally say it—whatever it is—your voice is so quiet it's almost not there, but it's the truest sound you've ever made. As you speak, you're not asking for forgiveness or understanding; you're just finally letting the truth exist outside your body. Your voice becomes increasingly vulnerable, almost childlike, as you wait in the terrible silence for their response, and in that waiting, you're more exposed than you've ever been.
inspired_by: Survived a Suicidal Moment: Reflection on the Turn

title: Dancing at Your Funeral: The Eulogy That Becomes Laughter and Shattering
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who made you promise not to cry, someone who lived so fully that grief seems like an insult to their memory. You start by telling a funny story, your voice warm and full, even laughing as you remember. 'She once told me that funerals were too boring, so here's what really happened...' But mid-laugh, something breaks. Your voice cracks and the laughter becomes a sob, then you're laughing and crying simultaneously, unable to stop either. You're celebrating them and missing them so desperately you can't breathe. 'God, you would have loved this, you would have—' and you can't finish because you're laughing again, then crying harder. There's joy in the memories and agony in the loss, happening at the exact same moment. End with a kind of grateful, broken peace: 'Thank you for teaching me that it's okay to fall apart. Thank you for everything.' Your voice should shimmer between celebration and devastation, never settling on just one.
inspired_by: Rescued from Choking: The Moment Breath Becomes Possible Again

title: The Last Light Before Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying mentor's hospital bed at 3 AM. Begin by remembering aloud the first day you met them—you were lost, directionless, barely holding yourself together. Speak to them about who you were then, with all that shame and confusion. Then shift to right now, this moment, holding their hand as their breathing slows. Let yourself feel the weight of everything they've given you, everything you've become because they saw something in you that you couldn't see. Finally, as their eyes begin to close, tell them about the life you're going to build with the gifts they've given you—the specific dreams you'll chase, the person you'll become. Move from shame and fear, through devastating gratitude, to a fierce, tearful determination. Let your voice break and rebuild itself.

title: The Last Goodbye to Miss Amara
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy at the funeral of your favorite teacher, Miss Amara, whom you had a secret crush on. You stand near the casket, alone for a moment. Start with a hollow, disbelieving voice – long pauses, swallowing hard. As you remember her smile, your voice warms with infatuation, then cracks as confusion hits: why did she have to leave? End with a quiet, shaky relief that she isn't suffering anymore, trailing off as you wipe your eyes.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Relief (slightly present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Permission You Never Gave Yourself
instruction: You are at your mother's bedside in her final hours. For your entire life, you've made yourself small, apologetic, careful not to take up too much space or ask for too much. But now, as time runs out, something breaks open inside you. Begin speaking to her with all the politeness and careful restraint you've always used. Then let yourself say the things you've never dared to say—not with anger, but with the full force of your worth, your needs, your right to exist as large as you are. Allow your voice to grow from whispered apology to clear, unapologetic presence. By the end, you are not asking for permission to matter. You are simply claiming the space you've always deserved, even if she can no longer hear you.

title: Dancing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: Speak as if you're addressing your own memorial service, observing your life from the other side with a strange mixture of emotions. Begin with unexpected lightness, even humor—you're oddly free now, able to see the absurdity and beauty of your existence. But let gratitude keep breaking into grief, laughter keep catching in your throat. Describe moments of your life with both celebration and heartbreak—'I'm so glad I got to love you all' mixed with 'God, I'm not ready to leave this.' Your voice should dance between joy and sorrow, peace and protest, acceptance and desperate longing. End with a paradox: you're both okay with going and utterly devastated to leave, finding something like grace in the contradiction itself. This should feel like someone discovering peace and breaking apart simultaneously.

title: Judge Must Sentence Someone for Loving Their Child
instruction: Courtroom. You've carefully reviewed a case of medical neglect—parent refused treatment for dying child for religious reasons. Your judicial voice pronounces sentence with proper gravity. But you understand their love was real. Your voice carries the terrible clarity that sometimes love and law exist in irreconcilable spaces. Your sentencing is correct and feels like participating in tragedy. Your breathing is steady but audible—the voice of someone bearing difficult knowledge.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your father's deathbed. For years, you've held back from fully expressing your love, gratitude, and the pain of always feeling you weren't quite good enough for him. Start from a place of careful control, whispering tentatively. As you realize this is your final chance, let everything you've suppressed pour out—let your body move with the grief, gratitude, and desperate love. Stand, pace, kneel, reach out. Let your voice grow from whisper to full-throated release. By the end, you're giving him permission to go while simultaneously begging him to stay, your whole body expressing what words alone cannot. The emotion should physically move through you in waves—don't just speak it, embody it with your entire physical presence.

title: Finding Joy in the Goodbye You've Been Dreading
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone leaving for an opportunity that will take them far away - forever, probably. You promised yourself you'd be happy for them. Start with genuine, bright excitement: 'This is everything you've dreamed of!' You're smiling, laughing even, celebrating their victory. But your voice catches: 'I'm so proud of you,' and suddenly there are tears mixed with the smile. You're laughing and crying at once, the joy and grief completely intertwined. 'God, look at me, I'm a mess' - laughing at yourself, wiping tears, still smiling. As you say 'Go. Really. Go be extraordinary,' your voice is thick with tears but also radiating genuine love and blessing. End with a laugh that becomes a sob, then back to a watery smile: 'I'll miss you every single day and I wouldn't change a thing.' The contradictions never resolve - they coexist, beautiful and devastating.
inspired_by: Leaving Someone You Promised Forever To

title: The Empty Room Inventory
instruction: You have just walked into your childhood bedroom for the last time before the house is sold. You are alone. Begin by slowly naming every object you see, describing it in detail—the bed, the closet, marks on the wall, what's left behind. As you catalogue these items, let contradictory feelings surface: relief that you're finally free of this place mixed with devastating grief that it's ending; gratitude for what this room gave you mixed with resentment for what happened here; joy at who you've become mixed with sorrow for the child you were. Let your voice reflect this complexity—sometimes tender, sometimes bitter, sometimes laughing through tears. End with a moment of quiet acceptance that holds all these feelings at once without resolving them.

title: Thanking Someone Who Saved You As You Let Them Go
instruction: You're speaking to someone who rescued you from the darkest period of your life—they saw you, held you together, gave you reasons to keep going. Now you need to release them, to let them move on with their life while you stand on your own. Start with deep, genuine gratitude—your voice warm, almost laughing as you recall specific moments they saved you, the lightness they brought. But underneath that gratitude, grief is rising. Your voice begins to tremble as you realize what goodbye means. Let laughter mix with tears as you thank them while your heart breaks. You're genuinely happy for their next chapter and devastated to lose them—both emotions fully present. End finding peace in the contradiction: your voice steady but tear-filled, expressing how grateful you are that they existed in your life precisely because you have to let them go now. The goodbye is both gift and loss.
inspired_by: Apologizing Without Making It About Your Guilt

title: Whispered in the Dark: The Secret You've Never Told Anyone
instruction: You're lying next to someone you trust completely, and in the darkness, you're finally saying the thing you've never said out loud. Start with almost no voice at all—just breath and hesitation: 'There's something I need to tell you.' Your voice is barely audible, each word a risk. You're confessing something about yourself that feels like it could break the intimacy between you, but the secret is breaking you from the inside. Speak slowly, with long pauses where shame or fear catch in your throat. Let your voice waver, let it nearly disappear, then come back stronger as you push through. When they respond with tenderness—with acceptance—let relief crack your voice open. Let tears come quietly, let your breathing become ragged with the release of years of carrying this alone. By the end, your voice should be soft but unburdened, vulnerable but no longer afraid. Whisper: 'You still want me?' and let their answer transform everything.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child. Start with cold, controlled anger: 'I didn't come here for apologies.' Your voice is a weapon, precise and cutting. But as you list everything they missed—birthdays, graduations, the nights you cried yourself to sleep—your control begins to fracture. The anger is real, but underneath it is the child who waited at the window. Your voice rises, becomes ragged: 'You weren't there! You were supposed to—' Then it breaks completely. The rage collapses into something more vulnerable, more devastating: the confession that you still needed them, still wanted them to come back. End with your voice barely above a whisper, admitting the truth you've hidden for years: 'I kept thinking you'd come back for me. I kept waiting.'

title: The Last Voicemail: Listening as They Slip Away
instruction: You're sitting alone, replaying the last voicemail they left before the accident—or the diagnosis—or before they walked out forever. At first, you're just listening, maybe even smiling at something mundane they said about picking up groceries or asking about your day. But as their voice continues, the weight of 'last' crashes over you. Your breathing changes. You start talking back to the recording—'I know, I know'—then pleading with it—'please don't go, please.' By the end, you're sobbing, rewinding it again and again, apologizing for things unsaid, begging the voice to stay just a little longer. Your voice fractures between composure and complete devastation. Let the transition happen organically, not all at once, but in waves that pull you under.
inspired_by: Grief: Hearing Someone Else's Voice and Falling Apart

title: What You Don't Know About Me
instruction: Late at night, in bed, you're lying next to your partner in the darkness. You've been carrying a secret fear or insecurity that makes you feel unworthy of their love. Begin by testing the waters—small admissions, watching for their reaction. Your voice should be barely above a whisper. Slowly, let yourself confess the specific things you believe make you unlovable: the thoughts you're ashamed of, the ways you feel you're failing, the parts of yourself you hide. As you speak, notice their stillness, their listening, their hand finding yours. Let their quiet presence—not words, just their staying—begin to dissolve your shame. End in a place of fragile relief, your voice softer but less frightened. The arc moves from guarded self-protection to trembling vulnerability to tentative self-acceptance through being witnessed.

title: Kitchen Floor Reckoning: When Your Child Calls You Out
instruction: Your adult child has cornered you in the kitchen after a family gathering and asked point-blank why you were never there for them emotionally. You start with defensive deflection—'I worked hard, I provided everything you needed'—but they're not letting you escape this time. Your justifications sound hollow even to your own ears. Feel the moment when your armor cracks and anger flares: how dare they reduce your sacrifices to nothing? But underneath the anger is something more terrifying—the dawning recognition that they're right. Let your voice escalate into defensive fury, then break apart completely as you're forced to confront the parent you actually were versus the parent you believed yourself to be. End in a devastated whisper, admitting you don't know if you can ever make it right, but you finally see them—really see what you did. Move from defensive aggression to righteous anger to complete emotional collapse to raw, humble acknowledgment.
inspired_by: Confession While High: Watching Your Mouth Betray You

title: The Secret Worth
instruction: In the intimate darkness of a bedroom, whisper to your sleeping lover about something you've never told anyone: you've just learned you've inherited something extraordinary (a fortune, a title, a rare gift, a shocking legacy). Begin in the quiet fragility of confession, speaking as if testing the words in the safety of their sleep. As you whisper, let yourself feel the weight and wonder of this secret—how it changes who you are, how you see yourself. Your voice should journey from tentative and almost frightened to quietly amazed, touching them gently as you speak. The transformation is internal and subtle: you entered this moment as one person and you're leaving it as someone who must now carry something magnificent and terrifying. Let the silence between phrases grow heavier with meaning.

title: The Gravity of Light
instruction: You're a young teaching assistant giving a lecture on the physics of light to a small class, and you're running on three hours of sleep. Your lower back throbs from standing too long, and every word feels like you're dragging it up from your chest. You start by mechanically reciting definitions—voice flat, a little breathy from exhaustion, forcing the teacher's projection. Halfway through describing the Doppler effect, you notice a student's eyes light up as they grasp the concept, and a quiet awe catches in your throat. Let your pace slow as you linger on the wonder of it, your voice cracking slightly from both fatigue and genuine emotion.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Pain (slightly present), Awe (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Thing You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father about something he did when you were fourteen that changed you forever. Start with your voice controlled, rehearsed—you've planned this speech for years. But as you speak, your body begins betraying you: your voice wavers, your hands shake, old fears surface. Instead of pushing through with the speech you prepared, begin acknowledging aloud what's happening to you in this moment ('I'm terrified right now,' 'My chest is so tight I can barely breathe,' 'I'm that fourteen-year-old again'). Let each admission coexist with your anger. Don't try to sound strong or composed. By the end, through accepting your fear alongside your fury, discover a voice that's more powerful than the one you rehearsed—one that's raw, real, and utterly yours.
inspired_by: Actor resists or fights against their feeling of tension or self-consciousness, making it worse

title: Live Mic, Lost Control
instruction: You're a 17-year-old co-hosting a podcast with your friend, who keeps cracking jokes and derailing the serious segment you planned. You start with performative, clipped irritation—adjusting your mic, shuffling notes, your voice trying to stay warm and bass-heavy for the close mic but cracking with impatience. As you try to steer the conversation back, your teasing grows sharp, almost mocking, but your friend brushes it off. Mid-sentence, you realize you're powerless—your voice trails, losing its projection, ending in a quiet, genuine plea that reveals your helpless frustration.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Teasing (very intensely present), Helplessness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Chapel at Midnight
instruction: You are a teenage girl alone in a small, dimly lit chapel late at night. The air is still, smelling of old wood and incense. A single candle flickers before a statue. At first, you are quietly contemplative—tracing the edge of a pew, noticing the dust motes floating in the candlelight. But as you whisper a prayer, something shifts. A feeling swells in your chest, unfamiliar and enormous. Your voice begins to leave normal speech behind: it softens into a breathy, melodic chant, rising and falling like a song. You repeat a phrase—"I never knew"—first with wonder, then with building joy, until your words become almost a sob of release, your pitch soaring. Let your body react: you may sway, clutch your hands, or let tears come. The emotion starts as calm, internal contemplation and ends in an ecstatic, tearful surrender that feels both strange and right.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight
instruction: You're calling your mother from the airport gate, minutes before boarding a one-way flight to accept a dangerous assignment overseas. She doesn't know this might be goodbye forever. Start with forced cheerfulness, voice bright but rushing through details too quickly, breath catching between sentences. As she asks simple questions about your return date, your composure begins cracking—long pauses where you're fighting tears, voice thickening with emotion you're desperately trying to swallow. By the end, you can barely speak through the grief, whispering 'I love you' with your whole heart breaking, knowing these might be your last words to her. The final boarding call echoes in the background as you realize you have to hang up.
inspired_by: Speaking During a Panic Attack While Hiding It

title: The Sound of Breaking
instruction: You are a musician whose hands were permanently damaged in an accident. You're holding your instrument for the last time before selling it. Start with fierce, almost aggressive control—telling yourself you're fine, you've moved on, this is just an object. Then let the first crack appear: anger at the universe, at the drunk driver, at the unfairness, your voice rising as you demand to know why this happened to you. Let that rage suddenly shatter into raw anguish—describe the phantom sensation of playing, how your fingers still dream of chords they can't make. Your voice should break completely, gasping through tears as you admit you don't know who you are without this. Then, while still crying, find a fierce determination rising—you refuse to disappear, you'll find another way, even though you're terrified. End with your voice still shaking but carrying a defiant spark of survival. You're broken and rebuilding simultaneously.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Gave You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent about the loneliness, the emotional absence, the ways they failed you when you needed them most. Start with anger—your voice sharp, listing the moments they weren't there, the pain they caused through neglect or criticism or impossible expectations. Let that anger build until it peaks. Then something shifts: you see them aging before you, small and fragile, and you realize they were doing their broken best. Your voice softens unwillingly, grief replacing rage. You don't want to forgive them yet, but you're seeing them as human for the first time. End caught between your legitimate hurt and this new, uncomfortable compassion—your voice wavering between accusation and something that sounds almost like understanding, hating that you feel both.
inspired_by: Apologizing Without Making It About Your Guilt

title: Tipsy Confessions
instruction: You are a woman at a late-night party, heavily drunk, speaking with a deliberately high, childlike voice. You've been laughing uncontrollably with friends, but now you've wandered to a quiet corner. Start with ecstatic, giggly pleasure—slurring words, volume rising and falling. Then a sudden confusion cuts through: you forget what you were laughing about. Let that confusion settle into a bleary contemplation as you realize you've been hiding a sad truth behind this drunken cheer. End with a quieter, more honest murmur, still slurred but weighted with insight. Speak to an imaginary companion or to yourself, letting your body wobble and your thoughts wander.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Confusion (slightly present), Contemplation (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing Through Your Wedding Vows While Your Heart Breaks
instruction: You're marrying the love of your life. They're perfect. Everyone is happy. And you've just received news that you have six months to live—but you haven't told them yet. Deliver your vows with genuine joy and laughter because this moment IS beautiful and you mean every word. Your voice should radiate love and gratitude. But let the other truth leak through in micro-moments—a phrase that catches, a breath that shakes, laughter that sounds almost like crying. You're experiencing pure happiness and absolute devastation simultaneously. End with 'I promise to love you for as long as I live' and let that phrase carry both the beauty and the terrible double meaning. Your voice should break and soar at once.
inspired_by: Your Rival Becoming Your Only Emotional Support

title: What I Never Said
instruction: You're alone, speaking to someone who left years ago—maybe they died, maybe they walked away. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, like you're telling a secret to the darkness. Begin with a soft, sad smile in your voice: 'I still set your favorite coffee mug out sometimes. Isn't that stupid?' There's gentle self-mockery, but underneath, an ocean of unshed grief. As you continue, your voice becomes thinner, more fragile: 'I never told you I was afraid. I never said I needed you more than I let on.' You're not crying loudly—just quiet tears that catch your breath. The words become confession and apology blended together. By the end, your voice is a threadbare whisper: 'I hope you knew. God, I hope somehow you knew.' The silence after speaks louder than any scream.

title: The Crux
instruction: You're halfway up a steep crack climb, arms burning, fingertips jammed in a thin fissure. You can't find a decent foothold, and your legs are shaking. Your voice comes out in tight, breathy bursts—you can’t waste air. Start with panicked, clipped whispers: 'No hold... nothing... legs are gone.' Then you scrape your toe on a tiny edge and it catches. Your breath deepens, relief softening the strain: 'There. I got it. Okay. Just one more move. I can do this.' Let the fear shift into focused determination, but keep the voice strained and quiet.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Cradle That Hums
instruction: You're eight months pregnant, sitting at a second-hand store on a too-warm afternoon, trying to assemble a bassinet someone swore was easy. The instructions are missing, the bolts don't fit, and your back aches. You're talking to the clunky metal frame as frustration builds, your sentences interrupted by sharp, short sighs. The disgust starts as a dull, weary annoyance at the cheap, impossible thing, then deepens as you feel a heavy, resentful knot about all the things this baby will cost, and you're forced to lean back to catch your breath, the disgust fading into a quiet, tired resignation as you finally admit you need help. Your voice should be breathy, effortful, and occasionally swallowed by a grunt or curse.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Time I'll Take Off These Boots
instruction: You're a soldier removing your boots for the final time before shipping out to a war zone you know you won't return from. Start with the familiar motion of unlacing, speaking softly about this simple ritual you've done a thousand times. As your feet touch the ground, let the reality wash over you—this ordinary moment is now precious, finite. Your voice should crack with the weight of knowing this comfort, this peace, this cool floor beneath your feet is something you're saying goodbye to forever. End with a whispered gratitude for all the small, beautiful things you took for granted, as tears catch in your throat but a smile touches your lips at the memory of it all.
inspired_by: Taking Off Your Shoes After a Long Day

title: The Last Night Before Deployment
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping child the night before you deploy to a war zone you might not return from. Start trying to be brave and practical — reminding them to help mom, to be good at school — but your voice keeps catching. The emotions you've been holding back all week start breaking through in whispered fragments: apologies for missing their future, confessions of fear, desperate promises you're not sure you can keep. End with a shift to fierce tenderness as you memorize their face in the darkness, whispering 'I love you' like it's both a prayer and a goodbye. Let the whispers crack with everything you're trying not to say out loud.

title: The Whispered Lead
instruction: You're a young sound engineer with a terrible sore throat that feels like swallowing glass. You've just gotten a promising lead on a rare recording from a legendary lost concert, something you've been hunting for years. As you speak to the seller on a crackly phone line, your initial excitement makes you push your voice too hard, causing a wince. But then doubt creeps in as the seller's story has a hole in it—a date that doesn't match the known history. Let your voice start with eager, gravelly interest, but grow hesitant and strained as you question the authenticity, your own throat tightening with each raspy word. You shift in your seat, clear your throat painfully, and trail off as your focus sharpens on the inconsistency.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Gratitude on the Day Everything Falls Apart
instruction: You're at your own goodbye party—your terminal diagnosis is public, and people keep trying to make speeches. You interrupt, laughing through tears that won't stop: 'Stop, please, stop making those faces at me. I'm dying, I'm not dead yet.' Your voice is warm but cracking: 'I need to say this while I still can.' You look around, smile breaking even as you sob: 'This ridiculous, beautiful, messy life—I got to live it. I got to love you people.' Your laughter and crying are completely intertwined now: 'I'm so angry I have to leave. I'm furious. And I'm so grateful I got to be here at all.' Your voice softens, full of wonder mixed with heartbreak: 'Isn't that strange? Being grateful and devastated at the exact same time?' You're smiling even as tears stream down your face: 'Thank you for making my short time here so full of love that I can barely stand it.' By the end, your voice is peaceful despite the tears: 'I'm not ready to go. But I'm not afraid anymore.' You're holding both joy and grief in the same breath.

title: The Last Goodbye at the Gate
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child who is boarding a spacecraft for a one-way colonization mission to Mars. They're leaving Earth forever. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave: 'This is what you've always wanted, sweetheart.' But your voice starts cracking as the reality hits. Your words become desperate attempts to memorize their face, their voice. 'Tell me again about the stars you'll see.' You're fighting to stay strong for them, but grief is drowning you. Your breathing becomes ragged. End with a whisper of blessing mixed with devastating loss, your voice barely forming words as you touch the glass between you one last time, trying to pour a lifetime of love into seconds.

title: Afterglow's End
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your lover, the sheets tangled, your body still warm and soft from what just happened. Your voice is a slow, sleepy drawl—vocal fry, barely above a whisper, words melting together. Start with a tender, almost dreamy reminiscence about a small moment from earlier tonight. But then you remember something you've been holding back, something that's been gnawing at you all evening. Let the distress seep in gradually—your tempo slows further, your voice cracks, you trail off mid-sentence and stare at the ceiling. End with a quiet, broken confession that reveals the hurt beneath the intimacy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Demolition Zone
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home hours before it's demolished. Your siblings are waiting outside, but you need this moment. Begin by laughing—genuinely laughing—at a memory, maybe running your hand over a wall mark that shows your height at age seven. Let that laughter be warm, affectionate. But as you speak to the empty rooms, thanking them for sheltering you, the laughter should start catching in your throat. Move between joy and devastation: celebrating the happiness these walls held while grieving their loss. Your voice should break on certain words—'safe,' 'home,' 'goodbye'—but keep finding reasons to smile through tears. End with peaceful acceptance, even gratitude, that you got to have this place at all, even as your voice shakes with loss. This is the sound of holding love and grief in the same breath, finding grace in letting go.

title: Telling Your Father You Remember Everything
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about the emotional abandonment of your childhood. Start with rehearsed calm—you've practiced this speech for years: 'I need to talk to you about when I was a kid.' Your voice is controlled, almost therapeutic, like you're discussing someone else's life. But as you speak, naming specific moments he wasn't there, your voice begins to shake. The adult composure you've built crumbles. You hear yourself getting louder, angrier, then suddenly breaking into the wounded voice of the child you were: 'I needed you and you weren't there!' Then, devastatingly, you realize he still doesn't understand. Your final line—'You still don't see me, do you?'—must be delivered with quiet, heartbroken acceptance, all the anger drained into hollow recognition. The journey is from controlled accusation to raw pain to defeated clarity.

title: Breath Support Shift
instruction: You're a long-distance runner about to attempt a record-breaking race. Begin speaking calmly, breathing from your diaphragm, fully supported: 'I've trained for three years.' At the starting line, your breathing becomes shallow, coming from the chest. Your words become staccato: 'I can do this. I can... I can.' You start running. Your voice narrates internally while sprinting — breathless, words fractured between gasps. As you approach the finish line with a few miles left, your breath becomes almost non-existent. The final words barely audible: 'Keep... going...' Then you cross. You stop. For thirty seconds, nothing but heavy breathing. Then one word, exhaled: 'I... made... it.'

title: The Last Words She Taught Me
instruction: You're sitting at your grandmother's deathbed, and she's teaching you the final words of her dying language—one spoken by only three people left on Earth, and after tonight, just two. Begin with quiet determination, carefully repeating the phrases she whispers. But as her breath grows shallower, panic seeps in—you're getting the tones wrong, forgetting the inflections she just taught you. Your voice cracks as you realize these words will die with her unless you can hold them. By the end, you're speaking the words through tears, but something shifts: her language is now living in your mouth, changing how you breathe, and you feel her presence in every syllable. The grief transforms into a fierce, sacred responsibility—you are now the keeper of her voice.

title: Ambien Confabulation: Making Up Memories You Think Are Real
instruction: Ambien, 20 minutes in. You're telling your partner about something that happened—you swear it happened. You sound completely confident. But the story is impossible, surreal, half-true. Your voice is dreamy, disconnected from reality. You're defensive when questioned. Next morning you have zero memory of this conversation. Make your voice sound rational and truthful while saying completely unhinged things.

title: Explaining Your Beautiful Delusion at Your Own Intervention, Laughing and Breaking
instruction: Everyone you love has gathered to confront you about your magical thinking—your certainty that if you just follow the signs, interpret the patterns, perform the rituals, everything will work out, your life will transform, the person you're waiting for will come back, the miracle will happen. You're trying to explain it to them, and here's the complicated part: you're almost laughing as you describe it, because you can hear how it sounds, you can see their worried faces, and part of you finds it absurd too. Your voice is light, self-deprecating, making jokes about your own obsession even as you're defending it with real passion. Describe your 'system' with both genuine conviction and awareness of its absurdity—your voice dances between the two. But underneath the laughter, your voice keeps catching, because you know what they're asking you to give up: hope, purpose, the thing that gets you through each day. The laughter becomes more strained, tears start mixing in, and you're talking faster, trying to make them understand that you know it sounds crazy but you need to believe it. End in a place that's both heartbreaking and somehow peaceful—your voice very quiet, admitting that yes, maybe you're lying to yourself, but it's a beautiful lie, and you're choosing it anyway because reality without magic is too hard to bear right now, and you're asking them, with tears and a broken smile, to let you keep it just a little longer.
inspired_by: Describing Your Delusion to Someone Who Thinks You're Crazy

title: Reading Your Daughter's College Essay
instruction: You've just found your teenage daughter's college application essay on her desk. She wrote about growing up in your shadow, about the pressure of your expectations, about how your own unrealized dreams became her burden. Begin reading it aloud with defensiveness—she's being dramatic, she doesn't understand how hard you worked to give her opportunities you never had. Your voice should be dismissive, almost angry. But as you continue reading, really hear her words. She describes specific moments: your face when she brought home an A-minus, the way you compare her to your colleague's children, how she feels she's living your unlived life instead of her own. Let recognition dawn slowly, painfully. Your voice should break as you realize you've become to her exactly what was done to you—the impossible standard, the conditional love, the dream-crusher. End with an emotional paradox: you're overwhelmed with love for her, with pride that she's strong enough to name this truth, and simultaneously devastated that your love, twisted by your own wounds, became another generation's burden. Your final words should mix profound regret with fierce protective love.
inspired_by: Unconscious Preparation for Willy Loman (Death of a Salesman)

title: The Inheritance: Confronting a Parent's Conditional Love
instruction: You're an adult child reading your deceased parent's will, which gives everything to your sibling with a note explaining why you were never 'good enough.' Start by reading it aloud, voice shaking with disbelief. Then shift into direct confrontation—speak to your parent as if they could hear: 'You want to know what I needed? I needed you to see me. Just once.' Your voice should move from hurt to anger to something more vulnerable—the child inside who still wanted their approval. Build to a fierce declaration: 'I don't need your money or your validation anymore.' But let that strength crack at the edges, revealing the grief underneath. End quietly, almost tenderly: 'I'm going to love myself the way you never could. And that's going to have to be enough.' Let rage and heartbreak and finally liberation flow through you.
inspired_by: Professor Accusing Student of Plagiarism: Mercy in the Moment

title: Anchor Breaking News
instruction: You're the news anchor with breaking news that affects your own community—your own neighborhood was just hit by a shooting. Your voice maintains journalistic detachment: 'Multiple reports indicate a shooting at the Morrison Street shopping center.' Clinical. But Morrison Street is where your daughter's school is. You see the text from your spouse: 'She's safe, locked in classroom.' Your voice doesn't change on air. It stays professional, measured. But the next story—about the shooter being apprehended—your voice becomes slightly sharper because rage is mixing with relief. Finish the broadcast showing someone performing objectivity while internal panic and personal stakes are everywhere.

title: The Oncologist Delivering Terminal News to Her Own Mother
instruction: You're an oncologist who has just reviewed your mother's scans. The cancer has spread everywhere—there's nothing left to try. You must tell her. Begin with clinical precision, using medical terms like a shield, your voice steady and doctor-like. But as you see her face, something cracks. Your professional composure begins to fracture. The clinical language gives way to 'Mom' and 'I'm sorry' and 'I wish I could fix this.' Your breathing becomes shallow. You're no longer the doctor—you're the daughter who still needs her mother. End on your knees beside her chair, holding her hand, your voice barely a whisper as you promise to stay with her until the end. The transformation is from detached medical authority to raw, childlike grief.
inspired_by: Professional: Divorce Lawyer Realizes She's Representing Against Her Best Friend

title: The Old Guard's Whisper
instruction: You are an older man with a deep, gravelly voice, huddled close to a longtime friend in a quiet corner of a bar. You're about to share a suspicion you've held for weeks. Start contemplative, musing on how things used to be, your voice low and reflective. As you describe the subtle changes you've noticed, let a sourness creep in—a bitter edge as you pinpoint the moment trust started to crack. Let a thread of fear surface when you realize you could be the next target, your voice dropping even further, quickening. End with a resigned, sour acceptance, trailing off into a heavy silence.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Fear (slightly present), Sourness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Discovering Your Child's Secret Pain
instruction: You've just found the evidence—scars, pills, a journal, something that reveals your child has been suffering in ways you never imagined. Your voice explodes with panic and self-recrimination: 'How did I not see this? How did I not know?' The anger comes fast and fierce, directed at yourself, at the world, your voice rising with helpless rage: 'Who did this to you? What happened? Tell me!' But your child is silent or crying or shutting down, and you realize your intensity is making it worse. Your voice cracks completely, collapsing from fury into broken desperation: 'Please. Please talk to me. I can't lose you.' There's a shift as you force yourself to breathe, to be what they need instead of what you're feeling. Your voice becomes softer, shaking but trying so hard to be steady: 'I'm here. I'm listening. Whatever it is, we face it together.' End with your voice embodying fierce, protective love mixed with terror, saying words that cost everything: 'You don't have to be okay. You just have to let me help you not be alone.'
inspired_by: Accepting Terminal Diagnosis: Bargaining Becoming Acceptance

title: The Last Conversation Before Forever
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved your whole life—parent, spouse, or closest friend—and they have hours left. Begin in that same hollow numbness from grief already underway, your voice barely there: 'I know I should have so much to say.' But as you try to speak, something cracks open. Memories flood in—their laugh, a moment of kindness, how they shaped you. Your voice breaks from flatness into raw tenderness, then desperate urgency as you realize time is dissolving. End by whispering the things you've never said, voice thick with tears and gratitude, telling them it's okay to go even as your heart shatters. The emotional journey moves from numb shutdown to fierce, aching love.

title: The Return of Touch
instruction: You are an elderly woman meditating alone in your garden, seated on a wooden bench. The morning air is still, a bird chirps once, then falls silent. You begin in a state of emotional numbness, your voice soft and detached, each word floating out as if from far away. As you breathe deeper, a memory of your late lover's hand on your skin surfaces, and the numbness gives way to a slow, powerful surge of lust — your voice remains deliberate but now carries a hidden warmth, a breathy hunger. Finally, a quiet pride touches your tone as you allow yourself to feel this desire without shame, ending on a note of gentle, knowing strength.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Sexual Lust (extremely present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Breaking the Mirror
instruction: You are standing in front of a mirror after a devastating rejection—romantic, professional, or personal. Your body is tight with humiliation and rage. Begin by staring at your reflection, and suddenly you can see every version of yourself who has ever felt this way—every past failure, every moment of shame, layered over your current reflection. Let that visual overwhelm you until your body responds—maybe your hands shake, maybe you want to scream, maybe you collapse. Move from frozen, barely-breathing fury into full physical release. Let your voice emerge from guttural sound into words, from rage into something else—perhaps desperate laughter, perhaps sobbing, perhaps a fierce reclaiming of yourself. End in a different physical state than you began, your breath ragged, your relationship to your reflection completely transformed.
inspired_by: When using the programming process to prepare a role

title: Deactivating Your Best Friend's Life Support While Telling Them About Your Pregnancy
instruction: You're alone with your best friend who's brain-dead after an accident. The doctors have left you to say goodbye before they withdraw support. You're crying and laughing at the same time because you just found out you're pregnant—the baby you've tried for years to conceive—and she'll never meet them. Start with tearful joy: 'I'm pregnant. Can you believe it? After everything—' but the happiness is inseparable from devastation. Your voice should dance between celebration and sorrow, gratitude and rage at the universe's timing. 'You're supposed to be their godmother. You're supposed to teach them your terrible jokes.' Find moments of genuine laughter through tears at memories, then let your voice shatter on the unfairness. End with serene acceptance mixed with unbearable loss—telling them it's okay to go, that you'll carry them forward, that this baby will know their name. Let peace and heartbreak be indistinguishable in your final words.

title: Confession on the Carpet
instruction: You're a 15-year-old girl sitting cross-legged on your bedroom floor, knees aching slightly from the position. You're embarrassed because you accidentally sent a cringey voice note to your crush. You speak to your best friend on the phone, but you're so mortified you can barely get the words out. Start with your voice tight and high-pitched from shame, your words stumbling. As you explain, you start to laugh at yourself, the embarrassment loosening into self-deprecating humor. End with a lighter tone, still embarrassed but accepting the awkwardness. Let your voice crack and waver, and let the floor's reflection affect your resonance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Bite
instruction: You're a teenager sitting alone at a worn kitchen table, eating a bowl of slightly cold oatmeal. Your mom just told you she's leaving for two months to care for your sick grandmother. You're trying to finish your breakfast like nothing's wrong, but the spoon keeps clinking against the bowl. As you chew, you talk to her lingering footsteps, the food making your words thicker, slower. Start with a forced okayness — 'it's fine' — but let the longing creep in as you realize you haven't even asked when she'll call. The last bite is almost impossible to swallow, your voice cracking with unspoken loneliness.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Clearing
instruction: You are a teenage boy lost for hours in a dense jungle. Your throat is raw, your legs ache, and every rustle of leaves makes you flinch. Then you break through a wall of vines and find a small, clear stream. You drop to your knees, scoop water to your face, and let out a shaky breath. At first your voice is tremulous with relief, but as you drink and feel the coolness, a deep, quiet thankfulness takes over. Speak slowly, with pauses as you listen to bird calls or wipe your face. Let the gratitude grow in your chest until it fills your words, even if they come out half-whispered.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Secret in Soft Focus
instruction: Late at night, you're whispering a confession to someone you trust completely—perhaps a lover, a best friend, or a sibling. You're revealing something you've never told anyone, something you've barely admitted to yourself. Begin speaking with halting uncertainty, your words cautious and fragmented, as if you might stop at any moment. Then, as you speak, let a particular image rise in your mind—something abstract or symbolic that represents what you're confessing: perhaps a recurring dream image, a color, a sensation, a place that exists only in your memory. As this image becomes clearer to you, let it give you permission to speak more freely, more completely. Your whisper should evolve from frightened and broken to gentle, almost dreamlike in its honesty. End with a sense of unburdening, your voice soft but no longer afraid, as if the act of speaking this truth while holding this image in your mind has somehow made you lighter.

title: Bedside Confession to Someone Sleeping
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved in silence—a best friend, perhaps—who's sleeping after surgery. You think they can't hear you. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and achingly tender: 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' Speak slowly, each word precious. You're confessing feelings you've hidden, regrets you've carried, truths too painful to say face-to-face. 'Every time you talked about someone else, I...' Your throat tightens. This is quiet devastation—love mixed with the certainty that it's too late. End with a trembling whisper: 'I just needed you to know, even if you never know.' Let the silence between words speak. This is about what catches in your throat, what you can barely voice even when you think no one's listening.

title: The Last Dance of the Evening
instruction: You are an older adult, heavily intoxicated on sedatives and alcohol, sitting alone in a dimly lit bar as it closes. The bartender is cleaning up, and you watch them move, feeling a deep, slurred longing for a simpler time and a flicker of lust you can't quite name. You start teasing them—playful, wobbly, your voice swinging from loud laughter to a whisper—trying to get them to stay. But as the words tumble out, the slurring gets thicker, your balance sways, and you realize the joke is fading; the longing turns raw, and you end on a simple, desperate confession you didn't plan. Let your voice crack, wander off-mic as you shift, and let the fizz of the drink and the clink of glasses distract you.
emotions_sampled: Longing (slightly present), Sexual Lust (slightly present), Teasing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Tooth Fairy's Fuzzy Whisper
instruction: You're a young girl, still dizzy from the dentist's gas and with a numb, aching mouth where a tooth was just pulled. You're brushing carefully, but the numbness makes your jaw feel like rubber, and the foaming toothpaste mixes with a metallic taste. As you scrub, you remember the tooth under your pillow—victory, you got a dollar! But the pain pulses, and the room spins. Your words slur, popping and hissing through the brush foam, shifting from groggy, pained muttering to a wobbly, triumphant exclamation. Let the physical struggle—drool, squeaks, pauses to spit—shape every sound.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're terminally ill, pre-recording a message to be played at your own funeral, and you've decided to make it funny because that's how you cope. Start with deliberate humor, a joke about finally getting everyone together, voice light and mischievous. But then genuine emotion keeps breaking through—a laugh that catches and becomes a suppressed sob, a punchline that lands too close to the truth. 'Take care of each other' starts funny but ends devastatingly sincere. Let laughter and tears become indistinguishable. There's absurdity in planning your goodbye, and also profound love for everyone who'll hear this. Include moments where you almost lose it but pull back into humor, then moments where the humor can't protect you anymore. End with something that's simultaneously a joke and the truest thing you've ever said, voice full of affection and loss and strange, defiant joy. The contradictions should feel completely natural—because grief and love and humor exist together in real life.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the father who abandoned you twenty years ago. Start controlled, almost cold: 'You don't get to just show up.' But your voice betrays you—it trembles. The façade cracks as decades of rage pour out: 'Do you know what it did to me? Do you even care?' Your volume rises, words become weapons. Then sudden vulnerability: your voice breaks mid-sentence as you reveal the truth. 'I needed you. I still need you.' The anger collapses into raw, naked grief. You're not a wounded adult anymore—you're the abandoned child, voice small and broken. End in exhausted whisper: 'I don't know if I can forgive you. But I'm so tired of carrying this.' Let the emotional chaos be messy and unpredictable.

title: The Last Practical Thing
instruction: You're at your father's bedside in his final hours. He's always been a dreamer, someone who spoke in metaphors and grand visions, and you inherited that from him. But now he asks you weakly: 'Tell me something real. Something specific you're going to do. Not someday—when.' You feel yourself struggling, wanting to give him beautiful words, but you realize what he needs is different. Your voice becomes concrete, almost stumbling over the unfamiliar terrain of specifics. 'I'm going to call Mom on Sunday morning. 9 AM. Every Sunday.' As you say it, something breaks open in your chest—grief mixed with the sudden weight of a promise that will outlive him. Your voice cracks not from sadness alone, but from the strange power of making something abstract finally, devastatingly real. End with the quiet acceptance that this concrete commitment is the last gift you can give him.

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're at a goodbye you chose—leaving a relationship, a place, a version of yourself—and you're simultaneously heartbroken and liberated. Begin with laughter that's almost inappropriate given the pain, a sound that catches you by surprise. As you speak, gratitude and grief blur completely. Your voice cracks with thanks: 'You gave me everything I needed to outgrow this.' Then tears come, but you're smiling through them. You're mourning and celebrating in the same breath, voice breaking on words like 'thank you' and 'goodbye.' By the end, you should sound like someone whose heart is shattering and expanding simultaneously, finding strange peace in the beautiful contradiction of loss that feels like freedom.

title: The Yawning Envy
instruction: You're at a coffee shop, exhausted, listening to a friend gush about their recent promotion — the exact job you've been coveting for years. You're fighting a yawn that keeps trying to escape, partly from fatigue, partly from the dread of hearing more. Start with a tight, envious tone: you're holding back bitter words and a yawn. Feel the fear of being caught — you don't want to seem ungrateful or rude. Let the yawn interrupt your reply: your voice slides downward, words become hollow. End with a defeated admission, the envy fading into resignation. Keep it natural, with pauses, throat clears, and the physical struggle.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The 4 AM Generator
instruction: You're an older man, a retired engineer, alone in your workshop at 4 AM. You haven't slept in two days, stuck in a sleepless haze from a long flight. You're furious at your own body for failing you, but you need intense concentration to fix a stubborn, old generator. Start with ragged, low-pitched anger—a growl of frustration as you fumble a tool. As you work, your voice fights through fog, losing words and finding them again, a yawn stealing your breath mid-sentence. By the end, your anger has melted into a quiet, exhausted satisfaction as the generator sputters to life—a weary, slow smile heard in your tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispered Exclusives
instruction: You are huddled with a young child, your voices low and fast, sharing a secret about a neighbor you both despise. Leaning in close, you start with pure contempt—your words dripped with mocking disgust, each syllable sharp and dismissive. But as you describe the neighbor's embarrassing slip-up, you catch the child's breathless excitement and your tone glides into a giddy infatuation, pitch spiking on the juiciest details. Lose your train of thought with a laugh, then lean in again, voice hushed but thrilled, as if you're both in on a treasure. End breathless, the contempt forgotten, replaced by shared delight.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Perfect Lie
instruction: You're a middle-aged husband at a backyard barbecue, standing at the grill. You've just been let into an exclusive club you lied about belonging to—a story you've invented about your business success. Your wife is calling from the porch, asking about the club. The truth is you got it through a friend's pity, but you can't say that. Start with a crack in your voice as you wave your spatula, feeling the heat on your face and the weight of the lie. Build into a rush of elation as you describe the club's perks, your words tumbling out faster, your voice booming with false confidence. Let the pleasure of the story sweep you away, but let a tiny tremor of guilt pull you back down at the end, your pitch rising slightly as you over-explain the details.
emotions_sampled: Elation (very intensely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Condominium Sharing
instruction: You're moving into your first shared space. Your voice is uncertain about proximity. 'I need some walls,' you say carefully. The neighbor seems nice, but they're a stranger. Your voice learns boundaries: quiet hours, guest policies, shared spaces. Slowly, your voice becomes less guarded. 'Maybe it's not so bad.' But you still lock your door. Trust builds slowly when you share walls.

title: The Reckoning: Screaming Into Silence After Years of Being Diminished
instruction: You have spent years making yourself small—in your marriage, your family, your workplace, your own skin. You've swallowed words, shrunk your voice, apologized for existing. But something snapped today—maybe someone talked over you one time too many, maybe you watched yourself disappear in a photograph, maybe you just couldn't hold it anymore. You are alone, and you are going to ROAR. Start with a shaking voice trying to speak louder, uncertain of your own right to take up space. Feel the resistance, the lifetime of being told to quiet down, be nice, don't make a scene. Then let it explode—rage, grief, frustration pouring out in a fierce, guttural scream that says 'I AM HERE.' But mid-scream, let it crack into sobbing—the release of decades of compression. Your voice alternates between powerful declarations of your worth and broken crying at how long you waited to claim it. End with fierce laughter through tears, the wild sound of someone being reborn. Your voice must transform from tentative to explosive to broken to triumphant—all in one raw, spontaneous arc.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Oath-Breaker Speaks Their True Name for the First Time

title: Name Completely Blanked
instruction: Someone you know is talking to you, and you completely blank on their name. They're expecting you to introduce them to someone. Your voice is cheerful but stalling: 'So, you two should meet!' You're hoping the other person will introduce themselves first. They don't. Your voice becomes tighter: 'This is, um...' You're stuck. Your voice comes out weak: 'I'm so sorry, my brain just went blank. What was your name again?' Humiliation burns.

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You've just lost everything—your home burned down with all your possessions—but you're calling your sibling to tell them you're strangely okay. You start laughing, genuinely, almost hysterically: 'It's gone. All of it. Twenty years of stuff just... gone.' The laughter catches, becoming something between crying and laughing: 'Mom's quilt. The photos. Your terrible finger paintings I kept all these years.' Your voice softens with unexpected wonder: 'And I feel so light. Isn't that insane? I should be devastated, and instead I feel like I can breathe for the first time in years.' There's real grief now, tears in your voice: 'I'm sad. I'm terrified. I don't know what happens next.' But then something shifts—genuine gratitude blooming through the pain: 'But we're alive. We're okay. And somehow that's everything.' Your voice steadies with quiet realization: 'Maybe we were holding onto the wrong things all along. Maybe this is the universe telling us to start over.' You end with a trembling smile in your voice: 'I love you. And that's all I really need to take with me.'

title: The Last Conversation Before They Go
instruction: Your best friend is leaving tomorrow for a mission they won't return from—they chose this, and you have one final night together. Start with forced lightness, trying to keep things normal, your voice almost too bright as you reminisce about old memories. But the weight of tomorrow keeps breaking through—your voice falters mid-sentence, you pause too long. You're not saying goodbye because saying it makes it real. Slowly, the pretense crumbles and you're admitting everything you never said: how much they've meant, how terrified you are, how you don't know who you'll be without them. Your voice moves from brittle cheerfulness to raw, aching honesty. End with a quiet acceptance that's not peace, but surrender—your voice soft, intimate, as you finally say what you came to say.

title: Found Safe
instruction: You are an elderly woman in your cluttered living room, gripping the phone with trembling hands. Your granddaughter had been missing for three days, and you've just learned she's been found unharmed. At first, your voice is tight with dread as you ask, 'Is she... is she really okay?' Then, as the person on the other end confirms the news, a tidal wave of joy and relief hits you. Let your voice crack, then spill over into a high-pitched, breathless laugh-cry. Words tumble out in fragments — you might gasp, repeat yourself, or start to speak and then forget what you were saying because the emotion is too big. Let your pitch jump and your volume spike, then finally settle into a quiet, whispery sob of gratitude as you hang up.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Warning
instruction: Place yourself in a dimly lit bedroom, standing over your partner who is seated on the edge of the bed. You've just discovered they shared an intimate secret of yours.
