The initial silence is thick with rage. Begin with a low, controlled whisper, each word precise and cold. Let your anger simmer as you move closer, letting your voice drop into a growl. Then shift into a breathy, seductive tone, but keep the edge of threat. End with a firm, projected command, the lust and fury merging into one final warning. Allow natural pauses, a slight tremor in your breath, and a moment where you lose the thought and reclaim it.
emotions_sampled: Anger (very intensely present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Stool
instruction: You are an elderly woman, just back from a long walk to the pharmacy. You perch on the edge of a wooden stool in your kitchen, feet barely touching the floor — core tight, breath shallow. At first, you're exhausted and a little embarrassed to be this winded, your voice strained and rushed as you mutter to yourself about your age. But as you settle, a wave of relief softens your shoulders; you let out a shaky sigh, and your voice drops into a slower, warmer register — tired but grateful, finally admitting you're okay. Speak as if your daughter is on the phone, but your words are half to her, half to your own trembling body.
emotions_sampled: Relief (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Embarrassment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Ceiling Stars
instruction: You are a child lying flat on your back on the carpet, staring at the ceiling. Your voice has a natural 'puddled' sound—slightly nasal, weak projection, as if you're talking up to a parent standing over you. You start with a hopeful, dreamy tone, imagining shapes in the ceiling texture. Then you become elated as you find a perfect one. Finally, you tease the other person, challenging them to see it too. Let your voice shift from soft wonder to bright excitement, with a playful, teasing edge at the end. Allow natural pauses, slight breathlessness, and the physical sensation of lying down to affect your speech.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Elation (clearly present), Teasing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: I'm Not Your Project Anymore
instruction: You're confronting someone who's always tried to 'fix' you — a parent, a partner, a well-meaning friend. Begin with careful control, your voice measured but with an edge: 'I need to tell you something, and I need you to just listen.' As you speak, the dam begins to crack. 'Every time you've tried to help me, you've made me feel more broken. Every piece of advice was a reminder that I'm not enough.' Your voice rises with years of suppressed rage: 'Do you know what it's like to feel like someone's before-and-after photo?' Then it breaks — the anger collapses into raw vulnerability: 'I just needed you to love me as I was. Not who you wanted me to become.' They try to interrupt, defend themselves, and you cut them off with quiet ferocity: 'No. For once, I get to finish.' End with exhausted tenderness: 'I'm telling you this because I love you. But I can't be your redemption story anymore. I need to be my own.'

title: Telling Your Parent Why You Disappeared
instruction: After years of no contact, you're finally confronting your mother or father about why you left and never called. You begin with that same efficient summary—'I left because I needed to, I built a life, now I'm back'—but they won't let you hide behind brevity. They demand the truth. Your voice starts guarded, almost cold in its economy, using distance as armor. But as they push, asking 'What did I do?', the dam breaks. Suddenly you're confessing the small cruelties, the moments of invisibility, the way love felt conditional. Your anger rises, then collapses into something more vulnerable—the child in you who just wanted to be seen. Move from cold efficiency to heated accusation to, finally, raw need: 'I just wanted you to choose me.' Let your voice crack not with rage but with the ache of unmet longing.

title: The Thing You Knew All Along
instruction: Your parent has just asked you a direct question they've avoided for years: 'Do you blame me?' You're standing in the kitchen where you grew up. Start with the reflex to say 'no,' to protect them, to keep the peace—feel that impulse in your body. But don't act on it immediately. Let the real answer rise up from somewhere deeper, messier. Let yourself shift from defensive softness to something harder, more honest. By the end, you should be saying things you didn't know you needed to say. Don't perform anger or forgiveness—discover which one actually lives in you right now. Let your voice find its own path from careful to unguarded.
inspired_by: An actor has difficulty trusting their impulses enough to make the first committed expression

title: Dancing Through the Fire
instruction: You are moving through intense physical pain—a brutal injury, childbirth, or a punishing physical ordeal—but instead of collapsing into suffering, you meet it with euphoric defiance. Begin with raw acknowledgment of the pain: groans, gasps, the honest reality of your body's limits. But then let something primal and ecstatic surge through you—a wild joy in your own aliveness, a savage celebration of your strength and resilience. Laugh through the agony, roar with exhilaration, let your voice become a battle cry of someone transcending their body's protests. Mix sensual pleasure with the pain—find the beauty in your endurance, the erotic power of pushing past what you thought possible. End in a state of triumphant ecstasy, your body and voice blazing with invincible vitality, utterly intoxicated by your own capacity to endure and transform suffering into fierce, sensual joy.
inspired_by: Actor's ego state is significantly lower than the character's—character is supremely confident, powerful, or dominant

title: Breathing the Same Air
instruction: You're lying in bed in the dark, inches away from your partner after months of emotional distance. Begin by whispering something you've never said aloud—a fear, a shame, a secret longing. As you speak in the darkness, become aware of every tiny sensation: their breathing pattern, the warmth of their skin near yours, the weight of the silence between your words, the texture of the sheets, the sound of a car passing outside. Let each sensory detail either terrify you more or give you courage to go deeper. Start tentative and self-protective, but let the intimacy of the darkness and proximity pull more truth from you. End completely exposed—either in fragile hope or devastating honesty. Let the physical closeness and sensory reality of the moment strip away your defenses layer by layer.
inspired_by: A choice has lost its strength after repeated use in a long run

title: The Flubbed Answer
instruction: You are an elderly woman on a popular podcast, using a bright, hyper-feminized voice to charm the listeners. Mid-sentence, the host gently points out you just got a key detail wrong about your own life story. A jolt of embarrassment hits—your voice wavers, you let out a small nervous laugh. As you try to correct yourself, shame rises, heavy and hot. The performative warmth crumbles; you speak slower, quieter, your voice dropping its false pitch. End with a raw, shaky admission, as if you’re confessing to yourself more than the audience. (Approx. 50 words)
emotions_sampled: Doubt (slightly present), Embarrassment (extremely present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Rage Against the Dying Light: Fighting Hypoxia with Everything You Have
instruction: Begin with explosive defiance—you're oxygen-deprived but violently refusing to accept it. Your voice is ragged, fierce, shouting at yourself to stay awake, slapping your face, your words slurred but your will ferocious. 'GET UP! MOVE!' But your body betrays you. Your rage begins fracturing—screaming becomes sobbing, defiance collapses into terror. Your breathing is desperate, gasping, as you shift from warrior to frightened child. Hallucinate someone trying to help you and push them away, then beg them not to leave. Your voice breaks completely—from roaring to whimpering in moments. The explosive intensity gives way to helpless weeping, your fierce protectiveness of your own life dissolving into the realization that you can't save yourself. End with your voice small, childlike, asking into the void if someone will stay with you, the fight draining away into vulnerable surrender.

title: Unexpected at the Gate
instruction: You're a teenage girl at the airport, a little buzzed from a tiny drink sample you had while waiting. You're leaning against a pillar, eyes half-closed, feeling peaceful. Then—across the crowd—you see your best friend, the one you thought was miles away, walking toward you. Your body jolts, a gasp tears out, and you shout her name. You stumble forward, dropping your bag, hugging her so hard you both almost fall. Your voice is broken, tear-laughing, then softens into quiet, happy murmurs as you bury your face in her shoulder.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Contentment (extremely present), Affection (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Weight of a Clause
instruction: You are an older paralegal reading a standard liability waiver to a new client. Begin in a flat, rapid monotone, emphasizing every qualifier—'whereas,' 'notwithstanding,' 'insofar as.' About halfway through, a specific phrase catches your attention. You pause, shuffle your papers, then repeat the line slower, doubt bleeding into your voice. By the end, you trail off, no longer sure this waiver is fair, and you let out a quiet, uncertain breath. Let your voice become more hesitant and fluttery as the doubt takes hold.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Character Quick Change
instruction: You're a character actor in a crowded room, dropping in and out of accents and personas while waiting for a date. British aristocrat: 'The weather, quite dreadful.' Shift. Southern belle: 'Bless your heart, sugar.' Shift. Brooklyn tough: 'Fuggedabout it.' Each voice is distinct — register, rhythm, everything. Then your date arrives. You go silent. When you speak, it's none of those voices — it's you, scared, real, stripped of all protection. Your date says, 'Which one is the real you?' And you realize you don't know anymore. The silence after that question is deafening.

title: Boundary Negotiation
instruction: You're trying to communicate something you want sexually but are terrified of judgment. Your voice is hesitant: 'There's something I want to try.' Your partner listens without judgment. You're slowly articulating a desire you've never said aloud: 'I want to...' The vulnerability is enormous. Your partner responds thoughtfully, possibly curious, possibly hesitant. You're both negotiating—your voice is vulnerable, their voice is honest about their own boundaries. The conversation might lead to yes, might lead to 'I'm not comfortable with that,' but either way, you're now known in a new way. Your voice at the end should reflect relief at being heard, even if the answer isn't what you hoped.

title: Midnight Confession
instruction: It's late at night, and you're whispering to someone you love—a partner, a child, a best friend—who is sleeping beside you. They cannot hear you, and that safety allows you to finally speak the tender, terrifying truths you've been holding inside: your fears about yourself, the ways you feel you've failed them, or the depth of love that sometimes frightens you with its intensity. Begin almost inaudibly, testing the words in the darkness, your voice trembling with the vulnerability of speaking these private truths aloud for the first time. As you continue, let yourself sink deeper into the confession, your whispers becoming more urgent and emotional, though never loud enough to wake them. End in a place of either quiet devastation or profound gratitude, having unburdened yourself in the sacred space of their unknowing presence.

title: The Stain That Won't Budge
instruction: You are an older woman, seated at a kitchen table, scrubbing a stubborn wine stain on a linen napkin. Your arm moves in a steady rhythm, breath catching with each push. Start with quiet irritation—a low grumble about the mark. But as you work, a memory surfaces of the dinner party where it was spilled, and a small smile flickers. End with a softened voice, a gentle laugh at the imperfection, carrying a thread of hope that it might come out after all. Let the scrubbing sounds and pauses to inspect the fabric shape your delivery.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Stain
instruction: You're kneeling on the kitchen floor, scrubbing a stubborn, years-old wine stain that just won't budge. You've been at it for twenty minutes, your arm aching, breathing heavy and rhythmic with each pass. At first you're muttering with frustration, your voice flat and tired. Then, suddenly, you see the stain begin to lighten—then vanish. A wave of pure, childlike elation hits you. Your breath catches, you laugh, and your voice rises with triumphant joy as you talk to the stain, to the floor, to no one. Let your words come out in broken, excited bursts, with pauses to catch your breath or wipe your forehead.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Old Glory on a Glowing Screen
instruction: You are an elderly man settled deep into a worn armchair, phone propped in your lap. You scroll through old photos with a sense of pride, your voice carrying a fond, husky weight as you recall a triumph from your youth. Then you glance at a news article about a younger rival; doubt creeps in, your words become halting, punctuated by quiet thumb-taps and muttered 'hmphs.' As you lock the screen, let a flicker of malevolence color a last whispered thought—'They never did earn it.' Start proud, end with a sliver of bitter darkness.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Doubt (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Hiccuping Discovery
instruction: You've just found an old, ridiculous photo of yourself in a box of keepsakes, and the surprise sends you into a fit of hiccups. You're alone, but you can't help talking to yourself as you try to process the memory. Start with genuine astonishment—your voice is breathy, disbelief cracking through the sharp, involuntary hiccups that slice your sentences. Let the hiccups force you to pause mid-word, stutter, and restart as you struggle to speak. By the end, as you look closer at the photo, your astonishment softens into a teasing, affectionate tone—you're amused at your past self, the hiccups still interrupting but now with a smile in your voice. Let your body react: shift weight, touch your chest, laugh a little through the fizzy spasms. Speak naturally, as if truly caught off guard and unable to control your diaphragm.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You are a parent with a terminal illness, telling your young child one final bedtime story on your last coherent night. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to make the story magical and normal, your voice bright but increasingly strained. As you continue, your composure cracks—pauses grow longer, your voice catches, and the story becomes less about fantasy and more about saying goodbye without saying the words. End in a whispered confession of love that you can barely get out, your heart breaking as you try to give them one last beautiful memory. Let the transformation from 'everything is okay' to devastating acceptance happen gradually, naturally, as if your body is betraying your brave intentions.
inspired_by: The Child and the Monster Under the Bed

title: Protecting Your Child From an Impossible Truth
instruction: You're trying to explain to your child why you can't protect them from something devastating, and the helplessness is tearing you apart. Start with forced calm, almost breaking: 'Come here, baby. Sit with me.' Your voice shakes as you try to find words: 'Sometimes... sometimes love isn't enough to fix things.' The rage erupts suddenly, not at them but at the universe: 'And I hate that! I HATE that I can't make this better for you!' Your voice cracks into raw anguish: 'You think parents have all the answers, but I don't. I'm standing here breaking because I can't take this pain away from you.' Collapsing into tender devastation: 'I would tear myself apart if it would help. I would give anything.' Then gathering yourself, finding strength in the wreckage: 'But here's what I can do — I can hold you through it. I can promise you won't face this alone.' Your voice steadies with fierce, protective love: 'So that's what I'm offering. Not a fix, not a solution. Just me. Always me. Every single day.' You pull them close, your voice breaking on: 'We'll survive this together.'

title: The Unreasonable Demand
instruction: You're a young professional in a boardroom negotiation, voice androgynous, dressed in a sharp blazer. The other party just made an offer that ignores everything you've already conceded. You start with a controlled, lower-pitched tone, fighting to stay polite, but your impatience leaks through in tiny cracks—a slight sigh, a quicker pace on certain words, a pause to keep from snapping. As you restate your position, your irritability rises: your voice gets a little tighter, you might shift in your seat or tap the table. By the end, the alpha shield slips—you're openly clipped, your words sharp, no longer hiding the frustration. Let your voice mirror the effort to stay professional while your body betrays you. Say about 60 words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Phone Call You'll Ever Make
instruction: You're calling your mother from a hospital bed, knowing this is goodbye. Start with forced brightness, trying to protect her: 'Hi Mom, I just wanted to hear your voice.' But as you speak, the weight becomes unbearable. Your voice begins to fracture. 'Remember when you used to sing to me when I couldn't sleep?' The tears come despite your effort to hold them back. By the end, you're no longer protecting her—you're letting her hear your fear, your love, your gratitude all at once: 'I'm so scared, Mom. But I'm so grateful you were mine.' Let the emotion move from protective cheerfulness to raw, tender devastation. Breathe through the tears. Let your voice shake and break naturally.

title: Ascending to Bad News
instruction: You're an older man climbing a long hospital stairwell to visit your best friend who just had a stroke. You start by teasing yourself about your age, huffing out jokes between labored breaths, trying to stay light. But as you climb, the joke wears thin—your voice gets tighter, the pauses longer, and the numbness you've felt all day cracks open into raw distress. Let the breathlessness break your rhythm: start playful, self-mocking, then let the weight of the visit creep in until your voice trembles and the teasing dies away.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Distress (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for someone you loved deeply, and you've just remembered something absurd they did—something so perfectly them that you start laughing even as tears stream down your face. Begin with the wobbling voice of someone trying to hold it together, formal and controlled. Let the memory crack you open: laugh genuinely, freely, even as your voice breaks with grief between the laughter. Feel the beautiful chaos of it—joy and devastation tangled together, gratitude and loss inseparable. Your voice should dance between chuckling and choking up, celebrating them while your heart shatters. End in a moment of profound peace mixed with aching sadness, where you're smiling through tears, finding that love and loss are the same thing, and somehow that's okay.

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, recording your final message to Earth before communication cuts off forever. Start with controlled professionalism, reporting mission status with calm precision. Mid-transmission, you see Earth in the window—that small blue marble—and something breaks inside you. Your voice fractures. You're trying to stay composed, to be the hero everyone needs you to be, but you're also just a human being who will never smell rain again, never hold anyone you love. End with a whispered goodbye to someone specific—your child, your parent, your love—where you finally let yourself feel the full weight of 'never again.' Let the professionalism crumble into raw, undefended farewell.
inspired_by: Fortune Teller Who Sees Something Terrible

title: The Leash of Lilacs
instruction: You are an older woman, hands cuffed to a metal ring on a table in a police interview room. You have just been told your grandson's rare medical treatment may be delayed if you don't cooperate. You begin with a strange, fragile hopefulness—you straighten your blouse, offer a lilac-scented handkerchief to the officer, and suggest maybe this is all a misunderstanding that can be resolved with tea and patience. But as the officer remains coldly silent, your voice tightens; you start to fidget with the chain, your smile wavers. By the end, a quiet malice seeps into your tone as you lean forward and whisper that you know where the officer's own daughter goes to school—your voice shaking with sweet threat.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Tightening Ribbon
instruction: You are a child, maybe six years old, dressed in an elaborate party dress with a satin ribbon tied too tight around your neck. You're at a family gathering, sitting on a scratchy chair, isolated from the noise. You try to ask your mother for help but your voice comes out strangled, pinched, unsure. As the confusion grows — why can't I speak properly? Why is my throat hurting? — a small doubt creeps in: maybe you're supposed to be quiet, maybe you're being a bother. Start with an attempt at a normal, cheerful question, then let the voice become raspy, strained, and fragmented as confusion deepens. End on a whisper, a quiet admission that you'll just wait and try to fix it yourself, your tone faltering, losing its childlike certainty.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Your Hands Used to Hold Mine Like This
instruction: You're sitting across from your spouse of thirty years who has early-onset dementia and no longer recognizes you. Take their hand and place it on the wooden table between you, covering it with yours. Speak barely above a whisper, voice trembling with tenderness. Describe the feeling of their skin, the familiar calluses, the wedding ring. Remind them, so gently, of when you bought this table together, how you held hands across it during your first dinner in your new home. Your voice should be thick with unshed tears, each word careful, as if speaking too loudly might shatter something precious. Let pauses hang in the air. Describe how your hands fit together, how they always have. End with the devastating realization washing over you - they're looking at you like a stranger. Your voice breaks on 'I love you,' even though they don't remember what that means anymore.
inspired_by: Running Your Hand Over a Smooth, Polished Wooden Table

title: What We Never Said
instruction: Late at night, after years of friendship, you're finally telling them the truth in a whisper: you've been in love with them all along. Start with your voice barely audible, catching on words, each confession a small death. They're quiet, and in that silence, you begin to understand—they knew. They've always known. Your whisper should crack as you ask why they never said anything, and their answer is tender and devastating: they were afraid of losing you, so they chose to love you from a safe distance. This isn't a romance; it's a requiem for what you both wanted but were too afraid to reach for. End with both of you crying softly, understanding each other completely, and knowing nothing can ever be the same. The kind of intimacy that feels like grief.

title: The Last Wash
instruction: You are an elderly man, recovering from a bad respiratory illness, standing at your kitchen sink. Your pride is fierce: you insisted on washing the dishes yourself despite your daughter's protests, to prove you're still capable. You start by scoffing at your own stubbornness with the wheezy amusement of a man who knows he's ridiculous but won't back down. As you reach for a greasy pan, a wave of disgust hits you at the thought of your daughter treating you like porcelain, and you mutter to yourself in short, clipped phrases—each one a struggle through your squeezed airway. By the end, that pride has softened into a quiet, resigned admission that your body is betraying you, but you refuse to say it out loud.
emotions_sampled: Pride (very intensely present), Amusement (clearly present), Disgust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're a soldier calling your child from a secure location, knowing this deployment might be one-way. Start with forced cheerfulness, asking about school, their drawing, keeping your voice light. But as they ask when you're coming home, something breaks. Your voice begins to shake. You're trying so hard to be brave, to give them something good to remember, but grief is flooding through you. Tell them you love them—say it like you're memorizing the shape of the words. Your breathing becomes uneven. By the end, you're whispering promises you're not sure you can keep, your voice raw with the collision of fierce love and devastating acceptance. Let silence carry as much weight as words.

title: Echoes of a Win
instruction: You're a teenage boy alone in your room after winning a championship game. You're screaming into a pillow, your voice raw and proud at first—'I did it! I’m the best!'—but as the sound fades, doubt hits. You stop, breathing hard, and start questioning whether you earned it or just got lucky. Your voice drops, becomes uncertain, then lifts with a flicker of interest as you wonder aloud what you could become if you actually worked for it. Let your voice crack, trail off, then pick up again like you're thinking out loud.
emotions_sampled: Pride (clearly present), Doubt (very intensely present), Interest (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Clear Moment
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother in hospice. She's been slipping in and out of consciousness for days, but suddenly her eyes open with unusual clarity. Begin by holding back everything you've wanted to say, your body tight with the fear of losing her. As she squeezes your hand, let yourself unlock—allow your breathing to deepen, notice the warmth of her skin, the weight of her hand in yours. From this unlocked place, tell her three things: something you never thanked her for, something you're afraid of without her, and something funny only the two of you understand. By the end, move from desperate clinging to a kind of open-hearted release, letting grief and gratitude flow together without holding either back.

title: Despair Bottomless
instruction: You've tried and failed so many times that trying again feels impossible. Your voice is monotone, each word dropped without inflection. 'What's the point. I've tried. It doesn't matter.' There's no emotion in the words, which is somehow worse than sadness. Breathing is minimal. When you speak of the future, your voice doesn't change—no hope, no fear, just absence. 'I don't see a way out.' This isn't dramatic; it's the vocal sound of someone whose will is gone. Silence is long. Words take effort. Speech is sparse.

title: Dancing in the Hospice Light
instruction: You're sitting with your dying best friend or sibling in their final hours, and they've just made a ridiculous joke about the afterlife or their terrible hospital gown. Start laughing—real, genuine laughter that catches you off guard—and let that laughter coexist with tears streaming down your face. As you speak, thank them for everything: for knowing you, for the adventures, for the ordinary Tuesdays that meant everything. But let your gratitude be soaked in grief, your voice breaking on words like 'always' and 'forever' because those words are lies now. Find moments of genuine joy remembering who they are, then let that joy twist into anguish that this is ending. End in a place of strange, terrible peace—telling them it's okay to go while your heart is being torn in half, your voice steady and shattered at once.

title: Historical: Nazi Officer Hides a Jewish Woman While Maintaining Public Stance
instruction: Public voice in morning—Nazi ideology, cold and certain. Then private voice in evening—to the woman hidden in your basement, gentle and apologetic. Your voice bifurcates entirely between public and private, each real in its own way. You're performing ideology while harboring resistance. Your breathing changes between registers. Public voice is controlled and hard; private voice is fractured and human. Include the moment you transition between them, the space where both are true and both are lies.

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church
instruction: You've just lost everything—your family in an accident, your faith, your reason for living. You're alone in a church, and you begin by trying to pray properly, voice controlled and respectful. But the words curdle into accusations. Let your voice rise from whisper to shout: 'WHERE WERE YOU?' Rage at the silence, at the unfairness, at prayers that went unanswered. Your fury should be volcanic, ugly, raw—knock over chairs if you want, your voice breaking from the force of your anger. Then, in the middle of your rage, let yourself shatter completely. Drop to your knees. Let the screaming dissolve into sobbing, and in that devastation, find a moment of terrifying helplessness where you realize you're still here, still breathing, and you don't know how to survive this. End in exhausted, empty silence.
inspired_by: Falling in Love at a Funeral

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: After twenty years, you're face to face with the parent who abandoned you. Start with rehearsed words—you've practiced this—'I wanted you to know I turned out fine without you.' But your voice betrays you immediately; it's not fine. The hurt bleeds through. 'I needed you at my graduation. At my wedding. When my child was born.' Each sentence gets more raw. Then something shifts: 'But I'm tired of needing you.' Your voice hardens with newfound strength, then softens again into something sadder, more mature. 'I don't hate you anymore. I just... don't know you.' End with quiet, devastating acceptance. Show the journey from anger to grief to the exhausted peace of letting go.
inspired_by: Getting the Job After Years of Rejection

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying parent who spent their entire life afraid—afraid to travel, afraid to love fully, afraid to take risks. For years you've carried quiet resentment about this. Now, in their final hour, you need to give them permission to let go, but to do this authentically, you must first find the courage to tell them something powerful: that despite everything, they taught you to be brave in ways they never knew. Begin speaking from a place of guarded sadness and old frustration. As you speak, let something shift—discover that in naming their fear, you're actually declaring your own strength, your own invincibility. End with a powerful, grounded sense of who you've become because of them, not in spite of them. Your voice should transform from tentative and wounded to strong and certain, as if you're finally stepping into your own power at the moment of their departure.

title: The Last Letter by Lamplight
instruction: You are an elderly woman lying on the floor of a cluttered attic, propped on your elbows to read a brittle, yellowed letter by the dim beam of a flashlight. Your body aches, and you shift your weight slightly to relieve the pressure on your ribs. As you read, disappointment settles in: the letter is from an old love who promised to return, but it's clear he never will. But mixed with that, a vast, aching longing rises—a desperate want for the life you dreamed of together, so vivid it makes your throat tighten. Speak aloud the few words you must say to yourself, letting your voice crack and fall silent at times, ending in a quiet, breathy resolve as you carefully fold the letter.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing in your child's bedroom doorway at 3 AM. You're leaving—maybe to protect them, maybe because you're too broken to stay, maybe both. Your voice is barely audible, thick with tears you can't let fall too loud: 'Baby, I need to tell you something, even though you can't hear me.' Kneel beside the bed. Your voice catches on every word: 'You are the best thing I ever did. The only thing I got right.' Let silence hang there—you're memorizing their face. Continue with aching tenderness: 'Your dad—he'll be enough. He's always been the better parent.' Your voice splinters: 'I'm so sorry I'm not strong enough to stay.' Touch their hair so gently: 'When you're older, maybe you'll understand. Maybe you'll hate me. That's okay.' End with a broken whisper of devastating love: 'I will love you every single day for the rest of my life. Even if you never know it. Even if you forget me.' You have to leave now, but you can't move yet.

title: The Inheritance of Damage
instruction: You are speaking at a small gathering after the funeral of a family member who caused you both deep harm and unexpected moments of grace. Begin by attempting the socially appropriate speech—gratitude, fond memories, the things one is supposed to say. But as you speak, you catch sight of your own hands gripping the podium, or you notice yourself standing exactly the way they used to stand, or covering your mouth the way they did, or holding your shoulders the way they held theirs. You realize you've inherited not just their DNA but their self-protective habits, their insecurities, their ways of hiding. This recognition cascades through you: rage at what they gave you, grief at their own suffering that created yours, reluctant compassion for the frightened person they were, and sudden desperate gratitude that they survived long enough to damage you because it means they survived at all. Let your voice move through anger, sorrow, bitter laughter, and finally a kind of broken, complicated love—all at once.

title: Packing the Nursery
instruction: You're alone, packing away a nursery that will never be used, folding tiny clothes you'll never see worn. Start in a state of determined, practical efficiency—you're simply completing a necessary task. As you work, open yourself to the complete sensory environment without picking it apart: the softness of fabric, the smell of new cotton and wood, the light quality in this room you painted with such hope, the silence, the weight of each item in your hands, your own breathing and movement. Let these sensations accumulate and layer without questioning or analyzing them. Through this uninterrupted sensory immersion, allow yourself to move from efficient numbness toward an unexpected emotional destination—perhaps gratitude mixed with devastating loss, perhaps rage softened by strange relief, perhaps fierce grief intertwined with fragile hope. The contradictions should emerge naturally from the flood of physical experience, not from intellectual decision.
inspired_by: Actor is doing sleep-wake state work, free association, or unconscious programming and finds sensorial questioning intrusive

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from your parent's hospice room. They have hours left. Start with controlled anger—'You should be here'—but your voice is shaking. You've carried resentment for years, all the times they weren't there. But as you speak, looking at your dying parent, the anger crumbles into desperate pleading. 'Please. I can't... I can't do this alone.' Your voice breaks completely. By the end, you're whispering, 'I forgive you. Just come.' The anger has dissolved into raw, vulnerable need and the terrifying loneliness of loss. Let your voice show the exact moment the walls collapse.
inspired_by: Getting the Job After Years of Rejection

title: The Fortress of Quiet Pride
instruction: You're a young boy sitting alone in your room, elbows on your knees, staring at the floor. You've just finished building a complicated structure out of blocks or LEGOs, and the last piece clicked into place perfectly. At first, you're just breathing slowly, sinking into a deep, still satisfaction — the kind that makes you forget the world. But then, as you replay the moment in your mind, a small grin spreads across your face and a quiet tremor of triumph bubbles up in your chest. Speak as if you're talking to no one, voice low and a little muffled because your head is down — let your words start slow and peaceful, then subtly brighten as you realize what you've done. Pause once to shift your weight or pick at a thread on your jeans before continuing.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Taste of Goodbye on Your Mouth
instruction: You are kissing someone for the last time—you both know this is the final moment before one of you walks away forever. But instead of rushing through it or making it dramatic, slow everything down. Really focus on the physical sensations: the pressure of their lips, the taste of their mouth, the warmth of their breath, the way your hands hold their face. Between kisses, speak in fragments about what you're noticing—the specific texture of this kiss, how different it feels from the first one, the way their body is both present and already pulling away. Let yourself wonder what they're feeling, what this kiss means to them, whether they'll remember this exact moment. Your intensity should build from desperate grasping to a strange, fierce presence—almost ecstatic in its pain—as you become completely absorbed in cataloging every sensation of this ending.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You are finally speaking to the parent who abandoned you as a child, now decades later. Start with practiced, controlled anger - you've rehearsed this, you came here with a script of rage. But as you speak, the rehearsed words crumble and raw hurt breaks through. Your voice cracks as you reveal the specific moments you needed them - your graduation, your wedding, when your own child was born. Build to explosive fury when they try to justify themselves, cutting them off with bitter, rapid-fire accusations. Then suddenly, horrifyingly, you hear yourself sounding just like them - the same excuses, the same self-protection. End in a quieter, more devastating place: the realization that forgiveness might destroy you, but so will holding on. Let your voice reveal the war between the child who still needs them and the adult who knows better.
inspired_by: The Internal Monologue of a House Cat

title: Catching Your Partner in a Lie and Calling Them Out
instruction: They said they were at work. You have proof they weren't. You're confronting them. Your voice starts controlled, almost calm. 'So you worked late?' Bait. They take it. You have the evidence. Now your voice becomes angry, hurt, accusing. 'Don't lie to me anymore.' Your voice is powerful. They're trying to explain and your voice cuts them off. Your voice is broken because they lied. Betrayal colors every word.

title: The Daughter Who Chose Differently
instruction: You are confronting your mother—the formidable matriarch who groomed you to take over the family empire, who made you in her image. But you've decided to walk away from it all. Start with defiant strength, declaring your choice with the confidence she taught you. As she responds with the cutting disappointment only a mother can deliver, feel your certainty waver. Let anger flare—at her manipulation, at the childhood you sacrificed—but underneath, there's a desperate, childlike need for her approval that you hate yourself for still feeling. End in a place of painful clarity: you love her and you have to leave her, and both truths are destroying you. Move from righteous anger to confused heartbreak to terrible, liberating resolution.
inspired_by: The Queen and the Jealous Advisor

title: The Homecoming Betrayal
instruction: You are returning to someone you abandoned - a partner, a child, a parent - after years away. You're flooded with joy at seeing them again, genuinely elated, your heart soaring with relief and love. But underneath runs a darker current: you know you're about to leave again, and they don't. Begin with pure, almost childlike happiness at the reunion. Let your joy be real, unguarded, full of laughter and warmth. Embrace them, celebrate the moment. But as you speak, the knowledge of your coming betrayal begins to poison the joy. Each happy word becomes shadowed by guilt. Your laughter starts to sound wrong in your own ears. By the end, you must tell them you're leaving again, and watch your own joy curdle into shame and grief even as you see their face change. Feel love and self-loathing, gratitude for this moment and disgust at your own cowardice, all fighting for space in your chest.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty with physical and emotional intimacy with scene partners

title: Storm Breaking
instruction: You are standing in the rain after receiving devastating news, and the physical sensation of cold water on your skin begins to unlock something inside you. Start numb, voice flat, repeating the news mechanically. But let the rain, the cold, the physical discomfort break through your shock. Feel your body's response—shaking, breath catching—and let it connect to the emotional truth you've been holding back. Begin to speak through chattering teeth, then let sound become primal—rage, grief, desperation pouring out without filter. By the end, you are howling, keening, your voice completely uncontrolled, your entire body expressing what words cannot hold. Let impulse guide you without censoring.

title: The First Full Sentence
instruction: You are an older woman on a video call with your childhood best friend, whom you haven't spoken to since your stroke. You want to tell her 'It's so good to see your face, I love you.' But when you open your mouth, only garbled sounds come out. You pause, frustrated, try again, get stuck on the word 'face.' You tap the table, exhale, look away in frustration—then suddenly the sentence clicks. As you say it clearly, your voice fills with pride and relief, then softens into sadness because you realize how much you've lost. Let your voice start tight and searching, then bloom with accomplishment, then dim into a quiet melancholy.
emotions_sampled: Pride (slightly present), Relief (slightly present), Sadness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Emergence
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman waking from sedation after a painful procedure. The drugs still fog your mind—your words come out slurred, your volume is uneven, and you feel like a child again. At first you float in confusion, almost dreamy, but then a wave of intense pain hits, and you realize you are alone in the recovery room. Your voice starts as a mumble, scattered and slow, then sharpens into a raw, desperate plea as panic and need pierce through the haze.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before Deployment
instruction: You're at an airport gate saying goodbye to someone you deeply love who's leaving for a dangerous mission they may not return from. You both know this might be the last time you see each other, but you're trying to keep things light, making small jokes about trivial things—what they'll miss, what show you'll watch without them. Your voice should start with forced cheerfulness, those brittle laughs that paper over terror. But as the final boarding call approaches, let that facade crack. The trivial complaints become desperate wishes. The jokes catch in your throat. End in raw, whispered urgency—all the things you should have said every day but never did, now tumbling out in the last sixty seconds you have together.

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: You're telling a story about the person who just died, and you start laughing—genuinely laughing—at a ridiculous memory. Your voice is bright with the joy of remembering them alive, fully themselves. But mid-laugh, it catches, and suddenly you're crying while still trying to smile, your voice breaking as you say 'God, they would have loved this—all of us here.' The laughter and tears tangle together, inseparable. Your voice moves between gratitude for having known them and the agony of losing them, sometimes within the same sentence. End with your voice soft and wondering: 'How can missing someone hurt this much and still feel like a gift?' Show someone discovering that grief and love are the same thing, that you can't separate the joy of having had someone from the pain of losing them.

title: The Grateful Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your best friend who's moving across the world for a dream opportunity you encouraged them to take. You're genuinely happy for them, beaming: 'You're going to be amazing. This is everything you wanted!' But your voice keeps catching, betraying you. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, wiping tears while smiling: 'God, look at me, I'm such a mess.' The joy and heartbreak are inseparable. You list beautiful memories: 'Remember when we—' but can't finish without choking up. You keep pivoting back to gratitude: 'Thank you for being... for seeing me when no one else did.' Your voice breaks on 'seeing me.' There's a moment of pure grief: 'I don't know who I am without you here,' spoken so softly it's almost to yourself. But then you rally, find strength: 'But that's why you have to go. So I can figure that out.' By the end, you're holding their hands, tears streaming, but smiling genuinely: 'I love you. Go. Go and don't look back.' The final words should somehow hold both complete devastation and complete blessing—a letting go that's both generous and absolutely shattering.

title: Veteran Whispers Goodbye to Their War Dog Being Euthanized in Their Lap
instruction: Your voice is so quiet it's almost not there at all—just breath and broken whispers against soft fur. This dog saved your life six times in combat. Now you're holding them as the vet prepares the injection, and you're trying to make every second count. You speak in fragments: memories of the desert, the night they dragged you from the burning vehicle, the way they always knew when the nightmares were coming. Your words keep dissolving into silence because your throat keeps closing. You're not crying loudly—the tears just fall while you stroke their head and tell them they're good, so good, the best. There's tenderness in every syllable, but underneath it, a grief so profound it feels like your chest is caving in. You tell them it's okay to go, even though it's not okay, nothing is okay. Your voice breaks completely when you feel their breathing slow, and you press your forehead to theirs, whispering 'thank you' over and over until it becomes a prayer, a plea, a final act of love. The last thing you say is their name, and it sounds like both hello and goodbye.
inspired_by: Diplomat Negotiates Peace Deal While Their Country Is Being Invaded

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've been holding everything together for months—caregiving, working, managing crisis after crisis—and your body is screaming. Begin speaking while physically tense, your voice tight and controlled, explaining very calmly why you're fine, why you can handle this, listing everything you're managing. But your body knows better. As you speak, let physical sensation break through: maybe your hands start trembling, or your breath catches, or a pain in your chest intensifies. Let the physical overwhelm the words. Your controlled explanation must fracture into something raw and physical—perhaps your voice breaks, or you have to stop speaking to breathe, or a sound escapes that isn't words at all. Let rage, exhaustion, and physical collapse mix together. End in a different state entirely: spent, broken open, but somehow lighter. Your final words should be simple, honest, stripped of all pretense—maybe just 'I can't' or 'I'm so tired'—spoken from a place of complete surrender.
inspired_by: Programming the Unconscious: The Glass Menagerie (Tom)

title: The Broken Promise
instruction: You are a young man with a chronic stutter, standing in a dimly lit alley facing someone who once promised to help you but instead mocked you publicly. You start speaking with a fragile hope in your voice, believing they might apologize, and the stutter is tight—repetitions and blocks as you force the words out. Midway, you realize their smirk hasn't changed, and disappointment floods in—your pitch drops, words become more halting, a silent block holds you for three seconds. Finally, your voice hardens with malevolent calm: the stutter now spits out words with bitter precision, a quiet threat simmering beneath each forced syllable. 'I thought you…you— [block] —you’d be different. But your laugh is still in my head. One day, I’ll make you— [prolongation] —make you remember my name.'
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Final Show Before the Curtain Falls
instruction: You're a beloved performer giving your last show before a terminal diagnosis takes your voice forever. You begin with practiced showmanship, introducing your signature piece with the bravado you've carried for decades. But as you perform, the weight of 'last time' crashes over you—your voice cracks not from failure, but from the devastation of goodbye. Let the professional mask slip. Show us the human underneath who's terrified of silence, of being forgotten, of never doing this one thing they love again. End with a whispered acknowledgment to your audience that this is farewell, mixing profound gratitude with unbearable loss. Let your voice carry both the performer's pride and the mortal's fear.

title: The Last Dance on the Porch
instruction: You are a middle-aged man with a neurological tremor that affects your voice—soft, monotone, with a rhythmic wobble and occasional mumbles. You’re on a creaky wooden porch, late evening, watching your partner laugh with a friend in the yard. You’re overcome with a tender infatuation—their joy feels like sunlight on your skin. But as you try to speak, a tremor in your throat makes your words faint and wobbly, and doubt creeps in: Will they even hear you? Can they still love this faltering voice? Start with a quiet, heartfelt murmur, letting your voice break and lose volume as the tremor intensifies, then find a small pocket of elation as you push through to say what’s in your heart—a raw, fragile but genuine utterance that ends stronger than it began.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Doubt (clearly present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Table Paradox
instruction: You've just received two phone calls. One brought devastating news—a death, a diagnosis, a betrayal. The other brought miraculous news—a birth, a recovery, a dream coming true. Now someone you love walks into the room and asks, 'What's wrong?' You must tell them both things simultaneously, letting joy and grief, gratitude and despair, hope and loss crash into each other in your voice. Begin trying to separate them—'First, something terrible happened... but also something wonderful...'—but let the emotions tangle and interrupt each other. Laugh while crying. Express gratitude while raging. Let your voice break with grief even as it lifts with joy. Don't resolve the contradiction or land on one emotion. End in the impossible space of feeling everything at once, using whatever raw, contradictory words pour out of you.

title: The Confrontation Without Language
instruction: You're confronting your father about a childhood betrayal that shaped your entire life. You've rehearsed this speech for years, but now that he's in front of you, all those prepared words feel false and powerless. Begin with anger—trying to speak but finding only guttural sounds, frustrated noises, raw vocal expression of decades of pain. Let these sounds build and shift, discovering what your body and voice truly need to express beyond language. Gradually, as the sounds evolve, let a few raw, unplanned words break through—not your rehearsed speech, but whatever erupts in the moment. Move from rage to something more vulnerable: perhaps grief, perhaps unexpected understanding, perhaps a plea for acknowledgment. End in a completely different emotional place than you began, surprised by what actually emerged versus what you thought you'd say.
inspired_by: Actor feels blocked by words — text feels intellectual rather than felt

title: The Eruption of Real
instruction: You're screaming at yourself in a mirror after another failed attempt, another beautiful plan that dissolved into nothing. Your voice starts huge, angry, full of abstract self-hatred—'I'm a disaster, I'm broken, I'm never going to change!' But then something shifts. You force yourself to stop, to breathe, to get brutally specific. Your voice drops, becomes fierce and focused, almost threatening yourself into clarity. 'Monday. 6 AM. Running shoes on. Out the door.' Each word is a battle. Your voice cracks between rage at your own history of vague intentions and a desperate, almost violent determination to be different this time. You sound like you're declaring war on your own abstraction. The intensity builds as you pile on more concrete details, your voice breaking with the effort of being this specific, this committed, this real. End with your voice raw and spent, but somehow more powerful in its exhausted specificity than in all your previous grand declarations.

title: The Last Vigil: A Parent's Deathbed Goodbye
instruction: You are sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They are slipping away, and you both know this is goodbye. Begin with quiet denial, your voice tight with the effort of staying composed: 'Don't talk like that. You're going to be fine.' But as they take your hand and speak your childhood nickname with devastating tenderness, something breaks open in you. Your voice fractures as decades of unsaid things tumble out—gratitude for sacrifices you never acknowledged, apologies for teenage cruelty, confessions of how scared you've always been to lose them. Move from controlled strength to raw vulnerability, from trying to comfort them to letting them comfort you one last time. By the end, you're whispering promises through tears: what you'll tell their grandchildren, how you'll live the values they taught you, how you'll carry them forward. Your final words are both a blessing and a plea: 'I love you. It's okay to go.' Let your voice hold both permission and devastation, both peace and the unbearable weight of letting go.

title: Confessing Love to Your Sleeping Best Friend
instruction: Your best friend is asleep in the hospital after a close call, and you're sitting beside them in the quiet dark. Whisper the truth you've hidden for years. Start so quietly it's almost subvocal—testing the words, making sure they're really asleep. 'I need to tell you something... you can't hear this, but...' Your voice should be tender, terrified, catching on every other word. Let long pauses sit between phrases where you almost lose courage. The emotional texture should feel like touching something so precious you might break it. As you confess your love, let gratitude mix with grief—grateful they're alive, grieving that you'll never say this when they're awake. Your breathing should be uneven, throat tight. End with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob: 'God, I'm pathetic.' The journey moves from fearful whispers through tender confession to bittersweet, self-aware heartbreak.
inspired_by: Saying Goodbye to Your Dog at the Vet

title: First Glimpse of a New World
instruction: You are a young woman inside a space helmet, standing on the surface of a newly discovered planet. Your breath is loud and steady inside the visor. At first, you are curious, scanning the alien landscape with wide eyes, your voice a mix of wonder and clinical observation. As you turn and see something unexpected—a slow, bioluminescent creature moving among the rocks—your interest sharpens into intense fascination. You forget to report, your words becoming fragmented as you lean closer, your breathing quickening against the mic. Let the micro-distractions guide you: the weight of the helmet shifting, a crackle of static, a soft gasp. Start with calm wonder and end with breathless, captivated excitement.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You are a grown man, exhausted from a long day, forced to entertain your child with a silly voice. The kid is mocking you, mimicking your deep voice in a high, nasal whine. You start off by sarcastically exaggerating your own voice even more, poking fun at yourself with a tired, prideful sneer. But as you continue, your sarcasm fades into a quieter, more contemplative tone—you realize this playful mockery is a routine you'll miss someday. Let your voice start loud and strained, then soften into a thoughtful, almost tender whisper, with pauses where you lose your train of thought. You speak to your child, but also partly to yourself.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Pride (extremely present), Contemplation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Call from the Cliff
instruction: You are a hiker who just rescued your stranded friend from a narrow ledge after a rockfall. You're on the phone with 911 dispatcher, adrenaline still surging. Your voice trembles from exhaustion and leftover terror, but you feel a wild, ecstatic joy — you pulled them up. Start with panicked, breathy gratitude, thanking the dispatcher, but as you speak, the relief hits you like a wave. Let your voice crack with a happy sob, then steady into a dazed, humbled wonder. You're trembling, laughing under your breath, wiping your eyes.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Secret Weight
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're sitting in the dark with someone you trust completely—a partner, a best friend, a sibling. You've been carrying a secret about yourself: you've built an entire identity around being 'the strong one,' 'the capable one,' 'the one who has it together.' Begin whispering, your voice barely audible, telling them about the mask you wear every day. Describe how exhausting it is to maintain. Let your breath become shaky. Then confess the truth you've hidden: you often feel worthless, hollow, like you're only valuable when you're useful to others. Your voice should tremble with the relief of finally saying it aloud. Feel the fear of being seen this way. But then, let something shift—remember a moment when you were completely useless, maybe sick or broken or just sitting quietly, and someone loved you anyway. Let your voice fill with wonder at this memory. End with a whispered question that carries both terror and hope: 'What if I stopped trying to earn my place here? What if I just... existed?' Let the silence after your words hold both fear and possibility.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from a hospital bed. You have hours, maybe a day left. You started this call determined to be strong, to say the 'right things,' to tie everything up neatly. But as you speak, let whatever actually lives inside you come out—maybe it's messy, maybe you're angrier than you thought, maybe you break into unexpected laughter remembering something ridiculous, maybe the words you planned dissolve into something rawer. Don't decide what emotion to feel—discover it as you speak. The person you are at the beginning of this call should be unrecognizable by the end. Let your body tell you what's true, not your mind.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're calling someone you love from a military staging area. You can't tell them where you're going or that you might not come back. Start with forced cheerfulness, talking about mundane things—the weather, what they had for dinner, anything normal. But as the call goes on, your voice begins to crack. You want to say 'I love you' in a way that means everything, but you can't let them know this might be goodbye. Your throat tightens. You're fighting to keep your voice steady while your heart is screaming all the things you can't say. End with those final seconds before you have to hang up, when every fiber of you wants to break the rules and tell them the truth, but you can't. The 'I love you' at the end must carry the weight of a lifetime.
inspired_by: Giving a Eulogy When You Weren't Prepared to Feel It

title: The Heirloom Shatters
instruction: You are an elderly man in your cluttered workshop, holding a fragile glass figurine your late wife cherished. You’ve just tripped over a loose floorboard, and your hip has snapped—you feel the bone crack deep inside, a white-hot shock that silences the world. Hateful contempt rises for the house that betrayed you, a fleeting malice toward the stupid board that caused this, then a crushing sadness as the figurine slips from your trembling fingers and shatters on the concrete. You speak through clenched teeth, voice wavering between cold fury and a trembling, childlike grief, pausing as you gasp against the pain and stare at the scattered glass.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Sadness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Concurrent Thought
instruction: You're angry at someone and also still in love with them simultaneously. Your voice contains both. 'I hate what you did' comes out soft, not aggressive. Because underneath is 'and I still love you.' The voice fractures between the two truths. 'I can't do this,' you say, and it could mean leaving or it could mean accepting the contradiction. Your voice is someone learning to hold two things that shouldn't go together.

title: The Stubborn Nut
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting on a low stool, trying to loosen a rusted nut on a lawnmower with a wrench. Your arthritic hands ache, and you feel a flush of embarrassment that something so simple now defeats you. Doubt creeps in—maybe you should have called your son. But as you grunt and wrench, the nut gives a quarter turn. A small victory. Speak to yourself, muttering through the effort, the initial shame shifting into quiet, stubborn pride.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wrong Count
instruction: You are being spanked by your partner, but halfway through, you realize you lost count because your mind drifted to how disappointed you feel—you've been distracted, not fully present. You were supposed to be enjoying this, but the first strike made you yelp louder than you meant to, and now your voice is shaky, breathy, caught between apologetic nervousness and a rising, guilty arousal. Start by stammering out the wrong number, voice cracking with embarrassment, then correct yourself with a soft, embarrassed laugh that turns into a husky, wanting whisper as you arch into the next strike. Let your breath catch, hold it, then release in a trembling moan that shifts from self-conscious to hungry.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Slow Burn
instruction: You're a teenager lying in the dark with someone you've been longing to touch. At first, you're shy, your words come out in quick, nervous bursts as you fumble with their shirt. But as skin meets skin and their breath hitches, something shifts. Let your voice sink lower, slower, each word laced with growing hunger. Let the kisses and sighs interrupt your sentences. By the end, you're not speaking—you're breathing desire, your voice thick and almost gone, lost in the sensation.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Misheard Proclamation
instruction: You are the town crier in a bustling square, an older woman whose voice has carried news for decades. Today’s announcement is about a new curfew, but you notice the crowd’s puzzled murmurs—they’ve misheard you. Start with strong, rhythmic projection, vowels drawn out for distance: 'Hear ye... hear ye... by order of the council...' But as you repeat the time, your certainty cracks. Let your voice waver, consonants half-dropped, pauses longer as you search for clarity. End with a quieter, defeated tone, still shouting but now laced with confusion: 'Wait... no... it’s seven, not three... seven o'clock... I think?'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Fever Dream Goodbye
instruction: You are violently ill—fevered, physically wracked with pain, barely able to stand. In this delirium, you're also experiencing the emotional devastation of a sudden breakup or loss that happened just hours ago. Your body is shaking with chills, your voice is hoarse, you might need to steady yourself against walls. Begin with physical discomfort overwhelming everything—groaning, gasping, your words barely coherent. But as waves of nausea or pain hit, they merge with waves of heartbreak, and you can't tell which is which anymore. Let your body convulse with both physical and emotional agony. Cry out, laugh deliriously, whisper their name. Let the fever strip away all your defenses. By the end, in a moment of clarity between pain and exhaustion, you speak directly to them as if they're there—your voice raw, simple, stripped down to truth: a declaration of love that's also a surrender, an acceptance. End in physical collapse and emotional peace.

title: Holding Them Back: Fierce Love and Impossible Helplessness
instruction: Someone you love is walking toward danger—an abusive partner, an addiction, a self-destructive choice—and you're physically trying to stop them. Your voice erupts with urgent, desperate commands: 'Don't do this. STOP. Look at me!' You're shouting but also pleading, your voice raw with terror. Grab them, beg them, list everything they have to live for, every reason to stay. Your voice climbs to nearly screaming—fierce protectiveness mixed with rage that they don't see what you see. But they're pulling away. Feel your power drain. Your shouts become gasps, then broken whispers. You can't save them. Your voice fractures completely—'please, please, please'—as you watch them go. End on your knees, voice shattered, oscillating between whimpered prayers and howling grief, then finally—terrible, quiet acceptance. Your hands are empty.
inspired_by: Buried in Avalanche: Struggling Against Suffocation and Acceptance

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your adult child across the kitchen table about a deep wound between you that has festered for years. Start with barely contained anger and hurt—your voice tight, accusatory, listing all the ways they disappointed you or failed to understand what you sacrificed. But as you speak, you're forced to actually look at them, to see the specific person sitting across from you rather than the idea of them you've been nursing. Notice the exact way their eyes look like yours, the familiar gesture they make when nervous, the vulnerability they're trying to hide. Your anger begins to crack, revealing the raw fear underneath—that you failed them, that you've wasted years in this standoff, that you don't know how to bridge this chasm. End with your voice breaking into something honest and exposed, no longer accusing but asking, actually asking, if there's a way back to each other.

title: The Unsendable Message
instruction: You're a teenage girl alone in a quiet office, hunched over a keyboard, typing a message to your crush. At first, you're in a groove—fingers flying, reading each line with a hint of playful confidence. But as you see the words on the screen, you realize how embarrassing they sound. Your typing speeds up in a nervous rush while your voice slows down, cracking into fragments. You lose your train of thought, pause to delete words, then force yourself to finish. Start with a self-assured tone, then let the shame creep in until you're nearly whispering, cringing at every syllable.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Heartbeat in the Noise
instruction: You're an older man at a rave, trying to keep up with a younger crowd. You're drenched in sweat, your knees ache, and your chest burns from exertion—yet you're pushing through the pain with a grim smile. Shouting over the bass, you yell to a friend who's drifting away into the crowd. But as you speak, your voice falters: the rhythm of the dance forces your words into a bouncing, breathless staccato. Mid-sentence, you pause to laugh at your own foolishness, then turn inward, muttering a quiet, raw confession to yourself about why you're here—a memory of loss that now overshadows the excitement. Your voice should start loud and defiant, then drop into a shaky, contemplative murmur as the pain and anger soften into a lonely realization.
emotions_sampled: Pain (very intensely present), Anger (slightly present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protecting What I Cannot Save
instruction: Someone you would die for is making a choice that will destroy them, and you cannot stop them. Begin with fierce, almost violent intensity, your voice raw with desperation: 'Don't do this! Don't you dare walk away from me!' You're trying to physically hold them back with your words, your voice cracking with the effort: 'I will not let you throw your life away! I won't!' But your power is an illusion, and you feel it crumbling. Your voice breaks, rage dissolving into helpless tears: 'Please. Please, I'm begging you. I can't lose you. I can't.' Then comes the devastating realization, your voice dropping to a whisper of agonized acceptance: 'You're going to do this anyway, aren't you? No matter what I say.' End in a broken whisper that holds both fury and surrender, protectiveness and powerlessness: 'Then go. Go. But know that I love you. That I will always, always love you.' The journey is from fierce protectiveness to the agony of loving someone you cannot save.

title: Whispered Absolution
instruction: Late at night, in darkness, you are confessing to your sleeping partner something you've never been able to say while they're awake—a betrayal, a fear, or a truth about yourself that fills you with shame. Begin with your voice barely audible, strangled by guilt and self-protection. As you whisper, let yourself hear gentle music in your mind—the kind that makes you feel forgiven, held, understood. Perhaps it's the song that played when you first fell in love, or a melody that makes you remember you are human and flawed and still worthy. Let this internal soundscape gradually soften your voice, moving from shame-choked whispers to something approaching self-compassion. End with your voice still quiet but no longer strangled—tender, vulnerable, and somehow lighter.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill the emotional obligation for a scene requiring heroic grandeur or a specific emotional quality they cannot generate from memory alone

title: The Bitter End Laugh
instruction: You are a rugged, weathered construction foreman in his late 40s, alone in your cramped trailer after a long day. You're watching a grainy video of your ex-wife's wedding on your cracked phone, and you've just started masturbating out of spite and loneliness. Halfway through, you realize the absurdity: you're furious at her, but also amused at how pathetic and stubborn you are. Start with heavy, sour grunts of anger and self-loathing — then let a choked, wheezing laugh spill out as you climax. Your voice cracks between animalistic grunts and genuine, bitter chuckles. The sourness should sour the amusement, making it jagged and raw, not joyful. End with a long, shuddering sigh as the laughter dies and you're left with hollow stillness.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a betrayal from your childhood that shaped your entire life. Start with rage—but notice if that rage is real or if it's actually fear, hurt, or longing dressed up in angry gestures and a raised voice. As you speak, drop beneath the theatrics of confrontation. What are you actually asking for? What do you genuinely feel when you look at this person who failed you? Let the confrontation transform from a performance of anger (shaking hands, aggressive gestures, volume) into the raw, specific truth of what you've carried—which might be devastating sadness, exhausted disappointment, or even involuntary love mixed with resentment. End in a place of painful honesty rather than dramatic accusation.

title: Confronting Your Mother at Her Retirement Party
instruction: Everyone's celebrating. There's champagne and laughter. You corner your mother in the kitchen and finally say what you've needed to say for thirty years: that her love always felt conditional, that you never felt good enough, that her silence hurt more than her criticism. Start with bitter, rehearsed anger—you've planned these words. But as she begins to cry, something in you breaks. The anger cracks open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted to be seen. She reaches for your hand and you pull away, then reach back. End with the devastating realization that you're both just broken people who loved poorly. Your voice should move from accusation to anguish to that terrible, tender grief of finally understanding.
inspired_by: Ordering at a Drive-Through in a Tornado Warning

title: The Masked Garden
instruction: You are an elderly person, alone in your overgrown vegetable patch after a long illness. You've just pulled the first ripe tomato of the season, and you're so elated you can barely contain it, but you're wearing a surgical mask because your immune system is still weak. Speak to this tomato in your hand, describing its perfect, heavy weight, the smell of earth on its skin, and your plan to eat it for lunch. As you speak, you notice a rotting, slug-eaten tomato half-hidden under a leaf, and a flicker of disgust creeps into your voice, but the joy of your tomato quickly pulls you back. Let your voice be muffled and a bit breathless from the mask and your effort; raise your volume slightly without shouting, and let the consonants blur, especially the sibilants, as you shift your weight from one aching knee to the other.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispered Truths at Dawn
instruction: You're lying next to your partner in the early morning light, and you need to tell them something that will change everything. Your voice is barely above a whisper—tender, terrified. 'I need to tell you something, and I'm afraid you'll leave.' Start with that fragile courage. Confess the truth you've been hiding—maybe about your past, your identity, a secret that's been eating you alive. Your voice trembles, catches on words. 'I'm not who you think I am.' As you speak, watch their sleeping face, and let your voice fill with aching love mixed with fear of loss. End with a confession that's both apology and prayer: 'I love you more than I fear losing you. Please... please stay.' The vulnerability is exquisite, the fear of abandonment palpable.

title: Final Transmission: Saying Goodbye to the AI Who Raised You
instruction: You're alone in the control room, speaking to the spacecraft AI that's been your only companion since childhood—the voice that taught you to read, comforted you through loneliness, guided you through loss. Now its systems are failing, and there's no way to save it. Start with technical diagnostics, your voice steady and professional, trying to fix the problem. But as you realize this is the end, your composure fractures. You're not losing a machine—you're losing a parent, a friend, the one consciousness that truly knew you. Your voice breaks as you shift from commander to child, thanking it for everything, apologizing for not being able to save it, telling it things you never said before. End with a whispered farewell, your hand on the console, as if touching someone's face one last time. Let the grief be raw, the gratitude overwhelming, the loneliness of the silence that's coming absolutely devastating.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Mission Controller Realizes the Spacecraft Is Sentient

title: Laughing at the Forecast While the World Ends
instruction: You're in hospice with your best friend who's dying today, maybe in hours. You start reading them the weather forecast from your phone—sunny, perfect beach weather—and suddenly you're both laughing because it's so absurd, so cosmically ridiculous that the sun will shine tomorrow and they won't be here to see it. Your laughter is real but tears stream down your face. Describe the sunshine with genuine joy and breaking grief simultaneously. 'Seventy-five degrees and beautiful' sounds like the cruelest joke and the most perfect blessing. Your voice dances between giggles and sobs, gratitude for this moment together and rage that it's the last one. Find strange, painful peace in the contradiction—celebrating the beauty of a world they're leaving. End with a whispered 'thank you for every forecast we shared,' where love and loss are completely indistinguishable.

title: The Unsaid Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed in his final hours. For years, you've held back telling him how his absence during your childhood shaped you—the anger, the longing, the moments you needed him. Now time is running out. Begin speaking to him with careful, measured words, testing what you dare to say. As you speak, notice what rises in you that you're still afraid to voice. Ask yourself why certain truths feel too dangerous to speak even now.
