Let the awareness of what you're holding back shift something inside you—perhaps the realization that your silence has been protecting you from vulnerability, not him from pain. By the end, allow one deeply honest thing you've never said to finally break through, transforming your careful control into raw, unguarded truth. Your emotion should move from guarded caution to undefended openness.

title: The Embers of a Broken Promise
instruction: You are an older woman sitting around a campfire with close friends. You’re telling a story about a cherished promise that was broken years ago. Begin with a teasing, almost wry tone, as if poking fun at the person who let you down. But as you speak, the old hurt creeps in—your voice may waver, you pause to poke the fire with a stick, or pull your shawl tighter. Let the disappointment and pain seep through, so by the end the humor is gone, leaving only quiet ache. Let the flames and the night air affect your delivery—maybe you cough slightly, or your voice cracks. End on a note of hollow acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (clearly present), Teasing (slightly present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Protecting What You Cannot Save
instruction: You're a doctor who just lost a child patient despite hours of desperate effort. You're calling their parents from outside the OR, your hands still shaking. Begin with professional control: 'This is Dr. Morrison. I need to talk to you about your daughter.' But as you try to say the words, your voice starts to fracture. The clinical distance you've maintained shatters. Suddenly you're not a doctor—you're someone who just held a dying child and couldn't save her. Your voice becomes fierce with rage: 'We did everything—' then breaks into anguish. You're cycling through fury at the universe, crushing guilt, helpless grief. Your professional composure is gone. You're apologizing, your voice raw and ragged: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry.' By the end, you're barely holding yourself together, voice reduced to shattered whispers, the cost of caring too much laid completely bare. Your voice should sound like someone whose armor has been obliterated.

title: Being Left Out
instruction: You've just found out that your friend group did something without inviting you. Your voice is hurt, trying to be casual: 'Oh, you guys hung out?' They're explaining themselves, and your voice becomes smaller: 'Why didn't you ask me?' They have explanations, but none of them feel genuine. Your voice becomes tight with hurt: 'Okay. Well, have fun next time without me.' By the end, you're alone, your voice is devastated.

title: Whispering to Someone Slipping Into Unconsciousness
instruction: You're holding someone you love as they fade—from injury, illness, or medication before surgery. Your voice starts gentle, reassuring, telling them everything will be okay, maintaining composure for their sake. As their responses slow and their grip weakens, your whispers become more desperate, tender, intimate—sharing secret memories, confessing small things you never said. 'Remember when we...' Your voice catches on half-finished sentences. You're trying to keep them present by the sound of your voice alone. Move into raw vulnerability: admitting your fear in barely audible whispers, voice breaking on words like 'don't go' or 'I need you.' End with a shift to acceptance—your whisper becomes a lullaby quality, giving them permission to rest, to let go, even as your voice trembles with the grief of releasing them.
inspired_by: Making Up After a Terrible Fight

title: The Empty Promise
instruction: You are a child around 8 or 9, alone in your messy bedroom after school. You just found a note from your best friend tucked under your pillow - they moved away without saying goodbye. At first, you stare at the note, numb, reading it over and over in a breathless whisper: 'You... you said you'd come over today.' Your fingers grip the paper too tight, and then your voice rises, cracking: 'Why didn't you tell me?' The anger surges just enough to make you slap the note down on the bed, but then it's swamped by confusion again as you trail off, 'I don't... I don't understand.' Let your words feel like they're stumbling out between shallow breaths, your eyes darting around the room as if searching for the friend who isn't there.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Clear Image
instruction: You are in a dim, quiet radiology suite, sitting on the edge of an exam table. A radiologist has just told you that the scan of your lungs shows no tumors, and now they are asking you standard follow-up questions—about your breathing, any pain. You are still trembling from the shock of relief. Speak your answers, but let your voice stumble and catch with that huge, unexpected release. Start with a shaky, breathless attempt at clinical politeness, and end with a collapsing, tearful whisper of relief as you fully let go.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Thanking Your Ex on What Would Have Been Your Wedding Day
instruction: You're alone, maybe with a glass of wine, on the day you would have married them—except they left six months ago. You start talking to them as if they were there, and strangely, you're laughing: 'We would have had gardenias, remember? You thought they smelled like feet.' The laughter is real but tears come too. You're genuinely grateful they left, genuinely devastated they left—both truths existing simultaneously. 'Thank you for knowing before I did. Thank you for being brave enough to break my heart.' Your voice moves fluidly between bitter humor, tender nostalgia, grief-stricken relief. End in an impossible emotional space: peaceful and destroyed at once, smiling through tears: 'I hope you're happy. I really, really do. And I really, really hate that I mean it.'
inspired_by: Realizing Someone You Love Doesn't Love You Back Anymore

title: Final Transmission from Deep Space: Losing Earth
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to the edge of the solar system, recording what you believe is your last message to your child back on Earth. Begin with forced optimism, trying to sound brave: 'Hey kiddo, Dad's just checking in from way out here.' But as you speak, the vast distance and isolation crack your composure. Your voice becomes smaller, more fragile. 'I can't... I can't remember what your laugh sounds like anymore.' Time dilation means years have passed for them while only months passed for you. They're grown now, maybe with children of their own, and you're dissolving into the realization that you're speaking to a stranger. End with a whispered confession of regret mixed with awe at what you've witnessed, your voice barely holding together: 'I saw things no human has ever seen, but I'd trade all of it for one more morning making you pancakes.' Let the silence of space seep into your pauses.
inspired_by: Sensory Deprivation Tank: Time Becoming Meaningless

title: Dust and Breath
instruction: You're a 16-year-old boy sanding down a heavy wooden table in a dusty garage. Early in the task, you're irritated and resentful—the respirator is hot, your goggles fog, and every breath feels like fighting through a wall. As you work, you notice a small groove taking shape under your hand, and you start to think about why you're doing this: building something for your mom's birthday. By the end, the sourness softens into a quiet contentment, and you pause mid-sentence to adjust the mask, speaking through its muffled seal with a thoughtful, almost proud tone.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Contemplation (clearly present), Contentment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone in complete darkness—a lover, a spouse, a close friend—and you're about to whisper something you've never said aloud to anyone. Start with something small and actually true about yourself, a fear or desire you rarely acknowledge. Let your voice be barely audible, intimate, as if the darkness makes honesty possible. As you continue, the confession deepens—maybe into shame, maybe into desperate hope, maybe into a truth that could change everything between you. Your breathing, your pauses, the catch in your throat—these matter more than volume. Move from tentative vulnerability to either profound relief or devastating exposure. Let silence hold as much weight as words. Draw on real secrets you carry, real moments when you've wanted to be truly seen.

title: Midnight Confession in a Hospital Chapel
instruction: You're alone in a hospital chapel at 3 AM while your child is in surgery. You're praying - or trying to - but you keep remembering something funny they said this morning, some silly thing that made you smile. Start whispering, trying to pray seriously, but the memory makes you want to smile even as terror grips your chest. Let your voice catch between the urge to laugh at the sweet memory and the choking fear of losing them. Speak softly, intimately, as if God or the universe might actually be listening. End with your voice barely above a whisper, the smile fading as the weight of 'what if' crushes down, your whispered words trailing into silence as you sit with the unbearable fragility of love and the terror of potential loss.
inspired_by: Suppressing Laughter During a Serious Moment

title: The Hinge Above the Sink
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman standing at the bathroom sink, chin tilted sharply upward, holding a screwdriver to the small hinge of a stubborn medicine cabinet door. The mirror reflects your strained neck and the ceiling. You're trying to fix it yourself because you can't afford a handyman, but your fingers are too thick for this tiny screw, and your arm is already trembling from the angle. Start with intense concentration — muttering to yourself, shifting your weight, adjusting your grip. As the screw refuses to catch, let helplessness creep in, then a deep, cold doubt: maybe you really can't do this anymore, maybe everything is falling apart. By the end, your voice should sound thinner, quieter, like you're losing the argument with yourself. Speak as if your jaw is tight, your throat is stretched, and you're barely holding back a wave of frustration. 'Come on, just... just catch. I had it. I had it a second ago. Maybe it's stripped. Maybe it's me. I don't... I don't even know why I'm trying.'
emotions_sampled: Concentration (very intensely present), Helplessness (very intensely present), Doubt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: My Body Remembers Wrong
instruction: You experienced something physically and emotionally devastating—a moment of humiliation, violation, or powerlessness where your body shut down or froze. Begin by physically embodying that original experience: shallow breath, collapsed posture, the sensory memory of helplessness flooding through you. Then, while moving your body, start speaking aloud a different version: the one where you fought back, where you screamed instead of going silent, where your body was powerful instead of frozen. Describe this revised physical experience in vivid sensory detail while actually moving your body that way—standing tall, using your full voice, feeling strength in your muscles. Repeat this embodied telling multiple times, each time more fierce, more convinced, more physically alive. Your voice should transform from weak and breaking to full-throated and powerful, even rageful. End with your body vibrating with reclaimed power, breath full and deep, the physical sensations of shame replaced by the physical sensations of fierce vitality. Journey from collapsed powerlessness to explosive, embodied strength.

title: The Explosion When Performing Finally Shatters
instruction: You've been the strong one, the reliable one, the one who handles everything with grace. You're mid-sentence, giving someone your usual reassuring response—your voice bright, capable, steady. Then something inside you detonates. Your voice suddenly rises, cracks wide open. You're shouting, but it's not controlled—it's messy, desperate, years of swallowed rage and exhaustion pouring out. You're saying things you've never allowed yourself to say. Your breath is ragged. You might be laughing harshly, crying, both at once. Then, just as suddenly, the fury collapses into something more fragile—your voice drops to almost nothing, shaking, as you realize how tired you are of being anything other than broken. End in near-whisper, utterly undone.
inspired_by: Realizing You Become Someone Different Around Specific People

title: The Kitchen Floor Confession
instruction: You're confronting your mother (or father, or grown child) late at night in the kitchen where you grew up. Begin by recounting a specific real memory from your childhood—something small and true—then build from there, layering in half-truths and invented grievances until you can no longer distinguish what actually happened from what you've carried as emotional truth for years. Start with controlled anger, the kind that's been rehearsed in your head a thousand times. As you speak, let the anger give way to something more vulnerable: the child inside you who needed something you never received. End not with resolution, but with the raw, exposed realization that you're still asking for the same thing you always needed, and the terrifying possibility that you might finally be heard.

title: The Last Thing I Never Said
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's conscious but fading. You arrive holding onto old resentment—she was never the warm, cookie-baking grandmother you wanted, always distant and critical. But as you look at her hands, you suddenly remember one specific moment: those same hands teaching you to tie your shoes when you were four, her rare patience that day. Let that single memory crack you open. Begin speaking with guarded distance in your voice, protection in your posture. As you focus on that one tender image of her hands, let it transform everything you're saying. By the end, you're no longer protecting yourself—you're raw, grateful, grieving the loss of what you did have, not what you didn't. Let one specific sensory detail (her hands, her smell, the way light hits her face) become the key that unlocks your heart.
inspired_by: Selective Emphasis is needed but the actor isn't sure how to apply it to a specific choice approach

title: Dancing with Dementia
instruction: Your parent with dementia suddenly recognizes you after months of blankness. They remember your name, a story from your childhood, how much they love you. You're laughing and crying at once—joy and grief are the same thing now. Your voice dances between celebration and devastation. You want to hold this moment forever, and you know it's already slipping away. Thank them for every sacrifice they made, for every time they showed up, while your heart shatters because you're also saying goodbye. They're here and already gone. Your voice carries gratitude that tastes like salt water. End as confusion clouds their eyes again—find peace in the wreckage, speaking tenderly to someone who no longer knows you, grateful for thirty seconds of recognition in an ocean of forgetting.

title: The Inheritance of Joy
instruction: You're cleaning out your best friend's apartment after their sudden death, and you find a letter they wrote to you—'If you're reading this, throw me a party, not a funeral.' You start reading it aloud, and you're laughing because they're still making jokes from beyond the grave, their voice so alive on the page. 'Remember when we got drunk and tried to steal that traffic cone?' Your laughter is real, full, the kind that comes from years of shared absurdity. But then the letter shifts to gratitude—'You made my life bearable'—and your laughter tangles with tears. You're trying to keep reading but you can't breathe right. The last line is 'Don't you dare be sad for long. I'm not there anymore, so live twice as hard.' You should be laughing and sobbing simultaneously, your voice a beautiful wreck of grief and joy and gratitude. End with you saying 'Okay, you ridiculous asshole, okay,' and it should sound like a promise, like grief, like love, like all of it at once. Let those contradictory emotions collide in your voice—celebration and devastation inseparable.

title: The Inventory of Skin
instruction: In the dark, in bed, whisper to your lover about your body—not seductively, but with devastating honesty. Begin with shame: describe the parts of yourself you hide, the angles you avoid in mirrors, the ways you've learned to disappear during intimacy. Your voice should be barely audible, fragile as paper. But as you continue this inventory of imperfection, let something unexpected happen: feel your lover's hands (real or imagined) touch each place you name. Let your whispered shame gradually, incrementally transform into whispered wonder—not at being beautiful, but at being touched anyway, at being chosen anyway. End in a place of breathless vulnerability where shame and desire are impossibly tangled, your voice breaking not from pain but from the shocking relief of being fully seen.
inspired_by: Actor wants to understand the full integrated system from Morris's perspective

title: What I Should Have Told You Yesterday
instruction: Someone you love is sleeping beside you. It's 3 AM. They don't know you're awake. You're watching them breathe, and you need to confess something you've been carrying—maybe an affair, maybe a terminal diagnosis, maybe that you're leaving. But you can't wake them, so you whisper it into the darkness as if they can hear. Your voice is barely audible, tender, terrified. Start with halting attempts to find the words. Let your voice catch on the truth. Feel how speaking it aloud—even to silence—makes it devastatingly real. By the end, you're crying silently, your whispers breaking apart. There's love in every word, and the knowledge that this truth will destroy everything. Your voice should be intimate, fragile, full of goodbye.
inspired_by: The Words You Can't Take Back

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're face-to-face with your parent after years—maybe at a funeral, maybe they reached out, maybe you finally cornered them. You came here with a speech prepared, a list of grievances, determined to finally tell them everything they did wrong. You start controlled, almost cold, listing the moments they missed, the ways they failed you. But as you speak, something shifts—the anger you've nursed for years starts crumbling into the grief of the child who just wanted to be seen. Your voice moves from accusatory to pleading, from rage to bewildered hurt. 'Why wasn't I enough?' slips out when you meant to stay strong. You're trying to wound them but you're the one bleeding, trying to make them accountable while revealing how much power they still have to hurt you. The confrontation that was supposed to free you is breaking you open instead.
inspired_by: Announcing Bad Diagnosis Out Loud for the First Time

title: Playing Cards in the Hospice Room
instruction: You're teaching your grandmother her favorite card game one last time, but her memory is fading and she keeps forgetting the rules she taught you as a child. Start patiently, gently reminding her with warmth in your voice. As she struggles to remember, let your whispers grow tender and thick with unshed tears. Describe the cards softly, tell her it's okay, remind her of when she taught you this on her kitchen table. Your voice should be intimate, close, like you're sharing a secret. Let quiet devastation live in every gentle word. End by telling her she won—even though the game never finished—and thank her for teaching you everything, your voice barely above a breath.

title: The Saluting Daisy
instruction: You are a 17-year-old girl, the daughter of a decorated general, who has just snuck three shots of vodka before being called to attention at a formal military ceremony. Your body is locked in a rigid, arms-at-sides stance, but your mind is swimming. You must recite a short, scripted tribute to your father's unit. Start with a sharp, metallic, overly projected voice that tries too hard to sound disciplined, but as the words go on, the alcohol loosens your tongue and your posture. Your voice wavers, you lose your place, you almost laugh, then catch yourself with a sad, quiet realization that you can't hold it together. End with a soft, slurred, almost tender whisper that betrays your fear and love.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Farewell You've Been Rehearsing for Months
instruction: Your partner is leaving for a mission they'll never return from - you both know it, though neither of you will say it. You've practiced staying strong for weeks, rehearsed being brave, but now they're standing in front of you for the last time. Start with the carefully constructed courage you planned to show - steady voice, reassuring smile, the strength you promised yourself you'd have. But as you try to say the words you prepared, that facade must crack and crumble. Let your voice break. Let the real grief, the terror of loss, the desperate wish to beg them to stay, all come flooding through the cracks of your rehearsed composure. End in a place of raw, unguarded truth - whether that's sobbing in their arms or a whispered confession of how afraid you really are. Your performance should feel like watching someone's heart break in real time despite their best efforts to hold it together.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Surprised at a Surprise Party You Discovered

title: The Revelation: Confronting Your Parent About the Adoption Secret
instruction: You've just discovered through a DNA test that you were adopted, and your parents never told you. Begin with confusion and hurt questions—voice tight, trying to understand why they lied for thirty years. As they remain silent or defensive, your pain sharpens into anger. Your voice rises with betrayal: every story about pregnancy, every family resemblance comment was a lie. But then something shifts—you hear the fear in their voice, see them as fragile humans who were terrified of losing you. Your rage collapses into something more complicated: grief for the birth parents you'll never know, and a painful, reluctant understanding of why they stayed silent. End with your voice breaking on forgiveness you're not sure you're ready to give, but love demands you try.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Explorer Discovers Humanity Was Seeded by Alien Civilization

title: The Hidden Splinter
instruction: You're sitting on the porch steps with a child, watching them play with a toy. You feel a deep contentment in this quiet moment, but as you shift your weight, a sharp pain from a splinter you barely noticed forces a wince. The child looks up and asks, 'Why did you make that face?' — you're confused by the question because you thought you hid it well, and you stumble over how to answer, caught between the lingering happiness and the sudden discomfort.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (clearly present), Pain (clearly present), Confusion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: When the Revolution Eats Its Children
instruction: You are screaming at your former mentor, the revolutionary leader who taught you to fight, to question everything, to burn down the old ways. But now they've become the very authority they taught you to resist. Start with explosive betrayal—your voice raw, fierce, cracking with rage. You're wielding their own words against them like weapons. Let your passion escalate until you're shaking. Then suddenly, they speak—and you hear exhaustion in their voice that stops you cold. Switch to the mentor: begin defending your compromises, but your voice wavers. You sound old, defeated. Admit you don't know if you were wrong to change or wrong to believe change was possible. Let your revolutionary fire reignite for just a moment, then collapse into doubt. Return to your own voice: your anger breaks. You realize you're not fighting them, you're grieving who they were, who you both were. End almost whispering, fierce protectiveness mixed with utter helplessness—trying to save them from their own surrender, knowing you can't.
inspired_by: The Elder and the Young Rebel

title: The Unspoken Weight
instruction: You're lying in bed in the dark next to someone you love deeply, and you need to tell them something you've been carrying alone—a diagnosis, a secret, a truth that will change everything. Your voice is almost inaudible at first, just breath and the beginning of words you can't quite say. You start with their name, whispered so tenderly it hurts. There's a long pause where you almost lose courage. When you finally begin, your words are halting, gentle, each one chosen carefully because you know they'll hurt. Your voice trembles with love and sorrow intertwined. You're trying to comfort them while breaking their heart, trying to be strong while falling apart. End with a confession of gratitude for the time you've had, your voice catching on the simplest words—'thank you' or 'I'm sorry'—barely more than a breath, filled with everything you can't say.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are confronting someone who hurt someone you love—maybe your child, your partner, your closest friend—and you're containing a rage so fierce it's making your whole body shake. Start with a voice that's too controlled, dangerous in its quietness, every word clipped and precise because if you let go, you'll explode. Your fury should be palpable but leashed. As you continue, let the dam begin to crack: your voice rises, words coming faster, harder, fueled by protective love turned into weapons. Let yourself escalate into full-throated anger—shouting, accusing, demanding answers. But then, right at the peak, let it shatter: your rage breaks into something rawer, and suddenly you're not shouting anymore but nearly sobbing with the helplessness of it all. Your voice should fracture as you realize that all your fury can't undo what was done, can't protect the person you love from having been hurt. The explosive energy collapses into something quieter but no less intense—a devastated admission of your own powerlessness. End in a place of fierce, broken love: you're still standing guard, but now with tears streaming down your face, voice hoarse and trembling, speaking from the most vulnerable part of your heart about what this person means to you and how their pain has become your own.

title: The Equation on the Board
instruction: You are a child in a quiet classroom, standing at the front to present a math problem you got wrong. Your voice must carry to the back of the room — use that teacher-like projection, slow your pace, and lean hard on the numbers. Start with a quavering, almost robotic delivery, forcing the words out over the hot shame crawling up your neck. As you explain your mistake, let sadness seep in — a heavier breath, a slight waver on the last sentence, like you’re holding back tears.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your funeral after your terminal diagnosis. Start with genuine laughter: 'God, this is weird, isn't it? Talking to you all after I'm...' The laugh catches, becomes bitter-sweet. 'I'm grateful—truly—for every ridiculous, beautiful moment we had.' Your voice is warm with gratitude but there's grief underneath. Then a laugh that's half-sob: 'I'm so pissed I won't see how your stories end.' The contradictions deepen—laughing through tears: 'Take care of each other, you idiots.' Voice breaking with love and loss simultaneously. End with peaceful acceptance wrapped in heartbreak: 'I was so lucky to love you all,' delivered with a smile you can hear, even as tears fall. The emotional arc weaves laughter, gratitude, grief, anger, love, and peace into something transcendent and real.
inspired_by: Someone Saying They Don't Trust You Anymore

title: The Last Conversation Before Dawn
instruction: Your father has hours left to live, and you're sitting beside his hospital bed at 3 AM. You begin by trying to say the prepared goodbye, the neat summary of your relationship, but it crumbles. You shift into confessing things you've never said: the moment you knew he loved you, the time you needed him and he wasn't there, how you've become him in ways that terrify and comfort you. Your voice moves from controlled and careful to raw and broken, then finds its way to something like peace—not resolution, but acceptance. End in a whisper, telling him something true you've never been brave enough to say. Let silence hang between phrases. This isn't about performing grief; it's about finding words when words feel impossible.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Lover What You Can Never Say Awake
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner is asleep beside you—you think they can't hear you, but they're actually awake, listening. Begin in barely audible whispers, confessing things you're too afraid to say in daylight: how lonely you feel even lying next to them, how you see them pulling away, how terrified you are of losing this. Your voice catches, throat tight with unshed tears. The words come slower, more fragile, admitting your own failures, your desperate love mixed with growing panic. End as you sense they might be awake—a moment of frozen vulnerability, your breath hitching as you wait to see if they'll respond or continue pretending to sleep. Journey from cautious confession to raw exposure to terrified hope.

title: The Purring of the Dark
instruction: You are a teenager with a chronic migraine, lying in a completely dark room with the blinds drawn. Your mom has just brought you a cold cloth for your head, and you're about to thank her. Begin by speaking as softly as possible, barely above a whisper, because any sound drills into your skull. Then your cat jumps onto the bed and starts purring against your hand. The pure, physical comfort of the warmth and vibration overwhelms you. Let your voice shift to a fragile, awed whisper of ecstasy as you describe the feeling—your words are for yourself, not for anyone else, trailing off as you sink into the relief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Stairwell Reckoning
instruction: You're on the third-floor landing of a concrete stairwell, 2 a.m., after a screaming match with your father. You're sitting on the cold steps, your voice bouncing off the walls as you replay your own harsh words. Start with raw shame—your breath is shallow, you're picking at a hangnail, and every echo feels like an accusation. Let the shame crack in your throat as you speak, then slowly transition into contemplation: you realize he was scared too, and your voice softens, trails off, searches for the right words amid the reverb. Say this aloud to yourself, as if testing the thought for the first time: 'I didn't mean it. Not like that. He just looked so tired... I saw it in his hands, the way they shook when he held the door. And I kept going. Why did I keep going?'
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your family home, destroyed by fire, and you've just found your grandmother's old music box still playing. Begin laughing - genuine, surprised laughter: 'It still works! Of course it does, she was too stubborn for anything she owned to break.' Let the laughter mix with tears as grief catches up: 'Everything's gone. Every photo, every...' But then you start humming along with the music box, swaying slightly, and gratitude wells up: 'But I remember. God, I remember everything.' Your voice breaks between laughter and crying as you spin once in the ash: 'She taught me to waltz right here. Right on this spot.' End in a place of bittersweet peace, voice full of wonder and loss simultaneously: 'The house is gone. But I'm still dancing. Grandma, I'm still dancing.' Let joy and devastation exist in the same breath, inseparable and true.

title: Cubicle Choke
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman on a personal call in your open-plan office. You're hunched over your desk, voice low to avoid eavesdroppers, but you're telling a friend about an incredibly awkward moment you had at a work event. In the middle of your whispered story, you suddenly realize how absurd the whole situation was — your voice wavers, a snort escapes, and you start shaking with suppressed laughter. Start with controlled embarrassment, your tone tight and self-conscious. Let the amusement swell until you can barely speak, pausing to cover your mouth, trying to regain composure while a giggle escapes. Your delivery should feel like you're physically cramping from holding it in, voice cracking, words trailing off as the laughter wins.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Unraveling Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed at 3am. Begin in exhausted numbness, barely able to form coherent thoughts after days of waiting. As you hold her hand, allow fragmented memories to surface without forcing them—her perfume, a childhood birthday, the pattern of her breathing, the weight of her hand, words you never said. Don't steer these images; let them come and go like waves. Speak to her as these sense-memories wash over you, your emotional state shifting from that initial fog into whatever emerges—perhaps unexpected anger, or sudden clarity, or overwhelming tenderness you've been holding back. Let the images lead your voice; end in a place utterly different from where you began, transformed by what surfaced unbidden.

title: The Gracious Pause
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a tender intimate moment with your long-term partner. Begin with a playful, breathy tone, then deliberately slow and clear your voice as you check in: 'Is this still okay for you?' Let there be a natural pause—maybe you hear a creak in the floor or adjust your position—as you wait for their response. When they affirm, let your voice soften with relief and genuine thankfulness, ending with a warm, almost tearful 'Thank you, my love.' Allow your gratitude to fill your voice, letting it catch slightly on the last words as you relax back into the moment.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to a Sleeping Child
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child who's sleeping peacefully, unaware that you're leaving forever—perhaps into witness protection, perhaps to treatment you won't survive, perhaps because staying would endanger them. Your voice is barely a whisper, each word carefully placed so as not to wake them: 'I need you to know something, even though you won't remember this.' You're memorizing their face in the dim light. 'You are the best thing I ever did. The only purely good thing.' Your voice catches, tears sliding silently: 'I wanted to watch you grow up. I wanted to be there for your first heartbreak, your graduation, your wedding day.' The grief is overwhelming but must stay quiet. 'Your life will be better without me in it, and that's the hardest truth I've ever had to accept.' You touch their hair with infinite gentleness: 'Be brave. Be kind. Be everything I couldn't be.' The final words are almost soundless: 'I love you. I will always, always love you.' You're breaking apart in complete silence.

title: The One That Got Away
instruction: You are a young woman with a naturally high, sweet voice, calling your ex-boyfriend after a painful breakup. You’re standing in your kitchen, clutching a cold mug of tea you haven’t touched. Start with forced steadiness and a note of pride — you want to show him you’re fine, that you don’t need him. But as you speak, the shame of how much you still love him slips through, and your voice starts to waver. Let a breath hitch break a sentence. Repeat words like 'I can't believe' or 'You were'. By the end, your proud mask crumbles completely, leaving only trembling affection and raw hurt. Let the last words sound like they physically ache. Say about 50 words.
emotions_sampled: Shame (very intensely present), Pride (extremely present), Affection (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent in their hospital room about a lifetime of emotional absence. Start with controlled, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, clinical even. 'I needed you to see me.' But as you list the moments they missed, the birthdays, the graduations, your voice hardens with decades of accumulated pain. Then something unexpected happens: they reach for your hand, and suddenly you're seven years old again, wanting so desperately to be loved. Your anger collapses into a child's pleading—'Why wasn't I enough?'—and you hate yourself for still needing their approval. End with the horrifying realization that even now, even after everything, you're begging for crumbs.

title: The Gilded Cage
instruction: You are lying on your back on a massage table or the foot of a bed, with your head hanging unsupported over the edge. Your neck is hyperextended, throat stretched, and each swallow is loud and hard. You are an older adult, and you are speaking to a younger person who stands above you—someone who has what you've always wanted. Start with a tight, envious edge in your voice, a defensive bitterness that clings to every word. As you continue, let that jealousy peel back into something softer: a weary, almost helpless admission of longing. Your voice may crack, thin out, or catch on a swallow—don't fight it.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Speaking Through Dental Numbing
instruction: You just left the dentist with half your face frozen and must make an important phone call. Your bilabial sounds (B, P, M) are disasters. You're drooling and trying to hide it. Over-compensate with the working side of your mouth. The harder you try to sound normal, the worse it gets. Include the frustration of repeating yourself, and the moment you give up and just text them instead — but narrate that decision through the numbed mouth.

title: The Last Afternoon Light
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandfather's hospital bed during his final hours. Begin by simply being present with him, noticing the small details—his breathing, the afternoon light, the weight of your hand in his. As you speak to him, let yourself discover what you truly need to say, moving from the surface of everyday comfort to the depths of what he meant to you. Your voice should transform from steady reassurance to raw, unguarded love. End in a place where gratitude and unbearable loss exist in the same breath. Don't perform grief—let it find you as you realize these are the last words you'll ever speak to him.
inspired_by: An actor is preparing a cold reading for an audition

title: The Numbed Response
instruction: You are an 8-year-old boy sitting in a stark, cold doctor's exam room. Your mother is beside you, but you've pulled so far inside yourself that her hand on your shoulder feels like faint pressure from far away. The doctor is asking you questions in a gentle, investigative voice—but you’re not really there. You feel a dull, heavy numbness, like your body is wrapped in thick wool. Start by answering with flat, clipped words, barely above a whisper. But as the questions keep coming and the doctor’s professional calm starts to feel like a cage, a flicker of irritation rises—your voice gets a little tighter, your answers a bit shorter, maybe you shift in your seat and let out a sigh. By the end, let that impatience crack through the numbness, making your final words snap with a sullen, irritable edge.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Melody You'll Never Hear
instruction: You are humming a lullaby to your newborn child who was born profoundly deaf. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate and achingly tender. Begin with pure love as you sing softly, then let reality creep in—the catch in your voice as you realize they'll never hear your voice, never hear music, never hear the song you wrote for them before they were born. Don't cry loudly; let tears live in your throat as you continue humming, your voice breaking on certain notes. Shift into whispered confessions of fear and inadequacy—how do you share your world with them? End with a fragile but determined tenderness as you promise to find new ways to sing to them, to make them feel music through your heartbeat, your touch. This is love mixed with grief, hope threaded through heartbreak.

title: Cheering at Your Father's Funeral
instruction: You've shown up to your estranged father's funeral still clinging to the coping mechanism you learned as a child - inappropriate cheerfulness, making jokes, treating serious moments like a game. Begin with that same oblivious, performative enthusiasm, trying to lighten the mood, telling stories like you're at a celebration. But as family members stare at you with confusion and pain, let their reactions pierce through your armor. Your voice should shake as the cheerfulness becomes harder to maintain, eventually shattering into raw anger at him for making you this way - for teaching you to never be serious, to never be real. End with a quiet, broken admission that you don't know how to grieve properly because he never taught you how to feel anything properly.

title: Fighting for Your Child Against the World
instruction: Your teenager came home broken—bullied, rejected, convinced they're worthless—and you're making them listen. Start fierce, almost angry in your protectiveness: 'Look at me. LOOK at me.' Let your voice shake with barely contained rage at whoever hurt them, then crack as you realize you can't fight this battle for them. Shift to desperate pleading: tell them exactly what you see when you look at them, listing specific moments of their beauty, courage, kindness. Your voice should break repeatedly, oscillating between fierce declaration and helpless tenderness. Let yourself become vulnerable—confess your own fears of failing them, of not knowing how to fix this. End with a whispered admission of your own powerlessness: 'I can't make them see what I see... but God, I wish I could,' then pull them close with words alone, your voice raw with a parent's ferocious, helpless love.
inspired_by: The Ex You Still Want: Running Into Them

title: Laughing Through the Eulogy You're Writing
instruction: Sit alone, writing a eulogy for someone who made you laugh until you cried, and let the memories make you do both now. Start reading aloud what you've written—a funny story about them, something ridiculous they did. Let yourself laugh genuinely, fully, the way they made you laugh. But the laughter should keep catching, breaking into tears, then back to laughter again. Your voice needs to ride this impossible wave of joy and grief. Share the absurd, beautiful, infuriating things about them—how they burned every meal, told terrible jokes, loved with reckless abandon. Midway through, hit the moment that breaks you: realizing you're using past tense, that these stories are all you have left. End in a place of profound gratitude that coexists with unbearable loss. Your final words should acknowledge the gift of having known them, even as your voice shatters on the reality that they're gone. Let the laughter and tears become indistinguishable.
inspired_by: Coma Visitor: Talking to Someone Who Can't Respond

title: Midnight Confession: The Secret That Has Been Eating You Alive
instruction: It's 3 AM and you've woken your best friend because you can't carry this secret another moment. Your voice is barely above a whisper, intimate and urgent in the darkness. You're confessing something you've hidden for years—something that if spoken aloud will change everything between you, possibly destroy it. Start with halting words, long pauses where shame chokes you silent. Your breathing is uneven; you keep almost backing away from the truth, then forcing yourself forward. As you speak, your voice oscillates between desperate need to be known and terror of being seen. There's tender gratitude mixed with devastating vulnerability—thanking them for their friendship even as you risk it. You're not asking for forgiveness, just bearing witness to your own truth. End with the exhausted, fragile relief of someone who has finally set down a crushing weight, uncertain what comes next but unable to carry it alone anymore.
inspired_by: Historical: Witness to Atrocity Must Testify Against Perpetrators Now in Power

title: Holding the Line
instruction: Your teenage child just told you they're planning to do something dangerous—run away, drop out, chase something reckless—and you're trying to stop them while your own panic threatens to overwhelm you. Start with explosive intensity, your voice loud with fear disguised as anger: 'Absolutely not! You have no idea what you're risking!' Let the volume escalate as they push back, your voice almost breaking with the force of your terror for them. But then something in their face stops you—you see their pain, their desperation. Your voice suddenly drops, becomes raw and unguarded: 'Please... please don't do this.' Now you're begging, your fierce protectiveness collapsing into helplessness. You're admitting your own limitations: 'I can't lose you. I couldn't survive it.' End with both rage and tenderness intertwined—your voice shaking with the impossible task of holding on while letting go: 'I'm so angry... and I love you so much I can't breathe.'

title: Pretending to Enjoy a Meal That Doesnt Taste Good
instruction: Youre dining with someone who cooked for you, but the food isnt to your liking. Internally, youre struggling with the taste, but you compliment it. Describe your internal reaction while taking another bite. Speak with a satisfied tone, masking your true feelings.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Lie They Chose
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about the affair that destroyed your childhood—and the fact that he knew your mother was innocent when he let everyone blame her. Begin with controlled anger, reciting facts like evidence: dates, moments, the things you noticed as a child. But as you speak, the professional detachment crumbles. 'You let me hate her. For fifteen years, you let me hate her.' Your voice becomes raw with betrayal, then suddenly breaks into something more vulnerable—the child who needed a parent. The anger doesn't disappear; it tangles with grief, with a desperate need for him to finally tell the truth. End not with rage but with a quiet, broken question that's more devastating than any accusation: 'Was it easier? Letting me hate the wrong person?'
inspired_by: Defense Closing Argument: Arguing Reasonable Doubt

title: The Jacket That Still Holds You
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're alone in your apartment wearing your deceased best friend's leather jacket—the one they died in six months ago, now cleaned and returned to you. You've finally found the courage to put it on. Begin in silence, becoming aware of how it sits on your shoulders, the weight of it, the scent of leather and something underneath that might be them or might be memory. Start whispering to them—tentative, testing if they can somehow hear you through this object. Share something you never got to tell them, something small and specific and true. As the jacket's presence intensifies around your body, let your whispers become more desperate, more honest. End with a confession of how you're failing without them, your voice barely audible but absolutely naked. Move from hesitant connection to complete surrender to grief.
inspired_by: Sense Memory with Emotionally Impacting Objects

title: Bedside Confession to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner lies sleeping beside you after a beautiful evening, and you're overwhelmed by a secret you can no longer carry—an affair, a terminal diagnosis, a truth that will end this peace forever. Speak in whispers so soft they barely disturb the air, as if quietness could somehow lessen the betrayal. Your breath catches constantly, not from physical distress but from the weight of what you're confessing to someone who cannot hear you. Let tears fall silently. Describe their sleeping face with heartbreaking tenderness even as you admit what will destroy them. The arc moves from desperate need to confess, through aching love for this moment of innocence, to the hollow realization that saying it aloud—even to the silence—has made it irreversibly real. End with your voice disappearing entirely into soundless grief.

title: The Ledger Lies
instruction: You are a retired schoolteacher, alone in your kitchen, going through the household accounts you've kept for forty years. Your daughter, who manages your finances, has been quietly siphoning money for months—you've just found the proof. Start with a quiet, stunned murmur as you see the numbers, a breathless 'No... that can't be right.' Let your voice tremble as you trace the dates, then shift to a rising, cracked accusation as you realize the depth of the betrayal. Your words should break apart—stops and starts, a dry throat, a sudden sharp laugh of disbelief before your tone hardens into raw, quiet fury.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering the Secret That's Been Eating You Alive
instruction: Late at night, lying next to someone you love, you finally confess the thing you've hidden—an addiction, a betrayal, an abortion, a trauma, something that's created a wall between you. Your voice is barely audible, thick with shame. Start almost inaudibly: 'I need to tell you something and I'm terrified you'll leave.' The words come haltingly, catching in your throat, each admission costing you everything. The emotion is suffocating tenderness mixed with self-loathing—you love this person so much, and you're certain this truth will destroy what you have. Let silence speak between phrases. End with your voice breaking on a question you're afraid to ask: 'Can you still love me knowing this?'
inspired_by: Realizing Your Coping Mechanism Has Become a Problem

title: Skin and Storm
instruction: You are in the grip of an overwhelming physical and emotional experience: perhaps the first touch after years of loneliness, or rage so complete your body shakes, or grief that makes you want to tear your own skin off, or ecstatic joy that feels like it might crack you open. Let your body respond without choreography—shaking, gasping, laughing, collapsing, whatever genuinely wants to happen. Don't perform the emotion; let sensation lead and emotion follow. Feel your heartbeat, the temperature of your skin, the actual physical impulses. Start in one intense state and let the physical reality of it transform you—rage might suddenly break into sobbing, passion might reveal unexpected fear, grief might shift into something almost transcendent. Trust your body's wisdom more than your mind's plan.

title: The Universal Language
instruction: You are an elderly woman trying to explain to a non-native speaker how to turn on the television. You start feeling a bit flustered – you've said the same thing three times and they still don't understand. Your voice gets louder, your sentences break into single words with pauses: "Press… button… red… there." Then, as you see their confusion turn to a tiny smile, you catch yourself. A wave of amusement rises. You laugh softly at the absurdity of it all and try a different approach – pointing and using a simple, warm tone. End with a chuckle and a gentle, resigned 'Never mind, let me show you.' The shift goes from impatient frustration to light-hearted, affectionate amusement.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Parent Who Chose to End Treatment
instruction: Your parent has decided to stop cancer treatment and enter hospice. You arrive at their bedside trying to be strong, voice steady as you say 'I brought your favorite flowers.' But as they take your hand and say they're ready to go, your composure fractures. The word 'Mom' or 'Dad' comes out broken. You cycle through trying to convince them to keep fighting, your voice rising with desperate energy, then collapsing into quiet acceptance as they explain why they need peace. By the end, you're whispering memories of childhood, your voice tender and thick with tears, telling them it's okay to let go even as your heart shatters. The journey moves from false brightness to desperate bargaining to finally, reluctantly, giving them permission to leave.
inspired_by: Your Partner Saying They Don't Want Children

title: Condescend Intentionally
instruction: This person has been arrogant, and you're about to cut them down with condescension. Your voice becomes honey-sweet and sharp. 'Oh, you didn't know that?' The implication: 'Everyone knows that.' You're being subtle about the cruelty. 'I'll explain it slowly for you.' Your voice is a weapon disguised as helpfulness. They hear every blade in it. You're winning this moment, but your voice will regret it later.

title: The Last Echo
instruction: You are standing alone in the middle of a vast, empty warehouse at dusk, having just learned that your child died in an accident hours ago, and you couldn't get there in time. For the first few seconds, your voice trembles and cracks as you try to form words — a choked, broken whisper of their name. Then it builds into a raw, wordless scream that rips from your chest, not directed at anyone or anything, just pure pain released into the concrete and steel. Your throat tears, your legs give out, and the scream tapers into a ragged sob as you slump to your knees, staring at nothing.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Gilded Cradle
instruction: You are an older woman in a sunlit Victorian parlor, scolding your adult son—who has just lied to you about his whereabouts—while your voice drips with cultivated sweetness. Begin with a honeyed, low-pitched tone, each word perfectly spaced, as if arranging teacups: 'My darling, I know you were not at the library.' Let contempt curl beneath the syrup, a cold, slow blade. Midway, your composure splinters—your teacup rattles in its saucer, your fingers tremble, and your tone hardens into gravel. End with a jagged whisper, voice cracking, as the mask drops entirely: 'Don't you dare use that phrase with me ever again.' Feel the weight of the china, the scent of lavender, the child you raised now a stranger.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Whispered at the Window
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're standing at a window, speaking softly to yourself or to someone who isn't there—a lost love, a version of yourself from years ago, a child you'll never have, or someone who died before you could say this. Your voice is barely above a whisper because these words feel too intimate for full volume, too private even for the empty room. Begin with tender confession—admitting something you've never said aloud, something that makes you feel exposed just to acknowledge. Let quiet grief seep in, the kind that sits in your chest like a stone, making your breath catch between words. Your voice should tremble not with drama but with the effort of staying composed while your heart breaks. End with a whispered acceptance or letting go, your voice soft but somehow more solid, like you've set down a weight you've been carrying. This should feel like overhearing someone's most private moment, never performed, achingly real.

title: Gratitude at the Goodbye Party
instruction: You're giving a toast at your mentor's retirement party—the mentor who built their entire career on the backs of people like you, who took your ideas and called them theirs, who's now being celebrated as a visionary. But you also genuinely learned from them. You also, despite everything, don't want them to leave. Speak with warmth and humor at first, praising their contributions, your voice full of genuine affection. But let the truth start bleeding through in moments of pointed observation—'You taught me that great leaders know how to recognize potential... even if they don't always acknowledge where ideas come from.' Laugh as you say it, but let the laughter have an edge. Move between real gratitude and veiled hurt, between celebration and reckoning. End in a moment of beautiful contradiction: your voice warm with actual love and appreciation, your eyes bright with unshed tears, your words both a genuine blessing for their future and a quiet acknowledgment of what you never got. Let the audience feel both your grace and your grief.
inspired_by: Suppressing Anger When Someone Takes Credit for Your Work

title: The Last Gift Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—a grandparent, mentor, or parent figure—in their final hours. They're drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin in quiet despair, feeling you never became the person they hoped you'd be, that you've disappointed them. But as you sit there in the dim light, you begin speaking to them—perhaps they can hear, perhaps not—and you start remembering out loud: the specific moments they shaped you, the qualities you have because of them, the small victories in your life that exist because they believed in you. Let your voice crack with grief, but also warm with gratitude. End in a place where sorrow and profound appreciation are inseparable—you're saying goodbye, but you're also saying thank you by showing them who you've become.

title: The Memory of Warmth
instruction: You are an older man lying curled on your side in bed, one lung pressed against the mattress, the other free. The room is quiet, late afternoon. At first, you’re thinking about the chill in the air and a minor ache in your hip—a slight, resigned weariness. But then a memory surfaces: of your wife’s hand on your forehead, the way she used to pull a blanket over you. As you speak that memory aloud to yourself, let your voice soften, your breath deepen, and the tension in your shoulders melt. The initial rumble of thought transforms into pure, quiet contentment. Let there be natural pauses, a little rustle, a shift of weight as you settle deeper into the mattress. Speak as if the words are for you alone, barely above a whisper.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dancing Alone to Their Song
instruction: A song comes on—the one that was yours and theirs—and suddenly your body remembers everything. Begin with just hearing the first notes, feeling them hit your chest. Let your body respond before your mind can plan: maybe you freeze, maybe you start moving, maybe your breath changes. As the song continues, allow the physical memory of dancing with them, holding them, losing them, to move through you. Don't choreograph this—let the music and the sensation of their absence or presence genuinely affect you. Your body might move with joy, then break with grief. You might laugh and cry in the same breath. Let pleasure and pain coexist in your moving body. By the song's end, be somewhere physically and emotionally different than where you started.

title: Dancing in the Ruins of Everything
instruction: You're standing in what used to be your home—maybe it burned down, maybe it's been foreclosed, maybe everyone who made it home is gone—and you're laughing. Start with wonder at the destruction: you're describing what's left with a voice full of strange joy, finding beauty in the debris, maybe humming a song that used to play here. Your laughter is real and frequent, punctuating your words. But gradually, as you touch objects that survived—a photo, a child's toy, a letter—the laughter begins to mix with tears. You're still smiling, still finding moments of lightness, but your voice is cracking. You're grateful for what you had, genuinely grateful, speaking with profound appreciation through tears that won't stop. The laughter and sobbing become indistinguishable. End in a place of profound peace mixed with devastating loss: your voice steady but wet with tears, expressing pure gratitude for the love that made the loss so painful, laughing softly through the words 'it was worth it' or 'I'm so glad I got to have this.'

title: The Mirror They Hold Up
instruction: Your parent/child confronts you about how you've shrunk yourself for years - always accommodating, always agreeable, never taking up space or voicing what you really want. They're not angry; they're heartbroken watching you erase yourself. Start defensive, insisting you're fine, that being easy-going is just who you are. Your voice is casual, dismissive, perhaps with a forced laugh. But as they persist - giving specific examples of times you disappeared your own needs, dreams, or boundaries - something cracks open. Feel the truth of what they're saying penetrate your defenses. Move from deflection to raw vulnerability as you admit, perhaps for the first time aloud, how exhausted you are from performing agreeability, how you don't even know what you actually want anymore. End with your voice breaking, no longer hiding behind pleasantness, finally allowing yourself to be seen as uncertain, lost, but desperately ready to reclaim yourself.

title: The Unexpected Toast
instruction: You're at a lively dinner with close friends, a few glasses in. The host suddenly reveals that the job you were anxious about came through—your friend got it instead, and you're genuinely thrilled for him. Your astonishment morphs into deep relief as you realize you dodged a bullet. Speak to the table, your voice slightly louder than necessary, turning to address different faces. Let the drink loosen your reactions, make you forget a word, then find it again. End with a sincere, almost shaky relief.

title: Confronting Your Father About Who You Really Are
instruction: You're finally telling your father something you've hidden for years - your true identity, your real dreams, a secret that changes everything between you. title: Rage Dissolving Into Light
instruction: You are in the grip of visceral, body-shaking rage at someone who betrayed you. Begin with your fury fully physical—fists clenched, jaw tight, breath ragged, voice raised. Notice specific details: the way tears cling to their eyelashes, a slight tremor in their hands, the exact color of their eyes in this light. Let your body's rage begin to drain away as wonder and recognition flood in. End in a place of strange, exhausted tenderness mixed with residual anger—your voice soft but your words still honest about the pain, now complicated by this new seeing.

title: The Revenge Gift
instruction: You are a teenage boy standing in your crush's backyard at night, holding a small, meticulously wrapped box. You've just watched them get humiliated by their ex at a party. But underneath it all is pure malice: this gift is a setup, designed to make them vulnerable and dependent on you. Start with a manic, breathless rush — your voice cracking, your heart pounding so loud you can barely hear yourself. As you explain what's in the box, let your words splinter. Stop twice. Once because a firework goes off nearby. Once because you realize they're crying, and the sound makes you feel both tender and triumphant. title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: You're lying next to your sleeping partner in the dark, believing they're asleep, and you finally allow yourself to whisper the truth you can't say when they're awake. title: The Body Keeps Score
instruction: You are experiencing intense physical sensation—passionate embrace, crushing grief that manifests as physical pain, rage that burns through your limbs, or illness that weakens you—while simultaneously receiving world-changing information. title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Wife After the Diagnosis
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your wife is finally asleep after days of insomnia. You're sitting on the edge of the bed, speaking barely above a breath so you don't wake her. But there's a tremor underneath—you're confessing something unbearable while trying to keep it gentle, like you're telling her the saddest bedtime story ever written. Your throat keeps catching. title: Confronting Your Mother About the Silence
instruction: You're finally telling your aging mother about the emotional neglect that shaped your entire childhood—the times you needed her and she wasn't there, the pain you've carried alone. title: The Reclamation
instruction: You're alone in a space where someone once made you feel powerless—physically, emotionally, or both. Transform from frozen victim-memory, through explosive physical and vocal rage, to grounded, embodied power.

instruction: You're calling your parent from the airport before boarding a one-way flight to take a job overseas—maybe forever. title: Choosing Your Child Over Your Dying Dream
instruction: You've just received the career opportunity of a lifetime - the role, the grant, the tour - but your child is struggling, barely holding on, and you have to choose. title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who shaped your entire life—a grandparent, mentor, or old friend—and they have hours left. instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your funeral - you know you're dying, you have weeks left, and you've decided to make it funny. title: The Secret Language
instruction: Late at night, you're whispering to your sleeping lover, revealing something you've never told anyone—perhaps about your childhood, a fear, or who you really are. instruction: You're doing one final walkthrough of the home where you built your life, and memories are crashing over you in waves that mix joy and devastation. title: Reading Your Sister's Eulogy While Wearing Her Favorite Dress
instruction: You're at your twin sister's funeral, and halfway through, you start laughing. Not from hysteria—from a memory that just hit you. instruction: You are confronting your father after twenty years of silence about something that shattered your childhood. Begin with controlled, cold anger—you've rehearsed this moment a thousand times in your mind, seeing yourself as calm and powerful. But the moment you start speaking, a specific image invades you unbidden: his hands, exactly as they looked when you were small, and suddenly you're not the powerful adult you imagined—you're utterly vulnerable. Let that image of his hands completely derail your planned speech. Feel your body rebel against the control you wanted to maintain. Move from icy, rehearsed confrontation into raw, unplanned emotional chaos, then finally into something quieter but more truthful than anything you intended to say. The images in your mind—of him, of yourself as a child, of the moment everything changed—should dictate where your words go, not your plan.
inspired_by: When using the hypnagogic state for character programming

title: The Breaking Point: Body and Heart
instruction: You are in the middle of an intense physical experience—running until your lungs burn, or in the grip of desire, or enduring physical pain—when emotional memories start erupting through your body without warning. Each physical sensation triggers a different emotional flashback: the burning in your chest suddenly becomes the moment you heard devastating news; the ache in your muscles transforms into the memory of being held; exhaustion becomes grief becomes rage becomes unexpected joy. Your breath, sounds, and words are pulled directly from this collision of physical and emotional sensation. Start from a place of pure physical focus, but let your body unlock emotional chambers you didn't know were there. End when the physical and emotional become so intertwined you can't tell them apart, and you collapse into something cathartic and raw.

title: A Parent's Final Gift: Teaching Your Child to Live Without You
instruction: You're in hospice, and your adult child has just arrived. You have maybe hours left, and there's so much you need to say—but you start with gentle humor, teasing them about finally showing up on time. As you speak, the lightness gives way to fierce urgency: practical advice about the boiler, about changing the air filters, about calling your sister when they feel alone. Your voice grows more fragile with each instruction, each piece of mothering or fathering you're trying to compress into minutes. The humor breaks into raw tenderness as you tell them the things you always assumed you'd have time to say. By the end, you're barely whispering, exhausted, but you need them to know: you're not afraid, and they shouldn't be either. Your last words are released like breath itself—light, certain, a permission to let you go.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Witch Casts a Spell Knowing It Will Cost Her Own Magic

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: You are lying in bed beside your partner of ten years, both awake in the darkness at 3am. You have a secret that's been eating you alive—an affair, a hidden child, a betrayal, a truth about your past. Begin with the overwhelming need to confess, to be known completely, to stop the exhausting performance of normalcy. Let this need make your voice shake as you whisper into the dark. But feel the obstacle: your terror of losing them, the weight of their trust, the fragile peace of this moment. Let these two forces—the desperate need to be fully seen and the paralyzing fear of destruction—create an excruciating tension. By the end, whether you've spoken the words or not, arrive at a different emotional place: perhaps devastating clarity about what you're willing to sacrifice, or a heartbroken understanding of the chasm between you.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill the emotional obligation but keeps playing surface emotion without the underlying need and passion

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Who I Pretended to Be
instruction: You're alone, maybe a little drunk, and you've just made a decision that will destroy the perfect life you built on borrowed dreams. Your voice starts with a laugh—bitter, a little manic. 'I quit today. Just walked out.' You're describing it almost giddily, the absurdity of it all. But the laughter keeps breaking into something else—grief, relief, terror all mixed together. You're crying and laughing at the same time: 'Twenty years! Twenty years of—of WHAT?' Your voice cracks with dark humor and devastating self-recognition. You feel insane and more sane than you've ever been. There's gratitude threading through the chaos—'Thank god, thank god'—but you're also mourning every year you lost. End with your voice soft, still thick with tears but also wonder: 'I have no idea what happens now.' You sound terrified. You also sound, impossibly, like yourself.

title: The Unsaid Goodbye
instruction: You are a young man on the phone with your dying father. Every time you try to say 'I love you,' the word gets stuck—repeating, prolonging, or a silent block. Your throat tightens, you blink hard, and your voice spikes when the word finally breaks free. Start with the intense pain of the struggle, feeling each block like a punch. By the end, after several failed attempts, your voice cracks into a raw, exhausted whisper as you finally force it out, the pain still there but now mixed with quiet surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Rage That Becomes Prayer
instruction: Your child has done something dangerous and self-destructive, and you're exploding with fury born from terror - you almost lost them. Start with fierce, volcanic anger, your voice loud and uncontrolled, words tumbling over each other. But mid-torrent, let the rage crack open to reveal the raw fear underneath. Your voice should break, your breath should sob, your fury should collapse into desperate love and helplessness. Grab them (metaphorically, through your voice) and shake them with anger, then pull them close with terrified tenderness. Move from 'How dare you!' to 'I can't lose you' to a whispered, broken 'Please don't leave me.' This is the contradiction of protective rage and absolute vulnerability - you're powerful and powerless simultaneously. Let yourself be messy, incoherent, wildly real. This is love that manifests as fury because you don't know what else to do with the terror.
inspired_by: Pretending to Agree While Internally Disagreeing

title: Protecting Someone You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone who's hurt - a child, a sibling, a friend - and they're asking 'Am I going to be okay?' Start with fierce, absolute certainty: 'Yes. Yes, you're fine. I've got you.' Your voice is strong, protective, full of love and determination. But as you keep reassuring them, reality is crashing in. Your certainty begins to crack. The reassurances become more desperate, louder, almost angry - angry at the universe, at your own helplessness. 'You're FINE. Do you hear me? You're FINE.' But your voice is breaking. By the end, you're still saying the words 'you're okay, you're okay' but they've become a prayer, a plea, whispered through tears as you rock them, your fierceness collapsing into the most devastating tenderness. Let us hear you trying to will them to survive through the sheer force of your love, even as you feel them slipping away.

title: The Last Tissue
instruction: You are a woman with a head cold so heavy your voice sounds stuffed and nasal. You are speaking to your young child, who also has a cold, and you are both sniffling and coughing. You just found the very last tissue in the house, and a wave of relief washes over you. Start by feeling the congestion and frustration in your throat, breaking off sentences to sniffle or clear your throat. As you explain to the child that you can finally wipe their nose, your voice lightens, gaining a tender, almost weepy gratitude. Let the relief crack through the stuffiness—your tone becomes softer, slower, and more present, as if each word is a little victory. Let the sound be affected by your blocked nose, but the warmth in your voice grows until the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Homecoming Paradox
instruction: You're returning home after years away, walking through the door of the house you grew up in. You're flooded with competing emotions: genuine joy at being back mixed with the weight of all the reasons you left, love for the people here tangled with resentment over old wounds, nostalgia colliding with the person you've become who no longer fits in this space. Don't choose one emotion—inhabit all of them simultaneously. Let your voice crack between laughter and something closer to tears. Feel gratitude and bitterness in the same breath. Start with the bright homecoming smile, but let every familiar smell, every unchanged room, every loving gesture from family complicate what you're feeling. By the end, you don't resolve these contradictions—you simply stand in the impossible middle of loving and grieving the same place, the same people, the same version of yourself you left behind.
inspired_by: Actor cannot find a choice for a scene obligation after trying the obvious options

title: The Goodbye You Can't Stop
instruction: Your adult child is cutting you out of their life, and you're trying desperately to stop them from leaving. Start with controlled panic, your voice tight and falsely calm: 'Please, let's just talk about this.' As they move toward the door, something primal erupts - your voice becomes loud, fierce, protective: 'I'm your mother/father! You don't just walk away!' They turn, and their coldness breaks you. Your voice cracks into raw pleading, all dignity abandoned: 'What did I do that was so terrible you can't forgive me?' You're sobbing now, rage and desperation and love all tangled together. Your voice drops to a broken whisper: 'I don't know how to lose you.' Finally, as the door closes, you collapse into helpless tears, alternating between fury at their cruelty and devastating self-blame, voice breaking: 'Come back. Please come back.'

title: Confronting the Ghost You Became
instruction: You are finally confronting your parent after years of silence, and they don't remember who you are anymore - dementia has taken that from both of you. Start with carefully controlled anger, listing all the ways they failed you, the birthdays missed, the promises broken, the coldness. But as you speak and they stare at you with confused, frightened eyes like a child, your rage must crumble into something more complicated - grief for the parent you needed and never had, and for the parent who is disappearing before you can ever get closure. Your voice should move from accusation to a desperate, breaking plea: 'Please, just remember me. Just once, see me.' Let your anger and love collide until you can't tell them apart anymore.

title: Parent Realizes Their Child's Suicide Note Is a Forgery—But Too Late to Stop the Funeral
instruction: You're reading your child's suicide note aloud to a grief counselor, trying to find meaning in their final words. Your voice is shattered but searching—desperate to understand, to find the moment you missed. Then mid-sentence, you see it: a phrase your child never used, a misspelling they'd never make, handwriting that's almost right but not quite. This isn't their note. Your voice explodes—not loud, but urgent, frantic. Someone did this. Your child didn't leave willingly. The grief detonates into rage, then terror, then back to grief because it doesn't matter—they're still gone. You're shouting and whispering in the same breath, demanding answers that can't come. Your voice becomes raw, animal, protective fury mixed with absolute helplessness. By the end, you collapse back into grief, but it's different now—not the grief of wondering why, but the grief of knowing someone took them, and you buried them yesterday believing a lie. Your final words are soft, fierce, broken: a vow spoken to your child that you will find the truth.
inspired_by: Scientist Realizes Her Breakthrough Comes from Data Her Competitor Stole

title: The Dream I Can't Stop Having
instruction: In bed, in darkness, whisper to your lover about a recurring dream that's been haunting you. Begin by trying to describe it matter-of-factly—just telling the story. But as you speak, start to realize what the dream actually means, what it's been trying to tell you about yourself, about them, about what you're afraid of or what you've been hiding. Let the act of speaking it aloud transform your understanding of it. Your voice should start casual, almost dismissive, but become increasingly vulnerable and raw as the truth reveals itself. By the end, you're not describing a dream anymore—you're confessing something you didn't know you needed to say.
inspired_by: Group Dream Sharing and Analysis (Workshop Format)

title: Lullaby Over the Body
instruction: You are a small, androgynous child lying contentedly in the lap of your most gentle caregiver.
