But as you speak, older memories start bleeding through—the smell of her perfume from a specific birthday, the sound of her voice from a night you pretended to sleep, the exact location where you stood when you first felt invisible to her. Let your voice shift from controlled to trembling to fierce. Stop trying to be fair. Let the symbols and fragments of your childhood tumble out: a blue plate, a slammed door, her hands, her silence. By the end, you're no longer asking for understanding—you're demanding to be seen, your voice raw with decades of unspoken need. Travel from careful politeness to volcanic truth-telling.

title: Burying Your Dead While Tasting Freedom
instruction: You're at a mass grave for the rebels who died to win freedom, and you're speaking over the bodies of your friends, your siblings, your lover—but the absurd beauty is that you're free now, you're standing in sunlight as a free person, and you can't reconcile the simultaneous joy and devastation. Start laughing through tears, your voice bright and broken at once, describing the morning—how the sky looks different now, how you woke up and forgot for a moment to be afraid. But the laughter keeps fracturing into sobs as you name the ones in the ground who will never see this day. Your voice moves fluidly between gratitude so profound it sounds like singing, and grief so deep it steals your breath. End with something impossible: thanking them while telling them goodbye, your voice full of wonder at the miracle of freedom and shattered by its cost, somehow holding both realities with equal intensity. Let your final words trail off into a sound that could be either laughing or crying—because in this moment, they're the same thing.

title: The Fine Print and a Familiar Face
instruction: You are an older man at a government benefits office, filling out a form while nursing a sharp lower back pain from sitting too long. Across the counter, you catch the eye of a caseworker you've seen before—someone you find quietly captivating. You begin reading the form's terms aloud in a clipped, monotone voice, focusing on accuracy, but the pain makes you wince and stammer on certain words. As you continue, your voice softens slightly, lingering on phrases that let you look up at her, and the bureaucratic drone becomes a hesitant, almost tender murmur by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Under the Grand Piano
instruction: You're an older man who crawled under your late wife's grand piano to retrieve a dropped heirloom. The piano shifted and now pins your chest — you can only take short, forced exhales. You initially doubt you can escape, gasping out fragments of worry. But as you lie there, you notice the absurdity: you're trapped under a piano, and you remember how your wife always said it would be the death of you. A dry chuckle escapes. Through pained breath, you speak to yourself, your doubt melting into weary amusement at the irony. Let your voice crack with the physical strain, but let the laughter bubble up despite it.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Butterfly's Wing
instruction: You are sitting alone in a quiet backyard, feeling the soft buzz of a cannabis high. You notice a butterfly landing on a flower nearby, and your focus sharpens intensely—you become utterly fascinated by the way its wing glitters. You talk to yourself or to the butterfly, your voice drifting, sticky with dry mouth, punctuated by small giggles. Start with pure, explosive elation and deep interest, describing every shimmer. As you watch, a wave of affection washes over you—for the butterfly, for this moment, for something unnamed. Let your voice soften, slow down, and end in a gentle, heartfelt sigh.
emotions_sampled: Elation (very intensely present), Affection (slightly present), Interest (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Finding Joy in the Ruins: Gratitude at the End
instruction: You're terminally ill or facing the end of something irreversible, and someone has brought you hot chocolate—something simple you never thought you'd taste again. Begin with surprised laughter, genuine delight breaking through pain, describing the taste with almost childlike wonder. But let that joy be shot through with awareness of loss—you're laughing and crying simultaneously. Your voice should crack between happiness and heartbreak, expressing profound gratitude for this small kindness while knowing it's one of your last experiences of simple pleasure. Let contradictory emotions wash over each other: peace and grief, acceptance and longing, gratitude and fury at what's being taken from you. End with a moment of transcendent clarity, voice soft but clear, finding unexpected beauty in this bittersweet instant—grateful for the hot chocolate, for whoever brought it, for being alive enough right now to taste it, even as you acknowledge the darkness coming. Let your final words hold both goodbye and thank you.
inspired_by: Sipping a Cup of Hot Chocolate on a Cold Day

title: Night-Scroll Drift
instruction: You're lying in the dark, phone propped on your chest, scrolling through old conversations. You've had enough to drink that your thoughts are fuzzy and your reactions are delayed. Start with a bitter, half-laugh as you swipe past a memory — your voice is low, directed at the screen, with quiet thumb-taps and long pauses where you lose your train of thought. Then you stop on something that sobers you: a photo of someone you miss. Let a vulnerable silence stretch, then speak again — this time softer, more raw, the bitterness fading into a quiet ache.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Jumping Through the Loss
instruction: You're a child doing a series of explosive jumps—maybe jump squats or leaps across a gym floor. Your coach told you to keep going even when you feel hollow. Start in a numb, automatic rhythm, landing with a flat thud, breath launching each word mid-air: 'I... don't... care.' Let the disappointment creep in with each landing—your voice catching, a slight crack on the next 'I... thought... I'd... win.' By the end, the numbness breaks, and the last fragmented words come out heavy, almost defeated, as you land one final time: 'But... I'm... still... jumping.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Gratitude That Destroys You
instruction: Your best friend is moving across the world tomorrow - following their dream, the one you helped them chase. You're meeting for goodbye drinks and you need to tell them what they mean to you. Begin trying to keep it light, almost joking - your voice has that false casualness people use when they're terrified of real emotion. But as you start listing what you're grateful for, something breaks open. Your voice shifts between genuine joy at their happiness and devastating grief at losing them. 'I'm so proud of you' becomes 'I don't know how to do life without you.' Laugh while tears choke your voice. Express pure, radiant gratitude while your heart audibly breaks: 'You saved my life and now I have to learn to live it without you in it every day.' End with contradictory peace and pain: 'This is right. This is so right. And it's killing me.' Let yourself smile through the devastation.
inspired_by: Child Discovering Death for the First Time

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Childhood They Stole
instruction: You're finally saying the things you've rehearsed for years but never had the courage to voice. Start with false calm, almost casual, as you begin listing specific memories—the recital they missed, the times you needed them and they weren't there. Feel your control slipping as old hurt surfaces. Your voice should shake with both anger and the childlike need for them to finally understand, finally apologize. Let rage build—not shouting, but intensely focused, each word a knife—then break unexpectedly into vulnerability, your adult voice cracking into the sound of the child you were. When they try to defend themselves, cut through with devastating clarity, but let your voice catch on the admission that you still love them, still wanted them to be different. End with quiet, exhausted honesty: you're done waiting for them to change, and that grief is heavier than the anger ever was.
inspired_by: Explaining Quantum Physics to a Five-Year-Old While High

title: Fierce and Failing
instruction: You're trying to protect someone you love from a threat—an addiction, an abusive relationship, a dangerous path—and you're watching helplessly as they choose it anyway. Start with explosive intervention, your voice loud with desperate urgency: 'Do you have any idea what this is doing to you? To us?' You're fierce, almost aggressive in your love. But as they resist you, as they defend their choices, your rage begins to splinter. Your voice cracks, oscillating wildly between shouting and breaking down—'I can't watch you destroy yourself!'—until you collapse into sobbing fury, then into something worse: helpless grief. Your voice drops to devastated quiet: 'I can't save you, can I? You have to want to be saved.' End with your voice hollowed out by powerlessness, still loving them, still terrified for them, but finally accepting you cannot force someone to survive.

title: The Hospital Room at 3 AM
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning hours. Begin by speaking to her about mundane, surface things—the weather, what you had for dinner—trying to keep everything normal and light, your voice controlled. As you hold her hand and look at her face, allow specific details to flood you: the exact way she used to smell when she hugged you as a child, the texture of her skin, the particular sound of her breathing when she laughed. Let these sense memories wash over you until you can no longer maintain the pretense of normalcy. Your voice should crack and transform as you finally tell her what she truly meant to you, moving from controlled distance to raw, unguarded love. End by speaking to her as if you are a child again, letting all your fear of losing her break through.
inspired_by: Imaging as Craft Technique with Endowments

title: Under the Desk
instruction: You are a middle-aged man crouched under your office desk, knees pulled tight to your chest, after a humiliating moment at work. Your breathing is shallow, your voice a strained whisper. You hear your daughter's footsteps approach and you shush her desperately, embarrassed at being seen like this. As she kneels down and peeks under, your tone shifts to tender affection, still hushed but warmer. Let your compressed body and anxiety crackle in the start, then let a soft smile bleed into your words without fully straightening up.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession - What I've Never Told You
instruction: It's late at night, and you're whispering to someone sleeping beside you - telling them things you can't say when they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, tender, catching on words. Begin with small truths: 'Sometimes I watch you sleep and feel so lucky it terrifies me.' Your breathing is soft, intimate. As you continue, deeper fears emerge - fears of losing them, of not being enough, of time running out. Your voice gets even quieter, as if speaking any louder would shatter something precious. Include long pauses where you almost can't continue. End with a confession of love so raw it hurts to say out loud, your voice breaking into silence as you realize they might have heard every word. The vulnerability is so complete it's almost unbearable.
inspired_by: Telling Someone You're Attracted to Them

title: Faith Shaking
instruction: Something happens that makes you question everything you thought was true about the universe, god, goodness, meaning. Your voice starts liturgical, then breaks. 'I prayed. I prayed and—' Words fail. Your breathing becomes heavy. When you try to articulate the betrayal, your voice gets raw: 'How could there be a god and allow this?' There's anger underneath, and anguish. Physical: you're holding yourself. Your voice doesn't recover to certainty; it opens, wounded, into genuine questioning. The vocal texture changes from assured to searching, lost.

title: Speaking Your Truth, Watching Your Parent Crumble
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about years of emotional absence, manipulation, or harm. Your voice starts controlled, rehearsed—you've practiced these words a thousand times. But as you speak, you watch them deflate, age before your eyes, become small and broken. Your voice gains power and momentum, fueled by decades of pain, growing sharper and more precise. Then you see them truly hearing you for the first time, and something shifts. Your anger doesn't disappear, but grief floods in alongside it. Your voice begins to shake not with rage but with the terrible realization that you're destroying someone you still, impossibly, love. The words keep coming—truths that need speaking—but now they're mixed with anguish. You're simultaneously the wounded child demanding recognition and the adult watching your parent's illusions about themselves shatter. Your voice must hold both the fierce need for accountability and the heartbreak of watching someone you needed realize they failed you.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Bard Sings a Prophecy That Becomes True as They Sing It

title: Ripping Off the Wedding Shoes
instruction: You're violently tearing off the expensive shoes you wore to your own wedding—a marriage you just discovered was built on lies. Start with explosive fury, yanking at straps and buckles, your voice raw with betrayal as you describe how these shoes pinched and hurt all day, just like this relationship. Let your rage be physical, visceral, your breathing ragged. Then let it shatter into sobbing as you realize how badly you wanted this to be real, how you ignored every warning sign. End with your voice oscillating between fierce anger at yourself for being fooled and helpless grief for the future you thought you'd have, barefoot and broken on the floor, not sure if you're more furious or heartbroken.
inspired_by: Taking Off Your Shoes After a Long Day

title: Fevered Longing
instruction: You are alone in a dim, stuffy room, your body wracked with chills and sweat from a high fever. Your thoughts swim between hazy hallucinations and a faint, unwanted pulse of sexual desire for a figure you can't quite recall. Speak to the empty air as if trying to summon them, but your voice cracks and wavers, words slipping and slurring. Begin with a whispered, ragged confession of lust, but let it dissolve into confusion, shivering, and a final, quiet surrender to exhaustion. Let the room feel stifling, your lips dry, your breath shallow—every micro-distraction (a creak, a shiver, a lost thought) is real.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Coffee Mug Knows Everything
instruction: You're confronting your mother/father across the kitchen table. There's a chipped coffee mug between you—the one they've used every morning for twenty years. Begin by staring at that mug, describing its stains, its chips, the way the handle is slightly crooked. Let the mug tell you what it has witnessed: every silent breakfast, every swallowed word, every lie of omission. As you speak to your parent, the mug becomes a witness you're calling to testify. Start with bitter, sarcastic observations about this 'stupid mug that's seen everything,' but as its history pours out—the mornings after their fights, the coffee they made you when you were sick, the day they drank from it while deciding whether to tell you the truth—let your anger crack open into something more complex. The mug doesn't take sides; it just holds everything. End in a place of raw, uncomfortable truth that you and your parent can finally share.

title: The Last Time I Saw Her
instruction: You're an older man leaning against the kitchen counter, weight on one hip, staring at a dusty photograph pinned to the fridge. The day has drained you—your joints ache, your eyes burn—but a deep, fierce longing pulls you into the memory of your daughter's laugh. Begin by concentrating on the photo, describing her smile with a tender, raspy voice that cracks with fatigue. As you talk, the longing intensifies, but exhaustion drags your words slower, softer. Finish by setting the photo down with a heavy sigh, your final words barely a whisper, as the longing fades into quiet resignation.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Concentration (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Splitting Laughter
instruction: You're a young woman in your backyard, working through a messy breakup by chopping a pile of wood. Each swing is a grunt of frustration, but after a few strikes, you start noticing how ridiculous you look—sweaty, swearing at a log. Between breaths, you mutter to yourself about your ex, then catch the absurdity and let out a raw, surprised laugh. Start with tight, angry effort—voice stretched from the overhead motion—then soften into a wry, amused chuckle as you realize you're actually having fun. Speak only between swings, with sharp grunts on impact, and let your words trail off as you reset for the next chop.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispered Goodnight to the Sleeping One You Can't Have
instruction: You're watching someone you're deeply in love with sleep — someone who belongs to another, someone you can never tell. Start by barely breathing, as if afraid to wake them, and whisper-sing a few lines of a song you associate with them, your voice gossamer-thin and aching. Let the tenderness in your voice carry all the love you'll never speak aloud. Midway through, your voice should catch and nearly break as the reality hits you — this is as close as you'll ever get. Breathe through the pain, then continue even softer, as if each word is a goodbye. Confess in the barest whisper: 'I hope they know how lucky they are.' Pause, listening to their breathing (imagined). End by pulling away, your final 'Goodnight' almost inaudible, weighted with resignation and heartbreak so profound it steals your voice. The last sound should be you steadying your breath, swallowing down everything you feel.
inspired_by: Crowded Subway: Two Strangers Share an Earbud

title: The Stolen Morning
instruction: It's 5 AM. You're lying next to your lover who's still asleep, and in three hours, they leave for a job overseas—gone for a year, maybe forever. You're watching them sleep in the dawn light, whispering things you've never said aloud, things you'll never say when they're awake. Begin in tender observation, describing the small details of their face, their breathing. Let yourself become more vulnerable, confessing your fears—that you're not brave enough for this, that you'll disappear without them. Speak so softly you're barely breathing the words. End with the terrifying intimacy of admitting you know this might be the end, and you're memorizing this moment because it may be all you get to keep. Your voice should be a whisper throughout, growing more fragile and precious.

title: Whispering the Truth in the Dark
instruction: It's 3am and you're lying next to your partner of many years. You can't sleep because you're carrying a secret that's destroying you from the inside. Your voice is barely audible, almost testing if you can say it: 'Are you awake? I need to... I can't carry this anymore.' Your words come out in fragments, throat tight with shame. 'When I was younger, before we met... something happened that I've never told anyone.' You're not crying loudly—instead, your voice keeps catching on itself, getting smaller. As you speak, your partner's hand finds yours in the darkness, and that simple touch nearly undoes you. Your voice breaks into something more raw: 'I thought if you knew, you'd see me differently.' But they whisper back with such tenderness that you feel something shift—permission to be broken and still loved. By the end, your voice is still fragile, still hurting, but there's a quality of being held in it, of not being alone in the dark anymore.
inspired_by: Telling Someone About Abuse for the First Time

title: Confronting Your Mother About Her Silence
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally saying what you've rehearsed for twenty years. You start controlled, listing facts: 'You knew. You saw the bruises. You heard me crying.' Your voice is measured, prosecutorial. But she won't look at you, and that silence—that same silence—breaks something open. Your voice rises, becomes raw: 'Look at me!' You're demanding she see you, really see you. Then suddenly you're begging, voice cracking with the desperation of a child who just wanted their mother to choose them. 'Why wasn't I enough? Why didn't you...' You can't finish. Your rage collapses into something more vulnerable. By the end, you're speaking softly, almost tenderly, because you realize: you're not angry anymore. You're grieving the mother you needed but never had. Your voice becomes quiet, resigned, heartbroken.

title: The Last Round
instruction: You're an older man alone at a worn-down bar, elbows on your knees, staring into the amber of your whiskey. You're three drinks in—your voice feels thick, your chest compressed, your breath shallow. At first you're just muttering to yourself about the weight of the week, the quiet, the ache in your back. But then you remember the moment your grandson took his first steps yesterday, how he wobbled and laughed, and a slow, stupid grin spreads across your face. Let that memory lift you—your words become lighter, your tone warms, and you end with a deep, satisfied sigh, nodding to the empty stool beside you as if he were still there.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Elation (clearly present), Contentment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've never been able to say to your parent. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay controlled. 'I need you to hear something I've never been able to tell you.' But as you speak, the anger you've buried for decades begins to surface. Your voice tightens, sharpens: 'You were so busy with your own purpose, your own mission, that you never once asked about mine.' Let the rage build, but then—unexpectedly—it breaks. Your voice drops to something raw and small: 'I just needed you to see me. Just once.' End in a place you didn't expect: not anger, not even asking for an apology, but a quiet, exhausted acceptance. 'I finally understand—your purpose was never about being my parent. And I have to let that be enough.'

title: Hospice Nurse Whispers Final Words to Unconscious Patient She Secretly Loved
instruction: It's 3 AM. The patient is unconscious, hours from death. You're alone with them. Your voice starts as a whisper—professional, gentle, the tone you use with all your patients. But then you confess what you've never said: you fell in love with them during these months of care. Not dramatically—quietly, in the way they listened to your stories, the way they said your name. Your voice is so soft it's almost not there, because this confession is just for you, really. You're not asking for anything. You're just letting yourself feel it before it's gone. Describe a moment you've held secret—when you almost touched their hand differently, when you stayed five minutes longer than you should have. Your voice catches, but you don't cry loudly. This is intimate grief, the kind that lives in your throat. By the end, you're thanking them for letting you care for them, and your voice is filled with gratitude and the quiet devastation of a love that existed only in the space between professionalism and goodbye.
inspired_by: Scientist Realizes Her Breakthrough Comes from Data Her Competitor Stole

title: The Vigil Confession
instruction: You are sitting beside your sleeping best friend in a hospital room at 3 AM, speaking truths you could never say to their face. Begin in a whisper, almost talking to yourself, describing how exhausting it's been to love them from the shadows while they loved someone else. Your voice is tender but tired, like you've carried this weight so long it's worn grooves into your bones. Let the words catch in your throat as you confess the specific moments—their wedding day, the birth of their child, every celebration where you smiled and died inside. Don't cry loudly; let the tears be silent, barely audible. Then shift: tell them you're grateful, that knowing them has been worth the heartbreak, but your voice fractures on the word 'grateful.' End by whispering goodbye—not because they're dying, but because you've finally decided to let go, to save yourself, and that feels like a different kind of death.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are experiencing an overwhelming physical sensation—perhaps the peak of passionate intimacy, or the moment of receiving devastating news that hits you like a physical blow, or sudden illness that brings you to your knees. Begin with your body reacting before your mind can process: breath catches, muscles seize, or surrender. Let physical sensation overtake you—don't perform it, EXPERIENCE it. Your voice emerges as raw sound: gasps, moans, half-words, your speech broken by the intensity of what your body feels. As the physical experience continues, it transforms: if it began as pain, let unexpected pleasure or release break through; if passion, let it crack open into vulnerable exposure or even grief. Speak through the physical experience—let words emerge that surprise you, things you didn't know you needed to say. By the end, your body has told you something your mind was afraid to know. Journey from pure physical reaction to emotionally-revealed truth spoken through the body.
inspired_by: Shyness Antidote: Public Speaking Fantasy Imaging

title: The Last Wave
instruction: You are a mother floating in the ocean with your young child at sunset. You've been treading water for a long time, waiting for rescue, and your arms are burning. Your daughter is scared, so you are faking contentment — humming little songs, splashing playfully, saying everything is fine. Your voice bobs up and down as your mouth dips underwater between words. You gasp and catch your breath mid-sentence. At first, you're all cheerful reassurance, but as you talk, you notice the sunset colors on the water and realize this might be your last peaceful moment together. Your fake contentment cracks into real, heart-wrenching gratitude — and you start crying while still trying to keep your voice light for her. Let your words be interrupted by splashes, gulps, and your own quiet sobs.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father in their kitchen—the same kitchen where you sat as a child waiting for them to notice you. Start with controlled fury, your voice tight: 'I need you to hear this. Just once, I need you to really hear me.' You list specific moments—the recital they missed, the night you called from college breaking down and they said they were busy, the way they'd light up for your sibling but look through you. Your anger is righteous, but midway through, it begins to crack. Your voice breaks not into tears but into something more devastating—the raw voice of the child you were, small and confused: 'Why wasn't I enough?' By the end, you're not yelling anymore. You're standing there, stripped bare, asking the question you've carried your whole life: 'Did you ever really see me?' The fury transforms into naked need, then finally into exhausted, grief-stricken acceptance that you might never get the answer you need.

title: You Don't Get to Hurt Them
instruction: Someone you fiercely love—a child, a younger sibling, a friend who trusted you—has been hurt, and you're confronting the person responsible. Start with rage: your voice is shaking but controlled, dangerously quiet. 'Do you know what they can do? Let me tell you.' Then launch into that euphoric description—but it's terrifying now. You're describing their miraculous qualities with the same wonder, but it's charged with protective fury. Your voice rises, becomes almost pleading: 'They draw these pictures and they're BRILLIANT and they showed you and you—' Then it collapses. The rage breaks into helplessness. Your voice cracks: 'I can't protect them from everything. I can't...' You're sobbing now, furious and powerless at once. End with your voice raw, desperate: 'They think the world is beautiful. They still think that. And you almost—' You can't finish. It's the devastation of fierce love meeting the limits of what you can shield them from.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who's Already Gone
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma—your lover, your closest friend, the person who knew you better than anyone—and the doctors have said it's time. You're holding their hand, and you need to say goodbye, but your voice barely works. Start with whispers that keep catching in your throat, words you planned that now seem impossible to say. Tell them the small things first—funny memories, ordinary moments—because the big things are too enormous. Your voice wavers between almost-normal and completely broken, like you're trying to be brave for them even though they can't hear you. As you move toward the real goodbye, your breathing changes; you're crying without sound, and the words come in fragments. There's a moment where you confess something you never said—'I knew, I always knew, and I loved you anyway'—and your voice is so tender it hurts. End with the simplest words, 'I release you,' barely audible, your voice simultaneously shattered and suffused with a love so vast it steadies you just enough to let them go.

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner in the darkness. You've been awake for hours, and you need to tell them something you've been hiding—something that could change everything between you. Begin in a whisper, your voice barely audible, testing each word before you release it. Your body is so tense you can barely breathe, and every syllable feels like stepping onto thin ice. As you confess, allow yourself to gradually soften, to let the relief of truth slowly untangle the knots in your chest. Your breathing should change, your voice should find a little more air, a little more space. End in a place of raw openness, where you've let yourself be completely seen for the first time, vulnerable but somehow lighter, waiting in the dark for their response.

title: Concoction Elaborate
instruction: You're making a potion for a friend—honey, vinegar, lemon, something unidentifiable. Your voice is theatrical, magical, like you're a witch. 'This needs intention.' You're genuinely trying to create something that might heal them. The concoction is ridiculous, but your voice is sincere. 'Drink this when you feel alone.' It won't cure anything, but the act of making it together, of ritual, of being cared for—that's the real concoction. Your voice is love disguised as magic.

title: Counting to Ten
instruction: You are in the middle of a scene with a partner, bent over their lap, about to receive a spanking. You've agreed to count each strike, but the first hit is sharper than you expected. Concentrate on keeping your voice steady and childlike, counting clearly, but as the rhythm continues, you feel a wave of helplessness wash over you—your breath catches, your pitch cracks on a count, and you end with a soft, surrendered whisper that admits you're losing control. Let your voice spike on the impact, then recover with a moan that blends pain and pleasure, and let your final words trail off as if the helplessness steals your breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are holding the hand of someone who raised you—a parent, grandparent, or guardian—as they lie dying. They have been holding on for days, and you suddenly realize they are waiting for your permission to let go. Begin in a state of desperate denial, insisting they will recover, reminding them of future plans you've made together. As you speak, allow yourself to feel the weight of what they need from you. Your emotional journey moves from frantic hope to the devastating, tender recognition that the greatest gift of love you can offer is release. End by giving them permission to leave, mixing gratitude for everything they were with the unbearable grief of saying goodbye. Let your voice soften from urgent to whispered, from pleading to blessing.

title: Sci-Fi: Soldier Realizes the War They've Been Fighting Is Based on False Intelligence
instruction: Receiving intelligence briefing. Your military voice is sharp and ready. Then you see the source analysis and realize—the enemy was fabricated. Your voice continues military response while your entire war becomes meaningless. Your breathing becomes confused. Everyone you've killed—killed for a lie. Your voice is the sound of moral ground collapsing. You must continue serving, but you've lost everything you thought you were serving. Your voice becomes someone living in permanent dissonance between function and morality.

title: The Pillow’s Promise
instruction: You are an elderly woman with chronic back pain, sitting on the edge of your bed, trying to get comfortable. You're talking on the phone to a friend who just sent you a new heating pad. Start with a sour, weary voice—complain about the ache, the sleepless nights, how you can't even turn over without a sharp pang. Mid-sentence, you shift and gasp, then catch yourself. Remember the gift. Let your voice soften with real gratitude, a small smile forming. End with a quiet hope: maybe tonight you'll sleep three hours straight. Let your words come haltingly, with sighs and tiny wincing breaths, but let the final sentence lift.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Call That Ended the Search
instruction: You are a father who has been frantic, sleepless, hunting for your missing child for three days. You just got a call — your child is safe. You are on your knees on the kitchen floor, phone still pressed to your ear, your whole body shaking. Start with a choked, nearly silent sob, the weight of all the terror and grief still crushing you. As you force out the words 'thank God,' your voice cracks, then slowly lifts — laughter and tears mixing — but deep sadness still clings to every breath. Let your words tumble out in broken, gasping sentences, then fade into a warm, exhausted whisper as you realize it's really over.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Concealing Knowledge
instruction: You know your best friend's partner is cheating. You're on a video call, and they're gushing about wedding plans. Your voice sounds normal, supportive, bright. But every word is a choice to lie. The strain builds silently. When they ask 'You're happy for me, right?'—your throat closes. You say yes, but it sounds like goodbye. Later, alone, your voice comes out strangled: 'I can't do this. I have to tell them.'

title: Softness Compassion
instruction: You're a hospice worker sitting with a patient who's actively dying. Your voice is soft, warm, full of compassion: 'You're safe. You're loved.' There's no hurry, no clinical distance. 'Your family is thinking of you right now.' Your voice is a physical comfort, like holding their hand. 'It's okay to let go. You don't have to hold on anymore.' The softness isn't weakness; it's strength channeled into pure compassion. You stay through their last breath, your voice the final thing they hear: 'Thank you for letting me be here with you.' The softness continues in the silence after. You sit with their body for an hour, weeping softly, your voice occasionally breaking into whispered prayers. The compassion is in every breath.

title: The Wall Hits
instruction: You're an older woman sitting alone in your car after a long meeting, the caffeine and sugar from that morning pastry suddenly crashing. You're leaving a voicemail for a friend, beginning with an irritable, resentful rant about the meeting's pointless arguments. As you speak, your voice slows, words drag, and you lose your train of thought. The irritation fades into a weary admission of how much your body aches—a dull, persistent pain you've been ignoring. Let your tone deflate, pause mid-sentence, then finish with a quiet, resigned sigh that acknowledges you're just exhausted.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Forgiveness in a Hospital Corridor
instruction: You're standing outside a hospital room, speaking in barely more than a whisper to someone who hurt you deeply years ago—a betrayal you thought you'd never forgive. They're dying, and you've come to say goodbye. Begin with words that feel rehearsed, mechanical, the forgiveness you think you should offer. But then something shifts. A memory surfaces—something small and tender you'd forgotten, a moment when they were kind, when they were human. Your voice should soften into something achingly genuine, almost a confession: you've been carrying this anger like armor, and now you're terrified to let it go because what if there's nothing underneath? Speak with the kind of tenderness that physically hurts, where every word feels like letting go of a piece of yourself.
inspired_by: Acting Brave to Encourage a Child

title: The Apology You'll Never Accept
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent who was never there for you, and they've just said the words you waited decades to hear: 'I'm sorry.' But instead of relief, you feel rage igniting. Start with that stunned silence, then let the anger pour out—all the birthdays they missed, the times you needed them and they chose something else. Your voice should crack with the violence of suppressed pain finally released. But halfway through your fury, you notice how small they look, how fragile. Your anger doesn't disappear, but something else enters: grief for the relationship you'll never have, for the parent they'll never be. End in a place between forgiveness and refusal, your voice shaking with the weight of loving someone who hurt you and knowing 'sorry' changes nothing and everything.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Prison
instruction: It's 4 AM and you're watching your six-year-old daughter sleep. In eight hours, you turn yourself in for a crime that will take you away for years. Your voice is barely audible, tender, each word a physical ache: 'Your hair still smells like the strawberry shampoo we used tonight.' You memorize her face, voice catching on details: 'The way your left eyebrow does that little... the freckle you got last summer.' Your whisper becomes even softer as you confess what she'll never hear: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.' You promise impossible things in a breaking voice: 'I'll be different when I come back. I'll be the father you...' But you can't finish. End in silence except for one sharp, suppressed sob you won't let yourself release fully because you might wake her.

title: The Legend We Became
instruction: You are whispering to your sleeping partner on your last night together before they leave for a dangerous mission they may not return from. Tell them the story of 'us'—how you met, the moment you knew, the life you imagined—but speak it as if it's already a legend, already in the past. Your voice should be barely audible, catching constantly in your throat, intimate as a prayer. Begin with tender nostalgia and gentle humor, remembering the small perfect moments. Gradually let grief seep in as you realize you're memorializing something that's still alive, still here in this bed beside you. End with a contradiction: speak of your future together with absolute conviction even as your voice breaks with the knowledge that this might be goodbye, finding strange comfort in the uncertainty, grateful for having had this at all.
inspired_by: The Elderly Storyteller and the Curious Child

title: Aftermath of the Storm
instruction: You've just survived something intense—a physical fight, passionate lovemaking, a moment of complete emotional breakdown, or shattering news. Your body is buzzing, hypersensitive, every nerve ending alive. Begin by touching yourself as if discovering your body is still intact, still here. Your breathing is ragged. As your hands move over your skin, sensations flood you—pleasure mixed with pain, relief mixed with shock, aliveness mixed with devastation. Let sounds pour out unfiltered—laughter that becomes sobbing, gasps that become moans. Your touch becomes more deliberate as you ground yourself back into your body. End with your hands pressed firmly against yourself, breath finally steadying, transformed from chaos into visceral, embodied survival.

title: The Last Sunset with Your Mother
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospice bed as golden hour light fills the room. She's awake and lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to make her smile by recounting a favorite childhood memory. But as she squeezes your hand weakly, the reality crashes over you and your voice begins to break. You oscillate between wanting to tell her everything you never said and just wanting to sit in silence, memorizing her face. End with a whispered confession of how terrified you are to live in a world without her, your voice raw and small, while simultaneously trying to give her permission to let go. The gratitude and the devastation must be inseparable.
inspired_by: Coming Down from MDMA: The Serotonin Crash

title: Fragile Strength
instruction: You are an elderly man in the midst of intimate sexual exertion with your partner. Fear drives you—fear that your aging body will fail, that you might hurt them, that you are not enough. Each thrust is a battle between wanting to be powerful and the tremor of doubt. Your breathing is locked to the rhythm, words coming out as broken, breathy commands or involuntary effort sounds. Start with tense, anxious control, each grunt laced with worry. Let the fear slowly transform into a raw, vulnerable tenderness as you feel your partner’s trust. End with a whisper of acceptance, breath slowing, the fear softening into fragile peace—a whispered 'I'm here.'
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Stole
instruction: You're finally saying the words you've rehearsed for twenty years, standing in your childhood kitchen. Start with your voice controlled, almost cold—you've prepared for this. Begin listing what she took: the safety, the innocence, the years you spent raising your siblings instead of being a child yourself. But as you speak, feel the control cracking. Your voice rises, becomes jagged with rage you didn't know you'd kept buried. Then something shifts—underneath the anger, hear the child you were, begging to know why you weren't enough, why she couldn't just love you. Let your voice break completely, oscillating between fury and desperate, raw need for her to acknowledge what she did. End with your breathing ragged, waiting for her to say something, anything, that makes this canyon between you crossable.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Cursed Being Realizes Breaking the Curse Requires Murdering Their Love

title: Dictating a Will on a Sinking Ship
instruction: The ship is going down and you're recording your last will on a waterproof device. Start with the formal legal language — 'I, being of sound mind...' — while water rises around you. The ship groans and tilts, making you stumble. Water splashes. Your composed legal voice becomes increasingly urgent, skipping formalities to get to what matters: who you love, what you regret. End with water at your chest, voice shaking, the last words swallowed by the sea.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your mother about a family secret she's kept for thirty years—something that has shaped your entire life without your knowing. Start from a place of controlled anger, the kind that's been rehearsed in your mind a thousand times, your voice sharp and accusing. But as you speak and she responds (imagine her responses), let the confrontation crack open something unexpected in you. Discover in real-time that beneath your rage is a terrified child who just needed to be protected. Allow your voice to break, to become younger, more vulnerable. End in a place of raw need rather than accusation—the adult facade completely stripped away, revealing the hurt child still living inside you.

title: The Mirror Breaks
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just revealed they're walking away from everything you built together—the family business, the legacy, the path you imagined. Start in betrayal and anger, ready to fight. But as you argue, they do something unexpected: they tell you, clearly and honestly, what they've always admired about you, the ways you've shaped them, the gifts you've given them they'll carry forever—even as they choose their own path. Let their genuine recognition of your worth clash with your fury. Feel the dissonance. Slowly, let something crack open. Move from righteous rage to a painful, reluctant understanding that loving someone means seeing who they truly are, not who you need them to be. End in a raw mixture of hurt and hard-won respect.

title: Laughing Through Your Mentor's Last Lesson
instruction: Your dying mentor is telling you one final story—something absurd and profound—and you're caught between grief and the irresistible humor that made you love them. Begin with genuine laughter, almost surprised it can still come: 'You're really telling this story now? Now?' Your voice dances between amusement and disbelief. But the laughter keeps catching on tears you're trying to suppress. You're holding their hand, and every chuckle is also a sob you're swallowing. The story gets funnier even as the moment gets more unbearable—you're laughing harder, but crying too, the sounds blending until you can't tell them apart: 'Stop, you're killing me... oh god, that's not...' Your voice breaks into something beautiful and terrible. By the end, you're thanking them through laughter-tears, finding perfect gratitude in perfect loss, your voice carrying both the joy of having known them and the devastation of goodbye, somehow holding both truths simultaneously without diminishing either.

title: The Barefoot Breaking Point
instruction: You're standing barefoot on cold tile after discovering a betrayal—a text message, a letter, evidence of something that shatters you. Begin in shock, your body rigid. Let your attention move freely across physical sensations: the cold floor burning your feet, the trembling in your hands, the weight of air in your lungs, the taste in your mouth. Don't force emotional progression; instead, allow images to surface from these physical experiences—memories of trust, moments of intimacy, images of the betrayer, sensations of past pain or pleasure. Your body and voice will shift as these uncontrolled associations arise. Let rage, grief, numbness, or unexpected tenderness emerge organically. End somewhere your body takes you—perhaps collapsed, perhaps frighteningly calm, perhaps in motion you didn't plan.

title: The Weight of Wonder
instruction: You're a child in your late 20s living with a chronic back condition, sitting on a park bench. Your new crush just sat down across from you, smiling. You want to talk, but every time you shift to lean forward, a sharp twinge makes you wince and breathe in through your teeth. Start with an attempt to hide the pain—your voice tight and careful—but as they speak, you forget yourself for a moment, and a wave of relief washes over you. End with a soft, contemplative sigh, your voice looser, almost dreamy, as you realize how good this feels despite the ache.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Relief (extremely present), Contemplation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Vigil Whispers
instruction: You're sitting beside your best friend's hospital bed at 3 AM. They're unconscious, machines breathing for them, and you know they can't hear you—but you need to say it anyway. Whisper your confession: that you've been in love with them for years, that you never said anything because you were terrified of losing the friendship, that you'd give anything for one more ordinary Tuesday of coffee and complaints. Your voice should be barely audible, catching on words, pausing when emotion threatens to break through. Let silence do the work between phrases. Include a moment where you almost laugh remembering something stupid you did together, but it dissolves into a sound that's half-sob, half-breath. End with the devastating gentleness of touching their hand and saying goodbye to someone who's already gone.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: Your parent is dying, and they've asked you to promise you'll take care of your sibling who broke you. You start gentle, holding their hand, wanting to give them peace. 'I can't promise that.' Your voice catches—not from anger, but from the impossibility of it. They're fading, and you're watching them go, and part of you wants to lie, to give them this one last gift. But you can't. The words come softer, breaking: 'I love you too much to lie to you now.' You're crying, but you're also free. You kiss their forehead. You're granting them a different permission—to let go without false promises. Your grief is enormous, but so is your integrity.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut recording your final message to Earth before embarking on a one-way mission to save the colony on Mars. You begin with forced optimism, reassuring your family that this is what you were born to do, your voice steady and rehearsed. But as you speak their names—your daughter's, your partner's—the facade starts crumbling. The words 'I won't see you grow up' catch in your throat. By the end, you're whispering the things you need them to remember about you, your voice raw and breaking, no longer the heroic explorer but just someone saying goodbye to everything they love. The transformation is from manufactured courage to devastating, tender honesty.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that defined your childhood. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, adult, controlled. But as you speak, decades of unmet needs begin flooding through. Your voice rises, cracks, becomes the voice of the child you once were, demanding to know why you were never enough. Then, seeing them diminish before you, something shifts. The anger collapses into grief—not for what you'll never have, but for what they never learned to give. End with a question asked in a voice so quiet it's almost tender: 'Did anyone ever teach you how to love?' Let the confrontation transform into heartbreaking understanding.

title: First Light Gravel
instruction: You're an elderly man waking at dawn. You sit on the edge of the bed, throat dry, voice cracked. First you're amused as you watch your cat knock a cup off the nightstand – a small chuckle escapes. Then a wave of disappointment hits as you remember the fishing trip you had to cancel yesterday, and you rub your face, muttering. Finally, you look out the window as the sun breaks through the clouds – a deep, silent awe seeps in, and your voice softens, almost breaking, as you whisper to no one: 'Look at that...' Let your gravelly morning voice warm up naturally through the arc – start with low fry and amusement, dip to tired disappointment, then lift into hushed wonder. Include natural pauses, a cough, or a stretch.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (clearly present), Disappointment (clearly present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Lull Between Waves
instruction: You are a woman in labor at home, waiting for your partner to grab the hospital bag. Between contractions, you speak to your sister on the phone, starting with amusement as you laugh at her frantic instructions. Your tone is light, warm, but distracted—you shift your weight, catch your breath. Then a contraction crests: your voice tightens, you groan, you breathe heavily through it, your words fragment. As the wave passes, you exhale, smile again, and finish the thought with weary humor. Let the pain pull you in and out of coherence, your amusement flickering through the struggle.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Perfect Cup That Hurts
instruction: You are curled up on your couch, nursing a toothache that has been throbbing for days. A friend just handed you a warm mug of herbal tea, and you want to thank them, but every word is a careful negotiation. You start by smiling gratefully, the warmth spreading through you, but the contentment is guarded—your lips barely part, your jaw stays tight. As you speak, you savor the comfort of the moment, but a shift in pressure makes you wince mid-sentence. By the end, the peacefulness fades into a quiet admission of pain, your voice softening as you surrender to the ache.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Betrayal in the Rain
instruction: You've just discovered your business partner has been embezzling from the company you built together—your dream, your financial security, your trust. You confront them in a parking garage as rain hammers the concrete. You start with cold, controlled fury—each word precise, cutting, lawyer-like. But as they make excuses, your control shatters. Your voice rises to a roar that echoes off the concrete walls. You're shouting over them, listing everything you sacrificed, every time you covered for them. Then suddenly—mid-rage—you realize you're not just angry. You're devastated. Your voice cracks and you're nearly sobbing, because you trusted them like family. The explosive anger collapses into something vulnerable and broken: 'How could you do this to me?' But then they say something dismissive, something that minimizes your pain, and a different kind of rage surfaces—protective, almost fierce—as you realize you're done grieving this relationship. End with you walking away through the rain, your voice shaking but final, knowing you'll never speak to them again.
inspired_by: Three Drinks Deep in an Ex's Kitchen

title: Rage Against the Dying of the Light
instruction: You've just received news that will change everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a loss—and you've come to this beach to fall apart. Start by trying to describe the peaceful scene, but let fury immediately fracture your words. The sand feels like it's burning, the waves sound violent and mocking. Let your voice escalate into raw, almost primal rage—screaming at the indifference of beauty, at how dare this place remain peaceful when your world is ending. Pound the sand, curse the waves. Then let the rage shatter completely into sobbing helplessness, your voice breaking into barely coherent fragments as you collapse from fury into grief, from feeling everything to feeling utterly powerless.

title: Upside-Down Plea
instruction: You are an older woman stuck in a handstand against a wall, your throat strained and voice thick as blood rushes to your head. Your granddaughter is about to walk into a dangerous situation, and you need to call out for help — but every word gurgles and slurs. Start with raw, panicked fear as you try to shout, but realize your voice is failing you. Over the next few seconds, struggle against the physical distortion, feeling the fear mix with frustration and then a desperate, quiet acceptance as you find a way to make yourself understood despite the gargling. Let your voice crack, swallow, and pulse with effort as you push through the compromised physiology.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Fantasy: Warrior Chooses Peace Over Victory
instruction: On the battlefield, victory is within reach. Your warrior voice is fierce and certain. Then you see the cost—endless more death. Your voice shifts mid-battle to offering peace. Your soldiers are confused; your voice is ordering them to stand down. Your breathing becomes the breathing of someone choosing something larger than winning. Your voice is mutiny against your own rage. You're choosing peace while violence roars around you. Your voice becomes the sound of choosing to be defeated rather than continue destroying. Your victory dies so killing can stop.

title: Confronting Your Dying Parent About the Childhood They Never Gave You
instruction: You're sitting by your parent's hospital bed, and after years of silence, the words finally come. Start with controlled anger—measured, careful accusations about the neglect, the absence, the pain they caused. But as you see their frail body, your rage begins to crack. The fury transforms into something more complex: grief for the relationship you never had, unexpected tenderness for the broken person before you, and anger at yourself for still caring. By the end, you're not sure if you're forgiving them or mourning the parent you needed them to be. Your voice should break in unexpected places—mid-accusation, during a memory, when you realize they're too weak to even defend themselves.
inspired_by: Therapist Hearing Themselves in a Patient's Story

title: 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's three in the morning, and you're lying in bed next to your partner who you believe is asleep. Begin by simply feeling the actual darkness around you, the weight of the blanket, the sound of their breathing. Let the real quiet and stillness of the room lead you into the safety of imagined privacy - they're asleep, you can speak without consequence. Start whispering a small truth you've never said aloud, something harmless. Let each whispered word embolden you to go deeper, confessing progressively more vulnerable truths: your fears, your secret shame, the way you really feel about the life you've built together, the part of yourself you keep hidden. Build from tentative half-thoughts to a full, breathless outpouring of everything you can never say when they're awake. End with the devastating realization that maybe you want them to be hearing this, that maybe you've known all along they weren't really sleeping.

title: Historical: Berlin Wall Communicant Realizes the Guard Is Their Sister
instruction: Morning, Eastern side of the Wall. You're planning escape. Then the guard shifts—you recognize your sister. Stationed on the opposite side for five years. Your voice drops to barely a whisper, speaking through the fence. Her voice is uncertain, also barely there. You're siblings separated by concrete and ideology. Your breathing is controlled fear mixed with overwhelming recognition. Neither of you can move, but both can speak. The silence between words is the Wall itself.

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You are giving a toast at a wedding—but it's for your ex-lover who is marrying someone else, or your child who is making a terrible mistake, or your best friend who is leaving your life behind. You must appear joyful and celebratory. Begin with the performance of happiness—big smile, champagne raised, loving words. But underneath, contradictory feelings are roiling. As you speak, let the truth leak through in ways you don't plan: a tremor in your voice you can't control, a genuine laugh breaking through your bitterness, unexpected tears of real joy mixed with grief, anger sharpening a word, love softening your face despite yourself. Follow each authentic impulse as it arises—the urge to break character and say what you really feel, or to mean the kind words more than you expected, or to find genuine celebration alongside your loss. Let the performance and the truth fight for control. End in a complex emotional place where multiple feelings coexist: perhaps bitter joy, loving rage, grateful devastation, or hopeful grief. The toast should be simultaneously real and false, generous and selfish, a goodbye and a blessing.
inspired_by: Strengthening Intuition and Learning from It

title: The Eruption: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You've just learned that someone you're fiercely protective of - a child, a sibling, a student - is in danger that you're powerless to prevent. They're making a choice that will harm them, or someone is threatening them and you can't stop it. Start speaking to them (or about them) with controlled urgency, trying to reason, to convince, your voice tight with barely restrained panic. Let that control shatter - build to raw, explosive desperation, your voice rising, breaking, words tumbling over each other. Then suddenly collapse into something else: helplessness, grief, maybe even anger at yourself for not being able to protect them. End in a place of broken tenderness - whispering that you love them, that you'd do anything, but knowing it's not enough. Take yourself through the full storm.
inspired_by: Acting Interested While Bored in a Conversation

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission, recording a final message to your child back on Earth. You won't see them grow up. Start with forced cheerfulness, telling them about the stars, trying to be brave for them. But as you describe what you're seeing out here in the infinite dark, your voice begins to fracture. 'I wish I could hold you one more time,' slips out before you can stop it. The grief crashes through your carefully maintained composure. Yet by the end, you find something—not peace, but a fierce, protective love that transcends the distance. 'You're going to do beautiful things,' you whisper, and you mean it with every fiber of your being, even as your heart shatters.

title: The Hollow Ritual
instruction: You are an older man alone in a dim bedroom, late at night. You begin masturbating out of habit, your voice flat and mechanical as you whisper a fantasy you've used for years. But as your body responds, doubt intrudes — a pause, a ragged breath, a murmured 'Is this still what I want?' The numbness of the routine cracks, replaced by a gnawing uncertainty that grows with each touch. Your voice becomes fragmented, vulnerable, the words barely audible as you question your own desire, until you finally stop, breathing heavily in the silence.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Doubt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Authority
instruction: You are a senior supervisor pulling aside a junior employee after a project failure. You stand with hands on hips, elbows out, chest puffed—trying to fill the room with authority. Your voice starts loud and probing, full of sharp interest in what went wrong. But halfway through your questioning, you realize the mistake was your own. The shame hits you like a wave. Your hands fall from your hips, your voice drops, and you stumble through a quiet confession. Let the shift be physical—your posture collapsing, your breath catching. Speak as if you're suddenly seeing yourself from the outside, embarrassed by the pose you were just holding.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Laughter at the Memorial
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who would have hated a somber funeral. Start by telling a ridiculous story about them that makes you genuinely laugh—let that laughter be real and full. But even as you're laughing, let us hear the grief underneath. Your voice should shimmer between joy at the memory and devastation that there will be no more memories. Tell funny stories while your voice cracks. Laugh while tears choke you. Express gratitude for having known them while your heart shatters that they're gone. The challenge is to hold both emotions simultaneously without letting either overwhelm the other—to be genuinely amused and genuinely destroyed at the same time. End with a sentence that could be taken as either funny or heartbreaking, your tone making it both. This is the complexity of real grief: we don't feel one thing at a time.

title: Protecting What You Cannot Save
instruction: You're a parent bathing your terminally ill child one last time, now wrapping them in a towel with unbearable gentleness. Start speaking with fierce, protective love—describing every careful motion, every soft touch, pouring all your devotion into making them comfortable. But let helplessness and rage crash through in waves: fury at the universe for this injustice, desperation to fight what cannot be fought. Your voice should oscillate between tender whispers and choked, barely-contained howls of protest. Let your words become promises you can't keep, apologies for failing to protect them, then collapse back into pure love. End in a place of broken surrender, still gentle but utterly devastated, knowing that all you can offer is this moment of warmth.
inspired_by: Wrapping Yourself in a Towel After a Shower

title: Inherited Obsession
instruction: You're confronting your parent in their cluttered home laboratory, surrounded by decades of failed experiments and broken promises. Start with bitter sarcasm as you mock their 'groundbreaking work,' your voice sharp with years of resentment over missed birthdays and lonely nights. But as your parent tries to explain—really explain—why this work consumed them, something shifts. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it becomes tangled with unwanted understanding, even reluctant compassion. You hate that you see yourself in their obsession, that you've inherited this same destructive focus. End torn between the child who needed them and the adult who finally, devastatingly, understands them. Your voice should move from cutting to cracking, from accusation to painful recognition.

title: Vagueness Uncertainty
instruction: You're a parent trying to explain something scary to your child, but you don't know how to tell them the truth. Your voice becomes vague, uncertain: 'Daddy's going to... be away for a while.' The vagueness isn't evasion; it's your own uncertainty bleeding through. 'It's not your fault. It's just... adult things.' You can hear yourself avoiding clarity, and it's breaking your voice. 'Everything's going to be... I don't know, sweetheart. I don't know.' The uncertainty is worse than certainty because your child hears it. They ask: 'Are you leaving forever?' And you have to choose between vague kindness and harsh truth. 'I don't know yet' is the answer you give, and it's the most honest thing you've said.

title: Gasping for You
instruction: You are an older adult doing box jumps in a home gym. This is your third set, your legs are burning, and your focus is intense — every rep demands every ounce of concentration to land steady. But across the room, someone you've been intensely but secretly lusting after just walked in, undressing you with their eyes. You're not supposed to stop; the workout is your alibi. As you jump, you try to speak between gasps and landings, your words chopped by each exertion. Your voice starts tight and breathless with effort, but as you steal glances, it grows thick with a raw, almost vulnerable desire. The final words tumble out on a landing, shaky and full of longing.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Interest (very intensely present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Voicing a Farewell Message While Overwhelmed With Gratitude and Grief
instruction: Your voice acting career is ending due to a progressive condition that will take your voice within months. You're recording a farewell message to your fans, your characters, the community that's been your family. But here's the paradox: you've never been happier. You've never felt more grateful. Start with genuine joy—maybe even laughter—as you thank them for letting you be a thousand different people, for loving the characters you brought to life. Let yourself feel the fullness of that blessing even as tears start to fall. The grief and gratitude become indistinguishable. You're laughing and crying at once, celebrating and mourning, finding peace in the losing. When you say 'This voice has had the most beautiful life,' your throat catches but there's a smile in it too. End in the strange, transcendent space where acceptance and heartbreak are the same thing, where you can mean both 'thank you' and 'goodbye' with your whole, breaking, grateful heart.
inspired_by: Voice Actor Recording a Death Scene of Their Own Character

title: Newscaster Breaking Their Own Story
instruction: You're a news anchor and the breaking story is about you — a scandal, a secret, something personal that's been leaked. Read the teleprompter in your news voice while the words describe your own life. The disconnect between the polished delivery and the personal devastation should be uncanny. Include the moment the camera catches a reaction — a blink too long, a swallow, a pause filled with an entire career ending in real-time. Resume reading. The show must go on.

title: Teaching Yourself to Float After the Divorce
instruction: You're alone in the lake for the first time since the divorce, finally attempting what your ex always said you couldn't do: float on your back without fear. Start with nervous laughter as you describe lying back, the absurdity of learning this at your age, the water cold against your neck. But as you begin to float, really float, something ridiculous and beautiful happens—you're crying and laughing at the same time. 'I'm doing it, I'm actually—' and your voice breaks with joy and grief tangled together. You're free and completely alone. You're terrified and exhilarated. Thank the water for holding you, but your gratitude is soaked in sadness for all the years you didn't believe you could. End with your voice trembling between celebration and heartbreak, finding peace in the contradiction of feeling whole while completely broken.
inspired_by: Floating on Your Back in a Calm Lake

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally speaking the truth you've carried for decades to a parent who was physically present but emotionally absent. Start with measured, almost careful words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay composed. Describe specific moments: the school play they missed, the night you needed them and they were somewhere else, the coldness you learned to mistake for love. As you speak, let your control begin to fracture. Your voice should shift from controlled explanation to raw accusation, then crack into the vulnerable child still inside you who just wanted to be seen. End with a question that's part plea, part demand: a need to know if they ever really loved you, asked with such naked vulnerability it hurts to hear.
inspired_by: Feeling the First Gentle Snowflakes Land on Your Face

title: The Last Handshake
instruction: You're a retired mob enforcer meeting your replacement in a dimly lit bar. He thinks you're passing a relic, but you've planted a bomb in the briefcase you're giving him. Your voice is flat, slow, almost friendly — you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, a flicker of real fear crosses your face: he's young, trusting, and you're about to destroy him. Start with cold satisfaction, then let the quiet devastation of what you're doing seep into your tone as you realize you've become the monster you hated.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Canvas
instruction: You're an elderly artist painting your final work, knowing you won't finish another. Begin with quiet, meditative focus: 'The light is perfect today.' Your hands shake slightly but your voice holds steady determination. As you paint, memories flood in—lovers, losses, triumphs—and your voice begins to crack with the weight of a lifetime: 'Every color I've ever mixed leads to this moment.' By the end, you step back and realize this piece holds everything you ever wanted to say but couldn't. Your final words—'I'm ready now. This is enough.'—carry both profound peace and the ache of goodbye. Let tears come naturally if they do, but don't force them. This is about finishing your life's sentence.

title: The Hollow Watch
instruction: You are an older, rugged man who hasn't slept in over a day, sitting in a hospital waiting room after your wife's emergency surgery. Your back is killing you from the hard plastic chair—each shift sends a spike of pain through your spine. You're talking to a nurse who just brought you coffee, but your words come out slow and slurred, with gaps where you blank out mid-sentence. Start with a gruff attempt at gratitude (pain in your voice), then let the exhaustion and helplessness seep in as you realize you can't control anything. End with a quiet admission of your fear, spoken almost to yourself, interrupted by a yawn.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Speech No One Wants to Hear
instruction: You're in a fluorescent-lit break room, chin pressed to your chest, staring at a coffee stain on the tile. You have to admit to a small, embarrassing mistake at work—you accidentally deleted a crucial file everyone else relied on. As you speak, a bitter sourness coats your tongue from the regret. But then, you remember: you spent all night rebuilding it from scratch, and it's actually better now. A tiny, weary triumph rises in your throat. Let your voice start creaky and ashamed, barely above a mumble, with pauses where you lose your nerve. As you recall the late-night fix, your voice gains a faint, gravelly warmth—still tired, but no longer defeated.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present), Triumph (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Words You Never Practiced
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. You've rehearsed what you'd say a thousand times in your head over the past week, but now that the moment is here, none of those words feel right. Begin with careful, almost formal attempts to say the 'right' thing—then let yourself abandon the script entirely. Let memories flood through you without planning them: that time you stole candy together, the secret you swore you'd never tell, the way they laughed. Your voice should shift from controlled and 'appropriate' to raw and completely unguarded. End in a place of unexpected peace—not acceptance, but something simpler: just being present with them, perhaps even laughing through tears at something ridiculous only the two of you would understand.
inspired_by: Actor has been cast in a major role and has weeks before rehearsal begins

title: Tiny General
instruction: You are a six-year-old girl in the backyard, absolutely determined to teach your imaginary army of stuffed animals the proper way to stand at attention. You start with intense concentration—hands on hips, elbows locked, voice louder and more commanding than your small frame suggests. Then you notice a loose toy soldier has flopped over, so your focus shifts to a mix of frustration and fierce resolve as you march over to fix it, your voice softening for a second before snapping back to command mode. Speak as a child who is deeply serious about this mission, letting your pitch rise and fall naturally as you shout orders and mutter corrections.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Mended Watch
instruction: You are an elderly man at a family dinner, seated apart, carefully repairing an old pocket watch while others celebrate your grandson's promotion. You are trying to concentrate on the tiny gears, but every compliment he receives makes your jaw tighten. Start by muttering to yourself about the watch's delicate spring, your voice controlled and focused, but as a laugh erupts from the table, your words turn clipped, bitter—a hollow 'good for him' slips out before you fall silent. Then, without looking up, you force yourself to speak again, this time with a fragile, weary finality, as if realizing the envy has drained you. Let your hands pause mid-motion, adjust your glasses, and let the last sentence trail off into the clatter of silverware.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Coffee
instruction: You're sitting across from your partner of thirty years at your kitchen table, the morning after receiving a terminal diagnosis. This is your last ordinary morning together before everything changes. Begin by fully experiencing the sensory details around you: the weight and warmth of the coffee mug in your hands, the specific bitter-sweet taste on your tongue, the sound of their breathing across the table, the morning light coming through the window hitting their face in that familiar way. Start in a state of forced normalcy, trying to pretend this is just another morning. As you build each sensory detail more vividly—the steam rising from the cup, the worn smoothness of the table under your fingertips, their particular scent—let the crushing weight of 'this is the last time' break through your composure. End in a place where you can no longer maintain the pretense, where every small detail becomes unbearably precious and painful.

title: The All-Nighter's Reward
instruction: You're a teenage boy who has stayed awake for 24 hours straight to finish a massive gaming tournament with friends. It's now 6 AM, and you're in your dark bedroom, slumped in your chair, speaking to a teammate on a voice call. You feel a deep, exhausted contentment — the tournament is over, you won, but your body is shutting down. Your words start clear and proud, but as you talk, yawns cut through your sentences, your tongue gets heavy, and you blank out for micro-moments. The emotion arcs from excited, sleepy pride into a weary, peaceful haze where you're barely holding onto the thought, trailing off mid-word before mumbling the rest.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Scream That Becomes a Sob
instruction: You've just received news that someone you love is in immediate danger—arrested, injured, missing—and you're powerless to help them. Start with explosive rage, shouting at whoever delivered the news, at the situation, at God, at the universe. Your voice should be fierce, almost feral, demanding answers and solutions. But mid-fury, let the helplessness crash over you. The rage should collapse into gasping, choking sobs as you realize there's nothing you can do. Bargain desperately, offer anything—your own life, your savings, your future—just to save them. End in a place of broken, animal grief mixed with fierce, protective love.
