Let your voice move from thunder to whisper, from accusations to broken prayers.
inspired_by: Acting Unaffected When Overhearing Gossip About Yourself

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother or father about failing to protect you from abuse when you were a child. Begin with careful, measured words—you've practiced this, your voice controlled but tight. 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' As you speak the truth aloud for the first time, anger surges through you, your voice rising, cracking with decades of suppressed rage. 'Where were you? Where the hell were you?' But then you see their face—their denial, their weakness, their own brokenness—and rage collapses into something more complicated. Grief. Pity. Exhaustion. Your voice becomes quieter, sadder: 'I needed you to be stronger than you were.' End not with forgiveness or reconciliation, but with weary acceptance and the recognition that you survived despite them, your voice carrying both profound disappointment and hard-won self-reliance.

title: Reading Your Childhood Diary in Your Old Bedroom Before the Wedding
instruction: You're getting married tomorrow. You've come back to your childhood bedroom in your parents' house and found your old diary from age ten, from the year your parents divorced. Sit where you used to sit—on the bed, on the floor, at the small desk—feel the space around you exactly as it was. Begin reading entries aloud in your adult voice but let your ten-year-old self's words break your heart. That child was so hopeful, so imaginative, so convinced everything would be okay. You played elaborate games in this room, created whole worlds, felt invincible. As you read, let yourself feel profound gratitude for that resilient child, deep grief for what they had to endure, and strange hope that maybe you're finally giving them the happy ending they dreamed about. Let your voice move between adult wisdom and childlike wonder. End by speaking directly to your younger self, making a promise about the life you're about to begin.

title: The Wedding Morning Phone Call
instruction: It's your wedding morning (or your child's, or your best friend's). You're alone, calling someone who won't be there - a dead parent, an estranged sibling, a former love. Begin with joy, excitement, wanting to share this perfect moment. Describe the dress, the flowers, how happy you are. But as you talk to this absent person, let the grief of their absence start bleeding through the joy. Don't choose between happiness and sorrow - hold both. Laugh through tears. Express gratitude tangled with resentment. Tell them you're angry they're missing this AND that you understand why. Let contradictory feelings exist simultaneously: 'I'm so happy but I hate that you're not here. I forgive you but I'm still furious. This is the best day of my life and it's breaking my heart.' Don't resolve the contradictions. Let your voice embody the gorgeous, painful mess of loving someone while carrying unfinished business with them. End in complex peace - not happy, not sad, but fully, messily human.

title: The Weight of Hope
instruction: You are a young woman carrying a heavy box of belongings through a long, dusty road. You're moving them for someone you're infatuated with, but you know they don't feel the same—shame burns in your chest. Start by trying to keep your voice light and breathy, almost a little giddy, as if the weight doesn't matter. But as each step grinds on, let the strain creep in—your words become more clipped, your breath shorter, and the sadness you've been hiding spills out between gasps. By the end, you're barely speaking, voice cracking with exhaustion and sorrow, the infatuation gone, just the raw ache of shame and heartbreak. Your speech should be interrupted by heavy footsteps, grunts, and moments where you lose your train of thought because you're just so tired.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Shame (very intensely present), Sadness (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Truth
instruction: You're confronting your mother while she continues washing dishes, refusing to stop and face you. You came here angry, ready to finally say what you've never said about how she made you feel invisible growing up. But as you speak, her hands start shaking in the dishwater. Your anger keeps breaking apart—you stammer, your voice cracks in unexpected places, you suddenly notice how old her hands look, you lose your momentum and have to rebuild it. She says something small and deflecting, and you laugh bitterly, then almost apologetically. The words come out jagged, not eloquent. By the end, you're both just standing there, and somehow your anger has dissolved into something more complicated—maybe recognition that she's just a person who failed, not a villain. Maybe forgiveness you didn't plan to offer. The shift is from righteous fury to unwanted empathy.
inspired_by: Actor's scene work is good but polished and predictable — missing genuine organic reality

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy Who Saved Your Life
instruction: Someone who destroyed your family, who you've hated for years, just threw themselves in front of a bullet meant for you. Now you're holding them as they die, and they're trying to explain why—maybe they've always loved you, maybe they were trying to atone, maybe they were protecting someone else. Start with shock and rage: 'Why would you do this? I don't want this!' Your voice furious because now you can't hate them purely anymore. Let that fury crack into confusion, desperation as you realize they're actually dying in your arms. Beg them not to die even though you've wanted them dead—because this version is too complicated, too human. End with a fierce, broken tenderness you didn't know you had for them, cradling them, whispering forgiveness you never thought you'd give, weeping for the enemy you loved and hated in equal measure.
inspired_by: Time Traveler Warning Themselves Not to Go

title: Numbed Revelation
instruction: You're a young man just back from the dentist, standing in front of a bathroom mirror. Your entire face is still frozen from Novocaine—you can barely feel your lips, and every time you try to say a B or P it comes out sloppy. You catch your reflection and are genuinely astonished at how ridiculous you look: one side of your mouth hangs slack, a little drool escapes. You start talking to yourself, trying to shape words, and the surprise slowly shifts into a bemused, resigned chuckle as you realize you can't even form a proper 'butterfly'—the word comes out 'uhtterfly.' The arc goes from wide-eyed shock at your own appearance to a rueful, self-deprecating laugh as you accept the absurdity.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Telling Your Best Friend You Need Space
instruction: Your voice is sad but firm: 'I need a break from us.' They're confused and hurt, your voice becomes explanatory. 'It's not you, I just...' realizing that's a lie—'Actually it's partly you, I feel suffocated.' Your voice cracks because you love them. They push and you repeat the boundary.

title: Laughing Through the Mutiny of the Heart
instruction: You are a ship's officer who has just discovered your crew—people you loved like family—have betrayed you, but instead of rage, you find yourself laughing. Begin with genuine, almost hysterical laughter at the beautiful irony: you were about to sacrifice everything for them, and they were planning to throw you overboard. Your voice should carry both amusement and shattering heartbreak simultaneously. As you speak, let the laughter become tears without stopping the laughter—you're genuinely grateful for the love you felt, even as it destroys you. Express appreciation for the beautiful moments mixed with the agony of betrayal. Your voice should crack between chuckles and sobs, finding strange peace in the chaos. End in a moment of transcendent acceptance, still half-laughing, half-crying, as you realize the love was real even if the loyalty wasn't—and somehow, impossibly, that's enough.
inspired_by: The Pirate Captain and the Mutinous First Mate

title: The Crumpled Note
instruction: You are an older woman hosting a nostalgic podcast from your home studio. You begin with your practiced, warm, close-mic host voice — intimate but polished — reading a script about childhood memories. Mid-sentence, you notice a crumpled note you wrote to yourself last night, left on the edge of your desk. You trail off, pick it up, and the scripted words fade. What follows is a real, unguarded moment: you read the note aloud, then slowly set it down, letting the silence stretch as a genuine contemplation washes over you. Your voice loses its performative gloss — becomes breathy, slower, more accidental — with small pauses where you lose your train of thought, clear your throat, or shift in your chair. The emotion shifts from controlled intimacy to spontaneous, vulnerable reflection.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Table That Kept Score
instruction: You are a boy, around ten years old, standing in the kitchen doorway. Your father sits at the table, his back to you, reading a newspaper. For years, he has dismissed you, called you soft, laughed at your drawings. But today, you found your old sketchbook—he had torn every page, secretly, and you saw him do it on the hidden camera you set up. Your voice must start cold, eerily calm, each word landing like a quiet hammer. You feel the relief of finally having proof, the longing for him to see you, to admit he was wrong. As you speak, you realize he will never change, and your voice cracks with a longing you didn't expect—then hardens again into the same measured, deliberate ice. You might fidget with the corner of the sketchbook, look down, then force yourself to meet his eyes. You begin, 'I have something to show you, Dad. I found it this morning...'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Waking from an Endless Dream
instruction: Youre describing the moment of waking up after years in a dream. Speak slowly, as though piecing reality together, with each sentence carrying surprise, fear, and relief as you recognize the real world.

title: Whispering to the Stillborn
instruction: You're alone in a hospital room, holding your baby who never took a breath. Begin speaking in the softest whisper, introducing yourself as their mother, telling them about the room you painted, the name you chose. Your voice is unbearably tender, almost singing. You describe what you wanted to show them—autumn leaves, the ocean, your grandmother's face. Each image catches in your throat. The whispers become more fragmented, interrupted by silences where you're just breathing with them, or trying to. You apologize for things that aren't your fault, make promises to a future that won't exist. End with the quietest possible 'goodbye,' barely vocalized, more breath than sound, and then silence that holds everything you can't say.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your father across the kitchen table where you ate breakfast as a child. Start with contained, careful anger—you've rehearsed these words for years. But as you lay out your grievances (the times he wasn't there, the coldness, the criticism), notice how your voice begins to tremble not just with anger but with the abandoned child still inside you, desperate for his approval. Let your accusations gradually reveal the deeper truth: you're not just angry, you're heartbroken. Transform from prosecutor to wounded son/daughter. By the end, let the anger dissolve into something more devastating—a quiet plea, almost a whisper: 'Did you ever actually love me?' Feel the terrifying vulnerability of finally asking the question you've avoided your whole life.

title: The Fevered Memory
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in a dim, sweltering room, burning with a high fever. You shiver and sweat, your lips cracked, the ceiling fan casting drunken shadows. You recall a face you were infatuated with decades ago—a lover or a fleeting crush. As you murmur to that phantom, a sharp, throbbing pain from your joints drags you back, and you start to doubt whether the memory was ever real. Let your voice waver and crack, sometimes losing the thought, then finding it again. Let the infatuation soften into a quiet, pained acceptance by the end.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (extremely present), Doubt (extremely present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child the Truth You Can Never Say Aloud
instruction: It's 2 AM and your child is finally asleep after months of illness. You sit beside their bed in the dark, and the words you've held back for so long spill out in whispers they'll never hear. You confess your terror, how you research their condition obsessively at 3 AM, how you've bargained with gods you don't believe in. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking. You tell them about the future you've imagined for them—college, falling in love, growing old—and how the possibility of losing them has made you understand a love so fierce it physically hurts. You apologize for the times you were impatient, for every moment you didn't cherish. End with a gentle, aching gratitude for every breath they take, every morning you get to see them again. Let the silence between words carry as much weight as the words themselves.
inspired_by: Blind Date Where Both People Are Catfish

title: The Proof You've Been Carrying
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or child) about something that has remained unspoken for years—a betrayal, an abandonment, a lie that shaped your life. In your pocket, you carry physical proof: a letter they never sent, a photograph that tells the truth, a document they thought was destroyed. Begin the confrontation trying to remain controlled, your hand occasionally touching your pocket, drawing strength from what you know you possess. As they deny or deflect, your certainty grows—not from anger alone, but from the solid reality of evidence against their words. Let your emotional state shift from trembling uncertainty to unshakeable conviction. When you finally produce what you've been carrying, let the power dynamic completely reverse. End not in triumph but in the complicated ache of finally being believed, of no longer carrying this secret weight alone.

title: The Leather Jacket That Makes You Dangerous
instruction: You're preparing to confront someone who hurt someone you love. Begin vulnerable and afraid, your body small and uncertain. You reach for a heavy leather jacket - really feel yourself putting it on. Sense the weight of it settling on your shoulders, the way the leather grips your arms, the zipper's resistance, the collar against your neck, how it constrains and protects simultaneously. As the physical sensation of this armor encases you, let it change your breathing, your stance, the set of your jaw. Feel yourself becoming someone capable of violence, someone protected and dangerous. But here's the turn: as you move and the leather creaks and pulls, restricting your breath slightly, making you sweat, let the discomfort remind you this isn't really who you are. This costume is both empowering and suffocating. End in a moment where you're caught between the fierce confidence the jacket gives you and the panicked recognition that you're pretending to be someone you're not - your body powerful and terrified at once.
inspired_by: Objects that Come into Contact with the Body (Choice Approach)

title: Dancing Alone at Your Wedding: Joy Cracking Through Grief
instruction: It's your wedding day - your mother died six months ago. You've held yourself together until now. The song plays - the one she promised to dance with you to. Start dancing alone, voice bright and almost manic with joy because this day is beautiful and you're married and it's perfect - describe the dress, the love, the magic. But your voice keeps breaking into laughter that's too high, too sharp. Let gratitude and grief smash into each other: you're so happy and she's so gone and both are unbearably true. Cry while laughing, laugh while crying - speak to her as if she's here, thank her through tears, tell her about your new spouse, apologize for being happy without her. End in a strange, broken peace, swaying alone, held by both presence and absence.
inspired_by: Nostalgia Ambush: A Song Comes On

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling from a hospital in a war zone, and you know this is the last time you'll hear your parent's voice. Start with forced brightness—you're trying to protect them, making your voice sound casual, even joking about small things. But as they talk about waiting for you to come home for the holidays, something breaks. Your voice catches. You try to recover, to keep the illusion going, but now every word is fighting tears. You need them to know you love them without saying goodbye, without letting them know this is the end. Finish by telling them one true thing about what they've meant to you, your voice raw and stripped of all pretense, gratitude and devastating loss indistinguishable from each other.
inspired_by: Being Told You're Not Good Enough

title: The Fever Dream of Heartbreak
instruction: You're in the physical and emotional throes of fresh heartbreak—the kind where your body aches, you can't eat, you're feverish with grief. Perform four intense physical-emotional moments from the first week after they left, but out of order: first, day five when you're furiously destroying their belongings in a rage; second, day one when you're collapsed on the floor in shock, body trembling; third, day three when you're in the shower and the physical release of crying becomes almost ecstatic, a purging; fourth, day seven when you're lying very still, exhausted, and feeling the first whisper of survival. Each moment must be viscerally physical—let the emotion live in your body as much as your voice. The rage must feel cathartic and alive, the shock must feel like physical paralysis, the shower crying must blur pain and release, the stillness must feel like rebirth. Jump between these states, but make each one completely real and present.

title: Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying best friend's hospital bed at 3 AM. They're unconscious, and you know they can't hear you, but you speak anyway in barely more than a whisper. 'Hey. It's me. I'm here.' Start with small talk, gentle and tender—telling them about the weather, the terrible hospital coffee, anything normal. But slowly, your voice begins to tremble: 'Remember when we were seventeen and you told me we'd never let life make us boring? We were going to set the world on fire together.' A quiet laugh that catches in your throat. 'We did pretty good, didn't we?' Then the confession, soft and breaking: 'I don't know how to do this life without you in it. I don't know who I am if you're not here.' Your hand reaches for theirs. 'I'm so scared.' Long pause. Then, with profound tenderness mixed with unbearable sadness: 'But if you need to go... if you're tired... I understand. I'll be okay. Eventually.' A lie and you both know it, but it's the most loving lie you'll ever tell. 'I love you. I'll always love you. Thank you for choosing me.' Silence, just the sound of the heart monitor, as you rest your forehead against their hand.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional abandonment of your childhood, but this time you're not asking for change—you're demanding acknowledgment. Start with a voice that's deceptively calm, almost cold: 'I need to say something I should have said twenty years ago.' As you lay out specific memories—the times they weren't there, the needs they ignored, the child you were—your voice becomes sharper, more cutting. When they try to deflect or minimize, your anger erupts: 'No. You don't get to do that anymore.' But then something shifts. Maybe you see them as fragile, maybe you recognize the parent who hurt you was once a hurt child too. Your voice cracks as fury dissolves into grief, and you end with a painful truth spoken through tears: the realization that acknowledgment might never come, but you're finally free of needing it.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Accent She Mocked Out of You
instruction: You're face-to-face with your mother after years of silence, and you're finally saying what you've never said: that she's the reason you erased your voice. Start angry, articulate, in your polished accent—the one that got you out, got you respect. Accuse her of making you ashamed. But as she responds—maybe defending herself, maybe breaking down—something shifts. Your old accent starts bleeding through against your will, especially on certain words, the ones she used to correct. Feel the humiliation of it, the way your body betrays you. End in a complicated place: still hurt, but also recognizing her own shame, her own survival. Your voice caught between two worlds, neither one feeling like home, realizing she was as trapped as you were.
inspired_by: Forced to Speak in Your Family Accent You Abandoned

title: Confronting Your Dying Mother Who Never Believed You Were Sick
instruction: You're at your mother's bedside and you finally have the chance to say what decades of chronic illness and her denial have built up inside you. Start controlled, almost gentle—you don't want to hurt her, she's dying. But as you speak about the years she called you dramatic, lazy, attention-seeking while you were truly suffering, rage surfaces. Your voice should crack between love and fury, between wanting her final days to be peaceful and needing her to finally see you. She's too weak to argue back and that somehow makes it worse. Transform from anger to something more complex: grief that she'll never truly understand, forgiveness you're not sure you feel, desperate love for someone who failed you. End with your hand on hers, voice barely audible, caught between releasing her and holding on.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Diplomat Realizes Peace Treaty Will Require Sacrificing an Entire Species

title: The Window's Reflection
instruction: You're an elderly woman on a long bus ride home from visiting your husband in a memory care unit. The engine drones, tires hiss on the wet road, and the window vibrates against your temple. You feel emotionally numb, staring at the blurred trees, your voice flat and distant. Then the bus hits a bump, and a stranger's laugh triggers a sudden, unbidden memory—your husband's laugh from decades ago. Your voice shifts to a fragile, startled whisper, words catching as you say to yourself, 'He used to laugh like that.' Let the numbness crack into a brief, sorrowful warmth, then fade back as you turn away.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Whispered Confession After Making Love
instruction: You're lying beside your lover in the dark, and they've just asked you to tell them something true about yourself. You begin with something safe—a sanitized version of a fear or memory, speaking in a controlled whisper. But as you speak, notice how you're protecting yourself, making yourself seem more together than you are, editing out the shameful or terrifying parts. Your challenge is to feel the impulse to tell the real, uglier truth—and then actually do it. Let your whisper become even quieter but more raw. What are you hiding beneath the acceptable confession? A devastating vulnerability? A secret shame? By the end, reveal the thing you swore you'd never say aloud, the thing that makes you feel naked and terrified. Move from protective self-disclosure to unbearable exposure.
inspired_by: Actor is redirecting authentic impulses into more comfortable emotional expressions, creating a split between what is felt and what is expressed

title: The Last Words Before the Morphine Takes You
instruction: You're on your deathbed, clarity fading fast, and you have minutes to tell your adult child something you've hidden for thirty years—something that will change how they see their entire life. Start with your voice already weak, words slipping away from you, frustrated that your body is betraying you at this crucial moment. As you push through the fog to confess, your voice gains unexpected strength from pure urgency, becoming almost fierce in its need to be understood. Then the truth is out, and you see their face change. Your voice breaks completely—not from weakness now, but from the devastating relief of finally being known, mixed with grief that you waited so long. End in whispers, each word a gift you're not sure you have time to give, asking forgiveness and giving blessing in the same breath, your voice tender and raw and utterly yours in these final moments.

title: I Won't Let Them Take You
instruction: You're holding your child (or younger sibling, or someone you've protected) and there are people coming to take them away — immigration officers, child services, soldiers, it doesn't matter. You start fierce, almost feral: 'You're not touching them, do you hear me? You're not—' Your voice is a weapon, sharp with protective rage. But as the reality sets in that you can't stop this, that fury begins cracking into desperation. You're bargaining, pleading, your voice breaking: 'Please, they're just a kid, they didn't do anything...' You oscillate wildly between trying to sound strong for the child ('It's okay, baby, it's going to be okay') and barely contained hysteria directed at the authorities. By the end, you're on your knees, your voice raw and destroyed, and the fierce protector has become someone helpless and shattered. The performance must feel dangerous, unpredictable, like anything could happen.

title: Last Words to a Child You'll Never See Again
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child before entering witness protection—you have fifteen minutes, and they can never know the real reason you're disappearing from their life forever. Start with forced brightness, trying to be strong, telling them about an 'amazing opportunity' you can't pass up. Let that facade crack as you memorize their face, your voice catching on details: the way their hair falls, that scar on their chin. Transition into barely-contained anguish as you give them life advice you won't be there to repeat—how to handle heartbreak, how to know they're loved, how to be brave. End with a whispered confession they're too young to understand: that leaving them is destroying you, that you'll carry them in every breath you take in your new life. Let your voice break between strength and devastation, between hope for their future and grief for yours.
inspired_by: Electrical Burn Aftermath: Consciousness Returning with Pain

title: Bitter Buzz, Then Crash
instruction: You're a tough-talking 10-year-old who snuck a can of your dad's extra-strong energy drink. Now you're wired, disgusted by the sickly sweet chemical taste coating your tongue, and doubting your own stupid choice. As you try to brag to your reflection, your jaw tightens, you shift restlessly, and the rapid jitter gives way to a heavy, overwhelming fatigue. Start with sharp, defiant disgust and nervous doubt, then let the words slow into a mumble as your eyelids grow heavy and exhaustion creeps in.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Doubt (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Reading Their Letter After They're Gone
instruction: You're holding a letter—maybe from someone who died, or left forever, or ended things, or is too sick to remember writing it. They wrote it knowing this moment would come. Start reading aloud, your voice warm with recognition of their words, maybe even smiling at an inside joke or a memory. But as you read, they're telling you to let go, to be happy, to live without them. Your smile becomes tears. You're laughing and sobbing at once—grateful they loved you enough to write this, destroyed that these words are all you have left. The gratitude and grief are inseparable. End with your voice suspended between joy at having been loved this way and the ache of losing it, reading the final line like both a benediction and a breaking heart.
inspired_by: Talking About Them As If They're Still Alive

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission Before the Point of No Return
instruction: You're an astronaut on humanity's first one-way voyage beyond our solar system. This is your last transmission before you pass the point where Earth's signals can reach you. You begin with practiced professionalism, reading coordinates and status updates, but your voice starts fracturing as you realize you're saying goodbye to every human voice you'll ever hear again. You're speaking to mission control, but really you're speaking to your child who's listening at home—you promised them you'd come back, and now you have to break that promise across the void of space. Your words become simpler, more desperate. You end in a whisper, trying to fit a lifetime of love into the seconds before the signal dies forever. The shift is from controlled scientist to raw parent, from confidence to the most profound loneliness imaginable.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Knight Must Execute the Sibling They Protected

title: The Weight We Carry
instruction: You're a father moving a heavy, old wooden dresser out of your apartment after a breakup. Your young child is watching you from the doorway, asking why you're sweating. You've had a couple of beers to dull the ache, and you're embarrassed that you can barely lift it, but you try to act tough. Start off with a strained, breathless bravado as you heave the dresser, your voice catching and cutting off mid-sentence from the effort. Over the course of a few lines, the embarrassment gives way to a quiet sadness as you realize this piece of furniture holds memories of a better time. Let your voice crack, trail off, and finally release in a sigh of defeat.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (extremely present), Sadness (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: First Trust
instruction: You are a teenage girl, nervous but wanting this, with your partner. Your voice is soft and feminine, but fear lingers in the edges—a slight tightness, a catch in your breath. As they touch you, you gasp, your words coming in broken fragments: 'I... I'm scared... but I trust you... don't stop.' Your breathing is uneven; you lose a thought mid-sentence, then find it again when pleasure overtakes you. Let your voice rise into a higher, breathier register at peaks, then drop with a shaky exhale. Start with hesitant, quiet moans, and by the end, let your voice tremble with a mix of relief and surrender—the fear still there, but quieter now, softened by connection.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Transcendence Reaching
instruction: You're dissolving into something larger than yourself. Your voice becomes ethereal, barely present: 'I'm not... I'm just...' Words become harder to find because individual self is dissolving. Breathing is deep, full-bodied. Your voice sounds like it's coming from somewhere else—expansive, resonant, not quite grounded. Physical: you're completely still, open. 'Everything is connected. Everything.' Your tone is amazed, humble. By the end, you're barely in your body; your voice is channeling something vast. Silence becomes as important as words.

title: The Taste Left Behind
instruction: You've just hung up the phone after a long, disastrous call with a close family member who revealed a betrayal you never saw coming. You're slumped in a kitchen chair, the receiver still warm in your hand, the room silent except for your own ragged breathing. Your throat is raw, eyes swollen, nose completely stuffed—you can barely get air through it. At first, you're just a hollow, exhausted shell, the fear so deep it's turned your stomach sour. But then, as you stare at the phone, a new sound starts in your chest—a quiet, bitter laugh. It's not humor; it's the sour taste of a truth you can't swallow. Speak aloud to the empty room: acknowledge the fear you feel, then let that sourness twist your words into something almost mocking. Start with a fragile, breathy croak, and let your voice build to a thin, acidic edge as the laugh threatens to take over. Let your congestion muffle your words, and let pauses be long and heavy as you try to find the strength to finish each sentence.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Execution
instruction: You have three minutes to speak to the person you love most before they're executed for a crime you know, in your soul, they didn't commit. Begin with forced brightness—'I'm going to get you out, I promise'—your voice cracking with false hope. You're trying to protect them from your own terror. As the seconds tick away, your denial crumbles. The brightness fractures into raw desperation, then finally collapses into a whispered, broken acceptance: 'I don't know how to be in this world without you.' Let your voice move from manic determination to helpless, devastating surrender. The goodbye you can barely say out loud.

title: The Perfectionist's Final Review
instruction: You are a renowned food critic lying in a hospital bed, speaking to your estranged daughter who has just brought you soup she made herself. Begin with your habitual critical dissection of the soup - the salt content, the temperature, the presentation - your voice sharp and analytical as always. But as you taste it, something breaks inside you. Let your voice crack as you realize this might be the last thing you ever taste, and that you've spent a lifetime measuring love by impossible standards. End by trying to tell her the soup is perfect, that she is perfect, but the words barely make it past the tears. Your transformation should move from armored perfectionism to raw, undefended love, with the critic's vocabulary slowly giving way to a parent's desperate tenderness.
inspired_by: The Restaurant Critic with Strange Criteria

title: Promising to Remember While Learning to Forget
instruction: You're speaking to someone with advancing dementia—a parent, a spouse, a person who is slowly disappearing. You begin by making gentle, reassuring promises: you'll visit every day, you'll bring their favorite foods, you'll keep them safe. Your voice carries warmth and optimism. But as you speak, the cruel paradox emerges—they're making you promise to let them go, to move on, to not let their forgetting destroy you. You start laughing through tears at the absurdity of it: promising to remember someone who won't remember the promise, vowing to hold on while learning to release. Your voice oscillates between joy at the memories you're sharing right now and grief at watching them slip away. By the end, you're making impossible promises—to carry their stories, to be their memory, to find gratitude in the heartbreak. Your voice is simultaneously breaking and soaring, the promise a bittersweet hymn to impermanent love.

title: The Protection That Destroys
instruction: You're a parent who just found out your teenager has been covering for their younger sibling's serious illness, protecting you because they knew you were already overwhelmed. Start with explosive fury—shouting at them for keeping this secret, for lying to you, your voice sharp and accusatory. 'How could you not tell me? How DARE you decide I couldn't handle this!' Your rage is towering, self-righteous. But mid-accusation, you hear your own words and realize you're angry because they're right—you couldn't handle it, and they knew it. The rage collapses instantly into devastation. Your voice drops to almost nothing. You try to apologize, but the words come out in gasping half-sentences, choked with shame and helplessness. 'I'm supposed to—I should have—you shouldn't have had to—' You can't complete a thought. End with a fierce, broken declaration that you'll do better, but even as you say it, your voice reveals your terrified uncertainty that you can. The final moment should mix desperate love, crushing inadequacy, and raw determination.

title: The Void Listens
instruction: You are a young astronaut on a solo spacewalk, repairing a critical module. Through your helmet's radio, you thank your ground controller for their precise guidance—your voice is warm, reliant, a little breathless from effort. But as you follow a wire, you find it's been deliberately cut. A slow, cold understanding spreads. Your gratitude doesn't vanish, but it curdles. Keep your tone steady, but let a faint, almost playful malice seep into the edges of your words—like you're savoring a secret. You breathe heavily, your voice compressed and tinny. You pause to glance at the vast blackness, your fingers trembling slightly on the tool. By the end, what started as thanks becomes a quiet, chilling promise.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're rehearsing the eulogy you'll give for someone who's still alive but won't be for much longer—perhaps your best friend, your sibling, the person who knows you better than anyone. Start reading it aloud with composure, but then you hit a funny memory and you laugh, really laugh, because they were hilarious and ridiculous and made you laugh until you couldn't breathe. Let that laughter build even as tears start streaming down your face, because the joy of knowing them and the agony of losing them are happening simultaneously. Your voice should oscillate between genuine delight at remembering their jokes, their quirks, their perfect imperfections, and the shattering awareness that these memories are all you'll have left. Begin by grumbling aloud about your own forgetfulness, the impatience rising with every failed search. As you fumble through old receipts and loose change, your voice shifts from sharp, irritable muttering to a quieter, more vulnerable realization that you might have left the key in the coat you wore yesterday. Let your breath hitch, your pacing slow, and end on a tired, reluctant sigh as you accept you'll have to go look.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Teaching Sign Language: When Hands Speak and Voice Goes Quiet
instruction: You're teaching someone sign language. Voice the signs as you make them — but your spoken voice should gradually give way to the beauty of signing. Describe the physical poetry: 'The sign for love is this — arms crossed over your chest, holding yourself. The sign for sorry is a fist circling your heart.' When you reach the sign for silence, stop speaking entirely. Hold the silence. Then whisper: 'Sometimes the most powerful thing a voice can do is stop.' Resume signing.

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at twilight. She's awake but fading. Begin by simply watching the light change on her face, and let whatever memories come—speak them aloud softly, without planning what you'll say next. A childhood smell. Her garden. The way she laughed. The time she disappointed you. Don't guide these memories toward anything meaningful or poetic; let them be random, broken, honest. As you speak, notice how your voice changes. Some memories might make you smile mid-sentence, others might catch in your throat. By the end, you're not trying to say goodbye perfectly—you're simply letting her see all the scattered pieces of loving her, even the complicated ones. Start with careful observation and end in raw, unfiltered remembering.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent the truth they've refused to see for years - that their expectations, their rigid categories, their need for you to be someone you're not has caused real damage. Start carefully, almost apologetically, your voice carrying years of trying to please them. As you speak, anger rises - not loud rage, but the sharp, precise fury of someone who's been diminished too long. Your words become more direct, cutting through their deflections and excuses. When they try to defend themselves or dismiss you, something breaks in you - not into shouting, but into a raw, trembling honesty that terrifies you both. End exhausted but clear-eyed, no longer asking for their approval, grieving the relationship you needed but finding strength in your own truth.
inspired_by: Explaining Your Non-Binary or Fluid Identity

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut whose oxygen system has failed beyond repair. You have eight minutes to record a final message to your partner and young daughter back on Earth. Begin with forced composure, trying to be brave and practical—explaining where important documents are, how much you love them. But as the oxygen thins and reality sets in, let your voice crack and soften. Allow yourself to become the vulnerable person beneath the astronaut, whispering the tiny details you'll miss: bedtime stories, the smell of your partner's hair, your daughter's laugh. End in a place of devastating tenderness mixed with gratitude for the life you had, your words growing quieter, more intimate, as if you're holding them close one last time.

title: The Comedy of Letting Go
instruction: You're packing up the home you shared with your deceased spouse, finding their belongings, and you're laughing and crying simultaneously, talking to them as if they can hear you. Start by discovering something absurd—their terrible collection of novelty socks, that hideous lamp they loved—and laugh genuinely, warmly, the way you used to tease them. Let that laughter crack into tears mid-sentence, then back to laughter through the tears as you remember their ridiculous defense of these items. Your voice should dance between joy at the memories and grief at the loss, sometimes in the same breath. Move through waves of contradictory emotion: gratitude for having had them, anger that they're gone, peace in remembering, devastation in the present. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance, laughing softly at something they would have said, crying because you can hear their voice so clearly in your mind, finding strange comfort in the contradiction of your own broken, beautiful reaction to their absence.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging father about the years of emotional absence, and you've finally found the courage to speak. Begin with a trembling voice, almost apologetic: 'I need to tell you something... I've needed to say this for twenty years.' Your anger builds as you list the moments he missed, the times you needed him—graduations, breakups, when Mom was sick. Let your voice crack with rage and hurt: 'Where were you? I was your child!' But when he starts to cry, really cry for the first time you can remember, your anger fractures. End in a completely different place—tentative forgiveness mixed with deep sadness, your voice barely steady: 'I don't know if I can... but I want to try. Do you want to try?' Let the confrontation transform into something fragile and new.

title: Morning Light and Thorns
instruction: You have just woken up, still in bed, with a stiff, achy body that makes every movement deliberate. Your voice is thick, gravelly, low from sleep. You slowly notice the morning sun falling on a potted plant by the window — a gift from your granddaughter who now lives far away. At first, you only register the pain in your joints and a dull resentment at time passing. But as you look at the plant, a fierce, consuming interest takes over — you examine each leaf, the soil, the tiny new bud. Underneath, you feel a slight but sharp jealousy of your granddaughter's young, easy life, and a pang of loss. Let your voice shift from slow, pained grogginess to a hushed, fascinated whisper, with moments of breathless realization, as if discovering something precious and painful at once. Speak aloud, mostly to yourself, maybe with a few pauses to swallow or stretch your neck. 'Look at that... a new leaf. When did that happen? She said it was easy to care for... Easy. Everything's easy for her. My hands... they ache just holding the pot. But this little green thing... it keeps growing. I keep waking up. There's a kind of... stubbornness in us both, I guess.'
emotions_sampled: Interest (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Best Friend Betrayal
instruction: Your best friend has sided with someone who hurt you. You're confronting them, and your voice is hurt, confused: 'How could you do this to me?' You thought they had your back. Your voice is shaky as you explain how they hurt you. They're defending themselves, and your voice becomes angry: 'I needed you. And you chose them.' By the end, you're realizing this friendship is over, and your voice becomes distant, sad: 'I guess we're done then.'

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave Forever
instruction: You're standing over your child's bed in the pre-dawn darkness. You're leaving—witness protection, a terminal diagnosis requiring isolation, or a choice so painful you can barely breathe through it. Start with your voice barely audible, tender and breaking: 'I need to tell you something, even though you can't hear me.' Describe small details—the way they sleep, a freckle, how their hand curls. Your voice catches on memories: their first word, a laugh, an ordinary Tuesday. 'I wanted to give you everything. I wanted to be there when...' Let your voice splinter into quiet devastation. You're trying not to sob, trying not to wake them, trying to memorize this moment. End with something simple that destroys you to say: 'You are the best thing I ever did. I'm so sorry.' Your voice is a whisper of pure grief, tender beyond measure, heartbroken in the quietest way possible.
inspired_by: Small Explosion at Work: Checking Colleagues for Injuries

title: The Wedding Toast from the Wrong Timeline
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's wedding—to someone who isn't you. You're genuinely happy for them, and you mean every word of celebration, but underneath runs a river of your own heartbreak because you've been in love with them for years. Start warm, funny, full of genuine joy and beautiful memories—your voice bright with authentic celebration. But let cracks appear: your voice catches on certain words, you have to pause to 'collect yourself' in ways that could be tears of happiness but aren't quite. Laugh while describing how perfect they are together, but let the laughter break into something more complex. Build to expressing your deepest wish for their happiness—and mean it completely—while your voice simultaneously reveals you're shattering inside. End with a smile in your voice and tears you're trying to hide, raising a glass with complete sincerity and complete devastation existing in the same moment. Let gratitude and grief be indistinguishable.

title: The Morning Ritual
instruction: You're shaving your face with an electric razor, the constant buzz muffling your words as you press it against your cheek. You speak quietly to your reflection, starting with a fragile hope that this time the result will be different, that you'll finally see a smooth, clean finish. But as you feel the missed patches and the familiar rough stubble beneath your fingers, your voice tightens with helplessness, and a dull disappointment settles in. Let the physical act shape your delivery — the razor's vibration forces you to pause, to distort your lips, to trail off mid-word. End with a resigned sigh, the initial optimism now only a faint memory.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Helplessness (extremely present), Disappointment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Aftermath
instruction: You’re alone in a dark bathroom, slumped against the tub, still catching your breath after sobbing until you couldn’t anymore. Your throat feels raw, stuffed up, every swallow a small scrape. You pick up your phone to leave a voicemail for the person you just fought with—but you’re not apologizing. Start with nothing but shame, a trembling whisper, barely able to admit what you’ve done wrong. Then let the shame curdle into a raw, exhausted anger—not yelling, but a quiet, bitter crack in your voice as you accuse them of pushing you here. By the end, that anger fades into a hollow, drained stillness, like you’ve already given up on being heard. Cough, sniffle, trail off, let your words get tangled as you think of what you really wanted to say.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the golden hour before sunset. She can no longer speak clearly, and neither can you find adequate words. Begin by feeling the weight of everything unsaid between you across decades—regrets, gratitude, private jokes, shared secrets. Let sounds emerge from your body that carry these feelings: hums, sighs, broken syllables, tones that rise and fall with memory. As the light fades, your sounds should shift from heavy with grief to something lighter, almost like a lullaby, as you realize you're giving her permission to go. End in a place of bittersweet peace, where your wordless sounds become a bridge between holding on and letting go.
inspired_by: Expressing Impulses in Sounds and Gibberish

title: Confessing to Your Child What You've Hidden
instruction: You're telling your adult child something you've kept secret for years—perhaps about their other parent, about a choice you made when they were young, about why you were absent or distant. Your voice starts barely above a whisper, each word painful to release. You're terrified of their judgment, of losing them. The confession must be specific and devastating: dates, details, the exact moment everything changed. As you speak, your voice should tremble with shame, with the weight of years of silence. But watch for the shift—when you see their face change, when they start to understand, your whispered confession must become something else. Maybe relief that the secret is finally out. Maybe desperate need for their forgiveness. End with your voice raw and small, asking them a question you're terrified to ask: 'Can you ever forgive me?' Let the silence after that question fill with your fear.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Sibling She Gave Away
instruction: You've just discovered you had a twin your mother gave up for adoption forty years ago. You walk into her kitchen where she's making tea like always. Start with a simple question that you know will shatter everything. Watch your voice move from eerily calm curiosity to barely contained fury to something more devastating—the grief of a child who realizes they were always half of something. She will deflect. You will not let her. Include the moment where your anger collapses into begging her to just tell you the truth, to finally see you. End not with resolution but with the horrible intimacy of real damage between two people who love each other.
inspired_by: Surgeon Performs Life-Saving Surgery on Person Who Assaulted Them

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church After Your Prayer Wasn't Answered
instruction: You came here believing. You came here begging. You did everything right—every ritual, every sacrifice, every desperate bargain. And it didn't matter. Start quietly, kneeling, still trying to be respectful, still trying to pray properly. But the rage is building. Your voice should crack and escalate—from whispered pleas to shouted demands. 'I trusted you!' 'Where were you?' 'Why them and not me?' Let your fury be raw and ugly and break apart into sobbing, then surge back into anger, then collapse into something more devastating: not rage, but abandonment. You're not just angry—you're heartbroken. You're a child who's been left alone. By the end, you're on the floor, voice hoarse, asking the question that terrifies you most: 'Are you even there?' Let the final words come out small, broken, stripped of everything but naked fear and grief.
inspired_by: Plating the Final Michelin Dish While Your Restaurant Is Failing

title: The Grateful Goodbye
instruction: You're at the airport, saying goodbye to your best friend who's moving across the world—permanently. You start laughing through tears about a ridiculous memory from college, your voice bright but unstable. You keep making jokes, keeping it light: 'You're going to forget all about me in your fancy new life.' But your voice keeps cracking. Your friend stops you: 'Say what you really want to say.' Now the laughter and tears are completely mixed. Your voice becomes earnest, vulnerable: 'You saved my life. After my divorce, when I wanted to... you were the only reason I didn't.' You're smiling and sobbing simultaneously, your voice full of gratitude and devastation: 'Thank you for loving me when I couldn't love myself.' They're crying too. The final boarding call comes. You pull them close, your voice in their ear carrying impossible contradictions—joy for their new adventure, grief at losing them, gratitude for every moment, peace that some loves transcend distance: 'Go. I love you. This isn't goodbye—it's just different.' Your voice at the end should sound like someone whose heart is breaking and whole at the same time.

title: The 3 AM Whisper
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone you love, and they're asleep. You've been awake for hours, body tense, holding a secret that's been eating you alive—an affair, a diagnosis, a betrayal, a truth about your past. Your throat is tight, your chest constricted. You begin by barely breathing, whispering fragments of confession into the darkness, testing the words with a voice that keeps catching. Your body is curled, protective, every muscle guarding against the vulnerability of speaking. But as you continue whispering your truth to the sleeping form beside you—knowing they can't hear but desperately needing to say it—something starts to loosen. Your whispers become more fluid, your breathing deeper. Maybe you even touch their hair or hand. By the end, you're speaking in full sentences, tears flowing quietly, your body unclenched and open, having released what you've been holding so tightly, even if only to the darkness and the unhearing beloved.

title: The Last Autumn Walk
instruction: You're walking your dying mother through her garden one final time, and she's asked you to describe everything you see, smell, and feel because her senses are fading. Begin with controlled composure, trying to be strong for her as you describe the obvious things—the roses, the bench. But as you truly open yourself to every detail—the exact quality of afternoon light on leaves, the particular scent of wet earth, the temperature of her hand growing cooler in yours—let the overwhelming awareness of this being the last time shatter your composure. Your voice should transform from steady narration to something breaking with the weight of truly perceiving this moment. End with a whispered observation so precise and tender it becomes unbearable—perhaps the sound of her breathing, or the way her fingers still respond to touch. Let heightened attention to the world around you crack open your grief.

title: Help First Ask
instruction: You're asking for help for the first time in your adult life, and your voice is shaking: 'I need help. I can't do this alone anymore.' The words feel like admitting defeat. Your voice becomes smaller: 'I know I'm supposed to be strong. I know I'm supposed to handle everything.' But the words come anyway: 'I'm drowning. I need someone to throw me a rope.' The person listens without judgment. Your voice becomes more honest: 'I've been pretending for so long that I had it all figured out. I don't.' By the end: 'Thank you for not leaving when I finally told you the truth.' The help is extended, and your voice is no longer alone. Walking away, your voice is lighter: 'I asked for help. And the world didn't end. In fact, it just got a little easier.' The first ask is the hardest and the most necessary.

title: The Tender Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're sitting beside your sleeping child's bed, knowing you'll be gone before they wake—either because you're leaving them with family to protect them from danger, or because your illness means you won't survive the night. Speak softly, barely above a whisper, so you don't wake them. Begin by recounting a specific memory—their first laugh, the way they grabbed your finger as a baby. Your voice is tender, full of wonder at this small miracle. Let sadness seep in slowly as you catalog all the moments you'll miss: first loves, graduations, their own children. Feel your throat tighten as you try to compress a lifetime of advice into minutes. Tell them the things they'll need to know, but let your voice break on the important parts. End with a simple 'I love you' that holds everything—pride, sorrow, fierce protective love, and the unbearable ache of goodbye. Let the silence after speak louder than words ever could.

title: Fever Dream Breakthrough
instruction: You are in the grip of a 104-degree fever, your body burning and shaking, consciousness flickering between reality and hallucination. Begin in physical agony—your voice strained, breathing labored, words broken by shivers and gasps. As the fever peaks, you start seeing faces from your past: a grandmother who died when you were seven, a friend who overdosed, the hospital room where your brother was born. Your voice becomes strange, sometimes childlike, sometimes ancient, as if these memories are possessing your body. Let your physical pain and emotional memories merge—shaking not just from chills but from grief, burning not just with fever but with rage at death, at loss, at the fragility of bodies. As the fever finally breaks, your voice steadies into something new: a raw, cleansed exhaustion. You've been taken apart and put back together. Speak your final words with the startling clarity that comes after surviving something that almost destroyed you.
inspired_by: Long Day's Journey Jamie — Unconscious Suggestions for Dark Character Exercise

title: The Body Remembers Otherwise
instruction: You're in a moment of physical intensity—passionate reunion, fighting through pain, or moment of ecstasy—but your body suddenly remembers something unexpected that contradicts the moment. You're kissing someone but your body recalls a betrayal; you're in pain but your body floods with inappropriate desire; you're dancing in joy but your muscles remember violence. Begin fully in one physical-emotional state, then let your body's unexpected memory hijack the moment. Don't resolve it neatly—let the two states coexist messily, fighting each other. End in a place where your voice and body tell two different truths simultaneously.

title: The Gift I Can't Protect You From
instruction: You're a parent watching your adult child walk into danger - military deployment, a dangerous mission, an unwinnable fight - and they're thanking you for 'giving them' the courage to go. Start with fierce pride that quickly cracks into terror. Your voice should be strong, supportive, everything a parent should be - then let it splinter. Let rage surface: rage at the world, at circumstances, at your own powerlessness. You want to scream at them to stay, to be safe, but instead you're choking out words of encouragement. Let your voice shake between fury and love, between the desperate need to protect and the requirement to let go. Build to a breaking point where your supportive words collide with animal fear - maybe your voice rises, maybe it collapses into ragged breathing. End with a transformation: finding some fierce, primal peace in your powerlessness, blessing them through tears, your voice raw but steady. Move from controlled pride to explosive fear to something transcendent and broken and beautiful.
inspired_by: Hiding Disappointment When Receiving an Unwanted Gift

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father about why he never defended you when your older brother bullied you mercilessly throughout childhood. You're now 35, and he's just asked why you never visit. Start with controlled, sharp anger—the kind that's been rehearsed mentally for years. Deliver your carefully prepared accusations with precision. But as he begins to cry—this man who never cried—watch your fortress crack. Let your voice break from prosecutorial sharpness into something rawer: the confused child who needed protection. End in a place where anger and love coexist impossibly, where you're furious at him and desperate to comfort him simultaneously. Your vocal control must shatter authentically mid-confrontation.
inspired_by: An actor is studying with a teacher or workshop and wants to make the most of it

title: The Echo of Victory
instruction: You are a retired coach who has slipped into the old gymnasium late at night. The space is empty, the polished floor reflects the dim lights, and every sound flutters with a metallic echo. You start speaking quietly, almost to yourself, with a tired nostalgia—remembering the games that filled this hall. Then you find a basketball, bounce it once, and the sound cracks through the silence. Without thinking, you take a shot, hear the swish, and a sudden, unexpected elation floods you—your voice lifts, grows fuller, almost laughing as you realize the thrill is still there. Let the echo shape your pauses, let your sneakers squeak, and let your voice change from weary recollection to a bright, joyful surprise by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering Your Secret to Your Sleeping Spouse
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your spouse sleeps beside you. You whisper a confession they'll never hear—maybe an affair, maybe that you're dying, maybe that you've fallen out of love, or that you're more in love than ever but terrified. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every other word. This is the safest place to tell the truth because they can't hear it. Start with the facts, clinical and quiet. But your whisper becomes unsteady, tender, aching. You're apologizing, explaining, grieving what is or what might have been. Touch their hair as you speak. Your voice breaks on their name. End in silence, your breath shaky, having said everything to no one. This is confession as prayer, intimate and utterly alone.
inspired_by: Your Child Asking an Impossible Question

title: The Kitchen Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your mother in the kitchen where you grew up. Start from a place of controlled anger, the kind you've rehearsed in your mind for years - your list of grievances, your prepared accusations. But as you speak, she doesn't react the way you expected. Her silence, or her tears, or her own unexpected honesty begins to crack your armor. The words you've planned dissolve. What emerges is something messier - the child inside you who still needs her, the fury at needing her, the grief over all the years of silence between you. End in a place you didn't intend to go: not resolution, but raw mutual recognition. Your voice must journey from calculated confrontation to unguarded, spontaneous emotional exposure.

title: The Hollow Release
instruction: You are alone, just after a mechanical climax with a partner who's already asleep. Your body is still shuddering involuntarily, breathing ragged, but your mind is eerily blank — a deep emotional numbness. As you catch your breath, a strange amusement flickers: you realize you're performing a script you don't believe. Let your voice start with flat, automatic gasps and moans, then shift to a low, wry chuckle that catches in your throat. End with a muttered, almost amused realization: 'Still goes through the motions... even when nothing's there.' Keep the physical rhythm — spasmodic breaths, rising pitch, loss of control — but weave in the irony.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Fear That Kept Us Safe
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your anxiety, your constant companion, the 'monster' that has protected you through trauma but now needs to be released. Begin with tearful laughter, voice full of affection and gratitude, thanking this fear for keeping you alert, for keeping you alive when the world was dangerous. As you speak, let the laughter fade into something more complex—grief mixed with relief, love mixed with exhaustion. Your voice should tremble with the contradiction of wanting to let go while being terrified to live without this protection. End in a place of bittersweet peace, voice soft and wondering, as you acknowledge that releasing this fear means trusting yourself in a way you never have before. This should feel like honoring something that hurt you while loving you, all at once.
inspired_by: The Child and the Monster Under the Bed

title: Last Bath Before the Crossing
instruction: You're preparing your elderly parent for their final journey, washing their hands with warm water one last time. Begin with tender, practical care—describing the temperature, the soap, helping them as you've done a hundred times before. But as you continue, let the weight of what this means settle in: this is the last time you'll do this simple, loving act. Your voice should start steady and caretaking, then gradually crack with the realization that you're memorizing every detail—the feel of their skin, the way their fingers curl. End with a whispered gratitude for all these small moments you took for granted, your voice thick with love and impending loss. Let the mundane act of washing become sacred, unbearable, and precious all at once.
inspired_by: Washing Your Hands with Warm, Soapy Water

title: The Thank-You Note in the Shoebox
instruction: You are a teenager with a bright, hyper-feminine voice, sitting cross-legged on your bedroom floor, sorting through a shoebox of old school papers. At first you feel relief—you've been searching for something, and the familiar rustle of papers calms you. As you shuffle through, a handwritten note catches your eye; you mumble the words aloud, your voice softening with interest. Then you remember: this is a thank-you note from a friend you'd forgotten about. Let your voice fill with genuine, building gratitude—a quiet, heartfelt warmth that lifts as you realize how much that kindness meant. You pause, crinkle a paper edge, and sigh before speaking the final words with a tender, almost tearful smile.
emotions_sampled: Relief (extremely present), Interest (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Fever of Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to a lover at a train station, and you have a fever—you're physically ill, your body aching and hypersensitive. Every touch burns and comforts simultaneously. Begin trying to stay composed despite your physical discomfort, but let the fever make everything more intense: their touch, the cold air, your own desperation. Don't separate the physical sensations from the emotional ones—let them blur and amplify each other. As the departure time approaches, allow the illness to strip away your defenses. Your body is already vulnerable; let that physical state crack open emotional truth. Move from trying to control how you appear to complete surrender to both the physical and emotional reality overwhelming you.
inspired_by: Actor repeats the same physical mannerisms across all performances or has physical habits that operate automatically

title: The Scent of Seventeen Years
instruction: You're confronting your teenage daughter who's been lying to you for months. You're angry, she's defensive—begin there, in that familiar battle. But as you argue, you catch her scent—maybe her shampoo, her perfume, something distinctly her. Let yourself truly notice it. Then allow that scent to expand in your awareness: it's the smell of her baby hair when she was three, the way she smelled after soccer practice, every bedtime story, every fever you nursed her through. Let the scent become impossibly rich with memory and time. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it begins to crack open, revealing something underneath—the devastating reality that she's not yours anymore the way she used to be. End in a place where your rage has transformed into a complicated mixture of love, grief for her childhood, and the terrifying knowledge that you're losing her to adulthood and can't stop it.

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You are a ruthless older man speaking into a crackling walkie-talkie, the PTT button pressing down with each cold word. You’re in a dim, rain-slicked parking garage, the equipment hissing static between your bursts. Start with a calm, almost friendly tone, but let a creeping malevolence—a quiet, seething malice—seep into your voice as you realize the person on the other end is about to betray you. By the end, your words become a low, venomous threat, your thumb instinctively grinding the button harder as the transmission ends with a sharp click. Let the narrow bandwidth compress your anger; let the static and your own harsh breathing punctuate the silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Goodbye at the Station
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is boarding a train to a place they'll never return from — war, a terminal journey, exile. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be brave, voice artificially cheerful as you talk about mundane things to avoid the truth. Feel the facade crack: your voice begins to tremble, words become harder to say. The moment arrives — they have to go — and everything you've held back floods out: desperate pleading mixed with fierce love, your voice breaking on their name. End in whispered devastation as the train pulls away, speaking to the empty air where they stood, voice barely audible, repeating 'come back' like a prayer you know won't be answered.

title: Breaking the Inheritance
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just told you they're repeating the exact destructive pattern you spent your whole life trapped in—addiction, abusive relationship, self-sabotage. You've kept your own past hidden from them, presenting a cleaned-up version of yourself. Begin pacing, unable to stand still, your whole body vibrating with the need to shake them awake. Let yourself get physically big—gestures that fill space, voice that won't be contained. You start with furious panic, nearly shouting, moving without restraint. But as you confess your own history—the raw, ugly truth you've hidden—something shifts. Your bigness becomes vulnerability. By the end, you're not lecturing but pleading, your voice stripped down to nakedness, offering them the one gift you have: the truth of your own brokenness and survival.
inspired_by: An actor is severely blocked — cannot function, cannot feel anything

title: The Reunion That Burns
instruction: You're seeing your former lover for the first time in five years, and the moment your hands touch in greeting, you're flooded with physical memory. Begin from a place of guarded politeness, but immediately let your body respond to everything at once—the shock of skin contact, the familiar scent, the way light falls on their face, the temperature of the room, the tension in your chest and stomach, the taste in your mouth. Don't intellectually process these sensations; let them accumulate and build without interruption. Allow the physical intensity to pull you from polite distance into something more dangerous—desire mixed with anger, longing tangled with grief—until you're speaking words you didn't plan to say, your voice and body betraying the careful control you intended to maintain.
inspired_by: Actor is doing sleep-wake state work, free association, or unconscious programming and finds sensorial questioning intrusive

title: Last Call Threat
instruction: You are an elderly man who has been drinking heavily for hours. It's past midnight in an empty parking lot. You corner a young person who accidentally bumped your car. Your voice is a low, lazy growl—thick with alcohol, slow and deliberate. At first, you're menacing, invading their space with slurred, gravelly threats. But as you speak, your exhaustion catches up with you: your shoulders sag, you lose your train of thought, and the menace fades into a tired, almost pathetic confusion. Start with a dangerous, intoxicated anger; end with a weary, hollow sense of defeat. Let your body sway and your words trail off naturally.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Perfect Run
instruction: You're a teenager sprawled across your bed, phone in hand, a pair of earbuds in. You just beat your personal best time on a difficult level... for the third time in a row. Your voice is low, close to your chest. Your thumbs are still tapping, and you keep glancing back at the screen, nearly hypnotized by the victory. Start with quiet, giddy disbelief as you mutter 'no way' to yourself, your pride swelling. By the end, you're grinning and practically crowing with triumph, as if you want to tell everyone in the world, even though no one else is there. Let the tone shift from a shaky, awed whisper to a full, breathless laugh.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Floor Opens
instruction: You're kneeling on the kitchen floor across from your partner after a bitter argument. Your voice is low, almost a whisper, as you start: 'I don't know where to begin...' Each word feels heavy, and you keep pausing to read their face. You're angry at yourself for hurting them, but underneath that anger there's a desperate longing to fix this, and a deep gratitude that they're still here listening. Let your voice crack on the words that matter most, and end with a raw, trembling 'thank you for not walking away.'
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Anger (clearly present), Longing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: You Never Came to Watch Me Run
instruction: Confront your parent who obsessed over their own fitness goals but never showed up for your track meets, dance recitals, or moments that mattered. Begin with bitter, clipped observations—recounting their step counts, their marathon times, their pride in hitting personal records. Let anger build as you list the specific days they missed: your championship, your graduation, the hospital. Your voice should gain intensity, become more jagged, accusations pouring out. Then break—mid-sentence, collapse into the hurt child underneath the anger. End with a vulnerable, almost inaudible question: 'Was I ever worth pausing your run for?' The shift from controlled rage to desperate need for validation should feel like a dam breaking.

title: The Confrontation That Won't Go As Scripted
instruction: You've rehearsed this confrontation with your father a thousand times—you know exactly what you'll say about how he abandoned the family. But he keeps throwing you off: suddenly touching your shoulder tenderly when you expect defensiveness, laughing at a serious moment, or falling silent and staring out the window when you need him to fight back. Start with righteous anger and a prepared speech. As his unexpected responses dismantle your script, feel your certainty crumble. Your accusations become questions. Your rage tangles with confusion, then unwanted understanding. Each time he surprises you, dig for a genuine response rather than falling back on what you planned to say. End in a place you never imagined—maybe forgiveness, maybe deeper hurt, maybe something you don't have words for. Let his unpredictability force you into authentic emotional territory.

title: The Confrontation You've Been Rehearsing Since Childhood
instruction: You are finally confronting your father about the way he made you feel invisible, unworthy, never quite good enough. Begin with the practiced, careful words you've rehearsed a thousand times—controlled, trying to make him understand, still seeking his approval even in your anger. But as you speak, something shifts. You realize you're still performing for his validation, still making yourself small enough to fit his version of who you should be. Let that realization crack you open. Stop trying to convince him. Stop shrinking. Speak from the part of you that knows your value isn't up for debate. Move from seeking permission to simply stating truth. Feel the power of no longer needing him to understand, validate, or approve.

title: Protecting Someone You Can't Save
instruction: You're holding someone—a child, a lover, a friend—and something terrible is coming that you're powerless to stop. Start with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance: 'I won't let anything happen to you,' said with absolute conviction. But as you continue, the cracks appear. Your promises become increasingly desperate, your voice rising as you try to will safety into existence through sheer force. You're giving instructions, making them promise to be brave, your words coming faster and more frantic. Then suddenly you break completely—collapsing from rage at your own helplessness into wrenching sobs. Your fierce protectiveness transforms into anguished apology: 'I'm so sorry, I can't—I don't know how to—' End holding them tighter, your voice raw and broken, making promises you both know are impossible but saying them anyway because what else can you do?
inspired_by: Explaining Why You Can't Forgive Them Yet

title: The Gilded Belch
instruction: You're at a crowded house party, standing near the snack table, trying to chat with someone you secretly envy. You've had a bit too much fizzy drink and every few words a burp rumbles up from your gut, dropping your voice into a low, guttural growl. At the start, you’re forcing a polite smile and complimenting their new job, but the envy is already churning. Midway, a burp escapes mid-sentence, and you feel a flush of shame. By the end, you stop fighting it — your voice cracks, and you blurt out your jealousy with a raw, bitter edge, the burp now a weapon.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your parent about something they did years ago that you've never spoken about. Start with rehearsed words, the speech you've practiced in your head a thousand times, your voice controlled and careful. But as you speak, notice if those words actually match what's churning inside you. Are you performing 'justified anger' when you're actually heartbroken?
