Are you trying to sound mature when you want to scream like a child? Halfway through, abandon the script in your head. Check in with your actual body, your actual feelings right now in this moment, and let the real accusation or plea or question come out—the one that's underneath the prepared statement. End somewhere you didn't plan to be, having said something true you didn't know you needed to say.
inspired_by: An actor feels disconnected from their moment-to-moment impulses during a scene

title: Standing Tall
instruction: You're refusing to break, no matter what pressure is applied. Your voice is the embodiment of that refusal. It's clear, strong, unmovable. You're facing something or someone that's trying to make you smaller, and you're refusing. Your voice doesn't waver. Physical threats might surround you, but your vocal composure is unwavering. There's power in this moment. Your voice carries the strength of conviction. By the end, you're still standing—metaphorically, maybe physically. Your voice is your proof that you couldn't be broken. The strength in your tone is not arrogance; it's the power of integrity.

title: The Runner's Vengeance
instruction: You just sprinted to catch the person who murdered your little sister. You are doubled over, gasping, hands on your knees. Between violent, heaving breaths, you start to speak. Your first words are barely audible, shaky whispers torn from a burning throat. You're terrified they might get away, that you'll lose them in the dark, but a sick, deep pleasure is rising through the pain. You begin with pure fear, desperate and ragged. By the end, your voice hardens into a jagged, breathless laugh, the malice and ecstasy of the hunt consuming you. Let your words be broken by gasps, your tone shift from shaky to venomous as you realize you have them.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Grateful for the Wreckage
instruction: You're saying goodbye to a relationship, a home, or a phase of your life that nearly destroyed you—but also made you who you are. Begin with a laugh that's almost genuine: 'I can't believe I'm going to miss this.' Your voice holds bewilderment at your own feelings. As you speak, let gratitude and grief become inseparable: 'You broke my heart, and somehow that was exactly what needed to happen.' There should be moments where you're almost smiling through tears, finding bizarre humor in the pain: 'What a beautiful disaster we were.' Your voice becomes warm with genuine thankfulness even as it shakes with loss. You're not being ironic—you really do mean both things at once. End with a voice that sounds simultaneously liberated and heartbroken, peaceful and grieving: 'Thank you for everything, even the parts that hurt. Especially the parts that hurt.' Let your final words sound like someone who just found freedom in the middle of goodbye.

title: Burnt Out Desire
instruction: You've just spent hours splitting firewood under a blazing sun. Your arms shake, your chest heaves, and every breath feels like dragging a weight. As you lean against the woodpile, your neighbor—someone you've secretly wanted for months—walks up in a thin tank top, smiling. You try to speak, but your voice is a wrecked rasp, each word costing you. Start from raw exhaustion and confusion at why your heart is racing even more, then let that confusion slowly ignite into unguarded, breathless lust. Let your voice crack, pause mid-sentence to gulp air, and let your words tumble out unevenly as desire overpowers your fatigue.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Stitch by Stitch
instruction: You're a young man knitting a scarf for your mother on a quiet Sunday afternoon. The rhythmic click of the needles and the soft wool ground you in a deep contentment. But as you near the end, you notice a small, mottled knot in the yarn—maybe from dirt or something worse. Your fingers slow, a flicker of disgust rises in your throat, but you keep knitting, trying to hold onto the peace you felt. Let your voice start warm and meditative, then let the disgust seep in like a sour note—a slight hitch in your breath, a harder swallow, a quieter tone as you push through.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Storm Inside the Kiss
instruction: You're standing in your ex-lover's doorway at midnight, drenched from rain. You came here furious—they betrayed you six months ago and you've been nursing rage ever since. You start by telling them exactly what you think of them, voice shaking with anger, fists clenched. But they're not fighting back. They're just looking at you with those same eyes, and suddenly your body remembers everything: their smell, the way they used to touch your face, every morning you woke up tangled together. The anger is still there but now it's colliding with devastating physical longing, and you hate yourself for it. Your voice catches. You step closer, still angry, but now your hands are trembling for a different reason. You're breathing harder. By the end, you're kissing them against the doorframe, and you don't know if you're trying to hurt them or consume them or both. The rage hasn't disappeared—it's mixing with desire, creating something fierce and almost painful. Let your voice and body carry both the violence and the need.

title: Crystal Cave Discovery
instruction: You are a young girl exploring a hidden underwater cave with your mother. You've just surfaced in a chamber filled with bioluminescent crystals, gasping and laughing as you tread water. Start with wild, almost breathless elation—splashing, giggling, and shouting about the colors. But as the water settles around you, and your mother's voice calms, you slow down. Feel the enormity of the silence, the cold stone, the ancientness of the light. End softly, in a hushed, wondering tone, as if the beauty has made you forget your own breathing. Let your voice go from frantic joy to a sacred, thoughtful whisper, with pauses where you swallow, cough, or let the water lap at your lips.
emotions_sampled: Elation (very intensely present), Contemplation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Inheritance You Never Wanted
instruction: You're sitting across from your terminally ill mother who just revealed she's leaving everything to your sibling - the one who abandoned the family. Start with a tight, controlled voice trying to be the good child: 'That's... that's your choice, of course.' But decades of swallowed resentment begin surfacing. Your voice sharpens as you list every sacrifice you made while they were gone, every hospital visit you took alone. The anger peaks, then shatters into something more vulnerable: the realization that you're not angry about the money at all - you're devastated that even now, even dying, she won't choose you. End with your voice breaking on: 'What did I do wrong?' Let the question hang, genuinely uncomprehending, like a child.

title: The Echo of Rescue
instruction: You are a young woman who has been lost in a deep cave for hours, cold and terrified. Suddenly, you see the flicker of a rescuer's headlamp far down the tunnel. You begin to call out, your voice shaky and desperate, almost lost in the deep, booming reverb of the cave. As the light draws closer and you realize they’ve found you, your relief swells into overwhelming, tearful gratitude. Let the natural echo carry your words, and let tears and trembling breath interrupt you. Your voice should shift from a panicked, pleading tone to a raw, soft, and deeply thankful one, almost whispering 'thank you' as your body finally slumps against the wet rock wall.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Kitchen Confrontation
instruction: You are confronting your father in the family kitchen about something he said to you fifteen years ago that has haunted you ever since. Start as the rational adult trying to have a 'calm discussion'—measured tone, explaining logically why his words hurt. Then let the angry teenager you once were take over: your voice rises, becomes accusatory, you stand differently, you're fighting for validation you never received. Next, allow the part of you that still desperately wants his approval to speak—voice softening, almost pleading, asking why you were never enough. Finally, access the voice of someone who has lived through this and survived: speak with hard-won clarity about what you've learned about yourself despite him, your tone carrying both disappointment in him and fierce self-respect. Each shift should feel like a different person inhabiting your body.

title: The Last Favor of a Tired Heart
instruction: You are an elderly woman nursing a persistent, dull toothache that has been gnawing at you for weeks. You sit in a worn armchair, cradling a warm mug of tea, but every sip makes you wince as the steam hits the sore spot. You are on the phone with a younger relative who has just asked for a large loan, and bitterness flickers in your chest as you recall how often you've been taken for granted. Yet, as you speak, you feel a deep, quiet contentment settling over you — a pleasure in being needed, in having something left to give. Let your voice be guarded, careful around the tooth; let your words come slowly, sometimes trailing off as you shift in your chair, but let the final note carry a worn smile.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Confession You Can Barely Whisper
instruction: It's late at night, dark, and you're confessing something to someone you cherish—a betrayal, a secret love, a truth that will change everything. Your voice is barely above a whisper because speaking louder would shatter you: 'There's something I need to tell you.' Every word costs you. Your breathing is uneven, catching. 'I've been carrying this and it's breaking me.' There's tenderness here, such tenderness it hurts: 'You're so good. You deserve better than this.' Your throat tightens. Long pauses where you almost can't continue. 'I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.' The emotion builds not through volume but through the weight of silence, the tremor in your breath. End with the actual confession—whatever it is—delivered so quietly, so brokenly, that it's almost a prayer. Transform from desperate secrecy to unburdened grief.

title: What I've Never Told You in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night. You're lying next to someone in the intimate darkness, and you're about to whisper something you've never said aloud. Begin with your breathing—just breath, settling into the vulnerability of night and closeness. Then start speaking about a real tender feeling you've held back in your actual life (it doesn't have to be about the person you're imagining—let it be a true pocket of unexpressed tenderness in you). Whisper it like a confession that terrifies you. As you speak, let the relief of finally saying it war with the fear of exposure. Your voice should be barely audible at times, trembling, catching on words. End by asking a question that makes you even more vulnerable than the confession itself.

title: The Shaken Prayer
instruction: You are a young boy, kneeling on a cold wooden floor in a dark room, hands clasped so tightly your knuckles ache. A storm rages outside—thunder rattles the window, and a loose shutter bangs every few seconds. You are praying, but it's not a gentle prayer. Your mother is sick, and you are furious at God for letting her suffer. Start with a trembling, hushed plea, your voice catching on each word as pain bleeds through—your head bowed, tears dripping onto your fists. But as you remember the sleepless nights watching her cough, the anger rises. Your jaw tightens, the rhythm of your words becomes sharper, more accusing. Let the storm outside punctuate your anger. End with a bitter, hissed demand, not a request—your faith cracking under the weight of your rage.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Silence
instruction: You're a young man sitting in a stark interview room, facing a police officer who barely speaks. The silence between each of your answers feels heavier than any accusation. You start nervously rambling, trying to fill the quiet with justifications and hedging phrases—'I mean, it wasn't really my fault, was it?'—but as the officer just stares, your voice fades. The nervous energy drains away, replaced by a hollow, crushing disappointment in yourself. Your speech becomes slower, quieter, laced with small pauses and sighs, as you admit the truth you've been avoiding: you let someone down, maybe yourself most of all.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Confession Against the Dark
instruction: You are in bed, tangled with someone you've just shared a moment of profound intimacy with. The room is dark, and the only sounds are your slow breathing and the rustle of sheets. You feel utterly exhausted, your body a heavy, malleable weight. As you lie there, a wave of distress creeps in — a specific, embarrassing memory from years ago, when a classmate saw you crying. You want to confess it, to be seen even in your shame, but the words feel thick and clumsy, coming out in slow, husky fragments. Start with the heavy, slow comfort of the silence, but let your voice become tight with the distress and embarrassment, finding its way to a raw, whispered revelation.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present), Distress (clearly present), Embarrassment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Quicksand Struggle: Fighting the Sinking with Diminishing Strength
instruction: You're sinking into quicksand and every movement makes you sink deeper. Your voice starts panicked, nearly screaming, as you describe the sensation of being pulled down. Your narration is frantic, movements described in almost real-time. Then you try the physics—stop moving, float, distribute weight—and your voice becomes desperate in a different way: controlled panic. 'I can't move I can't move.' Your voice cracks as you realize the solution (float, don't fight) requires a kind of surrender your fear won't allow. Include the moment where exhaustion starts replacing panic, where your voice becomes quieter, almost resigned. You're sinking. You can feel it. Your voice becomes almost meditative as you accept it, then suddenly frantic again as your body refuses to give up. This cycle repeats in your narration: desperate, resigned, desperate.

title: Running Through the Field to Save What You Cannot Save
instruction: You're running desperately through tall grass toward something or someone you're about to lose, fighting against time and fate itself. Begin breathless and fierce, describing the grass whipping against your legs like obstacles trying to slow you down, your voice urgent and defiant. Build explosive intensity as you push harder, your tone mixing rage at the unfairness with desperate hope—maybe you can make it, maybe you can change this. Let your voice rise with each sensation of the grass cutting your skin, the ground uneven beneath your feet, everything in the universe conspiring against you. Then break—mid-run, your voice should shatter from fierce determination into helpless sobbing as you realize you won't make it in time, that all your strength means nothing. End on your knees in the grass, describing how it feels against your palms as you collapse, your fierce protectiveness dissolving into whispered devastation and the terrible stillness of being too late.
inspired_by: Walking Through a Field of Tall Grass

title: The Couch Confession
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman slumped deep into a worn couch, legs splayed, head lolling against a cushion after an exhausting day. You're muttering to yourself, barely moving your jaw, voice mushy and lazy from your collapsed posture. Start with heavy doubt — replaying a conversation where you think you messed up, your voice slow, trailing off into sighs. Then a flicker of teasing, a wry half-smile as you mock your own overthinking. Finally, let the doubt dissolve into overwhelming relief as you realize it actually went fine — let your breath deepen, voice soften, and end with a slow, contented murmur. Keep the delivery natural, with pauses, shifts in weight, and distracted touches to your hair or the fabric.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (slightly present), Doubt (extremely present), Relief (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting your mother after finding letters she wrote but never sent to you during the fifteen years you were estranged. Start with cold, measured anger—reading phrases from her letters aloud in a voice dripping with controlled bitterness. 'You wrote that you missed me. You wrote that you were sorry.' You're holding every word like a weapon. But as you continue reading, you find a letter she wrote the day you were born, describing how afraid she was of failing you. Your voice wavers. The anger begins collapsing into something more complicated—hurt, longing, the grief of lost years. You try to pull the rage back, to protect yourself, but it's too late. End by asking her a simple question—'Why didn't you send them?'—and your voice is no longer angry at all. It's the voice of a child who just wanted to be reached for. Small. Aching. Still hoping.

title: The Guardian's Breaking Point
instruction: You're a fierce protector—a parent, a sibling, a soldier—holding someone you love who's been hurt, and you're trying to comfort them while rage tears through you. Start with forced gentleness, your voice tight and controlled, soothing them even though fury is coiling in your chest. But as you speak, the rage breaks through—you can't hold it. You start making promises, vows of vengeance, your voice rising to something almost savage. Then you look at their face, and everything shifts. The rage collapses into helplessness because you couldn't protect them, and that breaks you more than anything. By the end, you're sobbing, your voice destroyed, oscillating between whispered apologies and fierce declarations of love. You're both terrifying and utterly vulnerable. Let yourself be ferocious and shattered at the same time.

title: Unraveling the Inheritance: Confronting a Parent About a Lifetime of Silence
instruction: You've just discovered a family secret—an inheritance left to a sibling you never knew existed, a love affair your parent hid for decades, money stolen from your childhood savings. Confront your aging parent with this betrayal. Start with cold, measured anger—you came prepared, you rehearsed this. But as they remain silent or make excuses, let your control slip. Your voice should shift from prosecutorial and sharp to something more wounded and childlike: 'Why wasn't I enough? Why did you lie to me?' Let rage dissolve into the heartbroken confusion of a child who still, despite everything, desperately wants their parent's love and explanation. End not with resolution, but with the exhausted, throat-raw realization that you may never get the answer you need. Move from righteous fury to painful, vulnerable pleading.
inspired_by: Acting Calm During a Crisis to Reassure Others

title: The Tasting Room Turn Down
instruction: You're at a wine tasting gala, swirling a deep red in your glass. Across the room, you see your ex — the one who left you for someone younger — and they're laughing, arm draped around that new person. For a moment, you're lost in envy, your throat tight as you watch them. But then a stunning stranger slides up next to you, compliments your choice, and places a hand on your lower back. You feel a ripple of genuine pleasure — but you're not ready. Their hand lingers, and you have to turn them down without hurting them. Start with a tight, forced chuckle as you set your glass down, then speak. Your voice rises with nervous warmth at first, then hardens into a flat, deliberate 'no' — the wall slamming down. You shift weight, clear your throat, and find your center: 'I'm flattered, really. But I can't. Not tonight.' Let the envy and pleasure both color your words — the envy darkens your pause, the pleasure softens your refusal.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Echoes of Disappointment
instruction: You are walking down a long, dimly lit hallway after a painful argument with your child. Your footsteps slap against the hardwood floor, each one sending a small echo around you. At first, your voice is tight with raw disappointment — you mutter to yourself, frustrated, voice cracking slightly. As you reach the far end, the insulted quiet of the hallway makes you stop. You turn back, and your voice softens into a trembling, hollow resignation, fighting to hold back tears.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Lawyer Cross-Examination
instruction: You're cross-examining the prosecution's star witness—and you know they're lying because your investigator showed you the evidence. You're methodical, sharp, clinical, dismantling their testimony piece by piece. Your voice is that of someone skilled in legal violence. But then the witness starts crying, admitting they were coerced. Your voice becomes almost pitying. You press anyway because your job is to defend your client. Your voice maintains its ruthless efficiency even as you're watching someone break in real time. Show someone doing their job while hating themselves for being good at it.

title: What We Never Said
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the dark, and you need to confess something that will change everything between you. Begin in a whisper, your voice barely audible, testing whether you have the courage to continue. You're not angry, just heartbroken—maybe you've realized you're not in love anymore, or you've kept a devastating secret, or you've been pretending for so long you've forgotten who you really are. Your voice is gentle, aching, full of tenderness for what you're about to destroy. Every pause is loaded with all the years between you. By the end, you're crying softly, not for drama, but because love isn't always enough, and saying this truth out loud is both necessary and unbearable.

title: The Interview We Postponed
instruction: You're finally asking your estranged best friend, former spouse, or lost sibling the questions you should have asked before everything fell apart—but you're asking them now, in their absence, perhaps at their empty chair, their old apartment, their grave. Begin in bitter resentment, asking accusatory questions: Why did you leave? How could you? But as you continue this one-sided interview, let your questions become more honest, more vulnerable: What was I too afraid to ask you? What did you need from me? What question would have changed everything? Feel anger dissolving into grief, grief opening into gratitude for what you did share, gratitude mixing with devastating regret. End with one final question that contains both love and loss. Your voice should transform from sharp blame to breaking tenderness to bittersweet acceptance.

title: Fishbowl Farewell
instruction: You're in a sterile hospital room, a clear oxygen mask strapped over your mouth and nose. The hiss of air and the muffled plastic make every word a chore. You're speaking to a lover who just ended things—you have to stay calm because you can't even breathe without the machine. Start with a brittle, dismissive tone, your words clipped and tight with contempt. As you keep talking, the mask fogs, forcing you to pause, and the longing slips through, raw and unguarded, like a twitch you can't help. Let your voice crack with the ache of wanting them back, even as you force a hollow goodbye.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Hurt That Won't Stop Laughing
instruction: You're a father with a cracked rib, playing a tickle game with your four-year-old daughter. Every time you try to speak, the laughter rips through your chest like glass, but her giggles are so contagious you can't stop. Begin with a desperate, pained plea for her to stop—each word a squeezed-out wheeze, gasping for air—but as you hear her joy, the cringe of agony melts into a raw, ecstatic surrender. Let your voice crack and squeak, run out of breath mid-word, then find a new note of blissful exhaustion. End with a broken, breathless whisper that holds both the ache and the pure love.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Gratitude at the Edge of Loss
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love deeply—they're leaving for a journey they won't return from, or you're both aware this is the last time you'll see each other. Start by thanking them for specific moments, laughing through your words as you remember beautiful times together. Your voice is warm, almost light. But underneath, the grief is already there, threading through every word. As you continue, the laughter starts mixing with tears—you're crying and laughing at the same time, grateful and devastated. Halfway through, you break for a moment, trying to hold it together, but then you let yourself feel it all. By the end, you're speaking through sobs, but there's also profound peace, acceptance, even joy mixed with the heartbreak. 'Thank you' becomes both a celebration and a farewell. Let the contradictions live together in your voice.

title: The Shift Supervisor's Last Stand
instruction: You're an aging shift supervisor in a noisy warehouse, standing near a malfunctioning conveyor belt that's been clanking for hours. You feel helpless because management rejected your budget request for repairs, and bitter because this factory has worn you down for decades. Speak to your new assistant, trying to explain why you can't fix this machine anymore—your voice should start with forced calm, then crack with frustration and a dark, weary laugh as you realize there's no point in fighting. Let the echo of your words get swallowed by the machinery hum; pause when a forklift beeps nearby, and let your tone shift from pretended control to raw, quiet defeat.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Joy and Goodbye at the Hospice Window
instruction: You're sitting with someone you love who's choosing to end their suffering, and they've just told you the most beautiful, absurd joke from your shared past. You start laughing—real, genuine laughter that fills the room—and you can't stop even though tears are streaming down your face. Your voice dances between hilarity and heartbreak: 'Remember when we—' and you're laughing, then 'God, I'm going to miss—' and you're crying, then laughing again because they're laughing too. Let the contradictions live fully: gratitude for every ridiculous moment, grief that there won't be more, joy that you had this at all, devastation that it's ending. Your voice should crack between emotions seamlessly—not performed transitions, but the authentic chaos of feeling everything at once. End with a whispered 'thank you' that contains both perfect peace and absolute shattering, spoken while still smiling through tears.

title: The Last Drop
instruction: You are a young woman in a drought-stricken camp, severely dehydrated for days. Your lips are cracked, your throat burns, and each word is an effort—your voice comes out thin, scratchy, with audible clicks and sticky smacks. You are staring at a woman you once called a friend; she is casually sipping from a canteen, water trickling down her chin. At first, you feel nothing—just a hollow, numb exhaustion—as you speak about the heat and the dust. But as she refuses to share, a sharp, simmering jealousy rises in your chest, tightening your throat and making your words more bitter. Let the dryness physically break your voice, and let the envy crack through the numbness by the end. Speak: 'Hot today. Feels like the sky forgot us. You have a whole canteen... just for yourself. I remember when we shared everything. Guess that's gone now, too. Fine. I'll find my own.'
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: Your parent, who abandoned you as a child, has reached out after fifteen years wanting to reconnect. You've agreed to meet. Begin with controlled, cold politeness—you've rehearsed this, you won't give them the satisfaction of seeing your pain. As you speak, let the rehearsed words start to crumble. The hurt child inside you begins to surface—raw questions you've carried for years: 'Why wasn't I enough? Did you ever think about me? Do you have any idea what you did to me?' Let your voice move from icy distance to volcanic rage to something more devastating—the vulnerable, abandoned child still waiting to be chosen. End not with anger, but with the heartbreaking honesty of someone finally asking for what they needed all along.

title: Laughing Through the Farewell
instruction: You're packing up your childhood home for the last time, and your sibling just found the ridiculous matching Halloween costumes from 1987. You burst into genuine laughter: 'Oh my God, we actually wore these in public!' The laughter is real and bright, but tears are already forming: 'Mom kept everything, didn't she?' Your voice holds both joy and heartbreak: 'Remember how she'd save every terrible drawing, every failed science project?' You're smiling through tears now, the emotions inseparable: 'She thought everything we touched was precious.' The gratitude swells in your chest even as grief threatens to overwhelm you: 'How did we get so lucky to be loved like that?' Your voice breaks with the beautiful contradiction of it all: 'I'm so grateful and so angry that she's gone, and I don't know how to feel both things at once but here I am.' You hold up the costume, laughing and crying simultaneously: 'She'd tell us to stop being so serious. She'd say this is perfect—crying and laughing, just like life.' End with your voice full of wonder and devastation: 'I found peace in the chaos of missing her. She's everywhere in this house, and somehow that makes letting it go possible.' You're simultaneously destroyed and made whole by memory.

title: Dancing at Your Funeral
instruction: You are delivering a eulogy for someone who taught you joy, and you've decided to honor them by telling their funniest stories, even as your heart is shattering. Begin with genuine laughter—a memory so ridiculous and perfect you can't help but smile. But let the laughter catch, become entangled with tears you're trying to hold back. Your voice should oscillate between warm amusement and grief that threatens to overwhelm you. Include moments where you break into helpless laughter at their absurdity, then immediately feel the crushing weight that they're gone and will never be absurd again. End with profound gratitude that makes your voice rich and full even as it breaks—thank them for teaching you that sorrow and joy aren't opposites but can live in the same breath. Your final words should be both a celebration and a goodbye, laughter and tears inseparable.
inspired_by: Calling a Suicide Hotline: Both Sides

title: Chaos and Communion
instruction: You're attempting an impossibly complicated dish for your chosen family's gathering after surviving something terrible together—illness, loss, shared trauma. Everything goes spectacularly wrong: timers fail, ingredients spill, smoke fills the kitchen. But you're laughing, really laughing, even as tears stream down your face. Your narration bounces between frustrated curses and genuine joy, between 'This is a complete disaster' and 'I'm so grateful we're all still here to see this disaster.' Find the sweet spot where grief and celebration live together—where you're simultaneously mourning what you've lost and celebrating what remains. Let your voice break with emotion even as you giggle at the absurdity. End with profound gratitude spoken through both laughter and tears, acknowledging that the mess doesn't matter because you're together, you're alive, you survived.

title: The Wall Holds Me Up
instruction: You're leaning against a cold brick wall outside a dimly lit bar, arms crossed, trying to look casual. You're waiting for someone who owes you money — a man you once trusted but now fear. He's walking over, and you force a teasing grin to hide the tremor in your chest. Your voice comes out low and steady, but the wall behind you presses into your shoulder blades like a warning. As he gets closer, you catch a glint in his eye — maybe he's not here to fight. A wild hope flickers through your ribs, and your voice softens, losing its mockery. Say: 'Well, well. Took you long enough. Thought you'd crawl under a rock, Carl. But hey... maybe we can still work this out. Maybe.' Let the first part carry a sharp, trembly tease, then drop to something almost gentle and uncertain by the end.
emotions_sampled: Fear (extremely present), Teasing (very intensely present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Injured Child and Screaming at the Universe
instruction: Your child has been hurt—an accident, an attack, something sudden and terrible—and you're holding them, waiting for help that feels too far away. Start with fierce, protective tenderness: 'I've got you, baby, I've got you, you're okay, you're okay.' Your voice is shaking but strong—you're their rock. But underneath, panic is rising. As you keep talking to them—'Stay with me, keep your eyes open'—your terror starts breaking through. Your voice gets louder, more desperate. Suddenly you're not talking to them anymore—you're screaming at God, at fate, at whoever's listening: 'DON'T YOU TAKE THEM! NOT MY BABY!' Rage and helplessness explode out of you. Then you catch yourself, return to them, voice dropping back to tender but now broken, tears streaming: 'I'm here, I'm not going anywhere.' The arc moves from controlled strength to wild desperation to shattered devotion.
inspired_by: Talking to a Baby Who Just Said Their First Word

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child before leaving for a mission you know you won't return from. They don't know this is permanent. Start with forced brightness, packing their lunch, making jokes about being home for their birthday. But as they ask innocent questions—'Will you really be back in time?'—your voice begins to crack. You're memorizing their face, the way they say your name. By the end, you're holding them, whispering promises you can't keep, your voice breaking between 'I love you' and trying not to sob. The morning light feels unbearable. You must let go but you can't, and they can feel something is wrong even if they don't understand what.

title: The Floor's Confession
instruction: You are an older man, alone in your bedroom, lying curled on your side on the floor after a long day. Your voice is soft, breathy, and intimate, with one lung pressed against the carpet. You're replaying a memory from decades ago—a moment you've never told anyone about—and as you speak it aloud, you're startled by how funny it actually is. Start with a weary, distant tone, but as the memory unfolds, let amusement creep in, building until you're almost giggling to yourself, your body shaking slightly on the floor. Your voice should stay low and cozy, but the laughter leaks through, hiccupping in your chest, making you lose your train of thought and start again.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Bitter Bite
instruction: You are a tough, middle-aged man sitting alone at a cheap diner table. A plate of stale, rock-hard crackers sits before you — the only thing you can afford. As you force yourself to chew, each crunch feels like an insult. Start with a heavy, helpless sigh, then speak low and rough to yourself, disgusted by your situation. Let your voice crack with frustration as you mention being stuck here, trapped by bad luck. Midway, you pause to swallow hard, then continue, but your tone shifts to a quieter, sadder resignation — not giving up, just weary. Keep the chewing natural, with irregular pauses and sharp crunching sounds that interrupt your words. End with a long, defeated exhale.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Quiet Lullaby
instruction: You are a teenager, feminized and disoriented, lying in a soft bed after an intense scene. Your Dominant has left the room for a moment, and you hear their footsteps returning. Your voice is small, trembling, and childlike from the emotional drop — you feel a sliver of ecstasy from the release, but also a creeping disgust at what you just did. When they enter, whisper to them, mixing gratitude with a faint, malicious glee that you surrendered so fully. Let your voice crack, then soften, as you realize you’re safe. Speak as if you’re half-asleep, shivering under a blanket, and finishing a glass of water.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Disgust (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You're rehearsing aloud a toast for your ex-lover's wedding—someone you still ache for, someone who chose another. Begin performing the 'proper' version: gracious, warm, appropriately humorous, wishing them well with controlled elegance. But as you speak, let the mask slip. Repeat certain phrases with different inflections. A joke turns bitter. A blessing curdles into something else. Let genuine joy for their happiness war with your own grief. Your voice should break and rebuild multiple times—laughing genuinely at a shared memory, then choking on it. You're furious and grateful. You're devastated and sincerely happy for them. End in a place where all these contradictions exist simultaneously, where you're genuinely celebrating their joy while mourning your own loss, transformed from false composure into honest, messy, impossible complexity.
inspired_by: Actor has tried a choice but it isn't producing the desired emotional response

title: The Late Shift Confrontation
instruction: You're an older woman working a late-night shift at a small grocery store, running on pure adrenaline after 14 hours. You've hit that second wind—the kind where your voice gets fast, giggly, and a little manic. A customer has just accused you of overcharging them, and you're furious. Start with a bright, almost bubbly 'Oh, I'm sorry about that,' but as you notice their condescending tone, your anger spikes. Let your voice become sharp and scolding, your laughter turning bitter. End with a weary, clipped 'Next time, check your own math before blaming me,' as the energy crashes.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Protect Them Anymore
instruction: You're watching someone you love—a child, a partner, a sibling—make a choice that will destroy them, and you're powerless to stop it. Start with fierce protectiveness, your voice strong and urgent: 'Please, listen to me, you don't have to do this.' You're trying everything—pleading, reasoning, commanding—your voice rising with desperate intensity. But as you speak, you feel them pulling away, see the determination in their eyes, and the helplessness crashes over you like a wave. Your voice begins to crack and break, rage dissolving into tears: 'I can't lose you, I can't—' You're cycling rapidly between anger at them for not listening, fury at yourself for not knowing how to reach them, and devastating, overwhelming love. Let it all pour out—shouting that collapses into sobbing, fierce demands that become whispered begging. End with the terrible, quiet acceptance that you have to let them go, your voice raw and broken but finding one last thread of love to offer: 'I'll be here. Whatever happens, I'll be here.'

title: The Last Hour Before You Go
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love deeply who will leave forever in one hour—they're moving across the world, or this is a deathbed farewell, or circumstances are pulling you permanently apart. You cannot speak; perhaps they're sleeping, or words have all been said, or speaking would shatter you both. Sit with them. Let yourself feel everything—the weight of every shared moment, the approaching absence, the love, the unfairness, the gratitude for having known them. Begin with quiet denial or numbness, protecting yourself. As minutes pass, let the reality sink deeper into your body. Allow your emotional state to shift—perhaps from holding back to letting the grief move through you, or from desperate clinging to a kind of sacred acceptance. Let your breath, your stillness, your presence tell the story of loving someone you must release.

title: The Reunion: Seeing Them Again After Everything
instruction: You're face-to-face with someone you thought you'd lost forever—through estrangement, separation, or circumstances beyond your control. They're here, real, standing in front of you. Begin with disbelief: 'It's you. It's really you.' Your voice wavers between laughter and tears—you can't believe this is happening. Joy surges through you, almost manic with relief: 'You're here. Oh god, you're actually here.' But beneath the joy, there's an undercurrent of grief for all the lost time, all the moments you missed. Your laughter becomes tinged with sadness, your smile audible but breaking. You're trying to hold onto the happiness while acknowledging the pain: 'I thought I'd never—I thought we'd never—' Your voice cracks. Let gratitude and heartbreak coexist. End in a place of bittersweet peace, voice soft and wondering, as you simply say their name, holding both the joy of now and the ghost of everything that was lost.
inspired_by: Finding Shelter in a Blizzard: Relief Becoming Hypothermia Complacency

title: Confessing in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night, barely above a whisper. You're lying next to someone—maybe a spouse, maybe your closest friend—and you're finally saying the thing you've hidden for years. Start with your voice barely audible, testing the words in the darkness. Maybe it's 'I haven't loved you the way you needed for a long time' or 'I knew about your secret and said nothing' or 'I'm the reason everything fell apart.' Your throat tightens with shame. Long pauses where you can barely breathe. The words come in fragments, catching on tears you're trying to hold back. You're terrified of their response but also deeply relieved to finally speak truth. Your voice trembles between self-loathing and desperate hope for understanding. End with a raw, quiet plea that's barely more than breath: either 'Please don't leave me' or 'I understand if you do.' Every word should feel like it costs everything to say.
inspired_by: Meth Psychosis: Convincing Yourself of a Delusion

title: BDSM Aftercare: Coming Back Down
instruction: You've just finished an intense scene and are holding your partner. Your voice transitions from the commanding/playful scene voice to extreme tenderness. Speak softly, slowly, repetitively — 'You did so well,' 'I've got you,' 'You're safe.' Include sounds of blanket rustling, water sipping. The partner (also voiced by you) responds in a small, shaky, child-like voice. Show the vulnerability and trust in the acoustic intimacy. Both voices should be exhausted but warm.

title: Comprehending Finally
instruction: Your mother's dying words suddenly make sense. You're alone in the car. The meaning of what she said—something you've heard a thousand times—suddenly unlocks. Your voice goes quiet first, almost holding its breath. Then it cracks: a recognition so physical it's like getting punched. Words spill: 'Oh my God, she was telling me...' Panic, grief, gratitude all fighting in your throat. End standing still, understanding finally but too late.

title: Secrets Told to Sleeping Ears
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a hospital bed, someone who may or may not be able to hear you. You're confessing something you've carried alone for years—maybe a secret love, maybe a terrible choice you made, maybe forgiveness you never voiced. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and careful, as if the words themselves are fragile. Start with hesitant half-starts, clearing your throat, testing if you can even say this aloud. Let emotion accumulate slowly, your voice thickening with unshed tears, pausing to breathe through the tightness in your chest. End with a kind of broken relief, finally saying the thing that's lived in your throat for so long, your words dissolving into tears that are somehow both grief and strange, quiet peace.

title: The Rocket's Flicker
instruction: You are an elderly man in your living room, speaking rapidly to your daughter who just walked in. Your mind is racing — you’re convinced you’ve solved a major world problem, but you keep losing your thread. Start with manic confidence, your voice loud and fast, ideas spilling out. As you speak, a sudden confusion hits — you forget what you were saying. The energy collapses into a quiet, bewildered plea. Let your voice crack, slow down, and show the fragile core beneath the grandiosity. Speak as if you’re trying to hold onto a thought that keeps slipping away.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Spark in the Crowd
instruction: You’re an older activist on a worn wooden soapbox at a busy street corner, voice already hoarse from an hour of shouting. The crowd is restless, traffic noise bleeds through, and you have to project harder than you want. Watch the people—one young listener locks eyes with you, nodding. Your voice changes: the strain softens, a laugh catches in your throat, and you find yourself grinning between words, speaking faster, a trembling joy rising. End clear and bright, almost singing, as you realize this moment matters.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Long Walk Home
instruction: You are an older man walking down a long, empty corridor in an old school building after hours. At the far end, you spot a close friend you haven't seen in months. Your voice echoes off the walls as you start teasing them loudly, but as the sound bounces back and your footsteps fall into a rhythm, you feel a quiet relief washing over you. Let your teasing tone soften naturally with each step, until by the time you reach them, your voice is warm and deeply content, almost like a sigh. Allow the reverb to affect your pauses—maybe you chuckle at the echo, or slow down to savour the moment.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (clearly present), Relief (slightly present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Gratitude at the Moment of Unbearable Loss
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone leaving—whether to death, distance, or a choice that separates you forever. But instead of begging them to stay, you're thanking them. Start with your voice warm but unsteady, trying to smile through the words. List specific moments, specific gifts they gave you, ways they changed your life. Your gratitude must be genuine, detailed, real—but underneath it, your voice should quiver with suppressed grief. As you continue, the two emotions must coexist impossibly: you're laughing softly at a memory while tears are clearly in your voice. You're expressing joy for having known them while your heart audibly breaks. The contradiction should feel unbearable. End with the most devastating thank you—thanking them for loving you, even though that love is ending. Your final words should somehow hold both peace and devastation, acceptance and agony, gratitude and goodbye.

title: The Vigil: Confessing to Someone Who Can't Hear You
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma or deep sleep - maybe a lover, maybe an estranged sibling - and you're confessing something you've carried for years. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, tender and careful, telling them something beautiful about how you see them. Then let the confession come: the jealousy, the secret resentment, the way you've failed them, or the love you've hidden. Your voice should tremble and catch, emotions rising in your throat. End by admitting what you're most afraid of - that they'll wake up and things will go back to how they were, or that they won't wake up and you'll never get to say this when they can respond. Move from gentle admiration through guilty confession to raw, choking fear. Let silences speak. Let your breath shake.
inspired_by: The Final Words: What You'd Actually Say

title: Testimony of Skin
instruction: You are describing a moment of physical pain—an injury, illness, or intense bodily sensation—but you refuse to let it be only suffering. Start with your voice raw and strained, body tense, describing the hurt. But then, even as the pain continues, begin noticing: the strength of your heartbeat fighting, the warmth of your own blood, the miracle of your body's response, the hands that helped you, the air filling your lungs. Let your voice grow fiercer, more visceral—not denying the pain but claiming your aliveness within it. Your breath should become purposeful rather than panicked. Transform from victim of your body to warrior inhabiting it. End with your voice full of savage, physical gratitude for being alive enough to feel anything at all.

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You are confronting your mother across the kitchen table about why she stayed silent when you needed her protection as a child. Start with careful, controlled anger - you've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. Notice the chip in the table, the hum of the refrigerator, her hands folded in that familiar way. As you speak, create the specific memory in your mind - see yourself as that child, smell the house as it was then, feel what you felt. Let your controlled anger crack as the images become more vivid and real. By the end, you've moved through rage into something rawer - perhaps unexpected grief, or a desperate need for her to finally see you. The images you build should make the past present, until you're no longer just remembering - you're there again.
inspired_by: Glass Menagerie Walter Mitty Option — Scene 1 Fantasy Imaging Exercise

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye You've Rehearsed for Years
instruction: You're finally going no-contact with a toxic parent, and against all expectation, you're laughing. Start with genuine, slightly hysterical laughter—freedom mixed with disbelief. 'I'm actually doing this. After all these years, I'm finally choosing me.' Your voice should sound both liberated and on the edge of tears. Let the laughter keep breaking through even as you're saying painful truths: 'You'll never change, and that's okay now. That's actually okay.' The emotion should be beautifully contradictory—joy and grief happening simultaneously. End with your voice settling into something quieter, still smiling through tears: 'I'm going to be happy without you, and that feels like the saddest, most wonderful thing in the world.' The final words should carry both triumph and heartbreak.
inspired_by: Realizing You're Repeating Your Parent's Mistakes

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about why they were never there—not at graduations, not during your divorce, not when you needed them most. Begin with carefully controlled anger, words you've rehearsed for years, voice tight and measured. But as you speak, something shifts. You hear how old they sound, see how small they've become. Your accusations start to falter. The rage cracks open to reveal the child underneath who just wanted to be seen. Your voice breaks from sharp and cutting to pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in the awful space between anger and forgiveness, where you're asking them to explain the unexplainable, your voice stripped of all armor, just naked need.

title: The Unforgotten View
instruction: You're an older woman standing alone on your back porch at dusk, looking out over the garden you and your late husband planted forty years ago. The air is still, your hands rest on the railing, and for a moment, the quiet beauty of the evening wraps around you—clear, open, serene. But then a memory surfaces: a younger neighbor, shirtless, mowing his lawn earlier today, and the sudden, unwelcome flicker of desire in your chest—a reminder of years of loneliness after your husband's affair. Start with a soft, almost wistful reflection on the garden, but let your voice gradually tighten with bitterness as the lust feels like a betrayal. End on a sharp, dismissive sigh, as if shaking off a ghost that refuses to leave. You might pause to rub your arms against a chill, or clear your throat mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: I'm Laughing Because If I Don't, I'll Scream
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, hand on the old wooden table, just after your father's funeral. You've discovered he left the house to your sibling who abandoned the family years ago, while you stayed and cared for him. Start with an almost hysterical laugh - isn't it funny? This table where you sat doing homework while he criticized you, where you served him meals when he couldn't feed himself, where you held his hand and forgave him for everything. Your laughter should sound unhinged, wrong, catching in your throat. Run your fingers over the wood grain while you laugh-cry, voice swinging between bitter amusement and breaking grief. Describe touching this table every day for years, how the wood became smooth under your hands, how you earned every inch of it. Then your laughter dissolves entirely into something else - not quite peace, but a strange, exhausted gratitude. Your voice softens, almost serene. You don't need the table. You had him at the end. That's enough. Touch it one last time with genuine tenderness and walk away.
inspired_by: Running Your Hand Over a Smooth, Polished Wooden Table

title: What You Took From Me
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the childhood she stole by choosing addiction over you. Start with trembling restraint, voice tight: 'I need to say something I've held for twenty years.' Then let it build — the birthday parties she missed drunk, the times you walked yourself to school at seven years old, the shame of teachers asking where she was. Your voice rises not with volume but with decades of suppressed pain: 'I learned to cook because you were too high to feed me.' But midway through, something breaks. You realize she's smaller than your anger, just a broken person who couldn't be what you needed. The rage dissolves into something more painful — grief for both of you. End exhausted, voice barely there: 'I needed a mother. You needed help. We both lost.' You're not forgiving her, just finally releasing the weight.

title: Fever Dream
instruction: You are in the grip of intense physical sensation mixed with emotional overwhelm - perhaps fever and hallucination, perhaps passionate reunion after long separation, perhaps rage so physical it feels like your body is burning. Begin by locating actual sensations in your body right now - heat, tension, restlessness, softness. As you move and speak, track moment-to-moment what you're genuinely feeling: 'My hands are shaking... I feel power... I feel scared of how much I want this... I feel disgust... I feel exhilaration.' Let the physical and emotional blur together naturally. When you notice yourself indicating intensity rather than experiencing it, pause and ask what's really present in your body. Don't decide in advance whether this ends in surrender or rejection, ecstasy or exhaustion - follow the true progression of sensations and feelings to wherever they lead.

title: Why Won't She Answer?
instruction: You're a teenage girl, curled up on your bedroom floor, phone pressed to your ear. Your best friend — who you confessed your love to yesterday — isn't picking up. You've been sobbing for ten minutes, your breath catching in sharp, hiccup-like gasps. Through the mess of tears and phlegm, you try to leave a voicemail. At first, you're desperate and pleading, a high, wavering pitch cracking as you beg her to just talk to you. Then, a new, raw confusion breaks through: why would she just disappear? Your voice thickens with bewilderment, your words breaking off and starting again, as you try to piece together what you did wrong. By the end, your crying softens into a hollow, exhausted bewilderment that you're just not good enough to understand.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Fever Dream of Rage and Want
instruction: You're in the aftermath of a physical ordeal - a marathon you pushed through on a broken ankle, a night of dancing that became an exorcism, a fight you survived - and your body is simultaneously flooded with pain, exhaustion, and an almost transcendent aliveness. Your adrenaline is crashing, your muscles are shaking, and you need to speak to someone who isn't there - an ex-lover who destroyed you, a version of yourself you've outgrown, a ghost you're finally releasing. Begin with your breath ragged and uncontrolled, your voice raw and almost savage, your words emerging between gasps and groans of physical sensation. Let your fury and your desire tangle together - curse them while admitting what you still crave, laugh bitterly while crying, let your body's pain amplify every emotional wound. As your body begins to give out, let your voice soften into something primally honest. End in near-collapse, whispering words of release that are equally goodbye and gratitude, your physical and emotional exhaustion merging into something strangely sacred.
inspired_by: Actor needs to prepare instrumentally before a rehearsal

title: Holding Pattern
instruction: You are an elderly woman on the phone with a utility company, trying to correct a billing error that threatens your pension. You begin with your practiced, hyper-feminized 'customer service voice'—bright, high-pitched, full of polite uptalk—but as the representative puts you on hold repeatedly and dismisses your concerns, your mask cracks. Let your voice waver, lose its polish, and drop in pitch as fear and helplessness seep through. By the end, you are barely holding back tears, speaking in a raw, trembling whisper, no longer able to pretend. Speak naturally: fumble with a pen, let a sigh escape, pause as you hear muzak, and let the final plea come out broken.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: A Darkened Chapel
instruction: You are alone in a dimly lit chapel late at night. You kneel, hands clasped, but your mind is restless. Begin with a hushed, reverent tone, speaking to a presence you feel but cannot see. As you confess your shame, a flicker of anger rises – at yourself, at the silence. Let your voice waver, pause, and tighten as you struggle to maintain the rhythm of prayer. By the end, the anger dissipates into a weary plea.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Apple of Discord
instruction: You are a mother trying to get your child to put on their shoes while you eat a crisp apple. You're already running late, and each bite feels louder and more frustrating as your child dawdles. Start with sharp, irritable snaps between crunches, letting the hard sound of the apple underline your impatience. Midway, pause to swallow, then your voice softens — not with warmth, but with tired surrender as you realize you're exhausting yourself fighting. End with a quiet, resigned plea, the crunch fading as you stop chewing.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Rage Against the Storm That Took Everything
instruction: You're standing where your home once was, destroyed by the tornado three months ago. Start calmly describing distant thunder with bitter irony - you used to find peace in these sounds. But as the thunder grows, let your composure shatter. Your voice should explode with fury at the sky, at nature's indifference, screaming about how you trusted in the beauty of storms, how you found them peaceful, and they repaid you by taking everything - your house, your security, your child's favorite blanket, the ashes of your mother you can't find. Rage should crack into helpless sobbing as you realize you're screaming at clouds, that your anger is useless. End exhausted, voice hoarse, collapsing from fury into defeated whispers: 'I just want to feel safe during a storm again. I just want that back.'
inspired_by: Listening to the Distant Sound of Thunder on a Warm Evening

title: Thank You for Breaking My Heart
instruction: You're thanking someone who devastated you—a parent who failed you, a lover who betrayed you, a friend who abandoned you—and you mean it sincerely even as you're falling apart. Begin with genuine gratitude that feels almost serene, explaining with surprising clarity how their cruelty or absence forced you to become yourself. Let laughter bubble up as you describe the absurd freedom of having nothing left to lose. But weave grief through the gratitude—your voice catching on certain words, a tremor beneath the peace. Build to a moment where you're simultaneously crying and laughing, where 'thank you' and 'fuck you' become indistinguishable, where liberation and loss are the same feeling. End in quiet wonder at your own resilience, still heartbroken, still grateful, holding both truths at once with a voice that shakes but doesn't break.

title: Laughing Through Your Own Eulogy
instruction: You've been given six months to live, and you're recording your own eulogy—determined to make it funny, to leave people laughing instead of crying. You start with a joke about death, your voice bright with dark humor. You're riffing, making light, almost giddy with the absurdity. But then you mention someone specific—a friend, a partner, a child—and your voice wavers mid-laugh. The humor doesn't stop, but grief floods in underneath it. You're still trying to joke, but you're crying now, laughing and sobbing simultaneously. Your voice fractures between bitter comedy and raw heartbreak. 'I'm going to miss you so much' comes out like a punchline and a prayer. End with a laugh that's really a sob, or a sob that's really a laugh—the sound of someone finding the only way they can say goodbye.
inspired_by: Interviewer Asking About Your Worst Mistake

title: The Last Conversation Before the Journey
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is leaving tomorrow on a one-way mission to Mars—or entering hospice—and you're trying to say everything that matters in these final moments together. Start with forced cheerfulness, your voice bright but brittle: 'Remember when we...' You're protecting them from your devastation. Your breath keeps catching. Midway through, the facade cracks—a pause where you almost break, then: 'I don't know how to...' your voice drops to almost nothing, 'how to be in a world without you in it.' The last part is raw acceptance mixed with fierce gratitude: 'Thank you for every single day.' Your voice is simultaneously breaking and becoming whole, grief and love indistinguishable from each other.

title: Screaming the Love Confession You've Buried for Years
instruction: You're confronting someone who's about to marry another person—and you can't stay silent anymore. Start with your voice sharp, angry, accusatory: how dare they ask you to be happy for them. Your rage is a shield for the desperate truth underneath. As they try to respond, your voice explodes—all the years of swallowed feelings erupting in a torrent of furious, passionate confession. You're shouting your love at them like an accusation, like a wound, demanding to know if they ever felt it too. The ferocity cracks mid-sentence, your voice breaking from fury into pleading: stay, choose me, don't do this. End with your voice collapsing into raw vulnerability as you realize they're not going to choose you—the rage dissolving into devastated acceptance, the final words barely audible as you release them and the life you imagined together.
inspired_by: Admitting You Faked Orgasms for Years

title: Defending Someone Who Can't Defend Themselves
instruction: Someone is attacking a person you love—maybe your child, your sibling, your best friend—and they're not here to defend themselves. You start trying to stay reasonable, voice firm but controlled, correcting the lies. But as the attacks continue, as the other person speaks cruel specifics about someone precious to you, your control must explode. Let your voice rise to a roar—fierce, protective, almost feral in its intensity. You're listing everything beautiful about the person they're attacking, every way they're wrong, your words tumbling over each other. But then, mid-fury, you must break. Your rage collapses into helplessness because you can't actually protect them from this. Your voice should crack, become ragged with tears. End quietly, almost pleading, with the devastating admission: 'I can't lose them.' Your protective fury has transformed into naked, terrified vulnerability.

title: Whispering the Secret You've Carried for Years
instruction: Late at night, in the dark, you finally confess something you've never told anyone. Start so quietly they can barely hear you - this has been buried so deep, your body resists saying it aloud. 'I need to tell you something. I... I can't keep this anymore.' The words come in fragments, with long pauses where you almost can't continue. Each sentence requires gathering courage anew. This isn't dramatic confession - it's quiet unraveling. Your voice is tender, exhausted, relieved, and terrified all at once. By the end, you're crying softly, not from pain but from the unexpected lightness of finally being known. Let silence do as much work as words.
inspired_by: Saying 'I'm Fine' When You're Absolutely Not

title: The Last Mile
instruction: You're on your hands and knees at mile 20 of a marathon. The world sways; your daughter's face blurs in your mind. A stranger crouches, offering water. Start speaking in a hollow, confused whisper, struggling to process your collapse—words slur, breath comes in ragged gasps. As you accept the bottle, let a wave of intense gratitude overtake you, tinged with quiet sadness that you can't finish alone. Let your voice crack, pause to sob, and finish with a fragile, sincere 'thank you.'
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (very intensely present), Sadness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Joke That Stung
instruction: You're a teenage guy with a deep voice, sitting on the floor across from your best friend. You've been teasing them for the last five minutes, your voice loud and playful, grinning as you jab. But suddenly you see their eyes water, and the laughter dies in your throat. Now your voice drops—you literally feel yourself shrink, words coming out slower, quieter. You stumble through an apology, voice cracking, and at the end you let out a small, shaky exhale of relief when they nod. Start with the teasing energy still in your voice, then let it hollow out into genuine remorse, then end with a quiet, raw 'I'm sorry, man.'
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Contemplation (slightly present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Gently Swinging in a Porch Swing
instruction: Sit back, letting the porch swing move you gently back and forth. Describe the slow, easy rhythm, the slight breeze brushing against your face, and the light creak of the swing. Speak with a tone of relaxation and nostalgia, as if each swing brings a little more peace, like drifting into a pleasant daydream.

title: The Words We Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your parent in their hospital room about a lifetime of emotional absence, but they're sedated and can barely respond—just squeezing your hand occasionally. Start with careful, measured words: 'I need you to hear this before...' But your careful control dissolves. The years of rehearsed speeches fall away and what comes out is raw and unfiltered: the childhood moments they missed, the times you needed them and they chose work, success, their own pain over you. Your voice moves from quiet accusation to something closer to begging—'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay present?' But as their grip on your hand weakens, your anger transforms into something more complex: a desperate, aching need to forgive them before it's too late, mixed with fury that you're the one who has to do the forgiving. End with contradictory tenderness and unresolved pain.

title: Laughing at the Funeral of the Friend Who Saved Your Life
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for your best friend, the one who pulled you back from the edge years ago, and grief is colliding with absurd, inappropriate joy at the memories. Begin with a story that makes you smile, then laugh—genuinely laugh—at their ridiculous sense of humor: 'She showed up at my apartment with a kazoo and wouldn't leave until I played it. Who does that?' Let the laughter be real, warm, full of love. But mid-laugh, your voice should break. The smile should stay on your face even as tears start, creating that strange dissonance of laughing while crying. 'She saved my life and I couldn't save hers and somehow that's... I can't...' Your voice should oscillate between joy at the memories and devastation at the loss, sometimes in the same sentence. The emotional complexity is that you're genuinely grateful—so grateful you lived, so grateful you knew them—even as your heart is completely shattered. End with a tearful laugh: 'Thank you. God, thank you. I'm so angry you're gone. Thank you.' Let gratitude and grief be completely, simultaneously true.
inspired_by: Admitting You're Jealous of Your Partner's Success

title: Parent Discovering Child's Secret Self-Harm
instruction: You've just discovered evidence of your child's self-harm—scars, tools, something undeniable. You burst into their room, and the confrontation explodes immediately. Start with shock and rage: 'What is this? What the hell is this?' Your voice is loud, almost violent in its intensity—not because you're angry at them, but because you're terrified and don't know how to process it. Demand answers: 'How long? How long has this been happening?' But as they shrink away or try to explain, your fury collapses into desperate, helpless pleading. Your voice drops, becomes choked: 'Why didn't you tell me? Baby, why didn't you...' You're crying now, your voice completely broken. Try to reach for them: 'Let me see. Please let me see.' End with the unbearable recognition of your own failure to notice, to protect them from their own pain. Your final words are barely audible, destroyed: 'I'm your parent. I'm supposed to keep you safe. Even from yourself. Especially from yourself.' Let your voice carry both fierce love and devastating inadequacy.
inspired_by: Firefighter: After Successful Rescue Returns to Station

title: The Last Beam
instruction: You're an older construction worker finishing a late shift on a high-rise. The sun is setting, and the city lights are flickering on. For a moment, you stop tightening a bolt and just stare out between the beams. Your voice starts gruff and weary as you shout over the fading machinery to a coworker, but then you trail off, remembering a view you once shared with someone long gone. Let your voice drop—first harsh and loud, then quieter, more distant, as longing creeps in. Let the hard hat cup your words, and pause as you lose your thought, then find it again.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: A Discovery in the Drawer
instruction: You are an older woman sitting at your office desk, sifting through a stack of old letters. At first, you're mostly distracted, thinking about the day ahead. Then you find an envelope with no return address. As you open it, your interest sharpens. Speak aloud to yourself as you read. Let your voice reflect the shift from idle curiosity to complete absorption. Feel the weight of the paper in your hands. Pause to adjust your glasses or take a sip from your mug. Let your tone change subtly as you realize this letter contains a long-buried secret. End with a quiet, breathy fascination.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Call from the Station
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling from the train station before deployment to a war zone you both know you might not return from. Start with forced brightness—'Hey, I just wanted to hear your voice before I go'—trying to sound casual, almost cheerful. But as you speak, the facade cracks. Your voice becomes tender, urgent: 'Remember that time I promised I'd always protect you?' The memory floods you with love and devastating awareness that you can't keep that promise anymore. End in a whisper, trying not to cry: 'You're going to be okay without me. You have to be.' Let the goodbye remain unspoken but felt in every breath.

title: The Last Stretch
instruction: You are an elderly woman, bent over to pick up a fallen photograph from the floor, the blood rushing to your head, your diaphragm crushed. Start with a bitter edge as you mutter about how no one helps you anymore, your hyper-feminized voice strained and congested. Midway, a doubt creeps in—you question if you even deserve help, if you're just a burden. End with a quiet, trembling admission that maybe you've been pushing everyone away, your voice thick with reluctant, raw vulnerability. Let the physical strain affect your breath and tone, as if you're speaking through the effort of staying upright.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Lost on Market Street
instruction: You are a child, alone on a crowded city street at dusk, separated from your parent. You've been walking and calling for blocks, your voice hoarse from shouting over traffic and sirens. Start with a hopeful burst as you spot a familiar storefront, calling loudly 'Mom? Dad?', straining to be heard. But as the noise continues and no one answers, your energy drains. Let your voice become breathless, drop to a tired murmur; flinch as a siren wails nearby, pausing mid-thought. End softly, almost to yourself, saying you don't know what to do next.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Walking Through a Field of Tall Grass
instruction: Feel the grass brush gently against your legs as you walk, each blade soft and swaying. Describe the way it tickles your skin, moving with the breeze, as if the whole field is alive and breathing with you. Speak with a tone of quiet joy and connection to nature, as if each step through the grass fills you with a sense of freedom and grounding, and each touch is a reminder of the natural world around you.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your entire life. Start with your hands shaking, voice trying to stay measured, reasonable — you've rehearsed this. 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you list the specific moments they weren't there — the recital they missed, the night you needed them and they chose work, the way they never once asked how you really felt — your composure shatters. Your voice rises with decades of buried rage, then suddenly drops to something raw and young: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to stay?' Let the anger crack open to reveal the hurt child underneath. End in near-whisper, with a question that's haunted you forever: 'Did you even want me?' Feel the shift from controlled accusation to complete vulnerability, from fury to the most tender, devastating need.
inspired_by: Hearing Your Child Get Bullied and Intervening

title: The Fierce Protection That Comes Too Late
instruction: You've just discovered someone hurt your child, your younger sibling, or someone you were supposed to protect—and you weren't there to stop it. Start with confusion, voice shaking as you ask them to repeat what they just told you. Then explode into rage, voice rising, fierce and almost feral: 'Who? Who did this to you?' Feel the helpless fury of wanting to destroy someone but knowing it won't undo the harm. Your voice cracks as the rage collapses into anguished sobs: 'I should have known, I should have protected you, why didn't you tell me?' End on your knees, metaphorically or literally, voice raw and stripped bare, desperately promising 'I'm here now, I'm here now'—knowing it's both everything and not enough. The intensity must be visceral, your whole body in your voice.
inspired_by: Confronting Someone About Passive Aggressive Behavior

title: The Moth's Confession
instruction: In the darkness before dawn, whisper a confession to your sleeping lover about something you've kept hidden for years—perhaps a betrayal, a secret fear, or a truth about who you really are. Begin with the quality of something nocturnal and delicate: your movements barely perceptible, your breath light and hesitant, drawn toward their warmth but afraid to land fully. Your voice is almost inaudible, testing each word before releasing it. As you continue speaking in the darkness, something shifts—you become braver, slightly bolder, your whispers gaining substance. By the end, though still quiet, you're no longer fragile and fluttering; you've found a different kind of softness, one that's grounded and honestly tender rather than fearfully tentative. You touch them gently, finally, having transformed your fear into genuine intimacy.

title: The Moment You Realize You Can't Save Them
instruction: You're trying desperately to help someone—talking them down from a ledge, begging them not to leave, frantically explaining why they should stay—and your voice starts urgent, almost aggressive in its intensity. You're talking faster and faster, your voice rising, becoming almost frantic. But mid-sentence, something shifts. You realize nothing you're saying is working. Your fierce determination cracks and suddenly you're not shouting anymore—you're begging. Your voice breaks from powerful to utterly powerless in an instant. 'Please' becomes a whisper. Then rage floods back—at yourself, at them, at the situation—and your voice shakes with fury even as tears choke it. End in complete emotional collapse: your voice reduced to ragged breathing and broken fragments of words as you realize you're helpless. Let your voice show both the fighter and the person who's already grieving.
inspired_by: Speaking While Sexually Aroused and Trying to Hide It

title: Military Commander Realizes the Enemy Position Contains His Son's Unit
instruction: Battle coordinates coming across comms, your voice automatic with command authority. Then you hear the unit designation and recognize it—your son's battalion. Everything continues: you're giving orders, your voice steady. But now you're ordering your own child into potential death.
