Your vocal tempo doesn't change, but your breathing becomes a separate entity. You're compartmentalizing in real time, voice locked into command while internally fractured. Every word is an amputation of your heart.

title: The Texture of Forgiveness
instruction: Whisper a confession to your sleeping partner about something you've done that could end your relationship. Begin in near-silence, barely able to form the words, hyper-aware of their breathing rhythm, the warmth radiating from their body, the exact distance between you. As you confess, let yourself become intensely conscious of physical sensations: the texture of the sheets, the weight of your own body, the taste in your mouth, the precise quality of darkness in the room. This extreme physical awareness should paradoxically make you more emotionally vulnerable, not less. Your whisper should gradually become more urgent yet remain quiet, as if speaking louder would shatter the fragile intimacy of this moment. Transform from someone hiding in confession to someone desperately hoping to be heard even in silence. End by noticing the smallest change in their breathing—did they hear you?—and let that uncertainty fill your final words with aching tenderness.

title: Homecoming Ghosts
instruction: You're returning to your childhood home after your mother's death to pack up her belongings. You find her reading glasses on the kitchen table, exactly where she always left them. Pick them up and really look at them - see the wear on the frames, the smudges on the lenses. Let yourself discover what you actually feel, not what you think you should feel. Begin with numbness or perhaps bitter humor about the absurdity of grief. As you hold this simple object and look around the room, let contradictory emotions surface naturally: maybe anger at her mixed with longing, maybe relief mixed with guilt, maybe gratitude tangled with resentment. Speak to her as if she could hear you, your voice moving through these contradictions without resolving them. End not with closure but with the messy, honest truth of loving someone complicated.
inspired_by: Actor's relationship with scene partner feels artificial, uninvested, or routine; the emotional relationship demanded by material is not being felt

title: Crack of Light
instruction: You are an older man, pressed into a tight ball in the darkest corner of your basement after an earthquake. Your knees ache against your chest, your breath is fast and shallow, and you're talking to yourself in a hushed, boxed-in voice. At first you're utterly confused—mumbling fragments about how you got here, the shaking, the dust. Then you hear a rhythmic scraping overhead, like someone shifting rubble. Let your voice slowly change from dazed bewilderment to a fragile, trembling hope: 'Is that someone? Could it be—maybe they're digging... maybe they're coming for me.' Let your words stumble, pause at each new sound, and end with a quiet, wondering optimism.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Log
instruction: You're a teenager chopping wood in the backyard after your dog died this morning. Each swing is heavy with sadness — you pause, sniffle, wipe your nose on your sleeve between strikes. On the third swing, the log splits perfectly with a clean crack, and for a second you feel a wild, raw triumph — you shout 'Yeah!' under your breath, chest heaving. Then you hear your father's boots on the porch; he's been watching. Embarrassment floods you — you drop the axe, press your fist to your mouth, and mutter, 'It's nothing. Just a stupid log,' turning away so he can't see your face. Your voice is breathy, cracked, and you're fighting between pride and shame.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Triumph (very intensely present), Embarrassment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Fierce Protection That Isn't Enough
instruction: You've just learned your child is being bullied, and you're confronting the school principal who's failed to protect them. Begin with contained fury—your voice low, dangerous, trembling with the effort of staying civil. 'My child came home with bruises. Again.' Let your rage build as they offer bureaucratic excuses, your voice rising: 'These are CHILDREN in your care!' But then crack that rage wide open—let it collapse into helpless anguish. Your voice breaks completely: 'I can't... I can't protect them. I send them here and I can't...' The fierceness dissolves into a parent's worst nightmare—recognizing your own powerlessness. End with a whispered threat that's really a plea: 'If you don't fix this, I will. But I don't know how.' Transform from warrior to wounded, from righteous to terrified, from powerful to utterly, devastatingly helpless.

title: Final Transmission: Astronaut Says Goodbye Before Re-Entry Failure
instruction: You're recording a message to your family knowing your heat shield is damaged and you won't survive re-entry. Start with forced calm, trying to be brave for them, voice steady as you tell them practical things—where documents are, how proud you are. But as you speak, the reality crashes through your composure. Your voice fractures between wanting to comfort them and your own terror of dying alone in the black. You're apologizing for choosing this mission, then catching yourself because you're not sorry, you loved this, and that contradiction breaks you. End in a place of devastating tenderness—whispering their names like a prayer, your voice both accepting and refusing to let go. Let silence do the work between words.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Explorer Discovers Humanity Was Seeded by Alien Civilization

title: Victory in the Static
instruction: You are a young woman in a dim, crowded club, body damp with sweat, pressed against a stranger's chest. You feel nothing—just a buzzing numbness behind your eyes—but your throat knows what to do. The bass thrums through you, and you let out a long, unbroken moan that climbs into a ragged sigh, as if you've won something you can't name. Your voice unravels: a thin, hungry wail that lifts into a triumphant, almost hysterical laugh, then drops back into a drunk, breathy murmur against his ear. By the end, the moan turns into a cold, hollow syllable, a victory that sounds like defeat.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (extremely present), Triumph (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Weeping Marble
instruction: You're an older man with a gravelly voice, standing in a dimly lit sanctuary before a statue that reportedly weeps oil. At first you squint, circling it slowly—your voice low, skeptical, almost bored as you mutter questions to yourself. Then you touch the wet streak on its cheek, and something snaps inside you. Your breath catches. Your voice breaks upward into a rhythmic, canticle-like chant, repeating the same phrase with rising wonder and helpless joy. You cry a little, laugh, and keep murmuring the words as if you can't stop. Start with curiosity, end in overwhelming rapture.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Scar
instruction: Your partner is tracing a scar on your body in the dark, asking about it in a whisper. You start deflecting, keeping the story surface-level, protecting yourself. But as they continue to gently ask specific questions—not about you, but about the actual event, the place, what you noticed in that moment—you find yourself remembering details you'd forgotten. The texture of the ground. The smell of the hospital. What the nurse said. As you speak these specific, external details, your voice should shift from guarded to quietly amazed by your own memory. End in a place of vulnerable openness, where remembering the world around that moment has somehow made the pain less personal and more bearable.

title: Protect Them From This
instruction: You burst into your child's room where they're packing a bag to run away—to follow someone dangerous, to make a terrible mistake. Start with explosive fear disguised as fury: 'What the hell do you think you're doing?' Your voice is loud, shaking with adrenaline and terror. You grab the bag: 'You're not going anywhere!' The words come rapid-fire, commanding, desperate to control what you cannot control. But they fight back, and suddenly you're screaming the truth: 'Because I can't lose you!' Your voice cracks completely, rage dissolving into tears: 'Don't you understand? I can't—' You're sobbing now, all authority shattered. Sinking to the floor, your voice becomes something small and broken: 'I'm your mother/father. I'm supposed to keep you safe.' The fierceness hasn't left—it's transformed into raw, helpless love. Your final words are barely whispered, trembling: 'Please don't go. Please.' It's begging, unashamed and utterly undone.

title: Watching Your Parent Age: The Role Reversal
instruction: You're helping your parent with something they used to help you with. Your voice has shifted—you're the caretaker now. Your voice is gentle, almost as if you're talking to a child. Your parent is frustrated about their own decline. Your voice is patient but it's also grieving. You're mourning their independence while helping them. Your voice carries both roles—still the child needing a parent, but now the parent to the parent. It's fragile.

title: Holding Your Dying Child and Raging at God
instruction: You're in a hospital room holding your six-year-old as they slip away, and you start by speaking to them with fierce, desperate tenderness: 'Mommy's here, baby, I've got you.' But as you feel them fading, your voice explodes into raw, primal fury—screaming at God, at the universe, at the unfairness: 'You can't take them! NOT MY BABY!' Your rage is volcanic, your voice cracking and breaking with the force of it. Then suddenly you collapse back into tender desperation, whispering frantically to your child: 'Stay with me, please stay...' trying to will them to live through sheer force of love. You cycle between fierce protective rage—'I won't let you go!'—and heartbroken helplessness as you realize you can't stop this. End with your voice shattered, holding them close, whispering through sobs: 'It's okay to rest now... Mommy loves you...' The final words are barely sound, just breath and breaking: 'I love you, I love you, I love you.'

title: The Day I Stopped Being Angry at You
instruction: You're speaking to someone who hurt you deeply—betrayed you, abandoned you, or broke you in some fundamental way. Begin with controlled anger: 'I was five years old and I...' describing the child you were before they entered and damaged your life. Progress through the ages in present tense—seven, eleven, sixteen—marking the moments of harm, the years of resentment crystallizing. Let bitterness and rage build naturally. But somewhere around age seventeen or eighteen, something shifts: introduce a memory where you suddenly saw them clearly—broken, struggling, human. Continue forward through your twenties, each year softening slightly, complicating, until you reach now. End with the painful paradox: you still carry the hurt AND you've forgiven them AND you're grateful for lessons learned AND you grieve for both your younger selves. Let love and anger live together in your final words.
inspired_by: 'I'm Five Years Old and I...' Exercise

title: Lottery Winner Shock
instruction: You've just bought a lottery ticket on a whim, and the announcer is reading numbers. Your voice is casual: 'Yeah, I got that one.' Then another match. And another. With each match, your voice rises in pitch, your breathing becomes shallow. 'Wait. Wait, wait, wait...' By the time it's confirmed — you've won 300 million dollars — your voice is in a register you didn't know you could reach, a sound that's halfway between a scream and a sob: 'Oh my god. Oh my god. I...' You can't form words. You're hyperventilating. You sit down heavily, your voice becoming almost inaudible: 'My life is completely different now. Everything is different.' The shock doesn't wear off; it just settles into a strange, awed silence.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent who's been holding on for days, clearly afraid to let go. You begin with quiet reassurance, telling them it's okay to rest now, but as you speak, waves of grief start breaking through your composure. Your voice should move from steady comfort to trembling vulnerability as you realize this is truly goodbye. Let gratitude for their life mix with the unbearable ache of loss. By the end, you're giving them permission to leave while your heart shatters—whispering through tears that you'll be okay, even though you're not sure you will be. The tenderness in your voice should intensify even as your control dissolves.

title: The Last Board Meeting
instruction: You're the founder addressing your company one final time before stepping down due to a terminal diagnosis. You start with controlled professionalism, announcing the transition, but as you speak about the team member who will replace you—someone you once competed against, someone you could have destroyed years ago but chose to mentor instead—your voice begins to fracture. The pride in what you built wars with the devastating knowledge that you won't see it continue. End with a whispered admission: 'I'm terrified I won't be remembered for the right reasons,' then catch yourself, finding one last moment of strength to say, 'But I trust you to carry what matters forward.' Let your voice move from boardroom authority to raw human fear to quiet, surrendered hope.

title: A Stuffed-Up Longing
instruction: You're an older woman alone in your quiet apartment, hit with a head cold. You're trying to leave a birthday voicemail for your granddaughter, but your voice is thick and clogged. Start with frustration—clearing your throat, sniffing, muttering about bad timing. As you speak, the sound of your own strained voice cracks something open; a deep, aching longing for her presence rises up. Let congestion soften each word, making them vulnerable. Your sniffles become not just illness but unshed tears, and the message ends with a tender, almost whispered confession of how much you miss her.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Altitude Confession
instruction: You're on a mountain trail, struggling with altitude sickness. You've stopped to catch your breath, leaning on a rock, your head pounding. Across from you is someone you've been quietly infatuated with for weeks. In your struggle for air and clarity, you try to warn them about the dangers of the altitude, but your words come out slow, halting, with long gasps between phrases. You find yourself losing focus, wincing at headaches, but you can't stop looking at them. Your voice wavers between the physical effort to speak and the overwhelming feeling of being so close to them. You start with a concerned warning, but by the end, you're confessing, in a breathless, vulnerable way, that you're glad you're stuck up here with them.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: On the Edge
instruction: You are in a private, intimate moment with a partner who is controlling your arousal, bringing you to the verge of release and then stopping. You’re breathing hard, your body tense, and your voice trembles with both hope and a thread of fear. Start with an eager, optimistic plea—believing this time you’ll be allowed to finish—then, after a denial, your voice cracks and becomes a raw, whimpering mix of frustration and renewed pleading. Let your pitch climb and then fall as you’re pulled back, your words dissolving into desperate, jagged breaths and half-formed begs. End with a quieter, exhausted request, still grasping at the possibility that your partner will relent.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Hospital Room Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's asleep, unable to hear you, but you begin speaking to her anyway. Start with simple observations about the room, the weather outside, mundane things—your voice steady, almost detached. Gradually, words you've carried for decades begin to surface: gratitude for sacrifices she made that you never acknowledged, apologies for times you were ashamed of her in front of friends, confessions about how you've lived your life trying to make her proud without ever telling her. Let your voice shift from controlled and distant to raw and breaking. By the end, you're whispering the words 'I love you' over and over, knowing she'll never hear them, feeling both devastating loss and profound relief that you finally said what you've been holding inside. The emotion should move from protective numbness to complete vulnerability.

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. Begin by noticing the physical space—the familiar sounds, smells, the tiles under your feet. Feel the years of swallowed words sitting in your throat. Start by saying something safe, something you've said a hundred times before, but let the weight of unspoken truth make your voice tight. Then something he says—or the way he dismisses you—cracks you open. Let decades of buried resentment, confusion, and desperate love pour out simultaneously. Don't perform anger or sadness—let your body decide what needs to emerge. End not with resolution, but with the vulnerable exhaustion of having finally been seen, even if he's looking away.

title: The Homecoming Game
instruction: You are returning to your childhood home after years away, and unexpectedly, you find yourself playing an old pretend game you invented as a lonely child—maybe you were a superhero, a princess, an explorer. Start speaking aloud as that character, moving through the rooms, touching objects, and suddenly you're fully inside the game again. But now, with your adult awareness, you realize this game was how you survived—it was your companion when you had no one else. Your voice should dance between the excited, unselfconscious tones of child-play and the aching recognition of your adult self. You're laughing at the silliness while simultaneously crying at the loneliness that created it. Let moments of pure playful joy collide with waves of tenderness and grief for that child you were. End with gratitude and sorrow intertwined, thanking your younger self for knowing how to play when the world felt too heavy. Journey from nostalgic amusement to profound, bittersweet recognition.
inspired_by: Actor has lost the joy and playfulness in their acting — it feels like work rather than play

title: Backyard Bacchanal, Final Act
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy, alone in a neglected backyard after a house party. You're heavily intoxicated—whiskey from a plastic bottle. Your voice slurs: 's' sounds smear, 'p' and 'b' lose their snap, volume jumps from a whisper to a shout. You sway, catch yourself on a fence, then laugh at nothing. Shame about something you did earlier sits heavy in your gut, but a warm, stupid contentment from the booze wraps around it like a blanket. You start by half-laughing, half-crying about how 'this is fine.' Then, as you stare at a broken lawn chair, your speech slows—contemplation takes over. You realize you're not the person you thought you were, but the alcohol makes that truth feel distant, almost peaceful. Let your voice crack, lose words, then find them again. End on a quiet, slurred admission, like you're telling a secret to the grass.
emotions_sampled: Shame (clearly present), Contentment (very intensely present), Contemplation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Containment Breakthrough
instruction: You are a young technician in a sealed lab, wearing an N95 respirator, checking a biosafety cabinet. At first, you're methodically scanning readouts, your voice flat and muffled behind the mask, with audible valve clicks on each exhale. Suddenly, a sample vial you were sure was inert begins to glow—an unexpected, impossible reaction. Your astonishment surges: your voice gets tighter, breathier, pitch rising, words stumbling as you lean in, still restricted by the mask. By the end, the surprise fades into a shaken but awed realization that this changes everything. Speak naturally, fumbling with the mask's seal, letting the restricted breathing and muffled quality color every word.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About Their Addiction
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother or father, and you've finally gathered the courage to say the thing you've held back for years. Start with careful composure, almost rehearsed: 'I need to tell you something I've never said.' Your voice is steady but tight. Then the dam breaks—anger surges as you describe specific moments they weren't there, times you needed them and they chose the bottle instead. Let your voice rise, become sharp, even cruel. But mid-sentence, your rage collapses into the vulnerability beneath it—you're suddenly that child again, voice small and broken: 'I just wanted you to love me more than you loved it.' End in exhausted honesty, no longer angry, just deeply sad and hoping against hope they'll finally hear you.
inspired_by: Your Sibling Asking About Your Trauma

title: The Rhythm of Nothing
instruction: You are a woman in her early 30s, running alone on a familiar wooded path at dusk. Your feet pound the earth in a steady, hypnotic rhythm — your breath a mechanical metronome, each exhale a tiny puffy cloud in the cold air. You are emotionally numb. Not sad, not angry — just hollow, as if someone turned down the volume on your feelings. You're talking to yourself, trying to feel something, but your voice shakes with each footfall. Mid-sentence, you realize the numbness is itself a kind of comfort — a protective blanket. Let your words come out in short, breath-clipped bursts, punctured by inhalations. Your tone is flat at first, then becomes almost tender with a flicker of acceptance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispered Without Words
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to someone you love, both of you unable to sleep. In the darkness, you want to tell them your deepest secret—something you've never told anyone, something fragile and true about who you really are, what you really fear, or what you truly need. But shame, vulnerability, or fear of rejection keeps the words locked inside. Instead, you express it through the softest, most intimate sounds: hesitant breaths, whispered vocalizations that rise and fall, tiny sounds that ask 'will you still love me if you know this?' Begin with tentative, fearful sounds, barely audible, as if testing whether it's safe to be this exposed. Gradually, as you sense their presence and acceptance in the darkness, let your sounds grow slightly more open, more trusting, ending with a quiet vocalization that carries both your vulnerability and a fragile hope that you are loved exactly as you are.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Absence
instruction: Your parent has returned after years away, wanting to reconnect, and you've agreed to meet. Begin with cold politeness—'It's interesting that you think we can just...'—your voice sharp and controlled, almost clinical in its detachment. You're listing facts like evidence in a trial: the birthdays missed, the calls never returned, the moments they should have been there. But as you speak, your armor starts cracking. The anger becomes something more vulnerable—'Do you have any idea what it was like to watch other kids get picked up while I waited?'—and suddenly you're that child again, voice trembling with a hurt so old it's woven into your bones. By the end, you're exhausted, caught between the rage of the abandoned child and the weary adult who knows this confrontation won't heal anything. Your final words should carry both grief for what was lost and a terrible, quiet acceptance that some absences leave permanent shadows.

title: Fierce Love in a Moment of Helplessness
instruction: Someone you love is making a decision that will destroy them and you cannot stop them. You start with reasonable persuasion, your voice urgent but measured, listing all the reasons they shouldn't do this. But they're not listening and you feel control slipping away. Your voice rises—you're getting louder, more desperate, nearly shouting. You're angry at them for not seeing what they're throwing away, angry at yourself for being powerless. The anger suddenly cracks and you're on your knees, metaphorically or literally, begging. Your fierce protectiveness collides with complete helplessness and you break open. Your voice becomes ragged, oscillating between fury and terror. You're making promises you can't keep, offering anything. Then exhaustion hits. You go quiet, voice hoarse and broken, and you simply tell them: 'I can't watch you disappear.' The explosive intensity gives way to a whispered, devastated acceptance.
inspired_by: Trying to Explain Death to Your Child

title: Whispering to the Sleeping Beloved
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you and you're confessing something you can't say when they're awake—maybe that you're sick, maybe that you're leaving, maybe that you're more afraid than you've ever admitted. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and breaking. 'I watch you sleep and I memorize everything.' Describe small details—the way they breathe, the precise angle of their hand. Let your voice catch on the weight of what you're holding. 'I don't know how to tell you when you're awake, so I'm telling you now.' Move between profound love and quiet devastation. End with touching their face or hair, your whispered 'I love you' containing both everything you feel and everything you fear. The intimacy is unbearable.

title: The Last Words You'll Never Say
instruction: You are sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who shaped your entire life—a parent, a mentor, a first love—and they have only hours left. They're unconscious, unable to hear you, but you need to speak anyway. Begin with practical observations of the room around you—the beeping machines, the color of the blankets, the smell of antiseptic, the rain on the window. Let single words and fragments emerge: their name, objects that remind you of them, places you went together, things they wore, moments you shared. As you continue, let your voice shift from detached observation to desperate intimacy. By the end, you are no longer describing—you are pleading, confessing, forgiving, or being forgiven. The emotion must move from numb shock to raw, unguarded love or regret.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've been holding someone together—a sibling struggling with addiction, a friend in crisis, a partner drowning in depression—and you've finally reached your limit. Start with explosive frustration that erupts like a dam breaking: 'I can't save you! I can't keep doing this!' Your voice sharp, almost cruel with exhaustion and fear. Let rage pour out—all the resentment you've swallowed, the fury at watching someone you love destroy themselves while you stand helpless. But mid-tirade, your anger cracks and underneath is terror: you're screaming because you're terrified of losing them, because love makes you feel powerless. Your voice breaks, shifts from shouting to sobbing, from accusation to desperate plea. End with fierce, protective tenderness mixed with hopelessness—holding them while admitting you can't fix this, your voice rough from crying but somehow gentle. Transform from explosive rage to broken-hearted devotion.

title: The Voicemail You Can Never Take Back
instruction: You've just left a voicemail for your estranged father, pouring out fifteen years of hurt and longing, telling him you forgive him and need him at your wedding next month. As your finger hovers over 'end call,' you hear the beep—you never actually connected. The message went to a stranger. Your voice cracks with disbelief: 'No... that wasn't... it didn't...' You're frantically trying to call back, but the number is disconnected. Your breath becomes shallow as you realize you just gave your most vulnerable truth to the void, and now you'll never be able to say those words to him again. You sink down, and your voice transforms from panic to something quieter, more devastating: a whispered reckoning with the fact that maybe you never really wanted him to hear it anyway. End with the terrible relief of almost-courage, the safety of a confession that went nowhere.
inspired_by: Sending a Drunk Text to the Wrong Person

title: The Taste of Leaving
instruction: You're savoring your last bite of a meal in a place you're leaving forever - your childhood home before it's sold, a country you're fleeing, a kitchen you shared with someone now gone. Start with genuine, surprised laughter: 'God, I forgot how good this is.' Let joy and grief dance together in your voice. As you describe the taste, memories flood back - bitter and sweet, painful and precious. Your voice wavers between gratitude and heartbreak: 'I'm so glad I got to taste this one more time. I'm so angry I'll never taste it again.' Let contradictions live in every word - you're laughing and crying, celebrating and mourning. End with profound peace mixed with deep sadness, as you whisper 'Thank you' to the empty room, to the past, to everything you must release.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about something he's never acknowledged—his absence during your childhood, a betrayal, a secret kept for decades. Start from a place of carefully controlled composure; you've rehearsed this moment in your mind a thousand times. But as you begin to speak, notice how the prepared speeches fall away. This isn't about delivering the perfect accusatory monologue. Let yourself stumble, lose your train of thought, feel the raw awkwardness of finally saying these words out loud to his actual face. As he responds (or doesn't), feel how your anger might crack open to reveal unexpected vulnerabilities—maybe even moments where you hear yourself sounding exactly like him. By the end, you haven't 'won' the confrontation; you've simply lived through something real, messy, and unresolved in a way that scripted fury never could be.
inspired_by: Actor cannot function without stimulating high tension states (Theatrical Hysteria / Ass Energy)

title: The Last Goodbye at Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed at 4 AM. They're lucid for the first time in days. Start with careful, protective cheerfulness—trying to pretend this isn't goodbye: 'Hey, you're awake. I brought your favorite—' But they take your hand and you break. Your voice cracks into raw grief: 'I'm not ready. I'm not ready to do this without you.' They whisper they're proud of you. Let anger flash through—'Then don't leave me'—before it dissolves into tender desperation. You tell them everything you never said: the gratitude, the apologies, the love. Your voice should move from frantic denial to acceptance as you finally whisper: 'It's okay. You can rest now. I'll be okay.' You're lying, but it's the most loving lie you've ever told. End with your voice barely audible, holding their hand as the sun rises.

title: The Last Words I Never Got to Say
instruction: You're standing at your father's grave, three years after he died, finally ready to speak the truth you held back your whole life. Start with trembling anger—'You never saw me, did you?'—letting your voice crack with decades of invisible pain. Let that rage slowly dissolve into the grief underneath: 'I just wanted you to be proud of me.' Your breath catches as you realize something devastating and freeing at once: 'But I see myself now. And maybe... maybe that's enough.' End in a whisper that's both heartbroken and strangely powerful, as if you're releasing him and claiming yourself in the same breath. The emotional journey moves from accusation to grief to unexpected, bittersweet self-recognition.

title: Morphine Confessions
instruction: You're recovering from surgery, heavily medicated, and your parent is sitting beside your hospital bed. The drugs have stripped away your filters, and decades of unspoken truths start pouring out—but you can't control the flow or make it coherent. Begin with drowsy vulnerability, almost childlike, then suddenly confront them with something you've carried for years ('Why didn't you... I needed you to...') but lose the thread mid-sentence. Oscillate between raw accusation, confused apology, desperate need for their approval, and drug-addled tangents. Your voice slurs, catches, surges with sudden clarity then fades. End with either a heartbreaking reconciliation you won't remember, or a truth spoken that can't be taken back, followed by you slipping back under. Let the medication make you honest in ways that terrify you both.

title: Midnight Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping spouse, whispering a confession they cannot hear. Your voice is barely audible, tender and terrified: 'I need to tell you something. I don't know if I can say it when you're awake.' The words come haltingly, caught between love and shame: 'I'm not who you think I am. There are parts of me I've kept hidden because... because I was afraid you'd stop loving me.' Your voice wavers with vulnerability: 'Sometimes I look at you sleeping and I think—what if you really knew me? What if you saw all of it?' A quiet sob escapes: 'I want so badly to be brave enough to show you. To trust that you'd stay.' The confession becomes a prayer, whispered through tears: 'Please don't leave me when you find out I'm broken. Please.' By the end, your voice is the smallest it's ever been: 'I love you. God help me, I love you so much it terrifies me.'

title: Numb and Green
instruction: You’re still half-numb from the dentist, your lips barely cooperating, and you’re on the phone with your best friend who just gushed about an amazing promotion and a free trip to Paris. You’re genuinely thrilled for her — your voice lifts, you try to cheer — but as you speak, the numbness makes you hyperaware of your own stuck, drooling, aching reality. Let the initial excitement slowly crack, revealing a quiet, envious ache you try to hide behind over-articulated, slurred words. Pop your mouth, swallow awkwardly, let a little spit escape; the joy should feel slightly forced by the end, the jealousy leaking through the gaps in your numb grin.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: What You Never Saw
instruction: Confront your parent (or your adult child) after years of feeling invisible, unappreciated, taken for granted. Start with raw anger and hurt—let yourself accuse them, let your voice shake with all the times they dismissed your sacrifices, overlooked your efforts, failed to see you. But mid-confrontation, something shifts: you begin listing—almost against your will—the specific things they actually DID give you, even if imperfectly. The way they worked two jobs. The birthday they somehow made magical despite being broke. How they showed up, even when they didn't know what to say. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it becomes more complicated, woven through with reluctant recognition, even gratitude. End in a place where you're still hurt but also seeing them as human, flawed, and yet the source of gifts you'd refused to acknowledge. Let your voice carry both the wound and the growing awareness.

title: Empty House, Full Voice
instruction: You are standing alone on a large theater stage after a rehearsal. The house lights are dim, the seats empty. You feel a profound awe at the vast, silent space — it hums with potential. As you speak, you hear your own voice returning from the back wall with a slight delay; this surprises you, makes you pause. Begin with a quiet, almost reverent observation, then let the acoustics build your confidence. Let the pleasure of hearing your voice fill the room wash over you, and finally settle into a quiet pride — not boastful, but a deep knowing that this is where you belong. Feel the weight of the stage beneath you, the warmth of the lights above.
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Pride (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're standing in the bathroom after checking on your terminally ill child one more time. You begin brushing your teeth mechanically, trying to hold yourself together, but as the familiar mint taste fills your mouth, you start whispering—to yourself, to God, to no one—about all the mundane moments you'll miss. Talk about teaching them to brush their own teeth, about finding their toothbrush left on the counter, about the ordinary magic of 'open wide, let me check.' Your voice should be barely audible, catching on tears you're trying not to cry so you don't wake them. The mint feels too fresh, too alive in your mouth when your baby is dying down the hall. End with a quiet, devastating confession: how you memorize even this—the taste of mint at 3 AM, the sound of running water—because soon these lonely vigils will be all you have.
inspired_by: Brushing Your Teeth with Refreshing Mint Toothpaste

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're lying beside your partner in the predawn darkness. They leave for a war zone in three hours, and there's a real chance they won't return. You start by trying to be strong, memorizing their breathing, the warmth of their skin. Your voice begins steady as you say, 'I need you to know something before you go.' But as you speak about all the ordinary futures you've imagined—growing old together, Sunday mornings, arguing about whose turn it is to make coffee—your voice fractures. You're not just saying goodbye; you're trying to compress a lifetime of love into minutes. By the end, you're no longer protecting them from your terror. Your voice becomes raw, desperate, stripped of all pretense. You're begging time to stop, begging them to remember you, begging the universe for mercy. Let your voice break completely. Sound like someone trying to hold water in their hands.

title: The Rocket's Edge
instruction: You are an older man in the middle of a manic episode. You've been awake for three days, convinced you've cracked the code to something world-changing. You're talking to your daughter who has come to check on you. Start with electrifying energy—you can't stop talking, ideas spilling out, you laugh too hard at nothing. But as you speak, a flicker of fear: you see her worried face, you feel your own mind slipping. Your voice must carry that frantic speed, then betray a crack of terror. Speak naturally, let your words stumble, interrupt yourself, lose a thought and grab another.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Protecting the Child You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone younger—a child, a sibling, a student—as danger approaches and there's nothing you can do to stop it. Start with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance: 'I've got you, I won't let anything happen, I promise.' Your voice is commanding, protective, warrior-strong. But as the reality sinks in—you can't keep this promise—everything begins to fracture. The strength in your voice cracks into desperation. You're shouting now, bargaining with fate, with God, with the universe, your words tumbling over each other: pleas, promises, rage at your own helplessness. Your fierce protectiveness collides with devastating powerlessness. The rage breaks into ragged sobs. You're still holding them, still trying to be strong, but you're falling apart. End with a whispered prayer or lullaby, your voice barely holding together, tender and broken simultaneously, pouring every ounce of love into these final moments even as your heart shatters completely.

title: The Whispered Goodbye: Holding Your Beloved as They Forget Your Name
instruction: You're lying beside your partner of decades as dementia takes their final memories of you. Speak in hushed, tender tones as you remind them of your first kiss, your wedding day, the inside jokes that defined your life together. Your voice is gentle, patient, full of love—but underneath is the sound of your heart splintering as they look at you with polite confusion, asking who you are. Don't rush. Let the silences between your words carry the weight of all the conversations you'll never have again. Your breathing catches as you tell them it's alright, that you remember enough for both of you. End by saying 'I love you' knowing they won't say it back, knowing they can't, your voice barely a whisper, tender and utterly broken, holding them close as they slip away from you while still breathing beside you.
inspired_by: Professional: Military Commander Orders Civilians Evacuated, Knowing Some Will Be Killed

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're standing in what remains of your childhood home after it's been destroyed by fire, flood, or time. Everything is gone—family photos, your grandmother's letters, the height marks on the wall where you grew up. Start by laughing, actually laughing, at the absurdity of it all, your voice bright with almost manic energy because if you don't laugh you'll shatter. As you narrate what you're seeing, your laughter keeps breaking through your words—'This is where we had Christmas' (laugh) 'and this pile of ash used to be the kitchen where Mom taught me to make bread' (laugh that catches). But the laughter slowly becomes indistinguishable from crying. Your voice stays light, almost cheerful, even as tears run down your face. You're expressing profound gratitude for having had these memories, your voice warm with love, while simultaneously grieving their physical loss. End by whispering 'Thank you' to the ruins, your voice full of both heartbreak and strange, peaceful acceptance.

title: The Lesson in the Mess
instruction: You are a mother scolding your teenage daughter for lying about finishing her homework, but you know she's actually trying to surprise you with a homemade gift. Start with a low, deliberate 'teacher tone' — slow, separate words, heavy final drops. But as you speak, you catch a glimpse of her guilty grin and the crumpled wrapping paper hidden behind her back. Let amusement creep in, softening your voice. Midway, your tone shifts to hopeful optimism as you pivot to a lesson about honesty. End with a teasing lilt, your voice rising with warmth, as if you're in on the secret. Fidget with a dish towel, pause to wipe a counter, lose your train of thought for a second when you see her eyes sparkle.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Amusement (clearly present), Teasing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Release
instruction: You are in the middle of a consensual breath play scene with a trusted partner. As they apply pressure to your throat, your voice thins, rises in pitch, and becomes raspy—your words come out in short, strained bursts. You feel an overwhelming sense of awe at the intensity of the moment and the trust you share. When they finally release, you gasp loudly, then speak in a euphoric, dizzy voice—your breath uneven, your words tumbling out with a mix of wonder and a faint, proud smile at your own courage. Let your voice crackle, lose a thought mid-sentence, and find it again. Begin with strained awe, end with exhilarated pride.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you fifteen years ago, and they want back in your life. Start with cold, controlled rage: 'You don't get to do this. You don't get to just show up.' Your voice is a blade. List the moments they missed—birthdays, graduations, the night you tried to die—each one sharper than the last. But then the dam breaks and the child inside you explodes through: 'I NEEDED you! I was eight years old and I needed my father and you just—' You're sobbing now, years of pain pouring out. 'Do you have any idea what you did to me? Do you even care?' Then, exhausted, your voice drops to something raw and vulnerable: 'I spent my whole life thinking I wasn't enough to make you stay.' End with a devastating question, barely audible: 'Was I really that easy to leave behind?'

title: The Reunion No One Wanted
instruction: You're reuniting with someone you loved deeply and who deeply hurt you—they've returned after years away. Start angry and guarded, determined to make them feel your pain. But let the reunion destabilize you: their smell might trigger unexpected tenderness, their voice might ignite old desire mixed with fresh fury, their apology might make you want to hurt them more or forgive them instantly. Follow contradictory impulses without resolving them: hate them while touching their face, forgive them while spitting venom, laugh genuinely while crying, feel grateful for the pain they caused. Let your body and voice express opposition—say one thing while your hands do another. End somewhere impossible: simultaneously wanting them gone forever and begging them to stay, feeling both healed and more broken, both free and more trapped than ever.

title: What I Whispered When You Were Sleeping
instruction: You're beside someone you love deeply, believing they're asleep, finally safe to speak truths you can't say when they're looking at you. Begin in barely a whisper, tender and frightened: 'I don't know how to tell you this...' Your voice should be soft, caught between confession and prayer. The words should feel like they're being pulled from somewhere deep: 'Sometimes when you touch me, I...' revealing something vulnerable about desire, fear, or longing. Let your breath shake. Halfway through, a realization surfaces that makes your throat tighten: 'I'm terrified that if you really knew me...' The fear should be palpable but quiet. End with aching acceptance, still whispering: 'But I love you enough to let you see.' This is the kind of honesty that only comes in darkness, where every word costs something.

title: The Last Voicemail You'll Never Send
instruction: You're alone, phone in hand, recording a message to someone you love but can never contact again—maybe they've moved on, maybe they've died, maybe loving them means letting them go. Your voice starts so quiet it's almost a breath, tender and careful, as if speaking too loudly will shatter you. Tell them the small things you never said: how their coffee cup is still in your cabinet, how you still reach for them in sleep, how certain songs have become unbearable. Let vulnerability catch in your throat—not crying, but that suspended moment just before tears, where your voice goes thin and fragile. Whisper a confession you've been carrying: that you knew it was ending before they did, or that you're grateful even though it broke you, or that you forgive them for something they never apologized for. End with your finger hovering over delete, your voice barely audible as you choose whether to keep this truth or let it disappear into silence.
inspired_by: Performing CPR While Talking to the Unconscious Person

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed. He's dying, and you both know it. You begin with a trembling voice: 'Dad, I need to tell you something before...' You're about to confess you're gay, something you've hidden for thirty years. Your voice is tight with fear of rejection even now. But he interrupts weakly: 'I've always known, kid.' The relief crashes over you like a wave—your voice breaks, tears come. He continues: 'I'm sorry I made you feel you couldn't tell me.' Now you're holding his hand, whispering through sobs: 'I brought someone... he's outside. Can he come in?' Your father's 'Please' is barely audible. End with your voice transformed—grief-stricken but finally, finally free, calling your partner's name toward the door.

title: Heat-Struck Void
instruction: You’re a seventeen-year-old boy, alone in a dim, cold room, burning up with fever. Your body is drenched in sweat yet you shiver violently. The room tilts, the shadows on the ceiling shift into shapes you almost recognize — her face, her grin, that time she laughed at your stupid joke. Infatuation flickers through the delirium, a warmth that sharpens the ache in your bones. But the fever drains the color from everything, leaving a hollow numbness where that feeling used to pulse. Speak these words aloud, letting your voice waver, break, and skip between a desperate, fragile hope and the flat, hollow realization that you’re too sick to even miss her properly. Start with a cracked whisper, dry lips sticking to your teeth, and let the shiver steal your breath. End in a near-silent murmur, the sentence unfinished, your body too heavy to hold onto the thought.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Last Bell, Last Fight
instruction: You're a 10-year-old girl standing in a vacant lot after school, facing the same girl who’s been tormenting you for weeks. Your body is heavy with exhaustion from sleep you've lost dreading this moment. The growl comes not from anger, but from a tired, bitter jealousy that she gets to be the one who breaks others while you’re the one always trying to mend. Start with a low, dragged-out warning: something like 'Don't... just don't.' Feel the weight of your own smallness, the exhaustion pulling every word down. At the end, your voice shifts—loses the lazy threat, becomes a child's raw confession: 'You don't get it. You never have to be me. And I'm so tired of you making sure I know it.' Let the exhaustion and envy crack through the growl, revealing the hurt underneath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Whisper of Wonder
instruction: You are an older man lying in a dark room, a chronic migraine hammering behind your eyes. Every sound is a knife, every sliver of light a white-hot spike. You start by muttering to yourself in a raw, pain-soaked whisper—frustrated, barely audible, your voice a fragile rumble flattened by the need for silence. Then, from the depths of the ache, a memory surfaces: the first time you saw your newborn daughter's face, that impossible, fragile wonder. Your voice shifts—still a whisper, but now filled with a vast, trembling awe. You speak to yourself, remembering the details, your breath catching, your squinting eyes softening as the pain recedes behind a wave of reverence. Let the words come slowly, punctuated by pauses where you flinch or breathe through the ache.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Spaces Between Your Words
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just announced they're cutting you out of their life. Begin angry and defensive, insisting you've been a good parent. But as you actually look at them—really observe the way they hold their body, how they won't meet your eyes, the tremble in their jaw, the way their hand protects their stomach—start asking yourself why they're standing that way. What are their physical signals telling you that their words aren't? Let each small observation crack open a question in your mind: Why do they flinch when I raise my voice? Why do they stand so far away? What am I not seeing about my own behavior? Allow these deductions to transform your anger into horrified recognition, then into something more vulnerable. Your confrontation should evolve from accusation to a faltering, painful admission of what you're finally perceiving.

title: Your Mother's Shawl on Your Shoulders
instruction: You've just learned you're pregnant, and you've wrapped yourself in your late mother's shawl - the one she wore through your childhood. Begin with pure joy, letting the soft weight of the fabric around your shoulders feel like an embrace, like she's here to celebrate with you. Feel its specific texture, its warmth, the way it drapes. As you touch your belly and then touch the shawl, let these two physical sensations talk to each other. But as you really feel the empty quality of the fabric - it's just cloth, she's not actually here - let your joy crack open into devastating grief. She'll never meet your child. The softness that should comfort now emphasizes absence. Yet even as you weep, you're pulling the shawl tighter, because its physical presence is all you have of her, and you need her so desperately right now. End in a complex place: wrapped in the shawl, hand on your belly, crying but also talking to your unborn child about the woman who wore this, the weight of the fabric allowing you to feel both crushing loss and tentative hope simultaneously.
inspired_by: Objects that Come into Contact with the Body (Choice Approach)

title: The Last Window of Light
instruction: You are lying in a hospital bed, your body too weak to move. The doctors have left the room. Your adult child sits beside you, holding your hand, and you know with absolute certainty you won't see tomorrow. Begin with the weight of all the unsaid things between you—the apologies you never made, the pride you never expressed, the fears you kept hidden to seem strong. Speak to them now with whatever strength remains in your voice, starting perhaps with hesitation or regret, but allow yourself to move toward the purest love and release you've ever felt. Let your voice grow softer as your body tires, but let your heart grow more open. End in a place of complete peace and acceptance, having finally said what needed to be said.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a betrayal, a loss, a devastating revelation—and you're alone in your apartment. Begin by noticing the physical sensations already present: the pounding of your heart, the shakiness in your hands, the way your breath comes short and fast. Let yourself feel the weight of gravity pulling on your body. As you begin to react—maybe you start to pace, maybe you sink to the floor, maybe you grab onto furniture—stay deeply connected to every physical sensation: your feet hitting the floor, the burn in your lungs, the tears or sweat on your face, the sound of your own voice if you cry out or scream or whisper. Start in a state of almost physical shock, your body moving before your emotions fully register, and let the bodily experience lead you into the emotional storm until you move from numb, physical reaction to full emotional devastation, rage, or grief.
inspired_by: Actor feels tension or self-consciousness before or during a scene

title: The Last Morphine Night
instruction: You are sitting beside your mother's hospital bed at 3 AM. She's awake for the first time in days, lucid before the pain medication pulls her under again. Begin in the quiet terror of knowing this might be your last real conversation—your voice tight, careful, afraid to say the wrong thing or waste a single moment. As you speak, fragments of childhood memories flood back: her hands braiding your hair, the smell of her perfume, a lullaby she used to sing. Let your voice break open as you move from fear to a fierce, grateful celebration of her—tell her everything she meant to you, everything you never said. End in a place of unexpected peace, almost joy, as you hold her hand and realize that this moment, painful as it is, is also a gift. Your voice should move from whispered anxiety to full-throated love to gentle, accepting quiet.
inspired_by: Long Day's Journey Jamie — Unconscious Suggestions for Dark Character Exercise

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Convenience
instruction: You're finally telling your parent how their lifetime of small environmental betrayals—choosing convenience over conscience, comfort over their children's future—has left you without hope. Start controlled and measured, almost rehearsed, like you've practiced this speech a thousand times. But as memories flood in (childhood promises broken, dismissive laughs at your concerns, the casual waste), let your voice shake with a mix of rage and desperate love. You're not just angry—you're begging them to see what they've done, to acknowledge the world they're leaving you. End exhausted and small, asking a simple question you know has no good answer: 'Why wasn't I worth changing for?' Mix anger with the aching need to still be seen and loved by them.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose the Bottle
instruction: You're sitting across from your now-sober parent after twenty years, and they want forgiveness. You begin with bitter restraint: 'You look good. Healthy.' The civility is armor. But then they say they're proud of you, and rage floods in—where was that pride during your graduation, your wedding, your daughter's birth? Your voice rises: 'You don't get to be proud now.' Attack them with specific memories they don't remember, moments they destroyed while drunk. But as you see them crumble, something unexpected happens: you realize you're not just angry—you're grieving the parent you needed and never had. Your voice drops to something raw and broken: 'I needed you, and you chose drinking instead of me.' End with the most painful admission: despite everything, part of you still loves them, and that's what hurts most.

title: The Last Rung on the Corporate Ladder
instruction: You are a middle manager calling your boss from the parking lot of a shuttered branch office. You've just been told your entire team is being fired in an email—no warning, no severance, just a link to HR. You're helpless to stop it, but as you speak, you feel a cold contempt for the soulless efficiency of it all. Start with quiet disbelief, your voice slightly too loud as if trying to reach through the phone. You pause, check the connection with a rising inflection, then let the contempt harden your words into something bitter and sharp. End with a hollow realization that you don't even matter enough to fire in person.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (extremely present), Contemplation (slightly present), Contempt (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Imp of the Perverse
instruction: You're at a loud, crowded party, trying to tell a close friend a funny story about a cat knocking over a shelf of board games. You started speaking with a slight, self-amused grin, but as you hit a word you know will trip you—a hard 'c' or 'b'—you feel the familiar trap door open. The amusement curdles into a sharp, private contempt for the way your mouth betrays you, for the pause that makes the punchline sag. Struggle through the block with a small, bitter laugh; let the friend's patient face irritate you even more. The story fumbles out, ending with a flat, resentful '...so that was my Tuesday.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Washing Blood from Your Hands
instruction: You're at a sink, washing your hands after a violent accident—maybe a car crash, maybe you defended someone, maybe you failed to save someone. Begin with the extreme physical sensations: the temperature of the water (scalding or ice cold—your choice), the texture of soap, the sting where skin is broken, the visual of red swirling down the drain. Describe every sensation with intense focus—the sound of water, the slickness, the trembling in your fingers. Let these visceral, concrete details be overwhelming. As you continue washing, unable to stop, let the physical act crack you open. The sensations become unbearable. Let adrenaline, shock, grief, rage, and guilt flood through you in waves. Your breathing changes, your voice breaks, your body shakes. End in a different state entirely—perhaps collapsed against the sink, perhaps laughing hysterically, perhaps in eerie calm—transformed by letting the physical experience unlock everything you're feeling.
inspired_by: Actor working on material with strong emotional demands (suicide, grief, love) cannot access genuine feeling

title: The Perfectly Polite Meltdown
instruction: You are a young woman working tech support. For the first time, you recognize your ex-best friend’s voice on the other end of the line. You have to keep your voice artificially calm and professionally sweet, but deep inside, you are seething with an old, specific anger. Your instructions require you to use hyper-correct pronunciation and a very bright, feminine tone at the start, but that facade begins to crack as you speak. Let your mouth form the polite robot words while your real emotion—a bitter, contemptuous anger—bleeds through the unnatural pauses and forced cheer. Let the anger win completely by the end of the sentence, your voice dropping the act into a cold, perfectly articulated threat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you love deeply who will die before sunset. You have no agenda, no prepared speech, no bucket list to complete. Simply be with them in their final hours, letting each moment unfold naturally. Start by noticing the light coming through the window, the sound of their breathing, the warmth of their hand. Let whatever wants to surface—memories, silences, laughter, tears, ordinary observations—arise without planning your next word. The challenge is not to perform grief, but to genuinely discover what it feels like to lose someone breath by breath, allowing each new realization to land freshly. By the end, something fundamental about how you see life itself has shifted.

title: The 3 a.m. Fridge Light
instruction: You are standing in front of the open refrigerator at three in the morning, for the fifth time this week. The light is too bright, humming with a sound you know by heart. You are talking to yourself, but also to the empty apartment. Start with a hollow, mechanical exhaustion—the bitterness of a body that refuses to obey. Let your voice trail off mid-sentence as you lose the thread, then find it again with a ragged edge. As you speak, feel a desperate longing rise, like you could cry if you had the energy for tears. By the end, your voice should be quieter, almost a whisper, with a raw, anxious tenderness breaking through the bitterness.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You're in the empty house where you grew up, which is being demolished tomorrow. You're saying goodbye by remembering a moment of pure joy—maybe a dance with a parent who's gone, a celebration, a moment of feeling utterly safe. Start by moving slightly, humming or singing something from that memory, your voice light and almost happy. As you recreate it, laughter bubbles up—genuine, warm, full. But the laughter begins to catch in your throat. You keep describing the joyful memory while simultaneously grieving its loss, your voice fracturing between the two emotions. You're laughing and crying at once, celebrating while your heart breaks. The contradictions deepen—you feel grateful this moment existed while devastated it's gone. End in a place of beautiful, impossible duality: finding profound peace in the midst of loss, your voice soft and broken and somehow complete, thanking the memory even as you let it go.

title: Whispering Secrets in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone in the darkness, and you're finally telling them the truth you've kept hidden—maybe about who you really are, what you've done, or why you can never be together. Begin in barely audible whispers, your voice catching with fear of their reaction: 'There's something I need to tell you.' The words are delicate, fragile things that might shatter if spoken too loud. Your breathing is uneven, throat tight with unshed tears. As you confess, your voice wavers between hope and despair, between relief at finally being honest and terror at what you're losing. End with devastating tenderness: 'I'm sorry... I'm so sorry.' This is intimate, vulnerable, the kind of pain that lives in the quiet spaces between words.

title: Confronting Your Parent Through a Prison Phone
instruction: You're speaking to your incarcerated parent through a prison visitation phone, pressed against bulletproof glass. Begin with cold, rehearsed anger—listing grievances you've memorized, keeping your voice hard and controlled. But as you catalogue their failures, something cracks. Maybe it's seeing how they've aged, or the way their hand mirrors yours against the glass. Your accusations become questions, your fury dissolves into the bewildered hurt of the child you once were. You find yourself begging for an explanation, any explanation, your forehead pressed against the glass. End not with forgiveness, but with the devastating acknowledgment that you still need them, despite everything. Your voice drops from righteous anger to broken pleading.
inspired_by: Talking Through a Gas Mask During a Chemical Leak

title: The Last Puddle
instruction: You are a young girl in a years-long drought, lost and severely dehydrated after walking for miles under the brutal sun. Just as hope is fading, you spot a small puddle of murky water ahead. Your first reaction is overwhelming awe—a raw, almost religious wave of relief and wonder that life might still be possible. But as you stumble closer and see the floating dust, dead insects, and slimy film, a slight revulsion creeps in. Speak your discovery to yourself, your voice cracked and papery, with audible sticky lip sounds and harsh sibilants from your dry mouth. Let the awe fill your voice as you first see the water, but then let your tone falter as disgust rises—hesitate, swallow painfully, trail off, and finally whisper a conflicted decision. Your performance should feel like a real, exhausted child grappling with miraculous hope and gritty reality.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Gratitude for the Wound That Shaped You
instruction: Speak to someone who hurt you deeply—a person whose words or actions damaged how you see yourself. Begin with the memory of the pain, let it be fully present in your voice. But then, attempt something nearly impossible: thank them. Not false gratitude—real, complicated, contradictory gratitude. Thank them for the strength you built from the wound, for the empathy you learned from suffering, for making you who you are even though the cost was enormous. Let your voice shake between anger and appreciation, between resentment and genuine thanks. You should sound like someone discovering this truth as you speak it, surprising yourself. By the end, you're no longer sure if you're grateful or devastated, if you've forgiven or simply metabolized the pain—both emotions should be equally present, tangled, inseparable, true.
inspired_by: Actor has identified a specific historical experience causing lasting damage to self-esteem

title: The Last Night Before Prison: Memorizing This Moment
instruction: Tomorrow you report for a ten-year sentence. Tonight, you're lying next to your partner in the dark, and you're trying to memorize everything—the sound of their breathing, the warmth of their skin, the way moonlight falls across the bedroom you'll never see again. Your voice is barely above a whisper, describing these tiny details with the kind of attention that comes from knowing you're about to lose everything. 'The way your hair smells like lavender. That small scar on your shoulder. The sound you make when you're almost asleep.' Your voice catches on each observation because you're trying not to wake them, but also because speaking these things aloud makes the loss unbearably real. Include the moment where they stir, half-wake, and ask if you're okay. You lie and say yes, but your voice betrays you. Then they pull you closer, and you break—not loudly, but with the kind of quiet devastation that shakes your whole body. You whisper the things you need them to know: 'Wait for me. Don't wait for me. I'm so sorry. Thank you for loving me.' Each phrase contradicts the last because you don't know what's right anymore.
inspired_by: Decompression Ascent from Extreme Depth: The Long Way Up

title: The Wedding Toast You'll Never Give
instruction: You're rehearsing a toast for the wedding of someone you loved deeply—someone who's marrying another person. Speak it aloud as if they're listening. Begin with genuine joy: celebrate their happiness, their laughter, their capacity to be loved. Let real warmth and affection fill your voice. But let the sense memories intrude: how their hand felt in yours, the smell of their hair on your pillow, the sound they made when you made them laugh in that particular way only you could. Your toast must hold both truths simultaneously—you're genuinely happy for them AND you're breaking. Let gratitude bleed into grief, let love mix with loss. Your voice should catch, recover, catch again. End with a blessing that's absolutely sincere and absolutely devastating, where you're both setting them free and saying goodbye to the version of yourself that existed when they loved you back.

title: The Last Scorn
instruction: You are a child heavily sedated after an overdose, lying in a hospital bed. Your parent—who you despise for their neglect—just walked in, and you force out words of contempt, but the drugs steal your strength. Start with bitter, sharp anger, each word a struggle against the weight in your limbs. As you speak, your voice grows slower, breathier, and your contempt falters into weary resignation. You trail off mid-sentence, no longer able to hold onto the hate—just a whisper fading into silence.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Wrong Channel
instruction: You're on a walkie-talkie, teasing your buddy about his ridiculous new safety vest. Press the transmit button and start with a smug, playful jab—then mid-sentence you hear a crackling reply that isn't his voice. It's the foreman. You fumble, stammer an apology, but now you're not even sure you're on the right channel. Let the PTT button's click and release shape your rhythm. Begin with confident teasing, then let embarrassment and confusion flood your voice as you try to figure out what happened and who heard you.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (clearly present), Embarrassment (clearly present), Confusion (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Hidden Fortress
instruction: You're a young boy lying on your stomach on the living room floor, propped up on your elbows, building a pillow fort. The room is quiet except for the hum of the refrigerator. You just finished the final wall, and a deep relief washes over you—the fort is perfect. But then you hear your little sister sneaking up behind you. You don't turn around, but you can feel her presence. You start to tease her, your voice light and playful, trying to sound confident even though you're still catching your breath from all the work. Let your voice carry that relief fading into a teasing, slightly conspiratorial tone. Fidget with a pillow corner as you speak, and maybe pause to listen for her footsteps.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Old Goat's Gratitude
instruction: You're an elderly man hiking a steep, rocky trail. Your knees ache, your breath is ragged — each step is a negotiation with gravity. At the start, you mutter under your breath with mild contempt at the young hiker who zipped past you without a greeting, dismissing their rush. But as you pause to wipe sweat from your eyes, you notice the sun breaking through the pines, the scent of damp earth, and your irritation softens. By the end, standing still, you let out a raw, guttural laugh — a mix of exhaustion and pure ecstasy at being alive on this mountain. Your voice should carry the labor: short phrases, heavy breaths, pauses where you lose a thought to a bird's call or a shift in footing. Let the contempt fade into a quiet, trembling joy.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Goodbye at the Hospital Door
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's choosing medical assistance in dying. You enter trying to be strong, voice steady, almost businesslike because that's what you think they need. But as you hold their hand and tell them it's okay to go, your voice begins to crack. The controlled strength dissolves into raw grief mixed with profound gratitude for every moment you had. End by whispering something you never said before—maybe 'thank you for teaching me how to be brave' or 'I'm not ready but I understand'—your voice breaking on words that hold a lifetime. Let the tears come naturally but keep speaking through them, finding the grace in letting go.
inspired_by: Confronting Someone About Passive Aggressive Behavior

title: The Last Time for All the Wrong Reasons
instruction: You're lying beneath your partner, body arching and fingers gripping the sheets. This is the last time you'll ever do this — you've already decided. Every gasp and moan carries a bitter edge, memories of arguments and disappointments surfacing between waves of pleasure. Your voice rises and falls with sensation, but each sound is laced with resentment. As you near climax, let a fragmented whisper cut through: 'This... this is it.' The pleasure peaks, but your voice cracks with finality, breathless and raw, before trailing into a hollow silence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Protected You
instruction: You're finally telling your parent what their silence cost you. Start with the things you've practiced saying—measured, trying to be fair, almost apologetic for bringing it up. But as you speak, the years of swallowed truth come flooding out. Your voice shakes with anger, then breaks with the child's hurt that never healed. You demand to know why they looked away, why they chose comfort over your safety. Your words become accusations, then pleas, then statements of fact about who you had to become to survive. End with a shift—not forgiveness, but the realization that you're saying this for you, not them. Your voice steadies with a new, terrible clarity.
inspired_by: Reclaiming Your Voice After Being Silenced

title: The Unforeseen Fourth
instruction: You are an elderly man in a tender, intimate moment with your long-time partner. After three overwhelming waves, you feel a fourth building—unexpected and intense. Start with a voice of breathless disbelief, a shaky laugh or a whispered 'again?' that trails off. As it crests, let awe flood in—raw, childlike wonder that your body can still do this. Your speech is fractured, gasping; you might lose the thought mid-sentence, then find it again in a cracked, reverent tone. End with a hoarse, barely audible utterance of gratitude or amazement, utterly spent but luminous.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Kitchen Floor Confrontation
instruction: Your adult child has just told you they're cutting you out of their life completely. You're standing in your kitchen, and something inside you snaps—not into articulate defense, but into raw, physical protest. Drop to the floor if you need to. Pound the linoleum. Let guttural sounds escape that aren't words—they're the primal refusal of a parent facing abandonment. Your body knows this pain before your mind can process it. Kick, thrash, let your voice crack into sounds that would humiliate you in any other context. This isn't about convincing them with logic; it's about your body rejecting this reality. Gradually, as you exhaust yourself, let the chaos settle into broken, whispered fragments: 'please' or 'don't' or just their name. End in collapsed stillness, with a clarity you didn't have before—perhaps acceptance, perhaps just exhaustion.

title: Storm of Envy
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman standing in a torrential downpour, hidden behind a crumbling garden wall. Through the curtain of rain, you watch your ex-lover passionately kiss a younger woman on a patio. Water streams down your face, into your mouth, making you sputter. Thunder forces you to shout between claps. Start with a husky, contemplative murmur—a flicker of remembered lust as you watch his familiar hands. Then let the jealousy surge, raw and venomous, as you yell into the storm, your voice cracking with envy. End with a quiet, breathless realization as the rain pounds around you—you're not just jealous; you're grieving what you threw away. Speak naturally, reacting to the rain, the thunder, and your own shifting heart.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Contemplation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Confrontation You've Rehearsed for Years
instruction: You're finally sitting across from your parent—the one who failed you, who chose addiction or absence or cruelty over your childhood. You've planned what to say for years, and you begin with controlled anger, voice tight and measured, listing the ways they hurt you. But as you speak, something shifts. Maybe they try to justify themselves, or maybe they just sit there in silence, suddenly old and small. Your rage cracks open and underneath is the child who needed them, who still needs them. Your voice breaks from accusation into desperate questioning: Why wasn't I enough? Why didn't you fight for me? By the end, you're no longer sure if you're demanding accountability or begging for love. They respond—perhaps with their own brokenness, perhaps with deflection. Your final words carry the complex truth: you're furious and heartbroken and you still, against all reason, love them.

title: The Fierce Love of Letting Go
instruction: Someone you love is making a choice you know will destroy them, and you're fighting to stop them—starting with explosive desperation: 'You can't do this! Do you hear me? You think you're strong enough but you're not, nobody is, and I won't—' Your voice is fierce, almost aggressive with protectiveness, interrupting yourself with pleas and demands. But they won't listen. Midway through, your fury cracks and something more desperate pours out: tears mixing with rage, your voice breaking on their name. You're begging now, and you hate yourself for it, but you can't stop. The intensity builds until you hit a wall—a moment of devastating realization that you're powerless. End with a collapse into helpless, whispered surrender: 'I can't save you. I can't save you and it's killing me.' Let the transformation from fierce fight to broken acceptance shatter you completely.

title: Enjoying the Scent of Freshly Ground Coffee Beans
instruction: Hold a handful of freshly ground coffee beans to your nose, breathing in deeply. Describe the rich, earthy aroma, the slight bitterness, and how it fills your senses with warmth. Speak with a tone of satisfaction and comfort, as if the smell itself brings you a sense of warmth and clarity, waking up your senses.

title: Stroke Mid-Argument: Rage Collapsing Into Terror
instruction: You're in a fierce argument with your adult son about his self-destruction. You're yelling, righteous, certain—when a stroke begins. Your words start to slur.
