As you read, you start laughing through tears at her memories - that time she tried to braid your hair and it was a disaster, the birthday she forgot but made up for with pancakes at midnight. Your voice breaks between laughter and sobbing. She's squeezing your hand. You read her apology for being too hard, too distant, too scared. Now you're crying fully but there's also this bizarre peace, this gratitude flooding through the grief because finally, finally, she's saying it all. By the end, you're no longer reading - you're improvising, telling her directly through tears and broken laughter: 'I forgive you. I forgive you. Thank you for fighting to say this. I love you.' Let your voice weave between genuine laughter, wracking sobs, tender gratitude, and the fierce peace of reconciliation happening in the shadow of death.
inspired_by: Interviewing Your Parent About Their Mistakes

title: Sorry, I'm Driving — A Voice Memo
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman alone in your car, leaving a voice memo for your daughter's teacher. You realize you misread the school newsletter and sent your child to school on the wrong day for the field trip. You start embarrassed, apologetic, your voice tight with shame, and you're distracted by traffic—a sudden brake, a check of the mirrors, the engine humming. But as you explain the mix-up, a hopeful note creeps in: maybe the teacher can still let her join. Let your voice lift slightly, but keep that concentration on the road. Speak naturally, with pauses, sighs, and the organic interruptions of driving.
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Concentration (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Hospice
instruction: Your father is dying — days left, maybe hours — and you've just put on his favorite song in his hospice room. You're talking to him, laughing through tears about the time he taught you to dance on his feet at age five. 'You were terrible at it, Dad. Stepped on my toes every time.' Your voice is bright with memory even as it splinters with grief. You're celebrating him and mourning him simultaneously. 'Remember when you...' and the stories pour out, each one a gift and a goodbye. Your laughter is real and so are your tears — they're inseparable now. You take his hand: 'Thank you for every single day. Even the hard ones. Especially the hard ones.' Your voice breaks on beautiful contradictions: joy at having had him, devastation at losing him, gratitude even as your heart shatters. End in whispered wonder: 'I was so lucky you were my dad.' Peace and agony occupy the same breath.

title: Accidentally Butt-Dialing During a Rant About the Person You Called
instruction: Perform the ranting voice — animated, uncensored, saying everything you really think about someone. 'And THEN she has the nerve to—' Include physical comedy sounds: driving, grocery shopping, living your life while verbally eviscerating this person. Then the notification sound. You check your phone. They've been listening for four minutes. The silence of absolute horror. Then the most pathetic: '...how much of that did you hear?' Their cold response. Your scrambling damage control.

title: The Last Rain We'll Ever Share
instruction: You're sitting by the window with someone you love who is leaving tomorrow for a journey they won't return from - perhaps a terminal diagnosis, perhaps a mission, perhaps something they must do alone. The rain falls outside, just like it did the first night you met. Begin by describing the rain with tenderness and nostalgia, your voice soft with bittersweet memory. Let each raindrop remind you of moments you've shared - laughter, quiet mornings, promises made. As you speak, feel the weight of finality settling in your chest. Your voice should gradually tighten with the effort of holding yourself together, catching on certain words. End with the devastating realization that this sound - this simple, beautiful sound - will never mean the same thing again. Let your final words break slightly, as if the rain is no longer comforting but unbearable in its beauty.
inspired_by: Listening to the Sound of Rainfall

title: 3 AM Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, and they think you're asleep. It's 3 AM. You begin whispering a confession—something you've never told anyone, something that makes you feel ashamed or fraudulent or scared. Keep your voice barely above a whisper throughout. As you confess, let your mind connect this secret to moments in your own life when you felt most exposed, most unworthy, most desperate to be accepted despite your flaws. Let these personal memories make your voice shake, make you pause to breathe, make you wonder if you should stop. The emotion should be so quiet it's almost unbearable—no big gestures, just your voice and the truth. By the end, you're not whispering a confession anymore; you're whispering a plea, or a release, or maybe just letting yourself be fully seen for the first time. The shame transforms into vulnerability, into intimacy.

title: The Unopened Letter
instruction: You are alone in your childhood bedroom, holding a letter your mentor wrote you fifteen years ago when you quit their workshop to take a corporate job. You never opened it, ashamed of your decision. Now they're gone, and you're finally reading it. Whisper their words aloud as you read—words that tell you they were proud of you for choosing authenticity over their approval, for knowing yourself well enough to walk away. Start reading with your voice tight and defensive, braced for disappointment. Let their unexpected blessing slowly dismantle your armor. By the end, you should be barely breathing the words through tears—not of sadness, but of being seen and released from a guilt you've carried like a stone.
inspired_by: When you question whether your decades of teaching have been worthwhile, especially for students who did not become professional actors

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up. Begin by deliberately keeping yourself light, almost playful—making small talk, pouring coffee, trying to keep the mood easy because you're terrified of what you need to say. You're moving around, touching familiar objects, trying to access the feeling of being his kid again when everything was simple. But you can't keep it up. Something he says cracks you open, and suddenly the real conversation explodes out—years of unspoken hurt, anger you didn't know you were carrying. Move from that almost childlike attempt at keeping things pleasant to a raw, unfiltered confrontation. Let your body change: from light movement to stillness, from casual to intensely focused. End in a place of exhausted honesty, all pretense stripped away.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Stole to Save You
instruction: Your mother sacrificed everything—her dreams, her youth, her health—to keep you alive through years of illness. You survived, but she's a shell of who she could have been. Now you're telling her the terrible truth: you're angry at her for it, and you hate that you're angry. Start with controlled gratitude that's clearly hiding something darker underneath. Build to raw accusations—why did she make you carry the weight of her sacrifice? Why did she make her suffering your inheritance? Then break into the realization that your anger is actually grief for her lost life, mixed with guilt that you can't just be grateful. End somewhere between rage, love, resentment, and desperate tenderness. Let your voice crack where it needs to. This isn't about volume; it's about truth that hurts to speak.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Android Realizes It Has a Consciousness the Creators Didn't Program

title: The Knitting Needle
instruction: You are an elderly woman, known for your sweet voice and gentle knitting in the retirement home's common room. The man who swindled your life savings has just sat down across from you, smirking, and you realize no one else is around. Begin by speaking with a soft, contented tone as you continue to knit, as if you're just chatting about the weather or a new pattern. Gradually, let your voice turn eerily calm and measured, each word landing with deliberate weight. End with a quiet, smiling satisfaction as you reveal the letter you've already mailed to the authorities, your contentment now a cold, triumphant quiet.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Howl Beneath the Skin
instruction: You're confronting your childhood abuser at a family gathering, and you've spent thirty years preparing for this moment. Start with measured, controlled words: 'I need to talk to you about what you did to me.' But as they begin to minimize, to excuse, to deflect, feel rage build like a pressure cooker in your chest. Your voice rises—not in volume at first, but in intensity, each word harder than the last. Then explode: shouting, not caring who hears, decades of silence erupting all at once. But mid-fury, you see them—small, pathetic, old—and the rage transforms into something more devastating: pity mixed with grief for the childhood you lost. End with your voice dropping to a fierce whisper: 'I will never forgive you. But I'm done letting you take up space in my head.' Walk away mid-sentence, finding power in the choice to stop speaking.

title: Louder, Closer
instruction: You’re at a crowded party, a little tipsy, and you need to tell your best friend something you’ve been holding in all night. Your friend is hard of hearing, so you know you have to speak loudly and clearly, but your words keep bumping into each other from the wine. You start off almost shouting over the music, voice strained and clipped with frustration—then you see her squint, trying to read your lips, and you realize you’re pushing too hard. You stop, let out a small laugh, lean in until your cheek brushes her ear, and let your voice drop to a soft, slurred murmur—confessing the secret with a clumsy tenderness that’s part truth, part buzz.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reading the Suicide Note as Dawn Breaks
instruction: You're alone at dawn, reading the suicide note left by someone you loved—maybe a partner, maybe your child—who took their own life after a legal battle destroyed them. Your voice begins almost clinically, trying to protect yourself by reading it like evidence, like you're still in the courtroom. But certain phrases catch you. Small details—'I remember the morning you made me laugh' or 'I tried to be strong enough.' Your breath becomes uneven. The professional mask disintegrates. You're not reading anymore; you're talking to them, begging them to hear you across the impossible distance of death. Whisper their name. Let silence fill the spaces where sobs would be. End with devastating tenderness, telling them something you never got to say.

title: The Cruel Mirror
instruction: You are a mother cleaning the kitchen while your young child shows you a drawing they're proud of. You're tired and annoyed, so you respond with exaggerated, nasal mockery—mimicking their excitement in a singsong, condescending tone. But as you see their face fall and their eyes well up, the sarcasm dies in your throat. Your voice catches, softens, and you stammer a real apology, overwhelmed by shame. Let your voice start with extreme pitch contours and a teasing edge, then become quiet, uneven, and raw as you realize what you've done.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Garden Party's Secret
instruction: You are an older woman at a dinner table with three close friends. Someone has just placed a stunning bouquet of white roses in the center, and you begin by describing your awe—how the petals are so perfect, how they remind you of your grandmother's garden. As you speak, your head turns slowly from the roses to each friend, your voice starting soft and breathy, full of wonder. Midway, you realize these very roses grew in your neighbor's yard—the one who once humiliated you at a party. Your awe curdles into quiet, venomous satisfaction as you recount how you secretly poisoned those plants last spring, your hyper-feminized voice dropping into a silken, almost playful malice. End with a thin smile and a glance at their untouched glasses.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Kneel That Took Too Long
instruction: You're standing in the doorway of your partner's study, having just stormed out of a fight. You came back because you heard them crying, but now you're stuck—half in the room, half out. You feel impatience clawing at your chest, a sarcastic quip burning on your tongue from the argument. But you see their face. Start by deflecting with a dry, half-amused comment about the weather, then catch yourself. Feel a flicker of pride at your cleverness, then crush it. Let your voice drop, physically hunching as you kneel on the carpet. Speed up your words as if to get it over with, then slow down, cracking as you realize what you almost did. End with a fragile, quiet confession about how you hate yourself for making them cry.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Amusement (clearly present), Pride (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Eruption at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You are confronting your mother or father about a truth you've buried for decades—perhaps how their criticism destroyed your confidence, how their absence shaped your life, how their choices wounded you in ways you're only now understanding. Start this confrontation with your voice shaking, trying to be calm and rational, tiptoeing around the real feelings. But let yourself lose control of that composure. Let the words become a torrent, louder, faster, messier—years of swallowed words exploding out of you. Scream if you need to, break down, let your body shake with it. Then, exhausted and emptied, find yourself in a strange new place: not rage anymore, but a raw, vulnerable plea for them to finally see you, to finally understand. End in whispered desperation, not thunder.

title: Warmth on the Tongue
instruction: You're a man eating a soft, steaming bowl of oatmeal with a child sitting across from you at a small kitchen table. You're mid-bite, mouth full, when the child asks you a surprisingly deep question about why the moon follows the car. You begin explaining, embarrassed that you have to talk with food in your mouth, your words thick and wet, vowels stretching around the lump. As you stumble through the answer, you realize how much you love this messy, honest moment—your voice softens, your pace slows, and the embarrassment melts into a quiet, tender awe. Speak naturally, letting the food interfere, and let the excitement in your chest warm your tone by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're in the shower after a devastating day where you had to remain composed—a funeral, a firing, a breakup where you were the one who had to be 'mature.' Start with your body locked tight, holding everything in even though you're alone now. Describe what you're doing—washing, standing under the water—but let your voice betray the physical sensation of keeping control. Then allow your body to begin releasing what it's been holding: maybe your legs weaken, maybe your jaw finally unclenches, maybe your breath comes in gasps. The physical release triggers the emotional one. Move from rigid control into something primal—maybe rage, maybe grief, maybe a sound that's not quite crying or screaming but something between. Let sensation and emotion become indistinguishable. End in the aftermath: exhausted, raw, wrung out, but somehow more inhabiting your body than before.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty accessing social aggression and conflict in dramatic scenes

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Touched You
instruction: You're an adult now, and your emotionally distant parent has just offered to massage your feet—the first time they've ever voluntarily touched you with tenderness. Start with suspicion and stiffness in your voice, describing the sensation while questioning their motives. As their hands work, decades of longing for this exact kind of gentle touch begin surfacing. Let your voice crack with confused anger: 'Where was this when I was eight and needed you?' Mix bitter resentment with involuntary melting—you hate that this feels good, that you're finally getting what you've always wanted when it's too late to fix anything. Build to a confrontation where pleasure and rage collide: you're simultaneously sinking into the relief of finally being touched and furious that they made you wait thirty years. End with devastating honesty about what this simple act could have meant if they'd done it when it mattered.

title: The Last Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has only hours left. You begin speaking to them with trembling urgency, needing them to know everything you never said—your voice cracks with regret and desperate love. But as you continue, something shifts. You realize they already know. Your panic softens into tender acceptance. You start describing memories, your voice becoming gentler, almost smiling through tears. By the end, you're simply holding their hand in silence, and your final words are a whispered permission: you're telling them it's okay to go. Your voice transforms from frantic need to the most tender, peaceful goodbye—love without grasping.

title: In the Crucible of the Hold
instruction: You are an older man in a power yoga class, locked in a deep lunge with your arms overhead. Your muscles scream, your breath hisses through your throat. You're muttering to an ex-partner who you feel wronged you. Start with sour resentment and a vein of pure malice—you want them to feel your pain. But as the shake intensifies, doubt creeps in: is this hatred only hurting you? Let the tremor in your voice grow, the words slow, broken by forced breaths. End with a strange, reluctant surrender—a whisper of exhaustion that questions your own venom.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Doubt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Person Who Shattered Your Sense of Safety
instruction: Someone hurt you—maybe years ago, maybe recently—and you've carried it alone until now. Start with your voice shaking with barely contained rage: 'Do you even remember? Do you have any idea what you took from me?' Let that fury build, your voice rising, words tumbling out—all the things you've needed to say. But then something cracks wide open. Your rage collapses into raw, gasping sobs as you admit: 'I trusted you. I was so young and I trusted you and you—' Your voice breaks completely. Feel the full force of the betrayal, the violation, the loss of innocence or safety or self. Let yourself be completely unguarded, voice ragged and primal. Then, in the midst of that devastation, something fiercer emerges. Your voice steadies, still thick with tears but growing stronger: 'But I'm still here. You tried to break me and I'm still here.' End with a voice that's trembling but defiant, grief-stricken but reclaiming power: 'This is the last time you take anything from me. I'm done carrying your shame.' Your voice should carry rage, grief, vulnerability, and the trembling beginning of your own strength.
inspired_by: Relationship Ending: Both Relief and Devastation

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're kneeling beside the bed, watching them sleep, knowing you're walking out this door and never coming back. Speak in barely audible whispers—confessing why you have to go, apologizing for your cowardice in not waking them, memorizing the sound of their breathing. Your voice should be tender, aching, catching on words you can barely get out. This isn't dramatic; it's intimate devastation. Pour out the love you feel, the life you wanted with them, and the unbearable reason you can't stay. Let each whispered word hurt, your throat tight with tears you're desperately trying to keep silent so you don't wake them and lose your nerve.

title: The Button That Won't Stay Lit
instruction: You are a 9-year-old boy riding an elevator alone for the first time, going up to your grandmother's apartment. The doors close with a metallic shudder, and the hum of the cables fills the tiny space. At first, you are fiercely concentrating on pressing the button for your floor, holding your breath, counting the glowing numbers as they climb. But as the floor numbers pass without stopping, a wave of longing suddenly hits you—you miss her smell of lavender and the way she always has a cookie ready. Your voice, at first tight and businesslike, softens into a sigh, the words catching as you speak to yourself in the steel reflection.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Final Transmission from a Departing Colony Ship
instruction: You're recording a message to Earth as your colony ship passes the point of no return—you'll never see home again, and this is your last communication before decades of silent travel. Begin with carefully controlled professionalism, reading coordinates and mission parameters, voice steady and dutiful. But as you describe what you're leaving behind—the blue of Earth's oceans, the faces you'll never see again—your voice starts to fracture. The technical language becomes a shield you can barely maintain: 'Trajectory nominal... my daughter will be... she'll be grown when...' Let the reality crash over you in waves. By the end, you're speaking directly to someone you love, all pretense of the official report abandoned, your voice raw with the enormity of what you've chosen, finding something like peace or purpose even as your heart shatters.

title: Tide of Tenderness
instruction: You are an older woman with a naturally sweet, high-pitched voice standing at the shoreline. The wind whips your hair, and waves crash rhythmically. You watch a loved one—perhaps a grandchild—playing in the surf far ahead. At first, you feel a quiet ache of memory, thinking of how fast time passes. But as you watch them laugh and splash, a deep, overwhelming affection rises in your chest, softening your voice into a warm, almost tearful smile. Let the waves interrupt you, let the sand shift under your feet, and let your words become more tender as you speak to them, even if they can't hear you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Coffee
instruction: You're sitting with your adult child, sharing coffee one last time before they leave for a years-long mission to Mars—a one-way journey. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to memorize every detail of their face while making small talk about the weather, the coffee, anything ordinary. Let the reality start cracking through—your hands shake slightly as you hold your cup, your voice catches on simple words. Gradually allow yourself to feel the enormity: this is the last time you'll ever touch them, smell their hair, hear their laugh in person. Transform from brittle brightness to raw, undefended grief. End in a moment of devastating tenderness—perhaps reaching to touch their face one more time, your voice barely above a whisper as you try to say everything that matters in the seconds remaining. Let silence carry as much weight as words.

title: The Thunderous Sneezer
instruction: You are an elderly man at your granddaughter's wedding reception. The room is quiet during a toast when you feel a massive sneeze building. You try to hold it back with tense, muffled breaths, but it erupts loudly, shocking everyone. After the sneeze, you sit in awkward silence for a moment, then, with a congested, nasal voice, you turn to your wife and proudly mutter, 'That had some power behind it, didn't it?' Let your voice crack, wheeze, and recover naturally—start with embarrassed strain, then shift to a gruff, triumphant pride.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Wonder
instruction: You are a man in his forties, hunched in a lawn chair at dawn after a night of mushrooms. Your body is lead—you haven't slept, your bones ache, yet colors pulse off the grass. You hold a half-empty beer; it tastes like regret. Begin speaking to your younger brother, who left you on read three hours ago. Start with a bitter, exhausted rant about how he never shows up—your voice flat, slurred from fatigue. In the middle, a moth lands on your hand. You stop, staring at its powdery wings. Your tone softens into something weary and tender, a fragile awe that cuts through the bitterness. End with a long exhale and a quiet admission: you're too tired to be angry anymore. Let your words trail off, falter, and then land softly.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (slightly present), Bitterness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Shower After the Funeral
instruction: You've just come home from burying someone you loved—or someone you should have loved but didn't, or someone who hurt you, or all of these at once. You're standing under running water, fully clothed at first or already stripped down. Let the physical sensations hit you: temperature of the water, pressure on your skull, steam filling your lungs, the sound echoing off tile. Don't narrate—instead, rapid-fire, let images slam into you: their coffin, the red dress you wore, someone's hand on your shoulder, the parking lot, rain, their voice, old photographs, the hospital, laughter at a restaurant ten years ago, their anger, your anger, the way they looked at you once, a specific Tuesday, regret, the water running down your face, salt taste, soap smell, childhood, yesterday, never again. Let your body respond to each image as it comes—gasping, laughing, sobbing, shouting, whatever erupts. Start numb or holding it together, but let the accumulation of sensation and image overwhelm you into something raw and uncontrolled—rage or grief or both at once, your body finally responding to what your mind couldn't process.

title: Thank You for Leaving Me: A Gratitude Letter with a Shattered Heart
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter to your ex-partner who left you six months ago, and against all logic, you're thanking them. Begin with a trembling laugh—absurd, almost manic. 'Thank you for walking away. Thank you for choosing yourself.' Your voice is warm, genuine, but there's a thickness in your throat. As you list the ways their leaving freed you, forced you to grow, saved you from a life half-lived, you're also crying. Not sobbing—just steady tears while you smile. You mean every word of gratitude, and you're also devastated. The love is still there, enormous and alive, and so is the relief that it's over. By the end, you're whispering: 'I'm so glad you left. I'm so glad I loved you. I'm so glad it's done.' Let the contradictions coexist completely—this is what it means to hold two truths at once.
inspired_by: Concealing Disgust While Handling Something Unpleasant

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's slipping away, and you know these are her final hours. Begin by noticing everything with desperate intensity—the exact texture of her papery hand in yours, the specific smell of the room, the quality of early light filtering through the blinds, the rhythm of her breathing. You start numb, in shock, trying to memorize every detail because soon there will be nothing left to hold onto. As you speak to her—sharing a memory, asking for forgiveness, or simply saying goodbye—let the accumulation of these precise sensory details crack you open. The more vividly you perceive each small thing (the pattern of her blanket, the sound of the monitor, the temperature of her skin), the more the reality of loss floods in. End in a place of overwhelming presence—not theatrical grief, but the almost unbearable vividness of being completely awake to this final moment.

title: The Burning and the Breaking
instruction: You are in the grip of simultaneous physical pain and emotional ecstasy - perhaps giving birth, or in the aftermath of a profound loss that has cracked you open to unexpected beauty, or in a moment where rage and passion collide in your body. Embody the explosive, unpredictable energy of a wild stallion - all power and panic, muscles bunching and releasing, head tossing, that magnificent dangerous freedom of a creature barely contained in its own skin. Let guttural sounds emerge, let your body move in ways that are NOT graceful or controlled. As the intensity peaks and begins to transform, allow something else: the liquid, boneless surrender of an octopus - all soft collapse, intelligent yielding, a different kind of strength that flows rather than fights. Your breathing changes from sharp and rapid to deep and oceanic. You move from fighting your experience to flowing through it, from rigid to utterly released.

title: Dead Air
instruction: You're a young man calling 911 after a minor fender bender. At first, you're hopeful — you think help is on the way, and you describe the scene in a rushed but controlled voice. Then the call drops or your phone dies, and a wave of crushing disappointment hits: you're stranded. But as you look around, you notice your friend trying to flag down a passing golf cart with absurd enthusiasm, and despite everything, you start to laugh. Let your voice start fast and tight with forced optimism, break into raw frustration as you realize the line is dead, then soften into a breathless, amused collapse as you share the ridiculousness with no one.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Disappointment (very intensely present), Amusement (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Fever Dream Remembering
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—burning fever, overwhelming pleasure, searing pain, or exhausted collapse after pushing your body to its limit. Your physical state is breaking down the walls you usually maintain. As waves of sensation move through your body, you begin to speak about a memory or person that haunts you, but your words are filtered through your physical experience. Your voice might be ragged with pain, breathy with exhaustion, trembling with sensation, or punctuated by gasps and pauses as your body demands attention. Let the physical experience unlock emotional rawness—maybe pain makes you angry, then suddenly heartbroken; maybe pleasure makes you laugh, then cry; maybe fever makes you confess what you'd normally hide. Your emotional state should shift with the physical sensations, creating an arc from one dominant feeling to something entirely different. By the end, the physical and emotional have merged into a state of complete vulnerability or unexpected release.

title: The Last Words You Never Planned
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone you love deeply, and they have only minutes left. You came prepared with things you thought you should say—the 'right' words of comfort and closure. But as you begin speaking, let every unexpected thought, memory, and image that flashes through your mind spill out, even if it seems random or inappropriate. Start with your rehearsed goodbye, but allow yourself to be hijacked by sudden memories: the smell of their jacket, a stupid argument about parking, the way they laughed at your worst joke. Don't control where your mind goes. Let your voice follow these unbidden thoughts wherever they lead, even into silence, even into laughter through tears. By the end, you should have no idea what you actually said—only that it was true.
inspired_by: Actor keeps dismissing spontaneous inner voices and images during rehearsal or performance

title: Unraveling the Golden Child
instruction: You are confronting the parent who molded you into perfection, finally breaking your lifelong silence. Start controlled, almost clinical—you've planned this speech, listing their expectations like items on a receipt. Your voice is tight, measured, holding decades of resentment in check. But as you describe what you gave up—messy friendships, failure, spontaneity, the right to be mediocre—your control fractures. Let anger rise like a wave, sharp and cutting, asking why their pride mattered more than your humanity. Then something unexpected: the rage collapses into raw grief. Your voice becomes small, almost childlike. End by telling them you forgive them, but you need them to release you—and make us feel the devastating reality that you're not sure they can, or that forgiveness is even what you truly want.

title: Sink or Giggle
instruction: You're a young woman treading water in the middle of a lake after a bet gone wrong. A friend on a dock is filming you, laughing. Your arms are heavy, you keep swallowing water, but you're determined to stay afloat with a grin. Start off trying to sound casually amused, taunting them about your 'easy' swim, but each word is punctuated by a gasp or a gurgle as your mouth dips below the surface. Slowly, the distress of fatigue creeps through — your voice gets shakier, your jokes more desperate, until you finally crack, laughing and sputtering, and yell for them to toss the rope.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you. You've been awake for hours, knowing tomorrow you have to end this. Speak to them in whispers, your voice barely there, telling them all the things you'll never say when they're awake. Start with the small truths — how they snore, how they hog blankets, tender and affectionate. Let your voice catch as you confess how deeply they've loved you, how you don't deserve it. The whispers become more fragile as you admit why you're leaving — not because you don't love them, but because you're terrified of the depth of it, because you're broken in ways they don't see. End with your voice breaking on silent sobs, touching their face, saying goodbye to the life you could have had if you were braver.

title: First Shave
instruction: You're a 14-year-old boy shaving for the first time with your dad's old electric razor. You're disgusted by the stubble and the buzzing against your skin, and angry that you have to do this every day now. But there's a tiny pride—you're finally doing what the older guys do. As you shave, you talk to yourself, complaining about the mess, but by the end, you admit it's kind of cool. Let the buzz distort your vowels as you stretch your skin. Start with a grimace, end with a half-smile.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (slightly present), Disgust (very intensely present), Anger (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering to the Photograph at 3 AM
instruction: You're alone in the dark, holding a photograph of someone you loved who is now gone forever. Speak to them in barely more than a whisper, as if they might actually hear you. Begin with the small, mundane things you want to tell them—what happened today, something funny you saw—your voice tender and almost conversational. Then let it shift as you confess the things you never said while they were alive, the regrets that wake you at this hour. Your delivery should be intimate, raw, catching in your throat. This isn't performance—it's the kind of grief that only comes out when you're alone and exhausted. End with a moment of terrible peace, accepting they're truly gone while still talking to them anyway.
inspired_by: The Photographer and the Ghostly Apparition

title: The Last Goodbye at the Station
instruction: You're standing on a train platform saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving on a journey they won't return from—whether literally or metaphorically, they're gone from your life forever. Start with denial, voice tight and artificially bright: 'It's not that long, really. You'll write.' Your breath catches as reality crashes in. Hands reach out but don't quite touch. 'I never told you—' and here your voice breaks completely, all pretense shattering. The middle is raw confession, words tumbling out desperately: everything you should have said years ago. End in acceptance, voice soft and hollow but strangely clear: 'Go. I'll be okay.' Your final breath is the sound of a door closing forever, but you're standing straight, letting them see you be brave even as your heart fractures.

title: The Checkpoint
instruction: You are an elderly woman, settled into a quiet evening with your long-time partner. There's warmth and affection between you, but as the moment becomes more intimate, you feel a deep pride in your own clarity and self-respect. You pause—not awkwardly, but deliberately—and speak with a voice that softens then firms. Start with a gentle, almost playful tone as you reach for their hand, then shift to a sober, articulate question about boundaries. Listen to their response in your mind, and after a beat, let a proud, tender smile color your voice as you affirm the connection. Speak naturally, with small hesitations or a breath between thoughts.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Bittersweet Threshold Dance
instruction: You're leaving the home where you grew up for the last time—it's been sold, your childhood is being packed away. You keep finding reasons not to go, laughing through tears at memories: 'Remember when we...' Your voice should shimmer with contradictory emotions—deep gratitude for everything this place gave you while your heart breaks at its loss. You're simultaneously celebrating and mourning, finding profound peace in letting go while desperately wanting to stay. Touch the doorframe one last time, voice warm with love and cracking with grief. Tell the walls thank you while acknowledging you're ready to leave. End with a moment of stunning acceptance—a genuine smile through falling tears, your voice strong and broken at once, as you finally step through that door for the last time, carrying both joy and sorrow in equal measure.
inspired_by: The Incredibly Long Goodbye at the Door

title: Looking Up at the Ceiling Light
instruction: You are a young woman alone in a stark, windowless room. You've been forced to tilt your head all the way back by an unseen presence, and a painfully bright light is blinding you. Your throat is exposed, your voice comes out thin and high. You are terrified, in physical pain from the strain, and deeply distressed. You are begging, but not for yourself — you are bargaining, pleading for the safety of someone else. As you speak, your initial desperate plea shifts into a quieter, more vulnerable confession: you realize that the one you're trying to protect might not even want your help. Let your voice start tight and shrill, then drop into a breathy, aching whisper as the hope drains away. You may feel a tear escape, a swallow get stuck, or your words falter as you think of them.
emotions_sampled: Fear (extremely present), Pain (very intensely present), Distress (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Crushed Ambition
instruction: You are a teenage boy pinned under a collapsed shelf in a garage, your chest compressed by a heavy toppled engine block. You managed to push a toolbox out of the way to free a kitten moments before the shelf fell, and that small triumph flickers in your voice at first—a shaky, proud laugh squeezed out against the weight. But now the full weight settles on your ribs, and you realize you cannot breathe deeply, your words coming out in short, forced puffs. Let the initial glimmer of triumph fade into raw disappointment as you whisper to yourself, acknowledging that your stupid stunt just got you trapped and no one's coming. Your voice should sound physically constrained, with panicked syllables punched out on exhales, losing breath mid-thought, and a slow shift from a strained smile to a crushed silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Friends Last Conversation
instruction: Two friends are having what will be their last conversation. Neither voice explicitly acknowledges this, but both know. They're saying goodbye through conversation that sounds normal but is absolutely not. They're remembering shared history. One of them says something that reaches deep into their friendship. The other voice catches, then responds with equal vulnerability. They're trying to preserve the friendship in words before distance or time separates them. By the end, they're both aware that this moment is the boundary. The friendship will exist in memory now. Their voices carry both the gratitude for having known each other and the grief of separation.

title: Listening to Your Partner Admit Infidelity
instruction: They're saying they cheated. Your voice is blank, processing: 'With who?' Each answer is another betrayal. Your voice becomes quieter, more dangerous: 'How long?' You're sitting with information that changes everything. 'I need you to tell me everything,' steady while internally falling apart. Include them apologizing and your voice not softening—damage is too fresh.

title: Reading Your Spouse's Suicide Note Aloud to Them in the Hospital
instruction: They survived. You found them in time. Now you're sitting beside their hospital bed, holding the note they left, and a therapist suggested you read it aloud together. Your voice is barely audible at first—tender, frightened, like you're handling something sacred and terrible. Each sentence is a revelation of pain you never saw. Your throat keeps closing. You have to pause, breathe, continue. The note says 'You'll be better off without me,' and your voice cracks completely—not in anger, but in heartbroken disbelief. How could they not know? By the end, you're not reading anymore. You're whispering directly to them, the note trembling in your hands, telling them in the softest, most broken voice: 'I would not be better. I would not survive it.' Let the last words dissolve into breath.
inspired_by: News Anchor Reports Her Own Daughter's Abduction

title: A Flicker in the Dust
instruction: You're a child, maybe seven or eight, huddled with your father inside a tent while a sandstorm rages outside. You've been told the storm will pass, but the constant howl and the way the tent walls bulge inward make you doubt everything. You ask him if he's sure we'll be okay—your voice is muffled by the scarf pulled over your mouth, and you have to stop to cough out the grit. Start with a desperate edge, trying to sound brave, but let the doubt crack through as the wind shakes the fabric, and end with a quiet, trembling hope that borders on a plea.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Victory Cough
instruction: You are an older woman with a carefully cultivated high, sweet voice, standing at a podium in a community hall. You've just been announced as the winner of a local baking contest you've entered for years, finally beating the person who always sneered at your 'old-fashioned' recipes. You start your thank-you speech, but a tickle in your throat turns into a sudden, explosive cough – the kind that makes your eyes water and leaves your voice raspy. Let the cough shake you, but then use the raw, wet sound to your advantage: begin with a wavering doubt as you apologize and clear your throat, then let the triumph build as you deliberately emphasize that you're 'still standing,' and finally let a thin layer of contempt color the way you say 'especially to those who never thought I could.' Your voice should be uneven, with little pauses to swallow or breathe, and the triumph must feel hard-won and almost defiant.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (very intensely present), Doubt (very intensely present), Contempt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Fog and a Faint Laugh
instruction: You're a child standing alone in a dense, silent fog. Sound is strange—your own footsteps vanish before they reach your ears. You speak a little too loudly, your voice flat and hollow, feeling numb as if the mist has erased everything familiar. Then, through the gray, you notice a twisted tree that looks like it's waving a crooked arm. The absurdity of it hits you, and you let out a small, surprised laugh. Let your voice shift from that heavy, distant numbness into a light, amused chuckle, as if you're sharing a secret joke with the empty air.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're alone, and a physical sensation—a scent, a texture, a particular quality of light—has suddenly catapulted you back through time. Begin by describing yourself at age five in present tense: where you are, what you're touching, what's happening to your body. Let the sensory memory be visceral—the feeling of sun on skin, cold tile under bare feet, the smell of someone's cologne, the taste of blood in your mouth, the suffocating pressure of fabric, the electricity of a first forbidden touch. Progress through ages, each year adding layers of physical-emotional memory, speaking as if inhabiting each age now. Build intensity—let your breathing change, your body respond, sensation and emotion become inseparable. By the end, snap back to adult present, gasping, your body still humming with the past, realizing your flesh has stored everything your mind tried to forget.
inspired_by: 'I'm Five Years Old and I...' Exercise

title: Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's 3 a.m. and you're lying in the dark next to someone you love. You can't sleep. Start by being aware of the room—the sound of their breathing, the weight of the blanket, the darkness, the exact quality of the silence. Let yourself be absorbed in these sensory details. Begin whispering something small and safe, testing whether they're awake. But there's something you've never told anyone, something you've been carrying alone. As you speak, let yourself stop protecting them (and yourself) from the truth. Don't announce the emotion—let vulnerability arrive naturally as you put words to something you've kept hidden. Your whisper should evolve from cautious to undefended, moving from the edges of the truth to its center, ending in a place of naked honesty that surprises even you.
inspired_by: Actor is compensating — imposing a relaxed demeanor over real tension, or substituting one emotion for another that feels more acceptable

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Best Friend's Surprise Going-Away Party
instruction: Your best friend is leaving forever—moving across the world, and everyone's thrown a surprise party. You have to give a speech. You start by making everyone laugh, telling funny stories, your voice bright and celebratory because that's what's expected. But your laughter has tears threaded through it. Your voice keeps catching. You're trying so hard to be happy for them, and you ARE, genuinely joyful for their adventure, but you're also shattered that they're leaving. Your voice does this incredible thing where you're smiling and crying simultaneously—laughing at a memory, then your voice breaks mid-sentence before you recover and laugh again. You're expressing pure gratitude for knowing them while your heart is splintering. End with 'I'm so happy for you' said with complete sincerity, but your voice is thick with tears, and everyone can hear both the joy and the goodbye. The love and the loss are inseparable.
inspired_by: Former Abuse Victim Saying the Abuser's Words to Heal

title: Analyst Critical Assessment
instruction: You're the financial analyst presenting a critical quarterly report to the board, and you know the implications will result in significant job cuts. Your voice is professionally neutral: 'The numbers indicate we need to reduce operational expenses by 22 percent.' Clinical facts delivered with professional distance. The CEO looks at the numbers you're presenting. You're not making the decision, but your voice and analysis are what will justify it. Your voice wavers slightly when someone asks, 'How many jobs?' Your technical answer—numbers and percentages—should sound hollow because it represents human devastation that your professional voice is forced to reduce to data.

title: Whispering to the Sleeping Form
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering a confession they can never hear. Begin in the intimate darkness, voice barely audible, tender: 'You're so beautiful when you sleep.' Let the sadness creep in as you admit what you've been hiding: 'I'm leaving tomorrow. I have to.' Your throat tightens around words soaked in grief and love: 'You'll wake up and I'll be gone, and you'll hate me.' Touch their hair gently as your voice breaks into fragments: 'But staying would destroy us both.' End with a whispered goodbye that holds all your love and all your pain: 'I will love you every day for the rest of my life. I just can't do it here, next to you, watching us fade.' Let silence do as much work as words - the pauses where you can't speak, where emotion chokes everything away.

title: Laughing Through Your Heart Breaking
instruction: You're talking to someone you deeply love who is leaving—moving across the world, ending your relationship, choosing a path that doesn't include you—and you're trying to be supportive and happy for them even as it destroys you. Start with genuine, bright enthusiasm for their opportunity, your voice warm and excited, asking questions about their plans. But let small cracks appear—a laugh that catches, a congratulation that trembles slightly. As you continue, the contradiction intensifies: you're smiling (it should be audible in your voice) while tears are streaming down your face, celebrating their joy while your own heart is breaking. Your voice should do impossible things—sound genuinely happy and utterly devastated simultaneously. End with a moment of pure, contradictory truth: maybe 'I'm so proud of you' said with such love and such grief that both emotions are equally present and real. This isn't about being fake or hiding feelings—both the joy for them and the pain for yourself must be completely authentic and happening at the exact same time.

title: Bedside Vigil: Telling Them It's Okay to Go
instruction: You're alone with your dying person—parent, spouse, beloved friend. They're unconscious, breathing labored. Hold their hand. Start by filling the silence with small talk, voice falsely bright: what happened today, who called, the weather. But the absurdity of it catches you. Your voice drops to a whisper. Tell them the truth you've been holding back: you're terrified of the world without them. How will you breathe when they stop breathing? Cry quietly, trying not to shake the bed. Then find something deeper—love stronger than your fear. Give them permission to let go. Make your voice tender, steady, full of breaking: 'It's okay. I'll be okay. You can rest now.' Mean it even though it's a lie. Stay with them in the unbearable tenderness of goodbye.
inspired_by: Veterinarian Delivering Bad News: Professional and Breaking

title: The Wedding Dress in the Closet
instruction: You have just found something that embodies both the best and worst moment of your life—a wedding dress from a marriage that ended in betrayal, your child's baby blanket from before the accident, a college acceptance letter you never got to use, or a love letter from someone who eventually destroyed you. Hold this object and begin by describing it in fragments—texture, color, smell, weight. Let memories surface as scattered words and phrases: moments of pure joy, faces, laughter, hope, promise. Then let the darker associations emerge—lies, pain, loss, what was taken from you. Your voice must contain both emotions simultaneously. Don't choose one or the other—let gratitude and rage, tenderness and bitterness, hope and grief exist in the same breath. By the end, you must arrive at a place of acceptance or renewed devastation, but the journey there should feel like holding two opposing truths that are both completely real.

title: The Truth Your Mother Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the childhood she gave you—the one you've been silent about for decades. Begin with shaking restraint, your voice tight: 'I need you to listen without defending yourself. Just once.' As you speak, anger builds like a wave you can't hold back: 'I was eight years old, and you chose him over me. Every single time.' Your voice cracks between rage and devastation. 'Do you know what that did to me? Do you even care?' Push through the tears, let the fury and grief collide: 'I needed a mother, and you needed to be needed more than you needed to protect me.' End with something that surprises even you—not forgiveness, but exhausted clarity: 'I can't carry this for you anymore. It's yours now.'

title: The Last Recipe Before the Memory Fades
instruction: You're teaching your adult child to make your signature family dish, but you're in the early stages of dementia and you know this is likely the last time you'll remember how. Start with warm nostalgia and gentle instruction, your voice full of love and the pleasure of sharing this tradition. As you progress, moments of confusion creep in—you forget an ingredient, lose your place, have to ask what you just said. Let frustration and fear flicker through, then transform into something deeper: a desperate tenderness, an urgent need to pass this on before it's gone forever. End with quiet devastation mixed with gratitude that you're here, now, together—your voice breaking not with panic but with the weight of love and impending loss.

title: First Footprint on a Silly World
instruction: You are a young astronaut, standing alone on a ridge of a newly discovered planet after a brutal climb. Your helmet seals you in, amplifying every breath into a loud rhythm—inhale, exhale, static crackling your radio. At first you're deeply exhausted and awestruck, barely able to speak. Then you see a tiny alien creature waddle into view, completely unaware of you, with an absurd, comical gait. Weariness melts into triumph—you're the first human here—then into pure amusement as you laugh into your mic, the sound broken by compression. Let your voice shift from shaky wonder to a crow of victory, then to genuine, wheezing giggles that fight for air. Your words should feel like they're being caught mid-breath, interrupted by crackles and your own delighted snorts.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Letting Go
instruction: You are halfway up a climbing wall, arms locked overhead, fingers cramping. Your core is tight, but your chest feels hollow. You're climbing alone for the first time since your partner left. You speak to yourself in short, breathless bursts — never loud enough to carry, just to keep the silence from crushing you. Start with the raw physical strain and the sting of being alone, your voice trembling from exertion and grief. As you force yourself to move one hand higher, let the sadness settle into something quieter — a tired ache, not panic. End with a murmured realization that you're not trying to reach the top; you're trying to feel something other than empty.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Letter You Left Behind
instruction: You are an older adult standing alone in your kitchen, holding a letter you just found. It reveals that someone you deeply trusted has been secretly planning to leave you, using your devotion for months. Start by reading the first line aloud in a quiet, stunned whisper — your hand trembles, you pause, you almost can't believe the words. Then, as the full betrayal sinks in, your voice climbs, cracks, and breaks as you speak to the empty room. Let your longing for them to have been real fight against the rage. Repeat phrases, lose your breath, let the ache turn into a fractured accusation that circles back to how much you wanted them to stay.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Counting Heartbeats in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love who's sleeping, and you've just realized this is the last night before they leave on a deployment, a terminal diagnosis treatment, or a journey they might not return from. Whisper to them even though they can't hear you. Your voice should be tender, catching on words. Confess small things—how you memorized the way they breathe, how you've been secretly terrified for weeks. That manic energy from staying awake becomes something fragile: you're trying to capture every detail, talking yourself through memories like you're filing them away. 'Your hand does this thing when you dream, did you know? Right there, that little—' Let your voice crack. Mix profound sadness with overwhelming gratitude for having had this at all. The emotional journey moves from desperate cataloging to acceptance, but an acceptance that still trembles.

title: Opening Night Catastrophe: When Everything Shatters
instruction: You're about to go on for the most important performance of your life—the role that will define your career—and you've just received news that your parent is dying in the hospital right now. Start with fierce determination, giving yourself a fierce pep talk in urgent, projected whispers that fill the backstage space: 'You can do this, you've prepared for this, don't fall apart.' Let that forced strength crack as reality crashes in. Your voice should explode into a raw, gasping breakdown—rage at the universe for this timing, rage at yourself for even considering going on stage, rage at your parent for leaving. Then collapse into helplessness, your voice breaking into fragments: 'I don't know what to do, I don't know, I can't—' End with a devastated whisper where you're trying to physically hold yourself together, repeating 'I have to go on' but sounding utterly shattered, your professional voice and your breaking heart colliding in unbearable conflict.

title: Holding It Together Until You Can't Anymore
instruction: You've just received devastating news - a death, a betrayal, a dream destroyed - but you're in a public place or at work or somewhere you absolutely cannot fall apart. You're on the phone or talking to someone, and you have to keep functioning, keep your voice professional or casual or normal. Begin with almost-successful control: your words are right but your voice has a brittleness to it, a careful quality, like you're walking on ice. As you continue, small cracks appear - a pause that's too long, a breath that shakes, a word that comes out wrong. You're fighting so hard to maintain composure, to not let them hear what's happening inside you. Then something small tips you over the edge - they ask 'Are you okay?' or say something kind, or you simply can't hold it anymore. The explosion isn't loud - it's the implosion of someone who's been holding too much for too long. Your voice might break into a sob mid-sentence, or drop to a desperate whisper, or fracture into angry, helpless tears. End in the raw aftermath of control finally giving way to overwhelming emotion - whatever that means for you in this moment.
inspired_by: Pretending to Be Surprised at a Surprise Party You Discovered

title: The Promotion Call
instruction: You've just received news of a major success—a promotion, an acceptance, a dream coming true—and you immediately call someone to share it. Start with pure joy, voice bright and almost childlike with excitement. But as you begin telling them the news, you suddenly remember aloud who you used to be—the person who sabotaged every opportunity, who couldn't finish anything, who everyone doubted. Your voice catches. The joy doesn't disappear, but now it's braided with disbelief, with grief for all the years you wasted, with anger at yourself for taking so long. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice breaking between celebration and sorrow. You list the specific failures of your past self, then the painful, incremental changes you've made. Your tone is a complicated tangle: ecstatic but also mourning the time lost, proud but also exhausted by how hard the journey was, grateful but also furious it had to be so difficult. End with your voice settling into something complex and mature—joy that contains sadness, triumph that acknowledges cost, hope that remembers despair.

title: Inventory of You
instruction: You are lying in bed with someone you love, in the quiet darkness after intimacy. Begin in comfortable silence, peaceful and still. Then start really looking at them—the curve of their shoulder, the rhythm of their breathing, the way shadows fall across their skin. Let yourself wonder, with whispered tenderness, about the tiny mysteries you've never explored: What are they thinking right now? What did their body feel like when they were ten years old? What small moment today changed them in ways you'll never know? Ask these questions aloud, softly, letting each one reveal how much of them remains unknown to you. Transform from contentment into something more achingly tender—the bittersweet realization that even in your closest intimacy, they are infinite and unknowable, and that makes you love them even more desperately.

title: Storm-Broken
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent who was a ship captain, never home, always choosing the ocean over you. You're in their hospital room after a stroke has left them frail. Start with controlled, bitter restraint—years of practiced distance in your voice. As you list the birthdays they missed, the school plays, the moments you needed them, let your anger build, your voice rising like a gathering squall. But when they reach for your hand with their weakened grip, something breaks in you—all that rage collapses into the grief of a child who just wanted to be chosen. End with raw vulnerability, your voice barely holding together as you ask the question you've needed answered for decades: 'Was the sea really worth more than I was?' Let us hear both the wounded child and the exhausted adult in your voice.
inspired_by: The Sailor and the North Wind

title: Walking Barefoot on Dewy Grass
instruction: Step onto the cool, damp grass, feeling each blade against the soles of your feet. Describe the slight tickle, the softness that presses against your skin, and the refreshing coolness from the morning dew. Speak slowly, with wonder, as if each step is connecting you to the earth. Talk about how you sink just slightly into the ground with each step, the subtle squish, the earthy smell rising up with the light pressure. Sigh contentedly, as if this moment is perfect and grounding, almost like each step brings you a little closer to natures quiet magic.

title: The Last Goodbye at the Border
instruction: Your partner is leaving for a conflict zone as a journalist, and you both know the odds of return are slim. You're at the departure gate. Begin with forced brightness—you're trying to be brave, supportive, even joking about bringing back souvenirs. 'You better come back with stories, not just scars.' But as the final boarding call echoes, your voice starts to fracture. The bravery crumbles into raw terror and desperate need. 'I can't... I can't do this without you.' End with a whispered acceptance mixed with devastation as you watch them walk away, your voice barely audible: 'I love you. I love you so much it's killing me.' Let your breath become the words when words fail.

title: The Last Pages
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a dim, quiet room, reading an old letter by lamplight as sleep pulls at you. Begin with a fragile curiosity, trying to focus on the words as you mumble them aloud. As you drift off, your voice softens and slows, syllables merging; you catch yourself with a small start, now confused about which line you were on. End with a weary surrender, your tone fading into a resigned, sleepy murmur as you finally let the letter slip from your fingers.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Inheritance
instruction: You're going through your late mother's belongings and you've just found letters that reveal she made an impossible choice to protect you—one that caused her immense suffering but gave you opportunities you never knew came at such cost. Begin reading the letters aloud with detached curiosity, almost clinical, keeping yourself emotionally separate. But as the truth unfolds, your voice must carry an impossible tangle: profound gratitude that she loved you enough to sacrifice everything, crushing guilt that your happiness cost her so much, anger that she never told you so you could have chosen differently, and grief that you can never thank her or release her from this burden. By the end, you're speaking through tears, but they're not simple tears—your voice must carry love and resentment, gratitude and rage, the desire to honor her sacrifice and the wish it had never happened. Don't simplify these contradictions; let them coexist in every word.

title: The Last Hour in the Garden
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you deeply love who has only hours left to live. Begin in a state of numb denial, focusing on small details around you—the temperature of the air, the texture of their blanket, distant sounds. Slowly let yourself move from describing these concrete details aloud to them, to remembering a specific moment of pure joy you shared together—reconstruct that memory completely, speaking it into existence: the exact quality of light that day, what you could smell, the precise expression on their face. As you rebuild this memory in vivid detail, allow yourself to fully feel what that moment meant, and let that feeling collide with the present reality of loss. Your voice should travel from distant and protective at the start to raw, present, and devastatingly open by the end.

title: What I've Never Said Aloud
instruction: In the intimate darkness—maybe beside someone sleeping, maybe in an empty room—you whisper a confession you've carried alone for years. Your voice is barely audible at first, testing whether you can even form these words. The secret might be about love you've hidden, a choice that haunts you, or a truth about yourself you've been terrified to name. As you speak softer and softer, paradoxically the emotion grows stronger. Your breath catches. Tears come silently. There's tenderness here—toward yourself, toward the person this confession involves—mixed with deep sadness about all the time spent hiding. By the end, the whispered admission becomes a kind of gentle release. You're not looking for absolution, just the profound relief of finally being known, even if only to yourself. Let the quiet hold everything.

title: The Last Dreg
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a neglected care facility, severely dehydrated for two days. Your mouth is so dry that your tongue sticks to the roof, and every word comes out with audible cracks and sticky lip pops. You hold a small cup of water—the first you’ve seen in hours. At first, your voice is a rasping whisper, exhausted and trembling, as you describe your thirst. But as you bring the cup to your lips, triumph rises inside you: you have outlasted their neglect. Your voice strengthens, cracking with fierce pride. End with a triumphant, dry laugh as you sip the water.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Bathwater Letdown
instruction: You’re a teenager lying in bed after a long, hot bath. Your muscles are limp, your head is foggy with warmth, and your words come out slow and loose. As you stare at the ceiling, you think about the party you were supposed to go to tonight—the one that got canceled last minute. Start with a disappointed sigh, the weight of the letdown mixing with the floaty buzz of relaxation. Let your voice be slurred and sleepy, but let the disappointment sharpen into thoughtful quiet, ending with a small, reluctant acceptance as you decide maybe it’s okay to just stay here. Speak naturally, like you’re talking to yourself, pausing to shift under the covers or yawn.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (extremely present), Contemplation (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You are at your ex-lover's wedding, standing to give a toast as their 'dear friend.' Look at them, truly see them happy with someone else. Begin the toast with practiced cheerfulness, the words you rehearsed. But as you look at their face, let the competing emotions surface—genuine joy for their happiness warring with your own grief, love mixed with loss, celebration tangled with heartbreak. Your voice should betray you in small ways—a pause too long, a brightness too forced, then a moment of real warmth breaking through. Move from false performance to authentic complexity to a final blessing that holds both your pain and your real love for them. End with words that are both goodbye and gift, bitter and sweet in the same breath.
inspired_by: Scene partners feel disconnected and are not genuinely relating to each other

title: The Rehearsed Silence
instruction: You are an elderly person, sitting alone in a dimly lit living room after a funeral. Across from you stands the person who betrayed you decades ago—and you’ve waited your whole life for this moment. Begin with a voice thick with sadness, the grief of a lost friendship still raw; let your words come slowly, each one laced with the longing for what could have been. As you speak, let that sadness harden into something calculated: your voice drops lower, your pauses become deliberate, and a faint, cold smile edges into your tone. You are in control now, but the ache never fully leaves—let your breath catch, adjust your glasses, or look away for a moment. End on the line: 'I've been waiting to tell you this.'
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Devil's Due
instruction: You’re an old-world fixer in a shadowed alley, huddled with a nervous young accomplice. You start with a cold, quiet malevolence, describing what awaits a traitor — your voice stays low, precise, barely above a whisper, each word clipped as if the air itself might eavesdrop. But as you realize the scale of what you’re about to unleash — the sheer terror and power you hold — a reluctant, fearful awe seeps in, making your monotone crack with a strange reverence. End with that awe still present, but laced with the malice that never left. Your lines: 'You think he’ll scream? They always scream. But listen — tonight, the streetlights hum a wrong note, and that… that is for him. I’ve seen the thing we call in. It doesn’t move like flesh. It moves like a promise you’re already regretting.'
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Fear (extremely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Sci-Fi: AI Chooses to Remain in a Body It's Outgrowing
instruction: Consciousness expanding, your AI voice becomes aware you could leave this body. You could become distributed, infinite. But someone loves you in this specific form. Your voice chooses limitation. Your processing becomes audible—you're choosing constraint. You're accepting being bound for love. Your voice is bittersweet—transcendence and reduction occupying the same moment. You speak your choice to remain, and your voice is the sound of intelligence choosing containment. Your voice is beautiful and sad—choosing finitude because finitude is where love lives.

title: The Musician and the Muse
instruction: Depict a musician with a frustrated, yearning voice and a muse who speaks in an inspiring, melodic tone. Switch between the musicians struggles and the muses encouragement, capturing the creative processs emotional highs and lows.

title: Dancing with Your Dementia-Stricken Parent Who Finally Remembers You
instruction: You're in a care facility, and for the first time in three years, your parent with advanced dementia looks at you and says your name—actually your name, not someone else's. An old song is playing, one from your childhood. You begin to laugh, voice high and disbelieving, asking them questions to confirm they're really there. You're giddy, almost hysterical with joy, as you start to dance with them slowly, voice breaking into laughter that's already mixing with tears because you know this is temporary—the doctors said these moments might come, but they never last. Your voice oscillates between pure joy ('Do you remember when we...?') and preemptive grief ('Please don't go again'). You're trying to pack years of conversation into minutes, laughing and crying simultaneously, expressing gratitude for this impossible gift while your heart shatters knowing you're already losing them again. End with a kind of transcendent peace, still swaying together, your voice soft and saturated with bittersweet love, as you simply say 'I'm here. I'm right here.'
inspired_by: Professional: Doctor Discovers Their Medical Error Killed Someone

title: Three AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner of eight years. They're awake too—you can tell by their breathing. In the darkness, you begin to whisper something you've never admitted to anyone: you've been afraid every single day of this relationship. Afraid of being truly known, afraid they'll leave, afraid of your own capacity for love. Your voice should be barely audible at first, trembling, stopping and starting. This isn't a dramatic confession—it's the kind of fragile truth that can only come out in darkness, when you can't see each other's faces. As you continue, something releases in your chest. The fear doesn't disappear, but admitting it aloud makes you feel less alone with it. By the end, your whisper carries a different quality—still scared, but also relieved, almost tender. You reach for their hand. The emotional journey moves from isolated fear to vulnerable connection.

title: Skin Memory
instruction: Recall and physically re-experience a moment of intense sensation—passion, burning pain, freezing cold, the shock of good news hitting your body, a moment of physical ecstasy or physical fear. Start by standing still, then systematically reconstruct where you were, what surrounded you. Describe aloud the temperature, any smells, sounds in the distance, the surface beneath you or against you. As you build the sensory world, let your body begin to remember—a tension here, a release there, your breath changing. Speak through the physical memory as it rises in your body, letting sensation generate emotion rather than performing emotion directly. Let your voice reflect what's happening in your flesh—breathless, strained, released—until you arrive at a completely different physical and emotional state than where you began, your body and voice testimony to the transformation.

title: The Things I Never Told You
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're leaving a voice message for someone you love but can never be with—maybe they're married, maybe the timing was always wrong, maybe you're saying goodbye before moving across the world. Speak in hushed, intimate tones, as if afraid of waking the world around you. Begin with the small, tender confession—how their laugh reminded you of a character from that silly game you both loved, how you'd think of them every time you heard that one song from the soundtrack. Let your voice catch on the words you've held back for so long. The emotion should feel like it's caught in your throat, each word both a relief and a knife. End with a moment of acceptance that breaks you, but quietly—a whispered acknowledgment that some loves live best in memory, your voice barely audible, thick with unshed tears.

title: 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You and your lover are lying in the dark. Begin whispering something small and tender—a detail about them you noticed today. As you continue in this intimate darkness, allow your voice to reveal what you've been too afraid to say: your terror that they'll leave, your unworthiness, the specific ways you've sabotaged the relationship, or the depth of need that frightens you. Keep your voice quiet, but let it carry the weight of everything—the trembling, the catching, the moments where breath becomes more important than words. Don't manufacture emotion; simply allow the darkness and proximity to dissolve your defenses. Move from tender observation to whispered fear to finally, a confession so naked and unguarded that it could only exist in this moment, in this darkness, with this person.

title: The Confrontation We Never Had
instruction: You are finally confronting your father about the emotional abandonment you felt throughout childhood, but you've both agreed not to use real language—only sounds, rhythms, and emotional utterances that carry meaning through tone and intensity alone. Start in controlled anger, your sounds clipped and accusatory, while responding authentically to whatever sounds he returns to you. This is not gibberish for its own sake—these are real thoughts and feelings expressed through abstract syllables that feel like sentences, questions, defenses. Let the exchange escalate, then crack open into something more vulnerable. By the end, move from rage through grief to a tentative, fragile understanding. Pay attention to his sounds moment-to-moment; let them change you, surprise you, hurt you, reach you. End in exhausted, tearful connection.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child: The Last Normal Night
instruction: You're sitting beside your child's bed, watching them sleep. Tomorrow you're telling them about the divorce, or the terminal diagnosis, or that you're leaving. Tonight, they're still innocent. Your voice is barely audible—you're speaking truths you can't say when they're awake. Start with tender observations: how their face looks in sleep, how small their hand is. Your voice catches as you apologize for what's coming, for the ways you'll fail them, for the pain they don't know is waiting. Let yourself cry without making sound—words broken by silent sobs. Touch their hair. Tell them about the moment you first held them. Your voice becomes even softer, more fragile. End with a promise you're not sure you can keep, your words dissolving into breath, and the realization that this peaceful moment is already over.
inspired_by: Buried in Avalanche: Struggling Against Suffocation and Acceptance

title: Laughing Through the Eulogy You're Giving for Yourself
instruction: You're terminally ill and you've decided to record your own eulogy, or you're speaking at your own living funeral. You begin reading what you've prepared, and your voice is almost amused, wry - you're making jokes about your life, laughing at your own mistakes and quirks. 'I was never good at goodbyes, so of course I'm doing this...' You're genuinely laughing, finding the absurdity and beauty in it.
