title: The Protector Who Can't Protect
instruction: You're a parent/older sibling/guardian and something terrible has happened or is about to happen to someone under your protection—and you are utterly powerless to stop it. Start with fierce, explosive determination: 'I won't let them touch you. I'll fight every single one of them.' Your voice is a weapon, full of rage and protective fury. But reality intrudes—maybe they're being taken away by authorities, by illness, by circumstances beyond your control. The rage splinters into desperation. You're making promises you can't keep, your voice climbing, becoming almost feral with helplessness. Then it breaks completely—you collapse from warrior to devastated human. Your voice cracks into sobs of 'I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, I should have—' You cycle between attempting to rebuild your strength ('We'll fix this, I swear') and dissolving into the unbearable truth that you can't save them. End in a whispered, shattered vow that's more prayer than promise, mixing love, rage, and complete helplessness.
inspired_by: Meth Psychosis: Convincing Yourself of a Delusion

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're in the shower, and suddenly a smell, a sound, a sensation pulls you back into a memory your body has stored but your mind has tried to forget—a moment of humiliation, powerlessness, or violation. Begin with your breathing changing, your body tensing, reliving the frozenness, the silence, the inability to fight back. Feel the hot water on your skin as both present and past collapse together. But this time, your body does what it couldn't do then. Let yourself physically express what was locked inside—whether that's rage erupting in guttural sounds, fists pounding tile, or a scream that's been trapped in your throat for years. Your voice should be primal, uncontrolled, animal. Feel the release in your muscles, your jaw, your chest. As the water runs, let the intensity gradually transform into shaking, then crying, then finally a deep exhale. End with your body softer, emptied, reclaimed. The physical release should be palpable in your voice—from locked and tight to wild to finally, achingly open.

title: The Crown of the Night
instruction: You are lying in the dark, breath heaving, skin slick, after a long, intense encounter. Each orgasm has stolen more of your voice — now it's shot, cracked, barely a whisper. You try to murmur something to your partner through the aftershocks, but the words keep breaking off as another wave rolls through your body. Begin in a dazed, almost apologetic disbelief at your own stamina, then let the feeling of triumph creep in — a raw, animal pride that you lasted, that you gave everything. Let your voice fragment, hitch, and die mid-sentence, then come back in a rasp of satisfaction. The final line should be spoken with a hoarse, conqueror's smile, even as you shake.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Sunrise
instruction: You are an elderly man, lying on your side in a hospital bed, curled slightly toward the window. Outside, the first light of dawn breaks through the clouds, painting the room in gold. You just received news that your cancer is in remission—a miracle you didn't expect. As you watch the sunrise, allow the initial exhaustion and stillness to slowly give way to a quiet, trembling joy and awe. Your voice is soft, breathy, intimate—like a whisper meant only for the light. You speak haltingly, pausing to breathe, to let the tears or smiles interrupt. Let the words come from deep in your chest, surprised by the hope that feels so fragile and fierce all at once. End with a wonder that fills the air, even as your body stays still.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Touching Them One Last Time
instruction: You're touching the face or hand of someone in their final moments, or the preserved hand of someone already gone, and you're struck by the impossible wonder of their existence. Begin with your breath catching, barely able to speak: 'Your hands... I never memorized your hands.' There's tender discovery in your voice, intimate and hushed, as if speaking too loudly will shatter the moment. 'Every line. When did this scar...?' Let wonder mix with quiet devastation, your voice getting smaller, more fragile. 'You were here. You were real. You touched things.' End in a whisper that's both marveling and breaking: 'How can something so real just... stop?' Don't cry dramatically - let tears come like breath, involuntary, as you're overwhelmed by the ordinary miracle of a person who existed.

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Pretends Never Happened
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother, finally ready to speak about the neglect she's denied for decades. Begin measured, almost clinical - recounting specific memories with false calm. But as she starts her familiar deflections ('you were always so sensitive,' 'that's not how I remember it'), your voice hardens into something sharp and unforgiving. Detail a moment she left you alone, scared, waiting for her - and watch your voice crack on the word 'waiting.' Let anger and grief crash together as you demand she acknowledge what she did, but end with your voice breaking into something small and childlike: 'I just needed you to be my mom.' The final moment should contain both your adult rage and your child's desperate, still-unanswered need for her to see you.

title: The Last Toast
instruction: You are an older, androgynous person sitting alone in a dimly lit room, nursing a joint. But you're not just relaxed; you're nursing a deep resentment toward someone who wronged you long ago. As you speak to the empty room, start with a contemptuous, weary dismissal of them. Let your thoughts drift, giggle at a bitter memory, then let the malice surface clearly as you imagine their downfall. Your voice should be low, sticky, with long pauses where you lose your train of thought and find it again. End with a quiet, venomous promise.

title: Shouting into the Gale
instruction: You are an elderly man standing in the middle of a fierce, wet gale. Rain lashes sideways, and the wind rips at your coat. You have to tell your daughter that the old oak tree survived the storm — a sign that your family’s luck is turning. Your voice starts tight with frustration, nearly swallowed by the wind, each word a battle. But as you force the news out, your throat loosens and a raw, weary smile breaks through. Let the gusts steal your breath, turn your head to gulp air, and let the final words be almost sung, full of stubborn hope.

title: Goodbye at the Space Station Airlock
instruction: Your partner is boarding a one-way colonization ship to another star system. You'll never see them again—no video calls, no messages after they enter cryosleep. Start trying to be strong, reassuring them this is what they've always wanted. 'I'm happy for you, I really am.' But as the final boarding call echoes, your composure shatters. Your voice breaks as you try to memorize their face. The words catch in your throat: 'How do I let you go?' End in a whisper, touching the glass between you, as acceptance and devastation wash over you simultaneously. Let the silence after your last word carry as much weight as anything you've said.

title: The Storm Inside
instruction: You've just finished a marathon, body screaming with pain, and someone you once loved appears at the finish line—someone who shattered you years ago. Begin with your whole body in physical agony, breath ragged, muscles burning, mind spinning with confusion and resurfacing rage. Let the physical pain and emotional fury blur together. As you stand there, feeling sweat cooling on your skin, heart pounding in your chest, legs trembling, allow the sensation of your own strength—the fact that you just ran 26 miles—to flood your awareness. Feel your own power, your own endurance, the electric aliveness in your exhausted body. By the end, you're still hurting, still feeling everything, but you're laughing through tears—not at them, but at your own fierce survival, your own unbreakable vitality.

title: The Iron Confession
instruction: You are an elderly woman, trapped inside a heavy, visored helmet that was sealed shut as a cruel joke. It's hot, and your breath fogs the narrow slit. You're alone in a stone room, speaking to someone outside the door who you can't see, but who you know is listening. Begin with a frantic, muffled plea for help—your voice ringing off the metal as you rattle the visor. Let the helplessness mount as you realize no one is coming, but by the end, your voice softens into a quiet, defeated acceptance, the clank of the metal settling between your words as you say your final goodbye.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about the emotional absence that defined your childhood. Start measured, almost clinical—you've rehearsed this. 'I need to tell you something I should have said years ago.' But as you speak, old hurt surfaces. Your voice tightens with controlled anger. You list specific memories, each one making your voice sharper, more hurt. Then something shifts—mid-sentence, your anger cracks and underneath is the child who just wanted to be seen. Your voice breaks completely. You're no longer accusing; you're begging them to understand what their silence cost you. End with a question asked in a voice so vulnerable it's almost unrecognizable as yours: 'Did you ever actually see me?'
inspired_by: Narrator Triggered by Their Own Words

title: The Keys in Your Hand
instruction: You are holding the keys to your childhood home for the last time before it's sold. You've returned after your parent's funeral, and you're here alone to lock the door forever. Begin with practical efficiency—you're just here to finish this task, to be responsible, to do what needs to be done. But as you walk through empty rooms, you're ambushed by contradictory feelings: relief that this chapter is finally over, rage at everything that happened here, unexpected grief for the parent you never had, gratitude for the few good memories. Let these emotions collide and interrupt each other. End standing at the threshold, unable to simply lock the door and leave—trapped between the need to escape and the impossibility of really letting go.
inspired_by: Actor doesn't know what to do in a rehearsal

title: The Scent of Her Hairbrush
instruction: You're holding your mother's hairbrush three days after her funeral. Begin by feeling the weight of it in your hand—the cool smoothness of the handle, the worn bristle tips. Notice everything: the temperature, the texture against your palm, whether it's heavy or light. Bring it close and discover her scent still clinging to it—that specific combination of her shampoo, her perfume, something that is unmistakably her. Let this smell unlock a flood of memories. Start in numb grief, disconnected and hollow. As you explore every sensory detail of this object—really feeling it, smelling it, seeing the strands of her hair caught in the bristles—allow yourself to move from numbness into the full weight of your loss, until you're speaking to her through this object, asking her questions she'll never answer, finding both devastating sorrow and unexpected gratitude for having had her at all.

title: Summit of Resentment
instruction: You are standing alone at a mountain summit, wind tearing at your coat, your breath thin and ragged. You've hiked hours to this cliff edge, and now you shout at someone far below — a person who dismissed your dreams as foolish. Start with ragged, breathless doubt: your voice cracks as you ask if they were right, if your whole journey was a mistake. Then let bitterness rise like cold stone — your voice grows harder, more clipped, even as the wind steals your air. End with a raw, spiteful laugh that echoes off the cliffs before dying in the gusts.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Enjoying the Sound and Smell of a Crackling Fireplace
instruction: Sit by the fireplace, feeling its warmth and hearing the wood crackle. Describe the way the flickering light dances, the dry, slightly smoky scent filling the room, and the deep warmth radiating over your skin. Speak with a tone of coziness and contentment, as if each crackle brings you a little more peace, filling you with a sense of security and calm.

title: Crowned in Carpet
instruction: You're alone in your bedroom, having just won a fierce personal battle—maybe landing a dream role or finishing a project you poured your heart into. You kick off your shoes, sink into the soft carpet, and let out a giddy laugh as the victory washes over you. Start in that raw, breathless ecstasy—talk to yourself, whisper to the ceiling, let your voice tremble with pleasure as you relive the moment. Then as you stand and look in the mirror, let the feeling harden into triumph: a slow, confident smile, your voice dropping into a deeper, steadier tone as you claim your power. Fidget with your hair, hug a pillow, pause to catch your breath—make every micro-reaction real.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent the truth they've never wanted to hear: that their 'strength' was abandonment, that you needed them and they weren't there. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm. But as you speak, decades of suppressed need start breaking through. Your voice cracks on memories: 'I was seven years old and you didn't come home.' You're not yelling—this is rawer than anger. You're showing them the child inside you who's still waiting. Your words become both accusation and plea: you're demanding they finally see you, but you're also begging for something you know they can't give. End with exhausted tenderness, accepting that they did their broken best, even as your heart breaks for the child you were.

title: Dancing Between Fury and Desire
instruction: You've just discovered your ex-lover—the one who shattered you—waiting outside your apartment in the rain. Start in the doorway, confronting them with cold, controlled anger, every word sharp and cutting. But as they move closer, your body remembers them: the scent, the heat, the physical connection you've tried to forget. Allow a hungry, reckless part of yourself to rise up—the self that doesn't care about dignity or past pain, that just wants to feel alive and consumed. Your voice should roughen, your breath quicken. By the end, you're caught between two warring selves: one spitting rage at what they did, the other pulling them closer, your words mixing fury with desperate physical need, your body and voice expressing both violation and craving simultaneously.

title: The Unsung Lullaby
instruction: You are rocking your newborn niece in a quiet nursery, humming a soft tune. Your sister—her mother—just won an award you've been chasing for years, and her success gnaws at you. The baby's peaceful face mixes your adoration with a creeping bitterness. Let the rocking rhythm pulse through your voice as you whisper to her, starting with pure, fragile affection. Halfway through, let the envy seep in—your jaw tight, a shaky pause—so that by the end, you're confiding a confused ache, your tone hushed but strained.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (clearly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Bittersweet Becoming
instruction: You're speaking at the wedding or departure of someone you raised—a child, a younger sibling, a student—and you're overwhelmed by contradictory emotions. Begin with joy in your voice, genuine celebration: 'Look at you. Look at who you've become.' But even as you speak of pride and happiness, let your voice crack with the ache of letting go. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, your voice bright with gladness while trembling with loss. As you speak, move between reminiscing about who they were and marveling at who they are, your voice dancing between warm humor and throat-caught sorrow. End with gratitude that breaks your heart: 'Thank you for letting me be part of your story. Now go—go live it.' Your voice should sound like someone whose heart is both full and breaking, celebrating exactly what costs them, finding profound beauty in necessary goodbye.

title: The Frozen Forest Signal
instruction: You are alone in a sub-zero forest at dawn, having just stumbled upon a clearing where frost-rimed trees glitter under a pale sun. Your jaw is stiff from the cold, breath steaming, and your voice comes out tight and muffled. Start with a deep, awed whisper — barely able to speak — as you murmur to yourself about the unexpected beauty. Then, as you notice a broken animal track leading toward a frozen stream, your awe shifts into a quiet, desperate concern: you feel the weight of isolation and the fragility of life out here. Let your words slow, falter, and warm slightly with worry, but keep the cold pinching your throat.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Homecoming of the Divided Self
instruction: You are returning to embrace someone you both deeply love and furiously resent—perhaps a child you abandoned, a lover who betrayed you, or a friend whose success makes you burn with jealousy. Begin with your arms open, voice breaking with genuine joy and relief, moving toward them. But mid-embrace, feel your body start to fight itself: one part wants to hold them close, another wants to push them away. Let conflicting movements emerge—pulling in and shoving back simultaneously. Your voice cracks between laughter and snarling, between words of love and guttural sounds of anger. Allow your body to move in contradictory, almost animal-like ways—nuzzling then snapping, caressing then scratching the air. End in a trembling stillness where both emotions coexist, raw and unresolved.

title: Protective Fury Collapsing into Helplessness
instruction: You're confronting someone who hurt your child, your sibling, someone precious to you. Start with volcanic rage—your voice is a weapon. 'You had no RIGHT!' Every word is sharp, loud, dangerous. You're all fire and protection, righteous and ferocious. But mid-confrontation, something shifts: you realize your anger can't undo what happened. The fury cracks. Your voice wavers. 'Please... just tell me how to fix this.' Now you're begging, desperate, the fight draining out of you. By the end, you're quiet, almost broken: 'I couldn't protect them.' The admission is barely audible, all the rage collapsed into devastation and failure.

title: Whispering Your Secret Abortion to Your Best Friend in the Dark
instruction: It's 2am and you finally tell your best friend what you did three months ago, what you've been carrying alone. Your voice is barely audible, as if speaking louder would make it more real. Start with fragmented sentences, unable to complete thoughts, your breath catching. There's no drama here—just quiet, devastating honesty. Move through shame, relief, grief, and the terrible loneliness of a decision only you could make. Your voice trembles between needing to be heard and wishing you could take the words back. End with a simple, broken request: 'Please don't leave me alone with this.' Let silence do the heaviest work.
inspired_by: Professional: Activist Must Compromise Their Principles to Save Vulnerable People

title: I Won't Let Them Take You
instruction: You're a parent holding your sick child in the emergency room, and the doctors have just said there's nothing more they can do. Start fierce, almost aggressive—you won't accept this, you'll fight anyone, take them anywhere, sell everything. Your voice should shake with desperate determination. But as you make impossible promises ('We'll find another hospital, another country, I'll make this right'), let that ferocity crack and collapse into begging—begging God, fate, the universe. Rage should dissolve into helpless sobbing as you realize your strength means nothing here. End with your voice breaking completely as you whisper, 'I can't lose you, baby. I can't.' Transform from warrior to shattered supplicant.

title: The Unopened Letter
instruction: You're confronting your parent, holding a decades-old letter you found hidden in their belongings—a letter that reveals a life-altering secret they kept from you. Start with cold, controlled fury, your words precise and sharp like surgical instruments. You've rehearsed this confrontation in your mind for nights since discovering it, playing out every accusation. But as you speak, something shifts: flashes of recent dreams where you saw them as they were at your age, vulnerable and terrified of making the wrong choice. The anger begins to crack. You catch glimpses of their younger self in their aging face, and suddenly you're not just accusing—you're asking, pleading to understand. By the end, your rage has transformed into something more complicated: a raw, desperate need to reconcile the parent you thought you knew with this stranger before you. Let your voice move from steel to fracture to something achingly human.

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's the middle of the night, and you're lying next to someone—a lover, a spouse, a friend. You can't sleep because there's something you've never told them, something you're terrified to say. Begin by watching them in the darkness: the rise and fall of their breathing, the vulnerability of their sleeping face, the shape of their body beside yours. Wonder what they dream about, what secrets they carry, whether they'll still be here tomorrow. Your voice should start as barely a whisper, trembling, as you begin to speak—not sure if you want them to wake or stay sleeping. Confess something that could change everything between you. As you speak, really look at them, noticing every detail, and let your fear transform into relief, then into a fragile, desperate hope. End with your voice stronger but still quiet, having crossed a threshold you can't uncross, uncertain but unburdened.

title: Fury and Helplessness Rising
instruction: You're in an elevator with a coworker when you get a phone call—your teenager has been arrested. You answer, trying to stay composed: 'What? Where?' Your voice is controlled, professional, aware of the witness. But as details emerge (you're hearing them, we're not), your composure cracks. Your voice rises, shaking: 'They did WHAT to him?' Rage floods through you—protective, fierce, helpless. You're yelling now: 'I don't care about their procedures! He's sixteen!' But then something in what you hear deflates you completely. Your voice drops to broken: 'Was he scared? Did he ask for me?' Let the fury collapse into devastation. You're trying not to sob in front of this stranger: 'I should have been there. I should have...' The elevator reaches the lobby and you have to pull yourself together enough to run out, but your voice cracks on the final words to the coworker: 'I have to go. My baby needs me.' Exit in pieces, held together only by the urgency of love.

title: Professional: Scientist Realizes Her Research Is Being Used for Weapons
instruction: Meeting with military contractors. Your scientific voice presented your work with pride and precision. They're describing applications you didn't intend. Your voice becomes uncertain, then quiet. You've created something that will be weaponized. Your breathing becomes the breathing of someone realizing their creation is leaving their hands to be used for harm. Your voice shifts from proud scientist to horrified person. You're learning in real time that knowledge isn't neutral. Your vocal authority evaporates as you confront what you've enabled.

title: The Lost Key
instruction: You're a young man alone in your cluttered apartment, late at night. You're methodically searching for a small, important key you dropped an hour ago—and you're talking to yourself to stay focused. At first, it's a calm, almost tedious monologue as you retrace your steps, your voice low and lazy, sentences trailing off. But as your search becomes more frantic, your jaw tightens, and your voice rises with a mix of annoyance and desperation. End with a sudden, quiet realization that changes your mood entirely.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Dancing at Your Child's Wedding: Gratitude Wrapped in Grief
instruction: You're watching your child dance at their wedding, and you're alone for a moment. You start by whispering to your late spouse who should be here: 'You should see them. God, you should see them.' Your voice is full of wonder and joy—they're so happy, so radiant. You're almost laughing, describing the dress, the way they look at their partner. But then the laughter catches, becomes something else. Your voice cracks as you realize your spouse is missing this, that you're experiencing this enormous joy completely alone. You're crying and smiling at the same time, voice wavering between gratitude and heartbreak. 'They're perfect. We made someone so perfect, and you're not here to see it.' The emotions are impossibly tangled—pride, loss, love, loneliness, joy, grief all at once. Your voice finds this strange peace in the contradiction, accepting that the most beautiful moments can hurt the most, whispering 'thank you' to the universe, to your spouse, to the bittersweet gift of this moment.
inspired_by: Worst Case Scenario Spiraling: Catastrophizing Out Loud

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You've just received news that someone who once hurt you deeply—physically, emotionally, or both—has died. You're alone in your kitchen when you hear this news. Your body reacts before your mind can catch up. Start with the physical shock: your breath changes, your hands might shake, heat or cold floods through you. Don't think about how you 'should' feel. Let your body lead and discover what's actually there. Is it relief? Rage that they escaped without answering for what they did? Unexpected grief for what could have been? A complicated cocktail of all of these? As you move through this moment, let the physical sensations guide you into the emotional truth. By the end, you've allowed your body to express what your mind has been too afraid or too conditioned to acknowledge. This is about surrendering to what genuinely arises, not performing an emotion.

title: The Rescue Worker's Reunion: Finding Joy in the Rubble
instruction: You're a rescue worker who's been digging through earthquake rubble for 72 hours. You've found seventeen bodies. Now, impossibly, you've found someone alive—a child. You're radioing for medical, but your voice keeps breaking into something between laughter and weeping. You can't believe it. After so much death, here's life. Your instructions to the medical team are interrupted by gasps of relief, almost hysterical joy. But underneath runs a river of grief for all the ones you couldn't save, guilt that you're this happy when seventeen families are destroyed. Your voice oscillates—professional urgency, then wonder, then a sob, then laughter again. End by speaking directly to the child: a tender promise that everything's going to be okay now, your voice soaked in gratitude and sorrow simultaneously, barely able to form words through the contradictory emotions.
inspired_by: Air Traffic Controller: Two Planes on Collision Course

title: Holding Your Child Back from Danger with Your Bare Voice
instruction: Your teenager is walking toward a devastating mistake—an abusive relationship, addiction, a choice that will destroy them—and you have one chance to stop them. Start fierce and commanding: 'You are NOT doing this.' Pour everything into your voice—all your fear disguised as anger. Get louder, more desperate. But mid-sentence, your power collapses. Your voice cracks into pleading: 'Please, baby, please.' You're begging now, all authority gone, just a parent on their knees trying to save their child with nothing but love and terror. End sobbing through your words, telling them you can't watch them disappear. Let rage dissolve completely into helpless, aching love.
inspired_by: Celebrating Someone's Success While Drowning in Failure

title: Defending Your Child to a System That Won't Listen—Then Breaking
instruction: You're in an office, across from administrators or officials, and you start controlled, articulate, presenting your case with careful logic. 'If you look at the documentation...' But they're not listening. Your voice rises—not yelling yet, but louder, more insistent. 'You're not hearing me!' The fury builds as you realize they see your child as a file, a case number, a problem to manage. You explode—raw, protective rage of a parent watching their child be failed by people who don't care. But then, mid-sentence, the anger collapses. Your voice breaks completely. The shift from fierce to shattered should be sudden, devastating. End pleading, almost begging, voice small and broken: 'Please. They're just a kid. They're my kid.' The helplessness of loving someone you can't protect should be palpable.
inspired_by: Two People Breaking Up Over Assembling IKEA Furniture

title: I Will Burn It All Down
instruction: You're threatening to destroy something you've built—your company, your family legacy, your life's work—because you've discovered it's been poisoned from the beginning. Start with fierce, almost gleeful rage: 'I'll torch every piece of it. Watch me.' Your voice should crackle with wild energy, dangerous and uncontained. But as you detail what you'll destroy, let doubt and pain seep in. Your voice becomes less certain, more choked: 'My grandfather built this. My mother—' Break into ragged emotion, oscillating between fury and grief. Let protective love battle with helpless devastation. 'They used it to hurt people. Children. How do I—' Your voice should fracture completely, then rebuild into something quieter but more resolved. End with tearful determination, your voice rough but steady: 'I have to. Even if it destroys me too.'

title: The Last Story Before the Fog
instruction: You're in the early stages of dementia, sitting with your adult child, trying desperately to tell them one final important story about their childhood—something they need to know before you forget everything. Start with warm determination and clarity, but feel the story slipping away mid-sentence like sand through your fingers. Your emotion shifts from loving urgency to mounting panic as you lose the thread, then to heartbreaking acceptance mixed with tender apology. Let the gaps in your memory become moments of vulnerable silence. End with a whispered fragment of the story's ending that somehow captures everything, even as the details escape you. This isn't comedic—it's the devastating reality of watching your own mind betray you while trying to give one last gift to someone you love.

title: The Knot That Won't Untie
instruction: You are a middle-aged man alone in your apartment, suffering from a persistent abdominal cramp that has kept you curled on the couch for hours. You're trying to leave a voicemail for your doctor, but each word is a battle against the pain. Begin with a strained, frustrated effort to sound normal, but as the pain spikes mid-message, your voice crumbles into a low groan, and you admit to yourself and the machine that you can't keep pretending you're okay. Let your breath be shallow and guarded, your words weighted with the effort of speaking through the knot in your gut, ending in a weary, quiet plea.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Abuser Face to Face
instruction: You've spent years planning this. Now you're facing them. Your voice is shaking—from anger, fear, adrenaline. You're telling them what they did to you. Your voice becomes stronger as you speak your truth. But their denial makes your voice falter. 'You don't remember, do you?' Your voice cracks with the injustice. They're acting like it wasn't a big deal. Your voice becomes desperate—'It was a big deal to me.' Include the moment they're unmoved and your voice collapses.

title: The Rehearsal That Became Real
instruction: You and your romantic partner are playfully pretending to have the breakup conversation you've both been avoiding—treating it like a rehearsal, a game, something safe because it's 'not real.' Start light, even laughing, acting out exaggerated versions of what you might say. But as you continue, let the pretend words reveal actual truths. The imaginary grievances become real ones. The fake anger surfaces genuine hurt. Midway through, one or both of you should realize this isn't a game anymore—these are the actual words you needed to say. The playful tone must shatter and transform into raw confrontation. End having crossed a threshold you can't uncross, where the 'pretend' breakup has somehow become the real one, or where the honesty finally creates an opening for genuine intimacy you've never had.

title: Emergency Dispatcher Helpless on the Line During a Home Invasion
instruction: You're talking to a terrified caller hiding in a closet—you can hear the intruder ransacking the house, getting closer. Start with your training, your calm professional voice guiding them through staying quiet, staying safe, telling them police are coming. But the intruder finds them. You hear it happen—the scream, the struggle, sounds no training prepared you for. Your voice explodes from measured calm into desperate shouting, commanding them to stop, begging them, your professional distance completely obliterated. You're yelling into a phone miles away from someone being hurt while you listen, utterly powerless. Let your voice break from fierce authority to raw, helpless pleading to something almost feral—rage and terror and guilt all collapsing into chaos. End with the line going silent and you still talking, begging, your voice reduced to a whisper because you don't know what else to do.
inspired_by: Executioner Recognizes Victim's Parent Among the Crowd

title: The Farewell Party After the Funeral
instruction: You're at the gathering after burying someone who shaped your life—and you've just been told a story about them you never knew, something that completely reframes your understanding of who they were. You're holding a drink, surrounded by the low murmur of other mourners, and you begin speaking to someone (or to the air, or to the deceased) about this revelation. Start with the fresh, heavy grief of loss—your voice thick with it, slow, weighted down. But as you process this new information, other emotions flood in: anger at what was hidden, relief that explains old mysteries, guilt for judgments you made, unexpected laughter at a memory now seen differently, gratitude for a gift you didn't know you'd received. Let your voice ride these contradictory waves: sometimes you're smiling through tears, sometimes laughing bitterly, sometimes your voice breaks mid-sentence as grief and revelation collide. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance—the ache of missing them is now mixed with a strange, complicated gratitude for the fuller, more human picture of who they really were.
inspired_by: Actor fears exposing private feelings or being vulnerable in performance

title: The Confrontation: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the childhood they gave you—or didn't. Start with controlled, measured anger as you list specific moments of neglect, your voice steady but trembling underneath. As they try to defend themselves or remain silent, let your rage build and crack open, revealing the hurt child still inside you. Move through fury, accusation, and desperate questions—'Why wasn't I enough? Why didn't you see me?'—before collapsing into vulnerable pleading. Then something shifts: you see them as fragile, human, broken in their own way. End with a devastating mixture of compassion and grief, forgiving them while mourning what you'll never have. Your voice should break, rebuild, and break again—raw, messy, real.

title: What You Never Said at the Dinner Table
instruction: You're face-to-face with your parent (or your adult child) after years of swallowing truths that have calcified inside you. Start from a place of tight control—the lifelong habit of biting your tongue, of being 'good,' of keeping peace. But tonight, something has cracked that dam. Let the pressure build behind your careful words until language itself fails you, and raw sound becomes the only honest thing you have left. Move from controlled civility into volcanic release—not just anger, but the grief underneath it, the little child who needed something they never got, the adult who's tired of pretending. Let sounds carry what words have always failed to express. End in a place of shocking vulnerability you never intended to reach, completely exposed.

title: Watching Your Child Leave for Mars
instruction: You're at the space port, watching your adult child prepare to board a one-way mission to Mars. You'll never see them again—not in person, only through delayed video messages. Start with pride, forcing brightness into your voice as you tell them how brave they are, how proud you've always been. But as the final boarding call echoes, your voice begins to crack. You're remembering them as a child—their first steps, their laughter, the weight of them sleeping in your arms. Your words become fragmented, caught between wanting to hold them close and needing to let them go. You're describing their face right now, memorizing every detail, and your voice becomes tender, almost a whisper. By the end, you're saying goodbye—truly, finally, forever—and you must find a way to give them permission to leave while your heart is shattering. The last word catches in your throat.

title: Waiting on the Corner
instruction: You're a teenage girl stuck waiting for a friend who's twenty minutes late. You're leaning against a brick wall, one shoulder pressed into it, phone in your hand. Your voice has that clipped, slightly nasal hyper-feminized sound, and you begin with a huffed sigh and muttered complaint — sharp, impatient, your words bitten off. As you scroll through your phone and glance up the street, let the irritation grow, but then notice a crack in the pavement you've been staring at without seeing. Your voice softens, loses its edge, becomes tired and quiet. End with a flat, resigned decision to leave, the coolness of the wall against your back feeling like a final push.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Scrolling Through the Ache
instruction: You're a teenager lying on your bed, phone inches from your face, thumb lazily scrolling through social media. Your body is heavy, and there's a deep, gnawing pain in your chest — not physical, but the kind that sits behind your ribs and makes breathing feel like a chore. At first, you're half-distracted, muttering at posts, clearing your throat, shifting your weight. But as you keep scrolling, the pain swells — suddenly you can't swallow it anymore. Let your voice drop, get quieter, and break at the edges. End with a few words that crack open, like you're admitting it to no one but yourself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Villain Origin Justification
instruction: You're explaining why you did monstrous things, and you genuinely believe your own justifications. Your voice is persuasive, almost reasonable—you're trying to make the listener complicit. But underneath, there's the barely-suppressed fury of someone who was wronged and never recovered. You rationalize with surgical precision, but your voice cracks on the specific memory that broke you. You're articulate until you discuss your childhood, then you're slurring like you're drunk on old grief. You end trying to convince yourself, not the listener, that what you've become was necessary.

title: The Last Bedside Conversation
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent who has only hours left. You begin with forced brightness, trying to protect them: 'Remember when we used to...' But mid-sentence, your voice fractures. The pretense crumbles. Your breathing becomes ragged as you finally say what you've never said: 'I was so angry at you for so long.' Tears come but your voice strengthens with hard-won clarity. 'And I forgive you. I forgive us both.' Touch their hand. By the end, you're speaking with profound tenderness mixed with grief: 'Thank you for trying. Thank you for loving me the only way you knew how.' Let the last words be almost a whisper, filled with peace and unbearable sadness.

title: The Language You Chose
instruction: Your immigrant mother confronts you in her native tongue, asking why you speak it with an accent now, why you answer her in English, why you've become a stranger. Start defensive, switching to English to create distance—this is easier, more articulate, more you. She persists in her language, each word an accusation of abandonment. You fire back in English, angry, justified. She says one phrase in her language—something she used to say when you were small. You try to respond in English but can't. The words come out in her language, broken, childlike, and suddenly you're sobbing, apologizing in both languages at once, the grammar falling apart, admitting you don't know who you are anymore. End in her language, halting and imperfect, asking her to teach you how to come home.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your parent about the childhood you needed but never had, and they're finally—devastatingly—listening. Start with controlled anger, each word precise and sharp, listing the moments they weren't there, the ways they failed you. But as you speak, something shifts—you see them truly hearing you for the first time, and their face crumbles. Your anger begins to crack open, revealing the lonely child underneath who just wanted to be seen. They reach for you, and you have to decide: do you let them in now, after all these years? Your voice transforms from accusation to something more complex—a raw mixture of the rage you still carry and the desperate, aching need for them to finally be the parent you deserved. End with you allowing yourself to be vulnerable, voice breaking as you admit what you've never said before: 'I still need you. I hate that I still need you, but I do.'

title: Midwife Holding a Stillborn: The Silence After
instruction: You've just delivered a baby who didn't take their first breath. Begin in the terrible quiet after all the emergency efforts have ceased. Your voice is barely above a whisper, speaking to the tiny body you're cradling: 'You were so wanted. So, so wanted.' Your throat is tight with unshed tears. You must now bring the baby to the mother who's been asking 'Why can't I hear crying?' Your voice trembles as you try to be gentle: 'Sweetheart, I need you to listen carefully. Your baby is here, but...' You can't finish the sentence. Let the silence speak. Then, softly, with infinite tenderness: 'Would you like to hold your daughter? Take all the time you need.' As you place the baby in her mother's arms, you whisper the smallest, most devastating truth: 'She's beautiful. She looks just like you.' Your voice carries the weight of bearing witness to love and loss simultaneously, knowing you'll carry this moment forever.
inspired_by: Construction Foreman: Shutting Down After Accident

title: Gratitude at the Goodbye You Never Wanted
instruction: You're thanking someone who meant everything to you, but this is the last time you'll see them—they're dying, or leaving forever, or this is a goodbye that cannot be undone. Begin with genuine, almost light gratitude: 'Thank you for teaching me what real laughter sounds like.' Let yourself smile, even laugh softly at a memory. But feel the grief rising underneath—your voice starts to shake even as you're listing beautiful things. 'Thank you for seeing me when I was invisible to everyone else, including myself.' The thank-yous become more desperate, trying to fit a lifetime into moments. End with laughing and crying simultaneously: 'This is so unfair, I'm not ready, but God, I'm so grateful you existed.' Your final words are split perfectly between joy for having known them and agony at losing them.

title: Protecting What You've Already Lost
instruction: You're a parent who just discovered your child is in danger, and you're confronting the person responsible with explosive, protective fury. Start with volcanic rage—your voice should shake the air, threatening, demanding, towering in its intensity. Pour out every ounce of fierce parental instinct. But as you rage, the truth crystallizes: you're too late, the damage is done, and no amount of anger can undo it. Feel the fury crack open into helpless anguish. Your voice should break from roaring to sobbing mid-sentence, from threats to desperate bargaining. End in complete emotional collapse—still fierce in your love, but utterly powerless to protect them, your voice raw and destroyed.

title: Ancient Power Awakening
instruction: Something old and powerful is waking up inside you or around you. Your voice starts normal, then things shift. Harmonics appear that shouldn't be possible. Your breathing becomes ritualistic. You can feel the power moving through you, and your voice is amplified by it—you're speaking with authority that isn't natural. Your words carry weight. You're terrified of what you're becoming, but also seduced by the power. Your voice becomes almost musical. By the end, you're not sure if you're still human or if you're becoming something else entirely. Your final words might be in a language you don't remember learning.

title: Surgeon Narrating a Procedure While Exhausted
instruction: You're a surgeon dictating an operative report on hour 16 of a shift. Your voice should be clinical, precise, medical — 'Irrigating the wound bed, achieving hemostasis' — but exhaustion creates micro-pauses, the occasional wrong word self-corrected, a yawn suppressed mid-term. Your hands are steady but your voice wobbles. When the case gets complicated, adrenaline sharpens you temporarily, then fatigue crashes back. The patient's life depends on your focus.

title: First Voicemail to a Newborn
instruction: Your baby was just born and you're calling your own voicemail to save a message for them to hear someday. Your voice is wrecked — you've been crying happy tears for hours. Tell them about the moment they arrived. Describe their face, their tiny sounds, how the room felt. The voice should be raw, intimate, and aware that this recording is a time capsule. Include: 'I don't know who you'll be when you hear this. But right now you're perfect. You're the most perfect thing I've ever seen.'

title: Laughing Through the Goodbye at the Train Station
instruction: You're seeing off your best friend who's moving away permanently, and they're trying to keep it light by reminiscing about the time you both had panic attacks at a concert and had to leave together. Start by genuinely laughing at the memory, voice warm and bright: 'Remember how we thought we were dying? And it turned out we were just standing too close to the speakers?' But as the laughter continues, it begins mixing with tears, your voice cracking between giggles and sobs: 'We were such a mess. We're still such a mess.' The laughter becomes almost manic as the train announcement plays, covering devastating loss with humor: 'Who's going to have panic attacks with me now?' End with a smile in your voice even as you're clearly crying, finding genuine gratitude in the grief: 'Thank you for making my crazy feel less lonely. I'm going to miss you so much.' Your final words are whispered through tears but filled with love: 'Go. Before I fall apart for real.'

title: The Last Hour Before Deployment
instruction: You're a parent standing at the airport with your child in military uniform, about to board a flight to a war zone. Begin with forced cheerfulness—talking about practical things, reminding them to write, your voice bright and brittle like glass about to shatter. As the final boarding call approaches, your composure starts cracking. The practical advice becomes desperate whispers: 'Please be careful, please come home.' Your voice drops, becomes rawer. Then they hug you and you feel how much they've grown, how little they are underneath that uniform. You try to say 'I love you' but it comes out broken. After they walk through security and turn back one last time to wave, you wave back smiling through streaming tears, holding yourself together until they disappear. Then, alone in the terminal, you finally let yourself collapse into quiet, shaking sobs—grief mixed with pride, terror mixed with love, the awful beauty of letting go.

title: The Emergency Room Eruption
instruction: You're in the ER waiting room after your teenage child overdosed, and you've just been told they'll survive. Start with explosive rage at the doctors, the system, everyone who failed to see this coming—your voice sharp and accusatory, looking for someone to blame. Then turn that fury inward, your voice cracking as you confess your own blindness: the signs you missed, the conversations you avoided, the times you chose your phone over their pain. Let the anger dissolve into helpless, gasping sobs. But end with fierce, almost feral protectiveness—a whispered vow that combines desperate love with terrifying determination. Your voice should move from thunder to broken to steel, trembling with the force of nearly losing everything.

title: The Thank You Poisoned With Everything Else
instruction: You're thanking someone who saved your life or changed everything for you—but you also resent them for it, or you're furious at the cost, or you're devastated that you need to thank them at all. Start with attempts at genuine gratitude, but let it twist: speak your thanks in mocking tones, interrupt yourself with accusations, shift between sincere and sarcastic without warning. Distort the words until 'thank you' becomes a howl, a curse, a prayer, a joke. Let contradictory emotions bleed into each other so thoroughly that you can't tell what you actually feel. Physically embody this confusion—reach out then pull back, soften then harden. Through all this turbulence, arrive at a moment where all the contradictions exist simultaneously—where gratitude and rage and love and grief are finally, impossibly, the same thing speaking through you.

title: Reading Their Letter After the Funeral
instruction: You've just returned from your best friend's funeral and found a letter they wrote you before they died. Before you read it aloud, describe the letter itself: the paper's texture, their handwriting, a coffee stain, the specific way they folded it. Your hands are shaking. Begin reading their words—they're telling you they love you, they're grateful, they're saying goodbye. But between their sentences, your own responses break through. You start interrupting the letter with your own words: memories that flood back, things you wish you'd said, specific moments you shared. Describe sensory details: the exact shade of light on a particular afternoon you spent together, the sound of their specific laugh, the smell of their jacket. Let yourself swing wildly between emotions: laughing at something they wrote, then suddenly devastated, then angry they're gone, then grateful they existed, then broken that you can't respond. The letter is joyful and wise; your reaction is a storm of contradictions. By the end, you can barely read their words through your tears, but you're also smiling, your voice holding impossible opposites: complete devastation and profound gratitude existing in the same breath.

title: The Last Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, given five minutes for a final transmission to your child back on Earth. You start with careful excitement, trying to paint this as an adventure, your voice bright with forced optimism: 'Hey kiddo, guess what? I can see the whole Earth from here, it's smaller than my thumb!' But as the seconds tick down and the reality sets in that you'll never hold them again, never see them graduate, never meet their children, your voice begins to fracture. The excitement doesn't disappear—it mingles with devastating grief. You're still trying to smile through your words even as your throat closes. End by whispering something you need them to remember forever, your voice breaking on a truth you can barely speak. Let the shift happen gradually, naturally, like watching hope and heartbreak become the same thing.

title: Three in the Morning
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, unable to sleep, whispering a truth you've never told anyone. Begin with your guard up, voice barely audible, testing whether you can even say the words. As you speak, let your mind drift through sense-fragments: their breathing beside you, the weight of the blanket, a similar darkness you remember from childhood, a secret shame, a moment of grace, hands that held you, hands that hurt you. Don't connect these logically—just notice which images make your voice catch. Let vulnerability creep in through the cracks between these fragments. End in a place of complete exposure, your whisper now carrying the full trembling weight of being truly seen.
inspired_by: Actor needs to quickly elevate vulnerability or emotional availability before a scene

title: Reading Your Best Friend's Eulogy While Remembering the Stupid Fight You Never Resolved
instruction: You're standing at a funeral speaking about your best friend of twenty years, and you're supposed to share beautiful memories. You start strong, even managing to smile as you tell a funny story about the time you both got lost on a road trip. But then you remember the fight you had three months ago—something petty and stupid—and how you were both too proud to apologize. Your voice wavers as you continue praising them publicly while privately your heart is screaming with regret. You find yourself almost laughing at another memory, but the laugh turns into a choked sob. You're furious at them for dying before you could say sorry, grateful for every moment you had, destroyed by the ones you wasted. End with your voice breaking completely as you say their name, but somehow finding the strength to whisper 'I forgive you, and I hope you forgive me,' knowing they can't hear you but needing to say it anyway.
inspired_by: Flamenco Dancer Losing the Rhythm Because They Just Got Dumped

title: The Last Letter Before Deployment
instruction: You're recording a voice message to your child before leaving on a mission you might not return from. Start with forced cheerfulness, telling them about small memories: 'Remember when we couldn't get you to tie your shoes? Now you do it without thinking.' Your voice begins to crack as the weight of goodbye settles in. 'I'm so proud of how you've grown... how patient you've become.' The facade crumbles—you're now speaking through tears, but trying to hold it together: 'These little things—your laugh, the way you hum when you're concentrating—I carry them with me.' End with a whisper that's both tender and devastated: 'If I don't come back, know that watching you become yourself has been the greatest privilege of my life.' The emotional journey moves from protective cheerfulness to raw, unguarded love mixed with the terror of permanent goodbye.

title: The Last Sunrise Together
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying partner's hospital bed at dawn. They've just opened their eyes for what you both know is the last time. Start in numb, exhausted grief—you've been awake for days, hollowed out by helplessness. But as they squeeze your hand and smile at you, something shifts. Find the fierce gratitude rising from deep in your belly. Let your voice crack and soar as you tell them about all the mornings you watched the sun come up together, how they taught you to see beauty in ordinary things. Build from whispered memories to full-throated celebration of your love, your body leaning in, hands gripping theirs tighter. By the end, you're laughing through tears, almost shouting with joy about how lucky you were, how grateful you are, even as you're losing them. Pull this transformation from your core—let your entire body express the shift from empty despair to blazing thankfulness.

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to someone you love, in the middle of the night, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. Begin by feeling the specific texture of the sheets, the warmth of their body near yours, the quality of darkness, their breathing pattern. Don't describe these—let them support you. Start from shame and fear, your voice barely audible. As you confess, let the sensory safety of this moment—their warmth, the protective darkness, the intimacy of whispered breath—gradually transform your shame into fragile hope. By the end, let yourself feel the possibility of being fully known and still loved. The journey is from hiding to being seen.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use Verbalized Imaging but keeps describing images in words rather than experiencing them

title: Humming Through Tears: The Song You Couldn't Sing at Their Funeral
instruction: Begin humming—no words, just a melody that meant something profound to you and someone you lost. Your voice is barely audible, fragile as glass, because you couldn't do this at their funeral, couldn't make a sound when it mattered. This is the song you wished you could have sung as they lowered the casket. Start with your throat tight, notes barely escaping, each one a struggle against the weight in your chest. As you continue, the humming becomes increasingly interrupted by silent crying—your breath hitches, the melody stops and starts, but you force yourself to keep going because this is your goodbye. No dramatic crying, just quiet devastation. The humming gets even softer, more broken, until you're barely breathing the tune, and finally it dissolves into the silence you couldn't break when it mattered most.
inspired_by: Opera Singer Having an Emotional Breakdown Mid-Aria

title: The Last Sunset Together
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying spouse on a mountaintop they insisted on seeing one final time. As the sun begins to set, your voice is tight with forced cheerfulness: 'Look at those colors, baby. Just like our wedding day.' They squeeze your hand weakly, and something breaks inside you—your voice cracks: 'I don't know how to do this without you.' The tears come now, but you're trying to smile through them: 'Thirty-two years wasn't enough. A thousand years wouldn't be enough.' They whisper something you can barely hear, and your voice becomes fiercely protective yet utterly helpless: 'No, don't say goodbye yet. Not yet.' But as the sun touches the horizon, acceptance begins to wash over you. Your voice softens into something almost peaceful: 'Okay. Okay, my love. I'll be okay. You can let go now.' The sun disappears, and in the darkness, your voice is barely audible but filled with profound gratitude: 'Thank you for every single day.'

title: A Folded Note from Third Grade
instruction: You are alone at a cluttered desk, sorting through a dusty box of old school papers. Your hands shuffle and snap the dry pages, and you read aloud a note you wrote to yourself as a child. At first your voice is thick with doubt — you mumble through a bitter memory of a bad grade, your tone flat and tight. But as you read the child's hopeful promise to try harder, your voice softens, cracks with emotion, then rises with a fragile optimism. Let the sounds of paper and your own hesitant breath punctuate the reading.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (extremely present), Bitterness (clearly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The 3 AM Truth
instruction: It's three in the morning. You and your partner are lying in the dark after making love. You've been carrying a secret that's been slowly poisoning everything between you—maybe an affair, maybe a lie about your past, maybe something you did that betrayed them in a way they don't know. The intimacy of this moment has broken something open in you. Begin barely audible, testing the words in the darkness, your voice catching on fear. You don't want to destroy this moment, this feeling of closeness, but you can't live with the secret anymore. As you confess, let yourself feel their body beside you in the dark, not seeing their face, just sensing their breathing change. Your whisper grows more urgent, more naked. By the end, you're not asking for forgiveness—you're simply offering the truth, terrified and relieved at once, waiting in the silence for whatever comes next.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're facing your father after fifteen years of silence, and the words that have been locked inside you are finally breaking free. Start in cold, controlled fury—each word precise, cutting, a surgical exposure of every wound he left. You've rehearsed this confrontation a thousand times, and you're determined to make him feel everything he made you feel. But as you speak, something unexpected happens: beneath your rage, you discover a younger version of yourself, the child who just wanted to be seen. Let your voice crack and shift from accusatory to pleading, from adult to child, from anger to a raw, exposed longing. By the end, you're no longer destroying him—you're revealing yourself, asking the question you've always been afraid to ask: 'Why wasn't I enough?'

title: The Unraveling
instruction: You're shouting at someone you love who's about to make a terrible, irreversible mistake—leave the country, marry the wrong person, give up on something essential. Start with fierce, passionate conviction: 'You can't do this!' Your voice is powerful, certain, almost righteous. But as they remain silent or push back, your certainty splinters. The volume drops and rises erratically. You're grasping at arguments, cycling through rage, then pleading, then fury again. Your voice breaks. You're trying to be strong enough to save them, but you're collapsing under the helplessness of watching someone you love self-destruct. The explosive energy fractures into desperate, choking sobs. End in a whisper of defeat: 'I can't watch you do this.' The transformation is from fierce protector to broken witness—powerful to powerless.

title: Siblings Reconciliation
instruction: Two siblings who haven't spoken in years are reconciling. The first voice is distant, wary. The second voice is hopeful but bracing for rejection. They're tentatively stepping toward each other. The first sibling remembers something positive, and their voice softens. The second sibling admits to something they've regretted. There's a moment where both are on the verge of tears. They start remembering together, and their voices begin to harmonize. Old in-jokes appear. By the end, they're laughing in a way that feels like recovery. The estrangement wasn't erased, but the connection underneath it has been found.

title: Explosive Protectiveness: The Moment You Can't Save Them
instruction: Someone you love fiercely—your child, your sibling, your partner—is making a choice that will destroy them, and you're powerless to stop it. Begin with desperate reasoning, your voice tight with controlled panic: 'Please, just listen to me. Just once, listen.' But they won't. Your voice escalates into pleading, then rage—not at them, but at your own helplessness. 'I would take this from you if I could! I would carry it!' Your words become almost violent in their intensity, your voice cracking with the force of your love and fury. You're shouting truths you've never said: 'You are WORTH saving! Do you hear me?' But then you see it's not working. Nothing you say will change this. Your voice breaks completely. The rage collapses into raw, sobbing grief. You're on your knees emotionally. Your final words are whispered, devastated: 'I can't lose you. I can't.' The journey is from controlled fear to explosive desperation to helpless, broken love.
inspired_by: Extreme Altitude Climb: Lucidity Breaking Down in the Death Zone

title: The Numb Obedience
instruction: You are kneeling at your partner's feet, performing a routine task—adjusting the temperature of a drink or arranging a cushion. Your voice starts flat, hollow, obedient but emotionally numb, as if going through the motions. Midway, a wave of gratitude for the structure and care he provides breaks through—your breath catches, your tone warms, and the final words become soft and genuine. Let your voice shift from a compliant, almost mechanical high pitch to a tender, grateful sigh, with natural pauses and small movements as you adjust your posture or look down at your hands.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Letters I'll Never Send
instruction: You're a teenager in your bedroom, holding a stack of letters you wrote to your estranged mother over the past two years—angry, bitter, helpless letters you never mailed. You've just learned she won't be coming home, and you're laughing through tears, voice cracking and jumping as you read fragments aloud. Start with a raw, shaky bitterness, your words tumbling over each other, then let the sound turn wild and half-hysterical as you realize you're finally free of her poison. Let your voice spike and drop, let laughter and sobs blur, let the performance feel like a desperate, joyful exhale you can't control.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Lost in the Grit
instruction: You're a teenager searching for your little brother during a sudden sandstorm. You pull your scarf over your mouth and call his name, straining to see through the stinging air. At first, you're focused and determined, shouting his name between coughs. But as the wind howls and no answer comes, your voice cracks, your calls become quieter, and you end in a broken whisper, realizing you might not find him.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Prank That Burned
instruction: You're sitting around a campfire with a few close friends, the flames casting shadows on your face. You start telling a story about a cruel prank you played on someone you had a crush on in high school. Begin with a low, almost gleeful malevolence—relishing the details of their misery. As you describe your infatuation, let your voice soften, stumbling over a word, glancing away. Then, when you reach the moment you were caught, let shame flood your tone: hesitant, voice dropping, maybe a dry swallow. End with a quiet, hollow admission, the fire crackling in the pause.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Infatuation (slightly present), Shame (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Three AM Breathing
instruction: It's three in the morning and you're lying in bed next to your partner. You've been awake for an hour, and something inside you has finally broken open—you need to tell them the truth about why you've been so distant, so afraid. Begin by whispering their name in the darkness, gently waking them. Your voice should be barely audible, fragile, like you might shatter if you speak too loudly. As you confess your deepest fear—about inadequacy, about not being enough, about the terror of being truly seen—let your breath catch, let the words come in broken phrases. Feel their hand find yours in the dark. Notice how their listening changes you, how speaking the unspeakable makes you both more vulnerable and somehow stronger. By the end, you're still whispering, but there's a tentative relief, a raw openness that wasn't there before.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use a vivid or recurring dream as unconscious material for their work

title: Victory and Goodbye
instruction: You've just achieved the impossible thing—the goal that consumed years of your life—and you're describing it to someone on the phone, someone who sacrificed everything so you could pursue this dream. Start with breathless joy, laughing through exhausted tears, your voice crackling with triumph. But woven through every moment of celebration is the knowledge you're both avoiding: achieving this means leaving, means your lives diverge here, means goodbye. Your voice dances between exhilaration and heartbreak, between 'I did it!' and 'I'm so sorry.' Describe the winning moment with fierce pride, but let gratitude bleed into every word, the kind that hurts because it's attached to loss. End with trying to say thank you and I love you and I have to go all at once, your voice breaking on the contradiction of the best and worst moment of your life happening simultaneously.

title: The Homecoming
instruction: You are returning to your childhood home after many years, walking through rooms filled with memories. Begin by noticing everything with overwhelming intensity: the specific creak of the third step, the way light falls through the kitchen window exactly as it did twenty years ago, the smell of wood and dust and something ineffably familiar, the sound of wind through trees you climbed as a child, the texture of wallpaper under your fingertips. This heightened awareness brings flooding joy—you're HOME. But as you move deeper into the house, each sensation also triggers profound grief for time lost, for the people no longer here, for the child you were. Let these contradictory emotions build until they're inseparable. End in a moment where you're simultaneously laughing and crying, where every sensation is both comfort and knife-edge, where you cannot tell if you're being destroyed or made whole.

title: The Hologram in the Breakroom
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman sitting upright in an office chair at a small breakroom table. It’s just past lunch; the fluorescent light hums, you can hear someone typing in the next cubicle. You are mid-sentence, teasing a friend who just showed you a video — and you’re describing it as you watch it a second time. The awe sneaks in as the video goes on, cracking your teasing facade. Sip your coffee, lose your train of thought when the video gets chaotic, then let the wonder slip out with unguarded delight.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Garden
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She's sleeping, and you don't know if she'll wake again. Begin by noticing everything about this moment—the texture of the thin blanket under your palm, the rhythm of her breathing, the afternoon light coming through the window, the smell of her hand cream on the nightstand. Let yourself be genuinely curious about these details. As you sit, begin speaking to her softly—telling her about the garden she taught you to tend, how the tomatoes came in this year, which flowers bloomed. Start from a place of simply wanting to share these details with her, but let yourself arrive at the realization that you're also asking her permission to let her go. End in a place where gratitude and grief have become inseparable.

title: The Mirror Breaks
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just admitted they're walking away from everything you sacrificed to build for them. You start angry—righteous, certain, armed with every argument about duty and gratitude. But as you argue, something shifts. You catch a glimpse of yourself in their defiance, recognize your own younger face in their determination. The anger doesn't disappear—it transforms into something more complicated. Let yourself move from attacking to questioning, from certainty to confusion, from rage to a terrifying recognition that maybe you're not angry at them at all, but at the life you lived that they're refusing to repeat. End in a place where love and fury are inseparable, where your voice carries both blessing and accusation, where you're releasing them even as you want to hold on.
inspired_by: Actor struggles with a character very different from themselves

title: Telling Your Child You're Not Coming Back from the Mission
instruction: You're a soldier, astronaut, or aid worker speaking to your young child before a near-certain one-way journey. Begin with forced cheerfulness, voice bright and false: 'I'm going on a very special trip.' Your child asks when you'll be home and the brightness cracks. Move to tender reassurance that becomes increasingly fragile: 'You're going to do such amazing things.' They sense something is wrong and ask directly if you're coming back. The truth breaks through in a whisper, then stronger: 'No, sweetheart. I'm not.' End with desperate attempts to pack a lifetime of love into final words, your voice raw with the need to be remembered, to matter, to leave them something to hold onto when you're gone.
inspired_by: Admitting You've Been Using Substances to Cope

title: Toasting My Sister's Happily Ever After
instruction: You're a 17-year-old girl, a little tipsy from a glass of champagne, standing at your sister's wedding reception. You're supposed to give a toast, but the room feels huge and the microphone is making you nervous. Your voice starts shaky and contemplative: you pause too long, lose your place, let out an embarrassed laugh. But then you catch your sister's eye, she's smiling through tears, and a wave of pure warm contentment washes over you. Let your voice soften, slow down, slur just a bit from the champagne, and let the ending be full of natural, authentic happiness. Forget the crowd; you're just talking to her.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (very intensely present), Contemplation (clearly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Secret Garden of Breath
instruction: You are lying in bed with your lover in the dark, post-intimacy, bodies close. In a whisper, you begin describing an imaginary place—a secret garden that exists only in your mind, one you've never told anyone about. As you describe it in intimate detail, you're actually revealing your innermost self through metaphor: the hidden pond is your loneliness, the wild roses are your fierce desires, the locked gate is your fear of being truly known. Start with playful, sensual description, your voice soft and inviting. Gradually let the fantasy become more vulnerable, more revealing, until you realize you're no longer playing—you're confessing your deepest truth through this made-up world. End with a trembling admission that this garden is you, and you're terrified they'll stop loving what they find there. Journey from playful seduction to trembling, exposed vulnerability.
inspired_by: Actor has lost the joy and playfulness in their acting — it feels like work rather than play

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he never defended you as a child when others criticized you. Start with carefully controlled anger—the kind you've rehearsed in your mind for years, armed with specific examples and accusations. As you speak, notice his face, his silence, the way his hands shake. Let something unexpected happen inside you: the realization that your anger has been protecting you from seeing his own fear and inadequacy. Your voice should transform from prosecutorial sharpness to something more complicated—confusion mixed with unwanted compassion. End not with the cathartic release you expected, but with the disturbing discovery that understanding him doesn't heal you, and now you must decide what to do with this knowledge. The journey is from righteous fury to uncomfortable, unwanted empathy.
inspired_by: Actor wants to understand a character's physical mannerisms and actions beyond surface choices

title: Floor of Thanks
instruction: You are a teenage boy lying on your stomach on the carpet in your room. Your cheek is pressed against the floor, and each breath feels shallow, your ribcage squeezed. You start feeling calm and content, just watching dust motes in the light. Then a thought drifts in about your mom’s surprise dinner tonight—how she remembered your favorite dish. Let gratitude rise slowly, making your voice softer, quieter, each word falling with the weight of your body. End in a near-whisper, feeling genuinely thankful, as if talking to yourself on the ground.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (slightly present), Contemplation (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Sneeze of a Champion
instruction: You're a 14-year-old girl with terrible seasonal allergies, sitting in a crowded school hallway during a fire drill. Your nose is unstoppably running, eyes watering, and you're fighting a sneeze while trying to sound cool for a group of popular kids nearby. You notice a teacher making you move closer, and you have to deliver a defiant, proud statement about your allergies making you 'immune to everything' — but you keep getting interrupted by sneezes. Start with a shaky, congested bravado, then as you try to hold your ground, your voice cracks and you end up laughing at yourself, the pride dissolving into genuine, self-deprecating joy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Dancing at Your Own Goodbye Party
instruction: You have weeks to live, and your friends have thrown you a celebration of your life. You're giving an impromptu toast, but you're half-drunk and the morphine is making everything soft-edged. Start with genuine laughter and joy—share a ridiculous memory that has everyone cracking up. Your voice is light, almost giddy with the strange freedom that comes from having nothing left to lose. But mid-sentence, you're suddenly overwhelmed by the beauty of this moment, and tears start flowing even as you're still laughing. Your voice breaks as you tell them how grateful you are, how every friendship was a gift, but underneath the gratitude is the unbearable ache of having to leave. Let contradictions wash through you: rage that this is ending mixed with peace that you got to experience it at all. You're joking about death, then sobbing, then laughing again at your own tears. End with a moment of crystalline clarity where you tell them the truest thing you know, your voice stripped of everything but love and the fierce joy of being alive right now, even as you're dying.

title: Clutching Your Child's Blanket After They've Been Taken From You
instruction: You're holding the only thing you have left—their blanket, still carrying their scent. Begin in shock, your voice hollow, almost mechanical as you describe the fabric, the patterns, trying to stay in concrete details because the truth is too much. Then let the rage explode—scream at the injustice, at whoever took them, at God, at yourself. Let your voice shatter with fury and helplessness, the kind of primal sound that comes from a parent's worst nightmare. But then break entirely into desperation—beg for them back, plead with the universe, your voice cracking and dissolving into sobs.
