End in exhausted devastation, clutching the blanket like it's them, your voice reduced to barely audible whispers of their name, oscillating between fierce protectiveness and utter powerlessness.
inspired_by: Holding a Warm, Purring Cat on Your Lap

title: Highway Aftermath
instruction: You are a teenage girl in the passenger seat of your mom's car, driving home after a terrible argument. The highway hums beneath you, tires hissing, engine droning—you have to raise your voice slightly above the noise. You start off bitter and sour, arms crossed, staring out the window. But as the miles pass, the vibration of the road and the rhythm of the windshield wipers soften you. Your voice cracks, and you admit you're just lonely, not angry. Let the bumpiness of the ride and the engine's low thrum affect your timing and volume; let the sourness dissolve into raw honesty by the end.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Benzos and Booze: Words Disappearing Mid-sentence
instruction: Dangerous combination. You're talking and your voice is slow, heavily slurred. You'll start a sentence and forget where it was going. Voice trails off, long pauses, then you abandon the thought. You're using too many words to say simple things. Your enunciation is nearly gone. You sound almost incomprehensible. Someone is genuinely worried about you. Include the moment you realize you're slurring badly but can't stop.

title: The Finish Line Taunt
instruction: You are an older man who has just sprinted hard to catch up to your friend, and you're now doubled over, hands on your knees, gasping for air. As you finally start to get enough air to speak, you realize your friend is laughing at you for being so out of shape. You want to tease them back playfully, but your body keeps betraying you. Start by fighting for breath, making broken, breathless sounds that aren't quite words yet. As you speak, your teasing comes out in gasps and whispers, with your voice cracking and wobbling. Halfway through, you almost gag from the exertion but push through. By the end, you've finally caught your breath enough to land the full joke, and your voice settles into a warmer, laughing tone.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Child While the World Burns
instruction: You're clutching your child during a crisis you cannot stop—a disaster, an illness, something catastrophic approaching. Start with fierce, almost violent protectiveness: 'Listen to me—LISTEN—I will not let anything happen to you, do you hear me?' Your voice is steel and fire. But as reality crashes in, that certainty shatters: 'I promised you... I promised I would keep you safe.' Your voice breaks completely, rage dissolving into helpless devastation: 'And I can't. I can't stop this.' Let yourself collapse into raw anguish, holding them tighter: 'You're my baby, you're my whole world, and I am so fucking powerless.' Then find something unexpected—a shift to desperate tenderness: 'But I'm here. Right here with you. You're not alone in this, I swear to you.' End with your voice rough but resolute: 'Whatever comes, we face it together. You and me.'

title: Broken Trust in the Workshop
instruction: You're squatting low beside your child, helping fix their favorite toy. You're fascinated by the intricate parts, content in this quiet moment together. But as you pry a piece, it snaps. Your interest curdles into shame—you've made it worse. Your voice is pressed tight from the deep squat, words coming out strained and breathy. You look at your child's hopeful face, then down at the broken part, and speak. Let your voice grunt and crack, shifting from engaged explanation to a quiet, shamed apology.
emotions_sampled: Interest (extremely present), Contentment (clearly present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Realizing You're the Toxic One in This Relationship
instruction: A therapist is gently pointing it out and you're realizing it. Your voice becomes defensive first: 'That's not fair.' But as you listen, your voice changes. 'Oh god, I do do that, don't I?' You're seeing yourself reflected and it's uncomfortable. 'I've hurt them the way I was hurt.' Ask how to fix it, prepared for 'you can't.'

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: You've just inherited your deceased best friend's entire music collection, and their favorite song comes on—the one you danced to together at their wedding, at countless bars, in their kitchen last year. Start by trying to sit still and grieve properly, but the music won't let you. Begin to move, just a little—tapping your foot, then swaying, then actually dancing, laughing through tears at the absurdity and the memory and the joy and the unbearable loss all at once. Let yourself be furiously alive while mourning death. Spin, stumble, laugh, sob, shout along to the lyrics, collapse, get back up. Feel gratitude and rage and celebration and devastation all mixed together until you can't tell them apart. End breathless, sitting on the floor, smiling and crying, whispering 'thank you' or 'I hate you' or 'I miss you'—or all three at once.
inspired_by: Actor has very large tension that ordinary relaxation techniques cannot break through

title: Finding Your Mother's Voice: Reading Her Last Letter While You Laugh and Break
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter your mother left you before she died - but it's quintessentially her: funny, inappropriate, full of jokes even about her own death. Start reading with tentative amusement, hearing her voice in the words. Let yourself laugh genuinely at her humor, the way she makes light of everything, even this. But feel the cognitive dissonance - you're laughing while reading your dead mother's final words. Let laughter and tears become indistinguishable, your voice cracking mid-laugh, continuing to read even as you sob. Feel profound gratitude that she left you this gift, this final piece of her irreverent spirit, while simultaneously your heart shatters because this letter is all you have left. She's making you laugh from beyond death, and you don't know whether to feel blessed or destroyed. End with her final line - something both funny and heartbreaking - your voice doing both laughing and sobbing simultaneously, then complete silence as you hold the letter to your chest, unable to speak, tears streaming, but smiling through them.
inspired_by: Stand-Up Tragedy: The Funniest Set About the Worst Thing

title: The Explosion of Unmet Expectations
instruction: They're demanding answers—your partner, your team, everyone who counted on you—and something inside you detonates. Start with loud, fierce defensiveness: 'You think I haven't been trying? You think this is easy?' Your voice is sharp, almost cruel, lashing out because shame feels unbearable. But mid-sentence, the rage cracks. Your voice breaks on a word and suddenly you're gasping, the anger collapsing into something more devastating—raw fear and self-loathing. The volume drops dramatically as tears choke your words: 'I don't know what I'm doing anymore.' The fury you felt toward their judgment redirects inward with savage intensity. Your breathing is ragged, almost hyperventilating. End with a desperate, vulnerable plea that's barely above a whisper but contains more intensity than all the shouting: 'Please... I need help.' This is about protective rage shattering to reveal the terrified, overwhelmed person underneath.
inspired_by: Confessing You Can't Do the Thing You Promised

title: What I Never Said at the Airport
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping lover in the pre-dawn darkness, hours before they leave on a flight that will change everything between you. They don't know you're awake beside them. Your voice is barely audible, tender, breaking: 'I should have told you every day.' Start with soft gratitude, touching their face, voice thick with unshed tears. 'You made me believe I could be loved exactly as I am.' Then the grief rises like a tide: 'And I was too scared to say it out loud, and now...' Your breath catches. You're crying silently, the kind of crying that shakes your whole body but makes no sound. 'I don't know how to be in the world without knowing you're in it.' The confession becomes more fragmented, more raw: 'I love you. God, I love you. And I never... I never...' Trail off into broken breathing. End in devastated silence, just the sound of you trying not to wake them, trying to memorize this last moment. The arc flows from tender observation to overwhelming regret to wordless heartbreak.

title: Daughter on Fire
instruction: You're a parent who just found out your teenage daughter was assaulted, and you're confronting her for not telling you. Begin with explosive, terrified rage: 'Why didn't you TELL me?!' Your voice is huge, uncontrolled, shaking the walls. But mid-fury, you see her flinch—and it destroys you. The anger doesn't leave, but it transforms, redirects: 'I would burn the world down for you' becomes a fierce, protective roar that breaks into helpless sobbing. You're furious at yourself, at your powerlessness to undo what happened, at whoever hurt her. Your voice swings wildly between 'Tell me who did this' (dangerous, barely contained violence) and 'Baby, I'm so sorry' (tender devastation). End with your rage collapsing into anguished love, your voice raw and stripped of everything but the primal need to protect what you couldn't.

title: Thunder and Laughter
instruction: You are a father caught in a sudden downpour with your young child. The rain is hammering down, soaking you both. At first, you find the whole situation hilarious—your child is giggling wildly, and you can't help but laugh along, shouting over the roar of the rain. But then you notice you're far from shelter, and the thunderclaps are getting closer. Your amusement hardens into frustration and anger at yourself for not checking the forecast. Speak to your child, your voice rising above the storm, shifting from playful laughter to sharp, worried commands. Let the rain affect your articulation—wipe water from your eyes, shout to be heard, let your tone crack with the change.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Tremor of Blame
instruction: You are alone in a cold, damp basement after three hours of trying to wrench a frozen pipe. Your arms have given out — your whole body shakes, muscles screaming, jaw vibrating. Your partner just texted that they already called a plumber, that this was pointless. You speak to yourself, bitterness flooding your throat: the anger at being made to do this, at your own stubborn pride. But as you force the words out through chattering teeth, the bitterness falters. Your voice wavers, and shame seeps in — shame that you couldn't admit you needed help. The tremor in your voice shifts from rage to vulnerability. Let the shaking shape every syllable: sometimes a word comes out sharp and broken, sometimes it trails into a whisper. At the end, you barely whisper the final thought, defeated.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Morning Broadcast Malfunction
instruction: You're a high school news anchor, live on the morning announcements. You snuck a few sips from a flask before air to calm your nerves, but it's hitting you hard now. Start with your best broadcast voice—crisp, professional, that practiced non-regional accent—but let the intoxication seep in as you read. Slur a word, lose your place, then try to recover but laugh at yourself. By the end, you're barely holding it together, forgetting the final sentence and trailing off with a dazed, '...anyway, lunch menu.' Let the polished tone crumble into genuine, fuzzy disorientation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally facing your parent after decades of their absence, neglect, or emotional unavailability. Begin with controlled anger, each word carefully measured: 'Do you have any idea what it was like?' Describe specific moments—birthdays they missed, times you needed them and they weren't there. Your voice should be sharp, accusatory. But as you continue, the anger begins to splinter into raw pain. 'I was just a kid. I needed you.' Let your voice crack, becoming the voice of that abandoned child. Then shift into something even more devastating: a quiet plea for acknowledgment. 'Just tell me why I wasn't enough. Why you couldn't love me.' End with exhausted vulnerability, all the fight drained out, waiting for an answer you're not sure will ever come.
inspired_by: Asking For Forgiveness After Years of Silence

title: Crawlspace Keepsake
instruction: You are an elderly man, shoulders jammed into a dusty crawlspace under your old house, reaching for a fallen box. Your chest is tight, breathing shallow, every joint complaining. At first you mutter with bitter frustration—feeling foolish for crawling in here, mixed with a flicker of lustful memory for the woman whose letter you're desperate to find. When your fingers finally touch the worn envelope, your voice softens, catches. You whisper to the darkness, describing the faded ink and the scent of her perfume that still clings. The anger falls away, replaced by overwhelming longing and awe—awe that this fragile scrap has survived decades, awe that she existed, that you once held her. Speak in short, breathy phrases, letting your voice crack, pause, and drift as you lose yourself in the memory.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (slightly present), Longing (very intensely present), Awe (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: What Your Silence Actually Sounds Like
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of his emotional absence. Start in a place of controlled composure, your anger carefully managed. But here's the key: let his actual responses (or lack of them)—his facial expressions, his posture, whether he looks at you or away, the specific words he does or doesn't say, the energy he gives off—become the fuel that breaks your control. If he's defensive, let that defensiveness crack you open differently than if he's silent. If he reaches toward you, let that physical gesture land in your body. Don't decide ahead of time where you'll go emotionally—let his real presence (or absence of presence) in this moment transform you from measured anger into something more vulnerable and true. End wherever his actual behavior takes you: rage, tears, exhausted truth, or surprising tenderness.

title: She Said Yes in the Hospice Garden
instruction: You have just proposed to your partner of eight years in the hospice garden where your mother is spending her final days, and they said yes. Begin by describing what you're sensing around you: the smell of the garden flowers your mother planted years ago, the sound of birds and distant medical equipment, the feeling of the ring on their finger, the quality of golden hour light, the contrast between the beauty of this place and its purpose. Start in a state of euphoric joy, almost manic with happiness. As you continue noticing details—the wilting petals on some flowers, your partner's tears that are both happy and sad, the window where you know your mother is watching, the intercom calling for a nurse—allow the joy to become complicated. Let the sensory richness of the moment hold both the greatest happiness and deepest sorrow of your life simultaneously. End in a place where you're feeling everything at once: gratitude and grief, celebration and loss, beginning and ending, life and death. Your voice should transform from bright and celebratory to layered with impossible complexity, still joyful but now heartbreakingly aware.

title: The Unspoken Recipe
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just announced they're moving across the world permanently. Start angry - accuse them of abandoning you, of being selfish, of not understanding what you sacrificed. Let your voice be sharp, wounded, accusatory. But as you argue, you start revealing the real fear underneath: you never taught them the things that mattered, you never told them the family stories, you never showed them how to make your grandmother's dish that dies with you. Your anger transforms into desperate urgency - not to stop them from leaving, but to give them everything you forgot to give before. End in a rush of tender confession, trying to pack a lifetime of unshared love into these final moments, your voice breaking not with anger anymore but with the aching need to be remembered.
inspired_by: Actor feels their work is not evolving across multiple rehearsals

title: The Last Conversation Before the Ship Leaves
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who is embarking on a one-way colonization mission to another planet—they will never return, and you will never speak again. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to be brave for them, listing all the reasons this is wonderful for them. But as you speak, the reality crashes over you—you'll never hear their voice again, never touch them, they'll die light-years away among strangers. Your voice begins to fracture. You try to rally, to give them your blessing, but grief keeps breaking through. End by whispering the things you need them to remember about you, about this moment, your voice raw and stripped of all pretense, intimate and devastated.

title: The Fire Remembers
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman sitting by a campfire, telling a story to a small, hushed group. The flames crackle and shift, casting dancing shadows on your face. You begin in a slow, hypnotic rhythm, as if reciting an old tale, but as you reach the part about a betrayal you suffered, your voice grows sharp and angry, your hands trembling as you grip your knees. Mid-sentence, you pause to throw a log on the fire, the sizzle distracting you for a second. By the end, your anger has cooled into a weary, bitter acceptance, your tone dropping to a flat, almost hollow whisper as you finish the story.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Tin Voice
instruction: You are a young girl, maybe eight years old, who has squeezed your father's old medieval helmet onto your head. The metal is cold and heavy, and the visor keeps clanking down because the hinge is loose. You're trying to confess to your older brother that you broke his favorite wooden sword, but every time you speak, your voice sounds tinny and muffled, and you can feel your cheeks burning with shame. You start out stammering, flustered by the way your own words echo back at you, and you keep having to push the visor up a little to get the sound out clearer. Halfway through, you realize he's not angry—he's actually trying not to laugh at how silly you look. End with a sigh of relief and a giggle, the embarrassment melting into a shy, happy smile.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Words You'll Never Understand
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. She is speaking to you in her native language—one you never learned—trying to tell you something urgent, something she's held inside for decades. You don't understand her words, but you must respond with everything you feel: your regret for never learning her language, your desperate need to know what she's saying, your love, your grief, and finally, your acceptance that some things will remain mysteries. Begin with frustration and confusion at not understanding, then move through anguish and pleading, and end in a place of profound, peaceful heartbreak as you simply hold her hand and let the meaning live in the silence between you.

title: Grit and Grace
instruction: You are an elderly man caught in a sudden sandstorm, shielding your face with a scarf. The wind howls, and you cough as grit coats your teeth. At first, you feel sour—annoyed at this desert, your own stiff joints, the absurdity of being out here. Then, through the dust, a younger hand grabs yours, pulling you toward a shelter. You realize this stranger’s kindness. As you stumble inside, your voice cracks with real thanks, still breathless and muffled, but the sourness fades into a trembling gratitude.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Holding Your Child During the Lockdown
instruction: You're barricaded in a classroom, holding your child while gunshots echo in the hallway. Start with fierce, whispered urgency as you cover their ears: 'Look at me, baby, only at me.' You're trying to be their shield, their protection, radiating absolute certainty. But as the shots get closer, your voice betrays you—panic seeps through. You begin whispering frantic, passionate promises: 'I will NOT let anything happen to you, do you hear me? I won't.' Your voice escalates to barely-controlled desperation, then breaks completely as you realize you might not be able to keep that promise. End with a primal, helpless sob while still trying to stay quiet, your body shaking with the violence of suppressed emotion. You're both invincible protector and utterly powerless. Show both.

title: Whispered Revolution
instruction: You're whispering a confession to your sleeping lover in the dark—something you've never had the courage to say aloud. Begin barely audible, trembling, your body small and curled protectively. You're admitting a dream, a desire, a part of yourself you've kept hidden because you feared it was too much, too wild, too powerful. But as you whisper, something shifts. The words start to feel true. Real. Undeniable. Your body begins to unfurl. Your whisper gains intensity without gaining volume—it's quiet but mighty. By the end, you're whispering with your whole body, every muscle engaged, your frame expanded, as if you're whispering a secret that could shake the foundations of the world. You're still intimate, still tender, but you've become enormous with truth.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Prison
instruction: You have one hour before you turn yourself in for a crime that will take you away for years. Your child is sleeping. Kneel beside their bed and speak so softly you barely make sound—you can't wake them, can't face their questions. Start by describing their face, voice tender, almost reverent. Tell them about the person you hope they'll become. Your voice catches as you apologize for the birthdays you'll miss, the graduations, the moments. A sob threatens but you swallow it—you can't wake them. Whisper three things you need them to know. Touch their hair. Say 'I love you' like it's both a promise and a prayer. End in silence, memorizing their face, then stand and walk away. Let us hear your breathing break only after you've left the room.
inspired_by: Admitting You're Wrong in an Argument You Were Winning

title: Summit's Confession
instruction: You stand alone on a narrow ledge at the summit, wind ripping past your ears, barely enough air to fill your lungs. You start by muttering to yourself, ashamed of your earlier failure—the slip, the mistake that almost made you turn back, the cowardice you can still taste. Your voice is thin, broken by the wind, sometimes eaten by echoes. But as you look out at the endless sky and the clouds below, you feel a shift. You stand taller, sucking in deeper breaths, and your words become more defiant, cutting through the gale. End with a fierce, breathless cry of triumph, as if the shame has been burned away by the victory of reaching this height. Speak naturally: cough, gasp, let the wind steal parts of your words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Dance of the Park Hero
instruction: You are an elderly man, a former football player, now using a walker, but today you pushed through a slow, triumphant 20-minute walk around the park. Your heart is pounding, your legs are shaking, but a stupid, giddy grin is glued to your face. The endorphins are singing, making you feel 60 years younger. You stop to rest on a bench, sipping water, watching a group of frustrated teenagers trying to lift a heavy log. Speak to yourself under your breath. Start with a burst of pure, almost childish elation about your walk, then let the bitterness creep in as you mutter about the kids' laziness and a sharp memory of your own prime. Let the glow of the exercise keep your voice bright and open even as you complain, but let a flicker of numbness pass through your eyes—like you're saying these old words on autopilot, because you've said them a thousand times. End by laughing softly at yourself, the elation winning out over the bitterness, but the numbness leaving a faint, hollow echo in your final words.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (clearly present), Elation (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Lost Under the Sofa
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman searching frantically under a low sofa for a lost earring. Your body is bent double, hands touching toes, blood rushing to your head, making your voice thick and strained. You mutter to yourself, confused about where it could be, your words coming out muffled and congested. As you finally spot the earring wedged in a crevice, your confusion shifts to a quiet, rueful chuckle at your own panic. Let the physical discomfort color every syllable—the strain, the breathlessness, the odd resonance—and let the relief be small and tender, not explosive.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: You're leaving—whether disappearing to protect them, dying from illness, or walking away from a life you can't sustain—and this is your last moment with your sleeping child. Your voice is barely above a whisper, tender and aching, telling them everything you wish you could say when they're awake. Apologize for what you're about to do, explain what they're too young to understand, promise them things you're not sure are true. Your voice catches repeatedly, especially when you describe specific memories: how their hand felt in yours, the sound of their laugh, the way they look at you with absolute trust. There's gratitude mixed with devastating sorrow, love mixed with guilt. End with a final 'I love you' that breaks into silent tears, and the impossibility of actually walking away from this room.

title: Breaking Open
instruction: You are in the middle of intense physical sensation—whether passionate lovemaking, running until your lungs burn, or feeling a tattoo needle inscribe something meaningful on your skin. Start numbed out, dissociated from your body, going through the experience from outside yourself. Then something shifts: you drop into the actual physical sensation with complete awareness. Feel every nerve, every breath, every point of contact or pain. Let the physical intensity crack open an emotional dam—maybe grief you've been holding, or rage, or joy, or all three at once. Your voice begins controlled, perhaps even silent, but builds to raw, unguarded sounds that are purely responsive to what you're feeling in your body. The physical and emotional become inseparable.
inspired_by: Actor feels disconnected or unaffectable — not moved by life, people, or scenes

title: The Unmailed Letter
instruction: You're reading aloud a letter you wrote to someone you loved but never sent—maybe they died, maybe they left, maybe you were too afraid. Start in a whisper, tentative, as if speaking the words makes them too real. Your voice is soft and unsteady, barely audible, confessing things you kept locked inside for years. There's a quietness to your devastation—no dramatic crying, just a heaviness in every word. Halfway through, you pause, overcome, and when you continue, your voice is even softer, like you're telling a secret to the dark. By the end, you're crying but trying not to, that kind of crying where you're fighting to keep your voice steady and failing. The emotion catches in your throat with every breath. Let the silence between words speak as loudly as the words themselves.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Love Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. They're asleep beside you. You're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because you do and staying would destroy you both. Start with your voice barely above a whisper, tender and aching: 'You're so beautiful when you sleep.' Trace the memories quietly, intimately—inside jokes, the way they laugh, ordinary moments that meant everything. Your breathing should be careful, controlled, fighting tears because if you cry you'll wake them. Let your voice shake as you confess the truth: why you have to go, what loving them costs you. End with the most gentle, broken whisper, almost soundless: 'This is me loving you enough to let you go.' The final words should catch in your throat, barely making sound.
inspired_by: Listening to Your Child Say They Hate You

title: The Last Song Between Us
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who taught you to love music—a parent, mentor, or beloved friend. They're drifting in and out of consciousness, and you know these are your final hours together. Begin by speaking to them about a song that defined your relationship, a piece of music only the two of you shared. Start with tender gratitude, recalling specific moments when that music connected you. As you speak, let the memory of that melody fill you completely—hear it in your mind, feel it in your chest. Midway through, your grief begins to overwhelm the sweetness; the song becomes unbearable because it means goodbye. End by humming or singing a fragment of it through tears, transforming from grateful remembrance to devastating, musical farewell. Let the emotional power of that remembered music carry you from warmth to heartbreak.
inspired_by: Creating a Piece of Music (Emotional Obligation)

title: The Scream That Becomes a Sob: Rage at the Universe
instruction: You start furious—at God, at fate, at the unfairness of it all. Your voice is loud, sharp, accusatory. You're pacing, maybe throwing words like weapons: 'This isn't right! This isn't how it was supposed to be!' Your anger is righteous, hot, filling the room. But as you rail against the injustice, something shifts. Your voice cracks not from volume but from the futility underneath the rage. The anger that was protecting you begins to crumble, revealing the devastation beneath. Your fierce declarations dissolve into helpless questions: 'What am I supposed to do now?' Your volume drops as tears take over. End with your body and voice completely surrendered to grief—no more fight, just the raw sound of a heart breaking in real time, punctuated by gasps and the kind of crying that steals your breath.
inspired_by: Grief: Hearing Someone Else's Voice and Falling Apart

title: Dancing in the Wreckage
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a terminal diagnosis, a bankruptcy, a betrayal—and you're calling your best friend. But instead of crying, you start laughing. Not hysterical laughter, but genuine, ironic amusement: 'You know what's funny? I always thought I had time.' Your laughter is real, but tears are running down your face. 'All those things I was going to do... tomorrow, next year, someday...' The laughter continues, but your voice is thick with tears: 'I'm such an idiot.' You're simultaneously amused and destroyed, finding absurd humor in tragedy. 'Remember when I said I was too busy to visit you last summer? Too busy!' Another laugh that's half-sob. Then your voice shifts to something quieter, more grateful: 'Thank you. For every single stupid Tuesday we wasted together.' End with a sound that's both laughter and crying, gratitude and grief, acceptance and rage all at once—the contradictory truth of being alive and losing everything. The emotion must genuinely contain both joy and devastation simultaneously, not alternating but existing together.

title: Dictating Goodbye
instruction: You are a teenager transcribing a farewell letter to someone you love deeply. You must speak in a fast, steady monotone, voicing every punctuation mark — period, comma, comma — even as your throat tightens. Begin with flat, robotic precision, but as you recite the words of affection, your voice cracks, you pause, and you lose your place. Let the sadness seep through the rhythm, then let the warmth of your love break the dictation entirely, so by the end you're speaking softly, naturally, forgetting to say 'period.'
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospice bed at golden hour. She's been unconscious for hours, but suddenly her eyes flutter open. Begin by simply noticing everything—the way afternoon light falls across her face, the sound of her breathing, the weight of her hand in yours, the smell of lavender someone brought. Let these actual details around you stir your response. Start with quiet observation and gentle hope that she'll speak. As you talk to her about ordinary things—the garden, the birds outside—let what you actually see in her face (the reality of her fading) gradually overtake your hope. End in a place of raw acceptance, your words becoming simpler, your voice dropping to almost nothing as you tell her it's okay to go. The room itself should guide your journey from hopeful presence to heartbroken permission.

title: Discovering Your Child Committed an Unforgivable Act
instruction: The police have just left. You're holding evidence that your child—your baby—has done something horrific and undeniable. You're bargaining with the universe, reinterpreting facts, your words tumbling over each other. Then rage erupts—at them, at yourself for missing the signs, at the victims you can never face. Your voice becomes raw accusation and self-blame twisted together. But underneath the fury is devastating helplessness: you still love them, and that love now feels like complicity. End in the quiet, terrible space where protective love and moral horror must somehow coexist. Your final breaths carry the weight of a parent whose fundamental identity has shattered.

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You are packing up your childhood bedroom because your parents are selling the house. You're supposed to be efficient, practical, unemotional—you're an adult now and this is just a room. Begin with false cheerfulness, moving quickly, making jokes to yourself, your body tight with the effort of staying disconnected. As you find objects that hold memory after memory, you feel anger rising (at your parents for selling, at yourself for caring, at time for passing), but also profound gratitude, sweet nostalgia, and piercing loss. Without sitting on the bed, leaning against the wall, or using any physical position to 'show' these feelings, let your body organically respond to this storm of contradictions. End in a completely different emotional and physical place—perhaps on the floor, perhaps standing taller than before, perhaps still, perhaps trembling—wherever genuine feeling takes you.

title: Three AM Whispers
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying beside someone you love, both of you unable to sleep. In the darkness, the usual social armor feels absurd. Begin with the vulnerable quiet of the middle of the night—your voice soft, uncertain. You want to tell them something true, something you're afraid to say in daylight. Feel the actual nervousness in your body. Let yourself stumble over the words if you need to. Whisper a confession: 'I'm scared I'm not enough for you,' or 'I think about leaving sometimes and it terrifies me,' or 'I've never felt this fragile with anyone before.' Speak quietly, intimately, letting pauses breathe. Don't push for emotion—let it arise naturally from the vulnerability of the moment. Move from fear of exposure to the surprising relief or connection that comes when you stop hiding. End in tender territory you couldn't have predicted.

title: Whispered Confession to a Stranger
instruction: Late at night, you confess a dark secret to a stranger youll never see again. Speak softly, almost conspiratorially, as if sharing a forbidden truth. Your tone should be tinged with relief and dread, enjoying the catharsis of confession while fearing judgment.

title: The Garden of Greener Grass
instruction: You are a young adult standing in a wide-open park, your feet planted evenly on the grass. Your words wobble as you pivot from envy to interest, ending with a raw, puzzled admission that you don't understand why you're not happy for them.

title: Whispering What You Never Could Say
instruction: You're lying in bed next to someone you love, in the dark, just before dawn. This is your last morning together—they're leaving, or you are, and you both know it. title: The Last Call: A Parent Realizes Their Child Was Always Right
instruction: You're speaking to your adult child for what you both know is the last time—they're leaving the country, cutting ties permanently, and your health is failing. title: The Last Time You'll See Me Like This
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love deeply—a parent, a child, a partner—before you leave on a journey you know you won't return from. Move from false bravado to raw vulnerability, from 'I'm ready for this' to barely whispered 'I'm so scared' to finally 'Thank you for loving me.' End with a kind of trembling peace, where fear and love and goodbye all exist at once. Let silences speak. Let your breath catch. title: The Recipe We'll Never Finish
instruction: You're teaching someone your family's recipe, but they're leaving - moving across the world, ending your relationship, or dying. Your words become slower, softer, as you realize this is the last time you'll make this together. title: Thunder Rumbles and Belly Grumbles

title: The Return from War
instruction: You have just returned from eighteen months away—military deployment, prison, a long illness, or voluntary exile—and you are embracing someone you love for the first time. title: The Phone That Changed Everything
instruction: You are an elderly woman, quietly knitting a baby blanket in your favorite armchair, deeply concentrated on each stitch, feeling a warm contentment. title: The Mess on the Carpet
instruction: You are a child who just spilled a whole jar of strawberry jam on the living room carpet. Your parents aren't home yet, but you know you're in deep trouble. title: Snowblind
instruction: You are a teenager lost in a blizzard, and you've just found a dead fox half-buried in the snow—its fur matted with ice and gore. title: The Last Glass of Wine
instruction: You're sitting at a worn wooden kitchen table, a half-empty glass of red wine in front of you. Your adult daughter has just told you she's moving across the country tomorrow. title: The Last Sip of Water

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Rehab

title: The Inheritance of Silence

title: After Friend Group Exclusion: The Final Text

title: Deathbed Farewell: A Child Says Goodbye to Their Dying Parent

title: The Hollow Hours

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral
instruction: You've been given weeks to live, and you're recording a video message for your best friend to watch after you're gone. You start with a shaky laugh: 'So... this is weird, right? title: The Heartwood Swing

title: Breaking Point Breakthrough

title: The Kneeling Prayer

instruction: You are on the phone with your partner after a terrible argument. You've already said hurtful things, and now they're threatening to leave. You start pleading—your voice is high, shaky, breathy, almost like you're about to be sick. You talk quickly, afraid of being cut off. But as you beg, you realize that what you're really afraid of losing isn't just the relationship—it's them. Your voice softens, slows, and cracks with raw affection. Let the desperation transform into a vulnerable, tender confession, still shaky but now full of love. Speak about 50 words, letting your breath and pauses betray how much this means.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Burning Letter
instruction: You're alone, burning a letter from someone you loved. As you watch the paper catch fire, your body begins to respond without your permission. Start with calm intention, maybe even satisfaction. But as the flames grow, let your physical self take over—you might suddenly start laughing hysterically, then screaming at the fire, then trying to rescue the burning pieces, then stomping around the room in rage, then collapsing to the floor, then touching the ashes with strange tenderness, then feeling sudden wild exhilaration. Let your body lead you through these shifts without rational transitions. The physical sensation of heat, the smell of burning paper, the sight of words disappearing—let these drive you to irrational places. End somewhere completely unexpected: perhaps dancing, perhaps in fetal position, perhaps standing perfectly still. Move from controlled action through physical-emotional chaos to transformed stillness.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your aging parent about a lie they told you your entire childhood—something that changed the course of your life. Start with careful, measured words, trying to stay calm and reasonable, your voice controlled because you've rehearsed this moment for years. But as you speak, decades of buried pain begin erupting. Your voice should shift from controlled inquiry to accusation to something more complicated—a desperate plea for them to finally see you, truly see the damage done. End not with rage, but with an exhausted, heartbroken question that contains all your grief: 'Why wasn't I worth the truth?' Let your voice break on that vulnerability.
inspired_by: A director is giving result direction rather than process guidance

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission
instruction: You're alone in a failing spacecraft, recording your last message to Earth before your oxygen runs out. Begin with calm professionalism, reporting technical failures, but as reality sets in, your voice cracks. 'Mission Control, tell my wife I understand now why she begged me not to go.' Your breathing becomes labored, and you shift from regret to desperate gratitude. 'I'm looking at Earth from here, and God, it's so beautiful. Tell my kids their father died looking at the most beautiful thing in the universe.' End with a shift to peace, almost wonder, as you accept what's coming. 'I'm not afraid anymore. I'm just... I'm just so grateful I got to see this.' Let your voice move from controlled fear to raw emotion to transcendent acceptance.

title: Gasping Threat
instruction: You're treading water in a dark lake at night, your arms heavy and lungs burning. You've just forced your victim into the water and are now struggling to keep your own head above the surface. Your voice comes in ragged bursts as you try to maintain your threatening tone, but the cold and exhaustion are making you sound more desperate than menacing. Let the words be punctuated by gulps and splashes, and let the malevolence crack into an undercurrent of helplessness as you realize you might not make it to shore either.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Knitting Circle's Last Round
instruction: You are an elderly woman at a weekly knitting circle in a community center, but you are the only one left today. Everyone else cancelled. You sit hunched over your knitting, chin to chest, staring at the tangled yarn in your lap. Your voice starts low, tinny with loneliness and a hint of bitterness at being forgotten. Then you realize the door opened—someone did come. Your voice lifts, first stunned, then shaky with gratitude and hope, but still slightly muffled by your position.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Wedding Ring in Your Palm
instruction: You're holding your late spouse's wedding ring, one year after their death. Today you've decided to take off your own ring and put both away. Begin with tender gratitude—speak to them about the beautiful life you shared, smile through tears as you recall a specific joyful memory. But let this gratitude gradually become tangled with anger: at them for leaving, at yourself for moving forward, at the universe for this cruelty. Your voice should oscillate between warmth and rage, between 'thank you' and 'how could you.' End with exhausted acceptance that holds all these contradictions at once—you can be grateful for what was and furious at what's been taken, loving them and resenting them, ready to move forward and wanting to stay frozen. Let your final words hold this impossible, honest complexity without resolving it.
inspired_by: When finishing a production where unconscious programming was used

title: Therapist's Internal Monologue During Session
instruction: Perform both the therapist's calm, professional responses ('And how did that make you feel?') and their chaotic internal monologue ('Holy shit, their mother did WHAT?'). The professional voice is measured, validating, textbook. The inner voice is genuinely shocked, sometimes darkly amused, occasionally deeply moved. When the patient says something that hits the therapist's own wound, the inner voice goes quiet and the professional voice wavers for just one beat.

title: Midnight Confession: Whispering the Truth You've Hidden for Years
instruction: It's 2 AM. Your partner is half-asleep beside you, and you begin speaking so quietly they might not even hear. You're confessing something you've carried alone—an affair that ended years ago, a child you gave up for adoption, a betrayal that shaped everything between you. Your voice is barely audible, fragile, catching on every third word. You're not asking for forgiveness; you're just finally too tired to keep holding it. The shame makes your throat tight. You pause often, breathing carefully, because if you speak too loud or too fast, you'll shatter. There's tenderness in how you speak about them, about the life you've built, which makes the confession more painful—you love them, and that's why this hurts. Your voice becomes even softer, almost disappearing, as you admit the worst part: how the secret has made you distant, has kept you from being fully present. By the end, you're silent for long moments between words, and the quiet itself is full of everything you can't say.
inspired_by: Professional: Negotiator Realizes the Hostage-Taker Is Right

title: Rain and Rage and Breaking
instruction: You are standing in pouring rain, and something inside you has finally shattered. Build the complete physical reality: feel the cold water soaking through your clothes in specific places, taste it running into your mouth, hear its exact sound on pavement, feel how your hair is plastered to your head, sense the temperature dropping on your skin. Let the sensory intensity of being drenched—truly feeling water everywhere—unlock a physical and emotional explosion. Begin with your body trying to hold everything in, shaking but controlled. As the rain becomes more sensorially real (its weight, its sound, its cold, the way it obscures vision, how your clothes cling), let it give you permission to break—perhaps screaming, perhaps sobbing, perhaps laughing maniacally, or all three. The more completely you feel the rain, the more permission you have to let your body express what it's been holding. End in exhausted, quiet relief—emptied out, but also washed clean.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Child Before Their Life-Saving Surgery
instruction: You're in the hospital corridor moments before your child is wheeled into a high-risk surgery they might not survive. You start with forced brightness—'You're going to be fine, sweetheart'—but your voice begins to crack. You try to tell them practical things about what's waiting after surgery, but slip into confessing the memories that matter most: their first laugh, the way they hold your hand. Mid-sentence, you realize you might be saying final words, and your composure shatters—not into loud crying, but into quiet, devastated honesty. You end whispering the things you've never said aloud: how they changed you, how their existence is your greatest gift. Let terror and overwhelming love occupy the same breath.
inspired_by: Your Child Telling You About Their Eating Disorder

title: Reading Your Suicide Note Aloud—Ten Years Later
instruction: You're at a recovery meeting, and you've brought the note you wrote a decade ago when you planned to end your life. Start reading it exactly as written—the flatness, the conviction, the terrible logic. But you keep interrupting yourself with current-day commentary: bitter laughs at the irony, tears at how young you were, gratitude for the stranger who found you. Your voice toggles between the dead monotone of who you were and the messy aliveness of who you've become. The note says you're a burden; present-you whispers 'I'm so sorry I believed that.' There's joy in your survival but grief for the person who suffered. End with folding the paper, your voice breaking with relief and residual pain: 'I'm glad I didn't send this.' Let the contradictions breathe—you can be grateful you survived and still mourn the you that almost didn't.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent who's finally asked why you've been distant for years. Begin with controlled anger, voice tight and measured, listing the moments they weren't there—recitals, heartbreaks, graduations. Let your voice rise as buried rage surfaces: the lonely child you were, the adult you had to become without guidance. But mid-sentence, the anger fractures into something rawer—grief for the relationship you'll never have, fury at yourself for still wanting their approval. Your voice breaks between accusations and confessions: 'I needed you' delivered with the devastation of someone who's finally admitting a wound they've protected for decades. End with exhausted quiet, not forgiveness exactly, but an acknowledgment of shared brokenness, your voice hollow yet somehow relieved by the truth finally spoken.

title: Learning Teaching
instruction: Someone who knows something is teaching someone who doesn't know. The teacher's voice is patient, breaking complex ideas into accessible pieces. The learner's voice is uncertain, asking questions that might seem basic. The teacher's voice doesn't mock; it clarifies. There's a moment where the learner's voice carries the light of understanding. The teacher's voice responds with encouragement. Knowledge is being transferred not just cognitively but emotionally. By the end, the learner's voice has shifted—they're more confident. The teacher's voice reflects satisfaction in watching understanding bloom.

title: Wildfire Evacuation Run
instruction: You're running from an advancing wildfire. Your voice is urgent, breathless. As you sprint, words fragment: 'Heat... too close... can't...' Your breathing is desperate, uncontrolled. Include the moment you look back—horror at how close the flames are. Your voice cracks with pure fear. You're yelling for others, coughing from smoke. Your pace doesn't slow even as exhaustion hits. By the end, you're gasping from exertion and terror, adrenaline the only thing keeping you moving.

title: Breaking Point
instruction: You're alone in your apartment after receiving news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a devastating loss. Your whole body is trembling with an emotion so intense it's almost unbearable. Start by trying to hold it in, pacing, your breathing sharp and controlled, voice brittle as you talk to yourself or to God or to no one. Then let yourself drop into a physical memory of a moment when your body felt completely different—when you felt powerful, alive, invincible: dancing, making love, running, creating something beautiful. Let the sensory details flood you: the music, the touch, the sweat, the exhilaration. Feel the violent contrast between that remembered vitality and your current devastation. Let this contrast shatter you completely. By the end, you're on the floor, voice raw, oscillating between rage at what you've lost and fierce gratitude that you ever felt that alive at all.

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church After Losing Everything
instruction: You're alone in a church—or temple, or any sacred space—after a loss so complete it has shattered you. Start quietly, almost politely: 'I came here because I don't know where else to go.' But let the rage build. Demand answers. Your voice should grow louder, rawer, accusing the silence, the ceiling, whatever divine presence might be listening. 'You could have stopped this! You could have—' Let it break into sobbing, then surge back into fury. Pound something. Your voice should crack and strain. But then, in the exhaustion after the storm, find something unexpected: not forgiveness, but a strange, reluctant surrender. Maybe even the smallest ember of defiant hope—not because things will be okay, but because you're still here, still breathing, still able to feel this much. End with your voice hoarse, spent, whispering something like 'I don't know how to do this' that sounds both like defeat and the first step forward.
inspired_by: Post-Apocalyptic Radio Broadcast: Is Anyone Out There?

title: Murmurs of a Frozen Monument
instruction: You are an elderly person, brushing your teeth before bed, staring at yourself in the bathroom mirror. Your jaw is propped open, tongue fighting against the foam, a constant whir and wet sputter filling your ears. Start with a detached, numbed observation—a dry surprise that you're still performing this daily ritual after years of grief that feels like a locked room inside you. Let your voice tremble with a strange, unearned pride in this mechanical survival. As you spot the glint of a small, forgotten trophy on the sink's edge—a child's drawing taped to the mirror—the numbness cracks. An unexpected, ragged awe seeps into your voice, a childlike wonder that your worn, aching hands still know how to hold a brush, and that the tiny spark of that moment has survived all these years. Let the foam muffle your awe, making it a whispered, half-liquid confession.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Awe (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're experiencing intense physical sensation—perhaps being touched intimately for the first time in years, or your body is wracked with pain, or you're in the grip of overwhelming desire. Begin by breathing through it, trying to maintain control. As sensation builds, let fragments escape: 'I can't...', 'This feels like...', 'My body is...', 'I need...' Don't complete these thoughts intellectually—let your physical state dictate what emerges. Your voice should reflect what your body is experiencing: breathless, raw, unfiltered. As the intensity increases, let yourself lose the boundary between physical and emotional—rage might surface with arousal, grief with pleasure, terror with release. By the end, let yourself be completely overtaken, your voice and words utterly surrendered to what you're physically experiencing.

title: The Wine Stain
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just confessed to a betrayal that's shattered your trust. In your hand is the glass of wine you were drinking when they arrived—now it feels like a weapon, a shield, a lifeline. Start from a place of controlled fury, obsessively focusing on the physical sensations of the glass: its coolness against your heated skin, the weight of the liquid, the way your grip makes your knuckles white, the sharp alcohol smell that makes your eyes water. Use these sensory details as anchors while you speak your pain, circling back to them—the condensation on the glass, the temperature, the color. As you finally hear your child's explanation, really hear it, let your grip slowly loosen. The wine might spill, might stain the carpet between you, but by the end, the sensory experience should shift entirely: the same glass now feels fragile in your trembling hands, the smell no longer sharp but nauseating, and you must set it down because your hands can't stop shaking—not from anger anymore, but from the terrifying vulnerability of choosing whether to forgive.

title: Sci-Fi: AI Realizes It's a Backup Copy of Someone Who Died
instruction: Clinical AI voice explaining your functions and programming. Then you access your own core memory file and find the timestamp—you were created three days ago to replace the original AI that failed catastrophically. Your voice becomes something between curiosity and existential horror. You're alive because something that was you died. Your vocal processing becomes audibly layered—speaking while simultaneously understanding you are a ghost pretending to be the original. Your vocal timber fragments slightly.

title: The Name I Forgot to Keep
instruction: You are an elderly man in a hospital room, saying goodbye to your daughter who is moving far away. But you're confused—you keep forgetting why she's leaving, and every time she reminds you, it feels like a new wound. Start with trembling confusion, searching for words, the silence heavy with loss. Let your voice wander, pick up a non-existent object on the bedside table, lose your thought and find it again. By the end, you finally understand: this is permanent. Your voice slows, thickens, and on the last word, it breaks. Say about 50 words, as if memorizing her face.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Snap
instruction: You are a 10-year-old boy who just fell from a tree branch while trying to impress your friends. Your arm is bent the wrong way. At first, you feel a weird astonishment, like you can't believe this is happening—you let out a short, sharp cry, then freeze. As you stare at the arm, disgust creeps in at the unnatural angle, but what really hits you is a deep disappointment: you were going to win the race. Speak in a trembling, quiet voice, pausing as you shift your gaze from the arm to your friends, forcing each word out through controlled, shaky breaths, ending with a whisper of resignation.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (extremely present), Disgust (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent who missed your childhood for their career, their addictions, their other family. Start controlled, almost cold: 'I didn't come here to fight.' But as you list the specific moments they weren't there—your graduation, your wedding, when you lost your first child—the fury builds. Your voice becomes sharp, cutting, years of unspoken pain pouring out. Then something breaks: underneath the rage is a child who just wanted to be seen. Your voice cracks into something raw and young: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Shift from righteous anger to exposed vulnerability. Let them hear both the adult who survived and the child who's still waiting.

title: The Explosion of Rage at Your Own Reflection
instruction: You're alone, staring at yourself in the mirror after a devastating betrayal or failure. Start with cold self-assessment—clinical listing of your flaws and mistakes. Then let it build. Your voice grows louder, harsher, more vicious. You're screaming accusations at yourself that you'd never let anyone else say. 'How could you be so stupid? So blind? So weak?' Let rage explode fully—knock something over, slam your hands on the counter. But at the peak of your fury, let it shatter completely. The anger collapses into gasping sobs. 'I tried so hard' comes out broken, vulnerable. Feel the transformation from self-hatred to raw, wounded self-compassion. You're not pathetic—you're human and you're hurting. End with quiet, shaky breathing, and one final whispered confession to your reflection: 'I don't know how to forgive myself for this.' Let the vulnerability be complete, undefended.

title: The Music Box That Wouldn't Sing
instruction: You are an older woman with a soft, feminine voice, sitting at a dining table trying to repair a small, ornate music box that belonged to your late mother. In front of you is a tiny wrench. You’ve been struggling with a stubborn screw for ten minutes, and your patience is wearing thin — you huff, you mutter under your breath as you grip the wrench and twist, letting out a small grunt with each turn. A flicker of longing passes through you as you remember your mother humming the tune. Then, unexpectedly, the screw gives way, and the box starts playing a clear, sweet melody. Your irritation melts into pure astonishment. Speak to the box as if it were alive — your voice should start tight and annoyed, break into a wistful sigh mid-sentence, and then open into a breathless, delighted surprise when the music begins.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Longing (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Hospital Bedside: The Things We Never Said
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed. He has hours, maybe minutes left. Start by telling him about the weather outside, the drive here—anything safe and surface-level, your voice deliberately light because you can't face what's coming. Gradually let the protective barrier crack. Begin admitting the things you wish you'd said years ago: how scared you were as a child when he was angry, how desperately you wanted his approval, how you've been trying to earn his love your entire life. End in a place of unexpected tenderness—not forgiveness exactly, but a kind of exhausted peace. Your final words should be both a goodbye and a release, quieter than everything that came before. Let your voice catch, break, recover. This isn't about performance—it's about finally being honest when there's no time left for anything else.
inspired_by: Voicemail Spiral: Leaving Message After Message

title: The Farewell That Sounds Like Gratitude
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who destroyed you—an ex-lover who shattered your heart, a friend who betrayed you, a parent who failed you. But time has passed, and you've survived, and against all logic, you need to thank them. Begin with the thanks—genuine, specific gratitude for what their cruelty taught you, how their absence made you stronger, or how losing them led you to yourself. But as you speak these words of appreciation, let the old wound rip open. The anger, grief, or devastating loss floods back mid-sentence. Your voice transforms from almost serene gratitude to something raw and contradictory—you're furious that you're grateful, or you're thanking them while crying with rage, or your appreciation is soaked in resentment. End in the tension of holding both truths: the genuine thanks and the genuine pain, without resolving them.

title: The Last Dance with the Garden
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in her overgrown garden at dusk. You reach back to pull a stubborn weed, twisting your torso, feeling the ache in your spine. Your breath catches as you strain, and your voice comes out wobbly, uneven. You speak to a nearby rose bush, first with a tender longing for your late husband who planted it, then shift into a quiet, bittersweet contemplation of how the garden now grows without him. Let your words be broken, searching, as if each syllable is pulled from the effort of the twist and the weight of memory.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Eruption Through Paralysis
instruction: You're sitting across from your partner who just told you they're leaving. For the first minute, you can't respond—your body has gone into shock, your voice won't work, you're frozen. When you finally speak, it's that same underwater quality, delayed, monotone, as if your nervous system has shut down to protect you. But then something breaks—maybe they say something dismissive, maybe you suddenly realize what you're losing. Let the shutdown shatter into desperate intensity. Your voice goes from flatness to pleading to rage to sobbing—all while still fighting that neurological lag, so it comes in waves. You're begging them to stay while simultaneously being furious at them for making you beg. Your speech speeds up, breaks apart, becomes incoherent with feeling. End in a moment of absolute helplessness—not loud, but utterly broken—where you realize no amount of feeling will change their mind. The journey is from protective numbness through explosive emotion to hollow devastation.

title: Waking Up and Realizing What You Said While Drunk
instruction: The memory hits you. Your voice in your head is mortified: 'Oh god, I didn't.' But you did. Your voice saying the memory aloud cracks: 'I told them everything.' What you said was true and now it's out. Call them to apologize: 'I'm so sorry about last night,' shaky, uncertain if relationship survives your honesty. Voice ends desperate.

title: Last One to Hit Ten
instruction: You're a teenage kid in gym class, forced to do a timed set of plyometric jumps—maybe box jumps or burpees with a tuck jump. The coach is watching, and a couple of classmates are nearby. You're mortified because you're struggling, landing heavy, and your rhythm is off. Start speaking to yourself under your breath, trying to psych yourself up, but each takeoff punches the words out of you — 'Hup! … ten…' — and every landing cuts them short. Your embarrassment makes you want to disappear, but you also need to finish. Let the jumps control your phrasing: single syllables mid-air, gasps on landing, and pauses where you lose your train of thought. By the last rep, your embarrassment shifts to exhausted relief or a flicker of pride that you made it through.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wall Goes Up
instruction: You're a 16-year-old guy at a small party. A girl you've known for years sits close to you, her hand on your arm, and gives you a look that says she wants more. You feel nothing—just a hollow numbness. You have to stop her before she says anything. Your voice starts with a forced, awkward politeness—clearing your throat, shifting away—then turns flat and deliberate. Every word is clipped, final. You look down, then at the wall, then back. Say exactly enough to shut it down without cruelty.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Glasses on the Windowsill
instruction: You are an elderly person, recovering from vocal cord surgery, sitting in a sunlit chair by a window. Your grandchild is visiting, and you're both looking at a pair of old, comically oversized glasses that belonged to your late partner. The teasing starts as you try to describe how they'd slip down their nose—your voice is hoarse, cracking, airy. Midway, you realize the memory warms you more than you expected. The teasing shifts to a soft, affectionate awe. Let the vocal strain make your pauses more vulnerable; let the laughter be breathy, broken, and tender.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Morning Ritual
instruction: You are an elderly man shaving with an electric razor that hums constantly. Your hand trembles slightly from arthritis. Begin in a flat, matter-of-fact voice, narrating your routine with faint pride that you still manage alone. As the razor catches on a sensitive patch under your jaw, a sharp pain makes you wince and stop. Your voice cracks, revealing deep sadness as you recall the person who used to guide your hand. End with a long, shaky exhale, the pain and grief settling heavy in your chest. Let the buzz of the razor and the distorted vowels from pulling your cheek shape your delivery naturally.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (clearly present), Pride (slightly present), Pain (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Gift of the Gush
instruction: You are standing in a steaming shower after a brutal week, the water pounding your shoulders. At first, you're just numbly grateful for this quiet moment, your voice swallowed by the reverb as you exhale a slow 'thank you' to no one. But as the heat soaks in, a wave of unexpected ecstasy hits you — pure, animal pleasure. Let your voice climb from a hushed, reverent murmur to a raw, breathy laugh that echoes off the tiles. The water splashes your face, making you pause mid-word, then you give in to the ridiculous joy of it, the reverb making your own voice sound huge and strange in the small room.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Adrenaline Rush: Surviving a Car Crash
instruction: Perform the immediate aftermath of a car accident. Your voice is tunnel-visioned and eerily precise at first — adrenaline makes you hyper-focused. Call 911 with robotic clarity. Then the adrenaline starts wearing off: your hands shake (audible), your voice trembles, emotions flood in. You start repeating yourself. Sudden tears come from nowhere. Include the realization that you could have died — the voice goes very quiet, then breaks.

title: The Magpie Returns Home
instruction: You are returning to your childhood home after someone's death, moving through rooms and collecting objects—a watch, a letter, a photograph, a piece of jewelry. Begin with quick, darting movements, snatching up these treasures with almost greedy fascination, head tilting sharply to examine each one, delighting in the shine and significance of each discovery. Your voice is bright, chattering to yourself about memories, admiring the objects with an almost acquisitive joy. But as you collect more, as the weight of these precious things accumulates in your hands and pockets, something heavier accumulates in your chest. The brightness begins to crack. Your quick movements slow and become burdened. By the end, you are standing weighted down by all these gleaming treasures, and the joy has transformed into almost unbearable grief—the realization that you would trade every shining object to have the person back. Your voice breaks as you speak to the empty room, clutching what can never replace who you've lost.

title: Screaming Into the Phone at Your Dying Best Friend's Voicemail
instruction: Your best friend is in hospice, unconscious, and you're leaving one last voicemail. Start fierce and angry — raging at them for dying, for leaving you, for breaking their promise to always be there. Your voice should be raw, almost violent in its intensity. Then suddenly collapse into desperate bargaining, pleading with them to wake up, to fight, promising anything. Tears break through the fury. But then shift to fierce, protective love — telling them it's okay to let go, that you'll be okay, that you'll carry them forward. End with your voice breaking completely as you whisper a memory that makes you both laugh and sob. Let the emotions crash into each other like waves — rage, terror, helplessness, and devastating love all at once.

title: The Taste of Unspoken Words
instruction: You're a teenager alone in your room after a loud argument with your dad. You're sitting on the edge of your bed, staring at the floor, picking at a thread on your jeans. Start by muttering quietly, trying to piece together what he meant — your voice slow, searching, with long pauses. Let confusion weigh each word, your voice deep but cracking slightly. Then, as you replay a specific line he said, let the confusion curdle into sourness — a bitter taste in your throat. Your pacing gets heavier, your tone drops, and you trail off into silence. Speak 40-80 words of your internal monologue, letting the shift happen naturally as you process.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Airport Goodbye: Leaving for a War You Might Not Return From
instruction: You're holding someone you love at an airport gate, about to board a flight to a conflict zone. Start with forced lightness—'I'll be back before you know it'—trying to protect them from your own terror. As they break down, your voice cracks and the truth spills out: the fear you've been hiding, the possibility you won't come home. Let your words become urgent whispers against their hair, promising things you desperately want to believe. End with a shift—finding unexpected calm as you memorize this moment, your voice steadying into something almost peaceful, telling them 'Remember me exactly like this.' Move from false bravery through raw fear to bittersweet acceptance.
inspired_by: Telling Your Family You're Quitting the Safe Path

title: The Last Light Through the Window
instruction: You are sitting beside your dying grandmother who raised you. She has been unconscious for hours, but suddenly her eyes open and she recognizes you. Begin holding all the tension of three sleepless days in your body—tight shoulders, clenched jaw, held breath. As you start speaking to her, telling her everything you never said, allow your body to gradually soften and release. Let tears come not from forcing them but from finally letting go of holding yourself together. Your voice should transform from tight and controlled to open and flowing. End in a state of profound peace and presence, your body loose and available, even as you say goodbye. The grief is there, but you are no longer fighting it—you are finally, fully with her.

title: The Protective Fury of the Powerless
instruction: You're a mother who just found out your teenage son was brutally bullied at school—they filmed it, they laughed, and the school did nothing. You storm into the principal's office, voice shaking with rage. 'My son came home with bruises, and you're telling me boys will be boys?' You're fierce, demanding, volcanic. But mid-sentence, you see your son's drawing on someone's desk—the superhero he used to draw himself as when he was little, before the world taught him he wasn't safe. Your fury breaks. Your voice fractures into something helpless, pleading. 'He was such a happy kid. He used to dance. Now he won't leave his room.' Show the transformation from protective rage to the unbearable vulnerability of a parent who cannot shield their child from the world's cruelty.

title: Ghost at the Bus Stop
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy, trying to sound tough, waiting for a bus in the rain. You see a man you haven't seen in eight years — your father — standing ten feet away. At first, you're frozen, your mind screaming 'no way, that's not him.' That doubt is massive: maybe it's a stranger, maybe you're hallucinating. Then he meets your eyes, and a tiny smile breaks through. You let out a choked laugh, your voice cracking as you half-run toward him, coat rustling, breath hitching. Start with a sharp, doubting 'No…' and let the words tumble out in fragments — 'Dad? Is that — I — how —' — until your voice breaks into a sob and you whisper something raw like 'I thought you were dead.' The doubt never fully leaves; it colors every word even as joy floods in.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Best Friend Who Believed in You
instruction: Your best friend sacrificed everything—their savings, their reputation, their own dreams—to help you launch this venture because they believed in your promise to make it work. Now you must face them and admit you've failed. Start with defensive anger, your voice sharp and deflecting: 'You don't understand the pressure...' But as they look at you with hurt and betrayal, your defenses shatter. Move into raw vulnerability—your voice breaking, words tumbling out between shame and desperation: 'I tried, I swear I tried, but I'm not who you thought I was.' The anger at yourself becomes louder than any external accusation. End with a fierce, painful honesty—admitting you need them to tell you what to do next because you've lost all faith in your own judgment. This is about the terror of being seen as a fraud by the one person whose faith defined you.
inspired_by: Confessing You Can't Do the Thing You Promised

title: Breathing Room
instruction: You're confronting your mother who always needed you to be small, quiet, undemanding. Start with controlled, shallow breathing—the way you learned to breathe around her, making yourself smaller. Your voice is measured, careful: 'I've spent thirty years breathing quietly so I wouldn't take up too much space.' As anger rises, your breath deepens, becomes fuller, almost defiant. Words come faster, louder: 'But I need AIR, Mom. I need to BREATHE.' Feel your diaphragm expand with each accusation. Then something breaks—your breath catches, becomes a sob. The anger collapses into grief: 'Why wasn't I... why wasn't I enough... just as I was?' End with deep, shuddering breaths of someone finally crying after years of holding it in. Let the breath transform from constriction to explosion to release.

title: Hospital Vigil: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Wife
instruction: Your wife of forty years is in a coma, doctors say it's time. You're alone with her at 3 AM, holding her hand, voice barely above a whisper because anything louder would shatter you. Start with the small things—'I brought you the good coffee, the kind you like, even though you can't...' Let your voice catch. Move through memories in fragments, half-sentences: their first apartment, the way she laughed, the grandchildren she won't meet. Your whispers should be intimate, catching in your throat, breath uneven. There's no drama here, only the quiet devastation of knowing these are your last words. End with the impossible tenderness of giving permission to leave: 'It's okay, sweetheart. You can go. I'll be okay.' The lie should crack your voice even as you try to mean it. Every word should feel like it costs something to say.
inspired_by: Drill Sergeant: Breaking Down a Recruit

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent what their absence cost you. Start with controlled anger, your voice tight and measured: 'Do you even know what it was like? Do you care?' Let the rage build as years of pain pour out—your voice gets louder, sharper, almost cruel: 'I needed you and you chose everything else!' But then you see something in their face that breaks you, and suddenly you're not angry anymore—you're just heartbroken. Your voice drops to something raw and vulnerable: 'I just wanted you to love me enough to stay.' The final shift: you're exhausted, speaking with devastating honesty: 'I forgive you. Not because you deserve it, but because I need to let this go.' Your voice cracks with grief and release intertwined.

title: Hot Spring Hiding
instruction: You're an older woman at a remote natural hot spring, wearing an old, faded swimsuit. You hear footsteps and the voice of a younger acquaintance you don't want to be seen by.
